name: GPU Geometry Assembly and Coordinate Conversion
head: GPURenderer, GPURenderer Face Triangulation and Coordinate Conversion
body: This method converts raw voxel face data into typed arrays (position, normal, UV, index, color) suitable for direct upload to a GPU buffer (e.g., WebGL or WebGPU BufferGeometry). It solves the problem of transforming engine-internal voxel coordinates into a target graphics API coordinate system while ensuring correct triangle winding order. It differs from Voxel Face Mesh Generation by handling the coordinate system conversion and winding correction logic explicitly, whereas the parent method focuses on populating a generic MeshData buffer based on face direction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of raw voxel faces (obtained via engine.getFaces({ raw: true })), where each face contains vertex coordinates (v), a type (face.type), and optional style data. Output: A GPUGeometry object containing typed arrays: position (Float32Array, XYZ), normal (Float32Array, XYZ), uv (Float32Array, UV), index (Uint32Array, triangle indices), and optionally color (Float32Array, RGB). Data Structures: The GPUGeometry structure consists of: position: Float32Array, 3 floats per vertex. normal: Float32Array, 3 floats per vertex (flat-shaded). uv: Float32Array, 2 floats per vertex. index: Uint32Array, 3 indices per triangle. color: Float32Array, 3 floats per vertex (present only if options.color is true). faceCount: Number of quad faces encoded. vertexCount: Total vertices (faceCount 4). Parameters: yUp (boolean, default false): If true, converts from Heerich's Y-down/Z-into-screen space to Three.js Y-up/Z-toward-viewer space by negating Y and Z coordinates. This preserves winding order (determinant +1). scale (number, default 1): Uniform scale applied to vertex positions. color (boolean, default false): If true, parses face.style.fill and includes a color array. defaultColor (array, default [1,1,1]): Fallback color when parsing fails. Steps: 1. Initialize empty typed arrays for position, normal, uv, index, and optionally color. Determine array sizes based on the number of renderable faces. 2. Iterate through each face in the input list. 3. Skip faces where face.type is 'content' or if vertex data is absent. 4. Determine the face normal n: If face.n is present, use it. Otherwise, look up FACENORMALS[face.type]. If neither exists, default to [0, 0, 0]. 5. Determine the fill color: If options.color is true, parse face.style.fill using parseCSSColor. If parsing fails or color is disabled, use defaultColor. 6. For each of the 4 vertices v (indices 0–3) in the face quad: Compute ySign = yUp ? -1: 1 and zSign = yUp ? -1: 1. Compute position: x = v[0] scale y = v[1] scale ySign z = v[2] scale zSign Compute normal: nx = n[0] ny = n[1] ySign nz = n[2] zSign Compute UV: Look up QUADUVS[i] based on vertex index i. Compute color: If enabled, use the parsed fill color. Store these values in the respective arrays. 7. Determine winding order for the quad to ensure Counter-Clockwise (CCW) orientation: Let v0, v1, v2, v3 be the 4 vertices of the quad in order. Compute edge vectors: e1 = v1 - v0, e2 = v2 - v0. Compute cross product cross = e1 × e2. Compute dot product crossDotN = cross · n. Formula for crossDotN: \text{crossDotN} = (e{1y} e{2z} - e{1z} e{2y}) nx + (e{1z} e{2x} - e{1x} e{2z}) ny + (e{1x} e{2y} - e{1y} e{2x}) nz If crossDotN >= 0, the vertices are already CCW relative to the normal. Indices: [base, base+1, base+2, base, base+2, base+3]. If crossDotN < 0, flip the winding. Indices: [base, base+2, base+1, base, base+3, base+2]. Append these 6 indices to the index array. 8. Return the GPUGeometry object. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gpugeometryassembly(faces, options): yup = options.get('yUp', False) scale = options.get('scale', 1.0) enablecolor = options.get('color', False) defaultcolor = options.get('defaultColor', [1.0, 1.0, 1.0]) ysign = -1 if yup else 1 zsign = -1 if yup else 1 # Pre-calculate UVs for a quad (example mapping) quaduvs = [[0, 0], [1, 0], [1, 1], [0, 1]] # Estimate sizes facecount = 0 for face in faces: if face.type != 'content' and face.vertices is not None: facecount += 1 vertexcount = facecount 4 indexcount = facecount 6 position = [0.0] (vertexcount 3) normal = [0.0] (vertexcount 3) uv = [0.0] (vertexcount 2) indices = [0] indexcount color = [0.0] (vertexcount 3) if enablecolor else None vidx = 0 iidx = 0 for face in faces: if face.type == 'content' or face.vertices is None: continue # Determine normal if face.n is not None: n = face.n else: n = FACENORMALS.get(face.type, [0, 0, 0]) # Determine color if enablecolor: c = parsecsscolor(face.style.fill) if c is None: c = defaultcolor else: c = None verts = face.vertices # List of [x, y, z] # Process vertices for i in range(4): v = verts[i] # Position position[vidx 3] = v[0] scale position[vidx 3 + 1] = v[1] scale ysign position[vidx 3 + 2] = v[2] scale zsign # Normal normal[vidx 3] = n[0] normal[vidx 3 + 1] = n[1] ysign normal[vidx 3 + 2] = n[2] zsign # UV uvuv = quaduvs[i] uv[vidx 2] = uvuv[0] uv[vidx 2 + 1] = uvuv[1] # Color if enablecolor: color[vidx 3] = c[0] color[vidx 3 + 1] = c[1] color[vidx 3 + 2] = c[2] vidx += 1 # Winding check v0 = [position[vidx-43], position[vidx-43+1], position[vidx-43+2]] v1 = [position[vidx-33], position[vidx-33+1], position[vidx-33+2]] v2 = [position[vidx-23], position[vidx-23+1], position[vidx-23+2]] e1 = [v1[0]-v0[0], v1[1]-v0[1], v1[2]-v0[2]] e2 = [v2[0]-v0[0], v2[1]-v0[1], v2[2]-v0[2]] crossx = e1[1]e2[2] - e1[2]e2[1] crossy = e1[2]e2[0] - e1[0]e2[2] crossz = e1[0]e2[1] - e1[1]e2[0] crossdotn = crossxn[0] + crossyn[1] + crosszn[2] base = iidx if crossdotn >= 0: indices[iidx] = base indices[iidx+1] = base + 1 indices[iidx+2] = base + 2 indices[iidx+3] = base indices[iidx+4] = base + 2 indices[iidx+5] = base + 3 else: indices[iidx] = base indices[iidx+1] = base + 2 indices[iidx+2] = base + 1 indices[iidx+3] = base indices[iidx+4] = base + 3 indices[iidx+5] = base + 2 iidx += 6 return GPUGeometry(position, normal, uv, indices, color, facecount, vertexcount) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coordinate System Conversion: When converting from Heerich (X-right, Y-down, Z-into-screen) to Three.js (X-right, Y-up, Z-toward-viewer), both Y and Z must be negated (ySign=-1, zSign=-1) to preserve winding order (determinant +1). Using scale.y = -1 alone changes handedness and breaks winding. Winding Order: The winding check is critical for back-face culling. If the normal is zero or vertices are degenerate, the cross product may be zero, leading to undefined behavior. Color Parsing: parseCSSColor must handle various formats (#rgb, #rrggbb, rgb(), rgba()). If it fails, the default color must be used to avoid undefined values. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of exposed faces O(F), where F is the number of faces. Each face is processed once, with constant-time operations per vertex. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of vertices O(V), where V = 4F. The output arrays scale directly with the geometry size. Performance: Efficient for bulk geometry generation. The method avoids dynamic resizing by pre-calculating array sizes. Strengths: Handles coordinate system conversion and winding correction in a single pass. Produces ready-to-upload typed arrays. Limitations: Does not perform occlusion culling (this is handled by the engine's getFaces call). This method is part of the Heerich voxel engine's rendering pipeline, specifically the GPURenderer component. It bridges the gap between the engine's internal voxel representation and standard GPU graphics APIs. The method was introduced to support WebGL and WebGPU rendering, allowing for efficient batched geometry uploads. meodai/heerich, https://github.com/meodai/heerich, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Outline Generation
head: Line Outline Generation, Voxel Joint Outline
body: Voxel Outline Generation renders the edges of a voxel grid as line primitives to emphasize the blocky structure of the model. It solves the visual need for clear geometric definition in voxel art by drawing lines around the perimeter and holes of rectangular faces. It differs from Voxel Face Mesh Generation by emitting line segments instead of quads, and from Boolean Voxel Meshing by focusing on aesthetic edge highlighting rather than precise surface topology. Inputs: 2D color planes representing voxel layers (derived from the parent's neighbor check and face culling). Outputs: A list of line segments (pairs of 3D vertices). Data Structures: Color Planes: 2D arrays where each cell represents a voxel face color or empty state. Line Buffer: A dynamic list of vec3 pairs. Steps: 1. Iterate Planes: Process the 2D color planes used for face merging. 2. Generate Lines: For each rectangular face (including holes within larger faces), generate line segments around its perimeter. The algorithm examines the 12 edges of each voxel to determine if they should be drawn based on the presence and color of neighboring voxels. Alternatively, lines are generated directly around the perimeter and holes of the rectangular faces in the 2D planes. 3. Depth Bias: When rendering the lines, apply a slight depth buffer bias to avoid z-fighting and ensure lines are visible. Pitfalls: Duplicate Segments: The process generates duplicate line segments (exactly 2x) because adjacent faces share edges. These are typically not filtered out as the visual impact is negligible. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatevoxeloutlines(colorplanes): lines = [] # Iterate through each 2D color plane representing a slice of voxels for plane in colorplanes: # Identify rectangular faces and their holes # This step relies on the parent's face culling logic faces = extractrectangularfaces(plane) for face in faces: # Generate line segments around the perimeter and holes of the face perimeterlines = generateperimeterlines(face) lines.extend(perimeterlines) return lines def applydepthbias(line, biasfactor=0.001): # Adjust vertex positions slightly along the view direction to prevent z-fighting # Implementation depends on the specific renderer's depth buffer handling pass Draws a grid pattern on voxel faces using UV coordinates and a thickness uniform, without requiring a grid texture. Definition: A shader-based technique that overlays a grid on existing voxel faces. Steps: 1. If uGridThickness > 0.0: 2. Compute uv = fract(vModelUv). 3. Compute fromCenter = abs(uv - 0.5). 4. Compute isEdge = step(0.5 - uGridThickness, fromCenter). 5. Mix diffuseColor with materialColor + uGridColor weighted by max(isEdge.x, isEdge.y). Parameters: uGridThickness: float uniform controlling grid line width. uGridColor: vec3 uniform specifying the grid line color. Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of exposed faces. Performance: Generates significantly less geometry than face meshing (lines vs. quads). In a test with 226,036 voxels, it produced 4,682 lines compared to 29,666 triangles. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides clear visual separation between voxels; low memory footprint. Limitations: Does not filter duplicate edges, leading to redundant draw calls or vertex data; requires depth bias to avoid rendering artifacts. Originated from software rendering experiments for voxel models, specifically in the context of learning graphics programming. It is used in voxel art engines and educational graphics projects to provide a clean, blocky aesthetic. name: Topology-based Mesh Initialization
body: Topology-based Mesh Initialization generates initial 3D meshes for shape-from-projections optimization by parsing topology type and component/material counts from a dataset name string. It differs from voxel-based blocky meshing methods by constructing parametric primitives (tori, icospheres) rather than extracting geometry from a density field. This method is chosen when the target geometry is known to be composed of specific topological classes rather than arbitrary volumetric data. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A data string encoding topology type (last character) and number of components (characters at indices -3 to -1). Input: widthphysical (scene scale derived from detector spacing/count), radius (base radius factor, typically 0.4), subdivision (icosphere tessellation level, typically 3). Input: nmaterials (number of distinct attenuation values). Output: A list of meshes, each containing vertices, faces, and label pairs [labelv, labelf]. Data Structures: cc: A 10x3 numpy array of float32 defining predefined center offsets for inner components, scaled by 0.5. lflist: A list of label pairs [labelv, labelf] corresponding to each mesh component. Steps: 1. Parse Data String: Extract topologytype from data[-1] and ncomponents from data[-3:-1]. Pitfall: If data[-1] is not 'A'-'Z' or data[-3:-1] is not convertible to an integer, raise NotImplementedError. 2. Compute Radius: Calculate radius = widthphysical radius. 3. Initialize Offsets: Load predefined center coordinates cc (10 points). 4. Branch on Topology Type: 'A': Create single/multiple tori or icospheres based on ncomponents. 'B': Create ncomponents independent icospheres, offset by cc. 'C': Create nested icospheres for recursive materials. 'D': Create an outer shell with inner icospheres. 5. Generate Geometry: For each component, generate vertices and faces using the specified subdivision level and radius. 6. Assign Labels: Assign material labels to vertices and faces based on nmaterials and topology structure. 7. Save: Output meshes using utilmesh.savemesh or saveobjmesheslabels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def initmesh(data, widthphysical, radius=0.4, subdivision=3, nmaterials=1): # Parse topology type and component count topologytype = data[-1] try: ncomponents = int(data[-3:-1]) except ValueError: raise NotImplementedError("Invalid data string format") # Compute physical radius radius = widthphysical radius # Predefined center offsets (10x3 array, scaled by 0.5) # Note: Exact values of 'cc' are implementation-specific constants cc = np.array([ [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0.5, 0.0, 0.0], [-0.5, 0.0, 0.0], [0.0, 0.5, 0.0], [0.0, -0.5, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0, 0.5], [0.0, 0.0, -0.5], [0.5, 0.5, 0.0], [-0.5, -0.5, 0.0], [0.0, 0.5, 0.5] ]) 0.5 meshes = [] lflist = [] if topologytype == 'A': # Single/multiple tori or icospheres based on ncomponents # Implementation detail: Generate ncomponents icospheres at origin or distributed for i in range(ncomponents): verts, faces = generateicosphere(radius, subdivision) labelsv, labelsf = assignlabels(nmaterials, len(verts), len(faces)) meshes.append((verts, faces)) lflist.append((labelsv, labelsf)) elif topologytype == 'B': # ncomponents independent icospheres offset by cc for i in range(ncomponents): offset = cc[i % len(cc)] verts, faces = generateicosphere(radius, subdivision) verts += offset labelsv, labelsf = assignlabels(nmaterials, len(verts), len(faces)) meshes.append((verts, faces)) lflist.append((labelsv, labelsf)) elif topologytype == 'C': # Nested icospheres for recursive materials # Implementation detail: Generate concentric icospheres for i in range(ncomponents): scalefactor = 1.0 / (i + 1) verts, faces = generateicosphere(radius scalefactor, subdivision) labelsv, labelsf = assignlabels(nmaterials, len(verts), len(faces)) meshes.append((verts, faces)) lflist.append((labelsv, labelsf)) elif topologytype == 'D': # Outer shell with inner icospheres # Outer shell vertsshell, facesshell = generateicosphere(radius 2.0, subdivision) labelsvshell, labelsfshell = assignlabels(nmaterials, len(vertsshell), len(facesshell)) meshes.append((vertsshell, facesshell)) lflist.append((labelsvshell, labelsfshell)) # Inner icospheres for i in range(ncomponents): vertsinner, facesinner = generateicosphere(radius 0.5, subdivision) labelsvinner, labelsfinner = assignlabels(nmaterials, len(vertsinner), len(facesinner)) meshes.append((vertsinner, facesinner)) lflist.append((labelsvinner, labelsfinner)) else: raise NotImplementedError(f"Topology type {topologytype} not supported") return meshes, lflist def generateicosphere(radius, subdivision): # Placeholder for actual icosphere generation algorithm # Returns vertices (N, 3) and faces (M, 3) # This function is not defined in the source but is required for implementation pass def assignlabels(nmaterials, nverts, nfaces): # Placeholder for label assignment logic # Returns vertex labels (N,) and face labels (M,) # This function is not defined in the source but is required for implementation pass Time Complexity: Depends on the number of components and subdivision level. Icosphere generation is O(N) where N is the number of vertices. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of vertices and faces generated. Strengths: Provides clean, manifold geometry suitable for optimization-based shape reconstruction. Limitations: Limited to predefined topological classes (A-D). Cannot represent arbitrary shapes without complex nesting or combination. When to use: When the target object is known to be a combination of simple topological primitives (tori, spheres) and shape-from-projections optimization is used. When not to use: For arbitrary volumetric data or complex organic shapes not representable by the defined topology types. This method originates from the ShapeFromProjections repository by Jake Young. It is used in the context of differentiable volume rendering and shape-from-projections optimization, where initial mesh topology guides the optimization process. The method parses dataset names to automatically configure the initial geometry based on expected topology and component count. jakeoung/ShapeFromProjections, https://github.com/jakeoung/ShapeFromProjections, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Minkowski Sum Boundary Rendering via Primitive Culling
head: GPU-based Minkowski Sum Boundary Rendering via Primitive Culling, Minkowski Sum Rendering, Surface Primitive Culling
body: This method renders the outer boundary of the Minkowski sum of two 2-manifold triangular meshes, A and B, by generating a superset of surface primitives (triangles and quadrilaterals) and culling invalid ones using geometric propositions, without computing a complete boundary representation (B-rep). It differs from B-rep based algorithms by avoiding complex 3D Boolean operations and high combinatorial complexity, instead leveraging GPU rasterization and parallel culling to generate the volumetric representation. It builds on Blocky meshing by providing a geometric culling mechanism for Minkowski sum boundaries. Inputs: Two input polyhedra A and B, defined as 2-manifold triangular meshes. Let FA = \{fA\} and FB = \{fB\} be the boundary triangle sets, EA = \{eA\} and EB = \{eB\} be the edge sets, and VA = \{vA\} and VB = \{vB\} be the vertex sets of A and B respectively. Outputs: A Vertex Buffer Object (VBO) containing only valid surface primitives and their computed normals, ready for OpenGL rendering. Data Structures: 1. Flag Array: One entry per generated surface primitive. 0: Invalid (culled). 1: Valid triangle primitive. 1 or -1: Valid quadrilateral primitive (1 if normal is eA \times eB, -1 if normal is -eA \times eB). 2. Vertex Memory Layout: For coalesced global memory access, vertices are stored in a Structure of Arrays (SoA) format: all x-coordinates first, then all y-coordinates, then all z-coordinates (x1 \dots xn, y1 \dots yn, z1 \dots zn). Definitions: Valid Surface Primitive: A primitive is valid if its intersection with the Minkowski sum boundary has a non-zero area. Primitives sharing only an edge or vertex with the boundary are invalid (area zero). Concave Edge/Vertex: An edge or vertex is concave if the interior angle is greater than 180 degrees (or equivalently, the outward normals of incident faces point inwards relative to the edge/vertex geometry). Implementation typically involves checking the dot product of the edge direction with the cross product of incident face normals, or checking if the vertex lies inside the convex hull of its neighbors. Numbered Steps: 1. Generate Triangle Primitives: For each triangle fA \in FA and each vertex vB \in VB, compute the triangle primitive fA \oplus vB. The vertices of this primitive are \{vA + vB \mid vA \in fA\}. 2. Generate Quadrilateral Primitives: For each edge eA \in EA and each edge eB \in EB, compute the quadrilateral primitive eA \oplus eB. The vertices are \{uA + uB, uA + vB, vA + uB, vA + vB\} where eA = (uA, vA) and eB = (uB, vB). 3. Parallel Culling Test: For each generated primitive, determine validity using the following propositions. Perform this in parallel on the GPU. Proposition 1 (Triangle Culling): Given fA \in FA with outward normal nA, and ei the i-th incident edge of fA pointing away from vB. If fA \oplus vB is valid, then nA \cdot ei \le 0 for all ei. If nA \cdot ei > 0 for any ei, the primitive is invalid. Proposition 2 (Quadrilateral Culling): Given eA \in EA with incident triangles f0, f1 and edges e0, e1 pointing away from eA; and eB \in EB with incident triangles f2, f3 and edges e2, e3 pointing away from eB. If eA \oplus eB is valid, then either (eA \times eB) \cdot ei \le 0 for all i \in \{0,1,2,3\} OR (eA \times eB) \cdot ei \ge 0 for all i \in \{0,1,2,3\}. If the signs of (eA \times eB) \cdot ei differ among the four edges, the primitive is invalid. Proposition 3 (Quadrilateral Culling): If either eA or eB is a concave edge, then eA \oplus eB cannot be a valid quadrilateral primitive. Proposition 4 (Triangle Culling): If vB is a concave vertex, then fA \oplus vB cannot be a valid triangle primitive. 4. Compute Normals: For remaining valid primitives, compute the surface normal to enable back-face culling during rendering. For triangle fA \oplus vB, the normal is nA (outward normal of fA). For quadrilateral eA \oplus eB, the normal is eA \times eB if (eA \times eB) \cdot ei \le 0 for all ei, otherwise -eA \times eB. 5. Write Output: Write primitives with non-zero flags and their computed normals to a Vertex Buffer Object (VBO). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def minkowskisumboundaryrendering(meshA, meshB): """ Renders the boundary of the Minkowski sum of two triangular meshes. meshA, meshB: Objects containing vertices, triangles, and edges. Returns: List of valid primitives with normals. """ validprimitives = [] # Precompute concavity flags for vertices and edges of B # Concavity check: A vertex is concave if it is not convex. # An edge is concave if the dihedral angle is > 180 degrees (interior). # This requires access to incident faces. isvertexconcaveB = computevertexconcavity(meshB) isedgeconcaveB = computeedgeconcavity(meshB) isedgeconcaveA = computeedgeconcavity(meshA) # Process Triangle Primitives: fA + vB for fA in meshA.triangles: nA = fA.outwardnormal vAlist = fA.vertices # [v0, v1, v2] for vB in meshB.vertices: if isvertexconcaveB[vB.id]: continue # Prop 4 # Generate primitive vertices primverts = [vA + vB for vA in vAlist] # Prop 1 Check valid = True for vA in vAlist: # Incident edges of fA pointing away from vA (current vertex in loop context? # Note: Prop 1 says "incident edge of fA pointing away from vB". # The text implies ei are edges of fA. The condition is nA. ei <= 0. # The proof considers ei pointing away from vB? # Re-reading Prop 1: "ei the i-th incident edge of fA pointing away from vB". # This phrasing is slightly ambiguous. Usually, edges are defined by vertices. # In the proof, it considers a point P inside fA. # Standard interpretation: Check if any edge of fA points "outward" relative to the translation direction? # Actually, the proposition states: nA. ei <= 0. # Let's assume ei are the three edges of fA. pass # Correction on Prop 1 interpretation based on proof: # The proof considers ei as edges of fA. The condition nA. ei <= 0 must hold for ALL edges. # If nA. ei > 0 for ANY edge, it is invalid. for edge in fA.edges: if dot(nA, edge.vector) > 0: valid = False break if valid: validprimitives.append({ 'type': 'triangle', 'verts': primverts, 'normal': nA, 'flag': 1 }) # Process Quadrilateral Primitives: eA + eB for eA in meshA.edges: if isedgeconcaveA[eA.id]: continue # Prop 3 (partial) for eB in meshB.edges: if isedgeconcaveB[eB.id]: continue # Prop 3 (partial) # Generate primitive vertices # eA = (uA, vA), eB = (uB, vB) uA, vA = eA.vertices uB, vB = eB.vertices primverts = [uA + uB, uA + vB, vA + uB, vA + vB] # Prop 2 Check crossprod = cross(eA.vector, eB.vector) validsign = None isvalidprop2 = True # Get incident edges for eA and eB pointing away from the edge # Need to retrieve the 4 incident edges e0, e1 from f0, f1 of eA # and e2, e3 from f2, f3 of eB. incidentedgesA = getincidentedgesawayfromedge(eA, meshA) incidentedgesB = getincidentedgesawayfromedge(eB, meshB) allincident = incidentedgesA + incidentedgesB for ei in allincident: dotval = dot(crossprod, ei.vector) if dotval == 0: continue # Zero dot product doesn't violate sign consistency if validsign is None: validsign = 1 if dotval > 0 else -1 else: currentsign = 1 if dotval > 0 else -1 if currentsign != validsign: isvalidprop2 = False break if isvalidprop2: # Determine normal direction # If (eA x eB). ei <= 0 for all, normal is eA x eB # If (eA x eB). ei >= 0 for all, normal is -eA x eB # We need to check the sign of the dot products again to set the flag allnonpos = True allnonneg = True for ei in allincident: dotval = dot(crossprod, ei.vector) if dotval > 0: allnonpos = False if dotval < 0: allnonneg = False if allnonpos: normal = crossprod flag = 1 elif allnonneg: normal = -crossprod flag = -1 else: # Should have been caught by Prop 2 check, but for safety continue validprimitives.append({ 'type': 'quadrilateral', 'verts': primverts, 'normal': normal, 'flag': flag }) return validprimitives def computevertexconcavity(mesh): # Simple heuristic: A vertex is concave if it is not convex. # For a manifold mesh, this often requires checking the solid angle or # if the vertex lies inside the convex hull of its neighbors. # This is a placeholder for the specific geometric test. return {v.id: False for v in mesh.vertices} def computeedgeconcavity(mesh): # An edge is concave if the dihedral angle between incident faces is > 180. # Normal check: If the angle between the normals of the two incident faces # and the edge vector indicates an "inward" fold. return {e.id: False for e in mesh.edges} def getincidentedgesawayfromedge(edge, mesh): # Retrieve the two faces incident to the edge. # For each face, retrieve the edge opposite to the edge's vertices? # No, the proposition says "edges of f0/f1 pointing away from eA". # This likely refers to the other two edges of the triangle that share a vertex with eA? # Or the edges of the triangle that do not include eA? # In a triangle, if eA is one edge, the other two edges share vertices with eA. # "Pointing away" usually means oriented such that they diverge from the edge. # This function needs to return the specific vectors e0, e1, e2, e3. return [] This method computes the solid and surface voxelization of the Minkowski sum of two arbitrary polyhedra directly on the GPU, bypassing the construction of a complete boundary representation (B-rep). It differs from B-rep based algorithms by avoiding complex 3D Boolean operations and high combinatorial complexity, instead leveraging GPU rasterization and depth testing to generate the volumetric representation. It builds on Minkowski Sum Boundary Rendering via Primitive Culling by extending the primitive culling concept to a full volumetric voxelization pipeline. Time Complexity: The algorithm generates O(|FA||VB| + |EA||EB|) primitives. The culling step is parallelized on the GPU, with each primitive processed independently. The number of primitives is drastically reduced by culling. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the input meshes and the generated primitives. Memory optimization is achieved by using coalesced global memory access (SoA layout) and shared memory for block-local data (16 triangles/vertices or 32 edges). Performance: On a Quadro FX 5800 GPU (30 multiprocessors, compute capacity 1.3), the CUDA implementation achieves a 25-30x speedup over a sequential CPU implementation on a Pentium 4 at 3 GHz. Using coalesced global memory and shared memory provides an additional 3x speedup over an unoptimized GPU version. Culling Efficiency: For models with 500 triangles each, 1.82% of triangle primitives and 0.46% of quadrilateral primitives remain after culling. For models with 12,396 triangles each, 2.16% of triangles and 0.59% of quads remain. Strengths: Avoids complex B-rep construction; highly parallelizable; efficient culling reduces the number of primitives to render significantly. Limitations: The culling propositions provide necessary but not sufficient conditions for validity. Some invalid primitives (those hidden inside the boundary) may remain after culling, requiring a subsequent step (like 3D flood fill) if a complete solid voxelization is needed. The method was introduced in the paper "A GPU-based voxelization approach to 3D Minkowski sum computation". It is designed for applications such as motion planning, penetration depth computation, and polyhedron interpolation/morphing. The algorithm leverages the fact that the boundary of the Minkowski sum of two convex polyhedra consists of triangles and quadrilaterals derived from the faces and edges of the input polyhedra. name: GPU-based Voxelization of 3D Minkowski Sum
head: GPU Voxelization Approach, Voxelized Minkowski Sum Computation
body: This method computes the solid and surface voxelization of the Minkowski sum of two arbitrary polyhedra directly on the GPU, bypassing the construction of a complete boundary representation (B-rep). It differs from B-rep based algorithms by avoiding complex 3D Boolean operations and high combinatorial complexity, instead leveraging GPU rasterization and depth testing to generate the volumetric representation. It builds on Minkowski Sum Boundary Rendering via Primitive Culling by extending the primitive culling concept to a full volumetric voxelization pipeline. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Two polyhedra A and B, defined by their triangle facets FA, FB, vertices VA, VB, and edges EA, EB. Outputs: A 3D grid of binary voxels representing the solid Minkowski sum A \oplus B, and a surface voxelization derived from the exterior boundary. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D array of binary values (0 or 1) stored exclusively on the GPU. Each voxel represents a unit volume cell. The grid supports resolutions up to 1024^3. Primitive Buffers: Vertex Buffer Objects (VBOs) containing the generated triangle and quadrilateral primitives. Definitions: The Minkowski sum of two point sets A and B in \mathbb{R}^n is defined as: A \oplus B = \{a + b \mid a \in A, b \in B\} Equivalently, it can be viewed as sweeping object A along the boundary of B (or vice versa): A \oplus B = \bigcup{b \in B} Ab = \bigcup{a \in A} Ba where Ab is the translation of A by vector b. Primitives Generation: Any facet on the boundary of A \oplus B is generated by one of three operations: 1. Translating a triangle in FA by a vector in VB (Triangle Primitive). 2. Translating a triangle in FB by a vector in VA (Triangle Primitive). 3. Sweeping an edge in EA along an edge in EB (Quadrilateral Primitive). The total number of primitives is |FA| \times |VB| + |VA| \times |FB| triangles and |EA| \times |EB| quadrilaterals. Algorithm Steps: 1. Primitive Culling: Identify and remove surface primitives that lie entirely inside the Minkowski sum and will not contribute to the final boundary. This step significantly reduces the number of primitives to be rendered, lowering memory usage and rendering time. The criteria for culling are based on geometric propositions from [17] (referenced in). Note: The specific geometric predicates for culling are not detailed in the provided source text. 2. Rendering to Depth Textures: Render the remaining surface primitives to depth textures along six orthogonal directions (typically \pm X, \pm Y, \pm Z). This generates an initial solid voxelization. The graphics pipeline handles partially hidden primitives (those trimmed by others) automatically via depth testing, avoiding explicit intersection computations. 3. Flood Fill: Employ a fast flood fill algorithm on the voxel grid to identify all outside voxels. This step distinguishes the interior of the Minkowski sum from the exterior, ensuring a watertight solid voxelization without holes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeminkowskivoxelization(polyhedronA, polyhedronB, resolution): """ Computes the voxelized Minkowski sum of two polyhedra on the GPU. Args: polyhedronA: Object with attributes.facets (FA),.vertices (VA),.edges (EA) polyhedronB: Object with attributes.facets (FB),.vertices (VB),.edges (EB) resolution: Integer, side length of the cubic voxel grid (e.g., 1024) Returns: voxelgrid: 3D numpy-like array of binary values (0 or 1) """ # Step 1: Generate all potential surface primitives # Triangle primitives from translating FA by VB triprims1 = [] for tri in polyhedronA.facets: for vert in polyhedronB.vertices: # Translate triangle vertices by vector vert translatedtri = translatetriangle(tri, vert) triprims1.append(translatedtri) # Triangle primitives from translating FB by VA triprims2 = [] for tri in polyhedronB.facets: for vert in polyhedronA.vertices: translatedtri = translatetriangle(tri, vert) triprims2.append(translatedtri) # Quadrilateral primitives from sweeping EA along EB quadprims = [] for edgea in polyhedronA.edges: for edgeb in polyhedronB.edges: # Sweep edgea along edgeb to form a quadrilateral quad = sweepedges(edgea, edgeb) quadprims.append(quad) allprimitives = triprims1 + triprims2 + quadprims # Step 2: Cull primitives that lie entirely inside the Minkowski sum # Note: Specific culling criteria from [17] are not detailed in # Placeholder for culling logic: A primitive is culled if it is # strictly interior to the convex hull of the sum or fails visibility tests. remainingprimitives = cullinteriorprimitives(allprimitives) # Step 3: Render primitives to depth textures along 6 orthogonal directions # Initialize depth textures for each direction depthtextures = {} for direction in ['+X', '-X', '+Y', '-Y', '+Z', '-Z']: depthtextures[direction] = createdepthtexture(resolution) # Render each primitive to each depth texture # The GPU rasterizer handles depth testing for overlapping primitives for prim in remainingprimitives: for direction in depthtextures.keys(): renderprimitivetodepth(prim, depthtextures[direction], direction) # Step 4: Convert depth textures to initial voxel grid # Implementation detail: Sample the depth textures to populate the 3D grid. # Voxels intersected by any primitive are marked as 1. voxelgrid = initializevoxelgrid(resolution) for direction, texture in depthtextures.items(): voxelizedepthtexture(texture, voxelgrid, direction) # Step 5: Flood fill to determine solid interior # Find all outside voxels (exterior) and mark them as 0 # All other voxels are interior (1) exteriorvoxels = findexteriorvoxels(voxelgrid) for voxel in exteriorvoxels: voxelgrid[voxel] = 0 return voxelgrid def translatetriangle(triangle, vector): """Translates all vertices of a triangle by a given vector.""" return Triangle([v + vector for v in triangle.vertices]) def sweepedges(edgea, edgeb): """Sweeps edgea along edgeb to generate a quadrilateral primitive.""" # Implementation detail: The quadrilateral is formed by the four vertices: # edgea.start + edgeb.start, edgea.start + edgeb.end, # edgea.end + edgeb.start, edgea.end + edgeb.end v1 = edgea.start + edgeb.start v2 = edgea.start + edgeb.end v3 = edgea.end + edgeb.end v4 = edgea.end + edgeb.start return Quadrilateral([v1, v2, v3, v4]) def cullinteriorprimitives(primitives): """ Removes primitives that lie entirely inside the Minkowski sum. Specific criteria from [17] are not provided in. """ # Placeholder: In practice, this might involve checking if the primitive's # centroid is inside the bounding box of the sum and if it is occluded by # other primitives in all viewing directions. return primitives # Placeholder return def renderprimitivetodepth(primitive, depthtexture, direction): """Renders a primitive to a specific depth texture using GPU rasterization.""" # Implementation detail: This corresponds to OpenGL/DirectX draw calls # where the primitive is projected along the specified direction. pass def voxelizedepthtexture(depthtexture, voxelgrid, direction): """Populates the voxel grid based on depth texture samples.""" # Implementation detail: For each voxel, check if the depth value # indicates the voxel is intersected by a primitive. pass def findexteriorvoxels(voxelgrid): """Finds all voxels connected to the outside boundary.""" # Implementation detail: Standard flood fill from the grid boundaries. pass Parameters: Volumetric Resolution: The algorithm supports high resolutions, specifically tested at 1024^3. Primitive Counts: The number of primitives can reach millions for polyhedra with thousands of triangles, necessitating the culling step. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Usage: Without culling, rendering millions of primitives can exceed GPU memory limits (e.g., 1 GB limits inputs to a few thousand triangles). Partial Hiding: Primitives that are partially hidden by others are handled automatically by the graphics pipeline's depth test, avoiding the need for explicit intersection computation. Holes: The flood fill step ensures the resulting solid voxelization has no holes. Time Complexity: The algorithm avoids the high combinatorial complexity (O(m^3 n^3)) of convex-decomposition or convolution approaches for concave objects. It is at least one order of magnitude faster than existing B-rep based algorithms for computing Minkowski sums of objects with curved surfaces at similar accuracy. Memory Complexity: Volumetric data is stored and computed exclusively on the GPU. The culling step significantly reduces memory usage by limiting the number of primitives rendered to depth textures. Strengths: Easy to implement, avoids complex 3D Boolean operations, supports high volumetric resolution (1024^3), and leverages GPU parallelism. Limitations: The method is specific to polyhedral inputs. The culling criteria rely on external propositions [17] not detailed in the source. When to use: Motion planning, collision detection, and penetration depth computation. When not to use: When a precise boundary representation (B-rep) is required instead of a voxelized approximation. Origin: The method was presented in 2010 at the ACM Symposium of Solid and Physical Modeling (SPM ’10) by Li and McMain. Development: It builds on the concept that Minkowski sums can be generated by sweeping one object along the boundary of another. It addresses the limitations of previous methods like Ghosh's slope diagram approach, which is complex for concave objects. Usage: The voxelized Minkowski sums are used in applications such as motion planning and penetration depth computation. name: Bitmask-based Culling
head: Bitmask Culling, Bitwise Face Culling
body: Bitmask-based Culling is a family of optimizations for blocky meshing that reduces triangle count by using bitwise operations to determine which voxel faces are visible, replacing explicit neighbor coordinate lookups with parallel integer math. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Face Culling by operating on linear bitmasks to identify exposed surfaces in bulk, solving the performance bottleneck of naive neighbor-checking loops. The core mechanism relies on representing voxel states or geometric coverage as contiguous bitmasks (integers or arrays of integers). Visibility is determined by bitwise logical operations (AND, NOT, OR, XOR) and shifts, rather than iterative spatial checks. 1. State Representation Binary State: A single bit per voxel indicates solid (1) or empty/air (0). Coverage Mask: For partial shapes, a bitmask (e.g., 16-bit for a 4x4 grid) represents the geometric coverage of a face. 2. Visibility Logic Binary: A face is visible if the voxel is solid AND the neighbor is empty. This is computed as M \ \& \ (\sim M{shifted}). Coverage: A face is visible if the current block's coverage mask has bits set that are not covered by the neighbor's mask. This is computed as CurrentMask \ \& \ (\sim NeighborMask). 3. Implementation Constraints Data Layout: Requires data to be accessible in a linear or axis-aligned slice format to enable bitwise shifts. Precision: The integer type must be large enough to hold the entire slice or chunk dimension. For large chunks, arrays of integers are required. Determines visibility by comparing precomputed bitmasks of geometric coverage between adjacent blocks. It solves the problem where simple boolean flags are insufficient for partial shapes (stairs, slabs) that have mixed visible/hidden areas on a single face. Unlike binary methods, it retains accuracy for partial geometry while avoiding full CSG. Reduces face count by removing faces completely hidden by adjacent voxels using bitwise operations on a linear bitmask. It solves the performance bottleneck of random memory access by replacing it with parallel bitwise math on 1D slices. Unlike general face culling, it operates on linear bitmasks without explicit spatial lookups. A bitmask used to track which blocks in a chunk are 'buried' (fully surrounded by opaque blocks), allowing the renderer to skip mesh generation for those blocks. 1. Reset the buried bitmask for the chunk. 2. Create MappedAdjacentChunks for the current chunk position to access neighboring chunks. 3. Iterate through all blocks in the chunk (0 to CHUNKSIZE). For each block, determine if it is buried by calling block->isBuried(...) and set the corresponding flag in the bitmask. 4. If all blocks in the chunk are buried (checked via buriedBitmask->AreAllBlocksSet()), mark the mesh as empty and skip mesh generation. 5. When generating the mesh, skip any block that is air or has its buried flag set in the bitmask. Originating from the optimization techniques used in voxel-based games like Minecraft, this method evolved to handle the massive triangle counts generated by naive meshing. The specific "Buried Bitmask" variant is documented in the unofficial repository. The general bitwise approach for 1D slices is also described in unofficial sources. gabkhanfig/Cube, https://github.com/gabkhanfig/Cube, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Unofficial notes on Bitmask-based Culling, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Block Placement with Face Culling
head: Chunk Block Toggle, Dynamic Voxel Meshing
body: Voxel Block Placement with Face Culling is a technique for dynamically updating a voxel chunk's internal state and face visibility when blocks are placed or removed, using neighbor checks to toggle shared faces without regenerating the entire mesh. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A voxel chunk containing a flat array of block data, a block position (x, y, z), and a block ID. Output: Updated chunk state reflecting the presence/absence of the block and the visibility of adjacent faces. Data Structures: The chunk stores block data in a flat array: uint32t data[CHUNKSIZE CHUNKSIZE CHUNKSIZE] where CHUNKSIZE = 16. Element Size: Each element is 4 bytes; the source's "4096 bytes total" refers to the full chunk size 16^3 \times 4. Index Mapping: pos = x | (y << 4) | (z << 8). Block ID: Occupies the lower 6 bits (mask 0x3F), stored as 0x3F000000 | id. Face Visibility: Remaining bits track face visibility via Block::toggleBlockFace. Algorithm Steps: 1. Place Block: 1. Check bounds. If data[pos] == 0 and id > 0, set data[pos] = 0x3F000000 | id and increment blockCount. 2. For each of the 6 neighbors (directions \pm x, \pm y, \pm z): a. Call toggleFace on the neighbor. b. If the neighbor exists (within bounds), call toggleFace on the current block's corresponding opposite face. 2. Remove Block: 1. Check bounds. If data[pos] > 0 and id == 0, set data[pos] = 0 and decrement blockCount. 2. Call toggleFace on all 6 neighbors unconditionally to update their face states. 3. Neighbor Face Toggle: 1. If neighbor coordinates are within chunk bounds, compute neighbor pos. 2. If neighbor block exists (data[neighborpos] > 0), call Block::toggleBlockFace(data + neighborpos, side). 3. Return true if toggle occurred, false otherwise. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. CHUNKSIZE = 16 SIDEMASKS = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32] # 6 face masks OPPOSITE = [3, 2, 5, 4, 1, 0] # Opposite face indices def index(x, y, z): return x | (y << 4) | (z << 8) def isinbounds(x, y, z): return 0 <= x < CHUNKSIZE and 0 <= y < CHUNKSIZE and 0 <= z < CHUNKSIZE def toggleblockface(blockdata, side): # Toggles the visibility bit for the given side return blockdata ^ SIDEMASKS[side] def placeblock(chunkdata, x, y, z, blockid): pos = index(x, y, z) if not isinbounds(x, y, z): return currentval = chunkdata[pos] if currentval == 0 and blockid > 0: chunkdata[pos] = 0x3F000000 | blockid # Increment blockCount directions = [(1, 0, 0, 0), (-1, 0, 0, 3), (0, 1, 0, 1), (0, -1, 0, 4), (0, 0, 1, 2), (0, 0, -1, 5)] for dx, dy, dz, side in directions: nx, ny, nz = x + dx, y + dy, z + dz if isinbounds(nx, ny, nz): npos = index(nx, ny, nz) # Toggle face on neighbor chunkdata[npos] = toggleblockface(chunkdata[npos], side) # Toggle face on current block (opposite side) chunkdata[pos] = toggleblockface(chunkdata[pos], OPPOSITE[side]) def removeblock(chunkdata, x, y, z, blockid): pos = index(x, y, z) if not isinbounds(x, y, z): return currentval = chunkdata[pos] if currentval > 0 and blockid == 0: chunkdata[pos] = 0 # Decrement blockCount directions = [(1, 0, 0, 0), (-1, 0, 0, 3), (0, 1, 0, 1), (0, -1, 0, 4), (0, 0, 1, 2), (0, 0, -1, 5)] for dx, dy, dz, side in directions: nx, ny, nz = x + dx, y + dy, z + dz if isinbounds(nx, ny, nz): npos = index(nx, ny, nz) # Toggle face on neighbor unconditionally chunkdata[npos] = toggleblockface(chunkdata[npos], OPPOSITE[side]) def toggleface(chunkdata, x, y, z, side): # Wrapper matching evidence step 3 if not isinbounds(x, y, z): return False npos = index(x, y, z) if chunkdata[npos] > 0: chunkdata[npos] = toggleblockface(chunkdata[npos], side) return True return False Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Checks: Prevent out-of-bounds memory access when toggling faces at chunk edges. If a neighbor is outside the chunk, toggleFace returns false, correctly skipping the face update for that direction. Static Mesh Caching reduces draw calls and GPU data upload frequency by aggregating all voxel geometry into a single Mesh object. It differs from its parent Voxel Block Placement with Face Culling by ignoring shared face optimization; instead of toggling visibility, it rebuilds the full geometry of every visible voxel into one buffer. It differs from Dynamic Block Mesh Management by maintaining a single global mesh rather than managing multiple independent mesh objects. Dynamic Block Mesh Management is a technique for maintaining a dynamic list of block indices organized by spatial coordinates, allowing for efficient addition and removal of individual block faces without rebuilding the entire mesh. It solves the performance bottleneck of static mesh regeneration in voxel environments where the geometry changes frequently. Unlike Static Mesh Caching, which assumes immutable geometry, this method updates the index buffer in real-time by managing block-level data structures. Originating from the Shiranuit/VoxelEngine-0 project, this method is part of a broader effort in efficient voxel rendering. name: Static Mesh Caching
head: Mesh Caching, Voxel Mesh Caching
body: Static Mesh Caching reduces draw calls and GPU data upload frequency by aggregating all voxel geometry into a single Mesh object. It differs from its parent Voxel Block Placement with Face Culling by ignoring shared face optimization; instead of toggling visibility, it rebuilds the full geometry of every visible voxel into one buffer. It differs from Dynamic Block Mesh Management by maintaining a single global mesh rather than managing multiple independent mesh objects. Inputs: A world data structure containing a HashSet of active voxel positions (IVec3) and an optional cached Mesh field. Outputs: A single Mesh object containing vertices for all active voxels. Data Structures: The world state is represented by a World struct containing: voxels: A HashSet of 3D integer coordinates (IVec3) representing active voxel positions. mesh: An optional Mesh object. If none, the mesh is invalid or uninitialized. Steps: 1. Check Validity: During the render pass, check if world.mesh is not none. 2. Render Cached: If the mesh exists, upload it once and draw it using a single draw call. 3. Rebuild if Invalid: If world.mesh is none: a. Initialize an empty vertex list. b. Iterate through every position in world.voxels. c. For each position, generate the 36 vertices (6 faces × 6 vertices) of a unit cube centered at that position. d. Append these vertices to the list. e. Construct a new Mesh from the accumulated vertices and assign it to world.mesh. f. Draw the newly created mesh. 4. Invalidate on Change: Whenever a voxel is added or removed from world.voxels, set world.mesh to none to force a rebuild on the next render frame. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class World: voxels: set mesh: Optional[Mesh] def render(self): if self.mesh is not None: drawmesh(self.mesh) else: self.mesh = self.createmesh() drawmesh(self.mesh) def createmesh(self) -> Mesh: vertices = [] for voxelpos in self.voxels: # Generate 36 vertices for a unit cube at voxelpos and append to vertices pass return Mesh.fromvertices(vertices) def flipvoxel(self, position: IVec3): self.mesh = None if position in self.voxels: self.voxels.remove(position) else: self.voxels.add(position) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visual Discrepancies: Modifying world.voxels without setting world.mesh to none causes the renderer to display stale geometry. Performance Cost: Rebuilding the entire mesh is computationally expensive for large worlds. For example, a 2048x2048 world contains over 4 million cubes; rebuilding this geometry for a single block change is prohibitive. Splits the voxel world into independent chunks to allow localized mesh rebuilding, solving the performance bottleneck of global invalidation inherent in Static Mesh Caching. It differs from its parent by partitioning the single mesh object into multiple chunk-specific meshes, enabling independent updates per chunk rather than global invalidation. Time Complexity: O(V) for mesh creation, where V is the number of voxels. O(1) for rendering if the mesh is valid. O(1) for invalidation, but O(V) for the subsequent rebuild. Memory Complexity: O(V) to store vertex data for all voxels. Performance: Significantly reduces draw calls from V (or number of chunks) to 1. However, it incurs high CPU cost during updates. Strengths: Minimal draw call overhead; simple implementation. Limitations: Cannot handle dynamic worlds efficiently. Rebuilding the entire mesh for a single change is too slow for large resolutions (e.g., > 32x32). When to use: Small, static, or rarely changing voxel worlds. When not to use: Large, dynamic voxel worlds where frequent block placement/removal occurs. Originated in tutorials for building voxel engines from scratch, specifically highlighted in "Make yourself a Voxel Engine THIS weekend". It serves as a foundational optimization step before introducing more complex techniques like face culling or chunking. name: Chunked World Management
head: Chunk-based Mesh Caching
body: Chunked World Management splits a voxel world into smaller, independent sub-worlds called chunks to allow localized mesh rebuilding instead of processing the entire volume. This method builds on Static Mesh Caching by partitioning the single mesh cache into per-chunk meshes, enabling efficient updates when only a small portion of the world changes. It differs from Remesh Budget by focusing on spatial partitioning for data locality rather than time-budgeted dynamic simplification, and from Chunk-Based Parallel Voxel Culling & Rendering by handling the mesh generation and caching logic rather than just the GPU submission phase. Inputs and Outputs: Input: World coordinates of voxel edits (add/remove), world position for rendering. Output: Updated chunk data structures, per-chunk mesh objects, final rendered scene. Data Structures: The world is represented by a World struct containing a HashMap mapping chunk positions to Chunk objects. World: chunks: HashMap<IVec3, Chunk> mapping chunk coordinates to chunk instances. Chunk: voxels: HashSet<IVec3> storing local voxel positions within the chunk. mesh: Mesh? (optional) storing the generated geometry for the chunk. Parameters: Chunk size: 32 \times 32 \times 32 blocks. Steps: 1. Coordinate Conversion: When a voxel is edited at world position P, calculate the chunk position C and local position L. Use Euclidean division and remainder to handle negative coordinates correctly, ensuring consistent chunk boundaries across the entire grid. C = P \text{ div\euclid}(S) L = P \text{ rem\euclid}(S) Where S is the chunk size (32). 2. Chunk Access: Retrieve or create the Chunk object at position C in World.chunks. 3. Data Update: Invalidate the existing mesh for the chunk (set mesh to none) to mark it for regeneration. Update the chunk's voxels set: remove the voxel if it exists, or insert it if it does not. 4. Rendering: Iterate over all chunks in World.chunks. For each chunk, if mesh is none, generate the mesh by iterating over voxels and drawing cubes for each local position. Draw the mesh with an offset applied: Offset = C \times S. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. CHUNKSIZE = 32 class World: chunks: dict # Maps IVec3 -> Chunk class Chunk: voxels: set # Set of IVec3 (local positions) mesh: object # Mesh object or None class IVec3: x: int y: int z: int def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z def diveuclid(self, divisor): # Euclidean division for negative numbers # Returns (quotient, remainder) # In Python: divmod handles this correctly for negative numbers if using floor division # But explicitly: q = floor(x / d), r = x - q d # For IVec3, apply to each component return IVec3( self.x // divisor if self.x >= 0 else -((-self.x + divisor - 1) // divisor), # Simplified logic below self.y // divisor if self.y >= 0 else -((-self.y + divisor - 1) // divisor), self.z // divisor if self.z >= 0 else -((-self.z + divisor - 1) // divisor)) # More robust implementation for diveuclid and remeuclid def diveuclid(self, divisor): return IVec3( self.x // divisor if self.x >= 0 else -((-self.x + divisor - 1) // divisor), self.y // divisor if self.y >= 0 else -((-self.y + divisor - 1) // divisor), self.z // divisor if self.z >= 0 else -((-self.z + divisor - 1) // divisor)) def remeuclid(self, divisor): return IVec3( self.x % divisor if self.x >= 0 else divisor - ((-self.x) % divisor) if (-self.x) % divisor != 0 else 0, self.y % divisor if self.y >= 0 else divisor - ((-self.y) % divisor) if (-self.y) % divisor != 0 else 0, self.z % divisor if self.z >= 0 else divisor - ((-self.z) % divisor) if (-self.z) % divisor != 0 else 0) def getorcreatechunk(world: World, chunkpos: IVec3) -> Chunk: if chunkpos not in world.chunks: world.chunks[chunkpos] = Chunk() world.chunks[chunkpos].voxels = set() world.chunks[chunkpos].mesh = None return world.chunks[chunkpos] def flipvoxel(world: World, position: IVec3): # Calculate chunk and local positions using Euclidean division chunkpos = IVec3( position.x // CHUNKSIZE if position.x >= 0 else -((-position.x + CHUNKSIZE - 1) // CHUNKSIZE), position.y // CHUNKSIZE if position.y >= 0 else -((-position.y + CHUNKSIZE - 1) // CHUNKSIZE), position.z // CHUNKSIZE if position.z >= 0 else -((-position.z + CHUNKSIZE - 1) // CHUNKSIZE)) # Correct Euclidean remainder localpos = IVec3( position.x % CHUNKSIZE if position.x >= 0 else (CHUNKSIZE - (abs(position.x) % CHUNKSIZE)) % CHUNKSIZE, position.y % CHUNKSIZE if position.y >= 0 else (CHUNKSIZE - (abs(position.y) % CHUNKSIZE)) % CHUNKSIZE, position.z % CHUNKSIZE if position.z >= 0 else (CHUNKSIZE - (abs(position.z) % CHUNKSIZE)) % CHUNKSIZE) chunk = getorcreatechunk(world, chunkpos) # Invalidate mesh chunk.mesh = None # Update voxels if localpos in chunk.voxels: chunk.voxels.remove(localpos) else: chunk.voxels.add(localpos) def createmesh(chunk: Chunk) -> object: vertices = [] for voxelpos in chunk.voxels: # drawcube adds vertices for a unit cube at voxelpos drawcube(vertices, voxelpos) return Mesh.fromvertices(vertices) def drawmesh(mesh: object, offset: IVec3): # Apply offset to mesh vertices or transform matrix pass def renderworld(world: World): for chunkpos, chunk in world.chunks.items(): if chunk.mesh is None: chunk.mesh = createmesh(chunk) offset = IVec3( chunkpos.x CHUNKSIZE, chunkpos.y CHUNKSIZE, chunkpos.z CHUNKSIZE) drawmesh(chunk.mesh, offset) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Negative Coordinates: Standard integer division and modulus operations fail for negative numbers in many programming languages, resulting in incorrect chunk assignment and uneven chunk sizes (e.g., a chunk at the origin becoming double-sized). Euclidean division (diveuclid) and remainder (remeuclid) must be used to ensure consistent behavior across the entire grid. A manager class that handles spatial hashing, automatic job scheduling, world/local coordinate conversion, and smart meshing algorithm selection (blocky vs smooth). It selects the appropriate meshing algorithm (e.g., GreedyMeshingJob for blocky, MarchingCubesJob for smooth) based on voxel data and generates meshes automatically via Unity Jobs. It supports half-precision density to save 50% memory (68KB vs 128KB per 32^3 chunk). A remeshing strategy that rebuilds meshes only for a ring of chunks surrounding an edit, combined with pruning meshes for deleted chunks to prevent visual artifacts during undo. When an edit occurs, the owning chunk and any existing neighbor across a shared face are marked dirty. Meshes are rebuilt only for these dirty chunks. If a chunk is deleted during an undo operation, its mesh is explicitly pruned; without this, the chunk's quads would continue to draw, causing the undone stroke to remain visible on screen despite passing CPU assertions. Time Complexity: Mesh generation is localized to the affected chunk and its neighbors, reducing update time from O(N) to O(k) where k is the number of voxels in the affected chunk(s). Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the number of active chunks and their voxel counts. Using half-precision density can reduce memory per chunk by 50%. Performance: Localized updates prevent main-thread stalls associated with rebuilding the entire world mesh. Parallel job scheduling can further accelerate mesh generation. Strengths: Efficient handling of dynamic worlds with frequent localized edits; reduced draw calls compared to per-voxel rendering; modular architecture. Limitations: Requires careful handling of chunk boundaries and negative coordinates; potential for visual artifacts if dirty region logic or mesh pruning is not implemented correctly. When to Use: Suitable for voxel engines where the world is large and edits are frequent but localized. When Not to Use: Not ideal for static worlds where a single global mesh might be more efficient, or for worlds with extremely high-frequency global changes. Chunked World Management originated as a fundamental optimization in voxel engine development, allowing developers to build worlds out of independent "tiny worlds" (chunks) to enable efficient updates. It is widely used in modern voxel engines and games (e.g., Minecraft) to handle large, dynamic environments. name: Remesh Budget

body: Remesh Budget is a rendering optimization that processes dirty chunks nearest the camera first within a strict time budget per frame. It prevents main-thread stalls by limiting the number of sub-chunks remeshed per frame and capping the total time spent on geometry generation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of "dirty" chunks (sub-chunks containing modified voxel data) and the current camera position. Output: Updated GPU mesh data for a subset of dirty chunks, marked as "clean" in the world state. Data Structures: RemeshQueue: A collection of chunk indices ordered by distance to the camera (nearest first). ChunkMeshData: Contains Vertices (span of vertices), Indices (span of indices), VertexCount, and IndexCount. GpuMesh: Constructed from data[i].Vertices and data[i].Indices. Frame State: rebuildsThisFrame: Integer counter for chunks processed in the current frame. frameStarted: Timestamp recorded at the start of the frame using System.Diagnostics.Stopwatch.GetTimestamp(). MaxRebuildsPerFrame: Constant integer limit (typically 24). RebuildBudgetMs: Constant double limit (typically 6.0 ms). FrameBudget: Time budget for remeshing per frame (typically 3 ms). Transform Pipeline: VoxelBody mesh generation translates geometry to center, scales by voxel scale, rotates by quaternion, then translates to world position. Parameters: MaxRebuildsPerFrame: 24. RebuildBudgetMs: 6.0 ms. FrameBudget: 3 ms. Note: One sub-chunk always goes through even if the budget is exceeded. Steps: 1. BeginFrame: Reset rebuildsThisFrame to 0 and record frameStarted timestamp using System.Diagnostics.Stopwatch.GetTimestamp(). 2. RebuildAllowed: Returns true if rebuildsThisFrame < MaxRebuildsPerFrame AND (rebuildsThisFrame == 0 OR elapsed time since frameStarted < RebuildBudgetMs). 3. RebuildWithinBudget: Iterate through all chunk indices. If chunk is dirty and rebuild is allowed, increment rebuildsThisFrame, call Rebuild, and mark chunk clean. If rebuild is not allowed, set complete to false and continue. Return true if all dirty chunks were processed. 4. Prepare: If pending task exists and is not complete, return false. If complete, call FinishPending. Collect dirty chunk indices. If none, return true. Create a task on a worker thread that builds meshes for dirty chunks using a local MeshBuilder. Return false. 5. FinishPending: If pending task is not completed, return false. If completed, clear pending. If pending mode differs from current mode, return true (meshes are useless). Otherwise, upload each chunk's data and mark chunks clean. Pseudocode: Unverified code. self.framestarted if elapsedms >= self.rebuildbudgetms: return False return True def prepare(self): if self.pendingtask is not None: if not self.pendingtask["complete"]: return False self.finishpending() self.dirtychunks = [idx for idx in self.chunkdirtyflags if self.ischunkdirty(idx)] if not self.dirtychunks: return True self.dirtychunks.sort(key=lambda c: self.distancetocamera(c)) # self.pendingtask = {"chunks": self.dirtychunks, "complete": False, "mode": self.currentmode} # Create a task on a worker thread that builds meshes for dirty chunks using a local MeshBuilder return False def rebuildwithinbudget(self): if not self.dirtychunks: return True allprocessed = True firstchunk = True for chunkindex in self.dirtychunks: if not self.ischunkdirty(chunkindex): continue if self.isrebuildallowed() or firstchunk: # Always process at least one chunk self.rebuildsthisframe += 1 self.rebuildchunk(chunkindex) self.markchunkclean(chunkindex) firstchunk = False else: allprocessed = False break return allprocessed def finishpending(self): if self.pendingtask is None: return if not self.pendingtask["complete"]: return False pendingchunks = self.pendingtask["chunks"] pendingmode = self.pendingtask["mode"] self.pendingtask = None if pendingmode != self.currentmode: return True for chunkindex in pendingchunks: self.uploadchunkdata(chunkindex) self.markchunkclean(chunkindex) return True Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Mode Switch: Changing TerrainMode from Blocks to Smooth or vice versa marks all bodies dirty, triggering full remeshing over subsequent frames. Precision: Timestamps should use high-resolution counters (e.g., Stopwatch.GetTimestamp()) to accurately measure sub-millisecond budgets. Boundaries: The first chunk is always processed regardless of budget limits to ensure responsiveness. A queue-based system to batch and process chunk mesh rebuilds asynchronously or on tick. It defers mesh regeneration from immediate block modifications, processing them in a dedicated loop. Time Complexity: Bounded by the frame budget rather than total chunk count. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of queued dirty chunks. Measured Performance: In the Outpost scene (4 chunks, 10k triangles), the system handles 37 draws/200k triangles on Low, 114 draws/879k on Balanced, and 153 draws/1.87M on Ultra. Strengths: Prevents main-thread stalls during rapid block placement. Limitations: May leave some dirty chunks unprocessed in a single frame if the budget is exceeded. name: Chunk Mesh Rebuild Queue

body: A queue-based system to batch and process chunk mesh rebuilds asynchronously or on tick. It defers mesh regeneration from immediate block modifications, processing them in a dedicated loop. Inputs: RebuildQueue: List of ChunkIndex values pending regeneration. RebuildSet: Set of ChunkIndex values currently queued to prevent duplicates. ActiveChunks: Set of ChunkIndex values currently loaded. ChunkCache: Map from ChunkIndex to raw voxel block data. WorldMesh: Mesh manager object. PlayerPosition: 2D coordinates (x, y) of the player. Outputs: Updated meshes for processed chunks. Collision state updates for chunks near the player. Data Structures: ChunkIndex: 2D integer coordinate (x, y) or equivalent identifier. RebuildQueue: LIFO stack. RebuildSet: Hash set for O(1) lookup. Steps: 1. Enqueue Modification: When a chunk is modified, check if its ChunkIndex exists in RebuildSet. If not, add ChunkIndex to both RebuildSet and RebuildQueue. 2. Process Loop: Check if RebuildQueue is empty or WorldMesh is null. If so, terminate. 3. Pop Task: Retrieve the last element from RebuildQueue: ChunkIndex = RebuildQueue.Last(). Remove it from the queue: RebuildQueue.Pop(). Remove ChunkIndex from RebuildSet. 4. Validate Activity: Check if ChunkIndex is present in ActiveChunks. If not, return. 5. Retrieve Data: Fetch chunk data from ChunkCache using ChunkIndex. If data is missing, return. 6. Prepare Mesh: Generate geometry from the raw block data: Mesh = PrepareChunkMesh(Data). 7. Update Mesh: Replace the old mesh with the new one: WorldMesh.UpdateChunk(ChunkIndex, Mesh). 8. Collision Check: Determine if the chunk is near the player (within 1 chunk in X and Y axes). If true, enable collision for the chunk. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ProcessRebuildQueue(RebuildQueue, RebuildSet, ActiveChunks, ChunkCache, WorldMesh, PlayerPosition): if not RebuildQueue or WorldMesh is None: return ChunkIndex = RebuildQueue[-1] RebuildQueue.pop() RebuildSet.discard(ChunkIndex) if ChunkIndex not in ActiveChunks: return Data = ChunkCache.get(ChunkIndex) if Data is None: return Mesh = PrepareChunkMesh(Data) # Generates mesh geometry from raw block data WorldMesh.UpdateChunk(ChunkIndex, Mesh) if abs(ChunkIndex.x - PlayerPosition.x) <= 1 and abs(ChunkIndex.y - PlayerPosition.y) <= 1: ChunkCollisionState[ChunkIndex] = True # Enables collision flags for the chunk Edge Cases: Duplicate Modifications: The RebuildSet prevents adding the same chunk to the queue multiple times if multiple blocks change in the same frame. Unloaded Chunks: Chunks modified while outside the active view are skipped if they are not in ActiveChunks during processing. Null Mesh: If WorldMesh is not initialized, the queue processing halts immediately to prevent crashes. Asynchronous Chunk Loading offloads the computationally expensive process of generating chunk meshes from the main execution thread to a background thread pool, preventing frame stutter and maintaining frame rate in large voxel worlds. It solves the problem of blocking the game loop during mesh generation by using futures and task queues to synchronize data transfer between the generation thread and the rendering or game thread. Unlike synchronous loading, which halts execution until the mesh is ready, this method allows the player to continue interacting with the world while chunks are being generated in the background. Distributes terrain generation and meshing tasks across multiple CPU threads using a LIFO job queue with priority handling. It solves the bottleneck of synchronous chunk processing by decoupling job submission from execution, allowing the main thread to continue while workers process geometry. Unlike Asynchronous Chunk Loading which focuses on data transfer, this method focuses on CPU-intensive computation (generation and meshing). It builds on Chunk Mesh Rebuild Queue by providing the actual parallel execution engine. Time and memory complexity are not given in the sources.
