name: Face Coverage Mask Culling
head: Bitmask Culling, Culling Limitations, Partial Shape Culling
body: Face Coverage Mask Culling is a method for optimizing the mesh generation of voxel-based partial shapes (such as stairs, slabs, and walls) by determining face visibility using bitwise coverage masks rather than binary solid/empty flags. It solves the problem where a simple boolean solid flag is insufficient because partial shapes have mixed visible and hidden areas on a single face, preventing accurate culling of neighbor interactions. Unlike Binary Hidden-Face Culling, which treats faces as entirely solid or empty, this method distinguishes between fully occluded faces and partially visible ones, allowing for more accurate geometry reduction for complex shapes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A grid of voxel blocks, where each block has an associated shape definition. Each shape definition includes precomputed occlusion masks for all six faces and all possible rotations. Output: A set of triangle primitives for the visible boundary faces of the voxel chunk. Data Structures: The core data structure is the FaceMask, a 16-bit unsigned integer (u16) representing the geometric coverage of a 4x4 grid on a face boundary. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. #[derive(Clone, Copy)] struct FaceMask(u16); Two constants define the extremes of coverage: FULL: FaceMask(0xffff), representing a fully opaque face (e.g., a solid cube side). EMPTY: FaceMask(0x0000), representing a fully empty face. For transparent or cutout materials, the coverage is separated from material behavior using a FaceOcclusion struct: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct FaceOcclusion { coverage: FaceMask, mode: OcclusionMode, } Where OcclusionMode is an enum expressing behavior such as opaque, cutout, translucent, or never-occluding. Numbered Steps: 1. Precompute Masks: During library baking, determine the 4x4 coverage mask for each face of every shape in all allowed orientations. Store these in a lookup table shape.occlusion[rotation][face]. This eliminates runtime rotation calculations. 2. Iterate Faces: For each voxel in the chunk, iterate through its six faces. 3. Retrieve Masks: For the current face, retrieve the current block's coverage mask and the neighbor's opposite face mask: python currentmask = shape.occlusion[rotation][face] neighbormask = neighborshape.occlusion[neighborrotation][opposite(face)] If the neighbor is missing (e.g., outside the chunk boundary), treat the neighbor mask as EMPTY. 4. Check Occlusion: Determine if the current face is fully occluded by the neighbor using bitwise logic: python def fullyoccluded(current: FaceMask, neighbor: FaceMask) -> bool: return (current.0 & ~neighbor.0) == 0 Conceptually, this calculates visible = current coverage - neighbor coverage. 5. Handle Visibility: If fullyoccluded is true, the face is removed entirely. If fullyoccluded is false, the face is visible. The implementer must choose between: Keeping the original face geometry (accepting overdraw for hidden parts). Generating/subdividing geometry to only expose the uncovered region (reducing geometry but increasing mesher complexity). 6. Boundary Classification: Only geometry lying on the voxel cell boundary planes participates in neighbor culling. Internal triangles within a complex block are not tested against neighbors. A polygon is classified as a boundary polygon if all relevant vertices lie on the same cell boundary within a small tolerance. 7. Transparency Handling: For transparent materials, combine shape coverage with material occlusion behavior. Two adjacent glass blocks may geometrically cover each other, but the shared face's removal depends on material semantics. Formulas: Visibility Check: Visible = CurrentMask \ \& \ (\sim NeighborMask) Full Occlusion: FullyOccluded \iff (Visible == 0) Parameters: Grid Resolution: Typically 4x4 (16 bits), but depends on the shape vocabulary. FULL: 0xffff. EMPTY: 0x0000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Partial Occlusion Artifacts: If a cube touches a slab, the slab's side is culled, but the cube's side remains half-visible. The engine leaves triangles of the whole side visible, as sides are either fully culled or not culled. Transparency Issues: Transparency exposes underlying geometry due to culling limitations. There is no way to avoid this other than avoiding such situations in game design (e.g., no glass slabs in Minecraft). Missing Neighbors: If a neighbor chunk is not available, the engine must define a policy (e.g., treat as air, delay meshing, or use an unknown state). A geometry shader technique that generates cube faces from point primitives based on a bitmask, culling hidden faces to reduce overdraw and vertex processing. It builds on Face Coverage Mask Culling by using the bitmask to determine face visibility at the primitive generation stage. A face culling technique that uses per-face column arrays and opaque column arrays to determine visibility based on solid and transparent block transitions, allowing full per-face control over opacity. It extends Face Coverage Mask Culling by distinguishing between opaque and transparent surface contributions on partial shapes. Boundary Geometry Classification is a geometric filtering step used during octree construction and neighbor-based culling to distinguish surface geometry located on voxel cell boundary planes from internal geometry within complex blocks. It solves the problem where neighbor occlusion tests would incorrectly prune or interact with internal fragments of non-manifold or complex shapes by ensuring that culling logic only applies to polygons strictly lying on the six faces of the current voxel cell. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Face Coverage Mask Culling by operating at the individual polygon level to identify which geometry is eligible for neighbor interaction, rather than determining how to cull based on coverage masks. Discrete Polygonal Occlusion via 2D Boundary Coverage (VXL-044) is a synchronous mesh baking optimization that reduces polygon count by determining which inner shell polygons of a voxel cell are occluded by adjacent cells using discrete 2D coverage masks on cell boundaries. It solves the problem of replacing exact rational-coordinate geometric clipping with a deterministic, integer-based rasterization approach to verify if a boundary is fully enclosed by opaque neighbors. Unlike its siblings, which may rely on continuous geometry or per-frame GPU culling, this method operates on a fixed 1000x1000 integer grid per face during the model bake phase, ensuring deterministic results without floating-point precision issues. A method to handle culling for transparent or cutout materials by separating geometric coverage from material occlusion behavior. It uses a FaceOcclusion struct containing coverage: FaceMask and mode: OcclusionMode, where OcclusionMode expresses behavior such as opaque, cutout, translucent, or never-occluding. Time Complexity: O(1) per face for the culling check, as it involves only bitwise operations and table lookups. Memory Complexity: O(N \times F \times R) for precomputed masks, where N is the number of shapes, F is the number of faces (6), and R is the number of rotations. Performance: Very fast meshing due to precomputed bitmasks and minimal allocation in the inner loop. Strengths: Efficient culling for partial shapes; simple bitwise logic; precomputation reduces runtime cost. Limitations: Cannot perfectly cut out geometry like CSG; partial occlusion results in overdraw or complex geometry generation; transparency handling is limited. When to Use: When rendering voxel worlds with partial shapes (stairs, slabs) and performance is critical. When Not to Use: When exact geometric clipping is required, or when complex transparency interactions are necessary. Originating from voxel game engines like Minecraft, this method was developed to optimize the rendering of blocky terrains with partial shapes. The technique relies on precomputed bitmasks to quickly determine face visibility, avoiding the computational cost of full CSG operations. It is widely used in voxel-based games and editors where mesh generation performance is crucial. name: Face-Culling Geometry Shader
head: Bitmask Face Generation, Cube Face Culling
body: A geometry shader technique that generates cube faces from point primitives based on a bitmask, culling hidden faces to reduce overdraw and vertex processing. It builds on Face Coverage Mask Culling by using the bitmask to determine face visibility at the primitive generation stage. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single point primitive per voxel. Attributes are vertexColour (vec4) and faceBitmaskA (uint). The geometry shader receives these as arrays (vertexColour[], faceBitmaskB[]), where faceBitmaskB is a direct copy of faceBitmaskA. Output: A stream of triangle strips. The shader declares layout (trianglestrip, maxvertices = 48) out, allowing up to 48 vertices per input point. Data Structures: faceBitmaskA/faceBitmaskB: A 32-bit unsigned integer where specific bits correspond to face visibility: Bit 0 (0x01): Front face (z = +0.5). Bit 1 (0x02): Back face (z = -0.5). Bit 2 (0x04): Left face (x = -0.5). Bit 3 (0x08): Right face (x = +0.5). Bit 4 (0x10): Top face (y = +0.5). Bit 5 (0x20): Bottom face (y = -0.5). vertexColour: The color attribute passed from the vertex shader. Parameters: projection: A uniform 4×4 matrix applied to vertex positions. Steps: 1. The vertex shader passes the voxel position, color, and bitmask to the geometry shader. 2. The geometry shader receives the point primitive and checks each bit of faceBitmaskB against the corresponding face constant. 3. For each set bit, the shader emits two triangle strips forming a square face centered on the voxel's local coordinate system. 4. Vertices are generated by offsetting the input point position by ±0.5 in the relevant axes. 5. The projection matrix is applied to each vertex position before emission. 6. The vertex color is set to the input color for each emitted vertex. Formulas: P{out} = M{proj} \times (P{in} + \Delta), where P{in} is the input point position, M{proj} is the projection matrix, and \Delta is the face offset vector (\pm 0.5, \pm 0.5, \pm 0.5). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatecubefaces(position, color, mask, projection): """ Generates visible cube faces from a point primitive using a bitmask. position: tuple (x, y, z) color: tuple (r, g, b, a) mask: int (bitmask) projection: 4x4 matrix (list of 4 lists, each with 4 floats) Returns: list of vertex tuples (projectedpos, color) """ vertices = [] # Face constants and their corresponding vertex offsets relative to position # Each face emits two triangle strips (6 vertices total per face) faces = { 0x01: [ # Front (z=+0.5) (-0.5, -0.5, 0.5), (0.5, -0.5, 0.5), (0.5, 0.5, 0.5), (0.5, 0.5, 0.5), (-0.5, 0.5, 0.5), (-0.5, -0.5, 0.5) ], 0x02: [ # Back (z=-0.5) (-0.5, -0.5, -0.5), (-0.5, 0.5, -0.5), (0.5, 0.5, -0.5), (0.5, 0.5, -0.5), (0.5, -0.5, -0.5), (-0.5, -0.5, -0.5) ], 0x04: [ # Left (x=-0.5) (-0.5, -0.5, -0.5), (-0.5, -0.5, 0.5), (-0.5, 0.5, 0.5), (-0.5, 0.5, 0.5), (-0.5, 0.5, -0.5), (-0.5, -0.5, -0.5) ], 0x08: [ # Right (x=+0.5) (0.5, -0.5, -0.5), (0.5, 0.5, -0.5), (0.5, 0.5, 0.5), (0.5, 0.5, 0.5), (0.5, -0.5, 0.5), (0.5, -0.5, -0.5) ], 0x10: [ # Top (y=+0.5) (-0.5, 0.5, -0.5), (-0.5, 0.5, 0.5), (0.5, 0.5, 0.5), (0.5, 0.5, 0.5), (0.5, 0.5, -0.5), (-0.5, 0.5, -0.5) ], 0x20: [ # Bottom (y=-0.5) (-0.5, -0.5, -0.5), (-0.5, -0.5, 0.5), (0.5, -0.5, 0.5), (0.5, -0.5, 0.5), (0.5, -0.5, -0.5), (-0.5, -0.5, -0.5) ] } for bitmask, offsets in faces.items(): if mask & bitmask: for dx, dy, dz in offsets: localpos = (position[0] + dx, position[1] + dy, position[2] + dz, 1.0) projectedpos = applyprojection(localpos, projection) vertices.append((projectedpos, color)) return vertices def applyprojection(pos, projmatrix): # Standard matrix-vector multiplication for projection x, y, z, w = pos return ( projmatrix[0][0]x + projmatrix[1][0]y + projmatrix[2][0]z + projmatrix[3][0]w, projmatrix[0][1]x + projmatrix[1][1]y + projmatrix[2][1]z + projmatrix[3][1]w, projmatrix[0][2]x + projmatrix[1][2]y + projmatrix[2][2]z + projmatrix[3][2]w, projmatrix[0][3]x + projmatrix[1][3]y + projmatrix[2][3]z + projmatrix[3][3]w) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision and boundary handling are not specified in the sources. Degenerate input (e.g., zero direction components) is not addressed in the sources. Time Complexity: O(1) per voxel, proportional to the number of visible faces. Memory Complexity: O(1) per voxel for the bitmask and color. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple implementation, leverages GPU hardware for culling, reduces bandwidth and rasterization cost. Limitations: Requires a geometry shader capable of handling the output; the bitmask must be pre-computed. When to use: When reducing overdraw and vertex processing is prioritized and the bitmask is available. When not to use: When hardware lacks geometry shader support or bitmask generation is too costly. Not given in the sources. Vizaxo/voxel-game, https://github.com/Vizaxo/voxel-game, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Per-face Column-based Face Culling with Opacity Masks
head: Column-based Opacity Mask Culling
body: A face culling technique that uses per-face column arrays and opaque column arrays to determine visibility based on solid and transparent block transitions, allowing full per-face control over opacity. It extends Face Coverage Mask Culling by distinguishing between opaque and transparent surface contributions on partial shapes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: facecols: A 3D array of 64-bit integers representing general column data for each face. facecolsopaque: A 3D array of 64-bit integers representing opaque column data for each face. CHUNKSIZEP: The dimension size of the chunk along each axis. Outputs: colfacemasks: A 3D array of 64-bit integers storing the final visibility masks per face. Data Structures: The method uses three primary data structures indexed by faceindex, and two perpendicular dimensions depending on the axis. Each element is a 64-bit unsigned integer where each bit represents a voxel column along the depth axis. 1. facecols[faceindex][dim1][dim2]: General column mask. 2. facecolsopaque[faceindex][dim1][dim2]: Opaque column mask. 3. colfacemasks[faceindex][dim1][dim2]: Resulting face mask. The faceindex ranges from 0 to 5, corresponding to the 6 faces of a voxel chunk. The mapping of axes to face indices and array dimensions is as follows: Axis 0 (Y-axis faces): facepos = 0, faceneg = 1; Dimensions: [z][x]. Axis 1 (Z-axis faces): facepos = 2, faceneg = 3; Dimensions: [y][z]. Axis 2 (X-axis faces): facepos = 4, faceneg = 5; Dimensions: [y][x]. Algorithm Steps: 1. Iterate over each axis axis from 0 to 2. 2. For each axis, iterate over the two dimensions perpendicular to the axis (e.g., z and x for axis 0). The loop bounds are 0 to CHUNKSIZEP - 1. 3. Calculate the positive and negative face indices: facepos = 2 axis + 0 and faceneg = 2 axis + 1. 4. Retrieve the general column masks for the current position: colpos = facecols[facepos][dim1][dim2] and colneg = facecols[faceneg][dim1][dim2]. 5. Retrieve the opaque column masks for the current position: colopaquepos = facecolsopaque[facepos][dim1][dim2] and colopaqueneg = facecolsopaque[faceneg][dim1][dim2]. 6. Compute the effective opaque columns by intersecting general columns with opaque masks: effectiveopaquepos = colpos & colopaquepos and effectiveopaqueneg = colneg & colopaqueneg. 7. Detect solid transitions (solid to air) in the positive direction: soliddescending = colpos & ~(colpos << 1). 8. Detect solid transitions (solid to air) in the negative direction: solidascending = colneg & ~(colneg >> 1). 9. Detect opaque transitions (opaque to air) in the positive direction: opaquedescending = effectiveopaquepos & ~(effectiveopaquepos << 1). 10. Detect opaque transitions (opaque to air) in the negative direction: opaqueascending = effectiveopaqueneg & ~(effectiveopaqueneg >> 1). 11. Combine solid and opaque transitions to form the final face masks: colfacemasks[facepos][dim1][dim2] = soliddescending | opaquedescending and colfacemasks[faceneg][dim1][dim2] = solidascending | opaqueascending. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computefacemasks(facecols, facecolsopaque, colfacemasks, CHUNKSIZEP): # Axis 0: Y faces, dimensions z and x for z in range(CHUNKSIZEP): for x in range(CHUNKSIZEP): facepos, faceneg = 0, 1 colpos = facecols[facepos][z][x] colneg = facecols[faceneg][z][x] colopaquepos = facecolsopaque[facepos][z][x] colopaqueneg = facecolsopaque[faceneg][z][x] effectiveopaquepos = colpos & colopaquepos effectiveopaqueneg = colneg & colopaqueneg soliddescending = colpos & ~(colpos << 1) solidascending = colneg & ~(colneg >> 1) opaquedescending = effectiveopaquepos & ~(effectiveopaquepos << 1) opaqueascending = effectiveopaqueneg & ~(effectiveopaqueneg >> 1) colfacemasks[facepos][z][x] = soliddescending | opaquedescending colfacemasks[faceneg][z][x] = solidascending | opaqueascending # Axis 1: Z faces, dimensions y and z for y in range(CHUNKSIZEP): for z in range(CHUNKSIZEP): facepos, faceneg = 2, 3 colpos = facecols[facepos][y][z] colneg = facecols[faceneg][y][z] colopaquepos = facecolsopaque[facepos][y][z] colopaqueneg = facecolsopaque[faceneg][y][z] effectiveopaquepos = colpos & colopaquepos effectiveopaqueneg = colneg & colopaqueneg soliddescending = colpos & ~(colpos << 1) solidascending = colneg & ~(colneg >> 1) opaquedescending = effectiveopaquepos & ~(effectiveopaquepos << 1) opaqueascending = effectiveopaqueneg & ~(effectiveopaqueneg >> 1) colfacemasks[facepos][y][z] = soliddescending | opaquedescending colfacemasks[faceneg][y][z] = solidascending | opaqueascending # Axis 2: X faces, dimensions y and x for y in range(CHUNKSIZEP): for x in range(CHUNKSIZEP): facepos, faceneg = 4, 5 colpos = facecols[facepos][y][x] colneg = facecols[faceneg][y][x] colopaquepos = facecolsopaque[facepos][y][x] colopaqueneg = facecolsopaque[faceneg][y][x] effectiveopaquepos = colpos & colopaquepos effectiveopaqueneg = colneg & colopaqueneg soliddescending = colpos & ~(colpos << 1) solidascending = colneg & ~(colneg >> 1) opaquedescending = effectiveopaquepos & ~(effectiveopaquepos << 1) opaqueascending = effectiveopaqueneg & ~(effectiveopaqueneg >> 1) colfacemasks[facepos][y][x] = soliddescending | opaquedescending colfacemasks[faceneg][y][x] = solidascending | opaqueascending Parameters and Edge Cases: CHUNKSIZEP: Must be \le 64 to fit within a 64-bit integer. If the chunk size exceeds 64, this method requires modification to use wider integers or multiple words per column. Bitwise operations assume standard two's complement representation. The ~ operator inverts all bits, including those beyond the valid voxel range. Implementers must ensure that bits beyond CHUNKSIZEP are masked out or ignored to prevent false positives from garbage bits. The method assumes that facecols and facecolsopaque are correctly populated prior to this step. Time Complexity: O(F \cdot D^2), where F=6 is the number of faces and D is the chunk dimension size. The complexity is linear with respect to the number of voxels on the surface of the chunk. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for facecols, facecolsopaque, and colfacemasks. Each is 6 \cdot D^2 64-bit integers. Performance: Described as "definitely going to cost a bit more in terms of cycle time" compared to simpler culling, but "much faster than a non-binary meshing approach". It provides "very efficient" control over opacity. Strengths: Full per-face control over opacity; distinguishes between opaque and transparent surfaces. Limitations: Not given in the sources. This method was introduced in the context of binary greedy meshing for voxel rendering, specifically to support transparent voxel textures. It was discussed in a GitHub issue regarding a voxel meshing repository. Supporting Transparent Voxel Textures, https://github.com/TanTanDev/binarygreedymesherdemo/issues/5, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Boundary Geometry Classification
body: Boundary Geometry Classification is a geometric filtering step used during octree construction and neighbor-based culling to distinguish surface geometry located on voxel cell boundary planes from internal geometry within complex blocks. It solves the problem where neighbor occlusion tests would incorrectly interact with internal fragments of non-manifold or complex shapes by ensuring that culling logic only applies to polygons strictly lying on the six faces of the current voxel cell. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Face Coverage Mask Culling by operating at the individual polygon level to identify which geometry is eligible for neighbor interaction, rather than determining how to cull based on coverage masks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of vertices defining a single polygon, the axis of the cell boundary plane being tested, the coordinate value of that plane, and a tolerance epsilon. Output: A boolean indicating whether the polygon lies on the boundary plane. Data Structures: vertices: An array of 3D vectors (Vec3). axis: An integer index (0, 1, or 2) corresponding to the x, y, or z axis. plane: A floating-point scalar representing the coordinate value of the cell boundary. eps: A small floating-point tolerance value. Steps: 1. Check if all vertices of the polygon lie on the same cell boundary plane within the tolerance eps. 2. If the condition holds, classify the polygon as a boundary polygon; otherwise, classify it as internal. Formulas: For a vertex v and axis a \in \{0, 1, 2\}: |v{axis} - plane| \le \epsilon The polygon is a boundary polygon if: \forall v \in \text{vertices}, \quad |v{axis} - plane| \le \epsilon Parameters: eps: A small tolerance value used to determine if a vertex lies on the boundary plane. Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Chunk Borders: Chunk borders are not special semantically; a face on the edge of a chunk still has a normal voxel neighbor, and the mesher benefits from a read-only neighborhood view rather than embedding chunk-transition logic. Precision: Not given in the sources. Degenerate Input: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def liesonboundary(vertices, axis, plane, eps): """ Classify a polygon as a boundary polygon by checking if all its vertices lie on the same cell boundary plane within a small tolerance. """ for v in vertices: if abs(v[axis] - plane) > eps: return False return True A method to identify cells containing surface fragments smaller than the current subdivision level, ensuring neighbor-based culling does not incorrectly prune internal geometry of complex blocks. It is applied after basic inhomogeneity checks to decide if a cell must be subdivided further. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows arbitrary internal geometry to remain untouched while enabling efficient neighbor occlusion tests only on relevant boundary geometry. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Originating from techniques for face culling in voxel cube and partial shape rendering, this method was developed to optimize the rendering of complex shapes by separating boundary-relevant geometry from internal geometry. It addresses the limitation of simple boolean solid flags, which are insufficient for partial shapes with mixed visible/hidden areas on a single face, by providing a geometric criterion for neighbor interaction eligibility. name: Complex Face and Edge Criterion
head: Complexity Detection
body: The Complex Face and Edge Criterion is a geometric classification method used during octree construction to identify cells containing surface fragments smaller than the current subdivision level. It ensures that neighbor-based culling and simplification strategies do not incorrectly prune internal geometry of complex blocks by detecting non-manifold configurations and sub-cell-surface pieces. It is applied after basic inhomogeneity checks to decide if a cell must be subdivided further. Inputs: A voxel cell C in an octree and the implicit surface \partial V defined by a scalar field. Outputs: A boolean flag indicating if C is "complex" (requires subdivision or special handling). Data Structures: Cell Face: A square plane defined by 4 vertices of the cell. Homogeneous Face: A face where all 4 vertices are strictly inside (\phi > 0) or strictly outside (\phi < 0) the surface \partial V. Connected Component: A set of voxels on a face connected via shared edges or vertices. Steps: 1. Identify Homogeneous Faces: For each of the 6 faces of cell C, evaluate the scalar field \phi at the 4 corner vertices. If all 4 vertices have the same sign (all inside or all outside), the face is homogeneous. 2. Extract Connected Components: For each homogeneous face, extract the connected components of voxels contained within that face. 3. Complex Face Check: If a homogeneous face contains a connected component of surface intersection that is smaller than the current subdivision level, the cell is marked complex. 4. Complex Edge Check: For each of the 12 edges of cell C, determine if the edge intersects \partial V more than once. If an edge intersects \partial V multiple times, it induces a non-manifold surface configuration. 5. Result: If any face is complex or any edge is complex, the cell C is classified as complex. 6. Scope Restriction: Only check voxels belonging to cell faces to ensure all cells intersected by \partial V are processed. Parameters: Minimal Depth: The octree construction typically divides the space regularly until a user-defined minimal depth (usually 2 or 3) is reached before applying these criteria. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Accurate determination of vertex signs is critical. Floating-point errors near the zero-crossing can misclassify homogeneous faces. Boundary Geometry: The criterion ensures that only voxels belonging to cell faces are checked, ensuring all cells intersected by \partial V are processed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def iscellcomplex(cell, scalarfield, subdivisionthreshold): # Step 1: Identify homogeneous faces for face in cell.faces: vertexvalues = [scalarfield(v) for v in face.vertices] allinside = all(v > 0 for v in vertexvalues) alloutside = all(v < 0 for v in vertexvalues) if allinside or alloutside: # Step 2: Extract connected components of voxels on the homogeneous face # Sources do not specify the exact connectivity graph construction. components = [] visited = set() for voxel in face.voxels: if voxel not in visited: component = [] stack = [voxel] while stack: curr = stack.pop() if curr not in visited: visited.add(curr) component.append(curr) for neighbor in curr.neighbors: if neighbor in face.voxels and neighbor not in visited: stack.append(neighbor) components.append(component) # Step 3: Complex face check if any(len(c) < subdivisionthreshold for c in components): return True # Step 4: Complex edge check for edge in cell.edges: # Check if edge intersects ∂V more than once v0, v1 = edge.endpoints mid = (v0 + v1) / 2.0 s0, s1, sm = scalarfield(v0), scalarfield(v1), scalarfield(mid) changes = 0 if (s0 > 0 and sm < 0) or (s0 < 0 and sm > 0): changes += 1 if (sm > 0 and s1 < 0) or (sm < 0 and s1 > 0): changes += 1 if changes > 1: return True # Step 5 & 6: Result and scope restriction # Only voxels belonging to cell faces are checked to ensure all cells intersected by ∂V are processed. return False A post-processing step to prune small non-manifold branches (thin protrusions) and improve structural integrity by removing faces arising from locally inconsistent voxel configurations. It is applied after mesh extraction to handle artifacts that the lookup table (LUT) could not resolve without complicating the design. A face is removed if: (1) all three of its constituent vertices lie on either non-manifold edges or open boundary edges, AND (2) the face itself contains an open boundary edge. The process is repeated until no more faces can be removed. A local complexity test to verify that a candidate voxel contains a single, nearly planar surface patch, ensuring the pivot token is well-defined and numerically stable. It probes multiple sub-voxel locations within each candidate voxel and queries their closest surface points and corresponding triangle normals. A voxel is labeled as ambiguous if the normals exhibit strong directional inconsistency (indicating multi-sheet or topologically complex regions) or if the probed points deviate noticeably from a single plane (indicating high curvature). Parameters: Normal-consistency threshold: 0.9 (approx. 25° tolerance); Planarity tolerance: 5% of the voxel size. Pitfall: Voxels containing multi-sheet or topologically complex regions are filtered out to prevent ambiguous pivot placement. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method relies on a hash table to index octree cells for neighbor access, achieving almost constant access times. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method operates on individual cells and uses a hash table for neighbor indexing. Strengths: Ensures topological correctness by detecting non-manifold configurations and sub-cell surface fragments that simple inhomogeneity checks might miss. Limitations: Requires careful implementation of component extraction and intersection detection, which can be numerically sensitive near zero-crossings. The Complex Face and Edge Criterion was introduced in the context of adaptive surface extraction from anisotropic volumetric data using generalized octrees. It addresses the problem of cells that appear homogeneous at the vertex level but contain complex surface topology within their faces or edges, which would otherwise be incorrectly culled or simplified. The method is part of an iterative top-bottom octree construction algorithm.
