name: Discrete Polygonal Occlusion via 2D Boundary Coverage
head: Conditional InnerShell Emission, Couvertures discrétisées, Emission conditionnelle des innerShell selon les six voisins, VXL-044, VXL-044 Discrete Boundary Coverage, VXL-045, VXL-046, VXL-046 Conditional InnerShell Emission
body: Discrete Polygonal Occlusion via 2D Boundary Coverage (VXL-044) is a synchronous mesh baking optimization that reduces polygon count by determining which inner shell polygons of a voxel cell are occluded by adjacent cells using discrete 2D coverage masks on cell boundaries. It solves the problem of replacing exact rational-coordinate geometric clipping with a deterministic, integer-based rasterization approach to verify if a boundary is fully enclosed by opaque neighbors. Unlike its siblings, which may rely on continuous geometry or per-frame GPU culling, this method operates on a fixed 1000x1000 integer grid per face during the model bake phase, ensuring deterministic results without floating-point precision issues. Inputs: A Volume containing Cell objects, each referencing a Shape definition. A VoxelMesher instance capable of querying neighbor states via outsideCell. For each cell, the outerShell polygons of the current cell and its six immediate neighbors. Outputs: A Model containing the final mesh. For each cell: a boolean flag emitInnerShell determining whether to emit all inner shell polygons or none. OutsideCell Represents the state of a neighbor relative to the current cell. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct OutsideCell { enum class State { Empty, Occupied, Unknown }; State state; // Optional reference to the neighbor Cell }; State: Empty: The neighbor cell is empty or has no geometry. Occupied: The neighbor cell contains geometry that may occlude. Unknown: The neighbor state is not yet determined or accessible. 2D Coverage Mask A representation of the footprint of a polygon on a cell boundary. Resolution: 1000x1000 integer grid per boundary face. Representation: An exact union of axis-aligned 2D rectangles (AABBs) on this grid, derived by merging scanline intervals. Note: While a dense bit mask can be used internally, the logical representation must be equivalent to the union of rectangles. 1. Neighbor Query: For the current cell at position P, query the six neighboring cells in directions d \in \{+x, -x, +y, -y, +z, -z\}. Call outsideCell(P + offset(d)) to get the OutsideCell state. If the neighbor is Empty or Unknown, the boundary in direction d is considered open. 2. Coverage Derivation (VXL-044): For each neighbor that is Occupied, derive its 2D coverage mask on the boundary plane opposite to the connection. Identify outerShell polygons of the neighbor that are coplanar to the boundary plane. Rasterization: Rasterize the edges of these coplanar polygons onto the 1000x1000 integer grid using a deterministic Bresenham-like integer rule. Filling: Fill the surface defined by the rasterized edges. Edges alone are insufficient; the filled surface is required. Union: Represent the covered cells as an exact union of axis-aligned 2D rectangles (AABBs) on this grid, e.g., by merging scanline intervals. This union must be equivalent to the discretized mask, including for triangles. Orientation: Apply orientation/flip transformations to align the 2D coordinates of the neighbor's mask with the current cell's boundary plane. 3. Closure Test: Determine if a boundary direction d is closed (occluded). A direction is closed only if the neighbor's opaque outerShell coverage fully covers the entire 1000x1000 square of the boundary at the discrete resolution. The test uses only the neighbor's coverage, not a union with the current cell's outerShell. The neighbor's material must be fully opaque; non-totally opaque coverages (translucent, cutout) do not close the boundary. An AABB bounding box of a triangle or slope can only be used for early rejection, never as an exact coverage mask. 4. InnerShell Emission Decision (VXL-046): Check all six directions. If all six directions are closed (i.e., all six neighbors are Occupied and their opaque outerShell coverage fully covers the respective 1000x1000 boundary), then emitInnerShell = false. If at least one direction is open, partially covered, or unknown (i.e., neighbor is Empty, Unknown, or coverage is incomplete), then emitInnerShell = true. This rule applies even to Shapes with no outerShell polygons; they are not removed simply because their own outerShell coverages are empty. 5. Mesh Construction: Process outerShell visible fragments separately. If emitInnerShell is true, emit all innerShell polygons for the cell. If emitInnerShell is false, emit no innerShell polygons for the cell. Do not perform individual culling of inner polygons based on this rule; the decision is cell-wide. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bakecellmesh(volume, position): """ Bakes the mesh for a single cell, determining inner shell emission. """ # Step 1 & 2: Check neighbors and their coverage allsidesclosed = True for side in ALLSIXSIDES: # Query neighbor state neighbor = getoutsidecell(volume, position + offset(side)) # If neighbor is not occupied (Empty/Unknown), boundary is open if neighbor.state != State.Occupied: allsidesclosed = False break # Derive 2D coverage mask from neighbor's outerShell # This involves rasterizing coplanar polygons onto 1000x1000 grid # and computing the union of AABBs coveragemask = derive2dcoveragemask(neighbor.shape.outerShell, side) # Check if coverage fully covers the 1000x1000 boundary # Must account for orientation/flip of the neighbor if not isfullycovered(coveragemask, resolution=1000): allsidesclosed = False break # Step 4: Emission Decision emitinnershell = not allsidesclosed # Step 5: Construct Mesh mesh = Mesh() # Process outerShell visible fragments separately mesh.addpolygons(neighborculloutershell(volume, position)) # Emit innerShell based on decision if emitinnershell: mesh.addpolygons(getinnershellpolygons(position)) return mesh def derive2dcoveragemask(polygons, side): """ Rasterizes coplanar polygons onto a 1000x1000 grid and returns the union of AABBs representing the covered area. """ gridsize = 1000 # Initialize empty coverage structure (e.g., list of AABBs or bit mask) coveredcells = set() for poly in polygons: if iscoplanar(poly, side): # Rasterize edges using deterministic Bresenham-like integer rule edges = rasterizeedges(poly, gridsize) # Fill surface filled = fillsurface(edges, gridsize) # Add to covered cells coveredcells.update(filled) # Convert to union of AABBs (e.g., by merging scanline intervals) aabbunion = converttoaabbunion(coveredcells, gridsize) return aabbunion def isfullycovered(coveragemask, resolution): """ Checks if the coverage mask covers the entire resolution x resolution square. """ totalcells = resolution resolution # If using AABB union, check if union covers all cells # If using bit mask, check if all bits are set return countcoveredcells(coveragemask) == totalcells Grid Resolution: 1000x1000 integer grid per boundary face. Input Geometry Constraint: Source polygons are planar and convex. Complex/concave shapes are assemblies of such polygons. Empty/Unknown Neighbors: Do NOT close a boundary. A missing neighbor or non-opaque material means the boundary is open. Partial Coverage: Does NOT close a boundary. The test requires full coverage of the 1000x1000 square. AABB Bounding Box: Can only be used for early rejection, never as an exact coverage mask. Interior Cameras: This optimization is view-independent and may hide surfaces visible from inside a fully enclosed cavity. The behavior for interior cameras/cavities is an open issue not resolved by this spec. Degeneracy: Diagonals and very small fragments are quantized. Degeneracies, holes, and potential rasterization fissures require a shared deterministic boundary contract. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of polygons in the Shape's outerShell, per boundary face. Rasterization cost is constant per face (1000x1000 grid). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary per face for the union of rectangles, plus storage for the 6 masks if cached. Strengths: Deterministic rasterization; avoids floating-point precision issues of analytical clipping; simplifies implementation. Limitations: View-independent; may hide surfaces visible from inside a fully enclosed cavity; resolution-dependent (1/1000). When to Use: During synchronous mesh baking for static voxel models where deterministic occlusion is required. When Not to Use: For per-frame GPU culling or dynamic scenes requiring view-dependent optimization. Origin: VXL-044 and VXL-046 are part of the Sparkle voxel engine design specification (V0.1.4) by EreliaStudio. History: VXL-044 replaces exact rational-coordinate geometric clipping with discrete 2D grid coverage to simplify implementation and ensure deterministic rasterization. VXL-046 validates the conditional innerShell emission rule based on six-neighbor coverage. Usage: Used in the VoxelMesher bake phase of the Sparkle engine. V0.1.4 — Voxel engine design and implementation specification, https://github.com/EreliaStudio/Sparkle/pull/37, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Voxel Block Shape & Culling Configuration
head: Block trait interface, Shape enum system
body: Voxel Block Shape & Culling Configuration is a trait-based configuration system for voxel mesh generation that defines block geometry, transparency culling, and lighting per block type. It solves the problem of rigid, single-shape meshing by allowing each block type to specify its own shape (e.g., cube, ramp, fluid) and culling behavior (e.g., opaque, transparent merged, transparent unmerged). It sets itself apart from Face Culling by providing the rules for when and how faces are culled and shaped, rather than the geometric algorithm that removes adjacent faces. It differs from Voxel Block Placement with Face Culling by decoupling the block's logical identity and rendering properties from its physical placement logic. The system operates by associating a configuration object (often a trait or interface implementation) with each block type. This configuration dictates the geometry to generate, the culling mode to apply, and the lighting values to use. Input: A block type identifier (e.g., MyBlock::Glass) and the face orientation being evaluated (e.g., AlignedFace::PosZ). Output: A Shape enum value, a CullMode enum value, and lighting parameters (ambient occlusion, smooth light). The Shape enum defines the geometry to generate for a specific face of a block. Common variants include: WholeBlock: A full unit cube face. Cross(CrossInfo): A cross-shaped face, used for thin objects like chains or rails. CrossInfo fields: face: AlignedFace (e.g., PosZ, NegY). stretch: f32 (0.0 for standard cross, other values for stretched variants). Ramp: A sloped face (see Ramp Shape Geometry). Fluid: A fluid surface (see Fluid Surface Stitching). The CullMode enum determines how faces are culled based on neighbor transparency. Empty: The block is air; no geometry is generated. Opaque: The block is fully opaque. Faces are generated if the neighbor is empty or opaque. Shared faces between two opaque blocks are culled. TransparentMerged(T): The block is transparent. Faces are generated if the neighbor is empty or opaque. Crucially, shared faces between two transparent blocks are culled only if their TransparentGroup values are equal. This allows water to merge with water but not with glass. TransparentUnmerged: The block is transparent. Faces are generated if the neighbor is empty or opaque. Shared faces between two transparent blocks are never culled, even if they are the same type. This is used for blocks like leaves or cobwebs where internal structure visibility is desired or where merging causes visual artifacts. Vertices generated by the shape configuration include: pos: Vec4<f32> (position). uv: Vec2<f32> (texture coordinates). normal: Vec3<f32> (face normal). ao: f32 (per-vertex ambient occlusion, 0.0 = fully occluded, 1.0 = fully lit). smoothlight: f32 (per-vertex smooth light, 0.0..1.0). block: MyBlock (block type for render pass filtering). atlasoffset: f32 (pre-computed atlas tile offset). twosided: bool (whether the vertex belongs to a two-sided quad). uv: Vec2<f32>. normal: Vec3<f32>. atlasuoffset: f32. ao: f32. smoothlight: f32. 1. Block Configuration Lookup: For each non-empty block in the chunk, retrieve its configuration trait/interface. 2. Shape Determination: Call the shape(face) method on the configuration, passing the current face orientation. This returns a Shape enum variant. Example: MyBlock::ChainZ returns Shape::Cross(CrossInfo { face: AlignedFace::PosZ, stretch: 0 }). Example: MyBlock::Cobblestone returns Shape::WholeBlock. 3. Culling Mode Determination: Call the cullmode() method on the configuration. This returns a CullMode enum variant. Example: MyBlock::Glass returns CullMode::TransparentMerged(()). Example: MyBlock::Leaves returns CullMode::TransparentUnmerged. 4. Lighting Determination: Call the light(face) method on the configuration. This returns lighting values (ambient occlusion, smooth light) specific to the block and face. Example: MyBlock::Cactus on PosY returns 11.0, on NegY returns 12.0, otherwise 10.0. Example: MyBlock::Air returns 0.0. 5. Geometry Generation: Based on the Shape enum, generate the appropriate vertices and indices. For WholeBlock, generate a standard quad. For Cross, generate the cross-shaped geometry. For Ramp, generate the slope quad and side triangles. For Fluid, generate the stitched surface. 6. Culling Application: Apply the CullMode rules to determine if the generated geometry should be added to the mesh. If CullMode::Opaque, cull if neighbor is occupied. If CullMode::TransparentMerged(T), cull if neighbor is occupied AND neighbor's TransparentGroup == current block's TransparentGroup. If CullMode::TransparentUnmerged, cull only if neighbor is occupied (never cull shared transparent faces). 7. Mesh Assembly: Add vertices and indices to the chunk's linked list. Once all blocks are processed, transfer data to the GPU mesh object on the main thread. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateblockgeometry(block: MyBlock, face: AlignedFace, neighbor: MyBlock) -> Optional[Geometry]: """ Generate geometry for a single block face based on its configuration. """ # 1. Get configuration config = getblockconfig(block) # 2. Determine shape shape = config.shape(face) # 3. Determine culling mode cullmode = config.cullmode() # 4. Check culling if shouldcull(cullmode, block, neighbor): return None # 5. Generate vertices based on shape if shape == Shape.WholeBlock: vertices = generatewholeblockvertices(face) elif shape == Shape.Cross: vertices = generatecrossvertices(shape.info, face) elif shape == Shape.Ramp: vertices = generaterampvertices(face) elif shape == Shape.Fluid: vertices = generatefluidvertices(block, face) else: raise ValueError(f"Unknown shape: {shape}") # 6. Apply lighting ao, smoothlight = config.light(face) for v in vertices: v.ao = ao v.smoothlight = smoothlight v.block = block return Geometry(vertices) def shouldcull(cullmode: CullMode, block: MyBlock, neighbor: MyBlock) -> bool: """ Determine if a face should be culled based on culling mode and neighbor. """ if cullmode == CullMode.Empty: return True if neighbor == MyBlock.Air: return False if cullmode == CullMode.Opaque: # Cull if neighbor is occupied return True if cullmode == CullMode.TransparentMerged: # Cull if neighbor is transparent AND same transparent group if istransparent(neighbor) and gettransparentgroup(block) == gettransparentgroup(neighbor): return True return False if cullmode == CullMode.TransparentUnmerged: # Cull only if neighbor is occupied (never cull shared transparent faces) return True return False def istransparent(block: MyBlock) -> bool: """ Check if a block is considered transparent for culling purposes. """ return block in [MyBlock.Glass, MyBlock.Leaves, MyBlock.Cactus, MyBlock.SugarCane, MyBlock.Cobweb, MyBlock.Shrub, MyBlock.Ladder, MyBlock.Rail, MyBlock.ChainY, MyBlock.ChainX, MyBlock.ChainZ] def gettransparentgroup(block: MyBlock) -> int: """ Get the transparent group for a block. Blocks in the same group can merge. """ # Example: Water blocks might have group 1, Glass group 2, Leaves group 3 # This is implementation-specific. if block == MyBlock.Water: return 1 elif block == MyBlock.Glass: return 2 elif block == MyBlock.Leaves: return 3 else: return 0 # Default group FLUIDENABLED: Boolean flag. If true, fluid shapes are enabled. If false, fluids are treated as cubes. Setting FLUIDENABLED to true without implementing fluid shape causes a debug assertion failure rather than silently drawing fluids as cubes. TransparentGroup: Integer value assigned to each transparent block type. Used for TransparentMerged culling. Fluid Shape Implementation: Setting FLUIDENABLED to true without implementing the fluid shape logic causes a debug assertion failure. Threading: Unity3D functions must be called on the main thread. While vertex/index calculation is done on a background thread, the final Mesh object creation must be moved to the main thread. CullMode::TransparentMerged: This mode culls shared faces between two transparent blocks when their TransparentGroup values are equal, but does not replace Self: PartialEq for greedy meshing. This means greedy meshing must still handle the merging of identical transparent blocks correctly. A classification system for block IDs into three mutually exclusive layers ('opaque', 'water', 'transparentSolid') to determine rendering material and buffer assignment. It solves the insufficiency of a single boolean 'transparent' flag by distinguishing between fluids (water) requiring bespoke shaders and see-through solids (glass/leaves) requiring alpha blending. Unlike a boolean transparent flag which collapses water and glass/leaves into one category, this three-valued model allows water to use a bespoke shader (ripple, refraction) while glass/leaves use the ordinary block atlas with alpha blending. VoxelBlockyTypeLibrary is an alternative library type that contains a list of VoxelBlockyType objects instead of models directly. It defines a 'block type' with attributes representing states (e.g., orientation, pressed state), similar to Minecraft block states. It solves the problem of managing complex block behaviors by automatically generating unique numerical IDs for every combination of attribute values, similar to Minecraft's block state system. It differs from the standard VoxelBlockyLibrary by decoupling model identity from manual ID assignment, using a combinatorial attribute system instead. A shape representing a sloped block face, composed of a slope quad (2 triangles) and two side triangles (left and right). Instance creation: Iterate visible faces. If face is Left, Right, Top, or Front, set drawSlope = true and assign tint to tints[0] (Top/Front), tints[1] (Left), or tints[2] (Right). If a specific tint is Vector3.One, fallback to another face's tint. Add instances for slope, left triangle, and right triangle using respective shape IDs and tints. If face is Back or Bottom, add instance using cubeBackFaceShapeID or cubeBottomFaceShapeID. Slope vertices (6 vertices): (0,1,0) with UV[0], (0,0,1) with UV[1], (1,1,0) with UV[2], (1,1,0) with UV[3], (0,0,1) with UV[4], (1,0,1) with UV[5]. Left triangle vertices (3 vertices): (0,0,1) with UV[0], (0,1,0) with UV[1], (0,0,0) with UV[2]. Right triangle vertices (3 vertices): (1,0,0) with UV[0], (1,1,0) with UV[1], (1,0,1) with UV[2]. A mesh generation technique where fluid columns share a surface height field with neighbors, stitching surfaces when fluid IDs match. Two adjacent fluid blocks join their surfaces only when their FluidInfo::id (u8) values match. A design pattern using an interface to control the type of geometry created for each non-empty voxel, allowing different geometry types (cubes, ramps, X-shapes) to be generated via polymorphism without large switch statements. During mesh creation, call BuildGeometry() once for each non-empty block. Pass a reference to the chunk object to BuildGeometry(). Inside BuildGeometry(), use the chunk reference to add vertices and indices to the chunk's linked list. After BuildGeometry() has been called on every block for the chunk, place the vertex and index data into a Unity3D Mesh object on the main thread. Interface IGeometryBuilder contains a single function: BuildGeometry(). Unity3D functions must be called on the main thread. While vertex/index calculation is done on a background thread, the final Mesh object creation must be moved to the main thread. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of blocks in the chunk, as each block is processed once to determine its shape and culling status. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the vertex and index data for the chunk. Strengths: Flexible support for diverse block types (cubes, ramps, fluids, cross shapes). Efficient culling reduces triangle count. Decoupled configuration allows easy addition of new block types. Limitations: Requires careful implementation of culling modes to avoid visual artifacts. Threading constraints in Unity3D require careful management of mesh creation. Debug assertion failures can occur if fluid shapes are enabled but not implemented. When to use: When rendering voxel worlds with diverse block types requiring different geometries and culling behaviors. When not to use: When all blocks are simple cubes and no complex culling is needed; a simpler meshing algorithm may suffice. The concept of block-specific shape and culling configuration originated in voxel game development, particularly in Minecraft-like games, where different block types (water, glass, leaves, rails) require different rendering behaviors. The trait-based interface approach was formalized in projects like finnbear/voxmesh and rarefushion/Cubic-GridVoxelRenderer. The Geometry Builder pattern was introduced in academic work on procedural generation of voxel worlds, such as the thesis "Procedural Generation of Voxel Worlds with Castles", to manage complex geometry generation without large switch statements. finnbear/voxmesh, https://github.com/finnbear/voxmesh, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) rarefushion/Cubic-GridVoxelRenderer, https://github.com/rarefushion/Cubic-GridVoxelRenderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Procedural Generation of Voxel Worlds with Castles, https://researchcommons.waikato.ac.nz/entities/publication/70d98783-1629-43df-9d01-b973ddbb5d75, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Three-Valued Opacity Classification for Meshing
head: Mesh Layer Priority, Opaque/Water/TransparentSolid Classification, Occlusion Check
body: A classification system for block IDs into three mutually exclusive layers ('opaque', 'water', 'transparentSolid') to determine rendering material and buffer assignment. It solves the insufficiency of a single boolean 'transparent' flag by distinguishing between fluids (water) requiring bespoke shaders and see-through solids (glass/leaves) requiring alpha blending. Unlike a boolean transparent flag which collapses water and glass/leaves into one category, this three-valued model allows water to use a bespoke shader (ripple, refraction) while glass/leaves use the ordinary block atlas with alpha blending. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A block ID (integer). Output: A layer classification ('opaque', 'water', 'transparentSolid') or a layer index. Data Structures: MESHLAYERPRIORITY: A constant array defining the priority order: ['transparentSolid', 'water', 'opaque']. MESHLAYERS: A constant array defining the buffer emission order (draw order): ['opaque', 'water', 'transparentSolid']. lookup: A fixed-size typed array (e.g., Uint8Array) indexed by block ID, storing the layer index for each ID. OPAQUELAYER: The index of 'opaque' in MESHLAYERS. Steps: 1. Classify a block ID by checking membership in ordered sets: first check transparentSolidBlockIds, then waterBlockIds; if neither, return 'opaque'. 2. Return true if blockId is not AIR AND lookup[blockId] equals OPAQUELAYER index. Formula: Priority Order: transparentSolid > water > opaque. This order determines which layer a block ID belongs to if it appears in multiple sets. Occlusion Check: isoccluding(blockId) = (blockId != AIR) AND (lookup[blockId] == OPAQUELAYER). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def classifyblock(blockid, transparentsolidids, waterids): if blockid in transparentsolidids: return 'transparentSolid' if blockid in waterids: return 'water' return 'opaque' def isoccluding(blockid, lookup, opaquelayerindex, airid): if blockid == airid: return False return lookup[blockid] == opaquelayerindex Parameters: MESHLAYERPRIORITY: ['transparentSolid', 'water', 'opaque']. MESHLAYERS: ['opaque', 'water', 'transparentSolid']. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Using Effect's HashSet instead of native JavaScript Set for block ID lookups causes a 1.9x slowdown compared to native Set and 12.3x slowdown compared to Uint8Array lookup due to structural equality dispatch. Incorrectly classifying water or transparent solids as occluding causes the 'world is inside out' bug where inner surfaces render incorrectly. The Block ID Layer Lookup Table is a memory layout optimization that replaces hash-based set lookups with direct array indexing to classify block IDs into mesh layers during the inner meshing loop. It solves the performance bottleneck of iterating over Set or HashSet structures when processing hundreds of thousands of cells per chunk, by pre-computing a fixed-size typed array indexed by block ID. Unlike hash sets, which incur collision resolution overhead, this method provides O(1) access with minimal constant factors, specifically tailored for the three-valued opacity classification system. A mechanism that routes generated quads into specific layers (opaque, water, transparentSolid) based on the block ID and a pre-computed lookup table. The push function determines the layer index by calling layerAt(lookup, quad.blockId). If the layer index is 0, push the quad to the opaque array. If the layer index is 1, push the quad to the water array. Measured Performance: Using Uint8Array lookup is 12.3x faster than Effect's HashSet and 1.9x faster than native Set. Strengths: Enables distinct shaders for water and transparent solids; prevents occlusion bugs. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. nerima-games/mc-meshing, https://github.com/nerima-games/mc-meshing, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Block ID Layer Lookup Table
head: Block ID to Layer Lookup Table, Lookup Table Optimization for Meshing, MAX_BLOCK_ID Lookup
body: The Block ID Layer Lookup Table replaces hash-based set lookups with direct array indexing to classify block IDs into mesh layers during the inner meshing loop. It solves the performance bottleneck of iterating over Set or HashSet structures when processing hundreds of thousands of cells per chunk by pre-computing a fixed-size typed array indexed by block ID. Inputs: config: An object containing sets of block IDs for different material types. config.waterBlockIds: Set of block IDs classified as water. config.transparentSolidBlockIds: Set of block IDs classified as transparent solids. MAXBLOCKID: The maximum valid block ID value, inclusive. Outputs: lookup: A Uint8Array of size MAXBLOCKID + 1. Each index corresponds to a block ID, and the value at that index is an integer representing the mesh layer. Data Structures: MESHLAYERS: An ordered array of strings defining the layers: ['opaque', 'water', 'transparentSolid']. lookup: A Uint8Array where lookup[blockId] stores the index of the layer in MESHLAYERS. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize a lookup array of size MAXBLOCKID + 1 with default values of 0 (representing opaque). 2. Iterate over config.waterBlockIds and set lookup[blockId] to MESHLAYERS.indexOf('water') (which evaluates to 1). 3. Iterate over config.transparentSolidBlockIds and set lookup[blockId] to MESHLAYERS.indexOf('transparentSolid') (which evaluates to 2). 4. Validate that all blockId values in the configuration sets are \le MAX\BLOCK\ID before population to prevent out-of-bounds access. Formulas: Table size: N = MAX\BLOCK\ID + 1. Cells visited per chunk: C = FACES \times CHUNK\SIZE \times CHUNK\SIZE \times CHUNK\HEIGHT = 6 \times 16 \times 16 \times 256 = 393,216. Parameters: MAXBLOCKID: The maximum valid block ID, inclusive. The table size is exactly MAXBLOCKID + 1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Out-of-Bounds Access: If a block ID in the configuration exceeds MAXBLOCKID, direct array access will throw an error or corrupt memory. Sparse IDs: If MAXBLOCKID is very large but the number of unique block IDs is small, the table consumes significant memory. Default Behavior: IDs not explicitly listed in waterBlockIds or transparentSolidBlockIds default to 0 (opaque). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildlayerlookup(config, maxblockid): # Initialize lookup array of size maxblockid + 1 with default value 0 (opaque) lookup = [0] (maxblockid + 1) # Iterate over config.waterBlockIds and set lookup[blockId] = MESHLAYERS.indexOf('water') for blockid in config.waterBlockIds: lookup[blockid] = 1 # Iterate over config.transparentSolidBlockIds and set lookup[blockId] = MESHLAYERS.indexOf('transparentSolid') for blockid in config.transparentSolidBlockIds: lookup[blockid] = 2 return lookup Time and Memory Complexity: Build Time: O(W + T), where W is the number of water block IDs and T is the number of transparent solid block IDs. Lookup Time: O(1) per cell. Memory: O(MAX\BLOCK\ID) bytes. Measured Performance: The inner loop performs approximately 393,216 calls per chunk (6 face passes over a 16 \times 16 \times 256 cell grid). The lookup table method is faster than iterating a Set in the inner meshing loop because it uses array indexing instead of hash lookup. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Direct array indexing provides minimal constant factors for O(1) access. Limitations: Memory usage scales linearly with MAXBLOCKID. When to Use: Use when the inner meshing loop requires high-frequency lookups and block IDs are bounded. When Not to Use: Use hash sets or other sparse data structures if block IDs are sparse or the maximum ID is extremely large relative to the number of active block types. The Block ID Layer Lookup Table is an optimization for the inner meshing loop in voxel chunk processing. It addresses the performance bottleneck identified in earlier implementations that used Set or HashSet for block ID classification. nerima-games/mc-meshing, https://github.com/nerima-games/mc-meshing, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: VoxelBlockyTypeLibrary with Attributes
head: Minecraft-like block states, VoxelBlockyType
body: VoxelBlockyTypeLibrary is an alternative library type that contains a list of VoxelBlockyType objects instead of models directly. It defines a 'block type' with attributes representing states (e.g., orientation, pressed state), similar to Minecraft block states. It solves the problem of managing complex block behaviors by automatically generating unique numerical IDs for every combination of attribute values, similar to Minecraft's block state system. It differs from the standard VoxelBlockyLibrary by decoupling model identity from manual ID assignment, using a combinatorial attribute system instead. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of VoxelBlockyType definitions. Output: A library containing a mapping from type/attribute combinations to unique numerical model IDs, with functions to resolve these IDs at runtime. Data Structures: VoxelBlockyType: Defines a logical block type. Contains a name (StringName identifier) and a list of VoxelBlockyAttribute objects. VoxelBlockyAttribute: Represents a state variable. Contains a name (StringName identifier) and values between 0 and 255. Model ID Map: An internal mapping associating the canonical string identifier <typename>[attr1=val,attr2=val,...] to a unique integer ID. IDs are unique within the library instance but not portable across different worlds. Numbered Steps: 1. Define Block Types: Create VoxelBlockyType entries. Assign a name and a list of attributes. Types should usually have very few attributes. 2. Assign Attribute Values: Each attribute takes integer values between 0 and 255. Use built-in rotation attributes (VoxelBlockyAttributeAxis, VoxelBlockyAttributeDirection, VoxelBlockyAttributeRotation) for common geometric states. These attributes have predefined default rotations. Models are authored for the default rotation; the system generates rotated variants automatically. 3. Generate Variants: The system computes the Cartesian product of all attribute values for each type. For each combination, a unique model instance is created or referenced. If built-in rotation attributes are used, pre-rotated models are generated for all specified rotation axes/directions. Excluding unnecessary rotations (e.g., vertical for flat blocks) reduces memory cost, as VoxelBlockyAttributeRotation generates the highest number of variants. 4. Assign Numerical IDs: The system automatically assigns a unique integer ID to each generated variant. The ID is derived from the combination of type name and attribute values. Renaming a type or attribute changes the canonical identifier, effectively creating a new voxel type with a new ID. 5. Runtime Lookup: Use library functions to resolve model IDs from attribute values. Cache resolved IDs for performance if accessed frequently. Use VoxelTool to set the resolved ID into the voxel data. Formulas: Canonical Identifier Format: \text{ID}{\text{key}} = \text{type\name}[\text{attr}1=\text{val}1, \text{attr}2=\text{val}2, \dots] Where \text{val}i \in [0, 255]. Total Variants per Type: N{\text{variants}} = \prod{i=1}^{n} Vi Where n is the number of attributes and Vi is the number of possible values for attribute i. Example: Redstone dust has 1,296 variants. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class VoxelBlockyTypeLibrary: def init(self): self.types = {} # Map: StringName -> VoxelBlockyType self.idmap = {} # Map: CanonicalString -> int def addtype(self, typename, attributes): """Register a block type and generate all variant IDs.""" combinations = self.getattributecombinations(attributes) for combo in combinations: keyparts = [f"{attr.name}={val}" for attr, val in zip(attributes, combo)] canonicalkey = f"{typename}[{','.join(keyparts)}]" modelid = self.assignuniqueid(canonicalkey) model = self.generatemodelforstate(typename, attributes, combo) self.idmap[canonicalkey] = modelid self.storemodel(modelid, model) def getmodelindexwithattributes(self, typename, attrs): """Get model ID for a type and attribute values. Uses StringName for typename, standard strings for dict keys.""" keyparts = [f"{attrname}={val}" for attrname, val in attrs.items()] canonicalkey = f"{typename}[{','.join(keyparts)}]" return self.idmap.get(canonicalkey, -1) def getmodelindexsingleattribute(self, typename, attrval): """Shortcut for types with exactly one attribute.""" # Not given in the sources. pass def getmodelindexdefault(self, typename): """Get model ID for a type with no attributes, or its default state.""" # Not given in the sources. pass def getattributecombinations(self, attributes): """Generate Cartesian product of attribute values (0-255).""" # Not given in the sources. pass def generatemodelforstate(self, typename, attributes, combo): """Generate mesh for a specific state. Handles rotation attributes.""" # Not given in the sources. pass def assignuniqueid(self, canonicalkey): """Assign unique integer ID. IDs are unique within library but not portable across worlds.""" # Not given in the sources. pass def storemodel(self, modelid, model): """Store model reference internally for meshing.""" # Not given in the sources. pass Parameters: Attribute Values: Integers between 0 and 255. Attribute Count: Should be very low. Rotation Attributes: VoxelBlockyAttributeAxis, VoxelBlockyAttributeDirection, VoxelBlockyAttributeRotation. Default rotations are assumed for base models. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Complex States: If a block requires complex states (objects, lists), this system fails; fallback to voxel metadata and actual nodes (entities) is required. Large Variant Lists: Many attributes or states lead to a very large list of variants (e.g., redstone dust has 1,296 variants); conditional combination of models is preferred over a list of variants. Memory Cost: VoxelBlockyAttributeRotation has the highest number of variants and incurs significant memory cost for pre-rotated models; exclude unnecessary rotations (e.g., vertical) to reduce cost. ID Portability: Numerical IDs are not portable across worlds; renaming types or attributes changes IDs, breaking compatibility with saved worlds. Voxel IDs in VoxelBlockyLibrary act like tilemap tiles. For complex games, custom 'game block types' can be defined that map to one or multiple VoxelBlockyModel IDs. Minecraft examples include stairs (multiple IDs for orientations/appearances), crops (multiple IDs for growth stages), doors (2 voxels for top/bottom), and rails (many IDs for straight/slope/turn configurations). Managing the correspondence between game block IDs and voxel IDs is handled by the developer. Time Complexity: Lookup is O(1) after caching, or O(k) where k is the number of attributes for string construction. Variant generation is O(N{\text{variants}}). Memory Complexity: O(N{\text{types}} \times N{\text{variants}}). Memory usage scales with the number of attribute combinations; pre-rotated models increase the footprint significantly. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales poorly with high attribute counts or high value ranges per attribute; the redstone dust example (1,296 variants) illustrates the practical limit. Strengths: Automatic ID management, intuitive state representation (Minecraft-like), built-in rotation support. Limitations: Not suitable for complex states (objects/lists), high memory cost for rotations, non-portable IDs. When to use: Simple to moderately complex block states (orientation, on/off, basic connections). When not to use: Blocks requiring complex dynamic states, or when memory is extremely constrained and rotations are not needed. Originating from the Voxel Tools library for Godot, this system was inspired by Minecraft's block state system (specifically ForgeModLoader documentation). It was introduced as an alternative to VoxelBlockyLibrary to better handle the complexity of block states in voxel games. The system automates model generation and ID assignment, reducing manual configuration effort. Blocky terrains - Voxel Tools documentation, https://voxel-tools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/blockyterrain/, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Block Visibility Culling
head: Block Coordinate Change Detection, Block Rendering & Surface Orientation Culling, Camera-relative Block Culling, Visibility Culling via Normal Dot Product, renderBlock
body: Block Visibility Culling is an optimization technique that determines which voxel blocks or surface patches need to be rendered based on the camera's position and orientation, avoiding unnecessary mesh generation or update for geometry facing away from the viewer. It solves the problem of rendering invisible surfaces by evaluating the geometric relationship between face normals and the view direction. Unlike Voxel Block Placement with Face Culling which relies on adjacency to empty space, this method explicitly checks visibility relative to the camera. It differs from Opacity-based Mesh Culling by using geometric dot products rather than alpha thresholds. Inputs: Camera world position (Px, Py, Pz), camera rotation angles (typically yaw A in degrees, and optionally pitch/roll), and a set of voxel blocks or surface patches defined by their vertex coordinates and normals. Outputs: A boolean mask or list of visible faces/blocks for the current frame. Data Structures: BlockFace: An enumeration or bitmask representing the six faces of a voxel: YNeg (bottom), XPos (right), YPos (top), XNeg (left), ZNeg (back), ZPos (front). visibleFaces: An array or flag set associated with each block, storing which of the six faces are currently visible. previousCameraState: Stores the integer block coordinates of the camera and the "greatest direction" (primary viewing axis) from the previous frame. Steps: 1. Compute Camera Block Coordinates: Calculate the integer block coordinates containing the camera by flooring its world position: Cx = \lfloor Px \rfloor, \quad Cy = \lfloor Py \rfloor, \quad Cz = \lfloor Pz \rfloor 2. Optimization: Skip if Unchanged: Compare the current camera block coordinates (Cx, Cy, Cz) and the primary viewing direction with previousCameraState. If both match, skip the visibility update process for this frame. 3. Calculate View Direction: Compute the view vector components (vx, vy, vz) from the camera's rotation angles. For a 2D yaw angle A (in degrees): cs = \cos\left(\frac{A \pi}{180}\right), \quad sn = \sin\left(\frac{A \pi}{180}\right) The view direction in the horizontal plane is often derived as (-sn, 0, cs) or similar depending on coordinate system handedness. For full 3D, use pitch and roll to compute the full 3D view vector. 4. Determine Surface Orientation (Block-Level): For each block, determine its vertical orientation relative to the camera: Calculate block vertical bounds: Z{bottom} = Z{chunk} + z \cdot B, Z{top} = Z{bottom} + B, where B is block size. If Pz < Z{bottom}, orientation is Top (1). If Pz > Z{top}, orientation is Bottom (2). Otherwise, orientation is Side (0). Set cycle count: 2 if orientation != 0, else 1. 5. Compute Average Normal: For each surface or face, calculate the average normal \mathbf{n} as the mean of its vertex normals, then normalize it: \mathbf{n} = \frac{\sum{i=1}^{k} \mathbf{n}i}{\|\sum{i=1}^{k} \mathbf{n}i\|} 6. Visibility Check via Dot Product: Compute the view direction vector \mathbf{v} from the surface center to the camera position and normalize it: \mathbf{v} = \frac{P - C{center}}{\|P - C{center}\|} Calculate the dot product D = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v}. If D > 0, the surface is visible. If D \le 0, the surface is facing away and is culled. 7. Apply Face Flags (Implementation Specific): In block-based rendering, visibility flags are updated based on the dot product and orientation. For example, if a side face's normal dot view direction is positive, set block->visibleFaces[BlockFace::XPos] = true. These flags are checked before rendering: if (!block->visibleFaces[BlockFace::YNeg]) continue;. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updateblockvisibility(camerapos, camerayawdeg, blocks): # 1. Compute camera block coordinates camblockx = floor(camerapos.x) camblocky = floor(camerapos.y) camblockz = floor(camerapos.z) # 2. Check for state change (optimization) if (camblockx == prevcamblockx and camblocky == prevcamblocky and camblockz == prevcamblockz and camerayawdeg == prevcamerayawdeg): return # Skip update # 3. Calculate view direction components anglerad = camerayawdeg PI / 180.0 cosa = cos(anglerad) sina = sin(anglerad) # View direction vector (assuming standard right-handed system where camera looks down -Z or similar) # Adjust based on specific coordinate system; here we assume 2D yaw for horizontal visibility viewdirx = -sina viewdirz = cosa viewdiry = 0.0 # Simplified for 2D yaw; use pitch for full 3D for block in blocks: # 4. Determine orientation and update face flags # Example for a single block face facecenter = getfacecenter(block, facetype) facenormal = getfacenormal(facetype) # e.g., (1,0,0) for XPos # 5. Compute vector from face to camera vectocamx = camerapos.x - facecenter.x vectocamy = camerapos.y - facecenter.y vectocamz = camerapos.z - facecenter.z # Normalize view vector length = sqrt(vectocamx2 + vectocamy2 + vectocamz2) if length == 0: length = 1e-9 # Guard against division by zero normvecx = vectocamx / length normvecy = vectocamy / length normvecz = vectocamz / length # 6. Dot product test dotproduct = (facenormal.x normvecx + facenormal.y normvecy + facenormal.z normvecz) # 7. Set visibility flag if dotproduct > 0: block.visiblefaces[facetype] = True else: block.visiblefaces[facetype] = False # Update previous state prevcamblockx = camblockx prevcamblocky = camblocky prevcamblockz = camblockz prevcamerayawdeg = camerayawdeg Parameters: surfaceScale: Multiplier for floor/ceiling projection calculations, typically 120. BLOCKSIZE: Size of a voxel block, typically 16 units in some implementations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating point errors in dot product near 0 can cause flickering. A small epsilon threshold may be needed, though the sources strictly use > 0. Camera Inside Block: If the camera is inside a block, the view vector direction may be ambiguous for all faces. The orientation check (Step 4) helps distinguish top/bottom vs sides. Degenerate Input: If the camera position equals the face center, the view vector is zero-length. A guard value (e.g., 10^{-9}) should be used for normalization. Determines which of the six faces of a voxel block are visible by evaluating the geometric relationship between face normals and a reference direction. It solves the problem of rendering unnecessary geometry that faces away from the camera. Choose this when you need per-face visibility flags for block-based rendering. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of blocks or faces checked. The dot product calculation is constant time per face. The optimization in Step 2 can reduce this to O(1) if the camera state hasn't changed. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the visibleFaces flags for each block. Performance: Significantly reduces the number of triangles rendered by culling back-facing geometry. Performance gain depends on the scene complexity and camera movement frequency. Strengths: Simple to implement, low computational overhead per frame, effective for static or slowly moving cameras. Limitations: Does not account for occlusion by other objects (only back-face culling). Requires camera position and orientation. Less effective if the camera is moving rapidly or is inside the geometry. When to Use: Ideal for voxel-based games or terrain rendering where blocks are static or change infrequently. When Not to Use: When occlusion culling is required (use From-Region Visibility Preprocessing or Projection-based Culling). Block Visibility Culling is commonly used in voxel-based game engines and terrain rendering systems. It is implemented in projects like exolands, NeRF-Renderer, and Voxel1993. The technique leverages the fact that in many voxel scenarios, the majority of faces are internal or back-facing relative to the viewer, allowing for significant performance improvements by skipping their generation or rendering. kvxy/exolands, https://github.com/kvxy/exolands, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) matthxie/NeRF-Renderer, https://github.com/matthxie/NeRF-Renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) VidFurlan/Voxel1993, https://github.com/VidFurlan/Voxel1993, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Face Visibility Check
head: Back-Face Culling, Camera-relative Block Culling, Cube Face Culling, renderBlock
body: Voxel Face Visibility Check is a geometric optimization that determines which of the six faces of a voxel block are visible to the camera, allowing the renderer to skip generating or uploading geometry for faces pointing away from the viewer. It differs from Block Visibility Culling by operating at the individual face level within a block rather than discarding entire blocks, providing finer-grained culling for blocks near the camera or at viewing angles where only specific sides are occluded or back-facing. The method computes a visibility mask for the six faces of a cube based on the relative position of the camera (eye) to the block. Inputs: eyePt: Camera position in world space (float3). worldI: Inverse of the block's world transformation matrix (4x4). cubecenter: Center of the voxel block in world space (float3). cubesize: Side length of the voxel block (float). Outputs: visiblemask: An integer bitmask where bit i is set if face i is visible. OR facelist: A list of indices of visible faces. Data Structures: Face indices are typically mapped as: 0=Front, 1=Back, 2=Right, 3=Left, 4=Top, 5=Bottom. The visibility mask is a 6-bit integer. Steps: 1. Transform Eye Position: Convert the camera position from world space to the block's local space. \mathbf{e}{local} = \text{Transform}(\mathbf{e}{world}, \mathbf{M}{world}^{-1}) Where \mathbf{e}{world} is eyePt and \mathbf{M}{world}^{-1} is worldI. 2. Define Face Properties: Define the outward normal \mathbf{n}i and center offset for each of the six faces. Let h = \text{cube\size} / 2. Front: \mathbf{n}0 = (0, 0, 1), offset (0, 0, h) Back: \mathbf{n}1 = (0, 0, -1), offset (0, 0, -h) Right: \mathbf{n}2 = (-1, 0, 0), offset (-h, 0, 0) Left: \mathbf{n}3 = (1, 0, 0), offset (h, 0, 0) Top: \mathbf{n}4 = (0, 1, 0), offset (0, h, 0) Bottom: \mathbf{n}5 = (0, -1, 0), offset (0, -h, 0) (Note: Normal directions depend on the coordinate system convention. The above assumes a right-handed system where +Z is forward, consistent with. uses a bit-shifting logic that implies a specific axis mapping.) 3. Compute Face Centers: Calculate the world-space center of each face. \mathbf{c}i = \mathbf{e}{local} + \text{offset}i Correction: The visibility test should be based on the vector from the face center to the camera, or equivalently, the dot product of the face normal and the vector from the camera to the face center. However, explicitly states the test uses the dot product between the face center and its outward normal, which is geometrically equivalent to checking if the camera is in the half-space defined by the face plane if the origin is the camera. But notes a pitfall: using the world origin (0,0,0) as the reference point for the dot product is incorrect for arbitrary camera positions. The correct approach, implied by and standard graphics practice, is to use the local eye position. The correct visibility condition for face i is: vi = (\mathbf{c}i - \mathbf{e}{local}) \cdot \mathbf{n}i > 0 Since \mathbf{c}i - \mathbf{e}{local} is just the offset vector, this simplifies to checking if the camera is on the "outside" of the face. However, a more robust method used in checks the sign of the eye position component relative to the face's axis. Implementation from: The code in uses a bit-manipulation approach on the local eye position: python # localSpaceEyePt is the eye position transformed to local space # face is an integer 0..5 def isfacevisible(localSpaceEyePt, face): # Determine which axis and direction the face corresponds to # Mapping based on typical cube face bit packing: # 0: Front (+Z), 1: Back (-Z), 2: Right (-X), 3: Left (+X), 4: Top (+Y), 5: Bottom (-Y) # Note: The exact mapping depends on the engine's coordinate system. # Extract the relevant component of the eye position # face >> 1 gives the axis index (0=X, 1=Y, 2=Z) axisindex = face >> 1 viewcomp = localSpaceEyePt[axisindex] # face & 0x1 determines the sign/direction # If bit 0 is 1, we check if viewcomp > -1.0f (or < 1.0f depending on convention) # If bit 0 is 0, we check the opposite. # This logic effectively checks if the camera is "behind" the face plane relative to the block center. if (face & 0x1): return viewcomp > -1.0f else: return viewcomp < 1.0f Note: The thresholds -1.0f and 1.0f in suggest the block is centered at the origin with size 2 (i.e., h=1). For a general cubesize, the thresholds should be \pm h. Implementation from: python halfsize = cubesize / 2 normals = [ (0, 0, 1), # Front (0, 0, -1), # Back (-1, 0, 0), # Right (1, 0, 0), # Left (0, 1, 0), # Top (0, -1, 0) # Bottom ] visiblefaces = [] for i, normal in enumerate(normals): # Face center in local space relative to block center # The vector from the camera (local origin) to the face center is: # offset = normal halfsize # The dot product of the face center (relative to camera) and normal determines visibility # If the camera is outside the face, the vector from camera to face center should have a positive projection onto the normal? # Actually, formula: vi = ci. ni > 0 # If ci is the face center in local space (where camera is at 0,0,0), then ci = offset. # So we check if offset. normal > 0. # Since offset = normal halfsize, this is always halfsize (normal. normal) = halfsize > 0. # This implies ALL faces are visible, which is incorrect. # Correction based on pitfall: The source notes that using the world origin as reference is incorrect. # The correct logic is to check if the camera is on the negative side of the face plane. # Plane equation: (P - ci). ni = 0 # Camera is at 0. So: (0 - ci). ni < 0 => -ci. ni < 0 => ci. ni > 0 # This again leads to all faces being visible if ci is the face center. # The standard back-face culling for a block centered at origin with camera at E: # A face with normal N and center C is visible if (E - C). N < 0 # i.e., the camera is on the "inside" of the normal? No, the camera is on the "outside" if the dot product is negative? # Let's use the standard: Face is visible if the camera is in the half-space defined by the normal. # Vector from Face Center to Camera: V = E - C # If V. N > 0, the camera is in front of the face. # Let's stick to the logic which is proven to work in a renderer. pass Unified Algorithm: 1. Transform eye position to local space: \mathbf{e}{local}. 2. For each face i with normal \mathbf{n}i and center offset \mathbf{o}i (where \mathbf{o}i = \mathbf{n}i \times \text{half\size}): Compute vector from face center to camera: \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{e}{local} - \mathbf{o}i. If \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n}i > 0, the face is visible. 3. Set bit i in visiblemask if visible. Parameters: CPUCUBEFACECULL: Compile-time macro controlling culling mode. 0 = disabled, 1 = mask, 2 = list. GLCULLFACE: OpenGL flag that can enable hardware back-face culling, but this method is a software pre-culling step. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coordinate System Mismatch: The definition of face normals and axis mapping must match the rendering engine's coordinate system. and use different conventions. Camera Inside Block: If the camera is inside the block, all faces may be considered visible or none, depending on the implementation. The dot product test \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n}i > 0 will correctly identify faces where the camera is "outside" the plane. If the camera is inside, \mathbf{v} will point inwards, so \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n}i < 0 for all faces, meaning no faces are visible. This is a known issue in voxel rendering; usually, the camera is assumed to be outside the voxel grid or the block is treated as solid. Precision: Floating-point precision errors near the block boundaries can cause flickering. Using a small epsilon in the comparison is recommended. Incorrect Reference Point: Using the world origin instead of the camera position for the dot product is a common bug, as noted in. Time Complexity: O(1) per block, as it involves a fixed number of dot products (6) and vector transformations. Memory Complexity: O(1), storing only a few temporary vectors and a bitmask. Performance: Reduces the number of triangles sent to the GPU by up to 50% for blocks viewed from the side, and up to 83% for blocks viewed from a corner (only 2 faces visible). The overhead of the calculation is negligible compared to the cost of vertex processing and rasterization. Strengths: Simple to implement, effective for large voxel worlds, reduces GPU load. Limitations: Does not handle occlusion from other blocks (only back-face culling). Requires accurate camera position and block transformation. Back-face culling is a fundamental technique in computer graphics, dating back to the early days of 3D rendering. In the context of voxel rendering, it was adopted to optimize the high triangle counts associated with naive voxel meshing. It is commonly implemented in voxel games and engines, often in conjunction with frustum culling and greedy meshing. The specific implementation details in are from a DirectX 12 fluid simulation project, while provides a Python-based educational implementation. name: Extraction of Surface Points (Sobierajski)
head: Visible boundary voxel extraction
body: Extraction of Surface Points is a fast display method for the direct rendering of boundary surfaces by extracting only visible boundary voxels from volume data. It solves the problem of rendering speed in direct volume rendering by avoiding the processing of occluded geometry. It differs from its siblings, which often rely on block-based meshing or precomputed culling, by operating directly on individual voxel boundaries using orthographic visibility tests and 2D boundary tracing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume data (density values), viewing directions (typically six orthographic views), and lighting parameters. Output: A list of surface points (boundary voxels) with attributes (coordinates, normal vectors) ready for rendering, and the final image. Data Structures: Boundary Voxel List: A list of objects. Each object stores: coordinates: (x, y, z) integer indices of the voxel. normal: Surface normal vector \mathbf{n}. density: Original density value (for cutting plane support). Visibility Grid: Implicitly handled via 2D boundary tracing on slices. Steps: 1. Visibility Determination: Determine visibility using a set of viewing directions. Six orthographic views are sufficient for an approximate set of potentially visible boundary voxels; increasing the number of directions improves approximation. 2. 2D Boundary Tracing: Perform visibility calculations using a 2D boundary tracing algorithm on slices perpendicular to each coordinate axis. 3. Extraction and Deduplication: Extract boundary voxels. Remove duplicate elements from the generated list. Store attributes (coordinates, normal vectors) for each voxel. 4. Back-Face Culling: For a specific viewing direction, reduce the voxel list size. If the dot product of the surface normal \mathbf{n} and the viewing direction \mathbf{v} is positive, the voxel is a back face and is not rendered: \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v} > 0 \implies \text{discard}. 5. Projection: Pass the set of surface points to the rendering engine. Project each voxel onto several pixels depending on the viewing direction to avoid holes caused by adjacent voxels mapping to non-adjacent pixels. 6. Shading and Cutting Planes: Shade projected boundary surface points according to lighting conditions. If cutting planes are used, render voxels intersected by the cutting planes by projecting their original density values onto the image plane. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extractsurfacepoints(volume, viewingdirections): """ Extract visible boundary voxels using Sobierajski's method. volume: 3D array of density values. viewingdirections: List of 3D vectors (e.g., +/- x, y, z axes). Returns: List of SurfacePoint objects. """ boundaryvoxels = [] # Step 2: Visibility via 2D boundary tracing on slices # For each axis, trace boundaries on perpendicular slices for axis in [0, 1, 2]: # Identify boundary voxels where density changes significantly # This is implemented via 2D boundary tracing on slices perpendicular to 'axis' sliceboundaries = trace2dboundaries(volume, axis) for voxel in sliceboundaries: if voxel not in boundaryvoxels: boundaryvoxels.append(voxel) # Step 3: Remove duplicates (handled by 'if not in' check above, # but formally a deduplication step) uniquevoxels = removeduplicates(boundaryvoxels) # Step 4 & 5: Culling and Projection for each viewing direction renderedpoints = [] for vdir in viewingdirections: visiblevoxels = [] for voxel in uniquevoxels: # Calculate normal (simplified: gradient or face normal) normal = computenormal(voxel, volume) # Back-face culling if dot(normal, vdir) > 0: continue visiblevoxels.append(voxel) # Project each voxel to multiple pixels to avoid holes for voxel in visiblevoxels: projectedpixels = projecttopixels(voxel, vdir) for pixel in projectedpixels: renderedpoints.append(SurfacePoint( coordinates=voxel.coordinates, normal=voxel.normal, density=voxel.density, screenpos=pixel.screenpos)) return renderedpoints def trace2dboundaries(volume, axis): """ Perform 2D boundary tracing on slices perpendicular to the given axis. Returns list of boundary voxels. """ # Implementation detail: Iterate over slices perpendicular to axis. # For each slice, find contours where density transitions occur. # This is a standard 2D boundary tracing algorithm. # Specific 2D tracing algorithm (e.g., Moore-Neighbor) is not detailed in source, # but the method relies on this step for efficiency. pass def computenormal(voxel, volume): """ Compute surface normal for a boundary voxel. Typically computed via finite differences of density or by determining the face orientation relative to the neighbor. """ pass def projecttopixels(voxel, vdir): """ Project a voxel to multiple screen pixels to prevent holes. """ # The source states "one voxel is projected onto several pixels". # The exact projection geometry (e.g., splat radius) is not specified. pass Parameters: Viewing Directions: Typically six orthographic views (\pm x, \pm y, \pm z). More directions improve visibility approximation. Cutting Planes: Optional. Intersected voxels are rendered by projecting original density values. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Holes: Adjacent voxels may map to non-adjacent pixels. Mitigated by projecting each voxel onto several pixels. Precision: Not given in the sources. Degenerate Input: Not given in the sources. Trimmed Voxel Lists is a surface extraction algorithm that represents an iso-surface using 3D points as geometric primitives, projecting exactly one point per visible surface cell to ensure image coverage without recursive subdivision. It differs from Dividing Cubes by avoiding subdivision; instead, it allows a single projected point to span up to three pixels on the image plane to guarantee coverage. Saito's Fast Previewing Algorithm is a previewing algorithm based on extracting a subset of boundary voxels according to a uniform distribution to increase rendering speed. It extracts a subset of boundary voxels, converts them to geometrical primitives like crosslines perpendicular to the surface normal, and projects these primitives onto the image plane. Limitations: May produce holes if not projected to multiple pixels; approximation of visibility depends on the number of viewing directions. When to Use: When fast previewing or direct rendering of boundary surfaces is required, and approximate visibility is sufficient. When Not to Use: When high-fidelity, hole-free rendering is required without projection overhead, or when complex lighting/shading is needed beyond basic shading. name: Trimmed Voxel Lists
body: Trimmed Voxel Lists is a surface extraction algorithm that represents an iso-surface using 3D points as geometric primitives, projecting exactly one point per visible surface cell to ensure image coverage without recursive subdivision. It differs from Dividing Cubes by avoiding subdivision; instead, it allows a single projected point to span up to three pixels on the image plane to guarantee coverage. Inputs: Volumetric data grid. Iso-value threshold. Camera parameters (view and projection matrices). Outputs: A list of visible surface points, each associated with a 3D position and a normal vector. Data Structures: A list of surface points. Each entry contains: position: 3D coordinates (x, y, z) of the point in world space. normal: 3D normal vector (nx, ny, nz) at that position. Steps: 1. Identify Visible Surface Cells: Iterate through the volume grid to identify cells intersected by the iso-surface and filter out cells that are not visible from the current camera viewpoint. 2. Select One Point Per Cell: For each visible surface cell, compute a single representative 3D point on the iso-surface within that cell without subdividing the cell. 3. Project to Image Plane: Project the 3D point and its normal onto the 2D image plane, allowing the point to cover up to three pixels to guarantee coverage. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trimmedvoxellists(volumedata, isovalue, camera): surfacepoints = [] for cell in volumedata.cells: if not issurfacecell(cell, isovalue): continue if not isvisible(cell, camera): continue point = computesurfacepoint(cell, isovalue) normal = computenormal(cell, point) screenpos = projecttoscreen(point, camera) surfacepoints.append({'position': point, 'normal': normal, 'screenpos': screenpos}) return surfacepoints def issurfacecell(cell, isovalue): # Check if the cell intersects the iso-surface based on voxel values. # Not given in the sources. return False def isvisible(cell, camera): # Check if the cell is front-facing or occluded. # Not given in the sources. return False def computesurfacepoint(cell, isovalue): # Compute a representative point on the iso-surface. # Not given in the sources. return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def computenormal(cell, point): # Compute the gradient at the point to get the normal. # Not given in the sources. return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def projecttoscreen(point, camera): # Project 3D point to 2D screen coordinates. # Not given in the sources. return (0.0, 0.0) Parameters: Iso-value: The threshold for surface extraction. Camera: View and projection parameters. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coverage: The method relies on projecting a single point to cover up to three pixels. Accuracy: Since only one point per cell is used, the approximation of the surface may be less accurate than methods that subdivide cells. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of visible surface cells, as it avoids recursive subdivision. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of visible surface points, which is typically less than the total number of cells. Strengths: Fast rendering due to no subdivision. Limitations: Lower accuracy compared to subdivision-based methods; geometric primitives can only approximate surfaces and may require excessive primitives for adequate approximations. When to Use: Applications requiring efficient surface representation where a trade-off between accuracy and space requirements is acceptable. When Not to Use: Applications requiring high-precision surface geometry where subdivision-based methods are preferred. The Trimmed Voxel Lists method was introduced as an alternative to Dividing Cubes, which subdivides cells to ensure each subcell projects onto a single pixel. It is used in volume visualization for efficient surface rendering. name: Opacity-based Mesh Culling
head: Mesh Clipping, Opacity-based Mesh Filtering, Pre-rendering Mesh Extraction
body: Opacity-based Mesh Culling is a post-processing optimization for surface extraction that reduces triangle count by discarding geometric primitives associated with low-opacity regions. It solves the problem of excessive mesh complexity in radiance field representations by retaining only triangles that contribute significantly to the final image. It differs from its sibling Face Culling, which operates on voxel adjacency during generation, by operating on the final extracted polygonal mesh based on accumulated opacity values. The method operates on a pre-extracted polygonal mesh representation of a scene, typically derived from neural radiance fields or similar implicit representations. It filters triangles based on the opacity of their intersection points with rays, ensuring that only visually significant geometry is retained. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of triangular faces F extracted from a scene representation, where each face has associated vertex positions and opacity values at intersection points. Output: A filtered set of triangular faces F' and a transformed mesh aligned with real-world scale. Data Structures: Triangle: Defined by three vertices v1, v2, v3. Each vertex or intersection point on the face has an associated opacity value \alpha. Opacity Threshold: A scalar value \alpha{thresh} used to determine if a face is retained. Steps: 1. Ray Intersection and Opacity Sampling: For each triangular face in the input mesh, compute the intersection of rays with the polygon mesh. The traversal of light is halted when the cumulative opacity surpasses a maximum threshold (e.g., 0.8). 2. Face Clipping Decision: For each triangular face, evaluate the opacity of all intersection points on that face. If the opacity of all intersection points on the face is below the threshold \alpha{thresh}, the face is clipped (discarded). Otherwise, the face is retained. Formula: Retain face f if \exists p \in \text{points}(f): \alpha(p) \ge \alpha{thresh}. Typical Value: \alpha{thresh} = 0.3. 3. Coordinate Transformation: Perform a coordinate transformation to align the obtained mesh with real-world scale. This ensures the mesh vertices correspond to accurate physical positions. 4. UV Mapping: Map the vertex coordinates of the retained triangles to their corresponding positions in UV coordinates for texture mapping or further processing. Parameters: \alpha{thresh}: The opacity threshold for clipping. Typical value is 0.3. \alpha{max}: The cumulative opacity threshold for ray traversal halting. Typical value is 0.8. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Opacity values must be accurately sampled at intersection points. Inaccurate sampling may lead to incorrect clipping decisions. Degenerate Input: Faces with no intersection points or zero area should be handled explicitly, though the sources do not specify the exact behavior. Assume such faces are discarded to avoid rendering artifacts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def opacitybasedmeshculling(mesh, alphathresh=0.3, alphamax=0.8): """ Filters a mesh by clipping faces where all intersection points have opacity below alphathresh. Args: mesh: A list of triangles, each defined by vertices with associated opacity values. alphathresh: Threshold below which a face is clipped if all points are below it. alphamax: Cumulative opacity threshold for ray traversal. Returns: filteredmesh: A list of retained triangles. """ filteredmesh = [] for triangle in mesh: # Step 1: Compute intersections and sample opacities # Note: The exact ray casting and intersection logic is assumed to be provided # by the preceding mesh extraction step. We assume 'intersections' is a list # of objects with an 'opacity' attribute. intersections = computerayintersections(triangle, alphamax) # Step 2: Evaluate clipping condition # If all intersection points on the face have opacity below alphathresh, clip the face. if len(intersections) == 0: # Handle degenerate case: no intersections. Discard face. continue allbelowthreshold = True for point in intersections: if point.opacity >= alphathresh: allbelowthreshold = False break if not allbelowthreshold: # Retain the face filteredmesh.append(triangle) # Step 3: Coordinate Transformation # Align mesh with real-world scale. # Assuming a transformation matrix T is available or computed. # For each vertex v in filteredmesh: # v.transformed = T @ v.original # Step 4: UV Mapping # Map vertex coordinates to UV coordinates. # Assuming a UV mapping function is available. # For each triangle in filteredmesh: # triangle.uvcoords = maptouv(triangle.vertices) return filteredmesh This variant is used in the context of training neural radiance fields to produce mesh-compatible outputs. It prunes triangles with opacity below a threshold \tau{prune} during the final 5,000 training iterations, retaining only solid triangles. It introduces a loss term to encourage higher opacity and lower density \sigma, ensuring final triangles are mostly solid and opaque. After training, triangles are directly converted to standard mesh formats. This method achieves rendering speeds of 3,000 FPS at 1280×720 resolution on an RTX 4090. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of triangles in the input mesh, as each triangle is evaluated independently. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of retained triangles. The method reduces mesh count to 5% of the original in tested scenarios. Performance: In one implementation, the final extracted meshes accounted for only 5% of the original mesh count, significantly improving mesh utilization and inference speed. Another implementation achieved 3,000 FPS at 1280×720 resolution on an RTX 4090. Strengths: Significant reduction in triangle count, leading to faster rendering and reduced storage costs. Compatible with standard mesh-based renderers. Limitations: Requires pre-extracted mesh. The opacity threshold must be tuned for the specific scene and representation. When to use: When reducing mesh complexity for real-time rendering or storage efficiency is critical, and the underlying representation provides opacity values per triangle or intersection point. When not to use: When high-frequency details in low-opacity regions are visually important, as they may be discarded. The method originates from research on real-time rendering of large-scale scenes using neural radiance fields. The specific opacity threshold of 0.3 for clipping and 0.8 for ray traversal halting was introduced in the UE4-NeRF paper. The variant involving training-time pruning and loss terms was introduced in the Triangle Splatting paper. These methods aim to bridge the gap between neural radiance fields and traditional mesh-based rendering pipelines.
