The foundational volume rendering method used in volume illustration pipelines to simulate the appearance of translucent, gaseous, or semi-transparent media. It solves the problem of visualizing internal structures in volumetric data by combining an opacity transfer function with an atmospheric illumination model. Unlike surface-based rendering, it treats the volume as a continuous medium where light interacts with the scalar field values directly. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific reliance on an atmospheric (gaseous) lighting model rather than standard surface shading, though the framework is extensible to Phong illumination and linear accumulation. Computes light attenuation through a medium that absorbs all intercepted light without scattering or emitting. It solves for radiance decay along a ray, effectively simulating a cloud of black smoke or X-ray projection. Unlike the Emission-Absorption Model, it assumes zero scattering (\sigmas = 0) and surfaces that only emit light without reflecting or transmitting. Simulates a participating medium that adds light to a viewing ray via emission (e.g., hot tenuous gas, fluorescent stains) while neglecting absorption and scattering. It solves for the accumulated glow intensity along a ray, distinguishing itself from the Absorption-only model by adding radiance rather than attenuating it, and from the Standard volume rendering equation by omitting the exponential attenuation term. Unlike the Single Scattering Model, it assumes isotropic emission independent of incoming light. Computes the fraction of radiance that survives transmission through a participating medium with constant optical properties along a ray segment. It solves the problem of light attenuation in transparent or semi-transparent volumes by modeling the exponential decay of intensity due to absorption and out-scattering. It sets itself apart from Heterogeneous Medium Transmittance — Beer's Law by assuming a spatially constant extinction coefficient, and from Single Scattering Model by ignoring in-scattering contributions, focusing solely on the loss of radiance from the primary ray path. Approximates light transport in participating media by accounting only for light that undergoes zero or exactly one scattering event, ignoring multiple scattering and emitted radiance. It solves the problem of rendering volumetric effects like smoke or fluids efficiently by decomposing the outgoing radiance into direct transmission and a single-scattering term. It is distinguished from the Absorption-only model by including scattering phase functions and from the Standard volume rendering equation by truncating the infinite series of scattering events to the first order. Computes the color of a view ray by accumulating weighted contributions from samples along the ray, where each sample's contribution is modulated by the transmittance of all preceding samples. It treats opacity as a ray-dependent quantity representing the fraction of incoming light absorbed by each sample, distinguishing it from formulas that treat opacity as absolute and ray-independent. The Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) is an integro-differential equation that governs the behavior of light in participating media, describing the rate of change of radiance as it propagates through a medium that absorbs, emits, and scatters radiation. It serves as the fundamental physical model for light transport in volumes, accounting for extinction (absorption and out-scattering) and augmentation (in-scattering and emission). Unlike simplified models such as the Absorption-only model or Emission-only Model, the RTE captures the full complexity of light-matter interaction, including the redistribution of energy from all directions into the viewing direction via scattering. It is the generalization of the Standard volume rendering equation and Volume Rendering Equation to arbitrary media without surface boundaries. The fundamental optical model for light transport in participating media, calculating the color of a pixel by integrating emitted and in-scattered light along a ray, attenuated by transmittance. It generalizes the rendering problem by accounting for emission, absorption, and scattering within a volume grid (e.g., clouds, fog, flames). Unlike the Absorption-only model or Emission-only Model, it combines both effects into a single integral, and unlike the Single Scattering Model, it serves as the basis for approximating full radiative scattering. It differs from the Standard volume rendering equation primarily in its historical derivation context and specific notation regarding opacity \sigma as a product of density and cross-section, though they describe the same physical phenomenon. A deterministic method for rendering participating media where particles both occlude incoming light (absorption) and add their own glow (emission). It solves the volume rendering equation by integrating the combined differential equation along a ray, discretizing the solution into a back-to-front compositing loop. Unlike the Absorption-only model which only attenuates background light, or the Emission-only Model which lacks attenuation bounds, this model provides a physically bounded intensity result suitable for simulating clouds, flames, and segmented medical data. A method to visualize smoke flow realistically by integrating smoke opacity one grid plane at a time using a simple implementation of Beer's law in video hardware. An empirical optical model for volume rendering that captures the qualitative appearance of translucency and volumetric shadows by adding a blurred indirect light contribution to the direct light term, allowing interactive rates without full multiple scattering simulation. A model for light transport in scattering media that accounts for both absorption and scattering, solving the problem of computing reflectance and transmittance for homogeneous and inhomogeneous layers where simple extinction (Lambert-Bouguer) is insufficient. Generates cloud-like images that illustrate internal structure, instead of contour surfaces of the data. It uses an accurate light-scattering model to model scattering effects of light in a cloud and uses view rays as the basis for computing line integrals through the data to generate the color for each ray. A method to define participating media by summing multiple phase terms, each with its own density, phase function, and absorption, to produce a composite medium. It allows for complex scattering behaviors by combining terms like Rayleigh, Mie-Hazy, and Mie-Murky, with parameters including density (optical depth in RGB), phase function (directional scattering distribution applied per-channel), and absorption (optical depth of light absorption in RGB). The mathematical foundation of volume rendering lies in the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE), which has roots in astrophysics and nuclear engineering. In computer graphics, the field was formalized in the early 1980s. Sabella (1988) introduced ray-casting methods using accurate light-scattering models for clouds, building on Blinn (1982), Kajiya (1984), and Max (1986). The standard volume rendering equation, often attributed to Max, treats opacity as a ray-dependent quantity. Modern production rendering extends these physical models with empirical adjustments to achieve desired artistic looks. name: Base Gaseous Illumination Renderer
head: Base Gaseous Illumination Model, Physics-based illumination of gaseous phenomena
body: The Base Gaseous Illumination Renderer is the foundational volume rendering method used in volume illustration pipelines to simulate the appearance of translucent, gaseous media. It combines an opacity transfer function with an atmospheric illumination model to accumulate radiance along rays. It is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on an atmospheric lighting model rather than standard surface shading, though the framework can be replaced by Phong illumination and linear accumulation. Inputs: Volume dataset V containing scalar values vi for each voxel or sample point. Opacity transfer function parameters: k{os} (scalar controlling maximum opacity) and ke (exponent). Lighting configuration: Typically a single light source positioned above the volume and slightly toward the viewer. Base color assignment: Voxel colors c derived from transfer functions (e.g., mimicking tissue colors). Outputs: Final rendered image with shaded, segmented volume appearance. Data Structures: The volume is represented as a 3D grid of scalar values. For example, an abdominal CT volume may be 256 \times 256 \times 128 voxels. Each sample point xi has an associated scalar value vi. Steps: 1. Sample Volume Values: For each ray cast through the volume, retrieve the scalar value vi at the current sample position. 2. Compute Opacity: Calculate the opacity ov for the sample using the power function: ov = (k{os} vi)^{ke} where: vi is the volume sample value. k{os} is a scalar controlling maximum opacity. ke is an exponent. If ke < 1, volume differences are softened. If ke > 1, contrast within the volume is increased. 3. Assign Color: Determine the base color c for the sample using a transfer function (e.g., assigning voxel colors that mimic actual tissue). 4. Apply Illumination: Render the volume using an atmospheric illumination model. 5. Accumulate: Composite the samples along the ray to produce the final pixel color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def basegaseousilluminationrenderer(volumedata, kos, ke, lightdirection, viewdirection): """ Renders a volume using the base gaseous illumination model. Args: volumedata: 3D list or array of scalar values. kos: Scalar controlling maximum opacity. ke: Exponent for opacity transfer function. lightdirection: Normalized vector for the light source. viewdirection: Normalized vector for the camera view. Returns: 2D list of RGBA tuples. """ height, width, depth = len(volumedata), len(volumedata[0]), len(volumedata[0][0]) image = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): rayorigin, raydirection = castray(x, y) # Standard ray generation from pixel coordinates accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 t = 0.0 stepsize = 1.0 / depth # Uniform sampling step along depth axis while t < depth: samplepos = rayorigin + raydirection t vi = volumedata[int(samplepos[0])][int(samplepos[1])][int(samplepos[2])] # Compute opacity using the power function base = kos vi if base < 0: base = 0.0 # Guard against negative base for exponentiation ov = base ke # Assign base color c = assigncolor(vi) # Color transfer function implementation # Apply atmospheric illumination shadedcolor = applyatmosphericshading(c, lightdirection, viewdirection) # Atmospheric shading model # Front-to-back compositing alpha = ov accumulatedcolor = [accumulatedcolor[i] + (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) shadedcolor[i] for i in range(3)] accumulatedopacity = accumulatedopacity + (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) alpha if accumulatedopacity > 0.99: break t += stepsize image[y][x] = tuple(accumulatedcolor) + (accumulatedopacity,) return image Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Opacity Clamping: Ensure vi is non-negative before exponentiation if ke is not an integer, or clamp the result of k{os} vi to [0, 1] if the implementation expects normalized inputs. Lighting Setup: The default setup uses a single light source above and slightly toward the viewer. Deviating from this may require adjusting the atmospheric model parameters. The specific lighting model used in the base renderer. It simulates light scattering in gaseous media. Choose this when a soft, translucent appearance is desired. See Illumination and Tone Shading Models. An alternative base renderer mentioned in the sources. It uses standard surface shading (Phong) and linear accumulation instead of atmospheric illumination. Choose this when a more surface-like appearance is preferred. See Illumination and Tone Shading Models. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Demonstrated on an abdominal CT volume of 256 \times 256 \times 128 voxels. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides a good baseline for volume illustration. Limitations: Limited to gaseous or translucent appearances. When to Use: When creating volume illustrations that require a soft, atmospheric look; as a base for applying further illustration techniques. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The Base Gaseous Illumination Renderer was introduced in the paper "Non-Photorealistic Rendering of Volume Models" by Robert Hegele et al.. It serves as the foundational rendering method for the volume illustration toolkit described in the paper. The framework is designed to be flexible, allowing for the application of various illustration techniques in arbitrary combinations. name: Absorption-only model
head: Pure absorption, Absorption Model, Absorption-only Volume Rendering
body: The absorption-only model renders a participating medium composed of cold, perfectly black particles that absorb all intercepted light without scattering or emitting. It solves for light intensity attenuation along a ray, producing an X-ray-like projection or a "black smoke" obscuring a background. Unlike the Emission-only Model which adds radiance, or the Single Scattering Models which redirects light, this model considers only the exponential decay of incident radiance. Inputs and Outputs Input: A scalar field f(\mathbf{x}) representing density; a transfer function mapping f to the extinction coefficient \tau(\mathbf{x}); a camera ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}; and an incident radiance Li at the ray entry point (or background intensity I0). Output: The transmitted radiance Lo at the ray origin (or pixel). Data Structures Scalar Field: A 3D grid or continuous function f(\mathbf{x}). Extinction Coefficient: A scalar field \tau(\mathbf{x}) derived from f(\mathbf{x}) via a transfer function. Units are m^{-1}. Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (unit vector). Formulas The differential change in radiance L over a path length dt is governed by: \frac{dL}{dt} = -\tau(\mathbf{r}(t)) L(\mathbf{r}(t)) where \tau(\mathbf{r}(t)) is the extinction coefficient at position \mathbf{r}(t). The closed-form solution for radiance at the ray origin (t=0), given incident radiance Li at entry point t{entry} and exit point t{exit}, is: Lo = Li \exp\left( -\int{t{entry}}^{t{exit}} \tau(\mathbf{r}(t)) \, dt \right) If the ray intersects a surface at distance t{hit}, the incident radiance Li is the surface emission Le at that point. The term T = \exp\left( -\int \tau \, dt \right) is the transmittance. The opacity \alpha of a voxel of side l viewed parallel to an edge, assuming constant \tau, is: \alpha = 1 - \exp(-\tau l) For small voxels, this is often approximated as \alpha \approx \min(1, \tau l). Parameters \tau(\mathbf{x}): Extinction coefficient. Can be constant (homogeneous) or varying (inhomogeneous). I0 or Li: Initial intensity/radiance. Can be a constant background or pixel-dependent. Steps 1. Sample Ray: Generate a primary camera ray for the screen position. 2. Intersect Scene: Determine the entry and exit points of the ray within the volume or the intersection with a surface. If the ray hits a surface at t{hit}, calculate the transmittance from the ray origin to t{hit}. If the ray misses the scene, return 0 (or background). 3. Integrate Extinction: Compute the optical depth \tau{opt} = \int{t{entry}}^{t{exit}} \tau(\mathbf{r}(t)) \, dt. For homogeneous media, \tau{opt} = \tau \cdot (t{exit} - t{entry}). For inhomogeneous media, sample \tau along the ray and sum (e.g., trilinear interpolation of scalar field f mapped to \tau). 4. Compute Transmittance: Calculate T = \exp(-\tau{opt}). 5. Compute Output: If a surface was hit: Lo = T \cdot Le(\mathbf{p}{hit}). If no surface (background): Lo = T \cdot I0. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sampleprimary(camera, screenpos): return (camera.origin, normalize(camera.target - camera.origin)) def intersectscene(scene, rayorigin, raydirection): closest = None for prim in scene.primitives: t = rayintersectprimitive(rayorigin, raydirection, prim) if t is not None and (closest is None or t < closest[0]): closest = (t, prim.material, prim.islight) return closest def getbackground(screenpos): return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def renderabsorptiononly(screenpos, camera, scene, volume): origin, direction = sampleprimary(camera, screenpos) isect = intersectscene(scene, origin, direction) if isect: thit = isect[0] if volume.ishomogeneous: opticaldepth = volume.sigmaa thit else: opticaldepth = 0.0 t = 0.0 dt = volume.stepsize while t < thit: pos = origin + direction t # Interpolate scalar field f to get tau (e.g., trilinear) tau = samplescalarfield(volume.fgrid, pos) opticaldepth += tau dt t += dt transmittance = exp(-opticaldepth) Le = isect[1].emission if isect[2] else (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) return transmittance Le else: I0 = getbackground(screenpos) tfar = volume.farplanedistance if volume.ishomogeneous: opticaldepth = volume.sigmaa tfar else: opticaldepth = 0.0 t = 0.0 dt = volume.stepsize while t < tfar: pos = origin + direction t # Interpolate scalar field f to get tau (e.g., trilinear) tau = samplescalarfield(volume.fgrid, pos) opticaldepth += tau dt t += dt transmittance = exp(-opticaldepth) return transmittance I0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls Opacity vs. Extinction: Do not confuse the extinction coefficient \tau (units m^{-1}) with voxel opacity \alpha (dimensionless). \alpha depends on the path length through the voxel. If a voxel is scaled or viewed diagonally, the path length differs from the edge length l, making \alpha = 1 - \exp(-\tau l) invalid if \tau is treated as constant opacity. Thresholding: For binary volumes, \tau can be set to \infty for opaque regions and 0 for transparent ones. This allows rendering via z-buffer or painter's algorithm without integration. Precision: The exponential function can be computed once per pixel. In early implementations, gamma correction tables were used for this lookup. Simulates X-ray attenuation using Hounsfield Units directly, assuming single energy level and no scatter. Chosen for medical DR generation. Approximates absorption on triangle meshes by mapping depth to density. Chosen for dynamic surfaces without voxelization. The fundamental process of radiance reduction. Chosen as the base compositing step in more complex models. Simulates discrete black particles. Chosen for specific particle-based effects like smoke clouds. Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel, where N is the number of samples along the ray. For homogeneous media, O(1) if analytical integration is used. Performance: Fastest of the optical models. The exponential term can be precomputed or looked up. Strengths: Physically accurate for non-emitting, non-scattering media (e.g., X-rays, black smoke). Simple to implement. Limitations: Cannot render volumetric lighting, shadows, or color bleeding caused by scattering. Unsuitable for realistic clouds or fire. When to use: X-ray visualization, simple occlusion effects, or as a component in hybrid models. The absorption-only model is the simplest participating medium model, derived from the geometric optics of light interacting with particles. It was formalized in the context of direct volume rendering by Max and Blinn. The differential equation for intensity decay is analogous to neutron transport absorption cross-sections. Early implementations used Fourier methods (Malzbender, Totsuka/Levoy) to compute integrals rapidly via the projection slice theorem. name: X-ray simulation via ray integration
head: CT projection rendering, Digitally Reconstructed Radiograph, Simulated radiography, X-Ray Rendering
body: X-ray simulation via ray integration generates a Digitally Reconstructed Radiograph (DR) by integrating the linear attenuation coefficient along viewing rays from a source to a film plane, producing an X-ray-like projection image. Unlike standard direct volume rendering which maps scalar values to opacity for compositing, this method assumes a single energy level with no scatter, no beam hardening, and no detector response, relying strictly on the Beer-Lambert law to simulate physical attenuation. It is distinguished from its siblings by using actual Hounsfield Unit (HU) values directly in the attenuation calculation rather than arbitrary opacity mappings. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset where the scalar field f represents X-ray absorption density reconstructed by Computed Tomography (i.e., Hounsfield Units). Input: Camera parameters defining the source position s=0 and the film plane orientation. Input: Exposure control, which acts as a combined multiplier for tube output and detector gain. Output: A 2D simulated radiograph image. Data Structures: Volume: A 3D grid of floating-point values representing HU. Ray: Defined by origin (source) and direction vector. Step Size: A uniform constant uMmPerLangkah representing the integration step size in millimeters. Formulas: 1. Linear Attenuation Coefficient (\mu): Derived from the Hounsfield scale definition: \mu = \mu{water} \times \left(1 + \frac{HU}{1000}\right) Where \mu{water} = 0.0193 \, \text{mm}^{-1} at approximately 70 keV. 2. Attenuation Integral: The optical depth \tau along a ray is the integral of \mu over the path length l: \tau = \int{0}^{L} \mu(\mathbf{r}(l)) \, dl \approx \sum{i} \mui \cdot \Delta l Where \Delta l is the step size in millimeters (uMmPerLangkah). 3. Image Intensity (I): Using the Beer-Lambert law: I = I0 \cdot \text{Exposure} \cdot \exp(-\tau) Where I0 is the initial intensity (normalized to 1) and Exposure is the scalar control. Parameters: \mu{water}: 0.0193 \, \text{mm}^{-1}. Exposure: A scalar multiplier. It is NOT a dose in milligrays; no dose is computed. Step Size: Must be in millimeters. The multiplication by uMmPerLangkah is critical; removing it breaks the physics even if the uniform variable exists. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Step Size Integration: The integral must explicitly multiply the attenuation coefficient by the millimeter step size. A common implementation error is declaring the step size uniform but failing to use it in the summation, which causes incorrect attenuation values. Irrelevant Controls: Threshold controls and opacity-per-step sliders are irrelevant and should be hidden. Thresholds do not apply to attenuation-based calculation, and opacity-per-step is a volume-compositing factor not used in this single-pass integration. Physical Assumptions: The method assumes single energy. It does not account for scatter, beam hardening, or detector response characteristics. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def simulatexrayprojection(volume, camera, exposure, muwater=0.0193, stepsizemm=0.5): """ Simulates a radiograph by integrating attenuation along rays. Args: volume: 3D array of Hounsfield Units (HU) with.bounds and.sample(point) methods. camera: Object with 'rayforpixel(u, v)' returning (origin, direction). exposure: Scalar multiplier for tube output and detector gain. muwater: Linear attenuation coefficient of water in mm^-1. stepsizemm: Integration step size in millimeters. Returns: 2D image array. """ height, width = camera.imagesize image = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] volmin, volmax = volume.bounds for y in range(height): for x in range(width): origin, direction = camera.rayforpixel(x, y) # Normalize direction to ensure stepsizemm applies correctly along the ray dirlen = math.sqrt(direction[0]2 + direction[1]2 + direction[2]2) if dirlen > 0: direction = (direction[0]/dirlen, direction[1]/dirlen, direction[2]/dirlen) t = 0.0 integralmudl = 0.0 # Traverse until ray exits volume bounds while True: point = (origin[0] + direction[0]t, origin[1] + direction[1]t, origin[2] + direction[2]t) if not (volmin[0] <= point[0] <= volmax[0] and volmin[1] <= point[1] <= volmax[1] and volmin[2] <= point[2] <= volmax[2]): break hu = volume.sample(point) mu = muwater (1.0 + hu / 1000.0) integralmudl += mu stepsizemm t += stepsizemm intensity = exposure math.exp(-integralmudl) image[y][x] = intensity return image A GPU-based technique that renders geometric cells (hexahedra or tetrahedra) as separate layers using hardware rasterization to accumulate attenuation in a P-buffer. It handles unsorted, overlapping geometry by iteratively rendering non-overlapping subsets, minimizing expensive synchronization copies compared to sorted front-to-back methods. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Measured on a synthetic 700 HU sphere at 390x844 resolution, the method produces monotonic intensity changes with exposure (e.g., exposure x0.4 yields mean 7.7, x1 yields 14.6, x3 yields 22.2). Strengths: Physically accurate projection based on actual HU values; simple implementation; no need for complex transfer function tuning. Limitations: Assumes single energy; ignores scatter and beam hardening; does not model detector response. When to use: When generating standard X-ray projections from CT data for comparison with real radiographs or for basic visualization. When not to use: When high-fidelity spectral effects, scatter, or detector physics are required. The method originates from the application of optical models for direct volume rendering, specifically the absorption-only model where the transfer function is set to the identity function for X-ray absorption density. It integrates attenuation along viewing rays from arbitrary directions, using the identity transfer function for X-ray absorption density reconstructed by Computed Tomography. The specific implementation details, including the use of muwater = 0.0193 /mm at ~70 keV and the handling of exposure as a combined tube/detector gain factor, are documented in recent software development efforts for DICOM volume rendering. name: Hardware-Accelerated Simulated Radiography (Non-Emissive)
head: Hexahedral/Tetrahedral decomposition radiography, Layer-rendering algorithm, P-buffer accumulation, Unsorted Layer-Rendering Algorithm
body:
A GPU-based volume rendering technique for non-emissive objects that simulates X-ray radiography by accumulating attenuation coefficients in a floating-point off-screen P-buffer (accumulation buffer). It renders geometric cells (hexahedra or tetrahedra) as separate layers, using hardware-accelerated rasterization to compute the integral of attenuation along viewing rays. Unlike sorted front-to-back methods, this algorithm handles unsorted, overlapping geometry by iteratively rendering non-overlapping subsets of cells, minimizing expensive P-buffer-to-texture synchronization copies. Inputs: A volume decomposition into geometric cells (primarily hexahedra, subdivided into tetrahedra if necessary). Material properties for each cell, including density ho and elemental composition. X-ray source spectrum, discretized into N energy bands (typically N=4). Target image resolution (e.g., 512 	imes 512). Outputs: An attenuation image or simulated X-ray intensity image. Data Structures: Attenuation Table: Precomputed lookup table mapping material mixtures and energy bands to extinction coefficients \kappa
u. Cell List: A logically circular list of pointers to all cells, sorted or traversed in a specific order. Bounding Boxes: For each cell, the 2D image-plane bounding box of its projection. P-buffer: A floating-point off-screen framebuffer (texture) used to accumulate attenuation values. It has N channels (e.g., RGBA) to store attenuation for N energy bands in parallel. Test Buffer: A 1-bit per pixel buffer (represented in multi-bit words aligned per scan line) used to track which pixels have been covered by cells rendered in the current pass. Current Texture: A texture holding the accumulated attenuation from previous passes, used as input for interpolation. Formulas: The attenuation for a cell is computed based on the extinction coefficient and the path length through the cell: A = K
u \cdot t where K
u is the extinction coefficient for energy band 
u, and t is the thickness of the cell along the viewing ray. The extinction coefficient K
u is defined as: K
u = \kappa ho where \kappa is the opacity in 	ext{cm}^2/	ext{g} and ho is the density of the material. The final X-ray intensity I is derived from the total accumulated attenuation A{total} (sum of A across all cells and bands): I = e^{-A{total}} This exponential is applied during the final copy to the output buffer. Parameters: Number of energy bands: 4 (mapped to RGBA channels). Resolution: Typically 512 	imes 512 or similar. Threshold for pass termination: A fixed number of skipped cells due to overlap. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Read in volume data and compute the attenuation table for the specified energy bands and materials. For each cell, compute its 2D image-plane bounding box. If a hexahedron cannot be projected as a whole (e.g., due to non-convexity or self-intersection), subdivide it into five tetrahedra. Form a logically circular list of pointers to all cells. 2. Initialization: Initialize the P-buffer to zero. Initialize the Current Texture with the P-buffer data. 3. Iterative Rendering Passes: Traversal Order: Traverse the cell list in jumps of a size relatively prime to the list's length to ensure every cell is touched once before repetition and adjacent cells are not touched consecutively. Overlap Test: For each cell in the traversal: Clear the 1-bit Test Buffer at the start of the pass (or maintain it across the pass). Scan-convert the cell's bounding box into the Test Buffer format. The pattern along a scan line consists of a left partly filled word (from a lookup table), zero or more full words, and a right partly filled word (from a lookup table). Test the words involved in the bounding box against the Test Buffer using bitwise logical ANDs. If any result is non-zero, there is overlap with a cell already rendered in the current pass; skip this cell. If no overlap, use bitwise logical ORs to set the bits for the bounding box in the Test Buffer, mark the cell as completed in the list, and proceed to render. Rendering: Compute the attenuation for the current cell in software using geometry and K
u \cdot t. Interpolate the accumulated attenuation for the current cell from the Current Texture using hardware vertex data interpolation. Write the floating-point sum (accumulated attenuation) to the P-buffer. Pass Termination: If a threshold number of cells are skipped due to overlap, terminate the current pass. Copy the smallest rectangle in the P-buffer containing all rendered bounding boxes into the Current Texture. Start the next pass. 4. Final Output: When no cells are left (all cells rendered), copy the P-buffer (which contains the sum of all passes) to the output buffer. If an X-ray image is desired, compute the negative exponential e^{-A{total}} during this final copy. Draw the texture to the screen. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hardwareacceleratedradiography(cells, energybands, resolution): # Preprocessing attenuationtable = computeattenuationtable(cells, energybands) celllist = formcircularlist(cells) listlength = len(celllist) jumpsize = findrelativelyprimenumber(listlength) # Initialize buffers pbuffer = createfloatingpointbuffer(resolution, channels=len(energybands)) currenttexture = copytotexture(pbuffer) # Iterative passes while not allcellsrendered(celllist): testbuffer = create1bitbuffer(resolution) skippedcount = 0 threshold = 100 # Example threshold # Traverse with jump for i in range(0, listlength, jumpsize): cell = celllist[i % listlength] # Skip if already rendered in this pass if cell.renderedincurrentpass: continue # Overlap test bbox = cell.getimageplaneboundingbox() if checkoverlap(testbuffer, bbox): skippedcount += 1 continue # Render cell # 1. Compute attenuation for this cell attenuation = computecellattenuation(cell, attenuationtable) # 2. Interpolate accumulated attenuation from current texture # Hardware interpolation of vertex data accumulated = interpolatetexture(currenttexture, cell.vertices) # 3. Write sum to P-buffer writetopbuffer(pbuffer, cell, accumulated + attenuation) # 4. Mark as rendered in this pass cell.renderedincurrentpass = True setbitsintestbuffer(testbuffer, bbox) if skippedcount > threshold: break # Copy P-buffer to texture for next pass # Copy smallest rectangle containing rendered bounding boxes renderedrect = getrenderedrect(pbuffer) currenttexture = copyrecttotexture(pbuffer, renderedrect) # Reset rendered flags for next pass resetrenderedflags(celllist) # Final output if outputtype == 'xray': outputbuffer = applyexponential(pbuffer) else: outputbuffer = pbuffer drawtexture(outputbuffer) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Read-before-write artifacts: If the same framebuffer object is used for reading and writing, texture data may be used before it has been written out. This is handled by drawing a dummy textured square (e.g., 120 	imes 120 pixels) to flush the pipeline. Subdivision: Subdividing hexahedra into tetrahedra increases depth complexity, requiring more passes. Bounding Box vs. Actual Projection: Scanning the actual projection of the cell instead of its bounding box was tested but rejected because the extra cost of stepping along the edges balanced the speed-up from fewer layers, resulting in no net gain. Time Complexity: The method is bottlenecked by overlap determination and texture copying. The number of passes is related to the depth complexity of the volume decomposition. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the P-buffer, Current Texture, Test Buffer, and attenuation table. Measured Performance: On a dual processor 860 MHz Pentium4 Xeon PC with an nVidia 6800 GT graphics card, rendering 141,960 hexahedral cells (with some subdivided) at 512 	imes 512 resolution took 2.2 seconds for preprocessing and 35 seconds for rendering and copying. Using the same framebuffer object for read/write reduced rendering time to 7.4 seconds. Strengths: Hardware-accelerated rasterization; parallel accumulation of multiple energy bands; handles unsorted, overlapping geometry without sorting. Limitations: Bottlenecked by overlap determination and texture copying; requires multiple passes for complex scenes; subdivision increases depth complexity. When to use: When simulating X-ray radiography for non-emissive volumes with complex, overlapping geometry on hardware that supports floating-point framebuffers and efficient rasterization. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and the scene has high depth complexity; when emission is present (requires different model). Origin: Developed for simulating X-ray radiography in high-energy density physics experiments, such as hohlraum and capsule simulations. History: Validated against software raytrace packages used by scientists for simulation. The method uses EPDL database for atomic cross-sections. Usage: Used in scientific visualization for absorption-only radiographs of complex geometries. Hardware-Accelerated Simulated Radiography, https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc876978/?q=front-to-back compositing, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Spectral CT Simulation
head: Polychromatic Projection, Polychromatic spectral simulation, Spectralize
body: Spectral CT Simulation generates polychromatic X-ray projections by integrating monochromatic attenuation components weighted by an effective X-ray spectrum, applying material attenuation via the Beer-Lambert law, and adding Poisson noise to simulate detector statistics. It differs from monochromatic simulation by explicitly modeling the energy dependence of attenuation and the spectral shape of the source, which is critical for accurate beam-hardening artifacts and material decomposition studies. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume array vol (dtype float32, dimensions [vrt, mag, hrz]), geometry description geom, a list of material dictionaries mats, an energy grid E, an effective spectrum S, and a photon count parameter nphot. Output: A projection counts array counts (dtype float32), which must be converted to projection data using the negative logarithm: proj = -numpy.log(counts). Data Structures: mats: A list of dictionaries. Each dictionary contains keys 'material' (string), 'density' (float, g/cm³), and optionally other properties corresponding to labels in the phantom. E: 1D array of energy values in keV. S: 1D array of spectrum intensities corresponding to E. Parameters: kv: Tube voltage in kV. Default: 90. nphot: Total photon count for noise scaling. Default: 1e8 (typical forward projection value 1e6). filtr: Filter configuration (dict) containing material, density, and thickness. detector: Detector configuration (dict) containing material, density, and thickness. Method Steps: 1. Generate Effective Spectrum: Compute the effective spectrum S(E) based on the tube voltage kv, filtration filtr, and detector response. The spectrum represents the intensity distribution of X-ray photons across energies. 2. Compute Linear Attenuation: For each material in mats, compute the linear attenuation coefficient \mu(E) for each energy bin in E. This is done by retrieving the mass attenuation coefficient from a library (e.g., xraylib.CSTotalCP) and multiplying by the material density \rho: \mu(E) = \rho \cdot \frac{\mu{\text{mass}}(E)}{10} where \mu{\text{mass}} is in cm²/g and the factor 10 converts to mm⁻¹. 3. Ray Integration (Monochromatic): For each ray in the projection geometry, integrate the attenuation along the path through the volume. For a specific energy E, the transmitted intensity I{\text{mono}}(E) is calculated using the Beer-Lambert law: I{\text{mono}}(E) = S(E) \cdot \exp\left(-\sumi \mui(E) \cdot ti\right) where ti is the path length through material i. 4. Detector Response Accumulation: Sum the contributions across all energy bins. Assuming detector response is proportional to energy, the total detected signal before noise is: I{\text{total}} = \sumE E \cdot I{\text{mono}}(E) Note: The source notes describe I{\text{total}} = \sumE E \cdot I{\text{noisy}}(E), implying noise is added per energy bin before summation or the weighting applies to the noisy signal. The standard physical model sums intensities. The source formula suggests energy-weighted summation of noisy counts.. 5. Poisson Noise Application: Apply Poisson statistics to simulate detector noise. The noisy count I{\text{noisy}} is derived from the expected signal scaled by photon count N{\text{ph}}: I{\text{noisy}} = \frac{\text{Poisson}(I{\text{total}} \cdot N{\text{ph}})}{N{\text{ph}}} where \text{Poisson}(\lambda) draws a random integer from a Poisson distribution with mean \lambda. 6. Logarithmic Conversion: Convert the noisy counts to projection data (optical depth) for reconstruction: \text{proj} = -\ln(I{\text{noisy}}) Pitfall: If I{\text{noisy}} is zero, \ln(0) is undefined. A small epsilon or clamping is required in implementation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def spectralctsimulation(vol, geom, mats, E, S, nphot, kv=90, filtr=None, detector=None): """ Simulate spectral CT projections. Args: vol: numpy array [vrt, mag, hrz], float32 geom: geometry description mats: list of dicts with 'material', 'density' E: numpy array of energies in keV S: numpy array of spectrum intensities nphot: float, total photon count kv: float, tube voltage filtr: dict, filter properties detector: dict, detector properties Returns: proj: numpy array, projection data """ # 1. Precompute linear attenuation coefficients for all materials # mumap: dict mapping material name to numpy array of mu(E) in 1/mm mumap = {} for matinfo in mats: matname = matinfo['material'] rho = matinfo['density'] # g/cm^3 # Get mass attenuation from xraylib (CSTotalCP returns cm^2/g) # massatten: numpy array same shape as E massatten = getmassattenuation(E, matname) # Convert to linear attenuation in 1/mm: rho mass / 10 mumap[matname] = rho massatten / 10.0 # 2. Forward project for each energy bin # counts: numpy array matching projection geometry shape counts = np.zeroslike(geom.projectionshape, dtype=np.float32) # Get ray paths and material intersections from geometry # paths: list of tuples (materiallabel, pathlength) for each ray paths = getraypaths(geom, vol) for i, energy in enumerate(E): mue = np.array([mumap[m['material']][i] for m in mats]) # Not quite, need to map by label # Calculate attenuation for each ray # Imono = S(E) exp(- sum(mu t)) # We need to sum mu(E) t for each ray attenuation = np.zeros(geom.numrays, dtype=np.float32) for rayidx, raydata in enumerate(paths): for matlabel, pathlen in raydata: if matlabel in mumap: # Get mu for this energy # Note: mats list might not be ordered or indexed by label directly in this loop # Assuming a lookup table or dict for mumap by label muval = mumap[matlabel][i] attenuation[rayidx] += muval pathlen # Apply spectrum and Beer-Lambert # S[i] is intensity at energy E[i] Imono = S[i] np.exp(-attenuation) # Detector response: assume proportional to energy # Accumulate into counts # The source says: Itotal = sumE E Inoisy(E) # But noise is applied per energy? Or total? # Source: Inoisy = Poisson(Imono Nph) / Nph # Then Itotal = sum E Inoisy # Let's follow the source structure strictly: # 1. Scale by photon count expectedcounts = Imono nphot # 2. Add Poisson noise noisycounts = np.random.poisson(expectedcounts).astype(np.float32) / nphot # 3. Weight by energy and accumulate counts += energy noisycounts # 4. Convert to projection data # proj = -log(counts) # Guard against zero counts counts = np.maximum(counts, 1e-10) proj = -np.log(counts) return proj def getmassattenuation(energy, compound): """Wrapper for xraylib.CSTotalCP""" import xraylib energy = np.double(energy) if energy.size == 1: return xraylib.CSTotalCP(compound, energy) else: return np.array([xraylib.CSTotalCP(compound, e) for e in energy]) A forward projection method that simulates spectral CT data, accounting for material attenuation and detector response. It is chosen when generating synthetic projection data for a known volume and material composition, rather than reconstructing a volume from data. It differs from general spectral simulation by being a specific API call (model.forwardspectral) that encapsulates the geometry and material mapping logic. Typical parameters include nphot (1e6) and a list of material dictionaries mats. A key pitfall is that the output counts must be converted to projection data using the negative logarithm (proj = -numpy.log(counts)). Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays and the number of energy bins. O(N{\text{rays}} \cdot N{\text{energy}}). Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays and energy bins for storing intermediate attenuation and count arrays. Performance: Dependent on the efficiency of the ray integration and the speed of the X-ray library calls (e.g., xraylib). Strengths: Accurately models beam hardening and spectral effects, which are absent in monochromatic simulations. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to the integration over multiple energy bins. Requires accurate knowledge of the material composition and density in the volume. When to use: When simulating realistic CT data for algorithm development, especially for beam-hardening correction or material decomposition studies. When not to use: When speed is critical and spectral effects are negligible, or when the material composition is unknown. The method is implemented in the flexTOMO library, specifically within the cicwi/flexTOMO repository. It builds on the principles of X-ray physics, utilizing the Beer-Lambert law and Poisson statistics for noise modeling. The library uses xraylib for retrieving mass attenuation coefficients. cicwi/flexTOMO, https://github.com/cicwi/flexTOMO, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Prism Model
head: Smoke Surface (Prism Model), Surface-based thin volume model
body: The Prism Model is a surface-based optical model that simulates a thin participating volume by assigning an approximated depth to each triangle based on its orientation relative to the camera. It solves the problem of rendering volumetric absorption effects on dynamic, non-volumetric triangle meshes without requiring explicit voxelization or ray-marching through a 3D grid. It differs from its parent, the Absorption-only model, by replacing the physical particle density assumption with a geometric approximation where density is inversely proportional to triangle area and penetration depth is projected via the viewing angle. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangle mesh T representing the smoke surface; a viewing ray r; a design parameter k controlling initial density; an opacity multiplier function m{fade}; and a shape modifier function m{shape}. Output: The final absorption coefficient \alpha{final} for the pixel covered by the triangle. Data Structures: Ring Buffer: A data structure maintaining the topology of the mesh. It operates by removing the last (i.e., oldest) row of vertices from the visualization and reusing it as the new first (i.e., newest) row to simulate flow. Triangle Attributes: Each triangle t stores its vertices, computed normal n, area A(t), and current state for degeneration and fading. Numbered Steps: 1. Topology Update: At each frame, update the mesh topology using the ring buffer. Remove the last (oldest) row of vertices and reuse it as the new first (newest) row. 2. Ray Intersection: For each pixel, cast a ray r and determine intersection with triangle t at point p. 3. Geometry Calculation: Compute the triangle normal n. Compute the angle \gamma between n and r. Compute \operatorname{area}(t). 4. Degeneration Check: Evaluate the shape quality of t. If the triangle is degenerated (e.g., due to vertex movement in the ring buffer), calculate m{shape}(t) < 1. 5. Fade Check: Determine if triangle t is near the "seeding line" or "disappearance line" of the ring buffer cycle. Calculate m{fade}(t) to gently fade the triangle out. 6. Absorption Calculation: Compute \alpha(t) using the Prism Model formula. 7. Final Compositing: Apply modifiers to get \alpha{final} and composite the color. Formulas: 1. Prism Absorption: The base absorption coefficient \alpha(t) for a triangle t is defined as: \alpha(t) = 1 - e^{-\frac{k}{\cos(\gamma) \operatorname{area}(t)}} Where: k is a design parameter steering the initial density. \gamma is the angle between the triangle's face normal n and the viewing ray direction r. \operatorname{area}(t) is the geometric area of triangle t. Note: \cos(\gamma) represents the projected depth approximation. If the ray is parallel to the surface (\gamma = 90^\circ), the denominator approaches zero, requiring handling. 2. Final Absorption: The effective absorption is modified by fade and shape factors: \alpha{final} = \alpha(t) \cdot m{fade}(t) \cdot m{shape}(t) Parameters: k: Design parameter steering initial density. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Jagged Behavior (Fade In/Out): Sudden removal of vertices in the ring buffer causes entire rows of triangles to disappear instantly. This must be handled by modifying \alpha(t) with an opacity multiplier m{fade} to gently fade out triangles before they are removed from the buffer. Degeneration: Triangles change shape over time due to the ring buffer topology maintenance, leading to degenerated sections. A shape modifier m{shape} must decrease the triangle's contribution based on its level of degeneration. Back-facing Triangles: If \cos(\gamma) \le 0, the ray does not penetrate the "prism" in the expected direction. Standard culling or zero absorption should be applied. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeprismabsorption(triangle, raydirection, k, fadefactor, shapefactor): """ Computes the final absorption coefficient for a triangle using the Prism Model. Args: triangle: Object with attributes.vertices (list of 3 points),.normal (vector) raydirection: Normalized vector of the viewing ray k: Design parameter for initial density fadefactor: Multiplier [0, 1] for fade-in/out effects shapefactor: Multiplier [0, 1] for degeneration effects Returns: float: Final absorption coefficient alphafinal """ # 1. Get geometric properties area = computetrianglearea(triangle.vertices) normal = triangle.normal viewdir = raydirection # 2. Compute cosine of angle between normal and view ray # cos(gamma) = dot(normal, viewdir) cosgamma = dot(normal, viewdir) # Guard against division by zero or negative depth (back-facing) if cosgamma <= 0: return 0.0 # 3. Compute base absorption alpha(t) # Formula: alpha(t) = 1 - exp(-k / (cos(gamma) area(t))) denominator = cosgamma area if denominator == 0: return 0.0 # Avoid division by zero exponent = -k / denominator alphabase = 1.0 - exp(exponent) # 4. Apply modifiers alphafinal = alphabase fadefactor shapefactor return alphafinal def computetrianglearea(vertices): """Computes the area of a triangle given 3 vertices.""" v0 = vertices[0] v1 = vertices[1] v2 = vertices[2] # Vector cross product magnitude / 2 v01 = v1 - v0 v02 = v2 - v0 cross = crossproduct(v01, v02) return length(cross) 0.5 def crossproduct(a, b): """Returns the cross product of two 3D vectors.""" return [a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]] def dot(a, b): """Returns the dot product of two 3D vectors.""" return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def length(v): """Returns the Euclidean length of a 3D vector.""" return (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) 0.5 def exp(x): """Returns e raised to the power of x.""" import math return math.exp(x) Time Complexity: O(1) per triangle for absorption calculation, assuming area and normal are precomputed or cheaply computed. Memory Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of vertices in the mesh. The ring buffer stores a fixed number of rows. Strengths: Real-time capable; avoids expensive volume ray-marching; simple implementation on standard graphics pipelines. Limitations: Approximate depth; artifacts from topology changes (jaggedness, degeneration) require manual tuning of fade/shape modifiers; not physically accurate for complex scattering. When to use: Real-time visualization of vector fields or smoke-like effects on dynamic surfaces where performance is critical and physical accuracy of scattering is not required. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The Prism Model is a surface-based model that serves as the conceptual predecessor to smoke volume rendering. It was presented by Funck et al. [11] in the context of smoke surface rendering. The model interprets triangles as thin prisms to approximate volume information, allowing the use of optical absorption models on 2D surfaces. It is used for the exploration and analysis of unknown vector fields. Real-Time Smoke Volume Rendering, http://v22015081501727525.yourvserver.net/webpage/dirkfiles/betreutearbeiten/SowinskiMA2012.pdf, fetched 2026-10-31 (unofficial)

name: Absorption Attenuation
head: Absorption Coefficient Model, Absorption Coefficient, Absorption Model
body: Absorption Attenuation is the process by which light radiance is reduced as it travels through a participating medium due to the conversion of photon energy into other forms, such as heat. It calculates the surviving radiance along a ray segment in an absorption-only medium where no scattering or emission occurs. Unlike scattering-based models, this method considers only the exponential decay of incident light, serving as the foundational component for compositing in volume rendering and radiography [8074-transparency-and-opacity.md]. Inputs and Outputs Input: Incident radiance Li at the start of the segment, the absorption coefficient field \sigmaa(p, \omega), the start position p, the direction \omega, and the segment length d. Output: Exitant radiance Lo at the end of the segment. Data Structures The absorption coefficient \sigmaa represents the probability density that light is absorbed per unit distance traveled in the medium. Its units are reciprocal distance (m^{-1}). It can take any non-negative value and is not required to be between 0 and 1. It may vary with position p and direction \omega, though implementations often model it as purely a function of position. Exact storage layouts (fields, sizes, bit packing) are Not given in the sources. Formulas The differential change in radiance dL over a differential distance dt is given by: dL(p, \omega) = -\sigmaa(p, \omega) L(p, \omega) dt where L(p, \omega) is the radiance at position p in direction \omega, and \sigmaa(p, \omega) is the absorption coefficient. The surviving radiance after traveling distance d in direction \omega starting at point p is: L{surviving} = L{initial} \cdot e^{-\int0^d \sigmaa(p + t\omega, \omega) dt} The term in the exponent is the optical depth \tau: \tau(d) = \int0^d \sigmaa(p + t\omega, \omega) dt Thus, the transmittance T(d) is: T(d) = e^{-\tau(d)} And the exitant radiance is: Lo = T(d) Li Parameters \sigmaa: Absorption coefficient. It can take any non-negative value and is not required to be between 0 and 1. It may vary with position p and direction \omega, though many implementations (like pbrt) model it as purely a function of position. Steps 1. Initialize the accumulated optical depth \tau = 0. 2. Sample the absorption coefficient \sigmaa at the current position along the ray. 3. Add \sigmaa \cdot dt to \tau, where dt is the step size. 4. Repeat steps 2-3 for all steps along the ray segment of length d. 5. Compute the transmittance T = e^{-\tau}. 6. Compute the output radiance Lo = Li \cdot T. Edge Cases and Pitfalls If \sigmaa is zero, T=1 and no attenuation occurs. If \sigmaa is very large, T approaches 0, resulting in complete opacity. Numerical precision issues may arise if \tau is extremely large, causing e^{-\tau} to underflow to zero. The absorption coefficient is distinct from the absorption coefficient used in specifying indices of refraction of conductors. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def absorptionattenuation(Linitial, startpos, direction, length, numsteps): """ Calculate radiance after absorption attenuation. Args: Linitial: Incident radiance at startpos. startpos: 3D vector, starting point of the ray segment. direction: Normalized 3D vector, direction of propagation. length: Float, total distance to travel. numsteps: Integer, number of discrete steps for numerical integration. Returns: Lexitant: Radiance after attenuation. """ tau = 0.0 dt = length / numsteps for i in range(numsteps): currentpos = startpos + direction (i dt) # Sample absorption coefficient at currentpos # Not given in sources; implementation detail for integration sigmaa = 0.0 # Replace with actual sampling logic tau += sigmaa dt transmittance = math.exp(-tau) Lexitant = Linitial transmittance return Lexitant Defines transparency (transmittance) T(s) as the fraction of light remaining and opacity O(s) as the fraction absorbed (O(s) = 1 - T(s)). It is distinct from scattering-based models by considering only absorption. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sampling steps along the ray. If the absorption coefficient is constant, it is O(1). Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage of the absorption coefficient field. For a 3D grid, it is O(N^3) where N is the resolution. Strengths: Physically accurate for non-scattering media; computationally inexpensive compared to scattering models. Limitations: Does not account for light scattering or emission; requires accurate sampling of \sigmaa for inhomogeneous media. When to use: When modeling media where scattering is negligible (e.g., certain types of smoke, fog, or X-ray attenuation) or when compositing pre-computed attenuation maps. Absorption is one of the three main physical processes affecting radiance in participating media, alongside emission and scattering. Volume Rendering Volume Rendering, https://docslib.org/doc/1400821/volume-rendering, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) Volume Rendering in Offline Renderer · A Graphics Guy's Note, https://agraphicsguynotes.com/posts/volumerenderinginofflinerenderer/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) 11.1 Volume Scattering Processes, https://pbr-book.org/4ed/VolumeScattering/VolumeScatteringProcesses, fetched 2026-10-29 (book)

name: Transparency and Opacity
head: Opacity Calculation
body: Transparency and Opacity define the attenuation of light as it travels through a participating medium, quantifying how much incident radiance is preserved versus blocked by absorption. Transparency (or transmittance) T(s) represents the fraction of light surviving distance s, while Opacity O(s) represents the fraction blocked. This method serves as the foundational attenuation model for volume rendering, distinguishing itself from scattering models by considering only energy loss without redirection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Extinction coefficient \kappa(x, \omega) (units: inverse length), ray origin x, ray direction \omega, and integration distance s. Output: Transparency T(s) and Opacity O(s). Data Structures: Extinction Coefficient Field: A spatial field storing \kappa. In general volume rendering, this is a 3D texture or grid. In specific applications like X-ray radiography, it is stored in a table indexed by material number and energy group number. Formulas: The optical depth \tau(s) is the integral of the extinction coefficient along the ray: \tau(s) = \int0^s \kappa(x + t\omega, \omega) dt If \kappa is constant, \tau(s) = \kappa s. Transparency T(s) is defined as: T(s) = e^{-\tau(s)} = e^{-\int0^s \kappa(x + t\omega) dt} [ S1 ] Opacity O(s) is defined as: O(s) = 1 - T(s) [ S1 ] Pseudocode: The following Python-like pseudocode computes transparency and opacity for a constant extinction coefficient, handling the singularity at zero absorption. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computetransparencyopacity(sigma, s): """ Compute transparency and opacity for a constant extinction coefficient. Args: sigma (float): Absorption coefficient (extinction coefficient). s (float): Distance along the ray. Returns: tuple: (transparency, opacity) """ # Handle singularity where sigma is near zero to avoid division by zero # in more complex emission-absorption models, though pure transparency # T = exp(-sigmas) is well-defined at sigma=0. # However, if this function were part of an emission-absorption solver # (see Constant Intensity Model variant), the limit matters. # For pure transparency/opacity: tau = sigma s transparency = math.exp(-tau) opacity = 1.0 - transparency return transparency, opacity def computeextinctioncoefficientxray(sigmaE, u, A): """ Compute extinction coefficient from atomic cross-sections for X-rays. Args: sigmaE (float): Atomic cross-section interpolated at energy E (barns/atom). u (float): Atomic mass unit (1.6605402e-24 g). A (float): Atomic mass of the element in amu. Returns: float: Extinction coefficient kappaE. """ # 1 barn = 10^-24 cm^2 # kappaE = sigmaE / (u A) # Note: Units must be consistent. sigmaE in cm^2/atom, u in g, A in amu. # Resulting kappaE is in cm^2/g density? # Source defines kappaE directly via this formula for opacity. return sigmaE / (u A) def computegroupaverageopacity(kEfunc, Eg, Egplus1): """ Compute constant approximation for opacity over an energy group. Args: kEfunc (function): Function returning opacity kE' for energy E'. Eg (float): Lower energy of the group. Egplus1 (float): Upper energy of the group. Returns: float: Average opacity kg for the group. """ # kg = (1 / (Eg+1 - Eg)) integral from Eg to Eg+1 of kE' dE' # This requires numerical integration (e.g., Simpson's rule or trapezoidal) # as the exact function kE' is not provided in the general method. # Placeholder for numerical integration step. pass def computemixtureopacity(massfractions, elementopacities): """ Compute opacity of a mixture/compound from elemental opacities. Args: massfractions (list of float): mi, mass fraction of element i. elementopacities (list of float): Ki,g, opacity of element i for group g. Returns: float: Kmat,g, opacity of the mixture. """ Kmatg = 0.0 for i in range(len(massfractions)): Kmatg += massfractions[i] elementopacities[i] return Kmatg Parameters: Extinction Coefficient (\kappa): Not given in the sources for general volume rendering. In X-ray contexts, it is derived from cross-sections. Planck's Constant (h): 6.6263 \times 10^{-27} erg/s. Atomic Mass Unit (u): 1.6605402 \times 10^{-24} g. Barn: 10^{-24} cm^2. Electron Volt (eV): 1.60206 \times 10^{-12} erg. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity at Zero Absorption: In models combining emission and absorption (e.g., Constant Intensity Model), the term q/\sigma becomes undefined if \sigma \to 0. The sources provide a specific handling for this: if |\sigma| < 10^{-10}, use linear approximation I(s) = I0 + q \cdot s. Pure transparency T(s) = e^{-\sigma s} remains 1.0 at \sigma=0, which is numerically stable. Precision: Exponential decay can lead to underflow for large optical depths. Standard floating-point handling usually results in T(s) \approx 0, which is physically correct. Boundary Artifacts: In fuzzy surface rendering, lack of transparency attenuation can cause visual artifacts at object boundaries. Applying transparency decay (attenuation) can improve PSNR. A technique introduced to reduce visual artifacts at object boundaries in fuzzy surface rendering. It involves optimizing sample distribution and using view-dependent transparency to better capture fuzzy effects. Using transparency-decay resulted in a 2.13 dB PSNR gain on the Shelly scene compared to not using it. A procedure for obtaining extinction coefficients from calculated atomic cross-sections for X-rays, used to define material opacity for radiography. It involves interpolating cross-sections \sigmaE (in barns/atom) to compute element opacity \kappaE = \sigmaE / (uA), averaging over energy groups, and summing mass fractions for mixtures. Extinction coefficients are stored in a table indexed by material number and energy group number. A specific formulation for intensity I(s) along a ray with constant absorption coefficient \sigma and emission q. If |\sigma| < 10^{-10}, I(s) = I0 + q \cdot s. Otherwise, I(s) = I0 \cdot \exp(-\sigma s) + (q / \sigma) \cdot (-\text{expm1}(-\sigma s)). A set of modes in Phoenix for Maya determining how fire opacity is calculated. Use Smoke Opacity: Fire uses smoke's opacity; invisible where smoke is absent. Fully Visible: Fire renders with full opacity but no alpha; visible even without smoke. Uses additive blending. Not suitable for compositing fire mixed with smoke. Use Own Opacity: Custom varying opacity via diagram/texture. Don't Use Opacity Texture: Based entirely on Color and Opacity Curve. Multiply Opacity By Texture: Curve multiplied by texture. Fire Opacity From Texture: Based entirely on texture; curve ignored. Parameter: emAlphaTexture specifies the texture for Multiply or From Texture modes. Time Complexity: Computing transparency for a constant coefficient is O(1). For spatially varying \kappa, it requires numerical integration along the ray, proportional to the number of samples N (O(N)). Memory Complexity: Storing \kappa requires memory proportional to the volume resolution or the size of the material/energy group table. Strengths: Simple, physically grounded model for absorption. Essential for correct compositing in participating media. Limitations: Does not account for scattering. In X-ray radiography, requires pre-computed cross-section tables. In fire rendering, mode selection impacts compositing correctness. When to use: When absorption is the dominant light transport mechanism or when modeling non-scattering media like fog, smoke (absorption component), or X-rays. When not to use: When scattering is significant and must be modeled explicitly (requires full radiative transfer equation). The concepts of transparency and opacity are fundamental to the absorption-only model in volume rendering. The differential form of the light transport equation for absorption is dL/ds = -\kappa L, leading to the exponential decay solution. The specific formulas for X-ray extinction coefficients derive from atomic physics tabulations. The "Transparency Attenuation" variant was introduced in recent work on volumetric surfaces to handle fuzzy geometries. The "Constant Intensity Model" formula appears in HPC demonstrations. "Fire Opacity Texture Mode" is specific to the Phoenix for Maya software. name: Absorbing Particle Rendering
head: Direct Volume Rendering (Absorption Only)
body: Absorbing Particle Rendering simulates a participating medium composed of perfectly black particles that absorb all intercepted light without scattering or emitting. It solves for light intensity attenuation through a medium, resembling a cloud of black smoke or traditional X-ray imagery. Inputs: Initial light intensity I0 at the entry point of the volume. Extinction coefficient k of the medium. Distance x traveled through the medium. Outputs: Transmitted light intensity I(x) at the exit point. Data Structures: The method relies on scalar parameters derived from the medium's physical properties: A: Area of each particle. N: Number of particles per unit volume (number density). k: Extinction coefficient. \alpha: Opacity, where transparency is 1 - \alpha. Formulas: The change in light intensity I over a differential distance dx is governed by the differential equation: \frac{dI}{dx} = -k I where k is the extinction coefficient. The solution for intensity after traveling distance x is: I(x) = I0 e^{-k x} where I0 is the initial light intensity. The extinction coefficient k is derived from the particle properties. For a unit volume approximated as a small cylindrical slab with base area A and thickness dx, the intensity absorbed is determined by the total projected area of particles within that volume. The extinction coefficient is given by: k = N A where N is the number of particles per unit volume and A is the area of each particle. Parameters: r: Radius of the particles. Typical values depend on the scene scale; for example, discrete media simulations may use geometric mean radii \bar{r}g around 800 units in specific benchmark contexts. \etai: The imaginary part of the complex refractive index. Increasing \etai reduces the intensity of scattering, but in the pure absorption-only model, particles are assumed perfectly black. The extinction cross section must be slightly modified according to Ref. [65] to account for absorption. Steps: 1. Determine the area A of each particle. 2. Determine the number density N (particles per unit volume). 3. Compute the extinction coefficient: k = N \cdot A. 4. For a viewing ray traversing a segment of length x through the medium, compute the transmitted intensity: I(x) = I0 e^{-k x}. 5. If implementing discretely, accumulate opacity \alpha = 1 - e^{-k x} for compositing. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: For large optical depths (k x \gg 1), I(x) approaches 0. Standard floating-point precision is sufficient, but underflow to zero may occur for very dense media. Boundary Conditions: The model assumes a homogeneous medium with constant k. If N or A varies spatially, k must be integrated numerically along the ray. Degenerate Input: If N=0 or A=0, k=0 and I(x) = I0 (no attenuation). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def absorbingparticlerendering(I0, A, N, x): """ Calculate transmitted light intensity through an absorbing particle medium. Args: I0 (float): Initial light intensity at the start of the volume. A (float): Area of each particle. N (float): Number of particles per unit volume. x (float): Distance traveled through the medium. Returns: float: Transmitted light intensity I(x). """ # Step 3: Calculate extinction coefficient k = N A # Step 4: Calculate transmitted intensity using Beer-Lambert law # I(x) = I0 exp(-k x) Ix = I0 math.exp(-k x) return Ix Simulates attenuation using similar integration principles but accounts for energy-dependent absorption coefficients rather than discrete particle geometry. Choose when modeling monochromatic or energy-specific X-ray projections. X-ray simulation via ray integration Approximates the medium as a continuous distribution of light-absorbing prisms rather than discrete particles, offering different computational trade-offs. Choose when particle boundaries are less critical than continuous volume approximation. Prism Model A general term for the physical phenomenon of light reduction; this method is a specific implementation using discrete particle assumptions. Choose when explicitly modeling particulate media rather than continuous attenuation fields. Absorption Attenuation Time Complexity: O(1) per ray segment if k is constant. If k varies, it requires numerical integration along the ray, typically O(N{steps}) where N{steps} is the number of integration steps. Memory Complexity: O(1) if parameters are precomputed. O(N) if storing explicit particle positions for sparse sampling. Performance: Rendering time is minimal as it involves only exponential calculations. Benchmarks for discrete media show lowest rendering times at resolutions where there is roughly one particle per voxel (e.g., 60 \times 60 \times 60 for 2 \times 10^5 particles). Strengths: Computationally efficient; physically intuitive for dense, non-scattering media like smoke or X-ray attenuation. Limitations: Cannot represent scattering effects (glory, halos); assumes spherical particles; ignores emission. When to use: Simulating black smoke, fog, or X-ray projections where scattering is negligible. When not to use: When realistic lighting with shadows, caustics, or color bleeding from scattering is required. The absorption-only model is a foundational concept in Direct Volume Rendering, historically used to simulate media that only block light. It is derived from the Beer-Lambert law applied to discrete particulate media. The model assumes perfectly black particles that absorb light perfectly. name: Emission-only Model
head: Direct Volume Rendering (Emission Model), Emission Model, Glow Only Model, Glow model, Glowing transparent gas
body: The Emission-only Model renders a participating medium that adds light to the view ray via emission but neglects absorption and scattering. It solves for the accumulated glow intensity of a luminous medium, such as a hot tenuous gas or fluorescent stains, where the material is effectively transparent to its own light. Unlike the Absorption-only model which attenuates background light, or the Emission-Absorption Model which accounts for occlusion and depth ordering, the emission-only model is order-independent and assumes the contribution of each emitting particle is independent of others. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D scalar field f(\mathbf{x}) representing density or source strength; a viewing ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \boldsymbol{\omega}; an initial intensity I0 (typically background radiance). Output: Final radiance I(D) at distance D along the ray. Data Structures Scalar Field: A 3D grid or texture storing values f(\mathbf{x}). Transfer Function: A mapping g(f) that converts scalar values to emission intensity per unit length. Steps 1. Interpolate: For a sample point \mathbf{p} on the ray, interpolate the scalar field value f(\mathbf{p}). 2. Map to Source: Compute the source term g(s) using the transfer function applied to the scalar value: g(s) = g(f(\mathbf{p})). In many implementations, g is proportional to f. 3. Integrate: Accumulate the source term along the ray from the near clipping plane (s=0) to the far clipping plane (s=D). Formulas The change in radiance I over a differential path length ds is governed by the source term g(s): \frac{dI}{ds} = g(s) where g(s) is the added intensity per unit ray length. The solution to this ordinary differential equation is: I(s) = I0 + \int0^s g(t) \, dt where I0 is the initial intensity at the start of the ray. In terms of physical parameters, if the medium consists of perfectly glowing diffuse particles with intensity C per unit projected area and number density \rho, the source term is defined as: g(s) = C(s) \tau(s) where \tau(s) acts as a density proxy for emission (often \tau(s) = \rho(s) A, with A being the average projected area of particles). Thus: I(s) = I0 + \int0^s C(t) \tau(t) \, dt Parameters C (Emission Constant): Intensity per unit projected area. Must be scaled carefully to prevent overflow. g(f): Transfer function mapping scalar density to emission intensity. Does not account for direction or shadowing. Pitfalls and Edge Cases Unbounded Intensity: Because there is no attenuation term, the integral has no upper bound. Accumulated intensity can easily exceed the representable range of the output device (clipping). The constant C must be set small enough to avoid saturation at the center of dense regions. Order Independence: Like Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP), the result is commutative. Swapping parts of the ray does not change the final result, making it impossible to distinguish depth order between features. No Occlusion: Features in the "back" of the volume contribute equally to the "front," potentially overwhelming foreground details. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderemissiononly(rayorigin, raydirection, scalarfield, transferfunction, near, far, dt): """ Renders a volume using the emission-only model. Args: rayorigin: vec3, origin of the view ray. raydirection: vec3, normalized direction of the view ray. scalarfield: Function f(x) returning scalar value at position x. transferfunction: Function g(f) mapping scalar to emission intensity. near: float, start distance along ray. far: float, end distance along ray. dt: float, fixed integration step length ds. Returns: float, final intensity I(D). """ # Initial intensity (e.g., background color or 0) I = 0.0 # Iterate along the ray from near to far s = near while s < far: # 1. Interpolate scalar field position = rayorigin + raydirection s fval = scalarfield(position) # 2. Map to source term # g(s) is the added intensity per unit length gs = transferfunction(fval) # 3. Integrate (accumulate) # dI = g(s) ds I += gs dt s += dt return I Adds attenuation to the emission model. Choose this when depth ordering and occlusion are required, such as for smoke, clouds, or opaque surfaces in NeRFs. It solves the unbounded intensity problem of the emission-only model by introducing an exponential decay term. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of samples along the ray. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray, excluding the storage of the scalar field. Strengths: Computationally simple; order-independent; suitable for simulating glowing phenomena like flames, fluorescent stains, or tenuous gases where self-occlusion is negligible. Limitations: Prone to intensity overflow/clipping due to unbounded accumulation; lacks depth cues and occlusion. When to use: Visualization of transparent luminous media, neutron emission, or when a "glow" effect is desired without physical accuracy regarding occlusion. The emission-only model is a foundational concept in direct volume rendering, derived from the radiative transfer equation by neglecting extinction terms. It was formalized in the context of optical models for direct volume rendering by Max (1995), who described it as the limit where particle size or number density approaches zero while emission compensates, resulting in a transparent glowing medium. It is closely related to Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) in its order-independence. The model is historically used for visualizing neutron transport and fluorescent micrographs.
