name: Linear Distance Fog
head: Depth Cueing (Linear), Distance Fog, Light Diminishing, Linear Fog
body: Linear distance fog is a depth-cueing technique that attenuates surface brightness linearly with view distance, fading colors toward black with a brightness floor to simulate atmospheric density or limited visibility. Unlike Exponential Fog (Beer-Lambert), which models physical light absorption via exponential decay, linear fog is a geometric approximation implemented with integer or fixed-point arithmetic for performance. Inputs: dist (perpendicular distance from camera to surface in cells or world units), col (surface color in 24-bit RGB or 16-bit RGB565), FOGDIST (full fade distance), FOGMIN (brightness floor). Outputs: foggedcol (attenuated color). Data Structures: Precomputed row tables for floor/ceiling in raycasters: CEILROW and FLOORROW arrays of size H (screen height). Formula: shade = \max(FOG{MIN}, 256 - \lfloor \frac{dist \times 256}{FOG{DIST}} \rfloor) Where dist is the view distance, FOG{DIST} is the full fade distance, and FOG{MIN} is the brightness floor clamped between 0 and 256. The result shade is an integer in the range [FOG{MIN}, 256]. For floor and ceiling pixels in a raycaster, the distance depends only on the screen row y relative to the horizon (screen height H): d{row} = \frac{H / 2}{|y - H / 2|} If |y - H / 2| < 1, the distance is considered infinite and the shade is clamped to FOG{MIN}. Parameters: FOG{DIST} = 10 cells, FOG{MIN} = 36. Steps and Pseudocode: The implementation uses integer arithmetic to avoid floating-point costs. Wall shading folds directional side-darkening into the per-column fog shade. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fogshade(dist, fogdist=10, fogmin=36): attenuation = (dist 256) // fogdist shade = 256 - attenuation if shade < fogmin: shade = fogmin return shade def shadecolor24bit(col, shade): r = ((col & 0xff) shade) >> 8 g = (((col >> 8) & 0xff) shade) >> 8 b = (((col >> 16) & 0xff) shade) >> 8 return 0xff000000 | (b << 16) | (g << 8) | r def applyfog24bit(dist, col, fogdist=10, fogmin=36, side=0): shade = fogshade(dist, fogdist, fogmin) # Fold y-side directional darkening into the per-column factor if side == 1: shade = (shade 140) >> 8 return shadecolor24bit(col, shade) CEILROW = [0] FBH FLOORROW = [0] FBH for y in range(FBH): dy = abs(y - FBH / 2) shade = FOGMIN if dy < 1 else fogshade((FBH / 2) / dy) CEILROW[y] = shadecolor24bit(CEILCOLOR, shade) FLOORROW[y] = shadecolor24bit(FLOORCOLOR, shade) RGB565 Variant: This variant unpacks 16-bit RGB565, applies a linear factor, and repacks. Bitwise unpacking is mandatory because multiplying the raw 16-bit integer directly causes color channels to bleed into each other ("swimming" colors). The multipliers (8, 4, 8) adjust for the specific display driver's gamma or intensity. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applyfogrgb565(color16bit, dist, maxdist=12.0): r = (color16bit >> 11) & 0x1F g = (color16bit >> 5) & 0x3F b = color16bit & 0x1F if dist > maxdist: return 0 factor = 1.0 - (dist / maxdist) # Multipliers 8, 4, 8 compensate for display driver intensity rout = int(r factor 8) gout = int(g factor 4) bout = int(b factor 8) return (rout << 11) | (gout << 5) | bout Edge Cases and Pitfalls: 1. Integer Overflow: Multiplying an 8-bit color component by a shade value up to 256 produces a 16-bit intermediate value; arithmetic must support this before shifting. 2. Color Distortion in RGB565: Direct multiplication of the packed 16-bit integer causes channel bleeding; bitwise unpacking is required. 3. Floor/Ceiling Singularity: At the horizon line (y = H/2), d{row} approaches infinity; the code must handle |y - H/2| < 1 explicitly to avoid division by zero. 4. Side Darkening: Wall shading includes a directional component that folds into the fog shade via (shade 140) >> 8 for side walls. Standard 24-bit implementation using integer arithmetic and a brightness floor to ensure readability. Chosen for performance-critical raycasting engines using fixed-point math. Variant optimized for 16-bit LCD displays using floating-point factors and hardware-specific scaling multipliers (8, 4, 8) to compensate for display driver intensity. Chosen for embedded systems with limited color depth. Requires bitwise unpacking to prevent color distortion. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(H) for precomputed floor/ceiling row tables, otherwise O(1). Measured Performance: Extremely fast; the 24-bit integer version requires no floating-point unit, making it suitable for CPUs without FPU support. On embedded hardware, it runs efficiently on ESP8266-driven 16-bit LCDs. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Computationally inexpensive and cheap enough to add atmosphere to raycasted environments. Limitations: Does not model physical light scattering; linear fade is a geometric approximation rather than a physical model. When to use: Real-time raycasting or embedded graphics where performance is critical. When not to use: When physically accurate atmospheric scattering or volumetric light interaction is required. Origin: Introduced in later engines of the Wolfenstein 3D family to improve atmosphere, as the original game shipped with no depth cue except object size. Adapted for ESP8266 embedded projects as a "lantern effect" to simulate flashlight visibility on RGB565 displays. name: Absorption Adjustment
head: Opacity Adjustment
body: Absorption Adjustment corrects the opacity parameter \alpha used in planar smoke rendering to account for non-orthogonal viewing angles and variable plane spacing. It adjusts the absorption parameter \alpha for view directions not aligned with the axis orthogonal to the viewing planes, and when the distance between adjacent smoke planes changes or viewing planes are skipped. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Base absorption coefficient \alpha0 (derived from the medium's extinction coefficient and plane spacing), viewing direction vector, and plane normal vector. Output: Adjusted absorption parameter \alpha' suitable for OpenGL blending. Data Structures: The method operates on scalar values. In the source, \alpha is a float in the range [0.0, 1.0], where 0.0 represents completely transparent and 1.0 represents completely opaque. Steps: 1. Determine the angle \theta between the viewing direction and the plane normal. 2. Calculate the effective path length through the plane based on \theta. 3. Adjust the absorption coefficient if the viewing direction is not aligned with the axis orthogonal to the viewing planes. 4. Adjust the absorption coefficient if the distance between adjacent smoke planes changes or viewing planes are skipped. 5. Compute the final opacity for blending using the adjusted coefficient. Formulas: The base absorption parameter \alpha relates to the total mass extinction coefficient \sigmat and the distance between grid planes \Delta x via the Beer-Lambert law: \alpha = 1 - e^{-\sigmat \Delta x} When adjusting for view direction, the effective thickness scales by 1/\cos(\theta), yielding: \alpha' = 1 - e^{-\sigmat \frac{\Delta x}{\cos(\theta)}} If planes are skipped or spacing changes to \Delta x', the coefficient is recalculated using the new distance. Parameters: \sigmat: Total mass extinction coefficient (\sigmaa + \sigmas). \Delta x: Distance between adjacent grid planes. \theta: Angle between viewing direction and plane normal. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The calculation requires exponential operations. The source notes that ten million exponential operations per second are required to display smoke with corrected \alpha's at 10 frames per second for a simulation with grid dimensions of 100 \times 100 \times 100. Boundary Conditions: When \theta approaches 90^\circ (grazing angle), \cos(\theta) approaches 0, causing \alpha' to approach 1.0 (fully opaque), which requires clamping or capping to avoid numerical instability. Plane Skipping: If viewing planes are skipped, \alpha must be adjusted proportionally to the change in distance to maintain visual consistency. Extinction Falloff is a rendering shortcut that approximates the visual contribution of hundreds of additional scattering bounces by gently reducing the extinction coefficient with each real bounce. It allows scenes to achieve brighter, more realistic volumetric lighting (such as internal light spill in fire or smoke) while rendering faster than equivalent scenes without the technique, avoiding the need to increase trace depth. Time Complexity: The method requires exponential operations for each plane intersection. The source cites a requirement of ten million exponential operations per second for a 100 \times 100 \times 100 grid at 10 fps. Memory Complexity: Minimal, as it operates on scalar coefficients. Strengths: Corrects visual artifacts caused by oblique viewing angles and variable grid spacing in planar smoke rendering. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to the need for many exponential operations. Requires knowledge of the plane spacing and viewing geometry. When to use: When rendering smoke or fire using planar alpha-blending techniques where view direction varies or grid spacing is non-uniform. When not to use: When using continuous volume rendering methods that compute transmittance directly along the ray, or when performance is critical and visual accuracy of planar blending is not required. The method originates from the visualization of fire dynamics simulation data, specifically within the Smokeview tool. It addresses the need for accurate visual representation of smoke planes when viewed from arbitrary angles. The technique is described in the technical reference guide for Smokeview (Version 6). Smokeview (Version 6) A Tool for Visualizing Fire Dynamics Simulation Data Volume II: Technical Reference Guide, https://doi.org/10.6028/nist.sp.1017-2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Extinction Falloff
body: Extinction Falloff is a rendering shortcut that approximates the visual contribution of hundreds of additional scattering bounces by gently reducing the extinction coefficient with each real bounce. It allows scenes to achieve brighter, more realistic volumetric lighting (such as internal light spill in fire or smoke) while rendering faster than equivalent scenes without the technique, avoiding the need to increase trace depth. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The base extinction coefficient of the medium, the current scattering bounce count, and the Extinction Falloff Value parameter. Output: The modified extinction coefficient used for transmittance calculation at the current segment. Data Structures: The method operates on scalar values associated with the ray's current state and requires no complex data structures. Parameters: Extinction Falloff Value: A scalar parameter controlling the rate of extinction reduction. The default value is 0.2, described as a deliberate sweet spot. Method Steps: 1. Retrieve the base extinction coefficient for the current medium segment. 2. Determine the current scattering bounce count for the ray. 3. Apply a reduction to the extinction coefficient based on the bounce count and the Extinction Falloff Value parameter. 4. Use the modified extinction coefficient to calculate segment transmittance. 5. Proceed to the next scattering event or ray termination. Formulas: The sources describe the mechanism as a gentle reduction of extinction per bounce but do not provide an explicit mathematical formula. Implementers typically apply a multiplicative decay factor to the base extinction coefficient that scales with the bounce count and the falloff parameter. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Standard ray marching implementations should clamp the modified extinction coefficient to non-negative values to prevent numerical instability. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculateeffectiveextinction(baseextinction: float, bouncecount: int, falloffvalue: float) -> float: """ Calculates the effective extinction coefficient for a given bounce. Args: baseextinction: The medium's original extinction coefficient. bouncecount: The current scattering bounce number (1-based). falloffvalue: The Extinction Falloff Value parameter (default 0.2). Returns: float: The reduced extinction coefficient for this bounce. """ if baseextinction <= 0.0: return baseextinction # Formula not given in sources; standard geometric decay applied. reductionfactor = (1.0 - falloffvalue) (bouncecount - 1) effectiveextinction = baseextinction reductionfactor return max(effectiveextinction, 0.0) A companion shortcut that lowers the anisotropy parameter with every bounce to mimic van de Hulst’s similarity principle, making deeper rays scatter more isotropically. See Anisotropy Falloff. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The technique reduces overall rendering time by allowing the path tracer to terminate earlier while maintaining visual fidelity. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: In Redshift's cloud test, using the default value of 0.2 produced a brighter, more realistic result while rendering faster than the same scene without it. Strengths: Efficiently approximates multiple scattering effects without the computational cost of tracing hundreds of bounces. Limitations: It is an approximation that mimics the visual result of multiple bounces rather than physically simulating the exact radiative transfer. When to Use: When rendering participating media with significant multiple scattering (e.g., clouds, smoke, fire) and performance is a concern. When Not to Use: When strict physical accuracy is required over speed, or when the scene does not benefit from multiple scattering approximation. Extinction Falloff is a feature introduced in the Redshift Renderer by Maxon. It is part of a suite of shortcuts designed for experienced artists to achieve realistic volumetric results without excessive trace depths. The technique operates alongside Anisotropy Falloff, which draws inspiration from van de Hulst’s similarity principle in radiative transfer. What Is Volumetric Rendering? name: Non-Exponential Free Flight Model
head: Davis and Xu model, Generalized Boltzmann Equation (GBE) for non-exponential media, Generalized linear transport model for spatially correlated stochastic media
body: The Non-Exponential Free Flight Model simulates light transport in homogeneous participating media where scattering particles are spatially correlated, resulting in free path distributions with longer tails than the standard exponential decay of Beer's Law. Unlike Exponential Fog (Beer-Lambert), which assumes uncorrelated particle distributions, this model introduces "memory" into the photon transport process, allowing artistic control over light bleeding depth by adjusting a shape parameter. It is primarily used for subsurface scattering and volumetric effects where natural clustering or voids in particle distribution affect attenuation. The model adapts the Generalized Boltzmann Equation (GBE) from neutron transfer to computer graphics, assuming an isotropic medium without boundaries where the phase function and scattering albedo do not depend on distance. It modifies the standard Monte Carlo random walk by making the scattering probability a function of both the scattering cross-section and the distance traveled. Inputs: \sigmae: Extinction coefficient (constant for the homogeneous medium). \sigmas: Scattering coefficient (constant). a: Shape parameter controlling the tail of the distribution. \xi: Uniform random variable in [0, 1]. Outputs: s: Sampled free flight distance. Ta(s): Transmittance at distance s. S(s): Effective scattering coefficient at distance s. No complex data structures are required. The model relies on scalar values for coefficients and distances. The parameter a is often mapped to a user-friendly "bleed" parameter b such that a = 1/b. 1. Transmittance: Ta(s) = \frac{1}{(1 + \frac{\sigmae s}{a})^a} Where s is the distance traveled. 2. Probability Density Function (PDF): p(s) = \frac{\sigmae}{(1 + \frac{\sigmae s}{a})^{a+1}} This defines the likelihood of a scattering event occurring at distance s. 3. Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF): c(s) = \frac{1}{(1 + \frac{\sigmae s}{a})^a} Note that c(s) = Ta(s). 4. Inverse CDF (Sampling): To sample a distance s from a uniform random variable \xi \in [0, 1]: s(\xi) = \frac{a \cdot (\xi^{-1/a} - 1)}{\sigmae} This allows direct sampling of the free flight distance. 5. Modified Scattering Coefficient: In the Monte Carlo random walk, the scattering coefficient \sigmas is modified to depend on the distance traveled: S(s) = \frac{\sigmas}{1 + \frac{\sigmae s}{a}} This reflects the reduced probability of interaction as the photon travels further through correlated voids. a (Shape Parameter): Controls the shape of the distribution. As a \to \infty, the model converges to the exponential Beer's Law case. Smaller values of a (or larger "bleed" values) result in longer tails, allowing light to penetrate deeper. Bleed (b): A user-friendly parameter where a = 1/b. This maps the parameter to a meaningful unit range for artists. The following Python-like pseudocode implements the sampling and scattering logic for a single step in the random walk. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def samplenonexponentialfreeflight(sigmae, a, xi): """ Samples the free flight distance s for a non-exponential medium. Args: sigmae (float): Extinction coefficient. a (float): Shape parameter. xi (float): Uniform random number in [0, 1]. Returns: float: Sampled distance s. """ # Guard against xi = 0 to avoid division by zero or log(0) if xi <= 0.0: xi = 1e-9 # Inverse CDF: s = a (xi^(-1/a) - 1) / sigmae # Note: xi^(-1/a) is equivalent to (1/xi)^(1/a) term = math.pow(xi, -1.0 / a) s = (a (term - 1.0)) / sigmae return s def computetransmittance(sigmae, s, a): """ Computes the transmittance Ta(s) for the non-exponential model. Args: sigmae (float): Extinction coefficient. s (float): Distance traveled. a (float): Shape parameter. Returns: float: Transmittance value. """ denominator = 1.0 + (sigmae s) / a ta = 1.0 / (denominator a) return ta def geteffectivescatteringcoefficient(sigmas, sigmae, s, a): """ Computes the distance-dependent scattering coefficient S(s). Args: sigmas (float): Base scattering coefficient. sigmae (float): Extinction coefficient. s (float): Distance traveled. a (float): Shape parameter. Returns: float: Effective scattering coefficient S(s). """ denominator = 1.0 + (sigmae s) / a ss = sigmas / denominator return ss def montecarlostep(sigmae, sigmas, a, xi): """ Performs one step of the Monte Carlo random walk using the non-exponential model. Args: sigmae (float): Extinction coefficient. sigmas (float): Scattering coefficient. a (float): Shape parameter. xi (float): Uniform random number in [0, 1]. Returns: tuple: (distance s, transmittance Ta, effective scattering coeff Ss) """ # 1. Sample distance s = samplenonexponentialfreeflight(sigmae, a, xi) # 2. Compute transmittance ta = computetransmittance(sigmae, s, a) # 3. Compute effective scattering coefficient for this step ss = geteffectivescatteringcoefficient(sigmas, sigmae, s, a) return s, ta, ss Boundary Limitations: The original GBE theory assumes an isotropic medium without boundaries. While computer graphics adaptations eliminate some limitations, the model is strictly defined for homogeneous media in its basic form. Heterogeneous Media: Although the theory can conceptually support heterogeneous media, it does not provide a feasible solution, nor explain reciprocity and path integral form for such cases, so it cannot be directly applied to general light transport methods for heterogeneous volumes. Parameter Intuition: The raw parameter a can have unintuitive ranges. Using the mapped "bleed" parameter b (a=1/b) is recommended for usability. Precision: When \xi is very close to 0, numerical stability in the inverse CDF calculation must be handled (e.g., clamping \xi to a small positive value). A general, physically-based framework for modeling and rendering spatially-correlated media with non-exponential decay of transmittance, addressing both short-range and long-range correlations. It describes spatial correlations by introducing the fractional Gaussian field (FGF), a mathematical tool for modeling high-frequency noise-like fluctuations and k-th order fractional Brownian motion (fBm) with stochastic continuity. This method simulates different extents of randomness, resulting in a smooth transition in appearance from exponential falloff to complete transparency. It is the first method to address both short-range and long-range correlations using physically-based fluctuation models. Time Complexity: Sampling the distance s requires computing a power function and basic arithmetic, which is O(1) per step, similar to exponential sampling but slightly more expensive due to the exponentiation. Memory Complexity: O(1), as no additional data structures are needed beyond the coefficients and current distance. Performance: The model allows for artistic control over light bleeding. Strengths: Provides a simple parametric way to model non-exponential attenuation with longer tails, suitable for subsurface scattering and correlated volumetric effects. Limitations: Limited to homogeneous media in its standard implementation; does not natively support heterogeneous media with reciprocity in a feasible path-integral form. The "memory" effect is local to the free flight step and does not account for complex boundary interactions in the original formulation. When to Use: When simulating media with clustered or voided particle distributions (e.g., skin, clouds, fog) where Beer's Law is too aggressive in attenuation. When Not to Use: For heterogeneous media where a full path-integral solution or reciprocity is required, as the theory does not provide a feasible solution for such cases. The Non-Exponential Free Flight Model is based on the Generalized Boltzmann Equation (GBE) from the field of neutron transfer. It was developed by Davis and Xu in 2014, published in "A generalized linear transport model for spatially correlated stochastic media" in the Journal of Computational and Theoretical Transport. It was later adopted in production path tracing for subsurface scattering to provide intuitive artistic control over light bleeding. The Fractional Gaussian Field (FGF) framework was later proposed by Guo et al. in 2019 to extend these concepts to both short-range and long-range correlations. name: Heterogeneous Medium Transmittance — Beer's Law
head: Beam Transmittance, Beer's Law (Heterogeneous), Beer's Law with Optical Depth, Beer-Lambert Law, General Transmittance Equation, Transmittance (Beer-Lambert Law)
body: Heterogeneous Medium Transmittance calculates the fraction of radiance transmitted between two points through a participating medium where the extinction coefficient varies spatially. It generalizes the homogeneous case by integrating the extinction coefficient along the ray path to compute optical depth, then applying the exponential attenuation model. Unlike Homogeneous Medium Transmittance, which assumes a constant extinction coefficient, this method handles spatially varying density and composition, serving as the foundational attenuation term for light transport in complex participating media. Inputs: Start point \mathrm{p} (3D position). End point \mathrm{p}^\prime (3D position). Extinction coefficient function \sigma{\mathrm{t}}(\mathbf{x}, \omega), which returns the total extinction coefficient at position \mathbf{x} for direction \omega. This function may depend on position and direction, though often \omega is fixed for a single ray segment. Outputs: Transmittance \mathcal{T} (\mathrm{p} \to \mathrm{p}^\prime): A scalar in [0, 1] representing the fraction of light surviving attenuation. Optical depth \tau (\mathrm{p} \to \mathrm{p}^\prime): A scalar representing the integrated extinction along the path. Data Structures: No specific complex data structures are required for the definition itself, but implementation typically involves a numerical integration routine (e.g., trapezoidal rule, Simpson's rule, or adaptive quadrature) over the ray segment. The extinction coefficient function \sigma{\mathrm{t}} is usually accessed via a 3D texture, voxel grid, or analytical function. Steps: 1. Calculate the ray direction \omega and total distance d: \omega = \frac{\mathrm{p}^\prime - \mathrm{p}}{\lVert \mathrm{p}^\prime - \mathrm{p} \rVert} d = \lVert \mathrm{p}^\prime - \mathrm{p} \rVert If d = 0, return \mathcal{T} = 1 and \tau = 0. 2. Define the position along the ray at distance t from \mathrm{p}: \mathbf{x}(t) = \mathrm{p} + t \omega, \quad t \in [0, d] 3. Compute the optical depth \tau by integrating the extinction coefficient along the ray: \tau (\mathrm{p} \to \mathrm{p}^\prime) = \int0^d \sigma{\mathrm{t}} (\mathbf{x}(t), \omega) \; \mathrm{d}t In practice, this integral is approximated numerically. For a discrete set of samples ti with spacing \Delta t, a simple Riemann sum or trapezoidal rule is used: \tau \approx \sum{i} \sigma{\mathrm{t}} (\mathbf{x}(ti), \omega) \Delta ti 4. Compute the transmittance using the exponential of the negative optical depth: \mathcal{T} (\mathrm{p} \to \mathrm{p}^\prime) = \exp \left( - \tau (\mathrm{p} \to \mathrm{p}^\prime) \right) Formulas: General Transmittance: \mathcal{T} (\mathrm{p} \to \mathrm{p}^\prime) \equiv \exp \left( - \int0^d \sigma{\mathrm{t}} (\mathrm{p} + \omega t, \omega) \; \mathrm{d}t \right) where d = \lVert \mathrm{p}^\prime - \mathrm{p} \rVert and \omega = (\mathrm{p}^\prime - \mathrm{p}) / d. Optical Depth: \tau (\mathrm{p} \to \mathrm{p}^\prime) \equiv \int0^d \sigma{\mathrm{t}} (\mathrm{p} + \omega t, \omega) \; \mathrm{d}t. This is also written as \tau = \int{s=0}^d \sigmat(xs) ds where xs = x + s\omega. Extinction Coefficient Composition: The total extinction coefficient \sigma{\mathrm{t}} combines absorption \sigmaa and out-scattering \sigmas: \sigma{\mathrm{t}} = \sigmaa + \sigmas. Both absorption and out-scattering cause attenuation of the beam, and they are combined into a single term unless separate tracking is required. Multiplicative Property: Transmittance is multiplicative along a ray: \mathcal{T} (\mathrm{p} \to \mathrm{p}^{\prime \prime}) = \mathcal{T} (\mathrm{p} \to \mathrm{p}^\prime) \mathcal{T} (\mathrm{p}^\prime \to \mathrm{p}^{\prime \prime}). This follows from the linearity of the integral in the exponent. Parameters: \tau: Optical depth (or optical thickness). Not given in the sources as a fixed parameter, but a computed quantity. d: Distance traveled by the ray through the volume. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Distance: If \mathrm{p} = \mathrm{p}^\prime, d=0, transmittance is 1. Precision: For very large optical depths, \exp(-\tau) may underflow to 0. This is physically correct (opaque medium). Numerical Integration: The accuracy of \tau depends on the sampling density relative to the variation of \sigma{\mathrm{t}}. If \sigma{\mathrm{t}} varies rapidly, insufficient sampling leads to inaccurate transmittance. Direction Dependence: The extinction coefficient \sigma{\mathrm{t}} may depend on direction \omega (anisotropic media). The formula accounts for this by evaluating \sigma{\mathrm{t}}(\mathbf{x}, \omega). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def heterogeneoustransmittance(pstart, pend, sigmatfunc): """ Computes transmittance through a heterogeneous medium using Beer's Law. Args: pstart: 3D vector, start point of the ray. pend: 3D vector, end point of the ray. sigmatfunc: Function that takes (position, direction) and returns the total extinction coefficient sigmat. Returns: T: Transmittance (scalar in [0, 1]). tau: Optical depth (scalar). """ # Step 1: Calculate direction and distance direction = pend - pstart d = length(direction) # Edge case: zero distance if d == 0: return 1.0, 0.0 # Normalize direction omega = direction / d # Step 2: Numerical integration of optical depth # Note: The specific integration method (e.g., number of samples, # quadrature rule) is not specified in the sources. # A simple midpoint rule with N samples is provided as a common implementation. N = 100 # Number of samples. Not given in the sources. tau = 0.0 dt = d / N for i in range(N): # Sample at the midpoint of each interval t = (i + 0.5) dt position = pstart + t omega # Evaluate extinction coefficient at this position and direction sigmat = sigmatfunc(position, omega) # Accumulate optical depth tau += sigmat dt # Step 3: Compute transmittance T = exp(-tau) return T, tau This variant treats light as electromagnetic radiation with a spectral power distribution F(\lambda), typically limited to the visible spectrum \lambda \in [380\text{nm}, 770\text{nm}] or [400\text{nm}, 700\text{nm}]. It extends Beer's Law to wavelength-dependent extinction. For a homogeneous isotropic absorption filter, transmission follows Lambert's law: L(\lambda) = L0(\lambda) \cdot \exp(-s \cdot \tau(\lambda)), where \tau(\lambda) is the spectral extinction coefficient. Beer's extension for a liquid solution with solute concentration \nu and solute extinction coefficient \kappa(\lambda) is L(\lambda) = L0(\lambda) \cdot \exp(-s \cdot \nu \cdot \kappa(\lambda)). For depth correction, if transparency T(\lambda, \Delta) is known for a standard path length \Delta, the transparency for an arbitrary path length \delta is T(\lambda, \delta) = T(\lambda, \Delta)^{\frac{\delta}{\Delta}}, which can be rewritten for opacity as \alpha(\lambda, \delta) = 1 - (1 - \alpha(\lambda, \Delta))^{\frac{\delta}{\Delta}}. This is chosen when color accuracy and wavelength-dependent attenuation are critical. Time Complexity: Depends on the numerical integration method. For N samples along the ray, it is O(N) evaluations of \sigma{\mathrm{t}}. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory if \sigma{\mathrm{t}} is accessed on-the-fly (e.g., from a texture or analytical function). If precomputed optical depth is stored, it depends on the volume resolution. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Linear with ray length and sampling density. Strengths: Physically accurate for heterogeneous media; generalizes homogeneous case; multiplicative property allows efficient composition of transmittance over multiple segments. Limitations: Requires evaluation of \sigma{\mathrm{t}} at multiple points; numerical integration errors if sampling is insufficient; does not account for in-scattering (only attenuation). When to use: When the medium's extinction coefficient varies spatially and in-scattering is handled separately or ignored. When not to use: When the medium is homogeneous (use Homogeneous Medium Transmittance for efficiency); when in-scattering is significant and needs to be coupled with transmittance in a single step (requires full RTE solution). The Beer-Lambert law originates from the work of Bouguer (1727) and Lambert (1760) on absorption in filters, and Beer (1983) extended it to liquid solutions. In computer graphics, it is a fundamental component of the volume rendering equation, describing the attenuation of light as it travels through participating media. The general form for heterogeneous media is derived from the radiative transfer equation (RTE). It is widely used in offline renderers and real-time volume rendering for simulating fog, smoke, clouds, and biological tissues. From the Radiative Transfer Equation to the Volume Rendering Equation, https://scratchapixel.com/lessons/3d-basic-rendering/volume-rendering-for-developers/volume-rendering-summary-equations.html, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) Volumetric rendering fundamental concepts and terminology, https://computergraphics.stackexchange.com/questions/145/volumetric-rendering-fundamental-concepts-and-terminology, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) [Graphics] Volume Rendering - GitHub Pages, https://leeyngdo.github.io/blog/computer-graphics/2024-03-28-volume-rendering/, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Volume Rendering in Offline Renderer · A Graphics Guy's Note, https://agraphicsguynotes.com/posts/volumerenderinginofflinerenderer/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) Local and Global Illumination in the Volume Rendering Integral, https://avishek.net/assets/papers/nerfs/local-and-global-illumination-rendering-integral.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (book)

name: Maximum-Value Projection Shading Handling
head: Maximum Shader
body: Maximum-Value Projection Shading Handling is a method for rendering volumetric data where the final pixel color is determined by the highest scalar value encountered along the viewing ray, rather than an accumulation or average. It solves the problem of visualizing the outermost or most significant features in a volume while suppressing internal structures. It differs from Exponential Fog (Beer-Lambert) and Absorption Adjustment by discarding all intermediate data values and focusing solely on the extremum, and from Non-Exponential Free Flight Model by not modeling probabilistic light transport but rather deterministic data extraction. The method combines a data extraction shader with specific shading adjustments to ensure correct visibility of underlying geometry through the volume. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray cast through a volumetric cell containing scalar data values. Output: A single color value derived from the maximum scalar value found along the ray, processed through a transfer function. Data Structures: Ray: Defined by origin O and direction D. Cell: A volumetric element with an associated opacity O1 and scalar data values. Transfer Function: A mapping T(v) \rightarrow C that converts a scalar value v to a color C. Steps: 1. Ray Casting: Cast a primary ray through the volume. 2. Data Sampling: Examine all measured data values along the ray path within the current cell. 3. Maximum Extraction: Identify the maximum scalar value v{max} from the sampled data. 4. Color Mapping: Apply the transfer function to v{max} to determine the base color. 5. Shading Configuration: Turn off all shading effects except transmission. Set the index of refraction to 1. Calculate the transmission coefficient Tc using the opacity O1 of the maximum value: Tc = 1 - O1 where O1 is the opacity corresponding to the maximum value. 6. Intersection Handling (Recursive Prevention): If a transmission ray is cast from a maximum-value intersection point, the current cell must be turned "off" to prevent the ray from performing intersection calculations with it, thereby avoiding a recursive maximum-value intersection within the same object. Once the transmission ray intersects the target polygon, the cell must be turned "on" again to allow correct shadowing and reflection calculations for subsequent rays. Parameters: Index of Refraction: Set to 1. Transmission Coefficient: 1 - O1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Recursive Intersection: Naively casting a transmission ray from a maximum-value intersection without disabling the current cell results in another maximum-value intersection within the same object, causing visual artifacts or infinite loops. Opacity Handling: The transmission coefficient depends on the opacity of the maximum value. If the maximum value is opaque (O1 = 1), no transmission occurs, and underlying polygons are hidden. A shader that examines all measured data values along the ray and displays the maximum found using a transfer function. It is chosen when the user wants to visualize the most significant or outermost scalar values in a volume, such as the highest density or temperature, ignoring lower values. It is distinct from the Accumulation shader, which sums values, and the Cloud shader, which adds lighting functions. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples taken along the ray to find the maximum. Memory Complexity: Minimal, requiring storage for the current maximum value and the transfer function. Strengths: Provides clear visualization of dominant features; computationally efficient for data extraction. Limitations: Loses information about internal structures; sensitive to the transfer function definition. When to use: When the goal is to highlight the most extreme values in a dataset. When not to use: When internal details or average properties are of interest. The concept of the "Maximum shader" was introduced in the context of volume rendering in architecture, specifically for overlapping and combining 3D voxel volume data with 3D building models. The shading handling details, including the transmission coefficient formula and intersection management, were described in the context of volumetric ray tracing within the VolVis volume visualization system. Volumetric Ray Tracing, https://www.cs.drexel.edu/~david/Classes/Papers/p11-sobierajski.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) Volume Rendering in Architecture: Overlapping and combining 3d voxel volume data with 3d building models, https://doi.org/10.52842/conf.ecaade.2012.1.719, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Transmittance Calculation via Ratio Tracking
head: Ratio Tracking, Ratio Tracking Transmittance
body: Ratio Tracking is an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator for the transmittance function T(xi, x{i+1}) in heterogeneous media, proposed by Novák et al. [2014]. It is used within Pseudo-Marginal Metropolis Light Transport (PMLT) to provide a noisy but unbiased estimate of transmission where exact integration is intractable. Unlike deterministic methods such as Exponential Fog (Beer-Lambert) which assume homogeneous density, Ratio Tracking handles spatially varying extinction coefficients by sampling distances and evaluating the ratio of samples that exceed the target distance. Inputs: Ray segment endpoints xi and x{i+1}. Extinction coefficient function \sigmat(x), defined for all x along the segment. Bounding density \sigma{max} \ge \max(\sigmat(x)) along the segment. Number of samples N (integer > 0). Transmittance depth parameter \alpha (float, typically 1.0, range 0.1 to 10). Outputs: Estimated transmittance \hat{T} (float in [0, 1]). Data Structures: No persistent data structures required. The method is stateless per evaluation. Steps: 1. Compute the ray direction \omega = (x{i+1} - xi) / \|x{i+1} - xi\| and the segment length L = \|x{i+1} - xi\|. 2. Scale the target distance by the transmittance depth parameter: L{eff} = L \cdot \alpha. 3. Initialize a cumulative sum sumT = 0.0. 4. For each sample j from 1 to N: a. Initialize pos = xi, accumdist = 0.0, and prod = 1.0. b. Loop indefinitely: i. Sample a uniform random number u \in (0, 1]. ii. Compute free-flight distance d = -\ln(u) / \sigma{max}. iii. Update position: pos = pos + d \omega. iv. Update accumulated distance: accumdist += d. v. Multiply the running product by the ratio of actual to bounding density: prod = \sigmat(pos) / \sigma{max}. vi. Check if accumdist >= L{eff}. If true, break the loop. vii. Check if pos has exited the volume bounding box. If true, set prod = 0.0 and break the loop. c. Add prod to sumT. 5. Compute the raw estimate: \hat{T}{raw} = \text{sum\T} / N. 6. Clamp \hat{T}{raw} to [0, 1] and return as \hat{T}. Formulas: The transmittance T(xi, x{i+1}) represents the fraction of energy reaching x{i+1} from xi. T(xi, x{i+1}) = \exp\left(-\int{xi}^{x{i+1}} \sigmat(s) ds\right) The estimator \hat{T} is derived from N independent samples. Each sample estimates the transmittance by tracking the product of density ratios along a stochastic path until the scaled target distance is reached or the medium boundary is crossed. Parameters: \alpha (transmittance depth): Scales the transmittance distance, allowing adjustment of transmittance without changing density or distance estimation. Range observed: 0.1 to 10. Default is typically 1.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Changing \alpha affects the number of steps required to exit the volume bounding box because the code always checks if the ray position is still inside the medium boundaries. Precision issues may arise if \sigmat varies rapidly, requiring careful bounding density selection in delta tracking steps. If \sigmat(x) = 0 anywhere, \sigma{max} must still be positive to avoid division by zero in the ratio product. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def ratiotrackingtransmittance(xi, xiplus1, sigmat, sigmamax, N, alpha=1.0): """ Estimate transmittance using Ratio Tracking. Args: xi: Start point of the ray segment. xiplus1: End point of the ray segment. sigmat: Function returning extinction coefficient at a point. sigmamax: Bounding density, >= max(sigmat) along segment. N: Number of Monte Carlo samples. alpha: Transmittance depth parameter. Returns: Estimated transmittance. """ direction = normalize(xiplus1 - xi) segmentlength = length(xiplus1 - xi) targetdist = segmentlength alpha # Scale distance per sumT = 0.0 for in range(N): currentpos = list(xi) prod = 1.0 accumdist = 0.0 while True: u = random.random() if u == 0.0: u = 1e-9 # Guard against log(0) d = -math.log(u) / sigmamax accumdist += d # Update position currentpos = [currentpos[k] + d direction[k] for k in range(3)] # Update product with density ratio sigma = sigmat(currentpos) prod = sigma / sigmamax # Check if target distance is reached if accumdist >= targetdist: break # Check if currentpos is outside the volume bounding box if not isinsidevolume(currentpos): prod = 0.0 break sumT += prod rawestimate = sumT / N if N > 0 else 0.0 return max(0.0, min(1.0, rawestimate)) def normalize(v): l = length(v) return [c / l for c in v] if l > 0 else [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] def length(v): return math.sqrt(sum(cc for c in v)) def isinsidevolume(p): # Implementation depends on scene geometry; returns True if p is inside return True Computes transmittance using Beer's Law for constant density. Choose when density is uniform. Parent. Standard exponential decay model. Choose for simple, homogeneous attenuation. Sibling. Adjusts absorption based on path length. Choose for simple post-processing or simplified models. Sibling. Uses non-exponential distributions for free flight. Choose for media with non-standard scattering properties. Sibling. Applies Beer's Law with integration for varying density. Choose when exact integration is possible. Sibling. Time Complexity: O(N) per evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per evaluation. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with N. Strengths: Unbiased estimator; handles heterogeneous media; integrates well with MCMC methods like PMLT. Limitations: Noisy estimate. When to use: When unbiased transmittance estimation is required in heterogeneous media within a PMLT framework. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Ratio Tracking was proposed by Novák et al. in 2014 as part of the Pseudo-Marginal Metropolis Light Transport (PMLT) method. It was introduced to provide an unbiased estimate of transmittance in heterogeneous media, which is difficult to compute exactly. The method is based on the principle of ratio tracking, where the transmittance is estimated by the ratio of samples that survive the distance to the total number of samples. It has been used in research contexts involving complex light transport in participating media. Pseudo-marginal metropolis light transport, https://doi.org/10.1145/2820903.2820922, fetched 2026-10-30 Lighting And Transmittance, https://sergeneren.com/2019/04/26/lighting-and-transmittance/, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Light Decay Model
head: Light Decay Type, emLightsDecayType
body: The Light Decay Model controls the rate at which emissive light from a fire source fades as it travels through a participating medium or space. It defines the geometric attenuation function applied to light intensity based on distance from the emitter. It differs from Homogeneous Medium Transmittance, which handles absorption and scattering within the medium itself, by handling the vacuum-like geometric falloff of the source emission before medium interaction. The method applies a scalar decay factor to the emitted radiance based on the Euclidean distance d between the light source and the point of evaluation. Inputs: I{emit}: The initial intensity of the light source. d: The distance from the light source to the point being shaded. Outputs: I{decay}: The attenuated intensity at distance d. Data Structures: The decay type is represented by an integer or enumeration value: 0: None 1: Inverse 2: Inverse Square Steps: 1. Calculate the distance d from the light source origin to the current shading point. 2. Determine the decay factor F(d) based on the selected decay type. 3. Compute the final intensity: I{decay} = I{emit} \times F(d). Formulas: The decay factor F(d) is defined as: For None: F(d) = 1 The light intensity remains constant regardless of distance, unless obstructed by other geometry or medium transmittance. For Inverse: F(d) = \frac{1}{d} At a distance of 5 units, the intensity is 1/5 of the emitter intensity. For Inverse Square: F(d) = \frac{1}{d^2} At a distance of 5 units, the intensity is 1/25 of the emitter intensity. This model is physically correct for point sources in a vacuum. Parameters: emLightsDecayType: The selected decay mode. Typical values are Inverse Square for physical accuracy or Inverse/None for artistic control or specific simulation requirements. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Distance: If d=0, the Inverse and Inverse Square models result in division by zero. Implementations must clamp d to a minimum epsilon value or handle the singularity explicitly. Performance: Inverse Square decay is computationally slightly more expensive than Inverse due to the squaring operation, though negligible in modern hardware. Artifacts: Sharp circular banding artifacts may appear if the decay is too aggressive or if the sampling rate is insufficient. This is often addressed by adjusting the Light Cut-off parameter. A V-Ray specific control that specifies a threshold for light intensity below which the light will not be computed. This limits the effect of the Phoenix light to a certain distance around the simulator. Larger values cut away more light; lower values make the light range larger. At 0.0, the light is calculated for all surfaces, but rendering may slow down significantly. If sharp circular banding artifacts become visible, this parameter should be reduced. Time Complexity: O(1) per shading point for the decay calculation itself. However, the effective range of computation is limited by the Light Cut-off, potentially reducing the number of rays traced or surfaces illuminated. Memory Complexity: O(1). No additional data structures are required beyond the distance calculation. Strengths: Provides physically accurate lighting falloff (Inverse Square) or artistic control (Inverse/None). Limitations: Does not account for medium absorption or scattering; must be combined with Homogeneous Medium Transmittance for full participating media effects. When to use: Use Inverse Square for physically based rendering. Use Inverse or None for stylized effects or when the fire is embedded in a medium where geometric falloff is less relevant than volumetric scattering. The Light Decay Model is a feature of the Phoenix for Maya plugin, specifically within the V-Ray integration. It allows artists to control the visual behavior of emissive fire sources. The concept of inverse square law decay is a fundamental principle in physics (radiometry), while inverse and none are artistic approximations. Voxel Shader - Phoenix for Maya, https://documentation.chaos.com/space/PHX4MAYA/125768009, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Radiative Transfer Equation Formulation
head: Equation of Transfer, Light transport equation, Radiation Transport Equation, Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) for Participating Media, Radiative Transport Equation, Time-dependent RTE
body: The Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) is an integro-differential equation that governs the transport of radiance in participating media, describing how light changes as it propagates through a volume that absorbs, emits, and scatters radiation. It solves the fundamental problem of modeling light transport in arbitrary participating media (such as smoke, fog, clouds, or fire) by accounting for the balance of energy loss (extinction) and energy gain (emission and in-scattering) along a ray path. It differs from the Volume Rendering Integral by being the differential form from which the integral is derived, and from the Light Transport Equation by explicitly handling volumetric scattering rather than just surface interactions. Inputs and Outputs Input: The radiance field L(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}) at position \mathbf{x} and direction \boldsymbol{\omega}, along with medium properties: extinction coefficient \sigmat(\mathbf{x}), scattering coefficient \sigmas(\mathbf{x}), phase function fp(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}', \boldsymbol{\omega}), and emission term. Output: The directional derivative of radiance \frac{dL}{ds}, representing the change in radiance per unit distance traveled in direction \boldsymbol{\omega}. Data Structures The RTE operates on scalar fields defined over 3D space and the unit sphere of directions. Extinction Coefficient \sigmat(\mathbf{x}): A scalar field in \mathbb{R}^3, units m^{-1}. Defined as \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) = \sigmaa(\mathbf{x}) + \sigmas(\mathbf{x}), where \sigmaa is absorption and \sigmas is scattering. Phase Function fp(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}', \boldsymbol{\omega}): A function mapping incoming direction \boldsymbol{\omega}' and outgoing direction \boldsymbol{\omega} to a probability density, normalized such that \int{\mathbb{S}^2} fp(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}', \boldsymbol{\omega}) d\boldsymbol{\omega}' = 1. Often simplified to depend only on the dot product \boldsymbol{\omega} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}'. Emission: Defined as Le(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}) or volume emittance Le^V(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}). Formulas The differential form of the RTE describes the change in radiance L along a ray parameterized by distance s in direction \boldsymbol{\omega}: \frac{d L(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega})}{d s} = -\sigmat(\mathbf{x}) L(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}) + \sigmas(\mathbf{x}) \int{\mathbb{S}^2} fp(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}', \boldsymbol{\omega}) L(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}') d\boldsymbol{\omega}' + Le(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}) Where: \frac{d L}{d s} = \boldsymbol{\omega} \cdot \nabla L is the directional derivative. -\sigmat(\mathbf{x}) L(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}) is the extinction term (loss due to absorption and out-scattering). \sigmas(\mathbf{x}) \int{\mathbb{S}^2} fp(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}', \boldsymbol{\omega}) L(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}') d\boldsymbol{\omega}' is the in-scattering term (gain from other directions). Le(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}) is the emission term (internal light sources). Alternatively, using the source term Ls(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}) = Le(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}) + \sigmas(\mathbf{x}) \int{\mathbb{S}^2} fp(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}', \boldsymbol{\omega}) L(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}') d\boldsymbol{\omega}', the equation is: (\boldsymbol{\omega} \cdot \nabla) L(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}) = -\sigmat(\mathbf{x}) L(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}) + Ls(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}). Steps to Solve (Integral Form) To compute the radiance at a point \mathbf{x} along a ray from a surface intersection \mathbf{x}S in direction \boldsymbol{\omega}, the differential equation is integrated using the method of variation of parameters: 1. Calculate Transmittance: Compute the transmittance T(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x}) from a point \mathbf{x}' on the ray to the observation point \mathbf{x}: T(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x}) = \exp \left( -\int0^{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'\|} \sigmat(\mathbf{x}' + t\boldsymbol{\omega}) dt \right). 2. Integrate Source Term: Integrate the source term (emission + in-scattering) weighted by transmittance from the surface intersection \mathbf{x}S to \mathbf{x}: L(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}) = T(\mathbf{x}S, \mathbf{x}) L(\mathbf{x}S, \boldsymbol{\omega}) + \int0^{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}S\|} T(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x}) \left[ Le(\mathbf{x}', \boldsymbol{\omega}) + \sigmas(\mathbf{x}') \int{\mathbb{S}^2} fp(\mathbf{x}', \boldsymbol{\omega}', \boldsymbol{\omega}) L(\mathbf{x}', \boldsymbol{\omega}') d\boldsymbol{\omega}' \right] ds. Note: The incoming direction for in-scattering is often negated in implementation conventions (-\boldsymbol{\omega}') depending on coordinate system definitions. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def directionalderivativeradiance(x, omega, sigmat, sigmas, phasefunction, Le, Lfield): """ Computes the directional derivative of radiance dL/ds at position x in direction omega. Implements the differential form of the RTE. """ # 1. Extinction (Loss) extinction = -sigmat(x) Lfield(x, omega) # 2. In-scattering (Gain) # Integral over the unit sphere S^2 approximated by Monte Carlo inscattering = 0.0 numsamples = 1000 for in range(numsamples): # Sample a direction omegaprime uniformly on the unit sphere omegaprime = sampleuniformsphere() # Phase function fp(x, omega', omega) f = phasefunction(x, omegaprime, omega) # Incident radiance from direction omega' Lincident = Lfield(x, omegaprime) # Monte Carlo estimator: integral over sphere is approximated by sum / N 4pi inscattering += sigmas(x) f Lincident (4.0 math.pi / numsamples) # 3. Emission (Gain) emission = Le(x, omega) # Total derivative dL/ds dLds = extinction + inscattering + emission return dLds def computetransmittance(xstart, xend, sigmatfield): """ Computes transmittance T(xstart, xend) = exp(-integral of sigmat along path). """ pathvec = (xend[0]-xstart[0], xend[1]-xstart[1], xend[2]-xstart[2]) pathlength = math.sqrt(pathvec[0]2 + pathvec[1]2 + pathvec[2]2) if pathlength < 1e-6: return 1.0 direction = (pathvec[0]/pathlength, pathvec[1]/pathlength, pathvec[2]/pathlength) # Numerical integration of extinction along the path numsteps = 100 opticaldepth = 0.0 stepsize = pathlength / numsteps for i in range(numsteps): t = (i + 0.5) stepsize xmid = (xstart[0] + tdirection[0], xstart[1] + tdirection[1], xstart[2] + tdirection[2]) opticaldepth += sigmatfield(xmid) stepsize return math.exp(-opticaldepth) def solverteintegral(xobs, xsurface, omega, sigmatfield, sigmasfield, phasefunction, Lefield, Lsurface, Lfield): """ Computes the radiance at xobs by integrating the RTE along the ray from xsurface. Implements the integral form derived from the differential RTE. """ # 1. Calculate Transmittance from surface to observation point transmittancesurface = computetransmittance(xsurface, xobs, sigmatfield) termsurface = transmittancesurface Lsurface # 2. Integrate volumetric sources along the path pathvec = (xobs[0]-xsurface[0], xobs[1]-xsurface[1], xobs[2]-xsurface[2]) pathlength = math.sqrt(pathvec[0]2 + pathvec[1]2 + pathvec[2]2) volumetriccontribution = 0.0 numsteps = 100 stepsize = pathlength / numsteps for i in range(numsteps): t = (i + 0.5) stepsize xprime = (xsurface[0] + tomega[0], xsurface[1] + tomega[1], xsurface[2] + tomega[2]) # Transmittance from xprime to observation point transmittancevol = computetransmittance(xprime, xobs, sigmatfield) # Source term at xprime: Emission + In-scattering emission = Lefield(xprime, omega) # In-scattering integral approximation inscattering = 0.0 numscattersamples = 100 for in range(numscattersamples): omegaprime = sampleuniformsphere() f = phasefunction(xprime, omegaprime, omega) Lincident = Lfield(xprime, omegaprime) inscattering += sigmasfield(xprime) f Lincident (4.0 math.pi / numscattersamples) source = emission + inscattering volumetriccontribution += transmittancevol source stepsize return termsurface + volumetriccontribution def sampleuniformsphere(): """Samples a direction uniformly on the unit sphere S^2.""" u = random.uniform(0, 1) v = random.uniform(0, 1) theta = 2.0 math.pi u phi = math.acos(2.0 v - 1.0) return (math.sin(phi) math.cos(theta), math.sin(phi) math.sin(theta), math.cos(phi)) Parameters \sigmat: Total extinction coefficient (m^{-1}). \sigmas: Scattering coefficient (m^{-1}). \sigmaa: Absorption coefficient (m^{-1}), \sigmaa = \sigmat - \sigmas. fp: Phase function, normalized to 1 over the sphere. Le: Emission coefficient (W/(sr \cdot m^3)). \Lambda: Scattering albedo, \Lambda = \sigmas / \sigmat. Edge Cases and Pitfalls No Analytical Solution: The RTE is an integro-differential equation with no general analytical solution for arbitrary media. Numerical approximations (e.g., diffusion approximation, N-flux theory) are required. Neglected Physics: The RTE is based on geometrical optics and neglects diffraction, interference, wave character, and polarization. High Albedo: Smoke often has low albedo, allowing scattering terms to be simplified or eliminated for interactive rates. High albedo media require full multiple scattering solutions, which are computationally expensive. Coordinate Conventions: The direction of incoming light in the phase function integral may be negated (-\boldsymbol{\omega}') depending on the specific implementation's coordinate system. The Standard volume rendering equation computes the final pixel color by integrating emitted and scattered light along a camera ray, attenuated by extinction. It differs from the general RTE by typically assuming no explicit light transport simulation (in-scattering from other light sources) in its basic form, relying instead on direct emission or ambient approximation. The Volume Rendering Equation explicitly formulates the radiative transfer differential equation, allowing for the construction of emission and absorption fields directly from particle distributions or volume grids. Unlike the Standard equation, it handles the full RTE structure, enabling physically plausible gas cloud appearance from continuous density fields. Similarity Theory identifies equivalence classes within the RTE parameter space, where distinct sets of scattering parameters produce identical radiance fields if band-limited in the spherical harmonics domain. It enables replacing difficult-to-simulate scattering parameters (e.g., highly forward-scattering) with equivalent, easier-to-simulate ones, accelerating forward rendering. The Green's propagator G is the solution to the homogeneous RTE (source term Q=0) with an initial condition defined by a Dirac delta function representing a point source at position \mathbf{x}' and direction \boldsymbol{\omega}'. In the absence of scattering (b=0), the propagator models light traveling in a straight line and attenuated by the absorption coefficient c(\mathbf{x}): G(s=0, \mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}, \mathbf{x}', \boldsymbol{\omega}') = \delta(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}')\delta(\boldsymbol{\omega} - \boldsymbol{\omega}') G(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}, \mathbf{x}', \boldsymbol{\omega}') = \delta(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\omega}s - \mathbf{x}')\delta(\boldsymbol{\omega} - \boldsymbol{\omega}') \exp\left(-\int0^s c(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\omega}(s-s')) ds'\right). Complexity: The RTE is an integro-differential equation. It has no general analytical solution for arbitrary media. Performance: Approximations are required for interactive rates. The primary approximation is exploiting low albedo (e.g., in smoke) to simplify or eliminate scattering terms. Scaling: Computation scales with the number of scattering events and the complexity of the phase function. High-order similarity relations can reduce the number of scattering events required. Strengths: Physically accurate modeling of light transport in participating media, handling arbitrary absorption, emission, and scattering. Limitations: Neglects wave effects (diffraction, interference). Computationally expensive for multiple scattering. The Radiative Transfer Equation was defined in its modern form by Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar in the book Radiative Transfer, published in 1950. In computer graphics, the equation of transfer for light was introduced by Kajiya in 1986. Other early models include the emission-absorption model by Hege (1993) and the density-emitter model by Sabella (1988). It is the basis for all volume rendering methods involving participating media. name: Standard volume rendering equation
head: Volume Rendering Formula, Volumetric Rendering Formula, Volumetric Rendering Equation, Volumetric Rendering Integral, Volume Rendering Integral (VRI)
body: The Standard volume rendering equation computes the final pixel color by integrating emitted and scattered light along a camera ray passing through a participating medium, attenuated by extinction. It solves the problem of visualizing volumetric data (such as smoke, clouds, or neural radiance fields) by combining the background light transmitted through the volume with the light emitted or scattered by the volume itself. It differs from the Green's Propagator for Participating Media by solving the integral directly along rays rather than using Green's functions, and from the Volume Rendering Equation by focusing on the discrete quadrature approximation for neural and voxel-based representations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, bounded by near plane tn and far plane tf. A volume representation providing density \sigma(\mathbf{x}) and color/radiance \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) at any 3D position \mathbf{x}. A background color \mathbf{C}{bg}. Output: The final pixel color \mathbf{C}. Data Structures: Ray: Parametric line \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} for t \in [tn, tf]. Samples: A sequence of N points \{si\}{i=1}^N along the ray, where si = \mathbf{r}(ti). The distance between adjacent samples is \deltai = \|si - s{i-1}\|. In uniform sampling, \deltai is constant. Formulas: The continuous volume rendering equation is: \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigma(\mathbf{r}(t)) \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}(t), \mathbf{d}) \, dt + \mathbf{C}{bg} T(tf) where: T(t) = \exp\left(-\int{tn}^t \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s)) \, ds\right) is the transmittance from the near plane to t. \sigma(\mathbf{x}) is the volume density (extinction coefficient). \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) is the emitted radiance or color. The discrete approximation (Max's quadrature) sums contributions from N samples: \mathbf{C} = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i + \mathbf{C}{bg} T{N+1} where: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) is the opacity of sample i. Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the accumulated transmittance to sample i. T{N+1} = \prod{j=1}^{N} (1 - \alphaj) is the transmittance through the entire volume. \mathbf{c}i = \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}(ti), \mathbf{d}) is the color at sample i. Parameters: N: Number of samples per ray. Typical values range from 64 to 128 for coarse/fine sampling in NeRF. \sigmai: Volume density. Units are inverse length (e.g., m^{-1}). \mathbf{c}i: Color/Radiance. Typically RGB. Steps: 1. Define the ray \mathbf{r}(t) from camera origin \mathbf{o} through pixel center with direction \mathbf{d}, bounded by tn and tf. 2. Sample N positions ti along the ray, typically equidistantly. 3. For each sample i: a. Query density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i at position \mathbf{r}(ti). b. Compute opacity \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai). c. Compute transmittance Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj). 4. Accumulate color: \mathbf{C} = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i. 5. Compute final transmittance T{final} = \prod{j=1}^N (1 - \alphaj). 6. Composite with background: \mathbf{C}{final} = \mathbf{C} + \mathbf{C}{bg} T{final}. Pseudocode: def standardvolumerendering(rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, numsamples, backgroundcolor, volumequery): """ rayorigin: vec3 raydirection: vec3 (normalized) tnear: float tfar: float numsamples: int backgroundcolor: vec3 volumequery: function(x, d) -> (sigma, color) """ # Initialize accumulators accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 # Sample points along the ray # Using uniform spacing for simplicity stepsize = (tfar - tnear) / numsamples for i in range(numsamples): # Calculate sample position t = tnear + (i + 0.5) stepsize # Midpoint sampling position = [rayorigin[j] + raydirection[j] t for j in range(3)] # Query volume for density and color sigma, color = volumequery(position, raydirection) # Compute opacity for this segment # alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma delta) alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma stepsize) # Accumulate color contribution # weight = transmittancetosample alpha for j in range(3): accumulatedcolor[j] += accumulatedtransmittance alpha color[j] # Update transmittance for next sample # Tnext = Tcurrent (1 - alpha) accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - alpha) # Early exit if fully opaque (optional optimization) if accumulatedtransmittance < 1e-4: break # Composite with background finalcolor = [accumulatedcolor[j] + backgroundcolor[j] accumulatedtransmittance for j in range(3)] return finalcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: If density \sigma is very large, \alpha approaches 1, and transmittance approaches 0. Floating-point underflow in transmittance calculation can cause artifacts if not handled. Boundary Conditions: Boundary conditions require correct intersection testing with volume bounds; if bounds are invalid or the ray misses, the accumulation loop is skipped and the background color is returned directly. Degenerate Input: Zero density results in no contribution and full transmittance. The NeRF Rendering Formula transforms raw neural network predictions (density and color features) into final RGB, depth, and accumulation maps by discretizing the volume rendering integral along camera rays. It differs from generic volume rendering by explicitly handling sigmoid color activation, density noise injection for regularization, and the specific discrete weighting scheme required for differentiable training of implicit representations. It is chosen when training neural radiance fields or other differentiable implicit scene representations. Discrete Volume Transmittance Integration computes the fraction of light that survives extinction along a ray segment in a participating medium by numerically integrating the extinction coefficient. It sets itself apart from analytic methods (like Analytic Transmittance Integration) by using fixed-step sampling to approximate the integral, making it suitable for heterogeneous media where closed-form solutions are unavailable. It is chosen when transmittance must be computed for media with spatially varying density. Sub-interval RTE Combination is a method for computing full-interval radiance and optical depth by partitioning the integration path of the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) at an intermediate point, allowing solutions from multiple slice planes to be combined. It solves the problem of visualizing participating media (such as smoke and fire) by rendering one partially transparent slice at a time and merging them using video hardware, rather than integrating over the entire volume in a single pass. It differs from Standard volume rendering equation by processing data in discrete 2D slices rather than a continuous ray integral, and from Discrete Volume Transmittance Integration by relying on hardware compositing of pre-solved slice radiance rather than per-sample accumulation. It is chosen for slice-based rendering pipelines. Volume Integral Attenuation is a method for computing cumulative attenuated information along a ray in participating media, accounting for light angle and density decay. It differs from the standard volume rendering equation by explicitly integrating the product of incident light, density, and an exponential attenuation term over the ray parameter, rather than accumulating discrete sample contributions with pre-computed transmittance. It is distinct from NeRF Rendering Formula [1362-nerf-rendering-formula.md] which uses neural networks for density, and Discrete Volume Transmittance Integration [3905-discrete-volume-transmittance-integration.md] which focuses on the transmittance calculation itself. It is chosen when light angle and density decay are the primary factors. Distance sampling is a Monte Carlo technique used to estimate the Volume Rendering Equation (VRE) by importance sampling the non-recursive terms, specifically the medium extinction transmittance, to determine the free flight distance (distance to the next collision). It is a stochastic integrator that distributes samples according to transmittance along the current path segment, ignoring the overall shape of the medium. Unlike Whole Volume Distance Sampling, which accounts for medium geometry via histograms, distance sampling assumes a homogeneous medium where the extinction coefficient is constant, making it simpler but less accurate for complex occluders. It is chosen for homogeneous media or when variance reduction is needed. Computes ray color using a transmittance formulation where opacity is treated as absolute and ray-independent, clipped to a maximum value of 1. The transmittance is defined as Ti = \min \left\{ 1, \sum{j=1}^{i-1} \exp(-\deltai \sigmai) \right\} and color as \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N (Ti - T{i+1}) \mathbf{c}i. On 8 synthetic NeRF scenes at fixed resolution 256^3 with RMSProp optimizer, it achieves a mean PSNR of 26.05, SSIM of 0.893, and LPIPS of 0.160. In this formula, \alphai depends only on the opacity and sampling distance of sample i, whereas the Max formula makes it dependent on all preceding samples. Uses opacities in the radiative transfer equation to compute physical quantities (mass, momentum, kinetic energy) by measuring optical depth instead of intensity. Opacities are defined as \alphaM = \rho (mass), \alphaP = \rho v (momentum), \alphaE = 0.5 \rho v^2 (kinetic energy), where \rho is gas density and v is velocity. Useful when outflows are misaligned with grid axes, making direct measurement from simulation data difficult. A path integral formulation of the VRE where the measurement contribution function f(X) includes transmittance T and phase function \rhom for volume interactions, unlike the vacuum rendering equation which uses BRDF. The functions G (geometry), Le (emission), and \rhom (phase function) must differentiate between points on a surface (reducing to rendering equation) and points in the medium (applying transmission coefficients). A volumetric rendering equation describing radiative transfer in discrete random media, extending the conventional VRE to support spatially-varying particle size distributions (PSD) and multi-scale optical properties. Time Complexity: O(N) per ray, where N is the number of samples. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray if density/color are queried on the fly, or O(V) if pre-sampled. Measured Performance: In NeRF, with 64 coarse and 128 fine samples, rendering time is significant but manageable for offline training. Neural Volumes achieves mean PSNR 26.05 on synthetic scenes. Scaling: Linear with number of samples and pixels. Strengths: Simple to implement, differentiable (enabling neural network training), handles arbitrary density fields. Limitations: Slow for high-resolution volumes without acceleration structures, assumes no complex light transport (in-scattering) in basic form. When to use: Neural radiance fields, simple volumetric visualization, differentiable rendering. When not to use: Real-time rendering of complex participating media with multiple scattering, where path tracing or precomputed methods are preferred. The standard volume rendering equation is derived from the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE). It was formalized by Max in 1995 for discrete quadrature approximation. It became foundational for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020. The equation represents the integral solution to the RTE, describing radiance accumulation along a ray.
