name: NeRF Rendering Formula
head: Discrete Volumetric Rendering Equation, NeRF-style Volume Rendering, Radiance Field Rendering Formula, Standard Volumetric Rendering, Volume Rendering (NeRF-style), Volumetric RGB Rendering
body: The NeRF Rendering Formula is a discrete approximation of the volume rendering equation used to composite raw neural network predictions (color and density/opacity) into final pixel colors, depths, and accumulation maps. It differs from the continuous Standard volume rendering equation by operating on a fixed set of discrete sample points along a ray, assuming single-path light transport without explicit path tracing. It is the core reconstruction function for NeRFs and 3D Gaussian Splats, enabling differentiable rendering of implicit or explicit radiance fields. Inputs: rayso: Ray origins, shape (bs, 3). raysd: Ray directions, shape (bs, 3). zvals: Sample depths along the ray, shape (bs, K) where K is the number of samples per ray. implicitfn: A function (e.g., MLP or Gaussian field) that takes 3D positions and returns raw density \sigma{\text{raw}} and color features f. whitebkgd: Boolean flag to composite onto a white background. rawnoisestd: Standard deviation for noise added to density during training. backgroundcolor: Can be 'random', 'lastsample', 'black', 'white', or a Tensor of shape (3) or (bs, 3), default 'random'. Outputs: rgbmap: Composite RGB color, shape (bs, 3). depthmap: Expected depth, shape (bs,). accmap: Accumulated opacity, shape (bs,). Data Structures: raw: Tensor of shape (bs, K, 4) containing concatenated color features and density predictions from implicitfn. alpha: Tensor of shape (bs, K) containing computed opacity values. transmittance: Tensor of shape (bs, K) containing cumulative transmittance. weights: Tensor of shape (bs, K) containing the final rendering weights. Steps: 1. Sample and Predict: For each ray, sample K 3D positions xi along the ray using zvals and ray parameters. Pass xi through implicitfn to get raw density \sigma{\text{raw}} and color features f. \text{raw} = \text{implicit\fn}(x) \quad \text{shape: } (bs, K, 4) The first 3 channels are color features, the 4th is raw density. 2. Compute Raw Color: Apply sigmoid activation to the color features to bound them to [0, 1]. ci = \sigma(\text{raw}{i,:,:3}) 3. Compute Raw Density with Noise (Training Only): If rawnoisestd > 0, add Gaussian noise to the raw density to prevent overfitting to sparse samples. \sigma{\text{noisy}} = \text{relu}(\text{raw}{i,:, 3} + \mathcal{N}(0, \text{raw\noise\std})) If rawnoisestd is 0 or during inference, \sigma{\text{noisy}} = \text{relu}(\text{raw}{i,:, 3}). 4. Compute Segment Distances: Calculate the distance between adjacent samples. \text{dists}i = z{i, j+1} - z{i, j} \quad \text{for } j = 0 \dots K-2 Append a large value (10^{10}) for the last segment to approximate the infinite tail. \text{dists}i = \text{concat}(\text{dists}i, 10^{10}) Convert to real-world distance by multiplying by the norm of the ray direction (if directions are not unit length). \Delta ti = \text{dists}i \cdot \| \text{rays\d}i \| 5. Compute Opacity (\alpha): Convert density and segment length to opacity using the exponential attenuation model. \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigma{\text{noisy}, i} \cdot \Delta ti) Values are constrained between 0 and 1. 6. Compute Transmittance (T): Compute cumulative transmittance using exclusive cumulative product. Ti = \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) Implementation detail: Use cumprod on (1 - \alpha) with a small epsilon (10^{-10}) added for numerical stability, shifted to be exclusive. \text{ones} = \text{ones\like}(\alpha[:,:1]) T = \text{cumprod}(\text{concat}(\text{ones}, 1 - \alpha + 10^{-10}), \text{axis}=-1)[:,:-1] 7. Compute Weights (w): The weight for each sample is the product of transmittance and the opacity of the current sample. wi = Ti \cdot \alphai Alternatively expressed as w = T \cdot (1 - \exp(-\sigma \cdot \Delta t)). 8. Aggregate Outputs: Compute the final pixel color, depth, and accumulation map using the weights. \text{rgb\map} = \sum{i=0}^{K-1} wi \cdot ci \text{depth\map} = \sum{i=0}^{K-1} wi \cdot zi \text{acc\map} = \sum{i=0}^{K-1} wi 9. Background Composite (Optional): If whitebkgd is True, composite the result onto a white background using the accumulated opacity. \text{rgb\map} = \text{rgb\map} + (1 - \text{acc\map}) For packed samples (when rayindices is not None), use accumulatealongrays for comprgb and accumulatedweight. Raise NotImplementedError if backgroundcolor is 'lastsample' for packed samples. Check for global BACKGROUNDCOLOROVERRIDE and use it if set. Compute final RGB: \text{comp\rgb} + \text{background\color} \cdot (1.0 - \text{accumulated\weight}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def nerfrenderingformula(rayso, raysd, zvals, implicitfn, whitebkgd=False, rawnoisestd=0.0): """ rayso: (N, 3) ray origins raysd: (N, 3) ray directions zvals: (N, K) sample depths along rays implicitfn: callable returning (colorfeatures, density) for 3D points """ # 1. Compute 3D positions from ray origins, directions, and depths # x shape: (N, K, 3) x = rayso[:, None,:] + zvals[:,:, None] raysd[:, None,:] # 2. Predict raw density and color features # raw shape: (N, K, 4) raw = implicitfn(x) # 3. Compute Color via sigmoid rgb = torch.sigmoid(raw[...,:3]) # (N, K, 3) # 4. Compute Density with optional noise rawdensity = raw[..., 3] if rawnoisestd > 0: noise = torch.randnlike(rawdensity) rawnoisestd rawdensity = rawdensity + noise sigma = F.relu(rawdensity) # (N, K) # 5. Compute Distances between adjacent samples dists = zvals[:, 1:] - zvals[:,:-1] # (N, K-1) dists = torch.cat([dists, torch.oneslike(dists[:,:1]) 1e10], dim=-1) # (N, K) # Convert to real-world distance using ray direction norm dists = dists torch.norm(raysd, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # (N, K) # 6. Compute Alpha (opacity) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma dists) # (N, K) # 7. Compute Transmittance (exclusive cumprod) ones = torch.oneslike(alpha[:,:1]) transmittance = torch.cumprod(torch.cat([ones, 1.0 - alpha + 1e-10], dim=-1), dim=-1)[:,:-1] # (N, K) # 8. Compute Weights weights = alpha transmittance # (N, K) # 9. Aggregate outputs rgbmap = torch.sum(weights[..., None] rgb, dim=-2) # (N, 3) depthmap = torch.sum(weights zvals, dim=-1) # (N,) accmap = torch.sum(weights, dim=-1) # (N,) # 10. Background Composite if whitebkgd: rgbmap = rgbmap + (1.0 - accmap[..., None]) return rgbmap, depthmap, accmap Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Stability: When \alphai \approx 1, transmittance becomes 0, effectively switching off contributions from subsequent pixels. Adding epsilon (10^{-10}) to (1-\alpha) prevents cumprod from becoming exactly 0 too early due to floating-point errors, ensuring stable gradients. Opaque Surfaces: Once an opaque surface is encountered (\alphai \approx 1), Ti for subsequent samples becomes 0, effectively switching off contributions from behind the surface. Density Bounds: Raw density is passed through relu to ensure non-negative values, as negative density is physically invalid and breaks the exponential attenuation model. Infinite Distance: The last segment distance is set to a large value (10^{10}) to approximate the infinite tail of the ray, ensuring that if the last sample has non-zero density, it contributes to the final color. Packed Samples: The 'lastsample' background color mode is not implemented for packed samples (when rayindices is not None). A post-processing rendering technique for neural radiance fields that applies depth-of-field blur. name: Discrete Volume Transmittance Integration
head: Transmittance Calculation, Transmittance Integration, Visibility function, Volume Rendering Integral (Transmittance), getTransmittance, step-wise optical depth, tau integration
body: Discrete Volume Transmittance Integration computes the fraction of light that travels from a ray origin to a target point through a participating medium without being absorbed or scattered, by numerically integrating the extinction coefficient along the ray path. It solves the problem of determining visibility or attenuation in heterogeneous media where the density varies spatially, which cannot be solved analytically using the simple Beer-Lambert law. It sets itself apart from Analytic Transmittance Integration by using fixed-step numerical summation rather than closed-form solutions, and from Unbiased Line Integration by introducing bias through discretization to gain computational simplicity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized), start distance t{start}, end distance t{end}, extinction coefficient field \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) (or density \rho(\mathbf{x}) scaled by extinction cross-section), and number of integration steps N. Output: Transmittance T, a scalar value in [0, 1] representing the ratio of transmitted light. Data Structures: Extinction Field: A 3D grid or texture storing \sigmat or \rho at voxel centers. Access is typically trilinear or nearest-neighbor interpolated. Accumulator: A floating-point variable tau initialized to 0.0, storing the cumulative optical depth. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Validation: If the ray direction \mathbf{d} has zero length, return T=0 or handle as invalid. 2. Bounds Intersection: Calculate the intersection interval [t0, t1] of the ray with the volume's bounding box (e.g., AABB). If no intersection, return T=1 (fully transparent) or 0 depending on convention (usually 1 for empty space, but some implementations return 0 if the volume is strictly defined within bounds and the ray misses). Note: Source states "returns 0 transmittance" if no intersection, implying the volume is opaque or the function assumes the ray must hit the volume to compute valid transmittance within it. However, physically, missing the volume means no attenuation, so T=1. We follow the source's explicit pitfall note but note the physical contradiction.. 3. Step Size Calculation: Compute the step size \Delta t = (t1 - t0) / N. Some implementations apply an offset to t0 to align samples with the grid. 4. Initialization: Set tau = 0.0. 5. Integration Loop: For i from 0 to N-1: a. Calculate sample position: \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{o} + (\mathbf{o} + \mathbf{d} \cdot (t0 + i \cdot \Delta t)) \cdot \mathbf{d}? No, simpler: \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{o} + \mathbf{d} \cdot (t0 + i \cdot \Delta t). b. Sample the extinction coefficient: \sigmai = \sigmat(\mathbf{p}i). c. Update optical depth: tau += \sigmai \cdot \Delta t. 6. Exponentiation: Compute transmittance T = \exp(-\text{tau}). Formulas: The optical depth \tau is approximated by the Riemann sum: \tau \approx \Delta t \sum{i=0}^{N-1} \sigmat(\mathbf{p}i) The transmittance is: T = e^{-\tau} Where: \sigmat(\mathbf{p}i) is the extinction coefficient at sample point \mathbf{p}i. \Delta t is the step length along the ray. N is the number of steps. Parameters: StEPS (N): The number of integration steps. A typical value is 16. Higher values increase accuracy but cost more. Step Size: The distance between samples. In some implementations, this is a fixed global gStepSize multiplied by a factor (e.g., 2). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Ray Direction: If \|\mathbf{d}\| = 0, the function should return immediately to avoid division by zero or invalid sampling. No Intersection: If the ray does not intersect the volume bounds, behavior varies. Source states it returns 0 transmittance, which physically implies the volume is opaque or the function is strictly for computing attenuation within a hit volume. Physically, missing the volume should yield T=1. Precision: For large optical depths, tau can become very large, causing T to underflow to 0. Early termination can be used if tau exceeds a threshold (e.g., 10.0). Heterogeneous vs Homogeneous: Using the homogeneous Beer-Lambert law Ly = Lx e^{-\mu |x-y|} for heterogeneous media is incorrect because it fails to account for cumulative attenuation variations along the path. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computetransmittance(rayorigin, raydirection, volumebounds, extinctionfield, numsteps): """ Computes transmittance through a heterogeneous volume using discrete integration. Args: rayorigin (Vec3): Origin of the ray. raydirection (Vec3): Normalized direction of the ray. volumebounds (AABB): Axis-aligned bounding box of the volume. extinctionfield (Function): Function sigmat(point) returning extinction coefficient. numsteps (int): Number of integration steps (e.g., 16). Returns: float: Transmittance T in [0, 1]. """ # 1. Ray Validation if raydirection.length() == 0: return 0.0 # Or handle error # 2. Bounds Intersection tmin, tmax = volumebounds.intersect(rayorigin, raydirection) # If no intersection, return 1.0 (fully transparent) physically, # but source says return 0. We follow source for consistency with its implementation note. if tmin is None or tmax is None: return 0.0 # # 3. Step Size Calculation # Apply offset if necessary to align with grid tstart = tmin tend = tmax stepsize = (tend - tstart) / numsteps # 4. Initialization tau = 0.0 # 5. Integration Loop for i in range(numsteps): # Calculate sample position # Source uses i stepsize from p1. # Source iterates from t0 to t1. # We use the start of the interval for each step. tsample = tstart + i stepsize pos = rayorigin + raydirection tsample # Sample extinction coefficient sigmat = extinctionfield.sample(pos) # Update optical depth tau += sigmat stepsize # 6. Exponentiation transmittance = exp(-tau) return transmittance Computes transmittance between two points through a heterogeneous participating medium. It provides the geometric setup required before applying the discrete extinction summation and exponentiation logic of its parent, Discrete Volume Transmittance Integration. Analytic Transmittance Integration computes radiance along a ray with floating-point accuracy by integrating the radiative transfer equation analytically over each segment where optical properties (extinction coefficient and emission) are constant. It sets itself apart from discrete summation methods (like Iteration A or standard ray marching) by solving the integral of the transmittance term exactly, which prevents significant accuracy loss when the optical depth \tau \Delta s is large and transmittance varies significantly between samples. Unbiased Line Integration is a method for estimating the transmittance-weighted integral along a light ray in participating media, specifically designed to split primary rays and estimate contributions from both the volume and the surface boundary. It solves the problem of accurately computing the integral C defined in the radiative transfer context without the bias introduced by fixed-step ray marching. Unlike Analytic Transmittance Integration which relies on closed-form solutions, or Heterogeneous Medium Transmittance which may use different sampling strategies, this method uses transformed equidistant sampling to achieve smoothness approaching that of ray marching while remaining perfectly unbiased. Discrete Radiance Step Integration computes the outgoing radiance after traversing a small step of length ds through a participating medium with extinction coefficient \sigma and emission coefficient q, given incoming radiance I. It serves as the core update kernel for the discrete radiative transfer equation, iteratively applying the transport equation along a single ray to compute final intensity from initial intensity, absorption coefficient, and source term. It is distinct from sibling methods like Heterogeneous Medium Transmittance and Analytic Transmittance Integration by focusing on the per-step radiance update rather than just transmittance calculation, often employing a linear approximation for small optical depths to maintain precision. A technique for calculating the transmittance of a heterogeneous participating medium between an eye point and a surface intersection by discretely sampling the medium along the ray path, as an alternative to the analytical Beer-Lambert law used for homogeneous media. For homogeneous media, transmittance is calculated analytically using Ly = Lx e^{-\mu|x-y|}. For heterogeneous media, ray marching is required. Using the equation L(x, \omega) = \tau(x,y)Le(x,\omega) for heterogeneous absorption-only models is incorrect because it fails to account for the cumulative attenuation along the path, leading to incorrect images. Homogeneous media allow analytical calculation, whereas heterogeneous media require discrete ray marching. A method to compute light attenuation through a volume using a discrete sum of densities along a ray, replacing the continuous integral to account for line integrals through surfaces going to zero. It models the volume as a 'texel' model where each voxel contributes density. For each voxel, a ray is marched from the center in direction d until it leaves the volume, adding the density of each voxel hit scaled by the length of the ray that passed through it. The formula is T = e^{-r \sum{t{start}}^{t{end}} \rho (e+td)} where T is transparency, r is a constant (implied extinction coefficient), \rho is the 3D density function, e is the ray origin, d is the ray direction, and t is the parameter along the ray. The light is placed at infinity in the direction defined by vector d. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of integration steps per ray. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per ray, plus the storage for the extinction field. Measured Performance: With N=16 steps, the method is computationally inexpensive per ray but can be slow if many rays are traced through dense volumes. Performance scales linearly with N. Strengths: Simple to implement; handles heterogeneous media; robust. Limitations: Biased due to discretization; accuracy depends on N; may suffer from aliasing if N is too low. When to Use: When high performance is needed and moderate accuracy is acceptable; for heterogeneous media where analytic solutions are not feasible. When Not to Use: When unbiased results are required (use Unbiased Line Integration); when the medium is homogeneous (use Analytic Transmittance Integration or Beer-Lambert law). Discrete Volume Transmittance Integration is a fundamental technique in volume rendering, derived from the numerical integration of the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE). It is widely used in computer graphics for rendering fog, smoke, and other participating media. The method is often referred to as "ray marching" in the context of volume rendering. It is a core component of many volume rendering pipelines, including those in neural radiance fields (NeRFs). ainagutierrez01/Volumetric-Path-Tracing-, https://github.com/ainagutierrez01/Volumetric-Path-Tracing-, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) rbaravalle/webgl-volumetric, https://github.com/rbaravalle/webgl-volumetric, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) cgibson/Mr-Voxel, https://github.com/cgibson/Mr-Voxel, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Volume Rendering Integral: Definition & AI/ML Use, https://inferensys.com/glossary/neural-radiance-fields-and-spatial-computing/neural-scene-representations/volume-rendering-integral, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) How to do heterogeneous volume absorption using path tracing?, https://computergraphics.stackexchange.com/questions/5797/how-to-do-heterogeneous-volume-absorption-using-path-tracing, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF A Volumetric Approach to Rendering Microgeometry Using PRT, https://www.cs.umbc.edu/~ugrad/honors/theses/JohnKloetzli.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Heterogeneous Medium Transmittance
head: Transmittance Computation, computeTransmittance
body: Computes transmittance between two points through a heterogeneous participating medium. It provides the geometric setup required before applying the discrete extinction summation and exponentiation logic of its parent, Discrete Volume Transmittance Integration. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Start point p1, end point p2, scattering coefficient \mus, absorption coefficient \mua. Output: Transmittance T (scalar). Data Structures: Points p1, p2: 3D vectors. Coefficients \mus, \mua: Scalars. Steps: 1. Compute the direction vector: \vec{dir} = p2 - p1. 2. Compute the distance: dist = \|\vec{dir}\|. 3. Normalize the direction: \hat{dir} = \vec{dir} / dist. 4. Compute the extinction coefficient: \mut = \mus + \mua. 5. Compute the optical depth: \tau = \mut \times dist. 6. Compute transmittance: T = e^{-\tau}. Formulas: \vec{dir} = p2 - p1 dist = \|\vec{dir}\| \hat{dir} = \frac{\vec{dir}}{dist} \mut = \mus + \mua T = \exp(-\mut \cdot dist) Parameters: \mus: Scattering coefficient. \mua: Absorption coefficient. p1, p2: Endpoints of the ray segment. Edge Cases: If dist = 0, transmittance is 1.0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. It accumulates voxel contributions using the product of their individual AIV values to correctly handle positive and negative correlations between voxels, which traditional Beer-Lambert law fails to do. name: Transmittance Mapping
head: Moment-based Transmittance Approximation, Moment-based transmittance mapping, TM-n
body: Transmittance Mapping is a differentiable method for approximating volume transmittance (visibility) using bounds derived from the theory of moments. It solves the problem of computing visibility in inverse rendering tasks, such as pose recovery and 3D reconstruction, where gradients with respect to scene parameters are required. Unlike shadow mapping variants, which fail in empty space and suffer from geometric inaccuracies, Transmittance Mapping provides a principled, volume-based approximation that correctly reports constant 1 transmittance in free space while maintaining efficiency comparable to shadow mapping. It builds on Heterogeneous Medium Transmittance by providing a differentiable, moment-based approximation of the transmittance integral. Inputs: Density field \sigma(\mathbf{r}). Camera ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Light source position (point light assumed). Outputs: Approximated visibility V along the ray. Gradient of V with respect to scene parameters (e.g., pose, density). Data Structures: Transmittance Map: A 2D texture storing 2n + 1 values (moments m0, \dots, m{2n}) per pixel. The resolution determines spatial accuracy; coarse resolutions miss small structures. Parameters: Order n: Integer \ge 1 determining the number of moments (2n + 1). Higher orders increase accuracy but raise computational cost and numerical instability risks. Typical values range from 1 to 5. Density Scaling s: Controls the spread of volume density spikes, typically applied to implicit surfaces via \sigma(\mathbf{r}(t)) = \phis(g(\mathbf{r}(t))). Optimized from low to high values to balance gradient density and surface localization. Blending Parameter \beta: Scalar \in [0, 1] blending between lower and upper bounds. Steps: 1. Moment Integration: Compute moments mk = \int0^\infty z^k \sigma(\mathbf{r}(z)) \, dz for k = 0, \dots, 2n. 2. Bound Construction: Construct lower bound L(t) and upper bound U(t) for the absorbance A(t) = -\ln T(t) = \int0^t \sigma(\mathbf{r}(z)) \, dz using moment theory. 3. Transmittance Approximation: Blend the bounds to approximate transmittance: T(t) \approx \exp\left(-((1-\beta)L(t) + \beta U(t))\right). 4. Visibility Integration: Compute visibility V = \int0^\infty \sigma(\mathbf{r}(t)) T(t) \, dt. A direction-dependent normalization factor is omitted for brevity. 5. Gradient Propagation: Compute gradients of V with respect to scene parameters using automatic differentiation, leveraging the continuous differentiability of the moment bounds. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def transmittancemapping(rayorigin, raydirection, densityfield, densityscaling, ordern, lightposition, beta): """ Approximates volume transmittance and visibility using moment-based bounds. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, camera ray origin. raydirection: 3D vector, camera ray direction. densityfield: Callable, returns density sigma at 3D point. densityscaling: Float, parameter s controlling density spikes. ordern: Int, order of moment approximation (n). lightposition: 3D vector, position of the point light. beta: Float, blending parameter in [0, 1]. Returns: visibility: Float, approximated visibility V. """ # 1. Compute moments mk = integral0^inf z^k sigma(r(z)) dz # Numerical quadrature along the ray from 0 to maxdistance. maxdistance = 100.0 numsamples = 256 dz = maxdistance / numsamples moments = [0.0] (2 ordern + 1) for k in range(2 ordern + 1): integral = 0.0 for i in range(numsamples): z = (i + 0.5) dz point = rayorigin + raydirection z sigma = densityfield(point, densityscaling) integral += (z k) sigma dz moments[k] = integral # 2. Construct lower bound L(t) and upper bound U(t) for absorbance A(t). # The sources state bounds are derived from moment theory and are continuously differentiable, # but do not specify the exact polynomial root-finding or Hankel matrix solver. # Standard implementations solve the truncated moment problem to find valid bounding functions. Lt = constructlowerbound(moments, ordern) Ut = constructupperbound(moments, ordern) # 3. Evaluate transmittance approximation T(t) = exp(-((1-beta)L(t) + betaU(t))) # For visibility integration, we evaluate T(t) at quadrature points. visibilityintegral = 0.0 for i in range(numsamples): z = (i + 0.5) dz point = rayorigin + raydirection z sigma = densityfield(point, densityscaling) # Evaluate bounds at t = z Lval = Lt(z) Uval = Ut(z) # Approximate transmittance absorbanceapprox = (1.0 - beta) Lval + beta Uval Tt = math.exp(-absorbanceapprox) visibilityintegral += sigma Tt dz return visibilityintegral def constructlowerbound(moments, ordern): """Returns a callable L(t) for the lower absorbance bound.""" # Placeholder for the specific moment-problem solver. # In practice, this solves a constrained optimization or polynomial root-finding problem # to ensure L(t) <= A(t) for all t >= 0. def L(t): # Simplified linear bound for demonstration; real implementation uses moment matrices. return moments[0] t return L def constructupperbound(moments, ordern): """Returns a callable U(t) for the upper absorbance bound.""" # Placeholder for the specific moment-problem solver. # Ensures U(t) >= A(t) for all t >= 0. def U(t): # Simplified linear bound for demonstration; real implementation uses moment matrices. return moments[0] t return U Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Space: Shadow mapping fails in empty space because it is not volume-based; Transmittance Mapping correctly reports constant 1 transmittance. Numerical Instability: Higher-order moments lead to ill-conditioned matrices and difficult polynomial root finding; implementations must be designed around these constraints. Light Source Assumptions: The approach assumes point lights; area lights or image-based lighting are not supported. Resolution Dependence: If the transmittance map is too coarse, small structures are missed; memory requirements increase with resolution. Singularity Handling: Automatic differentiation implementations may generate undefined outputs and gradients if the query point is close to a singularity. Time Complexity: Equally efficient as shadow mapping, approximately 4× faster than shadow rays. Memory Complexity: Reasonable memory consumption; e.g., 10.55 GiB peak for 190x256 pixel views using 128 samples in multi-view 3D reconstruction. Memory increases with map resolution. Performance: In pose recovery tasks, TM-5 achieved a translation error (\Delta t) of 0.07 and Hausdorff distance (DH) of 0.09, compared to Tiwary et al.'s 0.50 and 0.33 respectively. In multi-view 3D reconstruction, TM-3 maintained a performance of one iteration per second. Strengths: More accurate than shadow mapping variants (Tiwary et al., VSM); handles free space correctly; differentiable; equally efficient as shadow mapping. Limitations: Numerical instability for higher orders; not supported for area lights or image-based lighting; quality depends on spatial discretization. When to Use: Differentiable shadow mapping and differentiable volumetric visibility for inverse rendering tasks like pose recovery, shadow art, and 3D reconstruction from low-density volumes. When Not to Use: When area lights or image-based lighting are required; when very high-order approximations are needed without careful numerical handling. Transmittance Mapping was introduced by Worchel and Alexa in 2025. It is based on the theory of moments, citing classical work in real-time graphics and moment shadow mapping. The method was developed to address the inaccuracies of shadow mapping in inverse rendering, particularly in pose recovery and 3D reconstruction tasks. It builds on previous work in differentiable volume rendering and shadow mapping. name: Analytic Transmittance Integration
head: Analytic segment integration, Exact segment integration, Iteration B
body: Analytic Transmittance Integration computes radiance along a ray with floating-point accuracy by integrating the radiative transfer equation analytically over each segment where optical properties (extinction coefficient and emission) are constant. It sets itself apart from discrete summation methods (like Iteration A or standard ray marching) by solving the integral of the transmittance term exactly, which prevents significant accuracy loss when the optical depth \tau \Delta s is large and transmittance varies significantly between samples. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An array of n segments along a ray. For each segment i (0 \le i < n), the inputs are the extinction coefficient \taui, the emission coefficient ci, and the geometric length \Delta si. A boundary term B (transmitted radiance from behind the volume) is also required. Output: The accumulated radiance E at the near end of the ray. Data Structures: Arrays tau, c, DeltaS of size n, containing floating-point values for extinction, emission, and segment length respectively. Scalar B for background radiance. Scalars E (accumulator) and T (current transmittance). Steps: 1. Initialize the accumulated radiance E = 0 and the current transmittance T = 1. 2. Iterate through each segment i from 0 to n-1: a. Compute the transmittance factor for the current segment: F = \exp(-\taui \Delta si). b. Update the accumulated radiance: E = E + T \cdot ci \cdot (1 - F). c. Update the current transmittance: T = T \cdot F. 3. After the loop, add the contribution from the background: E = E + T \cdot B. Derivation: The method solves the integral for a single segment [si, s{i+1}] with constant \taui and ci. The contribution to radiance is: \int{si}^{s{i+1}} T(si) \taui ci \exp(-\taui(s-si)) ds where T(si) is the transmittance entering the segment. Evaluating the integral: T(si) \taui ci \left[ \frac{\exp(-\taui(s-si))}{-\taui} \right]{si}^{s{i+1}} = T(si) ci (1 - \exp(-\taui \Delta si)) This matches the update step E = E + T \cdot ci \cdot (1 - F) where F = \exp(-\taui \Delta si). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def analytictransmittanceintegration(tau, c, deltas, B): n = len(tau) E = 0.0 T = 1.0 for i in range(n): F = math.exp(-tau[i] deltas[i]) E = E + T c[i] (1.0 - F) T = T F E = E + T B return E Parameters: \taui: Extinction coefficient. Must be non-negative. ci: Emission coefficient. \Delta si: Geometric length of the segment. B: Background radiance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If \taui \Delta si is large, discrete summation (Iteration A) suffers from precision loss or underestimation because T varies significantly. If \taui = 0, F = 1, and the term (1-F) becomes 0, correctly contributing no emission from that segment. For very small \taui \Delta si, standard floating point is sufficient. The method assumes \Delta si is pre-computed correctly for the ray traversal; it does not handle ray geometry or cell boundaries itself. Exactly integrates unoccluded single-scattering radiance in rectilinear box-shaped media with homogeneous density. It decomposes the intersection into trapezoid segments for closed-form evaluation. Computes transmittance integrals in skewed coordinate systems where geometric path length varies non-linearly, handling box face intersections efficiently. Uses analytical integration of density functions (e.g., exponential) for quasi-heterogeneous media, enabling real-time performance by rescaling distances. Accuracy: Higher than discrete Riemann sum methods (Iteration A) when \tau \Delta s is large, as it avoids the error introduced by assuming constant transmittance over the segment. Complexity: O(n) where n is the number of segments. Each step involves one exponential, one multiplication, and a few additions. Memory: O(1) auxiliary space if processing segments sequentially, or O(n) if storing segment parameters. Strengths: Floating-point accuracy for radiance accumulation; handles high optical depth segments without bias. Limitations: Requires segments to have constant optical properties. If properties vary within a segment, the segment must be subdivided. The method is described as "Iteration B" in contrast to "Iteration A" (Riemann sum approximation) in the context of volume rendering integrals. It addresses the inaccuracy of discrete sampling when transmittance varies significantly between samples. name: Trapezoid-based Radiance Integration in Box Coordinates
head: Analytic Integration, Analytic Integration of Unoccluded Single Scattering in Box-Shaped Medium, Integration of Unoccluded Radiance, Trapezoid Segment Integration, Unoccluded Single Scattering Integration
body: This method computes the exact integral of unoccluded single-scattering radiance for a homogeneous medium confined within a rectilinear box, using directional or collimated light. It differs from standard ray marching by decomposing the light-view plane intersection with the box into trapezoid segments, allowing the transmittance integral to be solved analytically in a single pass per segment. Unlike Analytic Transmittance Integration which handles general analytic forms, this method specifically exploits the linear geometry of box faces and the collimated nature of the light to reduce the integration domain to a skewed 2D plane. Inputs: Camera origin \mathbf{p}o and direction \omegao. Light origin \mathbf{p}{light} and direction \omegai (collimated/directional). Box geometry defined by transformation matrix B{3\times4} (orientation, scale, translation) and bounds [-1, 1]^3 in box coordinates. Extinction coefficient \sigmat (constant within the box). Emitted radiance Li from the light source. Outputs: Integrated unoccluded radiance contribution. Data Structures: Box Coordinates: A 3D space where the box is axis-aligned with bounds [-1, 1]. Skewed Coordinate System: Defined by axes corresponding to the camera ray direction and light ray direction, with the origin at the camera position. Algorithm Steps: 1. Coordinate Transformation: Transform the camera origin, light origin, and light direction into box coordinates using B{3\times4}. Camera origin in box coords: \tilde{\mathbf{p}}o = B{3\times4} [\mathbf{p}o, 1]^T. Light direction in box coords (non-normalized): \tilde{\omega}i = B{3\times4} [\omegai, 0]^T. Camera direction in box coords: \tilde{\omega}o = B{3\times4} [\omegao, 0]^T. 2. Intersection and Bounds: If the camera origin \tilde{\mathbf{p}}o is outside the box, move it to the first intersection point with the box, or assign 0 contribution if the ray does not intersect. Compute the light ray exit point \tilde{\mathbf{p}}L and distance dL: dL = \text{IntersectBox}(\tilde{\mathbf{p}}o, \tilde{\omega}i) \tilde{\mathbf{p}}L = \tilde{\mathbf{p}}o + dL \tilde{\omega}i \quad \text{} Compute the camera ray exit point \tilde{\mathbf{p}}C and distance tC: tC = \text{IntersectBox}(\tilde{\mathbf{p}}o, -\tilde{\omega}o) \tilde{\mathbf{p}}C = \tilde{\mathbf{p}}o - tC \tilde{\omega}o \quad \text{} If the camera ray does not intersect the box, return 0. 3. Face Vector Computation: Compute face vectors perpendicular to the box axes (x, y, z) and the light-view plane. These vectors define the traversal directions along the box edges. Determine the direction of progress towards the camera ray exit point \tilde{\mathbf{p}}C. If the light plane is parallel to the camera ray direction, skip traversal and compute the integral directly. If the vector connecting points is parallel to the light plane (|v| < \epsilon), select the direction along the camera ray instead of the face vector. The final face vector q is determined by multiplying the progress direction value v by the candidate vector a (q = v a). 4. Trapezoid Segment Integration Loop: Iterate up to 3 times (maximum number of edges in a box section). In each iteration k: a. Find Next Corner: Calculate progress along the current edge. Clamp progress to prevent overstepping the camera ray exit point: t{cut} = \min(1, g{progress}(\tilde{\mathbf{p}}C - \tilde{\mathbf{p}}, \tilde{\mathbf{w}})) where \tilde{\mathbf{p}} is the current position and \tilde{\mathbf{w}} is the current traversal direction. Compute the end point on the edge: \tilde{\mathbf{p}}{edge} = \tilde{\mathbf{p}} + t{cut} \tilde{\mathbf{w}} b. Compute Segment Geometry: Compute the projected distance along the camera ray for the edge end point: t{C,E} = g{progress}(\tilde{\mathbf{p}}{edge} - \tilde{\mathbf{p}}o, -\tilde{\omega}o) Compute the final point on the camera ray: \tilde{\mathbf{p}}{cam} \leftarrow \tilde{\mathbf{p}}o - t{C,E} \tilde{\omega}o Compute the distance from the camera ray to the edge: d{E,E} \leftarrow (\tilde{\mathbf{p}}{edge} - \tilde{\mathbf{p}}{cam}) \cdot \tilde{\omega}{i,s2} where \tilde{\omega}{i,s2} is the corrected incident light vector. Let t{C,S} and d{E,S} be the camera ray distance and edge distance at the start of the segment. c. Analytic Integration: Compute the trapezoid domain slope: c = 1 + \frac{d{E,E} - d{E,S}}{t{C,E} - t{C,S}} Compute the integral over transmittance for this trapezoid segment: \mathcal{I}{\text{trapezoid}} = e^{-(t{C,S}+d{E,S})\sigmat} (1 - e^{-\sigmat (t{C,E}-t{C,S})^c}) This can be expressed as EI (1 - Eu) where EI is the initial transmittance and Eu is the untransmitted portion. d. Accumulate: Add \mathcal{I}{\text{trapezoid}} to the total transmittance integral T{total}. 5. Final Result: The total integral is the sum of all segment integrals: T{total} = \sum{k=1}^{3} \mathcal{T}k The final radiance is Li \cdot T{total} (assuming uniform emitted radiance Li). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trapezoidintegration(po, wo, plight, wi, B3x4, sigmat, Li): # 1. Transform to box coordinates pobox = transformpoint(B3x4, po) wibox = transformvector(B3x4, wi) wobox = transformvector(B3x4, wo) # 2. Intersect with box # IntersectBox returns distance to intersection along ray # If no intersection, return 0 if not rayintersectsbox(pobox, wobox): return 0.0 # Move camera origin to first intersection if outside if not pointinbox(pobox): dist = intersectboxdistance(pobox, wobox) pobox = pobox + dist wobox # Light ray exit dL = intersectboxdistance(pobox, wibox) pL = pobox + dL wibox # Camera ray exit tC = intersectboxdistance(pobox, -wobox) pC = pobox - tC wobox # 3. Compute face vectors # Determine traversal directions based on progress towards pC # Handle parallel cases if isparallel(wibox, wobox): # Direct computation, skip loop return directintegral(pobox, pL, pC, sigmat) facevectors = computefacevectors(pobox, pC, wibox, wobox) # 4. Iterate up to 3 times totaltransmittance = 0.0 currentpos = pL # Start from light entry/exit depending on traversal direction # Note: The algorithm traverses the boundary outline of the light-view plane intersection # The starting point is determined by the intersection of the light ray with the box for k in range(3): # Find next corner # Determine which face vector to follow w = selectfacevector(currentpos, facevectors, pC) # Calculate progress to cut at camera ray exit # gprogress computes the parameter along the vector w to reach pC # This is a simplified representation of the geometric projection tcut = min(1.0, computeprogresstotarget(currentpos, w, pC)) pedge = currentpos + tcut w # Project edge point onto camera ray to get tC,E # gprogress(pobox, -wobox) gives distance along camera ray tCE = computeprogress(pedge - pobox, -wobox) # Point on camera ray pcam = pobox - tCE wobox # Distance from camera ray to edge # Corrected incident light vector needed here wis2 = correctlightvector(wibox, wobox) dEE = dot(pedge - pcam, wis2) # Previous segment values (tCS, dES) # For the first segment, these are derived from pL and pobox geometry # For subsequent segments, they are the current tCE and dEE if k == 0: tCS = computeprogress(pL - pobox, -wobox) dES = computedistancetocameraray(pL, pobox, wobox, wis2) else: tCS = tCEprev dES = dEEprev # Compute slope deltat = tCE - tCS if abs(deltat) < epsilon: deltat = epsilon # Guard against division by zero c = 1.0 + (dEE - dES) / deltat # Analytic integral # EI = exp(-(tCS + dES) sigmat) # Eu = exp(-sigmat (tCE - tCS)^c) # Itrapezoid = EI (1 - Eu) exponentterm = (tCS + dES) sigmat EI = exp(-exponentterm) difft = tCE - tCS exponentu = sigmat (difft c) Eu = exp(-exponentu) Itrapezoid = EI (1.0 - Eu) totaltransmittance += Itrapezoid # Update previous values for next iteration tCEprev = tCE dEEprev = dEE # Update current position for next corner currentpos = pedge return Li totaltransmittance Discretizes radiance and extinction individually to derive an analytic form, improving accuracy over Newton-Cotes rules for dense volumes with high extinction. Time Complexity: Constant time relative to the number of samples, as it requires only a single sample in unoccluded areas to compute the whole integral solution. The loop runs a maximum of 3 times regardless of resolution. Memory Complexity: Low, requiring storage for a few scalar values and vectors per ray. Strengths: Provides exact integration for unoccluded single scattering in box-shaped media, reducing variance compared to ray marching. It is efficient for real-time applications. Limitations: Restricted to rectilinear box-shaped media and collimated/directional light sources. Does not handle occlusion directly; requires a ratio estimator or other technique for visibility. When to use: Real-time rendering of homogeneous volumetric light scattering in box-constrained environments (e.g., indoor scenes, room-scale experiences). When not to use: Non-box geometries, non-collimated lights, or when occlusion is the primary concern without a complementary visibility estimator. This method was introduced by Zdravko Velinov and Kenny Mitchell from Disney Research Los Angeles. It is part of a set of algorithms for efficiently computing single scattering by box-constrained media, applicable to real-time volumetric lighting. The work extends to multiple scattering and convex media, and includes importance sampling schemes for Monte Carlo integration. name: Analytic Quadrature for Volume Radiance Integration
head: Analytic integration for volume slices, Proposed quadrature method
body: This method discretizes radiance L(s) and extinction \bar{\sigma}t(s) individually to derive an analytic form for the integrated radiance, improving accuracy over standard Newton-Cotes rules (which approximate the product Tr(s)L(s)) and speed over Simpson's rule, particularly for dense volumes with high extinction. Inputs: N: Number of intervals (slices) along the ray. sk: Position of the k-th sample point, for k=0 \dots N. L(sk): Radiance at position sk. \bar{\sigma}t(sk): Extinction coefficient at position sk. \deltak: Length of interval k, defined as |s{k+1} - sk|. Typically uniform (\deltak = \delta). Outputs: L(xi, \omegao): Total integrated radiance at point xi in direction \omegao. Data Structures: Arrays for L, \bar{\sigma}t, and positions s, indexed 0 \dots N. Scalar \delta for uniform interval length. Steps: 1. Compute Average Extinction: For each interval k \in [0, N-1], calculate the average extinction coefficient \bar{\sigma}{t,k} using the arithmetic mean of the endpoints: \bar{\sigma}{t,k} = \frac{1}{2} (\bar{\sigma}t(sk) + \bar{\sigma}t(s{k+1})) The extinction coefficient is assumed piecewise constant within the interval to avoid complex error functions of complex numbers, improving computational speed. 2. Compute Interval Radiance Contribution: For each interval k, calculate the integrated radiance contribution \bar{L}(k) using the analytic formula derived from piecewise linear radiance and piecewise constant extinction: \bar{L}(k) = \frac{2L(sk)}{\bar{\sigma}{t,k}\deltak} \left( e^{-\bar{\sigma}{t,k}\deltak} - 1 \right) + \frac{2L(s{k+1})}{\bar{\sigma}{t,k}\deltak} \left( e^{\bar{\sigma}{t,k}\deltak} - 1 \right) e^{-\bar{\sigma}{t,k}\deltak} Note: If \bar{\sigma}{t,k} \to 0, this formula approaches the trapezoid rule result. Implementation should handle the limit or use a small epsilon guard. 3. Compute Cumulative Throughput: Calculate the cumulative transmittance Tr(k) up to the start of interval k. For k=0, Tr(0) = 1. For k > 0, Tr(k) = \prod{l=0}^{k-1} e^{-\bar{\sigma}{t,l}\deltal}. This is computed iteratively as Tr(k) = Tr(k-1) \cdot e^{-\bar{\sigma}{t,k-1}\delta{k-1}}. 4. Sum Contributions: The total radiance is the sum of the interval contributions weighted by the cumulative throughput: L(xi, \omegao) = \sum{k=0}^{N-1} \bar{L}(k) Tr(k) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def analyticquadratureradiance(N, s, Lvals, sigmatvals, delta): """ Computes radiance using analytic quadrature for volume slices. Args: N: Number of intervals. s: Array of positions [s0,..., sN]. Lvals: Array of radiance values [L(s0),..., L(sN)]. sigmatvals: Array of extinction coefficients [sigmat(s0),..., sigmat(sN)]. delta: Interval length |s{k+1} - sk|. Assumed uniform. Returns: Total radiance L(xi, omegao). """ totalradiance = 0.0 cumulativethroughput = 1.0 for k in range(N): # 1. Average extinction for interval k sigmaavg = 0.5 (sigmatvals[k] + sigmatvals[k+1]) # 2. Interval radiance contribution Lbar(k) # Handle near-zero extinction to avoid division by zero if sigmaavg < 1e-8: # Limit as sigmaavg -> 0 corresponds to trapezoid rule # Integral of linear L(s) over [0, delta] is delta (L(0) + L(1)) / 2 lbark = delta (Lvals[k] + Lvals[k+1]) / 2.0 else: term1 = (2.0 Lvals[k] / (sigmaavg delta)) (math.exp(-sigmaavg delta) - 1.0) term2 = (2.0 Lvals[k+1] / (sigmaavg delta)) (math.exp(sigmaavg delta) - 1.0) math.exp(-sigmaavg delta) lbark = term1 + term2 # 3. Add to total with current cumulative throughput totalradiance += lbark cumulativethroughput # 4. Update cumulative throughput for next interval cumulativethroughput = math.exp(-sigmaavg delta) return totalradiance Parameters: \bar{\sigma}t(u): Piecewise constant approximation of extinction. This assumption is made to improve computational speed compared to piecewise linear extinction, which would require error functions of complex numbers. \deltak: Interval length. Typically uniform across all intervals. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Extinction: When \bar{\sigma}{t,k} \approx 0, the division in the \bar{L}(k) formula causes numerical instability. The method is theoretically identical to the trapezoid rule when \bar{\sigma}t = 0. A guard clause or L'Hôpital's rule application is required. High Extinction: The method maintains accuracy for high extinction values where standard Newton-Cotes rules (trapezoid/Simpson) fail because they approximate the product Tr(s)L(s) directly. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of intervals. It is faster than Simpson's rule because it avoids the more complex quadratic interpolation and dual integral calculations. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store radiance and extinction samples. Accuracy: Comparable to the trapezoid rule when extinction \bar{\sigma}t is low. Significantly more accurate than the trapezoid rule when \bar{\sigma}t is high, becoming comparable to Simpson's rule in accuracy. Strengths: Improved accuracy for dense volumes (e.g., flames in smoke) without the computational cost of Simpson's rule. Theoretically identical to the trapezoid rule when extinction is zero. Limitations: Requires sampling of both radiance and extinction at interval endpoints. Assumes piecewise constant extinction for speed. When to use: Rendering emissive inhomogeneous volumes with high extinction coefficients where standard quadrature rules lose accuracy. When not to use: When extinction is negligible and maximum speed is required (trapezoid rule is sufficient). Origin: Proposed by T. Kuge et al. in "Real-time Indirect Illumination of Emissive Inhomogeneous Volumes using Layered Polygonal Area Lights". History: Developed to address the inaccuracy of Newton-Cotes rules (trapezoid/Simpson) in dense participating media. These rules approximate the product of transmittance and radiance directly, leading to errors when extinction is high. The proposed method discretizes radiance and extinction individually to derive an analytic form for throughput. Usage: Used in real-time rendering of emissive volumes, such as flames inside dense smoke. Real‐time Indirect Illumination of Emissive Inhomogeneous Volumes using Layered Polygonal Area Lights, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.13851, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Trapezoid Integration for Transmittance
head: Linear Segment Integration
body: Trapezoid Integration for Transmittance computes the integral of transmittance over a linear segment within a skewed coordinate system, accounting for varying distances to the box boundary. It solves the problem of analytically integrating the radiative transfer equation over segments where optical properties are constant but the geometric path length through the medium varies non-linearly with respect to the camera ray parameter. It sets itself apart from standard constant-coefficient integration by handling the "skew" introduced by the intersection of a ray with a box face, allowing for efficient, closed-form evaluation without numerical quadrature. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: t{C,S}: Camera ray distance at the start of the segment. t{C,E}: Camera ray distance at the end of the segment. d{E,S}: Exit distance (distance to the box boundary along the light direction) at the start. d{E,E}: Exit distance at the end. \sigmat: Extinction coefficient (assumed constant over the segment). t{C,Surface}: Distance to any occluding surface along the camera ray. Outputs: \mathcal{I}{\text{trapezoid}}: The integrated transmittance contribution over the segment. Data Structures: The method operates on scalar values representing ray parameters and optical properties. Steps: 1. Clamp End Distance: Determine the effective end of the segment by clamping the geometric end distance t{C,E} against the surface occlusion distance t{C,Surface} and the start distance t{C,S}. t{C,B} = \text{clamp}(t{C,E}, t{C,S}, t{C,Surface}) If t{C,B} \le t{C,S}, the segment contributes zero transmittance. 2. Compute Slope c: Calculate the slope of the skewed coordinate system, which accounts for the change in exit distance relative to the camera ray distance: c = 1 + \frac{d{E,E} - d{E,S}}{t{C,E} - t{C,S}} 3. Handle Degenerate Cases: If the slope c approaches zero (|c| < \epsilon) or the segment size is negligible (t{C,E} - t{C,S} < \epsilon), use the linear approximation to avoid numerical instability: T = (t{C,B} - t{C,S}) EI where EI = e^{-(t{C,S} + d{E,S})\sigmat}. Return T. 4. Compute Exponential Terms: Calculate the precomputed exponential terms for efficiency: EI = e^{-(t{C,S} + d{E,S})\sigmat} Eu = e^{-\sigmat (t{C,B} - t{C,S})^c} 5. Compute Integral: Calculate the trapezoid integral using the derived formula: \mathcal{I}{\text{trapezoid}} = EI (1 - Eu) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def trapezoidintegration(tcs, tce, des, dee, sigmat, tcsurface): """ Computes the transmittance integral over a linear segment in a skewed coordinate system. Args: tcs: Camera ray distance at start. tce: Camera ray distance at end. des: Exit distance at start. dee: Exit distance at end. sigmat: Extinction coefficient. tcsurface: Distance to occluding surface. Returns: Integrated transmittance contribution. """ # Step 1: Clamp end distance tcb = min(max(tcs, tce), tcsurface) # If segment is invalid or zero length, return 0 if tcb <= tcs: return 0.0 # Step 2: Compute slope denom = tce - tcs if abs(denom) < 1e-9: # Avoid division by zero in slope calculation c = 1.0 else: c = 1.0 + (dee - des) / denom # Step 3: Handle degenerate cases (c -> 0 or small segment) segmentsize = tcb - tcs # Precompute common exponential term EI exponenti = -(tcs + des) sigmat ei = math.exp(exponenti) # Check for linear approximation condition if abs(c) < 1e-9 or segmentsize < 1e-9: return segmentsize ei # Step 4: Compute Eu exponentu = -sigmat (segmentsize c) eu = math.exp(exponentu) # Step 5: Compute Integral integralvalue = ei (1.0 - eu) return integralvalue Optimization Note: To reduce the number of exponential evaluations in consecutive segment evaluations, the product of the lower and upper bound parts (EI \cdot Eu) can be extracted outside the evaluation loop and assigned as the lower bound part (EI) for the next segment. Handles special cases where incident (\tilde{\omega}i) and outgoing (\tilde{\omega}o) light vectors are parallel or opposite, requiring separate solutions without traversing the box outline. Opposite Vectors: If \tilde{\omega}i \cdot \tilde{\omega}o < 0, the end distance is set to zero. Box transmittance is computed using trapezoid integration with parameters (0, tC, dL, 0). Same Direction: If vectors face the same direction, the end distance is the sum of distances to both exit points along the incident (dL) and outgoing (tC) vectors. Box transmittance is computed with parameters (0, tC, dL, dL + tC). Extends integration to collimated light sources with a gobo (convex binary map or stencil). Method: Offset the starting point of the integration to lie on the gobo edge and limit the integration to the far end of the gobo. The result is exponentially attenuated by the distance from the camera origin to the start of the gobo. Time Complexity: O(1) per segment, as it involves a constant number of arithmetic operations and exponential evaluations. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring only scalar storage for ray parameters and optical properties. Strengths: Provides an exact analytic solution for transmittance over skewed segments, avoiding the noise and convergence issues of Monte Carlo integration. It is compatible with distance sampling. Limitations: Requires careful handling of numerical edge cases (slope near zero, small segments) to maintain stability. Assumes homogeneous media within the segment. When to Use: When rendering participating media with homogeneous properties within bounding volumes (boxes) and high accuracy is required without stochastic noise. The method originates from the work on collimated whole volume light scattering in homogeneous finite media. It was developed to provide an efficient and accurate estimator for light transport in participating media, specifically addressing the challenges of shadowing and attenuation in complex geometries. The source compares this analytic approach against moment-based estimation, ratio estimation, and Monte Carlo integration.
