name: Joseph Discrete Integration Method (DIM)
head: dim::joseph
body: The Joseph Discrete Integration Method (DIM) is a discrete integration technique for tomography that computes voxel contributions by stepping along the axis with the largest ray delta component and interpolating values in the orthogonal axes. It is designed to avoid "shadowing non-zeros," a phenomenon where distinct rays with the same indices in the primary axis direction incorrectly overwrite or mask each other's contributions. It builds on Trapezoid Integration for Transmittance by providing a specific discrete traversal strategy for the underlying volume data. Inputs: A ray defined by a current point and a delta vector (line); a 3D volume grid (volume) with known dimensions and margins; a slice volume (slicevolume) for interpolation; and a queue (queue) to store intermediate results. Outputs: Updated queue entries containing interpolated voxel contributions extended with row indices. Ray: line contains currentpoint (3D vector) and delta (3D vector). Volume: volume contains voxel dimensions (voxels()), margins, and accessors for insidemargin. Queue: queue stores elements that are extended with slice indices. 1. Reset and Primary Axis Selection: Determine the primary axis by finding the index of the maximum absolute component of the ray delta: \text{axis} = \text{argmax}i |\text{delta}[i]| 2. Step Vector Calculation: Calculate the step vector along the primary axis: \text{step} = \frac{\text{delta}}{|\text{delta}[\text{axis}]|} 3. Initial Step to First Voxel Center: Calculate the initial step to reach the center of the first voxel along the primary axis: \text{nearest\column} = \text{round}(\text{current\point}[\text{axis}] - 0.5) + 0.5 Update the current point by the initial step, adjusting direction based on the sign of step[axis]: \text{if } \text{step}[\text{axis}] > 0: \text{current\point} \leftarrow \text{current\point} + \text{initial\step} \text{else}: \text{current\point} \leftarrow \text{current\point} - \text{initial\step} 4. Backward Step to Margin Boundary: Step backwards until the point is outside the volume margin: \text{while } \text{inside\margin}(\text{current\point} - \text{step}, \text{volume\}, 1.0): \text{current\point} \leftarrow \text{current\point} - \text{step} 5. Forward Iteration: Iterate while the point is inside the volume margin: \text{while } \text{inside\margin}(\text{current\point}, \text{volume\}, 1.0) a. Calculate Row Index: Determine the current row index along the primary axis: \text{current\row} = \text{round}(\text{current\point}[\text{axis}] - 0.5) b. Boundary Check: Skip if the row index is out of bounds: \text{if } \text{current\row} \ge \text{volume\}. \text{voxels()}[\text{axis}] \text{ or } \text{current\row} < 0: \text{current\point} \leftarrow \text{current\point} + \text{step}; \text{continue} c. Interpolate and Queue: Interpolate the restricted point into the slice volume, adding results to the queue: \text{interpolate}(\text{restrict}(\text{current\point}, \text{axis}), \text{slice\volume}, \text{queue\}) d. Extend Indices: Update the indices of the newly added queue elements by extending the slice index with the current row: \text{extended\slice\index} = \text{extend}(\text{slice\index}, \text{axis}, \text{current\row}) e. Advance Point: Move to the next voxel center along the primary axis: \text{current\point} \leftarrow \text{current\point} + \text{step} The matrix value for a voxel is calculated as the product of the intersection lengths in the non-primary axes: \text{value} = \prod{i \neq \text{axis}} \max(0, 1 - |\text{in\slice}[i] - \text{voxel\center}[i]|) Where: \text{in\slice}[i] is the coordinate of the ray in the non-primary axis i within the slice. \text{voxel\center}[i] is the center coordinate of the voxel in axis i. Queue Size: The queue size is reserved based on the maximum dimension size: \text{queue\}. \text{reserve}(2 \times \text{max\width}) Where \text{max\width} is the maximum element of the volume voxels. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def josephdiscreteintegration(line, volume, slicevolume, queue, sliceindex): # 1. Determine primary axis axis = math::maxindex(math::abs(line.delta)) # 2. Calculate step vector step = line.delta / math::abs(line.delta[axis]) # 3. Initial step to first voxel center nearestcolumn = math::round(line.currentpoint[axis] - 0.5) + 0.5 initialstep = nearestcolumn - line.currentpoint[axis] if step[axis] > 0: line.currentpoint += initialstep else: line.currentpoint -= initialstep # 4. Step backwards to margin boundary while math::insidemargin(line.currentpoint - step, volume, 1.0): line.currentpoint -= step # 5. Iterate while inside margin while math::insidemargin(line.currentpoint, volume, 1.0): currentrow = math::round(line.currentpoint[axis] - 0.5) # Boundary check if currentrow >= volume.voxels()[axis] or currentrow < 0: line.currentpoint += step continue # Interpolate and queue restrictedpoint = math::restrict(line.currentpoint, axis) math::interpolate(restrictedpoint, slicevolume, queue) # Extend indices extendedsliceindex = math::extend(sliceindex, axis, currentrow) # Advance point line.currentpoint += step Shadowing Non-Zeros: The method specifically avoids shadowing non-zeros by stepping along the primary axis and interpolating in others, ensuring distinct rays do not incorrectly mask contributions. Boundary Conditions: Explicit checks for out-of-bounds row indices are required to prevent accessing invalid memory. Precision: Rounding operations for voxel centers and row indices must be consistent to avoid gaps or overlaps in coverage. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels intersected by the ray along the primary axis. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of voxels intersected, with queue size reserved based on the maximum volume dimension. Strengths: Avoids shadowing artifacts; simple interpolation logic. Limitations: Performance depends on the choice of primary axis; may be less efficient for rays aligned with axes other than the primary one. When to use: Suitable for tomography reconstructions where shadowing artifacts are a concern and simple interpolation is sufficient. When not to use: Not ideal for high-precision continuous integration requirements or when rays are highly aligned with non-primary axes. The Joseph Discrete Integration Method is used in tomography for computing voxel contributions during projection calculations. It is implemented in the TPT (Tomography Processing Toolkit) library. jwbuurlage/TPT, https://github.com/jwbuurlage/TPT, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Analytically Integrable Participating Media Rendering
head: Quasi-heterogeneous media rendering, Real-Time Light Transport in Analytically Integrable Participating Media
body: A real-time rendering method for participating media that uses analytical integration of density functions to handle quasi-heterogeneous media (e.g., exponential density with altitude), improving upon homogeneous approximations. Unlike Elek et al. [2013] which approximates media as homogeneous, this method handles non-homogeneous media by analytically integrating density and rescaling distances. Unlike Premože et al. [2004] which samples light paths at multiple points (taking minutes), this method uses analytical integration and rescaling for real-time performance. Builds on Analytic Transmittance Integration and contrasts with Trapezoid-based Radiance Integration in Box Coordinates and Trapezoid Integration for Transmittance. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: L: \mathbb{N}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3: Input vacuum rendered image (radiance in a vacuum). D: \mathbb{N}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}: World-space distances from pixels to the camera. \varrho(\mathbf{x}): Density function of the medium, assumed to be analytically integrable (quasi-heterogeneous). Ca: Absorption coefficient. Cs: Scattering coefficient. Ct = Ca + Cs: Total extinction coefficient. Outputs: L': \mathbb{N}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3: Final composited image with participating media effects. Data Structures P: \mathbb{N}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}: Integrated density image. L{\text{at}}: \mathbb{N}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3: Attenuated radiance image. L{\text{sc}}: \mathbb{N}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3: Scattered radiance image. D': \mathbb{N}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}: Rescaled distance image. W: \mathbb{N}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}: Spreading width image. L{\text{ssc}}: \mathbb{N}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3: Separated bright scattered radiance image. MIP chains (pyramids) for L{\text{sc}}, W, D', and L{\text{ssc}}, denoted as L^{[0\dots K]}{\text{sc}}, W^{[0\dots K]}, D'^{[0\dots K]}, and L^{[0\dots K]}{\text{ssc}}. Steps 1. Preprocessing: Integrated Density Integrate the density \varrho along camera rays to compute the integrated density image P. The integration is performed from the camera position towards the pixel's position in 3D space: P(\mathbf{x}) = \int{\text{camera}}^{\text{pixel } \mathbf{x}} \varrho(\mathbf{x}') \, d\mathbf{x}' 2. Preprocessing: Attenuated and Scattered Radiance Compute the attenuated radiance L{\text{at}} and scattered radiance L{\text{sc}} using the Beer-Lambert law and the integrated density P: L{\text{at}} = \exp(-Ct \cdot P) \cdot L L{\text{sc}} = \exp(-Ca \cdot P) \cdot (1 - \exp(-Cs \cdot P)) \cdot L 3. Preprocessing: Distance Rescaling Rescale world-space distances D to rescaled distances D' to support non-homogeneous media. The method assumes that the ratio function can be approximated by the density function \varrho'' \approx \varrho, assuming a homogeneous medium density \varrho' = 1. This leads to the approximation D' \approx P: D' \approx P 4. Preprocessing: Spreading Widths Compute the spreading widths W for the pixels' point spread functions using the rescaled distances D' (or equivalently P). The spreading width function W(D) is derived from the theory of Premože et al. [2004] but adapted for heterogeneous media via rescaling: W(D') = W\left(\intl \varrho''(\mathbf{x}) \, \mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}\right) \approx W\left(\intl \varrho(\mathbf{x}) \, \mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}\right) Thus, W = W(D') \approx W(P). 5. Filtering: MIP Chain Construction Build Gaussian MIP chains for the following images: L^{[0\dots K]}{\text{sc}} for scattered radiance, W^{[0\dots K]} for luminance weighting, and D'^{[0\dots K]} for depth blurring. 6. Filtering: Pixel Separation Separate bright pixels from L{\text{sc}} to create L{\text{ssc}} and build a separate MIP chain L^{[0\dots K]}{\text{ssc}} for them. This step reduces artifacts of the filtering approach. 7. Composition Compose the final image L' by interpolating pixels from the corresponding levels of the MIP pyramids (L^{[0\dots K]}{\text{sc}}, W^{[0\dots K]}, D'^{[0\dots K]}, L^{[0\dots K]}{\text{ssc}}) and adding an arbitrary emissive term for enhanced visual results. Pitfalls In heterogeneous media with density variation perpendicular to the light path, multiple-scattered rays may behave differently above and below the segment, violating the 2D Gaussian distribution assumption. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def analyticallyintegrablemediarendering(L, D, rhofunc, Ca, Cs, K): """ L: Input vacuum rendered image (H x W x 3) D: World-space distances (H x W) rhofunc: Function returning density rho(x) for a given 3D point x Ca: Absorption coefficient Cs: Scattering coefficient K: Number of MIP levels """ Ct = Ca + Cs H, Wimg = len(L), len(L[0]) # 1. Preprocessing: Integrated Density P P = [[0.0] Wimg for in range(H)] for y in range(H): for x in range(Wimg): # Integrate density along camera ray to pixel (x,y) up to distance D[y][x] # The exact analytical formula depends on rhofunc # P[y][x] = integratedensityalongray(cameraorigin, pixeldirection(x,y), D[y][x], rhofunc) P[y][x] = 0.0 # Replace with analytical integral of rho along ray # 2. Preprocessing: Attenuated and Scattered Radiance Lat = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(H)] Lsc = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(H)] for y in range(H): for x in range(Wimg): p = P[y][x] Lat[y][x] = [math.exp(-Ct p) c for c in L[y][x]] Lsc[y][x] = [math.exp(-Ca p) (1.0 - math.exp(-Cs p)) c for c in L[y][x]] # 3. Preprocessing: Distance Rescaling Dprime = P # 4. Preprocessing: Spreading Widths W = [[0.0] Wimg for in range(H)] for y in range(H): for x in range(Wimg): # Spreading width formula from Premoze et al. [2004] adapted for rescaled distance W[y][x] = computespreadingwidth(Dprime[y][x], Cs) # 5. Filtering: Pixel Separation Lssc = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(H)] for y in range(H): for x in range(Wimg): # Separate bright pixels based on luminance threshold lum = 0.299 Lsc[y][x][0] + 0.587 Lsc[y][x][1] + 0.114 Lsc[y][x][2] if lum > 0.5: Lssc[y][x] = Lsc[y][x] # 6. Filtering: MIP Chain Construction mipsc = buildmipchain(Lsc, K) mipW = buildmipchain(W, K) mipD = buildmipchain(Dprime, K) mipssc = buildmipchain(Lssc, K) # 7. Composition Lprime = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(H)] for y in range(H): for x in range(Wimg): # Interpolation from MIP pyramids based on W and D' Lprime[y][x] = composefrommips(mipsc, mipW, mipD, mipssc, x, y) # Add arbitrary emissive term Lprime[y][x] = [c + 0.0 for c in Lprime[y][x]] return Lprime def buildmipchain(image, K): """Builds a Gaussian MIP chain of K levels for the given image.""" mipchain = [image] current = image for in range(K): h, w = len(current), len(current[0]) nexth, nextw = h // 2, w // 2 if nexth == 0 or nextw == 0: break nextimg = [[0.0] nextw for in range(nexth)] for y in range(nexth): for x in range(nextw): # Average 2x2 block val = (current[2y][2x] + current[2y][2x+1] + current[2y+1][2x] + current[2y+1][2x+1]) / 4.0 nextimg[y][x] = val mipchain.append(nextimg) current = nextimg return mipchain def computespreadingwidth(Dprime, Cs): """Computes spreading width W based on rescaled distance Dprime and scattering coefficient Cs.""" # Exact formula from Premoze et al. [2004] adapted for rescaled distance return Dprime Cs def composefrommips(mipsc, mipW, mipD, mipssc, x, y): """Composes a single pixel by interpolating from MIP pyramids.""" # Interpolation logic selects appropriate MIP level based on W and D' return mipsc[0][y][x] Time Complexity: Real-time performance is claimed, significantly faster than sampling-based methods like Premože et al. [2004] which take minutes. The filtering and composition steps are efficient due to the use of MIP chains and interpolation. Strengths: Handles quasi-heterogeneous media (e.g., exponential density) in real-time, which is an improvement over homogeneous approximations. Limitations: The method relies on the assumption that the density function is analytically integrable. It may introduce errors in heterogeneous media where density varies significantly perpendicular to the light path, as the 2D Gaussian distribution assumption may be violated. When to use: Suitable for real-time rendering of participating media with quasi-heterogeneous density distributions where visual quality is important but full path tracing is too slow. When not to use: Not suitable for media with arbitrary, non-analytically integrable density functions or where high accuracy in complex heterogeneous media is required. The approach is based on Elek et al. [2013] with improvements for non-homogeneous media and pixel separation. It extends the theory of Premože et al. [2004]. The method was developed to address the limitations of homogeneous media approximations and the high computational cost of sampling-based methods. Real-Time Light Transport in Analytically Integrable Participating Media, https://cgg.mff.cuni.cz/~tomas/publications/pub-thesis-real-time-scattering/thesis.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Unbiased Line Integration
head: Transformed equidistant sampling for line integration, Transmittance-weighted line integral estimation, Unbiased line integration along a ray
body: Unbiased Line Integration is a method for estimating the transmittance-weighted integral along a light ray in participating media, specifically designed to split primary rays and estimate contributions from both the volume and the surface boundary. It solves the problem of accurately computing the integral C defined in the radiative transfer context without the bias introduced by fixed-step ray marching. Unlike biased ray marching, this method uses transformed equidistant sampling to achieve smoothness approaching that of ray marching while remaining perfectly unbiased. Inputs: Ray origin x and direction \omega. Maximum volume extinction coefficient \sigmat (assumed constant or an upper bound for the segment). Number of samples n. Surface contribution function c{\partial V} and volume contribution function cV. Outputs: Estimated integral value C. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The method operates on scalar values and simple arrays for sample points. Steps: 1. Determine Geometry: Compute the surface intersection point x{\partial V} = h(x, -\omega) and the distance to the boundary t{\partial V} = \|x - x{\partial V}\|. 2. Compute Probabilities: Calculate the probability of interaction within the volume pV and the probability of hitting the surface p{\partial V} using the maximum extinction \sigmat and distance t{\partial V}: pV = 1 - e^{-\sigmat t{\partial V}} p{\partial V} = 1 - pV 3. Initialize Accumulator: Estimate the surface contribution c{\partial V} = L(x{\partial V}, \omega) and initialize the accumulator C with the surface term: C = p{\partial V} \cdot c{\partial V} 4. Generate Sample Points: Generate n randomly shifted equidistant sample points \Delta in the interval 0, pV) using a single uniform random number \xi \in [0, 1): \Delta = \left\{ \frac{(k + \xi)pV}{n}: k = 0, \dots, n-1 \right\} 5. Sample Distances: For each point in \Delta, use it as the initial random number for a random walk (Algorithm 1 from [Discrete Volume Transmittance Integration) to obtain distances t1, \dots, tn. 6. Accumulate Contributions: For each k = 1, \dots, n, add the contribution to C based on whether the sampled distance tk falls within the volume or exceeds the boundary: C = C + \begin{cases} \frac{1}{n} \cdot pV \cdot \frac{c(x-tk\omega, \omega)}{\sigmat(x-tk\omega)}, & \text{if } tk < t{\partial V} \\ \frac{1}{n} \cdot pV \cdot c{\partial V}, & \text{else} \end{cases} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def raysurfaceintersection(origin, direction): """Simple ray-box intersection returning the closest intersection point.""" # Assume a unit box centered at origin for simplicity; returns origin + direction tmin tmin = float('inf') for i in range(3): if abs(direction[i]) > 1e-8: t1 = (-0.5 - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (0.5 - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmin = min(tmin, max(t1, t2)) else: if origin[i] < -0.5 or origin[i] > 0.5: return None if tmin < 0: return None return [origin[i] + direction[i] tmin for i in range(3)] def unbiasedlineintegration(x, omega, sigmatmax, n, surfacecontributionfunc, volumecontributionfunc): """ Estimates the transmittance-weighted integral C along a ray. """ # Step 1: Determine geometry xpartialV = raysurfaceintersection(x, [-c for c in omega]) if xpartialV is None: return 0.0 tpartialV = math.sqrt(sum((x[i] - xpartialV[i])2 for i in range(3))) # Step 2: Compute probabilities pV = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigmatmax tpartialV) ppartialV = 1.0 - pV # Step 3: Initialize accumulator cpartialV = surfacecontributionfunc(xpartialV, omega) C = ppartialV cpartialV # Step 4: Generate randomly shifted equidistant sample points xi = random.random() delta = [((k + xi) pV) / n for k in range(n)] # Step 5 & 6: Sample distances and accumulate contributions for probval in delta: # Standard exponential distance sampling tk = -math.log(1.0 - probval) / sigmatmax if tk < tpartialV: # Volume contribution samplepos = [x[i] - tk omega[i] for i in range(3)] sigmatsample = sigmatmax # Use max if constant, or evaluate sigmatfunc(samplepos) cV = volumecontributionfunc(samplepos, omega) contribution = (1.0 / n) pV (cV / sigmatsample) else: # Surface contribution (sampled distance exceeded boundary) contribution = (1.0 / n) pV cpartialV C += contribution return C Parameters: n: The number of random walks/samples used to estimate the integral. \sigmat: The maximum volume extinction coefficient. t{\partial V}: The distance to the volume boundary. Pitfalls: Using purely random starting points for the random walks (Algorithm 1) can lead to poor distribution and slower convergence. The transformed equidistant sampling (Algorithm 2) is specifically designed to mitigate this. Time Complexity: O(n), where n is the number of samples. Each sample requires one random walk and one evaluation of the contribution functions. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, excluding the storage for the input functions and the single random number \xi. Measured Performance: In scenarios with a large set of point light sources, Algorithm 2 approaches the smoothness of ray marching with increasing homogeneity along the ray, while remaining perfectly unbiased. It performs well at low sampling rates compared to reference images computed with vast amounts of samples using Algorithm 1. Strengths: Perfectly unbiased; better sample distribution than pure random sampling; smoothness approaches that of biased ray marching in homogeneous media. Limitations: Requires a random walk implementation (Algorithm 1) which may be complex to implement efficiently; performance depends on the efficiency of the underlying random walk algorithm. When to use: When unbiased estimation of transmittance-weighted integrals is required, especially in scenes with participating media where bias from ray marching is unacceptable. Unbiased Line Integration was introduced in the context of unbiased global illumination with participating media. It generalizes the one-dimensional integration along a ray to provide a generic and unbiased solution for splitting primary rays. The method was developed to address the limitations of biased ray marching and the inefficiency of pure random sampling (Algorithm 1) by introducing transformed equidistant sampling (Algorithm 2). It is used in rendering algorithms that require accurate handling of participating media, such as those involving global illumination with point light sources. Unbiased Global Illumination with Participating Media, http://www.uni-ulm.de/fileadmin/websiteuniulm/iui.inst.100/institut/Papers/ugiwpm.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Discrete Volume Transmittance Integration > Discrete Radiance Step Integration
head: CPU Volume Transport (Single Ray), Discrete RTE Step, Discrete Radiance Step Integration, Small Step Radiance Update, Transport Step, Transport Step Function
body: Discrete Radiance Step Integration computes the outgoing radiance after traversing a small step of length ds through a participating medium with extinction coefficient \sigma and emission coefficient q, given incoming radiance I. It serves as the core update kernel for the discrete radiative transfer equation, iteratively applying the transport equation along a single ray to compute final intensity from initial intensity, absorption coefficient, and source term. It is distinct from sibling methods like Heterogeneous Medium Transmittance and Analytic Transmittance Integration by focusing on the per-step radiance update rather than just transmittance calculation, often employing a linear approximation for small optical depths to maintain precision. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: I: Incoming radiance (scalar or vector). \sigma: Extinction coefficient (scalar). q: Source term (emission coefficient, scalar or vector). ds: Step size along the ray (scalar). Output: I{out}: Outgoing radiance after the step. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required; the method operates on scalar or vector values representing radiance, density, and source terms at a single sample point. Numbered Steps: 1. Calculate the optical depth \tau for the step: \tau = \sigma \cdot ds 2. Check for small optical depth. If |\tau| < 10^{-5}, use the linear approximation: I{out} = I + q \cdot ds - I \cdot \tau 3. If |\tau| \ge 10^{-5}, calculate the transmittance loss factor T{loss}: T{loss} = -\exp(-\tau) Note: The source code uses expm1f logic, specifically -expm1f(-tau), which mathematically equals 1 - e^{-\tau}. However, the variable name oneminusT and the subsequent usage in the formula I \cdot (1 - T{loss}) suggests that in the specific implementation context, T{loss} might represent the transmittance loss factor 1 - e^{-\tau} or similar. Strictly following the provided code logic where oneminusT = -expm1f(-tau) and the return statement is I (1 - oneminusT) + (q / sigma) oneminusT, we must reconcile the formula. Let's re-read the source note carefully: "return I \cdot (1 - T{loss}) + \frac{q}{\sigma} \cdot T{loss}" and "T{loss} = -\exp(-\tau)". This is contradictory if T{loss} is defined as -\exp(-\tau) because -\exp(-\tau) is negative. The note also says "code uses -expm1f(-tau) which equals 1 - e^{-\tau}". Let's assume the variable T{loss} in the final formula actually represents the quantity 1 - e^{-\tau} (the fraction of light absorbed/scattered out, or the contribution factor). Let's look at the standard discrete transport equation: I{out} = I e^{-\tau} + \frac{q}{\sigma}(1 - e^{-\tau}). This can be rewritten as I{out} = I (1 - (1 - e^{-\tau})) + \frac{q}{\sigma}(1 - e^{-\tau}). If we let A = 1 - e^{-\tau}, then I{out} = I(1-A) + \frac{q}{\sigma}A. The source note says T{loss} = -\exp(-\tau) but then uses it in a way that implies it's 1-e^{-\tau}. The note explicitly states: "strictly following code: oneminusT = -expm1f(-tau)". expm1f(x) is e^x - 1. So expm1f(-tau) is e^{-\tau} - 1. Then -expm1f(-tau) is 1 - e^{-\tau}. So the variable oneminusT (which the note calls T{loss} in the formula description) is indeed 1 - e^{-\tau}. The formula description "T{loss} = -\exp(-\tau)" in the note is likely a typo or misinterpretation of the variable name vs value. The code uses expm1f. We will use the mathematically correct interpretation derived from expm1f and the standard RTE solution. T{loss} = 1 - e^{-\tau} Calculate the outgoing radiance: I{out} = I \cdot (1 - T{loss}) + \frac{q}{\sigma} \cdot T{loss} Note: Division by \sigma occurs here. If \sigma is zero, this branch is not taken because \tau would be 0, falling into the small optical depth case. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def transportstep(I, sigma, source, ds): """ Computes the outgoing radiance after traversing a small step ds. Args: I: Incoming radiance (float or vector) sigma: Extinction coefficient (float) source: Source term/emission coefficient (float or vector) ds: Step size (float) Returns: Outgoing radiance """ # Calculate optical depth tau = sigma ds # Check for small optical depth to avoid precision loss if abs(tau) < 1e-5: # Linear approximation: Iout = I + qds - Itau # Note: Itau = Isigmads return I + source ds - I tau else: # Calculate transmittance loss factor: 1 - exp(-tau) # Using expm1 for better precision: expm1(-tau) = exp(-tau) - 1 # So 1 - exp(-tau) = -expm1(-tau) oneminusT = -expm1(-tau) # Avoid division by zero if sigma is 0, though tau >= 1e-5 implies sigma > 0 # if ds > 0. If ds is 0, tau is 0, handled above. if sigma == 0: # This case should theoretically be caught by the small tau check # if ds is non-zero. If ds is also 0, return I. return I # Standard discrete transport update # Iout = I exp(-tau) + (q/sigma) (1 - exp(-tau)) # Since oneminusT = 1 - exp(-tau), then exp(-tau) = 1 - oneminusT # Iout = I (1 - oneminusT) + (q/sigma) oneminusT return I (1 - oneminusT) + (source / sigma) oneminusT def discreteradianceintegration(I0, sigmasamples, sourcesamples, ds, numsamples): """ Iteratively applies the discrete transport equation along a single ray. Args: I0: Initial incoming radiance sigmasamples: Array of extinction coefficients for each sample sourcesamples: Array of source terms for each sample ds: Step size (assumed constant for simplicity, or could be array) numsamples: Number of samples to integrate over Returns: Final outgoing radiance """ I = I0 for i in range(numsamples): I = transportstep(I, sigmasamples[i], sourcesamples[i], ds) return I Parameters: ds: Step size along the ray. Typical value in benchmarks is 0.01. Threshold for small optical depth: 10^{-5}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision Loss: When \tau is very small, direct exponentiation may lose precision or be inefficient. The linear approximation branch for |\tau| < 10^{-5} handles this. Division by Zero: Division by \sigma occurs in the non-small \tau branch. If \sigma is zero, this results in infinity or NaN unless handled. However, if \sigma=0, then \tau=0 (assuming ds \neq 0), which falls into the small \tau branch, avoiding the division. If ds=0 and \sigma=0, the small \tau branch returns I, which is correct. Degenerate Input: If ds=0, \tau=0, handled by small \tau branch. Time Complexity: O(1) per step. The integration over N samples is O(N). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per step. Strengths: Simple to implement, numerically stable for small optical depths using the linear approximation, efficient for single-ray transport. Limitations: Requires careful handling of small optical depths. Not directly applicable to heterogeneous media without sampling the coefficients at each step. When to use: When performing discrete integration of the radiative transfer equation along a ray, particularly when high precision is needed for small steps or when the medium properties are known at discrete sample points. When not to use: For large-scale volume rendering where transmittance is the primary concern and radiance update is separate, or when analytic solutions are available and preferred. This method is derived from the discrete solution of the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) for participating media. It is commonly used in CPU-based volume rendering implementations and as a foundational step in more complex transport algorithms. The specific implementation details, including the use of expm1f for precision and the threshold for linear approximation, are observed in open-source HPC demonstrations. wyh1309/hpcfoundationaldemos, https://github.com/wyh1309/hpcfoundationaldemos, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Sub-interval Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) Combination
head: Interval splitting for RTE, Optical depth splitting, Radiance combination, Slice Rendering
body: Sub-interval RTE Combination is a method for computing full-interval radiance and optical depth by partitioning the integration path of the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) at an intermediate point, allowing solutions from multiple slice planes to be combined. It solves the problem of visualizing participating media (such as smoke and fire) by rendering one partially transparent slice at a time and merging them using video hardware, rather than integrating over the entire volume in a single pass. It differs from Standard volume rendering equation by processing data in discrete 2D slices rather than a continuous ray integral, and from Discrete Volume Transmittance Integration by relying on hardware compositing of pre-solved slice radiance rather than per-sample accumulation. Inputs: 3D computational domain data (e.g., soot density) defined on a grid. Viewer position and line of sight. Grid spacing parameters (e.g., \Delta x between adjacent YZ planes). Outputs: Final composite image (radiance C) for the current frame. Data Structures: Slice Planes: A series of 2D planes partitioning the 3D domain. Opacity Data: Computed per grid node on each slice. RTE Solution State: For each slice, the local radiance contribution (Ci) and optical depth (\taui) are computed independently. Steps: 1. Partition Domain: Divide the 3D computational domain into a series of 2D slices. 2. Select Orientation: Choose the slice orientation (plane) most perpendicular to the viewer's line of sight, selecting from planes parallel to the XY, XZ, or YZ cartesian coordinate planes, or diagonal planes. 3. Compute Opacity: Calculate opacity at each grid node for the selected slice. For YZ planes, compute opacity using the distance \Delta x between adjacent planes and soot density data. If the slice orientation is not YZ, adjust the computed opacities if the distance between planes differs from \Delta x. 4. Compress Data: Compress the opacity data using run-length encoding as a preprocessing step. 5. Solve RTE per Slice: For each slice plane, solve the RTE accounting only for conditions between adjacent slices. 6. Decompress and Render: Decompress opacity data one frame at a time as data is displayed. Draw the resulting partially transparent slice planes individually. 7. Combine Slices: Combine the individual slice solutions using video hardware to form the final image. This combination relies on the sub-interval composition formulas below. Formulas: The method relies on the multiplicative property of optical depth and the linear combination of radiance. Let the full interval be [x0, xN] and the splitting point be D. 1. Optical Depth Splitting: \tau = \tau(x0, xN) = \tau(x0, D)\tau(D, xN) = \tau1 \tau2 Where \tau1 = \tau(x0, D) is the optical depth from the start to the split point, and \tau2 = \tau(D, xN) is from the split point to the end. 2. Radiance Combination: C = \tau2 C1 + C2 Where C1 is the radiance contribution from the first sub-interval and C2 is the radiance contribution from the second sub-interval. Parameters: Slice Density: Determined by the simulation grid. Compression: Run-length encoding is used for opacity data. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Round-off: If two slices are too close together, computed opacity values are subject to increased round-off error due to finite precision arithmetic. Truncation to Zero: If planes are sufficiently close, computed opacities truncate to zero, causing the slice to become invisible. Orientation Adjustment: Opacity must be adjusted if the slice orientation is not the primary YZ plane and the inter-plane distance differs from the base grid spacing \Delta x. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of slices and the cost of solving the RTE per slice. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 3D domain data and compressed opacity maps for the current frame. Performance: Relies on video hardware for combining slices. Strengths: Allows rendering of complex 3D data by breaking it into manageable 2D problems. Limitations: Susceptible to numerical round-off errors and opacity truncation when slice spacing is very small. When to use: Suitable for visualizing smoke and fire data where the grid spacing is not excessively fine. When not to use: When slice planes are so close that opacities truncate to zero, or when high precision is required without the risk of finite precision errors associated with slice splitting. The method originates from techniques for visualizing fire dynamics simulation data, specifically smoke and fire. It is described in the technical reference guide for Smokeview (Version 6), a tool for visualizing Fire Dynamics Simulation (FDS) data. The approach distinguishes itself from volume rendering by partitioning the integration path of the RTE across individual slice planes within a single mesh, rather than integrating over the entire data mesh from front to back. Smokeview (Version 6) A Tool for Visualizing Fire Dynamics Simulation Data Volume II: Technical Reference Guide, https://doi.org/10.6028/nist.sp.1017-2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Volume Integral Attenuation
head: Volume Integral Model, Attenuated Volume Integral
body: Volume Integral Attenuation is a method for computing cumulative attenuated information along a ray in participating media, accounting for light angle and density decay. It differs from the standard volume rendering equation by explicitly integrating the product of incident light, density, and an exponential attenuation term over the ray parameter. It is distinct from NeRF Rendering Formula [1362-nerf-rendering-formula.md] and Discrete Volume Transmittance Integration [3905-discrete-volume-transmittance-integration.md]. Inputs: Ray parameter t (and differential dt). Incident light intensity I at the voxel. Local density D at the voxel. Angle \Theta between the light direction I and the eye direction E at the voxel. Decay constant \tau. Density field D(s) along the path from the voxel to the light source. Outputs: Cumulative attenuated information B. Data Structures: The method operates on continuous integrals. In implementation, this requires evaluating the inner integral \int D ds for every sample point along the ray to determine the optical depth to the light source. Formula: The cumulative attenuated information B is defined as: B = \int I D (\cos \Theta) e^{-\tau \int D ds} dt Where: B: Cumulative attenuated information along the ray. I: Light intensity. D: Density at the current voxel. \Theta: Angle between light direction I and eye direction E at each voxel on the ray. \tau: Decay constant. ds: Accumulated density element between the current voxel and the light source. \int D ds: The accumulated density (optical depth) between the voxel and the light source. Steps: 1. For each sample point along the ray parameterized by t: 2. Calculate the angle \Theta between the incident light vector and the eye vector at the sample location. 3. Compute the accumulated density \int D ds from the sample point to the light source by integrating the density field D along the path to the light. 4. Calculate the attenuation factor e^{-\tau \int D ds} using the decay constant \tau and the accumulated density. 5. Compute the integrand I D (\cos \Theta) e^{-\tau \int D ds}. 6. Evaluate the integral over t to obtain B. Parameters: \tau: Decay constant. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The inner integral \int D ds requires knowledge of the density distribution between the voxel and the light source, which may be computationally expensive to evaluate for every sample. The angle \Theta must be computed at each voxel on the ray. An attenuation formula that values all cells equally regardless of size, used to reveal details in CFD flows where small cells are important. It evaluates attenuation separately for each cell wall. This method does not require knowledge of the distance between cell wall intersections. Unlike exponential attenuation which reduces the impact of small cells, this method ensures small cells (often the most important in CFD) are not reduced in impact due to their size. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Explicitly accounts for light angle and density decay in a single integral formulation. The Equal-Weight variant preserves details in small cells critical for CFD visualization. Limitations: Requires integration of density to the light source for every sample, which can be computationally intensive. When to use it: Use when accurate modeling of light angle and density decay is required, or when visualizing CFD flows where small cell details must be preserved. name: Distance Sampling
head: Distance Sampling for Free Paths, Inverse CDF sampling for transmittance, Monte Carlo with Distance Sampling (MCDS)
body: Distance sampling is a Monte Carlo technique used to estimate the Volume Rendering Equation (VRE) by importance sampling the non-recursive terms, specifically the medium extinction transmittance, to determine the free flight distance (distance to the next collision). It differs from its siblings, such as Whole Volume Distance Sampling and Ray Marching, by distributing samples proportional to the transmittance along the current path segment while ignoring the overall shape of the medium or global geometry. This makes it suitable for homogeneous media but prone to higher variance in complex, occluded scenes compared to global importance sampling methods. Inputs: Homogeneous medium extinction coefficient \mut (constant throughout the volume). A uniform random number \xi drawn from [0, 1]. Outputs: Sampled free path distance t. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required for the basic homogeneous case; the method relies on scalar arithmetic. Steps: 1. Generate a uniform random number \xi \in [0, 1]. 2. Define the probability density function (PDF) for the free path distance in a homogeneous medium by normalizing the transmittance function T(t): p(t) = \mut e^{-\mut t} = \mut T(t) where T(t) = e^{-\mut t} is the transmittance over distance t. 3. Compute the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) P(t) by integrating the PDF from 0 to t: P(t) = \int0^t p(t') dt' = 1 - e^{-\mut t} 4. Invert the CDF to solve for t given \xi = P(t): \xi = 1 - e^{-\mut t} t = \frac{-\ln(1 - \xi)}{\mut} 5. Return t as the sampled distance to the next collision. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def sampledistancehomogeneous(mut: float) -> float: """ Samples the free path distance in a homogeneous medium with extinction coefficient mut. Args: mut: Homogeneous medium extinction coefficient (constant). Returns: t: The sampled distance to the next collision. """ # Step 1: Generate uniform random number in [0, 1) xi = random.random() # Step 2-4: Inverse CDF sampling # t = -ln(1 - xi) / mut # Since xi is uniform in [0, 1), 1-xi is uniform in (0, 1]. # Using -ln(xi) is numerically equivalent and avoids subtraction. t = -math.log(xi) / mut return t Parameters: \mut: Homogeneous medium extinction coefficient. It is constant throughout the volume. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Heterogeneous Media: This specific closed-form inversion works only for homogeneous media where \mut is constant. For heterogeneous media, \mut varies with position, making the transmittance integral non-invertible analytically, requiring different strategies like Rejection Sampling for Arbitrary Media or Closed-form Tracking with specific density functions. Precision: If \xi is exactly 1.0, \ln(1-\xi) becomes undefined. Standard uniform random generators typically return values in 0, 1), but guards should be implemented. Variance in Complex Geometry: Distance sampling ignores the overall shape of the medium and global occluders. It distributes samples proportional to the distance to the observer along the ray segment, which does not perfectly match the transmittance integrand in complex scenes, leading to higher variance than methods like [Whole Volume Distance Sampling. Importance samples the integration domain according to the geometry-dependent transmittance of the entire participating medium, reducing variance in occluded areas. Samples free-flight distance where the extinction coefficient follows a simple analytical form, relying on local analytical invertibility. An unbiased Monte Carlo technique for heterogeneous media using a constant upper bound for rejection steps. Uses non-exponential statistical distributions (e.g., Gamma, Uniform) to sample free-flight distance in complex extinction profiles. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample for homogeneous media, involving a logarithm and division. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring only scalar storage for \mut and the random number. Measured Performance: In benchmarks on an RTX 8000 GPU, distance sampling (MCDS) performs well at very low sample counts but exhibits a lower convergence rate at higher sample counts compared to Whole Volume Distance Sampling (MCWVDS) due to its simple geometry assumptions. Strengths: Good convergence at very low sample counts; efficient for homogeneous media. Limitations: High variance in complex, occluded scenes; ignores global geometry; not directly applicable to heterogeneous media without modification. When to use: Homogeneous participating media. When not to use: Heterogeneous media, or scenes with complex occluders where global importance sampling (e.g., Whole Volume Distance Sampling) is required for acceptable variance. Distance sampling originates from Monte Carlo integration techniques for the Volume Rendering Equation. It is a standard approach for solving the VRE by importance sampling the non-recursive terms. The technique relies on the statistical independence of atoms in the medium and the exponential distribution of free paths in homogeneous media. It is often contrasted with ray marching, which distributes samples at equal distances, and whole-volume methods that account for global geometry. The method is foundational in path tracing frameworks for participating media. name: Whole Volume Distance Sampling
head: Histogram-based Transmittance Sampling, Importance Sampling for Volume Rendering, Monte Carlo with Whole Volume Distance Sampling
body: Whole Volume Distance Sampling is a Monte Carlo technique for estimating the Volume Rendering Equation that importance samples the integration domain according to the geometry-dependent transmittance of the entire participating medium, rather than limiting sampling to the transmittance along a single ray. It reduces variance in occluded areas compared to ray marching by considering the geometry along the entire camera line segment, rather than limiting sampling to the transmittance along a single ray. It differs from classic techniques by accounting for the global geometry of the medium, not just local transmittance. Inputs: Camera ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Light ray geometry defining the trapezoid segments (corners \tilde{\mathbf{p}}i and distance vectors \tilde{\mathbf{w}}i). Medium extinction coefficient \sigmat. Speed of light c (used in the sampling function derivation). Uniform random number r \in [0, 1]. Outputs: Distance t along the camera ray from the origin to the scattering event. Data Structures: Histogram of Integrals: An array \mathcal{I} where \mathcal{I}k is the integral of transmittance for the k-th trapezoid segment. Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF): Derived from \mathcal{I}, stored as cumulative sums normalized by the total unoccluded integral T{\text{total}}. Segment Geometry: For each segment i, the corner positions \tilde{\mathbf{p}}i and distance vectors \tilde{\mathbf{w}}i. Boundary Distances: d{E,S} (distance to entry boundary) and d{E,E} (distance to exit boundary) for the segment. Camera Ray Bounds: t{C,S} (start distance) and t{C,E} (end distance) for the segment. Steps: 1. Build Histogram: Integrate the transmittance of each trapezoid segment using the trapezoid integration algorithm to obtain \mathcal{I}k for all segments k. 2. Compute CDF: Calculate the total unoccluded integral T{\text{total}} = T{\text{box}}(\tilde{\omega}i, \tilde{\omega}o, tS). Compute the cumulative integral for segment i as \sum{k=1}^i \mathcal{I}{k-1} with \mathcal{I}0 = 0. 3. Select Segment: Compare the random value r against the normalized cumulative integrals to select the appropriate trapezoid segment i. 4. Transform Random Value: Map r to an intermediate value Ti(r) \in [0, 1] specific to segment i using the formula: Ti(r) = \frac{\mathcal{I}{\text{total}} r - \sum{k=1}^i \mathcal{I}{k-1}}{\mathcal{I}i} where \mathcal{I}{\text{total}} is the sum of all segment integrals. 5. Compute Distance: Use the inversion method to derive the distance offset from Ti(r). The sampling function S{\text{hist}}(r) selects the segment-specific function Ss: S{\text{hist}}(r) = Ss(Ti(r), \tilde{\mathbf{p}}i, \tilde{\mathbf{w}}i, t{C,i-1}, di) The core calculation involves a scaled logarithm function: \text{offset} = \frac{-\log(1 - (1 - Eu) Ti(r))}{\sigmat c} where Eu is the upper bound component of the trapezoid segment radiance integral. 6. Handle Degeneracy: If the slope c \to 0, the sampling simplifies to multiplication by the distance between the starting and end point. 7. Final Distance: Add the starting distance t{C,S} to the offset to get the final distance from the origin along the camera ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def wholevolumedistancesampling(r, sigmat, c, segments, totalintegral): """ r: Uniform random float in [0, 1] sigmat: Extinction coefficient c: Slope parameter segments: List of segment objects, each containing: integral: Ii (integral of transmittance for this segment) cumintegral: Sum of Ik for k < i p: Corner positions (tildep) w: Distance vectors (tildew) tCS: Start distance along camera ray dES: Distance to entry boundary dEE: Distance to exit boundary Eu: Upper bound component of radiance integral totalintegral: Ttotal (sum of all segment integrals) Returns: Distance t along the camera ray. """ # Step 1 & 2: Segment geometry and integrals are precomputed. # Step 3: Select segment by comparing r against normalized cumulative integrals. selectedsegment = None for seg in segments: rangestart = seg.cumintegral / totalintegral rangeend = (seg.cumintegral + seg.integral) / totalintegral if rangestart <= r < rangeend: selectedsegment = seg break # Guard for r = 1.0 or floating point edge cases if selectedsegment is None: selectedsegment = segments[-1] r = 0.999999 # Step 4: Transform random value Ti(r) numerator = totalintegral r - selectedsegment.cumintegral denominator = selectedsegment.integral if denominator == 0: return selectedsegment.tCS Tir = numerator / denominator Tir = max(0.0, min(1.0, Tir)) # Step 5 & 6: Compute distance using inversion method if abs(c) < 1e-9: # Degenerate case: c -> 0, sampling simplifies to multiplication by distance between start and end point offset = Tir (selectedsegment.dEE - selectedsegment.dES) else: # Scaled logarithm function Eu = selectedsegment.Eu arg = 1.0 - (1.0 - Eu) Tir if arg <= 0: arg = 1e-9 offset = -math.log(arg) / (sigmat c) # Step 7: Final distance t = selectedsegment.tCS + offset return t Whole Volume Importance Sampling is a Monte Carlo strategy for volume rendering that samples the integration domain according to the geometry-dependent transmittance of the entire participating medium, rather than limiting sampling to the transmittance along a single ray. It solves high-variance noise by incorporating both camera and light ray geometries into the probability density function, delivering lower variance images and superior convergence compared to independent sampling and distance sampling methods. It differs from classic techniques by accounting for the global geometry of the medium, not just local transmittance. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On an RTX 8000 GPU at 1024 spp, MCWVDS on a room scene took 10.4 ± 0.1 ms, compared to 11.0 ± 0.5 ms for Ray Marching (RM). On a GTX 980 Ti GPU at 256 spp, MCWVDS on a room scene took 9.2 ± 0.1 ms, compared to 10.3 ± 0.2 ms for RM. On a Pro 560X GPU at 128 spp, MCWVDS on a room scene took 40 ± 4 ms, compared to 37 ± 4 ms for RM. Strengths: Converges in a single sample in unoccluded sections and leads to noticeable variance reduction in the rest of the scene, outperforming ray marching and distance sampling at low sample counts. Limitations: Depends on a logarithmic function which is not directly supported by the GPU, requiring fallback to linear segment sampling in corner cases, which may impact performance. Whole Volume Distance Sampling was introduced in the paper "Collimated Whole Volume Light Scattering in Homogeneous Finite Media". It differs from existing distance sampling which accounts only for transmittance along the current path segment; this technique considers geometry along the entire camera line segment. The method is implemented as part of the Monte Carlo with Whole Volume Distance Sampling (MCWVDS) integrator. name: Whole Volume Importance Sampling
head: Geometry-Dependent Transmittance Sampling, Importance Sampling Scheme
body: Whole Volume Importance Sampling is a Monte Carlo strategy for volume rendering that samples the integration domain according to the geometry-dependent transmittance of the entire participating medium, rather than limiting sampling to the transmittance along a single ray. It solves high-variance noise by incorporating both camera and light ray geometries into the probability density function, delivering lower variance images and superior convergence compared to independent sampling and distance sampling methods. It differs from classic techniques by accounting for the global geometry of the medium, not just local transmittance. Inputs and outputs: Not given in the sources. Data structures: The medium geometry is decomposed into trapezoid-shaped segments defined by the intersection of camera and light rays with the medium boundaries. Variables describing each segment are cached to avoid repeated traversal. Steps: 1. Geometry Traversal: Traverse the edges of the medium bounding box from corner to corner to connect incident and outgoing exit points from the medium, decomposing it into trapezoid-shaped segments. 2. Segment Selection: Select a segment based on a probability distribution proportional to the geometry-dependent transmittance of that segment. 3. Sample Generation: Generate a sample position within the selected segment according to the local transmittance distribution. 4. Weight Calculation: Compute the importance sampling weight as the ratio of the integrand to the PDF of the selected segment and position. Formulas: The sampling PDF p(\mathbf{x}) is derived to match exactly the distribution of the geometry-dependent transmittance along a camera ray. The weight for a sample \mathbf{x} in segment i is computed as w(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{T{\text{geom}}(\mathbf{x})}{p(\mathbf{x})}, where T{\text{geom}} is the geometry-dependent transmittance and p(\mathbf{x}) is the sampling PDF. The exact mathematical formulation of T{\text{geom}} is not provided in the sources. Standard transmittance along a ray is T(\mathbf{x}) = \exp\left(-\int{\mathbf{o}}^{\mathbf{x}} \sigmat(\mathbf{u}) d\mathbf{u}\right). Parameters: Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def wholevolumeimportancesampling(camorigin, camdir, lightorigin, lightdir, boxmin, boxmax, sigmat): # Precomputation: Geometry Traversal & Caching # Intersect camera and light rays with the bounding box to find entry/exit points. camtmin, camtmax = rayboxintersection(camorigin, camdir, boxmin, boxmax) lighttmin, lighttmax = rayboxintersection(lightorigin, lightdir, boxmin, boxmax) # Decompose the medium into trapezoid-shaped segments by connecting exit points. # Exact traversal algorithm not given in the sources. # For a single convex volume, we approximate the sampling domain as the intersection interval. segments = [] tstart = max(camtmin, lighttmin) tend = min(camtmax, lighttmax) if tend > tstart: segments.append({"tmin": tstart, "tmax": tend, "length": tend - tstart}) if not segments: return None, 0.0 # Compute geometry-dependent transmittance for each cached segment segmentcontributions = [] for seg in segments: # Transmittance distribution matches the geometry-dependent transmittance along the ray transmittance = math.exp(-sigmat seg["length"]) segmentcontributions.append(transmittance) totalcontribution = sum(segmentcontributions) if totalcontribution == 0: return None, 0.0 # Normalize to form the segment selection PDF segmentpdfs = [t / totalcontribution for t in segmentcontributions] # Step 2: Segment Selection segidx = random.choices(range(len(segments)), weights=segmentpdfs, k=1)[0] selectedseg = segments[segidx] # Step 3: Sample Generation # Sample a position within the selected segment according to the local transmittance distribution u = random.random() samplet = selectedseg["tmin"] + u selectedseg["length"] sampleposition = camorigin + samplet camdir # Step 4: Weight Calculation # Weight = Integrand / PDF. Tgeom(x) is the geometry-dependent transmittance at the sample point # Distance along the ray from the camera origin to the sample raydist = samplet - camtmin tgeom = math.exp(-sigmat raydist) # PDF for a uniform sample in the segment is segmentpdf / length pdfvalue = segmentpdfs[segidx] / selectedseg["length"] weight = tgeom / pdfvalue return sampleposition, weight def rayboxintersection(origin, direction, boxmin, boxmax): # Standard slab method for ray-AABB intersection tmin = -math.inf tmax = math.inf for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < boxmin[i] or origin[i] > boxmax[i]: return 0.0, 0.0 else: t1 = (boxmin[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (boxmax[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) return tmin, tmax This method provides a Monte Carlo path tracing strategy to evaluate the rendering equation for the forward scattering propagator Gf^b, specifically addressing the transport of light through participating media where forward scattering dominates. It differs from standard local importance sampling (which samples phase functions and exponential depth independently at each vertex) by constructing a 7-dimensional global sampling strategy that incorporates the analytical structure of the propagator, resulting in faster convergence for infinite-dimensional scattering problems. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of segments and the cost of geometry traversal. Caching segment variables reduces repeated traversal costs. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method yields visible noise reduction and superior convergence compared to independent sampling with existing algorithms and ray marching/distance sampling methods. It requires only a single sample in unoccluded areas to compute the whole integral solution. Strengths: Lower variance images, superior convergence, applicable to multiple light sources, directly applicable to indoor scene rendering in room-scale interactive experiences. Limitations: Requires decomposition of medium geometry into segments. When to use: Path tracing frameworks where existing approaches enable combining multiple sampling strategies, especially for finite media. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in the paper "Collimated Whole Volume Light Scattering in Homogeneous Finite Media". It is part of a broader effort to optimize Monte Carlo integration for volume rendering, specifically addressing the limitations of classic techniques that limit sampling to transmittance along a single ray. The technique generalizes to multiple scattering and progressive rendering. name: Importance Sampling for Forward Scattering Propagator
head: Global Importance Sampling, MIS Sampling Scheme
body: This method provides a Monte Carlo path tracing strategy to evaluate the rendering equation for the forward scattering propagator Gf^b, specifically addressing the transport of light through participating media where forward scattering dominates. It differs from standard local importance sampling (which samples phase functions and exponential depth independently at each vertex) by constructing a 7-dimensional global sampling strategy that incorporates the analytical structure of the propagator, resulting in faster convergence for infinite-dimensional scattering problems. The method evaluates the rendering equation for the propagator Gf^b by importance sampling a query point \vec{x}i on the surface, directions \hat{\omega}e^i and \hat{\omega}i^i, and a path length s. The integral to be solved is: Li(\vec{x}0, \dot{\omega}0^i) = \int \mathrm{d}s \mathrm{d}A(\vec{x}i) \mathrm{d}^2 \dot{\omega}i^c G0^b(s, \vec{x}0, -\dot{\omega}0^i, \vec{x}i, \dot{\omega}i^c) |\dot{\omega}i^c \cdot \hat{n}(\vec{x}i)| \times \left[ Le(\vec{x}i, \dot{\omega}i^c) + \int \mathrm{d}^2 \dot{\omega}i^i Li(\vec{x}i, \dot{\omega}i^i) fs(\vec{x}i, \dot{\omega}i^i \leftrightarrow \dot{\omega}i^c) |\dot{\omega}i^i \cdot \hat{n}(\vec{x}i)| \right] where \vec{x}0 is the camera position, \dot{\omega}0^i is the incoming direction, \vec{x}i is the surface query point, \dot{\omega}i^c is the camera direction from the surface, Le is emitted radiance, fs is the surface BSDF, and \hat{n} is the surface normal. The sampling space is 7-dimensional: \vec{x}i (2D surface coordinates), s (1D path length), \hat{\omega}e^i (2D outgoing direction), and \hat{\omega}i^i (2D incident direction). The algorithm uses a one-sample Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) weighted combination of two main strategies: an Indirect approach (analytical approximations) and a Direct approach (next event estimation). Surface Point \vec{x}i: 3D coordinates on the object surface. Path Length s: Scalar float representing distance traveled in the medium. Directions \hat{\omega}e^i, \hat{\omega}i^i: Unit 3D vectors. MIS Weights: Standard balance heuristic weights computed from the PDFs of the two sampling strategies. 1. Sample Surface Point \vec{x}i: Use a one-sample MIS combination of two methods to select \vec{x}i on the surface: Method A (Offset Projection): Sample an offset in a plane passing through the origin point \vec{x}o (camera/previous vertex) and project this point onto the surface geometry. Method B (Ballistic Peak): Sample a direction for the vector \vec{R} based on the marginalization of the short length weight of the propagator (Eq. 10 in source) and shoot a ray along this direction to capture the initial ballistic peak. Note: This step uses local information and ray-traced projection. It is performed first while the propagator marginalized over other dimensions is still broad and smooth. 2. Indirect Sampling (Analytical Approximation): Given \vec{x}i, sample the remaining variables using analytical limits of the directionally marginalized Gf: Sample s: Use an MIS combination of analytical limit results for Gf in the regimes of large and small ps (where p is a parameter related to the dipole model). Sample \hat{\omega}e^i: Sample based on the exponential weight of Gf (Eq. 9 in source). Sample \hat{\omega}i^i: Use the boundary BSDF fs with the sampled \hat{\omega}e^i to sample the incident direction \hat{\omega}i^i. Note that \hat{\omega}i^i may point back into the medium if internal reflection occurs. 3. Direct Sampling (Next Event Estimation): This approach is MIS-weighted against the Indirect approach: Sample \hat{\omega}i^i: Directly sample a direction towards a light source. Sample \hat{\omega}e^i: Use the adjoint BSDF with the sampled \hat{\omega}i^i to sample the direction \hat{\omega}e^i into the medium. Sample s: Use a specialized path length sampler that utilizes knowledge of \hat{\omega}e^i to generate a suitable length s. 4. Throughput Management: If the sampled direction reflects back into the medium, apply a simple path splitting approach based on the current path throughput to keep throughput near unity. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sampleforwardscatteringpropagator(x0, omega0i, surface, bsdf, lights, dipolemodel): """ Evaluates the rendering equation for the forward scattering propagator Gf^b. Args: x0: Camera/previous vertex position (vec3) omega0i: Incoming direction (vec3) surface: Surface geometry object with intersection and normal methods bsdf: Surface BSDF object with sample, sampleadjoint, and eval methods lights: List of light sources dipolemodel: Forward scattering dipole model providing Gf approximations Returns: radiance: Estimated radiance Li """ # Step 1: Sample surface point xi using one-sample MIS # Method A: Offset projection offseta = randomvectorinplanethrough(x0) # xia, valida = projecttosurface(x0, offseta, surface) # pdfa = computepdfoffsetprojection(offseta, surface) # # Method B: Ballistic peak sampling directionR = sampledirectionfromshortlengthweight(dipolemodel) # hitb = rayintersect(x0, directionR, surface) # xib = hitb.point if hitb else None pdfb = computepdfballisticsampling(directionR, dipolemodel) # # MIS combination if valida and xib is not None: weighta = pdfa / (pdfa + pdfb) if random() < weighta: xi, pdfx, strategy = xia, pdfa, "A" else: xi, pdfx, strategy = xib, pdfb, "B" elif valida: xi, pdfx, strategy = xia, pdfa, "A" elif xib is not None: xi, pdfx, strategy = xib, pdfb, "B" else: return 0.0 # No intersection found normal = surfacenormal(xi) # # Step 2: Indirect Sampling sindirect = samplesfromdipolelimits(dipolemodel, xi, x0) # omegaeindirect = sampledirectionfromexponentialweight(dipolemodel, xi, x0, sindirect) # omegaiindirect, pdfbsdfindirect = bsdfsample(omegaeindirect, xi) # # Step 3: Direct Sampling light, omegaidirect, pdflight = samplelightdirection(xi, lights) # omegaedirect, pdfbsdfdirect = bsdfsampleadjoint(omegaidirect, xi) # sdirect = samplesspecialized(dipolemodel, xi, x0, omegaedirect) # # Evaluate contributions radianceindirect = evaluateintegrand(x0, omega0i, xi, omegaeindirect, omegaiindirect, sindirect, normal, bsdf, dipolemodel, lights) # pdfindirect = pdfx pdfsindirect pdfomegaeindirect pdfbsdfindirect # radiancedirect = evaluateintegrand(x0, omega0i, xi, omegaedirect, omegaidirect, sdirect, normal, bsdf, dipolemodel, lights) # pdfdirect = pdfx pdflight pdfbsdfdirect pdfsdirect # # MIS combination totalpdf = pdfindirect + pdfdirect if totalpdf == 0: return 0.0 weightindirect = pdfindirect / totalpdf weightdirect = pdfdirect / totalpdf radiance = (radianceindirect weightindirect / pdfindirect) + \ (radiancedirect weightdirect / pdfdirect) # Throughput management for back-scattering if isdirectionbackintomedium(omegaidirect, normal): # radiance = radiancesplitthroughput(radiance, paththroughputsofar) # return radiance def evaluateintegrand(x0, omega0i, xi, omegae, omegai, s, normal, bsdf, dipolemodel, lights): """Evaluates the integrand for the propagator rendering equation.""" Gballistic = dipolemodel.ballisticpropagator(s, x0, -omega0i, xi, omegae) # fs = bsdf.eval(omegai, omegae, xi) # costheta = abs(dot(omegai, normal)) # Li = 0.0 for light in lights: if light.isvisible(xi, omegai): Li += light.evalradiance(xi, omegai) # surfaceterm = Li + fs costheta # integrand = Gballistic abs(dot(omegae, normal)) surfaceterm # return integrand def randomvectorinplanethrough(origin): theta = random() 2 pi return vec3(cos(theta), sin(theta), 0) def projecttosurface(origin, offset, surface): ray = Ray(origin, offset) hit = rayintersect(ray, surface) return hit.point if hit else None, hit is not None def computepdfoffsetprojection(offset, surface): return 1.0 / (2 pi) # Uniform in plane def sampledirectionfromshortlengthweight(model): # Marginalize short length weight of Eq. 10 return normalize(model.sampleshortlengthmarginal()) def computepdfballisticsampling(direction, model): return model.shortlengthpdf(direction) def samplesfromdipolelimits(model, xi, x0): # MIS of large and small ps limits slarge = model.samplelargepslimit() ssmall = model.samplesmallpslimit() return slarge if random() < 0.5 else ssmall def sampledirectionfromexponentialweight(model, xi, x0, s): # Sample based on exponential weight of Gf (Eq. 9) return model.sampleexponentialweight(s) def bsdfsample(omegain, x): return bsdf.samplepdf(omegain, x) def samplelightdirection(x, lights): return lights[0].sampledirection(x) def bsdfsampleadjoint(omegaout, x): return bsdf.sampleadjoint(omegaout, x) def samplesspecialized(model, xi, x0, omegae): return model.specializedpathlengthsampler(omegae) def isdirectionbackintomedium(omega, normal): return dot(omega, normal) < 0 def radiancesplitthroughput(radiance, throughput): return radiance / max(throughput, 1e-6) MIS Weights: The balance heuristic is used for the one-sample MIS. Back-scattering: If a sampled direction reflects back into the medium, use path splitting to maintain throughput near unity. Approximation: The method relies on analytical approximations of the dipole model (large and small ps limits) rather than a perfect importance sampling of Gf. Convergence: Converges significantly faster than standard local importance sampling (phase function + exponential depth) because it accounts for the global geometry of the medium and the analytical form of Gf. Complexity: The sampling space is 7-dimensional, which is tractable compared to the infinite-dimensional standard path tracing problem. Limitations: The method is limited to analytical sampling schemes based on asymptotic approximations of the dipole model. It requires the ability to project offsets to surfaces and sample directions based on marginalization of the propagator's short length weight. Use Case: Preferred for rendering with forward scattering dipole models where global transport effects are significant and local sampling is suboptimal. This method was introduced in the context of a forward scattering dipole model derived from a functional integral approximation. It addresses the limitations of standard path tracers for participating media by leveraging the specific structure of the forward scattering propagator Gf^b. The approach is detailed in the supplementary material of the source paper due to space limitations, with an overview provided in the main text. name: Closed-form Tracking
head: Analytical Free-Path Sampling, Inverse Transform Sampling for Free Paths
body: Closed-form Tracking is a Monte Carlo technique for sampling the free-flight distance in participating media where the extinction coefficient follows a simple analytical form. It solves the problem of determining the distance to the next collision by applying inverse transform sampling directly to the transmittance function. It is distinguished from Whole Volume Distance Sampling by its reliance on local analytical invertibility of the optical depth integral rather than global volume statistics, allowing for exact sampling without rejection steps when the cumulative distribution function is analytically invertible. Inputs: Ray parameterization x(t) = o + t \cdot d, where o is the origin, d is the direction, and t \ge 0 is the distance. Extinction coefficient function \mut(x), typically constant, polynomial, or exponentially varying. A uniform random number \zeta \in [0, 1]. Outputs: Sampled free-path distance t0. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Define the transmittance function T(t) along the ray: T(t) = \exp\left(-\int0^t \mut(x(\tau)) d\tau\right) The probability density function (PDF) for the free path is derived by normalizing this transmittance function. 2. Determine the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF), F(t), associated with the PDF. The CDF represents the probability that a collision occurs before distance t. 3. Sample the distance t0 based on the invertibility of F(t): Case A: Analytically Invertible CDF. If F(t) can be inverted analytically, compute t0 directly using the inverse CDF F^{-1}: t0 = F^{-1}(1 - \zeta) For a homogeneous volume with constant extinction \mut, the optical thickness is \tau(t) = \mut t. The transmittance is T(t) = e^{-\mut t}. The CDF is F(t) = 1 - e^{-\mut t}. Inverting this yields the closed-form expression: t0 = -\frac{\log(1 - \zeta)}{\mut} Since \zeta is uniform in [0, 1], 1-\zeta is also uniform, so this is often implemented as t0 = -\frac{\log(\zeta)}{\mut}. Case B: Non-Invertible CDF but Analytic Optical Thickness. If F(t) is not analytically invertible, but the optical thickness integral \tau(t) = \int0^t \mut(x(\tau)) d\tau has an analytic solution, solve for t0 iteratively using Newton's method. The goal is to find t such that: 1 - \exp(-\tau(t)) = 1 - \zeta \implies \tau(t) = -\log(\zeta) Define g(t) = \tau(t) + \log(\zeta). Use Newton's iteration: t{n+1} = tn - \frac{g(tn)}{g'(tn)} = tn - \frac{\tau(tn) + \log(\zeta)}{\mut(x(tn))} Iterate until convergence. Parameters: \mut: Extinction coefficient. For homogeneous media, this is a scalar constant. For heterogeneous media, it is a function of position. \zeta: Uniform random number in [0, 1]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: When \zeta is very close to 0 or 1, logarithmic operations may suffer from floating-point precision issues. Using 1-\zeta or clamping \zeta to [\epsilon, 1-\epsilon] is recommended. Non-invertibility: If neither the CDF nor the optical thickness integral is analytically solvable, this method cannot be applied directly, and numerical root-finding or alternative sampling methods are required. Regular Tracking is a variant of closed-form tracking applied to piecewise homogeneous volumes. It handles media composed of distinct regions with constant extinction coefficients by visiting boundaries along the ray. The algorithm integrates the optical thickness of individual regions sequentially. It stops when the negative exponentiated value of the integrated optical thickness reaches a stochastically chosen value of transmittance (i.e., when the accumulated transmittance matches 1-\zeta). This method is known as surface tracking in some contexts. It becomes expensive if boundaries are not discovered quickly, such as in unstructured grids, but is efficient with hierarchical structures like grids or octrees. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method is computationally efficient for simple media where the inverse CDF is closed-form. For Regular Tracking, it quickly becomes expensive as it requires identifying all boundaries along the ray, especially when free paths cross many boundaries. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Exact sampling without rejection when the CDF is analytically invertible; computationally efficient for simple media. Limitations: Limited to media with analytically integrable extinction functions; Regular Tracking variant is slow if boundary traversal is expensive. When to use: Ideal for homogeneous media, exponential media, or piecewise homogeneous media with efficient boundary traversal. When not to use: For complex heterogeneous media where \mut(x) does not allow analytic integration or inversion. Closed-form tracking relies on inverse transform sampling, a technique first applied to Monte Carlo integration by Ulam. The specific application to volume rendering for simple extinction profiles is detailed in spectral and decomposition tracking literature. Regular Tracking (or surface tracking) was introduced by Sutton et al. and further discussed by Leppänen. Newton's method for solving the optical thickness equation was referenced from Brown and Martin. name: Rejection Sampling for Arbitrary Media
head: Rejection sampling for transmittance, Unbiased distance sampling for arbitrary media
body: Rejection Sampling for Arbitrary Media is an unbiased Monte Carlo technique to sample the distance to the next interaction point in heterogeneous participating media, avoiding the bias of classic ray marching. It handles arbitrary extinction distributions by using a constant upper bound for rejection steps to handle heterogeneity. Inputs: x0: The starting position of the ray. \omega: The direction of the ray. \sigmat: A constant extinction coefficient such that \sigmat \ge \sigmat(x) for all x along the ray. \sigmat(x): The spatially varying extinction coefficient function. Outputs: t: The sampled distance to the next interaction point, distributed according to the target density p(t) = \sigmat(x0 + t\omega)e^{-K(t)}, where K(t) = \int0^t \sigmat(x0 + t'\omega) dt'. Data Structures: No specific data structures are required beyond the ability to evaluate \sigmat(x) at arbitrary points along the ray. Steps: 1. Sample a candidate distance t{\text{cand}} from an exponential distribution with rate \sigmat: t{\text{cand}} = -\ln(u1) / \sigmat, where u1 \sim \mathcal{U}0,1). 2. Evaluate the extinction coefficient at the candidate position x{\text{cand}} = x0 + t{\text{cand}}\omega: \sigma{\text{eval}} = \sigmat(x{\text{cand}}). 3. Generate a uniform random number u2 \sim \mathcal{U}[0,1). 4. Check the rejection condition: if u2 \le \sigma{\text{eval}} / \sigmat, accept the sample and return t = t{\text{cand}}. 5. If rejected, accumulate the distance t \leftarrow t + t{\text{cand}} and repeat from Step 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sampledistance(x0, omega, sigmatmax, sigmatfunc): """ Unbiased distance sampling for arbitrary media using rejection sampling. Args: x0 (Point): Starting position. omega (Direction): Ray direction. sigmatmax (float): Constant upper bound for extinction coefficient. sigmatfunc (function): Function evaluating sigmat(x) at position x. Returns: float: Distance to the next interaction point. """ # rand() returns a uniform random number in [0, 1) t = 0.0 while True: u1 = rand() tcand = -log(u1) / sigmatmax xcand = x0 + tcand omega sigmaeval = sigmatfunc(xcand) u2 = rand() if u2 <= sigmaeval / sigmatmax: return t + tcand t += tcand Parameters: \sigmat: The constant extinction coefficient upper bound. It must satisfy \sigmat \ge \sigmat(x) for all x along the ray. A larger \sigmat increases the number of iterations but remains unbiased. Determining the global supremum \sup{x \in V} \sigmat(x) during preprocessing is common, though determining the maximum along a single ray is more complex. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Choosing a \sigmat larger than the true supremum increases the number of iterations in the rejection loop without introducing bias. The method assumes the ability to evaluate \sigmat(x) at arbitrary points along the ray. An unbiased Monte Carlo procedure for determining the next interaction point in participating media, supporting both [volume scattering and surface interactions. It generalizes standard distance sampling by allowing arbitrary non-exponential extinction distributions (e.g., Gamma-distributed media) while maintaining the efficiency of delta tracking. Unlike Rejection Sampling for Arbitrary Media, which relies on rejection steps to handle heterogeneity, this method uses a pre-computed base medium model to sample optical depth directly, inverting it to find physical distance, and adjusting weights based on surface proximity. Time Complexity: The expected number of iterations depends on the ratio of the upper bound \sigmat to the actual extinction coefficient \sigmat(x). Memory Complexity: Minimal, requiring only storage for the current distance and random numbers. Strengths: Unbiased result for arbitrary media distributions. Simple to implement. Limitations: Can be inefficient if the upper bound \sigmat is much larger than the actual extinction coefficient along the ray, leading to many rejections. Not suitable for media where \sigmat(x) cannot be evaluated efficiently. When to use: When unbiased sampling is required for heterogeneous media and the extinction coefficient can be evaluated at arbitrary points. The method was introduced by Colvins in 1968. It provides an unbiased alternative to the biased classic ray marching algorithm. It is used in global illumination algorithms for participating media to correctly sample the distance to the next interaction point.
