name: Energy-based Volume Rendering (Energy Engine)
head: Energy Mode Rendering, VTK-m Energy Tracing
body: Energy-based Volume Rendering is a deterministic ray-marching technique that separates absorption/scattering (primary field) and emission (secondary field) into distinct ray buffers, processed in ENERGYMODE by a connectivity-based ray tracer. It differs from standard emission-absorption ray marching by maintaining separate accumulation paths for primary optical depth and secondary emission energy. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A structured dataset containing scalar fields for absorption/scattering coefficients and optionally for emission coefficients. Output: A rendered image where pixel values represent the accumulated energy, derived from the primary absorption buffer and the secondary emission buffer. Data Structures: The method relies on the RenderSettings struct to configure the tracer. The layout is defined as follows: mrendermode: Enum (RenderMode). Controls the rendering pass type. mscatteringtype: Enum (ScatteringType). Defines the scattering model. mrayscope: Enum (RayScope). Defines the ray traversal scope. mcolortable: String identifier for the transfer function/color map (e.g., "cool2warm"). mprimaryfield: String name of the dataset array containing absorption/scattering coefficients. msecondaryfield: String name of the dataset array containing emission coefficients. An empty string disables emission. mvolumesettings: Struct containing volume-specific settings. menergysettings: Struct containing energy-specific settings. mpathlengths: Boolean flag (default false). Parameters: munitscalar: Float scaling factor for energy values during tracing. Default: 1.0. mrendermode: Default: volume (supports energy). mscatteringtype: Default: nonscattering. mrayscope: Default: globalrays. mcolortable: Default: "cool2warm". Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create a ConnectivityProxy from the input dataset. Set its render mode to ENERGYMODE. 2. Primary Field Assignment: Assign the dataset array specified by mprimaryfield to the tracer. This field represents the absorption/scattering coefficients. 3. Secondary Field Assignment: If msecondaryfield is not empty, assign the corresponding dataset array as the emission field. If empty, emission is disabled. 4. Primary Ray Buffer Setup: Initialize the primary ray buffer (index 0) with numbins channels. Set all initial values to 1.0. This buffer tracks the transmittance (energy remaining after absorption). 5. Emission Buffer Setup: If emission is enabled (step 3), allocate an emission buffer with numbins channels. Initialize all values to 0.0. This buffer accumulates emitted energy along the ray. 6. Ray Traversal: Execute the ray traversal and accumulation by calling PartialTrace on the tracer. The tracer uses the connectivity information to traverse the volume, updating the primary buffer based on absorption and the emission buffer based on emission contributions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class ConnectivityProxy: def init(self, dataset): self.dataset = dataset self.rendermode = None self.primaryfield = None self.secondaryfield = None self.primarybuffer = None self.emissionbuffer = None self.rendersettings = None def setrendermode(self, mode): self.rendermode = mode def assignfield(self, name, fieldtype): if fieldtype == "PRIMARY": self.primaryfield = name else: self.secondaryfield = name def setprimarybuffer(self, buf): self.primarybuffer = buf def setemissionbuffer(self, buf): self.emissionbuffer = buf def setrendersettings(self, settings): self.rendersettings = settings def partialtrace(self): # The sources do not provide the internal traversal and accumulation logic for PartialTrace. pass def getresult(self): return self.dataset def energybasedvolumerendering(dataset, primaryfieldname, secondaryfieldname=None, numbins=1): # 1. Create ConnectivityProxy from input dataset and set render mode to ENERGYMODE tracer = ConnectivityProxy(dataset) tracer.setrendermode("energy") # 2. Assign primary dataset array (absorption/scattering) to the tracer tracer.assignfield(primaryfieldname, "PRIMARY") # 3. Assign secondary dataset array as emission field if provided if secondaryfieldname is not None and secondaryfieldname != "": tracer.assignfield(secondaryfieldname, "SECONDARY") else: tracer.secondaryfield = "" # 4. Initialize primary ray buffer (index 0) with numbins channels, set all to 1.0 primarybuffer = [1.0] numbins tracer.setprimarybuffer(primarybuffer) # 5. Initialize emission buffer with numbins channels, set all to 0.0 if enabled if tracer.secondaryfield != "": emissionbuffer = [0.0] numbins tracer.setemissionbuffer(emissionbuffer) else: tracer.setemissionbuffer(None) # 6. Configure RenderSettings settings = { "mrendermode": "energy", "mscatteringtype": "nonscattering", "mrayscope": "globalrays", "mcolortable": "cool2warm", "mprimaryfield": primaryfieldname, "msecondaryfield": tracer.secondaryfield, "munitscalar": 1.0, "mpathlengths": False } tracer.setrendersettings(settings) # 7. Execute ray traversal and accumulation tracer.partialtrace() # 8. Retrieve results resultimage = tracer.getresult() return resultimage Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The implementation supports both single (vtkm::Float32) and double (vtkm::Float64) precision. Switching precision requires deleting and recreating the scheduler. MPI Parallelism: If MPI is enabled, the communication handle must be set correctly using setmpicommhandle. Empty Secondary Field: If msecondaryfield is empty, the emission buffer is not allocated, and no emission accumulation occurs. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays and the number of steps per ray (determined by volume resolution and ray length). Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of rays times the number of bins (numbins) for the primary and emission buffers, plus the storage for the input dataset arrays. Strengths: Separates absorption and emission logic, allowing for independent control and debugging of energy loss and gain. Suitable for scenarios where emission needs to be attenuated by the medium's absorption properties in a physically plausible way. Limitations: Requires managing two separate buffers. Performance may be impacted by the overhead of the connectivity proxy and buffer management compared to simpler single-buffer ray marchers. When to Use: Use when you need to render volumes where emission is significant and must be correctly attenuated by absorption, or when you need to analyze the separate contributions of absorption and emission. When Not to Use: Avoid for simple opacity-based rendering where emission is negligible or handled via standard compositing. Avoid if memory bandwidth is a critical bottleneck and single-buffer accumulation suffices. Energy-based Volume Rendering is implemented within the Rover framework, developed by Lawrence Livermore National Security, LLC. The method leverages the ConnectivityProxy and EnergyEngine components to handle the specific requirements of energy mode rendering, separating the optical depth calculation from the emission accumulation. llnl/rover, https://github.com/llnl/rover, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Neural Plasma Field Ray Casting with LUT Emissivity
head: Neural Plasma Field Ray Casting, Ray Sampling and Rendering Geometry
body: A forward rendering pipeline that casts rays through a normalized axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) to sample a neural plasma field and compute emissivity via a precomputed Look-Up Table (LUT). It solves the problem of synthesizing coronal images from neural network predictions of density and temperature, bridging the gap between implicit field representations and physical radiative transfer. It differs from its parent Emission-Absorption Ray Marching by explicitly handling the conversion of neural field outputs (log-density, log-temperature) into physical emissivity values using a specialized LUT, rather than relying on a fixed analytic emission model. It differs from Volumetric Liquid Rendering and Energy-based Volume Rendering (Energy Engine) by targeting solar coronal physics with specific coordinate transformations and atomic-line emissivity tables. Inputs: Neural plasma field function f\theta, which takes 3D Cartesian coordinates and outputs predictions for \log{10} ne and \log{10} Te. Emissivity Look-Up Table (LUT), a 3D tensor mapping (\log{10} ne, \log{10} Te, \log{10} r) to scalar Stokes-I emissivity. Camera parameters: heliocentric distance d \approx 215 R\odot, latitude 0^\circ, field of view (FOV) [-3, 3] R\odot. Step size \Delta s = 1/256 in AABB coordinates. Outputs: Rendered image with intensity in units of \text{photons s}^{-1} \text{cm}^{-2} \text{arcsec}^{-2}. Data Structures: 1. Neural Plasma Field f\theta: A neural network (e.g., MLP) taking input \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (AABB coordinates) and outputting a vector [\log{10} ne, \log{10} Te]. 2. Emissivity LUT: A PyTorch tensor of shape (128, 64, 32) representing the grid in (\log{10} ne, \log{10} Te, \log{10} r) space. The radial axis spans approximately \log{10}(1.001) to \log{10}(10). The tensor is implemented using torch.nn.functional.gridsample for trilinear interpolation. 3. Coordinate Systems: Physical: [-30, 30]^3 R\odot. AABB: [-1, 1]^3, obtained by dividing physical coordinates by 30 R\odot. Spherical: (r, \theta, \phi), where r = \|\mathbf{x}{\text{phys}}\|. Steps: 1. Camera Setup: For each pixel, construct a ray originating from the observer at distance d \approx 215 R\odot pointing toward the origin. The ray spans the FOV [-3, 3] R\odot. 2. Coronagraph Masking: Calculate the impact parameter of the ray. If the impact parameter is < 1 R\odot, discard the ray (mask it) to mimic a coronagraph and exclude the solar disk. 3. Ray-AABB Intersection: Compute the near (t{\text{near}}) and far (t{\text{far}}) intersection points of the ray with the normalized AABB [-1, 1]^3. 4. Sampling: Generate uniform sample points along the ray segment [t{\text{near}}, t{\text{far}}] with step size \Delta s = 1/256 in AABB coordinates. The number of samples N depends on the ray's intersection length. 5. Neural Field Query: For each sample point \mathbf{x}{\text{AABB}}: Convert to physical coordinates: \mathbf{x}{\text{phys}} = \mathbf{x}{\text{AABB}} \times 30 R\odot. Query the neural field: [\log{10} ne, \log{10} Te] = f\theta(\mathbf{x}{\text{AABB}}). Compute heliocentric radius: r = \|\mathbf{x}{\text{phys}}\|. 6. LUT Emissivity Lookup: Compute \log{10} r. Query the LUT at (\log{10} ne, \log{10} Te, \log{10} r). Clamping: If any coordinate is outside the LUT bounds, clamp to the nearest boundary value before interpolation. Let \epsilon{\text{raw}} be the interpolated value in units of \text{erg s}^{-1} \text{cm}^{-3} \text{sr}^{-1}. 7. Unit Conversion: Convert \epsilon{\text{raw}} to photon counts per arcsec^2: Convert from erg to photon counts. Convert from \text{sr}^{-1} to \text{arcsec}^{-2}. Let \epsilonc be the result in \text{photons s}^{-1} \text{cm}^{-3} \text{arcsec}^{-2}. 8. Differential Length: Compute the differential path length \Delta l for the sample segment. Scale the AABB step size \Delta s to physical units (R\odot) and then to cm. 9. Integration: Perform a midpoint Riemann sum integration along the ray: I = \sum{i=1}^{N} \epsilonc(\mathbf{x}i) \cdot \Delta li The final intensity I is in units of \text{photons s}^{-1} \text{cm}^{-2} \text{arcsec}^{-2}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def renderneuralplasmafield(ftheta, luttensor, lutbounds, cameraparams, stepsize=1/256): """ Render a single view using the Neural Plasma Field and LUT Emissivity. Args: ftheta: Neural network function returning [log10ne, log10Te] for AABB coords. luttensor: PyTorch tensor of shape (128, 64, 32) for LUT. lutbounds: Tuple of (min, max) for each LUT axis (log10ne, log10Te, log10r). cameraparams: Dict with 'distance', 'fov', 'resolution'. stepsize: Float, step size in AABB coordinates. Returns: image: Tensor of rendered intensities. """ # 1. Camera Setup # Observer at distance d, pointing to origin. FOV [-3, 3] Rsun. # Generate ray origins and directions for each pixel. # Note: Perspective rays are nearly parallel at 215 Rsun. rayorigins, raydirections = generateperspectiverays(cameraparams) # 2. Ray-AABB Intersection # AABB is [-1, 1]^3. tnear, tfar = intersectaabb(rayorigins, raydirections, aabbmin=-1.0, aabbmax=1.0) # 3. Coronagraph Masking # Calculate impact parameter for each ray. # Impact parameter < 1 Rsun -> mask out. impactparams = calculateimpactparameter(rayorigins, raydirections, observerdistance=215.0) validmask = impactparams >= 1.0 # 4. Sampling # Generate sample points along the ray segment [tnear, tfar] # Number of samples N depends on intersection length. # tsamples = torch.linspace(tnear, tfar, steps=N) # However, stepsize is fixed in AABB coords. # We calculate N based on length / stepsize. # For simplicity, assume we generate samples at uniform intervals of stepsize. # 5. Integration Loop # Initialize intensity accumulator intensities = torch.zeroslike(rayorigins[..., 0]) # Convert stepsize from AABB to physical (Rsun) # AABB range is 2 units (-1 to 1), Physical range is 60 Rsun (-30 to 30). # Scale factor: 30 Rsun per AABB unit. scalefactor = 30.0 deltasphysical = stepsize scalefactor # in Rsun # Convert Rsun to cm (approx 6.957e10 cm) Rsuntocm = 6.957e10 deltalcm = deltasphysical Rsuntocm # Process each valid ray for i in range(len(rayorigins)): if not validmask[i]: continue tstart = tnear[i] tend = tfar[i] # Calculate number of samples lengthaabb = tend - tstart numsamples = int(lengthaabb / stepsize) # Generate sample positions in AABB # Midpoint rule: samples are at tstart + (k + 0.5) stepsize sampleindices = torch.arange(numsamples) tsamples = tstart + (sampleindices + 0.5) stepsize # Get 3D coordinates in AABB # xaabb = rayorigins[i] + tsamples[:, None] raydirections[i] # Note: raydirections must be normalized for t to represent distance in AABB units? # The source says "step size 1/256 (AABB coordinates)". This implies t is in AABB units. # So raydirections should be normalized such that |direction| = 1 in AABB space? # Or t is just the parameter. Let's assume t is the parameter along the ray vector. # If raydirections are normalized to unit length in physical space, we need to adjust. # However, the source says "compute near and far bounds as intersections with the AABB". # Standard ray-AABB intersection returns t values. # Let's assume raydirections are normalized to unit length in AABB space for simplicity of stepsize. # If not, we must normalize. # Re-normalize direction to unit length in AABB space if necessary. # Assuming raydirections are already unit vectors in the coordinate system of t. xaabb = rayorigins[i] + tsamples[:, None] raydirections[i] # 6. Neural Field Query # Query ftheta for log10ne and log10Te # ftheta takes xaabb. log10ne, log10Te = ftheta(xaabb) # Shape: (numsamples, 2) # 7. LUT Emissivity Lookup # Compute radius r in physical units # xphys = xaabb 30 Rsun xphys = xaabb scalefactor r = torch.norm(xphys, dim=1) # Shape: (numsamples,) log10r = torch.log10(r) # Prepare LUT query coordinates # LUT axes: (log10ne, log10Te, log10r) # Grid coordinates for gridsample are typically normalized to [-1, 1] or [0, 1]. # We need to map log10ne, log10Te, log10r to grid indices. # Clamp to LUT bounds log10neclamped = torch.clamp(log10ne, min=lutbounds[0][0], max=lutbounds[0][1]) log10Teclamped = torch.clamp(log10Te, min=lutbounds[1][0], max=lutbounds[1][1]) log10rclamped = torch.clamp(log10r, min=lutbounds[2][0], max=lutbounds[2][1]) # Normalize to [0, 1] for gridsample # Assuming lutbounds are the min/max of the log values. def normalizeto01(val, vmin, vmax): return (val - vmin) / (vmax - vmin) coordsne = normalizeto01(log10neclamped, lutbounds[0][0], lutbounds[0][1]) coordsTe = normalizeto01(log10Teclamped, lutbounds[1][0], lutbounds[1][1]) coordsr = normalizeto01(log10rclamped, lutbounds[2][0], lutbounds[2][1]) # gridsample expects input of shape (N, C, H, W) or (N, C, D, H, W) for 3D. # And grid of shape (N,..., 3) for 3D. # Here we have 1D samples. We need to reshape for gridsample. # Let's assume we process in batches or reshape. # For simplicity, assume we can call a helper that handles the tensor reshape. # Create grid coordinates for gridsample # gridsample expects coordinates in [-1, 1]. coordsgrid = torch.stack([coordsne, coordsTe, coordsr], dim=-1) # (numsamples, 3) coordsgrid = 2.0 coordsgrid - 1.0 # Map [0,1] to [-1,1] # Reshape for gridsample: (1, 1, numsamples, 1, 1) for 3D? # Actually, gridsample for 3D takes input (N, C, D, H, W) and grid (N,..., 3). # We have 1D data. We can treat it as (1, 1, numsamples, 1, 1). # But the LUT is 3D. # Let's assume a helper function querylut handles the tensor operations. emissivityraw = querylut3d(luttensor, coordsgrid) # Shape: (numsamples,) # 8. Unit Conversion # Convert from erg/s/cm^3/sr to photons/s/cm^2/arcsec^2 # This involves physical constants and angular conversion. # Source says: "convert the raw LUT emissivity from erg to photon counts, and from steradian^-1 to arcsec^-2" # Let epsilonc be the converted value. epsilonc = convertemissivityunits(emissivityraw) # 9. Integration # Midpoint Riemann sum # I = sum(epsilonc deltal) # deltal is in cm. intensity = torch.sum(epsilonc deltalcm) intensities[i] = intensity return intensities def querylut3d(luttensor, coordsgrid): """ Query 3D LUT using gridsample. luttensor: (D, H, W) = (128, 64, 32) coordsgrid: (N, 3) in [-1, 1] """ # Reshape LUT for gridsample: (N, C, D, H, W) -> (1, 1, 128, 64, 32) # But gridsample expects input to have batch dimension. # We can process in batches. # For a single batch of N samples: # Input: (1, 1, 128, 64, 32) # Grid: (1, N, 1, 1, 3) -> (N, 1, 1, 3) ? # gridsample signature: input, grid # grid shape: (N,..., 3) # For 3D, grid is (N, Dout, Hout, Wout, 3). # We want to sample N points. So Dout=1, Hout=1, Wout=1. # Grid shape: (N, 1, 1, 1, 3). N = coordsgrid.shape[0] grid = coordsgrid.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1) # (N, 1, 1, 1, 3) # Input LUT: (1, 1, 128, 64, 32) inputlut = luttensor.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # (1, 1, 128, 64, 32) # gridsample # aligncorners=False is standard for gridsample in newer PyTorch. output = F.gridsample(inputlut, grid, aligncorners=False) # (1, 1, 1, 1, N) ? # Actually, gridsample output shape is (N, C, Dout, Hout, Wout) if input is (N, C, D, H, W). # Here input is (1, 1, 128, 64, 32). Grid is (N, 1, 1, 1, 3). # Output will be (N, 1, 1, 1, 1). # Wait, gridsample expects grid to be (N,..., 3). # If input is (1, 1, 128, 64, 32), and we want to sample N points. # We can treat N as the batch size? No, batch size is 1. # We can repeat the LUT N times? No. # We can use gridsample with batch size 1, but grid must match. # Actually, gridsample supports sampling multiple points per batch element. # Grid shape: (N, 1, 1, 1, 3). Input shape: (1, 1, 128, 64, 32). # This doesn't match batch dimensions. # Correct approach: Input (1, 1, 128, 64, 32). Grid (1, N, 1, 1, 3). # Output (1, 1, N, 1, 1). gridcorrect = coordsgrid.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(2).unsqueeze(3) # (1, N, 1, 1, 3) output = F.gridsample(inputlut, gridcorrect, aligncorners=False) # (1, 1, N, 1, 1) return output.squeeze() # (N,) A precomputed 3D table mapping \log{10} ne, \log{10} Te, and \log{10} r to scalar Stokes-I emissivity, used to convert neural field predictions into radiative values during rendering. It is constructed from PSI cube statistics and atomic-response ranges, storing values in log-space. The grid resolution is 128 \times 64 \times 32 along axes (\log{10} ne, \log{10} Te, \log{10} r). The radial LUT bounds are approximately 1.001 to 10 R\odot. Queries outside the tabulated domain are clamped to the nearest LUT boundary before interpolation, with a backstop that explicitly returns the nearest boundary value rather than zeros or linear extrapolation. It is implemented in PyTorch as a tensor-compatible structure using torch.nn.functional.gridsample for trilinear interpolation. This LUT is used both for synthetic observation generation (interpolating GT density/temperature on a spherical grid with periodic longitude wrapping) and for CoroNeRF rendering. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels and the number of samples per ray. The number of samples per ray depends on the ray's intersection length with the AABB. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the neural network weights and the LUT tensor (128 \times 64 \times 32 floats). Measured Performance: At production step size (\Delta s = 1/256), renders differ from a 4x-finer reference (\Delta s = 1/1024) by 7.5% in relative L2 error and 1.7 \times 10^{-3} in asinh image metric. Convergence is roughly first-to-second order. Strengths: Efficiently converts neural field predictions to physical emissivity; handles complex atomic physics via precomputed LUT; masks solar disk effectively. Limitations: Requires precomputation of LUT; discretization-dependent field recovery; assumes scalar Stokes-I emissivity, neglecting magnetic-field geometry terms. When to use: Synthetic dataset generation for solar corona; rendering neural plasma fields for visualization. When not to use: When high-fidelity magnetic field effects are required; when real-time rendering is critical and LUT precomputation is prohibitive. Originated in the context of neural tomography for solar corona reconstruction, specifically in the work "Image Fidelity is Not Field Fidelity: Joint Thermodynamic Reconstruction and Error Localization in Neural Tomography". The method uses oracle PSI density and temperature fields for synthetic dataset generation, which are identical to the ray sampling and integral procedures but replace the neural plasma field with ground truth fields. The oracle fields live on a spherical coordinate system, requiring transformation from AABB to spherical coordinates before sampling using spherical trilinear field interpolators. name: Emission-Absorption Volume Rendering
head: Back-to-Front Recursive Volume Rendering, Beer's Law Volume Rendering, Discrete Volume Rendering (Smokeview Approximation), Simple Volume Rendering, Smokeview RTE Discretization, Volumetric Rendering of Smoke
body: Emission-Absorption Volume Rendering is a method for visualizing participating media, specifically smoke and fire, by approximating the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) while neglecting the in-scattering integral term. It combines absorption and out-scattering into a total extinction coefficient and solves for radiance along a line of sight using a discrete back-to-front recursion based on Beer's Law. Unlike the Standard volume rendering equation which includes in-scattering, or Single Scattering Model which handles scattering explicitly, this method treats the medium as a non-scattering absorber with emission, making it computationally simpler and suitable for real-time visualization of smoke flow. It sets itself apart from Emission-Absorption Ray Marching by its specific discrete recursive formulation derived for grid-based data integration. Inputs and Outputs Input: A ray defined by origin and direction; a volumetric dataset providing extinction coefficient \sigmat, absorption coefficient \sigmaa, and emission term Ce at discrete sample points along the ray; background radiance C0 from behind the volume. Output: Final radiance CN at the observer. Data Structures The method operates on a discretized path of N segments. Sample Points: xi = x0 + i \Delta x for i = 0 \dots N, where x0 is the farthest point (background) and xN is the closest point (observer). Segment Length: \Delta x = (xN - x0) / N. Coefficients: \sigma{t,i} (total extinction), \sigma{a,i} (absorption), C{e,i} (emission) at each sample point xi. Segment Transparency: \taui for segment i, representing the fraction of light transmitted through that segment. Formulas and Definitions 1. Total Extinction: \sigmat(x) = \sigmaa(x) + \sigmas(x), combining absorption and out-scattering. 2. Approximate RTE: \frac{dC}{dx}(x) = -\sigmat(x)C(x) + \sigmaa(x)Ce(x). 3. Continuous Optical Depth: \tau(a, b) = \exp\left(-\int{a}^{b} \sigmat(s) ds\right). 4. Segment Transparency (Discrete): \taui = \exp(-\sigma{t,i} \Delta x). 5. Cumulative Transparency: \taui^{N-1} is the transparency from sample i to the closest end of the volume (N-1). 6. Emitted Radiance Contribution: \hat{C}{e,i} = \sigma{a,i} C{e,i} \Delta x. Algorithm Steps The solution is computed recursively from front to back (closest to farthest) to allow for early termination. 1. Initialize: Set cumulative transparency \tau{N-1}^{N-1} = 1 and partial radiance sum \hat{C}N^N = 0. 2. Iterate Forward (Closest to Farthest): For i from 0 to N-1: a. Compute segment transparency: \taui = \exp(-\sigma{t,i} \Delta x). b. Update cumulative transparency: \taui^{N-1} = \tau{i+1}^{N-1} \taui. c. Compute emitted contribution: \hat{C}{e,i} = \sigma{a,i} C{e,i} \Delta x. d. Update partial radiance sum: \hat{C}i^N = \hat{C}{i+1}^N + \taui^{N-1} \hat{C}{e,i}. e. Early Termination Check: If the remaining term \taui^{N-1} \hat{C}{e,i} is sufficiently small, terminate the loop. 3. Final Radiance: Compute the final radiance at the observer: CN = \tau0^{N-1} C0 + \hat{C}0^N where C0 is the background radiance. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def emissionabsorptionvolumerendering(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata, backgroundradiance, threshold=1e-4): """ Renders a ray through a volume using the emission-absorption approximation. Args: rayorigin: vec3, origin of the ray (camera position). raydirection: vec3, normalized direction of the ray. volumedata: Object providing sample(t) -> (sigmat, sigmaa, Ce) along the ray. backgroundradiance: vec3, radiance from behind the volume. threshold: float, minimum cumulative transparency to continue integration. Returns: vec3, final radiance at the observer. """ tstart = 0.0 tend = volumedata.maxdistance() numsamples = volumedata.numsamples() deltat = (tend - tstart) / numsamples taucumulative = 1.0 partialsum = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Iterate from closest (i=0) to farthest (i=numsamples-1) for i in range(numsamples): t = tstart + (i + 0.5) deltat pos = rayorigin + raydirection t sigmat, sigmaa, Ce = volumedata.sample(pos) tausegment = exp(-sigmat deltat) taucumulative = tausegment # Now taucumulative holds taui^{N-1} if taucumulative < threshold: break Chate = sigmaa Ce deltat partialsum += taucumulative Chate finalradiance = taucumulative backgroundradiance + partialsum return finalradiance Splitting Sub-intervals If the volume is composed of multiple meshes or sub-intervals, the method allows combining solutions. For an interval [x0, xN] split at D into [x0, D] and [D, xN], compute radiance C1 and optical depth \tau1 for the first interval and C2, \tau2 for the second. The combined radiance is derived by treating the output of the first interval as the background for the second. Solves the emission-absorption integral analytically using Gaussian primitives, eliminating discretization error for smooth transfer functions. Choose this when high accuracy for smooth data is required and analytical integration is feasible. A general ray-marching implementation of the emission-absorption model. Choose this for flexible, non-grid-based ray traversal or when using hardware ray tracing. Time Complexity: O(N) per ray, where N is the number of samples. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per ray, as the recursion is iterative. Performance: Fast and suitable for real-time visualization, as implemented in Smokeview. Performance depends heavily on the density of the medium; sparse media benefit greatly from early termination. Strengths: Simple implementation; efficient for smoke/fire visualization where in-scattering is negligible; supports early termination. Limitations: Neglects in-scattering, leading to inaccurate shadows and lighting interactions in dense, scattering media; discretization error depends on sample spacing. When to Use: Real-time visualization of smoke, fire, or thin clouds where in-scattering is not visually critical. When Not to Use: Scenes requiring accurate light transport with significant in-scattering, such as fog, thick clouds, or biological tissue. The method was first implemented in Smokeview (Version 6) for visualizing fire dynamics simulation data, inspired by the software tool "Frames" by James Sims. It approximates the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) by neglecting the in-scattering integral term and combining absorption and out-scattering into a total extinction coefficient. The derivation follows the Beer-Lambert law and is detailed in the NIST Technical Reference Guide for Smokeview. It is widely used in fire safety visualization tools. Smokeview (Version 6) A Tool for Visualizing Fire Dynamics Simulation Data Volume II: Technical Reference Guide, https://doi.org/10.6028/nist.sp.1017-2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Closed-Form Volume Rendering with Gaussian Transfer Functions
head: Analytically integrated segment with Gaussian TF, Closed-Form Approximation to the Volume Rendering Integral with Gaussian Transfer Functions, Gaussian primitive volume rendering
body: This method computes the emission-absorption volume rendering integral over a line segment in closed form by modeling the transfer function as a multivariate Gaussian primitive. It assumes linear variation of data values between sampled points, allowing the density integral to be solved analytically using the error function. By solving the integral analytically, the method avoids discretization errors associated with numerical sampling. Inputs: Segment endpoints in data space: \vec{v}1, \vec{v}2 (vectors of dimension N, typically 1D or multivariate). Gaussian transfer function parameters: Center \vec{c} (vector), Linear transformation matrix \mathbf{K} (matrix). Optical parameters: Constant color C, Extinction coefficient \tau. Segment length: l = b - a (physical length of the segment). Outputs: Pixel color I(a, b). The method operates on standard vectors and matrices. No specialized data structures are required. \vec{c}: Center of the Gaussian. \mathbf{K}: Linear transformation matrix defining the shape and orientation of the Gaussian. C: Emissive color (constant over the segment). \tau: Extinction coefficient (constant over the segment). l: Length of the ray segment in physical space (b-a). 1. Transform Endpoints: Compute the transformed endpoints \vec{v}'1 and \vec{v}'2 in the Gaussian's local space: \vec{v}'1 = \mathbf{K}(\vec{v}1 - \vec{c}) \vec{v}'2 = \mathbf{K}(\vec{v}2 - \vec{c}) 2. Compute Difference Vector: Calculate the difference vector \vec{d} in the transformed space: \vec{d} = \vec{v}'2 - \vec{v}'1 3. Compute Norm: Calculate the Euclidean norm of \vec{d}: \|\vec{d}\| = \sqrt{\vec{d} \cdot \vec{d}} 4. Compute Intermediate Scalars: A = \frac{\vec{d} \cdot \vec{v}'1}{\|\vec{d}\|} B = A + \|\vec{d}\| (equivalent to \frac{\vec{d} \cdot \vec{v}'2}{\|\vec{d}\|}) S = e^{-\|\vec{v}'1\|^2 + A^2} 5. Compute Average Density: Calculate the normalized density integral \rho'(v1, v2) using the error function: \rho'(v1, v2) = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2} \frac{S}{\|\vec{d}\|} (\text{erf}(B) - \text{erf}(A)) Note: The derivation assumes integration over t \in [0,1]. 6. Compute Opacity: Calculate the opacity \alpha for the segment: \alpha = 1 - e^{-\tau l \rho'(v1, v2)} 7. Compute Color: Calculate the final color contribution: I(a, b) = \frac{C \alpha}{\tau} The error function \text{erf}(z) is approximated numerically for z \geq 0 using the Abramowitz and Stegun approximation: \text{erf}(z) \approx 1 - (a1 t + a2 t^2 + a3 t^3) e^{-z^2} where: t = \frac{1}{1 + 0.47047 z} a1 = 0.3480242, \quad a2 = -0.0958798, \quad a3 = 0.7478556 For z < 0, use the odd symmetry property: \text{erf}(-z) = -\text{erf}(z). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def erfapprox(z): """Approximates erf(z) for z >= 0 using Abramowitz and Stegun.""" if z < 0: return -erfapprox(-z) a1, a2, a3 = 0.3480242, -0.0958798, 0.7478556 coeff = 0.47047 t = 1.0 / (1.0 + coeff z) poly = a1 t + a2 t2 + a3 t3 return 1.0 - poly math.exp(-z2) def segmentintegral(v1, v2, c, K, C, tau, l): """Computes the closed-form emission-absorption integral for one segment.""" v1prime = K @ (v1 - c) v2prime = K @ (v2 - c) d = v2prime - v1prime dnorm = math.sqrt(d @ d) if dnorm < 1e-10: density = math.exp(-v1prime @ v1prime) alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-tau l density) return (C / tau) alpha, alpha A = (d @ v1prime) / dnorm B = A + dnorm S = math.exp(- (v1prime @ v1prime) + A2) sqrtpiover2 = math.sqrt(math.pi) / 2.0 rhoprime = sqrtpiover2 (S / dnorm) (erfapprox(B) - erfapprox(A)) alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-tau l rhoprime) return (C / tau) alpha, alpha def renderray(origin, direction, stepsize, c, K, C, tau, maxsteps): """Front-to-back compositing loop. Sources do not specify the marching loop, so standard compositing is used.""" acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accalpha = 0.0 for i in range(maxsteps): v1 = origin + direction (i stepsize) v2 = origin + direction ((i + 1) stepsize) l = stepsize segcolor, segalpha = segmentintegral(v1, v2, c, K, C, tau, l) acccolor = [acccolor[j] + (1.0 - accalpha) segcolor[j] for j in range(3)] accalpha = accalpha + (1.0 - accalpha) segalpha if accalpha >= 0.999: break return acccolor Degenerate Segment: If \vec{v}1 = \vec{v}2, \|\vec{d}\| = 0. The division by \|\vec{d}\| in the density formula causes a singularity. In this case, the density is simply the value of the Gaussian at the point \vec{v}1. Error Function Domain: The Abramowitz and Stegun approximation is only valid for z \geq 0. Negative arguments must be handled by negating the result due to the odd symmetry of the error function. Precision: The term e^{-\|\vec{v}'1\|^2 + A^2} can underflow or overflow if the arguments are large. Care should be taken with numerical stability. Linear Variation Assumption: The method assumes data values vary linearly between samples. Time Complexity: O(1) per segment, dominated by the computation of the error function and matrix-vector multiplications. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Exact integration for Gaussian transfer functions; no sampling artifacts; efficient evaluation. Limitations: Limited to Gaussian-shaped transfer functions; assumes linear data variation; requires computation of the error function which may be slower than simple table lookups for non-Gaussian TFs. When to Use: When the transfer function can be well-approximated by a Gaussian and high accuracy is required without sampling noise. When Not to Use: For arbitrary, non-Gaussian transfer functions where numerical integration is more appropriate. The method was introduced by Joe Kniss, Simon Premoze, Milan Ikits, Aaron Lefohn, and Charles Hansen in 2003. It is part of the broader field of direct volume rendering, specifically addressing the integration of the emission-absorption equation. name: Kubelka-Munk Theory
head: KM theory, Kubelka-Munk model, One-dimensional Radiosity (Kubelka-Munk)
body: Kubelka-Munk Theory is a spectral optical model for light transport in scattering media that computes reflectance and transmittance by accounting for both absorption and scattering. It solves the problem of rendering homogeneous and inhomogeneous layers where simple extinction (Lambert-Bouguer law) is insufficient because it ignores the redirection of light. Unlike the Emission-Absorption Volume Rendering model which folds scattering into extinction, Kubelka-Munk restricts light transport to two opposing fluxes (incident and reflected) along a single axis, making it suitable for spectral volume rendering of layered materials. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Absorption coefficient K(\lambda), scattering coefficient S(\lambda), layer thickness X, and wavelength \lambda. Outputs: Reflectance R(\lambda) and Transmittance T(\lambda). Data Structures The method operates on scalar spectral values per layer. For inhomogeneous media, layers are represented as a sequence of tuples (Ki, Si, Xi). Formulas and Definitions The theory divides the volume into homogeneous elementary layers of thickness dx. It defines two fluxes: incident flux Ii(\lambda) flowing in direction x, and reflected flux Ir(\lambda) flowing in direction -x. The change in flux through an elementary layer is governed by: dIi(\lambda) = -K(\lambda)Ii(\lambda)dx - S(\lambda)Ii(\lambda)dx + S(\lambda)Ir(\lambda)dx \quad (7) dIr(\lambda) = -K(\lambda)Ir(\lambda)dx - S(\lambda)Ir(\lambda)dx + S(\lambda)Ii(\lambda)dx \quad (8) Note: Source contains a typo in equation (8) where the backscatter term is written as S(\lambda)Ir(\lambda)dx; physically, it must be S(\lambda)Ii(\lambda)dx to represent backscattering from the incident flux, consistent with equation (7) and the description "energy is also increased due to backscatter". For a layer of finite thickness X, the reflectance R(\lambda) and transmittance T(\lambda) are calculated using auxiliary parameters a(\lambda) and b(\lambda): a(\lambda) = \frac{S(\lambda) + K(\lambda)}{S(\lambda)} b(\lambda) = \sqrt{a(\lambda)^2 - 1} R(\lambda) = \frac{b(\lambda) \sinh(b(\lambda)S(\lambda)X)}{a(\lambda) \sinh(b(\lambda)S(\lambda)X) + b(\lambda) \cosh(b(\lambda)S(\lambda)X)} \quad (9) T(\lambda) = \frac{b(\lambda)}{a(\lambda) \sinh(b(\lambda)S(\lambda)X) + b(\lambda) \cosh(b(\lambda)S(\lambda)X)} \quad (10) The reflectance of an opaque medium (X \to \infty) is: R\infty(\lambda) = 1 + \frac{K(\lambda)}{S(\lambda)} - \sqrt{\left(\frac{K(\lambda)}{S(\lambda)}\right)^2 + 2\frac{K(\lambda)}{S(\lambda)}} Note: Source presents the square root term as squared in the text description but the square root symbol in the formula block. The standard Kubelka-Munk equation uses the square root. Inhomogeneous Layers (Composite Layers) For inhomogeneous layers, the theory combines two adjacent layers with properties (R1, T1) and (R2, T2) by considering infinite interactions between them: R(\lambda) = R1(\lambda) + \frac{T1(\lambda)^2 R2(\lambda)}{1 - R1(\lambda)R2(\lambda)} T(\lambda) = \frac{T1(\lambda)T2(\lambda)}{1 - R1(\lambda)R2(\lambda)} Algorithm: Spectral Volume Rendering To render a volume, the intersection of a ray with the volume is approximated as a series of homogeneous layers with thickness equal to the sampling distance. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sinh(x): return (math.exp(x) - math.exp(-x)) / 2.0 def cosh(x): return (math.exp(x) + math.exp(-x)) / 2.0 def kubelkamunklayer(K, S, X): """ Computes R and T for a single homogeneous layer. K: absorption coefficient S: scattering coefficient X: thickness """ if S == 0: # Fallback to Lambert-Bouguer if no scattering T = math.exp(-(K + S) X) R = 0.0 return R, T a = (S + K) / S b = math.sqrt(a2 - 1) if X == 0: return 0.0, 1.0 sinhval = sinh(b S X) coshval = cosh(b S X) denominator = a sinhval + b coshval R = (b sinhval) / denominator T = b / denominator return R, T def compositelayers(R1, T1, R2, T2): """ Combines two layers. """ denom = 1.0 - R1 R2 if abs(denom) < 1e-9: return 1.0, 0.0 Rnew = R1 + (T12 R2) / denom Tnew = (T1 T2) / denom return Rnew, Tnew def rendervolumelayered(Ksamples, Ssamples, Xsamples): """ Renders a volume by stacking layers. Ksamples: list of K for each layer Ssamples: list of S for each layer Xsamples: list of thicknesses for each layer """ if not Ksamples: return 0.0, 1.0 Rcurr, Tcurr = kubelkamunklayer(Ksamples[0], Ssamples[0], Xsamples[0]) for i in range(1, len(Ksamples)): Rnext, Tnext = kubelkamunklayer(Ksamples[i], Ssamples[i], Xsamples[i]) Rcurr, Tcurr = compositelayers(Rcurr, Tcurr, Rnext, Tnext) return Rcurr, Tcurr Edge Cases and Pitfalls S=0: If scattering is zero, the model reduces to the Lambert-Bouguer law (extinction only). Numerical Stability: For very large optical depths, \sinh and \cosh may overflow; use asymptotic limits (R \to R\infty). Directionality: The model assumes isotropic scattering within the two-flux approximation and does not account for anisotropic phase functions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Built-in distance attenuation; determines opacity and transparency optically based on K and S; suitable for spectral rendering. Limitations: Restricted to one-dimensional transport (no angular resolution). When to use: Spectral volume rendering of layered, scattering media (e.g., skin, paper, paint). When not to use: Not given in the sources. The Kubelka-Munk theory was originally proposed by Kubelka and Munk and built upon Schuster's two-flux concept. It was extended to inhomogeneous layers by Kubelka. In computer graphics, Abdul-Rahman and Chen adapted it for spectral volume rendering, presenting a spectral volume rendering integral that differs from the Lambert-Bouguer law by modeling absorption and scattering in only two directions (incident and reflected). name: Volume Rendering Integral
head: Levoy's Volume Rendering Integral
body: The Volume Rendering Integral computes the expected color I\lambda(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{r}) received at a point \mathbf{x} on the image plane from ray direction \mathbf{r}, assuming a low-albedo (single scattering) scenario where light scatters at most once before leaving the volume. It differs from its siblings by providing the foundational continuous formulation for full volume rendering, explicitly integrating emitted, transmitted, and reflected light contributions weighted by exponential attenuation along a ray path. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, ray length L, volume density field \sigma(\mathbf{p}), and color/emission field \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{p}) (or light contribution C\lambda(\mathbf{p})). Output: Expected color \mathbf{C} (or I\lambda) at the image plane. Data Structures The analytic integral cannot be computed efficiently in the general case, so practical algorithms discretize the ray into n sequential intervals of width \Delta s. Each segment i spans [ti, t{i+1}] with length \deltai = t{i+1} - ti, assuming constant density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i within the interval. Formulas The transmittance T(t), representing the probability that a ray passes through the medium up to distance t without interaction, is derived from the probabilistic fact that T(t+dt) = T(t)(1-\sigma(t)dt): T(t) = \exp\left(-\int0^t \sigma(s) ds\right) The probability that the first interaction (hit) occurs at distance t is the product of surviving up to t and interacting at t: P[\text{first hit at } t] = T(t)\sigma(t)dt = \exp\left(-\int0^t \sigma(s) ds\right) \sigma(t) dt The rendering equation for the expected color \mathbf{C} is the integral of the color contribution weighted by the probability of the first hit: \mathbf{C} = \int{t1}^{tN} T(t)\sigma(t)\mathbf{c}(t) dt In the low-albedo formulation, the light contribution C\lambda(s) at position s includes emission, transmission, and reflection: C\lambda(s) = E\lambda(s) + T\lambda(s) + R\lambda(s) where R\lambda(s) is computed via standard illumination equations involving light source color and distance: R(s) = kc Ca + kd Cl Co(s)(N(s) \cdot L(s)) + ks Cl(N(s) \cdot H(s))^{ns} Here Ca is ambient color, Cl is light source color, Co(s) is object color from density mapping, N(s) is the normal vector, L(s) is the light direction, H(s) is the half-vector, and ns is the Phong exponent. Algorithm Steps 1. Discretize the ray from t1 to t{n+1} into n segments of length \deltai. 2. Assume constant density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i within each segment. 3. Compute the opacity \alphai for segment i using the extinction coefficient and segment length: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) 4. Compute the front transmittance Ti at the start of segment i as the product of survival probabilities of all preceding segments: Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) 5. Approximate the integral using quadrature by summing the contributions of each segment: \mathbf{C} \approx \sum{i=1}^n Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def samplevolume(pos): """Standard volume sampling operation returning density and color at pos.""" # Returns (sigma, color) based on grid interpolation or neural query pass def volumerenderingintegral(rayorigin, raydirection, raylength, numsamples): """ Computes the expected color along a ray using the volume rendering integral. Assumes constant density and color per sample interval. """ deltat = raylength / numsamples tstart = 0.0 accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 expectedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(numsamples): pos = rayorigin + raydirection tstart sigma, color = samplevolume(pos) # Compute opacity for this segment if sigma deltat > 10.0: alpha = 1.0 else: alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma deltat) # Add contribution: Transmittance Opacity Color expectedcolor[0] += accumulatedtransmittance alpha color[0] expectedcolor[1] += accumulatedtransmittance alpha color[1] expectedcolor[2] += accumulatedtransmittance alpha color[2] # Update transmittance for the next segment accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - alpha) # Advance ray tstart += deltat return expectedcolor Parameters and Edge Cases \sigmai (Density): Must be non-negative. If \sigmai = 0, \alphai = 0 and the segment is transparent. Precision: The multiplicative transmittance update T{i+1} = Ti(1-\alphai) can underflow to zero for dense volumes, causing "black holes" where no light is seen. Low-Albedo Assumption: The standard integral assumes single scattering; multiple scattering requires recursive evaluation or approximations like the Single Scattering Model. Extends the integral to C-ToF cameras using complex-valued path length importance functions to handle multi-path interference and avoid wrap-around ambiguities. Choose when simulating C-ToF camera captures in participating media. An unbiased Monte Carlo estimator that decouples density queries from appearance evaluations, reducing computational cost by sampling a subset of points based on render weights. Choose when appearance evaluation is the bottleneck and slight variance increase is acceptable. Uses SH basis representation to simulate complex light-material interactions, supporting arbitrary light directions and full-sphere scattering for interactive DVR. Choose when simulating environmental effects like in-scattering and color bleeding in real-time applications. Transforms the integral from a ray-parameterization to a direct spatial volume integration, replacing directional queries with direct spatial coordinates. Choose when implementing path integral formulations or volume-based sampling strategies. Solves the integral by expressing incoming radiance as an infinite sum of contributions from light sources undergoing 0, 1, 2, \dots scattering events. Choose when avoiding angular basis approximations and operating directly on integral equation operators. Specializes the integrand for Computational Flow Imaging to project 3D gas density or refractive index distributions onto a 2D view plane for shadowgraph, schlieren, or interferometric visualization. Choose for optical flow diagnostics and flow field visualization. Computes acoustic impulse responses by treating sound propagation as volume rendering, explicitly modeling frequency-dependent attenuation and multiple bounces. Choose for acoustic scene simulation and impulse response field generation. Adds direct light attenuation to classic volume rendering to incorporate volumetric shadows and improve visual perception, considering approximations to phase functions and single/multiple forward scattering for interactive hardware-based visualization. Choose when real-time volumetric shadows are required without full physical scattering accuracy. Time Complexity: O(N) per ray for N samples, as each sample requires a density/color query and a constant-time update. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray with on-the-fly queries, or O(V) if the volume grid is stored in memory. Strengths: Differentiable with respect to density and color, enabling gradient-based optimization. Limitations: Assumes low-albedo (single scattering); inaccurate for highly scattering media without in-scattering extensions. Computing volumetric shadows adds significant computational complexity, making interactive hardware-based approaches necessary for real-time performance. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The volume rendering integral was formally derived by [152] (cited in) building on earlier descriptions by [14] and [98] (cited in). It is based on the conservation of energy for light passing through a participating medium. The probabilistic interpretation of the integral, linking transmittance to the probability of no hits, was popularized in modern computer graphics literature. name: Continuous-Wave ToF Phasor Model
head: C-ToF Phasor Model, Phasor Volume Rendering
body: The Continuous-Wave ToF Phasor Model extends the volume rendering integral to simulate images captured by continuous-wave Time-of-Flight (C-ToF) cameras by incorporating a complex-valued path length importance function. It differs from standard volume rendering by weighting contributions based on light travel distance and from depth-map-based methods by operating directly on complex phasor values, thereby avoiding wrap-around ambiguities and handling multi-path interference more robustly. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera origin \mathbf{x}, viewing direction \boldsymbol{\omega}0, modulation frequency f, speed of light c, scattering coefficient \sigma(\mathbf{x}t), incident light intensity Is(\mathbf{x}t, \boldsymbol{\omega}0), and transmittance T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}t) along the ray. Output: Complex-valued phasor radiance L{\text{ToF}}(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}0). Data Structures: The output is a complex number, typically stored as two floating-point values representing the real and imaginary components, or as magnitude and phase. Formulas: The core rendering equation for a C-ToF camera is: L{\text{ToF}}(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}0) = \int{tn}^{tf} \frac{T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}t)^2}{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}t\|^2} \sigma(\mathbf{x}t) Is(\mathbf{x}t, \boldsymbol{\omega}0) W(2\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}t\|) dt Where: tn, tf: Near and far clipping distances along the ray. \mathbf{x}t: Position on the ray at parameter t, defined as \mathbf{x}t = \mathbf{x} + t\boldsymbol{\omega}0. T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}t): Transmittance from camera \mathbf{x} to \mathbf{x}t. The square T^2 accounts for attenuation on both the outgoing and return paths. \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}t\|: Euclidean distance between camera and scene point. When \boldsymbol{\omega}0 is normalized, this distance equals t. The inverse-square term \frac{1}{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}t\|^2} models the geometric falloff of a point source. W(d): Path length importance function for distance d. For C-ToF, light travels distance d = 2\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}t\| (round trip). The phasor function W(d) is defined as: W(d) = \exp\left(i \frac{2\pi d f}{c}\right) Substituting d = 2\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}t\|: W(2\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}t\|) = \exp\left(i \frac{4\pi f}{c} \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}t\|\right) Where: f: Modulation frequency of the C-ToF signal. Typical value: 30 \text{ MHz}. c: Speed of light, \approx 3 \cdot 10^8 \text{ m/s}. i: Imaginary unit. Parameters: f: Modulation frequency. Typical value: 30 \text{ MHz}. This sets the unambiguous range to c/2f \approx 5 \text{ m}. Pseudocode: The following Python-like pseudocode computes the phasor radiance for a single ray. It assumes standard volume rendering integration is handled by the caller, and uses t directly as the distance \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}t\| (valid when \boldsymbol{\omega}0 is normalized). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import cmath def computectofphasing(distance, modulationfreq, speedoflight): """ Computes the complex phasor weight for a given one-way distance. Args: distance (float): One-way distance from camera to point (meters). modulationfreq (float): Modulation frequency f (Hz). speedoflight (float): Speed of light c (m/s). Returns: complex: The phasor weight W(2distance). """ # Round-trip distance d = 2.0 distance # Phase calculation: 2 pi f d / c phase = 2.0 math.pi modulationfreq d / speedoflight # Complex exponential: exp(i phase) return cmath.exp(1j phase) def renderctofray(rayorigin, raydirection, samples, modulationfreq=30e6, speedoflight=3e8): """ Renders a single ray using the C-ToF Phasor Model. Args: rayorigin (tuple): Camera position x (3D vector). raydirection (tuple): Viewing direction omega0 (3D vector, normalized). samples (list): List of tuples (t, sigma, Is, Tprev) sorted by t. modulationfreq (float): C-ToF modulation frequency. speedoflight (float): Speed of light. Returns: complex: The accumulated phasor radiance LTof. """ # Initialize accumulator phasorradiance = 0.0 + 0.0j # Small epsilon to avoid division by zero at the camera origin epsilon = 1e-6 for t, sigma, Is, Tprev in samples: # Distance from camera to point equals t for normalized direction dist = t # Guard against division by zero if dist < epsilon: dist = epsilon # Compute phasor weight for round-trip distance w = computectofphasing(dist, modulationfreq, speedoflight) # Transmittance squared (outgoing and return path) Tsquared = Tprev 2 # Inverse square falloff invdistsq = 1.0 / (dist 2) # Contribution: T^2 / dist^2 sigma Is W contribution = (Tsquared invdistsq sigma Is w) # Accumulate phasorradiance += contribution return phasorradiance Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multi-path interference: Multiple points along a ray contribute to the signal, resulting in a linear combination of phasor radiance values. This degrades depth quality, causing 'flying pixel' artifacts around depth edges or with semi-transparent/specular objects. Wrap-around errors: If deriving depth maps from phase, ranges > c/2f are ambiguous. Modeling raw phasor images avoids this. Noise: Depth values become unreliable when reflected light is small. Direct phasor modeling is more robust to sensor noise than derived depth maps. This model defines the radiance contribution from an ideal Time-of-Flight (ToF) camera that responds exclusively to light emitted by an infrared (IR) point source collocated with the camera lens, ignoring all ambient illumination. It sets apart from general volume rendering by enforcing a strict geometric constraint where the incident light direction \boldsymbol{\omega}i is identical to the viewing direction \boldsymbol{\omega}0 (backscattering along the same ray), and by incorporating the inverse-square falloff of a point source. Time Complexity: Same as standard volume rendering, O(N) where N is the number of samples per ray, plus the cost of complex arithmetic per sample. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray for the accumulator, plus the memory required for the scene representation (e.g., NeRF weights, grid). Strengths: Avoids wrap-around errors for ranges > c/2f; robust to sensor noise in dark objects; handles multi-path interference at depth edges better than deriving depth maps. Limitations: Multi-path interference can still cause 'flying pixel' artifacts; requires complex number arithmetic; unambiguous range is limited by modulation frequency f (e.g., \approx 5 \text{ m} for 30 \text{ MHz}). When to use: When simulating C-ToF camera behavior directly, especially for scenes with large depth ranges or where multi-path interference is a concern. When not to use: When only real-valued intensity or depth maps are needed and the scene depth is well within the unambiguous range, simpler models may suffice. The method originates from the TöRF paper, which extends volume rendering to simulate Time-of-Flight cameras. It builds on prior work in transient rendering frameworks [17, 39] and neural transient fields (NeTFs) [46] by incorporating a path length importance function. The specific phasor model for C-ToF cameras is derived from the physics of continuous-wave modulation, where the phase shift of the reflected signal encodes distance. TöRF: Time-of-Flight Radiance Fields for Dynamic Scene View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2109.15271, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Collocated Point Light Source Model
body: This model defines the radiance contribution from an ideal Time-of-Flight (ToF) camera that responds exclusively to light emitted by an infrared (IR) point source collocated with the camera lens, ignoring all ambient illumination. It builds on Continuous-Wave ToF Phasor Model by enforcing a strict geometric constraint where the incident light direction \boldsymbol{\omega}i is identical to the viewing direction \boldsymbol{\omega}0 (backscattering along the same ray), and by incorporating the inverse-square falloff of a point source. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: \mathbf{x}: Position of the light source/camera. \mathbf{x}t: Position along the ray at parameter t. I: Emitted radiant intensity of the source (scalar). \sigma(\mathbf{x}t): Extinction coefficient at \mathbf{x}t. f{\text{p}}(\mathbf{x}t, \boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}0, \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{x}t)): Scattering phase function depending on the local surface normal \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{x}t). T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}t): Transmittance from the source to the point \mathbf{x}t. tn, tr: Near and far clipping distances along the ray. Output: L(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}0): Radiance measured by the camera in direction \boldsymbol{\omega}0. Data Structures: Not specified in the sources. Formulas: The model assumes monochromatic radiance at a single wavelength (typically IR for ToF). 1. Incident Illumination: The incident radiance Li(\mathbf{x}t, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) from a point source at \mathbf{x} is modeled using a Dirac delta function to restrict illumination to the single direction from the source: Li(\mathbf{x}t, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) = \frac{I}{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}t\|^2} \delta \left( \frac{\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}t}{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}t\|} - \boldsymbol{\omega}i \right) T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}t) Here, \frac{1}{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}t\|^2} represents the inverse square light fall-off, and \delta(\cdot) ensures light arrives only from the direction of the source. 2. Scattering Phase Function Constraint: Because the source is collocated with the camera, the incident direction \boldsymbol{\omega}i is equal to the outgoing/viewing direction \boldsymbol{\omega}0. The phase function is evaluated as: IS(\mathbf{x}t, \boldsymbol{\omega}0) = f{\text{p}}(\mathbf{x}t, \boldsymbol{\omega}0, \boldsymbol{\omega}0, \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{x}t)) I This represents the emitted light reflected along the same ray. 3. Resulting Radiance: Substituting the incident illumination into the volume rendering integral yields the final radiance: L(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}0) = \int{tn}^{tr} \frac{T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}t)^2}{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}t\|^2} \sigma(\mathbf{x}t) IS(\mathbf{x}t, \boldsymbol{\omega}0) \, dt Note the squared transmittance T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}t)^2, accounting for attenuation on both the path from the source to the scattering point and from the scattering point back to the camera. Pitfalls: Forward Scattering: The model ignores forward scattering, which is reasonable if the scene consists mostly of completely opaque surfaces. Ambient Light: The model explicitly ignores ambient illumination and assumes the camera and light are at the exact same position. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def collocatedpointlightradiance(xsource, rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, getsigma, getnormal, getphasefunction, sourceintensity): """ Computes radiance for a collocated point light source model. Args: xsource: Vector, position of the light source (and camera). rayorigin: Vector, origin of the viewing ray (should equal xsource). raydirection: Vector, direction of the viewing ray. tnear: Float, near clipping plane distance. tfar: Float, far clipping plane distance. getsigma: Function, returns extinction coefficient sigma(x). getnormal: Function, returns surface normal n(x). getphasefunction: Function, returns fp(x, omegai, omegao, n). sourceintensity: Float, I. Returns: Float, radiance L(x, omega0). """ radiance = 0.0 numsamples = 100 # Implementation detail not in sources dt = (tfar - tnear) / numsamples for i in range(numsamples): t = tnear + (i + 0.5) dt xt = rayorigin + t raydirection # Distance from source to scattering point distsq = dot(xsource - xt, xsource - xt) # Avoid division by zero if source is on the ray origin if distsq < 1e-9: continue # Transmittance T(x, xt) = exp(-integral{x}^{xt} sigma(u) du) is computed via standard quadrature. T = computetransmittance(xsource, xt, getsigma) Tsquared = T T # Extinction sigma = getsigma(xt) # Phase function evaluation with omegai = omegao = raydirection normal = getnormal(xt) phaseval = getphasefunction(xt, raydirection, raydirection, normal) # Source intensity term IS = phaseval sourceintensity # Integrand: (T^2 / dist^2) sigma IS integrand = (Tsquared / distsq) sigma IS radiance += integrand dt return radiance def computetransmittance(xstart, xend, getsigma): """Standard transmittance calculation.""" numsamples = 10 dt = dot(xend - xstart, xend - xstart) / numsamples integral = 0.0 for i in range(numsamples): u = xstart + (i + 0.5) dt (xend - xstart) / dot(xend - xstart, xend - xstart) integral += getsigma(u) dt return exp(-integral) Complexity: The computational cost is dominated by the numerical integration of the volume rendering integral. It requires evaluating transmittance, extinction, and phase functions at each sample point along the ray. Strengths: Simple analytical form for idealized active illumination scenarios; correctly models inverse-square falloff and double-pass attenuation. Limitations: Invalid for scenes with significant ambient light or forward scattering in participating media. Assumes the camera and light are at the exact same position. This model originates from the TöRF (Time-of-Flight Radiance Fields) paper, which extends volume rendering to model images captured with Continuous-Wave ToF cameras. It is used to synthesize dynamic scenes by modeling the specific radiance contributions captured by ToF sensors, distinguishing them from standard RGB ambient illumination. TöRF: Time-of-Flight Radiance Fields for Dynamic Scene View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2109.15271, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Fast Cache Estimator
head: Categorical sampling estimator
body: The Fast Cache Estimator is an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator for the incoming radiance term in the volume rendering integral, designed to reduce computational cost by decoupling density queries from appearance evaluations. It reduces the number of expensive physically-based appearance evaluations from N to K \ll N samples drawn from a categorical distribution based on render weights, while still requiring density queries for all N points to determine those weights. Unlike the Volume Rendering Integral which typically sums over all sample points, this method approximates the integral using a subset of points, trading off the number of appearance evaluations for a slight increase in variance that is mitigated by importance sampling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{x}{origin}, ray direction \mathbf{d}{out}, number of density query points N, number of appearance evaluation points K. Output: Estimated incoming radiance \hat{L}i(\mathbf{x}{origin}, \mathbf{d}{out}). Data Structures: Render Weights: An array w of size N, where wj is the render weight for the j-th sample point along the ray. These weights are derived from the volume density queries at positions \mathbf{x}{pos}(tj). Sample Positions: An array of positions \mathbf{x}{pos}(t1), \dots, \mathbf{x}{pos}(tN) corresponding to the N density query locations. Steps: 1. Query Density: For each of the N sample points along the ray, query the volume density to compute the render weights w1, \dots, wN. 2. Normalize Weights: Ensure the weights w1, \dots, wN form a valid probability distribution (i.e., \sum{j=1}^N wj = 1). 3. Sample Indices: Draw K indices j1, \dots, jK independently from the categorical distribution defined by the weights w1, \dots, wN. 4. Evaluate Appearance: For each sampled index jk, evaluate the outgoing radiance Lo(\mathbf{x}{pos}(t{jk}), \mathbf{d}{out}) at the corresponding position. 5. Compute Estimator: Calculate the average of the evaluated outgoing radiances: \hat{L}i(\mathbf{x}{origin}, \mathbf{d}{out}) = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^{K} Lo(\mathbf{x}{pos}(t{jk}), \mathbf{d}{out}) Parameters: K: The number of appearance evaluations per ray. Typical value: K=1 is sufficient if the render weight distribution has a single peak. In practice, K=1 provides the best results in terms of PSNR for synthetic datasets. Pitfalls: Density Query Overhead: The method requires querying volume density for all N points to determine the weights, even though appearance is only evaluated at K points. This can be a bottleneck if density queries are expensive. Variance: If the render weight distribution is multimodal or complex, K=1 may result in high variance, requiring larger K for convergence. However, increasing K increases the number of secondary ray samples K \cdot M, which can be prohibitively expensive. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fastcacheestimator(rayorigin, raydirection, N, K, querydensity, evaluateappearance): """ Estimates incoming radiance using the Fast Cache Estimator. Args: rayorigin: Origin of the ray. raydirection: Direction of the ray. N: Number of density query points. K: Number of appearance evaluation points (K << N). querydensity: Function that returns render weight for a position. evaluateappearance: Function that returns outgoing radiance for a position and direction. Returns: Estimated incoming radiance. """ positions = [] weights = [] # Position tj is determined by the ray marching strategy (e.g., uniform or stratified sampling along the ray). for i in range(N): t = i / N # Placeholder for position sampling; actual implementation depends on ray marching pos = rayorigin + t raydirection positions.append(pos) weights.append(querydensity(pos)) # Ensure weights form a valid probability distribution. totalweight = sum(weights) if totalweight == 0: return 0.0 # Handle degenerate case where no density is encountered normalizedweights = [w / totalweight for w in weights] # Sample K indices from categorical distribution sampledindices = categoricalsample(normalizedweights, K) # Evaluate appearance and compute estimator totalradiance = 0.0 for idx in sampledindices: pos = positions[idx] radiance = evaluateappearance(pos, raydirection) totalradiance += radiance return totalradiance / K def categoricalsample(weights, K): """ Samples K indices from a categorical distribution defined by weights. """ import random indices = [] for in range(K): r = random.random() cumulative = 0.0 for i, w in enumerate(weights): cumulative += w if r <= cumulative: indices.append(i) break return indices This section provides the proof that the Fast Cache Estimator is an unbiased estimator for the volume rendering quadrature. The proof expands the expectation of the estimator and shows that it equals the sum of render weights multiplied by outgoing radiance. Steps: 1. Expand the expectation of the estimator: \mathbb{E}[\hat{L}i(\mathbf{x}{origin}, \mathbf{d}{out})] = \mathbb{E}[\frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^{K} Lo(\mathbf{x}{pos}(t{jk}), \mathbf{d}{out})]. 2. Substitute the categorical expectation, where jk \sim \operatorname{Cat}(w1, \ldots, wN): \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^{K} \sum{j=1}^{N} wj Lo(\mathbf{x}{pos}(tj), \mathbf{d}{out}). 3. Simplify the expression to the final sum: \sum{j=1}^{N} wj Lo(\mathbf{x}{pos}(tj), \mathbf{d}{out}), which is the quadrature value. Formula: \mathbb{E}[\hat{L}i(\mathbf{x}{origin}, \mathbf{d}{out})] = \sum{j=1}^{N} wj Lo(\mathbf{x}{pos}(tj), \mathbf{d}{out}) Parameters: w1, \ldots, wN: Render weights for the ray (\mathbf{o}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o). This section provides the proof that the Fast Cache Estimator is an unbiased estimator of the rendering equation, provided that the incoming illumination from the NeRF cache is correct. The proof leverages the unbiasedness of the estimator for the incoming radiance term. Steps: 1. Expand the expectation using the unbiasedness of the incoming radiance estimator: \int{\Omega} f(\mathbf{x}{pos}^t, \mathbf{d}{in}, \mathbf{d}{out}) \hat{L}i^{\text{NeRF}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}{in}) (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}{in}) d\mathbf{d}{in} + \int{\Omega} f(\mathbf{x}{pos}^t, \mathbf{d}{in}, \mathbf{d}{out}) (\hat{L}i^{\text{NeRF}} - \hat{L}i^{\text{fast}})(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}{in}) (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}{in}) d\mathbf{d}{in}. 2. Simplify to the final integral: \int{\Omega} f(\mathbf{x}{pos}^t, \mathbf{d}{in}, \mathbf{d}{out}) \hat{L}i^{\text{NeRF}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}{in}) (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}{in}) d\mathbf{d}{in}. Formula: \mathbb{E}[\hat{L}o] = \mathbb{E}[\hat{L}o^{\text{fast}}] + \mathbb{E}[\Delta \hat{L}o] Time Complexity: The method requires N density queries and K appearance evaluations per ray. Since K \ll N, the computational cost is dominated by the density queries. The total number of secondary ray samples is reduced from N \cdot M to K \cdot M, where M is the number of rays. Memory Complexity: Requires storing N render weights and N positions for each ray. Measured Performance: On the TensoIR-synthetic dataset, K=1 provides the best NVS PSNR (34.915) and Albedo PSNR (30.345) with the lowest MAE (3.355) compared to K=2, 4, 8. Strengths: Significantly reduces the number of expensive appearance evaluations. Unbiased estimator. Limitations: Still requires density queries for all N points. Variance can be high if the weight distribution is not peaked. When to use: When appearance evaluation is significantly more expensive than density queries, and the render weight distribution is peaked. When not to use: When density queries are also expensive, or when the weight distribution is multimodal and K=1 leads to high variance. The Fast Cache Estimator was introduced in "Flash Cache: Reducing Bias in Radiance Cache Based Inverse Rendering" by B. Attal et al.. It is part of a broader effort to accelerate volume rendering and inverse rendering by reducing the computational cost of Monte Carlo integration. The method builds on the idea of using importance sampling to reduce the number of samples needed for convergence.
