name: Spherical Harmonic Volume Rendering
head: Advanced Light Material Interaction for DVR, SH-based light material interaction, Spherical Harmonic (SH) Volume Rendering with Advanced Material Interaction
body: Spherical Harmonic Volume Rendering is a heuristic method for simulating advanced light-material interactions in interactive direct volume rendering (DVR) by incorporating complex material functions (reflectance and scattering) and colored area light sources using a unified Spherical Harmonic (SH) basis representation. Unlike slice-based techniques that are limited to headlights or cone-shaped scattering approximations, this approach supports arbitrary light directions and full-sphere scattering, enabling the simulation of environmental effects like in-scattering and color bleeding. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Volume data \tau(\mathbf{x}) (scalar field), material function M(\mathbf{x}, \omegai, \omegao) represented in SH coefficients, incident radiance Li(\mathbf{x}, \omegai) from area light sources, and emission EM(\mathbf{x}, \omegao). Outputs: Radiance L(\mathbf{x}, \omegao) leaving position \mathbf{x} in direction \omegao. Data Structures SH Coefficients: A vector of size (L+1)^2 containing the coefficients c{lm} for the spherical harmonic basis. For the standard implementation, L=3, resulting in 16 coefficients. Material Function: Defined over the whole sphere \Omega (not just the hemisphere) because volume data lacks an inherent surface normal. Mathematical Formulation The radiance L(\mathbf{x}, \omegao) leaving a position \mathbf{x} in direction \omegao is defined as: L(\mathbf{x}, \omegao) = EM(\mathbf{x}, \omegao) + \int{\Omega} M(\mathbf{x}, \omegai, \omegao) \cdot Li(\mathbf{x}, \omegai) d\omegai To compute this efficiently, functions on the sphere are represented using Spherical Harmonic basis functions Y{lm}(\vartheta, \phi). An infinite series representation of a function f(\vartheta, \phi) is: f(\vartheta, \phi) = \sum{l=0}^{\infty} \sum{m=-l}^{l} c{lm} Y{lm}(\vartheta, \phi) The basis functions Y{lm} use complex exponential functions for latitude variations and associated Legendre polynomials for longitude variations. For practical implementation, the representation is bandlimited to a maximum order L: \tilde{f}(\vartheta, \phi) = \sum{l=0}^{L} \sum{m=-l}^{l} c{lm} Y{lm}(\vartheta, \phi) The number of summands is (L+1)^2. The SH coefficients cj (where j indexes the basis function Yj) are computed via least square projection: cj = \int{S} Yj(s) f(s) ds Due to the orthonormality of the SH basis functions, the integration of two SH-projected functions \tilde{f} and \tilde{g} with coefficients ci and di respectively simplifies to a dot product: I(\tilde{f}, \tilde{g}) = \sum{i} ci di Parameters Maximum SH Order (L): Set to 3 for practical reasons, resulting in 16 coefficients. Algorithm Steps 1. Precompute Material SH Coefficients: For each voxel (or material category), compute the SH coefficients c{lm} representing the material function M. This involves projecting the material's reflectance and scattering properties onto the SH basis. 2. Project Incident Light: Represent the incident radiance Li(\mathbf{x}, \omegai) from colored area light sources as SH coefficients d{lm}. 3. Compute Interaction Integral: Calculate the local light-material interaction term by taking the dot product of the material SH coefficients and the light SH coefficients: \sum ci di. Note: As volume data lacks a surface normal, this modulation is not weighted by a clamped cosine term (\cos \theta). 4. Add Emission: Add the emission term EM(\mathbf{x}, \omegao) to the result from Step 3 to obtain the final radiance L(\mathbf{x}, \omegao). 5. Render: Use the computed radiance in the standard DVR compositing loop (e.g., front-to-back or back-to-front). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sphericalharmonicvolumerendering(volumedata, lightsources, maxorder=3): """ Renders volume data using SH-based light material interaction. Args: volumedata: 3D array of scalar values (density/opacity). lightsources: List of light source definitions (direction, color, intensity). maxorder: Maximum SH order L (default 3). Returns: Image buffer. """ numcoeffs = (maxorder + 1) 2 # Precompute SH coefficients for the material function M materialcoeffs = computematerialshcoefficients(volumedata, maxorder) # Project incident light Li into SH domain lightcoeffs = computelightshcoefficients(lightsources, maxorder) # Compute the interaction integral using dot product of SH coefficients interaction = dotproduct(materialcoeffs, lightcoeffs) # Add emission (EM) if present emission = getemission(volumedata) # Final radiance radiance = emission + interaction # Perform standard DVR compositing using the computed radiance return performdvrcompositing(volumedata, radiance) def dotproduct(a, b): """Computes the dot product of two coefficient vectors.""" return sum(ai bi for ai, bi in zip(a, b)) def norm(v): """Computes the Euclidean norm of a vector.""" return sum(x2 for x in v)0.5 def computematerialshcoefficients(volumedata, maxorder): """ Computes SH coefficients for the material function M. The sources do not specify the exact quadrature scheme or material evaluation function. Standard SH projection integrates Yj(s) M(s) over the sphere. """ coeffs = [0.0] ((maxorder + 1) 2) # Quadrature loop over sphere samples would compute: coeffs[j] += Yj(s) M(s) weight(s) return coeffs def computelightshcoefficients(lightsources, maxorder): """ Computes SH coefficients for the incident radiance Li. The sources do not specify the exact quadrature scheme for area lights. Standard SH projection integrates Yj(s) Li(s) over the sphere. """ coeffs = [0.0] ((maxorder + 1) 2) # Quadrature loop over sphere samples would compute: coeffs[j] += Yj(s) Li(s) weight(s) return coeffs def getemission(volumedata): """Retrieves emission values from the volume data or a separate texture.""" return 0.0 def performdvrcompositing(volumedata, radiance): """ Performs standard Direct Volume Rendering compositing. Uses front-to-back or back-to-front accumulation with opacity/density. """ return [0.0] Time Complexity: The core integration step is reduced to a dot product of SH coefficients, which is O((L+1)^2). With L=3, the dot product operates on 16-element vectors. Memory Complexity: Requires storing (L+1)^2 coefficients per material/light. For L=3, this is 16 floats per item. Performance: Implemented on the GPU to achieve interactive frame rates. Allows interactive changes to light and material properties. Strengths: Supports colored area light sources and arbitrary light directions. Handles scattering over the whole sphere, which is critical for area light sources with multiple spatial components. Limitations: It is a heuristic approach. The approximation of complex material functions with a limited SH order (L=3) may lose high-frequency details. The lack of surface normal weighting may produce physically inaccurate results for surface-like materials, but is consistent with the volume data definition. Origin: Proposed by Florian Lindemann and Timo Ropinski from the Visualization and Computer Graphics Research Group (VisCG), Department of Computer Science, University of Münster, Germany. Paper: "Advanced Light Material Interaction for Direct Volume Rendering" (2010). History: Previous techniques by Schott et al. and Patel et al. used slice-wise front-to-back compositing and only supported headlights. Techniques by Kniss et al. and Ropinski et al. assumed scattering was directed along one major axis (cone-shaped phase functions), which is a strong approximation, especially for area light sources. This method extends previous work by using SH basis functions to unify material and lighting representation, allowing for more realistic environmental effects. Advanced Light Material Interaction for Direct Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.2312/vg/vg10/101-108, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Change of Variables for Volume Rendering Integral
head: Change of Variables: Volume, Surface Integral Formulation of VRI, Volume Rendering Integral Change of Variables
body: This method transforms the volume rendering integral from a parameterization over ray direction and distance into a direct integration over the 3D spatial volume. It replaces directional queries with direct spatial coordinates, allowing the radiance contribution of all points in the participating medium to be summed directly rather than sampled along rays. This formulation is the volumetric analog of the surface integral change of variables, enabling path integral formulations where the integration domain is the volume \mathcal{V} rather than the solid angle \mathcal{S}^2 and distance r. The transformation relies on the Jacobian of the coordinate change from spherical coordinates (direction \bo and distance r) to Cartesian coordinates (position \bx'). Inputs and Outputs: Input: A view point \bx, a function f(\bx') representing the integrand (e.g., emitted and scattered light attenuated by transmittance), and the visibility function V(\bx' \to \bx). Output: The integral value over the volume \mathcal{V}. Data Structures: \bx: View point position (3D vector). \bx': Integration variable position (3D vector). \mathcal{V}: The volume domain of integration. Formula: The change of variables for the volume rendering integral is given by: \int{\mathcal{S}^2} \int0^{\|\raycast(\bx, \bo) - \bx\|} f(\bx + r\bo) \, dr \, d\bo = \int{\mathcal{V}} \frac{1}{\|\bx' - \bx\|^2} V(\bx' \to \bx) f(\bx') \, dV(\bx') Symbol Definitions: \mathcal{S}^2: The unit sphere of directions. \bx: The camera or sensor position. \bo: A unit direction vector on \mathcal{S}^2. r: Distance along the ray from \bx. \raycast(\bx, \bo): The intersection point of the ray starting at \bx in direction \bo with the boundary of the volume. f(\bx'): The integrand evaluated at position \bx'. In the context of the volume rendering equation, this typically includes emission and scattering terms attenuated by transmittance from \bx' to \bx. \mathcal{V}: The volume of the participating medium. \|\bx' - \bx\|: The Euclidean distance between the integration point \bx' and the view point \bx. V(\bx' \to \bx): The visibility function, which is 1 if the path from \bx' to \bx is unoccluded within the medium, and 0 otherwise. dV(\bx'): The differential volume element at \bx'. Derivation Logic: 1. Start with the integral over solid angle d\bo and distance dr. 2. The position \bx' is defined as \bx + r\bo. 3. The differential volume element in spherical coordinates centered at \bx is dV = r^2 dr d\bo = \|\bx' - \bx\|^2 dr d\bo. 4. Therefore, dr d\bo = \frac{1}{\|\bx' - \bx\|^2} dV(\bx'). 5. Substitute this into the integral. The limits of integration for r (from 0 to the boundary) become the extent of the volume \mathcal{V} along the ray, which is handled by the visibility function V(\bx' \to \bx) and the domain \mathcal{V}. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity at \bx' = \bx: The term \frac{1}{\|\bx' - \bx\|^2} becomes singular when the integration point coincides with the view point. In practice, this is handled by the behavior of f(\bx') (which may include transmittance T(\bx \to \bx') that goes to 1, but emission/scattering terms must be well-behaved) or by excluding a small neighborhood around \bx. Visibility Calculation: Computing V(\bx' \to \bx) for every point in the volume is computationally expensive and may require additional ray casting or precomputed visibility data. Boundary Handling: The original integral limits r to the boundary of the volume. The volume integral implicitly handles this via the domain \mathcal{V} and the visibility function. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def changeofvariablesvolumeintegral(viewpoint, volumedomain, integrandfunc, visibilityfunc): """ Computes the volume rendering integral using the change of variables formulation. Args: viewpoint (Vector3): The camera/sensor position bx. volumedomain (Volume): The 3D volume V to integrate over. integrandfunc (Function): A function f(bxprime) that returns the unattenuated radiance contribution at bxprime. visibilityfunc (Function): A function V(bxprime, bx) that returns 1 if bxprime is visible from bx, 0 otherwise. Returns: float: The value of the integral. """ # This is a conceptual representation. Actual implementation requires # a numerical integration method (e.g., Monte Carlo, quadrature) over the volume. totalintegral = 0.0 # Iterate over volume samples (e.g., via Monte Carlo sampling) for bxprime in volumedomain.sample(): distancesq = squaredlength(bxprime - viewpoint) # Avoid division by zero if sample coincides with view point if distancesq < epsilon: continue weight = 1.0 / distancesq visibility = visibilityfunc(bxprime, viewpoint) fvalue = integrandfunc(bxprime) # Estimate integral contribution # In Monte Carlo, this would involve importance sampling and PDF evaluation contribution = weight visibility fvalue totalintegral += contribution return totalintegral This is the surface analog of the volume change of variables. It transforms the integral over solid angle \mathcal{S}^2 to an integral over surface area \mathcal{M}. It replaces directional queries with direct spatial coordinates on the surface. Formula: \int{\mathcal{S}^2} f(\raycast(\bx, \bo)) \, d\bo = \int{\mathcal{M}} f(\bx') \frac{|\vec{n}' \cdot \bo{\bx \bx'}|}{\|\bx' - \bx\|^2} V(\bx' \to \bx) \, dA(\bx') Parameters: V(\bx' \to \bx): Visibility function (1 if visible, 0 if occluded). \bo{\bx \bx'}: Direction from \bx to \bx'. \vec{n}': Normal vector at \bx'. dA(\bx'): Differential area element at \bx'. Time Complexity: Depends on the numerical integration method used over the volume. For Monte Carlo, it scales with the number of samples. The evaluation of the visibility function V(\bx' \to \bx) can be a significant bottleneck if not precomputed or approximated. Memory Complexity: Depends on the representation of the volume \mathcal{V} and the visibility function. Strengths: Provides a unified framework for path integral formulations, treating volume and surface contributions similarly. It can simplify the analysis of light transport in participating media by removing the explicit ray parameterization. Limitations: The 1/\|\bx' - \bx\|^2 term can lead to high variance in Monte Carlo integration if not sampled carefully. The visibility function is difficult to compute efficiently for complex scenes. When to use: When formulating path integrals for participating media or when a direct spatial integration approach is preferred over ray marching. When not to use: For simple homogeneous volumes where analytical solutions exist, or when real-time performance is critical and ray marching is more efficient. This formulation is derived from the principles of light transport in participating media and is used in the context of the volume rendering equation. It is presented in the notes on the Volume Rendering Equation 2, which discusses the measurement equation and the path integral formulation of light transport. The concept is analogous to the surface integral formulation widely used in path tracing and bidirectional path tracing. ボリュームレンダリング方程式(Volume Rendering Equation) 2, https://rayspace.xyz/notes/VLTE2/, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Neumann Series Expansion
head: Neumann Series, Neumann Series Solution
body: The Neumann Series Expansion solves the Volume Rendering Integral by expressing the incoming radiance at a point as an infinite sum of contributions from light sources that have undergone 0, 1, 2, \dots scattering events. It operates directly on the integral equation operators rather than explicitly sampling path geometries. Inputs and Outputs: Input consists of the transport operator \mathbf{G}, the scattering operator \mathbf{K}, and the emitted radiance Le. The output is the incoming radiance Li at a specific point and direction. Data Structures: The method relies on continuous operator notation rather than discrete arrays. \mathbf{G} represents free-streaming and extinction. \mathbf{K} represents the integral over the unit sphere weighted by the phase function and scattering coefficient. Le represents emitted radiance from volume or surface sources. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute the direct term by applying \mathbf{G} to Le. 2. Iteratively compute higher-order terms by applying the composite operator \mathbf{G}\mathbf{K} to the result of the previous step. 3. Accumulate the terms into a sum until a chosen truncation depth N is reached. Formulas: The incoming radiance is defined as: Li = \sum{n=0}^\infty (\mathbf{G}\mathbf{K})^n \mathbf{G} Le = \mathbf{G} Le + \mathbf{G}\mathbf{K}\mathbf{G} Le + (\mathbf{G}\mathbf{K})^2 \mathbf{G} Le + \cdots. Symbol Definitions: n denotes the scattering order. \mathbf{G} Le represents light traveling from the source without scattering but still undergoing attenuation. \mathbf{G}\mathbf{K}\mathbf{G} Le represents light that scatters once. (\mathbf{G}\mathbf{K})^n \mathbf{G} Le represents light that has undergone n scattering events. Parameters: The truncation depth N controls the number of scattering terms computed; typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Attenuation via \mathbf{G} is applied even at n=0. Truncating the infinite series introduces bias into the result. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def neumannseriesexpansion(Le, G, K, maxterms): """ Computes incoming radiance Li using the Neumann Series Expansion. Args: Le: Emitted radiance function or value. G: Transport operator function (attenuation + streaming). K: Scattering operator function (integral over sphere). maxterms: Maximum number of scattering events to compute. Returns: Li: Approximated incoming radiance. """ Li = 0.0 term = G(Le) Li += term for in range(1, maxterms): term = G(K(term)) Li += term return Li Expresses the integral as a sum over paths of scattering events, allowing for arbitrary sequences of 2D surface locations and 3D positions in a participating medium. It transforms the measurement equation into a sum over path lengths k, where each term is an integral over a specific path space \mathcal{P}k^{\vec{c}}. It is a prerequisite for constructing participating medium-aware bidirectional integrators. Choose this when explicit path sampling is required for variance reduction in complex scenes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides a clear physical interpretation of light transport by separating contributions by scattering order. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. The Neumann Series Expansion is derived by recursively substituting the volume rendering equation into itself. Other historical details are not given in the sources. ボリュームレンダリング方程式(Volume Rendering Equation) 2, https://rayspace.xyz/notes/VLTE2/, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Path Integral Formulation
head: Generalized Path Space, Path Integral Representation, Path Space Integral
body: The Path Integral Formulation expresses the volume rendering integral as a sum over paths of scattering events, allowing for an arbitrary sequence of 2D surface locations and 3D positions in a participating medium. It transforms the measurement equation into a sum over path lengths k, where each term is an integral over a specific path space \mathcal{P}k^{\vec{c}}. This formulation is a prerequisite for constructing participating medium-aware bidirectional integrators. Inputs and Outputs Input: A scene defined by a surface manifold \mathcal{M} and a participating medium volume \mathcal{V}. Output: The measured radiance Ij for pixel j. Data Structures Path Type Vector \vec{c}: A binary vector \vec{c} \in \{0, 1\}^{k+1} of length k+1, where k is the path length. \vec{c}i = 0 indicates vertex \vxi is on the surface \mathcal{M}, and \vec{c}i = 1 indicates it is in the volume \mathcal{V}. Path Space \mathcal{P}k^{\vec{c}}: The Cartesian product of domains for each vertex based on \vec{c}, defined as \mathcal{P}k^{\vec{c}} = \prod{i=0}^{k} \{ \mathcal{M} \text{ if } \vec{c}i = 0, \mathcal{V} \text{ if } \vec{c}i = 1 \}. The total path space \mathcal{P} is the union of all path spaces for all lengths and types: \mathcal{P} = \bigcup{k=1}^\infty \bigcup{\vec{c} \in \{0,1\}^{k+1}} \mathcal{P}k^{\vec{c}}. The vertex \vx0 is the camera position, and \vxk is the light emission point. Generalized Scattering Distribution Function \bar{f} Combines surface BSDF and volumetric phase function with scattering coefficient: \bar{f}(\bx' \to \bx \to \bx''):= \begin{cases} fs(\bx' \to \bx \to \bx'') & \bx \in \mathcal{M} \\ \sigmas(\bx) fp(\bx' \to \bx \to \bx'') & \bx \in \mathcal{V} \end{cases} where fs is the surface BSDF, \sigmas is the scattering coefficient, and fp is the volumetric phase function. Measure d\mu The measure for a path \bar{\vx}k with type \vec{c} mixes area and volume elements: d\muk^{\vec{c}}(\bar{\vx}k):= \prod{i=0}^k \begin{cases} dA(\vxi) & \text{if } \vec{c}i = 0 \\ dV(\vxi) & \text{if } \vec{c}i = 1 \end{cases} where dA is the surface area element and dV is the volume element. Measurement Contribution Function fj For a path \bar{\vx}k = (\vx0, \vx1, \dots, \vxk), the integrand is: fj(\bar{\vx}k) = We^j(\vx1 \to \vx0) G(\vx1 \to \vx0) \prod{i=1}^{k-1} \left[ \bar{f}(\vx{i+1} \to \vxi \to \vx{i-1}) G(\vx{i+1} \to \vxi) \right] Le(\vxk \to \vx{k-1}) where We^j is the pixel weight function, G(\cdot \to \cdot) is the geometric term including visibility and attenuation, and Le is the emitted radiance. The product runs over the internal vertices i=1 to k-1. Algorithm The total radiance Ij is the sum over all path lengths k and all path types \vec{c}: Ij = \sum{k=1}^\infty \sum{\vec{c} \in \{0,1\}^{k+1}} \int{\mathcal{P}k^{\vec{c}}} fj(\bar{\vx}k) \, d\muk^{\vec{c}}(\bar{\vx}k) This can be written as a single integral over the total path space \mathcal{P}: Ij = \int{\mathcal{P}} fj(\bar{\vx}) \, d\mu(\bar{\vx}) Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatepathcontribution(path, c): """ Evaluates the integrand fj(vk) dmuk^c(vk) for a path of length k. path: tuple of vertices (v0, v1,..., vk) c: list of integers (0 or 1) indicating surface (0) or volume (1) for each vertex. Returns the product of the measurement contribution function and the measure differential. """ k = len(path) - 1 # Measurement contribution function fj contrib = scene.pixelweight(path[1], path[0]) scene.geometricterm(path[1], path[0]) for i in range(1, k): contrib = scene.generalizedscattering(path[i+1], path[i], path[i-1]) scene.geometricterm(path[i+1], path[i]) contrib = scene.emittedradiance(path[k], path[k-1]) # Measure differential dmuk^c measure = 1.0 for i in range(k + 1): if c[i] == 0: measure = scene.areadifferential(path[i]) else: measure = scene.volumedifferential(path[i]) return contrib measure Note: areadifferential and volumedifferential represent the infinitesimal elements dA and dV. In a Monte Carlo implementation, these are conceptually divided by the sampling PDF to estimate the integral. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Infinite Sum: The sum over k is infinite and must be truncated or terminated via Russian Roulette in practice. Path Type Explosion: The number of path types \vec{c} grows as 2^{k+1}, making explicit summation infeasible. Standard path tracing implicitly handles this by sampling the domain directly. Measure Definition: The measure d\mu mixes area and volume elements, requiring careful PDF matching during sampling. Special Cases: The case where \vec{c}i = 0 for all i reduces to the standard surface path integral. The case where \vec{c}i = 1 for all internal vertices represents paths entirely within the medium. The special case where \vec{c}i = 0 for all i, reducing to the standard surface path integral. The special case where \vec{c}i = 1 for all internal vertices, representing paths entirely within the medium. Complexity: The formulation is an exact mathematical identity. The complexity lies in the numerical integration via Monte Carlo methods. The number of path types grows exponentially with depth, but standard path tracing samples paths directly without enumerating types. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides a unified framework for handling both surface and volume scattering, enabling bidirectional integrators for participating media. Limitations: The infinite sum and high-dimensional integrals make direct evaluation impossible, relying on stochastic methods. The derivation of the medium-aware path integral is attributed to Pauly et al. (2000) and Chapter 3 of Jakob’s Ph.D. thesis (2013). It extends the surface path integral formulation to include participating media. Light Transport II: Volume Rendering / The Equation of Transfer, https://www.pbr-book.org/3ed-2018/LightTransportIIVolumeRendering/TheEquationofTransfer.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (book) ボリュームレンダリング方程式(Volume Rendering Equation) 2, https://rayspace.xyz/notes/VLTE2/, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Optical Modeling for CFI
head: CFI Optical Intensity Calculation, Shadowgraph/Schlieren/Interferometry Formulas
body: Optical Modeling for CFI is a theoretical framework for calculating optical intensities in Computational Flow Imaging (CFI) by performing line-of-sight integrations through a discrete three-dimensional flow field. It solves the problem of projecting 3D gas density or refractive index distributions onto a 2D view plane for visualization via shadowgraph, schlieren, or interferometric techniques. Unlike general volume rendering methods that compute radiative transfer, this model focuses on phase and intensity perturbations caused by refractive index gradients, building on the Volume Rendering Integral by specializing the integrand for optical flow diagnostics. Inputs: A discrete 3D field of gas density \rho(x,y,z) or refractive index n(x,y,z) on a grid. Integration limits z1, z2 defining the optical path length through the domain. Optical parameters: wavelength \lambda, reference refractive index n0, and glass plate angle difference \xi (or \xix, \xiy). Gladstone-Dale constant K (or species-specific constants for mixtures). Outputs: Optical intensity I for shadowgraph or schlieren modes. Fringe shift F(x,y) and resulting intensity I \propto \cos^2(\pi F) for interferometry. Data Structures: The input is a discrete 3D array. The integration is performed along the z-axis (line of sight) for each (x,y) pixel. The field is divided into n segments along the optical path. Formulas and Definitions: \xi: Difference of the angle of two glass plates P1 and P2. \lambda: Wavelength of the light source. n0: Refractive index of the reference field. z1, z2: Limits of integration representing the length along the optical path where the index of refraction varies. K: Gladstone-Dale constant. For mixtures, the text provides a garbled formula (2.8) involving mass fraction ai and species constant Ki. Standard physics implies a weighted sum, but the source text is ambiguous: "where a. is the mass fraction and Ki is the G-D constant of the specie.". Step-by-Step Method: 1. Determine Optical Mode: Select the appropriate intensity formula based on the imaging technique (Shadowgraph, Schlieren, or Interferometry). 2. Shadowgraph Intensity: Calculate the intensity proportional to the second derivative of density \rho integrated along z: I \propto \int{z1}^{z2} \left( \frac{\partial^2 \rho}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \rho}{\partial y^2} \right) dz In discrete form, using the trapezoidal rule or simple summation over n segments with step \Delta zi: I \propto \sum{i=1}^{n} \left( \frac{\partial^2 \rho}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \rho}{\partial y^2} \right)i \Delta zi 3. Schlieren Intensity: Calculate the intensity proportional to the first derivative of refractive index n integrated along z. Vertical knife-edge/filter: I \propto \int{z1}^{z2} \frac{\partial n}{\partial x} dz Horizontal knife-edge/filter: I \propto \int{z1}^{z2} \frac{\partial n}{\partial y} dz Discrete forms are implied by the trapezoidal rule application to the continuous integrals. 4. Interferometry Fringe Shift: Calculate the continuous fringe shift F(x,y): F(x,y) = \frac{2\xix}{\lambda} \int{z1}^{z2} [n(x,y,z) - n0] dz For discrete fields with n segments: F(x,y) = \frac{2\xix}{\lambda} \sum{i=1}^{n} [ni - n0] \Delta zi Alternatively, using the Gladstone-Dale equation n - 1 = K\rho, the fringe shift can be expressed in terms of density \rho and reference density \rho0 (where n0 - 1 = K\rho0): F(x,y) = \frac{2\xix K}{\lambda \rho0} \sum{i=1}^{n} \rhoi \Delta zi (Note: Source Eq 2.9 is garbled but this derivation follows from Eqs 2.6, 2.7, and 2.8). 5. Interferometry Intensity: Compute the final intensity: I \propto \cos^2(\pi F) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculatecfiintensity(fielddensity, fieldrefractiveindex, zlimits, dx, dy, dz, lambdawavelength, xix, xiy, n0, K, mode, usehorizontalschlieren=False): """ Calculate optical intensity for CFI modes. Args: fielddensity: 3D array (x, y, z) of density values rho. fieldrefractiveindex: 3D array (x, y, z) of refractive index values n. zlimits: Tuple (z1, z2) defining integration bounds. dx, dy, dz: Grid spacing in x, y, z directions. lambdawavelength: Wavelength lambda. xix, xiy: Glass plate angle differences. n0: Reference refractive index. K: Gladstone-Dale constant. mode: String, one of 'shadowgraph', 'schlieren', 'interferometry'. usehorizontalschlieren: Boolean, True for horizontal knife-edge, False for vertical. Returns: 2D array (x, y) of optical intensity or fringe shift. """ xdim, ydim, zdim = fielddensity.shape # Determine integration step and bounds # Assuming uniform grid for simplicity based on source description # The source mentions dividing path into n segments. # We iterate over z for each (x,y). intensitymap = np.zeros((xdim, ydim)) for x in range(xdim): for y in range(ydim): # Extract line-of-sight data # Note: Source implies integration along z. # We need to handle the derivatives for shadowgraph/schlieren. if mode == 'shadowgraph': # Calculate second derivatives in x and y # Using central differences for interior points, forward/backward for edges # d2rhodx2 if x == 0: d2rhodx2 = (fielddensity[x+1, y,:] - 2fielddensity[x, y,:] + fielddensity[x+1, y,:]) / (dx2) # Placeholder logic, source doesn't specify derivative scheme elif x == xdim - 1: d2rhodx2 = (fielddensity[x, y,:] - 2fielddensity[x, y,:] + fielddensity[x-1, y,:]) / (dx2) else: d2rhodx2 = (fielddensity[x+1, y,:] - 2fielddensity[x, y,:] + fielddensity[x-1, y,:]) / (dx2) # d2rhody2 if y == 0: d2rhody2 = (fielddensity[x, y+1,:] - 2fielddensity[x, y,:] + fielddensity[x, y+1,:]) / (dy2) # Placeholder logic elif y == ydim - 1: d2rhody2 = (fielddensity[x, y,:] - 2fielddensity[x, y,:] + fielddensity[x, y-1,:]) / (dy2) else: d2rhody2 = (fielddensity[x, y+1,:] - 2fielddensity[x, y,:] + fielddensity[x, y-1,:]) / (dy2) # Sum over z (integration) # Source Eq 2.1: sum of (d2rho/dx2 + d2rho/dy2) dz integrand = d2rhodx2 + d2rhody2 # Simple Riemann sum or Trapezoidal rule as per source mention integralvalue = np.sum(integrand dz) intensitymap[x, y] = integralvalue elif mode == 'schlieren': # Calculate first derivative of refractive index if usehorizontalschlieren: # Horizontal knife-edge: d/dy if y == 0: dndy = (fieldrefractiveindex[x, y+1,:] - fieldrefractiveindex[x, y,:]) / dy elif y == ydim - 1: dndy = (fieldrefractiveindex[x, y,:] - fieldrefractiveindex[x, y-1,:]) / dy else: dndy = (fieldrefractiveindex[x, y+1,:] - fieldrefractiveindex[x, y-1,:]) / (2dy) integrand = dndy else: # Vertical knife-edge: d/dx if x == 0: dndx = (fieldrefractiveindex[x+1, y,:] - fieldrefractiveindex[x, y,:]) / dx elif x == xdim - 1: dndx = (fieldrefractiveindex[x, y,:] - fieldrefractiveindex[x-1, y,:]) / dx else: dndx = (fieldrefractiveindex[x+1, y,:] - fieldrefractiveindex[x-1, y,:]) / (2dx) integrand = dndx integralvalue = np.sum(integrand dz) intensitymap[x, y] = integralvalue elif mode == 'interferometry': # Calculate fringe shift F # Eq 2.9: F = (2 xix K / (lambda rho0)) sum(rhoi dzi) # Note: Source uses xix for vertical fringes. # To get horizontal fringes, use xiy. # The source text for Eq 2.9 is garbled but links to density sum. # We need rho0. If not provided, assume derived from n0 and K? # n0 - 1 = K rho0 => rho0 = (n0 - 1) / K rho0 = (n0 - 1) / K # Sum of density along z rhosum = np.sum(fielddensity[x, y,:] dz) F = (2 xix K / (lambdawavelength rho0)) rhosum # Intensity intensitymap[x, y] = np.cos(np.pi F)2 return intensitymap Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Angle Difference (\xi = 0): If \xi = 0, the beams reach the photo plane with the same phase, resulting in no reference fringes (infinite-fringe mode). Non-Zero Angle Difference (\xi \neq 0): If \xi > 0 or \xi < 0, recombined beams interfere and produce reference fringes (finite-fringe mode). Fringe Orientation: The reference fringes in the standard equations are vertical. To obtain horizontal reference fringes, replace 2\xix with 2\xiy in the interferometry equations. Mixture Constants: The Gladstone-Dale constant K for gas mixtures is defined in the source with garbled text (Eq 2.8). Implementers should verify the exact mixing rule from primary physics literature if high accuracy is required, as the source text "A i P (2.8)" is unclear. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M \cdot L) where N, M are the spatial dimensions (x, y) and L is the number of segments along the optical path (z). Derivatives add a constant factor per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot M \cdot L) to store the 3D field. The output is O(N \cdot M). Strengths: Provides a direct, physically grounded mapping from CFD density fields to optical diagnostic images (shadowgraph, schlieren, interferometry). It is computationally efficient as it involves simple line integrations and derivatives. Limitations: Assumes paraxial approximation and straight-line light paths (no ray bending during integration). It does not account for multiple scattering or absorption, focusing only on refractive effects. The accuracy depends heavily on the grid resolution and the derivative approximation scheme. When to use: When visualizing flow fields using optical diagnostic techniques where density gradients are the primary observable. When not to use: For scenes with significant absorption, emission, or scattering (use Neumann Series Expansion or Volume Rendering Integral with extinction coefficients). For time-of-flight or phase-based depth sensing (use Continuous-Wave ToF Phasor Model). The method originates from research into Parallel Volume Rendering Algorithms for Computational Flow Imaging (CFI). It was developed to evaluate line-of-sight integrations through discrete three-dimensional fields for flow density measurement. The theoretical basis relies on classical optical diagnostics: shadowgraph (sensitive to second density derivatives), schlieren (sensitive to first refractive index derivatives), and interferometry (sensitive to optical path length differences). The Gladstone-Dale equation links gas density to refractive index, enabling the conversion of CFD density data into optical signals. The specific discrete integration algorithm using the trapezoidal rule was proposed to handle multizone or curvilinear grids common in CFD solutions. name: Acoustic Volume Rendering for Neural Impulse Response Fields
head: AVR
body: Acoustic Volume Rendering (AVR) computes the acoustic impulse response (RIR) of a 3D scene by treating sound propagation as a volume rendering problem, summing contributions from specular reflections, scattering, and diffraction along cast rays. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Continuous-Wave ToF Phasor Model and Neumann Series Expansion by explicitly modeling frequency-dependent material attenuation and multiple bounces within a unified quadrature framework, outperforming baselines such as NAF, INRAS, and AV-NeRF on standard datasets. Inputs: Scene geometry and material properties (reflection coefficient \beta, scattering coefficient \alpha). Source position and orientation. Receiver position and orientation. Simulation parameters: number of cast rays N\phi, number of angular samples N, maximum bouncing depth K{max}, number of volume steps Nr. Outputs: Frequency response H[f] for each source-receiver pair. Time-domain impulse response h(t) via inverse transform or direct summation. Data Structures: Material Properties: A lookup table mapping material names to frequency-dependent coefficients \beta(\omega) and \alpha(\omega). Ray Segment: Defined by near endpoint un and far endpoint uf. Volume Step: Defined by position um along the ray. Formulas: 1. Ray Sampling: The position of the m-th sample point p(um) along a ray segment from un to uf is: p(um) = pl + \left( \frac{uf - un}{Nr} m + un \right) \omega where pl is the ray origin and \omega is the ray direction. 2. Step Size: \Delta u = \frac{uf - un}{Nr} where Nr is the number of samples per ray. 3. Transmittance: The transmittance Tm to the m-th sample is: Tm = \exp \left( -\sum{x=1}^{m-1} \frac{uf - un}{\sigmax} \Delta u \right) where \sigmax is the extinction coefficient at step x. 4. Frequency Response per Ray: The contribution H\omega[f] for a specific frequency \omega is approximated by quadrature: H\omega[f] = F \sum{m=1}^{v} Tm (1 - \exp(-\sigmam \Delta u)) \frac{1}{tv} S(nT - \frac{um}{v}, \omega) where v is the number of volume steps, tv is a time scaling factor, S is the source/receiver directivity function, and F is a normalization constant. Note: The source text provides a slightly ambiguous summation index v vs Nr; we assume v=Nr for the quadrature sum. 5. Total Frequency Response: The total response H[f] sums over all rays i and angular samples j: H[f] = \sum{i=1}^{N\phi} \sum{j=1}^{N} G(\omega{ij}) H{\omega{ij}}[f] where G(\omega{ij}) is a weighting function. 6. Impulse Response (Time Domain): The impulse response h(t) is formulated as: h(t) = \sum{n=1}^{N} \frac{A}{dn} \delta{LP}\left(t - \frac{dn}{v}\right) \prod{k=1}^{K} (1 - \alpha{n,k})(-\beta{n,k}) where N is the number of paths, A is a constant, dn is the accumulated path length of the n-th path, v is the speed of sound, \alpha{n,k} and \beta{n,k} are the scattering and reflection coefficients for the k-th reflection of the n-th path, and \delta{LP} is a windowed sinc function. 7. Energy Update: For each reflection, the reflected wave's energy E' and scattered energy E'' are updated as: E' = (1 - \alpha)\beta E E'' = \alpha\beta E where E is the energy before interaction. Parameters: Maximum bouncing depth: 30. Number of cast rays: 10^6 (1e6). Grid size for loudness visualization: 0.1m. RIR duration: 0.32s. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeacousticvolumerendering(scene, source, receiver, params): """ Computes the acoustic impulse response using AVR. Args: scene: Object containing geometry and material lookup table. source: Source position and orientation. receiver: Receiver position and orientation. params: Dictionary with keys: Nphi: Number of cast rays (default 1e6) Nr: Number of samples per ray Kmax: Maximum bouncing depth (default 30) v: Speed of sound freqbands: List of frequency bands Returns: ht: Time-domain impulse response array. """ # Initialize total impulse response # Note: In practice, this might be accumulated in frequency domain then IFFT, # or directly in time domain as per Eq 23. We follow the time-domain formulation # for clarity of path summation. ht = [] # Cast rays for i in range(params['Nphi']): # Generate ray direction based on source orientation raydir = generateraydirection(source, i) rayorigin = source.position # Trace ray through scene path = traceray(rayorigin, raydir, scene, params['Kmax']) if path is None: continue # Calculate contribution for this path # Path consists of segments and reflections totallength = 0 attenuation = 1.0 reflections = [] currentpos = rayorigin for k, segment in enumerate(path.segments): dist = segment.length totallength += dist # Get material properties at intersection # Material properties are frequency-dependent material = scene.getmaterial(segment.intersectionpoint) # Retrieve coefficients for current frequency band # This loop is implicit in the frequency-domain formulation, # but for time-domain impulse response, we assume broadband coefficients # or sum over bands. Eq 23 uses specific alpha/beta. alpha = material.scatteringcoefficient beta = material.reflectioncoefficient # Update attenuation # Reflected energy: E' = (1 - alpha) beta E # Scattered energy: E'' = alpha beta E # The impulse response term uses (1-alpha)(-beta) # Note: The negative sign in (-beta) is due to phase inversion upon reflection attenuation = (1 - alpha) (-beta) reflections.append((alpha, beta)) # Check if receiver is hit (simplified) if segment.isreceiverhit: break # If path reached receiver or was terminated if path.reachedreceiver: # Calculate time delay timedelay = totallength / params['v'] # Calculate amplitude scaling # A / dn term from Eq 23 amplitude = params['A'] / totallength # Apply accumulated attenuation finalamplitude = amplitude attenuation # Create impulse contribution using windowed sinc # deltaLP is a windowed sinc function impulse = createwindowedsinc(finalamplitude, timedelay, params['v']) ht.append(impulse) # Sum all path contributions # In a real implementation, this would be a convolution or direct addition # depending on discretization. htfinal = sum(ht) return htfinal def createwindowedsinc(amplitude, timedelay, speedofsound): """ Creates a windowed sinc function for the impulse response. """ # deltaLP is defined similar to [39] in the source # Assuming a standard windowed sinc for acoustic simulation # This is a placeholder for the specific windowing function details # which are not fully specified in the provided text beyond "windowed sinc" # Implementation detail: Use a Hann-windowed sinc with bandwidth determined by simulation parameters. pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Scattering/Diffraction: The base equation assumes purely specular reflection. If scattering or diffraction occurs, the reflection term must be replaced with the corresponding scattering or diffraction attenuation. Precision: The exponential transmittance calculation can suffer from underflow for long paths or high extinction coefficients. Boundary Conditions: The ray tracing must correctly handle intersections with scene geometry to determine material properties. Time Complexity: Scales approximately linearly with the number of rays and the number of points sampled along each ray. Memory Complexity: Depends on the scene geometry and the number of rays stored for path tracing. Performance: On the RAF-Furnished dataset with a 0.32s RIR duration, AVR outperforms NAF, INRAS, and AV-NeRF across metrics including Phase, Amp, Env, T60, C50, and EDT errors. Strengths: Captures sound level differences caused by geometry occlusion and provides smoother spatial variation of loudness. Limitations: High computational cost due to the large number of rays (10^6) required for comprehensive path searching. Acoustic Volume Rendering (AVR) is based on the work presented in "Acoustic Volume Rendering for Neural Impulse Response Fields". It builds upon the Volume Rendering Integral [8682-volume-rendering-integral.md] and extends it to acoustic domains. The method is implemented in the AcoustiX platform, which is built on the Sionna ray tracing engine and supports reflection, scattering, and diffraction. Room models are created with Blender and exported in XML formats using the Mitsuba blender Add-on. name: Volume Shader
head: Participating Media Material, Principled Volume, Pyro Volume presets, Redshift Standard Volume shader, Standard Volume Material, Volume Material
body: A volume shader is a material definition for participating media that occupies space, instructing the render engine how light interacts with the medium at every point within a volume. It maps artistic parameters (Scattering, Absorption, Emission) to physical interactions, serving as the basis for implementations like the Standard Volume Shader Implementation and the Volumetric Scattering Model. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray position, ray direction, and spatial data (density, coefficients) at the current position. Output: Outgoing radiance contributed by the medium at that point. Data Structures The shader defines three primary ingredients per spatial point: 1. Scattering: The volume’s counterpart to a diffuse color, defining how much light bounces off microscopic particles and in which color (e.g., white for clouds, grey for smoke). 2. Absorption: The counterpart to transparency, defining how much light the medium swallows (e.g., making thick smoke dark). 3. Emission: The counterpart to incandescence, letting the medium give off light of its own (e.g., fire and explosions). Formulas Not given in the sources. Parameters Density: Multiplies the channel grid value, setting the overall thick or thin character of the medium. Scatter Color & Scale: Sets what the volume reflects and how brightly. Absorption: Defines the darkness or opacity of the volume. Emission: Defines self-illumination. Anisotropy Mode: Chooses the phase function: 'Henyey-Greenstein' (slider -1 to +1, all-rounder for isotropic smoke) or 'Jendersie-d’Eon' (cloud specialist modeling light through water droplets). Transparency Color & Depth: Implements per-wavelength travel distances. Measured in centimeters, set in relation to the real-world size of the volume. Darker means thicker, brighter means thinner, and any color tints the volume with its opposite at depth. Emission Channel & Mode: Points to the temperature grid for fire/explosions. 'Blackbody Mode' converts temperatures into physically correct colors on the Kelvin scale (deep red around 3,000 K to white/blue-white beyond 9,000 K). 'Color Mode' uses a classic black-to-red-to-yellow flame gradient for art-directed fire. Velocity Field: Input for motion blur in VDB sequences. Values far beyond 1,000 are normal. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Grid Name Case Sensitivity: The volume renders black or invisible if the grid name in the channel field is misspelled or has the wrong case, or if no light has volume contribution above zero. Insufficient Samples: The volume looks noisy if light samples are insufficient. Lights dominate volume noise; scattering-heavy media need more samples than absorption-heavy ones. Low Resolution: The volume looks blocky if simulation resolution is too low. Shader remapping can soften it, but higher resolution cache is required to truly fix it. VRAM Limits: The render aborts with an out of VRAM error if the VDB does not fit in GPU memory. Volumes are excluded from out-of-core systems. Flat Clouds: The cloud looks flat or grey if Volume Trace Depth is too low. Fix by raising depth with Brute Force GI, keeping Extinction Falloff at 0.2, and lowering Shadow Density Scale. Washed Out Fog: Fog washes out the frame if Environment Scattering value is too high. Reduce drastically; even small values are powerful. Benchmark Confusion: Do not confuse the volume shader material with 'Volume Shader BM', which is a GPU stress test benchmark, not a material. The Standard Volume Shader is a material definition for participating media that simulates light transport in heterogeneous environments where density varies per voxel, such as smoke, fog, or clouds. It distinguishes itself from subsurface scattering by applying random walk logic to non-polygonal, spatially varying density fields rather than uniform, bounded surfaces. It separates the geometric distribution of particles from their optical properties, using a scalar density grid for occupancy and distinct color channels for scattering albedo and wavelength-dependent absorption. Volumetric scattering models the interaction of light with participating media—substances like fog, smoke, clouds, and translucent solids (e.g., wax, skin) where the space itself participates in lighting. Unlike surface rendering, where radiance is constant along a ray between surfaces, participating media modify radiance through emission, absorption, out-scattering, and in-scattering. This method distinguishes itself by explicitly modeling the transport of light through volume using the radiative transfer equation, decomposed into extinction (absorption + out-scattering) and in-scattering terms, rather than approximating volume effects via surface shaders or simple opacity masks. Applying a volume shader to the world to fill the entire space. Most useful for night time or other dark scenes. Assumes the background is infinitely far away, which is inaccurate for modeling effects like fog or atmospheric scattering because most distance between light sources (e.g., sun) and objects is empty space; for such effects, a volume object surrounding the scene is better. Used to shade black smoke, colored glass objects, or mixed with Volume Scatter. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides a unified framework for defining complex volumetric behaviors (clouds, smoke, fire) through three intuitive parameters. Limitations: Requires gathering data at many positions within the volume for realistic rendering, which can be computationally expensive. The concept of the volume shader as a material for participating media is rooted in the physics of light transport in heterogeneous media. It is used by default for smoke and fire rendering when volume attributes are present. Modern render engines implement this through shaders like the Standard Volume shader, which supports scattering, absorption, and emission in a single node. name: Standard Volume Shader Implementation
head: RS Volume, Redshift Volume, Redshift Volume Shader
body: The Standard Volume Shader is a technique for rendering non-homogeneous participating media, such as smoke and fire, using voxel grids (typically OpenVDB) stored entirely in GPU memory. It differs from subsurface scattering by applying a random-walk light transport model to a heterogeneous medium where density varies at every voxel, rather than a uniform finite surface. It is built upon three shading components: Scatter (diffuse reflection), Absorption (transparency/extinction), and Emission (incandescence). Input: A volume object defined by an OpenVDB file or DCC volume grid, containing scalar channels (e.g., 'density', 'temperature'). Input: A scene containing at least one volume-affecting light with volume contribution scale > 0.0. Output: A rendered image where the volume interacts with light via scattering, absorption, and emission. The volume data is stored in GPU memory as a collection of grids. Each grid corresponds to a channel in the OpenVDB file. Grid Layout: A 3D array of voxels. Channel Data: Scalar values per voxel. Density Channel: Scalar description of particle count per voxel versus empty space. Temperature Channel: Scalar value representing heat, used for emission. Shader Parameters: scatterchannelname: String identifying the density channel. emissionchannelname: String identifying the temperature channel. scattercolor: RGB albedo of suspended particles. transparencycolor: RGB mean free path values (0 to 1). depth: Float multiplier converting transparency color to real-world distance in centimeters. anisotropy: Float controlling scattering directionality. scattercoefficient: Float scaling brightness. absorptioncoefficient: Float scaling opacity. emissionmode: Enum (Color Ramp or Blackbody). emissionramp: Gradient mapping channel values to emissive colors. blackbodytemperature: Float in Kelvin (default 6500K). blackbodyoffset: Float interpolating intensity (default 1.0). 1. Initialization: Load the OpenVDB file into GPU memory. If the data exceeds available VRAM, abort rendering. Identify the channels specified by scatterchannelname and emissionchannelname. If these are not set or do not exist, the volume renders as black/empty. Verify the presence of at least one light with volume contribution scale > 0.0. If absent, render black. 2. Ray Marching: For each pixel, cast a ray into the scene. Determine the entry and exit points of the ray within the volume bounding box. Step through the volume along the ray direction. The step size is determined by the voxel resolution or a fixed march step. At each step position P, sample the density grid to obtain the scalar density value d. 3. Optical Property Calculation: Scattering Coefficient (\sigmas): \sigmas = d \cdot \text{scatter\coefficient} Absorption Coefficient (\sigmaa): \sigmaa = d \cdot \text{absorption\coefficient} Total Extinction Coefficient (\sigmat): \sigmat = \sigmas + \sigmaa (Standard radiative transfer definition implied by coefficients) Single Scattering Albedo (\omega0): \omega0 = \frac{\sigmas}{\sigmat} (Derived from coefficients) Phase Function (p(\Omegai \to \Omegao)): If anisotropy \neq 0, use Henyey-Greenstein (default) or Jendersie-d’Eon (for cloud-like water). If anisotropy = 0, use isotropic scattering. 4. Emission Calculation: Sample the temperature channel at P to get value T{val}. If emissionmode is Color Ramp: Map T{val} through the emissionramp to get emissive color Le. If emissionmode is Blackbody: Calculate blackbody radiance L{bb} based on blackbodytemperature. Interpolate between channel value and calculated radiance using blackbodyoffset. Le = \text{lerp}(T{val}, L{bb}, \text{blackbody\offset}) (Interpretation of "interpolates... between channel value and calculated radiance") 5. Transmittance and Color Accumulation: Initialize transmittance T = 1.0 and accumulated color C = 0.0 (Standard volume rendering integral setup). For each step of length \Delta s: Calculate optical depth for the step: \tau = \sigmat \cdot \Delta s. Calculate transmittance through the step: t = e^{-\tau}. Calculate emitted and scattered light contribution: C{step} = T \cdot (Le + \sigmas \cdot \text{incident\light} \cdot p(\dots)) (Simplified single-bounce approximation; multiple scattering is handled via "Shadow Density Scale" trick or more complex integration not fully detailed in sources). Update accumulated color: C = C + C{step} \cdot t. Update transmittance: T = T \cdot t. If T < \epsilon (threshold), break loop. Final pixel color contribution: C{final} = C + T \cdot C{background}. 6. Wavelength-Dependent Absorption (Transparency Color): The transparencycolor defines the mean free path for each wavelength. Let M{rgb} be the transparencycolor vector (values 0 to 1). Let D be the depth parameter (real distance in cm). The effective mean free path for each channel is m{rgb} = M{rgb} \cdot D. The absorption coefficient for each wavelength is inversely proportional to the mean free path: \sigma{a, rgb} = \frac{1}{m{rgb}} \cdot d (Derived from "mean free path... average distance... before being extinguished" and "density grid... scalar description"). Note: Sources state that transparencycolor is an "artist friendly encoding" and depth multiplies these 0-1 values into real distances. The exact formula for integrating this into \sigmaa alongside absorptioncoefficient is not explicitly given, but the physical effect is that different wavelengths are absorbed at different rates, causing tinting. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervolumeray(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata, shaderparams): """ Renders a single ray through a volume using the Standard Volume Shader logic. """ # 1. Check for lights if not hasvolumeaffectinglights(): return Color(0, 0, 0) # 2. Initialize accumulation transmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = Color(0, 0, 0) # 3. Determine march bounds entrypoint, exitpoint = intersectvolumebbox(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata.bbox) if entrypoint is None: return raybackgroundcolor(raydirection) # 4. Ray march currentpos = entrypoint stepsize = volumedata.voxelsize # Or fixed step maxsteps = 1000 # Safety limit for i in range(maxsteps): if currentpos > exitpoint: break # Sample density density = volumedata.sampledensity(currentpos) # Skip empty space if density < 1e-6: currentpos += raydirection stepsize continue # Calculate coefficients sigmas = density shaderparams.scattercoefficient sigmaabase = density shaderparams.absorptioncoefficient # Apply wavelength-dependent absorption from transparency color # transparencycolor (0-1) depth (cm) = meanfreepath (cm) # sigmaawavelength = 1 / meanfreepath densityfactor? # Sources say transparencycolor encodes mean free path. # Let's assume sigmaa is modified by transparency color ratios. # Simplified: sigmaatotal = sigmaabase (1 / transparencycoloreffective) # But sources say "transparency color... represents travel distance". # We will apply the tinting effect via transmittance per channel. sigmat = sigmas + sigmaabase # Phase function phase = evaluatephasefunction(shaderparams.anisotropy, raydirection, lightdirection) # Emission tempval = volumedata.sampletemperature(currentpos) if shaderparams.emissionmode == 'Color Ramp': emissioncolor = shaderparams.emissionramp.map(tempval) else: # Blackbody bbradiance = blackbodyradiance(shaderparams.blackbodytemperature) emissioncolor = lerp(tempval, bbradiance, shaderparams.blackbodyoffset) # Incident light (simplified single scattering) incidentlight = getlightcontribution(currentpos, raydirection, volumedata) # Contribution # Lstep = T (E + sigmas Linc phase) # Note: Multiple scattering is approximated or handled by Shadow Density Scale stepcontribution = transmittance (emissioncolor + sigmas incidentlight phase) accumulatedcolor += stepcontribution exp(-sigmat stepsize) transmittance = exp(-sigmat stepsize) if transmittance < 0.001: break currentpos += raydirection stepsize # 5. Apply background finalcolor = accumulatedcolor + transmittance raybackgroundcolor(raydirection) # 6. Apply Shadow Density Scale (trick for multiple scattering approximation) # This parameter makes volume more/less opaque to shadow rays. # It is a post-process or ray-march modifier not fully detailed in formula. # finalcolor = applyshadowdensityscale(finalcolor, shaderparams.shadowdensityscale) return finalcolor Scatter Coefficient: Default 1.0. Increases brightness. Absorption Coefficient: Default 1.0. Increases opacity. Depth: Multiplies transparency color 0-1 values to real cm distances. Aware of scene scale. Anisotropy: Default 0 (isotropic). Positive values scatter forward (Henyey-Greenstein). Blackbody Temperature: Default 6500K. Blackbody Offset: Default 1.0. Shadow Density Scale: Advanced parameter to emulate multiple scattering by adjusting opacity to shadow rays. VRAM Limit: Volume objects must fit entirely in GPU memory. If they do not, rendering aborts with an out-of-VRAM error. Missing Channels: If scatterchannelname or emissionchannelname are not set or do not exist in the OpenVDB file, the volume will not render (renders black/empty). Missing Lights: If no volume-affecting lights are present (volume contribution scale \le 0.0), the volume renders black. Smoke/Fire Interference: Smoke (scatter/absorption) obstructs fire (emission). Adjustments to scatter/absorption must not interfere too much with emission. Temperature Range Remapping: Temperature channel ranges vary by 3D app. Range remapping may be necessary if the emission ramp does not align with the data range. Wavelength Tinting: Light traveling far through the medium becomes tinted with the opposite of the transparency color as other wavelengths are exhausted (e.g., deep water blue). Memory Complexity: O(V), where V is the total number of voxels in the OpenVDB file. All data must reside in GPU VRAM. Time Complexity: O(R \cdot M), where R is the number of rays and M is the number of march steps per ray. Cost increases with density and number of scattering bounces. Performance: Volumes are expensive due to the cost of ray marching and multiple scattering calculations. Single scattering is sufficient for thin media; multiple scattering requires more samples or tricks like Shadow Density Scale. Strengths: Artist-friendly parameters (transparency color, depth), physically plausible wavelength-dependent absorption, integration with OpenVDB. Limitations: High memory usage (no out-of-core support), sensitive to light setup, requires careful tuning of scatter/absorption/emission balance. Origin: The Standard Volume Shader is part of the Redshift renderer by Maxon. Development: It is described internally as a close relative of Random Walk Subsurface Scattering, adapted for heterogeneous media. Usage: Used for rendering smoke, fire, clouds, and fog in 3D applications like Cinema 4D, Maya, and Houdini via Redshift. name: Volumetric Scattering Model
head: Participating Media Physics, Participating Medium Rendering
body: Volumetric scattering models light interaction with participating media—substances like fog, smoke, clouds, and translucent solids where space participates in lighting. Unlike surface rendering where radiance is constant between surfaces, participating media modify radiance through emission, absorption, out-scattering, and in-scattering. This method distinguishes itself by explicitly modeling light transport through volume using the radiative transfer equation, decomposed into extinction and in-scattering terms, rather than approximating volume effects via surface shaders. It builds on Volume Shader and differs from the Standard Volume Shader Implementation by exposing the underlying physical coefficients directly. Inputs: Ray origin x and direction \omega. Volume definition (homogeneous or heterogeneous) providing spatially varying coefficients. Light sources for direct in-scattering. Environment map or indirect lighting cache for indirect in-scattering. Phase function parameters (e.g., anisotropy g, wavelength \lambda). Outputs: Radiance L(x, \omega) accumulated along the ray segment. The implementation relies on two primary abstractions: 1. Volume Class: evaluate(x): Returns a struct containing absorption coefficient \sigmaa(x), scattering coefficient \sigmas(x), emission E(x), and a phase function object. intersect(ray): Returns entry and exit distances or a bounding volume test. 2. Phase Function Class: evaluate(costheta): Returns probability density value. sample(costheta): Returns a sampled direction and PDF. The change in radiance dL along a differential path length ds is governed by four processes: 1. Emission: dL(x, \omega) = \frac{E(x) ds}{4\pi} Where E(x) is isotropic emission per unit length. 2. Absorption: dL(x, \omega) = -\sigmaa(x) L(x, \omega) ds Where \sigmaa is the absorption coefficient in units of 1/m. 3. Out-Scattering: dL(x, \omega) = -\sigmas(x) L(x, \omega) ds Where \sigmas is the scattering coefficient. 4. Extinction: Combining absorption and out-scattering: \sigmat(x) = \sigmaa(x) + \sigmas(x) dL(x, \omega) = -\sigmat(x) L(x, \omega) ds Absorption and out-scattering are combined into extinction. 5. Transmittance: The fraction of light surviving distance s: T(s) = e^{-\tau(s)} = e^{-\int0^s \sigmat(x + s'\omega) ds'} For homogeneous media, \tau(s) = \sigmat s. 6. In-Scattering: Light scattered into the ray direction from other directions \omegai: dL(x, \omega) = \sigmas(x) ds \int{4\pi} p(\omegai \cdot \omega) L(x, \omegai) d\omegai Where p(\cos \theta) is the phase function. The phase function p(\cos \theta) describes the angular distribution of scattered light. It must be reciprocal and energy-conserving. Isotropic: p(\cos \theta) = \frac{1}{4\pi} Scatters equally in all directions. Henyey-Greenstein: p(\cos \theta) = \frac{1 - g^2}{4\pi (1 + g^2 - 2g\cos \theta)^{1.5}} Uses anisotropy parameter g \in [-1, 1]. g=0 is isotropic; g>0 is forward-scattering; g<0 is back-scattering. Rayleigh (for particles d \ll \lambda): p(\cos \theta) = \frac{3}{16\pi} (1 + \cos^2 \theta) Scattering coefficient: \sigmas = \frac{2\pi^5 d^6}{3 \lambda^4} \frac{(n^2 - 1)^2}{(n^2 + 2)^2}. Empirical Mie Approximation: p(\cos \theta) = \frac{1}{4\pi} \frac{z+1}{2} \left( \frac{1 + \cos \theta}{2} \right)^z Controls forward scattering sharpness via parameter z (e.g., z=8, 32). The integral form of the radiative transfer equation is solved numerically via ray marching. 1. Discretization: Divide the ray segment inside the volume into finite segments. 2. Step Size: Use a maximum step size \Delta s{max}. Each actual step taken is a random number from 0 to 1 times the maximum step size. 3. Accumulation: For each segment, compute the change in radiance due to emission, absorption, out-scattering, and in-scattering. 4. In-Scattering Approximation: Li(x, \omega) \approx \frac{4\pi \sigmas(x)}{N} \sum{N} p(\omegai \cdot \omega) L(x, \omegai) Computed by tracing shadow rays to light sources (direct) and generating sample scattering rays traced into the environment (indirect). 5. Shadow Ray Calculation: Trace a ray to the light. First test for opaque surfaces. If nothing blocks, test for volumes. If the ray passes through volume, attenuate light by extinction, resulting in a [0, 1] scale factor. For homogeneous volumes, attenuate by total length. For inhomogeneous volumes, ray march through volume applying local extinction to each segment. 6. Update Rule: L(x + s\omega, \omega) \approx e^{-\sigmat(x) s} L(x, \omega) + E(x) s + Li(x) s Absorption and out-scattering are combined into extinction. Emission is approximated as emission at point x times length s. In-scattering at point x is represented by Li(x). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def raymarchvolume(rayorigin, raydirection, volume, lightsources, envmap, maxstep=0.1, numsamples=16): tentry, texit = volume.intersect(rayorigin, raydirection) if tentry is None: return 0.0 tcurrent = tentry currentradiance = 0.0 # Background radiance PI = math.pi while tcurrent < texit: # Each actual step taken is a random number from 0 to 1 times the maximum step size stepsize = random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) maxstep remaining = texit - tcurrent if stepsize > remaining: stepsize = remaining currentpos = rayorigin + tcurrent raydirection volprops = volume.evaluate(currentpos) sigmaa = volprops.sigmaa sigmas = volprops.sigmas sigmat = sigmaa + sigmas emission = volprops.emission # Absorption and out-scattering combined into extinction tau = sigmat stepsize segmenttransmittance = math.exp(-tau) # In-Scattering Approximation: Li(x, ω) ≈ (4π σs(x) / N) Σ p(ωi · ω) L(x, ωi) directsum = 0.0 indirectsum = 0.0 for in range(numsamples): # Direct in-scattering: trace shadow rays to light sources for light in lightsources: shadowdist = volume.intersect(currentpos, light.direction) if shadowdist is not None and shadowdist < light.distance: lightatten = math.exp(-sigmat shadowdist) directsum += light.intensity lightatten # Indirect in-scattering: generate sample scattering rays traced into environment envdir = sampleuniformsphere() indirectsum += envmap.sample(currentpos, envdir) # Evaluate phase function p(ωi · ω) for sampled directions phasevaldirect = volprops.phasefunction.evaluate(raydirection, lightsources[0].direction) phasevalindirect = volprops.phasefunction.evaluate(raydirection, envdir) lix = (4.0 PI sigmas / numsamples) ( phasevaldirect directsum + phasevalindirect indirectsum) # Update Rule: L(x + sω) ≈ e^(-σt s) L(x) + E(x) s + Li(x) s emissioncontrib = emission stepsize inscatteringcontrib = lix stepsize currentradiance = segmenttransmittance currentradiance + emissioncontrib + inscatteringcontrib tcurrent += stepsize return currentradiance Homogeneous vs. Heterogeneous: Homogeneous volumes allow computational shortcuts and closed-form transmittance (e^{-\sigmat s}). Heterogeneous volumes vary across space and require ray marching for every shadow ray and in-scattering calculation, significantly increasing cost. Single vs. Multiple Scattering: Single scattering (one event) is sufficient for thin haze and light beams, and for thicker volumes with high absorption like smoke. It is not sufficient for dense, low-absorption volumes like clouds where multiple scattering dominates. Precision: Small step sizes are needed for high-frequency heterogeneous volumes to avoid aliasing, but increase computational cost. Phase Function Sampling: Importance sampling the phase function is required for efficient Monte Carlo integration of in-scattering. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Physically accurate representation of light transport in participating media; handles complex lighting effects like light beams and subsurface scattering. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to the need for in-scattering integration; single scattering approximations fail for dense media. When to Use: Clouds, smoke, fog, translucent materials. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The volumetric scattering model is rooted in the physics of radiative transfer in participating media. Physicists call fog, smoke, and clouds participating media because the space itself participates in the lighting instead of leaving light alone until it hits a surface. Key developments include the Henyey-Greenstein phase function, a classic model from a 1941 astrophysics paper originally designed to model scattering in galactic dust clouds. Rayleigh scattering describes scattering by particles much smaller than the wavelength. Mie scattering approximates the true scattering of water droplets. The ray marching algorithm is a standard numerical solution for the radiative transfer equation in rendering. What Is Volumetric Rendering? name: World Volume
body: A World Volume applies a volume shader to the entire scene space, filling it with participating media. It differs from bounded volume objects by assuming the background is infinitely far away. This assumption is accurate for distant light sources like the sun but makes it unsuitable for effects like fog or atmospheric scattering, where most distance between light sources and objects is empty space. It is primarily useful for night-time or other dark scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume shader definition applied to the world context. Output: The final rendered image where the entire space is treated as a participating medium. Data Structures: The implementation relies on the standard Volume Shader data structures defined in the parent article Volume Shader. No additional global data structures are specified for the World Volume itself beyond the shader parameters. Steps: 1. Initialize the view ray for each pixel. 2. Treat the entire ray length as traversing the volume, ignoring world boundaries or background planes. 3. Evaluate the volume shader along the ray to compute transmittance and accumulated color. 4. Assume the background is at infinite distance. Formulas: The rendering follows standard front-to-back volume integration: T(t) = \exp\left(-\int0^t (\sigmaa(\tau) + \sigmas(\tau)) d\tau\right) C = \int0^{\infty} \sigmae(t) T(t) dt where \sigmaa is absorption, \sigmas is scattering, and \sigmae is emission. Parameters: Volume Shader: Contains scattering, absorption, and emission properties. Background Distance: Assumed to be infinite. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Infinite Background Assumption: The method assumes the background is infinitely far away. This is accurate for distant light sources like the sun but inaccurate for effects like fog or atmospheric scattering, where most distance between light sources and objects is empty space. Scene Darkness: Because the world background is assumed to be infinitely far away, using a World Volume causes the world surface shader or sun lights to have no effect if a volume shader is used. Geometry Holes: If scene geometry has holes or normals point in the wrong direction, the renderer is unable to decide what is the inside or outside of the volume, following the same rules as rendering glass refraction correctly. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderworldvolume(rayorigin, raydirection, volumeshader, stepsize): # World volume fills entire space; background is infinitely far away. # Standard front-to-back volume rendering integration. accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0) transmittance = 1.0 t = 0.0 maxdist = 1e6 # Represents infinite background assumption while t < maxdist: pos = rayorigin + raydirection t sigmaa = volumeshader.absorption(pos) sigmas = volumeshader.scattering(pos) emission = volumeshader.emission(pos) deltat = stepsize opticaldepth = (sigmaa + sigmas) deltat steptransmittance = exp(-opticaldepth) accumulatedcolor += emission transmittance (1.0 - steptransmittance) transmittance = steptransmittance t += deltat return accumulatedcolor A technique used in conjunction with World Volume rendering to composite the final image. It samples front-to-back (f2b) and back-to-front (b2f) accumulated volume textures at normalized screen coordinates (u\screen\size). The colors are blended using the formula color = f2b + b2f \times (1.0 - f2b.a). Finally, a transfer function is applied to the resulting color: gl\FragmentColor = texture(u\transfer, vec2(color.r, 0.0)). This method requires three sampler2D inputs: uf2b for the front-to-back accumulated volume texture, ub2f for the back-to-front accumulated volume texture, and utransfer for the transfer function texture. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Useful for night-time or dark scenes where global atmospheric effects are desired without explicit geometry. Limitations: Inaccurate for modeling fog or atmospheric scattering due to the infinite background assumption, which ignores the empty space between light sources and objects. Can cause scenes to become dark if it overrides world surface shaders or sun lights. When to use: Night-time scenes or dark environments. When not to use: Fog or atmospheric scattering effects where the distance between light sources and objects is significant. The World Volume concept is documented in the Blender Manual. It is part of the volume shader system, which allows materials to occupy space and interact with light through scattering, absorption, and emission. The specific pitfall regarding the infinite background assumption highlights the distinction between global volumes and bounded volume objects.
