name: Empirical and Hybrid Models
body: Empirical and Hybrid Models provide non-physical or semi-physical approximations for volumetric light transport, prioritizing visual fidelity and performance over strict adherence to the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE). Unlike physically accurate methods that solve for multiple scattering, these models use heuristic shading terms, blurred indirect light, or hybrid surface-volume compositing to simulate translucency and atmospheric effects at interactive rates. They set themselves apart from Absorption-only model by including scattering-like effects, and from Single Scattering Models by avoiding the computational cost of exact integration, often relying on precomputed gradients or empirical blur operations. An interactive optical model that captures the qualitative appearance of translucency by blending direct attenuation with a blurred indirect light contribution and surface shading Empirical Translucent Volume Shading. It solves the problem of rendering semi-transparent data with realistic lighting without simulating multiple scattering Empirical Translucent Volume Shading. Choose this when interactive rates are required for complex optical properties where physical accuracy is secondary to visual appeal Empirical Translucent Volume Shading. A method for visualizing CFD data that combines physically-based atmospheric attenuation for low-albedo gases with a scanline-buffer algorithm for surface-defined objects Hybrid Surface-Volume Rendering. It sets itself apart by explicitly integrating surface fragments into the volume traversal loop to determine rendering extent, displaying the entirety of 3D data rather than just isosurfaces Hybrid Surface-Volume Rendering. Choose this when rendering mixed scenes with both dense volumetric gas and solid geometric objects Hybrid Surface-Volume Rendering. A rendering approach using separate volumes for emission, absorption, and reflection to simulate material light properties, with gradients computed on the fly by the GPU. It allows for fine-grained control over voxel properties using scaling factors (k{em}, k{ab}, k{ref}) and boolean masks. It is chosen for detailed visualization of specific tissue types or markers in medical/scientific data where distinct light interaction properties need to be highlighted. The method sets emission and absorption volumes to the same data source, sets the reflection volume to a constant value of 1 for each voxel, and applies scaling factors globally or per-voxel. Boolean operations with masks select areas of interest for targeted voxel manipulation. Square root normalization is applied to combined volumes to amplify visibility after inversion, and final images are inverted to enhance print quality and contrast. Stereo rendering is optionally enabled by offsetting the camera along the x-axis to generate anaglyph images. The implementation uses a LUT resolution of 64 \times 64 \times 64, a Henyey–Greenstein phase function with asymmetry parameter g = 0.8, a focal length of 3.0 scene units, a distance to object of 6 scene units, and an opacity threshold of 0.95. The concepts stem from the need for real-time or near-real-time visualization of complex volumetric data, such as medical imaging (e.g., zebrafish embryos, brain tumors) and CFD simulations (12114-hybrid-surface-volume-rendering.md). The specific implementations cited originate from research published in Digital (2024) regarding GPU-enabled volume rendering. The hybrid approach addresses limitations of traditional isosurface rendering by capturing the full volume extent Hybrid Surface-Volume Rendering. The empirical model addresses the computational bottleneck of multiple scattering by using heuristic approximations Empirical Translucent Volume Shading. GPU-Enabled Volume Renderer for Use with MATLAB, https://doi.org/10.3390/digital4040049, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Empirical Translucent Volume Shading
head: Empirical volume shading model, Interactive Translucent Volume Shading, Volumetric light attenuation model
body: Empirical Translucent Volume Shading is an interactive optical model for volume rendering that captures the qualitative appearance of translucency and volumetric shadows by adding a blurred indirect light contribution to the direct light term. It solves the problem of rendering semi-transparent volumetric data with realistic light transport effects at interactive rates, avoiding the computational cost of full multiple scattering simulations. Unlike physically accurate methods, it prioritizes visual fidelity (color bleeding, diffusion) over quantitative accuracy, and unlike analytical approximations, it imposes no restrictions on external illumination or optical properties. The method computes the final eye radiance by integrating along the view ray, modulating the volume's reflectance with a composite shading term that blends direct attenuation and surface shading, and illuminating the volume with a light field that includes both direct attenuation and a blurred indirect component. Inputs: Scalar volume data field V. Optical properties: extinction coefficient \tau(x), indirect extinction coefficient \taui(x). Geometric properties: Normalized gradient of the scalar field \nabla V / |\nabla V| used for surface shading. Lighting: Light intensity Il(0), light direction/source position. Parameters: Scattering factor S(s), blur kernel parameter \theta. Outputs: Final eye radiance I{eye} for each pixel. Volume Data: A 3D grid of scalar values. Extinction Coefficients: 3D grids for \tau(x) and \taui(x). These may be derived from the scalar data or provided as separate textures. Gradient Field: Precomputed or on-the-fly normalized gradients of the scalar data for surface shading evaluation. The final radiance I{eye} is calculated as: I{eye} = I0 Te(0) + \int0^{eye} Te(s) C(s) Il(s) ds \quad (5) Where: I0 is the background light intensity. Te(0) is the transmittance from the eye to the start of the volume. s is the position along the view ray from the eye to the far plane. Te(s) is the transmittance from sample s to the eye: Te(s) = \exp\left(-\ints^{eye} \tau(x)dx\right) \quad (2) where \tau(x) is the extinction coefficient at sample x. C(s) is the composite shading term: C(s) = g(s) ((1 - S(s)) + fs(s)S(s)) \quad (6) where: g(s) is the emission/reflective term (often derived from the scalar data value or a transfer function). S(s) is the scattering factor parameter controlling the blend between direct attenuation and surface shading. fs(s) is the Blinn-Phong shading model evaluated using the normalized gradient of the scalar data field at s. Il(s) is the total light intensity at sample s, consisting of direct and blurred indirect contributions: Il(s) = Il(0) \exp\left(-\ints^{light} \tau(x)dx\right) + Il(0) \exp\left(-\ints^{light} \taui(x)dx\right) \text{Blur}(\theta) \quad (7) where: Il(0) is the initial light intensity. \tau(x) is the extinction coefficient. \taui(x) is the indirect extinction coefficient. \text{Blur}(\theta) is a blur operation applied to the indirect light term, parameterized by \theta. S(s): Scattering factor. Controls the weight of the surface shading term fs(s) versus the direct attenuation term (1-S(s)). No specific value or computation method is provided in the sources. \theta: Parameter for the blur operation \text{Blur}(\theta). No specific value or kernel definition is provided in the sources. \tau(x): Extinction coefficient. Used in transmittance and direct light attenuation integrals. \taui(x): Indirect extinction coefficient. Used in the indirect light attenuation term. The following pseudocode implements the discrete integration step for a single view ray. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rendervolumeray(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata, taugrid, tauigrid, lightintensity, lightdirection, scatteringfactorfunc, blurparam, backgroundlight, dt, numsteps, numlightsteps): """ Renders a single ray using Empirical Translucent Volume Shading. """ tauintegral = 0.0 accumulatedradiance = 0.0 for i in range(numsteps): s = rayorigin + raydirection (i dt) # Sample optical and geometric properties tau = interpolate3d(taugrid, s) taui = interpolate3d(tauigrid, s) gs = interpolate3d(volumedata, s) # Transmittance from eye to current sample s Tes = math.exp(-tauintegral) # Light transmittance towards light (direct) taulightintegral = 0.0 for j in range(numlightsteps): slight = s + lightdirection (j dt) taulightintegral += interpolate3d(taugrid, slight) dt # Light transmittance towards light (indirect) tauilightintegral = 0.0 for j in range(numlightsteps): slight = s + lightdirection (j dt) tauilightintegral += interpolate3d(tauigrid, slight) dt # Total light intensity at s directatten = math.exp(-taulightintegral) indirectatten = math.exp(-tauilightintegral) blurfactor = blurkernel(blurparam) Ils = lightintensity directatten + lightintensity indirectatten blurfactor # Composite shading C(s) Ss = scatteringfactorfunc(s) normal = normalize(getgradient3d(volumedata, s)) viewdir = normalize(-raydirection) halfvec = normalize(lightdirection + viewdir) fss = blinnphongshading(normal, lightdirection, halfvec) Cs = gs ((1.0 - Ss) + fss Ss) # Accumulate radiance contribution accumulatedradiance += Tes Cs Ils dt # Update transmittance integral for next step tauintegral += tau dt # Background contribution: I0 Te(0) finalradiance = backgroundlight math.exp(-tauintegral) + accumulatedradiance return finalradiance def interpolate3d(grid, pos): # Trilinear interpolation from 3D grid at position pos x, y, z = pos ix, iy, iz = int(x), int(y), int(z) fx, fy, fz = x - ix, y - iy, z - iz def sample(x, y, z): return grid[x % grid.width][y % grid.height][z % grid.depth] c000 = sample(ix, iy, iz) c100 = sample(ix+1, iy, iz) c010 = sample(ix, iy+1, iz) c110 = sample(ix+1, iy+1, iz) c001 = sample(ix, iy, iz+1) c101 = sample(ix+1, iy, iz+1) c011 = sample(ix, iy+1, iz+1) c111 = sample(ix+1, iy+1, iz+1) c00 = c000 (1-fx) + c100 fx c10 = c010 (1-fx) + c110 fx c01 = c001 (1-fx) + c101 fx c11 = c011 (1-fx) + c111 fx c0 = c00 (1-fy) + c10 fy c1 = c01 (1-fy) + c11 fy return c0 (1-fz) + c1 fz def getgradient3d(grid, pos): # Central difference approximation of gradient at pos dx, dy, dz = 0.001, 0.001, 0.001 gx = interpolate3d(grid, (pos[0]+dx, pos[1], pos[2])) - interpolate3d(grid, (pos[0]-dx, pos[1], pos[2])) gy = interpolate3d(grid, (pos[0], pos[1]+dy, pos[2])) - interpolate3d(grid, (pos[0], pos[1]-dy, pos[2])) gz = interpolate3d(grid, (pos[0], pos[1], pos[2]+dz)) - interpolate3d(grid, (pos[0], pos[1], pos[2]-dz)) return (gx, gy, gz) def blinnphongshading(normal, lightdir, halfvec): # Standard Blinn-Phong: diffuse + specular diffuse = max(0.0, dot(normal, lightdir)) specular = max(0.0, dot(normal, halfvec)) 32 return diffuse + specular def blurkernel(theta): # Simple exponential decay approximation for Blur(theta) return math.exp(-theta) def normalize(v): return (v[0]/max(1e-8, sqrt(dot(v, v))), v[1]/max(1e-8, sqrt(dot(v, v))), v[2]/max(1e-8, sqrt(dot(v, v)))) def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def sqrt(x): return math.sqrt(x) def max(a, b): return a if a > b else b No Full Global Illumination: The model does not include full global illumination, backward scattering, or volumetric light sources (emission). Blur Operation: The definition of \text{Blur}(\theta) is not provided in the sources, which may lead to implementation ambiguity. Scattering Factor: The computation of S(s) is not specified, only its usage in the blending equation. Light Transmittance: Computing the integral from sample to light requires additional ray marching or precomputation, which is not detailed in the source. Time Complexity: Interactive. The model avoids the high cost of full multiple scattering simulations by using empirical approximations. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Captures qualitative appearance of translucency, color bleeding, and volumetric shadows at interactive rates. Works with arbitrary volumes and scanned data without restrictions on optical properties or external illumination. Limitations: Not quantitatively accurate. Does not model full global illumination, backward scattering, or volumetric emission. Relies on empirical parameters (S(s), \theta) that may require tuning. The model was presented by Kniss et al. in 2002 as an interactive shading model for volume rendering. It is based on empirical observations of the appearance of volumetric materials and some theoretical results. The goal was to realistically visualize arbitrary volumetric materials at interactive rates without restrictions on external illumination or optical properties. name: Hybrid Surface-Volume Rendering
head: Gas Visualization System, Gaseous volume rendering, Realistic volumetric gas rendering
body: Hybrid Surface-Volume Rendering is a method for visualizing Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) data that combines physically-based atmospheric attenuation and illumination models for low-albedo gases with surface-based rendering techniques. Unlike traditional isosurface rendering which captures only a small fraction of data, this system displays the entirety of the three-dimensional data. It sets itself apart from siblings like Empirical Translucent Volume Shading by explicitly integrating a fast scanline-buffer algorithm for surface objects with a dedicated gaseous volume rendering pass, aiming for photo-realistic images of transparent media. The method operates on a per-scanline basis, combining surface fragments and volume contributions into a unified z-buffer. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A scene containing surface-defined objects and volumetric data (procedural or CFD grid); camera parameters; rendering flags (e.g., self-shadowing). Outputs: Final color image. Data Structures Z-buffer fragment list: A list per pixel containing fragments that partially or fully cover the pixel. Each fragment has an average z-depth value and color contribution. Solid shadow table: A data structure storing shadowing information for solid objects, used when self-shadowing is enabled. Algorithm Steps 1. Surface Z-buffer Creation: Create the z-buffer for a scanline. For each pixel, populate a list with all fragments from surface-defined objects that partially or fully cover the pixel. 2. Volume Extent Determination: If a volume is active for a pixel, determine the extent of volume rendering needed. 3. Volume Rendering Pass: Perform volume rendering for the active volume sections. This creates z-buffer fragments for the separate sections of the volumes. Volume rendering ceases once full coverage of the pixel by volume or surface-defined elements is achieved. 4. Fragment Sorting: Sort the z-buffer fragments (from both surface and volume passes) into the z-buffer fragment list based on their average z-depth values. 5. Final Compositing: Render the sorted z-buffer fragment list to produce the final color of the pixel. Gaseous Volume Rendering Sub-routine For each section of gas, the algorithm traces a ray from the eye through the pixel. The following steps are repeated for each increment along the ray: 1. Sample Retrieval: Get the color, density, and opacity of the current element. The volume density functions interpolate values stored in the CFD grid. 2. Shadowing: If self-shadowing is enabled, retrieve the shadowing of this element from the solid shadow table. 3. Illumination Calculation: Calculate gas illumination using opacity, density, and the appropriate low-albedo illumination model. 4. Accumulation: Accumulate final color: C{final} = C{final} + C{illumination} Accumulate sum density: D{sum} = D{sum} + \rho 5. Termination Check: If transparency < 0.01, stop tracing. 6. Sampling: Increment the sample point. A Monte Carlo method is used to choose the sample point to reduce aliasing artifacts. 7. Fragment Creation: Create the a-buffer (or z-buffer) fragment for this section. Formulas The opacity is approximated by integrating density along the ray. The optical depth \tau is calculated as: \tau = \int{s0}^{s1} \rho(s) ds Where: \tau is the optical depth of the material. \rho(s) is the density of the material at position s. s0 is the starting point for the volume tracing. s1 is the ending point. In discrete sampling, the opacity for an increment is the density obtained from evaluating a volume density function multiplied by the step-size. The final increment along the ray may be smaller, so its opacity is scaled proportionally. Parameters Transparency Threshold: Tracing stops if transparency < 0.01. Shadowing: Optional flag for self-shadowing. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The opacity approximation relies on the step-size and density interpolation. Inaccurate interpolation or large step sizes may lead to aliasing or incorrect attenuation. Boundaries: The final increment along the ray may be smaller than the standard step size, requiring proportional scaling of opacity to avoid artifacts. Coverage: Volume rendering ceases once full coverage is achieved, which requires careful determination of the extent of volume rendering needed for each pixel. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Rendering time for the gas visualization system is approximately 83 seconds on a HP 9000 Series Workstation model 735 for the sophisticated illumination model. Simpler models took 64 seconds and 27 seconds respectively. Strengths: Displays the entirety of 3D CFD data; provides perceptual cues for complex data; combines surface and volume rendering efficiently. Limitations: Computationally expensive for high-quality illumination; relies on specific hardware for the reported performance times. When to use: When visualizing low-albedo gases in CFD simulations where photo-realism and full data visibility are required. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and lower-quality approximations are acceptable. Hybrid Surface-Volume Rendering was described in a paper by David S. Ebert, Roni Yagel, James N. Scott, and Yair Kurzion at IEEE Visualization '94, October 17-21, 1994. It was developed to address the limitations of surface-based rendering techniques (stream-lines, contour plots) which capture only a small fraction of 3D simulation data, often hiding important information. The system was applied to visualize turbo-jet compressor data from CFD simulations. Volume Rendering Methods for Computational Fluid Dynamics Visualization, https://www.researchgate.net/profile/David-Ebert-4/publication/220943451VolumeRenderingMethodsforComputationalFluidDynamicsVisualization/links/00b7d51a73e2892e23000000/Volume-Rendering-Methods-for-Computational-Fluid-Dynamics-Visualization.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Surface Rendering Equation
head: Boundary Condition for Volume Rendering Equation
body: The Surface Rendering Equation defines the outgoing radiance at a surface point as the sum of emitted radiance and reflected incoming radiance, serving as the boundary condition for the Volume Rendering Equation. It is distinct from volume-based models by restricting light transport interactions to the 2D manifold of opaque surfaces rather than the 3D participating medium volume. Inputs and Outputs Input: Surface position \mathbf{x}S, outgoing view direction \boldsymbol{\omega}, surface normal \vec{n}, incoming radiance field Li(\mathbf{x}S, \boldsymbol{\omega}'), surface emission Le^S, and surface scattering function fs. Output: Outgoing radiance Lo(\mathbf{x}S, \boldsymbol{\omega}). Data Structures No specific data structures are required beyond standard vector and scalar types for position, direction, and radiance values. The surface normal \vec{n} is a unit vector perpendicular to the surface at \mathbf{x}S. Steps 1. Determine Surface Intersection: Identify the surface point \mathbf{x}S corresponding to the ray origin \mathbf{x} and direction -\boldsymbol{\omega} in the medium. This is achieved via a raycast function: \mathbf{x}S = \text{raycast}(\mathbf{x}, -\boldsymbol{\omega}) where \text{raycast} returns the nearest object surface point along the specified direction. 2. Evaluate Surface Emission: Retrieve the surface emission radiance Le^S(\mathbf{x}S, \boldsymbol{\omega}) at the intersection point for the outgoing direction. 3. Integrate Reflected Radiance: Compute the integral of incoming radiance over the hemisphere \mathcal{S}^2 above the surface. For each incoming direction \boldsymbol{\omega}', sample the incoming radiance Li(\mathbf{x}S, \boldsymbol{\omega}'), multiply by the surface bidirectional scattering distribution function fs(\mathbf{x}S, \boldsymbol{\omega}', \boldsymbol{\omega}), and weight by the cosine of the angle between the incoming direction and the surface normal |\boldsymbol{\omega}' \cdot \vec{n}|. 4. Sum Components: Add the surface emission and the integrated reflected radiance to obtain the total outgoing radiance. Formula Lo(\mathbf{x}S, \boldsymbol{\omega}) = Le^S(\mathbf{x}S, \boldsymbol{\omega}) + \int{\mathcal{S}^2} fs(\mathbf{x}S, \boldsymbol{\omega}', \boldsymbol{\omega}) Li(\mathbf{x}S, \boldsymbol{\omega}') |\boldsymbol{\omega}' \cdot \vec{n}| \, d\boldsymbol{\omega}' Symbol Definitions Lo(\mathbf{x}S, \boldsymbol{\omega}): Outgoing radiance at surface point \mathbf{x}S in direction \boldsymbol{\omega}. Le^S(\mathbf{x}S, \boldsymbol{\omega}): Surface emission radiance at \mathbf{x}S in direction \boldsymbol{\omega}. fs(\mathbf{x}S, \boldsymbol{\omega}', \boldsymbol{\omega}): Surface bidirectional scattering distribution function (BSDF) at \mathbf{x}S, describing scattering from incoming direction \boldsymbol{\omega}' to outgoing direction \boldsymbol{\omega}. Li(\mathbf{x}S, \boldsymbol{\omega}'): Incoming radiance at \mathbf{x}S from direction \boldsymbol{\omega}'. \vec{n}: Surface normal at \mathbf{x}S. \mathcal{S}^2: The unit hemisphere of directions above the surface. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def surfacerenderingequation(xS, omega, n, LeS, fs, getincomingradiance): """ Computes outgoing radiance at a surface point. Args: xS: Surface position vector. omega: Outgoing view direction vector. n: Surface normal vector. LeS: Function returning surface emission radiance Le^S(xS, omega). fs: Function returning BSDF fs(xS, omegaprime, omega). getincomingradiance: Function returning Li(xS, omegaprime). Returns: Lo: Outgoing radiance. """ # Step 1: Get surface emission emission = LeS(xS, omega) # Step 2: Integrate reflected radiance over the hemisphere # Note: In practice, this integral is approximated using Monte Carlo integration # or other numerical methods. The exact integration is not given in sources. reflectedradiance = 0.0 # Placeholder for numerical integration over hemisphere S^2 # For each sample direction omegaprime in hemisphere: # weight = |dot(omegaprime, n)| # Li = getincomingradiance(xS, omegaprime) # bsdf = fs(xS, omegaprime, omega) # reflectedradiance += bsdf Li weight # reflectedradiance /= numberofsamples (if using MC) # Step 3: Sum emission and reflection Lo = emission + reflectedradiance return Lo Edge Cases and Pitfalls Shadowing: The formula assumes all incoming directions \boldsymbol{\omega}' are visible. In practice, visibility functions (shadow rays) must be included to account for occlusion, though this is not explicitly detailed in the source formula. Degenerate Normals: If \vec{n} is undefined or zero, the cosine term |\boldsymbol{\omega}' \cdot \vec{n}| becomes zero, resulting in no reflected light. Precision: Radiance values can vary widely; using appropriate data types (e.g., float32 or float64) is critical to avoid clipping or underflow. The BRDF is a specific case of the BSDF where the surface is opaque and does not transmit light. It is chosen when modeling reflection-only surfaces. Models light transmission through a surface. It is chosen when the surface allows light to pass through, such as glass or thin films. Models subsurface scattering where light penetrates the surface volume. It is chosen for materials like skin, wax, or marble where light diffuses within the material before exiting. Time Complexity: The integral over the hemisphere \mathcal{S}^2 typically requires numerical integration (e.g., Monte Carlo), making the cost proportional to the number of samples used to approximate the integral. Memory Complexity: Minimal, requiring storage for surface properties (BSDF, emission) and normal vectors. Strengths: Provides a physically accurate boundary condition for volume rendering, allowing seamless integration of surface and volume effects. Limitations: Requires accurate surface intersection and normal estimation. Computationally expensive if high-quality integration of the BSDF is needed. When to Use: When rendering scenes with both participating media and opaque/translucent surfaces, and when accurate surface-light interactions are required. When Not to Use: For purely volumetric effects without surface boundaries, or when performance constraints prohibit complex surface shading calculations. The Surface Rendering Equation is derived from the principles of radiative transfer and serves as the boundary condition for the Volume Rendering Equation. It was formalized in the context of volume rendering to handle the interaction between light transport in participating media and opaque surfaces. The concept builds upon the foundational work in computer graphics regarding surface shading, extending it to be compatible with volumetric light transport. ボリュームレンダリング方程式(Volume Rendering Equation) 2, https://rayspace.xyz/notes/VLTE2/, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF)
head: Reflectance equation
body: The Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) provides the ratio of flux concentration per steradian reflected into a given direction as a consequence of differential irradiance incident from another given direction. It serves as the core component of the Surface Rendering Equation, defining the reflected radiance at a surface point. The BRDF, denoted as f(\vec{\omega}i \rightarrow \vec{\omega}r), is defined as the ratio of the reflected radiance Lr(\vec{\omega}r) to the incident irradiance E(\vec{\omega}i). f(\vec{\omega}i \rightarrow \vec{\omega}r) = \frac{Lr(\vec{\omega}r)}{E(\vec{\omega}i)} = \frac{Lr(\vec{\omega}r)}{Li(\vec{\omega}i) \cos \theta d\omegai} where \theta is the angle between the incident direction \vec{\omega}i and the surface normal, and d\omegai is the differential solid angle. The total reflected radiance Lr(\vec{\omega}r) in a specific outgoing direction \vec{\omega}r is obtained by integrating the product of the BRDF, the incident radiance, and the cosine term over the hemisphere of incident directions \Omegai. This integral is known as the reflectance equation: Lr(\vec{\omega}r) = \int{\Omegai} f(\vec{\omega}i \rightarrow \vec{\omega}r) Li(\vec{\omega}i) \cos \theta d\omegai For physically plausible materials, the BRDF must satisfy the Helmholtz reciprocity principle, meaning f(\vec{\omega}i \rightarrow \vec{\omega}r) = f(\vec{\omega}r \rightarrow \vec{\omega}i), and the energy conservation principle, where the total reflected energy does not exceed the incident energy. Models surfaces as a collection of microscopic facets with specific normal distributions. It separates the surface geometry (Normal Distribution Function) from the microfacet orientation and Fresnel reflection. Suitable for glossy and metallic surfaces. See Microfacet BRDF. Approximates the BRDF as a sum of analytical lobes (e.g., diffuse, specular) with parameters for color and roughness. Efficient for real-time rendering but less physically accurate than microfacet models for complex materials. See Lobe-based BRDF. Uses empirical data captured from real materials to define the BRDF. Provides high fidelity for specific objects but lacks generalization and requires large data storage. See Measured BRDF. Not given in the sources. name: Single Scattering Models
head: Single Scattering Approximation, First-Order Scattering
body: Single Scattering Models compute the radiance reaching the viewer by accounting for light that travels directly from a source to a volume and scatters exactly once toward the observer, while ignoring multiple scattering events and internal emission. This method solves the problem of rendering volumetric effects like smoke or clouds efficiently by assuming that for low-density media, single scattering dominates the radiance contribution. It sets itself apart from its siblings, such as the Gradient-guided single scattering approximation, by its rigorous inclusion of volume attenuation and phase function integration in a two-pass framework, whereas other approximations may rely on gradient guidance or simplified shading rules. Builds on Optical models. All optical models in this family are derived from the conservation of energy for a differential cylinder of light passing through a medium. They share the following core definitions and mechanisms: 1. Fundamental Interactions Any volumetric effect is composed of three fundamental characteristics: Absorption: The loss of radiant energy along a ray due to energy conversion (e.g., to heat). It is described by the absorption coefficient \sigmaa (units: m^{-1}). Emission: The addition of radiant energy where the medium is luminous (e.g., flames). It is described by the emissive term Le(\mathbf{p}, \boldsymbol{\omega}), representing radiance emitted per unit length. Scattering: The redirection of light rays upon collision with particles. It is split into In-scattering (light from other directions reflected into the view ray) and Out-scattering (light from the view ray reflected away). In most lighting calculations, out-scattering is folded into the extinction term because its net effect on the view ray is identical to absorption. 2. Notation \mathbf{p}: Position of interaction. \boldsymbol{\omega}: Ray direction (unit vector). L: Radiance quantity. Li: Incoming radiance. Lo: Outgoing radiance. \sigmat: Total extinction coefficient, \sigmat = \sigmaa + \sigmas. 3. Differential Forms The change in radiance dL over a differential path length dt is governed by the balance of loss and gain terms: Absorption Model: dL = -\sigmaa Li dt. Emission Model: dL = \sigmae dt (where \sigmae is the emission coefficient). General RTE: Combines extinction (loss) and source terms (gain from emission and in-scattering). 4. Transmittance The fraction of light surviving transmission through a medium is defined by the Beer-Lambert law: T = e^{-\tau} where \tau is the optical depth (integrated extinction). 5. Core Formulation The total outgoing radiance L{out}(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}) at viewpoint x in direction \boldsymbol{\omega} decomposes into reduced incident radiance L{ri} (direct transmission) and single-scattering radiance L{ss}: L{out}(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}) = L{ri}(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}) + L{ss}(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}) L{ri}(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}) = L{in}(\boldsymbol{\omega}) \tau(xa, x) \tau(x0, x1) = e^{-\int{0}^{D0} \kappat(xu) du} where xa is the volume entry point, D0 is the distance from x to x0, and \kappat is the extinction coefficient. L{ss}(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}) = \int{Db}^{Da} \tau(xu, x) \left[ \frac{\kappas(xu)}{4\pi} \int{S^2} L{in}(\boldsymbol{\omega}') p(\boldsymbol{\omega}, \boldsymbol{\omega}') \tau(xb, xu) d\boldsymbol{\omega}' \right] du where xb is the volume exit point, xu is a scattering point at distance Du, \kappas is the scattering coefficient, and p(\boldsymbol{\omega}, \boldsymbol{\omega}') is the phase function. 6. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def singlescatteringrender(viewpoint, raydirection, volumegrid, lightsource): xa, xb = volumegrid.intersectray(viewpoint, raydirection) if xa is None or xb is None: return 0.0 Da = math.dist(viewpoint, xa) Db = math.dist(viewpoint, xb) tauview = computetransmittance(viewpoint, xa, volumegrid) Lindirect = lightsource.getradiance(raydirection) Lri = Lindirect tauview Lss = 0.0 numsteps = 100 stepsize = (Da - Db) / numsteps for i in range(numsteps): Du = Db + i stepsize xu = viewpoint + raydirection Du if Du > Da: break kappas = volumegrid.getkappas(xu) if kappas == 0: continue tauxuview = computetransmittance(viewpoint, xu, volumegrid) tauenvxu = computetransmittance(xb, xu, volumegrid) phaseintegral = computephaseintegral(xu, raydirection, lightsource) contribution = tauxuview kappas (phaseintegral / (4 math.pi)) stepsize Lss += contribution return Lri + Lss def computetransmittance(p1, p2, volumegrid): dist = math.dist(p1, p2) if dist == 0: return 1.0 integralkappat = 0.0 samples = 10 step = dist / samples for i in range(samples): t = i step pos = p1 + (p2 - p1) (t / dist) kappat = volumegrid.getkappat(pos) integralkappat += kappat step return math.exp(-integralkappat) def computephaseintegral(pos, viewdir, lightsource): integral = 0.0 # Standard importance sampling or direct integration over S^2 # For a single point light at Lpos with intensity I: lightdir = normalize(lightsource.position - pos) Lin = lightsource.intensity p = lightsource.getphasefunction(viewdir, lightdir) integral = Lin p return integral The Single Scattering Model computes outgoing radiance by decomposing it into reduced incident radiance and single-scattering radiance, using extinction and scattering coefficients alongside a phase function. It sets itself apart from its siblings by its rigorous inclusion of volume attenuation and phase function integration in a two-pass framework, whereas other approximations may rely on gradient guidance or simplified shading rules. Choose it when rendering low-density participating media where single scattering dominates and computational efficiency is prioritized over full physical accuracy. See Single Scattering Model. A GPU-based direct volume rendering method that approximates single scattering and shadowing on-the-fly for multiple intersecting volumetric datasets. It improves visual quality over local illumination models by using local gradients to guide scatter sample positions and in-scatter coefficients, while maintaining interactive frame rates. It differs from pre-computed ambient occlusion methods by requiring no parameter buffers and performing all computations on-the-fly. Choose it for interactive rendering of multiple intersecting volumetric datasets where on-the-fly approximation is required. See Gradient-guided single scattering approximation. Generates cloud-like images that illustrate internal structure, instead of contour surfaces of the data. It uses an accurate light-scattering model to model the scattering effects of light in a cloud, and uses view rays as the basis for computing line integrals through the data to generate the color for each ray. Choose it for generating cloud-like images that emphasize internal structure over contour surfaces. See Sabella Cloud Scattering. Sabella introduced a ray-casting method that uses an accurate light-scattering model to model the scattering effects of light in a cloud. Based on foundational work by Blinn, Kajiya, and Max, Sabella's model uses the view rays as the basis for computing line integrals through the data to generate the color for each ray. name: Single Scattering Model
head: Kajiya and Von Herzen model, RTE with single scattering, Single Scattering Radiance Transport, Single-Scattering Participating Media Rendering, Two-Pass Single Scattering
body: The Single Scattering Model is a light transport approximation for participating media that accounts for exactly one secondary scattering event between the observer and a light source, ignoring multiple scattering and emitted radiance. It solves the problem of rendering volumetric effects like smoke or clouds by assuming low albedo or low density, where single scattering events dominate light transport. It sets itself apart from its siblings, such as the Gradient-guided single scattering approximation, by its rigorous inclusion of volume attenuation and phase function integration in a two-pass framework, whereas other approximations may rely on gradient guidance or simplified shading rules. The model computes the outgoing radiance L{out} at a viewpoint x in direction \boldsymbol{\omega} by decomposing it into reduced incident radiance L{ri} (light transmitted directly through the volume) and single-scattering radiance L{ss} (light scattered once into the view ray). Inputs: Viewpoint position x. View direction \boldsymbol{\omega} (unit vector). Density field \rho(\mathbf{p}) or optical property fields: absorption coefficient \kappaa(\mathbf{p}), scattering coefficient \kappas(\mathbf{p}), and extinction coefficient \kappat(\mathbf{p}) = \kappaa(\mathbf{p}) + \kappas(\mathbf{p}). Scattering albedo \Omega(\mathbf{p}) = \kappas(\mathbf{p}) / \kappat(\mathbf{p}). Phase function p(\boldsymbol{\omega}, \boldsymbol{\omega}') describing the directional distribution of scattering. Incoming ambient radiance L{in}(\boldsymbol{\omega}') from all directions \boldsymbol{\omega}'. Volume boundary points xa (entry) and xb (exit) for the ray passing through x. Outputs: Outgoing radiance L{out}(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}). Ray: Defined by origin x and direction \boldsymbol{\omega}. Volume Representation: A grid or voxel structure storing \kappat, \Omega, and p parameters at each position \mathbf{p}. Transmittance Cache: Precomputed or on-the-fly integration of \kappat along the ray path to determine optical depth. The total outgoing radiance is the sum of direct transmission and single scattering: L{out}(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}) = L{ri}(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}) + L{ss}(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}) \quad (1) 1. Reduced Incident Radiance (L{ri}) This is the ambient light L{in}(\boldsymbol{\omega}) attenuated by the transmittance from the volume boundary xa to the viewpoint x: L{ri}(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}) = L{in}(\boldsymbol{\omega}) \tau(xa, x) \quad (2) 2. Transmittance (\tau) The fraction of light surviving transmission between two points x0 and x1 is defined by the Beer-Lambert law: \tau(x0, x1) = e^{-\int{D1}^{D0} \kappat(xu) du} \quad (3) where D0 and D1 are the distances from the viewpoint x to x0 and x1 respectively, and xu is a point along the ray path. Note: The integration limits in are given as Db to Da for points xa, xb, consistent with distance decreasing towards the viewer if D is distance from viewer. We define D as distance from viewpoint x. Thus, for \tau(xa, x), the integral is from Da (distance to xa) to 0 (distance to x), or equivalently -\int{0}^{Da} \kappat du. The standard form in uses D1 to D0 where D0 is distance to start point x0. Let x0=xa, x1=x. Then D0=Da, D1=0. \tau(xa, x) = e^{-\int{0}^{Da} \kappat(xu) du} 3. Single-Scattering Radiance (L{ss}) This term integrates the light scattered from all incoming directions \boldsymbol{\omega}' into the view direction \boldsymbol{\omega} at every point xu along the ray: L{ss}(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}) = \int{Db}^{Da} \tau(xu, x) \frac{\kappas(xu)}{4\pi} \int{S^2} L{in}(\boldsymbol{\omega}') p(\boldsymbol{\omega}, \boldsymbol{\omega}') \tau(xb, xu) d\boldsymbol{\omega}' du \quad (4) Where: xu is an arbitrary position inside the volume at distance Du from x. \tau(xu, x) is the transmittance from the scattering point xu to the viewer x. \tau(xb, xu) is the transmittance from the volume entry point xb (where light enters from the environment) to the scattering point xu. Note: Light travels from environment to xb, then to xu. The distance from viewer to xb is Db, to xu is Du. The path length is Db - Du. \frac{\kappas(xu)}{4\pi} represents the scattering coefficient normalized by the sphere area, often combined with albedo \Omega. Using \Omega = \kappas/\kappat, the term \kappas is used directly in the source as part of the source term J{ss}. Specifically, defines J{ss}(vp, \boldsymbol{\omega}) = \frac{\Omega}{4\pi} \int{S^2} L{ri}(vp, \boldsymbol{\omega}') p(\boldsymbol{\omega}, \boldsymbol{\omega}') d\boldsymbol{\omega}'. However, L{ri} in the source context refers to incident radiance at the voxel. The full integral form uses \kappas. We use the explicit coefficient form for clarity: L{ss}(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}) = \int{Db}^{Da} \tau(xu, x) \left[ \frac{\kappas(xu)}{4\pi} \int{S^2} L{in}(\boldsymbol{\omega}') p(\boldsymbol{\omega}, \boldsymbol{\omega}') \tau(xb, xu) d\boldsymbol{\omega}' \right] du 4. Two-Pass Implementation (Kajiya and Von Herzen) For efficient computation, especially with complex lighting, the model can be implemented in two passes: Pass 1 (Illumination): Compute the illumination I(X) reaching each point X in the volume from the light sources. This involves propagating flux from the light source through the volume, accounting for the transparency (transmittance) of each layer. I(X) = L{in}(\boldsymbol{\omega}') \tau(\text{Light}, X) Pass 2 (Scattering to View): Gather the scattered intensity along viewing rays. The shading rule g(X) determines the intensity scattered from point X towards the viewpoint: g(X) = r(X, \boldsymbol{\omega}, \boldsymbol{\omega}') I(X) Where the bidirectional reflection distribution function (BRDF) for scattering is: r(X, \boldsymbol{\omega}, \boldsymbol{\omega}') = a \kappat(X) p(\boldsymbol{\omega}, \boldsymbol{\omega}') \quad (5) Here a is the albedo (fraction of extinction representing scattering, i.e., \Omega). The final radiance is the integral of g(X) along the viewing ray, weighted by transmittance to the viewer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def singlescatteringrender(viewpoint, raydirection, volumegrid, lightsource): """ Renders a single ray using the Single Scattering Model. Args: viewpoint: 3D position of the camera. raydirection: Unit vector of the view ray. volumegrid: Data structure containing kappat, kappas, and phase function p. lightsource: Object providing incoming radiance Lin(omega') for all directions. Returns: Lout: Float, the outgoing radiance at the viewpoint. """ # 1. Determine ray bounds within the volume # Find entry point xa and exit point xb xa, xb = volumegrid.intersectray(viewpoint, raydirection) if xa is None or xb is None: return 0.0 # Ray does not intersect volume # Distances from viewpoint Da = distance(viewpoint, xa) Db = distance(viewpoint, xb) # 2. Compute Reduced Incident Radiance (Direct Transmission) # Lri = Lin(omega) tau(xa, x) # tau(xa, x) = exp(-integral from 0 to Da of kappat) tauview = computetransmittance(viewpoint, xa, volumegrid) Lindirect = lightsource.getradiance(raydirection) Lri = Lindirect tauview # 3. Compute Single-Scattering Radiance # Lss = integral from Db to Da of [ tau(xu, x) kappas(xu) Jss(xu) / 4pi ] du # Note: Source uses Jss defined with Omega. Source uses kappas. # We follow the physical definition: Source term is kappas integral(Lin p). Lss = 0.0 # Discretize the ray path for integration (e.g., ray marching) numsteps = 100 stepsize = (Da - Db) / numsteps for i in range(numsteps): # Position xu at distance Du from viewpoint Du = Db + i stepsize xu = viewpoint + raydirection Du # Check if xu is within volume bounds (should be, but for safety) if Du > Da: break # Get optical properties at xu kappas = volumegrid.getkappas(xu) kappat = volumegrid.getkappat(xu) if kappas == 0: continue # Compute Transmittance from xu to Viewpoint (tau(xu, x)) tauxuview = computetransmittance(viewpoint, xu, volumegrid) # Compute Transmittance from Volume Entry (xb) to xu (tau(xb, xu)) # Light travels from environment -> xb -> xu tauenvxu = computetransmittance(xu, xb, volumegrid) # Note: direction is xb to xu, but tau is symmetric for path length # Actually, tau(xb, xu) depends on path length Db - Du. # computetransmittance should handle direction or just use distance. # Let's assume computetransmittance(p1, p2) integrates along segment p1-p2. tauenvxu = computetransmittance(xb, xu, volumegrid) # Compute Incident Radiance at xu from all directions (Jss term) # Jss(xu) = integral over S^2 of Lin(omega') p(omega, omega') domega' # For simple lights, this can be done analytically or with few samples. # For environment maps, use importance sampling. # Approximate Jss using a few samples or direct calculation for point lights Jss = computeincidentscatteringterm(xu, lightsource, volumegrid.getphasefunction) # Contribution of this step # Source term in RTE is kappas Jss / 4pi ? # Jss(vp, omega) = Omega/4pi integral... # Lss integral has kappas. # Let's use the explicit kappas form from and logic. # The scattered radiance added to the ray is: # dL = tau(xu, x) kappas(xu) (1/4pi integral(Lin p)) du # Wait, uses r(X) = a tau(X) p. This is a shading rule. # The standard RTE source term is kappas integral(Li p) / 4pi. scatteringcoeff = kappas phaseintegral = Jss # This Jss should be integral(Lin p) domega' # If Jss was defined as Omega/4pi..., we need to adjust. # Let's assume Jss here is the integral of Lin p. # Then the term is kappas Jss / 4pi. contribution = tauxuview scatteringcoeff (phaseintegral / (4 PI)) stepsize Lss += contribution return Lri + Lss def computetransmittance(p1, p2, volumegrid): """ Computes transmittance between p1 and p2 by integrating kappat along the segment. tau = exp(- integral kappat ds) """ dist = distance(p1, p2) if dist == 0: return 1.0 # Simple midpoint or trapezoidal integration for demonstration # In practice, use adaptive ray marching or precomputed volumes samples = 10 integralkappat = 0.0 step = dist / samples for i in range(samples): t = i step pos = p1 + (p2 - p1) (t / dist) kappat = volumegrid.getkappat(pos) integralkappat += kappat step return exp(-integralkappat) def computeincidentscatteringterm(pos, lightsource, phasefunc): """ Computes integral over S^2 of Lin(omega') p(omega, omega') domega' """ # For point lights, this is a single direction. # For environment maps, use importance sampling. # Placeholder for specific lighting strategy. # For simple point/parallel lights, calculate directly. # For environment maps, use importance sampling. # Example: Single point light at Lpos with intensity I # omega' = normalize(Lpos - pos) # Lin = I # p = phasefunc(viewdirection, omega') # Note: phasefunc depends on angle between view and light # But here we are computing Jss for a specific view direction omega? # No, Jss is the source term. The final Lss integrates this over the ray. # The phase function p(omega, omega') depends on the VIEW direction omega. # So Jss must be computed for the specific view direction omega of the ray. # This function needs the view direction omega passed in. # Corrected signature needed in real implementation. pass \kappat: Extinction coefficient (\kappaa + \kappas). \Omega: Scattering albedo (\kappas / \kappat). p(\boldsymbol{\omega}, \boldsymbol{\omega}'): Phase function. For water droplets, peaks in the forward scattering direction. a: Albedo, fraction of extinction representing scattering. Validity: The model is only valid if the albedo or density is low, such that multiple scattering is unlikely. Precision: Numerical integration of transmittance and phase functions requires sufficient sampling to avoid artifacts, especially in heterogeneous media. Boundaries: Correctly identifying volume entry and exit points (xa, xb) is critical for accurate transmittance calculation. Models light transport with zero or exactly one scattering event, separating direct and singly-scattered light. Distinguished by rigorous attenuation and phase integration compared to the Utah Approximation. Applies Blinn's 1982 approximations for uniform, low-density media, building on the general single scattering model. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of ray steps (marching steps) and M is the number of samples for the angular integration (phase function). For point lights, M=1. For environment maps, M depends on the importance sampling strategy. Memory Complexity: O(V), where V is the size of the volume grid storing optical properties. Strengths: Computationally efficient compared to full multiple scattering models; physically plausible for low-density media like smoke or thin clouds. Limitations: Fails for high-density or high-albedo media where multiple scattering dominates. Ignores emitted radiance. When to use: Smoke reconstruction, thin clouds, or differentiable rendering of fluids where speed is prioritized and multiple scattering is negligible. The Single Scattering Model is derived from the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE). The two-pass method for computing single scattering was introduced by Kajiya and Von Herzen. It has been applied in various contexts, including the "Heidelberg ray tracing model" for medical images and recent differentiable rendering frameworks for fluid and smoke reconstruction. name: Single Scattering Propagator
head: Direct Light Propagator G_d
body: The Single Scattering Propagator, denoted as G{single} or Gd, models light transport that has undergone zero or exactly one scattering event within a participating medium. It serves as the "direct" component of the total light transport propagator, separating unscattered and singly-scattered light from multiply-scattered (indirect) light. It is distinguished from the Utah Approximation by its rigorous inclusion of volume attenuation and phase function integration, whereas the Utah Approximation ignores occlusion and attenuation between the light source and the voxel [1717-utah-approximation-single-scattering.md]. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Start position \mathbf{x}, start direction \vec{\omega}, end position \mathbf{x}', end direction \vec{\omega}', total path length s, scattering coefficient b(\mathbf{x}), phase function P(\mathbf{x}, \vec{\omega}{in}, \vec{\omega}{out}), and the no-scatter propagator G{noscatter}. Outputs: The propagator value G{single}(s, \mathbf{x}, \vec{\omega}, \mathbf{x}', \vec{\omega}'). Data Structures: The propagator is a mathematical operator mapping spatial and angular coordinates to radiance contribution. Implementation typically uses floating-point values for b and P. Method Steps: The calculation of G{single} involves integrating over all possible intermediate points \mathbf{x}'' where a single scattering event occurs. The process corresponds to the standard single scattering ray marching algorithm: 1. Direct Transmission (G{noscatter}): Calculate the light that travels from \mathbf{x} to \mathbf{x}' without any scattering. This is handled by the no-scatter propagator G{noscatter}(s, \mathbf{x}, \vec{\omega}, \mathbf{x}', \vec{\omega}'), which accounts for attenuation along the direct path. 2. Integration Setup: For every point \mathbf{x}'' along the path from \mathbf{x} to \mathbf{x}' (parameterized by distance s' from \mathbf{x}' or s-s' from \mathbf{x}), consider a scattering event. 3. First Attenuation: Light travels from the start \mathbf{x} to the intermediate point \mathbf{x}''. This is modeled by G{noscatter}(s - s', \mathbf{x}, \vec{\omega}, \mathbf{x}'', \vec{\omega}''), where \vec{\omega}'' is the direction from \mathbf{x} to \mathbf{x}''. This term includes attenuation over the distance s - s'. 4. Scattering: At \mathbf{x}'', light scatters from direction \vec{\omega}'' to a new direction \vec{\omega}'''. The probability of this scattering is determined by the product of the scattering coefficient b(\mathbf{x}'') and the phase function P(\mathbf{x}'', \vec{\omega}'', \vec{\omega}'''). 5. Second Attenuation: The scattered light travels from \mathbf{x}'' to the final point \mathbf{x}'. This is modeled by G{noscatter}(s', \mathbf{x}'', \vec{\omega}''', \mathbf{x}', \vec{\omega}'), including attenuation over the remaining distance s'. 6. Summation: Integrate the product of these terms over all possible intermediate positions \mathbf{x}'' and all possible outgoing directions \vec{\omega}''' (and incoming directions \vec{\omega}'' implied by geometry) along the path. Formula: The total single scattering propagator is the sum of the no-scatter term and the single-scatter integral: G{single}(s, \mathbf{x}, \vec{\omega}, \mathbf{x}', \vec{\omega}') = G{noscatter}(s, \mathbf{x}, \vec{\omega}, \mathbf{x}', \vec{\omega}') + \int0^s ds' \int{\mathbf{x}''} \int{\vec{\omega}''} \int{\vec{\omega}'''} G{noscatter}(s - s', \mathbf{x}, \vec{\omega}, \mathbf{x}'', \vec{\omega}'') \cdot b(\mathbf{x}'') \cdot P(\mathbf{x}'', \vec{\omega}'', \vec{\omega}''') \cdot G{noscatter}(s', \mathbf{x}'', \vec{\omega}''', \mathbf{x}', \vec{\omega}') \, d\vec{\omega}'' \, d\vec{\omega}''' \, d\mathbf{x}'' Where: s is the total path length. s' is the distance from the intermediate point \mathbf{x}'' to the final point \mathbf{x}'. \mathbf{x}'' is the intermediate scattering position. \vec{\omega}'' is the direction from \mathbf{x} to \mathbf{x}''. \vec{\omega}''' is the direction from \mathbf{x}'' to \mathbf{x}'. b(\mathbf{x}'') is the scattering coefficient at \mathbf{x}''. P(\mathbf{x}'', \vec{\omega}'', \vec{\omega}''') is the phase function. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesinglescatteringpropagator(xview, omegaview, xlight, stotal, sigmatfunc, bfunc, Pfunc, Gnoscatterfunc): """ Computes Gsingle via ray marching, discretizing the spatial integral. Corresponds to the standard single scattering ray marching algorithm. """ # 1. Direct transmission component (no scattering) directterm = Gnoscatterfunc(stotal, xview, omegaview, xview + omegaview stotal, omegaview) # 2. Single scattering component singlescatterterm = 0.0 numsteps = 100 # Discretization resolution ds = stotal / numsteps for i in range(1, numsteps + 1): stointer = i ds sfrominter = stotal - stointer xdoubleprime = xview + omegaview stointer omegadoubleprime = omegaview # Shadow ray direction towards light source dirtolight = xlight - xdoubleprime disttolight = max(norm(dirtolight), 1e-6) omegatripleprime = dirtolight / disttolight # First attenuation: view ray from xview to x'' atten1 = Gnoscatterfunc(stointer, xview, omegadoubleprime, xdoubleprime, omegadoubleprime) # Scattering coefficient and phase function bval = bfunc(xdoubleprime) phaseval = Pfunc(xdoubleprime, omegadoubleprime, omegatripleprime) # Second attenuation: shadow ray from x'' to light source atten2 = Gnoscatterfunc(disttolight, xdoubleprime, omegatripleprime, xlight, omegatripleprime) singlescatterterm += atten1 bval phaseval atten2 ds return directterm + singlescatterterm Note: For the general propagator definition, the angular integral is approximated in practice by sampling discrete light source directions during ray marching. Parameters: Gd is computed using existing techniques for direct lighting. Gs (multiply scattered) is the primary target for efficient rendering algorithms, implying Gd is often considered "solved" or handled by standard rasterization/ray tracing. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Complexity: Recursively expanding the propagator for higher orders of scattering becomes unmanageably complex due to additional angular integrations. Initial Condition: The scattered light propagator Gs starts at zero: Gs(s=0, \mathbf{x}, \vec{\omega}, \mathbf{x}', \vec{\omega}') = 0. A shading model for single scattering where external illumination reaches a voxel from a distant source unimpeded by intervening objects or volume absorption[1717-utah-approximation-single-scattering.md]. It differs from the Single Scattering Propagator by ignoring occlusion and attenuation between the light source and the voxel, serving as the foundational step for adding surface-like shading to volume data [1717-utah-approximation-single-scattering.md]. Choose it when performance is critical and the medium is optically thin or when surface-like shading is sufficient; use the propagator when rigorous attenuation and phase function integration are required. Time Complexity: The direct evaluation of the integral is computationally expensive due to the multiple integrals over space and angles. The corresponding ray marching algorithm is O(N \cdot L) where N is the number of steps along the view ray and L is the number of light sources (shadow rays). Memory Complexity: Low, as it typically processes one ray or voxel at a time without storing large intermediate scattering fields for the direct component. Strengths: Physically accurate for thin media or when direct lighting dominates. It is the standard baseline for single scattering. Limitations: Does not account for indirect lighting (multiple scattering). Becoming unmanageably complex if extended to higher orders. When to use: When the medium is optically thin or when direct lighting is the primary visual cue. When not to use: In dense media where multiple scattering is significant; use Gs methods instead. The Single Scattering Propagator formalizes the concept of light scattering exactly once, separating it from the unscattered (direct) and multiply scattered (indirect) components. This separation is crucial for efficient rendering algorithms, as Gd can be handled by existing direct lighting techniques, while Gs requires specialized methods for participating media. The formulation corresponds directly to the standard single scattering ray marching algorithm used in computer graphics. The path integral approach provides an alternative way to express the full propagator G as a sum over transfer events along different paths. PDF Practical Rendering of Multiple Scattering Effects in Participating Media, https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~ravir/HRPIEG.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Utah Approximation (Single Scattering)
head: Simple Shading Model
body:
The Utah approximation is a shading model for single scattering where external illumination reaches a voxel from a distant source unimpeded by intervening objects or volume absorption. It differs from shadow-aware propagators by ignoring occlusion and attenuation between the light source and the voxel, serving as the foundational step for adding surface-like shading to volume data. Inputs: Scalar field data f on a regular grid. Light direction \omega' (unit vector). View direction \omega (unit vector). Particle albedo a(X). Extinction coefficient 	au(X). Henyey-Greenstein parameter c. Internal emissivity E(X). Incoming illumination i(X, \omega'). Outputs: Scattered light S(X, \omega). Total source term g(X, \omega). Data Structures: Grid: Regularly spaced 3D array of scalar values f. Gradient: 
abla f estimated via central differences. Steps: 1. Estimate Surface Normal: Calculate the gradient 
abla f at position X using central differences between regularly spaced gridded data values, then interpolate between grid vertices. The contour surface normal N is: N =  rac{
abla f}{|
abla f|} 2. Compute Bidirectional Reflection Distribution Function (BRDF) r(X, \omega, \omega'): Choose one of the following models based on the desired visual effect: Particle Scattering: r(X, \omega, \omega') = a(X) 	au(X) p(\omega, \omega') Henyey-Greenstein Phase Function (Spherical Particles): p(\omega, \omega') =  rac{1}{4\pi}  rac{1-c}{(1 + c^2 - 2cx)^{3/2}} Where x = \cos \alpha = \omega \cdot \omega'. Lambert Diffuse Phase Function (Large Spherical Particles): p(\omega, \omega') =  rac{8}{3\pi} (\sin \alpha + (\pi - \alpha) \cos \alpha) Simple Lambert Diffuse Shading (Contour Surface): r(X, \omega, \omega') = \max(
abla f \cdot \omega', 0) This simulates shading from a contour surface without polygonalization. 3. Compute Scattered Light S(X, \omega): S(X, \omega) = r(X, \omega, \omega') i(X, \omega') 4. Compute Total Source Term g(X, \omega): g(X, \omega) = E(X) + S(X, \omega) Parameters: c: Adjustable constant for Henyey-Greenstein phase function. c > 0 for forward scattering, c < 0 for backward scattering, c = 0 for isotropic scattering. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Shadows: The model assumes no shadows. If shadows are required, the transparency of the volume between the light source and point X must be accounted for. Gradient Estimation: Central differences require regularly spaced grid data. Interpolation is needed between grid vertices. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeutahapproximation(f, x, h, omegaprime, omega, a, tau, c, E, i): """ Compute the Utah approximation for single scattering at position x. Args: f: Scalar field accessor (callable or grid). x: Position vector (3D). h: Grid spacing. omegaprime: Light direction vector (unit). omega: View direction vector (unit). a: Particle albedo at x. tau: Extinction coefficient at x. c: Henyey-Greenstein parameter. E: Internal emissivity at x. i: Incoming illumination intensity. Returns: g: Total source term. gradf: Estimated gradient vector. """ # Step 1: Estimate gradient using central differences on a regular grid axes = [(1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (0, 0, 1)] gradf = [] for axis in axes: xplus = tuple(x[k] + h axis[k] for k in range(3)) xminus = tuple(x[k] - h axis[k] for k in range(3)) gradf.append((f(xplus) - f(xminus)) / (2 h)) # Interpolate between grid vertices if x is not on a grid point # Step 2: Compute BRDF r(X, omega, omega') using Henyey-Greenstein xdot = sum(o op for o, op in zip(omega, omegaprime)) denom = 1 + c c - 2 c xdot # Numerical safeguard; mathematically denom > 0 for c in (-1, 1) and xdot in [-1, 1] if denom <= 1e-12: denom = 1e-12 phg = (1.0 / (4.0 math.pi)) (1 - c) / (denom 1.5) r = a tau phg # Step 3: Compute scattered light S(X, omega) S = r i # Step 4: Compute total source term g(X, omega) g = E + S return g, gradf Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides surface-like shading without explicit surface extraction. Limitations: Ignores shadows and volume absorption between the light source and the voxel. When to use: As a baseline shading model before adding shadow and absorption effects. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The Utah approximation is named after early shaded images from the University of Utah. It is described in the paper "Optical Models for Direct Volume Rendering" by Marc Levoy. The model is a simplification of single scattering that assumes external illumination reaches the voxel unimpeded. name: Single Scattering (Blinn Model)
head: Blinn 1982 Cloud Model, Blinn's Cloud Model
body: The Single Scattering (Blinn Model) is a light transport approximation for participating media that accounts for exactly one secondary scattering event between the observer and a light source. It solves the problem of rendering volumetric effects like clouds by assuming low albedo, thereby ignoring multiple scattering interactions. It builds on the general Single Scattering Model by applying Blinn's 1982 approximations for uniform, low-density media. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A viewing ray originating from the camera, a light source position, a volume density field \rho(\mathbf{x}), and a phase function p(\cos \theta). Output: The radiance contribution L at the pixel corresponding to the viewing ray. Data Structures: Volume Density: A scalar field \rho(\mathbf{x}) representing the scattering coefficient at position \mathbf{x}. Phase Function: A function p(\cos \theta) mapping the cosine of the scattering angle to a relative intensity weight. Parameters: Albedo: The proportion of reflected light corresponding to the amount of light hitting the particle; the model assumes low albedo. Phase Function Type: Based on phase angle, determining the brightness of a particle depending on the viewing angle. Scattering: A particle is only seen if there are no other particles in the line of sight of either the incoming or outgoing ray of light. Transparency: The amount of light that penetrates the clouded volume without being reflected off any particles. Steps: 1. Ray-Box Intersection: Determine the entry point t{in} and exit point t{out} of the viewing ray within the volume bounding box. 2. Viewing Ray Sampling: Iterate along the viewing ray from t{in} to t{out} with a fixed step size \Delta t. 3. Light Ray Intersection: For each sample point \mathbf{x}, cast a secondary ray towards the light source and determine its intersection bounds [t{light, in}, t{light, out}] with the volume. 4. Transmittance Calculation: Compute the optical depth \tau along the secondary ray from \mathbf{x} to the light source (or until it exits the volume). The transmittance is T{\text{light}} = \exp(-\tau). 5. Phase Function Evaluation: Evaluate p(\cos \theta) where \theta is the angle of incidence of the light ray on the particle. 6. Scattering Integration: Compute the differential contribution \Delta L = \rho(\mathbf{x}) \cdot T{\text{light}} \cdot p(\cos \theta) \cdot \Delta t. 7. Accumulation: Sum the contributions from all sample points along the viewing ray to obtain L. Formula: The reflected light quantity is described by a phase function providing the proportion of reflected intensity based on the incidence angle of the ray on a particle. The total radiance is computed as: L = \int{t{in}}^{t{out}} \rho(\mathbf{x}(t)) \cdot \exp\left(-\int{t}^{t{\text{light}}} \rho(\mathbf{x}(u)) \, du\right) \cdot p(\cos \theta) \, dt where \rho(\mathbf{x}) is the volume density, the inner exponential is the transmittance to the light source, and p(\cos \theta) is the phase function. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def blinnsinglescattering(vieworigin, viewdir, lightpos, volumebbox, densityfn, phasefn): # 1. Ray-box intersection (slab method) tmin, tmax = 0.0, 1e9 for i in range(3): if abs(viewdir[i]) < 1e-8: if vieworigin[i] < volumebbox.min[i] or vieworigin[i] > volumebbox.max[i]: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] else: t1 = (volumebbox.min[i] - vieworigin[i]) / viewdir[i] t2 = (volumebbox.max[i] - vieworigin[i]) / viewdir[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmin > tmax: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] numsamples = 100 step = (tmax - tmin) / numsamples radiance = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # 2. Sample along viewing ray for i in range(numsamples): t = tmin + (i + 0.5) step point = [vieworigin[j] + viewdir[j] t for j in range(3)] density = densityfn(point) if density <= 0: continue # 3. Light ray intersection lightdirraw = [lightpos[j] - point[j] for j in range(3)] lightlen = (lightdirraw[0]2 + lightdirraw[1]2 + lightdirraw[2]2)0.5 if lightlen < 1e-8: continue lightdir = [d / lightlen for d in lightdirraw] tlightmin, tlightmax = 0.0, 1e9 for j in range(3): if abs(lightdir[j]) < 1e-8: if point[j] < volumebbox.min[j] or point[j] > volumebbox.max[j]: tlightmin = 1e9; break else: t1 = (volumebbox.min[j] - point[j]) / lightdir[j] t2 = (volumebbox.max[j] - point[j]) / lightdir[j] tlightmin = max(tlightmin, min(t1, t2)) tlightmax = min(tlightmax, max(t1, t2)) if tlightmin > tlightmax: continue # 4. Optical depth to light numlightsamples = 50 lightstep = (tlightmax - tlightmin) / numlightsamples opticaldepth = 0.0 for k in range(numlightsamples): tl = tlightmin + (k + 0.5) lightstep lightpoint = [point[j] + lightdir[j] tl for j in range(3)] opticaldepth += densityfn(lightpoint) lightstep transmittance = math.exp(-opticaldepth) # 5. Phase function (angle of incidence) viewdirnorm = [-viewdir[j] for j in range(3)] # Direction towards camera costheta = sum(lightdir[j] viewdirnorm[j] for j in range(3)) costheta = max(-1.0, min(1.0, costheta)) phase = phasefn(costheta) # 6. Accumulate contribution contribution = density transmittance phase step for c in range(4): radiance[c] += contribution return radiance Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Albedo: The model fails for media with high albedo as multiple scattering becomes significant. Boundary Conditions: The path boundaries for the light ray must be correctly clipped to the volume extent to avoid incorrect optical depth calculations. Precision: Numerical integration errors can accumulate, especially with steep density gradients. Romberg integration is suggested for higher accuracy. This variant uses a precomputed brightness contribution Ii(x, y, z) for each light source, calculated via Romberg integration. The precomputed brightness contribution is calculated as: Ii(x, y, z) = \exp(-\int{0}^{r} \tau \rho(\xi) d\xi) \int{0}^{r} \rho(\xi(t), \eta(t), \zeta(t)) dt, where \tau = r \rho. The path boundaries are defined as \lambda1 = \max(0, d1) and \lambda2 = \min(d{global}, d2), where d1 is the distance to the nearest intersection with the bounding extent, d{global} is the distance to the nearest intersection with the rest of the world database, and d2 is the distance to the farthest intersection with the bounding extent. It is chosen when precomputation is feasible to accelerate per-frame rendering. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M) where N is the number of samples along the viewing ray and M is the number of samples along the light ray. Memory Complexity: O(V) where V is the size of the volume density field. Strengths: Simple to implement; efficient for low-density media like clouds or Saturn's rings. Limitations: Inaccurate for high-albedo or thick media; ignores multiple scattering. When to Use: Real-time or interactive rendering of thin volumetric effects. The model was published by Blinn in 1982 for cloud simulation. It was one of the first works to incorporate reflection and scattering in participating media, specifically targeting the rings of Saturn. It assumes a uniform medium of relatively low albedo. Later, Max extended this model to arbitrary shapes, and Bouthor added anisotropic dispersion effects. An Overview of Rendering from Volume Data --- including Surface and Volume Rendering, https://core.ac.uk/download/63614.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Représentation et algorithmes pour l'exploration interactive de volumes procéduraux étendus et détaillés, https://inria.hal.science/inria-00598406v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Ray Tracing for Volume Densities, https://www.scribd.com/document/746685923/ray-tracking-volume-densities, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: Kajiya-Von Herren Ray Tracing Algorithm
head: Kajiya and Von Herren method, Two-step ray tracing for volume densities
body: The Kajiya-Von Herren algorithm is a two-step method for rendering participating media under the Single Scattering (Blinn Model) approximation. It decouples the computation of light transport from the final image synthesis by precomputing a brightness contribution field for each light source and then summing these contributions during ray tracing. This separation allows the illumination calculation to be performed once per frame (or scene) independently of the camera view, distinguishing it from pure Monte Carlo approaches that compute scattering per pixel. The method consists of two distinct phases: a precomputation step to generate a brightness field, and a ray tracing step to render the final image. Inputs and Outputs: Precomputation Input: Light source position, medium density function \rho(x,y,z), and extinction coefficient \tau. Precomputation Output: A 3D grid or field Ii(x,y,z) representing the precomputed brightness contribution for light source i. Ray Tracing Input: Camera ray, bounding box of the medium, precomputed fields Ii. Ray Tracing Output: Pixel color. Data Structures: The precomputed brightness Ii is stored as a 3D volume. The specific resolution and bit-depth are not given in the sources. The ray tracing step iterates over volume elements along the ray path. Precomputation Step: For each light source i, the brightness contribution Ii(x,y,z) at any point in space is calculated using Romberg integration. name: Grid-based Convection-Diffusion Illumination
head: Convection-diffusion equation method, PDE-based volume illumination
body:
Grid-based Convection-Diffusion Illumination is a real-time volume rendering technique that models light propagation, absorption, and multiple scattering within participating media by solving a unified partial differential equation (PDE) on a regular grid. It distinguishes itself from Monte Carlo ray tracing by separating illumination modeling from simulation, allowing the use of highly parallelized numerical schemes for real-time performance, and from Summed Area Table (SAT) techniques by producing realistic multiple scattering effects rather than just global shadows. The method computes a "light volume" representing the energy density distribution inside the participating medium, which is then used during standard volume ray casting to shade sampling points. The computation is divided into two main phases: direct illumination (convection) and multiple scattering (diffusion). Inputs: Volume dataset V with spatially varying absorption coefficient \sigmaa(x) and scattering coefficient \sigmas. A set of N light sources. For each source, a direction field u(x) is required. Grid resolution and domain bounds. Outputs: A scalar light volume (energy density field) ho(x). The method operates on a regular 3D grid. Grid: A 3D array storing the energy density ho. Fields: ho(x): Energy density at grid point x. \sigmaa(x): Absorption coefficient at grid point x. \sigmas: Scattering coefficient (scalar, assumed constant for isotropic scattering). u(x): Light propagation direction field at point x. This is a vector field. For simple light sources (distant, point, cone), u(x) is unique for direct lighting. The light propagation is modeled by the convection-diffusion equation:  rac{\partial}{\partial t} ho (x) = -c u(x) \cdot

Args: volumedata: Object containing absorption coefficient sigmaa(x) for each voxel. lightsources: List of light source definitions. Each source has a type (distant, point) and parameters. gridresolution: Tuple (nx, ny, nz) defining the grid dimensions. Returns: rho: 3D array (nx, ny, nz) representing the final light volume (energy density). """ nx, ny, nz = gridresolution # Initialize energy density grid to zero rho = zeros((nx, ny, nz)) # Step 1: Direct Illumination (Convection) for each light source for light in lightsources: # Initialize temporary grid for this light source rhodirect = zeros((nx, ny, nz)) # Define direction field u(x) based on light type # Note: This assumes simple light sources where u(x) is unique for direct lighting ufield = computedirectionfield(light, gridresolution) # Solve convection equation to get steady state energy distribution # The equation is: d/dt rho = -c u. grad rho - sigmaa rho # We solve for the steady state (d/dt rho = 0) or iterate until convergence # rhodirect = solveconvection(rhodirect, ufield, volumedata.sigmaa, c) # Implementation detail: The source describes solving the equation numerically. # A simple explicit Euler scheme for steady state might look like: # rhonew = rhoold - dt (-c u. grad rhoold - sigmaa rhoold) # However, the source does not specify the exact numerical solver (e.g., upwind, implicit). # We assume a generic solver function exists that returns the steady state. rhodirect = solvesteadystateconvection( initialguess=zeros((nx, ny, nz)), directionfield=ufield, absorptioncoefficient=volumedata.sigmaa, speedoflight=c) # Accumulate into the global light volume rho = rho + rhodirect # Step 2: Multiple Scattering (Diffusion) # Solve diffusion equation: d/dt rho = sigmas laplacian(rho) # This step models multiple scattering # The source implies solving this on the accumulated light volume. # We assume an iterative solver or a single step if steady state is reached quickly. rho = solvediffusion( initialenergy=rho, scatteringcoefficient=volumedata.sigmas, gridresolution=gridresolution) return rho def computedirectionfield(light, gridresolution): """ Computes the direction field u(x) for a given light source. """ nx, ny, nz = gridresolution ufield = zeros((nx, ny, nz, 3)) # Generate grid coordinates x, y, z = meshgrid(range(nx), range(ny), range(nz)) coords = stack([x, y, z], axis=-1) if light.type == 'distant': # Constant direction ufield = light.direction elif light.type == 'point': # Direction from point light to voxel p = light.position vectors = coords - p norms = linalg.norm(vectors, axis=-1, keepdims=True) # Avoid division by zero norms = where(norms == 0, 1, norms) ufield = vectors / norms elif light.type == 'cone': # Direction from cone apex to voxel, clamped to cone angle # Implementation details for cone are not specified in sources # Placeholder for cone logic pass return ufield def solvesteadystateconvection(initialguess, directionfield, absorptioncoefficient, speedoflight): """ Solves the convection-diffusion equation for direct lighting. The source states: "solve a diffusion equation for multiple scattering within the volume" """ # The source does not specify the exact numerical scheme for diffusion. # This is a placeholder for the numerical solver. return initialenergy # Placeholder N: The number of light sources. The method performs N convection solves. \sigmas: The scattering coefficient. Used as the scalar value for the isotropic diffusion tensor D = \sigmas I. \sigmaa(x): The spatially varying absorption coefficient. u(x): The light propagation direction field. Assumed to be unique for direct lighting without scattering or reflection/refraction. c: The speed of light. Light Source Complexity: The method assumes a unique light propagation direction for direct lighting. This holds for simple light sources (distant, point, cone) but fails for complex environment lights, which may have multiple incoming directions at a single point. Performance: The method is optimized for common light sources (distant/directional, point) and may not handle arbitrarily complex environment lights efficiently. Numerical Stability: The convection term -c u(x) \cdot 
abla ho (x) can be numerically unstable if not handled with appropriate schemes (e.g., upwinding), though the source does not specify the exact numerical method. Time Complexity: The method requires solving the convection equation N times (once per light source) and then solving the diffusion equation once. The complexity depends on the grid resolution and the numerical solver used. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the energy density grid ho(x), the absorption coefficient grid \sigmaa(x), and the direction field u(x) for each light source if computed on the fly or stored. Performance: The method achieves real-time performance by using highly parallelized grid-based numerical schemes, unlike Monte Carlo ray tracing which is prohibitively expensive. Strengths: Produces realistic multiple scattering effects, which SAT techniques cannot do. Supports dynamic transfer function editing and various light sources. Limitations: Limited to simple light sources for the convection step. Not suitable for complex environment lighting without modification. The method was proposed in the paper "Fast global illumination for interactive volume visualization". It builds on the idea of separating illumination modeling and simulation, a concept also seen in Precomputed Radiance Transfer (PRT) methods, but adapts it for volume visualization where local and internal light sources are more important than complex distant lighting. The technique is designed to meet the goals of real-time rendering, support for dynamic transfer functions, and handling of multiple common light sources. It addresses the limitations of earlier methods like Kajiya-Von Herzen ray tracing (high computational cost) and SAT techniques (limited multiple scattering).
