name: Gradient-guided single scattering approximation
head: GPU Based On-the-fly Light Emission-absorption Approximation, On-the-fly scatter approximation
body:
A GPU-based direct volume rendering method that approximates single scattering and shadowing on-the-fly for multiple intersecting volumetric datasets. It improves visual quality over local illumination models by using local gradients to guide scatter sample positions and in-scatter coefficients, while maintaining interactive frame rates. It differs from pre-computed ambient occlusion methods by requiring no parameter buffers and performing all computations on-the-fly. Inputs and Outputs Input: Multiple registered volumetric datasets (e.g., 256^3 grids), transfer functions defining opacity/scattering ratios, and a view ray. Output: Final radiance Lo for each pixel. Data Structures Voxel Grid: Standard 3D texture or volume grid storing density/extinction coefficients. Gradient Field: Not pre-computed; approximated on-the-fly from the voxel grid neighborhood. Parameters g: Average cosine of the scattering angle, ranging from -1 to 1. N{max}: Maximum number of scatter sample positions, set to 15. Algorithm Steps 1. Ray Marching: Cast a ray through the volume. For each step position \mathbf{p}: 2. Gradient Approximation: Compute the gradient 
abla V(\mathbf{p}) of the volume data at the current sampling point. 3. Determine Scatter Samples: Select up to N{max} = 15 scatter sample positions \mathbf{s}i in the local neighborhood of \mathbf{p}. The selection and weighting depend on the strength of the gradient at \mathbf{p}. Assume a strong gradient indicates a less scattering, more reflecting surface, and that the gradient points in the direction of less dense, more scattering media. 4. Calculate Scattering Angle: For each scatter sample \mathbf{s}i, compute its gradient 
abla V(\mathbf{s}i). Calculate the cosine of the scattering angle 	heta between the gradient at the current point 
abla V(\mathbf{p}) and the gradient at the scatter sample 
abla V(\mathbf{s}i). The cosine is zero only if the direction of the scatter sample gradient is identical to the current sampling point’s gradient vector. 5. Weighting: Weight the influence of each scatter sample position by: 1. The distance to the actual sampling point \mathbf{p}. 2. The gradient magnitude at the given scatter sampling position \|
abla V(\mathbf{s}i)\|. 6. Phase Function: Compute the phase function p(	heta) using the Henyey-Greenstein function: p(	heta) =  rac{1-g^2}{4\pi (1+g^2 +2g \cos	heta)^{3/2}} Where g < 0 indicates backward scattering, g > 0 indicates forward scattering, and g = 0 results in isotropic scattering. 7. Light Transfer: Calculate light transfer through the volumes using standard lighting absorption calculation as described in [Max95]. Combine the in-scattered light (weighted by p(	heta) and sample weights) with the direct illumination and absorption. 8. Compositing: Accumulate the result along the ray. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gradientguidedsinglescattering(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata, gparam): """ Approximates single scattering for a single ray. volumedata: 3D array of voxel values. gparam: Phase function parameter (average cosine of scattering angle). """ totaltransmittance = 1.0 accumulatedradiance = 0.0 # Standard ray marching parameters stepsize = 0.1 maxsteps = 1000 for step in range(maxsteps): currentpos = rayorigin + raydirection step stepsize currentval = trilinearinterpolate(volumedata, currentpos) # 1. Gradient Approximation at current position gradcurrent = computegradient(volumedata, currentpos) # 2. Determine scatter samples (up to 15) # Note: Exact selection logic for "up to 15" based on gradient strength # is not fully specified in sources beyond "depending on the strength". # We assume a fixed set of neighbors or a dynamic selection based on gradient magnitude. scattersamples = selectscattersamples(currentpos, gradcurrent, volumedata) inscatter = 0.0 for samplepos in scattersamples: # 3. Gradient at scatter sample gradsample = computegradient(volumedata, samplepos) # 4. Scattering Angle Cosine # Cosine is zero if directions are identical (parallel gradients) # Note: The source states "cosine... is zero only if... identical". # This implies the angle is between gradient vectors, not view directions. costheta = dotproduct(normalize(gradcurrent), normalize(gradsample)) # 5. Phase Function phase = heneygreenstein(costheta, gparam) # 6. Weighting dist = distance(currentpos, samplepos) gradmagsample = magnitude(gradsample) weight = (1.0 / (dist + epsilon)) gradmagsample # 7. Light Transfer (Simplified Absorption) # Using standard absorption calculation from Max95 # Assume sigmat is derived from volumedata or transfer function sigmat = getextinction(volumedata, samplepos) transmittancetosample = exp(-sigmat dist) # In-scatter contribution # Source implies in-scatter amount is defined by the angle and weights inscatter += phase weight transmittancetosample # 8. Accumulate # Standard emission-absorption model update # Lo = Li T + Le (1 - T) + InScatter # Here, InScatter is added to the radiance before absorption of the next step accumulatedradiance += inscatter totaltransmittance # Update transmittance for the next step sigmatcurrent = getextinction(volumedata, currentpos) totaltransmittance = exp(-sigmatcurrent stepsize) if totaltransmittance < epsilon: break return accumulatedradiance def heneygreenstein(costheta, g): """ Henyey-Greenstein phase function. """ numerator = 1.0 - g2 denominator = 4.0 pi (1.0 + g2 + 2.0 g costheta)1.5 return numerator / denominator def computegradient(volumedata, pos): """ Approximate gradient using central differences or finite differences. """ # Implementation detail: Standard finite difference gradient calculation dx = volumedata[pos.x+1, pos.y, pos.z] - volumedata[pos.x-1, pos.y, pos.z] dy = volumedata[pos.x, pos.y+1, pos.z] - volumedata[pos.x, pos.y-1, pos.z] dz = volumedata[pos.x, pos.y, pos.z+1] - volumedata[pos.x, pos.y, pos.z-1] return Vector3(dx, dy, dz) def selectscattersamples(currentpos, gradcurrent, volumedata): """ Select up to 15 scatter sample positions based on gradient strength. Note: Exact algorithm for selection is not detailed in sources. We assume a heuristic based on gradient magnitude. """ # Placeholder for specific selection logic not provided in # Typically involves sampling neighbors in the direction of the gradient samples = [] #... implementation depends on specific neighbor sampling strategy... return samples Time Complexity: Interactive. Performance depends on the number of scatter samples (up to 15) and the cost of gradient computation per voxel. Memory Complexity: Low. No pre-computed parameter buffers or ambient occlusion maps are required; computations are performed on-the-fly. Measured Performance: Tested on Intel QuadCore 3.16 GHz and two Nvidia Geforce 480 GPUs rendering two registered 256^3 datasets in a 1024 	imes 768 viewport. T1 (both opaque): L1 (no scattering) 45 fps, L2 (with scattering) 21 fps. T2 (1 opaque, 1 translucent): L1 11 fps, L2 9 fps. T3 (both half-opaque/half-scattering): L1 41 fps, L2 19 fps. T4 (both translucent): L1 41 fps, L2 11 fps. L1 = light transport only; L2 = light transport including scattering. Strengths: Improves visual quality over local illumination models (e.g., Phong) by capturing single scattering effects; maintains interactive frame rates; suitable for multi-volume rendering. Limitations: Approximation; relies on gradient direction which may not always accurately represent light transport paths; performance degrades with higher scattering ratios and translucent datasets. Origin: Presented by Rostislav Khlebnikov, Bernhard Kainz, Bernhard Roth, Judith Muehl, and Dieter Schmalstieg at EUROGRAPHICS 2011. History: The method builds on the emission-absorption model from Max [Max95] and uses the Henyey-Greenstein phase function from [HG41]. It was influenced by algorithms from Ropinski et al. [RDRS10] and Šoltészová et al. [ŠPBV10], which were not directly applicable to multi-volume rendering due to memory requirements or pre-computation needs. Usage: Used for direct multi-volume rendering of intersecting datasets, such as registered MRI and DTI-MRI of the brain. name: Simulated Fluorescence Process (SFP) Renderer
head: SFP Renderer, SFP volume rendering algorithm
body: The Simulated Flucescence Process (SFP) Renderer is a volume rendering algorithm that interprets image intensity as a distribution of fluorescent dye, modeling physical light-matter interaction to render scenes as they would appear under real fluorescence microscopy conditions. Unlike standard isosurface rendering or methods requiring surface detection and segmentation, SFP operates directly on 3D data by simulating two distinct light transport stages: excitation by a distant light source and subsequent emission propagation to the viewer. This approach allows for the visualization of internal structures with realistic shadowing and absorption effects without preprocessing. The SFP algorithm simulates the physical process of fluorescence in two sequential stages. It treats the input volume data as a distribution of fluorescent dye where intensity values determine absorption and emission properties. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D volume dataset (typically multi-channel microscopy data) where intensity represents dye concentration. Input: A light source located at infinity (directional). Input: A virtual table plane below the object. Input: Penetration Depth parameter (scalar). Output: A 2D image representing the scene as viewed by an observer. Data Structures The algorithm processes the volume as a grid of voxels. Each voxel v at position \mathbf{p} contains intensity values for one or more channels. Each channel is interpreted as a distinct dye with specific properties: transparency, color, and brightness. Parameters Penetration Depth (dp): A scalar parameter that sets the absorption and emission transparencies for all channels simultaneously. Low values: Objects appear solid with hard shadows; excitation light is absorbed immediately. High values: Light penetrates deeper, revealing internal structures with softer shadows. Algorithm Steps 1. Excitation Stage (Lighting): The fluorescent distribution is illuminated by a light source located at infinity. For each voxel in the volume, calculate the excitation intensity based on its orientation relative to the light source. Areas facing the light source are more excited because the dye absorbs the excitation light. Each voxel in the light beam is affected by shadowing from its predecessors along the light ray. Let L{exc}(\mathbf{p}) be the excitation intensity at position \mathbf{p}. This is determined by integrating the extinction of the excitation light through the volume from the light source to \mathbf{p}. 2. Emission Stage (Rendering): Light emitted by the object and the table below it propagates towards the viewer. Each voxel emits light proportional to its excitation intensity L{exc}(\mathbf{p}) and its channel-specific brightness. The emitted light travels along the view ray towards the camera. As the light passes through the dye, it gets absorbed. Objects can be obscured from view by other objects (shadowing from predecessors along the view ray). The final pixel color is the accumulated emission from all voxels along the view ray, attenuated by the absorption of the dye. Pseudocode The following pseudocode outlines the core logic. Note that specific integration formulas for optical depth are not provided in the source; standard Beer-Lambert integration is implied by the description of shadowing and absorption. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendersfp(volume, lightdirection, viewdirection, penetrationdepth, tableplane): """ Renders a volume using the Simulated Fluorescence Process. Args: volume: 3D array of intensity values (multi-channel supported). lightdirection: Unit vector for the light source at infinity. viewdirection: Unit vector for the camera view. penetrationdepth: Scalar controlling absorption/emission transparency. tableplane: Plane definition for the shadow-casting table. Returns: 2D image array. """ # Initialize output image image = zeroslike(viewdirection.xy) # Pre-calculate channel properties based on penetration depth # Note: Exact mapping of penetrationdepth to absorption coefficient is not specified # Assume absorption coefficient sigmaa is inversely proportional to penetrationdepth absorptioncoeff = 1.0 / penetrationdepth # Step 1: Excitation Stage # Calculate excitation intensity for each voxel, accounting for shadowing from light excitationmap = zeroslike(volume) # Ray march along lightdirection for each voxel to determine shadowing # This is a simplified representation; actual implementation requires efficient ray casting for voxel in volume: # Calculate transmittance from light source to this voxel # Texc = exp(-integral(sigmaa density) along light ray) # Standard exponential attenuation is implied by "absorbs excitation light" transmittance = calculatetransmittance(voxel.position, lightdirection, volume, absorptioncoeff) # Excitation is proportional to incident light and local dye concentration # Assuming linear relationship between intensity and dye concentration excitationmap[voxel] = voxel.intensity transmittance # Step 2: Emission Stage # Ray march along viewdirection for each pixel for pixel in image: accumulatedradiance = 0.0 currenttransmittance = 1.0 # March from near to far along view ray for voxel in volumealongray(pixel, viewdirection): # Emitted light from this voxel # Emission is proportional to excitation and channel brightness emittedlight = excitationmap[voxel] voxel.channelbrightness # Add contribution to pixel, attenuated by remaining path # dL = Le exp(-tau) dt accumulatedradiance += emittedlight currenttransmittance # Update transmittance for subsequent voxels (absorption of emission light) # Standard exponential attenuation currenttransmittance = exp(-absorptioncoeff voxel.density voxel.stepsize) # Check for table intersection to add table shadow/emission if applicable # "Light emitted by the object and a table below it propagates towards the viewer" if voxel.isontable: tableemission = gettableemission(voxel) accumulatedradiance += tableemission currenttransmittance image[pixel] = accumulatedradiance return image def calculatetransmittance(startpos, direction, volume, absorptioncoeff): """ Calculates the transmittance of light from the source to a point. """ # Standard ray marching for optical depth opticaldepth = 0.0 # Ray march from startpos backwards along -direction to infinity or volume boundary # Integrate absorption coefficient along the path # "Each voxel in the light beam is affected by shadowing from its predecessors" for voxel in volumealongray(startpos, -direction): opticaldepth += absorptioncoeff voxel.density voxel.stepsize return exp(-opticaldepth) Edge Cases and Pitfalls No Surface Detection Required: The algorithm does not require surface detection, sharp gradients, or segmentation, making it suitable for direct visualization of 3D microscopy data. Multi-Channel Interpretation: Each channel of a multi-channel image is interpreted as a dye with different properties (transparencies, color, brightness). Incorrect channel mapping may lead to unrealistic colors. Penetration Depth Sensitivity: Low penetration depth results in solid objects with hard shadows, potentially hiding internal details. High penetration depth reveals internal structures but may reduce contrast. An isosurface added to the SFP scene that acts as a completely impenetrable barrier for both excitation and emission light. The isosurface casts hard shadows on the SFP material beneath it and on the table. It is partially obscured by SFP material located in front of it. The isosurface can also cast shadows on itself, allowing for complex lighting interactions even without fluorescent material. This feature creates a greater sense of space and depth compared to standard surface rendering. Performance: The performance of the SFP Renderer greatly benefits from GPU acceleration. Strengths: Does not require surface detection, sharp gradients, or segmentation. Suitable for direct visualization of 3D microscopy data. Provides realistic lighting and shadowing effects (excitation and emission). Supports multi-channel data interpretation. Supports cutting planes (up to 6) for internal visualization. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that image intensity maps to fluorescent dye distribution. Specific performance metrics (FPS, memory usage) are not provided in the sources. When to use: Direct visualization of 3D microscopy data where realistic fluorescence appearance is desired without preprocessing. When not to use: When surface geometry is the primary focus and fluorescence effects are irrelevant. The SFP Renderer is part of the Huygens software suite by Scientific Volume Imaging (SVI). It was introduced in Huygens 19.10, which added features like cutting planes. The algorithm is designed for use with data acquired from microscopes, such as the Leica Digital Light Sheet microscope, and is often used in conjunction with deconvolution algorithms like CMLE. It is used in biological research, as evidenced by testimonials from institutions like Maastruth University and EMBL Heidelberg. name: Local illumination, shadows and ambient occlusion
head: Local shading, direct illumination in volumes, volumetric shadowing
body: This family covers techniques for computing direct visibility and local shading in volume rendering, addressing the problem of how light from sources interacts with participating media and opaque geometry to produce shadows, self-shadowing, and surface-like orientation cues. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Optical models by focusing on the geometric and visibility aspects of light transport (shadows, occlusion) rather than the physical scattering phase functions, and from Single and multiple scattering by typically ignoring or approximating indirect bounces. It differs from Real-time approximations in that it includes both offline precomputation methods (like Light Propagation Volumes) and real-time ray-marching techniques. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of evaluating visibility or illumination at a specific point \mathbf{p} within or on the boundary of a volume, based on a light source direction \mathbf{l} or environment. 1. Visibility/Transmittance Evaluation: The fundamental operation is determining how much light reaches \mathbf{p} from a source. This involves integrating the extinction coefficient \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) along a path from the source to \mathbf{p} (or vice versa). The transmittance T is calculated as: T = \exp\left(-\int{\mathbf{p}{source}}^{\mathbf{p}} \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) \, d\mathbf{x}\right) In discrete implementations, this integral is approximated by summing \sigmat \cdot \Delta s over samples along the ray. 2. Local Shading Models: For surface-like appearance in volumes, normals are approximated from the volume gradient \mathbf{g} = \nabla V. Usually, a simple absorption and emission model is used because it is relatively cheap to evaluate and gives good enough results. 3. Shadowing Approximation: Shadows are computed by testing occlusion along the direction to the light source. 4. Ambient Occlusion: Indirect illumination is approximated by integrating over the hemisphere or using simplified models (e.g., upward ray for sky light). The ambient contribution L{ambient} is often modulated by a shadowing factor based on local density: L{ambient} = L{sky} \cdot \exp(-D{up}) \cdot AO{factor} where D{up} is the integrated density along an upward ray. Lighting Models apply local illumination heuristics to scalar field data to enhance the perception of 3D structure and surface orientation. Unlike physically based light transport methods that solve the radiative transfer equation, these models modulate existing volume samples or pixel colors using diffuse and specular terms derived from the data gradient. This family distinguishes itself from siblings like Two-Pass Shadow Casting (Kajiya and Von Herzen) by focusing on local shading rather than global shadow computation, and from Path Tracing and Sampling by using deterministic or semi-analytical approximations instead of stochastic integration. Two-Pass Shadow Casting is a numerical algorithm for computing shadows in volume rendering by explicitly accounting for the transparency of participating media between a light source and a surface point, and between that point and the viewpoint. It solves the problem of realistic shadowing in scenes containing smoke, fog, clouds, or turbid water, where standard opaque shadow techniques fail to capture the attenuation of light through the volume. Unlike recursive ray tracing, which sends discrete "shadow feelers" to the light source at each point along the primary ray, this method integrates the shadowing effect continuously along the ray. It is distinguished from its sibling Shadow Ray Casting by its volumetric integration approach and from Shadow Mapping by its direct handling of participating media density rather than depth buffers. Ambient Light Approximation simulates indirect sky illumination in participating media by integrating the entire sky hemisphere into a single upward-pointing light value, weighted by local cloud density to simulate self-shadowing. Unlike full multiple scattering or complex irradiance tables, it uses a single precalculated or sampled upward ray to approximate the diffuse fill light, preventing the underside of clouds from appearing unnaturally dark. It differs from Ambient Occlusion via Geometry/Neighbors by relying on volumetric density rather than surface geometry, and from Bruneton-style Sky Irradiance by using a simplified single-ray model instead of a multi-dimensional lookup table. This method precomputes light intensities and shadows within a 3D volume based on a light source direction, color, decay, and a density mask, storing the result in a 3D texture for use during rendering. It differs from real-time ray marching by performing the light transport calculation offline (or in a dedicated compute pass) to decouple lighting cost from scene complexity, using density thresholding to filter noise and simulate god rays. Path Tracing and Sampling is a stochastic method for solving the rendering equation in participating media by simulating the random walk of light paths. It handles both direct and indirect illumination by recursively sampling scattering events and light sources. It differs from local illumination methods by accounting for multiple bounces and complex visibility, but at a significantly higher computational cost. Light Sampling for NEE is a technique for estimating direct illumination in participating media by explicitly sampling light sources and their surfaces to generate connection points for path tracing. It solves the problem of noisy direct lighting estimates by concentrating samples on bright emitters rather than relying solely on unidirectional shadow rays. It differs from Shadow Ray Casting by using probabilistic sampling with importance weighting and from Direct Light Sampling by focusing specifically on the geometry of light emission and the associated probability density functions (PDFs) required for unbiased Nearest Energy Estimation (NEE) in media. Shadow Ray Casting is a family of techniques that determine local visibility by casting rays from a point of interest toward light sources or into the environment to test for occlusion by geometry or participating media. It solves the problem of computing accurate shadows and ambient occlusion in volume rendering and surface shading, distinguishing itself from global illumination methods by evaluating direct visibility explicitly rather than through stochastic path exploration or precomputed light maps. Shadow Mapping is a technique to efficiently render shadows by rendering the scene from the light's point of view to generate a depth map (shadow map). It determines if a point is occluded by another object from the light's perspective. It differs from Shadow Ray Casting by using pre-rendered depth buffers instead of per-pixel ray traversal, and from Two-Pass Shadow Casting (Kajiya and Von Herzen) by relying on a single depth buffer comparison rather than geometric silhouette processing. Sampling a single light source to compute direct illumination, handling different light types and ensuring the path is not blocked by other geometry. Computes the final color of a terrain surface point by combining albedo, direct sunlight (modulated by shadow and cloud shadow), and hemispheric ambient light (sky and ground bounce modulated by AO). Computes ambient occlusion based on the geometric proximity of surrounding surfaces or neighbors, rather than volumetric density. Definition: Shading aims to enhance appearance by modeling effects like shadows, light scattering, and absorption. It depends on the chosen optical model. Parameter: A simple absorption and emission model is usually used because it is relatively cheap to evaluate and gives good enough results. Comparison: Local illumination shades each sample independently, ignoring the rest of the scene, so it cannot produce shadows or scattering but is cheap to compute. Global lighting simulates any effect for better results but is expensive and seldom used in real time. Definition: Approximating less scattered light at cloud fringes by reducing scattered light in low density areas using a powder function. Step: Multiply the increment to scattered light by powder(density stepsize). Code: glsl uniform float powderdecay; float powder(float d) { return 1.0 - exp(-powderdecay d); } Definition: Simulates first bounce indirect illumination by discretizing the scene into 3D cells in a continuous grid, where each cell holds a directional distribution of radiance. Step: Inject lighting into cells containing directly lit surfaces, using reflective shadow maps (or other methods) to find these cells. Form a radiance distribution around the normal, facing away from the surface, with color based on surface material. Propagate light from cell to cell: each cell analyzes the radiance field of its neighbors and modifies its own based radiance coming from all directions. Parameter: Encoding: 2nd order spherical harmonics are used to encode the directional distribution of radiance in each cell. Propagation steps: The number of steps allowed controls the light propagation. Definition: A technique that approximates the shape of unoccluded regions above the shading point via a cone to estimate occlusion of an area-light. Step: The set of 3D unoccluded directions is modeled as a circular aperture. Pitfall: If the set of unoccluded directions does not resemble an ellipse or a circle, it can produce incorrect shadowing results. Comparison: This method presents a lower storage requirement than horizon maps. Definition: Implements day/night sun cycle with scattering, soft shadows, and ambient occlusion. Step: Implements day/night sun cycle with sunset scattering, sun disc, halo and stars. Generates single-sample golden-angle PCF soft shadows jittered with interleaved gradient noise (TAA accumulates the penumbra). Computes bit-test ambient occlusion bilinearly interpolated across the hit face. Definition: Calculates sunlight contribution by casting a shadow ray from the surface towards the sun. If the shadow ray hits an object, the point is in shadow. Step: If SUNENABLED, calculate sunDir from sceneData. Calculate nDotL = max(dot(normal, sunDir), 0.0). If nDotL > 0, create shadowOrigin = position + normal 0.001. March shadow ray using March(shadowOrigin, sunDir, 64). If shadowRay.status != 2 (no hit), sunContribution = SUNCOLOR nDotL sceneData.sunIntensity. Definition: A pass that renders cloud shadows onto terrain and objects by rendering a sky plane from the light source's perspective. Step: Shadow intensity is determined by the coverage value in the Weather map. Definition: Computes and sets shader uniforms for up to 4 lights, eye position, and eye look direction in object space. Step: Compute the inverse of the actor's world matrix. Convert light position to object space. Set uniforms lightposition (array of 4 fvec3) and lightenable (array of 4 int). Compute eye look direction in object space. Local illumination and shadowing in volume rendering originated with the need to add realism to direct volume rendering (DVR) techniques, which initially relied on simple transfer functions without shading. Early work by Max [Max 1995] established the distinction between local and global illumination in the context of volume rendering, noting that local methods are cheap but lack shadows, while global methods are expensive. The Two-Pass Shadow Casting method by Kajiya and Von Herzen provided a foundational approach for computing shadows in participating media by separating illumination and gathering passes. Later developments, such as Light Propagation Volumes by Kaplanyan, extended these concepts to real-time indirect illumination. name: Direct Illumination with Shadow Rays
head: Direct Lighting with Shadows, Direct Lighting with Volume Transmittance, Direct Radiance with Volumetric Transmittance, Shadow Ray Illumination, Shadow Ray Lighting
body: Direct Illumination with Shadow Rays computes the direct lighting contribution at a surface point within or on the boundary of a volume, accounting for attenuation by heterogeneous participating media between the surface and the light source. It differs from Ambient Occlusion via Shadow Rays by explicitly evaluating directional light sources rather than approximating indirect hemispherical illumination, and from Lookup Table Shadow Rendering by performing real-time ray marching through the volume density field instead of relying on precomputed spatial data structures. Inputs: Surface point \mathbf{p} and surface normal \mathbf{n}. List of light sources, each defined by position \mathbf{l}i, color C{light, i}, and optionally area Ai. Volume density field (extinction coefficient \sigmat) accessible via a sampler. Surface material properties (diffuse color, specular parameters). Outputs: Direct radiance contribution L{direct} at \mathbf{p}. Data Structures: Light: Struct containing position (vec3), color (vec3), enabled (bool/uint), and area (float, for PDF calculation). Hit Surface: Struct containing hitpoint (vec3), normal (vec3), and material properties. Ray: Struct containing origin (vec3) and direction (vec3). Intersection Result: Struct containing t (distance to hit, -1 if none) and d (distance to light source for comparison). Steps: 1. Initialize Accumulator: Set direct lighting accumulator L{direct} = \mathbf{0}. 2. Iterate Lights: For each light source i in the light list: a. Skip Disabled: If light i is disabled, continue to next light. b. Compute Light Vector: Calculate vector \mathbf{L} = \mathbf{l}i - \mathbf{p} and distance d{light} = \|\mathbf{L}\|. c. Normalize Direction: \mathbf{w}i = \mathbf{L} / d{light}. d. Cast Shadow Ray: Create a shadow ray originating at \mathbf{p}{shadow} = \mathbf{p} + \epsilon \mathbf{n} (where \epsilon is a small offset, e.g., 0.01 \times \|\mathbf{n}\| or a fixed small value) in direction \mathbf{w}i. e. March Shadow Ray: Evaluate transmittance or occlusion along the shadow ray up to distance d{light}. Method A (Binary Occlusion): Perform ray marching (e.g., DDA or fixed steps). If an opaque object intersects the ray at distance t < d{light}, the point is in shadow. Method B (Volumetric Transmittance): Integrate extinction coefficient \sigmat along the ray from \mathbf{p}{shadow} to \mathbf{l}i. Compute transmittance T{light} = \exp(-\int \sigmat ds). f. Compute Visibility/Transmittance: If using Method A: Let V = 1 if no intersection found (or intersection is behind light), else V = 0. If using Method B: T{light} is the computed value. g. Compute Geometric Term: Calculate the dot product NL = \max(0, \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{w}i). h. Compute BRDF Contribution: Diffuse: L{diff} = C{light, i} \cdot C{diffuse} \cdot NL \cdot V \cdot T{light} / d{light}^2. (Note: includes a probability density term py = 1/Ai if sampling lights by area). Specular: If enabled, compute specular highlight using half-vector \mathbf{H} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{w}i + \mathbf{V}) where \mathbf{V} is view direction, and shininess \alpha. L{spec} = C{light, i} \cdot C{specular} \cdot T{light} \cdot \max(0, \mathbf{H} \cdot \mathbf{n})^\alpha. i. Accumulate: L{direct} += L{diff} + L{spec}. 3. Return: Return L{direct}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def directilluminationwithshadowrays(p, normal, lights, volumesampler, viewdir): """ Computes direct lighting at point p considering volume shadows. Args: p: vec3, surface position normal: vec3, surface normal lights: list of Light objects volumesampler: object with method extinctionat(pos) returning sigmat viewdir: vec3, view direction (for specular) Returns: vec3, direct lighting contribution """ directlight = vec3(0.0) for light in lights: if not light.enabled: continue # 1. Compute light vector and distance delta = light.position - p ldist = length(delta) if ldist < 1e-6: continue wi = normalize(delta) # 2. Cast shadow ray # Offset to avoid self-intersection epsilon = 0.01 length(normal) shadoworigin = p + epsilon normal shadowray = Ray(shadoworigin, wi) # 3. Evaluate transmittance/visibility # Method: Volumetric Transmittance via discrete integration numsamples = 16 opticaldepth = 0.0 deltas = ldist / numsamples for i in range(numsamples): pos = shadowray.origin + shadowray.direction (i deltas) sigmat = volumesampler.extinctionat(pos) opticaldepth += sigmat deltas Tlight = math.exp(-opticaldepth) # 4. Compute geometric term ndotl = max(0.0, dot(normal, wi)) # 5. Compute BRDF contribution (simplified diffuse + specular) # Diffuse diffuseterm = light.color ndotl Tlight / (ldist ldist) # Specular (Blinn-Phong) h = normalize(wi + normalize(viewdir)) ndoth = max(0.0, dot(normal, h)) shininess = 32.0 # Typical default if not specified specularterm = light.color Tlight pow(ndoth, shininess) # Accumulate # Note: includes 1/area for area lights. Assuming point lights here for simplicity. directlight += diffuseterm + specularterm return directlight Parameters: numsamples: Number of steps for shadow ray integration. Typical value: 16. epsilon: Offset for shadow ray origin. Typical value: 0.01 \times \|\mathbf{n}\| or a small fixed constant. MAXLIGHTS: Maximum number of lights to process. Value: 8. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-Shadowing: Failing to offset the shadow ray origin causes self-intersection artifacts. An offset \epsilon is required. Precision: In highly heterogeneous volumes, large step sizes \Delta s may miss thin high-density regions, leading to inaccurate transmittance. Adaptive stepping or higher numsamples mitigates this. Boundary Conditions: If the light source is inside the volume, the shadow ray integration must handle the exit from the volume boundary correctly. Degenerate Input: If \mathbf{n} is zero or \mathbf{L} is zero, the method is undefined. Guard against division by zero in distance and normalization. Estimates transmittance from a surface point to a distant light source through participating media using majorant sampling. It differs from the base method by using stochastic sampling (Russian Roulette) for transmittance estimation rather than deterministic integration, which is more efficient for large, sparse volumes. Choose this when performance is critical and the volume is large. Computes local illumination and shadows in voxel-based scenes by casting shadow rays from surface positions toward light sources. It differs from Shadow Ray Transmittance Estimation by using binary hit/miss results for shadowing rather than estimating transmittance through participating media. It builds on Direct Illumination with Shadow Rays by applying these concepts specifically to voxel geometry. Choose this for voxel-based rendering where binary occlusion is sufficient. A shadowing technique where shadow rays cross smooth glass in a straight line, and paths refracted to a light already reached that way do not count as reaching the light. This is a variant of shadow ray casting used in stylized voxel rendering (e.g., MagicaVoxel) to handle transparent materials without complex refraction tracing. Choose this for stylized rendering with transparent objects. Time Complexity: O(NL \cdot NS), where NL is the number of lights and NS is the number of samples per shadow ray. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per light, excluding the volume data structure. Performance: Performance scales linearly with the number of lights and shadow ray samples. For real-time applications, NS is often limited to 16–32 steps. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides accurate volumetric shadows for direct lighting; works with any volume representation accessible via sampling. Limitations: Does not account for multiple scattering or indirect illumination; noisy if NS is low in heterogeneous media; expensive for many lights. When to Use: Real-time or offline rendering where direct lighting shadows are required in participating media. When Not to Use: When full global illumination (multiple bounces) is needed; when the volume is extremely large and sparse (use Shadow Ray Transmittance Estimation instead). The method originates from early volumetric path tracing and ray marching techniques for participating media. It is a fundamental component of local illumination models in volume rendering, extending surface-based shadow ray casting to account for volumetric extinction. It is widely used in real-time voxel-based renderers (e.g., MagicaVoxel) and offline path tracers for accurate shadowing in fog, smoke, and clouds. ainagutierrez01/Volumetric-Path-Tracing-, https://github.com/ainagutierrez01/Volumetric-Path-Tracing-, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, https://github.com/unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) An Introduction to Raymarching - Maxime Garcia, https://typhomnt.github.io/teaching/raytracing/raymarchingintro/, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) cgibson/Mr-Voxel, https://github.com/cgibson/Mr-Voxel, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Milestone 13: MagicaVoxel look (.vox, DDA voxel grid, sun/sky, bloom, style voxel), https://github.com/adriendjn/mypbr/pull/10, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: Shadow Ray Transmittance Estimation
head: Majorant Transmittance Sampling
body: Estimates the transmittance from a surface point to a distant light source through participating media using majorant sampling. Inputs: Current position in the volume. Direction to the distant light source \omegai. Density grid and accessor. Total extinction coefficient \sigmat. Random number generator (RNG). Outputs: Estimated transmittance T{ray}. Data Structures: MajorantTransmittanceSampler: Initialized with intersection data, RNG, density grid, accessor, and total extinction coefficient. Tray: Floating-point accumulator initialized to 1.0. Steps: 1. Initialize transmittance T{ray} = 1.0. 2. Create a shadow ray from the current position in the direction of the distant light \omegai. 3. Intersect the shadow ray with the volume grid to obtain the entry and exit distances. 4. Initialize MajorantTransmittanceSampler with the intersection, RNG, density grid, accessor, and total extinction coefficient. 5. Loop through sampled points along the ray: update T{ray} with null event probabilities and apply Russian Roulette if T{ray} \le 0.05. 6. Multiply the phase function value (Henyey-Greenstein) by the estimated transmittance and light intensity to return radiance. Formulas: Step size sampling: \Delta t = -\frac{\ln(u)}{\sigmat}, where u \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1). Transmittance update: T{ray} \leftarrow T{ray} \cdot e^{-\sigmat \Delta t}. Parameters: Russian Roulette threshold: 0.05. Phase function: Henyey-Greenstein. Edge Cases: Precision issues when T{ray} approaches zero. Boundary conditions when the shadow ray exits the volume grid. Degenerate input when the density grid is empty or invalid. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rayaabbintersect(origin, direction, boxmin, boxmax): """Returns (t0, t1) for ray-box intersection. Handles zero direction components.""" t0 = 0.0 t1 = float('inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < boxmin[i] or origin[i] > boxmax[i]: return None else: tenter = (boxmin[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] texit = (boxmax[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] if tenter > texit: tenter, texit = texit, tenter t0 = max(t0, tenter) t1 = min(t1, texit) if t0 < t1: return t0, t1 return None def estimateshadowtransmittance(position, lightdirection, gridmin, gridmax, sigmat, rng): # 1. Initialize transmittance Tray = 1.0 # 2. Create shadow ray and 3. Intersect with volume grid t0, t1 = rayaabbintersect(position, lightdirection, gridmin, gridmax) if t0 is None or t0 >= t1: return 1.0 # Ray misses or is degenerate # 4. Initialize sampler (majorant sampling loop) t = t0 while t < t1: # Sample step size from exponential distribution with rate sigmat step = -math.log(rng.uniform()) / sigmat t += step if t >= t1: step = t1 - (t - step) t = t1 # 5. Update transmittance with null event probability: exp(-sigmat step) Tray = math.exp(-sigmat step) # Russian Roulette if transmittance is low if Tray <= 0.05: if rng.uniform() > Tray / 0.05: return 0.0 Tray = 0.05 # 6. Caller multiplies Tray by phase function and light intensity to return radiance return Tray This method estimates the transmittance from a surface point to a light source in participating media with wavelength-dependent scattering properties using null-scattering (delta-tracking). It differs from standard majorant sampling by selecting a specific RGB channel for the majorant at each step, allowing for tighter bounds per channel and reducing the variance caused by the global majorant in chromatic media. It is designed for Next Event Estimation (NEE) within volumetric path tracing. Shibodd/volumepathtracer, https://github.com/Shibodd/volumepathtracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

ee} \ = \exp(-	ext{majorant} 	imes t) 	imes  rac{	ext{majorant}}{\max(	ext{majorant})}. 3. Calculate 	ext{real\prob} =  rac{\sigmat}{	ext{majorant}}. 4. Update p{trans\dir} \ = \exp(-	ext{majorant} 	imes t) 	imes 	ext{majorant} 	imes (1 - 	ext{real\prob}) / \max(	ext{majorant}). 5. If \max(T{light}) \le 0, break. vii. Else (hit surface): 1. Update T{light} \ = \exp(-	ext{majorant} 	imes dt). 2. Update p{trans

ee}, p{trans\dir}. Parameters: maxnullcollisions limits the iteration count to prevent unbounded loops from numerical errors, with a default of 1000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical instability can cause unbounded loops without the iteration limit. Dividing by \max(	ext{majorant}) improves numerical robustness when \sigman is large relative to the majorant. If \sigman = 0, T{light} becomes zero and the loop breaks early to save computation. Usage in Path Throughput: When updating the path throughput, the Monte Carlo estimate of transmittance is divided by the average PDF over the RGB channels: currentpaththroughput = (Tlight / avg(ptransdir)). This normalization is required because the PDFs are scaled by \max(	ext{majorant}) for numerical robustness. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def chromaticnullscatteringnee(p, pprime, rng, maxnullcollisions, getmajorant, intersect, distance, clamp, exp, log, min, max): Tlight = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] ptransnee = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] ptransdir = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] accumt = 0.0 shadowray = Ray(p, pprime - p) isect = intersect(scene, shadowray) nextt = distance(p, pprime) if isect is not None: nextt = distance(p, isect.position) if shadowmediumexists: u = rng.next() channel = clamp(int(u 3), 0, 2) iteration = 0 while True: if majorant[channel] <= 0: break if iteration >= maxnullcollisions: break t = -log(1.0 - rng.next()) / majorant[channel] dt = nextt - accumt accumt = min(accumt + t, nextt) if t < dt: Tlight = exp(-majorant t) sigman / max(majorant) ptransnee = exp(-majorant t) majorant / max(majorant) realprob = sigmat / majorant ptransdir = exp(-majorant t) majorant (1.0 - realprob) / max(majorant) if max(Tlight) <= 0: break else: Tlight = exp(-majorant dt) ptransnee = exp(-majorant dt) ptransdir = exp(-majorant dt) break iteration += 1 return Tlight, ptransnee, ptransdir Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of null-scattering events, bounded by maxnullcollisions. Memory Complexity: Constant, per-ray. Strengths: Handles chromatic media efficiently by using channel-specific majorants, reducing the overestimation of the global majorant. Limitations: Requires precomputed channel-specific majorants and null-scattering coefficients. The hard iteration limit is an approximation. This method is described in the context of Volumetric Path Tracing homework assignments. It adapts null-scattering techniques for next-event estimation in participating media. name: Voxel Direct Lighting and Shadowing
body: Voxel Direct Lighting and Shadowing computes local illumination and shadows for voxel surfaces by casting shadow rays toward a light source. It builds on Direct Illumination with Shadow Rays and uses binary hit/miss results rather than the transmittance estimation used in Shadow Ray Transmittance Estimation. Inputs: pos: The 3D position of the surface point being shaded. normal: The surface normal at pos. material: A struct containing rgb (color) and a (emissive intensity). SUNDIR: The direction vector to the light source. traceuniforms.shadows: An integer flag indicating whether shadow casting is enabled. Outputs: color: The final RGB color of the surface point. shadow: A float value (0.0 or 1.0) representing the shadow factor. Data Structures: DirectLightningInfo: A struct containing color (vec3) and shadow (f32). shadowray: A ray structure initialized with origin pos and direction -normalize(SUNDIR). Steps: 1. Calculate Diffuse Lighting: Compute the diffuse lighting factor using the dot product of the surface normal and the normalized negative light direction. \text{diffuse} = \max(\text{dot}(\text{normal}, -\text{normalize}(\text{SUN\DIR})), 0.0) 2. Initialize Shadow Factor: Set the shadow factor to 1.0 (fully lit). 3. Cast Shadow Ray (if enabled): If traceuniforms.shadows is non-zero, cast a shadow ray from pos in direction -normalize(SUNDIR) using shootray(shadowray, 0.0, 0). Set shadow to 1.0 if the ray misses, or 0.0 if it hits. \text{shadow} = 1.0 \text{ if not } \text{shadow\hit.hit} \text{ else } 0.0 4. Calculate Emissive: If the material's emissive intensity a is non-zero, set the emissive color to the material's RGB color; otherwise, set it to black. \text{emissive} = \begin{cases} \text{vec3}(\text{material.rgb}) & \text{if } \text{material.a} \neq 0.0 \\ \text{vec3}(0.0) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 5. Combine Results: Compute the final color by multiplying the diffuse lighting by the shadow factor and adding the emissive component. \text{color} = \text{diffuse} \times \text{shadow} + \text{emissive} 6. Return: Return a DirectLightningInfo struct containing the computed color and shadow. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxeldirectlightingandshadowing(pos, normal, material, sundir, traceuniforms): # Assumes standard vector/math operations (dot, normalize, vec3, max) lightdir = -normalize(sundir) diffuse = max(dot(normal, lightdir), 0.0) # Step 2: Initialize shadow factor shadow = 1.0 # Step 3: Cast shadow ray if enabled if traceuniforms.shadows != 0: shadowray = Ray(origin=pos, direction=lightdir) # shootray performs voxel traversal and returns an object with a.hit boolean shadowhit = shootray(shadowray, 0.0, 0) shadow = 1.0 if not shadowhit.hit else 0.0 # Step 4: Calculate emissive emissive = vec3(material.rgb) if material.a != 0.0 else vec3(0.0) # Step 5: Combine results color = diffuse shadow + emissive # Step 6: Return return DirectLightningInfo(color=color, shadow=shadow) Parameters: traceuniforms.shadows: Typically 1 (enabled) or 0 (disabled). Edge Cases: Not given in the sources. A 5-step pipeline to render single scattering and volumetric shadows in real-time using GPU shaders and stencil buffer, with minimal texture memory cost. It differs from ray-marching approaches by leveraging conventional polygonal rendering and shadow volume logic. Not given in the sources. Described in an unofficial implementation for the Bevy voxel engine. ria8651/bevy-voxel-engine, https://github.com/ria8651/bevy-voxel-engine, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Hardware Implementation Pipeline
head: Single Scattering Rendering Pipeline, Volumetric Shadow Volume Method
body: The Hardware Implementation Pipeline is a five-step method for rendering single scattering and volumetric shadows in real-time using GPU shaders and the stencil buffer, designed for minimal texture memory cost. It differs from ray-marching approaches by leveraging conventional polygonal rendering and shadow volume logic, making it straightforward to integrate into traditional graphics engines. The pipeline consists of five steps that must be repeated for each light source. An initialization stage is required beforehand to obtain ambient lighting and the first depth map. Inputs: Scene geometry containing moving shadow casters, light source position (static or moving), and view ray direction. Outputs: Radiance L with direct single scattering (L{dss}) and volumetric shadows. Data Structures: Stencil Buffer: Integer buffer tracking occlusion status for shadow volume logic. Shadow Planes: Geometry derived from object silhouettes relative to the light source. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hardwarepipeline(scene, lights): # Initialization stage: obtain ambient lighting and first depth map initambientanddepthmap() for light in lights: # Step 1 (CPU) silhouettes = computesilhouettes(scene.shadowcasters, light.position) if light.ismoving: silhouettes = computesilhouettes(scene.shadowcasters, light.position) # Step 2 (GPU) rendersceneconventional() applyshadowplanesforsurfaceshadows() addambientfogforabsorptionandmultiplescattering() # Step 3 (GPU) setdepthtest(EQUAL) rendersceneagain() computedirectsinglescatteringpervertex() # Step 4 (CPU) shadowplanes = generateplanesfromsilhouettes(silhouettes) shadowplanes.sort(backtofront) # Step 5 (GPU) setdepthtest(LESS) setstenciltest(front: stencil==1, back: stencil==0) for plane in shadowplanes: if plane.isfrontfacing: addcontribution() stencildecrement() else: subtractcontribution() stencilincrement() Note: Helper functions for conventional rendering, fog application, and silhouette generation are standard graphics operations. Radiance Model: The observed radiance L along a view ray \vec{u} from point P is given by: L{\vec{u}\vec{P}} = L{dss}(\vec{u}\vec{P}) + e^{-kt OP} L(P) + La e^{-kt OP} + L{oiss}(\vec{u}\vec{P}) Where: L{dss}(\vec{u}\vec{P}): Direct single scattering term. L(P): Radiance at point P computed in steps 2 and 3. kt: Extinction coefficient. OP: Distance from observer to P. La: Ambient radiance. L{oiss}(\vec{u}\vec{P}): Other indirect single scattering terms. Parameters: The entire pipeline (steps 1-5) must be repeated for each light source. Pitfalls: Moving lights or objects require silhouette recomputation in Step 1. An initialization stage is mandatory before the main pipeline to obtain ambient lighting and the first depth map. Complexity: Real-time performance for classical graphics scenes. Memory: Minimal texture memory cost. Strengths: Easy to integrate into traditional engines; supports moving objects and lights. Limitations: Limited to single scattering and volumetric shadows; relies on stencil buffer operations which may have performance implications on some hardware. Measured Performance: Tested on scenes with up to 14,785 triangles, achieving approximately 30 frames per second with direct single scattering and shadows enabled. The method was proposed in "Single Scattering Effects for Computer Games". It follows the same strategy as the shadow volume algorithm, using only shaders and textures. Single Scattering Effects for Computer Games, https://hal.science/hal-00681726v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Lighting Models
body: Lighting models in volume rendering evaluate local illumination at a specific point \mathbf{p} to enhance the appearance of rendered objects by modeling effects like shadows, light scattering, and absorption. Unlike global light transport methods that simulate complex scattering, local lighting shades each sample independently, ignoring the rest of the scene, which makes it cheap to compute but unable to produce true shadows or scattering. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of evaluating visibility or illumination at a specific point \mathbf{p} within or on the boundary of a volume, based on a light source direction \mathbf{l} or environment. 1. Visibility/Transmittance Evaluation: The fundamental operation is determining how much light reaches \mathbf{p} from a source. This involves integrating the extinction coefficient \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) along a path from the source to \mathbf{p} (or vice versa). The transmittance T is calculated as: T = \exp\left(-\int{\mathbf{p}{source}}^{\mathbf{p}} \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) \, d\mathbf{x}\right) In discrete implementations, this integral is approximated by summing \sigmat \cdot \Delta s over samples along the ray. 2. Local Shading Models: For surface-like appearance in volumes, normals are approximated from the volume gradient \mathbf{g} = \nabla V. Usually, a simple absorption and emission model is used because it is relatively cheap to evaluate and gives good enough results. 3. Shadowing Approximation: Shadows are computed by testing occlusion along the direction to the light source. 4. Ambient Occlusion: Indirect illumination is approximated by integrating over the hemisphere or using simplified models (e.g., upward ray for sky light). The ambient contribution L{ambient} is often modulated by a shadowing factor based on local density: L{ambient} = L{sky} \cdot \exp(-D{up}) \cdot AO{factor} where D{up} is the integrated density along an upward ray. Applies local illumination calculations to enhance the perception of 3D shape and surface orientation within volumetric data. It sets itself apart from Gradient-based Shading with Phase Functions by using simplified local reflection rather than complex phase functions, and from Frequency Domain Directional Shading by operating in the spatial domain. Choose this method when a computationally efficient spatial-domain shading approximation is preferred over global phase function integration. Enables local diffuse illumination for semi-transparent volume rendering by utilizing multi-stage rasterization hardware (specifically register combiners) to compute lighting in a single pass. It differs from isosurface shading by using alpha blending instead of alpha testing, and from methods requiring 3D textures or multi-pass techniques by sacrificing real trilinear interpolation to fit gradient and color data into separate 2D textures. Choose this method when targeting early PC hardware with fixed-function register combiners for interactive frame rates. A physically based rendering (PBR) lighting model that uses the microfacet surface model to accurately represent real-world reflectance, distinguishing between metals and dielectrics. It sets itself apart from siblings like Shading models by explicitly separating diffuse and specular lobes with energy-conserving weights and using the Fresnel effect to vary reflectivity based on viewing angle. Choose this method when physically accurate specular highlights and energy conservation are required over simpler reflection models. Evaluates illumination at a surface point by combining ambient lighting with direct illumination from light sources, using shadow rays to determine visibility. It differs from its siblings by explicitly separating the computation of diffuse (Lambertian) and glossy (specular) reflection components, whereas Shading models provides a broader taxonomy, Shading for Semi-Transparent Volumes handles volume attenuation, and Cook-Torrance BRDF uses a more complex microfacet model for speculars. Choose this method when a straightforward ray-traced direct lighting model with shadow rays is sufficient. Approximates light transport in participating media by indexing a precomputed table with three angular parameters (\alpha, \beta, \gamma) derived from the surface normal, light direction, and view direction. It differs from sibling methods like Direct Illumination with Shadow Rays by replacing real-time integration of the scattering phase function with a fast trilinear texture lookup, allowing for complex scattering models (such as Henyey-Greenstein) to be evaluated efficiently on the GPU. Choose this method when real-time evaluation of complex phase functions is needed and precomputation memory is available. Computes the attenuation factor for a point light source that emits light within a specific cone direction, applying smooth falloff based on the angle between the light direction and the vector to the shading point. It is distinguished from area lights by its zero-size emission model and from uniform point lights by its angular dependency. Choose this method when directional intensity variation and cone-based falloff are required for local illumination. Shading aims to enhance appearance by modeling effects like shadows, light scattering, and absorption, depending on the chosen optical model. A simple absorption and emission model is usually used because it is relatively cheap to evaluate and gives good enough results. Local illumination shades each sample independently, ignoring the rest of the scene, so it cannot produce shadows or scattering but is cheap to compute. Under this model, each directional light shines in two directions: both the specified direction and the opposite direction. It is configured by setting the light color using vpSetLight with VPCOLOR and RGB components in range 0.0-1.0, setting the light direction with VPDIRECTION, enabling the light with vpEnable, and enabling two-sided lighting by calling vpEnable with the VPLIGHTBOTHSIDES option. A lighting model that attenuates light through the volume, providing simple but robust lighting without relying on a surface normal. It is used for multi-field gradients because the gradient orientation may not correspond to the surface of the classified region and can flip direction. Computes and sets shader uniforms for up to 4 lights, eye position, and eye look direction in object space. It involves computing the inverse of the actor's world matrix, converting light positions to object space, and transforming the eye look direction accordingly. Applies a simple day lighting model with sun, sky, and ambient components to a base color. The sky factor is S = 0 if nz < -0.5, 1 if nz > 0.5, else 0.5, and the direct factor is D = \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{s}, 0) \cdot V, resulting in C = B \cdot (A + S \cdot C{sky} + D \cdot C{sun}). Typical parameters include a sun direction of (-0.45, 0.35, 0.82), ambient color vec3(0.17, 0.20, 0.27), sky color vec3(0.23, 0.24, 0.21), and direct sun color vec3(0.88, 0.76, 0.61). The concept of lighting in volume rendering evolved from surface-based techniques, adapting local illumination models to scalar field data. Early methods focused on simple absorption and emission due to computational constraints. Modern implementations often combine these local shading models with shadow casting techniques to enhance depth perception. rokcej/volumetric-ray-casting, https://github.com/rokcej/volumetric-ray-casting, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Sample - Ray Marching and Signed Distance Functions, https://github.com/ComputeNode/cyfra/pull/13, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Advanced illumination and view-selection techniques for volume rendering and its application to medical imaging, http://hdl.handle.net/10803/371154, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) VolPack User's Guide, http://www-graphics.stanford.edu/software/volpack/vpuserguide.html, fetched 2026-10-28 Volume rendering multivariate data to visualize meteorological..., https://www.researchgate.net/publication/262237652Volumerenderingmultivariatedatatovisualizemeteorologicalsimulationsacasestudy, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) RaycastVolume.cpp, https://visualizationlibrary.org/documentation/raycastvolume8cppsource.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) aivv73/bend-voxel, https://github.com/aivv73/bend-voxel, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Shading models
head: Diffuse and Specular Shading for Volume Rendering
body:
Shading models for volume rendering apply local illumination calculations to enhance the perception of 3D shape and surface orientation within volumetric data. Unlike global illumination techniques that simulate light transport through participating media, this method approximates surface-like appearance by treating scalar field gradients as pseudo-normals and applying standard reflection models (diffuse and specular) to the volume samples. It sets itself apart from Gradient-based Shading with Phase Functions by using simplified local reflection rather than complex phase functions. The method evaluates shading contributions along a ray traversing the volume. It determines whether a region of the ray should be shaded based on data values and gradient magnitudes at the entry and exit points of that region. If shading is applied, it computes diffuse and specular components using averaged data values and gradients from the region boundaries. Inputs: Scalar volume data V. Ray segment defined by entry point \mathbf{p}{in} and exit point \mathbf{p}{out}. Shading parameters: diffuse amount kd, specular amount ks, specular shininess \alpha, shading opacity  eta, shading range [v{min}, v{max}], and minimum gradient threshold g{min}. Light direction \mathbf{l} (assumed uniform or local). View direction \mathbf{v} (assumed uniform or local). Outputs: Shading color contribution C{shade} (RGB). The implementation requires access to the scalar field V(\mathbf{x}) and its gradient 
abla V(\mathbf{x}). Scalar Value: v = V(\mathbf{x}). Gradient Vector: \mathbf{g} = 
abla V(\mathbf{x}) = [ rac{\partial V}{\partial x},  rac{\partial V}{\partial y},  rac{\partial V}{\partial z}]. Gradient Magnitude: |\mathbf{g}| = \sqrt{\mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{g}}. The gradient is typically computed as the derivative of the interpolation function used to sample the volume (e.g., trilinear interpolation). 1. Evaluate Boundary Properties: For the current ray segment (defined by entry \mathbf{p}{in} and exit \mathbf{p}{out}): Compute scalar values: v{in} = V(\mathbf{p}{in}), v{out} = V(\mathbf{p}{out}). Compute gradient vectors: \mathbf{g}{in} = 
abla V(\mathbf{p}{in}), \mathbf{g}{out} = 
abla V(\mathbf{p}{out}). Compute gradient magnitudes: g{in} = |\mathbf{g}{in}|, g{out} = |\mathbf{g}{out}|. 2. Determine Shading Eligibility: Shading is applied if: (v{in} \in [v{min}, v{max}] OR v{out} \in [v{min}, v{max}]) AND (g{in} > g{min} OR g{out} > g{min}). If not eligible, return C{shade} = \mathbf{0}. 3. Compute Averaged Data Value: Calculate the diffuse reflectivity value v{shade}: v{shade} =  rac{v{in} + v{out}}{2}. 4. Compute Averaged Gradient: Determine the shading normal \mathbf{n}: If both g{in} > g{min} and g{out} > g{min}: \mathbf{g}{avg} =  rac{\mathbf{g}{in} + \mathbf{g}{out}}{2} Else if only g{in} > g{min}: \mathbf{g}{avg} = \mathbf{g}{in} Else if only g{out} > g{min}: \mathbf{g}{avg} = \mathbf{g}{out} Else (should not happen if step 2 passed, but for safety): \mathbf{g}{avg} = \mathbf{0} Normalize the gradient to get the pseudo-normal: \mathbf{n} =  rac{\mathbf{g}{avg}}{|\mathbf{g}{avg}|}. 5. Calculate Diffuse Component: Diffuse color C{diff} is the color from the transfer function evaluated at v{shade}. Compute diffuse factor: Ld = \max(0, \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}). Diffuse contribution: C{diff\comp} = kd \cdot Ld \cdot C{diff}. 6. Calculate Specular Component: Specular color is assumed to be white (\mathbf{1}). Compute reflection vector \mathbf{r}: \mathbf{r} = 2(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l})\mathbf{n} - \mathbf{l} Compute specular factor: Ls = \max(0, \mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{v})^\alpha. Specular contribution: C{spec\comp} = ks \cdot Ls. 7. Combine and Apply Opacity: Total shading color: C{total} = C{diff\comp} + C{spec\comp}. Apply shading opacity  eta: C{shade} =  eta \cdot C{total}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def length(v): return math.sqrt(dot(v, v)) def normalize(v): l = length(v) if l == 0.0: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] return [v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l] def computeshading(pin, pout, volumedata, shadingparams, lightdir, viewdir): """ Computes shading for a ray segment in a volume. Args: pin: Entry point of the ray segment. pout: Exit point of the ray segment. volumedata: Object providing V(p) and gradV(p). shadingparams: Dict with keys: kd: float (diffuse amount) ks: float (specular amount) alpha: float (specular shininess) beta: float (shading opacity) vmin: float vmax: float gmin: float lightdir: Normalized vector. viewdir: Normalized vector. Returns: RGB color vector for shading contribution. """ vmin = shadingparams['vmin'] vmax = shadingparams['vmax'] gmin = shadingparams['gmin'] kd = shadingparams['kd'] ks = shadingparams['ks'] alpha = shadingparams['alpha'] beta = shadingparams['beta'] vin = volumedata.getvalue(pin) vout = volumedata.getvalue(pout) gin = volumedata.getgradient(pin) gout = volumedata.getgradient(pout) ginmag = length(gin) goutmag = length(gout) inrange = vmin <= vin <= vmax outrange = vmin <= vout <= vmax inthresh = ginmag > gmin outthresh = goutmag > gmin if not ((inrange or outrange) and (inthresh or outthresh)): return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] vshade = (vin + vout) / 2.0 if inthresh and outthresh: gavg = [(gin[i] + gout[i])/2.0 for i in range(3)] elif inthresh: gavg = gin elif outthresh: gavg = gout else: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] n = normalize(gavg) # Transfer function lookup at vshade cdiff = volumedata.gettransferfunctioncolor(vshade) ld = max(0.0, dot(n, lightdir)) cdiffcomp = [kd ld cdiff[i] for i in range(3)] r = [2.0 dot(n, lightdir) n[i] - lightdir[i] for i in range(3)] ls = max(0.0, dot(r, viewdir)) alpha cspeccomp = [ks ls for in range(3)] ctotal = [cdiffcomp[i] + cspeccomp[i] for i in range(3)] cshade = [beta ctotal[i] for i in range(3)] return cshade Diffuse Amount (kd): Controls the intensity of the diffuse reflection. Specular Amount (ks): Controls the intensity of the specular highlight. Specular Shininess (\alpha): Exponent for the specular term; higher values produce sharper highlights. Shading Opacity ( eta): Controls the transparency of the shading contribution, allowing it to blend with the underlying volume color. Shading Range ([v{min}, v{max}]): Scalar value range within which shading is considered. Minimum Gradient Threshold (g{min}): Minimum gradient magnitude required to apply shading, filtering out flat regions. Diffuse Color: Derived from the transfer function at the averaged data value v{shade}. Specular Color: Fixed to white. Gradient Discontinuity: Using the derivative of the trilinear interpolation function for gradients can cause discontinuities at shared cell faces, potentially introducing artifacts. Finite differences are an alternative but more expensive. Zero Gradient: If the averaged gradient is zero (e.g., in a perfectly flat region where both gradients are zero or cancel out), normalization fails. The logic in Step 4 handles cases where one gradient is valid, but if both are zero, the region is not shaded (Step 2). Out of Range Gradients: The logic explicitly handles cases where one boundary gradient is below the threshold and the other is above, using only the valid one. A technique for implementing directional diffuse reflection in volume rendering by performing shading computations entirely in the frequency domain. It solves the problem of applying shape cues without spatial differentiation overhead. Choose when computational efficiency in the frequency domain is preferred over spatial gradient calculation. A local illumination technique that modulates volumetric samples with diffuse and specular components, treating the gradient at the first significant surface intersection as a pseudo-surface normal. It differs by typically omitting shadow calculations for performance. Choose for fast, surface-like highlights in ray-cast volumes. Adds an illumination term to the emissive term to simulate single-scattering effects or computes shading for implicit iso-surfaces using phase functions like Henyey-Greenstein. Choose when angular scattering properties are important for the appearance of the volume. Computes diffuse lighting using the Lambertian reflectance model and enhances depth perception by casting shadow rays. It treats the volume as an opaque isosurface. Choose when only diffuse reflection and accurate shadows are needed, without specular highlights. A local illumination technique that calculates diffuse and specular contributions based on scalar data values and their gradients, managing the interplay between material opacity and light transport modes (indirect vs. direct) within a single shading pass. Choose when a comprehensive local shading model that handles both indirect and direct lighting components is required. A two-step rendering technique that generates colored, translucent shadows using stochastic sampling. It sets itself apart by producing softer, colored shadows with less memory than Deep Shadow Maps. Choose when accurate, colored, translucent shadows are needed for direct volume rendering. A local illumination technique for direct volume rendering that approximates surface lighting by estimating normals from the scalar field gradient and applying a Phong-like reflection model. It is computationally efficient but limited to local surface properties. Choose for fast, crisp depth cues in non-translucent media. Captures shadow information and global occlusion effects by branching a secondary ray towards the light source at each primary ray sample location. It computes transmittance at runtime. Choose when global ambient occlusion and runtime shadow computation are preferred over pre-computed shadow maps. A shading model that combines Lambertian diffuse lighting, ambient light, and rim lighting, modulated by a fire-colored palette driven by animated fBM noise. It computes the surface normal, light direction, diffuse factor, view direction, and rim light factor, then combines them with an ambient constant and maps the result through a fire palette. Choose when stylized, animated volumetric effects are required. Time Complexity: O(1) per shading evaluation, assuming gradient computation is O(1) (e.g., via trilinear derivative). Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for shading calculations. Measured Performance: Shading adds computational overhead to ray casting but is generally cheaper than global illumination techniques. It helps considerably in bringing out features and establishing orientations. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with the number of ray samples. Parallelization is effective as each ray's shading computation is independent. Strengths: Enhances perception of 3D shape and surface detail; computationally efficient; easy to implement within existing ray casting frameworks. Limitations: Approximates surface-like appearance; does not account for subsurface scattering or global light transport; gradient discontinuities may cause artifacts; limited to local illumination. When to Use: When enhancing visual clarity of features in volumetric data is prioritized over physical accuracy of light transport. When Not to Use: When accurate simulation of participating media light transport (e.g., subsurface scattering, global illumination) is required. The method was implemented within a ray casting volume renderer to calculate diffuse and specular contributions based on data values and gradients. It builds on the principle that shading helps considerably in bringing out features in the data and establishing orientations. The approach uses the derivative of the trilinear function as the gradient of the data, leveraging the fact that the function is already being used to model data at interior nodes of the tree.
