name: Frequency Domain Directional Shading
head: Frequency domain shading, Gradient moment shading, Gradient-Based Frequency Shading, Hemispherical Light Source Shading, Nusselt's analog shading
body:
Frequency Domain Directional Shading is a technique for implementing directional diffuse reflection in volume rendering by performing shading computations entirely in the frequency domain. It solves the problem of applying shape cues (shading) to volume data without the computational overhead of spatial domain differentiation or the nonlinearity of standard Lambertian models. Unlike Simplified Phong Lighting Model or Gradient-based Shading with Phase Functions which typically operate in the spatial domain, this method leverages the property that spatial differentiation is equivalent to frequency multiplication by a linear ramp, allowing the shading term to be computed as a moment of the spectrum. It builds on Shading models by replacing spatial gradient calculations with frequency domain operations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A premultiplied volume dataset f(x), where x is the spatial coordinate. The volume is assumed to be pre-multiplied by an opacity mask pm(x). Output: The shaded slice intensity I(s) for a specific projection direction, computed in the frequency domain before inverse transformation or during slice extraction. Data Structures: Volume Data: 3D grid of scalar values f(x). Frequency Spectrum: Complex-valued array F(s) representing the Fourier transform of the volume data. Interpolation Filter: A frequency-domain filter H(s) used to reconstruct the pure spectrum from the premultiplied volume. Parameters: C{amb}: Ambient color constant. L{amb}: Ambient light color. C{dif}: Directional shading strength constant. L{dif}: Directional light color. L: Unit light vector. Typically set perpendicular to the view vector V to maximize shading effect and eliminate adjustment terms in combined depth cueing/shading. s: Frequency coordinate vector. Method Steps: 1. Gradient Magnitude Pre-computation: Since the gradient magnitude |
abla f(x)| cannot be computed simply in the frequency domain, it must be computed in the spatial domain first. Compute the gradient vector 
abla f(x) in the spatial domain. Compute the magnitude |
abla f(x)|. Premultiply by the opacity mask: |
abla f(x)| pm(x). Compute the Fourier transform: G(s) = \mathcal{F}\{|
abla f(x)| pm(x)\}. 2. Volume Spectrum Preparation: Premultiply the volume data by the opacity mask: f(x) pm(x). Compute the Fourier transform: F{pre}(s) = \mathcal{F}\{f(x) pm(x)\}. 3. Filter Application: Apply the interpolation filter H(s) to reconstruct the pure spectrum of f from the premultiplied volume. F(s) = F{pre}(s) H(s). Similarly, apply the filter to the gradient magnitude spectrum: G{filtered}(s) = G(s) H(s). 4. Frequency Domain Shading Computation: Compute the shaded spectrum I(s) using the hemispherical light source model. The equation is derived from the linear approximation of diffuse reflection: I(s) = F(s) C{amb} L{amb} + F(s) i C{dif} L{dif} (s \cdot L) +  rac{1}{2} C{dif} L{dif} G{filtered}(s) Breaking this down into terms: Ambient Term: k1 = C{amb} L{amb}. Directional Shading Term: k2 = i C{dif} L{dif} (s \cdot L). This term represents the first moment of the spectrum, applying directional shading via frequency multiplication. Gradient Magnitude Term: k3 =  rac{1}{2} C{dif} L{dif}. This term scales the pre-computed gradient magnitude spectrum. The final frequency domain representation for the slice extraction is: I(s) = F(s) \cdot k1 + F(s) \cdot k2 + G{filtered}(s) \cdot k3 Note: The sources describe the combination as: \mathcal{F}\{f(x) pm(x)\} H(s) [C{amb} L{amb}] + \mathcal{F}\{f(x) pm(x)\} H(s) [i C{dif} L{dif} (s \cdot L)] +  rac{1}{2} C{dif} L{dif} \mathcal{F}\{|
abla f(x)| pm(x)\} H(s). 5. Slice Extraction: The shaded slice is obtained by applying the inverse Fourier transform or by extracting the relevant slice from the frequency domain representation during the rendering pipeline. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def frequencydomaindirectionalshading(volume, opacitymask, lightdirection, viewdirection, camb, lamb, cdif, ldif, interpolationfilterh): """ Computes directional shading for a volume slice in the frequency domain. Args: volume: 3D array of volume data f(x). opacitymask: 3D array of opacity mask pm(x). lightdirection: Unit vector L. viewdirection: Unit vector V (used to determine L if not provided). camb: Ambient color constant. lamb: Ambient light color. cdif: Directional shading strength constant. ldif: Directional light color. interpolationfilterh: 3D array representing H(s). Returns: shadedslice: 2D array representing the shaded slice. """ # Step 1: Compute gradient magnitude in spatial domain gradx = spatialderivative(volume, axis=0) grady = spatialderivative(volume, axis=1) gradz = spatialderivative(volume, axis=2) # Gradient magnitude |r(x)| gradmag = sqrt(gradx2 + grady2 + gradz2) # Premultiply gradient magnitude by opacity mask gradmagpremult = gradmag opacitymask # Step 2: Premultiply volume by opacity mask volpremult = volume opacitymask # Step 3: Fourier Transform both volumes Fpre = fft3(volpremult) G = fft3(gradmagpremult) # Step 4: Apply interpolation filter H(s) to reconstruct pure spectrum F = Fpre interpolationfilterh Gfiltered = G interpolationfilterh # Step 5: Define constants k1 = camb lamb k2coeff = 1j cdif ldif # i Cdif Ldif k3 = 0.5 cdif ldif # Step 6: Compute frequency domain shading terms # s is the frequency coordinate grid corresponding to F s = frequencycoordinategrid(F.shape) # Dot product s. L sdotL = dotproduct(s, lightdirection) # Term 1: Ambient termambient = F k1 # Term 2: Directional shading (First moment) termdirectional = F k2coeff sdotL # Term 3: Gradient magnitude contribution termgradient = Gfiltered k3 # Combine terms Is = termambient + termdirectional + termgradient # Step 7: Inverse FFT to get spatial slice shadedslice = inversefft3(Is) return shadedslice def spatialderivative(data, axis): """ Computes the spatial derivative along a specific axis using periodic boundaries. """ if axis == 0: return data[1:,:,:] - data[:-1,:,:] + data[0,:,:] - data[-1,:,:] elif axis == 1: return data[:, 1:,:] - data[:,:-1,:] + data[:, 0,:] - data[:, -1,:] elif axis == 2: return data[:,:, 1:] - data[:,:,:-1] + data[:,:, 0] - data[:,:, -1] else: raise ValueError("Invalid axis") def dotproduct(vec1, vec2): """ Computes dot product of two vectors. """ return sum(a b for a, b in zip(vec1, vec2)) def frequencycoordinategrid(shape): """ Generates frequency coordinate grid s for a given shape. Returns a tuple of 3D arrays (sx, sy, sz) scaled by 1/size. """ sx = [i / shape[0] for i in range(shape[0])] sy = [i / shape[1] for i in range(shape[1])] sz = [i / shape[2] for i in range(shape[2])] # Create meshgrid manually for pure Python compatibility sx = [[[sx[i] for in range(shape[1])] for in range(shape[2])] for i in range(shape[0])] sy = [[[sy[j] for in range(shape[2])] for j in range(shape[1])] for i in range(shape[0])] sz = [[[sz[k] for k in range(shape[2])] for j in range(shape[1])] for i in range(shape[0])] return (sx, sy, sz) def fft3(data): """Computes the 3D discrete Fourier transform.""" # Standard FFT algorithm (e.g., Cooley-Tukey) return fft3impl(data) def inversefft3(data): """Computes the inverse 3D discrete Fourier transform.""" return ifft3impl(data) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Magnitude Nonlinearity: The gradient magnitude |
abla f(x)| does not have a simple frequency domain representation. This necessitates computing the gradient in the spatial domain and requiring a second spectrum extraction, meaning two slices must be extracted from two volumes (one for f, one for |
abla f|). Sine Wave Depth Cueing: If depth cueing is implemented as a sine wave, its transform consists of two impulses. The filter H' must be computed by shifting H and adding three copies with complex weights, which increases the filter kernel size. Negative Values: A purely linear shading equation C{amb} L{amb} f(x) + C{dif} L{dif} 
abla f(x) can be derived but requires restricting the upper bound of C{dif} to prevent negative values, which restricts the shading effect. A local shading model that simulates diffuse reflection from a virtual hemisphere light source. It enhances shape perception by weighting volume points based on orientation relative to a light direction. It builds on Frequency Domain Directional Shading by computing directional shading in the frequency domain using an orientation field. Time Complexity: The method operates entirely in the frequency domain. Computing the moment (directional shading) incurs a few additional floating-point operations per sample on the slice, which is small relative to the convolution operations required for slice extraction. However, the requirement for a second spectrum (gradient magnitude) doubles the preprocessing cost for the gradient term. Memory Complexity: Requires storing two spectra: one for the volume f(x) and one for the gradient magnitude |
abla f(x)|. Due to the wide dynamic range and complex arithmetic of Fourier transforms, a pair of floating-point numbers is required for each voxel. Performance: The method is efficient for slice-based rendering as it avoids spatial domain differentiation during the projection step. The additional expense of moment computation is minor compared to convolution. Strengths: Avoids the nonlinearity of the MAX function used in Lambertian shading. Allows computation entirely in the frequency domain via moment computation. Easily extended to multiple light sources by adding moment terms. Limitations: Requires two slices to be extracted from two volumes due to the lack of a simple frequency domain representation for gradient magnitude. The shading effect is restricted if a single-volume linear equation is used to avoid the second spectrum, due to the need to prevent negative values. When to Use: Use when efficient frequency-domain volume rendering is required and directional shading is needed to enhance shape perception, particularly when avoiding spatial domain differentiation is beneficial. When Not to Use: Avoid if memory is constrained (due to the need for two spectra) or if a single-volume processing pipeline is strictly required without the overhead of pre-computing gradients. Frequency Domain Directional Shading was introduced by Takashi Totsuka and Marc Levoy in their 1993 paper "Frequency Domain Volume Rendering". The method is based on Nusselt's analog, which relates the irradiance on a surface to the projection of a hemispherical light source. It was developed to address the limitations of spatial domain shading techniques in frequency domain volume rendering, specifically the nonlinearity of the Lambertian MAX function. The technique has been used in volume rendering applications to provide directional illumination cues, enhancing the perception of shape and spatial relationships in volume projections. name: Hemisphere Illumination
head: Directional Shading (Hemisphere Illumination), Directional Shading via Hemispherical Illumination, Frequency Domain Directional Shading (Hemisphere Illumination)
body: Hemisphere Illumination is a local shading model for volume rendering that simulates diffuse reflection from a virtual hemisphere light source to provide directional illumination cues in volume projections. It enhances the perception of shape and spatial relationships by weighting volume points based on their orientation relative to a light direction, effectively treating the volume as a collection of diffusely reflecting surfaces. Unlike standard volume rendering which often lacks explicit shading cues, this method uses a hemisphere light source to provide directional illumination, though it remains a local approximation without global occlusion. It builds on Frequency Domain Directional Shading by computing directional shading in the frequency domain using an orientation field. Inputs: Volume data \Omega(x,y,z) (albedo/density). Orientation field N(x,y,z) = (Nx, Ny, Nz). Lighting direction L = (Lx, Ly, Lz), a unit vector. Source intensity Is (constant). Viewing direction V (normalized, pointing away from the eye). Outputs: Rendered image intensity I. Data Structures: The volume \Omega and orientation field N are represented in the frequency domain. Four 3D spectra are computed during precomputation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def precompute(volumeomega, orientationN, sourceintensity): # Create four copies of Is Omega volx = sourceintensity volumeomega orientationN.x voly = sourceintensity volumeomega orientationN.y volz = sourceintensity volumeomega orientationN.z volc = sourceintensity volumeomega # Compute 3D Fourier Transform of each to yield four 3D spectra specx = fft3d(volx) specy = fft3d(voly) specz = fft3d(volz) specc = fft3d(volc) return specx, specy, specz, specc def render(specx, specy, specz, specc, viewingdirectionV, lightingdirectionL): # Extract slices from spectra along viewing direction V slicex = extractslice(specx, viewingdirectionV) slicey = extractslice(specy, viewingdirectionV) slicez = extractslice(specz, viewingdirectionV) slicec = extractslice(specc, viewingdirectionV) # Compute constant c2 c2 = pi/2 - pi/2 (lightingdirectionL.x + lightingdirectionL.y + lightingdirectionL.z) # Combine slices intensity = lightingdirectionL.x slicex + lightingdirectionL.y slicey + lightingdirectionL.z slicez + c2 slicec return intensity def fft3d(volume): # Standard 3D discrete Fourier transform return transform3dfft(volume) def extractslice(spectrum, direction): # Projection-slice operation: extract 2D slice from 3D spectrum along direction return projectslice(spectrum, direction) Steps: 1. Precomputation: Create four copies of the product Is \Omega(x,y,z). Multiply the first copy by Nx(x,y,z), the second by Ny(x,y,z), the third by Nz(x,y,z), and leave the fourth copy as Is \Omega(x,y,z). Compute the 3D Fourier Transform of each of the four copies to yield four 3D spectra. 2. Rendering (for a given view and light direction): Extract the relevant slices from the four 3D spectra corresponding to the viewing direction V. Compute the image intensity I using the linear combination of the extracted slices: I = Lx \PiV \left[ \left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\pi}{2} Nx\right) Is \Omega \right] + Ly \PiV \left[ \left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\pi}{2} Ny\right) Is \Omega \right] + Lz \PiV \left[ \left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\pi}{2} Nz\right) Is \Omega \right] + c2 \PiV \left[ Is \Omega \right] Where: \PiV denotes the projection-slice operation along viewing direction V. c2 = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{2} (Lx + Ly + Lz). Formula Derivation Context: The weighting assigned to each point P(t) along a ray is based on the integral of the source intensity modulated by the diffuse reflection model: IP = \inta^b Is \Omega(P(t)) \left[ \frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\pi}{2} (N(P(t)) \cdot L) \right] dt This integral is decomposed into the linear combination shown above to allow efficient computation via the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem. Parameters: Light Hemisphere Direction: Typically placed on the right side of the picture, shining leftwards. This corresponds to a lighting direction L with a negative x-component in a standard right-handed coordinate system where the viewer looks down the negative z-axis or similar convention. Viewing Direction: V points away from the eye. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Padding: To avoid aliasing in the frequency domain, the input volume may need to be zero-padded. Increasing the volume width by a factor of k^2 (surrounding data with a margin of zeros of width N(k^2-1)/2) increases per-view processing time by a factor of k^2, memory by k^3, and preprocessing time by a factor of k^2. Orientation Field: The accuracy of the shading depends on the quality of the orientation field N. No Occlusion: The method does not account for occlusion between volume elements. A global illumination solution that models single-bounce light contribution from the sky by creating a virtual skybox of infinite directional lights and sampling it over the hemisphere directed away from the surface normal. Unlike typical raster renderers that model the sky as one or more directional lights (causing inaccurate shadowing and dark scenes), this method provides accurate shadowing and illumination by integrating radiance over the hemisphere. Time Complexity: Preprocessing time is proportional to the size of the zero-padded volume. Per-view processing time increases with the amount of zero padding. Memory Complexity: Memory requirements increase with the size of the zero-padded volume. Strengths: Provides strong directional shading cues that enhance shape perception and spatial relationships in volume data. Computed efficiently in the frequency domain via 3D Fourier transforms. Limitations: Does not model occlusion or global illumination effects like inter-reflections. Accuracy depends on the quality of the orientation field. When to Use: When directional shading cues are needed to improve shape perception in volume renderings, and computational efficiency is important. When Not to Use: When accurate shadows, occlusion, or global illumination effects are required. The method was described in the context of volume rendering using the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem. It was developed to generate realistically shaded renderings of volume data by simulating diffuse reflection from a hemisphere light source. The approach leverages the efficiency of frequency domain computations to apply complex shading models to volume data. Volume Rendering using the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem, https://graphics.stanford.edu/papers/fourier/fourier.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem in Volume Rendering, https://www.scribd.com/document/796298963/Marc-Levoy-Volume-rendering-using-the-Fourier-projection-slice-theorem, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Global Illumination via Hemisphere Sampling
head: Color Bleaching, Diffuse GI, Sky GI, Sky Global Illumination
body: A global illumination solution that models single-bounce light contribution from the sky by creating a virtual skybox of infinite directional lights and sampling it over the hemisphere directed away from the surface normal. Unlike typical raster renderers that model the sky as one or more directional lights (causing inaccurate shadowing and dark scenes), this method provides accurate shadowing and illumination by integrating radiance over the hemisphere. Inputs: Surface position p, surface normal n, surface roughness \alpha (for specular variant), temporal samples temporal\x, temporal\y \in [0, 1], sky radiance function s{sky}(\omegai), shadow hardness parameter k, diffuse weight kd, albedo c, specular coefficient ks, Cook-Torrance BRDF terms D, F, G, view direction \omegao. Outputs: Diffuse Global Illumination color contribution GI{diffuse} and/or Specular Global Illumination color contribution GI{specular}. Data Structures: temporalx: Float, temporal sample X coordinate. temporaly: Float, temporal sample Y coordinate. n: Normalized 3D vector, surface normal. T: 3D vector, tangent basis vector. B: 3D vector, bitangent basis vector. H: 3D vector, hemisphere sample direction in local space. omegai: 3D vector, world-space sample direction. Parameters: Shadow hardness k=3 for diffuse GI. Shadow hardness k = 3 + 1/\alpha for specular GI. Steps: 1. Construct Tangent Basis: Calculate the tangent vector T to avoid degeneracy when the normal is aligned with the Z-axis: T = \begin{cases} \{0, 0, 1\} \times n & \text{if } |nz| < 0.999 \\ \{1, 0, 0\} \times n & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Calculate the bitangent B: B = n \times T 2. Sample Direction: Depending on the variant (Diffuse or Specular), compute the sample direction \omegai using the respective sampling function. For Diffuse GI (Uniform Hemisphere Sampling): Compute spherical angles: \phi = 2\pi \cdot temporal\x \theta = 0.5\pi \cdot temporal\y Compute local hemisphere coordinates H: H = \{\cos\phi \sin\theta, \sin\phi \sin\theta, \cos\theta\} Transform to world space: \omegai = \{T, B, n\} \cdot H For Specular GI (GGX Importance Sampling): Compute \cos\theta based on roughness \alpha: \cos\theta = \frac{1 - temporal\x}{1 + (\alpha^2 - 1) temporal\y} Compute \phi = 2\pi \cdot temporal\x. Compute local hemisphere coordinates H: H = \{\cos\phi \sin\theta, \sin\phi \sin\theta, \cos\theta\} Transform to world space: \omegai = \{T, B, n\} \cdot H 3. Calculate Soft Shadow: Compute the soft shadow term SoftMarch(p, \omegai, k). 4. Compute Radiance Contribution: Diffuse GI: GI{diffuse} = \frac{kd c}{\pi} \int{\Omega{sky}} s{sky}(\omegai) SoftMarch(p, \omegai, 3) (n \cdot \omegai) d\omegai In practice, this is approximated by the single sample: GI{diffuse} \approx \frac{kd c}{\pi} s{sky}(\omegai) SoftMarch(p, \omegai, 3) (n \cdot \omegai) Specular GI: GI{specular} = ks \int{\Omega} \frac{D F G}{4 (\omegao \cdot n) (\omegai \cdot n)} s{sky}(\omegai) SoftMarch(p, \omegai, 3 + \frac{1}{\alpha}) (n \cdot \omegai) d\omegai In practice, approximated by the single sample: GI{specular} \approx ks \frac{D F G}{4 (\omegao \cdot n) (\omegai \cdot n)} s{sky}(\omegai) SoftMarch(p, \omegai, 3 + \frac{1}{\alpha}) (n \cdot \omegai) 5. Accumulate: Add GI{diffuse} to the pixel color of the first shading pass. Add GI{specular} to the pixel color computed from the first shading pass and diffuse GI pass. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computehemispheregi(p, n, alpha, temporalx, temporaly, ssky, k, kd, c, ks, D, F, G, wo): # 1. Construct Tangent Basis if abs(n[2]) < 0.999: T = cross([0, 0, 1], n) else: T = cross([1, 0, 0], n) B = cross(n, T) # 2. Sample Direction (Specular GGX formula used here; swap for Diffuse if needed) phi = 2 math.pi temporalx costheta = (1 - temporalx) / (1 + (alpha2 - 1) temporaly) sintheta = math.sqrt(1 - costheta2) H = [math.cos(phi) sintheta, math.sin(phi) sintheta, costheta] omegai = [dot(T, H), dot(B, H), dot(n, H)] # 3. Calculate Soft Shadow # Standard soft shadow factor based on ray distance and hardness t = raymarchdistance(p, omegai) shadow = 1.0 / (1.0 + (t / k)2) # 4. Compute Radiance Contribution ndotw = dot(n, omegai) diffuseterm = (kd c / math.pi) ssky(omegai) shadow ndotw specularterm = ks (D F G) / (4 dot(wo, n) dot(omegai, n)) ssky(omegai) shadow ndotw return diffuseterm, specularterm Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If |nz| \ge 0.999, the standard cross product for T might be degenerate or unstable; the code switches to using the X-axis vector \{1, 0, 0\} for the cross product. Using only one sample per frame produces a checkerboard pattern without Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA). Relies on TAA for accurate results because it uses Monte Carlo integration over time with limited samples. A reflection technique that samples the skybox using a specular lobe distribution based on the Cook-Torrance specular term and surface roughness \alpha, instead of uniform hemisphere sampling. It differs from diffuse GI by using a specular lobe distribution (GGX) dependent on roughness \alpha rather than uniform hemisphere sampling. It relies on Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) for accurate results because it uses Monte Carlo integration over time with limited samples. Complexity: Computationally expensive to integrate fully over the hemisphere, so it relies on single-sample Monte Carlo integration per frame. Performance: Requires Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) to converge to an accurate image within a few frames; without TAA, the result is noisy (checkerboard pattern). Strengths: Provides accurate shadowing and illumination from the sky, avoiding the dark scenes and inaccurate shadows caused by modeling the sky as simple directional lights in typical raster renderers. Limitations: Single-sample approach introduces noise without temporal accumulation; dependent on TAA stability. This method was implemented in a real-time renderer using CUDA, aiming to achieve visual fidelity comparable to offline high-fidelity techniques like ray tracing, while surpassing typical real-time raster renderers in quality. It addresses the limitation of engines like the Source Engine, which model the sky as directional lights (sun and sky lights) that fail to contribute accurate shadowing. The approach was evaluated at 1280 × 720 on an RTX 2080 Super, comparing against Blender Cycles and UE4. name: Simplified Phong Lighting Model
head: Phong Illumination, Phong Illumination Model, Phong Reflection Model, Simplified Phong Shading
body: The Simplified Phong Lighting Model is a local illumination technique used in volume rendering to enhance the perception of 3D shape and surface detail by modulating the color of volumetric samples with diffuse and specular lighting components. It solves the problem of flat, unstructured appearance in ray-cast volumes by treating the gradient of the scalar field at the first significant surface intersection as a pseudo-surface normal. Unlike Frequency Domain Directional Shading, which operates in the Fourier domain, or Gradient-based Shading with Phase Functions, which models complex light scattering, this method applies a standard local reflection model directly to the volume data. It differs from Lambert Shading with Shadow Rays by typically omitting shadow calculations to maintain performance, and from the Volume Shading Model by focusing on surface-like highlights rather than participating media absorption. The method calculates the color of a sample point by summing ambient, diffuse, and specular contributions. It requires a scalar volume dataset and a camera/lighting configuration. The core innovation for volume data is the estimation of the surface normal from the volume gradient at the point of interest, usually the first voxel where the value exceeds a threshold or the raymarched intersection point. Inputs: volume: A 3D scalar field (e.g., medical image data or SDF). point (p): The 3D position in world space being shaded. eye (e): The camera position. lightPos (l): The position of the light source. lightColor (CL): The color/intensity of the light. ambientLight (CA): The ambient light color/intensity. material: Coefficients for ambient (ka), diffuse (kd), specular (ks), and shininess (n or \alpha). Outputs: color: The final RGB color of the sample point. Normal Vector (N): A 3D vector (Nx, Ny, Nz), normalized to unit length. Light Vector (L): A 3D vector from the point to the light, normalized. View Vector (V): A 3D vector from the point to the eye, normalized. Reflection Vector (R): A 3D vector, calculated from L and N. Half Vector (H): (Optional, for Blinn-Phong variant) A 3D vector, calculated from L and V. 1. Estimate Normal: Compute the surface normal N at point p using finite differences of the scalar field or an annotation gradient volume. For opacity op(x,y,z), use central differences: N = \frac{1}{2} \begin{pmatrix} op(x + 1, y, z) - op(x - 1, y, z) \\ op(x, y + 1, z) - op(x, y - 1, z) \\ op(x, y, z + 1) - op(x, y, z - 1) \end{pmatrix} Then normalize N. For signed distance fields (SDFs), estimate via small scalar perturbations \epsilon: N = \text{normalize}(\text{SDF}(p + \epsilon) - \text{SDF}(p - \epsilon)). 2. Compute Vectors: Calculate L = \text{normalize}(lightPos - p), V = \text{normalize}(eye - p), and R = \text{reflect}(-L, N) = 2(N \cdot L)N - L. For the Blinn-Phong variant, compute H = \text{normalize}(L + V). 3. Calculate Dot Products: Compute dotLN = \max(N \cdot L, 0.0) and dotRV = \max(R \cdot V, 0.0). For Blinn-Phong, compute dotHV = \max(H \cdot N, 0.0). 4. Compute Components: Ambient: C{amb} = ka \times CA. Diffuse: C{diff} = kd \times CL \times dotLN. Specular (Phong): C{spec} = ks \times CL \times dotRV^n. Specular (Blinn-Phong): C{spec} = \max(H \cdot N, 0.0)^{\text{shininess}}. 5. Combine: Sum the components: Color = C{amb} + C{diff} + C{spec}. 6. Gamma Correction: Apply gamma correction to the final color: Color{final} = Color^{(1/2.2)}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def simplifiedphonglighting(p, eye, lightpos, lightcolor, ambientcolor, ka, kd, ks, shininess, volumefunc): # 1. Compute Vectors L = normalize(lightpos - p) V = normalize(eye - p) R = 2 dot(N, L) N - L R = normalize(R) # 3. Dot Products dotLN = max(dot(N, L), 0.0) dotRV = max(dot(R, V), 0.0) # 4. Components ambient = ka ambientcolor diffuse = kd lightcolor dotLN specular = ks lightcolor pow(dotRV, shininess) # 5. Combine and handle edge cases if dotLN < 0.0: return vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) if dotRV < 0.0: return ambient + diffuse color = ambient + diffuse + specular # 6. Gamma Correction return pow(color, vec3(1.0 / 2.2)) Shininess (n or \alpha): Controls the sharpness of the specular highlight. Typical values are 10 and 60. Higher values produce smaller, sharper highlights. Ambient Coefficient (ka): Typically 0.2. Diffuse Coefficient (kd): Typically 0.7. Specular Coefficient (ks): Typically 1.0. Ambient Light: Often set to 0.5 \times (1, 1, 1) or a soft gray. Light Intensity: Often set to 0.2–0.8 depending on scene brightness. Normal Estimation Noise: Finite difference normal estimation can be noisy in low-resolution volumes or near discontinuities. Smoothing or using higher-order differences may be required. Facing Away: If dotLN < 0, the light is behind the surface relative to the normal; return zero contribution. Reflection Vector Facing Away: If dotRV < 0, the reflection vector points away from the viewer; return only the diffuse component. Shadowing: Standard Simplified Phong does not include shadow rays. Self-shadowing is ignored, which can lead to unrealistic lighting in complex geometries. Ambient Term Deviation: Some implementations use a normalized color difference for the ambient term instead of a constant scalar, which deviates from the standard model. It solves the problem of rendering shiny surfaces in participating media without the recursive overhead of ray tracing or the approximation errors of numerical integration. Unlike Simple Reflections, which uses iterative raymarching, this approach relies on precomputed spectra and a linear combination of Fourier projections. It builds on Simplified Phong Lighting Model by adapting its local illumination term to the frequency domain. The Phong Shading Model for Volume Data applies local illumination calculations to volumetric scalar fields to provide 3-D shape cues without participating in the classification (opacity) operation. It treats the volume gradient at each sample point as a pseudo-surface normal to compute ambient, diffuse, and specular lighting components, typically combined with Beer-Lambert absorption for transparency. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Specular Reflections via Polynomial Expansion by using explicit gradient-based normals for standard Phong/Blinn-Phong terms rather than polynomial approximations of specular highlights, and differs from Phong Shading by operating on volumetric samples rather than polygonal meshes. Phong Shading is a local illumination model that approximates direct lighting by summing ambient, diffuse, and specular components. It solves the problem of rendering smooth, shiny surfaces by evaluating the lighting equation per fragment. It differs from its siblings by computing specular highlights based on the angle between the view direction and the reflection vector, whereas Blinn-Phong Shading Model uses the half-vector for computational efficiency, and Phong Shading Model for Volume Data adapts this to volumetric gradient-based shading. The Blinn-Phong Shading Model is a local illumination model used in volume visualization to calculate the emitted color of a sample voxel as the sum of ambient, diffuse, and specular components. It improves the perception of surface shape and fine details by modulating color from the transfer function with lighting intensity derived from the local surface normal, light direction, and view direction. It sets itself apart from its parent, the Simplified Phong Lighting Model, by using the half-vector (the normalized sum of the light and view directions) for specular calculation instead of the reflected light vector, which is computationally cheaper and produces smoother highlights. This method computes per-voxel illumination using the Blinn-Phong shading model and applies depth cueing to enhance the perception of volume density and depth. It differs from pure Blinn-Phong Shading Model by integrating lighting directly into the volume compositing loop with depth-based color modulation. This method renders non-Lambertian surfaces by approximating the Phong shading model using Spherical Harmonic (SH) lighting representations. It computes specular reflections in complex lighting environments by projecting the lighting into SH coefficients and applying approximated specular basis functions. It distinguishes itself from its parent, the Simplified Phong Lighting Model, by replacing explicit light source summation with SH domain operations, and from its sibling Specular Reflections via Polynomial Expansion by utilizing the specific SH approximation for the specular term rather than polynomial expansions of the reflection vector. This variant integrates Phong shading with texture mapping and reflection/refraction effects. It utilizes built-in trilinear texture interpolation to reconstruct normal vectors from attribute maps, which are then used for Phong shading. It also implements reflection and refraction using cube mapping, leveraging the continuous per-fragment correct normals. The final fragment color is set by summing contributions from lighting, texture mapping, reflectance mapping, and refraction mapping. In the context of medical imagery, this model provides a more convincing volumetric appearance. It estimates normals using central differences of opacity values op(x, y, z). The normal is calculated as: n(x, y, z) = \frac{1}{2} \begin{pmatrix} op(x + 1, y, z) - op(x - 1, y, z) \\ op(x, y + 1, z) - op(x, y - 1, z) \\ op(x, y, z + 1) - op(x, y, z - 1) \end{pmatrix} This normal is then used in the standard Phong illumination equation. This variant applies the Blinn-Phong model at the first surface intersection found during raymarching. It calculates the light direction L, view direction V, and halfway vector H = \text{normalize}(L + V). The specular intensity is computed as \max(H \cdot N, 0.0)^{\text{shininess}}, with a hardcoded shininess of 9.0 in some implementations. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample point for lighting calculation, assuming normal estimation is O(1) (finite differences). Total complexity depends on the number of samples per ray and rays per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for lighting vectors and coefficients. The volume data itself dominates memory usage. Performance: Very fast due to the lack of shadow rays and recursive reflections. Suitable for real-time or interactive volume rendering. Strengths: Simple to implement, computationally inexpensive, enhances shape perception significantly compared to unshaded volume rendering. Limitations: Does not account for self-shadowing or inter-reflections, which can lead to unrealistic lighting in complex scenes. Normal estimation can be noisy. When to Use: When performance is critical and the primary goal is to enhance shape perception of a single object or simple scene. When Not to Use: When realistic global illumination, shadows, or complex light transport effects are required. The Phong reflection model was originally developed by Bui Tuong Phong for polygonal meshes. Its adaptation to volume rendering leverages the gradient of the scalar field as a proxy for surface normals, allowing the same local illumination equations to be applied to volumetric data. This approach became popular in medical imaging and scientific visualization for its ability to provide intuitive 3D cues without the computational cost of full ray tracing. The "Simplified" variant refers to the omission of shadow calculations, as volume self-shadowing algorithms are expensive and rarely crucial. name: Specular Reflections via Polynomial Expansion
head: Fourier Projection-Slice Phong, Polynomial Phong Shading, Specular Reflections via Polynomial Approximation
body: This method extends the Fourier Projection-Slice volume rendering framework to handle specular highlights by analytically expanding the Phong specular term |N \cdot H|^n into a polynomial. It solves the problem of rendering shiny surfaces in participating media without the recursive overhead of ray tracing or the approximation errors of numerical integration. Unlike Simple Reflections, which uses iterative raymarching, this approach relies on precomputed spectra and a linear combination of Fourier projections. It builds on Simplified Phong Lighting Model by adapting its local illumination term to the frequency domain. Inputs: Volume data I\Omega(x,y,z). Surface normals N(x,y,z) (or derived from volume gradients). Light direction L and view direction V. Specular exponent n (integer). Outputs: Rendered image intensity I. Data Structures: Precomputed Spectra: A set of 3D Fourier transforms of the volume data filtered by specific polynomial basis functions. The count K is determined by the multinomial theorem. Spectral Slices: 2D slices extracted from the 3D Fourier volume along the viewing direction V for per-view rendering. Steps: 1. Polynomial Expansion: Expand the term (N \cdot H)^n into a sum of monomials using the multinomial theorem. Define vectors Hn and Nn containing the directional factors and coefficients from the expansion. 2. Integral Formulation: The specular contribution along a viewing ray P(t) from t=a to t=b is given by: IP = \inta^b I\Omega(P(t)) \left[ \frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\pi}{2} (N(P(t)) \cdot H)^n \right] dt The \frac{\pi}{2} constants implement hemispherical illumination to avoid the absolute value operator in |N \cdot H|^n. 3. Fourier Projection: Apply the Fourier projection-slice theorem to convert the integral into a linear combination of projections. The output image is: I = Hn \cdot \PiV \left[ \left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\pi}{2} Nn(x,y,z)\right) I\Omega(x,y,z) \right] + c4 \PiV [I\Omega(x,y,z)] where \PiV denotes the projection operator along view direction V, and c4 is a suitable constant accounting for the polynomial's constant term. 4. Per-View Rendering: Extract the required 2D slices from the precomputed 3D spectra corresponding to the current view direction V. Compute the inverse Fourier transform on each slice to obtain spatial domain projections. Weight the projections by the components of Hn and sum them to produce the final image intensity. Parameters: n: Specular exponent. Typical value is n=10. H: Halfway vector, H = \frac{L+V}{\|L+V\|}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision and Memory: The number of spectra grows rapidly with n. For n=10, 286 spectra are required. This leads to significant memory usage and slower rendering compared to conventional volume rendering. Degenerate Input: If N or H are undefined at boundaries or in homogeneous regions, the polynomial expansion may fail. Ensure normals are normalized and handle zero-length vectors by clamping or using a default normal. Hemispherical Illumination: The \frac{\pi}{2} constants assume a specific hemispherical illumination model. Deviations from this assumption require adjustment of the constant terms. Polynomial Depth Cueing is an adaptation of the specular reflection method to provide non-linear depth cueing (e.g., inverse square law falloff) by replacing the normal N and halfway vector H with the depth vector D and view vector V in the polynomial expansion. It is chosen when linear attenuation is insufficient to disambiguate depth in scenes with high depth complexity. For an inverse square law falloff, the term (D \cdot V)^2 is used, requiring 10 slices from 10 precomputed spectra. Time Complexity: Rendering time is proportional to the number of precomputed spectra, which is determined by the multinomial theorem for the exponent n. For n=10, 286 spectra are needed. Memory Complexity: Requires storing K 3D Fourier volumes, where K is the number of spectra. Measured Performance: The method is slower than conventional volume rendering due to the large number of spectra required, even for very large volumes. Strengths: Analytical evaluation of specular highlights; no recursive ray tracing; compatible with the Fourier projection-slice framework. Limitations: High memory and computational cost for large n; limited to polynomial approximations of the specular term. When to use: When analytical specular highlights are needed in a Fourier-based volume rendering pipeline and memory is not a constraint. When not to use: For real-time applications or when n is very large, due to the exponential growth in required spectra. The method originates from the work on Volume Rendering using the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem, specifically in the context of extending the technique to handle complex lighting models like Phong shading. It was developed to allow for the integration of local illumination effects, such as specular reflections, into the frequency-domain volume rendering framework. The approach leverages the linearity of the Fourier transform to decompose the non-linear Phong term into a sum of linear terms. name: Simple Reflections
head: Iterative Specular Reflections
body: Simple Reflections is a local illumination technique that approximates specular highlights by raymarching along the geometric reflection vector at a surface hit point and blending the resulting color with the base surface color. It calculates a simple reflection by raymarching off the surface normal and blending the result with the surface color. Unlike Specular Reflections via Polynomial Expansion, which uses polynomial expansion of the Phong term for analytical evaluation, Simple Reflections relies on iterative numerical raymarching. Inputs: color: The base surface color (RGB) at the hit point. point: The 3D coordinates of the surface hit point. direction: The incoming view direction vector (normalized). scene: The signed distance field or scene representation providing normal and raymarching queries. light: The light source definition. reflection-count: Integer, maximum number of bounces allowed (default 3). DRAW-DISTANCE: Float, maximum raymarch distance for a valid hit. Outputs: finalcolor: The blended RGB color including reflections. Data Structures: Vectors are 3-component floats (\mathbf{v} = [x, y, z]). Colors are 3-component floats in range [0, 1]. Steps: 1. Initialize state variables: p \leftarrow \text{point} d \leftarrow \text{direction} n \leftarrow \text{get-normal}(p, \text{scene}) i \leftarrow 0 \text{not-done?} \leftarrow \text{true} C{\text{out}} \leftarrow \text{color} 2. Loop while i < \text{reflection-count} AND \text{not-done?}: 1. Compute the reflection vector \mathbf{r} using the surface normal \mathbf{n} and incoming direction \mathbf{d}: \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{d} - 2(\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{n})\mathbf{n} 2. Raymarch from a point slightly above the surface to avoid self-intersection. Start position p{\text{start}} = p + \mathbf{n} \cdot \epsilon (implemented as above-surface-point in the source). 3. March ray in direction \mathbf{r} through the scene. Let the hit distance be distance and the hit color be hitcolor. 4. If distance < DRAW-DISTANCE: 1. Update position: p \leftarrow p + \mathbf{r} \cdot \text{distance}. 2. Update normal: n \leftarrow \text{get-normal}(p, \text{scene}). 3. Update direction: d \leftarrow \mathbf{r}. 4. Compute lightness L{\text{hit}} at the new point p. 5. Attenuate lightness by factor 0.5: l \leftarrow L{\text{hit}} / 2. 6. Blend colors. For each channel c \in \{R, G, B\}: c{\text{new}} = (c{\text{old}} + c{\text{hit}} \cdot l) \cdot 0.66 Update C{\text{out}} with these new channel values. 7. Increment bounce counter: i \leftarrow i + 1. 5. Else (ray did not hit within distance): 1. Set \text{not-done?} \leftarrow \text{false}. 3. Return C{\text{out}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def simplereflections(color, point, direction, scene, light, reflectioncount=3, drawdistance=100.0): """ Computes simple iterative specular reflections. Args: color: tuple (r, g, b) base surface color. point: vec3 hit point. direction: vec3 incoming view direction. scene: object with getnormal(p) and marchray(p, d) methods. light: object with pointlightness(p, scene) method. reflectioncount: int max bounces. drawdistance: float max raymarch distance. Returns: tuple (r, g, b) final color. """ # Initialize state p = list(point) d = list(direction) n = scene.getnormal(p) i = 0 notdone = True outcolor = list(color) while i < reflectioncount and notdone: # 1. Compute reflection vector r = d - 2(d. n)n dotdn = sum(d[j] n[j] for j in range(3)) r = [d[j] - 2 dotdn n[j] for j in range(3)] # 2. Raymarch from above surface point epsilon = 1e-4 startpoint = [p[j] + n[j] epsilon for j in range(3)] # 3. March ray distance, hitcolor = scene.marchray(startpoint, r) if distance < drawdistance: # 4. Hit found p = [p[j] + r[j] distance for j in range(3)] n = scene.getnormal(p) d = r # Compute lightness and attenuate lightness = light.pointlightness(p, scene) l = lightness / 2.0 # Blend colors newcolor = [] for j in range(3): cold = outcolor[j] chit = hitcolor[j] cnew = (cold + chit l) 0.66 newcolor.append(cnew) outcolor = newcolor i += 1 else: notdone = False return tuple(outcolor) Parameters: reflection-count: Maximum number of reflection bounces allowed. Default value in code is 3. 0.66: Color blending factor applied after adding hit color to prevent overflow and maintain brightness across bounces. 0.5: Light attenuation factor applied to reflection bounces to make them appear darker. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Infinite Recursion: Prevented by checking i < reflection-count and not-done?. Self-Intersection: The raymarch starts from above-surface-point (offset by normal) to prevent the ray from immediately hitting the surface it just reflected off. Language Limitations: In languages without a break statement (e.g., Fennel), the loop counter must be incremented manually at the end of each iteration, and not-done? must be used to exit early. Color Overflow: The multiplication by 0.66 ensures that the sum of base and reflected colors does not exceed 1.0, preventing clipping artifacts. Maps reflected directions to cube map texture coordinates following OpenGL specifications. It computes reflected directions using reflecteddirections = 2 surfacenormals sum(viewdirections surfacenormals, dim=-1, keepdim=True) - viewdirections. It finds the max absolute component index and value to determine the cube face, then computes texture coordinates by dividing the reflected direction by the max absolute value. Linear mapping is used for the third coordinate, and grid coordinates are constructed for each face based on the max index and sign, stacking (u, v, faceindex) where faceindex is mapped from 0-5 to -1 to 1. The cube map is sampled using nn.functional.gridsample and the output is permuted. This variant is chosen when environment mapping is preferred over iterative raymarching for reflections. Time Complexity: O(k \cdot m), where k is the number of reflection bounces (default 3) and m is the number of steps per raymarch. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel, as it only stores current state variables. Performance: Fast for low bounce counts. Performance degrades linearly with increased reflection-count. Strengths: Simple to implement, avoids environment maps by computing reflections via direct raymarching. Limitations: Approximate, limited by DRAW-DISTANCE. Not suitable for complex inter-reflections beyond the fixed bounce count. When to use: Real-time raymarched scenes with mirror-like surfaces. When not to use: High-fidelity rendering requiring accurate global illumination or infinite bounces. Originated in the context of raymarching signed distance fields (SDFs) for real-time graphics. The technique was popularized in blog posts and tutorials demonstrating SDF rendering with simple lighting models. It is a foundational technique for adding specular highlights to raymarched scenes without resorting to recursive ray tracing. name: Phong Shading Model for Volume Data
head: Direct Volume Rendering using Textures, Engel, Kraus & Ertl technique, Gradient-based Phong Shading, Heidelberg Raytracing, Texture Mapping Based Volume Rendering with Phong Illumination, VolumeClassifier Lighting Model
body:
The Phong Shading Model for Volume Data applies local illumination calculations to volumetric scalar fields to provide 3-D shape cues without participating in the classification (opacity) operation. It treats the volume gradient at each sample point as a pseudo-surface normal to compute ambient, diffuse, and specular lighting components, typically combined with Beer-Lambert absorption for transparency. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Specular Reflections via Polynomial Expansion by using explicit gradient-based normals for standard Phong/Blinn-Phong terms rather than polynomial approximations of specular highlights, and differs from Phong Shading by operating on volumetric samples rather than polygonal meshes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset, camera position \mathbf{E}, light source positions or directions, and rendering parameters (ambient/diffuse/specular coefficients, shininess, absorption coefficient). Output: A 2D image where each pixel color is the result of front-to-back compositing of shaded volume samples. Data Structures: Volume Data: Stored as a 3D texture or array. Light Structure: Contains direction, ambient color, and diffuse color. Gradient: Precomputed or computed on-the-fly. In precomputed variants, a gradient vector is stored for each voxel. In texture-mapping variants, normals may be encoded in RGB channels. Numbered Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Optional): Compute the gradient vector 
abla f for each voxel in the volume data. This is often done using central differences: 
abla f(xi, yj, zk) \approx  egin{bmatrix}  rac{f(x{i+1}, yj, zk) - f(x{i-1}, yj, zk)}{2} \  rac{f(xi, y{j+1}, zk) - f(xi, y{j-1}, zk)}{2} \  rac{f(xi, yj, z{k+1}) - f(xi, yj, z{k-1})}{2} \end{bmatrix} The surface normal \mathbf{N} is then the normalized gradient: \mathbf{N}(xi) =  rac{
abla f(xi)}{|
abla f(xi)|} 2. Ray Casting / Texture Mapping: Ray Casting: Cast rays from the camera through each pixel into the volume. Sample the volume at intervals dt. Texture Mapping: Render polygonal planes (oriented to object or view) containing the volume data as 3D textures. The fragment shader samples the 3D texture at the plane's position. 3. Lighting Calculation per Sample: For each sample point \mathbf{x} along the ray (or fragment): a. Retrieve Data: Get the scalar value val and opacity/alpha \alpha from the volume. b. Threshold Check: If val \le \Delta (a threshold, e.g., background), skip lighting and set emission to zero. c. Compute Normals: If precomputed, use the stored gradient vector. If encoded in texture, expand RGB values from [0,1] to [-1,1]: \mathbf{N} = 2 \cdot \mathbf{v}{rgb} - \mathbf{1}. If computed on-the-fly, estimate gradients (e.g., using Sobel operators for X/Y in specific hardware implementations). d. Compute Vectors: View direction \mathbf{V}: From sample to camera. For orthographic projection, this is constant. Light direction \mathbf{L}: From sample to light source. For parallel lights, this is constant. Halfway vector \mathbf{H}: \mathbf{H} =  rac{\mathbf{V} + \mathbf{L}}{|\mathbf{V} + \mathbf{L}|}. e. Compute Lighting Components: Ambient: \mathbf{C}a = ka \cdot \mathbf{c}p, where ka is the ambient reflection coefficient and \mathbf{c}p is the light color. Diffuse: \mathbf{C}d = kd \cdot (\mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{L}) \cdot \mathbf{c}p \cdot \max(0, \mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{L}),. Note: Some implementations use the light position directly in the dot product if not normalized correctly, but standard Phong uses normalized vectors. Specular: \mathbf{C}s = ks \cdot (\mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{H})^n \cdot \mathbf{c}p,, where ks is the specular coefficient and n is the shininess exponent. f. Combine: \mathbf{C}{light} = \mathbf{C}a + \mathbf{C}d + \mathbf{C}s. g. Apply Transfer Function: Multiply the lighting color by the visualization color derived from the scalar value and normal. 4. Absorption and Compositing: a. Transparency: Compute the transparency factor using the Beer-Lambert law: T = e^{-\kappa \cdot val \cdot dt}, where \kappa is the absorption coefficient. b. Accumulate: Update the accumulated color \mathbf{C}{out} and opacity \alpha{out} using front-to-back compositing: \mathbf{C}{out} = \mathbf{C}{out} + \mathbf{C}{light} \cdot (1 - \alpha{out}) \cdot \alpha{sample} \alpha{out} = \alpha{out} + \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{out}),. Note: In some implementations, light is attenuated twice (once on the way in, once on the way out). Pseudocode (Ray Casting Variant): Unverified code. samplepos[i] for i in range(3)]) V = normalize([camera.position[i] - samplepos[i] for i in range(3)]) H = normalize([V[i] + L[i] for i in range(3)]) Ca = [params.ka light.color[i] for i in range(3)] diff = max(dot(normal, L), 0.0) Cd = [params.kd diff light.color[i] for i in range(3)] spec = pow(max(dot(normal, H), 0.0), params.shininess) Cs = [params.ks spec light.color[i] for i in range(3)] lightcontribution = [lightcontribution[i] + Ca[i] + Cd[i] + Cs[i] for i in range(3)] # Step: Apply transfer function to get visualization color viscolor = getvisualizationcolor(val, normal) shadedcolor = [lightcontribution[i] viscolor[i] for i in range(3)] alphasample = 1.0 - Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Noise: The gradient operator is a high-pass filter. Raising it to a power (as in Gradient Shading variants) enhances high frequencies, causing aliasing if not filtered. Zero Gradient: At flat regions or boundaries, the gradient may be zero, leading to undefined normals. Handle by defaulting to a view-dependent normal or zeroing the lighting contribution. Performance: 3D texture accesses are slower than 2D due to irregular memory access patterns. Planes oriented to the view plane have lower performance than object-oriented planes. A set of three shading strategies applied during volume ray marching to compute lighting and shadows for each sample along a ray. They extend the Phong Shading Model for Volume Data by providing specific heuristics for handling illumination in participating media, distinguishing themselves through their approach to gradient estimation and shadow accumulation. The Blinn-Phong Lighting Model applies the Blinn-Phong shading approximation to volume rendering data, typically by computing surface normals from the scalar field gradient to simulate isosurface shading. It enhances the perception of depth and shape structure in volumetric data by combining ambient, diffuse, and specular lighting components, offering a computationally cheap alternative to full ray-traced shadows while providing stronger visual cues than unshaded volume rendering. A shading technique that modulates intensity by the strength of the local gradient raised to a power, similar to Phong shading in polygon rendering. It calculates the absolute value of the derivative (1D gradient) of the input signal, raises the gradient magnitude to a power to accentuate regions of rapid change, and multiplies the original input signal by the raised gradient result to select regions of rapid change. The exponent controls highlight width; higher powers narrow the highlight and introduce more high frequencies. A pitfall is that the gradient operator is a high-pass filter that enhances high frequencies; raising to a power further increases them, causing aliasing during resampling if not filtered. Measured Performance: In texture-mapping implementations, 3D texture accesses are slower than 2D due to irregular memory access patterns. Planes oriented to the view plane have substantially lower performance than those oriented to the object plane. Using fragment shaders (Cg) results in lower performance compared to the fixed-function pipeline of OpenGL. Strengths: Provides strong 3-D shape cues at a reasonable cost. Computationally cheap alternative to full ray-traced shadows. Limitations: Does not participate in classification. Shadows are approximated or absent unless specifically implemented (e.g., Heidelberg Raytracing). Gradient-based normals can be noisy. When to Use: When visual clarity of internal structures is prioritized over physical accuracy of light transport. When Not to Use: When accurate shadowing or complex light transport effects are required. The technique is used in systems like VolPack and VIRIM (Heidelberg Raytracing). It was presented for completeness in early volume rendering papers to provide a satisfactory illusion of smooth surfaces at a reasonable cost. It builds on the original Phong shading model for polygonal surfaces. name: Volume Shading Modes
body: Volume Shading Modes are a set of three shading strategies applied during volume ray marching to compute lighting and shadows for each sample along a ray. They extend the Phong Shading Model for Volume Data by providing specific heuristics for handling illumination in participating media, distinguishing themselves through their approach to gradient estimation and shadow accumulation. The method operates within a ray-marching loop, transforming rays to object space, sampling the volume, computing gradients, and applying shading based on the selected mode. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray origin and direction in world space, volume data, transformation matrices (world-to-object, object-to-world), shading parameters (shadingScale, gradientStep), and light parameters (ambient color, directional light color and direction). Output: Shaded color and accumulated alpha for the ray segment. Data Structures RadiancePayload: Contains rng (pointer to RandomTEA), alpha (float), and color (vec3f). Packaged via packPointer(&payload, u0, u1) for OptiX trace. Numbered Steps 1. Transform Ray: Transform ray origin and direction to object space: cpp const vec3f org = xfmPoint(wto, org); const vec3f dir = xfmVector(wto, dir); 2. Initialize Tracking (Single Shade Heuristic): If using SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC, initialize tracking variables: cpp vec3f highestContributionOrg = 0.f; vec3f highestContributionColor = 0.f; float highestContributionAlpha = 0.f; 3. March Ray: Iterate along the ray using raymarchingiterator(self, org, dir, tMin, tMax, self.step, & {... }). 4. Sample Position: Compute sample position with jitter: cpp const auto p = org + lerp(jitter, t.x, t.y) dir; 5. Compute Gradient: Compute gradient in object space. Negate it because opacity correlates to the scalar field, and the gradient points toward increasing values (outside), requiring a flip for correct lighting: cpp const vec3f No = -sampleGradient(self.volume, p, sampleValue, gradientStep); 6. Transform Normal: Transform gradient to world space: cpp const vec3f Nw = xfmNormal(otw, No); 7. Apply Shading: GRADIENTSHADING: Compute shaded color and blend: cpp const vec3f shadingColor = shadescivislight(dir, Nw, sampleColor, params.matgradientshading, params.lightambient, params.lightdirectionalrgb, params.lightdirectionaldir); sampleColor = lerp(shadingScale, sampleColor, shadingColor); SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC: Track the point with the highest contribution: cpp if (highestContributionAlpha < (1.f - payload.alpha) sampleAlpha) { highestContributionOrg = p; highestContributionColor = sampleColor; highestContributionAlpha = (1.f - payload.alpha) sampleAlpha; } 8. Continue Marching: Return payload.alpha < nearlyone to continue marching while alpha is below threshold. Parameters shadingScale: Controls the interpolation weight between base color and shaded color in lerp(shadingScale, base, shaded). gradientStep: Step size used for finite-difference gradient estimation in sampleGradient. Pitfalls Gradient Direction: The gradient direction must be negated (-sampleGradient) because the implementation assumes opacity directly correlates to the volume scalar field, meaning the gradient naturally points toward higher values (outside), requiring a flip for correct lighting. name: Blinn-Phong Lighting Model
head: Blinn-Phong Lighting on Isosurface, Blinn-Phong Shading, Blinn-Phong Shading for Volume Data, Blinn-Phong volume rendering, Isosurface Rendering with Blinn-Phong Shading, Isosurface Shading, Volume Illumination, Volumetric Shading
body: The Blinn-Phong Lighting Model applies the Blinn-Phong shading approximation to volume data, typically by detecting an isosurface during ray traversal and computing illumination at that hit point. It solves the problem of flat, unlit volume rendering by providing depth and shape cues through simulated diffuse and specular reflections. Unlike Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP), which projects the brightest voxel along the ray without lighting simulation, this method requires more computation power but yields visually more pleasing results with explicit surface shading. It builds on Phong Shading Model for Volume Data by using the half-vector approximation for specular highlights, which is computationally cheaper than calculating the reflection vector. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume texture V, a ray defined by origin O and direction D, a user-defined minimum threshold value T{min}, grid spacing g, and lighting parameters (ka, kd, ks, ia, id, is, \alpha, L). Output: The final pixel color C{final} incorporating ambient, diffuse, and specular components. Data Structures: Volume Texture: 3D texture containing scalar values. Optionally, precomputed gradient textures (X, Y, Z components) may be stored to avoid on-the-fly calculation. Lighting Parameters: ka, kd, ks: Scalar intensities for ambient, diffuse, and specular components. ia, id, is: Vector colors for ambient, diffuse, and specular components. \alpha: Shininess exponent (typically 64.0 in implementations, or user-defined). L: Normalized light direction vector. V{dir}: Normalized view direction vector (from surface to eye). Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Tracing and Isosurface Detection: Trace the ray through the volume. Sample the scalar value s(t) at each step. Stop the trace when s(t) \ge T{min}. If the ray exits the volume without exceeding the threshold, return the background color or handle as transparent. 2. Normal Computation: Compute the surface normal N at the hit point. This is done by calculating the gradient of the scalar field \nabla I using central differences between neighboring voxels: \nabla I = \left( \frac{I{right} - I{left}}{2g}, \frac{I{top} - I{bottom}}{2g}, \frac{I{front} - I{back}}{2g} \right) where I{right}, I{left}, etc., are the scalar values of the neighboring voxels, and g is the uniform voxel dimension. Normalize the gradient to obtain the unit surface normal N. Alternative: If precomputed gradient textures are available, fetch the gradient directly from the texture to save 6 texture fetches per calculation. 3. Lighting Calculation: Calculate the illumination I using the Blinn-Phong formula: I = ka ia + kd id (N \cdot L) + ks is \left( \left( \frac{L + V{dir}}{\|L + V{dir}\|} \right) \cdot N \right)^\alpha Where: N \cdot L is the dot product of the normal and light direction, clamped to [0, 1] for diffuse. H = \frac{L + V{dir}}{\|L + V{dir}\|} is the normalized half-vector. (H \cdot N)^\alpha is the specular term, clamped to [0, 1] before exponentiation. 4. Composition: The resulting color is combined with the volume color at the hit point. If using Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) composition, the shaded color is accumulated along the ray using front-to-back compositing. If strictly isosurface rendering, the pixel color is set to the calculated illumination multiplied by the material color at the hit point. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def blinnphongvolumeshading(rayorigin, raydirection, volumetexture, threshold, gridspacing, lightingparams): """ rayorigin: vec3 raydirection: vec3 volumetexture: function returning scalar value at 3D coordinate threshold: float, minimum scalar value to trigger shading gridspacing: float, distance between voxel centers lightingparams: dict containing ka, kd, ks, ia, id, is, alpha, lightdir """ # Step 1: Trace ray to find isosurface t = 0.0 stepsize = 0.01 # Implementation dependent maxdist = 10.0 # Bounding box or max ray length hitpoint = None while t < maxdist: currentpos = rayorigin + raydirection t scalarval = volumetexture(currentpos) if scalarval >= threshold: hitpoint = currentpos break t += stepsize if hitpoint is None: return vec3(0.0) # No surface hit # Step 2: Compute Normal via Central Differences dx = vec3(gridspacing, 0.0, 0.0) dy = vec3(0.0, gridspacing, 0.0) dz = vec3(0.0, 0.0, gridspacing) valright = volumetexture(currentpos + dx) valleft = volumetexture(currentpos - dx) valtop = volumetexture(currentpos + dy) valbottom = volumetexture(currentpos - dy) valfront = volumetexture(currentpos + dz) valback = volumetexture(currentpos - dz) gradx = (valright - valleft) / (2.0 gridspacing) grady = (valtop - valbottom) / (2.0 gridspacing) gradz = (valfront - valback) / (2.0 gridspacing) normal = normalize(vec3(gradx, grady, gradz)) # Step 3: Calculate Lighting L = normalize(lightingparams['lightdir']) V = normalize(-raydirection) # View direction is opposite to ray direction # Diffuse diffdot = max(dot(normal, L), 0.0) diffuse = lightingparams['kd'] lightingparams['id'] diffdot # Specular H = normalize(L + V) specdot = max(dot(normal, H), 0.0) specular = lightingparams['ks'] lightingparams['is'] pow(specdot, lightingparams['alpha']) # Ambient ambient = lightingparams['ka'] lightingparams['ia'] # Combine finalcolor = ambient + diffuse + specular return finalcolor Parameters: Threshold (T{min}): User-defined minimum scalar value. Determines which part of the volume is considered the "surface". Shininess (\alpha): Controls the sharpness of specular highlights. Default value of 64.0 is used in some implementations, but is user-modifiable. Lighting Coefficients (ka, kd, ks): Intensities for ambient, diffuse, and specular light. Default values in QuickVol are set for visual appeal but are user-modifiable. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normal Artifacts: Computing normals on-the-fly using central differences requires 6 texture fetches per sample, which can be expensive. Precomputing gradients on the host and storing them in the voxel data (e.g., packing X, Y, Z gradients into RGBA channels) increases texture memory usage by 4x but improves performance. Diagnostic Interference: Clinicians may deliberately disable illumination because shading can complicate diagnostic tasks by obscuring internal structures or introducing artifacts. Threshold Sensitivity: Choosing an inappropriate threshold may result in no surface being hit or noisy, fragmented surfaces. Time Complexity: Higher than MIP or simple DVR. Requires ray marching to find the isosurface. Normal calculation adds overhead: 6 texture fetches per hit if computed on-the-fly, or 0 extra fetches if precomputed. Memory Complexity: Standard volume texture size. If precomputed gradients are used, memory usage increases by 4x to store gradient components. Performance: Slower than MIP rendering due to the need for isosurface detection and lighting calculations. However, it is considered "quite cheap and simple to compute" compared to more complex global illumination methods. Strengths: Provides strong depth and shape cues, making it visually more pleasing and helpful for data exploration. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than unshaded methods. The approximation of normals from scalar gradients can be inaccurate for noisy data or thin structures. Not suitable for all diagnostic tasks where unobstructed view of intensity is required. The Blinn-Phong model was originally developed for polygonal surfaces by Jim Blinn. In the context of volume rendering, it was adapted to provide shading for isosurfaces detected within volumetric data. It is implemented in tools such as QuickVol to enhance the perception of anatomical structures. The technique is often compared to Phong shading, with Blinn-Phong being preferred for its computational efficiency in specular calculation. name: Phong Shading
head: Phong Illumination, Phong Illumination Model, Phong Model, Phong Reflection Model, Phong Shading Model
body: Phong Shading is a local illumination model that approximates the color of a surface point by summing ambient, diffuse, and specular components based on surface normals, light directions, and view directions. It is distinct from Phong Shading Model for Volume Data which adapts this model specifically for volume gradients. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Surface position \vec{x}, surface normal \vec{N} (unit vector), light direction \vec{L} (unit vector from point to light), view direction \vec{V} (unit vector from point to camera), material parameters (ka, kd, ks, n or \alpha), light parameters (Ia, Id, Is or colors), and object colors (Oa, Od, Os). Outputs: Final color I{total} at the surface point. Data Structures: The material is typically represented as a structure containing: ka: Ambient reflection coefficient (scalar). kd: Diffuse reflection coefficient (scalar or vector). ks: Specular reflection coefficient (scalar or vector). n or alpha: Shininess exponent (scalar). colorambient: Ambient color vector. colordiffuse: Diffuse color vector. colorspecular: Specular color vector. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Ambient Component: Calculate the ambient contribution using the ambient light intensity and the material's ambient reflection coefficient. I{amb} = Ia \cdot ka \cdot Oa Where Ia is the ambient light intensity/color, ka is the ambient reflection coefficient, and Oa is the object's ambient color. Note: Some implementations assume Oa = Od. 2. Compute Diffuse Component: Calculate the diffuse contribution using Lambert's cosine law. I{diff} = \sum{i} I{i,d} \cdot kd \cdot Od \cdot \max(\vec{L}i \cdot \vec{N}, 0) Where I{i,d} is the diffuse intensity of light source i, kd is the diffuse reflection coefficient, Od is the object's diffuse color, \vec{L}i is the unit vector from the surface point to light source i, and \vec{N} is the unit normal vector. If \vec{L}i \cdot \vec{N} < 0, the diffuse term is 0 (back-face culling for lighting). 3. Compute Specular Component: Calculate the specular highlight. There are two common variations cited in the sources: Reflection Vector Variant (Original Phong): Compute the reflection vector \vec{R} of the light direction about the normal. \vec{R} = 2(\vec{N} \cdot \vec{L})\vec{N} - \vec{L} Then calculate the intensity based on the angle between \vec{R} and the view direction \vec{V}: I{spec} = \sum{i} Ii \cdot ks \cdot Os \cdot \max(\vec{R} \cdot \vec{V}, 0)^n Where Ii is the intensity of light source i, ks is the specular reflection coefficient, Os is the object's specular color, \vec{V} is the unit view vector, and n is the shininess exponent. Half-Vector Variant (Blinn-Phong/Alternative): Compute the half-vector \vec{H} between the light direction \vec{L} and view direction \vec{V}. \vec{H} = \frac{\vec{L} + \vec{V}}{\|\vec{L} + \vec{V}\|} Then calculate the intensity based on the angle between \vec{H} and the normal \vec{N}: I{spec} = \sum{i} Ii \cdot ks \cdot Os \cdot \max(\vec{H} \cdot \vec{N}, 0)^n This variant is often attributed to Blinn but is cited in sources discussing the Phong model's implementation details. The sources note that the angle between \vec{R} and \vec{V} is twice the angle between \vec{N} and \vec{H}. 4. Combine Components: Sum the ambient, diffuse, and specular components to get the final color. I{total} = I{amb} + I{diff} + I{spec}. Parameters with Typical Values: Shininess (n or \alpha): Controls the size of the specular highlight. Typical values range from 10 to 128. A value of 10 is dull, 20 is shiny, 25 is very shiny/metallic. Default often cited as 64.0 or 100.0. Ambient Coefficient (ka): Typical default values range from 0.05 to 0.3 depending on the material. Diffuse Coefficient (kd): Typical default 0.7 to 1.0. Specular Coefficient (ks): Typical default 0.1 to 1.5. Light Colors: Often white (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) for simplicity. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Physical: The model is not physically sound; it does not conserve energy and L{phong} does not reflect genuine radiance but an approximated color. Glossy Term Discard: The specular term discards the \cos \thetas factor (projected surface area) because specular reflections are considered unaffected by it. Vector Normalization: All vectors (\vec{L}, \vec{V}, \vec{N}, \vec{R}, \vec{H}) must be normalized before dot products to ensure correct intensity. Back-Facing Surfaces: Diffuse and specular terms should be zero if the surface faces away from the light (\vec{N} \cdot \vec{L} < 0). Precision: In volume rendering, normals are computed via gradients (central differences), which can be noisy if the gradient step size is not small enough. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def phongshading(position, normal, lightposition, cameraposition, material, lights): """ Computes Phong shading for a single surface point. Args: position: vec3, world space position of the point. normal: vec3, normalized world space normal. lightposition: vec3, world space position of the light. cameraposition: vec3, world space position of the camera. material: dict or object with keys: ka, kd, ks, shininess, colorambient, colordiffuse, colorspecular. lights: list of dicts, each with keys: color (vec3), position (vec3). Returns: vec3, the final shaded color. """ # Initialize result color = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # 1. Ambient Component # Iamb = Ia ka Oa ambientlightcolor = vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # Default white ambient if not specified in lights ambientcontrib = ambientlightcolor material.ka material.colorambient color += ambientcontrib for light in lights: # 2. Diffuse Component # L = normalize(lightposition - position) lightdir = normalize(light.position - position) # Diffuse = Id kd Od max(N. L, 0) diffuseintensity = max(dot(normal, lightdir), 0.0) diffusecontrib = light.color material.kd material.colordiffuse diffuseintensity color += diffusecontrib # 3. Specular Component # V = normalize(cameraposition - position) viewdir = normalize(cameraposition - position) # Using Half-Vector variant as it is widely cited in the sources for Phong implementation halfdir = normalize(lightdir + viewdir) specularintensity = pow(max(dot(normal, halfdir), 0.0), material.shininess) specularcontrib = light.color material.ks material.colorspecular specularintensity color += specularcontrib return color Reflectance Map Shading is a technique that evaluates the Phong shading model per-pixel using cube map dependent texture reads, thereby avoiding the need to normalize vectors. It serves as an optimization to reduce lookup table size by replacing per-pixel dot-product calculations with a direct lookup into a pre-computed reflectance map organized as six n \times n tables. Phong Shading with Exponential Fog is a local illumination model that combines the standard Phong lighting components (ambient, diffuse, specular) with exponential depth cueing to simulate distance-based fading in volume rendering. It differs from its parent Phong Shading by explicitly integrating a distance-dependent attenuation factor into the final color calculation, and from Reflectance Map Shading by computing lighting dynamically per fragment rather than via precomputed textures. Time Complexity: O(1) per surface point per light source. The cost is dominated by vector operations (dot products, normalization, power function). Memory Complexity: O(1) for material and light parameters. Measured Performance: Fast enough for real-time rendering on standard hardware. Scaling: Linear with the number of light sources. Strengths: Computationally inexpensive; produces visually pleasing specular highlights; widely supported and understood. Limitations: Not physically based; does not account for occlusion or interreflection (local illumination only); specular highlights can appear sharp or unnatural if the shininess exponent is not tuned correctly. When to Use: Real-time rendering, volume visualization where performance is critical, and when approximate lighting is sufficient. When Not to Use: Physically based rendering requiring energy conservation, global illumination effects, or accurate shadowing. Phong Shading was developed by Bui Tuong Phong in 1975. It is a standard lighting model applied to SDF-rendered scenes and volume data, using surface positions, normals, material properties, and camera location. It is commonly used in ray casting to approximate lighting and in real-time OpenGL rendering. The model is an empirical approximation used because it can be efficiently computed.
