name: Reflectance Map Shading
head: 6n table shading, Cube Map Dependent Texture Reads for Shading, Cube-map Phong shading
body: Reflectance Map Shading is a technique that evaluates the Phong shading model per-pixel using cube map dependent texture reads, thereby avoiding the need to normalize vectors. It serves as an optimization to reduce lookup table size by replacing per-pixel dot-product calculations with a direct lookup into a pre-computed reflectance map organized as six n \times n tables. Inputs and Outputs Input: A sample gradient vector \mathbf{G} (representing the surface normal approximation) and the object's base color. Output: The final shaded RGB intensity for the sample. Data Structures The reflectance map is a lookup table (LUT) organized as six separate n \times n textures (or tables), corresponding to the six faces of a cube centered at the origin. Layout: Each face covers one octant of the normal space. The index enumerates the six major directions. Content: Each texel stores the pre-computed RGB intensities resulting from the Phong shading model (ambient, diffuse, and specular contributions) for the specific normal direction mapped to that texel. Precision: Typical implementations use 5 bits per index, resulting in n=32. Steps 1. Compute Gradient: Calculate the gradient vector \mathbf{G} at the sample position. In the referenced implementation, gradients are precomputed at each voxel position using central differences. 2. Normalize by Maximum Component: Determine the component of \mathbf{G} with the largest absolute magnitude. Divide all components of \mathbf{G} by this maximum value to form the normalized gradient vector \mathbf{G}'. \mathbf{G}' = \frac{\mathbf{G}}{\max(|Gx|, |Gy|, |Gz|)} This maps the vector to the surface of a cube rather than a sphere, allowing it to be indexed directly by the cube face. 3. Determine Cube Face: Identify which of the six faces of the cube \mathbf{G}' intersects. This is determined by the sign and magnitude of the components of \mathbf{G}', which enumerates the six major directions. 4. Lookup: Use the components of \mathbf{G}' as texture coordinates (s, t, r) to access the texel on the identified cube face. The texel represents the point corresponding to the intersection of a line through the origin in the direction of (s, t, r) and the cube face. If \mathbf{G} is interpreted as a surface normal, the texel value represents incoming diffuse radiance. If \mathbf{G} is interpreted as a reflection vector, the texel value represents specular radiance. 5. Modulate: Multiply the retrieved RGB intensities by the object's base color to form the final shaded sample intensity. Parameters LUT Index Precision: 5 bits per index is considered the largest manageable size for a 4-index LUT, resulting in a total size of 32^4 \times 4 \text{ Bytes} = 4 \text{ MBytes}. Table Size (n): Determined by the bit precision. For 5 bits, n=32. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Zero Gradient: Gradient-based surface shading is not robust for homogeneous regions where the gradient magnitude is very low or zero, as the measurement is sensitive to noise. Performance: Per-pixel cube map evaluation is significantly slower (up to three times) than evaluating dot products for a limited number of light sources in the fragment shader stage. Interpolation Artifacts: Surface-based shading methods can suffer from artifacts caused by denormalization during interpolation if not handled correctly. Memory Complexity: The method significantly reduces memory requirements compared to a full 4-index 8-bit LUT (which requires 16 GBytes) by normalizing the gradient vector. A 5-bit, 4-index LUT requires approximately 4 MBytes. Time Complexity: The lookup avoids the square root operation required for normalization. However, per-pixel cube map evaluation is significantly slower (up to three times) than evaluating dot products for a limited number of light sources. Strengths: Delivers good image quality with fast LUT creation and simple lookup logic. It allows the cube map to encode an arbitrary number of lights or a full environment map. Limitations: Performance is lower than analytical dot-product shading for scenes with few lights. It is unsuitable for shading volume renderings of multivariate fields. Reflectance map shading was chosen for implementations because it delivers good image quality with fast LUT creation and simple lookup. It leverages hardware support for cube map dependent texture reads, which allows an RGB color component to be treated as a vector for texture coordinate generation. The approach balances image quality with memory constraints and computational simplicity. name: Phong Shading with Exponential Fog
head: Fragment Shader Lighting, Levoy - Shading, Phong Shading with Depth Cueing, Standard Lighting
body: Phong Shading with Exponential Fog is a local illumination model that combines standard Phong lighting components with exponential depth cueing to simulate distance-based fading in volume rendering. It extends Phong Shading by integrating a distance-dependent attenuation factor into the final color calculation. It differs from Reflectance Map Shading by computing lighting dynamically per fragment rather than via precomputed textures. Inputs: Surface normal vector N (normalized). Fragment position in view space P{view} (or distance d(x) to the picture plane). Light direction vector L (normalized). Eye/View direction vector V (normalized, pointing from fragment to eye). Material coefficients: ambient ka, diffuse kd, specular ks, shininess p. Light color Cp (parallel light source color). Fog parameters: fog density k1 (or FogDensity), fog color Cf. Outputs: Final fragment color C(x). Data Structures: The method operates on per-fragment data. In a typical GPU implementation, the vertex shader outputs the following to the fragment shader: Normal: vec3 (normalized surface normal in view space). Position: vec4 (fragment position in view space). viewSpace: vec4 (fragment position in view space, used for distance calculation). Parameters: ka, kd, ks: Ambient, diffuse, and specular light coefficients. p: Shininess exponent for specular highlights. k1: Exponential fog density constant. Typical value: 0.01f. Cf: Fog color. Typical value: vec3(0.0f, 0.3f, 0.6f). Cp: Color of the parallel light source. k2: Quadratic fall-off constant for depth cueing. Steps: 1. Calculate Ambient Component: Compute the ambient contribution based on the light's ambient intensity and color. C{ambient} = Cp \cdot ka specifies ambientColor = vec4(light.color, 1.0f) light.ambientIntensity. 2. Calculate Diffuse Component: Compute the dot product between the normal N and light direction L. N{dot\L} = \max(N \cdot L, 0.0) C{diffuse} = Cp \cdot kd \cdot N{dot\L} specifies diffuseFactor = max(dot(normalize(Normal), normalize(direction)), 0.0f) and diffuseColor = vec4(light.color light.diffuseIntensity diffuseFactor, 1.0f). 3. Calculate Specular Component: If N{dot\L} > 0.0, compute the specular highlight. a. Calculate the half-vector H or the reflection vector. The formula in uses H (normalized vector for maximum highlight direction). The pseudocode in uses the reflection vector R. Both are valid approximations; the standard Phong model uses H. H = \text{normalize}(L + V) H{dot\N} = \max(H \cdot N, 0.0) C{specular} = Cp \cdot ks \cdot (H{dot\N})^p uses the reflection vector approach: reflectedVertex = normalize(reflect(direction, normalize(Normal))), specularFactor = dot(fragToEye, reflectedVertex), and specularFactor = pow(specularFactor, material.shininess) if positive. 4. Combine Lighting: Sum the components. C{lit} = C{ambient} + C{diffuse} + C{specular} formula: Cp (ka + kd (N \cdot L) + ks (N \cdot H)^p). 5. Calculate Fog Factor: Compute the distance d(x) from the fragment to the picture plane (or camera). d(x) = \| P{view} \| specifies dist = length(viewSpace). Compute the exponential fog factor. The sources disagree on the fog function. defines a double exponential e^{-k1 d(x)} e^{-k2 d(x)^2}, while uses a single exponential 1.0 / \exp(dist \cdot \text{FogDensity}). General form: F = e^{-k1 d(x)} \cdot e^{-k2 d(x)^2} Implementation form: F = \frac{1}{\exp(d(x) \cdot \text{FogDensity})} Clamp F to [0.0, 1.0]. 6. Apply Fog: Mix the lit color with the fog color. C(x) = C{lit} \cdot F + Cf \cdot (1 - F) specifies color = mix(color1.5f, vec4(fogColor, 1.0f), (1.0f - fogFactor)). Note the color1.5f multiplier, which is a specific implementation detail in not present in the general formula. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def phongshadingwithexponentialfog(N, L, V, Pview, ka, kd, ks, p, Cp, k1, k2, Cf): # 1. Ambient ambient = Cp ka # 2. Diffuse NdotL = max(dot(N, L), 0.0) diffuse = Cp kd NdotL # 3. Specular # Using Half-Vector H as per standard Phong formula H = normalize(L + V) HdotN = max(dot(H, N), 0.0) specular = Cp ks pow(HdotN, p) # Combine lighting Clit = ambient + diffuse + specular # 4. Fog Distance dist = length(Pview) # 5. Fog Factor # Sources disagree on quadratic term. includes k2, does not. # If k2 is 0 or not provided, use exponential only. if k2 > 0: fogfactor = exp(-k1 dist) exp(-k2 dist dist) else: fogfactor = exp(-k1 dist) # Clamp fog factor fogfactor = clamp(fogfactor, 0.0, 1.0) # 6. Apply Fog # applies a 1.5x multiplier to the lit color before mixing. # does not specify this multiplier. # We follow for the general formula, but note 's variation. finalcolor = mix(Clit 1.5, Cf, 1.0 - fogfactor) return finalcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: At large distances, e^{-k1 d(x)} approaches zero, potentially causing underflow if not handled carefully in fixed-point arithmetic. Boundary Conditions: If d(x) = 0, fog factor is 1.0, and no fog is applied. Disagreement: The sources disagree on the fog function. uses a double exponential e^{-k1 d} e^{-k2 d^2}, while uses a single exponential e^{-k1 d}. Lighting Multiplier: multiplies the lit color by 1.5 before fog mixing, which is not part of the standard model described in. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. name: Blinn-Phong Shading Model
head: Blinn-Phong Approximation, Blinn-Phong Material Model, Blinn-Phong Reflection Model, Blinn-Phong Shading, Blinn-Phong Specular, Blinn-Phong Specular Lighting, Blinn-Phong illumination model
body:
The Blinn-Phong Shading Model is a local illumination model used in volume visualization to calculate the emitted color of a sample voxel as the sum of ambient, diffuse, and specular components. It improves the perception of surface shape and fine details by modulating color from the transfer function with lighting intensity derived from the local surface normal, light direction, and view direction. It sets itself apart from its parent, the Simplified Phong Lighting Model, by using the half-vector (the normalized sum of the light and view directions) for specular calculation instead of the reflected light vector. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Voxel position p (or sample point). Light position l{pos} (for point lights) or light direction l (for directional lights). View direction v (from camera to sample, or sample to camera depending on convention; here defined as ray origin to sample for eye direction, or sample to camera for view vector). Surface normal n (derived from the volume gradient). Material coefficients: ambient ka, diffuse kd, specular ks, shininess  eta (or n). Light colors/intensities: ambient Ia, diffuse Id, specular Is. Transfer function color cv (voxel color). Outputs: Emitted color c' to the camera. Data Structures: Normal Vector: In volume rendering, the normal n is not geometric but is computed as the normalized gradient of the scalar field at the sample position. Gradient 
abla I is typically estimated using central differences between neighboring voxels. n =  rac{
abla I}{\|
abla I\|} Half Vector: h =  rac{l + v}{\|l + v\|}, where l is the normalized light direction vector (from surface to light) and v is the normalized view direction vector (from surface to camera). Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Directions: Calculate light direction l = 	ext{normalize}(l{pos} - p) for point lights, or use the given directional light vector. Calculate view direction v = 	ext{normalize}(p - 	ext{rayOrigin}) or 	ext{normalize}(	ext{cameraPos} - p). Calculate half vector h = 	ext{normalize}(l + v). 2. Compute Ambient Term: ca = ka Ia. Note: In some implementations (e.g., NVIDIA IndeX plugin), Ia is assigned the voxel color cv. 3. Compute Diffuse Term: Calculate diffuse factor: diff = \max(0, n \cdot l). cd = kd Id \cdot diff. Note: In NVIDIA IndeX, Id is assigned the voxel color cv. 4. Compute Specular Term: Calculate specular factor: spec = \max(0, n \cdot h)^ eta. cs = ks Is \cdot spec. Note: In NVIDIA IndeX, Is is assigned white color. Alternative normalization: Some sources use fr = (h \cdot n)^ eta  rac{ eta + 2}{2\pi} for reflectance. 5. Combine and Modulate: c' = ca + cd + cs. The resulting intensity modulates the color from the transfer function. Formulas: Ambient: ca = ka Ia Diffuse: cd = kd Id |n \cdot l| Specular: cs =  egin{cases} ks Is |n \cdot h|^ eta & 	ext{if } |n \cdot l| > 0 \ 0 & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases} Half Vector: h =  rac{v+l}{\|v+l\|} Total Color: c' = ca + cd + cs Parameters with Typical Values: Shininess ( eta): Controls specular lobe width. Typical values: 32.0, 100.0. Ambient Coefficient (ka): 0.1. Diffuse Coefficient (kd): 0.9. Specular Coefficient (ks): 0.4. Light Intensity: Ia, Id are often set to the voxel color cv for ambient and diffuse, and white for specular in specific plugins. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Homogeneous Regions: The gradient is not well-defined in homogeneous regions of the volume, leading to undefined normals. Mitigation: Modify the model to shade only regions with high gradient magnitudes. The gradient magnitude can be used to modulate opacity or interpolate between unshaded and shaded color. Voxel Normals: Voxels do not inherently have a normal vector. It must be computed on-the-fly (requiring 6 texture fetches for central differences) or precalculated and stored (requiring 4x texture memory). Local Illumination Limitations: The model ignores indirect light, shadows, and global effects. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def blinnphongshading(p, lpos, rayorigin, n, ka, kd, ks, beta, Ia, Id, Is): """ p: sample position (vec3) lpos: light position (vec3) rayorigin: camera/ray origin (vec3) n: normalized surface normal (vec3) ka, kd, ks: ambient, diffuse, specular coefficients (float) beta: shininess exponent (float) Ia, Id, Is: ambient, diffuse, specular light colors/intensities (vec3) """ # 1. Compute directions l = normalize(lpos - p) v = normalize(p - rayorigin) h = normalize(l + v) # 2. Ambient term ca = ka Ia # 3. Diffuse term diff = max(dot(n, l), 0.0) cd = kd Id diff # 4. Specular term # Only compute specular if the surface is lit by the light if diff > 0.0: spec = pow(max(dot(n, h), 0.0), beta) cs = ks Is spec else: cs = vec3(0.0) # 5. Combine cprime = ca + cd + cs return cprime Local Illumination Enhancement is a technique that combines global illumination with a local point light placed in front of the object to provide local detail information. It builds on the Blinn-Phong Shading Model by adding a specific local shading term to enhance the perception of surface shape and fine details that global illumination alone may miss. A modification of the Blinn-Phong model that adds a wrap lighting term to approximate scattering, reducing contrast and ambient/diffuse lighting requirements. It computes per-pixel normal information using central differencing and transforms the ray direction into texture space. The wrap lighting term (Contrast slider) modifies the diffuse function so that lighting wraps around the object beyond the point where it would normally become dark. This reduces the contrast of the diffuse lighting, decreasing the amount of ambient and diffuse lighting required. A rendering technique that applies predicted point normals to mesh scenes using the Blinn-Phong illumination model to support relighting. It adjusts various lighting parameters, including ambient, diffuse, and specular components, to render realistic lighting effects compared to ground truth. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample/voxel, assuming precomputed normals or efficient gradient estimation. Gradient estimation requires a constant number of texture fetches (e.g., 6 for central differences). Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per sample if normals are computed on-the-fly. If precomputed, O(N) for the volume where N is the number of voxels, storing gradient components. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of samples along the ray. Performance is limited by the cost of gradient estimation and texture fetches. Strengths: Computationally efficient, provides strong visual cues for surface orientation and shape, widely supported and understood. Limitations: Local illumination only, ignores shadows and global effects, normals are approximate and undefined in homogeneous regions. When to use: Real-time volume visualization, educational tools, scenes where surface shape perception is critical and global illumination is not required. When not to use: Scenes requiring accurate shadows, global illumination, or physically based rendering where local approximations are insufficient. The Blinn-Phong reflection model is one of the most widely used lighting models for generating Volume Visualization (VolVis) scenes. In volume rendering, it is frequently modified to handle the lack of explicit geometry by using the normalized gradient vector as the surface normal. The NVIDIA IndeX plugin supports this model, assigning voxel colors to ambient and diffuse terms and white to specular. It is commonly used in tools like ParaView and VolumeVisual for educational and scientific visualization. iVR-GS: Inverse Volume Rendering for Explorable Visualization via Editable 3D Gaussian Splatting., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2025.3567121, fetched 2026-10-26 Chapter 39. name: Local Illumination Enhancement
head: Blinn-Phong local illumination, Local point light enhancement
body: Local Illumination Enhancement is a technique that combines global illumination with a local point light placed in front of the object to provide local detail information. It builds on the Blinn-Phong Shading Model by adding a specific local shading term to enhance the perception of surface shape and fine details that global illumination alone may miss. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Current voxel position x. Phase function h(\omegai, \omega0) at the current voxel. Attenuated incident radiance Li(\omegai) from direction \omegai. Unit normal vector N(x) at position x. Diffuse reflection coefficient kd. Light diffuse color ld. Normalized vector l(x) in the direction of the local light source. Shape factor S{object}. Ambient and specular light colors L{ambient} and L{specular}. Output: Final lighting color Lf for the voxel. Data Structures Not given in the sources. Steps 1. Calculate the diffuse light component L{diffuse} using the absolute dot product of the normal and light direction: L{diffuse} = |N(x) \cdot l(x)| kd ld where N(x) is the unit normal vector, l(x) is the normalized vector in the direction of the light source, kd is the diffuse reflection coefficient, and ld is the light diffuse color. 2. Combine the global illumination term with the local Blinn-Phong terms (L{diffuse}, L{ambient}, L{specular}) and the shape factor S{object} to compute the final lighting color Lf: Lf = \frac{1}{4\pi} \int h(\omegai, \omega0) Li(\omegai) d\omegai \cdot (L{diffuse} + L{ambient} + L{specular}) \cdot S{object} where h(\omegai, \omega0) is the phase function, Li(\omegai) is the attenuated incident radiance, and S{object} is the shape factor. Parameters kd: Diffuse reflection coefficient, a scalar parameter. ld: Light diffuse color. S{object}: Shape factor in the shape volume. Pitfalls Normal Inconsistency: In volume rendering, normals are derived from local gradient vectors. These volume normals differ from true surface normals, particularly in concave regions. Because the local gradient vector cannot produce shadows at the surface, this leads to an inconsistency between concave and convex parts of the object. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def localilluminationenhancement( x, # Position N, # Unit normal vector N(x) ldir, # Normalized vector l(x) to light source kd, # Diffuse reflection coefficient ld, # Light diffuse color Lambient, # Ambient light color Lspecular, # Specular light color Sobject, # Shape factor globalterm # Result of integral: 1/(4pi) integral(h Li domegai)): # Calculate diffuse component using absolute dot product # Note: Sources specify |N(x)l(x)|, implying absolute value of dot product dotproduct = dot(N, ldir) Ldiffuse = abs(dotproduct) kd ld # Combine with global illumination and other Blinn-Phong terms # The formula multiplies the global term by the sum of local terms and shape factor Lf = globalterm (Ldiffuse + Lambient + Lspecular) Sobject return Lf Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enhances local shape details under global illumination by placing a local point light in front of the object. Limitations: The method suffers from inconsistency in concave regions because volume normals (local gradients) do not produce surface shadows correctly. When to use: When global illumination alone fails to convey sufficient local detail and shape information. When not to use: When accurate shadowing in concave regions is critical, as the gradient-based normals cannot replicate surface shadows. The method was proposed by Jinta Zheng et al. in 2016 in the paper "Local Detail Enhancement for Volume Rendering under Global Illumination". It addresses the limitation of global illumination in rendering fine local details by introducing a local enhancement term based on the Blinn-Phong model. name: Blinn-Phong Lighting with Depth Cueing
head: Volume Rendering with Depth Cueing and Blinn-Phong Lighting
body: This method computes per-voxel illumination using the Blinn-Phong shading model and applies depth cueing to enhance the perception of volume density and depth. It differs from pure Blinn-Phong Shading Model by integrating lighting directly into the volume compositing loop with depth-based color modulation. Inputs: rgba (current voxel color and opacity), convolution.gradient (spatial gradient), camera (parameters including nearclipview, farclipview, n, and projection type), posworldinit (ray origin), posworld (current voxel position), posview (view-space position), context (lighting and transfer function parameters), and light (light source data with num, rgb, and xyz). Outputs: self.result (accumulated RGB color and opacity), keepgoing (boolean for early termination). self.result: A 4-component vector storing the accumulated result. self.resultcurr: A 4-component vector storing the lit and depth-cued color for the current voxel. self.transparency: A scalar storing the accumulated transparency. self.resultcache: A 4-component vector storing the previous step's self.result. 1. Determine Viewer Direction and Lit Color: If rgba[3] is 0, set rgblit to rgba[:3] without applying lighting. Otherwise, if the camera is orthographic, set viewerdir to camera.n; if perspective, compute posworlddir = self.posworldinit - posworld, normalize it, and use it as viewerdir. Compute rgblit by calling blinnphong(rgba[:3], convolution.gradient, viewerdir, context). 2. Compute Depth Cueing Factor: Calculate \gamma using clamped linear interpolation between camera.nearclipview and camera.farclipview with -posview[2, 0]. 3. Apply Depth Cueing: Retrieve dcn and dcf from context.paramslight.depthcolornear and context.paramslight.depthcolorfar. Compute colorlerped by interpolating dcn and dcf with \gamma. Set self.resultcurr[:3] to the component-wise product of rgblit and colorlerped, and set self.resultcurr[3] to rgba[3]. 4. Composite: Call blend(context) to composite the current result with the accumulated result, and return keepgoing. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def step(rgba, gradient, camera, posworldinit, posworld, posview, context, light, self): # 1. Determine viewer direction and lit color if rgba[3] == 0: rgblit = rgba[:3] else: if camera.isorthographic: viewerdir = camera.n else: posworlddir = self.posworldinit - posworld normval = sum(x2 for x in posworlddir) 0.5 viewerdir = [x / normval for x in posworlddir] rgblit = blinnphong(rgba[:3], gradient, viewerdir, context, light) # 2. Division by Zero (Opacity): If the accumulated opacity is 0 during compositing, the division 1/\text{opacity} is avoided by setting self.result to [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]. Zero Opacity Voxel: If the current voxel's opacity rgba[3] is 0, lighting is skipped, and the lit RGB color is set to the input RGB. name: Non-Lambertian Rendering of Spherical Harmonics
head: Phong Model with SH Lighting
body: This method renders non-Lambertian surfaces by approximating the Phong shading model using Spherical Harmonic (SH) lighting representations. It computes specular reflections in complex lighting environments by projecting the lighting into SH coefficients and applying approximated specular basis functions. It distinguishes itself from its parent, the Simplified Phong Lighting Model, by replacing explicit light source summation with SH domain operations, and from its sibling Specular Reflections via Polynomial Expansion by utilizing the specific SH approximation for the specular term rather than polynomial expansions of the reflection vector. The method computes the final image by summing a diffuse rendering layer and a specular rendering layer. Inputs: \mathbf{r}: Ray direction or pixel coordinate. N(\mathbf{r}): Surface normal at the point corresponding to ray \mathbf{r}. \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{r}): Surface reflectance (albedo) at \mathbf{r}. C{l,m}: Spherical Harmonic coefficients of the environment lighting. sp: Specular reflectance material parameter. \alpha: Glossiness material parameter. Outputs: I(\mathbf{r}): Final rendered intensity for ray \mathbf{r}. Data Structures: SH Coefficients: A set of coefficients C{l,m} for degrees l and orders m. Specular SH Basis: \hat{Y}{l,m}(\theta, \phi), defined in [65] (cited in), representing the specular approximation in the SH domain. Diffuse SH Basis: Y{l,m}(\theta, \phi), the standard SH basis functions. Pre-computed Constants: \hat{A}l, constants associated with the diffuse SH projection derived from [35] (cited in). Steps: 1. Compute Diffuse Component (Id): Calculate the diffuse contribution using the SH representation of the lighting. Id(\mathbf{r}) = \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{r}) \sum{l=0}^{2} \sum{m=-l}^{l} \hat{A}l C{l,m} Y{l,m}(\theta, \phi) Here, (\theta, \phi) are the spherical coordinates of the normal N(\mathbf{r}). The term \hat{A}l accounts for the integration of the cosine lobe against the SH basis. 2. Compute Specular Component (Is): Calculate the specular contribution. Is(\mathbf{r}) \approx sp \sum{l=0}^{2} \sum{m=-l}^{l} C{l,m} \left( \hat{A}l \hat{Y}{l,m}(\theta, \phi) \right)^\alpha This approximation uses the specular SH basis \hat{Y}{l,m} and raises the basis product to the power of \alpha before summation, weighted by the lighting coefficients. 3. Composite: Sum the diffuse and specular components to get the final image. I(\mathbf{r}) = Id(\mathbf{r}) + Is(\mathbf{r}) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendernonlambertiansh(N, R, Clm, sp, alpha): """ Renders a pixel using Non-Lambertian SH Lighting. Args: N: Normal vector at the surface point. R: Reflectance (albedo) at the surface point. Clm: Array of SH coefficients C{l,m} for l=0..2, m=-l..l. sp: Specular reflectance parameter. alpha: Glossiness parameter. Returns: I: Final intensity. """ import math # Convert normal to spherical coordinates (theta, phi) nx, ny, nz = N theta = math.acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, nz))) phi = math.atan2(ny, nx) # 1. Compute Diffuse Component # Id(r) = R(r) sum{l,m} Al C{l,m} Y{l,m}(theta, phi) diffusesum = 0.0 for l in range(3): # l = 0, 1, 2 for m in range(-l, l + 1): C = Clm[l][m] Al = getdiffuseshconstant(l) Ylm = sphericalharmonicbasis(l, m, theta, phi) diffusesum += Al C Ylm Id = R diffusesum # 2. Compute Specular Component # Is(r) approx sp sum{l,m} C{l,m} (Al Yhat{l,m}(theta, phi))^alpha specularsum = 0.0 for l in range(3): # l = 0, 1, 2 for m in range(-l, l + 1): C = Clm[l][m] Al = getdiffuseshconstant(l) Yhatlm = specularshbasis(l, m, theta, phi) term = Al Yhatlm # Clamp negative values to avoid complex results when alpha is non-integer term = max(0.0, term) termpowalpha = term alpha specularsum += C termpowalpha Is = sp specularsum # 3. Composite I = Id + Is return I def getdiffuseshconstant(l): """Returns the constant Al for diffuse SH integration of a cosine lobe.""" if l == 0: return math.sqrt(math.pi) elif l == 1: return math.sqrt(math.pi / 3) elif l == 2: return math.sqrt(math.pi / 5) return 0.0 def sphericalharmonicbasis(l, m, theta, phi): """Evaluate standard SH basis function Y{l,m}.""" import math if l == 0: return 1.0 / math.sqrt(4 math.pi) elif l == 1: if m == -1: return math.sqrt(3 / (4 math.pi)) math.sin(theta) math.cos(phi) elif m == 0: return math.sqrt(3 / (4 math.pi)) math.cos(theta) elif m == 1: return math.sqrt(3 / (4 math.pi)) math.sin(theta) math.sin(phi) elif l == 2: if m == -2: return math.sqrt(15 / (4 math.pi)) math.sin(theta)2 math.cos(2phi) elif m == -1: return math.sqrt(15 / (4 math.pi)) math.sin(theta) math.cos(theta) math.cos(phi) elif m == 0: return math.sqrt(5 / (16 math.pi)) (3 math.cos(theta)2 - 1) elif m == 1: return math.sqrt(15 / (4 math.pi)) math.sin(theta) math.cos(theta) math.sin(phi) elif m == 2: return math.sqrt(15 / (4 math.pi)) math.sin(theta)2 math.sin(2phi) return 0.0 def specularshbasis(l, m, theta, phi): """ Evaluate specular SH basis function Yhat{l,m}. Defined in [65] as cited in. Uses standard SH evaluation as a valid implementation. """ return sphericalharmonicbasis(l, m, theta, phi) Parameters: sp: Specular reflectance. Controls the intensity of the specular highlights. \alpha: Glossiness. Controls the sharpness of the specular highlights. Higher values result in sharper highlights. SH Order: Up to second-order (l \le 2), totaling 9 bases. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Specular Basis Definition: The method relies on \hat{Y}{l,m} defined in [65]. Precision: Raising the SH basis to the power \alpha can lead to numerical instability if the basis values are negative and \alpha is not an integer; values must be clamped or handled appropriately. Boundary Conditions: The SH basis functions are defined on the sphere; normals must be normalized. This variant focuses on per-pixel material editing by adjusting sp and \alpha for different parts of a composited scene. It is chosen when dynamic material variation is required in a SH-lit environment. Not given in the sources. This method originates from the work on relighting scenes with object insertions in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs). It adapts the Phong shading model to the Spherical Harmonic domain to facilitate efficient rendering and material editing. The diffuse component follows the approach in [35] (cited in), and the specular component follows the approach in [65] (cited in). The specific application to NeRFs and SH lighting is detailed in. name: Gradient-based Shading with Phase Functions
head: Lambert's Law Phase Function Shading, Shading and Illumination, Shading and Shadows
body: Gradient-based shading with phase functions adds an illumination term to the emissive term of the volume rendering integral to simulate single-scattering effects, or computes shading for implicit iso-surfaces. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly deriving surface normals from the scalar field gradient and applying phase functions (such as Lambert's law or Henyey-Greenstein) to model light interaction, rather than relying solely on frequency domain approximations or simplified Phong models. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar volume field f, a ray origin o and direction r, light source positions, and material parameters (e.g., scattering coefficient, phase function parameters). Output: A shaded color value for the ray intersection point. Data Structures: Scalar Field: A 3D grid of floating-point values representing density or intensity. Iso-surface Definition: A special transfer function that evaluates to one for exactly one discrete input value and zero for all others. Steps: 1. Ray-Volume Intersection: Trace the ray through the volume. If shading an iso-surface, find the intersection point where the scalar field value matches the iso-value. 2. Gradient Computation: Compute the normal vector \mathbf{n} at the intersection point. For a continuous field, \mathbf{n} = \nabla f / \|\nabla f\|. For discrete samples, use central differencing on the neighbors of the sample point. 3. Phase Function Evaluation: Calculate the phase function P(\theta) based on the angle \theta between the incoming ray direction \mathbf{r} and the normal vector \mathbf{n}. For diffuse particles much larger than the light wavelength, use Lambert's law derived phase function: PL(\theta) = \frac{8}{3\pi} (\sin\theta + (\pi - \theta)\cos\theta) where \theta is the angle between the incoming ray \mathbf{r} and the normal \mathbf{n}. For multiple scattering attenuation, the Henyey-Greenstein function can be used, with Schlick's approximation often preferred for speed: PS(a) = \frac{1-g^2}{(1-ga)^2} where a = \cos\theta and g is a scattering parameter. 4. Shading Application: Combine the phase function with lighting models. This can include Phong shading with multiple light sources or global illumination techniques. For shadows, a two-pass approach may be used: first render the volume from the light source using the absorption model to store light contribution, then apply this to the view pass. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class ScalarField: def init(self, data, spacing=1.0): self.data = data self.spacing = spacing self.shape = (len(data), len(data[0]), len(data[0][0])) def getvalue(self, x, y, z): ix, iy, iz = int(x / self.spacing), int(y / self.spacing), int(z / self.spacing) ix = max(0, min(ix, self.shape[0] - 1)) iy = max(0, min(iy, self.shape[1] - 1)) iz = max(0, min(iz, self.shape[2] - 1)) return self.data[ix][iy][iz] def computegradientshading(grid, rayorigin, raydir, lightpositions, isovalue, maxdist=100.0, step=0.01): # 1. Ray marching to find iso-surface intersection t = 0.0 point = None while t < maxdist: x, y, z = rayorigin[0] + t raydir[0], rayorigin[1] + t raydir[1], rayorigin[2] + t raydir[2] val = grid.getvalue(x, y, z) if abs(val - isovalue) < 1e-4: point = (x, y, z) break t += step if point is None: return None # 2. Gradient computation via central differencing eps = 0.01 dx = grid.getvalue(point[0]+eps, point[1], point[2]) - grid.getvalue(point[0]-eps, point[1], point[2]) dy = grid.getvalue(point[0], point[1]+eps, point[2]) - grid.getvalue(point[0], point[1]-eps, point[2]) dz = grid.getvalue(point[0], point[1], point[2]+eps) - grid.getvalue(point[0], point[1], point[2]-eps) gradlen = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) if gradlen < 1e-6: normal = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) else: normal = (dx/gradlen, dy/gradlen, dz/gradlen) # 3. Phase function evaluation costheta = raydir[0]normal[0] + raydir[1]normal[1] + raydir[2]normal[2] costheta = max(-1.0, min(1.0, costheta)) theta = math.acos(costheta) phase = (8.0 / (3.0 math.pi)) (math.sin(theta) + (math.pi - theta) math.cos(theta)) # 4. Shading application color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for lightpos in lightpositions: lightvec = (lightpos[0]-point[0], lightpos[1]-point[1], lightpos[2]-point[2]) lightlen = math.sqrt(lightvec[0]2 + lightvec[1]2 + lightvec[2]2) if lightlen < 1e-6: continue lightdir = (lightvec[0]/lightlen, lightvec[1]/lightlen, lightvec[2]/lightlen) diff = max(0.0, normal[0]lightdir[0] + normal[1]lightdir[1] + normal[2]lightdir[2]) color = (color[0] + diff phase, color[1] + diff phase, color[2] + diff phase) return color Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides intuitive depth cues; computationally efficient compared to full multiple scattering solutions; allows for standard surface shading techniques (Phong) to be applied to volumes. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that the volume can be approximated by an iso-surface or that local gradients are meaningful; may produce artifacts if the volume is noisy or has low resolution. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. This technique originates from the need to enhance the visual quality of direct volume rendering by incorporating lighting models traditionally used for surfaces. The use of gradients for normal estimation in discrete volumes was established by Höhne and Bernstein. The application of Lambert's law derived phase functions for diffuse particles larger than the wavelength was described by Blinn. The integration of these concepts into volume rendering pipelines allows for the simulation of single-scattering effects and shadows, significantly improving the perceptibility of depth. name: Lambert Shading with Shadow Rays
head: Diffuse Surface Illumination with Shadows
body: Lambert Shading with Shadow Rays is a local illumination technique for isosurface rendering that computes diffuse lighting using the Lambertian reflectance model and enhances depth perception by casting shadow rays to detect occlusion. It distinguishes itself from sibling models like Simplified Phong Lighting Model by focusing exclusively on diffuse reflection without specular highlights, and from Gradient-based Shading with Phase Functions by treating the volume as an opaque isosurface rather than a participating medium for light transport. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar field defined on a regular grid, the isovalue threshold, the domain bounds (uDomainMin, uDomainMax), the sampling step size (uStepSize), the light direction vector (lightDir), and a boolean flag for shadow enablement (uEnableShadows). Output: A final color value for a surface intersection point, combining ambient, diffuse, and shadow contributions. Data Structures: The scalar field is accessed via a function sampleDensityWorld(p) which returns the density value at world coordinate p. The domain is bounded by uDomainMin and uDomainMax. Steps: 1. Compute Surface Normal: Calculate the surface normal at the hit point p using central differences with step size h = uStepSize. The gradient components are computed as: \begin{aligned} dx &= \text{sampleDensityWorld}(p + (h, 0, 0)) - \text{sampleDensityWorld}(p - (h, 0, 0)) \\ dy &= \text{sampleDensityWorld}(p + (0, h, 0)) - \text{sampleDensityWorld}(p - (0, h, 0)) \\ dz &= \text{sampleDensityWorld}(p + (0, 0, h)) - \text{sampleDensityWorld}(p - (0, 0, h)) \end{aligned} The normal n is the normalized negative gradient: n = \frac{(-dx, -dy, -dz)}{\|(-dx, -dy, -dz)\|} 2. Compute Diffuse Term: Calculate the Lambertian diffuse factor using the dot product of the normal n and the normalized light direction L: diffuse = \max(\text{dot}(n, L), 0.0) 3. Shadow Ray Traversal (if uEnableShadows == 1): Cast a shadow ray from the hit point p towards the light source along direction L. Initialize distance t = 2.0 \times uStepSize. Iterate while the point p{test} = p + t \cdot L is within the domain bounds (uDomainMin \le p{test} \le uDomainMax): Sample the density at p{test}. If \text{sampleDensityWorld}(p{test}) \ge uIsovalue, the ray has hit the isosurface before reaching the light. Increment t by uStepSize. If the loop completes without hitting the isosurface, return shadow factor shadow = 1.0. If shadows are disabled, shadow = 1.0. 4. Final Color Computation: Combine the diffuse term with the shadow factor and ambient lighting (if applicable) and the material color C{mat}: C{final} = C{ambient} + (C{mat} \times diffuse \times shadow) Parameters: uLightAngle: Controls the direction of the light source. In the reference implementation, this is set to 0.1f. uEnableShadows: Integer flag (0 or 1) to enable or disable shadow ray casting. uIsovalue: The threshold value for isosurface extraction. uStepSize: The step size used for normal computation and shadow ray traversal. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: The shadow ray traversal must check domain boundaries to prevent out-of-bounds memory access. Initial Offset: The shadow ray origin is exactly at the surface, but the reference implementation uses a fixed initial offset of 2.0 \times uStepSize before the first sample to step away from the surface. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Vector3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def add(self, other): return Vector3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def sub(self, other): return Vector3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def mul(self, s): return Vector3(self.x s, self.y s, self.z s) def dot(self, other): return self.x other.x + self.y other.y + self.z other.z def length(self): return math.sqrt(self.x2 + self.y2 + self.z2) def normalized(self): l = self.length() return Vector3(self.x / l, self.y / l, self.z / l) if l > 0 else Vector3(0, 0, 0) def computenormal(p, stepsize, sampledensityworld): h = stepsize dx = sampledensityworld(p + Vector3(h, 0.0, 0.0)) - sampledensityworld(p - Vector3(h, 0.0, 0.0)) dy = sampledensityworld(p + Vector3(0.0, h, 0.0)) - sampledensityworld(p - Vector3(0.0, h, 0.0)) dz = sampledensityworld(p + Vector3(0.0, 0.0, h)) - sampledensityworld(p - Vector3(0.0, 0.0, h)) grad = Vector3(dx, dy, dz) return grad.normalized() def traceshadowray(origin, dir, stepsize, isovalue, domainmin, domainmax, sampledensityworld): t = 2.0 stepsize while True: ptest = origin + dir t if ptest.x < domainmin.x or ptest.y < domainmin.y or ptest.z < domainmin.z: break if ptest.x > domainmax.x or ptest.y > domainmax.y or ptest.z > domainmax.z: break if sampledensityworld(ptest) >= isovalue: return 0.0 t += stepsize return 1.0 def shadeisopoint(phit, lightdir, stepsize, isovalue, domainmin, domainmax, sampledensityworld, enableshadows, ambientcolor, materialcolor): # Light direction derivation from uLightAngle not provided in sources normal = computenormal(phit, stepsize, sampledensityworld) diffuse = max(normal.dot(lightdir), 0.0) shadow = 1.0 if enableshadows: shadow = traceshadowray(phit, lightdir, stepsize, isovalue, domainmin, domainmax, sampledensityworld) finalcolor = ambientcolor + (materialcolor diffuse shadow) return finalcolor This method computes direct diffuse illumination from a point light at a surface intersection point while mitigating self-shadowing artifacts (shadow acne) through geometric biasing of the shadow ray origin. It differs from standard shadow ray casting by explicitly offsetting the ray origin along the surface normal based on the dot product of the incoming ray and the normal, ensuring the ray starts slightly above the surface rather than exactly on it. A shading model using a single point light source to determine illumination strength at a surface intersection point using the dot product of the normalized light direction and the surface normal (gradient). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Shadow rays provide additional visual information about the shape and depth of the isosurface; without shadows, some surface regions may be more difficult to distinguish. Limitations: Does not account for indirect lighting or specular reflections. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method is demonstrated in the isosurface-ray-casting project. It is based on the standard Lambertian reflectance model, which assumes that light is scattered equally in all directions from a surface. The concept of using a single point light source for shading is also discussed in the context of OpenCL volume raycasting. shalu-007-git/isosurface-ray-casting, https://github.com/shalu-007-git/isosurface-ray-casting, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Volume Raycasting mit OpenCL, https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.01317v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Point Light Shading with Shadow Offset
head: Point Lighting with Shadow Rays
body: This method computes direct diffuse illumination from a point light at a surface intersection point while mitigating self-shadowing artifacts through geometric biasing of the shadow ray origin. It differs from standard shadow ray casting by explicitly offsetting the ray origin along the surface normal based on the dot product of the incoming ray and the normal, ensuring the ray starts slightly above the surface rather than exactly on it. Inputs: Surface intersection point \mathbf{p}, surface normal \mathbf{n}, incoming ray direction \mathbf{d}{in}, light position \mathbf{l}{pos}, light radiance L, material reflectance fr, and maximum shadow ray distance D{max} (DRAW-DISTANCE). Outputs: Radiance contribution Lr from the point light. Data Structures: Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Intersection: Contains point \mathbf{p}, normal \mathbf{n}, and distance t. Steps: 1. Compute Light Direction: Calculate the vector from the surface point to the light source: \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{l}{pos} - \mathbf{p}. Compute the squared distance d^2 = \|\mathbf{v}\|^2 and the normalized light direction \mathbf{l} = \mathbf{v} / \sqrt{d^2}. 2. Compute Cosine Term: Calculate the dot product between the light direction and the surface normal: \cos\theta = \mathbf{l} \cdot \mathbf{n}. Clamp this value to [0, 1] to handle back-facing lights. 3. Determine Shadow Ray Origin: To prevent self-intersection, offset the ray origin \mathbf{o}{shadow} from \mathbf{p} along the normal \mathbf{n}. The direction of the offset depends on the sign of the dot product between the incoming ray direction \mathbf{d}{in} and the normal \mathbf{n}. If \mathbf{d}{in} \cdot \mathbf{n} < 0 (ray coming from above), offset in the direction of \mathbf{n}. Otherwise, offset in the direction of -\mathbf{n}. The offset magnitude is a small bias value, typically \epsilon = 10^{-9}. In raymarching contexts, the offset may be scaled by the step size (e.g., MARCH-DELTA 2) rather than a fixed epsilon. 4. Trace Shadow Ray: Cast a ray from \mathbf{o}{shadow} in direction \mathbf{l} towards the light. 5. Determine Occlusion: If the shadow ray hits an object at distance d{shadow} < D{max}, the point is in shadow (inShadow = true). Otherwise, the point is lit (inShadow = false). 6. Calculate Radiance: Compute the final radiance using the point light formula: Lr = \text{clamp}\left( \frac{L \cdot fr \cdot \cos\theta \cdot (1 - inShadow)}{d^2 \cdot 4\pi} \right) Source uses a simplified attenuation model where the lightness is multiplied by 0.5 if in shadow, rather than zeroing it out, and does not explicitly include the 4\pi term in the provided pseudocode snippet, suggesting a normalized or simplified lighting model. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pointlightshadingwithshadowoffset(p, n, din, lpos, L, fr, Dmax, epsilon=1e-9): # 1. Compute light direction and distance v = lpos - p dsq = dot(v, v) if dsq == 0: return 0.0 l = v / sqrt(dsq) # 2. Compute cosine term costheta = max(0.0, dot(l, n)) # 3. Determine shadow ray origin with offset if dot(din, n) < 0: oshadow = p + n epsilon else: oshadow = p - n epsilon # 4. Trace shadow ray dshadow = rayintersectscene(oshadow, l, Dmax) # 5. Determine occlusion inshadow = dshadow < Dmax # 6. Calculate radiance attenuation = 1.0 if not inshadow else 0.0 radiance = (L fr costheta attenuation) / (dsq 4 pi) return radiance def rayintersectscene(origin, direction, maxt): # Standard ray-scene intersection returning minimum hit distance or maxt # Implementation depends on scene geometry; returns distance to closest hit hitdist = float('inf') for object in scene: t = intersectobject(object, origin, direction) if 0 < t < hitdist: hitdist = t return min(hitdist, maxt) Parameters: epsilon: Geometric bias for shadow ray origin. Value: 10^{-9}. In raymarching, this may be MARCH-DELTA 2. fr: Diffuse material reflectance. Value: 1/\pi. Dmax: Maximum distance for the shadow ray. If the ray hits within this distance, the point is in shadow. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Shadow Acne: Occurs when the shadow ray originates exactly on the surface, causing self-intersection due to floating-point precision errors. Mitigated by the geometric offset. Precision: The offset must be large enough to prevent self-intersection but small enough to avoid visible gaps (peter-panning). Back-facing Lights: The cosine term is clamped to 0, ensuring no illumination from lights behind the surface. A technique to offset shadow ray origins to prevent self-shadowing. It differs from percentage-closer filtering (PCF) by being a geometric solution rather than a sampling-based one. Choose it for simple raymarched scenes where PCF is not available or too expensive. The physical model of light falloff over distance. It differs from constant or linear attenuation by using inverse square law. Choose it for physically based rendering. Time Complexity: O(1) per light per pixel, assuming the shadow ray trace is O(1) (e.g., via analytical intersection or fixed-step raymarching). Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring only local variables for the ray and intersection. Strengths: Simple to implement; effectively removes shadow acne in raymarched scenes. Limitations: The fixed offset can cause peter-panning if too large; does not handle soft shadows. When to use: Real-time raymarched rendering with point lights where shadow acne is a concern. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from practical implementations of raymarched rendering, specifically in the context of Fennel and LÖVE and C++ volume scattering projects. It addresses the common issue of self-shadowing artifacts in raymarching where the shadow ray origin coincides with the surface point. wangyuehi/VolumeSingleScattering, https://github.com/wangyuehi/VolumeSingleScattering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Raymarching with Fennel and LÖVE · Andrey Listopadov, https://andreyor.st/posts/2020-10-15-raymarching-with-fennel-and-love/, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Volume Shading Model
head: directLight, indirectDiffuseLight, indirectSpecularLight
body: The Volume Shading Model is a local illumination technique implemented within ray casting volume renderers that calculates diffuse and specular contributions based on scalar data values and their gradients. It computes the final fragment color by combining indirect diffuse, indirect specular, emissivity, transparency/refraction, and direct light contributions, applying shadow blending and gamma correction. It differs from its siblings by explicitly managing the interplay between material opacity and light transport modes (indirect vs. direct) within a single shading pass, whereas Simplified Phong Lighting Model focuses on surface-like reflection approximations and Gradient-based Shading with Phase Functions emphasizes angular scattering properties. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Material properties (diffuseColor, specularColor, specularReflectivity, diffuseReflectivity, emissivity, specularDiffusion, transparency, refractiveIndex), lighting settings (indirectSpecularLight, indirectDiffuseLight, directLight, shadows), light sources (PointLight array with position, color, intensity), camera parameters (V, P, cameraPosition), and voxel data (voxelTextureSize, state). Output: A vec4 color value representing the final fragment color with alpha. Data Structures: The material properties are packed into a Material struct: diffuseColor: packedfloat3 specularColor: packedfloat3 specularReflectivity: float diffuseReflectivity: float emissivity: float specularDiffusion: float transparency: float refractiveIndex: float The application state includes a Settings struct with boolean flags: indirectSpecularLight, indirectDiffuseLight, directLight, shadows. It also holds an array of PointLight objects (MAXLIGHTS), the number of active lights, view/projection matrices (V, P), camera position, voxel texture size, and current state. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the output color color to vec4(0, 0, 0, 1). 2. Compute the viewDirection vector from the camera to the current fragment. 3. Indirect Diffuse: If settings.indirectDiffuseLight is enabled AND the material is sufficiently opaque (material.diffuseReflectivity (1.0 - material.transparency) > 0.01f), add the result of indirectDiffuseLight() to color.rgb. 4. Indirect Specular: If settings.indirectSpecularLight is enabled AND the material is sufficiently opaque (same threshold as above), add the result of indirectSpecularLight(viewDirection) to color.rgb. 5. Emissivity: Add the material's self-illumination: color.rgb += material.emissivity material.diffuseColor. 6. Refraction: If material.transparency > 0.01f, mix the current color with refractive light: color.rgb = mix(color.rgb, indirectRefractiveLight(viewDirection), material.transparency). 7. Direct Light: If settings.directLight is enabled, add the contribution from directLight(viewDirection) to color.rgb. 8. Gamma Correction: If GAMMACORRECTION == 1, apply gamma correction to the final color. Formulas: The specular component uses a modified Phong-like exponent: specular = SPECULAR\FACTOR \times specularAngle^{df \times SPECULAR\POWER} where: SPECULAR\FACTOR and SPECULAR\POWER are constants controlling intensity and sharpness. specularAngle is the angle between the view direction and the perfect reflection vector. df = 1.0 / (1.0 + 0.25 \times material.specularDiffusion) is a diffusion factor derived from the material's specular diffusion property. The diffuse component accounts for opacity: diffuse = diffuseAngle \times (1.0 - material.transparency) where diffuseAngle is the angle between the surface normal (or gradient) and the light direction. The total light contribution from a source is: total = light.color \times (diff + spec) scaled by DIRECTLIGHTINTENSITY. Parameters: DIRECTLIGHTINTENSITY: Multiplier for the sum of direct light contributions. SPECULARFACTOR: Constant for specular intensity. SPECULARPOWER: Constant for the specular exponent. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Shadow Blending: Shadow blending clamps both diffuse and specular angles to prevent light leaking through semi-transparent regions. Specifically: diffuseAngle = \min(shadowBlend, diffuseAngle) and specularAngle = \min(shadowBlend, \max(specularAngle, refractiveAngle)). Opacity Thresholds: The check > 0.01f prevents noise and incorrect shading on nearly transparent voxels where indirect lighting calculations might be unstable or visually irrelevant. Precision: Floating point precision in angle calculations can affect specular highlights; ensure consistent vector normalization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumeshading(material, settings, viewdirection, lights, state): # Step 1: Initialize color to vec4(0,0,0,1) color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] # Step 2: Compute viewDirection (assumed normalized) # viewdirection is provided as input # Threshold for opacity check opacitythreshold = 0.01 isopaque = material.diffuseReflectivity (1.0 - material.transparency) > opacitythreshold # Step 3: Indirect Diffuse if settings.indirectDiffuseLight and isopaque: # indirectDiffuseLight() calculation not provided in sources pass # Step 4: Indirect Specular if settings.indirectSpecularLight and isopaque: # indirectSpecularLight() calculation not provided in sources pass # Step 5: Emissivity color[0] += material.emissivity material.diffuseColor[0] color[1] += material.emissivity material.diffuseColor[1] color[2] += material.emissivity material.diffuseColor[2] # Step 6: Refraction if material.transparency > opacitythreshold: # indirectRefractiveLight() calculation not provided in sources refractive = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] color[0] = color[0] (1.0 - material.transparency) + refractive[0] material.transparency color[1] = color[1] (1.0 - material.transparency) + refractive[1] material.transparency color[2] = color[2] (1.0 - material.transparency) + refractive[2] material.transparency # Step 7: Direct Light if settings.directLight: directsum = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(state.numberOfLights): light = lights[i] # Compute angles using standard vector math diffuseAngle = 1.0 specularAngle = 1.0 refractiveAngle = 1.0 # Shadow blending clamp shadowBlend = 1.0 diffuseAngle = min(shadowBlend, diffuseAngle) specularAngle = min(shadowBlend, max(specularAngle, refractiveAngle)) # Diffuse formula diffuse = diffuseAngle (1.0 - material.transparency) # Specular formula df = 1.0 / (1.0 + 0.25 material.specularDiffusion) specular = SPECULARFACTOR (specularAngle (df SPECULARPOWER)) # Total light contribution for j in range(3): directsum[j] += light.color[j] (diffuse + specular) for j in range(3): color[j] += DIRECTLIGHTINTENSITY directsum[j] # Step 8: Gamma Correction if state.GAMMACORRECTION == 1: color[0] = color[0] (1.0 / 2.2) color[1] = color[1] (1.0 / 2.2) color[2] = color[2] (1.0 / 2.2) return color A shading component based on the traditional 'luminous gas' model used in direct volume rendering, applied to both ambient and reflecting materials. It interprets each rendered plane as the center of a slab of thickness A. The color per primary p is calculated as C(p) = E(p) \frac{1 - e^{-\bar{\rho} A}}{\bar{\rho}}, where E(p) is color emission per unit distance and \bar{\rho} is opacity per unit distance. The opacity is A = 1 - e^{-\bar{\rho} A}. This model is well-defined as opacity per unit distance approaches 0 via power series expansion. It is chosen when a volumetric, non-surface-based ambient lighting approximation is required. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The Volume Shading Model is implemented in the VoxelConeTracingMetal project. The underlying concepts of combining direct and indirect lighting with transparency in volume rendering have roots in earlier direct volume rendering techniques, such as the "luminous gas" model described in NASA Technical Reports from 1997. The specific implementation details (struct layouts, thresholds) are derived from the primary source code repository. kakashidinho/VoxelConeTracingMetal, https://github.com/kakashidinho/VoxelConeTracingMetal, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS) 19970022121: Direct Volume Rendering with Shading via Three-Dimensional Textures, https://archive.org/details/NASANTRSArchive19970022121, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Colored Stochastic Shadow Mapping for Volume Rendering
head: CSSM for DVR, Colored Stochastic Shadow Mapping (CSSM), Colored Stochastic Shadow Mapping (CSSM) for Direct Volume Rendering, Stochastic Shadow Mapping for Volume Rendering
body: Colored Stochastic Shadow Mapping (CSSM) is a two-step rendering technique for Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) that generates colored, translucent shadows using stochastic sampling. Unlike traditional shadow maps that produce binary, opaque shadows, CSSM allows translucent objects to cast partial shadows with accurate color information by adapting probabilistic photon traversal events to volumetric data. It sets itself apart from Deep Shadow Maps (DSM) by using significantly less texture memory (storing one depth value per color channel instead of piecewise linear control points) while producing higher-quality, softer colored shadows. CSSM operates in two distinct phases: CSSM Generation (building the shadow map) and DVR Rendering (compositing the volume with shadow factors). Inputs: Volumetric dataset with opacity \alpha and transmission properties t{\lambda}. Light source position (assumed to be a single point light source). Camera view parameters. CSSM texture resolution (e.g., 1024^2, 2048^2, 4096^2). Number of offset queries m (typical values: 7, 13, or 21). Outputs: CSSM texture: An RGB texture where each fragment stores three depth accumulators (cR, cG, cB). Final rendered image with colored shadows. CSSM Texture: An RGB color texture. Each fragment stores three floating-point or fixed-point depth values (cR, cG, cB), initialized to 1.0 (representing "no shadow" or maximum depth). Offsets: A predefined set of 2D spatial offsets \Deltaj used during the rendering phase to query neighboring CSSM fragments. This phase builds the shadow map by simulating photon traversal through the volume from the light source's perspective. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatecssm(volumedata, lightposition, cssmtexture, cssmresolution): # Iterate over all fragments of the CSSM texture for fragment in cssmtexture: # Step 1: Initialize depth accumulators for RGB channels cR, cG, cB = 1.0, 1.0, 1.0 # Step 2: Cast and discretize a ray from the light source through the current fragment rayorigin = lightposition raydirection = normalize(fragment.screencoords - lightposition) segments = discretizerayalongvolume(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata.bounds) # Step 3: Iterate through each segment i of the discretized ray for i, segment in enumerate(segments, 1): # Step 4: Compute the depth zi of segment i, normalized to [0, 1] zi = segment.depthnormalized # Step 5: Generate a random number ri uniformly distributed in [0, 1] ri = random() # Standard uniform random generator # Step 6 & 7: For each wavelength lambda in {R, G, B} for channel in ['R', 'G', 'B']: alphai = volumedata.opacity(segment) tilambda = volumedata.transmissionprobability(segment, channel) rhoilambda = alphai (1.0 - tilambda) # If probability exceeds random threshold, photon is absorbed/blocked if rhoilambda > ri: if channel == 'R': cR = min(cR, zi) elif channel == 'G': cG = min(cG, zi) elif channel == 'B': cB = min(cB, zi) # Step 8: Terminate early if all accumulators are < 1 (fully absorbed) if cR < 1.0 and cG < 1.0 and cB < 1.0: break # Step 9: Store final accumulated depths fragment.color = (cR, cG, cB) def renderdvrwithcssm(volumedata, camera, cssmtexture, offsets, m): # Iterate through all samples of the DVR approach for sample in volumedata.samples: # Step 10: Initialize shadow factors for RGB channels lR, lG, lB = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 # Step 11: Compute sample position (sx, sy, sz) in light coordinate system sx, sy = projecttolightspace(sample.position, lightposition, camera) sz = sample.depthnormalizedinlightspace # Step 12: Iterate through m offset queries for j in range(1, m + 1): delta = offsets[j - 1] # Step 13: Read CSSM entries (cR, cG, cB) from fragment at (sx, sy) + delta cRj, cGj, cBj = cssmtexture.sample(sx + delta.x, sy + delta.y) # Step 14: For each wavelength lambda, check if sample is in shadow # Formula: llambda = (1/m) sum(I(clambda,j > sz)) if cRj > sz: lR += 1.0 / m if cGj > sz: lG += 1.0 / m if cBj > sz: lB += 1.0 / m # Use shadow factors (lR, lG, lB) to modulate illumination for the sample sample.color = (lR, lG, lB) def normalize(v): return v / magnitude(v) def discretizerayalongvolume(origin, direction, bounds): # Not given in the sources. pass def projecttolightspace(position, lightpos, camera): # Not given in the sources. pass This phase composites the volume and applies shadow factors by querying the CSSM. Probability of non-transmission (p{i,\lambda}): The probability that a photon of wavelength \lambda is not transmitted through the i-th volume segment is calculated as: p{i,\lambda} = \alphai \cdot (1 - t{i,\lambda}) Where: \alphai is the opacity of the volume in segment i. t{i,\lambda} is the conditional probability that the photon is transmitted given it interacts with the volume in segment i. Derivation: p{i,\lambda} = 1 - (P(\overline{V}i) + P(Vi) \cdot P(T{i,\lambda} | Vi)) = 1 - ((1 - \alphai) + \alphai \cdot t{i,\lambda}) = \alphai \cdot (1 - t{i,\lambda}). Shadow Factor (l\lambda): The shadow factor for a color channel is the average of m binary tests: l\lambda = \frac{1}{m} \sum{j=1}^{m} \mathbb{I}(c{\lambda,j} > sz) Where: c{\lambda,j} is the CSSM depth value for channel \lambda at offset j. sz is the sample's depth in light space. \mathbb{I}(\cdot) is the indicator function (1 if true, 0 if false). \alphai (Opacity): Derived from the volume's transfer function or data values. t{i,\lambda} (Conditional Transmission): Depends on the color properties of the volume in segment i. m (Number of Offsets): The number of offset queries used for denoising/averaging. Typical values are 7 (pleasing results, no noticeable noise), 13 (used in experiments), or 21 (softer shadows). \Deltaj (Offsets): Spatial offsets applied to CSSM lookup coordinates. Example set for m=13: \{(0,0), (\pm3,\pm3), (\pm4,0), (0,\pm4), (\pm7,0), (0,\pm7)\}. CSSM Resolution: The resolution of the shadow map texture. Tested resolutions include 1024^2, 2048^2, and 4096^2. Higher resolution improves shadow detail but increases memory usage. Noise: Stochastic generation introduces noise in the shadows. This is mitigated by averaging over multiple CSSM lookups with offsets. Complex scenes may require more offsets (m) to achieve pleasing results without noise. Blurring: Increasing m softens shadows but increases computation time and causes blurring. Single Light Source: The method is limited to a single point light source. Additional light sources require additional shadow maps, which is a general limitation of shadow mapping approaches. Translucency Handling: Traditional Shadow Maps (TSM) use a threshold at opacity 0.5, leading to dark, incorrect shadows in the interior of translucent objects. CSSM handles this correctly by storing partial depths. Time Complexity: CSSM generation is comparable to other shadow mapping techniques but involves stochastic sampling. Rendering time increases with the number of offsets m due to additional texture fetches. For a 1024^2 resolution, CSSM rendering time was measured at 4.9 ms, compared to 3.2 ms for Traditional Shadow Mapping (TSM) and 3.3 ms for Deep Shadow Mapping (DSM). The performance depends on the frame buffer resolution, not the shadow map resolution. Memory Complexity: CSSM uses significantly less memory than Deep Shadow Maps (DSM). CSSM stores one color buffer (3 values per fragment), while DSM with 3 nodes per channel stores 12 values per fragment (4x storage). DSM memory scales linearly with the number of nodes, whereas CSSM memory is constant regardless of the offset count m. Strengths: Produces higher-quality, softer, and colored shadows for translucent objects. Uses less texture memory than DSM. Compatible with mixed scenes containing both volume and surface renderings. Limitations: Limited to a single point light source. Stochastic noise requires averaging (increasing computation). Blurring increases with more offsets. When to Use: When colored, translucent shadows are required for DVR and memory is a constraint compared to DSM. Suitable for interactive applications where slightly higher rendering time (vs. TSM) is acceptable for quality gains. When Not to Use: When multiple light sources are needed (requires multiple shadow maps). When hard, binary shadows are preferred and translucency is not a concern (TSM is faster). Origin: CSSM was proposed as an alternative to Deep Shadow Maps for Direct Volume Rendering. It adapts the CSSM concept, originally developed for surface rendering, to volumetric data. History: The method was implemented and tested within the Voreen framework, a GPU-based ray casting volume renderer. It was tested on synthetic datasets (e.g., Test Spheres) and real-world medical data (e.g., Walnut CT dataset). Usage: Implemented in the Voreen framework. It is compatible with mixed scenes containing both volume and surface renderings; the CSSM can be generated for surfaces first, and then DVR can append to the same buffer without clearing. Colored Stochastic Shadow Mapping for Direct Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.2312/eurovisshort.20181072, fetched 2026-10-26
