name: Gradient-based shading
head: DVR.shader, Front-to-Back DVR with Gradient-Based Shading, Phong Shading model, VolumeDVR
body:
Gradient-based shading is a local illumination technique for direct volume rendering (DVR) that approximates surface lighting by estimating normals from the scalar field gradient and applying a Phong-like reflection model. It solves the problem of flat, "cloud-like" appearance in standard volume rendering by providing crisp depth cues and surface orientation information. Unlike volumetric shading which accounts for scattering and global occlusion, gradient-based shading is computationally efficient but limited to local surface properties, making it unsuitable for translucent media where subsurface scattering is significant. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D scalar volume texture (voxel values), a transfer function (TF) mapping values to color/alpha, light direction, and camera parameters. Output: A 2D image with accumulated color and alpha. Data Structures Volume Texture (VolumeTex): 3D texture, format RFloat (single channel float32). Memory order is x-fast, then y, then z. Transfer Function (TFTex): 2D texture, format RGBAFloat. Dimensions 256 	imes 1. The U coordinate maps to normalized intensity/label, V is fixed at 0.5. Metadata: Includes dimensions, voxel spacing, affine matrix, and normalization percentiles (P1, P99). Parameters StepSize: Distance advanced per sample. Range: 0.0005 to 0.02. Default: 0.003. Brightness: Global RGB multiplier. Range: 0 to 5. Default: 1.5. AlphaScale: Alpha multiplier before accumulation. Range: 0 to 2. Default: 0.5. LightDir: World-space light direction. Default: (0,0,1,0). LightIntensity: Diffuse intensity. Range: 0 to 5. Default: 1.0. Ambient: Ambient constant. Range: 0 to 1. Default: 0.2. IsLabelMap: Integer flag (1 or 0). 1 for discrete labels, 0 for continuous intensities. P1, P99: Percentiles for continuous normalization. MAXSTEPS: Maximum samples per ray. Default: 2048. Algorithm Steps 1. Ray Setup: Reconstruct camera position and fragment position in object space (cube [-0.5, +0.5]^3). Compute ray direction \vec{V}{obj} as normalized difference. Intersect ray with object-space bounding box [-0.5, 0.5]^3. If no intersection, return transparent black. Transform light direction \vec{L}{world} to object space \vec{L}{obj}. 2. Initialization: Set t = \max(t{enter}, 0.0). Initialize accumulators: 	ext{accRGB} = (0,0,0), 	ext{accA} = 0.0. 3. Raymarching Loop (iterate i from 0 to MAXSTEPS): Termination: Break if t > t{exit} or 	ext{accA} \ge 0.9999. Position: Compute object-space position \vec{p}{obj} = \vec{p}{cam, obj} + \vec{V}{obj} \cdot t. Coordinates: Convert \vec{p}{obj} to UVW coordinates in [0,1]^3: 	ext{uvw} = \vec{p}{obj} + 0.5. Break if any coordinate is outside [0,1]. Sampling: Sample volume texture at uvw. Extract red channel as voxel value val. Normalization: If IsLabelMap == 1: u =  rac{	ext{clamp}(	ext{round}(val), 0, 255)}{255}. If IsLabelMap == 0: u = 	ext{saturate}\left( rac{val - P1}{\max(P99 - P1, 10^{-6})}ight). Sample TF at (u, 0.5) to get 	ext{tf.rgb} and 	ext{tf.a}. Compute sample alpha: a{sample} = 	ext{tf.a} \cdot 	ext{\AlphaScale}. Shading (if a{sample} > 0.001): Normal Estimation: Compute gradient 
abla V using central differences with \epsilon = 0.002 in object space: 
abla V = [V(x+\epsilon, y, z) - V(x-\epsilon, y, z), V(x, y+\epsilon, z) - V(x, y-\epsilon, z), V(x, y, z+\epsilon) - V(x, y, z-\epsilon)] Estimate normal \vec{N} =  rac{
abla V}{\max(\|
abla V\|, 10^{-6})}. Lighting: Compute diffuse term: 	ext{lambert} = 	ext{saturate}(\vec{N} \cdot \vec{L}{obj}). Compute lighting: 	ext{lighting} = 	ext{\Ambient} + 	ext{\LightIntensity} \cdot 	ext{lambert}. Compute lit color: 	ext{litColor} = 	ext{tf.rgb} \cdot 	ext{lighting}. Note: The full Phong model includes specular terms ks i{m,s} (R \cdot V)^\alpha and attenuation A for point lights. Accumulation (if a{sample} > 0.001): 	ext{remain} = 1.0 - 	ext{accA} 	ext{accRGB} += 	ext{remain} \cdot 	ext{litColor} \cdot a{sample} 	ext{accA} += 	ext{remain} \cdot a{sample} Advance: t += 	ext{\StepSize}. 4. Final Output: 	ext{accRGB} = 	ext{\Brightness}. Return 	ext{float4}(	ext{accRGB}, 	ext{accA}). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gradientbasedshading(rayoriginobj, raydirobj, lightdirobj, volumetex, tftex, params): # 1. Ray-Box Intersection tenter, texit = intersectbox(rayoriginobj, raydirobj, bounds=[-0.5, 0.5]) if texit < 0 or tenter > texit: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) t = max(tenter, 0.0) accrgb = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) acca = 0.0 # 2. Loop for i in range(params.MAXSTEPS): if t > texit or acca >= 0.9999: break # 3. Position & Coordinates pobj = rayoriginobj + raydirobj t uvw = pobj + 0.5 if not (0.0 <= uvw.x <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= uvw.y <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= uvw.z <= 1.0): t += params.StepSize continue # 4. Sampling val = volumetex.sample(uvw) # Extract red channel # Normalization if params.IsLabelMap: u = clamp(round(val), 0, 255) / 255.0 else: denom = max(params.P99 - params.P1, 1e-6) u = saturate((val - params.P1) / denom) tfcolor, tfalpha = tftex.sample(u, 0.5) asample = tfalpha params.AlphaScale # 5. Shading if asample > 0.001: # Normal Estimation eps = 0.002 gradx = volumetex.sample(uvw + (eps, 0, 0)).x - volumetex.sample(uvw + (-eps, 0, 0)).x grady = volumetex.sample(uvw + (0, eps, 0)).x - volumetex.sample(uvw + (0, -eps, 0)).x gradz = volumetex.sample(uvw + (0, 0, eps)).x - volumetex.sample(uvw + (0, 0, -eps)).x gradnormsq = gradx2 + grady2 + gradz2 gradnorm = max(gradnormsq, 1e-6)0.5 N = normalize((gradx, grady, gradz)) # Lighting (Phong-like) lambert = saturate(dot(N, lightdirobj)) lighting = params.Ambient + params.LightIntensity lambert # Specular and Attenuation (Simplified in S2, Full in S1) # S2 uses only ambient + diffuse. S1 includes specular and attenuation. # Here we follow S2's explicit shader steps but acknowledge S1's model. litcolor = tfcolor lighting # 6. Accumulation remain = 1.0 - acca accrgb = accrgb + remain litcolor asample acca = acca + remain asample t += params.StepSize accrgb = accrgb params.Brightness return (accrgb[0], accrgb[1], accrgb[2], acca) This method performs direct volume raycasting using pre-computed Hounsfield Unit (HU) gradients for lighting direction, applying Phong shading only when a significant opacity change is detected along the gradient vector. It combines this hybrid lighting model with lasso-based voxel masking to selectively render regions of interest and cutting cube bounds to clip the volume. It differs from standard Phong shading by decoupling the lighting direction from the local sample gradient, relying instead on global HU gradients, and by gating the lighting contribution based on opacity thresholds to prevent shading artifacts on smooth structures like vessels. Hybrid Scattering is a stochastic shading technique for distance-field ray marching that switches between surface-based Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) and volumetric phase function scattering based on the local gradient magnitude. It solves the problem of rendering ambiguity in ill-defined regions by providing specular highlights where gradients are strong and volumetric scattering where gradients are weak, reducing sample variance compared to pure volumetric methods. Unlike conventional Phong shading, the underlying BRDF model is reciprocal and energy conserving. A technique to obtain crisp and solid-looking images from volume-rendered turbulent flow data by applying additional gradient shading, solving the problem of 'cloud like or fuzzy' images characteristic of direct volume rendering of space filling 3-D data. It applies solid-texture-mapping to map one velocity component onto another, then applies gradient shading with ambient, diffuse, specular, and glossiness contributions. Unlike geometrical rendering techniques, this preserves the full integrity of the original dataset, making it more adaptable to analysis. A shading technique that uses local gradients to simulate surface details, providing local shadowing and depth cues. It reflects local details and is often preferred for CT scans. The local gradient can be computed using either the opacity normal or the density normal; opacity gradient is particularly useful in medical images where tissues are made transparent. Unlike global shading, gradient shading reflects local details. It can be combined with volumetric shading or LAO, but not both simultaneously. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples per ray and the number of rays (pixels). Normal estimation requires 6 additional texture lookups per sample. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the volume texture and transfer function. The method itself uses minimal additional memory per ray. Performance: Generally faster than volumetric scattering or shadow ray techniques because it avoids secondary ray casts. Performance on a Stardent GS-1000 was demonstrated for 54 GB turbulent flow data. Strengths: Low computational cost, realistic surface lighting effects, easy adaptation to lighting scenarios, provides clear depth cues. Limitations: Cannot capture scattering effects of translucent materials or media occlusions. Can impose an overwhelmingly metallic feeling, making ultrasound data look unrealistic. Limited to local details, ignoring global lighting interactions. When to Use: When real-time performance is critical and the volume has well-defined surfaces or high-contrast boundaries. Suitable for CT scans and structural visualization. When Not to Use: For translucent media where subsurface scattering is important, or for noisy data like ultrasound where the metallic artifact is undesirable. Gradient-based shading was introduced as a widely used method to capture surface reflection in volume rendering by using the normalized surface gradient of scalar values. It is based on the Phong Shading model. The technique has been applied to various domains, including medical imaging (CT, MRI) and scientific visualization (turbulent flow). In medical visualization, it is often implemented in frameworks like VTK.js and Unity-based renderers (e.g., VolumeDVR.shader). The method addresses the "cloud-like" appearance of standard DVR by adding surface-like lighting cues. name: Hybrid Gradient Volume Raycasting with Lasso Masking
head: Colored Raycast Volume Render, HU Direction + Opacity Threshold Lighting
body: This method performs direct volume raycasting using pre-computed Hounsfield Unit (HU) gradients for lighting direction, applying Phong shading only when a significant opacity change is detected along the gradient vector. It combines this hybrid lighting model with lasso-based voxel masking to selectively render regions of interest and cutting cube bounds to clip the volume. It differs from standard Phong shading by decoupling the lighting direction from the local sample gradient, relying instead on global HU gradients, and by gating the lighting contribution based on opacity thresholds to prevent shading artifacts on smooth structures like vessels. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A 3D volume texture array of scalar density values (HU), a 1D Color Transfer Function (CTF) texture, a 3D lasso mask texture, and camera/model matrices. Outputs: A final RGBA color for each pixel. Data Structures The method uses a Uniforms struct passed to the shader. The layout is fixed as follows: modelMatrix: mat4x4<f32> viewMatrix: mat4x4<f32> projectionMatrix: mat4x4<f32> cameraPosition: vec3<f32> padding0: f32 numSlices: f32 stepSize: f32 densityScale: f32 padding1: f32 inverseModelMatrix: mat4x4<f32> padding2 to padding5: f32 (padding) voxelSpacing: vec3<f32> padding6: f32 toggleGradient: u32 (0 or non-zero) volumeWidth, volumeHeight, volumeDepth: u32 (Dimensions of the volume texture) xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax: f32 (Cutting cube bounds) Texture bindings: @binding(0): uniforms (Uniforms) @binding(1): volumeTexture (texture2darray<f32>) @binding(2): volumeSampler (sampler) @binding(3): gradientTexture (texture2darray<f32>) @binding(4): ctfTexture (texture1d<f32>) @binding(5): lassoMask (texture3d<u32>) Numbered Steps 1. Vertex Shader: Transform the input quad position to clip space using projectionMatrix viewMatrix modelMatrix. Pass the world position and a zero ray direction to the fragment shader. 2. Fragment Shader Initialization: Compute the camera position in cube space using the inverseModelMatrix. Set the ray origin to the camera position. Compute the ray direction by normalizing (worldPosition - cameraPosition) and scaling by voxelSpacing. 3. Ray-Box Intersection: Define the box bounds: boxMin = vec3(-1.0/voxelSpacing.x, -1.0/voxelSpacing.y, -1.0/voxelSpacing.z) and boxMax = vec3(1.0/voxelSpacing.x, 1.0/voxelSpacing.y, 1.0/voxelSpacing.z). Intersect the ray with this box to find tNear and tFar. Discard the pixel if tNear >= tFar or tFar <= 0. 4. Jitter: Compute a jitter value to reduce banding: \text{jitter} = \text{fract}(\sin(\text{dot}(\text{clipPosition.xy}, \text{vec2}(12.9898, 78.233))) \times 43758.5453) \times \text{stepSize}. 5. Ray Marching Loop: a. Initialize accumulatedColor = vec3(0.0), accumulatedAlpha = 0.0, t = tNear + jitter, and stepCount = 0. b. While accumulatedAlpha < 0.95 and t < tFar: i. Position Conversion: \text{scaledPos} = \text{rayOrigin} + \text{rayDir} \times t \text{pos} = \text{scaledPos} \times \text{voxelSpacing} \times 0.5 + \text{vec3}(0.5) This converts from cube space [-1, 1] to texture space [0, 1]. ii. Texture Bounds Check: If pos.x, pos.y, or pos.z is outside [0, 1], break the loop. iii. Lasso Mask Check: Compute voxel coordinates: \text{voxelCoord} = (\lfloor \text{pos.x} \times (\text{volumeWidth}-1) \rfloor, \lfloor \text{pos.y} \times (\text{volumeHeight}-1) \rfloor, \lfloor \text{pos.z} \times (\text{volumeDepth}-1) \rfloor) Load maskValue from lassoMask at voxelCoord. If maskValue == 0, increment t by stepSize and stepCount, then continue to the next iteration. iv. Volume Sampling: Sample the density using sampleVolumeFast(pos). This function performs trilinear interpolation across the 2D texture array slices. v. CTF Evaluation: Normalize the density to the HU range [-1024.0, 3071.0]: \text{normalized} = \text{clamp}\left(\frac{\text{density} - (-1024.0)}{3071.0 - (-1024.0)}, 0.0, 1.0\right) Map to texture index: \text{texelIndex} = \lfloor \text{normalized} \times 255.0 \rfloor Load ctfColor and sampleAlpha from ctfTexture at texelIndex. vi. Alpha Threshold: If sampleAlpha <= 0.001, skip lighting and accumulation. Increment t by stepSize and stepCount, then continue. vii. Alpha Normalization: \alpha = \text{sampleAlpha} \times \frac{\text{stepSize}}{0.006} \alpha = \text{clamp}(\alpha, 0.0, 1.0). viii. Lighting Calculation (Hybrid Gradient): If toggleGradient is non-zero: Sample the pre-computed gradient from gradientTexture at pos. Normalize the gradient to get the normal \mathbf{n}. Compute the Phong lighting term L(\mathbf{p}) using the standard model (ambient, diffuse, specular) with the view vector \mathbf{v} and light vector \mathbf{l}. Opacity Threshold Check: Calculate the opacity change along the gradient direction. If the opacity change is \le 0.15, set L(\mathbf{p}) = 1.0 (no shading). Otherwise, use the computed Phong lighting. This prevents shading on smooth vessels. If toggleGradient is zero, set L(\mathbf{p}) = 1.0. ix. Accumulation: \text{weight} = \alpha \times (1.0 - \text{accumulatedAlpha}) \text{accumulatedColor} += \text{ctfColor.rgb} \times L(\mathbf{p}) \times \text{weight} \text{accumulatedAlpha} += \text{weight} If accumulatedAlpha >= 0.95, break loop. x. Increment: t += \text{stepSize}, \text{stepCount} += 1. 6. Post-Processing: If accumulatedAlpha < 0.1, add a subtle ambient gray color to mask numerical errors: \text{accumulatedColor} += \text{vec3}(0.02) \times (0.1 - \text{accumulatedAlpha}). 7. Return: Return vec4(accumulatedColor, accumulatedAlpha). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def samplevolumefast(pos, volumetexture, volumesampler, numslices): coords = clamp(pos, vec3(0.0), vec3(1.0)) z = coords.z (numslices - 1.0) z0 = floor(z) z1 = min(z0 + 1.0, numslices - 1.0) zfrac = z - z0 sample0 = texturesamplelevel(volumetexture, volumesampler, coords.xy, int(z0), 0.0) sample1 = texturesamplelevel(volumetexture, volumesampler, coords.xy, int(z1), 0.0) return mix(sample0.r, sample1.r, zfrac) def evaluatectf(density, ctftexture): minhu = -1024.0 maxhu = 3071.0 normalized = clamp((density - minhu) / (maxhu - minhu), 0.0, 1.0) texelindex = int(normalized 255.0) return textureload(ctftexture, texelindex, 0) def intersectraybox(origin, direction, boxmin, boxmax): tmin = (boxmin - origin) / direction tmax = (boxmax - origin) / direction t1 = min(tmin, tmax) t2 = max(tmin, tmax) tnear = max(max(t1.x, t1.y), t1.z) tfar = min(min(t2.x, t2.y), t2.z) return tnear, tfar def computephonglighting(normal, lightdir, viewdir): ambient = vec3(0.1) diffuse = vec3(0.8) max(dot(normal, lightdir), 0.0) reflectdir = reflect(-lightdir, normal) spec = vec3(0.1) pow(max(dot(viewdir, reflectdir), 0.0), 32.0) return ambient + diffuse + spec def fragmentmain(worldpos, lightdir, viewdir): camerapos = inversemodelmatrix vec4(uniforms.cameraPosition, 1.0).xyz raydir = normalize(worldpos - camerapos) uniforms.voxelspacing rayorigin = camerapos boxmin = vec3(-1.0 / uniforms.voxelspacing.x, -1.0 / uniforms.voxelspacing.y, -1.0 / uniforms.voxelspacing.z) boxmax = vec3(1.0 / uniforms.voxelspacing.x, 1.0 / uniforms.voxelspacing.y, 1.0 / uniforms.voxelspacing.z) tnear, tfar = intersectraybox(rayorigin, raydir, boxmin, boxmax) if tnear >= tfar or tfar <= 0.0: return vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) jitter = fract(sin(dot(input.clipposition.xy, vec2(12.9898, 78.233))) 43758.5453) uniforms.stepsize accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 t = tnear + jitter stepcount = 0 while accumulatedalpha < 0.95 and t < tfar: scaledpos = rayorigin + raydir t pos = scaledpos uniforms.voxelspacing 0.5 + vec3(0.5) if pos.x < 0.0 or pos.x > 1.0 or pos.y < 0.0 or pos.y > 1.0 or pos.z < 0.0 or pos.z > 1.0: break voxelcoord = vec3( int(pos.x (uniforms.volumewidth - 1)), int(pos.y (uniforms.volumeheight - 1)), int(pos.z (uniforms.volumedepth - 1))) maskvalue = textureload(lassomask, voxelcoord, 0) if maskvalue == 0: t += uniforms.stepsize stepcount += 1 continue density = samplevolumefast(pos, volumetexture, volumesampler, uniforms.numslices) ctfresult = evaluatectf(density, ctftexture) ctfcolor = ctfresult.rgb samplealpha = ctfresult.a if samplealpha <= 0.001: t += uniforms.stepsize stepcount += 1 continue alpha = samplealpha (uniforms.stepsize / 0.006) alpha = clamp(alpha, 0.0, 1.0) lighting = 1.0 if uniforms.togglegradient != 0: grad = texturesamplelevel(gradienttexture, gradientsampler, pos, 0, 0.0) normal = normalize(grad) lighting = computephonglighting(normal, lightdir, viewdir) # Opacity change computation not provided in sources opacitychange = 0.0 if opacitychange <= 0.15: lighting = 1.0 weight = alpha (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) accumulatedcolor += ctfcolor lighting weight accumulatedalpha += weight t += uniforms.stepsize stepcount += 1 if accumulatedalpha < 0.1: accumulatedcolor += vec3(0.02) (0.1 - accumulatedalpha) return vec4(accumulatedcolor, accumulatedalpha) Parameters stepSize: f32 - Distance between samples along the ray. densityScale: f32 - Scaling factor for density values. voxelSpacing: vec3<f32> - Physical spacing between voxels in world units. toggleGradient: u32 - Boolean flag (0 or non-zero) to enable/disable gradient-based lighting. volumeWidth, volumeHeight, volumeDepth: u32 - Dimensions of the volume texture. numSlices: f32 - Number of slices in the volume texture array. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Numerical Errors: Very transparent regions (accumulatedAlpha < 0.1) may show black dots due to f16 numerical errors. This is mitigated by adding a subtle gray ambient color. Lasso Masking: Voxels inside the lasso contour (maskValue == 0) are skipped, allowing selective rendering. Gradient Threshold: Lighting is only applied if opacity change > 0.15. This prevents shading on smooth vessels but may reduce detail in low-contrast regions. Not given in the sources. This method is designed for medical volume rendering, specifically leveraging Hounsfield Unit (HU) gradients for lighting. The technique combines elements of direct volume raycasting, Phong shading, and lasso-based masking to provide an interactive and visually informative rendering experience. dongeronimo/webgpuvolumerendererdemo, https://github.com/dongeronimo/webgpuvolumerendererdemo, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Hybrid Scattering
head: Gradient-guided Hybrid Scattering
body: Hybrid Scattering is a stochastic shading technique for distance-field ray marching that switches between surface-based Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) and volumetric phase function scattering based on the local gradient magnitude. It solves the problem of rendering ambiguity in ill-defined regions by providing specular highlights where gradients are strong and volumetric scattering where gradients are weak, reducing sample variance compared to conventional ray casters. Unlike conventional Phong shading, the underlying BRDF model is reciprocal and energy conserving. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D volume texture (stored in CUDA texture memory), directional light vector, camera ray direction, sample position x, and gradient factor g \in [0, 1]. Output: Shaded color contribution integrated into the DVR accumulation loop. Data Structures: The transfer function is a 1D texture stored in CUDA texture memory with the following channels, each stored as a 16-bit unsigned short: 1. Opacity (ax) 2. Emission 3. Diffuse Color 4. Specular Color 5. Specular Roughness 6. Index of Reflection Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute Gradient: Calculate the local voxel gradient vector \nabla V(x) at sample position x on the fly using finite differences. Compute the normalized gradient magnitude D{+tn}(\tilde{x}) = \|\nabla V(x)\|. 2. Calculate BRDF Probability: Compute the probability P{brdf} that surface scattering will be used. The formula is: P{brdf} = ax \cdot (1 - e^{-25 \cdot g \cdot D{+tn}(\tilde{x})}) Where: ax is the opacity at position x retrieved from the transfer function. g is the gradient factor, a scalar in [0, 1] controlling the balance between surface and volumetric scattering. D{+tn}(\tilde{x}) is the normalized gradient magnitude. The constant 25 is hardcoded in the source. 3. Calculate Phase Probability: Compute the probability P{phase} for volumetric scattering: P{phase} = 1 - P{brdf} 4. Stochastic Selection: Draw a random number j from a uniform distribution U[0, 1]. If j < P{brdf}, select Surface Scattering. Otherwise, select Volumetric Scattering. 5. Shading Calculation: If Surface Scattering: Use the Fresnel Blend BRDF model. The model blends a diffuse Lambertian component and a glossy microfacet Blinn component. The blend is controlled by Schlick’s approximation to Fresnel reflectance. Parameters used: Diffuse color, Specular color, Specular roughness (Blinn exponent), and Index of Reflection from the transfer function. This model is reciprocal and energy conserving, unlike conventional Phong shading. If Volumetric Scattering: Use an isotropic phase function. (Note: Anisotropic functions like Schlick’s phase function could be used, but isotropic is the default implementation). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def hybridscattering(samplepos, lightdir, viewdir, gradientfactor, volumetexture): # Step 1: Compute gradient magnitude on the fly with finite differences dx = volumetexture.getvalue(samplepos + (1.0, 0.0, 0.0)) - volumetexture.getvalue(samplepos - (1.0, 0.0, 0.0)) dy = volumetexture.getvalue(samplepos + (0.0, 1.0, 0.0)) - volumetexture.getvalue(samplepos - (0.0, 1.0, 0.0)) dz = volumetexture.getvalue(samplepos + (0.0, 0.0, 1.0)) - volumetexture.getvalue(samplepos - (0.0, 0.0, 1.0)) gradientmagnitude = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) # Step 2: Retrieve opacity at sample position x opacity = volumetexture.getopacity(samplepos) # Step 3: Calculate BRDF probability exponent = -25.0 gradientfactor gradientmagnitude pbrdf = opacity (1.0 - math.exp(exponent)) # Step 4: Calculate phase probability pphase = 1.0 - pbrdf # Step 5: Stochastic selection j = random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) if j < pbrdf: # Surface Scattering: Fresnel Blend BRDF # Normal is derived from the computed gradient vector normal = normalize((dx, dy, dz)) return fresnelblendbrdf(lightdir, viewdir, normal, volumetexture) else: # Volumetric Scattering: Isotropic phase function return isotropicphasefunction(lightdir, viewdir) def normalize(v): length = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) if length == 0.0: return (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) return (v[0]/length, v[1]/length, v[2]/length) def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def fresnelblendbrdf(lightdir, viewdir, normal, volumetexture): # Retrieve parameters from transfer function diffusecolor = volumetexture.getdiffusecolor() specularcolor = volumetexture.getspecularcolor() roughness = volumetexture.getspecularroughness() ior = volumetexture.getindexofreflection() halfvector = normalize((lightdir[0] + viewdir[0], lightdir[1] + viewdir[1], lightdir[2] + viewdir[2])) # Schlick's approximation to Fresnel reflectance costheta = max(0.0, dot(viewdir, normal)) f0 = ((1.0 - ior) / (1.0 + ior)) 2 fresnel = f0 + (1.0 - f0) ((1.0 - costheta) 5) # Diffuse component (Lambert) diffuseterm = max(0.0, dot(normal, lightdir)) diffusecontribution = diffusecolor diffuseterm # Glossy component (Microfacet Blinn) coshn = max(0.0, dot(halfvector, normal)) glossyterm = coshn roughness glossycontribution = specularcolor glossyterm # Blend diffuse and glossy using Schlick's Fresnel shadedcolor = (1.0 - fresnel) diffusecontribution + fresnel glossycontribution return shadedcolor def isotropicphasefunction(lightdir, viewdir): # Isotropic phase function return 1.0 / (4.0 math.pi) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Noise: In regions with low signal-to-noise ratio, the gradient magnitude may be unreliable. The gradient factor g should be adjusted to mitigate this. Precision: The opacity and transfer function channels are stored as 16-bit unsigned shorts. Boundary Conditions: Finite difference gradient computation requires access to neighboring voxels. Boundary checks must be implemented to avoid out-of-bounds memory access. Complexity: The method adds a constant-time stochastic decision and gradient computation per sample to the standard DVR loop. The gradient computation involves six texture lookups and basic arithmetic. Performance: The method reduces sample variance compared to conventional ray casters. Strengths: Provides vivid specular highlights in well-defined regions while maintaining volumetric appearance in ill-defined regions. It is more physically plausible than Phong shading. Limitations: Requires on-the-fly gradient computation, increasing memory bandwidth usage. Hybrid Scattering was introduced in the "Exposure Render" framework, an interactive photo-realistic volume rendering system. The method was designed to integrate surface and volumetric scattering into stochastic volume rendering, addressing the limitations of conventional ray casters that use non-energy-conserving shading models like Phong. Exposure Render: An Interactive Photo-Realistic Volume Rendering Framework, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0038586, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Volumetric Shading
head: Fire Shader, Global Occlusion, Smoke Shader, Volumetric Render Settings, Volumetric Shadow, secondary scatter
body: Volumetric shading is a local illumination technique that captures shadow information and global occlusion effects in translucent participating media by branching a secondary ray towards the light source at each primary ray sample location. It differs from gradient-based shading (e.g., Gradient-based shading) by computing transmittance at runtime rather than using pre-computed shadow maps, thereby reducing memory occupancy while providing global ambient occlusion. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Primary ray sample position x', view direction \vec{o}, light source position xm, incident radiance Lm, phase function parameters, and user-defined parameters for ray reach and sampling distance. Outputs: Shaded radiance L{in}(x', \vec{o}) incorporating volumetric shadow effects. Data Structures: No specific complex data structures are required beyond standard ray traversal buffers; the method relies on runtime computation of transmittance along the secondary ray to avoid shadow map memory overhead. Parameters: GlobalIlluminationReach: The maximum length of the secondary ray to consider. VolumeShadowSamplingDistFactor: The sampling distance for the secondary rays; increasing this value speeds up rendering. Partial Shadow Ray: A setting where only a fraction (e.g., 10%) of the secondary ray length is considered, used to speed up rendering. Maximum proportion of the shadow ray: A user-adjustable parameter limiting the reach of the shadow ray; when small, the method is equivalent to local ambient occlusion with one sampled direction. Algorithm Steps: 1. For each sample point x' on the primary ray, branch a secondary ray towards the light source position xm. 2. Traverse the secondary ray from the sample position x0 to the end position x (or up to GlobalIlluminationReach) to calculate the global occlusion factor. 3. Compute the transmittance T(xm, x') along the secondary ray at runtime. 4. Evaluate the Henyey-Greenstein phase function \Phi(x', \vec{i}, \vec{o}) for the in-scatter direction \vec{i} (from light to sample) and out-scatter direction \vec{o} (from sample to viewer). 5. Integrate the shadow contribution using the formula below. 6. Sum the lighting effects over all light sources and their incident radiance Lm. Formula: The incident radiance L{in}(x', \vec{o}) due to volumetric shading L{vs} is calculated as: L{in}(x', \vec{o}) = L{vs} = \sum{m}^{lights} \int{x0}^{x} \Phi(x', \vec{i}, \vec{o}) Lm T(xm, x') dx' Where: \Phi(x', \vec{i}, \vec{o}) is the Henyey-Greenstein phase function. Lm is the incident radiance from light source m. T(xm, x') is the transmittance from the light source position xm to the sample x'. The integration is performed from the sample position x0 to the end position x. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def heneygreensteinphase(idir, odir, g): """Standard Henyey-Greenstein phase function.""" costheta = max(-1.0, min(1.0, dot(idir, odir))) g2 = g g denom = 1.0 + g2 - 2.0 g costheta return (1.0 - g2) / (4.0 math.pi (denom 1.5)) def volumetricshading(samplepoint, viewdirection, lights, volumedata, params): """ Calculate volumetric shading for a single sample point. Args: samplepoint: Position x' on the primary ray. viewdirection: Out-scatter direction o. lights: List of light sources, each containing position xm and incident radiance Lm. volumedata: Accessor to volume density/opacity data. params: Dictionary containing GlobalIlluminationReach, VolumeShadowSamplingDistFactor, etc. Returns: Shaded radiance contribution from volumetric shading. """ totalradiance = 0.0 for light in lights: lightpos = light.position lightradiance = light.radiance raydirection = normalize(lightpos - samplepoint) maxlength = params.get('GlobalIlluminationReach', float('inf')) if params.get('Partial Shadow Ray', False): maxlength = maxlength 0.1 stepsize = params.get('VolumeShadowSamplingDistFactor', 1.0) transmittance = 1.0 currentpos = samplepoint # Numerical integration of the shadow contribution along the secondary ray while distance(currentpos, lightpos) < maxlength: density = volumedata.getdensity(currentpos) # Update transmittance from light to currentpos as we step towards the light transmittance = math.exp(density stepsize) inscatterdirection = -raydirection phasevalue = heneygreensteinphase(inscatterdirection, viewdirection, params.get('phaseparams', 0.0)) # Accumulate integral contribution: Phi Lm T dx totalradiance += phasevalue lightradiance transmittance stepsize currentpos += raydirection stepsize return totalradiance Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noise Sensitivity: Small features are dampened by volumetric shading, which can be detrimental if the data contains significant noise. Performance: The method is computationally demanding; full shadow rays can lead to test failures on GPUs that are not powerful enough. Local vs Global: When the reach of the shadow ray is relatively small, the rendering method is equivalent to local ambient occlusion technique with one sampled direction. Time Complexity: Computationally demanding due to the traversal of secondary rays for every sample point. Render time does not necessarily increase linearly with file size; translucent tissues (more voxels traversed) require significantly more time (e.g., almost twice the render time for Head CT data compared to other datasets). Memory Complexity: Low memory occupancy compared to shadow map approaches, as transmittance is computed at runtime. Strengths: Captures global shadow effects and improves understanding of spatial relations and object size in translucent media. Reduces memory usage compared to shadow maps. Limitations: Can dampen small features and noise. Computationally expensive, potentially causing GPU test failures on weaker hardware. When to use: When global occlusion effects are desired in translucent media and memory is constrained, or when improving spatial perception in medical volume data is required. When not to use: When performance is critical and hardware is limited, or when preserving small noisy features is important. Volumetric shading was introduced as a relatively efficient technique to capture shadow information in participating media. It is often referred to as shadow ray or secondary scatter. Perceptual studies have shown that volumetric shadow improves understanding of spatial relations and object size. The method has been implemented in production rendering pipelines and in libraries such as VTK.js for in-browser cinematic volume rendering. Interactive, in-browser cinematic volume rendering of medical images, https://doi.org/10.1080/21681163.2022.2145239, fetched 2026-10-26 Cinematic Volume Rendering in Your Web Browser: VolView and VTK.js, https://www.kitware.com/cinematic-volume-rendering/, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Shading for Semi-Transparent Volumes
head: Local diffuse illumination for semi-transparent volumes, Semi-transparent volume shading with local diffuse illumination, Shaded semi-transparent volume rendering
body:
This method enables local diffuse illumination for semi-transparent volume rendering by utilizing multi-stage rasterization hardware (specifically register combiners) to compute lighting in a single pass. It solves the problem of achieving interactive frame rates for shaded volumes on early PC hardware by offloading the dot product calculation to fixed-function units. It differs from isosurface shading by using alpha blending instead of alpha testing, and from methods requiring 3D textures or multi-pass techniques by sacrificing real trilinear interpolation to fit gradient and color data into separate 2D textures. Inputs: 1. Gradient Texture (Texture 0): An RGB texture storing the voxel gradient vectors 
abla V. The RGB channels encode the normal components. 2. Color/Opacity Texture (Texture 1): An RGB texture (or paletted texture) storing the ambient color C{ambient} in RGB and opacity \alpha in the Alpha channel for each voxel. 3. Light Direction: A uniform vector \mathbf{l} representing the direction to the light source. 4. Diffuse Color: A uniform color C{diffuse} (e.g., white or light source color). 5. Ambient Color: A uniform color C{global\ambient} (used if per-voxel ambient is not enabled, though this method targets per-voxel). Outputs: A rendered image with semi-transparent shading, where each fragment's color includes ambient and diffuse contributions based on the local gradient. The method requires two distinct texture units bound to 2D textures (simulating 3D slices or using multi-texturing to bypass 3D texture limitations of the target hardware). Texture 0 (Gradient): Format: RGB (8-bit per channel typically). Content: 
abla Vx, 
abla Vy, 
abla Vz. Interpolation: Hardware trilinear interpolation is not performed on this texture in the combined sense because it is separate from the color texture. The source notes that "real trilinear interpolation is not possible" because hardware limits input textures to two at a time, and the gradient must be sampled separately from the color/opacity. Texture 1 (Color/Opacity): Format: RGBA (8-bit per channel) or Paletted RGB + Alpha. Content: C{ambient} (RGB), \alpha (Alpha). Note: If paletted, the RGB channels act as indices into a color lookup table, allowing per-voxel ambient color specification without consuming extra texture memory bandwidth for the color data itself. 1. Texture Binding: Bind the gradient data to Texture Unit 0 and the color/opacity data to Texture Unit 1. 2. Combiner Stage 0 (Dot Product): Configure the first register combiner stage to compute the dot product between the light direction and the gradient. Input A: Texture 0 (Gradient 
abla V). Input B: Light Direction \mathbf{l} (passed as a constant or varying). Input C: Zero. Operation: P = 
abla V \cdot \mathbf{l}. Output: P is passed to the next stage. 3. Final Combiner (Shading): Configure the final combiner to mix the ambient color and the diffuse contribution. Input A: Dot Product P from Stage 0. Input B: Diffuse Color C{diffuse} (passed as a constant). Input C: Zero. Input D: Texture 1 (Ambient Color C{ambient}). Operation: C{final} = P \cdot C{diffuse} + C{ambient}. Note on Hardware Specifics: The source describes the final combiner output as AB + (1-A)C + D. In this specific configuration: A is the dot product P. B is C{diffuse}. C is Zero. D is C{ambient}. Result: P \cdot C{diffuse} + 0 + C{ambient}. 4. Alpha Blending: Enable alpha blending using the alpha channel from Texture 1. The fragment shader/combiner output color is blended into the frame buffer based on the sampled \alpha. 5. Rendering: Render the volume slices (or ray-casted fragments) using the configured pipeline. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. ZEROVECTOR = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) LIGHTDIRECTION = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) # Uniform light direction DIFFUSECOLOR = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # Uniform diffuse color def setupcombiners(gradienttexture, coloropacitytexture): # Combiner Stage 0: Compute dot product # Input A: gradienttexture (RGB gradient) # Input B: LIGHTDIRECTION # Input C: ZEROVECTOR # Operation: dotproduct stage0output = dotproduct(gradienttexture, LIGHTDIRECTION) # Final Combiner: Compute shaded color # Input A: stage0output # Input B: DIFFUSECOLOR # Input C: ZEROVECTOR # Input D: coloropacitytexture (RGB ambient color) # Operation: combinergb -> A B + (1 - A) C + D # Since C is ZEROVECTOR, Output = A B + D finalcolor = stage0output DIFFUSECOLOR + coloropacitytexture return finalcolor def rendervolumeslice(gradienttexture, coloropacitytexture): # Bind textures to hardware units bindtextureunit(0, gradienttexture) bindtextureunit(1, coloropacitytexture) # Configure combiners finalcolor = setupcombiners(gradienttexture, coloropacitytexture) # Enable alpha blending for semi-transparency enablealphablending() setblendfunction(SRCALPHA, ONEMINUSSRCALPHA) # Draw volume slices/fragments drawprimitives(VOLUMESLICEGEOMETRY) Light Direction \mathbf{l}: Typically normalized. Diffuse Color C{diffuse}: Often white (1,1,1) or the color of the light source. Ambient Color C{ambient}: Per-voxel, stored in Texture 1. Opacity \alpha: Per-voxel, stored in Texture 1 Alpha channel. 1. Loss of Trilinear Interpolation: The primary limitation is that real trilinear interpolation of the volume data is not possible because the gradient and color/opacity data must reside in separate textures, and the hardware only supports two input textures at a time. This results in limited image quality compared to methods using 3D textures or multi-pass techniques. 2. No Per-Voxel Ambient Color with Trilinear Interpolation: If one attempts to keep trilinear interpolation, the RGB channels are used for the gradient vector and the Alpha channel for opacity. This leaves no channel for per-voxel ambient color, forcing the use of a globally defined ambient color. 3. Hardware Limits on Signed Vectors: Early hardware required workarounds for signed vector components (gradients). This method leverages hardware support for signed vectors, avoiding large-scale workarounds. 4. Limited Lighting: The described single-pass setup supports one diffuse light source efficiently. A second colored light source can be computed using unused registers (C and D of the first combiner stage), but this requires sacrificing either trilinear interpolation or separate ambient/diffuse color specification. Time Complexity: Single-pass rendering. The dot product is computed in hardware, avoiding CPU-side calculations for lighting. Memory Complexity: Requires two texture units. Memory requirements are similar to isosurface algorithms if paletted textures are used for color. Measured Performance: On a GeForce 256 with a 600x600 viewport: 128x128x64: 22.5 fps. 256x256x128: 4.1 fps. 256x256x256: 2.0 fps. Strengths: Interactive frame rates achieved via single-pass rendering; hardware-supported dot products; no large-scale workarounds for signed vectors. Limitations: Limited image quality due to missing real trilinear interpolation; limited to one primary diffuse light source in the basic configuration; hardware-dependent (relies on register combiners). When to Use: When interactive performance is required on hardware with register combiners and limited texture units, and high-fidelity interpolation is secondary. When Not to Use: When high-quality trilinear interpolation is critical, or when multiple complex light sources are needed without multi-pass rendering. This technique was developed for interactive volume rendering on standard PC graphics hardware in the early 2000s. It builds on the fast algorithm for displaying isosurfaces, adapting it for semi-transparent volumes by replacing alpha testing with alpha blending. The method was proposed as an alternative to implementations that required multi-pass rendering or complex workarounds for signed vectors. It anticipates future hardware improvements such as higher numbers of texturing units or native 3D-texturing capabilities. name: Cook-Torrance BRDF
head: Microfacet BRDF, GGX Cook-Torrance, Walter et al. BRDF
body: The Cook-Torrance BRDF is a physically based rendering model that represents the appearance of real-world opaque materials by combining diffuse and specular components based on microfacet theory. It distinguishes itself from simpler models like Phong by strictly conserving energy and using a statistical approximation of surface roughness to accurately simulate specular highlights, self-shadowing, and Fresnel effects. Unlike Shading models which may use empirical approximations, this method decomposes reflectance into physically meaningful terms: Normal Distribution, Geometry, and Fresnel. Inputs: Surface normal \mathbf{n} (unit vector). View direction \mathbf{v} (unit vector, pointing from surface to camera). Light direction \mathbf{l} (unit vector, pointing from surface to light source). Diffuse albedo \mathbf{c} (RGB color). Roughness parameter \gamma (scalar, typically [0, 1]). Base reflectivity F0 (RGB color, typically 0.04 for non-metals, or equal to \mathbf{c} for metals). Light radiance Li (RGB color). Emitted light Le (RGB color, optional). Outputs: Outgoing radiance Lo (RGB color). Data Structures: No complex data structures are required for the evaluation itself; it operates on scalar and vector primitives. Steps: 1. Calculate Halfway Vector: Compute the halfway vector \mathbf{h} between the view direction \mathbf{v} and the light direction \mathbf{l}: \mathbf{h} = \frac{\mathbf{l} + \mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{l} + \mathbf{v}\|} 2. Compute Normal Distribution Function (D): Use the Trowbridge-Reitz GGX approximation to determine the probability of microfacets aligning with \mathbf{h}. First, map roughness \gamma to \alpha: \alpha = \gamma^2 Then calculate D: D(\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{h}, \alpha) = \frac{\alpha^2}{\pi \left( (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{h})^2 (\alpha^2 - 1) + 1 \right)^2} Note: Some sources omit the square in the denominator's inner term or define \alpha differently, but the GGX form above is the standard implementation cited in. 3. Compute Geometry Function (G): Use Schlick-GGX with Smith's method to account for self-shadowing and masking. First, calculate the roughness-dependent coefficient k: k = \frac{(\alpha + 1)^2}{8} Then compute the Schlick geometry term for a vector \mathbf{i} (where \mathbf{i} is either \mathbf{v} or \mathbf{l}): G{\text{Schlick}}(\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{i}, k) = \frac{\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{i}}{(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{i})(1 - k) + k} The total geometry function is the product of the terms for view and light: G(\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{l}, \alpha) = G{\text{Schlick}}(\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{v}, k) \cdot G{\text{Schlick}}(\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{l}, k) 4. Compute Fresnel Function (F): Use the Fresnel-Schlick approximation to determine reflectivity at grazing angles: F(\mathbf{h}, \mathbf{v}, F0) = F0 + (1 - F0)(1 - \mathbf{h} \cdot \mathbf{v})^5 Note: uses a more complex exponential form for F, but the Schlick approximation is the standard for real-time PBR as cited in. 5. Compute Diffuse and Specular Weights: Ensure energy conservation. The specular weight ks is determined by the Fresnel term at the view angle (often approximated by F(\mathbf{h}, \mathbf{v}, F0) or simply F0 for simplicity in some implementations, but strictly ks = F in the energy-conserving split): ks = F(\mathbf{h}, \mathbf{v}, F0) kd = 1 - ks Note: defines the diffuse term directly as a/\pi without explicit kd weighting in the final sum formula (13), but explicitly use kd = 1-F to conserve energy. 6. Compute BRDF Components: Lambertian Diffuse: f{\text{Lambert}} = \frac{\mathbf{c}}{\pi} Cook-Torrance Specular: f{\text{CookTorrance}} = \frac{D(\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{h}, \alpha) F(\mathbf{h}, \mathbf{v}, F0) G(\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{l}, \alpha)}{4 (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v}) (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l})} 7. Combine and Integrate: The total outgoing radiance Lo is the sum of emitted light and the integral of reflected light over the hemisphere \Omega: Lo = Le + \int{\Omega} \left( kd f{\text{Lambert}} + ks f{\text{CookTorrance}} \right) Li (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}) \, d\omegai For a single directional light source, this simplifies to: Lo = Le + \left( (1 - F) \frac{\mathbf{c}}{\pi} + \frac{D F G}{4 (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v}) (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l})} F \right) Li (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}) Correction: The specular term already includes F. The standard form is: Lo = Le + \left( (1 - F) \frac{\mathbf{c}}{\pi} + \frac{D F G}{4 (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v}) (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l})} \right) Li (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cooktorrancebrdf(n, v, l, c, gamma, F0, Li, Le): # 1. Halfway vector h = normalize(l + v) # 2. Normal Distribution (GGX) alpha = gamma gamma nh = dot(n, h) denom = (nh nh) (alpha alpha - 1) + 1 D = (alpha alpha) / (pi denom denom) # 3. Geometry (Schlick-GGX) k = ((gamma + 1) 2) / 8 nv = dot(n, v) nl = dot(n, l) # Avoid division by zero if nv <= 0 or nl <= 0: return Le Gv = nv / (nv (1 - k) + k) Gl = nl / (nl (1 - k) + k) G = Gv Gl # 4. Fresnel (Schlick) hv = dot(h, v) F = F0 + (1 - F0) ((1 - hv) 5) # 5. Diffuse and Specular Weights # Energy conservation: kd = 1 - ks ks = F kd = 1 - ks # 6. Components fdiffuse = kd (c / pi) fspecular = (D F G) / (4 nv nl) # 7. Total Radiance # Note: Li is assumed to be pre-calculated radiance including attenuation Lo = Le + (fdiffuse + fspecular) Li nl return Lo Parameters: \gamma (Roughness): [0, 1]. 0 is perfectly smooth, 1 is very rough. F0 (Base Reflectivity): 0.04 for non-metals (dielectrics), equal to albedo \mathbf{c} for metals. \mathbf{c} (Albedo): RGB color, typically [0, 1]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Grazing Angles: When \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v} or \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l} approaches zero, the denominator in the specular term approaches zero. However, G and F also behave such that the term remains stable, but numerical precision issues may arise. Guard against negative dot products (back-face culling). Energy Conservation: Failing to multiply the diffuse term by (1 - F) results in energy creation, leading to overly bright surfaces. Roughness Mapping: Ensure \alpha is derived correctly from roughness. Some engines use \alpha = \text{roughness}^2, others use linear roughness. The GGX formula requires \alpha^2 in the numerator and \alpha^4 effectively in the denominator structure. A variant that specifically employs the anisotropic GGX Normal Distribution Function, Smith height-correlated geometry term, and Schlick Fresnel approximation. It distinguishes itself by supporting anisotropic roughness (different roughness in tangent and bitangent directions) and using a height-correlated geometry model for more accurate shadowing on rough surfaces. Choose this when rendering materials with directional scratches or brushed metals. It is a more advanced version of the standard isotropic Cook-Torrance model. Time Complexity: O(1) per light source per pixel. The evaluation involves a constant number of vector operations and trigonometric approximations (dot products, powers). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. Performance: Significantly more expensive than Phong or Blinn-Phong due to the calculation of D, G, and F, but still efficient enough for real-time rendering on modern GPUs. Strengths: Physically accurate, energy-conserving, handles a wide range of materials (metals, dielectrics, rough, smooth) with few parameters. Limitations: Does not account for subsurface scattering or complex inter-reflections (requires global illumination techniques like 3D Lookup Table Illumination Model or path tracing). The Schlick approximation for Fresnel is an approximation and may deviate from physical reality at extreme angles or for specific materials. When to use: Real-time rendering, PBR pipelines, when physical accuracy is required for surface appearance. When not to use: When subsurface scattering is dominant (use Shading for Semi-Transparent Volumes), or when performance is critically constrained and artistic control is preferred over physical accuracy. The Cook-Torrance BRDF was introduced by Richard L. Cook and Kenneth E. Torrance in 1982 in the paper "A Reflectance Model for Computer Graphics". It was one of the first models to apply microfacet theory to computer graphics, providing a physically based explanation for specular highlights. The model was later popularized in real-time rendering through the work of Walter et al. (2007) who introduced the GGX distribution, and Karis (2013) who simplified the Fresnel and geometry terms for real-time engines. It is now the standard for Physically Based Rendering (PBR) in modern graphics engines and libraries like Jrender. name: Cook-Torrance BRDF with Monte Carlo Integration
head: Monte Carlo Integration for Cook-Torrance BRDF, NDJIR Forward Rendering Model, Simplified Rendering Equation
body: This method computes the rendered color of a surface by integrating the diffuse and specular components of the Cook-Torrance BRDF over the upper hemisphere using Monte Carlo integration. It distinguishes itself by employing a simplified visibility function derived from the Filament model and utilizing importance sampling for the specular term to prevent light baking artifacts, which uniform sampling fails to mitigate. Inputs: \hat{\mathbf{x}}: Query point on the surface. \hat{\mathbf{n}}: Surface normal at \hat{\mathbf{x}}. \mathbf{v}: Viewing direction. \hat{\alpha}r: Roughness parameter. \mathbf{f}0: Specular reflectance (Fresnel coefficient at normal incidence). cb: Base color. \widehat{L}{pb}: Photogrammetric light intensity. LE(\mathbf{l}): Environment light intensity as a function of direction \mathbf{l}. \widehat{L}I(\hat{\mathbf{x}}): Implicit illumination term. N: Number of Monte Carlo samples. Outputs: \widehat{L}{out}: Estimated rendered color. Data Structures: Sample directions \mathbf{l}i: Vectors sampled from the upper hemisphere \Omega+, weighted by the specular distribution. Formulas: 1. Rendering Equation: The total radiance is estimated as: \widehat{L}{out} \approx \frac{\widehat{L}{pb} cb}{\pi N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \left( LV(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \mathbf{l}i) LE(\mathbf{l}i) (\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{l}i) + \widehat{L}I(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) \right) where LV is the soft visibility function. 2. Cook-Torrance Components: Normal Distribution Function (NDF) D: D = \frac{\hat{\alpha}r^2}{\pi \left( (\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{h})^2 (\hat{\alpha}r^2 - 1) + 1 \right)^2} Geometry Function G: G = \frac{2(\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{l})}{(\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{l}) + \sqrt{\hat{\alpha}r^2 + (1 - \hat{\alpha}r^2)(\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{l})^2}} \times \frac{2(\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{v})}{(\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{v}) + \sqrt{\hat{\alpha}r^2 + (1 - \hat{\alpha}r^2)(\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{v})^2}} Fresnel Term F: F = \mathbf{f}0 + (1 - \mathbf{f}0)(1 - (\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{h}))^5 3. Simplified Visibility Function V: The method uses a simplified visibility function V derived from the Filament model, which approximates the combined effect of G and other factors: V:= \frac{G}{4(\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{v})(\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{l})} = \frac{1}{(\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{l}) + \sqrt{\hat{\alpha}r^2 + (1 - \hat{\alpha}r^2)(\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{l})^2}} \times \frac{1}{(\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{v}) + \sqrt{\hat{\alpha}r^2 + (1 - \hat{\alpha}r^2)(\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{v})^2}} where \hat{\mathbf{n}} is the normal, \mathbf{v} is the viewing direction, \mathbf{l} is the light direction, and \hat{\alpha}r is roughness. 4. Half Vector \mathbf{h}: \mathbf{h} = \frac{\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{l}}{\|\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{l}\|} Steps: 1. Initialize sum S = 0. 2. For i = 1 to N: a. Sample a light direction \mathbf{l}i from the upper hemisphere \Omega+ using importance sampling based on the specular term (Eq. 6 in). b. Compute the half vector \mathbf{h}i = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{l}i). c. Compute Di, Gi, and Fi using the formulas above. d. Compute the simplified visibility Vi using the formula above. e. Evaluate the integrand: termi = Vi \cdot LE(\mathbf{l}i) \cdot (\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{l}i) + \widehat{L}I(\hat{\mathbf{x}}). f. Add to sum: S \leftarrow S + termi. 3. Compute final radiance: \widehat{L}{out} = \frac{\widehat{L}{pb} cb}{\pi N} S. Parameters: N: Number of samples. Typical values are not explicitly given, but increasing N reduces noise. \hat{\alpha}r: Roughness. Range [0, 1]. \mathbf{f}0: Specular reflectance. Typically 0.04 for dielectrics, higher for metals. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Uniform Sampling: Using uniform sampling instead of importance sampling causes "light baking," where high light intensity and specularity are incorrectly baked into the base color. Under/Overestimation: The method may underestimate or overestimate values in specific regions, such as the left cheek and chest of scan69 or the left jaw of scan65. Regularization: Strong regularization of the implicit illumination term can make the base color flatter, removing small details like dot eyes and thin mouths. Metalness: Metalness is not modeled in this method; metallic conversion is object-agnostic. Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel, where N is the number of Monte Carlo samples. Memory Complexity: O(1) per sample, assuming environment light and implicit illumination are accessible. Strengths: Importance sampling effectively models specularity and mitigates light baking artifacts compared to uniform sampling. Limitations: Can produce noisy artifacts or non-smooth geometry if dense voxel grid features are used without proper filtering. May under/overestimate in complex geometry regions. When to use: When accurate specular highlights are required and uniform sampling leads to baking artifacts. When not to use: When metalness needs to be physically modeled (not supported) or when high-frequency details are critical and regularization flattens them. The method is part of the NDJIR (Neural Direct and Joint Inverse Rendering) framework, proposed for geometry, lights, and materials of real objects tailored to photogrammetry settings. It builds on the Cook-Torrance BRDF model [12] and the rendering equation [30], adapting them for neural inverse rendering with simplified visibility and implicit illumination terms. NDJIR: Neural Direct and Joint Inverse Rendering for Geometry, Lights, and Materials of Real Object, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2302.00675, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Whitted-Style Shading with Diffuse/Glossy Materials
head: Diffuse Reflection, Lambertian Shading with Shadow Rays, Lambertian reflection, Volume Shading with Shadow Rays, Whitted-Style Shading
body: Whitted-Style Shading with Diffuse/Glossy Materials evaluates illumination at a surface point by combining ambient lighting with direct illumination from light sources, using shadow rays to determine visibility. It explicitly separates the computation of diffuse (Lambertian) and glossy (specular) reflection components, whereas Shading models provides a broader taxonomy, Shading for Semi-Transparent Volumes handles volume attenuation, and Cook-Torrance BRDF uses a more complex microfacet model for speculars. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Scene geometry (objects with materials) and light sources. Material properties: diffuse coefficient kd, glossy coefficient ks, albedo \mathbf{C}{albedo}, shininess exponent \alpha. Outputs: Final color \mathbf{C}{final} for the ray. Data Structures: Ray: Contains origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, min/max t bounds, and depth. Intersection data: Contains intersection point \mathbf{p}, surface normal \mathbf{n}, material reference, and distance t. Steps: 1. Intersection Test: Find the closest intersection between the input ray and the scene geometry. If no intersection is found, return the background color. If the hit is invalid, return a default background color, e.g., \{0.2, 0.6, 1.0\}. 2. Transform to World Space: If the intersection is in object space, transform the normal \mathbf{n}{obj} and position \mathbf{p}{obj} to world space using the object-to-world matrix \mathbf{M}{obj}: \mathbf{n} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{M}{obj} \mathbf{n}{obj}) \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{M}{obj} \mathbf{p}{obj} 3. Ambient Contribution: Calculate the ambient term. Implementations vary: one approach multiplies a constant factor by the diffuse coefficient, e.g., \{0.25, 0.25, 0.25\} \cdot kd. Another adds a small constant multiplied by the albedo, e.g., 0.003 \cdot \mathbf{C}{albedo}. 4. Direct Illumination Loop: For each light source in the scene: a. Light Direction: Compute the vector \mathbf{L} from the hit point \mathbf{p} to the light position \mathbf{p}L: \mathbf{L} = \mathbf{p}L - \mathbf{p} Compute the inverse squared distance: d^{-2} = \frac{1}{\|\mathbf{L}\|^2} Normalize the direction: \mathbf{l} = \frac{\mathbf{L}}{\|\mathbf{L}\|} b. Shadow Ray: Cast a shadow ray from \mathbf{p} towards the light. To prevent self-intersection (shadow acne), offset the origin slightly along the normal: \mathbf{o}{shadow} = \mathbf{p} + \epsilon \mathbf{n}, \quad \epsilon \approx 10^{-4} The shadow ray direction is \mathbf{l}. The maximum t is set to the distance to the light \|\mathbf{L}\|, though some implementations use an unbounded maximum distance. c. Visibility Check: Trace the shadow ray. If it hits an object before reaching the light, the point is in shadow (\mathbf{C}{direct} = \mathbf{0}). d. Diffuse Calculation: If not occluded, compute the Lambertian diffuse reflection. The BRDF fr is constant for diffuse surfaces, related to reflectance \rho by \rho = \pi fr. The reflected radiance is: \mathbf{C}{diffuse} = kd \cdot \mathbf{C}{albedo} \cdot \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}, 0) \cdot IL \cdot d^{-2} where IL is the light emission intensity. e. Glossy Calculation: If the material has a glossy component, compute the specular highlight. First, compute the perfect reflection vector \mathbf{R}: \mathbf{R} = 2(\mathbf{n} \cdot (-\mathbf{v}))\mathbf{n} - (-\mathbf{v}) where \mathbf{v} is the view direction (from \mathbf{p} to camera). The glossy term is: \mathbf{C}{glossy} = ks \cdot IL \cdot d^{-2} \cdot \max(\mathbf{R} \cdot \mathbf{v}, 0)^\alpha where \alpha is the shininess exponent. 5. Accumulate: Sum the ambient, diffuse, and glossy contributions: \mathbf{C}{final} = \mathbf{C}{ambient} + \sum{lights} (\mathbf{C}{diffuse} + \mathbf{C}{glossy}) Parameters: \alpha (shininess): Controls the sharpness of glossy highlights. Higher values yield narrower highlights. \epsilon (shadow offset): Prevents self-intersection artifacts. Typical value 10^{-4}. Light position: Typical value \{-3.0, 2.0, 5.0\}. Light emission: Typical value 20.0. Albedo: Typical value \{1.0, 1.0, 1.0\}. Edge Cases: Self-Intersection: Without the offset \epsilon, shadow rays may immediately hit the surface they originated from, causing incorrect shadows. Zero Distance: If the light is at the hit point, d^{-2} becomes infinite. Clamp or handle light positions carefully. Back-facing Normals: Ensure \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}, 0) handles cases where the light is behind the surface. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def whittedshading(ray: Ray, scene: Scene, lights: List[Light], material: Material) -> vec3: # 1. Intersection Test hit = scene.trace(ray) if not hit.valid: return vec3(0.2, 0.6, 1.0) # Background color # 2. Transform to World Space p = scene.objecttoworld @ hit.p n = normalize(scene.objecttoworld[:3,:3] @ hit.ng) color = vec3(0.0) # 3. Ambient Contribution color += vec3(0.25) material.diffusecoefficient color += 0.003 material.albedo # 4. Direct Illumination Loop for light in lights: L = light.position - p invdd = 1.0 / dot(L, L) l = normalize(L) # 4b. Shadow Ray shadoworigin = p + 1e-4 n shadowray = Ray(shadoworigin, l, 0.0, sqrt(dot(L, L))) # Distance to light occluded = scene.traceany(shadowray) if not occluded: # 4d. Diffuse Calculation diff = max(dot(n, l), 0.0) light.emission invdd material.albedo color += diff # 4e. Glossy Calculation if material.hasglossy: v = -ray.direction R = 2 dot(n, -v) n - (-v) spec = max(dot(R, v), 0.0) material.shininess color += spec light.emission invdd material.specularcoefficient return color Color Ramp Modulation is a shading technique that alters the diffuse and specular color components of a material by sampling a 1D color ramp texture, using light intensity values as texture coordinates. It differs from standard Whitted-style shading by introducing non-linear color mapping based on illumination intensity, allowing for stylized or physically-inspired color shifts (e.g., darkening shadows or brightening highlights) without changing the underlying light transport model. It builds on Whitted-Style Shading with Diffuse/Glossy Materials. Inter-reflection Modeling is a technique for approximating indirect illumination in inverse rendering by tracing a single ray from a surface point in its reflective direction to a secondary intersection point, computing the radiance at that point, and blending it into the primary point's output. Unlike methods such as IRON and WildLight that assume collocated camera and light sources, this approach accommodates variations in both incident and outgoing light directions, making it suitable for non-collocated capture setups. A simple shading model that returns either emissive radiance or diffuse reflectance based on the material properties of the intersected object, using shadow rays to determine visibility. Models reflections on rough surfaces by distributing outgoing rays around the perfect mirror reflection direction, controlled by a shininess exponent \alpha. The outgoing radiance follows Lr(\vec{\omega}r) = Lr d\omegar(\max(\vec{R} \cdot \vec{\omega}r), 0)^\alpha, where \vec{R} is the perfect mirror reflection vector and \vec{\omega}r is the view direction. Traces reflected rays to simulate mirror-like reflections, limited to a maximum recursion depth (e.g., 1 bounce). The main shade function calculates the reflection direction rd = -normalize(reflect(p, n)) and adds reflected color weighted by a specular coefficient. Water reflects the sky it is under rather than a static authored color, making low sun angles optimal for lake visuals. Swimming underwater limits sight distance to 34 meters and removes red light from the scene. An alternative lighting mode using quantized, pre-computed normals stored in a second Mixture Graph, as opposed to on-the-fly computed opacity gradients using discrete differences. Computes per-pixel normals for a hybrid surface consisting of an initial isosurface and a newly generated cut surface, using a Phong fragment shader to ensure illumination quality. Normals are interpolated at vertices for the initial isosurface, approximated from volume gradients for cut triangles in tetrahedra containing the isosurface, and handled separately for other cut triangles. Approximates the rendering equation via stochastic estimation, targeting mirror-like objects and higher frequency integrands at higher computational cost. MC estimators can exhibit high variance and produce noisy pixel gradients at low sample counts, requiring N > 1000 samples for rougher surfaces. MC is preferred for metallic surfaces (\beta \to 0) because reflected rays are concentrated, while spherical Gaussian shading is preferred for rough surfaces (\beta \to 1). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple to implement, fast for scenes with few lights. Limitations: No indirect illumination, noisy for rough surfaces if using MC variants, limited recursion depth for reflections. When to use: Real-time rendering with static lighting, simple materials, or as a base for more complex models. When not to use: Scenes requiring soft shadows, global illumination, or highly complex material interactions. Originated from Whitted's 1980 paper "An Improved Illumination Model for Shaded Display". It is a foundational technique in ray tracing, extending the basic ray-object intersection to include reflection and refraction. In volume rendering, it is adapted to handle local illumination on volume boundaries or implicit surfaces. name: Color Ramp Modulation
body: Modulates diffuse and specular colors using a color ramp texture based on light intensity values. It builds on Whitted-Style Shading with Diffuse/Glossy Materials. Inputs: mColorRamp: Color ramp texture. light: 2D vector where x is diffuse intensity and y is specular intensity. diffuseColor: Base material diffuse color. specularColor: Base material specular color. Outputs: modulatedDiffuseColor: Diffuse color after ramp modulation. modulatedSpecularColor: Specular color after ramp modulation. Data Structures: ColorRamp: Texture storing RGB color values. LightValues: 2D vector vec2(x, y). Steps: 1. Sample color ramp for diffuse: C{\text{diff\mod}} = \text{sample}(m{\text{ColorRamp}}, \text{vec2}(light.x, 0.0)).\text{rgb}. 2. Sample color ramp for specular: C{\text{spec\mod}} = \text{sample}(m{\text{ColorRamp}}, \text{vec2}(light.y, 0.0)).\text{rgb}. 3. Reset light values to 1.0 after modulation: light.x = 1.0, light.y = 1.0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Inter-reflection Modeling
head: Flashlight Inter-reflection, Secondary Intersection Point Ray Marching
body: Inter-reflection Modeling approximates indirect illumination in inverse rendering by tracing a single ray from a surface point in its reflective direction to a secondary intersection point, computing the radiance at that point, and blending it into the primary point's output. Unlike methods such as IRON and WildLight that assume collocated camera and light sources, this approach accommodates variations in both incident and outgoing light directions, making it suitable for non-collocated capture setups. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Surface point x, surface normal n at x, view direction \omegai, light source position, Signed Distance Field (SDF) of the scene, roughness value for the point, a neural network (MLP) that predicts a blending coefficient \gamma, and the flashlight's incoming radiance L{ind}. Outputs: Indirect illumination component f{ir} added to the shading model. Data Structures SDF: A function SDF(p) returning the distance to the nearest surface, where negative values indicate interior space or occlusion. Blending Coefficient Network: An MLP that takes roughness as input and outputs a scalar blending coefficient \gamma. Steps 1. Compute Reflective Direction: Given the view direction \omegai and surface normal n, calculate the reflective direction \omegar: \omegar = 2(n \cdot \omegai)n - \omegai Note: The source formula \omegar = 2 \times n - \omegai is a simplified notation; the standard vector reflection formula is used here for mathematical correctness. 2. Trace Secondary Intersection: Cast a ray from x in direction \omegar to identify the secondary intersection point x'. 3. Occlusion Check: Determine if x' is occluded from the light source: Uniformly sample 20 points along the path between the light source and x'. Evaluate the SDF at each sampled point. If any sampled point has an SDF value < 0, the light is considered occluded (o{x'} = 0). Otherwise, the light is unobstructed (o{x'} = 1). 4. Compute Outgoing Radiance: If x' is unobstructed, compute the outgoing radiance at x' using the flashlight's incoming radiance L{ind}. The implementation adheres to a roughplastic BRDF model with a GGX distribution parameter. 5. Compute Blending Coefficient: Input the roughness property of the 3D point into the MLP to obtain the blending coefficient \gamma. 6. Combine Indirect Illumination: Calculate the indirect illumination component f{ir} by combining the outgoing radiance at x' with the blending coefficient \gamma and the occlusion term. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def normalize(v): length = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 return (v[0]/length, v[1]/length, v[2]/length) def raymarchsdf(origin, direction, sdf, maxsteps=1000, stepmin=1e-4, tol=1e-3): t = 0.0 p = origin for in range(maxsteps): d = sdf(p) if d < tol: return t t += max(d, stepmin) p = (origin[0] + direction[0]t, origin[1] + direction[1]t, origin[2] + direction[2]t) return float('inf') def computeinterreflection(x, n, wi, lightpos, sdf, roughnessmlp, roughness, Lind): # Step 1: Compute reflective direction wr = (2.0 dot(n, wi) n[0] - wi[0], 2.0 dot(n, wi) n[1] - wi[1], 2.0 dot(n, wi) n[2] - wi[2]) wr = normalize(wr) # Step 2: Trace secondary intersection point x' tprime = raymarchsdf(x, wr, sdf) if tprime == float('inf'): return 0.0 xprime = (x[0] + wr[0]tprime, x[1] + wr[1]tprime, x[2] + wr[2]tprime) # Step 3: Occlusion check numsamples = 20 occluded = False for i in range(numsamples): t = (i + 1) / (numsamples + 1) samplepoint = (lightpos[0] + (xprime[0]-lightpos[0])t, lightpos[1] + (xprime[1]-lightpos[1])t, lightpos[2] + (xprime[2]-lightpos[2])t) if sdf(samplepoint) < 0: occluded = True break if occluded: return 0.0 # Step 4: Compute outgoing radiance at x' using flashlight's incoming radiance Lind # Step 5: Compute blending coefficient gamma from roughness via MLP gamma = roughnessmlp(roughness) # Step 6: Combine to represent indirect illumination component fir fir = gamma Lind return fir Parameters Occlusion Samples: 20 points uniformly sampled between the light source and x'. Blending Coefficient \gamma: Output of an MLP conditioned on roughness. BRDF Model: Roughplastic model with GGX distribution parameter. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Optimization Ambiguity: Detaching the roughness of x' from the gradient flow into the blending coefficient network prevents correlation-induced ambiguity, leading to more precise material decomposition. Geometric Reconstruction: Disabling the optimization of local geometry at x' reduces optimization complexity and improves geometric reconstruction, especially in concave regions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Training requires approximately 9 hours on a single RTX 3090 GPU with 24GB of memory. Strengths: Handles non-collocated camera and light setups, unlike IRON and WildLight. Improves geometric reconstruction in concave areas by disabling local geometry optimization at x'. Limitations: Approximates indirect illumination with a single bounce. Inter-reflection Modeling was introduced in the context of Photometric Inverse Rendering with Shading Cues Modeling and Surface Reflectance Regularization (PIR). It builds upon previous methods like IRON and WildLight, which used simplified BRDF models and assumed collocated camera and light sources. The method was developed to address deviations in capture setups where the camera and light are not collocated. PIR: Photometric Inverse Rendering with Shading Cues Modeling and Surface Reflectance Regularization, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv66043.2025.00055, fetched 2026-10-26
