name: 3D Lookup Table Illumination Model
head: Henyey-Greenstein LUT
body: The 3D Lookup Table (LUT) Illumination Model approximates light transport in participating media by indexing a precomputed table with three angular parameters (\alpha, \beta, \gamma) derived from the surface normal, light direction, and view direction. It differs from sibling methods like Direct Illumination with Shadow Rays by replacing real-time integration of the scattering phase function with a fast trilinear texture lookup, allowing complex scattering models such as Henyey-Greenstein to be evaluated efficiently on the GPU. Inputs: Voxel position \mathbf{p}, view position \mathbf{v}, and surface normal \mathbf{n} (approximated from volume gradient). List of light sources, each with position \mathbf{p}L and color \mathbf{c}L. LUT resolution n and scattering parameter g (for Henyey-Greenstein). Reflection factor a{\text{FactorReflection}} and voxel albedo a{\text{Color}}. Outputs: Radiance contribution L at \mathbf{p}. Data Structures: 3D LUT: A 3D texture array of size n \times n \times n. Values are normalized to [0, 1] for CUDA compatibility. Reflection Texture: A 2D or 3D texture indexed by sample position for reflection properties. Steps: 1. Compute Normal: Approximate the normal \mathbf{n} as the negative gradient of the volume density, normalized to unit length: \mathbf{n} = -\frac{\nabla V}{\|\nabla V\|} The gradient can be computed via finite differences or a library like vol∇. 2. Compute Direction Vectors: Incoming light direction: \mathbf{L}i = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{p}L - \mathbf{p}). Outgoing (view) direction: \mathbf{L}o = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{p}). 3. Compute Angles: \alpha: Angle between \mathbf{n} and \mathbf{L}i: \alpha = \arccos(\langle \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{L}i \rangle) \beta: Angle between \mathbf{n} and \mathbf{L}o: \beta = \arccos(\langle \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{L}o \rangle) Project \mathbf{L}i and \mathbf{L}o onto the plane orthogonal to \mathbf{n}: \mathbf{L}i' = \mathbf{L}i - \langle \mathbf{L}i, \mathbf{n} \rangle \mathbf{n} \mathbf{L}o' = \mathbf{L}o - \langle \mathbf{L}o, \mathbf{n} \rangle \mathbf{n} \gamma: Angle between the projected vectors \mathbf{L}i' and \mathbf{L}o': \gamma = \arccos\left( \frac{\langle \mathbf{L}i', \mathbf{L}o' \rangle}{\|\mathbf{L}i'\| \|\mathbf{L}o'\|} \right) Note: If \|\mathbf{L}i'\| or \|\mathbf{L}o'\| is zero (vectors parallel to normal), \gamma is undefined; handle as a degenerate case. 4. LUT Indexing: The angles are constrained to [0, \pi] due to symmetry. Map them to LUT coordinates a, b, c \in [0, n]: a = \frac{\alpha \cdot n}{\pi}, \quad b = \frac{\beta \cdot n}{\pi}, \quad c = \frac{\gamma \cdot n}{\pi} The LUT value is retrieved via trilinear interpolation: \text{light} = \text{TrilinearInterpolate}(\text{LUT}, a, b, c) The LUT is precomputed such that \text{LUT}(a, b, c) = HG(\theta, g), where \theta is the scattering angle derived from rotating \mathbf{L}o around \mathbf{n} by \gamma and computing the dot product with fixed \mathbf{L}i: \theta = \arccos(\langle R{\mathbf{n}} \mathbf{L}o, \mathbf{L}i \rangle). 5. Final Contribution: Combine the LUT lookup with reflection and albedo: \text{result} \leftarrow \text{result} + (a{\text{FactorReflection}} \cdot \text{ReflectionTexture}(\mathbf{p}) \cdot \text{light} \cdot \mathbf{c}L \cdot a{\text{Color}}) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def shade3dlut(aposition, aviewposition, asurfacenormal, acolor, alightsources, afactorreflection, luttexture, reflectiontexture, lutres): """ Calculate illumination at a voxel using 3D LUT. aposition: vec3, voxel position aviewposition: vec3, camera/view position asurfacenormal: vec3, normalized gradient normal acolor: vec3, voxel albedo alightsources: list of dicts with 'position' and 'color' afactorreflection: float, reflection scaling factor luttexture: 3D texture object, size lutres x lutres x lutres reflectiontexture: 2D/3D texture object lutres: int, LUT resolution """ result = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) n = normalize(asurfacenormal) for lightsource in alightsources: # 1. Compute directions lightout = normalize(lightsource['position'] - aposition) lightin = normalize(aviewposition - aposition) # 2. Compute angles alpha, beta, gamma alpha = acos(dot(n, lightout)) beta = acos(dot(n, lightin)) # Project vectors onto plane orthogonal to normal lightoutproj = lightout - dot(lightout, n) n lightinproj = lightin - dot(lightin, n) n normout = length(lightoutproj) normin = length(lightinproj) if normout > 1e-6 and normin > 1e-6: lightoutproj = lightoutproj / normout lightinproj = lightinproj / normin gamma = acos(dot(lightoutproj, lightinproj)) else: # Degenerate case: light or view is parallel to normal gamma = 0.0 # 3. Map angles to LUT coordinates [0, lutres] idxa = clamp(alpha lutres / pi, 0.0, lutres) idxb = clamp(beta lutres / pi, 0.0, lutres) idxc = clamp(gamma lutres / pi, 0.0, lutres) # 4. Lookup illumination (trilinear interpolation handled by sampler) lightintensity = luttexture.sampletrilinear(idxa, idxb, idxc) # 5. Lookup reflection reflection = afactorreflection reflectiontexture.sample(aposition) # 6. Accumulate result contribution = reflection lightintensity lightsource['color'] acolor result += contribution return result Parameters: n: LUT resolution. g: Henyey-Greenstein asymmetry parameter, used during LUT precomputation. Angle range: \alpha, \beta, \gamma \in [0, \pi]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parallel Vectors: If \mathbf{L}i or \mathbf{L}o is parallel to \mathbf{n}, the projection is zero, making \gamma undefined; the pseudocode handles this by setting \gamma=0. Precision: LUT values must be normalized to [0, 1] for CUDA texture sampling. Symmetry: The model relies on symmetry to restrict angles to [0, \pi], reducing LUT size. Time Complexity: O(1) per light source per voxel, dominated by texture lookups and vector math. Memory Complexity: O(n^3) for the LUT. Strengths: Fast evaluation of complex phase functions (e.g., Henyey-Greenstein); decouples scattering physics from rendering loop. Limitations: Approximation error depends on LUT resolution n; cannot handle anisotropic scattering beyond the parameterized model; requires precomputation. The method was introduced in a 2024 paper titled "GPU-Enabled Volume Renderer for Use with MATLAB". It builds on the principle that light-particle interaction can be fully described by three angles relative to the surface normal. The LUT is typically precomputed using the Henyey-Greenstein phase function, allowing the renderer to query pre-integrated scattering results. name: Spot Light with Cone Falloff
head: Delta Spot Light, Spot Light Falloff Computation
body: This method computes the attenuation factor for a point light source that emits light within a specific cone direction, applying smooth falloff based on the angle between the light direction and the vector to the shading point. It solves the problem of directional intensity variation in local illumination for participating media, treating the source as a delta light. It is distinguished from area lights by its zero-size emission model and from uniform point lights by its angular dependency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The light source direction vector \mathbf{d}{light} (a 4D vector where the w-component indicates spotlight status) and the light vector \mathbf{l} (the normalized direction from the shading point \mathbf{p} to the light source). Output: A scalar attenuation factor f{spot} \in [0, 1] representing the intensity multiplier. Data Structures: The light direction is stored as a 4D vector \mathbf{g}{LightDirection} = (x, y, z, w). If w \neq 0.0, the light is a spotlight. If w = 0.0, the light is a standard point light (no spot falloff applied). Steps: 1. Check Spotlight Status: Determine if the light is a spotlight by inspecting the w-component of the light direction vector. If g{LightDirection}.w == 0.0, the light is not a spotlight. Return attenuation factor 1.0 (or skip spot calculation). If g{LightDirection}.w \neq 0.0, proceed to compute falloff. 2. Compute Spot Falloff: Calculate the angular attenuation based on the dot product of the light direction and the light vector. Let \mathbf{d} be the normalized light direction (g{LightDirection}.x, g{LightDirection}.y, g{LightDirection}.z). Let \mathbf{l} be the normalized vector from the shading point to the light source. Compute the dot product: dot = \mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{l}. The sources indicate a "smooth cone falloff" is implemented. While the exact exponent or cutoff formula is not explicitly detailed in the provided text, standard implementations typically use a power function of the dot product relative to a cutoff angle \theta{cutoff}: f{spot} = \max(0.0, \frac{dot - \cos(\theta{cutoff})}{1.0 - \cos(\theta{cutoff})})^{\gamma} where \gamma is the exponent controlling the softness of the edge. The sources confirm the existence of this computation via computeSpotFalloff. 3. Optional IES Profile Blending: If an IES (Illuminating Engineering Society) profile is provided, blend the computed geometric spot falloff with the photometric profile data. The IES parser supports TILT=INCLUDE skipping and symmetry folding (0/90/180/360). The final attenuation is the product of the geometric spot falloff and the IES intensity value at the corresponding angle. 4. Discard if Zero: If the computed spot falloff f{spot} \leq 0.0, discard the lighting contribution entirely. Set the color to ambient only and return. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computespotfalloff(gLightDirection, lightVec): # gLightDirection is a 4D vector (x, y, z, w) # lightVec is the normalized direction from point to light # Step 1: Check if spotlight if gLightDirection.w == 0.0: return 1.0 # Not a spotlight, full intensity # Step 2: Compute geometric spot falloff # Extract 3D direction vector lightDir = normalize(Vector3(gLightDirection.x, gLightDirection.y, gLightDirection.z)) # Dot product between light direction and vector to point dot = dotproduct(lightDir, lightVec) # Smooth cone falloff implementation # Note: Exact cutoff angle and exponent are not specified in sources # Assuming standard smooth falloff logic cutoffcos = 0.5 # Placeholder for typical cutoff, e.g., 60 degrees exponent = 2.0 # Placeholder for typical exponent if dot < cutoffcos: spotFalloff = 0.0 else: # Linear interpolation in cosine space, raised to power ratio = (dot - cutoffcos) / (1.0 - cutoffcos) spotFalloff = pow(ratio, exponent) # Step 3: Blend with IES profile if available # IES lookup logic is not detailed in sources if hasiesprofile(): iesintensity = getiesintensity(lightDir) spotFalloff = iesintensity return spotFalloff def applyspotlighting(gLightDirection, lightVec, ambientColor): falloff = computespotfalloff(gLightDirection, lightVec) # Step 4: Discard if zero if falloff <= 0.0: return ambientColor # Direct lighting calculation (e.g., color falloff) is assumed # but not explicitly detailed in the provided snippets beyond the falloff directColor = computedirectlight(falloff) return ambientColor + directColor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Ensure the dot product is clamped to [-1.0, 1.0] before passing to inverse cosine or power functions to avoid NaNs. Boundary: The transition at the cone edge depends on the exponent; a low exponent creates a hard edge, while a high exponent creates a soft edge. Degenerate Input: If the light direction vector is zero, normalization will fail. Ensure \mathbf{d} is non-zero before normalization. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(1) per shading point. The calculation involves a few vector operations (dot product, normalization) and a power function. Memory: O(1) additional memory. No large data structures are required unless an IES profile is loaded, which is static per light source. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of shading points. Independent of scene complexity as it is a local illumination model. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Computationally cheap; provides realistic directional lighting effects; supports photometric accuracy via IES profiles. Limitations: Delta light approximation may cause aliasing in shadows if not sampled carefully; does not account for light scattering within the cone volume (only attenuation at the point). When to Use: Use when directional, focused lighting is required (e.g., spotlights, flashlights) in a volume rendering context. Avoid when soft, volumetric light beams (god rays) are needed, as this method only computes point attenuation, not volumetric scattering. Origin: The method is part of modern physically-based rendering engines that support volumetric effects. It is implemented in the photon-engine project, which adds volumetric rendering and advanced materials. History and Development: The implementation includes support for IES LM-63 profiles, allowing for real-world photometric data integration. The concept of spot lights with cone falloff is a standard technique in computer graphics, adapted here for delta lights in participating media. Where it is used: Used in the photon-engine for local illumination in volumetric scenes. Also referenced in the cubes project for basic spotlight functionality. destroflyer/cubes, https://github.com/destroflyer/cubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Add volumetric rendering, advanced materials, and imager effects, https://github.com/MihrimatriX/photon-engine/pull/3, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Two-Pass Shadow Casting (Kajiya and Von Herzen)
head: Kajiya and Von Herzen Method, Shadow Calculation via Illumination Pass, Shadow Casting via Two-Pass Method, Two-Pass Numerical Algorithm for Shadows, Two-Pass Numerical Shadow Algorithm
body: The Two-Pass Shadow Casting method, introduced by Kajiya and Von Herzen, computes shadows in participating media by decoupling light transport into an illumination pass and a gathering pass. It solves the problem of realistic shadowing in volume rendering, where light is attenuated by the medium itself, by propagating flux from the light source through the volume layer-by-layer before scattering it to the viewpoint. Unlike recursive ray tracing, which sends individual "shadow feelers" to the light source for every point along the viewing ray, this method integrates the shadowing effect globally along the ray, allowing the illumination pass to be amortized over multiple frames if only the viewpoint moves. The method evaluates the rendering equation for a single scattering event, accounting for the transparency of the volume between the light source and the point of interest, and between that point and the viewpoint. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volume density field \tau(\mathbf{x}) (extinction coefficient). Light source intensity L (assumed infinite/directional for the base formulation). Light direction -\omega' (unit vector pointing from the volume to the light). Viewpoint position \mathbf{X} and viewing direction -\omega (unit vector pointing from the volume to the camera). Shading rule r(\mathbf{x}, \omega, \omega') (phase function or reflectance model). Background intensity I0. Ray length D (distance from viewpoint to the far plane or volume boundary). Outputs: Final pixel intensity I(\mathbf{X}). Data Structures: The volume is typically represented as a 3D grid or voxel array where each cell stores the extinction coefficient \tau. The algorithm processes the volume "one voxel layer at a time" relative to the light direction. This implies iterating through the volume along the axis defined by the light direction \omega', or using a spatial partitioning structure that allows efficient traversal in that direction. Numbered Steps: 1. Pass 1: Illumination Calculation Compute the illumination i(\mathbf{X}, \omega') reaching each point \mathbf{X} in the volume from the light source. This involves propagating flux from the light source through the volume, accounting for the transparency of each layer before propagating to the next. The illumination at point \mathbf{X} from an infinite light source L in direction -\omega' is given by: i(\mathbf{X}, \omega') = L \exp\left(-\int0^\infty \tau(\mathbf{X} - t\omega') \, dt\right) In practice, the integral does not run to infinity but only to the edge of the data volume. Numerically, this is approximated by summing \tau \cdot \Delta s along the ray from the light source entry point to \mathbf{X}. 2. Pass 2: Gathering (Scattering to Viewpoint) Reflect or scatter the computed illumination i(\mathbf{X}, \omega') to the viewpoint using the shading rule g(\mathbf{X}, \omega) = r(\mathbf{X}, \omega, \omega') i(\mathbf{X}, \omega'). Gather the reflected intensity g(\mathbf{X}, \omega) along viewing rays. To simplify the integration, the ray parameterization is reversed so that the parameter s starts at the viewpoint \mathbf{X} and goes out in direction -\omega, reaching \mathbf{X} - s\omega at distance s. The final intensity I(\mathbf{X}) is calculated as: I(\mathbf{X}) = I0 \exp\left(-\int0^D \tau(\mathbf{X} - t\omega) \, dt\right) + \int0^D r(\mathbf{X} - s\omega, \omega, \omega') L \exp\left(-\int0^\infty \tau(\mathbf{X} - s\omega - t\omega') \, dt\right) \exp\left(-\int0^s \tau(\mathbf{X} - t\omega) \, dt\right) \, ds Here: The first term is the background intensity attenuated by the volume along the view ray. The integral term represents the light scattered from the volume into the view direction. The term \exp\left(-\int0^\infty \tau(\mathbf{X} - s\omega - t\omega') \, dt\right) represents the illumination i(\mathbf{X} - s\omega, \omega') at the scattering point \mathbf{X} - s\omega. The term \exp\left(-\int0^s \tau(\mathbf{X} - t\omega) \, dt\right) represents the transmittance from the scattering point to the viewpoint. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def twopassshadowcasting(taugrid, volumebounds, lightdir, viewdir, viewpoint, backgroundintensity, phasefunc, raylength, stepsize): """ Computes volumetric shadows using the Kajiya and Von Herzen two-pass method. Args: taugrid: 3D array of extinction coefficients tau(x). volumebounds: Tuple (minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz) defining the volume. lightdir: Unit vector omega' pointing from volume to light. viewdir: Unit vector omega pointing from volume to camera. viewpoint: 3D position of the camera X. backgroundintensity: Scalar I0. phasefunc: Function r(x, omega, omega') returning scattering coefficient. raylength: Distance D from viewpoint to far plane. stepsize: Sampling interval Delta s. Returns: Final intensity I(X). """ def sampletau(pos): x, y, z = pos if (volumebounds[0] <= x < volumebounds[1] and volumebounds[2] <= y < volumebounds[3] and volumebounds[4] <= z < volumebounds[5]): return taugrid[x, y, z] return 0.0 # Pass 1: Precompute Illumination Field # Propagate flux from light source through the volume, one voxel layer at a time. # We iterate over voxels sorted by projection onto lightdir to simulate layer traversal. illuminationfield = [[0.0 for in range(volumebounds[1]-volumebounds[0])] for in range(volumebounds[3]-volumebounds[2])] # Collect voxel centers and sort by light direction for layer-by-layer propagation voxels = [] for x in range(volumebounds[0], volumebounds[1]): for y in range(volumebounds[2], volumebounds[3]): for z in range(volumebounds[4], volumebounds[5]): voxels.append((x, y, z)) voxels.sort(key=lambda v: v[0]lightdir[0] + v[1]lightdir[1] + v[2]lightdir[2]) for X in voxels: opticaldepth = 0.0 pos = list(X) # March from X in direction lightdir to the volume boundary while (volumebounds[0] <= pos[0] < volumebounds[1] and volumebounds[2] <= pos[1] < volumebounds[3] and volumebounds[4] <= pos[2] < volumebounds[5]): opticaldepth += sampletau(tuple(pos)) stepsize pos[0] += lightdir[0] stepsize pos[1] += lightdir[1] stepsize pos[2] += lightdir[2] stepsize illuminationfield[X[0]-volumebounds[0]][X[1]-volumebounds[2]] = backgroundintensity exp(-opticaldepth) # Pass 2: Gather Scattered Light along view ray scatteringintegral = 0.0 transmittanceview = 1.0 currentpos = list(viewpoint) # Iterate s from 0 to raylength numsteps = int(raylength / stepsize) for s in range(numsteps): scatteringpoint = [viewpoint[0] - viewdir[0] s stepsize, viewpoint[1] - viewdir[1] s stepsize, viewpoint[2] - viewdir[2] s stepsize] if (volumebounds[0] <= scatteringpoint[0] < volumebounds[1] and volumebounds[2] <= scatteringpoint[1] < volumebounds[3] and volumebounds[4] <= scatteringpoint[2] < volumebounds[5]): # Retrieve precomputed illumination iscatter = illuminationfield[int(scatteringpoint[0]-volumebounds[0])][int(scatteringpoint[1]-volumebounds[2])] # Phase function evaluation rval = phasefunc(scatteringpoint, viewdir, lightdir) # Accumulate scattering integral: r i Tview ds scatteringintegral += rval iscatter transmittanceview stepsize # Update transmittance from camera to current scattering point tauval = sampletau(scatteringpoint) transmittanceview = exp(-tauval stepsize) currentpos[0] += viewdir[0] stepsize currentpos[1] += viewdir[1] stepsize currentpos[2] += viewdir[2] stepsize backgroundterm = backgroundintensity transmittanceview return backgroundterm + scatteringintegral Parameters: Light Intensity (L): Typically normalized to 1.0 or based on physical units. Ray Length (D): Determined by the volume bounds or camera clipping planes. Step Size (\Delta s): Determined by the voxel size or a fixed sampling rate. Smaller steps increase accuracy but cost more. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Scattering: The method is a single-scattering model. It is only valid if the albedo or density is low, so that multiple scattering is unlikely. It is not suitable for dense media like atmospheric clouds where multiple scattering is significant. Performance: The method takes only twice as long as the gathering pass without shadows. Amortization: The illumination pass can be amortized over several animated frames if only the viewpoint moves. Boundary Conditions: The integral for illumination runs to the edge of the data volume, not infinity. The Two-pass Spectral Rendering Integral is a method for computing volumetric shadows in participating media by adapting the Kajiya and von Herzen two-pass algorithm to spectral representation. It separates shadow computation (illumination phase) from radiance accumulation (radiation phase), allowing for the simulation of complex spectral effects such as fluorescence and phosphorescence. It is distinguished from its parent Two-Pass Shadow Casting (Kajiya and Von Herzen) by its explicit handling of wavelength-dependent opacity and emission spectra. Time Complexity: The method takes only twice as long as the gathering pass without shadows. This is significantly faster than recursive ray tracing for dense volumes, as it avoids sending shadow feelers for every sample point. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the illumination field for the entire volume, which is O(N) where N is the number of voxels. Strengths: Provides realistic shadows in participating media. Efficient for static lights and moving viewpoints, as the illumination pass can be amortized. Simpler to implement than full path tracing for single-scattering scenarios. Limitations: Single-scattering only; inaccurate for high-density or high-albedo media. Requires precomputing the illumination field, which can be memory-intensive for large volumes. Less flexible for dynamic lights compared to ray casting methods. When to Use: Suitable for medical imaging (e.g., Heidelberg ray tracing model) and scenes with low-density participating media where single scattering is a good approximation. When Not to Use: Unsuitable for atmospheric clouds or dense fog where multiple scattering is dominant. The two-pass numerical algorithm for shadows was suggested by Kajiya and Von Herzen. It was introduced as a more general approach to account for shadows in volume rendering, moving beyond simpler shading models that ignored volume transparency between the light and the point of interest. The method has been systematically applied to medical images in the "Heidelberg ray tracing model" by Meinzer et al.. While its utility in general volume rendering applications has been questioned due to the prevalence of multiple scattering in natural media like clouds, it remains a foundational technique for single-scattering shadow computation. name: Two-pass Spectral Rendering Integral
head: Noordmans Spectral Shadow Algorithm, Spectral Two-Pass Shadow Casting
body: The Two-pass Spectral Rendering Integral computes volumetric shadows in participating media by adapting the Kajiya and von Herzen two-pass algorithm to a spectral representation. It separates shadow computation from radiance accumulation, distinguishing itself from its parent method through explicit wavelength-dependent opacity and emission spectra. Inputs: Mass density field \rhom(x) for each material m. Spectral absorption attributes \kappam(\lambda) for each material m. Incident light spectrum It(x, \lambda) at the volume entry. Local emission spectrum Ie(x, \lambda). Step size \Delta x. Wavelengths \lambda. Outputs: Final radiance Ir(x, \lambda) for each sample point. Data Structures: Spectral opacity \tau(x, \lambda): Computed per sample point. Transmitted light It(x, \lambda): Accumulator for the illumination phase. Backward irradiance Ib(x, \lambda): Accumulator for the radiation phase. Radiance Ir(x, \lambda): Output accumulator. Spectral Opacity Definition: For a position x with M materials, the spectral opacity is defined as: \tau(x, \lambda) = \sum{m=1}^M \rhom(x) \cdot \kappam(\lambda) Algorithm Steps: 1. Illumination Phase (Shadow Computation): Propagate light flux through the volume using discrete front-to-back ray casting. For each sample step \Delta x at position x, update the transmitted light It: It(x + \Delta x, \lambda) = It(x, \lambda) \cdot (1 - \Delta x \cdot \tau(x, \lambda)) The resulting It at the end of the ray represents the shadowed incident light for the radiation phase. 2. Radiation Phase (Radiance Accumulation): Accumulate radiance using back-to-front ray casting. For each sample step \Delta x at position x, update the radiance Ir based on the local emission Ie and the backward irradiance Ib: Ib(x+\Delta x, \lambda) = Ir(x, \lambda) = Ie(x, \lambda) + Ib(x, \lambda) \cdot (1 - \Delta x \cdot \tau(x, \lambda)) Here, Ib(x, \lambda) acts as the accumulated background/transmitted light term. Parameters: Step size \Delta x: Not given in the sources. Number of materials M: Not given in the sources. Wavelength discretization: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The term (1 - \Delta x \cdot \tau(x, \lambda)) used in both phases is only an approximation. Degenerate inputs (e.g., zero density or infinite step size) require clamping to prevent negative or unphysical radiance values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def twopassspectralrendering(densities, absorptionattrs, incidentlight, stepsize, wavelengths): # densities: list of lists, densities[m][x] for material m at sample x # absorptionattrs: list of lists, absorptionattrs[m][w] for material m at wavelength w # incidentlight: list of floats, It at entry for each wavelength # stepsize: float Delta x # wavelengths: list of floats numsamples = len(densities[0]) numwavelengths = len(wavelengths) nummaterials = len(densities) # Precompute spectral opacity tau[x][w] tau = [[0.0] numwavelengths for in range(numsamples)] for x in range(numsamples): for w in range(numwavelengths): for m in range(nummaterials): tau[x][w] += densities[m][x] absorptionattrs[m][w] # Phase 1: Illumination (Front-to-Back) It = list(incidentlight) for x in range(numsamples - 1): for w in range(numwavelengths): It[w] = It[w] (1.0 - stepsize tau[x][w]) # Phase 2: Radiation (Back-to-Front) Ib = [0.0] numwavelengths Ir = [0.0] numwavelengths for x in range(numsamples - 1, -1, -1): # Sources do not specify the exact emission function formula. # Typically combines elastic scattering (material-specific spectral bands) # and inelastic scattering (fluorescence/phosphorescence). Ie = [0.0] numwavelengths for w in range(numwavelengths): Ir[w] = Ie[w] + Ib[w] (1.0 - stepsize tau[x][w]) Ib = list(Ir) return Ir Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows for spectral effects like fluorescence and material-specific absorption. Limitations: The linear approximation (1 - \Delta x \cdot \tau) is only an approximation. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was proposed by Noordmans et al., who adopted the Kajiya and von Herzen two-pass algorithm for volumetric shadows and adapted the notion of opacity to a spectral representation. It is described in the context of local and global illumination in the volume rendering integral. name: Ray-marched Volumetric Lighting with Density Thresholding
head: Light Intensity Volume, Volumetric Light Map Precomputation
body: This method precomputes light intensities and shadows within a 3D volume based on a global light source's direction, color, decay, and a density mask, storing the result in a 3D texture for use during rendering. It differs from its siblings by using a GPU compute shader to ray-march from each voxel in the light texture space towards the global light direction, accumulating density and applying exponential decay. Unlike Light Propagation Volume which propagates optical depth radially, or Pseudo Volume Textures with Per-Voxel Lighting which recomputes lighting per frame via secondary ray marches, this method performs a single precomputation pass per light source direction to generate a static light map volume. Inputs: lightdensitytexture: A 3D RenderTexture (format R8, wrap Clamp, filter Bilinear) of dimensions lightmapresolution (x, y, z). masktexture3D: A 3D texture representing the density mask, accessed via solver.densityrt with dimensions masktexturedims. noisetexture3D: A 3D texture containing noise data, accessed via worleynoisetexture. globallightdirection: A float3 vector defining the direction of the light source. globallightcolor: A float3 vector defining the color of the light. lightdecay: A float controlling the rate of exponential light attenuation per unit density. godraysintensity: A float scalar applied to simulate god rays. lightsamplecount: An integer determining the number of samples for light computation. densitythreshold: A float used to filter noise; densities below this value are treated as transparent unless god rays conditions are met. Outputs: lightdensitytexture: The resulting 3D volume where each voxel stores the computed light intensity. Data Structures: The core data structure is the lightdensitytexture, a 3D texture with R8 format. The dimensions are defined by lightmapresolution. The mask and noise textures are also 3D textures, accessed via specific indices mapped from the light texture coordinates. Parameters: lightmapresolution: Vector3 defining the resolution of the 3D light map volume. lightdecay: Float, range [0, 100]. godraysstrength: Float, range [0, 0.03f]. lightsamplecount: Integer, range [0, 128]. densitythreshold: Float, range [0, 1]. lightcolor: Vector3. lightdirection: Vector3. lighttexturedims: float3 dimensions of the light density texture space. masktexturedims: float3 dimensions of the mask texture. Steps: 1. Initialize: Create lightdensitytexture with dimensions lightmapresolution. Set format to R8, wrap to Clamp, filter to Bilinear. Enable random write. Bind to material property LightTexture. 2. Dispatch Kernel: Find kernel "computelightintensities". Set texture size params noisetexturesizex/y/z. Set light params lighttexturedims, globallightdirection, globallightcolor, lightdecay, godraysintensity, stepsize (calculated as 1.0f / lightsamplecount), densitythreshold. Bind lightdensitytexture to lightmap3D, noisetexture3D to worleynoisetexture, masktexture3D to solver.densityrt. Dispatch with thread groups Mathf.CeilToInt(lightmapresolution.x / 8), Mathf.CeilToInt(lightmapresolution.y / 8), Mathf.CeilToInt(lightmapresolution.z / 8). 3. Loop Initialization: For each voxel id in the 3D grid: currentcoordinates = id (voxel index). density = 0.0. densitysofar = 0.0. lightintensity = 1.0. normalizedlightdirection = normalize(globallightdirection). scaledstepsize = lighttexturedims.x stepsize. maxiteration = 256. 4. Ray Marching Loop: While !isfragoutboundries and maxiteration >= 0: Sample noisedensity from noisetexture3D at the current coordinates. Sample mask from masktexture3D at the current coordinates. Apply Mask and Threshold: density = min(1, mask - abs(densitythreshold)) noisedensity. Accumulate Density: densitysofar += density. Apply God Rays Logic: If density < densitythreshold and densitysofar < 0.5: density = godraysintensity. Else if density < densitythreshold: density = 0.0. Update Light Intensity: lightintensity = exp(-density lightdecay stepsize). Advance Ray: currentcoordinates += -normalizedlightdirection scaledstepsize. Check Boundary: isfragoutboundries = currentcoordinates.x >= lighttexturedims.x OR currentcoordinates.y >= lighttexturedims.y OR currentcoordinates.z >= lighttexturedims.z OR currentcoordinates.x < 0 OR currentcoordinates.y < 0 OR currentcoordinates.z < 0. 5. Write Result: lightdensitytexture[id] = lightintensity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computelightintensities(idx, idy, idz, lightmap3d, masktexture3d, noisetexture3d, lighttexturedims, globallightdirection, lightdecay, godraysintensity, stepsize, densitythreshold): # Initialize loop variables currentcoordinates = [idx, idy, idz] density = 0.0 densitysofar = 0.0 lightintensity = 1.0 normalizedlightdirection = [d / math.sqrt(sum(dd for d in globallightdirection)) for d in globallightdirection] scaledstepsize = lighttexturedims[0] stepsize maxiteration = 256 # Check initial boundary isfragoutboundries = ( currentcoordinates[0] >= lighttexturedims[0] or currentcoordinates[1] >= lighttexturedims[1] or currentcoordinates[2] >= lighttexturedims[2] or currentcoordinates[0] < 0 or currentcoordinates[1] < 0 or currentcoordinates[2] < 0) # Ray marching loop while not isfragoutboundries and maxiteration >= 0: maxiteration -= 1 # Sample textures at current coordinates noisedensity = noisetexture3d[currentcoordinates[0], currentcoordinates[1], currentcoordinates[2]] mask = masktexture3d[currentcoordinates[0], currentcoordinates[1], currentcoordinates[2]] # Apply mask and threshold filtering density = min(1.0, mask - abs(densitythreshold)) noisedensity # Accumulate density densitysofar += density # Apply god rays logic if density < densitythreshold and densitysofar < 0.5: density = godraysintensity elif density < densitythreshold: density = 0.0 # Update light intensity using exponential decay lightintensity = math.exp(-density lightdecay stepsize) # Advance ray currentcoordinates[0] -= normalizedlightdirection[0] scaledstepsize currentcoordinates[1] -= normalizedlightdirection[1] scaledstepsize currentcoordinates[2] -= normalizedlightdirection[2] scaledstepsize # Check boundary conditions isfragoutboundries = ( currentcoordinates[0] >= lighttexturedims[0] or currentcoordinates[1] >= lighttexturedims[1] or currentcoordinates[2] >= lighttexturedims[2] or currentcoordinates[0] < 0 or currentcoordinates[1] < 0 or currentcoordinates[2] < 0) # Write result lightmap3d[idx, idy, idz] = lightintensity This method implements direct volume rendering using 2D textures containing tiles that represent low-resolution 2D slices of the volume, referred to as 'pseudo volume textures'. It solves the problem of rendering dynamic volumetric data by allowing the volume to be "painted" at runtime. It differs from true 3D volume textures by restricting effective maximum volume resolution further, but distinguishes itself from its parent Ray-marched Volumetric Lighting with Density Thresholding by recomputing lighting for each frame via secondary ray marches for every voxel sample. Light Propagation Volume (LPV), specifically the Opacity Propagation Volume (OPV) variant, is a real-time method for precomputing the optical depth T(S,X) from each light source S to each cell X in a 3D grid. It solves the problem of efficiently calculating light attenuation (extinction) through heterogeneous participating media by propagating density information radially from light sources through a 3D volume on the GPU. Unlike standard radiance propagation which suffers from rapid scattering errors in dense media, OPV focuses on accurate optical depth integration, enabling correct shadowing and attenuation for subsequent ray-marched rendering. It builds on Ray-marched Volumetric Lighting with Density Thresholding by providing the precomputed attenuation data required for that rendering step. Time and Memory Complexity: The time complexity is proportional to the number of voxels in the light map volume multiplied by the number of samples per ray (lightsamplecount). The memory complexity is proportional to the size of the 3D light map texture (lightmapresolution.x lightmapresolution.y lightmapresolution.z bytes, assuming R8 format). Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method scales with the resolution of the light map volume and the number of samples. Higher resolutions and sample counts increase accuracy but also increase computation time and memory usage. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths include efficient precomputation of volumetric lighting and shadows, suitable for static or slowly changing volumes. Limitations include the static nature of the light map, which may not adapt well to dynamic lighting or rapidly changing volume densities without recomputation. When to Use: Use this method when rendering static or slowly changing volumetric scenes with a global light source, where precomputed lighting is acceptable and dynamic lighting is not required. When Not to Use: Do not use this method for dynamic volumetric scenes with changing light sources or rapidly changing densities, as the precomputed light map will become outdated. This method originates from the project "VolumetricSmoke" by furkanunsal42, an unofficial source. It is a GPU compute shader technique designed to simulate light attenuation through a volumetric medium by ray-marching from each voxel in the light texture space towards the global light direction, accumulating density and applying Beer-Lambert-like exponential decay. furkanunsal42/VolumetricSmoke, https://github.com/furkanunsal42/VolumetricSmoke, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Direct-volume raycasting, https://met3d.readthedocs.io/en/latest/05developermanual/03actors/algorithms/directvolumerendering.html, fetched 2026-10-27 Building beautiful worlds across platforms with PlayCanvas and the Magnopus Web Renderer; featuring volumetric lighting — Mag..., https://www.magnopus.com/blog/building-beautiful-worlds-across-platforms-with-playcanvas-and-the-magnopus-web-renderer-featuring-volumetric-lighting, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Pseudo Volume Textures with Per-Voxel Lighting
head: Custom Implementation (Pseudo Volume Textures with Per-Voxel Lighting), Direct Volume Rendering with Pseudo Volume Textures, Pseudo Volume Textures, YouTube tutorial series based on ShaderBits Blog
body: This method implements direct volume rendering using 2D textures containing tiles that represent low-resolution 2D slices of the volume, referred to as 'pseudo volume textures'. It solves the problem of rendering dynamic volumetric data by allowing the volume to be "painted" at runtime. It differs from true 3D volume textures by restricting effective maximum volume resolution further, but distinguishes itself from its parent Ray-marched Volumetric Lighting with Density Thresholding by recomputing lighting for each frame via secondary ray marches for every voxel sample. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D texture atlas (pseudo volume texture) containing tiled 2D slices of the volume data. Input: Primary ray direction and origin for the viewer. Input: Light source position and direction. Output: Final color buffer with per-voxel lighting. Data Structures: Pseudo Volume Texture: A 2D texture where each tile represents a 2D slice of the volume. The resolution is lower than a true 3D volume texture. Voxel Sample: A point along the primary ray intersecting the volume. Steps: 1. For each pixel in the screen space, cast a primary ray into the volume. 2. Sample the pseudo volume texture along the primary ray to obtain voxel density and color data. 3. For each voxel sample taken along the primary ray, perform a secondary ray march towards the light source. 4. Accumulate lighting along the secondary ray to determine the illumination for the current voxel sample. 5. Composite the lit voxel color into the final pixel color. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Tile size and resolution of the pseudo volume texture: Not given in the sources. Step size for primary and secondary ray marches: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Recomputing lighting per frame causes prohibitive performance impact for larger volumes. Effective maximum volume resolution is restricted compared to true volume textures. Adding a precomputed lighting cache that is only updated on voxel content or light source change would require an additional render pass and custom C++ and shader code, which is not straightforward anymore. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderpseudovolumetexture(pseudovolumetexture, primaryray, lightsource): # 1. Cast primary ray and sample volume voxelsamples = samplevolumealongray(pseudovolumetexture, primaryray) finalcolor = vec3(0.0) for sample in voxelsamples: # 2. Perform secondary ray march towards light source # This step is performed for each voxel sample taken along the primary ray lighting = computelightingviasecondaryraymarch(sample.position, lightsource) # 3. Composite lit color # Specific blending formula not given in sources samplecolor = sample.color lighting finalcolor = composite(finalcolor, samplecolor) return finalcolor def computelightingviasecondaryraymarch(voxelposition, lightsource): # Secondary ray march towards the light source # Accumulate density and apply lighting # Specific algorithm details not given in sources pass An optimization where lighting is precomputed and updated only on voxel content or light source changes. It requires an additional render pass and custom C++ and shader code. An existing plugin for Unreal Engine based on an implementation by Sundén and Ropinski. Time Complexity: Prohibitive for larger volumes due to the per-voxel secondary ray march for lighting. Memory Complexity: Restricted by the 2D texture atlas structure, limiting effective maximum volume resolution compared to true volume textures. Strengths: Allows runtime "painting" of the volume, making it fully dynamic. Limitations: Performance impact is prohibitive for larger volumes; effective maximum volume resolution is restricted. When to use: When dynamic volume painting is required and volume size is small enough to tolerate the performance cost of per-frame lighting recomputation. When not to use: For large volumes where performance is critical. This approach was used in the ARENA2 visualization dome. It is based on an implementation by Sundén and Ropinski. The technique is part of a survey on rendering large volume datasets in Unreal Engine 5. name: Light Propagation Volume (LPV) / Opacity Propagation Volume (OPV)
head: Cell-to-cell optical depth propagation, Crytek's algorithm, Opacity Propagation, Opacity Propagation Volume (OPV) Propagation, Opacity Propagation Volume (OPV) method, Propagation - Pixel shader
body: Light Propagation Volume (LPV), specifically the Opacity Propagation Volume (OPV) variant, is a real-time method for precomputing the optical depth T(S,X) from each light source S to each cell X in a 3D grid. It solves the problem of efficiently calculating light attenuation through heterogeneous participating media by propagating density information radially from light sources through a 3D volume on the GPU. Unlike standard radiance propagation which suffers from rapid scattering errors in dense media, OPV focuses on accurate optical depth integration, enabling correct shadowing and attenuation for subsequent ray-marched rendering. It builds on Ray-marched Volumetric Lighting with Density Thresholding by providing the precomputed attenuation data required for that rendering step. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of light sources S, each with a local extinction coefficient. A medium density model defined as a sum of Radial Basis Functions (RBFs). Output: An Opacity Propagation Volume (OPV) storing the optical depth integral T(X,S) for each cell X and light source S. Data Structures: 1. Extinction Volume (EV): A 3D texture storing the sampled density of the medium. Format: 3D 16-bit floating point texture. Dimensions: Same as the OPV. Content: Extinction coefficient values sampled from the RBF density model. 2. Opacity Propagation Volume (OPV): A 3D texture storing optical depth. Format: 3D 16-bit floating point texture. Dimensions: Same as the EV. Content: One optical depth integral per light source. One texture is needed per group of four lights. 3. Visited Texture: An additional texture used to mark texels that have already been computed or reached during propagation. Parameters: Grid Resolution: The dimensions of the 3D textures (e.g., 20^3 as used in the source experiments). Light Grouping: Lights are processed in groups of four to fit into a single OPV texture. Algorithm Steps: 1. Density Injection (EV Construction): Model the medium's extinction function as a sum of Radial Basis Functions (RBFs). Sample this density into the Extinction Volume (EV). 2. OPV Initialization: Clear the two OPV textures (ping-pong buffers) so that each texel starts with zero. For cells containing a light source S, initialize the corresponding texel in the OPV with the light source's local extinction coefficient. 3. Propagation Loop (Cell-to-Cell Optical Depth Propagation): The propagation originates from a single cell containing the light and advances radially like a wavefront. Use a ping-pong buffer approach with at least two copies of the OPV texture because reading and writing to the same texture in a shader is not available. Each single propagation step involves a plane sweep along the texture slices. Use the Visited Texture to discard cells which have already been computed or have not been reached yet, speeding up the process. The gathering algorithm is implemented in a fragment shader called on a fullscreen quad. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. for z in range(D): for y in range(H): for x in range(W): density = 0.0 for S in lightsources: # Standard RBF evaluation # density += evaluaterbf(S, x, y, z) density += 0.0 EV[x, y, z] = density for z in range(D): for y in range(H): for x in range(W): OPVread[x, y, z] = 0.0 OPVwrite[x, y, z] = 0.0 Visited[x, y, z] = False for S in lightsources: lsx, lsy, lsz = S.positioninvoxels OPVread[lsx, lsy, lsz] = S.extinctioncoefficient OPVwrite[lsx, lsy, lsz] = S.extinctioncoefficient Visited[lsx, lsy, lsz] = True currentread = OPVread currentwrite = OPVwrite while not all(Visited[z][y][x] for z in range(D) for y in range(H) for x in range(W)): # Plane sweep along texture slices for z in range(D): for y in range(H): for x in range(W): if Visited[x, y, z]: continue # The source describes a wavefront propagation using plane sweeps. # The exact cell-to-cell optical depth update formula is not provided in the sources. # Standard optical depth accumulation from visited neighbors would be applied here. # if reachablefromvisitedneighbor(x, y, z, currentread, EV): # currentwrite[x, y, z] = computenewopticaldepth(x, y, z, currentread, EV) # Visited[x, y, z] = True # Swap buffers currentread, currentwrite = currentwrite, currentread Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Texture Read/Write Conflict: Reading and writing to the same texture in a shader is not available, requiring ping-pong buffering with at least two copies of each OPV texture. Visited State: Correctly marking visited texels is crucial for performance and correctness, as it discards cells that have already been computed or have not been reached yet. Light Grouping: Lights must be grouped in sets of four to fit into a single OPV texture. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. name: Path Tracing and Sampling
body: Path Tracing and Sampling is a family of Monte Carlo algorithms that evaluate visibility and illumination at a point \mathbf{p} by recursively tracing rays from the camera into the scene to simulate global illumination, including direct lighting, shadows, and indirect bounces. It sets itself apart from local illumination methods by explicitly handling indirect light transport through recursive path generation, and from screen-space techniques by being view-independent and physically accurate. A real-time technique for rendering participating media (fog, smoke, dust) by simulating light interaction with particles, assuming light scatters only once before reaching the camera. It solves the problem of realistic volumetric lighting and light shafts by integrating the volume rendering equation along camera rays, using shadow maps for occlusion and fixed-length stepping for accumulation. It differs from screen-space god ray techniques by handling multiple light sources, varying density, and physically correct behavior from any viewing angle, and differs from Basic Volume Rendering and Ray Marching Loop with Absorption & Scattering by explicitly detailing the shadow map sampling and throughput accumulation logic for heterogeneous media. Choose it when real-time performance is required for heterogeneous media with single-scattering approximations. Calculates direct lighting from a spherical light source using Monte Carlo integration with various sampling strategies, including Importance Solid Angle, Importance Surface Area, Uniform Solid Angle, and others. It sets itself apart from siblings like Dwivedi Sampling by explicitly handling the geometry of a spherical light source through multiple distinct probability density functions (PDFs) rather than a single fixed approach, allowing the renderer to choose the most efficient estimator for the light's position relative to the shading point. Choose it when rendering scenes with prominent spherical area lights and varying distances to the shading point. A backward ray tracing algorithm that simulates light transport by recursively tracing rays from the camera, accumulating color contributions from surface interactions until a maximum bounce count is reached or a probabilistic termination condition is met. It is distinguished from its siblings by its explicit management of recursion depth combined with Russian Roulette termination based on the maximum component of the surface albedo, contrasting with methods that rely solely on fixed depth limits or discrete event sampling for sparse media. Choose it when strict control over path depth and unbiased termination via albedo-based survival probability is required. A Monte Carlo method that evaluates light transport by tracing rays from the camera into the scene, accumulating radiance through a sequence of interactions with surfaces and participating media. It solves the problem of computing global illumination by recursively sampling the next event in the light transport path, handling both surface scattering (BSDF) and volumetric scattering (medium sampling) within a single iterative loop. Unlike Explicit Path Tracing with Russian Roulette, which may separate the path construction logic more rigidly, or Path Tracing Extension with MIS, which explicitly combines multiple sampling strategies, standard unidirectional path tracing typically relies on direct light sampling or next-event estimation for direct illumination and simple Russian Roulette for path termination. It differs from Volumetric Path Tracing in that the latter explicitly extends the path tracer to handle complex multiple scattering in participating media using delta tracking, whereas the standard method often treats volumes as secondary interactions or uses simpler approximations unless extended. Choose it for standard global illumination pipelines requiring a unified loop for surface and volume interactions. This method extends a path tracing kernel by marching rays through sparse voxel data, shading intersections using albedo and geometric normals, and generating new ray directions via Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) between sun disk and cosine-weighted hemisphere sampling. It differs from standard path tracing by explicitly handling sparse voxel traversal for volume shading and decoupling the accumulation buffer from the pixel grid in its wavefront variant. Choose it when rendering sparse voxel environments with strong directional sunlight where variance reduction via MIS is critical. A path tracing algorithm that handles both surface and participating media intersections, using Russian Roulette for termination and power heuristic for light sampling. It evaluates multiple scattering in participating media, where light takes random paths through the medium until reaching a point, analogous to indirect illumination in surface rendering. It builds on Path Tracing and Sampling by integrating volume intersection logic and isotropic scattering models directly into the path generation loop. Choose it when accurate multiple scattering in participating media is required alongside surface interactions. Motion blur simulates the integration of light over a finite shutter interval [t0, t1], resulting in a blurred image when objects or the camera move during exposure. In path tracing, this is achieved by assigning a unique random time sample to each ray, naturally accumulating motion blur across samples. It differs from post-processing blur by preserving correct geometric occlusion and depth-of-field interactions at the sampled time instances. Choose it when physically accurate motion blur is needed without post-processing artifacts. This method enables differentiable path tracing by importance sampling shadow offsets using a Normal distribution kernel in parameter space. It allows for the computation of gradients with respect to scene parameters by treating shadowing as a convolution with a smooth kernel, rather than a hard binary visibility test. Unlike standard binary shadow mapping or hard-edged shadow volumes, this approach provides continuous visibility derivatives, which is essential for optimization tasks such as material parameter recovery or geometry refinement. Choose it when gradient-based optimization of scene parameters or geometry is required. IADDF Path Tracing is a Monte Carlo rendering method that solves the classical rendering equation using Intrinsic Appearance Differentiable Distance Fields (IADDF). It traces rays backwards from the eye to light sources, utilizing the DDF to find surface intersections and material/lighting fields to compute radiance. It is distinguished from standard path tracing by its reliance on differentiable implicit fields for geometry and appearance, allowing for continuous, analytic surface representation and shading without explicit mesh topology. Choose it when working with implicit geometry representations or differentiable appearance fields. A method for sampling edges for secondary visibility (shadow, reflection, global illumination) where the viewpoint is a shading point, analogous to many-lights sampling. Build a tree data structure over the set of geometric edges. For each node in the tree, collect summary statistics of the edges (e.g., total emission power, spatial bounding box, orientation ranges) to determine node importance. Traverse the tree to select edges, rejecting nodes that contain only non-silhouette edges relative to the current shading point. A method to calculate shading values for points in a scene by computing the probability of light rays from a source reaching the point and the probability of camera rays intersecting that point, leveraging light path reversibility. Select np points from the scene with high density. For a point light source at xl and a point x, sample ns points x1...xns along the path between xl and x, where xns = x. Compute qns by applying the same sampling procedure from the camera origin to x as used for the light source path. Utilize nc viewpoints with the lowest rate of missing values to obtain the shading vector in specific order. Obtain ns sampling points by projecting pixels from these viewpoints along camera rays, determining projection depth using formula 8. Apply post-processing to address holes in the shading map caused by occlusions and residual geometry details. Brightness formula: b = p{ns} \cdot \frac{I}{\|x - xl\|^2}, where b is brightness, p{ns} is the probability of ray propagation to x{ns}, I is light intensity, and \|x - xl\| is the distance. Shading formula: s = q{ns} \cdot b, where s is the shading value, q{ns} is the probability of a camera ray intersecting the point, and b is the brightness calculated previously. Path tracing was introduced by James Kajiya in 1986 as a generalization of the rendering equation to handle complex global illumination effects. The technique relies on Monte Carlo integration to estimate the integral of light transport, using Russian Roulette for unbiased termination of infinite path sequences. It has become a standard method for offline photorealistic rendering and is increasingly used in real-time graphics via techniques like Single Scattering Volume Rendering with Ray Marching and Path Tracing Extension with MIS. name: Single Scattering Volume Rendering with Ray Marching
head: Single Scattering Ray Marching, Volumetric Ray Marching, Single-Scattering Volume Rendering with Fixed-Length Ray Marching
body: Single Scattering Volume Rendering with Ray Marching is a real-time technique for computing volumetric light shafts (god rays) in participating media by numerically integrating the radiative transport equation under the assumption that light scatters only once before reaching the camera. It solves the problem of rendering physically plausible light interaction with fog, smoke, or dust while avoiding the prohibitive cost of multi-scattering simulations. Unlike screen-space god ray techniques which are limited to visible light sources and suffer from edge artifacts, this method steps along each camera ray through the volume, sampling shadow maps or distance fields to determine local illumination, thereby handling multiple light sources, varying density, and correct occlusion from any viewing angle. It builds on Basic Volume Rendering and Ray Marching Loop with Absorption & Scattering by explicitly integrating the light transport path from the volume sample to the light source, rather than relying on pre-computed ambient terms. The method approximates the radiative transport equation by ignoring multiple scattering, meaning the in-scattering term Li no longer depends on the unknown radiance L. The total radiance Li(c, -v) entering the camera at position c along direction -v is the sum of the attenuated surface radiance and the accumulated in-scattered light from volume emittance and light sources: Li(c,-v) = Tr(p,c)Lo(p,v) + \int{0}^{d} Tr(xt,c) \left[Le^V(xt,v) + \sigmas(xt)\int{S^2}fp(xt,w,v)Li(xt,w) dw \right]dt Where: c: Camera position. p: Surface point intersected by the camera ray. d = |c-p|: Distance from camera to surface. v = (c-p)/d: Unit direction from surface to camera. xt = c - vt: Sample point along the ray for 0 \leq t \leq d. Tr: Transmittance from point to camera. Lo(p,v): Surface radiance at p. Le^V(xt,v): Volume emittance (self-emission). \sigmas(xt): Scattering coefficient. fp(xt, w, v): Phase function describing scattering probability from direction w to v. Li(xt, w): Incident radiance at xt from direction w. Inputs: Camera position c, surface intersection point p, surface radiance Lo(p,v), volume density field (e.g., SDF or voxel grid), light positions and intensities, shadow maps (for opaque occlusion), and material parameters (\sigmaa, \sigmas, g). Outputs: Final pixel radiance L{final}. Ray Parameters: Origin c, direction v, length d. Accumulators: accumLight (in-scattering), transmittance (camera-to-point), tau (optical depth). Light Visibility: Computed via secondary ray march from sample point to light source. 1. Initialize Ray Parameters: Given camera c and surface p, calculate distance d = \text{length}(c-p), direction v = (c-p)/d, and step size step = d / n, where n is the number of march steps (typically 30). Initialize accumLight to 0 and transmittance to 1.0. 2. Iterate Along Camera Ray: Loop i from 0 to n-1: a. Calculate sample position: xt = c - v \cdot (i \cdot step). b. Compute Extinction: Query the extinction coefficient \sigmae(xt) = \sigmaa(xt) + \sigmas(xt). Update optical depth: \tau \leftarrow \tau + \sigmae(xt) \cdot step. c. Compute Transmittance: Calculate current transmittance from xt to camera: Tr(xt, c) = e^{-\tau}. d. Compute In-Scattering: i. Determine visibility from xt to each light source li. This involves a secondary ray march from xt towards the light to calculate absorption using the Beer-Lambert law, combined with shadow map lookups for opaque occlusion. Let fv(xt, p{lighti}) be this visibility function. ii. Calculate the phase function value fp(xt, li, v), typically using the Henyey-Greenstein function with parameter g. iii. Calculate scattering contribution: L{scat}(xt, v) = \pi \sigmas(xt) \sum{i=1}^{m} fp(xt, li, v) fv(xt, p{lighti}) L{lighti}(xt). iv. Add to accumulator: accumLight \leftarrow accumLight + Tr(xt, c) \cdot L{scat}(xt, v) \cdot step. e. Update Transmittance for Next Step: The transmittance variable in the simplified code is equivalent to Tr(xt, c) computed in step 2c. In the full formulation, Tr(xt, c) is derived from the accumulated \tau. 3. Compute Final Radiance: a. Calculate final surface transmittance: Tr(p, c) = e^{-\tau}. b. Compute surface contribution: L{surf} = Tr(p, c) \cdot Lo(p, v). c. Combine terms: La = \text{accumLight} + Le (where Le is volume emittance, if any). d. Return L{final} = L{surf} + La. Beer-Lambert Law (Absorption): A = e^{-c \cdot d}, where A is transmitted light fraction, c is absorption coefficient, d is distance. Transmittance: Tr(p,c) = e^{-\tau}, where \tau = \int{p}^{c} \sigmae(x) |dx|. Visibility Function: fv(xt, p{lighti}) = S(xi, p{lighti}) Tr(xi, p{lighti}), where S is shadow function (occlusion by opaque objects) and Tr is transmittance from light to point. In-Scattering Approximation: L{scat}(xt,v) = \pi \sigmas(xt) \sum{i=1}^n fp(xt,li,v)fv(xt,p{lighti})L{lighti}(xt). Ray march steps n: 30 for the main volume rendering loop. Shadow ray steps: 15 for computing transmittance in visibility/shadow calculations. Number of lights: 3 in the implementation example. Absorption Coefficient: Material parameter; low for clear volumes (water), high for thick volumes (milk). Phase Function Parameter g: Anisotropy factor for Henyey-Greenstein. Light Leaking: Opaque objects rendered before the volume do not account for volume shadowing, causing light to leak through the volume. Fix by calling GetLightVisibility for opaque object lighting calculations. Hard Edges: Volumes with sharp SDF boundaries appear unnatural. Soften edges by blending density based on distance to the volume boundary (e.g., using SDF value). Lack of Self-Shadowing: Without marching towards lights, all parts of the volume receive equal light. This is physically incorrect and must be fixed by computing light visibility via secondary ray marches. Precision: Summing L{is} and Le into an accumulator La before adding to L{surf} improves computational precision. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def singlescatteringvolumerendering(camerapos, surfacepoint, surfaceradiance, volumedensityfunc, lights, shadowmap, numsteps=30, shadowsteps=15): """ Computes single scattering volume rendering for a camera ray. """ # 1. Initialize Ray Parameters raydir = (camerapos - surfacepoint) raylength = length(raydir) raydir = normalize(raydir) stepsize = raylength / numsteps tau = 0.0 accumlight = vec3(0.0) # 2. Iterate Along Camera Ray for i in range(numsteps): t = i stepsize samplepos = camerapos - raydir t # Query extinction coefficient (sigmaa + sigmas) sigmae = volumedensityfunc.getextinction(samplepos) # Update optical depth tau += sigmae stepsize # Current transmittance from sample to camera transmittance = exp(-tau) # 2d. Compute In-Scattering lightcontribution = vec3(0.0) for light in lights: # Calculate visibility from sample to light # This involves a secondary ray march and shadow map check lightdir = normalize(light.position - samplepos) lightdist = length(light.position - samplepos) # Compute visibility function fv # fv = S Tr (Shadow Transmittance from light to sample) visibility = computelightvisibility(samplepos, lightdir, lightdist, volumedensityfunc, shadowmap, shadowsteps) if visibility > 0.0: # Phase function (e.g., Henyey-Greenstein) phase = heneygreenstein(dot(raydir, lightdir), g=0.8) # Scattering contribution sigmas = volumedensityfunc.getscattering(samplepos) lightradiance = light.intensity visibility # Lscat term approximation # Note: The pi factor in is often absorbed into phase normalization or light definition # Here we follow the structure: sigmas phase lightradiance scatter = sigmas phase lightradiance lightcontribution += scatter # Add to accumulator: Tr(xt, c) Lscat step accumlight += transmittance lightcontribution stepsize # 3. Compute Final Radiance # Final transmittance from surface to camera finaltransmittance = exp(-tau) surfaceradianceattenuated = finaltransmittance surfaceradiance # Combine surface and accumulated in-scattering # La = Lis + Le (assuming Le=0 for non-emissive volumes) finalradiance = surfaceradianceattenuated + accumlight return finalradiance def computelightvisibility(origin, direction, maxdist, volumedensityfunc, shadowmap, numsteps): """ Computes light visibility by marching from origin towards direction. Returns the fraction of light that reaches the point. """ stepsize = maxdist / numsteps currenttransmittance = 1.0 for i in range(numsteps): t = i stepsize pos = origin + direction t # Check if inside volume if volumedensityfunc.isinside(pos): sigmae = volumedensityfunc.getextinction(pos) currenttransmittance = exp(-sigmae stepsize) # Early exit if fully absorbed if currenttransmittance < 1e-5: return 0.0 # Check shadow map for opaque occlusion if shadowmap.isinshadow(pos, direction): return 0.0 return currenttransmittance Computes illumination by estimating light transport from volume sample to light source, solving for light shafts and silver linings. Differs by explicitly integrating the light path rather than using ambient terms. Focuses on performance via resolution reduction, temporal accumulation, and noise management. Differs by prioritizing efficiency over physical accuracy. Computes radiance by integrating absorption and out-scattering, ignoring direct in-scattering. Serves as the foundational transport mechanism. Complexity: O(n \cdot m \cdot k), where n is camera ray steps, m is number of lights, and k is light ray steps. Performance: More expensive than screen-space methods but handles multiple lights, colored fog, and varying density. Used in Unreal Engine 5, Unity HDRP, Red Dead Redemption 2, and The Last of Us Part II. Strengths: Physically correct behavior from any viewing angle, handles multiple light sources, supports varying density and colored fog. Limitations: High computational cost due to nested ray marches; single scattering approximation fails for dense media where multi-scattering is significant (e.g., thick fog blurring). Scaling: Performance degrades linearly with the number of lights and volume density. Optimizations like early termination and light visibility checks are critical. The method originates from the need for real-time volumetric lighting in games, where full Monte Carlo solutions to the radiative transport equation are too slow. It was popularized by techniques like those in Crysis (2007) for screen-space god rays, but evolved into ray marching approaches in engines like Unreal Engine 5 and Unity HDRP to support multiple lights and correct occlusion. The theoretical basis lies in the volume rendering equation, with single-scattering approximations allowing for real-time evaluation by decoupling the in-scattering term from unknown radiance. name: Volumetric Lighting with Phase Functions
head: Secondary Raymarching for Volumetric Lighting, Volumetric Lighting and Phase Functions
body: This method illuminates participating media by marching a short secondary ray toward a distant light source when volume density is non-zero, integrating optical thickness to compute solar attenuation. It applies the Henyey-Greenstein phase function to scatter light toward the camera, producing edge highlights and silver linings in single-scattering approximations. Inputs: 3D density field (e.g., Perlin-Worley noise texture). Camera position and view direction. Light source direction (assumed distant, e.g., the sun). Asymmetry parameter g for the phase function. Outputs: Illuminated color contribution for the current volume sample. Data Structures: Density sample: A scalar value representing optical depth or particle density at a 3D coordinate. If the density is zero, no lighting calculation is performed. Steps: 1. Density Check: Sample the primary 3D density field at the current view ray intersection point. If the density is zero, the contribution is zero. 2. Secondary Raymarching: Cast a short ray from the current volume sample toward the light source. This ray typically consists of 4 to 6 steps. 3. Optical Thickness Integration: Along the secondary ray, sample the density field and integrate the optical thickness d. The optical thickness is the integral of density along the light path. 4. Solar Attenuation: Calculate the transmittance T of light reaching the current point from the source using Beer's Law: T = \exp(-d) where d is the integrated light-path density. 5. Phase Function Evaluation: Calculate the scattering probability based on the angle \theta between the view ray (from camera to sample) and the sun ray (from sample to light). Use the Henyey-Greenstein phase function: P(\theta) = \frac{1 - g^2}{4\pi (1 + g^2 - 2g\cos\theta)^{1.5}} where g is the asymmetry parameter and \theta is the scattering angle. 6. Combine: Multiply the solar attenuation T by the phase function P(\theta) and the incident light intensity to get the final illumination contribution. Parameters: g (asymmetry parameter): Controls the directionality of scattering. Forward-scattering lobe: g \approx 0.8. Mild backward-scattering lobe: g \approx -0.2. Combining these lobes creates edge highlights and silver linings. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computevolumetriclighting(samplepos, viewdir, sundir, densityfield, gforward=0.8, gbackward=-0.2, numsteps=5, stepsize=1.0, lightintensity=1.0): density = densityfield.sample(samplepos) if density <= 0: return 0.0 opticalthickness = 0.0 for i in range(numsteps): marchpos = samplepos + sundir (i stepsize) opticalthickness += densityfield.sample(marchpos) stepsize transmittance = math.exp(-opticalthickness) costheta = math.dot(viewdir, sundir) pforward = (1 - gforward2) / (4 math.pi (1 + gforward2 - 2 gforward costheta)1.5) pbackward = (1 - gbackward2) / (4 math.pi (1 + gbackward2 - 2 gbackward costheta)1.5) # Source does not specify blending weights for the two lobes phase = (pforward + pbackward) / 2.0 return transmittance phase lightintensity Simulates volumetric light shafts for multiple spot lights by ray marching from the camera through the scene volume, integrating scattering contributions along the view ray. It operates as a post-processing compute shader pass that explicitly calculates light attenuation, spot cone factors, and phase function scattering at each sample point. Choose this when rendering multiple localized light sources in a post-process pipeline. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of volume samples requiring lighting and M is the number of secondary ray steps (typically 4-6). Memory Complexity: Low, as it only requires temporary storage for the optical thickness integral. Performance: Computationally intensive due to the secondary raymarching. Optimizations such as quarter-resolution raymarching, bilateral upsampling, and temporal reprojection are recommended to maintain frame rates. Strengths: Produces realistic edge highlights and silver linings in single-scattering approximations. Limitations: Only accounts for single scattering. Multi-scattering effects are not captured. Performance degrades with higher resolution or more secondary steps. This technique is part of the broader field of real-time volumetric rendering, specifically for simulating clouds and atmospheric effects. The use of Perlin-Worley noise for density generation and secondary raymarching for lighting is described in the context of OpenGL implementations. The Henyey-Greenstein phase function is a standard model in radiative transfer for anisotropic scattering.
