name: Volumetric Scattering via Ray Marching (Single Light)
head: Exponential Fog Light Shafts, Ray Marching Light Volume Integration, Ray Marching with Spot Factor, Tomas Ohlsson's volumetric shader, Volumetric.frag method
body: This method simulates volumetric light shafts for multiple spot lights by ray marching from the camera through the scene volume, integrating scattering contributions along the view ray. It operates as a post-processing compute shader pass that explicitly calculates light attenuation, spot cone factors, and phase function scattering at each sample point. The method reconstructs world-space positions from depth, then marches along the view vector to accumulate scattered light contributions. Inputs: inputTexture: Color buffer. depthTexture: Depth buffer. gInvProj: Inverse projection matrix. gInvView: Inverse view matrix. gCameraPos: Camera position in world space. gLights: Array of light structures containing Position, Direction, Range, Color, VolumetricStrength, outerCosine, innerCosine. Constants: absorptionTau, absorptionColor, scatteringSamples, scatteringTau, scatteringZFar, scatteringColor. Outputs: outputTexture: Accumulated volumetric scattering color. Constant Buffer 'VolumetricCB' Layout: c0.x: absorptionTau (float) c0.y: absorptionColor (float3) c1.x: scatteringSamples (int) c1.y: scatteringTau (float) c1.z: scatteringZFar (float) c2: scatteringColor (float3) c3-c6: gInvProj (matrix) c7-c10: gInvView (matrix) c11: gCameraPos (float3) c12+: gLights (array of Light structs) Light Struct Fields: Position: float3 Direction: float3 Range: float Color: float3 VolumetricStrength: float outerCosine: float innerCosine: float SpotPower: float Type: int 1. Reconstruct World Position: Get pixel dimensions, convert pixel coordinates to NDC (-1 to 1), multiply by inverse projection matrix, divide by w, multiply by inverse view matrix. 2. Initialize Ray March: Calculate vector from camera to fragment. If distance > scatteringZFar, clamp length to scatteringZFar. Calculate deltaStep = camToFrag / (scatteringSamples + 1). Offset start position by random value: x = gCameraPos + deltaStep random(worldPosition.xy + worldPosition.z). 3. Scattering Loop: For i from 0 to scatteringSamples-1: Calculate light vector L = x - light.Position. Calculate light distance dist = |L|. Calculate solid angle factor omega = 4 PI dist^2. Calculate incoming radiance Lin = Tabs(dist) visibility light.Diffuse light.SpotPower / omega. Calculate scattered radiance Li = Lin scatteringTau scatteringColor phaseFunction(normalize(L), normalize(gCameraPos - worldPosition)). Add to result: result += Li Tabs(|x - gCameraPos|) |deltaStep|. Advance x += deltaStep. 4. Main Dispatch: For each pixel, reconstruct world position. For each light, if Type == SPOTLIGHT and distance to light < FalloffEnd, add volumetricScattering result to output. Absorption Transmittance: T{abs}(dist) = C{abs} \times e^{-dist \times (\tau{abs} + \tau{scat})} Where: C{abs}: absorptionColor \tau{abs}: absorptionTau \tau{scat}: scatteringTau Phase Function: P(\theta) = \frac{0.5 + 16.5 \times x^{32}}{4\pi} Where: x = \frac{1 + \cos\theta}{2} \cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{inDir} \cdot \mathbf{outDir}}{|\mathbf{inDir}| |\mathbf{outDir}|}. absorptionTau: float, typical value -0.061. Controls absorption coefficient. scatteringTau: float, typical value 0.059. Controls scattering coefficient. scatteringSamples: int, typical value 16. Number of samples per view ray. scatteringZFar: float. Maximum distance for ray marching. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math SPOTLIGHT = 1 def length(v): return math.sqrt(sum(c c for c in v)) def dot(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def normalize(v): l = length(v) if l == 0: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] return [c / l for c in v] def random(co): return math.fmod(math.sin(dot(co, [12.9898, 78.233])) 43758.5453123, 1.0) def absorptiontransmittance(dist, absorptioncolor, absorptiontau, scatteringtau): return [c math.exp(-dist (absorptiontau + scatteringtau)) for c in absorptioncolor] def phasefunction(indir, outdir): cosangle = dot(indir, outdir) / (length(indir) length(outdir)) x = (1.0 + cosangle) / 2.0 return (0.5 + 16.5 (x 32)) / (4.0 math.pi) def volumetricscattering(worldposition, camerapos, light, scatteringsamples, scatteringtau, scatteringzfar, scatteringcolor, absorptiontau, absorptioncolor): camtofrag = [worldposition[i] - camerapos[i] for i in range(3)] distcf = length(camtofrag) if distcf > scatteringzfar: camtofrag = normalize(camtofrag) camtofrag = [c scatteringzfar for c in camtofrag] deltastep = [c / (scatteringsamples + 1) for c in camtofrag] fragtocamnorm = normalize([camerapos[i] - worldposition[i] for i in range(3)]) # HLSL quirk: worldPosition.xy + worldPosition.z adds scalar to vector components randval = random([worldposition[0], worldposition[1] + worldposition[2]]) x = [camerapos[i] + deltastep[i] randval for i in range(3)] result = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(scatteringsamples): lighttox = [x[i] - light['Position'][i] for i in range(3)] lightdist = length(lighttox) omega = 4.0 math.pi lightdist lightdist tabslight = absorptiontransmittance(lightdist, absorptioncolor, absorptiontau, scatteringtau) visibility = 1.0 # Simplified constant; sources note shadow maps should be used for correctness lin = [tabslight[i] visibility light['Diffuse'][i] light['SpotPower'] / omega for i in range(3)] pfunc = phasefunction(normalize(lighttox), fragtocamnorm) li = [lin[i] scatteringtau scatteringcolor[i] pfunc for i in range(3)] distxcam = length([x[i] - camerapos[i] for i in range(3)]) tabscam = absorptiontransmittance(distxcam, absorptioncolor, absorptiontau, scatteringtau) deltalen = length(deltastep) result = [result[i] + li[i] tabscam[i] deltalen for i in range(3)] x = [x[i] + deltastep[i] for i in range(3)] return result def computeshader(pixel, depth, inputtexture, outputtexture, invproj, invview, camerapos, lights, absorptiontau, absorptioncolor, scatteringsamples, scatteringtau, scatteringzfar, scatteringcolor): width, height = inputtexture.dimensions() u, v = pixel xndc = (u / width) 2.0 - 1.0 yndc = (v / height) -2.0 + 1.0 zndc = depth ndc = [xndc, yndc, zndc, 1.0] pview = [sum(ndc[j] invproj[j][i] for j in range(4)) for i in range(4)] pview = [pview[i] / pview[3] for i in range(3)] worldpos = [sum(pview[j] invview[j][i] for j in range(4)) for i in range(3)] volumetriccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for light in lights: if light['Type'] == SPOTLIGHT: distlight = length([light['Position'][i] - worldpos[i] for i in range(3)]) if distlight < light['FalloffEnd']: vol = volumetricscattering(worldpos, camerapos, light, scatteringsamples, scatteringtau, scatteringzfar, scatteringcolor, absorptiontau, absorptioncolor) volumetriccolor = [volumetriccolor[i] + vol[i] for i in range(3)] outputtexture[pixel] = [volumetriccolor[i] + inputtexture[pixel][i] for i in range(3)] Visibility: Setting visibility to a constant 1.0 ignores shadow maps and results in undesired output (light shafts appearing through occluders). Correct visibility calculation is critical. Light Direction Transformation: Multiplying light direction by the view matrix causes incorrect volume direction for vehicle headlights, while not multiplying causes incorrect direction for street lamps, and the correct transformation remains unclear in the source text. Precision: Using float for depth reconstruction can lead to precision issues at large distances. Boundary: Ray marching is clamped to scatteringZFar. Samples beyond this distance are ignored. A scan-line based method that deals with shadow volumes to take into account the glow in haze, computing the radiance reaching the eye by adding the contributions of single scattering of light in illumination volumes. It considers two scenarios: a light source at infinity illuminating a fog layer with constant or layered density with any phase function, and a point light source with a medium of constant density and isotropic scattering. Excessive frame drops occur when calculating visibility for 32 lights using shadow maps. Not given in the sources: exact time/memory complexity formulas, measured performance metrics, or scaling laws. This method is derived from post-processing techniques for simulating volumetric scattering in real-time graphics, referencing Tomas Ohlsson's volumetric shader (volumetric.frag) and concepts from GPU Gems 3, Chapter 13. It was developed as a compute shader approach for DirectX 12 to handle multiple spot lights efficiently. name: Optimization Strategies for Volumetric Lighting
head: God Rays Optimization Techniques, Real-time Volumetric Lighting Optimizations
body: This article details performance optimization strategies for real-time volumetric lighting, specifically addressing the high computational cost of ray marching in participating media. It solves the problem of excessive sample counts and memory bandwidth usage required to render soft, low-frequency light shafts (god rays) without sacrificing visual fidelity. Unlike Single Scattering Volume Rendering with Ray Marching, which focuses on the physical accuracy of light transport, these strategies prioritize rendering efficiency through resolution reduction, temporal accumulation, and noise management. The optimization pipeline modifies the standard ray marching loop to reduce per-frame computational load while maintaining visual continuity across frames. Inputs and Outputs Input: Full-resolution scene color buffer, depth buffer, light source position (screen-space or world-space), previous frame's volumetric lighting buffer, current frame index. Output: Optimized volumetric lighting buffer at reduced resolution, composited onto the final scene. Data Structures Reduced Resolution Buffer: A texture with dimensions W/2 \times H/2 or W/4 \times H/4 relative to the screen. Previous Frame Buffer: A texture storing the volumetric contribution from the prior frame, used for temporal blending. Blue Noise Texture: A 2D texture containing pre-generated blue noise values for dithering. Numbered Steps 1. Resolution Reduction: Initialize the ray marching loop to compute volumetric lighting at half or quarter screen resolution. The effect is inherently soft and low-frequency, allowing this reduction with minimal quality loss while achieving a 4x or greater performance gain. 2. Blue Noise Dithering: To mitigate banding artifacts caused by fewer samples, offset the ray march starting positions or sample intervals using blue noise. This converts structured aliasing into imperceptible high-frequency noise. \text{start\offset} = \text{blue\noise}(uv \times \text{scale}) \times \text{step\size} Where uv is the texture coordinate, \text{scale} adjusts noise frequency, and \text{step\size} is the ray march step length. 3. Temporal Reprojection: For each pixel, retrieve the volumetric contribution from the previous frame's buffer. Reproject this contribution to the current frame's coordinates using motion vectors or depth-based reprojection. Blend the current frame's computed result with the reprojected previous frame result. This effectively multiplies the sample count across frames while computing only a fraction per frame. C{final} = \alpha C{current} + (1 - \alpha) C{previous\reprojected} Where \alpha is the blending factor, typically determined by temporal stability or convergence rate. 4. Early Termination: During the ray marching loop, calculate the accumulated transmittance T. If T drops below a threshold (e.g., 0.01), terminate the march early. Samples beyond this point contribute negligibly to the final color, especially in dense media. \text{if } T < 0.01: \text{break} 5. Bilateral Upsampling: When compositing the reduced-resolution result onto the full-resolution scene, apply a depth-aware bilateral filter. This prevents halos and artifacts at depth discontinuities (object edges) by weighting samples based on both spatial proximity and depth similarity. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizevolumetriclighting(scenecolor, depthbuffer, lightpos, prevvolumetricbuffer, frameidx): # 1. Render at reduced resolution resw = scenecolor.width // 2 resh = scenecolor.height // 2 reducedvolumetric = emptytexture(resw, resh) for y in range(resh): for x in range(resw): uv = vec2(x / resw, y / resh) # 2. Blue noise dithering for starting position noiseval = bluenoisetexture.sample(uv 10.0) startoffset = noiseval raystepsize # Initialize ray ray = createrayfromscreen(uv, lightpos, startoffset) transmittance = 1.0 accumulatedlight = vec3(0.0) # 3. Ray marching with early termination for step in range(maxsteps): pos = ray.origin + ray.direction step raystepsize density = getdensityat(pos, depthbuffer) # Early termination check if transmittance < 0.01: break # Compute scattering contribution scatter = computescattering(pos, density, lightpos) accumulatedlight += scatter transmittance raystepsize transmittance = exp(-density raystepsize extinctioncoeff) reducedvolumetric.setpixel(x, y, accumulatedlight) # 4. Temporal reprojection # Reproject previous frame's volumetric buffer to current coordinates prevreprojected = reprojectbuffer(prevvolumetricbuffer, motionvectors) # Blend current reduced result with reprojected previous result blendedvolumetric = emptytexture(resw, resh) for y in range(resh): for x in range(resw): curr = reducedvolumetric.getpixel(x, y) prev = prevreprojected.getpixel(x, y) # Alpha blending factor alpha = 0.5 blendedvolumetric.setpixel(x, y, curr alpha + prev (1.0 - alpha)) # 5. Bilateral upsampling to full resolution fullvolumetric = emptytexture(scenecolor.width, scenecolor.height) for y in range(scenecolor.height): for x in range(scenecolor.width): uv = vec2(x / scenecolor.width, y / scenecolor.height) # Sample from blended reduced buffer with depth-aware weighting fullvolumetric.setpixel(x, y, bilateralupsample(blendedvolumetric, uv, depthbuffer)) return fullvolumetric Time Complexity: Reduced by a factor of 4x to 16x due to half/quarter resolution rendering. Temporal reprojection further reduces per-frame cost by allowing fewer spatial samples. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the reduced-resolution buffer, the previous frame's buffer, and blue noise texture. Bilateral upsampling may require additional temporary buffers for depth-aware filtering. Performance: Significant performance gain on GPU-bound scenarios. The trade-off is potential temporal instability if reprojection fails (e.g., at camera motion boundaries) and slight blurring due to resolution reduction. Strengths: Effective for soft, low-frequency effects like god rays. Minimal quality loss for the performance gain. Limitations: Not suitable for high-frequency volumetric details. Requires stable depth and motion vectors for effective temporal reprojection. These optimization strategies are standard practices in real-time graphics, particularly in high-end PC games and engines like Unreal Engine 5, which uses froxel grids with temporal reprojection for volumetric fog by default. The techniques address the inherent expense of volumetric lighting as a post-processing effect. name: Light Optimization via Light Volumes
head: Light coefficient optimization, Light volume method
body: Light Optimization via Light Volumes is a technique for optimizing light source coefficients in participating media by storing light transport residuals in dedicated volumetric structures rather than directly updating the coefficient vector. It solves the problem of atomic contention and serialization that occurs when multiple GPU threads attempt to write to the same light coefficient memory locations during ray traversal. Unlike direct residual accumulation, this method uses a gather-based approach via mipmapping to aggregate contributions, trading increased memory consumption for significantly higher performance and parallel efficiency. Inputs: V{ext}: The extinction volume (voxel grid). L{init}: Initial light coefficient vector of size N{coeffs}. T: The transmission matrix (or ray traversal operator) representing light transport from light sources to constraint pixels. I{target}: Target images (constraint pixels) for optimization. N{views}: Number of constraint views. N{coeffs}: Number of light basis functions (typically low, e.g., 16). R{vol}: Resolution of the light volumes (e.g., 128^3). Outputs: L{opt}: Optimized light coefficient vector. V{li}: Light volumes (one per coefficient or group) storing the influence of each coefficient. 1. Light Volume (V{li}): A 3D voxel grid of resolution R{vol} \times R{vol} \times R{vol}. For an isotropic phase function, the memory consumption is proportional to N{coeffs} \times R{vol}^3. Each voxel stores the accumulated light transport contribution for a specific coefficient. 2. Mipmap Pyramid: A hierarchical structure built over the light volume or the residual accumulation buffer to facilitate the gather operation. The highest level contains the aggregated values for the light coefficients. 1. Pre-computation of Light Volumes: For each light coefficient i (where i \in [0, N{coeffs}-1]): Treat the i-th light basis function as an emission source. Shoot rays through the volume V{ext} for all relevant directions. Compute the light transport result for each voxel. Store the result in the corresponding light volume V{li}. Note: This step is equivalent to lighting the volume with the i-th light source and storing the resulting lit volume. 2. Forward Pass (Gathering Influence): For each constraint pixel p in the target images: Shoot the corresponding ray through the volume V{ext}. For each light coefficient i, gather values from the pre-computed light volume V{li} along the ray path. Multiply the gathered values by the transmission T along the ray. Accumulate the influence of all coefficients to compute the current rendered pixel value I{current}(p). Compute the residual R(p) = I{target}(p) - I{current}(p). 3. Backward Pass (Distributing Residuals): Instead of adding residuals directly to L (which causes atomic contention), store the residuals with each ray. Perform a mipmapping procedure to gather all ray contributions. The multiplication with T^T (transpose of transmission) distributes the residuals to the light coefficients. Values are stored in the light volumes but targeted at the light coefficient vector. The highest level of the mipmap pyramid contains the aggregated values for L. 4. Update Light Coefficients: Extract the aggregated residuals from the highest level of the mipmap pyramid. Update L{init} to L{opt} using the aggregated residuals (e.g., via Conjugate Gradient or simple gradient descent). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizelightcoefficients(volumeext, targetimages, numcoeffs, volresolution, numviews): """ Optimizes light coefficients using light volumes to avoid atomic contention. """ # 1. Pre-compute Light Volumes # Vli[i] stores the transport result for the i-th light basis function Vli = [createzerovolume(volresolution) for in range(numcoeffs)] for i in range(numcoeffs): # Treat i-th light basis function as emission # Shoot rays through volumeext for all directions relevant to this basis # Store the lit result in Vli[i] Vli[i] = lightvolumeprecompute(volumeext, lightbasisfunction(i)) # 2. Initialize Light Coefficients L = [0.0] numcoeffs # 3. Optimization Loop (e.g., Conjugate Gradient) # Typically converges in 3-5 steps for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Forward Pass: Compute current render and residuals currentrender = [0.0] len(targetimages) residuals = [0.0] len(targetimages) for viewidx, targetimg in enumerate(targetimages): for pixel in targetimg: ray = getrayforpixel(pixel, viewidx) # Gather influence from all light volumes accumulatedlight = 0.0 for i in range(numcoeffs): # Gather values from Vli[i] along the ray # Multiply by transmission T along the ray influence = gatherfromlightvolume(Vli[i], ray) accumulatedlight += L[i] influence currentrender[viewidx] += accumulatedlight residuals[viewidx] = targetimg[pixel] - accumulatedlight # Backward Pass: Distribute residuals using Mipmapping # Instead of atomic adds to L, use gather-based aggregation # Initialize mipmap pyramid for aggregation mipmaplevels = buildmipmappyramid(residuals, numcoeffs) # The highest level contains aggregated residuals for each coefficient aggregatedresiduals = gethighestlevel(mipmaplevels) # Update Light Coefficients # Lnew = Lold + aggregatedresiduals (scaled by step size if necessary) for i in range(numcoeffs): L[i] += aggregatedresiduals[i] return L def gatherfromlightvolume(lightvol, ray): """ Shoots a ray through a light volume and accumulates values. Equivalent to multiplying with T (ray traversal). """ total = 0.0 for voxel in rayintersections(lightvol): total += voxel.value ray.transmissionto(voxel) return total Number of Light Coefficients (N{coeffs}): Typically low numbers (e.g., 16) are sufficient for acceptable computation times and good results. The flexibility of environmental lighting allows for low-frequency representation. Light Volume Resolution (R{vol}): Affects memory consumption significantly (N{coeffs} \times R{vol}^3 for isotropic phase function). Has minor impact on performance compared to ray marching steps. Light Basis Functions: In the cited work, 128 uniformly-distributed disc lights restricted to the upper hemisphere covering a constant solid angle with soft falloff were used for environment map stylization. However, only 16 coefficients were found sufficient for the final optimization. Ray Marching Steps: Twice the number of ray marching steps for the length of the diagonal as the number of voxels along an axis is a good choice for accurate integral estimation. Atomic Contention: Directly adding residuals to L during ray traversal causes serialization and low performance because multiple threads write to the same memory location. This is especially severe with few light coefficients. The light volume method avoids this by using a gather-based mipmapping approach. Isotropic Volume Filtering: An isotropic volume acts as a low-pass filter from the light source to the camera and vice versa. Consequently, high-frequency information (e.g., logos) in target images cannot be perfectly matched. The resulting environmental lighting is also low-frequency, justifying the use of a low number of light coefficients. Memory Usage: Memory consumption is significant (N{coeffs} \times R{vol}^3). If GPU memory is constrained, multiple ray traversals can be performed, keeping only a subset of V{li} in memory at once, though exchanging the set is costly. Time Complexity: Scales linearly with the number of light coefficients (N{coeffs}). The pre-computation time for light volumes also scales with N{coeffs} and resolution. Memory Complexity: Proportional to N{coeffs} \times R{vol}^3 for isotropic phase functions. Hardware: Intel X5650 CPU, nVidia 560Ti GPU. Volume Optimization: For 128^3 voxels, 256 ray marching steps, 460K constraint pixels (2 views), computation takes less than two seconds. With 2.3M constraint pixels (10 views), it takes seven seconds. Light Optimization: Optimizing for 16 light coefficients on a 128^3 volume with 2.3M constraint pixels (10 views) takes around three seconds. Pre-computation: For 256 coefficients and 128^3 resolution, pre-computation is ~5.39 seconds. Strengths: Avoids atomic operations and serialization, leading to high performance on GPUs. Preferred over direct residual accumulation despite higher memory usage. Limitations: High memory consumption. Cannot reproduce high-frequency details due to the low-pass filtering nature of isotropic volumes. Use when optimizing light source coefficients (e.g., environment maps) for volumetric scenes. Use when atomic contention is a bottleneck in direct coefficient updates. Use for stylizing environmental lighting, such as modifying environment maps for cloud scenes. Do not use if high-frequency detail reconstruction is required (e.g., matching logos). Do not use if GPU memory is extremely constrained and cannot accommodate the light volumes. The method was introduced in the paper "Property and Lighting Manipulations for Static Volume Stylization Using a Painting Metaphor". The technique was developed to address performance issues in volume stylization where artists modify renderings to reflect desired outputs. It was preferred over direct residual accumulation because it avoids atomic operations, despite higher memory usage. The method is particularly useful for modifying environmental illumination, such as in cloud scenes, where low-frequency lighting changes are sufficient. The method is used for stylizing environmental lighting, such as modifying environment maps for cloud scenes. It allows artists to produce desired target images using tools like Adobe Photoshop, and the optimization adjusts the light coefficients to match these targets. Property and Lighting Manipulations for Static Volume Stylization Using a Painting Metaphor, https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2014.13, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Basic Volume Rendering and Ray Marching Loop with Absorption & Scattering
head: Absorption and Scattering Integration, Single Scattering Ray Marching, Single-Scattering Volume Rendering with Fixed-Length Ray Marching, Transmittance Computation, Volume Rendering via Ray Marching, Volumetric Ray Marching
body: Basic volume rendering with ray marching computes the radiance along a camera ray by numerically integrating the changes in radiance due to absorption and out-scattering as the ray traverses a participating medium. It solves the problem of determining how much light is attenuated by a volume between the camera and a surface (or to infinity) when direct in-scattering is ignored or handled separately. Unlike analytical transmittance calculations which assume homogeneous media, this method subdivides space into discrete steps to handle heterogeneous density distributions, serving as the foundational transport mechanism for single-scattering approximations. Inputs: Camera ray origin o and direction \omega. Maximum ray extent s{max} (distance to the nearest surface intersection or scene boundary). Volume density function \sigmat(p), representing the total extinction coefficient (absorption + scattering) at point p. (Optional) Absorption coefficient \sigmaa(p) and scattering coefficient \sigmas(p) if separate tracking is required. Number of marching steps N. Outputs: Transmittance T(s{max}), the fraction of radiance surviving the traversal. Accumulated radiance (if in-scattering is included in the loop, though the basic loop primarily computes transmittance for single-scattering contexts). Ray: Defined by origin o and direction \omega. Step Size: \Delta t = s{max} / N. Sample Point: pi = o + (i + 0.5)\Delta t \omega, representing the midpoint of the i-th step. The change in radiance L due to absorption and out-scattering over a differential distance ds is given by: dL(p, \omega) = -\sigmat(p) L(p, \omega) ds where \sigmat(p) = \sigmaa(p) + \sigmas(p) is the total extinction coefficient. The transmittance T(s) over a distance s is defined as: T(s) = e^{-\tau(s)} where \tau(s) is the optical thickness (optical distance): \tau(s) = \int0^s \sigmat(p + t\omega) dt Since \sigmat varies spatially, \tau(s) is approximated numerically using ray marching with N steps: \tau(s) \approx \sum{i=0}^{N-1} \sigmat(pi) \Delta t where pi = o + (i + 0.5)\Delta t \omega. For homogeneous media, transmittance can be computed analytically as T(d) = \exp(-\sigmat d). N: Number of ray marching steps. Typical values depend on the desired accuracy and density variation; higher N reduces discretization error. \sigmaa: Absorption coefficient. \sigmas: Scattering coefficient. \sigmat: Extinction coefficient, \sigmat = \sigmaa + \sigmas. The following pseudocode implements the numerical integration of transmittance for a single ray segment. It assumes a function getdensity(p) that returns \sigmat(p) at point p. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computetransmittanceraymarch(o, omega, smax, N): """ Computes transmittance T(smax) for a ray from o in direction omega over distance smax using N ray marching steps. Args: o: Ray origin (vec3) omega: Ray direction (vec3) smax: Maximum distance to march N: Number of steps Returns: T: Transmittance value (float) """ if smax <= 0: return 1.0 deltat = smax / N opticalthickness = 0.0 for i in range(N): # Calculate sample point at the center of the step # pi = o + (i + 0.5) deltat omega tsample = (i + 0.5) deltat psample = o + tsample omega # Get extinction coefficient at sample point sigmat = getdensity(psample) # Accumulate optical thickness # tau += sigmat deltat opticalthickness += sigmat deltat # Transmittance T(s) = exp(-tau(s)) T = exp(-opticalthickness) return T If the method is integrated into a path tracer loop for single scattering with free-path sampling (as described in), the structure is: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pathtracevolumeray(o, omega, scene, maxdepth): """ Simplified path tracing loop for volume rendering with ray marching. """ throughput = vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) ray = Ray(o, omega) for depth in range(maxdepth): # Step 1: Ray intersection with geometry hit = rayintersect(scene, ray) if not hit: # Check if world contains scatter medium; if not, return if not scene.hasmedium(): return vec3(0.0) # If medium exists but no surface hit, march to infinity or boundary # This typically involves marching to a predefined boundary or # accumulating transmittance to a large distance. # For this basic loop, we assume we march to a boundary or # the loop terminates. break # Step 2: Distance sampling (free-path sampling) # For homogeneous medium, sample distance d before scattering event. # For heterogeneous, ray marching is used to evaluate transmittance # along the segment to the surface. # Calculate transmittance to the surface hit using ray marching disttosurface = hit.distance Ttosurface = computetransmittanceraymarch(ray.origin, ray.direction, disttosurface, N) # Update path throughput throughput = Ttosurface # If we want to simulate scattering events within the volume: # Sample a distance dscatter from the current ray origin. # If dscatter < disttosurface, a scattering event occurs. # Note: The basic "Absorption & Scattering Integration" loop # primarily computes the transmittance T(s) for the segment. # Full single-scattering integration requires adding in-scattering terms. # Step 3: If scattering event occurs (simplified logic from) # mediumevent = sampledistance(...) # if mediumevent: # ray.origin = mi.position # ray.direction = samplephasefunction(...) # throughput = transmittancevalue # Update ray for next intersection ray.origin = hit.point + hit.normal epsilon ray.direction = reflectorrefract(...) # Surface interaction return throughput Precision: In highly scattering media (high \sigmas, low \sigmaa), the path tracer estimator value approaches 1 (\frac{\sigmas}{\sigmas + \sigmaa} \approx 1), leading to poor convergence and high variance because a huge number of scattering events are required. Non-uniform Transmittance: Transmittance cannot be computed analytically for heterogeneous media; it must be evaluated via ray marching by subdividing space and multiplying the transmittance of each part. Computational Cost: Computing direct lighting in a volume is significantly more expensive than on surfaces because it requires integrating over the phase function distribution rather than a simple shadow ray test. Boundary Conditions: If the ray does not hit a surface, the algorithm must check if the world contains a scatter medium; if not, it returns immediately. Time: O(N) per ray, where N is the number of ray marching steps. The cost scales linearly with the number of steps and the number of rays. Memory: O(1) auxiliary memory per ray for the marching loop. The volume data structure itself (e.g., a 3D grid) requires O(V) memory, where V is the number of voxels. For a dense 3D grid with RGBA and density, storage can be significant (e.g., ~128 GB for a 4096^3 grid with 4 bytes/cell). Performance depends heavily on the resolution of the volume representation and the number of marching steps N. Higher resolutions and larger N improve accuracy but increase render time. In highly scattering media, convergence is slow, requiring many samples to reduce variance. Strengths: Simple to implement; handles heterogeneous media via numerical integration; foundational for more complex volume rendering techniques. Limitations: Computationally expensive for high-resolution volumes; poor convergence in highly scattering media; single-scattering approximation ignores multiple scattering effects, which are necessary for accurate appearance in dense media. Use for real-time volumetric rendering where single-scattering approximation is acceptable [Parent]. Use for scenes with moderate density variations where analytical transmittance is not feasible. Avoid for scenes requiring accurate multiple scattering effects (e.g., thick fog, dense clouds) without additional techniques. Avoid for highly scattering media if real-time performance is critical and variance is unacceptable. The method is based on the volume rendering equation, which describes radiance changes in participating media. The specific formulation of absorption and out-scattering cross-sections and the numerical integration via ray marching are detailed in Stanford CS248A lectures. The integration of this loop with path tracing and free-path sampling is discussed in community implementations. Volume rendering has evolved from simple ray marching for density visualization to complex Monte Carlo estimators for participating media. The distinction between single scattering (light scattering once) and multiple scattering (light scattering many times) is a key development in the field, with single scattering serving as a tractable approximation for real-time applications. Real-time volumetric lighting in games and interactive applications [Parent]. Medical imaging (e.g., CT scan visualization). Pre-computation for more advanced volume rendering techniques. name: Sphere Light Sampling with Multiple Strategies
head: getPixelColorWithSphereLightDBG
body: Calculates direct lighting from a spherical light source using Monte Carlo integration with various sampling strategies. It estimates direct illumination from a spherical light by sampling uniformly over the full 4π solid angle, ignoring the light's actual extent, or by using importance sampling techniques. Unlike Sphere Light Shading with Importance Solid Angle Sampling which samples the solid angle subtended by the light, or Importance Sampling for Sphere Surface Area which samples the physical surface points directly, this method provides a framework supporting multiple strategies including Uniform Solid Angle, Importance Solid Angle, Importance Surface Area, Importance Phong, and Cosine Weighted sampling. EquiAngular Sampling is a Monte Carlo integration technique used to estimate direct lighting from point lights in participating media by importance sampling the distance domain along a ray. It solves the high variance caused by the 1/r^2 geometric falloff and potential partial occlusion of the light source by sampling propagation distances proportional to the inverse squared length of the connecting edge. Unlike uniform solid angle or surface area sampling, which treat the light as a distant or extended object, this method re-parameterizes the integration into angular steps relative to the orthogonal projection of the light onto the ray, ensuring equal angular contributions. It is specifically designed for single scattering in homogeneous media. This method reduces variance and computation time when sampling directions for a procedural sky (modeled as a spherical light source) by concentrating samples in luminous regions, such as the sun, rather than using uniform sphere sampling. It achieves this by discretizing the sky's luminosity into 2D and 1D textures representing conditional and marginal probability distributions, allowing for efficient rejection-free sampling via inverse transform sampling. Unlike Importance Sampling for Sphere Surface Area which focuses on geometric surface area, or Sphere Light Shading with Importance Solid Angle Sampling which may use analytical approximations, this method relies on pre-integrated numerical CDFs derived directly from the procedural sky's color data. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot C) where N is the number of samples and C is the cost of ray intersection tests (shadow ray + light ray). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per sample. Performance: Depends heavily on the sampling strategy. Importance sampling strategies (Solid Angle, Surface Area) generally reduce variance for large lights compared to Uniform Solid Angle. Strengths: Supports multiple sampling strategies for different light sizes and material types. Handles self-intersection artifacts via offset. Limitations: Uniform Solid Angle is inefficient for small lights (low hit rate). Importance Surface Area requires careful geometric correction. When to use: When rendering scenes with spherical lights and varying material properties (diffuse/specular). When not to use: For very large lights where other approximations might be faster, or if the light is not spherical. name: Importance Sampling for Sphere Surface Area
head: Sphere Light Shading with Importance Surface Area Sampling, getSampleImportanceSolidAngle
body: Estimates direct illumination from a spherical light source by sampling points on its visible surface area, with a probability density function (PDF) proportional to the projected area. Unlike Sphere Light Shading with Importance Solid Angle Sampling which samples the solid angle subtended by the light, this method samples the physical surface points directly, requiring a geometric correction factor in the estimator to account for the varying projected area relative to the viewing direction. Inputs: Intersection point X on the shading surface, surface normal N at X, sphere light center C, sphere light radius R, and two uniform random numbers \eta1, \eta2 \in [0, 1). Outputs: Sample direction D from X to a point on the sphere surface, and the updated radiance estimator Lr. Data Structures: Vectors U, V, W form an orthonormal basis aligned with the local geometry, and scalar distance2XC stores the squared Euclidean distance between X and C. Steps: 1. Compute Geometry: Calculate the vector from the intersection point to the light center: \vec{XC} = C - X. Compute the squared distance: \text{distance2XC} = \|\vec{XC}\|^2. Compute the half-angle sine and cosine of the light cone: \sin\theta{\max} = R / \|\vec{XC}\|, \cos\theta{\max} = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2\theta{\max}}. 2. Construct Local Basis: Define the local coordinate system basis vectors: W = \vec{XC} / \|\vec{XC}\|, V = (W \times N) / \|W \times N\|, U = V \times W. If W and N are parallel, choose an arbitrary orthogonal vector for V to avoid division by zero. 3. Sample Angles: Generate two uniform random numbers \eta1, \eta2 \in [0, 1). Compute the polar angle \Theta and azimuthal angle \Phi: \Theta = \arccos(1 - \eta1 + \eta1 \sqrt{1 - R^2 / \text{distance2XC}}), \Phi = 2\pi \eta2. 4. Construct Direction: Construct the sample direction in the local coordinate system: D{\text{local}} = U (\cos\Phi \sin\Theta) + V (\sin\Phi \sin\Theta) + W \cos\Theta. Normalize and return D = D{\text{local}} / \|D{\text{local}}\|. 5. Estimator Update: Trace a ray from X in direction D to determine shadow status (1 - \text{inShadow}). Calculate the projected area factor: \text{Area} = 2\pi (1 - \sin\theta{\max}) R^2 / \text{distance2XC}. Update the radiance estimator: Lr += fr Li (1 - \text{inShadow}) \cos\thetai \cos\thetao \cdot \text{Area}. Average over N samples. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math PI = math.pi def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]) def normalize(v): l = math.sqrt(dot(v, v)) return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l) def samplespheresurfacearea(X, normal, lightcenter, lightradius, eta1, eta2): XC = (lightcenter[0]-X[0], lightcenter[1]-X[1], lightcenter[2]-X[2]) distance2XC = dot(XC, XC) dist = math.sqrt(distance2XC) sinthetamax = lightradius / dist W = normalize(XC) crossWN = cross(W, normal) lencrossWN = math.sqrt(dot(crossWN, crossWN)) if lencrossWN < 1e-6: # Degenerate case: W parallel to normal. Choose arbitrary orthogonal vector. if abs(W[0]) < 0.9: V = normalize(cross(W, (1.0, 0.0, 0.0))) else: V = normalize(cross(W, (0.0, 1.0, 0.0))) else: V = (crossWN[0]/lencrossWN, crossWN[1]/lencrossWN, crossWN[2]/lencrossWN) U = cross(V, W) term = math.sqrt(1.0 - (lightradius lightradius) / distance2XC) costheta = 1.0 - eta1 + eta1 term costheta = max(-1.0, min(1.0, costheta)) theta = math.acos(costheta) phi = 2.0 PI eta2 sintheta = math.sin(theta) cosphi = math.cos(phi) sinphi = math.sin(phi) Dlocal = ( U[0] (cosphi sintheta) + V[0] (sinphi sintheta) + W[0] math.cos(theta), U[1] (cosphi sintheta) + V[1] (sinphi sintheta) + W[1] math.cos(theta), U[2] (cosphi sintheta) + V[2] (sinphi sintheta) + W[2] math.cos(theta)) D = normalize(Dlocal) return D def updateestimator(X, normal, D, lightcenter, lightradius, fr, Li, inshadow, costhetao): XC = (lightcenter[0]-X[0], lightcenter[1]-X[1], lightcenter[2]-X[2]) distance2XC = dot(XC, XC) dist = math.sqrt(distance2XC) sinthetamax = lightradius / dist Area = 2.0 PI (1.0 - sinthetamax) (lightradius lightradius) / distance2XC costhetai = dot(normal, D) contribution = fr Li (1.0 - inshadow) costhetai costhetao Area return contribution A variant that explicitly loops to generate a point Y on the sphere surface and checks visibility. It generates \eta1, \eta2, computes \theta = \arccos(1 - 2\eta1) and \phi = 2\pi\eta2, then constructs Y = (R\sin\theta\cos\phi, R\sin\theta\sin\phi, R\cos\theta) + C. It computes the normal CY at Y and the vector YX = X - Y. If CY \cdot YX \le \epsilon, the sample is rejected and the loop repeats. This rejection sampling approach ensures the sampled point faces the shading point X. Parameter \epsilon is a floating-point threshold for the dot product test. Importance sampling is a variance reduction technique for Monte Carlo integration that accelerates convergence by selecting samples from a PDF p(x) that mimics the shape of the integrand f(x). Unlike uniform sampling, which treats all regions equally, this method concentrates computational effort on directions or values that contribute significantly to the final integral, such as light directions in rendering. It sets itself apart from its parent Importance Sampling for Sphere Surface Area by providing the general theoretical framework, while its sibling Occlusion-Aware vMF Importance Sampler applies specific geometric constraints to that framework. It solves the problem of approximating the true distribution of incoming light, including occlusions, by allowing the model to "turn off" lobes for light sources that are occluded from a specific point in space. It builds on Importance Sampling for Sphere Surface Area by adding spatial variation and occlusion awareness via the NGP, distinguishing it from static Importance Sampling strategies. name: Importance Sampling
body: Importance sampling is a variance reduction technique for Monte Carlo integration that accelerates convergence by selecting samples from a probability density function (PDF) p(x) that mimics the shape of the integrand f(x). Unlike uniform sampling, which treats all regions equally, this method concentrates computational effort on directions or values that contribute significantly to the final integral, such as light directions in rendering. It sets itself apart from its parent Importance Sampling for Sphere Surface Area by providing the general theoretical framework, while its sibling Occlusion-Aware vMF Importance Sampler applies specific geometric constraints to that framework. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An integrand function f(x) to be integrated over a domain \Omega, and a target PDF p(x) chosen to approximate f(x). Output: An unbiased estimator of the integral \int{\Omega} f(x) dx. Data Structures: No specific complex data structures are required for the core definition. The method relies on a random number generator capable of sampling from the distribution defined by p(x). Steps: 1. Select PDF: Choose a probability density function p(x) such that p(x) \approx c \cdot f(x) for some constant c, where p(x) > 0 whenever f(x) > 0. 2. Sample: Draw N independent samples X1, \dots, XN from the distribution p(x). 3. Estimate: Compute the Monte Carlo estimator FN using the formula: FN = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \frac{f(Xi)}{p(Xi)} Formulas: The estimator is defined as FN = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^n \frac{f(Xi)}{p(Xi)}. In the ideal case where p(x) = c f(x), the ratio \frac{f(Xi)}{p(Xi)} becomes constant \frac{1}{c}, resulting in zero variance. Parameters: N: The number of samples. The convergence rate is O(1/\sqrt{N}). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If p(x) = 0 where f(x) > 0, the estimator is undefined or biased. If p(x) poorly approximates f(x), variance reduction is minimal compared to uniform sampling. Precision issues may arise if p(Xi) is extremely small, leading to large weights. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def importancesamplingestimator(f, ppdf, psample, N): """ Estimate the integral of f using importance sampling. Args: f: The integrand function f(x). ppdf: The PDF function p(x). psample: A function that samples x from distribution p. N: Number of samples. Returns: The estimated integral value. """ total = 0.0 for i in range(N): # Sample x from p(x) x = psample() # Evaluate integrand and PDF at sample point fval = f(x) pval = ppdf(x) # Avoid division by zero if pval == 0: continue # Accumulate weighted contribution total += fval / pval return total / N The pseudocode assumes psample returns a valid sample and ppdf returns the density at that sample. In practice, psample often uses inverse transform sampling or rejection sampling based on the analytical form of p(x). Combines estimates from multiple PDFs to reduce variance when no single PDF matches the integrand well. Applies importance sampling specifically to the specular term in neural inverse rendering using GGX distributions. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of samples. Each sample requires evaluating f(x) and p(x). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per sample if processed sequentially. Performance: Convergence rate is O(1/\sqrt{N}), independent of dimensionality. Variance is significantly lower than uniform sampling when p(x) closely matches f(x). Strengths: Accelerates computation for integrals with sharp peaks or localized contributions. Limitations: Requires finding a suitable p(x) that is both easy to sample from and close to f(x). If p(x) is difficult to sample or evaluate, overhead may negate benefits. When to use: When the integrand has known high-contribution regions (e.g., light sources in rendering). When not to use: When no good approximation of f(x) is available, or when f(x) is smooth and uniform sampling is sufficient. Originating from Monte Carlo methods in statistics, importance sampling is widely used in computer graphics to accelerate light transport simulation. It is discussed in the context of null-scattering path integral formulations. The technique leverages the fact that sampling from a distribution similar to the integrand reduces the variance of the estimator, leading to faster convergence. name: Multiple Importance Sampling
head: Multi-sample estimator
body: Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) is a Monte Carlo integration technique that combines estimates from multiple sampling strategies to reduce variance when no single probability density function (PDF) adequately matches the integrand. Unlike standard importance sampling [9521-importance-sampling.md], MIS allows several specialized PDFs to be used simultaneously, weighting each sample to keep the combined estimator unbiased. Inputs: n: The number of distinct sampling strategies (PDFs) pi(x) being combined. ni: The number of samples generated by the i-th strategy. f(x): The integrand function (excluding the PDF). pi(x): The PDF of the i-th sampling strategy. x{i,j}: The j-th sample generated by the i-th strategy. Outputs: I{MIS}: The unbiased estimate of the integral \int{\Omega} f(x)g(x)dx. Data Structures: A list of n strategies, each storing its sample count ni, a sample generator, and a PDF evaluator. For each strategy i, an array of size ni storing tuples of (x{i,j}, \text{pdf\values}), where \text{pdf\values} is a list of length n containing pk(x{i,j}) for all k \in \{1, \dots, n\}. Steps: 1. For each strategy i from 1 to n, generate ni samples x{i,1}, \dots, x{i,ni} using the sampling distribution pi(x). 2. For each sample x{i,j}, evaluate all PDFs pk(x{i,j}) for k \in \{1, \dots, n\}. 3. Compute the balance heuristic weight for each sample: wi(x{i,j}) = \frac{ni pi(x{i,j})}{\sum{k=1}^n nk pk(x{i,j})} 4. Accumulate the estimator: I{MIS} = \sum{i=1}^n \frac{1}{ni} \sum{j=1}^{ni} wi(x{i,j}) \frac{f(x{i,j})}{pi(x{i,j})} Constraints on Weights: The weights wi(x) must satisfy two conditions to ensure an unbiased result: 1. \sum{i=1}^n wi(x) = 1 for all x where f(x) \neq 0. 2. wi(x) = 0 if pi(x) = 0. This implies that for any point x where the integrand is non-zero, at least one sampling strategy must have a non-zero probability of generating that sample. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multipleimportancesampling(strategies, integrand): """ strategies: list of tuples (ni, samplefunc, pdffunc) ni: number of samples for this strategy samplefunc: function that returns a sample x given random numbers pdffunc: function that returns p(x) for a given sample x integrand: function that returns f(x) for a given sample x """ totalestimate = 0.0 # Store samples and evaluate all PDFs at each sample point samples = [] # List of lists: samples[i][j] = (x, pdfvalueslist) for i, (ni, samplefunc, pdffunc) in enumerate(strategies): samples.append([]) for j in range(ni): x = samplefunc() pdfvalues = [pdfk(x) for k, (,, pdfk) in enumerate(strategies)] samples[i].append((x, pdfvalues)) for i, (ni, samplefunc, pdffunc) in enumerate(strategies): strategysum = 0.0 for j, (x, pdfvalues) in enumerate(samples[i]): fx = integrand(x) pix = pdfvalues[i] # Balance heuristic denominator: sumk(nk pk(x)) denominator = sum(nk pdfvalues[k] for k, (nk,,) in enumerate(strategies)) if denominator == 0: weight = 0.0 else: weight = (ni pix) / denominator if pix == 0: contribution = 0.0 else: contribution = weight (fx / pix) strategysum += contribution totalestimate += strategysum / ni return totalestimate Parameters: n: Number of sampling techniques. ni: Number of samples per technique. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If pi(x) = 0 for all i at a point where f(x) \neq 0, the estimator is undefined; the weight constraint requires at least one pi(x) > 0. Precision issues may arise if the denominator in the balance heuristic is very small. A variant that combines exponential and equiangular sampling for photon beam diffusion in participating media. It dedicates samples entirely to the superior PDF except in a small transition zone where it smoothly weights the two strategies, avoiding the wasteful standard balance heuristic. The weights are defined as w{exp}(ti, x) = \text{clamp}((x-a)/(b-a), 0, 1) and w{eq}(ti, x) = 1 - w{exp}(ti, x). The transition zone boundaries are a = 0.9/t0 and b = 1.1/t0, centered around one diffuse mean free path. With just 3 samples, this combined strategy matches the entire profile, including the peak and asymptotic tail behavior, making it preferable when standard MIS fails to capture both near-source and far-field contributions. A method to combine multiple guided sampling processes using MIS to improve estimation quality for boundary path integrals in differentiable rendering. It is used in primary-sample-space guiding techniques to efficiently estimate gradients, and is chosen when gradient estimation requires combining multiple importance sampling paths. A strategy that combines area-based and vertex-based probabilities to sample triangles during training, addressing inefficient convergence caused by non-uniform feature distribution. The sampling probability is p(i) = \eta \frac{A(i)}{A{total}} + (1 - \eta) \frac{N(i)}{N{total}}, where \eta controls the weighting factor. It is chosen when training convergence is bottlenecked by uneven feature density across mesh faces. Time Complexity: Proportional to \sum ni plus the cost of evaluating all PDFs for all samples to compute weights. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of strategies and samples, but PDF evaluation overhead grows with n. Strengths: Reduces variance by combining the strengths of different sampling strategies; remains unbiased. Limitations: Requires evaluating multiple PDFs for each sample, increasing computational cost per sample compared to single importance sampling. When to use: When no single PDF closely matches the integrand, or when different parts of the domain are better sampled by different strategies. When not to use: When a single PDF is known to be optimal, or when computational resources are extremely limited and the overhead of multiple PDF evaluations is prohibitive. Multiple Importance Sampling was introduced by Veach in 1997. It is widely used in computer graphics for rendering, particularly in path tracing and photon mapping, to handle complex lighting scenarios involving multiple light sources and materials. The balance heuristic for weights was also introduced by Veach. name: Importance Sampling for Specular Term
head: Inverse Transform Sampling for GGX-like Distribution, NDJIR Specular Term Sampling
body: This method computes the specular term in the Neural Direct and Joint Inverse Rendering (NDJIR) forward model using Monte Carlo integration with importance sampling. It accelerates convergence by sampling light directions according to a probability density function (PDF) derived from the GGX microfacet distribution D and geometric factors, rather than uniform hemisphere sampling. It is distinct from Importance Sampling in its specific application to the NDJIR specular integrand, and from Multiple Importance Sampling as it relies on a single, analytically invertible PDF for the specular component. Inputs: \zeta\phi, \zeta\theta: Uniform random numbers in 0, 1). \hat{\alpha}r: Roughness parameter (scalar). \hat{n}: Surface normal vector (world coordinates). \mathbf{v}: Viewing direction vector (world coordinates). \mathbf{f}0: Fresnel coefficient at normal incidence (vector/scalar depending on model). LV(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \mathbf{l}): Volume radiance at position \hat{\mathbf{x}} in direction \mathbf{l}. LE(\mathbf{l}): Emissive radiance of the light source in direction \mathbf{l}. V(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{l}, \hat{n}, \hat{\alpha}r): Visibility term. I(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{l}, \hat{n}): [Interaction term. \widehat{L}p: Pre-computed or estimated constant factor. NL: Number of light samples per pixel. Outputs: \mathbf{l}i: Sampled light direction vectors in the local coordinate system (where \hat{n} is the up-vector). \widehat{L}p: The estimated specular radiance contribution. Data Structures: Vectors \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{l}, \hat{n} are 3D Cartesian coordinates. Scalars \zeta, \hat{\alpha}r are floating-point values. Steps: 1. Sample Azimuthal Angle: Compute the azimuthal angle \phi using the first random number: \phi = 2\pi \zeta\phi 2. Sample Polar Angle: Compute the polar angle \theta using the second random number \zeta\theta and the roughness \hat{\alpha}r: \theta = \cos^{-1} \sqrt{\frac{1 - \zeta\theta}{(\hat{\alpha}r^2 - 1) \zeta\theta + 1}} Note: The PDF used for this inverse transform is derived from the GGX D term in solid angle representation: p(\theta, \phi) = \frac{\hat{\alpha}r^2}{\pi(\cos^2 \theta (\hat{\alpha}r^2 - 1) + 1)^2} \cos \theta \sin \theta 3. Construct Local Direction: Construct the light direction vector \mathbf{l}{local} in the local coordinate system where the normal \hat{n} aligns with the Z-axis (up-vector): \mathbf{l}{local} = (\cos \phi \sin \theta, \sin \phi \sin \theta, \cos \theta) 4. Transform to World Coordinates: Transform \mathbf{l}{local} to the world coordinate system. Let T(\hat{n}) be the rotation matrix that maps the local Z-axis to \hat{n}. The world direction \mathbf{l} is: \mathbf{l} = T(\hat{n}) \mathbf{l}{local} Implementation Note: T(\hat{n}) can be constructed using a basis where \hat{n} is the third column, and the other two columns are orthogonal vectors forming a right-handed system. 5. Compute Half Vector: Calculate the half vector \mathbf{h} between the viewing direction \mathbf{v} and the sampled light direction \mathbf{l}: \mathbf{h} = \frac{\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{l}}{\|\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{l}\|} 6. Evaluate Specular Term: For each sample i, compute the contribution using the discretized specular term formula: \text{Contribution}i = V(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{l}i, \hat{n}, \hat{\alpha}r) F(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{l}i, \mathbf{f}0) \frac{4(\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{h}i)}{(\hat{n} \cdot \mathbf{h}i)} LV(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \mathbf{l}i) LE(\mathbf{l}i) (\hat{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}i) I(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{l}i, \hat{n}) The final estimate is the average over NL samples: \widehat{L}p = \frac{\widehat{L}p}{NL} \sum{i=1}^{NL} \text{Contribution}i Note: The factor \frac{4(\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{h})}{(\hat{n} \cdot \mathbf{h})} arises from the ratio of the GGX D term (used in the PDF) and the geometric term in the BSDF, effectively canceling the PDF denominator. 7. Gradient Handling: Do not backpropagate gradients through the sampling process (steps 1-3) to avoid non-differentiable operations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def samplespeculardirection(zetaphi, zetatheta, alphar): """ Samples a light direction in the local coordinate system (normal is up). Args: zetaphi: Uniform random float in [0, 1). zetatheta: Uniform random float in [0, 1). alphar: Roughness parameter. Returns: llocal: numpy array [3] representing the direction in local coords. """ # Step 1: Sample Azimuthal Angle phi = 2.0 math.pi zetaphi # Step 2: Sample Polar Angle # Formula: theta = acos( sqrt( (1 - zetatheta) / ((alphar^2 - 1) zetatheta + 1))) numerator = 1.0 - zetatheta denominator = (alphar2 - 1.0) zetatheta + 1.0 # Guard against division by zero or negative sqrt if alphar is 1 or invalid if denominator <= 0: denominator = 1e-8 costheta = math.sqrt(numerator / denominator) theta = math.acos(costheta) # Step 3: Construct Local Direction sintheta = math.sin(theta) cosphi = math.cos(phi) sinphi = math.sin(phi) llocal = np.array([ cosphi sintheta, sinphi sintheta, costheta ]) return llocal def transformtoworld(llocal, normal): """ Transforms a local direction vector to world coordinates using the normal as the up-vector. Args: llocal: numpy array [3] in local coords. normal: numpy array [3] world normal (assumed normalized). Returns: lworld: numpy array [3] in world coords. """ # Construct orthonormal basis # We need two vectors tangent to the surface. # A robust way is to find a vector not parallel to normal, then cross. # Helper to create basis def createbasis(n): # Choose an arbitrary vector not parallel to n if abs(n[0]) > 0.9: aux = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) else: aux = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]) t1 = np.cross(aux, n) t1 = t1 / np.linalg.norm(t1) t2 = np.cross(n, t1) return t1, t2, n t1, t2, t3 = createbasis(normal) # llocal = x t1 + y t2 + z t3 lworld = llocal[0] t1 + llocal[1] t2 + llocal[2] t3 return lworld def computespecularterm(v, normal, alphar, f0, NL, getLv, getLE, getV, getI): """ Computes the specular term using importance sampling. Args: v: numpy array [3] viewing direction (world). normal: numpy array [3] surface normal (world). alphar: float roughness. f0: float or array Fresnel at normal incidence. NL: int number of samples. getLv: function returning volume radiance for a direction. getLE: function returning light emissive radiance for a direction. getV: function returning visibility term. getI: function returning interaction term. Returns: Lp: float estimated specular radiance. """ Lpsum = 0.0 for in range(NL): # Generate random numbers zetaphi = np.random.uniform(0, 1) zetatheta = np.random.uniform(0, 1) # Sample direction llocal = samplespeculardirection(zetaphi, zetatheta, alphar) l = transformtoworld(llocal, normal) # Compute half vector h = v + l hnorm = np.linalg.norm(h) if hnorm < 1e-8: continue # Degenerate case h = h / hnorm # Dot products vdoth = np.dot(v, h) ndoth = np.dot(normal, h) ndotl = np.dot(normal, l) # Guard against division by zero if ndoth < 1e-8: continue # Evaluate terms Vterm = getV(v, l, normal, alphar) Fterm = getF(v, l, f0) # Assuming a standard Fresnel function Lvterm = getLv(l) Leterm = getLE(l) Iterm = getI(v, l, normal) # Specular contribution # Formula: V F (4 (v.h) / (n.h)) Lv Le (n.l) I contribution = Vterm Fterm (4.0 vdoth / ndoth) Lvterm Leterm ndotl Iterm Lpsum += contribution # Average Lp = Lpsum / NL return Lp Parameters: NL: Number of light samples per pixel. Typical value: 128 (composed of 8 polar samples \times 16 azimuthal samples). \hat{\alpha}r: Roughness parameter. Range typically [0, 1]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradients: Gradients are not backpropagated through the sampling process to avoid non-differentiable operations. Degenerate Half Vector: If \mathbf{v} \approx -\mathbf{l}, the half vector \mathbf{h} is undefined or unstable. A guard is required. Roughness = 1: If \hat{\alpha}r = 1, the denominator in the polar angle sampling formula becomes \zeta\theta + 1, which is valid, but the PDF simplifies. The formula remains stable. Uniform Sampling for Diffuse: The diffuse term uses uniform sampling instead, where \theta = \cos^{-1}(1 - \zeta\theta). Do not confuse the two sampling strategies. Uses \theta = \cos^{-1}(1 - \zeta\theta) for the diffuse component, contrasting with the GGX-based importance sampling for specular. A baseline method mentioned in the source that separates the specular integral into pre-integrated BRDF and irradiance terms, differing from the direct Monte Carlo integration used here. Time Complexity: O(NL) per pixel, where NL is the number of light samples. Each sample requires trigonometric functions and vector operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per sample. Performance: Using 128 samples per pixel provides a balance between noise reduction and computational cost in the NDJIR experiments. Strengths: Reduces variance for the specular term by concentrating samples in directions where the GGX distribution is high, leading to faster convergence compared to uniform sampling for rough surfaces. Limitations: Requires the PDF to be analytically invertible, which limits the choice of BRDF models. Not applicable to the diffuse term in this specific implementation. This method is part of the Neural Direct and Joint Inverse Rendering (NDJIR) framework. It applies importance sampling to the specular term of the forward rendering model, deriving the PDF from the GGX microfacet distribution D and geometric factors. The approach avoids backpropagation through the sampler, following suggestions in reference [62] of the original paper. NDJIR: Neural Direct and Joint Inverse Rendering for Geometry, Lights, and Materials of Real Object, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2302.00675, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Occlusion-Aware vMF Importance Sampler
head: Spatially-varying vMF distribution, vMF mixture sampler
body: This method provides a lightweight importance sampler for incoming radiance in participating media and surface rendering, using a Neural Graphics Primitive (NGP) to predict a mixture of von Mises-Fisher (vMF) distributions. It solves the problem of approximating the true distribution of incoming light, including occlusions, by allowing the model to "turn off" lobes for light sources that are occluded from a specific point in space. Inputs: A 3D point \mathbf{x} in the scene. A trained NGP mapping \mathbf{x} to scalar parameters. A set of M sample directions \{\boldsymbol{\omega}^j{in}\}{j=1}^M generated by a proposal distribution p. Incident radiance estimates \hat{L}{NeRF}(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}^j{in}) from a NeRF cache or similar estimator. Outputs: A mixture of L vMF distributions parameterized by \{\lambda\ell(\mathbf{x}), \boldsymbol{\mu}\ell(\mathbf{x}), \kappa\ell(\mathbf{x})\}{\ell=1}^L. The probability density value \text{mixture}(\mathbf{d}; \mathbf{x}) for any direction \mathbf{d}. Data Structures: The NGP consists of: 1. Hash Grid: Maximum resolution 2048. 2. Hash Map: Fixed size 2^{19}. 3. MLP: 2-layer network with 64 hidden units. 4. Output: The MLP predicts 5L scalars for each point \mathbf{x}, interpreted as L sets of parameters \{\boldsymbol{\mu}'\ell(\mathbf{x}), \kappa\ell(\mathbf{x}), \lambda\ell(\mathbf{x})\}. Parameters: L = 128: Number of vMF lobes. NGP Resolution: 2048. MLP: 2 layers, 64 hidden units. Formulas: The mixture distribution is defined as: \text{mixture}(\mathbf{d}; \mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{Z} \sum{\ell=1}^{L} \lambda\ell(\mathbf{x}) \text{vMF}(\mathbf{d}; \boldsymbol{\mu}\ell(\mathbf{x}), \kappa\ell(\mathbf{x})) where Z = \sum{\ell=1}^{L} \lambda\ell(\mathbf{x}) is the partition function. The mean direction \boldsymbol{\mu}\ell(\mathbf{x}) is derived from the raw NGP output \boldsymbol{\mu}'\ell(\mathbf{x}) by normalizing the vector from the point \mathbf{x} to the predicted source location: \boldsymbol{\mu}\ell(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\boldsymbol{\mu}'\ell(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbf{x}}{\| \boldsymbol{\mu}'\ell(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbf{x} \|} This ensures the lobe points towards the light source. The parameters \lambda\ell (mixture weights) and \kappa\ell (concentration) are non-negative scalars predicted directly by the NGP. Training Objective: The parameters are optimized to match the true incoming radiance distribution, accounting for occlusions. The loss function is: \mathcal{L}{vMF} = \frac{1}{M} \sum{j=1}^{M} \frac{\| Z \cdot \text{mixture}(\boldsymbol{\omega}^j{in}; \mathbf{x}) - \bar{L}(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}^j{in}) \|^2}{p(\boldsymbol{\omega}^j{in})} where \bar{L}(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}^j{in}) = \| \hat{L}{NeRF}(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}^j{in}) \|^2 is the L2 norm of incident radiance across channels. p is the sampling distribution used to generate the samples, which combines the mixture distribution q and a standard material-based importance sampling distribution. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def vmfpdf(d, mu, kappa): """Computes the PDF of a 3D von Mises-Fisher distribution.""" d = d / np.linalg.norm(d) mu = mu / np.linalg.norm(mu) costheta = np.clip(np.dot(d, mu), -1.0, 1.0) if kappa == 0: return 1.0 / (4.0 math.pi) sinhkappa = np.sinh(kappa) if sinhkappa == 0: return 1.0 / (4.0 math.pi) cd = kappa / (4.0 math.pi sinhkappa) return cd np.exp(kappa costheta) def samplevmf(mu, kappa): """Samples from a 3D vMF distribution using standard rejection sampling.""" if kappa == 0: u1 = np.random.uniform(0, 1) u2 = np.random.uniform(0, 1) theta = 2 np.pi u1 phi = np.arccos(2 u2 - 1) return np.array([np.sin(phi)np.cos(theta), np.sin(phi)np.sin(theta), np.cos(phi)]) while True: u1 = np.random.uniform(0, 1) u2 = np.random.uniform(0, 1) u3 = np.random.uniform(0, 1) z = (1 - (1 + kappa) u1) / (1 + kappa u1) if z < -1 or z > 1: continue if u2 (1 - z2) <= (kappa z / (1 + kappa))2: break theta = 2 np.pi u3 costheta = z sintheta = np.sqrt(1 - z2) # Construct vector in local frame aligned with mu # Find orthogonal basis if abs(mu[2]) < 0.9: v1 = np.cross(mu, [0, 0, 1]) else: v1 = np.cross(mu, [1, 0, 0]) v1 = v1 / np.linalg.norm(v1) v2 = np.cross(mu, v1) return mu costheta + v1 sintheta np.cos(theta) + v2 sintheta np.sin(theta) def getngpparams(x, ngpmodel, L): """Retrieves the 5L parameters from the NGP for point x.""" rawoutput = ngpmodel.forward(x) muprime = rawoutput[:3L].reshape(L, 3) kappa = rawoutput[3L:4L] lambdaweights = rawoutput[4L:] return muprime, kappa, lambdaweights def computemixturepdf(d, x, ngpmodel, L): """Computes the mixture PDF for direction d at point x.""" muprime, kappa, lambdaweights = getngpparams(x, ngpmodel, L) Z = np.sum(lambdaweights) if Z == 0: return 0.0 totalpdf = 0.0 for l in range(L): diff = muprime[l] - x normdiff = np.linalg.norm(diff) if normdiff < 1e-8: mul = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) else: mul = diff / normdiff pdfl = vmfpdf(d, mul, kappa[l]) totalpdf += lambdaweights[l] pdfl return totalpdf / Z def computeloss(x, samples, radiancecache, ngpmodel, proposaldist, L): """Computes the LvMF loss.""" M = len(samples) muprime, kappa, lambdaweights = getngpparams(x, ngpmodel, L) Z = np.sum(lambdaweights) Lsum = 0.0 for j in range(M): omega = samples[j] mixturepdf = computemixturepdf(omega, x, ngpmodel, L) Lneurf = radiancecache(x, omega) Lbar = np.linalg.norm(Lneurf) 2 pomega = proposaldist(omega) if pomega == 0: continue term = (Z mixturepdf - Lbar) 2 / pomega Lsum += term return Lsum / M Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the predicted source location \boldsymbol{\mu}'\ell(\mathbf{x}) coincides with \mathbf{x}, the mean direction \boldsymbol{\mu}\ell is undefined A fallback to a uniform direction or a small epsilon perturbation is required. The parameters \lambda\ell and \kappa\ell must be non-negative The NGP output should be passed through a ReLU or softplus activation to enforce non-negativity, though the source states they are "nonnegative numbers" without specifying the activation. Time Complexity: Scales linearly with the number of lobes L and the NGP lookup cost. Memory Complexity: Determined by the NGP grid and hash map size 2^{19}. Performance: Described as lightweight. Strengths: Capable of modeling occlusions by turning off lobes and provides spatially varying distributions. Limitations: Requires training the NGP and depends on the quality of the NeRF cache for radiance estimation. The method originates from "Flash Cache: Reducing Bias in Radiance Cache Based Inverse Rendering" by Attal et al.. It is used within the Flash Cache framework for inverse rendering to approximate incoming radiance distributions. The use of vMF mixtures for directional distributions is adapted here for spatial variation and occlusion awareness. name: Sphere Light Shading with Importance Solid Angle Sampling
head: Importance Solid Angle Sampling for Sphere Lights
body: This method estimates direct illumination from a spherical light source using Monte Carlo integration over the solid angle subtended by the light. It samples directions uniformly within the cone defined by the light's extent at the shading point. It is a specific strategy within the broader Sphere Light Sampling with Multiple Strategies framework. Inputs: Shading point position X. Light center C and radius R{light}. Surface normal N. Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) fr. Incident radiance Li from the light. Shadow status inShadow. Outputs: Estimated reflected radiance contribution Lr. Data Structures: Standard 3D vector types for positions, directions, and normals. Random number generator for uniform samples \eta1, \eta2 \in [0, 1). Steps: 1. Compute Geometry: Calculate the vector from the shading point to the light center: \vec{d} = C - X. Compute the distance D = |\vec{d}|. 2. Determine Cone Parameters: Calculate the sine and cosine of the maximum half-angle \theta{max} subtended by the light sphere: \sin\theta{max} = \frac{R{light}}{D} \cos\theta{max} = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2\theta{max}}. 3. Sample Direction: Sample a direction \omegai uniformly within the solid angle of the cone. 4. Shadow Test: Trace a ray from X in direction \omegai with length D. If the ray hits the light sphere, set inShadow = 0; otherwise inShadow = 1. 5. Calculate PDF Weight: The solid angle subtended by the light is \Omega = 2\pi(1 - \cos\theta{max}). The PDF for uniform sampling over this solid angle is p(\omegai) = 1/\Omega, so the importance sampling weight is 2\pi(1 - \cos\theta{max}). 6. Update Estimator: Accumulate the radiance contribution: Lr \leftarrow Lr + fr \cdot Li \cdot \cos\thetai \cdot (1 - inShadow) \cdot 2\pi(1 - \cos\theta{max}) where \thetai is the angle between \omegai and the surface normal N. 7. Average: Repeat for N samples and divide by N. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def randf(): return random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) def length(v): return math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]) def normalize(v): l = length(v) return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l) def shadespherelightimportancesolidangle(X, C, Rlight, N, fr, Li, numsamples): """ Estimates direct lighting from a sphere using importance solid angle sampling. """ totalradiance = 0.0 # Vector from shading point to light center d = (C[0]-X[0], C[1]-X[1], C[2]-X[2]) dist = length(d) # Handle degenerate case where point is inside the light if dist <= Rlight: costhetamax = 1.0 else: sinthetamax = Rlight / dist costhetamax = math.sqrt(1.0 - sinthetamax2) # PDF constant (inverse of solid angle) pdfconstant = 2.0 math.pi (1.0 - costhetamax) for in range(numsamples): # 1. Sample direction uniformly within the cone subtended by the light phi = 2.0 math.pi randf() costheta = randf() (1.0 - costhetamax) + costhetamax sintheta = math.sqrt(1.0 - costheta2) # Construct local basis aligned with d if abs(d[0]) < 0.9: up = (1.0, 0.0, 0.0) else: up = (0.0, 1.0, 0.0) tangent = normalize(cross(d, up)) bitangent = cross(d, tangent) omegai = ( sintheta (math.cos(phi) tangent[0] + math.sin(phi) bitangent[0]) + costheta d[0], sintheta (math.cos(phi) tangent[1] + math.sin(phi) bitangent[1]) + costheta d[1], sintheta (math.cos(phi) tangent[2] + math.sin(phi) bitangent[2]) + costheta d[2]) omegai = normalize(omegai) # 2. Shadow test: Trace a ray from X in direction omegai with length dist # Source does not provide ray tracing implementation inshadow = 1.0 # 3. Calculate cosine term costhetai = max(0.0, dot(omegai, N)) # 4. Update estimator radiancecontribution = fr Li costhetai (1.0 - inshadow) pdfconstant totalradiance += radiancecontribution return totalradiance / numsamples Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Inside Light: If the shading point is inside the light sphere (D < R{light}), \sin\theta{max} > 1, leading to NaNs in \cos\theta{max}. Precision: For very distant lights, \theta{max} is small, and 1 - \cos\theta{max} may suffer from catastrophic cancellation. Estimates direct illumination from a spherical light by sampling directions weighted by the cosine of the angle with the surface normal. The probability density function is p(\omegai) = \frac{\cos\theta}{\pi}. The estimator update is Lr \leftarrow Lr + fr \cdot Li \cdot (1 - inShadow) \cdot \pi. Time Complexity: O(N) per shading point, where N is the number of samples. Each sample requires a shadow test. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. Strengths: Unbiased estimator; handles arbitrary light positions and sizes. Limitations: Requires a shadow test for each sample. This method is derived from standard Monte Carlo integration techniques for light transport. It is implemented in the VolumeSingleScattering repository by wangyuehi. wangyuehi/VolumeSingleScattering, https://github.com/wangyuehi/VolumeSingleScattering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)
