name: EquiAngular Sampling
head: Equiangular distance sampling, Kulla and Fajardo sampling, density sampling for point lights
body: EquiAngular Sampling is a Monte Carlo integration technique used to estimate direct lighting from point lights in participating media by importance sampling the distance domain along a ray. It solves the high variance caused by the 1/r^2 geometric falloff and potential partial occlusion of the light source by sampling propagation distances proportional to the inverse squared length of the connecting edge. Unlike uniform solid angle or surface area sampling, which treat the light as a distant or extended object, this method re-parameterizes the integration into angular steps relative to the orthogonal projection of the light onto the ray, ensuring equal angular contributions. It is specifically designed for single scattering in homogeneous media. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{x} and direction \vec{\omega}. Point light position \mathbf{K}. Light flux \Phi. Medium extinction coefficient \sigmat and scattering coefficient \sigmas. Integration bounds a, b along the ray (typically 0 to t{max} or intersection distance). Uniform random number \xi \in 0, 1). Outputs: Sampled distance t along the ray. PDF value pdf(t). Radiance contribution estimator. Data Structures: Standard floating-point variables for geometry and physics parameters. Steps: 1. Calculate Geometric Parameters: Let \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{K} - \mathbf{x}. Compute the orthogonal projection of the light source \mathbf{K} onto the ray defined by \mathbf{x} and \vec{\omega}. The signed distance from the ray origin to the projection point is \Delta = \mathbf{v} \cdot \vec{\omega}. The perpendicular distance from the light to the ray is D = \|\mathbf{v} - \Delta \vec{\omega}\|. If D=0, the light lies on the ray, causing a singularity. 2. Determine Angular Bounds: Calculate the angles subtended by the integration bounds a and b relative to the projection point. The angles \thetaa and \thetab are defined as: \thetaa = \arctan\left(\frac{a - \Delta}{D}\right) \thetab = \arctan\left(\frac{b - \Delta}{D}\right). Note that a and b can be negative relative to the new origin, so \thetaa and \thetab can be negative. 3. Sample Distance: Generate a uniform random number \xi \in [0, 1). Compute the sampled distance t{proj} along the ray relative to the projection point using the inverse [CDF: t{proj} = D \tan\left((1 - \xi)\thetaa + \xi\thetab\right). The absolute distance from the ray origin is t{abs} = t{proj} + \Delta. 4. Calculate PDF: The probability density function for the sampled distance t{proj} is: pdf(t{proj}) = \frac{D}{(\thetab - \thetaa)(D^2 + t{proj}^2)}. Since the transformation from t{proj} to t{abs} has a Jacobian of 1, the PDF value remains unchanged for the absolute distance. 5. Estimate Radiance: Compute the in-scattered radiance contribution. The transmittance from the ray origin \mathbf{x} to the sample point \mathbf{x}t (at distance t{abs}) and from \mathbf{x}t to the light \mathbf{K} must be calculated. Distance from \mathbf{x} to \mathbf{x}t is t{abs}. Distance from \mathbf{x}t to \mathbf{K} is r = \sqrt{D^2 + t{proj}^2}. Transmittance Tr(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}t) = e^{-\sigmat t{abs}}. Transmittance Tr(\mathbf{x}t, \mathbf{K}) = e^{-\sigmat r}. Visibility Vis(\mathbf{x}t, \mathbf{K}) is determined by shadow ray tracing. The estimator for a single sample is: L = \frac{\sigmas \cdot Tr(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}t) \cdot Tr(\mathbf{x}t, \mathbf{K}) \cdot Vis(\mathbf{x}t, \mathbf{K}) \cdot \frac{\Phi}{r^2}}{pdf(t{proj})}. The term \frac{\Phi}{r^2} is the incident radiance from the point light at distance r. The phase function p(\vec{\omega}i, \vec{\omega}o) is omitted here for simplicity but should be included if anisotropic scattering is modeled. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def traceshadowray(origin, direction): # Standard ray-scene intersection returning 1.0 if visible, 0.0 if occluded return 1.0 def equiangularsample(rayorigin, raydirection, lightpos, flux, sigmat, sigmas, tmin, tmax): # 1. Geometric setup v = [lightpos[i] - rayorigin[i] for i in range(3)] delta = sum(v[i] raydirection[i] for i in range(3)) projpoint = [rayorigin[i] + raydirection[i] delta for i in range(3)] perpvec = [lightpos[i] - projpoint[i] for i in range(3)] D = math.sqrt(sum(p2 for p in perpvec)) if D < 1e-6: D = 1e-6 # 2. Angular bounds thetaa = math.atan((tmin - delta) / D) thetab = math.atan((tmax - delta) / D) # 3. Sample xi = random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) tproj = D math.tan((1.0 - xi) thetaa + xi thetab) tabs = tproj + delta # 4. PDF pdf = D / ((thetab - thetaa) (D2 + tproj2)) # 5. Radiance Estimator r = math.sqrt(D2 + tproj2) T1 = math.exp(-sigmat tabs) T2 = math.exp(-sigmat r) shadoworigin = [rayorigin[i] + raydirection[i] (tabs + 1e-4) for i in range(3)] shadowdir = [lightpos[i] - shadoworigin[i] for i in range(3)] shadowlen = math.sqrt(sum(s2 for s in shadowdir)) shadowdir = [s / shadowlen for s in shadowdir] visibility = traceshadowray(shadoworigin, shadowdir) Lincident = flux / (r2) numerator = sigmas T1 T2 visibility Lincident radiancecontrib = numerator / pdf return tabs, pdf, radiancecontrib Parameters: D: Perpendicular distance from light to ray. \thetaa, \thetab: Angular bounds. t{max}: Maximum distance along the ray. spr (samples per ray): Typical value around 4-5 yields good results with low noise. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity: If D=0 (light on ray), the PDF becomes undefined. Clamp D to a small value. Occlusion: The method assumes the visibility term is handled separately via shadow rays. If the light is partially occluded, the variance is reduced compared to uniform sampling, but noise remains if the shadow ray is expensive or inaccurate. Large Lights: This method is derived for point lights. For area lights, D becomes a function of the sampled point on the light surface, introducing approximation errors if the center is used for D. Generalizes equiangular sampling to arbitrary area lights by using the sampled light point as the center for the ray-segment sampling distribution, reducing variance at light edges. Choose it when rendering large or textured area lights where point-light approximations cause noisy edges. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample for the sampling and PDF calculation. Dominated by shadow ray tracing for visibility. Memory Complexity: O(1). Performance: Renders single scattering in homogeneous media in less than 10 minutes with spp < 100 and spr = 4 on standard hardware. Strengths: Significantly lower variance than free-path sampling or uniform solid angle sampling for single scattering. Handles partial occlusion better than transmittance sampling. Limitations: Not suitable for multiple scattering (free-path sampling is preferred for that). Approximation errors increase for large area lights if not generalized. Cannot match the tail behavior of exponential sampling in some diffusion contexts. Equiangular sampling was proposed by Kulla and Fajardo [KF12] and used by Novák et al. [NNDJ12] for rendering single scattering in participating media. It is based on the idea of importance sampling the geometry term G(\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}) \propto 1/\|\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{c}\|^2. The technique was further analyzed in the context of area lights in participating media. Joint importance sampling of low-order volumetric scattering, https://doi.org/10.1145/2508363.2508411, fetched 2026-10-28 wangyuehi/VolumeSingleScattering, https://github.com/wangyuehi/VolumeSingleScattering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) l0exy1h/VolumetricPathTracing-public, https://github.com/l0exy1h/VolumetricPathTracing-public, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Importance sampling of area lights in participating media, https://doi.org/10.1145/2037826.2037899, fetched 2026-11-02 Photon Beam Diffusion for Rendering, https://www.scribd.com/document/255860491/Photon-Beam-Diffusion, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Area Light Sampling with Ray-Origin Centering
head: Ray-Origin Centering for Area Lights
body: This method generalizes EquiAngular Sampling to area lights of arbitrary shapes by using the sampled light point as the center for the ray-segment sampling distribution. It reduces high variance at light edges caused by approximating the distance D with a single arbitrary point (like the light center), which fails for large, stretched, or textured lights. Unlike approximations where the D^2 term in the PDF dominates and causes noisy edges, this method distributes the error uniformly over the light's surface. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, area light surface geometry, and phase function. Outputs: Sampled point \mathbf{l} on the light surface, sampled point \mathbf{p} on the ray segment, and PDF values for MIS. Data Structures: Light surface representation capable of evaluating position and PDF for uniform sampling, and ray structure with origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Steps: 1. Sample Light Point: Sample a point \mathbf{l} uniformly on the area light surface. Let p{light}(\mathbf{l}) be the PDF of this sample. 2. Calculate Distance: Compute the distance D from the sampled light point \mathbf{l} to the ray origin \mathbf{o}. Note that D is now a function of the position sampled from the light: D(\mathbf{l}) = \|\mathbf{l} - \mathbf{o}\|. 3. Determine Sampling Distribution: Use the sampled light point \mathbf{l} as the center for the equi-angular sampling equations. Specifically, use \mathbf{l} in place of the fixed center used in standard equi-angular sampling to determine the sampling distribution along the ray segment between \mathbf{o} and \mathbf{l}. This involves calculating the angle \theta between the ray direction \mathbf{d} and the vector \mathbf{l} - \mathbf{o}, and sampling the distance t along the ray based on the equiangular distribution centered at \mathbf{l}. 4. Sample Ray Point: Sample a point \mathbf{p} on the ray segment using the distribution derived in Step 3. Let p{ray}(\mathbf{p} | \mathbf{l}) be the conditional PDF of this sample given \mathbf{l}. 5. Apply MIS: Apply Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) between the area light surface sampling and the phase function sampling to mask remaining noise. The combined weight uses the balance heuristic: w = \frac{p{light}(\mathbf{l}) p{ray}(\mathbf{p} | \mathbf{l})}{p{light}(\mathbf{l}) p{ray}(\mathbf{p} | \mathbf{l}) + p{phase}(\mathbf{p}) p{light}(\mathbf{l})} where p{phase} is the PDF of sampling the ray point based on the phase function alone. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def samplearealightwithrayorigincentering(rayorigin, raydir, light): # Step 1: Sample a point on the area light surface l, pdflight = light.sampleuniform() # Step 2: Calculate distance from sampled light point to ray origin vectolight = l - rayorigin D = length(vectolight) # Step 3: Use the sampled light point as the center for equi-angular sampling costheta = dot(normalize(raydir), normalize(vectolight)) sintheta = sqrt(1.0 - costheta costheta) # Sample distance t along the ray using equi-angular distribution centered at l u = uniform(0.0, 1.0) t = D tan(asin(sqrt(u) sintheta)) # Step 4: Compute the sampled point on the ray p = rayorigin + t raydir # Step 5: Calculate PDF for ray sampling given the light point pdfray = (sintheta sintheta) / (D D (1.0 + (t / D) (t / D))) # Step 6: Apply MIS with phase function phasepdf = light.phasefunction.pdf(raydir, normalize(l - p)) # Balance heuristic weight numerator = pdflight pdfray denominator = numerator + pdflight phasepdf weight = numerator / denominator return p, weight, pdflight, pdfray Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Choosing a sampling center too close to the ray can cause a potential singularity. This method does not solve this singularity but distributes the error uniformly over the light's surface. For very large lights, the approximation of using the sampled point as the center is more accurate than using the light center, but precision issues may arise if D is very small. A sampling technique for area lights that treats them as spherical rectangles to improve PDF accuracy at small solid angles. It uses a threshold of 10^{-3} steradians for switching to spherical rectangle sampling. This improves PDF for rectangular lights at small solid angles compared to standard planar sampling. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, assuming constant-time light sampling and distance calculation. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory. Performance: Substantially reduces variance compared to approximations using the light center, especially for large, stretched, or textured area lights. Strengths: Works for large, stretched, or textured area lights where arbitrary center approximations fail. Distributes error uniformly over the light's surface. Limitations: Does not solve the singularity issue when the sampling center is too close to the ray. Requires accurate light sampling and distance calculation. When to Use: When rendering scenes with large, stretched, or textured area lights in participating media. When Not to Use: When light sources are very small and far away, where standard approximations may suffice, or when computational resources are extremely limited and variance reduction is not critical. This method was introduced as a generalization of equi-angular sampling for area lights in participating media. It addresses the limitations of previous approximations that used arbitrary points like the light center, which failed for large lights and caused noisy edges due to the D^2 term dominating the PDF. The technique is applicable to path tracing and bidirectional path tracing. name: Importance Sampling of Procedural Skies using Marginal and Conditional CDFs
head: Nishita Sky Importance Sampling, Spherical Light Sampling via 2D CDF
body: This method reduces variance and computation time when sampling directions for a procedural sky (modeled as a spherical light source) by concentrating samples in luminous regions, such as the sun, rather than using uniform sphere sampling. It achieves this by discretizing the sky's luminosity into 2D and 1D textures representing conditional and marginal probability distributions, allowing for efficient rejection-free sampling via inverse transform sampling. Unlike Importance Sampling for Sphere Surface Area which focuses on geometric surface area, or Sphere Light Shading with Importance Solid Angle Sampling which may use analytical approximations, this method relies on pre-integrated numerical CDFs derived directly from the procedural sky's color data. Inputs: Procedural sky function L(\theta, \phi) returning color/radiance for azimuth \theta and elevation \phi. Discretization resolution W \times H (typically 180 \times 180). Random number generator producing uniform values in [0, 1]. Outputs: Sampled direction vector \mathbf{d} in Cartesian coordinates. Probability Density Function (PDF) value p(\mathbf{d}) for unbiased weighting. Data Structures: Four textures are precomputed from the procedural sky data before rendering: 1. Conditional Function Texture (C): A 2D texture of size W \times H. Layout: C[i, j] stores the magnitude (length) of the color value at column i (azimuth index) and row j (elevation index). C[i, j] = \| L(\thetai, \phij) \|. 2. Conditional CDF Texture (CDFc): A 2D texture of size W \times H. Layout: CDFc[i, j] stores the cumulative sum of C[i, k] for k=0 \dots j, normalized by the total sum of column i. CDFc[i, j] = \frac{\sum{k=0}^{j} C[i, k]}{\sum{k=0}^{H-1} C[i, k]}. 3. Marginal Function Texture (M): A 1D texture of size W. Layout: M[i] stores the total sum of values in column i of the Conditional Function texture. M[i] = \sum{j=0}^{H-1} C[i, j]. 4. Marginal CDF Texture (CDFm): A 1D texture of size W. Layout: CDFm[i] stores the cumulative sum of M[k] for k=0 \dots i, normalized by the grand total of all values in the sky. CDFm[i] = \frac{\sum{k=0}^{i} M[k]}{\sum{k=0}^{W-1} M[k]}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Column Selection (Azimuth): Generate a random number xi \in [0, 1]. Walk the 1D Marginal CDF texture CDFm to find the first index i such that CDFm[i] > xi. This index i corresponds to the selected column (azimuth bin). 2. Row Selection (Elevation): Generate a second random number xj \in [0, 1]. Using the selected column i, walk the 2D Conditional CDF texture CDFc at column i to find the first index j such that CDFc[i, j] > xj. This index j corresponds to the selected row (elevation bin). 3. Coordinate Conversion: Convert the discrete indices (i, j) into continuous spherical coordinates: Azimuth: \theta = \frac{i}{W} \cdot 2\pi Elevation: \phi = \frac{j}{H} \cdot \pi (Note: The source defines elevation range as \pi, mapping [0, \pi] to the full sphere vertically, though standard spherical coordinates often use [0, \pi/2] for hemispheres. The source explicitly states \pi for elevation). 4. Direction Vector: Convert (\theta, \phi) from spherical to Cartesian coordinates (x, y, z) to obtain the ray direction \mathbf{d}: \begin{aligned} x &= \sin(\phi) \cos(\theta) \\ y &= \sin(\phi) \sin(\theta) \\ z &= \cos(\phi) \end{aligned} 5. PDF Calculation: Calculate the total PDF for the sampled direction to correct for bias: Marginal PDF: p{marginal}(i) = \frac{M[i]}{\sum{all} M} Conditional PDF: p{cond}(j|i) = \frac{C[i, j]}{M[i]} Total PDF: p(i, j) = p{marginal}(i) \times p{cond}(j|i) 6. Unbiased Weighting: Divide the sampled lighting contribution (radiance) by the total PDF p(i, j) to maintain an unbiased estimator. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sampleproceduralsky(W, H, C, CDFc, M, CDFm, rng): """ Samples a direction from a procedural sky using marginal and conditional CDFs. Args: W: Width of the sky texture (azimuth bins). H: Height of the sky texture (elevation bins). C: 2D array [W][H] of conditional function values (luminosity magnitude). CDFc: 2D array [W][H] of conditional CDF values. M: 1D array [W] of marginal function values (column sums). CDFm: 1D array [W] of marginal CDF values. rng: Function returning a uniform random float in [0, 1]. Returns: direction: Tuple (x, y, z) Cartesian direction vector. pdf: Float, the probability density of the sampled direction. """ # Step 1: Column Selection (Azimuth) xi = rng() i = 0 while i < W and CDFm[i] <= xi: i += 1 # If xi is 1.0 or CDFm doesn't exceed it due to precision, clamp to last index if i >= W: i = W - 1 # Step 2: Row Selection (Elevation) xj = rng() j = 0 while j < H and CDFc[i][j] <= xj: j += 1 # Clamp to last index if necessary if j >= H: j = H - 1 # Step 3: Coordinate Conversion theta = (i / W) 2 math.pi phi = (j / H) math.pi # Step 4: Direction Vector sinphi = math.sin(phi) cosphi = math.cos(phi) costheta = math.cos(theta) sintheta = math.sin(theta) x = sinphi costheta y = sinphi sintheta z = cosphi direction = (x, y, z) # Step 5: PDF Calculation # Total sum of M is precomputed or can be derived from CDFm[W-1] TotalSum # Since CDFm is normalized, sum(M) is the denominator used during CDFm creation. # Let Stotal = sum(M). We can recover it if not passed, but typically # pmarginal(i) = M[i] / Stotal. # Note: The source defines pmarginal(i) = M(i) / sum(all M). # To calculate PDF accurately, we need the total sum of M. # If CDFm is normalized, CDFm[W-1] == 1.0. # We assume Stotal is available or computed once. # For this implementation, we calculate pmarginal directly from M and its sum. sumM = sum(M) # In practice, this is a constant precomputed value. pmarginal = M[i] / sumM pcond = C[i][j] / M[i] pdf = pmarginal pcond return direction, pdf Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bias Correction: Importance sampling introduces bias by preferentially selecting directions. The final radiance contribution must be divided by the calculated PDF to ensure an unbiased estimator. Precision: Walking the CDF arrays requires careful handling of floating-point comparisons. If the random number equals the CDF value exactly, the loop condition <= ensures the next index is selected, which is consistent with standard inverse transform sampling definitions. Boundary Conditions: If the random number falls outside the range of the CDF (e.g., due to precision errors resulting in a value slightly > 1.0), the index should be clamped to the maximum valid index (W-1 or H-1). Time Complexity: Preprocessing is O(W \cdot H) to compute the textures. Sampling is O(W + H) in the worst case for walking the CDF arrays, though typically much faster if the CDFs are sampled via binary search (not specified in source, source describes linear walk). Memory Complexity: Requires storage for four textures: 2 \cdot W \cdot H floats for the 2D textures and 2 \cdot W floats for the 1D textures. For 180 \times 180, this is negligible. Performance: Significantly reduces the number of rays needed for the same quality compared to uniform sphere sampling by concentrating samples in luminous areas like the sun. Strengths: Efficiently handles procedural skies where analytical PDFs are difficult to derive. Reduces variance in scenes with bright localized light sources (sun). Limitations: Requires preprocessing time and memory for textures. Accuracy depends on the discretization resolution (180 \times 180 in the source). Linear walking of CDFs can be slow for high resolutions; binary search is recommended for production but not detailed in the source. When to use: When rendering procedural skies (e.g., Nishita model) in a path tracer where uniform sampling leads to high variance and slow convergence. When not to use: For simple directional lights (sun as a point) or when the sky is uniform. This method was implemented by Serkan Geren in a CUDA-based volumetric path tracer, specifically for the Nishita sky model implementation. The Nishita sky model uses Rayleigh and Mie scattering to achieve color and luminosity based on ray direction. The sampling strategy is inspired by the pbrt section on sampling light sources, adapting the marginal/conditional decomposition technique to the 2D discretization of a spherical sky. It was demonstrated in rendering clouds with a VPT (Volumetric Path Tracer) on an Nvidia GTX680. Sampling A Procedural Sky, https://sergeneren.com/2019/04/17/sampling-a-procedural-sky/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Explicit Path Tracing with Russian Roulette
head: Implicit Path Tracing, Monte Carlo Path Tracing, Path Tracing with Russian Roulette and Material Sampling
body: Explicit Path Tracing with Russian Roulette is a backward rendering algorithm that simulates light transport by recursively tracing rays from the camera, accumulating color contributions from surface interactions until a maximum bounce count is reached or a probabilistic termination condition is met. Unlike Single Scattering Volume Rendering with Ray Marching, which approximates volume effects via ray marching, this method handles discrete surface interactions and uses Russian Roulette to terminate paths based on surface albedo, balancing computational cost against variance. It differs from Unidirectional Path Tracing by explicitly managing the recursion depth and termination probability within the path generation loop rather than relying solely on fixed depth limits for all indirect terms. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Scene struct containing a Camera, a signed distance field map (SdfMap), and a background color function. Pixel coordinates (i, j), resolution (WIDTH, HEIGHT), and sample count per pixel. Output: A rendered image where each pixel contains the accumulated color C. Data Structures: Scene: camera: Camera struct. map: Box<dyn SdfMap> implementing ray intersection and normal retrieval. backgroundcolor: Function Fn(Vec3) -> Vec3 evaluating background radiance. Camera: position: Vec3 eye position. left, forward, up: Vec3 basis vectors. focallength: f32. aspectratio: f32. focusdist: f32. aperture: f32. Ray: origin: Vec3. direction: Vec3 (normalized). HitInfo: position: Vec3. material: Enum Material (e.g., Lambertian { color }, Emissive { color }, Specular { color, specularity, fuzziness }). Parameters: MAXBOUNCES: i32 = 4. Maximum recursion depth. SURFACEDIST: f32 = 0.001. Epsilon for shadow acne prevention. WIDTH: i32 = 800. Render width. HEIGHT: i32 = 600. Render height. SAMPLECOUNT: i32 = 100. Samples per pixel. Algorithm Steps: 1. Camera Ray Generation: For each pixel (i, j) and sample s: Generate jittered coordinates: x = \frac{-0.5 + (j + \text{jitter}x)}{WIDTH - 1.0} y = \frac{0.5 - (i + \text{jitter}y)}{HEIGHT - 1.0} where \text{jitter}x, \text{jitter}y \in [-0.5, 0.5] are uniform random floats. Compute ray origin and direction using Camera::getray: Sample aperture offset: (dx, dy) = \text{uniform\disk()}. offset = 0.5 \cdot aperture \cdot (dx \cdot left + dy \cdot up). origin = position + offset. direction = \text{normalize}(focus\dist \cdot (x \cdot \frac{left}{focal\length} + y \cdot \frac{up}{focal\length \cdot aspect\ratio} + forward) - offset). 2. Path Tracing Loop (castray): Initialize acc = Vec3::ONE (throughput) and bounces = 0. Loop indefinitely: Termination Check: If bounces > MAXBOUNCES, set acc = Vec3::ZERO and break. Ray Intersection: Query scene.map.rayintersection(origin, direction). Miss: If no hit, multiply acc by scene.backgroundcolor(direction) and break. Hit: Retrieve hitinfo. Emissive Material: If hitinfo.material is Emissive { color }, multiply acc by color and break (path terminates at light source). Lambertian Material: If Lambertian { color }: Multiply acc by color. Compute normal: n = \text{scene.map.normal}(hit\info.position). Offset origin: origin = hit\info.position + 2.0 \cdot SURFACE\DIST \cdot n. Sample new direction: direction = \text{cos\weighted\hemisphere}(n). Specular Material: If Specular { color, specularity, fuzziness }: Compute normal n. Offset origin: origin = hit\info.position + 2.0 \cdot SURFACE\DIST \cdot n. Generate random float \xi \in [0, 1). If \xi < specularity: Compute specular reflection: r = direction - 2.0 \cdot (direction \cdot n) \cdot n. Perturb: direction = \text{normalize}(r + fuzziness \cdot \text{uniform\ball}()). If direction \cdot n < 0.0, set acc = Vec3::ZERO and break. Else (diffuse component): Multiply acc by color. direction = \text{cos\weighted\hemisphere}(n). Russian Roulette / Depth Increment: Increment bounces by 1. Note: The provided source implements termination via MAXBOUNCES rather than explicit Russian Roulette probability based on albedo in the loop body, though the alias "Russian Roulette" suggests this concept is conceptually linked or implemented in variants. The source defines Russian Roulette as using Q = \max(color) as survival probability. In the absence of explicit RR code in 's loop, the loop relies on MAXBOUNCES for hard termination. If implementing the "Russian Roulette" aspect as per, one would check \xi < Q and terminate if false. 3. Accumulation: Sum all castray results for the pixel and divide by SAMPLECOUNT. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random MAXBOUNCES = 4 SURFACEDIST = 0.001 WIDTH = 800 HEIGHT = 600 SAMPLECOUNT = 100 def uniformdisk(): """Generate a uniform random point in the unit disk.""" while True: x = random.uniform(-1.0, 1.0) y = random.uniform(-1.0, 1.0) if xx + yy <= 1.0: return (x, y) def uniformball(): """Generate a uniform random point in the unit ball.""" # Implementation detail: reject sampling or normal distribution normalization # Standard approach: generate normal distribution and normalize while True: x = random.gauss(0, 1) y = random.gauss(0, 1) z = random.gauss(0, 1) length = math.sqrt(xx + yy + zz) if length > 1e-6: return (x/length, y/length, z/length) def cosweightedhemisphere(normal): """Sample a direction in the hemisphere defined by normal, weighted by cosine.""" # Generate random point on unit sphere u1 = random.uniform(0, 1) u2 = random.uniform(0, 1) z = math.sqrt(u1) theta = 2 math.pi u2 x = math.cos(theta) math.sqrt(1 - u1) y = math.sin(theta) math.sqrt(1 - u1) # Construct local basis # Assuming normal is (nx, ny, nz) # Create arbitrary tangent if abs(normal[0]) < 0.9: tangent = (1, 0, 0) else: tangent = (0, 1, 0) bitangent = ( normal[1]tangent[2] - It handles the intersection, shading, and recursion logic for a single light path segment. It is distinguished from non-recursive or iterative path tracers by its explicit handling of DDF queries (forward and backward passes) and its direct integration of Russian Roulette termination logic via the parent algorithm's bounce limit. A variance reduction technique using the scattering albedo to decide whether to continue tracing a scattered ray or terminate it. The scattering albedo is defined as \alpha = \sigmas / \sigmat, where \sigmas is the scattering coefficient and \sigmat is the extinction coefficient. If a random number \xi < \alpha, the path continues and the contribution is weighted by 1/\alpha; otherwise, the contribution is 0. Time Complexity: O(S \cdot B \cdot I), where S is the number of samples per pixel, B is the maximum number of bounces (MAXBOUNCES), and I is the cost of ray intersection. In practice, paths terminate early due to MAXBOUNCES or hitting emissive surfaces. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per ray, as the algorithm is iterative (or shallowly recursive) and does not store the full path history. Performance: Measured on a standard CPU implementation (Rust, single-threaded loop with parallel pixel processing via rayon), rendering 800x600 images with 100 samples takes several seconds to minutes depending on scene complexity. Strengths: Simple to implement; handles complex lighting via recursion; Russian Roulette (or bounce limits) prevents infinite loops. Limitations: High variance in scenes with deep shadows or complex indirect lighting; no explicit handling of volume scattering in the base algorithm; sensitive to MAXBOUNCES setting. When to use: General-purpose offline rendering for scenes with diffuse and specular surfaces. When not to use: Scenes requiring accurate volume rendering (use Path Tracing with Volume Interaction) or sparse participating media (use Path Tracing with Discrete Event Sampling). The algorithm originates from the implementation of a raymarching path tracer using Signed Distance Fields (SDFs). It combines standard path tracing concepts (recursive ray casting, BRDF sampling) with SDF-based intersection and Russian Roulette termination strategies. The specific implementation details, such as the MAXBOUNCES limit and material handling, are derived from the ollituohenmaa/raymarching-pathtracer repository. name: Path Tracing with Discrete Event Sampling
head: Null-Event Path Tracing, Russian Roulette with Discrete Events
body: Path Tracing with Discrete Event Sampling is a path tracing algorithm for participating media that replaces continuous Russian Roulette termination with a discrete probabilistic decision between absorption, scattering, and null events at each sampled point. Unlike Explicit Path Tracing with Russian Roulette, which uses continuous probability based on albedo/extinction ratios, this method explicitly handles null events (transmittance without interaction) to improve efficiency in sparse media by skipping non-interacting steps. It supports temperature-dependent emission and Henyey-Greenstein phase function scattering. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Volume grid providing density \sigmat(\mathbf{x}), temperature T(\mathbf{x}) (optional), and emission properties. Parameters: maxdepth, henyeygreensteing, lescale, temperaturescale, temperatureoffset, infinitelight. Random number generator (RNG). Outputs: Accumulated radiance L along the ray. Data Structures: MajorantTransmittanceSampler: Manages sampling of interaction points using a majorant extinction coefficient \sigmaM \ge \sigmat(\mathbf{x}). Stores current position, remaining distance, and step history. Event: Enum or integer representing {Null, Absorption, Scatter}. Steps: 1. Initialize: Set accumulated radiance L = 0 and terminated flag to false. Initialize pathdepth = 0. 2. Ray-Volume Intersection: Intersect the current ray with the volume grid. If no intersection, break the depth loop. 3. Sampler Initialization: Initialize MajorantTransmittanceSampler with the intersection, RNG, density grid, accessor, and total extinction coefficient. 4. Sample Points Loop: Loop through sampled points from the majorant sampler. a. Emission: If temperature grid is available, sample temperature at the point, convert to Kelvin (TK = t{norm} \times \text{temperature\scale} + \text{temperature\offset}), and add emission contribution: L \leftarrow L + pa \times \text{le\scale} \times \mathbf{L}e. b. Calculate Probabilities: Compute absorption probability pa and scattering probability ps based on the medium properties at \mathbf{x} and the ratio of coefficients to the majorant. Compute null probability: pn = \max(1.0 - pa - ps, 0.0). c. Sample Event: Sample a discrete event from {Null, Absorption, Scatter} with probabilities {pn, pa, ps} using a uniform random number u \in [0, 1). d. Null: If the event is Null, log it and continue to the next iteration of the path loop. e. Scatter: If the event is Scatter, check if maxdepth is reached. If so, log termination and break. Otherwise, recursively sample the scattered radiance L \leftarrow L + \text{sample\Ld}(...), sample a new direction using the Henyey-Greenstein phase function with parameter g, update the ray, log the scatter, and break the current loop iteration to continue the path. f. Absorption: If the event is Absorption, log it, mark as terminated, and break. 5. Termination Check: If the path terminates without scattering, break the outer loop. 6. Infinite Light: If the ray is not terminated (escapes to infinity), add infinite light contribution: L \leftarrow L + \text{params.infinite\light.xyz} \times \text{params.infinite\light.multiplier}. 7. Accumulate: Add the accumulated radiance to the film buffer, scaled by imagingratio, and increment the sample count. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pathtracingdiscreteevent(rayorigin, raydirection, params, grid, rng): L = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] terminated = False pathdepth = 0 currento = rayorigin currentd = raydirection while not terminated and pathdepth < params.maxdepth: hit = intersectvolumegrid(currento, currentd, grid.bbox) if not hit: break sampler = MajorantTransmittanceSampler(hit.t0, hit.t1, currentd, grid.densitygrid, grid.extinctiongrid, rng) while sampler.hasnext(): point, dist = sampler.nextsample() # Calculate extinction coefficients sigmat = grid.getextinction(point) sigmaa = grid.getabsorption(point) sigmas = sigmat - sigmaa sigmaM = sampler.majorant pa = sigmaa / sigmaM ps = sigmas / sigmaM pn = max(1.0 - pa - ps, 0.0) # Emission if grid.hastemperature(): tempnorm = grid.gettemperature(point) tempK = tempnorm params.temperaturescale + params.temperatureoffset le = blackbodyradiationxyz(tempK) L[0] += pa params.lescale le[0] L[1] += pa params.lescale le[1] L[2] += pa params.lescale le[2] # Sample event u = rng.uniform() if u < pn: continue elif u < pn + pa: terminated = True break else: if pathdepth >= params.maxdepth: terminated = True break pathdepth += 1 newdirection = samplehenyeygreenstein(currentd, params.henyeygreensteing, rng) currento = point currentd = newdirection # L accumulates across outer loop iterations break if terminated: break if not terminated: L[0] += params.infinitelight[0] params.infinitelight[1] L[1] += params.infinitelight[0] params.infinitelight[1] L[2] += params.infinitelight[0] params.infinitelight[1] return [x params.imagingratio for x in L] def intersectvolumegrid(origin, direction, bbox): # Returns hit object with t0, t1 or None if no intersection pass class MajorantTransmittanceSampler: def init(self, t0, t1, direction, densitygrid, extinctiongrid, rng): self.t0 = t0 self.t1 = t1 self.direction = direction self.densitygrid = densitygrid self.extinctiongrid = extinctiongrid self.rng = rng self.majorant = max(extinctiongrid.max(), 1e-6) self.currentt = t0 self.hasnextcalled = False def hasnext(self): return self.currentt < self.t1 def nextsample(self): # Sample distance using majorant exponential distribution u = self.rng.uniform() deltat = -math.log(1.0 - u) / self.majorant self.currentt += deltat point = self.currentt self.direction return point, deltat def blackbodyradiationxyz(temperaturek): h = 6.62606957e-34 c = 2.99792458e8 kb = 1.3806488e-23 # Simplified Planck's law for XYZ approximation lambdam = 5.0e-7 num = 2 h c c den = (lambdam 5) (math.exp((h c) / (lambdam kb temperaturek)) - 1) return [num / den, num / den, num / den] def samplehenyeygreenstein(direction, g, rng): # Standard Henyey-Greenstein phase function sampling pass Parameters: henyeygreensteing: Anisotropy parameter for the Henyey-Greenstein phase function. maxdepth: Maximum recursion depth for path tracing. lescale: Scaling factor for emission. temperaturescale, temperatureoffset: Parameters to convert normalized temperature samples to physical temperature (Kelvin). infinitelight: Directional light source properties (direction, intensity, multiplier). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Ensure pn is clamped to [0, 1] to avoid negative probabilities due to floating-point errors. Sparse Media: Null events are frequent in sparse media; skipping them efficiently is key. Majorant: The majorant must be \ge \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) everywhere; overestimating increases null events and reduces efficiency. Temperature Conversion: Ensure temperature conversion is physically accurate if using blackbody radiation. Accelerates path tracing in discrete participating media (e.g., sand) by replacing small-step integration with large-step sampling guided by precomputed probability densities. It differs from standard discrete event sampling by using spatial precomputation to determine scattering locations at larger distances, thereby reducing the number of sampling steps and improving convergence speed. Unlike methods for continuous media, it relies on the statistical independence of particle positions characteristic of discrete media. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of sampled points per ray segment and the depth of the path; null events allow skipping interactions, reducing the number of expensive scattering calculations in sparse media. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume grid (density, temperature, extinction) and the majorant; the sampler state is minimal. Performance: More efficient than continuous Russian Roulette in sparse media due to explicit null event handling; performance degrades in dense media where null events are rare. Strengths: Explicit handling of absorption and null events; supports temperature-dependent emission; efficient in sparse media. Limitations: Requires pre-computation or access to majorant; less efficient in dense media compared to methods that do not sample null events. When to Use: Sparse participating media, temperature-dependent emission, when explicit control over absorption/scattering/null events is desired. When Not to Use: Dense media where null events are rare, or when computational resources for pre-computing majorants/probabilities are limited. Originating from implementations like the unofficial volume path tracer by Shibodd, this method adapts path tracing for participating media by discretizing the interaction probabilities. It builds on the principles of Explicit Path Tracing with Russian Roulette but introduces discrete event sampling for better control and efficiency in specific media types. Shibodd/volumepathtracer, https://github.com/Shibodd/volumepathtracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Importance Sampling for Discrete Media
head: Concentric Spheres / Shells Precomputed Scattering, Moon et al. method, Precomputed Shell Importance Sampling, Shell Function Importance Sampling, Shell Tracing, Shell-based importance sampling for discrete media
body: This method accelerates path tracing in discrete participating media (e.g., sand) by replacing small-step integration with large-step sampling guided by precomputed probability densities. It differs from standard discrete event sampling by using spatial precomputation to determine scattering locations at larger distances, thereby reducing the number of sampling steps and improving convergence speed. The method consists of two phases: precomputation of scattering probabilities on concentric shells, and rendering via shell-guided sampling. Inputs: Medium properties: extinction coefficient \sigmat, albedo \omega0, and phase function p(\Omegai \to \Omegao). Scene geometry: a set of opaque surfaces defining the boundary of the medium. Precomputation resolution: number of concentric shells Ns and angular resolution per shell. Outputs: Precomputed probability density functions (PDFs) stored on concentric spheres/shells. Rendered image with reduced noise due to larger step sizes. The core data structure is a set of concentric shells centered at the current scattering position. Shell Structure: A shell is defined by its radius r and a 2D texture or array representing the PDF over the solid angle. PDF Storage: For each shell i with radius ri, the PDF pi(\Omega) is stored. Geometry Intersection: A spatial data structure (e.g., BVH or grid) is required to test if a sphere of radius r centered at a point intersects any scene geometry. 1. Center Selection: For a given scattering event at position \mathbf{x}, consider a set of concentric spheres centered at \mathbf{x} with radii r1, r2, \dots, r{Ns}. 2. PDF Calculation: For each radius ri, compute the probability density of the next scattering event occurring on the sphere of radius ri. This involves integrating the scattering probability over the sphere, accounting for attenuation through the medium and the phase function. 3. Storage: Store the computed PDFs for each shell. Materials with high albedo require longer computation times because particles are less likely to be absorbed, requiring more samples for accurate PDF estimation. 1. Ray Marching: When a ray hits a scattering event in the medium at position \mathbf{x}, the algorithm must determine the next scattering position. 2. Shell Selection: Find the sphere with the maximum radius r{max} centered at \mathbf{x} such that the sphere does not intersect any scene geometry. 3. Sampling: Sample the precomputed PDF associated with the selected shell r{max} to determine the direction \Omegao and distance r{max} to the next scattering event. The next position is \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} + r{max} \Omegao. The direction \Omegao is sampled from the stored angular PDF. 4. Weighting: Apply the appropriate Russian Roulette or weight adjustment based on the albedo and the ratio of the sampled PDF to the true PDF if importance sampling is not perfectly matched. The sources imply the precomputed PDF guides the sampling to reduce variance. 5. Iteration: Repeat from step 1 for the new position \mathbf{x}' until the path terminates or escapes the medium. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def precomputeshells(centerpoint, geometry, sigmat, albedo, numshells, angularresolution, deltar): shells = [] for i in range(numshells): r = (i + 1) deltar # Uniform radius spacing; deltar is not specified in sources # Check if sphere of radius r centered at centerpoint intersects any scene geometry if checkintersection(centerpoint, r, geometry): shells.append(Shell(radius=r, pdf=None)) continue pdfdata = computeshellpdf(r, sigmat, albedo, angularresolution) shells.append(Shell(radius=r, pdf=pdfdata)) return shells def samplenextscatter(centerpoint, precomputedshells): validshell = None # Iterate from largest radius to smallest to find the maximum non-intersecting sphere for shell in reversed(precomputedshells): if shell.pdf is not None: validshell = shell break if validshell is None: return None, None # Sample direction from the stored 2D PDF array using inverse transform or rejection sampling direction = validshell.pdf.sample() distance = validshell.radius nextposition = centerpoint + direction distance return nextposition, direction def computeshellpdf(r, sigmat, albedo, angularresolution): pdfarray = [0.0] angularresolution for idx in range(angularresolution): theta = (idx % 360) 3.14159 / 180.0 phi = (idx // 360) 3.14159 / 180.0 omega = [sin(phi)cos(theta), sin(phi)sin(theta), cos(phi)] # Evaluate the phase function p(omega) for the current direction pdfarray[idx] = evaluatephasefunction(omega) total = sum(pdfarray) # Normalize to form a valid probability distribution pdfarray = [p / total for p in pdfarray] return pdfarray def checkintersection(center, radius, geometry): # Standard geometry intersection test; implementation depends on scene representation return False # Placeholder for actual intersection logic Number of Shells: Not given in the sources. Depends on the spatial variation of the medium and geometry. Angular Resolution: Not given in the sources. Higher resolution reduces angular aliasing but increases memory. Albedo: High albedo materials require longer precomputation times. Geometry Intersection: If a sphere intersects geometry, it cannot be used for free-space sampling. The algorithm must select the largest non-intersecting sphere. Spatial Resolution: Concentric shells have lower spatial resolution, leading to poor representation on the axis and Mach banding effects if the number of samples is insufficient. Continuous Media: The method is designed for discrete media. When applied to continuous media, efficiency depends on the ratio of the mean-free-path to object size; it works better for smaller mean-free-paths (more opaque materials). A variant that combines accurate small-scale rendering with large-scale approximation. Meng et al. [68] variant: Uses path tracing with the shell-based method [69] for accurate rendering at small scales, and uses diffusion theory to approximate at large scales. Müller et al. [70] variant 1: Treats mixed media in multiple discrete participating media as equivalent continuous participating media to support mixed media rendering. Müller et al. [70] variant 2: Uses a particle scattering distribution function for small scale rendering and the method of Moon et al. [69] for large scale rendering. Time Complexity: Precomputation time depends on the number of shells, angular resolution, and albedo. High albedo materials require longer computation times. Rendering time is reduced compared to small-step tracing because fewer scattering events are sampled per path. Memory Complexity: Memory cost is determined by the number of shells and angular resolution. The sources note that memory costs are almost the same for different materials in their tests, but compression techniques (e.g., quadtree-based) can be used for adaptive representation. Performance: Reduces the number of sampling steps and improves convergence speed. However, it may suffer from Mach banding effects due to lower spatial resolution of concentric shells. Strengths: Efficient for discrete media like sand; reduces noise by taking larger steps. Limitations: Not suitable for continuous media without modification; suffers from aliasing/Mach banding; precomputation cost can be high for high-albedo materials. The method was proposed by Moon et al. [69] (also cited as [20] in some contexts) as an importance sampling approach for path tracing in discrete media via precomputation. It was designed to address the inefficiency of small-step integration in discrete media such as sand. The method has been further improved by Meng et al. [68] and Müller et al. [70] to support multi-scale rendering and mixed media scenarios. name: Recursive Trace Function
head: DDF-based recursive path tracing
body:
The Recursive Trace Function is the core recursive routine used in backward path tracing with Directed Distance Fields (DDF) to compute light transport for subsequent bounces. It handles intersection, shading, and recursion logic for a single light path segment. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: p: Origin point in \mathbb{R}^3. v: Incoming direction vector (pointing towards the eye, i.e., -v is the ray direction). \ell: Current bounce level (integer). Outputs: c: Radiance color vector (RGB) at p from direction v. Data Structures: DDF (d, \xi): A scalar field d(p, v) representing the distance to the surface along direction v from p, and a binary field \xi(p, v) indicating intersection (\xi < 0.5). Material Emission Field (ML): Queries emitted color cE at point q for direction \omegao. BRDF Field (fB): Queries reflectance B for incoming \omegai and outgoing \omegao. BRDF Sampling Distribution (\Psi): Samples outgoing direction vn given point q, outgoing direction \omegao, and normal n. Parameters: n{	ext{max}}: Maximum number of bounces (hyper-parameter). (Renamed from the source's n to avoid collision with the surface normal n) Steps: 1. Intersection Check: Evaluate \xi(p, v). If \xi(p, v) < 0.5, the ray does not intersect the scene geometry. Return the environment light EL(v). 2. Bounce Limit Check: If \ell \ge n{	ext{max}}, the maximum bounce depth is reached. Return the zero vector \vec{0}. 3. Forward Pass (Position): Compute the next scene point q along the ray direction -v: q = p + d(p, v)v 4. Backward Pass (Normal): Compute the surface normal n at q by taking the gradient of the distance field with respect to position: n = 	ext{Unit}(
ablap d(p, v)) 5. Direction Definitions: Outgoing direction (towards eye): \omegao = -v. Sample a light direction vn from the BRDF sampling distribution: vn \sim \Psi(q, \omegao \mid n). Incoming direction (into surface): \omegai = -vn. 6. Emission Query: Query the material emission field at q for direction \omegao: cE = ML(q, \omegao) 7. BRDF Query: Query the BRDF field at q for directions \omegai and \omegao: B = fB(q, \omegai, \omegao) 8. Recursive Call: Recursively call Trace with the new origin q, direction vn, and incremented bounce level \ell + 1: c{	ext{rec}} = 	ext{Trace}(q, vn, \ell + 1) 9. Weight Calculation: Compute the Monte Carlo weight wk for the sampled direction: wk = \Psi(vn \mid q, \omegao)^{-1} |n \cdot \omegai| 10. Return: Return the sum of emitted color and the weighted recursive color: c = cE + wk (B \odot c{	ext{rec}}) The source pseudocode shows B \odot 	ext{Trace}(\dots) inside the recursive call in Fig 25, but Fig 26 shows B \odot 	ext{Trace}(\dots) as part of the return calculation. Fig 26 is the specific definition of the recursive function. The return statement is cE + \Psi(vn \mid q, \omegao)^{-1} |n \cdot \omegai| c, where c is the result of B \odot 	ext{Trace}(\dots). Thus, the final formula is cE + wk (B \odot c{	ext{rec}}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def Trace(p, v, l, nmax, d, xi, gradd, ML, fB, Psi, EL): # 1. Intersection Check if xi(p, v) < 0.5: return EL(v) # 2. Bounce Limit Check if l >= nmax: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # 3. Forward Pass: Compute scene point q q = p + d(p, v) v # 4. Backward Pass: Compute surface normal n # gradd returns the gradient vector at p for direction v normal = normalize(gradd(p, v)) # 5. Direction Definitions omegao = -v # Sample outgoing direction from BRDF distribution vn = sample(Psi, q, omegao, normal) omegai = -vn # 6. Emission Query cE = ML(q, omegao) # 7. BRDF Query B = fB(q, omegai, omegao) # 8. Recursive Call crec = Trace(q, vn, l + 1, nmax, d, xi, gradd, ML, fB, Psi, EL) # 9. Weight Calculation # Psi returns the PDF value for the sampled direction vn pdf = Psi(q, omegao, normal, vn) weight = (1.0 / pdf) abs(dot(normal, omegai)) # 10. Return # B is multiplied element-wise with crec return cE + weight (B crec) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Precision: Computing 
ablap d(p, v) requires numerical or analytical gradients of the DDF. Small errors in the normal can cause shading artifacts. Zero PDF: If \Psi returns 0 for the sampled direction, division by zero occurs. The sampling distribution must be non-zero where the BRDF is non-zero. Recursion Depth: The function relies on the parent to manage the maximum bounce count n{	ext{max}}. If n{	ext{max}} is too small, paths terminate prematurely; if too large, performance degrades. Time Complexity: O(n{	ext{max}}) per path, where n{	ext{max}} is the maximum bounce depth. Each recursive call performs one forward pass (d(p, v)) and one backward pass (
ablap d(p, v)) on the DDF. Memory Complexity: O(n{	ext{max}}) stack space for recursion depth. Strengths: Integrates seamlessly with DDF-based rendering, avoiding explicit mesh intersection tests. Simple to implement as a recursive routine. Limitations: Recursion depth is limited by stack size. Performance depends heavily on the efficiency of the DDF queries. The Recursive Trace Function is defined in the context of "Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields for Ray-Based Shape Representations". It is part of a backward path tracing algorithm that uses DDFs to represent scene geometry and material properties. The method was introduced to enable efficient rendering of complex shapes represented by DDFs without explicit geometry. name: Unidirectional Path Tracing
head: Standard Path Tracing Lighting
body: Unidirectional Path Tracing is a Monte Carlo method for estimating the rendering equation by tracing sequences of connected rays (paths) from the camera into the scene, handling surface scattering and volumetric interactions via stochastic perturbation. It synthesizes the image by collecting all light paths that connect a pixel on the camera sensor to an emitter, updating a throughput vector at each bounce to accumulate emitted or reflected light. It sets itself apart from bidirectional methods by constructing paths solely from the camera side, and from pure rasterization by explicitly simulating global illumination through recursive ray tracing. Inputs: Camera ray (origin, direction), scene geometry (primitives, materials), medium stack (for volumetric regions), random number generator (sampler). Outputs: Radiance value L for the pixel. Data Structures: Ray: Struct containing origin (Vec3f), direction (Vec3f), throughput (Vec3f, initialized to (1,1,1)), and tmax (implied by intersection query). Medium: Stack of pointers representing the current volumetric environment. SurfaceInfo: Struct containing position, normal, shadingnormal, materialindex, and emission (Le). SceneData: Contains parameters including rayBounces (max depth), sunDir (vec3f), sunIntensity (f32), and sunEnabled (u32). MATERIALS: Constant array of size 5. Each material has specular (f32) and emissive (bool). Index 0: specular 0.0, not emissive. Index 1: specular 0.0, not emissive. Index 2: specular 0.0, emissive. Index 3: specular 0.9, not emissive. Index 4: specular 1.0, not emissive. Parameters: maxDepth: Maximum path length. Default value is 100. rayBounces: Controls the maximum number of ray bounces in SceneData. Algorithm: 1. Initialize radiance L = 0, throughput T = (1,1,1), and depth d = 0. 2. Loop while d < maxDepth: 3. Russian Roulette: If d > 0, calculate survival probability p = \min\left(\frac{Tr + Tg + Tb}{3}, 1.0\right). If sampler.getNext1D() \ge p, break loop. Otherwise, update T \leftarrow T / p. 4. Intersection: Intersect ray with scene primitives. If no intersection, return L. 5. Direct Light Check: If the hit primitive is an area light (emissive), add T \cdot Le to L and break loop. 6. BSDF Sampling: Sample the Bidirectional Scattering Distribution Function (BSDF) at the hit point. Compute incoming direction \omegai and outgoing direction \omegao (ray direction). Evaluate BSDF f(\omegai, \omegao) and PDF p(\omegao). Light Leak Guard: Check asymmetry of BSDF using shading normals (ns) and geometric normals (ng). If \omegai \cdot ng \cdot \omegai \cdot ns \le 0 or \omegao \cdot ng \cdot \omegao \cdot ns \le 0, return 0 (discard path). Update throughput: T{new} = T{old} \cdot \frac{f(\omegai, \omegao) \cdot |\cos \theta|}{p(\omegao)}, where \theta is the angle between the surface normal and the outgoing direction. Set flag isreflectedorrefracted = true. 7. Medium Update: Update the medium stack based on surface crossing using updateMedium(ray, dir, info). 8. Ray Update: Set ray origin to surfaceInfo.position and direction to the sampled \omegai. 9. Depth Increment: If isscattered or isreflectedorrefracted, increment d. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def unidirectionalpathtracing(cameraray, scene, sampler): radiance = Vec3f(0, 0, 0) throughput = Vec3f(1, 1, 1) depth = 0 maxdepth = 100 # Default value ray = cameraray ray.throughput = throughput while depth < maxdepth: # Russian Roulette if depth > 0: avgthroughput = (throughput.r + throughput.g + throughput.b) / 3.0 probability = min(avgthroughput, 1.0) if sampler.getnext1d() >= probability: break throughput = throughput / probability # Intersection surfaceinfo = scene.intersect(ray) if surfaceinfo is None: break # Direct Emission Check if surfaceinfo.isemissive: radiance += throughput surfaceinfo.emission break # BSDF Sampling # Sample BSDF: returns direction, pdf, and f wo, pdf, f = surfaceinfo.bsdf.sample( -ray.direction, surfaceinfo, FROMCAMERA, sampler) # Light Leak Guard wins = dot(wo, surfaceinfo.shadingnormal) wons = dot(wo, surfaceinfo.shadingnormal) # Note: source implies checking both wi and wo against normals # Source says: If wing wins <= 0 or wong wons <= 0, return 0 # Assuming wo is the outgoing direction from surface (incoming to ray) if dot(wo, surfaceinfo.geometricnormal) wins <= 0 or \ dot(wo, surfaceinfo.geometricnormal) wons <= 0: break # Discard path # Throughput Update costheta = abs(dot(wo, surfaceinfo.normal)) throughput = throughput (f costheta) / pdf # Medium Update updatemedium(ray, wo, surfaceinfo) # Ray Update ray.origin = surfaceinfo.position ray.direction = wo ray.throughput = throughput # Depth Increment depth += 1 return radiance A Monte Carlo method for simulating light transport in participating media, such as fog, smoke, and clouds, by modeling color-dependent absorption and scattering. It extends classical path tracing by allowing rays to enter volumetric regions, sample scattering events within the medium, and continue random walks after each scattering interaction to support multiple scattering. Unlike its sibling Unidirectional Volume Boundary Estimator, which focuses on boundary estimation, or Volumetric-Primitives Path Tracer, which uses primitives for acceleration, this method relies on delta tracking for volume sampling and does not perform explicit light sampling or handle surface scattering. It is primarily used for computing ground-truth results when debugging more sophisticated algorithms due to its simplicity and higher variance compared to light-sampling integrators. The Unidirectional Volume Boundary Estimator is a Monte Carlo method that samples volume boundary paths by building a main path from the detector to the light, then constructing side paths from main path vertices to the volume boundary and then to the light. It solves the problem of efficiently sampling paths where a scattering event occurs exactly on a volume boundary (interface). It sets itself apart from its sibling, the Bidirectional Volume Boundary Estimator, by constructing the path unidirectionally: it samples the main path first and then the boundary vertex, whereas the bidirectional variant samples the boundary vertex first and connects it to both light and camera. A forward rendering method for scattering and emissive media that models the scene as a collection of 3D kernel-based volumetric primitives and uses ray tracing to compute light transport, supporting multiple scattering via Next-Event Estimation. Unlike Volumetric Path Tracing which typically relies on voxel grids or implicit fields requiring numerical integration, VPPT provides closed-form analytical solutions for transmittance and free-flight sampling, eliminating Monte Carlo noise for single-scattering events and enabling efficient hardware-accelerated traversal. It maintains 3D volumetric density and integrates physically, preserving reciprocity and avoiding the view-dependent ordering artifacts and popping seen in delta-function approximations like 3D Gaussian Splatting. Unidirectional Differentiable Path Tracing is an algorithm to estimate the interior integral of the differential path integral using unidirectional path tracing, computing both the radiometric measurement L and its scene derivative \dot{L}. It sets itself apart from standard unidirectional path tracing by jointly estimating the measurement and its gradient with respect to scene parameters \pi using automatic differentiation, while carefully separating PDF terms from the differentiation graph to ensure correctness. It builds on Unidirectional Path Tracing. A rendering technique using a CPU-based volumetric path tracer with Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) to render generated volumetric data across different LoDs. It uses Woodcock’s Delta Tracking technique for transmittance estimation during the path tracing process. A technique to introduce correlation in path space by evaluating two states of the scene (current and previous) simultaneously during a single trace pass, enabling the use of control variates for variance reduction. It initializes radiance accumulators L{old}, L{new} to 0 and beta weights \beta{old}, \beta{new} to 1. It sets flag prev{bsdf\delta} to True. It intersects the ray with the scene; if no intersection, it returns L{old}, L{new}. If the previous BSDF was delta, it adds direct emission to both old and new paths using MIS weights, scaled by their respective beta weights. It samples the emitter, evaluating the BSDF for the current state (val) and previous state (val{old}), and adds emitter contribution to both paths, scaled by beta weights and MIS. It samples the BSDF, evaluating the current path for the previous state using eval{old}, and updates the prev{bsdf\delta} flag. It updates beta weights: if the previous BSDF was delta, it sets \beta{old} = 0; otherwise, it updates \beta{old} by multiplying by val{old}/pdf and \beta{new} by multiplying by val/pdf. The BSDF must be augmented to keep track of the previous parameter state, queryable via bsdf.evalold. Use of a path tracing integrator to reconstruct Principled BSDFs, providing an unbiased estimate of the rendering equation and allowing gradients to flow through all physically relevant light transport paths, including indirect bounces and coupled terms. Path tracing is required over compute-efficient integrators like Path Replay Backpropagation because translucent effects and nonlinear interactions with incoming light cannot be captured by the latter. Path tracing requires more samples per pixel to reconstruct textures used to parameterize the material. Complexity: Time complexity is proportional to the number of bounces and the cost of intersection queries. Memory complexity is dominated by the scene representation and the recursion stack (or explicit path buffer). Performance: Requires significant computational power; an RTX 3090 can run related voxel-based path tracing at 4K averaging around 120fps, but performance dips with scene complexity. Strengths: Physically accurate global illumination; unbiased estimator; handles complex lighting scenarios including indirect bounces and translucent effects. Limitations: High variance (noise) requiring many samples per pixel; slow convergence for scenes with complex light transport (e.g., caustics, deep shadows); requires more samples than compute-efficient integrators for material reconstruction. Usage: Useful for studying visible light and any type of electromagnetic radiation due to its ray-based nature. Essential for differentiable rendering and material reconstruction where gradients must flow through all light transport paths. Unidirectional path tracing is the standard algorithmic realization of ray tracing for lighting, tracing sequences of connected rays from the camera to synthesize images by collecting light paths connecting pixels to emitters. It is widely used in production rendering and research for its physical accuracy. It serves as the foundation for more advanced techniques like differentiable path tracing and volumetric path tracing. jamestkiernan/webgpu-voxel-raymarching, https://github.com/jamestkiernan/webgpu-voxel-raymarching, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) Differentiable visual computing for inverse problems and machine learning, https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-023-00743-0, fetched 2026-10-27 GitHub - yumcyaWiz/volpt: Volumetric path tracer written in C++, https://github.com/yumcyaWiz/volpt, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Fast Voxelization and Level of Detail for Microgeometry Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2604.13191, fetched 2026-10-26 Recursive Control Variates for Inverse Rendering, https://research.nvidia.com/labs/rtr/publication/nicolet2023recursive/, fetched 2026-11-08 MRD: Using Physically Based Differentiable Rendering to Probe Vision Models for 3D Scene Understanding, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2512.12307, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Volumetric Path Tracing
head: Path Tracing Volumes, Simple Volumetric Path Tracing, SimpleVolPathIntegrator, VolpathSimpleIntegrator, volpathsimple-basic, volpathsimple-drt
body: Volumetric Path Tracing is a Monte Carlo method for simulating light transport in participating media, such as fog, smoke, and clouds, by modeling color-dependent absorption and scattering. It extends classical path tracing by allowing rays to enter volumetric regions, sample scattering events within the medium, and continue random walks after each scattering interaction to support multiple scattering. Unlike its sibling Unidirectional Volume Boundary Estimator, which focuses on boundary estimation, or Volumetric-Primitives Path Tracer, which uses primitives for acceleration, this method relies on delta tracking for volume sampling and does not perform explicit light sampling or handle surface scattering. It is primarily used for computing ground-truth results when debugging more sophisticated algorithms due to its simplicity and higher variance compared to light-sampling integrators. Inputs: A camera ray r = (o, d) with origin o and normalized direction d. A scene containing a single participating medium with a convex bounding volume and a null BSDF at its boundary. Infinite light sources (e.g., environment maps or constant lights). A maximum path depth maxDepth. A sampler providing uniform random numbers. Outputs: The estimated radiance L along the ray. Data Structures: Ray: Struct with fields o (origin, Vec3) and d (direction, Vec3, normalized). MediumProperties: Contains absorption coefficient \sigmaa, scattering coefficient \sigmas, total extinction \sigmat = \sigmaa + \sigmas, and phase function. RNG: Random number generator initialized from hashed sampler values. Parameters: maxDepth: Integer, typically 5–10. \sigmaa, \sigmas: Coefficients per channel (R, G, B). \sigma{maj}: Majorant extinction coefficient, \sigma{maj} \ge \sigmat everywhere in the medium. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize radiance accumulator L = 0, path throughput \beta = 1.0, and depth depth = 0. 2. Terminate secondary wavelengths if spectral rendering is supported, estimating only the primary wavelength for simplicity. 3. Loop while depth < maxDepth: a. Intersection Test: Find the first intersection si of the current ray with the scene geometry. Determine t{max}, the distance to the nearest surface intersection or the ray's maximum range. b. Delta Tracking: If the ray is inside a medium: i. Initialize an RNG using two hashed samples from the main sampler: hash0 = Hash(sampler.Get1D()), hash1 = Hash(sampler.Get1D()), RNG rng(hash0, hash1). ii. Sample a uniform random number u and a mode selection number u{mode} from the sampler. iii. Perform delta tracking using the majorant \sigma{maj} to sample a distance t to the next interaction event. iv. At the sampled point p = o + d \cdot t, evaluate the medium properties \sigmaa, \sigmas, \sigmat and the transmittance T{maj} = \exp(-(\sigma{maj} - \sigmat)t). v. Compute event probabilities: p{Absorb} = \frac{\sigmaa}{\sigma{maj}} p{Scatter} = \frac{\sigmas}{\sigma{maj}} p{Null} = \max(0, 1 - p{Absorb} - p{Scatter}) vi. Select the event mode using discrete sampling with probabilities \{p{Absorb}, p{Scatter}, p{Null}\} based on u{mode}. vii. If Absorb: Add emission from the medium at p to L: L += \beta \cdot Le(p, \omega) (where Le is medium emission, often 0). Terminate the path. viii. If Scatter: If depth \ge maxDepth, terminate the path. Increment depth. Sample a scattering direction \omega' using the phase function p(\omega \to \omega') and two uniform random numbers. Update throughput: \beta = \beta \cdot \frac{p(\omega \to \omega')}{p{Scatter}}. Update ray: o = p, d = \omega'. Continue the loop to process the scattered ray. ix. If Null: Generate a new u{mode} from the RNG and continue delta tracking (sample a new distance). c. Termination Check: If the path was terminated in step 3b, return L. d. Surface Interaction: If a surface intersection si exists: i. Get the BSDF from the intersection. ii. If the BSDF exists and returns a valid sample (non-delta), the integrator issues an error because it does not support surface scattering. iii. If the BSDF is null or the intersection is skipped, proceed to emission accumulation. e. Emission Accumulation: i. If a surface intersection si exists and was not skipped, add surface emission: L += \beta \cdot Le(si, -d). ii. If no surface intersection exists, add emission from all infinite lights: L += \beta \cdot \sum{lights} Le(light, ray). iii. Return L. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def volumetricpathtracing(rayo, rayd, scene, sampler, maxdepth): L = 0.0 beta = 1.0 depth = 0 # Normalize direction invlen = 1.0 / math.sqrt(sum(cc for c in rayd)) rayd = [c invlen for c in rayd] while depth < maxdepth: si = scene.intersect(rayo, rayd) tmax = si.thit if si else float('inf') scattered = False terminated = False if scene.isinmedium(rayo, rayd): # Initialize RNG from hashed sampler values hash0 = hash(sampler.get1d()) hash1 = hash(sampler.get1d()) rng = random.Random(hash0 ^ hash1) u = sampler.get1d() umode = sampler.get1d() # Delta tracking loop while True: sigmamaj = scene.getmajorant(rayo, rayd, 0.0) t = -math.log(1.0 - rng.random()) / sigmamaj if t >= tmax: t = tmax break mp = scene.getmediumproperties(rayo, rayd, t) sigmat = mp.sigmaa + mp.sigmas pabsorb = mp.sigmaa / sigmamaj pscatter = mp.sigmas / sigmamaj pnull = max(0.0, 1.0 - pabsorb - pscatter) if umode < pabsorb: L += beta mp.emission terminated = True break elif umode < pabsorb + pscatter: depth += 1 u1, u2 = rng.random(), rng.random() ps = mp.phase.sample(-rayd, u1, u2) if not ps: terminated = True else: beta = ps.p / pscatter rayo = [rayo[i] + rayd[i] t for i in range(3)] rayd = ps.wi scattered = True break else: umode = rng.random() continue if terminated: return L if scattered: continue if si: bsdf = si.getbsdf(rayd) if bsdf and bsdf.hassample(): raise ValueError("SimpleVolPathIntegrator doesn't support surface scattering.") else: si.skipintersection(rayo, rayd, si.thit) if si: L += beta si.intr.le(-rayd) else: for light in scene.infinitelights: L += beta light.le(rayo, rayd) return L return L Extends the basic method by explicitly connecting path vertices to lights to solve inefficiency with small/distant lights, changing the integration domain to light surface area. Handles spectral wavelength sampling for dispersion effects using spectral MIS for channel selection. Derives the simplified Monte Carlo estimator for the generalized path contribution function, reducing the raw path integral to phase function ratios and emission. Computes single-scattering radiance by sampling distance directly from the transmittance distribution, handling surface intersections and light emission. Provides an unbiased estimator for first-order radiance derivatives, enabling differentiable rendering. Estimates derivatives of the RTE with respect to scene parameters (e.g., albedo) for inverse rendering. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of path vertices, but delta tracking can be inefficient if the majorant \sigma{maj} is much larger than the actual \sigmat, leading to many null scattering events. Memory Complexity: Low, as it avoids spatial acceleration structures for the volume itself. Performance: High variance (MSE) compared to light-sampling integrators like [VolPathIntegrator] because it does not sample lights directly. Requires many samples per pixel (e.g., 256–512) for reasonable noise reduction. Strengths: Simple implementation, robust for homogeneous and heterogeneous media within convex bounds, good for ground-truth generation. Limitations: Does not handle surface scattering, requires convex bounding volumes, assumes null BSDF at boundaries, and only supports infinite light sources. Inefficient for scenes with small or distant lights due to lack of explicit light sampling. Volumetric Path Tracing was developed as an academic exercise to study light transport in participating media compared to ray marching approaches. The SimpleVolPathIntegrator is described in the "Physically Based Rendering" (pbrt) book, Chapter 14, as a basic integrator for educational purposes. It uses delta tracking, a technique originally proposed by Keller for rendering participating media, to sample interaction events without requiring spatial acceleration structures for the volume itself. The method is often used as a baseline for more advanced integrators like VolPathIntegrator. ainagutierrez01/Volumetric-Path-Tracing-, https://github.com/ainagutierrez01/Volumetric-Path-Tracing-, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) MajorMeerkatThe3rd/VolumetricPathTracing, https://github.com/MajorMeerkatThe3rd/VolumetricPathTracing, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) https://github.com/rgl-epfl/unbiased-inverse-volume-rendering, https://github.com/rgl-epfl/unbiased-inverse-volume-rendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) 14.2 Volume Scattering Integrators, https://pbr-book.org/4ed/LightTransportIIVolumeRendering/VolumeScatteringIntegrators, fetched 2026-10-29 Volume Rendering and Scattering Theory, https://www.scribd.com/document/912805133/02941-Slides-07-Volumes, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Lighting And Transmittance, https://sergeneren.com/2019/04/26/lighting-and-transmittance/, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)
