name: Multiple Scattering Volume Path Tracing with Phase Function Sampling
head: VolPathIntegrator, Volumetric Path Integrator
body: A path tracing technique for simulating light transport in participating media where a ray enters a material, applies a BTDF, travels a distance determined by an exponential distribution, scatters according to a phase function, and repeats until exiting the material with another BTDF. It solves the problem of rendering multiple scattering events in homogeneous volumes by importance-sampling the distance to the next interaction and the scattering direction, supporting index-matched surfaces and Russian roulette termination. Unlike its parent Volumetric Path Tracing, which uses simple delta tracking, this method explicitly samples the phase function to handle multiple bounces efficiently. It differs from Volumetric Path Tracing with Transmittance Sampling by using majorant-based transmittance sampling to handle inhomogeneous or complex media boundaries robustly. Inputs: Camera ray, scene geometry, participating media definitions (scattering coefficient \sigmas, absorption coefficient \sigmaa, phase function), light sources, maximum depth maxDepth, Russian roulette depth rrdepth, and a sampler for random numbers. Outputs: Radiance L for the pixel. Data Structures: Ray: Origin o, direction d, time time, medium pointer. MediumProperties: \sigmaa (absorption), \sigmas (scattering), \sigmat = \sigmaa + \sigmas (extinction), phase function, emission Le. SampledSpectrum: Represents spectral data (e.g., RGB or sampled wavelengths). PhaseFunctionSample: Contains direction wi, PDF pdf, and phase function value p. BSDFSample: Contains direction wi, PDF pdf, BSDF value f, and flags (specular, transmission). Parameters: maxDepth: Integer limiting the maximum number of bounces/scattering events. If -1, infinite bounces are allowed (though Russian roulette terminates them). maxDepth=2 corresponds to single scattering. rrdepth: Controls when Russian roulette begins. RR starts when a light path has rrdepth + 1 vertices. regularize: Boolean flag; if true, BSDFs are regularized after non-specular bounces to prevent numerical instability. lightSampleStrategy: String specifying the light sampling strategy (default "bvh"). Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize state variables: L = 0 (Radiance) \beta = 1 (Path throughput weight) ru = 1 (Rescaled unidirectional probability) rl = 1 (Rescaled light-sampling probability) specularBounce = false anyNonSpecularBounces = false depth = 0 etaScale = 1 (Scalar multiplier for transmission refractive index) prevIntrContext = LightSampleContext (empty) 2. Main Loop: While true: a. Intersection: Intersect the current ray with the scene geometry to get intersection si. Let t{max} = si.t{hit} if an intersection exists, otherwise t{max} = \infty. b. Volumetric Sampling (if in medium): If the ray is inside a medium: i. RNG Initialization: Generate two 1D samples from the sampler, hash them to create hash0 and hash1, and initialize a local RNG rng(hash0, hash1). ii. Majorant Sampling: Sample the majorant transmittance T{maj} using SampleTmaj. This involves a callback that receives point p, medium properties mp, majorant cross-section \sigma{maj}, and transmittance T{maj}. iii. Medium Emission: If depth < maxDepth and the medium emits light (mp.Le): Compute PDF: pdf = \sigma{maj}[0] \cdot T{maj}[0]. Compute \beta' = \beta \cdot T{maj} / pdf. Compute rescaled absorption probability: re = ru \cdot \sigma{maj} \cdot T{maj} / pdf. If re is non-zero, add to radiance: L += \beta' \cdot mp.\sigmaa \cdot mp.Le / re.Average(). iv. Event Probabilities: Compute probabilities for absorption, scattering, and null scattering: p{Absorb} = \frac{\sigmaa[0]}{\sigma{maj}[0]} p{Scatter} = \frac{\sigmas[0]}{\sigma{maj}[0]} p{Null} = \max(0, 1 - p{Absorb} - p{Scatter}) v. Sample Event Type: Draw uniform random number um. Determine mode: mode = \text{SampleDiscrete}(\{p{Absorb}, p{Scatter}, p{Null}\}, um) vi. Handle Event: Absorption (mode == 0): Set terminated = true and return false from the callback to end the path. Scattering (mode == 1): If depth >= maxDepth, set terminated = true and return false. Increment depth. Compute PDF: pdf = T{maj}[0] \cdot mp.\sigmas[0]. Update \beta and ru: \beta \leftarrow \beta \cdot \frac{T{maj} \cdot mp.\sigmas}{pdf} ru \leftarrow ru \cdot \frac{T{maj} \cdot mp.\sigmas}{pdf} If \beta and ru are non-zero: Create MediumInteraction intr at point p with direction -ray.d. Sample direct lighting: L += \text{SampleLd}(intr, \text{nullptr}, \lambda, \text{sampler}, \beta, ru). Sample phase function: Generate 2D sample u. Call ps = intr.phase.Samplep(-ray.d, u). If ps is null or ps.pdf == 0, set terminated = true. Else: Update \beta and rl: \beta \leftarrow \beta \cdot \frac{ps.p}{ps.pdf} rl \leftarrow \frac{ru}{ps.pdf} Store prevIntrContext = LightSampleContext(intr). Set scattered = true. Update ray: ray.o = p, ray.d = ps.wi. Set specularBounce = false, anyNonSpecularBounces = true. Return false from callback. Null Scattering (mode == 2): Compute null scattering coefficient: \sigman = \text{ClampZero}(\sigma{maj} - mp.\sigmaa - mp.\sigmas). Compute PDF: pdf = T{maj}[0] \cdot \sigman[0]. Update \beta: \beta \leftarrow \beta \cdot \frac{T{maj} \cdot \sigman}{pdf} If pdf == 0, set \beta = 0. Update ru and rl: ru \leftarrow ru \cdot \frac{T{maj} \cdot \sigman}{pdf} rl \leftarrow rl \cdot \frac{T{maj} \cdot \sigma{maj}}{pdf} Return beta && ru (boolean result of validity). c. Post-Medium Handling: If terminated or \beta=0 or ru=0, return L. If scattered, continue to next iteration of the main loop. If unscattered (ray passed through medium without interaction): \beta \leftarrow \beta \cdot \frac{T{maj}}{T{maj}[0]} ru \leftarrow ru \cdot \frac{T{maj}}{T{maj}[0]} rl \leftarrow rl \cdot \frac{T{maj}}{T{maj}[0]} d. Surface Intersection Handling: If no intersection (!si): For each infinite light source: If light emits (Le): If depth == 0 or specularBounce: L += \beta \cdot Le / ru.Average() Else (MIS): Compute light PDF: lightPDF = lightSampler.PMF(prevIntrContext, light) \cdot light.PDF{Li}(prevIntrContext, ray.d, true). Update rl: rl \leftarrow rl \cdot lightPDF. L += \beta \cdot Le / (ru + rl).Average() If intersection exists (si): Get BSDF: bsdf = isect.GetBSDF(ray, \lambda, camera, scratchBuffer, sampler). If !bsdf, skip intersection and continue. Visible Surface Initialization: If depth == 0 and visibleSurf is set: Define 16 sample arrays ucRho and uRho (values hardcoded in). Compute albedo: albedo = bsdf.rho(isect.wo, ucRho, uRho). Set visibleSurf = VisibleSurface(isect, albedo, \lambda). Depth Check: If depth >= maxDepth, return L. Increment depth. Regularization: If regularize and anyNonSpecularBounces, call bsdf.Regularize(). Direct Lighting: If BSDF is non-specular: L += \text{SampleLd}(isect, &bsdf, \lambda, \text{sampler}, \beta, ru) Update prevIntrContext = LightSampleContext(isect). BSDF Sampling: Get outgoing direction wo = isect.wo. Generate 1D sample u and 2D sample. Sample BSDF: bs = bsdf.Samplef(wo, u, sampler.Get2D()). If !bs, break loop. Update \beta and rl: \beta \leftarrow \beta \cdot \frac{bs.f \cdot |n \cdot wi|}{bs.pdf} If bs.pdfIsProportional: rl = \frac{ru}{bsdf.PDF(wo, bs.wi)} Else: rl = \frac{ru}{bs.pdf} Update state: specularBounce = bs.IsSpecular(). anyNonSpecularBounces |= !bs.IsSpecular(). If transmission: etaScale = Sqr(bs.eta). Spawn new ray: ray = isect.SpawnRay(ray, bsdf, bs.wi, bs.flags, bs.eta). BSSRDF Handling: If BSSRDF exists and BSDF is transmission: Sample probe segment: probeSeg = bssrdf.SampleSp(uc, up). If !probeSeg, break. Initialize interactionSampler with seed. Intersect ray from p0 to p1. If intersection on same material, add to sampler with weight 1. If no sample, break. Get subsurface interaction ssi and sample bssrdfSample. Update \beta and ru using bssrdfSample.Sp and PDF. Sample BSDF at exit point pi: bs = Sw.Samplef(pi.wo, u, sampler.Get2D()). If !bs, break. Update \beta and rl: \beta \leftarrow \beta \cdot \frac{bs.f \cdot |n \cdot wi|}{bs.pdf} rl = \frac{ru}{bs.pdf} Set specularBounce, spawn new ray from pi. e. Russian Roulette: Compute rrBeta = \beta \cdot etaScale / ru.Average(). Generate u{RR}. If rrBeta.MaxComponentValue() < 1 and depth > 1: Compute q = \max(0, 1 - rrBeta.MaxComponentValue()). If u{RR} < q, break. Else, \beta /= 1 - q. 3. Return: Return L. Formulas: Extinction: \sigmat = \sigmas + \sigmaa. Rescaled Probabilities: r{u, \lambda, i}(\bar{p}n) = \frac{p{u, \lambda, i}(\bar{p}n)}{p{path}(\bar{p}n)} r{l, \lambda, i}(\bar{p}n) = \frac{p{l, \lambda, i}(\bar{p}n)}{p{path}(\bar{p}n)} MIS Weight (Unidirectional): wu(\bar{p}n) = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{m} \sum{i=1}^m r{u, \lambda, i}(\bar{p}n) + \sum{i=1}^m r{l, \lambda, i}(\bar{p}n)} Russian Roulette Probability: P{rr} = \min \left( \frac{\text{contrib}(\text{path})}{p(\text{path})}, 0.95 \right) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Double Counting: Do not apply Beer-Lambert attenuation e^{-\sigma x} explicitly to path weights if the distance was importance-sampled from the exponential distribution, as it is implicitly incorporated in the sampling probability. Zero PDF: If phase function sampling fails or returns zero PDF, terminate the path. If null scattering PDF is zero, explicitly set \beta=0 to prevent division by zero. Chromatic Media: For non-monochromatic coefficients, simulating all channels simultaneously is inefficient. Assign each ray a single wavelength or color channel and calculate scattering separately. Index-Matched Surfaces: Surfaces with materialid == -1 are index-matched. Pass through them, update the medium using updatemedium, and increment bounces. Adds direct lighting estimation by sampling points on light sources and tracing shadow rays. Solves inefficiency with small/distant lights. Extends to subsurface scattering by integrating BSSRDF probes into the path traversal loop. Handles translucent materials within media. Complexity: Time complexity depends on the number of scattering events, which is driven by the optical thickness of the medium. Memory complexity is linear in path depth. Performance: Robust for multiple scattering in homogeneous and inhomogeneous media. Majorant sampling handles complex boundaries but may be less efficient if the majorant is much larger than the actual extinction coefficient. Strengths: Handles multiple scattering, index-matched surfaces, and chromatic media. Rescaled probabilities prevent floating-point overflow/underflow. Limitations: Can be slow for very dense media due to many scattering events. Russian roulette introduces variance. When to use: Ground truth rendering, scenes with complex volumetric interactions, translucent materials. When not to use: Real-time rendering requiring approximations, very sparse media where simpler methods suffice. Originated from the need to simulate light transport in participating media accurately. The VolPathIntegrator is a key component of modern path tracers like PBRT, handling both surface and volume transport robustly. It builds on earlier work in Monte Carlo volumetric scattering and extends basic volumetric path tracing by incorporating rescaled probabilities and MIS for unidirectional and light sampling strategies. name: Next Event Estimation for Volumetric Path Tracing
head: NEE with transmittance, PathTracingNEE, Volumetric NEE, Volumetric Next Event Estimation with Index-Matching Surfaces, Volumetric Path Tracing 4, Volumetric Path Tracing with Next Event Estimation
body: Next Event Estimation (NEE) for volumetric path tracing is an optimization that adds direct lighting estimation to multiple scattering volume path tracing by sampling points on light sources and tracing shadow rays through participating media and index-matching surfaces. It solves the inefficiency of pure phase function sampling when light sources are small or distant by explicitly connecting path vertices to lights. Unlike its parent method, which only samples the phase function, this method changes the integration domain from the hemisphere to the light surface area, requiring the computation of transmittance through volumes and the handling of index-matched boundaries. It differs from Volumetric Path Tracing with BSSRDF and Medium Sampling by focusing on direct light connections via shadow rays rather than medium sampling for indirect illumination. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current scattering position \mathbf{p} in the medium, current medium extinction coefficient \sigmat, view direction \omegao, light sampler, and scene geometry including index-matching surfaces (surfaces with materialid == -1). Output: Direct lighting contribution Ls at \mathbf{p} from the sampled light, or 0 if blocked. Data Structures: Ray: Origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, medium reference. Intersection: Hit position \mathbf{p}{hit}, distance t, materialid (opaque if \ge 0, index-matching if -1). LightSampleContext: Contains surface interaction info for light sampling. Parameters: maxdepth: Maximum path depth (bounces + shadow bounces). ShadowEpsilon: Small offset to prevent self-intersection (e.g., 10^{-3} or 10^{-9} depending on implementation). Steps: 1. Light Sampling: Sample a light source and a point \mathbf{p}' on it. Sample light index: u1 = \text{sampler.Get1D()}. Sample point on light: u2 = \text{sampler.Get2D()}. Compute light PDF: p{light} = p{\text{selection}} \cdot p{\text{point}}. If no sample or Le(\mathbf{p}') = 0, return 0. 2. Shadow Ray Initialization: Direction to light: \mathbf{d}{light} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{p}' - \mathbf{p}). Initialize transmittance accumulator: T{light} = 1. Initialize shadow medium: \text{shadow\medium} = \text{current\medium}. Initialize shadow bounce counter: \text{shadow\bounces} = 0. Initialize MIS transmittance PDF factor: p{trans\dir} = 1. 3. Shadow Ray Tracing Loop: While \mathbf{d}{light} \neq \mathbf{0}: Create shadow ray: \mathbf{r} = \text{Ray}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{d}{light}). Intersect with scene: \text{isect} = \text{intersect}(\text{scene}, \mathbf{r}). Determine segment distance: If \text{isect} exists: t{seg} = \text{distance}(\mathbf{p}, \text{isect.position}). Else: t{seg} = \text{distance}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{p}'). Compute Transmittance: If \text{shadow\medium} is valid: T{light} \leftarrow T{light} \cdot \exp(-\sigmat \cdot t{seg}). p{trans\dir} \leftarrow p{trans\dir} \cdot \exp(-\sigmat \cdot t{seg}). Check Visibility: If no intersection: Light is visible. Break loop. If intersection exists: If \text{isect.material\id} \ge 0 (Opaque): Ray is blocked. Return 0. If \text{isect.material\id} == -1 (Index-Matching): Increment \text{shadow\bounces}. Check depth limit: If \text{bounces} + \text{shadow\bounces} + 1 \ge \text{max\depth}, return 0. (Note: Source uses \ge \text{max\depth} without the +1; implementations should follow their specific depth accounting convention). Update \text{shadow\medium} based on the surface intersection (entering/exiting volume). Advance position: \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} + t{seg} \cdot \mathbf{d}{light}. Continue loop. 4. Contribution Calculation: If T{light} > 0: Compute Geometry Term: G = \frac{|\mathbf{n}{\mathbf{p}'} \cdot \mathbf{d}{light}|}{\|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{p}'\|^2}. Evaluate Phase Function: fp = \text{phase}(\omegao, -\mathbf{d}{light}). Compute NEE PDF (Area measure): p{nee} = p{light} \cdot p{pos} \cdot \frac{|\cos \theta|}{d^2}. Compute Phase Function PDF (converted to area measure for MIS): p{phase\area} = p{\text{sample\phase}}(\omegao, -\mathbf{d}{light}) \cdot G \cdot p{trans\dir}. Compute Contribution: Ls = T{light} \cdot fp \cdot Le(\mathbf{p}') \cdot G. Apply Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) Weight (Power Heuristic): w = \frac{p{nee}^2}{p{nee}^2 + p{phase\area}^2}. Return w \cdot \frac{Ls}{p{nee}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nexteventestimation(p, currentmedium, phasefunction, lightsampler, scene, sampler, bounces, maxdepth): # 1. Sample Light u1 = sampler.get1d() u2 = sampler.get2d() # Sample light source and point on it sampledlight = lightsampler.sample(u1) if not sampledlight: return 0.0 light = sampledlight.light ls = light.sampleli(u2) if not ls or ls.L == 0 or ls.pdf == 0: return 0.0 lightpdf = sampledlight.p ls.pdf pprime = ls.plight Le = ls.L # 2. Initialize Shadow Ray State dlight = normalize(pprime - p) Tlight = 1.0 shadowmedium = currentmedium shadowbounces = 0 ptransdir = 1.0 # 3. Trace Shadow Ray while dlight != Vector3(0, 0, 0): shadowray = Ray(p, dlight) isect = scene.intersect(shadowray) # Determine segment length if isect: nextt = distance(p, isect.position) else: nextt = distance(p, pprime) # Compute transmittance for this segment if shadowmedium: sigmat = shadowmedium.sigmat Tlight = exp(-sigmat nextt) ptransdir = exp(-sigmat nextt) if not isect: # Light is visible break else: # Check if blocked if isect.materialid >= 0: # Opaque surface blocks the light return 0.0 else: # Index-matching surface: pass through shadowbounces += 1 # Source uses +1, Source uses >= without +1; follow implementation convention if maxdepth != -1 and bounces + shadowbounces + 1 >= maxdepth: return 0.0 # Update medium for the next segment shadowmedium = updatemedium(isect, shadowray, shadowmedium) # Advance position p = p + nextt dlight # 4. Compute Contribution if Tlight <= 0: return 0.0 # Geometry term distvec = pprime - p distsq = dot(distvec, distvec) if distsq == 0: return 0.0 G = abs(dot(ls.n, -dlight)) / distsq # Phase function evaluation fhat = phasefunction.p(-dlight, -dlight) # Placeholder for actual phase eval, usually depends on view dir too. # Note: In standard NEE, we evaluate phase at the scattering point p. # wo is the view direction (from p to camera), wi is from p to light (-dlight). # The pseudocode in implies f is evaluated at the scattering angle. # Let's assume standard phase function signature p(omegain, omegaout). # Here, we are estimating incoming radiance from light. # The term fp in is likely the phase function value. # Correct evaluation: phasefunction.p(-dlight, viewdirection) or similar. # Based on formula: rho(p, omega, omega'). omega is view, omega' is light direction. # So fp = phasefunction.p(-dlight, viewdirection) ? # Actually, the integral is over omega'. The estimator uses fp(omegao, omega'). # Let's stick to the variable names in: f is the scattering function. fhat = phasefunction.p(-dlight, -dlight) # Placeholder for actual phase eval, usually depends on view dir too. # Correction: The contribution is T f L G. f is the phase function. # The PDF in denominator is pnee. # MIS PDFs # pnee is the PDF of the light sample (area measure) pnee = lightpdf # pphase needs to be converted to area measure for MIS # pphasearea = pphasesample G ptransdir # We need the PDF of sampling the direction -dlight using the phase function pphasesample = phasefunction.PDF(-dlight, -dlight) # Placeholder pphasearea = pphasesample G ptransdir # Power heuristic w = (pnee pnee) / (pnee pnee + pphasearea pphasearea) # Contribution contrib = Tlight fhat Le G / pnee return w contrib Note: The pseudocode above simplifies the phase function evaluation. In practice, fhat should be phasefunction.p(omegao, -dlight) where omegao is the direction from the scattering point to the camera (or previous vertex). The pphasesample should be phasefunction.PDF(omegao, -dlight). A strategy for sampling the boundary term of the differential path integral using pre-processed importance grids to handle sparse, high-frequency integrands. It performs a photon mapping pass from light sources and an importon mapping pass from the sensor to assign importance values to grid cells, which are then used to sample the edge (1D manifold) and complete the light path (2D manifold direction). The integral is transformed to primary sample space variables u1 \in \mathbb{R} and u2 \in \mathbb{R}^2. A pitfall is that for complicated scenes, the grid resolution required becomes impractically high. Proposed by Weber et al., this method connects a point to the light source with sub-paths generated by perturbation, instead of one-segment connections. It is intended for multiple scattering in high-order scattering homogeneous participating media and is combined with a path tracer via MIS. It significantly reduces noise and increases performance in highly anisotropic, optically dense media but is unsuitable for participating media with boundaries. Time Complexity: Adds O(K) cost per scattering event, where K is the number of shadow ray bounces (index-matching surfaces) before hitting the light or an opaque surface. In dense media, transmittance computation dominates. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory, requiring only state variables for the shadow ray (T{light}, medium, bounces). Performance: Reduces inefficiency for scenes with small or distant lights compared to pure phase function sampling. Performance degrades if the shadow ray traverses many index-matching surfaces or if the medium is extremely dense (requiring many small steps for transmittance). Strengths: Handles index-matching surfaces correctly; provides unbiased direct lighting estimation; integrates with MIS to balance with phase function sampling. Limitations: Requires handling of index-matching surfaces explicitly; transmittance calculation can be expensive in heterogeneous media (though this method assumes homogeneous for the core algorithm, extends it with ratio tracking). Originating from the extension of volumetric path tracing to include direct lighting, this method was introduced as "Volumetric Path Tracing 4" in coursework from the University of California, San Diego. It addresses the limitation of previous methods that only sampled the phase function, which is inefficient for small light sources. The mathematical foundation is the change of variable from the spherical integral to the light surface area integral. It is used in unidirectional path tracing for participating media, particularly in educational and research contexts for rendering fog, smoke, and other homogeneous volumes with index-matched boundaries. name: Volumetric Path Tracing with MIS and Surface Lighting
body: This method extends volumetric path tracing to handle multiple monochromatic homogeneous volumes with absorption and multiple scattering, while integrating surface lighting via the full rendering equation. It combines phase function sampling, next event estimation (NEE), and null-scattering (delta tracking) to support heterogeneous media, using multiple importance sampling (MIS) to balance direct lighting contributions from light sources and indirect scattering. Unlike its predecessor Next Event Estimation for Volumetric Path Tracing, which only added NEE, this method fully replaces surface emission Le with the rendering equation and handles chromatic media by averaging probability densities over sampled color channels using one-sample MIS. Inputs: Screen pixel coordinates, random number generator state, scene description (volumes, surfaces, lights), and the majorant \sigmam for each volume. Output: Radiance value for the pixel. The algorithm maintains cache variables across path bounces to resolve PDFs for MIS that may originate from previous bounces, particularly when skipping index-matching surfaces. dirpdf: Float. PDF of the latest phase function sampling, measured in solid angle. Initialized to 0. neepcache: Position or None. The last position \mathbf{p} that can issue a next event estimation. If the position is on an index-matching surface, it cannot issue NEE. Initialized to None. multitranspdf: Float. Product PDF of transmittance sampling going through several index-matching surfaces from the last phase function sampling. Initialized to 1. currentpaththroughput: Float. Accumulated throughput of the path. Initialized to 1. radiance: Float. Accumulated radiance. Initialized to 0. bounces: Integer. Number of surface bounces. Initialized to 0. 1. Initialize: Set currentpaththroughput = 1, radiance = 0, bounces = 0, dirpdf = 0, neepcache = None, multitranspdf = 1. 2. Main Loop: a. Free Flight: Sample distance t0 using homogenized transmittance \taum. b. Event Handling: If t0 \ge t{\text{hit}} (Hit surface): Compute L{\text{surface}}. If real particle hit (Hit real particle): Probability \sigmat / \sigmam. Compute the scattering integral. If fake particle hit (Hit fake particle): Probability \sigman / \sigmam. Continue the ray in a straight line without scattering. If bounces == 0: Add emission directly: radiance += currentpaththroughput Le(isect). If bounces > 0: Perform NEE. Set lightpoint = isect. Compute pdfnee = pdfpointonlight(isect.light, lightpoint, neepcache, scene). Compute MIS weight w. The PDF for phase function sampling is dirpdf multitranspdf G. Add radiance: radiance += currentpaththroughput emission(vertex, -ray.dir, scene) w. Sample scattering direction from phase function. Update dirpdf to the PDF of the sampled direction. Update multitranspdf if crossing index-matching surfaces. Update currentpaththroughput with scattering coefficient and phase function value. Update bounces. c. Russian Roulette: Terminate path with probability based on throughput. The radiative transfer equation for participating media is: \frac{d}{dt} L(\mathbf{p}(t), \omega) = -\sigmat(\mathbf{p}(t)) L(\mathbf{p}(t), \omega) + \sigmas(\mathbf{p}(t)) \int{S^2} \rho(\omega, \omega') L(\mathbf{p}(t), \omega') d\omega' Integrating over distance yields the volume rendering equation: L(\mathbf{p}(t), \omega) = \int0^{t{\text{hit}}} \tau(\mathbf{p}(0), \mathbf{p}(t')) \left( \sigmas(\mathbf{p}(t')) \int{S^2} \rho(\omega, \omega') L(\mathbf{p}(t'), \omega') d\omega' \right) dt' + \tau(\mathbf{p}(0), \mathbf{p}(t{\text{hit}})) L{\text{surface}}(\mathbf{p}(t{\text{hit}})) where transmittance is \tau(\mathbf{p}(0), \mathbf{p}(t')) = \exp \left( - \int0^{t'} \sigmat(\mathbf{p}(t'')) dt'' \right). For heterogeneous media, null-scattering modifies the equation by adding and subtracting \sigman(\mathbf{p}(t)) L(\mathbf{p}(t), \omega): \frac{d}{dt} L(\mathbf{p}(t), \omega) = -(\sigmat(\mathbf{p}(t)) + \sigman(\mathbf{p}(t))) L(\mathbf{p}(t), \omega) + \sigman(\mathbf{p}(t)) L(\mathbf{p}(t), \omega) + \sigmas(\mathbf{p}(t)) \int{S^2} \rho(\omega, \omega') L(\mathbf{p}(t), \omega') d\omega' The homogenized transmittance is \taum(\mathbf{p}(0), \mathbf{p}(t')) = \exp(-\sigmam t'). For NEE, transmittance \taup is estimated via an exponential integrator. The ODE is transformed via \tilde{\tau}p(t') = \exp(\sigmam t') \taup(t'): \frac{d}{dt'} \tilde{\tau}p(t') = \sigman(\mathbf{p}(t')) \tilde{\tau}p(t'), \quad \tilde{\tau}p(0) = 1 This yields the recursive integral: \taup(t') = \exp(-\sigmam t') + \int0^{t'} \exp(\sigmam(t'' - t')) \sigman(\mathbf{p}(t'')) \taup(t'') dt'' Ratio tracking solves this integral by starting at z = t0, sampling zd with p(zd) \propto \exp(\sigmam zd), and updating z. If z reaches 0, evaluate the light source term \exp(-\sigmam z). Otherwise, evaluate the recursive term. The probability for the light source term is \exp(-\sigmam z). The probability density for the recursive term is \exp(-\sigmam zd) / \sigmam. MIS weight calculation uses the balance heuristic: w = \frac{(\text{dir\pdf\} \cdot \text{dir\pdf\})}{(\text{dir\pdf\} \cdot \text{dir\pdf\} + \text{pdf\nee} \cdot \text{pdf\nee})} where dirpdf = dirpdf multitranspdf G. dirpdf: The PDF of the latest phase function sampling, measured in solid angle. neepcache: The last position \mathbf{p} that can issue a next event estimation. multitranspdf: The product PDF of transmittance sampling going through several index-matching surfaces from the last phase function sampling. \sigmam: The majorant, defined as the upper bound of \sigmat(\mathbf{p}(t)) for all t, ensuring \sigman(\mathbf{p}(t)) \ge 0. Real particle probability: \sigmat / \sigmam. Fake particle probability: \sigman / \sigmam. Probability for light source term: \exp(-\sigmam z). Probability density for recursive term: \exp(-\sigmam zd) / \sigmam. Index-Matching Surfaces: NEE cannot be issued from positions on index-matching surfaces. PDF Caching: dirpdf and multitranspdf may refer to decisions made several bounces ago. Bounces == 0: MIS is not needed for the first surface hit because it is the only way to see the light source. Chromatic Sampling: When sampling distance for chromatic media, the PDF must be the average over all channels. Alternative Probability Assignment: Using \sigmas / (\sigmas + \sigman) for real/fake particle probabilities is avoided because \sigmas + \sigman can be 0, requiring corner case handling. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def L(screenpos, rng): # Initialize cache variables currentpaththroughput = 1.0 radiance = 0.0 bounces = 0 dirpdf = 0.0 # in solid angle measure neepcache = None multitranspdf = 1.0 # Generate primary ray rayorigin, raydirection = traceprimaryray(screenpos) while True: # 1. Free flight sampling using homogenized transmittance u = rng.uniform() t0 = -math.log(u) / sigmam # 2. Determine event type hitsurface = (t0 >= raylengthtosurface(rayorigin, raydirection)) hitreal = not hitsurface and (rng.uniform() < sigmat / sigmam) if hitsurface: isect = getsurfaceintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, t0) # Cache position for NEE if valid (not index-matching surface) if not isindexmatchingsurface(isect): neepcache = isect.position if bounces == 0: # Direct emission, no MIS radiance += currentpaththroughput Le(isect) else: # NEE with MIS lightpoint = isect.position pdfnee = pdfpointonlight(isect.light, lightpoint, neepcache, scene) # Combined PDF for phase function sampling path # G is the geometric term |cosθ|/r² dirpdf = dirpdf multitranspdf G(rayorigin, lightpoint) # MIS Weight w = (dirpdf dirpdf) / (dirpdf dirpdf + pdfnee pdfnee) # Add contribution radiance += currentpaththroughput emission(isect.vertex, -raydirection, scene) w # Surface lighting: Sample BSDF newdirection, bsdfpdf, bsdfvalue = samplebsdf(isect, rng) # Update cache variables for next bounce dirpdf = bsdfpdf multitranspdf = 1.0 # Reset if surface breaks continuity, or update if index-matching # Update throughput currentpaththroughput = bsdfvalue transmittancetosurface(rayorigin, isect.position) rayorigin = isect.position raydirection = newdirection bounces += 1 elif hitreal: # Hit real particle: Scatter newdirection, phasepdf = samplephasefunction(raydirection, rng) # Update cache variables dirpdf = phasepdf # Update multitranspdf for index-matching surfaces crossed multitranspdf = computesurfacetransmittancepdf(rayorigin, rayorigin + raydirection t0) # Update throughput currentpaththroughput = (sigmas / sigmam) phasevalue(raydirection, newdirection) rayorigin = rayorigin + raydirection t0 raydirection = newdirection else: # Hit fake particle: Continue straight # Update multitranspdf for index-matching surfaces crossed multitranspdf = computesurfacetransmittancepdf(rayorigin, rayorigin + raydirection t0) rayorigin = rayorigin + raydirection t0 # Russian Roulette p = min(1.0, currentpaththroughput) if rng.uniform() > p: break currentpaththroughput /= p return radiance Time Complexity: Depends on the density of the medium and the number of bounces. Delta tracking efficiency depends on the tightness of the majorant \sigmam. Ratio tracking for NEE can be expensive if \sigman is large. Memory Complexity: Low, primarily storing cache variables and scene data. Strengths: Handles heterogeneous media via null-scattering, integrates surface lighting, and uses MIS for robust direct lighting estimation. Limitations: Requires a valid majorant \sigmam. Ratio tracking for NEE can be slow if the medium is highly scattering or absorbing. When to use: Scenes with participating media and complex surfaces where direct lighting from volumes is significant. When not to use: Simple homogeneous media where closed-form solutions are sufficient, or when performance is critical and heterogeneity is low. This method is part of a series of volumetric path tracing implementations, specifically the fifth iteration, adding surface lighting and MIS to previous versions that handled phase function sampling and NEE. It builds on the concepts of null-scattering and delta tracking introduced in earlier works. The exponential integrator technique is named after a method in ODE literature. name: Manifold Next Event Estimation Improvement
head: Fermat's Principle NEE, Koerner et al. MNEE improvement, Volume-based Next Event Estimation Improvement
body: Manifold Next Event Estimation (MNEE) Improvement is an optimization for volumetric path tracing that estimates direct lighting by searching for a point within the participating medium that satisfies Fermat’s principle, rather than walking along surface boundaries. It addresses the limitations of standard NEE and original MNEE in scenes with refractive boundaries and complex geometry, specifically targeting highly directional, near-delta light distributions. It builds on Next Event Estimation for Volumetric Path Tracing by refining the connection strategy for media surrounded by refractive boundaries. The method improves upon Hanika et al.'s MNEE. Instead of walking along boundaries using geometric derivatives, it searches for a point in the volume that satisfies Fermat’s principle to connect the current path vertex to the light source. This avoids failures on detailed or displaced surfaces where derivative-based walking fails. The method can be integrated into a unidirectional path tracer using Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS). Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current path vertex position, direction, participating medium properties, and light source geometry. Output: A valid connection point on the light source and the transmittance along the path. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Fermat’s Principle Search: Search for a point \mathbf{x}v within the volume such that the optical path length to the light source is stationary, satisfying Fermat’s principle. 2. Connection: Connect the found volume point \mathbf{x}v to the light source. 3. Estimation: Estimate the direct illumination contribution using the connection, accounting for transmittance through the medium and boundaries. Formulas: Fermat’s principle implies the variation of the optical path length \delta \int n(\mathbf{r}) ds = 0. The exact optimization function is not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method is computationally expensive due to the optimization search. It is suitable for highly directional, near-delta distributions but may be inefficient for other cases. Original MNEE fails on detailed or displaced surfaces; the improvement mitigates this by searching in the volume, but the cost remains high. Manifold exploration is a mutation strategy for Metropolis light transport that improves sampling for paths involving specular and highly glossy surfaces, and is usable for participating media surrounded by refractive boundaries. The manifold exploration idea further benefits next event estimation (NEE) by enabling connections through multiple refracting surfaces. Time Complexity: High computational overhead due to the search for a volume point satisfying Fermat’s principle. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles refractive boundaries better than standard NEE; avoids failures on detailed or displaced surfaces where derivative-based surface walking fails. Limitations: Too expensive for general use; best suited for highly directional, near-delta light distributions. When to use: Scenes with participating media surrounded by refractive boundaries where standard NEE fails and surface-based MNEE is unstable or too costly due to geometry complexity. When not to use: Scenes with low-order scattering or non-directional lighting where the overhead is unjustified. Standard NEE is unsuitable for participating media with refractive boundaries. Hanika et al. proposed manifold next event estimation (MNEE), which leverages manifold exploration to connect to the light source through multiple refracting surfaces. The main drawback of MNEE is that the search for the boundary vertex may not succeed, and it relies on geometric derivatives that do not handle detailed or displaced surfaces well. Koerner et al. improved MNEE by searching for a point in the volume which satisfies Fermat’s principle instead of walking over the surface. Both methods can be integrated into a unidirectional path tracer using multiple importance sampling (MIS). name: Volumetric Path Tracing with BSSRDF and Medium Sampling
head: BSSRDF integration, Path Tracing with Subsurface Scattering and Participating Media, Subsurface Scattering Integration in Volumetric Path Tracing, Subsurface scattering in VolPathIntegrator, VolPathIntegrator with BSSRDF
body: This method extends volumetric path tracing to handle subsurface scattering by integrating BSSRDF (Bidirectional Surface Scattering Reflectance Distribution Function) probes directly into the path traversal loop, allowing light to enter a material, scatter internally, and exit at a different surface point before continuing as a standard surface interaction. It bridges surface geometry and participating media by treating the subsurface exit as a surface scattering event with direct and indirect illumination, distinct from Multiple Scattering Volume Path Tracing with Phase Function Sampling which focuses on homogeneous volume multiple scattering without explicit surface BSSRDF probes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current path state (beta, ru, ray, depth), surface intersection isect with an attached BSSRDF, scene geometry for intersection tests, sampler for random numbers, and MediumProperties for the current volume. Output: Updated path contribution L, updated path state (beta, ru, ray), and termination flags. Data Structures: BSSRDFProbeSegment: Contains entry point p0 and exit point p1 on the surface. WeightedReservoirSampler<T>: A reservoir sampling structure to select a random intersection from a stream of candidates with equal weight. BSSRDFSample: Contains the exit point interaction ssi, the scattering probability Sp, the PDF pdf, the outgoing direction wo, and the BSDF Sw at the exit point. MediumInteraction: Contains position p, incoming direction, time, medium reference, and phase function. Parameters: maxDepth: Maximum path depth. regularize: Boolean flag to regularize specular BSDFs to prevent infinite throughput spikes. lambda: Wavelength or spectral sample index. Formulas: The emission estimator for a medium scattering event at p' is \beta(\overline{pn} + p') \sigmaa(p') Le(p' \to pn). The incremental beta is computed as \beta(\overline{pn} + p') = \frac{\beta(\overline{pn}) T{maj}(pn \to p')}{pe(p') p{maj}(p' | pn, \omega)}, where pe=1 because absorption is sampled for emission. The MIS balance heuristic weight is we(\overline{pn} + p') = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{m} \sum{i=1}^m r{e, \lambdai}(\overline{pn} + p')}, where the denominator is computed using SampledSpectrum::Average(). Algorithm Steps: 1. Retrieve BSSRDF: Get the BSSRDF from the current intersection isect. If BSSRDF exists and is transmission, sample a probe segment: Float uc = sampler.Get1D(); Point2f up = sampler.Get2D(); pstd::optional<BSSRDFProbeSegment> probeSeg = bssrdf.SampleSp(uc, up); If no probe segment, break. 2. Reservoir Sampling for Exit Point: Initialize WeightedReservoirSampler<SubsurfaceInteraction> with seed MixBits(FloatToBits(sampler.Get1D())). Create base interaction at probeSeg->p0. Loop: spawn ray from base to probeSeg->p1, intersect against scene geometry. If intersection si exists and si->intr.material == isect.material, add SubsurfaceInteraction(si->intr) to reservoir with weight 1.0. Update base = si->intr. If no intersection, break. If reservoir has no samples, break. 3. Convert to BSSRDFSample: Get sampled SubsurfaceInteraction (ssi) from reservoir. Call bssrdf.ProbeIntersectionToSample(ssi, scratchBuffer) to get bssrdfSample. If !bssrdfSample.Sp or !bssrdfSample.pdf, break. 4. Update Path State: Calculate PDF: pdf = interactionSampler.SampleProbability() bssrdfSample.pdf[0]. Update throughput: beta = bssrdfSample.Sp / pdf. Update rescaled probability: ru = bssrdfSample.pdf / bssrdfSample.pdf[0]. Set surface interaction pi = ssi. Set outgoing direction pi.wo = bssrdfSample.wo. Set prevIntrContext = LightSampleContext(pi). 5. Regularize BSDF (Optional): If regularize is true, call Sw.Regularize() on BSDF from bssrdfSample. Set anyNonSpecularBounces = true. 6. Sample Direct Illumination: Call SampleLd(pi, &Sw, lambda, sampler, beta, ru) to add attenuated direct illumination to L. 7. Sample Indirect Subsurface Scattering: Generate u (1D) and v (2D). Call Sw.Samplef(pi.wo, u, v) to get bs. If no sample, break. Update throughput: beta = bs->f AbsDot(bs->wi, pi.shading.n) / bs->pdf. Update rescaled probability: rl = ru / bs->pdf. Set specularBounce = bs->IsSpecular(). Spawn new ray: ray = RayDifferential(pi.SpawnRay(bs->wi)). 8. Russian Roulette: If depth > 1, calculate rrBeta = beta etaScale / ru.Average(). If rrBeta.MaxComponentValue() < 1, generate uRR. If uRR < 1 - rrBeta.MaxComponentValue(), terminate. Else, beta /= 1 - q. 9. Sample Participating Medium: Determine tMax from next surface intersection or infinity. Initialize RNG with two 1D samples. Call SampleTmaj with lambda function. 10. Compute Medium Event Probabilities: Float pAbsorb = mp.sigmaa[0] / sigmamaj[0]; Float pScatter = mp.sigmas[0] / sigmamaj[0]; Float pNull = std::max<Float>(0, 1 - pAbsorb - pScatter); Sample mode m using um. 11. Handle Absorption (Mode 0): Set terminated = true, return false. 12. Handle Scattering (Mode 1): If depth >= maxDepth, set terminated = true, return false. Update beta and ru with transmittance and scattering PDF. If valid, add emission: L += betap sigmaa Le / re.Average() where betap = beta Tmaj / pdf and re = ru sigmamaj Tmaj / pdf. Note: Do not cancel Tmaj factors before MIS weighting. Sample direct lighting: L += SampleLd(intr, nullptr, lambda, sampler, beta, ru). 13. Sample Phase Function: ps = intr.phase.Samplep(-ray.d, u). If valid, update beta, rl, ray, and set scattered = true. 14. Handle Null Scattering (Mode 2): Compute sigman = ClampZero(sigmamaj - sigmaa - sigmas). Update beta and ru with null scattering PDF. If pdf == 0, set beta = 0. Return beta && ru. 15. Handle Terminated/Scattered/Unscattered Rays: If terminated or invalid beta/ru, return L. If scattered, continue to next path vertex. Else, update beta, ru, rl by Tmaj / Tmaj[0]. Pitfalls: Do not cancel out T{maj} factors between betap and re before MIS weighting, because the final estimator divides by the average of rescaled probabilities, not component-wise. Cancelling leads to incorrect results. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sampletmaj(ray, tmax, rng, eventlambda): sigmamaj = ray.medium.sigmamaj t = 0.0 while t < tmax: t += -log(1.0 - rng.uniform()) / sigmamaj[0] if t >= tmax: return Tmajval = exp(-sigmamaj[0] t) p = ray.o + t ray.d mp = ray.medium.getproperties(p) if not eventlambda(p, mp, sigmamaj, Tmajval): return def volumetricpathtracingwithbssrdf(isect, beta, ru, ray, depth, maxdepth, sampler, scene, lambdaidx, regularize, etascale=1.0, scratchbuffer=None): L = Spectrum(0.0) specularbounce = False anynonspecularbounces = False terminated = False scattered = False # Retrieve BSSRDF bssrdf = isect.getbssrdf(ray, lambdaidx) if bssrdf and bssrdf.istransmission(): uc = sampler.get1d() up = sampler.get2d() probeseg = bssrdf.samplesp(uc, up) if not probeseg: return L, beta, ru, ray, terminated, scattered seed = hash(sampler.get1d()) interactionsampler = WeightedReservoirSamplerSubsurfaceInteraction base = Interaction(probeseg.p0, ray.time, Medium()) while True: r = base.spawnrayto(probeseg.p1) si = scene.intersect(r, 1.0) if not si: break base = si.intr if si.intr.material == isect.material: interactionsampler.add(SubsurfaceInteraction(si.intr), 1.0) if not interactionsampler.hassample(): return L, beta, ru, ray, terminated, scattered ssi = interactionsampler.getsample() bssrdfsample = bssrdf.probeintersectiontosample(ssi, scratchbuffer) if not bssrdfsample.Sp or not bssrdfsample.pdf: return L, beta, ru, ray, terminated, scattered pdf = interactionsampler.sampleprobability() bssrdfsample.pdf[0] beta = bssrdfsample.Sp / pdf ru = bssrdfsample.pdf / bssrdfsample.pdf[0] pi = ssi pi.wo = bssrdfsample.wo previntrcontext = LightSampleContext(pi) Sw = bssrdfsample.Sw anynonspecularbounces = True if regularize: Sw.regularize() L += sampleld(pi, Sw, lambdaidx, sampler, beta, ru) u = sampler.get1d() bs = Sw.samplef(pi.wo, u, sampler.get2d()) if not bs: return L, beta, ru, ray, terminated, scattered beta = bs.f absdot(bs.wi, pi.shading.n) / bs.pdf rl = ru / bs.pdf specularbounce = bs.isspecular() ray = RayDifferential(pi.spawnray(bs.wi)) rrbeta = beta etascale / ru.average() urr = sampler.get1d() if rrbeta.maxcomponentvalue() < 1 and depth > 1: q = max(0.0, 1.0 - rrbeta.maxcomponentvalue()) if urr < q: terminated = True return L, beta, ru, ray, terminated, scattered beta /= 1.0 - q tmax = scene.intersect(ray, 1.0).thit if scene.intersect(ray, 1.0) else float('inf') hash0 = hash(sampler.get1d()) hash1 = hash(sampler.get1d()) rng = RNG(hash0, hash1) def mediumeventlambda(p, mp, sigmamaj, Tmajval): nonlocal scattered, terminated, beta, ru, rl, L, ray, specularbounce, anynonspecularbounces, previntrcontext if depth < maxdepth and mp.Le: pdfem = sigmamaj[0] Tmajval[0] betap = beta Tmajval / pdfem re = ru sigmamaj Tmajval / pdfem if re: L += betap mp.sigmaa mp.Le / re.average() pabsorb = mp.sigmaa[0] / sigmamaj[0] pscatter = mp.sigmas[0] / sigmamaj[0] pnull = max(0.0, 1.0 - pabsorb - pscatter) um = rng.uniform() mode = samplediscrete([pabsorb, pscatter, pnull], um) if mode == 0: terminated = True return False elif mode == 1: if depth >= maxdepth: terminated = True return False pdfsc = Tmajval[0] mp.sigmas[0] beta = Tmajval mp.sigmas / pdfsc ru = Tmajval mp.sigmas / pdfsc if beta and ru: intr = MediumInteraction(p, -ray.d, ray.time, ray.medium, mp.phase) L += sampleld(intr, None, lambdaidx, sampler, beta, ru) uphase = sampler.get2d() ps = intr.phase.samplep(-ray.d, uphase) if not ps or ps.pdf == 0: terminated = True else: beta = ps.p / ps.pdf rl = ru / ps.pdf previntrcontext = LightSampleContext(intr) scattered = True ray.o = p ray.d = ps.wi specularbounce = False anynonspecularbounces = True return False else: sigman = clampzero(sigmamaj - mp.sigmaa - mp.sigmas) pdfnull = Tmajval[0] sigman[0] beta = Tmajval sigman / pdfnull if pdfnull == 0: beta = Spectrum(0.0) ru = Tmajval sigman / pdfnull rl = Tmajval sigmamaj / pdfnull return beta and ru sampletmaj(ray, tmax, rng, mediumeventlambda) if terminated or not beta or not ru: return L, beta, ru, ray, terminated, False if scattered: return L, beta, ru, ray, False, False else: beta = Tmaj / Tmaj[0] ru = Tmaj / Tmaj[0] rl = Tmaj / Tmaj[0] return L, beta, ru, ray, False, False BSDF Sampling for Volumetric Paths handles the surface interaction component of path tracing within participating media, calculating indirect lighting contributions based on surface BRDFs and sampling strategies. It determines the new direction of a volumetric path upon hitting a surface, updating throughput and rescaled probabilities to account for the surface scattering event. Unlike pure volume integrators, this method bridges surface geometry and participating media by treating surface interactions as scattering events that redirect rays back into the medium or to other surfaces. Reference Path Tracing is an unbiased volumetric path tracer used as a ground-truth reference renderer for subsurface scattering and participating media. It solves the problem of accurate light transport in high-curvature surfaces and complex media by treating the subsurface layer as a volume, performing full random walks from entry to exit points. It sets itself apart from diffusion-based models by explicitly tracking geometric features for accurate shadowing and handling zero- and single-scatter events, while differing from sibling methods like BSDF Sampling for Volumetric Paths by relying on a pure random walk with Next-Event Estimation (NEE) rather than specialized BSDF sampling strategies. This method estimates the in-scattered radiance L{\text{ins}}(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}) for interior points x \in \Omega \setminus \partial \Omega and boundary points x \in \partial \Omega. It computes the angular integral of the source function by sampling directions according to the phase function. A technique to handle non-monochromatic media efficiently by using Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) between RGB channels during distance sampling, avoiding the inefficiency of picking a single wavelength. The probability of picking channel \lambda is P(\lambda), and the probability density for distance s given channel \lambda is P\lambda(s) = \sigma\lambda e^{-s\sigma\lambda}, where \sigma\lambda is the extinction coefficient for channel \lambda. The total probability density is P(s) = P(\lambda) P\lambda(s). The MIS weight using the balance heuristic for standard RGB renders is W\lambda(s) = \frac{P(\lambda)}{P(\lambdaR) + P(\lambdaG) + P(\lambdaB)}. To prevent fireflies from throughput spiking in deep paths with highly tinted extinction, P(\lambda) should be chosen using the current throughput instead of single scatter albedo. Time Complexity: O(N) per path vertex, where N is the number of intersections along the BSSRDF probe segment. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for the reservoir sampler state, assuming the scene intersection structure is pre-built. Strengths: Accurately handles subsurface scattering in complex scenes with participating media. Integrates seamlessly with existing path tracing infrastructure. Handles chromatic effects via MIS. Limitations: Performance depends heavily on the density of geometry along the BSSRDF probe segment. Reservoir sampling can be inefficient if few valid intersections are found. When to use: When rendering translucent materials (skin, wax, marble) in scenes with fog, smoke, or other participating media. When not to use: For purely opaque materials or purely volumetric effects without surface subsurface scattering. This method is described in "14.2 Volume Scattering Integrators" from the PBRT book. It builds upon the SimpleVolPathIntegrator and extends it to handle BSSRDFs. The chromatic MIS variant is described in "Path Traced Subsurface Scattering Model" from Pixar. 14.2 Volume Scattering Integrators, https://pbr-book.org/4ed/LightTransportIIVolumeRendering/VolumeScatteringIntegrators, fetched 2026-10-29 Path Traced Subsurface Scattering Model, https://www.scribd.com/document/965284472/Pixar-Path-Traced-SSS-Paper, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: BSDF Sampling for Volumetric Paths
head: GoTracer, Implicit Path Tracing with Volume Interaction, Ray Tracing in One Weekend Go Implementation, Surface scattering in volumetric path tracing
body: BSDF Sampling for Volumetric Paths handles the surface interaction component of path tracing within participating media, calculating indirect lighting contributions based on surface BRDFs and sampling strategies. It determines the new direction of a volumetric path upon hitting a surface, updating throughput and rescaled probabilities to account for the surface scattering event. Unlike pure volume integrators, this method bridges surface geometry and participating media by treating surface interactions as scattering events that redirect rays back into the medium or to other surfaces. Inputs: Incoming ray r (origin, direction). Scene geometry and materials (including participating media definitions). Current path throughput \beta. Random number generator state (for sampling directions and distances). Maximum recursion depth. Outputs: Scattered ray direction and origin. Updated throughput \beta'. Boolean flag indicating if the path terminates or continues. HitRecord: P: Vector, intersection point. Normal: Vector, surface normal at intersection. T: float64, distance along ray to intersection. FrontFace: bool, true if normal points against ray direction. Mat: Material, material properties at intersection. Material: Scatter: Function pointer, scattering function (e.g., Lambertian, Metal, Dielectric). Colour: Vector (RGB), albedo or emission color. Fuzz: float64, roughness factor for metallic reflections. Light: bool, true if the material is an emissive light source. ConstantMedium: Obj: Object, the enclosed geometry. Density: float64, density of the participating medium. Colour: Vector (RGB), color of the medium. Ray: Origin: Vector. Direction: Vector. 1. Ray-Scene Intersection: Cast the incoming ray against the scene. If the ray hits an object, retrieve the HitRecord containing the intersection point, normal, and material. If the ray hits a ConstantMedium, perform a two-step hit test against the inner object to determine entry and exit points, then sample the distance to the first scattering event within the medium using the density. 2. Surface Interaction Check: If a surface intersection occurs: If the material is emissive (Mat.Light is true), return the material's color as the direct lighting contribution and terminate the path. If the material is not emissive, proceed to BSDF sampling. 3. BSDF Sampling: Sample the Bidirectional Scattering Distribution Function (BSDF) to determine the outgoing direction wo. Generate random numbers u1, u2 from a uniform distribution 0, 1). Call the material's specific scatter function (e.g., LambertianScatter, MetalScatter, DielectricScatter) using the incoming direction wi, the surface normal, and the random numbers. The scatter function returns the scattered ray direction and the attenuation color. 4. Throughput Update: Update the path throughput \beta to account for the surface scattering. \beta' = \beta \cdot \frac{fr(wi, wo) \cdot |\cos \thetai|}{p(wo)} Where: fr(wi, wo) is the BSDF value (often hardcoded or derived from the material color, e.g., 1/\pi for Lambertian). \thetai is the angle between the surface normal and the outgoing direction. p(wo) is the probability density function (PDF) of the sampled direction. Note on PDFs: For [Uniform Hemisphere sampling: p(wo) = \frac{1}{2\pi}. For Cosine-Weighted Hemisphere sampling: p(wo) = \frac{1}{\pi}. For specific material implementations (like GoTracer), the PDF may be implicit in the scatter function, and the throughput update might simply multiply by the attenuation and cosine factor if the sampling is uniform over the hemisphere. 5. Rescaled Probabilities (Optional/Advanced): If using resampled path tracking or specific BSDF implementations that track proportional PDFs: If bs->pdfIsProportional is true: rl = ru / \text{bsdf.PDF}(wo, wi). Else: rl = ru / \text{bs->pdf}. This step is critical for unbiased estimation when using multiple importance sampling or resampling techniques. 6. State Update: Update specularBounce flag based on whether the BSDF sample is specular. Update anyNonSpecularBounces flag. If the interaction is a transmission (refraction), update the eta scale factor: \eta{scale} = \eta^2. Spawn the new ray with the updated direction and origin. 7. Recursive Path Tracing: Recursively call the path tracer with the new scattered ray, decrementing the depth counter. L{indirect} = \text{Color} \cdot \text{rayColour}(scattered\ray, scene, depth-1) \cdot \beta' Accumulate this indirect radiance into the pixel color. 8. Termination: If depth reaches 0, return black (0,0,0). If the BSDF sample fails (e.g., metal reflection dot product is negative), terminate the path. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycolour(ray, scene, depth, samplesperpixel): """ Recursively trace a ray through the scene. """ if depth <= 0: return Color(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) hitrecord = HitRecord() if scene.hit(ray, tmin=0.001, tmax=INF, rec=hitrecord): scatteredray = Ray() attenuation = Color(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Sample BSDF scattersuccess = hitrecord.mat.scatter(ray, hitrecord, attenuation, scatteredray) if scattersuccess: # Calculate throughput update # Note: In simple implementations like GoTracer, the scatter function # handles the direction, and attenuation is the color. # The PDF is often implicit or uniform. # Cosine factor costheta = abs(dot(hitrecord.normal, scatteredray.direction)) # PDF depends on sampling strategy. # For Lambertian: pdf = 1/pi. For Uniform: pdf = 1/(2pi). # GoTracer uses simple random vectors, implying uniform hemisphere sampling for Lambertian/Isotropic. # However, the throughput update in GoTracer is implicit in the recursive call # via the attenuation color multiplication. # General BSDF update: # betanew = betaold (fr costheta) / pdf # For GoTracer's Lambertian: # fr = color / pi # pdf = 1 / (2 pi) (if uniform hemisphere) # factor = (color / pi) costheta / (1 / (2 pi)) = 2 color costheta # But GoTracer simply multiplies by attenuation (color) and relies on # the random sampling distribution for unbiasedness. return attenuation.multiply(raycolour(scatteredray, scene, depth - 1, samplesperpixel)) if hitrecord.mat.light: return hitrecord.mat.colour return Color(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def renderrow(j, imagewidth, imageheight, samplesperpixel, maxdepth, invwidth, invheight, camera, scene, img): y = -j + imageheight for i in range(imagewidth): pixel = Color(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for s in range(samplesperpixel): u = (i + randomfloat()) invwidth v = (j + randomfloat()) invheight ray = camera.getray(u, v) pixel = pixel.add(raycolour(ray, scene, maxdepth, samplesperpixel)) img.writecolour(i, y, pixel) samplesPerPixel: Number of samples per pixel for anti-aliasing. Default: 300. maxDepth: Maximum recursion depth for path tracing. Default: 50. aperture: Depth of field aperture size. Default: 0.0. vfov: Vertical field of view in degrees. Default: 40.0. refractionIndex: Index of refraction for dielectric materials. Default: 1.5. Metal Scatter Direction: The reflected ray direction must have a positive dot product with the surface normal. If dot(normal, scattereddirection) <= 0, the ray is absorbed, and the path terminates. Dielectric Total Internal Reflection: If refractionRatio sinTheta > 1.0, total internal reflection occurs, and the ray is reflected instead of refracted. Constant Medium Hit Test: A small epsilon (0.0001) is added to the inner object's hit distance to avoid self-intersection when finding the second hit point. Lambertian Degeneracy: If the random unit vector added to the normal results in a near-zero vector, the scatter direction is clamped to the normal to avoid degenerate rays. Gamma Correction: Output values are gamma-corrected using sqrt(pixelvalue / samplesPerPixel) before display. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S \cdot D), where N is the number of pixels, S is the number of samples per pixel, and D is the maximum path depth. Each sample involves a recursive ray tracing process with potential intersections against scene geometry. Memory Complexity: O(D) for the recursion stack, plus O(G) for the scene geometry storage, where G is the number of primitives. Performance depends heavily on scene complexity and the number of samples. GoTracer uses parallelism via goroutines to process image rows in parallel, leveraging multi-core CPUs. Default settings (800x533 resolution, 300 samples, depth 50) provide high-quality images but require significant computation time. Strengths: Simple implementation, supports multiple surface types (Lambertian, Metal, Dielectric, Isotropic), handles participating media (Constant Medium), supports depth of field and anti-aliasing. Limitations: Limited to simple geometries (Spheres, Boxes, Rectangles), no advanced material models, no global illumination beyond path tracing, limited to constant density media. Suitable for educational purposes and simple volumetric rendering demonstrations. Not suitable for production-quality rendering due to limited material models and lack of advanced optimization techniques. The method is based on the "Ray Tracing in One Weekend" series by Peter Shirley, implemented in Go as "GoTracer" by hexhowells. It also draws concepts from the "Volume Single Scattering" project by wangyuehi and the theoretical framework of volume scattering integrators from the "Physically Based Rendering" (pbr-book) 4th edition. Ray Tracing in One Weekend: Popularized simple path tracing techniques for educational purposes. GoTracer: Extended the original C++ implementation to Go, adding parallelism and supporting participating media. Volume Single Scattering: Explored single scattering in volumes, providing a foundation for more complex volume rendering techniques. pbr-book: Provided the theoretical basis for volume scattering integrators, including BSDF sampling and throughput updates. Educational ray tracers. Simple volumetric rendering demonstrations. Research prototyping for volume rendering algorithms. wangyuehi/VolumeSingleScattering, https://github.com/wangyuehi/VolumeSingleScattering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) hexhowells/GoTracer, https://github.com/hexhowells/GoTracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) 14.2 Volume Scattering Integrators, https://pbr-book.org/4ed/LightTransportIIVolumeRendering/VolumeScatteringIntegrators, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Reference Path Tracing
head: Path Traced Subsurface Scattering, Random Walk SSS, ReferencePathTracer, Volume SSS
body: Reference Path Tracing is an unbiased volumetric path tracer used as a ground-truth reference renderer for subsurface scattering and participating media. It solves the problem of accurate light transport in high-curvature surfaces and complex media by treating the subsurface layer as a volume, performing full random walks from entry to exit points. It sets itself apart from diffusion-based models by explicitly tracking geometric features for accurate shadowing and handling zero- and single-scatter events, while differing from sibling methods like BSDF Sampling for Volumetric Paths by relying on a pure random walk with Next-Event Estimation (NEE) rather than specialized BSDF sampling strategies. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Surface entry point, surface normal, medium extinction coefficient \sigmat (assumed homogeneous for the basic model), geometry mesh for boundary intersection, maximum bounce count, and Russian roulette start threshold. Outputs: Radiance contribution from the path, weighted by the path throughput and surface response. Data Structures: The method is encapsulated in a struct ReferencePathTracer which inherits from VolumeIntegrationMethod. maxbounces::Int: Maximum number of scattering events per path. Default: 64. rrstart::Int: Number of bounces after which Russian roulette activation begins. Default: 3. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: At the surface entry point, choose the initial direction \omegai from a Lambertian distribution around the inverse surface normal -n. 2. Distance Sampling: Advance along the current direction by a distance s sampled from the transmittance distribution. For a homogeneous medium with extinction coefficient \sigmat, the transmittance T over distance s follows Beer's Law T = e^{-\sigmat s}. To sample the distance, draw a uniform random number \xi \in [0, 1) and invert the cumulative distribution function: s = -\frac{\ln(1 - \xi)}{\sigmat}. 3. Direction Update: For isotropic scattering, update the direction for the next step by drawing a sample from a uniform spherical distribution. 4. Boundary Intersection: Trace a ray from the current position along the new direction against the scene geometry to check for intersection with the exterior interface. 5. Termination Check (Exit): If the ray intersects the exterior interface at distance s{hit} < s{sampled}: Terminate the random walk. Compute direct illumination at the exit point using Next-Event Estimation (NEE). Weigh the incoming radiance by a Lambertian response function. Do not apply surface coloring effects (albedo) at this stage. Return the contribution. 6. Termination Check (Depth): If the path continues for a fixed depth limit (default 256 steps) without finding an exit point, deem the photon lost and set the final contribution to zero. 7. Termination Check (Russian Roulette): If the path has not exited and has not reached the fixed depth limit: If b \ge rr\start, apply Russian Roulette to terminate the path stochastically based on the path throughput to maintain unbiasedness. If the path survives, update the throughput and continue to Step 2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2]-a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0]-a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1]-a[1]b[0]) def normalize(v): l = math.sqrt(sum(cc for c in v)) return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l) def samplelambertian(n): u = random.uniform(-1, 1) v = random.uniform(-1, 1) if uu + vv > 1: u, v = -u, -v x = math.sqrt(1 - uu - vv) if abs(n[0]) < 0.999: s = (1,0,0) else: s = (0,1,0) t = normalize(cross(n, s)) b = cross(n, t) return (xt[0] + vb[0] + un[0], xt[1] + vb[1] + un[1], xt[2] + vb[2] + un[2]) def samplespherical(): phi = random.uniform(0, 2math.pi) cost = random.uniform(-1, 1) sint = math.sqrt(1 - cost2) return (sintmath.cos(phi), sintmath.sin(phi), cost) def computedirectillumination(point, normal): """Queries scene radiance at point for direction -normal.""" return 1.0 def referencepathtracing(entrypoint, normal, sigmat, geometry, maxbounces=64, rrstart=3, fixeddepth=256): """ Performs a reference random walk for subsurface scattering. geometry.traceray(origin, direction, maxdistance) returns (point, normal, dist) or None. """ throughput = 1.0 currentpos = entrypoint currentdir = samplelambertian((-normal[0], -normal[1], -normal[2])) bounces = 0 for step in range(fixeddepth): xi = random.uniform(0, 1) distance = -math.log(1.0 - xi) / sigmat hit = geometry.traceray(currentpos, currentdir, maxdistance=distance) if hit is not None: hitpoint, hitnormal, hitdist = hit transmittance = math.exp(-sigmat hitdist) radiance = computedirectillumination(hitpoint, hitnormal) return throughput transmittance radiance currentpos = (currentpos[0] + currentdir[0]distance, currentpos[1] + currentdir[1]distance, currentpos[2] + currentdir[2]distance) currentdir = samplespherical() bounces += 1 if bounces >= maxbounces: return 0.0 if bounces >= rrstart: prob = min(1.0, max(throughput)) if random.uniform(0, 1) > prob: return 0.0 throughput /= prob return 0.0 Parameters: maxbounces: 64. rrstart: 3. fixeddepth: 256. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision loss in math.log(1.0 - xi) occurs when \xi is extremely close to 1; using math.log1p(-xi) is recommended. Degenerate normals or zero-extinction coefficients require explicit guards to prevent division by zero. Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of scattering events and geometry intersection tests. Each step requires a ray trace against the geometry. Memory Complexity: Low, as it only stores the current path state and does not require storing large voxel grids or photon maps. Strengths: Explicitly handles high-curvature geometry and shadowing, which diffusion models fail at. Accurately models zero- and single-scatter events, preserving energy better than diffusion approximations. Unbiased. Limitations: Can be noisy due to the stochastic nature of random walks, especially for deep or highly absorbing media. The fixed depth limit of 256 may truncate paths in very thick media, though Russian Roulette mitigates this. Chromatic effects require wavelength-specific sampling which is inefficient if not handled carefully. When to use: When ground-truth accuracy is required for subsurface scattering, particularly for objects with high curvature or thin features where diffusion models are inaccurate. Reference Path Tracing originated as a method to provide a ground-truth reference for subsurface scattering in production renderers. It was developed to address the limitations of diffusion-based subsurface scattering models, which assume a semi-infinite flat slab and fail in areas of high curvature like the nose or ears of a human face. By treating the subsurface as a volume and using a random walk, it allows for the integration of standard volumetric path tracing techniques into subsurface scattering simulations. The specific implementation details, such as the ReferencePathTracer struct, are found in the Lyr.jl library. name: Monte Carlo estimation of in-scattered radiance
head: Monte Carlo In-scattering, Source Function Estimation
body: This method estimates the in-scattered radiance L{\text{ins}}(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}) for interior points x \in \Omega \setminus \partial \Omega and boundary points x \in \partial \Omega. It computes the angular integral of the source function by sampling directions according to the phase function. Inputs: Point x (position in 3D space). Direction \boldsymbol{\omega} (outgoing/view direction). Phase function fp(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}', \boldsymbol{\omega}) or p(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}', \boldsymbol{\omega}). Surface normal \mathbf{n}(x) (if x is on the boundary). Radiance evaluation function L(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}') (returns interior radiance). Boundary radiance function Ls(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}') (returns refracted surface radiance). Epsilon \epsilon (small scalar, \epsilon \to 0^+). Boolean isboundary (indicates if x \in \partial \Omega). Outputs: Estimated in-scattered radiance L{\text{ins}}. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Determine if x is in the interior (x \in \Omega \setminus \partial \Omega) or on the boundary (x \in \partial \Omega). 2. If x is in the interior: draw a direction \boldsymbol{\omega}' from the phase function distribution fp(x, -\boldsymbol{\omega}', \boldsymbol{\omega}) and set L{\text{ins}} \leftarrow L(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}'). 3. If x is on the boundary: define a point slightly inside the medium x{\text{in}} = x + \epsilon \boldsymbol{\omega}, draw \boldsymbol{\omega}' \sim fp(x{\text{in}}, -\boldsymbol{\omega}', \boldsymbol{\omega}), and check the dot product \langle \mathbf{n}(x), \boldsymbol{\omega}' \rangle > 0. 4. If \langle \mathbf{n}(x), \boldsymbol{\omega}' \rangle > 0, set L{\text{ins}} \leftarrow L(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}'); otherwise set L{\text{ins}} \leftarrow Ls(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}'). 5. Return L{\text{ins}}. Formulas: The source function J(s') represents in-scattering from all directions at s': J(s') = \int{4\pi} p(s', \boldsymbol{\omega}', \boldsymbol{\omega}) L(s', \boldsymbol{\omega}') \, d\boldsymbol{\omega}' The Monte Carlo estimator for the source function with M samples is: JN = \frac{1}{M} \sum{k=1}^M \frac{p(s', \boldsymbol{\omega}k', \boldsymbol{\omega}) L(s', \boldsymbol{\omega}k')}{\text{pdf}(\boldsymbol{\omega}k')} Importance sampling uses a pdf similar to the phase function to reduce variance. For isotropic media, p = \frac{1}{4\pi} and directions are sampled uniformly on the unit sphere. Parameters: M: Number of samples for the source function estimator. Value not given in the sources. \epsilon: Small positive scalar to offset boundary points into the interior, \epsilon \to 0^+. Value not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Boundary Precision: When x is on the boundary, sampling directly at x can cause incorrect normal evaluation or phase function sampling outside the medium. Offsetting by \epsilon along \boldsymbol{\omega} is required. Direction Validity: On the boundary, if the sampled direction \boldsymbol{\omega}' points out of the medium (\langle \mathbf{n}(x), \boldsymbol{\omega}' \rangle \le 0), the radiance must come from the surface source Ls(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}') rather than the interior volume L(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}'). Distance to Next Scatter: When estimating diffusion terms involving distance sampling, if the sampled distance to the next scattering event dj is greater than the distance to the surface s, the event corresponds to refraction (direct transmission), not an internal scatter. This method handles the angular part; the distance part is handled by the parent method's distance sampling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def estimateinscatteredradiance(x, omega, phasefunction, normal, Leval, Lseval, epsilon, isboundary): """ Estimates in-scattered radiance Lins(x, omega) for interior or boundary points. """ if not isboundary: # Interior point: x in Omega \ partial Omega omegaprime = samplephasefunction(phasefunction, x, -omega) Lins = Leval(x, omegaprime) else: # Boundary point: x in partial Omega xin = x + epsilon omega omegaprime = samplephasefunction(phasefunction, xin, -omega) if dot(normal, omegaprime) > 0: Lins = Leval(x, omegaprime) else: Lins = Lseval(x, omegaprime) return Lins def samplephasefunction(phasefunction, x, incomingdirection): """ Samples a direction omegaprime from the phase function fp(x, -omegaprime, incomingdirection). Importance sampling uses a pdf similar to the phase function. For isotropic media (p = 1/4pi), samples uniformly on the unit sphere. For anisotropic media, applies the specific inverse CDF or rejection sampling for the given phase function. """ # Standard uniform sampling on unit sphere phi = 2.0 math.pi random.random() costheta = 1.0 - 2.0 random.random() sintheta = math.sqrt(max(0.0, 1.0 - costheta costheta)) return vec3(sintheta math.cos(phi), sintheta math.sin(phi), costheta) def dot(v1, v2): return v1.x v2.x + v1.y v2.y + v1.z v2.z class vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z Samples the BSDF at the surface to determine the next direction, often used in conjunction with volume sampling for hybrid paths. A baseline implementation for validating the in-scattering estimator against a brute-force or analytical solution. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per evaluation. Strengths: Unbiased estimator for the in-scattering term. Importance sampling using a pdf similar to the phase function reduces variance. Limitations: High variance if the phase function is highly anisotropic and not sampled correctly. Requires accurate evaluation of L(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}') or Ls(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}'). Boundary handling requires offsetting by \epsilon along \boldsymbol{\omega}. The method estimates the source function J(s') in the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE). The first definitive text on radiative transfer was published by Chandrasekhar in 1950. The specific algorithm for estimating L{\text{ins}} at interior and boundary points, including the handling of discontinuities and side paths, is described in "A Differential Theory of Radiative Transfer". Phase function sampling techniques, such as for the Henyey-Greenstein phase function, are based on work by Henyey and Greenstein in 1940. A Differential Theory of Radiative Transfer, https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~ravir/diffrendering.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Volume Rendering and Scattering Theory, https://www.scribd.com/document/912805133/02941-Slides-07-Volumes, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)
