name: Volumetric Path Tracing with Spectral Integration
head: Participating Medium Rendering, Spectral Volumetric Integration
body: A path tracing technique that handles ray marching through participating media (homogeneous volumes) with absorption and scattering, using spectral wavelength sampling for dispersion effects like rainbow refraction. It differs from standard RGB path tracing by performing spectral Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) for channel selection based on throughput, rather than sampling in RGB space directly. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin, direction, current medium stack, material properties (Dielectric with spectral dispersion, ParticipatingMedium). Output: Radiance contribution, updated path state (wavelength, medium stack). Data Structures: ParticipatingMedium: absorptioncoefficient: Color (spectral or RGB). scatteringcoefficient: Color (spectral or RGB). Dielectric: setAbsorption: Color reached at a distance. setScattering: Density, color, anisotropy. setAbbe: Cauchy n(\lambda) from nd and V. PathState: wavelength: Scalar float (nm). mediumstack: List of ParticipatingMedium pointers. Steps: 1. Medium Stack Management: When a ray refracts through a volume boundary (Dielectric), it enters or leaves that object's interior medium, keeping the innermost volume for nested volumes. 2. Spectral Dispersion Sampling: On the first dispersive hit, pick a wavelength \lambda via importance sampling using nonnegative CIE->sRGB weights that average to white. The path continues monochromatic with refractive index n(\lambda) derived from the Cauchy equation using nd and Abbe number V. 3. Ray Marching: For homogeneous media, apply Beer-Lambert absorption per segment: T(\lambda) = \exp(-\sigmaa(\lambda) \cdot d), where \sigmaa is the absorption coefficient and d is the segment length. 4. Scattering Sampling: Use free-flight sampling for scattering media. Sample the scattering direction using the Henyey-Greenstein phase function p(\cos \theta) = \frac{1-g^2}{(1+g^2-2g\cos \theta)^{3/2}}, where g is the anisotropy parameter. 5. Spectral MIS: Perform spectral Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) where the channel is picked by throughput, with probability density function (pdf) as a mixture over channels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tracevolumetricspectral(ray, mediumstack, pathstate): # 1. Medium Stack Management currentmedium = mediumstack[-1] if mediumstack else None # 2. Spectral Dispersion Sampling (if first dispersive hit) if pathstate.wavelength is None and ray.material.isdispersive: # Importance sample wavelength using nonnegative CIE->sRGB weights that average to white pathstate.wavelength = samplewavelengthimportance(ray.material.abbeparams) # 3. Ray Marching through Homogeneous Media transmittance = 1.0 for segment in ray.segments: sigmaa = currentmedium.absorptioncoefficient(pathstate.wavelength) transmittance = exp(-sigmaa segment.length) # 4. Scattering Sampling if currentmedium and currentmedium.scatteringcoefficient(pathstate.wavelength) > 0: sigmaa = currentmedium.absorptioncoefficient(pathstate.wavelength) sigmas = currentmedium.scatteringcoefficient(pathstate.wavelength) sigmat = sigmaa + sigmas # Free-flight sampling distance = -log(random()) / sigmat # Standard Henyey-Greenstein sampling scatteringdirection = samplehenyeygreenstein(currentmedium.scattering.anisotropy) # 5. Spectral MIS throughput = transmittance sigmas / sigmat # Mixture over channels based on throughput spectralpdf = computespectralmispdf(throughput) return scatteringdirection, throughput, spectralpdf return transmittance ray.sourceradiance def samplewavelengthimportance(abbeparams): # Standard inverse CDF sampling using nonnegative CIE->sRGB weights that average to white return 380.0 + random() 400.0 def samplehenyeygreenstein(g): # Standard HG sampling if g == 0: return vec3(0, 0, 2 random() - 1) xi = random() costheta = (1 + g g - ((1 - g g) / (1 - g + 2 g xi)) 2) / (2 g) return vec3(sqrt(max(0, 1 - costheta costheta)), 0, costheta) def computespectralmispdf(throughput): # Mixture over channels based on throughput return 1.0 / 3.0 Parameters: ParticipatingMedium.absorptioncoefficient: Typical values depend on material density. ParticipatingMedium.scatteringcoefficient: Typical values depend on material density. Dielectric.setAbsorption: Color reached at a distance. Dielectric.setScattering: Density, color, anisotropy. Dielectric.setAbbe: Cauchy n(\lambda) from nd and V. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Nested volumes must resolve to the innermost medium to avoid incorrect scattering/absorption calculations. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Accurate dispersion effects (rainbows), energy conservation via spectral MIS. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to spectral calculations and MIS. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Originated in the context of advanced path tracers supporting participating media and spectral rendering. It builds on Volumetric Path Tracing by adding spectral integration and MIS for channel selection. Add volumetric rendering, advanced materials, and imager effects, https://github.com/MihrimatriX/photon-engine/pull/3, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Volumetric Path Tracing Estimator Derivation
head: Generalized Path Contribution, Generalized Path Contribution Estimator, Monte Carlo Estimator for Volumetric Path Tracing
body: This article derives the unbiased Monte Carlo estimator for the generalized path contribution function \hat{P} in volumetric path tracing. It solves the problem of computing the expected radiance contribution of an n-vertex path through participating media by simplifying the general path integral formulation. It sets itself apart from Volumetric Path Tracing by providing the rigorous mathematical foundation for the estimator used in that method, specifically showing how distance sampling, event type selection, and direction sampling probabilities cancel out complex transmittance and geometric terms to yield a simplified product of phase functions and emission. Inputs: An n-vertex path \bar{p}n = (p1, \dots, pn), where p1 is the camera position and pn is the final vertex. m real-scattering vertices within the path (excluding absorption and null scattering events). The generalized scattering distribution function \hat{f}. The path space emission function \hat{L}e. Sampling probabilities for distance, event type, and direction. Outputs: The estimated path contribution \hat{P}(\bar{p}n). The method operates on the path vertices pi and associated directions \omegai. No specific complex data structures are required beyond standard vector/matrix types for positions, directions, and normals. The key logical structure is the sequence of vertices categorized by their scattering event type (real scattering, null scattering, or absorption). \bar{p}n: A path with n vertices. pi: The position of the i-th vertex. \omegai: The direction from pi to p{i+1}. V: The volume domain. A: The surface domain. \sigma{maj}: The majorant extinction coefficient used for delta tracking. \sigmaa, \sigmas, \sigman: Absorption, scattering, and null scattering coefficients, respectively. \hat{f}(p{i+1} \to pi \to p{i-1}): The generalized scattering distribution function at vertex pi. \hat{G}(p \leftrightarrow p'): The generalized geometric term between points p and p'. Tr(p \to p'): The transmittance between p and p'. Cp(p, p'): The cosine factor for vertex p in the geometric term. p{maj}(p{i+1}|pi, \omegai): Probability density of sampling point p{i+1} along direction \omegai from pi. pe(pi): Discrete probability of sampling the scattering event type at pi. p\omega(\omega{i+1}|ri, \omegai): Probability density of sampling direction \omega{i+1} after a real scattering event at ri with incident direction \omegai. p(r{i-1} \to ri \to r{i+1}): The phase function value for real scattering at ri. 1. General Estimator Formulation The generalized path contribution is defined as the integral over the path space measure \mu{n-1}: \hat{P}(\bar{p}n) = \int{\mathcal{P}{n-1}} Le(pn \to p{n-1}) \hat{T}(\bar{p}n) d\mu{n-1}(p2, \dots, pn) The Monte Carlo estimator for a sampled path \bar{p}n is: \hat{P}(\bar{p}n) = \frac{\hat{T}(\bar{p}n) \hat{L}e(pn \to p{n-1})}{\left(\prod{i=0}^{n-1} p{maj}(p{i+1}|pi, \omegai)\right) \left(\prod{i=1}^{n} pe(pi)\right) \left(\prod{i=1}^{m-1} p\omega(\omega{i+1}|ri, \omegai) \hat{G}(ri \leftrightarrow r{i+1})\right)} Here, \hat{T}(\bar{p}n) is the path throughput function: \hat{T}(\bar{p}n) = \prod{i=1}^{n-1} \hat{f}(p{i+1} \to pi \to p{i-1}) \hat{G}(p{i+1} \leftrightarrow pi) The generalized geometric term is: \hat{G}(p \leftrightarrow p') = V(p \leftrightarrow p') Tr(p \to p') \frac{Cp(p, p') C{p'}(p', p)}{\|p - p'\|} where V is the visibility function, and Cp is the cosine factor: Cp(p, p') = \begin{cases} |\mathbf{n}p \cdot \frac{p - p'}{\|p - p'\|}| & \text{if } p \text{ is a surface vertex} \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} The generalized scattering distribution function is: \hat{f}(p{i+1} \to pi \to p{i-1}) = \begin{cases} \sigmas p(p{i+1} \to pi \to p{i-1}) & \text{if } pi \in V \\ f(p{i+1} \to pi \to p{i-1}) & \text{if } pi \in A \end{cases} 2. Distance Sampling Simplification Assume a single majorant \sigma{maj} is used for delta tracking. The probability density for sampling the distance t to the next interaction is: p{maj}(p{i+1}|pi, \omegai) = \sigma{maj} e^{-\sigma{maj} t} The term \hat{T} contains transmittance factors T{maj} derived from the majorant. When expanding \hat{T} and dividing by the product of p{maj} terms in the denominator, the exponential factors e^{-\sigma{maj} t} cancel out the T{maj} factors. Each vertex contributes a factor of 1/\sigma{maj}. Additionally, the \hat{G} factors in the numerator (from \hat{T}) cancel with the \hat{G} factors in the denominator (from the path space measure conversion). This leaves a factor of (\sigma{maj})^n in the denominator: \hat{P}(\bar{p}n) = \frac{\left(\prod{i=1}^{n-1} \hat{f}(p{i+1} \to pi \to p{i-1})\right) \hat{L}e(pn \to p{n-1})}{\left(\sigma{maj}\right)^n \left(\prod{i=1}^{n} pe(pi)\right) \left(\prod{i=1}^{m-1} p\omega(\omega{i+1}|ri, \omegai)\right)} 3. Event Type Simplification The discrete probability pe(pi) of choosing a specific event type (absorption, real scattering, or null scattering) at vertex pi is proportional to the corresponding coefficient divided by the majorant: pe(pi) = \frac{\sigma{\{a,s,n\}}(pi)}{\sigma{maj}} The product \prod{i=1}^{n} pe(pi) therefore contains a factor of (\sigma{maj})^{-n}. This cancels the (\sigma{maj})^n term in the denominator from the previous step. The estimator becomes: \hat{P}(\bar{p}n) = \frac{\left(\prod{i=1}^{n-1} \hat{f}(p{i+1} \to pi \to p{i-1})\right) \hat{L}e(pn \to p{n-1})}{\left(\prod{i=1}^{n} \sigma{\{a,s,n\}}(pi)\right) \left(\prod{i=1}^{m-1} p\omega(\omega{i+1}|ri, \omegai)\right)} 4. Specific Event Constraints In a standard path tracing setup, the first n-1 vertices are sampled as either real scattering or null scattering events (the path continues). The last vertex pn is sampled as an absorption event (the path terminates). Thus: For i = 1 \dots n-1, \sigma{\{a,s,n\}}(pi) is either \sigmas(pi) or \sigman(pi). For i = n, \sigma{\{a,s,n\}}(pn) is \sigmaa(pn). The estimator simplifies to: \hat{P}(\bar{p}n) = \frac{\left(\prod{i=1}^{n-1} \hat{f}(p{i+1} \to pi \to p{i-1})\right) \hat{L}e(pn \to p{n-1})}{\left(\prod{i=1}^{n-1} \sigma{\{s,n\}}(pi)\right) \sigmaa(pn) \left(\prod{i=1}^{m-1} p\omega(\omega{i+1}|ri, \omegai)\right)} 5. Phase Function and Null Scattering Cancellation Neglecting surface scattering, \hat{f} represents either regular volumetric scattering or null scattering. For real scattering at ri, \hat{f} = \sigmas p(r{i-1} \to ri \to r{i+1}). For null scattering at ni, \hat{f} = \sigman \cdot 1 (the Heaviside function for null scattering is 1). The term \sigma{\{s,n\}}(pi) in the denominator matches the \sigmas or \sigman factor in the numerator's \hat{f}. These cancel out for all i=1 \dots n-1. We restrict the product in the numerator to only the m real-scattering vertices r1, \dots, rm. The null scattering events contribute a factor of 1 and cancel their own \sigman terms. The estimator becomes: \hat{P}(\bar{p}n) = \frac{\left(\prod{i=1}^{m-1} p(r{i-1} \to ri \to r{i+1})\right) \hat{L}e(pn \to p{n-1})}{\sigmaa(pn) \left(\prod{i=1}^{m-1} p\omega(\omega{i+1}|ri, \omegai)\right)} Note: The product index for the phase functions corresponds to the real scattering vertices. If m=0, the product is empty (value 1). 6. Final Emission Cancellation The path space emission function \hat{L}e(pn \to p{n-1}) includes a factor of \sigmaa(pn) (the probability of absorption at the last vertex). This \sigmaa(pn) cancels with the \sigmaa(pn) in the denominator. The final simplified estimator is: \hat{P}(\bar{p}n) = \left(\prod{i=1}^{m-1} \frac{p(r{i-1} \to ri \to r{i+1})}{p\omega(\omega{i+1}|ri, \omegai)}\right) \hat{L}e(pn \to p{n-1}) This result shows that the path contribution is the emission at the last vertex scaled by the product of ratios of phase function values to sampling probabilities for all real scattering events. The following Python-like pseudocode computes the estimator for a given path. It assumes the path vertices have been sampled and categorized. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computevolumetricpathestimator(pathvertices, pathdirections, phasefunctions, samplingprobs, emissionatlastvertex): """ Computes the simplified volumetric path contribution estimator. Args: pathvertices: List of vertex positions [p1,..., pn] pathdirections: List of directions [omega1,..., omega{n-1}] phasefunctions: List of phase function values p(r{i-1} -> ri -> r{i+1}) for each real scattering vertex ri samplingprobs: List of direction sampling probabilities pomega(omega{i+1} | ri, omegai) for each real scattering vertex ri emissionatlastvertex: The value of Le(pn -> p{n-1}) including the sigmaa factor Returns: The estimated path contribution Phat """ # Identify real scattering vertices. # In a standard implementation, this is done during path traversal. # Here we assume phasefunctions and samplingprobs are aligned for the m real scattering events. m = len(phasefunctions) if m == 0: # No real scattering events. The product is empty (1). # The estimator is just the emission at the last vertex. # Note: emissionatlastvertex already includes sigmaa(pn) which cancels the denominator sigmaa. return emissionatlastvertex productratio = 1.0 for i in range(m): # For the first real scattering vertex (i=0), the phase function is p(r0 -> r0 -> r1) ? # The derivation uses indices 1 to m-1 for the product. # Let's align with the formula: product{i=1}^{m-1} # This implies the product is over the scattering events, excluding the first and last? # Re-reading: "Restrict to the remaining m real-scattering events in the numerator." # Formula: product{i=1}^{m-1} p(r{i-1} -> ri -> r{i+1}) / pomega(...) # This notation suggests r1... rm are the real scattering vertices. # The product runs from i=1 to m-1. # This means the first real scattering vertex r1 and the last real scattering vertex rm are NOT included in the product? # Let's re-read carefully. # "Our estimator simplifies to... product{i=1}^{m-1}..." # In the context of the derivation, the vertices are p1... pn. # The real scattering vertices are a subset. # The formula in Eq 14.19 is: # Phat = ( product{i=1}^{m-1} [ p(r{i-1} -> ri -> r{i+1}) / pomega(...) ]) [ Le / sigmaa ] # This implies that for the first real scattering vertex (index 1 in the real scattering list), # and the last real scattering vertex (index m in the real scattering list), the term is NOT in the product? name: Volumetric Path Tracing with Transmittance Sampling
head: Equiangular sampling (mentioned as alternative), Single-scattering volumetric path tracing
body: Volumetric Path Tracing with Transmittance Sampling is a unidirectional path tracing method that computes single-scattering radiance in participating media by sampling the distance to the next interaction event directly from the transmittance distribution. It differs from its parent, Volumetric Path Tracing, by explicitly handling surface intersections and light emission alongside volume scattering. Unlike Multiple Scattering Volume Path Tracing with Phase Function Sampling, this method does not handle multiple scattering events within the volume. Inputs: screenpos: 2D screen coordinates for the pixel. rng: Random number generator state. camera: Camera object providing ray generation. scene: Scene object providing surface intersection and light sampling. sigmat: Extinction coefficient of the homogeneous volume. sigmas: Scattering coefficient of the homogeneous volume. Outputs: L: Estimated radiance returning from the pixel. Data Structures: Ray: Struct with org (origin, vec3), dir (direction, vec3), thit (distance to nearest surface intersection, float). Intersection: Struct with thit (distance, float), surface (surface data, object), Le (emission, float or vec3). Steps: 1. Sample Primary Ray: Generate a camera ray from screenpos using the camera model and rng. 2. Intersect Scene: Find the distance to the nearest surface intersection, thit. 3. Sample Interaction Distance: Generate a uniform random number u \in [0, 1] from rng. Compute the sampled distance t to the next scattering event using the inverse CDF of the exponential transmittance distribution: t = \frac{\log(1-u)}{-\sigmat} 4. Determine Event Type: Compare t with isect.thit. Case A: Volume Scattering (t < \text{isect}.t{\text{hit}}): 1. Calculate the transmittance from the camera to the scattering point: T = \exp(-\sigmat \cdot t) 2. Calculate the probability density function (PDF) of the sampled distance: p(t) = \sigmat \exp(-\sigmat \cdot t) 3. Compute the scattering point position: p = \text{camera\ray.org} + t \cdot \text{camera\ray.dir} 4. Estimate the scattered radiance L{s1} by sampling a point on a light source and evaluating the phase function and geometry term. Let L{s1\estimate} be the radiance contribution and L{s1\pdf} be the PDF of the light sampling. 5. Return the radiance estimate weighted by the ratio of transmittance to the sampling PDF and the scattering coefficient: L = \frac{T}{p(t)} \cdot \sigmas \cdot \frac{L{s1\estimate}}{L{s1\pdf}} Case B: Surface Intersection (t \geq \text{isect}.t{\text{hit}}): 1. The ray hits a surface before the sampled scattering event. Calculate the transmittance to the hit point: T = \exp(-\sigmat \cdot \text{isect}.t{\text{hit}}) 2. Calculate the PDF for hitting the surface (probability that the next scattering event is beyond the surface): P(t \geq \text{isect}.t{\text{hit}}) = \exp(-\sigmat \cdot \text{isect}.t{\text{hit}}) 3. Retrieve the surface emission Le. If the hit surface is a light source, Le = \text{isect}.Le; otherwise, Le = 0. 4. Return the surface emission weighted by the ratio of transmittance to the PDF: L = \frac{T}{P(t \geq \text{isect}.t{\text{hit}})} \cdot Le Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def volpathtracingtransmittancesampling(screenpos, rng, camera, scene, sigmat, sigmas): # 1. Sample primary camera ray cameraray = sampleprimary(camera, screenpos, rng) # 2. Intersect scene isect = intersect(scene, cameraray) thit = isect.thit # 3. Sample distance to next scattering event u = next(rng) # u in [0, 1] t = -math.log(1 - u) / sigmat # 4. Determine if scattering or surface hit if t < thit: # Volume scattering transmittance = math.exp(-sigmat t) transpdf = sigmat math.exp(-sigmat t) # Compute scattering point p = cameraray.org + t cameraray.dir # Estimate scattered radiance from light source # Ls1(p, samplepointonlight(rng)) - sources do not provide full implementation Ls1estimate, Ls1pdf = samplelightandevalphase(p, rng, scene) # Return weighted estimate return (transmittance / transpdf) sigmas (Ls1estimate / Ls1pdf) else: # Surface intersection transmittance = math.exp(-sigmat thit) transpdf = math.exp(-sigmat thit) Le = 0 if islight(isect): Le = isect.Le return (transmittance / transpdf) Le def sampleprimary(camera, screenpos, rng): return Ray(camera.origin, camera.direction(screenpos), float('inf')) def intersect(scene, ray): tmin = float('inf') hit = None for surface in scene.surfaces: t, data = surface.intersect(ray) if 0 < t < tmin: tmin = t hit = data return Intersection(tmin, hit) def samplelightandevalphase(p, rng, scene): lightpos, lightpdf = scene.samplelight(rng) return lightpos.emission, lightpdf def islight(isect): return isect.surface is not None and isect.surface.isemissive Parameters: sigmat: Extinction coefficient. Assumed constant (homogeneous volume). sigmas: Scattering coefficient. Assumed constant (homogeneous volume). u: Uniform random number in [0, 1]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The sampling can generate t > t{\text{hit}}, meaning the ray hits a surface before the sampled scattering event. The method is noisy because it does not importance sample the geometry term \frac{|\omega \cdot n{p0}|}{\|p(t) - p0\|^2} along t. Extends this method to handle multiple scattering events within homogeneous media and index-matched surfaces. Choose this when multiple bounces are required. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method produces noisy images even at high sampling counts because it does not importance sample the geometry term. Strengths: Handles both volume scattering and surface emission in a unified framework. Limitations: High variance due to lack of geometry term importance sampling; limited to single scattering in homogeneous media. When to use: Debugging ground-truth results or simple single-scattering scenarios. When not to use: Scenes requiring multiple scattering or efficient single-scattering with low variance (use Equiangular sampling instead). This method is described in the homework assignment "Volumetric Path Tracing" from UCSD CSE 272 (Winter 2022). It is presented as a step towards more sophisticated volumetric path tracers, contrasting with equiangular sampling. Volumetric Path Tracing, https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~tzli/cse272/wi2022/homework2.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Volumetric Path Tracing with Transmittance Sampling and Multiple Scattering
head: Multi-scattering phase function sampling, Multiple Monochromatic Homogeneous Volumes with Multiple Scattering (Phase Function Sampling Only), Volumetric Path Tracing 3
body: This method extends volumetric path tracing to handle multiple scattering events within multiple homogeneous participating media, relying exclusively on phase function sampling for direction selection. It differs from its parent, Volumetric Path Tracing with Transmittance Sampling, by explicitly managing multiple bounces within volumes and handling index-matched surfaces that change the medium without reflecting or refracting light. Unlike methods that use Next Event Estimation (NEE) for surface lighting, this variant assumes surfaces only emit light and do not reflect or transmit it. Inputs: Camera ray origin and direction, scene geometry with medium assignments, volume absorption and scattering coefficients (\sigmaa, \sigmas), phase function \rho, surface emission Le, random number generator, maxdepth, and rrdepth. Outputs: Radiance value for the pixel. Intersection: Contains materialid, interiormedium, exteriormedium, geometrynormal, and position. Ray: Contains origin, direction, and tmax. Medium: Defined by absorption coefficient \sigmaa and scattering coefficient \sigmas. The method assumes monochromatic volumes where \sigmaa and \sigmas are identical across color channels. maxdepth: Controls the maximum number of bounces. If -1, bounces are infinite. Otherwise, the path can have at most maxdepth + 1 vertices. rrdepth: The bounce count at which Russian roulette begins. Russian roulette initializes when the path has rrdepth + 1 vertices. 1. Initialize ray, currentmedium, currentpaththroughput (1), radiance (0), and bounces (0). 2. If in a volume, sample distance t from the transmittance distribution, update ray origin, and update throughput by transmittance/transpdf. 3. If no scattering occurred (hit surface), add emission contribution to radiance. 4. If maxdepth is reached (and not infinite), break the loop. 5. If a surface was hit and is index-matched (materialid == -1), update the medium, increment bounces, and continue to the next iteration without sampling a new direction. 6. If scattering occurred, sample a new direction from the phase function and update throughput by phase function PDF and \sigmas. 7. Apply Russian roulette if bounces >= rrdepth. Terminate with probability P{rr}, otherwise divide throughput by P{rr}. 8. Increment bounces and return radiance. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def L(screenpos, rng, scene, camera, maxdepth, rrdepth): # Standard primary ray generation ray = Ray(origin=camera.origin, direction=sampleprimaryray(screenpos, rng)) currentmedium = camera.medium currentpaththroughput = 1.0 radiance = 0.0 bounces = 0 while True: scatter = False transmittance = 1.0 transpdf = 1.0 isect = intersect(scene, ray) # Standard scene intersection if currentmedium is not None: sigmat = currentmedium.sigmaa + currentmedium.sigmas # Sample t from p(t) ~ sigmat exp(-sigmat t) t = -math.log(1.0 - rng()) / sigmat transmittance = math.exp(-sigmat t) transpdf = sigmat math.exp(-sigmat t) if t < isect.thit: scatter = True ray.origin = ray.origin + t ray.direction currentpaththroughput = (transmittance / transpdf) else: ray.origin = isect.point if not scatter: # Hit a surface, include emission radiance += currentpaththroughput isect.emission if maxdepth != -1 and bounces == maxdepth - 1: break if isect.materialid == -1: # Index-matched surface: pass through, update medium, count as bounce currentmedium = updatemedium(isect, ray, currentmedium) bounces += 1 continue if scatter: # Sample phase function nextdir = samplephasefunction(-ray.direction, rng) phaseval = phasefunction(-ray.direction, nextdir) phasepdf = pdfsamplephase(-ray.direction, nextdir) currentpaththroughput = (phaseval / phasepdf) currentmedium.sigmas else: # Hit non-index-matched surface: terminate (no reflection/refraction) break # Russian Roulette rrprob = 1.0 if bounces >= rrdepth: # Prr formula from source # currentpaththroughput represents contrib(path)/p(path) relative to initialization rrprob = min(currentpaththroughput, 0.95) if rng() > rrprob: break else: currentpaththroughput /= rrprob bounces += 1 return radiance def updatemedium(isect, ray, currentmedium): # Only update on medium transition if isect.interiormedium != isect.exteriormedium: # Update based on ray direction relative to geometry normal if dot(ray.direction, isect.geometrynormal) > 0: return isect.exteriormedium else: return isect.interiormedium return currentmedium def dot(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) # Standard vector operation Index-matched surfaces: Surfaces with materialid == -1 do not reflect or refract but change the medium. The ray passes through them, counting as a bounce, and the medium is updated based on the ray direction relative to the geometry normal. Russian Roulette Cap: The termination probability P{rr} is capped at 0.95. Monochromatic Volumes: The method assumes \sigmaa and \sigmas are constant across color channels. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles multiple scattering in homogeneous volumes correctly. Simple to implement compared to methods requiring NEE or complex MIS weights for volume-surface interactions. Limitations: Only handles emission from surfaces; no reflection or refraction. Assumes homogeneous volumes. No next event estimation, which can lead to high variance in scenes with small light sources. When to use: Scenes with multiple homogeneous participating media where surfaces are emissive only. When not to use: Scenes with reflective/refractive surfaces, heterogeneous volumes, or where NEE is required for efficiency. This method handles multiple scattering in multiple homogeneous volumes with phase function sampling only. It builds upon previous volumetric path tracing methods that handled single scattering or transmittance sampling. name: Unbiased Monte Carlo Estimator for Radiance and Radiance Derivatives
head: Joint Estimation of L(1) and L̂(1)
body: This method provides an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator for the first-order radiance derivative \hat{L}^{(1)} and the radiance L^{(1)} in participating media, handling volumetric and interfacial scattering events separately based on the free-flight distance relative to the boundary distance D. It distinguishes itself from standard volumetric path tracing by explicitly propagating scene derivatives alongside radiance values, enabling the computation of gradients required for differentiable rendering. Unlike Volumetric Path Tracing, which computes only radiance, this estimator jointly tracks the sensitivity of the solution to scene parameters. Inputs: \mathbf{x}, \hat{\mathbf{x}}: Current position and its scene derivative. \omega, \hat{\omega}: Current direction and its scene derivative. n: Current path depth, used for Russian Roulette termination. Outputs: L^{(1)}: The estimated radiance. \hat{L}^{(1)}: The estimated radiance derivative. D: Distance from \mathbf{x} to the nearest boundary \partial \Omega along \omega. \hat{D}: Scene derivative of D. \tau: Sampled free-flight distance. \sigmas(\mathbf{x}): Scattering coefficient. \sigmat(\mathbf{x}): Extinction coefficient. \hat{\sigma}s(\mathbf{x}): Scene derivative of the scattering coefficient. \Sigmat(\mathbf{x}, \omega, \tau): Optical depth from \mathbf{x} to \mathbf{x} - \tau \omega. fp(\mathbf{x}, \omega', \omega): Phase function. \hat{f}p(\mathbf{x}, \omega', \omega): Scene derivative of the phase function. fs(\mathbf{x}, \omega', \omega): BSDF at the boundary. \hat{f}s(\mathbf{x}, \omega', \omega): Scene derivative of the BSDF. L^{(0)}(\mathbf{x}, \omega): Zero-order radiance (emission or direct illumination estimate). Russian Roulette: A survival probability is used to terminate paths stochastically to avoid infinite recursion during indirect term estimation. 1. Calculate Boundary Distance: Compute D and \hat{D} based on \mathbf{x}, \hat{\mathbf{x}}, \omega, \hat{\omega}. 2. Sample Free-Flight Distance: Draw \tau from the probability density p(\tau) = \sigmat(\mathbf{x}') T(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x}), where T is the transmittance. 3. Branch on Event Type: Volumetric Event (\tau < D): 1. Compute new position and derivative: \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} - \tau \omega and \hat{\mathbf{x}}' = \hat{\mathbf{x}} - \tau \hat{\omega}, ensuring \mathbf{x}' \in \Omega \setminus \partial \Omega. 2. Compute scattering ratio \alpha and derivative term \beta: \alpha = \sigmas(\mathbf{x}')/\sigmat(\mathbf{x}') and \beta = (\hat{\sigma}s(\mathbf{x}') - \Sigmat(\mathbf{x}, \omega, \tau)\sigmas(\mathbf{x}'))/\sigmat(\mathbf{x}'). 3. Draw new direction \omega' from the phase function fp(\mathbf{x}', -\omega', \omega). 4. Recursive Call: Call radiance(x', x̂', ω', 0) to obtain (L^{(1)}, \hat{L}^{(1)}) for the indirect term. 5. Initialize indirect radiance derivative \hat{L}{ins}: \hat{L}{ins} = \hat{L}^{(1)} + (\hat{f}p(\mathbf{x}', -\omega', \omega)/fp(\mathbf{x}', -\omega', \omega))L^{(1)}. 6. Estimate direct volumetric term L{ins} by integrating the source term over the hemisphere S^2: L{ins} \leftarrow L{ins} + \int{S^2} fp(\mathbf{x}', -\omega', \omega)L^{(0)}(\mathbf{x}', \omega') d\omega'. 7. Estimate direct derivative term \hat{L}{ins} by integrating the derivative of the source term: \hat{L}{ins} \leftarrow \hat{L}{ins} + \int{S^2} \partial\pi[fp(\mathbf{x}', -\omega', \omega)L^{(0)}(\mathbf{x}', \omega')] d\omega'. 8. Add the edge integral contribution to \hat{L}{ins} by calling edgeIntegral(x', x̂', ω, fp). 9. Compute final volumetric estimates: L^{(1)} = \alpha L{ins} and \hat{L}^{(1)} = \alpha \hat{L}{ins} + \beta L{ins}. Interfacial Event (\tau \ge D): 1. Compute intersection point and derivative: \mathbf{x}0 = \mathbf{x} - D \omega and \hat{\mathbf{x}}0 = \hat{\mathbf{x}} - D \hat{\omega}, ensuring \mathbf{x}0 \in \partial \Omega. 2. Draw new direction \omega' with probability p(\omega') from the local BSDF. 3. Compute BSDF ratio \alpha and derivative term \beta: \alpha = fs(\mathbf{x}0, \omega', \omega)/p(\omega') and \beta = \Sigmat(\mathbf{x}, \omega, D) + \hat{D}\sigmat(\mathbf{x}0). 4. Recursive Call: Call radiance(x0, x̂0, ω', 0) to obtain (L^{(1)}, \hat{L}^{(1)}) for the reflected/scattered radiance. 5. Compute reflected radiance L{rs} and its derivative \hat{L}{rs}: L{rs} = \alpha L^{(1)} and \hat{L}{rs} = \alpha \hat{L}^{(1)} + (\hat{f}s(\mathbf{x}0, -\omega', \omega)/p(\omega'))L^{(1)}. 6. Estimate direct interfacial term L{rs} by integrating the source term: L{rs} \leftarrow L{rs} + \int{S^2} fs(\mathbf{x}0, -\omega', \omega)L^{(0)}(\mathbf{x}0, \omega') d\omega'. 7. Estimate direct derivative term \hat{L}{rs} by integrating the derivative of the source term: \hat{L}{rs} \leftarrow \hat{L}{rs} + \int{S^2} \partial\pi[fs(\mathbf{x}0, -\omega', \omega)L^{(0)}(\mathbf{x}0, \omega')] d\omega'. 8. Add the edge integral contribution to \hat{L}{rs} by calling edgeIntegral(x0, x̂0, ω, fs). 9. Estimate the in-scattered radiance L{ins} at the boundary using the method from Appendix B. 10. Compute final interfacial estimates: L^{(1)} = L{rs} and \hat{L}^{(1)} = -\beta L{rs} + \hat{L}{rs} + \hat{D}\sigmas(\mathbf{x}0)L{ins}. 4. Return: Return (L^{(1)}, \hat{L}^{(1)}). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random import math def radiance(x, xhat, omega, omegahat, depth): """ Computes unbiased Monte Carlo estimates for radiance L(1) and its derivative Lhat(1). """ # 1. Calculate boundary distance D and its derivative Dhat D, Dhat = computeboundarydistance(x, xhat, omega, omegahat) # # 2. Sample free-flight distance tau from p(tau) = sigmat(x') T(x', x) tau = samplefreeflight(x, omega) # # Russian roulette to avoid infinite recursion if depth > 0 and random.random() > 0.5: # return 0.0, 0.0 if tau < D: # --- Volumetric Event --- xprime = x - tau omega xhatprime = xhat - tau omegahat sigmasp = getsigmas(xprime) sigmatp = getsigmat(xprime) alpha = sigmasp / sigmatp sigmatxtau = computeopticaldepth(x, omega, tau) sigmashatp = getsigmashat(xprime) beta = (sigmashatp - name: Differentiable Volumetric Path Tracing
head: Differential Theory of Radiative Transfer, Differentiable Volumetric Path Tracing for Albedo Gradient, unbiased Monte Carlo method for scene derivatives
body: Differentiable Volumetric Path Tracing is an unbiased Monte Carlo method used to numerically estimate derivatives of the radiative transfer equation (RTE) with respect to arbitrary scene parameterizations, specifically albedo. It solves the problem of computing gradients for inverse rendering in participating media, enabling the optimization of scene parameters such as material properties. Unlike standard volumetric path tracing which only estimates radiance, this method simultaneously computes radiance and its gradient with respect to a chosen parameter (e.g., albedo \alpha) along sampled paths. It sets itself apart from siblings like Multiple Scattering Volume Path Tracing with Phase Function Sampling by explicitly differentiating the path contribution weights to provide gradient information for regularization or optimization, rather than just reducing noise in the radiance estimate. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Scene geometry, participating media properties (extinction coefficient \sigmat, albedo \alpha, phase function p), light source definitions, camera parameters, and the specific scene parameter to differentiate with respect to (typically albedo \alpha). Outputs: Estimated radiance L(x, \omega) and its gradient \frac{\partial L}{\partial \alpha} for each pixel. Data Structures: Path State: A sequence of bounce points x0, x1, \dots, xK, where x0 is the camera position and xK is the endpoint (light source or termination). Path Contribution: A scalar value f(\tilde{p}) representing the unnormalized contribution of a path \tilde{p}. Accumulators: Per-pixel accumulators for radiance sum and gradient sum, initialized to zero. Formulas: The radiance L(x, \omega) is expressed as a path integral over a path space Sp containing all paths starting from x with direction \omega and ending at the light source: L(x, \omega) = \int{Sp} f(\tilde{p}) d\tilde{p} Using Monte Carlo sampling with M samples, the estimator is: L(x, \omega) = \frac{1}{M} \sum{i=1}^{M} \frac{f(\tilde{p}i)}{\text{pdf}(\tilde{p}i)} where \text{pdf}(\tilde{p}i) is the probability density function of sampling path \tilde{p}i. The contribution f(\tilde{p}i) for a path with K bounces is defined as: f(\tilde{p}i) = \prod{k=1}^{K} wk g(\omega{k-1}, \omegak) where wk is the weight at bounce k and g(\omega{k-1}, \omegak) is the scattering term. The weight wk depends on whether the bounce point xk is in a medium or on a surface: wk = \begin{cases} \alpha \sigmat \text{Tr}(x{k-1} \leftrightarrow xk) & \text{if } xk \in \text{medium} \\ \text{Tr}(x{k-1} \leftrightarrow xk) & \text{if } xk \in \text{surface} \end{cases} where \text{Tr}(x{k-1} \leftrightarrow xk) is the transmittance between x{k-1} and xk, \sigmat is the extinction coefficient, and \alpha is the albedo. The scattering term g(\omega{k-1}, \omegak) is defined as: g(\omega{k-1}, \omegak) = \begin{cases} p(\omega{k-1}, \omegak) & \text{if } xk \in \text{medium} \\ \frac{\rho(\omega{k-1}, \omegak) \cos(\thetak)}{4\pi} & \text{if } xk \in \text{surface} \end{cases} where p is the phase function, \rho is the bidirectional scattering distribution function (BSDF), and \thetak is the angle between the surface normal at xk and the direction \omegak. Parameters: M: Number of samples per pixel. Low sample counts are used for faster iterations in optimization. K: Maximum number of bounces. Not given in the sources. \alpha: Albedo parameter. The method often uses a modified lower albedo \alphas < \alphat to reduce noise variance. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize per-pixel accumulators for radiance L{sum} and gradient G{sum} to zero. 2. For each sample i from 1 to M: a. Sample a path \tilde{p}i from the camera through the scene to a light source, recording bounce points x0, \dots, xK and directions \omega0, \dots, \omegaK. b. Compute the path contribution f(\tilde{p}i) using the product of weights wk and scattering terms g(\omega{k-1}, \omegak) as defined above. c. Compute the gradient of the contribution with respect to albedo \alpha, \frac{\partial f(\tilde{p}i)}{\partial \alpha}, using automatic differentiation tools (e.g., Eigen C++ library) to compute both radiance and gradient simultaneously along the sampled path. d. Compute the importance sampling weight 1/\text{pdf}(\tilde{p}i). e. Update the pixel accumulators: L{sum} \leftarrow L{sum} + \frac{f(\tilde{p}i)}{\text{pdf}(\tilde{p}i)} G{sum} \leftarrow G{sum} + \frac{\frac{\partial f(\tilde{p}i)}{\partial \alpha}}{\text{pdf}(\tilde{p}i)} 3. After all M samples, compute the final radiance and gradient for the pixel: L = \frac{L{sum}}{M} G = \frac{G{sum}}{M} 4. Return L and G. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math PI = math.pi def differentiablevolumetricpathtracing(camera, scene, numsamples): radiancesum = 0.0 gradientsum = 0.0 for i in range(numsamples): # Sample a path from camera to light # Path sampling strategy (e.g., delta tracking) is not specified in the sources pathpoints = [] pathdirs = [] #... path generation logic... # For self-containment, assume pathpoints and pathdirs are populated # K is the number of bounces K = len(pathpoints) - 1 alpha = scene.albedo f = 1.0 dfdalpha = 0.0 for k in range(1, K + 1): xprev = pathpoints[k-1] xcurr = pathpoints[k] wprev = pathdirs[k-1] wcurr = pathdirs[k] # Compute transmittance Tr(x{k-1} <-> xk) # Assuming exponential transmittance: Tr = exp(-sigmat distance) dist = math.sqrt(sum((a-b)2 for a, b in zip(xcurr, xprev))) sigmat = scene.extinctioncoefficient(xcurr) tr = math.exp(-sigmat dist) # Determine weight wk # isinmedium check is not specified in the sources inmedium = True # Placeholder for medium check logic if inmedium: wk = alpha sigmat tr dwkdalpha = sigmat tr else: wk = tr dwkdalpha = 0.0 # Compute scattering term g if inmedium: g = scene.phasefunction(wprev, wcurr) dgdalpha = 0.0 else: bsdf = scene.bsdf(xcurr, wprev, wcurr) normal = scene.surfacenormal(xcurr) costheta = max(0.0, sum(nd for n, d in zip(normal, wcurr))) g = bsdf costheta / (4.0 PI) dgdalpha = 0.0 # Update contribution and gradient # fnew = fold wk g # dfnew = dfold wk g + fold dwkdalpha g fnew = f wk g dfdalphanew = dfdalpha wk g + f dwkdalpha g f = fnew dfdalpha = dfdalphanew # Compute PDF of the sampled path # Path PDF computation is not specified in the sources pdf = 1.0 # Placeholder for path PDF calculation if pdf == 0.0: continue weight = 1.0 / pdf radiancesum += f weight gradientsum += dfdalpha weight radiance = radiancesum / numsamples gradient = gradientsum / numsamples return radiance, gradient Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ideal Specular Surfaces: Discontinuities of radiance L(x, \omega) in \omega must include mirror images of geometric edges, which can be nontrivial to identify. Non-Exponential Transmittance: The derivations assume exponential transmittance. Supporting media with non-exponential transmittance requires adjustment of the derivations. Noise: Gradient images suffer from large amounts of noise, especially in media with high albedo where light paths are long and attenuation is slow. Temporal denoising or other regularization techniques may be required. The theoretical framework underlying the method, showing how the RTE can be differentiated with respect to arbitrary scene parameterizations. It handles volumetric absorption, single and multiple scattering, anisotropic phase functions, and heterogeneity. A post-processing technique used to reduce noise in gradient images by reprojection and blending with neighboring frames using motion vectors. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of samples M and the path length K. Similar to standard volumetric path tracing, but with additional overhead for computing gradients via automatic differentiation. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of pixels and the path length K for storing path states during computation. Measured Performance: The method produces better results than standard volumetric path tracing in terms of gradient accuracy for the same computational time, particularly in media with varying extinction coefficients. However, gradient images are noisy, requiring denoising or low sample counts for iterative optimization. Strengths: Unbiased estimation of radiance derivatives; handles complex volumetric phenomena; enables inverse rendering in participating media. Limitations: High variance in gradient estimates, especially for high albedo media; assumptions of exponential transmittance; difficulty with ideal specular surfaces. When to use: When gradients of radiance with respect to scene parameters (like albedo) are needed for inverse rendering or optimization in scenes with participating media. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method is based on the "Differential Theory of Radiative Transfer," introduced in a paper by. It was developed to enable inverse rendering in participating media by providing unbiased Monte Carlo estimators for scene derivatives. The technique has been applied to imaging-inspired and design-inspired inverse rendering examples, optimizing scene parameters such as material properties. Another related work by focuses on efficient participating media rendering by using differentiable volumetric path tracing to compute gradients with respect to albedo for temporal denoising in video rendering. name: Unidirectional Volume Boundary Estimator
head: Main-path side-path sampling, Unidirectional estimator
body: The Unidirectional Volume Boundary Estimator is a Monte Carlo method that samples volume boundary paths by building a main path from the detector to the light, then constructing side paths from main path vertices to the volume boundary and then to the light. It solves the problem of efficiently sampling paths where a scattering event occurs exactly on a volume boundary (interface). It sets itself apart from its sibling, the Bidirectional Volume Boundary Estimator, by constructing the path unidirectionally: it samples the main path first and then the boundary vertex, whereas the bidirectional variant samples the boundary vertex first and connects it to both light and camera. Inputs: Camera position (detector) p^D0. Scene geometry, including translucent objects with "null" interfaces \partial BV. Light sources. Medium properties (absorption, scattering coefficients, phase function). BSDF properties at surface vertices. Outputs: An unbiased estimate of the radiance contribution from volume boundary paths, \langle \mathbf{I}{\text{bnd}} \rangle. Data Structures: Main path: A sequence of vertices \vec{\mathbf{p}}^D = (p^D0, p^D1, \dots, p^DN). Side path: A sequence of vertices \vec{\mathbf{p}}^Sn = (p^S{n,0}, \dots, p^S{n,mn}) connecting the boundary to the light. Boundary vertex: p^Bn \in \partial BV. Steps: 1. Build Main Path: Construct a main path \vec{\mathbf{p}}^D = (p^D0, p^D1, \dots) starting from the detector p^D0 using standard unidirectional volume path tracing. 2. Russian Roulette for Side Paths: For each vertex p^Dn in the main path, stochastically decide whether to generate a side path using Russian roulette based on throughput. 3. Sample Direction: If generating a side path, draw a direction \omegan based on the BSDF or phase function at p^Dn. 4. Find Boundary Vertex: Trace a ray from p^Dn in direction \omegan and find the intersection p^Bn with all "null" interfaces \partial BV. 5. Connect to Light: Connect p^Bn to a light source via a subpath (p^S{n,0}, \dots, p^S{n,mn}) where mn \ge 0. 6. Form Volume Boundary Path: Form the volume boundary path (p^S{n,mn}, \dots, p^S{n,0}, p^Bn, p^Dn, \dots, p^D0) where p^Bn corresponds to a volume scattering event happening exactly on the boundary. Formula: The single-sample Monte Carlo estimator for the radiance contribution is: \langle \mathbf{I}{\text{bnd}} \rangle = \frac{f(\vec{\mathbf{p}}) \nu{\perp}(\mathbf{p}K)}{\text{pdf}(\vec{\mathbf{p}})} where: f(\vec{\mathbf{p}}) is the path contribution (product of BSDFs, phase functions, transmittances, and light emission). \nu{\perp}(\mathbf{p}K) is the perpendicular velocity at the boundary vertex \mathbf{p}K (equivalent to p^Bn). \text{pdf}(\vec{\mathbf{p}}) is the joint probability density of sampling the entire path \vec{\mathbf{p}}, including the main path, the direction \omegan, the boundary intersection, and the side path to the light. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def unidirectionalvolumeboundaryestimator(camerapos, scene, lightsources, maxdepth=10): # 1. Build main path from detector using unidirectional volume path tracing mainpath = [camerapos] throughput = 1.0 currentpos = camerapos for in range(maxdepth): # Sample next medium scattering or surface interaction hit, nextpos, weight, pdf = samplemediumorsurface(currentpos, scene) if not hit: break mainpath.append(nextpos) throughput = weight currentpos = nextpos # Terminate main path via Russian roulette if random.random() > throughput: break totalestimate = 0.0 for n, pDn in enumerate(mainpath): # 2. Stochastically decide whether to generate a side path based on throughput if random.random() > throughput: continue # 3. Draw a direction omegan based on the BSDF or phase function at pDn omegan = samplebsdforphase(pDn, scene) # 4. Trace a ray from pDn in direction omegan and find intersection pBn pBn = traceray(pDn, omegan, scene, interface="null") if pBn is None: continue # 5. Connect pBn to a light source via a subpath (p^S{n,0},..., p^S{n,mn}) where mn >= 0 sidepath = buildlightsubpath(pBn, lightsources, scene) if sidepath is None: continue # 6. Form the volume boundary path (p^S{n,mn},..., p^S{n,0}, p^Bn, p^Dn,..., p^D0) fullpath = sidepath[::-1] + [pBn] + mainpath[:n+1] # 7. Compute contribution using the estimator formula fp = computepathcontribution(fullpath, scene) nuperp = computeperpendicularvelocity(pBn, omegan) pdfp = computepathpdf(fullpath, scene) if pdfp > 0: totalestimate += (fp nuperp) / pdfp return totalestimate def samplemediumorsurface(pos, scene): # Returns (hit, nextpos, weight, pdf) for medium/surface sampling pass def samplebsdforphase(pos, scene): # Returns direction sampled from BSDF or phase function pass def traceray(origin, direction, scene, interface): # Returns intersection point with specified interface type pass def buildlightsubpath(pos, lights, scene): # Returns list of vertices connecting pos to a light source pass def computepathcontribution(path, scene): # Returns product of BSDFs, phase functions, transmittances, and light emission pass def computeperpendicularvelocity(point, direction): # Returns geometric term (e.g., cosine or Jacobian) at boundary pass def computepathpdf(path, scene): # Returns joint probability density of sampling the entire path pass Parameters: Russian roulette threshold: Not given in the sources. Typically based on throughput magnitude. Maximum path depth: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Boundary Intersection: If the ray from p^Dn does not intersect any null interface \partial BV, the side path generation is skipped. Multiple Intersections: The ray may intersect multiple null interfaces. The source specifies finding the intersection p^Bn with "all" null interfaces, but typically the closest one is used for the primary contribution, or all are sampled if the method supports it. The source does not specify handling of multiple intersections explicitly. PDF Calculation: The PDF must account for the probability of choosing the main path vertex p^Dn, the direction \omegan, the boundary intersection, and the side path. Misestimating this PDF leads to biased results. Samples the boundary vertex first, then connects to light and camera. Chosen when the boundary is hard to reach from the camera or when light sources are complex. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Depends on the length of the main path and the cost of finding boundary intersections and connecting to lights. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Linear in the length of the main path and side paths. Strengths: Efficiently samples volume boundary paths by leveraging the main path structure. Can handle complex media and anisotropic scattering. Limitations: May be inefficient if the boundary is rarely hit by rays from the main path vertices. Russian roulette introduces variance if not tuned properly. When to use: When volume boundary effects are significant and the camera has a good view of the boundary. When not to use: When the boundary is occluded or hard to reach from the camera. The Unidirectional Volume Boundary Estimator was introduced in the paper "Efficient Path-Space Differentiable Volume Rendering With Respect To Shapes" by Zhang et al.. It is part of a framework that supports the full radiative transfer model, including multiple scattering, anisotropic phase functions, and heterogeneity. The method is designed to be combined with a bidirectional estimator using Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) for robust rendering. name: Bidirectional Volume Boundary Estimator
head: Bidirectional estimator, EstimateBoundaryIntegral, Multi-Directional Boundary Integral Estimation, Multi-Directional Form of the Boundary Integral, Multi-directional estimation of the boundary integral, Multi-directional volume boundary sampling
body: A Monte Carlo estimator that samples volume boundary paths by first drawing the volume boundary vertex, then constructing two subpaths to connect it to the light source and the detector. It sets itself apart from its parent, the Unidirectional Volume Boundary Estimator, by decoupling the boundary integral from the interior term and building boundary light paths in a multi-directional manner to avoid costly silhouette edge searches. Unlike the unidirectional approach which builds paths from the detector, this method samples the boundary vertex first, enabling a symmetric construction of source and detector subpaths. The estimator computes the boundary integral contribution by sampling a boundary segment defined by a spatial point \mathbf{x}B and direction \boldsymbol{\omega}B, then estimating source and detector subpaths. Inputs: Probability density P(\mathbf{x}B, \boldsymbol{\omega}B) for sampling the boundary segment. Boolean direct: indicates whether to use Next-Event Estimation (NEE) for direct illumination or estimate indirect paths. Scene geometry M(\pi) and material properties. Outputs: The estimated boundary term contribution TS TB TD. Data Structures: Boundary segment vertices: \mathbf{p}0^S (source side), \mathbf{p}0^D (detector side). Spatial points: \mathbf{x}0^S = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{p}0^S, \pi), \mathbf{x}0^D = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{p}0^D, \pi). Boundary vertex: \mathbf{x}B on the silhouette. Direction: \boldsymbol{\omega}B. Steps: 1. Sample Boundary Segment: Draw (\mathbf{x}B, \boldsymbol{\omega}B) from the probability density P(\mathbf{x}B, \boldsymbol{\omega}B). Trace a ray from \mathbf{x}B in direction -\boldsymbol{\omega}B to find intersection \mathbf{x}0^S on the mesh. Trace a ray from \mathbf{x}B in direction \boldsymbol{\omega}B to find intersection \mathbf{x}0^D on the mesh. Note: The spatial counterpart of the boundary segment \mathbf{x}0^S \mathbf{x}0^D must intersect the evolving surface M(\pi) at exactly one point \mathbf{x}B besides the endpoints. 2. Validate Intersections: If \mathbf{x}0^S or \mathbf{x}0^D are invalid (no intersection or occlusion), return 0. 3. Compute Boundary Term (TB): Calculate the boundary contribution function \hat{f}B: \hat{f}B:= \Delta G(\mathbf{x}0^S \leftrightarrow \mathbf{x}0^D) V{\Delta B} where V{\Delta B} is the scalar normal velocity of \mathbf{p}0^D with \mathbf{p}0^S fixed. Compute the Jacobian JB(\mathbf{x}B, \boldsymbol{\omega}B). In the local parameterization where \mathbf{X}(\cdot, \pi0) and \mathbf{P}(\cdot, \pi0) are identity maps: JB(\mathbf{x}B, \boldsymbol{\omega}B) = \frac{\|\mathbf{x}0^D - \mathbf{x}0^S\|}{\|\mathbf{x}B - \mathbf{x}0^S\|} \frac{\sin \thetaB}{\sin \thetaD |\cos \thetaS|} where \thetaB is the angle between \boldsymbol{\omega}B and the face edge at \mathbf{x}B, \thetaD is the angle between \boldsymbol{\omega}B and the visibility boundary at \mathbf{x}0^D, and \thetaS is the angle between \boldsymbol{\omega}B and the surface normal at \mathbf{x}0^S. Compute TB: TB = \frac{\hat{f}B JB(\mathbf{x}B, \boldsymbol{\omega}B)}{P(\mathbf{x}B, \boldsymbol{\omega}B)}. 4. Compute Source Term (TS): Map spatial points to path space: \mathbf{p}0^S = \mathbf{P}(\mathbf{x}0^S, \pi) and \mathbf{p}0^D = \mathbf{P}(\mathbf{x}0^D, \pi). If direct is true: TS = Le(\mathbf{x}0^S \to \mathbf{x}0^D). Else: TS = \text{EstimateSourcePath}(\mathbf{p}0^S; \mathbf{p}0^D). 5. Compute Detector Term (TD): TD = \text{EstimateDetectorPath}(\mathbf{p}0^D; \mathbf{p}0^S). 6. Return Result: Return TS TB TD. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def EstimateBoundaryIntegral(Pboundary, direct, scene): """ Estimates the boundary integral using the bidirectional/multi-directional approach. Args: Pboundary: Function to sample (xB, omegaB) from probability density P(xB, omegaB). direct: Boolean, if True use Next-Event Estimation for direct illumination. scene: Object containing geometry M(pi) and material properties. Returns: Float: The estimated boundary term contribution TS TB TD. """ # Step 1: Sample boundary segment xB, omegaB = Pboundary() # Trace rays to find endpoints of the boundary segment x0S = scene.raytrace(xB, -omegaB) x0D = scene.raytrace(xB, omegaB) # Step 2: Validate intersections if x0S is None or x0D is None: return 0.0 # Step 3: Compute Boundary Term TB # Calculate geometric term Delta G deltaG = computedeltageometry(x0S, x0D) # VdeltaB: Scalar normal velocity of p0^D with p0^S fixed VdeltaB = scene.getnormalvelocity(x0D, x0S) fhatB = deltaG VdeltaB # Compute Jacobian JB # Angles: thetaB (omegaB vs face edge at xB), thetaD (omegaB vs visibility boundary at x0D), # thetaS (omegaB vs surface normal at x0S) thetaB = anglebetween(omegaB, getfaceedgeat(xB)) thetaD = anglebetween(omegaB, getvisibilityboundaryat(x0D)) thetaS = anglebetween(omegaB, getsurfacenormalat(x0S)) distx0Sx0D = norm(x0D - x0S) distxBx0S = norm(x0S - xB) # Handle degenerate cases where distances or cosines are zero if distxBx0S == 0 or abs(math.cos(thetaS)) < 1e-8: return 0.0 JB = (distx0Sx0D / distxBx0S) (math.sin(thetaB) / (math.sin(thetaD) abs(math.cos(thetaS)))) # Probability density of the sample pval = Pboundary.pdf(xB, omegaB) if pval == 0: return 0.0 TB = (fhatB JB) / pval # Step 4: Compute Source Term TS # Map to path space p0S = scene.projecttopathspace(x0S) p0D = scene.projecttopathspace(x0D) if direct: # Direct illumination: Emitter radiance from x0S to x0D TS = scene.emitterradiance(x0S, x0D) else: # Indirect illumination: Estimate source subpath # Standard unidirectional path tracing from p0S towards light, returning throughput TS. TS = estimatesourcepath(p0S, p0D, scene) # Step 5: Compute Detector Term TD # Standard unidirectional path tracing from p0D towards detector, returning throughput TD. TD = estimatedetectorpath(p0D, p0S, scene) # Step 6: Return product return TS TB TD def norm(v): return math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]) def normalize(v): n = norm(v) return (v[0]/n, v[1]/n, v[2]/n) if n > 1e-8 else (0, 0, 0) def anglebetween(a, b): costheta = dot(a, b) / (norm(a) norm(b)) costheta = max(-1.0, min(1.0, costheta)) return math.acos(costheta) def computedeltageometry(p1, p2): # Standard geometric term for visibility between two points on a surface n1 = getsurfacenormalat(p1) n2 = getsurfacenormalat(p2) d = p2[0]-p1[0], p2[1]-p1[1], p2[2]-p1[2] distsq = norm(d)2 if distsq == 0: return 0.0 return dot(n1, d) dot(n2, (-d[0], -d[1], -d[2])) / distsq def getfaceedgeat(point): # Returns a tangent vector on the mesh face at point return (1.0, 0.0, 0.0) def getvisibilityboundaryat(point): # Returns a tangent vector along the visibility boundary at point return (0.0, 1.0, 0.0) def getsurfacenormalat(point): # Returns the surface normal at point return (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) def estimatesourcepath(p0S, p0D, scene): # Standard unidirectional path tracing from p0S towards light return scene.tracepath(p0S, p0D, direction='light') def estimatedetectorpath(p0D, p0S, scene): # Standard unidirectional path tracing from p0D towards detector return scene.tracepath(p0D, p0S, direction='detector') Parameters: V{\Delta B}: Scalar normal velocity of \mathbf{p}0^D with \mathbf{p}0^S fixed. direct: Boolean flag for using NEE. Pitfalls: Identifying silhouette edges is costly. The method avoids this by sampling \mathbf{x}B and \boldsymbol{\omega}B directly, ensuring the segment intersects the surface at \mathbf{x}B. Precision issues may arise if \mathbf{x}B is very close to \mathbf{x}0^S or if \cos \thetaS is near zero. The method assumes the boundary segment's spatial counterpart intersects the evolving surface at exactly one point \mathbf{x}B besides the endpoints. Reparameterizes the boundary segment from two independent endpoints to an interior point and a direction, guaranteeing endpoints lie on each other's visibility boundary by construction. Combines the unidirectional and bidirectional volume boundary estimators using path-level MIS with the balanced heuristic to reduce variance. Time Complexity: Depends on the cost of sampling the boundary segment and tracing rays. Avoids explicit silhouette search, which is costly for complex geometries. Memory Complexity: Low, as it does not require storing large silhouette edge lists. Strengths: Unbiased estimation without expensive silhouette identification. Conceptually similar to multi-directional techniques for ordinary boundary paths but applied to volume boundary paths. Limitations: Requires careful sampling of the boundary segment to ensure valid intersections. Performance depends on the efficiency of the source and detector path estimation subroutines. When to use: When dealing with complex geometries where silhouette identification is prohibitive, or when unbiased boundary path sampling is required. When not to use: If direct silhouette information is already available and cheap to use, other methods might be simpler. Originated in the context of path-space differentiable rendering. The bidirectional estimator is conceptually similar to the multi-directional technique introduced by Zhang et al. [ZMY 20] for sampling ordinary boundary paths. It addresses the challenge of costly silhouette edge identification in prior unbiased methods. name: Multi-Directional Sampling of Boundary Paths
head: Interior-to-Boundary Reparameterization for Boundary Estimator, Zhang et al. 2020 boundary sampling
body: Multi-Directional Sampling of Boundary Paths is a Monte Carlo technique for estimating the boundary integral in volume rendering that avoids explicit silhouette detection by decoupling the boundary segment from the source and detector subpaths. It samples a point on the evolving surface and a direction to reconstruct the boundary segment endpoints via ray tracing, guaranteeing that the endpoints lie on each other's visibility boundary by construction. Inputs and Outputs Input: Scene geometry M(\pi) defined by a reference map P (or motion X) transforming material points to spatial positions; a parameter \pi defining the current state of the geometry. Output: A boundary path consisting of a boundary segment \mathbf{p}{0S}\mathbf{p}{0D}, a source subpath \bar{\mathbf{p}}S connecting \mathbf{p}{0S} to the light source, and a detector subpath \bar{\mathbf{p}}D connecting \mathbf{p}{0D} to the detector. Data Structures Boundary Segment: Defined by two material points \mathbf{p}{0S}, \mathbf{p}{0D} and their corresponding spatial positions \mathbf{x}{0S}, \mathbf{x}{0D}. Sampling Variables: A spatial point \mathbf{x}B \in M(\pi) and a direction \boldsymbol{\omega}B \in S^2. The point \mathbf{x}B is not a vertex of the final path but lies in the interior of the spatial segment \mathbf{x}{0S}\mathbf{x}{0D}. Numbered Steps 1. Sample Boundary Segment Parameters: Draw a point \mathbf{x}B on the evolving surface M(\pi) and a direction \boldsymbol{\omega}B on the unit sphere S^2. 2. Compute Spatial Endpoints: Perform ray tracing from \mathbf{x}B in directions -\boldsymbol{\omega}B and \boldsymbol{\omega}B to find the spatial endpoints of the boundary segment: \mathbf{x}{0S} = \text{rayIntersect}(\mathbf{x}B, -\boldsymbol{\omega}B) \mathbf{x}{0D} = \text{rayIntersect}(\mathbf{x}B, \boldsymbol{\omega}B) By construction, \mathbf{x}{0S} and \mathbf{x}{0D} are guaranteed to be on the visibility boundary of each other, eliminating the need for explicit silhouette detection. 3. Map to Material Space: Convert the spatial endpoints \mathbf{x}{0S} and \mathbf{x}{0D} back to material points \mathbf{p}{0S} and \mathbf{p}{0D} using the inverse of the reference map P (or motion X). 4. Construct Source Subpath: Using standard path sampling methods (e.g., unidirectional or bidirectional path tracing), construct the source subpath \bar{\mathbf{p}}S starting from \mathbf{p}{0S} towards the light source. 5. Construct Detector Subpath: Using standard path sampling methods, construct the detector subpath \bar{\mathbf{p}}D starting from \mathbf{p}{0D} towards the detector. Formulas The method relies on a change of variables to rewrite the boundary integral. The original integral over material boundary points is transformed into an integral over \mathbf{x}B and \boldsymbol{\omega}B: \iiint \hat{f}S d\mu(\bar{\mathbf{p}}S) \hat{f}B JB(\mathbf{x}B, \boldsymbol{\omega}B) \hat{f}D d\mu(\bar{\mathbf{p}}D) d\boldsymbol{\omega}B d\mathbf{x}B where \hat{f}S and \hat{f}D are the source and detector subpath densities, and \hat{f}B is the boundary term density. The Jacobian determinant JB(\mathbf{x}B, \boldsymbol{\omega}B) is the product of two determinants: 1. The change of variables from spatial endpoints (\mathbf{x}{0S}, \mathbf{x}{0D}) to (\mathbf{x}B, \boldsymbol{\omega}B). 2. The change of variables from material points (\mathbf{p}{0S}, \mathbf{p}{0D}) to spatial ones (\mathbf{x}{0S}, \mathbf{x}{0D}). Parameters P: The reference map of the motion X, transforming a material point to its spatial representation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Sampling Difficulty: Efficiently sampling \mathbf{x}B and \boldsymbol{\omega}B remains highly nontrivial. Interior Constraint: The method assumes that \mathbf{x}B lies strictly in the interior of the segment \mathbf{x}{0S}\mathbf{x}{0D}. Specular Surfaces: Connecting the resulting boundary segments to lights and cameras is difficult when highly specular surfaces (mirror, glass) exist between the segment's endpoints and the target, resembling the Specular-Diffuse-Specular light path sampling problem. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sampleboundarypath(scene, pi): # Step 1: Sample boundary segment parameters # The sources do not specify the exact sampling distribution for xB and omegaB. xB = samplepointonsurface(scene.M(pi)) omegaB = sampledirectiononsphere() # Step 2: Compute spatial endpoints via ray tracing x0S = scene.rayintersect(xB, -omegaB) x0D = scene.rayintersect(xB, omegaB) if x0S is None or x0D is None: return None # Step 3: Map to material space p0S = scene.inversereferencemap(x0S, pi) p0D = scene.inversereferencemap(x0D, pi) # Step 4: Construct source subpath # The sources do not specify the exact subpath sampling algorithm. pbarS = samplesourcesubpath(scene, p0S, pi) # Step 5: Construct detector subpath # The sources do not specify the exact subpath sampling algorithm. pbarD = sampledetectorsubpath(scene, p0D, pi) # Compute Jacobian determinant JB(xB, omegaB) # The sources do not provide the explicit analytical form for the determinants. JB = computeboundaryjacobian(xB, omegaB, x0S, x0D, p0S, p0D, scene, pi) return BoundaryPath(sourcesubpath=pbarS, boundarysegment=(p0S, p0D), detectorsubpath=pbarD, jacobian=JB) def samplepointonsurface(surface): # The sources do not specify the exact sampling distribution for xB. pass def sampledirectiononsphere(): # Standard uniform sampling on S^2. pass def samplesourcesubpath(scene, p0S, pi): # The sources do not specify the exact subpath sampling algorithm. pass def sampledetectorsubpath(scene, p0D, pi): # The sources do not specify the exact subpath sampling algorithm. pass def computeboundaryjacobian(xB, omegaB, x0S, x0D, p0S, p0D, scene, pi): # The sources do not provide the explicit analytical form for the determinants. pass An alternative method by Zhang et al. that samples a path segment directly from an edge and connects it to cameras and light sources, avoiding per-shading-point edge selection. It randomly selects a point and direction on an edge to form a segment, then selects directions such that all points on the direction recognize the edge as a silhouette. It uses a hash grid where cell importance is estimated using photon mapping to select edges efficiently. A key pitfall is the difficulty of connecting edge segments to lights/cameras when highly specular surfaces exist between the segment's endpoints and the target, resembling the Specular-Diffuse-Specular light path sampling problem. Time Complexity: Avoids the prohibitively expensive explicit silhouette detection required by methods like Li et al. (2018), which must detect silhouettes at each vertex of a light path. However, efficient sampling of \mathbf{x}B and \boldsymbol{\omega}B remains highly nontrivial. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Guarantees that endpoints are on each other's visibility boundary by construction, simplifying the boundary segment sampling process. Limitations: The method does not solve the problem of connecting boundary segments to lights/cameras in the presence of highly specular surfaces. When to use: When explicit silhouette detection is too expensive for complex geometry. When not to use: When the scene contains many highly specular surfaces between the boundary segment and the light/camera, as connection becomes difficult. The method was proposed by Zhang et al. in 2020 as part of path-space differentiable rendering. It addresses the challenge of estimating the boundary integral in differentiable rendering without the computational cost of Monte Carlo edge sampling, which requires detecting object silhouettes at each vertex of a light path. The technique is a key component of the Multi-Directional Sampling of Boundary Paths approach, enabling efficient sampling of boundary segments by decoupling them from the source and detector subpaths. name: Multiple Importance Sampling for Boundary Paths
head: MIS for direct boundary paths
body: This method combines the unidirectional and bidirectional volume boundary estimators using path-level Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) with the balanced heuristic to reduce variance in differentiable volume rendering. It addresses the limitation of single-estimator approaches by allowing independent sampling of boundary paths from both strategies and weighting their contributions based on their respective sampling probabilities. Unlike the unidirectional estimator which traces from the detector, or the bidirectional estimator which connects a sampled boundary vertex to both light and detector, this method treats the boundary path as a complete entity sampled by either strategy and blends them. Inputs: Scene geometry, participating media properties (optical density, phase function), and light sources. Two independent volume boundary paths: \tilde{\mathbf{p}}1 sampled by the unidirectional estimator and \tilde{\mathbf{p}}2 sampled by the bidirectional estimator. Outputs: The combined radiance estimate for the boundary path contribution. Data Structures: Path structures containing vertices \mathbf{p}0, \dots, \mathbf{p}K, boundary vertex \mathbf{p}B, and light source vertex \mathbf{p}{S0}. Probability density values \text{pdf}1(\tilde{\mathbf{p}}) and \text{pdf}2(\tilde{\mathbf{p}}) associated with each path. Steps: 1. Sample Unidirectional Path: Generate a volume boundary path \tilde{\mathbf{p}}1 using the unidirectional estimator. Starting from a detector vertex \mathbf{p}0, build a main path, then for each vertex \mathbf{p}D^n, explicitly draw a volume boundary vertex \mathbf{p}B^n \in \partial BV and connect it to a light source via a subpath (\mathbf{p}{S^n,0}, \dots, \mathbf{p}{S^n,mn}). 2. Sample Bidirectional Path: Generate a volume boundary path \tilde{\mathbf{p}}2 using the bidirectional estimator [Parent]. This involves first drawing the volume boundary vertex \mathbf{p}B, then constructing two subpaths to connect it to the light source and the detector [Parent]. 3. Compute PDFs: Calculate the probability density \text{pdf}1(\tilde{\mathbf{p}}1) for the unidirectional path and \text{pdf}2(\tilde{\mathbf{p}}2) for the bidirectional path. Note that computing these PDFs is difficult when delta tracking is used to sample free-flight distances. 4. Apply Balanced Heuristic: Weight the contribution of each path using the balanced heuristic formula: \langle \hat{\mathbf{l}}{\text{bnd}} \rangle{\text{mis}} = \frac{f(\tilde{\mathbf{p}}1) v{\perp}(\mathbf{p}{K1})}{\text{pdf}1(\tilde{\mathbf{p}}1) + \text{pdf}2(\tilde{\mathbf{p}}1)} + \frac{f(\tilde{\mathbf{p}}2) v{\perp}(\mathbf{p}{K2})}{\text{pdf}1(\tilde{\mathbf{p}}2) + \text{pdf}2(\tilde{\mathbf{p}}2)} Where: f(\tilde{\mathbf{p}}) is the path throughput (product of phase functions, transmittance, and emission). v{\perp}(\mathbf{p}{K}) is the geometric term involving the perpendicular component of the boundary segment. \mathbf{p}{K1} and \mathbf{p}{K2} are the final vertices of the respective paths. The paths can have varying lengths, so K1 does not have to equal K2. Parameters: The MIS estimator is used only for objects with homogeneous optical densities. For objects with spatially varying albedo, the bidirectional estimator alone is used. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Delta Tracking: Computing \text{pdf}1 and \text{pdf}2 is difficult when delta tracking is used to sample free-flight distances. Occlusion in Direct Sampling: When estimating the direct component, sampling the direction \omegaB by first drawing a point on an area light can yield invalid (occluded) directions in complex illumination (e.g., image-based lighting). In such cases, directly sampling the direction \omegaB is more efficient. This variant combines MIS with primary-sample-space guiding to estimate the boundary segment contribution in differentiable volume rendering. It addresses the issue where light-source sampling yields invalid directions due to occlusion. It differs from a full 5D MIS sampler by applying guiding separately to two lower-dimensional mappings (light-source and direct direction), thereby avoiding the computational expense of guiding a higher-dimensional space while maintaining unbiased estimation. See Multiple Importance Sampling for Boundary Segments. Complexity: The method requires generating two independent paths (unidirectional and bidirectional) and computing their respective PDFs. Strengths: Reduces variance by combining the unidirectional and bidirectional estimators using MIS. Limitations: Requires computing PDFs for both estimators, which is non-trivial with delta tracking. Restricted to homogeneous optical densities for the MIS combination; spatially varying albedo requires the bidirectional estimator alone. When to use: When rendering translucent objects with homogeneous optical densities where both unidirectional and bidirectional sampling strategies are viable. The technique combines unidirectional and bidirectional estimators using MIS. It builds upon the unidirectional and bidirectional volume boundary estimators which support the full radiative transfer model including multiple scattering, anisotropic phase functions, and heterogeneity. The implementation in the source literature is based on the system developed by Yu et al. [YZN 22] utilizing the Enzyme automatic differentiation framework. Zhang et al. (2020) decompose the boundary integral into direct and indirect terms using next-event estimation.
