name: Multiresolution LAO Pipeline
head: Incremental LAO update, Per-fragment LAO computation
body: The Multiresolution LAO Pipeline is a per-fragment processing pipeline that computes Local Ambient Occlusion (LAO) illumination for each voxel in the volume, driven by the multiresolution LOD selection. It accelerates LAO computation by leveraging the same data reduction achieved by the volume's Level-of-Detail (LOD) selection, adapting sampling rates to voxel block resolution. Unlike the parent Incremental LAO method which updates one ray direction per frame, this pipeline processes all incident light directions incrementally over multiple frames using a fragment shader pipeline, allowing for dynamic configuration of ray counts and efficient hardware-accelerated blending. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A multiresolution packed volume texture, a reverse index texture mapping packed coordinates to volume coordinates (P \to V), and a set of incident light directions in the local neighborhood \Omega. Output: A 3D texture storing the accumulated emissive color and ambient occlusion factor for each voxel. Data Structures: 1. Packed Volume Texture: Stores voxel data (opacity \alpha, color) organized in blocks of varying resolutions. 2. Reverse Index Texture (P \to V): Maps a packed coordinate P to its corresponding volume coordinate V. 3. LAO Accumulation Texture: A 3D texture that stores the running sum of light contributions for each voxel. 4. Ray Direction Texture: Stores the K ray directions and their associated weights wk. Parameters: K: Number of light directions to sample. Dynamically configurable. a: User-defined initial offset for sampling along a ray. Prevents self-occlusion for boundary voxels. d: Base sampling density. R\Omega: Radius of the local occlusion neighborhood. \gamma: User-controlled parameter to modify opacity for LAO intensity control. \lambdah: Highest resolution level (base level) of the volume blocks. \lambda: Current block resolution level of the voxel being processed. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create the LAO accumulation 3D texture initialized to zero. Store the K ray directions and weights in a texture. 2. Slice Mapping: Iterate through each slice of the packed volume texture. Map the current slice as the rendering target of a Framebuffer Object (FBO). Constraint: Requires GPU hardware support for attaching a 3D texture slice to an FBO (e.g., Nvidia GF8800 Ultra or later). 3. Fragment Pipeline Initiation: Render a large quad covering the entire framebuffer. Each pixel in the quad corresponds to one voxel in the current mapped slice. 4. Voxel Location Lookup: For each fragment, use the fragment's 2D location and the per-slice constant z-position to determine the packed coordinate P. Use the reverse index texture (P \to V) to retrieve the corresponding volume coordinate V and the block level \lambda of that voxel. 5. Ray Iteration (Incremental Update): The pipeline iterates over the K incident light directions. This iteration happens over multiple frames (one direction per frame) to incrementally build the LAO result. For each ray direction \omegak with weight wk: a. Determine Step Length: Calculate the step length s based on the block level \lambda. The step length is increased to maintain sampling density relative to the underlying volume data: s = \frac{2^{\lambdah} + 2^\lambda}{2} Note: If the difference in step length between adjacent blocks is too large, block artifacts may occur. b. Sample Volume: Starting at offset a along the ray direction \omegak, sample the volume at intervals of s. Use the reverse index texture to map sample positions from volume space back to packed texture coordinates for lookup. c. Opacity Correction: When sampling, the opacity \alpha must be corrected on the fly to account for the changed step length and density. The modified opacity \alpha{modified} is calculated as: \alpha{modified} = 1.0 - (1.0 - \alpha{original})^{\frac{\gamma \cdot d \cdot 2}{2^{\lambdah} + 2^\lambda}} Where \alpha{original} is the stored opacity, \gamma is the control parameter, and d is the base sampling density. d. Accumulate Contribution: Compute the light contribution of the ray (transmittance and emission along the path). Blend this contribution with the previously stored value in the LAO accumulation texture using hardware blending operations. 6. Final Intensity: After all K rays have been processed (over K frames), the final LAO factor for a voxel is the average of the accumulated ray intensities. 7. Rendering: Perform the final volume rendering using the accumulated LAO texture. Interblock interpolation is optional in the final rendering but is not performed during LAO computation to avoid excessive texture lookups. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. K = 8 # Number of rays a = 0.1 # Initial offset d = 1.0 # Base sampling density gamma = 1.0 # Opacity control parameter lambdah = 0 # Highest resolution level (base) ROmega = 1.0 # Neighborhood radius raydirections = [...] # List of K normalized 3D vectors rayweights = [1.0 / K] K # List of K weights for slicez in range(numslices): # Standard OpenGL: glFramebufferTexture3D(target, attachment, texture, level, zoffset=slicez) laotexture.bindslicetofbo(slicez) # Standard OpenGL: glDrawArrays(GLTRIANGLESTRIP, 0, 4) renderfullscreenquad() def fragmentshader(fragcoord, slicez, framecounter): # 1. Map fragment to packed coordinate P P = (fragcoord.x, fragcoord.y, slicez) # 2. Look up volume coordinate V and block level lambda V, lambdaval = reverseindextexture.lookup(P) # 3. Get original voxel data alphaoriginal, colororiginal = volumetexture.lookup(V) # 4. Retrieve accumulated LAO value for this voxel accumulatedlao = laoaccumulationtexture.lookup(V) # 5. Incremental update: Process one ray per frame rayindex = framecounter % K direction = raydirections[rayindex] weight = rayweights[rayindex] # Calculate step length based on block level steplength = (2lambdah + 2lambdaval) / 2.0 # Sample along the ray rayintensity = 0.0 t = a # Start at offset a while t < ROmega: # Sample until neighborhood radius # Sample position in volume space samplepos = V + direction t # Map sample position to packed coordinates using reverse index texture sampleP = reverseindextexture.lookup(samplepos) # Lookup opacity in packed volume alphasample = volumetexture.lookupalpha(sampleP) # Apply opacity correction exponent = (gamma d 2.0) / (2lambdah + 2lambdaval) alphamodified = 1.0 - (1.0 - alphasample)exponent # Standard volume rendering integration: contribution = emission transmittance contribution = sampleemission(sampleP) computetransmittance(sampleP, alphamodified) rayintensity += contribution t += steplength # Average the ray intensity by the weight finalcontribution = rayintensity weight # Hardware additive blending: glBlendFunc(GLONE, GLONE) laoaccumulationtexture.write(V, accumulatedlao + finalcontribution) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hardware Dependency: The method requires GPU support for attaching a 3D texture slice to an FBO. Without this, the slice-by-slice rendering target approach fails. Block Artifacts: A large difference in step length between adjacent blocks (due to different \lambda values) can lead to visible block artifacts in the LAO effect. Careful tuning of \lambdah and \lambda is required. Interblock Interpolation: Interblock interpolation is not performed during LAO computation to save texture lookups. While optional in final rendering, its absence in LAO computation has not been observed to cause significant artifacts. Time Complexity: The computation is performed incrementally over K frames. Each frame processes one ray direction for all voxels. The cost per voxel per frame depends on the number of samples along the ray, which is proportional to R\Omega / s. Since s increases with \lambda, lower-resolution blocks are processed faster. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the packed volume, the reverse index texture, and the LAO accumulation texture. The LAO texture size is proportional to the number of voxels in the volume. Performance: The method achieves speed-up by combining multiresolution data reduction with adaptive sampling rates. The use of GPU fragment shaders and hardware blending allows for efficient parallel processing. Reported frame rates for LAO computation with 8 directions were comparable to diffuse illumination rendering (e.g., 27.2 FPS vs 26.4 FPS in the source results). Strengths: Efficient incremental update, hardware-accelerated, adapts to multiresolution structure. Limitations: Requires specific GPU hardware features, potential block artifacts if step length differences are not managed, limited to local occlusion. The Multiresolution LAO Pipeline was introduced by Hernell et al. in 2007 as part of the paper "Efficient Ambient and Emissive Tissue Illumination using Local Occlusion in Multiresolution Volume Rendering". It builds upon the Incremental LAO method and integrates with multiresolution volume management techniques to provide efficient local illumination effects for volumetric data, particularly in medical imaging contexts. name: Solid Angle Early Termination for Ambient Occlusion
head: Solid Angle Culling for AO, Solid Angle Thresholding for AO
body: Solid Angle Early Termination for Ambient Occlusion accelerates shadow ray traversal in sparse voxel structures by stopping traversal when a node subtends a solid angle below a specified threshold, effectively using a lower level-of-detail representation for distant points. Inputs: A sparse voxel structure (e.g., Sparse Voxel Octree or DAG); a shading point P; a cone angle threshold \theta{\text{thresh}}. Outputs: A traversal decision indicating whether to continue or terminate traversal for the current branch. Data Structures: The method operates on nodes of the sparse voxel hierarchy. Steps: 1. Project the node onto the unit hemisphere centered at P. 2. Calculate the solid angle \Omega subtended by the node. 3. If \Omega < \Omega{\text{thresh}}, stop traversal. 4. Otherwise, continue traversal to children or process the node. Formulas: The threshold is defined by a cone angle \theta{\text{thresh}}, where \Omega{\text{thresh}} = 2\pi(1 - \cos(\theta{\text{thresh}})). Parameters: Cone angle threshold: 9^\circ (corresponding to 0.07 sr). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method results in images that are darker than ground-truth because distant contributions are ignored. Despite the darkening, it maintains high quality for near-contact occlusion. Precision requirements are not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def shouldtraverse(node, pointP, thetathreshrad): # Vector from shading point to node center u = node.center - pointP distsq = dot(u, u) if distsq == 0: return True # Point inside node, always traverse dist = sqrt(distsq) # Project node onto unit hemisphere and calculate solid angle solidangle = computesolidanglebox(node, pointP) # Threshold in steradians omegathresh = 0.07 if solidangle < omegathresh: return False return True def computesolidanglebox(box, point): # Standard geometric calculation for solid angle of an AABB from a point # Implementation projects the 8 corners to the unit sphere and computes # the area of the resulting spherical polygon using the spherical excess formula. corners = [] hx, hy, hz = box.dimensions.x / 2, box.dimensions.y / 2, box.dimensions.z / 2 for dx in [-hx, hx]: for dy in [-hy, hy]: for dz in [-hz, hz]: corners.append(vec3(box.center.x + dx, box.center.y + dy, box.center.z + dz)) # Project to unit sphere unitcorners = [normalize(c - point) for c in corners] # Compute spherical polygon area (solid angle) by decomposing faces into triangles solidangle = 0.0 faces = [ (0, 1, 3, 2), (4, 5, 7, 6), (0, 1, 5, 4), (2, 3, 7, 6), (0, 2, 6, 4), (1, 3, 7, 5) ] for f in faces: v1, v2, v3, v4 = unitcorners[f[0]], unitcorners[f[1]], unitcorners[f[2]], unitcorners[f[3]] solidangle += solidangletriangle(v1, v2, v3) solidangle += solidangletriangle(v1, v3, v4) return abs(solidangle) def solidangletriangle(v1, v2, v3): # Oosterom and Strackee formula for solid angle of a triangle from origin u1, u2, u3 = normalize(v1), normalize(v2), normalize(v3) numerator = dot(u1, cross(u2, u3)) denominator = 1.0 + dot(u1, u2) + dot(u2, u3) + dot(u3, u1) return 2.0 atan2(numerator, denominator) Computes multiple scattering contributions in participating media by traversing an octree of volume samples to identify a "tree cut" of nodes that significantly influence a camera sample point. It addresses the computational cost of evaluating light transport from distant or less relevant volume samples by combining solid angle thresholds with phase function checks. It builds on Solid Angle Early Termination for Ambient Occlusion by extending early termination logic to higher-order scattering events. Time and Memory Complexity: The method reduces traversal time by skipping distant nodes. The DAG representation decreases total memory consumption compared to a sparse voxel octree due to a significant reduction in node counts. Measured Performance: In the SANMIGUEL scene, the method provides faster traversal speed for AO rays compared to full traversal. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Faster than standard traversal; maintains high quality for near-contact occlusion. Limitations: Results in images that are darker than ground-truth. When to Use: Use when performance is critical and slight darkening in distant areas is acceptable. The method was introduced in the context of high-resolution sparse voxel DAGs. It leverages the properties of the SVO and DAG scene representations to optimize shadow ray casting. name: Octree Subdivision for Multiple Scattering
body: This method computes multiple scattering contributions in participating media by traversing an octree of volume samples to identify a "tree cut" of nodes that significantly influence a camera sample point. It addresses the computational cost of evaluating light transport from distant or less relevant volume samples by combining solid angle thresholds with phase function checks. It builds on Solid Angle Early Termination for Ambient Occlusion by extending early termination logic to higher-order scattering events. Inputs: Camera sample position Pk. Camera ray direction \hat{o}. Octree cell C with center C.r and incoming light direction C.d. Volume sample positions vi associated with nodes in the hierarchy. Scattering coefficient \sigmas. Extinction coefficient \sigmai for each sample i. Phase function p(\cdot, \cdot). Precomputed multiple scattering table. Thresholds \epsilon1 and \epsilon2. Outputs: Multiple scattering contribution to the radiance at Pk in direction \hat{o}. Data Structures: Octree Cell: Contains center position C.r, incoming light direction C.d, references to child cells, and a reference to the volume sample vi stored at the leaf. Volume Sample: Contains position vi, intensity I{vi}, and extinction coefficient \sigmai. Steps: 1. Traverse the octree hierarchy starting from the root node. 2. For each cell C at sample point Pk, compute \mathbf{u} = Pk - C.r and \hat{u} = \mathbf{u}/\|\mathbf{u}\|. 3. Compute the solid angle \Omega(Pk, C) subtended by C at Pk. 4. Apply subdivision criteria: if \Omega(Pk, C) > \epsilon1, subdivide and process children. Else if \Omega(Pk, C) > \epsilon2 and (p(\hat{o}, \hat{u}) > \pi/4 or p(\hat{u}, C.d) > \pi/4), subdivide. Otherwise, add C to the tree cut. 5. For each node vi in the tree cut, compute double scattering using the formula: \text{double}(Pk) = \sigmas^2 \sum{vi} \frac{e^{-\sigmai ri} I{vi}}{ri^2} p(\hat{\alpha}, \hat{r}i) p(\hat{r}i, \hat{\alpha}{vi}) where \mathbf{r}i = Pk - vi, ri = \|\mathbf{r}i\|, \hat{r}i = \mathbf{r}i/ri, \hat{\alpha} = \hat{o}, and \hat{\alpha}{vi} = C.d. 6. Handle weak singularities caused by 1/ri^2 by clamping the denominator. 7. Use the same tree cut to compute higher-order multiple scattering via a precomputed table generated by Monte Carlo simulation of photon propagation in an infinite medium. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computemultiplescattering(Pk, ohat, octreeroot, epsilon1, epsilon2, sigmas, phasefunction, precomputedtable): treecut = [] def solidangle(cell, point): # Computes the solid angle subtended by the cell's bounding box at point # Standard geometric implementation omitted for brevity return 0.0 def traverse(node): uvec = Pk - node.center uhat = uvec / length(uvec) omega = solidangle(node, Pk) if omega > epsilon1: for child in node.children: traverse(child) elif omega > epsilon2: cond1 = phasefunction(ohat, uhat) > math.pi / 4 cond2 = phasefunction(uhat, node.incominglightdir) > math.pi / 4 if cond1 or cond2: for child in node.children: traverse(child) else: treecut.append(node.sample) else: treecut.append(node.sample) traverse(octreeroot) doublescattering = 0.0 for sample in treecut: rvec = Pk - sample.position rdist = length(rvec) rhat = rvec / rdist # Clamp denominator to handle weak singularities from 1/r^2 denom = max(rdist 2, 1e-6) term = (sigmas 2) (exp(-sample.extinction rdist) sample.intensity / denom) term = phasefunction(ohat, rhat) term = phasefunction(rhat, sample.incominglightdir) doublescattering += term return doublescattering Parameters: \epsilon1: Threshold for solid angle to force subdivision. \epsilon2: Secondary threshold for solid angle combined with phase function check. \sigmas: Scattering coefficient. \sigmai: Extinction coefficient for sample i. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Weak Singularities: The 1/ri^2 term in the double scattering formula can cause numerical instability when ri is very small. This is handled by clamping the denominator. Degenerate Input: If Pk coincides with a sample position, ri = 0. Clamping prevents division by zero. This variant focuses specifically on the double scattering component, computing only the first two scattering events (sample to Pk to camera) using the tree cut mechanism. It explicitly evaluates the 1/r^2 attenuation and phase functions for each node in the cut. The stopping criterion uses the solid angle sustained by the node from Pk and the phase function between the outgoing direction \hat{o} and the direction from Pk to the node center vi. The double scattering contribution is calculated as \text{double}(Pk) = \sigmas^2 \sum{vi} \frac{e^{-\sigmai ri} I{vi}}{ri^2} p(\hat{\alpha}, \hat{r}i) p(\hat{r}i, \hat{\alpha}{vi}). Weak singularities from 1/r^2 are handled by clamping. Time Complexity: Depends on the depth of the octree and the number of nodes in the tree cut; worst case traverses the entire tree, but solid angle and phase checks prune it significantly. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficiently approximates multiple scattering by ignoring distant or poorly oriented samples and reduces the number of expensive phase function and attenuation calculations. Limitations: Accuracy depends on the thresholds \epsilon1 and \epsilon2; poorly chosen thresholds can lead to over-subdivision or under-subdivision artifacts. When to Use: When simulating participating media with significant multiple scattering and performance is a concern. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from point-based rendering for homogeneous participating media with refractive boundaries. It extends the PBGI (Point-Based Global Illumination) approach to multiple scattering events. The tree cut mechanism is inspired by solid angle-based early termination techniques used in ambient occlusion. The precomputed table for higher-order scattering is generated via Monte Carlo simulation of photon propagation in an infinite medium. name: Zhukov Ambient Occlusion
head: Ambient Occlusion (Empirical Model), Geometric Obscurance, Obscurance
body: Zhukov Ambient Occlusion is an empirical local illumination model that simulates indirect lighting by computing the geometric obscurance of a surface point, representing how open the point is to the environment. It differs from radiosity by measuring the degree of occlusion (lack of secondary light) rather than the intensity of secondary reflections, making it computationally cheaper and aesthetically driven rather than physically correct. It builds on Ambient Occlusion via Shadow Rays by approximating the hemisphere integral of visibility weighted by the cosine of the incident angle. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Surface point x, surface normal n, scene geometry (for visibility queries). Output: Ambient Occlusion factor OA(x, n) \in [0, 1]. Data Structures: The visibility function V(x, \omega) is typically implemented via ray casting or ray marching. For a given direction \omega, it returns 1 if an occluder is found within a certain distance or range, and 0 otherwise. Formula: The ambient occlusion factor is defined as the integral over the hemisphere \Omega oriented with normal n centered at x: OA(x, n) = \frac{1}{\pi} \int{\Omega} V(x, \omega) |\omega \cdot n| d\omega Where: V(x, \omega) is the visibility function (1 if occluder found, 0 otherwise). |\omega \cdot n| is the absolute value of the dot product between the direction vector \omega and the normal n. Note: The original source notation uses a floor operator \lfloor \omega \cdot n \rfloor, but it is interpreted as the absolute value for consistency with standard hemisphere sampling formulations. \Omega is the hemisphere oriented with n centered at x. Parameters: OA(x, n) range: 0 to 1. A value of 1 denotes full occlusion (repressed), and 0 denotes no occluding geometry influencing the point. Steps: 1. For the surface point x and normal n, define the hemisphere \Omega of directions. 2. Sample directions \omega uniformly or quasi-randomly over \Omega. 3. For each direction \omega, cast a ray from x in direction \omega. 4. Determine V(x, \omega): If the ray intersects geometry within the scene, V(x, \omega) = 1. Otherwise, V(x, \omega) = 0. 5. Compute the dot product |\omega \cdot n|. 6. Estimate the integral using Monte Carlo integration: OA(x, n) \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} V(x, \omegai) |\omegai \cdot n| Where N is the number of samples. 7. Multiply the constant ambient term of the Phong model by (1 - OA(x, n)) to approximate global illumination effects. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The visibility function V(x, \omega) is binary in this basic model, leading to potential aliasing if not sampled sufficiently. The interpretation of the dot product term as absolute value is an assumption based on consultation with standard practices, as the original paper's use of a floor operator is unclear. Generalizes standard binary ambient occlusion by replacing the visibility function with a distance suitability function, providing a smooth gradient of darkening based on proximity. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples N and the cost of visibility queries (ray casting/marching). Memory Complexity: Low, as it typically computes values per vertex or pixel without storing large buffers, though results may be stored as vertex attributes or texture maps for later use. Strengths: Computationally cheaper than radiosity; aesthetically pleasing; simulates indirect illumination effects effectively for local geometry. Limitations: Not physically correct; ignores indirect bounces; considers only local geometry. When to use: When real-time or fast offline rendering is required, and aesthetic quality of local shadows/occlusion is prioritized over physical accuracy. When not to use: When physically accurate global illumination is required. The method was introduced by Zhukov et al. in [ZIK98] as an empirical ambient light illumination model aiming to achieve illumination effects of occlusion similar or correct up to a certain degree to those acquired from radiosity but in a shorter time period. It has been a basis for many other works, such as [IKSZ03] and [KL05], and has become quite popular in the movie industry under the influence of which it has undergone some refinement. Kontkanen et al. mention that ambient occlusion is considered a special case, a simplification of the model proposed by Zhukov et al.. name: Zhukov Obscurance
head: Ambient Occlusion (Zhukov et al.), Ambient Occlusion Approximation (Zhukov et al.), Distance Ambient Effect, Geometric Obscurance, Obscurance, Obscurance Illumination Model
body: Zhukov Obscurance is a local illumination approximation that attenuates ambient light based on the distance to the nearest occluding geometry, generalizing standard binary ambient occlusion by replacing the visibility function with a distance suitability function. Unlike standard ambient occlusion which yields a binary 0 or 1, this method provides a smooth gradient of darkening based on proximity, allowing for "Distance Ambient Effect" calculations. It is distinct from global illumination techniques as it ignores indirect bounces, considering only local geometry. Inputs: Surface point position x. Surface normal n. Distance to the first intersection d(x, \omega) for rays \omega in the hemisphere \Omega above n. Parameter \tau > 0 controlling decay rate. Ambient light intensity Ia. Diffuse reflectance ka(x). Outputs: Obscurance value W(x) \in [0, 1]. Final ambient intensity I(x). Data Structures: The method operates on scalar values derived from ray casting. No specific complex data structure is defined in the sources for the core formula, though implementation typically requires a ray-marching or ray-casting routine to determine d(x, \omega). Steps: 1. For the surface point x and normal n, sample directions \omega over the hemisphere \Omega defined by n. 2. For each direction \omega, cast a ray from x and determine d(x, \omega), the distance to the first intersection with any geometry. If no intersection is found, d(x, \omega) \to +\infty. 3. Compute the distance suitability \rho(d(x, \omega)) for each intersection distance. 4. Integrate the product of \rho(d(x, \omega)) and the cosine of the angle between \omega and n over the hemisphere, normalized by \pi. 5. Compute the final intensity using the ambient light and reflectance. Formulas: The obscurance value W(x, n) is defined as: W(x, n) = \frac{1}{\pi} \int{\Omega} \rho(d(x, \omega)) |\omega \cdot n| d\omega where: W(x, n) is the obscurance value, ranging from 0 (fully occluded) to 1 (fully open). \Omega is the hemisphere of directions above the surface normal n. \rho(d) is the distance suitability function. d(x, \omega) is the distance to the first intersection in direction \omega. The distance suitability function \rho(d) is typically modeled as: \rho(d) = 1 - e^{-\tau d} where: \tau is a positive parameter defining the decay rate. Properties of \rho(d): \rho(0) = 0 (fully occluded). \rho(+\infty) = 1 (fully open). \rho'(d) > 0 (monotonically increasing). \rho''(d) < 0 (monotonically decreasing derivative/smoothness). The final reflected intensity I(x) is calculated as: I(x) = Ia ka(x) W(x) where: Ia is the ambient light intensity. ka(x) is the diffuse reflectance for ambient light. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def zhukovobscurance(x, n, raycaster, tau): """ Computes Zhukov Obscurance for a surface point. Args: x: Point position (vec3). n: Surface normal (vec3). raycaster: Function that returns distance to first intersection for a ray origin and direction. Returns infinity if none. tau: Positive decay rate parameter. Returns: W: Obscurance value in [0, 1]. """ # Hemisphere sampling # In practice, this is approximated by Monte Carlo integration or # pre-computed lookup tables as noted in related works. # Here we show the conceptual integral evaluation. numsamples = 100 # Not given in sources; typical implementation detail integralsum = 0.0 for i in range(numsamples): # Sample direction omega in hemisphere above n omega = samplehemisphere(n) # Get distance to first intersection d = raycaster(x, omega) # Compute distance suitability rho(d) # rho(d) = 1 - exp(-tau d) # Handle infinity: if d is infinity, rho is 1 if d == float('inf'): rho = 1.0 else: rho = 1.0 - math.exp(-tau d) # Cosine term |omega. n| costheta = abs(dot(omega, n)) # Accumulate integral # Note: Monte Carlo integration divides by probability density. # For uniform hemisphere sampling, pdf = 1 / (2pi). # The formula has 1/pi. # Integral approx: (1/numsamples) sum(rho costheta) # To match 1/pi factor: sum(rho costheta) / numsamples (2pi) / pi # = sum(rho costheta) / numsamples 2 # However, standard MC for hemisphere integral of f(w) dw is: # (Area / N) sum(f(wi) / pdf(wi)) # Area of hemisphere = 2pi. pdf = 1/(2pi). # So factor is 2pi. # The formula is (1/pi) Integral. # So result = (1/pi) (2pi/N) sum(rho costheta) # = (2/N) sum(rho costheta) integralsum += rho costheta W = (2.0 / numsamples) integralsum # Clamp to [0, 1] to handle numerical errors W = max(0.0, min(1.0, W)) return W def computeambientintensity(x, n, raycaster, tau, Ia, ka): W = zhukovobscurance(x, n, raycaster, tau) I = Ia ka W return I Parameters: \tau: Positive parameter defining the decay rate. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The exponential function e^{-\tau d} may underflow for large d, resulting in \rho(d) \approx 1, which is correct behavior. Boundaries: If d=0, \rho(0)=0, correctly indicating full occlusion. Degenerate Input: The method does not account for indirect illumination, making it physically inaccurate for scenes where indirect light is significant. The broader category of techniques using Zhukov's obscurance model. Zhukov Obscurance is the specific illumination model within this family. Link Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples used to approximate the hemisphere integral. Each sample requires a ray intersection test. Memory Complexity: Low, as it computes values per point. Can be pre-computed and stored in texture maps or vertex attributes for static scenes. Strengths: Provides smooth, distance-based occlusion gradients; computationally efficient for static scenes if pre-computed; does not depend on light sources. Limitations: Not physically accurate as it ignores indirect illumination; only considers local geometry. When to use: When a smooth, distance-based ambient darkening is desired for static geometry, and performance is critical. When not to use: When physically accurate global illumination is required. Zhukov Obscurance was introduced by Zhukov, Iones, and Kronin in 1998. It was developed as an approximation for global illumination through occlusions, determining the occlusion of ambient light at interpolated points. The technique was later elaborated upon by Iones et al. in 2003, who defined the distance suitability function properties and the exponential decay model. It is used in computer graphics for simulating indirect illumination effects in real-time or pre-computed contexts. name: Spatially Cached Raytraced Ambient Occlusion
head: Spatial Hashing for Raytraced Ambient Occlusion
body:
Spatially Cached Raytraced Ambient Occlusion (SC-RTAO) is an optimization for raytraced ambient occlusion that stores accumulated occlusion values in spatial cells within a hashmap. Since ambient occlusion is view-independent, these values can be accumulated into a cell without reprojection when the camera moves, reducing redundant ray tracing for static geometry across frames. It distinguishes itself from naive RTAO by caching results to avoid redundant ray tracing, and from sibling methods like Evans AO or Zhukov AO by relying on spatial hashing and atomic accumulation rather than different sampling or approximation strategies. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Face position (facepos), face normal (normal), pixel coordinate (pixel), frame index (uniforms.frameindex), cell size, hash map parameters. Outputs: Updated hash map payloads (occlusion count and sample count); final AO value derived from the hash map in a separate shading pass. Data Structures: 1. spatialhashkey: A struct containing two 32-bit unsigned integers: hash (spatial hash key derived from position and normal) and checksum (checksum for collision verification). 2. hashpayloads: An array of 32-bit unsigned integers. The layout packs two 16-bit values: upper 16 bits store occlusioncount (number of rays that hit geometry), and lower 16 bits store raycount (total number of rays cast for this cell, typically VXAORAYSPERPIXEL). 3. hashchecksums: An array of 32-bit unsigned integers storing the checksum for each hash slot. 4. hashframes: An array of 32-bit unsigned integers storing the last frame index in which each hash slot was accessed. Parameters: VXAOHASHMASK: Mask for the hash map size (e.g., for 16 million elements, this is 0xFFFFFF if power-of-two, or specific mask for the chosen size). VXAOMAXCELLAGE: Maximum age (in frames) before a cell is considered expired. VXAOSAMPLELIMIT: Maximum number of samples allowed per hash cell before stopping accumulation. VXAORAYSPERPIXEL: Number of rays cast per pixel for the AO calculation. cellsize: Size of the spatial cell for hashing. Hash map size: 16 million elements (recommended to prevent running out of space during rapid camera movement at 4k resolutions). Steps: 1. Generate Key: Compute the spatial hash key from the face position and normal: key = makespatialhashkey(facepos, normal, cellsize). 2. Lookup/Insert: Call spatialhashfindorinsert(key) to find the index in the hash map. 3. Check Validity: If the returned index is 0xFFFFFFFF (not found/failed) or the current sample count in the payload exceeds VXAOSAMPLELIMIT, return immediately without casting rays. 4. Offset Ray Origin: Calculate the ray origin by offsetting the face position along the normal: pos = offsetray(facepos, normal). 5. Generate Frame Seed: Create a seed based on the current frame index to vary the sampling pattern across frames: 	ext{frame\seed} = (	ext{frame\index} 	imes 0x9E3779B9, 	ext{pcg}(	ext{frame\index} \oplus 0xA511E9B3)) 6. Generate Pixel Noise: Compute a 2D noise vector based on the pixel coordinate and frame seed: 	ext{pixel

Generate Key key = makespatialhashkey(facepos, normal, uniforms.cellsize) # 2. Lookup/Insert index = spatialhashfindorinsert(key, uniforms, hashchecksums, hashframes, hashpayloads) # 3. Check Validity currentraycount = hashpayloads[index] & 0xFFFF if index == 0xFFFFFFFF or currentraycount >= VXAOSAMPLELIMIT: return # 4. Offset Ray Origin pos = offsetray(facepos, normal) # 5. Atomic Update updatevalue = (occlusioncount << 16) | VXAORAYSPERPIXEL hashpayloads[index] += updatevalue def spatialhashfindorinsert(key, uniforms, hashchecksums, hashframes, hashpayloads): frame = uniforms.frameindex index = key.hash & VXAOHASHMASK for probe in range(VXAOHASHPROBECOUNT): # Simulate InterlockedCompareExchange: if slot is empty (0), claim it with key.checksum exchecksum = hashchecksums[index] if exchecksum == 0: hashchecksums[index] = key.checksum exchecksum = 0 if exchecksum == 0 or exchecksum == key.checksum: # Simulate InterlockedExchange for frame hashframes[index] = frame return index exframe = hashframes[index] # Check age if frame - exframe > VXAOMAXCELLAGE: # Simulate InterlockedExchange for checksum, payload, and frame hashchecksums[index] = key.checksum hashpayloads[index] = 0 hashframes[index] = frame return index # Linear probe index = (index + 1) & VXAOHASHMASK return 0xFFFFFFFF Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hash Map Saturation: At 4k resolutions, the algorithm may fail to find a free slot older than 20 frames if the hash map is too small. A size of 16 million elements is recommended to mitigate this. Atomic Overhead: The hashmap lookup involves multiple atomic operations (InterlockedCompareExchange, InterlockedExchange, InterlockedAdd), which add overhead compared to regular buffer reads. Register Allocation: Maintaining many float3 variables during the computation can bloat register allocation, reducing shader occupancy (e.g., from ~40% to ~20% in some implementations). Time Complexity: Hash map lookup is O(1) average case but with a high constant factor due to atomic operations and potential linear probing. Ray casting scales linearly with the number of rays per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(M) where M is the hash map size (16 million elements). Requires storage for hashpayloads, hashchecksums, and hashframes. Measured Performance: On a Macbook Air (M2) with the Sponza scene at 4k resolution: Baseline RTAO: 39.04 FPS (46.16 ms). With SC-RTAO (Cell size 5->10): 71.73 FPS (23.50 ms), a ~83.72% improvement. Further optimizations (checkerboard update, rasterized brick coordinates) pushed FPS to ~72.00 (19.33 ms). Strengths: Significant performance improvement in static or slowly moving scenes by avoiding redundant ray tracing. View-independent accumulation allows for smooth camera movement without reprojection artifacts. Limitations: High memory usage for the hash map. Atomic operations can become a bottleneck. Performance degrades if the camera moves rapidly, causing frequent cache misses and overwrites. Precision issues with float3 can impact shader occupancy. When to Use: Scenes with significant static geometry where AO is a major performance bottleneck. When Not to Use: Highly dynamic scenes with rapid camera movement or frequent geometry changes, as the cache invalidation overhead may negate benefits. Spatially Cached Raytraced Ambient Occlusion was introduced in August 2026 as an optimization for a voxel raytracer, documented in the "Voxel Raytracer Devlog" by the author of the nelari.us blog. The method was added in commit 4a6c4b7 to address performance issues in the RTAO hashmap update pass. It builds on the concept of spatial hashing for raytraced ambient occlusion, leveraging the view-independence of AO to cache results across frames. name: Lookup Table Shadow Rendering
head: One-pass Shadow with Lookup Tables, Shadow Rendering, VolPack Shadow Algorithm
body: Lookup Table Shadow Rendering is a fast, one-pass shadowing technique implemented within the VolPack volume rendering system. It solves the problem of computing shadows for participating media efficiently by precomputing shadow contributions into lookup tables, avoiding the per-voxel ray casting overhead of standard shadow ray methods. Unlike Shadow Ray Casting, which evaluates visibility per sample or per voxel via explicit integration, this method accelerates the process by mapping shadow conditions to pre-calculated values, trading flexibility for speed. The method relies on the VolPack API to configure and execute the shadow pass. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset (voxels), light source parameters, and rendering context. Output: A rendered image with shadows applied to the volume. Data Structures: Lookup Table: The specific layout of the lookup table is not defined in the sources. It is implied to store shadow factors or transmittance values indexed by depth or density. VolPack Context: A state structure managed by the VolPack library. Steps: 1. Initialize VolPack Context: Create and configure the VolPack rendering context. 2. Configure Shadow Lookup Shader: Call vpSetShadowLookupShader to define how shadows are computed using lookup tables. The specific parameters for this function are detailed in the VolPack man page. 3. Set Image Buffer: Declare the array where the result will be stored using vpSetImage. python def setimagebuffer(context, imagearray, width, height, bytesperscan, pixeltype): """Declares the array that VolPack should store the image into.""" # vpSetImage(vpc, image, width, height, bytesperscan, pixeltype) context.imagebuffer = imagearray context.imagewidth = width context.imageheight = height context.bytesperscan = bytesperscan context.pixeltype = pixeltype 4. Render: Execute the rendering pass. VolPack internally uses the lookup table to apply shadow factors to the volume data. Formulas: The transparency of the fog (which is modulated by shadowing) is calculated as: T = front\factor \cdot \exp(-density \cdot depth) Where: T is the transparency of the fog. front\factor is a scaling factor (1.0 or larger to brighten the foreground). density controls the "density" of the fog, determining how rapidly objects recede into darkness. depth is the distance from the front plane of the viewing volume (0 at the front, 1 at the back). Each voxel color component is multiplied by the fog transparency T during rendering. Parameters: Density: Controls fog density. Typical values are not specified. Front Factor: Typically 1.0, but can be larger to brighten the foreground. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The exact implementation details of the lookup table generation and indexing are not provided in the sources. Precision issues related to the lookup table resolution are not discussed. A shadowing algorithm that casts rays from a light source to each voxel to determine if it is in shadow, darkening the voxel index accordingly. It is distinct from Lookup Table Shadow Rendering as it performs explicit ray casting per voxel rather than using precomputed tables. Choose this method when explicit control over voxel-level shadowing is required and performance constraints are less critical than in large-scale volume rendering. Steps: 1. Iterate x from 0 to xsize-1, y from 0 to ysize-1, and z from 0 to zsize-1. 2. Retrieve the current voxel's palette index: voxel = getvoxelpal(x, y, z). 3. If the voxel is not empty (voxel != 0), cast a ray from the light position (lx, ly, lz) to the voxel position (x, y, z) using throwraytopos. Let the result be (hx, hy, hz, i), where i is the index of the first non-empty voxel hit along the ray. 4. If the ray hit a voxel (i \neq 0), darken the current voxel by subtracting depth: voxel = voxel - depth. 5. Write the modified voxel index back: setvoxelpal(x, y, z, voxel). Parameters: lx, ly, lz: The world coordinates of the light source. depth: The amount to darken the voxel index if in shadow, typically between 1 and 32. xsize, ysize, zsize: The dimensions of the current level in voxels. Pitfalls: The voxel index must not drop below the lower bound of its tone group. Calculate colormargin = math.floor((voxel-1)/32)32 + 1. If voxel < colormargin, clamp it to colormargin. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The lookup table approach is described as "fast" and "one-pass". Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The lookup table size is not specified. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Fast, one-pass shadowing for volume rendering. Limitations: Limited flexibility due to the use of lookup tables; specific implementation details are opaque. When to use: When rendering volumes with VolPack and performance is a priority. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from the VolPack volume rendering system. VolPack is a software library for volume rendering that provides this shadowing technique. The Voxel Shadow Raycasting variant originates from the Doommy voxel engine, an unofficial CPU-based renderer. VolPack User's Guide, http://www-graphics.stanford.edu/software/volpack/vpuserguide.html, fetched 2026-10-28 jabberx/doommy, https://github.com/jabberx/doommy, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Recursive Ray Tracing
head: Higher-order Rays, Secondary Ray Shooting, Whitted shading, Whitted-style Ray Tracing
body: Recursive Ray Tracing extends basic ray casting by handling diffuse reflection, specular reflection, and transmission (refraction) through the recursive tracing of rays upon intersection with objects. It solves the problem of limited visual realism in simple ray casting by adding global illumination effects such as shadows, reflections, and refractions, distinguishing itself from its parent Shadow Ray Casting by explicitly generating secondary rays for surface interactions rather than just testing visibility for shadowing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A camera ray (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}), a scene description containing a list of geometric primitives, material properties for each primitive (diffuse, specular, transmission coefficients, refractive index \eta), and a maximum recursion depth D{max}. Output: A final color value \mathbf{C} for the pixel associated with the input ray. Data Structures: Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized). Intersection: Contains the hit point \mathbf{p}, the surface normal \mathbf{n}, the intersected object reference, and the distance t from the ray origin. Material: Contains flags for specular/transmission properties, color/albedo, and refractive index \eta. Numbered Steps: 1. Primary Ray Intersection: Trace the primary ray from the camera into the scene. Find the closest intersection point \mathbf{p} with any primitive. If no intersection is found, return the background color. 2. Shadow Ray Casting (Visibility): For each light source, construct a shadow ray from \mathbf{p} towards the light source. The maximum distance for this ray is the distance between \mathbf{p} and the light source. If another primitive intersects this shadow ray before reaching the light, the visibility factor Vi is 0 (shadow); otherwise, it is 1. 3. Diffuse Shading: Calculate the diffuse contribution using the surface normal \mathbf{n}, the view direction, and the incident light direction \mathbf{l}. The contribution is proportional to the dot product \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l} and the light intensity. 4. Specular Reflection: If the material has specular properties, compute the ideal reflection direction \mathbf{r} using the incident direction \mathbf{d}{in} and normal \mathbf{n}: \mathbf{r} = 2.0 (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}{in}) \mathbf{n} - \mathbf{d}{in} Trace a new ray in direction \mathbf{r} recursively. 5. Transmission (Refraction): If the material has transmission properties, compute the refraction direction using Snell's law. Determine if the ray is entering or exiting the medium by checking \mathbf{d}{in} \cdot \mathbf{n}. If exiting (\mathbf{d}{in} \cdot \mathbf{n} < 0), flip the normal (\mathbf{n} = -\mathbf{n}) and invert the refractive index ratio (\eta = 1.0 / \eta). 6. Refracted Direction Calculation: Compute the discriminant k: k = 1.0 - \eta^2 (1.0 - (\mathbf{d}{in} \cdot \mathbf{n})^2) If k < 0, total internal reflection occurs; compute the reflection direction instead. If k \ge 0, the refracted direction \mathbf{t} is: \mathbf{t} = \eta \mathbf{d}{in} + (\eta (\mathbf{d}{in} \cdot \mathbf{n}) - \sqrt{k}) \mathbf{n} Trace a new ray in direction \mathbf{t} recursively. 7. Recursion and Termination: Recursively call the ray tracing function for the new rays (reflection/refraction). The recursion stops if the current depth exceeds D{max} or if the contribution of the ray becomes negligible. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def traceray(rayorigin, raydirection, scene, depth, maxdepth): """ Recursively trace a ray and compute color. rayorigin: (x, y, z) tuple raydirection: (x, y, z) tuple, normalized scene: dict with keys 'shapes', 'lights', 'bgcolor' depth: int, current recursion depth maxdepth: int, maximum allowed recursion depth """ # Base case: max depth reached or no intersection intersection = scene.getclosestintersection(rayorigin, raydirection) if intersection is None or depth >= maxdepth: return scene.bgcolor p, normal, material = intersection.point, intersection.normal, intersection.material color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # 1. Diffuse Shading & Shadow Rays for light in scene.lights: lightdir = normalize(light.position - p) shadoworigin = add(p, scale(normal, 1e-4)) shadowray = (shadoworigin, lightdir) shadowhit = scene.getclosestintersection(shadowray[0], shadowray[1], maxt=distance(p, light.position)) visibility = 0.0 if shadowhit is not None else 1.0 if visibility > 0: dotproduct = dot(normal, lightdir) if dotproduct > 0: diffuseterm = scale(material.diffusecolor, light.intensity dotproduct) color = add(color, scale(diffuseterm, visibility)) # 2. Specular Reflection if material.hasspecular: reflectiondir = add(scale(normal, 2.0 dot(normal, raydirection)), scale(raydirection, -1.0)) reflorigin = add(p, scale(normal, 1e-4)) reflectedcolor = traceray(reflorigin, reflectiondir, scene, depth + 1, maxdepth) color = add(color, scale(material.specularcolor, reflectedcolor)) # 3. Transmission (Refraction) if material.hastransmission: cosi = dot(scale(raydirection, -1.0), normal) entering = cosi > 0.0 n = normal eta = material.refractiveindex if not entering: n = scale(normal, -1.0) eta = 1.0 / eta cosi = dot(scale(raydirection, -1.0), n) k = 1.0 - eta eta (1.0 - cosi cosi) if k < 0.0: refractdir = add(scale(n, 2.0 dot(n, raydirection)), scale(raydirection, -1.0)) else: refractdir = add(scale(raydirection, eta), scale(n, eta cosi - math.sqrt(k))) refractorigin = add(p, scale(n, 1e-4)) refractedcolor = traceray(refractorigin, refractdir, scene, depth + 1, maxdepth) color = add(color, scale(material.transmissioncolor, refractedcolor)) return color def add(a, b): return (a[0]+b[0], a[1]+b[1], a[2]+b[2]) def scale(v, s): return (v[0]s, v[1]s, v[2]s) def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def normalize(v): l = math.sqrt(dot(v, v)) return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l) def distance(a, b): return math.sqrt(dot((a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1], a[2]-b[2]), (a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1], a[2]-b[2]))) Parameters: Recursion Depth (D{max}): A pre-defined level limiting ray tracing, as contribution diminishes with each level. Recursion may also stop if the contribution is too small. Refractive Index (\eta): Ratio of speeds of light in two media. Default refraction ratio is 0.75, which is inverted to 1.5 when the ray exits a medium. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Total Internal Reflection: Occurs when the discriminant in Snell's law is negative. Must be handled by switching to reflection. Precision Errors: Intersection points \mathbf{p} may cause self-intersection artifacts. An epsilon offset along the normal is typically required. Infinite Recursion: If the scene contains mirrors facing each other, recursion may not terminate naturally. A depth limit is a standard stopping condition. A GPU-friendly implementation that replaces function calls with an explicit loop to compute ray color, reducing register pressure and shader inlining overhead. Time Complexity: Exponential in the worst case (O(b^d) where b is branching factor and d is depth) due to recursive branching for reflections and refractions. Memory Complexity: Linear in recursion depth O(d) for the call stack. Strengths: Produces highly realistic images with accurate reflections, refractions, and shadows. Simple to implement for basic scenes. Limitations: Computationally expensive for deep recursion. Does not handle diffuse inter-reflection (global illumination) natively without extensions like path tracing. When to use: Realistic rendering of scenes with glossy/specular surfaces and transparent objects. When not to use: Scenes requiring soft global illumination or complex diffuse bounces (use Path Tracing instead). Recursive Ray Tracing was introduced as an extension to basic ray casting to add visual cues like shadows, reflections, and refractions. It is often referred to as Whitted-style ray tracing after Turner Whitted's seminal 1980 paper, which formalized the recursive approach for specular and transparent surfaces. It builds on Shadow Ray Casting by adding the generation of secondary rays for surface interactions. name: Iterative Ray Tracing
head: Bounce-Level Ray Looping, Iterative Ray Color Calculation, Non-recursive Ray Tracing
body: Iterative Ray Tracing is a GPU-friendly implementation of recursive ray tracing that replaces function calls with an explicit loop to compute ray color. It solves the problem of limited or absent recursion support in GPU shading languages like GLSL, while reducing register pressure and shader inlining overhead by consolidating ray tracer calls into a single loop per bounce level. It builds on Recursive Ray Tracing. Inputs: r: Current ray (origin, direction). O: Set of objects in the scene. b: Remaining bounce count (integer). sec\rays: Number of secondary rays to spawn per bounce (typically 1 or 2, stored in sphereRays). Outputs: color: The computed radiance/color for the ray. Data Structures: sphereRays: An array storing 1 or 2 rays per bounce level. c: Accumulator for material color, initialized to 1 (identity for Hadamard product). Formulas: Hadamard Product (\circ): Element-wise multiplication of vectors/matrices of same dimensions. (a, c, e) \circ (b, d, f) = (ab, cd, ef). Ray Point: p = \text{origin}(r) + t \cdot \text{direction}(r), where t is the intersection distance. Steps: 1. Initialize accumulator c \leftarrow 1. 2. Enter an infinite loop. 3. Check if b < 0. If true, return 0. 4. Find object o \in O with minimum intersection distance t > 0 from current ray r. o \leftarrow \arg \min{o \in O} \{ t \mid t = \text{intersection test}(r, o) \land t > 0 \}. 5. If no object is hit (o = \emptyset), return \text{bg}(r) \circ c, where \text{bg}(r) is the background color. 6. Compute intersection point p using r and t. 7. Compute valid bounce direction d at p on object o given incoming ray r. 8. Update ray r \leftarrow \text{ray}(p, d). 9. Update accumulator c \leftarrow c \circ \text{color material}(p, o). 10. Decrement b (implicit in the loop structure for next iteration, or handled by loop counter). 11. Repeat from step 2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def iterativeraycolor(r, O, b, secrays): c = 1 # Accumulator initialized to identity for Hadamard product while True: if b < 0: return 0 # No more bounces allowed # Find closest intersection o = None mint = infinity for obj in O: t = intersectiontest(r, obj) if t > 0 and t < mint: mint = t o = obj if o is None: # No hit: return background color modulated by accumulated material color return backgroundcolor(r) c # Using to denote Hadamard product as per # Compute intersection point t = intersectiontest(r, o) p = r.origin + t r.direction # Compute bounce direction d = validbouncedir(p, o, r) # Update ray for next iteration r = Ray(p, d) # Accumulate material color c = c materialcolor(p, o) # Hadamard product # Decrement bounce counter b = b - 1 Parameters: secrays: Number of secondary rays per bounce. Typically 1 or 2. b: Maximum bounce depth. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Recursion Limit: GPUs like GLSL do not support recursion, necessitating this iterative approach. Register Pressure: By inlining only 2 walks per level and looping over sphereRays, register usage is reduced compared to recursive inlining of 6 grid walks. Background Color: If no object is hit, the background color is returned, modulated by the accumulated material color. The parent method using function calls. Choose iterative when GPU recursion is unsupported or register pressure is high. Recursive Ray Tracing A simpler form of ray tracing for shadows. Iterative ray tracing generalizes this to full global illumination with multiple bounces. Shadow Ray Casting Time Complexity: Linear in the number of bounces b and the number of objects O per bounce. Total complexity O(b \cdot |O|). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per ray, excluding the scene structure O. Performance: Reduces shader inlining overhead by consolidating calls. In one implementation, inlining 2 walks per level (vs 6 in recursive) held fewer registers, improving performance. Strengths: Compatible with GPU languages lacking recursion; reduced register pressure; easier to maintain than multiple hardcoded bounce functions. Limitations: Fixed maximum bounce depth; less flexible than recursive for varying bounce counts per ray. When to Use: GPU implementations of ray tracing where recursion is unsupported or problematic. When Not to Use: CPU implementations where recursion is efficient and flexible; scenes requiring highly variable bounce depths. Iterative Ray Tracing was developed as a practical solution for implementing global illumination on GPUs, specifically in GLSL, which lacks recursion support. It was adopted as the most common method to avoid the maintenance burden of defining separate functions for each bounce level. It is used in real-time ray tracing applications and educational implementations of global illumination. name: Soft Shadows via Area Lights
head: Area Light Shadow Sampling, Area Light Shadows, Partial Occlusion, Shadow Occlusion
body: This method models shadows cast by light sources with spatial extent, allowing points in space to be partially occluded, unlike point sources which cast sharp shadows. It differs from its parent Shadow Ray Casting by replacing the single boolean visibility test with an integration over the light source area to compute natural soft shadows with penumbra. Inputs: Point \mathbf{p} in the volume or on the surface. Light source geometry defining an area A. Volume density field (for participating media) or distance field (for solid geometry). Number of samples N for the light source area. Outputs: Shadow factor S \in [0, 1] representing the fraction of the light source visible from \mathbf{p}. Data Structures: Light source area representation: A parametric surface or a set of sample points \{\mathbf{l}i\}{i=1}^N distributed over A. Volume sampler: Provides extinction coefficient \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) or distance to nearest surface d(\mathbf{x}). Steps: 1. Sample the Light Source: Generate N sample points \mathbf{l}i uniformly (or according to a distribution) over the light source area A. 2. Cast Shadow Rays: For each sample \mathbf{l}i, cast a shadow ray from \mathbf{p} towards \mathbf{l}i. 3. Evaluate Visibility: If using a distance field (solid geometry): Compute the distance di from \mathbf{p} to the nearest surface along the direction \mathbf{v}i = \mathbf{l}i - \mathbf{p}. If di < \|\mathbf{l}i - \mathbf{p}\|, the sample is occluded. If using a volume density field: Compute the transmittance Ti from \mathbf{p} to \mathbf{l}i using the method from Shadow Ray Casting. 4. Accumulate Shadow Factor: S = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} Vi where Vi = 1 if the sample is unoccluded, and Vi = 0 (or Ti) if occluded. 5. Apply Shadow Factor: Modulate the direct illumination contribution by S. Parameters: N: Number of samples. Typical values range from 4 to 64 depending on desired quality and performance. Higher N reduces noise but increases cost. Edge Cases: Small Light Sources: If the light source is small relative to the distance, N may need to be increased to avoid aliasing. Large Light Sources: If the light source is very large, the shadow factor approaches 1, and soft shadows become negligible. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise when \mathbf{p} is very close to the light source or occluding geometry. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computearealightshadow(p, lightsamples, distancefield): """ Computes soft shadow factor for point p given light samples and a distance field. Args: p: Point in space (tuple of 3 floats). lightsamples: List of sample points on the light source area (list of tuples of 3 floats). distancefield: Object with method query(origin, direction) returning distance to nearest surface. Returns: Shadow factor S in [0, 1]. """ nsamples = len(lightsamples) if nsamples == 0: return 1.0 visiblecount = 0.0 for l in lightsamples: direction = (l[0] - p[0], l[1] - p[1], l[2] - p[2]) disttolight = math.sqrt(direction[0]2 + direction[1]2 + direction[2]2) if disttolight < 1e-6: visiblecount += 1.0 continue unitdir = (direction[0] / disttolight, direction[1] / disttolight, direction[2] / disttolight) # Standard distance field ray marcher query disttosurface = distancefield.query(p, unitdir) # If the surface is closer than the light, the sample is occluded if disttosurface < disttolight: visiblecount += 0.0 else: visiblecount += 1.0 return visiblecount / nsamples This method generates soft shadows from area light sources by tracing coherent packets of shadow rays from primary ray hit points to samples on the light source. It differs from hard shadow casting by enabling smooth transitions between shadowed and unshadowed regions, providing visual cues about object positioning. Unlike rasterization-based impostor approaches, this technique integrates global effects easily due to its ray tracing basis. A shader function that applies shadow rays from surface points to a point light, handling plane intersections and soft shadows via Gaussian filtering. It differs from its parent Soft Shadows via Area Lights by modeling a single point source rather than an area, and from Soft Shadows via Ray Tracing by using a specific plane-intersection refinement and post-process Gaussian blur rather than direct area-light sampling. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of light samples and M is the number of steps per shadow ray. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per sample. Strengths: Produces physically plausible soft shadows with penumbra. Works well with dynamic geometry. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to multiple shadow rays per point. Noise can appear with low sample counts. When to use: When realistic soft shadows are required and performance allows for multiple shadow rays. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and hard shadows are acceptable, or when the light source is effectively a point source. The concept of soft shadows arises from the observation that real-world light sources have spatial extent, leading to partial occlusion and penumbra. Early implementations in rasterization used distance-based low-pass filters on shadow maps. In ray tracing, the approach of sampling the light source area instead of performing a single boolean test was introduced to achieve more natural appearing soft shadows. This method is particularly relevant in volume rendering and raymarching, where distance fields can be used to approximate soft shadows efficiently. name: Soft Shadows via Ray Tracing
head: Packet-based Soft Shadow Ray Tracing
body: This method generates soft shadows from area light sources by tracing coherent packets of shadow rays from primary ray hit points to samples on the light source. It differs from hard shadow casting by enabling smooth transitions between shadowed and unshadowed regions, providing visual cues about object positioning. Unlike rasterization-based impostor approaches, this technique integrates global effects easily due to its ray tracing basis. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Primary ray hit points (P), area light source geometry (defined by a set of samples or a parametric surface), and a user-defined number of shadow rays (N) per hit point. Output: Shadow factor (visibility) for each hit point, resulting in soft shadow boundaries. Data Structures: Ray Packet: A structure containing N rays sharing a common origin P. Each ray i (0 \le i < N) has a direction vector \vec{d}i pointing towards a specific sample Li on the area light source. Layout: origin (3 floats), directions (array of N vectors, each 3 floats). Steps: 1. Generate Shadow Ray Packets: For each primary ray hit point P, generate N shadow rays. Each ray i connects P to a sample Li on the area light source. The direction \vec{d}i is calculated as: \vec{d}i = \frac{Li - P}{\|Li - P\|} where Li is the position of the i-th sample on the light source. 2. Traverse Shadow Rays: Traverse the generated shadow rays in a manner identical to primary ray packets. Since all rays in the packet share the common origin P, they can be processed together using coherent traversal logic. 3. Evaluate Occlusion: For each ray i in the packet, determine if it intersects any occluder in the scene before reaching Li. 4. Compute Shadow Factor: The shadow factor for hit point P is the ratio of unoccluded rays to the total number of rays N. If k rays are unoccluded, the factor is k/N. Parameters: Number of shadow rays (N): Controls the quality of the soft shadow. Higher N yields smoother shadows but increases computational cost. Controlled interactively by the user. Light Source Size: The spatial extent of the area light source. Larger sources produce softer shadows. Controlled interactively by the user. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: When P is very close to the light source, numerical instability may occur in direction calculation. Degenerate Input: If the light source has no samples or N=0, the method fails. Generates soft shadows by organizing shadow rays into coherent packets to maintain traversal efficiency. It builds on this method by specifically structuring the rays for optimized traversal. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot T), where N is the number of shadow rays per hit point and T is the cost of traversing the scene for one ray. The coherent traversal of packets may reduce T due to cache efficiency. Memory Complexity: O(N) per hit point to store the ray packet. Performance: Performance depends heavily on the number of shadow rays and the complexity of the scene. The coherent traversal approach improves efficiency compared to independent shadow rays. Strengths: Easy integration of global effects; smooth shadow transitions; interactive control over quality/performance trade-off. Limitations: Computationally expensive for high N; requires ray tracing infrastructure. When to use: When soft shadows from area lights are required and ray tracing is available. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and N must be very low, or when hard shadows suffice. This method is part of the broader field of ray tracing for volume rendering and light transport. It was discussed in the context of coherent grid traversal approaches for visualizing particle data, where soft shadows were generated to enhance visual quality. The approach leverages the inherent flexibility of ray tracing to handle complex lighting effects that are difficult to implement in rasterization systems. name: Soft Shadows via Ray Packets
head: Area Light Shadows, Ray Packet Soft Shadows, Soft Shadows via Coherent Shadow Rays, Soft Shadows with Ray Packets
body: Soft Shadows via Ray Packets generates soft shadows from area light sources by creating packets of coherent shadow rays. This method leverages the ray tracing basis of the underlying system to support global illumination effects that are difficult to implement in rasterization-based pipelines. It differs from hard shadow casting by tracing secondary ray packets from primary ray hit points to multiple samples on an area light source, producing smooth transitions between shadowed and unshadowed regions that provide visual cues about relative object positioning. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Primary ray hit point on a surface or particle; area light source definition; scene geometry (particle dataset); grid structure for traversal. Output: Shadow visibility factor for the primary ray, used to modulate local illumination. Data Structures: Shadow Ray Packet: A collection of N \times N shadow rays sharing a common origin at the primary ray hit point. Each ray is defined by its origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Area Light Samples: N \times N points distributed over the area light source. The light source area is specified as 5% of the solid angle subtended by the bounding box of the scene. One source notes the area as 5% of the bounding box area instead. Numbered Steps: 1. Shadow Ray Generation: For each primary ray that intersects a surface or particle, generate a packet of coherent shadow rays by connecting the hit point to N \times N samples on the area light source. The direction \mathbf{d}i for each shadow ray i is calculated as: \mathbf{d}i = \frac{\mathbf{l}i - \mathbf{o}}{\|\mathbf{l}i - \mathbf{o}\|} where \mathbf{o} is the hit point and \mathbf{l}i is the i-th sample point on the area light. 2. Packet Traversal: Trace the secondary ray packet through the scene using the modified Coherent Grid Traversal (CGT) algorithm. Because all rays in the packet share a common origin, they exhibit high spatial coherence, allowing them to traverse the grid identically to primary ray packets. 3. Shadow Determination: For each ray in the packet, traverse the grid to determine if it intersects any occluding geometry before reaching the light source. 4. Shading: Modulate the local illumination (e.g., simple Lambertian shading) by the computed shadow visibility. Parameters: Packet Size (N \times N): Tested sizes are 2x2 (4 rays), 4x4 (16 rays), and 8x8 (64 rays). The number of shadow ray samples is interactively controlled by the user to permit performance-for-quality trade-offs. Light Source Area: 5% of the solid angle subtended by the bounding box of the scene. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coherence Dependency: Interactive performance with soft shadows depends heavily on the coherence exhibited by secondary ray packets. Performance Scaling: The performance impact is sublinear in the number of shadow rays traced, but large packets can still cause significant frame rate degradation. Light Size: The tested configurations use a large light source area, which affects the angular spread of shadow rays. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesoftshadow(hitpoint, lightsamples, grid, particles): """ Compute soft shadow factor for a primary ray hit point using ray packets. Args: hitpoint (Vector3): Origin of the shadow ray packet. lightsamples (List[Vector3]): NN sample points on the area light. grid (Grid): The coherent grid structure for traversal. particles (List[Particle]): The particle dataset. Returns: float: Shadow factor (0.0 to 1.0). """ numrays = len(lightsamples) occludedcount = 0 for lightsample in lightsamples: # Calculate shadow ray direction direction = lightsample - hitpoint direction = direction / length(direction) # Trace shadow ray using modified CGT # Returns True if the ray is occluded before reaching the light isoccluded = traceshadowray(hitpoint, direction, grid, particles) if isoccluded: occludedcount += 1 # Shadow factor is the ratio of unoccluded rays shadowfactor = 1.0 - (occludedcount / numrays) return shadowfactor def traceshadowray(origin, direction, grid, particles): """ Trace a single shadow ray through the grid to check for occlusion. Uses the modified CGT algorithm for coherent traversal. """ # Initialize traversal state currentcell = grid.getcellat(origin) # Traverse grid cells along the ray direction while not rayreacheslight(origin, direction): # Check for particle intersections in current cell for particle in currentcell.particles: # Standard ray-primitive intersection test if raysphereintersect(origin, direction, particle): return True # Occluded # Move to next cell using CGT traversal logic nextcell = grid.getnextcell(origin, direction, currentcell) if nextcell is None: break currentcell = nextcell return False # Not occluded def rayreacheslight(origin, direction): """Check if the ray has traveled far enough to reach the light source.""" # Standard distance check based on light bounds return dot(origin, direction) > LIGHTDISTANCETHRESHOLD def raysphereintersect(origin, direction, particle): """Standard ray-sphere intersection test.""" # Standard geometric intersection calculation return True # Placeholder for standard intersection logic Time and Memory Complexity: Time Complexity: The performance impact is sublinear in the number of shadow rays traced due to packet coherence. Memory Complexity: Memory usage depends on the grid structure and particle storage, similar to primary ray casting. No additional significant memory is required for the shadow rays themselves beyond the packet storage. Measured Performance: Performance was measured on a test machine with 16 threads, rendering 1024x1024 images. Frame rates for various datasets and shadow settings are as follows: | Dataset | No shadows | 2x2 (4 rays) | 4x4 (16 rays) | 8x8 (64 rays) | |-------------|------------|--------------|---------------|---------------| | Cylinder | 100.20 fps | 14.91 fps | 10.47 fps | 5.34 fps | | JP8 | 99.88 fps | 16.31 fps | 12.21 fps | 6.65 fps | | Bullet | 126.93 fps | 19.55 fps | 13.69 fps | 6.56 fps | | Thunder | 40.86 fps | 14.07 fps | 10.74 fps | 6.45 fps | | Foam | 14.34 fps | 4.38 fps | 2.51 fps | 1.17 fps | | BulletTorso | 18.30 fps | 7.39 fps | 6.09 fps | 3.82 fps | The performance degradation ranges from a factor of 2.42 (for 2x2 packets) to 19.35 (for 8x8 packets). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Integrates easily into ray tracing-based visualization systems; provides smooth, realistic shadows; performance impact is sublinear in the number of shadow rays; user-controllable quality/performance trade-off. Limitations: Performance is highly dependent on ray coherence; large packets can significantly reduce frame rates; not suitable for real-time applications requiring high frame rates with large shadow packets. When to Use: Use when soft shadows are needed for visual clarity in particle-based simulations and interactive performance is acceptable with moderate packet sizes (e.g., 2x2 or 4x4). Avoid when high frame rates are critical and large shadow packets are required, or when ray coherence is low. Origin: The method was introduced in the referenced papers on coherent grid traversal for particle visualization. The work extends the modified Coherent Grid Traversal (CGT) algorithm to support soft shadows via ray packets. History and Development: The technique builds on previous research in coherent ray tracing and grid traversal for particle visualization. The specific approach of using ray packets for soft shadows leverages the coherence of shadow rays sharing a common origin to maintain traversal efficiency. Applications: The method is used in interactive visualization systems for particle-based simulation data, such as fluid dynamics and molecular dynamics simulations, where soft shadows provide important visual cues about object positioning and depth. A coherent grid traversal approach to visualizing particle-based simulation data, https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/4293019/, fetched 2026-10-25 A Coherent Grid Traversal Approach to Visualizing Particle..., https://www.sci.utah.edu/~thiago/papers/pcgtrevised.pdf, fetched 2026-10-25

name: Point Light Shadow Shader
body: A shader function that applies shadow rays from surface points to a point light, handling plane intersections and soft shadows via Gaussian filtering. Inputs: rays: A Rays object containing origins (N, 3), dirs (N, 3), and distmax. rb: A render buffer object containing hit (N, bool), depth (N, 1), xyz (N, 3), normal (N, 3), and rgb (N, 4). pipeline: An object with a tracer method and a nef (neural implicit field) representation. pointlight: Position of the point light, default [1.5, 4.5, 1.5]. miny: Location of the xz plane, default -2.0. rate: Scalar divisor for plane intersection calculation, definition not given in the sources. Data Structures: Rays: Contains origins, dirs, distmin, distmax. rb (Render Buffer): Contains boolean hit, float depth, float xyz, float normal, float rgb. Steps: 1. Compute delta: \delta = \text{rays.origins}[:, 1] - \text{min\y}. 2. Compute plane parameter: t = \delta / \text{rate}. 3. Identify potential plane hits: planehit is True where t > 0 and t < 500. 4. Refine planehit: planehit = planehit & (t < \text{rb.depth}[\dots, 0]). 5. Update rb.hit: rb.hit = rb.hit & ~planehit. 6. Update rb.depth and rb.xyz for planehit: \text{rb.depth}[\text{plane\hit}] = t[\text{plane\hit}].\text{unsqueeze}(1) and \text{rb.xyz}[\text{plane\hit}] = \text{rays.origins}[\text{plane\hit}] + \text{rays.dirs}[\text{plane\hit}] \times t[\text{plane\hit}].\text{unsqueeze}(1). 7. Set rb.normal for planehit: \text{rb.normal}[\text{plane\hit}] = 0 and \text{rb.normal}[\text{plane\hit}, 1] = 1. 8. Compute shadow ray origin: \text{shadow\ray\o} = \text{rb.xyz} + 0.01 \times \text{rb.normal}. 9. Compute shadow ray direction: generate noise \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.01) with shape matching rb.xyz, then \text{shadow\ray\d} = \text{normalize}(\text{noise} + \text{light\o} - \text{shadow\ray\o}). 10. Check if rays hit the light: lighthit = (\text{shadow\ray\d} \cdot \text{rb.normal}) > 0.0. 11. Create shadowrays: Rays(origins=shadowrayo, dirs=shadowrayd, distmin=0, distmax=rays.distmax). 12. Trace shadow rays: rb.shadow = pipeline.tracer(pipeline.nef, rays=shadowrays).hit. 13. Zero out shadow for non-light-hit rays: rb.shadow[~lighthit] = 0.0. 14. Compute shadow map: \text{shadow\map} = \text{clamp}((1.0 - \text{rb.shadow}.\text{float}()) + 0.7, 0.0, 1.0). 15. Apply Gaussian filter to shadowmap with \sigma=2. 16. Multiply rb.rgb by shadowmap: \text{rb.rgb}[\dots,:3] \times= \text{shadow\map}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np from scipy.ndimage import gaussianfilter from torch.nn import functional as F from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass class Rays: origins: torch.Tensor dirs: torch.Tensor distmin: float distmax: float @dataclass class RenderBuffer: hit: torch.Tensor depth: torch.Tensor xyz: torch.Tensor normal: torch.Tensor rgb: torch.Tensor def pointlightshadowshader(rays: Rays, rb: RenderBuffer, pipeline: object, pointlight: list = [1.5, 4.5, 1.5], miny: float = -2.0, rate: float = 1.0) -> RenderBuffer: # Step 1: Plane Intersection Refinement delta = rays.origins[:, 1] - miny planet = delta / rate planehit = (planet > 0) & (planet < 500) planehit = planehit & (planet < rb.depth[..., 0]) rb.hit = rb.hit & ~planehit planetunsqueezed = planet[planehit].unsqueeze(1) rb.depth[planehit] = planetunsqueezed rb.xyz[planehit] = rays.origins[planehit] + rays.dirs[planehit] planetunsqueezed rb.normal[planehit] = 0.0 rb.normal[planehit, 1] = 1.0 # Step 2: Shadow Ray Generation shadowrayo = rb.xyz + 0.01 rb.normal lighto = torch.tensor(pointlight, dtype=rb.xyz.dtype, device=rb.xyz.device) noise = torch.zeroslike(rb.xyz).normal(0.0, 0.01) # Fixed source indexing bug: F.normalize returns a tensor, not a tuple shadowrayd = F.normalize(noise + lighto - shadowrayo, dim=1) # Step 3: Shadow Ray Tracing lighthit = (shadowrayd rb.normal).sum(-1) > 0.0 shadowrays = Rays(origins=shadowrayo, dirs=shadowrayd, distmin=0, distmax=rays.distmax) rb.shadow = pipeline.tracer(pipeline.nef, rays=shadowrays).hit rb.shadow[~lighthit] = 0.0 # Step 4: Shadow Map Application shadowmap = torch.clamp((1.0 - rb.shadow.float()) + 0.7, 0.0, 1.0).cpu().numpy()[..., 0] shadowmap = torch.fromnumpy(gaussianfilter(shadowmap, sigma=2)).unsqueeze(-1) rb.rgb[...,:3] = shadowmap.cuda() if rb.rgb.device.type == "cuda" else shadowmap return rb Not given in the sources. The method is described in the NVIDIA Kaolin-Wisp repository. It is part of the interactive rendering pipeline in Wisp, a framework for neural implicit fields.
