name: Light Injection Pass
head: Light-Space Rendering Pass, Light/Volume two-pass, Main Rendering Pass, Precomputed Lighting Pass, Volumetric Light (Sun Shafts and Lamp Glow), Wave D volumetric light
body: The Light Injection Pass is a GPU fragment-stage algorithm that computes volume illumination by traversing light rays from the light source's perspective, determining visibility via a binary search on an opacity shadow map (A-Buffer), and compositing light samples into camera space. It is specifically implemented as a post-processing pass that marches rays from the eye to the depth buffer to add light scattered by air (sun shafts and lamp glow), executed only when rrealtimeLighting is set to 2. It builds on Ray Marching with Shadow Mapping by precomputing in-scattered radiance into a 3D texture using shadow maps, which is then integrated during the view-ray march. Unlike Shadow Volume Rendering which uses geometric volumes, or Deep Shadow Maps which store depth distributions, this method relies on a two-pass approach: an injection pass to populate lighting data and a rendering pass to composite it. The method consists of two distinct phases: the Light Injection Pass (populating the 3D texture with lighting data) and the Main Rendering Pass (compositing light into the final image). Inputs: 3D texture (voxel grid) storing extinction coefficient and in-scattered radiance. Shadow maps (cascaded for directional lights, cubemaps for point lights). Camera view and projection matrices. Light source parameters (position, color, range, type). Volume parameters: density, anisotropy (g), range. Outputs: Updated 3D texture with in-scattered radiance. Final image with volumetric lighting effects (sun shafts, lamp glow). 3D Texture: Stores extinction coefficient (\sigmat) and in-scattered radiance (L{in}). Accessed via image load/store (glBindImageTexture). A-Buffer (Visibility Buffer): Stores visibility (v) and distance (d) to the camera for each sample along the ray. The number of layers is 2^k - 1, where k is manually specified or set via data variation analysis. Shadow Maps: Cascaded shadow maps (4 cascades) for directional lights; shadow cubemaps for point lights. This pass calculates the incoming radiance for each voxel based on light sources. 1. World Position Reconstruction: For each voxel at 3D grid index (x, y, z), map to clip space, apply the inverse view-projection matrix, and divide by w to determine the world-space center of the cell. 2. Shadow Map Sampling: Sample standard shadow maps (cascaded for directional, cubemaps for point lights) to check for occlusion. 3. In-Scattering Calculation: For all unshadowed lights, evaluate light color, attenuation, and the phase function p(\theta). Store the resulting in-scattered radiance alongside the extinction coefficient in the 3D texture using image load/store. This pass traverses light rays from the light source, determines visibility, and projects light into camera space. 1. Define Ray: Define a ray from front to back (from the light source). 2. Loop for Samples: For all samples s along the ray: a. Read Voxel: Read/classify voxel at s to get color/opacity c. b. Check Opacity: If opacity in c > 0: i. Project to Camera: Project s to camera space and get texture coordinate t. ii. Calculate Distance: Calculate distance d to camera (in volume space). iii. Binary Search: Retrieve closest layers to s based on t and d using binary search in the A-Buffer. Optimize by checking against first and last layer before initiating search. iv. Calculate Visibility: Calculate visibility v through linear interpolation between closest layers with respect to d. v. Compositing: Perform front-to-back compositing along the ray into r. vi. Compute Color/Opacity: Compute color/opacity as seen from the camera. vii. Project to Covered Pixels: Project s onto camera to determine covered pixels c. viii. Atomic Add: For all pixels p in c, add contribution to pixels in the resulting image using atomic add operations (requires OpenGL 4.0 or GLNVshaderatomicfloat extension for floats). ix. Determine Next Position: Determine next position or if done (early ray termination enabled). c. Compensate Perspective: Compensate for perspective projection by changing light sample footprint (similar to splat footprint or cone tracing). Oversampling light rays is used as a simpler alternative. Sun (Directional Light): March 16 steps along the ray from the eye to the depth buffer. At each step, sample the shadow from the finest of the four cascades that contains the sun. Stop the sun ray march when the distance reaches rvolumetricRange (3000 units). Lamps (Point Lights): Determine the segment of the ray that lies inside the lamp's reach using a ray-sphere test. March 4 steps along the selected lamp ray segment. Use equi-angular sampling (Kulla & Fajardo 2012) to spread the steps by the angle at the lamp, which cancels the 1/d^2 light falloff against the sampling density. Apply the same shade, cone, and fade terms used by RtLightParticle, plus one sample from the lamp's cube shadow map. Lamp Culling: Lamps whose upper-bound contribution is below the visible threshold are skipped. The upper-bound contribution is calculated as C = \pi / h, where h is the distance from the ray to the lamp center. Use the Henyey-Greenstein phase function for forward scattering with an anisotropy parameter g of 0.5. The phase function p(\theta) is defined as: p(\theta) = \frac{1 - g^2}{4\pi (1 + g^2 - 2g \cos \theta)^{3/2}} where \theta is the angle between the view vector and the light direction. Apply per-pixel interleaved-gradient jitter during sampling. Smooth the result using an existing depth-aware blur pass. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mainrenderingpass(lightsource, camera, volumetexture, abuffer): # Define ray from front to back (from light source) ray = definerayfromlight(lightsource) # Loop for all samples s along the ray for s in ray.samples: # Read/classify voxel at s to color/opacity c c = readvoxel(volumetexture, s) if c.opacity > 0: # Project s to camera space and get texture coord t t = projecttocameraspace(s, camera) # Calculate distance d to camera (in volume space) d = calculatedistancetocamera(s, camera) # Retrieve closest layers to s based on t and d (binary search) # Optimize: check against first and last layer before search closestlayers = binarysearchabuffer(abuffer, t, d) # Calculate visibility v through linear interpolation v = interpolatevisibility(closestlayers, d) # Perform compositing front-to-back along ray into r r = compositefronttoback(r, c, v) # Compute color/opacity as seen from camera coloropacity = computecoloropacity(r) # Project s onto camera to determine covered pixels c coveredpixels = projecttocoveredpixels(s, camera) # Add contribution to pixels in resulting image (atomic add) for p in coveredpixels: atomicadd(p, coloropacity) # Determine next position or if done (early ray termination) if isdone(r): break def lightinjectionpass(lightsource, volumetexture, shadowmap): # World Position Reconstruction for x, y, z in volumetexture.grid: worldpos = reconstructworldposition(x, y, z) # Shadow Map Sampling isshadowed = sampleshadowmap(shadowmap, worldpos, lightsource) if not isshadowed: # In-Scattering Calculation radiance = calculateinscatteredradiance(lightsource, worldpos) # Store in 3D texture using image load/store writetovolume(volumetexture, x, y, z, radiance) A variant that renders the shadow map from the light's point of view and reconstructs the world position of each shadow map texel to traverse down an octree data structure, calculating reflected radiance (assuming diffuse reflection) and writing it to 3D texture bricks. It uses a cascade shadow map with 4 cascades, with the last cascade used for light injection. Slope scale depth bias is disabled to ensure the reconstructed world position is exactly inside the voxel. Pitfalls include shadow map instability causing flickering during cone tracing when the camera moves, and low shadow map resolution causing light injection artifacts where only a subset of voxels are filled. Time Complexity: The pass is performed individually for each light source with no restriction on computation order and no increase in memory usage, as light is additive. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 3D texture, shadow maps, and the A-Buffer (visibility buffer) with 2^k - 1 layers. Measured Performance: On a GTX 1080 at 2560×1440 with rrealtimeLighting 2 and MSAA 4×: 'm3l2 house room' scene (sun through windows/door): 0.91 ms total, with 0.41 ms for sun and blur. 'Tech demo lamp hall' scene (48 colored lamps): 0.93 ms total, with 0.44 ms for sun and blur. Scaling: Performance improved from 4.4 ms (half-size march, 8 uniform steps, 4-tap shadows) to 0.9 ms (quarter resolution, equi-angular sampling, 4 steps, real culling, 1-tap shadows). Strengths: Efficient for sun shafts and lamp glow; supports perspective (point lights) and orthogonal (directional lights) projections; area lights can be simulated using fish-eye lenses. Limitations: Does not support froxel or temporal accumulation (would allow more steps); does not link density to a map's fog; does not include extinction (the scene isn't dimmed by the haze). When to Use: When real-time volumetric lighting for sun shafts and point lights is required, and performance is critical. When Not to Use: When global illumination or complex scattering effects are needed, or when the scene requires extinction effects. This approach is based on the method used by Frostbite and UE4 before the introduction of froxels. The equi-angular sampling technique is attributed to Kulla & Fajardo (2012). It is implemented as part of the Wave D volumetric light feature in the OpenMOHAA project. feat(render): the light in the air: sun shafts and the glow round lamps, in their shadows (rvolumetric), https://github.com/ssshoshi/openmohaa/pull/116, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Volumetric Fog Using 3D Textures in OpenGL - opengl, https://salivity.github.io/opengl/article/volumetric-fog-using-3-d-textures-in-open-gl, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Multimodal Volume Illumination, https://www.uni-ulm.de/fileadmin/websiteuniulm/iui.inst.100/institut/Papers/viscom/2015/sunden15multimodal.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Implementing Voxel Cone Tracing, http://simonstechblog.blogspot.com/2013/01/implementing-voxel-cone-tracing.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Inject Direct Lighting Pass
head: Direct Light Injection, Voxel Direct Lighting Injection
body: The Inject Direct Lighting Pass populates a voxelized scene's data structure with direct illumination data, enabling subsequent global illumination calculations (such as voxel cone tracing). It solves the problem of transferring light transport information from a standard rasterized shadow map into a 3D volumetric representation. It differs from its sibling, the Light Injection Pass, which operates in the GPU fragment stage using camera-space ray traversal and A-Buffer visibility; this pass operates in world space by traversing an octree from shadow map texels. Inputs: A voxelized scene represented as an octree data structure, stored in 3D texture bricks. A shadow map rendered from the light's point of view. Light direction and position. Outputs: Updated 3D texture bricks containing reflected radiance values at leaf nodes. Data Structures: Octree: Hierarchical structure where leaf nodes correspond to voxels. Each leaf stores radiance data. Shadow Map: 2D texture storing depth information from the light's perspective. Steps: 1. Render Shadow Map: Render the scene from the light's point of view to generate a shadow map. 2. Iterate Shadow Map Texels: For each pixel (texel) in the shadow map: a. Reconstruct World Position: Convert the shadow map texel coordinates and depth value back into world-space coordinates. b. Traverse Octree: Traverse the octree data structure to locate the voxel(s) corresponding to the reconstructed world position. c. Calculate Reflected Radiance: Compute the direct lighting contribution. The method assumes the surface reflects diffusely. d. Write to Bricks: Write the calculated radiance value into the 3D texture bricks associated with the leaf nodes of the octree. Parameters: Cascade Shadow Map: Uses a cascade shadow map with 4 cascades. The last cascade is specifically used for the light injection pass. Slope Scale Depth Bias: Disabled. This ensures that the reconstructed world position is exactly inside the voxel, preventing misalignment artifacts. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Shadow Map Instability: If the shadow map moves relative to the scene (e.g., due to camera movement), it causes flickering during the subsequent cone tracing step. Stabilization is required, such as computing the directional light position from the view camera. Unfilled Voxels: Stabilizing the shadow map may result in some voxels remaining unfilled with lighting data if the shadow map resolution is low or not fully utilized. Resolution Artifacts: Low shadow map resolution leads to incomplete light injection. Launching one thread per shadow map texel means only voxels aligned with texel centers receive light. For example, in a vertical column of 5 voxels, a low-resolution shadow map might only inject light into 3 of them, leaving gaps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def injectdirectlighting(octree, shadowmap, lightdirection, lightposition): # Step 1: Shadow map is assumed to be already rendered from light's POV # Step 2: Iterate over shadow map texels for y in range(shadowmap.height): for x in range(shadowmap.width): # Get depth from shadow map depth = shadowmap.sample(x, y) # Reconstruct world position from shadow map texel # Requires inverse projection and view matrices of the light worldpos = reconstructworldposition(x, y, depth, lightviewmatrix, lightprojmatrix) # Traverse octree to find leaf node(s) at worldpos leafnodes = octree.traverse(worldpos) for leaf in leafnodes: # Calculate reflected radiance assuming diffuse reflection # Note: Specific shading model details (e.g., albedo, NdotL) are not provided in sources # Assuming standard diffuse direct lighting calculation radiance = calculatediffuseradiance(lightdirection, leaf.normal, leaf.albedo) # Write radiance to 3D texture brick leaf.writeradiance(radiance) A GPU fragment-stage algorithm that renders volume illumination by traversing light rays, computing visibility via binary search on the A-Buffer, and compositing light samples into camera space. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of shadow map texels. Each texel triggers an octree traversal. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the shadow map and the 3D texture bricks. Strengths: Integrates well with existing shadow mapping infrastructure. Limitations: Highly sensitive to shadow map resolution. Low resolution causes visible gaps in lighting (unfilled voxels). Requires careful stabilization to avoid flickering. When to use: When a voxelized scene is already available and direct lighting needs to be baked into the voxel structure for subsequent global illumination passes like cone tracing. When not to use: When high-resolution shadow maps are not feasible, or when camera-relative lighting accuracy is critical without stabilization overhead. This method is part of the Voxel Cone Tracing pipeline, specifically the step that injects direct lighting into the voxel data structure. It was described in the context of implementing voxel cone tracing in a custom engine, utilizing cascade shadow maps and octree traversal. Implementing Voxel Cone Tracing, http://simonstechblog.blogspot.com/2013/01/implementing-voxel-cone-tracing.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Variance Shadow Mapping for NeRFs
head: NeRF shadow mapping, VSM for NeRFs
body: Variance Shadow Mapping for NeRFs is a shadow rendering method for neural radiance fields that uses spherical Gaussians (SGs) to render cast shadows, inspired by traditional variance shadow mapping. It avoids the cumulative transmittance of light along sampling points on shadow rays by comparing depth inconsistencies from light and camera views. The method transforms discontinuous depth from the light perspective into continuous depth, producing soft shadows with visibility values in [0, 1] rather than the hard shadows produced by naive depth comparison. Inputs: A trained NeRF model. Camera parameters (intrinsics and extrinsics) for the view being rendered. Light source position and orientation (defining a virtual camera at the light source). A depth map D rendered from the camera view. A box filter kernel size (typically small, e.g., 3\times3 or 5\times5). Outputs: A visibility factor V(\mathbf{r}) \in [0, 1] for each pixel \mathbf{r} in the camera view. The final pixel color I(\mathbf{r}) incorporating the shadow. Data Structures: 1. Depth Map (X): A 2D array of floats, where each element X(\mathbf{r}c) represents the depth z of the surface point at camera pixel \mathbf{r}c. 2. Squared Depth Map (X^2): A 2D array of floats, where each element X^2(\mathbf{r}c) = (X(\mathbf{r}c))^2. 3. Filtered Depth Map (\mu(X)): The result of applying a box filter to X. 4. Filtered Squared Depth Map (\mu(X^2)): The result of applying a box filter to X^2. 5. Variance Map (\sigma^2): A 2D array of floats computed from the filtered maps. Steps: 1. Reconstruct 3D Points: For each pixel \mathbf{r} in the camera view, use the depth map value z(\mathbf{r}) and the camera parameters to reconstruct the 3D coordinate \mathbf{P} of the surface point. 2. Render Light View Maps: Set a virtual camera at the light source. Transform the depth map from the camera view to this new light view to obtain z(\mathbf{r}). Render the squared map of the depth, denoted as X^2, and the depth map X directly from the light view. 3. Filter the Light View Maps: Apply a box filter (uniform average) to both X and X^2 to obtain \mu(X) and \mu(X^2). 4. Calculate Variance: For each pixel \mathbf{r}l in the light view, calculate the variance \sigma^2(\mathbf{r}l) using the filtered maps. 5. Map Camera Point to Light View: For the 3D point \mathbf{P} reconstructed in Step 1, project it into the light camera's coordinate system to find the corresponding pixel \mathbf{r}l in the light view. 6. Compute Visibility: Calculate the visibility V(\mathbf{r}) for the camera pixel \mathbf{r} using the Chebyshev inequality-based formula. 7. Final Rendering: Combine the visibility with the NeRF's radiance to compute the final pixel color. Formulas: Variance: \sigma^2(\mathbf{r}l) = \mu(X^2)(\mathbf{r}l) - \mu^2(X)(\mathbf{r}l). Visibility: V(\mathbf{r}) = \begin{cases} 1, & z(\mathbf{r}) \leq \mu(X)(\mathbf{r}l) \\ \frac{\sigma^2(\mathbf{r}l)}{\sigma^2(\mathbf{r}l) + (z(\mathbf{r}) - \mu(X)(\mathbf{r}l))^2}, & z(\mathbf{r}) > \mu(X)(\mathbf{r}l) \end{cases}. Final Color: I(\mathbf{r}) = Id(\mathbf{r}) + Is(\mathbf{r}) + V(\mathbf{r})\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{r})S{SG}(\mathbf{r}). Where \mathbf{r}l is the correspondence pixel of \mathbf{r} in the light view, z(\mathbf{r}) is the depth of the shaded point as seen from the light, \mu(X)(\mathbf{r}l) is the filtered mean depth at \mathbf{r}l, and \sigma^2(\mathbf{r}l) is the variance at \mathbf{r}l. Id and Is are diffuse and specular components, \mathcal{R} is the BRDF, and S{SG} is the light source intensity. Parameters: Box Filter Kernel Size: Not explicitly given in the sources, but typical for VSM is small (e.g., 3\times3 to 5\times5). Larger kernels produce softer shadows but more blur. Variance Clamp: A small epsilon (e.g., 10^{-6}) to prevent division by zero or negative variance due to numerical noise. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Negative Variance: Due to numerical precision, \mu(X^2) can be slightly less than \mu(X)^2. Clamp variance to \ge 0. Light Frustum Bounds: Points outside the light's view frustum cannot be projected. These should default to fully visible (V=1) or be handled based on scene requirements. Depth Discontinuities: VSM handles soft shadows well, but sharp edges may still exhibit artifacts if the filter size is too small. NeRF Depth Definition: The "depth" in NeRFs is ambiguous (surface vs. volume). The source implies using a depth map, which suggests a surface extraction or a specific depth metric (e.g., mean depth) was used to generate the initial depth map. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def boxfilter(image, kernelsize=3): """Apply a uniform box filter to a 2D image.""" pad = kernelsize // 2 padded = np.pad(image, pad, mode='edge') h, w = image.shape kernel = np.ones((kernelsize, kernelsize)) / (kernelsize kernelsize) filtered = np.zeroslike(image) for i in range(h): for j in range(w): filtered[i, j] = np.sum(padded[i:i+kernelsize, j:j+kernelsize] kernel) return filtered def varianceshadowmappingfornerf(nerfmodel, cameraparams, lightparams, depthmap, kernelsize=3): """ Compute shadow visibility for a NeRF rendering. """ h, w = depthmap.shape ucam, vcam = np.meshgrid(np.arange(w), np.arange(h)) # Step 1: Reconstruct 3D points from depth map xcam = (ucam - cameraparams['cx']) depthmap / cameraparams['fx'] ycam = (vcam - cameraparams['cy']) depthmap / cameraparams['fy'] zcam = depthmap pointscam = np.stack([xcam, ycam, zcam, np.oneslike(zcam)], axis=-1) camtoworld = np.linalg.inv(cameraparams['extrinsics']) points3d = np.einsum('ij,...j->...i', camtoworld, pointscam[...,:3]) # Step 2: Render Light View Maps # Project 3D points to light camera space to get depth and 2D coordinates lightworldtocam = lightparams['worldtocam'] pointslightcam = np.einsum('ij,...j->...i', lightworldtocam, points3d) xl, yl, zl = pointslightcam[..., 0], pointslightcam[..., 1], pointslightcam[..., 2] # Project to light view pixel coordinates ul = (xl / zl) lightparams['fx'] + lightparams['cx'] vl = (yl / zl) lightparams['fy'] + lightparams['cy'] # Create light view depth maps (simplified accumulation for pseudocode) lighth, lightw = lightparams['height'], lightparams['width'] lightdepth = np.full((lighth, lightw), np.inf) lightdepthsq = np.full((lighth, lightw), np.inf) # Scatter points to light view grid, keeping closest depth ulint = np.clip(ul.astype(int), 0, lightw - 1) vlint = np.clip(vl.astype(int), 0, lighth - 1) valid = (zl > 0) & (ul >= 0) & (ul < lightw) & (vl >= 0) & (vl < lighth) lightdepth[vlint[valid], ulint[valid]] = np.minimum(lightdepth[vlint[valid], ulint[valid]], zl[valid]) lightdepthsq[vlint[valid], ulint[valid]] = np.minimum(lightdepthsq[vlint[valid], ulint[valid]], zl[valid] 2) # Step 3: Filter Light View Maps mulightdepth = boxfilter(lightdepth, kernelsize) mulightdepthsq = boxfilter(lightdepthsq, kernelsize) # Step 4: Calculate Variance variance = mulightdepthsq - mulightdepth 2 variance = np.maximum(variance, 1e-6) # Step 5 & 6: Compute Visibility # Retrieve filtered mean depth at the projected light-view coordinates muatpoint = mulightdepth[vlint, ulint] varatpoint = variance[vlint, ulint] diff = zl - muatpoint visibility = np.oneslike(diff) occludedmask = diff > 0 visibility[occludedmask] = varatpoint[occludedmask] / \ (varatpoint[occludedmask] + diff[occludedmask] 2) # Handle invalid pixels visibility[~valid] = 1.0 return visibility Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of pixels, dominated by the projection and filtering steps. The filtering is O(N \cdot K^2) where K is kernel size. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the depth maps and filtered maps. Performance: Efficient compared to ray-traced shadows or cumulative transmittance methods, as it avoids per-ray shadow ray traversal. Strengths: Produces soft shadows, efficient, easy to implement with standard graphics primitives. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the depth map from the NeRF. Artifacts may occur if the depth map is noisy or if the NeRF representation is not surface-like. This method is inspired by Variance Shadow Mapping (VSM) from traditional computer graphics. It was proposed for NeRFs in the context of relighting scenes with object insertions, aiming to provide realistic shadow effects without the computational overhead of volumetric shadow ray marching. name: Variance Shadow Mapping
head: VSM
body: Variance Shadow Mapping (VSM) is a shadow mapping technique that smoothens depth values to calculate the probability of shadows using Chebyshev's inequality, producing soft shadow edges instead of the abrupt 0/1 values of naive shadow mapping. It sets itself apart from its siblings by trading the binary occlusion test of Shadow Mapping for a statistical bound on visibility, allowing for efficient soft shadows with minimal overhead compared to standard shadow mapping. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A depth map D (or two maps for moments), a query point zq (depth of the fragment from the light's perspective), and a bias b. Output: A shadow factor s \in [0, 1] representing the probability that the fragment is lit. Data Structures: VSM requires storing two depth maps instead of one: 1. Mean Map (M1): Stores the first moment (mean depth) E[z]. 2. Second Moment Map (M2): Stores the second moment E[z^2]. These maps are typically stored in floating-point formats (e.g., GLRGBA32F or similar) to preserve precision for the variance calculation. Steps: 1. Render Depth Moments: Render the scene from the light's perspective. For each pixel, compute the mean depth z and the squared depth z^2. Store z in M1 and z^2 in M2. 2. Filtering (Optional but Recommended): Apply a low-pass filter (e.g., Gaussian blur) to M1 and M2 to anti-alias the shadow edges. Let the filtered values be \mu = M1(x,y) and \mu2 = M2(x,y). If filtering is skipped, \mu = z and \mu2 = z^2 of the nearest depth. 3. Calculate Variance: Compute the variance \sigma^2 of the depth distribution at the query location: \sigma^2 = \mu2 - \mu^2 Clamp \sigma^2 to a small positive value (e.g., 10^{-6}) to prevent division by zero or numerical instability when \mu2 \approx \mu^2. 4. Calculate Distance: Compute the distance between the query depth zq and the mean depth \mu: d = zq - \mu 5. Apply Bias: Adjust the distance by a bias term b to prevent self-shadowing artifacts (shadow acne): d' = d + b 6. Compute Probability Bound: Use Chebyshev's inequality to find the upper bound on the probability that the fragment is in shadow. Let p be the confidence level (typically p=0.8 or similar, but often simplified to a fixed threshold in implementations). The standard VSM formula uses a single-sided Chebyshev bound: s = \frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + d'^2} This formula provides the probability that the depth is greater than zq (i.e., occluded). If d' \le 0, the fragment is definitely lit (or the bias handles it), so s=0. In practice, if d' < 0, return 1.0 (lit). Otherwise, return \min(1.0, \frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + d'^2}). Parameters: Bias (b): A small positive value to prevent self-shadowing. Typical values depend on the scene scale and depth precision. Common range: 10^{-4} to 10^{-2} in normalized device coordinates. Confidence Level (p): The probability threshold. The source does not specify a fixed p, but the formula \frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + d'^2} corresponds to a specific bound derivation. Standard implementation often omits explicit p and uses the raw bound. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Light Leaking: VSM can suffer from light leaking (shadow appearing where it shouldn't) because Chebyshev's inequality is a loose bound. Precision: Floating-point precision in the depth maps is critical. Bias Tuning: Too little bias causes shadow acne; too much causes "Peter Panning" (shadows detached from objects). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def varianceshadowmapping(meanmap, secondmomentmap, zquery, bias): """ Calculate shadow factor using Variance Shadow Mapping. Args: meanmap: 2D array of mean depths (E[z]) secondmomentmap: 2D array of second moments (E[z^2]) zquery: float, depth of the fragment from light's perspective bias: float, bias to prevent self-shadowing Returns: float: Shadow factor in [0, 1] (0 = lit, 1 = shadow) """ # Retrieve moments at the current pixel (assuming 2D lookup) mu = meanmap[currentpixel] mu2 = secondmomentmap[currentpixel] # Calculate variance sigma2 = mu2 - mu mu # Guard against numerical instability if sigma2 < 1e-6: sigma2 = 1e-6 # Calculate distance with bias d = zquery - mu + bias # If the fragment is behind the mean depth (with bias), it is lit if d <= 0: return 0.0 # Chebyshev's inequality bound # Probability that z > zquery is <= sigma^2 / (sigma^2 + d^2) shadowprob = sigma2 / (sigma2 + d d) return min(1.0, shadowprob) Moment Shadow Mapping (MSM) is a differentiable shadow mapping technique that uses higher-order moments (e.g., n=2 for 4 moments) to provide a sharper bound to visibility, reducing light leaking compared to VSM. It sets itself apart from VSM by using a polynomial bound (Chebyshev-Cantelli or similar higher-order bounds) which is tighter than the single-variance bound, resulting in more accurate albedo textures in inverse rendering pipelines. It is chosen when differentiable rendering requires precise visibility gradients and reduced light leaking. recommends a bias value of \alpha = 5 \times 10^{-7} for n=2, but implementations often use at least twice this value to avoid singular Hankel matrices. MSM runtime is similar to VSM, but it requires slightly more memory. A PyTorch AD implementation of MSM may fail to converge due to NaN outputs near singularities, whereas C++/CUDA implementations are stable. Variance Occlusion Maps (VOM) approximate the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) of voxel values within a spherical region using only the first two statistical moments (mean and variance) to determine the percentage of occluding voxels for ambient occlusion and soft shadows. Unlike naive shadow mapping or standard variance shadow mapping which operate on 2D depth buffers, VOM operates directly on 3D volume data, allowing for spatially varying soft shadows and ambient occlusion that respect the underlying geometry's density distribution. It sets itself apart from its sibling Variance Shadow Mapping by extending the moment-based approximation into volumetric space, enabling occlusion queries against isosurfaces rather than just depth planes. Time Complexity: O(1) per fragment for the lookup and calculation, assuming pre-filtered maps. Rendering the depth maps is O(N) where N is the number of pixels. Memory Complexity: 2 \times the size of a standard depth map (for mean and second moment). Measured Performance: VSM produces soft shadows with minimal overhead compared to standard shadow mapping. MSM implementation runtime is similar to VSM. Strengths: Efficient soft shadows; differentiable (MSM); minimal overhead over hard shadow mapping. Limitations: Light leaking (VSM); requires careful bias tuning; loose bounds can cause artifacts. When to use: When soft shadows are desired and performance is critical, and light leaking is acceptable or mitigated by other means. When not to use: When high-fidelity, artifact-free shadows are required (use ray tracing or MSM with careful tuning). Variance Shadow Mapping was introduced as a method to smooth depth values and calculate shadow probabilities using Chebyshev's inequality. It is selected as a method for shadow generation in pipelines where soft shadows are needed with minimal overhead. Moment Shadow Mapping is a more recent development in the context of differentiable rendering, aiming to reduce light leaking and provide better gradients for inverse rendering tasks. name: Variance Occlusion Maps
head: Variance Ambient Maps
body: Variance Occlusion Maps (VOM) approximate the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) of voxel values within a spherical region using only the first two statistical moments (mean and variance) to determine the percentage of occluding voxels for ambient occlusion and soft shadows. Unlike naive shadow mapping or standard variance shadow mapping which operate on 2D depth buffers, VOM operates directly on 3D volume data, allowing for spatially varying soft shadows and ambient occlusion that respect the underlying geometry's density distribution. It sets itself apart from its sibling Variance Shadow Mapping by extending the moment-based approximation into volumetric space, enabling occlusion queries against isosurfaces rather than just depth planes. Input: A scalar volume dataset (e.g., density field, distance field, or MRI data). Output: A mip-mapped two-channel floating-point texture (the Variance Ambient Map) storing the first and second moments, and rendered images with ambient occlusion and/or soft shadows applied to the extracted isosurface. The core data structure is the Variance Ambient Map, stored as a mip-mapped two-channel floating-point texture. Layout: Each texel stores two values: Channel 1: M1 (First moment, mean). Channel 2: M2 (Second moment, mean of squared values). Mip-map Generation: The map is generated by iteratively doubling the Gaussian kernel size and down-sampling the volume by a factor of two. This allows the representation of large filter regions at lower resolutions. The method relies on Chebyshev's inequality to bound the probability of occlusion. 1. First Moment (M1): M1 = E(x) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} x p(x) dx Where x is the voxel value and p(x) is the probability density function. 2. Second Moment (M2): M2 = E(x^2) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} x^2 p(x) dx 3. Mean (\mu) and Variance (\sigma^2): Derived from the stored moments: \mu = M1 \sigma^2 = M2 - M1^2 4. Chebyshev Bound for Occlusion Probability (p{max}): Given a threshold t (the isovalue), the upper bound on the probability that a voxel value x is less than t (i.e., occluding) is: p{max}(t) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } t \le \mu \\ \frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + (t-\mu)^2} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Blur Kernel: A 5 \times 5 \times 5 separable Gaussian kernel is used during preprocessing. Down-sampling Factor: 2 (kernel size doubles, resolution halves at each mip level). Isovalue Offset: Samples for occlusion calculation are taken one half of a voxel under the surface in the direction of the gradient. 1. Moment Calculation: Create a new volume where each voxel contains the original value (x) and the squared value (x^2). 2. Separable Convolution: Perform separable convolutions with the Gaussian kernel on the moment volumes to generate local distributions centered at each voxel. 3. Mip-map Construction: For each subsequent mip level: Double the Gaussian kernel size. Down-sample the current volume by a factor of two. Store the resulting M1 and M2 values in the two-channel texture. Initialize the base level (highest resolution) by convolving the original volume moments with the base 5 \times 5 \times 5 kernel. 1. Surface Search: Ray march from the camera to the isosurface. Perform a binary search to refine the surface intersection point P. 2. Gradient Calculation: Calculate the surface normal (gradient) at P using central differencing on the original volume data. 3. Isovalue Determination: To handle partial volumes (where one material meets another), take an extra sample at P{iso} = P + 0.5 \cdot \Delta \cdot \nabla, where \Delta is the voxel size and \nabla is the normalized gradient direction. Use the value at P{iso} as the effective isovalue t for the occlusion query. 4. Occlusion Query: Sample the Variance Ambient Map at four mip levels (typically the first 4 levels) in the direction of the surface normal. For each sample, retrieve M1 and M2. Calculate \mu and \sigma^2 from the moments. Evaluate p{max}(t) using the Chebyshev bound formula for each mip level. 5. Final Occlusion: Take the maximum occlusion value among the sampled mip levels. This ensures that the finest detail that fits within the query radius is used, preventing over-occlusion from coarser approximations. 1. Ray Casting: Cast a ray from the surface point P in the direction of the light source L. 2. Stepwise Evaluation: Advance the ray in steps (e.g., every 4 steps or based on distance). At each step, query the Variance Ambient Map. Logarithmically increase the mip level as the ray travels further towards the light to simulate area light sources (larger filter regions for distant occluders). Evaluate p{max}(t) for the current sample. 3. Termination: Stop when the ray leaves the volume or the occlusion probability reaches 1 (fully occluded). 4. Final Shadow: The shadow factor is determined by the occlusion probability at the point of interest, typically taking the maximum occlusion encountered along the path or the value at the surface. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def calculatemoments(volume): """ Preprocessing: Calculate M1 and M2 and build mip-maps. volume: 3D array of scalar values. Returns: list of 2-channel textures [(M1level0, M2level0), (M1level1, M2level1),...] """ # Initialize base level moments m1 = volume.copy() m2 = (volume 2).copy() mipmaps = [] # Store base level mipmaps.append((m1, m2)) currentm1 = m1 currentm2 = m2 # Iteratively build mip-maps while currentm1.shape[0] > 1: # Double kernel size implicitly by increasing blur extent # Perform separable Gaussian convolution currentm1 = gaussianseparableconvolve(currentm1, kernelsize=5) # Kernel size conceptually doubles relative to previous step's coverage currentm2 = gaussianseparableconvolve(currentm2, kernelsize=5) # Down-sample by factor of 2 currentm1 = downsampleby2(currentm1) currentm2 = downsampleby2(currentm2) mipmaps.append((currentm1, currentm2)) return mipmaps def chebyshevbound(mu, sigmasq, t): """ Calculate the upper bound of occlusion probability using Chebyshev's inequality. mu: mean of the distribution sigmasq: variance of the distribution t: isovalue (threshold) """ if t <= mu: return 1.0 else: return sigmasq / (sigmasq + (t - mu) 2) def queryambientocclusion(mipmaps, surfacepoint, gradient, isovalueoffsetfactor=0.5): """ Calculate ambient occlusion for a surface point. mipmaps: List of (M1, M2) tuples for each level. surfacepoint: 3D coordinate (x, y, z) gradient: Normalized gradient vector at surfacepoint isovalueoffsetfactor: Fraction of voxel size to offset for isovalue determination """ # Determine the effective isovalue t # Sample one half of a voxel under the surface in the direction of the gradient # Note: In a real implementation, voxelsize must be known. Assuming normalized coordinates or known delta. voxelsize = 1.0 # Placeholder for actual voxel dimension offsetpoint = surfacepoint + (gradient voxelsize isovalueoffsetfactor) # Get the value at the offset point from the original volume (not the mip map) # This serves as the threshold t for the Chebyshev bound t = trilinearsample(originalvolume, offsetpoint) maxocclusion = 0.0 # Sample the first 4 mip levels (or all available if fewer) numlevels = min(4, len(mipmaps)) for i in range(numlevels): m1tex, m2tex = mipmaps[i] # Sample M1 and M2 from the mip map at the surface point m1val = trilinearsample(m1tex, surfacepoint) m2val = trilinearsample(m2tex, surfacepoint) # Calculate mean and variance mu = m1val sigmasq = m2val - (m1val 2) # Ensure variance is non-negative (numerical stability) if sigmasq < 0: sigmasq = 0.0 # Calculate occlusion bound occlusion = chebyshevbound(mu, sigmasq, t) # Take the maximum occlusion value if occlusion > maxocclusion: maxocclusion = occlusion return maxocclusion def querysoftshadow(mipmaps, origin, lightdirection, maxsteps=100): """ Calculate soft shadow using ray casting. mipmaps: List of (M1, M2) tuples. origin: Surface point. lightdirection: Normalized vector towards light. """ currentpos = origin maxocclusion = 0.0 for step in range(maxsteps): # Logarithmically increase mip level based on distance distance = step 0.1 # Arbitrary step size miplevel = int(math.log2(distance + 1)) # Example logarithmic mapping miplevel = max(0, min(miplevel, len(mipmaps) - 1)) m1tex, m2tex = mipmaps[miplevel] # Sample moments m1val = trilinearsample(m1tex, currentpos) m2val = trilinearsample(m2tex, currentpos) # Calculate moments mu = m1val sigmasq = m2val - (m1val 2) if sigmasq < 0: sigmasq = 0.0 # The isovalue t is typically the density threshold defining the surface # For shadows, we check if the ray is inside the occluder. # Assuming t is a fixed global isovalue for the volume t = globalisovalue occlusion = chebyshevbound(mu, sigmasq, t) if occlusion > maxocclusion: maxocclusion = occlusion if maxocclusion >= 1.0: break # Advance ray currentpos = currentpos + (lightdirection 0.1) # Check if out of bounds (simplified) if not isinsidevolume(currentpos): break return maxocclusion Aliasing: Using a hemispherical filter region with cosine weighting requires non-separable blurring based on surface normal. This causes aliasing artifacts under linear interpolation of neighboring samples, especially at lower resolutions. VOM avoids this by using a radially symmetric kernel and offsetting the sampling location from the surface. Accuracy Degradation: The approximation becomes less accurate as the chosen isovalue moves towards the mean of the distribution. This is particularly problematic for non-bimodal data like MRI or distance fields, where the distribution is not clearly separated into "occluder" and "non-occluder" modes. Concentration Bias: Because a radially symmetric kernel is used instead of a normal-dependent hemispherical one, the occlusion becomes slightly more concentrated in the direction of the surface normal. Preprocessing: O(N \cdot K^3) where N is the number of voxels and K is the kernel size. The mip-map structure reduces memory usage significantly; at half resolution, the map is roughly 0.6 \times the size of the original volume (including mipmaps) for a two-channel 32-bit float texture. Rendering (AO): Constant time per pixel, requiring a fixed number of samples (e.g., 4) from the mip-mapped texture. Rendering (Shadows): Linear in the number of steps along the ray cast towards the light. Tested on a Mac Pro with a single NVIDIA GeForce 8800 GTS. Preprocessing can be greatly accelerated on the GPU. Lighting is calculated as a post-process, independent of volume size, except for soft shadows which require an extra ray cast. Strengths: Produces soft shadow edges and ambient occlusion without explicit ray tracing of every voxel. Efficient memory footprint due to mip-mapping and moment storage. Allows for view-dependent ambient occlusion by adjusting surface normals during interactive rendering. Limitations: Accuracy is compromised for non-bimodal data distributions. Occlusion is biased towards the surface normal direction due to the use of spherical kernels. Not suitable for highly detailed, non-clustered data where the mean is a poor separator. Variance Occlusion Maps were introduced by Eric Penner and Ross Mitchell in the paper "Isosurface Ambient Occlusion and Soft Shadows with Filterable Occlusion Maps" (2008). The method builds upon the technique described by Donnelly et al. [DL06] for representing image distributions using the first two moments. The technique extends the concept of Percentage Closer Filtering (PCF) and Variance Shadow Mapping from 2D depth buffers to 3D volume data. It addresses the need for efficient, filterable occlusion queries in volumetric rendering, particularly for isosurfaces. The authors noted that while hemispherical filters are theoretically more accurate for surface lighting, the computational cost of non-separable blurring based on normals led to aliasing, prompting the adoption of the radially symmetric kernel approach. The method was implemented and demonstrated on medical imaging data (MRI) and synthetic volumes to show its applicability in generating realistic ambient occlusion and soft shadows for isosurfaces. name: Reflective Shadow Maps
head: Virtual Point Lights (VPL) via Shadow Maps
body: Reflective Shadow Maps (RSM) approximate single-bounce indirect illumination in real-time rendering by reusing data from a shadow map pass. Unlike standard shadow mapping, which only determines visibility for direct lighting, RSM stores surface properties alongside depth to treat texels as virtual point lights during the final shading pass. This distinguishes it from Light Propagation Volumes, which discretize the scene into 3D cells encoded with spherical harmonics, by operating directly on screen-space texels. Inputs: Scene geometry and light source(s). Outputs: Final shaded image with direct and single-bounce indirect lighting. Data Structures: Reflective Shadow Map (RSM) textures containing depth, albedo, normal, and direct illumination per texel. Steps: 1. Direct Lighting Pass: Render the scene from the light's point of view, storing depth, albedo, normal, and direct illumination into the RSM textures. 2. Virtual Point Light (VPL) Generation: Treat texels of the RSM as point lights to provide single-bounce indirect illumination. 3. Screen-Space Splatting (Optimization): Reverse the processing by creating lights based on the entire map and splatting them in screen-space. 4. Final Shading: Combine the direct lighting with the accumulated indirect lighting from the splatted VPLs to produce the final image. Formulas: The exact irradiance calculation is not given in the sources. The contribution of each VPL is derived from its stored direct illumination and albedo, projected onto the screen. Parameters: RSM resolution determines the number of potential VPLs. Heuristic thresholds are used to select which texels become VPLs to balance performance and quality. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Using all texels as VPLs leads to excessive performance cost, requiring heuristics to choose regions of the map. An insufficient number of selected lights causes temporal stability issues and flickering when lights or cameras move. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderreflectiveshadowmaps(scene, light, camera): # Step 1: Render RSM from light's perspective rsmdepth = rendershadowmapdepth(scene, light) rsmalbedo = rendershadowmapalbedo(scene, light) rsmnormal = rendershadowmapnormal(scene, light) rsmdirectlight = rendershadowmapdirectlight(scene, light) # Step 2: Select VPLs from RSM # Heuristic: Select texels with direct illumination above a threshold to avoid excessive cost vpllist = [] threshold = 0.0 # Implementation-dependent threshold for y in range(rsmdepth.height): for x in range(rsmdepth.width): if rsmdirectlight[y, x] > threshold: worldpos = texeltoworldposition(x, y, rsmdepth[y, x], light.viewmatrix) vpllist.append({ 'position': worldpos, 'normal': rsmnormal[y, x], 'albedo': rsmalbedo[y, x], 'intensity': rsmdirectlight[y, x] }) # Step 3: Splat VPLs to screen space # Reverse processing: project VPLs and splat contribution to covered pixels indirectbuffer = zerobuffer(camera.resolution) for vpl in vpllist: screenpos = worldtoscreen(vpl.position, camera.viewmatrix, camera.projectionmatrix) radius = calculateinfluenceradius(vpl.intensity) for dy in range(-radius, radius + 1): for dx in range(-radius, radius + 1): px, py = screenpos.x + dx, screenpos.y + dy if 0 <= px < camera.width and 0 <= py < camera.height: distsq = distancesquared(vpl.position, pixelworldposition(px, py, camera)) if distsq > 0: contribution = vpl.intensity vpl.albedo / distsq indirectbuffer[py, px] += contribution # Step 4: Final composite directimage = renderdirectlighting(scene, light, camera) finalimage = directimage + indirectbuffer return finalimage def rendershadowmapdepth(scene, light):... # Standard depth pass def rendershadowmapalbedo(scene, light):... # Standard albedo pass def rendershadowmapnormal(scene, light):... # Standard normal pass def rendershadowmapdirectlight(scene, light):... # Standard direct lighting pass def texeltoworldposition(x, y, depth, viewmatrix):... # Inverse view-projection transform def worldtoscreen(pos, viewmatrix, projmatrix):... # View-projection transform def calculateinfluenceradius(intensity):... # Intensity-based falloff def distancesquared(p1, p2): return sum((a-b)2 for a, b in zip(p1, p2)) def pixelworldposition(px, py, camera):... # Ray origin reconstruction def zerobuffer(resolution): return [[0.0]resolution.width for in range(resolution.height)] def renderdirectlighting(scene, light, camera):... # Standard direct lighting pass Beer Shadow Maps are a variant used primarily for volumetric cloud shadowing in Unreal Engine. They use cascaded shadow maps to support far shadow distances for clouds and ground casting. Compared to ray-marched shadows, they are faster and support far distances but lack volumetric self-shadow color and accuracy. They are recommended for console platforms like Xbox One and PlayStation 4. Parameters include Cloud Shadow Ray Sample Count Scale (drives sample count), Cloud Shadow Map Resolution Scale (drives resolution and sunlight shaft cost), and Cloud Shadow Extent (reduces map radius for sharper results). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance scales with the number of selected VPLs and the splatting resolution. Memory Complexity: Requires storing additional textures (albedo, normal, direct light) in the RSM, increasing memory usage compared to standard shadow mapping. Strengths: Efficient approximation of single-bounce indirect illumination; compatible with existing shadow map infrastructure; real-time performance with heuristics. Limitations: Flickering due to temporal instability; limited to single-bounce; performance sensitive to VPL count. When to Use: Real-time applications requiring diffuse interreflection where full global illumination is too expensive. When Not to Use: Scenarios requiring multi-bounce GI or accurate volumetric shadows. Reflective Shadow Maps were inspired by the Virtual Point Lights technique used in the production of Shrek 2. Tabellion and Lamorlette utilized a direct lighting pass and cached lighting to create one-bounce indirect lighting. Dachsbacher and Stamminger formalized this into the Reflective Shadow Maps technique, rendering from the light's perspective and storing surface properties to treat texels as point lights. The method was optimized by reversing the processing to splat lights in screen-space. Kaplanyan's Light Propagation Volumes also aim for first-bounce GI but use 3D cells and spherical harmonics, contrasting with RSM's texel-based VPLs. name: Shadow Caching
body: Shadow Caching exploits the inherent coherence of shadow rays for a point light source that are occluded by the same object to avoid redundant ray traversal. It stores occlusion results in a spatial data structure, replacing expensive shadow ray casts during rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scene subdivision, light source position, and transfer function. Output: A cached shadow lookup structure and the final rendered image. Data Structures: 1. Shadow Cache (3D Texture): A volumetric texture storing the shadow status for each spatial region relative to the light source. 2. Shadow Feelers: Precomputed rays used to populate the cache. Steps: 1. Subdivide the scene into cells or spatial regions. 2. For each cell, generate shadow feelers by casting rays from representative points toward the light source. 3. Traverse the feelers to determine if the cell is fully occluded, fully visible, or partially visible to the light. 4. Store the occlusion status in the spatial cache, such as a 3D texture. 5. During rendering, query the cache for the cell containing the shading point. 6. If the cache indicates fully occluded or fully visible, return the cached result immediately. 7. If partially visible or a cache miss occurs, perform a full shadow ray traversal. Parameters: Light Source Position: Must be known during preprocessing. Cache Resolution: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Shadow feelers must be recomputed if the light source position changes or if the transfer function changes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildshadowcache(scenecells, lightposition): cache = {} for cell in scenecells: status = "FULLYVISIBLE" # Generate shadow feelers from cell representative points toward the light feelers = [(cell.center, lightposition)] for start, end in feelers: # Standard ray-scene intersection to detect occluders pass cache[cell.id] = status return cache def rendershadowcaching(voxels, cache, lightposition): for voxel in voxels: # Standard spatial grid indexing to map position to cell cellid = tuple(int(p) for p in voxel.position) status = cache.get(cellid, "PARTIALLYVISIBLE") if status == "FULLYOCCLUDED": voxel.light = 0.0 elif status == "FULLYVISIBLE": voxel.light = 1.0 else: # Standard shadow ray traversal for partial visibility voxel.light = 0.0 This variant uses 3D textures to store shadow results, gaining performance through fast texture lookups instead of ray traversal. It requires preprocessing of shadow feelers. A key pitfall is that shadow feelers need to be recomputed if the light source position changes or if the transfer function changes. Time and memory complexity are Not given in the sources. Strengths include exploiting shadow ray coherence to reduce redundant computations. Limitations include preprocessing overhead and costly cache invalidation when the light source or transfer function changes. Usage guidelines are Not given in the sources. Fernandez et al. [104] subdivided the scene and maintained lists of light sources per region as fully occluded, fully visible, or partially visible using shadow ray approximations. Pharr et al. [94] introduced ray queues for scene cells. The 3D texture variant was explored by Ropinski for GPU-based volume raycasting. name: PCF Shadow Lookup with Slope Scaling and Edge Fade
head: PCF with Slope Scaling and Edge Fade
body: This method computes sun shadow occlusion at a world position using Percentage-Closer Filtering (PCF) with a dynamic kernel, slope-scaled depth bias, and distance-based edge fading. It prevents peter-panning by offsetting geometry along the surface normal rather than the light direction, and avoids hard shadow cutoffs at the shadow map boundaries by fading occlusion based on UV distance from the map center. It differs from standard PCF Shadow Mapping by dynamically scaling the depth bias with surface orientation and applying a distance-based fade instead of a fixed bias and uniform kernel. Inputs and Outputs: worldpos: The 3D world-space position of the fragment being shaded. normal: The surface normal at worldpos, normalized. lightdir: The direction from the surface towards the light, normalized. scene.lightviewproj: The 4x4 view-projection matrix transforming world space to light clip space. scene.shadowparams: A uniform vector containing texel size (x), base normal offset magnitude (y), shadow strength multiplier (z), and kernel radius in texels (w). shadowmap: A 2D depth texture bound as a comparison sampler. Output: occlusion, a float in [0.0, 1.0] representing final shadow intensity (0.0 = fully lit, 1.0 = fully shadowed). Data Structures: shadowmap: Declared as layout(set = 0, binding = 2) uniform sampler2DShadow shadowmap;. The comparison sampler returns 1.0 if the stored depth is greater than the provided depth, and 0.0 otherwise. Parameters: SHADOWPCFMAXRADIUS = 4: Integer constant limiting the kernel half-width to a 9x9 grid. SHADOWSLOPEOFFSET = 2.0: Float constant for the slope-scaled bias multiplier. SHADOWFADESTART = 0.85: Float constant representing the fraction of the map half-width where edge fading begins. Numbered Steps and Formulas: 1. Calculate the dot product between the surface normal and the light direction: ndotl = clamp(dot(normal, lightdir), 0.0, 1.0). 2. Compute the slope-scaled normal offset: offset = scene.shadowparams.y (1.0 + SHADOWSLOPEOFFSET (1.0 - ndotl)). 3. Transform the offset world position to light clip space: lightclip = scene.lightviewproj vec4(worldpos + normal offset, 1.0). 4. Perform perspective division to obtain Normalized Device Coordinates: ndc = lightclip.xyz / lightclip.w. 5. Map NDC to texture UV space: uv = ndc.xy 0.5 + 0.5. 6. Retrieve texel size and clamp the kernel radius: texel = scene.shadowparams.x and radius = clamp(int(scene.shadowparams.w + 0.5), 0, SHADOWPCFMAXRADIUS). 7. Initialize occlusion = 0.0 and loop y from -radius to radius, x from -radius to radius. Compute tap = uv + vec2(x, y) texel and accumulate occlusion += 1.0 - texture(shadowmap, vec3(tap, ndc.z)). 8. Average the accumulated occlusion: occlusion /= float((2 radius + 1) (2 radius + 1)). 9. Compute the edge distance from the UV center: edge = max(abs(uv.x - 0.5), abs(uv.y - 0.5)) 2.0. 10. Compute the fade factor: fade = 1.0 - smoothstep(SHADOWFADESTART, 1.0, edge). 11. Return the final result: occlusion fade scene.shadowparams.z. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If ndc.z <= 0.0 || ndc.z >= 1.0, the point is outside the light's view frustum; return 0.0. If uv falls outside [0, 1], the point is outside the shadow map bounds; return 0.0 to avoid black walls at volume edges. Offsetting along the surface normal instead of the light direction keeps contact points fixed and prevents peter-panning. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pcfshadowlookupwithslopescalingandedgefade( worldpos: vec3, normal: vec3, lightdir: vec3, lightviewproj: mat4, shadowparams: vec4, shadowmap: sampler2DShadow, SHADOWPCFMAXRADIUS: int = 4, SHADOWSLOPEOFFSET: float = 2.0, SHADOWFADESTART: float = 0.85) -> float: # 1. Light Direction Dot Product ndotl = clamp(dot(normal, lightdir), 0.0, 1.0) # 2. Slope-Scaled Normal Offset offset = shadowparams.y (1.0 + SHADOWSLOPEOFFSET (1.0 - ndotl)) # 3. Transform to Light Clip Space lightclip = lightviewproj vec4(worldpos + normal offset, 1.0) # 4. Convert to NDC ndc = vec3(lightclip.x / lightclip.w, lightclip.y / lightclip.w, lightclip.z / lightclip.w) # Edge case: Outside light frustum if ndc.z <= 0.0 or ndc.z >= 1.0: return 0.0 # 5. Compute UV Coordinates uv = vec2(ndc.x 0.5 + 0.5, ndc.y 0.5 + 0.5) # Edge case: Outside shadow map bounds if uv.x < 0.0 or uv.x > 1.0 or uv.y < 0.0 or uv.y > 1.0: return 0.0 # 6. Initialize PCF Kernel texel = shadowparams.x radius = clamp(int(shadowparams.w + 0.5), 0, SHADOWPCFMAXRADIUS) # 7. Accumulate Occlusion occlusion = 0.0 kernelsize = 2 radius + 1 for y in range(-radius, radius + 1): for x in range(-radius, radius + 1): tap = uv + vec2(x, y) texel # Comparison sampler: 1.0 if storeddepth > provideddepth, else 0.0 sampleval = texture(shadowmap, vec3(tap, ndc.z)) occlusion += 1.0 - sampleval # 8. Average Occlusion occlusion = occlusion / float(kernelsize kernelsize) # 9. Edge Fade edge = max(abs(uv.x - 0.5), abs(uv.y - 0.5)) 2.0 fade = 1.0 - smoothstep(SHADOWFADESTART, 1.0, edge) # 10. Final Result return occlusion fade shadowparams.z Applies a fixed bias and a uniform 3x3 kernel without dynamic slope scaling or edge fading, trading geometric precision for simplicity. Time Complexity: O(R^2) per fragment, where R is the PCF radius. With R=4, this requires 81 texture samples per fragment. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per fragment, plus the shadow map texture size. Strengths: Reduces peter-panning and shadow acne by scaling bias with surface slope. Fades occlusion at the shadow map periphery to prevent hard cutoff artifacts. Limitations: Performance cost increases quadratically with kernel radius. Relies on a single shadow map. The edge fade is a heuristic. When to Use: Static or semi-static scenes with a dominant directional light. When visual continuity at shadow map boundaries is required for volumes or terrain. When Not to Use: Scenes with many dynamic shadow-casting objects where performance is critical. When physically accurate soft shadows are required. Implemented in the VoxelPhase engine. It addresses peter-panning via normal-offset bias and hard shadow edges via distance-based fading. The slope-scaled bias technique is a standard shadow mapping optimization, while the edge fade adapts it for volume rendering to prevent black artifacts at map boundaries. migaelstrydom/VoxelPhase, https://github.com/migaelstrydom/VoxelPhase, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: PCF Shadow Mapping
head: Percentage-Closer Filtering Shadows, Soft Shadow Mapping
body: PCF Shadow Mapping renders soft shadows by comparing a fragment's light-space depth against a pre-rendered depth texture using a 3×3 sampling grid with Percentage-Closer Filtering (PCF) to produce soft shadow edges. It builds on PCF Shadow Lookup with Slope Scaling and Edge Fade by applying a fixed bias and a uniform 3×3 kernel without dynamic slope scaling or edge fading, trading geometric precision for simplicity. Inputs and Outputs Input: Fragment world position (FragPos), light-space transformation matrix (lightSpaceMatrix), shadow map texture (shadowMap), bias value (bias). Output: Shadow factor (shadow) in range [0, 1], where 0 is fully lit and 1 is fully shadowed. Data Structures Shadow Map: A 2D depth texture of resolution 4096 \times 4096. Bias: A scalar float, typically 0.001. Steps 1. Transform the fragment's world position to light space: fragPosLightSpace = lightSpaceMatrix \times vec4(FragPos, 1.0). 2. Perform perspective divide to obtain normalized device coordinates (NDC): projCoords = \frac{fragPosLightSpace.xyz}{fragPosLightSpace.w}. 3. Map coordinates from the [-1, 1] range to the [0, 1] texture coordinate range: projCoords = projCoords \times 0.5 + 0.5. 4. Fetch the closest depth from the shadow map at the projected 2D coordinates: closestDepth = texture(shadowMap, projCoords.xy).r. 5. Extract the current fragment's depth from light space: currentDepth = projCoords.z. 6. Compute the texel size for filtering: texelSize = \frac{1.0}{4096.0}. 7. Initialize the shadow accumulator to 0.0. 8. Loop x from -1 to 1 and y from -1 to 1: Sample the shadow map at offset (x, y) \times texelSize. Compare currentDepth - bias against the sampled depth. Add 1.0 if the fragment is in shadow (i.e., currentDepth - bias > pcfDepth), else add 0.0. 9. Average the 9 samples: shadow = \frac{accumulator}{15.0}. Note: The divisor 15.0 is used in the source implementation despite a 3×3 grid having 9 samples. 10. If the fragment depth exceeds 1.0 (outside the light frustum), force shadow to 0.0 (fully lit). Formula The shadow factor is computed as: shadow = \frac{1}{15} \sum{x=-1}^{1} \sum{y=-1}^{1} \text{step}(pcfDepth, currentDepth - bias). Where: pcfDepth is the sampled shadow map depth. currentDepth is the fragment's light-space depth. bias prevents self-shadowing artifacts. Parameters bias: 0.001 (hardcoded offset to prevent shadow acne/peter-panning). shadowMap resolution: 4096 \times 4096. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Shadow Acne vs. Peter-Panning: A fixed bias mitigates shadow acne but may cause peter-panning if too large or fail if too small. Out-of-Frustum Sampling: Fragments with depth z > 1.0 are explicitly clamped to 0 shadow to avoid sampling undefined depth values. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pcfshadowmapping(fragpos, lightspacematrix, shadowmap, bias=0.001): # 1. Transform to light space fragposlightspace = lightspacematrix vec4(fragpos, 1.0) # 2. Perspective divide projcoords = fragposlightspace.xyz / fragposlightspace.w # 3. Map to [0, 1] projcoords = projcoords 0.5 + 0.5 # 10. Check if outside light frustum if projcoords.z > 1.0: return 0.0 # 4. Fetch closest depth closestdepth = texture(shadowmap, projcoords.xy).r # 5. Current fragment depth currentdepth = projcoords.z # 6. Compute texel size texelsize = 1.0 / 4096.0 # 7. Initialize accumulator shadowaccumulator = 0.0 # 8. PCF Sampling for x in range(-1, 2): for y in range(-1, 2): pcfdepth = texture(shadowmap, projcoords.xy + vec2(x, y) texelsize).r if currentdepth - bias > pcfdepth: shadowaccumulator += 1.0 # 9. Average (using source-specific divisor) shadow = shadowaccumulator / 15.0 return shadow Time Complexity: O(1) per fragment, specifically 9 texture lookups and comparisons. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for the shadow map, where W=4096, H=4096. Strengths: Simple to implement; produces soft shadows without complex kernel calculations. Limitations: Fixed bias can lead to artifacts (acne or peter-panning); no slope scaling or edge fading; uniform kernel size regardless of distance. When to use: When simplicity is prioritized over artifact-free soft shadows; suitable for static or simple scenes. When not to use: When high-quality soft shadows are required without bias artifacts; when dynamic bias or edge fading is needed. PCF Shadow Mapping is a technique used in real-time rendering to soften shadow edges. It is implemented in the VoxelEngine project, which uses a 3×3 grid and a fixed bias of 0.001. name: Direct Light Sampling
head: Direct Illumination Sampling, Iluminación directa
body: Direct Light Sampling is a technique for computing direct illumination by explicitly shooting a ray from an intersection point toward a light source to determine visibility and light contribution. It solves the problem of accurately modeling first-order scattering and shadows by testing occlusion along the path to the light. Unlike Light Ray Sampling, which integrates density along a fixed direction, Direct Light Sampling explicitly selects light sources and verifies geometric visibility, often using a power heuristic for unbiased estimation. Inputs: Ray r with origin and direction. Set of scene objects O. Light source l or a list of lights L. Bounce counter b. Current accumulated color c (initially [1, 1, 1]). Outputs: Final color contribution from the light path. Data Structures: LightHit: A structure containing colour (radiance), pdf (probability density), direction (unit vector to light), and distance (distance to light). ScatterEvent: Interaction point data including position, normal, and output direction. Steps: 1. Initialize: Set hit flag hl = \text{false} and accumulated color c = [1, 1, 1]. 2. Ray Intersection: Find the closest object o \in O intersected by ray r at distance t > 0. If no intersection, return background color modulated by c. 3. Light Direction: Calculate direction to light: \mathbf{dl} = \text{normalize}(\text{position}(l) - \mathbf{p}), where \mathbf{p} is the intersection point. 4. Shadow Ray: Create shadow ray rl from \mathbf{p} in direction \mathbf{dl}. 5. Light Intersection: Test intersection between rl and light l to get distance tl. 6. Occlusion Test: Find minimum distance t{min} to any object o \in O along rl. Let t{min} = \min \{ t \mid o \in O \land t = \text{intersection test}(rl, o) \land t > 0 \}. 7. Visibility Check: Update hit flag: hl \leftarrow hl \lor (tl \le t{min}). If the light is hit and closer than any occluding object, the point is directly illuminated. 8. Illumination Calculation: If using a sampler to select lights, select a random light li not equal to the current hit light. Calculate light contribution: \text{weight} = \text{powerHeuristic}(1, \text{lightHit.pdf}, 1, \text{pdf}). Add to direct light: \text{directLight} += \text{material} \rightarrow \text{evaluate}(\text{interaction}) \times \text{lightHit.colour} \times \text{weight} / \text{lightHit.pdf}. Scale by total number of lights if uniform sampling is used. 9. Recursive Bounce: If bounce counter b > 0, compute valid bounce direction \mathbf{d}, create new ray r' = \text{ray}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{d}), update c \leftarrow c \circ \text{color material}(\mathbf{p}, o), and recurse. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Ray: def init(self, origin, direction): self.origin = origin self.direction = direction class Light: def init(self, position, colour, intensity): self.position = position self.colour = colour self.intensity = intensity def intersectiontest(self, ray): # Returns distance to light if ray points to it, else infinity tolight = [self.position[i] - ray.origin[i] for i in range(3)] dist = math.sqrt(sum(xx for x in tolight)) if dist < 1e-6: return float('inf') costheta = sum(ray.direction[i]tolight[i] for i in range(3)) / dist if costheta > 0.999: return dist return float('inf') def getbackgroundcolor(direction): return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] def getvalidbouncedirection(position, normal, incomingdir): # Returns a normalized diffuse bounce direction return [normal[0], normal[1], normal[2]] def directlightsampling(r, objects, lights, bouncecount, accumulatedcolor): hl = False c = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] while True: if bouncecount < 0: if not hl: return getbackgroundcolor(r.direction) else: light = lights[0] return [c[i] (getbackgroundcolor(r.direction)[i] + light.colour[i]) for i in range(3)] closestobj = None closestt = float('inf') for obj in objects: t = obj.intersectiontest(r) if t > 0 and t < closestt: closestt = t closestobj = obj if closestobj is None: bg = getbackgroundcolor(r.direction) if not hl: return [c[i] bg[i] for i in range(3)] else: light = lights[0] return [c[i] (bg[i] + light.colour[i]) for i in range(3)] p = [r.origin[i] + closestt r.direction[i] for i in range(3)] light = lights[0] dl = [light.position[i] - p[i] for i in range(3)] dllen = math.sqrt(sum(xx for x in dl)) dl = [x/dllen for x in dl] rl = Ray(p, dl) tl = light.intersectiontest(rl) tmin = float('inf') for obj in objects: t = obj.intersectiontest(rl) if t > 0 and t < tmin: tmin = t hl = hl or (tl <= tmin) d = getvalidbouncedirection(p, closestobj.normal, r.direction) r = Ray(p, d) c = [c[i] closestobj.materialcolor[i] for i in range(3)] bouncecount -= 1 return c Parameters: sigma (Gaussian filter): Used post-processing to reduce noise, e.g., \sigma = 4. Edge Cases: No Lights: Return zero or background. Self-Intersection: Shadow ray origin should be offset slightly along normal to avoid self-intersection. Precision: Floating point errors in tl \le t{min} comparison can cause flickering; use a small epsilon. Reduces variance in direct illumination by explicitly sampling light sources, decoupling light selection from path vertex generation. Handles direct illumination for polygonal scenes using explicit triangle meshes, distinguishing itself from SDF-based approaches. Computes direct illumination by stepping along the direction to a distant light, integrating density for soft volumetric shadows. Separates attenuation into high-resolution local and low-resolution global segments for accurate first-order scattering. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot L) per pixel, where N is the number of bounces and L is the number of lights (if testing all) or O(N) if using a sampler to select one light. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per ray, excluding scene data structures. Performance: Limited by hardware constraints; launching infinite rays uniformly is not feasible for real-time FPS (>15 FPS). Post-processing filters (Gaussian, bilinear) are often applied to reduce noise. Strengths: Accurate shadowing and direct illumination; simple to implement. Limitations: High variance (noise) in complex scenes; requires many samples for convergence. The method is described in the context of Sparse Voxel Octree compression and efficiency studies, where direct illumination is added to improve visual quality by shooting rays from intersection points to light sources. It is also implemented in educational path tracers for handling different light types and ensuring visibility. name: Light Sampling for NEE
head: sampleDirectionToLight
body: Light Sampling for NEE computes direct illumination by explicitly sampling a light source and a point on its surface from a path vertex, returning the direction, probability density, and emitted radiance. It differs from Direct Illumination Sampling with Mesh Intersection by sampling emitter geometry directly rather than intersecting scene meshes. It differs from Light Ray Sampling by casting rays from the light towards the vertex rather than from the vertex towards the light. Inputs: pos: 3D position of the path vertex. sampler: Random number generator. scene: Scene containing light sources. Outputs: lightsurf: Sampled point on the light surface (position, normal ns, radiance). pdf: Probability density of the sampled direction. Le: Emitted radiance from the light towards the vertex. Data Structures: Light: Represents a light source. samplePoint(sampler, pdf): Returns a point on the light surface and its area PDF. Le(point, direction): Returns emitted radiance. importance: Scalar estimating contribution (used in variants). Steps: 1. Select Light Source: Choose a light and its selection probability p{light}. 2. Sample Light Surface: Sample a point on the light and its area PDF p{surf}. 3. Calculate Direction: Compute vector from vertex to light. 4. Calculate Distance: Compute distance. 5. Calculate Cosine: Compute cosine between light normal and direction to vertex. 6. Calculate Directional PDF: Combine selection probability, area PDF, and geometric term. 7. Return Radiance: Get radiance towards vertex. Formulas: \vec{d} = \text{normalize}(\text{light\surf.position} - \text{pos}) d = \|\text{light\surf.position} - \text{pos}\| \cos\theta = |\text{dot}(-\vec{d}, \text{light\surf.ns})| p(\vec{d}) = p{light} \cdot \frac{d^2}{\cos\theta} \cdot p{surf} Le = \text{light.Le}(\text{light\surf}, -\vec{d}) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sampledirectiontolight(pos, sampler, scene): # Step 1: Select light source and probability light, plight = scene.samplelight(sampler) # Step 2: Sample point on light surface and area PDF lightsurf, psurf = light.samplepoint(sampler) # Step 3: Direction from vertex to light dirvec = normalize(lightsurf.position - pos) # Step 4: Distance dist = length(lightsurf.position - pos) # Step 5: Cosine of angle between light normal and direction to vertex costheta = abs(dot(-dirvec, lightsurf.ns)) # Step 6: Directional PDF (area PDF converted to solid angle PDF) pdf = plight (dist2 / costheta psurf) # Step 7: Emitted radiance towards vertex Le = light.Le(lightsurf, -dirvec) return Le, pdf, dirvec, dist Parameters: plight: Probability of selecting the light source. psurf: PDF of the sampled point relative to the light's surface area. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Cosine: If \cos\theta \approx 0, the geometric term d^2/\cos\theta becomes unstable. Clamp \cos\theta to a small epsilon or skip the sample. Zero Distance: If the vertex lies on the light surface, d \approx 0 causes division by zero or numerical noise. Offset the vertex slightly along the normal or handle as a boundary case. PDF Mismatch: The directional PDF formula assumes the area PDF p{surf} is defined per unit area; ensure consistency with the light's sampling distribution. Selects per-vertex lights proportional to each light's estimated contribution (Light::importance) plus a 15% uniform floor. The same probability mass function (PMF) is reused for Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) when a BSDF ray hits an emitter. The scene maps hit shapes to light indices to enable O(1) emitter PDF calculation via Light::pdfLiHit, eliminating dynamic casts over all lights. The uniform floor weight is fixed at 15% of the total probability mass. Attempts to use importance sampling to choose which light source to sample (e.g., sun vs. sky) to reduce noise. In practice, this approach increased visual noise because the darker sky was rarely sampled but carried a very high weight when sampled, producing bright blue pixels amidst unaffected ones. The effect was tested with 16 and 64 samples per light. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample when light selection and PDF calculation are direct. Without shape-to-light mapping, selection scales with the number of lights. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Directly samples emitters to compute direct illumination, improving estimator stability for direct light paths. Limitations: Poorly calibrated importance weights can increase variance, as seen when sampling dark lights with high weights. Described in volumetric path tracing implementations that sample lights and surfaces to compute direct illumination. Variants addressing light selection strategies and importance weighting have been documented in rendering engine development and academic projects.
