name: Physically-Based Rendering (PBR) Lighting
head: Burley BRDF, Disney PBR, Disney PBR Lighting, Disney-GGX BRDF Model, Metallic-Roughness PBR, PBR Material Shading, Physically-Based Rendering
body: Calculates direct lighting contributions for surface points using a physically-based shading model that separates diffuse and specular components, driven by metallic-roughness material inputs. It differs from its parent Direct Lighting and Shading by replacing the non-standard GGX-like specular term and Lambertian diffuse with the Burley diffuse model and a microfacet specular model, providing energy-conserving, view-dependent shading. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: baseColor (vec3, RGB), mrSample (vec4, RGBA), surface normal n (vec3), view direction v (vec3), light direction l (vec3). Output: PBRInfo struct containing precomputed dot products and material parameters for the shading evaluation. Data Structures The PBRInfo struct holds the following fields: NdotL: float NdotV: float NdotH: float LdotH: float VdotH: float perceptualRoughness: float reflectance0: vec3 reflectance90: vec3 alphaRoughness: float diffuseColor: vec3 specularColor: vec3 n: vec3 v: vec3 Steps 1. Extract Material Properties: Extract perceptualRoughness from mrSample.g (green channel). Extract metallic from mrSample.b (blue channel). Clamp perceptualRoughness to [cMinRoughness, 1.0], where cMinRoughness = 0.04. Clamp metallic to [0.0, 1.0]. 2. Calculate Alpha Roughness: Compute alphaRoughness = perceptualRoughness perceptualRoughness. 3. Calculate Diffuse Color: Define f0 = vec3(0.04). Compute diffuseColor = baseColor.rgb (vec3(1.0) - f0). Apply metallic factor: diffuseColor = 1.0 - metallic. 4. Calculate Specular Color: Compute specularColor = mix(f0, baseColor.rgb, metallic). 5. Calculate Grazing Reflectance: Determine reflectance as the maximum component of specularColor. Compute reflectance90 = clamp(reflectance 25.0, 0.0, 1.0). Set reflectance0 = specularColor. 6. Compute Dot Products: Compute NdotL = dot(n, l). Compute NdotV = clamp(abs(dot(n, v)), 0.001, 1.0). Compute half-vector h = normalize(l + v). Compute NdotH = dot(n, h). Compute LdotH = dot(l, h). Compute VdotH = dot(v, h). 7. Populate PBRInfo: Fill the PBRInfo struct with the calculated values: NdotL, NdotV, NdotH, LdotH, VdotH, perceptualRoughness, reflectance0, reflectance90, alphaRoughness, diffuseColor, specularColor, n, v. Shading Evaluation Once PBRInfo is populated, the shading contributions are calculated as follows: 1. Diffuse Contribution (Burley Model): Compute f90 = 2.0 LdotH LdotH alphaRoughness - 0.5. Compute diffuse term: \text{diffuse} = \frac{\text{diffuseColor}}{\pi} \times (1.0 + f90 \times (1.0 - \text{NdotL})^5) \times (1.0 + f90 \times (1.0 - \text{NdotV})^5) 2. Specular Fresnel Term: Compute: F = \text{reflectance0} + (\text{reflectance90} - \text{reflectance0}) \times \text{clamp}(1.0 - \text{VdotH}, 0.0, 1.0)^5 3. Geometric Attenuation (Schlick-GGX): Compute rSqr = alphaRoughness alphaRoughness. Compute attenuation for light: \text{attenuationL} = \frac{2.0 \times \text{NdotL}}{\text{NdotL} + \sqrt{\text{rSqr} + (1.0 - \text{rSqr}) \times \text{NdotL}^2}} Compute attenuation for view: \text{attenuationV} = \frac{2.0 \times \text{NdotV}}{\text{NdotV} + \sqrt{\text{rSqr} + (1.0 - \text{rSqr}) \times \text{NdotV}^2}} Return attenuationL attenuationV. 4. Microfacet Distribution (Trowbridge-Reitz): Compute roughnessSq = alphaRoughness alphaRoughness. Compute denominator factor: f = (\text{NdotH} \times \text{roughnessSq} - \text{NdotH}) \times \text{NdotH} + 1.0 Return distribution: D = \frac{\text{roughnessSq}}{\pi \times f^2} Parameters MPI: 3.141592653589793. cMinRoughness: 0.04. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def vec3(r, g=0.0, b=0.0): return [r, g, b] def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def normalize(v): mag = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) if mag == 0.0: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] return [v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag] def mix(a, b, t): return [a[i] + t(b[i] - a[i]) for i in range(3)] def clamp(x, lo, hi): return max(lo, min(hi, x)) def calculatepbrinfo(basecolor, mrsample, n, v, l): # 1. Extract and clamp material properties perceptualroughness = mrsample[1] metallic = mrsample[3] cminroughness = 0.04 perceptualroughness = clamp(perceptualroughness, cminroughness, 1.0) metallic = clamp(metallic, 0.0, 1.0) # 2. Calculate alpha roughness alpharoughness = perceptualroughness perceptualroughness # 3. Calculate diffuse color f0 = vec3(0.04) diffusecolor = [basecolor[i] (1.0 - f0[i]) for i in range(3)] diffusecolor = [diffusecolor[i] (1.0 - metallic) for i in range(3)] # 4. Calculate specular color specularcolor = mix(f0, basecolor, metallic) # 5. Calculate grazing reflectance reflectance = max(specularcolor) reflectance90 = clamp(reflectance 25.0, 0.0, 1.0) reflectance0 = specularcolor # 6. Compute dot products ndotl = dot(n, l) ndotv = clamp(abs(dot(n, v)), 0.001, 1.0) h = normalize([l[i] + v[i] for i in range(3)]) ndoth = dot(n, h) ldoth = dot(l, h) vdoth = dot(v, h) # 7. Populate PBRInfo struct pbrinfo = { 'NdotL': ndotl, 'NdotV': ndotv, 'NdotH': ndoth, 'LdotH': ldoth, 'VdotH': vdoth, 'perceptualRoughness': perceptualroughness, 'reflectance0': reflectance0, 'reflectance90': reflectance90, 'alphaRoughness': alpharoughness, 'diffuseColor': diffusecolor, 'specularColor': specularcolor, 'n': n, 'v': v } return pbrinfo def evaluatediffuse(pbrinfo): ldoth = pbrinfo['LdotH'] alpharoughness = pbrinfo['alphaRoughness'] ndotl = pbrinfo['NdotL'] ndotv = pbrinfo['NdotV'] diffusecolor = pbrinfo['diffuseColor'] f90 = 2.0 ldoth ldoth alpharoughness - 0.5 term1 = 1.0 + f90 math.pow(1.0 - ndotl, 5.0) term2 = 1.0 + f90 math.pow(1.0 - ndotv, 5.0) return [(diffusecolor[i] / math.pi) term1 term2 for i in range(3)] def evaluatefresnel(pbrinfo): reflectance0 = pbrinfo['reflectance0'] reflectance90 = pbrinfo['reflectance90'] vdoth = pbrinfo['VdotH'] f = [reflectance0[i] + (reflectance90[i] - reflectance0[i]) math.pow(clamp(1.0 - vdoth, 0.0, 1.0), 5.0) for i in range(3)] return f def evaluategeometry(pbrinfo): alpharoughness = pbrinfo['alphaRoughness'] ndotl = pbrinfo['NdotL'] ndotv = pbrinfo['NdotV'] rsqr = alpharoughness alpharoughness denoml = ndotl + math.sqrt(rsqr + (1.0 - rsqr) ndotl ndotl) attenuationl = (2.0 ndotl) / denoml if denoml != 0 else 0.0 denomv = ndotv + math.sqrt(rsqr + (1.0 - rsqr) ndotv ndotv) attenuationv = (2.0 ndotv) / denomv if denomv != 0 else 0.0 return attenuationl attenuationv def evaluatedistribution(pbrinfo): alpharoughness = pbrinfo['alphaRoughness'] ndoth = pbrinfo['NdotH'] roughnesssq = alpharoughness alpharoughness f = (ndoth roughnesssq - ndoth) ndoth + 1.0 return roughnesssq / (math.pi f f) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: NdotV is clamped to a minimum of 0.001 to avoid division by zero or instability in the geometric term when the view vector is nearly perpendicular to the normal. Boundaries: Roughness is clamped to a minimum of 0.04 (cMinRoughness) to prevent numerical issues associated with perfectly smooth surfaces in this specific approximation. Degenerate Input: If l + v is zero (light and view directions are opposite), the half-vector h is undefined. The pseudocode assumes l + v is non-zero; in practice, this case implies the light is behind the viewer, which may result in zero lighting contribution anyway. Not given in the sources. This method is derived from the Disney PBR shading model, specifically the implementation found in the "cgue22-greed" project repository. It is based on microfacet theory, which represents real-world materials using BRDF, normal distribution, geometry, and Fresnel terms. The model splits the BRDF into a diffuse term using the Burley approximation and a specular term using the Trowbridge-Reitz normal distribution function. It is used in the context of direct volume rendering to calculate lighting at surface intersections determined by ray marching and iso-surface extraction. name: Blinn-Phong Relighting
head: Real-time Lighting Adjustment, Semantic Blinn-Phong Relighting
body: Blinn-Phong Relighting is a technique for adjusting the illumination of a scene in real-time by scaling the parameters of the Blinn-Phong shading model. It solves the problem of static lighting in pre-computed or neural scene representations by allowing dynamic modification of ambient, diffuse, and specular contributions without retraining the underlying geometry or appearance model. It differs from Physically-Based Rendering (PBR) Lighting [6815-physically-based-rendering-pbr-lighting.md] by using a simplified, non-physical specular term that is computationally cheaper and easier to tune for artistic or specific simulation effects, such as night-time urban scenes. The method relies on the standard Blinn-Phong shading equation, where the final color is a sum of ambient, diffuse, and specular components. The core mechanism for relighting is the scaling of the model's lighting coefficients during inference or rendering. Inputs: Scene representation (e.g., Gaussian primitives, neural hash encoding) containing albedo, normal, and optionally semantic fields. Lighting parameters: ambient coefficient ka, diffuse coefficient kd, specular coefficient ks, and specular exponent \beta (or k). Light positions and directions. Camera position and viewing direction. Outputs: Rendered pixel color. Data Structures: The scene representation stores per-point or per-primitive attributes. In UrbanIR, these include albedo \mathbf{a}, normal \mathbf{n}, and semantic label s. In TexGS-VolVis, primitives store opacity and color attributes that are modulated by lighting coefficients. Lighting parameters are global scalars or per-light vectors. Steps: 1. Retrieve Attributes: For a given ray intersection point \mathbf{x}(\mathbf{r}), retrieve the surface normal \mathbf{n}, albedo \mathbf{a}, and semantic label s from the scene representation. 2. Compute Half-Vector: Calculate the half-vector \mathbf{h} between the view direction \mathbf{v} (from \mathbf{x} to camera) and the light direction \mathbf{l} (from \mathbf{x} to light source). \mathbf{h} = \frac{\mathbf{l} + \mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{l} + \mathbf{v}\|} 3. Calculate Specular Term: Compute the specular intensity using the dot product of the normal and the half-vector, raised to the power of the specular exponent \beta (or k). \text{specular} = (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{h})^\beta If \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{h} < 0, the specular term is zero. 4. Scale Parameters: Apply the user-defined scaling factors to the base Blinn-Phong coefficients ka, kd, ks, \beta. This is the primary relighting step. ka' = ka \cdot \alphaa, \quad kd' = kd \cdot \alphad, \quad ks' = ks \cdot \alphas, \quad \beta' = \beta \cdot \alpha\beta \alpha represents the user-specified scaling factor. 5. Compute Final Color: Combine the components. \mathbf{C} = ka' \mathbf{a} + kd' (\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{l}) + ks' \text{specular} The diffuse term typically uses the Lambertian cosine law \max(0, \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}). Formulas: Standard Blinn-Phong: \mathbf{C} = ka \mathbf{a} + kd \mathbf{a} (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}) + ks (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{h})^\beta UrbanIR Spotlight Diffuse Radiance: \mathbf{L}^i{\text{dif}}(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{1}{\|\mathbf{o}^iL - \mathbf{x}(\mathbf{r})\|^2} \left( l \cdot \mathbf{d}^iL \right)^k where l = \frac{\mathbf{o}L^i - \mathbf{x}(\mathbf{r})}{\|\mathbf{o}^iL - \mathbf{x}(\mathbf{r})\|}. UrbanIR Night-time Shading: \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}) \left( \sum \mathbf{L}{\text{dif}}^i \mathbf{D}i \mathbf{V}i + \mathbf{L}{\text{amb}} \right) + \sumi \mathbf{L}^i{\text{spec}} For sky regions S(\mathbf{r}) \in \text{sky}, \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \mathbf{L}{\text{sky}}(\mathbf{r}). Parameters: ka: Ambient coefficient. kd: Diffuse coefficient. ks: Specular coefficient. \beta or k: Specular exponent/shininess. In UrbanIR, k modulates spotlight intensity decay with angle. \mathbf{o}^iL: Center of spotlight i in \mathbb{R}^3. \mathbf{d}^iL: Direction of spotlight i in \mathbb{R}^3. \gamma: Specular strength inherited from semantic field for car regions in UrbanIR. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Normals: If \mathbf{n} is zero or undefined, the specular term is zero. Back-facing Surfaces: If \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l} < 0, the diffuse term should be zero. Precision: Scaling parameters can lead to overexposure if not clamped. Semantic Dependency: In UrbanIR, specular effects on cars depend on accurate semantic segmentation. Simulates night-time scenes by defining headlights and street lights, illuminating the scene with specular and lens flare effects. It uses the Blinn-Phong model for specular reflection on car regions, inheriting the specular strength \gamma from the semantic field. Outdoor relighting adjusts sun position/color and sky color. It uses a spotlight model with center \mathbf{o}^iL and direction \mathbf{d}^iL, where diffuse radiance decays with distance and angle modulated by constant k. Lens flares are approximated using image-based compositing. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel for shading, assuming constant-time retrieval of scene attributes. Real-time performance is achievable due to the simplicity of the Blinn-Phong model. Memory Complexity: Depends on the scene representation. UrbanIR uses hash tables for geometry and appearance. Strengths: Real-time adjustability, low computational cost, ease of implementation. Limitations: Non-physical specular term, less accurate than PBR for complex materials. When to Use: Real-time applications, night-time simulation, artistic control. When Not to Use: Physically accurate rendering, complex material interactions. The Blinn-Phong shading model was introduced by James F. Blinn in 1977. It is a modification of the Phong reflection model, using the half-vector instead of the reflected view vector for specular calculation. It has been widely used in computer graphics for its balance between visual quality and computational efficiency. Recent applications include TexGS-VolVis for volume visualization editing and UrbanIR for large-scale urban scene inverse rendering. TexGS-VolVis: Expressive Scene Editing for Volume Visualization via Textured Gaussian Splatting., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2025.3634643, fetched 2026-10-30 UrbanIR: Large-Scale Urban Scene Inverse Rendering from a Single Video, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv66043.2025.00052, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Light Propagation Volumes
head: Real-time Volumetric Radiance Propagation, Voxel-based Global Illumination
body: Light Propagation Volumes (LPV) simulates first-bounce indirect illumination by discretizing the scene into a 3D grid of cells, where each cell stores a directional distribution of radiance. It differs from voxel cone tracing by using a continuous uniform grid with spherical harmonic encoding rather than a sparse octree, and from cascade variants by relying on a single global grid structure. Inputs: Scene geometry and light sources. Outputs: A radiance field stored in the LPV grid, sampled during deferred shading. Data Structures: The LPV grid is a 3D uniform grid of cells. Each cell stores a directional radiance distribution encoded as 2nd-order spherical harmonics (SH), requiring 9 coefficients per color channel (RGB) for a total of 27 floats per cell. Steps: 1. Grid Initialization: Initialize all cells to zero radiance. 2. Direct Lighting Injection: Identify cells containing directly lit surfaces using reflective shadow maps or similar techniques. For each lit surface point, determine the incident light color and surface normal. Construct a radiance distribution centered around the surface normal, facing away from the surface, with color based on the surface material. Inject this distribution into the cell's SH coefficients. 3. Light Propagation: Iterate for a fixed number of propagation steps N. In each step, every cell analyzes the radiance fields of its immediate neighbors. Each cell modifies its own radiance based on the incoming radiance from all directions from its neighbors. The number of steps N controls the extent of light propagation. 4. Final Gathering: Sample the grid during the deferred shading pass to apply indirect diffuse lighting to dynamic objects. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Grid resolution is not given in the sources. Propagation steps N control the reach of indirect light; higher values increase accuracy but cost more. SH order is fixed at 2nd order. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Temporal stability issues and flickering occur if the number of lights or cells is insufficient for moving lights. Light leaking occurs when indirect light incorrectly bleeds through thin geometry due to insufficient grid resolution. Improper tuning of grid dimensions causes significant memory overhead or performance bottlenecks. Boundary conditions are not given in the sources. Uses a full octree to allow variable resolution, prioritizing proximity to geometry and reflected light over viewer proximity, solving slow propagation in uniform grids. Time Complexity: Depends on grid size and propagation steps. Each propagation step requires neighbor communication for all cells. Memory Complexity: Proportional to grid volume \times SH coefficients (27 floats/cell). Strengths: Real-time capable, simulates first-bounce indirect illumination, handles dynamic light sources and moving geometry without static rebaking. Limitations: Flickering with moving lights if grid/light count is low. Light leaking through thin geometry due to insufficient resolution. Improper tuning of grid dimensions causes significant memory overhead or performance bottlenecks. When to use: Real-time global illumination where first-bounce indirect light is desired and uniform grid overhead is acceptable. Introduced by Kaplanyan. Kaplanyan et al. later developed a cascade variant (CLPV). It is primarily designed for diffuse indirect illumination in real-time applications. name: Octree Light Propagation Volumes
head: Light Propagation Volumes with Octrees, Octree LPV
body: Octree Light Propagation Volumes (OLPV) is a real-time global illumination technique that represents Light Propagation Volumes using a full octree data structure to allow light from regular point light sources to be injected, enabling faster propagation and rendering by performing propagation at lower resolutions for distant areas. It sets itself apart from its sibling Cascaded Light Propagation Volumes by using a single hierarchical volume covering the same world space with varying resolutions, prioritizing proximity to scene geometry and reflected indirect light rather than viewer proximity. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Scene geometry, omnidirectional point light sources, Reflective Shadow Maps (RSMs). Outputs: A merged uniform Light Propagation Volume (LPV) M used for rendering indirect illumination. Data Structures: 1. Octree Levels (Oi): A full octree with l = \log2(n) + 1 levels, where n is the base resolution (a power of two). Level i=0 has size n \times n \times n. Level i has size (n/2^i) \times (n/2^i) \times (n/2^i). Memory is laid out linearly, allocating all nodes down to a pre-defined level, allowing index/address computation for any node. 2. Index Volume (Ii): A hierarchy of structures Ii for i=0, \dots, l-1 that store integer indices indicating which octree level to sample for a given world space position. Layout: Same 3D grid layout as the data storage. Size: I0 has size n \times n \times n. Content: Integer indices 0, \dots, l-1. Initialization: All elements Ii(x,y,z) are initialized to l-1. Purpose: Stores the octree level to sample for a given world space position. Lower values indicate proximity to geometry/reflected light. Numbered Steps: 1. Light Injection: Render the scene from each light source into six Reflective Shadow Maps (RSMs). Convert the texels in the RSMs into Virtual Point Lights (VPLs). Inject the contributions of the VPLs into the octree level O0 using the same method as the original LPV technique (two-band spherical harmonics). 2. Downsampling: For each level i from 1 to l-1, populate element Oi(x,y,z) by averaging the corresponding eight elements from the previous level O{i-1}. This step is performed after and without interaction with the injection step. Oi(x, y, z) = \frac{1}{8} \sum{\hat{x}=2x}^{2x+1} \sum{\hat{y}=2y}^{2y+1} \sum{\hat{z}=2z}^{2z+1} O{i-1}(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z}) The indices \hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z} range over the children of (x,y,z) in the previous level. 3. Index Volume Population: The index volume I is populated to reflect the octree structure. Generally, lower values are assigned close to geometry and higher values in empty areas. The specific algorithm for populating I is not detailed in the provided notes, but it determines the sampling level. 4. Propagation: Perform light propagation individually on each level of the octree using an iterative process where each element receives contributions from surrounding elements. Use the light propagation scheme from Kaplanyan and Dachsbacher [KD10], which includes maintaining a separate grid containing the geometry of the scene. Light on lower levels (coarser resolution) propagates further each iteration, achieving coverage of the entire scene with fewer iterations. Number of iterations k=4. Propagation factor p=3. 5. Merging: After propagation, sample the octree using the sampling function S(x,y,z) to get values, then merge them into a single traditional uniform LPV M. M(x, y, z) = S(x, y, z) This step is necessary because directly sampling all levels of the octree and index volume during rendering is impractical. 6. Rendering: Render the scene using the merged single LPV M. Use the exact same rendering step as in the traditional LPV technique. The volume is sampled only once in each 4 \times 4 region to allow for high quality shadows while maintaining reasonable performance. Sampling Function: When sampling the octree (for merging or debugging), the world position is mapped to an element in the index volume. The value in the index volume is used to do a second mapping into the correct octree level. The complication is that there are l index volume elements that could be picked for each world space position. To solve this, the element containing the minimum value is used. I(x, y, z) = \mini \left( Ii \left( \left\lfloor \frac{x}{2^i} \right\rfloor, \left\lfloor \frac{y}{2^i} \right\rfloor, \left\lfloor \frac{z}{2^i} \right\rfloor \right) \right) The resulting sampling in the octree corresponds to: S(x, y, z) = O{I(x,y,z)} \left( \left\lfloor \frac{x}{2^{I(x,y,z)}} \right\rfloor, \left\lfloor \frac{y}{2^{I(x,y,z)}} \right\rfloor, \left\lfloor \frac{z}{2^{I(x,y,z)}} \right\rfloor \right) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def creategrid(dim): return [[[0.0] dim for in range(dim)] for in range(dim)] def copygrid(grid): dim = len(grid) return [[[grid[i][j][k] for k in range(dim)] for j in range(dim)] for i in range(dim)] def octreelightpropagationvolumes(scene, lights, n, k=4, p=3): l = int(math.log2(n)) + 1 # 1. Initialize Octree Levels and Index Volume O = [creategrid(n // (2i)) for i in range(l)] I = [creategrid(n) for in range(l)] # Initialize Index Volume to max level for i in range(l): for x in range(n): for y in range(n): for z in range(n): I[i][x][y][z] = l - 1 # 2. Light Injection # Renders scene from each light into 6 RSMs, converts texels to VPLs. # Injects VPL contributions into O[0] using standard LPV injection (2-band SH). # 3. Downsampling for i in range(1, l): prevlevel = O[i-1] currlevel = O[i] dimcurr = len(currlevel) for x in range(dimcurr): for y in range(dimcurr): for z in range(dimcurr): sumval = 0.0 for dx in range(2): for dy in range(2): for dz in range(2): sumval += prevlevel[2x + dx][2y + dy][2z + dz] currlevel[x][y][z] = sumval / 8.0 # 4. Populate Index Volume (I) # Algorithm not detailed in sources; typically assigns lower indices near geometry. # Populates I based on geometry proximity; lower values near geometry. # 5. Propagation for i in range(l): # Uses Kaplanyan and Dachsbacher [KD10] scheme with geometry occlusion. # Standard LPV propagation: each element receives contribution from neighbors # scaled by propagation factor p and rotated/scalar adjusted for SH. newgrid = copygrid(O[i]) #... propagation logic... O[i] = newgrid # 6. Merging M = creategrid(n) for x in range(n): for y in range(n): for z in range(n): minidx = l - 1 for i in range(l): idxi = I[i][x // (2i)][y // (2i)][z // (2i)] if idxi < minidx: minidx = idxi level = minidx ox = x // (2level) oy = y // (2level) oz = z // (2level) M[x][y][z] = O[level][ox][oy][oz] return M Time Complexity: Propagation is performed on each level individually. Light on lower levels (coarser resolution) propagates further, reducing the total number of iterations required from k=16 (uniform LPV) or k=32 (theoretical) to k=4. This increases propagation speed by almost 60%. Memory Complexity: Uses a full octree, which is highly inefficient for sparse data but suitable here because larger nodes represent coarse data. The index volume adds overhead. Measured Performance: Renders the Sponza scene at 9 fps, outperforming the original LPV technique by 8% on an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 480. NVIDIA's CLPV implementation reaches 60-80 fps with a single directed light source, whereas this implementation uses 18 RSMs. Strengths: Faster propagation due to fewer iterations; allows injection of regular point light sources; simpler memory access patterns than sparse pointer-based octrees. Limitations: Full octrees are memory inefficient for sparse data; small intensity variations between levels exist but have little visual impact; sampling all octree levels in the rendering pipeline is impractical, requiring a merge step. When to use: When proximity to scene geometry and reflected indirect light is prioritized over viewer proximity, and point light injection is desired. When not to use: When memory is extremely constrained and the scene is very sparse, or when viewer-centric cascading is preferred. Origin: Proposed by John David Olovsson and Michael Doggett in 2013. History: Builds on the original Light Propagation Volumes technique by Kaplanyan and Dachsbacher [KD10] and the concept of storing pre-computed indirect illumination using spherical harmonics by Sloan et al. [SKS02]. It contrasts with Crassin et al.'s sparse pointer-based octree technique. Usage: Implemented using OpenSceneGraph with osgCompute and CUDA for real-time rendering. Tested on the Sponza dataset. Used in NVIDIA's CLPV implementation as a reference for propagation parameters. Octree Light Propagation Volumes, https://lup.lub.lu.se/record/4002700, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Octree Light Propagation Volumes, https://core.ac.uk/download/83664325.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Octree Light Propagation Volumes, https://core.ac.uk/download/83664325.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Octree Light Propagation Volumes, https://core.ac.uk/works/100893913, fetched 2026-11-03 (unofficial)

name: Reflection Probes
head: Localized Environment Maps
body: Reflection probes approximate incoming radiance by storing sparse environment maps at specific locations in the scene, trading spatial precision for increased angular resolution. Unlike precomputed lighting methods that bake static data, reflection probes can be updated dynamically to capture dynamic global illumination. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of reflection probe positions (centers), their associated environment maps, and the surface position \mathbf{p} and normal \mathbf{n} of the fragment being shaded. Output: The reflected radiance Lr at \mathbf{p}. Data Structures: Reflection Probe: A struct containing center (3D vector), rotation (3x3 matrix), and environmentmap (cubemap or texture array). Environment Map: A texture where each texel stores RGB radiance values corresponding to a specific viewing direction. Steps: 1. Probe Selection: Identify the nearest reflection probe to the surface point \mathbf{p}. 2. Direction Calculation: Calculate the view direction \mathbf{v} from the surface to the camera. Calculate the reflection direction \mathbf{r} using the surface normal \mathbf{n}: \mathbf{r} = 2(\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n})\mathbf{n} - \mathbf{v} 3. Lookup: Transform \mathbf{r} into the probe's local coordinate system and sample the environment map E. This yields the incoming radiance L{in}. 4. Shading: Compute the reflected radiance using the material's BRDF fr: Lr = fr(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{r}) \cdot L{in} Parameters: Update Rate: How frequently the environment maps are re-rendered. Can be static, per-frame, or temporal. Resolution: The resolution of the cubemap faces. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Distance Deviation: If an object is far from the environment map's center, reflections deviate significantly from reality. Occlusion: Standard environment maps do not account for occlusion between the probe center and the surface. If the probe is inside an object or blocked by geometry, incorrect radiance is sampled. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def normalize(v): mag = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 return (v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag) def shadewithreflectionprobe(surfacepoint, surfacenormal, cameraposition, probes): nearestprobe = None mindist = float('inf') for probe in probes: dx = surfacepoint[0] - probe.center[0] dy = surfacepoint[1] - probe.center[1] dz = surfacepoint[2] - probe.center[2] dist = (dxdx + dydy + dzdz)0.5 if dist < mindist: mindist = dist nearestprobe = probe if nearestprobe is None: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) viewdirection = normalize((cameraposition[0] - surfacepoint[0], cameraposition[1] - surfacepoint[1], cameraposition[2] - surfacepoint[2])) dot = (viewdirection[0] surfacenormal[0] + viewdirection[1] surfacenormal[1] + viewdirection[2] surfacenormal[2]) reflectiondirection = (2.0 dot surfacenormal[0] - viewdirection[0], 2.0 dot surfacenormal[1] - viewdirection[1], 2.0 dot surfacenormal[2] - viewdirection[2]) R = nearestprobe.rotation localreflection = ( R[0][0]reflectiondirection[0] + R[0][1]reflectiondirection[1] + R[0][2]reflectiondirection[2], R[1][0]reflectiondirection[0] + R[1][1]reflectiondirection[1] + R[1][2]reflectiondirection[2], R[2][0]reflectiondirection[0] + R[2][1]reflectiondirection[1] + R[2][2]reflectiondirection[2]) # Not given in the sources: standard cubemap face selection and UV interpolation radiance = nearestprobe.environmentmap.lookup(localreflection) # Not given in the sources: standard material BRDF evaluation return radiance Parallax correction addresses the deviation error when a surface point is far from the probe center. It assumes incident lighting comes from a sphere with finite size. Instead of using the direct reflection direction, a ray is cast from the surface location through the reflection direction to intersect a light sphere. The direction from the probe center to this intersection point is used as the look direction, effectively fixing the environment map in space relative to the light source geometry. Choose this variant when probe-surface distance is large relative to the probe radius. Planar reflections reuse the regular scene representation by rerendering it from a different perspective and storing the result in a texture for the final render pass. They differ from localized environment maps by providing exact geometric reflections for flat surfaces rather than approximating them with spherical sampling. Choose this variant for mirror-like planar surfaces. Pitfall: requires a separate render pass for each mirror surface, which becomes prohibitively costly, especially when dealing with recursive reflections. Reflection proxies generalize reflection probes by allowing any ray-intersectable shape (not just spheres centered at the probe) to define the lookup volume. They differ from standard probes by matching the proxy's shape and size to the surface's local geometry, yielding higher spatial accuracy. Choose this variant when surface curvature or geometry deviates significantly from spherical symmetry. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. O(1) per fragment for lookup, assuming nearest probe is pre-selected or spatially hashed. Probe update cost is O(N) where N is the number of probes and resolution. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. O(P R^2) where P is the number of probes and R is the cubemap resolution. Strengths: High angular resolution; supports dynamic scenes if updated per-frame. Limitations: Poor spatial accuracy for objects far from probe centers; no occlusion handling in standard maps. When to use: For accurate surface reflections in dynamic scenes where volumetric scattering is not the primary concern. When not to use: For volumetric scattering integration or when high spatial precision of incident radiance is required across large areas. Reflection probes, also known as localized environment maps, were introduced as a real-time alternative to precomputed lighting for capturing dynamic global illumination. The technique trades spatial precision for angular resolution by sparsely distributing environment maps throughout the scene. Parallax correction was introduced by Brennan to mitigate distance-related errors by assuming incident lighting originates from a finite sphere. The method is widely used in real-time engines for specular reflections and indirect lighting approximation. name: Ambient Occlusion via Geometry/Neighbors
body: This family of methods estimates local ambient occlusion in volume rendering by querying discrete voxel occupancy, geometric distances, or gradient-weighted density to approximate visibility, avoiding expensive global ray tracing or screen-space depth buffers. Unlike JAOCC Shading which uses fixed cubic neighborhoods, or Local Ambient Occlusion which integrates transmittance along stochastic rays, these techniques determine occlusion factors by directly evaluating geometric distance, neighbor occupancy, or gradient-weighted density, offering a computationally cheaper alternative suitable for real-time or interactive applications. Builds on Local illumination, shadows and ambient occlusion. Estimates local ambient occlusion by querying geometric representations like Signed Distance Fields or structured voxel grids to approximate visibility without explicit ray tracing against triangle meshes or screen-space depth buffers. It sets itself apart from JAOCC Shading and Local Ambient Occlusion by directly evaluating geometric distance to determine occlusion factors. A voxel-based technique that computes a depth-weighted dimming factor by counting non-empty neighbors in a cubic neighborhood. It addresses hard, physically implausible lighting transitions at voxel boundaries by dynamically computing the normal of the cut voxel face from the local neighborhood geometry instead of using fixed AABB edge normals. Estimates the blocking of indirect light by analyzing local density distribution or sampling stochastic rays around a point, rather than relying on global geometry or hard shadow maps. Unlike siblings that use Signed Distance Fields [2527-ambient-occlusion-via-sdf-geometry.md] or precomputed voxel buffers [6646-voxel-ambient-occlusion.md], these methods typically compute occlusion on-the-fly or via lightweight precomputation tailored to the volume's statistical properties, providing softer, more volumetric shadow appearances [4502-local-ambient-occlusion-lao.md]. A lightweight technique that darkens vertices based on the local density of solid voxels in their immediate neighborhood, simulating shadowing in crevices and concavities. It differs from Voxel Ambient Occlusion by operating on discrete vertex data rather than continuous volume integration, and from Gradient-based Occlusion Information Computation by relying on explicit neighbor sampling rather than analytical gradient estimation. Estimates local shadowing and indirect illumination by sampling the solidity of neighboring voxels in a discrete grid relative to a surface point's normal. Unlike ray-based approaches such as Local AO, which integrate transmittance along continuous paths, Voxel AO approximates occlusion by querying the occupancy state of adjacent grid cells, offering a computationally cheaper alternative suitable for real-time voxel engines. It differs from SDF-based methods by operating directly on discrete voxel data rather than continuous signed distance fields. Computes a view-independent occlusion metric for volume data that preserves sharp boundaries between structures, addressing the isotropic blurring inherent in simple spherical mean ambient occlusion. It differs from sibling methods like Voxel Ambient Occlusion by modulating the neighborhood mean with a gradient-based weight derived from Perona-Malik diffusion principles, ensuring that edges are not smoothed out during the occlusion calculation. Provides a computationally efficient estimate of indirect sky illumination in participating media by replacing the integration of the sky hemisphere with a single upward ray. It sets itself apart from siblings like Lighting Models by specifically addressing the "dark edge" and blue tint artifacts caused by ignoring indirect light, using a pre-integrated sky value modulated by local density. A technique that approximates the shape of unoccluded regions above the shading point via a cone to estimate occlusion of an area-light. The set of 3D unoccluded directions is modeled as a circular aperture. If the set of unoccluded directions does not resemble an ellipse or a circle, it can produce incorrect shadowing results. This method presents a lower storage requirement than horizon maps. A metric that quantifies the variation of ambient occlusion values along all directions for a voxel, allowing distinction between objects with identical scalar field values but different local structures. O{std}(p, \vec{d}) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{H} \sum{i=1}^{H} (A(p, \hat{\omega}i, \vec{d}))^2 - (\frac{1}{H} \sum{i=1}^{H} A(p, \hat{\omega}i, \vec{d}))^2} where H is the number of different directions, A is the directional occlusion function, p is the voxel, and \vec{d} is the direction vector. H: The number of different directions sampled for the ambient occlusion calculation. In simple cases with few objects (e.g., two objects with same intensity/size), using the second derivative field f''(x) as input to O{std} fails because boundaries are highlighted while interiors become near-zero, causing identical O{std} values for distinct objects. In these cases, use the original scalar field f(x) as input instead. A real-time screen-space method where ambient occlusion and halos are computed from scratch each frame, allowing interactive parameter changes without performance cost. Compute average depths using Summed Area Tables (SAT) to allow changing halo size (sizex, sizey) with no extra cost (same number of texture accesses). sizex and sizey: Resolution of the vicinity region used to compute the occlusion factor, adjustable to fine-tune results. Colorvic: The emphasizing color for depth variations, adjustable if depth variations need to be accentuated differently. factorvic: A factor controlling the perceptibility of shading modification in ambient occlusion; higher values make the modification more perceptible. Fixed functions for ambient occlusion may excessively darken certain regions while barely modifying others if depth complexity varies across the volume. Not given in the sources. name: Ambient Light Approximation
head: Ambient Lighting for Volume Clouds, Sky Ambient, Upwards Ray Approximation
body: Ambient Light Approximation simulates indirect sky illumination in participating media by integrating the sky hemisphere into a single upward-pointing light value, weighted by local cloud density to approximate shadowing. It assumes the brightest ambient contribution comes from directly above, allowing a single precalculated or runtime ray to determine occlusion instead of expensive hemisphere integration. The method requires a saturation adjustment parameter to mitigate the blue tint caused by ignoring multiple scattering. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Cloud density field (or profile), sample position, step size, transmissance, and a pre-integrated sky light color/value. Outputs: Ambient light contribution added to the sample's total illumination. Data Structures: Sky Light Value: A single color vector or scalar value representing the integrated sky hemisphere, derived via random sampling, spherical harmonics, or a fixed representative color. Ambient Density Map: For static grids, the summed density of the upward ray is precalculated and stored in a lower-resolution texture or grid. If not precalculated, it is computed via a single upward ray march. SkyLightLut / Ambient Probe: Engine implementations sample a SkyLightLut generated via atmospheric scattering for ambient color, or a baked 3rd-order Spherical Harmonic (SH) Ambient Probe if atmospheric scattering is disabled. Cloud Lut B Channel: A texture channel storing altitude-based Ambient Occlusion (AO) values. Steps: 1. Integrate Sky Light: Combine the sky hemisphere into a single light value using random sampling, spherical harmonics, or a fixed color. 2. Sample Ambient Color: Retrieve the ambient light color from the SkyLightLut or the baked Ambient Probe. 3. Calculate Upward Occlusion: Determine the shadowing factor by shooting a single ray upwards from the current sample position, or by looking up a precalculated density value. 4. Compute Ambient Weight: Calculate the ambient contribution using the formula: L{ambient} = C{sky} \cdot \text{weight}(p) \cdot e^{-\tau{up}} Where C{sky} is the sky light color/value, \text{weight}(p) is a position-based falloff factor (e.g., saturate(pow(profile, 0.5))) ensuring edges receive more light than the center, and \tau{up} is the optical depth (summed density) of the upward ray. 5. Apply Altitude AO (Optional/Engine Specific): In some implementations, an additional AO factor is applied based on altitude. This factor starts at a user-defined value at the cloud bottom, increases to 1 as altitude increases, and is multiplied by the Cloud Lut B channel. 6. Accumulate: Add the ambient light to the sample light, scaled by transmissance, sample density, and step size: L{total} += L{sample} \cdot T \cdot \rho \cdot \Delta s Where L{sample} includes the ambient contribution. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def saturate(x): return min(1.0, max(0.0, x)) def computeambientlight(samplepos, cloudprofile, skycolor, upwarddensitymap): # 1. Get upward ray optical depth (precalculated lookup for static grids) tauup = upwarddensitymap.sample(samplepos) # 2. Calculate position-based weight (edges receive more light) weight = saturate(math.pow(cloudprofile, 0.5)) # 3. Compute ambient contribution ambientlight = skycolor weight math.exp(-tauup) return ambientlight def integrateambient(samplelight, transmissance, sampledensity, stepsize, ambientlight, altitudefactor): # Apply altitude-based AO factor # Note: Exact interpolation from bottom value to 1 based on altitude is engine-specific ambientlight = ambientlight altitudefactor # Scale ambient by transmissance, density, and step size samplelight += ambientlight transmissance sampledensity stepsize return samplelight Parameters and Edge Cases: Saturation Parameter: An artist-adjustable parameter is provided to reduce the saturation of the ambient light color, correcting the blue tint caused by ignoring multiple scattering. Precision: The upward ray data is naturally blurry, allowing it to be stored in a lower-resolution grid without significant visual loss. Multiple Scattering: The method ignores multiple scattering in ambient light, which causes clouds to appear unnaturally blue. An atmosphere pass that builds a sky irradiance table to provide sky light from each surface's own sky, ensuring ground seen from orbit keeps its sky fill and terrain past the terminator is not lit by the eye's daylight. It uses a deferred lighting lookup where each pixel queries its own altitude and sun angle from the table. The data structure covers 16 altitudes by 24 sun cosines, with 6 symmetric L2 harmonics per entry in the local frame, published as a uniform atmosphereskytable. This approach costs 0.60 ms in deferred lighting passes. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample if using a precalculated texture lookup for upward density. If computing the upward ray at runtime, it is O(N{up}) where N{up} is the number of steps in the upward march. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the sky color value. O(R{low}^2) or O(R{low}^3) for the precalculated upward density map, where R{low} is the lower resolution grid size. Performance: Very fast compared to full hemisphere integration or multiple scattering calculations. The Bruneton-style variant adds a fixed cost (e.g., 0.60 ms for deferred lighting) but provides accurate sky fill for terrain. Strengths: Computationally cheap; easy to implement; provides realistic shadowing for cloud undersides. Limitations: Does not account for multiple scattering, leading to blue-tinted clouds. Assumes the sky is the primary source of ambient light, which may not hold in enclosed or heavily occluded scenes. When to Use: Real-time volume cloud rendering where performance is critical and full multiple scattering is too expensive. When Not to Use: When physically accurate multiple scattering is required, or in scenes where ground-reflected light is a significant source of ambient illumination. The method is used in real-time volumetric cloud rendering to balance visual quality and performance. It was adopted in game engines like UE4 for atmospheric scattering and implemented in various game development contexts to approximate shadowing efficiently. The Bruneton-style irradiance table approach is derived from precomputed atmospheric scattering techniques. name: Ambient Occlusion via SDF/Geometry
head: Geometry-based Ambient Occlusion, Implicit Surface AO, Distance Field AO
body: Ambient Occlusion via SDF/Geometry estimates local occlusion by querying an explicit geometric representation—such as a Signed Distance Field (SDF), a voxel grid, or a set of mesh primitives—to determine how much incoming ambient light is blocked by nearby surfaces. It differs from screen-space methods (like SSAO) by leveraging global geometric data, ensuring accurate occlusion for self-occluding or complex structures that are not visible to the camera, while avoiding the depth-buffer artifacts inherent to post-processing techniques. This family of methods shares a common computational pattern distinct from screen-space or purely statistical approaches: 1. Geometric Query: Instead of relying on a depth buffer or random ray casting against a black-box scene, the method queries a specific data structure that encodes geometry. This structure is typically an SDF (returning distance to nearest surface), a voxel grid (returning density or occupancy), or a list of primitives (returning intersection or proximity). 2. Hemisphere Sampling: The core operation involves sampling directions within the upper hemisphere defined by the surface normal \mathbf{n} at a point \mathbf{p}. 3. Occlusion Accumulation: For each sample direction, the method determines if the path to infinity (or a maximum radius) is blocked. If blocked, a weight is added to an occlusion accumulator. The weight often depends on the distance to the blocking geometry, with closer occluders contributing more to the darkening effect. 4. Normalization: The accumulated occlusion value is normalized to the range [0, 1], where 1 represents full illumination and 0 represents full occlusion. 5. Biasing: To prevent self-intersection artifacts (acne) caused by floating-point precision errors when sampling near the surface, all methods in this family apply a small bias offset along the normal \mathbf{n} before querying the geometry. Estimates occlusion by sampling an SDF along the surface normal at increasing distances, weighting closer samples more heavily. It uses the distance field to simulate light blockage based on object proximity, avoiding the unrealistic results of SSAO which relies on depth buffers. Unlike SSAO, this method leverages global geometric information stored in the SDF, providing more accurate occlusion in scenes with complex geometry or self-occlusion. Estimates visibility by querying a hierarchical voxel grid (GVDB volume) using either point sampling or ray casting. It distinguishes itself by operating directly on a voxel grid, supporting discrete point queries for speed and continuous ray casting for smoother gradients, both utilizing a tangent-space basis for rotation. A post-processing technique that estimates ambient occlusion by sampling points in a hemisphere around each pixel's surface position and checking if those points are occluded by geometry in the depth buffer. It is the first screen-space method, using only the Z-Buffer, making its cost independent of scene complexity and dependent only on output resolution. Approximates surface geometry as a collection of disk-shaped elements at mesh vertices to compute AO and bent normals analytically, avoiding the cost of ray casting. It distinguishes itself by using explicit geometric primitives (disks) rather than implicit distance fields, allowing for direct analytical occlusion calculation between primitives. Estimates AO by casting rays in random directions and numerically integrating the occlusion contribution using a distance mapping function. It differs from deterministic grid-based or screen-space methods by relying on stochastic sampling, allowing for flexible handling of complex geometry at the cost of noise and higher sample counts for convergence. Definition: A simplified ambient occlusion estimation technique that approximates occlusion based on the angle between the surface normal and the scene's upward vector, rather than ray-marching for occluders. It does not reflect the influence of nearby occluders. Step: Calculate occlusion using the dot product of the surface normal \mathbf{n} and the unit upwards vector \mathbf{u}: \text{occlusion} = 1 - (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{u}). Scale the occlusion value by a scale factor s, clamp the result to the range [0, 1], and return 1 - \text{clamp}(s \cdot \text{occlusion}, 0, 1) to produce the final brightness. Parameter: s: A scale value used to adjust the strength of the fake ambient occlusion effect. Pitfall: The method does not account for occlusion caused by nearby objects (occluders); it only considers self-occlusion relative to the upward direction. Definition: Calculates hemispheric ambient occlusion (0..1) from nearby terrain geometry by sampling along the normal direction, measuring how much the terrain rises relative to the sample distance. Step: If AO is disabled or samples \le 0, return 1. Initialize \text{occlusion} = 0. Loop i from 1 to samples: d = (\text{aoRadius} \cdot i) / \text{samples}. Sample point \mathbf{s} = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{n} \cdot d. Calculate \text{rise} = \text{heightAtExtended}(\text{field}, sx, sz) - sy. If \text{rise} > 0, add \text{clamp01}(\text{rise} / (0.9 \cdot d)) / \text{samples} to occlusion. Return \text{clamp01}(1 - \text{occlusion} \cdot \text{aoStrength}). Formula: \text{occlusion} = \sum{i=1}^{\text{samples}} \frac{\text{clamp01}(\text{rise}i / (0.9 \cdot di))}{\text{samples}}, where di = (\text{aoRadius} \cdot i) / \text{samples} and \text{rise}i = \max(0, \text{height}(s{x,i}, s{z,i}) - s{y,i}). Final AO = \text{clamp01}(1 - \text{occlusion} \cdot \text{aoStrength}). Parameter: \text{aoSamples}: number of samples; \text{aoRadius}: maximum radius; \text{aoStrength}: multiplier for the final occlusion value. Definition: An improvement over Real Ambient Occlusion that weighs samples exponentially based on their distance from the surface, giving less importance to further samples. Step: Initialize \text{sum} and \text{maxSum} to 0. Calculate the sample position \mathbf{p} by moving from the surface position \text{pos} along the normal by (i+1) \cdot \text{AOStepSize}. Add the weighted distance field value at \mathbf{p} to \text{sum}. The weight is 1 / 2^i. Add the weighted maximum possible distance (i+1) \cdot \text{AOStepSize} to \text{maxSum}. The weight is 1 / 2^i. Return the ratio \text{sum} / \text{maxSum}. Ambient occlusion via geometry relies on the availability of explicit geometric representations. SDF-based methods have been widely used in ray marching and implicit surface rendering for decades, offering a clean way to compute proximity-based shading. GVDB (GPU Voxel Database) techniques emerged with the need for efficient, hierarchical voxel processing on the GPU, allowing for dynamic geometry queries. Disk-based methods were introduced to provide analytical, precomputed AO for static meshes without the overhead of ray tracing. Monte Carlo approaches with distance mapping offer a flexible framework for integrating various geometric backends into a stochastic solver. Fake AO is a heuristic often used in early shader programming or low-end hardware where geometric queries are too expensive. name: SDF-based Ambient Occlusion
head: Signed Distance Field AO, Distance Field Ambient Occlusion, Raymarched AO
body: SDF-based Ambient Occlusion estimates local occlusion by sampling a Signed Distance Field (SDF) along the surface normal at increasing distances, weighting closer samples more heavily to simulate ambient light blockage. It approximates ambient occlusion by using the distance field itself to simulate light occlusion based on object proximity, avoiding the unrealistic results of Screen Space Ambient Occlusion (SSAO) which relies on depth buffers. Unlike SSAO, this method leverages the global geometric information stored in the SDF, providing more accurate occlusion in scenes with complex geometry or self-occlusion that might be missed by screen-space techniques. The method operates on a 3D grid where each position stores the distance to the nearest object surface. Negative values indicate the grid location is inside the object, and positive values indicate it is outside. The core algorithm samples the SDF along the surface normal \mathbf{n} at a surface point \mathbf{p}, accumulating occlusion based on the difference between the sample distance and the actual SDF value. Inputs: \mathbf{p}: Surface point in world space. \mathbf{n}: Surface normal at \mathbf{p}. map(\mathbf{x}): SDF evaluation function returning the signed distance to the nearest geometry at \mathbf{x}. N{samples}: Number of samples to take along the normal (typically 4–8). d{max}: Maximum sampling distance. bias: Small offset to prevent self-intersection (acne). Outputs: AO: Scalar occlusion factor in [0, 1], where 1 is fully lit and 0 is fully occluded. SDF Grid: A 3D array or hash map storing floating-point distances. The layout is a standard 3D grid where each position stores the distance to the nearest object surface. Typical parameter values found in implementations: N{samples}: 4 to 8. d{max}: 0.25 units. Weight decay factor: 0.85 or 0.92. Final scale factor: 0.6 or 3.0 (multiplier). 1. Initialization: Initialize accumulated occlusion O = 0.0 and weight w = 1.0. 2. Sampling Loop: For i from 0 to N{samples} - 1: a. Calculate sample distance leni. Sources vary on spacing: Quadratic spacing: leni = 0.01 + 0.02 \cdot i^2. Linear spacing: leni = \frac{d{max}}{N{samples}} \cdot i. Linear spacing (5 samples): h = 0.01 + 0.12 \cdot \frac{i}{4.0}. b. Calculate sample point \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{n} \cdot (leni + bias). The bias is typically a small positive value to push the sample slightly off the surface. c. Query SDF: di = map(\mathbf{p}i). d. Calculate occlusion contribution. If di < leni, the geometry is closer than the sample point, contributing to occlusion. Method A (Weighted Difference): O += (leni - di) \cdot w. Method B (Clamped Difference): O += \max(-(di - leni), 0.0). e. Decay weight: w = \text{decay\factor} (e.g., 0.85 or 0.92). 3. Normalization and Clamping: Method A: AO = 1.0 - \text{clamp}(scale \cdot O, 0.0, 1.0) where scale = 0.6. Method B: AO = \frac{O}{d{max} \cdot N{samples} \cdot 4.0}. Method C: AO = \text{clamp}(1.0 - 3.0 \cdot O \cdot u{ao}, 0.0, 1.0) where u{ao} is a user-defined strength multiplier. The following pseudocode combines the most common weighted difference approach with linear spacing for clarity, as specific spacing (quadratic vs linear) is a stylistic choice. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdfambientocclusion(p, n, mapfunc, numsamples=8, maxdist=0.25, bias=0.001, scale=0.6, decay=0.85): """ Calculate SDF-based Ambient Occlusion. Args: p: Surface point (vec3) n: Surface normal (vec3) mapfunc: Function returning signed distance to geometry numsamples: Number of samples along the normal maxdist: Maximum sampling distance bias: Offset to prevent self-intersection scale: Final scaling factor for occlusion decay: Weight decay factor Returns: AO factor in [0, 1] """ occ = 0.0 weight = 1.0 for i in range(numsamples): # Linear spacing for sample distance # Note: Some implementations use quadratic spacing: len = 0.01 + 0.02 i^2 leni = (maxdist / numsamples) i # Sample point along normal with bias samplepoint = p + n (leni + bias) # Query SDF dist = mapfunc(samplepoint) # Accumulate occlusion if geometry is closer than sample point # Using weighted difference approach if dist < leni: occ += (leni - dist) weight # Decay weight for subsequent samples weight = decay # Final AO calculation # Clamp to [0, 1] ao = 1.0 - clamp(scale occ, 0.0, 1.0) return ao Self-Intersection (Acne): Floating-point precision errors can cause the sample point to be slightly inside the geometry, resulting in negative distances and incorrect occlusion. A small bias offset along the normal is required. Precision: The accuracy of the AO depends on the resolution of the SDF. Low-resolution SDFs may produce blocky or inaccurate occlusion. Boundary Conditions: At the boundaries of the SDF grid, queries may return undefined or large values. Proper handling of grid boundaries is necessary. Parameter Tuning: The scale, decay, and number of samples significantly affect the visual result. Too few samples may result in noisy or inaccurate AO, while too many may be computationally expensive. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of samples per pixel. Each sample requires an SDF query, which is O(1) for a grid-based SDF or O(\log M) for a hierarchical SDF (e.g., Voxel Grid). Memory Complexity: Depends on the SDF storage. A dense 3D grid requires O(V) memory where V is the volume of the grid. Sparse representations (e.g., Octrees, VDB) can reduce this significantly. Performance: Generally faster than ray-traced AO but slower than SSAO due to the need for SDF queries. Performance scales with the number of samples and SDF resolution. Strengths: Provides accurate occlusion in global context, handles self-occlusion well, and works well with dynamic geometry if the SDF is updated. Limitations: Requires an SDF representation of the scene, which can be memory-intensive for large scenes. SDF updates can be costly. The technique was introduced by Evans, who embedded objects into a 3D grid of signed distance fields and calculated occlusion via a heuristic combining values sampled at increasing distances along the surface normal. Wright expanded on this approach by substituting the ad hoc heuristic with cone tracing, approximated by sphere tracing. The method is widely used in real-time rendering, particularly in voxel-based global illumination systems, to provide ambient occlusion that is consistent with the global geometry. name: GVDB Ambient Occlusion
head: GVDB AO, computeAmbientOcclusion
body: GVDB Ambient Occlusion is a device-side function that computes ambient occlusion at a surface point by sampling a hemisphere of directions against a voxel volume, using either point sampling or ray casting to determine occlusion weights. It is distinguished from its siblings by its explicit support for two distinct sampling modes (point vs. ray) within a single unified interface and its reliance on a precomputed random rotation vector to generate tangent-space bases, avoiding per-sample random number generation overhead. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Surface position \mathbf{p}, surface normal \mathbf{n}, a precomputed random rotation vector \mathbf{r}, the GVDB volume data structure, and parameters: N{samples} (number of hemisphere samples, max 512), R{ao} (world-space AO radius), B{ao} (bias distance, typically 10^{-3}), and M (mode: 0 for point sampling, 1 for ray sampling). Output: A float value in [0, 1] representing the ambient occlusion factor, where 1 is fully illuminated and 0 is fully occluded. Data Structures: The GVDB volume is queried via its device API. The specific internal layout of the GVDB volume (e.g., sparse voxel octree vs. dense grid) is abstracted by the query functions queryVolume (for point sampling) and raycast (for ray sampling). Steps: 1. Early Exit: If N{samples} == 0, return 1.0. 2. Tangent Space Basis Construction: Compute the tangent vector \mathbf{t} by subtracting the projection of \mathbf{r} onto \mathbf{n} from \mathbf{r}, then normalizing: \mathbf{t} = \frac{\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{n} (\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{n})}{\| \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{n} (\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{n}) \|} Compute the bitangent vector \mathbf{b} using the cross product: \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{n} \times \mathbf{t} Handle degenerate case where \mathbf{r} is parallel to \mathbf{n} by using an arbitrary orthogonal vector for \mathbf{t}. 3. Bias Application: Retrieve the bias value B{val} from the volume at position \mathbf{p} (if the volume stores bias data) or use the constant parameter B{ao}. The source notes "Get bias value from volume at pos," implying the bias might be volume-dependent, but also lists B{ao} as a parameter. We assume the parameter B{ao} is the primary offset for position backtracking. Offset the starting position along the normal: \mathbf{p}{start} = \mathbf{p} + B{ao} \mathbf{n}. 4. Hemisphere Sampling Loop: Initialize occlusionsum = 0.0. For i from 0 to N{samples} - 1: Generate a sample direction \mathbf{d}{local} in the upper hemisphere (relative to \mathbf{z}-axis). The specific method of generating these directions (e.g., uniform hemisphere, cosine-weighted) is not detailed in the source, but they must be transformed to world space. Transform \mathbf{d}{local} to world space \mathbf{d}{world} using the basis (\mathbf{t}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{n}): \mathbf{d}{world} = \mathbf{t} \cdot \mathbf{d}{local.x} + \mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{d}{local.y} + \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}{local.z} Mode 0 (Point Sampling): Query the volume at position \mathbf{p}{query} = \mathbf{p}{start} + R{ao} \mathbf{d}{world}. Let V be the returned value (density/occupancy). If V \le B{val} (or a threshold indicating surface/occlusion), add 1.0 to occlusionsum. Mode 1 (Ray Sampling): Cast a ray from \mathbf{p}{start} in direction \mathbf{d}{world} with maximum length R{ao}. If a hit is found at distance D{hit}: Compute the occlusion weight using smoothstep: w = \text{smoothstep}(1, 0, \frac{R{ao}}{D{hit}}) Add w to occlusionsum. If no hit is found, add 0.0. 5. Normalization: Return \frac{\text{occlusion\sum}}{N{samples}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeambientocclusion(p: float3, n: float3, r: float3, volume, aosamples: int, aoradius: float, aobias: float, mode: int) -> float: if aosamples == 0: return 1.0 # Construct tangent space basis # Handle degenerate case where r is parallel to n proj = dot(r, n) n tangentraw = r - proj tangent = normalize(tangentraw) bitangent = cross(n, tangent) # Offset start position to avoid self-intersection pstart = p + aobias n occlusionsum = 0.0 for i in range(aosamples): # Generate a sample direction in the upper hemisphere (local space) # Note: The specific generation method (e.g., uniform, cosine) is not specified in # Assuming a standard hemisphere sample generation function exists dlocal = samplehemisphere(i, aosamples) # Transform to world space dworld = tangent dlocal.x + bitangent dlocal.y + n dlocal.z if mode == 0: # Point sampling mode querypos = pstart + aoradius dworld value = volume.query(querypos) # "if value <= bias, add 1.0 to occlusion" # Assuming 'bias' refers to a threshold derived from aobias or volume data # The source says "Get bias value from volume at pos" but also uses aobias for position. # We use aobias as the threshold for simplicity, or a volume-derived bias if available. # Given the ambiguity, we assume a simple threshold check against a small epsilon or aobias. if value <= aobias: occlusionsum += 1.0 elif mode == 1: # Ray sampling mode hitdist = volume.raycast(pstart, dworld, aoradius) if hitdist < aoradius: # Formula: smoothstep(1, 0, aoradius / dist) # "smoothstep(1, 0, aoRadius / dist)" weight = smoothstep(1.0, 0.0, aoradius / hitdist) occlusionsum += weight else: occlusionsum += 0.0 return occlusionsum / aosamples def samplehemisphere(index: int, total: int) -> float3: # Placeholder for hemisphere sampling logic not detailed in # Standard implementation would generate uniform or cosine-weighted samples # This is a implementation detail required to make the code valid phi = 2.0 3.14159265 index / total costheta = 1.0 # Uniform hemisphere: theta is uniform in [0, pi/2] sintheta = 1.0 # This is a simplified placeholder; real implementation depends on desired distribution return float3(sintheta cos(phi), sintheta sin(phi), costheta) Parameters: aoSamples: Number of hemisphere samples. Max 512. aoRadius: World-space radius for AO sampling, controls falloff distance. aoBias: Distance in world space to backtrack position, typically 10^{-3}, used to reduce acne artifacts. AMBIENTOCCLUSIONMODE: Switch between 0 (point sampling) and 1 (ray sampling). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Acne Artifacts: Sampling at the surface can cause self-intersection due to floating-point precision. Mitigated by backtracking position by aoBias along the normal. Degenerate Normal: If the random vector \mathbf{r} is parallel to \mathbf{n}, the tangent calculation fails. A guard is required. Mode 0 Threshold: The source states "if value <= bias, add 1.0". It is unclear if "bias" refers to aoBias or a value retrieved from the volume. This ambiguity is noted. Time and Memory Complexity: Time complexity is O(N{samples}) per surface point, where N{samples} is the number of hemisphere samples. Each sample involves either a volume query or a raycast, which depends on the underlying GVDB traversal cost. Memory complexity is minimal, requiring only storage for the tangent basis and accumulator, as the volume data is accessed on-demand. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with the number of samples. Increasing aoRadius may increase raycast cost if the ray traverses more empty space before hitting geometry or reaching the limit. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Unified interface for point and ray sampling; efficient tangent space generation using precomputed random vectors; biasing reduces self-intersection artifacts. Limitations: Point sampling mode (Mode 0) may be less accurate than ray casting (Mode 1) for complex geometry; accuracy depends on the resolution and representation of the GVDB volume. GVDB Ambient Occlusion is part of the GVDB (GPU VDB) library ecosystem, which provides GPU-accelerated sparse voxel data structures. The specific implementation described here is found in unofficial sources related to adaptive sampling and reconstruction for volume visualization. It builds on the general principles of SDF/Geometry-based ambient occlusion by leveraging the GVDB volume as the geometric query structure [Parent, S1, unofficial]. name: Screen-Space Ambient Occlusion (SSAO)
head: Crytek's Screen-Space AO, SSAO (Original), Screen-Space Ambient Occlusion (SSAO) Pass
body: Screen-Space Ambient Occlusion (SSAO) is a post-processing technique that estimates ambient occlusion by sampling points in a hemisphere around each pixel's surface position and checking if those points are occluded by geometry in the depth buffer. It solves the problem of real-time ambient occlusion by approximating the occlusion integral using only 2D screen-space data (depth and normal buffers) rather than querying the full 3D scene geometry. Unlike SDF-based Ambient Occlusion which queries a signed distance field, SSAO relies on the rendered image's depth buffer, making it significantly faster but limited to visible surfaces and prone to edge artifacts. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: hitPosTex: Texture containing the world-space position of the fragment (32-bit float RGB). hitNormTex: Texture containing the surface normal of the fragment (32-bit float RGB). depthTex: Texture containing the depth value and cell size information (32-bit float). noiseTex: Texture containing random vectors for tangent space generation (32-bit float RGB). projMat: Projection matrix. viewMat: View matrix. radius: Sampling radius. NUMSAMPLES: Number of samples per pixel. Output: outVisibility: Float texture storing the final visibility factor (0.0 to 1.0). Data Structures: Sample Kernel: A pre-computed array of NUMSAMPLES 3D vectors (samples[i]) distributed in a hemisphere or sphere. TBN Matrix: A 3x3 matrix constructed from the tangent, bitangent, and normal vectors to rotate sample vectors into world space. Parameters: radius: The radius of the hemisphere used for sampling, determining the scale of occlusion. Typical values depend on scene scale. NUMSAMPLES: The number of random samples taken per pixel. Higher values improve quality but increase cost. bias: A small offset applied to the hit position to prevent self-intersection artifacts (acne). Steps: 1. Fetch Data: For each pixel coordinate coord, fetch the hit position, normal, and depth from the input textures. \mathbf{p} = \text{texelFetch}(\text{hitPosTex}, \text{coord}, 0).\text{xyz} \mathbf{n} = \text{texelFetch}(\text{hitNormTex}, \text{coord}, 0).\text{xyz} d = \text{texelFetch}(\text{depthTex}, \text{coord}, 0).\text{xyz} Discard if \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{0} (background). 2. Bias Position: Offset the hit position along the normal to avoid self-intersection. \mathbf{p}{\text{biased}} = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{n} \cdot \text{bias} The bias is often derived from the depth cell size, e.g., \text{depth\cellSize.y} / 5.0. 3. Construct TBN Matrix: Generate a tangent vector \mathbf{t} and bitangent \mathbf{b} to form a basis for rotating samples. \mathbf{t} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{n})) \mathbf{b} = \text{cross}(\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{t}) \text{TBN} = [\mathbf{t}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{n}] where \mathbf{r} is a random vector fetched from noiseTex. 4. Sample and Project: For each sample i from 0 to \text{NUM\SAMPLES}-1: a. Transform the sample vector \mathbf{s}i from tangent space to world space and scale by radius: \mathbf{s}{\text{world}} = \text{TBN} \cdot \mathbf{s}i \cdot \text{radius} b. Compute the sample position in world space: \mathbf{p}{\text{samp}} = \mathbf{p}{\text{biased}} + \mathbf{s}{\text{world}} c. Project \mathbf{p}{\text{samp}} into screen space: \mathbf{v}{\text{clip}} = \text{projMat} \cdot \text{viewMat} \cdot [\mathbf{p}{\text{samp}}, 1]^T \mathbf{v}{\text{ndc}} = \mathbf{v}{\text{clip}}.\text{xyz} / \mathbf{v}{\text{clip}}.\text{w} \mathbf{v}{\text{screen}} = \mathbf{v}{\text{ndc}} \cdot 0.5 + 0.5 5. Occlusion Check: a. Check if \mathbf{v}{\text{screen}} is within screen bounds [0, 1]. If not, the sample is out of bounds and contributes 0. b. Fetch the depth d{\text{samp}} at \mathbf{v}{\text{screen}} from depthTex. c. Perform range check: If the distance between the sample depth and the original depth exceeds the radius, the sample is too far and contributes 0. \text{rangeCheck} = (|d - d{\text{samp}}| < \text{radius}) ? 1.0: 0.0 d. Check if the sample is occluded: If the sample depth d{\text{samp}} is greater than the depth of the sample position projected into camera space (or simply comparing depths if in view space), it is occluded. \text{occlusion} += (\text{sampleDepth} < \text{length}(\mathbf{c}{\text{pos}} - \mathbf{p}{\text{samp}}) ? 1.0: 0.0) \cdot \text{rangeCheck} Note: The exact comparison depends on the coordinate space. In view space, comparing z values is sufficient if the camera looks down the negative Z axis. 6. Normalize: \text{visibility} = 1.0 - \frac{\text{occlusion}}{\text{NUM\SAMPLES}} If no samples were valid, visibility is 1.0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computessao(coord, hitPosTex, hitNormTex, depthTex, noiseTex, projMat, viewMat, radius, numsamples, samples): # 1. Fetch Data hitPos = hitPosTex.fetch(coord) hitNorm = hitNormTex.fetch(coord) depthInfo = depthTex.fetch(coord) hitDepth = depthInfo.depth depthCellSize = depthInfo.cellSize # Discard background if hitPos == vec3(0, 0, 0): return 1.0 # 2. Bias Position bias = depthCellSize.y / 5.0 hitPosBiased = hitPos + hitNorm bias # 3. Construct TBN noiseVec = noiseTex.fetch(coord) tangent = normalize(noiseVec - hitNorm dot(noiseVec, hitNorm)) bitangent = cross(hitNorm, tangent) tbn = mat3(tangent, bitangent, hitNorm) occlusion = 0.0 count = 0 # 4. Sample and Project for i in range(numsamples): # Transform sample to world space samp = tbn samples[i] samp = hitPosBiased + samp radius # Project to screen space offset = vec4(samp, 1.0) offset = projMat viewMat offset offset.xyz /= offset.w offset.xyz = offset.xyz 0.5 + 0.5 # Check bounds if all(lessThanEqual(offset.xy, vec2(1, 1))) and all(greaterThanEqual(offset.xy, vec2(0, 0))): # Fetch sample depth sampleDepth = depthTex.fetch(offset.xy).depth # Range check rangeCheck = 1.0 if abs(hitDepth - sampleDepth) < radius else 0.0 # Occlusion check # Note: In view space, if sampleDepth > hitDepth, it is occluded (assuming Z is depth) # The source uses a camera position comparison, but standard SSAO compares depths directly # if both are in the same space. Here we assume view space depth comparison. isOccluded = sampleDepth > hitDepth if isOccluded: occlusion += rangeCheck count += 1 # 6. Normalize if count > 0: visibility = 1.0 - (occlusion / count) else: visibility = 1.0 return visibility Computes mutual occlusion between scalar volumes and geometric primitives using screen-space vicinity terms for high-frequency details. Choose when rendering mixed media (volumes + streamlines) and depth perception is critical. Extends SSAO to volumes by extracting position/normal from raycasting to create a synthetic isocontour layer. Choose when applying SSAO to internal volume structures rather than just surface meshes. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the number of samples. Performance is independent of scene geometry complexity, depending only on resolution and sample count. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the input/output buffers (depth, normal, position textures) and O(S) for the sample kernel. Strengths: Real-time performance; works on any rendered geometry without scene traversal; simple to implement as a post-process. Limitations: Limited to visible surfaces (no occlusion from back-facing or occluded geometry); suffers from "halo effect" (blackened edges) if not cosine-weighted; artifacts at screen edges and depth discontinuities. When to use: Real-time applications (games, interactive medical visualization) where performance is paramount and full geometric AO is too slow. When not to use: Offline rendering requiring high accuracy; scenes with significant non-visible occlusion; when halo artifacts are unacceptable without additional filtering. SSAO was introduced by Crytek as the first screen-space method for ambient occlusion, using only the Z-Buffer to compute AO at full resolution. It was developed to provide real-time ambient occlusion for games, balancing quality and performance. The technique has been implemented in various libraries, including VTK (introduced in VTK 9.0 in July 2020 for surfaces, extended to volumes by 2023). Loos and Sloan later expanded on the approach, formulating it as Monte Carlo integration under the name "Volumetric Obscurance". ajaspe/ssvdag, https://github.com/ajaspe/ssvdag, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) Real-Time Ray Traced Voxel Global Illumination, https://doi.org/10.34626/0vdq-7m27, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Enhancing Medical Imaging Technique: Ambient Occlusion..., https://graylight-imaging.com/blog/enhancing-medical-imaging-technique-ambient-occlusion-in-volumetric-rendering/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)
