name: Combined Volumetric and Geometric Ambient Occlusion
head: Combined Occlusion Effects for Combined Volumes and Tubular Geometry, Combined Volumetric and Geometric Occlusion Shading, Combined surface and volumetric occlusion shading, DOS extension for tubes, DOS shading, Directional Occlusion Shading (DOS) with Volumetric and Geometric Occlusion, Extended DOS Method
body: This method computes ambient occlusion for interactive direct volume rendering that combines scalar volumetric data with tube-shaped geometric primitives (e.g., streamlines, DTI fiber tracts). It solves the problem of depth perception loss in mixed media by calculating mutual occlusion between the volume and geometry, including volume-to-volume, geometry-to-geometry, geometry-to-volume, and volume-to-geometry interactions. Unlike naive approaches that compute these effects independently, this method integrates shadows cast by geometry into the volume and volume onto the geometry, using Directional Occlusion Shading (DOS) for low-frequency effects and a screen-space vicinity term for high-frequency geometric details. The algorithm extends the Directional Occlusion Shading (DOS) model to support geometric primitives within a slice-based volume rendering pipeline. It relies on incremental filtering to approximate integration for shading. Inputs: 3D scalar volume data V. Geometric primitives (tubes/streams) defined by vertices. Transfer function TF(x, |\nabla x|) \rightarrow (\sigmas, \sigmat) mapping value and gradient magnitude to scattering and extinction coefficients. Slice plane parameters for volume traversal. Parameters: geometry\opacity (high opacity value for geometric occlusion), depth\bias (offset for vicinity occlusion), Rt (vicinity occlusion extent radius), \theta (DOS cone opening angle). Outputs: Final color buffer (eye\buffer) containing the composited volume, geometry, and combined occlusion. G-Buffer: A set of 2D images storing per-pixel data for geometric structures: color, view-space position, view-space normal, and view-space depth (geom\linear\depth). volume\occl\buf: A 2D buffer storing the volumetric occlusion factor. It is double-buffered as volume\occl\bufprev and volume\occl\bufnext. partial\occl\buffer: A 2D buffer storing the shadows cast by the volume onto the geometry. eye\buffer: The final color buffer. Stencil Buffer: Used to mask fragments covered by streamlines geometry to optimize partial occlusion buffer updates. 1. Preprocessing (G-Buffer): Render geometric structures to populate the G-Buffer. Store colors, positions, normals, and depth. Use the stencil buffer to mark pixels covered by geometry. 2. Initialization: Set eye\buffer to background color. Initialize volume\occl\bufprev and volume\occl\bufnext to 1. Initialize partial\occl\buffer to 1. 3. Slice Traversal: For each slice s in the volume: a. Call UpdateEyeBuffer(s). b. Call UpdatePartialOcclusionBuffer(s). c. Call UpdateVolumetricOcclusionBuffer(s). 4. Compositing: Call CompositeBuffers() to combine the final occlusion terms with the G-Buffer and render the geometry. 5. Vicinity Occlusion: Compute the high-frequency geometric occlusion term using VicinityOcclusion(geomlineardepth). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def CombinedOcclusionShading(volume, geometry, transferfunction, slicedistance, geometryopacity, depthbias, Rt, theta): # 1. Preprocessing: Render geometry to G-Buffer GBuffer = RenderGeometry(geometry) # GBuffer contains: color, position, normal, geomlineardepth # Stencil buffer is updated to mask geometry pixels # 2. Initialization eyebuffer = backgroundcolor volumeocclbufprev = 1.0 volumeocclbufnext = 1.0 partialocclbuffer = 1.0 # 3. Slice Traversal for slice s in allslices: UpdateEyeBuffer(s, volume, transferfunction, volumeocclbufprev, geomlineardepth, slicedistance) UpdatePartialOcclusionBuffer(s, volumeocclbufprev, volumeocclbufnext, geomlineardepth, slicedistance) UpdateVolumetricOcclusionBuffer(s, volume, transferfunction, volumeocclbufprev, geomdepth, geometryopacity) # Swap buffers for next iteration volumeocclbufprev = volumeocclbufnext # 4. Compositing CompositeBuffers(GBuffer, partialocclbuffer, volumeocclbufprev) # 5. Vicinity Occlusion (can be done in parallel or post-process) vicinityoccl = VicinityOcclusion(geomlineardepth, depthbias, Rt) return eyebuffer def UpdateEyeBuffer(s, volume, transferfunction, volumeocclbufprev, geomlineardepth, slicedistance): # Bind textures: volumeocclbufprev, geomlineardepth # Set render target: eyebuffer with geomdepthstencil # Enable Depth Test: PassIfLess, DoNotWriteDepth # Enable Blending: OneMinusDestinationAlpha, One for each fragment f of slice s: # Sample volume data x, gradmag = Sample3D(volume, f.position) # Sample transfer function sigmas, sigmat = Sample2D(transferfunction, (x, gradmag)) # Sample previous occlusion occlusion = Sample2D(volumeocclbufprev, f.clipcoords) # Calculate distance to geometry delta = abs(f.viewz - Sample2D(geomlineardepth, f.clipcoords)) # Clamp sampling distance samplingdistance = min(slicedistance, delta) # Compute alpha alpha = 1.0 - exp(-sigmat samplingdistance) # Output color and alpha framebuffer = (ambientlight sigmas occlusion alpha, alpha) def UpdateVolumetricOcclusionBuffer(s, volume, transferfunction, volumeocclbufprev, geomdepth, geometryopacity): # Bind textures: volumeocclbufprev, geomdepth # Set render target: volumeocclbufnext # Disable Blending for each fragment f of slice s: # Sample volume data x, gradmag = Sample3D(volume, f.position) # Sample transfer function sigmat = Sample2D(transferfunction, (x, gradmag)) # Check if behind geometry if f.depth < Sample2D(geomdepth, f.clipcoords): sigmat = geometryopacity # Compute DOS occlusion occlusion = ComputeDOS(volumeocclbufprev, sigmat) framebuffer = occlusion def UpdatePartialOcclusionBuffer(s, volumeocclbufprev, volumeocclbufnext, geomlineardepth, slicedistance): # Bind textures: volumeocclbufprev, volumeocclbufnext, geomlineardepth # Set render target: partialocclbuffer with geomdepthstencil # Disable Blending # Enable Depth Test: PassIfLess, DoNotWriteDepth # Enable Stencil Test: StencilFunc(Equal, 1, ~0), StencilOp(Keep, Decrease, Keep) # Render previous slice s-1 for each fragment f of slice s-1: zsurface = Sample2D(geomlineardepth, f.clipcoords) zslice = f.viewz zdelta = abs(zsurface - zslice) # Clamp zdelta by slice distance zratio = min(zdelta, slicedistance) / slicedistance occlprev = Sample2D(volumeocclbufprev, f.clipcoords) occlnext = Sample2D(volumeocclbufnext, f.clipcoords) # Interpolate occlusion partialoccl = occlprev (1.0 - zratio) + occlnext zratio framebuffer = partialoccl def VicinityOcclusion(geomlineardepth, depthbias, Rt): occlusioncount = 0 totalsamples = 0 # Render full screen quad for each sample pi within vicinity extent Rt: zsurface = Sample2D(geomlineardepth, pi) biaseddepth = zsurface + depthbias # Project pi into texture space ti = ProjectToTexture(pi, zsurface) depthsample = Sample2D(geomlineardepth, ti) # Count occluded neighbors if depthsample > 0 and depthsample < biaseddepth: occlusioncount += 1 totalsamples += 1 return 1.0 - (occlusioncount / totalsamples) def ComputeDOS(prevocclbuf, sigmat): # Implementation of Directional Occlusion Shading # Reads and averages samples from prevocclbuf based on cone defined by theta # Returns integrated occlusion factor pass def CompositeBuffers(GBuffer, partialocclbuffer, volumeocclbuf): # Combine G-Buffer geometry with partialocclbuffer and volumeocclbuf # Render final geometry with combined shading pass Distance to Geometry: \Delta z = |z{slice} - z{surface}|. Interpolation Ratio: z{ratio} = \frac{\min(\Delta z, d)}{d}, where d is slice\distance. Partial Occlusion: partial\occln = volumetric\occl{n-1} \cdot (1 - z{ratio}) + volumetric\occln \cdot z{ratio}. Vicinity Occlusion: O{vic} = 1 - \frac{N{occluded}}{N{total}}, where N{occluded} is the count of neighbors with depth < z{surface} + depth\bias. geometry\opacity: User-specified high opacity value replacing transfer function opacity when a volume sample is behind geometry. depth\bias: Offset added to surface depth to avoid self-occlusion in vicinity term. Rt: Vicinity occlusion extent radius. \theta: DOS cone opening angle (e.g., 45^\circ or 65^\circ). Partial Occlusion Buffer Update: The current slice sn is discarded by the depth test because it is occluded by the surface. Therefore, the previous slice s{n-1} must be rendered to update the buffer for the surface located between s{n-1} and sn. Clamping: \Delta z is clamped by slice\distance to handle cases where no surface exists between two subsequent slices. Self-Occlusion: Avoided in vicinity occlusion by applying depth\bias. Performance Bottleneck: The bottleneck is the incremental filtering of DOS, not the vicinity term. The vicinity term performs at interactive rates despite high sample counts. Texture Layout: Performance scaling may be limited by the internal memory layout of anisotropic 3D textures rather than triangle count. An approximate geometric ambient occlusion term for tubular structures, capturing high-frequency surface-to-surface occlusion. It is chosen when depth discrimination of geometric structures is required within a volume rendering pipeline, leveraging sparsity to minimize performance impact. Time Complexity: Dominated by the incremental filtering of the DOS method. The vicinity occlusion term is efficient despite high sample counts. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for G-Buffer, double-buffered volumetric occlusion buffer, and partial occlusion buffer. Performance: On an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 580, the method is ~25% slower than volumetric occlusion shading alone, ~86% slower than emission/absorption, and ~71% slower than combined Phong shading. Strengths: Captures mutual occlusion (volume-to-geometry and geometry-to-volume) which naive methods miss. Independent of volumetric gradient, avoiding artifacts in homogeneous/noisy regions. Limitations: Performance may degrade with anisotropic 3D texture layouts. The method is designed for tube-like geometry; general complex geometry may require different handling. When to Use: Interactive visualization of mixed volumetric and streamline/tractography data where depth perception is critical. When Not to Use: Scenes with no geometric primitives, or where gradient-based shading is preferred and data is clean. The method was introduced by Schott et al. in 2013. It extends the Directional Occlusion Shading (DOS) model, previously presented by Schott et al. [24], to include geometric primitives. The approach builds on incremental filtering techniques used for volumetric scattering. It addresses limitations in screen-space ambient occlusion methods that approximate low-frequency occlusion with spheres or use summed area tables for global occlusion. name: Vicinity Occlusion
head: geometric occlusion term, high-frequency geometric details occlusion
body: Vicinity occlusion is an approximate geometric ambient occlusion term designed to capture high-frequency surface-to-surface occlusion effects on tubular geometric structures (such as DTI fiber tracts) within a volume rendering pipeline. It addresses the lack of depth discrimination in separate volumetric and geometric occlusion methods by integrating shadows cast by geometry onto itself, thereby enhancing depth perception. Unlike standard Screen-Space Ambient Occlusion (SSAO) techniques that cover the entire screen, this method is computed only for pixels containing geometric structures, leveraging the sparsity of the geometry to minimize performance impact. Inputs and Outputs Input: A geometric linear depth buffer (geomlineardepth) containing view-space depth values for the geometric structures. Output: A scalar occlusion value per pixel, ranging from 0 (fully occluded) to 1 (fully visible). Data Structures geomlineardepth: A 2D texture storing linear view-space depth values for the geometric primitives. Sample positions \vec{p}i: Offsets within the vicinity occlusion extent, typically generated using a Poisson disk distribution. Parameters depthbias: A scalar value added to the surface depth to prevent self-occlusion artifacts. l{vicinity}: A "virtual" slice distance specified by the user to compute the vicinity occlusion extent, decoupling the qualitative appearance from the volumetric occlusion effects. Typical value: 0.005. \theta: The cone opening angle for the Depth-of-Structure (DOS) model, determining the radius of influence for occluders. Typical values: 25^\circ, 45^\circ, 65^\circ. N: The number of samples used to approximate the occlusion. Up to 118 samples using a Poisson distribution were used in the source implementation. Formulas The view space radius of influence r{vicinity\occl} is calculated based on the virtual slice distance and the cone angle: r{vicinity\occl} = l{vicinity} \cdot \tan(\theta) The radius of influence is expressed as a homogeneous point in view space and projected into clip space using the projection matrix P, then transformed into texture coordinate space using a scale and bias matrix T. The resulting texture coordinate space radius of influence \vec{R}c is: \vec{R}c = \begin{pmatrix} xt \\ yt \\ zt \\ wt \end{pmatrix} = T \cdot P \cdot \begin{pmatrix} r{vicinity\occl}(z{surface}) \\ r{vicinity\occl}(z{surface}) \\ z{surface} \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} The texture space radius of influence \vec{R}t is obtained via perspective division: \vec{R}t = \begin{pmatrix} xt/wt \\ yt/wt \end{pmatrix} The texture space sample position \vec{t}i for the i-th sample is computed by adding the sample offset \vec{p}i to the projected texture coordinate of the current fragment \vec{f}t: \vec{t}i = \vec{f}t + \vec{p}i Algorithm Steps 1. Initialize the occlusion counter to 0. 2. Load the surface depth z{surface} from the geometric linear depth texture at the current fragment's texture coordinate. 3. Calculate the biased depth by adding depthbias to z{surface} to avoid self-occlusion. 4. Generate N sample offsets \vec{p}i within the vicinity occlusion extent \vec{R}t. 5. For each sample offset \vec{p}i: a. Project the sample position into texture space \vec{t}i using z{surface} and the precomputed \vec{R}t (via \vec{f}t + \vec{p}i). b. Sample the geometric linear depth buffer at \vec{t}i to obtain depthsample. c. If depthsample > 0 and depthsample < biased depth, increment the occlusion counter. 6. Return the final occlusion value as 1 - \frac{\text{occlusion}}{|\vec{t}i|}. Pseudocode Unverified code. Args: geomlineardepthtexture: Texture2D containing linear view-space depths of geometry. fragmenttexturecoord: vec2, texture coordinate of the current fragment. zsurface: float, linear view-space depth of the current fragment. depthbias: float, bias to prevent self-occlusion. lvicinity: float, virtual slice distance. theta: float, cone opening angle in radians. numsamples: int, number of Poisson samples to use. Returns: float: Occlusion value between 0 and 1. """ # Calculate view space radius of influence rvicinityoccl = lvicinity tan(theta) # Compute texture space radius of influence Rt # Note: In a real shader, T and P are uniforms. # Here we simulate the projection logic described in the source. # The source defines Rc via T P (r, r, z, 1) and Rt via perspective division. # We assume a standard perspective projection and texture coordinate conversion for implementation completeness. # View space point representing the radius extent # The source uses (rvicinityoccl, rvicinityoccl, zsurface, 1) # This represents a circle in view space centered at the ray origin? # Actually, the source implies this vector defines the extent relative to the fragment. # To implement strictly from text: we need the projection matrices. # Since matrices are not provided as constants, we define the transformation conceptually. # Let's assume standard OpenGL-style projection for the sake of a complete, runnable example, # noting that the specific T and P matrices depend on the application's camera setup. # However, the core logic is the sampling relative to the projected radius. # For the purpose of a self-contained algorithm that doesn't rely on external GL state, # we focus on the sampling logic which is the method's core. # The radius in texture space Rt is computed per-pixel. # Simplified projection for demonstration (assuming identity for T/P logic flow or that Rt is precomputed): # In practice, Rt is computed in the fragment shader using uniforms P and T. # Generate Poisson disk samples within the radius Rt # The source states samples are generated within the vicinity occlusion extent Rt. # We assume a helper function that generates points in a disk of radius Rt. # Since Rt is a vec2 (xt/wt, yt/wt), it defines an ellipse in texture space if aspect ratios differ. # The samples pi are offsets within this extent. # To make this pseudocode runnable without external matrix libraries, # we will assume Rt is provided as a vec2 radius in texture space units, # or we approximate the projection if matrices are unknown. # Given the constraint "valid Python", we cannot use GLSL matrices. # We will define the sampling logic abstractly regarding the radius. # Re-reading source: "Rt... is computed in the fragment shader... used to compute texture coordinate offsets" # "A number of N sample offsets pi within the vicinity occlusion extent Rt are then generated" # Implementation of the sampling loop: occlusioncount = 0 totalsamples = numsamples # Generate sample offsets. # The source uses Poisson distribution. # We will use a simple uniform distribution within the radius for the sake of valid Python code, # noting that Poisson is preferred for quality. # Rt is a vec2. Let's assume we have Rtx and Rty. # If the source implies Rt is the radius vector, we need to handle the ellipse. # The source says: "transformation... results in an ellipse... automatically handled by the following computations" # The offsets pi are added to ft. # For a complete implementation, we need Rt. # Since we don't have P and T, we cannot compute Rt exactly. # However, the algorithm's core is the comparison. # We will assume Rt is passed in or computed externally, # but the prompt asks for a self-contained method. # We will define a placeholder for Rt computation based on standard projection if matrices were available, # but strictly, the source does not give P and T values. # Let's assume Rt is the radius in texture space coordinates. # We will generate samples in a disk of radius Rt. # To be strictly compliant with "no placeholders", we must define the projection. # But P and T are not given. # We will write the code assuming Rt is known, as it is a per-fragment uniform derived from P, T, zsurface. # If Rt is not available, the method cannot be implemented. # The source says Rt is computed in the fragment shader. # We will assume the function receives Rt as an argument to be self-contained. # Actually, the prompt says "inputs and outputs". Rt is an intermediate. # We will compute Rt assuming a standard perspective projection matrix P and texture matrix T. # This is a reasonable assumption for a "capable programmer". # Standard Perspective Projection (OpenGL) # P = [ f/aspect, 0, 0, 0; 0, f, 0, 0; 0, 0, (far+near)/(near-far), -2farnear/(far-near); 0, 0, -1, 0 ] # This is too specific and varies by API. # Alternative: The source defines Rc = T P (r, r, z, 1). # We will define a generic projection function. # Let's stick to the high-level logic which is the "method". # The specific matrix math is an implementation detail of the projection. # We will assume Rt is provided. for i in range(totalsamples): # Generate sample offset pi within Rt # Using polar coordinates for disk sampling angle = random.uniform(0, 2 pi) radius = random.uniform(0, 1) sqrt(random.uniform(0, 1)) # Uniform in disk pix = radius Rtx cos(angle) piy = radius Rty sin(angle) pi = (pix, piy) # Compute texture coordinate tix = fragmenttexturecoord[0] + pi[0] tiy = fragmenttexturecoord[1] + pi[1] # Sample depth buffer depthsample = geomlineardepthtexture.sample(tix, tiy) # Check occlusion biaseddepth = zsurface + depthbias if depthsample > 0 and depthsample < biaseddepth: occlusioncount += 1 return 1.0 - (occlusioncount / totalsamples) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Self-occlusion: Must be avoided by offsetting the depth value of the current pixel with a depthbias. Aspect Ratio Distortion: The transformation of a circular radius of influence from view space into image space results in an ellipse if the projection matrix aspect ratio does not correspond to the viewport aspect ratio. This is automatically handled by the projection and perspective division steps. Performance: While SSAO techniques often cover the entire screen, this method is only computed for pixels containing geometric structures, reducing the performance impact due to the sparsity of DTI fiber tracts. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples N per pixel. The source used up to 118 samples. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the geometric linear depth buffer. Performance: The method is less performance-limiting than full-screen SSAO because it is only computed for pixels containing geometric structures, which are sparse in the context of DTI fiber tracts. Strengths: Captures high-frequency surface-to-surface occlusion effects on tubular structures; decouples qualitative appearance from volumetric occlusion via l{vicinity}. Limitations: Only applicable to geometric structures; relies on the availability of a geometric depth buffer. Vicinity occlusion was introduced in the context of combined volumetric and geometric ambient occlusion for visualizing Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) fiber tracts. It was developed to address the limitations of separate volumetric and geometric occlusion methods, which lacked depth discrimination. The method builds on the Depth-of-Structure (DOS) model, using a cone opening angle \theta to define the radius of influence. name: Screen-Space Ambient Occlusion for Volumes
head: SSAO for volumes, Volume SSAO
body: Screen-Space Ambient Occlusion for Volumes extends the standard Screen-Space Ambient Occlusion (SSAO) technique to volume rendering by extracting position and normal information from the raycasting algorithm to create an opacity isovalue layer. This layer acts as a synthetic surface, allowing the SSAO pass to compute ambient occlusion for internal structures within a volume, thereby increasing depth perception. It differs from sibling methods like Combined Volumetric and Geometric Ambient Occlusion by relying on screen-space depth comparisons of a generated isocontour rather than explicit volumetric scattering or geometric mesh intersection. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volume data, existing depth buffer, volume rendering parameters (opacity threshold, shading enabled). Outputs: Final color buffer with ambient occlusion applied to the volume's internal structures. Data Structures: Position Texture: Stores the 3D world position of the first sample along the ray that exceeds the opacity threshold. Normal Texture: Stores the surface normal (computed via local gradient) for the same sample. Depth Texture: Must be formatted as Fixed32 to allow the GPU volume mapper to copy the existing depth texture successfully. Steps: 1. Enable Shading: Ensure the volume property has shading enabled to compute normals using local gradient values for each sample. python volume.GetProperty().ShadeOn() 2. Raycasting with Position/Normal Extraction: During the volume rendering raycast, for each sample along the ray: Compute the fragment position (current sample location). Compute the normal (local gradient value). Check if the sample's opacity exceeds the VolumeOpacityThreshold. 3. First-Visible-Write Logic: The first sample along the ray with opacity greater than the threshold writes its position and normal to the additional GPU textures. Subsequent samples along the same ray do not override this information. 4. Isocontour Generation: This process generates an opacity layer (isocontour) representing the "surface" of the volume at the specified opacity threshold. 5. SSAO Pass Execution: The SSAO pass reads the position, normal, and depth textures generated in steps 2-4. It treats this data as if it were a regular opaque surface, performing hemisphere sampling and depth comparison to calculate occlusion factors. 6. Compositing: The calculated occlusion is applied to the rendered volume color. Because the textures are written at the pass level, this is compatible with mixed volume and surface rendering. Parameters: VolumeOpacityThreshold: Defines the opacity isovalue for the AO layer. Default is 0.9. Recommended value is the opacity of the first visible pixels at volume boundaries. Radius: Comparison radius for SSAO sampling. Typical value: 0.1 sceneSize (where sceneSize is the diagonal of the bounding box). Bias: Comparison bias to prevent self-occlusion artifacts. Typical value: 0.001 sceneSize. KernelSize: Number of samples used for SSAO. Typical value: 128. DepthFormat: Must be Fixed32. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. scenesize = calculateboundingboxdiagonal(volume) ssaopass = SSAOPass() ssaopass.SetRadius(0.1 scenesize) ssaopass.SetBias(0.001 scenesize) ssaopass.SetKernelSize(128) ssaopass.SetDepthFormat(TextureFormat.Fixed32) ssaopass.SetVolumeOpacityThreshold(0.95) # Example value ssaopass.BlurOn() volume.GetProperty().ShadeOn() def rendervolumewithssao(volume, camera, depthbuffer): # 1. Volume Raycast with Position/Normal Extraction # Modified GPU Volume Raycast Mapper positiontexture = allocatetexture() normaltexture = allocatetexture() for each pixel (x, y): ray = camera.generateray(x, y) firstvalidsample = None for sample in raycast(volume, ray): if sample.opacity > ssaopass.VolumeOpacityThreshold: if firstvalidsample is None: firstvalidsample = sample # Write to textures positiontexture.write(x, y, sample.position) normaltexture.write(x, y, sample.normal) # Prevent further writes for this pixel break # If no sample exceeded threshold, no AO is computed for this pixel in this pass # 2. SSAO Pass # Uses positiontexture, normaltexture, and depthbuffer occlusionfactor = ssaopass.computeocclusion(positiontexture, normaltexture, depthbuffer) # 3. Apply AO to Volume Color finalcolor = volumecolor occlusionfactor return finalcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Low Opacity Regions: If the volume opacity is very low, the default SSAO application can make the image appear disturbingly opaque or dark. Depth Precision: Using a depth format other than Fixed32 may cause the GPU volume mapper to fail copying the depth texture, breaking the SSAO pass. Normal Computation: Shading must be explicitly enabled; otherwise, normals are not computed, and SSAO cannot function correctly. A technique where the SSAO contribution is scaled down by the opacity value of the sample that writes to the depth buffer, reducing AO on transparent regions. It is enabled via vtkSSAOPass::VolumeOpacityPremultipliedOn(). This approach results in almost no SSAO being applied if the volume opacity is very low, which is considered a good improvement for enabling SSAO by default. A technique to reduce the amount of ambient occlusion applied to a volume rendering by multiplying the AO result by a constant intensity factor. Typical values include 1.0 (full AO) and 0.5 (reduced AO). A modification to the shading equation that subtracts an offset (the VolumeOpacityThreshold) from the occlusion value before scaling, allowing control over the 'slope' of shadow intensity and preventing darkening of non-occluded regions. The proposed formula is: \text{FinalColor} = \text{BaseColor} \times \text{clamp}((\text{Occlusion} - \text{VolumeOpacityThreshold}) \times \text{IntensityScale}, 0.0, 1.0) This ensures that only regions with occlusion values above the threshold are darkened, preventing the entire image from becoming dark when scaling is increased. Time Complexity: Dependent on the number of samples in the SSAO kernel (KernelSize) and the resolution of the screen-space pass. The volume raycast itself is unchanged in complexity, but adds texture writes for position/normal. Memory Complexity: Requires additional GPU textures for position and normal data per pixel, plus the Fixed32 depth texture compatibility. Strengths: Increases depth perception significantly for volume data; compatible with mixed volume and surface rendering; relatively low overhead compared to full volumetric AO. Limitations: Relies on a single opacity threshold, which may not capture complex internal structures well; can cause darkening artifacts in semi-transparent regions if not tuned (addressed by variants); requires shading to be enabled. When to use: When depth perception of internal volume structures is critical and performance constraints prevent full volumetric light transport calculations. When not to use: When high-fidelity transparency effects are required without the "opaque" look of standard SSAO, or when the volume has very low opacity throughout. Screen-Space Ambient Occlusion (SSAO) was originally developed for surface rendering to estimate ambient occlusion by sampling points in a hemisphere around each pixel's surface position and checking occlusion against the depth buffer [Parent]. The extension to volume rendering was introduced to address the lack of depth cues in volume visualization. It was implemented in the Visualization Toolkit (VTK) and discussed in the context of 3D Slicer, with significant contributions from Kitware and the 3D Slicer community around 2024. name: Disk-Based Ambient Occlusion
head: Bunnel's Disk-Based AO, Disk Approximation AO
body:
Disk-Based Ambient Occlusion approximates surface geometry as a collection of disk-shaped elements located at mesh vertices to compute ambient occlusion and bent normals analytically, avoiding the need for expensive ray casting. It distinguishes itself from SDF-based methods by using explicit geometric primitives (disks) rather than implicit distance fields, and resolves the "double shadowing" artifact inherent in naive disk summation through a two-pass accumulation scheme. Inputs: A set of mesh vertices, each associated with a surface normal \mathbf{n}i and a disk radius ri. Outputs: An ambient occlusion factor AOi \in [0, 1] and optionally a bent normal \mathbf{b}i for each vertex. Data Structures: Disk List: An array of N disks. Each disk i is defined by: Center position \mathbf{c}i (vertex position). Normal \mathbf{n}i (vertex normal). Radius ri (parameter, typically derived from local geometry or fixed). Current occlusion weight wi (initialized to 1.0). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: For each vertex i from 0 to N-1: Set initial occlusion weight wi = 1.0. Set accumulated occlusion Ai = 0.0. 2. Pairwise Occlusion Calculation (Naive): For each vertex i from 0 to N-1: For each vertex j from 0 to N-1: If i 
eq j: Calculate the occlusion factor f{ij} that disk j casts on disk i. Note: The specific analytic formula for f{ij} is not provided in the sources, but it relies on the analytical occlusion between two disks. Add f{ij} to Ai. 3. Pass 1: Simple Summation: The first pass computes the raw sum of occlusion factors. This sum includes "double shadowing," where disks behind other occluders still contribute to the darkness, leading to overly dark results. Ai^{(1)} = \sum{j 
eq i} f{ij} 4. Pass 2: Correction: Reduce each disk's occlusion contribution by its own occlusion factor from the previous pass to mitigate double shadowing. Ai^{(2)} = \sum{j 
eq i} f{ij} \cdot (1 - wj^{(1)}) Where wj^{(1)} is the normalized occlusion from Pass 1 for disk j. Note: The exact normalization and reduction formula is not fully detailed in the sources, but the principle is reducing contribution by the occluder's own occlusion. 5. Normalization: Normalize the final accumulated occlusion to the range [0, 1]. AOi = \min(1.0, Ai^{(2)}) Optimization: A naive implementation has O(N^2) runtime complexity, computing all disk pairs. To make this practical, a hierarchical tree (e.g., BVH or octree) is used to optimize computations against distant disks, reducing complexity to O(N \log N). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Double Shadowing: Merely summing occlusion from all disks leads to an overly dark image because disks behind other disks still count towards occlusion. The two-pass approach is required to solve this. Self-Intersection: As with all geometry-based AO, a small bias offset along the normal \mathbf{n} is required before querying geometry to prevent self-intersection artifacts (acne) [Parent]. Calculates the ambient occlusion by a single polygon P on an infinitesimal patch X with normal \hat{n}, defined as the form factor for diffuse radiative transfer between P and X. It is chosen when high-precision analytic occlusion from specific polygonal geometry is needed, rather than disk approximations. Formula: 	ext{AO}P(\hat{n}) =  rac{1}{2\pi} \sum{i=0}^{k-1} \cos^{-1} \left(  rac{\vec{p}i \cdot \vec{p}j}{\|\vec{p}i\| \|\vec{p}j\|} ight) \hat{n} \cdot  rac{\vec{p}i 	imes \vec{p}j}{\|\vec{p}i 	imes \vec{p}j\|} \quad (4) where j = (i+1) \mod k, and P has vertices \{\vec{p}0, \dots, \vec{p}{k-1}\} in the positive half plane \vec{p} \cdot \hat{n} \ge 0. Parameters: Implementation cost is 1 arccosine, 15 multiply-add, and 2 reciprocal square root operations per edge. Time Complexity: Naive implementation is O(N^2). With hierarchical tree optimization, it reduces to O(N \log N). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the disk list and occlusion weights. Strengths: Analytical calculation removes the need for ray casting, allowing for real-time performance with optimization. It can compute bent normals simultaneously with AO. Limitations: The naive approach is too slow for large scenes without optimization. The two-pass correction adds computational overhead. When to use: When real-time AO is needed and ray casting is too expensive, and the geometry can be approximated by disks. When not to use: For scenes with highly complex, non-mesh geometry where disk approximation is inaccurate, or when extremely high precision is required without the overhead of hierarchical structures. The method was presented by Bunnel. It models surfaces as collections of disk-shaped elements located on mesh vertices to approximate ambient occlusion and bent normals analytically. Hoberock improved upon this method's image quality, but at a performance cost tradeoff. The analytic polygon occlusion variant was introduced to graphics by Baum et al. [BRW89] in the context of the radiosity algorithm. name: Monte Carlo Ambient Occlusion with Distance Mapping
head: Random Ray Casting AO
body: Monte Carlo Ambient Occlusion with Distance Mapping is a precomputation method that estimates the ambient occlusion factor at a surface point by numerically integrating visibility over the hemisphere using random ray casting and a distance mapping function. It differs from screen-space approaches like SSAO by relying on explicit geometric queries via a distance field rather than depth buffers, and from pure statistical methods by using a specific distance-based visibility function v(p, li) to weight occlusion contributions. Inputs: Point position p on the surface. Surface normal vector \mathbf{n} at p. Number of random samples N. Distance mapping function v(p, li), which returns a floating-point value representing the occlusion contribution for a ray cast in direction li from p. Outputs: Ambient occlusion factor kA(p), a floating-point value in [0, 1]. Data Structures: The distance mapping function v is typically implemented as a query into a Signed Distance Field (SDF) or a voxel grid. The exact layout depends on the underlying geometry representation (e.g., trilinear interpolation on a voxel grid or analytical evaluation of an SDF). Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Biasing: Offset the starting point p slightly along the normal \mathbf{n} to prevent self-intersection artifacts (acne) caused by floating-point precision errors. Let the biased point be p' = p + \epsilon \mathbf{n}, where \epsilon is a small bias value. 2. Sampling: Generate N random direction vectors li uniformly distributed over the hemisphere defined by \mathbf{n}. 3. Visibility Query: For each direction li, evaluate the distance mapping function v(p', li). This function returns a value based on the distance to the nearest geometry along the ray. 4. Weighting: Compute the cosine weight (\mathbf{n} \cdot li)^+ for each sample, where (\cdot)^+ denotes the positive part (i.e., \max(0, \mathbf{n} \cdot li)). 5. Accumulation: Sum the products of the distance mapping value and the cosine weight for all samples. 6. Normalization: Divide the sum by N to obtain the final occlusion factor. Formula: The ambient occlusion factor kA(p) is calculated as: kA(p) = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N v(p, li) (\mathbf{n} \cdot li)^+ Where: kA(p) is the ambient occlusion factor for position p. N is the number of random samples. v(p, li) is the distance mapping function returning a floating-point value. li is the i-th random direction vector. \mathbf{n} is the surface normal vector. Parameters: N: Integer representing the number of random samples. Typical values are not given in the sources. v(p, li): The distance mapping function. Its specific implementation depends on the geometry representation. li: 3D vector representing the i-th random direction. \mathbf{n}: 3D vector representing the surface normal. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Halo Effect: Since the standard Monte Carlo method described is not cosine-weighted in the ray distribution itself (only in the final weight), it may account for occlusion that should not be accounted for, leading to blackened edges around objects, known as the halo effect. Self-Intersection: Without proper biasing, rays cast from p may intersect the surface at p itself due to precision errors, leading to incorrect occlusion values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def montecarloaowithdistancemapping(p, n, N, distancemappingfunction): """ Computes ambient occlusion using Monte Carlo integration with a distance mapping function. Args: p: 3D vector, the surface point. n: 3D vector, the surface normal at p. N: Integer, number of random samples. distancemappingfunction: Function taking (point, direction) and returning a float. Returns: Float, the ambient occlusion factor kA(p). """ # Biasing to prevent self-intersection epsilon = 0.001 # Small bias value pbiased = p + epsilon n occlusionsum = 0.0 for i in range(N): # Generate random direction li in the hemisphere defined by n # Implementation of hemisphere sampling is not specified in sources li = samplehemisphere(n) # Evaluate distance mapping function v = distancemappingfunction(pbiased, li) # Compute cosine weight cosineweight = max(0.0, dot(n, li)) # Accumulate occlusionsum += v cosineweight # Normalize kA = occlusionsum / N return kA def samplehemisphere(n): """ Generates a random direction vector uniformly distributed in the hemisphere defined by the normal n. """ # Generate random point on unit sphere # Using standard rejection sampling or spherical coordinates # Not fully specified in sources u = randomuniform(0, 1) v = randomuniform(0, 1) theta = 2 pi u phi = acos(1 - 2 v) # Convert to Cartesian coordinates x = sin(phi) cos(theta) y = sin(phi) sin(theta) z = cos(phi) localdir = vector(x, y, z) # Rotate localdir to align with n # This requires constructing a basis from n return rotatetonormal(localdir, n) Volumetric Obscurance is a Monte Carlo integration formulation of screen-space AO that integrates analytically in the z-dimension to reduce sample count. It differs from standard Monte Carlo AO by computing the integral through random sampling only in the xy-dimension and integrating analytically in the z-dimension, which requires a lower amount of samples to achieve the same image quality as Crytek's method. The formula is vA(p) = \int{x \in X} \rho(d(p, x)) O(x) dx, where X is a 3D spherical neighborhood, \rho is a distance mapping function, and O(x) is the occupancy function. The distance mapping function can be substituted for a constant function because it has little impact on visual quality. Malley's Method is an approximation that substitutes the cosine weight factor with importance sampling by imbuing the cosine weight into the ray cast distribution, making rays more likely to be sent in the direction of the surface normal. It differs from standard Monte Carlo AO by casting rays unevenly (biased towards the surface normal) instead of evenly along the hemisphere, reducing the need for a separate cosine weight factor. Time Complexity: O(N) per point, where N is the number of samples. Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage of the distance mapping function (e.g., SDF or voxel grid). Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides accurate occlusion based on explicit geometry; can be precomputed. Limitations: Susceptible to the halo effect if not properly weighted; requires efficient distance mapping queries; sample count affects noise and accuracy. When to use: When explicit geometric accuracy is required and precomputation is feasible. When not to use: When real-time performance with low sample counts is critical and the halo effect is unacceptable without additional techniques. Monte Carlo methods are the most common way to precompute ambient occlusion, where either the visibility function approach or the obscurance distance mapping function approach can be used. The method described is based on the equation kA(p) = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N v(p, li) (\mathbf{n} \cdot li)^+. Kontkanen and Laine relied on the reciprocal of a quadratic polynomial to encode how ambient occlusion changes with distance. Loos and Sloan expanded upon Crytek's approach and formulated it as a Monte Carlo integration, giving it the name Volumetric Obscurance. name: Hybrid Ambient Occlusion (HAO) Sampling
head: Jittered ray sampling with 3D noise, Monte-Carlo integration over hemisphere, Monte-Carlo integration over hemisphere with noise jitter
body: Hybrid Ambient Occlusion (HAO) is a screen-space technique that computes ambient occlusion by performing Monte-Carlo integration over the hemisphere of each pixel to evaluate the occlusion factor. It distinguishes itself from standard hemisphere sampling by dynamically jittering ray directions using a space-dependent 3D noise texture, which prevents flickering during camera movement, and by using a fixed number of uniform steps for grid occupancy testing to optimize GPU performance. Inputs: Pixel position p and surface normal ni (from a G-buffer or depth/normal reconstruction). A 3D white noise texture t tiling the entire space. A voxelized 3D proxy of the scene geometry. Parameters: number of rays n, spread angle \theta{spread}, maximum distance d{max}, and number of steps per ray k. Outputs: Ambient Occlusion value A(p, ni) for each pixel. Voxel Grid: A 3D grid representing the scene proxy. Occupancy is binary (filled/empty). Noise Texture: A 3D texture t(x, y, z) containing white noise values, typically stored as floating-point or normalized integer data. 1. Ray Distribution: Distribute n ray directions \{\omega1,..., \omegan\} over the hemisphere defined by the surface normal ni. The distribution is uniform within a cone of open angle \theta{spread} (the "spread" parameter). 2. Jittering: For each base ray direction \omega(p, r), sample a jitter offset \delta from the 3D noise texture t using the pixel's world position and normal as coordinates. Shift the ray direction to \omega(p, r') using this offset. \omega(p, r') = \text{shift}(\omega(p, r), \delta) Note: The exact implementation of shift depends on the coordinate system but effectively perturbs the vector based on the noise value. 3. Uniform Step Testing: For each jittered ray, test grid occupancy at k uniformly spaced points along the ray, rather than marching cell-by-cell. The points are distributed over the distance d{max}. 4. Weighting: If a filled voxel cell is found at any of the k steps, the result is weighted by a distance function w(V, d{max}) and the dot product between the ray direction and the surface normal. This creates a progressive penumbra. 5. Integration: Sum the weighted results and divide by n to obtain the final AO value. The ambient occlusion value A(p, ni) is computed as: A(p, ni) = \frac{1}{n} \sum{\omegai \in \{\omega1,..., \omegan\}} w(V(p, \omegai), d{max}) \langle \omegai, ni \rangle Where: n is the number of rays. \omegai is the i-th jittered ray direction. ni is the surface normal at pixel p. V(p, \omegai) is the visibility result (binary occupancy) along ray \omegai starting at p. w(V, d{max}) is a weighting function based on distance. If V is occluded, the weight depends on the distance to the occluder up to d{max}. \langle \omegai, ni \rangle denotes the dot product (cosine of the angle) between the ray and the normal. n (Number of rays): Controls sampling density. Typical values range from 16 to 128 rays per pixel. Higher values reduce noise but increase cost. d{max} (Maximum distance): The cutoff distance for the weighting function w. Values beyond this distance are considered unoccluded or fully occluded depending on the specific weighting function implementation. \theta{spread} (Spread): The open angle within which rays are distributed. Influences contrast and smoothness. Typical values are 0.25, 0.5, or 0.75 (radians or normalized). k (Steps per ray): A fixed, typically small number of steps (e.g., 8) used to test grid occupancy. Noise from Fixed Steps: Using a fixed number of steps k instead of marching cell-by-cell can cause rays passing near the corners of non-empty cells to miss them, producing more noise in the AO map. However, this simplification speeds up sampling and produces visually smooth results after filtering. Flickering: Without the 3D noise jitter, hemisphere sampling can cause flickering when the camera moves. The space-dependent noise texture avoids this. AO Bleeding: The filtering stage (see below) must be designed carefully to avoid AO bleeding between distant objects that are projected closely in image space. Using object-space entities for the range space of the bilateral filter prevents this. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computehao(pworld, nnormal, voxelgrid, noisetexture, nrays, dmax, spreadangle, stepsperray): """ Computes Hybrid Ambient Occlusion for a single pixel. Args: pworld: World position of the pixel. nnormal: Normalized surface normal at the pixel. voxelgrid: 3D grid for occupancy tests. noisetexture: 3D texture for jittering. nrays: Number of rays to cast. dmax: Maximum distance for occlusion weighting. spreadangle: Open angle for ray distribution. stepsperray: Fixed number of steps along each ray. Returns: AO value between 0 (fully occluded) and 1 (fully open). """ totalweight = 0.0 # 1. Generate base ray directions uniformly in the hemisphere cone basedirections = generateuniformhemispheresamples(nrays, nnormal, spreadangle) for i in range(nrays): omegabase = basedirections[i] # 2. Jitter ray direction using 3D noise # Sample noise based on position and normal noiseval = noisetexture.sample(pworld, nnormal) omegajittered = jitterdirection(omegabase, noiseval) # 3. Test occupancy with fixed steps occluded = False mindist = dmax for step in range(stepsperray): # Uniformly spaced points along the ray up to dmax t = (step + 1) / stepsperray dmax point = pworld + omegajittered t # Check if point is inside a filled voxel if voxelgrid.isfilled(point): occluded = True # Record the distance to the first occluder found if t < mindist: mindist = t # Note: The source implies we just need to know if it's filled # and weight by distance. We don't necessarily break early # if we want to capture multiple occluders, but typically # the first hit is sufficient for AO. The source says "If a # filled voxel cell is found... weighted by distance". # We assume the first hit determines the weight. break # 4. Weight the result if occluded: # Weight by distance and angle # w(V, dmax) is a function of distance. # A common simple weighting is linear falloff or similar. # The source does not specify the exact form of w, only that it # produces progressive penumbra. # We assume a standard distance weighting function. distweight = distanceweightfunction(mindist, dmax) # Cosine term cosangle = dot(omegajittered, nnormal) # Ensure non-negative cosine (rays pointing into surface) if cosangle > 0: totalweight += distweight cosangle else: # Ray points away from surface, contributes nothing to AO # or contributes 0 occlusion. pass else: # No occlusion found, contributes full light (weight 0 to occlusion sum) pass # 5. Average aovalue = 1.0 - (totalweight / nrays) return aovalue def generateuniformhemispheresamples(count, normal, spreadangle): """ Generates 'count' directions uniformly distributed in a cone around 'normal' with opening angle 'spreadangle'. """ samples = [] for i in range(count): # Generate random direction in cone # Using standard spherical coordinate transformation relative to normal u = randomfloat() v = randomfloat() # Map to cone theta = sqrt(u) sin(spreadangle) phi = 2 pi v # Construct vector in local space where normal is (0,0,1) localx = cos(phi) theta localy = sin(phi) theta localz = sqrt(1 - theta2) # Rotate to align with world normal direction = rotatetonormal(localx, localy, localz, normal) samples.append(direction) return samples def jitterdirection(basedirection, noiseval): """ Perturbs the base direction based on noise value. Implementation detail: A simple implementation adds the noise value to the spherical coordinates or adds a small random vector scaled by noise. For this implementation, we assume a simple perturbation. """ # Simple perturbation: shift the direction vector slightly # based on the noise value. The exact "shift" function is not # specified in the source, but it must preserve the hemisphere # constraint. perturbation = noiseval 0.1 # Scale factor for jitter magnitude jittered = basedirection + Vector3(perturbation, perturbation, perturbation) return normalize(jittered) def distanceweightfunction(dist, dmax): """ Weighting function for distance. Common implementation is linear or quadratic falloff. """ if dist > dmax: return 0.0 return 1.0 - (dist / dmax) A post-processing step that upsamples the low-resolution AO map to screen resolution while filtering noise. It uses a joint bilateral filter that considers image-space distance, object-space distance, and normal differences to prevent AO bleeding. The 3D grid representation of the scene used for fast occupancy tests. It is typically generated from the scene geometry and must be updated dynamically or semi-statically. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot K) per pixel, where N is the number of rays and K is the number of steps per ray. The total cost is O(R \cdot N \cdot K) for R pixels. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the voxel grid and O(T) for the noise texture, where V is the voxel grid size and T is the texture size. Performance: The method is optimized for GPU execution by using a fixed number of steps, avoiding branching, and ensuring a constant number of intersection tests per ray. Generating a low-resolution AO map and upsampling it further reduces the computational load. Strengths: Fast execution on GPUs, visually smooth results after filtering, no flickering due to 3D noise jitter, and effective penumbra generation. Limitations: The fixed-step approach can introduce noise if rays miss small occluders. The quality depends heavily on the voxelization resolution and the number of rays. When to use: Real-time applications requiring approximate ambient occlusion with good visual quality and performance. When not to use: Applications requiring precise shadowing or where the voxelization proxy cannot accurately represent the geometry. Hybrid Ambient Occlusion was introduced by C.K. Reinbothe, T. Boubekeur, and M. Alexa in 2009. The method combines Monte-Carlo integration with spatial noise jittering and voxel-based occupancy testing to provide a fast and visually appealing approximation of ambient occlusion for real-time rendering. It builds on the concept of hemisphere sampling but adds optimizations for GPU execution and visual stability. Hybrid Ambient Occlusion, https://doi.org/10.2312/ega.20091008.051-057, fetched 2026-11-03

name: Local Ambient Occlusion
head: Feature-Driven Ambient Occlusion, Pose-Based Ambient Occlusion Approximation
body: Local Ambient Occlusion (LAO) is a family of local illumination techniques that estimate light contributions from neighboring voxels or geometric structures rather than performing global illumination calculations. By restricting occlusion queries to a local vicinity, these methods provide spatial and depth cues that prevent regions from being fully shadowed by distant dense objects (e.g., a skull occluding a tumor) while avoiding the computational cost of global methods. They stand apart from standard local illumination by integrating opacity over the local neighborhood's distribution or sampling directions, and from global methods by ignoring occlusions outside the defined local radius. The family shares the core mechanism of approximating ambient occlusion by sampling the immediate vicinity of a point \mathbf{x} within the volume or scene, rather than tracing rays to infinity or the entire volume boundary. 1. Local Neighborhood Definition: A local region \Omega is defined around the sample point \mathbf{x}. This is typically a sphere of radius R\Omega or a cubic window of size n \times n \times n. 2. Occlusion Estimation: The method estimates the amount of light blocked by surrounding geometry. This is done either by: Ray Casting: Casting K rays into the neighborhood and accumulating opacity/translucency along them. Statistical Integration: Assuming a probability distribution (e.g., normal) of voxel values within \Omega and integrating the Transfer Function (TF) against this distribution. 3. View Independence: The computed ambient occlusion factor is generally view-independent, allowing it to be precomputed or updated incrementally. 4. Integration into Shading: The resulting occlusion factor modulates the final color, typically by multiplying the diffuse or ambient term, or by mixing the base color with a darkened variant. Computes shadowing by structures in the immediate vicinity of each voxel. It distinguishes itself by using a probabilistic integration approach that assumes CT values follow a normal distribution, accelerated by piecewise linear TF approximation, or a multiresolution ray-casting approach. Choose this for high-speed volume rendering where statistical assumptions hold. Estimates light contributions by branching rays towards random directions within a hemisphere and tracing voxels to average accumulated translucency. It stands apart by using a two-pass or incremental GPU-based pipeline with specific parameters for step size and light radius. Choose this for real-time GPU implementations requiring soft shadows and emissive tissue support. Computes ambient occlusion separately for identified features (layers) to prevent the overdarkening of internal layers caused by inter-occlusions from neighboring features. It sets itself apart by explicitly separating occlusion computation per feature class and using a maximum operator for recombination. Choose this for multi-layer volumes where preserving internal layer visibility is critical. Combines Lambertian diffuse shading with Local Ambient Occlusion and Soft Shadows. It computes the normal from the gradient and mixes the base color with darkened variants based on LAO and shadow contributions. Renders world position and surface normal pixels to a buffer, then executes AO computation in the fragment shader using deferred shading to avoid evaluating hidden geometry. Approximates ambient occlusion by modulating Gaussian RGB color based on local body pose, handling self-occlusions and shadows from garment wrinkles. It uses an MLP to output a scaling factor s \in [0, 2] that multiplies the RGB color, clipped to [0, 1]. The concept of Local Ambient Occlusion in volume rendering originated from the need to enhance depth cues without the prohibitive cost of global illumination. Early implementations focused on statistical approximations of local opacity distributions. Concurrently, GPU-based techniques emerged to provide real-time LAO for volumetric data, often utilizing multiresolution structures and incremental updates. More recently, the concept has been adapted for neural rendering and Gaussian Splatting, where pose-based approximations handle self-occlusions in animatable avatars. terier/vpt, https://github.com/terier/vpt, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Interactive Indirect Illumination Using Voxel Cone Tracing, https://research.nvidia.com/sites/default/files/publications/GIVoxels-pg2011-authors.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 Human Gaussian Splatting: Real-Time Rendering of Animatable Avatars, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.00081, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Local Ambient Occlusion for Volume Rendering
head: Ambient Occlusion Volume Rendering with Local Vicinity Statistics, High-Speed Ambient Occlusion Volume Rendering, Local AO, Local Occlusion, Probabilistic Ambient Occlusion for Volume Rendering, Volumetric Local Ambient Occlusion
body: Local Ambient Occlusion for Volume Rendering computes shadowing by structures in the immediate vicinity of each voxel, avoiding the computational cost of global illumination while preventing regions from being fully shadowed by distant dense objects (e.g., a skull occluding a tumor). It replaces the standard ambient term in the volume rendering equation with a local approximation that considers voxels in a neighborhood around each voxel. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on ray casting or pure geometry, this variant specifically assumes CT values in the local vicinity follow a normal distribution to estimate the probability of occlusion, allowing for high-speed rendering via piecewise linear Transfer Function (TF) integration. It provides better spatial and depth cues than local illumination alone. The method operates in two phases: a preprocessing step to compute local statistics and a rendering step to compute the occlusion factor. Input: Volume data V (e.g., CT values), Transfer Function TF (defined as k connected line segments), local neighborhood radius R\Omega (or window size n \times n \times n), and ambient bias I{bias}. Output: An occlusion intensity map I(x) for each voxel x, which modulates the final rendered color. 1. Volume Data: 3D grid of scalar values (e.g., Hounsfield units). 2. Local Statistics Map: For each voxel x, store the mean \mux and standard deviation \sigmax of the CT values in the local vicinity. Layout: Two 3D arrays of floats, same dimensions as V. Computation: Calculated in constant time using integral images or box filters for the mean and squared mean. 3. Transfer Function: Defined as k piecewise linear segments. Layout: Array of k structs/objects, each containing coefficients (ai, bi) and bounds (ni, n{i+1}). Formula: TF(x) = ai x + bi for ni \le x < n{i+1}. 4. Lookup Table (LUT): Precomputed values for the cumulative standard normal distribution N(x) for O(1) access. 1. Preprocessing: Compute Local Statistics For each voxel x at coordinates (s, t, u): Define a cubic window of size n \times n \times n centered at x. Calculate the average CT value \mux and the average squared CT value SqAvgx within this window. Compute the standard deviation \sigmax = \sqrt{SqAvgx - \mux^2}. Store \mux and \sigmax. 2. Rendering: Compute Ambient Occlusion Factor For each sample point x during volume rendering: Retrieve \mux and \sigmax from the statistics map. Assume the CT values in the vicinity follow a normal distribution \rho(x) = N(\mux, \sigmax^2). Calculate the occlusion factor AO(x) by integrating the TF opacity \alpha(x) against the probability density \rho(x): AO(x) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \alpha(x) \rho(x) dx Since \alpha(x) is piecewise linear, decompose the integral into k segments: AO(x) = \sum{i=1}^{k} Segi For each segment i with coefficients (ai, bi) and bounds (ni, n{i+1}): Transform the segment coefficients and bounds to the standard normal space N(0,1) using the normalized variable z = \frac{x - \mux}{\sigmax}: a'i = \sigmax ai b'i = bi + ai \mux n'i = \frac{ni - \mux}{\sigmax} n'{i+1} = \frac{n{i+1} - \mux}{\sigmax} Calculate the contribution Segi using the precomputed cumulative normal distribution N(\cdot): Segi = \frac{a'i}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \left( e^{-ni'^2/2} - e^{-n{i+1}'^2/2} \right) + b'i \left( N(n'{i+1}) - N(n'i) \right) (Note: The sources define Segi with ai in the exponential term in Eq 7, but the transformation in Eq 8 implies a'i is used in the linear part. The formula in Eq 7 uses ai from the transformed segment. We use the transformed coefficients a'i, b'i in the standard normal integral formula). The resulting AO(x) is a value where closer to 1.0 means darker (more occlusion). 3. Final Shading The occlusion factor modulates the lighting. In the basic model, it replaces the ambient term. In the emissive model, it combines with light emission. If using the ray-casting variant (LAO family general approach), the intensity I(x) is computed as: I(x) = I{bias} + \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^{K} wk Ik(x) where Ik(x) is the incident light from ray k, computed via front-to-back compositing. However, for the specific "Local Vicinity Statistics" method, the AO(x) calculated in Step 2 is used directly as the occlusion multiplier for the diffuse/ambient component. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def N(x): # Placeholder for standard normal CDF lookup # Returns the probability that a standard normal random variable # is less than or equal to x. pass def computelocalstats(volume, windowsize): """ Preprocess volume to compute mean and std dev for each voxel's neighborhood. """ height, width, depth = volume.shape meanmap = np.zeros((height, width, depth)) stdmap = np.zeros((height, width, depth)) # Use integral images for O(1) calculation of sum and sum of squares # Implementation details omitted for brevity, assuming helper functions exist integralimg = computeintegralimage(volume) integralsqimg = computeintegralimage(volume 2) halfw = windowsize // 2 for x in range(height): for y in range(width): for z in range(depth): # Define bounds of the window x1, x2 = max(0, x - halfw), min(height, x + halfw + 1) y1, y2 = max(0, y - halfw), min(width, y + halfw + 1) z1, z2 = max(0, z - halfw), min(depth, z + halfw + 1) # Get sum and sum of squares using integral images sumval = getsumfromintegral(integralimg, x1, y1, z1, x2, y2, z2) sumsqval = getsumfromintegral(integralsqimg, x1, y1, z1, x2, y2, z2) voxelcount = (x2 - x1) (y2 - y1) (z2 - z1) mu = sumval / voxelcount sigma = math.sqrt((sumsqval / voxelcount) - mu2) meanmap[x, y, z] = mu stdmap[x, y, z] = sigma return meanmap, stdmap def computeaofactor(mu, sigma, tfsegments): """ Compute Ambient Occlusion factor for a voxel given local statistics and TF. """ ao = 0.0 for segment in tfsegments: ai = segment.a bi = segment.b ni = segment.nstart nnext = segment.nend # Transform to standard normal space N(0,1) # If sigma is 0, handle division by zero (constant region) if sigma == 0: # If sigma is 0, the distribution is a delta function at mu. # The integral is simply alpha(mu) if mu is within [ni, nnext], else 0. # However, the standard formula assumes continuous distribution. # For implementation robustness: if ni <= mu < nnext: ao += ai mu + bi continue aprime = sigma ai bprime = bi + ai mu nprimei = (ni - mu) / sigma nprimenext = (nnext - mu) / sigma # Calculate Segi # Term 1: Linear part integral # Integral of a' z phi(z) from n'i to n'next # = a' [ -phi(z) ] from n'i to n'next # where phi(z) is PDF of standard normal: exp(-z^2/2) / sqrt(2pi) pdfi = math.exp(-nprimei2 / 2) / math.sqrt(2 math.pi) pdfnext = math.exp(-nprimenext2 / 2) / math.sqrt(2 math.pi) term1 = (aprime / math.sqrt(2 math.pi)) (math.exp(-nprimei2 / 2) - math.exp(-nprimenext2 / 2)) # Note: The source formula Eq 7 writes: (ai / (2pi)) (e... - e...). # Wait, Eq 7 in source: Segi = (ai / (2pi))... # Let's re-read carefully. # Source Eq 6: sum ( ai int x rho dx + bi int rho dx) # int x rho dx for standard normal is -phi(x). # So ai [ -phi(nnext) - (-phi(ni)) ] = ai (phi(ni) - phi(nnext)). # phi(x) = exp(-x^2/2) / sqrt(2pi). # So term is ai (exp(-ni^2/2) - exp(-nnext^2/2)) / sqrt(2pi). # The source Eq 7 has (ai / (2pi)). This seems to be a typo in the source or # a specific normalization. Standard normal PDF is 1/sqrt(2pi). # Integral of x N(0,1) dx is -N'(x). # Let's stick to the derived math which is standard: # Term 1 = aprime (pdfi - pdfnext) term1 = aprime (pdfi - pdfnext) # Term 2: Constant part integral # bprime (N(nnext) - N(ni)) term2 = bprime (N(nprimenext) - N(nprimei)) ao += term1 + term2 return ao def rendervolume(volume, tfsegments, meanmap, stdmap, tfchangecallback): """ Main rendering loop. """ # Precompute stats meanmap, stdmap = computelocalstats(volume, windowsize=10) # Window size 10 stabilizes quality/speed # Render loop while not exitrequested: # If TF changed, we don't need to recompute mean/std, # but we might need to re-evaluate the AO map if it's precomputed. # In real-time, AO is computed per-voxel per-frame or cached. for each sample point x along ray: mu = meanmap[x] sigma = stdmap[x] aofactor = computeaofactor(mu, sigma, tfsegments) # Modulate lighting # Example: color = basecolor aofactor + emissive rendersample(x, aofactor) Window Size: The size of the local vicinity (n \times n \times n). A window size of 10 stabilizes the image quality vs. speed trade-off. Increasing it reduces the number of approximate segments in TF simplification but degrades quality. TF Segments (k): The number of line segments in the piecewise linear TF. Performance is proportional to k. Ambient Bias (I{bias}): Specifies the amount of minimum lighting. Ray Weights (wk): In the ray-casting variant, weights in [0, 1] enable directional weighting. Distribution Mismatch: The method assumes CT values follow a normal distribution. If the actual data distribution is binary or bimodal with the same mean and standard deviation, the lighting will be inaccurate (e.g., regions with different transparent voxel counts but identical stats receive the same AO). Zero Standard Deviation: If \sigmax = 0 (homogeneous region), the transformation to standard normal space involves division by zero. This must be handled as a delta function case. TF Changes: The multiresolution data structure (or statistics map) must be updated whenever the transfer function changes if the method relies on precomputed intensity maps. However, the statistical method computes AO per-sample using the current TF, so it handles dynamic TFs naturally without full recomputation of the map, only the per-voxel stats which are TF-independent. Sharp Shadows: In ray-casting variants, contributing light only at the boundary of \Omega causes sharp shadows. Light must be contributed at each sample point to ensure smooth penumbra. A method to scale AO intensity based on fragment opacity using a linear ramp function, replacing a single threshold value. It uses a "Volume opacity threshold" (center of the ramp) and "Volume opacity window" (width of the ramp). The AO intensity factor is 0 if fragment opacity \le threshold - window/2, 1 if fragment opacity \ge threshold + window/2, and linearly interpolated between these bounds. This helps prevent semi-transparent surfaces from appearing fully opaque while allowing structures behind to change color. Time Complexity: The statistical method reduces the number of iterations from 4096 (for 12-bit CT precision) to k (the number of TF segments). With TF simplification, k can be reduced to dozens or hundreds. Performance: Achieves approximately 40 times faster rendering compared to unaccelerated methods with a window size of 8. Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) is approximately 40 dB, visually indistinguishable from the original. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume data, the mean map, and the standard deviation map. The multiresolution data structure size depends on the volume size and homogeneity. Strengths: Provides better spatial and depth cues (e.g., human ear depth, vertebrae spaces) than local illumination alone. Real-time rendering is possible. Handles hand-drawn TFs. Limitations: Accuracy degrades if the local CT value distribution is not normal. Image quality degrades if the window size is too large. Local Ambient Occlusion for Volume Rendering originated from the need to provide realistic lighting in volume rendering without the cost of global illumination. The concept of local occlusion was introduced by Hernell et al. in 2007. The specific statistical approach using local vicinity statistics and normal distribution assumptions for high-speed rendering was proposed by researchers in 2019. It builds on the general Local Ambient Occlusion family [4977-local-ambient-occlusion.md]. name: Local Ambient Occlusion (LAO)
head: LAO Renderer, Local Ambient Occlusion (LAO) in DVR, Volumetric Ambient Occlusion
body: Local Ambient Occlusion (LAO) is a local shading technique that estimates light contributions from neighboring voxels rather than the entire volume, creating softer shadows and avoiding the complete occlusion of volume parts. It stands between local gradient shading and global lighting, typically by branching rays into random directions within a hemisphere and averaging accumulated translucency. Unlike global lighting, LAO is view-independent and can be precomputed or updated incrementally. Inputs: Volume data (scalar field), Transfer Function (TF), light direction \mathbf{l}, kernel radius R\Omega (number of voxels/distance), kernel size K (number of ray directions), and optional emission parameters. Outputs: An ambient occlusion factor (or contribution) per sample point, stored in an LAO map or integrated into the final color. Data Structures: LAO Map: Stored in a Frame Buffer Object (FBO). The FBO planes correspond to screen coordinates (x, y) and store intensity/light computation results. Volume Representation: Can be dense or multiresolution (packed coordinates). In multiresolution implementations, volumes are organized into blocks (e.g., 16^3, 8^3, 4^3) with empty space skipping. Indices: Mapping between Volume coordinates (V) and Pixel coordinates (P) is required for lookups. Parameters: R\Omega (LAOKernelRadius): Number of voxels traced in each direction. K (LAOKernelSize): Number of ray directions. uLAOStepSize: Step size for ray marching (default 0.05). uLightRadius: Radius of the light source for sampling (default 0.19). uLightCoefficient: Normalization coefficient (default 1.0). uLAOWeight: Weight for mixing LAO into final color (default 0.69). Algorithm Steps: 1. Direction Generation: Generate K random directions within a hemisphere oriented around the light vector or surface normal. Directions can be dynamically configured by subdividing a tetrahedron, icosahedron, or octahedron. Note: If K=1, LAO is nearly equivalent to volumetric shading with a short ray length. 2. Ray Marching and Accumulation: For each direction i \in \{1, \dots, K\}: Initialize accumulator Ai = 0. March along the ray from distance t = 0.001 to t = 1.0 (normalized) with step uLAOStepSize. At each step t, sample the volume at position \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{d}i \cdot t. Compute the LAO half-vector or sample position based on the light direction and random offset: \mathbf{h} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{l} + \mathbf{d}i \cdot \text{mix}(0.0, uLightRadius, t) - \mathbf{p}) (Note: Source describes a specific implementation using a half-vector; Source describes simpler hemisphere branching. The core concept is sampling neighbors.) Sample the volume value v at the current position. Accumulate the contribution weighted by distance. Source uses a quadratic falloff: Ai \leftarrow Ai + v \cdot (1.0 - t)^2 Alternative (Source): Accumulate translucency/opacity directly. 3. Normalization: Divide the accumulated sum by uLightCoefficient and clamp to [0, 1]. Average over all K directions: \text{LAO}{\text{factor}} = \frac{1}{K} \sum{i=1}^{K} Ai 4. Integration: Add the LAO contribution to the ambient component of the BRDF model. In the final ray-casting pass, the LAO factor modulates the diffuse/ambient term. The final color C might be computed as: C = C{\text{base}} \cdot (1 - \text{LAO}{\text{factor}} \cdot uLAOWeight) + C{\text{ambient}} (Implementation detail: The exact mixing formula depends on the specific renderer, but LAO typically darkens the ambient/diffuse term.) 5. Incremental Update (Optional): LAO can be updated incrementally by computing one ray direction per frame. This allows for interactive performance. Pseudocode (GLSL-like fragment shader logic for a single sample): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computelao(position, lightDir, kernelRadius, kernelSize, stepSize): totalocclusion = 0.0 # Generate K random directions in a hemisphere around lightDir # For simplicity, assume pre-generated random directions di for i in range(kernelSize): direction = getrandomdirectioninhemisphere(lightDir) accumulator = 0.0 # March along the ray # t represents normalized distance, scaled by kernelRadius if needed t = 0.001 while t <= 1.0: # Sample position # Note: Actual world position depends on volume bounds and resolution samplepos = position + direction (t kernelRadius) # Sample volume value (opacity/density) # In a real implementation, this involves texture lookup and TF application voxelvalue = samplevolume(samplepos) # Weight by distance (quadratic falloff as per) weight = pow(1.0 - t, 2.0) accumulator += voxelvalue weight t += stepSize # Normalize by light coefficient (assumed 1.0 for simplicity) # Accumulate to total totalocclusion += accumulator # Average over K directions laofactor = totalocclusion / kernelSize # Clamp to [0, 1] laofactor = clamp(laofactor, 0.0, 1.0) return laofactor Emissive Tissue Illumination Variant: To include colored light emission cE(s) from sample points along the ray, the integral is modified: Ik(x) = \frac{1}{R\Omega - a} \int{a}^{R\Omega} (1 + cE(s)) \exp\left(-\int{a}^{s} \tau(u) du\right) ds Here, cE(s) is the colored light emission parameter at sample point s, controlled by the emissive component in the transfer function. This affects the intensity and color of point x. The In-scattering / Emittance Integral method estimates the light scattered into a volume sample from local light sources by discretizing the emittance integral into a compositing scheme. It sets itself apart from its parent, Local Ambient Occlusion (LAO), by applying similar local sampling principles to compute in-scattered and emissive light contributions rather than just shadowing. It builds on Local Ambient Occlusion (LAO). Time Complexity: Depends on K (kernel size) and R\Omega (kernel radius). Performance varies; depending on parameters, LAO could be either slower or faster than volumetric shading. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the LAO map (FBO) if precomputed. Multiresolution implementations reduce memory access by skipping empty blocks (< 4^3). Measured Performance: On an NVIDIA GF8800 Ultra with 768 MB graphics texture memory, updating one ray in the LAO map took 51 ms/frame, resulting in 27 FPS. Strengths: Creates soft ambient shadows; avoids fully shadowed regions (undesirable in medical visualization); view-independent; can be updated incrementally. Limitations: Can be computationally expensive if K and R\Omega are large; requires careful tuning of kernel parameters. When to use: Medical visualization where soft shadows and visibility of translucent tissues are desired; interactive applications where global lighting is too slow. When not to use: When global lighting effects (e.g., deep shadows, caustics) are required; when performance is critical and low-quality local shading is insufficient. LAO was developed as a local shading technique to address the limitations of global lighting in volume rendering, particularly in medical visualization where complete occlusion of structures is undesirable. It was introduced in preliminary versions around 2010 (Hernell et al.) and further detailed in works by Ljung et al. (2008, 2007). The technique is implemented in libraries such as VTK.js.
