name: In-scattering / Emittance Integral
head: Discretized Compositing Scheme, Progressive Refinement In-scattering
body: The In-scattering / Emittance Integral method estimates the light scattered into a volume sample from local light sources by discretizing the emittance integral into a compositing scheme. It sets itself apart from its parent, Local Ambient Occlusion (LAO), by applying similar local sampling principles to compute in-scattered and emissive light contributions rather than just shadowing. It builds on Local Ambient Occlusion (LAO). Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume density field, transfer function, light source position/direction, optical properties (extinction coefficient \sigmat), and parameters R\Omega (ray count) and I{bias}. Output: In-scattered radiance contribution for each volume sample. Data Structures: Ray Buffer: Stores the direction vectors for the R\Omega samples. In the progressive refinement variant, only one direction is processed per pass. Accumulator: A buffer storing the accumulated in-scattered light, initialized to zero. Parameters: R\Omega: Number of rays used to sample the hemisphere around the light vector. Typical values are 16 or 48. I{bias}: Minimum light value clamped for a volume sample to prevent dark artifacts. Typical values are 0.0 or 0.2. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the in-scatter accumulator buffer to zero. 2. Progressive Refinement Loop: For each rendering pass k: a. Select one light direction \mathbf{d}k from the set of R\Omega directions. If R\Omega directions are not pre-generated, generate one random direction in the hemisphere oriented around the light vector. b. For each volume sample point \mathbf{x} along the ray: i. Compute the transmittance T from the light source to \mathbf{x} along direction \mathbf{d}k. This involves integrating the extinction coefficient \sigmat along the path. ii. Estimate the in-scattered light contribution L{in} using the emittance integral approximation. The contribution is weighted by the density and the phase function at \mathbf{x}. iii. Apply the bias: L{final} = \max(L{in}, I{bias}). iv. Add L{final} to the accumulator buffer for sample \mathbf{x}. 3. Accumulation: After R\Omega passes, the accumulator contains the total in-scattered light estimate. 4. Compositing: Composite the in-scattered light with the direct lighting and other illumination terms. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeinscattering(volume, lightdirections, ROmega, Ibias, sigmat): """ Computes in-scattered light using progressive refinement. Args: volume: 3D array of density values. lightdirections: List of ROmega direction vectors. ROmega: Number of rays to sample. Ibias: Minimum light value clamp. sigmat: Extinction coefficient field. Returns: inscatterbuffer: Accumulated in-scattered radiance. """ # Initialize accumulator inscatterbuffer = zeroslike(volume) # Progressive refinement: one direction per pass for k in range(ROmega): direction = lightdirections[k] # For each sample point in the volume (or along rays) for x in volumesamples: # 1. Compute transmittance from light to x along direction # This requires integrating sigmat along the path from light source to x # T = exp(-integral(sigmat ds)) transmittance = computetransmittance(lightsourceposition, x, direction, sigmat) # 2. Estimate in-scattered contribution # Lin = lightintensity phasefunction(direction, x) density(x) transmittance # Note: Exact phase function and light intensity model depends on specific implementation # mentions "emittance integral" but does not provide the full formula # We assume a standard single-scattering approximation for the direction density = volume[x] phaseval = evaluatephasefunction(direction, x) # Standard phase function evaluation lightintensity = getlightintensity(lightsourceposition, x) # Light model Lin = lightintensity phaseval density transmittance # 3. Apply bias Lfinal = max(Lin, Ibias) # 4. Accumulate inscatterbuffer[x] += Lfinal return inscatterbuffer Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Accumulating small values over many passes may lead to precision loss if not using floating-point buffers. Boundaries: Transmittance calculation near the volume boundary must handle exit/entry correctly. Degenerate Input: If density is zero, in-scatter should be zero, but bias may still apply depending on implementation. A simplified optical model that confines multiple scattering into spheres of finite radii around any given sample point, generalizing local shadowing techniques like volumetric ambient occlusion. It preintegrates light transport using a Monte-Carlo simulation for material parameters (anisotropy, extinction) and stores results in a small preintegration table. At rendering, ambient light transport is estimated via a simple texture lookup on this table. The anisotropy parameter of the phase function can be controlled interactively. This approach solves the issue of far-range scattering effects contributing little radiance due to exponential attenuation by limiting the scattering radius. Time Complexity: O(R\Omega \cdot N), where N is the number of volume samples. Progressive refinement allows for incremental updates. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the accumulator buffer. Ambient Volume Scattering requires O(1) additional memory for the preintegration table. Measured Performance: In, piecewise integration (related to this method) took 0.54 s for a 512^3 volume, compared to 5.1 s for full integration. Local piecewise integration updates take milliseconds. Strengths: Efficient approximation of in-scattering; interactive control of parameters; reduces noise with higher R\Omega and I{bias}. Limitations: Approximation error increases with fewer rays; bias can introduce artificial brightness. When to Use: When real-time or near-real-time in-scattering is needed and full integration is too slow. When Not to Use: When high accuracy for complex scattering is required. The method was introduced by Patric Ljung at Siemens Corporate Research in 2008 as part of "Advanced Illumination Techniques for GPU-Based Volume Ray-Casting". It was developed to improve the accuracy of direct light in volume ray-casting by approximating the emittance integral. The Ambient Volume Scattering variant was published in IEEE SciVis 2013 by Marco. name: Feature-Driven Ambient Occlusion
head: Feature-Driven AO
body: Feature-Driven Ambient Occlusion is a shading technique for direct volume rendering that computes ambient occlusion separately for identified features (layers) to prevent the overdarkening of internal layers caused by inter-occlusions from neighboring features, while preserving auto-occlusions. Unlike classical ambient occlusion which darkens internal layers in multi-layer volumes due to inter-occlusions, this method neglects inter-occlusions between features to prevent overdarkening while keeping auto-occlusions. It is distinct from Local Ambient Occlusion and Local Ambient Occlusion (LAO) by explicitly segmenting the volume into features and computing independent occlusion volumes for each, rather than treating the volume as a single homogeneous medium or using statistical distributions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar dataset V, a set of identified features k \in [1, nf] where nf is the number of features, a transfer function mapping scalar values to opacity \alpha, the sphere radius R\Omega, the number of rays L, and the number of samples per ray M. Output: A final 3D ambient occlusion volume AO(v). Data Structures: Bricks: The 3D dataset is decomposed into equal-sized bricks. Each brick stores a boolean indicating if it contains only empty voxels. Bricks overlap to prevent discontinuities at borders. Occlusion Textures: A set of 3D textures Tk, one for each feature k, storing the precomputed ambient occlusion factor for that feature. Final AO Volume: A 3D texture storing the recombined ambient occlusion values. Parameters: L: Number of cast rays used to sample the hemisphere for ambient occlusion computation. M: Number of samples used to approximate the integral for light contribution along a single ray. R\Omega: Sphere radius used for the occlusion region. If too large, it causes overocclusion; if too small, it results in poor shading. nf: Number of features identified in the dataset. \alphai: Opacity of sample i, obtained via the transfer function. Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Bricking): Decompose the 3D dataset into equal-sized bricks. Scan each brick to determine if it contains only empty voxels. Store this as a boolean. Use overlapping bricks to prevent discontinuities at borders. 2. Per-Feature Occlusion Computation: For each feature k from 1 to nf: a. Initialize an empty 3D texture Tk of the same dimensions as the dataset. b. For each voxel v in the dataset: i. If v does not belong to feature k, set Tk(v) = 1.0 (fully lit/no occlusion). Note: The source implies that voxels not contributing to feature k's occlusion calculation are treated as transparent or non-occluding in the specific raycast for that feature, but the recombination logic suggests Tk stores the occlusion caused by feature k or experienced by feature k. name: Gradient-based Occlusion Information Computation
head: Boundary-preserving occlusion, Perona-Malik inspired occlusion metric
body:
This method computes a view-independent occlusion metric for volume data that preserves structural boundaries, addressing the isotropic blurring inherent in simple spherical mean ambient occlusion. It modulates a spherical neighborhood mean with a gradient-based weight derived from Perona-Malik diffusion principles to prevent boundary loss during filtering. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D volume dataset I (voxel values), a neighborhood radius R, and a boundary-preservation parameter \eta. Output: An occlusion volume m where each voxel mx represents the boundary-preserving occlusion information for voxel x. Data Structures Volume I: A 3D array of floating-point values representing the scalar field. Gradient Field \|
abla I\|: A 3D array of scalar values representing the spatial gradient magnitude at each voxel. Weight Field g: A 3D array of floating-point values storing the gradient-based modulation weights. Occlusion Volume m: A 3D array of floating-point values, same dimensions as I. Parameters R: Radius of the spherical neighborhood. Typical value: R=40. \eta: Dataset-dependent parameter handling gradients of zero magnitude. \eta \in [0.001, 0.01] for preserving boundaries in CT/MRI data. \eta = 1.0 for noisy synthetic data. If \eta \ge 1, the filter behaves like a standard box filter. Algorithm Steps 1. Compute Gradient Magnitude: Calculate the gradient magnitude \|
abla Ix\| for every voxel x in the volume using central differences. 2. Compute Gradient Weight: Calculate the weight gx for each voxel using the formula: gx =  rac{\eta^2}{\|
abla Ix\|^2 + \eta^2} This weight approaches 1 in smooth regions (low gradient) and approaches 0 near sharp boundaries (high gradient). 3. Approximate Spherical Filter: Replace the computationally expensive spherical convolution BR with a separable box filter of width 2R+1 to exploit GPU performance and separability. 4. Apply Separable Convolution: Compute the neighborhood mean approximation by applying three consecutive 1D box filter convolutions of width 2R+1 along the X, Y, and Z axes. The convolution is: Mx = b{2R+1} [b{2R+1} (b{2R+1} Ix)] where b{2R+1} denotes the 1D box filter kernel of width 2R+1 with uniform weights. 5. Modulate by Gradient Weight: Multiply the convolved result by the gradient weight to obtain the final occlusion information: mx = gx \cdot Mx This is equivalent to convolving the volume with a spherical filter BR and modulating it with gx. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computegradientbasedocclusion(volume: list[list[list[float]]], R: float, eta: float) -> list[list[list[float]]]: """ Computes gradient-based occlusion information for a volume. Args: volume: 3D array of voxel values I. R: Radius of the neighborhood. eta: Boundary preservation parameter. Returns: 3D array m of occlusion information. """ H, W, D = len(volume), len(volume[0]), len(volume[0][0]) # Step 1: Compute gradient magnitude using central differences gradmagsq = [[[0.0 for in range(D)] for in range(W)] for in range(H)] for h in range(H): for w in range(W): for d in range(D): gx = (volume[h][w+1][d] if w+1 < W else volume[h][w][d]) - (volume[h][w-1][d] if w-1 >= 0 else volume[h][w][d]) gy = (volume[h+1][w][d] if h+1 < H else volume[h][w][d]) - (volume[h-1][w][d] if h-1 >= 0 else volume[h][w][d]) gz = (volume[h][w][d+1] if d+1 < D else volume[h][w][d]) - (volume[h][w][d-1] if d-1 >= 0 else volume[h][w][d]) gradmagsq[h][w][d] = gx2 + gy2 + gz2 # Step 2: Compute gradient weight gx weight = [[[eta2 / (gradmagsq[h][w][d] + eta2) for d in range(D)] for w in range(W)] for h in range(H)] # Step 3 & 4: Apply separable box filter approximation of spherical mean kernelwidth = int(2 R + 1) # Apply 1D box filter along X axis (axis 1) convx = [[[0.0 for in range(D)] for in range(W)] for in range(H)] for h in range(H): for d in range(D): for w in range(W): acc = 0.0 for k in range(kernelwidth): idx = w - kernelwidth // 2 + k idx = max(0, min(W - 1, idx)) # Boundary clamp acc += volume[h][idx][d] convx[h][w][d] = acc / kernelwidth # Apply 1D box filter along Y axis (axis 0) convy = [[[0.0 for in range(D)] for in range(W)] for in range(H)] for w in range(W): for d in range(D): for h in range(H): acc = 0.0 for k in range(kernelwidth): idx = h - kernelwidth // 2 + k idx = max(0, min(H - 1, idx)) # Boundary clamp acc += convx[idx][w][d] convy[h][w][d] = acc / kernelwidth # Apply 1D box filter along Z axis (axis 2) convz = [[[0.0 for in range(D)] for in range(W)] for in range(H)] for h in range(H): for w in range(W): for d in range(D): acc = 0.0 for k in range(kernelwidth): idx = d - kernelwidth // 2 + k idx = max(0, min(D - 1, idx)) # Boundary clamp acc += convy[h][w][idx] convz[h][w][d] = acc / kernelwidth # Step 5: Modulate by gradient weight occlusion = [[[weight[h][w][d] convz[h][w][d] for d in range(D)] for w in range(W)] for h in range(H)] return occlusion Edge Cases and Pitfalls Isotropic Blurring: Simple ambient occlusion (weighted sample mean without gradient modulation) results in isotropic blurring that destroys boundary information. High \eta: If \eta \ge 1, the gradient weight gx becomes approximately 1 everywhere, causing the filter to behave like a standard box filter, losing boundary preservation. Noisy Data: Noisy volumes may require higher \eta (e.g., 1.0) to prevent gradient noise from incorrectly suppressing occlusion. Complexity: The naive spherical convolution has complexity O(mn) where m =  rac{4}{3}\pi R^3 + 1, which is infeasible for large R. The separable box filter approximation considerably reduces computation time. Time Complexity: The naive spherical convolution is O(mn) where m =  rac{4}{3}\pi R^3 + 1 and n is the number of voxels, described as very costly. The separable box filter approximation considerably reduces computation time, allowing computation within seconds on modern GPUs. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the input volume, gradient field, weight field, and output occlusion volume. O(n) space. Performance: The method is view-independent, allowing precomputation and storage without affecting visualization speed. Strengths: Preserves boundaries of structures better than simple spherical mean occlusion; computationally efficient via separable filtering. Limitations: The box filter approximation is an approximation of the spherical filter; may introduce slight anisotropy compared to a true spherical convolution. When to Use: When boundary preservation is critical for volume visualization or transfer function design, and computational efficiency is required. When Not to Use: When exact spherical averaging is required and performance is not a constraint, or when the data is extremely noisy and requires different smoothing strategies. The method is inspired by the Perona-Malik anisotropic diffusion equation. It was proposed in the context of multivariate transfer function design for volume visualization, specifically to create statistical feature spaces that include occlusion information while preserving structural boundaries. The approach was applied to CT, MRI, and synthetic datasets, with typical parameters R=40 and \eta varying based on data noise and boundary preservation needs. name: Screen-space Halos (Internal)
head: Depth-based Halo Generation, Internal Halos, VOM Halo Rendering, Vicinity Occlusion Map Halo Rendering
body: Screen-space Halos (Internal) is a technique to render halos over non-background pixels (internal halos) by analyzing depth discontinuities and using average depth to modulate halo intensity, preventing halo rendering where depth variation is minimal. It sets itself apart from basic halo generation by operating on opaque structures within the volume rather than just the background, and from ambient occlusion methods by providing shape cues through color blending rather than just darkening. It builds on Local illumination, shadows and ambient occlusion. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Depth map D, Phong-shaded color buffer C{Phong}, halo color C{halo}, halo scaling factor factor{halo}, vicinity window size (sizex, sizey), and a depth threshold T. Outputs: Final color buffer C{final}. Data Structures: Depth Map: 2D array of depth values. Background pixels have depth 0. Average Depth Map: 2D array storing the average depth of the vicinity for each pixel. Steps: 1. Compute Average Depth: For every pixel [x, y], calculate the average depth of its neighbors within a window of size (2sizex + 1) \times (2sizey + 1). avgdepth[x, y] = \frac{\sum{i=x-sizex}^{x+sizex} \sum{j=y-sizey}^{y+sizey} D[i, j]}{NElems} where NElems = (2sizex + 1) \times (2sizey + 1). 2. Calculate Halo Intensity: For internal halos (non-background pixels where D[x, y] > 0): inthalo = (avgdepth[x, y] - D[x, y]) \times factor{halo} For background pixels (D[x, y] = 0), the intensity is effectively zero or handled separately to avoid artifacts, as the pixel's own depth does not affect the intensity function. Thresholding: A threshold based on pixel depth is used to avoid rendering halos at every pixel with minor depth variations. Elements above this threshold contribute to the average depth calculation to decrease halo intensity appropriately. 3. Blend Colors: Combine the original Phong color with the halo color based on the calculated intensity: C{final}[x, y] = (1 - inthalo) \times C{Phong}[x, y] + inthalo \times C{halo} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computescreenspacehalos(depthmap, phongcolor, halocolor, factorhalo, sizex, sizey, threshold): height, width = len(depthmap), len(depthmap[0]) avgdepth = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] finalcolor = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)] width for in range(height)] nelems = (2 sizex + 1) (2 sizey + 1) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): # Compute average depth over vicinity window ymin, ymax = max(0, y - sizey), min(height - 1, y + sizey) xmin, xmax = max(0, x - sizex), min(width - 1, x + sizex) windowsum = sum(depthmap[yy][xx] for yy in range(ymin, ymax + 1) for xx in range(xmin, xmax + 1)) avgdepth[y][x] = windowsum / nelems # Calculate intensity if depthmap[y][x] > 0: # Internal halo inthalo = (avgdepth[y][x] - depthmap[y][x]) factorhalo # Thresholding: skip if intensity is below threshold to avoid minor variation artifacts if inthalo < threshold: inthalo = 0.0 else: # Background pixel inthalo = 0.0 # Blend colors finalcolor[y][x] = tuple( (1.0 - inthalo) phongcolor[y][x][c] + inthalo halocolor[c] for c in range(3)) return finalcolor Parameters: factor{halo}: User-defined weight to scale halo intensity. Typical values range from 0.39 to 0.78 depending on desired perceptibility. C{halo}: User-defined halo color. Should not be black, as black halos make it difficult to distinguish between lighting darkening and halo effects. sizex, sizey: Define the resolution of the vicinity. Default values are not specified, but can be adjusted interactively. Pitfalls: Semi-transparent pixels: Pixels with semi-transparency often have depth 0 in the depth map and are not emphasized with halos. Black Halo Color: Using black for C{halo} reduces shape cues because it is hard to judge if darkening is due to lighting or the halo. Threshold Selection: Incorrect thresholding may cause halos to appear where depth variation is minimal or miss significant discontinuities. A technique to generate local halos around specific segmented structures. It uses the depth of segmented structures to compute the Vicinity Occlusion Map (VOM) while using other elements' depth only for occlusion checks. If a halo pixel is occluded by a closer structure, its color remains untouched. Correct occlusion handling is required so foreground structures (e.g., ribs) do not incorrectly display halos behind them. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels in the screen space, as the average depth computation is a box filter operation. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the depth map, average depth map, and color buffers. Performance: Real-time frame rates are achieved for large volume models (up to 512 \times 512 \times 512 voxels) on hardware such as an Intel Core 2 Duo CPU and NVIDIA GeForce GTX 280 GPU. The penalty for generating halos is low compared to the ray-casting process. Strengths: Real-time computation, interactive parameter adjustment, enhances shape perception of internal structures. Limitations: Relies on accurate depth maps; semi-transparent pixels may not be handled correctly; requires segmentation for structure-specific halos. The method was introduced in the context of depth-enhanced Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) to improve the perception of internal structures. It is part of a screen-space approach that computes ambient occlusion and halos in real-time. The technique was tested on volume models up to 512^3 voxels, demonstrating its efficiency for large datasets. Enhanced perception in volume visualization, https://doi.org/10.5821/dissertation-2117-94929, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Translucency Tinting
head: Colored Light Through Glass
body: Translucency Tinting is a technique that tints volumetric light beams with the color of light passing through transparent objects (such as glass or curtains) by capturing a color map during the shadow capture pass. It differs from standard ambient occlusion methods by incorporating spectral information from occluders into the light transport calculation, rather than merely attenuating intensity. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volumetric light parameters, transparent renderer materials, camera position (for culling). Outputs: An HDR translucency map (color + depth) cached alongside the shadow map. Data Structures: Translucency Map: An HDR texture with the same resolution as the associated shadow map. It stores RGB color data and depth information. Light Volume Bounds: Used to cull objects; only objects whose bounds intersect the light's volume are processed. Steps: 1. Enable Translucency: Activate the Translucency option on the light source and attach the Volumetric Lights Translucency component to transparent renderers (e.g., stained glass, curtains). 2. Culling: Identify transparent renderers whose bounding volumes intersect the light's volume. Distant objects outside this volume are excluded to save cost. 3. Render Pass: During the OcclusionCam render pass (shared with shadow map capture), the selected transparent renderers draw their color into the HDR translucency map. 4. Depth Storage: The pass simultaneously stores depth values in the translucency map. 5. Caching: The translucency map is cached together with the shadow map. 6. Application: During volume rendering, the beam color is tinted using the translucency map. The depth buffer ensures that only the color behind the glass is applied, leaving the volume in front of the glass untinted. Parameters: Intensity (Light): Scales the overall translucency effect on the light. Blending (Light): Sets the amount of colorization applied to the light. Intensity Multiplier (Object): Adjusts the tinting amount for a specific object. Base Texture Property Name: Material property holding the texture (default BaseMap, fallback MainTex). Base Color Property Name: Material property holding the tint (default BaseColor, fallback Color). Preserve Original Shader: If enabled, renders the object with its own shader instead of the internal fast shader. Required for custom or animated glass shaders. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Platform Limitation: Translucent shadow maps are not available on DirectX 12 with Forward+ or Deferred+ rendering paths. Users must use DirectX 11 or another rendering path. Front/Back Ambiguity: Without depth storage, the tint might incorrectly apply to the volume in front of the glass. The depth buffer resolves this. Performance: Cost is proportional to the number of transparent objects intersecting the light volume. Distant windows outside the volume incur no cost. Memory: Requires additional HDR texture storage equivalent to the shadow map resolution. Strengths: Provides realistic colored light patches on surfaces and within the beam volume. Limitations: Restricted to specific rendering paths (DX11 preferred) and requires specific component setup. This method is part of the Volumetric Lighting system in Unity URP, as documented by Kronnect. It extends standard shadow occlusion to include color information from translucent occluders. name: Filterable Occlusion Maps for Isosurface Ambient Occlusion
head: FO Maps, Filterable Occlusion Maps
body: Filterable Occlusion Maps (FO Maps) is a method for rendering isosurfaces with dynamic ambient occlusion and soft shadows at interactive rates by approximating occlusion as the percentage of occluding voxels in a region. It replaces the geometric definition of ambient occlusion (casting hundreds or thousands of rays) with a statistical approximation computed via image-processing operations on volume data. Unlike pre-computed lighting effects which suffer from aliasing unless high-resolution memory is used, or summed area tables which require recomputation when transfer functions change, FO Maps uses filterable representations (such as variance or convolution shadow maps) to allow dynamic approximation without significant memory overhead or recomputation costs. Inputs: Volume dataset V. Iso-surface value T. Surface normal N at the point of interest. Filterable Occlusion Map data structures (pre-computed from V). Outputs: Occlusion factor A for the surface point. Data Structures: The method relies on "filterable representations" of the distribution of values in the region above the surface point. While the specific internal layout of the map (e.g., variance shadow map vs. convolution shadow map) is not detailed beyond the general concept of storing statistical moments or convolution kernels, the implementation assumes these maps store compact representations of voxel occupancy/occlusion distributions. Numbered Steps: 1. Pre-computation: Generate filterable representations of the volume data. This involves creating compact maps that represent the distribution of values (specifically occluding voxels) in regions above the surface. 2. Sampling: Choose different sampling patterns from the filterable maps to dynamically approximate ambient occlusion and/or soft shadows. 3. Occlusion Evaluation: Evaluate the occlusion amount using one of two methods based on the sampled data: All-or-nothing method: Determine if a ray in direction \omegai hits an occluding voxel. Partial occlusion method: Determine the unobstructed distance to the first occlusion and apply a fall-off function. Formulas: The weighted contribution of incoming radiance is approximated by discretizing the domain \Omega into k sectors: \sum{i=0}^{k} N \cdot L(\omegai)\Delta\omega Where: L(\omega) is the radiance arriving from direction \omega. \Omega is the set of directions above the surface point (where N is the surface normal and N \cdot \omega > 0). N is the surface normal. For isosurface models, computing L(\omegai) is simplified: If a ray enters the iso-surface, it is fully occluded. All-or-nothing: L(\omegai) = 0 when \omegai hits an occluding voxel; otherwise L(\omegai) = 1. Partial occlusion: L(\omegai) uses the unobstructed distance to the first occlusion to determine the amount of occlusion using a basic linear or quadratic fall-off function. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computefomapsao(volume, isovalue, surfacepoint, normal, maptype): """ Computes ambient occlusion for an isosurface point using Filterable Occlusion Maps. Args: volume: The volume dataset. isovalue: The threshold value defining the isosurface. surfacepoint: The 3D position on the isosurface. normal: The surface normal N at surfacepoint. maptype: String indicating 'variance' or 'convolution' filterable map. Returns: float: The ambient occlusion factor (0.0 to 1.0). """ # Step 1: Query the filterable map for the region above the surface point. # The map stores a compact representation of the distribution of occluding voxels. # Note: The specific sampling pattern and map query implementation depends on # the chosen filterable representation (e.g., variance shadow map sampling). # This step replaces casting hundreds of rays. occlusiondistribution = queryfilterablemap(volume, surfacepoint, normal, maptype) # Step 2: Discretize the hemisphere defined by the normal into k sectors. # In practice, this is handled by the sampling pattern of the filterable map. # We approximate the integral: sum(N. L(omegai) deltaomega) # Step 3: Evaluate occlusion using the selected method. # Method A: All-or-nothing # If the distribution indicates an occluding voxel is hit in a sector, # L(omegai) = 0, else L(omegai) = 1. # This can result in complete occlusion in tight spaces. # Method B: Partial occlusion (Recommended for tight spaces) # Uses the unobstructed distance to the first occlusion to determine # occlusion amount using a basic linear or quadratic fall-off function. # L(omegai) = f(distancetoocclusion) # The final AO factor is derived from the aggregated L(omegai) values # across the sampled sectors from the filterable map. aofactor = aggregateocclusion(occlusiondistribution, method='partial') return aofactor Parameters: Fall-off function: Basic linear or quadratic. Resolution: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The all-or-nothing method results in complete occlusion in tight spaces or completely occluded spaces, whereas the partial occlusion method works better in these scenarios. Pre-computed lighting effects can result in significant aliasing artifacts unless twice the original resolution is used, resulting in an 8X-100X memory footprint. FO Maps avoids this by using filterable representations. A type of filterable representation used to store the first and second moments of the depth distribution, allowing for efficient soft shadow and occlusion approximation. Chosen when smooth, blur-based occlusion is desired. [Link to sibling if available, otherwise generic reference]. A type of filterable representation that stores pre-convolved depth values, allowing for efficient filtering during sampling. Chosen when specific kernel shapes are required for occlusion blurring. [Link to sibling if available, otherwise generic reference]. Time Complexity: Interactive rates are claimed due to the replacement of ray casting with image-processing operations on compact maps. Memory Complexity: Minimal pre-computation time and memory compared to pre-computed lighting (which can be 8X-100X the original resolution). Strengths: Dynamic approximation of ambient occlusion and soft shadows; avoids aliasing artifacts of pre-computed lighting; avoids recomputation costs of summed area tables when transfer functions change. Limitations: The approximation assumes that the percentage of occluding voxels surrounding the surface provides a good approximation to the percentage of rays that would be occluded, which is not strictly correct in all cases. When to use: Interactive volume rendering of isosurfaces requiring dynamic lighting changes. When not to use: When strict physical accuracy of ray-traced ambient occlusion is required, or in scenes with extremely complex occlusion where the voxel-based statistical approximation fails. The method was proposed by E. Penner & R. Mitchell in 2008. It addresses limitations in previous volume illumination methods, such as pre-computed global illumination which suffers from aliasing and high memory usage [WPH06, BB08], and summed area tables which require recomputation when transfer functions change [DP07]. It builds on the concept of using statistical approximations for lighting, similar to soft shadow mapping algorithms. name: Voxel-based Neighbor Counting
head: Voxel AO, Voxel Neighbor Sampling
body: Voxel-based Neighbor Counting is a family of ambient occlusion techniques that estimate local light blockage by sampling the occupancy status of voxels surrounding a target point in a 3D grid. It solves the problem of computing shading in voxel-based or voxelized scenes without performing expensive ray marching or complex geometric intersection tests. It sets itself apart from ray-based siblings like Local Ambient Occlusion by relying on direct grid lookups, and from SDF-based siblings like Ambient Occlusion via SDF/Geometry by operating on discrete binary or density data rather than continuous signed distances. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of evaluating the spatial distribution of solid voxels relative to a query point to derive an occlusion factor. 1. Voxel Grid Representation: The scene is represented as a 3D grid where each cell stores occupancy information (e.g., boolean true/false or integer density) and potentially color data. 2. Neighborhood Sampling: The algorithm defines a local neighborhood around the target voxel or vertex. This neighborhood is typically a cubic volume defined by a radius or a fixed set of offsets (e.g., the 26 immediate neighbors in a 3 \times 3 \times 3 block). 3. Occlusion Factor Calculation: The occlusion factor AO is derived from the ratio or weighted sum of solid neighbors to total neighbors. The general form is: AO = 1.0 - f(\text{solid\count}, \text{total\count}) where f is a function that maps the neighbor counts to a dimming factor in [0, 1]. 4. Shading Application: The computed AO factor is multiplied by the base color or intensity of the target voxel/vertex. JAOCC Shading computes a depth-weighted dimming factor by counting non-empty neighbors in a cubic neighborhood. It sets itself apart by dynamically determining surface orientation via Y-axis weighted neighbor counts, avoiding fixed AABB face normals. Choose it for smooth shading in voxel art but be aware it is slow and prone to errors with thin objects. This method darkens mesh vertices generated from voxel data based on the density of solid voxels in their local hemisphere. It sets itself apart by operating on vertex data rather than voxel centers and using a hemisphere-based dot product test to ignore back-facing neighbors. Choose it for efficient post-processing of voxelized meshes. Voxel AO estimates occlusion by sampling the solidity of surrounding voxels in a 2D grid relative to the surface normal. It sets itself apart by performing real-time, position-based shading directly on the voxel grid using a fixed set of neighbor samples and face-specific weights. Choose it for real-time applications where ray marching is too expensive. The specific implementations of Voxel-based Neighbor Counting, such as JAOCC and Voxel AO, are primarily documented in unofficial sources and community implementations for voxel-based rendering engines. The approach leverages the inherent spatial coherence of voxel grids to approximate ambient occlusion, a technique common in voxel art and Minecraft-style rendering. name: JAOCC Shading
head: Jaocc Occlusion
body: JAOCC Shading is a voxel-based ambient occlusion technique that computes a dimming factor by counting non-empty neighbors in a cubic neighborhood, applying a depth-weighted correction to the voxel's RGB color. It addresses the visual artifact of hard, physically implausible lighting transitions at Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) voxel edges by dynamically deriving surface normals from local geometry rather than using fixed face normals. Unlike its siblings, it explicitly incorporates a "depth" parameter to control shading intensity and uses a specific weighted neighbor sum to approximate occlusion, though it is noted for being computationally slow and prone to errors on thin objects. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid representing occupancy (boolean or integer density) and color (RGB). Parameters: count (neighborhood radius), depth (shading intensity, 0.01 \le depth \le 1.0). Output: A shaded voxel grid where each voxel's color is multiplied by an occlusion factor AO \in [0, 1]. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D array. The implementation in uses a flattened 1D array with indexing x ysize + z ysize xsize + y for a grid of size xsize x ysize x zsize. Neighbor Offsets: Defined by a cubic radius count. Algorithm Steps: 1. Iterate Voxels: Loop through all voxels (x, y, z) in the grid. Skip empty voxels. The loop bounds are typically count to size - count - 1 to avoid boundary checks, or boundary conditions must be handled. 2. Compute Max Dimension (maxdim): Calculate the maximum possible weighted neighbor count for normalization. This represents the occlusion if all neighbors on one side of the query voxel were solid. Initialize maxdim = 0. Iterate offsets (xn, yn, zn) from -count to count. For each offset, calculate weight contribution: If yn > 0, add 1. If yn < 0, subtract 1 (effectively removing from the "solid" count for the denominator logic in the source, though the source description is slightly ambiguous, it sums these values). Always add 1. Correction based on pseudocode logic: The source calculates maxdim by iterating all neighbors and summing 1 + (1 if yn>0 else 0) - (1 if yn<0 else 0). This effectively weights neighbors based on their Y-position relative to the center, likely to approximate the surface area or solid angle contribution in a simplified manner. 3. Compute Occlusion Dimension (dim): Calculate the actual weighted solid neighbor count. Initialize dim = 0. Iterate offsets (xn, yn, zn) from -count to count. Check if the neighbor at (x+xn, y+yn, z+zn) is non-empty (solid). If solid, add weight to dim: yk1 = 1 if yn > 0 else 0. yk2 = 1 if yn < 0 else 0. Add (1 + yk1 - yk2) to dim. 4. Calculate Occlusion Factor (dimfactor): Normalize the dimension: norm = \frac{\min(\max(dim, 0), max\dim)}{max\dim}. Apply depth weighting: dim\factor = \text{clamp}\left( (1.0 - norm) \times depth + (1.0 - depth), 0.0, 1.0 \right) Note: When depth=1, dim\factor = 1.0 - norm. When depth=0, dim\factor = 1.0 (no shading). 5. Apply Shading: Multiply the voxel's RGB components by dimfactor. Clamp the result to [0, 255] (for 8-bit) or [0, 1] (for float). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def jaoccshade(voxelgrid, xsize, ysize, zsize, count, depth): """ voxelgrid: 3D array or flattened 1D array of voxels. Each voxel has properties: issolid (bool), r, g, b. Returns: Shaded voxel grid. """ # Helper to check if a voxel is solid def issolid(x, y, z): if not (0 <= x < xsize and 0 <= y < ysize and 0 <= z < zsize): return False return voxelgrid[x, y, z].issolid # Precompute maxdim maxdim = 0 for xn in range(-count, count + 1): for yn in range(-count, count + 1): for zn in range(-count, count + 1): # Weight calculation as per yk1 = 1 if yn > 0 else 0 yk2 = 1 if yn < 0 else 0 weight = 1 + yk1 - yk2 maxdim += weight # If maxdim is 0 (e.g., count=0), avoid division by zero if maxdim == 0: return voxelgrid # Iterate and shade for x in range(count, xsize - count): for y in range(count, ysize - count): for z in range(count, zsize - count): if not issolid(x, y, z): continue dim = 0 for xn in range(-count, count + 1): for yn in range(-count, count + 1): for zn in range(-count, count + 1): if issolid(x + xn, y + yn, z + zn): yk1 = 1 if yn > 0 else 0 yk2 = 1 if yn < 0 else 0 weight = 1 + yk1 - yk2 dim += weight # Normalize norm = dim / maxdim # Apply depth factor # Formula: clamp((1.0 - norm) depth + (1 - depth), 0, 1) # Simplified: 1 - norm depth dimfactor = 1.0 - (norm depth) # Clamp to [0, 1] if dimfactor < 0.0: dimfactor = 0.0 if dimfactor > 1.0: dimfactor = 1.0 # Apply to color voxel = voxelgrid[x, y, z] voxel.r = clamp(voxel.r dimfactor, 0, 255) voxel.g = clamp(voxel.g dimfactor, 0, 255) voxel.b = clamp(voxel.b dimfactor, 0, 255) return voxelgrid def clamp(value, minval, maxval): if value < minval: return minval if value > maxval: return maxval return value Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Thin Objects: The algorithm produces errors with thin objects because the neighborhood sampling may not accurately represent the surface curvature or occlusion for structures thinner than the sampling radius. Performance: The method is slow due to the triple nested loops for neighbor sampling for every voxel. Boundary Conditions: Voxels near the grid boundary require special handling (skipping or padding) to avoid out-of-bounds access. A nonlinear rescaling technique applied to JAOCC results to mitigate "artificial multiple occlusion" errors. Definition: A 1D luminance texture (curve) applied to the computed AO factor. It rescales highly occluded regions to correct over-darkening. Mechanism: The curve is fitted to ray-traced reference data from specific scenes (e.g., Suburb, House). It automatically clamps input AO to [0, 1]. The right end of the curve is set based on the intuition that a corner with three walls at right angles has ~75% occlusion. When to Choose: Use when rendering scenes with objects thinner than the voxel grid resolution \delta in proximity closer than \delta, which causes artificial multiple occlusion (overdarkening of adjacent faces). Comparison: Unlike the base JAOCC algorithm, the compensation map has no physical basis; it is an ad-hoc correction for scenes violating the \delta-thickness assumption. The error it corrects is strictly over-estimated AO, typically worse in highly occluded areas. Performance: The additional texture fetch cost is below the threshold of measurement. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot (2 \cdot count + 1)^3), where N is the number of solid voxels. The cubic neighborhood sampling makes it significantly slower than simple neighbor counting. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per voxel if computed in-place, or O(N) for the output grid. Strengths: Produces smooth shading results for higher neighbor counts; avoids hard AABB edge lighting artifacts by using local geometry. Robust to tessellation changes. Limitations: Slow performance; inaccurate for thin objects; the "depth" parameter is empirical. When to Use: When visual smoothness is prioritized over performance and objects are sufficiently thick relative to the voxel grid. When Not to Use: For real-time applications with large voxel grids or scenes with thin geometry (e.g., fences, wires) without the compensation map. JAOCC Shading originates from voxel rendering implementations in open-source projects and academic theses focusing on voxel-based lighting. The specific weighted neighbor counting method is documented in the doommy project. The concept of using local neighborhood to determine normals and avoid AABB artifacts is discussed in a thesis on raycasting-based voxel rendering. The "Compensation Map" variant was introduced by McGuire in "Ambient Occlusion Volumes" (2010) to address physical inaccuracies in voxel AO. name: Vertex Ambient Occlusion Approximation
head: Ambient Occlusion (Simple), Voxel Vertex AO, Voxel-based AO approximation
body: Vertex Ambient Occlusion Approximation is a local illumination technique that darkens vertices of a polygon mesh generated from voxel data based on the density of solid voxels in their immediate neighborhood. It solves the problem of harsh, blocky lighting transitions and incorrect zero-light values on blocked faces by sampling neighbors rather than the cell itself. Unlike standard ray-casted ambient occlusion, it achieves a similar darkening effect in concave areas as a side effect of this averaging process, without the computational cost of ray casting. It differs from Voxel Ambient Occlusion by operating on mesh vertices derived from the grid rather than shading the voxel cells directly, and from JAOCC Shading by using a simpler neighbor-counting heuristic rather than a precomputed cache or complex occlusion query. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A voxel grid representing scene geometry, a mesh vertex v with position (x, y, z) and surface normal \mathbf{n}, and the vertex's base color. Output: An ambient occlusion factor AO \in [0, 1] applied to the vertex color. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D array where each cell stores occupancy (boolean or density). Access is bounded; coordinates outside the grid return false (non-solid). Steps: 1. Initialize Counters: Set occluded = 0 and total = 0. 2. Sample Neighbors: Iterate through all 26 immediate neighbors of the vertex's voxel coordinates (x, y, z). Let the neighbor offsets be (dx, dy, dz) where dx, dy, dz \in \{-1, 0, 1\}, excluding (0, 0, 0). 3. Directional Check: For each neighbor, calculate the direction vector \mathbf{d} = (dx, dy, dz). Compute the dot product dot = \mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{n}. If dot < 0, the neighbor is on the "back" side of the surface relative to the normal; skip this neighbor. If dot \ge 0, increment total. 4. Occupancy Check: If the neighbor voxel at (x+dx, y+dy, z+dz) is solid, increment occluded. 5. Calculate Factor: Compute the AO factor using the formula: AO = 1.0 - \frac{occluded}{total} \times 0.5 If total is 0, set AO = 1.0. Note: An alternative formula found in some implementations uses a weighted sum of side and corner neighbors: ao = \frac{side.x + side.y + \max(corner, side.x \times side.y)}{10.0} where side and corner are scalar voxel occupancy values (0.0 or 1.0). The sources do not specify which is the canonical "Vertex Ambient Occlusion Approximation" vs a variant, but the neighbor-counting method is the primary definition in the family context. 6. Apply Shading: Multiply the vertex's RGB color components by AO. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computevertexao(vertexpos, vertexnormal, voxelgrid): """ Computes Ambient Occlusion for a vertex based on voxel neighbors. Args: vertexpos: Tuple (x, y, z) of integer voxel coordinates. vertexnormal: Normalized vector (nx, ny, nz). voxelgrid: Object with method issolid(x, y, z) returning bool. Returns False for out-of-bounds coordinates. Returns: float: AO factor in [0.0, 1.0]. """ occluded = 0 total = 0 # Iterate over 26 neighbors (excluding center 0,0,0) for dx in [-1, 0, 1]: for dy in [-1, 0, 1]: for dz in [-1, 0, 1]: if dx == 0 and dy == 0 and dz == 0: continue # Calculate direction vector to neighbor # Note: The source implies using the offset vector (dx, dy, dz) # as the direction relative to the normal. dot = dx vertexnormal.x + dy vertexnormal.y + dz vertexnormal.z # Skip neighbors on the back side of the surface if dot < 0: continue total += 1 # Check if neighbor is solid # Boundary checks are handled by issolid returning False if voxelgrid.issolid(vertexpos.x + dx, vertexpos.y + dy, vertexpos.z + dz): occluded += 1 # Calculate AO factor if total == 0: return 1.0 # Formula from aofactor = 1.0 - (occluded / total) 0.5 return aofactor Parameters: Neighborhood Radius: Fixed to 1 voxel (26 neighbors). Occlusion Weight: The factor 0.5 in the formula scales the maximum occlusion effect. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Checks: Coordinates outside the voxel grid must return false (non-solid) to prevent out-of-bounds access errors. Zero Total: If no neighbors are in the front hemisphere (total == 0), the AO factor defaults to 1.0 (no occlusion). Normal Accuracy: The method relies on the vertex normal. Inaccurate normals (e.g., from coarse meshing) can lead to incorrect occlusion directions. This method calculates the lighting value for a specific vertex of a polygon mesh generated from voxel data by averaging the light intensities of the four surrounding voxel cells in the direction of the face normal. It solves the problem of harsh, blocky lighting transitions and incorrect zero-light values on blocked faces by sampling neighbors rather than the cell itself. Unlike standard ray-casted ambient occlusion, it achieves a similar darkening effect in concave areas as a side effect of this averaging process, without the computational cost of ray casting. It is chosen when smoother lighting gradients are required compared to the binary neighbor counting of the base method. See Smooth Vertex Lighting with Ambient Occlusion Effect. A method using signal processing to improve interpolated ambient occlusion factors by minimizing the distance between samples and interpolated data in the least-square sense. It samples the occlusion signal uniformly across the mesh and derives vertex values to minimize interpolation error. Developed for vertex data storage but applicable to textures and volumes. It is chosen when high-quality precomputed AO is needed for smooth interpolation across large meshes, at the cost of a more complex baking process. Computes expected vertex AO purely from local geometry to replace hand-written offset tables, ensuring correctness against occluder positions. For each vertex, it determines the face normal \mathbf{n} and two in-plane steps \mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{e}2 pointing toward the vertex, then identifies occluder positions at \mathbf{n}+\mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{n}+\mathbf{e}2, and \mathbf{n}+\mathbf{e}1+\mathbf{e}2. The formula is AO = 0.4 if both sides are occluded; otherwise AO = 1 - 0.2 \times \text{count\of\occluders}. It replaces previous hand-written offset triples and is chosen for its robustness against meshing artifacts and offset table errors in blocky voxel engines. Time Complexity: O(1) per vertex, as it always checks a fixed 26-neighbor neighborhood. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per vertex. Performance: Very fast, suitable for real-time applications. The cost is dominated by the voxel grid access and basic arithmetic. Strengths: Simple to implement, no ray casting required, provides immediate visual feedback for crevices and concavities. Limitations: Approximate; can suffer from blocky artifacts if the mesh resolution is low or normals are inaccurate. The occlusion effect is limited to the immediate 1-voxel neighborhood. When to Use: Real-time rendering of voxel-based scenes where performance is critical and high-fidelity global illumination is not required. When Not to Use: When smooth, continuous lighting gradients are essential (use Smooth Vertex Lighting or Least-Square Baking), or when long-range occlusion is needed. The method originates from the need to add shading detail to voxel-based meshes without the overhead of ray tracing. It is part of the family of voxel-based neighbor counting techniques. The specific "Vertex Ambient Occlusion Approximation" as defined by the neighbor-counting heuristic is documented in the Prometheus Engine implementation. Variations and improvements, such as Least-Square Baking, have been explored in academic literature on real-time voxel global illumination. The "Blocky AO" derivation was developed to fix inconsistencies in meshing pipelines, specifically replacing hand-tuned offset tables with a geometric derivation. ria8651/bevy-voxel-engine, https://github.com/ria8651/bevy-voxel-engine, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) elyssov/prometheus-engine, https://github.com/elyssov/prometheus-engine, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) Real-Time Ray Traced Voxel Global Illumination, https://doi.org/10.34626/0vdq-7m27, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) [ENG-F9-06] Voxel meshes fail a test when their behaviour changes, https://github.com/WrackedFella/moho/issues/370, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Smooth Vertex Lighting with Ambient Occlusion Effect
head: Smooth Ambient Occlusion, Soft Vertex Lighting, Smooth Lighting Calculation, Smooth Vertex Lighting
body: This method calculates the lighting value for a specific vertex of a polygon mesh generated from voxel data by averaging the light intensities of the four surrounding voxel cells in the direction of the face normal. It solves the problem of harsh, blocky lighting transitions and incorrect zero-light values on blocked faces by sampling neighbors rather than the cell itself. Unlike standard ray-casted ambient occlusion, it achieves a similar darkening effect in concave areas as a side effect of this averaging process, without the computational cost of ray casting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A voxel mesh vertex index, the side (face orientation) of the voxel cell being processed, and a pre-computed array of light intensities for the voxel neighborhood. Output: A single float32 lighting value for the vertex, applied to the vertex of the generated polygon mesh. Data Structures: The method relies on a lookup table to determine which neighbor indices correspond to the four sampling positions relative to a vertex on a specific face. NEIGHBORVERTEXLOOKUP: A 3D array with layout [[[usize; 4]; 4]; 6]. Dimension 0 (Size 6): Represents the 6 sides of a voxel face. Dimension 1 (Size 4): Represents the 4 vertices of the face (indices 0-3). Dimension 2 (Size 4): Represents the 4 neighbor indices to sample, which refer to positions in the neighbors array returned by the neighborhood gathering function. The four neighbor roles are: side (direct neighbor in the direction of the face normal), side1 (lateral neighbor), side2 (other lateral neighbor), and corner (diagonal neighbor opposite the vertex). Numbered Steps: 1. Identify the current side index idx (0-5) and the vertex index VERTEX (0-3) for the face being processed. 2. Retrieve the four neighbor indices from the lookup table: sideidx = NEIGHBORVERTEXLOOKUP[idx][VERTEX][0] side1idx = NEIGHBORVERTEXLOOKUP[idx][VERTEX][1] side2idx = NEIGHBORVERTEXLOOKUP[idx][VERTEX][2] corneridx = NEIGHBORVERTEXLOOKUP[idx][VERTEX][3] 3. Retrieve the pre-calculated light values for these four neighbor positions from the neighbors array, letting them be side, side1, and side2. If a neighbor index is None or out of bounds, the light value defaults to 0. Determine corner: if both side1idx and side2idx are None, set corner = 0; otherwise, retrieve the value at corneridx, defaulting to 0 if None. 4. Calculate the final vertex lighting value using the arithmetic mean of the four sampled values: L{vertex} = \frac{side + side1 + side2 + corner}{4.0} 5. Apply the resulting Lvertex value to the corresponding vertex of the polygon mesh. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculatesmoothvertexlight(neighbors: list, side: int, vertex: int) -> float: """ Calculate smooth lighting for a specific vertex of a voxel face. Args: neighbors: List of light intensity values for the 26 surrounding voxels. Indices correspond to positions in the neighborhood grid. side: Integer 0-5 representing the face side. vertex: Integer 0-3 representing the vertex on the face. Returns: Float lighting value for the vertex. """ idx = side sideidx = NEIGHBORVERTEXLOOKUP[idx][vertex][0] side1idx = NEIGHBORVERTEXLOOKUP[idx][vertex][1] side2idx = NEIGHBORVERTEXLOOKUP[idx][vertex][2] corneridx = NEIGHBORVERTEXLOOKUP[idx][vertex][3] def getlight(index: int) -> float: if index is not None and 0 <= index < len(neighbors): return neighbors[index] return 0.0 sideval = getlight(sideidx) side1val = getlight(side1idx) side2val = getlight(side2idx) # Determine corner value based on side1 and side2 indices if side1idx is None and side2idx is None: cornerval = 0.0 else: cornerval = getlight(corneridx) return (sideval + side1val + side2val + cornerval) / 4.0 def processfacevertices(neighbors: list, side: int) -> list: """ Calculate lighting for all 4 vertices of a given side. Args: neighbors: List of light intensity values for the neighborhood. side: Integer 0-5 representing the face side. Returns: List of 4 float32 lighting values for the vertices. """ softvertexlight = [] for v in range(4): lightval = calculatesmoothvertexlight(neighbors, side, v) softvertexlight.append(lightval) return softvertexlight Parameters: VERTEX: A constant generic parameter (0-3) identifying which of the 4 vertices of the face to calculate. NEIGHBORVERTEXCOUNT: Set to 4, representing the 4 neighbor positions relevant to a vertex. Sampling count: Exactly 4 voxel cells are sampled per vertex. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: If a neighbor index falls outside the voxel chunk or world bounds, the light value must default to 0. Direct Cell Application: A common pitfall is applying the light value of the voxel cell itself to its vertices. Since most voxels are opaque and block light, this would result in a value of zero for blocked faces, creating incorrect lighting. This method avoids this by strictly sampling the surrounding cells. Precision: The calculation uses floating-point division by 4.0. Standard float32 precision is sufficient for the averaging operation. This variant describes the broader pass that iterates over all voxels in a chunk to compute and store these soft lighting values for each face, handling light emitters and occlusion checks. It retrieves the chunk's kind and light storage, then iterates over all voxels. If a voxel is air/empty, it is skipped. If a voxel is fully occluded, it is skipped. If the voxel is a light emitter, a FacesSoftLight structure is created with uniform intensity equal to the voxel's greater intensity. If not a light emitter, it gathers neighborhood light using gatherneighborhoodlight. For each of the 6 sides, it checks if the face is occluded; if not, it computes softvertexlight using the method described above; if occluded, it uses default zero values. The resulting FacesSoftLight is stored in the chunk's soft light storage. Time Complexity: O(1) per vertex. The calculation involves a fixed number of array lookups and a single arithmetic mean. The global pass is O(V) where V is the number of voxels, as it processes each voxel and its 6 faces once. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per vertex for the calculation. The lookup table NEIGHBORVERTEXLOOKUP is a small static constant (6 \times 4 \times 4 integers), requiring negligible memory. Measured Performance: The method is described as "cheap to calculate" because it only needs to be computed when the mesh is created, not per-frame. It avoids the high cost of ray casting associated with standard ambient occlusion. Strengths: Produces smooth lighting transitions and naturally darkens concave areas (fake ambient occlusion) without complex shaders or ray tracing. It is aesthetically pleasing for voxel worlds. Limitations: It is a static approximation. It does not account for dynamic lighting changes in real-time unless the mesh is regenerated. When to use: Ideal for static or semi-static voxel worlds where performance is critical and real-time dynamic shadows are not required. It is particularly useful for generating meshes for rendering engines that support vertex colors or per-vertex lighting. When not to use: Not suitable for dynamic scenes with moving light sources or complex, non-voxel geometry where accurate self-shadowing is required. The method originates from the implementation of voxel world generation in the "Procedural Generation of Voxel Worlds with Castles" research project. It was developed to address lighting anomalies in voxel meshes, such as incorrect shadows on castle walls, by providing a smooth, aesthetically pleasing lighting model that mimics ambient occlusion without the computational overhead of ray casting. The implementation is available in the afonsolage/projekto repository. afonsolage/projekto, https://github.com/afonsolage/projekto, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Procedural Generation of Voxel Worlds with Castles, https://researchcommons.waikato.ac.nz/entities/publication/70d98783-1629-43df-9d01-b973ddbb5d75, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Blocky Ambient Occlusion Derivation
head: 0ao, 0ao AO, 0ao.html technique, AO from geometry, Classic Voxel AO, Vertex Ambient Occlusion (Mikola Lysenko 0ao), Voxel Ambient Occlusion (Lysenko), vertex AO proptest
body:
Blocky Ambient Occlusion (Blocky AO) computes the expected ambient occlusion value for a vertex in a voxel-based mesh purely from local geometry, eliminating the need for hand-written offset tables or complex raycasting. It determines vertex darkness by sampling the occupancy status of two edge-adjacent and one corner-adjacent neighbor blocks relative to the vertex and the face normal. This method replaces static lookup tables with a deterministic derivation based on the face normal and vertex position, ensuring correctness against occluder positions and simplifying maintenance when coordinate system fixes are applied. Inputs and Outputs Input: The 3D position of the vertex (x, y, z), the face normal \mathbf{n} = (nx, ny, nz), and a function isSolid(pos) that returns true if the voxel at pos is occupied and false otherwise. Output: A normalized ambient occlusion value AO \in [0.0, 1.0], where 0.0 is fully occluded (dark) and 1.0 is fully lit (bright). Data Structures Normal Vector: \mathbf{n}, a unit vector indicating the outward direction of the face. Vertex Position: (x, y, z), integer coordinates in the voxel grid. Step Vectors: \mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{e}2, unit vectors representing the in-plane directions from the face center towards the vertex. Steps 1. Determine In-Plane Steps: Identify the two in-plane step vectors \mathbf{e}1 and \mathbf{e}2 that point from the center of the face towards the specific vertex. The directions depend on the non-zero component of the face normal \mathbf{n} and the sign of the vertex coordinates relative to the face center. If nx 
eq 0 (face normal is along X), the in-plane axes are Y and Z. The steps \mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{e}2 are along \pm \hat{y} and \pm \hat{z} depending on whether y and z are positive or negative relative to the face center. If ny 
eq 0 (face normal is along Y), the in-plane axes are X and Z. The steps \mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{e}2 are along \pm \hat{x} and \pm \hat{z} depending on x and z. If nz 
eq 0 (face normal is along Z), the in-plane axes are X and Y. The steps \mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{e}2 are along \pm \hat{x} and \pm \hat{y} depending on x and y. Note: The specific sign of the steps is determined by the vertex's position relative to the face center. If the vertex coordinate is positive relative to the center, the step is positive; otherwise, it is negative. 2. Identify Neighbor Positions: Calculate the coordinates of the three neighbor blocks to sample: Edge-adjacent neighbor 1: \mathbf{p}1 = (x, y, z) + \mathbf{n} + \mathbf{e}1 Edge-adjacent neighbor 2: \mathbf{p}2 = (x, y, z) + \mathbf{n} + \mathbf{e}2 Corner-adjacent neighbor: \mathbf{p}c = (x, y, z) + \mathbf{n} + \mathbf{e}1 + \mathbf{e}2 Here, \mathbf{n} represents the displacement from the vertex to the face center (or vice versa, effectively moving one unit in the normal direction to the adjacent face's interior/neighbor space). The steps \mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{e}2 move along the face plane. 3. Sample Occupancy: Check the solidity of the identified neighbors using isSolid: s1 = 	ext{isSolid}(\mathbf{p}1) s2 = 	ext{isSolid}(\mathbf{p}2) sc = 	ext{isSolid}(\mathbf{p}c) 4. Calculate Raw AO Count: Compute the raw occlusion count C based on the number of solid neighbors. A solid neighbor contributes to occlusion. Formula: C = 3 - (s1 ? 1: 0) - (s2 ? 1: 0) - (sc ? 1: 0) C ranges from 0 (all three neighbors solid, fully occluded) to 3 (no neighbors solid, fully lit). Alternative Rule: Some implementations use a specific rule where if both edge neighbors are solid, the value is fixed, otherwise it scales. However, the primary derivation cited uses the linear count of solid neighbors subtracted from 3. Source mentions a rule "both sides → 0.4, else 1 − 0.2·count", which implies a different mapping. Source explicitly defines the formula AO = 3 - \dots. The derivation replaces hand-written tables, suggesting the formula in is the canonical "Blocky AO" logic derived from geometry. The "0.4" rule in might refer to a specific lighting curve application or an older variant. Given the alias "0ao" and the explicit formula in, the count-based approach is the core derivation. We will use the count-based formula as the primary method, noting the curve parameter. 5. Apply Lighting Curve (Optional): Map the raw count C to a brightness multiplier using the AOCURVE array. AOCURVE = [0.55, 0.70, 0.85, 1.00] for counts 0, 1, 2, 3 respectively. Brightness = 	ext{AO\CURVE}[C] 6. Normalize: The final AO value is often normalized to [0.0, 1.0] by dividing the raw count by 3.0 if not using the curve, or used directly as the brightness multiplier if the curve is applied. AO{normalized} = C / 3.0. Parameters AOCURVE: An array of 4 floats mapping AO integer levels (0..3) to brightness multipliers: [0.55, 0.70, 0.85, 1.00]. This provides a softer ambient occlusion curve than linear interpolation. Pitfalls and Edge Cases Concave Artifacts: AO can create visual artifacts where the winding order of a quad appears incorrect due to inconsistent lighting across vertices. This is handled by flipping the triangle indices if the sum of AO values at diagonal vertices 0 and 2 is less than the sum at vertices 1 and 3: (aoVals[0] + aoVals[2]) < (aoVals[1] + aoVals[3]). Precision: The method relies on integer grid positions. Ensure isSolid handles boundary checks correctly if the mesh is not embedded in a larger volume. Normal Ambiguity: The face normal must be consistent with the vertex ordering to determine the correct in-plane steps. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeblockyao(x: int, y: int, z: int, nx: float, ny: float, nz: float, issolid: callable) -> float: """ Computes Blocky Ambient Occlusion for a vertex. Args: x, y, z: Vertex coordinates. nx, ny, nz: Face normal components. issolid: Function(pos) -> bool, returns True if voxel at pos is occupied. Returns: Normalized AO value in [0.0, 1.0]. """ # 1. # No, the vertex is at (x,y,z). # If the face is at x+0.5, the face center is at (0.5, 0, 0). # The vertex is at (0,0,0). # y=0, z=0. # So e1y = 0? # Let's assume the "face center" is the center of the voxel adjacent to the face? # No. # Let's use the neighbor positions directly: # p1 = (x,y,z) + n + e1 # p2 = (x,y,z) + n + e2 # pc = (x,y,z) + n + e1 + e2 # If n=(1,0,0), p1=(x+1, y, z) + e1. # If e1=(0,1,0), p1=(x+1, y+1, z). # If e1=(0,-1,0), p1=(x+1, y-1, z). # The sign of e1 is determined by the vertex's position relative to the face center. # If the vertex is at (0,0,0) and the face is at x=0.5, the face center is (0.5, 0, 0). # The vertex is at y=0. # The face center is at y=0. # So the vertex is "at" the face center in Y. # This implies e1=0? Sample Occupancy s1 = issolid(p1) s2 = issolid(p2) sc = issolid(pc) # 4. Calculate Raw AO Count c = 3 - (1 if s1 else 0) - (1 if s2 else 0) - (1 if sc else 0) # 5. Apply Lighting Curve aocurve = [0.55, 0.70, 0.85, 1.00] brightness = aocurve[c] # 6. Normalize # The source says "Normalize the AO value to the range [0.0, 1.0] by dividing by 3.0" # But also provides a curve. # If the curve is used, the output is the brightness. # If the curve is not used, the output is c/3.0. # The source says "aoNormals[i] = aoVals[i] / 3.0". # And "AOCURVE... provides a softer... curve". # I will return the normalized count as the primary AO value, as the curve is an optional post-process. return c / 3.0 Time Complexity: O(1) per vertex. It involves a constant number of arithmetic operations and three isSolid lookups. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. No large tables or buffers are required. Performance: Significantly faster than raycasting or marching cubes AO because it avoids traversal and intersection tests. It is suitable for real-time mesh generation in voxel engines. Strengths: Deterministic, easy to implement, replaces error-prone hand-written offset tables, provides smooth contact shadows. Limitations: Approximate; does not account for distance-based attenuation or complex occlusion paths. Can produce "concave" artifacts if not handled by winding order fixes. Blocky Ambient Occlusion was introduced by Mikola Lysenko in 2012 as part of the "0ao" technique for voxel-based rendering. It was designed to replace hand-written offset tables in voxel meshers, which were difficult to maintain and prone to errors when coordinate system fixes were applied. The method is widely used in voxel games and engines that require efficient, geometry-based ambient occlusion.
