name: Voxel Ambient Occlusion
head: Voxel AO, computeAO
body: Voxel Ambient Occlusion (Voxel AO) estimates ambient occlusion for a surface point by sampling the solidity of surrounding voxels in a 2D grid relative to the surface normal, simulating light blockage from adjacent geometry. It sets itself apart from its siblings by operating on a 2D projection of the 3D voxel neighborhood aligned with the surface normal, allowing for efficient face-based occlusion calculation without full 3D ray marching. Unlike Histogram-based Voxel Ambient Occlusion which uses vector quantization, or Vicinity Occlusion Mapping which operates in screen space, Voxel AO computes occlusion directly from voxel occupancy data in world space. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid storing occupancy (solidity) data, a query point hitPos on the surface, and the surface normal normal at that point. Output: A scalar ambient occlusion factor AO \in [0, 1]. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D array or hash map mapping integer coordinates (x, y, z) to a boolean or integer solidity value (1 for solid, 0 for empty). Offset Array: A 2D array axes of 4 elements representing the corners of a unit square in the local 2D plane: (1,1), (-1,1), (-1,-1), (1,-1). Steps: 1. Base Position Calculation: Determine the integer voxel coordinate of the hit surface by rounding the hit position offset by the normal to prevent self-intersection: basePos = \lfloor hitPos + normal \cdot 0.01 \rfloor 2. Neighbor Sampling: Define side vectors sideA and sideB based on the dominant axis of the normal to establish the local 2D plane: If |normal.x| > 0: sideA = (0, offset.x, 0), sideB = (0, 0, offset.y) Else if |normal.y| > 0: sideA = (offset.x, 0, 0), sideB = (0, 0, offset.y) Else: sideA = (offset.x, 0, 0), sideB = (0, offset.y, 0) Sample 4 side neighbors using offsets d1 and d2 (derived from axes): side.x = get\voxel(pos + d1) side.y = get\voxel(pos + d2) side.z = get\voxel(pos - d1) side.w = get\voxel(pos - d2) Sample 4 corner neighbors: corner.x = get\voxel(pos + d1 + d2) corner.y = get\voxel(pos - d1 + d2) corner.z = get\voxel(pos - d1 - d2) corner.w = get\voxel(pos + d1 - d2) 3. Face AO Calculation: Compute AO for each of the 4 faces using a helper function vertexao which takes two side values and one corner value: ao.x = vertex\ao(side.xy, corner.x) ao.y = vertex\ao(side.yz, corner.y) ao.z = vertex\ao(side.zw, corner.z) ao.w = vertex\ao(side.wx, corner.w) The vertexao function calculates the contribution ao for a face: If both side voxels are solid (1u): ao = 0.9 Otherwise: ao = side1 \cdot 0.4 + side2 \cdot 0.4 + corner \cdot 0.2 4. Accumulation and Finalization: Initialize aoSum to 0.0. Loop i from 0 to 3 (4 iterations). For each iteration, get offset = axes[i]. Accumulate the AO contributions: aoSum += ao[i]. Return the final AO value: AO = \text{clamp}(1.0 - (aoSum / 4.0), 0.0, 1.0) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computevoxelao(hitpos: Vec3, normal: Vec3, getvoxel: Callable[[Vec3], int]) -> float: # Step 1: Base position basepos = floor(hitpos + normal 0.01) # Step 2: Define axes for 2D plane axes = [(1, 1), (-1, 1), (-1, -1), (1, -1)] # Determine side vectors based on dominant normal axis if abs(normal.x) > 0: sidea = (0, 1, 0) sideb = (0, 0, 1) elif abs(normal.y) > 0: sidea = (1, 0, 0) sideb = (0, 0, 1) else: sidea = (1, 0, 0) sideb = (0, 1, 0) # Helper for vertex AO def vertexao(s1: int, s2: int, c: int) -> float: if s1 == 1 and s2 == 1: return 0.9 return s1 0.4 + s2 0.4 + c 0.2 aosum = 0.0 # Step 3 & 4: Sample and accumulate for i in range(4): offsetx, offsety = axes[i] # Calculate corner offset corneroffset = (sidea[0]offsetx + sideb[0]offsety, sidea[1]offsetx + sideb[1]offsety, sidea[2]offsetx + sideb[2]offsety) # Sample sides and corner relative to basepos # Note: The source defines side/corner sampling explicitly with d1/d2 # We map axes to d1/d2 for clarity d1 = (offsetx, 0, 0) if abs(normal.x) > 0 else ((1,0,0) if abs(normal.y)>0 else (1,0,0)) # Simplified mapping d2 = (0, offsety, 0) if abs(normal.x) > 0 else ((0,0,1) if abs(normal.y)>0 else (0,1,0)) # Re-implementing S2's explicit sampling for robustness # S2 samples: side.x = pos+d1, side.y = pos+d2, side.z = pos-d1, side.w = pos-d2 # And corners: pos+d1+d2, pos-d1+d2, pos-d1-d2, pos+d1-d2 # To align with S1's loop structure, we iterate axes and compute contributions # However, S2's structure is more explicit. We follow S2's logic for sampling # but aggregate as S1 suggests. # Let's stick to the S2 explicit sampling for accuracy of neighbors pass # See below for refined loop # Refined Loop based on S2's explicit neighbor definition # S2 defines 4 sides and 4 corners. # We will compute the 4 face AOs directly. # Define d1, d2 based on normal dominance for the 2D plane if abs(normal.x) > 0: d1 = (1, 0, 0) # X axis d2 = (0, 0, 1) # Z axis elif abs(normal.y) > 0: d1 = (1, 0, 0) # X axis d2 = (0, 0, 1) # Z axis else: d1 = (1, 0, 0) # X axis d2 = (0, 1, 0) # Y axis # Sample sides s1 = getvoxel(basepos + d1) s2 = getvoxel(basepos + d2) s3 = getvoxel(basepos - d1) s4 = getvoxel(basepos - d2) # Sample corners c1 = getvoxel(basepos + d1 + d2) c2 = getvoxel(basepos - d1 + d2) c3 = getvoxel(basepos - d1 - d2) c4 = getvoxel(basepos + d1 - d2) # Compute AO for each face (xy, yz, zw, wx mapping to sides/corners) # S2: ao.x = vertexao(side.xy, corner.x) -> side.xy implies s1,s2? corner.x implies c1? # Mapping: # Face 1 (xy): sides s1, s2; corner c1 # Face 2 (yz): sides s2, s3; corner c2? (Note: S2 says side.yz, corner.y) # Face 3 (zw): sides s3, s4; corner c3? # Face 4 (wx): sides s4, s1; corner c4? ao1 = vertexao(s1, s2, c1) ao2 = vertexao(s2, s3, c2) ao3 = vertexao(s3, s4, c3) ao4 = vertexao(s4, s1, c4) aosum = ao1 + ao2 + ao3 + ao4 return clamp(1.0 - (aosum / 4.0), 0.0, 1.0) Parameters: Epsilon offset: 0.01 (used to prevent self-intersection). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-Intersection: Rays or samples starting exactly on the surface may hit the surface itself. An epsilon offset (normal 0.01) is required. Normal Dominance: The choice of side vectors depends on the dominant axis of the normal. If the normal is aligned with an axis, the 2D plane must be chosen correctly to avoid degenerate sampling. Histogram-based Voxel Ambient Occlusion is a local illumination technique for volume rendering that approximates ambient occlusion, color bleeding, and basic scattering effects by modulating precomputed intensity distributions (local histograms) with the transfer function during rendering. Unlike ray-based approaches such as Local AO, it uses vector quantization clustering to store these distributions in a 2D texture table, allowing real-time updates via GPU texture blending with only two additional texture lookups compared to standard gradient-based shading. Vicinity Occlusion Mapping (VOM) is a screen-space technique that incorporates view-dependent ambient occlusion and halo effects into volume rendered images by utilizing two Summed Area Tables (SATs) computed from a depth map. It sets itself apart from its siblings, such as Histogram-based Voxel Ambient Occlusion, by operating in image space rather than volume space, allowing for real-time performance without the high preprocessing costs and memory footprint of 3D density SATs. Unlike Crytek's screen-space ambient occlusion which relies on subsampling patterns that cause noise artifacts and require filtering, VOM computes the average depth of pixel vicinities in constant time using SATs, eliminating the need for filtering. This method renders only visible voxel faces by culling internal voxels and applying ambient occlusion based on the presence of neighbouring voxels. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by using a Moore neighbourhood to determine visibility and a Von Neumann neighbourhood mask for occlusion calculations, implemented via instance rendering with precomputed neighbour masks. A stochastic method to estimate ambient occlusion by casting rays into a hemisphere oriented around the surface normal, using cosine-weighted sampling. It loops i from 0 to maxSamples (default 8), calculates a seed from fragCoord and time, generates random numbers, and samples a local direction transformed to world space using tangent, bitangent, and normal basis. It performs a voxel mesh query (ray march) from hitPosition + normal epsilon and increments a hit counter if a hit is found. The occlusion factor is 1.0 - (hit / maxSamples). An ambient occlusion technique for voxel scenes that samples the 4 corners of the voxel face adjacent to the hit point, weighted by the surface normal's dominant axis. It calculates basePos using floor(hitPos + normal 0.01), defines 4 corner offsets (1,1), (-1,1), (-1,-1), (1,-1), and sums the solidity of the 4 corners, dividing by 4.0 to get the AO factor. Converts each vertex's world-space position to voxel grid coordinates by subtracting the grid offset and dividing by the voxel scale, casting to i32. It computes the AO factor by querying the voxel neighborhood at the grid coordinates (vx, vy, vz) and the vertex normal, then modulates the vertex RGB color channels by multiplying each channel by the computed AO factor. An approximation of color bleeding where the color appearance of a surface is affected by colored nearby objects, modeled by including the voxel color C{RGB} in the attenuation integral. It reformulates the AO integral by multiplying the extinction coefficient \tau(t) by the color C{RGB}(t) before integration: I{AORGB}(s) \approx IA \cdot e^{-\int{t \in \mathbb{N}(s)} \frac{\tau(t) C{RGB}(t)}{|s-t|^2} dt} where I{AORGB} is a vector describing intensity per color, C{RGB}(t) is the color at position t depending on the Transfer Function (TF), and other terms are as in Eq. 4. A CUDA-based implementation to compute Vicinity Occlusion Maps on the GPU, using a column-then-row summation strategy for Summed Area Tables. It analyzes the source depth map by columns on the GPU and sums the resulting values by rows. Performance tests on an Intel Core 2 Duo CPU and NVidia GeForce GTX 280 GPU showed VOM construction times of 2.427ms (CPU) vs 1.450ms (GPU) for 512x512 viewport, but frame rates were similar (5.67 fps vs 7.21 fps for Body dataset) due to data transfer overhead. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample point, as it involves a fixed number of voxel lookups (typically 8-12 neighbors). Memory Complexity: O(N) for the voxel grid, where N is the number of voxels. No additional large buffers are required for the basic method. Performance: The method is lightweight and suitable for real-time applications. The cost is dominated by voxel grid access, which can be optimized with spatial hashing or uniform grids. Strengths: Simple to implement, fast, and provides plausible occlusion results for voxel-based scenes. Limitations: Approximate; does not account for distance attenuation beyond immediate neighbors (unless modified). Quality depends on voxel resolution. Voxel Ambient Occlusion is a technique used in voxel-based rendering to approximate the dimming of light in crevices and corners. It builds on the principles of voxel-based neighbor counting [17927-voxel-based-neighbor-counting.md]. The method is commonly used in real-time voxel engines and games to add depth and realism to voxel graphics. name: Histogram-based Voxel Ambient Occlusion
head: Dynamic Ambient Occlusion, Histogram-based AO, Precomputed local histograms for ambient occlusion, Ropinski et al
body:
Histogram-based Voxel Ambient Occlusion is a local illumination technique for volume rendering that approximates ambient occlusion, color bleeding, and basic scattering effects by modulating precomputed intensity distributions (local histograms) with the transfer function during rendering. Unlike ray-based approaches such as Local AO, it uses vector quantization clustering to store these distributions in a 2D texture table, allowing real-time updates via GPU texture blending with only two additional texture lookups compared to standard gradient-based shading. Inputs and Outputs Input: Scalar volume data set, transfer function (mapping intensity to transparency 	au\alpha and emissive color 	au{rgb}), and precomputed clustering data. Output: Final pixel color incorporating ambient occlusion, environmental color (color bleeding), and glow effects. Data Structures 1. Cluster ID Volume: A scalar volume data set where each voxel stores an integer ID. This ID associates the voxel with a specific row in the 2D texture table. 2. 2D Texture Table: Stores representative local histograms for clusters of similar voxels. The texture is indexed by the cluster ID. Each entry represents a normalized local histogram LH. Parameters \OmegaR: Radius of the region for which local histograms LH have been precomputed. b: Data bit depth. The number of bins in the local histogram is 2^b. 	au\alpha(j): Transparency assigned to intensity bin j. 	au{rgb}(j): Emissive color of voxels having intensity j. Algorithm Steps 1. Precomputation (Offline): 1. For each voxel in the volume, compute a local histogram of intensities within the neighborhood defined by radius \OmegaR. 2. Normalize these histograms. 3. Perform similarity-based clustering (vector quantization) on the histograms to group similar neighborhoods. 4. Store the representative histogram for each cluster in a 2D texture table. 5. Generate the Cluster ID Volume, assigning each voxel the ID of its corresponding cluster. Note: This stage is computationally expensive. Interactive clipping is not supported because changing the clipping plane would alter the density distribution in the voxel neighborhoods, invalidating the precomputed histograms. 2. Rendering (Per Voxel/Sample): 1. Retrieve the cluster ID for the current voxel 	ilde{x} from the Cluster ID Volume. 2. Look up the representative local histogram LH{	ilde{x}} from the 2D Texture Table using the cluster ID. 3. Modulate the histogram bins based on the transfer function transparency 	au\alpha(j) for each bin j. 4. Compute the local occlusion factor O{env} using the modulated histogram: O{env}(	ilde{x}, 
abla	au(f(	ilde{x}))) =  rac{2}{3} \cdot  rac{1}{\pi \OmegaR} \sum{0 \le j < 2^b} 	au\alpha(j) \cdot LHj(	ilde{x}) where LHj(	ilde{x}) is the value of the histogram bin j for the voxel's cluster. 5. Compute the environmental color E{env} (for color bleeding) by modulating the histogram with the transfer function color 	au{rgb}(j): E{env}(	ilde{x}, 
abla	au(f(	ilde{x}))) =  rac{2}{3} \cdot  rac{1}{\pi \OmegaR} \sum{0 \le j < 2^b} 	au\alpha(j) \cdot 	au{rgb}(j) \cdot LHj(	ilde{x}). 6. For Isosurface Rendering: Compute the ambient intensity L{amb} using the ambient light coefficient ka: L{amb}(	ilde{x}) = 1.0 - O{env}(	ilde{x}, 
abla	au(f(	ilde{x}))) \cdot ka. 7. For Direct Volume Rendering: Compute the diffuse color coefficient kd by blending the transfer function color 	au{rgb} and the environmental color E{env} using O{env} as the blend factor. This simulates color bleeding, where the voxel's color is affected by its environment. 8. Glow Effect: An additional mapping function can be used to modulate the local histograms to produce a simple glow effect, highlighting specific regions. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def precompute(volumedata, radiusOmegaR, bitdepthb): rawhistograms = [] numbins = 2 bitdepthb for voxel in volumedata: # Standard 3D grid iteration to collect intensities within radius ΩR neighborhoodintensities = getvoxelneighbors(voxel, radiusOmegaR) hist = [0.0] numbins for intensity in neighborhoodintensities: binidx = int(intensity) % numbins hist[binidx] += 1.0 # Normalize histogram total = sum(hist) if total > 0: hist = [h / total for h in hist] rawhistograms.append(hist) # Apply vector quantization (e.g., k-means) to group similar histograms clusters = performvectorquantization(rawhistograms) clusterids = [c.id for c in clusters] # Build 2D texture table and cluster ID volume texturetable = [c.representative for c in clusters] clusteridvolume = [c.id for c in clusters.assignments] return texturetable, clusteridvolume def rendervoxel(voxelpos, texturetable, clusteridvolume, tfalpha, tfrgb, OmegaR, bitdepthb): clusterid = clusteridvolume[voxelpos] histogram = texturetable[clusterid] numbins = 2 bitdepthb normalizationfactor = (2.0 / 3.0) / (math.pi OmegaR) sumocclusion = 0.0 sumenvcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for j in range(numbins): hj = histogram[j] ta = tfalpha[j] tc = tfrgb[j] modulatedh = ta hj sumocclusion += modulatedh sumenvcolor[0] += modulatedh tc[0] sumenvcolor[1] += modulatedh tc[1] sumenvcolor[2] += modulatedh tc[2] Oenv = normalizationfactor sumocclusion Eenv = normalizationfactor sumenvcolor # Standard 3D grid lookup to retrieve intensity at voxelpos currentvoxelcolor = tfrgb[getvoxelintensity(voxelpos)] kd = [ currentvoxelcolor[0] (1.0 - Oenv) + Eenv[0] Oenv, currentvoxelcolor[1] (1.0 - Oenv) + Eenv[1] Oenv, currentvoxelcolor[2] (1.0 - Oenv) + Eenv[2] Oenv ] return kd Performance: Interactive rendering performance is achieved. It requires only two additional texture lookups compared to standard gradient-based shading. Update Speed: Illumination update time is very low because histogram modulation is performed through GPU texture blending. Precomputation Cost: The precomputation stage (computing local histograms and performing clustering) is expensive. However, CUDA-based optimizations can reduce precomputation times by a factor of up to 10. Limitations: Interactive clipping is not supported because it would affect the density distribution in the voxel neighborhoods used for histogram precomputation. Only local shadows with a soft appearance are supported. The set of precomputed local histograms may become too large for large datasets, increasing memory requirements. Strengths: Allows real-time updates of occlusion information and supports ambient occlusion, color bleeding, basic scattering, and glow effects in a unified framework. The method was introduced by Ropinski et al. in 2008 as "Dynamic Ambient Occlusion". It was originally presented in the context of volume ray-casting. The approach was later discussed in the context of interactive volume rendering with volumetric illumination. A follow-up CUDA-based approach by Mess and Ropinski (2010) improved precomputation performance. name: Vicinity Occlusion Mapping (VOM)
head: Vicinity Occlusion Map
body: Vicinity Occlusion Mapping (VOM) is a screen-space technique that incorporates view-dependent ambient occlusion and halo effects into volume rendered images by utilizing two Summed Area Tables (SATs) computed from a depth map. It sets itself apart from its siblings, such as Histogram-based Voxel Ambient Occlusion, by operating in image space rather than volume space, allowing for real-time performance without the high preprocessing costs and memory footprint of 3D density SATs. Unlike Crytek's screen-space ambient occlusion which relies on subsampling patterns that cause noise artifacts and require filtering, VOM computes the average depth of pixel vicinities in constant time using SATs, eliminating the need for filtering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A depth map generated from a volume rendering pass, where depth values are encoded in the range [0, 1] (0 is the furthest point, 1 is the closest point). Background pixels are assigned depth 0. Output: A modified color map with ambient occlusion and/or halo effects applied. Data Structures: The VOM consists of two 2D textures (Summed Area Tables): 1. SAT{depth}: Stores the accumulated depth for each pixel. Each cell (x, y) stores the sum of depth values from (0, 0) to (x, y). 2. SAT{Ndepth}: Stores the count of contributed values in the neighborhood. It is computed from a bitmap where non-background pixels are 1 and background pixels are 0. Numbered Steps: 1. Stage 1 (GPU): Perform ray casting on the 3D texture to generate a color map (using Phong shading) and a depth map. The depth map encodes the depth of the first sample that reaches full opacity along the viewing rays. 2. Stage 2 (CPU): Compute SAT{depth} from the depth map and SAT{Ndepth} from the bitmap (0 for background, 1 otherwise). Store these as two 2D textures. The 2D SAT is computed incrementally during a single pass. The value of each cell is computed as: SAT{image}(x, y) = \sum{i=0, j=0}^{x,y} p{i,j} where p{i,j} is the value at cell (i, j). 3. Stage 3 (GPU): Load the VOM textures. For each pixel [x, y] where the volume model is projected (background pixels are excluded), evaluate the average depth of the vicinity. 4. Evaluate Occlusion: Determine if the pixel is occluded by comparing the average depth of the vicinity (avgdepth[x, y]) with the pixel's depth (depth[x, y]). If avgdepth[x, y] > depth[x, y], the vicinity is closer to the observer, indicating occlusion. 5. Calculate Occlusion Factor: If occluded, calculate the occlusion factor occ: occ = (avgdepth[x, y] - depth[x, y]) \times factor{vic} where factor{vic} is a user-defined scaling factor. 6. Smooth Occlusion: Smooth the occlusion value using smoothstep to obtain dark{vic}: dark{vic} = smoothstep(0., 0.99, occ) 7. Modify Color: Apply the occlusion to the original Phong shading color Phong[x, y] using a user-defined RGB triplet Color{vic}: Color[x, y] = (1 - dark{vic}) \times Phong[x, y] + dark{vic} \times Color{vic} 8. Halo Rendering (Optional): To render halos, consider the average depth from the neighborhood. If the structure in the pixel lies outside the object, render a halo color that decays with respect to the distance to the object. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x): t = max(0.0, min(1.0, (x - edge0) / (edge1 - edge0))) return t t (3.0 - 2.0 t) def getsat(S, x, y): if x < 0 or y < 0: return 0.0 return S[y, x] def applyvom(colormap, depthmap, satdepth, satndepth, factorvic, colorvic, sizex, sizey): height, width = depthmap.shape resultcolor = colormap.copy() for y in range(height): for x in range(width): # Skip background pixels if depthmap[y, x] == 0: continue # Define vicinity bounds x1 = max(0, x - sizex) x2 = min(width - 1, x + sizex) y1 = max(0, y - sizey) y2 = min(height - 1, y + sizey) # Calculate sum of depths in vicinity using SAT (4 texture accesses) sumdepth = (getsat(satdepth, x2, y2) - getsat(satdepth, x1 - 1, y2) - getsat(satdepth, x2, y1 - 1) + getsat(satdepth, x1 - 1, y1 - 1)) sumcount = (getsat(satndepth, x2, y2) - getsat(satndepth, x1 - 1, y2) - getsat(satndepth, x2, y1 - 1) + getsat(satndepth, x1 - 1, y1 - 1)) # Calculate average depth if sumcount > 0: avgdepth = sumdepth / sumcount else: avgdepth = depthmap[y, x] # Check for occlusion (higher depth value means closer) if avgdepth > depthmap[y, x]: # Calculate occlusion factor occ = (avgdepth - depthmap[y, x]) factorvic # Smooth occlusion darkvic = smoothstep(0.0, 0.99, occ) # Modify color phongcolor = colormap[y, x] resultcolor[y, x] = (1.0 - darkvic) phongcolor + darkvic colorvic return resultcolor Parameters: factor{vic}: User-defined scaling factor controlling the intensity of the ambient occlusion effect. Color{vic}: User-defined RGB triplet for darkening or changing the color of occluded pixels. sizex, sizey: Define the vicinity resolution, resulting in a (2sizex + 1) \times (2sizey + 1) pixel neighborhood. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The depth map only encodes the depth of the first sample that reaches full opacity. Consequently, only opaque structures and semi-transparent ones contributing to full opacity are considered for occlusion and halos. Computations are performed only for pixels where the volume model is projected; background pixels are excluded. The 3D Density Summed Area Table (DSAT) is a view-independent ambient occlusion technique for volume rendering that simulates occlusion at the voxel level by evaluating the local density environment. It supports semi-transparent structures and is more accurate than 2D image-space approaches, though it incurs higher preprocessing costs and memory usage. It sets itself apart from opacity-based SATs by storing raw density values, allowing the occlusion factor to update dynamically when the transfer function changes without recomputing the table. Calculate occlusion factor occ if the vicinity is closer to the observer (avgdepth[x, y] > depth[x, y]): occ = (avgdepth[x, y] - depth[x, y]) \times factor{vic}. Smooth the occlusion value using smoothstep: dark{vic} = smoothstep(0., 0.99, occ). The average depth is computed as avgdepth[x, y] = \frac{\sum{i=x-sizex}^{x+sizex} \sum{j=y-sizey}^{y+sizey} depth[i, j]}{NElems |depthElem > 0}, where sizex and sizey define the vicinity resolution ((2sizex +1)\times(2sizey +1) pixels), and NElems|depthElem > 0 is the count of non-background pixels in the vicinity. The final color is Color[x, y] = (1 - dark{vic}) \times Phong[x, y] + dark{vic} \times Color{vic}, where Phong[x, y] is the original Phong shading color and Color{vic} is a user-defined RGB triplet for darkening/changing color. factor{vic} is a user-defined scaling factor controlling the intensity of the ambient occlusion effect. Computations are performed only for pixels where the volume model is projected; background pixels are excluded. Time Complexity: The 2D SAT computation cost increases linearly with the number of cells. Evaluating a region sum requires only four texture accesses to the corners of the regions. Memory Complexity: Requires storing two 2D textures for the VOM. Measured Performance: Enables real-time ambient occlusion and halo rendering. Only one ray casting process is required in the whole pipeline. Strengths: View-dependent, real-time performance, no filtering required, simple implementation using SATs. Limitations: Only considers structures that reach full opacity, view-dependent (requires recomputation if view changes significantly, though the VOM itself is computed per frame), higher memory footprint compared to simple shading. When to use: When real-time view-dependent ambient occlusion and halos are needed for opaque or fully opaque-contributing semi-transparent volumes. When not to use: When view-independent occlusion is required, or when accurate occlusion for semi-transparent structures that do not reach full opacity is needed. Vicinity Occlusion Mapping (VOM) was introduced by Diaz et al. [DYV08] as a method to effectively utilize two SATs computed from the depth map to incorporate view-dependent ambient occlusion and halo effects in volume rendered images. It was presented as an alternative to screen-space ambient occlusion techniques that rely on subsampling and filtering. name: 3D Density Summed Area Table
head: 3D SAT Occlusion, 3D SAT for AO, Density SAT, Density Summed Area Table, Volumetric Ambient Occlusion (DSAT)
body: The 3D Density Summed Area Table (DSAT) is a view-independent ambient occlusion technique for volume rendering that simulates occlusion at the voxel level by evaluating the local density environment. It supports semi-transparent structures and is more accurate than 2D image-space approaches, though it incurs higher preprocessing costs and memory usage. It sets itself apart from opacity-based SATs by storing raw density values, allowing the occlusion factor to update dynamically when the transfer function changes without recomputing the table. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset V of density values with dimensions W \times H \times D. Output: A 3D Density Summed Area Table (DSAT) of the same dimensions, and a rendered volume image with ambient occlusion applied to opaque samples. Data Structures: Volume V: A 3D array where V[x, y, z] represents the density at voxel coordinates (x, y, z). DSAT: A 3D array of the same size as V. Each cell DSAT[x, y, z] stores the cumulative sum of density values from the origin (0, 0, 0) to (x, y, z). Formulas: The DSAT is defined recursively to allow efficient region queries: DSAT[x, y, z] = \sum{i=0}^{x} \sum{j=0}^{y} \sum{k=0}^{z} V[i, j, k] \quad \text{} To compute the sum of density values for an arbitrary cuboid region defined by corners (x1, y1, z1) and (x2, y2, z2), eight queries on the DSAT are required: Sum = DSAT[x2, y2, z2] - DSAT[x1-1, y2, z2] - DSAT[x2, y1-1, z2] - DSAT[x2, y2, z1-1] + DSAT[x1-1, y1-1, z2] + DSAT[x1-1, y2, z1-1] + DSAT[x2, y1-1, z1-1] - DSAT[x1-1, y1-1, z1-1] \quad \text{} (Note: Terms with negative indices are treated as 0.) The average density \bar{d} of the vicinity region is calculated as: \bar{d} = \frac{Sum}{N} where N is the number of voxels in the cuboid region. The occlusion factor O is derived by applying the current transfer function's opacity mapping T to this average density: O = T(\bar{d}) \quad \text{} Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing (CPU): 1. Load the volume density data V. 2. Construct the 3D DSAT incrementally. For each voxel (x, y, z), compute the sum based on previously computed DSAT values. The incremental construction follows the standard 3D prefix sum logic, similar to the 2D case but extended to three dimensions. 3. Store the resulting DSAT in memory. 2. Rendering (GPU): 1. Pass the DSAT and the volume model V to the GPU. 2. Perform ray casting through the volume. 3. For each sample point along the ray that is classified as opaque (based on the transfer function): a. Define a vicinity cuboid region around the sample point. b. Query the DSAT using the eight-corner formula to obtain the sum of densities in this region. c. Calculate the average density \bar{d} by dividing the sum by the number of voxels in the region. d. Map \bar{d} to an opacity value using the current transfer function T(\bar{d}). e. Modify the shading of the sample by reducing its lighting contribution according to the occlusion factor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compute3dsat(volume): """ Computes the 3D Density Summed Area Table from a volume. volume: 3D list of density values V[x, y, z] Returns: 3D list DSAT[x, y, z] """ W, H, D = len(volume), len(volume[0]), len(volume[0][0]) dsat = [[[0.0 for in range(D)] for in range(H)] for in range(W)] for x in range(W): for y in range(H): for z in range(D): current = volume[x][y][z] fromx = dsat[x-1][y][z] if x > 0 else 0 fromy = dsat[x][y-1][z] if y > 0 else 0 fromz = dsat[x][y][z-1] if z > 0 else 0 fromxy = dsat[x-1][y-1][z] if x > 0 and y > 0 else 0 fromxz = dsat[x-1][y][z-1] if x > 0 and z > 0 else 0 fromyz = dsat[x][y-1][z-1] if y > 0 and z > 0 else 0 fromxyz = dsat[x-1][y-1][z-1] if x > 0 and y > 0 and z > 0 else 0 dsat[x][y][z] = current + fromx + fromy + fromz - fromxy - fromxz - fromyz + fromxyz return dsat def queryregionsum(dsat, x1, y1, z1, x2, y2, z2): """ Computes the sum of values in the cuboid defined by (x1,y1,z1) to (x2,y2,z2) using the 3D DSAT. """ def getval(x, y, z): if x < 0 or y < 0 or z < 0: return 0 return dsat[x][y][z] return (getval(x2, y2, z2) getval(x1-1, y2, z2) getval(x2, y1-1, z2) getval(x2, y2, z1-1) + getval(x1-1, y1-1, z2) + getval(x1-1, y2, z1-1) + getval(x2, y1-1, z1-1) getval(x1-1, y1-1, z1-1)) def applyaosample(x, y, z, dsat, vicinitysize, transferfunction): """ Calculates ambient occlusion for a single sample point. """ halfsize = vicinitysize // 2 x1, y1, z1 = max(0, x - halfsize), max(0, y - halfsize), max(0, z - halfsize) x2, y2, z2 = min(len(dsat)-1, x + halfsize), min(len(dsat[0])-1, y + halfsize), min(len(dsat[0][0])-1, z + halfsize) densitysum = queryregionsum(dsat, x1, y1, z1, x2, y2, z2) numvoxels = (x2 - x1 + 1) (y2 - y1 + 1) (z2 - z1 + 1) avgdensity = densitysum / numvoxels occlusionfactor = transferfunction(avgdensity) return occlusionfactor Parameters and Edge Cases: Vicinity Size and Density Variability: The size of the cuboid region queried for average density affects accuracy; if density values vary significantly within the vicinity, the assigned opacity may differ from the real one, causing artifacts. Transfer Function Changes: Since DSAT stores density, not opacity, changing the transfer function does not require recomputing the DSAT. View Independence: The DSAT is view-independent, so it does not need to be recomputed when the camera view changes. Time Complexity: Preprocessing is O(W \times H \times D) for constructing the DSAT. Per-sample rendering requires 8 texture accesses to estimate the region sum. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the DSAT, resulting in a larger memory footprint. Performance: Higher preprocessing cost on the CPU compared to screen-space methods. However, it avoids GPU-CPU transfers during rendering, leading to higher frame rates in interactive scenarios compared to dynamic screen-space approaches. Accuracy: More accurate than 2D image-space approaches because it considers the full 3D neighborhood, including semi-transparent structures. Limitations: Artifacts can occur if the density variability in the vicinity is high, as the average density may not map correctly to the actual local opacity. The 3D Density Summed Area Table was introduced as a method to enhance volume visualization by providing view-independent ambient occlusion. It builds upon the concept of Summed Area Tables used in 2D image processing and extends it to 3D volumes. The method was described in the context of enhancing perception in volume visualization, specifically addressing the limitations of depth-based screen-space occlusion methods that fail to account for semi-transparent structures. It is related to other SAT-based techniques such as those by Desgranges and Engel. name: Voxel Culling and Ambient Occlusion
head: Moore/Von Neumann Neighbourhood Culling, Sparse Voxel Rendering with AO
body: This method renders only visible voxel faces by culling internal voxels and applying ambient occlusion based on the presence of neighbouring voxels. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by using a Moore neighbourhood to determine visibility and a Von Neumann neighbourhood mask for occlusion calculations, implemented via instance rendering with precomputed neighbour masks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A voxel grid organized into chunks of size CHUNKSIZE (128). Input: A list of visible voxels, each storing a linear index and a Von Neumann neighbour mask. Output: Rendered scene with visible voxel faces and ambient occlusion applied. Data Structures: VONNEUMANNMASK: A constant u32 bitmask (4281360) representing the 6 Von Neumann neighbours (indices 4, 10, 12, 14, 16, 22 in the Moore neighbourhood). visiblevoxels: A buffer storing pairs of (linearindex, neighboursmask) for each visible voxel. TRIVERTICES: Array of vertex offsets for the 6 faces of a voxel. TRINORMALS: Array of normal vectors for the 6 faces of a voxel. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Moore Neighbourhood: For each voxel position v, compute its Moore neighbourhood using mooreneighbourhood(v). 2. Check Visibility: A voxel is visible if it is VOXELFULL AND (on the chunk boundary OR has at least one empty Von Neumann neighbour). 3. Store Visible Voxels: If visible, atomically increment a counter and store the voxel's linear index and Von Neumann neighbour mask in the visiblevoxels buffer. 4. Calculate Occlusion Factor: In the vertex shader, for each instance (voxel), calculate the occlusion factor by counting the number of set bits in the intersection of the current face's Moore mask and the voxel's Von Neumann mask, then dividing by 3.0. 5. Calculate Lighting Intensity: Calculate lighting intensity as the diffuse component (max(dot(norm, lightdir), 0.0)) minus the ambient occlusion term (AMBIENT occlusion). Formulas: Occlusion Factor: O = \frac{\text{countOneBits}(m \cap n)}{3.0}, where m is the Moore mask for the specific triangle face and n is the Von Neumann neighbour mask of the voxel. Lighting Intensity: I = \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}, 0.0) - \text{AMBIENT} \times O, where \mathbf{n} is the face normal, \mathbf{l} is the normalized light direction, and AMBIENT is 0.25. Parameters: CHUNKSIZE: 128. AMBIENT: 0.25. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The Moore neighbourhood linear index calculation assumes a specific ordering of the 27 neighbours. The mooretovonneumann function hardcodes the mapping from Moore indices to Von Neumann indices. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. CHUNKSIZE = 128 AMBIENT = 0.25 VONNEUMANNMASK = 4281360 # Precomputed bitmask for Von Neumann neighbours def moorelinearindex(v): """Compute linear index in the 3x3x3 Moore neighbourhood.""" return (v.x + 1) + 3 (v.y + 1) + 9 (v.z + 1) def chunkvectorindex(i): """Convert linear chunk index to 3D vector.""" s = CHUNKSIZE CHUNKSIZE z = i // s y = (i % s) // CHUNKSIZE x = (i % s) % CHUNKSIZE return (x, y, z) def isvisible(v, neighbours): """Check if a voxel is visible.""" i = linearindex(v) return (voxels[i] == VOXELFULL) and (isboundary(v) or hasemptyneighbour(neighbours)) def mooreneighbourmask(v, n): """Compute Moore mask for a specific face.""" # Hardcoded mapping from Moore indices to Von Neumann indices # This function returns a bitmask of occupied Von Neumann neighbours # for the given face normal n at position v pass # Implementation details depend on specific Moore ordering def countonebits(mask): """Count set bits in a u32 mask.""" return bin(mask).count('1') def vertexshader(voxelindex, neighboursmask, vertexindex): translation = chunkvectorindex(voxelindex) v = TRIVERTICES[vertexindex] n = TRINORMALS[vertexindex] m = mooreneighbourmask(v, n) occlusion = countonebits(m & neighboursmask) / 3.0 fragpos = v + translation norm = n lightdir = normalize(lightpos - fragpos) intensity = max(dot(norm, lightdir), 0.0) intensity -= AMBIENT occlusion return intensity def fragmentshader(intensity): return (AMBIENT + intensity) vec3(0.3, 0.2, 0.1) Time Complexity: Visibility check is O(1) per voxel. Occlusion calculation is O(1) per face. Total time is proportional to the number of visible voxels. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing visible voxels, where N is the number of visible voxels. Performance: Efficient for sparse voxel grids as it culls internal voxels. Performance scales with the number of visible voxels rather than total voxels. Strengths: Simple implementation, efficient culling, real-time capable. Limitations: Approximate occlusion (only considers immediate neighbours), fixed AMBIENT value may not suit all scenes. When to Use: Real-time rendering of sparse voxel terrains or environments where performance is critical. When Not to Use: When high-quality global illumination or accurate shadowing is required. This method is derived from the wgpu-voxel-terrain project by statusfailed, which implements a voxel terrain renderer using WebGPU. It builds on the concept of voxel ambient occlusion by incorporating neighbour-based culling and occlusion calculations. statusfailed/wgpu-voxel-terrain, https://github.com/statusfailed/wgpu-voxel-terrain, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Positional & Normal-Based Voxel Shadowing
head: Block Position Shadowing, Deterministic Voxel Shadowing
body: Positional & Normal-Based Voxel Shadowing calculates a per-face shadow multiplier for voxel blocks using deterministic rules based on block position, block type, and face normal to simulate directional shading without ray tracing. It differs from ray-traced or ray-marched shadowing methods (such as Two-Pass Shadow Casting or Shadow Ray Casting) by avoiding expensive visibility integration along light rays, instead relying on static geometric heuristics to approximate occlusion. Inputs: blockPos: The 3D integer coordinates (X, Y, Z) of the voxel block. block: The unique identifier (ID) of the block type (e.g., ushort). faceNormal: The direction of the face being shaded (e.g., Top, Bottom, Left, Right, Front, Back). Outputs: shadow: A float multiplier in the range [0, 1] representing the shadow intensity applied to the face. Data Structures: transparencylookup: An array or map indexed by block ID, storing the transparency mode for each block type. shadowIntensity: A scalar float parameter defining the darkness of the shadow when conditions are met. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize shadow to 1.0. 2. Determine if the block is transparent by checking transparencylookup[block] against the opaque state. 3. Evaluate shadow conditions in the following order: Depth Shadow: If Y < -2, apply shadow. Z-Offset Shadow: If Y \le 0 AND Z \neq 0 AND |X| \pmod{10} > 5, apply shadow. X-Offset Shadow: If Y \le 0 AND X \neq 0 AND |Z| \pmod{14} > 7, apply shadow. Bottom Face Shadow: If faceNormal is Bottom AND the block is opaque, apply shadow. 4. Return shadow. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import enum class Direction(enum.Enum): Bottom = "Bottom" Top = "Top" Left = "Left" Right = "Right" Front = "Front" Back = "Back" class TransparencyMode(enum.Enum): Opaque = "Opaque" Transparent = "Transparent" def getshadow(blockpos: tuple, blockid: int, facenormal: Direction, shadowintensity: float, transparencylookup: dict) -> float: """ Calculates the shadow multiplier for a voxel face based on position and normal. Args: blockpos: (X, Y, Z) coordinates of the block. blockid: ID of the block type. facenormal: Direction of the face being shaded. shadowintensity: The multiplier value when shadowed. transparencylookup: Dict mapping blockid to TransparencyMode. Returns: Shadow multiplier (1.0 if no shadow, shadowintensity if shadowed). """ shadow = 1.0 isopaque = transparencylookup.get(blockid, TransparencyMode.Opaque) != TransparencyMode.Transparent # Condition 1: Depth shadow (below a certain Y threshold) if blockpos[1] < -2: return shadowintensity # Condition 2: Z-offset shadow (checkerboard-like pattern along Z) elif blockpos[1] <= 0 and blockpos[2] != 0 and abs(blockpos[0]) % 10 > 5: return shadowintensity # Condition 3: X-offset shadow (checkerboard-like pattern along X) elif blockpos[1] <= 0 and blockpos[0] != 0 and abs(blockpos[2]) % 14 > 7: return shadowintensity # Condition 4: Bottom face shadow (only for opaque blocks) elif facenormal == Direction.Bottom and isopaque: return shadowintensity return shadow Parameters: shadowIntensity: The multiplier applied when any shadow condition is met. Exact value not defined in the source snippet. blockPos: Integer vector (X, Y, Z). faceNormal: Enum representing one of the six cardinal directions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Grass Blocks: Blocks with ID 1 (Grass) require an additional dirt face (ID 5) to be rendered when side faces are visible. This must be handled before tint calculation to prevent visual artifacts. Transparent Blocks: Bottom faces of transparent blocks do not receive the bottom-face shadow, but may still receive position-based shadows if they meet the Y or offset criteria. Noise-Driven Face Tinting applies a procedural color tint to visible block faces using 2D noise, modulated by the calculated shadow multiplier from Positional & Normal-Based Voxel Shadowing. It is used to add visual variation to specific block types (e.g., Grass ID 1, Stone ID 6) based on their position. Definition: Interpolates between two colors based on a 2D noise sample at the block's X/Z coordinates. Steps: 1. Initialize tint to white (1, 1, 1) and doTint flag to false. 2. Determine if tinting is enabled: If block == 1 (Grass) AND faceNormal != Direction.Bottom, set doTint = true. If block == 6 (Stone) AND faceNormal == Direction.Top, set doTint = true. 3. If doTint is true: Sample 2D noise at (blockPos.X, blockPos.Z). Normalize the noise sample to [0, 1]. Interpolate between color1 and color2 using the normalized noise value. 4. Multiply the resulting tint by the shadow multiplier from GetShadow. Parameters: color1: Base tint color (0.8, 0.7, 1.0). color2: Target tint color (0.0, 1.0, 1.0). noise: A FastNoiseLite instance (or equivalent procedural noise generator). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getshadedtint(blockpos: tuple, blockid: int, facenormal: Direction, shadow: float, noisegenerator, color1: tuple, color2: tuple) -> tuple: """ Calculates the final tint color for a voxel face, modulated by shadow. """ tint = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) dotint = False # Determine if this block/face combination requires tinting if blockid == 1 and facenormal != Direction.Bottom: dotint = True elif blockid == 6 and facenormal == Direction.Top: dotint = True if dotint: # Sample 2D noise at X/Z coordinates noiseval = noisegenerator.getnoise2d(blockpos[0], blockpos[2]) # Normalize to [0, 1] assuming noise output is [-1, 1] normalizednoise = (noiseval + 1.0) / 2.0 # Interpolate between color1 and color2 tint = ( color1[0] + (color2[0] - color1[0]) normalizednoise, color1[1] + (color2[1] - color1[1]) normalizednoise, color1[2] + (color2[2] - color1[2]) normalizednoise) # Apply shadow multiplier finaltint = (tint[0] shadow, tint[1] shadow, tint[2] shadow) return finaltint Depth-based Colored Halos uses a data structure based on summed area tables to simulate ambient occlusion and generate depth-based colored halos around structures of interest during ray casting visualization. The method filters seeds from a previous stage, assigns colors and opacities to halo regions, and composites the halos into the volume rendering. It is primarily applied in Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) medical visualization to provide contextual depth cues that the maximum operator alone lacks. Time Complexity: O(1) per face, as the method involves a fixed number of arithmetic comparisons and modulo operations independent of scene size or light distance. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory, requiring no ray buffers, depth maps, or accumulation buffers. Performance: Extremely fast, suitable for real-time rendering of large voxel worlds on low-end hardware or mobile devices. Strengths: Deterministic, artifact-free (no ray marching errors or shadow acne), and easily parallelizable. Limitations: Shadows are static and do not change with light position or time, and do not account for actual occlusion by other blocks, only heuristic rules. Soft shadows are not supported natively. When to use: When performance is critical, and approximate, stylized shading is acceptable. When not to use: When dynamic lighting, realistic soft shadows, or global illumination effects are required. This method is defined in a public voxel renderer repository. It is designed for efficient voxel rendering in game engines, specifically targeting Minecraft-like block worlds. The approach simplifies lighting by decoupling shadow calculation from ray tracing, using block position and type as proxies for occlusion. rarefushion/Cubic-GridVoxelRenderer, https://github.com/rarefushion/Cubic-GridVoxelRenderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Enhanced perception in volume visualization, https://doi.org/10.5821/dissertation-2117-94929, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Flat Corner Lighting for Greedy Merged Quads
head: computeGreedyCornerLighting
body: Flat corner lighting calculates per-vertex lighting values for greedy merged quads to allow the GPU to interpolate a smooth light gradient across the face, avoiding broken ambient occlusion (AO) artifacts that occur when lighting is computed per-face. It builds on Positional & Normal-Based Voxel Shadowing by providing the specific corner samples required for that shading model. Inputs: world: The voxel world context providing block state and lighting queries. face: The greedy merged quad geometry, containing getStepX(), getStepY(), getStepZ() (integer offsets from the block origin) and the face normal/orientation. worldX, worldY, worldZ: The integer coordinates of the block origin for this face. cornerIndex: The index of the specific corner being computed (0–3 for a quad). scratch: A temporary storage structure with fields brightness[4] and lightmap[4]. Outputs: Updates scratch.brightness[cornerIndex] and scratch.lightmap[cornerIndex] with the computed lighting values for the specified corner. Data Structures: scratch: An array-like structure of size 4 for brightness and lightmap. cornerState: The BlockState retrieved from the world. packedLight: An integer or packed float representing the combined light and AO value. Steps: 1. Calculate the sample position for the corner: \text{samplePos} = (\text{worldX} + \text{face.getStepX()}, \text{worldY} + \text{face.getStepY()}, \text{worldZ} + \text{face.getStepZ()}) 2. Retrieve the block state at the sample position: \text{cornerState} = \text{world.getBlockState}(\text{samplePos}) 3. Compute the packed light value for the corner: \text{packedLight} = \text{greedyMeshing}\.getLightColor(\text{world}, \text{cornerState}, \text{samplePos}) 4. Compute the directional shade for the face using the parent method: \text{shade} = \text{world.getShade}(\text{face}, \text{scratch.applyDirectionalShade}) 5. Store the results in the scratch buffer: \text{scratch.brightness}[\text{cornerIndex}] = \text{shade} \text{scratch.lightmap}[\text{cornerIndex}] = \text{packedLight} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeGreedyCornerLighting(world, face, worldX, worldY, worldZ, cornerIndex, scratch): # Step 1: Determine sample position based on face step offsets sampleX = worldX + face.getStepX() sampleY = worldY + face.getStepY() sampleZ = worldZ + face.getStepZ() samplePos = (sampleX, sampleY, sampleZ) # Step 2: Get block state at the corner sample position cornerState = world.getBlockState(samplePos) # Step 3: Compute packed light color for the corner packedLight = world.getLightColor(cornerState, samplePos) # Exact implementation not specified # Step 4: Compute directional shade for the entire face shade = world.getShade(face, scratch.applyDirectionalShade) # Step 5: Store results in scratch buffer scratch.brightness[cornerIndex] = shade scratch.lightmap[cornerIndex] = packedLight Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The sample position is derived from the face's step offsets, not the corner's local offset within the quad. This ensures consistent lighting across merged geometry. Fills lighting for an entire merged face by sampling light at a specific position, handling emissive blocks correctly to avoid dark rendering through translucent blocks. It differs from corner lighting by using a single sample position for the whole face rather than per-corner samples. Choose this when the face is uniform and emissive blocks are present. The logic is: if state.getLightEmission() > 0, set samplePos to (worldX, worldY, worldZ); else, set samplePos to (worldX + face.getStepX(), worldY + face.getStepY(), worldZ + face.getStepZ()). Then get faceState = world.getBlockState(samplePos), compute packedLight = greedyMeshinggetLightColor(world, faceState, samplePos), compute shade = world.getShade(face, scratch.applyDirectionalShade), and fill scratch.brightness and scratch.lightmap arrays with shade and packedLight respectively. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides smooth lighting gradients on large merged quads, reducing visual artifacts compared to flat face lighting alone. Limitations: Requires access to the world's block state and lighting system. May not be suitable for non-voxel-based geometry. When to use: When using greedy meshing for voxel-based geometry and smooth lighting is desired. When not to use: When emissive blocks are present and flat face lighting is preferred to avoid dark rendering through translucent blocks, or when the geometry is not voxel-based. This method is part of the Greedy Meshing Mod for Minecraft, which optimizes rendering by merging adjacent faces of the same block type. The specific lighting techniques are designed to maintain visual fidelity while reducing draw calls. The mod addresses issues with fancy grass mods and translucent geometry sorting. name: Volume Ambient Occlusion
head: AO Field, Occlusion Field
body: Volume Ambient Occlusion computes a scalar occlusion field from a density field, quantifying how much of the surrounding environment each voxel can "see". It is primarily used to accelerate cloud rendering by approximating multiple scattering effects through a remapped occlusion field, offering a balance between efficiency and visual quality despite not being physically accurate. Unlike Positional & Normal-Based Voxel Shadowing, which calculates directional shading based on face normals and block types, this method computes a holistic, non-directional occlusion value per voxel. Inputs and Outputs Input: A volume or VDB density field. Output: The input density field with an additional scalar field named occlusion. The occlusion field stores values where 0 indicates no occlusion and 1 indicates full occlusion. Data Structures Density Field: The source field containing density values. Occlusion Field: A scalar field with the same spatial domain as the density field (or a downsampled version based on Resolution Ratio). VDB Structure: If the input is a VDB, the occlusion field is stored within the VDB structure. The Expand Voxels parameter applies here to pad the active area. Parameters Resolution Ratio: Defines the occlusion field resolution as a ratio of the density field resolution. A value of 0.5 yields half resolution. Smaller values are more efficient but less accurate. Expand Voxels: Expands the active area of the occlusion field by a specified number of voxels to prevent sampling outside the computed area during interpolation at render time. This parameter is only considered for VDBs; dense volumes are not affected. Density Scale: A multiplier applied to the density field for the occlusion computation only. The original density field remains untouched. A value of 0.1 makes the density appear ten times more transparent to the computation. Transmission Cutoff: The transmittance threshold below which a ray is considered fully occluded, terminating the marching process. A value of 0.005 means an occlusion value of 0.995 is treated as fully occluded. Larger values improve efficiency but reduce accuracy. Algorithm: Volume Marching The occlusion value for each voxel is computed by marching rays in multiple directions through the density field. 1. Initialize: For each voxel v in the target grid: Let d{scale} be the Density Scale. Let t{cutoff} be the Transmission Cutoff. Initialize total occlusion O = 0. Define a set of ray directions \mathcal{D} (typically a uniform distribution over the sphere, though the specific directions are not detailed in the source). 2. Marching: For each direction \vec{d} \in \mathcal{D}: Start a ray at voxel v in direction \vec{d}. Initialize transmittance T = 1.0. March along the ray through the density field. At each step, sample the density \rho from the input field. Apply the scale: \rho' = \rho \times d{scale}. Update transmittance: T = T \times e^{-\rho' \Delta s}, where \Delta s is the step size. If T < t{cutoff}, break the loop (ray is fully occluded). 3. Accumulate: The occlusion contribution for this direction is 1 - T. Accumulate: O = O + (1 - T). 4. Normalize: The final occlusion value is the average over all directions: \text{occlusion}(v) = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|} \sum{\vec{d} \in \mathcal{D}} (1 - T{\vec{d}}) Clamp the result to [0, 1]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls VDB Padding: When using VDBs, failing to set Expand Voxels may cause the renderer to sample undefined values at the boundaries during interpolation, leading to artifacts. Density Scale Interaction: A high Density Scale will cause rays to terminate quickly, potentially underestimating occlusion in sparse regions if Transmission Cutoff is not adjusted accordingly. Resolution Trade-off: Lower Resolution Ratio speeds up computation but reduces the accuracy of the occlusion field, which may result in blocky or inaccurate shading. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of voxels in the occlusion field multiplied by the number of ray directions and the average ray length. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the input density field and the output occlusion field. For VDBs, the Expand Voxels parameter increases the memory footprint of the active area. Performance: Smaller Resolution Ratio and larger Transmission Cutoff values improve efficiency but reduce accuracy. Strengths: Significantly accelerates cloud rendering by approximating multiple scattering effects. Limitations: Not physically accurate; relies on post-processing remapping for visual effect. Volume Ambient Occlusion was initially created to accelerate cloud rendering. It allows for the approximation of multiple scattering by remapping the occlusion field at render time, mapping dark values to cloud edges and bright values to the cloud interior. This technique was introduced in Houdini version 20.0. Volume Ambient Occlusion - SideFX, https://www.sidefx.com/docs/houdini/nodes/sop/volumeambientocclusion.html, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Gaussian Splatting Shadows
head: Nearly-Soft Shadows for Gaussian Splashing, Shadow Rendering
body: This method renders nearly-soft dynamic shadows for scenes represented by Gaussian splats by projecting the splats into a light-view space and performing depth-based occlusion testing. It differs from traditional volumetric shadow ray casting by leveraging the explicit Gaussian kernel representation to generate a depth image directly, avoiding the need for ray-marching through a density field. Unlike hard shadow mapping, it computes shadowing probabilities using Chebyshev’s inequality to approximate soft shadow edges, balancing performance and visual quality for dynamic particle systems. Inputs: A set of N Gaussian kernels \{Gi\}, where each kernel i is defined by mean position \mathbf{\mu}i, covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma}i, opacity \alphai, and color \mathbf{c}i. A point light source position \mathbf{l}{pos} and direction \mathbf{l}{dir}, where the direction is aligned with the significantly bright light in the environment map. Original image resolution (W, H). Outputs: A shadow map containing shadowing probabilities for each pixel. A final composited image with soft shadows applied. Data Structures: Light-View Depth Buffer: A 2D array of size (3W, 3H) storing depth values from splatted Gaussian kernels from the light's perspective. Shadow Map: A 2D array storing computed shadowing probabilities for each pixel. Steps: 1. Light-View Setup: Position a virtual camera at the point light's location \mathbf{l}{pos}. Align the camera's view direction with \mathbf{l}{dir}, determined as the direction of the significantly bright light in the environment map. Set the light-view image resolution to (3W, 3H) to mitigate under-sampling artifacts. 2. Splatting to Light-View: Splat all Gaussian kernels \{Gi\} to the light-view camera to generate a depth image D{light}. 3. Reprojection: Reproject points seen in the original camera view to the light-view space to obtain their coordinates and depth values. 4. Occlusion Comparison: Compare the reprojected points' depths to the previously splatted light-view depth image D{light}. If a point's depth is larger than the light-view depth, it is occluded by a nearer point and casts a shadow. 5. Shadow Probability Computation: Compute the shadowing probability using Chebyshev’s inequality to create a robust variance method. Softer shadows can be achieved by blurring and averaging the light-view depth image. Store the computed shadowing probabilities in a shadow map. 6. Compositing: Composite the rendered image with the shadow map to achieve nearly-soft dynamic shadows. Parameters: Light-View Resolution: 3 \times original image resolution. This factor is chosen to address visual discrepancies caused by under-sampling. Pitfalls: Under-sampling: Using a light-view resolution equal to or lower than the original image can cause visual discrepancies in shadows. This is mitigated by using a light-view resolution three times that of the original image. A two-pass rendering technique that uses splatting primitives during the passes to compute and project shadow information, producing both hard and soft shadows. It is chosen when a simple two-pass pipeline is preferred over depth-comparison methods. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. This method is derived from the "nearly-soft shadows" technique, re-engineered for use with Gaussian splatting in the context of the "Gaussian Splashing" framework for unified particle motion synthesis and rendering. It was introduced to enhance visual realism in dynamic fluid and particle simulations by providing efficient, soft shadowing. Gaussian Splashing: Unified Particles for Versatile Motion Synthesis and Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR52734.2025.00057, fetched 2026-10-29 Enhanced perception in volume visualization, https://doi.org/10.5821/dissertation-2117-94929, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Minecraft-style Static Lighting Algorithm
head: Global Illumination Approximation, Minecraft Lighting Algorithm, VoxBox Lighting
body: This method approximates global illumination in voxel-based environments by baking static lighting data directly into mesh vertices. It solves the problem of efficient indirect illumination in large, dense voxel worlds by decoupling direct sunlight calculation from indirect light diffusion. Unlike dynamic lighting systems that recalculate illumination every frame, this approach precomputes light values, offering a significant performance trade-off for static scenes at the cost of inability to handle dynamic light sources or moving geometry. It is distinct from Light Propagation Volumes in its use of a discrete, iterative diffusion pass rather than continuous volume propagation, and from Two-Pass Shadow Casting (Kajiya and Von Herzen) by operating on a discrete grid with integer light levels rather than continuous ray marching. The algorithm operates in two distinct passes: a direct sunlight pass and an indirect light spread pass. It assumes a static world divided into chunks, where each chunk contains a 3D array of voxels. Input: A voxel grid representing the world geometry. Each voxel has a boolean property BlocksLight (true if opaque/occluding, false if transparent/translucent). Output: A 3D array of integer light values, one per voxel, with values ranging from 0 (no light) to 16 (full light). This array is typically baked into the vertex colors of the chunk mesh. Voxel Grid: A 3D array Voxel[x][y][z]. The specific implementation in the source uses a chunk-based system where chunks are stored in a hash map keyed by chunk coordinates. Each chunk is a fixed-size cube (e.g., 16 \times 16 \times 16 voxels). Light Array: A 3D array Light[x][y][z] of integers, same dimensions as the voxel grid. Initialized to 0. 1. Initialize Light array to 0 for all voxels. 2. For each column (x, z) in the world/chunk: 3. Trace from the highest y (sky) down to the lowest y (ground). 4. For each voxel (x, y, z) encountered: 5. If Voxel[x][y][z].BlocksLight is true, stop tracing this column. 6. Otherwise, set Light[x][y][z] = 16. Note: The source describes this as "decrementing as it goes down, or simply setting to 16 until blocked". The implementation uses a constant 16 for all unblocked voxels in the column. This pass simulates the diffusion of light from lit voxels to their neighbors. It runs for a fixed number of iterations equal to the maximum light spread distance. 1. Set MaxSpread = 16. 2. For pass from MaxSpread down to 1: 3. For each voxel (x, y, z) in the grid: 4. If Light[x][y][z] == pass: 5. For each of the 6 neighbors (nx, ny, nz): 6. If Voxel[nx][ny][nz].BlocksLight is false: 7. If Light[nx][ny][nz] < Light[x][y][z] - 1: 8. Set Light[nx][ny][nz] = Light[x][y][z] - 1. The core update rule for indirect lighting is: L{neighbor} = \max(L{neighbor}, L{current} - 1) Subject to the condition that the neighbor does not block light. The algorithm iterates from high light values to low values to ensure that light propagates correctly from sources outward. Light Range: 16 blocks. This is the maximum distance indirect light spreads. Light Levels: Integers from 0 to 16. Chunk Size: Typically 16 \times 16 \times 16 voxels, but can be configured. Opaque Blocks: Voxels with BlocksLight = true do not receive light from neighbors in Pass 2, nor do they transmit light. Marshalling Errors: When implementing this in native code (e.g., C/C++ DLLs from C#), incorrect handling of multidimensional array boundaries or memory layout can cause lighting anomalies and incorrect shadows. Precision: The use of integer arithmetic avoids floating-point precision issues but limits the granularity of light levels to 17 distinct values. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculatestaticlighting(voxelgrid, chunksize=16): """ voxelgrid: 3D list/array of objects with attribute 'blockslight' (bool) chunksize: size of the chunk in each dimension Returns: 3D list/array of integers representing light levels """ # Initialize light array with 0 lightgrid = [[[0 for in range(chunksize)] for in range(chunksize)] for in range(chunksize)] # Pass 1: Direct Sunlight (trace from top y down to bottom y) for x in range(chunksize): for z in range(chunksize): for y in range(chunksize - 1, -1, -1): if voxelgrid[x][y][z].blockslight: break else: lightgrid[x][y][z] = 16 # Pass 2: Indirect Light Spread maxspread = 16 for passval in range(maxspread, 0, -1): for x in range(chunksize): for y in range(chunksize): for z in range(chunksize): if lightgrid[x][y][z] == passval: # Check 6 neighbors neighbors = [ (x+1, y, z), (x-1, y, z), (x, y+1, z), (x, y-1, z), (x, y, z+1), (x, y, z-1) ] for nx, ny, nz in neighbors: # Check bounds if 0 <= nx < chunksize and 0 <= ny < chunksize and 0 <= nz < chunksize: # Check if neighbor blocks light if not voxelgrid[nx][ny][nz].blockslight: # Update neighbor light if it's lower than current - 1 if lightgrid[nx][ny][nz] < lightgrid[x][y][z] - 1: lightgrid[nx][ny][nz] = lightgrid[x][y][z] - 1 return lightgrid Time Complexity: Pass 1 is O(N) where N is the number of voxels. Pass 2 is O(N \cdot K) where K is the light spread distance (16). Total complexity is O(N). Memory Complexity: O(N) for the light array. The source notes that storing chunk positions explicitly saves memory compared to storing coordinates for every voxel, but the light array itself is dense. Performance: In the source implementation, calculating lighting for 5,214 chunks (approx. 20 million voxels) took 11.79 seconds on an i7-4712HQ, or ~2.26ms per chunk. A native C version was 2-3x faster but suffered from bugs. Strengths: Very fast for static scenes; simple to implement; low memory overhead per voxel (1 byte for light level). Limitations: Cannot handle dynamic light sources or moving geometry; limited to 17 light levels; indirect light spread is limited to 16 blocks; no attenuation based on distance beyond the integer step. The algorithm is adapted from the lighting system used in the game Minecraft. It was implemented in the VoxBox project, a procedural voxel world generator. The system is described as a "crude global illumination approximation" baked into chunk mesh vertices. The source notes that dynamic lighting is handled separately by the Unity3D engine, while this static system handles the bulk of the illumination for the voxel geometry. The implementation details, including the 16-pass diffusion and the specific pitfalls of native code marshalling, are documented in a thesis from the University of Waikato. name: Layered Polygonal Area Lights
head: Layered Polygonal Area Light (LPAL) Integration, Volume slicing with area lights
body: Layered Polygonal Area Lights (LPAL) is a real-time rendering technique for computing the indirect illumination of emissive, inhomogeneous participating media as reflected off glossy surfaces. It solves the problem of efficiently evaluating the volume integral for light transport from a volume to a surface point by decomposing the volume into parallel planar slices, each treated as a virtual area light. Unlike Voxel Cone Tracing (VCT) or sparse VPL sampling, LPAL analytically integrates light contributions over these cutting sections while accounting for extinction within the intervals between slices, providing higher visual quality for glossy reflections at comparable computational costs. The method approximates the total radiance reflected from a point \mathbf{x}i on a reflective surface by integrating contributions from all vertices \mathbf{v} within the volume domain V. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D texture representing the volume domain V (typically an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box, AABB); surface point \mathbf{x}i with normal \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{x}i) and BRDF fr; camera center \mathbf{x}e; volume gravity center \mathbf{c}V. Output: Radiance L(\mathbf{x}i, \omegao) reflected towards the camera direction \omegao = (\mathbf{x}e - \mathbf{x}i) / \|\mathbf{x}e - \mathbf{x}i\|. Data Structures: Volume Domain V: Defined by an AABB. If multiple disjoint volumes exist, they should be stored in individual bounding boxes to avoid excessive slicing. LPAL Layers: A set of parallel planes perpendicular to a cutting direction \omegac. The number of layers is a parameter; more layers retain detail for sparse or distant volumes. Cutting Direction: The direction \omegac defines the cutting sections. In practice, it is chosen as the line connecting the reflection point \mathbf{x}i and the gravity center of the domain V. Let s be the signed distance from \mathbf{x}i along \omegac. Let A(s) be the plane intersecting \omegac perpendicularly at distance s. Formulas: The total radiance is the integral over the volume V: L(\mathbf{x}i, \omegao) = \intV L(\mathbf{v} \to \mathbf{x}i \to \mathbf{x}e) \, d\mathbf{v} where the radiance from a single vertex \mathbf{v} is: L(\mathbf{v} \to \mathbf{x}i \to \mathbf{x}e) = \frac{I(\mathbf{v}, -\omegai)}{\|\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{x}i\|^2} \text{Tr}(\mathbf{v} \to \mathbf{x}i) fr(\mathbf{x}i; \omegai, \omegao) |\omegai \cdot \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{x}i)| Here, \omegai = (\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{x}i) / \|\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{x}i\| is the incident direction, I is radiant intensity, and \text{Tr} is transmittance. The method decomposes this into an integral over slices s: L(\mathbf{x}i, \omegao) \approx \int L(s) \, ds where L(s) is the contribution from plane A(s): L(s) = \int{A(s)} L(\omegai) fr(\mathbf{x}i; \omegai, \omegao) |\omegai \cdot \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{x}i)| \, d\omegai This integral is separated into a surface term ID and a light term IL: L(s) \approx ID \cdot IL ID = \int{A(s)} fr(\mathbf{x}i; \omegai, \omegao) |\omegai \cdot \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{x}i)| \, d\omegai IL = \frac{\int{A(s)} L(\omegai) fr(\mathbf{x}i; \omegai, \omegao) |\omegai \cdot \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{x}i)| \, d\omegai}{\int{A(s)} fr(\mathbf{x}i; \omegai, \omegao) |\omegai \cdot \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{x}i)| \, d\omegai} The term ID is computed analytically using Linearly Transformed Cosine (LTC) integration in clamped cosine space. The term IL is approximated by filtering the area light with Gaussian functions and storing the result in a MIP map. The transmittance \text{Tr}(\mathbf{v} \to \mathbf{x}i) is approximated using an average extinction coefficient \bar{\sigma}t over the slice: \text{Tr}(\mathbf{v} \to \mathbf{x}i) \approx e^{-\bar{\sigma}t \|\mathbf{v}{//}(s) - \mathbf{x}i\|} where \mathbf{v}{//}(s) = \mathbf{x}i + s\omegac is the vertex on the reflected ray at distance s. Algorithm Steps: 1. Define Volume Domain: Identify the AABB enclosing the emissive volume V. If multiple volumes are present, use separate bounding boxes. 2. Determine Cutting Direction: Calculate \omegac as the vector from \mathbf{x}i to the gravity center of V. 3. Slice Volume: Divide the volume along \omegac into N parallel planes (LPALs) at distances sk. 4. Compute Average Extinction: For each slice k, calculate the weighted average extinction coefficient \bar{\sigma}t(sk). Simple averaging is insufficient; the method weights the integration based on the BRDF lobe shape, considering properties of the volume near the regularly reflected ray. 5. Evaluate Light Term (IL): For each slice, approximate the light integral IL by filtering the area light contribution with Gaussian functions, utilizing a pre-computed MIP map. 6. Evaluate Surface Term (ID): Compute the BRDF integral ID analytically using LTC in clamped cosine space. 7. Accumulate Radiance: Sum the contributions ID \cdot IL across all slices, applying the transmittance attenuation e^{-\bar{\sigma}t \Delta s} between slices. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computelpalradiance(xi, n, omegao, volumetexture, volumecenter, numslices): # 1. Setup geometry omegac = normalize(volumecenter - xi) # Project volume AABB bounds onto omegac to find signed distance range mins = dot(volumetexture.aabbmin - xi, omegac) maxs = dot(volumetexture.aabbmax - xi, omegac) slicestep = (maxs - mins) / numslices totalradiance = 0.0 # Pre-compute LTC parameters for the surface BRDF ltcmatrix = computeltcmatrix(n, omegao) for k in range(numslices): # Sample at slice centers for Riemann sum integration s = mins + (k + 0.5) slicestep # 2. Get slice properties: weighted average extinction coefficient # Sources do not specify the exact sampling routine; average extinction weighted by BRDF lobe shape over the slice plane sigmatavg = 0.0 # 3. Compute Transmittance from slice to surface dist = abs(s) transmittance = exp(-sigmatavg dist) # 4. Compute Light Term (IL) # Sources do not specify the exact MIP map filtering routine; filter area light with Gaussian functions lightterm = 0.0 # 5. Compute Surface Term (ID) # Sources do not specify the exact LTC integration routine; analytic integration of BRDF in clamped cosine space surfaceterm = 1.0 # 6. Accumulate sliceradiance = surfaceterm lightterm transmittance totalradiance += sliceradiance slicestep return totalradiance def computeltcmatrix(n, omegao): # Sources do not specify the exact LTC matrix construction; standard linear transformation for BRDF lobe return identitymatrix() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Black Margins: Standard 3D textures have black (zero) margins. If the volume data is in the center of the AABB, these margins cause insufficiently blurred reflections on highly rough surfaces because the LTC integration considers the zero-emission margin. The method requires handling or eliminating black margins, e.g., by filling the domain with uniform emittance or disabling domain transforms that introduce margins. High Roughness: High roughness values cause deviations from path tracing due to the black margin issue in the LTC-based surface integration. Simple Averaging: Using a simple average for extinction coefficients fails to account for spatial variance of density and albedo, inappropriately attenuating light from the sides when the BRDF has a sharp lobe. Multiple Volumes: If multiple volumes are stored in a single large bounding box, they require more slices to retain detail. Storing them in individual bounding boxes is recommended. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of slices N. The per-slice cost involves texture lookups and LTC evaluation, which is constant time. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume texture and potentially a MIP map for the filtered light terms. Performance: Designed for real-time rendering. It is significantly faster than path tracing and provides better visual quality than VPL sampling with limited samples (e.g., 64 VPLs). Strengths: Accurately calculates area integration over cutting sections; considers light extinction within intervals; applicable to surfaces with arbitrary shapes and roughness. Limitations: Relies on observation-based approximations rather than pure physics; sensitive to black margins in 3D textures; less accurate for very high roughness compared to path tracing. When to Use: Real-time rendering of participating media indirectly visible over reflective surfaces, especially for glossy materials. When Not to Use: When strict physical accuracy is required for highly rough surfaces, or when the volume is extremely sparse and requires a very high number of slices for detail, potentially negating performance benefits. The Layered Polygonal Area Lights (LPAL) method was proposed by T. Kuge et al. in 2019. It was introduced as a real-time technique for indirect illumination of emissive inhomogeneous volumes. The method builds upon the Linearly Transformed Cosine (LTC) model for surface integration. It addresses the limitations of Voxel Cone Tracing (VCT) and VPL sampling in the context of glossy reflections from participating media. Real‐time Indirect Illumination of Emissive Inhomogeneous Volumes using Layered Polygonal Area Lights, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.13851, fetched 2026-10-26
