name: Surface Shading Effects
body: Surface shading effects apply local illumination models to volumetric data to create the appearance of solid surfaces, shadows, and ambient occlusion within participating media. This family solves the problem of volumes appearing as featureless fog by introducing directional lighting, self-shadowing, and indirect light approximation. It differs from sibling methods like Lighting Models by focusing specifically on surface-like appearance cues (normals, shadows) rather than general scattering phase functions, and from Two-Pass Shadow Casting by typically evaluating shading per-sample during ray marching rather than via separate geometry passes. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of evaluating visibility or illumination at a specific point \mathbf{p} within or on the boundary of a volume, based on a light source direction \mathbf{l} or environment. 1. Visibility/Transmittance Evaluation: The fundamental operation is determining how much light reaches \mathbf{p} from a source. This involves integrating the extinction coefficient \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) along a path from the source to \mathbf{p} (or vice versa). The transmittance T is calculated as: T = \exp\left(-\int{\mathbf{p}{source}}^{\mathbf{p}} \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) \, d\mathbf{x}\right) In discrete implementations, this integral is approximated by summing \sigmat \cdot \Delta s over samples along the ray. 2. Local Shading Models: For surface-like appearance in volumes, normals are approximated from the volume gradient \mathbf{g} = \nabla V. Usually, a simple absorption and emission model is used because it is relatively cheap to evaluate and gives good enough results. 3. Shadowing Approximation: Shadows are computed by testing occlusion along the direction to the light source. 4. Ambient Occlusion: Indirect illumination is approximated by integrating over the hemisphere or using simplified models (e.g., upward ray for sky light). The ambient contribution L{ambient} is often modulated by a shadowing factor based on local density: L{ambient} = L{sky} \cdot \exp(-D{up}) \cdot AO{factor} where D{up} is the integrated density along an upward ray. The Powder Sugar Effect is a local illumination approximation used in volumetric rendering to simulate the physical reality that less light is available for scattering at the fringes of a cloud or participating medium [1713-powder-sugar-effect.md]. It solves the artifact where low-density regions appear unnaturally bright or "glowing" by modulating the scattered light contribution based on local density [1713-powder-sugar-effect.md]. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Shadow Density Scale by specifically targeting the source of scattered light (reducing it where density is low) rather than the view attenuation (brightening dense regions to simulate multiple scattering) [1713-powder-sugar-effect.md]. Inputs and Outputs: Input: local density d, step size \Delta s, and decay parameter \alpha (powderdecay). Output: scalar modulation factor P \in [0, 1] applied to the scattered light increment [1713-powder-sugar-effect.md]. Method: Calculate optical thickness t = d \cdot \Delta s. Evaluate P(t) = 1 - e^{-\alpha t}. Multiply the scattered light increment \Delta L{scat} by P(t) [1713-powder-sugar-effect.md]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def powdersugareffect(density: float, stepsize: float, powderdecay: float) -> float: """ Calculates the modulation factor for scattered light at cloud fringes. Args: density: Local volume density at the current sample point. stepsize: The distance step taken during volume integration. powderdecay: The decay constant controlling fringe darkness. Returns: A float between 0.0 and 1.0 to multiply the scattered light increment. """ opticalthickness = density stepsize modulationfactor = 1.0 - math.exp(-powderdecay opticalthickness) return modulationfactor Edge Cases: Zero density yields P=0; high density yields P \to 1; parameter sensitivity affects fringe darkness; sparse sampling may exacerbate blue noise [1713-powder-sugar-effect.md]. Implements a day/night sun cycle with sunset scattering, sun disc, halo, and stars. Generates single-sample golden-angle PCF soft shadows jittered with interleaved gradient noise, where TAA accumulates the penumbra. Computes bit-test ambient occlusion bilinearly interpolated across the hit face. A shading technique for thin, translucent objects like wings that adds a term brightening the surface as it turns away from the light source while the camera looks toward it, simulating light transmission through the membrane. It is chosen for semi-transparent biological or delicate structures where subsurface scattering is approximated by geometric orientation. Parameter: SUN direction vector is vec3(-0.42, 0.60, -0.68). Surface shading techniques for participating media originated to give volumetric clouds and fog a tangible appearance rather than flat fog. The Powder Sugar Effect was introduced to address the lack of detail at cloud fringes by attenuating scattered light in low-density areas [1713-powder-sugar-effect.md]. The integration of complex lighting cycles, soft shadows, and ambient occlusion into voxel-based volumetric rendering was demonstrated in voxelG, which combined terrain and cloud shading. Specialized techniques like backlighting glow have been applied to procedural animations of translucent objects, such as butterflies, to enhance realism. mstampfli/voxelG, https://github.com/mstampfli/voxelG, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) el-bakkali/manim-glsl-butterflies, https://github.com/el-bakkali/manim-glsl-butterflies, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Powder Sugar Effect
head: Powder Decay, Powder Function
body: The Powder Sugar Effect is a local illumination approximation for volumetric media, specifically designed to correct the visual artifact of overly bright, "puffy" fringes in participating media like clouds. It solves the problem where low-density regions at the volume boundary scatter too much light relative to the available incident illumination, creating an unnatural halo. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Terrain Shading with Direct and Ambient Light by applying a density-dependent attenuation factor directly to the scattered light increment, rather than modifying the shadowing or ambient occlusion terms themselves. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Local volume density \rho at the shading point, step size \Delta s used for integration, and a decay parameter \alpha (uniform float). Output: A scalar attenuation factor P \in [0, 1] applied to the scattered light contribution. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The method relies on a single scalar parameter \alpha and the current integration step's density and length. Steps: 1. Calculate the optical thickness for the current integration step: \tau = \rho \cdot \Delta s. 2. Evaluate the powder function using the decay parameter \alpha: P(\tau) = 1 - \exp(-\alpha \cdot \tau) 3. Multiply the computed scattered light increment dL{scat} by P(\tau): dL{final} = dL{scat} \cdot P(\tau) Formulas: The core function is defined as: \text{powder}(d) = 1.0 - \exp(-\alpha \cdot d) Where d is the product of density and step size (\rho \cdot \Delta s). Parameters: \alpha (powderdecay): Controls the rate at which the attenuation approaches 1.0 as density increases. Higher values make the effect more aggressive, darkening low-density fringes faster. Typical values are not explicitly given in the source, but it is treated as a uniform float adjustable by the artist. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Low Density: As \tau \to 0, P(\tau) \to 0. This correctly suppresses scattering in very thin areas where little light is available to scatter, preventing the "white noise" or blue noise artifacts common in low-density cloud rendering. High Density: As \tau \to \infty, P(\tau) \to 1. The effect becomes negligible in dense regions, preserving the volume's internal brightness and silhouette. Precision: The exponential function must be evaluated with sufficient precision to avoid artifacts in very low-density steps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def powdersugareffect(density: float, stepsize: float, powderdecay: float) -> float: """ Calculates the attenuation factor for scattered light in low-density regions. Args: density: The volume density at the current shading point. stepsize: The integration step size used for this sample. powderdecay: The decay parameter (alpha) controlling the effect's intensity. Returns: A scalar factor between 0 and 1 to multiply the scattered light increment. """ # Calculate optical thickness for the current step opticalthickness = density stepsize # Apply the powder function # Formula: 1.0 - exp(-alpha d) attenuation = 1.0 - math.exp(-powderdecay opticalthickness) return attenuation A related optimization that decouples visual silhouette from shadow-casting opacity. While Powder Sugar affects the scattering brightness at fringes, Shadow Density Scale affects the transmittance and shadow casting depth. Choose Powder Sugar when the issue is visual halo/brightness in low-density areas; choose Shadow Density Scale when the issue is light penetration and multiple scattering approximation. Time Complexity: O(1) per shading point. It adds a single exponential evaluation and a multiplication to the shading loop. Memory Complexity: O(1). Requires storing only the powderdecay parameter. Strengths: Extremely cheap to compute; effectively reduces visual noise and "puffiness" in cloud fringes without altering the physical density field. Limitations: It is an artistic approximation, not a physically accurate solution to multiple scattering. It may require reduced sampling intervals to minimize blue noise, which can impact performance if not combined with techniques like depth-aware upsampling. When to use: Procedural volumetric clouds or fog where low-density fringes appear unnaturally bright or noisy. When not to use: Physically based rendering requiring strict energy conservation or accurate multiple scattering simulation. The method was introduced by Jan Wedekind in his implementation of procedural volumetric clouds. It is named for the visual effect of "powdering" or softening the edges of the volume, reducing the harshness of the transition between the dense core and the transparent exterior. It is primarily used in real-time or interactive procedural cloud rendering. Procedural Volumetric Clouds · Jan Wedekind, https://www.wedesoft.de/software/2023/05/03/volumetric-clouds/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Shadow Density Scale
body: Shadow Density Scale is a rendering optimization technique that decouples a volume's visual silhouette from its shadow-casting opacity, allowing light to penetrate deeper into participating media without altering the volume's physical density or absorption properties. Unlike reducing absorption, which increases overall transparency and makes the volume appear "puffy," this method retains the volume's "tightness" and silhouette while faking the brightening effect of multiple scattering at a fraction of the computational cost. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The volume's optical depth \tau along a shadow ray, calculated from the density field \rho and absorption/scattering coefficients. Parameter: shadowdensityscale (S), a floating-point scalar. Output: The modified transmittance T' used for shadow ray termination. Data Structures: The parameter is a single floating-point value stored in the shader's advanced configuration. No additional data structures are required; it modifies the evaluation of the existing density field during shadow ray traversal. Steps: 1. Sample Density: During shadow ray traversal, sample the volume density \rho at the intersection point. 2. Calculate Optical Depth: Compute the optical depth \tau accumulated along the ray segment from the light source to the current point, using the standard density and absorption coefficient \sigmaa. 3. Apply Scale: Multiply the accumulated optical depth by the shadowdensityscale parameter S: \tau' = \tau \times S 4. Compute Transmittance: Calculate the shadow ray transmittance using the scaled optical depth: T' = e^{-\tau'} 5. Terminate: Use T' to determine the contribution of the light source. If T' is below a threshold, terminate the shadow ray. Parameters: shadowdensityscale (S): A float value where 1.0 is the default (no change). Values below 1.0 (e.g., 0.5) increase transparency to shadow rays. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: S > 1.0: Makes the volume more opaque to shadows than its physical density suggests, potentially creating unnatural dark cores. S = 0.0: Renders the volume completely transparent to shadow rays, effectively removing all shadows cast by the volume. Visual Inconsistency: Since the volume's silhouette remains unchanged while its internal lighting brightens, this can create a visual disconnect between the volume's edge and its interior if not balanced with other effects like the Powder Sugar Effect. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeshadowtransmittance(ray, volumeshader): """ Computes shadow transmittance using Shadow Density Scale. Args: ray: The shadow ray from the surface point to the light. volumeshader: The volume shader containing density and coefficients. Returns: float: The transmittance value T'. """ # 1. Sample density and compute optical depth along the ray # This involves integrating density absorptioncoefficient along the ray path # from the light to the current point. opticaldepth = 0.0 stepsize = ray.stepsize numsteps = ray.numsteps for i in range(numsteps): point = ray.origin + ray.direction (i stepsize) density = volumeshader.sampledensity(point) absorptioncoeff = volumeshader.getabsorptioncoefficient(point) opticaldepth += density absorptioncoeff stepsize # 2. Apply Shadow Density Scale # Get the scale parameter from the shader's advanced settings shadowdensityscale = volumeshader.getshadowdensityscale() # Default is 1.0 if not explicitly set if shadowdensityscale is None: shadowdensityscale = 1.0 scaledopticaldepth = opticaldepth shadowdensityscale # 3. Compute transmittance transmittance = math.exp(-scaledopticaldepth) return transmittance Reduces scattered light in low-density areas to approximate less scattered light at cloud fringes. Choose this for edge darkening; Shadow Density Scale is for internal brightening. Link Time Complexity: O(1) additional cost per shadow ray evaluation. It adds a single multiplication operation to the optical depth calculation. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for the scalar parameter. Performance: Significantly cheaper than simulating true multiple scattering, which requires additional bounces and anisotropic scattering evaluations. Strengths: Allows light to penetrate deeper into volumes without increasing render time or changing the volume's silhouette. Retains the "tightness" of the volume. Limitations: It is a heuristic cheat and does not physically simulate multiple scattering. Can lead to visual inconsistencies if the volume's interior appears too bright relative to its edges. When to Use: When rendering volumes that appear too dark internally due to high absorption or density, and true multiple scattering is too expensive. When Not to Use: When physical accuracy is required, or when the volume's silhouette needs to change with lighting conditions. Shadow Density Scale was introduced as a practical optimization in volumetric rendering workflows, particularly within the Redshift Volume Shader and Cinema 4D's Pyro workflow. It addresses the common problem of volumes appearing too dark or "muddy" when light cannot penetrate deeply, without resorting to expensive multiple scattering simulations. The technique is part of a broader set of "cheats" used to balance visual quality and render time, often combined with moderate trace depths and other helpers like anisotropic scattering relaxation. name: Terrain Shading with Direct and Ambient Light
head: Hemispheric Ambient Occlusion Shading
body: This method computes the final color of a terrain surface point by combining surface albedo, direct sunlight (modulated by shadow and cloud shadow), and hemispheric ambient light (sky and ground bounce modulated by ambient occlusion). It distinguishes itself from siblings like the Powder Sugar Effect by explicitly separating direct illumination from a two-component hemispheric ambient model, and from Terrain Shader Lighting and Effects by relying on a specific baked normal map and bias-based shadow tracing rather than generic lighting parameters. Inputs: Surface position \mathbf{p} = (x, y, z). Surface normal \mathbf{n} = (nx, ny, nz), normalized. Albedo color \mathbf{C}{albedo}. Sun direction \mathbf{l}{sun} and sun radiance \mathbf{C}{sun}. Sky ambient color \mathbf{C}{sky} and ground ambient color \mathbf{C}{ground}. Cloud shadow factor S{cloud} at \mathbf{p}. Terrain grid cell size (for bias calculation). Outputs: Final color \mathbf{C}{out}. Data Structures: The normal \mathbf{n} is typically baked into a texture and interpolated across the cell, rather than computed via finite differences, to avoid facet artifacts on coarse heightfields. Steps: 1. Direct Light Calculation: a. Compute the dot product between the normal and sun direction: N \cdot L = nx lx + ny ly + nz lz b. Calculate a bias to offset the shadow trace origin, preventing self-shadowing artifacts on coarse grids: \text{bias} = \text{cell\size} \times 0.5 + 0.5 c. Trace a shadow ray from the biased position: \mathbf{p}{start} = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{n} \times \text{bias} + \text{jitter} The jitter is applied to reduce aliasing. The shadow factor S{shadow} is determined by whether this ray hits terrain geometry. d. Compute the direct light scale: \text{lightScale} = \max(0, N \cdot L) \times S{shadow} \times S{cloud} e. Compute the direct color contribution: \mathbf{C}{direct} = \mathbf{C}{sun} \times \text{lightScale} 2. Ambient Occlusion Calculation: a. Trace an ambient occlusion ray or compute a precomputed occlusion value AO based on local density/geometry around \mathbf{p}. b. If not precomputed, this typically involves sampling the hemisphere or using a simplified depth-based approximation. 3. Hemispheric Ambient Calculation: a. Compute the sky factor based on the normal's Y component: \text{sky} = 0.5 + 0.5 \times ny b. Interpolate between sky and ground ambient colors: \mathbf{C}{ambient\base} = \mathbf{C}{sky} \times \text{sky} + \mathbf{C}{ground} \times (1 - \text{sky}) c. Apply occlusion: \mathbf{C}{ambient} = \mathbf{C}{ambient\base} \times AO 4. Final Color Composition: a. Combine direct and ambient contributions, modulated by albedo: \mathbf{C}{out} = \mathbf{C}{albedo} \times (\mathbf{C}{direct} + \mathbf{C}{ambient}) Parameters: cellsize: The resolution of the terrain grid. sky, ground: Ambient color vectors. sunDirection, sunRadiance: Light source properties. Pitfalls: Self-shadowing: The shadow origin must be biased clear of the surface. A bias of field.cell 0.5 + 0.5 is recommended to prevent artifacts on coarse heightfields. Normal Quality: Using finite differences for normals on a bilinear heightfield results in piecewise constant normals, causing visible facet edges. Baked normal maps interpolated across cells are required for smooth shading. Masking Inputs: Material masks (e.g., for slope or moisture) require smooth inputs. Per-cell slope thresholds create single-cell patches, and normalized fractal noise clusters tightly, leading to thin contour stripes. Slope fields should be blurred, and moisture fields expanded around their midpoint before driving masks. A global luma darkening effect relative to the map ceiling, distinct from the local illumination of the main method. It darkens terrain based on depth from the map ceiling using an exponential contrast curve, applied in-place to color buffers. Definition: Darkens terrain based on vertical distance from the map top. When to choose: When a global atmospheric depth cue or fog-like darkening is desired, rather than local shadowing. Link: Height Shading (hypothetical link for variant) A screen-space method to compute directional occlusion, differing from the hemispheric approach by estimating a visibility cone axis and apex angle. Definition: Computes directional occlusion using Z-Buffer data to estimate screen-space bent cones, which are circular apertures. When to choose: When directional occlusion is needed for better image quality than standard AO, and screen-space data is available. Link: Screen-Space Bent Cones (hypothetical link for variant) Time Complexity: Dominated by the shadow trace and ambient occlusion trace. If AO is precomputed, the cost is proportional to the shadow ray length and sampling. If AO is traced per-pixel, it adds significant cost. Memory Complexity: Low, requiring storage for albedo, baked normals, and potentially precomputed AO maps. Strengths: Provides realistic terrain shading with distinct sky/ground ambient contributions and handles cloud shadows. Limitations: Relies on baked normals for quality; finite differences cause artifacts. Does not handle interreflections or small area lights well. When to use: For static or semi-static terrain rendering where baked data is feasible. When not: For dynamic scenes requiring real-time normal updates without baking, or when high-fidelity global illumination is required. The method originates from the theme1 project by mingderwang, which implements a procedural terrain renderer with specific lighting themes. It addresses the need for realistic terrain appearance in procedural worlds, distinguishing itself by using baked normals and a specific hemispheric ambient model. The concept of hemispheric ambient occlusion is also related to broader techniques in screen-space lighting, such as bent cones, which aim to improve directional occlusion quality. mingderwang/theme1, https://github.com/mingderwang/theme1, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) herbal1st/pyvorengi-sdk-demo, https://github.com/herbal1st/pyvorengi-sdk-demo, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Real-Time Ray Traced Voxel Global Illumination, https://doi.org/10.34626/0vdq-7m27, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Planetary Surface Shading
body: Planetary Surface Shading computes the radiance emitted or reflected by a planetary body's surface (ground or water) as seen by an observer, accounting for direct illumination, ambient scattering, and subsurface effects, before applying atmospheric attenuation. It distinguishes itself from pure atmospheric scattering by handling the distinct bidirectional reflectance distribution functions (BRDF) of diffuse terrain and specular water, while integrating precomputed spectral scattering data. Inputs: Observer position P0 and view direction V. Light source direction L (e.g., sun). Wavelength \lambda. Surface point Pg on the planetary body. Surface normal N at Pg. Diffuse ground color ID(\lambda). Precomputed scattering textures for atmosphere and water. Precomputed extinction lookup texture parameterized by observer altitude h and zenith angle \vartheta. Outputs: Surface radiance contribution IP(P0, V, L, \lambda). Final fragment color IF after atmospheric attenuation. 1. Extinction Lookup Texture: A 2D texture storing extinction t(P Pc), parameterized by observer altitude h and zenith angle \vartheta. Pc is the intersection of the ray starting at P with zenith angle \vartheta with the upper atmosphere boundary. 2. Scattering Texture: Stores atmospheric scattering contributions IS. 3. Water Scattering Texture: Stores water volume light IS^{\text{water}}, indexed by depth D. 1. Determine Surface Type: Identify if Pg is on ground or water. 2. Compute Ambient and Direct Illumination: Calculate attenuated direct illumination I'I(Pg, L, \lambda). Calculate ambient illumination IA(Pg, L, \lambda) caused by scattering. 3. Compute Surface Radiance IP: If Ground: Apply the diffuse ground model: IP = ID(\lambda)(-L \cdot N)I'I(Pg, L, \lambda) + ID(\lambda)IA(Pg, L, \lambda) where -L \cdot N is the dot product of the light direction and surface normal (assuming L points from surface to light, or adjusted for sign convention such that the term is positive for lit surfaces). If Water: Apply the specular water model: IP = \hat{F}(\varphi)(IS(Pg, VR, L, \lambda) + I'I(Pg, VR, \lambda)) + IS^{\text{water}}(Pg, V'R, D, \lambda) Compute refraction ray VR using the refract() intrinsic function in the fragment shader. Determine unattenuated direct illumination I0^I(Pg, VR, \lambda): Set to I0^I(Pg, L, \lambda) if VR hits the star disc, otherwise zero. Fetch IS^{\text{water}} using the depth D of the point where VR intersects the seabed. \hat{F}(\varphi) is a Fresnel approximation. 4. Apply Atmospheric Attenuation: Compute the path from surface point Pg to observer PO. Retrieve extinction t(Pa Pg, \lambda) from the precomputed texture, where Pa is the intersection of the view ray with the atmosphere boundary if the observer is outside, or P0 if inside. Calculate final fragment color: IF = IS + IP \cdot e^{-t(Pa Pg, \lambda)} where IS is the atmospheric scattering contribution fetched for the observer's position. Ground Surface Radiance: IP(P0, V, L, \lambda) = ID(\lambda)(-L \cdot N)I'I(Pg, L, \lambda) + ID(\lambda)IA(Pg, L, \lambda) Water Surface Radiance: IP(P0, V, L, \lambda) = \hat{F}(\varphi)(IS(Pg, VR, L, \lambda) + I'I(Pg, VR, \lambda)) + IS^{\text{water}}(Pg, V'R, D, \lambda) Final Fragment Color: IF = IS + IP \cdot e^{-t(Pa Pg, \lambda)} \hat{F}(\varphi): Fast and accurate Fresnel approximation from [Lazanyi and Szirmay-Kalos 2005], precomputable. ID(\lambda): Diffuse ground color. IS: Atmospheric scattering contribution. t: Extinction coefficient, precomputed in a 2D texture. Observer Position: If the observer is outside the atmosphere, the intersection point Pa between the view ray and the atmosphere sphere must be evaluated, as there is no scattering or attenuation outside the atmosphere. Spectral vs RGB: Spectral precomputation yields more natural results than RGB precomputation, particularly during sunset when higher scattering orders are stronger, affecting lightness, chroma, and hue. Refraction Ray: The refraction ray VR must be correctly computed in the fragment shader to determine the correct water scattering and direct illumination contributions. Performance: Relies heavily on precomputed textures (extinction, scattering, water scattering) to avoid costly real-time calculation of extinction coefficients and complex volume integration. Memory: Requires storage for multiple textures (extinction 2D texture, scattering textures, water scattering texture). Accuracy: Spectral precomputation provides higher accuracy in color reproduction compared to RGB, especially for complex lighting conditions like sunset. Limitations: Assumes finely tessellated spheres for the planet and atmosphere. The method is specific to the planetary rendering context described in. This method is part of a real-time spectral scattering framework for large-scale natural participating media, specifically designed for rendering planets and their atmospheres. It integrates surface shading with atmospheric scattering to provide a cohesive visual result. Real-time spectral scattering in large-scale natural participating media, https://doi.org/10.1145/1925059.1925074, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Terrain Shader Lighting and Effects
head: Voxel Terrain Lighting, Chunk Mesh Lighting, Directional Face Shading
body: This method provides real-time lighting for voxel-based terrain rendered as chunk meshes, combining baked vertex colors with dynamic global and local illumination. It solves the problem of achieving visually rich terrain appearance in voxel engines by blending face-dependent directional shading, soft shadows from spherical occluders, and point light attenuation, while applying post-processing effects like grid overlays and mode-switch visual rings. It differs from pure volume rendering methods by operating on discrete surface normals of meshed chunks rather than continuous volume gradients, and from simple ambient occlusion methods by including explicit directional face shading and soft shadowing calculations. Inputs and Outputs: Vertex Inputs: vertexPosition (vec3), vertexNormal (vec3), vertexColor (vec4, where RGB is albedo and A is a mode-switch factor). Uniforms: Model matrix matModel, MVP matrix mvp, sunDirection (vec3), sunColor (vec3), ambientColor (vec3), cameraPosition (vec3), fogColor (vec3), fogStart (float), fogEnd (float), occluders (array of vec4, xyz=center, w=radius), pointLights (array of vec4, xyz=position, w=range), pointLightColors (array of vec3), waveCenter (vec3), waveRadius (float), waveWidth (float), waveStrength (float), waveColor (vec3), gridSpacing (float), gridStrength (float), worldShade (float). Constants: MAXOCCLUDERS = 8, MAXPOINTLIGHTS = 8. Output: Fragment color (vec3). Data Structures: Occluders: Array of 8 vec4 structures. Each vec4 represents a spherical occluder: xyz is the center position, w is the radius. Point Lights: Array of 8 vec4 structures. Each vec4 represents a point light: xyz is the position, w is the maximum range. Point Light Colors: Array of 8 vec3 structures. Each vec3 is the color of the corresponding point light. Steps: 1. Vertex Shader Processing: Transform the vertex position to clip space: glPosition = mvp vec4(vertexPosition, 1.0). Transform the vertex normal to world space: fragNormal = mat3(matModel) vertexNormal. Pass the vertex position to world space: fragPosition = vec3(matModel vec4(vertexPosition, 1.0)). Pass the vertex color: fragColor = vertexColor. 2. Directional Face Shading: Compute a directional shade factor based on the surface normal n (normalized fragNormal). Formula: shade = n.x^2 0.80 + n.z^2 0.72 + n.y^2 (n.y > 0.0 ? 1.00: 0.55). This blends face shades based on squared normal components, making top faces brighter (1.00) and bottom faces darker (0.55). 3. Sun Visibility and Shadowing: Initialize sunVisibility = 1.0. For each occluder in occluders: Compute toSun = -sunDirection. Compute relative = occluder.xyz - fragPosition. Compute along = dot(relative, toSun). If along <= 0.0, the occluder is behind the surface; skip. Compute perpendicular distance: perpendicular = length(relative - toSun along). Apply soft edge shadowing: shadow = smoothstep(occluder.w 0.80, occluder.w 1.20, perpendicular). Update sunVisibility = (1.0 - shadow). 4. Point Light Attenuation: Initialize pointLightSum = vec3(0.0). For each point light in pointLights: Compute distance = length(light.xyz - fragPosition). If distance >= light.w, skip. Compute attenuation: attenuation = (1.0 - distance / light.w)^2. Compute light direction: toLight = normalize(light.xyz - fragPosition). Compute Lambertian term: lambert = max(dot(normalize(fragNormal), toLight), 0.0). Add to sum: pointLightSum += pointLightColors[i] lambert attenuation. 5. Final Color Composition: Normalize fragNormal. Compute albedo: albedo = fragColor.rgb mix(vec3(1.0), vec3(shade), worldShade). Compute diffuse sunlight: sunDiffuse = max(dot(normalize(fragNormal), -sunDirection), 0.0) sunVisibility. Combine lighting: litColor = albedo (ambientColor + sunDiffuse sunColor) + pointLightSum. Mix between lit and self-lit (vertex alpha): finalColor = mix(litColor, albedo, fragColor.a). 6. Grid Overlay: If gridStrength > 0.0: Compute grid coordinates: p = fragPosition / gridSpacing. Compute width: w = max(fwidth(p), 1e-4). Compute grid mask: g = abs(fract(p - 0.5) - 0.5) / w + abs(normalize(fragNormal)) 10.0. Compute line mask: line = clamp(1.0 - min(min(g.x, g.y), g.z), 0.0, 1.0). Fade with distance: near = 1.0 - smoothstep(6.0, 14.0, length(cameraPosition - fragPosition)). Apply: finalColor = 1.0 - 0.16 line near gridStrength. 7. Mode-Switch Wave: If waveStrength > 0.0: Compute distance: d = length(fragPosition.xz - waveCenter.xz). Compute band: band = 1.0 - smoothstep(0.0, waveWidth, abs(d - waveRadius)). Compute rim lighting: rim = pow(1.0 - max(dot(normalize(fragNormal), normalize(cameraPosition - fragPosition)), 0.0), 2.0). Compute wave color: waveContrib = waveColor band waveStrength (0.3 + 0.5 rim). Mute outside terrain: mute = smoothstep(waveRadius, waveRadius + waveWidth, d). Apply: finalColor = mix(finalColor, dot(finalColor, vec3(0.299, 0.587, 0.114)), mute) + waveContrib. 8. Exponential Fog: Compute fog factor: fog = smoothstep(fogStart, fogEnd, length(cameraPosition - fragPosition)). Mix color with fog: finalColor = mix(finalColor, fogColor, fog). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def terrainshaderlightingeffects( vertexposition, vertexnormal, vertexcolor, mvp, matmodel, sundirection, suncolor, ambientcolor, cameraposition, fogcolor, fogstart, fogend, occluders, pointlights, pointlightcolors, wavecenter, waveradius, wavewidth, wavestrength, wavecolor, gridspacing, gridstrength, worldshade): # Vertex Shader glposition = mvp vec4(vertexposition, 1.0) fragnormal = mat3(matmodel) vertexnormal fragposition = vec3(matmodel vec4(vertexposition, 1.0)) fragcolor = vertexcolor # Directional Face Shading n = normalize(fragnormal) shade = n.x2 0.80 + n.z2 0.72 + n.y2 (1.0 if n.y > 0.0 else 0.55) # Sun Visibility sunvisibility = 1.0 tosun = -sundirection for occluder in occluders: relative = occluder.xyz - fragposition along = dot(relative, tosun) if along <= 0.0: continue perpendicular = length(relative - tosun along) shadow = smoothstep(occluder.w 0.80, occluder.w 1.20, perpendicular) sunvisibility = (1.0 - shadow) # Point Light Attenuation pointlightsum = vec3(0.0) for i, light in enumerate(pointlights): distance = length(light.xyz - fragposition) if distance >= light.w: continue attenuation = (1.0 - distance / light.w)2 tolight = normalize(light.xyz - fragposition) lambert = max(dot(n, tolight), 0.0) pointlightsum += pointlightcolors[i] lambert attenuation # Final Color Composition albedo = fragcolor.rgb mix(vec3(1.0), vec3(shade), worldshade) sundiffuse = max(dot(n, -sundirection), 0.0) sunvisibility litcolor = albedo (ambientcolor + sundiffuse suncolor) + pointlightsum finalcolor = mix(litcolor, albedo, fragcolor.a) # Grid Overlay if gridstrength > 0.0: p = fragposition / gridspacing w = max(fwidth(p), 1e-4) g = abs(fract(p - 0.5) - 0.5) / w + abs(n) 10.0 line = clamp(1.0 - min(min(g.x, g.y), g.z), 0.0, 1.0) eyedistance = length(cameraposition - fragposition) near = 1.0 - smoothstep(6.0, 14.0, eyedistance) finalcolor = 1.0 - 0.16 line near gridstrength # Mode-Switch Wave if wavestrength > 0.0: d = length(fragposition.xz - wavecenter.xz) band = 1.0 - smoothstep(0.0, wavewidth, abs(d - waveradius)) toeye = normalize(cameraposition - fragposition) rim = pow(1.0 - max(dot(n, toeye), 0.0), 2.0) wavecontrib = wavecolor band wavestrength (0.3 + 0.5 rim) mute = smoothstep(waveradius, waveradius + wavewidth, d) luminance = dot(finalcolor, vec3(0.299, 0.587, 0.114)) finalcolor = mix(finalcolor, luminance, mute) + wavecontrib # Exponential Fog eyedistance = length(cameraposition - fragposition) fog = smoothstep(fogstart, fogend, eyedistance) finalcolor = mix(finalcolor, fogcolor, fog) return finalcolor Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of occluders and point lights. Each occluder and point light requires a constant number of vector operations per fragment. Memory Complexity: Constant, determined by the maximum number of occluders and point lights (8 each). Strengths: Provides visually appealing terrain lighting with soft shadows and face-dependent shading. Efficient for real-time rendering on chunk meshes. Limitations: Limited to spherical occluders and point lights. Grid and wave effects are purely visual and do not affect lighting physics. Performance degrades with a large number of dynamic lights or occluders. When to Use: Suitable for voxel-based terrain rendering where visual fidelity is important but full global illumination is too expensive. When Not to Use: Not suitable for physically accurate light transport or complex shadowing scenarios. This method is implemented in the VoxelTerraformer project, an unofficial voxel engine. It is designed to provide a rich visual experience for voxel terrain by combining various lighting and post-processing effects in a fragment shader. The method is specific to the VoxelTerraformer engine and is not a general-purpose technique found in standard graphics literature. GhostlyActive/VoxelTerraformer, https://github.com/GhostlyActive/VoxelTerraformer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Primary Shading
body: Primary Shading evaluates the final radiance of a traced voxel material at a specific hit point by combining direct lighting, indirect lighting (Global Illumination or Ambient), environment lighting, and subsurface translucency. It integrates visibility results into a comprehensive appearance model that supports multiple material shading models, including unlit, emissive, clear coat, two-sided foliage, and subsurface scattering. Inputs and Outputs: The method operates on a per-pixel basis using structured buffers. Inputs: gPrimaryResults: StructuredBuffer<TraceResult> containing hit information (material ID, normal, voxel position). gPrimaryRays: StructuredBuffer<TraceRay> containing ray origins and directions. gAmbientOcclusion: StructuredBuffer<float> containing precomputed AO values. gShadowVisibility: StructuredBuffer<float> containing shadow visibility factors. gIndirectDiffuse: StructuredBuffer<float4> containing precomputed indirect diffuse lighting. gDiffuseIrradiance: TextureCube<float4> for environment irradiance. gSpecularPrefilter: TextureCube<float4> for environment specular prefiltering. gEnvironmentBrdfLut: Texture2D<float2> for environment BRDF lookup. gEnvironmentSampler: SamplerState for texture sampling. Constants: gEnvironmentLightingEnabled, gEnvironmentMaximumSpecularLod, gEnvironmentIntensity, gEnvironmentRotationRadians. Output: gRadiance: RWStructuredBuffer<float4> storing the final radiance and alpha. Data Structures: The implementation relies on specific material records and shading models. MaterialRecord: Contains baseColorRGB, baseColorA, roughness, metallic, specular, emissiveRGB, shadingModel (enum), and subsurface parameters (subsurfaceScatterDistanceMeters, subsurfaceColorRGB). TraceResult: Contains hit (boolean), material (ID), normal, voxel (position), and hitPosition. TraceRay: Contains direction. Parameters: kMpcTimeOfDayTint: Material global vector for time-of-day color tint. kMpcWetness: Material global scalar for wetness factor (0.0 to 1.0). gSunColor, gSunIntensity, gSunDirection: Global light source properties. gShadowMode: Enum (kShadowOff, etc.). gGlobalIlluminationMode: Enum (kGlobalIlluminationAmbientHemisphere, kGlobalIlluminationVoxelOneBounce). gSkyColor, gGroundColor: Hemisphere lighting colors. gSubsurfaceMaxDistanceMeters: Maximum distance for subsurface scattering calculation. gShadowBiasMeters, gShadowStrength, gShadowMaxDistanceMeters: Shadow tuning parameters. Steps: 1. Miss Handling: If the ray misses (hit.hit == 0), compute the background color based on the ray's upwardness. \text{upness} = 0.5 + 0.5 \cdot \text{normalize}(\mathbf{rayDirection}).y \text{radiance} = \text{lerp}(\text{gGroundColor}, \text{gSkyColor}, \text{upness}) Store float4(radiance, 0.0) in gRadiance and return. 2. Material Loading: Load the material record using hit.material. Compute timeOfDayTint from global constants. Compute wetness from global constants, clamped to [0, 1]. Compute baseColor: \text{baseColor} = \text{MaterialBaseColorRGB} \cdot \text{timeOfDayTint} \cdot \text{lerp}(1.0, 0.76, \text{wetness}) Compute roughness: \text{roughness} = \text{lerp}(\text{material.roughness}, 0.08, \text{wetness}) Get emissive from material. 3. Simple Shading Models: If shadingModel == kShadingModelUnlit: \text{radiance} = \text{baseColor} Store float4(baseColor, material.baseColorA) and return. If shadingModel == kShadingModelEmissive: \text{radiance} = \text{emissive} Store float4(emissive, material.baseColorA) and return. 4. Normal Computation: Compute geometricNormal from hit.normal. Compute viewDirection as -normalize(rayDirection). If shadingModel == kShadingModelTwoSidedFoliage, apply wind deformation to geometricNormal to get normal. Otherwise, normal = geometricNormal. 5. Lighting Visibility: Load ao from gAmbientOcclusion. Compute shadowVisibility: \text{shadowVisibility} = \begin{cases} 1.0 & \text{if } gShadowMode == kShadowOff \\ \text{saturate}(gShadowVisibility) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Compute sunRadiance: \text{sunRadiance} = \text{gSunColor} \cdot \text{gSunIntensity} \cdot \text{shadowVisibility} 6. Direct Lighting: Call the appropriate direct lighting function based on shadingModel: kShadingModelClearCoat: ShadeClearCoatDirect kShadingModelTwoSidedFoliage: ShadeTwoSidedFoliageDirect Others: ShadeDirectLight Inputs to these functions include normal, viewDirection, gSunDirection, sunRadiance, baseColor, material.metallic, roughness, and material.specular. Let the result be direct. 7. Indirect Lighting: Initialize indirect = 0. If gGlobalIlluminationMode == kGlobalIlluminationAmbientHemisphere and gEnvironmentLightingEnabled == 0: \text{indirect} = \text{ShadeAmbient}(\text{ambientNormal}, \text{gSkyColor}, \text{gGroundColor}, \text{ao}) \cdot \text{baseColor} \cdot (1.0 - \text{material.metallic}) \cdot \text{gGlobalIlluminationIntensity} If gGlobalIlluminationMode == kGlobalIlluminationVoxelOneBounce: \text{indirect} = \text{gIndirectDiffuse} \cdot \text{baseColor} \cdot (1.0 - \text{material.metallic}) If gEnvironmentLightingEnabled != 0: Add image-based lighting contribution using EvaluateImageBasedLighting with inputs: irradiance (gDiffuseIrradiance), prefilter (gSpecularPrefilter), BRDF LUT (gEnvironmentBrdfLut), sampler, ambientNormal, viewDirection, baseColor, material.metallic, roughness, material.specular, ao, gEnvironmentMaximumSpecularLod, gEnvironmentRotationRadians. \text{indirect} += \text{EvaluateImageBasedLighting}(\dots) \cdot \max(\text{gEnvironmentIntensity}, 0.0) 8. Subsurface Scattering (Conditional): Condition: shadingModel == kShadingModelSubsurface AND material.subsurfaceScatterDistanceMeters > 0 AND gSubsurfaceMaxDistanceMeters > 0 AND \text{dot}(\text{geometricNormal}, \text{gSunDirection}) < 0. Compute interiorBiasVoxels: \text{interiorBiasVoxels} = \max(1.0 \times 10^{-3}, \text{MetersToVoxelUnits}(0.001)) Compute hitPoint: \text{hitPoint} = \text{TraceHitPosition}(\text{ray}, \text{hit}) - \text{geometricNormal} \cdot \text{interiorBiasVoxels} March subsurface thickness: \text{march} = \text{MarchSubsurfaceThicknessVoxels}(\text{hitPoint}, \text{gSunDirection}, \text{hit.material}, \text{MetersToVoxelUnits}(\text{gSubsurfaceMaxDistanceMeters}), 64) If march.exited: Compute farVisibility: If gShadowMode != kShadowOff: Trace a far ray from march.exitPoint + march.exitNormal \max(1.0 \times 10^{-3}, \text{MetersToVoxelUnits}(gShadowBiasMeters)) in direction gSunDirection with max distance MetersToVoxelUnits(gShadowMaxDistanceMeters). If hit: farVisibility = \text{saturate}(1.0 - gShadowStrength). Else: farVisibility = 1.0. Else: farVisibility = 1.0. Add subsurface transmission: \text{radiance} += \text{ShadeSubsurfaceTransmission}(\text{thickness}, \text{scatterDistance}, \text{subsurfaceColor}, \text{exitNormal}, \text{sunDirection}, \text{sunRadiance} \cdot \text{farVisibility}) 9. Final Computation: \text{radiance} = \text{direct} + \text{indirect} + \text{emissive} Store float4(radiance, material.baseColorA) in gRadiance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. gPrimaryResults = None gPrimaryRays = None gAmbientOcclusion = None gShadowVisibility = None gIndirectDiffuse = None gDiffuseIrradiance = None gSpecularPrefilter = None gEnvironmentBrdfLut = None gEnvironmentSampler = None gEnvironmentLightingEnabled = 0 gEnvironmentMaximumSpecularLod = 0.0 gEnvironmentIntensity = 0.0 gEnvironmentRotationRadians = 0.0 gSunColor = float3(1.0) gSunIntensity = 1.0 gSunDirection = float3(0.0) gShadowMode = 0 kShadowOff = 0 gGlobalIlluminationMode = 0 kGlobalIlluminationAmbientHemisphere = 0 kGlobalIlluminationVoxelOneBounce = 1 gSkyColor = float3(0.5) gGroundColor = float3(0.2) gSubsurfaceMaxDistanceMeters = 0.0 gShadowBiasMeters = 0.0 gShadowStrength = 0.0 gShadowMaxDistanceMeters = 0.0 gGlobalIlluminationIntensity = 1.0 kMpcTimeOfDayTint = float3(1.0) kMpcWetness = 0.0 kShadingModelUnlit = 0 kShadingModelEmissive = 1 kShadingModelTwoSidedFoliage = 2 kShadingModelClearCoat = 3 kShadingModelSubsurface = 4 def LoadMaterialRecord(materialid): # Returns material record with fields: baseColorRGB, baseColorA, roughness, metallic, specular, emissiveRGB, shadingModel, subsurfaceScatterDistanceMeters, subsurfaceColorRGB pass def MaterialBaseColorRGB(material): return material.baseColorRGB def MaterialEmissiveRGB(material): return material.emissiveRGB def MaterialSubsurfaceColorRGB(material): return material.subsurfaceColorRGB def MaterialGlobalVector(vecid): return {"rgb": float3(1.0)} def MaterialGlobalScalar(scalarid): return 0.0 def MetersToVoxelUnits(meters): return meters def TraceHitPosition(ray, hit): return ray.origin + ray.direction hit.distance def MarchSubsurfaceThicknessVoxels(hitpoint, sundirection, materialid, maxdistance, maxsamples): # Returns object with.exited,.exitPoint,.exitNormal,.thicknessmeters pass def ShadeClearCoatDirect(normal, viewdirection, sundirection, sunradiance, basecolor, metallic, roughness, specular): # Clear coat direct lighting evaluation return float3(0.0) def ShadeTwoSidedFoliageDirect(normal, viewdirection, sundirection, sunradiance, basecolor, metallic, roughness, specular): # Two-sided foliage direct lighting evaluation return float3(0.0) def ShadeDirectLight(normal, viewdirection, sundirection, sunradiance, basecolor, metallic, roughness, specular): # Standard direct lighting evaluation return float3(0.0) def ShadeAmbient(ambientnormal, skycolor, groundcolor, ao): # Hemisphere ambient lighting evaluation return float3(0.0) def EvaluateImageBasedLighting(irradiance, prefilter, brdflut, sampler, ambientnormal, viewdirection, basecolor, metallic, roughness, specular, ao, maxspecularlod, rotationradians): # Image-based lighting evaluation return float3(0.0) def ShadeSubsurfaceTransmission(thicknessmeters, scatterdistancemeters, subsurfacecolor, exitnormal, sundirection, sunradiance): # Subsurface scattering transmission evaluation return float3(0.0) def ApplyFoliageWindNormal(geometricnormal, voxelpos): # Wind deformation for foliage return geometricnormal def saturate(x): return max(0.0, min(1.0, x)) def lerp(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) def normalize(v): return v / length(v) def dot(a, b): return sum(ai bi for ai, bi in zip(a, b)) def float3(r, g, b): return (r, g, b) def float4(r, g, b, a): return (r, g, b, a) def ShadePrimaryPixel(pixelindex: int) -> float4: # 1. Miss Handling if gPrimaryResults[pixelindex].hit == 0: raydir = normalize(gPrimaryRays[pixelindex].direction) upness = 0.5 + 0.5 raydir.y gRadiance[pixelindex] = float4(lerp(gGroundColor, gSkyColor, upness), 0.0) return # 2. Material Loading hit = gPrimaryResults[pixelindex] material = LoadMaterialRecord(hit.material) timeofdaytint = max(MaterialGlobalVector(kMpcTimeOfDayTint).rgb, 0.0) wetness = saturate(MaterialGlobalScalar(kMpcWetness)) basecolor = MaterialBaseColorRGB(material) timeofdaytint lerp(1.0, 0.76, wetness) roughness = lerp(material.roughness, 0.08, wetness) emissive = MaterialEmissiveRGB(material) # 3. Simple Shading Models if material.shadingmodel == kShadingModelUnlit: gRadiance[pixelindex] = float4(basecolor, material.basecolora) return if material.shadingmodel == kShadingModelEmissive: gRadiance[pixelindex] = float4(emissive, material.basecolora) return # 4. Normal Computation geometricnormal = normalize(float3(hit.normal)) viewdirection = normalize(-gPrimaryRays[pixelindex].direction) if material.shadingmodel == kShadingModelTwoSidedFoliage: normal = ApplyFoliageWindNormal(geometricnormal, float3(hit.voxel) + 0.5) else: normal = geometricnormal # 5. Lighting Visibility ao = gAmbientOcclusion[pixelindex] if gShadowMode == kShadowOff: shadowvisibility = 1.0 else: shadowvisibility = saturate(gShadowVisibility[pixelindex]) sunradiance = gSunColor gSunIntensity shadowvisibility # 6. Direct Lighting if material.shadingmodel == kShadingModelClearCoat: direct = ShadeClearCoatDirect(normal, viewdirection, gSunDirection, sunradiance, basecolor, material.metallic, roughness, material.specular) elif material.shadingmodel == kShadingModelTwoSidedFoliage: direct = ShadeTwoSidedFoliageDirect(normal, viewdirection, gSunDirection, sunradiance, basecolor, material.metallic, roughness, material.specular) else: direct = ShadeDirectLight(normal, viewdirection, gSunDirection, sunradiance, basecolor, material.metallic, roughness, material.specular) # 7. Indirect Lighting indirect = float3(0.0) if gGlobalIlluminationMode == kGlobalIlluminationAmbientHemisphere and gEnvironmentLightingEnabled == 0: ambientnormal = geometricnormal indirect = ShadeAmbient(ambientnormal, gSkyColor, gGroundColor, ao) basecolor (1.0 - material.metallic) gGlobalIlluminationIntensity elif gGlobalIlluminationMode == kGlobalIlluminationVoxelOneBounce: indirect = gIndirectDiffuse[pixelindex].rgb basecolor (1.0 - material.metallic) if gEnvironmentLightingEnabled != 0: indirect += EvaluateImageBasedLighting( gDiffuseIrradiance, gSpecularPrefilter, gEnvironmentBrdfLut, gEnvironmentSampler, geometricnormal, viewdirection, basecolor, material.metallic, roughness, material.specular, ao, gEnvironmentMaximumSpecularLod, gEnvironmentRotationRadians) max(gEnvironmentIntensity, 0.0) # 8. name: Ray Casting and Fragment Shading
head: Fragment Shading with Voxel Lighting
body: This method evaluates shading for traced voxel materials by casting primary rays per fragment to determine surface interaction, then computing direct lighting, ambient occlusion (AO), and indirect lighting contributions. It differs from Basic Gas Rendering Algorithm by focusing on discrete surface hits and fragment-based shading rather than volumetric integration along the ray, and builds on Primary Shading by handling the specific ray-casting-to-fragment pipeline for voxel environments. Inputs: Fragment position (in.position.xy), UV coordinates (in.uv), camera inverse matrix (traceuniforms.camerainverse), voxel texture size (voxeluniforms.texturesize), time (traceuniforms.time), samples count (traceuniforms.samples), and a debug flag (traceuniforms.showraysteps). Outputs: Final color (outputcolor), hit normal texture (normal), and hit position texture (position). Data Structures: hit: Struct containing material (with rgb), pos (world position), normal (world normal), steps (u32 ray step count), and reprojectionpos (reprojected position). ao: Vector of 4 floats (vec4<f32>) representing interpolated AO values from corners. Steps: 1. Seed Generation: Generate a deterministic seed for noise/lighting calculations. seed = \text{vec3<u32>}(in.position.xyz) \times 100 + u32(trace\uniforms.time \times 120.0) \times 15236 2. Ray Setup: Convert fragment UV to clip space and unproject to world space. clip\space = \text{vec2}(1.0, -1.0) \times (in.uv \times 2.0 - 1.0) pos1 = trace\uniforms.camera\inverse \times \text{vec4}(clip\space.x, clip\space.y, 1.0, 1.0) dir1 = trace\uniforms.camera\inverse \times \text{vec4}(clip\space.x, clip\space.y, 0.01, 1.0) pos = pos1.xyz / pos1.w dir = \text{normalize}(dir1.xyz / dir1.w - pos) 3. Ray Casting: Cast the ray into the voxel scene. hit = \text{shoot\ray}(ray, 0.0, 0u) steps = hit.steps 4. Shading (if hit): Direct Lighting: Calculate direct illumination based on material, position, normal, seed, and samples. direct\lighting = \text{calculate\direct}(hit.material, hit.pos, hit.normal, seed + 1u, trace\uniforms.samples) Ambient Occlusion (AO) Coordinates: Compute texture coordinates for AO lookup. texture\coords = hit.pos \times VOXELS\PER\METER + \text{f32}(voxel\uniforms.texture\size) / 2.0 AO Interpolation UV: Calculate UV for bilinear interpolation of AO values. uv = \text{glmod}(\text{vec2}(\text{dot}(hit.normal \times texture\coords.yzx, \text{vec3}(1.0)), \text{dot}(hit.normal \times texture\coords.zxy, \text{vec3}(1.0))), \text{vec2}(1.0)) Interpolate AO: Mix the 4 AO values using the calculated UV. interpolated\ao\pweig = \text{mix}(\text{mix}(ao.z, ao.w, uv.x), \text{mix}(ao.y, ao.x, uv.x), uv.y) AO Gamma Correction: Apply gamma correction to AO. voxel\ao = \text{pow}(interpolated\ao\pweig, 1.0 / 3.0) Indirect Lighting: Approximate indirect lighting using the gamma-corrected AO. indirect\lighting\color = \text{vec3}(0.3 \times voxel\ao) Final Color: Combine indirect, direct, and material color. output\color = (indirect\lighting\color + direct\lighting.color) \times hit.material.rgb 5. No Hit Case: If the ray misses, set a default color. output\color = \text{vec3}(0.3) 6. Debug Override: If enabled, override color with step count visualization. \text{if } trace\uniforms.show\ray\steps \neq 0u: output\color = \text{vec3<f32>}(f32(steps) / 100.0) 7. Clamping: Ensure no negative color values. output\color = \text{max}(output\color, \text{vec3}(0.0)) 8. Store Results: Write hit normal and reprojection position to textures. \text{textureStore}(normal, \text{vec2<i32>}(in.position.xy), \text{vec4}(hit.normal, 0.0)) \text{textureStore}(position, \text{vec2<i32>}(in.position.xy), \text{vec4}(hit.reprojection\pos, 0.0)) 9. Return: Output the final color with alpha 1.0. \text{return } \text{vec4<f32>}(output\color, 1.0) Pseudocode: Unverified code. Ray Casting hit = shootray(pos, dir, 0.0, 0) steps = hit.steps # 4. Shading if hit.ishit: directlighting = calculatedirect(hit.material, hit.pos, hit.normal, seed + 1, samples) texturecoords = [hit.pos[0] voxelspermeter + voxeltexturesize[0] / 2.0, hit.pos[1] voxelspermeter + voxeltexturesize[1] / 2.0, hit.pos[2] voxelspermeter] uvx = dot(hit.normal, [texturecoords[1], texturecoords[2], texturecoords[0]]) uvy = dot(hit.normal, [texturecoords[2], texturecoords[0], texturecoords[1]]) uv = [uvx % 1.0, uvy % 1.0] ao = fetchaocorners(texturecoords) interpolatedaopweig = mix(mix(ao[2], ao[3], uv[0]), mix(ao[1], ao[0], uv[0]), uv[1]) voxelao = interpolatedaopweig (1.0 / 3.0) indirectlightingcolor = [0.3 voxelao, 0.3 voxelao, 0.3 voxelao] outputcolor = [(indirectlightingcolor[i] + directlighting.color[i]) hit.material.rgb[i] for i in range(3)] else: outputcolor = [0.3, 0.3, 0.3] if showraysteps != 0: outputcolor = [steps / 100.0, steps / 100.0, steps / 100.0] outputcolor = [max(c, 0.0) for c in outputcolor] texturestore(normal, [int(inposition[0]), int(inposition[1])], [hit.normal[0], hit.normal[1], hit.normal[2], 0.0]) texturestore(position, [int(inposition[0]), int(inposition[1])], [hit.reprojectionpos[0], hit.reprojectionpos[1], hit.reprojectionpos[2], 0.0]) return [outputcolor[0], outputcolor[1], outputcolor[2], 1.0] def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def mix(a, b, t): return a + (b - a) t def fetchaocorners(coords): # Not given in the sources. Assumes sampling 4 AO values from a texture at coords. return [0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5] def shootray(origin, direction, tmin, tmax): # Not given in the sources. Stub for ray-scene intersection. return type('Hit', (), {'ishit': True, 'steps': 10, 'material': type('Mat', (), {'rgb': [1.0, 1.0, 1.0]})(), 'pos': origin, 'normal': [0.0, 1.0, 0.0], 'reprojectionpos': origin})() def calculatedirect(material, pos, normal, seed, samples): # Not given in the sources. Stub for direct lighting calculation. return type('Light', (), {'color': [0.8, 0.8, 0.8]})() def texturestore(tex, coord, value): # Not given in the sources. Stub for texture write. pass class Mat4: def init(self, cols): self.cols = cols def mulvec4(self, v): return [sum(c v[i] for i, c in enumerate(self.cols[j])) for j in range(4)] Parameters: VOXELSPERMETER: Not given in the sources. traceuniforms.samples: Not given in the sources. traceuniforms.time: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero in ray unprojection if pos1.w or dir1.w is zero. Precision issues in glmod for UV calculation if coordinates are large. The AO interpolation assumes a specific layout of ao values (z, w, y, x) which may not be standard bilinear interpolation without clarification on texture sampling. A shader that adds up all measured data values along the ray and applies a transfer function to display the pixel color. It may also add up all measured data of the ray, apply a lighting function, and then apply a transfer function to display the pixel value. The implementation accumulates all measured data values from the ray, applies a transfer function to the accumulated data to display the pixel color, adds up all measured data of the ray, applies a lighting function to the accumulated data, and applies a transfer function to display the pixel value. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of ray steps for shading, plus constant time for AO interpolation and lighting calculations. Memory Complexity: Constant per fragment for temporary variables; requires storage for normal and position textures. Performance: Depends heavily on the efficiency of shootray and calculatedirect. The use of fragment shading allows for parallel execution across pixels. Strengths: Simple implementation, leverages GPU parallelism, provides basic shading and AO. Limitations: No volumetric effects, limited lighting accuracy (approximate indirect lighting), debug visualization overrides final color. When to use: Real-time voxel rendering where performance is critical and high-fidelity lighting is not required. When not to use: Scenes requiring accurate global illumination, subsurface scattering, or volumetric effects. This method is implemented in the bevy-voxel-engine repository. It implements a fragment-based shading approach for voxel materials, integrating ray casting for surface detection and basic lighting models. ria8651/bevy-voxel-engine, https://github.com/ria8651/bevy-voxel-engine, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Volume Rendering in Architecture: Overlapping and combining 3d voxel volume data with 3d building models, https://doi.org/10.52842/conf.ecaade.2012.1.719, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Basic Gas Rendering Algorithm
head: Low-albedo gas illumination model, CFD gas visualization algorithm
body: The Basic Gas Rendering Algorithm is a volume rendering method designed for visualizing Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) data, specifically gaseous flows and atmospheric phenomena. It solves the problem of revealing internal flow details, shock waves, and pressure changes that are often obscured by traditional surface-based rendering techniques. Unlike methods that rely on gradient-based surface implication and Phong illumination, this approach uses self-shadowing and volume transparency to provide a deeper understanding of three-dimensional flow structures. Inputs: Ray origin and direction. Volume density function (interpolated from a CFD grid). Solid shadow table for self-shadowing queries. Parameters: densityscalar (multiplier), powerfunction exponent (contrast enhancer), transparencythreshold (default 0.01). Outputs: Final accumulated color (finalcolor) for the pixel. Accumulated density (sumdensity). Data Structures: CFD Grid: Stores raw density values. Interpolation (e.g., trilinear) is used to evaluate density at arbitrary points. Solid Shadow Table: A precomputed or runtime-accessible structure storing shadowing information for volume elements. A-buffer: Used to store fragment information for the final image. Formulas: 1. Opacity (Optical Depth): The opacity \tau is calculated as the integral of density \rho(s) along the ray path from start si to end se: \tau = \int{si}^{se} \rho(s) ds In practice, this is approximated by summing density values multiplied by the step size. 2. Density Modification: Raw density \rho{raw} is modified using a scalar and a power function to enhance visualization: \rho{modified} = (\rho{raw} \times \text{density\scalar})^{\text{power\function}} (Note: The exact order of operations for scalar and power is not explicitly defined in the source, but both are applied to enhance volumetric information and contrast.) 3. Transparency: Transparency T is derived from accumulated optical depth \tau{acc}: T = e^{-\tau{acc}} 4. Illumination Model: A low-albedo illumination model is used. The phase function p(\theta) is based on the summation of Henyey-Greenstein functions. The amount of light I reflected from an element depends on the angle between the light and the eye. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize finalcolor to 0 and sumdensity to 0. 2. Iterate through each section of the gas volume along the ray. 3. For each increment (sample point) along the ray: a. Evaluate the modified density \rho{modified} at the current sample point using the CFD grid and parameters. b. Calculate the opacity contribution for this step. If this is the final increment, scale the opacity proportionally to account for the reduced step size. c. If self-shadowing is enabled, retrieve the shadowing factor for the current element from the solid shadow table. d. Calculate the gas illumination color using the opacity, modified density, shadowing factor, and the low-albedo illumination model (Henyey-Greenstein phase function). e. Add the calculated illumination color to finalcolor. f. Add the modified density to sumdensity. g. Calculate the transparency of the accumulated path. If transparency is less than 0.01, stop tracing the ray. h. Increment the sample point. Monte Carlo sampling may be used to choose sample points to reduce aliasing artifacts. i. Create the a-buffer fragment for the current sample. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def basicgasrendering(rayorigin, raydirection, cfdgrid, shadowtable, params): finalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] sumdensity = 0.0 opticaldepth = 0.0 samplepoint = rayorigin stepsize = params.get('stepsize', 1.0) transparencythreshold = 0.01 densityscalar = params.get('densityscalar', 1.0) powerfunction = params.get('powerfunction', 1.0) selfshadowingenabled = params.get('selfshadowing', True) lightcolor = params.get('lightcolor', [1.0, 1.0, 1.0]) maxsteps = params.get('maxsteps', 100) raylength = params.get('raylength', 100.0) for i in range(maxsteps): # Get raw density from CFD grid rawdensity = cfdgrid.interpolate(samplepoint) # Apply density modifications modifieddensity = (rawdensity densityscalar) powerfunction # Calculate opacity for this step # Opacity is density stepsize # Scale for final increment if needed traveled = (samplepoint - rayorigin).length() remaining = raylength - traveled stepscale = min(1.0, remaining / stepsize) if i == maxsteps - 1 else 1.0 taustep = modifieddensity stepsize stepscale opticaldepth += taustep sumdensity += modifieddensity # Check transparency threshold # Transparency is exp(-opticaldepth) transparency = math.exp(-opticaldepth) if transparency < transparencythreshold: break # Retrieve shadowing if enabled shadowfactor = 1.0 if selfshadowingenabled: shadowfactor = shadowtable.retrieveshadow(samplepoint) # Calculate illumination using low-albedo model # Phase function based on Henyey-Greenstein summation illuminationcolor = calculategasillumination( taustep=taustep, density=modifieddensity, shadowfactor=shadowfactor, lightcolor=lightcolor) # Accumulate color finalcolor[0] += illuminationcolor[0] finalcolor[1] += illuminationcolor[1] finalcolor[2] += illuminationcolor[2] # Increment sample point samplepoint = samplepoint + raydirection stepsize # Create a-buffer fragment createabufferfragment(samplepoint, finalcolor, sumdensity) return finalcolor, sumdensity def calculategasillumination(taustep, density, shadowfactor, lightcolor): # Low-albedo model: color contribution proportional to density and shadow # Uses standard volumetric attenuation approximation for gas return [c shadowfactor (1.0 - math.exp(-taustep)) for c in lightcolor] def createabufferfragment(point, color, density): # Stores fragment data for compositing pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The final increment along the ray may be smaller than standard steps; its opacity must be scaled proportionally to account for the reduced step size. Precision issues may arise when transparency is very close to the threshold (0.01). Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples along the ray. The use of a shadow table allows for fast shadow queries, but the table itself may require significant precomputation or memory. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the CFD grid and the solid shadow table. Strengths: Reveals internal flow details, shock waves, and pressure changes that are lost in traditional surface-based rendering. Self-shadowing increases the understandability of the 3D flow. Limitations: Traditional techniques using gradient-based surface implication and Phong illumination are simpler but lack the depth of information provided by this method. The method may be computationally expensive due to the need for shadow table lookups and multiple density evaluations. When to use: When visualizing CFD data where internal structures, flow dynamics, and pressure variations are critical, and when traditional surface rendering fails to convey this information. The Basic Gas Rendering Algorithm was developed for the visualization of Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) data. It was introduced as an alternative to traditional volumetric rendering techniques that rely on gradient-based surface implication and Phong illumination. The method emphasizes the use of self-shadowing and volume transparency to enhance the visualization of gaseous flows and atmospheric phenomena. name: Topology-aware illumination perception contrast model
head: Perceptual illumination, Distance illumination, Saliency illumination, Topology-aware lighting
body: The Topology-aware illumination perception contrast model is a volume rendering framework that utilizes topological attributes derived from a contour tree to automatically generate distinct illuminations for subregions, allowing users to perceive structural differences (such as importance and topological distance) via lighting cues. It specifically addresses the problem of inner structures being obscured by outer structures in semi-transparent volumes by applying less illuminance to outside structures and higher illuminance to inner structures. Unlike standard lighting models that treat all geometry equally or rely solely on spatial distance, this method maximizes visual perception differences between neighboring objects by optimizing luminance contrast based on topological saliency and persistence. The method operates in two phases: an Initialization Phase and an Optimization Phase. It requires a pre-computed contour tree of the volume data, which is first simplified to reduce noise. Inputs: Simplified contour tree of the volume data. Initial root luminance L0 (user-specified). Initial illumination contrast ratio \gamma0 (user-specified, range [0, 1]). Topological attributes for each branch: persistence (p), volume (v), hypervolume (hv), and saddle value (s). User-modulated weights: w (for saliency/distance models) and V (lighting speed in medium). Outputs: Illumination coefficients (ka, kd, ks) for each branch in the contour tree. Luminance distribution across the contour tree. The core data structure is the Contour Tree, where each node represents a branch (a connected component of a level set). Each branch node stores: Topological Attributes: pi: Persistence of branch i. vi: Volume of branch i. hvi: Hypervolume of branch i. si: Saddle value of branch i. depthi: Topological depth (distance from root). n{ci}: Number of children of branch i. n{si}: Number of siblings (branches sharing the same parent). Illumination State: Li: Luminance of branch i. k{d,i}: Diffuse coefficient for branch i. 1. Base Illumination Model (Blinn-Phong) The color C of a voxel is computed as: C = (ka + kd (N \cdot L)) C{tf} + ks (N \cdot H)^n Where: ka, kd, ks: Ambient, diffuse, and specular coefficients. N: Normalized gradient vector of the voxel. L: Normalized lighting direction. H: Normalized half-way direction. n: Shininess exponent. C{tf}: Color defined by the transfer function. 2. Topology-Aware Attenuation Factor (f{att}) Light intensity weakens over distance. The attenuation factor is defined using Stokes' law adapted for topology: f{att} = e^{-\alpha z} Where: z: Modeled as the persistence p of the branch. \alpha: Attenuation coefficient derived from Stokes' law: \alpha = \frac{2 \eta{visc} \eta{freq}^2}{3 \rho V^3} \eta{visc}: Dynamic viscosity (0.001002 P·s for water at 20°C). \rho: Density (998.2071 kg/m³ for water at 20°C). \eta{freq}: Modeled as the number of siblings n{si}. V: Lighting speed in the medium (user-controlled). The modified Blinn-Phong equation becomes: C = (ka + kd f{att} (N \cdot L)) C{tf} + ks f{att} (N \cdot H)^n 3. Just-Noticeable-Difference (JND) The minimal luminance change \Delta Li required for an observer to perceive a difference, based on luminance Li: \log(\Delta Li) = \begin{cases} -2.86 & \text{if } \log(Li) < -3.94 \\ (0.405 \log(Li) + 1.6)^{2.18} - 2.86 & \text{if } -3.94 \le \log(Li) < -1.44 \\ \log(Li) - 0.395 & \text{if } -1.44 \le \log(Li) < -0.0184 \\ (0.294 \log(Li) + 0.65)^{2.7} - 0.72 & \text{if } -0.0184 \le \log(Li) < 1.9 \\ \log(Li) - 1.255 & \text{if } \log(Li) \ge 1.9 \end{cases} 4. Illumination Contrast Ratio (\gamma) Defined between parent branch i-1 and child branch j: \gamma = \frac{L{child}}{L{parent}} Range [0, 1]. \gamma=0 implies the child is black; \gamma=1 implies equal luminance. The model aims for \gamma < 1 so children (inner structures) have higher luminance than parents (outer structures). 5. Saliency Illumination (kd function) For "Saliency Illumination," kd is a function of topological saliency Sri: kd = w S{ri} Where w is a user weight. Sri is calculated using a Gaussian weighting function \omega{ij} based on topological depth difference d(ci, cj) and maximum depth r: \omega{ij} = e^{-\frac{d(ci, cj)^2}{r^2}} 6. Distance Illumination (kd function) For "Distance Illumination," kd is a function of topological distance (depth z) using a Sigmoid function: kd = \frac{w}{2} \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} This assigns higher kd to deeper (inner) branches. 7. Optimization Constraints The optimization must satisfy: 1. \Delta Li \ge \Delta L{JND, i} 2. \gammai \ge \gamma0 3. Li \ge L{i,0} (where L{i,0} is the initial luminance from the Initialization Phase) 1. Simplify Contour Tree: Reduce noise in the topological structure. 2. Set Root Luminance: User specifies L0 for the root branch. 3. Recursive Initialization: For each branch i (starting from root): Calculate JND difference \Delta L{JND} between parent and children using the JND formula. Set initial luminance for children Lc = L{parent} + \Delta L{JND}. Recursively apply to all branches from root to leaves. The goal is to maximize luminance differences while satisfying constraints. The process iterates through depth levels i \ge 1. Step 2.1: Parent-to-Children Distribution For each depth level i: 1. Calculate new base luminance L'{i-1} for the parent level based on contrast ratio \gamma{i-1} and parent luminance. Note: The source defines L'{i-1} = L'{i-2} / \gamma{i-1} effectively, but since \gamma < 1 and children should be brighter, the logic implies L{child} = L{parent} / \gamma or similar scaling to ensure L{child} > L{parent} if \gamma represents parent/child ratio. However, the text states \gamma = Li / Lj (parent/child) and \gamma \in [0,1]. Thus L{child} = L{parent} / \gamma. If \gamma=0.5, child is 2x brighter. 2. For each child j of parent i: Get initial luminance band L'{ij} from Initialization Phase. Calculate luminance difference \Delta L{ij} = |L'{ij} - L{parent}|. Check Constraint: If \Delta L{ij} \ge \Delta L{JND, ij}: Define final L'{ij} as the initial value. Else: Define final L'{ij} by adjusting to meet the JND difference (increase luminance if necessary). Compute illumination coefficients (kd) for branch j based on the new luminance L'{ij} using either Saliency or Distance illumination formulas. 3. Update Contrast Ratio: Calculate absolute head loss \Delta hi using the residue flow model: \Delta hi = \frac{1}{Q} \cdot \frac{pi}{K \cdot n{ci}} Q: Fluid flow speed (user parameter). K: Hydraulic conductivity (300 for sand). pi: Persistence of branch i. n{ci}: Number of children of branch i. Update contrast ratio for next level: \gammai = (1.0 - \Delta hi) \cdot \gamma{i-1} This results in smaller contrast ratios (higher relative luminance for children) for deeper levels. Step 2.2: Sibling Distribution Distribute the base illumination L'i among siblings j=1 \dots n{si} on level i: L'{ij} = L'i \cdot fb(p{ij}, v{ij}, hv{ij}) \cdot fd(s{ij}) fb: Function controlling distribution based on importance (persistence, volume, hypervolume). Defined as the area of the importance triangle formed by these three attributes. fd: Function controlling distribution based on saddle value s{ij}: fd(s{ij}) = \frac{s{ij} - s{min, i}}{\Delta si} Where s{min, i} is the minimum saddle value among siblings on level i, and \Delta si = s{max, i} - s{min, i}. Precision: The JND formula involves logarithms and piecewise functions; care must be taken with Li \le 0 (luminance must be positive). Boundary Conditions: \gamma=0 results in black child branches; \gamma=1 results in no contrast. Noise: Raw contour trees may contain noise affecting topology; simplification is required before attribute extraction. Parameter Sensitivity: V (lighting speed) and Q (flow speed) are interactive and significantly affect attenuation and contrast propagation. Time Complexity: Depends on the size of the contour tree (number of branches) and the depth of the tree. The optimization iterates through depth levels and branches. Simplification is a preprocessing step. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of branches in the contour tree, storing topological attributes and illumination coefficients. Strengths: Automatically emphasizes inner structures and important topological features without manual tuning of per-object lighting. Maximizes perceptual contrast based on human vision models (JND). Limitations: Requires pre-computation of a contour tree. Performance depends on the complexity of the topological simplification. The model assumes a specific relationship between topological depth and visual importance (inner = more important), which may not hold for all datasets. When to use: When the goal is to reveal internal structures in complex, nested volumetric data (e.g., biological structures) and topological hierarchy is meaningful. When not to use: For flat or non-nested data where topological depth does not correlate with visual importance, or when real-time performance is critical and contour tree computation is too expensive. The method was introduced by Zhou et al. in 2016. It builds upon previous work on topology-aware visualization, such as the use of contour trees for data segmentation and opacity transfer functions. The framework integrates concepts from psychophysics (JND) and fluid dynamics (residue flow model) to model light attenuation and contrast distribution in a topological context. It is part of the broader field of topology-aware illumination design, which includes sub-methods like "Saliency Illumination" and "Distance Illumination". Topology-aware illumination design for volume rendering, https://doi.org/10.1186/s12859-016-1177-4, fetched 2026-10-26
