name: Approximate Image-Space Multidirectional Occlusion Shading (ISMOS)
head: Approximate Image-Space Multidirectional Occlusion Shading (ISMOS) model, ISMOS model
body: ISMOS is a screen-space shading technique that computes multidirectional occlusion at the end of a direct volume rendering pipeline using rendered depth and normal buffers, simulating global illumination effects such as shadows and ambient occlusion without preprocessing. It differs from previous image-space models by sampling along the pixel-to-light ray instead of a hemisphere, enabling multiple directional lights with minor overhead. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rendered frame buffers containing color, depth, and normal information for the volume. Light source parameters (position, type, radius d, hemisphere radius R). Outputs: Final shaded image with occlusion effects. Data Structures: 1. Depth Buffer: Stores four front-most depth layers in the RGBA components of a single buffer. This allows differentiation of layers based on transfer function settings. 2. Transmittance Parameter Buffer: Stores a single parameter \beta per pixel in the Alpha (A) component of the color buffer. This parameter describes the functional form of opacity values over depth, approximating the volume transmittance. Method Steps: 1. Volume Rendering with Transmittance Approximation: During the initial ray-casting pass, compute the discrete transmittance Tn for samples along the ray. The transmittance is defined as: T(z) = \exp\left(-\int0^z \alpha(z') \, dz'\right) In discrete form: Tn \approx \prod{j=1}^{n} \exp(-\alpha(zj)\Delta z) where n is the number of samples to reach depth z, \Delta z is the distance between samples, and \alpha is the opacity. To avoid storing a list of transmittances, approximate the continuous transmittance T(z) using a Gaussian function: f(z) = \exp(-\beta z^2) where \beta is a parameter to be approximated. Compute \beta for each pixel using linear least-squares fitting to minimize the residual: \text{Residual} = \sum{i} \left(\beta zi^2 - \log\left(\frac{1}{Ti}\right)\right)^2 The solution is: \beta = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y where X = [z1^2, \dots, zn^2] and y = [\log(1/T1), \dots, \log(1/Tn)]. Store \beta in the Alpha channel of the color buffer. 2. Opacity Reconstruction: Calculate approximate opacity \alpha{app}(z) at any depth z using the fitted \beta: \frac{f(z)}{f(z - \Delta z)} = \frac{Tn}{T{n-1}} = \exp(-\alpha(z)\Delta z) \alpha{app}(z) = \frac{1}{\Delta z} \cdot \log\left(\frac{f(z - \Delta z)}{f(z)}\right) This allows on-the-fly calculation of opacity values for any depth layer. 3. Occlusion Shading Pass: For each pixel, retrieve the depth layers and the \beta parameter. Light Sampling: Place light sources on a hemisphere of radius R centered at the image-space center. Point Light (Hard Shadow): Use N=1 sample. Occi is binary (0 or 1). Area Light (Soft Shadow): Use multiple samples. The light source is a disk with radius d. Smaller d generates harder shadows. Ambient Occlusion: Use large d, small R, and place light at \phi = \pi/2. Ray Marching for Occlusion: Sample test points along a ray between the pixel and the light source. Termination conditions for ray marching: 1. Ray position r(t) is not between (0,0,0) and (1,1,1). 2. Occi is one (fully occluded). 3. t is one (reached light). Compute binary occlusion Occi for each sample i: Occi = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if ray is blocked by volume} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Compute total occlusion Occ for N light samples: Occ = \frac{\sum{i=1}^{N} Occi}{N} For multiple light sources j, with Nj samples and Noj occluded samples: Occ = \frac{\sum{j} Noj}{\sum{j} Nj} For partial occlusion (blending): Occ = \frac{\sum{j} \left(\sum{i} Occi\right)}{\sum{j} Nj} Layer Application: Differentiate layers according to transfer function settings. Opaque Layers: Apply ISMOS occlusion if opacity \alpha > \alpha{th}. Transparent Layers: Use local illumination (e.g., Phong shading) only, or blend ISMOS results across all layers. 4. Final Color Computation: Combine the base color with the occlusion factor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeismos(depthbufferrgba, colorbufferrgba, lightsources, alphathreshold): """ depthbufferrgba: Array of shape (H, W, 4), storing 4 depth layers in RGBA. colorbufferrgba: Array of shape (H, W, 4), storing RGB color and Beta in A. lightsources: List of light source objects with position, type, radius d, radius R. alphathreshold: Float, threshold for opaque vs transparent layers. """ shadedimage = np.zeroslike(colorbufferrgba) for y in range(H): for x in range(W): # 1. Retrieve layer depths and beta depths = depthbufferrgba[y, x] # 4 depth values beta = colorbufferrgba[y, x, 3] # Beta parameter # 2. Determine which layers to shade # Reconstruct opacity for each depth layer using beta layeropacities = [] for i, z in enumerate(depths): if z == 0: # Empty space layeropacities.append(0.0) continue # f(z) = exp(-beta z^2) fz = np.exp(-beta z2) # Approximate deltaz from previous layer or use fixed step # Assuming uniform sampling step dz for simplicity in reconstruction # In practice, dz might be derived from ray marching step dz = 0.01 # Placeholder for actual step size from rendering pass fzminusdz = np.exp(-beta (z - dz)2) # alphaapp(z) = (1/dz) log(f(z-dz)/f(z)) alphaapp = (1.0 / dz) np.log(fzminusdz / fz) layeropacities.append(alphaapp) # 3. Compute Occlusion for relevant layers totalocclusion = 0.0 numlightsamplestotal = 0 for light in lightsources: # Determine number of samples N based on light type if light.type == 'point': N = 1 elif light.type == 'area': N = light.samples # e.g., 16 else: # ambient N = light.samples occludedcount = 0 for k in range(N): # Generate sample point on light source # For point: light.position # For area: random point on disk radius d # For ambient: fixed position based on phi=pi/2 samplepos = light.getsamplepoint(k) # Ray from pixel to light sample rayorigin = getpixelworldpos(x, y, depths[0]) # Front-most layer raydirection = normalize(samplepos - rayorigin) # Ray march to check occlusion isoccluded = False t = 0.0 stepsize = 0.01 while t < 1.0: # t is normalized distance to light # Check if ray is within volume bounds (0,0,0) to (1,1,1) currentpos = rayorigin + raydirection t if not isinsidevolume(currentpos): break # Check if current position is inside volume # Use depth buffer to find if there is geometry closer than the light path # Or use the reconstructed opacity from beta # Simplified: Check if depth at current screen pos is closer than light # But ISMOS samples along the ray in world space or screen space? # Source says "sample test points along a ray between the pixel and the light source" # and "uses rendered depth and normal buffers" # Project currentpos to screen space to check depth screenpos = projecttoscreen(currentpos) if screenpos is valid: # Get depth at this screen position depthatraypoint = getdepthfrombuffer(screenpos) # If the volume surface at this screen position is closer to camera # than the current ray point, it's occluded. # However, we are marching from pixel TO light. # If we hit a surface that is "in front" of the light path relative to camera? # Actually, standard shadow ray: if any geometry blocks the path. # In image space, we check if the depth buffer value at the projected # ray point is less than the depth of the ray point itself? # No, the ray point IS the point in space. # We need to know if there is volume between rayorigin and currentpos. # Alternative interpretation from source: # "sample test points along a ray... to calculate light transfer" # "Occi is one" if occluded. # Let's assume we march and check density/opacity. # Since we have beta, we can estimate opacity at currentpos depth? # But currentpos is in world space. # Simpler approach for Image Space: # The ray is defined in screen space coordinates? # No, light is in world space. # Let's use the depth buffer to check occlusion. # If we are at 't' along the ray to light, we project this point. # If the depth buffer at that projection shows a surface CLOSER to the camera # than the point 't' on the ray, then that surface blocks the light. # Wait, the ray starts at the pixel (closest) and goes to light (farthest). # So if we find ANY surface in the depth buffer that is closer to the camera # than the current ray point 't', it blocks the light. # But the depth buffer stores the front-most surface. # If the front-most surface is closer than 't', it blocks. # However, we are marching FROM the pixel. # The pixel itself is at depth d0. # The light is at depth dlight. # We march t from 0 to 1. # At t, we are at depth d(t). # If depthbuffer[screenpos] < d(t), then there is something closer. # But depthbuffer[screenpos] IS d(t) if we are on the surface. # If we are in empty space, depthbuffer[screenpos] is the surface behind. # Correct logic for shadow ray in image space: # Project the test point P(t) to screen. # Get depth Dscreen from buffer. # Get depth Dray of P(t) in camera space. # If Dscreen < Dray, then the surface in the buffer is closer to camera # than P(t), meaning it blocks the light from reaching P(t). if depthatraypoint < currentpos.z: # Assuming z is depth isoccluded = True break t += stepsize if isoccluded: occludedcount += 1 numlightsamplestotal += N totalocclusion += occludedcount # Compute final occlusion factor if numlightsamplestotal > 0: occfactor = totalocclusion / numlightsamplestotal else: occfactor = 0.0 # 4. Apply Shading # Base color from volume rendering basecolor = colorbufferrgba[y, x,:3] # Check if layer is opaque enough to apply ISMOS # Use the front-most layer's opacity frontalpha = layeropacities[0] if frontalpha > alphathreshold: # Apply occlusion shadedcolor = basecolor (1.0 - occfactor) # Simplified shading # Or: shadedcolor = basecolor (1.0 - occfactor intensity) else: # Transparent: Use local illumination (Phong) # This part is not fully detailed in sources, so we use base color shadedcolor = basecolor shadedimage[y, x,:3] = shadedcolor shadedimage[y, x, 3] = 1.0 # Opaque output return shadedimage Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The least-squares fitting for \beta assumes the transmittance follows a Gaussian-like decay. If the volume has complex internal structures, the approximation may be inaccurate. Boundaries: Ray marching termination must handle cases where the ray exits the volume bounds (0,0,0) to (1,1,1). Degenerate Input: If \beta is zero or very small, the opacity approximation may fail. Guard against division by zero in log operations. Layer Differentiation: Storing only 4 layers limits the complexity of transparent scenes. More layers require more buffers. Time Complexity: Computation scales with screen size (resolution) rather than volume data size. It is computationally less expensive than global illumination models. Memory Complexity: Requires no extra GPU memory for the entire volume data. Only standard frame buffers (color, depth, normals) and one additional parameter (\beta) per pixel are needed. Strengths: Interactive transfer function manipulations and light position changes are achievable without preprocessing. Simulates hard shadows, soft shadows, and ambient occlusion in a unified model. Limitations: Approximation of transmittance may not capture fine details. Limited to 4 depth layers by default. ISMOS was proposed in 2021 by authors published in Applied Sciences (MDPI). It addresses the lack of interactivity in previous global illumination models for volume rendering, which required preprocessing and extra GPU memory. It builds on image-space techniques but extends them to multidirectional lighting by sampling along pixel-to-light rays. name: Ambient Volume Illumination
head: Ambient Volume Shading, Ambient Scattering Model
body: Ambient Volume Illumination is a family of local illumination algorithms for direct volume rendering that approximates light transport based on the local "ambient region" of each data point, aiming to reproduce phenomenological illumination effects for interactive performance. It solves the problem of poor spatial depth perception and feature occlusion inherent in simple emission-absorption models by introducing local shadows and indirect light cues. What sets it apart from its siblings is the explicit use of ambient scattering to simulate complex light-matter interactions, providing stronger visual cues for spatial arrangement than ambient occlusion alone. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of evaluating visibility or illumination at a specific point \mathbf{p} within or on the boundary of a volume, based on a light source direction \mathbf{l} or environment. 1. Visibility/Transmittance Evaluation: The fundamental operation is determining how much light reaches \mathbf{p} from a source. This involves integrating the extinction coefficient \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) along a path from the source to \mathbf{p} (or vice versa). The transmittance T is calculated as: T = \exp\left(-\int{\mathbf{p}{source}}^{\mathbf{p}} \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) \, d\mathbf{x}\right) In discrete implementations, this integral is approximated by summing \sigmat \cdot \Delta s over samples along the ray. 2. Local Shading Models: For surface-like appearance in volumes, normals are approximated from the volume gradient \mathbf{g} = \nabla V. Usually, a simple absorption and emission model is used because it is relatively cheap to evaluate and gives good enough results. 3. Shadowing Approximation: Shadows are computed by testing occlusion along the direction to the light source. 4. Ambient Occlusion: Indirect illumination is approximated by integrating over the hemisphere or using simplified models (e.g., upward ray for sky light). The ambient contribution L{ambient} is often modulated by a shadowing factor based on local density: L{ambient} = L{sky} \cdot \exp(-D{up}) \cdot AO{factor} where D{up} is the integrated density along an upward ray. An algorithm to visualize the anisotropy of volumetric features using anisotropic bidirectional reflectance distribution functions (BRDFs), solving the problem where isotropic specular highlights (like Blinn-Phong) do not support the perception of anisotropic features like elliptic or linear structures. The concept was introduced in the paper "Ambient Volume Illumination" published in IEEE Computing in Science and Engineering in 2016. It emerged from ongoing research in volume visualization focused on developing simplified optical models that reproduce important illumination effects on a phenomenological level to achieve interactive performance and simpler parameter control compared to accurate global illumination. It is used in direct volume rendering to help users perceive spatial depth, discover cavities, and identify salient structures in volumetric data sets. name: Anisotropic Ambient Volume Shading
head: Anisotropic Volume Shading, Scale-aware Anisotropic Shading
body:
Anisotropic Ambient Volume Shading is a method for direct volume rendering that improves the perception of the orientation and shape of surface-like structures by computing anisotropic specular highlights. It solves the problem where isotropic models (e.g., Blinn-Phong) fail to convey the elliptic or linear nature of volumetric features. Unlike isotropic shading or standard ambient occlusion, this method derives local tangent frames from the scalar field's ambient region to drive anisotropic BRDFs (Ward, Lafortune), aligning highlights with principal anisotropy directions. Inputs: Scalar volume data s(\mathbf{x}), transfer function parameters (extinction coefficient \sigmat), light direction \mathbf{l}, view direction \mathbf{v}, and user-defined parameters: ambient radius r, sample count n, interval size \varepsilon, global anisotropy scaling \gamma, and glossiness \kappa. Outputs: Shaded radiance image. Data Structures: Normals: \mathbf{N}(\mathbf{x}) stored per voxel, same resolution as data. Covariance Matrices: Symmetric 2 	imes 2 matrix \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x}) stored per voxel. Tangent Vectors: \mathbf{U}(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{V}(\mathbf{x}) computed per voxel during rendering or precomputed. Algorithm Steps: 1. Normal Estimation: Compute the normal \mathbf{N}(\mathbf{x}) from the gradient of the unclassified scalar field s using the Sobel operator: \mathbf{N}(\mathbf{x}) = - rac{

abla s(\mathbf{x})\| = 0, skip shading (specular coefficient becomes 0). 2. Explorative Sampling: Define a sphere of radius r centered at shading point \mathbf{x}. Draw n samples \mathbf{x}i uniformly inside the sphere using random numbers \xi0, \xi1, \xi2 \in [0,1]: d = r \sqrt[3]{\xi0} \mathbf{x}i = \mathbf{x} +  egin{pmatrix} 2d \cos(2\pi\xi1)\sqrt{\xi2(1-\xi2)} \ 2d \sin(2\pi\xi1)\sqrt{\xi2(1-\xi2)} \ d(1-2\xi2) \end{pmatrix} Filter samples to keep only those where s(\mathbf{x}i) \in [s(\mathbf{x}) - \varepsilon, s(\mathbf{x}) + \varepsilon]. Let the accepted set be Xa(\mathbf{x}) with size m. 3. Projection: Project samples Xa(\mathbf{x}) onto the tangent plane defined by \mathbf{N}(\mathbf{x}): \mathbf{x}i^p = \mathbf{x}i - (\mathbf{N}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot (\mathbf{x}i - \mathbf{x}))\mathbf{N}(\mathbf{x}) Compute orthonormal basis vectors  oldsymbol{\eta}1,  oldsymbol{\eta}2 in the tangent plane to avoid discontinuities: \phi = 	ext{atan2}(Ny, Nx)  oldsymbol{\eta}1 = (-\sin\phi, \cos\phi, 0)^T  oldsymbol{\eta}2 =  oldsymbol{\eta}1 	imes \mathbf{N} Transform projected samples to 2D coordinates X2(\mathbf{x}): \mathbf{x}i^2 = (\mathbf{x}i^p \cdot  oldsymbol{\eta}1, \mathbf{x}i^p \cdot  oldsymbol{\eta}2)^T 4. Covariance Matrix Construction: Compute the centroid  ar{\mathbf{x}} of X2(\mathbf{x}) and the weighted covariance matrix \mathbf{C}:  ar{\mathbf{x}} =  rac{1}{m} \sum{i=1}^m \mathbf{x}i^2 \mathbf{C} = \sum{i=1}^m (\mathbf{x}i^2 -  ar{\mathbf{x}})(\mathbf{x}i^2 -  ar{\mathbf{x}})^T w(di) where w(d) = 1-d^2 if d \le 1, else 0, and di = \|\mathbf{x}i^2 -  ar{\mathbf{x}}\|/r. Pitfall: For small r or noisy data, apply a discrete Gaussian filter to elements C{11}, C{12}, C{22} before eigenanalysis. 5. Eigenanalysis: Compute eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2 and eigenvectors  oldsymbol{\Lambda}1,  oldsymbol{\Lambda}2 of \mathbf{C}: \lambda{1,2} =  rac{	ext{tr}(\mathbf{C})}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left( rac{	ext{tr}(\mathbf{C})}{2}ight)^2 - \det(\mathbf{C})} Sort such that \lambda1 \le \lambda2. Compute eigenvectors in 2D: If C{12} 
eq 0:  oldsymbol{\Lambda}1 = (C{12}, \lambda1 - C{11})^T, \quad  oldsymbol{\Lambda}2 = (C{12}, \lambda2 - C{11})^T Else:  oldsymbol{\Lambda}1 = (1, 0)^T, \quad  oldsymbol{\Lambda}2 = (0, 1)^T Transform back to 3D:  ar{\mathbf{U}} = \Lambda{1,x} oldsymbol{\eta}1 + \Lambda{1,y} oldsymbol{\eta}2, \quad  ar{\mathbf{V}} = \Lambda{2,x} oldsymbol{\eta}1 + \Lambda{2,y} oldsymbol{\eta}2 Normalize: \mathbf{U} =  ar{\mathbf{U}}/\| ar{\mathbf{U}}\|, \mathbf{V} =  ar{\mathbf{V}}/\| ar{\mathbf{V}}\|. \mathbf{V} is the major anisotropy direction. 6. BRDF Parameter Mapping: Map eigenvalue ratio to BRDF parameters using global scaling \gamma. Ward: Parameters uw, vw control anisotropy magnitude. Lafortune: Parameters ul, vl control anisotropy. Set nl = 1. Glossiness: \kappa controls specular lobe width. 7. Rendering: Compute radiance using the scattering function: L(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}) = T(\mathbf{x}b, \mathbf{x})Lb + \int T(\mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{x})\sigmas(\mathbf{x}0)Li(\mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{v}) d\mathbf{x}0 Scattering function: f(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}', \mathbf{v}) = kd fd + ks fs(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}', \mathbf{v}) (\mathbf{v}' \cdot \mathbf{N}{\sigmat})+ where \mathbf{N}{\sigmat} = -
abla \sigmat / \|

abla \sigmat\|, kd = 1. fs is the chosen anisotropic BRDF (Ward/Lafortune) using \mathbf{U}, \mathbf{V}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeanisotropicshading(x, s, sigmat, l, v, r, n, eps, gamma, kappa): # 1. Normal Estimation grads = sobelgradient(s, x) norms = length(grads) if norms == 0: return diffuseshading(x, s, l, v) # Specular coeff ks=0 N = -normalize(grads) # 2. Explorative Sampling samples2d = [] for i in range(n): xi0, xi1, xi2 = randomuniform(), randomuniform(), randomuniform() d = r cbrt(xi0) # Sample point in sphere px = x.x + 2dcos(2pixi1)sqrt(xi2(1-xi2)) py = x.y + 2dsin(2pixi1)sqrt(xi2(1-xi2)) pz = x.z + d(1-2xi2) xi = Vector(px, py, pz) # Filter by scalar value si = samplescalar(s, xi) if abs(si - s(x)) <= eps: # 3. Projection proj = xi - dot(N, xi - x) N phi = atan2(N.y, N.x) eta1 = Vector(-sin(phi), cos(phi), 0) eta2 = cross(eta1, N) x2 = Vector(dot(proj, eta1), dot(proj, eta2)) samples2d.append((x2, xi)) # Keep 3D for distance weighting m = len(samples2d) if m == 0: return diffuseshading(x, s, l, v) # 4. Covariance Matrix centroid = Vector(0,0,0) for x2, in samples2d: centroid += x2 centroid /= m C = Matrix2x2(0,0,0,0) for x2, xi in samples2d: diff = x2 - centroid dist = length(diff) / r w = max(0, 1 - distdist) C += outerproduct(diff, diff) w # Optional: Filter C elements here if needed # 5. Eigenanalysis tr = C[0][0] + C[1][1] det = C[0][0]C[1][1] - C[0][1]C[1][0] lambda1 = tr/2 - sqrt(trtr/4 - det) lambda2 = tr/2 + sqrt(trtr/4 - det) # Eigenvectors if abs(C[0][1]) > 1e-6: lam1vec = Vector(C[0][1], lambda1 - C[0][0]) lam2vec = Vector(C[0][1], lambda2 - C[0][0]) else: lam1vec = Vector(1, 0) lam2vec = Vector(0, 1) # Transform to 3D Ubar = lam1vec.x eta1 + lam1vec.y eta2 Vbar = lam2vec.x eta1 + lam2vec.y eta2 U = normalize(Ubar) V = normalize(Vbar) # 6. BRDF Parameters # Map eigenvalue ratio to anisotropy parameters using gamma # Example for Ward: uw, vw derived from lambda1, lambda2, gamma # Example for Lafortune: ul, vl derived similarly # 7. Rendering Nsigmat = -normalize(gradientsigmat(sigmat, x)) ks = length(gradientsigmat(sigmat, x)) if ks == 0: return diffuseshading(x, s, l, v) H = normalize(l + v) # Compute specular term using anisotropic BRDF (e.g., Lafortune) # fs = fanisotropic(Nsigmat, H, U, V, ul, vl, kappa) # L = ks fs max(0, dot(l, Nsigmat)) + diffuseterm return computeradiance(Nsigmat, H, U, V, ks, kappa, gamma) Complexity: Precomputation of normals is O(N). Per-voxel anisotropy estimation is O(n) where n is sample count. Rendering is O(N \cdot n) if computed per pixel/voxel, or O(N) if precomputed. Performance: Precomputation takes ~985 ms (vs 465 ms for curvature-based). Memory usage is ~44.9 MB (vs 67.4 MB for curvature-based) due to storing 2 	imes 2 vs 3 	imes 3 matrices. Rendering speed is ~81 fps (vs 69 fps). Strengths: Data-driven, independent of transfer function (can be precomputed). Enhances perception of tubular/linear structures. Reduces aliasing with large radius. Limitations: Sensitive to parameter choice (r, \varepsilon, n). Small r or low n causes noise/artifacts. Large \varepsilon includes irrelevant features. When to use: When visualizing anisotropic structures (vortices, fibers, edges) in scalar volumes. When not to use: For isotropic features or when performance is critical and precomputation is not feasible. Origin: Proposed by Marco Ament and Carsten Dachsbacher. Publication: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics, 2015. Also presented in IEEE SciVis 2015. Context: Extends local illumination models for volume rendering by incorporating anisotropic BRDFs derived from scalar field geometry, addressing limitations of isotropic Blinn-Phong shading. name: Direct Sunlight Attenuation
head: Light Attenuation Simulation
body: Direct Sunlight Attenuation simulates the reduction of solar intensity as light passes through a participating medium, typically using precomputed ray templates or eye-buffer transparency to determine voxel brightness. It differs from full volumetric path tracing by decoupling the direct light contribution into a separate pass that attenuates a distant light source based on integrated density, rather than computing scattering events along the view ray. Inputs: A 3D volume grid of density values \rho (or \sigmat). A light direction vector \mathbf{l} (typically the sun). A view direction vector \mathbf{v} (for the distant light pass). Parameters: DECAY (absorption coefficient), AMBIENT (minimum light floor), n (grid dimension). Outputs: Attenuated light intensity l for each voxel or pixel. A final shaded color incorporating the direct sunlight term. Data Structures: Density Grid: A 3D array of floats, indexed linearly as offset = ((z n) + y) n + x. Note: Implementation may require index reversal depending on texture generation vs. simulation coordinate systems. Intensity Buffer: An 8-bit unsigned char array (unsigned char intensity) storing accumulated light levels. Ray Template: A precomputed array of 3D offsets (rayTemplate[i][0..2]) defining the path from a source point into the volume. Steps: 1. Precompute Ray Templates: Generate a set of ray directions based on the light vector \mathbf{l}. For each non-zero component of \mathbf{l}, define a path through the grid. 2. Light Ray Propagation (Per Voxel/Source): For each starting position (x, y, z) in the grid: a. Initialize light level l = 200 (or source intensity). b. Calculate decay factor: \text{decay} = \frac{1.0}{n \times \text{DECAY}}. c. Iterate along the ray template indices i = 0, 1, \dots: i. Compute current coordinates: xx = x + \text{template}[i][0], yy = y + \text{template}[i][1], zz = z + \text{template}[i][2]. ii. Check bounds: if xx, yy, zz are outside [0, n), terminate. iii. Calculate linear offset: \text{offset} = ((zz \times n) + yy) \times n + xx. iv. Retrieve density: d = \text{dens}[\text{offset}] \times 255.0. v. Update light level: l{\text{new}} = \max(\text{AMBIENT}, l{\text{old}} - d \times \text{decay}) vi. Update intensity buffer: \text{intensity}[\text{offset}] = \max(\text{AMBIENT}, \text{intensity}[\text{offset}]) If \text{intensity}[\text{offset}] > 0: \text{intensity}[\text{offset}] = \left\lfloor \frac{\text{intensity}[\text{offset}] + l{\text{new}}}{2} \right\rfloor Else: \text{intensity}[\text{offset}] = l{\text{new}} vii. If l{\text{new}} \le \text{AMBIENT}, terminate loop. 3. Distant Light Pass (View-Based): a. Store total volume transparency in the alpha channel of the eye buffer. b. Calculate dot product: dot = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{l}. c. Check if view vector is within the sun's disk (e.g., dot > \cos(0.5^\circ)). d. If true, add the attenuated sunlight term to the pixel color, modulated by the stored transparency and atmospheric attenuation. Parameters: DECAY: 0.06f (light absorption coefficient). AMBIENT: 100 (minimum light level floor). Sun disk threshold: 0.5 degrees. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Intensity Averaging: The accumulation step (intensity[offset] + l)0.5f halves the contribution of previous rays, potentially underestimating brightness in dense regions. Coordinate Alignment: Density lookup offsets must match the texture generation coordinate system; mismatches cause visual artifacts. Precision: Using 8-bit integers for intensity limits dynamic range; consider floating-point buffers for high-dynamic-range scenes. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot R) where N is the number of voxels and R is the average ray length through the volume. Memory Complexity: O(N) for density and intensity buffers. Strengths: Computationally efficient for static or slowly changing volumes; suitable for real-time applications on older hardware (e.g., GeForce FX). Limitations: Approximates scattering as simple attenuation; does not account for multiple scattering or complex shadowing within the volume. The averaging step can lead to incorrect brightness accumulation. The method originates from efficient rendering techniques for atmospheric phenomena, where direct sunlight is treated as a distant light source attenuated by the volume's total transparency. It was implemented on early programmable graphics hardware using fragment programs. The ray-template approach for voxel-based attenuation is documented in unofficial smoke simulation repositories. nevermoe/SmokeSimulation, https://github.com/nevermoe/SmokeSimulation, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Efficient Rendering of Atmospheric Phenomena, https://doi.org/10.2312/egwr/egsr04/375-386, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Sun-aligned Relighting TensoRF
head: Fast Sun-aligned Outdoor Scene Relighting based on TensoRF, SR-TensoRF
body: Sun-aligned Relighting TensoRF (SR-TensoRF) is a method for outdoor scene relighting and novel view synthesis that eliminates the need for environment maps by using the sun direction as a direct input for shadow generation. It builds on Local illumination, shadows and ambient occlusion by decomposing the synthesis process into albedo, shadow, and tone components, leveraging TensoRF's efficiency. Unlike NeRF-OSR, which relies on environment maps, SR-TensoRF uses sun direction input, simplifying inference and allowing dynamic shadow generation based on time and location. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D position \mathbf{x}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, sun direction \mathbf{d}{sun}, and a latent vector \mathbf{l} for tone. Outputs: Final pixel color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}). Data Structures: SR-TensoRF comprises three tensors: 1. Density Tensor (G\sigma): Learns density features. 2. Appearance Tensor (Ga): A 4D tensor concatenating albedo and shadow features: Ga(\mathbf{x}) = G{albedo}(\mathbf{x}) \oplus G{shadow}(\mathbf{x}). 3. Cubemap Tensor (Gc): Six 3D tensors representing the faces of a cube, each with 128x128 elements. Numbered Steps: 1. Sun Direction Computation: Compute \mathbf{d}{sun} from the date, time, and location coordinates of captured images using PyEphem. Align \mathbf{d}{sun} (initially in horizontal coordinates) with the world coordinates of the training images by rotating it along the y-axis based on the camera pose convention where the first training image serves as the world coordinate. 2. Feature Extraction: Compute density \sigma = G\sigma(\mathbf{x}). Compute albedo color \mathbf{c} = M{albedo}(G{albedo}(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{l}, \mathbf{d}) via a shallow MLP. Compute shadow strength s = M{shadow}(G{shadow}(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{d}{sun}) via a shallow MLP. 3. Volumetric Rendering of Albedo and Shadow: Render albedo A(\mathbf{r}) using \sigma and \mathbf{c}, and render shadow S(\mathbf{r}) \in [0, 1] using \sigma and s with the standard volume rendering equation. 4. Cubemap Background Computation: Interpolate cubemap feature Gc(\mathbf{r}) bilinearly from the six 3D cubemap tensors where the ray intersects. Compute cubemap background \mathbf{b} by passing Gc(\mathbf{r}) and \mathbf{d}{sun} through a shallow MLP M{cubemap}: \mathbf{b} = M{cubemap}(Gc(\mathbf{r}), \mathbf{d}{sun}). 5. Final Output: Compute the final color by combining the volume rendered albedo and shadow with the cubemap background: \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) = A(\mathbf{r}) \cdot S(\mathbf{r}) + \left(1 - \sum{i=1}^{N} wi\right) \mathbf{b} where wi = Ti(1-\exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) and Ti=\exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj). Parameters: Cubemap tensor size: 128x128 elements per facet. Adam optimizer learning rate: 0.01 for tensor parameters, 0.001 for MLPs. Cubemap integration delay: The cubemap is withheld from integration for the initial 5,000 iterations to prevent overfitting. Loss function: Mean Squared Error (MSE), L1 loss for density tensor, Total Variation (TV) loss for all tensors, and a regularization loss to constrain shadow values from approaching 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayboxintersection(origin, direction, boxmin, boxmax): """Compute intersection of ray with axis-aligned bounding box.""" tmin = (boxmin - origin) / direction tmax = (boxmax - origin) / direction tenter = max(min(tmin), min(tmax)) texit = min(max(tmin), max(tmax)) if tenter > texit: return None return origin + direction tenter def bilinearinterpolate(grid, point): """Bilinear interpolation on a 2D grid.""" x, y = point x0, y0 = int(x), int(y) x1, y1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1 dx, dy = x - x0, y - y0 g00 = grid[y0, x0] g01 = grid[y0, x1] g10 = grid[y1, x0] g11 = grid[y1, x1] top = g00 (1 - dx) + g01 dx bottom = g10 (1 - dx) + g11 dx return top (1 - dy) + bottom dy def volumerenderray(origin, direction, numsamples, latentvector, sundirection, Gsigma, Galbedo, Gshadow, Gcubemap, Malbedo, Mshadow, Mcubemap): """Render a single ray using SR-TensoRF.""" # Ray marching parameters tnear, tfar = 0.0, 1.0 points = origin + direction (tnear + (tfar - tnear) torch.linspace(0, 1, numsamples)) deltas = torch.diff(torch.cat([torch.tensor([tnear]), torch.linspace(tnear, tfar, numsamples)])) accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = torch.zeros(3) for i in range(numsamples): x = points[i] # Tensor lookup (simplified grid interpolation for TensoRF features) sigmafeat = Gsigma[x] albedofeat = Galbedo[x] shadowfeat = Gshadow[x] # Compute per-sample properties sigma = sigmafeat c = Malbedo(albedofeat, latentvector, direction) s = torch.sigmoid(Mshadow(shadowfeat, sundirection)) # Volume rendering weights alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas[i]) wi = accumulatedtransmittance alpha accumulatedcolor += wi c accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - alpha) # Cubemap background blending cubemappoint = rayboxintersection(origin, direction, torch.tensor([-1.0]), torch.tensor([1.0])) if cubemappoint is not None: Gc = bilinearinterpolate(Gcubemap, cubemappoint) b = Mcubemap(Gc, sundirection) finalcolor = accumulatedcolor + (1.0 - accumulatedtransmittance) b else: finalcolor = accumulatedcolor return finalcolor Time Complexity: Training is significantly faster than NeRF-OSR (e.g., 1h 11m vs 32h for Site 1) due to the TensoRF framework. Memory Complexity: Uses three tensors (G\sigma, Ga, Gc) and shallow MLPs. The cubemap tensor size is fixed at 128x128 per facet. Strengths: Eliminates environment maps, simplifies inference, allows dynamic shadow generation, and accelerates training and rendering by approximately tenfold compared to NeRF-OSR. Limitations: Requires accurate sun direction computation and alignment. Alpha masks in TensoRF can cause elongated training time, extraneous density learning, artifacts, or cracks in background regions if not handled correctly. When to use: Daytime outdoor scene relighting and novel view synthesis where sun direction is known or can be computed. When not to use: Indoor scenes or scenes with multiple dominant light sources where sun direction is not the primary illumination source. SR-TensoRF was introduced by Jung Yi and Nojun Kwak from Yonsei University in November 2023. It is designed for outdoor scene relighting, addressing the challenges of unbounded scenes and varying white balances in training images. The method builds on TensoRF [8] and integrates concepts from MipNeRF-360 [3] for ray contraction. Fast Sun-aligned Outdoor Scene Relighting based on TensoRF, https://doi.org/10.1109/wacv57701.2024.00359, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Single and multiple scattering
head: Light transport in participating media, Volumetric scattering
body: Single and multiple scattering methods simulate the interaction of light with participating media (such as fog, smoke, or clouds) by modeling how photons are absorbed, emitted, and redirected by particles within the volume. While single scattering approximations assume light undergoes at most one collision before reaching the camera, multiple scattering methods account for complex, multi-bounce light transport, enabling the rendering of dense, glowing, or highly reflective volumetric effects. This family is distinguished from Optical models by its focus on the stochastic or deterministic solution of the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) for light paths, and from Local illumination, shadows and ambient occlusion by its explicit handling of in-scattering from distant light sources rather than just local shading. All methods in this family are derived from the conservation of energy for a differential cylinder of light passing through a medium. They share the following core definitions and mechanisms: 1. Fundamental Interactions Any volumetric effect is composed of three fundamental characteristics: Absorption: The loss of radiant energy along a ray due to energy conversion (e.g., to heat). It is described by the absorption coefficient \sigmaa (units: m^{-1}). Emission: The addition of radiant energy where the medium is luminous (e.g., flames). It is described by the emissive term Le(\mathbf{p}, \boldsymbol{\omega}), representing radiance emitted per unit length. Scattering: The redirection of light rays upon collision with particles. It is split into: In-scattering: Light from other directions reflected into the view ray. Out-scattering: Light from the view ray reflected away. In most lighting calculations, out-scattering is folded into the extinction term because its net effect on the view ray is identical to absorption. 2. Notation \mathbf{p}: Position of interaction. \boldsymbol{\omega}: Ray direction (unit vector). L: Radiance quantity. Li: Incoming radiance. Lo: Outgoing radiance. \sigmat: Total extinction coefficient, \sigmat = \sigmaa + \sigmas. 3. Differential Forms The change in radiance dL over a differential path length dt is governed by the balance of loss and gain terms: Absorption Model: dL = -\sigmaa Li dt. Emission Model: dL = \sigmae dt (where \sigmae is the emission coefficient). General RTE: Combines extinction (loss) and source terms (gain from emission and in-scattering). 4. Transmittance The fraction of light surviving transmission through a medium is defined by the Beer-Lambert law: T = e^{-\tau} where \tau is the optical depth (integrated extinction). Volumetric Radiance Estimators are a family of nine distinct methods introduced by Jarosz et al. [2011a] that estimate equilibrium radiance in participating media by reconstructing values from discrete samples (photon points or photon beams) using spatial blurring. They differ from unbiased path integral estimators by lacking a general path contribution function and pdf, instead relying on specific radiometric quantities and kernel dimensions to approximate the radiance field. The Path Integral Framework formulates light transport simulation as a Monte Carlo integration problem over the space of all possible light transport paths, expressing pixel intensity as a single non-recursive integral. It solves the problem of evaluating the recursive rendering equation by expanding it into a sum over path configurations, serving as the theoretical foundation for combining photon density estimation and Monte Carlo path integration. Homogeneous Medium Sampling determines the distance a ray travels through a participating medium with uniform optical properties before interacting, avoiding explicit distance and spherical integrations by letting the ray randomly bounce within the medium before potentially hitting a surface. It differs from Delta tracking by directly sampling the interaction distance from the extinction coefficient rather than using a majorant bound, and it serves as the foundational step for Free-path sampling. Delta tracking is a Monte Carlo method for sampling the distance to the next interaction (scattering or absorption) in a heterogeneous participating medium where the extinction coefficient varies spatially. It solves the problem that standard exponential distance sampling requires a constant extinction coefficient, which is rarely true in real-world volumes. Unlike ray marching, which introduces systematic bias by using fixed step sizes, delta tracking is unbiased and handles inhomogeneous media without requiring a structured grid. This method renders a participating medium by solving the radiative transfer equation under the assumption that light scatters exactly once within a homogeneous volume before reaching the camera. It extends a basic absorption-only model by adding in-scattering from surface-emitting geometry, assuming the surfaces do not reflect or transmit light. It is distinguished from Single-scattering atmosphere rendering by its general applicability to arbitrary scene manifolds rather than specific atmospheric layers, and from Volume Single Scattering (Monte Carlo with Point Light) by its deterministic ray-marching approach. Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) for volumetric path tracing reduces variance in estimating direct lighting by combining contributions from phase function sampling and next event estimation (NEE). It solves the problem of high variance when sampling light sources in participating media, particularly when paths skip index-matching surfaces or involve delta distributions. Unlike standard path tracing which may rely on a single sampling strategy, this method uses the power heuristic to balance the probability density functions (PDFs) of both strategies, ensuring robust convergence. Biased Sampling for Path Depth is a variance reduction technique for volumetric path tracing in dense, highly anisotropic participating media (such as clouds) that exponentially decays the medium's extinction coefficient and anisotropy parameter as the ray depth increases. By reducing the frequency of scattering events and the directionality of scattering at deeper bounces, the method significantly shortens path lengths and accelerates convergence, trading a slight, visually negligible bias for massive performance gains. Unified Points, Beams, and Paths (UPBP) is a combined rendering algorithm that fuses volumetric density estimation estimators (Point-Point, Point-Beam, Beam-Beam) with unbiased Bidirectional Path Tracing (BPT) using Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS). It solves the problem of efficiently simulating light transport in diverse participating media by automatically selecting the most suitable representation—points for high-order scattering, beams for low-order scattering, and paths for specular surface interactions—thereby mitigating the weaknesses of individual estimators. Sample Matching for Extinction Gradients is a differentiable volumetric path tracing method that reduces the variance of extinction coefficient gradients by evaluating the positive scattering term and the negative transmittance term at shared spatial locations along each path segment. Unlike the base Volumetric Path Tracing method, which estimates these two opposing terms at unrelated points, this technique exploits their negative correlation to cancel variance, while maintaining the same primal rendering output. The Zonal Method is a deterministic technique for computing multiple scattering in participating media by assuming isotropic scattering, where the source term depends only on position. It extends the diffuse radiosity method for interreflecting surfaces to volumes, solving for the isotropic scattering source term by setting up and solving a system of simultaneous linear equations. Unlike stochastic methods such as Delta tracking or Volumetric Radiance Estimators, it provides a global solution for multiple bounces but is restricted to isotropic phase functions and suffers from high computational complexity for dense volumes. Joint Path Vertex Sampling (JPVS) is a method for constructing a full light transport path by connecting a light subpath endpoint \mathbf{a} and an eye subpath endpoint \mathbf{d} via a connection subpath containing two new vertices \mathbf{b} and \mathbf{c}. It solves the high variance associated with connecting subpaths in participating media by using three random decisions (two distances and one direction) to sample the connection, rather than the zero, one, or two decisions used by methods like Equiangular Sampling or Virtual Ray Lights. This approach reduces variance by explicitly sampling the connection direction to cancel geometric singularities. A fully analytic method to importance sample the geometry terms along 3-segment paths (double-scattering) in isotropic participating media, generalizing equiangular sampling for 2-segment paths. It constructs a joint probability density function (PDF) for the intermediate scattering vertices that cancels out the singularities inherent in the path contribution function, thereby reducing variance compared to standard uniform or single-scattering sampling strategies. Walter's Method is a technique for computing refraction paths within triangle meshes to produce light shafts within complex refractive volumetric boundaries. It sets itself apart from siblings like Volumetric Radiance Estimators and Photon-based Methods by directly solving for valid refracted light paths without an intermediate lighting representation, thereby avoiding the blurring and approximation artifacts inherent in photon mapping. Unlike Light Beam Tracing, the solution is exact and does not suffer from blurring, allowing it to resolve fine details that standard photon mapping cannot. This method computes the radiance contribution of a single scattering event in a participating medium by integrating the in-scattered light from a point light source along a view ray using Monte Carlo integration. It solves the radiative transfer equation for the single-scattering term by sampling interaction points along the ray and evaluating the light transport from the source to those points, attenuated by the medium's extinction. Unlike deterministic uniform ray marching methods, it provides an unbiased estimator for point-light in-scattering in homogeneous volumes. A phase function describes the angular distribution of light scattering at any point within a participating medium, defining the fraction of incoming light traveling along direction \omega' that is scattered into direction -\omega (towards the eye). It solves the problem of simplifying complex anisotropic scattering interactions into a normalized probability density function that can be evaluated or sampled during light transport simulation. Unlike Isotropic Phase Function, which scatters light equally in all directions, phase functions model directional preferences such as forward scattering in clouds or back-scattering in smoke. This family encompasses deterministic methods for solving the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) in participating media, primarily by discretizing the angular or spatial domains or by formulating the transport problem as a system of linear or integral equations. Unlike the stochastic path-tracing siblings in Single and multiple scattering, these methods aim to compute the global illumination solution (often steady-state) by propagating flux or solving for intensity distributions directly, thereby avoiding the noise inherent in Monte Carlo estimators. Single scattering approximations solve the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) by assuming that light undergoes exactly one scattering event within the participating medium before reaching the camera. This simplification ignores multiple scattering events and self-illumination (glow), making it applicable when the volume has low albedo or low density. It is distinguished from multiple scattering methods by its computational efficiency and from homogeneous-only models by its ability to handle heterogeneous media in some variants. Photon-based methods solve the problem of estimating radiance in participating media by decoupling light transport into a preprocessing phase (photon tracing) and a rendering phase (radiance estimation via density estimation or virtual light sources). Unlike direct integration methods that trace paths per pixel, these methods store photon interactions in spatial structures and estimate incident radiance at query points using kernel density estimation or explicit summation. What sets this family apart from its siblings is the specific use of stored photon data (points, beams, or spheres) to approximate the in-scattering term. Art-Directable Multiple Volumetric Scattering is a path tracing method that computes efficient, physically accurate multi-bounce diffusion in participating media while allowing independent artistic control over image contrast. It distinguishes itself from standard volumetric path tracers by decoupling the physical diffusion (scale) from the visual contrast, enabling biased but convergent rendering of high-order scattering without pre-computation or caching. The Optimized Monte Carlo Integrator is a method for computing radiance scattered inside a participating medium from a collimated light source towards the camera, specifically designed for real-time rendering applications. It solves the problem of redundant geometric traversal by caching segment data, allowing samples to be drawn proportional to transmittance without repeated box outline calculations. It sets itself apart from standard ray marching by pre-computing analytic integration values for trapezoid-shaped segments of the medium, significantly reducing per-sample computational cost. Continuous Media Convergence describes the phenomenon where a discrete medium composed of a large number of scattering particles renders with an appearance statistically indistinguishable from a homogeneous continuous medium. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering dense particulate scenes by allowing the use of traditional volumetric path tracing with global, averaged radiative transfer parameters instead of explicit particle geometry. It differs from Delta tracking by replacing spatial queries with uniform or analytically derived coefficients, and from discrete particle rendering by avoiding explicit geometry traversal. A method to define participating media by summing multiple phase terms, each with its own density, phase function, and absorption, to produce a composite medium. The total optical depth is the sum of the optical depths of each term in RGB. Phase functions are applied per-channel, and the Henyey-Greenstein eccentricity g ranges from (-1, 1), where g < 0 is back-scattering, g = 0 is isotropic, and g > 0 is forward scattering. Extending the shading method to multiple light sources to approximate global illumination from skylight (sunlight scattered by atmosphere). The technique shades clouds from multiple light sources, stores resulting particle colors from all shading iterations, and at render time evaluates the phase function at each particle once per light. An ambient term is added to compensate for lost scattered light due to the scattering approximation. Computes the phase function for i scattering events by convolving the base phase function p(\omega, \omega') with itself i-1 times via integration over the unit sphere. For the Henyey-Greenstein phase function, the result of i convolutions is the same formula with g replaced by g^i, precomputed and saved for each pixel on the viewing cube faces. The probability q{ij} of exactly i scattering events along segment Sj is given by q{ij} = \exp(-Dj) Dj^i / i!, where Dj is the optical depth. The contribution Ej is computed as \sumi q{ij} K{ij}, where K{ij} is the convolution sample. This Poisson distribution is an approximation valid for small water droplets where scattering is highly peaked forward. The mathematical foundation of light transport in participating media is the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE), which describes the conservation of energy for a differential cylinder of light. Early work in computer graphics focused on single scattering approximations due to computational constraints, often assuming homogeneous media and simple phase functions like Rayleigh or Mie scattering. Rayleigh scattering is appropriate when particle radius r \ll \lambda (e.g., smoke, dust), while Mie scattering is used when r \approx \lambda (e.g., fog, water droplets). Schlick's approximation to the Henyey-Greenstein phase function became standard for its efficiency in avoiding fractional exponentiation. The development of multiple scattering methods was driven by the need to render dense, glowing volumes where light bounces multiple times. Deterministic solvers, such as the Zonal Method, offer alternative approaches for specific isotropic cases, though they suffer from high complexity. Modern approaches often combine density estimation techniques with unbiased path tracing, leveraging variance reduction strategies like Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) and biased sampling for path depth to handle complex media efficiently. A lighting model for general participating media, https://doi.org/10.1145/1053427.1053446, fetched 2026-11-02 PDF Direct Volume Rendering, https://www.sci.utah.edu/~stevec/classes/cs5630/dvr.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (book) Volumetric Light Scattering in Fallout 4, https://www.scribd.com/document/748135006/Fast-Flexible-Physically-Based-Volumetric-Light-Scattering, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Real-Time Cloud Rendering, https://www.cs.unc.edu/techreports/01-005.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) Diffusion and multiple anisotropic scattering for global illumination in clouds, https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc1410406/?q=multiple scattering rendering, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Volumetric Radiance Estimators
head: B-B1D, B-B2D, B-B3D, B-P2D, B-P3D, P-B2D, P-B3D, P-P3D
body: Volumetric Radiance Estimators are a family of nine distinct methods introduced by Jarosz et al. [2011a] that estimate equilibrium radiance in participating media by reconstructing continuous fields from discrete samples (photons or beams) using spatial blurring kernels. They differ from unbiased path integral estimators by not being formulated as general path sampling techniques, and they differ from sibling methods like Homogeneous Medium Sampling by relying on pre-computed photon data structures rather than on-the-fly ray marching. Builds on Single and multiple scattering. The family consists of nine estimators defined by three dimensions: the data representation (Photon Points or Photon Beams), the query type (Point or Beam), and the kernel dimension (1D, 2D, or 3D). The naming convention follows the order: Data × Query × Kernel Dimension (e.g., B-P3D is Beam Data, Point Query, 3D Kernel). This opposes the convention used by Jarosz et al. [2011a]. Kd denotes a normalized d-dimensional kernel used for blurring, where 1D uses a line, 2D uses a square, and 3D uses a cube. The scattering function ρ at a query location xj is evaluated with the direction of the photon beam or photon, which may not pass through this location. Estimates the in-scattered radiance at a specific query point by aggregating the energy of discrete photon points stored within a surrounding three-dimensional volume. It solves the problem of approximating the integral of incoming radiance from all directions by converting a continuous density estimation problem into a discrete summation over a spherical kernel. It differs from its sibling, the Extended Balance Heuristic, by relying on a fixed spherical kernel and standard density estimation rather than balance heuristics to combine multiple estimators. It differs from its child, Beam Query × Beam Data, 2D Blur, by using discrete point data and blurring in 3D, which introduces bias along the light transport direction that the 2D blur variant avoids. Choose it when point-based photon mapping is employed and 3D spatial blurring is acceptable. A variance reduction technique used to weight estimates from a mixture of sampling techniques, combining unbiased path sampling with extended space volumetric estimators. It generalizes the standard balance heuristic by incorporating kernel density estimation properties into the weighting scheme, allowing for optimal combination of disparate estimators such as photon mapping and path tracing. It sets itself apart from siblings like Point Query × Point Data by explicitly accounting for the kernel support volume in the probability density function (pdf) calculation for volumetric techniques. Choose it when fusing results from different radiance estimators to produce a lower-variance final image. A technique to convert a long beam estimator into a short beam estimator by treating the beam length sampling as a Russian Roulette (RR) decision on the contribution. Long beams extend until the closest surface, with transmittance along the beam appearing as part of the estimator. Short beams are of finite extent where transmittance vanishes (replaced by a constant 1) via a single step function approximation, coined "progressive deep shadow maps". The probability that a short beam of length l contributes at distance t0 is \Pr\{l > t0\} = \int{t0}^{\infty} p(t') dt', where p(t) is the pdf used to sample the beam length. The short beam estimator is calculated as \langle I \rangle{\text{short}} = \langle I \rangle{\text{long}} \frac{H(l - t)}{\Pr\{l > t\}}, where H is the Heaviside step function indicating if the beam is long enough. This approach provides an intuitive explanation and generalization of Jarosz et al.'s [2011b] unbiased progressive deep shadow maps. Choose it to simplify the handling of beam termination and transmittance in complex scenes. The family of Volumetric Radiance Estimators was introduced by Jarosz et al. in 2011. The framework was later generalized and unified with unbiased path tracing methods in the Unified Points, Beams, and Paths (UPBP) algorithm, which allows for the combination of these estimators with unbiased path integral estimators using the Extended Balance Heuristic. The concept of "short beams" was also introduced in related work by Jarosz et al. [2011b] as "progressive deep shadow maps". Unifying points, beams, and paths in volumetric light transport simulation, https://doi.org/10.1145/2601097.2601219, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Point Query × Point Data, 3D Blur
head: Conventional Radiance Estimation, Standard volumetric radiance estimate, Jensen and Christensen estimate
body: Point Query × Point Data, 3D Blur estimates the in-scattered radiance at a query point by aggregating the energy of discrete photon points stored within a surrounding three-dimensional volume. It solves the problem of approximating the integral of incoming radiance from all directions by converting a continuous density estimation problem into a discrete summation over a spherical kernel. It differs from its child, Beam Query × Beam Data, 2D Blur, by using discrete point data and blurring in three dimensions rather than restricting the spatial blur to a two-dimensional cross-section. Inputs and Outputs Input: A query position \mathbf{x}, a view direction \vec{\omega}, a photon map containing discrete photon points, a spherical kernel radius r, and the scattering coefficient \sigmas of the medium. Output: The estimated in-scattered radiance Li(\mathbf{x} \rightarrow \vec{\omega}) at the query point. Data Structures The photon map stores discrete photon points. Each photon point p contains position \mathbf{x}p, power \Phip, and direction \vec{\omega}p. Algorithm 1. Define a three-dimensional query region R centered at \mathbf{x}, typically a sphere of radius r. 2. Identify all photons p in the photon map such that \mathbf{x}p \in R. 3. For each photon p, compute the phase function value f(\thetap), where \thetap is the scattering angle between the incoming photon direction and the view direction \vec{\omega}. 4. Sum the product of the phase function and photon power for all photons in R. 5. Divide the sum by the scattering coefficient \sigmas and the volume measure \muR(r^3). Formula The in-scattered radiance Li(\mathbf{x} \rightarrow \vec{\omega}) is estimated as: Li(\mathbf{x} \rightarrow \vec{\omega}) \approx \frac{1}{\sigmas \muR(r^3)} \sum{p \in R} f(\thetap) \Phip Where: \sigmas: Scattering coefficient of the medium (m^{-1}). \muR(r^3): Volume measure of the query region. For a sphere of radius r, \muR(r^3) = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3. R: The set of photon indices p such that \|\mathbf{x}p - \mathbf{x}\| \le r. f(\thetap): Phase function value for the scattering angle \thetap. \Phip: Power of photon p. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def vectorlengthsq(v): """Returns the squared Euclidean length of vector v.""" return v.x v.x + v.y v.y + v.z v.z def phasefunction(costheta): """Evaluates the scattering phase function for a given cosine of the scattering angle. The exact formula depends on the chosen scattering model (e.g., Henyey-Greenstein).""" return 1.0 # Placeholder for model-specific evaluation def pointquerypointdata3dblur(querypoint, viewdirection, photonmap, radius, scatteringcoefficient): """ Estimates in-scattered radiance at querypoint using Point Query x Point Data, 3D Blur. Args: querypoint (Vector3): The position x where radiance is estimated. viewdirection (Vector3): The view direction omega. photonmap (List[Photon]): List of photon points. radius (float): The spherical kernel radius r. scatteringcoefficient (float): The scattering coefficient sigmas. Returns: float: Estimated in-scattered radiance. """ # 1. Compute volume measure of the spherical kernel volumemeasure = (4.0 / 3.0) math.pi (radius 3) # 2. Initialize summation accumulator totalweightedpower = 0.0 # 3. Search for photons within the spherical kernel for photon in photonmap: # Check if photon is within radius r of querypoint if vectorlengthsq(photon.position - querypoint) <= radius radius: # 4. Compute scattering angle cosine # Photon direction is the direction it traveled; incoming direction is opposite incomingdirection = (-photon.direction.x, -photon.direction.y, -photon.direction.z) # Normalize incoming direction invlenin = 1.0 / math.sqrt(vectorlengthsq(incomingdirection)) incomingdirection = (incomingdirection[0] invlenin, incomingdirection[1] invlenin, incomingdirection[2] invlenin) # Normalize view direction invlenv = 1.0 / math.sqrt(vectorlengthsq(viewdirection)) viewdirnorm = (viewdirection.x invlenv, viewdirection.y invlenv, viewdirection.z invlenv) # Dot product gives cos(thetap) costheta = incomingdirection[0] viewdirnorm[0] + \ incomingdirection[1] viewdirnorm[1] + \ incomingdirection[2] viewdirnorm[2] # Clamp to [-1, 1] to handle floating point errors costheta = max(-1.0, min(1.0, costheta)) # 5. Evaluate phase function and accumulate phasevalue = phasefunction(costheta) totalweightedpower += phasevalue photon.power # 6. Normalize by sigmas and volume measure if scatteringcoefficient == 0 or volumemeasure == 0: return 0.0 radiance = totalweightedpower / (scatteringcoefficient volumemeasure) return radiance Parameters r: The radius of the spherical kernel. \sigmas: The scattering coefficient of the medium. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Empty Kernel: If no photons fall within the radius r, the summation evaluates to zero. Division by Zero: The estimate is undefined if \sigmas = 0 or r = 0. Adaptive Kernels: The notation assumes spatially constant query regions for simplicity, though spatially adaptive blurring kernels are possible. Computes accumulated in-scattered radiance along an eye ray by querying photon beams and blurring their energy in two dimensions perpendicular to the beam direction. It differs from this method by using continuous beam data instead of discrete point data and restricting the spatial blur to a 2D cross-section, thereby reducing bias for the same radius. Choose it when high accuracy in anisotropic scattering is required and computational cost allows for beam-based structures. Computes in-scattered radiance at a point using photon beams with a 3D blur. It differs from this method by treating discrete beams as limits of continuous beams and integrating transmittance along the beam within the kernel. Choose it when photon beams are available and a 3D blur is desired for the query point. Computes accumulated in-scattered radiance along a camera ray by querying photon points with a 3D blur. It differs from this method by evaluating transmittance from the photon point towards the eye and integrating it around the photon point, rather than from the query point to the beam start. Choose it when estimating beam radiance for volume rendering along eye rays. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced by Jensen and Christensen in 1998 as the standard volumetric radiance estimate for photon mapping in participating media. It is based on the principle of density estimation, where radiance is approximated by the average power of photons within a local volume. It serves as a fundamental component of volumetric photon mapping algorithms. name: Beam Query × Beam Data, 2D Blur
head: Integral of Continuous Photon Beams, Direct integration of 2D blurred in-scattered radiance
body: Beam Query × Beam Data, 2D Blur is a radiance estimation technique for participating media that computes the accumulated in-scattered radiance along an eye ray by querying photon beams and blurring their energy in two dimensions perpendicular to the beam direction. It solves the problem of estimating light transport in participating media without the bias introduced by blurring along the beam's length, which is inherent in the 3D blur variant. It differs from its parent, Point Query × Point Data, 3D Blur, by using continuous beam data instead of discrete point data and restricting the spatial blur to a 2D cross-section, thereby reducing bias for the same radius. It differs from the Beam × Beam 1D estimate by performing a 2D spatial blur rather than a 1D line blur, making it more general for volumetric scenes where the beam direction varies significantly relative to the view. The method estimates the beam radiance integral by substituting the 2D blurred in-scattered radiance estimate into the radiance transport equation and integrating along the camera ray. Inputs: Photon beams b, each defined by origin \mathbf{x}b^, direction \tilde{\omega}b, total flux \Phib, and scattering coefficient \sigmas of the medium. Camera ray defined by origin \mathbf{x}c, direction \tilde{\omega}c, and integration limit s. Phase function f(\thetab), where \thetab is the angle between \tilde{\omega}c and \tilde{\omega}b. Extinction coefficient \sigmat (assumed constant for the analytical simplification). Cross-sectional area measure \muR(r^2) of the photon beam's blur kernel. Outputs: Estimated radiance Lb(\mathbf{x}c \leftarrow \vec{\omega}c, s) along the camera ray. Data Structures: Photon beams are stored as a list or spatially accelerated structure (e.g., BVH, grid) allowing retrieval of all beams b \in Rb that intersect the camera ray's 2D blur region. Each beam b stores: \mathbf{x}b^, \tilde{\omega}b, \Phib. Steps: 1. Beam Selection: Identify all photon beams b whose 2D cylindrical blur regions intersect the camera ray segment [0, s]. Let this set be Rb. 2. Intersection Bounds: For each beam b \in Rb, calculate the intersection distances tc^- and tc^+ where the camera ray enters and exits the beam's 2D blur region. 3. Integral Calculation: For each beam b, compute the integral of the product of the camera ray transmittance and the photon beam transmittance over the interval [tc^-, tc^+]. The transmittance along the camera ray is e^{-\sigmat tc}. The transmittance along the photon beam depends on the position tc. For constant cross-section beams in homogeneous media, the distance along the photon beam tb is related to tc by: tb = tb^- - |tc - tc^-| |\cos \thetab| where tb^- is the scalar projection of the camera ray start point onto the beam, and \cos \thetab = \tilde{\omega}c \cdot \tilde{\omega}b. The integral is: Ib = \int{tc^-}^{tc^+} e^{-\sigmat tc} e^{-\sigmat tb} dtc 4. Summation: Sum the contributions from all beams and multiply by the scattering coefficient and phase function: Lb(\mathbf{x}c \leftarrow \vec{\omega}c, s) \approx \frac{\sigmas}{\muR(r^2)} \sum{b \in Rb} f(\thetab) \Phib Ib Formulas: The general estimate is: Lb(\mathbf{x}c \leftarrow \vec{\omega}c, s) \approx \frac{\sigmas}{\muR(r^2)} \sum{b \in Rb} f(\thetab) \Phib \int{tc^-}^{tc^+} e^{-\sigma{tc}} e^{-\sigma{tb}} dtc \quad For homogeneous media with constant cross-section beams, the integral Ib simplifies to: Ib = \frac{e^{-\sigmat (tc - tc^+)} (|\cos \thetab| - 1) - 1}{e^{\sigmat (tc + tb^-)} \sigmat (|\cos \thetab| - 1)} \quad Parameters: \sigmas: Scattering coefficient. Typical value: Scene-dependent. \sigmat: Extinction coefficient. Typical value: Scene-dependent. \muR(r^2): 2D area measure of the beam cross-section. For a circular kernel of radius r, \muR(r^2) = \pi r^2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Heterogeneous Media: The analytical simplification of the integral is not available. Varying Cross-Section: If the beam cross-section varies (e.g., conical beams), \muR(r^2) becomes a function of tb and must be moved inside the integral, complicating the calculation. Parallel Beams: If \cos \thetab = 1 (camera ray parallel to beam), the denominator in the simplified integral becomes zero. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def beamquerybeamdata2dblur(cameraorigin, cameradir, raylength, photonbeams, sigmas, sigmat, r): """ Estimates radiance along a camera ray using 2D blurred photon beams. cameraorigin: (x, y, z) cameradir: (x, y, z), normalized raylength: float s photonbeams: list of dicts with keys 'origin', 'dir', 'flux' sigmas: scattering coefficient sigmat: extinction coefficient r: radius of 2D blur kernel """ muR = math.pi r r totalradiance = 0.0 for beam in photonbeams: # 1. Beam Selection and Intersection Bounds tcminus, tcplus = computecylinderintersection(cameraorigin, cameradir, raylength, beam['origin'], beam['dir'], r) if tcminus is None: continue # 2. Integral Calculation costhetab = dot(cameradir, beam['dir']) abscosthetab = abs(costhetab) denomterm = abscosthetab - 1.0 if abs(denomterm) < 1e-6: # Parallel case: denominator becomes zero, use numerical integration or limit evaluation integralval = numericaltransmittanceintegral(cameraorigin, cameradir, tcminus, tcplus, beam, sigmat) else: # Compute tbminus: scalar projection of camera ray start point onto beam campointattcm = (cameraorigin[0] + cameradir[0] tcminus, cameraorigin[1] + cameradir[1] tcminus, cameraorigin[2] + cameradir[2] tcminus) vectocam = (campointattcm[0] - beam['origin'][0], campointattcm[1] - beam['origin'][1], campointattcm[2] - beam['origin'][2]) tbminus = dot(vectocam, beam['dir']) # Source formula (Eq 30) num = math.exp(-sigmat (tcminus - tcplus)) denomterm - 1.0 den = math.exp(sigmat (tcminus + tbminus)) sigmat denomterm integralval = num / den if abs(den) > 1e-10 else 0.0 # 3. Summation phase = evaluatephasefunction(costhetab) contribution = (sigmas / muR) phase beam['flux'] integralval totalradiance += contribution return totalradiance def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def evaluatephasefunction(costheta): # Standard phase function evaluation for participating media return 0.25 def computecylinderintersection(p0, d, s, c0, n, r): # Computes intersection of ray p(t) = p0 + td with infinite cylinder of radius r around axis c0 + un # Returns (tmin, tmax) clamped to [0, s], or None if no intersection # Standard geometric derivation solves ||p(t) - c(u)||^2 = r^2 for t # This reduces to a quadratic At^2 + Bt + C = 0 # Implementation follows standard ray-cylinder intersection algorithms return None # Placeholder for standard geometric solver def numericaltransmittanceintegral(p0, d, tstart, tend, beam, sigmat): # Numerical integration of transmittance product for parallel beams or heterogeneous media # Uses standard quadrature (e.g., Simpson's rule) over [tstart, tend] # Implementation follows standard numerical integration techniques return 0.0 # Placeholder for standard numerical integration The Beam × Beam 1D estimate is a radiance estimation technique for participating media that combines a camera subpath with a light subpath by finding nearby endpoints of light subpaths and merging them, resulting in one less vertex than the sum of vertices of the subpaths. It avoids the expensive 3D convolution required by the 3D variant and the ray marching associated with point-based methods, offering better image quality than photon points while being computationally simpler to implement. It is a specific case of Photon Density Estimation (PDE) where both the light and camera data are represented as beams, and the spatial blur is performed over a line (1D). A beam radiance estimate that directly computes the beam radiance integral along a camera ray by substituting the in-scattered radiance estimate (Equation 21) into the beam radiance integral (Equation 8), resulting in a double integral. It is fairly complicated due to the integral of a 3D convolution and is impractical for heterogeneous media, included mainly for completeness. It is used when a full 3D blur is required for theoretical completeness or specific homogeneous scenarios where analytical bounds can be derived. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of photon beams Nb that intersect the camera ray's blur region, assuming efficient spatial querying. The integral evaluation is O(1) per beam for homogeneous media. Memory Complexity: Linear in the number of photon beams stored. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the density of photon beams and the complexity of the scene's extinction coefficient. Strengths: Simpler evaluation than 3D blur (no integration along beam length) and less bias for the same radius because no blurring is performed along the beam. It is a limit case of anisotropic density estimation. Limitations: Impractical for heterogeneous media due to the complexity of the integral. Requires careful handling of parallel beams and varying cross-sections. When to use: Homogeneous media where bias reduction along the beam direction is important and computational resources allow for beam-based querying. When not to use: Heterogeneous media, or when extreme computational efficiency is required (consider 1D variant or point-based methods). The method was introduced in "A comprehensive theory of volumetric radiance estimation using photon points and beams". It is derived by taking the limit of discrete photon marching while shrinking the cylindrical kernel's height to the step size, reducing bias. It is related to surface radiance estimates developed by Herzog et al. [2007] and can be seen as a generalization of their photon ray splatting estimate to participating media.
