2 for k in range(maxk + 1): for s in range(len(lightsubpath)): t = k + 1 - s if t < 0 or t >= len(eyesubpath): continue yend = lightsubpath[s] zend = eyesubpath[t] # Check occlusion if not isvisible(yend, zend, scene): continue # Compute connection terms Tconn = computetransmittance(yend, zend, scene) Gconn = computegeometryfactor(yend, zend) # Compute full subpath PDFs and transmittances py = computesubpathpdf(lightsubpath[:s+1], scene) pz = computesubpathpdf(eyesubpath[:t+1], scene) Ty = computesubpathtransmittance(lightsubpath[:s+1], scene) Tz = computesubpathtransmittance(eyesubpath[:t+1], scene) # BPT estimator Le = emittedradiance(lightsubpath[0], scene) We = camerasensitivity(camera) rhoy = scatteringfunction(yend, scene) rhoz = scatteringfunction(zend, scene) radiance = (Le (Ty / py) rhoy Tconn Gconn rhoz (Tz / pz) We) # Balance heuristic weight weight = py / (py + pz) totalradiance += radiance weight return totalradiance def samplelightposition(rng): return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def samplelightdirection(pos, rng): return (0.0, 1.0, 0.0) def sampledistance(pos, dir, scene, rng): return 1.0 def isinmedium(pos, scene): return True def schlickphasefunction(dir, rng): return 0.5 def scatterdirection(dir, phase, rng): return dir def scatteringprobability(scene, pos): return 0.5 def samplecameradirection(camera, rng): return (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) def isvisible(p1, p2, scene): return True def computetransmittance(p1, p2, scene): return 1.0 def computegeometryfactor(p1, p2): return 1.0 def computesubpathpdf(path, scene): return 1.0 def computesubpathtransmittance(path, scene): return 1.0 def emittedradiance(pos, scene): return 1.0 def camerasensitivity(camera): return 1.0 def scatteringfunction(pos, scene): return 1.0 Bidirectional Path-Space Differentiable Rendering computes gradients of a rendering equation with respect to scene parameters by constructing a differentiable path space using both light and eye subpaths. It sets itself apart from unidirectional differentiable methods by leveraging the bidirectional structure of Bidirectional Path Tracing to reduce variance in gradient estimation for complex light transport, specifically addressing the discontinuities inherent in path-space derivatives [7618-bidirectional-path-space-differentiable-rendering.md]. A data layout for storing the primary sample vector \bar{u} in Bidirectional Path Tracing (BDPT) to ensure that small changes in the sample space U correspond to small changes in the path space P. It solves the problem of sample correlation in heterogeneous participating media by separating random numbers for eye/light subpaths and between scattering/propagation steps, unlike standard BDPT which uses successive dimensions of U directly. UPBP Recursive Weight Calculation is a method for efficiently computing Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) weights in Bidirectional Path Tracing (BPT) and Photon Density Estimation (PDE) estimators within participating media. It solves the problem of expensive path weight re-evaluation by caching partial sums that remain constant as subpaths are extended, avoiding the storage of full path weights. Unlike methods that store full path weights, UPBP stores only the recursive d-quantities, which are updated incrementally as the subpath is traced [10612-unified-path-based-photon-path-upbp-recursive-weight-calcula.md]. An adaptation of BDPT for participating media where propagation densities pi are approximated because they are not analytically computable in heterogeneous media. To preserve the good properties of the heuristics without introducing bias, \tau is approximated by a deterministic quadrature rule, ensuring weights produced by the power heuristic sum up to one. The multi-sample estimator is: F = \sum{i=1}^n \frac{1}{ni} \sum{j=1}^{ni} w{ij}(x{i,j}) \frac{f(x)}{pi(x{i,j})} The power heuristic uses an exponent \beta, where \beta=1 is the balance heuristic and \beta \to \infty is the maximum heuristic. A pitfall is that using Algorithm 2 to approximate \tau for density estimation in MIS fails condition (17) (weights summing to 1 in expectation) for all but the maximum heuristic. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of subpath vertices and the number of connections attempted. A k-length path yields k+2 sampling techniques. Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage of subpath vertices. Since subpaths are traced independently, memory usage is linear with respect to subpath length. Measured Performance: In short times, BPT provides a usable, view-dependent approximation, unlike light tracing which produces partial solutions that are not useful. It improves convergence rate for light transport with refractive boundaries. Strengths: Unbiased for anisotropic media. View-dependent, allowing for progressive refinement. Combines light shooting and light gathering. Limitations: High variance due to vertex-vertex connections (infinite variance in some cases). When to use: Scenes with refractive boundaries, anisotropic media, or where view-dependent progressive rendering is required. When not to use: Scenes where unidirectional methods are sufficient and computational resources are limited, or where the infinite variance of vertex connections is a critical issue. Bidirectional Path Tracing was introduced by Lafortune and Willems to improve convergence rates for light transport with refractive boundaries. It expands on the ideas of path tracing to a bidirectional approach, combining light shooting (random walks from light sources) and light gathering (random walks from the eye point). It is an image-based method. The method uses the balance heuristic to combine illumination contributions from different subpath connections. It is cited as the only existing unbiased method for anisotropic media in the context of the surveyed techniques. name: Bidirectional Path-Space Differentiable Rendering
head: I.1 (unidirectional variant), I.2 (bidirectional variant), Our deriv
body: Bidirectional Path-Space Differentiable Rendering computes gradients of a rendering equation with respect to scene parameters by constructing a differentiable path space using both light and eye subpaths. It sets itself apart from unidirectional differentiable methods by leveraging the bidirectional structure of Bidirectional Path Tracing to reduce variance in gradient estimation for complex light transport, specifically addressing the discontinuities inherent in path-space derivatives. The method relies on a discretized representation of the joint probability density function (PDF) of the connection segment in path space. Let \mathbf{x}B be the position and \boldsymbol{\omega}B be the direction of the connection segment between the light subpath endpoint and the eye subpath endpoint. The joint PDF P(\mathbf{x}B, \boldsymbol{\omega}B) is discretized as a regular 3D grid precomputed before rendering. The preprocessing step involves generating two maps: 1. A photon map: Generated by tracing photons carrying radiance information from the light source. 2. An importon map: Generated by tracing importons carrying importance information from the detector. For each cell Ci in the grid, the integral of the product of the path contribution FB(\mathbf{x}B, \boldsymbol{\omega}B) and the PDF is computed by uniformly sampling \mathbf{x}B and \boldsymbol{\omega}B within the cell: Pi = \int{Ci} FB(\mathbf{x}B, \boldsymbol{\omega}B) \, d\boldsymbol{\omega}B \, d\mathbf{x}B This provides a piecewise constant representation of the path-space density. The gradient computation utilizes this precomputed structure to handle the non-differentiable connections in path tracing by smoothing or approximating the derivative within the discretized cells. A variant that computes gradients using only the light subpath or eye subpath structure, effectively reducing the bidirectional complexity to a unidirectional path tracing framework while maintaining the path-space differentiation technique. It is chosen when computational resources for bidirectional sampling are limited or when the scene geometry favors one direction of light transport. Validation shows derivatives estimated with this method closely match finite-difference approaches for parameters like rotation angles. The full bidirectional implementation that utilizes both the photon map and importon map to compute gradients across the complete bidirectional path. It is chosen for scenes with complex multiple scattering or when high-fidelity gradient estimation is required for both light and camera parameters. It builds on the shared principles of grid-based path-space discretization. The method originates from research on path-space differentiable rendering, specifically aiming to extend differentiable rendering techniques to bidirectional path tracing scenarios. The approach was introduced in the paper "Path-Space Differentiable Rendering". The technique addresses the challenge of computing gradients in path tracing where the connectivity between subpaths is non-differentiable. By discretizing the path space using photon and importon maps, it provides a robust way to estimate derivatives for optimization tasks in computer graphics. name: Primary Sample Space Transformation Layout
head: Array of Arrays for Primary Samples, BDPT Primary Sample Layout
body: A data layout for storing the primary sample vector \bar{u} in Bidirectional Path Tracing (BDPT) to ensure that small changes in the sample space U correspond to small changes in the path space P. It solves the problem of sample correlation in heterogeneous participating media by separating random numbers for eye/light subpaths and between scattering/propagation steps, unlike standard BDPT which uses successive dimensions of U directly. Inputs: The primary sample vector \bar{u}. Outputs: A structured array-of-arrays layout mapping indices to specific sampling operations within the BDPT algorithm. Data Structure: The primary sample \bar{u} is stored as an array of arrays. The i-th row vector provides input to the sampling done at the |i|-th vertex of the respective subpath. Elements within each row are accessed in sequential order. Indices are assigned as follows: positive indices (i > 0) for eye subpath vertices, negative indices (i < 0) for light subpath vertices, and index 0 for transmittance estimation. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize the primary sample structure as an empty array of arrays. 2. For each vertex generation step in the BDPT algorithm, determine the vertex index i based on the subpath type (positive for eye, negative for light) and the vertex order. 3. Retrieve the row vector corresponding to index i. 4. Consume random values from the row vector sequentially for the specific sampling operation (e.g., distance or direction sampling). 5. If the row is exhausted, append new random values to the row. 6. For transmittance estimation between deterministic connections, use the row vector at index 0 and consume random values sequentially. Formulas: Let P be the path space and U be the primary sample space. The transformation s: U \rightarrow P must satisfy \|\Delta U\| \text{ small} \implies \|\Delta P\| \text{ small}. This is achieved by ensuring that random numbers driving distinct parts of path generation are separated. Parameters: Index mapping: positive for eye, negative for light, 0 for transmittance. Access pattern: sequential within each row. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Heterogeneous Media: The amount of random input needed for distance sampling in heterogeneous media cannot be determined in advance. Each deterministic connection between subpaths requires an additional unknown amount of random values for transmittance estimation. The array-of-arrays layout handles this by allowing variable-length rows. Transmittance Smoothness: Large variations in random values driving transmittance estimation have little effect on the result because transmittance is fairly smooth in realistic settings. Therefore, further separation within the transmittance row (index 0) is not necessary. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class PrimarySampleSpaceLayout: def init(self): # Array of arrays to store primary samples # Index 0: Transmittance # Index > 0: Eye subpath vertices # Index < 0: Light subpath vertices self.samples = {} def getsample(self, index, count): """ Retrieve 'count' random values for the given index. Consumes values sequentially from the row. """ if index not in self.samples: self.samples[index] = [] row = self.samples[index] if len(row) < count: # PRNG generation not specified in sources newvalues = [0.0] (count - len(row)) row.extend(newvalues) # Consume values sequentially values = row[:count] del row[:count] return values def sampleeyevertex(self, vertexindex, count): """Sample a vertex on the eye subpath.""" return self.getsample(vertexindex, count) def samplelightvertex(self, vertexindex, count): """Sample a vertex on the light subpath.""" # Use negative index for light subpath return self.getsample(-vertexindex, count) def sampletransmittance(self, count): """Sample transmittance between subpath connections.""" return self.getsample(0, count) A method that constructs two independent subpaths and connects their endpoints deterministically. This layout is a specific data organization technique for BDPT's primary samples that ensures path space smoothness. Choose it when using BDPT in participating media to maintain sample continuity. A sibling method that extends BDPT to differentiable rendering. The primary sample space transformation layout may be relevant for ensuring smooth gradients in differentiable contexts, though specific details are not provided in the sources. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Ensures small changes in U cause small changes in P, which is crucial for robustness in participating media. Handles variable-length random number requirements for heterogeneous media. Limitations: Requires managing variable-length arrays. Not given in the sources for specific performance trade-offs compared to other layouts. When to use: When using BDPT in scenes with participating media, especially heterogeneous media, to ensure sample space smoothness. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Originated in the paper "Unbiased Global Illumination with Participating Media". The method was developed to address the limitations of standard BDPT in participating media, where the fixed mapping of random numbers to path vertices fails to ensure smoothness in path space due to the variable nature of distance sampling in heterogeneous media. name: Unified Path-based Photon Path (UPBP) Recursive Weight Calculation
head: Recursive d-quantities, UPBP Recursive MIS Weight Computation, UPBP Recursive Weight Calculation, Unified Path-Based Path Tracing recursive weight
body: UPBP Recursive Weight Calculation is a recursive algorithm for computing the Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) weight w{v,s,t} for a light path formed by connecting a light subpath with s vertices and a camera subpath with t vertices using technique v. It solves the problem of efficiently computing path weights by caching partial sums that remain constant as subpaths are extended, avoiding the storage of full path weights. Unlike methods that store full path weights, UPBP stores only the recursive d-quantities, which are updated incrementally as the subpath is traced. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Light subpath vertices \bar{\mathbf{y}} with s vertices, camera subpath vertices \bar{\mathbf{z}} with t vertices, technique v (BPT or PDE), and estimator-specific parameters. Output: MIS weight w{v,s,t} for the light path formed by connecting the subpaths. Data Structures: For each vertex i in a subpath, store three scalar quantities: di^{\text{shared}}: Shared recursive quantity. di^{\text{BPT}}: BPT-specific recursive quantity. di^{\text{PDE}}: PDE-specific recursive quantity. Definitions: pi^{\rightarrow}: PDF of vertex i in the forward direction (light or camera subpath generation). gi^{\leftarrow}: Geometric term for the connection from vertex i to the previous vertex in the reverse direction. fi: Phase function or scattering term at vertex i. p{\tau,i-2}^{\leftarrow}: Transition probability term for vertex i-2 in reverse direction. p{\omega,i-2}^{\leftarrow}: Solid angle term for vertex i-2 in reverse direction. n{\text{BPT}}: Number of light paths used in the BPT estimator normalization. nv: Estimator-specific term for technique v. e{v,s}: Estimator-specific term for technique v on a light subpath with s vertices. e{v,t}: Estimator-specific term for technique v on a camera subpath with t vertices. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization (i=1): Compute initial values for the first stored vertex (i=1): d1^{\text{shared}} = 1/p1^{\rightarrow} d1^{\text{BPT}} = g0^{\leftarrow}/(p0^{\rightarrow} p1^{\rightarrow}) d1^{\text{PDE}} = (g0^{\leftarrow} n{\text{BPT}})/(p0^{\rightarrow} p1^{\rightarrow}) Store these values. Note that the first vertices \mathbf{y}0 and \mathbf{z}0 are not stored. 2. Recursive Update (i > 1): For each subsequent vertex i, update the quantities using the previous vertex's values (i-1): di^{\text{shared}} = 1/pi^{\rightarrow} di^{\text{BPT}} = \frac{g{i-1}^{\leftarrow}}{pi^{\rightarrow}} \left( \frac{fi}{n{\text{BPT}}} + d{i-1}^{\text{shared}} + p{\tau,i-2}^{\leftarrow} p{\omega,i-2}^{\leftarrow} d{i-1}^{\text{BPT}} \right) di^{\text{PDE}} = \frac{g{i-1}^{\leftarrow}}{pi^{\rightarrow}} \left( fi + n{\text{BPT}} d{i-1}^{\text{shared}} + p{\tau,i-2}^{\leftarrow} p{\omega,i-2}^{\leftarrow} d{i-1}^{\text{PDE}} \right) Store these values for vertex i. 3. Weight Construction: When connecting a light subpath with s vertices and a camera subpath with t vertices, compute the partial weights using the stored d-quantities at vertices s-1 and t-1: For BPT: \bar{w}{v,s-1}(\bar{\mathbf{y}}) = p{s-1}^{\leftarrow} \left( \frac{fs}{n{\text{BPT}}} + d{s-1}^{\text{shared}} + p{\tau,s-2}^{\leftarrow} p{\omega,s-2}^{\leftarrow} d{s-1}^{\text{BPT}} \right) \bar{w}{v,t-1}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}) = p{t-1}^{\leftarrow} \left( \frac{ft}{n{\text{BPT}}} + d{t-1}^{\text{shared}} + p{\tau,t-2}^{\leftarrow} p{\omega,t-2}^{\leftarrow} d{t-1}^{\text{BPT}} \right) For PDE: \bar{w}{v,s-1}(\bar{\mathbf{y}}) = \frac{1}{nv e{v,s}} (n{\text{BPT}} d{s-1}^{\text{shared}} + p{\tau,s-2}^{\leftarrow} p{\omega,s-2}^{\leftarrow} d{s-1}^{\text{PDE}}) \bar{w}{v,t-1}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}) = \frac{1}{nv e{v,t}} (n{\text{BPT}} d{t-1}^{\text{shared}} + p{\tau,t-2}^{\leftarrow} p{\omega,t-2}^{\leftarrow} d{t-1}^{\text{PDE}}) These equations hold for s > 1 and t > 1. 4. Final MIS Weight: Compute the total weight as: w{v,s,t} = 1/(w{v,s}^{\text{light}} + w{v,s}^{\text{local}} + w{v,s}^{\text{camera}}) where w{v,s}^{\text{light}} depends only on light subpath vertices, w{v,s}^{\text{local}} depends on local connection/merge information, and w{v,s}^{\text{camera}} depends only on camera subpath vertices. For BPT, w{v,s}^{\text{local}} = 1. For PDE, w{v,s}^{\text{local}} is given by specific estimator formulas. Parameters: n{\text{BPT}}: Number of light paths used in the BPT estimator normalization. nv: Estimator-specific term for technique v. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: First Vertices: The first vertices \mathbf{y}0 and \mathbf{z}0 are not stored. Equations (43)-(46) only hold for s > 1 and t > 1. Special handling is required for s \leq 1 or t \leq 1. PDF Zero Conditions: BPT PDF must be zero when \mathbf{y}{s-1} or \mathbf{z}{t-1} is on a specular surface. B-B1D, P-B2D, and P-P3D PDFs must be zero when \mathbf{y}{s-1} or \mathbf{z}{t-1} are not in media. P-P2D PDF must be zero when \mathbf{y}{s-1} or \mathbf{z}{t-1} are in media or on a specular surface. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializedquantities(p0forward, p1forward, g0reverse, nBPT): dshared = 1.0 / p1forward dbpt = g0reverse / (p0forward p1forward) dpde = (g0reverse nBPT) / (p0forward p1forward) return dshared, dbpt, dpde def updatedquantities(piforward, gprevreverse, fi, ptauprev2reverse, pomegaprev2reverse, dsharedprev, dbptprev, dpdeprev, nBPT): dshared = 1.0 / piforward dbpt = (gprevreverse / piforward) ( (fi / nBPT) + dsharedprev + (ptauprev2reverse pomegaprev2reverse dbptprev)) dpde = (gprevreverse / piforward) ( fi + (nBPT dsharedprev) + (ptauprev2reverse pomegaprev2reverse dpdeprev)) return dshared, dbpt, dpde def computebptweights(psminus1reverse, ptminus1reverse, fs, ft, dsharedsminus1, dbptsminus1, dsharedtminus1, dbpttminus1, ptausminus2reverse, pomegasminus2reverse, ptautminus2reverse, pomegatminus2reverse, nBPT): wlight = psminus1reverse ( (fs / nBPT) + dsharedsminus1 + (ptausminus2reverse pomegasminus2reverse dbptsminus1)) wcamera = ptminus1reverse ( (ft / nBPT) + dsharedtminus1 + (ptautminus2reverse pomegatminus2reverse dbpttminus1)) return wlight, wcamera def computepdeweights(nv, evs, evt, dsharedsminus1, dpdesminus1, dsharedtminus1, dpdetminus1, ptausminus2reverse, pomegasminus2reverse, ptautminus2reverse, pomegatminus2reverse, nBPT): wlight = (1.0 / (nv evs)) ( (nBPT dsharedsminus1) + (ptausminus2reverse pomegasminus2reverse dpdesminus1)) wcamera = (1.0 / (nv evt)) ( (nBPT dsharedtminus1) + (ptautminus2reverse pomegatminus2reverse dpdetminus1)) return wlight, wcamera def computemisweight(wlight, wlocal, wcamera): return 1.0 / (wlight + wlocal + wcamera) The recursive update performs O(1) work per vertex, yielding linear time complexity relative to the number of subpath vertices. Memory usage is constant per vertex, storing only three scalar quantities instead of full path weights. The method efficiently computes MIS weights for BPT and PDE estimators in participating media by caching partial sums. It requires careful handling of edge cases for short subpaths (s \leq 1 or t \leq 1) and enforces specific PDF zero conditions for different estimators. UPBP Recursive Weight Calculation was introduced in the paper "Efficient Hardware Acceleration of Robust Volumetric Light Transport Simulation". It is part of the Unified Path-based Photon Path (UPBP) framework, which aims to efficiently simulate light transport in participating media using hardware-accelerated ray tracing. The method builds on Bidirectional Path Tracing by providing an efficient way to compute MIS weights for various connection techniques in media. name: Unidirectional Importance Sampling for Double-Scattering
head: Analytic unidirectional PDF sampling, Joint importance sampling of low-order volumetric scattering (unidirectional)
body: A fully analytic method to importance sample the geometry terms along 3-segment paths (double-scattering) in isotropic participating media. It constructs a joint probability density function (PDF) for the intermediate scattering vertices that cancels out the singularities inherent in the path contribution function, thereby reducing variance compared to standard uniform or single-scattering sampling strategies. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Two fixed endpoints \mathbf{a} and \mathbf{c} (defining the first and third vertices of the path), and a ray origin \mathbf{d} with direction \boldsymbol{\omega}{dc} (defining the fourth vertex's location). The medium is assumed to be isotropic. Outputs: The intermediate vertex \mathbf{b} and the distance t{dc} along the ray from \mathbf{d}. Data Structures No specific complex data structures are required beyond standard vector arithmetic. The method relies on geometric primitives: Points \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Directions \boldsymbol{\omega} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (unit vectors). Distances t \in \mathbb{R}. Random numbers \xi, \xi1, \xi2 \in 0, 1). Numbered Steps 1. Define Local Frame: Establish a local coordinate system where the direction from \mathbf{c} to \mathbf{a} is the z-axis. Let \boldsymbol{\omega}{ca} = \frac{\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{c}}{\|\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{c}\|}. 2. Sample Direction \boldsymbol{\omega}{cb}: Generate two uniform random numbers \xi1, \xi2 \in [0, 1). Then: t{dc} = t{da}^{\perp} + h{da}^{\perp} \sinh\left( \xi \Delta + \text{arsinh}\left(\frac{-t{da}^{\perp}}{h{da}^{\perp}}\right) \right) where \Delta = \text{arsinh}\left(\frac{t{dc}^{\max} - t{da}^{\perp}}{h{da}^{\perp}}\right) - \text{arsinh}\left(\frac{-t{da}^{\perp}}{h{da}^{\perp}}\right). 5. Formulas Direction Sampling: \theta{cb} = \pi(1 - \sqrt{\xi1}) \phi{cb} = 2\pi\xi2 Distance t{cb} Sampling (Equiangular): t{cb} = t{ca}^{\perp} + h{ca}^{\perp} \tan\left(\xi(\pi - \theta{cb}) + \theta{cb} - \frac{\pi}{2}\right) Distance t{dc} PDF: p(t{dc} | \Xi) = \frac{1}{C{t{dc}}^{\max}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{h{da}^2 + (t{da} - t{dc})^2}} Normalization Constant C{\Xi} (for t{dc}): C{\Xi} = \frac{1}{C{t{dc}}^{\max}} = \frac{1}{\text{arsinh}\left(\frac{t{dc}^{\max} - t{da}^{\perp}}{h{da}^{\perp}}\right) - \text{arsinh}\left(\frac{-t{da}^{\perp}}{h{da}^{\perp}}\right)} Joint PDF: p(\mathbf{b}, t{dc} | \Xi) = \frac{G(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}) G(\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c})}{\pi^3 C{t{dc}}^{\max}} The constant C{t{dc}}^{\max} incorporates the product of the three [isotropic phase functions (4\pi)^{-3}. Parameters t{dc}^{\max}: Maximum sampling distance along the ray (\mathbf{d}, \boldsymbol{\omega}{dc}). This is required because the integral of the PDF diverges at infinity. This singularity is present in the path contribution function as well. By sampling from this specific PDF, the singularity is cancelled out, reducing variance. Divergence at Infinity: The integral for the normalization constant C{\Xi} diverges at infinity. A maximum sampling distance t{dc}^{\max} must be set to obtain an analytical expression. name: Tabulated Importance Sampling for Anisotropic Scattering
head: Adaptive tabulation of geometry and phase functions, Tabulated unidirectional/bidirectional factorization
body: A method to efficiently tabulate target probability density functions (PDFs) for unidirectional and bidirectional factorizations to handle anisotropic scattering in participating media. It solves the problem of analytically unavailable conditional PDFs for double-scattering paths by precomputing accurate approximations in a compact 2D table, avoiding the limited accuracy and overhead of on-the-fly tabulation. Unlike Unidirectional Importance Sampling for Double-Scattering which relies on analytic formulations for isotropic media, this method supports general anisotropic phase functions by exploiting symmetries to reduce dimensionality. Inputs: Ray origin c and direction \omega{cb}. Previous vertex a and incoming direction \omega{dc} (encoded in \Xi). Phase function \rho(\cdot), assumed to be circularly-symmetric 1D (depending only on deflection angle); isotropic scattering is the special case \rho = 1/4\pi. Outputs: Sampled scattering distance t{cb} and direction \omega{cb} (for unidirectional factorization). Corresponding PDF values for importance sampling. Data Structures: 2D Lookup Table: Indexed by canonical spherical coordinates (\theta{la}, \phi{la}) of the direction vector \omega{la}. Table Entries: Each entry is a piecewise-linear approximation of a 1D PDF over \theta \in [0, \pi]. Table Construction (Unidirectional Factorization): 1. Canonical Coordinate System: For a given ray (c, \omega{cb}) and vertex a: rescale the problem such that the distance between the line defined by (c, \omega{cb}) and vertex a is one; place the origin at a; align the z-axis with the ray direction \omega{cb}; align the x-axis in the plane containing a and the ray. 2. Indexing: The table is indexed by the direction vector \omega{la} (the direction from a to the scattering point b), represented by spherical coordinates (\theta{la}, \phi{la}) in the canonical system. 3. PDF Definition: The target PDF for the distance t{cb} is proportional to the product of geometry and scattering terms: p(t{cb} \mid \omega{cb}, t{dc}, \Xi) \propto G(a,b) \rho(a) \rho(b), where G(a,b) is the geometry term and \rho is the phase function. 4. Reparameterization: To handle sharp peaks or singularities in the geometry term, the infinite line is mapped to a finite angular domain using \theta = \text{arccot } u, where u is the signed distance from the projection of a onto the line. 5. Tabulated Function: Each entry stores a piecewise-linear approximation of p(\theta(u)) = p(u) \left| \frac{du}{d\theta} \right| = p(u) \frac{1}{G(a,b(u))} \propto \rho(a) \rho(b(u)). This transformation analytically eliminates geometric variations, improving tabulation accuracy. 6. Adaptive Refinement: The 1D PDF p(\theta) is approximated using adaptive refinement over \theta \in [0, \pi]. Sampling (Unidirectional Factorization): 1. Coordinate Setup: Construct the canonical coordinate system for the specific ray (c, \omega{cb}) and vertex a as described in construction. 2. Table Lookup: Index the 2D table using the canonical spherical coordinates of \omega{la}. 3. Angle Sampling: Draw an angle \thetab from the retrieved tabulated PDF, constrained to the interval \thetab \in [0, \text{arccot } uc], where uc is the canonical distance from the projection of a to the ray origin c. 4. Distance Conversion: Transform the sampled angle to a canonical distance: ub = \cot \thetab. Compute the scattering distance: t{cb} = -uc + ub. 5. PDF Transformation: Transform the PDF from the angular measure to the Euclidean length measure for the final importance sampling weight: p(ub) = p(\thetab) \left| \frac{d\thetab}{dub} \right| = p(\thetab) [G(a,b) h{ca^\perp}], where h{ca^\perp} is the distance between a and the ray. Pitfalls: Geometric Singularities: Geometric terms can have sharp peaks or singularities, which reduce tabulation accuracy; the reparameterization \theta = \text{arccot } u is critical to analytically eliminate these variations. Precision: The mapping from infinite line to finite angular domain requires careful handling of boundaries, particularly near \theta = 0 and \theta = \pi. Time Complexity: Precomputation is done once per configuration family; sampling is O(1) table lookup and inversion, significantly faster than on-the-fly tabulation. Memory Complexity: Compact 2D table of 1D PDFs; dimensionality is reduced by exploiting symmetries, storing only the necessary angular parameters. Accuracy: Achieves nearly ideal importance sampling of the product of geometry and scattering terms, outperforming on-the-fly methods. Strengths: Handles anisotropic scattering; avoids analytic formulation requirements; high accuracy with low sampling overhead. Limitations: Requires precomputation; assumes circularly-symmetric phase functions. Introduced in to tabulate target PDFs for anisotropic scattering without requiring analytic formulations, extending on-the-fly tabulation approaches. The method is part of a broader effort to efficiently sample double-scattering paths in participating media, building on Unidirectional Importance Sampling for Double-Scattering but generalizing to anisotropic cases. name: Walter's Method
head: Walter et al. Refraction Technique, Walter et al, direct algorithm
body: Walter's Method is a technique for computing refraction paths within triangle meshes to produce light shafts within complex refractive volumetric boundaries. It sets itself apart from siblings like Volumetric Radiance Estimators and Photon-based Methods by directly solving for valid refracted light paths without an intermediate lighting representation, thereby avoiding the blurring and approximation artifacts inherent in photon mapping. Unlike Light Beam Tracing, the solution is exact and does not suffer from blurring, allowing it to resolve fine details that standard photon mapping cannot. Inputs: Triangle mesh representing the refractive boundary surface. Light source definition. Volume medium definition (extinction, phase function). Camera ray parameters. Outputs: Radiance contribution at individual points in the volume along camera rays. Data Structures: Triangle mesh data structure supporting ray-triangle intersection tests. Surface normal data (shading normals \hat{\mathbf{N}}s and geometric normals \hat{\mathbf{N}}g). Method Steps: 1. Path Finding: For a given light source and a volume point V, solve for points P on the boundary triangle mesh such that light from the source refracts through P to reach V. 2. Normal Handling: Utilize a refractive half-vector \hat{\mathbf{H}} formulation to satisfy Snell's law relative to the shading normal \hat{\mathbf{N}}s, accommodating cases where \hat{\mathbf{N}}s differs from the geometric normal \hat{\mathbf{N}}g. 3. Point-wise Radiance: Compute the light contribution at the specific volume point V based on the found refracted path. 4. Ray Marching Integration: Perform numerical integration (ray marching) along the camera ray to accumulate the in-scattered radiance from all volume points. 5. Clamping: Apply clamping to the accumulated radiance values to avoid bright pixels and noise resulting from insufficient ray marching samples. Formulas: Transmittance along the path follows the standard Beer-Lambert law. Snell's law is enforced via the half-vector formulation \hat{\mathbf{H}} \parallel \hat{\mathbf{N}}s. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision and Boundaries: The method requires an expensive numerical solver for robustness. Degenerate Input: Restricted to a single specular bounce; it cannot handle multiple refractions or total internal reflection within the volume. Bias: Although theoretically unbiased, the method requires clamping in practice to avoid noise, which introduces unbounded bias due to loss of energy. Noise: Ray marching for accumulated in-scattered radiance results in visible noise if not enough samples are taken. This method finds points P on a boundary surface that refract light from a source L to a scatter point V, specifically handling cases where the shading normal \hat{\mathbf{N}}s differs from the geometric normal \hat{\mathbf{N}}g. It sets itself apart from standard Fermat’s principle approaches by using a refractive half-vector \hat{\mathbf{H}} to enforce Snell's law relative to the shading normal, allowing for accurate path finding on surfaces with interpolated normals or normal maps. Time Complexity: Performance is tied to the geometric complexity of the boundary mesh. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Rendered in 3 times as long as photon beams on one core, measured on an 8-core, 2.83 GHz machine with dual Intel Xeon 5440 chips. Strengths: Exact solution without blurring or approximation artifacts; resolves fine details not possible with standard photon mapping. Limitations: Requires an expensive numerical solver for robustness; restricted to a single specular bounce (cannot simulate volume caustics from multiple refractions or total internal reflection); requires ray marching leading to visible noise; requires clamping causing arbitrary energy loss; operates only on triangle meshes. When to use: When exact refracted light paths within complex triangle mesh boundaries are required and fine detail resolution is critical. When not: For scenes requiring multiple bounces, total internal reflection, or arbitrary surface representations (implicit/procedural); for performance-critical applications where noise and bias from clamping are unacceptable. Walter's Method was developed by Bruce Walter and colleagues in 2009. It was designed to compute refraction paths within triangle meshes, producing light shafts within complex refractive volumetric boundaries. The method was notably used to render the lighthouse scene [Jarosz et al. 2008] and underwater sun rays. It serves as a precursor to more advanced techniques like photon beams, which address its limitations regarding multiple bounces and noise. name: Half-vector formulation for refracted path finding
head: Half-vector based formulation
body: This method finds points P on a boundary surface that refract light from a source \mathbf{L} to a scatter point \mathbf{V}, specifically handling cases where the shading normal \hat{\mathbf{N}}s differs from the geometric normal \hat{\mathbf{N}}g. It sets itself apart from standard Fermat’s principle approaches by using a refractive half-vector \hat{\mathbf{H}} to enforce Snell's law relative to the shading normal, allowing for accurate path finding on surfaces with interpolated normals or normal maps. Inputs: Source position \mathbf{L} (3D vector). Scatter/view position \mathbf{V} (3D vector). Candidate point P on the boundary (3D vector). Shading normal at P, \hat{\mathbf{N}}s (unit 3D vector). Relative index of refraction \eta = \eta{in}/\eta{out} (scalar). Outputs: Boolean validity of P as a refraction point. The half-vector \hat{\mathbf{H}} used for validation. Data Structures: Vectors are stored as 3-component floating-point arrays or standard vector types. Normals are unit vectors. Steps: 1. Compute the direction vector from P to V: \hat{\omega}V = \frac{\mathbf{V} - \mathbf{P}}{\|\mathbf{V} - \mathbf{P}\|} The source text contains a typo in Equation (1) writing \mathbf{V} \cdot \mathbf{P}, but context and Equation (2) confirm subtraction is required for direction vectors. 2. Compute the direction vector from P to L: \hat{\omega}L = \frac{\mathbf{L} - \mathbf{P}}{\|\mathbf{L} - \mathbf{P}\|} 3. Compute the unnormalized half-vector sum: \mathbf{H}{\text{raw}} = \eta \hat{\omega}V + \hat{\omega}L. The source text uses \hat{\omega}{\text{A}} in Equation (3), which contextually refers to \hat{\omega}{\text{V}} (the internal direction). 4. Normalize to get the half-vector: \hat{\mathbf{H}} = \frac{\mathbf{H}{\text{raw}}}{\|\mathbf{H}{\text{raw}}\|} 5. Validate the point P. P is a valid solution if and only if both conditions are met: Normal Alignment: \hat{\mathbf{H}} = -\hat{\mathbf{N}}s. Side Constraints: (\mathbf{V} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{N}}s) \leq (\mathbf{P} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{N}}s) \leq (\mathbf{L} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{N}}s). The normal alignment ensures Snell's law is obeyed relative to the shading normal. The side constraints ensure that V and L lie on opposite sides of the local tangent plane defined by \hat{\mathbf{N}}s. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def halfvectorformulation(L, V, P, Ns, eta): """ L: Source position (vec3) V: Scatter/View position (vec3) P: Candidate point on boundary (vec3) Ns: Shading normal at P (vec3, unit length) eta: Relative index of refraction (float) Returns: (isvalid: bool, H: vec3) """ # Step 1: Direction from P to V dirV = V - P normV = length(dirV) if normV == 0: return False, vec3(0, 0, 0) omegaV = dirV / normV # Step 2: Direction from P to L dirL = L - P normL = length(dirL) if normL == 0: return False, vec3(0, 0, 0) omegaL = dirL / normL # Step 3 & 4: Compute normalized half-vector H Hraw = omegaV eta + omegaL normH = length(Hraw) if normH == 0: return False, vec3(0, 0, 0) H = Hraw / normH # Step 5: Validation # Condition 1: H must be anti-parallel to shading normal isaligned = abs(dot(H, -Ns) - 1.0) < 1e-6 # Condition 2: V and L must satisfy the side constraint inequality projV = dot(V, Ns) projP = dot(P, Ns) projL = dot(L, Ns) isbetween = (projV <= projP) and (projP <= projL) isvalid = isaligned and isbetween return isvalid, H Parameters: \eta: Relative index of refraction. Not given in the sources. Epsilon for floating point comparison: 10^{-6} is typical for normal alignment checks. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If P = V or P = L, the direction vectors are undefined and the method fails. Typo Correction: The source text contains typos in Equations (1) and (3) (\mathbf{V} \cdot \mathbf{P} and \hat{\omega}{\text{A}}). Implementers must use subtraction for direction vectors and substitute \hat{\omega}{\text{V}} for \hat{\omega}{\text{A}}. Normal Orientation: The side constraint (\mathbf{V} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{N}}s) \leq (\mathbf{P} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{N}}s) \leq (\mathbf{L} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{N}}s) assumes a specific orientation of \hat{\mathbf{N}}s. A geometric pruning test to determine if a position bounding box and normal bounding cone can satisfy refraction conditions. It uses 3D boxes for positions instead of 2D triangles. An iterative method to find the point P on a triangle boundary using the half-vector formulation. It uses a specific heuristic for the initial guess and clamping, applicable when shading normals are constant (Case 1). Computes single scattering by treating it as a deterministic search problem using interval Newton optimization to find all valid refraction points. Time Complexity: O(1) per candidate point P. Memory Complexity: O(1). Strengths: Handles varying shading normals (\hat{\mathbf{N}}g \neq \hat{\mathbf{N}}s) which Fermat's principle does not support directly. Limitations: Requires a candidate point P to validate and functions as a validation step rather than a search algorithm. When to use: When rendering refractive caustics in participating media with complex surface normals (normal maps, interpolated normals). The half-vector formulation was introduced by Walter et al. in 2007. It was developed to address the limitations of Fermat's principle in handling shading normals that differ from geometric normals, such as those found in triangles with interpolated normals or normal maps. This method is a core component of Walter's Method for accurate single scattering in refractive media. name: Sidedness Test
body: The Sidedness Test is a geometric pruning test used to determine if a position bounding box and a normal bounding cone can possibly satisfy the refraction conditions for a light transport path. It ensures that the view vector V lies on the negative side of the shading normal and within the critical angle cone defined by \arcsin(1/\eta). It differs from the smooth normal pruning test only in that positions are bounded by a 3D box rather than a 2D triangle; the test logic is otherwise identical. Inputs: Position bounding box B (axis-aligned, defined by min/max extents). Normal bounding cone C (defined by axis A and semi-angle \alpha). Light direction vector L (pointing from surface to light). View direction vector V (pointing from surface to viewer). Refraction index ratio \eta (relative to the medium). Outputs: Boolean: True if the box/cone pair might contain a valid refraction point; False if it can be safely pruned. Method: The test verifies three conditions for any potential point P in B with a shading normal N in C: L \cdot N > 0 (light on the positive side), V \cdot N < 0 (viewer on the negative side), and the angle between V and N is less than the critical angle \thetac = \arcsin(1/\eta). To perform this efficiently without sampling, the algorithm computes bounds on the angles between the cone axis A and the vectors L and V as seen from any point in the position bounding box. These bounds are offset by the semi-angle of the normal bounding cone to check if it is possible for the respective angles to lie within the required ranges. 1. Compute angular bounds for L: Calculate the angle between the cone axis A and the vector from each corner of B to L. The bounds are [\psi{L,\min}, \psi{L,\max}] clamped to [0, \pi]. 2. Compute angular bounds for V: Similarly, calculate the angle between A and the vector from each corner of B to V. The bounds are [\psi{V,\min}, \psi{V,\max}] clamped to [0, \pi]. 3. Offset by normal cone semi-angle: The actual shading normal N can deviate from the cone axis A by at most \alpha. Adjust the ranges: [\theta{L,\min}, \theta{L,\max}] = [\max(0, \psi{L,\min} - \alpha), \min(\pi, \psi{L,\max} + \alpha)] and [\theta{V,\min}, \theta{V,\max}] = [\max(0, \psi{V,\min} - \alpha), \min(\pi, \psi{V,\max} + \alpha)]. 4. Check validity ranges: Light Condition: The light is on the positive side if the angle is < \pi/2. The test passes if the minimum possible angle satisfies \theta{L,\min} < \pi/2. Viewer Condition: The viewer is on the negative side if the angle is > \pi/2. The test passes if the maximum possible angle satisfies \theta{V,\max} > \pi/2. Critical Angle Condition: The viewer must be within the critical angle cone. The test passes if the minimum possible angle satisfies \theta{V,\min} < \arcsin(1/\eta). 5. Result: Return True if all three checks pass. Otherwise, return False. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def normalize(v): invlen = 1.0 / math.sqrt(dot(v, v)) return (v[0]invlen, v[1]invlen, v[2]invlen) def anglebetween(a, b): costheta = max(-1.0, min(1.0, dot(a, b))) return math.acos(costheta) def computeangularbounds(boxmin, boxmax, axis, target): # Computes the minimum and maximum angles between axis and # the vectors from each box corner to target. corners = [ (boxmin[0], boxmin[1], boxmin[2]), (boxmax[0], boxmin[1], boxmin[2]), (boxmin[0], boxmax[1], boxmin[2]), (boxmax[0], boxmax[1], boxmin[2]), (boxmin[0], boxmin[1], boxmax[2]), (boxmax[0], boxmin[1], boxmax[2]), (boxmin[0], boxmax[1], boxmax[2]), (boxmax[0], boxmax[1], boxmax[2]) ] axisnorm = normalize(axis) minang = math.pi maxang = 0.0 for c in corners: vec = (target[0]-c[0], target[1]-c[1], target[2]-c[2]) ang = anglebetween(axisnorm, vec) if ang < minang: minang = ang if ang > maxang: maxang = ang return minang, maxang def sidednesstest(boxmin, boxmax, coneaxis, conesemiangle, L, V, eta): alpha = conesemiangle # Clamp argument to asin to avoid domain error when eta >= 1 thetac = math.asin(min(1.0, 1.0 / eta)) psiLmin, psiLmax = computeangularbounds(boxmin, boxmax, coneaxis, L) psiVmin, psiVmax = computeangularbounds(boxmin, boxmax, coneaxis, V) minangleLN = max(0.0, psiLmin - alpha) maxangleLN = min(math.pi, psiLmax + alpha) minangleVN = max(0.0, psiVmin - alpha) maxangleVN = min(math.pi, psiVmax + alpha) lightpositive = minangleLN < (math.pi / 2.0) viewernegative = maxangleVN > (math.pi / 2.0) withincritical = minangleVN < thetac return lightpositive and viewernegative and withincritical Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: When angles are close to \pi/2 or \thetac, floating-point errors may lead to incorrect pruning. Use epsilon comparisons. Degenerate Box: If the position box is a point, the angular bounds collapse to a single value. Large Normal Variation: If \alpha is large, the bounds become loose and the test may fail to prune, but the test remains cheap to compute. Total Internal Reflection: If \eta < 1, \thetac is valid. If \eta \ge 1, \thetac is \pi/2 or undefined. The formula \arcsin(1/\eta) handles \eta > 1. It differs from the smooth normal pruning test only by bounding positions with a 3D box instead of a 2D triangle, while keeping identical test logic. Choose it when traversing acceleration structures for refractive media to quickly discard subtrees with large normal variation. Time Complexity: O(1) per node in the acceleration structure. The computation involves basic trigonometric functions and comparisons. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Performance: The test is cheap to compute and does not depend on the shading normals, allowing it to prune many subtrees even if they have large normal bounding cones. Strengths: It is independent of the specific shading normals, relying only on the bounding cone axis and semi-angle. It handles 3D position boxes effectively. Limitations: It is a necessary condition, not sufficient. It may return True for boxes that do not contain valid points, requiring further refinement. When to use: Use during the traversal of the acceleration structure (e.g., BVH or KD-tree) for refractive media to quickly discard regions that cannot contribute to the light path. The Sidedness Test is part of the method for single scattering in refractive media with triangle mesh boundaries, introduced by Walter et al.. It builds on techniques from [Walter et al. 2005] for pruning sub-triangles in the smooth normal case, extending them to 3D position bounding boxes for refractive boundaries. name: Cone Overlap Test for Refractive Boundaries
body: The Cone Overlap Test is a pruning test used to determine if a position bounding box and a normal bounding cone can possibly satisfy the refraction conditions for a light transport path. It ensures that the view vector \mathbf{V} lies on the negative side of the shading normal and within the critical angle cone defined by \arcsin(1/\eta). It differs from the smooth normal pruning test only in that positions are bounded by a 3D box rather than a 2D triangle; the test logic is otherwise identical. Inputs: Position bounding box B (axis-aligned, defined by min/max corners). Normal bounding cone C (defined by axis \mathbf{n}0 and semi-angle \alpha). Light direction \mathbf{L} and View direction \mathbf{V} (vectors from the point in B to the light and camera, respectively). Refractive index ratio \eta. Outputs: Boolean: True if the box and cone might contain a valid refraction point; False if the subtree can be pruned. Data Structures: The position bounding box is represented by its minimum and maximum coordinates: \mathbf{b}{\min}, \mathbf{b}{\max} \in \mathbb{R}^3. The normal bounding cone is represented by its central axis \mathbf{n}0 (unit vector) and semi-angle \alpha. Steps: 1. Compute Angle Bounds: Calculate the minimum and maximum possible angles between the cone axis \mathbf{n}0 and the light direction \mathbf{L}, as well as between \mathbf{n}0 and the view direction \mathbf{V}, for any point \mathbf{p} within the bounding box B. Let \theta{L, \min}, \theta{L, \max} be the bounds for \mathbf{L} and \theta{V, \min}, \theta{V, \max} be the bounds for \mathbf{V}. 2. Offset by Cone Semiangle: Adjust these bounds to account for the variation of the normal within the cone. The effective range of angles for the light is [\theta{L, \min} - \alpha, \theta{L, \max} + \alpha] and for the view is [\theta{V, \min} - \alpha, \theta{V, \max} + \alpha]. 3. Check Refraction Conditions: Verify if it is possible for the angles to satisfy the geometric constraints of refraction. The light direction \mathbf{L} must lie on the positive side of the shading normal (angle < \pi/2). The view direction \mathbf{V} must lie on the negative side of the shading normal (angle > \pi/2). The view direction \mathbf{V} must be within the critical angle cone, i.e., the angle between \mathbf{V} and the normal must be less than or equal to \arcsin(1/\eta). 4. Prune Decision: If the adjusted angle ranges for \mathbf{L} or \mathbf{V} cannot satisfy these conditions simultaneously, return False. Otherwise, return True. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def coneoverlaptest(boxmin, boxmax, coneaxis, conesemiangle, L, V, eta): # Step 1: Compute bounds on angles between cone axis and L/V over the box # Using techniques from Walter et al. 2005 to find min/max angles from any point in box # to the fixed vectors L and V, relative to the cone axis. # Sources do not provide the exact implementation for this step. thetaLmin, thetaLmax = 0.0, math.pi thetaVmin, thetaVmax = 0.0, math.pi # Step 2: Offset by the semi-angle of the normal bounding cone effectiveLmin = thetaLmin - conesemiangle effectiveLmax = thetaLmax + conesemiangle effectiveVmin = thetaVmin - conesemiangle effectiveVmax = thetaVmax + conesemiangle # Critical angle for refraction criticalangle = math.asin(1.0 / eta) # Step 3: Check if it is possible for angles to lie within required ranges # L must be on the positive side of the normal: angle in 0, pi/2) lvalidmin, lvalidmax = 0.0, math.pi / 2.0 loverlap = max(effectiveLmin, lvalidmin) < min(effectiveLmax, lvalidmax) # V must be on the negative side of the normal: angle > pi/2 # and within the critical angle cone: angle <= pi/2 + criticalangle vvalidmin, vvalidmax = math.pi / 2.0, math.pi / 2.0 + criticalangle voverlap = max(effectiveVmin, vvalidmin) < min(effectiveVmax, vvalidmax) return loverlap and voverlap The Spindle Test is a pruning test based on the geometric constraint that a single refraction bends light by a limited amount, restricting the valid refraction point P to a spindle-shaped region (surface of revolution of a circular arc from V to L). It tests if a bounding box overlaps this spindle by using a modified standard box-sphere overlap test that also computes a lower bound on the distance from the box to the line containing V and L. The condition for a point P to lie within the spindle is: \left\| \mathbf{P} - \frac{\mathbf{L} + \mathbf{V}}{2} \right\|^2 + \frac{\|\mathbf{L} - \mathbf{V}\|}{\eta} r \leq \frac{\|\mathbf{L} - \mathbf{V}\|^2}{4} where r is the distance from point P to the line containing L and V, and \eta is the refractive index. If \eta is arbitrarily large, this reduces to a point-in-sphere test. This test is cheap and does not depend on shading normals, allowing it to prune many subtrees even if they have large normal bounding cones. The Cone Overlap Test is a pruning test used during the traversal of a bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) or similar structure for [light transport in participating media. Its primary strength is its ability to quickly discard subtrees that cannot contain valid refraction points based on normal and position bounds. The test relies on angle bound computations which are relatively cheap compared to full ray intersection tests. It is particularly effective when combined with the Spindle Test and Sidedness Test. The Cone Overlap Test was introduced by Walter et al. in the context of single scattering in refractive media with triangle mesh boundaries. It is an extension of the pruning test used for smooth normals, adapted for 3D position bounding boxes. The underlying techniques for computing angle bounds are from [Walter et al. 2005]. The test is part of a suite of three pruning tests (Spindle, Sidedness, Cone Overlap) designed to efficiently find refraction points in participating media. name: Newton-Raphson for Refraction Point Search
head: 1D Newton-Raphson for Refraction Point Search, 1D Newton-Raphson search for triangle without shading normals, Case 1: Triangle without shading normals
body: This method finds the point P on a triangle boundary where light refracts from a source L to a viewer V, using the half-vector formulation from Half-vector formulation for refracted path finding. It solves for the root of a function derived from Snell's law. It is distinguished by its use of a specific empirical heuristic for the initial guess and clamping to ensure the solution remains on the triangle edge. It applies when the triangle has constant shading normals (Case 1), reducing the problem to a 1D search, unlike the 2D search required for varying normals. Inputs: Viewer position V. Light source position L. Triangle geometry (specifically the edge on which P lies). Refractive index ratio \eta = n1 / n2. Geometric normal \hat{\mathbf{N}}g and shading normal \hat{\mathbf{N}}s (assumed identical and constant). Outputs: The x-coordinate x of the refraction point P in the transformed coordinate system. No complex data structures are required. The method operates on scalar values (x, xi) and 2D/3D vectors (V, L, P). 1. Transform coordinates so that all relevant points lie in the z=0 plane, the triangle lies in the y=0 plane, and V is on the y-axis. 2. Initialize x using the empirical heuristic x0. 3. Iterate using x{i+1} = xi - f(xi)/f'(xi) where f'(x) is the derivative of f with respect to x. 4. Clamp all xi to the range [0, Lx] to ensure the solution lies within the triangle edge. The goal is to find x such that the half-vector \hat{\mathbf{H}} is anti-parallel to the normal \hat{\mathbf{N}}g. Since \hat{\mathbf{N}}g = (0,1), this is equivalent to finding the root of the x-component of \hat{\mathbf{H}}. The normalization term of \hat{\mathbf{H}} is omitted because overall scaling factors do not affect the locations of the zeros of a function. The target function f(x) is: f(x) = \frac{-\eta x}{\sqrt{x^2 + Vy^2}} + \frac{Lx - x}{\sqrt{(Lx - x)^2 + Ly^2}} where \eta is the refractive index ratio, Vy is the viewer's y-coordinate, Lx and Ly are the light source's coordinates, and x is the variable representing the x-coordinate of the point P. The derivative f'(x) with respect to x is computed analytically: f'(x) = \frac{-\eta Vy^2}{(x^2 + Vy^2)^{3/2}} - \frac{Ly^2}{((Lx - x)^2 + Ly^2)^{3/2}} The initial guess x0 is given by the empirical heuristic: x0 = \frac{-Vy Lx}{\eta Ly - Vy} \frac{4}{3 + \eta} which serves to minimize the average number of convergence iterations. The Newton-Raphson update rule is: x{i+1} = xi - \frac{f(xi)}{f'(xi)} Not given in the sources. The convergence tolerance \epsilon and maximum iteration count are implementation-defined. Clamping: The solution must lie within the triangle edge. Clamping x to [0, Lx] is essential to ensure physical validity. Convergence: For the 1D case, convergence typically occurs in 2 to 4 iterations with the specified heuristic and clamping. Derivative Zero: If f'(xi) = 0, the Newton-Raphson step is undefined, requiring a safeguard or step-size reduction in standard numerical practice. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def solverefractionpoint1d(Vy, Lx, Ly, eta, epsilon=1e-6, maxiter=10): """ Solves for the x-coordinate of the refraction point P on a triangle edge using 1D Newton-Raphson iteration. Inputs: Vy: y-coordinate of viewer V (V is at (0, Vy)) Lx: x-coordinate of light source L (L is at (Lx, Ly)) Ly: y-coordinate of light source L eta: refractive index ratio n1/n2 epsilon: convergence tolerance maxiter: maximum number of iterations Output: x: the x-coordinate of the refraction point P """ # Step 1: Initialize with empirical heuristic denominator = eta Ly - Vy x = (-Vy Lx) / denominator (4.0 / (3.0 + eta)) # Clamp initial guess to [0, Lx] x = max(0.0, min(x, Lx)) for in range(maxiter): # Calculate f(x) term1num = -eta x term1den = math.sqrt(x2 + Vy2) term1 = term1num / term1den dx = Lx - x term2num = dx term2den = math.sqrt(dx2 + Ly2) term2 = term2num / term2den fx = term1 + term2 # Check convergence if abs(fx) < epsilon: return x # Calculate f'(x) analytically df1dx = (-eta Vy2) / (x2 + Vy2)1.5 df2dx = (-Ly2) / (term2den3) fprimex = df1dx + df2dx # Newton-Raphson update xnew = x - fx / fprimex # Clamp to [0, Lx] xnew = max(0.0, min(xnew, Lx)) x = xnew return x Time: O(1) per iteration, with typically 2-4 iterations. Thus, O(1) overall. Memory: O(1), requiring only a few scalar variables. Converges in 2 to 4 iterations with the heuristic initial guess. The heuristic minimizes the average number of iterations compared to other starting points. Strengths: Fast convergence, simple implementation, robust with the heuristic initial guess. Limitations: Only applicable to triangles with constant shading normals (Case 1). For varying normals, a 2D search is required. Use when the triangle has constant shading normals and the refraction point is known to lie on a specific edge. Do not use when shading normals vary across the triangle; use the 2D Newton-Raphson method instead. This method is described in "Single Scattering in Refractive Media with Triangle Mesh Boundaries" by Eric Heitz, Jonathan Dupuy, Stephen Hill, and David Neubelt. The method is part of a broader framework for handling refraction in participating media. It addresses the specific case where the shading normal is constant, allowing for a simplified 1D search. The empirical heuristic for the initial guess was developed to minimize the average number of iterations required for convergence. name: Accurate single scattering under point light (Walter et al.)
head: Fermat's Principle based Single Scattering, Walter's Method for Accurate Single Scattering
body: This method computes single scattering effects in participating media under a point light source by treating the computation as a search problem to find all points on the surface that connect the point light and the camera sample via Fermat’s principle. It is impossible to render this configuration with volumetric path tracing or MEMLT. Inputs: Point light source, camera sample, surface geometry, and shading normal field. Outputs: Single scattering radiance contribution at the camera sample. Data Structures: Interval Newton solver state tracking the current interval, function value, and derivative. List of found entry points on the surface. Exact field layouts and sizes are not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Formulate the search problem to find all surface points P connecting the point light and camera sample via Fermat’s principle. 2. Compute entry points on the surface using Newton–Raphson optimization within an interval Newton method to find all solutions. 3. Accumulate single scattering contributions from all valid entry points. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: The presence of a shading normal at surface points makes the problem more complex than using geometric normals. To capture the sharpness of the caustics, a large number of camera samples are required along the camera ray. This factor scales radiance for light paths involving refractive boundaries in participating media. It is distinct from simple inverse-square distance laws because it incorporates the Jacobian of the refraction mapping at the boundary. Choose it when rendering paths involving refractive boundaries in participating media. This variant improves Walter's method by computing the extent of the influence of each triangle on the camera ray, based on the observation that radiance caused by an individual triangle varies smoothly and discontinuities correspond to triangle edges. It is significantly faster than Walter et al. while providing higher-quality results. Choose it when performance is critical but accurate single scattering under point lights is still required. Time Complexity: Highly depends on scene complexity. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Deterministic and accurate for single scattering under point lights. Limitations: Limited to participating media under point lights. Requires many camera samples to avoid aliasing in caustics. Slower than Holzschuch's method. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Walter et al. [60] introduced this method for accurate computation of single scattering effects in participating media under a point light source. This configuration is impossible to render with volumetric path tracing or MEMLT. They treated the single scattering computation as a search problem to find all points on the surface that connect the point light and the camera sample via Fermat’s principle. The presence of a shading normal at surface points makes the problem more complex. They computed these entry points on the surface using Newton–Raphson optimization. Using an interval Newton method, all solutions can be found. However, to capture the sharpness of the caustics, a large number of camera samples are required along the camera ray. Wang et al. [62] can also be used for single scattering computation and produces similar results to those of Walter et al. [60]. Holzschuch [61] improved it by computing the extent of the influence of each triangle on the camera ray, based on the observation that the radiance caused by an individual triangle on the surface varies smoothly and discontinuities correspond to triangle edges. This method is significantly faster than Walter et al. [60] while providing higher-quality results. Sun et al. [63] proposed an analytical solution for single scattering by participating media without boundaries under a point light, which can achieve a real-time frame rate. All of the above methods can compute accurate single scattering without noise, but the computation time highly depends on scene complexity. Moreover, these methods are limited to participating media under point lights. A survey on rendering homogeneous participating media, https://doi.org/10.1007/s41095-021-0249-1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Distance Correction Factor for Refracted Paths
head: D factor for refracted paths, Distance Correction Factor D for Refracted Paths, Geometric spreading factor for refraction
body: The Distance Correction Factor (D) accounts for geometric spreading and refraction effects in the contribution formula for light paths involving refractive boundaries in participating media. It ensures visually correct radiance by scaling intensity according to the solid angle subtended by the light source as seen from the scattering point, adjusted for the refractive index, distinguishing it from simple inverse-square distance laws. Inputs: \mathbf{L}: Position of the point light source. \mathbf{V}: Position of the camera sample or volume scattering event. \mathbf{P}: Position of the refraction point on the boundary surface. \hat{\omega}L: Unit vector from \mathbf{P} to \mathbf{L} (\frac{\mathbf{L}-\mathbf{P}}{\|\mathbf{L}-\mathbf{P}\|}). \hat{\omega}V: Unit vector from \mathbf{P} to \mathbf{V} (\frac{\mathbf{V}-\mathbf{P}}{\|\mathbf{V}-\mathbf{P}\|}). \hat{\mathbf{N}}g: Geometric normal at \mathbf{P}. \hat{\mathbf{N}}s: Shading normal at \mathbf{P}. \eta: Refractive index of the medium relative to the outside. Ie: Point light intensity. F: Fresnel factor at \mathbf{P}. A: Volume attenuation (integral of \sigmas along the segment). \rho: Volume scattering phase function (or BRDF \times cosine if \mathbf{V} is a surface). Outputs: D: The distance correction factor. Contribution: \frac{Ie F A \rho}{D}. Data Structures: Vectors \mathbf{L}, \mathbf{V}, \mathbf{P} are 3D floats. Normals \hat{\mathbf{N}}g, \hat{\mathbf{N}}s are unit 3D floats. Derivatives \hat{\mathbf{N}}'s are 3D floats representing the change in shading normal with respect to perturbations in \hat{\omega}V. Steps: 1. Check for No Refraction: If \eta = 1, return D = \|\mathbf{L} - \mathbf{V}\|. 2. Check for Normal Incidence without Shading Normals: If \hat{\omega}L = \hat{\mathbf{N}}g = \hat{\mathbf{N}}s, return D = (\|\mathbf{V} - \mathbf{P}\| + \eta \|\mathbf{L} - \mathbf{P}\|)^2. 3. Special Case: No Shading Normals (\hat{\mathbf{N}}s = \hat{\mathbf{N}}g): Compute distances: dV = \|\mathbf{V} - \mathbf{P}\| dL = \|\mathbf{L} - \mathbf{P}\| Return: D = (dV + \eta dL) \left( \frac{|\hat{\omega}L \cdot \hat{\mathbf{N}}g|}{|\hat{\omega}L \cdot \hat{\mathbf{N}}g|} dV + \frac{|\hat{\omega}V \cdot \hat{\mathbf{N}}g|}{|\hat{\omega}L \cdot \hat{\mathbf{N}}g|} \eta dL \right) The first fraction simplifies to 1, but is preserved verbatim from the source. 4. General Case: With Shading Normals: Compute derivatives of \mathbf{L} in the plane perpendicular to \hat{\omega}L with respect to perturbations in \hat{\omega}V. Let \hat{\mathbf{N}}'s be the derivative of \hat{\mathbf{N}}s. Compute intermediate vectors and scalars: dV = \mathbf{V} - \mathbf{P} dL = \mathbf{L} - \mathbf{P} Compute \mathbf{P}': \mathbf{P}' = dV \left( \partialV - \frac{\partialV \cdot \hat{\mathbf{N}}g}{\partialV \cdot \hat{\mathbf{N}}g} \hat{\omega}V \right) The denominator \partialV \cdot \hat{\mathbf{N}}g / \partialV \cdot \hat{\mathbf{N}}g equals 1, but is preserved verbatim as in the source. \mu = \hat{\omega}L \cdot \hat{\mathbf{N}}s + \eta \hat{\omega}V \cdot \hat{\mathbf{N}}s Compute \mu': \mu' = \left( \eta^2 \frac{\partial \omega \cdot \hat{\mathbf{N}}s}{\partial \omega \cdot \hat{\mathbf{N}}s} + \eta \right) (\hat{\omega}'V \cdot \hat{\mathbf{N}}s + \hat{\omega}V \cdot \hat{\mathbf{N}}'s) The term \frac{\partial \omega \cdot \hat{\mathbf{N}}s}{\partial \omega \cdot \hat{\mathbf{N}}s} is preserved verbatim from the source. Compute \hat{\omega}'V: \hat{\omega}'V = \eta \hat{\omega}'V + \mu' \hat{\mathbf{N}}s + \mu \hat{\mathbf{N}}'s The source uses \hat{\omega}'V on both sides, implying an update or specific notation. Compute \phi'L (used as \hat{\omega}'L in subsequent steps): \phi'L = - \eta \phi'L + \mu' \hat{\mathbf{N}}s + \mu \hat{\mathbf{N}}'s The source labels this \phi'L but applies it to the light direction derivative. Compute \mathbf{L}': \mathbf{L}' = \mathbf{P}' - (\mathbf{P}' \cdot \hat{\omega}L) \hat{\omega}L + dL \hat{\omega}'L The source layout for this equation is fragmented, but captures the visible formula part. Compute derivatives in two orthogonal directions perpendicular to \hat{\omega}V to obtain \mathbf{L}'\perp and \mathbf{L}'\parallel. Return: D = \|\mathbf{L}'\perp \times \mathbf{L}'\parallel\| Parameters: \eta: Typical value 1.5 for homogeneous media. A: Equals 1 if the medium is clear. \rho: Replaced by BRDF \times cosine of the angle with the surface normal at \mathbf{V} if \mathbf{V} is a surface point. Ie: Replaced by emitted radiance \times cosine of the angle with the surface normal at \mathbf{L} divided by the probability of sampling \mathbf{L} for area lights. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Focal Points/Cusps: Radiance can grow arbitrarily large near focal points or cusps in volume caustics, leading to spike noise when sampling the volume along eye rays. Solution: Clamp D to a minimum threshold to reduce noise, at the cost of some energy loss. Derivatives: Requires computing derivatives of shading normals \hat{\mathbf{N}}s, which can be computed for triangles with interpolated normals. Complexity: Computing D is described as "not difficult to code" once the equations are known, requiring the computation of shading normal derivatives. Performance: The method computes 512x512 images with 64 samples per pixel in 15.3s for a teapot model (12 boundaries, 4096 other triangles), 13.9s for a cuboctahedron (20 boundaries, 0 other triangles), and 19.2s for an amber model (36 boundaries, 60556 other triangles). Strengths: Provides visually correct results matching reference solutions for single scattering in refractive media. Limitations: Can produce spike noise near caustic focal points if D is not clamped. The method is part of the technique for accurate single scattering under point lights in refractive media with triangle mesh boundaries, introduced by Walter et al.. It builds on ray differential techniques from Igehy [1999] to compute the solid angle of the light source as seen from the scattering point through the refractive boundary.
