name: Mie Phase Function Calculation
head: Mie Theory Phase Function, MiePlot Calculation
body: Calculates the phase function for homogeneous spheres significantly larger than the wavelength of light, specifically modeling scattering by rain and cloud particles. It distinguishes itself from Rayleigh scattering (which handles particles smaller than the wavelength) by capturing complex interference phenomena such as the strong forward peak, rainbow angles, and the glory effect. Inputs: Particle radius distribution parameters (lognormal distribution). Wavelength of incident light. Refractive index of the particle material (water for clouds/rain). Angular resolution for discretization (typically 0.1 degrees). Outputs: A discrete phase function P(\Theta) sampled at the specified angular resolution, where \Theta is the scattering angle. Data Structures: The output is typically a 1D array or texture mapping scattering angle \Theta to phase function value P(\Theta). Steps: 1. Define Particle Size Distribution: Model the collection of randomly distributed particles using a lognormal distribution. The parameters for this distribution are derived from empirical data described by Pruppacher and Klett. 2. Compute Single-Particle Scattering: For a given spherical particle of radius r and refractive index m, calculate the scattering amplitudes S1(\Theta) and S2(\Theta) using Mie theory. This involves solving Maxwell's equations via infinite series expansions of spherical vector wave functions. 3. Calculate Phase Function for Single Particle: Compute the phase function for a single sphere using the scattering amplitudes: P{single}(\Theta) = \frac{|S1(\Theta)|^2 + |S2(\Theta)|^2}{2k^2} where k is the wavenumber. Note: Standard Mie theory normalizes this such that \int P(\Theta) d\Omega = 1. 4. Integrate Over Size Distribution: Convolve the single-particle phase function with the lognormal particle size distribution to obtain the ensemble phase function: P{ensemble}(\Theta) = \int0^\infty P{single}(\Theta, r) f(r) dr where f(r) is the lognormal probability density function. 5. Sample at Required Resolution: Evaluate the resulting ensemble phase function at the specified angular resolution (e.g., 0.1 degrees). Parameters: Angular resolution: 0.1 degrees. Particle size distribution: Lognormal, parameters per Pruppacher and Klett. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Refractive Index: Must be complex for absorbing media; for water droplets, it is primarily real with a small imaginary part. Size Parameter: The method assumes particles are "much larger" than the wavelength. If particles approach the wavelength scale, Mie theory remains valid but computational cost increases significantly due to the number of terms required in the series expansion. Numerical Stability: The infinite series in Mie theory must be truncated at a sufficiently high order (n{max} \approx kr + 4(kr)^{1/3}) to ensure convergence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculatemiephasefunction(wavelength, refractiveindex, sizeparams, angularresolutiondeg): """ Calculates the Mie phase function for a lognormal distribution of spheres. Args: wavelength: float, wavelength of light in meters. refractiveindex: complex, refractive index of the sphere material. sizeparams: tuple, (meanradius, sigma) for lognormal distribution. angularresolutiondeg: float, angular step size in degrees. Returns: angles: array of scattering angles in degrees. phasevalues: array of phase function values. """ # 1. Define angular grid anglesdeg = numpy.arange(0, 180.1, angularresolutiondeg) anglesrad = numpy.radians(anglesdeg) # 2. Define lognormal size distribution parameters # Parameters derived from Pruppacher and Klett [PK00] # Note: Exact parameters depend on specific cloud/rain type meanradius = sizeparams[0] sigma = sizeparams[1] # 3. Precompute constants k = 2 numpy.pi / wavelength refractiveindexm = refractiveindex / 1.0 # relative to air # 4. Initialize ensemble phase function accumulator ensemblephase = numpy.zeroslike(anglesrad) # 5. Integrate over particle sizes # Discretize the lognormal distribution numsizes = 100 radii = numpy.logspace(numpy.log10(meanradius 0.1), numpy.log10(meanradius 10), numsizes) weights = lognormalpdf(radii, meanradius, sigma) weights = weights / numpy.sum(weights) # Normalize for i, r in enumerate(radii): # Calculate single-particle phase function for radius r singlephase = computesinglemiephase(anglesrad, r, wavelength, refractiveindexm) # Accumulate weighted contribution ensemblephase += weights[i] singlephase return anglesdeg, ensemblephase def computesinglemiephase(anglesrad, radius, wavelength, refractiveindexm): """ Computes the Mie phase function for a single homogeneous sphere. Uses Bohren and Huffman's implementation [BH83]. """ k = 2 numpy.pi / wavelength x = k radius # Size parameter # Initialize scattering amplitudes S1 = numpy.zeroslike(anglesrad, dtype=complex) S2 = numpy.zeroslike(anglesrad, dtype=complex) # Determine maximum order for series expansion nmax = int(x + 4 x(1/3) + 10) # Compute Mie coefficients an and bn # This involves Bessel and Hankel functions # Implementation details per Bohren and Huffman [BH83] an, bn = computemiecoefficients(x, refractiveindexm, nmax) # Compute scattering amplitudes for i, theta in enumerate(anglesrad): sintheta = numpy.sin(theta) costheta = numpy.cos(theta) # Series expansion for S1 and S2 sumS1 = 0 sumS2 = 0 for n in range(1, nmax + 1): pin = computepin(n, costheta) taun = computetaun(n, costheta) sumS1 += (2 n + 1) / (n (n + 1)) (an[n] pin + bn[n] taun) sumS2 += (2 n + 1) / (n (n + 1)) (an[n] taun + bn[n] pin) S1[i] = sumS1 S2[i] = sumS2 # Calculate phase function # Normalization factor ensures integral over sphere is 1 # P(theta) = (|S1|^2 + |S2|^2) / (2 k^2 integral(|S|^2 dOmega)) # However, standard Mie code returns normalized phase function directly intensity = (numpy.abs(S1)2 + numpy.abs(S2)2) # Normalize so that average over 4pi steradians is 1 # Integral of phase function over solid angle is 4pi # P(theta) = intensity / (2 k^2 normalization) # The standard definition is P(theta) = (|S1|^2 + |S2|^2) / (2 k^2) # But this is not normalized. We need to normalize by the total scattering cross section. # For a single sphere, the phase function is defined as: # P(theta) = (|S1|^2 + |S2|^2) / (2 k^2 Qsca pi r^2) # where Qsca is the scattering efficiency. # Simplified: Most implementations return the normalized phase function directly. # We assume computesinglemiephase returns the normalized value. return intensity / (2 k2) # Placeholder for actual normalization per [BH83] def computepin(n, costheta): """Compute the Legendre function of the first kind derivative term.""" if n == 1: return costheta # Recursive relation or direct computation # pin(x) = n x pi{n-1}(x) - (n + x^2) pi{n-2}(x) / (n - 1) # This is a simplified placeholder. Actual implementation requires careful recursion. return 0 # Placeholder for actual Legendre function computation def computetaun(n, costheta): """Compute the Legendre function of the second kind derivative term.""" return n costheta computepin(n, costheta) - n computepin(n-1, costheta) # Simplified def lognormalpdf(x, mean, sigma): """Lognormal probability density function.""" return 1 / (x sigma numpy.sqrt(2 numpy.pi)) numpy.exp(-(numpy.log(x) - numpy.log(mean))2 / (2 sigma2)) Provides a practical technique for evaluating the Mie phase function in real-time volume rendering by precomputing values into a 1D texture, trading memory bandwidth for speed while preserving diffraction and interference features. Time Complexity: Calculating the Mie phase function analytically is computationally expensive due to the infinite series expansions required for scattering amplitudes. The complexity depends on the size parameter x = kr and the required accuracy. Memory Complexity: If precomputed, the lookup table requires memory proportional to the angular resolution (e.g., 1800 entries for 0.1-degree resolution). Strengths: Accurately models complex scattering phenomena like rainbows and glories, which simpler approximations (e.g., Henyey-Greenstein) cannot capture. Limitations: High computational cost for real-time applications if calculated on the fly; requires accurate knowledge of particle size distribution and refractive index. When to Use: When visual fidelity of atmospheric phenomena (rainbows, glories) is critical and offline precomputation or lookup tables are feasible. Mie theory was developed by Gustav Mie in 1908 to describe the scattering of electromagnetic radiation by spherical particles. The implementation used in this context is based on Bohren and Huffman's [BH83] code, widely regarded as the standard reference for Mie scattering calculations. Philip Laven’s MiePlot [Lav] provides a practical implementation of this theory for atmospheric phenomena. The specific application to cloud and rain particles uses lognormal size distributions described by Pruppacher and Klett [PK00]. name: Mie Phase Function Lookup
head: Mie Phase Function Image Lookup, Mie PF EXR Lookup
body: This method provides a practical technique for evaluating the Mie phase function in real-time volume rendering, specifically for clouds and participating media containing microscopic water droplets. It addresses the computational cost of calculating Mie scattering analytically by precomputing the phase function values into a 1D texture (OpenEXR image) and sampling it via a dot-product-derived coordinate. It sets itself apart from analytical calculation methods by trading memory bandwidth for speed, and from generic phase function approximations (like Henyey-Greenstein) by preserving the specific diffraction and interference features of Mie theory, such as the strong forward peak and silver lining effect. Inputs: Eye direction vector I (view direction). Light direction vector L (direction to the light source). Precomputed scattering data derived from Antoine Bouthors’ thesis. Outputs: Phase function value p(\theta) for the given scattering angle. RGB color values if the phase function is spectrally resolved (though typically treated as luminance or grayscale in standard implementations, the source notes normalization over RGB channels). Phase Function Storage: A 1800 \times 1 pixel OpenEXR image. Format: OpenEXR (high dynamic range). Resolution: 1800 pixels in the U (horizontal) dimension, 1 pixel in the V (vertical) dimension. Content: The scattering values of the combined Mie phase function. Rationale: VEX arrays in Houdini have size limits that cause compilation errors when storing the full 1800 values; the EXR image serves as a portable, efficient alternative. 1. Preprocessing (Offline): Retrieve the split scattering data files Mie0.txt and MiePF3.txt from Antoine Bouthors’ thesis. These represent a general-purpose droplet size distribution found in clouds. Combine the split data (forward peak and rest) into a single set if importance sampling is not being used for the phase function itself. The split is intended for sampling efficiency, but for simple weighting, they are summed. Normalize the combined data so that it sums to 1.0 over the RGB channels. Generate the 1800 \times 1 OpenEXR image containing these normalized values. 2. Runtime Evaluation: Calculate the angle \theta between the eye direction I and the light direction L. Compute the U coordinate for texture sampling using the formula below. Sample the OpenEXR image at the computed U coordinate to retrieve the phase function value. The U coordinate is calculated by normalizing the dot product of the eye and light directions, mapping the angle to the range [0, 1]: U = \frac{\arccos(\text{normalize}(I) \cdot \text{normalize}(L))}{\pi} Where: I is the eye direction vector. L is the light direction vector. \text{normalize}(v) returns the unit vector in the direction of v. \arccos returns the angle in radians. \pi is the mathematical constant pi. Data Source: Mie0.txt and MiePF3.txt from Antoine Bouthors’ PhD thesis, Realistic rendering of clouds in realtime. Texture Resolution: 1800 samples. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def samplemiephasefunction(exrimage, eyedir, lightdir): """ Samples the Mie phase function from a 1D EXR image. Args: exrimage: A 1D texture (1800x1) containing normalized Mie scattering data. eyedir: Vector3, the view direction (I). lightdir: Vector3, the direction to the light source (L). Returns: float: The phase function value p(theta). """ # 1. Normalize directions I = eyedir.normalized() L = lightdir.normalized() # 2. Calculate cosine of the angle between I and L costheta = I.dot(L) # 3. Clamp to [-1, 1] to handle floating point errors costheta = max(-1.0, min(1.0, costheta)) # 4. Calculate U coordinate: angle / pi # arccos returns radians in [0, pi] angle = math.acos(costheta) u = angle / math.pi # 5. Sample the EXR image # U is in [0, 1]. Assuming standard texture coordinates where 0 is left, 1 is right. # The EXR image is 1800 pixels wide. # Note: Exact sampling method (linear vs nearest) depends on the renderer. # For high precision, linear interpolation between texels is preferred. phasevalue = exrimage.sample1d(u) return phasevalue Array Size Limits: In Houdini VEX, arrays of a handful of floats work, but full arrays of 1800 values cause compilation errors. Using an EXR image avoids this limitation. Forward Scattering Intensity: The Mie phase function is heavily forward-scattering, with over 90% of energy scattered in the forward direction. This causes the volume to appear dark from angles other than directly in front of the light. Dynamic Range: The intensity difference between the strong forward peak (silver lining) and backward/sideways scattering is extreme. High dynamic range (HDR) lighting and tone mapping (or gamma correction) are required to visualize the weaker scattering components without clipping the peak. Multiple Scattering: Single scattering alone is insufficient for realistic cloud rendering. Multiple scattering must be added to fill out the overall light in the volume. A common approximation is to add a weak isotropic phase function, as higher-order scattering tends toward isotropy. The analytical computation of the phase function using Mie theory for homogeneous spheres. This is the source of the data used in the lookup method. Mie Phase Function Calculation The broader context of calculating phase function coefficients, of which Mie theory is a specific, physically accurate case for spherical particles. Classical Phase Function Coefficient Calculation Time Complexity: O(1) per sample. The lookup involves a dot product, an arccos, and a texture sample. This is significantly faster than analytical Mie calculation, which involves infinite series summations. Memory Complexity: O(N) where N=1800. The storage is minimal (a single 1D texture). Strengths: Physically accurate representation of cloud scattering (forward peak, diffraction effects). Fast evaluation suitable for real-time rendering. Portable across renderers (EXR is a standard format). Limitations: Requires precomputation and storage of the texture. Does not inherently handle multiple scattering; requires additional techniques (e.g., isotropic fake) to appear realistic. The strong forward peak requires careful handling of HDR and tone mapping to avoid visual artifacts (darkness in non-forward directions). When to Use: Real-time cloud rendering where physical accuracy of the single-scattering lobe is desired, and analytical Mie calculation is too slow. When Not to Use: When multiple scattering is the dominant effect and a simple isotropic approximation is sufficient, or when memory bandwidth is extremely constrained and even a 1D texture lookup is prohibitive (though unlikely). The method originates from practical real-time rendering of clouds, as described by the author of the blog post "Rendering clouds with the Mie phase function". It builds upon the work of Antoine Bouthors, whose PhD thesis Realistic rendering of clouds in realtime provided the Mie scattering data (Mie0.txt, MiePF3.txt) generated using Mieplot. The technique was developed to overcome the limitations of simpler phase functions (like Henyey-Greenstein) and the computational cost of analytical Mie calculation, specifically addressing the "silver lining" effect and the anisotropic nature of cloud scattering. The use of an EXR image was a pragmatic solution to Houdini VEX array size limitations. Rendering clouds with the Mie phase function, https://mattebb.com/blog/weblog/rendering-clouds-with-the-mie-phase-function/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Phase Function Interface
head: pbrt PhaseFunction
body: The Phase Function Interface defines the abstract contract for phase functions in the pbrt rendering system, requiring implementations to evaluate the scattering probability density and sample new scattering directions. It distinguishes itself from sibling implementations by enforcing a specific direction convention where both incident and outgoing vectors point away from the scattering point, differing from standard scattering literature. Inputs and Outputs: The interface operates on unit direction vectors \omegao (outgoing) and \omegai (incident) and random variables u. It outputs a scalar probability density value or a sampled direction. Data Structures: The core data structure is the abstract base class PhaseFunction. It contains two pure virtual methods: 1. p(const Vector3f &wo, const Vector3f &wi): Returns the phase function value p(\omegao, \omegai). 2. Samplep(const Vector3f &wo, Vector3f wi, const Point2f &u): Samples a new incident direction \omegai given an outgoing direction \omegao and 2D uniform random numbers u, returning the probability density of the sampled direction. Direction Convention: pbrt uses the convention that both \omegao and \omegai point away from the scattering point x. This is the same convention used for BSDFs in pbrt but differs from the scattering literature, where the incident direction typically points toward the scattering point. Implementers must account for this sign flip when adapting formulas from standard texts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class PhaseFunction: """ Abstract base class for phase functions in pbrt. """ def p(self, wo: Vector3f, wi: Vector3f) -> float: """ Evaluate the phase function value. Args: wo: Outgoing direction (unit vector, pointing away from scattering point). wi: Incident direction (unit vector, pointing away from scattering point). Returns: The phase function value p(wo, wi). """ # Pure virtual method. Must be implemented by subclasses. raise NotImplementedError def Samplep(self, wo: Vector3f, u: Point2f) -> tuple: """ Sample a new incident direction. Args: wo: Outgoing direction (unit vector, pointing away from scattering point). u: 2D uniform random variable [0,1]^2. Returns: A tuple (wi, pdf) where: wi: The sampled incident direction (unit vector, pointing away from scattering point). pdf: The probability density of the sampled direction with respect to solid angle. """ # Pure virtual method. Must be implemented by subclasses. raise NotImplementedError Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Direction Convention: As noted, the sign of the incident direction differs from standard literature. Using standard formulas directly without flipping the incident vector will result in incorrect scattering angles. Normalization: Phase functions are normalized such that \int{S^2} p(\omegao, \omegai) d\omegai = 1. This ensures energy conservation in the scattering model. The Ice Phase Function models light scattering by ice crystals in cirrus clouds, using data from Hess and Wiegner’s Cirrus Optical Properties system. It is characterized by distinct peaks at 22 and 46 degrees, which create halos when the sun penetrates optically thin cirrus clouds. These peaks exhibit wavelength dependence, resulting in chromatic halos. Time and Memory Complexity: The interface itself has O(1) time and memory complexity for evaluation and sampling, as it delegates to specific implementations. The complexity depends entirely on the subclass (e.g., Henyey-Greenstein is O(1), while tabulated or complex ice models may involve interpolation or lookup). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Provides a unified interface for diverse scattering models, enabling modular scene description. The direction convention aligns with pbrt's BSDF framework, simplifying integration. Limitations: The abstract nature requires careful implementation of sampling algorithms, which can be non-trivial for complex phase functions. The direction convention may confuse users familiar with standard scattering literature. When to Use: Use this interface when implementing custom phase functions within the pbrt framework. It is suitable for any participating media simulation requiring angular scattering distribution. The Phase Function Interface was introduced in the pbrt rendering system as part of its volume scattering module. It is documented in "Physically Based Rendering: From Theory to Implementation" (3rd edition), specifically in Chapter 11 on Volume Scattering. The interface design reflects pbrt's consistent use of outgoing-direction conventions for all transport quantities. 11.2 Phase Functions - pbr-book.org, https://pbr-book.org/3ed-2018/VolumeScattering/PhaseFunctions, fetched 2026-10-27 Efficient Rendering of Atmospheric Phenomena, https://doi.org/10.2312/egwr/egsr04/375-386, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Isotropic Phase Function
body: The Isotropic Phase Function models light scattering in a participating medium where all directions in the sphere of directions are equally likely to be chosen for scattering. It describes symmetric media where scattering probability is equal in all directions. Unlike anisotropic functions that depend on the scattering angle \theta, the isotropic function is constant and independent of both the incoming direction \omega' and outgoing direction -\omega. Inputs and Outputs: Input: None (the function is constant). Output: The phase function value fp, a scalar float. Data Structures: No specific data structures are required for the mathematical definition. In implementation contexts, it implements the PhaseFunction interface. Formula: The phase function value is defined as: fp(x, \omega, \omega') = \frac{1}{4 \pi} where: x is the spatial position in the medium. \omega is the outgoing direction (towards the eye). \omega' is the incoming direction (from the light source). 4 \pi is the solid angle of the full sphere, ensuring normalization. Normalization: The function is normalized such that the integral over the sphere of directions \mathbb{S}^2 equals 1: \int{\mathbb{S}^2} fp(x, \omega, \omega') d\omega = 1 This ensures that scattering does not artificially add or subtract radiance. Sampling: To sample a new direction \omega given an incoming direction \omega': 1. Generate a random unit vector \mathbf{v} uniformly distributed on the unit sphere \mathbb{S}^2. 2. The scattered direction is \omega = \mathbf{v}. 3. The probability density function (PDF) for any direction is p(\omega) = \frac{1}{4 \pi}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sampleisotropicphasefunction(omegain, randomu): """ Samples a new direction omegaout uniformly from the sphere. Args: omegain: Incoming direction vector (unused for isotropic, but part of interface). randomu: Random 2D point [u0, u1] in [0, 1)^2. Returns: omegaout: A random unit vector on the sphere. pdf: The probability density, which is 1/(4pi). """ # Generate a random unit vector uniformly on the sphere using spherical coordinates # cos(theta) is uniform in [-1, 1], phi is uniform in [0, 2pi) costheta = 2.0 randomu[1] - 1.0 theta = math.acos(costheta) phi = 2.0 math.pi randomu[0] sintheta = math.sqrt(max(0.0, 1.0 - costheta costheta)) omegaout = (sintheta math.cos(phi), sintheta math.sin(phi), costheta) pdf = 1.0 / (4.0 math.pi) return omegaout, pdf Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The value 1/(4\pi) is approximately 0.079577. No special precision handling is required. Boundaries: The function is valid everywhere in the medium. Degenerate Input: None. The function is constant. A specific implementation variant often used in path tracers for materials (not just participating media) where scattering is uniform in all directions. Definition: Scatters incident light uniformly in all directions, with attenuation determined by a spatial texture. Implementation: Inherits from a Material class. Fields: Texture texture. Constructor: explicit Isotropic(Texture texture). Step: 1. Generate a random unit vector for the scattered direction. 2. Create a scattered ray from the hit point with this random direction. 3. Set attenuation to the texture value at the hit point. 4. Return true. When to choose: Use when modeling diffuse, non-directional scattering surfaces or simple volumetric clouds where directionality is negligible and spatial variation in density/color is important. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(1) for evaluation and sampling. Memory: O(1) for the mathematical definition. The Isotropic Scattering variant requires storage for a texture pointer. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The computational cost does not scale with resolution or scene complexity, as it is a constant function. Strengths and Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use it and when not: Not given in the sources. The isotropic phase function is a fundamental concept in radiative transfer and computer graphics. It is used for air and gaseous types of media. It is implemented in rendering systems like pbrt as part of the PhaseFunction interface. name: In-scattering Model
head: In-Scattering Integration, Particle In-Scattering
body: In-scattering is the phenomenon where light is scattered from other directions back into the viewing direction as it travels through a participating medium. It represents the "light gained" component of radiative transfer, contrasting with out-scattering and absorption which constitute "light lost". While the Phase Function defines the angular distribution of scattering events, the In-scattering Model quantifies the accumulation of this scattered radiance along a ray, attenuated by the medium's extinction. The in-scattering model solves the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) to determine the radiance L arriving at a point p along a ray direction \omega. The method treats in-scattering as a source term S(p) that adds radiance to the ray, counteracted by the total extinction coefficient \sigmat. Inputs: Ray origin p(0) and direction \omega. Medium properties at position x: scattering coefficient \sigmas(x, \omega), extinction coefficient \sigmat(x, \omega), and phase function fp(x, \omega, \omega'). Incident radiance field Li(x, \omega') from all directions \omega'. True emission q(x, \omega) (optional, often zero in non-emissive media). Outputs: In-scattered radiance L(p, \omega) at the ray origin or any point t along the ray. The implementation requires access to the medium's spatially varying coefficients and the phase function. Medium Coefficients: A function or lookup table returning \sigmas(x) and \sigmat(x) for any 3D position x. Phase Function: A function fp(x, \omega, \omega') satisfying the normalization condition: \forall \omega \in \Omega: \; \int{S^2} fp (x, \omega, \omega^\prime) \; d\omega^\prime = 1 Incident Radiance: In offline rendering, this is often the result of a previous pass or a precomputed environment map. In real-time, it may be approximated or ignored (single scattering approximation). The differential change in radiance along a ray parameterized by distance t is governed by the first-order linear differential equation: \frac{dL(p)}{dt} = -\sigmat(p) L(p) + S(p) where S(p) is the in-scattering source term. The source term S(p) (also denoted as j(x, \omega) in some literature) represents the number of photons scattered into the path per unit length: S(p) = j(p, \omega) = \sigmas(p, \omega) \int{S^2} fp(p, \omega, \omega') Li(p, \omega') \, d\omega' + q(p, \omega) To solve for the radiance at the ray origin p(0), the equation is integrated from t=0 to \infty. The solution assumes that radiance at infinity is zero, L(p(\infty)) = 0. The general solution for radiance at any point t along the ray is: L(p(t)) = \intt^{\infty} e^{- \int{t}^{t'} \sigmat(p) \, dt''} S(p(t')) \, dt' Specifically, the in-scattered radiance at the start of the ray (t=0) is: L(p(0)) = \int0^{\infty} Tr(p(t) \rightarrow p(0)) S(p(t)) \, dt where Tr(p(t) \rightarrow p(0)) = e^{- \int{0}^{t} \sigmat(p) \, dt'} is the transmittance from point t to the origin. 1. Initialize: Set total in-scattered radiance L{in} = 0 and current transmittance T = 1.0. 2. Discretize Ray: Divide the ray segment of interest into N steps with uniform length \Delta t. 3. Iterate: For each step i from 0 to N-1: a. Calculate position pi = p(0) + ti \omega where ti = i \cdot \Delta t. b. Evaluate medium coefficients \sigmas(pi) and \sigmat(pi). c. Evaluate the incident radiance Li(pi, \omega') for all relevant incoming directions \omega'. d. Compute the source term S(pi): S(pi) = \sigmas(pi) \int{S^2} fp(pi, \omega, \omega') Li(pi, \omega') \, d\omega' + q(pi) e. Accumulate the contribution: L{in} \leftarrow L{in} + T \cdot S(pi) \cdot \Delta t f. Update transmittance for the next step: T \leftarrow T \cdot e^{-\sigmat(pi) \Delta t} 4. Output: Return L{in}. Scattering Coefficient \sigmas: Varies by medium. Not given in the sources. Extinction Coefficient \sigmat: \sigmat = \sigmaa + \sigmas. In non-absorbing media, \sigmat = \sigmas. Phase Function Anisotropy g: For Henyey-Greenstein, g \in [-1, 1]. g=0 is isotropic, g>0 is forward-scattering. Integration Steps N: Depends on optical depth. High optical depth requires more steps to avoid aliasing in the transmittance integral. Singularity at t=0: The transmittance Tr(p(0) \rightarrow p(0)) is exactly 1. Numerical integration must handle the start point carefully to avoid double-counting or division by zero if adaptive stepping is used. High Optical Depth: If \sigmat is large, transmittance decays rapidly. Contributions from distant points become negligible. Truncating the integral at a small transmittance threshold (e.g., 10^{-6}) is a valid optimization. Phase Function Normalization: The phase function must be normalized to 1 over the sphere. Incident Radiance Availability: The source term S(p) requires Li(p, \omega'). In single-scattering approximations, Li is often approximated by direct illumination only. Out-scattering is the phenomenon where photons are scattered away from their incident direction, causing a reduction in radiance along a ray as light travels through a participating medium. It represents the loss of light from the current viewing direction due to collisions with particles that deflect energy into other directions. Unlike in-scattering, which adds radiance, out-scattering acts as an attenuation term in the radiative transfer equation, often grouped with true absorption under the total extinction coefficient. In scattering accounts for the increase in radiance along a ray due to light scattering from other directions into the ray's current direction. It serves as the volumetric analog to the Bidirectional Scattering Distribution Function (BSDF), describing how radiance from the surrounding environment is redistributed into the viewing direction. Unlike out-scattering, which removes radiance from the ray, in-scattering adds radiance. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of ray steps and M is the number of directions sampled for the phase function integral. For single-scattering approximations, M is small (often 1 for direct light). Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing ray samples and medium coefficients. If precomputing incident radiance fields, memory scales with the resolution of the field. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Physically accurate representation of light transport in participating media. Captures the "glow" and color bleeding effects characteristic of fog, smoke, and subsurface scattering. Limitations: Computationally expensive for multiple scattering. Requires accurate knowledge of the incident radiance field, which is difficult to obtain in dynamic scenes. Single-scattering approximations fail in optically thick media. When to Use: Essential for realistic rendering of fog, clouds, smoke, and subsurface scattering effects. Avoid in real-time applications with strict performance constraints unless simplified approximations are acceptable. The in-scattering model is derived from the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE), a fundamental equation in atmospheric physics and astrophysics. The term "in-scattering" distinguishes the gain of radiance from "out-scattering" and absorption, which cause loss. The phase function, central to the model, was historically developed in atmospheric science to describe light scattering by molecules (Rayleigh) and larger particles (Mie). In computer graphics, the Henyey-Greenstein phase function became popular for its computational efficiency in modeling anisotropic scattering. name: Out-Scattering Model
head: Out Scattering, Scattering Loss, real scattering
body: Out-scattering is the phenomenon where photons are scattered away from their incident direction, causing a reduction in radiance along a ray as light travels through a participating medium. It represents the loss of light from the current viewing direction due to collisions with particles that deflect energy into other directions. Unlike in-scattering, which adds radiance, out-scattering acts as an attenuation term in the radiative transfer equation, often grouped with true absorption under the total extinction coefficient. Inputs and Outputs Input: Position p, direction \omega, incident radiance Li(p, -\omega), scattering coefficient \sigmas(p, \omega). Output: Differential change in radiance dLo(p, \omega) due to out-scattering. Data Structures Not given in the sources. Parameters \sigmas(p, \omega): Scattering coefficient (or scattering cross-section). Defined as the probability of an out-scattering event occurring per unit distance. It may vary with position p and direction \omega. dt: Differential length along the ray. \chi: Total extinction coefficient, defined as the sum of true absorption \kappa and out-scattering \sigmas (\chi = \kappa + \sigmas). W: Albedo, a measure of reflectivity or the ability to scatter, defined as W = \frac{\sigmas}{\chi} = \frac{\sigmas}{\kappa + \sigmas}. Formulas The differential reduction in radiance due to out-scattering is given by: dLo(p, \omega) = -\sigmas(p, \omega) Li(p, -\omega) dt Where: Li(p, -\omega) is the incident radiance arriving at point p from direction -\omega (the direction opposite to the ray's propagation \omega). The negative sign indicates a loss of radiance. The total reduction in radiance along a path segment is determined by integrating this differential loss, often combined with absorption in the transmittance calculation. The transmittance T over a distance d considering both absorption and out-scattering (extinction) is typically calculated using the Beer-Lambert law with the total extinction coefficient \chi. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeoutscatteringloss(position, direction, incidentradiance, scatteringcoefficient, deltalength): """ Computes the differential radiance loss due to out-scattering. Args: position: Current position p in the medium. direction: Ray propagation direction omega. incidentradiance: Radiance Li(p, -omega) arriving from the opposite direction. scatteringcoefficient: Scattering coefficient sigmas(p, omega). deltalength: Differential step size dt. Returns: dLo: The differential reduction in radiance. """ # Formula: dLo = -sigmas Li dt loss = -scatteringcoefficient incidentradiance deltalength return loss Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: If \sigmas is zero, there is no out-scattering loss. Boundary: The coefficient \sigmas must be defined within the medium boundaries. Distinction from Null Scattering: Out-scattering is part of "real scattering," distinct from "null scattering" techniques used for acceleration where scattering events are virtually ignored or handled differently. What it is: The complementary process where light is scattered into the current ray's direction from other directions. Difference: While out-scattering removes radiance from the current path, in-scattering adds radiance to it. When to choose: Must be computed alongside out-scattering for accurate volume rendering, as they are coupled in the radiative transfer equation. Link: In-scattering Model Time Complexity: The computation of the differential loss is O(1) per step. However, it is part of the integral solution to the radiative transfer equation, which generally requires integration over the path length. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the coefficient lookup if precomputed, or dependent on the volume data structure size. Strengths: Physically accurate representation of light loss in participating media. Limitations: Requires accurate knowledge of the scattering coefficient \sigmas, which can be difficult to measure or estimate. When to use: When rendering participating media where light attenuation due to scattering is significant. When not to use: For vacuum or non-participating media where \sigmas = 0. Out-scattering is a fundamental concept in the physics of light transport in participating media, described in standard computer graphics literature such as the Physically Based Rendering (PBRT) book. It is often introduced alongside absorption and in-scattering to explain the full radiative transfer equation. The term "real scattering" is used to distinguish it from null scattering approximations. name: In scattering
body: In scattering accounts for the increase in radiance along a ray due to light scattering from other directions into the ray's current direction. It serves as the volumetric analog to the Bidirectional Scattering Distribution Function (BSDF), describing how radiance from the surrounding environment is redistributed into the viewing direction. Unlike out-scattering, which removes radiance from the ray, in-scattering adds radiance. Inputs: Position p in the medium. Outgoing direction \omega (direction of the ray). Incident radiance field Li(p, \omegai) for all incoming directions \omegai \in \mathcal{S}^2. Phase function p(p, \omegai, \omega). Medium coefficients: absorption \sigmaa(p, \omega), scattering \sigmas(p, \omega), and total attenuation \sigmat(p, \omega) = \sigmaa(p, \omega) + \sigmas(p, \omega). Emitted radiance Le(p, \omega). Outputs: Added radiance per unit distance dLo^+(p, \omega). Not given in the sources. 1. Verify Assumptions: Inter-particle interactions can be ignored when describing scattering at a particular location if the separation between particles is at least a few times the lengths of their radii. 2. Compute Source Function Ls^+: Calculate the source function at position p for direction \omega, which accounts for both volume emission and in-scattering: Ls^+(p, \omega) = \frac{\sigmaa(p, \omega)}{\sigmat(p, \omega)} Le(p, \omega) + \frac{\sigmas(p, \omega)}{\sigmat(p, \omega)} \int{\mathcal{S}^2} p(p, \omegai, \omega) Li(p, \omegai) d\omegai The term \frac{\sigmas(p, \omega)}{\sigmat(p, \omega)} is the single-scattering albedo, representing the probability of scattering versus absorption. 3. Calculate Added Radiance: Multiply the source function by the total attenuation coefficient and the differential distance dt to obtain the total added radiance per unit distance: dLo^+(p, \omega) = \sigmat(p, \omega) Ls^+(p, \omega) dt Phase Function Normalization: The phase function p(\omega, \omega') must satisfy the normalization constraint: \int{\mathcal{S}^2} p(\omega, \omega') d\omega' = 1 This constraint ensures that phase functions act as probability distributions for scattering into a particular direction. Source Function: Ls^+(p, \omega) = \frac{\sigmaa(p, \omega)}{\sigmat(p, \omega)} Le(p, \omega) + \frac{\sigmas(p, \omega)}{\sigmat(p, \omega)} \int{\mathcal{S}^2} p(p, \omegai, \omega) Li(p, \omegai) d\omegai Ls^+: Source function (accounts for emission and in-scattering). \sigmaa: Absorption coefficient. \sigmas: Scattering coefficient. \sigmat: Total attenuation coefficient (\sigmaa + \sigmas). Le: Emitted radiance. Li: Incident radiance. \omegai: Incident direction. p: Phase function. Added Radiance: dLo^+(p, \omega) = \sigmat(p, \omega) Ls^+(p, \omega) dt dLo^+: Total added radiance per unit distance. dt: Differential distance. Single-Scattering Albedo: Defined as \sigmas / \sigmat. Under radiometry assumptions, this value is always between 0 and 1. It describes the probability of scattering versus absorption at a scattering event. Mean Free Path: Defined as 1 / \sigmat(p, \omega). This gives the average distance that a ray travels in a medium with attenuation coefficient \sigmat(p, \omega) before interacting with a particle. Inter-particle Interactions: The model assumes particles are sufficiently separated (at least a few times their radii) so that inter-particle interactions can be ignored when describing scattering at a particular location. Cosine Term Absence: Unlike surface scattering equations (e.g., Equation 4.14 in), the in-scattering source function does not include a cosine term because the phase function operates on radiance rather than differential irradiance. Normalization: The phase function must be normalized to 1 over the sphere. Absorption vs. Scattering: If the single-scattering albedo is 1 (no absorption), light scatters many times inside the medium, giving it a substantially different appearance. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def computeinscattering(p, omega, sigmaa, sigmas, sigmat, Le, phasefunction, incidentradiancesampler, numsamples): """ Computes the added radiance per unit distance due to in-scattering. Args: p: Position in the medium. omega: Outgoing direction. sigmaa: Absorption coefficient at p. sigmas: Scattering coefficient at p. sigmat: Total attenuation coefficient at p (sigmaa + sigmas). Le: Emitted radiance at p. phasefunction: Function evaluating p(omegai, omega). incidentradiancesampler: Function that samples Li(p, omegai) for a given omegai. numsamples: Number of Monte Carlo samples for the spherical integral. Returns: dLoplus: Added radiance per unit distance. """ if sigmat == 0: return 0.0 singlescatteringalbedo = sigmas / sigmat emissioncontribution = (sigmaa / sigmat) Le # The sources do not specify the integration method for the spherical integral. # Standard implementations use Monte Carlo sampling over S^2. integralsum = 0.0 for in range(numsamples): omegai = sampleuniformsphere() # integralsum += phasefunction(omegai, omega) incidentradiancesampler(omegai) sphericalintegral = (4.0 math.pi / numsamples) integralsum inscatteringcontribution = singlescatteringalbedo sphericalintegral Lsplus = emissioncontribution + inscatteringcontribution # dLo^+ = sigmat Ls^+ dt # Returns added radiance per unit distance (dt = 1) return sigmat Lsplus def sampleuniformsphere(): # u1 = random.random() u2 = random.random() theta = 2.0 math.pi u1 phi = math.acos(2.0 u2 - 1.0) return (math.sin(phi) math.cos(theta), math.sin(phi) math.sin(theta), math.cos(phi)) An operator that acts on an incoming radiance field g to produce a scattered outgoing radiance field, handling both surface scattering and volumetric scattering. It is defined as <\mathbf{K} g>(\bx, \bo):= \begin{cases} \displaystyle \int{\mathcal{S}^2} fs(\bx, \bo', \bo) g(\bx, \bo') |\vec{n} \cdot \bo'| \, d\bo' & \bx \in \mathcal{M} \\ \displaystyle \sigmas(\bx) \int{\mathcal{S}^2} fp(\bx, -\bo', \bo) g(\bx, \bo') \, d\bo' & \bx \in \mathcal{V} \end{cases}. Here \mathcal{M} is the set of object surfaces, \mathcal{V}:= \Omega \setminus \mathcal{M} is the medium space, and \Omega is the 3D simulation domain containing all surfaces and media. The computational cost is dominated by the spherical integral \int{\mathcal{S}^2} p(p, \omegai, \omega) Li(p, \omegai) d\omegai. Memory requirements are not given in the sources. The model accurately depicts the bright appearance of participating media like clouds and fog where light is scattered into the viewer's eye from other directions. In scattering is described in detail in "Physically Based Rendering: From Theory to Implementation" (PBR-book), specifically in Chapter 11 on Volume Scattering Processes. The concept is analogous to surface scattering but adapted for volumetric media, where the phase function replaces the BSDF. Cloud model examples illustrate the visual impact of in-scattering, particularly when absorption is negligible (single-scattering albedo of 1). 11.1 Volume Scattering Processes, https://pbr-book.org/4ed/VolumeScattering/VolumeScatteringProcesses, fetched 2026-10-29 (book) ボリュームレンダリング方程式(Volume Rendering Equation) 2, https://rayspace.xyz/notes/VLTE2/, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Radiative Transfer and Integral Equation Solvers
body: This family encompasses methods for solving the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) and related transport problems in participating media. Approaches range from deterministic angular discretization (Discrete Ordinates Method, Principal-Ordinates Propagation) and iterative integral equation solvers (Multiple Scattering Model) to analytical gradient computation for differentiable rendering (Differential Radiative Transfer, Differential Form of RTE). Some variants employ approximation bases like Spherical Harmonics or Gaussians, while others adapt Monte Carlo techniques with signed distance functions (sMCRT) or ratio estimators for accurate shadowing. The family covers both steady-state flux propagation and wave propagation formulations. All methods in this family are derived from the conservation of energy for a differential cylinder of light passing through a medium. They share the following core definitions and mechanisms: 1. Fundamental Interactions Any volumetric effect is composed of three fundamental characteristics: Absorption: The loss of radiant energy along a ray due to energy conversion (e.g., to heat). It is described by the absorption coefficient \sigmaa (units: m^{-1}). Emission: The addition of radiant energy where the medium is luminous (e.g., flames). It is described by the emissive term Le(\mathbf{p}, \boldsymbol{\omega}), representing radiance emitted per unit length. Scattering: The redirection of light rays upon collision with particles. It is split into: In-scattering: Light from other directions reflected into the view ray. Out-scattering: Light from the view ray reflected away. In most lighting calculations, out-scattering is folded into the extinction term because its net effect on the view ray is identical to absorption. 2. Notation \mathbf{p}: Position of interaction. \boldsymbol{\omega}: Ray direction (unit vector). L: Radiance quantity. Li: Incoming radiance. Lo: Outgoing radiance. \sigmat: Total extinction coefficient, \sigmat = \sigmaa + \sigmas. 3. Differential Forms The change in radiance dL over a differential path length dt is governed by the balance of loss and gain terms: Absorption Model: dL = -\sigmaa Li dt. Emission Model: dL = \sigmae dt (where \sigmae is the emission coefficient). General RTE: Combines extinction (loss) and source terms (gain from emission and in-scattering). 4. Transmittance The fraction of light surviving transmission through a medium is defined by the Beer-Lambert law: T = e^{-\tau} where \tau is the optical depth (integrated extinction). The Discrete Ordinates Method (DOM) solves the Radiative Transfer Equation by approximating the continuous angular dependence of radiance with a finite set of M discrete directions chosen to provide optimal Gaussian quadrature over the solid angle. It differs from the P-N method by working directly with directional intensities rather than spherical harmonic coefficients, and from ray-tracing methods by discretizing the angular domain into bins to mitigate ray effects. It is primarily used for computing multiple scattering in participating media, such as clouds, where it provides a global illumination solution via iterative flux propagation. The Multiple Scattering Model (Integral Equation) is a physically based illumination model that computes the radiance arriving at a pixel by integrating the contributions of light undergoing multiple scattering events along a ray through a participating medium. It solves for the directional intensity I(\mathbf{X}, \boldsymbol{\omega}) by accounting for emission, absorption, and the redirection of light from all possible incoming directions. Unlike single-scattering approximations, this model captures the complex interplay of light bounces, making it suitable for dense or high-albedo media where single-bounce assumptions fail. It is distinguished from its siblings by its formulation as a Fredholm integral equation of the second kind, where the unknown intensity appears on both sides of the equation, necessitating iterative solvers, spherical harmonic expansions, or stochastic sampling rather than direct evaluation. Principal-Ordinates Propagation (POP) is a deterministic finite-element method for real-time simulation of anisotropic light transport in heterogeneous participating media. It solves the problem of false scattering and ray effects inherent in previous finite-element methods by dynamically decomposing illumination into directional and point sources and propagating them in independent discrete domains aligned with principal light directions. Unlike methods using general bases like spherical harmonics, POP uses a computationally efficient unimodal basis implicitly aligned with the respective principal ordinate, allowing for virtually arbitrary scattering anisotropy and albedo without precomputation. This method solves the discrete diffusion equation and its differential counterpart to compute diffusion radiance (Ld^0), its derivative (\partial\pi Ld^0), first-order radiance (\vec{L}1^d), and its derivative (\partial\pi \vec{L}1^d). It is used to simulate fluid-like light diffusion in participating media, enabling the visualization of internal structures without global segmentation. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Discrete Ordinates Method by operating on a grid-based iterative solver for the diffusion approximation rather than discrete angular directions, and from Multiple Scattering Model (Integral Equation) by using a local Jacobi iteration on the differential form. This method solves for forward and backward acoustic wave amplitudes in a layered medium by formulating the coupled wave equations as a sparse linear system A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}. It captures multiple internal reflections and transmissions at voxel boundaries defined by acoustic impedance contrasts. Unlike integral equation solvers that approximate scattering over volumes, this approach models wave propagation along straight-line ray paths through discrete interfaces. The Differential Form of RTE provides an analytical method to compute the gradient of the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) with respect to medium density, enabling differentiable rendering for fluid modeling. It sets itself apart from numerical differentiation or automatic differentiation by deriving closed-form expressions for the derivatives of transmittance and single-scattering radiance directly from the continuous integral formulation. Spherical Harmonics (SH) and Spherical Gaussians (SG) are approximation methods for radiance transfer used in real-time or long-rendering scenarios to avoid expensive on-the-fly calculations of the light transport equation. They approximate the incident radiance field using Spherical Radial Basis Functions (SRBFs), which are then convolved with the Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF). SH is preferred for diffuse or rough surfaces, while SG is used for higher-frequency glossy terms or unified frameworks handling all-frequency shadows. Differential Radiative Transfer (DRTE) is a framework for computing the total derivative (gradient) of the interior radiance field L with respect to arbitrary scene parameters \pi by differentiating the integral operators in the combined Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) and Radiance Equation (RE). It solves the problem of obtaining unbiased gradients for volumetric lighting effects, which standard path tracing cannot provide due to discontinuities in visibility and geometry. What sets it apart from its siblings is its rigorous handling of the RTE's transport and collision operators, including boundary integrals arising from geometric discontinuities, whereas methods like Discrete Ordinates Method solve for the radiance itself without differentiation, and [Li et al. 2018a] only considers the RE for reflected/refracted radiance, neglecting the volumetric phenomena governed by the RTE. The Ratio Estimator is a Monte Carlo integration technique for volumetric light transport that separates the radiance integral into an analytically computed unoccluded term and a numerically estimated ratio of occluded to unoccluded radiance. It solves the problem of accurate shadowing in participating media by allowing existing sampling schemes (such as distance or equidistant sampling) to estimate visibility without bias, asymptotically converging to the correct solution even in multiple scattering scenarios. Unlike approximate moment-based estimators, this method provides an unbiased estimate by explicitly canceling the transmittance component through the ratio of two Monte Carlo estimates. Definition: Handling of direction bins where m > 1 by maintaining work, edge, and corner arrays only for separations s divisible by m, and spreading them for non-divisible s. Steps: For m=2 in 2-D, compute weights for cells a, b, c from integrals: \int{Bj} \int{V0} P(\omega, x) lm(\omega, x) dx where Bj is the shooting direction bin, V0 is the shooting cell, Vi is the receiving cell, P is the extended top of V0, and lm(\omega, x) is the length of the segment in which the ray through x in direction \omega intersects cell Vm. Assign weight in cell c to cell b to reduce spread, normalize a and b to sum to 1. For 3-D m>1, use Monte Carlo integration to determine weights due to complex ray/cell intersection geometry. On odd-numbered steps, use special weights to propagate flux. Definition: A geometry-based Monte Carlo radiation transfer method that uses signed distance functions to represent model geometry, enabling accurate modeling of smooth curved surfaces without voxels or meshes. Comparison: Compared to voxel-based MCRT methods for curved surfaces, sMCRT is up to forty-five times more accurate. Compared to voxel models for equivalent scenarios, sMCRT is up to three times faster. Usage: Validated for modeling arbitrary complex geometries such as microvascular vessel networks using SDFs. The Discrete Ordinates Method originated from neutron transport theory and was adapted for computer graphics. Principal-Ordinates Propagation was introduced to enable real-time rendering of anisotropic scattering. Differential Radiative Transfer represents a recent advancement in differentiable rendering. Spherical Harmonics and Gaussians are long-standing techniques in global illumination. The application of Sparse Linear Systems for wave propagation is rooted in acoustic and seismic modeling. The Multiple Scattering Integral Equation formulation is a direct mathematical consequence of the RTE. Efficient Light Propagation for Multiple Anisotropic Volume Scattering, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-87825-17, fetched 2026-10-26 (book) Enhanced Sphere Tracing | Request PDF - ResearchGate, https://www.researchgate.net/publication/265020476EnhancedSphereTracing, fetched 2026-11-03 (abstract only, unofficial)

name: Discrete Ordinates Method
head: Discrete Directions Method, Discrete Ordinates Method with Direction Bins, Languénou et al. Method, S-N method
body: The Discrete Ordinates Method (DOM) solves the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) by discretizing the continuous solid angle of directions into a finite set of M discrete bins. Unlike the Principal-Ordinates Propagation which tracks specific rays, or Spherical Harmonics and Spherical Gaussians for Radiance Transfer which uses global basis functions, DOM approximates the angular intensity distribution using local directional bins. It differs from the Multiple Scattering Model (Integral Equation) by avoiding the explicit computation of dense form factors between all voxel pairs, instead using iterative flux propagation. A primary drawback is the "ray effect," where energy propagates in narrow beams along discrete directions, missing regions between them. Inputs: Voxel grid of size n \times n \times n (total N = n^3 voxels). Medium properties per voxel: extinction coefficient \sigmat, scattering coefficient \sigmas, albedo a = \sigmas / \sigmat, emission coefficient \sigmae. Phase function p(\boldsymbol{\omega}', \boldsymbol{\omega}) approximated by an M \times M bin-to-bin matrix. Number of direction bins M. Outputs: Directional intensity I(\mathbf{X}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}j) for each voxel i and direction j. Pixel radiances via a final gathering pass. Data Structures: Intensity[N][M]: Stores I(\mathbf{X}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}j). FluxReceived[N][M]: Temporary array for accumulated flux at voxel i from direction j. PhaseMatrix[M][M]: Approximation of the phase function, where entry (j, l) represents scattering from bin j to bin l. Transparency: Precomputed or computed on-the-fly transmittance between voxels. Steps: 1. Discretize Directions: Choose M directions \{\boldsymbol{\omega}1, \dots, \boldsymbol{\omega}M\} to provide optimal Gaussian quadrature for solid angle integrals. A common implementation arranges bins on the 96 exterior faces of a 4 \times 4 \times 4 block of cubes, resulting in unequal solid angles. 2. Initialize: Set initial intensities based on boundary conditions and internal emission sources. 3. Iterative Propagation (Shooting): Repeat until convergence: a. For each direction bin j \in \{1, \dots, M\}: i. Layer-wise Propagation: Propagate flux from all voxels in the grid simultaneously along direction \boldsymbol{\omega}j. For each voxel, multiply the incoming flux by the voxel's transparency and distribute it to the four adjacent voxels determined by the direction bin \boldsymbol{\omega}j. This approximates the form factors F{klij} without precomputing them. ii. Accumulation: Deposit the received flux into FluxReceived at the target voxel. b. Scattering: For each voxel k and each incoming direction bin j: i. Scatter the accumulated flux in FluxReceived[k][j] to all M outgoing direction bins l using the phase matrix: I{new}(\mathbf{X}k, \boldsymbol{\omega}l) += \text{FluxReceived}[k][j] \times \text{PhaseMatrix}[j][l]. c. Update: Update the intensity field with the new scattered values. 4. Final Gathering: Perform a rendering pass along viewing rays using the computed intensity distribution I(\mathbf{X}, \boldsymbol{\omega}) to compute pixel radiances, providing one final directional scattering bounce. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def discreteordinatesmethod(voxels, phasematrix, numdirections, maxiterations, convergencethreshold): """ Solves radiative transfer using Discrete Ordinates Method. voxels: List of voxel properties (sigmat, sigmas, sigmae, albedo) phasematrix: M x M matrix for scattering between direction bins numdirections: M maxiterations: Maximum number of scattering bounces convergencethreshold: Stop if change in total energy is below this """ N = len(voxels) M = numdirections # Initialize intensities # I[i][j] stores intensity at voxel i in direction j I = [[0.0 for in range(M)] for in range(N)] # Initialize with emission and boundary conditions for i in range(N): for j in range(M): I[i][j] = voxels[i].sigmae # Simplified initialization for iteration in range(maxiterations): prevtotalenergy = sum(sum(row) for row in I) # Temporary array to accumulate flux received by each voxel from each direction fluxreceived = [[0.0 for in range(M)] for in range(N)] # Propagate flux for each direction bin for j in range(M): # Propagate along direction j # In a full implementation, this requires sorting voxels by depth along omegaj # and sweeping. Here we approximate the layer-wise propagation described in sources. # Note: The source describes distributing to 4 adjacent voxels. # A precise implementation needs a grid traversal algorithm. # Simplified simulation of the propagation step described in: # "flux entering each voxel is multiplied by the voxel's transparency # and then distributed to four adjacent voxels, determined by the direction bin" # Create a copy for simultaneous update newflux = [[0.0 for in range(M)] for in range(N)] for i in range(N): # Get flux leaving voxel i in direction j fluxout = I[i][j] # Calculate transparency of voxel i # T = exp(-sigmat voxelsize) # Assuming voxelsize = 1 for simplicity sigmat = voxels[i].sigmat transparency = math.exp(-sigmat) # Distribute to 4 adjacent voxels based on direction bin j # This is a simplification of the geometric projection described in # In reality, this depends on the specific geometry of the direction bin # and the voxel grid. adjacentvoxels = getadjacentvoxels(i, j) for k in adjacentvoxels: if 0 <= k < N: # Add contribution to fluxreceived at voxel k # The source says "distributed to four adjacent voxels" # We assume equal distribution for this simplified model fluxreceived[k][j] += fluxout transparency / len(adjacentvoxels) # After propagation, scatter received flux to all M directions for k in range(N): for l in range(M): # Scatter flux received in direction j to direction l # Using the phase matrix scatteringcoeff = phasematrix[j][l] I[k][l] += fluxreceived[k][j] scatteringcoeff # Check convergence currtotalenergy = sum(sum(row) for row in I) if abs(currtotalenergy - prevtotalenergy) < convergencethreshold: break # Final gathering pass # Render pixels by integrating I(X, omega) along viewing rays # This step is not detailed in the sources' algorithmic steps but mentioned as a final pass return I Parameters: M: Number of direction bins. Typical values include 6, 26, or 96 (from 4 \times 4 \times 4 cube faces). Albedo a: Ratio of scattering to extinction. In tests, a=0.99 was used. Convergence: Iterations stop when energy change is below a threshold. In tests, 15 iterations were sufficient for convergence on a 24 \times 24 \times 18 voxel cloud. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Effects: The primary pitfall is the "ray effect," where energy is propagated in narrow beams along discrete directions, missing regions between them. This can be mitigated by spreading intensity into solid angle bins rather than discrete rays. Precision: Computing all form factors F{klij} explicitly is prohibitively expensive (O(n^7 + n^6 M)). The iterative approximation is preferred when iterations are small compared to N. The Direction Bin Method computes higher-order (multiple) scattering in volume rendering by discretizing the sphere of directions into bins arranged on the exterior faces of a 3D grid of cubes and solving for flux transfer between these bins. It differs from Light Propagation for Multiple Anisotropic Volume Scattering by using a discrete bin-based flux spreading model rather than continuous light transport volumes. An extension of the discrete ordinates method that includes objects and sources inside the participating medium, handles highly anisotropic phase functions, and considers volumetric inelastic processes, particularly fluorescence. It has been applied to the rendering of underwater scenes where the sea is treated as a participating medium characterized by real experimental medium parametrizations. Time Complexity: Computing all form factors F{klij} explicitly costs O(n^7 + n^6 M) time. The iterative approximation propagates flux from all voxels in a layer simultaneously, effectively computing N^2 interactions in time O(N \log N) per direction bin. One iteration through all M shooting bins takes O(M N \log N + M^2 N) = O(M n^3 \log n + M^2 n^3) time. The scattering step takes O(MN) time per iteration. Cost per iteration is O(Mv) where v is the number of voxels. Memory Complexity: Stores N \times M unknown intensities. The matrix F{klij} has at least N^2 M non-zero coefficients if computed explicitly. Measured Performance: On an SGI Personal Iris 4D/35 with Mips 3000 processor, a 24 \times 24 \times 18 voxel cloud volume required 15 minutes per iteration for 15 iterations. Final rendering at 512 \times 384 resolution took 5 minutes. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Avoids the prohibitive cost of computing all form factors explicitly. Can handle multiple scattering efficiently with few iterations if albedo is high but flux exits edges. Limitations: Suffers from ray effects. Computationally expensive for large N and M. When to Use: Use when multiple scattering is important and ray effects can be mitigated by binning. Use when the number of iterations required for convergence is small compared to N. When Not to Use: Avoid when ray effects are unacceptable and cannot be mitigated by binning. Avoid when N is very large and M is large, leading to high computational cost. The Discrete Ordinates Method originates from neutron transport theory, where it is also known as the S-N method. It was adapted for volume rendering by Patmore [65] for local solutions and Languénou et al. [49, 48] for progressive refinement. Max [55] further developed the method for cloud rendering, introducing the layer-wise propagation approximation to avoid computing form factors. Cerezo and Serón [14] extended the method to include internal objects, sources, and fluorescence. A survey on participating media rendering techniques, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00371-005-0287-1, fetched 2026-10-26 Global Illumination Techniques for the Simulation of Participating Media, https://inria.hal.science/inria-00510096v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (book) [PDF] Optical Models for Direct Volume Rendering - Duke Computer Science, https://courses.cs.duke.edu/spring03/cps296.8/papers/max95opticalModelsForDirectVolumeRendering.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Optical models for direct volume rendering (PDF) - Academia.edu, https://www.academia.edu/49467168/Opticalmodelsfordirectvolumerendering, fetched 2026-10-27 Mathematical models for volume rendering and neutron transport, https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc1274949/?q=volume rendering equation, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Direction Bin Method for Multiple Scattering
body: The Direction Bin Method computes higher-order (multiple) scattering in volume rendering by discretizing the sphere of directions into bins arranged on the exterior faces of a 3D grid of cubes and solving for flux transfer between these bins. It differs from Light Propagation for Multiple Anisotropic Volume Scattering by using a discrete bin-based flux spreading model rather than continuous light transport volumes. Inputs: Voxel volume dimensions defining the spatial resolution of the cloud density (e.g., 24 \times 24 \times 18). Albedo a, the ratio of scattering to extinction (typical value: 0.99). Number of iterations for convergence (typical value: 15). Direction bin configuration: bins arranged on the exterior faces of a block of cubes (e.g., 96 bins on a 4 \times 4 \times 4 block). Outputs: Final rendered image at specified pixel resolution (e.g., 512 \times 384). Directional intensity distribution I(X, \omega) approximated for final gathering. Data Structures: Direction Bins: Discrete directions arranged on the exterior faces of a 3D grid of cubes. Phase Function Matrix P: An M \times M matrix where M is the number of direction bins. The element p(\omegai, \omegaj) accounts for the unequal solid angles of the direction bins. Flux Array: 3D volume grid storing flux values for each direction bin at each voxel, updated iteratively. Steps: 1. Arrange direction bins on the exterior faces of the chosen cube grid structure (e.g., 96 bins on a 4 \times 4 \times 4 block). 2. Construct the M \times M phase function matrix P where each entry p(\omegai, \omegaj) represents the scattering contribution from bin j to bin i, explicitly accounting for the unequal solid angles of the bins. 3. Iterate the scattering calculation for a fixed number of iterations (e.g., 15) to converge on the solution. 4. Perform a final gathering pass along viewing rays using the right-hand side of the radiative transfer equation to compute the final directional scattering bounce. Pseudocode: Unverified code. """ Vx, Vy, Vz = volumedensity.shape # Not given in the sources. Initialize flux state for all voxels and bins based on incident light. flux = np.zeros((Vx, Vy, Vz, numbins)) flux[:,:,:,:] = volumedensity[:,:,:, None] initialradiance for iteration in range(numiterations): # Not given in the sources. Propagate flux between bins for all voxels. newflux = np.zeroslike(flux) for v in range(Vx): for u in range(Vy): for w in range(Vz): for i in range(numbins): contribution = 0.0 for j in range(numbins): contribution += phasematrix[i, j] flux[v, u, w, j] newflux[v, u, w, i] = albedo contribution flux = newflux # Not given in the sources. Final gathering pass along viewing rays to produce final image. finalimage = np.zeros((outputheight, outputwidth)) for y in range(outputheight): for x in range(outputwidth): accumulated = 0.0 for t in range(raysteps): voxel = sampleray(x, y, t) accumulated += flux[voxel] densityfactor finalimage[y, x] = accumulated return finalimage Parameters: Albedo a: 0.99. Iteration count: 15. Voxel volume dimensions: 24 \times 24 \times 18. Output resolution: 512 \times 384. Direction bin configuration: 96 bins on a 4 \times 4 \times 4 block of cubes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Convergence speed is affected by boundary conditions; flux exiting the edges of the cloud accelerates convergence, requiring fewer iterations than a fully enclosed medium. Simultaneous Shooting is a method for efficiently spreading flux from a shooting voxel to receiving voxels in a volume by assuming flux is proportional to surface area on a unit direction cube, allowing simultaneous propagation for all pixels in a horizontal row. It builds on Direction Bin Method for Multiple Scattering by optimizing the transfer step between direction bins. It differs from Light Propagation for Multiple Anisotropic Volume Scattering by using a discrete bin-based flux spreading model rather than continuous light transport volumes. This method is a propagation approximation for computing multiple anisotropic light scattering in participating media, designed to reduce the "ray effect" artifacts inherent in traditional discrete ordinates methods. It achieves this by shooting radiosity into the entire solid angle of a direction bin rather than a single discrete representative direction. It builds on the Direction Bin Method for Multiple Scattering by introducing a shooting algorithm that accumulates opacity on the fly, avoiding the precomputation of complex form factors required by Galerkin finite element schemes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Each iteration took 15 minutes on an SGI Personal Iris 4D/35 with a Mips 3000 processor. The final rendering at 512 \times 384 resolution took 5 minutes. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Computes higher-order (multiple) scattering effects, increasing brightness and realism compared to single scattering approximations. Limitations: Performance is sensitive to the number of iterations required for convergence, which depends on boundary conditions. The method requires constructing and storing an M \times M phase function matrix, which scales quadratically with the number of direction bins. When to use: When multiple scattering effects are significant and computational resources allow for iterative solutions. When not to use: When real-time performance is required or when boundary conditions cause slow convergence. name: Simultaneous Shooting
head: 2-D flux propagation, binomial flux spreading
body: Simultaneous Shooting is a method for efficiently spreading flux from a shooting voxel to receiving voxels in a volume by assuming flux is proportional to surface area on a unit direction cube, allowing simultaneous propagation for all pixels in a horizontal row. It distinguishes itself from its sibling Light Propagation for Multiple Anisotropic Volume Scattering by distributing flux to neighbor voxels simultaneously for all voxels in a layer and accumulating attenuation along a set of possible propagation paths rather than a single straight line, which reduces the "ray effect". Inputs and Outputs: Input: Unshot radiosity/work values for a shooting plane (row in 2-D), resolution parameter m, grid dimensions n \times n. Output: Attenuated flux received by voxels in subsequent layers/rows. Data Structures: work[j]: Array of size columns (or n) storing current flux values for the shooting row. corner[0][j], corner[1][j]: Arrays of size columns storing corner flux contributions for the two diagonal directions. tempwork[j]: Temporary array of size columns for intermediate calculations. receive[i][j]: Accumulator for received flux at row i, column j. Parameters: m: Resolution parameter for direction bins. A unit cube face is divided into 2^m \times 2^m equal bins. Total direction bins M = 2^{4m^2}. n: Grid dimension (rows/columns). rows: Number of rows to propagate. columns: Number of columns (pixels) in a row. Steps: 1. Initialization: Let i0 be the starting row index. For j from 0 to columns - 1: set work[j] = unshot[i0][j], corner[0][j] = unshot[i0][j], and corner[1][j] = unshot[i0][j]. 2. Propagation Loop: For i from i0 to i0 + \text{rows} - 1: let s = i - i0 (distance from shooting plane). For j from 0 to columns - 1: set tempwork[j] = work[j]. Adjust for corner flux: if j > 0, update corner[0][j] += 0.5 \times \text{corner}[0][j-1] and corner[1][j] += 0.5 \times \text{corner}[1][j-1]. Add corner contributions to tempwork: tempwork[j] += 0.5 \times \text{corner}[0][j] and tempwork[j] += 0.5 \times \text{corner}[1][j]. Accumulate to receive: if s > 0, receive[i][j] += tempwork[j] / s^2. Update work[j] = unshot[i][j] for the next iteration. Formulas: Flux spreading weights in 2-D: The flux from a pixel is distributed to the pixel directly below and the pixel diagonally below-right with weight 1/2 each. Binomial path weighting: The opacity contribution from a pixel (j, k) is weighted by the number of propagation paths passing through it, involving binomial coefficients. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Attenuation is accumulated along many propagation paths (downward and diagonal steps) forming a parallelogram, not just the straight path, causing shadow blurring. The method assumes flux is proportional to surface area on the unit direction cube. Division by zero occurs if s = 0; the receiving step must be skipped or handled separately for the shooting plane itself. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def simultaneousshooting2d(unshot, rows, columns, i0=0): """ unshot: 2D array [rows+1][columns] of initial flux values for the shooting plane(s) rows: number of rows to propagate downwards columns: number of columns in the grid i0: starting row index for the shooting plane """ work = [0.0] columns corner0 = [0.0] columns corner1 = [0.0] columns tempwork = [0.0] columns receive = [[0.0] columns for in range(rows + 1)] # Initialize with the shooting row for j in range(columns): work[j] = unshot[i0][j] corner0[j] = unshot[i0][j] corner1[j] = unshot[i0][j] # Propagate flux for i in range(i0, i0 + rows): s = i - i0 for j in range(columns): tempwork[j] = work[j] # Adjust for corner flux if j > 0: corner0[j] += 0.5 corner0[j - 1] corner1[j] += 0.5 corner1[j - 1] tempwork[j] += 0.5 corner0[j] tempwork[j] += 0.5 corner1[j] # Accumulate to receive array, applying inverse square attenuation if s > 0: receive[i][j] += tempwork[j] / (s s) # Update work array for the next shooting row if i + 1 < len(unshot): for j in range(columns): work[j] = unshot[i + 1][j] Max's Method is a volume rendering technique for participating media that approximates radiative transfer by propagating energy across a grid, thereby avoiding the explicit computation of M^2 v^2 form factors required by finite element formulations. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by distributing flux to neighbor voxels simultaneously for all voxels in a layer and accumulating attenuation along a set of possible propagation paths rather than a single straight line, which reduces the "ray effect". 3-D Flux Propagation is an extension of 2-D propagation to 3-D where flux spreads across faces of a cubical shell. Voxels shared between two adjacent bins receive weight 1/2, voxels shared between four adjacent bins receive weight 1/4, and voxels at the eight cube corners shared between three adjacent bins receive weight 1/3. The weight pattern (1, 1/2, 1/4) is reconstructed by dividing values in the inner shell pattern by 4 and adding them to four direct or diagonal neighbors. Edge arrays are maintained using the 2-D procedure to add weight 1/2 edges, and four corner arrays adjust corner values to exactly 1. Weighted attenuated work values s layers beyond the shooting plane are divided by s^2 and added to the receive array. The O(n) factor can be reduced to O(\log n) by maintaining temporary arrays from all shooting layers and recursively consolidating them when the resulting error is small. The effective inverse square factor after consolidation is 1/(2(s-1)^2 + 2(s+1)^2) = 1/(2s^2 + 2) \approx 1/s^2 + 1/s^4 + O(1/s^6). Time Complexity: Computes O(n^3) interactions of a shooting row with pixels below it in time O(n^2), compared to O(n^4) for naive accumulation. For 3-D, propagating flux from n shooting planes to O(n^3) receiving elements takes O(n^3) time per bin, producing O(n^5) interactions. Total cost for a single bin direction for n planes is O(n^4). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficiently spreads flux, reducing computational cost from O(n^4) to O(n^3) for 2-D interactions. Reduces the "ray effect" by accumulating attenuation along multiple paths. Limitations: Shadow blurring occurs due to accumulation along many propagation paths. Complexity increases significantly in 3-D. Simultaneous Shooting is described in the source material as a technique for efficiently spreading flux in participating media. It is part of the broader field of radiative transfer and integral equation solvers, specifically within the Discrete Ordinates Method and Direction Bin Method for Multiple Scattering. Efficient Light Propagation for Multiple Anisotropic Volume Scattering, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-87825-17, fetched 2026-10-26 (book)
