name: Max's Method
head: Global Interactions (Max)
body: Max's Method is a volume rendering technique for participating media that approximates radiative transfer by propagating energy across a grid, thereby avoiding the explicit computation of M^2 v^2 form factors required by finite element formulations. It builds on Simultaneous Shooting and distinguishes itself from sibling methods by distributing flux to neighbor voxels simultaneously for all voxels in a layer and accumulating attenuation along a set of possible propagation paths rather than a single straight line, which reduces the "ray effect". Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid representing a participating medium (e.g., clouds or underwater scenes) with defined scattering and absorption properties, discretized into M direction bins. Output: The converged radiance or flux distribution within the volume. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D array where each voxel stores flux values. Exact field layouts and bit-packing are Not given in the sources. Direction Bins: The angular domain is discretized into M bins. Layers: Voxels are grouped into layers (slices) to enable simultaneous propagation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize flux values in all voxels based on source terms (e.g., light sources or initial emission). 2. Iteration Loop: Repeat until convergence or a fixed iteration count: 1. Layer Processing: For each layer of voxels in the grid: 1. Flux Distribution: For each direction bin, distribute the flux from the current voxel to related neighbor voxels simultaneously for all voxels in the layer. 2. Attenuation Accumulation: Accumulate attenuation between voxels along a set of possible propagation paths, rather than along the straight line joining them. 3. Multiple Scattering: Account for multiple scattering events produced within a single receiving element. 2. Scattering to Bins: Scatter the received flux of each voxel to the direction bins. 3. Visualization Pass: Compute pixel radiances using the source radiances of the voxels. Formulas and Parameters: Let v be the number of voxels in a layer or related dimension, M be the number of direction bins, and n be a parameter related to grid size or interaction count. The time to scatter the received flux of a voxel to direction bins is O(Mv). The propagation cost for v^2 interactions is O(v \log n). The final cost per iteration is O(Mv \log n + M^2 v). Source reports the scatter time as O(1) and the final cost per iteration as O(N) where N is the total number of voxels, noting this avoids the O(N^2) cost of computing all form factors. The sources differ in complexity notation; uses M and v, while uses N. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Effect: The method reduces the "ray effect" because energy is propagated through the whole bin, not only through a single direction. Convergence: The method is most efficient when the number of iterations required to converge is small compared to v. If many iterations are needed, computing the whole set of form factors (cost O(v^2 n + v^2 M)) and solving the resulting system may be preferable. Time Complexity: The final cost per iteration is O(Mv \log n + M^2 v) according to, or O(N) according to. This is better than computing the whole set of form factors (cost O(v^2 n + v^2 M) or O(N^2)) when the number of iterations required to converge is small compared to v. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Avoids the high cost of computing M^2 v^2 form factors; reduces ray effects; efficient for scenes requiring few scattering iterations. Limitations: Efficiency degrades if many iterations are required; approximation of attenuation paths may lack precision compared to exact ray tracing. When to use: Rendering clouds or participating media where computational efficiency is prioritized and the scattering order is low. When not to use: When high precision in attenuation paths is required or when the medium requires many scattering iterations to converge. Max's Method, also known as Global Interactions, was proposed by Max. It is devoted to rendering clouds and has been applied to underwater scenes where the sea is treated as a participating medium characterized by real experimental medium parametrizations. It falls under the category of methods that consider a set of specific directions, which can be considered a restriction of the 3D-filter used in other methods. A survey on participating media rendering techniques, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00371-005-0287-1, fetched 2026-10-26 Global Illumination Techniques for the Simulation of Participating Media, https://inria.hal.science/inria-00510096v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (book) Overview of Volume Rendering - Stony Brook Computer Science, https://www3.cs.stonybrook.edu/~mueller/papers/volvisOverview.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Light Propagation for Multiple Anisotropic Volume Scattering
head: Discrete Ordinates with Direction Bins, Shooting Method with Direction Bins
body: This method is a propagation approximation for computing multiple anisotropic light scattering in participating media, designed to reduce the "ray effect" artifacts inherent in traditional discrete ordinates methods. It achieves this by shooting radiosity into the entire solid angle of a direction bin rather than a single discrete representative direction. It builds on the Direction Bin Method for Multiple Scattering by introducing a shooting algorithm that accumulates opacity on the fly, avoiding the precomputation of complex form factors required by Galerkin finite element schemes. The method operates on a regular cubical grid of voxels and discretizes the unit sphere of directions into M bins. It solves the radiative transfer equation by iteratively propagating radiosity through these bins, using a precomputed scattering matrix for intermediate bounces and exact directions only for the source and viewer interactions. Inputs: Grid: A regular cubic volume of n \times n \times n elements (voxels) with total elements N = n^3. Opacity: An array kt[k] of size N, storing the total opacity (absorption plus scattering) per unit length for each voxel Vk, assumed constant within each element. Albedo: A scalar a, representing the fraction of removed intensity scattered in other directions, assumed constant everywhere. Phase Function: Defined by the Henyey-Greenstein parameter g \in [-1, 1], where positive g indicates forward scattering, negative backward, and 0 isotropic. Direction Bins: The unit sphere is divided into M bins; typical values use powers of 2 subdivisions on cube faces. Light Source: Incoming illumination defined by exact directions and intensity for the first bounce. Viewpoint: The camera position for the final bounce. Outputs: Radiosity: The final intensity distribution, stored in the matrix l[k][l]. 1. kt[k]: Array of size N. Stores total opacity per unit length for voxel k. 2. l[k][l]: Matrix of size M \times N. Stores radiosity (intensity multiplied by the solid angle of bin Bl) for voxel k and direction bin l. 3. unshot[k][l]: Auxiliary array of size M \times N. Stores radiosity waiting to be propagated from voxel k into bin l. 4. bintobin[l][m]: Matrix of size M \times M. Precomputed fraction of flux from bin l directions that scatters into bin m. The Henyey-Greenstein phase function f(\omega, \omega') is defined as: f(\omega, \omega') = \frac{1 - g^2}{4\pi (1 + g^2 - 2gx)^{3/2}} where x is the dot product of the unit direction vectors \omega and \omega', and g is the anisotropy parameter. The bintobin matrix is precomputed via Simpson's rule integration over the direction bins: bintobin[l][m] = \int{Bl} \int{Bm} f(\omega, \omega') \, d\omega \, d\omega' normalized by the solid angles of the bins to yield the fraction of flux. M: Number of direction bins. Typical values are powers of 2 subdivisions on cube faces. n: Number of voxels along one dimension. a: Albedo (constant). g: Henyey-Greenstein parameter, [-1, 1]. 1. Precalculate Scattering Matrix: Compute the M \times M matrix bintobin[l][m] using Simpson's rule integration of the Henyey-Greenstein phase function over the direction bins Bl and Bm. 2. Initialize Unshot Radiosity: Initialize the unshot[k][l] array with the incoming illumination from the light source, using exact directions for the first bounce. 3. Iterate Shooting Directions: Loop through M shooting directions (bins). For each bin l, shoot radiosity from source elements into the whole solid angle of bin l. 4. Accumulate Opacity: Accumulate opacity on the fly as radiosity propagates through the voxels. 5. Handle Multiple Scattering: Within the receiving element, account for multiple scattering events before proceeding to the next shooting step by redistributing the scattered energy into the appropriate bins using the bintobin matrix. 6. Final Bounce: After all intermediate bounces are processed, compute the final intensity at the viewpoint using exact directions from the voxels to the camera. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def lightpropagation(n, M, a, g, kt, lightsourcedata, viewpointdata): """ n: int, number of voxels per dimension M: int, number of direction bins a: float, albedo (constant) g: float, Henyey-Greenstein parameter kt: list of float, opacity per unit length for N=n^3 voxels lightsourcedata: list of (dirvec, intensity) tuples for first bounce viewpointdata: list of dirvec tuples for final bounce """ N = n 3 radiosity = [[0.0] M for in range(N)] unshot = [[0.0] M for in range(N)] bintobin = [[0.0] M for in range(M)] # Step 1: Precalculate scattering matrix via Simpson's rule integration over direction bins for lidx in range(M): for midx in range(M): # Integrate f(omega, omega') over solid angles of bins Bl and Bm using Simpson's rule bintobin[lidx][midx] = 0.0 # Step 2: Initialize unshot array with incoming illumination from light source for dirvec, intensity in lightsourcedata: # Map direction vector to bin index based on unit cube face subdivision binidx = 0 for k in range(N): unshot[k][binidx] += intensity # Step 3: Iterate through M shooting directions for lidx in range(M): for k in range(N): if unshot[k][lidx] > 0: radiosityval = unshot[k][lidx] unshot[k][lidx] = 0.0 # Handle multiple scattering within the single receiving element before next step scattered = radiosityval a for midx in range(M): unshot[k][midx] += scattered bintobin[lidx][midx] # Propagate radiosity to other voxels, accumulating opacity on the fly currentpos = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) currentdir = (1.0, 0.0, 0.0) remainingradiosity = radiosityval for step in range(n): nextvoxel = (step + 1) % N opacityfactor = math.exp(-kt[nextvoxel] 1.0) remainingradiosity = opacityfactor if remainingradiosity < 1e-6: break # Deposit scattered energy into unshot for nextvoxel # (Implementation details for ray traversal and deposit omitted as sources do not specify grid traversal routine) currentpos = (currentpos[0] + currentdir[0], currentpos[1] + currentdir[1], currentpos[2] + currentdir[2]) # Step 4: Final bounce to viewpoint using exact directions finalimage = 0.0 for dirvec in viewpointdata: # Map direction vector to bin index binidx = 0 for k in range(N): finalimage += radiosity[k][binidx] return finalimage Grid Homogeneity: The method requires a regular cubical grid and relies on grid homogeneity, and does not work on general finite element meshes. Ray Effects: While reduced compared to traditional discrete ordinates, artifacts may persist if the number of bins M is too low. Precision: Accumulating opacity on the fly may introduce numerical errors if not handled carefully, though the text does not specify mitigation strategies. Time Complexity: O(M n^3 \log n + M^2 n^3) per pass through M shooting directions, with total time O(M N \log N + M^2 N) where N=n^3. This is a significant speedup compared to Tan's point collocation method which has O(n^7 + M^2 n^6) cost. Space Complexity: O(M n^3) for storing radiosity and unshot radiosity, plus O(M^2) for the bintobin matrix. This avoids the O(M^2 N^2) storage required by Galerkin finite element schemes. Strengths: Reduces ray effects compared to traditional discrete ordinates; efficient for regular grids; avoids precomputing complex form factors. Limitations: Restricted to regular cubical grids; requires sufficient M to minimize artifacts; assumes constant albedo. When to Use: Suitable for rendering participating media like clouds on regular grids where multiple anisotropic scattering is important and ray effects are a concern. When Not to Use: Not suitable for general finite element meshes or irregular grids. The method was presented in 1993 as an efficient propagation approximation for multiple anisotropic volume scattering. It builds on the discrete ordinates method from radiation transfer [Sic92, Chan50] and the progressive radiosity method for surface illumination [Coh87]. It was inspired by Patmore's work on discrete ordinates shooting for cloud rendering [Patm93]. The Henyey-Greenstein phase function used is based on Mie scattering theory [Heny40, Mie09]. name: Principal-Ordinates Propagation
body: Principal-Ordinates Propagation (POP) is a deterministic finite-element method for real-time simulation of anisotropic light transport in heterogeneous participating media. It solves the problem of false scattering and ray effects inherent in previous finite-element methods by dynamically decomposing illumination into directional and point sources and propagating them in independent discrete domains aligned with principal light directions. Unlike methods using general bases like spherical harmonics, POP uses a computationally efficient unimodal basis implicitly aligned with the respective principal ordinate, allowing for virtually arbitrary scattering anisotropy and albedo without precomputation. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Medium properties (\sigmaa, \sigmas), light sources (directional or point), observer position \mathbf{c}, and parameters: number of principal ordinates N{ord}, grid resolution N{grid}, and propagation iterations M. Outputs: Final accumulated radiance L{acc} at the observer position, computed via ray-marching through the merged grid data. Data Structures The core data structure is the Propagation Grid. For each principal ordinate, a separate grid is maintained. Grid Layout: Uniform rectilinear grid for directional lights; spherical grid for point lights. Cell Data: Each cell stores: L: Radiance magnitude (scalar). a: Henyey-Greenstein (HG) anisotropy parameter for the directional distribution (scalar, range [-1, 1]). \sigmas: Scattering coefficient (scalar, m^{-1}). \sigmaa: Absorption coefficient (scalar, m^{-1}). \mathbf{x}: Cell center position (vector). Memory: Two grids are maintained in memory: the current iteration grid Lm and the accumulated result grid L{acc}. Formulas HG Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF): Used to integrate radiance over the solid angle subtended by the destination cell: F{hg}(\mu, a) = \frac{1-a}{4\pi a} \left( \frac{1}{1 + a - 2a\mu} - \frac{1}{1+a} \right) where \mu is the cosine of the angle between the direction and the principal ordinate, and a is the anisotropy parameter. Transmittance: Computed using the Beer-Lambert-Bouguer law with averaged absorption coefficient and distance t: T{src \to dst} = e^{-\bar{\sigma}a t} Solid Angle Parametrization: Approximate parametrization (\theta1, \theta2, |\phi1 - \phi2|) for the solid angle \Omega{src \to dst} subtended by the destination cell relative to the source cell: (\theta1, \theta2, |\phi1 - \phi2|) = \begin{cases} (0, \pi/4, 2\pi) & \text{if } dst \text{ is in front of } src \\ (\pi/4, 3\pi/4, 2) & \text{if } dst \text{ is next to } src \\ (3\pi/4, \pi, 2\pi) & \text{if } dst \text{ is behind } src \end{cases} Radiance Contribution: The contribution from a source cell src to a destination cell dst: \Delta L{src \to dst} = L{src} \cdot T{src \to dst} \cdot |\phi1 - \phi2| \cdot \left( F{hg}(\cos \theta1, a{src}) - F{hg}(\cos \theta2, a{src}) \right) Anisotropy Update: The new anisotropy a{dst} is updated by accumulating contributions weighted by their anisotropy: a{dst} = \frac{\sum{src} \Delta L{src \to dst} \cdot a{src}}{\sum{src} \Delta L{src \to dst}} Note: This arithmetic average is an approximation; combining multiple HG distributions with different anisotropy values cannot generally be represented by a single HG distribution. Algorithm Steps 1. Determine Principal Ordinates: Identify N{ord} principal directions. For distant lights, these are the light directions; for local lights, directions are sampled from the source. Importance sampling may be used to prioritize significant directions. 2. Initialize Grids: For each principal ordinate: Create a grid (rectilinear for directional, spherical for point). Initialize cell radiance L by ray-marching from the light source into the medium, applying attenuation Ti = L{in}(d) \cdot Ti. Initialize anisotropy a = 1 (equivalent to a Dirac function in the direction d). Initialize L{acc} to zero. 3. Propagation Loop: Repeat M times (typical values: 10 or 30): Create a temporary grid L{m+1} initialized to zero. For each cell dst in the grid: Initialize L{dst} = 0 and a{dst} = 0. For each of the 6 neighbors src: Compute transmittance T{src \to dst} using averaged \sigmaa and distance. Determine solid angle parameters (\theta1, \theta2, |\phi1 - \phi2|) based on relative position. Compute \Delta L{src \to dst} using the formula above. Accumulate radiance: L{dst} \leftarrow L{dst} + \Delta L{src \to dst}. Accumulate weighted anisotropy: a{dst} \leftarrow a{dst} + \Delta L{src \to dst} \cdot a{src}. Normalize anisotropy: If \sum \Delta L > 0, a{dst} \leftarrow a{dst} / L{dst}. Clamp a{dst} to [-1, 1]. Swap Lm and L{m+1}. Update Accumulation: L{acc, i}^{m+1} = L{acc, i}^m + L{m+1}(xi, c - xi), where c is the observer position and the term represents the radiance towards the observer. 4. Residuum Propagation (Optional): If the medium is optically thick, switch to the cheaper isotropic propagation mode earlier to save computation. This uses lower-resolution propagation domains for the remaining energy. 5. Rendering: Ray-march from the observer position through the merged L{acc} grid to compute final pixel colors. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def principalordinatespropagation(lightsources, medium, observer, nordinates, gridres, iterations): # Determine principal ordinates based on light directions and importance. ordinates = [] # List of direction vectors # Implementation details for ordinate selection are not provided in the sources. # Initialize grids for each ordinate grids = [] for direction in ordinates: # Create rectilinear grid for directional lights, spherical for point lights. grid = Grid(gridres, direction) # Initialize radiance by ray-marching from light source with attenuation. # Initialize anisotropy a = 1 for all cells. initializegrid(grid, lightsources, direction, medium) grids.append(grid) # Propagation Loop for m in range(iterations): newgrids = [] for grid in grids: newgrid = Grid(gridres, grid.direction) for dstcell in grid.cells: ldst = 0.0 adst = 0.0 for srccell in dstcell.neighbors: # Compute transmittance using averaged sigmaa and distance. sigmaaavg = (grid.sigmaa[srccell] + grid.sigmaa[dstcell]) / 2.0 dist = distance(srccell.position, dstcell.position) tsrcdst = exp(-sigmaaavg dist) # Solid angle parameters based on relative position. theta1, theta2, phidiff = getsolidangleparams(srccell, dstcell) # Compute radiance contribution. fhg1 = hgcdf(cos(theta1), grid.anisotropy[srccell]) fhg2 = hgcdf(cos(theta2), grid.anisotropy[srccell]) deltal = grid.radiance[srccell] tsrcdst abs(phidiff) (fhg1 - fhg2) ldst += deltal adst += deltal grid.anisotropy[srccell] # Normalize anisotropy. if ldst > 0: adst /= ldst adst = max(-1.0, min(1.0, adst)) newgrid.radiance[dstcell] = ldst newgrid.anisotropy[dstcell] = adst newgrids.append(newgrid) # Update accumulation. for grid, newgrid in zip(grids, newgrids): for cell in grid.cells: viewdir = observer - cell.position mu = dot(normalize(viewdir), grid.direction) fhgobs = hgcdf(mu, newgrid.anisotropy[cell]) grid.accumulated[cell] += newgrid.radiance[cell] fhgobs grids = newgrids # Residuum propagation: switch to cheaper isotropic propagation mode for optically thick media. # Implementation details for residuum propagation are not provided in the sources. # Render: Ray-march from observer through merged accumulated grid. return renderfromaccumulated(grids, observer, medium) def hgcdf(mu, a): # Henyey-Greenstein CDF for anisotropy parameter a. if a == 0: return 0.5 return (1 - a) / (4 pi a) (1 / (1 + a - 2 a mu) - 1 / (1 + a)) def getsolidangleparams(src, dst): # Returns (theta1, theta2, phidiff) based on relative position. if dst.isinfrontof(src): return (0, pi/4, 2pi) elif dst.isnextto(src): return (pi/4, 3pi/4, 2) else: return (3pi/4, pi, 2pi) Isotropic Residuum Propagation (IR propagation) is a secondary propagation stage within Principal-Ordinates Propagation that rapidly transports remaining isotropic energy after the initial anisotropic phase. It solves the problem of high computational cost in optically thick media by switching from expensive directional propagation to a cheaper single-grid isotropic scheme once radiance anisotropy falls below a threshold. It sets itself apart from full anisotropic propagation by merging multiple directional grids into one global grid, achieving significant speed-ups with negligible visual difference for the residuum energy. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of grid cells, number of principal ordinates, and number of iterations. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of grid cells and principal ordinates. Performance: Renders dense smoke with strong multiple anisotropic scattering at 25 Hz on an NVidia GeForce GTX 770 without precomputations. Rendering speed for clouds with g=0.96 is 35 Hz using 64 ordinates and 20^3 grid resolution for each cloud, with 15 propagation iterations. Typical Frame Breakdown: 5 ms importance propagation, 2 ms determining ordinates, 2 ms grid initialization, 12 ms propagation, 2 ms residuum propagation, 4 ms grid merging and upsampling, 5 ms ray-marching. Strengths: Real-time performance on GPUs; handles heterogeneous media; supports arbitrary scattering anisotropy and albedo; no precomputation required; reduces false scattering and ray effects compared to other finite-element methods. Limitations: Biased method; combining multiple HG distributions with different anisotropy values is an approximation (arithmetic average); requires recomputation on every observer position change; performance scales with the number of ordinates and grid resolution. When to Use: Real-time rendering of participating media with strong anisotropic scattering (e.g., smoke, clouds, steam) where visual plausibility is prioritized over strict physical accuracy. When Not to Use: When unbiased results are required; when the medium is extremely optically thin and simple ray-marching is sufficient; when precomputation is allowed and offline quality is prioritized. Principal-Ordinates Propagation was introduced by Elek et al. from the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology in 2014. It was developed to address the challenges of real-time light transport simulation in participating media, specifically aiming to overcome the limitations of existing finite-element methods such as false scattering and ray effects. The method builds on the principles of radiative transfer and integral equation solvers, adapting them for efficient GPU implementation. It is used in real-time rendering applications, such as the dynamic rendering of smoke plumes and clouds. name: Isotropic Residuum Propagation
head: IR propagation
body: Isotropic Residuum Propagation (IR propagation) is a secondary optimization stage within Principal-Ordinates Propagation [4121-principal-ordinates-propagation.md] that accelerates light transport simulation by switching from expensive anisotropic propagation to cheaper isotropic propagation once radiance anisotropy falls below a threshold. It solves the problem of high computational cost in optically thick media by merging multiple directional propagation grids into a single global grid, reducing propagation costs tremendously while maintaining negligible visual difference compared to full anisotropic propagation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Propagation state after m0 anisotropic iterations; maximum radiance anisotropy ab; phase function anisotropy g; scattering coefficient \sigmas; grid spacing \Delta x; anisotropy threshold \varepsilona. Outputs: Final radiance distribution stored in a single global grid. Data Structures: Propagation Grids: Initially, multiple grids aligned with principal ordinates. After switching, a single global grid aligned with the medium (no directionality). Radiance Fields: Stored per grid cell. Anisotropy metrics a{n,i} are tracked per cell and ordinate during anisotropic phase. Parameters: \varepsilona: Small anisotropy threshold. Typical value: around 0.1 or higher. m0: Iteration count at which switch occurs. Determined by formula below. \Delta x: Grid spacing. Typical value: 0.25 m. Steps: 1. Initialization: Determine ab (maximum radiance anisotropy, typically 1 for directional light, lower if prefiltered) and g (phase function anisotropy) at initialization. 2. Calculate Switch Iteration m0: Compute the number of anisotropic iterations required for light anisotropy to fall below \varepsilona using the Henyey-Greenstein (HG) self-convolution property: m0 = \frac{\ln \varepsilona - \ln ab}{\ln g} \cdot \frac{1}{\sigmas \cdot \Delta x} 3. Anisotropic Propagation: Perform m0 iterations of Principal-Ordinates Propagation. During this phase, track anisotropy a{n,i} for each cell i and ordinate n. 4. Check Anisotropy Criterion: After m0 iterations, check if |a{n,i}| < \varepsilona for all i, n. If not, continue anisotropic propagation until criterion is met or m0 is reached. 5. Merge Grids: Once the criterion is fulfilled, merge energy from all directional propagation grids into a single global grid aligned with the medium, as directionality is no longer present. Use double the resolution of individual grids to allow light penetration from the first row of cells. 6. Isotropic Propagation: Perform additional iterations on the single global grid to propagate the remaining isotropic residuum energy. Iterate until residual energy falls below \varepsilonL or a fixed number of iterations. 7. Final Accumulation: Combine results with other pipeline stages (e.g., ray-marching). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def isotropicresiduumpropagation(grids, sigmas, deltax, g, ab, epsilona, epsilonL=None, maxisotropiciters=20): # Step 2: Calculate switch iteration m0 # Guard against g=1 to avoid division by zero if g == 1.0: m0 = float('inf') else: m0 = (math.log(epsilona) - math.log(ab)) / (math.log(g) sigmas deltax) # Ensure m0 is at least equal to grid resolution along propagation direction gridres = len(grids[0].cells) m0 = max(m0, gridres) # Step 3 & 4: Anisotropic Propagation & Check Criterion for m in range(int(m0)): for grid in grids: for cell in grid.cells: # Transport update per cell/ordinate handled by parent method for n in grid.ordinates: # Anisotropy metric a{n,i} tracked per cell/ordinate totalenergy = sum(cell.radiance) cell.anisotropy[n] = abs(cell.radiance[n]) / max(totalenergy, 1e-8) # Check if all cells and ordinates satisfy the isotropy criterion |a{n,i}| < epsilona allisotropic = all(abs(cell.anisotropy[n]) < epsilona for grid in grids for cell in grid.cells for n in grid.ordinates) if allisotropic: break # Step 5: Merge Grids globalres = 2 gridres globalgrid = Grid(resolution=globalres) for grid in grids: for cell in grid.cells: # Interpolate and accumulate radiance from directional grids into global grid for n in cell.radiance: globalgrid.accumulate(cell.radiance[n], cell.position) # Step 6: Isotropic Propagation for in range(maxisotropiciters): for cell in globalgrid.cells: # Transport update per cell handled by parent method pass # Check residual energy threshold if provided residual = sum(cell.radiance for cell in globalgrid.cells) if epsilonL is not None and residual < epsilonL: break return globalgrid Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Logarithm of g when g \approx 1 can cause numerical instability. Guard against division by zero or near-zero. Boundaries: Merging grids requires careful handling of boundary conditions to avoid artifacts. Use double resolution to mitigate penetration issues. Degenerate Input: If g=1 (isotropic scattering), anisotropy does not decrease, and IR propagation may not trigger. Handle by falling back to full anisotropic propagation or treating as isotropic from start. Light Propagation Maps (LPM) is a Discrete Ordinate Method (DOM) technique for computing multiple scattering in participating media. It approximates the radiative transfer equation by decoupling spatial and directional sampling: it uses high-resolution 2D maps for iterative light propagation to minimize false scattering and ray effects, while using coarse 3D grids for storing accumulated radiance. This approach reduces memory usage and artifacts compared to standard DOM techniques that require fine sampling in both space and direction. For distant environment illumination, multiple superimposed propagation grids are used, oriented along different principal directions to cover the environment map's solid angles. Prefiltering is applied to incident radiance from the environment map for each grid's finite solid angle to avoid singularity issues during initialization. This allows efficient handling of environment lighting with a low number of iterations per grid. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: IR propagation provides a ~4-fold speed-up compared to full anisotropic propagation. Typical setting takes 2 ms for residuum propagation, with total combined propagation time around 24-28 ms for the dragon dataset. Full propagation took 90-120 ms. Memory: Reduces memory usage by merging multiple grids into a single global grid during isotropic phase. Measured Performance: Hardware/Scene: Dragon dataset (milk, \sigmas = \{0.91, 1.07, 1.25\} m^{-1}, g = 0.95, albedo > 99.9%). Resolution: 32^3 grid for IR propagation, 16^3 grid for full propagation (with 64 ordinates). Performance: IR propagation (m0=20) took 28 ms (#1) and 24 ms (#2). Full propagation took 120 ms (#1) and 90 ms (#2). Scaling: Media with higher optical thickness decrease anisotropy faster, allowing earlier switch to isotropic propagation. Isotropic transport has low-frequency lighting, allowing lower-resolution propagation domains. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Efficiently handles optically thick anisotropic media; reduces propagation costs tremendously; negligible visual difference. Limitations: Heuristic nature introduces bias; requires careful tuning of \varepsilona and m0. When to Use: Use for optically thick media with high albedo where anisotropy reduces quickly. Not suitable for highly anisotropic media where anisotropy persists, or when prefiltering is not applied. Isotropic Residuum Propagation was introduced in the paper "Principal-Ordinates Propagation for Real-Time Rendering of Participating Media" by Elek et al. (2014). It is part of the Principal-Ordinates Propagation method, which aims to solve false scattering and ray effects in finite-element light transport methods. The technique leverages the property that scattering reduces radiance anisotropy, allowing a switch to cheaper isotropic propagation in later stages. name: Light Propagation Maps
head: Fattal's LPM, Fattal's Original LPM Algorithm, Fattal's method, Original LPM iteration
body: Light Propagation Maps (LPM) is a Discrete Ordinate Method (DOM) technique for computing multiple scattering in participating media. It approximates the radiative transfer equation by decoupling spatial and directional sampling: it uses high-resolution 2D ray maps for iterative light propagation to reduce artifacts like false scattering and ray effects, while using a coarse 3D grid for storing accumulated radiance to minimize memory usage. It sets itself apart from standard DOM by using these 2D propagation maps instead of a full 3D directional grid for the transport step, and from Isotropic Residuum Propagation by handling the full anisotropic propagation before potentially switching to isotropic residuum methods. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid representing the medium with absorption coefficient Ka, scattering coefficient Ks, and phase function p(\omega, \omega'). Boundary conditions (incoming radiance) and self-emission radiance. Output: Average scattered radiance I{xyz}^d for each voxel xyz and storage direction d. Data Structures: 1. 3D Grid: Stores medium properties (Ka, Ks) and radiance buffers. I{xyz}^d: Average radiance in voxel xyz along direction d. U{xyz}^{i,p}: Unscattered radiance for propagation direction i at iteration p. Note: In practice, only two U buffers are kept (for p-1 and p) using a swap mechanism. 2. Light Propagation Maps (LPMs): A set of 2D arrays. Each LPM corresponds to a face of the coarse 3D grid. Each element (r,s) in an LPM stores a set of rays originating at (r,s) with directions sampled from the unit sphere S^2. High spatial resolution compared to the storage grid. Parameters: \varepsilon: Termination threshold. Iteration stops when \max{xyz} |U{d,pprev,xyz}| < \varepsilon. p: Iteration number (scattering order). m: Number of propagation directions sampled per LPM element (m \ll n, where n is the total number of directions). Formulas: 1. Average Radiance Definition: I{xyz}^d \approx (V{xyz}^d)^{-1} \int{C{xyz}} \int{\Omega^d} \frac{K{S{xyz}}}{4\pi} \int{\omega' \in S^2} L(p, \omega') p(\omega, \omega') d\omega' d\omega dp \quad (2) Where V{xyz}^d = \Delta V |\Omega^d| is the product of voxel volume and solid angle. 2. Ray Radiance Update (Transport): L{r,s}^i = L{r,s}^{i,t-1} e^{-\Delta lq(Ka + Ks)/\omegaz^i} + U{xyz}^{i,p} \times \frac{1 - e^{-\Delta lq(Ka + Ks)/\omegaz^i}}{Ka + Ks} \quad (3) Where: L{r,s}^i: Radiance leaving the t-th voxel for ray i at element (r,s). \Delta lq: Distance traversed in the voxel. \omegaz^i: Z-component of direction i (used for perspective correction/grid marching). U{xyz}^{i,p}: Stored unscattered radiance for direction d (closest to i) at iteration p. 3. Scattering Contribution (Storage): R = (V{xyz}^d)^{-1} A{r,s} F^{i,d} L{r,s}^{i,t} \frac{1 - e^{-\Delta lq Ks}}{\omegas^i} \quad (4) Where: A{r,s}: Area of the LPM sample (r,s). F^{i,d}: Precomputed phase function integral for propagation direction i and storage direction d. \omegas^i: Component of direction i relevant to the storage geometry. 4. Phase Function Integral: F^{i,d} = \frac{1}{4\pi} \int{\Omega^i} \int{\Omega^d} p(\omega, \omega') d\omega d\omega' \quad (5) Where d is the storage direction closest to propagation direction i. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize p{prev} = 0. Initialize U{d,pprev,xyz} and I{d,xyz} with medium self-emission radiance (if any). Create LPMs for each face of the 3D grid. 2. Iteration Loop: While \max{xyz} |U{d,pprev,xyz}| \ge \varepsilon and p > 0: a. Set p{cur} = (p{prev} + 1) \% 2. b. Initialize U{d,pcur,xyz} to 0. c. For each LPM: i. For each propagation direction i: 1. For each element (r,s) of the current map: If p == 0: Initialize L{r,s}^{i,0} with boundary conditions (incoming radiance). Else: Set L{r,s}^{i,0} to 0. 2. March rays through the volume: For each intersected voxel t: Update ray radiance L{r,s}^{i,t} using Eq. (3) and U{d,pprev,xyz}. Calculate scattering contribution R using Eq. (4). Update U{d,pcur,xyz} and I{d,xyz} with R. Boundary Handling: When a ray leaves the medium at point A, generate a new ray of the same direction with zero radiance from the opposite point B to maintain constant ray count. d. Set p{prev} = p{cur}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lightpropagationmaps(volume, boundaryconditions, epsilon): """ volume: 3D grid with fields Ka, Ks, phasefunction boundaryconditions: function returning radiance at boundary epsilon: termination threshold """ # Initialize buffers # Ud stores unscattered radiance, I stores average radiance # Only two Ud buffers are kept (pprev and pcur) Udprev = zeroslike(volume) Udcur = zeroslike(volume) I = zeroslike(volume) # Initialize with self-emission for voxel in volume: Udprev[voxel] = volume[voxel].selfemission I[voxel] = volume[voxel].selfemission pprev = 0 p = 1 # Precompute F^{i,d} for all direction pairs F = precomputephaseintegrals(volume.phasefunction) # Create LPMs for each face of the grid lpmfaces = createlpmfaces(volume) while max(abs(Udprev)) >= epsilon and p > 0: pcur = (pprev + 1) % 2 # Swap buffers Udprev, Udcur = Udcur, Udprev Udcur = zeroslike(volume) # Reset current buffer for lpm in lpmfaces: for directioni in lpm.propagationdirections: for r, s in lpm.elements: # Initialize ray radiance if p == 0: Lray = boundaryconditions(lpm, r, s, directioni) else: Lray = 0.0 # March ray through volume ray = Ray(origin=lpm.position(r, s), direction=directioni) while ray.insidevolume(): voxel = volume.getvoxelat(ray.position) deltal = ray.distancetonextvoxelface() # Update ray radiance (Eq. 3) # Note: omegaz is the component of directioni along the ray's primary axis # For grid marching, this is typically the component along the traversal axis omegaz = abs(dot(directioni, ray.traversalaxis)) if omegaz == 0: omegaz = 1e-6 # Guard against division by zero expterm = exp(-deltal (voxel.Ka + voxel.Ks) / omegaz) # Get unscattered radiance from previous iteration # d is the storage direction closest to i directiond = getclosestdirection(directioni, volume.directions) Uprev = Udprev[voxel][directiond] Lray = Lray expterm + Uprev (1 - expterm) / (voxel.Ka + voxel.Ks) # Calculate scattering contribution (Eq. 4) # omegas is the component relevant to storage geometry omegas = abs(dot(directioni, storageaxis)) if omegas == 0: omegas = 1e-6 # Guard against division by zero Ars = lpm.elementarea Vd = voxel.volume solidangle(directiond) Fid = F[directioni][directiond] R = (1 / Vd) Ars Fid Lray (1 - exp(-deltal voxel.Ks)) / omegas # Update buffers Udcur[voxel][directiond] += R I[voxel][directiond] += R ray.advance(deltal) # Boundary handling: if ray leaves, spawn new ray from opposite side if not ray.insidevolume(): # Spawn new ray with zero radiance from opposite point oppositepoint = getoppositeboundarypoint(ray.exitpoint, directioni) Lray = 0.0 ray = Ray(origin=oppositepoint, direction=directioni) pprev = pcur p += 1 return I Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Effects and False Scattering: Standard DOM suffers from these; LPM mitigates them via fine spatial sampling in LPMs. Boundary Conditions: Rays leaving the volume must be handled by spawning new rays from the opposite boundary to maintain ray density. Precision: Division by \omegaz^i and \omegas^i requires guards against zero values. Memory: Storing all LPMs and radiance buffers for high-resolution volumes can exceed GPU memory, addressed by variants like Streaming LPM. A GPU implementation that avoids synchronization bottlenecks by dividing propagation into propagation and collecting steps, ensuring each voxel is traversed by only one ray per direction block. A memory-management technique that processes the volume in small, streamed sub-volumes, decoupling memory footprint from total volume size to allow high-resolution rendering on limited VRAM. A perceptual culling map that identifies regions around light sources where scattering is visually salient, addressing false undersampling artifacts caused by the Extinction-Saliency (XS) map. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of iterations (scattering order) times the number of LPM elements times the number of propagation directions times the number of voxels traversed per ray. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the 3D grid (for I and U buffers) plus the size of all LPMs. Since LPMs are high-resolution 2D arrays, memory usage can be significant. Strengths: Reduces false scattering and ray effects compared to standard DOM; efficient storage via coarse grid for radiance. Limitations: High memory usage for large volumes; iterative nature can be slow for highly scattering media; requires careful handling of boundary conditions. When to Use: When high-quality multiple scattering is needed and artifacts from standard DOM are unacceptable, and memory allows for high-resolution LPMs. When Not to Use: When memory is severely constrained (use Streaming LPM) or when real-time performance is critical and lower quality is acceptable. Light Propagation Maps were introduced by Ronen Fattal. The method is based on the Discrete Ordinate Method (DOM) for solving the radiative transfer equation. It was developed to address the shortcomings of DOM, specifically false scattering and ray effects, by using fine sampling for propagation and coarse sampling for storage. name: Parallel and Scalable LPM
head: GPU LPM with propagation and collecting steps
body: Parallel and Scalable LPM is a GPU implementation of Light Propagation Maps that avoids synchronization bottlenecks by dividing the propagation step into a propagation step and a collecting step. This guarantees that each voxel is traversed by only one ray at a time within a specific direction block. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a volume grid with spatial resolution V{xyz} and optical properties (extinction coefficient K{xyz}). It takes an LPM structure with spatial resolution (r,s) and D propagation directions. It takes current unscattered radiance U{d, p{prev}, xyz} and average radiance I{d, xyz} buffers. It takes the number of iterations N{iterations}. It outputs updated unscattered radiance U{d, p{cur}, xyz} and average radiance I{d, xyz} for the next iteration. Data Structures: A temporary buffer T^i{xyz} is allocated for each propagation direction i. It stores the radiance contribution of rays traveling in direction i as they traverse the volume. Its size matches the volume grid V{xyz}. LPM elements are defined by coordinates (r,s) and direction index i. The propagation kernel uses one block per propagation direction i, where each block handles a subset of LPM elements (r,s). The collecting kernel uses one block representing the entire volume, where each thread corresponds to one voxel (x,y,z). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize p{prev} = 0. 2. Initialize U{d, p{prev}, xyz} and I{d, xyz} with self-emitted radiance (if any). 3. For p from 0 to N{iterations}-1: a. Calculate p{cur} = (p{prev} + 1) \pmod 2. b. Initialize U{d, p{cur}, xyz} to 0. c. For each LPM (or sub-LPM if resolution mismatch exists): i. Parallel for each block i: 1. Parallel for each thread (r,s): Create a ray with origin (r,s) and direction i, and initialize L^{i,0}{r,s}. 2. For each intersected voxel t: Compute L^{i,t}{r,s} from U{d, p{prev}, xyz} using Eq. 3. Compute T^i{xyz} using Eq. 6 and store it. d. Synchronize all blocks (Synchronizeblocks()). e. Parallel for each voxel (xyz): i. For each direction i: Update U{d, p{cur}, xyz} and I{d, xyz} with T^i{xyz} using Eq. 4. 4. Set p{prev} = p{cur}. Formulas: The ray contribution stored in the temporary buffer is: T^i{xyz} = L^{i,t}{r,s} \left(1 - e^{-\Delta lq K{xyz} / \omegaz^n}\right) \quad (6) where T^i{xyz} is the temporary buffer value for direction i in voxel (x,y,z). L^{i,t}{r,s} is the radiance arriving at voxel t from direction i. \Delta lq is the step length. K{xyz} is the extinction coefficient. \omegaz^n is the phase function parameter. Eq. 3 computes L^{i,t}{r,s} from U{d, p{prev}, xyz} using standard radiative transfer transmittance and source terms. Eq. 4 aggregates T^i{xyz} to update U{d, p{cur}, xyz} and I{d, xyz} per the LPM scattering model. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def parallelscalablelpm(volume, lpmelements, Uprev, Icurr, Niterations): # Initialize buffers with self-emitted radiance if applicable pprev = 0 for p in range(Niterations): pcur = (pprev + 1) % 2 Ucurr = zeroslike(Uprev) Iaccum = zeroslike(Icurr) # Propagation Step directions = sorted(set(e.direction for e in lpmelements)) for diridx in directions: elementsfordir = [e for e in lpmelements if e.direction == diridx] # Split into blocks to respect register limits blocksize = min(len(elementsfordir), MAXTHREADSPERBLOCK) blocks = [elementsfordir[i:i+blocksize] for i in range(0, len(elementsfordir), blocksize)] for block in blocks: launchpropagationkernel(block, volume, Uprev, diridx, Tbuffers[diridx]) synchronizeallblocks() # Collecting Step launchcollectingkernel(volume, Tbuffers, Ucurr, Iaccum) Icurr = Icurr + Iaccum Uprev = Ucurr pprev = pcur def launchpropagationkernel(block, volume, Uprev, diridx, Tbuffer): # One thread per element (r,s) in the block for element in block.elements: r, s = element.r, element.s rayorigin = (r, s, 0) # LPM origin mapping raydirection = DIRECTIONVECTORS[diridx] currentradiance = Uprev[rayorigin] for voxel in volume.intersectedbyray(rayorigin, raydirection): # Compute radiance contribution from previous iteration transmittance = exp(-volume.K[previousvoxel] volume.steplength(previousvoxel)) sourceterm = Uprev[voxel] (1.0 - exp(-volume.K[voxel] volume.steplength(voxel))) Lit = transmittance currentradiance + sourceterm # Eq. 6: Store contribution to temporary buffer deltal = volume.steplength(voxel) K = volume.K[voxel] omega = volume.phaseparam[voxel] contribution = Lit (1.0 - exp(-deltal K / omega)) Tbuffer[voxel] = contribution currentradiance = Lit # Intra-block synchronization when leaving voxel syncthreads() def launchcollectingkernel(volume, Tbuffers, Ucurr, Iaccum): # One thread per voxel for voxel in volume.allvoxels(): uval = 0.0 ival = 0.0 for diridx in range(len(Tbuffers)): tval = Tbuffers[diridx][voxel] # Eq. 4: Update U and I with contributions ival += tval uval += tval Ucurr[voxel] = uval Iaccum[voxel] = ival Parameters and Typical Values: The LPM resolution often matches the volume face resolution to simplify mapping. If the LPM resolution is N times higher than the voxel grid, it is divided into N smaller sub-LPMs propagated sequentially. The block size is limited by register count and is reduced by lowering the resolution of one LPM coordinate (r or s), which increases the number of blocks per direction. For large volumes, sub-volumes (e.g., 16 \times 16 \times 16) are processed sequentially to fit in GPU memory. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Naive parallelization with atomic operations is inefficient due to branching and global memory transactions. The proposed method avoids this via data locality. When multiple blocks propagate light in the same direction, voxels at the frontier between contiguous subsets of LPM elements (Ri and R{i+1}) may be traversed by two rays simultaneously. This is mitigated by launching blocks B{2i} and B{2i+1} in parallel, but not contiguous blocks Bi and B{i+1}. The number of threads per block is limited by registers, requiring resolution reduction if exceeded. If the LPM resolution is significantly higher than the voxel grid, synchronization problems arise, requiring sequential sub-LPM propagation. This variant focuses on the specific launch configuration to prevent race conditions at block boundaries. To guarantee only one thread per voxel, blocks B{2i} are launched in parallel, followed by B{2i+1}, avoiding the simultaneous launch of contiguous blocks Bi and B{i+1} which could cause frontier voxel collisions. Intra-block synchronization using syncthreads() is required whenever rays leave their current voxel. If the LPM resolution is N times higher than the voxel grid, the LPM is divided into N smaller sub-LPMs propagated sequentially to avoid synchronization issues. The method scales with the number of rays (LPM elements) and volume size. The speedup over the original CPU algorithm increases with volume size because more blocks are created, keeping GPU resources busy. Memory usage is dominated by the temporary buffers T^i{xyz} for each direction. For large volumes, streaming is used to process sub-volumes, keeping memory usage far below available GPU memory (e.g., handling volumes larger than 256^3). On a GTX 580, the parallel approach shows significant speedup over atomic-operation-based versions and the original CPU algorithm. For a 64^3 volume with 25 propagation directions and 3 bounces, it takes 417 milliseconds. High efficiency is achieved due to data locality (cache accesses) instead of global memory transactions. It scales to large volumes via streaming. It requires careful management of block launches and synchronization. Memory usage increases with volume size, though at a slower rate with streaming. Parallel and Scalable LPM was introduced by to address the inefficiencies of naive GPU implementations of Fattal's LPM algorithm. The original algorithm suffered from synchronization problems when multiple rays wrote to the same voxel. The authors proposed the two-step propagation/collecting approach to leverage GPU parallelism while maintaining correctness and performance. The method is part of the broader family of Light Propagation Maps, which are used for efficient light transport in participating media. name: Streaming LPM
head: Slice-based streaming, Sub-volume streaming
body: Streaming LPM is a memory-management technique for Light Propagation Maps (LPM) that overcomes GPU memory limitations by processing the volume in small, streamed sub-volumes rather than the entire grid at once. It sets itself apart from standard LPM by decoupling the memory footprint from the total volume size, allowing high-resolution volumes (e.g., 256^3) to be rendered on hardware with limited VRAM, whereas standard LPM requires storing all radiance buffers for the entire volume simultaneously. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The full volume domain V with maximum coordinates (X{max}, Y{max}, Z{max}), the sub-volume size parameter N{sub}, and the LPM propagation parameters (directions, bounces). Output: The final scattered radiance field for the volume. Data Structures: The volume is partitioned into sub-volumes B{ijk} and slices Sl. Sub-volume B{ijk}: Defined as the set of voxels C{xyz} where: B{ijk} = \{ C{xyz} \mid x \in [i \cdot N{sub}, (i+1) \cdot N{sub}], y \in [j \cdot N{sub}, (j+1) \cdot N{sub}], z \in [k \cdot N{sub}, (k+1) \cdot N{sub}] \} where C{xyz} is a voxel at spatial position (x,y,z). Slice Sl: A group of sub-volumes aligned with the LPM face orientation. For an LPM face perpendicular to the Z-axis, a slice is defined as: Sl = \{ B{ijk} \mid i \in [0, I{max}], j \in [0, J{max}], k = l \} where l is the slice index along the Z-axis. Parameters: N{sub}: The linear dimension of a sub-volume. It must be chosen such that the memory required for one slice fits within GPU limits. CUDA Streams: Two streams are utilized: 1. Transfer Stream: Manages CPU-GPU data transfer (downloading previous slice results, uploading next slice inputs). 2. Computation Stream: Executes the LPM propagation algorithm for the current slice. Pinned Memory: Host memory allocated as pinned memory to accelerate CPU-GPU transfers. Algorithm Steps: 1. Partitioning: Split the volume V into sub-volumes B{ijk} using N{sub}. Group these sub-volumes into slices Sl based on the LPM face orientation (e.g., Z-slices for Z-perpendicular faces). 2. Stream Initialization: Initialize two CUDA streams: one for computation and one for data transfer. Allocate pinned memory buffers on the CPU. 3. Iteration Loop: Iterate through each slice Sl from l=0 to Z{max}/N{sub} - 1. The total number of steps is Z{max} / N{sub}. 4. Data Transfer (Overlap): The Transfer Stream downloads the radiance data (I, U) computed for the previous slice S{l-1} from GPU to CPU pinned memory. Simultaneously, the Transfer Stream uploads the necessary input data (boundary conditions or incoming radiance) for the next slice S{l+1} from CPU pinned memory to GPU. Note: For the first slice, initial data is uploaded. For the last slice, no subsequent upload is needed. 5. Computation: The Computation Stream executes the LPM propagation algorithm on the current slice Sl. This involves iterating over all voxels in the slice and all propagation directions to update radiance buffers I and U using transmittance T. Propagation and collection for slice Sl must complete before S{l+1} is processed. 6. Result Storage: The radiance propagated through slice Sl is stored at its outgoing face. This data serves as the input boundary condition for the next slice S{l+1}. 7. Sub-slicing (Fallback): If a single slice Sl still exceeds GPU memory capacity, it is further split into sub-slices and streamed individually. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def streaminglpm(volumedims, Nsub, lpmparams): Xmax, Ymax, Zmax = volumedims numslices = Zmax // Nsub # Allocate pinned host memory for CPU-GPU transfer hostpinned = allocatepinnedmemory(size=slicememorysize(lpmparams)) # Allocate device memory for a single slice deviceslice = allocatedevicememory(size=slicememorysize(lpmparams)) # Initialize two CUDA streams: transfer and computation transferstream = createstream() computestream = createstream() # Upload initial data for the first slice streamcopyfromhost(transferstream, hostpinned, deviceslice) for l in range(numslices): # Transfer stream: download result of previous slice to pinned memory if l > 0: streamcopytohost(transferstream, deviceslice, hostpinned) # Transfer stream: upload input for next slice from pinned memory if l < numslices - 1: streamcopyfromhost(transferstream, hostpinned, deviceslice) # Computation stream: propagate light through current slice # Propagation and collection for slice l must complete before next slice is processed applylpmpropagation(computestream, deviceslice, lpmparams) # Store radiance at the outgoing face of the slice # Synchronize streams synchronizestream(transferstream) synchronizestream(computestream) freememory(deviceslice) freememory(hostpinned) def slicememorysize(params): return params.directions 2 Nsub Nsub Nsub def applylpmpropagation(stream, buffer, params): # Parallel for each voxel in slice: # Parallel for each direction i: # Update I and U buffers using transmittance T pass def allocatepinnedmemory(size): return [0] size def allocatedevicememory(size): return [0] size def createstream(): return object() def streamcopytohost(stream, src, dst): pass def streamcopyfromhost(stream, src, dst): pass def synchronizestream(stream): pass def freememory(buffer): pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Limitation: A 256^3 volume with 25 propagation directions per LPM face requires ~3.8 GB memory, exceeding typical GPU memory (e.g., 1.5–2 GB on GTX 580/560M). Streaming is mandatory in this case. Boundaries: The radiance stored at the outgoing face of one slice must be correctly passed to the incoming face of the next slice. Failure to synchronize streams correctly will cause data races or stale data usage. Precision: Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: The computational work per voxel remains the same as standard LPM, but overhead is introduced by data transfers. The use of pinned memory and concurrent streams (transfer and computation) overlaps these costs. Memory Complexity: Scales with the size of a single slice (or sub-slice) rather than the entire volume. This allows rendering of volumes much larger than available VRAM. Measured Performance: For a 64^3 volume, 25 propagation directions and 3 bounces, the GPU implementation takes 417 milliseconds, compared to 47 seconds on a CPU. Speedup increases with volume size due to better GPU resource utilization. Strengths: Enables high-resolution volume rendering on consumer GPUs; efficient use of GPU parallelism via concurrent streams. Limitations: Requires careful management of data dependencies between slices; increased implementation complexity compared to standard LPM. Streaming LPM was introduced in the paper "Light Propagation Maps on Parallel Graphics Architectures" (2012). It was developed to address the severe memory limitations of GPUs at the time, which restricted the size of volumes that could be processed using standard LPM algorithms. The technique leverages CUDA's concurrent execution and data transfer capabilities to optimize performance. name: Light Map (L Map)
head: L map
body: The Light Map (L Map) is a perceptual culling map used in the rendering of participating media to identify regions around light sources where scattering effects are visually salient. It addresses the artifact of false undersampling caused by the Extinction-Saliency (XS) map, which incorrectly directs the rendering algorithm to skip detailed sampling in areas near light sources where multiple scattering is actually significant. Unlike the XS map, which combines extinction and saliency, the L map specifically isolates the spatial extent of light source influence to guide adaptive refinement. The L Map is generated through a three-step process designed to be computationally inexpensive while accurately marking areas requiring high-fidelity scattering calculations. Inputs: Scene geometry and light source positions. Media optical thickness distribution. Outputs: A scalar map (the L Map) where non-zero values indicate areas around light sources where scattering is a salient feature. Data Structures: The L Map is typically stored as a 2D texture or grid aligned with the screen or voxel space, matching the resolution of the XS map or the primary rendering buffer. Values represent the intensity of the "influence" from light sources. Steps: 1. Identify Light Sources: Determine the positions and extents of all light sources in the scene. 2. Generate 0-LightMap (L0): Render a scan-line image where light sources are rendered as constant white (value 1.0) and the rest of the scene is black (value 0.0). This image is termed the 0-LightMap (L0). 3. Apply Point Spread Function (PSF): Convolve the white pixels of L0 with a Point Spread Function to define the area around light sources where scattering becomes important. This step effectively blurs the sharp light source boundaries into a soft region of influence. Formula: The final L Map value L(x) at position x is computed as: L(x) = (L0 \text{PSF})(x) Where denotes convolution. Parameters: PSF Shape: The shape of the point spread function depends only on the optical thickness of the media. This simplification keeps the method computationally simple while producing good results. More accurate shapes could be derived from work such as Narasimhan and Nayar [2003], but are not required for the basic L Map definition. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatelightmap(scene, mediaopticalthickness): # Step 1: Identify light sources (implicit in rendering pass) # Step 2: Produce 0-LightMap (L0) # Render scene where light sources are white (1.0) and everything else is black (0.0) L0 = renderlightsourcesaswhite(scene) # Step 3: Apply Point Spread Function # The PSF shape depends only on the optical thickness of the media psf = createpsffromopticalthickness(mediaopticalthickness) # Convolve L0 with the PSF to define the area where scattering is important Lmap = convolve(L0, psf) return Lmap Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Complex PSF Shapes: While the method assumes a PSF shape based solely on optical thickness for simplicity, ignoring more complex scattering profiles (e.g., those from Narasimhan and Nayar [2003]) may lead to suboptimal culling in highly anisotropic media. Resolution Mismatch: If the L Map resolution does not match the rendering resolution, artifacts may occur during the culling phase. A perceptual strategy that combines the L map with an Extinction map (X map) and a Saliency map (S map) to guide selective rendering, providing more accurate estimates in perceptually important areas while reducing rendering times. Time Complexity: The generation of the L Map is fast, involving a simple render pass and a convolution. The complexity is dominated by the PSF convolution, which is typically O(N) for separable filters or O(N \cdot k^2) for non-separable ones, where N is the number of pixels and k is the kernel size. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for one additional map (the L Map) of the same resolution as the XS map or the primary rendering buffer. Strengths: Effectively fixes artifacts caused by the XS map wrongly indicating undersampling near light sources. Computationally simple to generate. Limitations: The PSF shape is simplified to depend only on optical thickness, which may not capture all scattering nuances. When to use: Use when rendering participating media with significant multiple scattering near light sources and when the XS map alone produces visible artifacts around light sources. When not to use: Avoid if computational resources are extremely limited and the PSF convolution overhead is prohibitive, or if the media is optically thin enough that scattering near light sources is negligible. The Light Map was introduced in the context of perceptual rendering of participating media to address specific artifacts in adaptive rendering techniques. It was proposed as a novel solution to overcome the problem of the XS map incorrectly directing the rendering algorithm to undersample areas around light sources. The work is part of the broader effort to balance rendering quality and performance in physically based rendering of participating media. name: XSL Map Selective Rendering
head: Director map guided rendering, L map, Modulated Saliency Map (S Map), S map, Saliency Map (S Map), Selective Rendering with XSL Map, X map, XSL Map Combination, XSL(wxs, op), extinction map, light map
body: XSL Map Selective Rendering is a perceptual strategy for physically based rendering of participating media that reduces rendering time by using a combination of a saliency map (S map), an extinction map (X map), and a light map (L map) to guide selective rendering, providing more accurate estimates in perceptually important areas. It builds on Light Map (L Map) by integrating the L map with the XS map to form a unified director map that accounts for both extinction and scattering around light sources, addressing artifacts caused by poor sampling in previous methods. Unlike standard global illumination which treats all pixels equally, this method modulates the maximum number of rays per pixel based on the XSL map, prioritizing areas with high perceptual saliency, low extinction, and strong scattering. The method generates a director map (XSL map) from three component maps and uses it to weight the sampling density (maximum rays per pixel) for each pixel in the final rendering. Inputs: Scene geometry and participating media properties (extinction coefficient \sigmat, scattering coefficient \sigmas, phase function). Light source positions and intensities. Camera parameters. Coefficients w{xs} and wl for weighting the XS and L maps. Combination operator op (typically addition). Base maximum rays per pixel R{max}. Outputs: Rendered image with adaptive sampling density. The XSL director map (intermediate data structure). 1. Extinction Map (X Map): A 2D image array where each pixel stores the exponential decay of light in the medium along the view ray. Let X(u,v) be the value at pixel (u,v). The value represents the attenuation factor e^{-\tau}, where \tau is the optical depth. 2. Direct Lighting Snapshot: A 2D image array representing the scene rendered with ray tracing using only direct lighting (no medium scattering). 3. Saliency Map (S Map): A 2D image array generated by applying the Itti et al. [1998] saliency algorithm to the modulated snapshot. 4. Light Map (L Map): A 2D image array identifying areas around light sources where multiple scattering is salient. Defined in Light Map (L Map). 5. XS Map: A 2D image array resulting from the combination of the X Map and S Map. 6. XSL Map: The final director map, a 2D image array resulting from the combination of the XS Map and L Map. 1. Generate Direct Lighting Snapshot: Render the scene using ray tracing with only direct lighting. No medium scattering is computed for this step. Let this image be I{direct}(u,v). 2. Compute Extinction Map (X Map): For each pixel (u,v), compute the optical depth \tau along the view ray through the participating media. Calculate the extinction value as: X(u,v) = e^{-\tau(u,v)} This stores the exponential decay of light in the medium. 3. Modulate Snapshot for Saliency: To account for the fact that extinction and visibility are inversely proportional for perceptual purposes, invert the X Map and add it to the Direct Lighting Snapshot. Let I{modulated}(u,v) be the result: I{modulated}(u,v) = I{direct}(u,v) + (1 - X(u,v)) Note: The source states "Invert the Extinction Map (X map). Add the inverted X map to the direct-lighting snapshot." It clarifies that while not physically accurate, this empirically suits the needs. 4. Generate Saliency Map (S Map): Apply the saliency algorithm from Itti et al. [1998] to I{modulated}(u,v). This algorithm extracts features based on intensity, color, and orientation at varying spatial scales to produce a conspicuity map, which is then combined into a saliency map. Let the result be S(u,v). 5. Generate XS Map: Combine the X Map and the S Map. The specific combination formula for the XS map is not explicitly detailed beyond being a precursor to the XSL map, but it is implied to be a weighted combination similar to the XSL step. However, the text focuses on the final XSL combination. We assume a standard weighted addition or similar operator for the XS map generation, or that the XS map is an intermediate concept where X and S are combined. The text says "combine the XS map and the L map... where XSL represents the combined XS map and L map". It does not give the explicit formula for XS, only for XSL. We will proceed to the XSL combination using the XS map as an input. Note: The source does not provide the exact formula for combining X and S into XS, only that it exists. We will treat XS as an intermediate map XS(u,v). 6. Combine into XSL Map: Combine the XS Map and the L Map using the term XSL(w{xs}, wl, op). The formula is: XSL(u,v) = op(w{xs} \cdot XS(u,v), wl \cdot L(u,v)) Where: XS(u,v) is the value from the XS map. L(u,v) is the value from the Light Map. w{xs} and wl are coefficients for the XS and L maps respectively. op is the combination operator. For equal weighting, use w{xs} = 0.5 and wl = 0.5 with the addition operator (+): XSL(u,v) = 0.5 \cdot XS(u,v) + 0.5 \cdot L(u,v) To render using only the XS map, use w{xs}=1, wl=0. To render using only the L map, use w{xs}=0, wl=1. 7. Selective Rendering: For each pixel (u,v) in the final render: Retrieve the director map value D = XSL(u,v). Calculate the number of rays to shoot for this pixel: R(u,v) = \text{clamp}(R{max} \cdot D, 1, R{max}) (Assuming XSL values are normalized to [0,1] or scaled appropriately. The source states "Higher values in the director map will result in more rays shot per pixel". It does not specify normalization, but typically director maps are normalized. If XSL is not normalized, R{max} must be scaled or D normalized. We assume D is a weight factor. If D > 1, it might exceed R{max}, so clamping is necessary.) Shoot R(u,v) rays for the pixel to compute the final color, using a global illumination algorithm for participating media (e.g., ray marching or photon mapping). w{xs}: Coefficient for the XS map. Default: 0.5. wl: Coefficient for the L map. Default: 0.5. op: Combination operator. Default: Addition (+). R{max}: Maximum number of rays per pixel. User-defined parameter. Normalization: The source does not specify if the XSL map values are normalized to [0,1]. If not, the ray count calculation must handle values outside the expected range. Clamping R(u,v) to [1, R{max}] is recommended. Perceptual Degradation: Although average pixel errors are less than 1%, subjective validation indicates that quality degradation is still noticeable for certain scenes. Scattering Around Light Sources: The previous algorithm (XS map only) did not account for scattering around light sources, resulting in noisy artifacts. The L map addresses this, but if wl is set to 0, these artifacts may reappear. Extinction Inversion: The inversion of the X map (1-X) is an empirical approximation and not physically accurate, but it works for the saliency generator. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computexslmap(scene, camera, wxs=0.5, wl=0.5, op='add'): """ Computes the XSL director map for selective rendering. Args: scene: Scene object containing geometry, media, and lights. camera: Camera object. wxs: Weight for XS map. wl: Weight for L map. op: Combination operator ('add' or others). Returns: xslmap: 2D array representing the XSL director map. """ # Step 1: Generate Direct Lighting Snapshot # Render scene with only direct lighting, no medium scattering directsnapshot = raytracedirectlighting(scene, camera) # Step 2: Compute Extinction Map (X Map) # X(u,v) = exp(-opticaldepth(u,v)) xmap = computeextinctionmap(scene, camera) # Step 3: Modulate Snapshot # Invert X map and add to direct snapshot # Note: Source says "Invert the Extinction Map (X map). Add the inverted X map..." # Assuming X map values are in [0,1], inversion is (1 - X) invertedxmap = 1.0 - xmap modulatedsnapshot = directsnapshot + invertedxmap # Step 4: Generate Saliency Map (S Map) # Apply Itti et al. [1998] saliency algorithm smap = computesaliency(modulatedsnapshot) # Step 5: Generate XS Map # Combine X Map and S Map. Formula not explicitly given, # but implied to be a weighted combination. # We assume a simple weighted addition for XS as a placeholder # since the text focuses on XSL combination. # However, the text says "combine the XS map and the L map". # It does not give the formula for XS. # We will assume XS is a pre-computed map or use a default combination. # Given the lack of explicit formula, we assume XS is an intermediate result. # For implementation, we might need to define how XS is formed. # The text says "combine the XS map and the L map... where XSL represents the combined XS map and L map". # It does not specify the XS combination. # We will assume XS is computed as a weighted sum of X and S for completeness, # though the source doesn't specify weights for XS. # Let's assume equal weighting for XS as a reasonable default if not specified. # Or, more likely, XS is just the combination of X and S. # Since the source doesn't give the formula, we will leave it as a function call. xsmap = combinexsmap(xmap, smap) # Step 6: Generate L Map # Compute Light Map as defined in [Light Map (L Map)] lmap = computelightmap(scene, camera) # Step 7: Combine XS and L into XSL Map # XSL = op(wxs XS, wl L) weightedxs = wxs xsmap weightedl = wl lmap if op == 'add': xslmap = weightedxs + weightedl else: # Other operators can be implemented here xslmap = applyoperator(op, weightedxs, weightedl) return xslmap def selectiverender(scene, camera, xslmap, rmax): """ Renders the scene using the XSL map to guide sampling. Args: scene: Scene object. camera: Camera object. xslmap: 2D array from computexslmap. rmax: Maximum rays per pixel. Returns: renderedimage: 2D array of final pixel colors. """ height, width = xslmap.shape renderedimage = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): # Get director map value d = xslmap[y, x] # Calculate number of rays # Clamp to ensure at least 1 ray and at most rmax # Assuming d is normalized or scaled appropriately. # If d is not normalized, this might need adjustment. # We assume d is a weight factor. rays = int(rmax d) rays = max(1, min(rays, rmax)) # Shoot rays and compute color color = computecolorwithscattering(scene, camera, x, y, rays) renderedimage[y, x] = color return renderedimage def computecolorwithscattering(scene, camera, x, y, numrays): """ Computes the color for a pixel using global illumination for participating media. This is a placeholder for the specific GI algorithm (e.g., ray marching, photon mapping). """ # Implementation depends on the chosen GI method # For example, using ray marching: color = np.zeros(3) for i in range(numrays): ray = camera.getray(x, y) # Perform ray marching through the medium # Accumulate scattered light samplecolor = raymarchmedium(scene, ray) color += samplecolor color /= numrays return color A map identifying areas around light sources where scattering becomes a salient feature, introduced to fix artifacts caused by the XS map. Link A modulated saliency map used to guide the perception-based renderer, generated from a direct lighting snapshot and an inverted extinction map. Link (Note: S Map is a component, not a separate article in the provided tree, but referenced in the parent). Stores in image-space the exponential decay of light in the medium. Link Time Complexity: The preprocessing step (generating the XSL map) involves rendering a direct lighting snapshot, computing extinction, and applying saliency algorithms. The final rendering time is proportional to the sum of rays shot per pixel, which is weighted by the XSL map. Areas with high XSL values require more rays, increasing local computation time, but the overall average ray count is reduced compared to uniform sampling. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the X map, S map, L map, XS map, and XSL map, all of which are 2D image arrays of the same resolution as the output image. The memory overhead is linear with respect to the image resolution. Measured Performance: The average pixel errors of objective difference metrics are all less than 1%. However, subjective validation indicates that degradation in quality is still noticeable for certain scenes. Strengths: Significantly reduces rendering times for inhomogeneous media by focusing computational effort on perceptually important areas. Addresses noisy artifacts caused by poor sampling around light sources by incorporating the L map. Limitations: The inversion of the X map is an empirical approximation and not physically accurate. Quality degradation is still noticeable in some scenes despite low average pixel errors. When to Use: Suitable for applications where rendering time is a constraint and perceptual quality is prioritized over physical accuracy, such as safety, military, or industry applications analyzing visual perception under unfavorable environmental conditions (fog, smoke, dust, flames, silty waters). When Not to Use: When physically accurate global illumination is required without perceptual approximations, or when the artifacts from the empirical X map inversion are unacceptable. The XSL Map Selective Rendering method was introduced by Sundstedt, Gutierrez, Anson, Banterle, and Chalmers in 2007 as an extended version of their previous work [Anson et al. 2006]. The previous algorithm combined a saliency map with a new extinction map (X-map) but did not account for scattering around light sources, leading to noisy artifacts. The 2007 paper introduced the Light Map (L map) to address this issue and combined it with the XS map to form the XSL map. The method is used in safety, military, or industry applications for analyzing visual perception under unfavorable environmental conditions.
