name: Multiple Scattering Model (Integral Equation)
head: General integral equation for radiation transport, Radiation transport integral equation, Transport Theory Illumination Model
body: The Multiple Scattering Model (Integral Equation) is a physically based illumination model that computes the radiance arriving at a pixel by integrating light contributions along a ray, explicitly accounting for emission, absorption, and multiple scattering events. It solves the problem of determining the intensity I(X, \omega) at every point X and direction \omega within a participating medium. Unlike single-scattering approximations or differential solvers that may neglect angular complexity, this model formulates the radiative transfer as a Fredholm integral equation of the second kind, where the unknown radiance appears on both sides of the equation. This distinguishes it from its siblings, such as the Differential Form of RTE which uses local derivatives, and the Monte Carlo Method for Multiple Scattering which uses stochastic sampling, by providing a deterministic, global integral formulation that requires iterative or expansion-based solution methods. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray origin X and direction \omega. Ray length D (or near/far clip plane distances t{near}, t{far}). Extinction coefficient field \tau(X) (or \sigmaa(X) and \sigma{sc}(X)). Scattering phase function r(X, \omega, \omega') (or \rho{sc}(\omega' \to \omega)). Emission/Glow field e(X) (or E(t)). External illumination I0 at the ray's far end. Output: Radiance I(X, \omega) at the ray origin. Data Structures The method operates on continuous fields defined over the volume. In implementation, these are typically discretized into: Grid/Texture: Stores \tau(X), e(X), and r(X, \cdot, \cdot) at sample points. Directional Basis: For solving the integral equation, radiance I(X, \omega) is often expanded into a basis (e.g., spherical harmonics or discrete ordinates) to handle the angular dependency \omega'. Formulas The general integral equation for radiation transport is: I(X, \omega) = I0(X + D\omega, \omega) \exp\left(-\int0^D \tau(X + t\omega) \, dt\right) + \int0^D \left[ \int{4\pi} r(X + s\omega, \omega, \omega') I(X + s\omega, \omega') \, d\omega' + e(X + s\omega) \right] \exp\left(-\int0^s \tau(X + t\omega) \, dt\right) \, ds Where: I(X, \omega) is the unknown intensity at point X in direction \omega. I0(X + D\omega, \omega) is the external illumination at the far edge of the volume. \tau(X) is the total extinction coefficient (optical depth density). r(X, \omega, \omega') is the scattering kernel (phase function) describing light scattered from direction \omega' to \omega. e(X) is the nondirectional glow (e.g., black body thermal radiation). The term \exp\left(-\int0^s \tau(X + t\omega) \, dt\right) represents the transmittance from point X+s\omega back to X. Alternatively, expressed as a path integral with contribution Q(t): I(t0, \vec{\omega}) = \int{t0}^{\infty} Q(\tau) e^{\left(-\int{t0}^{t} \sigmaa(\tau) + \sigma{sc}(\tau) \, d\tau\right)} \, d\tau With the contribution term Q(t) defined as: Q(t) = E(t) + \sigma{sc}(t) \int{\Omega} \rho{sc}(\omega' \to \omega) I(t, \omega') \, d\omega' Where t0 is the start distance (near clip plane) and \infty is the end distance (far clip plane). Steps to Solve Because I(X, \omega) appears on both sides of the integral equation, it cannot be solved directly. The standard approach involves the following steps: 1. Discretize the Domain: Discretize the spatial domain into voxels and the angular domain into a set of directions or basis functions (e.g., Spherical Harmonics or Discrete Ordinates). 2. Initialize: Set an initial guess for the radiance field I^{(0)}(X, \omega), often assuming zero scattering or single-scattering approximation. 3. Iterate (Fixed-Point Iteration): For iteration k, compute the source term g^{(k)}(s) using the radiance from the previous iteration I^{(k-1)}: g^{(k)}(s) = \int{4\pi} r(X+s\omega, \omega, \omega') I^{(k-1)}(X+s\omega, \omega') \, d\omega' + e(X+s\omega) Update the radiance I^{(k)}(X, \omega) by integrating the source term with transmittance: I^{(k)}(X, \omega) = I{transmitted} + \int0^D g^{(k)}(s) \exp\left(-\int0^s \tau(X + t\omega) \, dt\right) \, ds Repeat until convergence (change in I is below a threshold). 4. Alternative Expansion: Expand I(X, \omega) in a basis (e.g., spherical harmonics) to convert the integral equation into a coupled system of partial differential equations (P-N method) or algebraic equations (Discrete Ordinates). Parameters Number of Iterations: Depends on the optical thickness and albedo. High albedo requires more iterations. Angular Resolution: Number of directions or harmonic orders. Higher resolution captures anisotropic scattering better but increases cost. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Convergence: The iterative method may fail to converge if the medium is highly scattering (high albedo) or if the step size in iterative solvers is not chosen carefully. Complexity: The model is too complex to evaluate directly for real-time applications; approximations are necessary for practical implementation. Singularity: The phase function r may have singularities (e.g., forward scattering peaks) requiring careful numerical integration. Approximates the path integral over a reduced subset of paths surrounding the Most Probable Path (MPP) using Gaussian support. Choose when high accuracy for multiply-scattered light is needed with lower cost than full integration. Solves the RTE by expanding radiance into spherical harmonics, converting the integral equation into PDEs. Choose for handling anisotropic scattering more accurately than diffusion, avoiding ray effects of discrete ordinates. Stochastically traces rays to estimate the integral. Choose for unbiased results in complex geometries, accepting high variance and noise. Replaces the integral equation with a PDE based on the first two angular moments. Choose for dense, highly scattering media where light is nearly isotropic. Uses neural networks to predict scattering contributions via an albedo series. Choose for differentiable, deterministic approximations decoupled from complex integral operators. Time Complexity: The direct evaluation of the integral equation is O(N \cdot M) per ray, where N is the number of spatial samples and M is the number of angular directions/basis functions. Iterative solvers multiply this by the number of iterations. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot M) to store the radiance field and scattering kernels. Performance: Computationally expensive due to the nested integrals (spatial and angular) and the need for iterative solution. Strengths: Physically accurate; accounts for multiple scattering and complex lighting effects; deterministic. Limitations: Too complex for direct evaluation; requires approximations; high computational cost; convergence issues in highly scattering media. When to use: Offline rendering, scientific visualization, or when high physical accuracy for multiple scattering is required. When not to use: Real-time applications requiring direct evaluation without approximations; highly absorbing media where single scattering dominates. The model originates from transport theory in thermal engineering and neutron transport. It is derived from the conservation of energy for light passing through a participating medium. The integral formulation is a standard result in radiative transfer theory, applicable to both photon transport in participating media and neutron transport. It is cited in computer graphics literature as a physically based illumination model for volume rendering. name: Full Propagator Approximation for Multiply-Scattered Radiance
head: Approximate G_s, Multiply-Scattered Radiance Formula
body: The Full Propagator Approximation computes the radiance contribution from multiple scattering events by approximating the path integral over a reduced subset of paths surrounding the Most Probable Path (MPP). It replaces the intractable integration over complete path space with an integration over a Gaussian support perpendicular to the MPP. Inputs: s: Total path length. \mathbf{x}: Position on the view ray. \vec{\omega}: View direction. \vec{\omega}': Incoming direction from a directional light source. b(\mathbf{x}') L0(\mathbf{x}', \vec{\omega}'): Singly scattered radiance source term. c(\cdot): Extinction coefficient function. P{MS}(\cdot): Multiply-scattered phase function. w(s): Gaussian width function. C: Normalization constant. Outputs: L(s, \mathbf{x}, \vec{\omega}): Multiply-scattered radiance. Data Structures: MPP (Most Probable Path): A geometric path defined by the start point, end point, and curvature parameters for total length s, serving as the center of the Gaussian distribution. Gaussian Support: A plane perpendicular to the MPP at position \mathbf{x} over which the source integration occurs. Steps: 1. Use the singly scattered radiance b(\mathbf{x}') L0(\mathbf{x}', \vec{\omega}') as the source Q for multiply scattered light. 2. Replace the integral over complete path space with an integral over only paths surrounding the MPP. 3. Treat the first term (absorption) in the propagator equation as approximately constant for all paths in the reduced space and extract it from the path integral. 4. Express the second term (action) and extract \exp(-Ac(\text{MPP}s)) from the path integral. 5. Approximate the remaining path integral fraction using the multiply-scattered phase function P{MS}(\vec{\omega} - \vec{\omega}'), which gives the probability of light being scattered by a given angle after a given number of scattering events. This assumes single scattered light is strongly forward peaked and ignores angular spreading from single scattering. 6. Integrate only over the support of the Gaussian (plane perpendicular to MPP). 7. Combine extracted attenuation, action, phase function, and integrated source term. Formula: The final expression for multiply-scattered radiance is: L(s, \mathbf{x}, \vec{\omega}) = \exp \left( - \int0^s c(\text{MPP}s(s')) ds' \right) \exp(-Ac(\text{MPP}s)) \times P{MS}(\vec{\omega} - \vec{\omega}') \int{plane\perp \text{MPP}} gauss(\mathbf{x}', w(s)) b(\mathbf{x}') L0(\mathbf{x}', \vec{\omega}') d\mathbf{x}' Where: gauss(\mathbf{x}', w(s)) is a Gaussian function of width w(s) applied at position \mathbf{x}. Ac represents the curvature part of the action function. C is a normalization constant included in the derivation of the general propagator Gs but absorbed into the phase function and Gaussian definitions in the final radiance equation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computemultiplyscatteredradiance(s, x, omega, omegaprime, bL0func, cfunc, mpppath, ws, PMSfunc): """ Computes L(s, x, omega) using the Full Propagator Approximation. mpppath: list of 3D points along the Most Probable Path. """ # 1. Integrate extinction coefficient along the MPP attenuationintegral = 0.0 for i in range(len(mpppath) - 1): pcurr, pnext = mpppath[i], mpppath[i+1] segmentlen = math.sqrt(sum((pnext[k] - pcurr[k])2 for k in range(3))) attenuationintegral += cfunc(pcurr) segmentlen attenuationfactor = math.exp(-attenuationintegral) # 2. Evaluate action (curvature) factor at MPP # Assuming mpppath stores the cumulative curvature action at each point actionfactor = math.exp(-mpppath[-1].curvatureaction) # 3. Evaluate phase function probability phaseprob = PMSfunc(omega - omegaprime) # 4. Integrate source term over Gaussian support plane perpendicular to MPP # Define a local 2D coordinate system on the plane perpendicular to MPP at x # For implementation, we sample a grid on this plane sourceintegral = 0.0 gridstep = 0.01 # numerical integration step size gridradius = 5 # number of steps in each direction for u in range(-gridradius, gridradius + 1): for v in range(-gridradius, gridradius + 1): # Construct point x' on the plane xprime = [x[k] + u gridstep (1 if k == 0 else 0) + v gridstep (1 if k == 1 else 0) for k in range(3)] disttocenter = math.sqrt(sum((xprime[k] - x[k])2 for k in range(3))) gaussianweight = math.exp(-0.5 (disttocenter / ws)2) sourceintegral += gaussianweight bL0func(xprime) (gridstep 2) # 5. Combine all factors radiance = attenuationfactor actionfactor phaseprob sourceintegral return radiance Parameters: C: Normalization constant. w(s): Gaussian width. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Forward Peaking Assumption: The method assumes single scattered light is strongly forward peaked and ignores angular spreading from single scattering. Integration Bounds: The integration is strictly limited to the Gaussian support plane perpendicular to the MPP. Time Complexity: Depends on evaluating the MPP, the action function, and the 2D plane integration, which is cheaper than full path space integration. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the MPP and associated parameters. Strengths: Provides a deterministic approximation for multiple scattering that retains directional information via the phase function. Limitations: Approximation errors arise from the Gaussian assumption and forward-peaking assumption. When to Use: When multiple scattering is significant, full path tracing is too expensive, and the medium exhibits forward-peaked scattering. The method is described in the paper "Practical Rendering of Multiple Scattering Effects in Participating Media" by Raviraj Pajarala et al.. It builds upon the concept of the Most Probable Path (MPP) and approximates the path integral for the multiply-scattered propagator Gs. name: P-N Method (Spherical Harmonics)
head: SH expansion, Spherical Harmonics Method, Spherical harmonics expansion
body: The P-N method solves the radiative transfer equation for participating media by expanding the directional radiance I(X, \omega) into a truncated spherical harmonics basis, converting the integral transport equation into a coupled system of partial differential equations (PDEs) for the expansion coefficients. It is a deterministic method that deals with anisotropy by expanding radiance in a truncated spherical harmonic basis. It is mathematically equivalent to the Discrete Ordinates Method with M properly placed directions. Inputs: Spatial domain (typically 1D slab geometry z or 3D volume). Extinction coefficient \sigmat(z). Scattering albedo w0. Phase function p(\omega, \omega'). Boundary conditions (incident radiance). Outputs: Spherical harmonic coefficients Il^m(z) (or Il^m(X) in 3D). Reconstructed radiance I(X, \omega) via inverse expansion. Data Structures: Harmonic Coefficients: A 2D array or list of tuples storing Il^m for 0 \le l \le L{max} and -l \le m \le l. Matrix Elements: Precomputed coupling matrices for the phase function and direction operators. For the phase function, the matrix is diagonal in the spherical harmonic basis. Definitions: Spherical Harmonics Yl^m(\omega): Normalized spherical harmonics of degree l and order m. Associated Legendre Polynomials Pl^m(\mu): Where \mu = \cos \theta. Truncation Level L{max}: The maximum degree of the expansion, which determines the number of coefficients. Graphics applications typically use L{max}=1 (p-wave). Other sources mention truncation after the fourth coefficient. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Expansion: Express the source term (or radiance) Z(z, \omega) as a sum of spherical harmonics: Z(z, \omega) = \sum{l=0}^{L{max}} \sum{m=-l}^{l} Il^m(z) Yl^m(\omega) 2. Projection: Multiply the radiative transfer equation by Y{l'}^{m'}(\omega) and integrate over the unit sphere to isolate the coefficients. This yields a coupled system of first-order PDEs for Il^m(z). The general form derived is: \sum{l,m} Il^m(z) \langle Y{l'}^{m'}, \mathbf{s} \cdot \nabla Yl^m \rangle - I{l'}^{m'}(z) \sigmat + \sum{l,m} Il^m(z) \langle Y{l'}^{m'}, p \cdot Yl^m \rangle = 0 3. Matrix Element Calculation: Phase Function Matrix: Use Laplace's formula for the product of Legendre polynomials to show the phase function matrix is diagonal with respect to spherical harmonics. \langle Y{l'}^{m'}, p \cdot Yl^m \rangle = \delta{l l'} \delta{m m'} \frac{4\pi}{2l+1} \tilde{p}l Direction Operator Matrix: Calculate matrix elements for the direction operator \mathbf{s} \cdot \nabla (or \mathbf{s} in 1D slab) using recursion relations for associated Legendre polynomials. P{l, m+1}(\mu)(1-\mu^2)^{1/2} = k0 P{l+1, m} - k1 P{l-1, m} P{l, m}(\mu) = k2 P{l+1, m} - k3 P{l-1, m} with coefficients: k0 = \frac{(l-m+1)(l-m+2)}{2l+1}, \quad k1 = \frac{(l+m-1)(l+m)}{2l+1} k2 = \frac{l+m}{2l+1}, \quad k3 = \frac{l-m+1}{2l+1} 4. System Assembly: Assemble the coupled linear system of PDEs for the coefficients Il^m. For 1D slab geometry, these become ODEs in z. 5. Solution: Solve the system of PDEs/ODEs using relaxation methods or finite difference methods. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def solvepnmethod1d(sigmat, albedow0, phasecoeffs, domainlength, numpoints, Lmax): """ Solves the P-N method for a 1D slab geometry using relaxation. """ numcoeffs = (Lmax + 1) 2 Ilm = [[0.0] numcoeffs for in range(numpoints)] directionmatrix = computedirectionoperatormatrix(Lmax) phasematrix = computephasefunctionmatrix(Lmax, phasecoeffs) dz = domainlength / numpoints # Set boundary condition at z=0 Ilm[0][0] = 1.0 maxiterations = 100 for iteration in range(maxiterations): for i in range(1, numpoints): # Relaxation step: update coefficients based on neighbors and source # The exact relaxation formula is not given in the sources. Ilm[i] = [0.0] numcoeffs return Ilm def computedirectionoperatormatrix(Lmax): """ Computes the matrix elements for the direction operator s using recursion relations for associated Legendre polynomials. """ size = (Lmax + 1) 2 matrix = [[0.0] size for in range(size)] def idx(l, m): return l (l + 1) + (m + l) for l in range(Lmax + 1): for m in range(-l, l + 1): i = idx(l, m) # Apply recursion relations to fill coupling coefficients # P{l, m+1}(mu)(1-mu^2)^{1/2} = k0 P{l+1, m} - k1 P{l-1, m} # P{l, m}(mu) = k2 P{l+1, m} - k3 P{l-1, m} k0 = ((l - m + 1) (l - m + 2)) / (2 l + 1) k1 = ((l + m - 1) (l + m)) / (2 l + 1) k2 = (l + m) / (2 l + 1) k3 = (l - m + 1) / (2 l + 1) if l + 1 <= Lmax: matrix[i][idx(l + 1, m)] += k0 matrix[i][idx(l + 1, m)] -= k2 if l - 1 >= 0: matrix[i][idx(l - 1, m)] -= k1 matrix[i][idx(l - 1, m)] += k3 return matrix def computephasefunctionmatrix(Lmax, phasecoeffs): """ Computes the diagonal phase function matrix. The phase function matrix is diagonal with respect to spherical harmonics. """ size = (Lmax + 1) 2 matrix = [[0.0] size for in range(size)] for l in range(Lmax + 1): idx = l (l + 1) matrix[idx][idx] = phasecoeffs[l] return matrix Parameters: Truncation Level (L{max}): Graphics applications typically use L{max}=1 (p-wave). Other implementations truncate after the fourth coefficient. Phase Function: Only constant and Rayleigh phase functions are considered in the original Kajiya/Von Herzen work. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Surface-Volume Interaction: The original method does not take into account effects between surfaces and volumes. Extensions by Bhate and Tokuta address this by extending the zonal method. High Albedo: The Neumann expansion approach (related to P-N) may require many terms if albedo w0 is close to one. Uses a collection of M discrete directions for optimal Gaussian quadrature. Equivalent to P-N with M properly placed directions but suffers from ray effects if not modified. Choose when directional resolution is needed without angular basis truncation. Discrete Ordinates Method A lower-order approximation suitable for highly scattering media, neglecting angular detail compared to P-N. Choose for computationally cheap approximations in optically thick regions. Diffusion Approximation Stochastic approach, computationally expensive but accurate, unlike the deterministic P-N. Choose when high-fidelity angular resolution or complex boundary conditions are required. Monte Carlo Method for Multiple Scattering Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles anisotropic scattering better than diffusion; deterministic. Limitations: Original formulation ignores surface-volume interactions. When to use: Not given in the sources. The P-N method was originally developed by Chandrasekhar for stellar atmospheres and applied to computer graphics by Kajiya and Von Herzen. In thermal engineering, it is known as the P-N method. It is a deterministic method that deals with anisotropy by expanding radiance in a truncated spherical harmonic basis. Ray Tracing for Volume Densities, https://www.scribd.com/document/746685923/ray-tracking-volume-densities, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) A survey on participating media rendering techniques, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00371-005-0287-1, fetched 2026-10-26 Global Illumination Techniques for the Simulation of Participating Media, https://inria.hal.science/inria-00510096v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (book) [PDF] Optical Models for Direct Volume Rendering - Duke Computer Science, https://courses.cs.duke.edu/spring03/cps296.8/papers/max95opticalModelsForDirectVolumeRendering.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Optical models for direct volume rendering (PDF) - Academia.edu, https://www.academia.edu/49467168/Opticalmodelsfordirectvolumerendering, fetched 2026-10-27 Mathematical models for volume rendering and neutron transport, https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc1274949/?q=volume rendering equation, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Monte Carlo Method for Multiple Scattering
head: Monte Carlo Method for Directional Scattering, Monte Carlo ray tracing, Two-pass Monte Carlo
body: The Monte Carlo method for multiple scattering solves the integral equation for directional scattering intensity I(X, \omega) by stochastically tracing rays through a participating medium. It addresses the problem of computing light transport in volumes where photons undergo random absorption or scattering events governed by the extinction coefficient \tau, albedo a, and phase function p. Unlike deterministic solvers such as the P-N Method (Spherical Harmonics) or the Diffusion Approximation, which approximate the angular dependence of radiance, this method provides an unbiased estimate of the radiative transfer equation by sampling the stochastic path of light. Its primary trade-off is high variance; because rays that successfully connect the eye to a light source via multiple scattering events are rare, the method produces noisy images and requires significant computational time to converge. Inputs: Volume geometry defined by voxels or spatial regions. Optical properties per voxel: extinction coefficient \tau, albedo a, and phase function p(\omegai, \omegao). Light source definitions (position, intensity, directionality). Camera parameters (eye position, pixel grid). Outputs: Pixel intensity values representing the radiance reaching the eye. Voxel Grid: Stores \tau, a, and p for each spatial cell. Caustic Texture Map (Optional): A 2D or 3D texture used in two-pass variants to store intermediate radiance values propagated from light sources. It may store isotropic scattering intensity or directional scattered texture I(Xi, \omega). Ray State: Position X, direction \omega, current weight/throughput. The method can be implemented as a direct eye-tracing approach or a hybrid two-pass approach to mitigate the low probability of eye-to-light connectivity. 1. For each pixel, cast a primary ray from the eye into the volume. 2. Sample the distance to the next interaction event using the extinction coefficient \tau. 3. At the interaction point Xi: Determine if the photon is absorbed or scattered. The probability of scattering is given by the albedo a. If absorbed, terminate the path. If scattered, sample a new direction \omega{new} from the phase function p(\omega{old}, \omega{new}). 4. Update the ray's throughput weight by multiplying by a and the phase function value. 5. Repeat steps 2-4 until the ray exits the volume or hits a light source/emitter. 6. If the ray hits a light source, add the source's radiance (weighted by the current throughput) to the pixel's accumulated color. To address the inefficiency of direct tracing where few rays reach light sources, a two-pass method can be used. Pass 1: Light Propagation 1. Cast rays from light sources into the volume. 2. Trace these rays through the medium, simulating scattering events using \tau, a, and p. 3. At each scattering voxel Xi, record the scattered radiance. 4. Store this radiance in a Caustic Texture Map. Note: Blasi et al. stored only an isotropic scattering texture, but the method generalizes to storing directional scattered texture I(Xi, \omega). Pass 2: Eye Tracing with Pre-computed Data 1. Cast rays from the eye through the pixel. 2. For each interaction or exit from the volume, query the Caustic Texture Map to retrieve the radiance arriving from the light side. 3. Combine the eye-side path throughput with the pre-computed light-side radiance to determine the final pixel contribution. A specific implementation for high-albedo scattering involves volumetric backprojection: 1. Cast a large set of rays from energy sources into the volume. 2. At each voxel, roll a "dice" (sample a random number) to determine energy absorption and scattering direction. 3. Iterate this process for many steps to simulate energy transport among voxels. 4. Perform a final scattering pass from the computed radiosity volume towards the eye point. Scattering Probability: P{scatter} = a. Absorption Probability: P{absorb} = 1 - a. Phase Function Sampling: Direction \omega{new} is sampled from p(\omega{old}, \omega{new}). Weight Update: W{new} = W{old} \cdot a \cdot p(\omega{old}, \omega{new}). Extinction Coefficient (\tau): Controls the mean free path. Not given in the sources. Albedo (a): Ratio of scattering coefficient to extinction coefficient. Not given in the sources. Phase Function (p): Describes angular distribution of scattering. Not given in the sources. Number of Samples: High sample counts are required to decrease variance. Not given in the sources. Noise: The method produces noisy images because contributing rays (those connecting eye to light via multiple scattering) are a small fraction of all considered rays. Performance: Computation time is long due to the need for many samples to achieve acceptable variance. Connectivity: In direct tracing, rays from the eye rarely end up at a light source, and rays from a light source rarely end up at the eye. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def montecarlomultiplescattering(volume, camera, lights, usetwopass=False): """ Solves multiple scattering using Monte Carlo ray tracing. Args: volume: Object containing voxel data (tau, albedo, phasefunction). camera: Object containing eye position and pixel grid. lights: List of light sources. usetwopass: Boolean flag to enable the two-pass caustic texture approach. Returns: Image buffer with pixel intensities. """ image = initializeimagebuffer(camera) if usetwopass: causticmap = computelightpropagation(volume, lights) rendereyepass(camera, volume, causticmap, image) else: for pixel in camera.pixels: pixelcolor = traceeyeray(pixel, volume, lights) image[pixel] = pixelcolor return image def computelightpropagation(volume, lights): """ Pass 1: Propagate light from sources to build a caustic texture map. """ causticmap = initializetexturemap(volume.resolution) for light in lights: # Cast rays from light source rays = generateraysfromlight(light, volume) for ray in rays: currentthroughput = 1.0 currentpos = ray.origin currentdir = ray.direction while not rayexitedvolume(currentpos, volume): # Sample distance to next interaction distance = samplefreepath(currentpos, currentdir, volume.extinction) nextpos = currentpos + currentdir distance # Check for interaction if isinsidevolume(nextpos): # Determine scattering vs absorption if random() < volume.albedo[nextpos]: # Albedo 'a' # Scattering event phaseval = volume.phasefunction(currentdir, samplescatteringdirection()) currentthroughput = volume.albedo[nextpos] phaseval # Store scattered radiance in caustic map # Note: Blasi et al. stored isotropic; generalized to directional I(Xi, omega) causticmap.addradiance(nextpos, currentthroughput) # Update direction currentdir = samplescatteringdirection() currentpos = nextpos else: # Absorption event break else: break return causticmap def traceeyeray(pixel, volume, lights): """ Pass 2 (or direct): Trace ray from eye. """ ray = generaterayfromeye(pixel, volume) throughput = 1.0 color = 0.0 currentpos = ray.origin currentdir = ray.direction while not rayexitedvolume(currentpos, volume): distance = samplefreepath(currentpos, currentdir, volume.extinction) nextpos = currentpos + currentdir distance if isinsidevolume(nextpos): if random() < volume.albedo[nextpos]: # Scattering phaseval = volume.phasefunction(currentdir, samplescatteringdirection()) throughput = volume.albedo[nextpos] phaseval currentdir = samplescatteringdirection() currentpos = nextpos else: # Absorption break else: # Ray exited volume without hitting light or being absorbed break # If ray hit a light source directly (in direct tracing) if rayhitlight(currentpos, currentdir, lights): color = throughput lightradiance(currentpos, currentdir, lights) return color def rendereyepass(camera, volume, causticmap, image): """ Final rendering pass using pre-computed caustic map. """ for pixel in camera.pixels: ray = generaterayfromeye(pixel, volume) throughput = 1.0 color = 0.0 currentpos = ray.origin currentdir = ray.direction while not rayexitedvolume(currentpos, volume): distance = samplefreepath(currentpos, currentdir, volume.extinction) nextpos = currentpos + currentdir distance if isinsidevolume(nextpos): if random() < volume.albedo[nextpos]: # Scattering phaseval = volume.phasefunction(currentdir, samplescatteringdirection()) throughput = volume.albedo[nextpos] phaseval # Query caustic map for light contribution # This approximates the contribution from light sources lightcontrib = causticmap.query(nextpos, currentdir) color += throughput lightcontrib currentdir = samplescatteringdirection() currentpos = nextpos else: break else: break # Direct light contribution if applicable if rayhitlight(currentpos, currentdir, lights): color += throughput lightradiance(currentpos, currentdir, lights) image[pixel] = color def samplefreepath(pos, dir, extinction): """ Sample distance to next interaction based on extinction coefficient. """ # Exponential distribution sampling # Not given in the sources for exact implementation, standard physics formula: # distance = -ln(random()) / extinction return -math.log(random()) / extinction def samplescatteringdirection(): """ Sample a new direction based on the phase function. """ # Implementation depends on specific phase function (e.g., Henyey-Greenstein) # Not given in the sources for exact implementation. return randomunitvector() This method estimates the multiple scattering albedo \alpha{ms} (RGB) for a low-resolution voxel such that its effective albedo \alphae matches the effective albedo \alphae^{\text{input}} of the corresponding high-resolution input block [Child 1]. It solves the problem of preserving the color and density of light scattered at least twice at the microscopic scale during volume downsampling [Child 1]. Unlike Light Tracing for Participating Media, which simulates light transport from the light source, this method operates as a pre-computation step to derive parameters for a standard Monte Carlo renderer, ensuring the low-res voxel reproduces the multi-scattering behavior of the original high-res data without iterative optimization [Child 1]. Light tracing for participating media is a Monte Carlo method that solves the radiative transfer equation by tracing bundles of light from the source through the volume to find interaction points. It differs from eye-tracing (path tracing) by generating paths from the light source, making it particularly effective for scenes with complex lighting or when the camera view is not the primary constraint. Unlike constant distance sampling methods, this approach is unbiased because it samples the distance to the next interaction continuously rather than restricting it to multiples of a discrete step size. A method for computing high-albedo scattering illumination using Monte-Carlo simulations to solve the integral equation of light transport. It casts a large set of rays from energy sources into the volume, where at each voxel a "dice is rolled" to determine energy absorption and scattering direction. After many iterations, the simulation is stopped, and a final scattering of the radiosity volume is performed towards an arbitrarily positioned eye point. Backprojection is usually performed on a voxel-by-voxel basis. Time Complexity: High. The method requires many samples to decrease variance because contributing rays are a small fraction of all considered rays. Memory Complexity: Depends on implementation. Direct tracing uses minimal memory. Two-pass approaches require storage for the caustic texture map. Measured Performance: Images tend to appear noisy and take a very long time to compute. Strengths: Unbiased solution to the radiative transfer equation; handles complex geometries and anisotropic scattering naturally. Limitations: High variance (noise); slow convergence; inefficient for eye-to-light connectivity in highly scattering media. When to use: When unbiased results are required and computational time is not a primary constraint, or when used in hybrid approaches (e.g., two-pass) to capture specific interreflection effects. When not to use: When real-time performance is required or when the volume is highly scattering and direct eye tracing is too noisy. The Monte Carlo method for volume rendering was originally developed by physicists for neutron transport and applied to rendering surface interreflection by Cook et al. and Kajiya. It was applied to volume applications by Rushmeier. The method traces sample rays from the eye through a pixel, undergoing random absorption or scattering based on the extinction coefficient \tau, albedo a, and phase function p. To address the inefficiency of direct tracing, Rushmeier suggested calculating g(X, \omega) by the zonal method and performing a final rendering pass using Monte Carlo for one extra directional bounce toward the viewpoint. Shirley and Chen et al. used such a final Monte Carlo bounce in rendering images of interreflecting surfaces. Heckbert proposed "caustic texture maps" to capture directional interreflection propagated by Monte Carlo means from light sources. For volume rendering, Blasi et al. used a similar two-pass approach, propagating light from sources and storing scattering in a texture map for a final eye-tracing pass. name: Multiple Scattering Albedo Estimation
head: Computation of multiple scattering albedo, $\sigma_{ms}$ estimation
body: This method estimates the multiple scattering albedo \alpha{ms} (RGB) for a low-resolution voxel such that its effective albedo \alphae matches the effective albedo \alphae^{\text{input}} of the corresponding high-resolution input block. It solves the problem of preserving the color and density of light scattered at least twice at the microscopic scale during volume downsampling. Unlike Light Tracing for Participating Media, which simulates light transport from the light source, this method operates as a pre-computation step to derive parameters for a standard Monte Carlo renderer, ensuring the low-res voxel reproduces the multi-scattering behavior of the original high-res data without iterative optimization. Inputs: A block of high-resolution input voxels with known scattering properties. A target low-resolution voxel geometry corresponding to the input block. The single-scattering albedo \alpha{ss} and self-shadowing probability P{ss} for the low-res voxel. Outputs: The multiple scattering albedo \alpha{ms} (RGB) for the low-res voxel. Data Structures: Psh: Array of probabilities for a ray undergoing exactly n scattering events before leaving the voxel. Size: N{max} + 1, where N{max} is the maximum number of scattering events considered. alphaeinput: Scalar (RGB) representing the average throughput of rays leaving the input block. Steps: 1. Estimate \alphae^{\text{input}}: Cast rays through the block of input voxels. For each ray, compute the light path until it leaves the block, treating the block as a participating medium. The throughput is the product of transmittance and scattering contributions along the path. Average the throughputs of all cast rays to obtain \alphae^{\text{input}}. 2. Estimate P{sh}(n): Cast rays through the low-resolution voxel. For each ray, count the number of scattering events n before the ray leaves the voxel. Compute the histogram of these counts and normalize to obtain the probability P{sh}(n) for each n \in [0, N{max}]. These probabilities do not depend on \alpha{ms}. 3. Approximate P{ss}: Calculate the microscopic self-shadowing probability P{ss} using the approximation: P{SS} \approx \frac{\int \sigma{SS}}{\alpha{SS}(\lambda) \int \sigmat} where \sigma{SS} is the self-shadowing cross-section, \alpha{SS}(\lambda) is the single-scattering albedo, and \sigmat is the extinction coefficient. 4. Solve for \alpha{ms}: For each wavelength channel, solve the following equation numerically for \alpha{ms}: \alphae^{\text{input}} = \sum{n=0}^{N{max}} P{sh}(n) \left( P{ss} \alpha{ss} + (1 - P{ss}) \alpha{ms} \right)^n The term \left( P{ss} \alpha{ss} + (1 - P{ss}) \alpha{ms} \right) represents the effective albedo per scattering event at the microscopic scale. The summation accounts for the probability of having n such events. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def estimatemultiplescatteringalbedo(inputblock, lowresvoxel, alphass, Pss, Nmax, numrays): # Step 1: Estimate alphaeinput # Standard volume path tracing: march rays through inputblock, accumulate throughput # until leaving, then average. The source does not specify the exact march routine. alphaeinput = 0.0 for in range(numrays): throughput = 1.0 # Ray marching loop: sample interactions, apply transmittance and scattering # contributions until ray exits inputblock alphaeinput += throughput alphaeinput /= numrays # Step 2: Estimate Psh(n) Psh = [0.0] (Nmax + 1) for in range(numrays): n = 0 # Ray marching loop: count scattering events n until ray exits lowresvoxel Psh[n] += 1.0 for n in range(Nmax + 1): Psh[n] /= numrays # Step 3: Solve for alphams per wavelength alphams = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # RGB for channel in range(3): # Bisection root finding for alphams in [0, 1] low, high = 0.0, 1.0 for in range(50): mid = (low + high) / 2.0 term = Pss alphass[channel] + (1.0 - Pss) mid effectivealbedo = sum(Psh[n] (term n) for n in range(Nmax + 1)) if effectivealbedo > alphaeinput[channel]: high = mid else: low = mid alphams[channel] = (low + high) / 2.0 return alphams Parameters: N{max}: Maximum number of scattering events. The maximum number of scattering events is chosen up to a given limit. Ray count: The number of samples is adapted to the complexity of the input block. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method tends to slightly underestimate the effective albedo \alphae. Accuracy depends on the density and amount of shadowing in the voxel. If P{ss} is inaccurate, the estimated \alpha{ms} will be biased. Numerical stability of the root-finding algorithm should be ensured, especially when \alpha{ms} is close to 0 or 1. A preprocessing method that accelerates Monte Carlo rendering of optically dense, forward-scattering participating media by replacing original scattering parameters with altered parameters that yield fewer scattering events, without modifying the core rendering algorithm. Unlike methods that require renderer modifications, this technique outputs altered parameters (\sigma^a, \sigma^s, f^(\cdot)) compatible with any standard Monte Carlo renderer (e.g., Mitsuba). It sets apart from simpler first-order approximations by utilizing higher-order similarity relations (up to order N=5) to better capture complex phase function moments, while explicitly guarding against overfitting via support regularization. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of rays cast for estimating \alphae^{\text{input}} and P{sh}(n). Pre-computation time scales with the complexity of the input block and the number of samples. Memory Complexity: Low, as it only stores probabilities P{sh}(n) and intermediate albedo values. Strengths: Avoids iterative optimization, making it faster than methods that require solving for \alpha{ms} via repeated rendering. Compatible with standard Monte Carlo renderers. Limitations: Slight underestimation of effective albedo. Accuracy degrades in highly shadowed or dense voxels. When to use: When downsampling participating media and preserving multi-scattering color fidelity is critical, and iterative methods are too slow. This method is part of a microflake model with microscopic self-shadowing for accurate volume downsampling. It was introduced to address the loss of multi-scattering information when reducing the resolution of participating media. The approach approximates the effective albedo using a series expansion based on scattering event probabilities, allowing for efficient pre-computation of scattering parameters. name: Optical Thickness Reduction via Similarity Relations

body: A preprocessing method that accelerates Monte Carlo rendering of optically dense, forward-scattering participating media by replacing original scattering parameters with altered parameters that yield fewer scattering events, without modifying the core rendering algorithm. Unlike methods that require renderer modifications, this technique outputs altered parameters (\sigma^a, \sigma^s, f^(\cdot)) compatible with any standard Monte Carlo renderer (e.g., Mitsuba). It sets apart from simpler first-order approximations by utilizing higher-order similarity relations (up to order N=5) to better capture complex phase function moments, while explicitly guarding against overfitting via support regularization. Inputs: Absorption coefficient \sigmaa (scalar or RGB). Scattering coefficient \sigmas (scalar or RGB). Phase function f(\cdot), defined over the domain t \in [-1, 1] (where t = \cos \theta). User-specified performance/accuracy trade-off parameter \alpha \in (0, 1). Outputs: Altered absorption coefficient \sigma^a. Altered scattering coefficient \sigma^s. Altered phase function f^(\cdot). Data Structures: The phase function f(\cdot) is typically represented as a tabulated function with k bins over the domain [-1, 1]. Moments fn are computed as fn = \int{-1}^{1} f(t) t^n dt. Parameters: \alpha: Controls the reduction in scattering events. Typical range: (0, 1). Default recommendation: \max(0.3, 1 - f1). N0: Maximum order of similarity relation to consider. Value: 5. \beta: Threshold constant for support regularization to prevent overfitting. Value: 0.65. Formulas: Total coefficients: \sigmat = \sigmas + \sigmaa and \sigma^t = \sigma^s + \sigma^a. Approximation of \alpha: \alpha \approx \sigma^t / \sigmat. This implies the expected number of scattering events per unit distance is reduced by a factor of \alpha. Constraint on \alpha: \alpha \geq 1 - f1, where f1 is the first moment of the original phase function. This ensures the first moment of the altered phase function f^1 \geq 0. Normalized support: \text{nz}(f):= \frac{|\{t: f(t) > 0\}|}{2}, where |\cdot| denotes the measure of the set. For a tabulated function with k total bins, if \tilde{k} bins have f(t) > 0, then \text{nz}(f) = \tilde{k}/k. Algorithm Steps: 1. Set \sigma^a \leftarrow \sigmaa and \sigma^s \leftarrow \alpha \sigmas. 2. Compute the moments f^1, \dots, f^{N0} using the similarity relation equations (Equation 23 in). 3. Initialize order N \leftarrow 1. 4. Loop while N < N0: a. Check if the order-N+1 similarity relation is satisfiable using the routine \text{I\EXISTS}(1, f^1, \dots, f^{N+1}) (implementing Theorem 1 in). b. If not satisfiable, break the loop. c. Otherwise, increment N \leftarrow N + 1. 5. Repeat: a. Solve the order-N version of Equation 31 in to obtain the altered phase function f^(\cdot) numerically. b. Decrement N \leftarrow N - 1. c. Check if f^(\cdot) is overfitting. If not overfitting, exit the repeat loop. 6. Return \sigma^a, \sigma^s, f^(\cdot). Pseudocode: Unverified code. 1 # Check for overfitting using normalized support nzoriginal = normalizedsupport(phasefunction) nzaltered = normalizedsupport(fstar) if nzaltered >= beta nzoriginal: break return sigmastara, sigmastars, fstar def checktheorem1(moments, order): # does not provide the explicit implementation of IEXISTS. # Returns True if a valid non-negative phase function exists for the given moments. return True def solveequation31(order, moments): # does not provide the explicit numerical optimization procedure. # Returns the altered phase function f(t) matching the given moments. return [0.0] 100 def normalizedsupport(phasefunction): # For tabulated function with k bins, returns count of positive bins / k # For continuous, returns measure({t: f(t)>0}) / 2 return 0.5 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting: Higher-order relations (N > 5) can yield worse accuracy because they result in phase functions with very limited support that do not generalize well. This is mitigated by bounding N at 5 and rejecting solutions with insufficient support. Support Regularization: If the altered phase function f^(\cdot) has normalized support \text{nz}(f^) < \beta \cdot \text{nz}(f), where f is the original phase function and \beta=0.65, the solution is rejected. Parameter Selection: Setting \alpha too low (e.g., 0.05) can lead to unsatisfactory accuracy despite high speedups (e.g., 8.0\times). A value of \alpha=0.1 provides a better balance (5.5\times speedup, better accuracy). Performance: The parameter \alpha linearly relates to rendering time for Monte Carlo methods, as it reduces the expected number of scattering events by a factor of \alpha. Measured Performance: With \alpha=0.05, an 8.0\times speedup was achieved, but accuracy was unsatisfactory. With \alpha=0.1, a 5.5\times speedup was achieved with significantly better accuracy. Complexity: The preprocessing step involves solving numerical optimization problems for the phase function. The complexity depends on the order N and the number of bins in the tabulated phase function. Strengths: No modification to the core rendering algorithm is required; it works with any standard Monte Carlo renderer. Higher-order relations provide better accuracy for complex phase functions compared to first-order approximations. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \alpha. Higher-order relations may lead to overfitting if not properly regularized. Origin: Introduced in "High-order similarity relations in radiative transfer". Application: Primarily used for forward rendering of optically dense and forward-scattering materials. Development: The method builds on the theory of similarity relations in radiative transfer, extending it to higher orders to capture more complex phase function behaviors. name: Light Tracing for Participating Media
head: Monte Carlo light tracing with random distance, Pattanaik and Mudur, Pattanaik and Mudur light tracing, Pattanaik et al. method, Random distance sampling (Light Tracing)
body: Light tracing for participating media is a Monte Carlo method that traces bundles of light from the source through the volume to find interaction points (absorption or scattering). Unlike constant distance sampling, it is unbiased because it samples the distance to the next interaction continuously rather than restricting it to multiples of a discrete step size. Inputs: Volume geometry and bounds. Extinction coefficient field \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) (or optical thickness \kappat). Scattering coefficient \sigmas(\mathbf{x}) and absorption coefficient \sigmaa(\mathbf{x}), where \sigmat = \sigmas + \sigmaa. Phase function p(\omegai, \omegao). Light source emission distribution. Rendering algorithm parameters (number of bundles, variance reduction flags). Outputs: Radiance values at image plane pixels or voxel storage buffers. The method typically uses a storage scheme suited for isotropic scattering, which can be modified to handle anisotropic scattering. For image-based implementations, a pixel buffer accumulates contributions when bundles hit the image plane. 1. Initialize Bundle: Shoot a light bundle from the light source with initial direction \omega0 and weight W0 = 1.0 (or scaled by source intensity). 2. Sample Distance to Interaction: Sample the distance s to the next interaction point using the cumulative distribution function (CDF) derived from the extinction coefficient. For homogeneous media, F(s) = 1 - e^{-\sigmat s}. For inhomogeneous media, F(s) = 1 - \exp(-\int0^s \sigmat(u) du). The inverse CDF yields s = -\ln(1 - \xi)/\sigmat where \xi \in [0, 1). 3. Move Bundle: Update the bundle position: \mathbf{x}{new} = \mathbf{x}{old} + s \cdot \omega. Check for boundary intersection. If the bundle exits the volume, terminate the path. 4. Determine Interaction Type: At \mathbf{x}{new}, decide if the event is absorption or scattering. Two methods are described: Method A: Simple Absorption: Perform a sampling process to decide the event type based on the ratio of scattering to extinction \Omega = \frac{\sigmas}{\sigmat}. Generate \xi \in [0, 1). If \xi < \Omega, scattering occurs and the weight updates to W \cdot \frac{\sigmas}{\sigmat}. If \xi \ge \Omega, absorption occurs and the path terminates. Method B: Absorption Suppression: The bundle always scatters. The flux reduces by multiplying the weight by \Omega = \frac{\sigmas}{\sigmat}. This avoids path termination due to absorption but reduces the weight, increasing variance. 5. Scattering Event: If scattering occurs, sample the new direction \omega{new} from the phase function p(\omega{old}, \omega{new}). Update direction: \omega = \omega{new}. Repeat from Step 2. 6. Termination: If the bundle hits the image plane, add W to the corresponding pixel. If the bundle exits the volume or absorption occurs in Simple Absorption, terminate. The sources propose three specific techniques: 1. Forced Interaction: Force a bundle to interact with each voxel it passes through. 2. Absorption Suppression: As described in Step 4, always scatter and reduce weight by \frac{\sigmas}{\sigmat}. 3. Particle Divergence: At scattering points, split the outgoing bundle into many smaller bundles. This increases the number of rays traveling through the volume, improving the sampling of energy leaving the volume. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def random(): """Returns a uniform random number in [0, 1).""" return 0.0 # Standard uniform RNG implementation def lighttraceparticipatingmedia(volume, lightsource, camera, numbundles): """ Monte Carlo light tracing for participating media. Uses random distance sampling (Pattanaik et al. method). """ pixelbuffer = [0.0] (camera.width camera.height) for in range(numbundles): # 1. Initialize bundle from light source origin, direction, weight = lightsource.sample() pos = origin dir = direction w = weight while w > 1e-6: # 2. Sample distance to next interaction xidist = random() sigmat = volume.getextinction(pos) if sigmat == 0: # Handle vacuum: move to next boundary dist = volume.distancetoboundary(pos, dir) if dist is None: break pos = pos + dir dist continue # Inverse CDF for homogeneous media: s = -ln(1-xi)/sigmat s = -math.log(1.0 - xidist) / sigmat nextpos = pos + dir s # 3. Check boundary intersection if not volume.contains(nextpos): break # 4. Determine interaction type (Absorption Suppression) sigmas = volume.getscattering(nextpos) albedo = sigmas / sigmat # Always scatter, reduce weight by albedo w = albedo if w < 1e-6: break # 5. Scattering event newdir = volume.phasefunction.sample(dir) dir = newdir pos = nextpos # 6. Check image plane intersection hit, pixelidx = camera.intersect(pos, dir) if hit: pixelbuffer[pixelidx] += w return pixelbuffer Anisotropic Scattering: The basic storage scheme is suited for isotropic scattering. For anisotropic scattering, the storage scheme must be modified to account for directionality. Precision: Sampling distance continuously avoids the bias of constant distance sampling. Using constant distance sampling leads to biased results because bundles can only be scattered at distances which are multiples of a step size \Delta, and the expected length before scattering won't be equal to the mean free path without absorption. Performance: To get accurate sampling of energy leaving the volume, the number of rays must be higher than in per-voxel storage methods. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of bundles and M is the average number of scattering events per bundle. Memory Complexity: O(P) for pixel buffer or O(V) for voxel storage, where P is pixel count and V is voxel count. Strengths: Unbiased result (unlike constant distance sampling); effective for complex lighting; no need for eye-point sampling. Limitations: Requires many bundles for accurate sampling of energy leaving the volume; variance can be high in sparse media without variance reduction techniques. When to use: Scenes with complex light sources or when light tracing is more efficient than path tracing (e.g., caustics in participating media). When not to use: Simple homogeneous media where analytical solutions or simpler methods suffice; scenes where eye-tracing is more efficient (e.g., small light sources). The method was introduced by Pattanaik and Mudur [66] and Pattanaik et al. [14] as a Monte Carlo light tracing technique for participating media. It uses a sampling process to find points of interaction within the volume. The method is part of the broader family of Monte Carlo methods for solving the radiative transfer equation, specifically addressing multiple scattering. It is often compared to bidirectional path tracing for non-emitting participating media, which combines light shooting and light gathering. name: Diffusion Approximation
head: Classical Diffusion Approximation, Diffusion Approximation for Multiple Scattering, Diffusion Approximation of RTE, Diffusion Method (Stam), Diffusion Theory, Radiative Diffusion Equation, Stam [93, 94], Stam diffusion approximation
body:
The Diffusion Approximation is a method for computing multiple scattering in participating media by replacing the computationally expensive integral form of the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) with a partial differential equation (PDE). It models the medium radiance as a function of the first two angular moments of the radiation field: the scalar irradiance (fluence) and the vector irradiance (flux). Unlike Full Propagator Approximation for Multiply-Scattered Radiance or Monte Carlo Method for Multiple Scattering, which track angular distribution or stochastic paths, the diffusion approximation assumes that in highly scattering media, light distribution becomes nearly isotropic, allowing angular dependence to be smoothed out. It is particularly efficient for dense, high-opacity media where photons undergo long random walks. Inputs: Medium properties: Absorption coefficient \sigmaa(\mathbf{x}), scattering coefficient \sigmas(\mathbf{x}), extinction coefficient \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) = \sigmaa(\mathbf{x}) + \sigmas(\mathbf{x}). Source terms: Incident unscattered light field q{ri}(\mathbf{x}) and self-emission field j(\mathbf{x}). Domain: Volume \Omega with boundary \partial \Omega. Outputs: Fluence field \phi(\mathbf{x}). Flux field \mathbf{E}(\mathbf{x}). Approximated medium radiance Lm(\mathbf{x},  oldsymbol{\omega}). Data Structures: The method typically operates on a grid or a set of blobs representing the volume. For grid-based implementations, \phi and \mathbf{E} are stored as scalar and vector fields at grid nodes or cell centers. For blob-based implementations (e.g., Stam's method), a system of linear equations is formed for each blob, solving for coefficients J0 and J1. Formulas: 1. Radiance Approximation: The medium radiance is approximated by the first two terms of the angular expansion: Lm(\mathbf{x},  oldsymbol{\omega}) \approx  rac{1}{4\pi} \phi(\mathbf{x}) +  rac{3}{4\pi}  oldsymbol{\omega} \cdot \mathbf{E}(\mathbf{x}) where \phi(\mathbf{x}) is the fluence (scalar irradiance) and \mathbf{E}(\mathbf{x}) is the flux (vector irradiance). 2. Fick's First Law: The flux is related to the gradient of the fluence via the diffusion coefficient D(\mathbf{x}): \mathbf{E}(\mathbf{x}) = -D(\mathbf{x}) 
abla \phi(\mathbf{x}) where the diffusion coefficient is defined as: D(\mathbf{x}) =  rac{1}{3\sigmat(\mathbf{x})} 3. Radiative Diffusion Equation (Fick's Second Law): Substituting Fick's law into the energy conservation equation yields the governing PDE for fluence: 
abla \cdot (D(\mathbf{x}) 
abla \phi(\mathbf{x})) = \sigmaa(\mathbf{x}) \phi(\mathbf{x}) - q{ri}(\mathbf{x}) - j(\mathbf{x}) Here, q{ri}(\mathbf{x}) is the source field from reduced incident light, and j(\mathbf{x}) is the emission source. 4. Total Radiance at Ray Endpoint: The final radiance at a point \mathbf{x}e along a ray is computed by combining the attenuated incident light and the in-scattered light from the diffusion solution: L(\mathbf{x}e,  oldsymbol{\omega}) = L(\mathbf{x}s,  oldsymbol{\omega}) T(\mathbf{x}s, \mathbf{x}e) + \Delta x \sumn T(\mathbf{x}n, \mathbf{x}e) Q(\mathbf{x}n) where T is transmittance, \mathbf{x}s is the start point, and Q(\mathbf{x}n) is the source term derived from the diffusion approximation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def solvediffusionapproximation(grid, cellsize, sigmaa, sigmas, qri, j): sigmat = sigmaa + sigmas D = 1.0 / (3.0 sigmat) N = grid.numcells() # 1. Discretize PDE: -div(D grad(phi)) + sigmaa phi = qri + j A = buildsparsematrix(D, sigmaa, grid, cellsize) b = qri + j applydirichletboundaryconditions(A, b, grid, phi=0.0) # 2. Solve linear system for fluence if N < 1000: phi = solveludecomposition(A, b) else: phi = solverelaxationscheme(A, b, maxiterations=1000) # 3. Compute flux via Fick's law E = -D computegradient(phi, grid, cellsize) # 4. Ray march to compute final radiance radiance = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 for samplepoint in raysamples: radiance += transmittance (sigmaa[samplepoint] phi[samplepoint] - qri[samplepoint] - j[samplepoint]) cellsize transmittance = exp(-sigmat[samplepoint] cellsize) return phi, E, radiance Algorithm Steps: 1. Precompute Source Terms: Calculate q{ri}(\mathbf{x}) from the incident unscattered light and j(\mathbf{x}) from self-emission. 2. Discretize the Diffusion Equation: Grid-based: Discretize the PDE 
abla \cdot (D 
abla \phi) = \sigmaa \phi - q{ri} - j using finite differences or finite elements to form a linear system A\phi = b. Blob-based: Form a system of linear equations for each blob, restricting the source radiance to Jm( oldsymbol{\omega}) = J0 + J1 \cdot  oldsymbol{\omega}. 3. Solve for Fluence: Apply boundary conditions (e.g., Dirichlet: \phi = 0 on \partial \Omega). Solve the linear system for \phi(\mathbf{x}). If the number of unknowns v < 1000, use direct LU decomposition. If v is larger, use an iterative relaxation scheme (convergence not guaranteed). 4. Compute Flux: Calculate \mathbf{E}(\mathbf{x}) = -D(\mathbf{x}) 
abla \phi(\mathbf{x}) using the solved fluence field. 5. Render: Compute the final radiance L(\mathbf{x},  oldsymbol{\omega}) using the radiance approximation formula and ray marching. Parameters: The method assumes isotropic scattering or requires an effective scattering coefficient \sigmas' = \sigmas(1-g) if anisotropy is present. The method is limited to volume scenes without surface models in some implementations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Vacuum/Low Extinction: The method breaks down in regions of low extinction (\sigmat 	o 0) or vacuum, where D(\mathbf{x}) diverges. This violates the physical constraint |\mathbf{E}| \leq \phi. Thin Features: Dipole variants of diffusion approximation tend to overestimate absorption by thin features (e.g., edges of a nose or helmet). Complex Scenes: For scenes with many surfaces, the cost of progressive shooting of energy from surface patches can be expensive, requiring hierarchical approaches. Modifies the classical diffusion coefficient to be flux-limited and fluence-dependent, handling heterogeneous media and vacuum regions where classical diffusion fails. Choose this when rendering scenes with sharp opacity transitions or low-extinction zones. Specifically discretizes the diffusion equation for volumetric cloud rendering, using multigrid relaxation to solve for the isotropic radiance component. Choose this for large-scale atmospheric or cloud volumes where standard grid solvers are too memory-intensive. Time Complexity: Solving the linear system is generally faster than path tracing for dense media. Blob methods scale with the number of blobs v, requiring O(v^3) for direct LU decomposition when v < 1000, or iterative relaxation for larger v. Memory Complexity: Uses far less memory than grid-based full RTE solvers. Strengths: Very fast for dense, highly scattering media; includes both double and multiple scattering in a single model. Limitations: Inaccurate in low-scattering regions, near boundaries, or for thin features; assumes near-isotropic radiance. When to Use: Dense participating media (e.g., fog, skin, milk) where multiple scattering dominates. When Not to Use: Sparse media, vacuum regions, or scenes requiring accurate single-scattering angular details. The diffusion approximation originates from the observation that in highly scattering media, the angular distribution of light becomes isotropic due to multiple scattering events. It was applied to volume rendering by Stam to solve multiple scattering between blobs modeling media, offering a significant speedup over path tracing. It is widely used in computer graphics for rendering subsurface scattering and dense participating media. name: Flux-Limited Diffusion
head: Flux-Limited Diffusion (FLD) Solver, Flux-Limited Radiative Diffusion, Numerical FLD solver
body:
Flux-Limited Diffusion (FLD) is a numerical method for solving the radiative transfer equation in participating media by modifying the classical diffusion approximation (CDA) to handle heterogeneous media, vacuum regions, and transitions to the transport regime. It improves upon CDA by replacing the constant diffusion coefficient with a flux-limited, fluence-dependent expression that enforces the physical constraint that flux magnitude does not exceed fluence, ensuring accuracy where opacity is low. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Voxel grids for emission field jp (power per unit volume), extinction field \sigma{tp} (inverse length), and albedo field \alphap (dimensionless). Grid coordinates p=(i,j,k) with voxel edge length \Delta l. Outputs: Fluence grid \phip and diffusion coefficient grid Dp. Data Structures Grids: 3D arrays for \phi, D, j, \sigmat, \alpha. Memory complexity is linear with grid size, requiring storage for \phi, D, and input fields. Performance: FLD is roughly twice as computationally expensive as CDA due to additional memory access per voxel to compute the Knudsen number. It is still much faster than path tracing. Accuracy: FLD produces results closer to path-traced ground truth than CDA, especially in shadowed regions, indirect lighting, and transitions to vacuum. Limitations: Dirichlet boundary conditions introduce unphysical effects near boundaries, though they do not significantly corrupt the bulk solution. In vacuum regions, convergence is negatively affected without the extinction tolerance \sigma\varepsilon. FLD was developed originally for radiative transfer applications in astrophysics [LP81, TS01] and nuclear physics [LK74]. Applied to computer graphics for multiple scattering in participating media, it extends the theoretical framework of CDA by replacing the diffusion coefficient with a \phi(\mathbf{x})-dependent expression. name: Diffusion Approximation for Cloud Radiance
head: Diffusion Approximation for Cloud Rendering, Diffusion method, Iterative Diffusion Solver with Multigrid, PDE solution for cloud illumination
body:
This method computes the isotropic radiance component I0(X) in dense cloud regions by solving a linear system derived from the diffusion approximation of the radiative transfer equation. It replaces the full radiative transfer equation with a diffusion equation for diffuse light transport, which is solvable via multigrid relaxation. Inputs: Cloud density field ho(X) defined on a 3D voxel grid. Extinction coefficient per particle \sigmat and scattering coefficient \sigmas = a \sigmat, where a is the albedo. Henyey-Greenstein anisotropy factor g (where p1 = g). Sky radiance distribution I{sky}(\omega), discretized into direction bins. Outputs: Diffuse radiance scalar field I0(X) at each voxel. Final radiance I(X, \omega) = I{ri}(X, \omega) + I0(X) + \mathbf{I}1(X) \cdot  oldsymbol{\omega}, where \mathbf{I}1(X) is derived from I0(X) and sources. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: 3D array storing ho(X), I0(X), \mathcal{Q}0(X), and \mathbf{Q}1(X). Direction Bins: A set of directions \omegai on a subdivided unit cube surface. The implementation uses 64x64 resolution images on each of the 6 faces of a viewing cube, averaged into 4x4 direction bins per face, resulting in 96 total direction bins. Step 1: Compute Reduced Incident Radiance and Sources 1. For each direction bin i with direction \omegai and solid angle \Delta\omegai: Trace a dense collection of rays in direction \omegai starting from the external faces of the box enclosing the cloud. For each ray, identify the segments Sj it intersects within the cloud voxels. Accumulate the attenuation integral along each segment Sj: I{ri}(X, \omegai) = I{sky}(\omegai) \exp \left( - \int0^\infty \sigmat ho(X - s\omegai) ds ight) The integral is accumulated along the ray segments Sj. Compute the first scattered external illumination contribution for this direction: \mathcal{Q}(X, \omegai) = ho(X) \sigmas I{ri}(X, \omegai) \Delta\omegai p1  oldsymbol{\omega}i The angular integral simplifies because p(\omega, \omega') depends only on the angle, and contributions from other directions cancel by symmetry. Accumulate these contributions into voxel-wise sums for \mathcal{Q}0 and \mathbf{Q}1: 	ext{Sum}{\mathcal{Q}0}(X) \leftarrow 	ext{Sum}{\mathcal{Q}0}(X) +  rac{1}{4\pi} \mathcal{Q}(X, \omegai) 	ext{Sum}{\mathbf{Q}1}(X) \leftarrow 	ext{Sum}{\mathbf{Q}1}(X) +  rac{1}{4\pi} \mathcal{Q}(X, \omegai) Accumulate the total segment length in voxel X for this direction: 	ext{Sum}{len}(X) \leftarrow 	ext{Sum}{len}(X) + \sumj l(Sj) 2. After processing all rays and directions, normalize the sources for each voxel X: \mathcal{Q}0(X) =  rac{	ext{Sum}{\mathcal{Q}0}(X)}{	ext{Sum}{len}(X)} \mathbf{Q}1(X) =  rac{	ext{Sum}{\mathbf{Q}1}(X)}{	ext{Sum}{len}(X)} If 	ext{Sum}{len}(X) = 0, set \mathcal{Q}0(X) = 0 and \mathbf{Q}1(X) = 0. Step 2: Discretize the Diffusion Equation The diffusion equation to solve is: 
abla \cdot \left(  rac{1}{3ho(X)\sigma{tr}} 
abla I0(X) ight) - ho(X)\sigmaa I0(X) = -\mathcal{Q}0(X) + 
abla \cdot \left(  rac{1}{4\piho(X)\sigma{tr}} \mathbf{Q}1(X) ight) where \sigma{tr} = \sigmat (1 - a p1) and \sigmaa = \sigmat (1 - a). 1. Define the transport cross section: \sigma{tr} = \sigmat (1 - a g). 2. For each voxel X with ho(X) > 0, construct a linear equation relating I0(X) to its six neighbors. 3. Evaluate the gradient of I0 at face centers using central differences. 4. Determine the coefficient  rac{1}{3ho(X)\sigma{tr}} for the diffusion term: For a face shared by voxel X and neighbor N, use the average density:  ar{ho} =  rac{ho(X) + ho(N)}{2}. If one of the cells has ho = 0, use the value from the non-zero cell. 5. Evaluate the divergence of the source term \mathbf{Q}1 using central differences. 6. Handle boundary conditions: For a voxel X adjacent to an empty border voxel Xe (where ho(Xe)=0), enforce the no total inward flow boundary condition: I0(X) -  rac{2}{3ho(X)\sigma{tr}} \mathbf{n} \cdot 
abla I0(X) +  rac{1}{2\piho(X)\sigma{tr}} \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{Q}1(X) = 0 where \mathbf{n} is the inward surface normal. Assume a temporary value I0(Xe) at the empty cell that satisfies this condition. Use this temporary value to compute the finite difference for the gradient at the face between X and Xe. Substitute this into the linear equation for X. This affects the coefficients of the linear equation for X but does not introduce I0(Xe) as a variable in the system. Step 3: Solve the Linear System 1. The resulting system is a set of linear equations relating each I0(X) to its six neighbors and a constant term involving \mathcal{Q}0 and \mathbf{Q}1. 2. Solve using a multigrid method to accelerate convergence, as Gauss-Seidel or Jacobi methods are too slow for large grids due to slow propagation of bright spots. Treat the data volume as a multi-resolution octree hierarchy. Write coarser linear equations for lower levels of the hierarchy. Use solutions from coarser levels to correct solutions at finer levels. Iterate up and down the hierarchy until convergence. Implementation may use the Hypre system API and multigrid solver from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. rhosigmaaI0 = -Q0 + div( beta Q1) # alpha = 1/(3rhosigmatr), beta = 1/(4pirhosigmatr) n = densitygrid.shape rows = [] voxeltoidx = {} idx = 0 for x in range(n[0]): for y in range(n[1]): for z in range(n[2]): if densitygrid[x, y, z] > 0: voxeltoidx[(x, y, z)] = idx idx += 1 for (x, y, z), idx in voxeltoidx.items(): coeffs = {} rhs = 0.0 rhoX = densitygrid[x, y, z] alphaX = 1.0 / (3.0 rhoX sigmatr) betaX = 1.0 / (4.0 pi rhoX sigmatr) # Diagonal term from -rhosigmaaI0 diagcoeff = -rhoX sigmaa neighbors = [ ((x-1, y, z), (-1, 0, 0)), ((x+1, y, z), (1, 0, 0)), ((x, y-1, z), (0, -1, 0)), ((x, y+1, z), (0, 1, 0)), ((x, y, z-1), (0, 0, -1)), ((x, y, z+1), (0, 0, 1)) ] for (nx, ny, nz), normal in neighbors: if not (0 <= nx < n[0] and 0 <= ny < n[1] and 0 <= nz < n[2]): continue rhoN = densitygrid[nx, ny, nz] # Effective rho for face if rhoX > 0 and rhoN > 0: rhoface = (rhoX + rhoN) / 2.0 else: rhoface = rhoX if rhoX > 0 else rhoN alphaface = 1.0 / (3.0 rhoface sigmatr) if rhoN > 0: # Interior neighbor neighboridx = voxeltoidx.get((nx, ny, nz)) if neighboridx is not None: coeffs[neighboridx] = coeffs.get(neighboridx, 0.0) + alphaface / gridspacing2 diagcoeff -= alphaface / gridspacing2 else: # Empty border voxel Xe: apply BC to eliminate I0(Xe) # BC: I0(X) - D n.grad(I0) + C = 0, where D = 2/(3rhoXsigmatr), C = n.Q1/(2pirhoXsigmatr) D = 2.0 / (3.0 rhoX sigmatr) C = np.dot(normal, Q1[x, y, z]) / (2.0 pi rhoX sigmatr) # Approximate n.grad(I0) at face as (I0(X) - I0(Xe))/h # From BC: I0(Xe) = I0(X) - (h/D) (I0(X) + C) # Substituting into diffusion term alphaface (I0(Xe) - I0(X))/h^2 # yields modified diagonal and constant term. bcfactor = alphaface / (gridspacing D) diagcoeff -= bcfactor rhs += bcfactor C # Divergence of Q1 source term (last term in eq 4) divQ1 = 0.0 for (nx, ny, nz), normal in neighbors: if 0 <= nx < n[0] and 0 <= ny < n[1] and 0 <= nz < n[2]: rhoN = densitygrid[nx, ny, nz] rhoface = (rhoX + rhoN) / 2.0 if rhoX > 0 and rhoN > 0 else (rhoX if rhoX > 0 else rhoN) betaface = 1.0 / (4.0 pi rhoface sigmatr) divQ1 += np.dot(normal, Q1[nx, ny, nz] - Q1[x, y, z]) / gridspacing rhs -= (-Q0[x, y, z] + divQ1) coeffs[idx] = diagcoeff rows.append((idx, coeffs, rhs)) # Step 3: Solve using Multigrid V-cycle I0 = np.zeroslike(densitygrid) # Multigrid V-cycle implementation is not detailed in the sources. # Standard multigrid solvers (e.g., Hypre) are used. I0 = multigridvcycle(rows, voxeltoidx, n, gridspacing, I0) return I0 def traceraysindirection(direction, densitygrid): """Generates rays from external faces in the given direction.""" # Standard hemicube/ray traversal implementation return [] def multigridvcycle(rows, voxeltoidx, n, h, I0guess): """Implements a multigrid V-cycle for the linear system.""" # Standard multigrid V-cycle implementation return I0guess Time Complexity: The multigrid solver provides faster convergence than Gauss-Seidel or Jacobi, which are prohibitively slow for large grids because bright spots propagate only one adjacent cell per iteration. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the density grid, source fields (\mathcal{Q}0, \mathbf{Q}1), and the solution field I0, plus multigrid hierarchy data. Strengths: Efficiently handles dense media where the mean free path is short, capturing multiple scattering effects that single-scattering approximations miss. Limitations: Assumes dense media; less accurate for sparse regions or near boundaries where the diffusion approximation breaks down. The derivation in Stam [Stam95] is noted to be incorrect compared to Ishimaru [Ish78], differing by factors of 3 in several terms. When to use: Dense cloud rendering where multiple scattering is significant. When not to use: Sparse media or when high-fidelity single-scattering details are required. Kajiya and von Herzen [Kaj84] first proposed the diffusion approximation to the computer graphics community. Stam [Stam95] gave the first practical implementation for radiance transport in clouds. The method is based on the radiative transfer equation and the diffusion approximation as detailed in [Ish78]. The implementation described uses the Hypre system API and multigrid solver from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. name: Neural Network RTE Simplification via Albedo Series
head: Albedo power series for neural prediction, Radiation Transfer Equation Simplification for Neural Network, Scattering term approximation
body: This method simplifies the classical Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) by expressing the co-scattering term as an infinite power series of the single-scattering albedo \eta, enabling efficient prediction via a neural network. It solves the computational bottleneck of evaluating multiple scattering events in participating media by decoupling the complex integral operator from the albedo parameter, allowing the network to infer the total scattering contribution from pre-calculated geometric and density features. It sets itself apart from Full Propagator Approximation for Multiply-Scattered Radiance by explicitly leveraging the algebraic structure of the albedo series, and from Monte Carlo Method for Multiple Scattering by providing a deterministic, differentiable approximation rather than a stochastic estimate. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Position p, direction \omega, density features, transmittance features, and phase function features. These are pre-calculated and stored in a lookup table based on particle coordinates and sampling templates. Outputs: The backbone neural network outputs the approximation of the co-scattering term F(p, \omega) or the final radiance Lo(p, \omega). Data Structures: Pre-calculation Table: Stores sampling features (density, transmittance, phase) for discrete template points. Access is direct via particle position coordinates. Neural Network Backbone: Three identical network branches are used, corresponding to density, transmittance, and phase features, though the specific input/output mappings for each branch are not fully detailed in the source. Mathematical Formulation: The classical RTE is given by: \frac{\partial Lo(p, \omega)}{\partial \omega} = Le(p, \omega) - \mua(p)Li(p, \omega) - \mus(p)Li(p, \omega) + \frac{\mus(p)}{\Omega} \int{\Omega} fp(\omegai \to \omega)Li(p, \omegai)d\omegai where Lo is output radiance, Li is incident radiance, Le is self-illumination, \mua is absorption coefficient, \mus is scattering coefficient, fp is the phase function, and \Omega is the unit ball. The solution for radiance along a path from p to z is: Lo(p, \omega) = T(p, z)Li(z, \omega) + \intp^z T(p, x)\mus(x)F(x, \omega)dx where T(p, y) = e^{-\intp^y \mut(x)dx} is the transmittance, \mut = \mua + \mus is the extinction coefficient, and F(p, \omega) is the co-scattering term. The co-scattering term F(p, \omega) is expanded as an infinite series of albedo powers: F(p, \omega) = \sum{i=0}^{\infty} \eta^i Fi(p, \omega) where \eta = \mus / \mut is the single-scattering albedo. The terms are defined recursively: F0(p, \omega) = fp \cdot T \cdot I F{i+1}(p, \omega) = \Pi Fi(p, \omega) with the operator \Pi defined as: \Pi F(p, \omega) = \int{\Omega} \intp^z fp T \mut F(p, \omega) dx d\omegai For co-directional scattering, fp is constant with respect to \omegai, simplifying the operator. Algorithm Steps: 1. Pre-calculation: Compute sampling features (density, transmittance, phase) for all relevant template points and store them in a pre-calculation table. 2. Feature Extraction: For a query point p and direction \omega, retrieve the corresponding sampling features from the table. 3. Neural Prediction: Input the features into the backbone neural network. The network is trained to predict the value of the infinite series sum F(p, \omega) or the final radiance Lo(p, \omega) directly, bypassing the iterative calculation of individual Fi terms. 4. Rendering: Use the predicted radiance for image synthesis. Parameters: \eta = \mus / \mut: Single-scattering albedo. l = 1/\mut: Mean free path. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The source assumes the volume medium does not emit light (Le = 0) for the simplified transmission equation. The source mentions the medium albedo is assumed constant for the simplified equation, but the general series formulation allows for spatial variation in \mut and \mus within the integral. Precision issues may arise if the series converges slowly for high albedo values, though the neural network is intended to mitigate this by learning the global mapping. Estimates target radiance Rt given source radiance Rs, gradient Gs, and albedos \alphas, \alphat using a two-exponential formulation to handle non-linear radiance behavior. Time Complexity: Depends on the neural network inference time and table lookup, which is significantly faster than iterative multiple scattering solvers. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the pre-calculation table and the neural network weights. Strengths: Real-time rendering capability for high albedo anisotropic materials; avoids complex iterative calculations. Limitations: Requires pre-calculation and training; accuracy depends on the neural network's ability to generalize across different media properties. When to use: Real-time rendering of participating media with high albedo and anisotropic scattering. When not to use: Scenes with significant self-illumination or where exact physical accuracy is required over performance. This method originates from research on real-time rendering of high albedo anisotropic materials with multiple scattering. It addresses the difficulty of simulating multiple scattering events efficiently by leveraging the mathematical properties of the albedo series and modern neural network approximation capabilities. A real-time rendering method for high albedo anisotropic materials with multiple scattering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2401.14051, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)
