name: Participating Media Regularization (Prediction Function)
head: Novel prediction function, Two-exponential prediction
body: This method estimates the target radiance Rt for a participating media scene given a rendered source radiance Rs, its gradient Gs at a source albedo \alphas, and a target albedo \alphat. It solves the problem that linear and log-linear prediction functions fail to capture the complex, non-linear behavior of radiance with respect to albedo changes in participating media, particularly across varying mean free paths and extinction coefficients. It sets itself apart by using a two-exponential formulation that adapts to both high/low albedo regimes and small/large mean free paths, providing a better fit to ground truth than simpler models. Inputs: Rs: Source radiance (pixel value) at source albedo. Gs: Source gradient (rate of change of radiance with respect to albedo) at source albedo. \alphas: Source albedo. \alphat: Target albedo. \sigmat: Extinction coefficient of the medium. Outputs: Rt: Predicted target radiance. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required; the method operates on scalar values per pixel or per light transport path segment. Parameters: c\beta: A constant used to scale the mean free path (\sigmat^{-1}). It must satisfy 0 < c\beta \le \sigmat \alphas to ensure \beta \le 1. In practice, c\beta is set to 0.5 or searched for around 0.5. Formulas: The target radiance is computed as: Rt = Rs + Gs \beta \left( e^{(\alphat - \alphas)/\beta} - 1 \right) e^{-\gamma Rs (\alphat - \alphas)} The parameters \beta and \gamma are defined as: \beta = \frac{c\beta \ln(\sigmat + 1)}{\sigmat \alphas} \gamma = \frac{5}{1 - \alphas} Step-by-Step Procedure: 1. Calculate \beta using the extinction coefficient \sigmat, source albedo \alphas, and constant c\beta. 2. Calculate \gamma using the source albedo \alphas. 3. Compute the first exponential term component: E1 = e^{(\alphat - \alphas)/\beta} - 1. 4. Compute the second exponential term component: E2 = e^{-\gamma Rs (\alphat - \alphas)}. 5. Compute the predicted radiance: Rt = Rs + Gs \cdot \beta \cdot E1 \cdot E2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def predictradiance(Rs, Gs, alphas, alphat, sigmat, cbeta=0.5): """ Predict target radiance Rt given source radiance Rs, gradient Gs, source albedo alphas, target albedo alphat, and extinction coefficient sigmat. Args: Rs: Source radiance (float) Gs: Source gradient (float) alphas: Source albedo (float) alphat: Target albedo (float) sigmat: Extinction coefficient (float) cbeta: Scaling constant for mean free path (float, default 0.5) Returns: Rt: Predicted target radiance (float) """ # Calculate beta # beta = (cbeta ln(sigmat + 1)) / (sigmat alphas) # Note: Ensure sigmat alphas is not zero to avoid division by zero. # If alphas is 0, the behavior is undefined in this formulation. beta = (cbeta math.log(sigmat + 1)) / (sigmat alphas) # Calculate gamma # gamma = 5 / (1 - alphas) # Note: If alphas approaches 1, gamma approaches infinity. # The term (1 - alphas) in the exponent of the second exponential # helps control the amplification. gamma = 5.0 / (1.0 - alphas) # Calculate the first exponential term part # term1 = exp((alphat - alphas) / beta) - 1 exponent1 = (alphat - alphas) / beta term1 = math.exp(exponent1) - 1.0 # Calculate the second exponential term part # term2 = exp(-gamma Rs (alphat - alphas)) exponent2 = -gamma Rs (alphat - alphas) term2 = math.exp(exponent2) # Calculate final radiance # Rt = Rs + Gs beta term1 term2 Rt = Rs + Gs beta term1 term2 return Rt Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Albedo and Small Mean Free Path: In these cases, \beta approaches 0. This causes the factor multiplying Gs to become significantly large, amplifying small differences in Gs among neighboring pixels and leading to discontinuities in the predicted result. The second exponential term (controlled by \gamma) is specifically designed to alleviate this amplification. Albedo near 1: As \alphas \to 1, \gamma \to \infty. However, the term (1-\alphas) in the denominator of \gamma is balanced by the (\alphat - \alphas) term in the exponent of the second exponential. When Rs is close to 0, Gs is also close to 0, so the attenuation effect of the second exponential term is restrained. Zero Extinction or Albedo: The formula for \beta involves division by \sigmat \alphas. If \alphas = 0 or \sigmat = 0, the formula is undefined. The sources do not specify a fallback for these degenerate cases. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel, as it involves a constant number of arithmetic operations and exponential evaluations. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel, requiring storage for Rs, Gs, \alphas, \alphat, \sigmat and intermediate variables. Performance: The method is designed to work for a wide range of materials, from large mean free path (mfp) to small mfp. It fits ground truth better than linear and log-linear prediction functions across varying mfp and extinction coefficients. Strengths: Handles complex non-linear albedo behavior; adapts to different scales of mean free path; reduces discontinuities in high-albedo/small-mfp scenarios compared to simpler models. Limitations: Requires accurate estimation of Gs (gradient); performance depends on the choice of c\beta; undefined for \alphas = 0 or \sigmat = 0. When to use: When rendering participating media with varying albedo and needing to predict radiance for a target albedo from a source albedo, especially when linear/log-linear models fail to capture the complexity. When not to use: When \alphas is 0 or \sigmat is 0; when computational cost of evaluating exponentials is prohibitive (though it is generally low). The method was proposed in the context of efficient participating media rendering with differentiable volumetric path tracing. It addresses the challenge that rendering participating media with high albedo is difficult due to slow light path attenuation, leading to noisy results. The prediction function is part of a regularization technique that uses source pixel values and gradients to predict target pixel values, avoiding the need for expensive re-rendering at the target albedo. The design was inspired by observations of radiance and gradient curves as functions of albedo for different pixels and extinction coefficients. The authors implemented their algorithm in Mitsuba 0.5. name: Jacobi Iterative Method for Diffusion
head: Computing Diffusion Radiance and Derivative, Diffusion Solver
body:
This method solves the discrete diffusion equation and its differential counterpart to compute diffusion radiance (Ld^0), its derivative (\partial\pi Ld^0), first-order radiance (\vec{L}1^d), and its derivative (\partial\pi \vec{L}1^d). It sets itself apart from sibling methods by operating on a grid-based iterative solver for the diffusion approximation rather than discrete angular directions. Inputs: Ld^0: Diffusion radiance field (uninitialized or previous iteration). \partial\pi Ld^0: Derivative of diffusion radiance field. \vec{L}1^d: First-order radiance field. \partial\pi \vec{L}1^d: Derivative of first-order radiance field. S: Source term field. \kappa: Optical coefficient field. \kappaa: Absorption coefficient field. h: Grid spacing. error	hreshold: Convergence threshold for Mean-Square Error (MSE). Outputs: Ld^0: Converged diffusion radiance. \partial\pi Ld^0: Converged derivative of diffusion radiance. \vec{L}1^d: First-order radiance. \partial\pi \vec{L}1^d: Derivative of first-order radiance. Data Structures: Fields Ld^0, \partial\pi Ld^0, \vec{L}1^d, \partial\pi \vec{L}1^d, S, \kappa, \kappaa are 3D arrays indexed by (i, j, k) corresponding to voxel coordinates. Values are floating-point numbers representing radiance or optical coefficients. Definitions: Discrete gradient approximation: 
abla F{ijk} \approx  rac{F{i+1,j,k} - F{i-1,j,k}}{2h}. Discrete Laplacian approximation: 
abla^2 F{ijk} \approx  rac{F{i+1,j,k} + F{i-1,j,k} - 2F{i,j,k}}{h^2}. \Sigma^1{ijk}, \Sigma^2{ijk}, \Sigma^6{ijk}: Intermediate terms derived from the expansion of 
abla \partial\pi \kappa \cdot 
abla Ld^0, 
abla \kappa \cdot 
abla \partial\pi Ld^0, and other diffusion terms. The exact expansion is defined in the source's Appendix B. Steps: 1. Initialization: If Ld^0, \vec{L}1^d, \partial\pi Ld^0, and \partial\pi \vec{L}1^d are uninitialized, assign them random values. 2. Solve for Diffusion Radiance (Ld^0): Repeat until convergence: Compute L^{new}{ijk} using the discrete diffusion equation (Equation 25). Calculate error: error = MSE(L^{new}, Ld^0). Update: Ld^0 \leftarrow L^{new}. Stop when error < error	hreshold. 3. Compute First-Order Radiance (\vec{L}1^d): Compute \vec{L}1^d using Equation 5. 4. Solve for Derivative of Diffusion Radiance (\partial\pi Ld^0): Repeat until convergence: Compute \partial\pi L^{new}{ijk} using the differential diffusion equation (Equation 29). Calculate error: error = MSE(\partial\pi L^{new}, \partial\pi Ld^0). Update: \partial\pi Ld^0 \leftarrow \partial\pi L^{new}. Stop when error < error	hreshold. 5. Compute Derivative of First-Order Radiance (\partial\pi \vec{L}1^d): Compute \partial\pi \vec{L}1^d using Equation 30. 6. Return: Ld^0, \vec{L}1^d, \partial\pi Ld^0, \partial\pi \vec{L}1^d. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def DiffusionSolver(L0d, dL0d, L1d, dL1d, S, kappa, kappaa, h, errorthreshold): def randomfill(shape): import random return [[[random.random() for in range(shape[2])] for in range(shape[1])] for in range(shape[0])] def computemse(a, b): n = len(a) len(a[0]) len(a[0][0]) return sum((a[i][j][k] - b[i][j][k])2 for i in range(len(a)) for j in range(len(a[0])) for k in range(len(a[0][0]))) / n # 1. Initialization if L0d is None or L1d is None or dL0d is None or dL1d is None: shape = (10, 10, 10) # Not given in the sources. L0d = randomfill(shape) if L0d is None else L0d L1d = randomfill(shape) if L1d is None else L1d dL0d = randomfill(shape) if dL0d is None else dL0d dL1d = randomfill(shape) if dL1d is None else dL1d # 2. Solve for Diffusion Radiance (L0d) while True: # Equation 25: Discrete diffusion equation for L0d # The source does not provide the explicit formula for Equation 25. # Standard 7-point Jacobi update for -∇·(κ∇L) + κa L = S Lnew = [[[[0.0 for in range(len(L0d[0][0]))] for in range(len(L0d[0]))] for in range(len(L0d))] for i in range(len(L0d)): for j in range(len(L0d[0])): for k in range(len(L0d[0][0])): laplacian = ( (L0d[i+1][j][k] if i+1 < len(L0d) else L0d[i][j][k]) + (L0d[i-1][j][k] if i-1 >= 0 else L0d[i][j][k]) + (L0d[i][j+1][k] if j+1 < len(L0d[0]) else L0d[i][j][k]) + (L0d[i][j-1][k] if j-1 >= 0 else L0d[i][j][k]) + (L0d[i][j][k+1] if k+1 < len(L0d[0][0]) else L0d[i][j][k]) + (L0d[i][j][k-1] if k-1 >= 0 else L0d[i][j][k]) - 6 L0d[i][j][k]) / (h h) Lnew[i][j][k] = (S[i][j][k] + kappa[i][j][k] laplacian) / (kappaa[i][j][k] + 6 kappa[i][j][k] / (h h)) error = computemse(Lnew, L0d) L0d = Lnew if error < errorthreshold: break # 3. Compute First-Order Radiance (L1d) # Equation 5 is not provided in the notes. # Direct computation from L0d and kappa for i in range(len(L0d)): for j in range(len(L0d[0])): for k in range(len(L0d[0][0])): L1d[i][j][k] = L0d[i][j][k] # 4. Solve for Derivative of Diffusion Radiance (dL0d) while True: # Equation 29: Differential diffusion equation for dL0d # The note provides the explicit formula for this update. dLnew = [[[[0.0 for in range(len(dL0d[0][0]))] for in range(len(dL0d[0]))] for in range(len(dL0d))] for i in range(len(dL0d)): for j in range(len(dL0d[0])): for k in range(len(dL0d[0][0])): # Sigma terms from Appendix B sigma1 = 0.0 # Not given in the sources. sigma2 = 0.0 # Not given in the sources. sigma3 = 0.0 # Not given in the sources. sigma6 = 0.0 # Not given in the sources. denominator = h h kappaa[i][j][k] + 6 kappa[i][j][k] numerator = 0.25 (sigma1 + sigma2) + kappa[i][j][k] sigma3 - h h kappaa[i][j][k] dL0d[i][j][k] + h h sigma6 dLnew[i][j][k] = numerator / denominator error = computemse(dLnew, dL0d) dL0d = dLnew if error < errorthreshold: break # 5. Compute Derivative of First-Order Radiance (dL1d) # Equation 30 is not provided in the notes. # Direct computation from dL0d and L1d for i in range(len(L0d)): for j in range(len(L0d[0])): for k in range(len(L0d[0][0])): dL1d[i][j][k] = dL0d[i][j][k] return L0d, L1d, dL0d, dL1d Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Uninitialized Values: The method requires random initialization if fields are not provided. Convergence: The method stops when the MSE between iterations falls below errorthreshold. Missing Formulas: Equations 5, 25 (for Ld^0), 30, and the definitions of \Sigma^1, \Sigma^2, \Sigma^6 are referenced but not fully detailed in the provided notes, requiring implementation from the source's Appendix B or other sections. This method approximates light transport in participating media by reducing the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) to a diffusion equation, enabling interactive, iterative resolution via per-voxel kernels. It visualizes structures and regions of interest in volumes without requiring global segmentation by simulating fluid-like light diffusion based on light transport. Unlike ray-tracing or path-tracing, which are view-dependent and require recomputation on camera move, or photon mapping, which incurs high memory costs for storing the full photon map, this implicit representation allows efficient per-voxel implementation and avoids full-volume storage of light paths. Time Complexity: Iterative, dependent on the number of iterations required for convergence (MSE < threshold). Each iteration involves a pass over the volume grid. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for Ld^0, \partial\pi Ld^0, \vec{L}1^d, \partial\pi \vec{L}1^d, and intermediate fields (S, \kappa, \kappaa). Strengths: Efficiently computes diffusion radiance and its derivatives for participating media visualization. Limitations: Requires convergence of iterative solver; performance depends on errorthreshold and grid resolution. When to use: When interactive visualization of volume structures via diffusion approximation is needed. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method is part of a differential diffusion theory for participating media. It was introduced in the paper "A Differential Diffusion Theory for Participating Media". name: Iterative Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) Solver for Light Diffusion
head: Diffusion Approximation for Volume Rendering, Diffusion Equation Method, Iterative RTE Solver, Light Diffusion, Light Diffusion Solver
body:
This method approximates light transport in participating media by reducing the Radiance Transfer Equation (RTE) to a diffusion equation, enabling interactive, iterative resolution via per-voxel kernels. It visualizes structures and regions of interest in volumes without requiring global segmentation by simulating fluid-like light diffusion based on light transport. Unlike ray-tracing or path-tracing, which are view-dependent and require recomputation on camera move, or photon mapping, which incurs high memory costs for storing the full photon map, this implicit representation allows efficient per-voxel implementation and avoids full-volume storage of light paths. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset defining material properties (extinction, scattering, emission). Output: A 3D buffer containing the computed fluence rate \phi and potentially the irradiance vector \vec{E}, representing the diffused light field. Data Structures: Two 3D buffers are used in a Ping Pong scheme to store the diffusion result during iterative resolution. This scheme allows access to data from a previous step during computation. Memory usage requires 256 bits per voxel to store the diffusion result, in addition to the original data. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize two 3D buffers for ping-pong iterative resolution. 2. Apply a finite difference scheme with forward time and central space pattern to solve the diffusion equation. 3. Update the fluence rate \phi iteratively. 4. Control parameters D, Ka, and dt via transfer functions or automatic values based on the scattering albedo \alpha. Formulas with Symbols Defined: The Radiance Transfer Equation (RTE) describes light transport:  rac{1}{c}  rac{\partial L(p,t,\vec{\omega})}{\partial t} + \vec{\omega} \cdot 
abla L(p,t,\vec{\omega}) = -Kt(p) \cdot L(p,t,\vec{\omega}) + Qe(p,t,\vec{\omega}) +  rac{Ks(p)}{4\pi} \int{\Omega2} P(p,\vec{\omega},\vec{\omega}') Li(p,t,\vec{\omega}') d\vec{\omega}' Where L(p,t,\vec{\omega}) is radiance, Kt(p) is the extinction coefficient (m^{-1}), Qe(p,t,\vec{\omega}) is volumetric emission (W.m^{-3}), P(p,\vec{\omega},\vec{\omega}') is the phase function (sr^{-1}), and Ks(p) is the scattering coefficient. The Diffusion Approximation assumes radiance L is a combination of an isotropic term \phi(p) and a direction-dependent term: L(p,\vec{\omega}) =  rac{1}{4\pi}\phi(p) +  rac{3}{4\pi}\langle\vec{\omega}, \vec{E}(p)angle Where \phi(p) is the fluence rate (spherical integral of radiance) and \vec{E}(p) is the irradiance vector (flux). Taking the moments of order 0 and 1 of the RTE and applying the steady-flux approximation ( rac{\partial \vec{E}}{\partial t} \approx 0) leads to the Diffusion Equation for fluence rate \phi:  rac{1}{c}  rac{\partial \phi(p,t)}{\partial t} = D(p)\Deltap \phi(p,t) - \langle
ablap D(p), 
ablap \phi(p,t)angle - Ka(p)\phi(p,t) + \phie(p,t) Where D(p) =  rac{1}{3Kt'(p)} is the diffusion coefficient, Ka(p) is the absorption coefficient, and \phie(p,t) is emission. Parameters: D(p): Diffusion coefficient, defined as  rac{1}{3Kt'(p)}. Controlled via predefined functions or custom transfer functions. Ka(p): Absorption coefficient. Controlled indirectly using an automatic value based on D or by using the scattering albedo \alpha (van de Hulst, 1981). dt: Time step. Must be set according to the discretization spatial step to ensure convergence of the method. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Instability: Numerical schemes for steady/unsteady RTE (e.g., finite element with main axis projection, finite differences with first/second order angular moment) are often unstable or lead to grid pattern artifacts. The unsteady RTE with diffusion approximation is chosen for stability. Overflow: Insufficient constraint on diffusion parameters causes light to overflow the structure it was emitted in. Under-diffusion: Excessive constraint on diffusion parameters limits the diffusion, preventing full identification of structures (e.g., veins). Positivity: To ensure radiance is positive, \phi \ge ||\vec{E}|| must hold. The implementation should guard against negative fluence values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. buffera = [[[0.0] Nz for in range(Ny)] for in range(Nx)] bufferb = [[[0.0] Nz for in range(Ny)] for in range(Nx)] dt = 0.01 # Exact stability condition not given in sources D = [[[0.0] Nz for in range(Ny)] for in range(Nx)] # D(p) = 1 / (3 Ktprime(p)) Ka = [[[0.0] Nz for in range(Ny)] for in range(Nx)] # Controlled indirectly via D or albedo alpha for iteration in range(maxiterations): readbuf = buffera if iteration % 2 == 0 else bufferb writebuf = bufferb if iteration % 2 == 0 else buffera for x in range(1, Nx - 1): for y in range(1, Ny - 1): for z in range(1, Nz - 1): # Central difference Laplacian for phi laplacian = (readbuf[x+1][y][z] + readbuf[x-1][y][z] + readbuf[x][y+1][z] + readbuf[x][y-1][z] + readbuf[x][y][z+1] + readbuf[x][y][z-1] - 6 readbuf[x][y][z]) # Central difference gradients for D and phi gradDx = (D[x+1][y][z] - D[x-1][y][z]) / 2 gradDy = (D[x][y+1][z] - D[x][y-1][z]) / 2 gradDz = (D[x][y][z+1] - D[x][y][z-1]) / 2 gradphix = (readbuf[x+1][y][z] - readbuf[x-1][y][z]) / 2 gradphiy = (readbuf[x][y+1][z] - readbuf[x][y-1][z]) / 2 gradphiz = (readbuf[x][y][z+1] - readbuf[x][y][z-1]) / 2 gradientterm = gradDx gradphix + gradDy gradphiy + gradDz gradphiz phiold = readbuf[x][y][z] phie = volumedata.emission[x][y][z] # Emission term not specified in sources newphi = phiold + dt (D[x][y][z] laplacian - gradientterm - Ka[x][y][z] phiold + phie) # Guard: Ensure positivity if required by physical model if newphi < 0: newphi = 0 writebuf[x][y][z] = newphi finaldiffusionfield = buffera if maxiterations % 2 == 0 else bufferb Time Complexity: Computation time scales linearly with the number of voxels. For a 128 	imes 128 	imes 128 voxel dataset, it requires an additional 2.5ms per iteration. For larger volumes, this hinders interactivity. Memory Complexity: Requires 256 bits per voxel to store the result of the diffusion, in addition to the original data. Strengths: Efficient per-voxel kernel implementation using compute shaders; avoids full-volume storage of light paths; provides fluid-like diffusion for exploration without global segmentation. Limitations: Tuning constraints is difficult; trade-off between overflow and under-diffusion is hard to find; memory and computation costs limit interactivity for large volumes. When to use: When interactive exploration of light transport in participating media is needed, and global segmentation is undesirable. When not to use: For high-fidelity, view-dependent rendering requiring exact path tracing, or for very large volumes where memory and linear scaling time exceed interactive thresholds. The Diffusion Approximation was introduced in Computer Graphics by Stam [Sta95] and later used by [JMLH01]. The method is inspired by fluoroscopy imaging, where fluorescent liquid or gas is injected and tracked to visualize propagation inside organs. The specific iterative RTE solver for light diffusion described here was proposed by D. Murray, J. Baril, and X. Granier. Volume Exploration with Light Diffusion, https://inria.hal.science/hal-03272284v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Sparse Linear System Solver for Wave Propagation
body: This method solves for forward and backward acoustic wave amplitudes in a layered medium by formulating the coupled wave equations as a sparse linear system A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}. It captures multiple internal reflections and transmissions at voxel boundaries defined by acoustic impedance contrasts. Unlike integral equation solvers that approximate scattering over volumes, this approach models wave propagation along straight-line ray paths through discrete interfaces. Inputs: N: Number of voxels along the ray path. Z: Array of acoustic impedances Z0, \dots, ZN for each voxel. c: Speed of sound, constant at 1540 m/s for soft tissue. Outputs: Vector \mathbf{x}: Wave amplitudes at each interface. Data Structures: The unknown vector \mathbf{x} has size 2N+2 and layout: \mathbf{x} = [g0, d0, g1, d1, \dots, gN, dN]^T where gi is the forward-traveling amplitude and di is the backward-traveling amplitude at interface i. The system matrix A is a sparse matrix of size (2N+2) \times (2N+2). The right-hand side vector \mathbf{b} has size 2N+2. Step 1: Compute Interface Coefficients For each interface i between voxel i and voxel i+1 (where i = 0, \dots, N-1), calculate the reflection and transmission coefficients: R{i \rightarrow i+1} = \left| \frac{Z{i+1} - Zi}{Z{i+1} + Zi} \right| T{i \rightarrow i+1} = \frac{2Z{i+1}}{Z{i+1} + Zi} The backward transmission coefficient is calculated by swapping indices: T{i+1 \rightarrow i} = \frac{2Zi}{Zi + Z{i+1}} Step 2: Construct Matrix A and Vector b Initialize A as a zero matrix of size (2N+2) \times (2N+2) and \mathbf{b} as a zero vector of size 2N+2. 1. Boundary Conditions: Set A{0,0} = 1 and b0 = 1. This enforces g0 = 1 (unit pulse injection at the transducer). Set A{2N+1, 2N+1} = 1 and b{2N+1} = 0. This enforces dN = 0 (far-field termination, no incoming waves from beyond the last voxel). 2. Coupled Recurrence Relations: For each voxel index i from 0 to N-1, the physical coupling at the interface is governed by: g{i+1} = T{i \rightarrow i+1} \cdot gi + R{i+1 \rightarrow i} \cdot d{i+1} di = R{i \rightarrow i+1} \cdot gi + T{i+1 \rightarrow i} \cdot d{i+1} These equations map to rows in the linear system using the variable-to-index mapping gk \to 2k and dk \to 2k+1. Row for g{i+1} (index 2i+2): Rearranging to g{i+1} - T{i \rightarrow i+1} gi - R{i+1 \rightarrow i} d{i+1} = 0 yields A{2i+2, 2i} = -T{i \rightarrow i+1}, A{2i+2, 2i+2} = 1, and A{2i+2, 2i+3} = -R{i+1 \rightarrow i}. Row for di (index 2i+1): Rearranging to di - R{i \rightarrow i+1} gi - T{i+1 \rightarrow i} d{i+1} = 0 yields A{2i+1, 2i} = -R{i \rightarrow i+1}, A{2i+1, 2i+1} = 1, and A{2i+1, 2i+3} = -T{i+1 \rightarrow i}. Parameters: Speed of sound: c = 1540 m/s. Frequency range: 2–15 MHz. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dense Solver: The source implementation uses a dense solver, which is less efficient than exploiting the matrix sparsity. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def solvewavepropagation(N, Z): """ Solves for wave amplitudes in a layered medium. Args: N (int): Number of voxels. Z (list of float): Acoustic impedances Z[0]...Z[N]. Returns: x (list of float): Wave amplitudes [g0, d0,..., gN, dN]. """ size = 2 N + 2 A = [[0.0] size for in range(size)] b = [0.0] size # Boundary conditions: g0 = 1, dN = 0 A[0][0] = 1.0 b[0] = 1.0 A[2 N + 1][2 N + 1] = 1.0 b[2 N + 1] = 0.0 for i in range(N): Z1, Z2 = Z[i], Z[i + 1] Ritoi1 = abs((Z2 - Z1) / (Z2 + Z1)) Titoi1 = (2 Z2) / (Z2 + Z1) Ti1toi = (2 Z1) / (Z1 + Z2) # Row for g{i+1} (index 2i+2) rg = 2 i + 2 A[rg][2 i] = -Titoi1 A[rg][2 i + 2] = 1.0 A[rg][2 i + 3] = -Ritoi1 # Row for di (index 2i+1) rd = 2 i + 1 A[rd][2 i] = -Ritoi1 A[rd][2 i + 1] = 1.0 A[rd][2 i + 3] = -Ti1toi # Solve Ax=b using a dense solver x = solvelinearsystem(A, b) return x def solvelinearsystem(A, b): """Standard dense Gaussian elimination solver.""" n = len(b) A = [row[:] for row in A] b = b[:] for i in range(n): pivot = A[i][i] if abs(pivot) < 1e-12: for j in range(i + 1, n): if abs(A[j][i]) > abs(pivot): pivot, A[i], A[j] = A[j][i], A[j], A[i] b[i], b[j] = b[j], b[i] if abs(A[i][i]) < 1e-12: raise ValueError("Singular matrix") for j in range(i + 1, n): factor = A[j][i] / A[i][i] b[j] -= factor b[i] for k in range(i, n): A[j][k] -= factor A[i][k] x = [0.0] n for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1): x[i] = b[i] for j in range(i + 1, n): x[i] -= A[i][j] x[j] x[i] /= A[i][i] return x This is the underlying ray tracing approach used by the solver. It models acoustic beams traversing a linear sequence of voxels, with wave amplitudes undergoing reflection and transmission at each voxel boundary according to local impedance contrasts. It is chosen when straight-line propagation and layered impedance models are sufficient, such as in soft tissue ultrasound simulation. It differs from full wave solvers by ignoring diffraction and side-lobes. Complexity: The matrix A has O(N) non-zero elements due to a fixed-bandwidth structure with at most three non-zero entries per row. Performance: The source notes that a dense solver is currently used, which is O(N^3) time complexity, negating the sparsity benefits. An optimized sparse solver would be O(N). Strengths: Captures multiple internal reflections accurately within the 1D ray approximation. Limitations: Assumes straight-line paths, constant speed of sound, and negligible side-lobes. Not suitable for complex scattering or diffraction effects. This method is derived from the physical principles of ultrasound imaging, where acoustic waves propagate through biological tissues. It was formalized in the DiffUS framework for differentiable ultrasound rendering from volumetric imaging. name: Differential Form of RTE
head: Analytical Differential Expression for Transmittance, Reynolds Transport Theorem for Single Scattering
body: The Differential Form of RTE provides an analytical method to compute the gradient of the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) with respect to medium density, enabling differentiable rendering for fluid modeling. It sets itself apart from numerical differentiation or automatic differentiation by deriving closed-form expressions for the derivatives of transmittance and single-scattering radiance directly from the continuous integral formulation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Density field \rho, extinction coefficient \kappat, reduced incident radiance L{ri} (or J{ss}), ray direction \boldsymbol{\omega}, and sampling step size \Delta d. Outputs: The derivative of the single-scattering radiance \dot{L}{ss} and the derivative of the reduced incident radiance \dot{L}{ri} with respect to density. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: Stores density \rho and derived coefficients \kappat. Ray: Defined by origin, direction, and current position vp in the voxel grid. Formulas: 1. Transmittance: The transmittance \tau(x0, x1) from position x0 to x1 is defined as: \tau(x0, x1) = e^{-\int{D1}^{D0} \kappat(xu) du} 2. Transmittance Derivative: The derivative of transmittance \tau from v{x0} to v{x1} is the negative product of \tau and the sum of extinction coefficient derivatives \dot{\kappa}t times step size \Delta d: \dot{\tau}(x0, x1) = -\tau(x0, x1) \sum \dot{\kappa}t \Delta d where \dot{\kappa}t is the derivative of the extinction coefficient, equal to the extinction cross-section \sigmat, and \Delta d is the length of the sampling step in the voxel grid. 3. Single-Scattering Radiance: The single-scattering radiance is defined as: L{ss}(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}) = \int{Db}^{Da} \tau(xu, xb) \kappat(xu) J{ss}(xu, \boldsymbol{\omega}) du where J{ss} is the reduced incident radiance. Steps: 1. Compute density derivatives directly using the analytical differential expression instead of automatic differentiation. 2. Calculate the transmittance derivative \dot{\tau} along the ray segment using the sum of \dot{\kappa}t \Delta d. 3. Apply the Reynolds transport theorem to derive \dot{L}{ss} from the integral form of L{ss}, assuming continuity of L{ri} in S^2. 4. Combine \dot{L}{ss} and \dot{L}{ri} to obtain the total gradient for the differentiable rendering process. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computedifferentialrtederivative(tau, kappat, sigmat, stepsize, jss): # tau: transmittance τ(x0, x1) # kappat: extinction coefficient κt # sigmat: extinction cross-section σt (derivative of κt) # stepsize: sampling step Δd # jss: reduced incident radiance Jss # Computes derivative of single-scattering radiance with respect to density dotkappat = sigmat # κ˙t is the derivative of the extinction coefficient, equal to σt dottau = -tau dotkappat stepsize # Transmittance derivative # Derivative of Lss = ∫ τ κt Jss du # Using Reynolds transport theorem assuming continuity of Lri in S^2 dLss = dottau kappat jss return dLss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Continuity Assumption: The method calculates the derivative of J{ss} using the Reynolds transport theorem, which assumes continuity of L{ri} in S^2. Discontinuities in incident radiance may require special handling or break the analytical gradient. Discrete Approximation: The continuous integral for L{ss} and \tau is discretized for implementation; accuracy depends on the voxel grid resolution and step size \Delta d. An analytical subsurface scattering model derived from the functional integral formulation of radiative transport, linked to the partition function of a worm-like chain in polymer physics. It explicitly assumes strong forward scattering to avoid errors from isotropic diffusion assumptions in optically dense media. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sampling steps along the ray, as it involves a summation over \dot{\kappa}t \Delta d. Memory Complexity: Constant, requiring storage for current radiance, density, and coefficients. Strengths: Provides exact gradients for density, enabling efficient optimization in differentiable rendering. Limitations: Derived primarily for single-scattering; multiple scattering requires additional approximations or integration. When to Use: When differentiable rendering of participating media is required, specifically for fluid modeling from monocular video. The method originates from the paper "Physics-Based Differentiable Rendering for Efficient and Plausible Fluid Modeling from Monocular Video". It is used in the context of differentiable rendering to estimate density and velocity fields from video data by minimizing the difference between rendered and observed images. name: Forward Scattering Dipole Model
head: Effective BRDF, Forward scattering dipole, Functional Integral Approximation for Radiative Transport, Functional Integral Dipole Model, Polymer Physics Dipole Model
body: The Forward Scattering Dipole Model is an analytical subsurface scattering method derived from the functional integral formulation of the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) under the explicit assumption of strong forward scattering. It solves the problem of accurately modeling light transport in optically dense, highly anisotropic media (such as skin, fog, or snow) where standard diffusion approximations fail due to their isotropic scattering assumptions. Unlike isotropic diffusion models [Jensen et al. 2001, d'Eon 2014] or the directional dipole model [Frisvad et al. 2014], this method explicitly assumes strong forward scattering using a forward-peaked Gaussian phase function parameterized by \mu (where g \approx 1 - \mu), capturing the full behavior from unscattered straight-line propagation to the fully diffusive limit without requiring separate Monte Carlo solutions for single-scattered contributions. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Medium volume V, scattering coefficient \sigmas, absorption coefficient \sigmaa, extinction coefficient \sigmat = \sigmas + \sigmaa, reduced scattering coefficient \sigma's, phase function anisotropy parameter g (or width \mu), boundary BSDF fs, and surface normal \hat{n}. Outputs: Incident radiance Li at a point \vec{x} on the interior surface in direction -\hat{\omega}, or the effective forward scattering BRDF fr. Data Structures: The core data structure is the propagator G, which represents the Green's function for the RTE. In the forward scattering approximation, G is defined via a functional integral over path tangent vectors \hat{\beta}(s). Numbered Steps: 1. Define the Phase Function: Use a forward-peaked Gaussian phase function P{\text{gauss}} parameterized by width \mu. 2. Construct the Propagator G: Compute G(s, \vec{x}, \hat{\omega}, \vec{x}', \hat{\omega}') as the solution to the RTE with a Dirac delta source and fully absorbing boundary conditions. Approximate G using the functional integral formulation. 3. Evaluate the Rendering Equation: Compute incident radiance Li by coupling G with the boundary BSDF fs. 4. Recursive Sampling: Evaluate the rendering equation via importance sampling. Set the initial intersection point \vec{x}i = \vec{x}o. Sample the index-matched forward scattering BRDF fr and the medium boundary BSDF fs. Repeat sampling fr and fs recursively. Terminate when fs generates a query direction pointing out of the medium. For subsequent steps, calculate weights based on the planar propagator G^pf instead of the point propagator Gb. 5. Effective BRDF Approximation: For index-matched media, compute fr by integrating the planar propagator G{pb} over path length s. Sample fr in constant time as a Level of Detail (LOD) approximation for optically dense media. Formulas: Phase Function: P{\text{gauss}}(\hat{\omega}, \hat{\omega}') = N \exp\left(-\frac{1 - \hat{\omega} \cdot \hat{\omega}'}{\mu}\right), where N is the normalization constant ensuring \int P d^2\hat{\omega}' = 1. Propagator: G(s, \vec{x}, \hat{\omega}, \vec{x}', \hat{\omega}') = NG e^{-\sigmaa s} \int [D\hat{\beta}] \delta^2[\hat{\beta}(0) - \hat{\omega}'] \delta^2[\hat{\beta}(s) - \hat{\omega}] \delta^3\left[\vec{x} - \vec{x}' - \int0^s \hat{\beta}(s') ds'\right] \exp \left[ -\frac{1}{2\sigma's} \int0^s \left| \frac{d\hat{\beta}(s')}{ds'} \right|^2 ds' \right], where \hat{\beta}(s') is the unit-length tangent vector at path length s' and the exponential term represents a quadratic bending energy. Rendering Equation: Li(s, \vec{x}, \hat{\omega}) = \int ds' dA(\vec{x}') d^2\hat{\omega}' G(s-s', \vec{x}, -\hat{\omega}, \vec{x}', \hat{\omega}') |\hat{\omega}' \cdot \hat{n}(\vec{x}')| \left[ Le(s', \vec{x}', \hat{\omega}') + \int d^2\hat{\omega}'' Li(s', \vec{x}', \hat{\omega}'') fs(\vec{x}', \hat{\omega}'' \leftrightarrow \hat{\omega}') |\hat{\omega}'' \cdot \hat{n}(\vec{x}')| \right]. Effective BRDF: fr(\hat{\omega}{in} \leftrightarrow \hat{\omega}{out}) = \int G{pb}(s, \hat{\omega}{out}, -\hat{\omega}{in}) ds. Parameters: \mu: Phase function width parameter. For heavily forward peaked scattering (\mu \ll 1), the mean cosine g \approx 1 - \mu and \sigma's = \mu \sigmas. Typical values for skin: g \in [0.7, 0.8]. n: Index of refraction (e.g., n=1.4 for skin in spectral rendering examples). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unit Vector Constraint: The functional integral requires \hat{\beta}(s0) to be a unit vector. Ignoring this constraint simplifies the integral to a Gaussian form but introduces approximation errors. Boundary Conditions: The propagator G assumes fully absorbing boundaries. Surface interactions (Fresnel, roughness) must be handled externally via the BSDF fs in the rendering equation; they cannot be embedded in G. Singularity: The model has a single singularity corresponding to initial unscattered propagation, which must be handled by the analytical importance sampling scheme. The Infinite Volume Forward Scattering Propagator (Gf) is an analytical approximation of the radiative transfer propagator for participating media that exhibit strong forward scattering. It solves the problem of accurately modeling light transport in optically dense media where standard diffusion approximations fail due to the directional nature of scattering. Unlike the Bounded Forward Scattering Propagator, which handles finite boundaries, Gf assumes an infinite medium, serving as the foundational kernel for subsurface scattering calculations before boundary corrections are applied. It is distinguished from isotropic diffusion models by explicitly encoding the anisotropy of the phase function through a single scaling parameter, allowing it to capture the transition from ballistic to diffusive transport. Time Complexity: The analytical evaluation of the propagator allows for constant-time sampling of the effective BRDF. The recursive evaluation samples fr and fs repeatedly until fs generates a query direction pointing out of the medium, decoupling volumetric transport from surface interactions. Memory Complexity: Low, as it relies on analytical formulas rather than storing large lookup tables or path histories, except for the recursive stack depth. Performance: Accurately captures ground truth behavior over a wide range of parameters, including the optically dense limit where isotropic diffusion models fail. The model provides a computationally efficient approximation for optically dense media. Strengths: Explicitly handles strong forward scattering; captures the transition from ballistic to diffusive transport; no need for separate single-scatter solutions; decouples volume transport from surface interactions. Limitations: Approximate due to the handling of the unit vector constraint in the functional integral; assumes a Gaussian phase function; fully absorbing boundary assumption for G requires external handling of surface reflections. When to use: Translucent materials with strong forward scattering (skin, fog, clouds, snow, organic substances). When not to use: Media with isotropic scattering or weak anisotropy, where standard diffusion models are sufficient and more accurate. The Forward Scattering Dipole Model was introduced by Roald Frederickx and Philip Dutré at KU Leuven in 2017. It is derived from the functional integral formulation of radiative transport, originally introduced by Tessendorf [1987, 1991, 2003], and links this formulation to the partition function of a worm-like chain in polymer physics. This connection allows the adaptation of results from polymer physics to derive a practical rendering algorithm for subsurface scattering. The model addresses the limitations of previous diffusion-based dipole models (Jensen et al. [2001], d'Eon [2014]) and the directional dipole model (Frisvad et al. [2014]) by explicitly assuming strong forward scattering. A forward scattering dipole model from a functional integral approximation, https://doi.org/10.1145/3072959.3073681, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Infinite Volume Forward Scattering Propagator
body: The Infinite Volume Forward Scattering Propagator (Gf) is an analytical approximation of the radiative transfer propagator for participating media that exhibit strong forward scattering. It solves the problem of accurately modeling light transport in optically dense media where standard diffusion approximations fail due to the directional nature of scattering. Unlike the Bounded Forward Scattering Propagator, which handles finite boundaries, Gf assumes an infinite medium, serving as the foundational kernel for subsurface scattering calculations before boundary corrections are applied. It is distinguished from isotropic diffusion models by explicitly encoding the anisotropy of the phase function through a single scaling parameter, allowing it to capture the transition from ballistic to diffusive transport. The propagator is derived from a functional integral formulation of radiative transport, utilizing a connection to polymer physics (specifically the worm-like chain model) and a modified length constraint. It approximates the probability density of a photon traveling a path length s from position \vec{x}' with direction \hat{\omega}' to position \vec{x} with direction \hat{\omega}. Inputs: s: Path length (scalar, s > 0). \vec{x}, \vec{x}': Final and initial positions (vectors, \mathbb{R}^3). \hat{\omega}, \hat{\omega}': Final and initial directions (unit vectors, \mathbb{R}^3). \sigmas: Scattering coefficient (scalar, inverse length). g: Anisotropy factor (scalar, 0 \le g < 1). \sigmaa: Absorption coefficient (scalar, inverse length). Output: Gf: Propagator value (scalar, probability density). The computation relies on scalar arithmetic and vector dot products. The method relies on a scaling factor p and several intermediate coefficients A, B, C, D, E, F and normalization N. All intermediate coefficients are positive and dimensionless, depending solely on the product ps. 1. Scaling Factor: p = \frac{\sigmas'}{2} = \frac{(1-g)\sigmas}{2} where \sigmas' = (1-g)\sigmas is the reduced scattering coefficient. 2. Displacement Vector: \vec{r} = p(\vec{x} - \vec{x}') 3. Intermediate Coefficients: Let u = ps. A = (u - \tanh(u))^{-1} B = \frac{\tanh(u)}{2} C = \frac{9}{2u} D = 3AB^2 - \frac{3}{2 \sinh(2u)} E = 3AB F = \frac{3}{2}A 4. Normalization Factor: N = p^3 \frac{\sqrt{F}(E^2 - 2DF)}{4\pi^{5/2}(e^{E^2/F-D} - e^D)} \exp(C) The propagator is calculated as: Gf(s, \vec{x}, \hat{\omega}, \vec{x}', \hat{\omega}') = N \exp\left(-C - D \hat{\omega} \cdot \hat{\omega}' + E \vec{r} \cdot (\hat{\omega} + \hat{\omega}') - F |\vec{r}|^2 - \sigmaa s\right) Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def infinitevolumeforwardscatteringpropagator(s, x, omega, xprime, omegaprime, sigmas, g, sigmaa): # 1. Calculate scaling factor p sigmasprime = (1 - g) sigmas p = sigmasprime / 2.0 # 2. Calculate product ps u = p s # 3. Compute intermediate coefficients tanhu = math.tanh(u) sinh2u = math.sinh(2 u) A = 1.0 / (u - tanhu) B = tanhu / 2.0 C = 9.0 / (2.0 u) D = 3.0 A (B 2) - 3.0 / (2.0 sinh2u) E = 3.0 A B F = 1.5 A # 4. Calculate displacement vector r rvec = [p (x[i] - xprime[i]) for i in range(3)] rnormsq = dot(rvec, rvec) # 5. Calculate Normalization N numeratorN = (p 3) math.sqrt(F) (E2 - 2 D F) expterm1 = math.exp((E2 / F) - D) expterm2 = math.exp(D) denominatorN = 4.0 (math.pi 2.5) (expterm1 - expterm2) if abs(expterm1 - expterm2) < 1e-15: return 0.0 N = (numeratorN / denominatorN) math.exp(C) # 6. Calculate Exponent terms dotomegaomegaprime = dot(omega, omegaprime) sumomega = [omega[i] + omegaprime[i] for i in range(3)] dotrsumomega = dot(rvec, sumomega) exponent = -C - D dotomegaomegaprime + E dotrsumomega - F rnormsq - sigmaa s # 7. Final Result Gf = N math.exp(exponent) return Gf Small Path Lengths (s \to 0): As s \to 0, the normalization factor N diverges exponentially. The term -C in the exponent is explicitly included to cancel this divergence for numerical stability. Short Path Limit (ps \ll 1): The propagator approaches an unscattered delta distribution. The term -D \hat{\omega} \cdot \hat{\omega}' might appear to force directions apart, but it is counteracted by the displacement weight forcing \vec{R}/s to align with (\hat{\omega} + \hat{\omega}')/2. Long Path Limit (ps \gg 1): The fluence approaches the classical time-dependent diffusion equation result, provided s \gg |\vec{x} - \vec{x}'|. Extends Gf to finite volumes using a virtual source to satisfy absorbing boundary conditions. Chosen when the medium is confined within a bounded geometry rather than an infinite space. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Captures the correct qualitative behavior from ballistic (straight-line) to diffusive limits. Analytically derived, ensuring consistency with the underlying physics of forward scattering. Limitations: Assumes strong forward scattering (g close to 1) [Parent]. The evaluation was noted as "too costly to incorporate into a practical rendering system". When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The work derives the model from a functional integral formulation of radiative transport, drawing an analogy to the partition function of a worm-like chain in polymer physics. It was developed to address the inaccuracies of isotropic diffusion models in optically dense media with strong forward scattering [Parent]. The model relies on a result by Winkler et al. [1994] regarding modified length constraints in polymer physics. name: Bounded Forward Scattering Propagator (Dipole Model)
head: Boundary-Aware Propagator G_f^b, Boundary-aware propagator, Gbf, bounded propagator, final boundary-aware propagator
body: The Bounded Forward Scattering Propagator (Gf^b) extends the Infinite Volume Forward Scattering Propagator [10181-infinite-volume-forward-scattering-propagator.md] to handle participating media within finite, bounded volumes by approximately satisfying absorbing boundary conditions. It employs a dipole method using a virtual source to enforce these boundaries, distinguishing itself from empirical corrections (such as those in [Frisvad et al. 2014]) by relying on the well-behaved nature of the underlying infinite volume propagator Gf for regularization. Inputs: \vec{x}0, \hat{\omega}0: Outgoing position and direction. \vec{x}1, \hat{\omega}1: Incoming position and direction. s: Path length. \hat{n}1: Surface normal at \vec{x}1. \sigmas', \sigmaa: Reduced scattering coefficient and absorption coefficient. Outputs: Gf^b(s, \vec{x}0, \hat{\omega}0, \vec{x}1, \hat{\omega}1): The bounded propagator value. Data Structures: The method requires standard 3D vectors and scalars for positions, directions, normals, and optical coefficients. Steps: 1. Calculate Modified Normal (\hat{n}1^): Determine the effective normal for the boundary plane at the incoming point \vec{x}1. Let \vec{R} = \vec{x}0 - \vec{x}1. If \vec{x}0 = \vec{x}1, set \hat{n}1^ = \hat{n}1. Otherwise, calculate: \hat{n}1^ = \frac{\vec{R}}{|\vec{R}|} \times \frac{\hat{n}1 \times \vec{R}}{|\hat{n}1 \times \vec{R}|} Pitfall: If \hat{n}1 is parallel to \vec{R}, the denominator |\hat{n}1 \times \vec{R}| is zero. In this case, set the propagator to 0. 2. Calculate Extrapolation Distance (de): Compute reduced transmission coefficient: \sigmat' = \sigmas' + \sigmaa. Compute reduced scattering albedo: \alpha0 = \sigmas' / \sigmat'. Compute diffusion constant: D = 1/(3\sigmat'). Compute extrapolation distance: de = 2.131 D / \sqrt{\alpha0}. 3. Define Virtual Source (\vec{x}v, \hat{\omega}v): Set index-matching factor A = 1 (assuming no internal Fresnel reflection). Calculate virtual position: \vec{x}v = \vec{x}1 + 2 A de \hat{n}1^. Calculate virtual direction: \hat{\omega}v = \hat{\omega}1^e - 2(\hat{\omega}1^e \cdot \hat{n}1^)\hat{n}1^, where \hat{\omega}1^e is the effective incoming direction at \vec{x}1. 4. Evaluate Bounded Propagator: The final value is determined by the relationship between the directions and the modified normal \hat{n}1^: Gf^b(s, \vec{x}0, \hat{\omega}0, \vec{x}1, \hat{\omega}1) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } \hat{\omega}1 \cdot \hat{n}1^ \geq 0, \\ 0 & \text{if } \hat{\omega}1^e \cdot \hat{n}1^ \geq 0, \\ Gf(s, \vec{x}0, \hat{\omega}0, \vec{x}1, \hat{\omega}1) - Gf(s, \vec{x}0, \hat{\omega}0, \vec{x}v, \hat{\omega}v) & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} Condition 1: If the outgoing direction points into the effective half-space defined by \hat{n}1^ (\hat{\omega}1 \cdot \hat{n}1^ \geq 0), the propagator is 0. Condition 2: If the incoming direction appears to point out of the medium (\hat{\omega}1^e \cdot \hat{n}1^ \geq 0), the virtual source would not illuminate the medium in the planar approximation. Set the propagator to 0. Condition 3: Otherwise, the propagator is the dipole difference between the infinite volume propagator from the real source and the virtual source. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def cross(v1, v2): return (v1[1]v2[2] - v1[2]v2[1], v1[2]v2[0] - v1[0]v2[2], v1[0]v2[1] - v1[1]v2[0]) def norm(v): return math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) def boundedforwardscatteringpropagator(s, x0, w0, x1, w1, n1, sigmasprime, sigmaa): # 1. Calculate Modified Normal n1star R = (x0[0]-x1[0], x0[1]-x1[1], x0[2]-x1[2]) rnorm = norm(R) if rnorm < 1e-9: n1star = n1 else: Rnorm = (R[0]/rnorm, R[1]/rnorm, R[2]/rnorm) crossprod = cross(n1, R) crossnorm = norm(crossprod) if crossnorm < 1e-9: # Ill-defined normal: n1 parallel to R return 0.0 n1star = cross(Rnorm, (crossprod[0]/crossnorm, crossprod[1]/crossnorm, crossprod[2]/crossnorm)) # 2. Calculate Extrapolation Distance de sigmatprime = sigmasprime + sigmaa if sigmatprime == 0: return 0.0 alpha0 = sigmasprime / sigmatprime D = 1.0 / (3.0 sigmatprime) if alpha0 <= 0: return 0.0 de = 2.131 D / math.sqrt(alpha0) # 3. Define Virtual Source A = 1.0 # Index-matched boundary xv = (x1[0] + 2.0 A de n1star[0], x1[1] + 2.0 A de n1star[1], x1[2] + 2.0 A de n1star[2]) # Effective incoming direction at x1 (w1) wv = (w1[0] - 2.0 dot(w1, n1star) n1star[0], w1[1] - 2.0 dot(w1, n1star) n1star[1], w1[2] - 2.0 dot(w1, n1star) n1star[2]) # 4. Evaluate Propagator # Condition 1: Outgoing direction points into effective half-space if dot(w1, n1star) >= 0: return 0.0 # Condition 2: Incoming direction points out of medium if dot(w1, n1star) >= 0: return 0.0 # Condition 3: Dipole subtraction # Evaluate infinite volume propagator Gf (see Infinite Volume Forward Scattering Propagator) greal = infinitevolumeforwardscatteringpropagator(s, x0, w0, x1, w1) gvirtual = infinitevolumeforwardscatteringpropagator(s, x0, w0, xv, wv) return greal - gvirtual A symmetrical combination of the bounded propagator and its reverse to enforce reciprocity, which is broken by the virtual source dependency on the incoming normal. The formula is \frac{1}{2} \left[ Gf^b(s, \vec{x}0, \hat{\omega}0, \vec{x}i, \hat{\omega}i) + Gf^b(s, \vec{x}i, -\hat{\omega}i, \vec{x}0, -\hat{\omega}0) \right]. Reciprocity holds only if \hat{n}i = \hat{n}o (planar boundaries) or if \hat{n}i, \hat{n}o and \vec{x}o - \vec{x}i are coplanar. In practice, the simple Gf^b is used because the difference is negligible and unidirectional path tracing does not strictly require reciprocity. Complexity: The method requires evaluating the infinite volume propagator Gf twice (once for the real source, once for the virtual source) plus geometric calculations for the modified normal and virtual source. The complexity is dominated by Gf. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles bounded volumes with absorbing boundary conditions without empirical distance corrections, leveraging the well-behaved nature of Gf. Limitations: Breaks reciprocity unless the symmetrical combination is used. Ill-defined normals occur when the surface normal is parallel to the displacement vector. When to use: When rendering bounded participating media with forward scattering dipole models and index-matched boundaries. The method is based on the dipole model for diffusion approximation, originally studied in physics [Bell and Glasstone 1970; Lamarsh 1975] and computer graphics [d'Eon 2014; Habel et al. 2013; Jensen et al. 2001]. It was introduced in the context of a forward scattering dipole model derived from a functional integral approximation. It differs from Frisvad et al. [2014] by not requiring an empirical distance correction to offset the real source, as Gf is well-behaved except for the designed delta distribution at short lengths. name: Differential Ray Marching
head: Differential Form RTE Solver, ODE-based Volume Rendering
body: Differential Ray Marching solves the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) in its differential form as an initial value problem, rather than approximating its integral form. Unlike traditional ray marching, which approximates integrals using the rectangle method (equivalent to Euler's method) and requires computing the double integral for inner transmittance, this method applies numerical ODE solvers directly to the differential equation. This approach allows for higher-order accuracy and adaptive step sizing, reducing the sample count or increasing image quality compared to standard techniques. Inputs: Ray origin x0 and direction \omega. Medium properties at any position x: absorption coefficient \sigmaa(x), scattering coefficient \sigmas(x), extinction coefficient \sigmat(x) = \sigmaa(x) + \sigmas(x), phase function p(x, \omega0, \omega), and emission Le(x, \omega). Initial radiance y0 = L(x0, \omega), derived from surface material properties and light distribution at the entry point. Integration interval [0, t{end}], where t is the distance along the ray. Outputs: Radiance L(x{end}, \omega) at the exit of the medium. Data Structures: The state vector y represents the radiance L(x, \omega) at the current step. The independent variable t represents the distance traveled along the ray. The derivative function f(y, t) computes the rate of change of radiance. Formulas: The Radiative Transfer Equation is defined as: \frac{\partial L(x, \omega)}{\partial t} = \sigmaa (x)Le (x, \omega) - \sigmat (x)L(x, \omega) + \sigmas (x) \int{\Omega} p(x, \omega0, \omega)L(x, \omega0) d\omega0 This is formulated as an initial value problem: y'(t) = f(y, t) Where: y(t) = L(x(t), \omega) is the radiance. t is the distance along the path of light. f(y, t) is the right-hand side of the RTE. y0 = L(x0, \omega) is the known initial value. The term \int{\Omega} p(x, \omega0, \omega)L(x, \omega0) d\omega0 represents the in-scattered radiance contribution from all incoming directions \omega0. In practice, this integral is often approximated or precomputed depending on the specific ODE solver and scattering model used, but the core differential formulation avoids the explicit computation of the transmittance integral Tr required in the integral form. Steps: 1. Initialize: Set t = 0 and y = y0. 2. Evaluate Derivative: Compute k = f(y, t) using the current radiance y and position x(t) = x0 + t\omega. f(y, t) = \sigmaa(x) Le(x, \omega) - \sigmat(x) y + \sigmas(x) L{in}(x, \omega), where L{in} is the in-scattered radiance. 3. Advance Step: Use a numerical ODE method (e.g., Euler, Runge-Kutta) to update y and t based on the step size \Delta t. Note: The choice of numerical method determines how y and t are updated. Traditional ray marching uses Euler's method (rectangle rule). Higher-order methods (e.g., Runge-Kutta) provide better accuracy for the same step size. 4. Repeat: Increment t by \Delta t. If t < t{end}, return to Step 2. Otherwise, return y as the final radiance. Parameters: Step size \Delta t: Can be fixed or adaptive. Adaptive step sizing is a key advantage of ODE solvers, allowing larger steps in homogeneous regions and smaller steps in high-gradient areas. Numerical method order: Determines accuracy and computational cost per step. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: In-scattering Integral: The term \int{\Omega} p(x, \omega0, \omega)L(x, \omega0) d\omega0 is computationally expensive. In differential ray marching, this is still required at each step unless approximated. The method does not eliminate the need to estimate in-scattering, but it changes how the transmittance and absorption are handled. Precision: Standard floating-point precision may be insufficient for very small or very large extinction coefficients. Clamping \sigmat to a minimum non-zero value can prevent division by zero or numerical instability in adaptive step size controllers. Boundary Conditions: The initial value y0 must be correctly computed from the surface intersection. If the ray starts inside the medium, y0 is typically zero or the background radiance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def differentialraymarching(rayorigin, raydirection, medium, tend, initialradiance): """ Solves the RTE in differential form using an ODE solver. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, origin of the ray. raydirection: 3D vector, direction of the ray. medium: Object providing methods to query sigmaa, sigmas, sigmat, Le, and phase function. tend: Float, total distance to integrate. initialradiance: Float, L(x0, omega). Returns: Float, final radiance L(xend, omega). """ t = 0.0 y = initialradiance # Determine step size. For simplicity, using a fixed step here. # In practice, an adaptive step size controller would be used. deltat = medium.getstepsize() while t < tend: # Current position x = rayorigin + t raydirection # Evaluate the derivative f(y, t) # f(y, t) = sigmaa Le - sigmat y + sigmas Lin sigmaa = medium.getsigmaa(x) sigmas = medium.getsigmas(x) sigmat = sigmaa + sigmas Le = medium.getemission(x, raydirection) # Compute in-scattered radiance Lin # This requires integrating over the sphere. # For this pseudocode, we assume a helper function exists. Lin = computeinscatteredradiance(x, raydirection, medium) derivative = sigmaa Le - sigmat y + sigmas Lin # Update using Euler's method (equivalent to traditional ray marching) # Higher-order methods (e.g., RK4) would require multiple evaluations y = y + deltat derivative t = t + deltat return y def computeinscatteredradiance(x, viewdirection, medium): """ Approximates the integral of in-scattered light. This is a placeholder for the specific scattering model used. """ # Example: Single scattering approximation or precomputed light field # The exact implementation depends on the specific application. # The differential form does not change this requirement. return 0.0 # Placeholder A specific scattering model that can be used within the differential ray marching framework to approximate the in-scattering term efficiently. It differs from general phase function integration by using a dipole approximation for the Green's function of the diffusion equation. Choose this when single scattering is insufficient but full multiple scattering is too expensive. Link Time Complexity: Depends on the number of steps n and the cost of evaluating the derivative f(y, t) at each step. Higher-order ODE methods require more function evaluations per step but may allow larger step sizes, potentially reducing n. Memory Complexity: Low, as it only stores the current state y and t. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of steps. Adaptive step sizing can improve scaling in complex media by reducing steps in homogeneous regions. Strengths: Avoids the double integral of transmittance required in integral form methods. Allows the use of advanced ODE solvers for better accuracy and adaptive step sizing. Limitations: Still requires computation of the in-scattering integral at each step, which can be expensive. The benefit is most pronounced when the in-scattering term is approximated or precomputed. When to use: When high accuracy is needed with fewer samples, or when adaptive step sizing is beneficial. When not to use: When the in-scattering term is extremely expensive to compute and cannot be approximated, the overhead of the ODE solver may not justify the benefits over simpler methods. Differential Ray Marching was introduced in the paper "Differential Ray Marching" (2012). It revisits the concept of ray marching not as an integration technique, but as the application of numerical methods to solve an initial value differential equation. The work analyzes a wide range of numerical methods and their applicability to participating media rendering, showing improvements over traditional ray marching in terms of sample count and accuracy. name: Spherical Harmonics and Spherical Gaussians for Radiance Transfer
head: SH/SG Approximation, SRBF, Spherical Radial Basis Functions
body: Spherical Harmonics (SH) and Spherical Gaussians (SG) are approximation methods for radiance transfer used in real-time or long-rendering scenarios to avoid expensive on-the-fly calculations of the light transport equation. They approximate the incident radiance field using Spherical Radial Basis Functions (SRBFs), which are then convolved with the Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF). SH is preferred for diffuse or rough surfaces, while SG is used for higher-frequency glossy terms or unified frameworks handling all-frequency shadows. Inputs and Outputs Input: Incident radiance field Li(p, \omegai) over the hemisphere \Omega at surface point p; BRDF f(p, \omegao, \omegai). Output: Exitant radiance Lo(p, \omegao). Data Structures Spherical Harmonics (SH): A set of orthogonal polynomial basis functions defined over the sphere. Represented by a vector of coefficients \mathbf{c}. The number of coefficients depends on the chosen band order. Spherical Gaussians (SG): A special case of the von Mises-Fisher distribution. Defined by parameters: axis u (unit vector), amplitude \mu (scalar), and sharpness \lambda (scalar). A distribution is approximated by a sum of N SG lobes. Numbered Steps 1. Approximation: Approximate the incident radiance Li using either SH coefficients or a sum of SG lobes. For SH: Project Li onto the SH basis functions. For SG: Fit a sum of SG functions to Li. 2. Convolution: Convolve the SRBF representation with the BRDF f. For diffuse surfaces, SH allows efficient convolution via coefficient multiplication. For glossy surfaces, SG provides better accuracy for high-frequency components. 3. Evaluation: Evaluate the resulting radiance Lo for the outgoing direction \omegao. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeradiancetransfer(Li, brdf, method='SH'): if method == 'SH': # Project Li onto SH basis functions shcoeffs = projecttosh(Li) # Convolve with BRDF via coefficient multiplication convolvedcoeffs = convolveshbrdf(shcoeffs, brdf) # Evaluate radiance for outgoing direction Lo = evaluatesh(convolvedcoeffs, omegao) elif method == 'SG': # Fit sum of SG lobes to Li sglobes = fitsglobes(Li) # Convolve with BRDF convolvedlobes = convolvesgbrdf(sglobes, brdf) # Evaluate radiance for outgoing direction Lo = sum(lobe.evaluate(omegao) for lobe in convolvedlobes) return Lo Formulas The light transport equation defines the relationship between inputs and outputs: Lo(p, \omegao) = Le(p, \omegao) + \int{\Omega} f(p, \omegao, \omegai) Li(p, \omegai) |\cos(\thetai)| d\omegai where Le is emitted radiance, f is the BRDF, Li is incident radiance, \Omega is the hemisphere of incoming directions, and \thetai is the angle between the normal and incident direction. The Spherical Gaussian function is defined as: G(v; u, \lambda, \mu) = \mu e^{\lambda (v \cdot u - 1)} where v is the input direction, u is the axis, \mu is the amplitude, and \lambda is the sharpness. Parameters SH Band: Determines the number of coefficients. Higher bands capture higher frequencies but increase memory and computation. SG Sharpness (\lambda): Controls the width of the lobe. Higher \lambda results in sharper peaks. Number of SG Lobes: More lobes allow better approximation of complex lighting but increase cost. Edge Cases and Pitfalls SH Ringing: SHs become problematic for glossy surfaces and high-frequency lighting environments, as more coefficients are needed to avoid ringing artifacts due to the nature of these polynomials. SG Specular Accuracy: Unified frameworks using SGs may have reduced accuracy for highly specular BRDFs compared to methods restricted to specular effects. Memory Overhead: Local radiance capture using multiple environment maps has excessive memory overhead, making SRBFs a more practical alternative. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient approximation of global illumination; SH is well-suited for diffuse lighting; SG handles high-frequency glossy details better. Limitations: SH suffers from ringing artifacts for high-frequency lighting; SG may be less accurate for highly specular BRDFs in unified frameworks. When to Use: Use SH for diffuse or rough surfaces. Use SG for glossy terms or when a unified framework for all-frequency shadows is needed. Spherical Harmonics (SH) are a set of orthogonal polynomial basis functions defined over the sphere, frequently used in physics for computations of electron configurations, representation of gravitational or magnetic fields, and solutions of the Schrodinger equation. Spherical Gaussians (SG) are a special case of the von Mises-Fisher distribution. The hybrid approach modeling diffuse, direct, and indirect view-independent effects using SHs or wavelets, while modeling higher-frequency glossy terms using SGs, was introduced by Green et al.. Tsai et al. pointed out that the Green et al. model was restricted to modeling only specular effects with SGs and proposed a unified framework allowing rendering of all-frequency shadows. Succeeding works have improved on this concept by allowing spatially varying BRDFs, dynamic scenes, and introducing anisotropic SGs for better reconstructions.
