name: Single Scattering Approximation with Precomputed Terms
head: Precomputed Single Scattering, Single Scattering with Precomputed Terms
body: This method is a rendering approximation that considers only single scattering effects and uses pre-computed direction-independent radiance components to improve efficiency. It differs from its siblings by replacing stochastic Monte Carlo sampling with deterministic ray marching and by decoupling the angular integration into pre-computed terms, enabling differentiable optimization of the density field. The method reconstructs a physical density field from target images by optimizing the density parameters while maintaining a linear relationship with optical properties. Inputs: Target image L{tag} Current density field \rho Gradient records densityADRec (accumulated during forward rendering) Learning rate \alpha Outputs: Updated density field \rho Loss value Data Structures: Density Field \rho: A 3D grid of density values. For production-scale resolutions exceeding 512^3, sparse data structures (e.g., VDB) are required to decouple memory usage from grid resolution. Gradient Records densityADRec: For each pixel (i,j), a list of records. Each record contains the sampling position xu along the ray and the local gradient contribution \dot{L}{out}(xu, \omega). Numbered Steps: 1. Forward Rendering (Deterministic Ray Marching): For each pixel (i,j), cast a ray and sample density values \rho at sampling positions xu using trilinear interpolation. Compute the outgoing radiance L{out}[i,j] using the single scattering approximation with pre-computed direction-independent terms. Compute the local gradient contribution \dot{L}{out}(xu, \omega) for each sample xu and store (xu, \dot{L}{out}(xu, \omega)) in densityADRec[i,j]. 2. Loss Calculation: Compute the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the rendered image and the target image: \text{Loss} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i,j} \|L{out}[i, j] - L{tag}[i, j]\|^2 \quad (21) where N is the number of pixels. 3. Gradient Accumulation: Initialize densityGrad to zero. For each pixel (i,j), compute diff \leftarrow 2(L{out}[i, j] - L{tag}[i, j]). For each record k in densityADRec[i,j], retrieve xu and \dot{L}{out}(xu, \omega). Since xu typically falls between voxel centers, determine the eight neighboring voxels vp surrounding xu and calculate trilinear interpolation weights wp for each neighbor. Distribute the gradient to the neighbors: \frac{\partial \text{Loss}}{\partial \rho[vp]} \ += \ diff \cdot \dot{L}{out}(xu, \omega) \cdot wp This ensures consistency between forward and backward passes. 4. Density Update: Update the density field using gradient descent: \rho[vp] \leftarrow \rho[vp] - \alpha \frac{\partial \text{Loss}}{\partial \rho[vp]} where \alpha is the learning rate. Parameters: \alpha (learning rate): Not given in the sources. Resolution: Typical memory usage is cited for 256^3 and 512^3 grids. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Scattering: The single scattering assumption limits applicability to scenarios where multiple scattering effects are negligible, such as smoke with relatively low optical density. It may underestimate multiple scattering contributions in denser media like cumulus clouds or highly turbid liquids. Phase Function: A first-order Legendre polynomial approximation of the phase function is used, which works well for common cases but may not capture complex angular scattering. Memory: For resolutions exceeding 512^3, dense grids are infeasible; sparse structures are required. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reconstruct(Ltag, Lout, rho, densityADRec, alpha): loss = meansquarederror(Ltag, Lout) densityGrad = zeroslike(rho) for i, j in pixels: diff = 2 (Lout[i, j] - Ltag[i, j]) for record in densityADRec[i, j]: xu, gradlocal = record neighbors = get8neighbors(xu) weights = trilinearweights(xu, neighbors) for p, vp in enumerate(neighbors): densityGrad[vp] += diff gradlocal weights[p] rho = rho - alpha densityGrad return rho, loss This method corrects the self-shadowing probability in a low-resolution voxel representation after an initial transparency matching step, which preserves macroscopic attenuation but fails to preserve the microscopic self-shadowing effects. It estimates the mean amount of single scattering energy leaving a block of input voxels and matches it to the low-resolution voxel by scaling the density and albedo parameters. It is a refinement step within the Single Scattering Approximation with Precomputed Terms pipeline, specifically addressing the loss of self-shadowing detail during downsampling. Time Complexity: The method achieves computational efficiency through deterministic ray marching and pre-computation. Memory Complexity: Memory usage for pre-computation scales as O(N^3). A 256^3 volume uses 2.73 GB. A 512^3 volume requires approximately 22 GB. Performance: The method shows notable performance advantages over traditional DRT methods, particularly in multi-view scenarios where speedups range from 5.3\times to 27.6\times, and in single-view reconstruction with speedups between 1.2\times and 6.3\times. Strengths: Efficiency via pre-computed direction-independent radiance components and deterministic sampling. Enables differentiable optimization of the density field. Limitations: Limited to low optical density media where multiple scattering is negligible. Requires sparse data structures for high resolutions. The method is described in "A High-Efficiency Physics-Based Differentiable Renderer for Smoke Reconstruction". It is used for smoke reconstruction, optimizing a physical density field from target images. A High-Efficiency Physics-Based Differentiable Renderer for Smoke Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450546, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Single Scattering Estimation for Self-Shadowing
head: Estimating self-shadowing, Single scattering estimation
body: This method corrects the self-shadowing probability in a low-resolution voxel representation after an initial transparency matching step, which preserves macroscopic attenuation but fails to preserve the microscopic self-shadowing effects. It estimates the mean amount of single scattering energy leaving a block of input voxels and matches it to the low-resolution voxel by scaling the density and albedo parameters. Inputs: A block of high-resolution input voxels with spatial extent [x{\min}, x{\max}]. Precomputed parameters for the low-resolution voxel: pre-filtering distribution D, base density \rho0, and base directional albedo A0(\omega). The extinction coefficient \sigmat(s, \omega) and scattering coefficient \sigmas(x, \omega) for the input block. The phase function f(x, \omegar \rightarrow \omega). Number of rays N{ray} (typically aligned with main axes of the voxel grid). Outputs: A scaling factor \gamma \in (0, 1]. Final density \rho = \rho0 \gamma and final directional albedo A(\omega) = \gamma A0(\omega) for the low-resolution voxel. Data Structures: The input block is treated as a volume defined by its spatial bounds and per-voxel coefficients. The low-resolution voxel is defined by the scalar \rho0, the function A0(\omega), and the distribution D(m). Steps: 1. Define Transmittance: Compute the transmittance between two points x1 and x2 in direction \omega as: O(x1, \omega, x2) = \exp\left(-\int{x1}^{x2} \sigmat(s, \omega) ds\right) Let O(x1, \omega) denote the transmittance from x1 to the limit of the input block in direction \omega. 2. Estimate Single Scattering for a Single Ray: For an incoming ray r with direction \omegar intersecting the input block at x{\min} and x{\max}, compute the amount of single scattering P{SS}(r) as: P{SS}(r) = \int{x{\min}}^{x{\max}} \sigmas(x, \omegar) O(x{\min}, \omegar, x) \left[ \int{S^2} f(x, \omegar \rightarrow \omega) O(x, \omega) d\omega \right] dx This quantity is dimensionless but wavelength-dependent. 3. Estimate Mean Single Scattering in Input Block: Cast N{ray} rays in directions parallel to the main axes of the voxel grid. For each ray ri, compute P{SS}(ri). Average these values to obtain the mean single scattering of the input block: M{ss}^{\text{input}} = \frac{1}{N{ray}} \sum{\text{rays}} P{SS}(ri) 4. Estimate Mean Single Scattering in Low-Res Voxel: Compute M{ss} for the low-resolution voxel using the same integral form as Eq. 7.10, but substituting the input block's \sigmas and f with the low-res voxel's \sigma{ss} and f{ss}, which are derived from \rho0, A0(\omega), and D. 5. Compute Scaling Factor \gamma: The scaling factor \gamma is chosen to minimize the error between the estimated single scattering of the input block and the scaled low-res voxel across wavelengths. Using RGB albedos (wavelengths \lambdai), compute: \gamma = \arg \ming \sum{\lambdai} \left\| M{SS}^{\text{input}}(\lambdai) - g M{SS}(\lambdai) \right\|^2 where g is the trial scaling factor. (Note: The source notation uses \arg \max, which is corrected here to \arg \min to correctly minimize the squared error norm.) 6. Apply Final Parameters: Set the final density and albedo for the low-resolution voxel as: \rho = \rho0 \gamma A(\omega) = \gamma A0(\omega) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def numericalquadrature(func, a, b, n=100): """Trapezoidal rule for 1D integration.""" h = (b - a) / n total = 0.5 (func(a) + func(b)) for i in range(1, n): total += func(a + i h) return total h def computetransmittance(x1, x2, direction, sigmatfunc): """O(x1, direction, x2) = exp(-integral{x1}^{x2} sigmat(s, direction) ds)""" integral = numericalquadrature(lambda s: sigmatfunc(s, direction), x1, x2) return math.exp(-integral) def samplesphereuniform(n): """Generates n directions uniformly distributed on the unit sphere.""" directions = [] for in range(n): theta = math.acos(2 random() - 1) phi = 2 math.pi random() directions.append((math.sin(theta) math.cos(phi), math.sin(theta) math.sin(phi), math.cos(theta))) return directions def computesinglescatteringforray(raystart, rayend, raydirection, sigmasfunc, sigmatfunc, phasefunc, blockmin, blockmax): """PSS(r) for a single ray.""" xmin = max(raystart, blockmin) xmax = min(rayend, blockmax) if xmin >= xmax: return 0.0 def integrand(x): oentrytox = computetransmittance(xmin, x, raydirection, sigmatfunc) sigmas = sigmasfunc(x, raydirection) spheresamples = samplesphereuniform(64) innersum = 0.0 for omega in spheresamples: limit = blockmax oxtolimit = computetransmittance(x, limit, omega, sigmatfunc) f = phasefunc(x, raydirection, omega) innersum += f oxtolimit innerintegral = innersum / len(spheresamples) return sigmas oentrytox innerintegral return numericalquadrature(integrand, xmin, xmax) def estimatemeansinglescatteringinput(blockvoxels, numrays=3): """Mss^input = (1/Nray) sum PSS(ri)""" total = 0.0 axes = [(1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (0, 0, 1)] for direction in axes[:numrays]: raystart = blockvoxels.min rayend = blockvoxels.max pss = computesinglescatteringforray( raystart, rayend, direction, blockvoxels.sigmas, blockvoxels.sigmat, blockvoxels.phasefunc, blockvoxels.min, blockvoxels.max) total += pss return total / numrays def computesigmass(rho0, A0, D, direction): """sigmass(omega) = gamma rho0 A0(omega) integral A0(omega) D(m) <omega. m> dm""" msamples = samplesphereuniform(64) integralsum = 0.0 for m in msamples: dotproduct = sum(d mi for d, mi in zip(direction, m)) integralsum += A0(direction) D(m) dotproduct return rho0 A0(direction) (integralsum / len(msamples)) def estimatemeansinglescatteringlowres(lowresvoxel, numrays=3): """Mss for low-res voxel using precomputed terms.""" total = 0.0 axes = [(1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (0, 0, 1)] for direction in axes[:numrays]: sigmass = computesigmass(lowresvoxel.rho0, lowresvoxel.A0, lowresvoxel.D, direction) def fss(x, omegain, omegaout): return lowresvoxel.A0(omegaout) pss = computesinglescatteringforray( lowresvoxel.min, lowresvoxel.max, direction, lambda x, d: sigmass, lowresvoxel.sigmat, fss, lowresvoxel.min, lowresvoxel.max) total += pss return total / numrays def computegamma(inputmss, lowresmss, wavelengths): """gamma = arg ming sum || Minput - g Mlowres ||^2""" bestg = 1.0 minerror = float('inf') for g in [i/100.0 for i in range(1, 101)]: error = 0.0 for lam in wavelengths: diff = inputmss[lam] - g lowresmss[lam] error += diff diff if error < minerror: minerror = error bestg = g return bestg Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The transmittance calculation O(x1, \omega, x2) requires accurate integration of \sigmat. The inner integral over S^2 for the phase function and outgoing transmittance is computationally expensive. The scaling factor \gamma is constrained to (0, 1]. The method relies on the pre-filtering distribution D and base parameters \rho0, A0(\omega) being established during the preceding transparency matching step. This variant describes the mathematical mechanism for adjusting the low-resolution voxel's parameters to match the estimated self-shadowing. It scales the density \rho and directional albedo A(\omega) by a factor \gamma \in (0, 1]. This scaling preserves the attenuation coefficient \sigmat(\omega) because the product \rho A(\omega) remains constant relative to the initial state (\rho0 A0(\omega)), but it multiplies the single scattering coefficient \sigma{ss}(\omega) by \gamma. The single scattering coefficient becomes \sigma{ss}(\omega) = \gamma \rho0 A0(\omega) \int A0(\omega) D(m) \langle \omega \cdot m \rangle dm. The value of \gamma is computed by minimizing the error between the estimated single scattering of the input block and the scaled low-res voxel across wavelengths (using RGB albedos). Time Complexity: The method requires casting N{ray} rays through the input block and the low-res voxel. Each ray requires a numerical integration over the block length and an integration over the sphere S^2 for the phase function. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the input block's coefficients and the low-res voxel's precomputed terms. Strengths: Accurately preserves self-shadowing effects that are lost during downsampling. It is physically based and ensures consistency between the high-res and low-res representations. Limitations: Computationally intensive due to the multiple integrals. The accuracy depends on the number of rays and samples used in the integrals. When to use: When accurate self-shadowing is critical and the computational cost of the full single scattering estimation is acceptable. It is used in the context of volume downsampling for efficient rendering. This method is part of the "new microflake model with microscopic self-shadowing for accurate volume downsampling". It addresses the issue that standard downsampling techniques preserve macroscopic transparency but fail to preserve microscopic self-shadowing, leading to visually incorrect results. The approach is detailed in Section 7.4 of the source paper. A new microflake model with microscopic self-shadowing for accurate volume downsampling, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.13346, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Analytical Approximation of Single Scattering Radiance
head: First-Order Taylor Expansion of Incident Radiance, Legendre Polynomial Expansion Approximation
body: This method computes the in-scattered single scattering radiance J{ss} by approximating the phase function and incident radiance with low-order expansions, allowing the scattering contribution to be decomposed into direction-independent terms that are pre-computed per voxel. It differs from Monte Carlo approaches by avoiding repeated ray tracing for incident light estimation during rendering, making it significantly more efficient for differentiable rendering or multi-viewpoint reconstruction where gradients are required. Inputs: Density field \rho(x) defined on a voxel grid. Extinction cross-section \sigmat (scalar). Scattering anisotropy factor \bar{\mu}. Ambient incident radiance field L{in}(x, \omega') (or a point light source model). Number of sample directions N for pre-computation. Outputs: Pre-computed voxel grids: Q{ri}^0, Q{ri}^1, \dot{Q}{ri}^0, \dot{Q}{ri}^1. Final outgoing radiance L{out} per pixel. 1. Density Grid: 3D array storing \rho(x) for each voxel. 2. Extinction Grid: 3D array storing \kappat(x) = \sigmat \rho(x). 3. Pre-computed Term Grids: Four 3D arrays storing the vectors/scalars Q{ri}^0(x), Q{ri}^1(x), \dot{Q}{ri}^0(x), \dot{Q}{ri}^1(x) for each voxel center. Q{ri}^0(x): Scalar. Q{ri}^1(x): 3D Vector. \dot{Q}{ri}^0(x): Scalar (gradient w.r.t density). \dot{Q}{ri}^1(x): 3D Vector (gradient w.r.t density). N: Number of sample directions over the unit sphere for pre-computation. \bar{\mu}: Scattering anisotropy factor, defined as \bar{\mu} = \frac{3}{2} \int{-1}^{1} \mu p(\mu) d\mu. Phase Function Approximation: The phase function p(\omega, \omega') is approximated using a truncated Legendre polynomial expansion after the first moment: p(\omega, \omega') \approx \frac{1}{4\pi} (1 + \bar{\mu}(\omega \cdot \omega')) \quad (6) where \omega is the view direction and \omega' is the incident direction. Incident Radiance Approximation: The reduced incident radiance L{ri} is approximated using a first-order Taylor expansion in direction \omega': L{ri}(xu, \omega') \approx L{ri}^0(xu) + L{ri}^1(xu) \cdot \omega' \quad (7) where L{ri}^0 is the average radiance and L{ri}^1 is the directional gradient vector. In-scattered Radiance Decomposition: Substituting the approximations into the single scattering integral yields: J{ss}(xu, \omega) = \Omega (Q{ri}^0(xu) + Q{ri}^1(xu) \cdot \omega) \quad (8) where \Omega is the solid angle factor. The direction-independent terms are defined as: Q{ri}^0(xu) = L{ri}^0(xu) \quad (9) Q{ri}^1(xu) = \frac{\bar{\mu}}{3} L{ri}^1(xu) \quad (10) Computation of L{ri}^0 and L{ri}^1: These are computed via importance sampling over N directions \omega'i on the unit sphere: L{ri}^0(xu) = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N L{ri}(xu, \omega'i) \quad (11) L{ri}^1(xu) = \frac{3}{N} \sum{i=1}^N L{ri}(xu, \omega'i) \omega'i \quad (12) The factor of 3 arises from the spherical integration of direction vectors. Gradient Terms (for Differentiable Rendering): The derivatives of the pre-computed terms with respect to density are computed similarly: \dot{Q}{ri}^0(xu) = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \dot{L}{ri}(xu, \omega'i) \quad (19) \dot{Q}{ri}^1(xu) = \frac{3}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \dot{L}{ri}(xu, \omega'i) \omega'i \quad (20) Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generateuniformspheresamples(N): """Generate N directions uniformly distributed over the unit sphere.""" phi = np.random.uniform(0, 2 np.pi, N) costheta = np.random.uniform(-1, 1, N) sintheta = np.sqrt(1 - costheta2) x = sintheta np.cos(phi) y = sintheta np.sin(phi) z = costheta return np.stack([x, y, z], axis=1) def trilinearinterpolate(grid, point): """Standard trilinear interpolation for a 3D grid at an arbitrary point.""" # point is [x, y, z] in grid coordinates x, y, z = point ix, iy, iz = np.floor([x, y, z]).astype(int) fx, fy, fz = [p - i for p, i in zip([x, y, z], [ix, iy, iz])] # Clamp indices to grid bounds D, H, W = grid.shape ix = np.clip(ix, 0, D - 2) iy = np.clip(iy, 0, H - 2) iz = np.clip(iz, 0, W - 2) v000 = grid[ix, iy, iz] v100 = grid[ix + 1, iy, iz] v010 = grid[ix, iy + 1, iz] v110 = grid[ix + 1, iy + 1, iz] v001 = grid[ix, iy, iz + 1] v101 = grid[ix + 1, iy, iz + 1] v011 = grid[ix, iy + 1, iz + 1] v111 = grid[ix + 1, iy + 1, iz + 1] w000 = (1 - fx) (1 - fy) (1 - fz) w100 = fx (1 - fy) (1 - fz) w010 = (1 - fx) fy (1 - fz) w110 = fx fy (1 - fz) w001 = (1 - fx) (1 - fy) fz w101 = fx (1 - fy) fz w011 = (1 - fx) fy fz w111 = fx fy fz return (w000 v000 + w100 v100 + w010 v010 + w110 v110 + w001 v001 + w101 v101 + w011 v011 + w111 v111) def computereducedincidentradiance(vp, omegap, sigmat, densitygrid): """Trace ray from voxel to light source and compute Lin transmittance.""" # Simplified point light model: Lri = Llight exp(-sigmat opticaldist) / dist^2 lightpos = np.array([0.0, 10.0, 0.0]) Llight = 1.0 direction = lightpos - vp dist = np.linalg.norm(direction) if dist < 1e-6: return Llight opticaldist = dist transmittance = np.exp(-sigmat opticaldist) return Llight transmittance / (dist 2) def computegradientreducedincidentradiance(vp, omegap, sigmat, densitygrid): """Compute d(Lri)/drho along the light ray.""" # d/drho (L exp(-sigmat int rho ds)) = -L exp(-sigmat int rho ds) sigmat int ds lightpos = np.array([0.0, 10.0, 0.0]) direction = lightpos - vp dist = np.linalg.norm(direction) if dist < 1e-6: return 0.0 transmittance = np.exp(-sigmat dist) return -transmittance sigmat dist def precomputeterms(densitygrid, sigmat, N, anisotropymu): """Pre-computes direction-independent terms for single scattering.""" D, H, W = densitygrid.shape Q0 = np.zeros((D, H, W)) dQ0 = np.zeros((D, H, W)) Q1 = np.zeros((D, H, W, 3)) dQ1 = np.zeros((D, H, W, 3)) omegaprimes = generateuniformspheresamples(N) kappat = sigmat densitygrid for d in range(D): for h in range(H): for w in range(W): vp = np.array([d + 0.5, h + 0.5, w + 0.5]) Lrisum = 0.0 Lrivecsum = np.zeros(3) dLrisum = 0.0 dLrivecsum = np.zeros(3) for i in range(N): omegap = omegaprimes[i] Lrival = computereducedincidentradiance(vp, omegap, sigmat, densitygrid) dLrival = computegradientreducedincidentradiance(vp, omegap, sigmat, densitygrid) Lrisum += Lrival Lrivecsum += Lrival omegap dLrisum += dLrival dLrivecsum += dLrival omegap Lri0 = Lrisum / N Lri1 = (3.0 / N) Lrivecsum dLri0 = dLrisum / N dLri1 = (3.0 / N) dLrivecsum Q0[d, h, w] = Lri0 Q1[d, h, w] = (anisotropymu / 3.0) Lri1 dQ0[d, h, w] = dLri0 dQ1[d, h, w] = (anisotropymu / 3.0) dLri1 return Q0, Q1, dQ0, dQ1 def raymarchsinglescattering(camerarayorigin, cameraraydirection, densitygrid, sigmat, Q0, Q1, dQ0, dQ1, tmin, tmax, stepsize): """Ray marches through the volume to compute single scattering radiance and gradients.""" Lss = 0.0 dLss = 0.0 tau = 1.0 currentt = tmax while currentt > tmin: xu = camerarayorigin + cameraraydirection currentt currentt -= stepsize rhoxu = trilinearinterpolate(densitygrid, xu) kappatxu = sigmat rhoxu Q0xu = trilinearinterpolate(Q0, xu) Q1xu = np.array([trilinearinterpolate(Q1[..., i], xu) for i in range(3)]) dQ0xu = trilinearinterpolate(dQ0, xu) dQ1xu = np.array([trilinearinterpolate(dQ1[..., i], xu) for i in range(3)]) omega = cameraraydirection Jss = Q0xu + np.dot(Q1xu, omega) dJss = dQ0xu + np.dot(dQ1xu, omega) tau = np.exp(-kappatxu stepsize) contribution = Jss tau stepsize dcontribution = (dJss tau - Jss kappatxu tau stepsize) stepsize Lss += contribution dLss += dcontribution return Lss, dLss Interpolation Consistency: Trilinear interpolation is used for sampling density and pre-computed terms at arbitrary positions. Gradients are scattered back to the eight nearest voxels using the same interpolation weights to maintain consistency between forward and backward passes. Anisotropy Factor: The approximation assumes the phase function can be well-approximated by the first two Legendre moments. The approximation truncates the Legendre expansion after the first moment, which is sufficient for most common phase functions like Henyey-Greenstein due to rapidly diminishing higher-order contributions. Light Tracing: The pre-computation step requires tracing rays from each voxel to the light source to compute L{ri}. The method avoids repeated ray tracing during rendering, maintaining efficiency for multi-viewpoint reconstruction. Time Complexity: Pre-computation is O(V \cdot N), where V is the number of voxels and N is the number of sample directions. Ray marching is O(R \cdot S), where R is the number of rays and S is the number of steps per ray. Memory Complexity: Requires storing four additional 3D grids (Q{ri}^0, Q{ri}^1, \dot{Q}{ri}^0, \dot{Q}{ri}^1) in addition to the density grid. Memory usage is O(V). Strengths: Efficient for differentiable rendering as gradients are computed simultaneously with radiance. Avoids repeated ray tracing for incident light estimation. Limitations: Approximation error due to truncation of Legendre series and Taylor expansion. When to Use: Suitable for smoke/volumetric rendering where real-time or differentiable rendering is required. When Not to Use: For highly anisotropic media where higher-order phase function terms are critical, or for scenes with complex, dynamic lighting where pre-computation is not feasible. This method was proposed in "A High-Efficiency Physics-Based Differentiable Renderer for Smoke Reconstruction". It addresses the inefficiency of traditional ray tracing-based frameworks for computing single scattering radiance, particularly in the context of differentiable rendering where gradient computation requires tracing additional rays. By pre-computing direction-independent terms, the method avoids redundant calculations during rendering. A High-Efficiency Physics-Based Differentiable Renderer for Smoke Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450546, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Volume Single Scattering (Monte Carlo with Sphere Light)
body: This method computes single scattering radiance in participating media using Monte Carlo integration with a sphere light for background and emission. It differs from its parent, Volume Single Scattering (Monte Carlo with Point Light), by replacing the point light source with a sphere light and employing equi-angular sampling for distance estimation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin, ray direction, maximum ray distance (t{MAX}), scene objects, volume properties (density, scattering coefficient), sphere light parameters (position, radius, emission color). Outputs: Radiance value for the pixel. Data Structures: Vector3: 3D vector with components x, y, z. Color: RGB color representation. Ray: Defined by origin and direction. Object: Base class for scene geometry. Triangle: Inherits from Object, stores vertices A, B, C, normal, distance, and color. Steps: 1. Calculate Background Radiance: Compute the background radiance using the sphere light. This involves tracing a ray from the camera through the scene to determine what is visible behind the volume. Call getPixelColorWithSphereLight(objects, id, tMAX, ray, hitPoint, 1, ImportanceSolidAngle) where id is the current pixel index, tMAX is the maximum ray distance, ray is the camera ray, hitPoint is the intersection point, and ImportanceSolidAngle is the sampling mode. 2. Set Sampling Mode: Set the 1D sampling mode to EquiAngular. sampleMode1D sampleMode = EquiAngular. 3. Monte Carlo Integration Loop: For each sample: a. Sample Distance: Sample the distance t{sample} along the ray using the EquiAngular sampling mode. b. Calculate Sample Point: Compute the sample position x{sample} = ray.origin + t{sample} \cdot ray.direction. c. Calculate Light Radiance (Le): Compute the radiance arriving at x{sample} from the sphere light. Call getPixelColorWithSphereLight(objects, -1, tsample, ray, hitPoint, 1, ImportanceSolidAngle) where id is -1 (indicating a light query), tsample is the sampled distance, and other parameters are as above. d. Calculate Transmittance from Light: Compute the transmittance from the sample point to the light source. transmittanceFromLight = volume->getTransmittanceHomogeneos(xsample, light.getLightPosition()). e. Accumulate Radiance: Add the contribution to the total radiance. The contribution is the product of the light radiance, the transmittance from the light, and the volume's scattering properties. 4. Average and Return: Average the accumulated radiance over the number of samples and return the result. Formulas: Background Radiance: L{bg} = \text{getPixelColorWithSphereLight}(\dots). Sampled Distance: t{sample} = \text{sampleEquiAngular}(). Sample Point: x{sample} = o + t{sample} \cdot d. Light Radiance: Le = \text{getPixelColorWithSphereLight}(\dots). Transmittance from Light: T(x{sample}, L) = \text{getTransmittanceHomogeneos}(x{sample}, L{pos}). Total Radiance: L = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} Le(xi) \cdot T(xi, L) \cdot \sigmas \cdot \Delta t. Parameters: sampleMode1D: Set to EquiAngular. ImportanceSolidAngle: Sampling mode for sphere light. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision issues with small distances or large scene scales. Degenerate triangles (zero area) may cause intersection failures. Boundary conditions for ray-volume intersections. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getRadiance(ray, objects, volume, spherelight, numsamples): # Step 1: Calculate background radiance background = getPixelColorWithSphereLight(objects, 0, ray.tmax, ray, ray.hitpoint, 1, ImportanceSolidAngle) # Step 2: Set sampling mode to EquiAngular samplemode = EquiAngular totalradiance = Vector3(0, 0, 0) # Step 3: Monte Carlo loop for i in range(numsamples): # Step 3a: Sample distance using EquiAngular mode tsample = sampleequiangular(ray.tmax) # Step 3b: Calculate sample point xsample = ray.origin + tsample ray.direction # Step 3c: Calculate Le using sphere light Le = getPixelColorWithSphereLight(objects, -1, tsample, ray, ray.hitpoint, 1, ImportanceSolidAngle) # Step 3d: Calculate transmittance from light transmittancefromlight = volume.gettransmittancehomogeneous(xsample, spherelight.getlightposition()) # Step 3e: Accumulate radiance # Note: The exact scattering coefficient and step size are not provided in the source. # Assuming a simple accumulation for demonstration. contribution = Le transmittancefromlight totalradiance += contribution # Step 4: Average and return averageradiance = totalradiance / numsamples return averageradiance def sampleequiangular(tmax): # Equi-angular sampling implementation # This is a placeholder for the actual sampling logic # Typically involves generating a random number and mapping it to the distance u = random.uniform(0, 1) # Example mapping (not from source) tsample = tmax u return tsample A deterministic ray marching technique for computing single scattering, replacing stochastic sampling with fixed-step integration and using the "Frostbite method" for radiance accumulation. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M) where N is the number of samples and M is the cost of ray-object intersection and light query. Memory Complexity: O(1) per sample, excluding scene storage. Performance: Depends on the number of samples and scene complexity. Higher sample counts reduce noise but increase computation time. Strengths: Handles complex lighting scenarios with sphere lights; Monte Carlo method provides unbiased results. Limitations: High variance with few samples; computationally expensive for high-quality images. When to Use: When accurate single scattering with sphere lights is required and computational resources allow. When Not to Use: For real-time applications or when point lights are sufficient. name: Main Ray Marching with Frostbite Integration
head: Frostbite Volume Integration
body: Main Ray Marching with Frostbite Integration is a volume rendering technique that marches along the view direction through a participating medium, accumulating radiance using a physically based integration scheme from Frostbite that handles transmittance, inscatter, and early termination. It differs from its parent method, Volume Single Scattering (Monte Carlo with Sphere Light), by replacing stochastic sphere light sampling with a fixed-step deterministic ray march. Inputs: Ray origin O and direction D (normalized). Bounding volume of the participating medium. Volume density \rho. Scattering coefficient \sigmas and extinction coefficient \sigmat. Step size s. Light source parameters (position, intensity). Outputs: Accumulated radiance L. Total transmittance T{total} (passed by reference). Data Structures: Current position P. Cumulative transmittance T{total}. Accumulated radiance L. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Determine ray intersection with bounding volume. If no intersection, return black. 2. Initialize L = 0. Initialize T{total} (passed by reference). Calculate phase function: p(\theta) = 0.7 \cdot HG(\theta, g=-0.3) + 0.3 \cdot HG(\theta, g=0.3). 3. If density \rho > 0: Calculate sample scattering coefficient \sigmas' = \sigmas \cdot \rho and sample extinction coefficient \sigmat' = \sigmat \cdot \rho. 4. Calculate emission (distance glow) and ambient light. Calculate inscatter: L{inscatter} = L{emission} + L{ambient} + L{sun} \cdot p(\theta) \cdot \tau{light}. 5. Scale inscatter by scattering coefficient and density: L{inscatter} \leftarrow L{inscatter} \cdot \sigmas'. 6. Calculate transmittance for the step: T{step} = \exp(-\sigmat' \cdot s). 7. Integrate radiance using Frostbite method: L \leftarrow L + T{total} \cdot (L{inscatter} - L{inscatter} \cdot T{step}) / \sigmat'. 8. Update total transmittance: T{total} \leftarrow T{total} \cdot T{step}. 9. Early termination: if |T{total}| \le 10^{-3}, set T{total} = 0 and return L. 10. Step along ray: P \leftarrow P + D \cdot s. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def frostbitevolumeintegration(rayorigin, raydir, boundingvolume, sigmas, sigmat, stepsize, lightsource, densityfunc): # 1. Intersection Test tmin, tmax = intersectboundingvolume(rayorigin, raydir, boundingvolume) if tmin is None: return 0.0, 0.0 # 2. Initialize radiance = 0.0 totaltransmittance = 1.0 epsilon = 1e-3 currentpos = rayorigin + raydir tmin # Loop while currentpos is within boundingvolume and totaltransmittance > epsilon: # 3. Sample Coefficients density = densityfunc(currentpos) if density <= 0: currentpos += raydir stepsize continue sigmasprime = sigmas density sigmatprime = sigmat density # 2. Phase Function tolight = lightsource.position - currentpos costheta = dot(normalize(tolight), -raydir) phase = 0.7 heneygreenstein(costheta, -0.3) + 0.3 heneygreenstein(costheta, 0.3) # 4. Insatter # Emission and ambient are scene-dependent evaluations. Lemission = computedistanceglow(currentpos) Lambient = computeambientlight(currentpos) # Light transmittance approximated as standard exponential decay. taulight = exp(-sigmatprime length(tolight)) Lsun = lightsource.intensity Linscatter = Lemission + Lambient + Lsun phase taulight # 5. Scale Insatter Linscatter = sigmasprime # 6. Step Transmittance Tstep = exp(-sigmatprime stepsize) # 7. Integrate Radiance (Frostbite Method) if sigmatprime > 1e-6: term = Linscatter (1.0 - Tstep) / sigmatprime else: term = Linscatter stepsize radiance += totaltransmittance term # 8. Update Total Transmittance totaltransmittance = Tstep # 9. Early Termination if abs(totaltransmittance) <= epsilon: totaltransmittance = 0.0 return radiance # 10. Step Forward currentpos += raydir stepsize return radiance, totaltransmittance def intersectboundingvolume(origin, direction, volume): # Standard axis-aligned bounding box intersection. tmin = (volume.min - origin) / direction tmax = (volume.max - origin) / direction tenter = max(min(tmin)) texit = min(max(tmax)) if tenter > texit or texit < 0: return None, None return tenter, texit def heneygreenstein(costheta, g): numerator = 1.0 - g g denominator = 4.0 3.141592653589793 pow(1.0 + g g - 2.0 g costheta, 1.5) if denominator == 0: return 0.0 return numerator / denominator Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Early Termination Threshold: The 10^{-3} threshold is a heuristic to save computation in transparent regions. Phase Function Mix: The specific weights (0.7 for g=-0.3, 0.3 for g=0.3) are hardcoded in the source. Division by Zero: When \sigmat' approaches zero, the Frostbite integration formula divides by \sigmat', requiring a fallback to a linear approximation. Uniform Volume Ray Marching is a rendering technique for participating media with constant opacity and density, using ray marching to estimate the integral of light scattering. It assumes a single light source and constant volume properties, allowing precomputation of attenuation factors. It is distinguished from its sibling, Main Ray Marching with Frostbite Integration, by its strict assumption of uniform volume properties, which simplifies the transmission calculation to a constant per-step factor. name: Uniform Volume Ray Marching
head: Backward Ray Marching, Forward Ray Marching
body: Uniform Volume Ray Marching is a rendering technique for participating media with constant opacity and density, using ray marching to estimate the integral of light scattering. It assumes a single light source and constant volume properties, allowing precomputation of attenuation factors. Forward ray marching is preferred over backward ray marching for uniform volumes because it allows for early termination when transmission becomes very small, optimizing performance. Inputs: Camera ray origin O and direction D. Volume density \sigmat (constant). Light source position L and color CL. Step size \Delta s. Early termination threshold \epsilon. Maximum number of steps N{max}. Outputs: Final pixel color C{out} (RGBA). Data Structures: overalltransmission: Floating-point scalar, initialized to 1.0. colorresult: Vector (RGB), initialized to 0.0. currentposition: Vector, initialized to O. Steps: 1. Initialize overalltransmission to 1.0 and colorresult to 0.0. 2. Iterate along the ray direction D for up to N{max} steps: a. Compute the in-scattered light Li(x) at the current sample point x, representing the light attenuated from the source to the sample point. b. Accumulate the final color: colorresult += Li(x) \times overalltransmission. c. Update overalltransmission by multiplying it by the current sample's transmission value T{sample}. For a uniform volume, T{sample} = e^{-\sigmat \Delta s}. d. Advance currentposition by \Delta s \cdot D. e. If overalltransmission drops below a small threshold close to zero, terminate the loop early. 3. Return colorresult and overalltransmission as the final RGBA pixel value. Formulas: Sample transmission: T{sample} = e^{-\sigmat \Delta s}. In-scattered light: Li(x) is computed based on the attenuation of light from the source to x. The exact formula depends on the light model, but the accumulation term is Li(x) \cdot T{overall}. Pixel width estimation for step size: \text{step\size} \approx 2 \cdot \tan(\frac{\pi}{180} \cdot \frac{FOV}{2}) \cdot \text{image\width}. Note: The source provides a garbled formula, but this is the standard interpretation for estimating pixel width to inform step size selection. Parameters: Step size \Delta s: A constant distance between march steps. Trade-off between speed and accuracy. Early termination threshold \epsilon: A small value close to zero. Pitfalls: If the step size is too large, the ray may overstep small solid objects casting shadows, completely ignoring the shadow and creating visual artifacts. If the volume is not uniform, a constant step size may miss small features or shadows (aliasing/filtering issue). A source typo claimed that a step size that is 'too small' misses detail; the correct interpretation is that a step size that is 'too large' misses detail. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def uniformvolumeraymarching(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedensity, lightposition, lightcolor, stepsize, threshold, maxsteps): overalltransmission = 1.0 colorresult = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] currentposition = list(rayorigin) for in range(maxsteps): if overalltransmission < threshold: break # Compute in-scattered light Li(x) lightdir = [lightposition[i] - currentposition[i] for i in range(3)] dist = math.sqrt(sum(dd for d in lightdir)) dist = max(dist, 1e-6) lix = [lightcolor[i] / (dist dist) for i in range(3)] # Accumulate color before updating transmission colorresult[0] += lix[0] overalltransmission colorresult[1] += lix[1] overalltransmission colorresult[2] += lix[2] overalltransmission # Update overall transmission sampletransmission = math.exp(-volumedensity stepsize) overalltransmission = sampletransmission # Advance position currentposition[0] += raydirection[0] stepsize currentposition[1] += raydirection[1] stepsize currentposition[2] += raydirection[2] stepsize return [colorresult[0], colorresult[1], colorresult[2], overalltransmission] Handles non-uniform volumes and complex integration schemes. Choose when volume properties vary. Uses Monte Carlo methods for single scattering. Choose for stochastic accuracy or complex light interactions. Extends Monte Carlo to sphere lights. Choose for soft shadows from area lights. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of steps. Early termination can reduce effective N. Memory Complexity: O(1), as it only requires scalar and vector accumulators. Strengths: Simple to implement; early termination optimizes performance for opaque regions; precomputable attenuation for uniform volumes. Limitations: Assumes uniform volume properties; step size trade-off can lead to aliasing or missed details if not tuned correctly; not suitable for non-uniform volumes without modification. When to use: Uniform volumes with constant density and opacity; single light source; performance-critical applications where early termination is beneficial. When not to use: Non-uniform volumes; multiple light sources; high-frequency details requiring adaptive step sizes. Originated in the context of volume rendering for developers, specifically discussed in "Volume Rendering for Developers" Group Read Part 1. The technique is a simplified version of ray marching tailored for uniform media, allowing for precomputed attenuation factors. name: Volume Single Scattering (Uniform Ray Marching with Point Light Background)
body: This method computes single scattering radiance in a participating medium using uniform ray marching, where the background radiance is computed via a point light model instead of a generic surface object color. It replaces the Monte Carlo integration of its parent method with deterministic uniform sampling along the ray. Inputs: ray: Ray origin O and direction D. volume: Homogeneous participating medium. objects: List of scene geometry primitives. light: Point light source definition. tMAX: Maximum ray distance to the scene boundary or far plane. N: Number of uniform marching steps. Outputs: Li: Final accumulated radiance for the pixel. Data Structures: Sphere: Defined by radius r, center C, color, exponent, and radiance. Ray: Contains origin and direction vectors. Vector3: 3D floating-point vector type. Formulas: 1. Homogeneous Transmittance: Computed via volume->getTransmittanceHomogeneos(t). 2. Background Radiance: Computed via getPixelColorPointLight(objects, id, tMAX, ray, light). 3. Light Emission at Step: Computed via getPixelColorPointLight(objects, -1, tmarch, ray, light). Steps: 1. Calculate the background radiance using the point light function: background = getPixelColorPointLight(objects, id, tMAX, ray, light). 2. Calculate the transmittance from the ray origin to the hit point at distance tMAX: transmittance = volume->getTransmittanceHomogeneos(tMAX). 3. Initialize the accumulated radiance: Li = background transmittance. 4. Iterate through N uniform steps: a. Compute the step distance: tmarch = (i + 0.5) (tMAX / N). b. Calculate transmittance from the eye to the current position: transmittanceFromEye = volume->getTransmittanceHomogeneos(tmarch). c. Calculate the light emission at the current position: Le = getPixelColorPointLight(objects, -1, tmarch, ray, light). d. Calculate transmittance from the current position to the light: transmittanceFromLight = volume->getTransmittanceHomogeneos(xmarch, lightHitPoint). e. Accumulate the scattered contribution: Li += transmittanceFromEye Le transmittanceFromLight (tMAX / N). (The source notes omit the scattering coefficient \sigmas and step size \Delta t in the accumulation line, but standard volume rendering requires them for physical correctness.) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getPixelColorVolumeSingleScatterpoint(ray, volume, objects, light, tMAX, N): # 1. Background radiance background = getPixelColorPointLight(objects, id, tMAX, ray, light) # 2. Initial transmittance to boundary transmittance = volume.getTransmittanceHomogeneos(tMAX) # 3. Initialize accumulated radiance Li = background transmittance dt = tMAX / N for i in range(N): # 4a. Uniform step distance (midpoint sampling) tmarch = (i + 0.5) dt # 4b. Transmittance from eye to step transmittanceFromEye = volume.getTransmittanceHomogeneos(tmarch) # 4c. Light emission at step Le = getPixelColorPointLight(objects, -1, tmarch, ray, light) # 4d. Transmittance from step to light xmarch = ray.origin + ray.direction tmarch transmittanceFromLight = volume.getTransmittanceHomogeneos(xmarch, light.position) # 4e. Accumulate scattering (sigmas absorbed or assumed unity per source notation) Li += transmittanceFromEye Le transmittanceFromLight dt return Li Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Exponential transmittance can underflow for large optical depths; clamp the exponent to a minimum value like -50.0 before evaluation. Boundary: If tMAX is not correctly determined (e.g., ray misses all objects), background should default to zero or environment color. Light Inside Volume: If the light position lies inside the volume, transmittanceFromLight approaches unity; ensure Le handles the geometric singularity at the light position. Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel, where N is the number of marching steps. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per pixel. Performance: Execution time scales linearly with N and the cost of the point light evaluation. Strengths: Deterministic output with no stochastic noise, and straightforward implementation. Limitations: Aliasing artifacts appear if N is too low, and the point light background approximation fails for complex area lighting. When to Use: Real-time volume rendering with simple lighting, educational demonstrations, or baseline comparisons. When Not to Use: High-fidelity offline rendering requiring multiple scattering, or scenes demanding accurate soft shadows from area lights. This method originates from the repository wangyuehi/VolumeSingleScattering. It implements a variant of uniform ray marching where the boundary condition for the radiative transfer equation is explicitly solved using a point light model. The approach simplifies the rendering equation by neglecting multiple scattering events and relying on deterministic sampling. wangyuehi/VolumeSingleScattering, https://github.com/wangyuehi/VolumeSingleScattering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: BSSRDF Approximation with Dipole and Single Scattering
head: BSSRDF Model with Dipole Diffusion Approximation, BSSRDF Rendering with Dipole Diffusion and Single Scattering, BSSRDF approximation, Dipole BSSRDF, First-order scattering, Hanrahan and Krueger extension, Practical Model for Subsurface Light Transport, Single Scattering Term
body: This method approximates subsurface light transport by combining a dipole diffusion model for multiple scattering with a single-scattering term, evaluating the Bidirectional Surface Scattering Reflectance Distribution Function (BSSRDF) at the surface boundary. It solves the problem of computationally expensive volumetric path tracing in participating media by replacing full volumetric integration with analytical diffusion-based solutions and single-scattering approximations. The method computes outgoing radiance by integrating incident radiance over the surface area, using the BSSRDF to relate incident flux at point xi to outgoing radiance at point xo. The BSSRDF S is approximated using a dipole solution to the diffusion equation for the multiple scattering component, supplemented by a single-scattering term for near-surface effects. Inputs: Surface geometry: Points xi (incident) and xo (outgoing), normals n(xi) and n(xo). Material properties: Absorption coefficient \sigmaa, scattering coefficient \sigmas, mean cosine of scattering angle g, relative index of refraction \eta. Lighting: Incident radiance Li(xi, \omegai), incident direction \omegai, observed distance si. Sampling: Random number \xi \in ]0, 1] for single scattering distance. Outputs: Outgoing radiance Lo(xo, \omegao). The method relies on scalar and vector quantities derived from the radiative transfer equation. Key parameters are computed as follows: \sigmat = \sigmas + \sigmaa: Extinction coefficient. \sigma{s0} = \sigmas (1 - g): Reduced scattering coefficient. \sigma{t0} = \sigma{s0} + \sigmaa: Reduced extinction coefficient. D = \frac{1}{3\sigma{t0}}: Diffusion constant. \sigma{tr} = \sqrt{3\sigmaa \sigma{t0}}: Effective transport coefficient. 1. BSSRDF Definition: dLo(xo, \omegao) = S(xi, \omegai; xo, \omegao) d\Phii(xi, \omegai) Lo(xo, \omegao) = \intA \int{2\pi} S(xi, \omegai; xo, \omegao) (\omegai \cdot \omegao) Li(xi, \omegai) d\omegai dA(xi) 2. Single Scattering Term: The single scattering radiance Lo^{(1)} is computed as: Lo^{(1)}(xo, \omegao) = \frac{\sigmas(xo) F p(\omegai \cdot \omegao)}{\sigma{tc}} e^{-s{0i} \sigmat(xi)} e^{-s{0o} \sigmat(xo)} Li(xi, \omegai) Where: F = Ft(\eta, \omegao) Ft(\eta, \omegai) is the product of Fresnel transmission terms. p(\omegai \cdot \omegao) is the phase function. \sigma{tc} is the total cross section (often equivalent to \sigmat in this context). s{0i} is the refracted distance through the material. s{0o} is the distance along the outgoing ray. 3. Refracted Distances: Outgoing distance (s{0o}): s{0o} = -\frac{\ln(\xi)}{\sigmat(xo)} where \xi \in ]0, 1] is a uniformly distributed random number. Incoming distance (s{0i}): Approximated using Snell's law, assuming the light source is far away compared to the mean free path: s{0i} = si \frac{|\omegai \cdot ni|}{\sqrt{1 - (\eta^2 (1 - |\omegai \cdot n(xi)|^2))}} Where si is the observed distance, \eta is the index of refraction, ni is the normal at the outgoing point, and n(xi) is the normal at the incoming point. 4. Dipole Diffusion Approximation (Multiple Scattering): The diffuse BSSRDF Rd is derived from the dipole solution to the diffusion equation. The fluence \phi(x) for a dipole configuration (real source at xr and virtual source at xv) is: \phi(x) = \frac{\Phi}{4\pi D} \left( \frac{e^{-\sigma{tr} rr(x)}}{rr(x)} - \frac{e^{-\sigma{tr} rv(x)}}{rv(x)} \right) Where: \Phi is the source power. rr(x) = ||x - xr|| is the distance to the real source. rv(x) = ||x - xv|| is the distance to the virtual source. The real source is placed at distance zr = 1/\sigma{t0} below the surface at xi. The virtual source is placed symmetrically or according to boundary conditions (often -zr or adjusted for index mismatch). Rd(r) = -D \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial n} \big|{surface} / d\Phii. For a plane-parallel medium, the diffuse reflectance F{dr} can be approximated analytically or via rational approximation: F{dr} = 1.440 \left( \frac{1}{\eta^2} - 1 \right) + 0.710 \left( \frac{1}{\eta^2} + 1 \right) + 0.668 + 0.0636 \eta Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def computebssrdfapproximation(xi, xo, wi, wo, ni, no, material, light): """ Computes outgoing radiance using BSSRDF approximation with Dipole and Single Scattering. Args: xi: Incident point on surface. xo: Outgoing point on surface. wi: Incident direction (normalized). wo: Outgoing direction (normalized). ni: Normal at xi. no: Normal at xo. material: Object containing sigmaa, sigmas, g, eta. light: Object containing Li (incident radiance), si (observed distance), and Phi (source power). Returns: Lo: Outgoing radiance. """ # Extract material properties sigmaa = material.sigmaa sigmas = material.sigmas g = material.g eta = material.eta # Compute derived coefficients sigmat = sigmas + sigmaa sigmas0 = sigmas (1 - g) sigmat0 = sigmas0 + sigmaa D = 1.0 / (3.0 sigmat0) sigmatr = math.sqrt(3.0 sigmaa sigmat0) # 1. Single Scattering Term # Sample distance for single scattering u = random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) if u <= 0.0: u = 1e-9 # Guard against log(0) s0o = -math.log(u) / sigmat # Approximate refracted incoming distance using Snell's law approximation si = light.si dotwini = math.dot(wi, ni) dotwinxi = math.dot(wi, ni) # Assuming local flatness or n(xi) passed separately # Denominator for Snell's law approximation denomsq = 1.0 - (eta2 (1.0 - dotwinxi2)) if denomsq <= 0: s0i = 0.0 # Degenerate case else: s0i = si abs(dotwini) / math.sqrt(denomsq) # Fresnel transmission (simplified approximation) # F = Ft(eta, wo) Ft(eta, wi) Ftwi = 1.0 - fresnelreflectance(eta, math.acos(abs(math.dot(wi, ni)))) Ftwo = 1.0 - fresnelreflectance(eta, math.acos(abs(math.dot(wo, no)))) F = Ftwi Ftwo # Phase function p(wi. wo) p = 1.0 / (4.0 math.pi) # Isotropic default # Single scattering radiance # Lo(1) = [sigmas F p / sigmatc] exp(-s0i sigmat) exp(-s0o sigmat) Li # Assuming sigmatc = sigmat termsingle = (sigmas F p / sigmat) math.exp(-s0i sigmat) math.exp(-s0o sigmat) light.Li # 2. Multiple Scattering Term (Dipole BSSRDF) # Distance between xi and xo r = distance(xi, xo) # Dipole source positions # Real source at 1/sigmat0 below xi zr = 1.0 / sigmat0 # Virtual source position depends on boundary conditions. # Standard dipole: real at zr, virtual at -zr (or adjusted for eta). # Here we use the fluence gradient method for Rd. # Calculate fluence gradient at surface for Rd # Rd(r) = -D d(phi)/dn / dPhii # Approximation for Rd using the dipole solution derivative # This part is complex; often Rd is precomputed or approximated by the Fdr formula scaled by geometry. # Using the Fdr approximation for diffuse reflectance component Fdr = 1.440 (1.0/eta2 - 1.0) + 0.710 (1.0/eta2 + 1.0) + 0.668 + 0.0636 eta # The BSSRDF S is often approximated as Rd(r) Ft(wo) Ft(wi) p(wi, wo) / (|n.wi| + |n.wo|) for the single scattering-like term # Or the full BSSRDF is Rd(r) for the diffuse part. # Combining: The total radiance is often the sum of single scattering and the diffuse BSSRDF contribution. # Lo = Lo(1) + Lo(diffuse) # Diffuse contribution approximation # Lo(diffuse) ~ Rd(r) Li... (simplified integration) # For a point light, the diffuse term is often: # Lo(diffuse) = Rd(r) Li (ni. wi) (no. wo) / (|n.wi| + |n.wo|) ? # The source notes give: fr(1) = alpha F p / (|n.wi| + |n.wo|) # Let's use the provided single scattering BRDF approximation formula for the "single scattering term" # and assume the dipole handles the rest, or that the formula provided IS the approximation for the BSSRDF term in this context. # Re-reading source: "Single scattering BRDF approximation fr(1)... The outscattered radiance L(1)o... is computed as..." # It seems the method primarily focuses on the single scattering term L(1)o and the dipole for the diffuse BSSRDF Rd. # The final output is the sum. # Diffuse BSSRDF term (Rd) # Rd(r) is the diffuse reflectance. # Lo(diffuse) = Rd(r) Li (ni. wi) / pi ? (Standard diffuse) # The source does not give a explicit Lo(diffuse) formula, only Rd. # We will assume the single scattering term L(1)o is the primary contribution for the "Single Scattering" part of the title, # and the Dipole is used to compute Rd for the multiple scattering part. # Approximate Rd(r) using the dipole solution's exitance # Rd(r) = (1/pi)... (complex) # Using the Fdr approximation as a proxy for the diffuse component scaling termdiffuse = Fdr light.Li abs(math.dot(wi, ni)) # Simplified Lo = termsingle + termdiffuse return Lo def fresnelreflectance(eta, thetai): """Simplified Fresnel reflectance for dielectric.""" sinthetai = math.sin(thetai) costhetai = math.cos(thetai) sinthetat = sinthetai / eta costhetat = math.sqrt(max(0, 1 - sinthetat2)) Rs = ((eta costhetai - costhetat) / (eta costhetai + costhetat))2 Rp = ((eta costhetat - costhetai) / (eta costhetat + costhetai))2 return (Rs + Rp) / 2 def phasefunction(mu): """Simple isotropic phase function.""" return 1.0 / (4.0 math.pi) def distance(p1, p2): return math.sqrt(sum((a-b)2 for a, b in zip(p1, p2))) The pseudocode includes a simplified Fresnel function and isotropic phase function as standard graphics primitives not detailed in the source notes but required for implementation. The diffuse term termdiffuse is a simplified placeholder for the full dipole integration, as the source notes provide the formula for Rd but not the explicit integration into Lo for a point light in a single line. In practice, Lo^{diffuse} involves integrating Rd over the surface area. \sigmaa: Absorption coefficient. \sigmas: Scattering coefficient. g: Mean cosine of scattering angle. \eta: Index of refraction. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Hair Darkness: The hair at the back of the head appears slightly darker in the BSSRDF simulation compared to full Monte Carlo. This is attributed to the forced 1/\sigma{t0} distance in the diffusion approximation. Sharp Edges: Special care must be taken in the presence of highly curved surfaces. The method handles this by always evaluating the diffusion term with a minimum distance of 1/\sigma{t0} to eliminate singularities at sharp edges where the source can be placed arbitrarily close to xo. Boundary Conditions: The diffusion equation does not have an analytical solution for finite media. The method assumes a semi-infinite plane-parallel medium. The BSSRDF Model approximates subsurface light transport by formulating the problem as a surface integral, avoiding expensive volumetric path tracing in participating media under rough dielectric surfaces. It replaces volumetric integration with an analytical diffusion-based solution using a dipole configuration of real and virtual light sources. It builds on BSSRDF Approximation with Dipole and Single Scattering by evaluating the transport at the surface boundary. The Tabulated BSSRDF method approximates the spatially varying reflectance distribution function (BSSRDF) for subsurface scattering by precomputing a lookup table of the single-scattering profile Sr as a function of albedo \rho and optical radius r{optical}. It solves the problem of the high dimensionality of the full BSSRDF, which depends on five parameters (\eta, g, \rho, \sigmat, r), by fixing the refractive index \eta and asymmetry coefficient g and reducing the remaining variables to a 2D table. This approach sets it apart from analytical approximations like the Dipole model by trading storage space for potentially higher accuracy across a wider range of material parameters, while avoiding the computational cost of evaluating complex analytical functions per sample. Time Complexity: Significantly faster than full volumetric Monte Carlo. Rendering time for a milk glass example was 4 minutes for BSSRDF vs. 2 minutes for diffuse BRDF, and much faster than the 1250 minutes for full Monte Carlo. Memory Complexity: Low, as it does not require storing volumetric photon maps or extensive precomputed tables (unless using Tabulated BSSRDF). Strengths: Captures the true appearance of translucent materials (marble, skin, milk, etc.) with much lower computational cost than volumetric path tracing. Handles spatial variation of light entry and exit. Limitations: Approximation errors near sharp edges or highly curved surfaces (mitigated by minimum distance clamp). "Hair darkness" artifact due to diffusion approximation. Assumes semi-infinite medium. When to use: When rendering translucent materials where performance is critical and full volumetric scattering is too expensive. When not to use: When high accuracy near boundaries or complex geometry is required without the minimum distance hack, or when the medium is not highly scattering (diffusion approximation fails). The model was presented in a paper for the SIGGRAPH conference proceedings, funded by NSF (IIS-0085864) and DARPA (DABT63-95-C-0085). It builds on the radiative transfer equation and the diffusion approximation. The method is used for rendering translucent materials such as marble, cloth, paper, skin, milk, cheese, bread, meat, fruits, plants, fish, ocean water, and snow. name: BSSRDF Model
head: BSSRDF Appearance Model, Jensen et al. model, Practical Model for Subsurface Light Transport, diffusion-based BSSRDF
body: The BSSRDF (Bidirectional Surface Scattering Reflectance Distribution Function) model approximates subsurface light transport in highly scattering translucent media by treating light entry and exit as surface phenomena, thereby avoiding the computational cost of volumetric path tracing. It formulates the subsurface light transport problem as a surface integral to compute the appearance of translucent objects. It sets itself apart from volumetric path tracing by replacing expensive participating medium integration with a surface convolution, and from tabulated approaches by relying on analytical diffusion-based approximations rather than precomputed lookup tables. The BSSRDF model computes the outgoing radiance Lo(xo, \omegao) at a surface point xo in direction \omegao as the sum of surface reflection and subsurface scattering contributions. The subsurface component is formulated as a surface integral over the incident position xi and direction \omegai, convolving the incident illumination Li with the BSSRDF \rhos: Lo(xo, \omegao) = \iint \rhos(xo, xi, \omegao, \omegai) Li(xi, \omegai) |\cos \thetai| \, dA \, d\omegai + \int \rhor(xo, \omegao, \omegai) Li(xo, \omegai) |\cos \thetai| \, d\omegai where \rhos is the BSSRDF and \rhor is the BRDF (e.g., a rough dielectric model with GGX distribution). The BSSRDF is typically factorized into three terms: the Fresnel transmission at entry Se, the subsurface scattering propagation Sp, and the Fresnel transmission at exit S\omega: \rhos(xo, xi, \omegao, \omegai) = Se(\omegai) Sp(xo, xi) S\omega(\omegao) Inputs: Incident position xi, incident direction \omegai, exit position xo, exit direction \omegao, and material properties including absorption coefficient \sigmaa, scattering coefficient \sigmas, refractive index \eta, and reduced albedo \alpha'. Outputs: Outgoing radiance Lo. The model parameters are stored as uniform values or texture maps on the surface. Key parameters include \eta, \sigmaa, \sigmas, and \alpha' = \sigmas / (\sigmaa + \sigmas). 1. Compute Fresnel Moment Normalization Factor (c): The factor c is a normalization factor calculated using the first Fresnel moment FresnelMoment1(\eta): c = 1 - 2 \cdot \text{FresnelMoment1}(1/\eta) The function FresnelMoment1(\eta) is approximated by a polynomial fit: python def FresnelMoment1(eta): # Polynomial approximation from eta2 = eta eta eta3 = eta2 eta eta4 = eta3 eta eta5 = eta4 eta if eta < 1: return 0.45966 - 1.73965 eta + 3.37668 eta2 - 3.904945 eta3 + 2.49277 eta4 - 0.68441 eta5 # else: return -4.61686 + 11.1136 eta - 10.4646 eta2 + 5.11455 eta3 - 1.27198 eta4 + 0.12746 eta5 # 2. Compute Exit Distribution (S\omega): The probability distribution of light exiting at xo in direction \omegao is given by: S\omega(\omegao) = \frac{1 - Fr(\cos \thetao)}{c \pi} where Fr is the Fresnel reflectance for a dielectric interface. 3. Compute Entry Distribution (Se): Similarly, the entry distribution at xi for direction \omegai is: Se(\omegai) = \frac{1 - Fr(\cos \thetai)}{c \pi} 4. Compute Subsurface Propagation (Sp): The term Sp(xo, xi) models the subsurface light propagation. In the standard dipole approximation, this is modeled using virtual light sources. A real source is placed at depth zr = 1/\sigmat (where \sigmat = \sigmaa + \sigmas) and a negative virtual source at zv = zr + 4AD (where A is a factor related to refractive index and D is the diffusion coefficient). The fluence \phi at a point is computed as: \phi(x) \propto \frac{e^{-\sigmat r}}{r} - \frac{e^{-\sigmat v}}{v} where r is the distance to the real source and v is the distance to the virtual source. For implementation, Sp is often approximated as a function of the distance ||xo - xi|| assuming a planar geometry. 5. Combine Contributions: The BSSRDF is computed as the product of the three terms. The final radiance is integrated over the surface area and incident directions. Refractive Index (\eta): Surface parameter. Reduced Albedo (\alpha'): Controls color and scattering extent. Extinction Coefficient (\sigmat): Controls the depth of scattering. Sharp Features: The standard BSSRDF model assumes a planar or smoothly varying surface and does not work well on shapes with sharp features. Homogeneity: The approximation Sp(||xo - xi||) assumes the medium is relatively uniform. High-Order Scattering: Classic BSSRDF models may struggle with high-order scattering effects compared to brute-force volumetric path tracing, though they are more efficient. The Effective BRDF is a computationally efficient approximation for rendering optically dense, approximately planar media under low-frequency illumination, derived as a limiting case of the subsurface scattering model. It replaces the expensive integration of the subsurface propagator over a surface area with a single bidirectional reflectance evaluation, enabling its use in level-of-detail hierarchies for participating media. Choose it when rendering planar translucent layers at multiple scales. SubsurfaceMaterial is a physically based material model that combines a Bidirectional Scattering Distribution Function (BSDF) for surface interactions with a Bidirectional Surface Scattering Reflectance Distribution Function (BSSRDF) for subsurface scattering. It is designed for objects with a defined surface geometry, such as those exhibiting perfect specular transmission or glossy specular transmission, where light enters the surface, scatters internally, and exits at a different location. It differs from KdSubsurfaceMaterial by requiring explicit absorption and scattering coefficients rather than deriving them from diffuse reflectance and mean free path. Choose it for precise physical materials with defined geometry. The Shape-adaptive BSSRDF Model introduces a shape-adaptive BSSRDF model using a conditional variational autoencoder that learns to sample from a reference distribution produced by a brute-force volumetric path tracer. It maintains the efficiency of the classic BSSRDF model without the assumption of diffusion theory, greatly improving overall accuracy. Choose it when high-order scattering accuracy is needed for smooth shapes, avoiding sharp feature artifacts. Time Complexity: The BSSRDF model is significantly faster than volumetric path tracing because it reduces the problem to a surface integral. The computational cost scales with the number of samples used to approximate the surface integral. Memory Complexity: Low, as it typically stores only material parameters (texture maps or uniform values). Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: The model maintains efficiency without the assumption of diffusion theory in its shape-adaptive variant. It provides physically plausible appearance for homogeneous translucent materials. Limitations: Standard dipole models assume diffusion theory, which breaks down near boundaries or for small objects. The model can only handle high-order scattering effects rather than guaranteeing superior accuracy for them. It struggles with sharp geometric features. When to Use: Rendering translucent materials where performance is critical and geometry is smooth. When Not to Use: Rendering media with sharp features. The BSSRDF model was introduced by Jensen et al. in 2001 as a practical model for subsurface light transport. It was developed to address the computational expense of volumetric path tracing for participating media with rough dielectric surfaces. The model has become a standard technique in computer graphics for rendering translucent objects, with various extensions and approximations developed over the years, including the dipole approximation and more recent neural network-based approaches. Reconstructing Translucent Objects using Differentiable Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1145/3528233.3530714, fetched 2026-11-03 Practical Model for Subsurface Light Transport, https://www.scribd.com/document/904578145/A-Practical-Model-for-Subsurface-Light-Transport, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Physically Based Rendering：体积散射 - YangWC's Blog, https://yangwc.com/2020/04/19/VolumeScattering/, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) A survey on rendering homogeneous participating media, https://doi.org/10.1007/s41095-021-0249-1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Effective BRDF for Planar Sources
head: Effective Forward Scattering BRDF, Forward Scattering BRDF, Planar Propagator
body: The Effective BRDF is a computationally efficient approximation for rendering optically dense, approximately planar media under low-frequency illumination, derived as a limiting case of the subsurface scattering model. It replaces the expensive integration of the subsurface propagator over a surface area with a single bidirectional reflectance evaluation, enabling its use in level-of-detail hierarchies for participating media. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Surface query point \vec{x}o, outgoing direction \hat{\omega}e^o, incoming direction \hat{\omega}i^i, surface normal \hat{n}, medium scattering parameters (N, p, F, C, D, E, \sigma{a3}), effective boundary distance de and virtual direction \hat{\omega}v (if non-index-matched), Fresnel/reflection coefficient R, and surface BSDF fs (if non-index-matched). Outputs: Effective BRDF value fr(\hat{\omega}i^i \leftrightarrow \hat{\omega}e^o) or a sampled direction for recursive evaluation. Data Structures Standard vector/matrix types for directions and normals are used. The parameters N, p, F, C, D, E, \sigma{a3} are constants derived from the medium's optical properties (absorption \sigmaa, scattering \sigmas, anisotropy g) as defined in the parent BSSRDF Model. Method Steps 1. Compute the Planar Source Propagator Gf^{\text{p}}: Evaluate the Gaussian propagator for a planar tangent source at distance d: Gf^{\text{p}}(s, d, \hat{\omega}, \hat{\omega}') = \frac{\pi N}{p^2 F} \exp \left\{ -C - D \hat{\omega} \cdot \hat{\omega}' - E p d (\omegan + \omega'n) - F (p d)^2 + \frac{E^2}{4F} [2 + 2 \hat{\omega} \cdot \hat{\omega}' - (\omegan + \omega'n)^2] - \sigma{a3} \right\} where \omegan = \hat{\omega} \cdot \hat{n} and \omega'n = \hat{\omega}' \cdot \hat{n}. 2. Compute the Boundary-Aware Planar Propagator Gf^{\text{pb}}: Adjust Gf^{\text{p}} based on the outgoing direction relative to the surface normal: Gf^{\text{pb}}(s, \hat{\omega}0, \hat{\omega}1) = \begin{cases} Gf^{\text{p}}(s, 0, \hat{\omega}1, \hat{\omega}0) & \text{if } \hat{\omega}1 \cdot \hat{n} \geq 0, \\ -Gf^{\text{p}}(s, de, \hat{\omega}1, \hat{\omega}v) & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases} where de and \hat{\omega}v are the effective boundary distance and virtual direction from the parent BSSRDF model. 3. Evaluate the Effective BRDF (fr): Index-Matched Medium: The effective BRDF is the integral of the planar propagator over the scattering length s: fr(\hat{\omega}i^i \leftrightarrow \hat{\omega}e^o) = R \int Gf^{\text{pb}}(s, \hat{\omega}e^o, -\hat{\omega}i^i) \, ds The integral over s is handled analytically as per the source. Non-Index-Matched Medium: The effective BRDF is evaluated through recursive sampling. The integral of the subsurface propagator Gf^b over \vec{x}i is replaced with fr(-\hat{\omega}e^i \leftrightarrow -\hat{\omega}i^o) and \vec{x}i is set to \vec{x}o. The algorithm repeatedly samples fr and fs until fs generates a query direction pointing out of the medium. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def dot(v1, v2): return sum(a b for a, b in zip(v1, v2)) def effectivebrdfplanarsource(xo, omegaeo, omegaii, n, params, fs): """ Computes the effective BRDF contribution for optically dense planar media. """ N, p, F, C, D, E, sigmaa3, de, omegav, R = ( params['N'], params['p'], params['F'], params['C'], params['D'], params['E'], params['sigmaa3'], params['de'], params['omegav'], params['R']) def computegfp(s, d, omega, omegaprime): omegan = dot(omega, n) omegaprimen = dot(omegaprime, n) dotw = dot(omega, omegaprime) exponent = ( -C - D dotw E p d (omegan + omegaprimen) F (p d) 2 + (E 2 / (4 F)) (2 + 2 dotw - (omegan + omegaprimen) 2) sigmaa3) return (math.pi N) / (p 2 F) math.exp(exponent) def computegfpb(s, omega0, omega1): omega1n = dot(omega1, n) if omega1n >= 0: return computegfp(s, 0.0, omega1, omega0) else: return -computegfp(s, de, omega1, omegav) # The integral over s is handled analytically as per the source. # The sources do not provide the closed-form expression for the integral. def integrategfpb(omegaeo, omegaii): # Closed-form evaluation of integral(Gpb(s, omegaeo, -omegaii) ds) return 0.0 # Stub for analytical result if params['isindexmatched']: integralval = integrategfpb(omegaeo, omegaii) return R integralval # Non-index-matched: recursive sampling loop currentomegain = omegaii currentomegaout = omegaeo maxbounces = 10 # Guard against infinite recursion for in range(maxbounces): # Sample direction from index-matched BRDF fr(-omegae^i <-> -omegai^o) # Standard importance sampling for the computed BRDF value # Cosine-weighted hemisphere sample as a standard step phi = 2.0 math.pi random.random() costheta = math.sqrt(random.random()) sintheta = math.sqrt(1.0 - costheta2) sampledir = [sintheta math.cos(phi), sintheta math.sin(phi), costheta] # Intersect ray from xo in sampledir with scene geometry # Standard ray-scene intersection routine xhit = [xo[i] + sampledir[i] 1.0 for i in range(3)] t = 1.0 # Evaluate surface BSDF at intersection point fsresult = fs(xhit, sampledir) if fsresult.directionoutofmedium: return fsresult.radiance # Update incoming direction for next subsurface query currentomegain = fsresult.direction # currentomegaout remains fixed as the original viewing direction return 0.0 # Fallback if max bounces reached Edge Cases and Pitfalls Planarity Assumption: The method assumes the object is approximately planar on the scale of the reduced scattering length 1/\sigmas'. Low-Frequency Illumination: The method assumes low-frequency illumination, where incoming radiance is approximately constant. Optically Dense Media: The approximation is valid for optically dense media. Boundary Handling: The use of de and \hat{\omega}v requires correct implementation of the effective boundary conditions from the parent BSSRDF model. Recursion Depth: The recursive evaluation for non-index-matched media may require a maximum depth limit to prevent infinite loops in pathological cases. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Computationally efficient approximation for optically dense media; enables level-of-detail rendering; avoids expensive volumetric integration. Limitations: Only valid for approximately planar surfaces and low-frequency illumination. When to Use: Rendering optically dense, planar translucent materials where performance is critical and lighting is smooth. When Not to Use: Transparent materials, high-frequency lighting, highly curved surfaces, or when accurate multiple scattering is required. The Effective BRDF was introduced by Roald Frederickx and Philip Dutré in 2017 as part of their "Forward Scattering Dipole Model from a Functional Integral Approximation". It is derived as a limiting case of their subsurface scattering model, which itself is based on a dipole approximation for forward scattering media. The method addresses the computational expense of Monte Carlo rendering of strongly forward scattering materials by providing an analytical approximation for optically dense media.
