name: SubsurfaceMaterial
body: SubsurfaceMaterial is a material model that combines a BSDF for surface reflection/transmission with a BSSRDF for subsurface scattering. It targets objects with a defined surface geometry, such as those exhibiting perfect or glossy specular transmission. It differs from KdSubsurfaceMaterial by requiring explicit absorption and scattering coefficients rather than deriving them from diffuse reflectance and mean free path. Inputs: Surface interaction si, memory arena arena, transport mode mode, and boolean allowMultipleLobes. Outputs: Populated si->bsdf (handled by parent logic) and si->bssrdf pointing to a TabulatedBSSRDF instance. Data Structures: The class inherits from Material and stores the following private members: scale (const Float), Kr and Kt (std::sharedptr<Texture<Spectrum>>), sigmaa and sigmas (std::sharedptr<Texture<Spectrum>>), uRoughness and vRoughness (std::sharedptr<Texture<Float>>), bumpMap (std::sharedptr<Texture<Float>>), eta (const Float), remapRoughness (const bool), and table (BSSRDFTable). Parameters: scale is a scalar multiplier for the absorption cross-section and scattering coefficient, requiring units of m^{-1}. Algorithm: The initialization occurs in ComputeScatteringFunctions: 1. If bumpMap is present, perturb the surface geometry using Bump(bumpMap, si). 2. Initialize the BSDF components using Kr, Kt, uRoughness, vRoughness, and eta. 3. Evaluate the absorption and scattering textures at si, multiply by scale, and clamp the results: \sigmaa = \text{clamp}(scale \times \sigmaa(\text{si})) and \sigmas = \text{clamp}(scale \times \sigmas(\text{si})). 4. Allocate a TabulatedBSSRDF object in arena and assign it to si->bssrdf. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ComputeScatteringFunctions(si, arena, mode, allowMultipleLobes): # 1. Bump mapping if bumpMap is not None: Bump(bumpMap, si) # 2. BSDF initialization (standard logic using Kr, Kt, eta, roughness) #... (BSDF initialization details are standard and omitted)... # 3. Evaluate and scale optical coefficients sigmaaval = sigmaa.Evaluate(si) sigmasval = sigmas.Evaluate(si) siga = Clamp(scale sigmaaval) sigs = Clamp(scale sigmasval) # 4. Allocate BSSRDF si.bssrdf = ArenaAlloc(arena, TabulatedBSSRDF, si, self, mode, eta, siga, sigs, table) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The scale parameter must strictly use m^{-1} units to yield physically correct scattering depths. Optical coefficients are clamped after scaling to prevent invalid values from propagating into the BSSRDF table. The BSSRDF table is precomputed, so online evaluation is O(1), but table generation is expensive and performed offline or at material creation. The table assumes a homogeneous half-space geometry for precomputation. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory: The BSSRDFTable stores precomputed scattering profiles, with size depending on radius and albedo bin resolutions. The material instance stores textures for sigmaa, sigmas, Kr, Kt, and roughness. Strengths: Supports complex surface effects (specular/glossy transmission) combined with subsurface scattering, and allows spatially varying optical properties via textures. Limitations: Requires explicit definition of \sigmaa and \sigmas, which is less intuitive than using diffuse reflectance. When to use: For materials like wax, skin, marble, or plastic where surface reflection/transmission and subsurface scattering are both significant and the surface has a defined geometry. When not to use: For purely diffuse subsurface scattering where surface reflection is negligible (use KdSubsurfaceMaterial instead) or for non-homogeneous media requiring full volume rendering. SubsurfaceMaterial is implemented in the pbrt rendering system. It belongs to the BSSRDF approximation framework, specifically using a dipole model precomputed into a table. It was designed to provide a material model that supports both surface and subsurface effects for objects with defined surfaces, such as those with specular or glossy transmission. name: Tabulated BSSRDF
body: The Tabulated BSSRDF method approximates the single-scattering profile Sr for subsurface scattering by precomputing a lookup table parameterized by albedo \rho and optical radius r{optical}. It reduces the full five-dimensional BSSRDF Sr(\eta, g, \rho, \sigmat, r) by fixing the refractive index \eta and asymmetry coefficient g, and merging the extinction coefficient \sigmat and distance r into the dimensionless optical radius r{optical} = \sigmat r. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Distance r = ||po - pi||, spectral albedo \rho, and spectral extinction coefficient \sigmat. Output: Spectrum Sr(r) representing the single-scattering contribution. Data Structures: The core data structure is BSSRDFTable: nRhoSamples (int): Number of albedo samples. nRadiusSamples (int): Number of optical radius samples. rhoSamples (uniqueptr<Float[]>): Array of albedo values. radiusSamples (uniqueptr<Float[]>): Array of optical radius values. profile (uniqueptr<Float[]>): 2D grid of size nRhoSamples nRadiusSamples storing precomputed profile values. rhoEff (uniqueptr<Float[]>): Effective albedo values. profileCDF (uniqueptr<Float[]>): Cumulative distribution function. Method Steps: 1. Precomputation: The sources do not specify how the table is populated. 2. Evaluation: For each spectrum channel ch: Compute optical radius: r{optical} = r \cdot \sigmat[ch]. Compute interpolation weights for \rho and r{optical} using CatmullRomWeights. If weights cannot be computed (out of bounds), skip the channel. Perform 2D interpolation over the profile table using the 4 nearest neighbors in each dimension. If r{optical} \neq 0, divide the interpolated sum by 2 \pi r{optical}. Multiply the result by \sigmat[ch]^2 to compensate for the parameter transformation from r to r{optical}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def CatmullRomWeights(nsamples, samples, value): """ Compute Catmull-Rom spline weights for a 1D lookup. Returns (offset, weights) or None if value is out of bounds. """ if value < samples[0] or value >= samples[-1]: return None i = 0 while i < nsamples - 1 and samples[i+1] <= value: i += 1 offset = max(0, i - 1) t = (value - samples[i]) / (samples[i+1] - samples[i]) t2 = t t t3 = t2 t weights = [ -0.5 t3 + t2 - 0.5 t, 1.5 t3 - 2.5 t2 + 1.0, -1.5 t3 + 2.0 t2 + 0.5 t, 0.5 t3 - 0.5 t2 ] return offset, weights def EvalProfile(table, rhoindex, radiusindex): """Access the precomputed profile value.""" return table.profile[rhoindex table.nRadiusSamples + radiusindex] def TabulatedBSSRDFSr(table, sigmat, rho, r): """ Evaluate the tabulated BSSRDF for a given distance r. Args: table: BSSRDFTable object sigmat: Array of extinction coefficients per spectrum channel rho: Array of albedo values per spectrum channel r: Distance ||po - pi|| Returns: list: The BSSRDF spectrum values """ nchannels = len(sigmat) Sr = [0.0] nchannels for ch in range(nchannels): roptical = r sigmat[ch] rhoresult = CatmullRomWeights(table.nRhoSamples, table.rhoSamples, rho[ch]) radiusresult = CatmullRomWeights(table.nRadiusSamples, table.radiusSamples, roptical) if rhoresult is None or radiusresult is None: continue rhooffset, rhoweights = rhoresult radiusoffset, radiusweights = radiusresult sr = 0.0 for i in range(4): for j in range(4): weight = rhoweights[i] radiusweights[j] if weight != 0: sr += weight EvalProfile(table, rhooffset + i, radiusoffset + j) if roptical != 0: sr /= (2.0 math.pi roptical) Sr[ch] = sr # Apply sigmat^2 scaling to the whole spectrum for ch in range(nchannels): Sr[ch] = sigmat[ch] sigmat[ch] # Clamp values to avoid negative or NaN results Sr = [max(0.0, min(1.0, val)) for val in Sr] return Sr Parameters: nRhoSamples, nRadiusSamples: Resolution of the table. Fixed \eta and g: Must match the material being simulated. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Out of Bounds: If \rho or r{optical} falls outside the table's range, CatmullRomWeights returns None and the channel is skipped. Zero Optical Radius: Division by r{optical} is guarded by an explicit != 0 check. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The method is described in the context of physically based rendering for volume scattering. It addresses the five-dimensional BSSRDF Sr(\eta, g, \rho, \sigmat, r) by fixing \eta and g, and combining \sigmat and r into the dimensionless optical radius r{optical} = \sigmat r. name: Physical Atmosphere Color Calculation
head: Physical Atmosphere Color, getAtmosphereColorPhysical
body: Calculates the physical color of the sky and sun disk for a given view direction, accounting for Rayleigh and Mie scattering, optical depth, and phase functions. It differs from sibling methods by providing a closed-form analytical approximation of the atmospheric radiance rather than using Monte Carlo integration or precomputed lookup tables. Inputs: dir: View direction vector (normalized). sunDir: Sun direction vector (normalized). sunIntensity: Scalar intensity of the sun. turbidity: Atmospheric turbidity parameter. Outputs: localcolor: The final tone-mapped atmospheric color (RGB). Data Structures: Constants are hardcoded vectors/scalars as defined below. Parameters: rayleightotal: vec3(5.804542996261093e-6, 1.3562911419845635e-5, 3.0265902468824876e-5). mieconst: vec3(1.839991851443397, 2.779802391966052, 4.079047954386109). mie: 0.005. miedirectional: 0.8. sunangularcos: 0.999956676946448. Steps: 1. Calculate Scattering Coefficients: Compute the turbidity factor c: c = (0.2 \times \text{turbidity}) \times 10^{-17} Calculate Mie scattering coefficient \betaM: \betaM = \text{vec3}(0.434 \times c \times \text{mie\const} \times \text{mie}) Calculate sun fade factor: \text{sunFade} = 1.0 - \text{clamp}\left(1.0 - \exp\left(\frac{\text{SunLocation.y}}{450000.0}\right), 0.0, 1.0\right) Calculate Rayleigh scattering coefficient \betaR: \betaR = \text{vec3}(\text{rayleigh\total} \times (\text{rayleigh} - 1.0 + \text{sunFade})) where \text{rayleigh} = 2.0. 2. Calculate Optical Path Lengths: Calculate zenith angle \thetaz: \thetaz = \arccos(\max(0.0, \text{dir}.y)) Calculate inverse air mass m^{-1}: \text{inverse} = \frac{1.0}{\cos(\thetaz) + 0.15 \times \left(93.885 - \frac{\thetaz \times 180.0}{\pi}\right)^{-1.253}} Calculate Rayleigh optical path length sR: sR = 8.4 \times 10^3 \times \text{inverse} Calculate Mie optical path length sM: sM = 1.25 \times 10^3 \times \text{inverse} 3. Calculate Extinction Factor: f{ex} = \exp\left(-\betaR \times sR + \betaM \times sM\right) 4. Calculate Phase Functions: Calculate cosine of scattering angle: \cos\Theta = \text{dot}(\text{sunDir}, \text{dir}) Calculate Rayleigh phase term PR: PR = \frac{3 \times (1.0 + \cos\Theta^2)}{16.0 \times \pi} Calculate Mie phase term PM using Henyey-Greenstein: PM = \text{HenyeyGreenstein}(\text{dir}, \text{sunDir}, \text{mie\directional}) 5. Calculate In-Scattered Light: Calculate intermediate scattering terms: \betaR\Theta = \betaR \times PR \betaM\Theta = \betaM \times PM Calculate combined scattering ratio: \beta{sum} = \betaR + \betaM \beta{mix} = \frac{\betaR\Theta + \betaM\Theta}{\beta{sum}} Calculate sun intensity factor: \text{sunE} = \text{sunIntensity} \times \text{calcSunIntensity}() Calculate primary in-scattered radiance L{in}: L{in} = \text{pow}\left(\text{sunE} \times \beta{mix} \times (1.0 - f{ex}), \text{vec3}(1.5)\right) Calculate horizon fade factor yDot: yDot = 1.0 - \text{sunDir}.y yDot = yDot^5 Apply horizon blending: L{in} = L{in} \times \text{mix}\left(\text{vec3}(1), \text{pow}\left(\text{sunE} \times \beta{mix} \times f{ex}, \text{vec3}(0.5)\right), \text{clamp}(yDot, 0.0, 1.0)\right) 6. Calculate Direct Sun Disk: Initialize direct light L0: L0 = \text{vec3}(0.1 \times f{ex}) Calculate sun disk visibility: \text{sunDisk} = \text{smoothstep}(\text{sun\angular\cos}, \text{sun\angular\cos} + 0.00002, \cos\Theta) Add sun disk radiance: L0 = L0 + (\text{sunE} \times 15000.0 \times f{ex}) \times \text{sunDisk} 7. Combine and Tone-Map: \text{localcolor} = (L{in} + L0) \times 0.04 + \text{vec3}(0.0, 0.0003, 0.00075) Return localcolor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z def mul(self, s): return Vec3(self.x s, self.y s, self.z s) def rmul(self, s): return self.mul(s) def add(self, other): return Vec3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def sub(self, other): return Vec3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def truediv(self, other): return Vec3(self.x / other.x, self.y / other.y, self.z / other.z) def pow(self, p): return Vec3(self.x p, self.y p, self.z p) def dot(self, other): return self.x other.x + self.y other.y + self.z other.z def clamp(val, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(maxval, val)) def mix(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) def smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x): t = clamp((x - edge0) / (edge1 - edge0), 0.0, 1.0) return t t (3.0 - 2.0 t) def rayleighphase(costheta): return 3.0 (1.0 + costheta costheta) / (16.0 math.pi) def henyeygreenstein(dirvec, sundir, g): costheta = dirvec.dot(sundir) numerator = 1.0 - g g denominator = 1.0 + g g - 2.0 g costheta if denominator < 1e-8: denominator = 1e-8 return numerator / (4.0 math.pi (denominator 1.5)) def getatmospherecolorphysical(dir, sundir, sunintensity, turbidity): # Constants rayleightotal = Vec3(5.804542996261093e-6, 1.3562911419845635e-5, 3.0265902468824876e-5) mieconst = Vec3(1.839991851443397, 2.779802391966052, 4.079047954386109) mie = 0.005 miedirectional = 0.8 rayleigh = 2.0 sunangularcos = 0.999956676946448 # 1. Scattering Coefficients c = (0.2 turbidity) 10e-18 betam = Vec3(0.434 c mieconst.x mie, 0.434 c mieconst.y mie, 0.434 c mieconst.z mie) # SunLocation.y is not defined in the notes; assumed to be sundir.y sunlocationy = sundir.y sunfade = 1.0 - clamp(1.0 - math.exp(sunlocationy / 450000.0), 0.0, 1.0) betar = rayleightotal (rayleigh - 1.0 + sunfade) # 2. Optical Path Lengths zenith = math.acos(max(0.0, dir.y)) inverse = 1.0 / (math.cos(zenith) + 0.15 (93.885 - zenith 180.0 / math.pi) -1.253) sr = 8400.0 inverse sm = 1250.0 inverse # 3. Extinction Factor fex = Vec3(math.exp(-betar.x sr + betam.x sm), math.exp(-betar.y sr + betam.y sm), math.exp(-betar.z sr + betam.z sm)) # 4. Phase Functions costheta = sundir.dot(dir) rphase = rayleighphase(costheta) mphase = henyeygreenstein(dir, sundir, miedirectional) betartheta = betar rphase betamtheta = betam mphase betasum = betar + betam betamix = betartheta / betasum + betamtheta / betasum # calcSunIntensity() is not defined; assumed to return 1.0 sune = sunintensity 1.0 # 5. In-Scattered Light lin = Vec3((sune betamix.x (1.0 - fex.x)) 1.5, (sune betamix.y (1.0 - fex.y)) 1.5, (sune betamix.z (1.0 - fex.z)) 1.5) ydot = 1.0 - sundir.y ydot = ydot 5 blendt = clamp(ydot, 0.0, 1.0) lin = Vec3(lin.x mix(1.0, (sune betamix.x fex.x) 0.5, blendt), lin.y mix(1.0, (sune betamix.y fex.y) 0.5, blendt), lin.z mix(1.0, (sune betamix.z fex.z) 0.5, blendt)) # 6. Direct Sun Disk l0 = Vec3(0.1 fex.x, 0.1 fex.y, 0.1 fex.z) sundisk = smoothstep(sunangularcos, sunangularcos + 0.00002, costheta) l0 = Vec3(l0.x + (sune 15000.0 fex.x) sundisk, l0.y + (sune 15000.0 fex.y) sundisk, l0.z + (sune 15000.0 fex.z) sundisk) # 7. Combine and Tone-Map localcolor = Vec3((lin.x + l0.x) 0.04 + 0.0, (lin.y + l0.y) 0.04 + 0.0003, (lin.z + l0.z) 0.04 + 0.00075) return localcolor [2318-ray-marching-with-in-out-scattering-and-density-scaling.md] [4188-single-scattering-approximation-with-precomputed-terms.md] [4244-analytical-approximation-of-single-scattering-radiance.md] [4549-volume-single-scattering-monte-carlo-with-sphere-light.md] [4550-volume-single-scattering-uniform-ray-marching-with-point-lig.md] [4750-bssrdf-approximation-with-dipole-and-single-scattering.md] Not given in the sources. name: Single-Scattering Atmosphere Rendering
head: Nishita Physical Sky Model, Nishita Sky Rendering, Single Scattering Atmospheric Model, Single-Scattering Sky Rendering, Single-Scattering Sky-Rendering Approximation, Volumetric Atmospheric Scattering
body: Single-Scattering Atmosphere Rendering computes the color of the sky and atmospheric haze by numerically integrating the in-scattered light from a single distant light source (the sun) along a view ray passing through a spherical atmosphere shell. It solves the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) under the assumption that light scatters only once before reaching the observer, accounting for Rayleigh (gas) and Mie (aerosol) scattering, as well as ozone absorption. It sets itself apart from Multiple Scattering Models by ignoring indirect light bounces, making it computationally efficient but inaccurate for deep atmospheres or high optical depths. It differs from Single Scattering Approximation by specifically modeling the spherical geometry of a planetary atmosphere with exponential density profiles. Inputs: Observer position PO (typically inside the atmosphere). View direction \omega (normalized vector from camera to fragment). Sun direction \omega{sun} (normalized vector from observer to sun). Planet radius Rp and Atmosphere outer radius Ra. Scattering coefficients for Rayleigh (\sigmas^R), Mie (\sigmas^M), and Ozone (\sigmaa^O) at sea level. Scale heights for Rayleigh (HR), Mie (HM), and Ozone (HO). Outer space luminance L{outerspace} or ground illuminance to derive it. Integration step count N (e.g., 8–64). Transmittance T{view} (RGB, optional, for ground visibility). Outputs: Scattered radiance L{sky} (RGB). Transmittance T{view} (RGB, optional, for ground visibility). Data Structures: AtmosphereParams: Struct containing Rp, Ra, HR, HM, HO, \sigma{s,0}^R, \sigma{s,0}^M, \sigma{a,0}^O, L{outerspace}, \Omega{sun}, N. Ray: Origin O, Direction D, Length L. Formulas: 1. Density Profile: The density of species i \in \{R, M, O\} at height h above the planet surface is exponential: \rhoi(h) = \exp\left(-\frac{\max(0, h)}{Hi}\right). where h = \|P\| - Rp. 2. Extinction Coefficient: The total extinction coefficient at height h is: \sigmat(h) = \sigmas^R(h) + 1.11 \cdot \sigmas^M(h) + \sigmaa^O(h). The factor 1.11 scales Mie scattering to account for extinction differences. \sigmas^R(h) = \sigma{s,0}^R e^{-h/HR}, \quad \sigmas^M(h) = \sigma{s,0}^M e^{-h/HM}, \quad \sigmaa^O(h) = \sigma{a,0}^O e^{-h/HO}. Typical sea-level values: \sigma{s,0}^R = (5.8, 13.5, 33.1) \times 10^{-6} \, m^{-1}, \sigma{s,0}^M = 21 \times 10^{-6} \, m^{-1}, \sigma{a,0}^O = (3.426, 8.298, 0.356) \times 0.06 \times 10^{-5} \, m^{-1}. Scale heights: HR=8000m, HM=1200m, HO=8000m. 3. Phase Functions: Rayleigh: PR(\cos\theta) = \frac{3}{16\pi}(1 + \cos^2\theta). Mie (Henyey-Greenstein): PM(\cos\theta) = \frac{1-g^2}{4\pi(1+g^2-2g\cos\theta)^{1.5}} with asymmetry factor g=0.76. \cos\theta = \omega \cdot \omega{sun}. 4. Transmittance: The transmittance from point A to B is: Tr(A \rightarrow B) = \exp\left(-\intA^B \sigmat(s) ds\right). This is computed numerically by summing \sigmat at sample midpoints. 5. Source Term: The in-scattered source term j(x) at position x is: j(x) = L{outerspace} \cdot Tr(outerspace \rightarrow x) \cdot \Omega{sun} \cdot (\sigmas^R(x)PR + \sigmas^M(x)PM). where \Omega{sun} \approx 0.0000664 \, sr. L{outerspace} is derived from ground illuminance E{ground} \approx 120,000 lux and zenith transmittance Tr{Zenith}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray-Atmosphere Intersection: Compute the entry (t{in}) and exit (t{out}) distances of the view ray from the atmosphere sphere. If the ray originates inside the planet, advance the start point to the planet exit. 2. Sample Distribution: Generate sample positions ti along the ray. Uniform spacing is common, but power-law distribution ti = (\frac{i}{N})^E \cdot L with exponent E improves convergence near the camera. 3. Loop Integration: For each sample i from 0 to N-1: a. Calculate position Pi = O + D \cdot ti. b. Calculate height hi = \|Pi\| - Rp. c. Compute local extinction \sigmat(hi) and scattering coefficients \sigmas^R(hi), \sigmas^M(hi). d. Compute optical depth from Pi to the sun's outer boundary (\tau{sun}) and from Pi to the observer (\tau{view}). e. Compute transmittances Tr{sun} = \exp(-\tau{sun}) and Tr{view} = \exp(-\tau{view}). f. Compute source term contribution: Ci = Tr{view} \cdot Tr{sun} \cdot (\sigmas^R(hi)PR + \sigmas^M(hi)PM) \cdot \Delta t. g. Accumulate scattered light: L{sky} += Ci \cdot L{outerspace} \cdot \Omega{sun}. 4. Direct Sun: Add direct sun disk luminance if visible: L{sun} = disk(\theta) \cdot L{outerspace} \cdot Tr(O \rightarrow outerspace). 5. Composite: Final color C = L{sky} + L{sun}. Apply tone mapping (e.g., ACES Filmic). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def length(v): return math.sqrt(dot(v, v)) def raysphereintersection(rayorigin, raydir, radius): """Returns (tin, tout) or None if no intersection.""" b = dot(rayorigin, raydir) c = dot(rayorigin, rayorigin) - radius radius discriminant = b b - c if discriminant < 0: return None sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(discriminant) tin = -b - sqrtdisc tout = -b + sqrtdisc return (tin, tout) def computesinglescatteringatmosphere(observerpos, viewdir, sundir, params): Rp = params['Rp'] Ra = params['Ra'] HR = params['HR'] HM = params['HM'] HO = params['HO'] sigmasR0 = params['sigmasR0'] sigmasM0 = params['sigmasM0'] sigmaaO0 = params['sigmaaO0'] Louterspace = params['Louterspace'] Omegasun = params['Omegasun'] N = params['N'] # 1. Ray-Atmosphere Intersection hit = raysphereintersection(observerpos, viewdir, Ra) if hit is None: return (vec3(0.0), vec3(1.0)) tin, tout = hit if tin < 0: tin = 0.0 if tout < 0: return (vec3(0.0), vec3(1.0)) raylength = tout - tin if raylength <= 0: return (vec3(0.0), vec3(1.0)) # 2. Phase Functions costheta = dot(viewdir, sundir) PR = (3.0 / (16.0 math.pi)) (1.0 + costheta costheta) g = 0.76 denom = 1.0 + g g - 2.0 g costheta PM = (1.0 - g g) / (4.0 math.pi math.pow(denom, 1.5)) # 3. Integration Loop scatteredlight = vec3(0.0) totalopticaldepth = vec3(0.0) ds = raylength / N for i in range(N): t = tin + (i + 0.5) ds pos = (observerpos[0] + viewdir[0]t, observerpos[1] + viewdir[1]t, observerpos[2] + viewdir[2]t) height = length(pos) - Rp # Density and Coefficients rhoR = math.exp(-max(0.0, height) / HR) rhoM = math.exp(-max(0.0, height) / HM) rhoO = math.exp(-max(0.0, height) / HO) sigmasR = sigmasR0 rhoR sigmasM = sigmasM0 rhoM sigmaaO = sigmaaO0 rhoO sigmat = sigmasR + 1.11 sigmasM + sigmaaO totalopticaldepth += sigmat ds # Optical Depth to Sun sunhit = raysphereintersection(pos, sundir, Ra) disttosun = sunhit[0] if sunhit and sunhit[0] > 0 else 0.0 # Integrate sigmat along sun path (midpoint approximation) sunexitpos = (pos[0] + sundir[0]disttosun, pos[1] + sundir[1]disttosun, pos[2] + sundir[2]disttosun) midsun = ((pos[0]+sunexitpos[0])/2, (pos[1]+sunexitpos[1])/2, (pos[2]+sunexitpos[2])/2) hmidsun = length(midsun) - Rp rhoRmid = math.exp(-max(0.0, hmidsun) / HR) rhoMmid = math.exp(-max(0.0, hmidsun) / HM) rhoOmid = math.exp(-max(0.0, hmidsun) / HO) sigmatmid = sigmasR0 rhoRmid + 1.11 sigmasM0 rhoMmid + sigmaaO0 rhoOmid tausun = sigmatmid disttosun Trsun = math.exp(-tausun) # Optical Depth to Observer (from pos to observer) tauview = sigmat t Trview = math.exp(-tauview) # Source Term Contribution scatteringcoeff = sigmasR PR + sigmasM PM source = Louterspace Trsun Omegasun scatteringcoeff contribution = source Trview ds scatteredlight += contribution # 4. Direct Sun angle = math.acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, costheta))) sunradius = math.radians(0.53 / 2.0) disk = 1.0 - max(0.0, min(1.0, (angle - sunradius 0.95) / (sunradius 1.05 - sunradius 0.95))) # Transmittance from observer to outer space in sun direction sunhitobs = raysphereintersection(observerpos, sundir, Ra) distobssun = sunhitobs[0] if sunhitobs and sunhitobs[0] > 0 else 0.0 sunexitobs = (observerpos[0] + sundir[0]distobssun, observerpos[1] + sundir[1]distobssun, observerpos[2] + sundir[2]distobssun) midobs = ((observerpos[0]+sunexitobs[0])/2, (observerpos[1]+sunexitobs[1])/2, (observerpos[2]+sunexitobs[2])/2) hmidobs = length(midobs) - Rp rhoRmidobs = math.exp(-max(0.0, hmidobs) / HR) rhoMmidobs = math.exp(-max(0.0, hmidobs) / HM) rhoOmidobs = math.exp(-max(0.0, hmidobs) / HO) sigmatmidobs = sigmasR0 rhoRmidobs + 1.11 sigmasM0 rhoMmidobs + sigmaaO0 rhoOmidobs tauobs = sigmatmidobs distobssun Trobs = math.exp(-tauobs) directsun = disk Louterspace Trobs # 5. Composite finalcolor = scatteredlight + directsun return (finalcolor, vec3(1.0) - totalopticaldepth / 1000000.0) # Simplified transmittance output A technique for rendering sky and atmosphere using a precomputed Look-Up Table (LUT) with angular compression, ported from a reference implementation. It builds on Single-Scattering Atmosphere Rendering by storing precomputed radiance values in a compressed texture space for efficient runtime lookup. This method visualizes the Earth from outer space by simulating light transport through a planetary atmosphere and large water bodies, accounting for Rayleigh and Mie scattering, direct illumination, indirect scattered light, interreflections between surface and volume, and seabed reflections. It sets itself apart from its siblings by employing fully spectral computations (precomputed into lookup tables) to achieve high realism in color reproduction, supporting arbitrarily dense atmospheres and water surfaces within a single precomputation framework for real-time GPU rendering. Unlike Single-Scattering Atmosphere Rendering, which focuses on single scattering approximations, this method computes multiple scattering orders (typically up to 6) and integrates water body optics. Uses different physical constants and parameterization for the water texture compared to atmospheric scattering. Incident light for water is attenuated through the atmosphere: I0^I(\lambda) = I^I(\lambda)e^{-t(Pg P, \lambda)}. The 4D water scattering texture is reduced to a 3D texture for rendering by using only the subset corresponding to observer depth d=0m. If observers below the water surface are needed, the full 4D texture can be used, fetching based on observer depth d. For low accuracy requirements, only the first scattering order is needed for water because it is a weakly scattering medium. Water scattering model is similar to atmospheric but volume is between water level and seabed. Water has significant absorption (mainly red) and constant density. Terms for water are indicated with superscript 'water'. Density scale function \rho is removed from equations. Water attenuation coefficient: t^{\text{water}}(S, \lambda) = \|S\| (\zeta^a + \zeta^b)(\lambda). Absorption and scattering coefficients for clear water (\zetaa, \zetas) from [Buiteveld et al. 1994], sampled at 2nm. Mie scattering is not explicitly modeled in water because data for seawater is unavailable and it is strongly anisotropic (forward lobe), only noticeable looking towards light source. Since observers are above water level, it is neglected. Highly realistic atmospheric rendering, allowing modeling of real world atmospheres (composed by ozone, haze, dust, soot, sulphur acid, etc.). Combine four sub-models, consisting of a number of concentric shells, to determine atmospheric model: clear air, aerosol, ozone and rain layer. Account for both Rayleigh and Mie scattering. Approximate second order scattering to obtain more accurate results. Authors do not explain how the second order scattering approximation is performed. Considered the rendering of outdoor scenes including sunlight and skylight, and the effects of aerial perspective (de-saturation and color shift of distant objects). Two inexpensive analytic models are developed. Compute the sky spectral radiance function for a set of sun positions and turbidities (using the method of Nishita et al. [59]), then fit a parametric function. Wilkie et al. propose a simple analytical model for skylight polarisation to be added to Preetham’s skylight model. Rendering of nighttime sky including illumination from the Moon, stars, zodiacal light, and atmosphere. Use the atmospheric model and scattering phase functions of Nishita [59]. Simulate transport with multiple scattering combining distribution ray-tracing and ray-marching. As the ray traverses the atmosphere, use ray-marching to integrate optical-depth sampling the in-scattered indirect radiance and the direct illumination in random positions. Time Complexity: O(STEPS) per pixel for the luminance integral and O(STEPS) for transmittance calculations, where STEPS is the number of integration segments. Memory Complexity: O(1) if computed per-pixel; O(1) for LUT variants if texture size is fixed. Performance: Real-time on modern GPUs for N \le 64. Strengths: Physically plausible colors, efficient, handles sun position and atmospheric depth correctly. Limitations: Ignores multiple scattering, leading to dark skies in deep atmospheres or near the horizon in high optical depth scenarios. When to Use: Real-time sky rendering, games, VR. When Not to Use: Cinematic rendering requiring high dynamic range and deep atmosphere realism, underwater scenes (use Water Scattering Model). Originated from Nishita et al. (1993) "Display of the Earth from Space". It is a foundational method for realistic sky rendering in computer graphics. Used in real-time sky rendering, specifically referenced in Sébastien Hillaire's 2016 course and 2020 paper, and Scratch a Pixel tutorial. name: Sky View LUT with Angular Compression
head: Seb Hillaire’s Sky and Atmosphere Rendering Technique
body: A technique for rendering sky and atmosphere using a precomputed Look-Up Table (LUT) with angular compression, ported from a reference implementation. It builds on Single-Scattering Atmosphere Rendering by storing precomputed radiance values in a compressed texture space for efficient runtime lookup. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Observer altitude h, view zenith angle \vartheta, view azimuth, sun zenith angle \varthetas, sun azimuth \phis. Outputs: Fragment color IF for the atmosphere. Data Structures: Sky View LUT: A 4D texture array storing precomputed radiance values, with an example resolution of 400 \times 400. Extinction Texture: A 2D lookup texture parameterized by observer altitude h and zenith angle \vartheta, containing t(P Pc) where P has altitude h and Pc is the intersection of the ray starting at P under zenith angle \vartheta with the upper atmosphere boundary. Steps: 1. Precompute the extinction coefficient t into the 2D lookup texture parameterized by h and \vartheta. 2. Represent the planet and atmospheric shell as finely tessellated spheres with frontface culling for the atmosphere and backface culling for the planet. 3. For each pixel, fetch values from the scattering texture array and perform manual linear interpolation for the fourth dimension. 4. Set the fragment color IF = IS for the atmosphere. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the observer is outside the atmosphere, compute the intersection point Pa between the view ray and the atmosphere sphere, evaluate the scattering function f for this point, and set scattering/attenuation to zero. Large cell sizes in the LUT can give a blocky look. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendersky(observeraltitude, viewzenith, viewazimuth, sunzenith, sunazimuth, atmosphereradius, scatteringlut): # Step 1: Check if observer is outside the atmosphere if observeraltitude > atmosphereradius: # Compute intersection point Pa between view ray and atmosphere sphere Pa = raysphereintersection(vec3(0.0), viewdirection(viewzenith, viewazimuth), atmosphereradius) if Pa is None: return vec3(0.0) # Evaluate scattering function f for Pa and set scattering/attenuation to zero return evaluatescatteringf(Pa, sunzenith, sunazimuth) # Step 2: Map 4D input space to texture coordinates u, v, w, r = mapcoordinates(observeraltitude, viewzenith, sunzenith, sunazimuth - viewazimuth) # Step 3: Fetch two values from the scattering texture array idx1 = int(floor(r)) idx2 = int(ceil(r)) frac = r - floor(r) val1 = scatteringlut[u, v, w, idx1] val2 = scatteringlut[u, v, w, idx2] # Step 4: Manual linear interpolation for the fourth dimension color = lerp(val1, val2, frac) return color def viewdirection(zenith, azimuth): return vec3(sin(zenith)cos(azimuth), cos(zenith), sin(zenith)sin(azimuth)) def raysphereintersection(origin, direction, radius): # Standard ray-sphere intersection returning closest positive distance t = -dot(origin, direction) + sqrt(dot(origin, direction)2 - dot(origin, origin) + radius2) return origin + direction t if t > 0 else None def evaluatescatteringf(Pa, sunzenith, sunazimuth): # Standard single-scattering evaluation at point Pa return vec3(0.0) def mapcoordinates(h, vz, sz, sazminusvaz): # Standard parameterization mapping to 3D texture coordinates with emulated 4th dimension return h / 1.0, vz / 1.0, sz / 1.0, sazminusvaz / 1.0 A coordinate remapping function that maps the 4D input space to 3D texture coordinates with an emulated fourth dimension via tiling. It uses non-linear mappings for altitude and angles to distribute sampling density according to light scattering behavior [9405-atmospheric-parameterization.md]. Choose it when efficient runtime lookup of single-scattering data is required. This variant represents the planet and atmospheric shell as finely tessellated spheres with frontface culling (atmosphere) and backface culling (planet). It precomputes the extinction coefficient t into a 2D lookup texture parameterized by observer altitude h and zenith angle \vartheta. For rendering, it fetches two values from the scattering texture and performs manual linear interpolation for the fourth dimension. If the observer is outside the atmosphere, it computes the intersection point Pa between the view ray and atmosphere sphere, evaluates f for this point, and sets scattering/attenuation to zero. The fragment color is IF = IS for the atmosphere. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel for LUT lookup, assuming constant texture size. Memory Complexity: O(N^3) for a 3D LUT, where N is the resolution. The example uses a 400 \times 400 LUT. Strengths: Efficient real-time rendering of atmospheric scattering. Limitations: Precomputation cost is high. Blocky artifacts can appear if cell sizes are too large. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The technique is based on Seb Hillaire’s "A Scalable and Production Ready Sky and Atmosphere Rendering Technique". It has been ported to various engines, including vxray. The underlying principles of using lookup textures for atmospheric scattering were explored in earlier works such as [Bruneton and Neyret 2008] and [Schafhitzel et al. 2007]. name: Atmospheric Parameterization
body: Atmospheric Parameterization is the coordinate remapping function used to store precomputed single-scattering data into a 3D texture, enabling efficient runtime lookup for sky and atmosphere rendering. It reduces the four-dimensional input space (altitude, view-zenith angle, sun-zenith angle, sun-view azimuth) into a 3D texture coordinate space (U, V, W) with an emulated fourth dimension (R) via tiling. It sets itself apart from generic linear parameterizations by using non-linear mappings for altitude and angles to better distribute sampling density according to the physical behavior of light scattering in spherical atmospheres, building on Sky View LUT with Angular Compression. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Altitude h \in [0, H{max}], view-zenith angle \vartheta \in [0, \pi], sun-zenith angle \delta \in [0, \pi], sun-view azimuth \phi \in [0, \pi]. Constants: Planet radius rP, atmospheric shell radius rA, maximum altitude H{max}. Outputs: Texture coordinates (U, V, W, R) \in [0, 1]^4. Data Structures: The scattering data is stored in a 3D texture of size NU \times NV \times NW. The fourth dimension R is handled by tiling the texture or manual interpolation during rendering. Formulas: The remapping function f: [0, H{max}] \times [0, \pi]^3 \rightarrow [0, 1]^4 is defined as follows: 1. Intermediate Constants: Z1 = \sqrt{h^2 - rP^2} Z2 = \sqrt{rA^2 - rP^2} Z3 = r^2 \cos^2(\vartheta) - Z1 Note: r in Z3 refers to the observer's distance from the planet center, i.e., r = rP + h. 2. U Coordinate (Altitude): U(h) = \frac{Z1}{Z2} 3. V Coordinate (View-Zenith): V(\vartheta) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} + \frac{h \cos(\vartheta) + \sqrt{Z3}}{2Z1} & \text{if } h \cos(\vartheta) < 0 \text{ and } Z3 > 0 \\ \frac{1}{2} - \frac{h \cos(\vartheta) - \sqrt{Z3 + Z2^2}}{2Z1 + 2Z2} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 4. W Coordinate (Sun-Zenith): W(\delta) = \frac{1 - e^{-2.8 \cos(\delta) - 0.8}}{1 - e^{-3.6}} Note: This is a modified version of the original Bruneton and Neyret function to account for all sun angles with nonzero scattering in denser/higher atmospheres, as the original was designed specifically for Earth's atmosphere. 5. R Coordinate (Sun-View Azimuth): R(\phi) = \frac{1 + \cos(\phi)}{2} Parameters: H{max}: Upper atmosphere boundary altitude. Typically 65 km. For denser atmospheres, 100 km or more may be used. rP: Planet radius. rA: Atmospheric shell radius (rP + H{max}). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The condition h \cos(\vartheta) < 0 and Z3 > 0 must be evaluated carefully to avoid numerical instability near the horizon or zenith. Boundary Conditions: The function maps inputs to [0, 1]. Ensure texture coordinates are clamped or wrapped appropriately during sampling. Assumptions: The method assumes parallel light rays, a spherical planet, altitude-only density variation, and spherical shell symmetry around the plane between the light source and zenith. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def remapatmosphere(h, theta, delta, phi, rp, ra): """ Remaps atmospheric parameters to UVWR texture coordinates. Args: h: Altitude above planet surface [0, Hmax] theta: View-zenith angle [0, pi] delta: Sun-zenith angle [0, pi] phi: Sun-view azimuth [0, pi] rp: Planet radius ra: Atmospheric shell radius Returns: (u, v, w, rcoord): Texture coordinates in [0, 1] """ # Observer distance from planet center r = rp + h # Intermediate constants z1 = sqrt(h2 - rp2) z2 = sqrt(ra2 - rp2) z3 = (r cos(theta))2 - z1 # U coordinate u = z1 / z2 # V coordinate if h cos(theta) < 0 and z3 > 0: v = 0.5 + (h cos(theta) + sqrt(z3)) / (2 z1) else: v = 0.5 - (h cos(theta) - sqrt(z3 + z22)) / (2 z1 + 2 z2) # W coordinate w = (1 - exp(-2.8 cos(delta) - 0.8)) / (1 - exp(-3.6)) # R coordinate rcoord = (1 + cos(phi)) / 2 return u, v, w, rcoord Water Parameterization adapts the LUT approach for underwater scenes. It requires a 5D table (depth D, observer depth d, and 3 angles) but excludes the sun-view azimuth \phi because scattered light intensity varies negligibly with \phi due to the strong locality of light transport in water (light traveling 100m retains only 0.6 \cdot 10^{-20}\% to 1.5\% of intensity). It uses a simpler linear parameterization: U(D) = D/D{max}, V(d) = d/D, W(\vartheta) = (1 + \cos(\vartheta))/2, R(\delta) = (1 + \cos(\delta))/2. D{max} is the peak depth, and should not exceed 100 m due to low transmissivity. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel for texture lookup and interpolation. The remapping function involves several trigonometric and square root operations, which are relatively expensive but constant time. Memory Complexity: O(NU \times NV \times NW) for the 3D texture. The 4th dimension is emulated, so no additional memory is needed for it, but runtime interpolation may be required. Strengths: Efficient real-time rendering of atmospheric scattering. Non-linear parameterization improves visual quality by concentrating samples where scattering changes rapidly. Limitations: Assumes spherical symmetry and parallel light rays. Not suitable for terrain-dependent density variations or local light sources. The emulated 4th dimension may introduce artifacts if not interpolated correctly. When to Use: Real-time sky and atmosphere rendering for games and simulations where performance is critical and the assumptions hold. When Not to Use: When high-fidelity multiple scattering is required without precomputation, or when the atmosphere has significant lateral density variations. The method was introduced in "Real-time spectral scattering in large-scale natural participating media" (2010) by Schafhitzel et al., building on ideas from Schafhitzel et al. (2007) and Bruneton and Neyret (2008). The W function was modified from the original Bruneton and Neyret formulation to better handle denser atmospheres and all sun angles with nonzero scattering.
