name: Spectral Scattering Model for Atmosphere
head: Nishita, Nishita et al. Earth from Outer Space Method, Nishita et al. sky rendering, Physical Model for Atmospheric Light Transport, Spectral Scattering with Water Bodies and Tone Mapping
body: This method visualizes the Earth from outer space by simulating light transport through a planetary atmosphere and large water bodies, accounting for Rayleigh and Mie scattering, direct illumination, indirect scattered light, interreflections between surface and volume, and seabed reflections. It sets itself apart from its siblings by employing fully spectral computations (precomputed into lookup tables) to achieve high realism in color reproduction, supporting arbitrarily dense atmospheres and water surfaces within a single precomputation framework for real-time GPU rendering. Unlike Single-Scattering Atmosphere Rendering, which focuses on single scattering approximations, this method computes multiple scattering orders (typically up to 6) and integrates water body optics. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Viewpoint position PO, view direction V, light source direction L (Sun/stars), atmospheric density profiles, water body geometry (seabed depth), and spectral parameters. Outputs: Final spectral color IF for each pixel. Data Structures: The method relies on precomputed lookup tables (LUTs) generated via CPU-based spectral integration. These tables store spectral data for real-time GPU sampling. Atmospheric Scattering Texture: 4D table packed into a 32 \times 128 \times 256 3D texture with resolution 32 \times 128 \times 32 \times 8. Water Scattering Texture: 3D texture with resolution 32 \times 64 \times 64. Extinction Texture: 2D texture with resolution 256 \times 512. Ambient Texture: 1D texture with size 256. Precision: 16-bit floating-point values per channel, consuming ~10MB total memory. Parameters: Rayleigh Scale Height (HR): \approx 8 km. Mie Scale Height (HM): \approx 1.2 km. Mie Anisotropy (g): Range [-1, 1]. Spectral Sampling: 15 evenly distributed samples across the visible spectrum. Numerical Integration: Regular trapezoidal rule with 30 samples per integral. Scattering Orders: 6 orders for convergence; up to 10 for very dense atmospheres. Formulas: 1. Scattering Coefficients: The scattering coefficients for Rayleigh (\sigmaR) and Mie (\sigmaM) are calculated based on mean particle polarizability \alpha{\{R,M\}}, index of refraction ne, molecular number density N{\{R,M\}}, and wavelength \lambda. \sigmaM is wavelength-independent. 2. Density Scale Function: The density at altitude h is modeled exponentially: p{\{R,M\}}(P) = \exp(-H{\{R,M\}}) where H{\{R,M\}} is the scale height expressing the altitude where density scales down by 1/e. 3. Phase Functions: Rayleigh Phase Function FR(\theta): FR(\theta) = \frac{3}{4}(1 + \cos^2(\theta)) where \theta is the scattering angle. Mie Phase Function FM(\theta, g): Improved Henyey-Greenstein approximation by Cornette and Shanks [1992]: FM(\theta, g) = \frac{3(1-g^2)}{2(2+g^2)} \frac{(1+\cos^2(\theta))}{(1+g^2-2g\cos(\theta))^{3/2}} where g describes anisotropy. 4. Optical Depth: The optical depth t(S, \lambda) along path length S is the sum over scattering types i \in \{R, M\}: t(S, \lambda) = \sum{i \in \{R, M\}} \sigmai(\lambda) \int0^S pi(s') ds' Computed via trapezoidal integration of sampled density. The atmosphere is non-uniformly subdivided into concentric spherical layers where density variation between layers is below a threshold, using linear interpolation for density at sampling points. 5. Single Scattering Intensity: The intensity I{S{\{R,M\}}}^{(1)}(PO, V, L, \lambda) reaching observer PO is: I{S{\{R,M\}}}^{(1)}(PO, V, L, \lambda) = R(PO, V, L, \lambda) + II(\lambda) F{\{R,M\}}(\theta) \cdot \frac{\sigma{\{R,M\}}(\lambda)}{4\pi} \int{Pa}^{Pb} \rho{\{R,M\}}(P) e^{-t(P Pc, \lambda) - t(Pa Pb, \lambda)} ds Where II(\lambda) is incident light intensity, \rho{\{R,M\}}(P) is the density scale function, and t represents optical depths along segments. Note: The source provides conflicting versions of Eq. 8; the integral form above is the detailed version provided. 6. Water Refraction and Scattering: Compute refraction ray V{0R} in the fragment shader using refract(). Determine incident light I0I(Pg, VR, \lambda): if VR hits the star disc, I0I(Pg, VR, \lambda) = I0I(Pg, L, \lambda); otherwise, it is zero. Obtain water scattering IS by fetching the water scattering texture using the depth D of the intersection point with the seabed. Light transmission through water molecules is considered analytically. 7. Final Color and Tone Mapping: The final color IF is the sum of surface color IS and the attenuated participating medium contribution IP: IF = IS + IP \cdot e^{-t(Pa Pg, \lambda)} Due to high dynamic range, tone mapping is applied using exposure constant E: IF = 1 - \exp(-E \cdot IF). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def precomputespectralluts(): wavelengths = [400.0 + i (700.0 - 400.0) / 14.0 for i in range(15)] atmscattertex = [[[[0.0 for in range(8)] for in range(32)] for in range(128)] for in range(32)] waterscattertex = [[[0.0 for in range(64)] for in range(64)] for in range(32)] extinctiontex = [[0.0 for in range(512)] for in range(256)] ambienttex = [0.0 for in range(256)] for order in range(1, 7): for w in wavelengths: sigmaR = computescatteringcoeff(w, type="Rayleigh") sigmaM = computescatteringcoeff(w, type="Mie") for s in range(30): pR = math.exp(-h / 8000.0) pM = math.exp(-h / 1200.0) t = (sigmaR pR + sigmaM pM) (s / 30.0) # Accumulate scattering contributions and store in LUTs pass return atmscattertex, waterscattertex, extinctiontex, ambienttex def computescatteringcoeff(w, type): if type == "Mie": return 0.0001 # Wavelength-independent placeholder for Mie return 5.0e-6 (550.0 / w) 4 # Rayleigh approximation def renderspectralatmosphere(viewpos, viewdir, lightdir, depthbuffer): atmlut = sample3dtexture(atmscattertex, viewpos, viewdir) waterlut = sample3dtexture(waterscattertex, depthbuffer.getwaterdepth()) extlut = sample2dtexture(extinctiontex, viewpos, viewdir) tatm = computeopticaldepth(viewpos, viewdir, extlut) IP = computesinglescattering(viewpos, viewdir, lightdir, atmlut) if depthbuffer.iswater(): V0R = refract(viewdir, depthbuffer.getnormal(), 1.33) Iincident = spectralintensity(lightdir) if hitsstardisc(V0R, lightdir) else 0.0 D = depthbuffer.getwaterdepth() Iwater = sample3dtexture(waterlut, D) IS = computesurfacereflection() + Iwater twater = computewateropticaldepth(D) IF = IS + IP math.exp(-twater) else: IS = computesurfacecolor() IF = IS + IP math.exp(-tatm) E = 1.0 IFfinal = 1.0 - math.exp(-E IF) return IFfinal def sample3dtexture(tex, x, y, z): return tex[int(x) % len(tex)][int(y) % len(tex[0])][int(z) % len(tex[0][0])] def sample2dtexture(tex, x, y): return tex[int(x) % len(tex)][int(y) % len(tex[0])] def refract(ray, normal, eta): return [ray[i] eta for i in range(3)] def hitsstardisc(ray, light): return math.dot(ray, light) > 0.99 def computeopticaldepth(pos, dir, tex): return sample2dtexture(tex, pos[0], pos[1]) def computesinglescattering(pos, dir, light, tex): theta = math.acos(math.dot(dir, light)) FR = 0.75 (1 + math.cos(theta)2) return FR sample3dtexture(tex, pos[0], pos[1], pos[2]) def computesurfacereflection(): return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] def computesurfacecolor(): return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] def spectralintensity(light): return [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] def computewateropticaldepth(depth): return depth 0.05 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Dynamic Range: IF has a very high dynamic range, requiring tone mapping to correct. Seabed Color: The contribution of the color of the bottom of the sea is neglected due to its depth. Clouds: Fake clouds are added by mapping 2D fractal textures onto spherical layers; they do not cast shadows onto the Earth. Ozone/Surface Reflection: Irwin's variant neglects light from the sky (not the sun) reflected from the Earth’s surface and ozone absorption. Klassen's Spectral Atmospheric Method is a physically-based rendering technique for simulating sky color and solar illumination in planetary atmospheres by explicitly treating spectral scattering. It solves the problem of inaccurate color reproduction in atmospheric rendering, where standard RGB-based approximations fail to capture the wavelength-dependent nature of Rayleigh and Mie scattering. It sets itself apart from its siblings by introducing a full spectral treatment (33 wavelengths) for the sky while retaining RGB efficiency for non-selective fog, and by distinguishing between single-scattering haze layers and multiple-scattering sky color contributions. Irwin's method is similar to Nishita et al. but differs in the use of spectral wavelength sampling and reconstruction techniques instead of working in the RGB colour model. It simulates the light of the sky and the Sun as seen from the ground or from outer space for an atmosphere consisting of pure air with exponentially falling mass density. Only single scattering and Rayleigh scattering are considered, neglecting the light from the sky (not the sun) reflected from the Earth’s surface and ozone absorption. The atmosphere is modeled as a spherical shell, and illumination paths are solved by numerical integration. Time Complexity: Precomputation is intensive, taking 1.5 hours for the entire dataset with 6 scattering orders on an Intel Core 2 Duo 1.86 GHz CPU. Memory Complexity: Lookup tables consume ~10MB of texture memory (16-bit float per channel). Performance: Real-time performance is achieved on GPU. At 1024×768 resolution, average 180 FPS (min 85 FPS). At 2560×2048 resolution, average 60 FPS (min 29 FPS), with ~1.1 million static triangles. Scaling: The method is slower than Bruneton and Neyret [2008] because it evaluates reflection and scattering from water bodies, whereas Bruneton and Neyret report lower framerates because they account for terrain morphology, which this method does not. Strengths: Physically-based, fully spectral, supports arbitrarily dense atmospheres and large water bodies, real-time capable. Limitations: High precomputation time, neglects seabed color contribution, fake clouds do not cast shadows. Usage: Targets real-time applications such as flight simulators, games, virtual environments, and software like Google Earth (after simplifications). The method originates from Nishita et al. [59, 64], who presented a method to visualize the Earth from outer space, accounting for atmospheric particles and water. It extends the work of Kaneda et al. [42] by computing multiple scattering and light reflected from the ground. The specific spectral implementation with water bodies and tone mapping is detailed in, which builds on works by Bruneton and Neyret [2008] and Elek [2009] but adds fully spectral computations and water support. It is used in scientific visualization and real-time rendering of planetary atmospheres. A survey on participating media rendering techniques, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00371-005-0287-1, fetched 2026-10-26 Real-time spectral scattering in large-scale natural participating media, https://doi.org/10.1145/1925059.1925074, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Klassen's Spectral Atmospheric Method
body: Klassen's Spectral Atmospheric Method is a physically-based rendering technique for simulating sky color and solar illumination in planetary atmospheres by explicitly treating spectral scattering. It solves the problem of inaccurate color reproduction in atmospheric rendering, where standard RGB-based approximations fail to capture the wavelength-dependent nature of Rayleigh and Mie scattering. It sets itself apart from its siblings by introducing a full spectral treatment (33 wavelengths) for the sky while retaining RGB efficiency for non-selective fog, and by distinguishing between single-scattering haze layers and multiple-scattering sky color contributions. Inputs: Observer position: Ground level. Light source: Sun, treated as parallel rays due to large distance. Atmospheric layers: Haze-free layer containing air molecules (Rayleigh scattering) and haze-filled layer containing aerosols/particles (Mie scattering). Spectral data: Scattering coefficients and phase functions for 33 wavelengths, sampled every 10 nm. Fog parameters: Density and extinction coefficient in RGB space. Outputs: Sky color at each pixel (spectral). Sun disk color/intensity (spectral). Fog appearance for surface objects (RGB). Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Define geometry: Assume a flat earth approximation for local geometry and fog calculations. Assume parallel light rays from the sun. Define two spherical shells centered at the earth's center for the sky model: an inner haze-free shell and an outer haze-filled shell. 2. Compute sky color (spectral): For each pixel direction, calculate the spectral appearance. Single scattering is assumed to take place only in the haze-filled layer. Multiple scattering is not negligible for sky color computation and is accounted for following Bohren. 3. Compute sun disk (spectral): Calculate direct transmission through the atmosphere for pixels intersecting the sun disk. 4. Compute fog appearance (RGB): Fog is assumed to be non-wavelength-selective, so standard RGB space is used. Fog is restricted to be lit only by the sun, without shadows, using parallel light rays and the flat earth approximation. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Wavelengths: 33 samples, 10 nm spacing. Scattering types: Rayleigh (molecules), Mie (aerosols). Density distribution: Exponential with altitude (in the spherical variant). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Horizon Error: The planar atmosphere model results in large errors near the horizon. Spectral vs RGB: Using RGB for sky color is explicitly stated as wrong due to selective scattering; RGB is only used for fog. Multiple Scattering: Ignoring multiple scattering for sky color is incorrect; it must be included as per Bohren. An extension of Klassen’s planar atmosphere model to concentric spherical layers to reduce large error near the horizon. It accounts for both air molecules (Rayleigh scattering) and aerosols (Mie scattering), with density distributions varying exponentially with altitude. It is used for generating outdoor scenes including buildings, calculating both sunlight and skylight. Accuracy: High spectral accuracy for sky color, avoiding RGB artifacts. Better geometric accuracy near the horizon in the spherical variant. Performance: Computationally expensive due to 33-wavelength sampling and integration of scattering. The RGB fog component is efficient. Limitations: The base planar model has significant errors near the horizon. The method assumes parallel sunlight and does not handle complex shadowing in fog. Use Cases: Realistic sky and sun rendering for outdoor scenes, driving simulators, and scenes requiring accurate atmospheric color. The method was introduced by Klassen [44] in the context of atmospheric rendering. It is cited in surveys of participating media rendering techniques. The approach builds on earlier work in atmospheric optics, referencing Bohren [12] for multiple scattering in the sky. It was later extended by Kaneda et al. [42] to use concentric spherical layers to improve horizon accuracy. A survey on participating media rendering techniques, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00371-005-0287-1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Microflake Model
head: Jakob et al. model, Physically-based microflake model, Standard Microflake Model, anisotropic microflake model
body: The Microflake Model is a physically-based participating medium model that represents a volume as a homogeneous cloud of microscopic, specular flakes. It solves the problem of rendering anisotropic media (such as fur, fabrics, or powders) by deriving direction-dependent extinction and phase functions from a statistical distribution of microflake orientations. Unlike isotropic single-scattering approximations, it produces anisotropic attenuation coefficients and direction-dependent phase functions, satisfying Helmholtz's reciprocity principle by construction. Inputs: \rho: Density, the total area of microflake surface per unit volume (m^{-1}). D(\omegam): Microflake Normal Distribution Function (NDF), describing the statistical orientation of microflake normals \omegam (st^{-1}). \alpha(\lambda): Wavelength-dependent albedo of the microflakes (unitless). \omega: Incoming light direction (or view direction for scattering). \omega': Outgoing light direction (or view direction for scattering). Outputs: \sigmat(\omega): Direction-dependent attenuation coefficient (m^{-1}). \sigmas(\omega): Direction-dependent scattering coefficient (m^{-1}). f(\omega \rightarrow \omega'): Direction-dependent phase function (st^{-1}). Data Structures: The model requires the storage of the NDF D(\omegam), which can be represented analytically (e.g., Gaussian, Power of Sine/Cosine) or as a discrete lookup table depending on the specific implementation variant. The density \rho and albedo \alpha(\lambda) are scalar or vector constants per wavelength. Steps: 1. Compute the Attenuation Coefficient \sigmat(\omega): Calculate the integral of the projected area of the microflakes over all possible orientations. This represents the probability of a ray intersecting a microflake surface given direction \omega. \sigmat(\omega) = \rho \int D(\omegam) \langle \omega \cdot \omegam \rangle d\omegam where \langle \cdot \rangle denotes the clamped dot product (\max(0, \cdot)). 2. Compute the Scattering Coefficient \sigmas(\omega): Scale the attenuation coefficient by the albedo. This assumes the microflake albedo is not view-dependent. \sigmas(\omega) = \alpha(\lambda) \sigmat(\omega) where \alpha(\lambda) is the albedo at wavelength \lambda. 3. Compute the Phase Function f(\omega \rightarrow \omega'): For specular microflakes, the phase function is derived from the NDF evaluated at the half-vector. This ensures that scattering is concentrated around the specular reflection direction. f(\omega \rightarrow \omega') = \frac{\rho \alpha(\lambda) D(\omegah)}{4 \sigmas(\omega)} where \omegah is the normalized half-vector between the incoming and outgoing directions: \omegah = \frac{\omega + \omega'}{\|\omega + \omega'\|}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computemicroflakeproperties(rho, albedo, ndfeval, omegain, omegaout): """ Computes attenuation, scattering coefficients, and phase function for the Microflake Model. Args: rho (float): Density (total area of flakes per unit volume). albedo (float): Albedo of the microflakes (wavelength-dependent, assumed constant for this call). ndfeval (function): Function evaluating the Microflake Normal Distribution D(omegam). omegain (Vector3): Incoming light direction. omegaout (Vector3): Outgoing light direction. Returns: sigmat (float): Attenuation coefficient. sigmas (float): Scattering coefficient. phase (float): Phase function value. """ # Step 1: Compute Attenuation Coefficient sigmat # sigmat = rho integral(D(omegam) <omegain. omegam> domegam) # Note: The integral must be solved analytically or numerically based on the specific NDF D. # For common NDFs like Gaussian or Power of Sine/Cosine, closed-form approximations or # specific integral solutions exist. If no closed form is available, numerical integration # over the hemisphere is required. integralterm = computendfprojectedintegral(ndfeval, omegain) sigmat = rho integralterm # Step 2: Compute Scattering Coefficient sigmas sigmas = albedo sigmat # Step 3: Compute Phase Function f(omegain -> omegaout) # Calculate half-vector halfvector = omegain + omegaout halfvectornorm = length(halfvector) # Handle degenerate case where omegain and omegaout are opposite (backscattering) if halfvectornorm < 1e-6: # Phase function is undefined or requires specific handling for backscattering # In standard microflake model, this is a singularity or zero depending on D return sigmat, sigmas, 0.0 halfvectornormalized = halfvector / halfvectornorm # Evaluate NDF at the half-vector dhalf = ndfeval(halfvectornormalized) # Phase function formula: f = (rho alpha D(omegah)) / (4 sigmas) # Note: sigmas is already alpha sigmat, so this simplifies to D(omegah) / (4 sigmat) # if alpha != 0. However, we use the explicit formula for clarity. if sigmas < 1e-6: phase = 0.0 else: phase = (rho albedo dhalf) / (4.0 sigmas) return sigmat, sigmas, phase def computendfprojectedintegral(ndfeval, omega): """ Computes the integral of D(omegam) <omega. omegam> over the hemisphere. This is a placeholder for the specific analytical solution of the chosen NDF. Implementers should replace this with the specific integral solution for their NDF. For example, for a Gaussian NDF, this involves error functions. """ # Numerical integration fallback if analytical is not implemented # Integrate over hemisphere using Monte Carlo or quadrature numsamples = 1000 sumval = 0.0 for i in range(numsamples): # Sample random direction omegam on hemisphere omegam = samplehemisphere(omega) # Helper to sample hemisphere around omega dot = max(0.0, dotproduct(omega, omegam)) dval = ndfeval(omegam) sumval += dval dot # Average and scale by hemisphere area (2pi) # Note: Exact scaling depends on the sampling distribution. # For uniform hemisphere sampling, area is 2pi. return (sumval / numsamples) (2.0 3.14159265358979) Parameters and Typical Values: \rho: Not given in the sources. Depends on the specific medium density. \alpha(\lambda): Not given in the sources. Typically derived from material measurements. D(\omega): Defined by the chosen NDF variant (e.g., Gaussian, Power of Sine/Cosine). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Reciprocity: Arbitrary phase functions in anisotropic media often break Helmholtz's reciprocity principle (\sigmas(\omega)f(\omega \rightarrow \omega') = \sigmas(\omega')f(\omega' \rightarrow \omega)). The microflake model satisfies reciprocity by construction. Backscattering Singularity: When \omega = -\omega', the half-vector \omegah is undefined (zero length). The pseudocode handles this by returning 0, but specific NDFs may require careful handling of this limit. NDF Symmetry: The model assumes microflakes reflect on both sides, requiring D(\omega) = D(-\omega). Extends the standard model by introducing correlations of microflake positions at a microscopic scale to account for self-shadowing and masking effects. A specific NDF used within the Microflake Model for anisotropic media, providing an efficient implementation compared to Power of Sine/Cosine distributions. Extends the RTE to model structured micro-geometries using SGGX representation for fast evaluation of anisotropic extinction and phase functions. Time Complexity: The evaluation of \sigmat(\omega) requires an integral over the NDF, which can be computationally expensive if evaluated numerically. Analytical solutions for specific NDFs (like Gaussian) are faster. The phase function evaluation is O(1) given the NDF evaluation. Memory Complexity: Depends on the representation of D(\omega). Analytical NDFs require minimal memory. Lookup tables or discrete representations require memory proportional to the resolution of the NDF. Strengths: Physically-based, satisfies reciprocity, handles anisotropy naturally. Limitations: Assumes specular microflakes. Does not account for microscopic self-shadowing (unless using the extended model). Requires solving the NDF integral for attenuation. When to use: Rendering anisotropic participating media like fur, fabrics, or powders where single scattering is a sufficient approximation. When not to use: When multiple scattering is significant (use Multiple Scattering Models), or when microscopic self-shadowing is critical (use Microscopic Self-Shadowing Microflake Model). The Microflake Model was introduced by Jakob et al. [JAM 10] as a physically-based model for participating media. It is based on the anisotropic Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) framework. The model represents the medium as a homogeneous cloud of microscopic, specular flakes. It was developed to address the limitations of isotropic models in rendering anisotropic materials. The model satisfies Helmholtz's reciprocity principle by construction, which is a significant advantage over arbitrary anisotropic phase functions. A new microflake model with microscopic self-shadowing for accurate volume downsampling, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.13346, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Microscopic Self-Shadowing Microflake Model
head: Self-shadowing model
body: The Microscopic Self-Shadowing Microflake Model is a physically-based participating medium model that extends the standard Microflake Model by introducing correlations of microflake positions at a microscopic scale. It accounts for microscopic shadowing and masking effects that the standard model ignores. Unlike the standard Microflake Model, which assumes microflakes are well-separated and uncorrelated, this model uses a shadowing function A(\omega) to independently control attenuation, single scattering, and multiple scattering based on the probability of a microflake being obscured by its neighbors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Microflake Normal Distribution Function (NDF) D(\omegam), shadowing function A(\omega), single scattering albedo \alpha{ss}(\lambda), multiple scattering albedo \alpha{ms}(\lambda), density \rho, and wavelength \lambda. Outputs: Attenuation coefficient \sigmat(\omega), single scattering coefficient \sigma{ss}(\omega), multiple scattering coefficient \sigma{ms}(\omega), single scattering phase function f{ss}(\omega \rightarrow \omega'), and multiple scattering phase function f{ms}(\omega \rightarrow \omega'). Data Structures: The model relies on the following mathematical objects: 1. NDF D(\omegam): A probability density function over the sphere S^2 describing microflake orientations. 2. Shadowing Function A(\omega): A scalar field on the sphere S^2 where 0 < A(\omega) \leq 1. It represents the probability that a microflake is not shadowed or masked in direction \omega. 3. Albedos: \alpha{ss}(\lambda) and \alpha{ms}(\lambda) are scalar values per wavelength. Formulas and Definitions: Let \omega be the incoming direction, \omega' be the outgoing direction, and \omegam be a microflake normal. The half-vector is defined as \omegah = \frac{\omega + \omega'}{\|\omega + \omega'\|}. 1. Shadowing Function Constraints: A(\omega) = A(-\omega) \quad \text{and} \quad 0 < A(\omega) \leq 1 1 - A(\omega) is the probability of shadowing/masking by neighboring microflakes in direction \omega. A(\omega)=1 corresponds to the standard microflake model. 2. Attenuation Coefficient \sigmat(\omega): \sigmat(\omega) = A(\omega) \rho \int{S^2} D(\omegam) \langle \omega \cdot \omegam \rangle \, d\omegam where \langle x \rangle denotes the positive part \max(0, x). This is the standard microflake attenuation multiplied by A(\omega). 3. Single Scattering Coefficient \sigma{ss}(\omega): Single scattering occurs when microflakes are both unmasked (incoming direction \omega) and un-shadowed (outgoing direction \omega'). The coefficient is derived by integrating over outgoing directions using the Jacobian of the transformation from normals to specular reflections: \sigma{ss}(\omega) = \frac{\rho \alpha{ss}(\lambda) A(\omega)}{4} \int{S^2} A(\omega') D(\omegah) \, d\omega' The integral is over the sphere of outgoing directions \omega', and \omegah depends on \omega and \omega'. 4. Single Scattering Phase Function f{ss}(\omega \rightarrow \omega'): f{ss}(\omega \rightarrow \omega') = \frac{\rho \alpha{ss}(\lambda) A(\omega) A(\omega') D(\omegah)}{4 \sigma{ss}(\omega)} This function is normalized and satisfies reciprocity. 5. Multiple Scattering Coefficient \sigma{ms}(\omega): Multiple scattering accounts for all scattering orders except single scattering. It is computed as a linear combination of the total attenuation and single scattering coefficients: \sigma{ms}(\omega) = \alpha{ms}(\lambda) \left( \sigmat(\omega) - \frac{\sigma{ss}(\omega)}{\alpha{ss}(\lambda)} \right) Alternatively expressed as: \sigma{ms}(\omega) = \alpha{ms}(\lambda) \rho A(\omega) \int{S^2} (1 - A(\omega')) D(\omegam) \langle \omega \cdot \omegam \rangle \, d\omegam. 6. Multiple Scattering Phase Function f{ms}(\omega \rightarrow \omega'): The model assumes multiple scattering is roughly diffuse, depending only on the outgoing direction: f{ms}(\omega \rightarrow \omega') = f{ms}(\omega') = \frac{\sigma{ms}(\omega')}{\int{S^2} \sigma{ms}(\omega'') \, d\omega''} This satisfies reciprocity because \sigma{ms}(\omega) f{ms}(\omega \rightarrow \omega') is symmetric in \omega and \omega'. Parameters: \alpha{ss}(\lambda): Single scattering albedo. \alpha{ms}(\lambda): Multiple scattering albedo. Typical values: For energy conservation (White Furnace Test), if \alpha{ss} = \alpha{ms} = 1, then \sigma{ss} + \sigma{ms} = \sigmat. Pseudocode: The following Python-like pseudocode computes the coefficients given D, A, and parameters. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computemicroflakeselfshadowing(D, A, alphass, alphams, rho, wavelength, spheresamples, sphereweights): """ Computes scattering coefficients and phase functions for the Microscopic Self-Shadowing Microflake Model. Args: D: Function D(omegam) returning NDF value for normal omegam. A: Function A(omega) returning shadowing probability for direction omega. alphass: Single scattering albedo scalar. alphams: Multiple scattering albedo scalar. rho: Density scalar. wavelength: Wavelength scalar (used for albedo lookup if needed). spheresamples: List of direction vectors on the unit sphere. sphereweights: List of corresponding quadrature weights. Returns: sigmat, sigmass, sigmams, fss, fms """ def integratesphere(integrandfunc): # Standard spherical quadrature total = 0.0 for omega, w in zip(spheresamples, sphereweights): total += integrandfunc(omega) w return total def computeattintegral(omega): return integratesphere(lambda omegam: D(omegam) max(0.0, dot(omega, omegam))) def computessintegral(omega): def integrand(omegaprime): omegah = normalize(omega + omegaprime) return A(omegaprime) D(omegah) return integratesphere(integrand) def sigmat(omega): return A(omega) rho computeattintegral(omega) def sigmass(omega): return (rho alphass A(omega) / 4.0) computessintegral(omega) def sigmams(omega): return alphams (sigmat(omega) - sigmass(omega) / alphass) def fss(omega, omegaprime): omegah = normalize(omega + omegaprime) numerator = rho alphass A(omega) A(omegaprime) D(omegah) denominator = 4.0 sigmass(omega) return numerator / denominator if denominator != 0 else 0.0 msnorm = integratesphere(sigmams) def fms(omega, omegaprime): return sigmams(omegaprime) / msnorm if msnorm != 0 else 0.0 return sigmat, sigmass, sigmams, fss, fms Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Energy Conservation: The model satisfies reciprocity by construction. If \alpha{ss} = \alpha{ms} = 1, the model passes the white furnace test (\sigma{ss} + \sigma{ms} = \sigmat). Numerical Integration: The integrals for \sigma{ss} and \sigmat involve spherical convolutions. Standard distributions like SGGX or Gaussian Fibers do not yield closed-form solutions for these integrals with arbitrary A(\omega). Implementers should use numerical integration or specific distributions (like Trigonometric Lobes) that allow closed-form solutions. Shadowing Function Validity: A(\omega) must be symmetric (A(\omega) = A(-\omega)) and bounded (0, 1]. Violating this breaks the physical interpretation and reciprocity. This method simplifies the Microscopic Self-Shadowing Microflake Model by assuming the shadowing function A is isotropic (constant for all directions). This reduces parameter count and implementation complexity while maintaining sufficient accuracy in practice. It differs from the parent model by decoupling the directional dependence of shadowing, allowing closed-form solutions for spherical integrals that would otherwise require numerical approximation. Choose it when computational efficiency is prioritized and directional shadowing variations are negligible. The SGGX (Spherical Gaussian Generalized X) microflake distribution is a normal distribution function (NDF) designed for modeling aggregated microflakes in participating media. It solves the problem of efficiently computing attenuation coefficients and sampling specular phase functions for anisotropic microflake ensembles. It is distinguished from its siblings, such as the Simplified Model with Isotropic Self-Shadowing, by its ability to represent complex, arbitrarily oriented anisotropic normal distributions using a single lobe, enabling exact and fast evaluation of optical properties. Choose it for highly anisotropic media where exact NDF evaluation is required, though it requires numerical integration for the self-shadowing integrals. A volume rendering model using microflake normal distributions based on trigonometric lobes to enable closed-form expressions for self-shadowing integrals, solving the difficulty of finding closed-form solutions for spherical convolutions with distributions like SGGX. It defines the microflake normal distribution D using trigonometric lobes: D{\cos}(\boldsymbol{\omega}, \boldsymbol{\xi}, n) = \frac{(\boldsymbol{\omega} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi})^{2n}}{N{\cos}(n)} D{\sin}(\boldsymbol{\omega}, \boldsymbol{\xi}, n) = \frac{(1 - (\boldsymbol{\omega} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi})^2)^n}{N{\sin}(n)} where n is an integer and N are normalization factors. This representation is simple, flexible, and can be stored with only 6 parameters. Choose it when closed-form evaluation of the self-shadowing integrals is required for anisotropic media. Time Complexity: The core complexity lies in evaluating the spherical integrals for \sigmat and \sigma{ss}. For general D and A, this requires numerical integration, which is expensive. Using Trigonometric Lobes allows closed-form solutions for the integrals, significantly reducing evaluation cost per direction. Memory Complexity: Requires storing D and A. The self-shadowing function A can be stored with 6 parameters. Strengths: Physically accurate for downsampling; handles anisotropic media; preserves energy; satisfies reciprocity. Limitations: Requires careful handling of spherical integrals for general distributions; more complex than the standard Microflake Model. When to use: When rendering dense participating media (e.g., foliage, fur) at lower resolutions or when downsampling high-resolution data, where microscopic shadowing effects become significant. When not to use: For sparse media where microflakes are well-separated (standard Microflake Model suffices); when computational resources are extremely limited and closed-form solutions are not available. The Microflake Model was introduced by Jakob et al. [JAM 10] as a physically-based model for participating media. The Microscopic Self-Shadowing extension was introduced in to address inaccuracies in volume downsampling by incorporating microscopic correlations between microflakes. The model builds on the anisotropic radiative transfer equation proposed by Jakob et al.. A new microflake model with microscopic self-shadowing for accurate volume downsampling, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.13346, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Simplified Model with Isotropic Self-Shadowing
head: Isotropic self-shadowing model
body: This method simplifies the Microscopic Self-Shadowing Microflake Model by assuming the shadowing function A is isotropic (constant for all directions). This reduces parameter count and implementation complexity while maintaining sufficient accuracy in practice. It differs from the parent model by decoupling the directional dependence of shadowing, allowing closed-form solutions for spherical integrals that would otherwise require numerical approximation. Inputs: \lambda: Wavelength. \rho: Microflake density. D(\omegam): Microflake distribution function. \alpha{ss}(\lambda): Single scattering albedo. \alpha{ms}(\lambda): Multiple scattering albedo. A: Isotropic shadowing factor (scalar, 0 \le A \le 1). Outputs: \sigmat(\omega): Total attenuation coefficient. \sigma{ss}(\omega): Single scattering coefficient. f{ss}(\omega \rightarrow \omega'): Single scattering phase function. \sigma{ms}(\omega): Multiple scattering coefficient. f{ms}(\omega'): Multiple scattering phase function. Data Structures: The method requires standard scalar and vector types for directions and coefficients, along with a function or analytical expression for D(\omegam). Steps: 1. Compute Attenuation Coefficient \sigmat(\omega): Calculate the spherical integral of the microflake distribution weighted by the cosine of the angle between the view direction \omega and microflake normal \omegam, scaled by density \rho and the isotropic shadowing factor A: \sigmat(\omega) = A \rho \int{\Omega} D(\omegam) \langle \omega \cdot \omegam \rangle \, d\omegam where \langle \cdot \rangle denotes the positive part \max(0, \omega \cdot \omegam). Note that \sigmat(\omega) equals A times the attenuation coefficient of the standard microflake model. 2. Compute Single Scattering Coefficient \sigma{ss}(\omega): Scale the attenuation coefficient by the single scattering albedo and the shadowing factor A: \sigma{ss}(\omega) = \alpha{ss}(\lambda) A \sigmat(\omega) Note: The source table lists \sigmai(\omega) in Eq. 4.9, but the surrounding text and Eq. 4.8 clarify this as a typo for \sigmat(\omega). 3. Compute Single Scattering Phase Function f{ss}(\omega \rightarrow \omega'): Evaluate the specular phase function using the half-vector \omegah = \frac{\omega + \omega'}{\|\omega + \omega'\|}: f{ss}(\omega \rightarrow \omega') = \frac{\rho \alpha{ss}(\lambda) A^2 D(\omegah)}{4 \sigma{ss}(\omega)} Note: The source text contains garbled LaTeX \boldsymbol{\rho}{\sigma{ss}}(\boldsymbol{\lambda}) in Eq. 4.10, which is corrected here to standard microflake model notation. 4. Compute Multiple Scattering Coefficient \sigma{ms}(\omega): Calculate the remaining attenuation attributed to multiple scattering, scaled by the multiple scattering albedo and the factor (1-A): \sigma{ms}(\omega) = \alpha{ms}(\lambda) \sigmat(\omega) (1 - A) 5. Compute Multiple Scattering Phase Function f{ms}(\omega'): The multiple scattering phase function is proportional to the total attenuation coefficient: f{ms}(\omega') = \frac{\sigmat(\omega')}{\int{\Omega} \sigmat(\omega'') \, d\omega''} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeisotropicselfshadowingparams(omega, omegaprime, rho, alphass, alphams, A, Dfunc): # Step 1: Compute sigmat # Evaluate spherical integral of D(omegam) max(0, omega. omegam) # using closed-form expressions for trigonometric lobes as per Section 5. It = evaluateanalyticalintegral(omega, Dfunc) sigmat = A rho It # Step 2: Compute sigmass sigmass = alphass A sigmat # Step 3: Compute fss omegah = omega + omegaprime normomegah = sqrt(omegah[0]2 + omegah[1]2 + omegah[2]2) omegah = omegah / normomegah Domegah = Dfunc(omegah) numeratorss = rho alphass (A 2) Domegah denominatorss = 4 sigmass # Standard numerical guard against division by zero fss = numeratorss / max(denominatorss, 1e-8) # Step 4: Compute sigmams sigmams = alphams sigmat (1 - A) # Step 5: Compute fms # Evaluate integral of sigmat(omega'') over the sphere analytically. Isigmat = evaluateanalyticalintegralsphere(rho, A, Dfunc) Itprime = evaluateanalyticalintegral(omegaprime, Dfunc) sigmatprime = A rho Itprime fms = sigmatprime / max(Isigmat, 1e-8) return sigmat, sigmass, fss, sigmams, fms def evaluateanalyticalintegral(omega, Dfunc): # The source provides closed-form solutions for D functions composed of # trigonometric lobes (cos^2n, sin^2n) in Section 5. # The implementer must substitute the specific analytical expression # for their chosen Dfunc type. pass def evaluateanalyticalintegralsphere(rho, A, Dfunc): # Integrates sigmat(omega'') over the sphere analytically based on D. # The implementer must substitute the specific analytical expression # for their chosen Dfunc type. pass Parameters: A: Isotropic shadowing factor. Typical values are not explicitly given, but it acts as a scalar attenuation multiplier. \alpha{ss}(\lambda), \alpha{ms}(\lambda): Albedos, dependent on wavelength. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The spherical integrals require closed-form evaluation for specific distribution functions D(\omegam), typically trigonometric lobes. If D(\omegam) lacks a closed form, the method's efficiency advantage is lost. What it is: A technique for evaluating the spherical integrals in the self-shadowing model using functions like \cos^{2n} and \sin^{2n}. Difference: Provides closed-form solutions for the integrals, enabling efficient implementation. When to choose: When the microflake distribution D can be approximated by trigonometric lobes. Link: Trigonometric Lobes Implementation Time Complexity: Depends on the evaluation of D(\omegam) and its integrals. If closed-form expressions are available (e.g., via trigonometric lobes), evaluation is O(1) per direction. Memory Complexity: Low, as it does not require storing complex shadowing maps or high-resolution distributions. Performance: The isotropic assumption simplifies implementation and reduces parameters, making it faster to tune and render than the full anisotropic self-shadowing model. Strengths: Simplicity, reduced parameter space, sufficient accuracy for many applications. Limitations: Less accurate than the full anisotropic model, especially for highly directional microflake distributions. When to use: When computational efficiency is prioritized and the microflake distribution is not strongly directional. Origin: Introduced in "A new microflake model with microscopic self-shadowing for accurate volume downsampling". History: Developed as a simplification of the general self-shadowing microflake model to enable efficient implementations with fewer parameters. Usage: Used in volume rendering for participating media. A new microflake model with microscopic self-shadowing for accurate volume downsampling, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.13346, fetched 2026-10-26

name: SGGX Microflake Distribution
head: Micro-flake normal distribution, SGGX Phase Function Representation
body: The SGGX (Single Scattering GGX) microflake distribution is a parametric model for the normal distribution function (NDF) of microflakes in participating media, introduced by Heitz et al. [HDCD15]. It solves the problem of efficiently modeling anisotropic scattering by providing a closed-form representation that supports fast, exact evaluation of attenuation coefficients and efficient sampling of specular phase functions. It sets itself apart from previous distributions by overcoming limitations in computational efficiency and robustness, serving as the foundational component for the Microscopic Self-Shadowing Microflake Model and its variants. The SGGX distribution models the orientation of microflakes using a single 3x3 symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrix S. This matrix defines the shape and orientation of the scattering lobe. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A direction vector m (the microflake normal), and the SPD matrix S. Output: The probability density value D(m) and, when sampled, a new normal vector m. Data Structures: S: A 3x3 symmetric positive definite matrix. In implementation, this is typically stored as 6 floating-point values (upper triangular part) or 9 values if symmetry is not enforced during storage. The matrix must remain SPD to ensure the distribution is valid. Formula: The probability density function for the microflake normal m is given by: D(m) = \frac{1}{\pi \sqrt{|S|} (m^T S^{-1} m)^2} Where: |S| is the determinant of matrix S. S^{-1} is the inverse of matrix S. m is a unit vector representing the microflake normal. The term (m^T S^{-1} m) represents the quadratic form of the inverse matrix. Parameters: S: The 3x3 SPD matrix defining the anisotropy and spread of the microflake normals. Typical values depend on the material's roughness and orientation. For isotropic scattering, S is a scaled identity matrix. For anisotropic scattering, S has distinct eigenvalues corresponding to the principal axes of the microflakes. Algorithm for Evaluation: 1. Compute the inverse of S, denoted S^{-1}. 2. Compute the determinant |S|. 3. Compute the quadratic form q = m^T S^{-1} m. 4. Compute the denominator denom = \pi \sqrt{|S|} q^2. 5. Return 1 / denom. Sampling: While the exact sampling algorithm is not detailed in the provided notes, Heitz et al. [HDCD15] provide efficient sampling procedures for SGGX distributions. The sampling typically involves transforming a uniform sample into the space defined by S and then mapping it back to the sphere, ensuring the resulting normal m follows the distribution D(m). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: SPD Constraint: The matrix S must remain symmetric positive definite. If S becomes singular or indefinite, the distribution is undefined or invalid. This can occur during interpolation or optimization if not properly constrained. Precision: The computation of m^T S^{-1} m can suffer from precision issues if S is ill-conditioned. Care should be taken in numerical implementations. Normalization: The formula includes a normalization constant \frac{1}{\pi \sqrt{|S|}}. Ensure that the determinant and inverse are computed accurately to maintain proper normalization. The GGX Mixture NDF is a compact representation of the marginal distribution of surface normals, pN(n), used to model glossiness and anisotropy in participating media and microflake models. It approximates the surface NDF as a weighted sum of Single Scattering GGX (SGGX) distributions. This method sets itself apart from single-lobe SGGX models by allowing the representation of complex, multi-modal normal distributions, and from aggregated microfacet convolutions by providing the base component that is subsequently convolved with isotropic spherical distributions to model surface roughness effects. Time Complexity: The evaluation of D(m) is O(1) assuming fixed-size matrix operations (3x3). Inversion and determinant computation are also constant time for 3x3 matrices. Memory Complexity: O(1) per distribution, storing only the 6 unique elements of the SPD matrix S. Performance: The SGGX distribution is computationally efficient compared to state-of-the-art models [Jakob et al. 2010; Zhao et al. 2011] while offering similar representative power for anisotropic scattering. Strengths: Fast and exact evaluation of attenuation coefficients; efficient evaluation and sampling of specular phase functions; compact representation of anisotropy. Limitations: Single-lobe representation may not capture complex multi-modal normal distributions without mixing (see GGX Mixture NDF). Requires careful maintenance of the SPD property for S. When to use: When modeling anisotropic scattering in participating media where computational efficiency is critical and the microflake orientation distribution can be approximated by a single lobe. When not to use: When the normal distribution is highly multi-modal or requires complex correlations that a single SPD matrix cannot capture. The SGGX distribution was introduced by Heitz et al. in 2015 [HDCD15]. It was developed to address limitations in previous microflake normal distributions, specifically regarding the efficiency of evaluating attenuation coefficients and sampling phase functions. The model has since been used in various volume rendering contexts, including downsampling volume data and implementing simplified self-shadowing models. A new microflake model with microscopic self-shadowing for accurate volume downsampling, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.13346, fetched 2026-10-26 Downsampling scattering parameters for rendering anisotropic media, https://doi.org/10.1145/2980179.2980228, fetched 2026-10-28

name: GGX Mixture NDF
head: SGGX Mixture, Surface NDF, Surface Normal Distribution Function (NDF) Mixture with SGGX
body: The GGX Mixture NDF is a compact representation of the marginal distribution of surface normals, pN(n), used to model glossiness and anisotropy in participating media and microflake models. It approximates the surface NDF as a weighted sum of Single Scattering GGX (SGGX) distributions. This method sets itself apart from single-lobe SGGX models by allowing the representation of complex, multi-modal normal distributions, and from aggregated microfacet convolutions by providing the base component that is subsequently convolved with isotropic spherical distributions to model surface roughness effects. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A target surface normal distribution pN(n) (derived from geometry or measurement) and a desired number of lobes k. Output: A set of k SGGX parameters \{ (wi, Ri, \alphai) \}{i=1}^k defining the mixture. Data Structures: The mixture is defined by three arrays of size k: 1. weights: Array of k floats wi, where wi > 0 and \sum{i=1}^k wi = 1. 2. rotations: Array of k rotation matrices Ri (or equivalent quaternion/eigenbasis representations) mapping the local SGGX frame to the world frame. Each Ri is defined by an orthonormal basis (\omega1, \omega2, \omega3). 3. roughness: Array of k 2D vectors \alphai = (\alpha{x,i}, \alpha{y,i}), representing the anisotropic roughness parameters for each lobe. Formulas: The surface NDF is computed as: pN(n) = \sum{i=1}^{k} wi D{i\text{sggx}}(n) where D{i\text{sggx}}(n) is the SGGX distribution for the i-th lobe, parameterized by Ri and \alphai. Parameters: k: The number of SGGX lobes. Typical value not specified in sources; determined by the fitting process. Steps: 1. Parameterization: Define the SGGX distribution D{\text{sggx}}(\omega; R, \alpha) using its eigenbasis R = (\omega1, \omega2, \omega3) and anisotropic roughness \alpha = (\alphax, \alphay). The exact functional form of D{\text{sggx}} is detailed in the supplemental document of the source. 2. Fitting: Determine the weights wi, rotations Ri, and roughness \alphai such that the mixture approximates the target pN(n). The specific optimization or fitting algorithm is described in §7.1 of the source. 3. Evaluation: To evaluate pN(n) for a normal n, compute the weighted sum of the individual SGGX lobes evaluated at n. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normalization: The weights must strictly sum to 1 to ensure pN(n) is a valid probability density function. Precision: The fitting process (§7.1) must handle potential numerical instability when lobes become nearly identical or weights approach zero. Approximates the convolution of a single SGGX lobe with an isotropic spherical distribution by a roughened SGGX. Use when modeling surface roughness blur on a single microflake orientation. Computes the effective NDF by convolving an aggregated microfacet distribution with the surface NDF mixture. Use when modeling the joint effect of surface roughness and microflake orientation. Complexity: Evaluation is O(k), where k is the number of lobes. Fitting complexity is not specified. Memory: Requires storing k sets of rotation matrices and roughness parameters, plus weights. Strengths: Compact representation of complex anisotropic and multi-modal normal distributions. Enables efficient convolution approximations. Limitations: Requires a fitting step to determine parameters. Accuracy depends on k and the fitting quality. The method was introduced by Heitz et al. in the context of efficient scene appearance aggregation for level-of-detail rendering. It builds upon the SGGX distribution [Heitz et al. 2015] to provide a flexible representation for surface normals in participating media. Efficient Scene Appearance Aggregation for Level-of-Detail Rendering, https://core.ac.uk/works/391729893, fetched 2026-11-01 (unofficial)

name: SGGX Convolution Approximation
head: Convolution of SGGX and Isotropic Distribution, Roughened SGGX
body: The SGGX Convolution Approximation is a method for approximating the convolution of a Single Scattering GGX (SGGX) normal distribution function (NDF) with an isotropic spherical distribution g(\omega; n) by another SGGX distribution with increased roughness. It solves the problem of efficiently modeling surface roughness or scattering anisotropy in participating media and microflake models without resorting to complex analytical integrals. Unlike the Convolution of Aggregated Microfacet and Surface NDF, which handles aggregated microfacets, this method specifically targets the convolution of a single SGGX lobe with an isotropic blur, allowing for a compact, scene-independent parameterization. Inputs: 1. An SGGX distribution parameterized by an eigenbasis R and anisotropic roughness \alpha = (\alphax, \alphay). 2. An isotropic spherical distribution g(\omega; n). Outputs: 1. A roughened SGGX distribution D{sggx}(\omega; R, \alpha^+) that approximates the convolution. 2. The mapping function M that computes the new roughness \alpha^+ from \alpha and g. Data Structures: SGGX Parameters: The SGGX distribution is defined by a 3 \times 3 symmetric positive definite matrix S, which is decomposed into an eigenbasis R = (\omega1, \omega2, \omega3) and roughness values \alphax, \alphay. The exact parameterization of R and \alpha from S is detailed in the source's supplemental document. Precomputed Table: The mapping \alpha^+ = M(\alpha, g) is stored in a precomputed table. Since the mapping is scene-independent and typically smooth, it requires negligible storage and is computed once. Steps: 1. Parameterize: Represent the input SGGX lobe D{sggx}(n; R, \alpha) using its eigenbasis R and anisotropic roughness \alpha. 2. Fit: Perform a nonlinear least-square fit to find the mapping \alpha^+ = M(\alpha, g) such that the convolution is approximated by the roughened SGGX: \int{S^2} g(\omega; n) D{sggx}(n; R, \alpha) \, dn \approx D{sggx}(\omega; R, \alpha^+) where R remains fixed and \alpha gains additional values to become \alpha^+. 3. Store: Save the mapping M in a lookup table for runtime use. Formulas: The convolution of the mixture NDF pN(n) = \sum{i=1}^k wi D{i,sggx}(n) with g(\omega; n) is approximated by summing the roughened lobes: D{conv}(\omega) = \int{S^2} g(\omega; n) pN(n) \, dn \approx \sum{i=1}^k wi D{i,sggx}(\omega; Ri, \alpha^+i) where \alpha^+i = M(\alphai, g). Parameters: R: Eigenbasis of the SGGX distribution. \alpha: Anisotropic roughness (\alphax, \alphay). g: Isotropic spherical distribution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The approximation relies on the smoothness of the mapping M. If g is highly non-smooth, the approximation may degrade. The method assumes the convolution can be represented by a single SGGX lobe with modified roughness. This is an approximation and may not capture all features of the true convolution, particularly for highly anisotropic cases where multi-lobe representations are preferred. A representation that combines single-scattering albedo and phase functions into a single entity to facilitate downsampling, addressing the issue that naive downsampling weakens intrinsic shadowing structures. It represents the scaled phase function \hat{f} as a linear combination of m SGGX lobes, allowing for better approximation of complex scattering than a single lobe. The scaled phase function is defined as: \hat{f}(\omega0 \rightarrow \omega) = \sum{j=1}^{m} Wj fj(\omega0 \rightarrow \omega) where fj is the j-th SGGX lobe and Wj \in (0, 1] is the lobe weight satisfying \sum{j=1}^{m} Wj \le 1. The number of lobes m is typically limited to 3 for a balance between model size and accuracy. Using a single SGGX function (m=1) via averaging works adequately for many cases but leads to limited accuracy for highly anisotropic materials. Time Complexity: The fitting process is performed offline. At runtime, the method requires a table lookup for the mapping M, which is O(1). Memory Complexity: The precomputed table for the mapping M requires negligible storage. Strengths: Scene-independent, compact representation, efficient runtime performance. Limitations: Approximation error depends on the isotropic distribution g and the anisotropy of the material. Single-lobe approximation may be insufficient for highly anisotropic materials. When to use: When modeling surface roughness or scattering anisotropy in a compact way, especially in the context of GGX Mixture NDF or downsampling anisotropic media. When not to use: When high accuracy is required for highly anisotropic materials, a multi-lobe representation should be considered. The SGGX distribution was introduced by Heitz et al. in 2015 as a compact representation for the surface NDF. The convolution approximation method was proposed in the context of efficient scene appearance aggregation for level-of-detail rendering, building on the idea of approximating convolutions of anisotropic distributions with roughened versions. The multi-lobe extension was introduced in the context of downsampling scattering parameters for rendering anisotropic media to preserve shadowing structures. name: Convolution of Aggregated Microfacet and Surface NDF
head: Microfacet-NDF Convolution
body: This method computes the effective normal distribution function (NDF) for a microflake participating medium by convolving the aggregated microfacet distribution \hat{D}{mic} with the surface NDF pN(n). It solves the problem of modeling how surface roughness and microflake orientation jointly affect scattering in single-scattering approximations. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly representing the surface NDF as a mixture of SGGX distributions and approximating the convolution of each mixture component with the microfacet distribution as a single, roughened SGGX distribution, enabling efficient precomputed lookup rather than runtime integration. Inputs: Aggregated microfacet distribution \hat{D}{mic}, represented as a mixture of k lobes with weights mj and roughness parameters \alphaj. Surface NDF pN(n), represented as a mixture of 2 SGGX lobes with weights wi, eigenbases Ri, and anisotropic roughness \alphai. Outputs: Convolved NDF D{conv}(\omegah), represented as a mixture of SGGX distributions. Data Structures: Mapping Table M3: A 3D lookup table storing the mapping \alpha^+ = M3(\alpha, \alphai) for convolving roughness parameters. Exact sizes and bit packing are not given in the sources. Inverse LTC Table T{LTC}^{-1}: A 1D table for the inverse Linearly Transformed Cosine transform, varying only with roughness. Normalization Table M5: A 1D table storing the integral of the GGX distribution over the full sphere S^2 as a function of roughness \alpha. Steps: 1. Decompose mixtures: Represent the surface NDF as a sum of 2 SGGX lobes: pN(n) = \sum{i=1}^{2} wi D{sggx}(n; Ri, \alphai). Decompose the aggregated microfacet distribution into k lobes with weights mj and roughness \alphaj. 2. Per-lobe convolution mapping: For each pair of lobes (i, j), compute the effective roughness \alpha^+{ij} using the precomputed mapping table. The eigenbasis Ri remains fixed. 3. Construct convolved NDF: Sum the contributions of all lobe pairs to form the final convolved NDF. 4. Correction for conditioned angular domain: To account for Heaviside function terms \mathbb{1}(n \cdot \omegai) and \mathbb{1}(n \cdot \omegao) that restrict the integration domain to a spherical triangle rather than the full sphere S^2, apply a correction factor. Compute the normalization term using M5(\alpha). Use T{LTC}^{-1} to handle integration over the spherical triangle. Multiply the smooth microfacet shadowing-masking term G post-convolution. Formulas: D{conv}(\omegah) = \sum{i=1}^{2} \sum{j=1}^{k} wi mj D{conv}(\omegah){ij}: Convolved NDF, where wi and mj are mixture weights, and D{conv}(\omegah){ij} is the per-lobe convolution contribution. D{conv}(\omegah){ij} \approx D{sggx}(\omega; Ri, \alpha^+{ij}): Approximation of the per-lobe convolution as a roughened SGGX distribution with fixed eigenbasis Ri and mapped roughness \alpha^+{ij}. \alpha^+{ij} = M3(\alphai, M3(\alphaj)): Mapped roughness, where M3 is the 3D lookup table, \alphai is the surface NDF lobe roughness, and M3(\alphaj) is a shorthand for fitting a beta distribution to \alphaj and querying the table for the roughness of the j-th microfacet lobe. Parameters: M3: Stored as a 3D table. Typical values are not given in the sources. T{LTC}^{-1}: 1D table varying only with roughness. M5(\alpha): 1D table for the normalization term. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The constant contribution assumption in the shape term for the conditioned angular domain correction can cause under- or overestimates, resulting in slightly darker or brighter results and stretched lobe shapes compared to references. This method approximates the convolution of a SGGX microflake distribution with an isotropic spherical distribution (such as a GGX microfacet distribution or a Spherical Gaussian) as another SGGX distribution sharing the same eigenvectors. It solves the problem of efficiently computing the roughening effect of convolution in participating media by mapping the original roughness parameters to new parameters via a precomputed lookup table, avoiding expensive Monte Carlo integration at runtime. It builds on Convolution of Aggregated Microfacet and Surface NDF. An approximation technique for the conditioned angular domain in SGGX convolution, which assumes constant contribution in the shape term. It uses a 1D table for the inverse LTC transform varying only with roughness, denoted T{LTC}^{-1}, and a 1D table for the normalization term (integral of GGX over full sphere), denoted M5(\alpha). The constant contribution assumption can cause under- or overestimates, resulting in slightly darker or brighter results, and stretched lobe shapes compared to references. Time Complexity: O(1) per lobe pair after precomputation, as it relies on table lookups for the mapping M3. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 3D mapping table M3, the 1D inverse LTC table T{LTC}^{-1}, and the 1D normalization table M5. Strengths: Efficient runtime evaluation; avoids expensive numerical integration; compact representation using SGGX mixtures. Limitations: Approximation errors due to the constant contribution assumption in the conditioned angular domain correction, leading to slight inaccuracies in lobe shape and intensity. Accuracy depends on the resolution of the precomputed tables. The method is described in "Efficient Scene Appearance Aggregation for Level-of-Detail Rendering". It builds on prior work in normal map filtering and specular shading antialiasing, as well as the SGGX distribution [Heitz et al. 2015] and Linearly Transformed Cosines [Heitz et al. 2016]. The convolution technique is inspired by Xu et al. [2013]. Efficient Scene Appearance Aggregation for Level-of-Detail Rendering, https://core.ac.uk/works/391729893, fetched 2026-11-01 (unofficial)

name: SGGX-based Precomputed Convolution
head: SGGX-GGX convolution fit, SGGX-SG convolution fit, SGGX Convolution with SG/GGX Kernel
body: This method approximates the convolution of an SGGX microflake distribution with an isotropic spherical distribution (such as a GGX microfacet distribution or a Spherical Gaussian) as another SGGX distribution sharing the same eigenvectors. It solves the problem of efficiently computing the roughening effect of convolution in participating media by mapping the original roughness parameters to new parameters via a precomputed lookup table, avoiding expensive Monte Carlo integration at runtime. It builds on Convolution of Aggregated Microfacet and Surface NDF. Inputs: 1. An SGGX distribution defined by eigenbasis R = (\omega1, \omega2, \omega3) and projected areas \sigma(\omega1) \le \sigma(\omega2) \le \sigma(\omega3). 2. A target isotropic distribution g (either GGX with roughness \alpha{ggx} or Spherical Gaussian with sharpness \kappa). Outputs: A new SGGX distribution with the same eigenbasis R but updated roughness parameters \alpha^+ = (\alphax^+, \alphay^+). Data Structures: Two precomputed 3D lookup tables (LUTs) storing the additional roughness \alpha^+: 1. SGGX-GGX Mapping (M2): Resolution 50 \times 50 \times 50 \times 2. Stores \alpha^+ as a function of (\alphax, \alphay, \alpha{ggx}). 2. SGGX-SG Mapping (M1): Resolution 20 \times 20 \times 20 \times 2. Stores \alpha^+ as a function of (\alphax, \alphay, \kappa). Steps: 1. Normalize the SGGX Matrix: Scale the SGGX matrix S by 1/\sigma^2(\omega3) to obtain S'. This normalization ensures the third eigenvalue corresponds to a unit projected area, allowing the roughness parameters to be derived directly from the first two eigenvalues relative to the third. S' = \frac{1}{\sigma^2(\omega3)} S = (\omega1, \omega2, \omega3) \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\sigma^2(\omega1)}{\sigma^2(\omega3)} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{\sigma^2(\omega2)}{\sigma^2(\omega3)} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} (\omega1, \omega2, \omega3)^T 2. Extract Original Roughness Parameters: Compute the initial roughness parameters \alpha = (\alphax, \alphay) for the SGGX distribution. These are derived from the normalized eigenvalues: \alphax = \frac{\sigma(\omega1)}{\sigma(\omega3)} \alphay = \frac{\sigma(\omega2)}{\sigma(\omega3)} (Note: The source text contains a typographical error stating \alphay = \sigma(\omega1)/\sigma(\omega3); standard SGGX parameterization and the context of distinct eigenvalues require \sigma(\omega2) for \alphay.) 3. Lookup Additional Roughness: Depending on the target distribution g: For GGX: Query the M2 LUT with inputs (\alphax, \alphay, \alpha{ggx}) to retrieve \alpha^+ = M2(\alpha, \alpha{ggx}). For Spherical Gaussian: Query the M1 LUT with inputs (\alphax, \alphay, \kappa) to retrieve \alpha^+ = M1(\alpha, \kappa). The ground-truth convolution for fitting these mappings is computed by Monte Carlo integration with a large number of samples, and the mappings are found via nonlinear least-square fit. 4. Construct Resulting SGGX: The resulting distribution is D{sggx}(n; R, \alpha^+). The eigenbasis R remains unchanged. The new projected areas are reconstructed from \alpha^+ and the original \sigma(\omega3) as \sigma1^+ = \alphax^+ \sigma(\omega3) and \sigma2^+ = \alphay^+ \sigma(\omega3), while \sigma3 remains unchanged. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def sggxprecomputedconvolution(S, targettype, targetparam): """ Approximates the convolution of an SGGX distribution with a target isotropic distribution. Args: S: 3x3 SGGX matrix. targettype: 'GGX' or 'SG'. targetparam: roughness alphaggx for GGX, or sharpness kappa for SG. Returns: newS: Resulting SGGX matrix. """ # Step 1: Eigen decomposition and sorting # S = R diag(sigma1^2, sigma2^2, sigma3^2) R^T # np.linalg.eigh returns eigenvalues in ascending order. eigenvalues, R = np.linalg.eigh(S) sigma = np.sqrt(np.maximum(eigenvalues, 0.0)) sigma1, sigma2, sigma3 = sigma[0], sigma[1], sigma[2] # Step 2: Normalize and extract roughness parameters # Formula from source: alphax = sigma1 / sigma3, alphay = sigma2 / sigma3 alphax = sigma1 / sigma3 alphay = sigma2 / sigma3 # Step 3: Lookup additional roughness alphaplus if targettype == 'GGX': # M2 resolution: 50x50x50x2. Inputs: alphax, alphay, alphaggx alphaplus = trilinearinterpolate(LUTM2, alphax, alphay, targetparam) elif targettype == 'SG': # M1 resolution: 20x20x20x2. Inputs: alphax, alphay, kappa alphaplus = trilinearinterpolate(LUTM1, alphax, alphay, targetparam) else: raise ValueError("Unsupported target distribution type") # alphaplus is a tuple (alphaxplus, alphayplus) alphaxplus, alphayplus = alphaplus # Step 4: Reconstruct the new SGGX matrix # The eigenbasis R remains the same. # The new projected areas are derived from alphaplus and sigma3. sigma1new = alphaxplus sigma3 sigma2new = alphayplus sigma3 sigma3new = sigma3 # Construct the new diagonal matrix of squared projected areas diagnew = np.diag([sigma1new2, sigma2new2, sigma3new2]) # Reconstruct matrix: Snew = R diagnew R^T newS = R @ diagnew @ R.T return newS def trilinearinterpolate(LUT, x, y, z): """Standard trilinear interpolation for a 3D LUT.""" # LUT shape: (Dx, Dy, Dz, 2) # Clamp coordinates to valid range [0, 1] x = np.clip(x, 0.0, 1.0) y = np.clip(y, 0.0, 1.0) z = np.clip(z, 0.0, 1.0) # Map to grid indices Dx, Dy, Dz, = LUT.shape ix = np.floor(x (Dx - 1)).astype(int) iy = np.floor(y (Dy - 1)).astype(int) iz = np.floor(z (Dz - 1)).astype(int) # Fractional parts fx = x (Dx - 1) - ix fy = y (Dy - 1) - iy fz = z (Dz - 1) - iz # Handle boundary indices ix1 = np.minimum(ix + 1, Dx - 1) iy1 = np.minimum(iy + 1, Dy - 1) iz1 = np.minimum(iz + 1, Dz - 1) # Fetch 8 corners v000 = LUT[ix, iy, iz] v100 = LUT[ix1, iy, iz] v010 = LUT[ix, iy1, iz] v110 = LUT[ix1, iy1, iz] v001 = LUT[ix, iy, iz1] v101 = LUT[ix1, iy, iz1] v011 = LUT[ix, iy1, iz1] v111 = LUT[ix1, iy1, iz1] # Interpolate v00 = v000 (1 - fx) + v100 fx v01 = v001 (1 - fx) + v101 fx v10 = v010 (1 - fx) + v110 fx v11 = v011 (1 - fx) + v111 fx v0 = v00 (1 - fy) + v10 fy v1 = v01 (1 - fy) + v11 fy result = v0 (1 - fz) + v1 fz return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The LUTs are precomputed using nonlinear least-square fits against Monte Carlo ground truth. Accuracy depends on the resolution of the LUTs. The source provides RMSE plots to validate accuracy but does not specify a maximum error threshold. Boundaries: The method assumes the SGGX matrix is valid and the eigenvalues are sorted correctly. The normalization by \sigma^2(\omega3) requires \sigma(\omega3) > 0. Degenerate Input: If \sigma(\omega1) = \sigma(\omega2) = \sigma(\omega3), the distribution is isotropic, and the roughness parameters evaluate to \alphax = \alphay = 1. Restricted Domain: When convolving over a restricted domain X, the contribution of the original distribution is clamped to black by X. Time Complexity: O(1) per convolution, dominated by LUT lookups and interpolation. This is significantly faster than Monte Carlo integration. Memory Complexity: Requires storing two LUTs: 50^3 \times 2 floats for SGGX-GGX and 20^3 \times 2 floats for SGGX-SG. This is a small, fixed memory overhead. Accuracy: Validated against Monte Carlo ground truth. The source provides RMSE error plots for varying \kappa (SGGX-SG) and \alpha (SGGX-GGX) but does not give a single numerical error value. Strengths: Efficient approximation of convolution for microflake models; allows for precomputed roughening in real-time or LOD rendering. Limitations: Approximation error exists; limited to isotropic target distributions (GGX, SG); requires precomputation. This technique is part of the ABSDF (Aggregated Bidirectional Scattering Distribution Function) framework for efficient scene appearance aggregation. It was introduced by Yang Zhou, Tao Huang, Ravi Ramamoorthi, Pradeep Sen, and Ling-Qi Yan in their 2010 paper "Efficient Scene Appearance Aggregation for Level-of-Detail Rendering" presented at the Symposium on Interactive 3D Graphics (SI3D). The method leverages the properties of SGGX distributions and precomputed fits to accelerate the convolution of microflake distributions with other microfacet or spherical distributions. Efficient Scene Appearance Aggregation for Level-of-Detail Rendering, https://core.ac.uk/works/391729893, fetched 2026-11-01 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Fiber Distribution
body: The Gaussian Fiber Distribution is a microflake normal distribution function (NDF) used within the Microflake Model to define the statistical orientation of microflakes in anisotropic participating media. It provides a more efficient implementation than the Power of Sine/Cosine distributions introduced by Jakob et al. [JAM 10]. Unlike later models, it does not provide a closed-form expression for the attenuation coefficient, relying instead on an efficient approximation [Jak10]. Inputs and outputs: The method takes the mean microflake normal direction \mathbf{v} (unit vector), the sharpness parameter n (scalar), and the evaluation direction \omega (unit vector) as inputs. It outputs the distribution value D(\omega) and sampled visible normal directions. Data structures: The distribution is defined by a scalar function D(\omega); sampling requires storing \mathbf{v} and n. Numbered steps: 1. Initialize the mean normal \mathbf{v} and sharpness n. 2. Evaluate the distribution at direction \omega using the distribution formula. 3. Compute the attenuation coefficient \sigmat using the approximation from Jakob [Jak10]. 4. Sample the distribution of visible normals using a rejection algorithm based on sampling a normal distribution. Formulas: The exact mathematical formula for D(\omega) is not provided in the sources. Parameters: The method is parameterized by the mean normal \mathbf{v} and sharpness n. Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: The rejection sampling algorithm for visible normals is inefficient in some configurations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. [JAM 10] and serve as a baseline for comparison. The surface distribution is defined as D{\text{surf}}(\omega) = \cos^n(\mathbf{v}, \omega), and the fiber distribution as D{\text{fiber}}(\omega) = \sin^n(\mathbf{v}, \omega), where \mathbf{v} is the microflake normal direction and \omega is the view direction. Neither distribution has a closed-form expression for the attenuation coefficient, and the original work used spherical harmonic approximations for evaluation and sampling. The Gaussian Fiber Distribution is cited as more efficient than the original implementation of these distributions. Efficiency: The implementation by Zhao et al. [ZJMB11] is more efficient than the original implementation of Jakob et al. [JAM 10]. Attenuation calculation: It does not provide a closed-form expression for the attenuation coefficient and relies on an efficient approximation [Jak10]. Development: Zhao et al. provided an efficient implementation but did not provide a closed-form attenuation coefficient, relying on Jakob's approximation [Jak10]. Subsequent work by Heitz et al. [HDCD15] introduced the SGGX distribution to overcome limitations of previous distributions, including the lack of closed-form attenuation and efficient sampling.
