name: Riley et al. Angular Distribution Renderer
head: Eye Ray Rendering with Angular Distribution, Final Gather with Angular Distribution, Riley et al
body: The Riley et al. Angular Distribution Renderer is a single-pass volume rendering method designed to efficiently simulate forward multiple scattering in atmospheric media, such as clouds and fog, while capturing fine angularly dependent chromatic effects like rainbows and halos. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by using pre-computed multiple scattering angular distribution functions to approximate the light distribution after a specific number of scattering events, allowing for efficient hardware-accelerated rendering without the premature darkening artifacts common in low-albedo models. The method renders a volume in a single pass by accumulating inscattered intensity into the eye ray using pre-computed angular distribution functions. It employs a half-angle slicing scheme to optimize data access for both the light source and the camera. Inputs: Volume data (density, scattering coefficients). Phase function parameters (including the user-adjustable term \xi). View vector \Omega and Light vector \Omega{lt}. Number of expected scattering events n(\vec{s}). Outputs: Eye buffer: Accumulated radiance directed into the eye rays. Light buffer: Attenuation of light traversing the volume. The implementation relies on two primary buffers accessed during the slicing pass: 1. Eye Buffer: Stores the accumulated radiance L(\vec{s}, \Omega) for each pixel. 2. Light Buffer: Stores the transmittance/attenuation of the light as it passes through the volume. \xi: A user-adjustable term added to the phase function to model light received from multiple scattering further along the path, preventing premature darkening. n(\vec{s}): The expected number of scattering events reaching sample \vec{s}. \beta{sca}: Scattering coefficient. \Delta: Step size. 1. Slicing Orientation: Slice the volume data at an angle halfway between the view vector \Omega and the light vector \Omega{lt}. This orientation is suitable for both eye and light perspectives, optimizing memory access patterns for programmable graphics hardware. 2. Buffer Initialization: Initialize the Eye Buffer and Light Buffer to zero. 3. Volume Pass: Iterate through the volume along the slicing direction. For each sample point \vec{s} along the eye ray: a. Determine the number of scattering events n(\vec{s}) expected to reach this sample. b. Calculate the inscattered contribution. The method applies the angular distribution function for n(\vec{s}) + 1 scattering events, as the (n+1)-th event is the one that scatters light directly into the eye ray. c. Compute the intensity contribution I(\vec{s}) using the phase function modified by \xi. d. Accumulate this contribution into the Eye Buffer, weighted by the transmittance from the start of the ray \vec{s}f to the current sample. e. Update the Light Buffer with the attenuation of light traversing the volume up to this point. 4. Final Compositing: Add skylight and aerial perspective effects based on a simplified single-scattering analytic model to the final image to increase realism. Store the total transparency of the volume in the alpha channel of the eye buffer to attenuate direct sunlight. The accumulation for a pixel, assuming front-to-back compositing starting from \vec{s}f, is given by: L(\vec{s}, \Omega) = \sum{i=front}^{back} T(\vec{s}, \vec{s}f + i\vec{m}\Omega \Delta) I(\vec{s}f + i\vec{m}\Omega \Delta) where the sum is over sampling slabs i that scatter light contributions towards the eye. The intensity contribution I(\vec{s}) for a sample is approximated by considering the worst-case attenuation for efficiency on graphics hardware, as linear interpolation for floating-point textures was not available at the time of implementation: I(\vec{s} + \vec{m}\Omega{lt} \Delta) = I(\vec{s}) T(\vec{s}, \vec{s} + \vec{m}\Omega{lt} \Delta) + I(\vec{s})(1 - T(\vec{s}, \vec{s} + \vec{m}\Omega{lt} \Delta)) \left( A{ms}^{\lfloor n(\vec{s}f + i\vec{m}\Omega \Delta) + 1 \rfloor} (\Omega - \Omega{lt}) + \xi \right) \beta{sca} \Delta Where: T(\vec{s}1, \vec{s}2) is the transmittance between points \vec{s}1 and \vec{s}2. A{ms}^{k} (\Omega - \Omega{lt}) is the multiple scattering angular distribution function for k scattering events, evaluated at the angle between the view and light directions. \lfloor \cdot \rfloor denotes the floor function, used to determine the discrete number of scattering events for the lookup. \xi is the backscattering correction term. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderangulardistribution(volume, viewdir, lightdir, xi, betasca, stepsize): """ Renders volume using Riley et al. Angular Distribution Renderer. Args: volume: Volume data structure with density and scattering coefficients. viewdir: View vector Omega. lightdir: Light vector Omegalt. xi: User-adjustable backscattering term. betasca: Scattering coefficient. stepsize: Delta. Returns: eyebuffer: Accumulated radiance. lightbuffer: Attenuation buffer. """ # Initialize buffers eyebuffer = zeroslike(viewdir) lightbuffer = zeroslike(lightdir) # Determine slicing direction (halfway between view and light) slicedir = normalize(viewdir + lightdir) # Iterate through volume along slice direction for samplepoint in volume.iteratealong(slicedir, stepsize): # Calculate expected scattering events at this sample # Note: n(s) calculation depends on specific volume density integration ns = calculateexpectedscatteringevents(samplepoint, volume) # Determine number of scattering events for angular distribution # We use n(s) + 1 because the (n+1)-th event scatters into the eye numscatterevents = ns + 1 # Get angular distribution function value # Ams is the pre-computed multiple scattering angular distribution anglediff = anglebetween(viewdir, lightdir) angulardist = Ams.lookup(numscatterevents, anglediff) # Calculate transmittance from ray start to current sample # T(s, sf) represents attenuation from the beginning of the ray transmittancetosample = calculatetransmittance(samplepoint, volume.startpoint, volume) # Calculate intensity contribution # Using worst-case attenuation approximation for hardware efficiency # I(s) = I(sprev) T + I(sprev) (1 - T) (AngularDist + xi) betasca Delta # Note: I(sprev) is the incoming intensity, which includes direct light attenuation incomingintensity = lightbuffer.getattenuation(samplepoint) # Transmittance over the step steptransmittance = exp(-volume.density(samplepoint) betasca stepsize) # Insattered light contribution # The term (angulardist + xi) models the phase function with backscattering correction inscattered = incomingintensity (1 - steptransmittance) (angulardist + xi) betasca stepsize # Accumulate into eye buffer # Weighted by transmittance from the start of the ray to the current sample eyebuffer.add(samplepoint, transmittancetosample inscattered) # Update light buffer with attenuation lightbuffer.updateattenuation(samplepoint, steptransmittance) # Add skylight and aerial perspective effects eyebuffer.addskylight(volume, viewdir, lightdir) return eyebuffer, lightbuffer Premature Darkening: Rendering without backscattered light causes the region where light first strikes the cloud to appear unnaturally dark. This is corrected by adding the term \xi to the phase function. Hardware Limitations: The original implementation avoided linear interpolation for floating-point textures due to hardware limitations of the time, instead using a worst-case attenuation approximation for efficiency. Accuracy: The model is least accurate in dense inner regions of the cloud. Time Complexity: Single pass through the volume, making it highly efficient for real-time or near-real-time rendering. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for Eye Buffer and Light Buffer, plus pre-computed angular distribution functions. Strengths: Efficient rendering on programmable graphics hardware; captures fine angularly dependent chromatic effects (rainbows, halos, glories); avoids premature darkening artifacts. Limitations: Least accurate in dense inner regions of the cloud; relies on pre-computed angular distribution functions which may limit flexibility for arbitrary phase functions. When to use: Suitable for atmospheric phenomena like clouds and fog where forward multiple scattering and chromatic effects are important, and hardware efficiency is a priority. When not to use: Not suitable for highly dense, optically thick media where the single-pass approximation breaks down in inner regions. The method was proposed by Riley et al. [76] as part of a multiple model system for fast rendering of atmospheric effects. It was designed to handle the forward multiple scattering behavior of large water and ice atmospheric particles. The core idea is to use multiple scattering angular distribution functions to approximate the distribution of light after a certain number of scattering events. It builds on the half-angle slicing scheme introduced by Kniss et al. [45]. The method is cited in surveys on participating media rendering as an example of efficient, hardware-accelerated approaches for atmospheric phenomena. Efficient Rendering of Atmospheric Phenomena, https://doi.org/10.2312/egwr/egsr04/375-386, fetched 2026-10-26 A survey on participating media rendering techniques, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00371-005-0287-1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: 3D-Filter / Concrete Directions
head: 3D-Filter / Nishita, Nishita et al. 3D-Filter, 3D-Filter / N Directions, Concrete Directions Method
body: The 3D-Filter method approximates multiple scattering in participating media by representing the directional distribution of radiance using extended form factors within a voxel grid. It solves the problem of computationally prohibitive multiple scattering integration by precomputing a "contribution-ratio pattern" (the 3D-filter) that encodes how energy from neighboring voxels contributes to the radiance of a center voxel in the viewing direction. Unlike sibling methods that may use diffusion equations or stochastic path tracing for the full angular distribution, this approach restricts the solution to specific scattering orders (typically up to third order) and exploits the forward-scattering nature of media like clouds to accelerate the calculation of these form factors. Inputs: A voxelized representation of the participating medium (e.g., a cloud or snow volume). The viewing direction \omegav. The sunlight direction \omegas. The mean density of the cloud \bar{\rho}. Single scattering radiance contribution L{ss}. Outputs: Total radiance L(x) at each voxel x in the viewing direction. The method relies on a 3D grid of voxels. The space including the medium is subdivided into voxels, with the viewing direction defined as the principal axis of the grid. 1. Voxel Grid: Stores the density and optical properties of the medium. 2. 3D-Filter (Contribution-Ratio Pattern): A precomputed data structure representing the extended form factors. It stores the contribution ratios to the radiance of a center voxel from other voxels, taking into account the sunlight direction. Layout: For a center voxel, the filter contains weights corresponding to neighboring voxels that effectively contribute to the radiance in the viewing direction. Content: The filter stores the light scattered due to second and third-order scattering in the viewing direction. 1. Voxelization: Subdivide the space including the medium into voxels, aligning the viewing direction as the principal axis. 2. Define Reference Space: Set up a smaller reference space characterized by the mean density of the cloud \bar{\rho}. This simplifies the computation of form factors by assuming uniform density for the filter generation. 3. Compute 3D-Filter (Precomputation): Calculate the contribution ratios to the radiance of a center voxel (in the viewing direction) from other voxels in the reference space, considering the sunlight direction. This calculation constitutes the "contribution-ratio pattern" or 3D-filter. Optimization: Since scattering in media like clouds is mainly forward, energy scattered at a point lies within a small solid angle. Use this fact to compute extended form factors faster by concentrating effort on voxels that effectively contribute to the center voxel for paths with one or two scatterings. Selection: Use a stochastic method to select the voxels that effectively contribute to the center voxel. Orders: Consider only the first three orders of scattering for multiple scattering of sunlight to save computation time. Second-order scattering is explicitly handled in the filter. 4. Apply Filter to Medium: Apply the precomputed 3D-filter to the voxels in the whole space. For each voxel, multiply the form factors (from the filter) by the energy at the related points (neighboring voxels). Accumulate these results to obtain the multiple scattering radiance component L{ms}(x). Store the light scattered due to second and third-order scattering in the viewing direction for each voxel. 5. Compute Single Scattering: Compute the single scattering contribution L{ss}(x) separately. 6. Accumulate Radiance: Combine the single scattering and multiple scattering components to obtain the final radiance L(x). L(x) = L{ss}(x) + L{ms}(x) Radiance: L(x) is the total radiance at position x in the viewing direction. Multiple Scattering Orders: The method considers only the first three orders of scattering for sunlight. Order 1: Single scattering (computed separately). Order 2 & 3: Handled by the 3D-filter. Contribution Ratio: The weight w{ij} in the 3D-filter represents the ratio of radiance contribution from voxel j to voxel i in the viewing direction, given the sunlight direction. Energy Accumulation: L{ms}(xi) = \sum{j} w{ij} \cdot Ej where Ej is the energy at voxel j. Scattering Orders: Typically limited to the first three orders (single, second, third) to save computation time. Mean Density: The reference space uses the mean density of the cloud \bar{\rho}. Stochastic Selection: A stochastic method is used to select contributing voxels. The specific number of directions or samples is not detailed in the sources, but the method relies on selecting voxels that effectively contribute. Forward Scattering Assumption: The method relies on the fact that scattering is mainly forward (e.g., in clouds) to optimize the form factor calculation. This may be less accurate for media with strong backward scattering. Mean Density Approximation: Using a smaller space with mean density for the filter may introduce errors if the density distribution is highly heterogeneous. Limited Scattering Orders: By considering only the first three orders, the method may underestimate radiance in very thick or highly scattering media where higher-order scattering is significant. Time Complexity: The precomputation of the 3D-filter is optimized by focusing on contributing voxels and using stochastic selection, reducing the cost compared to computing form factors between all voxel pairs. The application of the filter is a convolution-like operation over the voxel grid. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the voxel grid and the 3D-filter data structure. Strengths: Efficiently handles multiple scattering in media like clouds and snow by exploiting forward scattering and limiting scattering orders. Limitations: Approximate nature due to limited scattering orders and mean density assumption; less suitable for media with non-forward scattering characteristics. When to Use: Suitable for rendering clouds and snow where multiple scattering is significant and forward scattering dominates. The 3D-Filter method was proposed by Nishita et al.. It was originally developed to display clouds taking into account multiple scattering and sky light. The method computes radiance from a cloud reaching the eye as sunlight multiple scattered plus skylight single scattered by the particles of the cloud. It has also been applied to render snow, which has a high albedo and looks white due to multiple scattering, with shape and density distribution modeled using metaballs. The approach is part of a broader family of methods that use implicit representations of directional distribution, such as scattering patterns and diffusion equations. name: Multiple Scattering
head: Multiple Scattering Simulation
body: Multiple scattering simulates light transport where photons undergo more than one scattering event within a participating medium. It solves the problem of rendering dense media, such as thick clouds or smoke, which appear dark and lifeless under single scattering approximations because they fail to capture the internal light bouncing that contributes significantly to their brightness and color. It is distinguished from single scattering by its ability to model the recursive dependency of radiance on itself, though it incurs a multiplicative computational cost for each additional bounce. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volume density fields (extinction \sigmat, scattering \sigmas, absorption \sigmaa), phase function p(\omega', \omega), and a "Volume Trace Depth" parameter controlling the maximum number of scattering bounces. Outputs: Final radiance L at the camera pixel, accounting for light that has scattered multiple times before escaping the volume. Data Structures: The method builds on the standard volume rendering data structures defined in the parent article [10687-multiple-scattering-models.md], specifically the radiative transfer equation (RTE) and optical depth calculations. Steps: 1. Ray Marching: Cast a ray from the camera into the volume. 2. Bounce Simulation: For each scattering event encountered, determine the new direction based on the phase function. 3. Recursive Integration: Instead of terminating the path after one scatter (single scattering), continue tracing the ray for up to N bounces, where N is the Volume Trace Depth. 4. Accumulation: Accumulate the scattered radiance from each bounce, weighted by the transmittance and scattering albedo \omega0 = \sigmas / \sigmat. 5. Termination: Stop when the maximum bounce depth is reached. Parameters: Volume Trace Depth: Controls the number of scattering bounces simulated. Typical tested values include 1 (single scattering), 5, and 31. Scattering Strength: The scattering coefficient must be sufficiently high for the intensity of the scattered light to be visible. Pitfalls: Noise: Unbiased rendering of multiple scattering can be noisy due to the high variance in path contributions. Performance: Every added bounce multiplies the computational work, making dense media rendering significantly slower. Denoising Difficulty: Volumes are harder to denoise than surfaces because helper data like surface normals does not exist inside a cloud. Degenerate Input: If scattering strength is too low, multiple scattering effects will be invisible regardless of the trace depth. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendermultiplescattering(rayorigin, raydirection, volume, maxbounces, rng): """ Simulates multiple scattering for a given ray. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, camera ray origin. raydirection: 3D vector, camera ray direction. volume: Object with methods getsigmat(pos), getsigmas(pos), getsigmaa(pos), getphase(pos), getemissive(pos). maxbounces: The Volume Trace Depth parameter. rng: Random number generator returning uniform [0, 1). Returns: L: Accumulated radiance [R, G, B]. """ L = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] throughput = 1.0 currentpos = rayorigin currentdir = raydirection for bounce in range(maxbounces): # 1. Sample distance to next scattering event using optical depth sigmat = volume.getsigmat(currentpos) if sigmat <= 0: # Empty space: advance far or break depending on volume bounds currentpos += 1000.0 currentdir continue # Exponential sampling for free path length: t = -ln(1 - rand) / sigmat t = -log(1.0 - rng()) / sigmat # 2. Check volume boundary if t > 1000.0: break currentpos += t currentdir # 3. Calculate transmittance to this point: T(t) = exp(-sigmat t) transmittance = exp(-sigmat t) # 4. Sample scattering direction using phase function p(omega', omega) # For isotropic phase function p = 1/(4pi), sample uniformly on sphere # omegas = samplephasefunction(volume.getphase(currentpos), currentdir, rng) # Simplified: assume isotropic scattering for self-containment omegas = currentdir # 5. Update throughput with scattering albedo omega0 = sigmas / sigmat sigmas = volume.getsigmas(currentpos) omega0 = sigmas / sigmat if sigmat > 0 else 0.0 throughput = transmittance omega0 # 6. Accumulate contribution from this bounce emissive = volume.getemissive(currentpos) L[0] += throughput emissive[0] L[1] += throughput emissive[1] L[2] += throughput emissive[2] # 7. Continue ray for next bounce currentdir = omegas return L Note: The pseudocode above is a simplified path-tracing representation. The sources do not provide a specific closed-form formula for the multiple scattering integral solution, but describe the process as following rays through many bounces. Link Link Link Link Link Time Complexity: Computational work multiplies with every added bounce. Rendering time increases significantly with higher Volume Trace Depth values. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: In Blender's Cycles, unbiased rendering of multiple scattering is noisy and often disabled by default due to performance costs. Strengths: Accurately renders dense media like clouds and smoke, which appear realistic with many scattering bounces. Limitations: Noisy results; high computational cost; difficult to denoise due to lack of surface normals. When to use: For dense participating media like clouds, smoke, or thick fog where single scattering appears too dark. When not to use: For thin media like light haze, where single scattering is sufficient and faster; for materials like skin or milk, where subsurface scattering is more efficient. Multiple scattering is a fundamental concept in radiative transfer theory, essential for simulating real-world effects like scattering in clouds and subsurface scattering. The term "multiple scattering" refers to the effect resulting from more than one scattering bounce. In computer graphics, it has been a challenge due to its computational expense, leading to the development of various approximations and hybrid methods. The concept is widely used in volume rendering engines, though often limited by default settings to maintain performance. name: Hybrid Hair/Fur Rendering Strategy
head: Hybrid Hair/Fur Rendering with Volumetric Multiple Scattering Approximation, Hybrid Rendering Strategy for Hair/Fur, Hybrid light transport estimator, Volumetric Approximation for Hair/Fur Multiple Scattering
body: This method approximates multiple scattering in dense hair and fur by combining explicit geometric rendering for direct illumination with a volumetric participating medium model for higher-order scattering. It solves the computational bottleneck of simulating dozens of light bounces between fibers by treating the aggregate hair volume as an anisotropic medium, preserving high-frequency strand details while efficiently capturing soft volumetric glow. Unlike microflake models that assume opaque particles, this approach normalizes the hair BCSDF to define the phase function, preserving complex transmission paths. The method employs a hybrid geometric–volumetric representation. Explicit fiber geometry handles direct lighting and first-bounce interactions to preserve fine details, while an equivalent anisotropic participating medium approximates the low-frequency, multi-bounce transport. Inputs: Hair/fur geometry (strands), hair scattering model (BCSDF), lighting environment, camera parameters. Outputs: Rendered image with direct and multiple scattering contributions. 1. Volumetric Medium: Derived from voxelized hair geometry. Fields: Local fiber density, average fiber orientation (tangent), extinction coefficient \sigmat, absorption coefficient \sigmaa, scattering coefficient \sigmas, and anisotropic phase function P. Layout: Heterogeneous grid where properties vary per voxel based on local strand density and orientation. 2. Albedo Map: Precomputed 1D function of incident inclination angle \thetai relative to local fiber direction, derived from the hair BCSDF. N: Number of octaves in the multiple scattering summation. a: Scalar controlling effective attenuation, allowing deeper light penetration for higher-order terms. \gamma: Scalar gain in [0, 2] to moderate excessive color saturation. c: Parameter in [0, 1] controlling the rate at which higher-order scattering becomes isotropic. Base Model: Yan et al. [2017a] double-cylinder fur model (accounts for cuticle, cortex, medulla). 1. Precomputation (Voxelization): Voxelize the hair geometry to compute local fiber densities and average orientations. Derive the equivalent volumetric medium properties (\sigmat, \sigmas, \sigmaa, P) from the hair fiber distribution. The albedo is precomputed as a function of the incident inclination angle \thetai. 2. Rasterization Pass: Accumulate per-pixel visibility and hair density in screen space. 3. First Geometric Interaction (Direct Lighting): Trace camera rays to find the first intersection with explicit hair geometry. Compute direct illumination using an arbitrary hair BCSDF and standard next-event estimation. Ensure the same scattering model is used consistently for the subsequent volumetric representation. 4. Transition to Medium: Sample an outgoing direction from the hair BCSDF at the first hit. Propagate the light path into the surrounding hair volume. Restrict geometric interactions to at most one; all subsequent transport is handled exclusively in the equivalent participating medium. 5. Single Scattering in Medium: Sample a scattering point p along the view ray using delta tracking in the heterogeneous medium. Select a random light direction \omegai. March along \omegai to evaluate transmittance and direct illumination at p. Evaluate the transmittance T along the shadow ray using ray marching through the medium: T = \exp \left( -\int0^t \sigmat(x(s), \omegai) ds \right) This yields the single-scattering estimate L{single}. 6. Multiple Scattering Approximation: Reweight the single-scattering estimate to approximate higher-order scattering. The total volumetric contribution L is a sum of N octaves: L = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} Li where each octave Li is defined as: Li = \sigmas(p, \omegai) (\gamma \cdot \text{Albedo}(p, \omegai))^i L{light}(\omegai) P'i(\omegai, \omegao) Ti L{light}(\omegai): Incident radiance from the light source. \text{Albedo}(p, \omegai): Local RGB albedo at point p for direction \omegai. Using RGB albedo (rather than a scalar) preserves spectral energy redistribution. P'i(\omegai, \omegao): Modified phase function for octave i. Ti: Transmittance for octave i, using parameter a to control attenuation: Ti = \exp \left( -ai \int0^t \sigmat(x(s), \omegai) ds \right) Modified Phase Function: Linearly interpolate between the original hair phase function P and an isotropic phase function P{iso}: P'i(\omegai, \omegao) = \text{lerp}(P(\omegai, \omegao), P{iso}, 1 - c^i) Here, c \in [0, 1] controls the rate of isotropization. Evaluation: The summation is evaluated stochastically by sampling a single octave i according to its relative contribution, or deterministically by accumulating all terms. 7. Compositing: Combine the direct geometric contribution and the approximated multiple scattering contribution to produce the final pixel color. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderhairfur(cameraray, hairgeometry, lightsources, mediumparams): # 1. First Geometric Interaction hit = hairgeometry.intersect(cameraray) if hit is None: return backgroundcolor # Compute direct illumination on explicit geometry directradiance = 0.0 for light in lightsources: shadowray = hit.point + light.direction distance # Standard next-event estimation with hair BCSDF directradiance += evaluatebcsdf(hit, light, shadowray) # 2. Transition to Medium # Sample outgoing direction from BCSDF outgoingdir = samplebcsdfoutgoing(hit, cameraray.direction) # 3. Single Scattering in Equivalent Medium # Sample scattering point p using delta tracking p = deltatrack(cameraray, mediumparams.sigmatmax) if p is not None: # Select random light direction lightsample = randomlightdirection(lightsources) # Ray march to evaluate transmittance and direct illumination # This corresponds to the single-scattering estimate transmittance = raymarchtransmittance(p, lightsample, mediumparams.sigmat) incidentradiance = evaluatelightsource(lightsample) # Base single scattering term sigmas = mediumparams.sigmas(p, lightsample) albedo = mediumparams.albedo(p, lightsample) # RGB albedo phase = mediumparams.phase(p, lightsample, outgoingdir) singlescatteringestimate = sigmas albedo incidentradiance phase transmittance # 4. Multiple Scattering Approximation # Stochastic evaluation: sample one octave octaveindex = sampleoctave(mediumparams.N) # Calculate octave-specific parameters # Gamma moderates saturation albedoterm = (mediumparams.gamma albedo) octaveindex # Modified phase function: lerp between original and isotropic # c controls isotropization rate isotropicphase = 1.0 / (4.0 pi) originalphase = mediumparams.phase(p, lightsample, outgoingdir) modifiedphase = lerp(originalphase, isotropicphase, 1.0 - mediumparams.c octaveindex) # Attenuation parameter 'a' allows deeper penetration for higher orders # ai is derived from base 'a' and octave index ai = mediumparams.a (1.0 + octaveindex 0.1) # Heuristic for ai scaling octavetransmittance = exp(-ai raymarchopticaldepth(p, lightsample, mediumparams.sigmat)) multiplescatteringcontribution = sigmas albedoterm incidentradiance modifiedphase octavetransmittance # Composite finalradiance = directradiance + multiplescatteringcontribution else: finalradiance = directradiance return finalradiance Spectral Variation: The derived phase function is spectrally varying. However, the method avoids per-channel sampling by evaluating the phase function only for a deterministic outgoing direction during single-scattering estimation. Color Saturation: Using a scalar contribution factor instead of local RGB albedo leads to severe color loss. Repeated application of albedo can cause excessive saturation, mitigated by the gain parameter \gamma. Tightly Coiled Hair: The method struggles to reproduce localized bright spots from intense multiple backscattering in highly scattering, tightly coiled hair (e.g., white Afro), approximating them as macroscopic energy distribution instead. Performance: Achieves a 7.1× to 11.06× speedup compared to ground truth path tracing at the same noise level. It is 2.7× to 3.26× faster than Extended Dual Scattering. Timing: On human hair, renders an image in 1.17 minutes on average, compared to 9.98 minutes for path tracing (8.53× speedup) and 2.27 minutes for Dual Scattering (1.94× speedup). On fur scenes, achieves an average speedup of 3.84× (1.17 minutes vs. 4.49 minutes) compared to Extended Dual Scattering. Samples: Requires 256 SPP for equal visual quality, whereas path tracing and Dual Scattering require 512 SPP. Strengths: Preserves high-frequency details via explicit geometry while efficiently capturing soft volumetric glow. Robust under various lighting conditions (studio, environment, directional, spot). Limitations: Cannot reproduce localized bright spots from intense multiple backscattering in tightly coiled hair. Assumes dense hair/fur behaves as a continuous medium, which may fail for sparse or lifted flyaway strands where voxel-based accumulation underestimates scattering. The method was proposed by Hu, Zhu, Lin, and Zhang, building on the observation that dense hair aggregates behave like an anisotropic participating medium. It addresses the limitations of prior approximations like Dual Scattering and Fur BSSRDF, which often yield dry or blurred appearances in dense hair. The implementation was demonstrated in Mitsuba 0.6. Parameters were obtained via numerical optimization using Ceres Solver with an L1 loss on a scene with three area lights. Efficient Fur and Hair Multiple Scattering Using Volumetric Approximation, https://doi.org/10.1145/3811343, fetched 2026-11-01

name: Optically Thin Approximation Correction
head: Exospheric Optical Depth Correction, Self-absorption and Secondary Scattering Correction
body: The Optically Thin Approximation Correction improves the accuracy of the single-scattering approximation by modeling photon loss due to absorption and secondary scattering along the light path. It addresses the error introduced when assuming no attenuation between the light source, the scattering volume, and the observer. Unlike the base Single Scattering Approximation, it applies exponential reduction factors for optical depth along the Sun-to-scatterer path and the scatterer-to-observer path. Inputs: Density field \rho defined on a voxel grid. Line-of-sight (LOS) parameterization S for each pixel, defined by origin, direction, and step size \Delta l. Index arrays r, e, a defining the voxel traversal along S. Cross-section \sigma, dependent on local exospheric temperature. Forward tomographic operator F (or its sunward variant F1). Outputs: Corrected radiance I{corr} for each pixel. Data Structures: Arrays r, e, a: Indices mapping the LOS traversal to the voxel grid. Size: N{steps} per LOS. Array \Delta l: Step lengths along the LOS. Size: N{steps} per LOS. Array \rho: Density values at voxel centroids. Size: N{voxels}. Formulas: The corrected radiance is given by: I{corr} = \int F \rho e^{-\tau1} e^{-\tau2} dl where: F is the forward tomographic operator. \tau1 is the optical depth along path S1 (Sun to scattering point Ps). \tau2 is the optical depth along path S2 (scattering point Ps to spacecraft). The optical depths are calculated as cumulative sums of \sigma \rho \Delta l along the respective paths. Steps: 1. Calculate \tau1 for each scattering point Ps along the LOS. This requires a sunward ray trace from Ps to the Sun. 2. Calculate \tau2 for each scattering point Ps along the LOS. This is the optical depth from Ps to the observer along the LOS S. 3. Compute the correction factors e^{-\tau1} and e^{-\tau2}. 4. Discretize the integral as an inner product using the custom raytracer operator F1 and cumulative summation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeopticallythincorrection(rho, indices, deltal, sigma): """ Computes the optically thin approximation correction. rho: density array [Nvoxels] indices: list of arrays [r, e, a] for each LOS, each of length Nsteps deltal: step lengths array [Nsteps] sigma: cross-section array [Nvoxels] """ import math Nsteps = len(deltal) Npixels = len(indices) Icorr = [] for i in range(Npixels): r, e, a = indices[i] # Step 1: Compute tau2 (Secondary scattering / Observer path) # Reuse LOS arrays r, e, a and deltal because S2 lies along S tau2steps = [sigma[r[j]] rho[r[j]] deltal[j] for j in range(Nsteps)] # Cumulative sum from the end to get optical depth from point to observer tau2 = [0.0] Nsteps runningsum = 0.0 for j in range(Nsteps - 1, -1, -1): runningsum += tau2steps[j] tau2[j] = runningsum tau2[-1] = 0.0 # Step 2: Compute tau1 (Self-absorption / Sun path) # F1 is a custom raytracer operator with LOS originating at voxel centroid and propagating sunwards # Approximation: voxel centroids do not lie directly on path S1 tau1 = [0.0] Nsteps for j in range(Nsteps): # The sources do not specify the exact voxel traversal algorithm for F1 tau1[j] = 0.0 # Step 3: Compute correction factors correction = [0.0] Nsteps for j in range(Nsteps): correction[j] = math.exp(-tau1[j]) math.exp(-tau2[j]) # Step 4: Discretize integral as inner product # Icorr = F rho correction. deltal sourceterm = [sigma[r[j]] rho[r[j]] correction[j] for j in range(Nsteps)] Icorrval = sum(sourceterm[j] deltal[j] for j in range(Nsteps)) Icorr.append(Icorrval) return Icorr Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Voxel Centroid Approximation: The operator F1 is an approximation because voxel centroids do not lie directly on the path S1 (Sun to scatterer). This introduces geometric error. Temperature Dependence: The cross-section \sigma depends on local exospheric temperature. Performance: Computing \tau1 requires a separate ray trace for each scattering point, which is computationally expensive. Time Complexity: O(N{pixels} \cdot N{steps}) for the base approximation. The correction adds O(N{pixels} \cdot N{steps}) for \tau2 (reuse of LOS arrays) and O(N{pixels} \cdot N{steps\sunward}) for \tau1 (sunward ray trace). The sunward trace is the bottleneck. Memory Complexity: O(N{voxels}) for density and cross-section arrays. Additional O(N{steps}) per pixel for intermediate calculations. Strengths: Improves accuracy of optically thin approximations in planetary exospheres by accounting for self-absorption and secondary scattering. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to the need for sunward ray tracing. Approximation error from voxel centroid alignment. When to use: When high accuracy is required for optically thin media, such as planetary exospheres, and computational resources allow for additional ray tracing. When not to use: For real-time applications where performance is critical, or for optically thick media where multiple scattering dominates. The method was introduced by J. H. Zoennchen et al. (2024) in the context of the TomoSphero framework for planetary and solar tomography. It extends the single-scattering approximation to better model photon loss in exospheric environments. TomoSphero: Fast Differentiable Projector for Planetary and Solar Tomography on Spherical Grids, https://doi.org/10.3847/1538-4357/ae6db5, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Photon-based Methods
body: Photon-based methods solve the problem of estimating radiance in participating media by decoupling light transport into a preprocessing phase (photon tracing) and a rendering phase (radiance estimation via density estimation or virtual light sources). Unlike direct integration methods that trace paths per pixel, these methods store photon interactions in spatial structures and estimate incident radiance at query points using kernel density estimation or explicit summation. What sets this family apart from its siblings is the specific use of stored photon data (points, beams, or surfaces) to approximate the integral of the radiance transfer equation, differing from the explicit path tracing of Compute Shader Photon Integration and the boundary-segment sampling of Grid-based Importance Sampling for Boundary Segments. Inherits core definitions and mechanisms from Single and multiple scattering. Solves the problem of computing realistic in-scattering and indirect illumination by decoupling light transport simulation from final image synthesis. Unlike direct integration methods, it stores photon interactions in a spatial data structure and estimates radiance via density estimation or direct contribution summation. Distinguished from Photon Beam Mapping and Adaptive Beam Tracing for Volume Caustics by using discrete point-based representations, and from Instant Radiosity / Virtual Point Lights (VPLs) by explicitly tracking photon paths through scattering events rather than approximating them as point light sources. Provides a preprocessing-based importance sampling strategy for boundary path integrals in differentiable rendering. It addresses the difficulty of analytically computing the probability density P(\mathbf{x}B, \boldsymbol{\omega}B) by discretizing it into a regular 3D grid. Unlike standard path guiding, it is specifically designed for the boundary integrals required for gradient computation. It builds on Photon-based Methods by applying photon/importon map concepts to the low-dimensional boundary space. Replaces discrete photon points with continuous photon beams to create a more compact representation of light transport. By storing light transport as beams rather than points, it achieves faster convergence for media such as fog compared to standard photon mapping. It operates in two phases: a lighting pass that stores light transport as photon beams, and a rendering pass that uses a beam-to-beam estimator to gather contributions. A real-time algorithm for rendering surface and volume caustics in single-scattering participating media. It solves the problem of efficiently capturing high-frequency light transport patterns formed by specular reflections and refractions without the prohibitive cost of path tracing. Unlike sibling methods which trace individual rays or photons, this method traces volumetric beams of light. It differs from Grid-based Importance Sampling for Boundary Segments by generating beams adaptively from a projected grid in light space, refining resolution based on geometric discontinuities and beam contribution, thereby reducing fill-rate in defocused regions. Computes indirect illumination by approximating the global illumination solution by treating stored photons as discrete light sources rather than using density estimation. It solves the problem of efficiently calculating diffuse interreflection and caustics on surfaces by replacing the complex integral of incoming radiance with a summation of contributions from a smaller set of virtual point lights. Unlike sibling methods such as Photon-based Estimation, which rely on kernel density estimation to smooth photon contributions, VPLs require explicit visibility computation for each light, resulting in significantly fewer samples but introducing singularity artifacts at close distances. Extends photon beam tracing to handle multiple scattering events by spawning new discrete beams from existing ones. 1. For a discrete beam b0, choose a random propagation distance ts for the scattering event location. 2. In homogeneous media, compute ts = -\log(1-\xi)/\sigmat. 3. In heterogeneous media, use inversion method or delta-tracking. 4. Initiate a new discrete beam b1 with origin x{b1} = x{b0} + ts \tilde{\omega}{b0}, direction \tilde{\omega}{b1} sampled from f(\theta), and starting power \Phi{b1} = (\sigmas/\sigmat) \Phi{b0}. 5. Continue photon marching of the parent beam b0 to the media's boundary. The scattering distance ts is determined by the probability density function pdf(ts) = \sigmat e^{-\sigmat ts}, leading to the inverse transform sampling formula: ts = -\frac{\log(1-\xi)}{\sigmat} where \xi is a uniform random number in 0, 1) and \sigmat is the total extinction coefficient. The scattering albedo \sigmas/\sigmat is used for [Russian roulette. If the scattering event is accepted, the starting power of the new beam simplifies to \Phi{b1} = \Phi{b0} in grey media. A new technique based on the lattice-Boltzmann method able to deal with diffusion processes involved in participating medium illumination problems. It uses a simple grid-based photon transport model able to handle complex boundary conditions. No interaction between light and surfaces is considered. Not given in the sources. A comprehensive theory of volumetric radiance estimation using photon points and beams, https://doi.org/10.1145/1899404.1899409, fetched 2026-10-26 A survey on participating media rendering techniques, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00371-005-0287-1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Photon-based Estimation
body: Photon-based estimation methods solve the light transport problem in participating media by decoupling the simulation of light paths from the final image synthesis. Instead of integrating the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) directly via ray marching or path tracing, these methods store photon interactions (positions, directions, and energy) in a spatial data structure and estimate radiance at render time via density estimation. Density estimation approaches are the most commonly used solutions for participating media rendering, since they support all types of scattering. Photon-based estimation relies on the following shared mechanisms and mathematical foundations: 1. Photon Emission and Tracing: Photons are emitted from light sources and traced through the scene. When a photon enters a participating medium, it undergoes a random walk. The step size t between interactions is sampled from the extinction coefficient \sigmat: t = -\frac{\ln(r)}{\sigmat} where r is a uniform random number in [0, 1]. 2. Interaction Handling: At each step, the photon's fate is determined by the ratio of absorption \sigmaa and scattering \sigmas to the total extinction \sigmat = \sigmaa + \sigmas. Scattering: The photon's direction is updated using a phase function p(\omegai, \omegao), and its energy is attenuated by the scattering albedo \omega = \sigmas / \sigmat. Absorption: The photon is terminated or its energy is reduced. Null Collisions: In heterogeneous media, a majorant \sigma{\text{max}} \ge \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) is used. Steps are sampled using \sigma{\text{max}}, and a null collision occurs with probability P{\text{null}} = (\sigma{\text{max}} - \sigmat)/\sigma{\text{max}}, where the photon continues without interaction but with transmittance adjustment. 3. Storage: Interactions are stored in a spatial data structure tailored to the specific variant. Implementations use KD-trees for nearest-neighbor queries, volume textures for GPU acceleration [2190-volumetric-photon-mapping.md], or bounding volume hierarchies for beam-based representations [2275-photon-beam-storage-in-bvh.md]. 4. Density Estimation (Gathering): During rendering, for a point \mathbf{x} on a camera ray, the in-scattered radiance Ls(\mathbf{x}) is estimated by gathering nearby stored photons. The general form is: Ls(\mathbf{x}) \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \frac{Pi}{Vi} K\left(\frac{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}i\|}{r}\right) p(\omegai, \omegao) where N is the number of photons in the search radius r, Pi is the power of the i-th photon, Vi is the volume of influence or a normalization factor, K is a kernel function, and p(\omegai, \omegao) is the phase function. 5. Integration: The estimated in-scattered radiance is integrated along the camera ray using the transmittance T: L(\mathbf{x}0, \omega0) = L0 T(\mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{x}n) + \sum{j=1}^{n} T(\mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{x}{j-1}) \sigmas(\mathbf{x}j) Ls(\mathbf{x}j) \Delta sj. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def photonbasedestimationsharedpipeline(scene, camera, numphotons): # Phase 1: Photon Emission and Tracing photonmap = [] for in range(numphotons): photon = emitphoton(scene.lightsources) while photonalive(photon): sigmat = scene.extinction(photon.position) step = -math.log(random()) / sigmat photon.position += photon.direction step # Interaction handling (simplified) if random() < scene.scatteringalbedo(photon.position): photon.direction = samplephasefunction(scene.phase, photon.direction) photon.energy = scene.scatteringalbedo(photon.position) else: photonalive = False photonmap.append(photon) # Phase 2: Density Estimation and Integration image = zeros(camera.resolution) for pixel in camera.rays: ray = pixel.ray totalradiance = 0.0 t = 0.0 while t < ray.maxdistance: samplepos = ray.origin + ray.direction t gatheredenergy = densityestimation(photonmap, samplepos, searchradius=0.7) transmittance = exp(-scene.extinction(samplepos) t) totalradiance += transmittance gatheredenergy scene.scatteringcoefficient(samplepos) stepsize t += stepsize image[pixel] = totalradiance return image A GPU-accelerated Monte Carlo method that processes photons in parallel using compute shaders. It differs from traditional photon mapping by directly updating radiance feedback buffers per-frame rather than storing photons in a spatial structure for later density estimation. Suitable for dynamic scenes and real-time feedback. A global illumination technique that decouples indirect illumination simulation from direct illumination. Solves realistic in-scattering and absorption in complex volumes by storing photon interactions in a spatial data structure and estimating radiance via density estimation. Sets itself apart from beam-based methods by using discrete point-to-point density estimation. Organizes photon beams into a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) to accelerate spatial queries during volumetric radiance estimation. Solves efficient retrieval of all beams intersecting a specific eye ray. Modifies BVH construction to handle highly overlapping beams by splitting them into sub-beams with unit aspect ratios. A global illumination method for homogeneous translucent materials with refractive boundaries. Decorrelates scene complexity from illumination computation by replacing the scene with a shaded point cloud (volume samples) for indirect illumination. Computes single, double, and multiple scattering contributions separately using precomputed light surface and volume samples, handling refraction at boundaries which breaks screen-space coherence. A method by Deng et al. that generalizes photon planes to photon surfaces, introducing estimators like photon cone, cylinder, and sphere, combined with Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) for robustness. Couples the light and camera subpaths using a delta kernel to avoid bias. Reduces variance significantly compared to prior work and handles any scattering event, including single scattering. However, it is unable to handle medium interactions immediately following scattering from a surface, such as volumetric caustics. Photon-based methods for participating media originated from the adaptation of photon mapping techniques, originally developed for surface rendering by Jensen. Early applications focused on homogeneous media, but the complexity of heterogeneous media and multiple scattering led to the development of specialized estimators. The survey by highlights the evolution from simple photon planes to more complex photon surfaces and beam-based representations to handle singularities and improve variance. The method is widely used in offline rendering for realistic effects like caustics in fog or smoke, and in real-time applications via GPU-accelerated variants like Compute Shader Photon Integration. A survey on rendering homogeneous participating media, https://doi.org/10.1007/s41095-021-0249-1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Compute Shader Photon Integration
head: MCM Renderer, MCCRenderer
body: Compute Shader Photon Integration is a GPU-accelerated Monte Carlo photon integration method that simulates light transport through participating media by processing photons in parallel using global invocation IDs. It differs from CPU-based photon mapping by leveraging compute shaders to perform random walk steps, handling absorption, scattering, and null collisions via probability checks, while accumulating radiance in a feedback buffer. Unlike traditional photon mapping which stores photons in a spatial data structure for later density estimation, this method directly updates radiance buffers per-frame, making it suitable for dynamic scenes or real-time feedback. Inputs: Photon Buffer: A storage buffer (std430) containing photon state structures. Volume Texture: A 3D texture storing volume density/color information. Environment Map: A 2D texture for sampling background radiance when photons exit the volume. Uniforms: uMajorant: Global majorant extinction coefficient. uAbsorptionCoefficient: Base absorption multiplier. uScatteringCoefficient: Base scattering multiplier. uAnisotropy / uScatteringBias: Henyey-Greenstein asymmetry parameter g. uMaxBounces: Maximum scattering events allowed. uSteps: Fixed number of null-collision steps per photon per frame. uColorBias, uAlphaBias, uAlphaTransfer: Blending factors for transfer function application. uMvpInverseMatrix, uInverseResolution, uBlur: Parameters for ray unprojection and jittering. Outputs: Radiance Image: A rgba32f write-only image buffer (image2D) storing the accumulated radiance. Photon State Buffers (G-buffers): Four 2D textures storing photon state for the next frame or feedback: oPosition (vec4): xyz = position, w = unused (or 0). oDirection (vec4): xyz = direction, w = bounce count. oTransmittance (vec4): rgb = transmittance, w = unused (or 0). oRadiance (vec4): rgb = accumulated radiance, w = sample count. The photon state is typically stored in a flat buffer or structured buffer accessible via std430 layout. The structure Photon contains: position: vec3 direction: vec3 transmittance: vec3 radiance: vec3 bounces: uint samples: uint 1. Dispatch and Indexing: The compute shader is dispatched with a grid size matching the number of photons. Each work item calculates its global index: \text{globalIndex} = \text{gl\GlobalInvocationID.x} + \text{gl\GlobalInvocationID.y} \times \text{gl\WorkGroupSize.x}. It loads the photon state from sPhotons[globalIndex]. 2. Photon Initialization (Reset): Generate a random ray origin and direction using unprojectRand. Set photon.direction = normalize(to - from). Intersect the ray with the volume cube (unit cube [0,1]^3) using intersectCube to get tbounds. Set photon.position = from + tbounds.x photon.direction. Reset state: photon.transmittance = vec3(1), photon.bounces = 0, photon.radiance = vec3(0), photon.samples = 0. 3. Random Walk Loop: Iterate i from 0 to uSteps - 1. Step Sampling: Sample a random number rx and compute step size: t = -\frac{\ln(rx)}{\sigma{\text{majorant}}} where \sigma{\text{majorant}} is uMajorant. Advance Position: photon.position += t photon.direction. Boundary Check: If photon.position is out of bounds (any component < 0 or > 1): Sample environment map: envSample = sampleEnvironmentMap(photon.direction). Compute radiance contribution: radiance = photon.transmittance envSample.rgb. Update radiance incrementally: L{\text{new}} = L{\text{old}} + \frac{L{\text{sample}} - L{\text{old}}}{N} where N is photon.samples. Increment photon.samples and reset photon state (return to Step 2). Volume Sampling: Sample volume color at photon.position using sampleVolumeColor. Let the result be volumeSample (vec4). Coefficient Calculation: Compute absorption coefficient: \mu{\text{absorption}} = \text{volumeSample.a} \times \text{uAbsorptionCoefficient}. Compute scattering coefficient: \mu{\text{scattering}} = \text{volumeSample.a} \times \text{uScatteringCoefficient}. Compute null coefficient: \mu{\text{null}} = \sigma{\text{majorant}} - \mu{\text{absorption}} - \mu{\text{scattering}}. Adjust majorant: \sigma{\text{majorant}}' = \mu{\text{absorption}} + \mu{\text{scattering}} + |\mu{\text{null}}|. Compute probabilities: P{\text{null}} = \frac{|\mu{\text{null}}|}{\sigma{\text{majorant}}'} P{\text{absorption}} = \frac{\mu{\text{absorption}}}{\sigma{\text{majorant}}'} P{\text{scattering}} = \frac{\mu{\text{scattering}}}{\sigma{\text{majorant}}'}. Note: Some implementations use a simplified probability model based on volume alpha and max RGB: P{\text{scattering}} = \text{volumeSample.a} \times \max(\text{volumeSample.rgb}) if bounces < uMaxBounces, else 0; P{\text{absorption}} = 1 - P{\text{null}} - P{\text{scattering}}. The majorant-based approach is more rigorous for null-collision Monte Carlo. Interaction Selection: Sample a random number ry. If ry < P{\text{absorption}}: Absorption: Update transmittance: \text{photon.transmittance} \times= 1.0 - \frac{\mu{\text{absorption}}}{\sigma{\text{majorant}}' \times P{\text{absorption}}}. (Alternatively, set radiance contribution to 0 and reset). Reset photon state (return to Step 2). Else if ry < P{\text{absorption}} + P{\text{scattering}}: Scattering: Update transmittance: \text{photon.transmittance} \times= \text{volumeSample.rgb} \times \frac{\mu{\text{scattering}}}{\sigma{\text{majorant}}' \times P{\text{scattering}}}. Sample new direction using Henyey-Greenstein phase function with parameter g (uAnisotropy). Compute \cos\theta = \frac{1 + g^2 - c^2}{2g}, where c = \frac{1 - g^2}{1 - g + 2gU} and U is a uniform random number. Compute new direction \mathbf{d}' using a random vector \mathbf{u}. Increment photon.bounces. Else: Null Collision: Update transmittance: \text{photon.transmittance} \times= \frac{\mu{\text{null}}}{\sigma{\text{majorant}}' \times P{\text{null}}}. Continue loop without changing direction or bounces. 4. Output: Write the final photon state to the output buffers (oPosition, oDirection, oTransmittance, oRadiance). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeshader(globalInvocationID, glWorkGroupSize, sPhotons, oPosition, oDirection, oTransmittance, oRadiance, volumeTexture, envMap, uMajorant, uAbsorptionCoefficient, uScatteringCoefficient, uAnisotropy, uMaxBounces, uSteps, uMvpInverseMatrix, uInverseResolution, uBlur): globalIndex = globalInvocationID.x + globalInvocationID.y glWorkGroupSize.x photon = sPhotons[globalIndex] # Reset Photon: Ray generation from screen coordinates with jitter frompos, todir = unprojectRand(uMvpInverseMatrix, uInverseResolution, uBlur) photon.direction = normalize(todir - frompos) # Ray-unit cube intersection [0,1]^3 invdir = 1.0 / photon.direction t0 = (0.0 - frompos) invdir t1 = (1.0 - frompos) invdir tbounds = min(t0, t1), max(t0, t1) photon.position = frompos + max(tbounds[0], 0.0) photon.direction photon.transmittance = vec3(1.0) photon.bounces = 0 photon.radiance = vec3(0.0) photon.samples = 0 for i in range(uSteps): rx = rand() t = -log(rx) / uMajorant photon.position += t photon.direction if any(c < 0.0 or c > 1.0 for c in photon.position): envsample = sampleenvironmentmap(envMap, photon.direction) radiancecontrib = photon.transmittance envsample.rgb N = float(photon.samples) photon.radiance = photon.radiance + (radiancecontrib - photon.radiance) / N photon.samples += 1 break volumesample = samplevolumecolor(volumeTexture, photon.position) muabs = volumesample.a uAbsorptionCoefficient muscat = volumesample.a uScatteringCoefficient munull = uMajorant - muabs - muscat sigmamajorantprime = muabs + muscat + abs(munull) Pnull = abs(munull) / sigmamajorantprime Pabs = muabs / sigmamajorantprime Pscat = muscat / sigmamajorantprime ry = rand() if ry < Pabs: photon.transmittance = 1.0 - muabs / (sigmamajorantprime Pabs) photon.radiance = vec3(0.0) photon.samples += 1 break elif ry < Pabs + Pscat: photon.transmittance = volumesample.rgb muscat / (sigmamajorantprime Pscat) # Henyey-Greenstein direction sampling U = rand() c = (1.0 - uAnisotropy2) / (1.0 - uAnisotropy + 2.0 uAnisotropy U) costheta = (1.0 + uAnisotropy2 - c2) / (2.0 uAnisotropy) photon.direction = samplehenyeygreenstein(uAnisotropy, photon.direction, costheta) photon.bounces += 1 else: photon.transmittance = munull / (sigmamajorantprime Pnull) oPosition[globalInvocationID.xy] = vec4(photon.position, 0.0) oDirection[globalInvocationID.xy] = vec4(photon.direction, float(photon.bounces)) oTransmittance[globalInvocationID.xy] = vec4(photon.transmittance, 0.0) oRadiance[globalInvocationID.xy] = vec4(photon.radiance, float(photon.samples)) def unprojectRand(uMvpInverseMatrix, uInverseResolution, uBlur): # Generates ray origin and direction from screen space with jitter pass def samplevolumecolor(texture, pos): # Fetches vec4 from 3D texture pass def sampleenvironmentmap(map, dir): # Fetches vec3 from environment map pass def samplehenyeygreenstein(g, currentdir, costheta): # Constructs new direction vector from costheta and currentdir pass uMajorant: Global majorant coefficient. Must be \ge \sigmat(\mathbf{p}) for all \mathbf{p} in the volume. uSteps: Fixed number of steps per photon. Higher values increase accuracy but cost more. uMaxBounces: Limits scattering depth. Set to 0 for single-scattering approximation. uAnisotropy: Henyey-Greenstein g parameter. g=0 is isotropic, g>0 is forward-scattering. Out-of-Bounds: If photon.position is out of bounds, sampling the volume texture may cause undefined behavior or division by zero if not checked. Always check bounds before sampling. Majorant Selection: If uMajorant is too close to the local extinction coefficient, variance increases. If too large, null collisions dominate, reducing efficiency. Precision: Using rgba32f for radiance accumulation is standard to support high dynamic range. Time: O(N \times S), where N is the number of photons and S is uSteps. Each step involves texture sampling and random number generation. Memory: O(N) for photon storage plus O(W \times H) for output buffers, where W, H are screen dimensions. Performance depends heavily on GPU compute throughput and memory bandwidth. Parallel processing of photons allows high throughput on modern GPUs. Scaling is linear with the number of photons and steps. Strengths: Fully parallelizable on GPU; suitable for dynamic scenes; no need for complex spatial data structures like BVH or KD-trees for photon storage. Limitations: High variance with few photons; requires many samples for convergence; null collisions can be inefficient if the majorant is poorly chosen. Use for real-time or near-real-time volume rendering where dynamic changes are expected. Avoid for static scenes requiring high-quality offline rendering where traditional photon mapping or path tracing might offer better convergence with spatial caching. Compute Shader Photon Integration is an implementation of Monte Carlo photon integration using GPU compute shaders. It is associated with the "MCM Renderer" and "MCCRenderer" projects. The method leverages the parallel processing capabilities of modern GPUs to accelerate photon transport simulation, which was traditionally done on CPUs. The use of null-collision Monte Carlo allows for efficient handling of heterogeneous media. name: Volumetric Photon Mapping
head: Photon Mapping in Participating Media, Real-time volume rendering for three-dimensional fetal ultrasound using volumetric photon mapping, Screen-space volumetric photon mapping, Volume Photon Map Creation, Volumetric Photon Mapping (VPM) for Fetal Ultrasound, Volumetric Photon Mapping (VPM) for Real-Time Fetal Ultrasound, Volumetric photon mapping with screen-space destiny estimation
body: Volumetric Photon Mapping (VPM) is a global illumination technique for participating media that simulates light transport by decoupling the simulation of indirect lighting from the final image synthesis. It solves the problem of efficiently capturing complex scattering effects, such as caustics and subsurface scattering, in dense media by storing photon interactions in a spatial data structure and estimating radiance during a subsequent gathering pass. Unlike direct integration methods that require expensive Monte Carlo sampling at render time, VPM pre-computes photon paths, and it is distinguished from its sibling Beam Radiance Estimate by storing discrete photon packets rather than continuous beam radiance estimates. Volumetric Photon Mapping operates in two distinct phases: a preprocessing phase to build the photon map, and a rendering phase to estimate radiance. Inputs: Scene geometry, participating media properties (extinction \sigmat, scattering \sigmas, absorption \sigmaa, phase function p), light source positions and intensities, and camera parameters. Outputs: A photon map data structure containing stored photon interactions, and a final rendered image with direct and indirect illumination. The core data structure is the Photon Map. While traditional implementations use KD-trees for nearest-neighbor queries, specific real-time implementations for ultrasound data store photons in a 3D Volume Texture to minimize storage space and accelerate gathering by avoiding time-consuming tree traversals. Volume Texture Layout: Stores photon position, incidence direction, and power (flux). Dimensions match the volume resolution or a lower-resolution grid. Fields per voxel: Position (3 floats), Direction (3 floats), Power (1 float). Standard Photon Map Layout (KD-Tree variant): Each node stores: Position (3 floats), Direction (3 floats), Power (1 float). 1. Photon Emission: Photons are emitted from light sources into the volume. To prevent wastage, photons are cast onto the volume’s boundary voxels. 2. Photon Tracing (Markov Random Walk): A photon travels through the medium. The step size t is sampled from the extinction coefficient \sigmat: t = -\frac{\ln(r)}{\sigmat} where r is a uniform random number in [0, 1]. At each step, the photon's fate is determined by the scattering albedo \omega = \sigmas / \sigmat. Scattering: If scattered, the photon's direction is updated using the phase function p(\omegai, \omegao), and its energy is attenuated by \omega. The Henyey-Greenstein phase function is commonly used: p(\theta) = \frac{1-g^2}{(1+g^2-2g\cos\theta)^{2/3}} where g \in [-1, 1] is the anisotropy coefficient. Absorption: The photon is terminated or its energy is reduced. Null Collisions: In heterogeneous media, a majorant \sigma{max} \ge \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) is used. Steps are sampled using \sigma{max}, and a null collision occurs with probability P{null} = (\sigma{max} - \sigmat)/\sigma{max}. Russian Roulette: After a certain number of interactions (e.g., three), the photon may be terminated with a probability (e.g., 50%) to limit path length. 3. Storage: When a photon interacts with the volume (scatters or is absorbed), its state is recorded. Data recorded: Position \mathbf{x}, incoming direction \omegai, and power P. These are stored in the Photon Map (Volume Texture or KD-Tree). GPU Optimization: To improve emission efficiency, threads co-complete emission tasks using a shared counter Count, initialized to 0, incremented by 1 each time a thread emits a photon, until it equals the total number of photons. 1. Ray Casting: For each pixel, a camera ray is cast into the volume. 2. Direct Illumination: Calculated separately via single scattering (SS). L{ss}(x', \omega0) = \int{\Omega} s(x', \omegai, \omega0) Li(x', \omegai) d\omegai where s is the material shading function and Li is attenuated incident radiance. 3. Indirect Illumination (Gathering): The ray is sampled at discrete points xj. For each sample point, nearby photons are gathered to estimate in-scattered radiance L{ms} (multiple scattering). Screen-Space Destiny Estimation: A novel method proposed for real-time ultrasound rendering to accelerate computation. It avoids complicated storage structures by estimating radiance in screen space. Standard Gathering (Point-to-Point): L{ms}(x') \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \frac{Pi}{Vi} K\left(\frac{\|x' - pi\|}{r}\right) p(\omegai, \omega0) where N is the number of photons in search radius r, Pi is photon power, Vi is volume of influence, K is a kernel function, and p is the phase function. Implementation Note (Pseudocode Logic): In some implementations, a search radius sqRadius (e.g., 0.7) is used. Photons within this radius contribute to the energy accumulator. The weight may be calculated based on distance and normal alignment, though specific implementations may simplify this (e.g., overwriting weight with power/numvol). 4. Integration: The total radiance along the ray is integrated using transmittance T: L(xs, \omega0) = L0(x0, \omega0)T(x0, xs) + \int{x0}^{xs} \lambdas(x') Ls(x', \omega0) T(x', xs) dx' where \lambdas is the scattering coefficient and Ls = L{ss} + L{ms}. Transmittance between samples xi and xj: T(xi, xj) = e^{-\int{xi}^{xj} \taut dt} where \taut is the extinction coefficient. For discrete samples xj: L{xn} = \sum{j=1}^{n} \prod{i=j}^{n-1} T(xi, x{i+1}) \int{x{j-1}}^{xj} T(x', xj) \sigmas(x') L{ms}(x') dx'. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumetricphotonmapping(scene, camera, numphotons): # Phase 1: Preprocessing photonmap = VolumeTexture(scene.volumeresolution) # Initialize shared counter for GPU thread co-completion count = 0 # Emit photons for photonid in range(numphotons): photon = emitphotonfromlightsource(scene) currentenergy = photon.power currentpos = photon.position currentdir = photon.direction # Trace photon through volume while currentenergy > 0 and photonalive: # Sample step size sigmat = scene.getextinction(currentpos) step = -log(random()) / sigmat # Move photon nextpos = currentpos + currentdir step # Check for interaction (simplified for homogeneous media) # In heterogeneous media, use null collisions with sigmamax if isinsidevolume(nextpos): # Determine fate sigmas = scene.getscattering(currentpos) sigmaa = scene.getabsorption(currentpos) sigmat = sigmas + sigmaa # Russian Roulette for termination if photonbounces > 3: if random() > 0.5: photonalive = False break # Scattering if random() < sigmas / sigmat: # Store photon interaction photonmap.store(currentpos, currentdir, currentenergy) # Update direction using phase function (e.g., Henyey-Greenstein) g = scene.anisotropy theta = samplephasefunction(g) currentdir = rotatedirection(currentdir, theta) # Attenuate energy currentenergy = sigmas / sigmat photonbounces += 1 else: # Absorption photonalive = False break else: # Hit surface or exit handlesurfaceinteraction(currentpos, currentdir, currentenergy) break count += 1 # Phase 2: Rendering image = createimage(camera.resolution) for pixel in camera.rays: ray = pixel.ray totalradiance = 0.0 # Direct Illumination (Single Scattering) directL = calculatedirectscattering(ray, scene) # Indirect Illumination (Multiple Scattering via Photon Map) indirectL = 0.0 t = 0.0 rayorigin = ray.origin # Ray march through volume while t < ray.maxdistance: samplepos = rayorigin + ray.direction t # Gather photons for density estimation gatheredenergy = 0.0 searchradius = 0.7 # Example value # Query photon map for nearby photons nearbyphotons = photonmap.querysphere(samplepos, searchradius) for photon in nearbyphotons: distsq = distancesq(samplepos, photon.position) if distsq < searchradius searchradius: # Calculate weight (simplified from) # Note: Some implementations use normal-based weighting, # but volume textures may simplify this. weight = photon.power / len(nearbyphotons) gatheredenergy += weight # Integrate indirect radiance # Lms contribution added to total indirectL += gatheredenergy scene.scatteringcoefficient(samplepos) stepsize t += stepsize # Combine direct and indirect transmittance = calculatetransmittance(rayorigin, rayorigin + ray.direction t, scene) finalradiance = directL transmittance + indirectL transmittance # Apply HDR tone mapping image[pixel] = applyhdr(finalradiance, exposure=0.4) return image Anisotropy coefficient g: Controls scattering direction. g \in [-1, 1]. Negative for back-scattering, 0 for isotropic, positive for forward-scattering. Exposure: Luminance value assigned to each photon. Typical values: 0.3 to 0.4. Number of Photons: Controls realism vs. speed. Higher counts improve realism but reduce FPS. Large datasets require higher counts. Samples: Number of samples per ray. Fixed at 800 in tested datasets. Search Radius: Used in gathering. Example value: 0.7. Speckle Noise: In ultrasound images, speckle noise degrades signal-to-noise ratio and makes gradient-based normal calculation unreliable. VPM is less sensitive to this than local illumination methods. Storage Overhead: Traditional KD-tree storage is memory-intensive and slow for gathering. Using volume textures mitigates this but may reduce precision. GPU Thread Scheduling: Creating a thread per photon can lead to resource wastage. Co-completing emission tasks with a shared counter improves efficiency. Normal Weighting Bug: In some implementations, the normal vector N is initialized to zero, rendering normal-based weighting ineffective. The weight is overwritten by power/numvol. Emission Term: For fetal ultrasound, emission is often ignored, simplifying the radiance transport equation. The Beam Radiance Estimate (BRE) is a photon-based technique for estimating accumulated in-scattered radiance along an entire camera ray in participating media, serving as the core gathering step for Volumetric Photon Mapping. Unlike conventional volumetric photon mapping, which estimates incident radiance at discrete points along a ray via spherical neighborhood queries, BRE queries all photons intersecting the ray line simultaneously, replacing Dirac delta and Heaviside functions with a 2D smoothing kernel perpendicular to the ray. This approach eliminates redundant photon gathering and noise associated with large step sizes in ray marching, concentrating computational effort only where photons intersect the viewing path. Photon Emission and Storage is the preprocessing phase of Volumetric Photon Mapping that generates photon paths from light sources and records their positions, directions, and energy densities into spatial data structures for both surface intersections and volumetric scattering events. It solves the problem of efficiently capturing indirect lighting and caustics in participating media by decoupling the complex light transport simulation from the final image synthesis, allowing for density estimation during a subsequent gather pass. Unlike direct integration methods, it pre-computes photon interactions, and it is distinguished from its sibling Beam Radiance Estimate by storing discrete photon packets rather than continuous beam radiance estimates. Progressive Photon Mapping is a volumetric light transport method developed by Hachisuka et al. that uses a multipass rendering technique to continuously emit photons into the image, gradually reducing inaccuracy. It builds on Volumetric Photon Mapping by applying a multipass strategy to photon emission and accumulation. It differs from sibling methods like Beam Radiance Estimate by refining illumination through iterative photon passes rather than beam-based approximations. Volumetric Photon Mapping with Radiance Transfer is a rendering technique that integrates volumetric photon mapping into a pre-designed radiance transfer procedure to achieve real-time, realistic volume rendering. It distinguishes itself from standard volumetric photon mapping by explicitly separating direct and indirect lighting computations within a radiance transfer framework, allowing for effective updates to the photon map when transfer functions change. Unlike Beam Radiance Estimate which focuses on density estimation via beam kernels, this method prioritizes the structural integration of photon data into a transfer-based rendering pipeline to handle wide intensity ranges. Time Complexity: Preprocessing is O(N) for N photons, depending on the traversal speed of the medium. Rendering is O(R \cdot S \cdot K), where R is the number of rays, S is samples per ray, and K is the cost of gathering photons (dependent on the data structure, e.g., O(1) for volume texture lookup vs O(\log N) for KD-tree). Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing N photons. Memory costly due to the requirement of a huge volumetric photon map. Volume textures reduce overhead compared to KD-trees but still require significant memory for high-resolution volumes. Measured Performance: On Intel E5, 8GB RAM, GPU: Fetus 1 (289x212x266, 800 samples, exposure 0.4, 17 photons) -> 217 FPS; Fetus 2 (183x115x126, 800 samples, exposure 0.4, 22 photons) -> 222 FPS; Fetus 3 (209x175x209, 800 samples, exposure 0.3, 18 photons) -> 218 FPS; Fetus 4 (196x128x122, 800 samples, exposure 0.4, 20 photons) -> 220 FPS. Real-time performance is maintained even when photon count increases to ten million. Strengths: Simulates realistic global illumination effects (scattering, shadows) in participating media; handles heterogeneous media; less sensitive to speckle noise in ultrasound images compared to local illumination methods. Limitations: High memory usage for large photon maps; requires GPU acceleration for real-time performance; insufficient photons on large volumes produce unrealistic results; traditional KD-tree gathering is slow. When to Use: Real-time volume rendering of participating media where global illumination effects are critical, such as medical ultrasound visualization or foggy scenes. When Not to Use: When memory is severely constrained and a simplified local illumination model is acceptable; when real-time performance is not required and path tracing is preferred for accuracy. Volumetric Photon Mapping was developed as an extension of the original photon mapping algorithm by Jensen [29], which was designed for surface global illumination. Jensen and Christensen generalized the algorithm from light travel between object surfaces to light transport in participating media by storing volumetric interactions as photons and estimating density using a 3D kernel. Later, Jarosz et al. improved convergence by gathering along camera rays (point-to-beam) and replacing photons with photon beams. The method has been applied to real-time volume rendering for 3D fetal ultrasound to overcome the limitations of local illumination methods, which produce plastic-like visuals and fail to differentiate tissues due to noise sensitivity.
