body: The Beam Radiance Estimate (BRE) is a photon-based technique for estimating accumulated in-scattered radiance along an entire camera ray in participating media, serving as the core gathering step for Volumetric Photon Mapping. Unlike conventional volumetric photon mapping, which estimates incident radiance at discrete points along a ray via spherical neighborhood queries, BRE queries all photons intersecting the ray line simultaneously, replacing Dirac delta and Heaviside functions with a 2D smoothing kernel perpendicular to the ray. This approach eliminates redundant photon gathering and noise associated with large step sizes in ray marching, concentrating computational effort only where photons intersect the viewing path. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A photon map (set of photons with position \mathbf{x}i, direction \vec{\omega}i, and weight \alphai), a camera ray defined by origin \mathbf{x}, direction \vec{\omega}, and length s, and scattering properties (\sigmas, \sigmaa). Outputs: The accumulated in-scattered radiance Lb along the ray segment [0, s]. Data Structures: 1. Photon Map: Traditionally stores 20 bytes per photon. For BRE with Variable Kernel (VK) radii, each photon stores an additional 7 floating-point values (radius and bounding box coordinates), increasing size to 46 bytes per photon. 2. Bounding-Box Hierarchy (BBH): A hierarchy constructed over "photon discs" (the 2D blur area of each photon perpendicular to the ray). It reuses the balanced kd-tree structure of the photon map. Each node stores a bounding box enclosing its photon's radius and the bounding boxes of its children. Algorithm Steps: 1. Shoot Photons: Shoot photons from light sources into the scene, recording interactions. 2. Construct kd-Tree: Build a balanced kd-tree for the photon positions. 3. Assign Photon Radius: For fixed-width kernels, use a constant radius r. For Variable Kernel (VK) method, estimate local density to assign a per-photon radius ri. Compute the distance d{i,m} to the m-th nearest neighbor in the kd-tree. Estimate the radius for n neighbors assuming uniform density: ri = d{i,m} \sqrt[3]{\frac{n}{m}} where m \ll n is a search parameter (default m = \sqrt{n}) and n controls blur amount. 4. Construct BBH: Traverse the kd-tree from leaves to root. For each node p, compute its bounding box B as the union of the bounding box of its photon disc and the bounding boxes of its children. Store B in p.bbox. The kd-tree can be freed after BBH construction. 5. Render (Gathering): For each camera ray, traverse the BBH to find all photons whose bounding spheres intersect the ray. For each intersecting photon i, compute its contribution using the radiance estimate equation. Formulas: The beam radiance estimate for a ray \mathbf{x} with direction \vec{\omega} and length s is: Lb(\mathbf{x} \leftarrow \vec{\omega}, s) \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N Ki(\mathbf{x}, \vec{\omega}, s, \mathbf{x}i, ri) Tr(\mathbf{x} \leftrightarrow \mathbf{x}'i) \sigmas(\mathbf{x}'i) p(\mathbf{x}i, \vec{\omega}, \vec{\omega}i) \alphai Where: N is the total number of photons (normalization factor for the Monte Carlo estimator). Ki is the per-photon smoothing kernel. Tr(\mathbf{x} \leftrightarrow \mathbf{x}'i) is the transmittance between the ray origin and the photon's projection. \sigmas(\mathbf{x}'i) is the scattering coefficient at the projection point. p(\mathbf{x}i, \vec{\omega}, \vec{\omega}i) is the phase function. \alphai is the photon weight. Cylindrical Coordinates: Photons are evaluated in cylindrical coordinates (ti, \thetai, ri) about the ray: ti = (\mathbf{x}i - \mathbf{x}) \cdot \vec{\omega}: Projected distance along the ray. \mathbf{x}'i = \mathbf{x} + ti \vec{\omega}: Projection of photon position onto the ray. di = \|\mathbf{x}i - \mathbf{x}'i\|: Shortest distance from photon to ray. Kernel Function: The 2D biweight kernel is used: K(\mathbf{x}, \vec{\omega}, s, \mathbf{x}i, ri) = \begin{cases} ri^{-2} K2\left(\frac{di}{ri}\right) & \text{if } di \in [0, ri] \text{ and } 0 \le ti \le s \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} K2(u) = \frac{3}{\pi}(1-u^2)^2 This kernel is normalized for 2D because the integration along the ray is handled explicitly, blurring only perpendicular to the ray. Heterogeneous Media Transmittance: For heterogeneous media, precompute transmission terms Tr(x \leftrightarrow x'i) by marching along the ray and storing values in a 1D lookup table. Interpolate within this table during gathering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computetransmittancetable(rayorigin, raydir, raylength, sigmatfunc, numsamples=100): """Marches along the ray to compute transmittance T(t) = exp(-int0^t sigmat dt).""" table = [] dt = raylength / numsamples currentt = 0.0 opticaldepth = 0.0 table.append((0.0, 1.0)) for i in range(1, numsamples + 1): currentt = i dt pos = (rayorigin[0]+raydir[0]currentt, rayorigin[1]+raydir[1]currentt, rayorigin[2]+raydir[2]currentt) opticaldepth += sigmatfunc(pos) dt table.append((currentt, math.exp(-opticaldepth))) return table def interpolatetransmittance(table, t): """Linear interpolation of transmittance from the lookup table.""" if t <= table[0][0]: return table[0][1] if t >= table[-1][0]: return table[-1][1] for i in range(len(table) - 1): if table[i][0] <= t <= table[i+1][0]: t0, v0 = table[i] t1, v1 = table[i+1] return v0 + (v1 - v0) (t - t0) / (t1 - t0) return table[-1][1] def createbboxsphere(center, radius): """Creates an axis-aligned bounding box from a sphere center and radius.""" return (center[0]-radius, center[1]-radius, center[2]-radius, center[0]+radius, center[1]+radius, center[2]+radius) def unionbbox(b1, b2): """Computes the union of two axis-aligned bounding boxes.""" return (min(b1[0], b2[0]), min(b1[1], b2[1]), min(b1[2], b2[2]), max(b1[3], b2[3]), max(b1[4], b2[4]), max(b1[5], b2[5])) def rayintersectsbbox(rayorigin, raydir, bbox): """Standard slab method for ray-AABB intersection.""" invdir = (1.0/raydir[0], 1.0/raydir[1], 1.0/raydir[2]) t1 = (bbox[0] - rayorigin[0]) invdir[0] t2 = (bbox[3] - rayorigin[0]) invdir[0] t3 = (bbox[1] - rayorigin[1]) invdir[1] t4 = (bbox[4] - rayorigin[1]) invdir[1] tmin = max(max(t1, t2), max(t3, t4)) t1 = (bbox[2] - rayorigin[2]) invdir[2] t2 = (bbox[5] - rayorigin[2]) invdir[2] tmax = min(max(t1, t2), tmin) return tmax >= tmin def rayintersectssphere(rayorigin, raydir, center, radius): """Checks if a ray intersects a sphere.""" oc = (rayorigin[0]-center[0], rayorigin[1]-center[1], rayorigin[2]-center[2]) a = raydir[0]2 + raydir[1]2 + raydir[2]2 b = 2.0 (oc[0]raydir[0] + oc[1]raydir[1] + oc[2]raydir[2]) c = oc[0]2 + oc[1]2 + oc[2]2 - radius2 discriminant = b2 - 4ac return discriminant >= 0 def evaluatephase(omegain, omegaout): """Standard phase function evaluation (e.g., Henyey-Greenstein).""" return 1.0 / (4.0 math.pi) def constructbbh(node): """Recursively constructs Bounding Box Hierarchy from kd-tree.""" bbox = createbboxsphere(node.position, node.radius) if node.leftchild is not None: leftbbox = constructbbh(node.leftchild) bbox = unionbbox(bbox, leftbbox) if node.rightchild is not None: rightbbox = constructbbh(node.rightchild) bbox = unionbbox(bbox, rightbbox) node.bbox = bbox return bbox def traversebbh(node, rayorigin, raydir, results): """Traverses BBH to find photons whose bounding spheres intersect the ray.""" if node is None: return if not rayintersectsbbox(rayorigin, raydir, node.bbox): return if node.photon is not None: if rayintersectssphere(rayorigin, raydir, node.photon.position, node.photon.radius): results.append(node.photon) traversebbh(node.leftchild, rayorigin, raydir, results) traversebbh(node.rightchild, rayorigin, raydir, results) def beamradianceestimate(rayorigin, raydir, raylength, bbhroot, sigmatfunc, N): """Estimates radiance along a ray using BBH traversal.""" totalradiance = 0.0 photonsfound = [] traversebbh(bbhroot, rayorigin, raydir, photonsfound) transmittancetable = computetransmittancetable(rayorigin, raydir, raylength, sigmatfunc) for photon in photonsfound: ti = (photon.position[0]-rayorigin[0])raydir[0] + \ (photon.position[1]-rayorigin[1])raydir[1] + \ (photon.position[2]-rayorigin[2])raydir[2] if ti < 0.0 or ti > raylength: continue xprime = (rayorigin[0]+tiraydir[0], rayorigin[1]+tiraydir[1], rayorigin[2]+tiraydir[2]) di = math.sqrt((photon.position[0]-xprime[0])2 + (photon.position[1]-xprime[1])2 + (photon.position[2]-xprime[2])2) if di > photon.radius: continue u = di / photon.radius kernelval = (1.0 - uu)2 (3.0 / math.pi) / (photon.radius2) tr = interpolatetransmittance(transmittancetable, ti) phase = evaluatephase(raydir, photon.direction) contribution = kernelval tr photon.sigmas phase photon.weight totalradiance += contribution return totalradiance / N Adaptive Beam Width is a technique for estimating radiance in participating media that uses photon differentials to dynamically adjust the smoothing kernel width of photon beams. It solves the problem of over-blurring and banding artifacts inherent in fixed-width beam estimates, particularly in regions with sharp lighting features like volume caustics. Unlike fixed-width methods, it allows for small beam widths in focused regions and larger widths in sparse regions, enabling crisp reconstruction of sharp details with significantly fewer photons. Time Complexity: BBH construction is linear in the number of photons. Adaptive kernel width computation is inexpensive, typically <1–2% of total render time. Memory Complexity: Increases photon storage from 20 bytes to 46 bytes per photon due to BBH and radius data. Performance: More efficient than conventional volumetric photon mapping for scenes with concentrated lighting (e.g., caustics) because it avoids redundant gathering and large step-size noise. Strengths: Eliminates ray marching noise; handles heterogeneous media via lookup tables; adaptive kernels improve quality in focused regions. Limitations: Biased due to kernel blurring; requires preprocessing for radii and BBH; small m values in radius computation can cause noisy radii. Developed by Henrik Wann Jensen and colleagues, building on the theory of volumetric radiance estimation using photon points and beams. It reformulates Volumetric Photon Mapping by treating photon contributions as 2D discs perpendicular to the query ray, derived from the measurement equation in ray space. head: Photon Beams, Continuous Photon Beams, Beam Radiance Estimation, 2D Beam Radiance Estimate, Varying Kernel Beam Estimate, Jarosz et al. estimate, Photon Beam Rendering with Adaptive Width, Adaptive Beam Width via Photon Differentials
body: Adaptive Beam Width is a radiance estimation technique that models photon energy as continuous beams and integrates their contribution along a camera ray, using photon differentials to determine the beam's cross-sectional size and shape. It sets itself apart from fixed-width beam methods by adapting the blur kernel based on the geometric footprint of photon differentials, thereby avoiding the over-blurring and banding artifacts common in focused regions like volume caustics. Unlike the 3D beam estimate which averages transmittance through the kernel depth, this method evaluates transmittance at the intersection point and divides by the 2D area, making it more practical for heterogeneous media. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera ray origin \mathbf{x}c and direction \vec{\omega}c; a set of photon beams B, where each beam b has a central position/direction, power \Phib, phase function f(\theta), and differential rays defining its geometry. Output: Estimated radiance Lb(\mathbf{x}c \leftarrow \vec{\omega}c, s) along the camera ray segment s. Data Structures: A photon beam is defined by: 1. Central Ray: Origin \mathbf{x}, direction \vec{\omega}. 2. Differential Rays: Two auxiliary rays with origins \mathbf{x}u, \mathbf{x}v and directions \vec{\omega}u, \vec{\omega}v. These form a conical frustum with the central ray. 3. Heterogeneous Storage (Optional): For heterogeneous media, store a 1D transmittance function along each beam, analogous to deep shadow maps. Parameters: Beam Width Factor (\alpha): A global multiplier for the computed beam widths to adjust the tradeoff between banding and blur. Typical value: 3.0. Kernel: Biweight kernel K(x) = \frac{15}{16}(1 - x^2)^2 for x \in [0, 1]. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute Beam Cross-Section: For a query point at distance t along the central beam ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{x} + t\vec{\omega}, compute the positions on the differential rays: \mathbf{r}u(t) = \mathbf{x}u + t\vec{\omega}u and \mathbf{r}v(t) = \mathbf{x}v + t\vec{\omega}v. The semi-major and semi-minor axes of the elliptical cross-section are the Euclidean distances: a(t) = \|\mathbf{r}(t) - \mathbf{r}u(t)\| and b(t) = \|\mathbf{r}(t) - \mathbf{r}v(t)\|. The 2D measure for the circular cross-section approximation is \muR(r^2) = \pi r^2. 2. Query Photons: Identify all photon beams b that intersect the camera ray's search region. This is accelerated using a BVH over all beams. 3. Compute Transmittance and Integration: For each photon beam b, determine the overlap interval [tb^-, tb^+] along the beam and the corresponding interval [tc^-, tc^+] along the camera ray. If the media is homogeneous, the integral of the two transmittance terms can be solved analytically: \int{tc^-}^{tc^+} e^{-\sigmat tc} e^{-\sigmat tb^c} dtc = \frac{e^{-\sigmat (tc^- - tc^+)} (|\cos \thetab| - 1) - 1}{e^{\sigmat (tc^- + tb^-)} \sigmat (|\cos \thetab| - 1)} where tb^c = tb^- - (tc - tc^-)|\cos \thetab| is the projected distance along the photon beam, and \cos \thetab = \vec{\omega}c \cdot \vec{\omega}b. If the media is heterogeneous, evaluate the transmittance e^{-\sigmat t{p,c}} at the intersection point using ray marching, and divide by the 2D measure \pi r^2. 4. Sum Contributions: Sum the contributions of all intersecting beams. For the 2D estimate: Lb(\mathbf{x}c \leftarrow \vec{\omega}c, s) \approx \frac{1}{\pi r^2} \sum{p \in R} f(\thetap) \Phip e^{-\sigma{t{p,c}}} where r is the beam radius at the intersection, scaled by \alpha. 5. Handle Singularities: For secondary scattering or area lights, ensure the beam start cross-section is non-zero to avoid division by zero. Use the differential footprint to induce a conical frustum shape. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def estimateradiance(cameraorigin, cameradir, photonbeams, alpha, sigmatfunc): """ cameraorigin: (x, y, z) cameradir: (dx, dy, dz) normalized photonbeams: list of dicts with keys 'origin', 'dir', 'originu', 'diru', 'originv', 'dirv', 'power' alpha: float (global width multiplier) sigmatfunc: callable returning extinction coefficient at a point """ radiance = 0.0 # 1. Query intersecting beams (simplified linear scan; replace with BVH traversal in practice) for beam in photonbeams: # 2. Compute cross-section at intersection # Assume intersection parameter tc along camera ray is known from BVH query tc = 0.0 intersectionpt = (cameraorigin[0] + tc cameradir[0], cameraorigin[1] + tc cameradir[1], cameraorigin[2] + tc cameradir[2]) # Project intersection point onto beam direction to find tb dx = intersectionpt[0] - beam['origin'][0] dy = intersectionpt[1] - beam['origin'][1] dz = intersectionpt[2] - beam['origin'][2] tb = (dx beam['dir'][0] + dy beam['dir'][1] + dz beam['dir'][2]) # Get differential ray positions at tb rcenter = (beam['origin'][0] + tb beam['dir'][0], beam['origin'][1] + tb beam['dir'][1], beam['origin'][2] + tb beam['dir'][2]) ru = (beam['originu'][0] + tb beam['diru'][0], beam['originu'][1] + tb beam['diru'][1], beam['originu'][2] + tb beam['diru'][2]) rv = (beam['originv'][0] + tb beam['dirv'][0], beam['originv'][1] + tb beam['dirv'][1], beam['originv'][2] + tb beam['dirv'][2]) # Semi-axes a = math.sqrt(sum((rcenter[i] - ru[i])2 for i in range(3))) b = math.sqrt(sum((rcenter[i] - rv[i])2 for i in range(3))) # Effective radius for 2D measure, scaled by alpha reff = alpha math.sqrt(a b) area = math.pi reff reff # 3. Compute Transmittance # For 2D estimate, evaluate transmittance at the intersection point sigmat = sigmatfunc(intersectionpt) dist = math.sqrt(sum((intersectionpt[i] - beam['origin'][i])2 for i in range(3))) transmittance = math.exp(-sigmat dist) # 4. Add contribution # Phase function evaluation (dot product of directions) dotprod = (cameradir[0] beam['dir'][0] + cameradir[1] beam['dir'][1] + cameradir[2] beam['dir'][2]) phase = 0.25 math.pi (1.0 - dotprod2) # Standard isotropic approximation radiance += (phase beam['power'] transmittance) / area return radiance This variant defines the initial geometry of photon beams based on the light source type to ensure tight packing and correct angular coverage. Singularity Lights (Point/Spot): Differential ray origins are set to the light source location. Directions are set to cover the angular extent with minimal overlap, where the solid angle per beam is 1/(pdf(\omega) \cdot N). Area Lights: The surface is discretized into a jittered grid. Central ray origins are at grid centers, differential origins at grid edges. Directions follow the angular emission PDF. For multiple scattering events, beam widths are set to cylinders with widths equal to the footprint of the parent beam at the scattering location \mathbf{x}. The differential rays are always parallel to the parent beam. Unlike pdf-based or pilot density estimate methods which produced visibly biased results due to extreme spreading, this automatic cylinder method produces reasonable results. Compute locations along the refracted incident beam during numerical integration. The explicit integration formulation allows choosing any \vec{\omega} not orthogonal to the surface normal without modifications. Similar to Yan et al. [YZXW12] who formulated QD for oblique angles by offsetting Gaussian centers, this method uses explicit integration to handle angles. Treat each sample (summand of Equation 8) as a dipole and mirror it at the extrapolated boundary to perform a multipole extension for a finite slab, similar to Donner and Jensen [DJ05]. When close to \mathbf{x}=0, placing dipoles directly on reflective or transmissive boundaries can cause issues. The equiangular sampling in the MIS strategy avoids placing dipoles directly on these boundaries, allowing for very thin slabs without drawbacks. Time Complexity: Dominated by the BVH traversal for beam intersection. Memory Complexity: Linear in the number of photon beams. Heterogeneous media require storing 1D transmittance functions, which can be significantly compressed for efficient storage. Performance: Converges significantly faster than photon points for sharp features. In a volume caustic scene, 32k beams converged in 43 seconds, while 512k photons took nearly twice as long and produced a noisier, over-blurred result. Strengths: Eliminates shadow rays by reusing visibility from photon tracing; handles area lights and multiple bounces naturally; avoids singularities via finite cross-sections. Limitations: Adaptive width based on differentials works well for single scattering and caustics but is less successful for multiple scattering. Fixed-width beams cause banding. Adaptive Beam Width is part of the photon beam framework introduced by Jarosz et al. [2008] as a generalization of photon mapping. It builds on the concept of photon differentials from Igehy [1999] and surface-based methods [Schjøth et al. 2007; Fabianowski and Dingliana 2009]. The method was developed to provide a compact, expressive intermediate representation for lighting in participating media, allowing for efficient radiance estimation without shadow rays. name: Photon Emission and Storage
head: Photon Mapping with Volume Storage, emitPhotons
body: Photon Emission and Storage is the preprocessing phase of Volumetric Photon Mapping that generates photon paths from light sources and records their positions, directions, and energy densities into spatial data structures for both surface intersections and volumetric scattering events. It solves the problem of efficiently capturing indirect lighting and caustics in participating media by decoupling the complex light transport simulation from the final image synthesis, allowing for density estimation during a subsequent gather pass. Unlike direct integration methods, it pre-computes photon interactions, and it is distinguished from its sibling Beam Radiance Estimate by storing discrete photon packets rather than continuous beam radiance estimates. Inputs: Light source position Light (Vector3). Light source radius lightbulbr (double, 0.1). Scene geometry defined by a list of objects objects with types (e.g., TYPESPHERE) and optical properties. Room boundary constraints (e.g., |x| \le 1.5, |y| \le 1.2, z \ge 0). Total photon count nrPhotons (int). Maximum bounces nrBounces (int). Reflection limit reflectionlimit (int, 4). Rendering mode flag view3D (bool). Outputs: Surface photon map: Array of photons stored at intersection points with position, direction, and color. Volume photon map (volphotons): Array of photons stored in volume buffers for volumetric scattering or direct visualization. Data Structures: volphotons: A dynamic array or buffer storing volume photons. Each entry contains: volphotons[i][0]: Position (Vector3). volphotons[i][1]: Direction (Vector3). volphotons[i][2]: Energy/Color (Vector3). numvol: Integer counter for the number of stored volume photons. numPhotons[t]: Integer array tracking photon counts per object t. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Reset photon counters: numPhotons[t] = 0 for all objects, numvol = 0. Determine total photons to emit: numphoton = nrPhotons 3.0 if view3D is true, else nrPhotons. Initialize random seed for reproducibility if required (e.g., srand(0)). 2. Optional Fixed Source Emission (Testing/Specific Objects): Emit a fixed number of photons (e.g., 100) from a specific object (e.g., objects[5]). For each photon: Generate random direction ray = randDir(1.0). Calculate start position: from = Light + stepout(ray, lightbulbr) + epsilon. Store photon at from in volume buffer: storePhotonvol(from, ray, rgb). Store photon at intersection with objects[5]: storePhoton(objects[5], pnt, ray, rgb). 3. Main Photon Emission Loop: Iterate i from 0 to numphoton - 1: Step 3.1: Photon Generation Initialize color rgb = white (1.0, 1.0, 1.0). Initialize bounce counter bounces = 1. Generate random direction ray = randDir(1.0). Generate initial position from: Start at Light. If from.y() >= Light.y(), regenerate from = randDir(1.0) + Light until from.y() < Light.y(). Step 3.2: Validation Check if from is outside the room boundaries (e.g., |x| > 1.5 or |y| > 1.2). If so, mark invalid: bounces = nrBounces + 1. Check if from is inside any object (e.g., sphere). For each object ob: If ob is a sphere and distance(from, center) < radius, mark invalid: bounces = nrBounces + 1. If invalid, continue to next photon. Step 3.3: Volume Storage (Initial) If valid, store the initial photon state in the volume buffer: storePhotonvol(from, ray, rgb). Step 3.4: Ray Tracing and Bouncing Trace ray from from with direction ray to find first intersection istat. While istat.dist < NOTINTERSECTED and bounces <= nrBounces: Calculate intersection point pnt = from + ray istat.dist. Handle optical interactions (reflection/refraction) based on istat.obj.getOptics() up to reflectionlimit. If the optics loop breaks due to no intersection, skip storage and continue to next iteration. Update color: col = mulColor(rgb, istat.obj). Attenuate color by bounces: rgb = col (1.0 / sqrt(bounces)). Store photon at intersection: storePhoton(istat.obj, pnt, ray, rgb). Trace shadow ray: shadowPhoton(ray, pnt) to determine visibility and store shadow photon if applicable. Reflect/Refract ray: ray = reflect(istat.obj, pnt, ray, from). Update from = pnt. Trace next intersection: istat = raytrace(ray, from). If no next intersection, break loop. Increment bounces. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random class Vector3: def init(self, x=0.0, y=0.0, z=0.0): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def add(self, o): return Vector3(self.x+o.x, self.y+o.y, self.z+o.z) def sub(self, o): return Vector3(self.x-o.x, self.y-o.y, self.z-o.z) def mul(self, s): return Vector3(self.xs, self.ys, self.zs) def rmul(self, s): return self.mul(s) def truediv(self, s): return Vector3(self.x/s, self.y/s, self.z/s) def normalize(self): l = math.sqrt(self.x2 + self.y2 + self.z2) if l > 0: self.x, self.y, self.z = self.x/l, self.y/l, self.z/l return self def dot(self, o): return self.xo.x + self.yo.y + self.zo.z def distanceto(self, o): return math.sqrt((self.x-o.x)2 + (self.y-o.y)2 + (self.z-o.z)2) def randDir(s): tmp = [random.uniform(-s, s) for in range(3)] v = Vector3(tmp) v.normalize() return v def stepout(ray, radius): return ray radius def distance(a, b): return a.distanceto(b) def mulColor(rgb, obj): return rgb obj.color def reflect(obj, pnt, ray, frompos): normal = obj.getnormal(pnt) # return ray - 2 ray.dot(normal) normal def raytrace(ray, origin): closestdist = float('inf') closestobj = None for obj in objects: d = obj.intersect(ray, origin) if d is not None and d < closestdist: closestdist = d closestobj = obj return {'dist': closestdist, 'obj': closestobj} def storePhoton(obj, pnt, ray, rgb): obj.photons.append({'pos': pnt, 'dir': ray, 'rgb': rgb}) def storePhotonvol(pnt, ray, rgb): volphotons.append([pnt, ray, rgb]) def shadowPhoton(ray, pnt): pass # NOTINTERSECTED = float('inf') TYPESPHERE = 1 OPTNONE = 0 def emitPhotons(Light, lightbulbr, objects, nrPhotons, nrBounces, reflectionlimit, view3D): numPhotons = [0] len(objects) numvol = 0 volphotons = [] numphoton = nrPhotons 3.0 if view3D else nrPhotons white = Vector3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # Optional fixed emission for testing for i in range(100): ray = randDir(1.0) rr = stepout(ray, lightbulbr) pnt = rr + Light + Vector3(0.0001, 0.0001, 0.0001) rgb = Vector3(50, 50, 50) storePhoton(objects[5], pnt, ray, rgb) storePhotonvol(pnt, ray, rgb) numvol += 1 numPhotons[5] += 1 for i in range(numphoton): bounces = 1 rgb = white ray = randDir(1.0) frompos = Light while frompos.y() >= Light.y(): frompos = randDir(1.0) + Light if abs(frompos.x()) > 1.5 or abs(frompos.y()) > 1.2: bounces = nrBounces + 1 for dx in range(len(objects)): ob = objects[dx] if ob.getType() != TYPESPHERE: continue center = Vector3(ob.coords) radius = ob.coords[3] if distance(frompos, center) < radius: bounces = nrBounces + 1 break if bounces > nrBounces: continue storePhotonvol(frompos, ray, rgb) numvol += 1 istat = raytrace(ray, frompos) while istat['dist'] < NOTINTERSECTED and bounces <= nrBounces: pnt = frompos + ray istat['dist'] ref = 0 while istat['obj'].getOptics() != OPTNONE and ref < reflectionlimit: ray = reflect(istat['obj'], pnt, ray, frompos) ref += 1 frompos = pnt istat = raytrace(ray, frompos) if istat['dist'] >= NOTINTERSECTED: break else: pnt = frompos + ray istat['dist'] if istat['dist'] >= NOTINTERSECTED: continue col = mulColor(rgb, istat['obj']) rgb = col (1.0 / math.sqrt(bounces)) storePhoton(istat['obj'], pnt, ray, rgb) numPhotons[istat['obj'].getIndex()] += 1 shadowPhoton(ray, pnt) ray = reflect(istat['obj'], pnt, ray, frompos) frompos = pnt bounces += 1 istat = raytrace(ray, frompos) return volphotons, numPhotons Parameters: nrBounces: Maximum number of bounces. Value not explicitly defined in sources, but used as a threshold. reflectionlimit: Maximum number of optical interactions per bounce, typically 4. lightbulbr: Light source radius, typically 0.1. collectr: Radius for photon collection during density estimation, typically 0.7. power: Photon power scaling factor, typically 500. exposure: Exposure factor for lighting calculation, value not specified. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Use a small epsilon (e.g., 1.0e-5) when checking intersection distances to avoid self-intersection artifacts. Boundary Conditions: Photons starting outside the room or inside objects are discarded by setting bounces to an invalid value. Degenerate Input: If nrBounces is 0, no photons are stored. Extends surface-based photon mapping to handle light transport within volumetric media by decoupling light transport simulation from final image synthesis. It is distinguished by specific handling of volumetric scattering events and a distinct radiance estimate formula for volume photons. Choose it when rendering complex indirect lighting and caustics in non-homogeneous participating media. Uses continuous beam radiance estimates instead of discrete photon packets for density estimation. Choose it when higher throughput is needed for participating media with less emphasis on discrete caustic paths. Traces beams of photons rather than single rays to improve efficiency in participating media. Choose it when volumetric density is high and single-ray sampling is too noisy. Iteratively refines the photon map and radius to converge to the correct solution. Choose it when bias-free convergence is required over multiple rendering passes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: For real-time applications or scenes with dynamic geometry where pre-computation is not feasible. Photon Emission and Storage is part of the Volumetric Photon Mapping technique, an extension of the surface-based Photon Mapping algorithm by Henrik Wann Jensen. The specific implementation described in the sources is from an unofficial repository by jacklv123, which adapts the technique for participating media by storing photons in volume buffers. The method builds on the principles of global illumination by storing photon paths in a spatial data structure for later density estimation. jacklv123/Volumetric-photon-mapping, https://github.com/jacklv123/Volumetric-photon-mapping, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Photon Mapping for Participating Media
head: Jensen and Christensen, Nonlinear RTE photon mapping, Photon Maps for Participating Media, Volume Photon Map, nl-RTE PM
body: Photon Mapping for Participating Media extends the surface-based photon mapping algorithm to handle light transport within volumetric media, introducing a distinct volume photon map to estimate radiance via density estimation. Unlike methods that rely on straight-line shadow rays for single scattering, this approach uses Monte Carlo photon tracing to account for spatially varying optical properties and general phase functions, making it suitable for non-homogeneous materials. It is primarily distinguished by its separation of the volume photon map (used for indirect illumination) from the surface photon map and its reliance on final gathering to reconstruct inscattered light. The method consists of two main passes: a photon tracing preprocess and a final gather rendering pass. Inputs: Light source definitions (position, flux, spectrum), scene geometry, participating media properties (extinction coefficient \sigmat, scattering coefficient \sigmas, albedo, phase function p), and camera parameters. Outputs: A rendered image with indirect illumination and inscattered light from participating media. 1. Volume Photon Map: A spatial data structure (typically a kd-tree) storing photons that have interacted with the media. Fields per photon: Position \mathbf{x}: 3D coordinates. Direction of incidence \boldsymbol{\omega}i: 3D vector (required for anisotropic scattering to recover source radiance toward the eye). Flux W: Scalar energy value. Wavelength/Color: RGB or spectral data. Storage Criteria: Only photons representing indirect illumination are stored. This includes: Photons reflected or transmitted by surfaces before entering the media. Photons that have been scattered at least once within the media. Photons stored after the first bounce in refractive media (see Subtopics). 1. Emit Photon: Generate a photon from a light source with initial flux W and direction \boldsymbol{\omega}0. 2. Trace through Scene: Trace the photon ray through the scene. If the photon intersects a surface, apply surface reflection/refraction. If the photon enters a participating medium, begin volume interaction. Volume Interaction: Calculate the distance to the next scattering event s using the extinction coefficient \sigmat(\mathbf{x}): s = -\frac{\ln(r)}{\sigmat(\mathbf{x})} where r is a uniform random number in (0, 1]. Move the photon to \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} + s \boldsymbol{\omega}. Check for Scattering: If the photon is inside a medium: Determine if scattering occurs (based on albedo \omega = \sigmas / \sigmat). If scattering occurs: Store the photon in the Volume Photon Map at \mathbf{x}'. Record position, incidence direction \boldsymbol{\omega}, flux W, and color. Select a new scattering direction \boldsymbol{\omega}' using the phase function p(\boldsymbol{\omega}, \boldsymbol{\omega}') (e.g., Schlick phase function). Update flux: W \leftarrow W \cdot \sigmas / \sigmat (or similar energy conservation step depending on specific implementation details not fully specified in sources, but generally proportional to scattering probability). Continue tracing from \mathbf{x}' in direction \boldsymbol{\omega}'. If absorption occurs (photon does not scatter): Absorb the photon (terminate trace) or reduce flux to zero. If the photon exits the medium, continue tracing as a surface ray. Repeat until the photon is absorbed, escapes the scene, or a maximum bounce count is reached. 1. View Ray Tracing: For each pixel, cast a view ray from the camera. 2. Identify Interaction Points: Find points \mathbf{x} on the view ray that lie within participating media. 3. Radiance Estimation: For each point \mathbf{x}, query the Volume Photon Map for the k nearest photons. Estimate the inscattered radiance Li(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}) using density estimation: Li(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}) \approx \frac{1}{\pi rk^2} \sum{j=1}^{k} \frac{Wj}{\sigmat(\mathbf{x})} p(\boldsymbol{\omega}j, \boldsymbol{\omega}) Note: The exact formula for density estimation in volume photon mapping is derived by Jensen and Christensen. The sources cite the derivation but do not provide the explicit final summation formula with all constants (like n^2 for refractive media) in the general case. For refractive media, the relationship involves n^2. For anisotropic scattering, use the stored incidence direction \boldsymbol{\omega}j to correctly evaluate the phase function p(\boldsymbol{\omega}j, \boldsymbol{\omega}). 4. Composite: Combine the estimated inscattered radiance with direct illumination and surface contributions to form the final pixel color. Number of Photons (N): High number required for accurate convergence; the method is slow due to this requirement. Number of Nearest Neighbors (k): Used in density estimation. Not given in the sources. Phase Function: e.g., Schlick phase function. Maximum Bounce Depth: Not given in the sources. Overestimation: The method overestimates radiance inside participating media because energy conservation is not enforced within the volume, only at the surface via a nonsymmetric BTDF. Performance: The method can be slow because many photons are required for accurate convergence. Refractive Media: In continuously refractive media, straight shadow rays cannot be used for single scattering. Photons must be stored after the first bounce, increasing the required photon count. Nonlinear Dependency: The squared refractive index n^2 creates a strong nonlinear dependency that cannot be compensated by simple rescaling of light source fluxes. A variant of photon mapping for participating media that handles single-scattered light in continuously refractive media where straight shadow rays are insufficient. It stores photons after the first bounce (unlike nonrefractive media which store after at least two bounces) to solve single scattering via radiance estimation from the photon map. The key distinction is the handling of basic radiance \tilde{L}i and scattered radiance Li via the squared refractive index n^2: \tilde{L}i(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}, v, t) = \frac{1}{n^2} Li(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i, v, t) This relationship is derived from the distribution function and energy conservation principles. The drawback is that the necessary amount of photons to obtain high-quality results increases significantly due to this approach. The strong nonlinear dependency of n^2 cannot be compensated by simple rescaling of light source fluxes. Time Complexity: Slow. Requires a large number of photons for accurate convergence, making the preprocessing step computationally expensive. Memory Complexity: High. Stores a large volume photon map containing positions, directions, and fluxes for all scattered photons. Strengths: Handles non-homogeneous materials, spatially varying optical properties, and general phase functions effectively. Straightforward handling of single-scattered light in refractive media. Limitations: Overestimates radiance inside the medium due to lack of volume energy conservation. Performance degrades with complex refractive media due to increased photon requirements. When to Use: Scenes with complex participating media, non-homogeneous materials, or refractive media where single scattering is significant and cannot be handled by simple shadow rays. When Not to Use: Real-time applications or scenes requiring strict energy conservation within the volume. Photon Mapping for Participating Media was introduced by Henrik Wann Jensen and Per Christensen. It extends the original photon mapping method, which was limited to surfaces, to participating media by introducing a volume photon map. The method uses Monte Carlo simulation of photon transport from light sources, accounting for spatially varying optical properties and general phase functions. It was developed to address the limitations of previous methods that were less useful for volume rendering of spatially varying data. The approach has been used in research for simulating fog effects and other atmospheric phenomena. name: Progressive Photon Mapping
head: Multipass Photon Mapping
body: Progressive Photon Mapping is a volumetric light transport method developed by Hachisuka et al. that uses a multipass rendering technique to continuously emit photons into the image, gradually reducing inaccuracy. It builds on Volumetric Photon Mapping by applying a multipass strategy to photon emission and accumulation. It differs from sibling methods like Beam Radiance Estimate by refining illumination through iterative photon passes rather than beam-based approximations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scene geometry, participating media properties, camera parameters, and a total number of passes N{passes}. Not given in the sources. Output: A rendered image with progressively refined illumination. Data Structures: Photon Map: A dynamic list or array storing photon records with fields for position (3D vector), energy (scalar), and direction (3D vector). In this method, it is updated or rebuilt per pass. A standard spatial acceleration structure (e.g., KD-tree or grid) is typically used for neighbor search during density estimation, though specific implementation details are not provided in the source. Steps: 1. Initialize the photon map. 2. For each pass i from 1 to N{passes}: a. Emit a batch of photons from light sources into the scene. b. Trace photons through the participating media, storing interactions in the photon map. c. Update the photon map with the new photons. d. Render the image using the current photon map state. 3. Gradually reduce inaccuracy by increasing the number of photons or refining the search radius in subsequent passes. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Number of passes N{passes}: Not given in the sources. Photons per pass: Not given in the sources. Search radius: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Convergence: The method relies on gradual reduction of inaccuracy; insufficient passes may result in noisy images. Precision: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def progressivephotonmapping(scene, camera, numpasses): photonmap = [] accumulatedimage = zeroslike(camera.resolution) for passidx in range(1, numpasses + 1): # Emit and trace photons for light in scene.lights: for in range(photonsperpass): rayorigin, raydirection = samplelightemission(light) pos = rayorigin while pos inside scene: step = marchstep(pos, scene.media) pos += step raydirection photonmap.append(Photon(pos, scene.media.extinction step, raydirection)) # Render using current photon map for ray in camera.rays: radiance = 0.0 for photon in photonmap: if distance(photon.position, ray.origin) < searchradius: radiance += photon.energy / (pi searchradius2) accumulatedimage += radiance return accumulatedimage / numpasses Progressive Photon Beam Mapping is a memory-efficient volumetric light transport method that replaces the large, static photon map with a series of small, iteratively generated photon maps. It addresses the high memory costs associated with storing huge volumetric photon maps in participating media. Unlike standard photon mapping which requires storing all photons, this method discards the photon map after each iteration, significantly improving practicality for large scenes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Gradual convergence through multipass photon emission. Limitations: Requires multiple passes for high quality. When to use: Real-time realistic volume rendering and interactive character updates. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Progressive Photon Mapping was developed by Hachisuka et al.. It was proposed as a multipass rendering technique to continuously emit photons into the image to gradually reduce inaccuracy. The method builds on earlier photon mapping techniques and adapts them for volumetric rendering. name: Progressive Photon Beam Mapping
body: Progressive Photon Beam Mapping is a volumetric light transport method that eliminates the memory limitations of traditional photon mapping by replacing the single huge volumetric photon map with many small, iteratively generated photon maps. It builds on Progressive Photon Mapping by applying a multipass strategy where each small photon map is used to update shading point contributions and then discarded, thereby improving practicality for participating media. Shading Point Accumulator: Stores the accumulated radiance contribution for each shading point across iterations. Steps: 1. Initialize: Set up the scene and shading points. Initialize accumulators for radiance to zero. 2. Iterative Loop: For each iteration i = 1, 2, \dots, N: a. Generate Small Photon Map: Iteratively generate a small photon map. b. Update Contributions: Use the small photon map to update the contribution of the shading points. The estimator operates on a beam-to-beam basis. c. Discard: Discard the small photon map. 3. Finalize: Return the accumulated radiance values at the shading points. Pseudocode: Unverified code. body: Transient Progressive Photon Beams is a volumetric light transport simulation method that uses photon beams to estimate transient radiance in participating media. It builds on Progressive Photon Beam Mapping by optimizing the convergence rate of the estimator through analytical minimization of the Asymptotic Mean Squared Error (AMSE). Not given in the sources. The method relies on small photon maps generated iteratively by the parent method. Each photon beam carries position, direction, energy, time, and weight. 1. Initialization: Set \alpha = 2/3, \betaT = 1/2, \beta{Rb} = 1/2, and initial bandwidths \mathcal{T}1, R{b1}. 2. Iteration Loop (for n = 1 to N): Update Kernel Bandwidths: Calculate current temporal bandwidth \mathcal{T}n and spatial radius R{bn} using the decay formulas: \mathcal{T}n = \mathcal{T}1 (n \alpha \text{B}(\alpha, n))^{-\betaT} R{bn} = R{b1} (n \alpha \text{B}(\alpha, n))^{-\beta{Rb}} where \text{B}(x, y) is the Beta function. Photon Transport & Storage: Shoot photon beams from the light source and store them in the current small photon map. Estimate Radiance: Accumulate contributions from all stored photon beams using the current bandwidths \mathcal{T}n and R{bn} for spatial and temporal smoothing. 3. Convergence: The estimator \hat{L}n converges to the true transient radiance with an optimal AMSE rate of O(n^{-2/3}). The variance of the estimator \hat{L}n is decomposed into signal variance and noise variance: \text{Var}[\hat{L}n] = \frac{1}{n} \text{Var}[\Psi L] + \frac{1}{n^2} \sum{j=1}^n \text{Var}[\Psi \epsilonj] Expanding this, and assuming independence between the signal \Psi and noise \epsilonj: \text{Var}[\hat{L}n] = \frac{1}{n} \text{Var}[\Psi L] + \text{Var}[\Psi] \frac{1}{n^2} \sum{j=1}^n \text{Var}[\epsilonj] + \text{E}[\Psi]^2 \frac{1}{n^2} \sum{j=1}^n \text{Var}[\epsilonj] + \text{Var}[\Psi] \frac{1}{n^2} \sum{j=1}^n \text{E}[\epsilonj]^2 The variance of the noise term \epsilonn at iteration n is approximated as: \text{Var}[\epsilonn] \approx \frac{\text{Var}[\epsilon1]}{(2 - \alpha)n^\alpha} = O(n^{-1}) + O(n^{-\alpha}) = O(n^{-\alpha}) The expected bias E[\epsilonj] at iteration j is a sum of three terms involving photon flux E[\Phi], probabilities p{Rb} and pT, constants CT^{ij}, C1^{ij}, initial bandwidths \mathcal{T}1, Rb, and decay factors: E[\epsilonj] = E[\Phi]p{Rb}CT^{ij}\mathcal{T}1^{-\alpha}\Theta(j^{-\alpha})^{-2\betaT} + E[\Phi]pTC1^{ij}Rb^2\Theta(j^{-\alpha})^{-2\beta{Rb}} + E[\Phi]CT^{ij}C1^{ij}\mathcal{T}1^{-\alpha}Rb^2\Theta(j^{-\alpha})^{-2(\betaT+\beta{Rb})} The asymptotic expected bias E[\epsilonn] for the final estimator is: E[\epsilonn] = O(n^{1-\alpha})^{-2\betaT} + O(n^{1-\alpha})^{-2\beta{Rb}} + O(n^{1-\alpha})^{-2(\betaT + \beta{Rb})} Using the equality \beta{Rb} = 1 - \betaT, the bias simplifies to: E[\epsilonn] = O(n^{1-\alpha})^{-2\betaT} + O(n^{1-\alpha})^{2\betaT - 2} The Asymptotic Mean Squared Error (AMSE) is the sum of variance and squared bias: AMSE(\hat{L}n) = O(n^{-\alpha}) + \left( O(n^{1-\alpha})^{-2\betaT} + O(n^{1-\alpha})^{2\betaT - 2} \right)^2 The convergence is governed by three decay parameters and two initial bandwidths: 1. \alpha: Iteration count scaling exponent. Optimal value: \alpha = 2/3. 2. \betaT: Temporal kernel bandwidth decay exponent. Optimal value: \betaT = 1/2. 3. \beta{Rb}: Spatial kernel radius decay exponent. Constrained by \beta{Rb} = 1 - \betaT, yielding \beta{Rb} = 1/2. 4. \mathcal{T}1: Initial temporal bandwidth. 5. R{b1}: Initial spatial radius. name: Transient Progressive Photon Beams Convergence Analysis
head: Asymptotic Analysis of Transient Progressive Photon Beams, TPPB Convergence
body: This method provides the theoretical foundation for optimizing the convergence rate of the radiance estimator in Transient Progressive Photon Beams. It analyzes the asymptotic behavior of the estimator's variance and bias to derive the optimal parameters that minimize the Asymptotic Mean Squared Error (AMSE). It sets itself apart from its sibling Transient Progressive Photon Beams by providing the mathematical proof for why specific parameter schedules (\alpha=2/3, \betaT=1/2) are chosen, rather than just describing the algorithmic steps. The analysis decomposes the Mean Squared Error (MSE) of the radiance estimator \hat{L}n after n iterations into variance and bias components, then optimizes the kernel evolution parameters to minimize the asymptotic limit of this error. Inputs: The iteration count n, the variance decay parameter \alpha, and the kernel bandwidth decay parameter \betaT. Outputs: The optimal parameter values \alpha^ and \betaT^ that minimize the AMSE, and the resulting convergence rate. The analysis relies on the following symbolic variables: \hat{L}n: The radiance estimator at iteration n. \Psi: The photon weight or throughput factor. \epsilonj: The error term introduced at iteration j. \mathcal{T}j: The kernel bandwidth at iteration j. R{bj}: The kernel radius at iteration j. \mathcal{T}1, R{b1}: Initial kernel bandwidth and radius. B(x, y): The Beta function. E[\cdot]: Expectation operator. \text{Var}[\cdot]: Variance operator. 1. Variance Decomposition Assuming the random variables \Psi and \epsilonj are independent, the variance of the estimator is modeled as: \text{Var}[\hat{L}n] = \frac{1}{n} \text{Var}[\Psi L] + \frac{1}{n^2} \sum{j=1}^n \text{Var}[\Psi \epsilonj] Expanding the second term using independence yields: \text{Var}[\hat{L}n] = \frac{1}{n} \text{Var}[\Psi L] + \text{Var}[\Psi] \frac{1}{n^2} \sum{j=1}^n \text{Var}[\epsilonj] + \text{E}[\Psi]^2 \frac{1}{n^2} \sum{j=1}^n \text{Var}[\epsilonj] + \text{Var}[\Psi] \frac{1}{n^2} \sum{j=1}^n \text{E}[\epsilonj]^2 \quad (36) 2. Variance Approximation Following established techniques, the variance of the error term at iteration n is approximated as a function of the first iteration's variance: \text{Var}[\epsilonn] \approx \frac{\text{Var}[\epsilon1]}{(2 - \alpha)n^\alpha} = O(n^{-\alpha}) \quad (37) Substituting this into the variance decomposition and applying asymptotic simplifications yields the asymptotic variance of the estimator: \text{Var}[\mathcal{L}n] \approx \frac{1}{n} \text{Var}[\Psi L] + \text{E}[\Psi^2] \text{Var}[\epsilon1] \approx \frac{1}{n} \text{Var}[\Psi L] + \frac{\text{Var}[\epsilon1]}{(2 - \alpha)n^\alpha} = O(n^{-1}) + O(n^{-\alpha}) = O(n^{-\alpha}) \quad (38) 3. Kernel Evolution The kernel bandwidth \mathcal{T}j and radius R{bj} evolve according to the following schedules, where B(\alpha, j) is the Beta function: \mathcal{T}j = \mathcal{T}1(j \alpha B(\alpha, j))^{-\beta{\mathcal{T}}} \quad (39) R{bj} = R{b1}(j \alpha B(\alpha, j))^{-\beta{Rb}} \quad (40) 4. Bias Analysis The expected error E[\epsilonj] at iteration j is modeled as a function of initial kernel parameters and constants E[\Phi], p{Rb}, CT^{ij}, C1^{ij}: E[\epsilonj] = E[\Phi]p{Rb}CT^{ij}\mathcal{T}1^{-\alpha}\Theta(j^{-\alpha})^{-2\beta\tau} + E[\Phi]pTC1^{ij}Rb^2\Theta(j^{-\alpha})^{-2\beta{Rb}} + E[\Phi]CT^{ij}C1^{ij}\mathcal{T}1^{-\alpha}Rb^2\Theta(j^{-\alpha})^{-2(\beta\tau+\beta{Rb})} \quad (41) Using the summation property \sum{j=1}^n \Theta(j^x) = O(n^{1+x}), the asymptotic bias E[\epsilonn] is derived: E[\epsilonn] = O(n^{1-\alpha})^{-2\beta\tau} + O(n^{1-\alpha})^{-2\beta{Rb}} + O(n^{1-\alpha})^{-2(\beta\tau + \beta{Rb})} By applying the constraint \beta{Rb} = 1 - \betaT, this simplifies to: E[\epsilonn] = O(n^{1-\alpha})^{-2\betaT} + O(n^{1-\alpha})^{2\betaT - 2} \quad (42) 5. AMSE Optimization The Asymptotic Mean Squared Error (AMSE) is the sum of asymptotic variance and squared bias: AMSE(\hat{L}n) = O(n^{-\alpha}) + \left( O(n^{1-\alpha})^{-2\betaT} + O(n^{1-\alpha})^{2\betaT - 2} \right)^2 \quad (43) To minimize AMSE, we first optimize \betaT. Since the variance term is independent of \betaT, we differentiate the bias term in Eq. 42 with respect to \betaT, apply asymptotic simplifications, and equate to zero. This yields the optimal bandwidth decay parameter: \betaT = 1/2 Substituting \betaT = 1/2 into Eq. 43 yields: AMSE(\hat{L}n) = O(n^{-\alpha}) + O(n^{-2(1-\alpha)}) \quad (44) Finally, we optimize \alpha. The optimal convergence rate is achieved when the variance and bias terms decay at the same rate, or by balancing the exponents. The analysis identifies the optimal parameters as: \alpha = 2/3, \quad \betaT = 1/2 Resulting in the optimal convergence rate: AMSE(\hat{L}n) = O(n^{-2/3}) \quad (45) The following Python-like pseudocode calculates the optimal parameters and convergence rate based on the derived formulas. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def betafunction(x, y): """ Computes the Beta function B(x, y) = Gamma(x) Gamma(y) / Gamma(x + y). """ return math.gamma(x) math.gamma(y) / math.gamma(x + y) def analyzetppbconvergence(): """ Analyzes the convergence of Transient Progressive Photon Beams. Returns optimal parameters and convergence rate. """ # Step 1: Determine optimal betaT # Derived from minimizing the bias term in Eq. 42. # The bias terms are O(n^(1-alpha)^(-2betaT)) and O(n^(1-alpha)^(2betaT-2)). # Equating the exponents for balanced decay or differentiating yields betaT = 0.5. betaTopt = 0.5 # Step 2: Determine optimal alpha # Substitute betaT into AMSE (Eq. 44): AMSE = O(n^-alpha) + O(n^-2(1-alpha)) # We want to minimize the dominant term. The optimal balance occurs when # the derivative of the combined error is minimized. # The source explicitly states alpha = 2/3 yields O(n^-2/3). alphaopt = 2.0 / 3.0 # Step 3: Calculate Convergence Rate # AMSE = O(n^-alpha) + O(n^-2(1-alpha)) # With alpha = 2/3: # Term 1: O(n^-2/3) # Term 2: O(n^-2(1-2/3)) = O(n^-2(1/3)) = O(n^-2/3) # Both terms decay at rate 2/3. convergencerate = alphaopt return { "alpha": alphaopt, "betaT": betaTopt, "convergencerate": convergencerate, "amseorder": f"O(n^{-convergencerate})" } if name == "main": results = analyzetppbconvergence() print(f"Optimal Alpha: {results['alpha']}") print(f"Optimal BetaT: {results['betaT']}") print(f"Convergence Rate: {results['amseorder']}") \alpha: Kernel radius decay parameter. Optimal value: 2/3. \betaT: Kernel bandwidth decay parameter. Optimal value: 1/2. \mathcal{T}1: Initial kernel bandwidth. Not given in the sources. R{b1}: Initial kernel radius. Not given in the sources. Precision: The asymptotic analysis assumes n is sufficiently large for the O(\cdot) notation to hold. For small n, the actual convergence may deviate from the theoretical rate. Independence Assumption: The variance decomposition (Eq. 36) assumes \Psi and \epsilonj are independent. If this assumption is violated in specific scene configurations, the variance estimate may be inaccurate. Beta Function Calculation: Computing B(\alpha, j) for large j may require careful numerical implementation to avoid overflow or underflow, though the source does not specify a particular numerical method. Time Complexity: The analysis itself is O(1) as it involves closed-form mathematical derivations. The application of these parameters in the rendering algorithm follows the complexity of Transient Progressive Photon Beams. Memory Complexity: The analysis requires no additional memory beyond storing the symbolic parameters. Strengths: Provides a rigorous theoretical basis for parameter selection, ensuring optimal convergence rates (O(n^{-2/3})) for the radiance estimator. Limitations: The analysis is asymptotic and does not provide guidance for early iterations where the asymptotic behavior has not yet stabilized. It relies on the validity of the independence assumption between photon weights and error terms. The convergence analysis for Transient Progressive Photon Beams was presented in the paper "Progressive Transient Photon Beams". The variance approximation technique follows the work of Kaplanyan and Dachsbacher (2013) [KD13], which was originally developed for Progressive Photon Mapping [KZ11]. The base method, Progressive Photon Beams, was introduced by Jarosz et al. (2011) [JNT11]. This analysis extends those concepts to the transient (time-of-flight) domain. name: Volumetric Photon Mapping with Radiance Transfer
body: Volumetric Photon Mapping with Radiance Transfer is a rendering technique that integrates volumetric photon mapping into a pre-designed radiance transfer procedure to achieve real-time, realistic volume rendering. It distinguishes itself from standard volumetric photon mapping by explicitly separating direct and indirect lighting computations within a radiance transfer framework, allowing for effective updates to the photon map when transfer functions change. Unlike Beam Radiance Estimate which focuses on density estimation via beam kernels, this method prioritizes the structural integration of photon data into a transfer-based rendering pipeline to handle wide intensity ranges. The method operates in two main phases: photon map construction and radiance transfer rendering. Inputs: Scene geometry and participating media properties (scattering coefficient \sigmas, absorption coefficient \sigmaa, phase function p). Light source positions and intensities. Camera parameters. Transfer function for volume visualization. Outputs: Rendered image with direct and indirect illumination. Data Structures: Photon Map: A spatial data structure (e.g., k-d tree) storing photons emitted from light sources. Each photon record typically contains: Position (x, y, z) Direction (\omegai, \omegao) Power P Additional metadata for radiance transfer weighting, such as local density or path length, if required by the specific transfer function implementation. Steps: 1. Photon Emission and Storage: Emit photons from light sources into the volume. Ray march through the participating media, simulating scattering events. Store photon interactions (positions, directions, power) in the photon map. The storage format is designed to allow effective updates to the photon map when scene areas affected by altering the transfer function are assessed. 2. Direct Illumination Computation: Cast rays from the camera into the scene. Compute direct lighting contributions along the ray path using standard volume rendering integration techniques. 3. Indirect Illumination Computation (Radiance Transfer): For each pixel/ray, query the photon map for nearby photons. Use the stored photon data to estimate indirect illumination. Integrate this indirect contribution into the radiance transfer procedure. The volumetric photon mapping algorithm is incorporated into the customary predesigned radiance transfer procedure. This allows the method to tackle the wide range of intensities resulting from varying light conditions by leveraging the transfer function's ability to map radiance to color/opacity. 4. Final Image Assembly: Combine direct and indirect illumination results. Apply the transfer function to produce the final visual output. Parameters: Number of photons: Not given in the sources. Search radius for photon map queries: Not given in the sources. Transfer function parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Intensity Range: The method is designed to handle wide ranges of intensities, but improper scaling of the radiance transfer function may lead to loss of detail in bright or dark regions. Transfer Function Updates: Changing the transfer function requires assessing affected scene areas to update the photon map effectively; failure to do so may result in visual artifacts or incorrect lighting. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method is designed to produce an interactive character for real-time realistic volume rendering. Strengths: Real-time capability; effective handling of wide intensity ranges; modular integration of photon mapping into radiance transfer. Limitations: Dependence on the pre-designed radiance transfer procedure; potential complexity in updating the photon map when transfer functions change. When to use: Real-time volume rendering applications, such as medical imaging (e.g., fetal ultrasound), where interactive performance is critical and lighting conditions vary. When not to use: Offline rendering where higher accuracy is prioritized over speed, or when the scene does not benefit from the specific radiance transfer framework. The method was proposed by Zhang et al.. It builds upon the foundational work of Daniel et al. [35] in creating data formats for assessing scene areas affected by altering transfer functions, and incorporates the volumetric photon mapping algorithm into a customary radiance transfer procedure. The primary application cited is real-time volume rendering for three-dimensional fetal ultrasound. name: Photon Mapping for RRTE
head: Extended Photon Mapping, RRTE-based photon mapping, Refractive radiative transfer equation-based photon mapping
body: Photon Mapping for the Refractive Radiative Transfer Equation (RRTE) is a two-pass rendering algorithm designed to simulate light transport in participating media with spatially varying refractive indices. It solves the integral form of the RRTE using basic radiance to ensure energy conservation, addressing the limitation of standard photon mapping which assumes a constant index of refraction. Unlike standard photon mapping, this method computes curved photon and ray trajectories analytically or numerically to model continuous refraction, producing altered caustic shapes and more accurate reflections. The method consists of two passes: Photon Tracing and Radiance Estimation. It handles both steady-state and transient scenarios. Inputs: Light source definitions (position, direction, flux). Medium properties: extinction coefficient \sigmat(\mathbf{x}), scattering coefficient \sigmas(\mathbf{x}), phase function p(\boldsymbol{\omega}, \boldsymbol{\omega}'), and spatially varying index of refraction n(\mathbf{x}). Geometry of the scene. For transient mode: Time step \Delta t and total simulation time. Outputs: A photon map storing virtual photons with their positions, directions, flux, and (for transient mode) Time of Flight (TOF). Final rendered image with physically correct global illumination. Photon Map Entry: Each stored photon contains: Position \mathbf{x}. Direction \boldsymbol{\omega}. Flux W (or weight). Radius r (for beam radiance estimation). Bounding box of the photon disc (for acceleration structure). Transient only: Time of Flight (TOF). Transient only: Unique light source identifier. Acceleration Structure: A bounding box hierarchy (e.g., BVH) built over the photon discs to accelerate density estimation during the second pass. Index of Refraction Models: 1. Linear vertical profile: n(y) = (1.0 - y) \cdot n{bottom} + y \cdot n{top} where y \in [0, 1] is the normalized vertical axis position. 2. Heterogeneous material mix: n(\mathbf{x}) = Cg(\mathbf{x}) \cdot ng + Cj(\mathbf{x}) \cdot nj where Cg(\mathbf{x}) \in [0, 1] is the concentration of material g, Cj(\mathbf{x}) = 1.0 - Cg(\mathbf{x}) is the concentration of material j, and ng, nj are their respective refractive indices. Group Velocity (Transient): vg(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{c}{n(\mathbf{x})} where c is the speed of light in vacuum. Spatial Step Size (Transient): \Delta s(\mathbf{x}) = vg(\mathbf{x}) \Delta t where \Delta t is the time step size. \Delta t: Step size for numerical integration in transient photon tracing. Photon radius: Assigned to each photon for beam radiance estimation. Number of photons N: Determines the weight of each emitted photon as 1/N. Virtual photons are emitted from light sources and traced through the medium. 1. Emit Photon: For each light source, emit a photon with initial weight W = 1/N and a unique source ID (if transient). 2. Trace Trajectory: Compute the curved path \mathbf{x}(s) through the medium with varying n(\mathbf{x}). Steady-State: Use the fourth-order Runge-Kutta (RK4) method to solve the ray equation. Transient: Solve for position \mathbf{x}(t) and velocity \mathbf{v}(t) numerically using step size \Delta s(\mathbf{x}) = vg(\mathbf{x})\Delta t. Accumulate TOF by adding \Delta t at each step. 3. Interaction Sampling: Determine if the photon interacts with the medium using the inversion method or Woodcock tracking based on \sigmat(\mathbf{x}). 4. Store Photon: If an interaction occurs, store the photon in the photon map. Scattering Handling: Store photons after the first bounce (single scattering) as well as subsequent bounces. This is necessary because curved trajectories prevent general shadow ray tracing to sample direct lighting. 5. Russian Roulette: Use Russian roulette to decide if the photon is absorbed or scattered. If scattered, update direction \boldsymbol{\omega} based on the phase function and reduce weight W by the albedo. 6. Repeat: Continue tracing until the photon is absorbed or escapes the scene. Ray march from the camera to solve the integral form of the transfer equation. 1. Ray Marching: For each pixel, cast a ray into the scene. Sample points along the ray. 2. Density Estimation: At each sample point, query the photon map to find nearby photons within the assigned radius. 3. Radiance Calculation: Estimate the in-scattered radiance using the stored photon fluxes and the beam radiance estimation method. 4. Accumulate: Accumulate the estimated radiance along the ray, accounting for extinction. Unverified code. """ c = 299792458.0 # Speed of light pos = lightsource.position dir = lightsource.direction flux = 1.0 / lightsource.numphotons currentweight = flux tof = 0.0 while currentweight > 0.01: # 1. Determine free path distance # Not given in sources: Implementation of free path sampling deltas = samplefreepath(pos, sigmat) # 2. Compute spatial step based on group velocity nval = nfield.evaluate(pos) vg = c / nval deltasactual = vg deltat # Use the smaller of the two steps step = min(deltas, deltasactual) # 3. Move photon # Not given in sources: Numerical integration of x(t) and v(t) newpos = integratetransient(pos, dir, nfield, step) # 4. Update TOF tof += deltat # 5. Check interaction if interacted: photon = Photon(newpos, dir, currentweight, radius=0.0, tof=tof, sourceid=lightsource.id) photonmap.insert(photon) # Russian Roulette if random() < sigmas / sigmat: dir = samplephasefunction(dir, phasefunc) currentweight = sigmas / sigmat pos = newpos else: break else: pos = newpos return photonmap def estimateradiance(cameraray, photonmap, radius): """ Estimate radiance at a point along the camera ray using photon map. """ radiance = 0.0 # Find nearby photons within radius nearbyphotons = photonmap.queryballpoint(cameraray.position, radius) for photon in nearbyphotons: # Beam radiance estimation # Not given in sources: Exact kernel function for beam radiance estimation contribution = estimatecontribution(photon, cameraray.direction) radiance += contribution return radiance Curved Trajectories: Curved paths prevent the use of shadow rays to connect arbitrary points, making path tracing slow due to lack of direct lighting sampling. Photon mapping is chosen to handle this. Single Scattering Storage: Storing photons after the first bounce increases the necessary amount of photons to obtain high-quality results compared to non-refractive media. Concentration Profile Errors: Discrepancies between rendered and real-world results occur if the measured concentration profile deviates from the assumed distribution, causing blurring or trajectory errors near bounces. Precision: Numerical integration of curved trajectories requires careful handling of precision, especially with steep refractive index gradients. Time Complexity: Render time increases due to the more expensive computation of curved trajectories and intersection points with geometry. Measured increases: Cocktail scene 2:21 h to 3:16 h; Sphere scene 1:26 h to 2:19 h; Fluid sim cup scene ~3 h to 4:41 h. Memory Complexity: Requires storing photons with additional data (radius, bounding box, TOF, source ID) and building a bounding box hierarchy over photon discs. Strengths: Produces noticeably different global illumination, altered caustic shapes/positions, and more accurate reflections due to curved trajectories compared to standard photon mapping. Conserves energy using basic radiance. Limitations: Higher computational cost. Requires more photons for high-quality results due to single scattering storage. Sensitive to inaccuracies in the refractive index profile. When to use: When simulating participating media with spatially varying refractive indices where accurate caustics and refraction effects are critical. When not to use: When performance is critical and constant refractive index is a sufficient approximation. Photon Mapping for RRTE was developed by Zhang et al. as an extension of standard photon mapping to handle the Refractive Radiative Transfer Equation. It builds on the work of Gutierrez et al. [2005] on bending light in participating media and Jarosz et al. [2008] on beam radiance estimation. The method was introduced to conserve energy in participating media with spatially varying refractive indices, a problem not fully addressed by previous approaches that did not account for transient effects or basic radiance. It is used in computer graphics for physically based rendering of complex fluids and heterogeneous materials.
