name: Photon Beam Storage in BVH
body: Photon Beam Storage in BVH accelerates the gathering phase of photon-based radiance estimation by organizing photon beams into a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH). Unlike KD-Trees or grid-based storage, which struggle with the high overlap of volumetric photon paths, this method uses a BVH constructed with the Surface Area Heuristic (SAH) to efficiently cull non-interacting beams during camera ray intersection. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Volumetric Photon Mapping by explicitly handling beam geometry and overlap through sub-beam splitting, enabling rapid retrieval of all beams intersected by an eye ray. Inputs: A set of photon beams generated during the photon tracing phase. Outputs: A BVH data structure containing the photon beams, ready for runtime intersection queries. Data Structures: The core data structure is a BVH where each leaf node contains one or more photon beams. To handle the inefficiency of naive BVH application caused by overlapping beams (e.g., multiple beams emanating from a point light source), the storage structure splits original photon beams into smaller segments called sub-beams. Each sub-beam is enclosed in a bounding volume for BVH traversal. Construction Algorithm: 1. Beam Splitting: During BVH construction, each photon beam is split into sub-beams. The splitting length is determined automatically by the construction algorithm to ensure that each sub-beam has an approximately unit aspect ratio. This improves the partitioning quality of the BVH. 2. BVH Construction: The sub-beams are inserted into a BVH using the Surface Area Heuristic (SAH) for node splitting. Runtime Query: 1. Ray Intersection: For each pixel, a camera ray is cast. 2. BVH Traversal: The camera ray is intersected with the BVH. 3. Beam Retrieval: All leaf nodes (and thus all sub-beams) intersected by the camera ray are collected. 4. Radiance Estimation: The radiance is estimated using the gathered beams, applying the standard photon density estimation formula from the parent Parent, using the power and phase function of the intersected beams. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def sub(self, o): return Vec3(self.x-o.x, self.y-o.y, self.z-o.z) def dot(self, o): return self.xo.x + self.yo.y + self.zo.z def length(self): return math.sqrt(self.x2 + self.y2 + self.z2) class PhotonBeam: def init(self, start, end, power, direction): self.start = start self.end = end self.power = power self.direction = direction self.boundingvolume = self.computeaabb() def computeaabb(self): return { 'min': Vec3(min(self.start.x, self.end.x), min(self.start.y, self.end.y), min(self.start.z, self.end.z)), 'max': Vec3(max(self.start.x, self.end.x), max(self.start.y, self.end.y), max(self.start.z, self.end.z)) } class BVHNode: def init(self, boundingvolume, children=None, beams=None): self.boundingvolume = boundingvolume self.children = children if children else [] self.beams = beams if beams else [] def splitbeam(beam, targetaspectratio=1.0): diff = beam.start - beam.end length = diff.length() numsplits = max(1, int(length / targetaspectratio)) subbeams = [] for i in range(numsplits): t0 = i / numsplits t1 = (i + 1) / numsplits s = Vec3(beam.start.x + (beam.end.x - beam.start.x)t0, beam.start.y + (beam.end.y - beam.start.y)t0, beam.start.z + (beam.end.z - beam.start.z)t0) e = Vec3(beam.start.x + (beam.end.x - beam.start.x)t1, beam.start.y + (beam.end.y - beam.start.y)t1, beam.start.z + (beam.end.z - beam.start.z)t1) subbeams.append(PhotonBeam(s, e, beam.power, beam.direction)) return subbeams def buildbvh(beams, maxdepth=10): if not beams or maxdepth == 0: bv = beams[0].boundingvolume if beams else None return BVHNode(boundingvolume=bv, beams=beams) minx = min(b.boundingvolume['min'].x for b in beams) maxx = max(b.boundingvolume['max'].x for b in beams) miny = min(b.boundingvolume['min'].y for b in beams) maxy = max(b.boundingvolume['max'].y for b in beams) minz = min(b.boundingvolume['min'].z for b in beams) maxz = max(b.boundingvolume['max'].z for b in beams) extents = (maxx - minx, maxy - miny, maxz - minz) axis = extents.index(max(extents)) centroids = [] for b in beams: cx = (b.boundingvolume['min'].x + b.boundingvolume['max'].x) / 2 cy = (b.boundingvolume['min'].y + b.boundingvolume['max'].y) / 2 cz = (b.boundingvolume['min'].z + b.boundingvolume['max'].z) / 2 centroids.append(((cx, cy, cz)[axis], b)) centroids.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) mid = len(centroids) // 2 leftbeams = [c[1] for c in centroids[:mid]] rightbeams = [c[1] for c in centroids[mid:]] leftnode = buildbvh(leftbeams, maxdepth - 1) rightnode = buildbvh(rightbeams, maxdepth - 1) mergedmin = Vec3(min(leftnode.boundingvolume['min'].x, rightnode.boundingvolume['min'].x), min(leftnode.boundingvolume['min'].y, rightnode.boundingvolume['min'].y), min(leftnode.boundingvolume['min'].z, rightnode.boundingvolume['min'].z)) mergedmax = Vec3(max(leftnode.boundingvolume['max'].x, rightnode.boundingvolume['max'].x), max(leftnode.boundingvolume['max'].y, rightnode.boundingvolume['max'].y), max(leftnode.boundingvolume['max'].z, rightnode.boundingvolume['max'].z)) mergedbv = {'min': mergedmin, 'max': mergedmax} return BVHNode(boundingvolume=mergedbv, children=[leftnode, rightnode]) def rayintersectsaabb(rayorigin, raydirection, aabb): tmin = (aabb['min'].x - rayorigin.x) / raydirection.x if raydirection.x != 0 else float('-inf') tmax = (aabb['max'].x - rayorigin.x) / raydirection.x if raydirection.x != 0 else float('inf') if tmin > tmax: tmin, tmax = tmax, tmin tymin = (aabb['min'].y - rayorigin.y) / raydirection.y if raydirection.y != 0 else float('-inf') tymax = (aabb['max'].y - rayorigin.y) / raydirection.y if raydirection.y != 0 else float('inf') if tymin > tymax: tymin, tymax = tymax, tymin if (tmin > tymax) or (tymin > tmax): return False tmin = max(tmin, tymin) tmax = min(tmax, tymax) tzmin = (aabb['min'].z - rayorigin.z) / raydirection.z if raydirection.z != 0 else float('-inf') tzmax = (aabb['max'].z - rayorigin.z) / raydirection.z if raydirection.z != 0 else float('inf') if tzmin > tzmax: tzmin, tzmax = tzmax, tzmin if (tmin > tzmax) or (tzmin > tmax): return False return True def rayintersectsbeam(rayorigin, raydirection, beam): diff = beam.end - beam.start denom = raydirection.dot(diff) if abs(denom) < 1e-9: return False t = ((beam.start - rayorigin).dot(diff)) / denom if t < 0 or t > 1: return False # Exact intersection depends on beam cross-section (cylinder/sphere), assumed point-like here return True def querybvh(bvhroot, rayorigin, raydirection): intersectedbeams = [] def traverse(node): if not rayintersectsaabb(rayorigin, raydirection, node.boundingvolume): return if node.children: for child in node.children: traverse(child) else: for beam in node.beams: if rayintersectsbeam(rayorigin, raydirection, beam): intersectedbeams.append(beam) traverse(bvhroot) return intersectedbeams Parameters: Aspect Ratio: Target aspect ratio for sub-beams is approximately 1.0. Heuristic: Surface Area Heuristic (SAH) is used for BVH construction. Edge Cases: High Overlap: Naive BVH application is inefficient when many beams overlap the same region (e.g., from a point light). Sub-beam splitting mitigates this. Precision: Not given in the sources. Accelerates photon queries by formulating spatial search as a ray-tracing problem using hardware-accelerated BVHs (e.g., NVIDIA OptiX). It stores geometric bounding volumes (cylinders/spheres) for kernel support, leveraging GPU ray-tracing cores for culling. Choose this when hardware acceleration is available and photon densities are high. Performance: Measured on a MacBook Pro with a 3.06 GHz Intel Core 2 Duo processor and 4 GB of RAM. The reference implementation uses only one core, but radiance estimation is a read-only operation and can be parallelized in an optimized implementation. Test scenes include the Cornell box, bumpy sphere, and sphere caustic at 512 pixels across their larger dimension. Strengths: Efficient handling of overlapping beams; fast runtime retrieval of intersected beams; effective partitioning via SAH and sub-beam splitting. Limitations: Construction overhead from splitting and BVH building; the reference study uses a single-core implementation. This method was explored by the authors of as an acceleration scheme for volumetric radiance estimation using photon points and beams. After experimenting with KD-Trees, BVHs, and grids, they found that a BVH with modifications (sub-beam splitting) performed well for their problem domain. The BVH construction uses the Surface Area Heuristic. A comprehensive theory of volumetric radiance estimation using photon points and beams, https://doi.org/10.1145/1899404.1899409, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Photon Query Using Ray Tracing (BVH Acceleration)
head: OptiX Photon Query, Ray Tracing Photon Query
body: This method accelerates photon queries for Path Derivative Estimation (PDE) estimators by formulating the spatial search as a ray-tracing problem using hardware-accelerated Bounding Volume Hierarchies (BVH), such as those provided by NVIDIA OptiX. It stores geometric bounding volumes (cylinders or spheres) representing the kernel support of photon points and beams, allowing the GPU's ray-tracing cores to efficiently cull non-interacting photons before executing software-based intersection tests. Unlike brute-force linear scans, this approach leverages the BVH structure to reduce query overhead, trading off ray-tracing setup for speedups in scenes with many photons. Inputs: A set of stored photons (points or beams) with associated kernel radii r. A query entity: either a camera beam (ray) or a camera point. A ray-tracing framework (e.g., OptiX) with hardware-accelerated BVH support. The specific PDE estimator type (B-B1D, P-B2D, P-P3D, or P-P2D). Outputs: A list of interacting photons (those within the kernel radius) and their geometric intersection details required for density estimation. The BVH stores instances of bounding volumes. The layout depends on the estimator type: 1. B-B1D (Beam-Beam, 1D blur): Volume: A cylinder centered on the photon beam axis. Radius: Equal to the 1D kernel width r. Storage: The BVH stores an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) of this cylinder. To reduce empty space, an instance transform of a unit cylinder is used for an initial Oriented Bounding Box (OBB) rejection test in hardware, followed by a software test. 2. P-B2D (Point-Beam, 2D blur): Volume: A sphere centered on the photon point. Radius: Equal to the kernel width r. Storage: The BVH stores the AABB of this sphere. 3. P-P3D / P-P2D (Point-Point, 3D/2D blur): Volume: A sphere centered on the photon point. Radius: Equal to the kernel width r. Storage: The BVH stores the AABB of this sphere. Kernel Width (r): The maximum distance between points or beams considered by the estimator. This value is set according to Vévoda [Vév14]. 1. BVH Construction: For each photon (point or beam), compute the bounding volume (cylinder or sphere) with radius r. Insert the AABB of this volume into the hardware-accelerated BVH. For B-B1D, also store the instance transform for the unit cylinder OBB test. 2. Query Formulation: If the query is a camera beam, define a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} corresponding to the beam direction. If the query is a camera point (P-P3D/P-P2D), define a ray with origin at the camera point, an arbitrary direction, and a very small extent (effectively a point query). 3. BVH Traversal (Hardware): Trace the query ray against the BVH. The hardware checks for intersections with the stored AABBs (and OBBs for B-B1D). If no intersection is found, the photon is outside the kernel radius. Skip evaluation. If an intersection is found, invoke the software Intersection Program. 4. Intersection Program (Software): Perform a precise geometric test to confirm if the query entity interacts with the photon's kernel support. The test depends on the estimator: B-B1D: Check if the camera beam ray intersects the plane perpendicular to the photon beam. P-B2D: Check if the camera beam ray intersects the disk centered at the photon point and perpendicular to the ray. P-P3D/P-P2D: Check if the camera point lies within the sphere (distance \le r). 5. Estimator Evaluation: If the intersection program confirms a valid geometric interaction, evaluate the PDE estimator using the photon data and the intersection geometry (e.g., finding points \mathbf{b} and \mathbf{c} for B-B1D). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def photonqueryraytracing(estimatortype, queryentity, kernelradius, bvh): """ Accelerates photon query using BVH ray tracing. Args: estimatortype: 'B-B1D', 'P-B2D', 'P-P3D', or 'P-P2D' queryentity: For B-B1D/P-B2D: A Ray representing the camera beam. For P-P3D/P-P2D: A Vector3 representing the camera point. kernelradius: float, r bvh: BVH structure containing photon bounding volumes Returns: List of interacting photons with intersection details. """ interactingphotons = [] # Step 2: Formulate Query Ray if estimatortype in ['P-P3D', 'P-P2D']: # Point query requires a ray with very small extent queryorigin = queryentity querydirection = Vector3(1.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Arbitrary direction queryextent = 1e-6 # Very small extent queryray = Ray(queryorigin, querydirection, queryextent) else: # Beam query uses the camera beam directly queryray = queryentity # Step 3: BVH Traversal # Hardware checks AABB (and OBB for B-B1D) # Returns list of candidate photon indices that intersect the bounding volume candidateindices = bvh.intersect(queryray) for idx in candidateindices: photon = bvh.getphoton(idx) isvalid = False if estimatortype == 'B-B1D': # Cylinder center is photon beam axis # Check if queryray intersects the plane perpendicular to photon beam isvalid = checkbb1dintersection(queryray, photon, kernelradius) elif estimatortype == 'P-B2D': # Sphere center is photon point # Check if queryray intersects the disk centered at photon point # perpendicular to queryray direction isvalid = checkpb2dintersection(queryray, photon, kernelradius) elif estimatortype in ['P-P3D', 'P-P2D']: # Sphere center is photon point # Check if queryorigin (camera point) is inside the sphere isvalid = checkppintersection(queryray.origin, photon.position, kernelradius) # Step 5: Evaluate Estimator if isvalid: # Evaluate PDE estimator using photon and query data # The sources do not specify the exact estimator evaluation formula. interactingphotons.append({'photon': photon, 'valid': True}) return interactingphotons def checkbb1dintersection(ray, photon, radius): """ Checks if ray intersects the perpendicular plane of the photon beam. Photon beam is defined by origin and direction. """ planenormal = photon.direction planeorigin = photon.origin t = intersectplane(ray, planeorigin, planenormal) if t is None: return False intersectionpoint = ray.origin + t ray.direction # Check if intersection point is within radius of photon beam axis vec = intersectionpoint - photon.origin proj = dot(vec, planenormal) planenormal perpdistsq = lengthsq(vec - proj) return perpdistsq <= radius radius def checkpb2dintersection(ray, photon, radius): """ Checks if ray intersects the disk centered at photon point, perpendicular to ray direction. """ diskcenter = photon.origin disknormal = ray.direction t = intersectplane(ray, diskcenter, disknormal) if t is None: return False intersectionpoint = ray.origin + t ray.direction distsq = lengthsq(intersectionpoint - diskcenter) return distsq <= radius radius def checkppintersection(point, spherecenter, radius): """Checks if point lies within sphere.""" return lengthsq(point - spherecenter) <= radius radius def intersectplane(ray, planeorigin, planenormal): """Returns t if ray intersects plane within ray extent, else None.""" denom = dot(ray.direction, planenormal) if abs(denom) < 1e-8: # Parallel case return None t = dot(planeorigin - ray.origin, planenormal) / denom if t < 0 or t > ray.maxt: return None return t def dot(a, b): return a.xb.x + a.yb.y + a.zb.z def lengthsq(v): return dot(v, v) def Vector3(x, y, z): return type('Vector3', (), {'x': x, 'y': y, 'z': z}) def Ray(origin, direction, maxt): return type('Ray', (), {'origin': origin, 'direction': direction, 'maxt': maxt}) B-B1D Parallel Beams: The camera beam may be parallel to the photon beam. In this case, the ray intersects the cylinder but not the perpendicular plane. The intersection program must explicitly reject this case. P-B2D Ray Origin/Endpoint in Sphere: The ray origin or endpoint may lie inside the sphere (bounding volume) without intersecting the actual disk (kernel support). The intersection program must verify disk intersection, not just sphere intersection. P-P3D/P-P2D Point Query: Ray tracing frameworks require a ray, but the query is a point. The remedy is to trace a ray with origin at the camera point, arbitrary direction, and very small extent. Time Complexity: The method relies on hardware BVH traversal for coarse culling and software intersection programs for precise geometric tests. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the BVH structure and the bounding volumes (AABBs/OBBs) for all photons. Strengths: Leverages hardware-accelerated ray tracing (RTX) for efficient culling and reduces the number of expensive software-based geometric tests. Limitations: Requires a ray-tracing capable GPU and framework (e.g., OptiX). The bounding volumes (especially cylinders for B-B1D) may have empty space, requiring additional OBB tests or software checks. This method accelerates PDE estimators within the Unified Photon Beam Path (UPBP) framework for volumetric light transport simulation. It builds on the concept of photon beam storage in BVH [Parent] and adapts it for hardware ray tracing using RTX GPUs. The kernel radii follow Vévoda [Vév14]. Efficient Hardware Acceleration of Robust Volumetric Light Transport Simulation, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14802, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Point-Based Light Transport in Participating Media
head: Point-Based Global Illumination in Participating Media, Point-Based Global Illumination for Participating Media, Point-Based Light Transport for Participating Media with Refractive Boundaries, PBGI for homogeneous media with refractive boundaries
body: Point-Based Light Transport in Participating Media is a global illumination method for homogeneous translucent materials with refractive boundaries that decorrelates scene complexity from illumination computation by replacing the scene with a shaded point cloud (volume samples) for indirect illumination, while keeping polygonal representation for direct visibility. It computes single, double, and multiple scattering contributions separately, handling refraction at boundaries which breaks screen-space coherence. It sets itself apart from its siblings Compute Shader Photon Integration and Volumetric Photon Mapping by using a precomputed multiple scattering table and a specific tree-cut traversal for double scattering, rather than density estimation or beam-based storage. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Scene geometry (polygonal mesh), material properties (index of refraction \eta, scattering coefficient \sigmas, absorption coefficient \sigmaa, phase function p(\hat{i}, \hat{o})), light source positions and intensities. Outputs: Radiance L for each camera ray sample. Data Structures: 1. Light Surface Samples: Layout: Position \mathbf{x}s, diffuse intensity Is. Storage: Organized in an octree spatial hierarchy. 2. Light Volume Samples: Layout: Position \mathbf{x}v, incoming light direction \mathbf{d}v, incoming light intensity Iv, Oriented Bounding Box (OBB) defining the volume of influence Vv. The OBB is computed using the surface area around the originating surface sample and the length of the sampling interval on the incoming ray. Storage: Organized in an octree spatial hierarchy. Each node stores the average position, average direction of incoming light, and combined bounding box of its descendants. 3. Multiple Scattering Table: Layout: 4D table Lo(\rho/\ell, z/\ell, \theta, \phi). Storage: Initially a 2D grid of 512 \times 512 cells. Each cell stores a lobe in spherical coordinates (\theta, \phi) sampled with 18 directions for \theta and 36 for \phi. Compressed using a bottom-up quadtree: replace four neighboring cells with identical lobes with a single cell storing the same lobe. Precomputation Steps: 1. Surface Sampling: Place blue-noise surface samples on the object surface. If enclosed in transparent layers, place samples on the outer layer, connect to the light source, trace the refracted ray through transparent layers to the participating media, and remove samples too close to others to ensure minimal distance. Store indirect diffuse illumination and indirect illumination from inside the material after multiple bounces. 2. Volume Sampling: Connect surface samples to the light source. Compute the refracted ray inside the material (including internal reflections) and sample this ray. Each volume sample stores \mathbf{x}v, \mathbf{d}v, Iv, and its OBB. 3. Hierarchy Construction: Build an octree over light surface samples. Build an octree over light volume samples. 4. Table Generation: Simulate photon propagation in an infinite medium with a point light source sending photons in a single direction. Accumulate results to form a table of material response. Store response in cylindrical coordinates (\rho, z) indexed by distances divided by mean-free-path \ell. Store outgoing radiance in spherical coordinates (\theta, \phi) relative to the current frame. Rendering Steps: 1. Ray Tracing: Trace rays from the camera. When a ray reaches a translucent object, compute the refracted ray inside the object with direction \mathbf{o}. 2. Sample Placement: Place sample points Pk on the refracted ray, defined by depth dk from the entry point. If the camera ray reaches the media directly or after specular events, place k{max} samples with exponential depth distribution. If it reaches after diffuse interactions, sample randomly with a smaller number of samples (as low as one). 3. Contribution Computation: For each sample point Pk, compute single, double, multiple, and bounced contributions, then sum them. Formulas: Transmittance: Tr(\mathbf{x} \leftrightarrow \mathbf{x}t) = e^{-\sigmat \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}t\|}. Sample Depth: dk = -\frac{1}{\sigmat} \log\left(1 - \frac{k(1 - e^{-\sigmat d{max}})}{k{max}}\right), where d{max} is the exit point depth, k is the sample index (1 to k{max}), and \sigmat = \sigmas + \sigmaa. Single Scattering at Pk: \text{single}(Pk) = e^{-\sigmat dk} \frac{1}{Nv} \sum{i} \sigmas p(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}{vi}) I{vi} where Nv is the number of leaf nodes whose bounding box contains Pk, and the sum is over leaf nodes vi containing Pk. Double Scattering at Pk: \text{double}(Pk) = e^{-\sigmat dk} \sum{i} \frac{e^{-\sigmat ri} I{vi}}{ri^2} \sigmas^2 p(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{m}i) p(\mathbf{m}i, \mathbf{d}{vi}) where ri = \|Pk - vi\|, \mathbf{m}i = (Pk - vi)/ri, and the sum is over nodes in the tree cut. Weak singularities caused by r{12} are handled by clamping. Multiple Scattering at Pk: \text{mult}(Pk) = e^{-\sigmat dk} \sum{i} \frac{Lo\left(\frac{\rhok}{\ell}, \frac{zk}{\ell}, T{(vi, \mathbf{d}i)}(\mathbf{o})\right)}{vi} where zk = (Pk - vi) \cdot \mathbf{d}i, \rhok = \|(Pk - vi) - zk \mathbf{d}i\|, \ell is mean-free-path, Lo is outgoing radiance from the precomputed table, and T{(vi, \mathbf{d}i)}(\mathbf{o}) is direction \mathbf{o} in the frame defined by (vi, \mathbf{d}i). Bounced Multiple Scattering: \text{bounced}(Pk) = e^{-\sigmat dk} \sum{j} \frac{e^{-\sigmat qj} I{sj}}{qj^2} fr(\mathbf{t}j) \sigmas p(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{t}j) where qj = \|Pk - sj\|, \mathbf{t}j = (Pk - sj)/qj, and the sum is over surface samples in the tree cut. Total Radiance: L = \sumk (\text{single}(Pk) + \text{double}(Pk) + \text{mult}(Pk) + \text{bounced}(Pk)). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def precomputesurfacesamples(mesh, lights): # Place blue-noise samples on surface samples = [] for light in lights: # Connect to light, trace refracted ray if enclosed in transparent layers # Remove samples too close to others samples.extend(generatebluenoisesamples(mesh, light)) return buildoctree(samples) def precomputevolumesamples(surfaceoctree, lights): volumes = [] for surfacesample in surfaceoctree.flatten(): # Connect to light, compute refracted ray inside material # Include internal reflections ray = tracerefractedray(surfacesample.position, lights) # Sample the ray for t in sampleray(ray): volume = { 'position': ray.point(t), 'direction': ray.direction, 'intensity': computeintensity(ray, t), 'obb': computeobb(surfacesample, t) } volumes.append(volume) return buildoctree(volumes) def precomputemultiplescatteringtable(material): # Simulate photon propagation in infinite medium # Point light source sending photons in single direction grid = creategrid(512, 512) for photon in tracephotonsinfinitemedium(material): rho, z = tocylindrical(photon.position, photon.direction) theta, phi = tospherical(photon.outgoingdirection, photon.direction) grid[rho, z].addlobe(theta, phi, photon.energy) # Compress using bottom-up quadtree return compressquadtree(grid) def rendercameraray(cameraray, surfaceoctree, volumeoctree, table, material): # Compute refracted ray inside object refractedray = tracerefraction(cameraray, material) # Determine sampling strategy if cameraray.isdirectorspecular(): kmax = 64 # Example value dmax = refractedray.exitdepth samples = [] for k in range(1, kmax + 1): dk = -1.0 / material.sigmat math.log(1 - k (1 - math.exp(-material.sigmat dmax)) / kmax) samples.append({'point': refractedray.point(dk), 'depth': dk, 'index': k}) else: # Random sampling with fewer points samples = [generaterandomsample(refractedray)] totalradiance = 0.0 for sample in samples: pk = sample['point'] dk = sample['depth'] # Single Scattering single = computesinglescattering(pk, refractedray.direction, volumeoctree, material) # Double Scattering double = computedoublescattering(pk, refractedray.direction, volumeoctree, material) # Multiple Scattering multiple = computemultiplescattering(pk, refractedray.direction, volumeoctree, table, material) # Bounced Multiple Scattering bounced = computebouncedscattering(pk, refractedray.direction, surfaceoctree, material) totalradiance += single + double + multiple + bounced return totalradiance def computesinglescattering(pk, o, volumeoctree, material): # Traverse octree, stop if bounding box does not contain pk leafnodes = getleafnodescontaining(volumeoctree, pk) if not leafnodes: return 0.0 sumcontrib = 0.0 for vi in leafnodes: sumcontrib += material.sigmas phasefunction(o, vi.direction) vi.intensity return math.exp(-material.sigmat pk.depth) sumcontrib / len(leafnodes) def computedoublescattering(pk, o, volumeoctree, material): # Traverse octree until tree cut criterion is met # Criterion: solid angle phase function treecut = gettreecut(volumeoctree, pk, o) sumcontrib = 0.0 for vi in treecut: ri = distance(pk, vi.position) mi = normalize(pk - vi.position) # Clamp weak singularities caused by r12 if ri < epsilon: ri = epsilon contrib = (math.exp(-material.sigmat ri) vi.intensity / (ri ri)) \ (material.sigmas 2) \ phasefunction(o, mi) phasefunction(mi, vi.direction) sumcontrib += contrib return math.exp(-material.sigmat pk.depth) sumcontrib def computemultiplescattering(pk, o, volumeoctree, table, material): # Use same tree cut as double scattering treecut = gettreecut(volumeoctree, pk, o) sumcontrib = 0.0 for vi in treecut: # Cylindrical coordinates around (vi, di) axis zk = dot(pk - vi.position, vi.direction) rhok = norm((pk - vi.position) - zk vi.direction) # Transform outgoing direction o to frame of (vi, di) otransformed = transformdirection(o, vi.position, vi.direction) # Extract from table lo = table.query(rhok / material.meanfreepath, zk / material.meanfreepath, otransformed) sumcontrib += lo / vi.volume return math.exp(-material.sigmat pk.depth) sumcontrib def computebouncedscattering(pk, o, surfaceoctree, material): # Use same tree cut as double scattering treecut = gettreecut(surfaceoctree, pk, o) sumcontrib = 0.0 for sj in treecut: qj = distance(pk, sj.position) tj = normalize(pk - sj.position) if qj < epsilon: qj = epsilon contrib = (math.exp(-material.sigmat qj) sj.intensity / (qj qj)) \ brdf(sj.normal, tj, o) material.sigmas phasefunction(o, tj) sumcontrib += contrib return math.exp(-material.sigmat pk.depth) sumcontrib This method extends point-based light transport for participating media with refractive boundaries by replacing fixed kernel sizes with dynamic kernels predicted by the local light field's frequency content. It solves the problem of over-blurred single scattering in high-frequency volume caustics by using the determinant of a covariance matrix to adaptively shrink the sampling kernel where light transport is complex, allowing fewer samples to capture sharp details. It sets itself apart from its parent method Point-Based Light Transport in Participating Media by specifically optimizing the single scattering pass with frequency analysis, while retaining the parent's approach for double and multiple scattering. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples k{max} and the depth of the octree traversal. The tree cut optimization reduces the number of nodes visited for double and multiple scattering. Memory Complexity: The precomputed multiple scattering table is compressed from 8.4 GB to approximately 100 MB using the quadtree compression. The octrees for surface and volume samples add additional memory proportional to the number of samples. Measured Performance: Up to 60x faster than UPBP (Unified Points, Beams and Paths) with similar quality. Rendering time was 41 minutes for an olive oil scene compared to 6 hours for UPBP. The GPU implementation yields 30 fps when moving the viewpoint and 25 fps when editing light position or material parameters. Strengths: Fast convergence with little noise. Handles refractive boundaries which break screen-space coherence. Supports editing of material properties and light position. Suitable for interactive rendering applications. Limitations: Assumes homogeneous materials; extension to heterogeneous materials requires further work. Does not consider visibility when summing contributions, resulting in over-estimation when there is occlusion. Point-based methods are biased. Cannot handle multiple refractions caused by concave geometries; only handles light paths with a single refraction on the camera ray and a single refraction on the light ray. Origin: The method was introduced by Beibei Wang, Jean-Dominique Gascuel, and Nicolas Holzschuch from INRIA and Université Grenoble-Alpes in 2016. History: It builds upon point-based global illumination techniques. It addresses limitations of previous methods such as BDPT, BRE, and UPBP by providing a faster alternative with a smaller memory footprint. It also differs from dipole methods by targeting a wide range of albedos and from screen-space methods by handling refractive interfaces. Usage: Used for translucent materials with low albedo and large mean-free-path, where low-order scattering effects dominate. Suitable for rendering applications needing limited rendering cost and interactive rendering applications. name: Covariance Driven Single Scattering Computation
head: Frequency Analysis for Single Scattering, Kernel Prediction with Covariance
body: This method extends point-based light transport for participating media with refractive boundaries by replacing fixed kernel sizes with dynamic kernels predicted by the local light field's frequency content. It solves the problem of over-blurred single scattering in high-frequency volume caustics by using the determinant of a covariance matrix to adaptively shrink the sampling kernel where light transport is complex, allowing fewer samples to capture sharp details. It sets itself apart from its parent method Point-Based Light Transport in Participating Media by specifically optimizing the single scattering pass with frequency analysis, while retaining the parent's approach for double and multiple scattering. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A homogeneous participating media enclosed in refractive boundaries; surface samples distributed on the media boundary; extinction coefficient \sigmat; parameters Ck and \alpha. Outputs: Single scattering radiance for camera rays. Data Structures: Volume Sample: Stores radiance, position, and the determinant of the covariance matrix (\eta). Spatial Hierarchy: An octree or tree structure organizing volume samples. Each node contains an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB). Leaf nodes contain the actual volume samples and their Oriented Bounding Boxes (OBB). Precomputation: 1. Distribute surface samples on the media boundary. 2. Refract light rays from surface samples into the volume. 3. Sample refracted rays to create volume samples. 4. For each volume sample, compute the covariance matrix \Sigma of the local light field. Initialize \Sigma at the light source. Update \Sigma using transport operators: free space travel, projection, boundary refraction, and medium travel. 5. Compute the frequency factor \eta as the square root of the determinant of \Sigma: \eta = \sqrt{|\Sigma|} The value \eta ranges from 0 to 1, where higher values indicate larger frequency content (sharper caustics). 6. Store \eta and radiance for each volume sample. 7. Organize samples into a spatial hierarchy (octree/tree) with AABBs for internal nodes and OBBs for leaf nodes. Rendering: 1. Refract the camera ray into the volume. 2. Sample the refracted camera ray at regular intervals to create camera samples. 3. For each camera sample, traverse the volume sample hierarchy from the root: Check if the node's AABB contains the camera sample. If not, discard the node. If yes, recursively descend until leaf nodes are reached. 4. For each leaf node whose AABB contains the camera sample, perform a kernel test using the leaf's OBB. 5. If the OBB contains the camera sample, the volume sample contributes to the radiance. 6. Calculate the kernel multiplier ki to adjust the kernel size based on frequency: ki = Ck (\alpha \cos(\eta \pi) + (1 - \alpha)) where 0 < \alpha < 1. 7. Update the radiance of the volume sample by multiplying it with ki to conserve energy. 8. Evaluate single scattering radiance using the adjusted kernel. Parameters: Ck: Constant factor controlling kernel size. Value: 20 \times \text{clamp}(\sigmat, 0.3, 0.8), where \sigmat is the extinction coefficient. \alpha: Tweakable parameter. Typical value: 0.4. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The determinant calculation for \eta must be stable. \eta is normalized to the range [0, 1]. Boundaries: The method assumes homogeneous media and refractive boundaries. Degenerate Input: If \eta = 0 (uniform distribution), the kernel size is maximized (ki \approx Ck). If \eta = 1 (high frequency), the kernel size is minimized (ki \approx Ck(1-\alpha)). A framework for frequency analysis of light transport that represents the Fourier spectrum of the local light field using a covariance matrix to predict frequency content and adapt sampling/reconstruction. The local light field is defined as a 4D function parameterized by two spatial coordinates (\delta x, \delta y) and two angular coordinates (\delta \theta, \delta \phi) around a central ray. It computes eigenvectors and eigenvalues of \Sigma to determine principal spreading directions and variance. Transport operators (free space, reflection, refraction) are applied as matrix operations on \Sigma to propagate frequency information. The covariance matrix \Sigma is defined as: \Sigma{i,j} = \frac{\int{\Omega} (x \cdot ei)(x \cdot ej) f(x) dx}{\int{\Omega} f(x) dx}, \quad \forall (i, j) \in \{1, \dots, 4\}^2 where ei is the i-th vector of the canonical basis of the 4D space \Omega and x \cdot y is the dot product. This framework is used to compute the covariance matrix for volume samples in the main method. Time Complexity: Approximately twice as fast as Wang et al. [3] for equal quality requirements. Memory Complexity: Uses one-fifth of the memory cost of Wang et al. [3] for equal quality. Measured Performance: Tested on a 2.20GHz Intel Xeon (16 cores), 24 GB RAM, at 512x512 resolution. Strengths: Produces sharper results (visually identical to UPBP reference) with equal computation time compared to Wang et al. [3], which produces over-blurred results. Limitations: Performance may vary with scene complexity; however, it is less dependent on scene complexity than Holzschuch [2]. When to Use: When rendering homogeneous participating media with refractive boundaries and high-frequency volume caustics, especially when memory or computation time is constrained compared to the original point-based method. Scope: The method is designed for homogeneous participating media with refractive boundaries. The underlying frequency analysis framework was introduced by Durand et al. [4], with the covariance matrix approximation by Belcour et al. [5, 6]. This specific method extends Wang et al. [3] for point-based light transport in participating media with refractive boundaries. The authors implemented the algorithm in the Mitsuba Renderer [14] and compared it against Wang et al. [3], Holzschuch [2], and Unified Points, Beams and Paths (UPBP) by Křivánek et al. [16]. Fast Computation of Single Scattering in Participating Media with Refractive Boundaries Using Frequency Analysis, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2019.2909875, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Photon Beam Tracing
head: Photon beams
body: Photon Beam Tracing is a volumetric radiance estimation method where photon paths are stored as beams (segments) rather than points, allowing for density estimation via beam intersection. It differs from standard volumetric photon tracing by storing beam segments up to the point of intersection with solid objects, rather than discarding the photon. Inputs and Outputs: Photons are shot from light sources into the scene. The output is a photon beams map containing beam segments and their associated radiance/weight information. Data Structures: The photon beams map stores beam segments. Each segment is defined by: 1. Start Point: A 3D vector (\mathbf{p}{start}) representing the origin of the beam. 2. End Point: A 3D vector (\mathbf{p}{end}) representing the termination of the beam segment. 3. Direction: A normalized 3D vector (\mathbf{d}) indicating the direction of propagation from \mathbf{p}{start} to \mathbf{p}{end}. 4. Radiance/Weight: A scalar or vector value representing the energy carried by the photon at that segment. Steps: 1. Photon Shooting: Shoot photon paths from light sources into the scene. 2. Propagation: Propagate the photon through the participating medium. 3. Scattering: If a scattering event occurs within the medium before the propagation distance limit is reached, record the current segment from the previous position (or light source) to the scattering point. Update the photon's position and direction based on the phase function and proceed to the next segment. 4. Object Intersection: If the photon path intersects a solid object before the propagation distance limit is reached: Calculate the intersection point \mathbf{p}{intersect}. Store a beam segment from the current position (or light source) to \mathbf{p}{intersect}. Unlike standard volumetric photon tracing which discards the photon upon object intersection, photon beam tracing retains this segment. 5. Termination: If the photon reaches its propagation distance limit without intersecting an object or scattering, store the final segment from the last position to the limit point. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Beam Radius: The radius of the cylindrical kernel used for density estimation. Propagation Distance: The maximum distance a photon travels before being terminated or stored as a segment. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fixed Beam Width: Choosing a single blurring width that works well for the whole domain is often impossible. Adaptive beam width is a known challenge. Density Estimation: To estimate radiance at a query point \mathbf{q}, a Beam × Point 3D estimate is used. This involves determining the local density of beams intersecting or near \mathbf{q}. The theory assumes an abstract, fixed blurring kernel, which can be implemented by interpreting each photon beam as a cylinder of a specified radius. A minor modification to the standard Point × Point 3D beam radiance estimate (BRE) is required to obtain the Beam × Point 3D estimate. Volume Photon Map Lookup is the process of estimating inscattering contribution during eye ray traversal using the pre-computed volume photon map. For each step during eye ray traversal, a lookup is performed in the volume photon map. Unlike surface photon map lookups which always use final gathering, volume photon map lookups are performed without a final gather step. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Captures light transport up to object boundaries, providing more complete information about indirect illumination near surfaces and in complex scenes with both participating media and solid geometry. Limitations: Density estimation is more complex than point-based methods due to the need to handle beam intersections and potentially varying beam widths. Fixed beam widths may lead to inaccurate estimates in regions with varying photon densities. When to use: Scenes with participating media and solid objects where light transport near boundaries is important. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Photon Beam Tracing was introduced by as a comprehensive theory for volumetric radiance estimation using photon points and beams. It extends standard volumetric photon mapping by incorporating beam segments. The method allows for efficient implementation of standard Point × Point 3D and Beam × Point 2D beam radiance estimates (BRE). It can be easily integrated into existing volumetric photon mapping implementations. A comprehensive theory of volumetric radiance estimation using photon points and beams, https://doi.org/10.1145/1899404.1899409, fetched 2026-10-26 CS348b Final Project - Rendering Underwater Scenes, http://www.graphics.stanford.edu/courses/cs348b-competition/cs348b-04/underwater/index.html, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Grid-based Importance Sampling for Boundary Segments
head: Photon/importon map sampling
body: This method provides a precomputed importance sampling distribution for boundary path integrals in differentiable rendering by discretizing the integrand onto a regular 3D grid. It solves the problem of efficiently sampling the low-dimensional boundary space (\mathbf{x}B, \boldsymbol{\omega}B) where the integrand is complex and potentially discontinuous, making uniform sampling inefficient. Unlike Instant Radiosity / Virtual Point Lights (VPLs) which uses point sources, this method constructs a continuous density field using bidirectional path tracing data (photons and importons) to guide the sampling of boundary segments. Inputs: Light source radiance distribution. Detector importance distribution. Scene geometry (e.g., polygonal meshes). Outputs: A regular 3D grid storing weights Pi for each cell Ci, representing the discretized probability density P(\mathbf{x}B, \boldsymbol{\omega}B). Data Structures: Regular 3D Grid: A fixed-resolution 3D array. Each cell Ci stores a scalar weight Pi. Photon Map: Stores photons traced from the light source, carrying radiance information. Importon Map: Stores importons traced from the detector, carrying importance information. Steps: 1. Precomputation: Before rendering, generate a photon map by tracing photons carrying radiance from the light source. 2. Precomputation: Generate an importon map by tracing importons carrying importance from the detector. 3. Discretization: Define a regular 3D grid that covers the domain of the boundary variables. The total dimensionality of the domains for \mathbf{x}B and \boldsymbol{\omega}B is 3 (1D for \mathbf{x}B on mesh edges, 2D for \boldsymbol{\omega}B on a subset of the sphere of directions). 4. Weight Calculation: For each cell Ci in the grid, compute the weight Pi by integrating the boundary integrand FB(\mathbf{x}B, \boldsymbol{\omega}B) over the cell volume using uniform sampling: Pi = \int{Ci} FB(\mathbf{x}B, \boldsymbol{\omega}B) \, d\boldsymbol{\omega}B \, d\mathbf{x}B This provides a piecewise constant representation of the probability density P(\mathbf{x}B, \boldsymbol{\omega}B). 5. Sampling: During rendering, sample boundary segments (\mathbf{x}B, \boldsymbol{\omega}B) by first selecting a cell Ci proportional to Pi, then sampling uniformly within that cell. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def precomputegrid(photonmap, importonmap, gridresolution): """ Precompute the importance sampling grid for boundary segments. """ # Initialize grid with zeros gridweights = zeros(gridresolution) # Define the 3D domain covering xB (1D edge parameter) and omegaB (2D direction) domainbounds = getdomainbounds() # Iterate over all cells in the grid for i in range(gridresolution): cell = gridcells[i] # Uniformly sample xB and omegaB within the cell # Note: xB is 1D (edge parameter), omegaB is 2D (direction on sphere subset) samples = uniformsamplecell(cell) # Compute the integral of FB over the cell using the samples # FB depends on radiance from photonmap and importance from importonmap integralsum = 0.0 for sample in samples: xB, omegaB = sample radiance = evaluateradiance(xB, omegaB, photonmap) importance = evaluateimportance(xB, omegaB, importonmap) FB = radiance importance # Simplified interaction term integralsum += FB # Normalize by number of samples to approximate the integral Pi = integralsum / len(samples) gridweights[i] = Pi return gridweights def sampleboundarysegment(gridweights, gridcells): """ Sample a boundary segment using the precomputed grid. """ # Select a cell proportional to its weight cellindex = weightedchoice(gridweights) cell = gridcells[cellindex] # Sample uniformly within the selected cell xB, omegaB = uniformsamplecell(cell) return xB, omegaB Parameters: Grid resolution: Not given in the sources. Number of uniform samples per cell for integration: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method assumes the total dimensionality of the domain is low (3D) to make the regular grid feasible. If the AABBs used for spatial partitioning are not small enough, the assumption of at most one intersection per sample point on the proxy curve may be violated, introducing bias. This method efficiently estimates boundary path integrals in differentiable rendering by constructing Kd-trees over the 3D primary sample space to importance sample boundary segments. It addresses the challenge that the integrand is complex and potentially discontinuous, making uniform sampling inefficient. Unlike forward rendering path guiding, which accelerates unidirectional path tracing, this technique focuses on the unique boundary integrals required for gradient computation in differentiable rendering. It builds on Grid-based Importance Sampling for Boundary Segments by replacing the rigid regular grid with an adaptive Kd-tree structure that automatically refines based on the local structure of the approximated integrand. This method provides a compact, piecewise-constant representation of the importance function \tilde{k}(t) along a ray, enabling efficient importance sampling for Monte Carlo volume rendering. It solves the problem of maintaining an accurate sampling distribution without storing every individual sample, thereby reducing memory usage and accelerating the binary search required for sampling. It differs from naive accumulation by actively discarding redundant samples and splitting segments when importance values change, ensuring the data structure remains a refined approximation of the true importance function. A simple regular-grid-based scheme used to guide the sampling of boundary paths for implicit surfaces, helping to find un-occluded regions of light. Regular-grid-based guiding has difficulties handling reflections off of highly glossy surfaces. It assumes at most one intersection for each sample point on the proxy curve, which may be violated when AABBs are not small enough, introducing bias. Time Complexity: Precomputation requires tracing photons and importons and integrating over grid cells. Sampling is O(1) after precomputation. Memory Complexity: Depends on grid resolution and the size of the photon/importon maps. Strengths: Exploits the low dimensionality (3D) of the boundary domain. Provides a continuous density field for importance sampling. Limitations: Struggles with highly glossy surfaces due to the regular grid structure. Bias can occur if spatial partitioning (AABBs) is too coarse. When to use: When efficient gradient estimation for boundary integrals in differentiable rendering is required, and the boundary domain is low-dimensional. When not to use: For scenes with highly glossy reflections where regular grids fail to capture the complex importance distribution. Originated in the context of path-space differentiable rendering. The method is inspired by standard path guiding using photon maps [Jensen 1995]. It was developed to address the challenges of sampling boundary paths efficiently in differentiable rendering, particularly for implicit surfaces. name: Primary-Sample-Space Guiding with Kd-Trees
head: Kd-tree guided sampling of boundary segments, Kd-tree importance sampling for boundary segments, Primary-sample-space guiding
body: This method efficiently estimates boundary path integrals in differentiable rendering by constructing Kd-trees over the 3D primary sample space to importance sample boundary segments. It addresses the challenge that the integrand is complex and potentially discontinuous, making uniform sampling inefficient. Unlike forward rendering path guiding, which accelerates unidirectional path tracing, this technique focuses on the unique boundary integrals required for gradient computation in differentiable rendering. It builds on Grid-based Importance Sampling for Boundary Segments by replacing the rigid regular grid with an adaptive Kd-tree structure that automatically refines based on the local structure of the approximated integrand. Inputs: Scene geometry \mathcal{M}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) and material parameters. Pre-computed photon maps (or importon maps) to approximate source and detector contributions. Error threshold \epsilon for Kd-tree leaf termination. Number of samples N{\text{fit}} for fitting the integrand (typically 32). Outputs: A global list of Kd-tree leaf nodes, each containing a trilinear fit of the approximated integrand \tilde{F} and its integrated probability mass. A discrete distribution over these leaf nodes for sampling. Data Structures: Kd-Tree Node: Contains an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) in the primary sample space, a boolean flag isleaf, and if a leaf, a trilinear fit coefficient vector and a scalar mass (integral of the fit over the AABB). Global Leaf List: A list of all leaf nodes in the tree, used to build the discrete sampling distribution. Definitions: The boundary segment is defined by a point \mathbf{x}B on a mesh edge and a direction \boldsymbol{\omega}B. The mapping from primary samples (u1, \mathbf{u}2) \in [0,1)^3 to (\mathbf{x}B, \boldsymbol{\omega}B) is continuous within intervals corresponding to mesh edges. The integrand F(u1, \mathbf{u}2) is defined as: F(u1, \mathbf{u}2):= \hat{f}^B(\mathbf{p}0^S, \mathbf{p}0^D) J^B(u1, \mathbf{u}2) h^S(\mathbf{p}0^S, \mathbf{p}0^D) h^D(\mathbf{p}0^S, \mathbf{p}0^D) where: J^B is the Jacobian determinant of the change of variable from (\mathbf{x}B, \boldsymbol{\omega}B) to (u1, \mathbf{u}2). \mathbf{p}0^S and \mathbf{p}0^D are the source and detector boundary points, derived from primary samples: \mathbf{p}0^S = \mathbf{x}^{-1} \left( \text{rayIntersect} \left( \mathbf{x}^{\mathbf{B}}(u1), -\boldsymbol{\omega}^{\mathbf{B}}(u2) \right), \boldsymbol{\theta} \right) \mathbf{p}0^D = \mathbf{x}^{-1} \left( \text{rayIntersect} \left( \mathbf{x}^{\mathbf{B}}(u1), \boldsymbol{\omega}^{\mathbf{B}}(\mathbf{u}2) \right), \boldsymbol{\theta} \right) where \mathbf{x}^{-1} is the inverse mapping from scene geometry to reference configuration. h^S and h^D are source and detector contributions, approximated by \hat{h}^S and \hat{h}^D using photon mapping. The method approximates the absolute value of the integrand as: \tilde{F}(u1, \mathbf{u}2) = \left| \hat{f}^B(\mathbf{p}0^S, \mathbf{p}0^D) \right| J^B(u1, \mathbf{u}2) \hat{h}^S(\mathbf{p}0^S, \mathbf{p}0^D) \hat{h}^D(\mathbf{p}0^S, \mathbf{p}0^D) This approximation is used only to construct the PDF; the estimator remains unbiased. Algorithm Steps: 1. Pre-partitioning: Partition the first dimension u1 \in [0,1) into intervals such that each interval corresponds to a specific edge of a polygonal face in the mesh. This ensures that the mapping from u1 to \mathbf{x}B is continuous within each interval. 2. Kd-Tree Construction: For each interval [a, b), build a Kd-tree over the subspace [a, b) \times [0, 1)^2 using the function \tilde{F}. The construction is recursive: Start with the root node covering the subspace [a, b) \times [0, 1)^2. At each node r with AABB, draw N{\text{fit}} samples uniformly from the AABB. Compute a trilinear fit of \tilde{F} using these samples. Calculate the fitting error err. If err \le \epsilon, make r a leaf node. Compute the integral of the trilinear fit over the AABB to determine the node's mass. Add r to the global leaf list. If err > \epsilon, split the node: For each axis ax \in \{x, y, z\}, split the AABB in half along ax. Compute the trilinear fit and total fitting error err{ax} for both child regions. Select the axis ax^ that maximizes the total fitting error err{ax}. Split the AABB along ax^ into two child AABBs. Create two child nodes and recurse. 3. Discrete Distribution Creation: After building all Kd-trees, create a discrete distribution over the global leaf list. The probability mass of each leaf node is proportional to its mass (the integral of the trilinear fit of \tilde{F} over its AABB). 4. Sampling at Render Time: Select a leaf node from the global list using the discrete distribution. Draw primary samples (u1, \mathbf{u}2) within the selected node's AABB using the inversion method based on the trilinear fit of \tilde{F} associated with that node. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random from typing import List, Tuple class KdNode: def init(self, aabbmin: Tuple[float, float, float], aabbmax: Tuple[float, float, float]): self.aabbmin = aabbmin self.aabbmax = aabbmax self.isleaf = False self.fitcoeffs = None self.mass = 0.0 self.children = [] def trilinearfit(samples: List[Tuple[float, float, float]], values: List[float]) -> Tuple[float,...]: # Solves a linear system for 8 trilinear basis functions over the AABB. raise NotImplementedError("Standard linear algebra routine") def evaluatetrilinear(coeffs: Tuple[float,...], u: Tuple[float, float, float]) -> float: u0, u1, u2 = u c = coeffs return (c[0](1-u0)(1-u1)(1-u2) name: Importance Segment Data Structure and Estimation
head: Importance Segment Data Structure
body: This method provides a compact, piecewise-constant representation of the importance function \tilde{k}(t) along a ray, enabling efficient importance sampling for Monte Carlo volume rendering. It solves the problem of maintaining an accurate sampling distribution without storing every individual sample, thereby reducing memory usage and accelerating the binary search required for sampling. It differs from naive accumulation by actively discarding redundant samples and splitting segments when importance values change, ensuring the data structure remains a refined approximation of the true importance function. Inputs: A camera ray defined by origin \mathbf{x} and direction \omega; a target number of initial samples N. Outputs: A data structure representing the importance function \tilde{k}(t) and precomputed integrals, used for Woodcock tracking and transmittance estimation. Data Structure Layout: The data structure is a list of segments. Each segment Ai stores a tuple containing: 1. ti: The location along the ray (lower bound position) of the segment. 2. li: The length of the segment. 3. ki: The importance value (constant within the segment). 4. Ki: The precomputed integral of the squared importance from the ray start to ti, defined as Ki = \int{0}^{ti} \tilde{k}(s)^2 ds. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize an empty data structure for the current ray. 2. Sampling: Draw N random samples of the importance function along the ray, resulting in pairs (t'i, k'i) for i = 1 \dots N. 3. Insertion: Insert the samples into the data structure. This involves merging new samples with existing segments, splitting segments where importance values change, and discarding redundant samples to maintain a compact piecewise-constant representation. 4. Integral Accumulation: Compute and accumulate the integrals for each segment. For empty regions at the beginning and end of the ray, assume the border has an importance of 0. The integral K{i+1} for the next segment is computed by accumulating the integral of the current segment and any preceding empty regions. 5. Tracking: Perform Woodcock tracking using the optimized extinction derived from the data structure until a scattering or absorption event is reached. 6. Light Sampling: In case of a scattering event, sample light sources and compute the (optionally visibility optimized) transmittance. 7. Multiple Scattering (Optional): Calculate the multiple-scattering contribution if required. 8. Progressive Refinement: Repeat steps 2–6 for progressive rendering updates. Computation of h(\mathbf{y}): During rendering, the function h(\mathbf{y}) (where \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x} + t \cdot \omega) is computed using the precomputed integrals: 1. Perform a binary search to find the segment [ti, t{i+1}) containing the current sample location t. 2. Look up the integral to the left of this segment, which is stored with ti as Ki. 3. Add the integral inside the segment up to t. This is calculated as (t - ti) \cdot ki^2. 4. Interpolation Edge Case: If t lies between two segments [t{i-2}, t{i-1}) and [ti, t{i+1}) such that t{i-1} \le t < ti, linearly interpolate between: The stored integral of the segment to the right (Ai). The integral stored for the left segment (A{i-2}) plus the integral of the left segment itself. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeh(y, rayorigin, raydirection, segments): """ Computes h(y) for a point y on a ray using the Importance Segment Data Structure. Args: y: 3D point in world space. rayorigin: 3D point, origin of the ray. raydirection: 3D vector, direction of the ray. segments: List of tuples (ti, li, ki, Ki). Returns: float: The value of h(y). """ # Calculate t, the distance along the ray from origin to y # Assuming raydirection is normalized t = dot(y - rayorigin, raydirection) # Binary search to find the segment index i such that t is in [ti, t{i+1}) # segments are sorted by ti i = binarysearchsegment(segments, t) if i is None: # Handle case where t is outside all defined segments # Based on notes, empty regions at ends have importance 0 return 0.0 ti, li, ki, Ki = segments[i] # Check if t lies strictly between segments (gap case) # Condition: t{i-1} <= t < ti # This implies t is in the gap after segment i-1 and before segment i if i > 0: tprevend = segments[i-1][0] + segments[i-1][1] if segments[i-1][0] <= t < ti: # Linear interpolation between stored integral of Ai and # (integral of A{i-2} + integral of left segment) # Note: The source mentions A{i-2}, implying a specific interpolation scheme # across a gap. We need K{i-2} and the integral of segment i-1. # Get K for the segment before the previous one (i-2) if i >= 2: Kprevprev = segments[i-2][3] else: Kprevprev = 0.0 # Assuming start of ray # Integral of the segment i-1 (which is empty or has different k) # The note says "integral stored for the left segment (A{i-2}) plus the integral of the left segment" # This phrasing is slightly ambiguous. It likely means: # Interpolate between Ki and (K{i-2} + Integral(A{i-1})) # However, K{i-1} is already K{i-2} + Integral(A{i-1}). # So we interpolate between Ki and K{i-1}. Kleft = segments[i-1][3] # Linear interpolation factor # The gap is from t{i-1} (end of i-1) to ti (start of i) # But t is in [t{i-1}, ti). # Let's assume linear interpolation of the integral value over the gap. tgapstart = segments[i-1][0] + segments[i-1][1] tgapend = ti if tgapend == tgapstart: Kinterp = Kleft else: alpha = (t - tgapstart) / (tgapend - tgapstart) Kinterp = (1 - alpha) Kleft + alpha Ki return Kinterp # Standard case: t is within segment i # Integral = Ki (integral up to ti) + integral from ti to t # Integral inside segment = (t - ti) ki^2 integralinside = (t - ti) (ki 2) return Ki + integralinside def binarysearchsegment(segments, t): """ Finds the index i such that segments[i].ti <= t < segments[i].ti + segments[i].li """ low = 0 high = len(segments) - 1 result = None while low <= high: mid = (low + high) // 2 ti, li,, = segments[mid] tend = ti + li if ti <= t < tend: return mid elif t < ti: high = mid - 1 else: low = mid + 1 return result This method constructs and maintains a compact, piecewise-constant representation of the importance function \tilde{k}(t) along a ray by merging newly sampled points with an existing list of segments. It solves the problem of efficiently updating the importance sampling distribution during rendering without storing every individual sample, thereby reducing memory usage and accelerating the binary search required for sampling. It differs from naive accumulation by actively discarding redundant samples and splitting segments when importance values change, ensuring the data structure remains a refined approximation of the true importance function. Time Complexity: The initial construction involves sorting and merging N samples, which is O(N \log N) or O(N) depending on the insertion strategy. During rendering, the binary search for a segment is O(\log M), where M is the number of segments. Woodcock tracking steps depend on the variance of the importance function but are accelerated by the optimized extinction. Memory Complexity: O(M), where M is the number of segments. This is significantly less than storing N individual samples if M \ll N. Strengths: Compact representation reduces memory footprint. Precomputed integrals allow fast evaluation of h(\mathbf{y}). Progressive refinement allows for adaptive quality improvement. Limitations: Requires careful handling of gaps between segments. The quality of the approximation depends on the number of initial samples N and the merging strategy. When to use: Suitable for Monte Carlo volume rendering where importance sampling is critical for variance reduction, especially in scenes with complex participating media. When not to use: Not suitable for real-time rendering where O(\log M) lookup overhead is prohibitive, or for scenes where the importance function is trivial. The Importance Segment Data Structure was introduced in the context of view-dependent visibility optimization for Monte Carlo volume visualization. It builds on the parent method Grid-based Importance Sampling for Boundary Segments by providing a more efficient way to manage the importance function along rays. The method was developed to address the computational cost of maintaining accurate sampling distributions in participating media. name: Construction and Update of Importance Segments
head: Importance Segment Data Structure and Estimation
body: This method constructs and maintains a compact, piecewise-constant representation of the importance function \tilde{k}(t) along a ray by merging newly sampled points with an existing list of segments. It solves the problem of efficiently updating the importance sampling distribution during rendering without storing every individual sample, thereby reducing memory usage and accelerating the binary search required for sampling. It differs from naive accumulation by actively discarding redundant samples and splitting segments when importance values change, ensuring the data structure remains a refined approximation of the true importance function. Inputs and Outputs Input: A sorted list of existing segments list of size n, a new candidate sample cand (containing position t{cand} and importance k{cand}), and a user-defined merge distance threshold d. Output: The updated list of segments, and a flag indicating if the candidate was processed or needs later processing (specifically, null if processed, or an index if deferred). Data Structures Each segment Ai in the list is defined by: ti: The start position of the segment. li: The length of the segment. ki: The constant importance value for the segment. Ki: The accumulated integral of importance up to the end of this segment (or the start of the next). The list is sorted by position ti. The merge distance threshold d determines if two samples are considered "close enough" to form or extend a segment. Algorithm Steps The update process merges the new candidate into the existing list using four merge rules: 1. Empty List: If the list is empty (n=0), insert the candidate as the first segment and return. 2. Same Importance, Close Proximity (Extension): If the new candidate cand has the same importance value as the last segment in the list (curr), and the distance between the end of curr (t{curr} + l{curr}) and the start of cand (t{cand}) is less than d, extend the last segment. Set the end of curr to the end of cand (t{curr} + l{curr} \leftarrow t{cand} + l{cand}). 3. Same Importance, Internal (Discard): If two existing samples form a segment (distance < d) and have the same importance value as the new candidate cand, and cand lies strictly between them (ti < t{cand} < t{i+1}), discard cand. 4. Different Importance, Internal (Split): If the new candidate cand lies on an existing segment [ti, t{i+1}] but has a different importance value, store cand and split the segment [ti, t{i+1}] into two new segments at the location of cand. 5. Otherwise (Insert): If none of the above conditions are met, insert the new segment into the list. Integral Computation Along with merging, the algorithm precomputes the integral Ki for each segment Ai: For unsampled regions between segments, the importance is approximated as the mean of the two surrounding segments' importance values: k{gap} = \frac{ki + k{i+1}}{2}. For empty regions at the beginning and end of the ray, the border importance is assumed to be 0. Integrals are accumulated for each segment and empty region, and the result is stored in the next segment A{i+1}. Pseudocode The following Python-like pseudocode implements the insertion logic described in Algorithm 1 of. It assumes list is a list of segment objects with attributes importance, right() (end position), and left() (start position). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updateimportancesegments(list, cand, d): """ Updates the list of importance segments with a new candidate. Args: list: List of existing segment objects. cand: Candidate segment object with 'importance', 'left()', 'right()'. d: Merge distance threshold. Returns: None if processed, or an index if deferred (simplified to None for this implementation). """ n = len(list) # Rule 1: Empty list if n == 0: list.append(cand) return None curr = list[n - 1] # Rule 2: Same importance and close proximity -> Extend if curr.importance == cand.importance: # Check if the gap between the end of the current segment and the start of the candidate is < d if cand.left() - curr.right() < d: # Extend the current segment to include the candidate curr.right(cand.right()) return None # Rule 3: Same importance, internal -> Discard # Check if there is a previous segment that forms a segment with curr if n > 1: prev = list[n - 2] # If prev and curr form a segment (distance < d) and have same importance if (curr.right() - prev.right()) < d and prev.importance == curr.importance: # If cand lies between them and has same importance if prev.right() < cand.left() < curr.right() and cand.importance == curr.importance: return None # Discard cand # Rule 4: Different importance, internal -> Split # Check if cand lies within an existing segment for i in range(n): seg = list[i] # Check if cand is inside the segment [seg.left(), seg.right()] if seg.left() <= cand.left() < seg.right(): if cand.importance != seg.importance: # Split the segment # Create new segment for the part before cand newseg1 = createsegment(seg.left(), cand.left(), seg.importance) # Create new segment for the part after cand (cand itself) newseg2 = cand # Replace the old segment with the two new ones list[i] = newseg1 list.insert(i + 1, newseg2) return None # Rule 5: Otherwise -> Insert # Insert cand into the list maintaining sorted order # Find correct position insertpos = 0 for i in range(n): if cand.left() < list[i].left(): insertpos = i break else: insertpos = i + 1 list.insert(insertpos, cand) return None def createsegment(start, end, importance): """Helper to create a segment object.""" class Segment: def init(self, start, end, importance): self.start = start self.end = end self.importance = importance self.length = end - start def left(self): return self.start def right(self): return self.end def right(self, val): self.end = val self.length = val - self.start return Segment(start, end, importance) Parameters Merge distance threshold d: A user-defined threshold. If the distance between two samples is less than d, they are considered close enough to provide a sufficient approximation, and redundant samples of the same importance are omitted. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The comparison cand.left() - curr.right() < d relies on floating-point arithmetic. Care must be taken with boundary conditions where samples are exactly at distance d. Empty Regions: The assumption of 0 importance at ray boundaries and mean importance in gaps is a simplification that may introduce bias in regions with sharp importance gradients. Degenerate Input: If the list is empty, the first sample is always inserted. Time Complexity: The insertion involves a linear scan of the list to find the correct position or check for splits, resulting in O(n) time per update, where n is the number of segments. Memory Complexity: The data structure stores only the segments, not every sample, leading to significant memory savings compared to storing all samples. Strengths: Reduces memory footprint; accelerates sampling via binary search on the accumulated integrals. Limitations: The approximation of unsampled regions using mean importance may be inaccurate for highly variable importance functions. When to Use: When rendering participating media with varying importance and memory is a constraint. When Not to Use: When the importance function is extremely complex and requires high-fidelity sampling without approximation. This method is part of the "View-Dependent Visibility Optimization for Monte Carlo Volume Visualization" framework. It was developed to optimize the sampling process in volume rendering by maintaining a compact representation of the importance function along rays. The approach builds on the concept of importance sampling, where samples are concentrated in regions of high contribution to the final image.
