name: Art-Directable Multiple Volumetric Scattering
head: Art-Directable Multi-bounce Scattering
body: Art-Directable Multiple Volumetric Scattering is a path tracing method that computes efficient, physically accurate multi-bounce diffusion in participating media while allowing independent artistic control over image contrast. It distinguishes itself from standard volumetric path tracers by decoupling the physical diffusion (scale) from the visual contrast, enabling biased but convergent rendering of high-order scattering without pre-computation or caching. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Camera ray, volume density field, extinction coefficients (\sigmat, \sigmas), phase function p, light sources, random number generator, contrast control parameter ai, and bounce depth limit. Outputs: Radiance Lo for the camera ray. Data Structures Volume: A voxel grid storing density values. Access is via interpolated voxel values. Random Numbers: A stream of uniform random variables \xi0, \xi1, \xi2 \in 0, 1). Parameters ai: Absorption/attenuation factor for contrast control at bounce i. Bounce limit: The maximum number of scattering events. Example: 16 bounces. Rays per pixel: Example: 256. Algorithm Steps 1. Initial Scatter Selection: Choose the first scatter event along the camera ray using the [density sampling technique from [Kulla and Fajardo 2012]. This technique samples positions proportional to the local density, avoiding the need for a full Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) construction. 2. Random Walk Initialization: Set current position \mathbf{p} and direction \boldsymbol{\omega} based on the initial scatter. 3. Loop for Bounces (i = 0 to N): a. Step Length Selection: For subsequent bounces, approximate Woodcock Tracking by setting the maximum extinction d{max} equal to the local density d at the current position. Calculate the step length l: l = \frac{-\ln(\xi0)}{d} where \xi0 is a uniform random number. Note: This is not mathematically rigorous Woodcock tracking but provides a reasonable measure of maximum extinction in the sample region. b. Move: Advance position \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} + l \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}. c. Scatter Direction: Choose the new outgoing direction \mathbf{v}0 by inverting the phase function p: \mathbf{v}0 = p^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\omega}, \xi1, \xi2) where \xi1, \xi2 are uniform random numbers. d. Direct Light Contribution (Contrast Approximation): Calculate the direct light contribution Li at this bounce using the contrast approximation formula: Li = e^{-ai \int0^t \sigmat(s) ds} \cdot \sigmas \cdot bi \cdot L{light}(\boldsymbol{\omega}i) \cdot p(\boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o, \mathbf{c}i) \cdot g Where: ai: Contrast control parameter at bounce i. \int0^t \sigmat(s) ds: Optical depth along the path segment. \sigmas: Scattering coefficient. bi: A bias or weight factor. L{light}(\boldsymbol{\omega}i): Radiance from the light source in direction \boldsymbol{\omega}i. p(\boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o, \mathbf{c}i): Phase function value at point \mathbf{c}i. g: A geometric or normalization factor. e. Accumulate: Add Li to the total radiance. f. Update: Set \boldsymbol{\omega} \leftarrow \mathbf{v}0 for the next iteration. 4. Return: The accumulated radiance from all bounces. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def artdirectablemultiplescattering(rayorigin, raydirection, volumegrid, sigmat, sigmas, phasefunc, lights, rng, ai, maxbounces): """ Renders a camera ray using art-directable multiple volumetric scattering. """ totalradiance = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] currentpos = rayorigin currentdir = raydirection # Step 1: Initial scatter selection via density sampling # Standard density sampling along ray (Kulla & Fajardo 2012) # Simulate sampling a position proportional to local density currentpos = rayorigin + 0.5 raydirection # Placeholder for actual density sampling logic for i in range(maxbounces): # Step 2: Step length selection using local density approximation localdensity = volumegrid.interpolate(currentpos) if localdensity <= 0.0: break xi0 = rng.uniform(0.0, 1.0) steplength = -math.log(xi0) / localdensity # Step 3: Move and compute optical depth along segment nextpos = currentpos + steplength currentdir opticaldepth = sigmat steplength # Constant sigmat approximation for integral # Step 4: Scatter direction inversion xi1 = rng.uniform(0.0, 1.0) xi2 = rng.uniform(0.0, 1.0) newdir = phasefunc.inverse(currentdir, xi1, xi2) # Step 5: Direct light contribution (Contrast Approximation) # Standard shadow ray trace to lights lightrad = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] # Placeholder for actual light radiance phaseval = phasefunc.evaluate(currentdir, newdir, nextpos) bi = 1.0 # Bias factor, not specified in sources g = 1.0 # Geometric factor, not specified in sources contrastfactor = math.exp(-ai opticaldepth) directcontrib = contrastfactor sigmas bi lightrad phaseval g totalradiance = [totalradiance[j] + directcontrib[j] for j in range(3)] # Step 6: Update for next bounce currentpos = nextpos currentdir = newdir return totalradiance Time Complexity: High. Rendering times for a cloud scape with 16 bounces and 256 rays/pixel were 63m 11s, compared to 5m 16s for single scattering and 6m 4s for the contrast approximation alone. Memory Complexity: Low. The method requires no pre-computation or caching, making it memory-efficient and suitable for static and animated volumes. Strengths: Independent control over contrast and diffusion; works without pre-computation; independent of volume resolution. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to the number of indirect rays; the step length approximation is not mathematically rigorous. When to use: When artistic control over contrast is needed in high-albedo media like clouds or whitewater, and performance is secondary to visual quality. The method was developed by Pixar Animation Studios for use in the production of The Good Dinosaur. It was presented at ACM SIGGRAPH 2015. The approach builds on density sampling techniques from [Kulla and Fajardo 2012]. Art-directable multiple volumetric scattering, https://doi.org/10.1145/2775280.2792512, fetched 2026-10-31

name: Continuous Media Convergence
body: Continuous Media Convergence describes the phenomenon where a discrete medium composed of a large number of scattering particles renders with an appearance statistically indistinguishable from a homogeneous continuous medium. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering dense particulate scenes by allowing the use of traditional volumetric path tracing with global, averaged radiative transfer parameters instead of explicit particle geometry. Inputs: Particle radius r. Total particle count N{tot}. Bounding volume V containing the particles. Single-particle extinction coefficient Ct(r). Single-particle scattering coefficient Cs(r). Outputs: Rendered image using standard volumetric path tracing. Data Structures: Global extinction coefficient \sigmat: A scalar value derived from particle density. Global scattering coefficient \sigmas: A scalar value derived from particle density. Phase function table: Stores the computed phase function for sampling. Steps: 1. Derive Global Coefficients: Calculate the effective extinction and scattering coefficients for the continuous medium based on the particle distribution: \sigmat = \frac{Ct(r) N{tot}}{V} \sigmas = \frac{Cs(r) N{tot}}{V} Where Ct(r) and Cs(r) are the extinction and scattering cross-sections for a single particle of radius r. 2. Compute Phase Function: Calculate the phase function in a similar way and store it in a table. 3. Render: Use the derived global properties to render using traditional volumetric path tracing. Parameters: N{tot}: The number of particles. Convergence to the continuous appearance is observed when N{tot} = 10^7. For very dense media (r = 400\ \mu\text{m}, N{tot} = 10^8), the method produces a smooth appearance matching that from a continuous medium. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Low Density: When N{tot} is small, individual particles lit by lamps are clearly visible, and the appearance differs from the continuous limit. Distribution Assumption: The coefficient derivation assumes a uniform particle distribution within volume V. A simplification for differentiating pixel intensities in homogeneous media with \pi-invariant parameters where \nabla \sigmas = \nabla \sigmat \equiv 0. This causes the gradient term \beta to vanish in Lines 7 and 20 of Algorithm 1. The derivative of the zeroth-order radiance \hat{L}^{(0)} becomes \hat{L}^{(0)}(x, \omega) = e^{-\sigmat D} \hat{L}{es}(x0, \omega) - \hat{D}{\sigmat} L{es}(x0, \omega). The derivative of the first-order radiance \hat{L}^{(1)} becomes \hat{L}^{(1)}(x, \omega) = \int0^D e^{-\sigmat \tau} \sigmas \hat{L}{ins}(x', \omega) d\tau + [e^{-\sigmat D} D \hat{L}{rs}(x0, \omega) + \hat{D}{\sigmas} L{ins}(x0, \omega) - \sigmat L{rs}(x0, \omega)]. Time Complexity: Equivalent to standard volumetric path tracing with homogeneous media. Memory Complexity: Low. Only global coefficients and a phase function table are stored, independent of N{tot}. Performance: Rendering time is constant regardless of particle count once the continuous approximation is valid. Strengths: Efficiently renders extremely dense media (N{tot} \ge 10^7) without geometric overhead. Limitations: Fails to render the "grainy" appearance of sparse particle distributions or resolve individual particle occlusion when N{tot} is small. When to use: When the particle count is high enough that the medium appears hazy or smooth, and individual particle visibility is not required. The concept originates from the observation that discrete participating media converge to continuous media in the limit of particle concentration. Rendering discrete participating media using geometrical optics approximation, https://doi.org/10.1007/s41095-021-0253-5, fetched 2026-10-26 PDF A Differential Theory of Radiative Transfer, https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~ravir/diffrendering.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Volume Scatter
body: Volume Scatter is a volumetric shading component that models the redirection of light as it interacts with particles within a participating medium. It simulates how light propagates through semi-transparent media like smoke or clouds by scattering incoming radiance into other directions. Inputs and Outputs The method takes incident radiance Li and medium properties to compute the scattered radiance contribution. Key inputs are the density (total extinction coefficient \sigmat), the anisotropy parameter g, and the medium color. The output is the scattered radiance added to the ray's accumulated color. Data Structures The implementation relies on a scalar field for density and a scalar or vector for color. The anisotropy is stored as a single floating-point value. Method Steps 1. Sample Interaction Distance: Determine the distance to the next scattering event using the medium's extinction coefficient \sigmat. 2. Evaluate Phase Function: Sample a new direction \boldsymbol{\omega}s based on g. For g=0, use a uniform distribution over the sphere. For g \neq 0, use a biased phase function. 3. Compute Scattering Contribution: Calculate radiance scattered into the view direction by multiplying Li, the scattering coefficient \sigmas, the phase function value p(\boldsymbol{\omega}i \to \boldsymbol{\omega}s), and the transmittance to the interaction point. 4. Accumulate: Add the scattered radiance to the accumulated color, accounting for the transmittance of the remaining path to the camera. Formulas The total extinction coefficient is defined as \sigmat = \sigmaa + \sigmas, where \sigmaa is the absorption coefficient and \sigmas is the scattering coefficient. The transmittance over a path length t is T(t) = e^{-\tau}, where \tau = \int0^t \sigmat \, dt is the optical depth. Parameters Anisotropy (g): Controls scattering directionality. g = 0 scatters evenly in all directions (similar to a diffuse BSDF). g < 0 scatters mostly backwards. g > 0 scatters mostly forwards. Density: Defines how much light interacts with the volume (absorbed or scattered) versus passing through. Typical values are not given in the sources. Pitfalls Anisotropy Range: Values outside [-1, 1] may cause physical inaccuracies or numerical instability. Density Scaling: High density without field scaling can make volumes opaque, obscuring scattering from absorption. A control parameter that limits the number of diffuse bounces light undergoes inside the volume. Definition: Equivalent to the surface diffuse limit property, controlling internal light bounces. Parameter: Volume limit (integer). Default is 0 (no bounces, volume does not transmit light from behind). Can be increased to 1, 2, 3, or 4 for more bounces. Usage: Increasing the value makes the volume brighter by transmitting more light. Pitfalls: The visual difference between 0 and 1 is dramatic, while 1 to 2 is much less. Values should generally not exceed 4 due to diminishing returns and increased render time. Complexity: Cost is proportional to sampled scattering events, depending on optical depth and path depth limit. Performance: Higher anisotropy (forward scattering) may require more samples to resolve sharp phase function peaks. Higher Volume limit values significantly increase render time by tracing additional bounces. Strengths: Provides physically plausible scattering for smoke and clouds. Limitations: Without multiple scattering approximations or high bounce limits, volumes may appear too dark or lack internal illumination. Volume Scatter is a standard component in volumetric shading systems. It is based on the physical principle that light interacts with particles in a medium, redirecting energy according to the medium's properties. The concept of anisotropy in scattering is rooted in radiative transfer theory. It is commonly used to shade white smoke or clouds. Volumes — Blender Manual, https://www.blender.org/manual/nb/3.6/render/materials/components/volume.html, fetched 2026-10-26 Rendering volumes - SideFX, https://www.sidefx.com/docs/houdini/render/volumes.html, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Volume Rendering Equation with Extinction and Inscattering
head: Beer-Lambert with Inscattering, Physical Volume Model
body: This method computes the radiance arriving at a camera by integrating the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE), accounting for light attenuation via extinction (absorption and out-scattering) and light gain via emission and in-scattering. It differs from the Absorption-only model by including scattering effects and from the Single Scattering Model by integrating over the full sphere of directions for in-scattering, providing a physically accurate solution for participating media. Inputs: Camera ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \boldsymbol{\omega} (unit vector pointing from eye to scene). Volume density field \rho(\mathbf{p}) (scalar field, typically 0 to 1). Absorption coefficient \sigmaa (base value, units m^{-1}). Scattering coefficient \sigmas (base value, units m^{-1}). Emissive term Le(\mathbf{p}, \boldsymbol{\omega}) (radiance emitted per unit length). Incident radiance Li(\mathbf{p}, \boldsymbol{\omega}') from light sources, attenuated through the volume. Phase function p(\boldsymbol{\omega}, \boldsymbol{\omega}'). Outputs: Final radiance Lo at the camera. Data Structures: Extinction Coefficient \sigmat: A scalar value computed per sample. Layout: \sigmat = \sigmaa + \sigmas. Phase Function p: A scalar value in range [0, 1]. Depends on the angle \theta between view direction \boldsymbol{\omega} and light direction \boldsymbol{\omega}'. For isotropic scattering: p = \frac{1}{4\pi}. Normalization: \int{\Omega} p(\boldsymbol{\omega}, \boldsymbol{\omega}') d\omega' = 1 to conserve energy. Parameters: \sigmaa: Absorption coefficient. Represents light absorbed by the volume. \sigmas: Scattering coefficient. Represents probability of light scattering outwards. \sigmat: Extinction coefficient. Sum of \sigmaa and \sigmas, used in Beer's Law. Density: A global scaling variable for \sigmaa and \sigmas to adjust volume opacity uniformly. Steps: 1. Compute Extinction: Calculate the total extinction coefficient \sigmat as the sum of absorption and scattering coefficients: \sigmat = \sigmaa + \sigmas Apply global density scaling if applicable. 2. Compute Transmittance: Use \sigmat in the Beer-Lambert law to compute transmission for the camera ray and the ray to the light source: T = e^{-\tau} = e^{-\int \sigmat dt} This accounts for both absorption and out-scattering (light lost from the view ray). 3. Check Density: If the local density is zero, skip accumulation for this sample. No light is accumulated, and no in-scattering is added. 4. Compute In-Scattering: Calculate the in-scattering contribution Li(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}) by integrating incident radiance over the sphere of directions: Li(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}) = \int{\Omega} p(\boldsymbol{\omega}, \boldsymbol{\omega}') L(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}') d\omega' Where: x is the sample position. \boldsymbol{\omega} is the view direction. \boldsymbol{\omega}' is the light direction (opposite to radiance flow, from light to particle). L(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}') is the incident radiance at x from direction \boldsymbol{\omega}', attenuated through the volume. p(\boldsymbol{\omega}, \boldsymbol{\omega}') is the phase function, determined by the angle \theta between \boldsymbol{\omega} and \boldsymbol{\omega}' (via dot product and cosine). 5. Accumulate: Add the in-scattering term and emission term to the result, weighted by the transmittance from the camera to the sample point. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervolumeray(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedensity, sigmaabase, sigmasbase, Le, Lincident, phasefunction): """ Renders a single ray through a participating medium using the volume rendering equation with extinction and inscattering. Args: rayorigin: vec3, origin of the camera ray. raydirection: vec3, direction of the camera ray (unit vector). volumedensity: function(p) -> float, returns density at position p. sigmaabase: float, base absorption coefficient. sigmasbase: float, base scattering coefficient. Le: function(p, omega) -> vec3, emissive term at position p in direction omega. Lincident: function(p, omega) -> vec3, incident radiance from lights, attenuated. phasefunction: function(omega, omegaprime) -> float, returns scattering probability. Returns: vec3, final radiance. """ # Constants MAXSTEPS = 100 STEPSIZE = 0.1 # Example step size, depends on resolution accumulatedradiance = vec3(0.0) transmittance = 1.0 # Ray marching for i in range(MAXSTEPS): # Current sample position pos = rayorigin + raydirection (i STEPSIZE) # Get density at current position density = volumedensity(pos) # Edge case: If density is zero, no interaction occurs if density == 0.0: continue # Compute extinction coefficient # Density scales the base coefficients globally sigmaa = sigmaabase density sigmas = sigmasbase density sigmat = sigmaa + sigmas # Compute transmittance for this step # T = exp(-sigmat dt) steptransmittance = exp(-sigmat STEPSIZE) # Compute in-scattering # Li(x, omega) = integral over sphere of p(omega, omega') L(x, omega') domega' # In practice, this is approximated by sampling light directions inscattering = vec3(0.0) # Example: Single light source approximation for inscattering # Note: Full integration requires sampling the sphere, which is computationally expensive. # Here we assume Lincident provides the attenuated light from specific directions. # For a single light, we might sample the direction to the light. lightdirection = normalize(lightposition - pos) # Phase function value # theta is angle between view direction and light direction # p depends on theta pval = phasefunction(raydirection, lightdirection) # Incident radiance from light, already attenuated through volume # L(x, omega') is the light reaching this point from the light source Llight = Lincident(pos, lightdirection) # In-scattering contribution for this direction # Note: The integral is over all directions. This is a simplification. inscattering += pval Llight # Add emission emission = Le(pos, raydirection) # Accumulate radiance # dL = (sigmas Li + sigmae) T dt # Here, sigmas Li is the inscattering term, sigmae is emission # We multiply by the transmittance from the camera to this point (transmittance) # And the transmittance of the current step (steptransmittance) # The term (sigmas inscattering + emission) represents the source term # multiplied by the step length (implicitly handled by integration) # Correct accumulation formula: # Lo = integral from 0 to tmax of T(0, t) (sigmas Li(t) + sigmae(t)) dt # Discretized: # accumulatedradiance += transmittance (sigmas inscattering + emission) STEPSIZE # transmittance = steptransmittance # However, the source notes emphasize that sigmas is used for transmission calculation too. # And that result is premultiplied by opacity. # Let's follow the standard volume rendering integral: # C = integral T(t) sigmas Li(t) dt + integral T(t) sigmae(t) dt accumulatedradiance += transmittance (sigmas inscattering + emission) STEPSIZE transmittance = steptransmittance # Early termination if transmittance is negligible if transmittance < 0.001: break return accumulatedradiance Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Density: If density is zero, no light is accumulated, and no in-scattering is added. Phase Function Normalization: The phase function must be normalized such that its integral over the sphere equals 1 to conserve energy. Anisotropic Scattering: Most volumes are anisotropic, scattering light biased towards certain directions (e.g., forward scattering). Isotropic scattering (p = 1/4\pi) is a simplification. Computational Cost: Integrating over the sphere of directions for in-scattering is expensive. Approximations (like single scattering or gradient-guided approximations) are often used. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of samples per ray and M is the number of light directions sampled for in-scattering integration. Full integration over the sphere is O(N \cdot S), where S is the number of samples over the sphere. Memory Complexity: O(V), where V is the size of the volume density field. Strengths: Physically accurate; handles complex lighting interactions; accounts for both absorption and scattering. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to the integration over the sphere of directions for in-scattering; sensitive to noise if not enough samples are used. When to Use: High-quality offline rendering; scenes with significant scattering effects (fog, smoke, clouds). When Not to Use: Real-time applications with limited computational resources; scenes where scattering effects are negligible. The volume rendering equation with extinction and inscattering is derived from the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE), a fundamental equation in physics describing light transport in participating media. It generalizes the Beer-Lambert law by including scattering and emission terms. The method is widely used in computer graphics for rendering volumetric effects like fog, smoke, and clouds. The phase function concept, introduced to model directional scattering, is central to this model. name: Volume Rendering (Single Scattering Stratified)
head: Homogenous volume rendering, Participating media rendering, Single Scattering Stratified Sampling
body: This method renders participating media (fog, smoke, smog) by numerically integrating the radiance transfer equation along view rays using stratified sampling. It solves the problem of light attenuation and in-scattering in volumetric scenes by decomposing the rendering equation into separate attenuation and augmentation terms, estimating the latter via single scattering from direct light sources. It is distinguished from general single scattering methods by its use of stratified sampling to reduce variance in the 1D light transfer integral, and from multiple scattering methods by its neglect of indirect lighting contributions. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: View ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; media properties (attenuation coefficient \sigmat, scattering coefficient \sigmas, emission Le, phase function p); light source positions and intensities; step size \Delta t for ray marching. Outputs: Final radiance L at the camera pixel. Data Structures Ray Segment: Defined by start parameter t{start}, end parameter t{end}, and length \Delta t = t{end} - t{start}. Sample Point: A position \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{o} + t \mathbf{d} within the segment, determined by a stratified offset. Accumulators: mask (float): Accumulated transmittance T. Initialized to 1.0. color (vector): Accumulated in-scattered radiance. Initialized to 0. Formulas 1. Radiance Transfer Equation: \frac{dL}{ds} = -\sigmat L + \sigmas \int{4\pi} p(\omega, \omega') L(\omega') d\omega' + Le Where \sigmat is the attenuation coefficient (absorption + out-scattering), \sigmas is the scattering coefficient, p is the phase function, and Le is media emission. 2. Homogenous Attenuation (Beer's Law): T(s) = \exp(-\sigmat s) Derived from solving \frac{dT}{ds} = -\sigmat T. 3. Henyey-Greenstein Phase Function: p(\cos \theta) = \frac{1}{4\pi} \frac{1 - g^2}{(1 + g^2 - 2g \cos \theta)^{3/2}} Where g is the asymmetry parameter ranging from -1 to 1 (e.g., 0.7 for forward scattering). For isotropic media, p = \frac{1}{4\pi}. 4. Rendering Equation Decomposition: L = T \cdot L{background} + \int{t{near}}^{t{far}} T(t) \left( \sigmas \int{4\pi} p L{incident} d\omega' + Le \right) dt Computed as: color += mask augmentationterm \Delta t; mask = transmittance. Parameters Step Size (\Delta t): Determines ray marching resolution. Smaller values increase accuracy but cost more. Asymmetry Parameter (g): Controls scattering polarity. g=0 is isotropic, g>0 is forward, g<0 is backward. Numbered Steps 1. Initialize: Set mask = 1.0, color = 0. Generate a random stratified offset for the current ray. 2. Ray Marching Loop: For each segment along the view ray from t{near} to t{far} with step size \Delta t: a. Calculate Transmittance: Compute T{seg} = \exp(-\sigmat \Delta t) assuming homogenous media within the segment. b. Update Mask: mask = mask T{seg}. c. Estimate Augmentation (In-scattering): i. Determine sample position \mathbf{x} within the segment using the stratified offset. ii. Perform Next Event Estimation (NEE): For each light source, shoot a shadow ray from \mathbf{x} to the light. iii. If visible, calculate incident radiance L{incident} from the light. iv. Evaluate phase function p(\omega{light}, \omega{view}) at \mathbf{x}. v. Compute augmentationterm = \sigmas \cdot p \cdot L{incident} + Le. vi. color = color + mask augmentationterm \Delta t. d. Advance: Increment t by \Delta t. Generate a new random offset for the next ray (stratified sampling resets per ray). 3. Composite: Add mask backgroundcolor to color. 4. Output: Return color. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Indirect Lighting: This method neglects indirect lighting in in-scattering. This is acceptable as indirect contributions are often weak, but causes inaccuracies in highly reflective or enclosed scenes. Precision: Using exponential functions for transmittance requires care with very small \sigmat \Delta t to avoid precision loss, though standard exp is usually sufficient. Homogeneity Assumption: The Beer's law application assumes constant coefficients within \Delta t. If media density varies rapidly, \Delta t must be small enough to approximate homogeneity. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def heneygreenstein(costheta, g): """ Henyey-Greenstein phase function. costheta: cosine of the angle between incident and view direction. g: asymmetry parameter (-1 to 1). """ if abs(1 - g g) < 1e-9: return 1.0 / (4.0 math.pi) denom = 1 + g g - 2 g costheta if denom < 1e-9: denom = 1e-9 return (1 - g g) / (4 math.pi (denom 1.5)) def volumerendersinglescatteringstratified(rayorigin, raydir, mediasigmat, mediasigmas, mediaLe, lights, stepsize, backgroundcolor): """ Renders volume using single scattering and stratified sampling. """ mask = 1.0 color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Generate random offset for stratified sampling for this ray # The offset is uniform in [0, stepsize) offset = random.uniform(0, stepsize) t = 0.0 while t < 100.0: # Arbitrary far plane limit # Determine segment bounds tstart = t tend = t + stepsize # Calculate transmittance for this segment (Beer's Law) # T = exp(-sigmat s) transmittanceseg = math.exp(-mediasigmat stepsize) # Update accumulated mask mask = transmittanceseg # Calculate sample point within segment using stratified offset # The offset is applied relative to the start of the segment # Note: In strict stratified sampling for 1D integral, # we might use a fixed offset pattern or randomize per ray. # Source says: "assigns same offset for each segment and randomizes # the offset for a new ray". This implies the offset is constant # across segments for a single ray, or reset per ray. # We use the ray-level offset. tsample = tstart + offset # Clamp sample to segment if tsample > tend: tsample = tend # Position of sample samplepos = [ rayorigin[0] + tsample raydir[0], rayorigin[1] + tsample raydir[1], rayorigin[2] + tsample raydir[2] ] # Estimate augmentation term (In-scattering + Emission) augmentation = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Add emission augmentation[0] += mediaLe[0] augmentation[1] += mediaLe[1] augmentation[2] += mediaLe[2] # Single scattering from direct lights (Next Event Estimation) for light in lights: # Vector to light lightdir = [ light.pos[0] - samplepos[0], light.pos[1] - samplepos[1], light.pos[2] - samplepos[2] ] disttolight = math.sqrt(lightdir[0]2 + lightdir[1]2 + lightdir[2]2) # Normalize if disttolight < 1e-9: continue lightdirnorm = [d / disttolight for d in lightdir] # Shadow ray check # Simple implementation: assume visible if no occlusion check provided # In a real engine, this would involve a ray-march or BVH query isvisible = True # Placeholder for shadow ray logic if isvisible: # Cosine of phase function angle # Angle between view direction (raydir) and light direction (lightdirnorm) # Note: raydir is incoming to surface, lightdirnorm is outgoing from sample to light # Phase function usually takes angle between incoming light and outgoing view # Here, view direction is -raydir (from sample to camera) # Light direction is lightdirnorm (from sample to light) # Dot product of (-raydir) and lightdirnorm costheta = - (raydir[0]lightdirnorm[0] + raydir[1]lightdirnorm[1] + raydir[2]lightdirnorm[2]) # Evaluate phase function # g is assumed to be a property of the media, e.g., 0.7 g = 0.7 phase = heneygreenstein(costheta, g) # Incident radiance from light # Lincident = light.intensity / dist^2 (simplified point light) incidentL = light.intensity / (disttolight 2) # Add to augmentation: sigmas p Lincident augmentation[0] += mediasigmas phase incidentL[0] augmentation[1] += mediasigmas phase incidentL[1] augmentation[2] += mediasigmas phase incidentL[2] # Accumulate color # color += mask augmentation deltat color[0] += mask augmentation[0] stepsize color[1] += mask augmentation[1] stepsize color[2] += mask augmentation[2] stepsize # Advance ray t += stepsize # Stratified sampling note: # "assigns same offset for each segment" -> offset is constant for the ray. # "randomizes the offset for a new ray" -> offset is regenerated per ray. # So we do NOT change offset here. # Composite with background color[0] += mask backgroundcolor[0] color[1] += mask backgroundcolor[1] color[2] += mask backgroundcolor[2] return color Time Complexity: O(N \cdot L), where N is the number of ray march steps and L is the number of light sources. Each step requires a shadow ray cast to each light. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per ray, excluding scene data structures for lights and media. Measured Performance: Performance is heavily dependent on scene density and number of lights. Stratified sampling reduces variance, allowing for fewer samples per pixel compared to standard Monte Carlo, but the single-scattering approximation limits visual fidelity in dense media. Strengths: Physically plausible for thin to medium density media; efficient due to single scattering approximation; stratified sampling provides smoother results than naive Monte Carlo. Limitations: Neglects indirect lighting, leading to dark shadows and lack of color bleeding in dense scenes; assumes homogeneity within step size; computationally expensive for many lights due to NEE. When to Use: Real-time or interactive rendering of fog, smoke, or clouds where indirect lighting is negligible or can be approximated by ambient terms. When Not to Use: Dense, optically thick media where multiple scattering dominates; scenes requiring accurate global illumination within the volume. The method is based on the integro-differential equation of transfer for participating media, originally described by Chandrasekhar (1960). The use of the Henyey-Greenstein phase function dates to Henyey and Greenstein (1941). The specific application of stratified sampling for volume rendering to reduce variance in the 1D light transfer integral is attributed to Pauly (1999). This approach is a standard technique in computer graphics for rendering participating media, often implemented in real-time engines and offline renderers for effects like fog and smoke. name: Monte Carlo Sampling and Estimation
body: Monte Carlo methods solve the transport equation by means of random sampling, using random paths along interaction points. They are distinguished from deterministic approaches by their reliance on stochastic path generation rather than spatial discretization. All methods in this family rely on the statistical estimation of the integral form of the radiative transfer equation. The core mechanism involves generating random paths through the medium and estimating the contribution of each path to the final image. 1. Path Generation Paths are constructed by sampling interaction points (scattering or absorption events) along rays. The distance to the next interaction is sampled from a probability density function (PDF) defined by the extinction coefficient \sigmat. For heterogeneous media, techniques sample the continuous distribution exactly without grid constraints. 2. Estimator Formulation The radiance L is estimated as an average of N independent samples Xi: L \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \frac{f(Xi)}{p(Xi)} where f(Xi) is the path contribution (including emission, scattering, and transmittance) and p(Xi) is the probability of generating that path. Unbiased estimators require that E[L] = L{\text{true}}. 3. Variance Reduction To improve convergence, methods employ variance reduction techniques: Importance Sampling: Sampling interaction points or directions according to a distribution that approximates the integrand's shape, such as sampling near light sources or boundaries. Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS): Combining multiple sampling strategies (e.g., light sampling vs. path sampling) to reduce variance in difficult lighting scenarios. Biased Sampling: Deliberately biasing the random walk to exit the medium faster to reduce the number of "lost" paths, accepting a small bias for significant variance reduction. The Path Integral Framework expresses light transport as a non-recursive integral over the space of all possible light transport paths \mathcal{P}, unrolling the infinite series of scattering events into a single high-dimensional integral. It sets itself apart from recursive formulations by enabling the application of general Monte Carlo integration techniques and MIS. Choose it when a rigorous mathematical measure is required for variance reduction methods. See Path Integral Framework. Delta tracking is a Monte Carlo free-path sampling method that finds the first real collision point in a heterogeneous participating medium by sampling tentative collisions from a fictitious homogeneous medium with a constant maximum extinction coefficient (majorant). It sets itself apart from ray marching by providing an unbiased estimator through probabilistic acceptance/rejection. Choose it for efficiently sampling interaction distances in spatially varying media without structured grids. See Delta tracking. Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) for volumetric path tracing reduces variance by combining contributions from unidirectional path sampling (phase function sampling) and light sampling (Next Event Estimation). It sets itself apart from standard path tracing by balancing strategies using the power heuristic, requiring careful PDF caching across index-matching surfaces. Choose it when paths frequently terminate near light sources or when light sources are small. See Multiple Importance Sampling for Volumetric Path Tracing. Unified Points, Beams, and Paths (UPBP) is a combined rendering algorithm that fuses volumetric density estimation estimators (Point-Point, Point-Beam, Beam-Beam) with unbiased bidirectional path tracing using MIS. It sets itself apart by automatically selecting the most suitable representation—points for high-order scattering, beams for low-order scattering, and paths for volume effects with specular surfaces. Choose it for efficiently simulating light transport in diverse participating media. See Unified Points, Beams, and Paths (UPBP). Dwivedi Sampling is a variance reduction technique that biases the random walk to exit the medium as quickly as possible. It sets itself apart from standard distance sampling by approximating the local geometry as a slab to analytically estimate the light field, thereby reducing "lost" paths. Choose it for high-scattering scenarios where paths tend to terminate deep inside opaque objects. See Dwivedi Sampling. The Optimized Monte Carlo Integrator computes radiance scattered inside a homogeneous, box-shaped participating medium from a collimated light source. It sets itself apart from standard ray marching by pre-computing a cumulative distribution histogram of trapezoidal segments to select interaction points directly, and from Delta Tracking by exploiting convex box geometry for analytic integration. Choose it for real-time single-scattering estimation in box-shaped volumes. See Optimized Monte Carlo Integrator. A stochastic method sampling interaction points from a function of \kappa t. A technique used to address the computational challenge of rendering fire smoke, specifically handling multiple scattering directions. A multiple scattering scheme based on Metropolis-Hasting sampling, analyzed in the thesis. The survey by categorizes stochastic methods by how they set interaction points, distinguishing between those using a constant step distance and those sampling a function of optical depth \kappa t. Methods sampling a function of \kappa t include light tracing, bidirectional path-tracing, photon maps, and Metropolis Light Transport. A survey on participating media rendering techniques, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00371-005-0287-1, fetched 2026-10-26 Visualization of Smoke and Fire Data Based on the Fire Dynamics Simulation Model, https://doi.org/10.13016/m2bm1b, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Path Integral Framework
head: Path Space Formulation, Veach's path-integral formulation, Path Integral Formulation of the Rendering Equation
body: The Path Integral Framework expresses light transport in participating media as a non-recursive integral over the space of all possible light transport paths \mathcal{P}, where the pixel intensity I is the sum of contributions from every path connecting a light source to the camera. It sets itself apart from recursive formulations (like the standard rendering equation) by unrolling the infinite series of scattering events into a single high-dimensional integral, enabling the application of general Monte Carlo integration techniques and variance reduction methods such as Multiple Importance Sampling. Unlike Delta tracking, which focuses on sampling techniques for heterogeneous media, the Path Integral Framework provides the rigorous mathematical measure and contribution function definition that these samplers estimate. Inputs and Outputs Input: A scene geometry \mathcal{M} (union of surfaces and volumes), light source emission functions Le, surface scattering functions (BSDFs) \rhos, volumetric scattering functions (phase functions) \rhop and scattering coefficients \sigmas, extinction coefficients \sigmat, and camera response function We. Output: The estimated pixel intensity I. Data Structures A path \bar{\mathbf{x}} is represented as an ordered sequence of vertices \bar{\mathbf{x}} = (\mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{x}1, \dots, \mathbf{x}k), where k \ge 1 is the path length (number of segments) and k+1 is the number of vertices. \mathbf{x}0: Vertex on a light source. \mathbf{x}k: Vertex on the camera sensor. \mathbf{x}i (0 < i < k): Intermediate vertices, which may lie on surfaces or within participating media. Each vertex \mathbf{x}i contains spatial coordinates \mathbf{p}i, surface normal \mathbf{n}i (if on surface), and direction vectors relative to adjacent segments. Formulas The pixel intensity is defined as the integral over the path space \mathcal{P}: I = \int{\mathcal{P}} f(\bar{\mathbf{x}}) d\mu(\bar{\mathbf{x}}) where f(\bar{\mathbf{x}}) is the measurement contribution function and d\mu(\bar{\mathbf{x}}) is the differential path measure. The measurement contribution function is the product of emitted radiance, path throughput, and detector sensitivity: f(\bar{\mathbf{x}}) = Le(\mathbf{x}0) T(\bar{\mathbf{x}}) We(\mathbf{x}k) The path throughput T(\bar{\mathbf{x}}) accounts for geometric attenuation, volumetric transmittance, and scattering at intermediate vertices: T(\bar{\mathbf{x}}) = \left[ \prod{i=0}^{k-1} G(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1}) T{\mathbf{r}}(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1}) \right] \left[ \prod{i=1}^{k-1} \rho(\mathbf{x}i) \right] The geometry term G(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) for a segment between \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{y} is: G(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = V(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) \frac{D(\mathbf{x} \rightarrow \mathbf{y}) D(\mathbf{y} \rightarrow \mathbf{x})}{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\|^2} where V(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) is the binary visibility function (1 if unobstructed, 0 otherwise). The factor D accounts for surface orientation: D(\mathbf{x} \rightarrow \mathbf{y}) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \mathbf{x} \text{ is in a medium} \\ \mathbf{n}{\mathbf{x}} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}{\mathbf{x}\mathbf{y}} & \text{if } \mathbf{x} \text{ is on a surface} \end{cases} where \boldsymbol{\omega}{\mathbf{x}\mathbf{y}} = (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x}) / \|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x}\| is the unit direction vector from \mathbf{x} to \mathbf{y}, and \mathbf{n}{\mathbf{x}} is the surface normal at \mathbf{x}. The scattering function \rho(\mathbf{x}i) at an intermediate vertex depends on whether the vertex is on a surface or in a medium: \rho(\mathbf{x}i) = \begin{cases} \rhos(\mathbf{x}{i-1} \rightarrow \mathbf{x}i \rightarrow \mathbf{x}{i+1}) & \text{if } \mathbf{x}i \text{ is on a surface} \\ \rhop(\mathbf{x}{i-1} \rightarrow \mathbf{x}i \rightarrow \mathbf{x}{i+1}) \sigmas(\mathbf{x}i) & \text{if } \mathbf{x}i \text{ is in a medium} \end{cases} where \rhos is the BSDF, \rhop is the phase function, and \sigmas is the scattering coefficient. The differential path measure d\mu(\bar{\mathbf{x}}) is a product measure corresponding to area integration for surface vertices and volume integration for medium vertices. Steps 1. Sample Path Length: Determine the number of segments k for the path, typically by sampling from a geometric distribution based on the albedo or scattering probability. 2. Generate Vertices: Sample \mathbf{x}0 on a light source according to the emission distribution. For i = 0 to k-1: Sample the distance to the next interaction \Delta s from the extinction coefficient \sigmat(\mathbf{x}i) along the current direction. Determine the next vertex position \mathbf{x}{i+1} = \mathbf{x}i + \Delta s \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}. If \mathbf{x}{i+1} is in a medium, sample a new direction using the phase function \rhop. If \mathbf{x}{i+1} is on a surface, sample a new direction using the BSDF \rhos. Check visibility V(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1}). If obstructed, terminate the path (contribution is 0). Ensure \mathbf{x}k lies on the camera sensor. 3. Compute Throughput: Calculate T(\bar{\mathbf{x}}) using the product of geometry terms G, transmittance terms T{\mathbf{r}} (often combined with visibility in G or handled separately as e^{-\int \sigmat ds}), and scattering functions \rho for all intermediate vertices. 4. Compute Contribution: Calculate f(\bar{\mathbf{x}}) = Le(\mathbf{x}0) T(\bar{\mathbf{x}}) We(\mathbf{x}k). 5. Estimate: Average the contributions of N independent paths: I \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum{j=1}^N \frac{f(\bar{\mathbf{x}}j)}{p(\bar{\mathbf{x}}j)}, where p(\bar{\mathbf{x}}j) is the probability density of generating path \bar{\mathbf{x}}j. Parameters k: Path length. Not given in the sources. \sigmat: Extinction coefficient. Not given in the sources. \sigmas: Scattering coefficient. Not given in the sources. We: Camera response function. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Infinite Dimensionality: The path space is infinite-dimensional, making the differential measure \mathcal{D}x highly complex and non-intuitive. Visibility: Computing V(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) accurately in complex scenes is computationally expensive and prone to aliasing if not handled with robust shadow rays. Path Length Constraints: The formulation strictly defines paths with k \ge 1 segments and k+1 vertices; direct illumination (k=0) is not part of the standard path space measure. Approximates the path integral by integrating only over paths near the Most Probable Path (MPP), valid for sparse/inhomogeneous media. Extends the path space to include null-scattering vertices, enabling rigorous measure definition for heterogeneous media and MIS. Uses MCMC to sample paths proportional to their contribution, handling complex lighting and multiple scattering efficiently. The foundational numerical technique for estimating the high-dimensional path integral. Formulates transport for media with spatially correlated scatterers, replacing the standard exponential Beer-Lambert law. Time Complexity: Depends on the sampling strategy and path length. Generally O(N \cdot k), where N is the number of samples and k is the average path length. Memory Complexity: O(k) per path for storing vertex data. Strengths: Provides a unified framework for combining different sampling strategies (e.g., light sampling, path tracing) via MIS. Handles general geometry and participating media. Limitations: Convergence can be slow in scenes with complex lighting or deep multiple scattering due to high variance. The infinite-dimensional nature of the path space makes analytical solutions impossible for most scenes. When to use: When a general, unbiased estimator for light transport in participating media is required, especially when combining multiple sampling techniques. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and variance reduction techniques are insufficient, or when the medium is extremely dense and diffusion approximations are more appropriate. The Path Integral Framework was introduced by Eric Veach in his 1997 thesis and further developed by Pauly et al. in 2000 for volumetric light transport. It reformulates the recursive rendering equation into a non-recursive integral over path space, derived via von Neumann series expansion. This formulation has become the theoretical basis for modern path tracing and unidirectional/bidirectional integrators in computer graphics. It is applied in NLOS imaging, differentiable rendering, and robust volumetric simulation. name: Surrounding Path Contribution (WKB Expansion)
head: Gaussian Weighting of Paths, WKB Expansion
body: Surrounding Path Contribution approximates the complete path integral in participating media by integrating only over paths in the vicinity of the Most Probable Path (MPP). It solves the problem of efficiently estimating radiance by replacing the infinite-dimensional integral with a Gaussian-weighted sum of "surrounding" paths. Inputs: The Most Probable Path (MPP) for a single-sided boundary condition (fixed start point and direction, e.g., eye position and primary viewing ray). The action function A(\text{path}) associated with the light transport equation. A parameterization vector \vec{\xi} representing deviations from the MPP, where \vec{\xi} = \vec{0} at the MPP. Outputs: An approximation of the radiance contribution, dominated by the MPP term and a Gaussian integral over the re-parameterized path space. Data Structures: The scalar action value A(0) for the MPP and the Hessian matrix \mathbf{H} (second derivatives of A with respect to \vec{\xi}) evaluated at the MPP. Steps: 1. Identify the MPP for the specified single-sided boundary condition and compute its action value A(0). 2. Parameterize the family of nearby paths using a vector \vec{\xi} such that \vec{\xi} = \vec{0} corresponds to the MPP. 3. Perform a Taylor series expansion of the action A(\vec{\xi}) around \vec{\xi} = \vec{0}. Since A has a global minimum at the MPP, the linear term is omitted. The expansion is: A(\xi) = A(0) + \frac{1}{2}\xi^2 \frac{\partial^2 A}{\partial \xi^2} + \dots For a vector parameterization, this generalizes to a quadratic form involving the Hessian matrix \mathbf{H}. 4. Substitute the expanded action into the path integral weight \exp(-A(\text{path})). The weight for a surrounding path becomes: \exp(-A(\text{path})) \sim \exp(-A(MPP)) \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\xi^2 \frac{\partial^2 A}{\partial \xi^2}\right) This yields a Gaussian form that weights nearby paths according to their "distance" from the MPP. 5. Evaluate the integral over the re-parameterized path space. The propagator G is approximated as: G \sim \exp(-A(MPP)) \int{\xi} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (\xi \nabla{\xi})^2 A \right) d\xi where (\xi \nabla{\xi})^2 A represents the quadratic form \vec{\xi}^T \mathbf{H} \vec{\xi} derived from the Hessian. 6. Use this expression to estimate properties of the radiance distribution, such as radiation blurring, which is measured by the spatial width of the contributing paths. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def surroundingpathcontribution(mppaction, hessianmatrix): """ Approximates the path integral using WKB expansion around the MPP. Args: mppaction (float): The action value A(0) of the Most Probable Path. hessianmatrix (list of lists): The Hessian matrix H of the action at the MPP. Returns: float: Approximated radiance contribution (propagator G). """ # Step 1: Compute the MPP contribution factor mppfactor = math.exp(-mppaction) # Step 2: Evaluate the Gaussian integral over the re-parameterized path space. # The integral is of the form int(exp(-0.5 xi^T H xi)) dxi. # For an n-dimensional Gaussian integral, the analytical result is (2pi)^(n/2) / sqrt(det(H)). n = len(hessianmatrix) # Compute determinant of Hessian analytically for small dimensions if n == 1: detH = hessianmatrix[0][0] elif n == 2: detH = hessianmatrix[0][0] hessianmatrix[1][1] - hessianmatrix[0][1] hessianmatrix[1][0] else: # For n > 2, compute det(H) using LU decomposition or standard linear algebra routines. detH = 1.0 # Guard against non-positive definite Hessian or zero determinant if detH <= 0: raise ValueError("Hessian must be positive definite for a valid Gaussian integral.") gaussianintegral = (2 math.pi) (n / 2) / math.sqrt(detH) # Step 3: Combine MPP contribution with the Gaussian integral result = mppfactor gaussianintegral return result Parameters: Radiation blurring along the path is measured by the spatial width of contributing paths. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The expansion assumes A has a global minimum at the MPP, so the linear term is omitted. The integration space is still infinite-dimensional, but properties are estimated by keeping some parameters fixed. The WKB-based Multiple Scattering Approximation is a method for computing multiply-scattered light in participating media by replacing the integration over the complete initial path space (x0, \tilde{\omega}0) with an integration over a reduced subset defined by Multiple Path Points (MPPs). It is distinguished from the diffusion approximation by its validity in sparse and inhomogeneous media, though it assumes strongly forward-peaked phase functions and ignores backscattering. Strengths: Efficiently models radiation blurring by considering the contribution of surrounding paths via WKB expansion and Gaussian weighting. Limitations: The integration space remains infinite-dimensional, requiring approximation by fixing parameters. The Surrounding Path Contribution method is based on the WKB (Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin) expansion of the path integral. It was introduced in the context of practical rendering of multiple scattering effects in participating media. The method builds on the Path Integral Framework [873-path-integral-framework.md]. The WKB expansion allows for the approximation of the path integral by focusing on the neighborhood of the Most Probable Path (MPP). name: WKB-based Multiple Scattering Approximation
head: Multiple Path Point (MPP) method, WKB expansion of the path integral
body: The WKB-based Multiple Scattering Approximation computes multiply-scattered light in participating media by replacing explicit integration over the complete initial path space (x0, \tilde{\omega}0) with integration over a reduced subset selected by Multiple Path Points (MPPs). It differs from diffusion approximations by remaining valid in sparse and inhomogeneous media, though it assumes strongly forward-peaked phase functions and ignores backscattering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Total path length s, current position \mathbf{x}, current direction \vec{\omega}, extinction coefficient c(\cdot), source/scattering term b(\mathbf{x}'), incident radiance L0(\mathbf{x}', \vec{\omega}'), and the set of MPPs for length s. Output: Radiance L(s, \mathbf{x}, \vec{\omega}) at the current point. Data Structures: MPP (Multiple Path Point): Represents a specific path configuration for a given total length s, defining the center of the reduced integration subset. Gaussian Width w(s): Scalar width of the Gaussian distribution applied at position \mathbf{x}0 for length s. Curvature Action Ac(MPPs): Scalar representing the curvature part of the action function for the MPP. Steps: 1. Construct MPPs: For a given total path length s, identify the set of MPPs that define the reduced integration subset, relying on the assumption that the single-scattered light distribution is strongly forward-peaked. 2. Compute Extinction: Evaluate the exponential extinction term along the path defined by the MPP: \exp \left( - \int0^s c(MPPs(s')) ds' \right). 3. Compute Curvature Action: Evaluate the curvature part of the action function, Ac(MPPs), for the given MPP. 4. Evaluate Phase Function: Compute the multiply-scattered phase function P{MS}(\vec{\omega} - \vec{\omega}'), which gives the probability of light being scattered by a given angle after a given number of scattering events. 5. Integrate Over Reduced Support: Perform the integration over the plane perpendicular to the MPP direction, weighted by a Gaussian of width w(s), the source term b(\mathbf{x}'), and the incident radiance L0(\mathbf{x}', \vec{\omega}'): \int{plane\perp MPP} gauss(\mathbf{x}', w(s)) b(\mathbf{x}') L0(\mathbf{x}', \vec{\omega}') d\mathbf{x}'. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeradiance(s, x, omega, c, b, L0, mppset): # Select MPP for the given total path length s mpp = mppset[s] # 1. Extinction along the MPP path extterm = math.exp(-integrate(lambda sp: c(mpp.path(sp)), 0, s)) # 2. Curvature action part acterm = math.exp(-mpp.curvatureaction) # 3. Multiply-scattered phase function PMS(omega - omega') phase = PMS(omega - mpp.direction) # 4. Integration over the plane perpendicular to the MPP # gauss(x', w(s)) is a Gaussian of width w(s) applied at x0 # integrate, planeperpendicular, dA are standard numerical/geometric routines integralval = 0.0 for xprime in planeperpendicular(mpp): gaussval = gauss(xprime, w(s)) integralval += gaussval b(xprime) L0(xprime, mpp.direction) dA return extterm acterm phase integralval Formula: The final radiance is computed as: L(s, \mathbf{x}, \vec{\omega}) = \exp \left( - \int0^s c(MPPs(s')) ds' \right) \exp(-Ac(MPPs)) \times P{MS}(\vec{\omega} - \vec{\omega}') \int{plane\perp MPP} gauss(\mathbf{x}', w(s)) b(\mathbf{x}') L0(\mathbf{x}', \vec{\omega}') d\mathbf{x}' Parameters: w(s): Gaussian width determined by the WKB approximation at position \mathbf{x}0 and length s. Ac(MPPs): Curvature part of the action function. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Phase Function Assumption: Relies on the assumption that the single-scattered light distribution is strongly forward-peaked. Integration Support: The method replaces explicit integration over the complete (x0, \tilde{\omega}0)-space with integration only over the support of the Gaussian, which may limit accuracy if the Gaussian support is too narrow or misaligned. Premoze et al. path integration is an approximation for simulating light transport in participating media that utilizes the WKB (Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin) approximation to compute multiply-scattered light. It is distinguished from the diffusion approximation by its validity in sparse and inhomogeneous media, though it assumes strongly forward-peaked phase functions and ignores backscattering. Choose this variant when rendering sparse or highly inhomogeneous media where diffusion fails, but avoid it for isotropic scattering or scenes requiring accurate backscattering. Strengths: Replaces integration over complete (x0, \tilde{\omega}0)-space with a reduced subset selected by MPPs, reducing computational cost. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that the single-scattered light distribution is strongly forward-peaked. The method is introduced in as a practical approach for rendering multiple scattering effects in participating media. It is also known as the Multiple Path Point (MPP) method or the WKB expansion of the path integral. name: Premoze et al. Path Integration
head: Premoze et al
body: Premoze et al. path integration is an approximation for simulating light transport in participating media that utilizes the WKB (Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin) approximation to compute multiply-scattered light. It is distinguished from the diffusion approximation by its validity in sparse and inhomogeneous media, though it assumes strongly forward-peaked phase functions and ignores backscattering. It builds on WKB-based Multiple Scattering Approximation. The method approximates light transport by finding the most probable path for light propagation and analytically integrating scattered radiance along this path and its neighborhood, including quadratic fluctuations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume density/scattering coefficients, phase function (assumed strongly forward-peaked and uniform), light sources, camera position. Output: Rendered image or radiance distribution. Data Structures: Pre-computed Attenuation: A lookup table or grid storing light attenuation values at all possible depths to accelerate direct component calculation. Exact layout details are not given in the sources. Numbered Steps: 1. Pre-compute Direct Attenuation: Calculate and store light attenuation through the volume for all possible depths to speed up the direct lighting component. 2. Construct Most Probable Path: Identify the path of highest probability for light transport from source to camera, leveraging the WKB approximation. 3. Ray-Marching: Implement the integration using ray-marching along the constructed path. 4. Uniform Scattering Steps: March along the path in discrete steps such that the number of scattering events is uniform per step. 5. Local Integration: At each sampling point along the path, compute the contribution from several directions over the sphere. No new rays are spawned for further tracing. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Scattering coefficients must vary smoothly. Phase function must be strongly forward-peaked and uniform throughout the medium. Pitfalls: Fails for media with non-smoothly varying scattering coefficients. Inaccurate for media where the phase function is not strongly forward-peaked. Ignores backscattering effects entirely. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The pre-computation of attenuation speeds up direct component calculation. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Valid for sparse and inhomogeneous media where diffusion approximation fails. Limitations: Ignores backscattering; requires smooth coefficients and forward-peaked phase functions. Usage: Applied to simulation of scattering in clouds and subsurface scattering. Premoze et al. [74] presented this approximation to simulate light transport in volumes. The method exploits the WKB approximation, which computes multiply-scattered light by finding the most probable path and integrating radiance along it with quadratic fluctuations. In a subsequent paper [75], Premoze et al. applied the mathematical path integration framework again, focusing on fast rendering algorithms that are qualitatively correct rather than numerically precise, leveraging the observation that multiple scattering causes blurring and attenuation of incident radiance. name: Null-Scattering Path Integral Framework
head: Generalized Path Space for Volume Rendering, Path Integral with Null Scattering
body: The Null-Scattering Path Integral Framework formulates light transport in participating media as a Monte Carlo integration problem over a generalized path space that explicitly includes null-scattering vertices. It solves the problem of defining a rigorous measure for path integrals in heterogeneous media where standard delta tracking or majorant sampling does not naturally fit into a path-space summation, enabling the application of variance reduction techniques like multiple importance sampling and bidirectional integrators. It differs from standard path tracing by treating null-scattering events as distinct vertex types in the path configuration, allowing the path throughput to be decomposed into majorant transmittance and scattering terms that can be sampled independently. The framework defines a path space over sequences of vertices that can be of three types: surface locations (A), real scattering positions in the medium (V), and null-scattering positions in the medium (V\emptyset). The framework takes a path \bar{p}n of length n and a configuration vector \mathbf{c} \in \{0, 1, 2\}^n defining vertex types as input, and outputs the path contribution estimator \hat{P}(\bar{p}n) and the throughput weight \beta(\bar{p}n). The path \bar{p}n is a sequence of n vertices p1, \dots, pn. Each vertex pi has a type determined by the configuration vector \mathbf{c}: ci = 0: Surface vertex (pi \in A). ci = 1: Real scattering vertex (pi \in V). ci = 2: Null-scattering vertex (pi \in V\emptyset). The subset of vertices representing real scattering is denoted ri. Note that the index of a real-scattering vertex in the full path \bar{p}n may differ from its index in the subset r. The set of paths for a specific configuration \mathbf{c} is the Cartesian product: \mathcal{P}n^{\mathbf{c}} = \prod{i=1}^{n} \begin{cases} A & \text{if } ci = 0 \\ V & \text{if } ci = 1 \\ V\emptyset & \text{if } ci = 2 \end{cases} The set of all paths of length n is the union over all configuration vectors: \mathcal{P}n = \bigcup{\mathbf{c} \in \{0, 1, 2\}^n} \mathcal{P}n^{\mathbf{c}} The measure \mun for a domain D \subseteq \mathcal{P}n sums over configurations \mathbf{c} \in \{0, 1, 2\}^n: \mun(D) = \sum{\mathbf{c} \in \{0, 1, 2\}^n} \mun^{\mathbf{c}}(D \cap \mathcal{P}n^{\mathbf{c}}) where the differential measure d\mun^{\mathbf{c}} uses dA(pi) if ci=0, dV(pi) if ci=1, and dV\emptyset(pi) if ci=2. The measure dV\emptyset incorporates a Dirac delta distribution to restrict integration to the line segment between successive real-scattering vertices. The generalized path contribution function is: \hat{P}(\bar{p}n) = \int{\mathcal{P}{n-1}} \hat{L}e(pn \to p{n-1}) \hat{T}(\bar{p}n) d\mu{n-1}(p2, \dots, pn) where the emitted radiance term \hat{L}e is: \hat{L}e(pn \to p{n-1}) = \begin{cases} Le(\dots) & \text{if } pn \in A \\ \sigmaa(pn) Le(\dots) & \text{if } pn \in V \end{cases} The generalized path throughput \hat{T}(\bar{p}n) is: \hat{T}(\bar{p}n) = \left( \prod{i=1}^{n-1} \hat{f}(p{i+1} \to pi \to p{i-1}) \right) \left( \prod{i=0}^{n-1} T{maj}(pi \to p{i+1}) \right) \left( \prod{i=1}^{m-1} \hat{G}(ri \leftrightarrow r{i+1}) \right) where m is the number of real-scattering vertices. The generalized scattering distribution \hat{f} is: \hat{f}(p{i+1} \to pi \to p{i-1}) = \begin{cases} f(\dots) & \text{if } pi \in A \\ \sigmas(pi) p(\dots) & \text{if } pi \in V \\ \sigman(pi) H((pi - p{i+1}) \cdot (pi - p{i-1})) & \text{if } pi \in V\emptyset \end{cases} where \sigman is the null-scattering coefficient, H is the Heaviside function, and p(\dots) is the phase function. The generalized geometric term \hat{G} is: \hat{G}(p \leftrightarrow p') = V(p \leftrightarrow p') \frac{Cp(p, p') C{p'}(p', p)}{\|p - p'\|} where Cp(p, p') = |np \cdot \frac{p - p'}{\|p - p'\|}| if p \in A, and 1 if p \in V. Note that Cp is only evaluated for real-scattering vertices ri. The Monte Carlo estimator is: \hat{P}(\bar{p}n) = \frac{\hat{T}(\bar{p}n) \hat{L}e(pn \to p{n-1})}{p(\bar{p}n)} where p(\bar{p}n) is the probability density of sampling the path with respect to the generalized measure. The volumetric path throughput weight is: \beta(\bar{p}n) = \frac{\hat{T}(\bar{p}n)}{p(\bar{p}n)}. The following pseudocode outlines the evaluation of the path throughput and emitted radiance term for a given path \bar{p}n and its configuration \mathbf{c}. It assumes access to scene queries for \sigmaa, \sigmas, \sigma{maj}, T{maj}, and surface normals. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def distance(a, b): return math.sqrt(sum((x - y)2 for x, y in zip(a, b))) def evaluatenullscatteringpathintegral(path, config): """ Evaluates the path throughput and emitted radiance term for a path in the null-scattering framework. Args: path: List of vertices p0,..., p{n-1}. Each vertex is a dict with 'pos' (vector), 'type' (int: 0=surface, 1=real, 2=null), 'normal' (vector, if surface), 'emittedradiance' (float), 'bsdf' (float), 'phasefunction' (float), 'absorptioncoefficient' (float), 'scatteringcoefficient' (float), 'nullscatteringcoefficient' (float). config: List of integers c0,..., c{n-1} matching vertex types. Returns: That: Generalized path throughput. Lehat: Emitted radiance term at the endpoint. """ n = len(path) if n < 2: return 1.0, 0.0 # 1. Calculate Emitted Radiance Term Lhate at the last vertex p{n-1} pn = path[-1] cn = config[-1] if cn == 0: # Surface Lehat = pn.get('emittedradiance', 0.0) elif cn == 1: # Real Volume sigmaa = pn.get('absorptioncoefficient', 0.0) Lehat = sigmaa pn.get('emittedradiance', 0.0) else: # Null Volume (cn == 2) Lehat = 0.0 # 2. Calculate Generalized Path Throughput That That = 1.0 # Product 1: Generalized Scattering Distribution fhat over intermediate vertices # Corresponds to \prod{i=1}^{n-2} \hat{f}(p{i+1} \to pi \to p{i-1}) in 0-based indexing for i in range(1, n - 1): pprev = path[i-1] pcurr = path[i] pnext = path[i+1] ccurr = config[i] if ccurr == 0: # Surface fhat = pcurr.get('bsdf', 1.0) elif ccurr == 1: # Real Volume sigmas = pcurr.get('scatteringcoefficient', 0.0) phase = pcurr.get('phasefunction', 1.0) fhat = sigmas phase elif ccurr == 2: # Null Volume sigman = pcurr.get('nullscatteringcoefficient', 0.0) # Heaviside function H checks if the direction is consistent (no backtracking) dotproduct = dot(pcurr['pos'] - pnext['pos'], pcurr['pos'] - pprev['pos']) H = 1.0 if dotproduct >= 0 else 0.0 fhat = sigman H else: fhat = 0.0 That = fhat # Product 2: Majorant Transmittance Tmaj over all segments # Corresponds to \prod{i=0}^{n-2} T{maj}(pi \to p{i+1}) for i in range(n - 1): pcurr = path[i] pnext = path[i+1] dist = distance(pcurr['pos'], pnext['pos']) # Majorant extinction is typically constant or per-segment; here assumed per-vertex for simplicity sigmamaj = pcurr.get('majorantextinction', 0.0) That = math.exp(-dist sigmamaj) # Product 3: Generalized Geometric Term Ghat for consecutive real scattering vertices realscatterindices = [i for i, c in enumerate(config) if c == 1] for j in range(len(realscatterindices) - 1): idxcurr = realscatterindices[j] idxnext = realscatterindices[j+1] pcurr = path[idxcurr] pnext = path[idxnext] dist = distance(pcurr['pos'], pnext['pos']) if dist > 0: # Cp and Cp' are 1 for volume vertices. Visibility V is scene-dependent. # Assuming V=1 and cosines=1 for the base framework evaluation. That = 1.0 / dist else: That = 0.0 return That, Lehat Dirac Delta: The measure dV\emptyset restricts null-scattering vertices to the line between real-scattering vertices. Heaviside Function: Ensures that null-scattering directions are consistent with the path direction (no backtracking). Configuration Vector: The framework handles arbitrary sequences of surface, real, and null vertices. An unbiased algorithm that uses the framework to sample distances from the majorant distribution and explicitly maintains the majorant transmittance factor, ensuring unbiased estimates even with significant majorant overestimation. A sibling method that uses a WKB expansion to approximate the path contribution, differing in its approach to handling multiple scattering and variance reduction. Complexity: The complexity depends on the sampling strategy. The framework itself is a formulation, not a specific sampler. The number of path vertices n and the number of real-scattering vertices m affect the cost of evaluating \hat{T}. Performance: The framework enables variance reduction techniques like MIS, which can significantly improve performance in complex scenes with heterogeneous media. Strengths: Rigorous path-space formulation allows for bidirectional and multi-bounce integrators in participating media. Handles heterogeneous media via the majorant and null-scattering terms. The framework was introduced in the context of the Path Tracing book (PBR Book), specifically in Section 14.1.4, to express the null-scattering integral equation of transfer as a sum over paths. It builds on the surface path space formulation from Section 13.1.4 and extends it to include volume and null-scattering vertices. name: Null-Scattering Volumetric Path Tracing
head: Volumetric Path Tracing with Null Scattering
body: Null-Scattering Volumetric Path Tracing is an unbiased algorithm for rendering participating media that uses a homogeneous majorant medium with an added null-scattering term to sample distances along a ray. It solves the problem of efficiently sampling interaction points in sparse or heterogeneous media by treating absorption, scattering, and null-scattering as mutually exclusive events with probabilities proportional to their coefficients. It differs from standard delta tracking by explicitly maintaining a majorant transmittance factor T{maj} and sampling distances from the majorant distribution, ensuring unbiased estimates even when the majorant significantly overestimates the physical extinction. It builds on the Null-Scattering Path Integral Framework. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin p0, direction \omega0, medium properties (absorption coefficient \sigmaa, scattering coefficient \sigmas, emission Le, phase function p), majorant coefficient \sigma{maj}, and scene geometry. Output: Radiance Li(p0, \omega0) along the ray. Data Structures: Majorant Iterator: Provides piecewise-constant \sigma{maj} segments along the ray. State: Current position p, current direction \omega, accumulated majorant transmittance T{maj}, and current segment index in the majorant iterator. Parameters: \sigma{maj}: The majorant coefficient, defined as \sigmaa(p) + \sigmas(p) + \sigman(p). It must be greater than or equal to the sum of absorption and scattering coefficients at all points in the medium. \sigman: The null-scattering coefficient, defined as \sigma{maj} - \sigmaa(p) - \sigmas(p). Steps: 1. Initialize: Set current position p = p0, direction \omega = \omega0, and accumulated majorant transmittance T{maj} = 1.0. 2. Sample Distance: Sample a distance t from the exponential distribution p(t) = \sigma{maj} e^{-\sigma{maj} t} using the current \sigma{maj} value. 3. Check Geometry: Let t{geom} be the distance to the nearest surface intersection along \omega. If t > t{geom}, return surface radiance Lo(ps, \omega0) where ps = p + t{geom}\omega. 4. Update Position: Set p' = p + t\omega. Update T{maj} by multiplying by e^{-\sigma{maj} t}. 5. Evaluate Null-Scattering Source: Evaluate Ln(p', -\omega). This involves selecting one of three terms based on probabilities \sigmaa(p')/\sigma{maj}, \sigmas(p')/\sigma{maj}, and \sigman(p')/\sigma{maj}: Absorption: Return Le(p', \omega0) and terminate the path. Scattering: Sample a new direction \omega' from the phase function p(p', \omega', \omega0). Recursively evaluate Li(p', \omega') and return \frac{\sigmas(p')}{\sigma{maj}} \frac{p(p', \omega', \omega0)}{q(\omega')} Li(p', \omega') where q(\omega') is the PDF of the sampled direction. Null-Scattering: Recursively evaluate Li(p', \omega0) and return \frac{\sigman(p')}{\sigma{maj}} Li(p', \omega0). 6. Return: Return the result from step 5. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nullscatteringpathtrace(p0, omega0, majorantiterator, geometry): Tmaj = 1.0 p, omega = p0, omega0 while True: sigmamaj = majorantiterator.currentsigmamaj() t = sampleexponential(sigmamaj) tgeom = geometry.distancetointersection(p, omega) if t > tgeom: ps = p + tgeom omega return Tmaj geometry.evalradiance(ps, omega, -omega) p = p + t omega Tmaj = exp(-sigmamaj t) sigmaa = majorantiterator.sigmaa(p) sigmas = majorantiterator.sigmas(p) sigman = sigmamaj - sigmaa - sigmas r = random() if r < sigmaa / sigmamaj: return Tmaj majorantiterator.emission(p, omega) elif r < (sigmaa + sigmas) / sigmamaj: omegaprime = samplephasefunction(p, omega) Lrec = nullscatteringpathtrace(p, omegaprime, majorantiterator, geometry) return Tmaj (sigmas / sigmamaj) (phasefunction(p, omegaprime, omega) / pdfphase(omegaprime)) Lrec else: Lrec = nullscatteringpathtrace(p, omega, majorantiterator, geometry) return Tmaj (sigman / sigmamaj) Lrec Note: The sources do not provide exact code for advancing through piecewise-constant majorant segments; implement a loop that clamps t to segment boundaries and updates T{maj} with partial exponentials. Formulas: Majorant Transmittance: T{maj}(p' \rightarrow p0) = e^{-\sigma{maj} d}. Null-Scattering Source Function: Ln(p0, \omega0) = \frac{\sigmaa(p0)}{\sigma{maj}} Le(p0, \omega0) + \frac{\sigmas(p0)}{\sigma{maj}} \intS p(p0, \omegai, \omega0) Li(p0, \omegai) d\omegai + \frac{\sigman(p0)}{\sigma{maj}} Li(p0, \omega0) PDF for Distance Sampling: p(t) = \sigma{maj} e^{-\sigma{maj} t}. Recursive Estimator: Li(p0, \omega0) \approx Ln(p', -\omega0). Accumulated Transmittance: T{maj}(p0 \rightarrow p') = T{maj}^1(p0 \rightarrow p1) T{maj}^2(p1 \rightarrow p2) \dots T{maj}^n(p{n-1} \rightarrow p'). Pitfalls: The majorant \sigma{maj} is often piecewise-constant along a ray. The transmittance T{maj} is continuous but has discontinuous first derivatives at segment boundaries. Sampling must account for these segments by updating \sigma{maj} and T{maj} correctly at each segment transition. If \sigma{maj} is not constant, the simple exponential sampling p(t) = \sigma{maj} e^{-\sigma{maj} t} is invalid across segment boundaries. The algorithm must sample within the current segment and handle transitions explicitly. Generalizes the equation of transfer to enable unbiased sampling from a modified transmittance equation using a constant majorant extinction coefficient. Solves efficient sampling in sparse or heterogeneous media by homogenizing density. Differs from standard delta tracking by maintaining T{maj} and applying Russian Roulette based on null density ratio. Choose when media density varies significantly along rays and standard tracking becomes inefficient. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources.
