name: Non-exponential transport kernel via macroscopic optical depth
head: Base transport kernel decomposition, Heterogeneity model
body: This method models light transport in non-exponential, heterogeneous participating media by decomposing the medium description into an explicit 3D macroscopic density field \sigma(\mathbf{x}) and a 1D base transport kernel T{\text{base}}(t) that captures statistical correlations. It solves the problem of rendering heterogeneous media with non-exponential attenuation by reducing the complex ensemble-averaged transport kernel to a function of the macroscopic optical depth alone. Unlike the fully homogenized model of Larsen and Vasques, which assumes identical statistics everywhere, this method allows for arbitrary spatial distribution of the macroscopic density while assuming the underlying correlation structure is statistically homogeneous. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Macroscopic extinction coefficient field \sigma(\mathbf{x}). Base transport kernel functions \text{ff}(t), \text{pf}(t), and \text{pp}(t). Two spatial points \mathbf{x}i and \mathbf{x}{i+1} defining a segment. Output: The transport kernel value \tilde{T}(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1}) for the segment. Data Structures: The base kernel functions are typically stored as 1D lookup tables or parametric functions mapping optical depth t to a scalar value. The macroscopic density \sigma(\mathbf{x}) is a 3D field (e.g., a voxel grid or analytical function). Definitions: \tau(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1}): The macroscopic optical depth between \mathbf{x}i and \mathbf{x}{i+1}, calculated as \int0^{\|\mathbf{x}{i+1}-\mathbf{x}i\|} \sigma(\mathbf{x}s) ds. \partial\mathcal{V}: The boundary of the volume. \mathcal{V}: The interior of the volume. \text{ff}(t): Base kernel for boundary-to-boundary segments, defined as \langle \text{Tr}(t) \rangle. \text{pf}(t): Base kernel for mixed segments, defined as \langle \text{Tr}(t)\rho\mu(\mathbf{x}t) \rangle. \text{pp}(t): Base kernel for interior-to-interior segments, defined as \langle \text{Tr}(t) \sigma{\mu}(\mathbf{x}t) \rho{\mu}(\mathbf{x}t) \rangle. Note that \text{pp}(t) acts as a PDF. Steps: 1. Calculate the macroscopic optical depth \taui = \tau(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1}) by integrating the macroscopic extinction coefficient \sigma(\mathbf{x}) along the segment from \mathbf{x}i to \mathbf{x}{i+1}. 2. Determine the location of the endpoints \mathbf{x}i and \mathbf{x}{i+1} relative to the volume boundary \partial\mathcal{V} and interior \mathcal{V}. 3. Select the appropriate base function based on the endpoint locations: If \mathbf{x}i \in \partial\mathcal{V} and \mathbf{x}{i+1} \in \partial\mathcal{V}, select \text{ff}. If \mathbf{x}i \in \mathcal{V} and \mathbf{x}{i+1} \in \mathcal{V}, select \text{pp}. Otherwise (one point on boundary, one in interior), select \text{pf}. 4. Evaluate the selected base function at the calculated optical depth \taui to obtain the transport kernel value \tilde{T}(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computetransportkernel(xi, xnext, sigmafield, basekernelff, basekernelpf, basekernelpp): """ Computes the non-exponential transport kernel for a segment. Args: xi: Start point of the segment. xnext: End point of the segment. sigmafield: Function or data structure providing macroscopic extinction coefficient sigma(x). basekernelff: Function evaluating ff(t). basekernelpf: Function evaluating pf(t). basekernelpp: Function evaluating pp(t). Returns: The transport kernel value T(xi, xnext). """ # Step 1: Calculate macroscopic optical depth taui # Integrate sigma(x) along the segment from xi to xnext. # For a uniform sigma, this is sigma distance. # For a heterogeneous sigma, numerical integration (e.g., trapezoidal rule) is required. taui = integratesigma(xi, xnext, sigmafield) # Step 2: Determine location of endpoints # isboundary(x) returns True if x is on the volume boundary, False if in interior. # This depends on the specific volume definition. onboundaryi = isboundary(xi) onboundarynext = isboundary(xnext) # Step 3: Select base function and evaluate if onboundaryi and onboundarynext: # Boundary-to-Boundary kernelvalue = basekernelff(taui) elif not onboundaryi and not onboundarynext: # Interior-to-Interior # Note: pp is a PDF, but the Jacobian factor sigma(xnext) is handled by the # path integral formulation (cancels division by sigma), so we return the raw pp value. kernelvalue = basekernelpp(taui) else: # Mixed (Boundary-to-Interior or Interior-to-Boundary) kernelvalue = basekernelpf(taui) return kernelvalue def integratesigma(xstart, xend, sigmafield): """ Computes the macroscopic optical depth between two points. Assumes a simple linear path. For implementation, sample sigma along the line. """ # Placeholder for numerical integration logic # Example: sample N points along the segment, sum sigma(x) deltat return 0.0 # Not given in the sources. Implement numerical integration of sigma(x) along the segment. def isboundary(x): """ Checks if point x is on the volume boundary. """ # Placeholder for boundary check logic return False # Not given in the sources. Implement based on volume geometry. Parameters: \sigma(\mathbf{x}): Macroscopic extinction coefficient. Represents large-scale heterogeneous variation. Determines the local stretching of the base medium. Base kernel functions (\text{ff}, \text{pf}, \text{pp}): Derived from the statistical properties of the micro-scale fluctuations. For statistically homogeneous media, these are functions of distance t only. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Jacobian Factor: The function \text{pp}(t) is a PDF. When transforming variables, it incurs a Jacobian factor of \sigma(\mathbf{x}{i+1}). This factor cancels the division by \sigma from the equivalent of Eq 22 in the source, resulting in the simple transport kernel form used here. Statistical Homogeneity Assumption: The method assumes that while the macroscopic density \sigma(\mathbf{x}) varies, the underlying correlations (captured by the base kernels) are the same throughout the medium. If correlations vary spatially, this decomposition is invalid. This variant explicitly refers to the decomposition of the medium description into a heterogeneous macroscopic density \sigma(\mathbf{x}) and a 1D transport kernel T{\text{base}}(t). It assumes statistical homogeneity of correlations throughout the medium, meaning the base kernels depend only on distance. This model lies between the fully homogenized model of Larsen and Vasques (identical statistics everywhere) and the general heterogeneous model (no assumptions about correlation distribution). Time and Memory Complexity: The method reduces the transport kernel to 1D, making it practical to estimate numerically or derive analytically. The evaluation of the kernel is O(1) if the base kernels are precomputed lookup tables or simple functions, plus the cost of integrating \sigma(\mathbf{x}) along the segment. Memory usage depends on the storage of \sigma(\mathbf{x}) and the base kernel tables. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method scales with the complexity of the macroscopic density field \sigma(\mathbf{x}) and the accuracy of the numerical integration of optical depth. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Enables practical rendering of heterogeneous media with non-exponential attenuation. Separates explicit density variations from statistical fluctuations, allowing for "plug-in" correlation functions. Limitations: Relies on the assumption of statistical homogeneity of correlations. If correlations vary spatially, the model is inaccurate. When to Use: Use when rendering heterogeneous media where the macroscopic density varies significantly, but the micro-scale statistical properties (correlations) are uniform throughout the volume. When Not to Use: Do not use if the medium's correlation structure varies spatially, or if a fully homogenized model (Larsen and Vasques) is sufficient and simpler. Origin: The method was introduced in "A radiative transfer framework for non-exponential media". History and Development: The work positions itself between the fully homogenized model of Larsen and Vasques and general heterogeneous models, seeking a middle ground that combines the benefits of both. It was motivated by the difficulty of numerically rendering the path integral form for non-exponential media and the need to support heterogeneous media widely used in graphics. Where it is Used: Rendering of participating media with non-exponential attenuation, particularly in heterogeneous environments. name: Ensemble-averaged transmittance via characteristic functions
head: CF-based transmittance, Probabilistic ensemble-averaging
body: This method computes the ensemble-averaged transmittance of non-exponential media by modeling the line-averaged micro-scale density as a random variable and evaluating its characteristic function (CF). It solves the problem of computing light transport in heterogeneous media with spatial correlations without instantiating billions of discrete particles, providing a closed-form alternative to tabulation-based approaches. Unlike the Non-exponential transport kernel via macroscopic optical depth which relies on macroscopic optical depth approximations, this method explicitly derives the transmittance from the probability distribution of the line-averaged extinction coefficient. Inputs: Distance t along the ray segment. Medium parameters \psi = \{\mu\sigma, C, \beta\}, where \mu\sigma is the mean extinction coefficient, C controls the amplitude of variation, and \beta is the spectral exponent. The probability density function (PDF) of the line-averaged micro-scale density \bar{\sigma}\mu(t), derived from the chosen stochastic model (e.g., 1/f^\beta noise). Outputs: The ensemble-averaged transmittance \text{ff}(t) for a boundary-to-boundary segment of length t. Data Structures: Parameter vector \psi: A tuple or struct containing three floating-point values: musigma (mean extinction), C (amplitude constant), and beta (spectral exponent). Characteristic Function \varphi: A mathematical function mapping a complex argument to a complex value, specific to the chosen PDF of \bar{\sigma}\mu. Steps: 1. Model Micro-Scale Density: Define the micro-scale density field \sigma\mu(\mathbf{x}) as a random process, typically modeled as a 3D fractal where 1D transects are characterized by 1/f^\beta fractal noise. The parameter \beta controls spatial correlations: \beta=0 is uncorrelated white noise, \beta>0 is positively correlated, and \beta<0 is negatively correlated. 2. Determine Line-Averaged PDF: Determine the probability density function \text{pd}(\bar{\sigma}\mu \mid t) for the line-averaged density \bar{\sigma}\mu(t) over distance t given parameters \psi. The variance of this distribution is controlled by \beta, with lower \beta leading to more rapid decay of variance with distance. 3. Identify Characteristic Function: Identify the characteristic function \varphi{\bar{\sigma}\mu(t)}(r) corresponding to the PDF from Step 2. The characteristic function is defined as the Fourier transform of the PDF: \varphiX(r) = \langle e^{irX} \rangle. 4. Evaluate Transmittance: Evaluate the characteristic function at the imaginary argument r = ti to obtain the closed-form transmittance \text{ff}(t). Formulas: The ensemble-averaged transmittance is the expectation of the exponential attenuation weighted by the PDF of the line-averaged density: \text{ff}(t) = \left\langle e^{-t\bar{\sigma}\mu(t)} \right\rangle = \int0^\infty e^{-t\bar{\sigma}\mu} \text{pd}(\bar{\sigma}\mu \mid t) \, d\bar{\sigma}\mu \quad (30) By Jensen's inequality, this value is greater than or equal to the exponential of the mean optical depth, resulting in longer transmittance tails for heterogeneous media: \left\langle e^{-t \overline{\sigma}\mu(t)} \right\rangle \geq e^{-t \langle \overline{\sigma}\mu(t) \rangle} \quad (29) The integral in Equation (30) is equivalent to the characteristic function \varphi of the random variable \bar{\sigma}\mu(t) evaluated at ti: \text{ff}(t) = \varphi{\overline{\sigma}\mu(t)}(ti) \quad (32) where i = \sqrt{-1}. Parameters: \mu\sigma: Mean extinction coefficient. C: Constant controlling overall amplitude of variation. \beta: Spectral exponent, ranging from -1 (blue noise) to 1 (pink noise). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Homogeneous Limit: If \sigma\mu(t) is constant (no density fluctuations), the inequality in (29) becomes an equality, and the method reduces to standard exponential transmittance. Negative Extinction: Standard Gaussian approximations for the PDF may allow negative extinction values, which are physically invalid. Variants like the Gamma-distributed model are required to ensure strictly non-negative extinction. Parametric Control: While avoiding discrete particle instantiation, parametric control can be cumbersome if the CF does not have a simple closed form or requires tabulation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecftransmittance(t: float, psi: dict) -> float: """ Computes ensemble-averaged transmittance using the characteristic function. Args: t: Distance along the ray segment. psi: Dictionary containing medium parameters {musigma, C, beta}. Returns: The ensemble-averaged transmittance ff(t). """ musigma = psi['musigma'] C = psi['C'] beta = psi['beta'] # Step 2: Determine the PDF of the line-averaged density. # The specific PDF depends on the chosen stochastic model (e.g., Gamma or Gaussian). # For a general implementation, one must select the appropriate PDF class # based on the physical constraints (e.g., non-negative extinction). pdf = getlineaveragedpdf(t, musigma, C, beta) # Step 3 & 4: Identify the Characteristic Function and evaluate at ti. # The CF is the Fourier transform of the PDF. # For many common distributions (like Gamma), the CF has a known closed form. # Here we assume a helper function that returns the CF value for the specific PDF. # The argument is r = t i. # Note: The exact CF formula depends on the PDF chosen in Step 2. # For example, if the PDF is Gamma-distributed, the CF is (1 - it/scale)^(-shape). # This implementation assumes the PDF object provides a method to compute its CF. cfvalue = pdf.characteristicfunction(r=t 1j) return cfvalue.real # Transmittance is real-valued Computes ensemble-averaged transmittance by modeling line-averaged micro-scale density as a Gamma-distributed random variable. It ensures strictly non-negative extinction coefficients, making it suitable for heterogeneous media with low mean extinction relative to variance. Uses a Gaussian distribution for line-averaged extinction derived from 1/f^\beta fractal noise. It offers a simpler analytic solution but allows negative extinction values, which is a physical inconsistency. Time Complexity: O(1) per segment if the characteristic function has a closed-form expression. If tabulation is required, it depends on the resolution of the table. Memory Complexity: O(1) for closed-form CFs. O(N) if tabulation is used, where N is the number of precomputed values. Strengths: Avoids the complexity of instantiating billions of discrete particles; provides closed-form solutions for transmittance; naturally handles spatial correlations via the spectral exponent \beta. Limitations: Parametric control can be cumbersome if closed-form CFs are not available; requires careful selection of PDF to avoid unphysical negative extinction values. When to use: When rendering non-exponential media with spatial correlations and a closed-form CF is available for the chosen density distribution. When not to use: When the medium's density distribution does not have a well-known characteristic function or when high-fidelity discrete particle effects are required. The method was introduced in the context of a radiative transfer framework for non-exponential media. It builds on the observation that ensemble-averaged transmittance can be viewed as the expectation of the exponential attenuation over the probability distribution of the line-averaged density. The approach leverages the mathematical properties of characteristic functions to derive closed-form solutions, avoiding the need for stochastic sampling of individual scatterers. The modeling of micro-scale density as 1/f^\beta fractal noise follows the work of Davis and Mineev-Weinstein. name: Gamma-distributed 1/f^β noise transmittance model
head: Gamma distribution transmittance
body: This method computes the ensemble-averaged transmittance of participating media by modeling the line-averaged micro-scale density as a Gamma-distributed random variable. It solves the problem of non-physical negative extinction coefficients inherent in Gaussian approximations. Unlike the Gaussian 1/f^β noise transmittance model, which allows negative values, the Gamma model ensures strictly non-negative extinction, making it suitable for heterogeneous media where the mean extinction is low relative to the variance. Inputs: \mu\sigma: Mean extinction coefficient. C: Amplitude of variation (noise strength). \beta: Spectral exponent (color of noise). t: Path length. Outputs: \text{ff}\Gamma(t \mid \psi): Ensemble-averaged transmittance. Data Structures: No persistent data structures are required. The method computes parameters on the fly. Steps: 1. Compute the variance of the line-averaged density, \nu{\overline{\sigma}\mu}(t), based on the Gaussian model's variance scaling (derived from the parent method's characteristic function framework). 2. Calculate the shape parameter \alpha(t) using the mean and variance: \alpha(t) = \frac{\mu\sigma^2}{\nu{\overline{\sigma}\mu}(t)} 3. Compute the transmittance using the characteristic function of the Gamma distribution: \text{ff}\Gamma(t \mid \psi) = \left(1 + \frac{\mu\sigma t}{\alpha(t)}\right)^{-\alpha(t)} Parameters: \mu\sigma > 0: Mean extinction. C \ge 0: Amplitude. \beta \ge 0: Spectral exponent. Edge Cases: Homogeneous/White Noise: If C=0 or \beta=0, the variance vanishes, \alpha \to \infty, and the model reduces to the standard exponential transmittance e^{-\mu\sigma t}. Precision: For very large \alpha, numerical stability of (1 + x/\alpha)^{-\alpha} should be handled using exp(-x) or logarithmic evaluation to avoid precision loss. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gammatransmittance(musigma, C, beta, t): """ Compute ensemble-averaged transmittance using the Gamma-distributed 1/f^beta noise model. Args: musigma: Mean extinction coefficient. C: Amplitude of variation. beta: Spectral exponent. t: Path length. Returns: Transmittance value. """ # Step 1: Compute variance nusigmamu(t) # The variance scaling is derived from the Gaussian model's characteristic function. # From Eq 34 in, the variance scales as: # nusigmamu(t) = (C musigma t)^(beta + 1) / (2 t^2) ? # Note: The source Eq 35 shows the Gaussian exponent term as (Cmusigmat)^(beta+1)/2. # The variance nu is the second moment term in the exponent expansion. # Specifically, for the Gaussian model, the exponent is -mut + nut^2/2. # Eq 35: exp(-mut + (Cmut)^(beta+1)/2). # Thus, nu t^2 / 2 = (C mu t)^(beta+1) / 2 # nu = (C mu t)^(beta+1) / t^2 = C^(beta+1) mu^(beta+1) t^(beta-1) if t == 0: return 1.0 # Calculate variance nusigmamu(t) # nu = C^(beta+1) mu^(beta+1) t^(beta-1) # Using log-exp for stability if needed, but direct computation for typical values: nu = (C (beta + 1)) (musigma (beta + 1)) (t (beta - 1)) # Step 2: Calculate shape parameter alpha(t) # alpha = mu^2 / nu if nu == 0: # Variance is zero, alpha is infinite, returns exponential return math.exp(-musigma t) alpha = (musigma 2) / nu # Step 3: Compute transmittance # ff = (1 + (mu t) / alpha)^(-alpha) # Substitute alpha: mut/alpha = mut nu / mu^2 = t nu / mu # ff = (1 + t nu / mu)^(-alpha) term = 1.0 + (t nu) / musigma # Use log to compute power for numerical stability # logff = -alpha log(term) # ff = exp(logff) if term <= 0: # Should not happen for positive inputs, but guard against precision issues return 0.0 logff = -alpha math.log(term) return math.exp(logff) A special case where the spectral exponent \beta = 1 (pink noise). In this scenario, the distribution of extinction values becomes independent of the path length t. The shape parameter \alpha becomes constant: \alpha = C^{-\beta-1} = C^{-2} The transmittance reduces to the characteristic function of the static probability density function: \text{ff}{\text{pink}}(t) = \varphi{\bar{\sigma}\mu}(t) = \int0^\infty e^{-t\bar{\sigma}\mu} \text{pdf}(\bar{\sigma}\mu) \, d\bar{\sigma}\mu This scale-invariant property simplifies the model to a single-parameter family determined by C and \mu\sigma. Time Complexity: O(1) per path length evaluation. Requires basic arithmetic operations and a logarithm/exponential. Memory Complexity: O(1). No storage required. Strengths: Guarantees non-negative extinction coefficients, avoiding the non-physical artifacts of the Gaussian model. Provides a closed-form solution for non-exponential transmittance. Limitations: More complex than the exponential model. Requires tuning of three parameters (\mu\sigma, C, \beta). When to use: When simulating heterogeneous media with significant density fluctuations where the mean extinction is not sufficiently high to make negative Gaussian samples negligible. The Gamma-distributed model was proposed by Davis and Mineev-Weinstein [2011] to address the limitations of the Gaussian approximation in the path integral framework for non-exponential media. It is part of the broader effort to model light transport in participating media with fractal 1/f^\beta noise density distributions. body:
The Gaussian 1/f^β noise transmittance model is a closed-form method for computing the ensemble-averaged transmittance in participating media where the line-averaged extinction coefficient follows a Gaussian distribution derived from 1/f^β fractal noise. It differs from the Gamma-distributed 1/f^β noise transmittance model by assuming a symmetric normal distribution for the density fluctuations, which allows for a simpler analytic solution but introduces the physical inconsistency of allowing negative extinction values. Inputs: t: The distance along the ray (scalar, t \ge 0). \mu\sigma: The mean extinction coefficient of the medium (scalar, \mu\sigma > 0). C: The noise amplitude parameter (scalar, C > 0).  eta: The spectral exponent of the fractal noise (scalar, typically -1 \le  eta \le 3 for the resulting fBm properties). Outputs: \mathbf{f}{\mathcal{N}}(t \mid  oldsymbol{\psi}): The ensemble-averaged transmittance (scalar, 0 \le \mathbf{f}{\mathcal{N}} \le 1). Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The model relies on scalar parameters  oldsymbol{\psi} = \{\mu\sigma, C,  eta\}. While the source notation \overline{\sigma}{\mu}(t) is ambiguous regarding whether it represents standard deviation or variance, the derivation of the final transmittance formula (Equation 35) implies that the variance term in the characteristic function exponent is 
u(t) = (C\mu\sigma)^{ eta+1}t^{ eta+1}. Specifically, the term (C\mu\sigma t)^{ eta+1}/2 in the exponent of the transmittance corresponds to r^2

Args: t (float): Distance along the ray. musigma (float): Mean extinction coefficient. C (float): Noise amplitude parameter. beta (float): Spectral exponent. Returns: float: Transmittance value. """ # Step 1: Mean attenuation term meanatten = musigma t # Step 2: Noise variance term base (C musigma t) noisebase = C musigma t # Step 3: Exponent correction term: (C musigma t)^(beta + 1) / 2 # Note: If noisebase is 0 and beta+1 < 0, this may result in inf. # Guard against negative base with non-integer exponent if necessary, # though physical parameters C, musigma, t are positive. exponentcorrection = 0.5 (noisebase (beta + 1)) # Step 4: Total exponent totalexponent = -meanatten + exponentcorrection # Step 5: Transmittance return math.exp(totalexponent) Parameters and Typical Values: \mu\sigma: Must be sufficiently high to ensure the probability of negative extinction is negligible. C: Controls the magnitude of density fluctuations.  eta: The spectral exponent. The model is derived from 1/f^β noise which produces fractional Brownian motion (fBm) with  eta + 2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Negative Extinction: The Gaussian distribution is supported on the entire real line, meaning it assigns non-zero probability to negative extinction coefficients (\sigma\mu < 0), which are nonphysical. The model is only reasonable when \mu\sigma is set sufficiently high and the variance (controlled by C and  eta) is sufficiently low such that negative values are statistically unlikely. Precision: For large t, the term (C\mu\sigma t)^{ eta+1} may grow rapidly, potentially causing overflow in the exponent if  eta+1 > 0. Conversely, if  eta+1 < 0 and t is small, precision issues may arise. Time Complexity: O(1). The model involves a constant number of arithmetic operations and a single exponential evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1). No storage is required beyond the input parameters. Strengths: Provides a closed-form analytic solution, avoiding numerical integration or sampling. It is computationally very efficient. Limitations: The assumption of a Gaussian distribution allows for negative extinction values, which is physically invalid. This limits the model's applicability to scenarios where the mean extinction is high relative to the variance. It is an approximation of the true transmittance for 1/f^β noise media. When to use: Use when computational efficiency is critical and the medium parameters allow for the Gaussian approximation (high mean, low variance relative to mean). The model is based on the work of Davis and Mineev-Weinstein [2011], who formally derived the dependence of the Gaussian distribution of line-averaged density on distance and medium parameters. The approach is part of a broader framework for non-exponential path integrals in volume rendering, specifically addressing media modeled as fractal noise. name: Ensemble Transport Kernel
head: T(x, four transport functions
body: The Ensemble Transport Kernel (ETK) is a method for estimating light transport in non-exponential stochastic media by replacing the classical transmittance term with an ensemble-averaged transport kernel T(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1}). It solves the problem of computing the path integral expectation \langle I\mu \rangle by decorrelating path segments, allowing the ensemble average to be computed independently for each segment rather than over the entire path. Unlike the Non-exponential transport kernel via macroscopic optical depth which relies on macroscopic optical depth approximations, or Ensemble-averaged transmittance via characteristic functions which uses characteristic functions, the ETK explicitly defines four distinct transport functions (\text{pp}, \text{fp}, \text{pf}, \text{ff}) based on the boundary configuration of segment endpoints. Inputs: Path vertices \bar{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{x}0, \dots, \mathbf{x}k. Macroscopic extinction coefficient field \sigma(\mathbf{x}) = \langle \sigma\mu(\mathbf{x}) \rangle. Phase function f(\mathbf{x}) and geometry term G(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1}). Outputs: Estimated path throughput \langle g\mu(\bar{\mathbf{x}}) \rangle. Data Structures: The method requires evaluating the transport kernel T(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1}). The kernel is not a single function but a set of four functions determined by the location of the endpoints relative to the medium volume \mathcal{V} and its boundary \partial\mathcal{V}: 1. \text{pp}(t): Interior-to-Interior (\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1} \in \mathcal{V}). 2. \text{ff}(t): Boundary-to-Boundary (\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1} \in \partial\mathcal{V}). 3. \text{pf}(t): Interior-to-Boundary (\mathbf{x}i \in \mathcal{V}, \mathbf{x}{i+1} \in \partial\mathcal{V}). 4. \text{fp}(t): Boundary-to-Interior (\mathbf{x}i \in \partial\mathcal{V}, \mathbf{x}{i+1} \in \mathcal{V}). Steps: 1. Define \Sigma(\mathbf{x}): For each vertex, determine the scaling factor \Sigma(\mathbf{x}): \Sigma(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} \sigma(\mathbf{x}) & \text{if } \mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{V} \\ 1 & \text{if } \mathbf{x} \in \partial\mathcal{V} \end{cases} 2. Evaluate Transport Kernels: For each segment i from \mathbf{x}i to \mathbf{x}{i+1}, select the appropriate kernel function based on endpoint locations: If \mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1} \in \mathcal{V}, use T(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1}) = \text{pp}(\|\mathbf{x}i - \mathbf{x}{i+1}\|). If \mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1} \in \partial\mathcal{V}, use T(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1}) = \text{ff}(\|\mathbf{x}i - \mathbf{x}{i+1}\|). If \mathbf{x}i \in \mathcal{V}, \mathbf{x}{i+1} \in \partial\mathcal{V}, use T(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1}) = \text{pf}(\|\mathbf{x}i - \mathbf{x}{i+1}\|). If \mathbf{x}i \in \partial\mathcal{V}, \mathbf{x}{i+1} \in \mathcal{V}, use T(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1}) = \text{fp}(\|\mathbf{x}i - \mathbf{x}{i+1}\|). Note: The specific mathematical definitions of \text{pp}, \text{fp}, \text{pf}, \text{ff} depend on the underlying stochastic medium model (e.g., Poisson Boolean model) and are derived from the ensemble average of the classical free-flight PDFs. 3. Compute Throughput: Calculate the estimated path throughput using the product of phase functions, geometry terms, and transport kernels: \langle g\mu(\bar{\mathbf{x}}) \rangle \approx \left[ \prod{i=1}^{k-1} f(\mathbf{x}i) \Sigma(\mathbf{x}i) \right] \left[ \prod{i=0}^{k-1} G(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1}) \right] \left[ \prod{i=0}^{k-1} T(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1}) \right] Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Reciprocity: The standard ETK is not reciprocal, i.e., T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) \neq T(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{x}) in the general case. This occurs because free-flight PDFs (like \text{pp}) are not generally reciprocal, and swapping endpoints changes the case statement (e.g., \text{fp} vs \text{pf}). This can cause issues in bidirectional rendering methods that rely on reciprocity. A variant that modifies the standard kernel to satisfy reciprocity by dividing by the boundary scaling factor \Sigma(\mathbf{y}). It sets itself apart by evaluating only averages of transmittance for all four segment configurations, guaranteeing T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = T(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{x}). Choose this variant when implementing bidirectional rendering methods that require symmetric kernel evaluation. It differs from the exponential case only by replacing transmittance with \tilde{T}, allowing direct integration into existing renderers. Time and Memory Complexity: Reduces ensemble averaging from path-wide to segment-wise, allowing independent computation per segment. Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Explicitly handles general heterogeneity, supporting varying macroscopic density and scattering correlations. Integrates easily into existing bidirectional renderers when using the reciprocal variant. Limitations: Standard kernel lacks reciprocity, requiring the modified \tilde{T} formulation for bidirectional methods. Accuracy relies on the segment decorrelation assumption. When to use: Non-exponential participating media where segment decorrelation holds and bidirectional methods are needed (use reciprocal variant). When not to use: Scenarios requiring strict reciprocity without the \tilde{T} modification, or where segment decorrelation is invalid. Introduced in "A radiative transfer framework for non-exponential media". It builds on the General Boltzmann Equation of Larsen and Vasques. The method decorrelates path segments to enable independent ensemble averaging. It is used in volume rendering for participating media that do not follow exponential transmittance laws. A radiative transfer framework for non-exponential media, https://doi.org/10.1145/3272127.3275103, fetched 2026-11-08

name: Delta tracking
head: Delta Tracking with Null Collisions, Null Collision Method, Null-scattering sampling, Woodcock Tracking
body: Delta tracking is a Monte Carlo free-path sampling method that finds the first real collision point (scattering or absorption) in a heterogeneous participating medium by sampling tentative collisions from a fictitious homogeneous medium with a constant maximum extinction coefficient (majorant). It solves the problem of efficiently sampling interaction distances in spatially varying media without requiring a structured grid or expensive memory accesses at every step. Unlike ray marching, which introduces systemic statistical bias by using fixed steps, delta tracking provides an unbiased estimator by probabilistically accepting or rejecting tentative collisions based on the ratio of local to maximum extinction. It sets itself apart from siblings like Dwivedi Sampling by strictly maintaining unbiasedness through rejection sampling, whereas Dwivedi Sampling introduces bias to reduce variance. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{w} (normalized), maximum distance t{max} (or volume bounds), majorant extinction coefficient \bar{\mu} (or \sigmat^{max}), and a function to evaluate local extinction coefficient \sigmat(\mathbf{x}). Output: Distance to the first real collision t, or t{max} if no collision occurs within the volume. Data Structures Majorant (\bar{\mu}): A scalar value representing the upper bound of the total extinction coefficient over the entire volume or a specific region. It must satisfy \bar{\mu} \ge \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) for all \mathbf{x} along the ray. Local Extinction Function: A query function that returns \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) = \sigmaa(\mathbf{x}) + \sigmas(\mathbf{x}) at any position \mathbf{x}. Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: Set current distance t = 0 (or t{min}). Compute the inverse majorant invMajorant = 1 / \bar{\mu}. 2. Sample Tentative Distance: Generate a uniform random number \xi \sim U[0, 1). Sample the distance to the next tentative collision from the exponential distribution defined by the majorant: t \leftarrow t - \frac{\ln(1 - \xi)}{\bar{\mu}} 3. Boundary Check: If t > t{max}, the ray exits the volume without a collision. Return t{max} (or the remaining distance). 4. Evaluate Local Extinction: Compute the position \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{o} + t \mathbf{w}. Evaluate the local total extinction coefficient \sigmat(\mathbf{x}). Pitfall: If the evaluation returns NaN (e.g., out-of-bounds access), skip the rejection test and continue to the next step to avoid incorrect shading. 5. Acceptance/Rejection Test: Generate a new uniform random number \xi' \sim U[0, 1). Calculate the acceptance probability: p{accept} = \frac{\sigmat(\mathbf{x})}{\bar{\mu}} If \xi' < p{accept}, the collision is real. Return t as the distance to the first real collision. Pitfall: If \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) > \bar{\mu} due to numerical error or incorrect majorant, p{accept} > 1, breaking the logic. Ensure \bar{\mu} is a strict upper bound. 6. Null Collision: If \xi' \ge p{accept}, the collision is a null collision (fictitious).. The ray passes through without interaction.. Continue from Step 2 with the current t. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def randomuniform(): return random.random() def deltatracking(rayorigin, raydirection, tmax, majorant, getlocalextinction): """ Finds the first real collision distance in a heterogeneous volume. Args: rayorigin: list of 3 floats, origin of the ray. raydirection: list of 3 floats, normalized direction of the ray. tmax: float, maximum distance to search for a collision. majorant: float, upper bound on extinction coefficient (sigmatmax). getlocalextinction: function, returns sigmat(x) at position x. Returns: float: Distance to the first real collision, or tmax if none found. """ if majorant <= 0: return tmax invmajorant = 1.0 / majorant t = 0.0 while True: # Step 2: Sample tentative distance xi = randomuniform() t += -math.log(1.0 - xi) invmajorant # Step 3: Boundary check if t >= tmax: return tmax # Step 4: Evaluate local extinction position = [rayorigin[i] + raydirection[i] t for i in range(3)] localextinction = getlocalextinction(position) # Pitfall: Handle NaN from invalid positions if math.isnan(localextinction): continue # Step 5: Acceptance/Rejection test xiprime = randomuniform() acceptanceprob = localextinction / majorant # Clamp probability to [0, 1] to handle floating point errors acceptanceprob = max(0.0, min(1.0, acceptanceprob)) if xiprime < acceptanceprob: # Real collision found return t else: # Null collision, continue loop pass Parameters Majorant (\bar{\mu}): The tighter the majorant is to the actual extinction, the fewer null collisions occur. A global maximum is simple but inefficient for sparse volumes; local majorants (e.g., per voxel or brick) reduce null collisions but add overhead. Typical values depend on the volume's density scale. Random Numbers: Two independent uniform random numbers per step are required: one for distance sampling, one for acceptance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Large Empty Spaces: If the volume has large regions of zero density but a high global majorant, the algorithm wastes samples on null collisions. Incorrect Majorant: If \bar{\mu} is not a true upper bound, the estimator becomes biased. NaN Values: Accessing invalid memory or out-of-bounds coordinates can produce NaN, which must be handled to prevent propagation. Accumulates a continuous product of null-scattering ratios for transmittance estimation, avoiding binary visibility tests. Choose when low-variance transmittance is needed in heterogeneous media. Uses spatially varying upper bounds (local majorants) to reduce null collisions in sparse areas. Choose when the volume has significant density variation and global majorant is too loose. Simplified version using a single global majorant. Choose for homogeneous media or when implementation simplicity outweighs performance in sparse volumes. Maps medium interaction depths between camera viewpoints using majorant optical depth. Choose for multi-view rendering and sample reuse. Separates scattering event sampling (delta tracking) from transmittance estimation (ratio tracking). Choose for GPU implementations requiring distinct handling of emission/absorption. Relaxes the majorant constraint, allowing \bar{\mu} < \mut by using statistical weights. Choose when a tight majorant is hard to compute but variance from weights is acceptable. Manages majorants for volumes changing over time or optimization steps. Choose for inverse rendering or animation. Time Complexity: Expected number of steps is proportional to the ratio of the majorant to the average extinction coefficient. In sparse volumes with a loose majorant, this can be very high. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory beyond the volume data structure and the majorant. No need for structured grids or precomputed transmittance tables. Measured Performance: On the HACC dataset (51 million particles), delta tracking path tracing achieved 1.44 MR/s, compared to 6.0 MR/s for ray casting, but with higher quality and unbiasedness. Rendering a cloud with delta tracking and Next Event Estimation took 248s for 10 samples per pixel. Strengths: Unbiased, handles arbitrary heterogeneous media (including particle volumes and unstructured grids), no need for voxelization. Limitations: High variance in sparse volumes with loose majorants; many null collisions waste computation. When to Use: When unbiased rendering of complex, unstructured, or highly heterogeneous media is required, and performance constraints allow for higher sample counts. When Not to Use: For homogeneous media (use analytical transmittance) or when real-time performance is critical and bias is acceptable (use ray marching). Delta tracking, also known as Woodcock tracking, was initially developed in the 1950s and 1960s by Butcher and Messel (1958, 1960), Zerby et al. (1961), Bertini (1963), Woodcock et al. (1965), Miller (1967), and Coleman (1968). In computer graphics, it has been adopted for unbiased volumetric path tracing to handle complex participating media without the bias of ray marching. It is implemented in systems like OSPRay using ISPC and exposed via the Open VKL API for volume rendering of RBF particle data. name: Ratio Tracking with Null Scattering
head: Novák et al. Transmittance Estimation, Ratio Tracking, Ratio-Tracking Transmittance Estimation
body: Ratio tracking with null scattering is a Monte Carlo method for estimating transmittance in participating media that avoids the high variance of binary visibility tests by accumulating a continuous product of null-scattering ratios. Unlike standard delta tracking, which terminates paths upon real scattering or absorption events, ratio tracking continues sampling along the ray, multiplying the estimate by the ratio of actual to majorant extinction at each step, thereby providing an unbiased, low-variance estimator for heterogeneous media. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin o, direction \omega, parametric bounds [t{min}, t{max}], medium properties (extinction \sigmat, absorption \sigmaa, scattering \sigmas, or albedo a), and a majorant extinction coefficient \sigmam \ge \sigmat(x) for all x in the medium. Output: Estimated transmittance T (Spectrum), and optionally PDFs for Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS). Data Structures: Spectrum: A vector of 3 floats (R, G, B) used to track transmittance and PDFs independently per channel. Majorant (\sigmam): A constant Spectrum representing the upper bound of the extinction coefficient. Null Scattering Coefficient (\sigman): Computed as \sigman = \max(0, \sigmam - \sigmat). Parameters: maxnullcollisions: Integer limit to prevent infinite loops from numerical errors. Default: 1000. RR Threshold: Float threshold for Russian roulette. Default: 0.05. RR Survival Probability: Float 1-q. Default: 0.25 (termination probability q=0.75). ShadowEpsilon: Small float subtracted from 1.0 to define max ray distance, preventing self-intersection. Steps: 1. Initialize: Set transmittance accumulator T{ray} = 1.0, rescaled path probabilities rl = 1.0 (for unidirectional/delta tracking PDF) and ru = 1.0 (for null scattering/NEE PDF). Initialize RNG with hash of ray origin and direction. 2. Sample Channel: Generate uniform random u \in [0,1]. Select channel c = \text{clamp}(\lfloor u \times 3 \rfloor, 0, 2) for distance sampling. 3. Loop: While iteration count < \text{max\null\collisions}: a. Sample Distance: Sample free path distance t using the majorant for the selected channel: t = -\ln(1 - \text{rng}()) / \sigmam[c]. b. Check Bounds: Calculate remaining distance dt = t{max} - t{current}. If t \ge dt, the ray reaches the endpoint/surface. Update T{ray} = \exp(-\sigmam \cdot dt), update PDFs, and break loop. c. Compute Null Coefficient: At position xt, compute \sigman = \max(0, \sigmam - \sigmaa - \sigmas). d. Update Estimators: Compute PDF of majorant sampling: pdf = T{maj}[0] \times \sigmam[0] (where T{maj} is the majorant transmittance \exp(-\sigmam t)). Update transmittance: T{ray} = T{maj} \times \frac{\sigman}{pdf}. Update rescaled probabilities: rl = T{maj} \times \frac{\sigmam}{pdf} and ru = T{maj} \times \frac{\sigman}{pdf}. e. Russian Roulette: Compute test value Tr = T{ray} / (rl + ru).\text{Average()}. If \max(Tr) < 0.05, terminate with probability q=0.75 (set T{ray}=0) or survive with probability 1-q (divide T{ray} by 1-q). f. Advance: Update accumulated distance t{current} = \min(t{current} + t, t{max}). 4. Final Segment: After the loop, update accumulators for the final segment from the last sampled point to t{max} by multiplying by \frac{T{maj}}{T{maj}[0]}. 5. Return: Return T{ray} normalized by the average PDFs if used for MIS. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ratiotracking(rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax, medium, sigmamaj, rng): """ Estimates transmittance using ratio tracking with null scattering. """ # Helper functions for Spectrum (list of 3 floats: R, G, B) def makespectrum(val): return [val, val, val] def clampzero(x): return [max(0.0, c) for c in x] def expspectrum(x): return [exp(c) for c in x] def avgspectrum(x): return sum(x) / len(x) def maxcomponent(x): return max(x) Tray = makespectrum(1.0) rl = makespectrum(1.0) ru = makespectrum(1.0) tcurrent = tmin iteration = 0 maxnullcollisions = 1000 while iteration < maxnullcollisions: # 1. Sample a color channel for distance sampling u = rng.uniform(0.0, 1.0) channel = int(u 3) if channel > 2: channel = 2 if sigmamaj[channel] <= 0.0: break # 2. Sample distance using majorant t = -log(1.0 - rng.uniform(0.0, 1.0)) / sigmamaj[channel] dt = tmax - tcurrent # 3. Check if we reached the end of the segment if t >= dt: # Reached surface/endpoint Tmaj = expspectrum([-sigmamaj[c] dt for c in range(3)]) Tray = [Tray[c] Tmaj[c] for c in range(3)] rl = [rl[c] Tmaj[c] for c in range(3)] ru = [ru[c] Tmaj[c] for c in range(3)] break # 4. Update accumulated distance tcurrent = min(tcurrent + t, tmax) # 5. Compute null scattering coefficient at current position sigmaa = medium.getsigmaa() sigmas = medium.getsigmas() sigman = clampzero([sigmamaj[c] - sigmaa[c] - sigmas[c] for c in range(3)]) # 6. Compute PDF of the majorant sampling Tmaj = expspectrum([-sigmamaj[c] t for c in range(3)]) pdf = [Tmaj[c] sigmamaj[c] for c in range(3)] # 7. Update transmittance and rescaled probabilities Tray = [Tray[c] Tmaj[c] (sigman[c] / pdf[c]) for c in range(3)] rl = [rl[c] Tmaj[c] (sigmamaj[c] / pdf[c]) for c in range(3)] ru = [ru[c] Tmaj[c] (sigman[c] / pdf[c]) for c in range(3)] # 8. Russian Roulette for low transmittance avgpdf = avgspectrum(rl) + avgspectrum(ru) if avgpdf > 0: Tr = [Tray[c] / avgpdf for c in range(3)] else: Tr = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] if maxcomponent(Tr) < 0.05: q = 0.75 if rng.uniform(0.0, 1.0) < q: Tray = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] break else: Tray = [Tray[c] / (1.0 - q) for c in range(3)] iteration += 1 # 9. Update for final segment (if loop broke early or for last segment logic) # In some implementations, this handles the segment from last sample to tmax # if the loop didn't break on 't >= dt' but on max iterations. # However, standard ratio tracking usually breaks on endpoint. # If using the callback structure from, this update happens inside SampleTmaj. return Tray Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Instability: Without normalization, transmittance and PDF values can explode because \sigman can be large. The method divides by \max(\sigmam) (implicitly via the PDF ratio) to maintain robustness. Chromatic Media: Distance sampling uses a single channel, but PDFs are tracked for all channels to enable MIS. The final estimate uses the average of channel PDFs. Russian Roulette: Setting survival probability equal to transmittance transforms the method into delta tracking (binary 0/1 outcome), losing variance reduction benefits. A fixed, less aggressive probability (q=0.75) is used. Infinite Loops: Numerical errors can cause unbounded loops. A maximum iteration count (1000) is enforced. This method estimates transmittance between two points in a participating medium using ratio tracking to connect real-scattering vertices in a path integral framework. Unlike delta tracking which terminates on collision, ratio tracking continues until the endpoint is reached, accumulating a product of ratios to estimate total transmittance. It is chosen when connecting vertices in null-scattering path tracing to avoid binary visibility variance. The Weighted Next-Fight Estimator is a Monte Carlo method for estimating transmittance using null scattering that explicitly adds the transmittance through the rest of the combined medium at each step. It is distinguished from Real-scattering vertex connection by correcting for initial underestimation of uncollided radiance via a modified RTE. A method to estimate transmittance for next event estimation by solving an ODE derived from the transmittance definition, avoiding unbiased estimation of exponentials. It transforms the transmittance ODE \frac{dT}{dt'} = -\sigmat T into \frac{d}{dt'} \tilde{T} = \sigman \tilde{T} to enable Monte Carlo sampling. It is used when unbiased estimation of \exp(X) is invalid due to Jensen's inequality. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of null scattering events, which depends on the ratio \sigman / \sigmam. In highly heterogeneous media with tight majorants, performance approaches that of delta tracking. Memory Complexity: Low, requiring only storage for the transmittance accumulator, PDFs, and current position. Variance: Significantly lower than binary delta tracking for transmittance estimation, as it avoids the high variance of Russian roulette termination on absorption. Strengths: Unbiased, handles heterogeneous media efficiently, reduces noise in transmittance estimation. Limitations: Can be slower than delta tracking if the number of scattering events increases significantly due to non-termination on absorption. Requires careful tuning of Russian roulette parameters to avoid bias. When to Use: When accurate, low-variance transmittance estimation is required in heterogeneous media, especially for next-event estimation or vertex connection in path tracing. Ratio tracking was originally analyzed by Cramer in 1978. It was reinvented and studied by Novák et al. in 2014 in the context of rendering, where it was applied to transmittance estimation in participating media. The method is a key component of null-scattering path integral formulations, enabling unbiased light transport in heterogeneous volumes. name: Real-scattering vertex connection with ratio tracking
head: Delta Tracking for Transmittance Estimation, Ratio Tracking Volumetric Sensor, Ratio Tracking with Null Scattering, RatioVolumetricSensor, Real-scattering vertex connection
body: This method estimates the transmittance between two points p1 and 2 in a participating medium using ratio tracking, which accumulates a product of null-scattering ratios rather than terminating on collision. It is used to connect real-scattering vertices on camera and light subpaths in a null-scattering path integral framework. Unlike delta tracking for sampling which terminates on collision, ratio tracking continues until the endpoint is reached, accumulating a product of ratios to estimate the total transmittance. Inputs: p1, p2: Start and end points of the segment. sampler: A random number generator providing uniform samples in 0, 1). majorant: The homogenized extinction coefficient \hat{\mu}t (stored as self.majorant). throughput: The current path throughput, initialized by undoing transmittance from previous interactions. attenuation: The accumulated transmittance from previous segments. tprev: The distance traveled in the previous segment. nscat: The number of scattering events in the history. sigmas: The scattering coefficient. sigmaa: The [absorption coefficient (derived from sigmat and sigmas). sigmat: The total extinction coefficient at the current position. em: The emission coefficient. sa: The absorption coefficient (\sigmaa = \sigmat - \sigmas). st: The total extinction coefficient \sigmat. weight: The initial weight for the contribution, calculated as throughput exp(-st tprev). bbox: The bounding box of the medium grid. voxelsize: The size of each voxel in the grid. mfilm: The volumetric film to write contributions to. δL.array: The differentiable array for gradient storage. Outputs: transmittance: The estimated transmittance product. contrib: The contribution written to the film. VolumetricFilm: A tensor of shape (resz, resy, resx, channels) where channels is 2 if surfaceaware is true, else 1. Container: Stores medium properties including sigmat, albedo, and mediumphase. 1. Initialize Throughput and Scattering History: Undo transmittance from previous interactions and adjust for scattering history: python throughput = dr.detach(attenuation dr.exp(mei.sigmat tprev)) throughput = dr.select(mei.sigmas != 0, dr.rcp(dr.detach(mei.sigmas) nscat), 1.) 2. Setup Segment: Calculate the distance to the endpoint: distToEnd = length(p1 - p2). Initialize t = 0 and transmittance = (1, 1, 1). Create a ray from p1 to p2. 3. Ratio Tracking Loop: While the ray is active: a. Sample Distance: Sample a collision-free distance s using the majorant: python # Using uniform sample u in [0, 1) u = sampler.next1d(active) # Ensure u is not exactly 1 to avoid log(0) u = dr.clamp(u, 0.0, 0.9999999) sampledt = - dr.log(1.0 - u) / self.majorant Alternatively, using invMajorant: python s = - dr.log(dr.max(1.0 - sampler.getNext1D(), 0.0)) invMajorant sampledt = s b. Update Position: Update the ray position t: python t[active] += sampledt c. Check Bounds: Check if the ray is still within the maximum distance maxt (or distToEnd): python active &= t < maxt # or t < distToEnd If t > distToEnd, break the loop and return transmittance. d. Voxel Lookup: Determine the current voxel index: python currentvoxel = mi.Vector3i(dr.floor((p - self.bbox.min) / self.voxelsize)) isinsidegrid = dr.all(currentvoxel >= 0) & dr.all(currentvoxel < self.res) idx = computeflatindex(currentvoxel, self.res, self.surfaceaware) Compute the local density/extinction coefficients at ray(t). Let \sigmat be the total extinction and \sigmas be the scattering coefficient at the current position. e. Update Transmittance: Compute the null-scattering ratio and update the transmittance product: python sigman = self.majorant - sigmaa - sigmas # Ratio tracking accumulates the ratio of null-scattering probability # to the majorant sampling probability. # The term (sigman / majorant) represents the probability of a null event. transmittance = (sigman invMajorant) Note: Some implementations accumulate the product of ratios directly as the estimator for transmittance. f. Compute Contribution (for Sensor/Connection): If performing a connection (e.g., Next-Event Estimation), compute the contribution: python # sa = sigmat - sigmas # st = sigmat # weight = throughput exp(-st tprev) contrib = dr.select( active & isinsidegrid, weight em sa / st (1 - st / self.majorant) ninteractions st / self.majorant, 0.) Here, n{interactions} is the number of steps taken in the ratio tracking loop. g. Write to Film: In primal mode, write the contribution to the film: python self.mfilm.write(contrib, idx, active & isinsidegrid) 4. Automatic Differentiation: Forward Mode: Scatter the gradient: python dr.scatterreduce(dr.ReduceOp.Add, δL.array, dr.forwardto(contrib), idx, active & isinsidegrid) Reverse Mode: Gather the gradient and backpropagate: python grad = dr.gather(mi.Spectrum, δL.array, idx, active & isinsidegrid) dr.backwardfrom(contrib grad) The path PDF for connecting real-scattering vertices on camera and light subpaths with s and t vertices respectively is: p{s,t} (x) = p{dt} (x{r0}...x{r{t-1}}) p{rt}(x{r{t-1}}, x{r{r-s+1}}) p{dt}(x{rr}...x{r{r-s+1}}) where p{dt}(x) is the delta-tracking path PDF: p{dt}(x) = p(x0) \prod{i=1}^{k} p(\omegai |x{i-1}, \omega{i-1}) p(xi |x{i-1}, \omegai) P(e{xi}) \prod{i=1}^{k-1} G(x{ri}, x{ri+1}) The transition probabilities are: p(\omega' |x, \omega) \propto \rho(\omega, x, \omega'), \quad p(y|x, \omega) = T(x, y)\mut(y), \quad P(ex) = \frac{\mu{ex}(x)}{\mut(x)} where ex \in \{a, s, n\} denotes the event type (absorption, scattering, or null-scattering). For the full path PDF including the connection segment: p(x) = p{dt}(x0...x{r{r-1}}) p(\omegar |x{r{r-1}}, \omega{r{r-1}}) p(xk) p{ea}(x{r{r-1}}|x{r{r-2}}, \omega{r{r-1}}, xk) \cdot p{rt}(x{r{r-2}}, x{r{r-1}}) p{rt}(x{r{r-1}}, xk) G(x{r{r-2}}, x{r{r-1}}) The equiangular sampling PDF for the connection is: p{ea}(x{r{r-1}}|x{r{r-2}}, \omega{r{r-1}}, xk) \propto G(x{r{r-1}}, xk) = \frac{1}{\|x{r{r-1}} - xk\|^2} majorant: The majorant density \hat{\mu}t used for ratio tracking sampling. s: Number of vertices on the camera subpath (real-scattering). t: Number of vertices on the light subpath (real-scattering). Precision: Logarithms of values close to 1 or 0 can cause precision issues. Clamp sampler outputs away from 1.0. Boundaries: Ensure voxel indices are within grid bounds before accessing data. Degenerate Input: If sigmas is 0, avoid division by zero in throughput initialization. Termination: Ratio tracking must continue until the endpoint is reached, unlike standard delta tracking which stops at the first collision. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of ratio tracking steps, which depends on the ratio of the majorant to the local extinction coefficient. Higher majorants lead to more steps but lower variance per step. Memory Complexity: Depends on the grid resolution for storing medium properties and the film buffer. Strengths: Unbiased estimation of transmittance in heterogeneous media without requiring spatial coherence or bounding volume hierarchies for acceleration structures. Limitations: Can be slow if the majorant is much larger than the local extinction coefficient, leading to many null-scattering events. When to use: When estimating transmittance between two points in a participating medium within a null-scattering path integral framework, especially for connecting real-scattering vertices. This method is part of the null-scattering path integral formulation of light transport. It builds on the concept of ratio tracking introduced for transmittance estimation. The implementation details are found in the Dr. TVAM project for inverse rendering in volumetric additive manufacturing. Dr. TVAM – Inverse Rendering for Tomographic Volumetric Additive Manufacturing, https://github.com/rgl-epfl/drtvam, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) GitHub - yumcyaWiz/volpt: Volumetric path tracer written in C++, https://github.com/yumcyaWiz/volpt, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) A Null-Scattering Path Integral Formulation of Light Transport, https://www.scribd.com/document/1067625811/A-Null-scattering-Path-Integral-Formulation-of-Light-Transport, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Weighted Next-Fight Estimator
head: Integral Formulation of Transmittance Estimators, Next-flight estimator
body: The Weighted Next-Fight Estimator is a Monte Carlo method for estimating transmittance (uncollided radiance) in participating media by modifying the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) to account for losses and a point source of unit radiance. It sets itself apart from standard delta tracking by explicitly adding an underestimated uncollided contribution at each collision point and using null collision sampling to correct for the initial underestimation, thereby providing an unbiased estimator for the transmittance term in light transport. It builds on Ratio Tracking with Null Scattering by utilizing the null scattering framework to handle heterogeneous media. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Starting position \mathbf{x}0, direction \omega, remaining distance to the point source di, combined extinction coefficient function \bar{\mu}(\mathbf{x}) = \mut(\mathbf{x}) + \mun(\mathbf{x}), null collision coefficient function \mun(\mathbf{x}), and PDF of sampled free paths p(t). Output: The estimated transmittance L(\mathbf{x}0, \omega). Data Structures: No specific complex data structures are required beyond the coefficient functions \bar{\mu} and \mun, which are typically accessed via volume lookup or analytical evaluation. The estimator maintains a running weight product and a sum of scores. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize the Monte Carlo score sum W = 0 and the current weight product w{prod} = 1. 2. Set the current position \mathbf{x}{curr} = \mathbf{x}0 and remaining distance d{rem} = di. 3. Sample a free path distance t from the PDF p(t). If p(t) is not explicitly provided, standard exponential sampling t = -\ln(\xi)/\bar{\mu}{max} is used, where \xi \in (0,1) is a uniform random number and \bar{\mu}{max} is the maximum combined extinction coefficient. 4. Update the current position: \mathbf{x}{next} = \mathbf{x}{curr} + t\omega. 5. Calculate the transmittance from \mathbf{x}{curr} to \mathbf{x}{next} through the combined medium: T{curr} = \exp\left(-\int0^t \bar{\mu}(\mathbf{x}s) \, ds\right) where \mathbf{x}s = \mathbf{x}{curr} + s\omega for s \in [0, t]. 6. Add the underestimated uncollided contribution to the score. If the path segment does not exceed the remaining distance to the source (t \le d{rem}), the contribution is: \text{score\add} = T{curr} \times w{prod} If the path segment exceeds the remaining distance (t > d{rem}), the contribution is the transmittance to the source: \text{score\add} = \exp\left(-\int0^{d{rem}} \bar{\mu}(\mathbf{x}s) \, ds\right) \times w{prod} Update the total score: W \leftarrow W + \text{score\add}. 7. If the path segment exceeds the remaining distance (t > d{rem}), terminate the estimator and return W. 8. Update the weight product for the next iteration by multiplying by the ratio of null collision to combined extinction at the collision point \mathbf{x}{next}: w{prod} \leftarrow w{prod} \times \frac{\mun(\mathbf{x}{next})}{\bar{\mu}(\mathbf{x}{next})} 9. Update the remaining distance: d{rem} \leftarrow d{rem} - t. 10. Update the current position: \mathbf{x}{curr} \leftarrow \mathbf{x}{next}. 11. Repeat from step 3. Formulas: The estimator is derived from the modified RTE: (\omega \cdot \nabla) L(\mathbf{x}, \omega) = -[\mut(\mathbf{x}) + \mun(\mathbf{x})]L(\mathbf{x}, \omega) + \delta(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}d) + \mun(\mathbf{x}) \int{S^2} \delta(\omega - \bar{\omega}) L(\mathbf{x}, \bar{\omega}) d\bar{\omega} where \mathbf{x}d = \mathbf{x}0 - d\omega is the position of the point source of unit radiance. The integral formulation is: L(\mathbf{x}, \omega) = \exp\left(-\int0^{di} \bar{\mu}(\mathbf{x}s) \, ds\right) + \int0^{di} p(t) \frac{\mun(\mathbf{x}t)}{\bar{\mu}(\mathbf{x}t)} L(\mathbf{x}t, \omega) \, dt The Monte Carlo score for a path \mathbf{X} = \{\mathbf{x}0, \dots, \mathbf{x}k\} where k is the index of the first collision after exceeding distance d from \mathbf{x}0 is: w(\mathbf{X}) = \sum{i=0}^{k-1} \exp\left(-\int0^{di} \bar{\mu}(\mathbf{x}s) \, ds\right) \prod{j=1}^i \frac{\mun(\mathbf{x}j)}{\bar{\mu}(\mathbf{x}j)} Parameters: \bar{\mu}(\mathbf{x}): Combined extinction coefficient. Must be known or bounded. \mun(\mathbf{x}): Null collision coefficient. Must satisfy \mun(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0 and \bar{\mu}(\mathbf{x}) \ge \mut(\mathbf{x}). p(t): PDF of sampled free paths. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The integrals \int \bar{\mu} ds must be computed accurately. In heterogeneous media, this may require numerical integration or precomputed lookup tables. Boundaries: The estimator assumes the point source is at a finite distance di. If di \to \infty, the transmittance term vanishes, and the estimator may become inefficient or require modification. Degenerate Input: If \bar{\mu}(\mathbf{x}) = 0 anywhere along the path, the transmittance is 1, and the weight product update becomes undefined if \mun(\mathbf{x}) is also 0. Handle this by checking for zero extinction and skipping weight updates or treating it as a vacuum. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def weightednextflightestimator(x0, omega, di, mutfunc, munfunc, psamplefunc, maxsteps=1000): """ Estimates transmittance using the Weighted Next-Fight Estimator. Args: x0: Starting position (vector). omega: Direction (vector, normalized). di: Remaining distance to the point source (scalar). mutfunc: Function returning true extinction coefficient at position. munfunc: Function returning null collision coefficient at position. psamplefunc: Function sampling free path distance t from PDF p(t). maxsteps: Maximum number of collision steps to prevent infinite loops. Returns: Estimated transmittance L(x0, omega). """ W = 0.0 wprod = 1.0 xcurr = x0 drem = di for step in range(maxsteps): # Sample free path t = psamplefunc() # Check if path exceeds remaining distance if t > drem: # Calculate transmittance to the source # Integral from 0 to drem # Assuming a simple numerical integration or analytical form is available # For demonstration, we use a placeholder for the integral calculation integralval = computetransmittanceintegral(xcurr, omega, drem, mutfunc, munfunc) Ttosource = exp(-integralval) W += Ttosource wprod break # Calculate transmittance for the sampled path # Integral from 0 to t integralval = computetransmittanceintegral(xcurr, omega, t, mutfunc, munfunc) Tcurr = exp(-integralval) # Add score W += Tcurr wprod # Update position xnext = xcurr + t omega # Update weight product munnext = munfunc(xnext) mutnext = mutfunc(xnext) muncombinednext = mutnext + munnext if muncombinednext == 0: # Handle zero extinction case # If combined extinction is zero, weight product doesn't change # because the ratio is 0/0, but physically it means no interaction. # However, the formula uses mun / mucombined. If both are 0, ratio is undefined. # In practice, if mut=0 and mun=0, the medium is vacuum, so no scattering. # The weight product should remain unchanged. pass else: wprod = (munnext / muncombinednext) # Update remaining distance and current position drem -= t xcurr = xnext if drem <= 0: break return W def computetransmittanceintegral(xstart, omega, distance, mutfunc, munfunc): """ Computes the integral of combined extinction along a ray segment. This is a placeholder for the actual integration method. In practice, this might involve numerical quadrature or volume traversal. """ # Simple midpoint rule for demonstration numsamples = 10 step = distance / numsamples integral = 0.0 for i in range(numsamples): t = (i + 0.5) step x = xstart + t omega mut = mutfunc(x) mun = munfunc(x) integral += (mut + mun) step return integral Sampling Proportional to Transmittance is a technique for generating free-flight distances distributed according to the transmittance function T(t), rather than the standard extinction-weighted distribution. It solves the problem of needing to sample from T(t) for unbiased inverse volume rendering estimators without requiring explicit evaluation of the normalization constant C = \int0^{ts} T(t') dt', which is generally intractable. It sets itself apart from standard delta tracking by producing samples proportional to T(t) directly, whereas standard delta tracking produces samples proportional to \sigmat(t)T(t) (the probability of the first interaction). It builds on Weighted Next-Fight Estimator by providing the specific sampling distribution required for the uncollided radiance term. Time Complexity: The complexity depends on the number of collisions k before exceeding the distance d. In homogeneous media, k is small. In highly heterogeneous media with many null collisions, k can be large, leading to higher computational cost. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory, assuming the coefficient functions are accessible in O(1) time. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance degrades in media with high variance in extinction coefficients, as the number of null collisions increases. Strengths: Provides an unbiased estimator for transmittance. Integrates naturally with null scattering methods. Limitations: Can suffer from high variance if the null collision coefficient is not chosen optimally. Requires accurate evaluation of the transmittance integral. When to use: When estimating uncollided radiance in participating media, especially in conjunction with null scattering methods. When not to use: When the medium is homogeneous and simple analytical solutions are available, or when the computational cost of evaluating the transmittance integral is prohibitive. The Weighted Next-Fight Estimator was presented by Cramer in 1978. This document claims it is the first derivation of the next-flight estimator directly from a modified version of the RTE and its first description in computer graphics literature. It is used in volume rendering for estimating transmittance, which is a key component in solving the radiative transfer equation for participating media.
