name: Spectral Multiple Importance Sampling
head: Chromatic Media Sampling with MIS, Single-sample MIS for Spectra, Spectral Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) for Wavelengths, Spectral Volume Sampling
body: Spectral Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) is a technique for handling spectrally varying participating media in path tracing by sampling a single wavelength channel while correctly weighting contributions across all spectral bands. It solves the high-variance problem that arises when a single sampling probability density function (PDF), derived from one wavelength's medium properties, is used to evaluate integrands at other wavelengths where that PDF may be a poor match or zero-valued. Inputs: Current path vertex position x. Throughput vector \beta (RGB or n spectral samples). Medium properties: absorption coefficient \sigmaa(\lambda) and scattering coefficient \sigmas(\lambda) for n spectral samples (typically n=3 for RGB). Majorant extinction coefficient \sigma{maj} (scalar upper bound for the sampled channel's transmittance). Random number generator state. Outputs: Sampled wavelength index k \in \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}. PDF values p{\lambdai}(x) for all i \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}. Updated throughput and path termination status. Data Structures: throughputalbedo: A vector of size n, where each element i is \betai \cdot \frac{\sigma{s,\lambdai}}{\sigma{a,\lambdai} + \sigma{s,\lambdai}}. DiscreteEmpiricalDistribution1D: A discrete distribution object constructed from the throughputalbedo vector, mapping a continuous uniform random variable to a channel index based on relative spectral contributions. pmf: An array of size n storing the probability density values p{\lambdai}(x) for each wavelength. Steps: 1. Compute Spectral Weights: Calculate the product of the current throughput and the single-scattering albedo for each wavelength channel. 2. Construct Discrete Distribution: Create a discrete distribution object using the computed weights. 3. Sample Channel Index: Draw a uniform random number u \in 0, 1) and use it to sample an index k from the discrete distribution. 4. Sample Distance: Sample the distance t to the next [interaction using the majorant extinction coefficient \sigma{maj}. 5. Evaluate PDFs: For the sampled distance t and position x, compute the PDF for the sampled channel p{\lambdak}(x) and the PDFs for all other channels p{\lambdai}(x) for i \neq k. 6. Compute MIS Weights: Apply the balance heuristic for single-sample MIS. 7. Update Throughput: Multiply the throughput by the MIS weight and the appropriate spectral terms (albedo, phase function, etc.) for the sampled channel. 8. Continue Path: Proceed with the path tracing algorithm using the sampled distance and updated throughput. Formulas: Albedo: \alpha{\lambdai} = \frac{\sigma{s,\lambdai}}{\sigma{a,\lambdai} + \sigma{s,\lambdai}}. Discrete weights: wi = \betai \cdot \alpha{\lambdai}. MIS weight (balance heuristic): w{\lambdak}(x) = \frac{p{\lambdak}(x)}{\sum{i=1}^{n} p{\lambdai}(x)}. Discrete probability: q = 1/n, where n is the number of spectral samples. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def spectralmissamplemedium(x, throughput, sigmaa, sigmas, sigmamaj, rng): """ Sample a medium interaction using Spectral MIS. Args: x: Current position. throughput: Current path throughput (vector of size n). sigmaa: Absorption coefficients for n wavelengths (vector of size n). sigmas: Scattering coefficients for n wavelengths (vector of size n). sigmamaj: Scalar majorant extinction coefficient. rng: Random number generator with uniform() method. Returns: t: Distance to next interaction. newthroughput: Updated throughput. terminated: Boolean indicating if path is terminated. pmf: PDFs for all wavelengths. """ n = len(sigmaa) sigmat = [sigmaa[i] + sigmas[i] for i in range(n)] albedo = [sigmas[i] / sigmat[i] if sigmat[i] > 0 else 0.0 for i in range(n)] weights = [throughput[i] albedo[i] for i in range(n)] # Construct discrete distribution from weights cumweights = [0.0] n cumweights[0] = weights[0] for i in range(1, n): cumweights[i] = cumweights[i-1] + weights[i] totalweight = cumweights[-1] # Sample channel index k u = rng.uniform() k = 0 while k < n - 1 and cumweights[k] < u totalweight: k += 1 # Sample distance using scalar majorant t = -math.log(1.0 - rng.uniform()) / sigmamaj # Evaluate PDFs for all channels at distance t pmf = [sigmat[i] math.exp(-sigmamaj t) for i in range(n)] # Compute MIS weight for the sampled channel (balance heuristic) sumpmf = sum(pmf) misweight = pmf[k] / sumpmf if sumpmf > 0 else 0.0 # Update throughput for all channels newthroughput = [0.0] n for i in range(n): newthroughput[i] = throughput[i] (misweight if i == k else 0.0) albedo[i] (sigmat[i] / sigmamaj) terminated = False # Absorption check depends on event sampling, not detailed here return t, newthroughput, terminated, pmf Parameters: n: Number of spectral samples. Typical value: 3 (RGB). q: Discrete probability of sampling a specific wavelength. Value: 1/n if uniform. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Extinction: If \sigma{t,\lambdai} = 0, the albedo is undefined. Handle by setting albedo to 0 or 1 depending on whether the medium is purely scattering or empty. Infinite Variance: If the majorant for one wavelength is much larger than the true extinction for another, the variance can be high. Precision: Floating-point round-off errors in PDF calculations should be clamped to zero to avoid negative probabilities. This method extends null-scattering free-flight sampling to handle spectrally varying (chromatic) participating media by sampling a single color channel (R, G, or B) for distance determination while averaging the probability density functions (PDFs) across all channels to maintain unbiasedness. It solves the problem where a single sampling PDF based on one wavelength is a poor match or invalid for other wavelengths, causing high variance in spectral path tracing. It differs from standard monochromatic null-scattering by introducing channel selection logic and PDF averaging, and from full spectral sampling by reducing the per-step computational cost to a single channel's majorant evaluation. A technique to avoid infinite variance when sampling transport equations for multiple wavelengths simultaneously by limiting the extinction coefficient to a single scalar value shared across all wavelengths. It enforces the constraint that for every pair of wavelengths \lambda1, \lambda2, the total extinction coefficients are equal: \sigma{a,\lambda1}(x) + \sigma{s,\lambda1}(x) = \sigma{a,\lambda2}(x) + \sigma{s,\lambda2}(x) = \sigmat(x). This approach is suitable when extinction depends only on particle density/size (color varies via BSDF-like probabilities). For atmospheric scattering, solving transport equations separately for each wavelength is preferred. If \sigma{t,\lambda2} > \sigma{t,\lambda1} and sampling is done using density p{\lambda2}, the variance on wavelength \lambda1 can be arbitrarily high or infinite. Specifically, variance is infinite if \sigma{t,\lambda2} \geq 2\sigma{t,\lambda1}. Time Complexity: O(n) per interaction, where n is the number of spectral samples. Memory Complexity: O(n) to store the spectral coefficients and PDFs. Performance: Reduces variance compared to monochromatic sampling with a single majorant. Strengths: Unbiased, handles spectrally varying media effectively. Limitations: Can still suffer from high variance if the majorant is a poor match for the sampled channel's true extinction. When to Use: Suitable for general participating media with moderate spectral variation. Spectral Multiple Importance Sampling was developed to address the challenges of rendering spectrally varying participating media. The technique is discussed in the context of volumetric path tracing and multiple importance sampling for wavelengths. The scalar extinction constraint was introduced to handle infinite variance issues in multi-wavelength sampling. The method is part of the broader field of unbiased global illumination with participating media. name: Chromatic Null-Scattering Free-Flight Sampling
head: One-sample multiple importance sampling for chromatic media, RGB channel sampling for null scattering
body: This method extends null-scattering free-flight sampling to handle spectrally varying (chromatic) participating media by sampling a single color channel (R, G, or B) for distance determination while averaging the probability density functions (PDFs) across all channels to maintain unbiasedness. It solves the problem where a single sampling PDF based on one wavelength is a poor match or invalid for other wavelengths, causing high variance in spectral path tracing. It differs from standard monochromatic null-scattering by introducing channel selection logic and PDF averaging, and from full spectral sampling by reducing the per-step computational cost to a single channel's majorant evaluation. Inputs: Ray origin, direction, and t{hit} (distance to next surface intersection). Medium properties: extinction coefficient \sigmat (vector of size 3, e.g., RGB), scattering coefficient \sigmas, absorption coefficient \sigmaa. Majorant \sigmam (vector of size 3), precomputed as the element-wise maximum of \sigmat over the medium's domain. Random number generator rng. maxnullcollisions: integer limit for loop termination (default 1000). Outputs: scatter: boolean, true if a real particle interaction occurred. transmittance: spectrum (vector of size 3), accumulated transmittance. transdirpdf: spectrum (vector of size 3), PDF for free-flight sampling (used in path throughput). transneepdf: spectrum (vector of size 3), PDF for next event estimation (used in light transmittance). Data Structures: Vectors are 3-element arrays representing R, G, B channels. makeconstspectrum(v): creates a vector [v, v, v]. max(v): returns the maximum element of vector v. avg(v): returns the arithmetic mean of vector elements \frac{1}{3}\sum vi. clamp(x, min, max): clamps x to [min, max]. Formulas: Real particle probability: p{real} = \frac{\sigmat}{\sigmam} (element-wise division). Null-scattering coefficient: \sigman = \sigmam (1 - p{real}) = \sigmam - \sigmat. Distance sample: t = -\frac{\log(1 - u)}{\sigmam[channel]}, where u \in [0, 1). Parameters: maxnullcollisions: Default 1000. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize scatter = False, transmittance = [1, 1, 1], transdirpdf = [1, 1, 1], transneepdf = [1, 1, 1]. 2. If the ray is inside the medium: a. Retrieve \sigmam for the current ray segment. b. Sample u \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1). c. Determine channel index: c = \text{clamp}(\lfloor u \times 3 \rfloor, 0, 2). d. Initialize accumt = 0, iteration = 0. 3. Loop indefinitely: a. If \sigmam[c] \le 0, break (no scattering possible in selected channel). b. If iteration \ge maxnullcollisions, break (prevent unbounded loops due to numerical error). c. Sample distance t = -\frac{\log(1 - \text{next}(rng))}{\sigmam[c]}. d. Compute remaining distance to surface: dt = t{hit} - \text{accum\t}. e. Update accumulated distance: \text{accum\t} = \min(\text{accum\t} + t, t{hit}). f. If t < dt (interaction occurs before surface): i. Compute p{real} = \frac{\sigmat}{\sigmam}. ii. Sample v \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1). iii. If v < p{real}[c] (hit real particle): Set scatter = True. Update transmittance \leftarrow transmittance \times \frac{\exp(-\sigmam \cdot t)}{\max(\sigmam)}. Update transdirpdf \leftarrow transdirpdf \times \frac{\exp(-\sigmam \cdot t) \cdot \sigmam[c] \cdot p{real}[c]}{\max(\sigmam)}. Break loop. iv. Else (hit fake/null particle): Update transmittance \leftarrow transmittance \times \frac{\exp(-\sigmam \cdot t) \cdot \sigman[c]}{\max(\sigmam)}. Update transdirpdf \leftarrow transdirpdf \times \frac{\exp(-\sigmam \cdot t) \cdot \sigmam[c] \cdot (1 - p{real}[c])}{\max(\sigmam)}. Update transneepdf \leftarrow transneepdf \times \frac{\exp(-\sigmam \cdot t) \cdot \sigmam[c]}{\max(\sigmam)}. g. Else (reach surface, t \ge dt): Update transmittance \leftarrow transmittance \times \exp(-\sigmam \cdot dt). Update transdirpdf \leftarrow transdirpdf \times \exp(-\sigmam \cdot dt). Update transneepdf \leftarrow transneepdf \times \exp(-\sigmam \cdot dt). Break loop. h. Increment iteration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def chromaticnullscatteringfreeflight(ray, medium, rng, maxnullcollisions=1000): scatter = False transmittance = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] transdirpdf = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] transneepdf = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] if inmedium(ray.origin, medium): sigmam = getmajorant(medium, ray) u = next(rng) channel = clamp(int(u 3), 0, 2) accumt = 0 iteration = 0 while True: if sigmam[channel] <= 0: break if iteration >= maxnullcollisions: break t = -log(1 - next(rng)) / sigmam[channel] dt = ray.thit - accumt accumt = min(accumt + t, ray.thit) if t < dt: realprob = sigmam[0] / sigmam[0] # Placeholder: sigmat / sigmam # Note: sigmat must be retrieved from medium at current position sigmat = getsigmat(medium, ray.origin + ray.direction accumt) realprob = sigmat / sigmam if next(rng) < realprob[channel]: scatter = True transmittance = [t (exp(-sigmam[i] t) / max(sigmam)) for i, t in enumerate(transmittance)] transdirpdf = [p (exp(-sigmam[i] t) sigmam[i] realprob[i] / max(sigmam)) for i, p in enumerate(transdirpdf)] break else: sigman = [sigmam[i] (1 - realprob[i]) for i in range(3)] transmittance = [t (exp(-sigmam[i] t) sigman[i] / max(sigmam)) for i, t in enumerate(transmittance)] transdirpdf = [p (exp(-sigmam[i] t) sigmam[i] (1 - realprob[i]) / max(sigmam)) for i, p in enumerate(transdirpdf)] transneepdf = [p (exp(-sigmam[i] t) sigmam[i] / max(sigmam)) for i, p in enumerate(transneepdf)] else: transmittance = [t exp(-sigmam[i] dt) for i, t in enumerate(transmittance)] transdirpdf = [p exp(-sigmam[i] dt) for i, p in enumerate(transdirpdf)] transneepdf = [p exp(-sigmam[i] dt) for i, p in enumerate(transneepdf)] break iteration += 1 return scatter, transmittance, transdirpdf, transneepdf The pseudocode above assumes helper functions getsigmat and getmajorant which are standard in volume rendering implementations. The element-wise operations are explicitly written out for clarity. The formula for sigman is derived from \sigmam(1 - \sigmat/\sigmam).] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unbounded Loops: Numerical errors can cause infinite loops if the majorant is very small or zero. The loop is terminated when iteration reaches maxnullcollisions (default 1000). Numerical Overflow: Values can blow up to infinity if not normalized because \sigman can be large. Both transmittance and PDFs are divided by \max(\sigmam) to improve numerical robustness. Zero Majorant: If \sigmam[channel] \le 0, the loop breaks immediately to avoid division by zero. Time Complexity: O(k) per free-flight step, where k is the number of null-scattering events before a real interaction or surface hit. k depends on the ratio \sigmat / \sigmam. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per ray, storing vectors of size 3. Performance: Reduces variance compared to monochromatic sampling in chromatic media by ensuring the PDF is non-zero and well-matched for all wavelengths. Strengths: Unbiased spectral rendering; handles arbitrary chromatic media; robust against numerical instability via normalization. Limitations: Requires precomputed majorants; increased computational cost per step due to vector operations and channel selection; potential for unbounded loops if not capped. When to Use: Spectral path tracing with chromatic participating media where variance from monochromatic sampling is unacceptable. When Not to Use: Monochromatic media (use standard null-scattering); real-time rendering where performance is critical and chromatic accuracy is not required. Origin: Introduced in the context of volumetric path tracing for chromatic media, specifically addressing the limitations of monochromatic null-scattering in spectral rendering. History: Developed as part of the broader effort to enable unbiased spectral path tracing, building on null-scattering techniques. Usage: Used in offline spectral renderers for accurate simulation of colored participating media. Volumetric Path Tracing, https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~tzli/cse272/wi2022/homework2.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Wavelength Sampling via Balance Heuristic MIS
head: channel sampling for subsurface scattering
body: This method selects a single wavelength channel (e.g., R, G, B) for volumetric path tracing steps proportional to the product of the ray's spectral throughput and the medium's single scattering albedo. It addresses the variance caused by spectrally varying medium properties, where a single sampling PDF based on one wavelength may be a poor match or invalid for others. It sets itself apart from Spectral Multiple Importance Sampling by reducing the problem to a discrete categorical selection of channels rather than continuous spectral integration, and from Chromatic Null-Scattering Free-Flight Sampling by using a balance heuristic on the albedo/throughput product rather than null-scattering coefficients. Inputs: albedo: Single scattering albedo as a 3-component vector (\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^3), representing weights for the three wavelength channels. throughput: Ray throughput as a 3-component vector (T \in \mathbb{R}^3), representing the accumulated spectral weight of the path up to the current step. rand: A uniform random number in [0, 1). Outputs: channelindex: An integer in \{0, 1, 2\} indicating the selected wavelength channel. pdf: A 3-component vector containing the probability density for each channel. Data Structures: weights: A 3-component vector storing the unnormalized sampling probabilities. sumweights: A scalar storing the sum of the weights. Steps: 1. Calculate the unnormalized weights for each channel by taking the absolute value of the element-wise product of throughput and albedo: wi = |Ti \cdot \alphai| \quad \text{for } i \in \{x, y, z\} 2. Compute the sum of the weights: S = \sum{i \in \{x, y, z\}} wi 3. Determine the PDF for each channel: If S > 0: pi = \frac{wi}{S} If S = 0 (degenerate case where all weights are zero): pi = \frac{1}{3} \quad \text{for all } i 4. Select the channel index using cumulative distribution sampling with rand: If \text{rand} < px, return 0. Else if \text{rand} < px + py, return 1. Else, return 2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def samplewavelengthchannel(albedo: Vector3, throughput: Vector3, rand: float) -> Tuple[int, Vector3]: """ Sample a wavelength channel proportional to throughput and single scattering albedo. Args: albedo: Single scattering albedo (float3). throughput: Ray throughput (float3). rand: Uniform random number in [0, 1). Returns: channelindex: Selected channel index (0, 1, or 2). pdf: Probability density for each channel. """ # Calculate weights: absolute value of throughput albedo weights = Vector3( abs(throughput.x albedo.x), abs(throughput.y albedo.y), abs(throughput.z albedo.z)) # Sum the weights sumweights = weights.x + weights.y + weights.z # Determine PDF if sumweights > 0.0: pdf = Vector3( weights.x / sumweights, weights.y / sumweights, weights.z / sumweights) else: # Fallback to uniform sampling if all weights are zero pdf = Vector3(1.0 / 3.0, 1.0 / 3.0, 1.0 / 3.0) # Select channel based on cumulative PDF if rand < pdf.x: return 0, pdf elif rand < pdf.x + pdf.y: return 1, pdf else: return 2, pdf Parameters: albedo: Input single scattering albedo. Typical values depend on the material, ranging from 0 to 1 per channel. throughput: Input ray throughput. Values are typically between 0 and 1, decreasing with distance and absorption. rand: Uniform random number. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Throughput/Albedo: If all components of throughput albedo are zero, the sum of weights is zero. The method falls back to uniform sampling (1/3 per channel) to avoid division by zero. Precision: Using fabs ensures non-negative weights, handling potential negative values from numerical errors or specific throughput representations. Discrete vs Continuous: This method samples a discrete channel, not a continuous wavelength. It is intended for RGB path tracing where spectral variation is approximated by channel-wise weights. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample. The calculation involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1). Only a few temporary vectors and scalars are required. Performance: Significantly reduces noise in volumetric path tracing, especially with many bounces, by prioritizing channels with higher throughput and albedo. Strengths: Simple to implement, computationally inexpensive, effective for reducing variance in RGB-based volumetric rendering. Limitations: Only applicable to discrete channel-based rendering (e.g., RGB). Does not handle continuous spectral rendering directly. The balance heuristic assumes that the importance of a channel is well-approximated by the product of throughput and albedo. When to use: Volumetric path tracing with RGB wavelengths where spectral variation is significant and noise reduction is desired. When not to use: Continuous spectral rendering, or when the medium properties do not vary significantly across channels. The method is derived from the technique described in "Practical and Controllable Subsurface Scattering for Production Path Tracing" by Matt Jen-Yuan Chiang, Peter Kutz, and Brent Burley (SIGGRAPH 2016). It is implemented in production renderers such as Blender Cycles to handle subsurface scattering and volumetric effects efficiently. The approach uses a balance heuristic to sample color channels proportional to throughput and single scattering albedo, which helps in managing the variance introduced by spectrally varying medium properties. 2018 年, ナウでヤングな path tracing based subsurface scattering を実装する, https://qiita.com/syoyo/items/a5469f9e399f80fc62df, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Forward Vertex PDFs
head: Forward PDF, Unidirectional Path Segment PDF
body: Forward Vertex PDFs define the probability density function (PDF) for a unidirectional path segment sampled in the same direction as the random walk. They are used to assign weights when combining multiple sampling strategies in volumetric path tracing. This method differs from Reverse Vertex PDFs, which sample in the opposite direction, by establishing the likelihood of a path sequence generated from the camera or light source outward. Inputs and Outputs Input: A subpath \bar{\mathbf{y}} consisting of s vertices \mathbf{y}0, \dots, \mathbf{y}{s-1}. Output: The forward vertex PDF pi^{\rightarrow}(\bar{\mathbf{y}}) for each vertex index i \in [0, s-1]. Data Structures The path is represented as an ordered list of 3D positions \mathbf{y}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Definitions p(\cdot): Unconditional PDF with respect to Euclidean volume on \mathbb{R}^3. p{\omega}(\cdot): Directional PDF with respect to solid angle measure. p{\tau}(\cdot): Distance PDF with respect to Euclidean length on \mathbb{R}^1. G(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}): Geometry factor converting the solid angle \times length product measure to a volume measure. Formulas The forward vertex PDF for vertex i is defined as: pi^{\rightarrow}(\bar{\mathbf{y}}) = \begin{cases} p(\mathbf{y}0) & \text{if } i = 0, \\ p{\omega,i}^{\rightarrow}(\bar{\mathbf{y}})gi^{\rightarrow}(\bar{\mathbf{y}})p{\tau,i}^{\rightarrow}(\bar{\mathbf{y}}) & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} The directional component p{\omega,i}^{\rightarrow} depends on the vertex index: p{\omega,i}^{\rightarrow}(\bar{\mathbf{y}}) = \begin{cases} p{\omega}(\mathbf{y}0 \rightarrow \mathbf{y}1) & \text{if } i = 1, \\ p{\omega}(\mathbf{y}{i-2} \rightarrow \mathbf{y}{i-1} \rightarrow \mathbf{y}i) & \text{if } i > 1. \end{cases} The geometry factor and distance PDF are defined as: gi^{\rightarrow}(\bar{\mathbf{y}}) = G(\mathbf{y}{i-1}, \mathbf{y}i) p{\tau,i}^{\rightarrow}(\bar{\mathbf{y}}) = p{\tau}(\mathbf{y}{i-1} \rightarrow \mathbf{y}i) The total PDF of a subpath \bar{\mathbf{y}} with s vertices is the product of its forward vertex PDFs: ps(\bar{\mathbf{y}}) = \prod{i=0}^{s-1} pi^{\rightarrow}(\bar{\mathbf{y}}) Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeforwardvertexpdf(vertices, s): """ Computes the forward vertex PDFs for a path segment. Args: vertices: List of 3D positions [y0, y1,..., y{s-1}] s: Number of vertices in the path Returns: List of forward vertex PDF values [p0, p1,..., p{s-1}] """ pdfs = [] for i in range(s): if i == 0: # p(y0): unconditional PDF w.r.t Euclidean volume. # Implementation depends on camera/light emission model. Not given in the sources. pi = computeunconditionalpdf(vertices[0]) else: if i == 1: # pomega(y0 -> y1) pomega = computedirectionalpdf(vertices[0], vertices[1]) else: # pomega(y{i-2} -> y{i-1} -> yi) pomega = computedirectionalpdf(vertices[i-2], vertices[i-1], vertices[i]) g = computegeometryfactor(vertices[i-1], vertices[i]) ptau = computedistancepdf(vertices[i-1], vertices[i]) pi = pomega g ptau pdfs.append(pi) return pdfs def computeunconditionalpdf(y0): # Not given in the sources. return 1.0 def computedirectionalpdf(yprev, ycurr, yprevprev=None): # Not given in the sources. return 1.0 def computegeometryfactor(yprev, ycurr): # Standard geometry factor: cos(theta) / r^2 or similar. # Not given in the sources. return 1.0 def computedistancepdf(yprev, ycurr): # Not given in the sources. return 1.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The product of multiple PDFs can lead to underflow for long paths. Log-space arithmetic may be required. Boundaries: The geometry factor G involves division by distance squared. If vertices are coincident (\mathbf{y}{i-1} = \mathbf{y}i), the value is undefined. Degenerate Input: Paths with s < 2 vertices do not have i > 1 cases. Reverse Vertex PDFs define the PDF for a path sampled in the opposite direction of the random walk. They are needed to assign weights when combining multiple sampling strategies. The directional component p{\omega,i}^{\leftarrow} is defined as: p{\omega,i}^{\leftarrow}(\bar{\mathbf{y}}) = \begin{cases} p{\omega}(\mathbf{y}{k-1} \leftarrow \mathbf{y}k) & \text{if } i = k-1, \\ p{\omega}(\mathbf{y}i \leftarrow \mathbf{y}{i+1} \leftarrow \mathbf{y}{i+2}) & \text{if } i < k-1, \end{cases} where k is the total number of vertices in the path. The full reverse vertex PDF follows the same structure as the forward PDF but uses reverse directional and geometry terms. Not given in the sources. Forward Vertex PDFs are part of the theoretical framework for unidirectional sampling in volumetric light transport simulation. name: Direct Lighting with MIS in VolPathIntegrator
head: Direct Lighting with MIS
body: Direct Lighting with MIS in VolPathIntegrator is a method to sample direct illumination in volumetric media by combining unidirectional path sampling and light path sampling using Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS). It solves the high variance problem in spectral volumetric path tracing by allowing the estimator to leverage the strengths of both sampling strategies—phase function sampling for direction and light source sampling for geometry—while correctly accounting for the different PDFs introduced by ratio tracking in participating media. Unlike standard MIS which assumes a single sampling distribution, this method evaluates path PDFs at all wavelengths to enable MIS over wavelengths, significantly reducing color noise and variance compared to unsampled spectral approaches. The method estimates the direct lighting contribution at a path vertex p{n-1} by generating two candidate paths: one via unidirectional sampling and one via light path sampling. It computes the MIS weight for each based on their respective probabilities and combines them. Inputs: Path vertex p{n-1} and its throughput \beta. Scattering coefficient \sigmas(p{n-1}) and null scattering coefficient \sigman(p{n-1}) at the vertex. Majorant scattering coefficient \sigma{maj} (constant or spatially varying upper bound). Phase function p\omega(\omega). Light source geometry and emission Le. Wavelengths \lambda (typically spectral samples). Outputs: Estimated direct lighting contribution L{dir}. Path Vertex: Contains position p, incoming direction \omega{in}, and accumulated throughput \beta. Spectral Coefficients: Arrays or vectors for \sigmas(\lambda), \sigman(\lambda), and \sigma{maj}(\lambda). MIS Weights: Scalar values wu and wl computed via the power heuristic. 1. Initialize Common Path State: For the current path \bar{p}{n-1}, the throughput \beta and the path PDF pu(\bar{p}{n-1}) are identical for both sampling strategies up to this vertex. 2. Unidirectional Path Sampling (pu): a. Sample a direction \omegan from the phase function p\omega(\omegan) at p{n-1}. b. Use delta tracking to find the next real-scattering vertex pn along \omegan. This involves sampling null-scattering events. c. The probability of a path segment from pi to pj with m intermediate null-scattering vertices is: p{null}(pi, pj) = \left( \prod{k=1}^{m} \sigman(p{i+k}) T{maj}(p{i+k-1} \rightarrow p{i+k}) \right) T{maj}(p{i+m} \rightarrow pj) where the acceptance probability for a null scattering event at p{i+k} is: pe(p{i+k}) = \frac{\sigman(p{i+k})}{\sigma{maj}} and the majorant PDF for the distance is: p{maj}(p{i+k-1} \rightarrow p{i+k}) = \sigma{maj} T{maj}(p{i+k-1} \rightarrow p{i+k}) d. The full unidirectional path PDF is: pu(\bar{p}n) = pu(\bar{p}{n-1}) \frac{\sigmas(p{n-1})}{\sigma{maj}} p\omega(\omegan) p{null}(p{n-1}, pn) 3. Light Path Sampling (pl): a. Sample a point on a light source and compute the direction \omega{light} towards p{n-1}. b. Trace a shadow ray from p{n-1} towards the light. c. Use ratio tracking to estimate the transmittance along this segment. The PDF for a path sampled between points pi and pj with m intermediate vertices using ratio tracking is: p{ratio}(pi, pj) = \left( \prod{k=1}^{m} T{maj}(p{i+k-1} \rightarrow p{i+k}) \sigma{maj} \right) T{maj}(p{i+m} \rightarrow pj) d. The full light path PDF is: pl(\bar{p}n) = pu(\bar{p}{n-1}) \frac{\sigmas(p{n-1})}{\sigma{maj}} p{l,\omega}(\omegan) p{ratio}(p{n-1}, pn) where p{l,\omega} is the PDF of the light direction sampling. 4. Spectral Evaluation: The VolPathIntegrator samples both types of paths according to the first wavelength \lambda1 but evaluates the PDFs pu and pl at all wavelengths \lambda to enable MIS over wavelengths. 5. MIS Weighting: Compute weights wu(\bar{p}n) and wl(\bar{p}'n) using the power heuristic (typically \frac{w^2}{wu^2 + wl^2}) based on the evaluated PDFs at each wavelength. 6. Estimator Combination: The final contribution is the sum of the weighted contributions from both strategies: L{dir} = wu(\bar{p}n) \frac{\hat{T}(\bar{p}n) Le(pn \rightarrow p{n-1})}{p{u, \lambda1}(\bar{p}n)} + wl(\bar{p}'n) \frac{\hat{T}(\bar{p}'n) Le(p' \rightarrow p'{n-1})}{p{l, \lambda1}(\bar{p}'n)} where \hat{T} is the estimated transmittance. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def directlightingmis(pnminus1, sigmas, sigman, sigmamaj, phasefunc, lightsampler): """ Computes direct lighting contribution at pnminus1 using MIS. name: Spectral+NEE MIS (Shadow Connection Routine)
head: MIS for chromatic media, Spectral MIS, Spectral Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS), Spectral Multiple Importance Sampling with Next-Event Estimation, Spectral NEE with MIS
body: Spectral+NEE MIS is a shadow connection routine used in volumetric path tracing to estimate direct illumination in chromatic participating media. It reduces variance by combining unidirectional path sampling and next-event estimation (NEE) using Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) across spectral samples. Unlike standard spectral MIS, which can suffer from high variance or color noise in heterogeneous media, this method uses ratio tracking to handle null scattering events, allowing robust connections through dense or thin media while maintaining color fidelity. Inputs: Current path vertex position x and incoming direction \omega. Selected component index \tilde{c} for distance sampling. Current path contribution accumulator f (vector of spectral values). Current path probability density function (pdf) p. Outputs: Updated path contribution f. Updated path pdf p. MIS weight for combining unidirectional and NEE estimators. Spectral Vector: A vector of size n (number of spectral samples) representing radiance or contribution at each wavelength. Extinction Coefficients: \mut^c(x) for each component c \in \{1, \dots, N\} at position x. Null Scattering Coefficients: \mun^c(x) for each component c. Phase Function: \rhom(\omega, x, \omega') for the medium. 1. Sample Light Direction: Sample a direction \omega' toward the light source and compute its pdf p{\omega'}. 2. Update Contributions: Update the path contribution accumulator f by multiplying with the medium phase function value \rhom(\omega, x, \omega'). 3. Initialize PDFs: Initialize the next-event path pdf p{nee} as p \cdot p{\omega'}. Initialize the unidirectional path pdf p{uni} as p \cdot \rhom(\omega, x, \omega'). 4. Ratio Tracking Loop: Begin ratio tracking along the shadow ray in direction \omega'. Sample distance t using the extinction coefficient of the selected component \tilde{c}: t = -\frac{\ln(1-\xi)}{\mut^{\tilde{c}}} where \xi \in [0, 1) is a uniform random number. Intersect the ray at distance t to find point y. If surface hit: If y exists (surface hit), return the average of p{uni} and p{nee} (2N techniques). If no hit: Update contributions f with null-scattering transmittance for all components c: f \leftarrow f \circ \langle Tc^1(t)\mun^1(x), \dots, Tc^N(t)\mun^N(x) \rangle where \circ denotes component-wise multiplication and Tc^k(t) is the transmittance for component k over distance t. Update p{nee} with extinction/transmittance ratios for all components. Update p{uni} with null-scattering ratios for all components. Repeat loop. MIS Weight: The balance heuristic weight for wavelength sample \lambda1 is: w{\lambda1}(x) = \frac{p{\lambda1}(x)}{\sum{i=1}^{n} p{\lambdai}(x)} Estimator: The combined estimator for spectral samples is: \frac{p{\lambda1}(x)}{\frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^{n} p{\lambdai}(x)} \left[ \frac{f{\lambda1}(x)}{p{\lambda1}(x)}, \frac{f{\lambda2}(x)}{p{\lambda1}(x)}, \dots, \frac{f{\lambdan}(x)}{p{\lambda1}(x)} \right] = \frac{\left[ f{\lambda1}(x), f{\lambda2}(x), \dots, f{\lambdan}(x) \right]}{\frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^{n} p{\lambdai}(x)} n: The number of spectral samples. q: The discrete probability of sampling using wavelength \lambda1, uniform at 1/n. High Variance in Heterogeneous Media: Estimating every component separately can lead to color noise, which the MIS combination remedies. Extreme Variance: Sampling distances according to a single component with low extinction can lead to extreme variance if other components have much higher extinction, which ratio tracking mitigates. Surface Hit: If a surface is hit, the routine returns the average of the two path pdfs, effectively combining 2N techniques. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spectralneemisshadowconnection(x, omega, ctilde, f, p, nspectralsamples): """ Perform Spectral+NEE MIS shadow connection. Args: x: Current vertex position. omega: Incoming direction. ctilde: Selected component index for distance sampling. f: Current path contribution (vector of size nspectralsamples). p: Current path pdf. nspectralsamples: Number of spectral samples. Returns: f: Updated path contribution. p: Updated path pdf. weight: MIS weight. """ # 1. Sample light direction omegaprime, pomegaprime = samplelightdir(x) # 2. Update path contributions with phase function rhom = mediumphasefunction(omega, x, omegaprime) f = f rhom # 3. Initialize PDFs pnee = p pomegaprime puni = p rhom # 4. Ratio tracking loop while True: # Sample distance using selected component xi = randomuniform() mutctilde = extinctioncoefficient(x, ctilde) t = -log(1 - xi) / mutctilde # Intersect ray y = intersectray(x, omegaprime, t) # If surface hit, return average of pdfs if y is not None: weight = 0.5 (puni + pnee) return f, p, weight # Update contributions with null-scattering transmittance nullscatteringfactors = [] for c in range(1, nspectralsamples + 1): Tct = transmittance(x, omegaprime, t, c) munc = nullscatteringcoefficient(x, c) nullscatteringfactors.append(Tct munc) f = f nullscatteringfactors # Update pnee with extinction/transmittance ratios pneeratios = [] for c in range(1, nspectralsamples + 1): mutc = extinctioncoefficient(x, c) Tct = transmittance(x, omegaprime, t, c) # Ratio tracking update for NEE pdf ratio = mutc / (mutctilde Tct) pneeratios.append(ratio) pnee = pnee pneeratios # Update puni with null-scattering ratios puniratios = [] for c in range(1, nspectralsamples + 1): munc = nullscatteringcoefficient(x, c) Tct = transmittance(x, omegaprime, t, c) # Ratio tracking update for unidirectional pdf ratio = munc / (mutctilde Tct) puniratios.append(ratio) puni = puni puniratios def samplelightdir(x): """Sample direction toward light source and return pdf.""" # Standard light sampling strategy return (vec3(0.0), 1.0) def mediumphasefunction(omega, x, omegaprime): """Compute medium phase function value.""" # Standard phase function evaluation return 1.0 def extinctioncoefficient(x, c): """Get extinction coefficient for component c at x.""" return 1.0 def nullscatteringcoefficient(x, c): """Get null scattering coefficient for component c at x.""" return 0.0 def transmittance(x, omega, t, c): """Compute transmittance for component c over distance t.""" mut = extinctioncoefficient(x, c) return exp(-mut t) def intersectray(x, omega, t): """Intersect ray at distance t. Returns point or None.""" # Standard ray-scene intersection return None def randomuniform(): """Return uniform random number in 0, 1).""" return 0.5 def log(x): """Natural logarithm.""" import math return math.log(x) def exp(x): """Exponential function.""" import math return math.exp(x) A sibling method that uses spectral MIS with unidirectional path tracing but without the NEE shadow connection routine. It is chosen when NEE is not required or when unidirectional sampling is sufficient. [Spectral MIS with Unidirectional Path Tracing Time Complexity: The ratio tracking loop length varies depending on the medium density and extinction coefficients. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for spectral vectors and extinction/null scattering coefficients for each component. Measured Performance: In a test scene (Fig. 9 right plume), Spectral+NEE MIS achieved RMSE: 0.016 and LTUV: 0.08M lookups, outperforming Spectral MIS (RMSE: 0.029, LTUV: 1.09M). Strengths: Reduces variance significantly in chromatic media and handles both back-lit thin media and side-lit dense media robustly. Limitations: Can be computationally expensive due to the ratio tracking loop and spectral calculations. When to Use: When rendering chromatic volumetric media with complex lighting and where variance reduction is critical. When Not to Use: When computational resources are limited and approximate results are acceptable, or when the medium is non-chromatic. Origin: The method is part of the VolPathIntegrator, which uses multiple importance sampling for direct illumination in volumetric media. History: The specific combination of spectral MIS with NEE and ratio tracking was integrated into null-scattering path integral formulations for light transport to handle heterogeneous media and reduce color noise. Usage: Implemented in the VolPathIntegrator. 14.2 Volume Scattering Integrators, https://pbr-book.org/4ed/LightTransportIIVolumeRendering/VolumeScatteringIntegrators, fetched 2026-10-29 A Null-Scattering Path Integral Formulation of Light Transport, https://www.scribd.com/document/1067625811/A-Null-scattering-Path-Integral-Formulation-of-Light-Transport, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Spectral MIS with Unidirectional Path Tracing
head: Spectral MIS, Unidirectional Spectral MIS
body: Spectral MIS with Unidirectional Path Tracing is a volumetric path tracing method that reduces computational time by sampling a single random color channel (e.g., RGB) of the scatter coefficient at each step instead of using the majorant of the entire spectrum. This approach combines unidirectional path sampling and light path sampling using Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) to estimate direct illumination in participating media. Unlike spectral tracking or delta tracking which use the majorant of the spectrum, this method uses a random channel, resulting in larger sampled distances when the selected channel value is small, leading to fewer steps inside the volume and faster convergence. The method estimates the radiance contribution for each color component c \in \{c1, \dots, cN\} (typically N=3 for RGB) by maintaining per-component path contributions and probability density functions (PDFs). It avoids computing a conservative majorant for all channels simultaneously by selecting one channel \tilde{c} per interaction and weighting the results via MIS. Inputs: Current position x and direction \omega. Spectral extinction \mut(x), scatter \mus(x), absorption \mua(x), and null \mun(x) coefficients for each color component. Maximum density of the volume maxdensity. Inverse maximum density imaxdensity. Emission coefficient Le(x, \omega). Phase function \rhom(\omega). Outputs: Estimated radiance contribution for the path segment. Path Contribution Vector f: A vector of size N storing the accumulated transmittance and event weights for each color component. Initialized to \langle 1, \dots, 1 \rangleN. Path PDF Vector p: A vector of size N storing the accumulated PDFs for each color component. Initialized to \langle 1, \dots, 1 \rangleN. Selected Channel \tilde{c}: An index or identifier for the randomly chosen color component for the current step. maxdensity: The maximum density value in the volume, computed as densityvol->maxvoxel object->densitymult. imaxdensity: The inverse of the maximum density, computed as 1.0f / maxdensity. N: Number of color components (typically 3). 1. Initialize: Set path contributions f \leftarrow \langle 1, \dots, 1 \rangleN and path PDFs p \leftarrow \langle 1, \dots, 1 \rangleN. 2. Select Channel: Select a random color component \tilde{c} from \{c1, \dots, cN\}. 3. Sample Distance: Sample the medium interaction distance t using the extinction coefficient of the selected component \tilde{c}: t = -\frac{\ln(1-\xi)}{\mut^{\tilde{c}}(x)} where \xi \in [0, 1) is a uniform random number. 4. Check Boundary: If t is greater than the maximum distance to the volume edge, exit the loop. 5. Update Position: Move to the new position x \leftarrow x + t\omega. 6. Sample Event: Sample the event type e \in \{a, s, n\} (absorption, scattering, null) using SampleEvent with probabilities normalized by the max density. The probabilities are computed using the sampled channel of \mua, \mus, \mun. Specifically, the probability of event e is proportional to \mue^{\tilde{c}}(x). 7. Update Contributions: Update path contributions f component-wise with transmittance and event coefficient: f \leftarrow f \circ \langle T(t)\mue^{c1}(x), \dots, T(t)\mue^{cN}(x) \rangle where T(t) is the transmittance over distance t. 8. Update PDFs: Update path PDFs p by multiplying with the ratio of the true PDF to the sampled PDF for each component. For component ci, this ratio is \frac{\mut^{ci}(x)}{\mut^{\tilde{c}}(x)}T(t). 9. Handle Event: If e = a (absorption): Update f with emission Le(x, -\omega) and return the average of f across all N components using the balance heuristic. If e = s (scattering): Sample incoming direction \omega' from the phase function \rhom(\omega) and continue the path walk. If e = n (null): Continue the path walk. 10. Return: Return the average of the path contributions f across all N components using the balance heuristic. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spectralmisunidirectional(x, omega, maxdensity, imaxdensity, N, mut, mua, mus, mun, Le, rhom, maxdistancetoedge): # Initialize per-component path contributions and PDFs f = [1.0] N p = [1.0] N # Select a random color component index ctilde = random.randint(0, N - 1) while True: # Sample medium interaction distance using the selected channel's extinction xi = random.random() t = -math.log(1 - xi) / mutctilde # Check if distance exceeds volume boundary if t > maxdistancetoedge(x, omega): break # Update position x = x + t omega # Sample event type (absorption, scattering, null) # Probabilities proportional to the sampled channel's coefficients probs = mua[ctilde, musctilde, munctilde] e = sampleevent(probs) # Compute transmittance over distance t Tt = math.exp(-mutctilde t) # Update path contributions component-wise for i in range(N): coeff = muai if e == EVENTABSORB else (musi if e == EVENTSCATTER else muni) f[i] = Tt coeff # Update path PDFs by ratio of true PDF to sampled PDF for i in range(N): p[i] = (muti / mutctilde) Tt # Handle event if e == EVENTABSORB: # Add emission contribution for i in range(N): f[i] = Le(x, -omega) # Return average using balance heuristic return sum(f) / N elif e == EVENTSCATTER: # Sample phase function omega = samplephasefunction(rhom, omega) # Continue path walk continue elif e == EVENTNULL: # Continue path walk continue # If loop exits without absorption/scattering, return accumulated contribution return sum(f) / N Convergence/Accuracy: The method has problems with convergence or accuracy in certain scenarios, leading the authors to decide to use the mean of the spectrum values instead of the random channel selection, although the random channel method remains faster than precedent algorithms. Precision: The use of a random channel can lead to higher variance if the selected channel has a very low coefficient, resulting in large steps and potentially missing important interactions. Boundaries: The method must correctly handle volume boundaries to avoid sampling distances that exceed the volume extent. Time Complexity: The method reduces computational time compared to spectral tracking and delta tracking by sampling a single random channel, leading to larger sampled distances and fewer steps inside the volume. Memory Complexity: Requires storing per-component path contributions and PDFs, which is O(N) where N is the number of color components. Measured Performance: In a 1D medium experiment, Spectral MIS achieved a reduction of color noise comparable to spectral tracking but at a lower cost (fewer medium lookups). In the left plume of Fig. 9 (high density, low albedo green channel), Spectral MIS achieved RMSE: 0.047 and LTUV: 4.12M lookups, outperforming Spectral tracking (RMSE: 0.055, LTUV: 5.82M) and Independent tracking (RMSE: 0.077, LTUV: 11.5M). In the right plume of Fig. 9 (similar spectral variation), Spectral MIS achieved RMSE: 0.029 and LTUV: 1.09M lookups, outperforming Spectral tracking (RMSE: 0.035, LTUV: 1.51M). In the malachite material (Fig. 10), Spectral MIS achieved RMSE: 0.032 and LTUV: 0.56M lookups, outperforming Spectral tracking (RMSE: 0.042, LTUV: 2.85M). Strengths: Faster convergence than spectral tracking and delta tracking in heterogeneous volumes with spectrally varying coefficients. Limitations: Potential convergence issues in certain scenarios, requiring the use of mean spectrum values for stability. Origin: The method was proposed by Miller et al.. History: It is an improvement over spectral tracking and delta tracking, which use the majorant of the spectrum. Usage: Used in volumetric path tracing for rendering participating media with spectrally varying coefficients. An extension that combines Spectral MIS with Next-Event Estimation (NEE) using a shadow connection routine to further reduce variance in dense media. Choose this when high accuracy is needed in dense volumes with complex lighting. name: Unknown Distance PDF and MIS
head: Distance PDF Cancellation for MIS
body: A technique to enable Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) for path-construction strategies, such as Next Event Estimation (NEE) or bidirectional methods, in rejection-based volumetric trackers where the free-path sample probability density function (PDF) cannot be evaluated exactly. It solves the problem of combining strategies by ensuring the unknown distance PDFs cancel out in the MIS weight calculation, allowing the weight to be computed based solely on directional PDFs. This sets it apart from general MIS applications by relying on the structural identity of the sampling tracker rather than explicit PDF evaluation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two path-construction strategies (e.g., free-path sampling and transmittance sampling/NEE) using the same unbiased rejection-based tracker. Output: MIS balance-heuristic weight for combining the strategies. Data Structures: Directional PDFs: p\Omega(\omega) for the sampled directions. Steps: 1. Ensure Tracker Identity: Use the exact same unbiased rejection-based tracker implementation for both the free-path sampling (generating the path segment) and the transmittance sampling (evaluating the contribution, e.g., in NEE). This ensures the distance PDFs are identical. 2. Compute Directional PDFs: Evaluate the directional PDFs, p{\Omega,1}(\omega1) and p{\Omega,2}(\omega2), for the directions sampled by each strategy. 3. Calculate MIS Weight: Compute the balance-heuristic weight using only the directional PDFs, as the distance PDFs have cancelled out. w1 = \frac{p{\Omega,1}(\omega1)}{p{\Omega,1}(\omega1) + p{\Omega,2}(\omega2)} The power heuristic is also valid under these conditions. 4. Apply Weight: Multiply the contribution of the path segment by the computed weight w1 (or w2 = 1 - w1). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeunknowndistancemisweight(pdir1, pdir2): """ Computes MIS weight when distance PDFs are unknown but identical. Uses the balance heuristic based on directional PDFs. """ total = pdir1 + pdir2 if total == 0.0: return 0.5 return pdir1 / total Parameters: Tracker Consistency: The same tracker must be used for both sampling passes. Heuristic Type: Balance or Power heuristic. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Different Trackers: If different trackers are used for free-path and transmittance sampling, the distance PDFs will not cancel, and this method fails. Other Heuristics: The cancellation property holds for balance and power heuristics but does not generalize to other MIS heuristics. Spectral Tracking: The distance PDFs are not wavelength-dependent in the spectral tracker, so the cancellation holds even for spectral tracking. Approximation: If cancellation conditions are not met, a near-optimal weight can be computed using a deterministic approximation of the PDF, e.g., via an extra ray-marching pass. Extends MIS to handle more complex sampling scenarios. Choose when standard MIS is insufficient for complex path constructions. Uses Multiple Weighted Importance Sampling for multi-view consistency. Choose when rendering from multiple viewpoints. A general technique for weighting samples. Choose when unbiasedness is not required or for variance reduction in specific contexts. Applies MIS to direct lighting in volumetric path tracing. Choose for combining direct lighting strategies. Strengths: Enables MIS in rejection-based trackers where distance PDFs are unknown. Works for spectral tracking. Limitations: Requires identical trackers for all strategies. Only works for balance/power heuristics. Does not generalize to other heuristics or different trackers. When to Use: When using rejection-based trackers and combining strategies like NEE where distance PDFs are unknown but can be made identical. When Not to Use: When different trackers are necessary for different strategies, or when using MIS heuristics other than balance/power. Developed for use in rejection-based trackers where the free-path sample PDF cannot be evaluated exactly. It allows for the combination of multiple path-construction strategies using MIS, such as in next-event estimation (NEE) or bidirectional techniques. The method is particularly useful for spectral tracking because the distance PDFs are not wavelength-dependent. name: Unified Points, Beams, and Paths (UPBP)
body: Unified Points, Beams, and Paths (UPBP) is a combined rendering algorithm that fuses volumetric density estimation estimators (Point-Point, Point-Beam, Beam-Beam) with unbiased bidirectional path tracing (BPT) using Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS). It solves the problem of efficiently simulating light transport in diverse participating media by automatically selecting the most suitable representation—points for high-order scattering, beams for low-order scattering, and paths for volume effects with specular surfaces—thereby mitigating the weaknesses of individual estimators. Unlike its siblings, UPBP subsumes the methods of Georgiev et al. [2012] and Hachisuka et al. [2012] by treating them as special cases within a unified MIS framework. UPBP operates in two distinct stages per iteration: a light subpath generation stage and a camera subpath evaluation stage. Inputs: Scene geometry, participating media properties (extinction \sigmat, scattering \sigmas, phase function p), light sources, camera parameters, maximum path length k, and number of light subpaths nv for each technique v. Outputs: Radiance estimate for each pixel. The algorithm maintains specific data structures to accelerate density estimation queries during the camera stage: 1. Hashed Grids: Separate hashed grids for surface vertices and medium vertices to support Point-Point (P-P) estimators. 2. Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH): Built over medium vertices to support Point-Beam (P-B) estimators. 3. Uniform Grid: Organizes photon beams to support Beam-Beam (B-B) estimators. This was found faster than a BVH for beam queries, though query performance is suboptimal. The implementation uses a subset of estimators to balance bias and computational cost: P-P3D: Point-Point 3D for medium vertices. P-B2D: Point-Beam 2D for medium vertices (specifically using short photon beams and long query beams, denoted P-Bl2D in some contexts, but formally P-B2D in the estimator family). B-B1D: Beam-Beam 1D (specifically short-beam variant Bs-Bl1D) for medium segments. P-P2D: Point-Point 2D for surface vertices. BPT: Bidirectional Path Tracing for unbiased connections. Long-beam variants and P-B3D are excluded due to high construction/query costs or similar PDFs to other estimators. Stage 1: Light Subpath Generation and Storage 1. Generate n{BPT} light subpaths \bar{\bf y}. 2. For each light subpath, store vertices on surfaces and vertices/beams in media. 3. Build the hashed grids over surface and medium vertices. 4. Build the BVH over medium vertices. 5. Organize photon beams in a uniform grid. Stage 2: Camera Subpath Evaluation 1. For each pixel, generate one camera subpath \bar{\bf z}. 2. Stochastically terminate light and camera subpaths up to the user-defined maximum path length k. 3. For each vertex s on the camera subpath (where 0 \le s \le k+1 for BPT, 2 \le s \le k for PDE): BPT Evaluation: Connect the camera vertex to all vertices of a randomly chosen stored light subpath to evaluate the BPT estimator \langle I \rangle{BPT,s}. PDE Evaluation: Query the data structures for nearby beams/points to evaluate PDE estimators: If the vertex is on a surface, evaluate P-P2D \langle I \rangle{P-P2D,s}. If the vertex is in the medium, evaluate P-P3D \langle I \rangle{P-P3D,s}. 4. For each segment (beam) on the camera subpath passing through a medium: Evaluate P-B2D \langle I \rangle{P-B2D,s} and B-B1D \langle I \rangle{B-B1D,s} estimators by querying the BVH and uniform grid respectively. 5. Compute the MIS weight w{v,s,t}(\bar{\bf x}) for each technique v and path configuration (s,t). 6. Accumulate the weighted contributions to the pixel value. The total radiance estimate is the sum of contributions from all techniques v \in \{BPT, B-B1D, P-B2D, P-P3D, P-P2D\}: \langle I \rangle{UPBP} = \sum{v} \frac{1}{nv} \sum{i=1}^{nv} \sum{s} w{v,s,t}(\bar{\bf x}i) \langle I \rangle{v,s}(\bar{\bf x}i) Where: nv is the number of light subpaths for technique v. s is the number of vertices on the light subpath. t is the number of vertices on the camera subpath. For BPT: t = k + 1 - s. For PDE (volumetric estimators): t = k + 2 - s. Note that PDE techniques require at least two vertices (2 \le s \le k) as they cannot be evaluated on light sources or camera lenses. \langle I \rangle{v,s} is the radiance estimate from technique v at light subpath vertex s. The MIS weight uses the extended balance heuristic: w{v,s,t}(\bar{\bf x}) = \frac{nv p{v,s}(\bar{\bf x})}{gv(\bar{\bf x})} gv(\bar{\bf x}) = \sum{j=0}^{k+1} n{BPT} p{BPT,j}(\bar{\bf x}) + \sum{j=2}^k n{B-B1D} p{B-B1D,j}(\bar{\bf x}) + n{P-B2D} p{P-B2D,j}(\bar{\bf x}) + \sum{j=2}^k n{P-P3D} p{P-P3D,j}(\bar{\bf x}) + n{P-P2D} p{P-P2D,j}(\bar{\bf x}) Where p{v,s}(\bar{\bf x}) is the probability density function of generating the path configuration with technique v and light subpath length s. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class HashedGrid: def init(self): self.cells = {} def insert(self, vertex): self.cells[hash(vertex.position)].append(vertex) def query(self, point, radius): return [v for v in self.cells[hash(point)] if dist(v.position, point) < radius] class BVH: def init(self): self.root = None def insert(self, vertex): self.root = buildbvh([vertex]) # Standard BVH construction def query(self, ray, maxdepth): return traversebvh(self.root, ray, maxdepth) # Standard ray-BVH traversal class UniformGrid: def init(self, cellsize): self.cellsize = cellsize; self.cells = {} def insert(self, beam): self.cells[hash(beam.center)].append(beam) def query(self, ray, radius): return [b for b in self.cells[hash(ray.origin)] if dist(b.center, ray.origin) < radius] def generatelightsubpath(scene, maxk): # Generates light subpath ybar, stores vertices and beams vertices, beams = [], [] origin = samplelightsource(scene) for in range(maxk): vertices.append(Vertex(origin, issurface=issurface(origin))) if not vertices[-1].issurface: nextpos = sampleinteraction(origin, scene.extinction) beams.append(Beam(vertices[-1].position, nextpos)) origin = nextpos else: break return vertices, beams def generatecamerasubpath(camera, maxk): # Generates camera subpath zbar per pixel vertices, beams = [], [] origin = samplecamerarays(camera) for in range(maxk): vertices.append(Vertex(origin, issurface=issurface(origin))) if not vertices[-1].issurface: nextpos = sampleinteraction(origin, scene.extinction) beams.append(Beam(vertices[-1].position, nextpos)) origin = nextpos else: break return vertices, beams def computepdfbpt(s, t, path): return standardbptpdf(s, t, path) # Computes BPT PDF def computepdfbb1d(s, t, path): return standardbb1dpdf(s, t, path) # Computes B-B1D PDF def computepdfpb2d(s, t, path): return standardpb2dpdf(s, t, path) # Computes P-B2D PDF def computepdfpp3d(s, t, path): return standardpp3dpdf(s, t, path) # Computes P-P3D PDF def computepdfpp2d(s, t, path): return standardpp2dpdf(s, t, path) # Computes P-P2D PDF def evaluatebpt(vertex, lightsubpath): return connectcameratolight(vertex, lightsubpath) # Connects camera vertex to light subpath vertices def evaluatepp2d(vertex, grid): return densityestimate(vertex, grid.query(vertex.position, radius=0.0)) # Queries surface grid for P-P2D def evaluatepp3d(vertex, grid): return densityestimate(vertex, grid.query(vertex.position, radius=0.0)) # Queries medium grid for P-P3D def evaluatepb2d(beam, mediumgrid, bvh): return densityestimate(beam, mediumgrid.query(beam.origin, radius=0.0)) # Queries for P-B2D def evaluatebb1d(beam, beamgrid): return densityestimate(beam, beamgrid.query(beam.origin, radius=0.0)) # Queries for B-B1D def upbprender(scene, camera, maxk, nv): # Initialize data structures surfacegrid = HashedGrid() mediumgrid = HashedGrid() mediumbvh = BVH() beamgrid = UniformGrid(cellsize=0.1) # Stage 1: Light Subpath Generation lightsubpaths = [] for in range(nv['BPT']): ybar = generatelightsubpath(scene, maxk) for vertex in ybar[0]: if vertex.issurface: surfacegrid.insert(vertex) else: mediumgrid.insert(vertex); mediumbvh.insert(vertex) for beam in ybar[1]: beamgrid.insert(beam) lightsubpaths.append(ybar) # Stage 2: Camera Subpath Evaluation for pixel in camera.raster: pixelvalue = 0.0 zbar = generatecamerasubpath(camera, maxk) # Evaluate BPT and PDE estimators at vertices for s, vertex in enumerate(zbar[0]): # BPT: t = k + 1 - s; PDE: t = k + 2 - s tbpt = maxk + 1 - s tpde = maxk + 2 - s # BPT Estimator ybar = lightsubpaths[hash(pixel) % len(lightsubpaths)] bptcontrib = evaluatebpt(vertex, ybar) bptweight = (nv['BPT'] computepdfbpt(s, tbpt, zbar)) / computedenominator(s, maxk, nv) pixelvalue += bptweight bptcontrib # PDE Estimators (if not on light/camera lens) if 2 <= s <= maxk: if vertex.issurface: pp2dcontrib = evaluatepp2d(vertex, surfacegrid) pp2dweight = (nv['P-P2D'] computepdfpp2d(s, tpde, zbar)) / computedenominator(s, maxk, nv) pixelvalue += pp2dweight pp2dcontrib else: pp3dcontrib = evaluatepp3d(vertex, mediumgrid) pp3dweight = (nv['P-P3D'] computepdfpp3d(s, tpde, zbar)) / computedenominator(s, maxk, nv) pixelvalue += pp3dweight pp3dcontrib # Evaluate PDE estimators on beams (segments) for s, beam in enumerate(zbar[1]): tpde = maxk + 2 - s pb2dcontrib = evaluatepb2d(beam, mediumgrid, mediumbvh) pb2dweight = (nv['P-B2D'] computepdfpb2d(s, tpde, zbar)) / computedenominator(s, maxk, nv) pixelvalue += pb2dweight pb2dcontrib bb1dcontrib = evaluatebb1d(beam, beamgrid) bb1dweight = (nv['B-B1D'] computepdfbb1d(s, tpde, zbar)) / computedenominator(s, maxk, nv) pixelvalue += bb1dweight bb1dcontrib pixel.value = pixelvalue def computedenominator(s, maxk, nv): # Computes gv(x) from the extended balance heuristic denom = 0.0 for j in range(0, maxk + 2): denom += nv['BPT'] computepdfbpt(j, maxk + 1 - j, None) for j in range(2, maxk + 1): denom += nv['B-B1D'] computepdfbb1d(j, maxk + 2 - j, None) denom += nv['P-B2D'] computepdfpb2d(j, maxk + 2 - j, None) denom += nv['P-P3D'] computepdfpp3d(j, maxk + 2 - j, None) denom += nv['P-P2D'] computepdfpp2d(j, maxk + 2 - j, None) return denom Maximum Path Length (k): User-defined limit for stochastic termination of light and camera subpaths. Number of Light Subpaths (nv): Number of light subpaths generated for each technique v. Representation Choice: Photons for high-order scattering, beams for low-order scattering, paths for volume effects with specular surfaces. PDE Evaluation Constraints: PDE techniques cannot be evaluated on a light source or camera lens, requiring subpaths to have at least two vertices (2 \le s \le k). Beam Query Performance: The uniform grid for photon beams is faster to build than a BVH but has suboptimal query performance. Long Beams: Long photon beams have high construction and query costs, which are rarely compensated by variance reduction; thus, short photon beams are preferred. A full GPU implementation leveraging NVIDIA RTX hardware for path generation and accelerated data structures (BVH) for density estimation, achieving significant speedups over CPU baselines by adapting Point-Point and Beam-Beam estimators to ray-tracing acceleration structures. Time Complexity: Dominated by the generation of light subpaths and the construction of acceleration structures (hashed grids, BVH, uniform grid) in Stage 1, and the evaluation of multiple estimators per camera vertex/segment in Stage 2. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of stored light subpath vertices and beams, as well as the size of the acceleration structures. Strengths: Automatically selects the best estimator for the scene (points for high-order, beams for low-order, paths for specular volumes), subsuming previous methods like VCM and Photon Mapping. Limitations: High computational cost per pixel due to the evaluation of multiple estimators and the overhead of managing multiple data structures. Query performance for beam-based estimators can be suboptimal. When to Use: Scenes with diverse participating media where no single estimator (pure BPT, pure Photon Mapping, or pure Beam Tracing) is efficient across the entire scene. When Not to Use: Simple scenes where a single estimator suffices, or when memory is severely constrained due to the storage of multiple data structures. UPBP was introduced by Křivánek et al. in 2014. It builds on the observation that different representations (points, beams, paths) are suitable for different types of light transport in participating media. The method unifies Bidirectional Path Tracing (BPT) with Volumetric Density Estimation (VDE) estimators (P-P, P-B, B-B) using Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS). It subsumes the methods of Georgiev et al. [2012] and Hachisuka et al. [2012].
