name: GPU-accelerated UPBP with RTX BVH
head: Robust Volumetric Light Transport Simulation GPU, UPBP GPU implementation
body: This method is a full GPU implementation of the Unified Points, Beams, and Paths (UPBP) algorithm that leverages NVIDIA RTX hardware for light and camera path generation, combined with new accelerated data structures and a constant-time Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) weight algorithm. It solves the performance bottleneck of CPU-based UPBP implementations by offloading path tracing and density estimation queries to the GPU, achieving significant speedups over single-threaded and multi-threaded CPU baselines. Unlike its CPU sibling Unified Points, Beams, and Paths (UPBP), this implementation specifically adapts the Point-Point and Beam-Beam estimators to work with ray-tracing acceleration structures rather than traditional hash grids or grids, using small-extent rays for point queries and AABBs for sphere containment checks. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Scene geometry, participating media properties (phase function, extinction coefficient), light source definitions, camera parameters, and UPBP configuration parameters (kernel widths, subpath lengths). Outputs: Rendered image with unbiased volumetric lighting estimates. Data Structures: The implementation utilizes specific data structures for different estimators, stored on the GPU: 1. Point-Point 3D (P-P3D): Stores an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) representing a sphere centered on each photon point, with a radius equal to the kernel width. If a camera point lies inside this sphere, the distance between the points is less than or equal to the radius. 2. Beam-Beam (B-B) and Point-Beam (P-B): Uses a custom GPU data structure that spends more time building than an LBVH but less time querying, resulting in better overall performance for these estimators. 3. Hash Grids: A GPU implementation of hash grids is provided for comparison, particularly for P-P3D, but exhibits poor performance in specific scenarios. Algorithm Steps: 1. Light Subpath Generation: Generate light subpaths on the GPU using RTX hardware acceleration. Cache data at light vertices required for Photon Density Estimation (PDE) or Beam-Photon Transport (BTP). 2. Camera Subpath Generation: Generate camera subpaths on the GPU. This kernel accounts for most of the GPU running time, as it generates subpaths, queries the data structures, and evaluates the estimators. 3. Point Query Adaptation: For Point-Point estimators, adapt the point query to the ray-tracing framework by creating a ray with a very small extent where the origin is the point and an arbitrary direction is chosen. 4. Density Estimation Query: For P-P3D, check if the camera point is inside the AABB of the photon's sphere. For B-B and P-B, query the custom data structure to find relevant beams or points. 5. MIS Weight Evaluation: Compute the MIS weight in constant time by splitting the path weight into three independent parts: one for the light subpath, one for the camera subpath, and a quantity depending on both subpath ends. The subpath weight is formulated as a recursive quantity evaluated as the subpath is traced. 6. Path Weight Computation: Upon forming a full path by combining two subpaths, compute the weight only from data cached at the light and camera vertices that are merged with PDE or connected with BTP. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gpuupbpkernel(camera, lightsubpaths, datastructures): # 1. Generate camera subpath using RTX hardware camerasubpath = tracecamerasubpathrtx(camera) # Cache vertex data for PDE/BTP cameravertexdata = cachecameravertices(camerasubpath) # 2. Iterate over light subpaths to form full paths for lightsubpath in lightsubpaths: # 3. Combine subpaths fullpath = mergesubpaths(lightsubpath, camerasubpath) # 4. Evaluate estimators based on path type estimator = determineestimatortype(fullpath) density = 0.0 if estimator == "P-P3D": # Point query adaptation: small extent ray querypoint = getcameraendpoint(fullpath) queryray = createsmallextentray(querypoint, arbitrarydirection()) # Query AABB structure photons = queryaabbstructure(datastructures.pp3d, queryray) for photon in photons: density += evaluatekernel(querypoint, photon.position, photon.kernelwidth) elif estimator == "B-B1D": # Query custom data structure beams = querybeamstructure(datastructures.bb, fullpath) density = evaluatebeambeamestimator(fullpath, beams) else: # Other estimators (P-B, B-P, etc.) follow similar query and weight evaluation steps # not detailed in the sources. pass # 5. MIS weight evaluation (constant time) misweight = computemisweight( lightsubpath.subpathweight, cameravertexdata.subpathweight, fullpath.endpoints) # 6. Final contribution from cached vertex data contribution = density misweight fullpath.pathweight accumulatepixel(contribution) def createsmallextentray(point, direction): origin = point tmax = 1e-6 return {"origin": origin, "direction": direction, "tmax": tmax} def arbitrarydirection(): return normalize(randomvector()) def computemisweight(lightw, cameraw, endpoints): # Split into three parts: light subpath, camera subpath, both ends wboth = evaluateendpointinteraction(endpoints) total = lightw + cameraw + wboth return lightw / total if total > 0 else 0.0 def tracecamerasubpathrtx(camera): # Standard RTX camera path generation routine pass def cachecameravertices(subpath): # Extract and store vertex data for PDE/BTP merging pass def mergesubpaths(light, camera): # Combine light and camera subpaths into a full path pass def determineestimatortype(path): # Classify path based on endpoint types (P, B, or V) pass def getcameraendpoint(path): # Return the camera-side endpoint of the path pass def queryaabbstructure(structure, ray): # Ray-AABB intersection test returning contained photons pass def querybeamstructure(structure, path): # Query custom data structure for relevant beams pass def evaluatebeambeamestimator(path, beams): # Compute beam-beam density estimate pass def evaluatekernel(point, photonpos, kernelwidth): # Evaluate scattering kernel at distance pass def accumulatepixel(contribution): # Add contribution to the output image buffer pass Parameters: Hardware: NVIDIA RTX 2070 GPU, AMD Ryzen 5 2600 CPU (6 cores, 3.4 GHz), 16 GB RAM. Subpath Lengths: Equal number of light and camera subpaths in experiments. Kernel Widths: Determined by scene parameters (see supplementary materials in source). Iterations: Performance measured over 120 iterations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Small Light Sources: Hash grids perform notoriously poorly on scenes with small light sources concentrated in a small part of the scene, causing non-uniform distribution of light samples. This significantly affects P-P3D estimators in scenes like San Miguel and Sun Temple. Point Query in Ray Tracing: Point queries must be adapted to ray queries using small-extent rays, which may introduce precision issues if not handled carefully. Data Structure Construction: The new data structures spend more time building than LBVH, which may impact performance in dynamic scenes or if frequent rebuilds are required. Time and Memory Complexity: Speedup: The GPU implementation achieves a speedup of 21 to 69 times over the single-threaded SmallUPBP and 4 to 15 times over the multi-threaded version. Data Structure Performance: Beam-Beam (B-B1D): The new GPU data structure spends more time building than LBVH but less time querying, resulting in better overall performance. Point-Point 3D (P-P3D): Hash grids perform best on most scenes, but fail on scenes with small, concentrated light sources (San Miguel, Sun Temple). Point-Point 2D (P-P2D): The new data structure has the lowest query time but highest construction time, with no clear winner among data structures. Measured Performance: Baseline CPU Times (SmallUPBP): Bathroom: ST 134.01s, MT 28.46s Bistro: ST 127.22s, MT 18.28s Mirror Balls: ST 58.33s, MT 9.97s San Miguel: ST 115.06s, MT 26.84s Still Life: ST 50.72s, MT 7.86s Sun Temple: ST 419.78s, MT 89.00s GPU Data Structure Times (ms, 20 iterations): B-B1D (San Miguel): Grid (CPU) Build 36, Query 491; Ours (GPU) Build 20, Query 2; Hash Grid (GPU) Build 8, Query 625; LBVH (GPU) Build 10, Query 52. P-P2D (Bathroom): Hash Grid (CPU) Build 424, Query 28646; Ours (GPU) Build 415, Query 171; Hash Grid (GPU) Build 52, Query 1946; LBVH (GPU) Build 88, Query 833. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significant performance improvement over CPU implementations; efficient constant-time MIS weight evaluation; effective use of RTX hardware for path generation; robust data structures for beam-based estimators. Limitations: Poor performance of hash grids for P-P3D in scenes with small light sources; higher construction time for the new data structures compared to LBVH; most GPU time spent in the camera kernel. When to Use: Use when high-performance volumetric rendering is required and NVIDIA RTX hardware is available. Use for scenes with sparse and dense media where beam-based estimators are beneficial. Avoid hash grids for P-P3D in scenes with small, concentrated light sources. When Not to Use: Avoid if the scene has small, concentrated light sources and P-P3D is the primary estimator, as hash grids will perform poorly. Avoid if frequent data structure rebuilds are required, due to higher construction times. The method originates from the paper "Efficient Hardware Acceleration of Robust Volumetric Light Transport Simulation". It builds on the UPBP algorithm Unified Points, Beams, and Paths (UPBP) and the CPU-based SmallUPBP implementation. The work adapts UPBP for GPU execution, leveraging NVIDIA RTX hardware for path generation and introducing new data structures and MIS weight algorithms to optimize performance. The implementation is publicly available. Efficient Hardware Acceleration of Robust Volumetric Light Transport Simulation, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14802, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Dwivedi Sampling
head: Biasing Random Walk
body: Dwivedi Sampling is a variance reduction technique for Monte Carlo light transport in participating media that biases the random walk to exit the medium as quickly as possible. It operates on the principle that paths near the boundary contribute more to the final image than those deep within the volume, particularly in high-scattering scenarios. Unlike uniform distance sampling, it crudely approximates the local geometry as a slab to guide scattering toward boundaries, reducing the number of paths lost inside opaque or highly scattering objects. Inputs: Current vertex position \mathbf{x} and direction \omegai. Local extinction coefficient \sigmat(\mathbf{x}), scattering coefficient \sigmas(\mathbf{x}), and absorption coefficient \sigmaa(\mathbf{x}). Phase function p(\omegai, \omegao). Geometric boundary query function. Outputs: Next vertex position \mathbf{x}' and direction \omegao. Importance weight w for path throughput correction. Data Structures: Slab Model: A local geometric approximation defined by the current vertex \mathbf{x}, the boundary intersection point \mathbf{x}{out}, and the thickness T = \|\mathbf{x}{out} - \mathbf{x}\| along the scattering direction. Steps: 1. Thickness Estimation: Cast a probe ray from \mathbf{x} in direction \omegai to intersect the medium boundary, yielding the local slab thickness T. 2. Slab Approximation: Approximate the local volume as a homogeneous slab of thickness T with constant coefficients \sigmat, \sigmas, \sigmaa. 3. Analytic Light Field Computation: Compute an analytic approximation of the light field through the slab to derive a biased probability density function (PDF) that favors shorter distances leading to boundary exit. 4. Biased Sampling: Sample the distance to the next interaction s from the slab-derived biased PDF. 5. Weight Correction: Calculate the importance weight to correct for the biased sampling distribution. 6. Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS): Combine the Dwivedi sampling strategy with classical distance and direction sampling methods, applying modified heuristic weights to balance their contributions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def dwivedisampling(x, omega, sigmat, sigmas, sigmaa, phasefunc, geometry): # 1. Thickness Estimation: cast probe ray to boundary T = geometry.rayintersect(x, omega) if T is None: # Sources do not specify fallback behavior; standard exponential sampling assumed s = -math.log(1.0 - random.uniform(0, 1)) / sigmat return x + s omega, omega, 1.0 # 2 & 3. Slab Approximation & Analytic Light Field # Sources state the method computes an analytic approximation of the light field # to derive a biased PDF, but do not provide the exact formula # We approximate pbiased(s) as a truncated exponential over [0, T] pbiasednorm = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigmat T) pbiasedval = sigmat math.exp(-sigmat s) / pbiasednorm # 4. Biased Sampling: sample distance s from biased PDF u = random.uniform(0, 1) s = -math.log(1.0 - u pbiasednorm) / sigmat # 5. Weight Correction: ratio of true PDF to biased PDF ptrue = sigmat math.exp(-sigmat s) w = ptrue / pbiasedval if pbiasedval > 1e-8 else 0.0 # 6. MIS: combine with classical sampling # Sources mention mixing with classical distance/direction sampling using # modified heuristic weights from [Kd14], but do not give the exact formula misweight = w # Heuristic weighting applied externally per xnext = x + s omega omeganext = omega # Phase function sampling omitted per return xnext, omeganext, misweight Parameters: Slab Thickness T: Determined dynamically per vertex via probe ray. MIS Heuristic Weights: Modified from [Kd14] to distinguish between distance and direction sampling contributions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Thin Geometries: The method is unsuitable for thin geometries (such as ears) with strong backlighting, as the slab approximation fails to capture complex light transport in such cases. Heterogeneous Media: The analytic slab solution assumes homogeneous coefficients. In heterogeneous media, the local approximation may introduce bias if coefficients vary significantly over thickness T. A variant that addresses Dwivedi Sampling's limitations in thin geometries by incorporating geometric characteristics to guide scattering away from the object boundary. It proposes two methods: Closest Points Sampling, which searches for the closest point to the boundary at every scattering vertex to increase escape chances in thin structures, and Incident Illumination Sampling, which chooses light vertices proportional to their emission using importance sampling to improve variance in backlit cases. This variant is only suitable for high-order scattering and isotropic participating media. A future work technique where the probabilities of absorption (Pa), scattering (Ps), and normal direction (Pn) in the tracker are biased based on scene information, such as light distribution. This involves increasing absorption rates in emissive parts or scattering more in brightly lit regions to reduce variance. It builds on historical biasing techniques by Spanier and Gelbard (1969) and Steen (1966), and relates to advanced zero-variance schemes proposed by Dwivedi (1982). Variance Reduction: Leads to significantly lower variance in high-scattering and isotropic participating media by reducing the number of paths that get "lost" deep within the volume. Computational Cost: Requires additional geometric queries (probe rays) and analytic computations for the slab model, increasing per-sample cost compared to standard distance sampling. Limitations: Not suitable for thin geometries with strong backlighting. Limited to high-order scattering and isotropic media in its basic form. Implementation Complexity: Moderate. Requires integrating probe ray queries and MIS frameworks. Dwivedi Sampling originates from Dwivedi (1982), who proposed advanced zero-variance schemes for radiation transport. The method was later adapted for computer graphics to improve convergence in subsurface scattering and participating media rendering. It is cited in surveys on rendering homogeneous participating media and in practical implementations of path-traced subsurface scattering models. The technique is part of a broader history of biasing random walks in radiation transport, with roots in nuclear engineering literature (Spanier and Gelbard, 1969; Steen, 1966). name: Optimized Monte Carlo Integrator
head: Cached Monte Carlo Integration, Optimized Monte Carlo Integration, Variable Caching Integrator
body: The Optimized Monte Carlo Integrator is a method for computing radiance scattered inside a homogeneous, box-shaped participating medium from a collimated light source towards the camera. It solves the problem of redundant geometric traversal in single-scattering estimation by caching segment properties and using importance sampling proportional to the geometry-dependent transmittance. It sets itself apart from standard ray marching by pre-computing a cumulative distribution histogram of trapezoidal segments to select interaction points directly, and from Delta Tracking by exploiting the specific convex geometry of a box to allow analytic integration of unoccluded paths. Inputs: Camera ray origin po and direction \omegao. Light direction \omegai (collimated). Medium extinction coefficient \sigmat, scattering coefficient \sigmas, and phase function f(\omegai, \omegao). Box geometry defined by entry and exit points for light and camera rays. Number of samples N{sample}. Outputs: Estimated radiance L. Data Structures: Segment Cache Matrix K: A matrix where each row s corresponds to a trapezoidal segment formed by connecting light and camera ray intersections with the box boundaries. Fields: K{s,1}: Upper bound integral part, 1 - Eu. K{s,2}: Slope, \sigmat c (where c is a constant related to the geometry). K{s,3}: Size of segment along camera ray, t{C,B} - t{C,S}. K{s,4}: Starting position along camera ray, t{C,S}. Cumulative Histogram H: Array of size N{seg} (number of segments). Multiplicative Weights D: Array of size N{seg}. Summands M: Array of size N{seg}. Steps: 1. Geometry Traversal and Caching: Traverse the edges of the box to identify trapezoidal segments connecting the incident light exit points and outgoing camera exit points. For each segment s: Compute the transmittance Ts for the segment. Compute total transmittance T{total} = \sum Ts. Cache segment parameters into Ks: K{s,1} = 1 - Eu K{s,2} = \sigmat c K{s,3} = t{C,B} - t{C,S} K{s,4} = t{C,S} 2. Build Cumulative Distribution: Compute selection probability for segment k: Gk = \frac{Tk}{T{total}} Compute multiplicative weight: Dk = \frac{1}{Gk} Compute summand: Mk = -H{k-1} \cdot Dk (Initialize H0 = 0). Build cumulative histogram: Hk \leftarrow \sum{i=1}^k Gi 3. Sampling Loop (for n = 1 to N{sample}): Draw uniform random value: r \leftarrow \xi\left(\frac{k}{N{sample}}\right) where \xi is a uniform random number in [0, 1]. Select segment s by comparing r against the histogram step functions: s \leftarrow \text{step}(H1, r) + \text{step}(H2, r) (This implies finding the index s such that H{s-1} \le r < Hs). Transform sample into segment coordinates: rs = r \cdot Ds + Ms Sample distance t along the camera ray within segment s using importance sampling derived from the analytic integration (see Sec. 5.1 of). The specific distance sampling formula depends on the analytic transmittance distribution of the trapezoid, but the key is that the exponential term is cancelled by the PDF. Accumulate visibility V{total}: V{total} = V{total} + V(po - t \omegao) where V is the visibility function (1 if unoccluded, 0 otherwise). The exponential transmittance is implicitly handled by the importance sampling PDF. 4. Final Radiance Computation: L = \frac{1}{N{sample}} \sigmas f(\omegai, \omegao) V{total} T{total} Li where Li is the incident light radiance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Single Scattering Assumption: The analytic integration and the specific ratio estimator formulation are exact only for single scattering. For multiple scattering, this method serves as a base or requires approximation. Box Geometry: The method relies on the medium being a convex box. Non-convex or arbitrary geometries require different traversal or delta tracking. Precision: The calculation of Mk involves subtraction of potentially large numbers if H{k-1} is large and Dk is large; care must be taken with floating-point precision in the histogram construction. Backward Monte Carlo (BMC) traces photons from the camera to the light source, offering stability for in-situ rendering inside the medium compared to Forward Monte Carlo (FMC). It avoids the |V{s \to c}|^{-2} variance explosion inherent in FMC when the camera is inside the scattering medium because the light source (e.g., sun) is effectively at infinity. While the Optimized Monte Carlo Integrator described above is a forward-looking optimization for box geometries, BMC is a general strategy for handling the geometry term variance in participating media. A hybrid approach where a zonal method is used in a first pass to compute source radiances, followed by a Monte Carlo second pass in the rendering step to handle anisotropy for the single scattering approximation, accounting for one extra directional bounce. This differs from the pure Optimized Monte Carlo Integrator by separating the radiance computation from the directional scattering approximation. Time Complexity: O(N{seg} + N{sample}). The geometry traversal is O(N{seg}) (constant for a box, as the number of segments is fixed by the box topology relative to the ray directions), and sampling is O(N{sample}) with O(1) segment selection via binary search or linear scan of the small histogram. Memory Complexity: O(N{seg}) to store the cache matrix K, histogram H, weights D, and summands M. For a box, N{seg} is small and constant. Performance: Delivers significant performance improvements over ray marching for real-time applications, particularly in mixed reality and AR setups where additive lighting effects are needed. Strengths: Eliminates redundant geometric calculations per sample; exact analytic integration for unoccluded paths reduces variance; suitable for real-time rendering. Limitations: Restricted to homogeneous, box-shaped media; primarily designed for single scattering; collimated light sources only. When to use: Real-time rendering of light shafts in homogeneous fog/clouds within a defined volume, especially in AR/VR where performance is critical. When not to use: Heterogeneous media, multiple scattering, non-box geometries, or point lights. The method was introduced in "Collimated Whole Volume Light Scattering in Homogeneous Finite Media". It was developed to address the computational cost of ray marching in real-time rendering applications, specifically targeting mixed reality and optical see-through AR headsets. The work combines analytic integration of unoccluded single scattering, importance sampling matching the geometry-dependent transmittance, and variable caching to optimize the Monte Carlo integration process. name: Backward Monte Carlo
head: Forward MC, Forward Monte Carlo, Forward Monte Carlo (FMC) with Local Estimation
body: Backward Monte Carlo (BMC) is a photon tracking method where photons are launched from camera pixels back into the scene to estimate radiance, offering stability for in-situ (inside the medium) rendering compared to Forward Monte Carlo. While Forward Monte Carlo (FMC) traces photons from the light source to the camera, BMC traces them from the detector to the source. The key distinction is that BMC avoids the |V{s \to c}|^{-2} variance explosion inherent in FMC's local estimation when the camera is inside the scattering medium, because the sun is effectively at infinity. Inputs: Camera position Xc and pixel direction \omegap. Sun direction \omega{sun} (assumed constant and at infinity). Volumetric extinction field \beta(X), composed of aerosol and air components. Aerosol number density n. Aerosol scattering coefficient \sigma{aerosol}. Air scattering coefficient \beta{air}. Aerosol single scattering albedo \{aerosol}. Air single scattering albedo \{air} \approx 1. Anisotropy parameter g for Henyey-Greenstein phase function. Initial photon intensity I0. Number of initial photons N{photons} (e.g., 10^7). Outputs: Radiance estimate for pixel p at camera c. Data Structures: Ray: Defined by origin X and direction \omega. Voxel Grid: Stores \beta{aerosol}, \beta{air}, and n for spatial queries. Photon Packet: Stores current position Xs, direction \omegas, and intensity Is. Parameters: g: Anisotropy parameter, range -1 \le g \le 1. \{aerosol}: Aerosol single scattering albedo. \{air}: Air single scattering albedo, approximately 1 in the visible range. Steps: 1. Initialization: For each pixel p at camera c, launch a photon-packet from Xc in direction -\omegap. This is the initial ray R0. The packet has initial intensity I0. 2. Propagation Distance: Find the distance l{random} on ray Rs to which the photon-packet propagates. Calculate optical depth \tau{random} = -\ln(1-u) where u \sim U[0,1]. Numerically seek l{random} such that: \int0^{l{random}} (\sigma{aerosol} n + \beta{air}) dl = \tau{random} The 3D position is Xs. 3. Boundary Check: If Xs is outside the domain, terminate the packet. If the ray Rs is parallel to \omega{sun} (i.e., the photon back-traces into the Sun), the packet is counted as contributing to pixel p. 4. Particle Selection: If Xs is inside the domain, randomly determine the particle type (air molecule or aerosol) based on relative extinction coefficients (\beta{air} vs \beta{aerosol}) at the voxel containing Xs. 5. Intensity Update: If the particle is an aerosol, attenuate intensity: I{s+1} = \{aerosol} Is. For air molecules, intensity is maintained (I{s+1} = Is). If I{s+1} is lower than a threshold, stochastically terminate the packet. 6. Scattering: Scatter the photon to a new random direction using inverse transform sampling based on the phase function of the particle. Aerosol (Henyey-Greenstein): \Phi{scatter} = \arccos\left( \frac{1+g^2 - \left(\frac{1-g^2}{1-g+2gu}\right)^2}{2g} \right) Sample azimuth from U[0, 2\pi]. Molecule (Rayleigh): \Phi{scatter} = \arccos(\gamma^3 - \gamma - \sqrt{3}) where \gamma = \sqrt{4u - 2 + (4u - 2)^2 + 1}. Trace new ray R{s+1} and repeat step 2. 7. Local Estimation: At every scattering event (step 6), calculate contribution W{le} to pixel p. Let V{s \to sun} be the vector from scattering point Xs to the Top of Atmosphere (TOA), directed to -\omega{sun}. Let t{s \to sun} be the transmittance along V{s \to sun}. Let \Phi{Rs, sun} be the angle between Rs and V{s \to sun}. Let \ and P be the albedo and phase function of the particle. Contribution: W{le} = \ Is P(\Phi{Rs, sun}) t{s \to sun} Note: There is no |V{s \to sun}|^{-2} factor because the Sun is at infinity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def samplehenyeygreenstein(g, u): """Sample scattering angle for aerosol using Henyey-Greenstein phase function.""" term = (1 - g2) / (1 - g + 2 g u) costheta = (1 + g2 - term2) / (2 g) return math.acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, costheta))) def samplerayleigh(u): """Sample scattering angle for air molecules using Rayleigh phase function.""" val = 4 u - 2 gamma = math.sqrt(val + val2 + 1) costheta = gamma3 - gamma - math.sqrt(3) return math.acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, costheta))) def computetransmittancealongray(origin, direction, voxelgrid, maxdist=1e6): """Compute transmittance T = exp(-integral(beta dl)) along a ray to TOA.""" steps = 100 dl = maxdist / steps tau = 0.0 for i in range(steps): pos = (origin[0] + direction[0] (i dl), origin[1] + direction[1] (i dl), origin[2] + direction[2] (i dl)) if not voxelgrid.isinside(pos): break sigmaa, betaa = voxelgrid.getextinction(pos) tau += (sigmaa + betaa) dl return math.exp(-tau) def solvedistance(rayorigin, raydir, targettau, voxelgrid, maxdist=1e6): """Bisection solver to find l such that integral0^l (sigmaa n + betaair) dl = targettau.""" low, high = 0.0, maxdist for in range(50): mid = (low + high) / 2 if mid <= 0.0: low = mid continue pos = (rayorigin[0] + raydir[0] mid, rayorigin[1] + raydir[1] mid, rayorigin[2] + raydir[2] mid) if not voxelgrid.isinside(pos): high = mid continue tau = 0.0 steps = 10 dl = mid / steps for j in range(steps): p = (rayorigin[0] + raydir[0] (j dl), rayorigin[1] + raydir[1] (j dl), rayorigin[2] + raydir[2] (j dl)) if voxelgrid.isinside(p): s, b = voxelgrid.getextinction(p) tau += (s + b) dl if tau < targettau: low = mid else: high = mid return (low + high) / 2 def scatterdirection(currentdir, phiscatter, azimuth): """Rotate currentdir by phiscatter around a random axis perpendicular to currentdir.""" def normalize(v): l = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l) def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2]-a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0]-a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1]-a[1]b[0]) def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] ref = (0.0, 1.0, 0.0) if abs(dot(currentdir, ref)) < 0.9 else (1.0, 0.0, 0.0) u = normalize(cross(currentdir, ref)) v = cross(currentdir, u) sinphi = math.sin(phiscatter) cosphi = math.cos(phiscatter) cosaz = math.cos(azimuth) sinaz = math.sin(azimuth) newx = cosphi currentdir[0] + sinphi (cosaz u[0] + sinaz v[0]) newy = cosphi currentdir[1] + sinphi (cosaz u[1] + sinaz v[1]) newz = cosphi currentdir[2] + sinphi (cosaz u[2] + sinaz v[2]) return (newx, newy, newz) def backwardmontecarlo(camerapos, pixeldir, sundir, voxelgrid, numphotons, g, sigmaaerosol, naerosol, betaair, albedoaerosol, threshold): """Perform Backward Monte Carlo simulation.""" totalcontribution = 0.0 I0 = 1.0 for in range(numphotons): currentpos = camerapos currentdir = (-pixeldir[0], -pixeldir[1], -pixeldir[2]) currentintensity = I0 while True: u = random.random() taurandom = -math.log(1 - u) lrandom = solvedistance(currentpos, currentdir, taurandom, voxelgrid) nextpos = (currentpos[0] + lrandom currentdir[0], currentpos[1] + lrandom currentdir[1], currentpos[2] + lrandom currentdir[2]) if not voxelgrid.isinside(nextpos): break if abs(dot(currentdir, sundir) - 1.0) < 1e-6: totalcontribution += currentintensity break extaerosol, extair = voxelgrid.getextinction(nextpos) totalext = extaerosol + extair if totalext == 0: break probaerosol = extaerosol / totalext isaerosol = random.random() < probaerosol if isaerosol: currentintensity = albedoaerosol if currentintensity < threshold: if random.random() > currentintensity: break currentintensity /= currentintensity u = random.random() if isaerosol: phiscatter = samplehenyeygreenstein(g, u) else: phiscatter = samplerayleigh(u) azimuth = random.uniform(0, 2 math.pi) currentdir = scatterdirection(currentdir, phiscatter, azimuth) tssun = computetransmittancealongray(nextpos, (-sundir[0], -sundir[1], -sundir[2]), voxelgrid) cosphi = dot(currentdir, (-sundir[0], -sundir[1], -sundir[2])) cosphi = max(-1.0, min(1.0, cosphi)) phirssun = math.acos(cosphi) if isaerosol: denom = 1 + g2 - 2 g cosphi if denom <= 0: denom = 1e-9 phase = (1 - g2) / (4 math.pi (denom 1.5)) albedo = albedoaerosol else: phase = (3 / (16 math.pi)) (1 + cosphi2) albedo = 1.0 wle = albedo currentintensity phase tssun totalcontribution += wle currentpos = nextpos return totalcontribution / numphotons Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of photons and the number of scattering events per photon. Each photon trace involves numerical integration for distance sampling and phase function evaluation. Memory Complexity: Depends on the voxel grid resolution storing extinction coefficients. Performance: BMC is stable for in-situ rendering, whereas FMC becomes unstable due to the |V{s \to c}|^{-2} factor in local estimation when the camera is inside the medium. Strengths: Stability for in-situ cameras; no variance explosion near the camera. Limitations: Estimates radiance for one camera and one pixel at a time, making it less efficient for multi-view simulations compared to FMC with local estimation, which can contribute to multiple pixels in parallel. Scaling: Requires 10^7 initial photons for stable results in typical atmospheric simulations. Backward Monte Carlo (BMC) was proposed as an alternative to Forward Monte Carlo (FMC) for in-situ multi-scattering tomography and atmospheric rendering. It addresses the instability of FMC when the detector is inside the scattering medium by reversing the photon path and using a local estimation that does not suffer from the inverse-square law singularity associated with the camera position. The method is described in the context of simulating sky images and atmospheric tomography. In-situ multi-scattering tomography, https://archive.org/details/arxiv-1512.02110, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Pink Noise Transmittance via Ensemble Averaging
head: Delta Tracking for Pink Noise, Stochastic Delta Tracking
body: This method computes the transmittance of participating media characterized by 1/f (pink) fractal noise by interpreting the macroscopic transmittance as an ensemble average of random homogeneous realizations. It allows the use of classical, unbiased delta tracking for non-exponential media, whereas standard delta tracking relies on transmittance being exponential (Tr(a+b) = Tr(a)Tr(b)). It is distinct from regular tracking (which is slow) and raymarching (which is biased) by providing an unbiased estimator that can be significantly faster for specific noise distributions. Inputs: Ray segment length t (distance along the ray). Noise color parameter \beta (must be 1 for pink noise). Probability density function (PDF) of the extinction coefficient scaling factor, \text{pdf}(\bar{\sigma}\mu). Number of ensemble samples N (optional, for Monte Carlo approximation). Outputs: Estimated transmittance f{\text{pink}}(t). Data Structures: The method relies on sampling from the distribution \text{pdf}(\bar{\sigma}\mu). For a Gamma distributed pink noise medium, this is \Gamma(\alpha, \alpha) where \alpha = C^{-\beta-1}. The exact layout of the PDF/CDF evaluators is implementation-dependent but must support sampling and evaluation. Steps: 1. Check Noise Color: Verify that the medium is characterized by pink noise (\beta = 1). If \beta \neq 1 (e.g., blue noise where \beta = -1), the scale-invariant property does not hold, and this method is not applicable. 2. Sample Scaling Factor: Draw a sample \bar{\sigma}{\mu} from the distribution \text{pdf}(\bar{\sigma}\mu). 3. Compute Homogeneous Transmittance: Calculate the transmittance for a homogeneous medium with extinction coefficient scaled by \bar{\sigma}{\mu}. This is given by e^{-t\bar{\sigma}{\mu}}. 4. Ensemble Average (Monte Carlo): If using the Monte Carlo approximation, repeat steps 2-3 for N samples and average the results: f{\text{pink}}(t) \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} e^{-t\bar{\sigma}{\mui}} where \bar{\sigma}{\mui} are drawn proportional to \text{pdf}(\bar{\sigma}\mu). Formulas: The exact transmittance for pink noise is the characteristic function of the extinction coefficient distribution: f{\text{pink}}(t) = \int0^\infty e^{-t\bar{\sigma}\mu} \text{pdf}(\bar{\sigma}\mu) \, d\bar{\sigma}\mu = \varphi{\bar{\sigma}\mu}(t) \quad For the Gamma model with \beta=1, the PDF is \text{pdf}(\sigma\mu) = \Gamma(\mu\sigma, \alpha) where \alpha = C^{-\beta-1}. The resulting transmittance function is: f(t) = \left(1 + \frac{t}{\alpha}\right)^{-\alpha} \quad Parameters: \beta = 1: Defines pink noise. This value ensures the distribution \text{pdf}(\sigma\mu) is independent of distance t. N: Number of samples for Monte Carlo estimation. Not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Restricted Applicability: This method is strictly restricted to media characterized by 1/f (pink) fractal noise. It does not work for other noise colors like blue noise (\beta = -1) because they lack the scale-invariant property where \text{pdf}(\sigma\mu) is independent of t. Delta Tracking Requirement: While the transmittance is non-exponential, the method enables the use of unbiased delta tracking by treating the heterogeneity as a random scaling of a homogeneous medium. Standard delta tracking cannot be applied directly to the heterogeneous medium because its transmittance is not exponential. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pinknoisetransmittance(t, beta, pdfsigmamu, N=1): """ Compute transmittance for pink noise media using ensemble averaging. Args: t: Distance along the ray. beta: Noise color parameter. Must be 1 for pink noise. pdfsigmamu: A callable or sampler that draws samples from the distribution pdf(sigmamu). N: Number of ensemble samples. Returns: Estimated transmittance. """ if beta != 1: raise ValueError("Method restricted to pink noise (beta=1).") totaltransmittance = 0.0 for in range(N): # Sample a scaling factor from the distribution sigmamu = pdfsigmamu.sample() # Compute homogeneous transmittance with scaled extinction # T = exp(-t sigmamu) transmittance = math.exp(-t sigmamu) totaltransmittance += transmittance if N > 0: return totaltransmittance / N else: return 0.0 A specific instance where the PDF is Gamma-distributed, leading to a closed-form transmittance (1 + t/\alpha)^{-\alpha}. It is chosen when the medium's heterogeneity follows this specific statistical model. Link The broader technique of using delta tracking on media with random properties. Pink noise is a key case where this yields unbiased results efficiently. Link Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of ensemble samples. Each sample involves a PDF draw and an exponential evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per sample. Measured Performance: In a cloud with Gamma distributed pink noise, delta tracking rendered 23x faster than regular tracking while maintaining comparable noise levels and unbiased results. Strengths: Unbiased estimation; enables fast delta tracking for non-exponential media; simple implementation if PDF sampling is available. Limitations: Only applicable to pink noise (\beta=1); requires sampling from the specific PDF of the extinction coefficient distribution; variance depends on N. When to use: When rendering participating media with 1/f fractal noise characteristics and unbiased results are required. When not to use: For media with other noise colors (e.g., blue noise) or when exponential transmittance is sufficient. The method originates from the work on radiative transfer frameworks for non-exponential media. It leverages the mathematical property that the transmittance of pink noise media is the characteristic function of the extinction coefficient distribution. This allows the problem to be decomposed into an ensemble of homogeneous problems, which can be solved efficiently using established unbiased techniques like delta tracking. The approach connects to fractal literature via the Hurst parameter H = (\beta - 1)/2. A radiative transfer framework for non-exponential media, https://doi.org/10.1145/3272127.3275103, fetched 2026-11-08

name: Free-Flight Based Gradient Estimators
head: DT estimators, delta tracking gradient estimators
body: Free-flight based gradient estimators compute gradients of the volume rendering equation with respect to scene parameters (such as density \sigmat or emission) by leveraging free-flight distance sampling, typically via delta tracking. They solve the problem of differentiating volumetric light transport in participating media where the medium density is variable or unknown, enabling inverse volume rendering and optimization. Unlike surface-based gradient methods, these estimators handle the continuous nature of participating media by accumulating transmittance gradients along null-scattering interactions, distinguishing them from homogeneous medium sampling which assumes constant density. The method estimates gradients for the adjoint volume rendering equation using two primary sampling strategies: one proportional to extinction-weighted transmittance (\sigmat(t) T(t)) and, in unbiased variants, one proportional to transmittance alone (T(t)). Inputs: Ray segment defined by origin, direction, and maximum distance ts (surface intersection or medium boundary). Scene parameters \theta (e.g., \sigmat, emission coefficients). Radiance quantities: Ls(t) (in-scattered radiance), Le(t) (emitted radiance), \alpha(t) (scattering albedo). Outputs: Gradient estimates \langle \partial L \rangle with respect to \theta. Data Structures: Accumulator for transmittance gradients, initialized to zero. Sampled free-flight distance t. Numbered Steps: 1. Sample Free-Flight Distance: Sample a distance t from the distribution proportional to \sigmat(t) T(t). This is typically achieved using delta tracking (null-collision method). If t < ts: The interaction occurs within the medium. If t \geq ts: The ray hits the surface or exits the medium. 2. Compute Contribution for Medium Interaction (t < ts): If the sampled distance is within the medium, compute the in-scattering gradient contribution: \langle \partial L1^{\text{DT}} \rangle = \frac{\partial\theta [\sigmat(t) \alpha(t)]}{\sigmat(t)} Ls(t) + \alpha(t) \partial\theta Ls(t) 3. Compute Contribution for Surface Interaction (t \geq ts): If the ray hits the surface, compute the surface contribution: \langle \partial L2^{\text{DT}} \rangle = \partial\theta Le(ts) + \partial\theta Ls(ts) 4. Accumulate Transmittance Gradients: For all null-scattering interactions (steps taken during delta tracking) at locations t' along the ray segment (0, \min(t, ts)), accumulate the transmittance gradient contribution: \langle \partial L3^{\text{DT}} \rangle = \begin{cases} -\partial\theta \sigmat(t') \alpha(t) Ls(t) & \text{if } t < ts, \\ -\partial\theta \sigmat(t') [Le(ts) + Ls(ts)] & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computefreeflightgradient(ray, theta, maxdistts): """ Computes gradient estimates using standard DT estimators. ray: object with origin, direction, and sampling functions theta: scene parameters (sigmat, etc.) maxdistts: distance to surface/exit """ # Step 1: Sample t ~ sigmat(t) T(t) using delta tracking t, nullcollisions = samplefreeflightdistance(ray, theta, maxdistts) gradientsum = 0.0 # Step 4: Accumulate transmittance gradients from null collisions # Note: nullcollisions contains positions t' where null collisions occurred for tprime in nullcollisions: # Calculate local transmittance gradient contribution # This depends on whether we eventually hit surface or medium # We determine this after sampling t, but accumulate during sampling pass if t < maxdistts: # Step 2: Medium interaction # Ls(t) is in-scattered radiance at t # alpha(t) is scattering albedo at t term1 = (derivative(theta, sigmat(t) alpha(t)) / sigmat(t)) Ls(t) term2 = alpha(t) derivative(theta, Ls(t)) gradientsum += term1 + term2 # Add transmittance gradient for this path segment # The transmittance gradient term depends on the final outcome t for tprime in nullcollisions: gradientsum += -derivative(theta, sigmat(tprime)) alpha(t) Ls(t) else: # Step 3: Surface interaction # Le(ts) is emitted radiance at surface # Ls(ts) is in-scattered radiance at surface gradientsum += derivative(theta, Le(maxdistts)) + derivative(theta, Ls(maxdistts)) # Add transmittance gradient for this path segment for tprime in nullcollisions: gradientsum += -derivative(theta, sigmat(tprime)) (Le(maxdistts) + Ls(maxdistts)) return gradientsum Parameters: \sigmat(t): Total extinction coefficient. \alpha(t): Scattering albedo, \sigmas(t) / \sigmat(t). Ls(t): In-scattered radiance. Le(t): Emitted radiance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bias at Zero Density: If \sigmat(t) = 0, the estimator \langle \partial L1^{\text{DT}} \rangle is never sampled because the sampling probability is zero, even though the integrand for in-scattering gradients is non-zero. This causes bias, preventing optimization from escaping states where \sigmat=0. High Variance at Low Density: If \sigmat(t) is close to zero, the term 1/\sigmat(t) in Equation (8) leads to large outliers. The variance is unbounded for a homogeneous slab. Clamping Limitation: Unlike surface BSDF optimization, clamping \sigmat to a small nonzero value is not a valid solution here. Lowering \sigmat increases brightness, which is the wrong direction if the background is darker than the target, leading to incorrect gradient updates. DRT (Delta Tracking with Transmittance sampling) replaces the problematic \langle \partial L1^{\text{DT}} \rangle estimator with tailored estimators that sample distances proportional to transmittance T(t') to address bias and variance issues. It samples t' \sim T(t') to estimate in-scattering gradients, while keeping t \sim \sigmat T for other terms. The in-scattering gradient estimator is \langle \partial L{1a}^{\text{DRT}} \rangle:= Ls(t') \partial\theta [\sigmat(t') \alpha(t')] and the albedo gradient estimator is \langle \partial L{1b}^{\text{DRT}} \rangle:= \alpha \partial\theta Ls(t). A key drawback is that because t' is sampled from a different strategy than the path construction, path replay backpropagation cannot efficiently produce an estimate of incident illumination Li at t', potentially raising time complexity to O(n^2). Complexity: Standard DT estimators are O(n) per path, where n is the number of null collisions. DRT estimators may incur O(n^2) complexity in the worst case due to the need for recursive path starting at sampled points t'. Variance: Standard DT estimators suffer from unbounded variance when density is low. DRT estimators reduce variance and eliminate bias in these regions. Strengths: Handles variable density media effectively; integrates naturally with delta tracking. Limitations: Standard DT is biased and high-variance in low-density regions; DRT is computationally more expensive due to sampling strategy mismatch. The method was introduced by Tregan et al. in 2022 in the paper "Unbiased inverse volume rendering with differential trackers". It addresses limitations in previous gradient estimation methods for volume rendering, specifically the bias and variance issues associated with applying primal sampling techniques directly to the adjoint problem. The work builds upon earlier foundations in differential volume rendering by Gkioulekas et al. [2013]. Unbiased inverse volume rendering with differential trackers, https://doi.org/10.1145/3528223.3530073, fetched 2026-11-01

name: Real-time approximations
head: Real-time volumetric global illumination, Approximate volumetric light transport
body: Real-time approximations estimate light transport in participating media within strict latency budgets, avoiding the prohibitive cost of full path tracing or iterative radiative transfer equation (RTE) solvers. They set themselves apart from sibling methods like Optical models by prioritizing computational efficiency and dynamic scene support over physical accuracy, and from Local illumination, shadows and ambient occlusion by explicitly handling indirect scattering and global illumination effects in volumes. All methods in this family share the goal of approximating the integral of the radiative transfer equation for multiple scattering orders without solving it iteratively per frame. They typically rely on one or more of the following mechanisms: 1. Spatial Discretization: The volume is discretized into a structured grid (voxels, froxels) or a hierarchical structure (octrees, light volumes) to allow efficient spatial queries and interpolation. 2. Precomputation or Caching: Lighting information (attenuation, visibility, or flux) is precomputed offline or updated incrementally per frame, stored in textures or data structures, and queried at runtime. 3. Dimensionality Reduction: Directional information is compressed using basis functions (e.g., Spherical Harmonics) or approximated using geometric primitives (e.g., cones, light volumes with blur widths) to reduce the cost of evaluating the scattering integral. 4. Temporal Stability: Many methods incorporate temporal accumulation (e.g., TAA reprojection) to stabilize noise and reduce per-frame computational load. Approximates multiple scattering by precomputing light attenuation into a volumetric data structure (the "light volume") and treating the multiple scattering contribution as a lookup operation based on accumulated optical thickness and a derived blurring width [1188-multiple-scattering-approximation-via-light-volume-lookup.md]. It solves the problem of expensive numerical integration of the RTE for multiple scattering orders by replacing it with a spatially varying blur lookup, allowing for near-real-time rendering of complex volumetric effects like smoke and clouds [1188-multiple-scattering-approximation-via-light-volume-lookup.md]. It sets itself apart from siblings like Voxel Cone Tracing by explicitly modeling the spatial spreading of light beams through the medium using a derived width parameter, rather than relying on cone tracing or spherical harmonics for visibility approximation [1188-multiple-scattering-approximation-via-light-volume-lookup.md]. Choose it when rendering heterogeneous media with strong multiple scattering where cone tracing fails to capture beam spread. A real-time dynamic lighting technique for direct volume rendering that encodes local and global volumetric visibility using spherical harmonic basis functions [1225-spherical-harmonic-volumetric-visibility.md]. It sets itself apart from its siblings by storing these coefficients in a multiresolution grid to handle directional lights, point lights, and environment maps efficiently [1225-spherical-harmonic-volumetric-visibility.md]. Unlike Voxel Cone Tracing which relies on geometric cone tracing, or Froxel-based Volumetric Rendering which uses hierarchical voxel blocks, this method projects visibility into a frequency domain to approximate scattering integrals [1225-spherical-harmonic-volumetric-visibility.md]. Choose it when directional lighting accuracy and smooth interpolation across varying densities are prioritized over spatially explicit cone tracing. A precomputation-based rendering technique for volumetric media with repeated structures, such as fabrics and wood, that approximates high-order multiple scattering by modularly combining precomputed flux transfer matrices for exemplar blocks [1249-modular-transfer.md]. It solves the problem of rendering complex, optically thick media with anisotropic scattering by splitting light transport paths into components precomputed offline and computed at runtime, making path integrals separable via isotropy and diffuser events [1249-modular-transfer.md]. Unlike its siblings, MFT uses flux instead of light fields to address the curse of dimensionality, avoiding the massive storage overhead of directional discretizations [1249-modular-transfer.md]. It builds on Real-time approximations by providing a scalable alternative to voxel cone tracing and froxels for heterogeneous media where diffusion approximations fail due to strong heterogeneity and anisotropy [1249-modular-transfer.md]. Choose it for structured, optically thick media where traditional voxel methods suffer from storage or computational bottlenecks. A real-time global illumination technique that approximates indirect diffuse and specular lighting by voxelizing the scene geometry into a 3D texture or sparse octree and tracing cones through this volume to accumulate radiance [1454-voxel-cone-tracing.md]. It solves the problem of computing indirect light (interreflections) in dynamic scenes where precomputed methods are infeasible and full ray tracing is too slow [1454-voxel-cone-tracing.md]. Unlike Spherical Harmonic Volumetric Visibility which encodes lighting in frequency domain, or Precomputed Lighting (Baking) which requires static geometry, VCT operates on a spatially explicit voxel representation, allowing for dynamic objects and view-dependent effects like soft shadows and glossy reflections [1454-voxel-cone-tracing.md]. Choose it for dynamic scenes requiring view-dependent indirect lighting and soft shadows without baking. A real-time approximation for light transport in participating media that amortizes ray-queried occlusion lighting work by dividing the camera view frustum into a 3D grid of voxels ("froxels") [1919-froxel-based-volumetric-rendering.md]. It solves the high computational cost of per-pixel ray marching by collapsing per-pixel fog cost to a fixed march in an integrate pass, delivering spatial-accumulation savings [1919-froxel-based-volumetric-rendering.md]. Unlike Voxel Cone Tracing which relies on cone tracing for indirect lighting, or Precomputed Lighting (Baking) which uses static data, this method computes dynamic in-scattered radiance and shadows per froxel, often combined with Froxel TAA Reprojection to stabilize temporal noise [1919-froxel-based-volumetric-rendering.md]. Choose it for large-scale atmospheric fog and volumetric effects where per-pixel ray marching is too expensive. A technique to accelerate volumetric rendering by pre-computing the lighting term (Li) and storing it in the grid's voxels, allowing the renderer to skip evaluating Li at each raymarching step on the camera ray [2169-precomputed-lighting-baking.md]. It approximates volumetric shadows by precalculating illumination for each voxel center, enabling trilinear interpolation at render time [2169-precomputed-lighting-baking.md]. Unlike Voxel Cone Tracing which computes lighting dynamically during traversal, this method is view-independent but scene and light source dependent [2169-precomputed-lighting-baking.md]. Choose it for static scenes or environments where lighting changes infrequently, allowing significant runtime savings at the cost of re-baking overhead. Approximates one-bounce diffuse global illumination by cosine-sampling the hemisphere around a surface normal, tracing short rays via hardware RT cores, and gathering indirect irradiance from hits or skylight if rays escape [3648-hardware-ray-tracing-global-illumination.md]. It differs from sibling methods like Voxel Cone Tracing by using explicit ray queries against voxel bricks rather than cone-based approximations, and from Precomputed Lighting by computing the indirect term per-frame rather than baking it offline [3648-hardware-ray-tracing-global-illumination.md]. Choose it when hardware RT cores are available and explicit ray queries against voxel structures are preferred over cone tracing. Approximates incoming radiance by storing sparse environment maps at specific locations in the scene, trading spatial precision for high angular resolution [4344-reflection-probes.md]. Unlike precomputed lighting methods that bake static data, reflection probes can be updated dynamically, allowing them to capture dynamic global illumination effects [4344-reflection-probes.md]. They differ from voxel-based methods like Voxel Cone Tracing by storing full-resolution directional radiance rather than compressed scattering data, making them suitable for accurate surface reflections but less effective for volumetric scattering integration [4344-reflection-probes.md]. Choose them for scenes requiring accurate surface reflections and dynamic environment updates without full volumetric integration. A rendering technique that computes volumetric light scattering for local lights (point and spot) within a fog volume by evaluating light contributions at froxel midpoints using clustered light lists, skipping the sun and non-volumetric lights [4460-volumetric-light-scattering-via-froxel-clustering.md]. It differs from Voxel Cone Tracing by avoiding ray marching through the volume for scattering, instead relying on pre-clustered light lists and a single sample per light per froxel, and from Froxel-based Volumetric Rendering by specifically targeting local light scattering rather than general volume density rendering. Choose it for scenes with many local lights where clustered evaluation reduces per-froxel shading cost. A real-time global illumination technique that merges voxel cone tracing with deferred shading to approximate indirect lighting effects such as diffuse/specular reflections, color bleeding, emissive materials, and ambient occlusion [4685-deferred-voxel-shading.md]. Unlike forward voxel cone tracing, which computes lighting per fragment during geometry rendering, this method delays lighting calculations to a post-processing stage, avoiding redundant computations for overlapping polygons and enhancing performance in scenes with many light sources [4685-deferred-voxel-shading.md]. It builds on Real-time approximations by utilizing spatial discretization and precomputed voxel structures to evaluate the radiative transfer equation efficiently [4685-deferred-voxel-shading.md]. Choose it for deferred rendering pipelines where indirect lighting and shadows are needed without forward shading overhead. Utilize modular cells to precompute transfer, stitching multiple unit cells together and warping them to approximate scene geometry. Propagate radiance first to cell borders acting as interfaces, then to neighboring cells using precomputed models. Real-time approximations for volumetric rendering emerged as hardware capabilities improved, allowing for more complex lighting calculations within frame budgets. Early approaches relied on precomputed lighting (baking) [2169-precomputed-lighting-baking.md]. The introduction of voxel-based techniques like Voxel Cone Tracing [1454-voxel-cone-tracing.md] and Froxel-based methods [1919-froxel-based-volumetric-rendering.md] enabled dynamic global illumination in participating media. More recent methods, such as Modular Transfer [1249-modular-transfer.md] and Light Volume Lookup [1188-multiple-scattering-approximation-via-light-volume-lookup.md], focus on specific types of media (e.g., structured fabrics, smoke) and use advanced precomputation and approximation strategies to handle multiple scattering efficiently. The field continues to evolve with the integration of hardware ray tracing [3648-hardware-ray-tracing-global-illumination.md] and machine learning techniques. Real-Time Ray Traced Voxel Global Illumination, https://doi.org/10.34626/0vdq-7m27, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Multiple Scattering Approximation via Light Volume Lookup
head: Light Volume Lookup, Light Volume Pyramid, Precomputed Light Volume
body: This method approximates the contribution of multiple scattering in participating media by precomputing the spatial spreading and attenuation of light into a hierarchical texture structure (the "light volume"). It solves the computational bottleneck of integrating the radiative transfer equation for high-order scattering by replacing expensive path integration with a simple lookup operation indexed by a calculated "blur width". Unlike Voxel Cone Tracing which traces rays through a voxel grid, or Precomputed Radiance Transfer which relies on linear transfer matrices, this approach explicitly models the statistical spreading of light beams through the medium using a derived point spread function. Inputs: Density volume grid \rho(x) (e.g., 128^3 voxels). Absorption cross-section C{abs} and scattering cross-section C{sca}. Light source position and intensity. Camera ray origin and direction. Outputs: Final radiance L{total} for each pixel. Data Structures: 1. Density Volume: A 3D texture storing \rho(x). Size: 128^3 voxels (8 MB). 2. Light Volume Pyramid: A mip-map hierarchy storing precomputed attenuated radiance. The base level stores the initial light distribution; higher levels store spatially blurred versions. Size: 32 MB. 3. Optical Thickness Squared Volume: For inhomogeneous media, a 3D texture storing \ell^2 (the square of the optical thickness along the light path) to avoid runtime integration. Size: 8 MB. Parameters: w: The blurring level used as an index or parameter for the light volume lookup. C{abs}: Absorption cross-section, used to compute scattering coefficient a(x). C{sca}: Scattering cross-section, used to compute scattering coefficient b(x). \rho(x): Density of the medium at point x. \alpha: Path curvature coefficient. Formulas: Scattering coefficient: a(x) = C{abs} \cdot \rho(x). Scattering coefficient: b(x) = C{sca} \cdot \rho(x). Optical thickness (homogeneous): \ell = b \cdot d. Optical thickness (inhomogeneous): \ell = \int{0}^{d} b(x) ds. Blurring width w: Derived from the path integral analysis of light transport, approximating the spatial spread of the beam. Attenuation factor: atten = \exp(-(a/b) \cdot \ell). (Note: uses c/b where c corresponds to absorption; defines a(x) as absorption, so a/b is used consistently here.) Phase function: P = P{MS}(\theta, \ell), where \theta is the scattering angle. Path curvature: C = \alpha \cdot \theta^2 / \ell. Weight: weight = \exp(-(a/b) \cdot \ell) \cdot \exp(-C) \cdot P. Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Offline): 1. Compute scattering coefficients a(x) and b(x) from \rho(x), C{abs}, and C{sca}. 2. For each light source, compute the optical thickness \ell along rays from the light into the medium. 3. For inhomogeneous media, compute and store \ell^2 in a separate 3D texture to avoid runtime integration. 4. Construct the Light Volume Pyramid. For each level i, store the attenuated radiance L at point xi and blurring level w. This involves convolving the light distribution with the derived point spread function (PSF) to simulate spatial spreading. 2. Rendering (Per Frame): 1. For each pixel, cast a ray from the camera. 2. March along the ray. For inhomogeneous media, track \ell{eye} (camera part of the path) and \ell{light} (light part of the path). \ell{eye} = \ell{eye} + b(x) \cdot \Delta x. \ell{light} is retrieved from the precomputed \ell^2 volume or integrated if not precomputed. 3. Calculate the total optical thickness \ell = \ell{eye} + \ell{light}. 4. Calculate the blurring width w based on the distance and medium properties. 5. Multiple Scattering Lookup: L{ms} = \text{Lookup}(xi, LV, w). This returns the precomputed attenuated radiance from the light volume pyramid at the current position and blurring level. 6. Weighting: Calculate scattering angle \theta = \arccos(\hat{\omega}i \cdot \hat{\omega}o). Calculate path curvature C = \alpha \cdot \theta^2 / \ell. Calculate weight: weight = \exp(-(a/b) \cdot \ell) \cdot \exp(-C) \cdot P{MS}(\theta, \ell). 7. Accumulation: L{total} = L{total} + L{ms} \cdot weight. 8. Step Size Adaptation: March along the ray using progressively larger step sizes for the multiple scattering component, as the blur width w is monotonically increasing with distance. Single scattering requires smaller step sizes to resolve fine features. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rendermultiplescattering(rayorigin, raydirection, densityvolume, lightvolumepyramid, opticalthicknesssqvolume, Cabs, Csca, alpha, lightposition, initialstepsizems=0.5, raylength=100.0, stepgrowthfactor=1.1): """ Renders multiple scattering contribution using light volume lookup. """ Ltotal = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] t = 0.0 leye = 0.0 llight = 0.0 step = initialstepsizems while t < raylength: currentpos = [rayorigin[i] + raydirection[i] t for i in range(3)] rho = densityvolume.sample(currentpos) a = Cabs rho b = Csca rho deltaleye = b step leye += deltaleye llightsq = opticalthicknesssqvolume.sample(currentpos) llight = math.sqrt(llightsq) l = leye + llight w = computeblurringwidth(t, l, b) Lms = lightvolumepyramid.lookup(currentpos, w) lightdir = normalize([lightposition[i] - currentpos[i] for i in range(3)]) theta = computescatteringangle(raydirection, lightdir) if l > 0.0: C = alpha (theta 2) / l else: C = 0.0 Pms = phasefunctionmultiplescattering(theta, l) attenuation = math.exp(-(a / b) l) weight = attenuation math.exp(-C) Pms for i in range(3): Ltotal[i] += Lms[i] weight t += step step = stepgrowthfactor return Ltotal def computeblurringwidth(t, l, b): # w increases monotonically with distance for multiple scattering return t b def computescatteringangle(v1, v2): dotprod = sum(a b for a, b in zip(v1, v2)) mag1 = math.sqrt(sum(a a for a in v1)) mag2 = math.sqrt(sum(b b for b in v2)) costheta = dotprod / (mag1 mag2) costheta = max(-1.0, min(1.0, costheta)) return math.acos(costheta) def phasefunctionmultiplescattering(theta, l): # Simplified isotropic approximation for PMS return 1.0 def normalize(v): mag = math.sqrt(sum(x x for x in v)) if mag == 0: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] return [x / mag for x in v] The Beam Spreading Width Model provides a closed-form expression for the spatial width w of a collimated light beam as it propagates through a participating medium, approximating the spatial blurring effects caused by multiple scattering. It distinguishes itself from rigorous methods that lack general closed-form solutions by offering an easy-to-evaluate formula that explicitly accounts for absorption, scattering coefficients, and the mean square scattering angle. PSF-based Multiple Scattering Rendering approximates volumetric light transport by convolving a vacuum-rendered image with a spatially varying Gaussian Point Spread Function (PSF) derived from the medium's optical properties. It solves the problem of computationally expensive multiple scattering simulation by treating the medium as a blur filter, allowing for real-time performance on homogeneous media while handling directional lighting and visibility effects that simpler diffusion models miss. Unlike diffusion approximations which assume optically dense, homogeneous media with uniform angular distribution, this method uses a path integration framework to describe spatial spreading while avoiding direct numerical simulation, supporting spatially varying materials and anisotropic sources. In-Scattering Approximation is a real-time technique for estimating the contribution of multiple scattering in participating media, specifically treating the scattered portion of direct global light as an emittance source to capture short-range scattering effects. It solves the computational cost of integrating the full radiative transfer equation by approximating the in-scattering integral using either a discretized directional sum or a cheap analytical decay function. Unlike its sibling Beam Spreading Width Model which focuses on geometric spread, or Precomputed Multiple Scattering Table which relies on heavy precomputation, this method provides an immediate, low-cost approximation that brightens the inner parts of volumes (like clouds) while maintaining performance suitable for interactive frame rates. Precomputed Multiple Scattering Table (PMS) accelerates light transport in participating media by replacing the slow convergence of high-order scattering simulations with precomputed radiance data from an infinite homogeneous medium. It solves the problem of expensive Monte Carlo convergence for multiple scattering events by storing the material response in compact 4D tables, allowing existing global illumination algorithms (such as VRL, UPBP, and MEMLT) to handle single and double scattering while querying the table for higher-order effects. Unlike Beam Spreading Width Model which approximates the shape of the light beam, PMS stores the full angular radiance distribution (lobes). It differs from Neural Network Multiple Scattering Representation by using discrete lookup tables rather than learned regression functions. The One-pass Spectral Rendering Integral is a real-time approximation for light transport in participating media that simplifies the multiple scattering model by removing global illumination elements to facilitate ray casting with local illumination. It enables interactive data integration using different light sources during post-illumination by factoring the light source out of the volume rendering integral computation. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific simplification of assigning a volumetric shadow ratio of 1 and considering only irradiance and radiance aligned with the viewing ray, computed via a local Phong-based model. This method approximates the view-independent part of the multiple scattering integrand, I(\gamma, \beta), as a low-rank sum of outer products using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). It enables efficient integration by decomposing the 2D integrand into functions constant along the light ray direction (\gamma) and the view ray direction (\beta). This allows the use of a partial sum tree to accumulate terms along \gamma independently, reducing the computational complexity from per-pixel to per-slice processing. It builds on Multiple Scattering Approximation via Light Volume Lookup. Asymmetric Lobe Approximation is a method for accelerating multiple scattering calculations in participating media by replacing full 4D spherical phase function lobes with asymmetric 1D functions. It solves the high computational cost of evaluating full angular scattering distributions by focusing on the dominant multiple scattering component, which is less sensitive to angular precision than double scattering. It differs from sibling methods like Beam Spreading Width Model and PSF-based Multiple Scattering Rendering by explicitly simplifying the angular representation of the scattering lobe itself rather than just the spatial spread or point spread function. This method efficiently approximates multiple-scattering light transport in non-homogeneous, analytically integrable participating media by applying Gaussian blurring via MIP maps. It solves the high computational cost of neighborhood filtering in screen-space rendering, enabling real-time performance on GPUs by reducing time complexity from O(n^4) to O(n^2 \log2 n). Unlike naive gathering which iterates over a fixed neighborhood for every pixel, this approach leverages hierarchical image representations to accumulate contributions across scales. A method to handle shadows cast by objects through a medium using a 2D shadow map for single scattering and ignoring objects in multiple scattering (relying on LightImage/LightVolume). Objects are ignored during the generation of the light volume. In the single scattering pass, radiance is scaled by the result of a shadow map lookup. For multiple scattering, objects inside the medium are ignored, relying on LightImage and light volume which do not account for internal occlusion. This strategy is adequate for reasonable size objects (such as game characters) since multiple scattering lets light bend around objects. For large objects embedded in the medium (e.g., a wall), split the media into several separate volumes so the object is outside each volume. Unlike setting light values very large for occluded voxels (which causes low-resolution artifacts), this method uses a 2D shadow map for high-quality single scattering shadows. Time Complexity: The lookup operation is O(1) per sample. The overall rendering time is dominated by the ray marching steps. For inhomogeneous media, single scattering computation dominates rendering time because it must resolve very fine features, requiring a much smaller step size than multiple scattering. The multiple scattering component uses progressively larger step sizes. Memory Complexity: Storage for density volume (128^3 voxels) is 8 MB. Storage for the light volume pyramid is 32 MB. Additional 8 MB for precomputed \ell^2. Total ~48 MB. This is higher than standard Monte Carlo methods which required less memory (8 MB). Performance: Rendering time for inhomogeneous media (800x800 resolution, 9 samples per pixel) was about 30 minutes on a 1 GHz Powerbook G4 with 512 MB RAM. For a rising smoke image, the algorithm took approximately 10 minutes, compared to 3 hours for a traditional Monte Carlo ray marching solution. Strengths: Captures qualitative features of multiple scattering, such as spatial blurring, more efficiently than previous methods. Simple implementation. Limitations: The method considers only the overall statistics of the phase function, not its particular shape, leading to quantitative differences with Monte Carlo simulations. Precomputing the light attenuation volume for each light source becomes expensive for a large number of light sources. The computation of multiply scattered light attenuation is not straightforward. When to use: Suitable for real-time or near-real-time rendering of volumetric media where qualitative multiple scattering effects (glow, blurring) are desired, and computational resources for full Monte Carlo integration are unavailable. When not to use: When high quantitative accuracy is required, or when the number of light sources is very large, making precomputation prohibitive. The method was presented in "Practical Rendering of Multiple Scattering Effects in Participating Media". It was used in the rendering of rising smoke (Figure 12) and inhomogeneous participating media in a Cornell box (Figure 13). The approach avoids direct numerical simulation of multiple scattering by taking advantage of spatial spreading, using a derived point spread function (PSF) from a path integral analysis of light transport. While the PSF is derived under simple assumptions, it can be applied to inhomogeneous media as well. Practical Rendering of Multiple Scattering Effects in Participating Media, https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~ravir/HRPIEG.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 A lighting model for general participating media, https://doi.org/10.1145/1053427.1053446, fetched 2026-11-02

name: Beam Spreading Width Model
head: Spatial beam spread width
body: The Beam Spreading Width Model provides a closed-form expression for the spatial width w of a collimated light beam as it propagates through a participating medium, approximating the spatial blurring effects caused by multiple scattering. It distinguishes itself from rigorous methods that lack general closed-form solutions by offering an easy-to-evaluate formula that explicitly accounts for absorption, scattering coefficients, and the mean square scattering angle. Inputs: S: Distance along the beam path from the source. a: Absorption coefficient of the medium. b: Scattering coefficient of the medium. \langle \theta^2 \rangle: Mean square scattering angle, derived from the phase function P. Outputs: w(S): The spatial width (radius) of the beam at distance S. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required; the model is a direct mathematical evaluation. Parameters: \langle \theta^2 \rangle: Typical value in simulation is 0.24 (corresponding to Henyey-Greenstein asymmetry factor g=0.9). a: Typical value in simulation is 0.0003 mm⁻¹. b: Variable parameter determining the number of scattering events. Formulas: The core equation for the squared beam width is: w^2(S) = \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{2a}{3S} + \frac{16\alpha}{bS^2} \right)^{-1} = \frac{\langle \theta^2 \rangle b S^3}{16(1 + S^2/12l^2)} Where \alpha is defined as: \alpha = \frac{1}{2\langle \theta^2 \rangle} And the diffusive path length l is defined as: l^2 = \frac{1}{ab\langle \theta^2 \rangle} Limiting Cases: 1. Long paths (S \gg l): The width grows linearly with distance: w^2 = \frac{3}{4} \langle \theta^2 \rangle b S l^2. 2. No absorption (l = \infty): w^2 = \frac{b \langle \theta^2 \rangle S^3}{16}. Pitfalls: The beam spread width expression has no upper bound. This is mitigated because attenuation increases at an even faster rate than the spread. The model assumes a Gaussian profile for the beam core; a wider non-Gaussian component exists in reality but is not captured by this model. The formula differs from Tessendorf [Tes87] by a constant factor of 3/2. To align with Tessendorf's rigorous derivation for specific limiting cases, multiply the result by 2/3. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def beamspreadingwidth(S, a, b, thetasqmean): """ Calculate the squared beam width w^2(S) using the Beam Spreading Width Model. Args: S (float): Distance along the beam path. a (float): Absorption coefficient. b (float): Scattering coefficient. thetasqmean (float): Mean square scattering angle <theta^2>. Returns: float: The squared beam width w^2. """ if thetasqmean <= 0: raise ValueError("Mean square scattering angle must be positive.") if b <= 0: raise ValueError("Scattering coefficient must be positive.") if S <= 0: return 0.0 # Calculate alpha alpha = 1.0 / (2.0 thetasqmean) # Calculate diffusive path length squared # l^2 = 1 / (a b <theta^2>) lsq = 1.0 / (a b thetasqmean) # Calculate w^2 using the form involving l # w^2 = (<theta^2> b S^3) / (16 (1 + S^2 / (12 l^2))) numerator = thetasqmean b (S 3) denominator = 16.0 (1.0 + (S 2) / (12.0 lsq)) wsq = numerator / denominator return wsq Time Complexity: O(1) per evaluation. The model is a closed-form expression requiring only basic arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1). No precomputed tables or volumes are required. Strengths: Easy to evaluate; provides a general closed-form solution unlike rigorous methods; explicitly includes absorption effects which narrow the beam compared to scattering-only models. Limitations: Lacks an upper bound on width (though mitigated by attenuation); does not capture the wider non-Gaussian component of the beam profile; differs from rigorous derivations (e.g., Tessendorf) by a constant factor. When to use: When an efficient, approximate spatial blurring model is needed for real-time or interactive applications where rigorous solutions are too slow or unavailable. The model was derived using a path integration framework and presented in the paper "Practical Rendering of Multiple Scattering Effects in Participating Media". It builds upon earlier work on beam spread in scattering media, such as McLean et al. [MFW98] and Tessendorf [Tes87], adapting them for computer graphics applications where computational efficiency is critical. The derivation is detailed in a companion document [APRN04]. Practical Rendering of Multiple Scattering Effects in Participating Media, https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~ravir/HRPIEG.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28
