name: One-pass Spectral Rendering Integral
head: Bergner Spectral Rendering, Spectral Volume Rendering Integral
body: The One-pass Spectral Rendering Integral is a real-time approximation for light transport in participating media that simplifies the multiple scattering model by removing global illumination elements to facilitate ray casting with local illumination. It enables interactive data integration using different light sources during post-illumination by factoring the light source out of the volume rendering integral computation. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific simplification of assigning a volumetric shadow ratio of 1 and considering only irradiance and radiance aligned with the viewing ray, computed via a local Phong-based model. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Light source spectral power distribution L(\lambda), viewing direction \omega, sampling position x, entry point d (where the light ray first enters the volume), distance D = |x - d|, spectral extinction coefficient \tau(x, \lambda), and local material reflectance properties for the Phong model. Outputs: Irradiance Ii(x, \omega, \lambda) at position x. Data Structures: Spectral extinction coefficient \tau(x, \lambda): Defined per voxel and wavelength. Local material reflectance: Parameters for the Phong model (ambient, diffuse, specular coefficients). Formulas: The irradiance Ii(x, \omega, \lambda) is computed as: Ii(x, \omega, \lambda) = L(\lambda) \cdot \tilde{I}i(x, \omega, \lambda, D) where \tilde{I}i is the proportion of light arriving at x from the entry point d: \tilde{I}i(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}, \boldsymbol{\lambda}) = \tilde{I}i(x - D\boldsymbol{\omega}, \boldsymbol{\omega}, \boldsymbol{\lambda}) \cdot T(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}, \boldsymbol{\lambda}, D) + \int0^D \tilde{I}r(x - s\boldsymbol{\omega}, \boldsymbol{\omega}, \boldsymbol{\lambda}) \cdot T(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}, \boldsymbol{\lambda}, s) ds The spectral extinction function T is defined as: T(x, \omega, \lambda, s) = \exp\left(-\int0^s \tau(x-t\omega, \lambda) dt\right) The scattered radiance term \tilde{I}r is computed using a local illumination model based on the Phong model. Steps: 1. Determine the entry point d where the light ray first intersects the volume boundary for the given direction \omega. 2. Calculate the distance D from the sampling position x to the entry point d. 3. Evaluate the spectral extinction integral \int0^s \tau(x-t\omega, \lambda) dt for s ranging from 0 to D, discretized along the ray segment from d to x. 4. Compute the transmission T(x, \omega, \lambda, s) using the exponential of the negative extinction integral. 5. Compute the scattered radiance \tilde{I}r at each point along the ray using the local Phong illumination model, calculating diffuse and specular contributions based on local material properties and the light direction, ignoring global shadows (shadow ratio = 1). 6. Evaluate the integral \int0^D \tilde{I}r(x - s\omega, \omega, \lambda) \cdot T(x, \omega, \lambda, s) ds using numerical quadrature over the sampled points. 7. Compute the boundary term \tilde{I}i(x - D\omega, \omega, \lambda) \cdot T(x, \omega, \lambda, D), where \tilde{I}i(x - D\omega, \omega, \lambda) represents the irradiance proportion just outside the volume, which is 1. 8. Sum the boundary term and the integral result to get \tilde{I}i(x, \omega, \lambda). 9. Multiply by the light source spectral power L(\lambda) to obtain the final irradiance Ii(x, \omega, \lambda). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def onepassspectralrenderingintegral(x, omega, Llambda, taufunction, phongparams, normalfunc, numsamples): # x: sampling position (list of 3 floats) # omega: light ray direction (list of 3 floats, normalized) # Llambda: light source spectral power distribution (list of floats) # taufunction(p, wavelengths) -> list of floats: spectral extinction coefficient # phongparams: dict with 'ka', 'kd', 'ks', 'shininess' # normalfunc(p) -> list of 3 floats: surface normal at p # numsamples: integer N for discretization # Returns: Ii (list of floats) D = 1.0 # Distance from x to entry point d, assumed known from ray-volume intersection d = [x[i] - D omega[i] for i in range(3)] if D <= 0.0: return [0.0] len(Llambda) ds = D / numsamples numw = len(Llambda) # Precompute cumulative optical depth and transmission T(s) tauoptical = [0.0] numw Ts = [[0.0] numw for in range(numsamples + 1)] for i in range(numsamples + 1): s = i ds ps = [x[j] - s omega[j] for j in range(3)] taus = taufunction(ps, list(range(numw))) if i > 0: for k in range(numw): tauoptical[k] += taus[k] ds for k in range(numw): Ts[i][k] = exp(-tauoptical[k]) # Compute scattered radiance Ir at each sample point using local Phong model Ir = [[0.0] numw for in range(numsamples + 1)] for i in range(numsamples + 1): s = i ds ps = [x[j] - s omega[j] for j in range(3)] n = normalfunc(ps) dotnl = dot(n, omega) # Diffuse term diffuse = [phongparams['kd'] (dotnl if dotnl > 0.0 else 0.0) Llambda[k] for k in range(numw)] # Specular term reflectdir = [omega[j] + 2.0 (-dotnl) n[j] for j in range(3)] # View direction is assumed to be -omega for local evaluation per simplification (ii) viewdir = [-w for w in omega] dotrv = dot(reflectdir, viewdir) specular = [phongparams['ks'] pow(dotrv if dotrv > 0.0 else 0.0, phongparams['shininess']) Llambda[k] for k in range(numw)] # Ambient term ambient = [phongparams['ka'] Llambda[k] for k in range(numw)] for k in range(numw): Ir[i][k] = ambient[k] + diffuse[k] + specular[k] # Evaluate integral term: int0^D Ir T ds using trapezoidal rule integralterm = [0.0] numw for i in range(numsamples): Iravg = [(Ir[i][k] + Ir[i+1][k]) 0.5 for k in range(numw)] Tavg = [(Ts[i][k] + Ts[i+1][k]) 0.5 for k in range(numw)] for k in range(numw): integralterm[k] += Iravg[k] Tavg[k] ds # Boundary term: Ii(d) T(x, omega, D) # Ii(d) is the proportion of light at entry, which is 1.0 boundaryterm = [1.0 Ts[numsamples][k] for k in range(numw)] # Combine Ii = [boundaryterm[k] + integralterm[k] for k in range(numw)] # Final irradiance return [Llambda[k] Ii[k] for k in range(numw)] def dot(a, b): return sum(a[i] b[i] for i in range(len(a))) def exp(x): import math return math.exp(x) def pow(base, exp): import math return math.pow(base, exp) Parameters: N: Number of samples along the ray segment. Typical value: 64. Phong parameters (ka, kd, ks, shininess): Material-specific. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The exponential function in the extinction term can lead to underflow for large optical depths. Use clamping or log-space arithmetic if necessary. Boundaries: The entry point d must be correctly identified. If the ray does not enter the volume, the result is zero. Degenerate Input: If D=0, the integral is zero. Spectral Precomputation is a variant that uses full spectral computation instead of RGB to simulate light scattering, resulting in smoother, less saturated, and more natural colors. It uses an array of 4D textures to emulate a spectral texture with M spectral channels, requiring \lceil (M+1)/4 \rceil textures (the +1 is for storing I{SM}). Constants must be spectral (sampled at more than three wavelengths), and incident light intensity is calculated as blackbody radiation at 5778K according to Planck's law. All textures in the array are fetched using exactly the same texture coordinates for both reading and writing. Spectral color values are converted to CIE XYZ space using standard XYZ primaries, then moved to sRGB gamut and converted to sRGB by multiplication with an XYZ→sRGB conversion matrix. The final sRGB result is stored in a single 4D texture for use in rendering. A key pitfall is that RGB precomputation values cannot be used directly as RGB color components; they must be treated as 3-sample spectra and converted via the spectral-to-RGB pipeline. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples along the ray N and the number of wavelengths M. The precomputation step (if used) is offline. Memory Complexity: Depends on the volume resolution and the number of spectral channels. The spectral precomputation variant uses an array of 4D textures, which can be memory-intensive. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with resolution and spectral samples. Strengths: Enables interactive rendering with different light sources via post-illumination; more natural colors than RGB methods. Limitations: Simplifications (shadow ratio = 1, local illumination only) reduce accuracy for complex lighting scenarios; spectral computation is more expensive than RGB. When to use: Real-time applications requiring natural-looking spectral effects with local lighting. When not to use: Applications requiring accurate global illumination or shadowing. The One-pass Spectral Rendering Integral was developed by Bergner et al. [7, 8] as part of their work on spectral volume rendering. It is based on a simplified multiple scattering model described in Section 4.1 of their work. The method was designed to facilitate ray casting with local illumination and post-illumination with different light sources by removing global illumination elements from the model. Local and Global Illumination in the Volume Rendering Integral, https://avishek.net/assets/papers/nerfs/local-and-global-illumination-rendering-integral.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (book) Real-time spectral scattering in large-scale natural participating media, https://doi.org/10.1145/1925059.1925074, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Variation Along and Across Light Rays (SVD Approximation)
head: Low-rank SVD approximation of light transport, SVD Approximation
body: This method approximates the view-independent part of the multiple scattering integrand, I(\gamma, \beta), as a low-rank sum of outer products using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). It enables efficient integration by decomposing the 2D integrand into functions constant along the light ray direction (\gamma) and the view ray direction (\beta). This allows the use of a partial sum tree to accumulate terms along \gamma independently, reducing the computational complexity from per-pixel to per-slice processing. It builds on Multiple Scattering Approximation via Light Volume Lookup. Inputs: The integrand function I(\gamma, \beta), which encodes all integration terms excluding visibility. The integration grid resolution for \gamma and \beta. The number of singular values N to retain. Outputs: Singular vectors \Gammai(\gamma) and Bi(\beta) for i=1 \dots N. Singular values \sigmai. Data Structures: Partial Sum Tree: A hierarchical structure where each node stores an N-dimensional vector instead of a scalar. The tree supports O(\log n) updates and queries for interval sums. Singular Vectors: Stored as 1D arrays, upsampled to the integration grid resolution. Steps: 1. Sample the Integrand: Sample I(\gamma, \beta) at discrete values to form a matrix M. The rows correspond to \gamma samples and columns to \beta samples. 2. Compute SVD: Compute the Singular Value Decomposition of M: M \approx U \Sigma V^T The columns of U correspond to \Gammai(\gamma), the columns of V correspond to Bi(\beta), and the diagonal elements of \Sigma are the singular values \sigmai. Optimization: To reduce cost, compute the SVD on a 64 \times 64 subsampled matrix. Linearly upsample the resulting singular vectors \Gammai(\gamma) and Bi(\beta) to the resolution of the actual integration grid. Multiply the singular values \sigmai into Bi(\beta) so that Bi(\beta) \leftarrow \sigmai Bi(\beta). 3. Handle Symmetry and Reuse: Because \beta is parametrized by angle, slices are symmetric around the light direction. For uniform scattering phase functions, I does not depend on the azimuthal angle \alpha. Therefore, the same SVD can be reused for all slices. Compute the SVD once per frame rather than once per slice. 4. Initialize Partial Sum Tree: The algorithm integrates the products of each \Gammai(\gamma) and the visibility function. The tree stores the sum \sum \Gammai(\gamma)V(\gamma, \beta) for each i. Textured Light Sources: If incident radiance \tilde{L}{in} depends on \alpha and \gamma (but not \beta), initialize the tree with the element-wise product \tilde{L}{in}(\alpha, \gamma)\Gammai(\gamma) instead of just \Gammai(\gamma). 5. Integrate and Sum: For each view ray \beta, query the partial sum tree to obtain the accumulated values for each i. The final result is computed as: \text{Result}(\beta) = \sum{i=1}^N Bi(\beta) \times (\text{tree query result for } i) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesvdapproximation(integrandmatrix, numsingularvalues=4, gammares=256, betares=256): # 1. Subsample to 64x64 for SVD computation subsampledmatrix = integrandmatrix[::gammares//64,::betares//64] # 2. Compute SVD using standard linear algebra routine U, S, Vt = svd(subsampledmatrix) # 3. Select top N singular values/vectors Gammasub = U[:,:numsingularvalues] # Shape: (64, N) Bsub = Vt[:numsingularvalues,:] # Shape: (N, 64) sigma = S[:numsingularvalues] # Shape: (N,) # 4. Linearly upsample singular vectors to integration grid resolution def linearupsample1d(vec, newlen): oldlen = len(vec) return [vec[int(i oldlen / newlen)] for i in range(newlen)] Gamma = [[linearupsample1d(Gammasub[r, c], gammares) for c in range(numsingularvalues)] for r in range(gammares)] B = [[linearupsample1d(Bsub[r, c], betares) for c in range(betares)] for r in range(numsingularvalues)] # 5. Multiply singular values into B for i in range(numsingularvalues): B[i] = [B[i][j] sigma[i] for j in range(betares)] return Gamma, B def integratewithpartialsumtree(Gamma, B, N, visibilityintervals, texturedlightradiance=None): # Initialize tree to store N-dimensional vectors # Tree structure supports update and query operations tree = [0.0] (len(visibilityintervals) 4) # Array-based partial sum tree # Determine initialization term if texturedlightradiance is not None: # Lin depends on alpha and gamma, but not beta initterm = [[texturedlightradiance[g] Gamma[g][i] for i in range(N)] for g in range(len(Gamma))] else: initterm = Gamma # Update tree with visibility-weighted terms for g in range(len(visibilityintervals)): for i in range(N): val = initterm[g][i] visibilityintervals[g] updatetree(tree, g, val) # Query the tree for each view ray beta results = [] for b in range(len(B[0])): # Query returns an N-dimensional vector representing sumi (Gammai V) treequeryresult = [querytree(tree, b) for in range(N)] # Final result is sumi Bi(beta) treequeryresult[i] result = sum(B[i][b] treequeryresult[i] for i in range(N)) results.append(result) return results def svd(M): import numpy.linalg U, S, Vt = numpy.linalg.svd(M, fullmatrices=False) return U, S, Vt def updatetree(tree, idx, val): # Standard point update for hierarchical sum tree tree[idx] += val p = (idx + 1) // 2 - 1 while p >= 0: tree[p] += val p = (p + 1) // 2 - 1 def querytree(tree, idx): # Standard interval query for hierarchical sum tree s = 0 i = idx + 1 while i > 0: s += tree[i-1] i -= (i & -i) return s Parameters: N: Number of singular values. N=4 is sufficient for high-quality results in a uniform medium. The magnitude of the 4th singular value never exceeds 1/40th of the 1st, even in extreme configurations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Epipole Singularity: View rays and light rays are parallel at the epipole, causing the rectification mapping derivative ds/d\gamma to go to infinity. This can throw off the SVD. Mitigation: Render results within a small ring (about two degrees) around the epipole using a ray marcher. Run the SVD algorithm on the remainder of the image. Precision: The SVD computation should be performed on a subsampled matrix to avoid numerical instability and high cost, then upsampled. Enables interactive rendering of multiple scattering in non-homogeneous participating media by approximating the scattering phase function using SVD. Solves the discrete transport equation iteratively on GPU hardware. Approximates the multiple scattering integral in volumetric shadowing by decomposing the view-independent part of the integrand using SVD in epipolar coordinates. Reduces complexity from per-pixel to per-slice. Time Complexity: The SVD computation is performed once per frame (due to symmetry), not per slice. The integration cost is reduced from per-pixel to per-slice, allowing massive parallelism. Memory Complexity: The partial sum tree stores N-dimensional vectors. Memory usage scales with N and the size of the integration grid. Performance: N=4 provides high-quality results with minimal performance overhead. The 4th singular value is negligible (magnitude < 1/40th of the 1st). Strengths: Efficient handling of multiple scattering in uniform media. Reuse of SVD across slices reduces computational cost. Limitations: Requires uniform scattering phase function for full SVD reuse. Degenerate at the epipole, requiring special handling. This method was introduced in the paper "A hierarchical volumetric shadow algorithm for single scattering". It builds on the concept of decomposing the integrand into separable functions to enable efficient integration using hierarchical data structures. The use of SVD allows for a low-rank approximation of the integrand, which is crucial for real-time rendering applications. name: SVD-Approximated Iterative Transport Equation for Multiple Scattering
head: Interactive Multiple Scattering with Separable Phase Function, Interactive Rendering of Multiple Scattering in Participating Media Using Separable Phase Function, SVD Factorization for Transport Equation, SVD-based phase function approximation, Separable phase function rendering
body: This method enables interactive rendering of multiple scattering in non-homogeneous participating media by approximating the scattering phase function using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). It solves the discrete transport equation iteratively on GPU hardware, replacing expensive angular integrals with efficient texture lookups. Unlike particle-based methods that require path recalculation upon movement, this grid-based approach allows for dynamic scene rendering without recomputing scattering paths. Inputs: Density Texture: A 3D texture storing the density values \rho(x) at each point in the volume. Emission Density: Le(x, \omega0), the emitted radiance at position x and direction \omega0. Phase Function Parameters: The anisotropy factor g for the Henyey-Greenstein phase function. Precomputed Textures: Incident-Direction Texture: 2D texture storing \xik uk(\omega0). Outgoing-Direction Texture: 2D texture storing \xik vk(\omegai). Initial Radiance: L0(x, \omega0), typically from single scattering or the previous frame's solution. Outputs: Radiance Texture: A 3D texture storing the converged radiance L(x, \omega0) for all positions and directions. The method relies on specific texture layouts to facilitate GPU-based iteration: 1. Incident-Direction Texture: A 2D texture indexed by column k \in \{1, \dots, N\} (SVD term index) and row i \in \{1, \dots, D\} (direction index). It stores values \xik uk(\omega0). 2. Outgoing-Direction Texture: A 2D texture indexed by column k \in \{1, \dots, N\} and row i \in \{1, \dots, D\}. It stores values \xik vk(\omegai). 3. Radiance Texture: A flat 3D texture storing Ln(x, \omegad) for the current iteration n. 4. Temporary Outgoing Texture: A flat 3D texture used to accumulate \sum{d=1}^{D} L{n+1}(x, \omegad) \xik vk(\omegad) for each k during the direction loop. The differential transport equation for radiance L is: \frac{dL(x, \omega0)}{dx} = \kappaa(x)Le(x, \omega0) - \kappaa(x)L(x, \omega0) - \kappas(x)L(x, \omega0) + \frac{\kappas(x)}{4\pi} \int{\Omega} L(x, \omegai)p(\omega0, \omegai)d\sigma{\omegai} Where \kappaa(x) is the absorption coefficient, \kappas(x) is the scattering coefficient, \kappat(x) = \kappaa(x) + \kappas(x) is the extinction coefficient, Le(x, \omega0) is the emission density, and p(\omega0, \omegai) is the phase function. The Henyey-Greenstein (HG) phase function is defined as: p(\theta) = \frac{1}{4\pi} \frac{1-g^2}{(1+g^2-2g\cos\theta)^{3/2}} Where g \in (-1, 1) is the asymmetry parameter and \theta is the angle between incident direction \omegai and outgoing direction \omega0. The SVD approximation of the phase function is: p(\omega0, \omegai) \approx \sum{k=1}^{N} \xik uk(\omega0) vk(\omegai) Where N is the number of retained terms, \xik are the singular values, and uk, vk are the left and right singular vectors, respectively. The discrete transport equation, solved iteratively, is: L{n+1}(x+dx, \omega0) \approx Ln(x, \omega0) + \kappaa(x)Le(x, \omega0)dx - \kappat(x)Ln(x, \omega0)dx + \frac{\kappas(x)}{4\pi D} \sum{d=1}^{D} Ln(x, \omegad) p(\omega0, \omegad)dx Substituting the SVD approximation into the in-scattering term transforms the equation to: L{n+1}(x+dx, \omega0) \approx Ln(x, \omega0) + \kappaa(x)Le(x, \omega0)dx - \kappat(x)Ln(x, \omega0)dx + \frac{\kappas(x)}{4\pi} \sum{k=1}^{N} \xik uk(\omega0) \left[ \sum{d=1}^{D} Ln(x, \omegad) \xik vk(\omegad) \right] dx N (SVD Terms): Number of terms in the SVD approximation. Typical values are 8 or 24. For g=0.5, 24 terms yield approximately 10% RMSE. Higher g requires more terms. D (Directions): Number of discrete directions used to discretize the angular domain. Typical values are 128 or 256. g (Anisotropy): The asymmetry factor of the HG phase function. Typical value is 0.5. Albedo: Single-scattering albedo \kappas / \kappat. Typical value is 0.9. dx: Step size along the ray. The following pseudocode describes the logic within the fragment program for a single direction d and the accumulation logic. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. N = 24 # Number of SVD terms D = 128 # Number of directions dx = 1.0 # Step size (normalized) def fragmentprogram(currentdirectionindex d, currentiteration n): wd = getdirectionfromindex(d) # Retrieve physical coefficients from Density Texture rho = sample3dtexture(DensityTexture, currentposition) kappaa = rho absorptioncoefficientconstant # kappas = rho scatteringcoefficientconstant # kappat = kappaa + kappas # Retrieve emission Le = sampleemission(currentposition, wd) # Retrieve previous radiance Ln(x, wd) Lnwd = sampleradiance(RadianceTexture, currentposition, wd) # Calculate in-scattering sum using precomputed Outgoing Texture from iteration n inscatteringsum = 0.0 for k in range(1, N + 1): ucoeff = sample2dtexture(IncidentTexture, k, getdirectionindex(wd)) outgoingsum = sample3dtexture(OutgoingTexture, currentposition, k) inscatteringsum += ucoeff outgoingsum # Update Radiance Lnplus1wd = Lnwd + kappaa Le dx - kappat Lnwd dx + (kappas / (4.0 3.14159265)) inscatteringsum dx # Write L{n+1}(x, wd) to Radiance Texture writeradiance(RadianceTexture, currentposition, wd, Lnplus1wd) # Accumulate for the NEXT iteration's Outgoing Texture for k in range(1, N + 1): vcoeff = sample2dtexture(OutgoingTexture, k, getdirectionindex(wd)) contribution = Lnplus1wd vcoeff addtotexture(TempOutgoingTexture, currentposition, k, contribution) def renderiteration(n): cleartexture(TempOutgoingTexture) for d in range(1, D + 1): fragmentprogram(d, n) swaptextures(OutgoingTexture, TempOutgoingTexture) Approximation Error: The SVD approximation generally yields smaller reconstructed values than the original phase function, leading to darker rendered images, especially in thick parts of the medium. Convergence in Dynamic Scenes: For highly dynamic scenes, the transport equation may not converge before the scene changes, causing errors to accumulate. Precision: The method relies on flat 3D textures. Precision issues may arise from texture sampling interpolation if not handled carefully. Boundary Conditions: The method assumes a volume grid. Boundary conditions for the volume must be defined, typically as zero radiance outside the volume. Time Complexity: Per iteration: O(D \cdot N \cdot V), where V is the number of voxels. The SVD approximation reduces the complexity of the in-scattering integral from O(D^2) to O(D \cdot N) per voxel per iteration, assuming N \ll D. Memory Complexity: O(V \cdot D) for the Radiance Texture. O(V \cdot N) for the Outgoing and Temporary Outgoing Textures. O(N \cdot D) for the Incident and Outgoing Direction Textures (negligible compared to volume textures). Measured Performance: On an NV7800GT graphics card with 64x64x64 volume resolution and D=128, the scene is simulated at 2fps. With D=256, 1.5fps is achieved. Compared to the unfactorized model (no SVD), this method achieves a rendering speed of 1.5fps vs 0.2fps on the same hardware (NV7800GT, 64x64x64 resolution, D=256). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Interactive rendering rates; handles dynamic scenes; little constraints on lighting conditions compared to other near real-time algorithms like Harris (2001) and Sloan (2002). Limitations: Approximation error leads to darker images; convergence issues in highly dynamic scenes; accuracy depends on N and g. When to Use: Use for interactive rendering of multiple scattering in participating media where dynamic scenes are required and high accuracy is not critical. Avoid for highly dynamic scenes where convergence cannot be achieved, or when precise physical accuracy of the phase function is required. Origin: The method was proposed by Gong Z., Ren Z., Wang Z., and Peng Q. in 2007. It is based on the application of Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to the scattering phase function in the transport equation. History and Development: Separable decomposition techniques were introduced by Kautz (1999) for BRDF rendering. Wang (2004) and Liu (2004) applied SVD to glossy BRDFs in PRT. Wang (2005) introduced SVD to the approximation of BSSRDFs by separating the Henyey-Greenstein phase function. This method extends these ideas to interactive multiple scattering in participating media. Usage: Implemented in a Direct3D/HLSL environment. Interactive Rendering of Multiple Scattering in Participating Media Using Separable Phase Function, https://www.scitepress.org/PublishedPapers/2007/20840/, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Epipolar Coordinate Integral Approximation
head: SVD-based integrand approximation
body: This method approximates the multiple scattering integral in volumetric shadowing by decomposing the view-independent part of the integrand using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) in epipolar coordinates. It reduces the computational cost from per-pixel to per-slice by processing each camera ray independently, which enables massive parallelism compared to methods that maintain interdependent partial sum trees across rays. It builds on Variation Along and Across Light Rays (SVD Approximation). Inputs: Camera depth map (unrectified). Light depth map (rectified into epipolar coordinates, stored as shadow map S). Volume density \sigmat, scattering coefficient \sigmas, phase function \rho, and incoming light L{\text{in}}. Number of singular vectors N (typically 4). Outputs: Radiance L(\alpha, \beta) for each camera pixel (\alpha, \beta). Data Structures: Rectified Shadow Map S: A 2D array where S[\alpha, \gamma] stores the \beta coordinate (height) of the camera ray at which the light ray (\alpha, \gamma) is blocked. Singular Value Decomposition Components: Left singular vectors Bi(\beta) and right singular vectors \Gammai(\gamma), precomputed once per frame on the CPU. Prefix Sum Tables: For each singular vector i \in [1, N], a 1D prefix sum table of \Gammai(\gamma) \Delta \gamma is computed. Steps: 1. Change of Variables: Rewrite the scattering integral in epipolar coordinates (\alpha, \beta, \gamma). The radiance L(\alpha, \beta) for a camera ray defined by (\alpha, \beta) is: L(\alpha, \beta) = \int0^{D(\alpha, \beta)} e^{-\sigmat s(\beta, \gamma)} V(\alpha, \beta, \gamma) \sigmas \rho(\beta, \gamma) L{\text{in}}(\beta, \gamma) \frac{ds}{d\gamma} d\gamma where D(\alpha, \beta) is the \gamma coordinate of the light ray at which the camera ray (\alpha, \beta) is blocked. 2. Separate Visibility: Define the view-independent integrand \mathcal{I}(\beta, \gamma) containing all terms except visibility V: \mathcal{I}(\beta, \gamma) = e^{-\sigmat s(\beta, \gamma)} \sigmas \rho(\beta, \gamma) L{\text{in}}(\beta, \gamma) \frac{ds}{d\gamma} The integral becomes: L(\alpha, \beta) = \int0^{D(\alpha, \beta)} V(\alpha, \beta, \gamma) \mathcal{I}(\beta, \gamma) d\gamma 3. SVD Approximation: Sample \mathcal{I}(\beta, \gamma) on a 64 \times 64 grid. Compute the SVD of this sampled matrix on the CPU. Select the top N singular values and their corresponding left singular vectors Bi(\beta) and right singular vectors \Gammai(\gamma). Approximate the integrand as: \mathcal{I}(\beta, \gamma) \approx \sum{i=1}^N Bi(\beta) \Gammai(\gamma) Substitute this into the integral: L(\alpha, \beta) \approx \sum{i=1}^N \left( Bi(\beta) \int0^{D(\alpha, \beta)} V(\alpha, \beta, \gamma) \Gammai(\gamma) d\gamma \right) 4. Discretization and Visibility: Approximate the inner integral as a Riemann sum. Visibility V(\alpha, \beta, \gamma) is 1 if the point is lit, 0 otherwise. In epipolar coordinates, a point (\alpha, \beta, \gamma) is lit if \gamma < D(\alpha, \beta) and S[\alpha, \gamma] > \beta. The radiance is: L(\alpha, \beta) \approx \sum{i=1}^N \left( Bi(\beta) \sum{\substack{\gamma < D(\alpha, \beta) \\ S[\alpha, \gamma] > \beta}} \Gammai(\gamma) \Delta \gamma \right) 5. Parallel Evaluation: For each camera ray (\alpha, \beta), identify the lit segments along \gamma where S[\alpha, \gamma] > \beta. Use 1D min-max mipmaps to accelerate finding these segments. Compute the sum over each segment using the precomputed prefix sum tables for \Gammai(\gamma) \Delta \gamma. Multiply by Bi(\beta) and sum over i=1 \dots N. Parameters: N: Number of singular vectors. Typical value: 4. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The camera depth map does not need to be rectified, simplifying the pipeline. Precision issues may arise if the SVD approximation error is high for complex lighting; however, smooth variation of \mathcal{I} usually allows small N to suffice. Time Complexity: Reduces computational cost from per-pixel to per-slice. Instead of maintaining a partial sum tree for each \beta (as in incremental integration), it computes only N prefix sum tables per frame. Each ray is processed independently, enabling massive parallelism on the GPU. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the rectified shadow map, N prefix sum tables, and the SVD components. The SVD computation is done on the CPU once per frame. Strengths: Massive parallelism due to independent ray processing; reduced computational overhead compared to incremental integration. Limitations: Approximation error depends on the number of singular vectors N and the smoothness of the integrand. This method is part of the "Real-Time Volumetric Shadows using 1D Min-Max Mipmaps" technique, which uses epipolar coordinates and SVD to approximate multiple scattering in participating media. It was introduced by to address the performance bottlenecks of previous real-time volumetric shadowing methods. name: Asymmetric Lobe Approximation
body: Asymmetric Lobe Approximation is a method for accelerating multiple scattering calculations in participating media by replacing full spherical coordinate lobes with asymmetric lobes. It reduces the computational cost of evaluating full angular scattering distributions by focusing on the dominant multiple scattering component, which is less sensitive to angular precision than double scattering. It differs from sibling methods like Beam Spreading Width Model and PSF-based Multiple Scattering Rendering by explicitly simplifying the angular representation of the scattering lobe itself rather than just the spatial spread or point spread function. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Full spherical coordinate scattering lobes (phase functions) for light transport interactions. Output: Asymmetric 1D lobe functions that retain the essential energy distribution for multiple scattering events. Data Structures: The method replaces the full spherical coordinate lobe representation with an asymmetric 1D function representation. The exact bit-packing or memory layout is not specified in the sources. Steps: 1. Identify the Scattering Lobe: Extract the full spherical coordinate scattering lobe for the current light transport interaction. 2. Apply Asymmetric Approximation: Replace the full spherical lobe with an asymmetric 1D function to reduce computational cost. 3. Evaluate for Multiple Scattering: Use the approximated 1D lobe in the light transport simulation, specifically targeting multiple scattering events. Formulas: The sources do not provide a specific mathematical formula for the asymmetric 1D function itself, only describing it as a replacement for the full spherical lobe. Parameters: Approximation Type: Asymmetric 1D. Target: Multiple scattering. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Double Scattering: The approximation is less accurate for double scattering, which has a more pronounced elliptic shape. PSNR Impact: There is a small decrease in Peak Signal to Noise Ratio (PSNR) due to the approximation, but the visual impact is not visible in rendered images because the method focuses on multiple scattering. Mean-Free-Path (MFP): The method works better for smaller mean-free-path (more opaque materials) where more scatter events are saved, but provides quality over the entire MFP range. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def asymmetriclobeapproximation(sphericallobe): """ Approximates a full spherical scattering lobe with an asymmetric 1D function. Args: sphericallobe: The original scattering lobe data structure defined over spherical coordinates. Returns: approximated1dlobe: The simplified 1D asymmetric lobe function. """ # Step 1: Identify the scattering lobe # Extract angular dependencies from the full spherical coordinate representation. angles = sphericallobe.angles weights = sphericallobe.weights # Step 2: Apply Asymmetric Approximation # Replace the full spherical lobe with an asymmetric 1D function. # The exact mathematical transformation is not specified in the sources. # In practice, this involves projecting or integrating angular dependencies # to reduce dimensionality while preserving energy distribution. # Not given in the sources. approximated1dlobe = None # Step 3: Evaluate for Multiple Scattering # Return the approximated lobe for use in the light transport simulation. return approximated1dlobe Integral Lobe Encoding (ILE) is a technique to featurize incoming rays within a roughness-adaptive specular lobe to reduce computational cost in neural illumination fields. It constructs a positional encoding of all coordinates within a specular lobe around the reflection direction lr, using a multivariate Gaussian to approximate the integration over conical frustums. It is chosen when efficient learning of high-frequency variations related to roughness is required in a NeRF-style environment. It differs from standard positional encoding by incorporating the lobe width and vMF distribution correlated to the incoming direction. Definition: ILE featurizes incoming rays within a roughness-adaptive specular lobe. It uses a multivariate Gaussian to approximate the integration over conical frustums. Steps: 1. Define the specular lobe based on the reflection direction lr and material roughness \rho. 2. Divide the specular lobe into a series of conical frustums. 3. Compute the mean (\mu) and covariance (\Sigma) of the conical frustum obtained by surface point xs and reflection direction lr. 4. Use the features encoded by ILE as input to the ambient MLP network R to output the density and color of the NeIF. Formula: The ILE is formulated as a sum of sinusoids weighted by the Gaussian: ILE = \left\{ \sin(\mu) \exp(-2\ell^{-1}) \text{diag}(\Sigma(\rho)) \right\}{\ell=0}^{L-1} combined with cosine terms, where \Sigma(\rho) is decided by material roughness. Parameters: lr: Reflection direction (center axis of the lobe). \rho: Material roughness (controls angular width). xs: Surface point. L: Number of sinusoidal frequencies. Time and Memory Complexity: The sources do not provide explicit time or memory complexity formulas for Asymmetric Lobe Approximation. For Integral Lobe Encoding, the method reduces computational cost by featurizing rays within a lobe, but specific complexity metrics are not given. Measured Performance: Asymmetric Lobe Approximation: In the UPBP method, using the approximation resulted in a rendering time of 53s with a PSNR of 34.54, compared to 180s with a PSNR of 37.4 for the full 4D lobe. The approximation provides better quality over the entire mean-free-path range. Integral Lobe Encoding: The sources do not provide specific performance metrics for ILE, only stating it reduces computational cost. Scaling: The method provides consistent quality over the entire mean-free-path range. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significant speedup with visually imperceptible quality loss for multiple scattering. Works well for smaller mean-free-path materials. Limitations: Small decrease in PSNR. Less accurate for double scattering due to its pronounced elliptic shape. When to Use: Use Asymmetric Lobe Approximation when real-time or rapid light simulation in participating media is required, and the focus is on multiple scattering effects. Use Integral Lobe Encoding when training neural illumination fields with rough materials to efficiently capture high-frequency variations. Origin: Asymmetric Lobe Approximation was introduced in the paper "Precomputed Multiple Scattering for Rapid Light Simulation in Participating Media". Integral Lobe Encoding was introduced in "A Pre-convolved Representation for Plug-and-Play Neural Illumination Fields". History and Development: Asymmetric Lobe Approximation is part of the UPBP (Unbiased Path-Based Precomputation) method for light simulation in participating media. Integral Lobe Encoding is part of a neural illumination field framework that combines material properties and NeIF radiance fields. Where it is Used: Asymmetric Lobe Approximation is used in rapid light simulation for participating media. Integral Lobe Encoding is used in photo-realistic rendering and view synthesis applications involving neural rendering. name: MIP map filtering for multiple scattering
head: Elek et al. MIP map filtering, Filtering-based real-time multiple scattering, MIP map Gaussian blurring, Real-time GPU filtering method
body: This method efficiently approximates multiple-scattering light transport in non-homogeneous, analytically integrable participating media by applying Gaussian blurring via MIP maps. It solves the high computational cost of neighborhood filtering in screen-space rendering, enabling real-time performance on GPUs by reducing time complexity from O(n^4) to O(n^2 \log2 n). Unlike naive gathering which iterates over a fixed neighborhood for every pixel, this approach leverages hierarchical image representations to accumulate contributions across scales. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A screen-space image representing single-scattering or vacuum-rendered lighting, where each pixel is treated as an independent light source. Input: A density function \varrho(x) that is analytically integrable, allowing for non-homogeneous media (e.g., exponential density variations). Output: The filtered image after applying MIP map convolution. Data Structures: MIP Map Pyramid: A set of images Lk where L0 has resolution n \times n. Higher levels Lk have resolutions decreasing exponentially until 1 \times 1, yielding a total of O(\log2 n) levels. Kernel: A constant-sized Gaussian kernel G used for convolution at each level. Parameters: n: Image resolution (width or height). m: Neighborhood radius. In HDR images where a pixel blurs into the whole image, m = n. Target Performance: Higher than 25 FPS at 1280x720 resolution (HD). Steps: 1. Generate MIP Map Pyramid: Construct the MIP map levels L0 to L{max} from the input image. The total number of levels is O(\log2 n). 2. Iterate Levels: For each MIP map level k > 0: a. Perform convolution of the current level's image with the constant-sized Gaussian kernel G. b. For each pixel in the level, iterate through the constant-sized neighborhood defined by the kernel. c. Accumulate weighted contributions from the neighborhood pixels. 3. Handle Non-Homogeneous Media: Use analytically integrable density functions (e.g., derived from the barometric formula) to calculate transmittance efficiently between points. Formulas: Barometric Formula for Pressure: Used to derive density functions for non-homogeneous media: p(z) = p(0) \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{mgz}{kT}\right) Where: p(z) is pressure at altitude z. p(0) is pressure at z=0. m is molecular mass. g is gravitational constant. k is Boltzmann constant. T is temperature. Density \varrho(z) is derived similarly, as it is directly related to pressure. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def mipmapfiltering(inputimage, kernelradius): """ Applies MIP map filtering for multiple scattering. Args: inputimage: 2D list of floats, resolution n x n. kernelradius: Half-width of the constant-sized Gaussian kernel G. Returns: filteredimage: Resulting multiple-scattering approximation. """ n = len(inputimage) # Step 1: Generate MIP Map Pyramid miplevels = [inputimage] current = inputimage while len(current) > 1: h, w = len(current), len(current[0]) nexth, nextw = (h + 1) // 2, (w + 1) // 2 nextlevel = [[0.0] nextw for in range(nexth)] for i in range(0, h, 2): for j in range(0, w, 2): val = 0.0 count = 0 for di in range(2): for dj in range(2): if i + di < h and j + dj < w: val += current[i + di][j + dj] count += 1 if count > 0: nextlevel[i // 2][j // 2] = val / count miplevels.append(nextlevel) current = nextlevel # Step 2: Iterate Levels and Convolve # The source describes convolving each level k > 0 with a constant kernel G # and accumulating weighted contributions. filteredimage = [[0.0] n for in range(n)] halfk = kernelradius for k in range(1, len(miplevels)): level = miplevels[k] h, w = len(level), len(level[0]) blurredlevel = [[0.0] w for in range(h)] for i in range(h): for j in range(w): contribution = 0.0 for di in range(-halfk, halfk + 1): for dj in range(-halfk, halfk + 1): ni, nj = i + di, j + dj # Clamp boundaries ni = max(0, min(ni, h - 1)) nj = max(0, min(nj, w - 1)) weight = gaussianweight(di, dj, kernelradius) contribution += level[ni][nj] weight blurredlevel[i][j] = contribution # Upsample blurred level back to original resolution for accumulation upscaled = upscaletooriginal(blurredlevel, n) for i in range(n): for j in range(n): filteredimage[i][j] += upscaled[i][j] return filteredimage def gaussianweight(dx, dy, radius): """Computes Gaussian weight for a given offset.""" sigma = radius / 2.0 exponent = -((dx 2 + dy 2) / (2 sigma 2)) return math.exp(exponent) def upscaletooriginal(blurredlevel, targetn): """Bilinear upsampling to match original resolution n x n.""" h, w = len(blurredlevel), len(blurredlevel[0]) scaleh = targetn / h scalew = targetn / w upscaled = [[0.0] targetn for in range(targetn)] for i in range(targetn): for j in range(targetn): srci = i / scaleh srcj = j / scalew i0, i1 = int(math.floor(srci)), int(math.ceil(srci)) j0, j1 = int(math.floor(srcj)), int(math.ceil(srcj)) i0, i1 = max(0, min(i0, h - 1)), max(0, min(i1, h - 1)) j0, j1 = max(0, min(j0, w - 1)), max(0, min(j1, w - 1)) fi, fj = srci - i0, srcj - j0 val = ((1 - fi) (1 - fj) blurredlevel[i0][j0] + fi (1 - fj) blurredlevel[i1][j0] + (1 - fi) fj blurredlevel[i0][j1] + fi fj blurredlevel[i1][j1]) upscaled[i][j] = val return upscaled Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: The pseudocode assumes clamping for neighborhood iteration; the source does not specify. Non-Analytic Densities: The method requires analytically integrable density functions; arbitrary density functions cannot be handled efficiently. Artifacts: While MIP map filtering reduces artifacts compared to naive gathering, some visual artifacts may still be present, though significantly reduced. Screen-Space Approximation: The method treats every pixel as an independent light source, disregarding attenuation or scattering before surface reflection for simplicity. Time Complexity: O(n^2 \log2 n), where n is the image resolution. This is a significant improvement over naive gathering's O(n^4) to O(n^6) for HDR images where m=n. Memory Complexity: O(n^2) for storing the MIP map pyramid, as the sum of geometric series n^2 + (n/2)^2 + \dots converges to O(n^2). Measured Performance: On a GeForce GTX 760M, the method achieved 2 milliseconds per frame for a sample image, compared to 30 seconds for the gathering algorithm and 15 hours for path-tracing reference. Target Performance: Higher than 25 FPS at 1280x720 resolution (HD). Strengths: Real-time performance on GPUs; handles non-homogeneous media; significantly faster than naive gathering. Limitations: Requires analytically integrable density functions; screen-space approach disregards attenuation/scattering before surface reflection; potential for residual visual artifacts compared to more accurate but slower methods. When to Use: Real-time rendering of multiple scattering in non-homogeneous media where performance is critical and approximate results are acceptable. When Not to Use: When high accuracy is required (e.g., offline rendering), or when density functions are not analytically integrable. Origin: Proposed by Elek et al. [2013] as a solution to reduce visual artifacts and computational cost in multiple-scattering light transport. History: The method is part of a broader effort to enable real-time rendering of complex light transport effects in participating media. It builds on the concept of treating screen-space pixels as light sources and applying filtering to approximate multiple scattering. Usage: Implemented in fragment shaders for GPU execution, tested on hardware like the GeForce GTX 760M. It is used in contexts requiring real-time performance, such as video games or interactive applications, where traditional path-tracing is too slow. name: Multiple Scattering Table Representation
head: 4D Look-up Table, Radiance table
body: This method stores precomputed double and multiple scattering radiance in a regularly sampled 4D structure to serve as an intermediate representation for neural network-based light transport. It solves the problem of expensive per-sample neural network queries by allowing fast table lookups and accumulation. It differs from its siblings by explicitly discretizing the spatial (z, \rho) and angular (\theta, \phi) domains into a fixed grid with specific culling and accumulation steps, whereas variants like Precomputed Multiple Scattering Table may use different discretizations or Variation Along and Across Light Rays (SVD Approximation) use low-rank decompositions. Inputs: Material properties (scattering coefficients, phase function parameters). Precomputed neural network model for radiance estimation. Outputs: A 1D GPU buffer containing the 4D radiance table. A culling mask indicating valid lobes. Data Structures: The table is a 4D structure indexed by (z, \rho, \theta, \phi), stored as a 1D buffer on the GPU. Spatial Domain: z (axial distance) and \rho (radial distance) are sampled per mean-free path (mfp). The maximum spatial distance is 32 mfp. Angular Domain: \theta and \phi are sampled every 10 degrees. Storage: The 4D array is flattened into a 1D buffer. Indices are mapped linearly. Steps: 1. Extraction: Extract precomputed table data from the neural network model for the given material. This involves computing the double and multiple scattering radiance for each grid point. 2. Summation: Sum the double and multiple scattering tables to form the total scattering radiance table. 3. Culling: For each cell (lobe) in the table, check the precomputed radiance values. If 90% of the directions in the lobe have low radiance values, discard the lobe (mark it as invalid/culled) to reduce memory and access costs. 4. Accumulation (Segment-to-Segment): To encode camera ray length, accumulate the contribution along the direction (\thetai, \phii) with a length of 5 \times \text{mfp}. This transforms the segment-to-point table into a segment-to-segment table. This step is accelerated using the GPU. 5. Rendering Query: During rendering, query the table for the current ray's parameters. Interpolate the multiple scattering radiance from the table and add it to direct illumination and single scattering. Formulas: Culling Condition: Let L(\theta, \phi) be the radiance for a given lobe. If \frac{\text{count}(\theta, \phi: L(\theta, \phi) < \epsilon)}{\text{total directions}} \ge 0.9, the lobe is discarded. Accumulation Length: L{acc} = 5 \times \text{mfp}. Parameters: Max spatial distance: 32 mfp. Angular sampling: 10 degrees. Culling threshold: 90% of directions in lobe must have low radiance. Accumulation length: 5 \times \text{mfp}. Pitfalls: Training the Segment-to-Segment contribution directly with a neural network tends to overestimate contributions. Precision issues may arise if the 1D buffer indexing is not carefully managed for the 4D structure. A table representing multiple scattering from a point (zi, \rhoi) with direction (\thetai, \phii) and length 5 \times \text{mfp}, created by accumulating contributions along the direction. It is chosen when the camera ray length needs to be encoded into the scattering approximation. The accumulation is performed by summing contributions along the direction (\thetai, \phii) with length 5 \times \text{mfp}. A key pitfall is that training this table directly with a neural network tends to overestimate contributions. Time Complexity: Query time is O(1) for table lookup, but requires interpolation. Precomputation involves neural network inference and GPU accumulation. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the 4D grid size (32 \times \text{mfp} spatial, 36 \times 36 angular). Culling reduces effective memory usage. Performance: Reduces the cost of per-sample neural network computations (3 matrix multiplications and trigonometric evaluations per query). Strengths: Fast rendering queries; reduces expensive neural network calls. Limitations: Fixed resolution limits accuracy; culling may remove valid data if thresholds are too aggressive. When to use: When real-time performance is critical and material properties are fixed. When not to use: When dynamic materials or varying mfp are required without recomputing the table. Originated in the work on Interactive Simulation of Scattering Effects in Participating Media Using a Neural Network Model. It builds on Virtual Ray Lights (VRL). The method was developed to address the high computational cost of neural network-based light transport simulation by precomputing and storing scattering data in a structured format. Interactive Simulation of Scattering Effects in Participating Media Using a Neural Network Model, https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2019.2963015, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Spherical Harmonic Volumetric Visibility
head: SH Volumetric Visibility, Spherical Harmonics in Volume Rendering
body: Spherical Harmonic Volumetric Visibility is a real-time dynamic lighting technique for direct volume rendering that encodes local and global volumetric visibility using spherical harmonic basis functions. It solves the problem of computing incident radiance in participating media by representing light source radiance and transparency (visibility) as basis functions, allowing dynamic light changes without expensive visibility updates. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly compressing the directional occlusion and lighting information into spherical harmonics stored in a multiresolution grid, reducing the rendering overhead to a few texture lookups and scalar products. Unlike Voxel Cone Tracing which uses geometric cones, or Froxel-based Volumetric Rendering which uses spatial clustering, this method relies on frequency-domain representation of visibility. Inputs: Volume density data \rho(\mathbf{x}). Light source definitions (directional, point, or environment maps). Transfer function mapping density to color/opacity. Clip planes (if used). Outputs: Rendered image with dynamic volumetric illumination. Data Structures: Multiresolution Grid: A hierarchical data structure (e.g., octree or mipmapped 3D texture) storing spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients for visibility. The grid allows sampling at different levels of detail (LOD), where the LOD decreases as the sampling distance from the voxel increases. SH Coefficients: For each voxel, a vector of coefficients representing the visibility function. The number of coefficients determines the frequency of the representation. Method Steps: 1. Precomputation of Local Visibility: For each voxel, compute local visibility over a small neighborhood. Send rays uniformly distributed on the sphere from the voxel center. Evaluate visibility along these rays over the small neighborhood. Note: This step is expensive if the transfer function or clip planes change. 2. Precomputation of Global Visibility: Perform piecewise integration of the local visibility to compute global visibility. Traverse the multiresolution data structure with increasing step sizes, sampling at decreasing LODs as distance from the voxel increases. Store the resulting spherical harmonic coefficients in the multiresolution grid. 3. Light Source Representation: Represent the light source radiance Ll using spherical harmonics. For dynamic lights, the light source representation must be recomputed or rotated, which is generally fast and can be performed in real-time. 4. Rendering (Ray-casting): During ray-casting, sample the multiresolution grid at the current ray position. Retrieve the precomputed SH coefficients for visibility. Compute the spherical integral over the product of the area light source and voxel occlusion efficiently using the precomputed occlusion information. Use a modified spherical harmonic projection approach tailored for volume rendering to realize non cone-shaped phase functions. The final incident radiance is computed via dot products between the light SH coefficients and the visibility SH coefficients. Formulas: The incident radiance Li is computed by projecting the product of light radiance and visibility onto the SH basis. Let V(\omega) be the visibility function and L(\omega) be the light radiance. The SH coefficients of the visibility cV and light cL are used to compute the integral: \int{S^2} V(\omega) L(\omega) d\omega \approx \sum{l,m} c{V,l,m} \cdot c{L,l,m} where l is the degree and m is the order of the spherical harmonics. Note: The exact projection formula for non-cone-shaped phase functions is described in but not explicitly detailed in the provided notes. Parameters: SH Degree: Determines the number of coefficients. Higher frequencies allow better accuracy but increase storage and computation. LOD Levels: The number of levels in the multiresolution grid. Neighborhood Size: The size of the local neighborhood for local visibility computation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Transfer Function Changes: Visibility must be recomputed when the transfer function changes, which is expensive. Clip Plane Changes: Visibility must be recomputed when clip planes change, which is expensive. Light Source Position: Light sources are generally constrained to be outside the volume, unless local visibility is used. Storage Requirements: High memory consumption due to storing SH coefficients for each voxel. An extra 3D texture for the SAT (Spherical Attenuation Texture) can be of lower resolution than the volume data. Accuracy Limits: Storage and computation time limit the accuracy, restricting illumination to low-frequency effects. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def precomputevisibility(volumedata, transferfunction, clipplanes, lightsources): shgrid = MultiresolutionGrid() for voxel in volumedata: # 1. Compute Local Visibility # Send rays uniformly distributed on the sphere over a small neighborhood localvisibilitycoeffs = computelocalvisibility(voxel, volumedata, transferfunction, clipplanes) # 2. Compute Global Visibility via Piecewise Integration # Traverse multiresolution structure with increasing step size, decreasing LOD globalvisibilitycoeffs = computeglobalvisibility(localvisibilitycoeffs, shgrid) # 3. Store Coefficients shgrid.set(voxel.position, globalvisibilitycoeffs) return shgrid def computelocalvisibility(voxel, volumedata, transferfunction, clipplanes): # Send rays uniformly distributed on the sphere directions = getuniformraysonsphere() occlusionsamples = [] for dir in directions: # Evaluate visibility along ray direction over small neighborhood occlusion = evaluatevisibilityalongdirection(voxel, dir, volumedata, transferfunction, clipplanes) occlusionsamples.append(occlusion) # Project samples to SH coefficients return projecttosh(occlusionsamples) def computeglobalvisibility(localvisibilitycoeffs, shgrid): # Piecewise integration of local visibility to compute global visibility # Sources do not specify the exact piecewise integration algorithm for global visibility. globalvisibility = localvisibilitycoeffs[:] #... integration logic... return globalvisibility def renderraycasting(volumedata, shgrid, lightsources): for pixel in pixels: rayorigin, raydirection = generateray(pixel) t = 0.0 step = getstepsize() accumulatedradiance = 0.0 # Use midpoint sampling to avoid boundary artifacts and fix accumulation errors while t < volumeboundary(rayorigin, raydirection): pos = rayorigin + raydirection (t + step / 2) # Sample volume and retrieve precomputed SH visibility coefficients visibilitycoeffs = shgrid.get(pos) lightcoeffs = getlightshcoefficients(lightsources, pos) # Compute incident radiance via dot product incidentradiance = dotproduct(visibilitycoeffs, lightcoeffs) # Integrate radiance along ray accumulatedradiance += integrateradiance(incidentradiance, step) t += step return accumulatedradiance A two-step, GPU-friendly technique that estimates spherical scattered radiance, projects it into SH, and uses it for single scattering. It sets itself apart by splitting the scattered radiance integral into volume-independent and volume-dependent factors to reduce the triple product cost to a dot product. Encodes full spherical irradiance information using SH basis functions for surface lighting. It sets itself apart by focusing on surface normal-dependent irradiance rather than volumetric light transport. Encodes directional volumetric visibility using SH basis functions. It sets itself apart by encoding the absence of light (occlusion) in the frequency domain. Time Complexity: Interactive rendering time, requiring only 1-4 extra texture lookups and scalar products per voxel. Precomputation of visibility is expensive, especially when the transfer function or clip planes change. Memory Complexity: High memory requirements as each SH coefficient needs to be stored for the visibility in the volume. An extra 3D texture for SAT is required, which can be of lower resolution than the volume data. Strengths: Supports dynamic light changes without expensive visibility updates. Supports an arbitrary number of dynamic directional light sources, environment maps, area lights, and point lights. Allows switching between local and global visibility during rendering. Limitations: Restricted to low-frequency illumination effects due to storage and computation limits. Light sources are generally constrained to be outside the volume. Visibility recomputation is expensive when transfer functions or clip planes change. When to Use: Real-time dynamic lighting in direct volume rendering where light sources are dynamic and outside the volume. When Not to Use: When high-frequency lighting effects are required, or when the transfer function/clip planes change frequently. The method was developed by Kronander et al. in 2011 to achieve real-time dynamic lighting in direct volume rendering by encoding local and global volumetric visibility using spherical harmonic basis functions stored in a multiresolution grid. It builds on earlier work by Ritschel (2007) for spherical harmonic projection and Ljung et al. (2006) for sparse volume representation. The technique allows for the support of directional lights, point lights, and environment maps. It is used in applications requiring interactive volume rendering with advanced light setups. name: Real-Time Image-Based Volume Lighting
body: Real-Time Image-Based Volume Lighting is a two-step, GPU-friendly technique for the real-time rendering of heterogeneous participating media under distant environment lighting. It estimates spherical scattered radiance at discrete points in the medium, projects this function into spherical harmonics (SH), and uses this cached information to compute single scattering via ray-marching. It sets itself apart from its parent Spherical Harmonic Volumetric Visibility by explicitly splitting the scattered radiance integral into a volume-independent factor and a volume-dependent factor to reduce the computational cost of the triple product inherent in SH-based scattering to a simple dot product. Unlike Spherical Harmonics Irradiance Encoding, which typically encodes irradiance at surface points, this method encodes scattered radiance within the volume itself to handle self-shadowing and heterogeneous density. Inputs: Heterogeneous participating medium defined by extinction \sigmat(\mathbf{p}) = \sigmaa(\mathbf{p}) + \sigmas(\mathbf{p}) and phase function p(\mathbf{p}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) within a bounding box. Distant environment lighting L(\boldsymbol{\omega}i) provided as an HDR image. Camera ray direction \boldsymbol{\omega}o for each pixel. Outputs: Radiance L(\mathbf{p}{\text{in}}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) for each pixel, representing the light reaching the camera after single scattering through the medium. Reduced Intensity Record: A structure storing the SH coefficients for a specific location in the medium. coeffs: Array of 9 half-precision floating-point numbers (SH coefficients for L=2). position: 3D vector (x, y, z) representing the center of the grid cell. Record Grid: A coarse uniform grid subdividing the medium's bounding box. Implemented as multiple 2D floating-point textures. Each texel in these textures stores the 9 SH coefficients for one grid cell. Empty cells (cells where volume density is null at all sample points) are eliminated from the grid to save memory and computation. SH Order: Typically L=2, resulting in 9 coefficients. This is sufficient because scattering acts as a low-pass filter, making high-frequency detail loss visually innocuous. Grid Resolution: The size of the coarse uniform grid (e.g., 10^3, 50^3, 100^3). Smaller cells converge to the reference solution but are slower. Sampling: HEALPix distribution is used for evenly distributed samples around the sphere. Single Scattering Radiance: The radiance reaching a point \mathbf{p}{\text{in}} due to single scattering along direction \boldsymbol{\omega}o is: L(\mathbf{p}{\text{in}}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) = \int{\mathbf{p}{\text{in}}}^{\mathbf{p}{\text{out}}} RS(\mathbf{p}n, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) e^{\int{\mathbf{p}{\text{in}}}^{\mathbf{p}n} -\sigmat(\mathbf{p}) d\mathbf{p}} d\mathbf{p}n where RS is the scattered radiance at sample point \mathbf{p}n, and the exponential term is the attenuation from \mathbf{p}{\text{in}} to \mathbf{p}n. Scattered Radiance: RS(\mathbf{p}n, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) = \sigmas(\mathbf{p}n) \int{\Omega} p(\mathbf{p}n, \boldsymbol{\omega}o, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) L(\boldsymbol{\omega}i) e^{\int{\mathbf{p}n}^{\mathbf{k}{\text{in}}} - \sigmat(\mathbf{k}) d\mathbf{k}} d\boldsymbol{\omega}i Note: The source text contains a typo in the exponent integral limits (\mathbf{p}n to \mathbf{p}n), which is corrected here to represent transmittance from the light source entry point \mathbf{k}{\text{in}} to \mathbf{p}n. Factorization: To avoid the costly triple product in SH space, the integrand is split into two factors: 1. Volume-Independent Factor (F{Ind}): For isotropic media, this is the incoming lighting L(\boldsymbol{\omega}i) projected into SH. 2. Volume-Dependent Factor (F{Dep}): For isotropic media, this is the product of the reduced intensity and the phase function: F{Dep}(\mathbf{p}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) = \frac{1}{4\pi} e^{\int{\mathbf{k}{\text{in}}}^{\mathbf{p}} - \sigmat(\mathbf{k}) d\mathbf{k}} For general anisotropic media: F{Dep}(\mathbf{p}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) = p(\mathbf{p}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) e^{\int{\mathbf{k}{\text{in}}}^{\mathbf{p}} - \sigmat(\mathbf{k}) d\mathbf{k}} The scattered radiance is then computed as a dot product of the SH coefficients of F{Ind} and F{Dep}. SH Basis Functions: Real spherical harmonics are defined as: Yl^m(\theta, \phi) = \begin{cases} \sqrt{2}Kl^m \cos(m\phi) Pl^m(\cos(\theta)) & m > 0 \\ \sqrt{2}Kl^m \sin(|m|\phi) Pl^{|m|}(\cos(\theta)) & m < 0 \\ \sqrt{2}Kl^0 Pl^0(\cos(\theta)) & m = 0 \end{cases} where Pl^m are associated Legendre polynomials and Kl^m is a normalization constant. SH Dot Product: The integral of the product of two functions f and g represented by SH coefficients \mathbf{f} and \mathbf{g} is: \int f(s)g(s)ds = \sum{l=0}^N \sum{m=-l}^{l} \mathbf{f}l^m \mathbf{g}l^m This reduces the computation to a simple dot product of coefficient vectors. This step is performed once per frame for dynamic lighting/media, or once for static configurations. 1. Generate Samples: Generate direction samples \boldsymbol{\omega}i using the HEALPix distribution. These samples are arranged in discrete rings of constant latitude. 2. Evaluate Legendre Polynomials: Evaluate associated Legendre polynomials Pl^m(\cos(\theta)) once per row (latitude) to optimize computation. 3. Iterate Grid Cells: For each cell in the coarse uniform grid: a. Empty Check: Probe the cell by evaluating volume density \sigmat at sample points. If density is null everywhere, mark the cell as empty and skip. b. Get Cell Center: Let \mathbf{p} be the center of the current cell. c. Compute Reduced Intensity: For each HEALPix direction \boldsymbol{\omega}i: i. Compute the intersection \mathbf{k}{\text{in}} between the ray (\mathbf{p}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) and the medium's bounding box. ii. Ray-march along the path from \mathbf{k}{\text{in}} to \mathbf{p} to compute the transmittance T = e^{\int{\mathbf{k}{\text{in}}}^{\mathbf{p}} - \sigmat(\mathbf{k}) d\mathbf{k}}. iii. Compute the phase function value p(\mathbf{p}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) if anisotropic. For isotropic media, p = 1/4\pi. iv. Compute F{Dep}(\boldsymbol{\omega}i) = p \cdot T. d. Project to SH: Project the computed F{Dep} values for all \boldsymbol{\omega}i into SH coefficients \mathbf{g}. e. Store Record: Pack \mathbf{g} and \mathbf{p} into a Reduced Intensity Record and store it in the Record Grid (textures) at the index corresponding to the cell. For each pixel in the output image: 1. Cast Ray: Cast a ray from the camera origin in direction \boldsymbol{\omega}o. 2. Intersect Bounding Box: Find entry point \mathbf{p}{\text{in}} and exit point \mathbf{p}{\text{out}} of the ray with the medium's bounding box. If no intersection, return background color. 3. Initialize Accumulator: Set accumulated radiance L{acc} = 0 and accumulated transmittance T{acc} = 1. 4. Ray March: Sample the ray along the path |\mathbf{p}{\text{in}} \mathbf{p}{\text{out}}| at discrete points \mathbf{p}n. a. Find Cell: Determine which cell in the Record Grid contains \mathbf{p}n. b. Fetch Coefficients: Retrieve the SH coefficients \mathbf{g} for that cell from the Record Grid textures. c. Compute Scattered Radiance: i. Project the incoming environment lighting L(\boldsymbol{\omega}i) into SH coefficients \mathbf{f} (precomputed or computed on the fly). ii. Compute scattered radiance RS = \mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{g} (dot product). d. Accumulate: i. Compute attenuation from \mathbf{p}{\text{in}} to \mathbf{p}n: T{path} = e^{\int{\mathbf{p}{\text{in}}}^{\mathbf{p}n} -\sigmat(\mathbf{p}) d\mathbf{p}}. ii. Add contribution: L{acc} += RS \cdot T{acc} \cdot T{path} \cdot \Delta s. iii. Update transmittance: T{acc} = T{path}. e. Emission (Optional): If the medium is emissive, add self-emission E(\mathbf{p}n) to L{acc} during the march. 5. Output: Return L{acc} as the pixel color. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def shbasis(l, m, theta, phi): if m > 0: return math.sqrt(2) K(l, m) math.cos(m phi) P(l, m, math.cos(theta)) elif m < 0: return math.sqrt(2) K(l, abs(m)) math.sin(abs(m) phi) P(l, abs(m), math.cos(theta)) else: return math.sqrt(2) K(l, 0) P(l, 0, math.cos(theta)) def K(l, m): norms = {(0,0): 0.282095, (1,0): 0.488603, (1,1): 0.488603, (2,0): 1.092548, (2,1): 0.546274, (2,2): 0.946175} return norms.get((l, m), 1.0) def P(l, m, x): if l == 0 and m == 0: return 1.0 if l == 1 and m == 0: return x if l == 1 and m == 1: return -math.sqrt(1 - x2) if l == 2 and m == 0: return 0.5 (3 x2 - 1) if l == 2 and m == 1: return -3 x math.sqrt(1 - x2) if l == 2 and m == 2: return 3 (1 - x2) return 0.0 def shdot(fcoeffs, gcoeffs): return sum(f g for f, g in zip(fcoeffs, gcoeffs)) def projecttosh(directions, values): coeffs = [0.0] 9 for omega, val in zip(directions, values): theta = math.acos(omega[2]) phi = math.atan2(omega[1], omega[0]) for l in range(3): for m in range(-l, l+1): idx = ll + l + m coeffs[idx] += val shbasis(l, m, theta, phi) solidangle = 4.0 math.pi / len(directions) return [c solidangle for c in coeffs] def generatehealpixsamples(nsamples=100): samples = [] for i in range(nsamples): phi = 2 math.pi i / nsamples theta = math.acos(1 - 2 (i + 0.5) / nsamples) samples.append((math.sin(theta)math.cos(phi), math.sin(theta)math.sin(phi), math.cos(theta))) return samples def intersectraybox(origin, direction, bboxmin, bboxmax): tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < bboxmin[i] or origin[i] > bboxmax[i]: return None, None else: t1 = (bboxmin[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (bboxmax[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 if t1 > tmin: tmin = t1 if t2 < tmax: tmax = t2 if tmin > tmax: return None, None if tmax < 0: return None, None tenter = max(tmin, 0.0) texit = tmax return origin + direction tenter, origin + direction texit def computetransmittance(pstart, pend, medium, steps=10): totalsigmat = 0.0 dist = (pend - pstart).length() dt = dist / steps for i in range(steps): p = pstart + (pend - pstart) (i / steps) sigmat = medium.extinction(p) totalsigmat += sigmat dt return math.exp(-totalsigmat) def precomputerecords(medium, boundingbox, gridresolution, envradiancefunc): healpixsamples = generatehealpixsamples() grid = {} cellsize = (boundingbox.max - boundingbox.min) / gridresolution for x in range(gridresolution): for y in range(gridresolution): for z in range(gridresolution): center = boundingbox.min + cellsize (0.5 + x, 0.5 + y, 0.5 + z) if not medium.isempty(center, radius=cellsize): depvalues = [] for omegai in healpixsamples: kin, = intersectraybox(center, omegai, boundingbox.min, boundingbox.max) if kin is None: continue transmittance = computetransmittance(kin, center, medium) phase = 1.0 / (4.0 math.pi) depvalues.append(phase transmittance) gcoeffs = projecttosh(healpixsamples, depvalues) grid[(x, y, z)] = {'coeffs': gcoeffs, 'position': center} return grid def render(medium, boundingbox, grid, gridresolution, cellsize, envradiancefunc, camera): findcoeffs = projecttosh(generatehealpixsamples(), [envradiancefunc(omega) for omega in generatehealpixsamples()]) imagewidth, imageheight = camera.resolution outputimage = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(imageheight)] for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): raydir = camera.getraydirection(x, y) pin, pout = intersectraybox(camera.origin, raydir, boundingbox.min, boundingbox.max) if pin is None: continue accumulatedradiance = 0.0 accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 numsamples = 100 stepsize = (pout - pin).length() / numsamples for i in range(numsamples): t = i stepsize pn = pin + raydir t cellidx = ( int((pn[0] - boundingbox.min[0]) / cellsize), int((pn[1] - boundingbox.min[1]) / cellsize), int((pn[2] - boundingbox.min[2]) / cellsize)) if cellidx in grid: gcoeffs = grid[cellidx]['coeffs'] rs = shdot(findcoeffs, gcoeffs) tpath = computetransmittance(pin, pn, medium) accumulatedradiance += rs accumulatedtransmittance tpath stepsize accumulatedtransmittance = tpath accumulatedradiance += medium.emission(pn) accumulatedtransmittance tpath stepsize outputimage[y][x] = accumulatedradiance return outputimage Memory Usage: Storing 9 half-precision coefficients for every voxel in a high-resolution grid (e.g., 512^3) requires ~2.25 GB of graphics memory. Using a coarse uniform grid (e.g., 50^3) mitigates this. Precision: Using half-precision floats for SH coefficients may introduce quantization errors, but is generally acceptable for real-time rendering. Empty Cells: Failing to eliminate empty cells leads to unnecessary computation and memory usage. Probing cells for null density is essential. Anisotropic Media: For dynamic anisotropic media, F{Dep} must be recomputed every frame as it depends on the viewing direction \boldsymbol{\omega}o. For static anisotropic media, F{Ind} can represent the phase function, and F{Dep} stores the product of reduced intensity and lighting, allowing F{Dep} to be recomputed only when lighting changes. Typo in Source Formula: The source text contains a typo in the exponent integral limits for scattered radiance (\mathbf{p}n to \mathbf{p}n). This is corrected to represent transmittance from the light source entry point to the sample point. Time Complexity: Precomputation: Depends on the number of grid cells, HEALPix samples, and ray-marching steps per sample. For a 50^3 grid, it is manageable in real-time. Rendering: Linear with respect to the number of ray-marching steps per pixel. The dot product is constant time (9 multiplications and additions). Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of non-empty cells in the coarse grid. A 50^3 grid uses significantly less memory than a per-voxel grid. Measured Performance: Hardware: Intel Xeon X5680 3.36GHz, GeForce GTX580. Resolution: 1280x720. Grid Resolution vs FPS (Dynamic Lighting): 10^3: 28.00 fps 50^3: 10.70 fps 100^3: 3.81 fps Grid Resolution vs FPS (Static Lighting): 10^3: 31.90 fps 50^3: 31.90 fps 100^3: 31.90 fps. Strengths: Real-time performance for dynamic lighting and media. No precomputation required for dynamic scenes. Handles heterogeneous media, self-shadowing, and emission. Simple implementation using GPU shaders. Limitations: Single scattering only. Multiple scattering is not supported. Quality depends on grid resolution. Coarse grids may introduce artifacts. Anisotropic media requires more complex factorization or recomputation. When to Use: Real-time applications requiring dynamic lighting and heterogeneous media. When single scattering is sufficient for the visual effect. When Not to Use: Offline rendering requiring high accuracy and multiple scattering. Scenes with very fine-scale density variations that require a very fine grid, leading to performance issues. Origin: The method was proposed in the paper "Real-Time Image-Based Volume Lighting" presented at the EG 2013 Short Papers. History and Development: The technique builds upon the use of spherical harmonics for caching directional data in volume rendering. It addresses the computational bottleneck of the triple product in SH-based scattering by factorizing the integrand. The use of HEALPix for sampling and coarse uniform grids for caching are key innovations for real-time performance. Applications: Real-time rendering of participating media in interactive applications, such as video games and virtual reality, where dynamic lighting and heterogeneous media are required. name: Spherical Harmonics Irradiance Encoding
head: Good and Taylor Spherical Harmonics
body: Spherical Harmonics Irradiance Encoding is a technique for encoding full spherical irradiance information using spherical harmonic basis functions, serving as the most generic method to represent directional surface lighting. It solves the problem of modeling how irradiance changes with surface normal, which is required to provide indirect lighting for dynamic objects where the lighting value must be known for every possible surface orientation. Inputs: Incoming radiance/irradiance field over the sphere. Outputs: Spherical harmonic coefficients stored in textures. Data Structures: SH Texture: A texture array or multi-channel texture storing the coefficients. 2nd Order: 4 coefficients per texel. 3rd Order: 9 coefficients per texel. Steps: 1. Basis Selection: Choose the order of spherical harmonics (L). For L=2, use 4 coefficients. For L=3, use 9 coefficients. 2. Projection: Project the incoming irradiance signal onto the chosen spherical harmonic basis functions to compute the coefficients. 3. Storage: Store the computed coefficients in a texture map. 4. Evaluation: At runtime, for a given surface normal \mathbf{n}, evaluate the spherical harmonic basis functions at \mathbf{n} and dot product with the stored coefficients to reconstruct the irradiance. Parameters: Order (L): L=3: High quality, significant storage and bandwidth cost. L=2: Lower cost, but loss of subtleties, reduced lighting contrast, and less pronounced normal maps. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ringing: Both spherical harmonics and H-Basis approaches can exhibit ringing artifacts. Prefiltering can mitigate this but leads to unwanted smoothing of the lighting. Cost: Both approaches present relatively high memory and bandwidth costs. A variation of spherical harmonic encoding utilized in Halo 3 to achieve the quality level of 3rd order spherical harmonics at a much lower cost. It extracts the most dominant light and stores it separately as color and direction. The residual data is then encoded in 2nd order spherical harmonics. This results in very little quality loss at a much lower cost compared to full 3rd order encoding. Memory/Bandwidth: High. 3rd order requires 9 coefficients per texel; 2nd order requires 4. Quality: 3rd order provides very high quality; 2nd order loses subtleties and contrast. Artifacts: Susceptible to ringing artifacts, requiring prefiltering which smooths lighting. Good and Taylor presented the approach of encoding full spherical irradiance information using spherical harmonics. Chen and Liu presented a variation of this method, which they utilized in Halo 3.
