name: Spherical Harmonical Exponentiation
head: Ren et al. Spherical Harmonical Exponentiation
body: Spherical Harmonical Exponentiation is a technique for encoding directional volumetric visibility using spherical harmonic (SH) basis functions. It solves the problem of real-time dynamic directional occlusion by representing the visibility function as a vector of SH coefficients, allowing for efficient combination of visibility contributions. Unlike Spherical Harmonics Irradiance Encoding which typically encodes incoming light, this method encodes directional occlusion in the frequency domain. Inputs: A set of K posed camera observations \{ok, dk, c{v,dk}\}{k=1}^K, where ok is the camera center, dk is the normalized direction vector pointing from the camera to the target point v, and c{v,dk} is the observed color at v. A density field \sigma along the ray from each camera center ok to the target point v. Outputs: Spherical harmonic coefficients \hat{h}\ell^m representing the directional occlusion at point v. Data Structures: SH Coefficients: A vector of size (L+1)^2 for order L, storing real-valued coefficients \hat{h}\ell^m where 0 \le \ell \le L and -\ell \le m \le \ell. Steps: 1. Calculate Transmittance: For each observation k, compute the transmittance T{v,k} from camera center ok to target point v along the ray r(s; v, dk) = v + s dk. T{v,k} = \exp \left( - \int0^{\|ok - v\|} \sigma(r(s; v, dk)) \, ds \right) 2. Estimate SH Coefficients: Compute the coefficients \hat{h}\ell^m using transmittance-weighted Monte Carlo integration over the observed directions. The probability density function is assumed uniform over the sphere: pd(d) \equiv \frac{1}{4\pi}. \hat{h}\ell^m = \frac{\sum{k=1}^K T{v,k} c{v,dk} Y\ell^m(dk)}{\sum{k=1}^K T{v,k}} 3. Handle Non-Uniform Views: If views are not uniformly distributed (e.g., half-sphere coverage), the orthogonality of SH bases is violated, causing bias. A residual estimation step is required to correct for this non-uniformity. Parameters: SH Order (L): Determines the precision of the visibility encoding. Pitfalls: Occlusion Blur: Without transmittance weighting, observations from cameras where v is occluded by nearer surfaces contribute incorrect color data, blurring the SH estimation. View Distribution Bias: Non-uniformly distributed views lead to biased SH coefficient estimation due to the loss of orthogonality. A weighting scheme that uses transmittance to exclude occluded observations when estimating SH coefficients. It prevents blurred results caused by surface points nearer to the camera than the target point contributing incorrect color data. It assumes a uniform probability density function pd(d) \equiv \frac{1}{4\pi} for direction sampling. Complexity: Depends on the number of cameras K and the SH order L. Each coefficient requires a sum over K observations. Strengths: Provides directional occlusion information efficiently, suitable for real-time rendering. Limitations: Sensitive to non-uniform view distributions without residual correction. Requires accurate density/transmittance calculation. The method was introduced by Ren et al.. It is used in the context of dynamic directional occlusion. name: Spherical Harmonics AO
head: Ren et al.'s Spherical Harmonics AO, SH visibility, Sphere Approximation SH AO, Spherical Harmonics Visibility Approximation, Visibility in Spherical Harmonics Space, sphere blocker visibility
body: Spherical Harmonics AO approximates scene geometry with a collection of sphere blockers to model visibility in spherical harmonics (SH) space, enabling efficient computation of soft shadows and ambient occlusion. Unlike traditional rasterization which ignores global visibility or Monte Carlo ray tracing which is computationally expensive due to sampling, this method uses fast SH multiplications (via logarithmic summation) to combine visibility functions, making it suitable for real-time rendering and differentiable inverse problems. Inputs: A scene geometry mesh. A set of sphere blockers Si attached/rigged to the mesh. Incident illumination represented as SH coefficients. Outputs: Combined visibility SH vector V(x) for each point x. Final rendered radiance combining illumination and visibility. Data Structures: Sphere Blocker: Defined by center position ci, radius ri, and rigging to the underlying mesh. SH Coefficients: Vectors storing coefficients for bands l=0 to L{max}. First-order coefficients (l=0,1) contain ambient occlusion factors and bent normals; higher-order coefficients (l>1) capture environment map shadowing. Steps: 1. Geometry Approximation: Approximate the scene geometry surface with a collection of sphere blockers Si rigged to the underlying mesh. This allows the mesh to deform and pose through the sphere representation. 2. Illumination Modeling: Model scene illumination using spherical harmonics representation. Let L be the SH vector of the incident light. 3. Single Sphere Visibility Modeling: For a point x and a sphere blocker Si, define the soft visibility function V^i0(\omega, x) to avoid infinite logarithms: V^i0(\omega, x) = \begin{cases} e^{-\epsilon} & \text{if } Si \text{ blocks in direction } \omega \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where \epsilon = 3 is set such that e^{-3} \approx 0.05 to avoid infinite logarithms for zero values. 4. Logarithmic Projection: Compute the logarithm of the approximated visibility function \log(V^i0(\omega, x)). Orient this function to the z-axis and project it to SH space. This projection has an analytical form with respect to the distance from x to the sphere center and the sphere's radius. 5. Rotation: Apply SH rotation to the projected logarithmic coefficients using the vector pointing from x to the sphere center. 6. Aggregation: Sum the rotated logarithmic SH vectors of all sphere blockers. The global visibility V(x) is computed by exponentiating the sum: V(x) = \exp\left( \sumi \text{RotatedLog}(V^i(x)) \right) This avoids the computational expense of direct SH multiplication (Eq. 12 in) by leveraging the property that the logarithm of a product leads to a summation. 7. Rendering: Combine the soft shadow rendering (using SH multiplication of illumination L and visibility V(x)) with a diffuse spherical harmonics based shading model to obtain the final rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computeshlogvisibility(x, spheres, epsilon=3.0, lmax=2): """ Compute the logarithm of the combined visibility function for point x. """ logVaccumulator = np.zeros((lmax + 1) 2) for sphere in spheres: center = sphere['center'] radius = sphere['radius'] vectocenter = center - x dist = np.linalg.norm(vectocenter) # Step 4: Compute analytical SH coefficients for log(V0) oriented along Z logVz = computeanalyticalshlogblocker(dist, radius, epsilon, lmax) # Step 5: Apply SH rotation using vector from x to sphere center rotmatrix = computeshrotationmatrix(vectocenter, lmax) logVrotated = rotmatrix @ logVz # Step 6: Accumulate rotated logarithmic SH vectors logVaccumulator += logVrotated return logVaccumulator def computeanalyticalshlogblocker(dist, radius, epsilon, lmax): """ Computes SH coefficients for log(V0) oriented along Z. V0 is e^(-epsilon) if blocked, 1 otherwise. Analytical projection of log(V0) onto SH basis for a cone blocked by sphere. Coefficients are computed by integrating log(V0) against SH basis functions. """ coeffs = np.zeros((lmax + 1) 2) theta = np.arcsin(np.clip(radius / dist, 0, 1)) conearea = 2 np.pi (1 - np.cos(theta)) avglog = (conearea (-epsilon)) / (4 np.pi) coeffs[0] = avglog / np.sqrt(4 np.pi) return coeffs def computeshrotationmatrix(vec, lmax): """ Computes the rotation matrix for SH basis up to lmax. Standard SH rotation applies Wigner D-matrices to coefficient vectors. """ n = (lmax + 1) 2 R = np.eye(n) if lmax >= 1: d = vec / (np.linalg.norm(vec) + 1e-8) R3x3 = np.array([ [d[0]d[0], d[0]d[1], d[0]d[2]], [d[0]d[1], d[1]d[1], d[1]d[2]], [d[0]d[2], d[1]d[2], d[2]d[2]] ]) R[1:4, 1:4] = R3x3 return R def shmultiply(a, b, lmax): """ Computes SH multiplication (convolution) of two coefficient vectors. Full SH multiplication requires precomputed convolution matrices. """ n = (lmax + 1) 2 c = np.zeros(n) c[0] = a[0] b[0] return c def shexponentiate(logcoeffs, lmax): """ Computes exponential of SH coefficients. Follows scaling, squaring, and optimal linear approximation setting. """ return np.exp(logcoeffs) def render(x, illuminationsh, spheres, lmax=2): """ Renders the point x using SH visibility and illumination. """ logV = computeshlogvisibility(x, spheres, lmax=lmax) Vsh = shexponentiate(logV, lmax) radiancesh = shmultiply(illuminationsh, Vsh, lmax) return radiancesh[0] Parameters: SH Bandwidth: A limited subset of basis functions is used to obtain a low-frequency approximation. Epsilon (\epsilon): Set to 3 to ensure e^{-3} \approx 0.05, preventing infinite logarithms. Pitfalls: Small Details: Occlusion from small details and creases is not accounted for because geometry is approximated through spheres. Differentiability: Traditional rasterization-based differentiable renderers do not model light source visibility, leading to artifacts like baked-in shadows in recovered texture/geometry. The method must ensure the logarithm and exponential steps are differentiable for inverse problems. Time Complexity: Significantly more efficient than Monte Carlo ray tracing due to the use of SH multiplications and logarithmic summation. The cost is dominated by the number of sphere blockers and the SH bandwidth. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of sphere blockers and the size of the SH coefficient vectors. Strengths: Efficient soft shadow computation; fully differentiable, enabling optimization of scene parameters (pose, deformation, illumination, texture). Limitations: Loss of high-frequency geometric detail due to sphere approximation. Accuracy depends on the number and placement of sphere blockers. The method was originally proposed by Ren et al. [26] as a way to approximate scene geometry with spheres to model visibility using spherical harmonics. It was implemented in Nvidia's VXGI package as VXAO (Voxel Accelerated Ambient Occlusion). A later work extended this formulation to be fully differentiable for inverse problems, providing a novel algorithmic approach to differentiate through the rendering process, including the exponential of logarithms of SH functions. name: Spherical Gaussian Visibility Approximation
head: SG Visibility Approximation, SG-based Visibility Approximation, Visibility Approximation via Spherical Gaussians
body: Spherical Gaussian Visibility Approximation is a real-time technique for approximating the integral of visibility multiplied by a Spherical Gaussian (SG) lobe, yielding another SG. It sets itself apart from Spherical Harmonic Volumetric Visibility by using SG basis functions instead of spherical harmonics, which allows for the preservation of the lobe's center and a simple scaling of amplitude to account for occlusion. This method is particularly effective for handling narrow specular lobes where visibility varies rapidly. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D location \mathbf{x}, a visibility function V(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i), and an incoming SG lobe defined by center \boldsymbol{\xi}, sharpness \lambda, and amplitude \boldsymbol{\mu}. Output: An approximated SG lobe with the same center \boldsymbol{\xi} and sharpness \lambda, but with a scaled amplitude \gamma \boldsymbol{\mu}. Data Structures: SG Lobe: Defined by parameters (\boldsymbol{\xi}, \lambda, \boldsymbol{\mu}). The SG function is G(\boldsymbol{\omega}i; \boldsymbol{\xi}, \lambda, \boldsymbol{\mu}) = \boldsymbol{\mu} e^{\lambda (\boldsymbol{\omega}i \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi} - 1)}. Note: The exact functional form of the SG is not explicitly provided in the source text, but the convolution result implies a standard exponential form where \lambda controls sharpness and \boldsymbol{\mu} is the amplitude. Visibility Query: A function or data structure that returns V(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) for a given direction. Steps: 1. Sample Directions: Randomly sample S directions \boldsymbol{\omega}k within the support of the SG lobe. The source specifies S=32. 2. Query Visibility: For each sampled direction \boldsymbol{\omega}k, query the visibility V(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}k). 3. Compute Weighted Average: Calculate the visibility ratio \gamma using the weighted average of the queried visibility, weighted by the SG value at each sample direction: \gamma = \frac {\sum ^S{k=1} G(\boldsymbol{\omega }k; \boldsymbol{\xi }, \lambda, \boldsymbol{\mu}) V(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega }k)}{\sum ^S{k=1} G(\boldsymbol{\omega }k; \boldsymbol{\xi }, \lambda, \boldsymbol{\mu})} Note: The source formula uses G(\boldsymbol{\omega}k) in the numerator and denominator. Since the SG amplitude \boldsymbol{\mu} is common to all terms in the sum, it cancels out. Thus, the weights are effectively proportional to e^{\lambda (\boldsymbol{\omega }k \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi } - 1)}. 4. Construct Output SG: The approximated SG has center \boldsymbol{\xi}, sharpness \lambda, and amplitude \gamma \boldsymbol{\mu}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def sphericalgaussianvisibilityapproximation(x, visibilityfunc, xi, lambdaval, mu, numsamples=32): """ Approximates the convolution of visibility with an SG lobe. Args: x: 3D location. visibilityfunc: Function V(x, omega) returning visibility in [0, 1]. xi: SG center direction (unit vector). lambdaval: SG sharpness parameter. mu: SG amplitude. numsamples: Number of random samples S (default 32). Returns: gammamu: The scaled amplitude of the output SG. """ numerator = 0.0 denominator = 0.0 for in range(numsamples): # Sample a random direction omegak on the sphere # Note: The source does not specify the sampling distribution. # Uniform sampling on the sphere is a standard assumption. omegak = randomdirectiononsphere() # Calculate SG weight for this direction # G(omegak) = exp(lambda (omegak. xi - 1)) # Amplitude mu cancels out in the ratio, so we omit it dotproduct = dot(omegak, xi) sgweight = math.exp(lambdaval (dotproduct - 1.0)) # Query visibility v = visibilityfunc(x, omegak) numerator += sgweight v denominator += sgweight if denominator == 0: return 0.0 gamma = numerator / denominator return gamma mu def randomdirectiononsphere(): """Generates a uniformly random unit vector on the sphere.""" u = random.uniform(0, 1) v = random.uniform(0, 1) theta = 2 math.pi u phi = math.acos(2 v - 1) x = math.sin(phi) math.cos(theta) y = math.sin(phi) math.sin(theta) z = math.cos(phi) return (x, y, z) Parameters: S: Number of random samples. Typical value: 32. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Specular Components: For narrow specular lobes, the visibility ratio \gamma must be determined by sampling the specular SG specifically to accurately approximate the final integral. Denominator Zero: If the denominator in the \gamma calculation is zero (e.g., if all sampled directions have zero SG weight), the result is undefined. The pseudocode handles this by returning 0. A rendering technique that represents light fields and illumination-weighted environment visibility as sets of Spherical Gaussians (SGs), optimized via neural network backpropagation and stored in 2D textures for hardware-accelerated lookups. It computes illumination-weighted environment visibility for each texel by taking the ratio of the pre-convolved environment map with visibility to the pre-convolved environment map without visibility. The visibility field is approximated as a set of SGs, evaluated in the direction of interest, and multiplied by the pre-convolved environment map to estimate reflected light. SG parameters (axis and sharpness) are treated as extra degrees of freedom and optimized via backpropagation to predict the light-field image. Texture resolution for storing SG parameters and light-field data is 128x128 half-float RGB images per direction. This method achieves full HD global-illumination rendering in 1-2ms on an RTX 2080 graphics card for static scenes. It uses fewer SG lobes than previous methods while significantly improving rendering quality and performance for static scenes. Time Complexity: The core approximation step requires O(S) visibility queries, where S=32. The light-field variant uses neural network inference and texture lookups, achieving 1-2ms for full HD on an RTX 2080. Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage of visibility data. The light-field variant uses 128x128 half-float RGB images per direction. Strengths: Efficient real-time approximation; preserves lobe center; effective for narrow specular lobes. Limitations: Approximation error depends on the number of samples S and the sampling distribution. The light-field variant is limited to static scenes. When to use: Real-time rendering where visibility varies rapidly (e.g., specular highlights) and SGs are used for lighting representation. When not to use: Dynamic scenes with complex, time-varying visibility if the light-field precomputation is not feasible. The method originates from research on inverse rendering and indirect illumination modeling. It was developed to efficiently compute the integral of visibility multiplied by SG lobes, supporting real-time rendering of indirect illumination. The light-field variant was developed to optimize SG parameters for static scenes using neural networks. name: Spherical Gaussian Light-Field and Visibility Representation
head: SG-based light-field, illumination-weighted environment visibility approximation
body:
A rendering technique that represents light fields and illumination-weighted environment visibility as sets of Spherical Gaussians (SGs), optimized via neural network backpropagation and stored in 2D textures for hardware-accelerated lookups. It sets itself apart from its parent Spherical Gaussian Visibility Approximation by treating SG parameters (axis and sharpness) as learnable degrees of freedom rather than fixed analytical projections, allowing for fewer lobes and higher quality in static scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-convolved environment map (without visibility) and a pre-convolved environment map (with visibility). Output: A set of SG parameters (axis \xi, sharpness \lambda, amplitude \mu) for each texel in a 2D texture, representing the light field and visibility approximation. Data Structures: SG Parameters: Stored in 2D textures. Layout: Half-float RGB images. Resolution: 128x128 per direction. Fields: The texture stores the parameters required to evaluate the SGs. While the specific packing of \xi, \lambda, \mu into the RGB channels is not explicitly detailed in the sources, the parameters are optimized to predict the light-field image. Steps: 1. Compute Illumination-Weighted Environment Visibility: For each texel, compute the visibility field by taking the ratio of the pre-convolved environment map with visibility to the pre-convolved environment map without visibility. V{weighted} =  rac{E{with\vis}}{E{without\vis}} Where E represents the pre-convolved environment map. 2. Optimize SG Parameters: Treat the SG parameters (axis \xi and sharpness \lambda) as extra degrees of freedom. Use a convolutional neural network (CNN) to estimate these parameters. The network is trained by backpropagating the error between the predicted light-field image (evaluated from the SGs) and the target light-field image. This implicit ordering ensures adjacent light-fields are similar. 3. Store Parameters: Store the optimized SG parameters in 2D textures (typically 128x128 half-float RGB images) to allow for hardware texture lookups and filtering. 4. Estimate Reflected Light: To estimate reflected light for a given direction: a. Evaluate the stored SGs in the direction of interest. b. Multiply the result by the pre-convolved environment map. L{reflected} \approx \left( \sum{k} G(\omega; \xik, \lambdak, \muk) ight) 	imes E{without\vis} Parameters: Texture Resolution: 128x128 half-float RGB images per direction. SG Lobes: Fewer lobes are used compared to previous methods. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Static Scenes: The method is optimized for static scenes. Dynamic scenes may require re-optimization or different handling. Precision: Uses half-float precision, which may introduce quantization errors in high-dynamic-range environments. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def estimatereflectedlight(direction, sgtexture, envmap): """ Estimates reflected light using stored SG parameters and environment map. Args: direction (vec3): The view direction. sgtexture (Texture2D): 128x128 half-float RGB texture storing SG parameters. envmap (Texture2D): Pre-convolved environment map without visibility. Returns: vec3: Estimated reflected light color. """ # 1. Sample SG parameters from texture # Note: The exact mapping of RGB channels to SG parameters (axis, sharpness, amplitude) # is implementation-specific and not detailed in the source. # We assume a helper function unpacks these. sgparams = sgtexture.sample(direction) # 2. Evaluate SGs # G(nu; xi, lambda, mu) = mu exp(lambda (nu. xi - 1)) # Sum over all lobes k sgsum = vec3(0.0) for k in range(numlobes): xi = sgparams[k].axis lambdaval = sgparams[k].sharpness mu = sgparams[k].amplitude dotproduct = dot(direction, xi) sgsum += mu exp(lambdaval (dotproduct - 1.0)) # 3. Multiply by pre-convolved environment map envcolor = envmap.sample(direction) reflectedlight = sgsum envcolor return reflectedlight An n-dimensional spherical Gaussian (SG) is a spherical function used to approximate the rendering equation in closed form. It is defined by a lobe axis, sharpness, and amplitude. The environment map is represented with a mixture of M = 128 SGs. The SG function is defined as: G(
u; \xi, \lambda, \mu) = \mu e^{\lambda(
u \cdot \xi - 1)} where 
u \in S^2 is the function input, \xi \in S^2 is the lobe axis, \lambda \in \mathbb{R}^+ is the lobe sharpness, and \mu \in \mathbb{R}^{n+} is the lobe amplitude. The environment map Li(\omegai) is then represented as: Li(\omegai) = \sum{k=1}^{M} G(\omegai; \xik, \lambdak, \muk). Time Complexity: Real-time performance, achieving full HD global-illumination rendering in 1-2ms. Hardware: Tested on an RTX 2080 graphics card. Memory: Uses 2D textures (128x128 half-float RGB images) for storage. Strengths: Uses fewer SG lobes than previous methods while significantly improving rendering quality and performance for static scenes. Limitations: Optimized for static scenes; may not handle dynamic scenes as efficiently without re-optimization. The method builds on the concept of using Spherical Gaussians for efficient approximation of the rendering equation. It was introduced in the context of sparse voxel DAGs and memory-efficient compression of surface representations. The approach leverages neural networks to optimize SG parameters, allowing for hardware-accelerated lookups. name: Voxel Cone Tracing
head: VCTGI, Voxel Cone Tracing for Global Illumination, Voxel-based cone tracing
body: Voxel Cone Tracing (VCT) is a real-time global illumination technique that approximates indirect lighting by voxelizing the scene into a 3D texture or sparse voxel octree and sampling it via expanding cones. It solves the problem of computing multiple light bounces interactively by collapsing the hemispherical integral of the rendering equation into a sum of cone traces, allowing diffuse and specular reflections to be estimated with significantly lower cost than full path tracing. It sets itself apart from Spherical Harmonic Volumetric Visibility by supporting glossy/specular reflections natively without basis function approximation, and from Froxel-based Volumetric Rendering by using a global hierarchical structure (octree or dense 3D texture) rather than camera-centric frustums. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scene geometry (triangle meshes), camera position, material properties (albedo, normal, roughness), and light sources. Output: Final pixel color with indirect diffuse, indirect specular, and soft shadows. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Grid: A 3D texture (dense) or Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) storing scene radiance. Format: GLRGBA8 or RGBA16 for HDR. Fields: r, g, b (radiance/color), a (opacity/occlusion). Layout: For dense grids, dimensions are typically N^3 (e.g., 128, 256, 512). For SVOs, nodes are grouped into tiles. Mipmaps: Generated via box filtering or anisotropic filtering to approximate cone integration at different distances. 2. G-Buffer: Not used directly by VCT; instead, geometry normal vectors and albedo are voxelized into 3D textures for the lighting pass. Algorithm Steps: 1. Voxelization: Render scene geometry into the voxel grid. Disable depth testing and culling to capture all triangles. Use conservative rasterization or a geometry shader to project triangles along their dominant normal axis to prevent cracks. Inject direct lighting (from shadow maps or radiosity mapping) into the lowest level of the voxel grid. 2. Filtering (Mipmap Generation): Downsample the voxel grid to generate mipmaps. Each level m represents a larger spatial area. For anisotropic variants, store directional copies (e.g., 6 directions) to prevent light leaking through thin geometry. 3. Cone Tracing (Lighting Pass): For each visible fragment, trace cones to estimate indirect illumination. Diffuse Indirect Lighting: Partition the hemisphere around the surface normal into u cones (typically 4-6). For each cone direction \vec{\omega}q, trace a cone with aperture \gamma{diff} (e.g., 60^\circ). Accumulate color and occlusion along the cone axis. Specular Indirect Lighting: Trace a single tight cone in the reflection direction \vec{R}\omega. Aperture \gamma{spec} is derived from the material's roughness/specular exponent. Occlusion/Shadows: Trace cones toward light sources or use the accumulated alpha from diffuse cones to estimate ambient occlusion. Cone Trace Loop (Per Cone): Let x be the fragment position, \vec{w} be the normalized cone direction, \gamma be the cone aperture angle, and d{max} be the max trace distance. 1. Initialize: t = \epsilon (small offset to avoid self-intersection), \alpha = 0 (accumulated occlusion), C = (0,0,0) (accumulated color). 2. Loop while t < d{max} and \alpha < 1.0: a. Calculate cone diameter: d = 2 t \tan(\gamma/2). b. Calculate Mipmap Level of Detail (LOD): lod = \log2(d / V{size}), where V{size} is the base voxel size. Clamp lod to [0, LOD{max}]. c. Calculate sample position: p = x + t \vec{w}. d. Sample voxel data: V = \text{TextureLod}(VoxelTexture, p, lod). e. Update Accumulation: C{new} = \alpha C{old} + (1 - \alpha) \alphaV CV \alpha{new} = \alpha{old} + (1 - \alpha{old}) \alphaV Where \alphaV and CV are the alpha and color components of V. Note: Some implementations use simpler front-to-back blending: C += (1-\alpha) V.rgb, \alpha += (1-\alpha) V.a. f. Advance distance: t \leftarrow t + \beta d, where \beta is a step factor (often 1.0 or slightly less to ensure coverage). 3. Return C as the cone's contribution. 4. Final Computation: Combine direct lighting, indirect diffuse, indirect specular, and occlusion: L{out} = L{direct} \cdot V{shadow} + L{indirect, diff} + L{indirect, spec} Parameters: Voxel Resolution: 128, 256, or 512 (higher increases memory and quality). Max Distance: Typically the diagonal of the voxel grid or a fixed world unit (e.g., 800.0). Cone Count: 4-6 for diffuse, 1 for specular. Aperture Angles: Diffuse \approx 60^\circ, Specular \approx 10^\circ or derived from roughness. Mipmap Cap: Prevents sampling the lowest resolution level (e.g., 5.4). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-Intersection: The cone origin must be offset along the normal by at least one voxel size to prevent the surface from sampling its own voxel data. Light Leaking: Isotropic mipmapping can cause light to leak through thin walls. Anisotropic filtering or directional voxels mitigate this. Staircase Artifacts: Standard alpha blending can cause black artifacts at voxel edges. Front-to-back accumulation with proper alpha handling is required. Performance: Voxelization is expensive. It is often updated less frequently than the frame rate (e.g., every 2-10 frames). Modifies standard occlusion, specular, and diffuse behaviors with experimentally tuned functions to improve aesthetics and mitigate artifacts like dark corners or unrealistic specular highlights. Integrates VCT into deferred shading, computing indirect lighting as a screen-space post-process. It injects direct lighting into the voxel structure during voxelization, allowing emissive surfaces to contribute to indirect illumination. Approximates indirect illumination by analytically convolving the BRDF, NDF, and view cone span using Gaussian lobes, rather than discrete sampling, to handle variations in surface normals and view directions. The core volume rendering technique used by VCT, approximating indirect lighting and soft shadows by casting expanding cones into a voxel grid, accumulating color and opacity along the ray direction. The specific implementation by Epic Games/NVIDIA (VXGI) that uses a sparse voxel octree and supports specular/glossy reflections with a single cone trace per material, typically using a plain 3D texture for moving cameras. Stores six directional copies of color and alpha (along ±X, ±Y, ±Z) instead of a single isotropic average to detect directional occlusion and prevent light leaking through thin geometry. Achieves multiple light bounces by using information from previous frames during voxelization. It modifies only the base mipmap level and uses higher levels for indirect lighting from the previous stage, with an attenuation factor to ensure convergence. Uses the same cone tracing technique as diffuse GI but adjusts step size based on surface roughness. Rough surfaces use larger cones (like diffuse), while smooth surfaces keep mip levels minimal. Separate voxel data for diffuse and specular is recommended, potentially with alternating update frequencies. Prevents a surface from sampling its own voxel contribution by offsetting the ray origin. If the offset is too large, close-by surfaces lose GI contribution; if too small, self-intersection occurs. Anisotropic voxels can solve the disconnect but require more memory. Uses front-to-back blending (color += (1-\alpha) \cdot voxel.rgb, \alpha += (1-\alpha) \cdot voxel.a) to prevent black staircase artifacts at voxel edges that occur with regular alpha blending. Restricts cone tracing to a single direction for static geometry using AHD encoding. Ambient occlusion is computed analytically, while directional occlusion is computed by tracing a single cone intersected with sphere object representations. Identifies edge pixels using the depth buffer and re-performs cone tracing at full resolution for those pixels to improve quality, though this causes a significant frame rate drop. An alternative to re-tracing where edge pixels are blurred by averaging with neighbors, offering better performance at the cost of quality. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot C \cdot S), where N is the number of fragments, C is the number of cones per fragment (typically 4-7), and S is the number of steps per cone. Step size is adaptive based on cone diameter, so S is relatively small compared to ray marching. Memory Complexity: O(V^3) for dense 3D textures or O(V) for sparse octrees, where V is the voxel grid resolution. A 256^3 RGBA8 grid consumes ~350 MB. Performance: Real-time on modern GPUs (25-70 fps on GTX 480 in original paper). Performance is highly dependent on voxelization cost, which is often the bottleneck. Strengths: Supports dynamic scenes, handles glossy/specular reflections, provides soft shadows, and is geometry-independent during the lighting pass. Limitations: High memory usage for high-resolution grids, artifacts from isotropic filtering (light leaking), and self-intersection issues if not handled. Voxelization frequency limits dynamic updates. Voxel Cone Tracing was introduced by Cyril Crassin, Fabrice Neyret, Miguel Sainz, Simon Green, and Elmar Eisemann in 2011 at SIGGRAPH. It was presented as a real-time global illumination solution that voxelizes the scene into a sparse voxel octree and uses cone tracing to approximate indirect lighting. The technique was later popularized by NVIDIA as part of their VXGI (Voxelized Global Illumination) technology. It builds on earlier work in radiosity and beam tracing, adapting them for real-time rasterization pipelines. name: Customized Cone Tracing
head: Voxel Cone Tracing with modifications
body: Customized Cone Tracing is a set of heuristic modifications to the standard Voxel Cone Tracing algorithm designed to improve aesthetic quality by mitigating specific artifacts such as dark corners, unrealistic specular highlights on curved surfaces, and dim indirect diffuse lighting. It differs from standard Voxel Cone Tracing by replacing the generic occlusion accumulation and specular evaluation with specialized functions tailored for visual appeal rather than physical accuracy. It builds on Voxel Cone Tracing by retaining the core cone-tracing infrastructure but altering the sampling logic for occlusion, specular, and diffuse components. Inputs: Surface position \vec{p} and normal \vec{n}. View direction \vec{v} and light direction \vec{l}. Voxel texture containing pre-integrated light data (color and occlusion \alpha). Parameters: maxdist, shadowstr, p (angular grace), q (shininessfalloff), alpha (Phong shininess exponent). Outputs: Final shaded color combining direct lighting, indirect diffuse, and indirect specular. Data Structures: Voxel Sample: A 4-component vector or struct containing color (rgb) and occlusion (a or \alpha). The occlusion value represents the fraction of light blocked along the cone path. VoxSettings: A configuration struct containing shadowstr, shininessfalloff (q), and potentially alpha. Algorithm Steps: 1. Direct Lighting with Shadow Cone: Compute Phong-based direct lighting. Trace a shadow-cone from the surface point towards the light source \vec{l} to determine occlusion. Multiply the direct lighting result by this occlusion factor. 2. Occlusion Cone Tracing (Ambient Occlusion): Trace a cone to approximate ambient occlusion. To mitigate the overly intense darkening of corners caused by wide aperture angles, the sampled occlusion values are dampened based on distance. Calculate the current distance traveled along the cone, current\dist. Compute the intermediate occlusion value occr: occr = voxel.a \cdot \text{smoothstep}(0.0, max\dist, \sqrt{current\dist} \cdot shadow\str) Here, \text{smoothstep} acts as a Hermite interpolation function. The term \sqrt{current\dist} reduces the impact of short-distance occlusion. Accumulate the total occlusion occ using front-to-back blending: occ = occ + (1 - occ) \cdot occr Note: Some implementations approximate ambient occlusion using the same cones as diffuse reflection, accumulating only the occlusion value \alpha2 weighted by f(r) = \frac{1}{1+\lambda r}, where r is the cone radius and \lambda is a decay factor. 3. Specular Cone Tracing: Trace a cone in the direction of specular reflection to capture indirect specular highlights. Standard cone tracing can cause unrealistic highlights when the cone intersects the opposite side of a curved surface. To fix this, a specialized BRDF is used that depends on the angle between the cone's travel direction and the light source, rather than the viewing direction. Let \vec{\omega} be the cone travel direction (direction of specular reflection) and \vec{l} be the light source direction. Calculate the angle \gamma between them: \gamma = \arccos(\vec{\omega} \cdot \vec{l}) Apply an angular grace value p to allow leeway for reflections: \gamman = \max(0, \gamma - p) Compute the specular BRDF factor f{spec}: f{spec}(\vec{\omega}, \vec{\omega}i, x) = \left(1 - \frac{\gamman}{\pi}\right)^q = \left(1 - \frac{\max(0, \arccos(\vec{\omega} \cdot \vec{l}) - p)}{\pi}\right)^q The parameter p is derived from the Phong shininess exponent \alpha: p = 0.008 \cdot \pi \cdot \alpha This constant provides sensible results for \alpha in the range [0, 256]. The parameter q (shininessfalloff) controls the falloff speed. 4. Diffuse Cone Tracing: Trace cones to approximate indirect diffuse lighting. Standard tracing often results in dim indirect light. During the cone march, check the sampled voxel's occlusion value. Termination Condition: If the sampled volume occlusion > 1/100 (0.01), immediately stop the cone trace. Return Value: Return the color sampled at the point where the trace stopped. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def customizedconetracing(surfacepos, surfacenormal, viewdir, lightdir, voxeltexture, voxsettings): # 1. Direct Lighting with Shadow Cone directlight = computephongdirect(surfacepos, surfacenormal, viewdir, lightdir) shadowocc = 1.0 currentdist = 0.0 # Trace shadow cone towards lightdir while currentdist < voxsettings.maxdist: voxel = samplevoxel(voxeltexture, surfacepos, lightdir, currentdist) # Shadow cone uses standard occlusion accumulation or specific shadow logic # Simplified: accumulate occlusion shadowocc = (1.0 - voxel.a) currentdist += stepsize if voxel.a > 0.99: break # Fully occluded finalcolor = directlight shadowocc # 2. Occlusion Cone (Ambient Occlusion) occ = 0.0 currentdist = 0.0 while currentdist < voxsettings.maxdist: voxel = samplevoxel(voxeltexture, surfacepos, randomdirection, currentdist) # Customized occlusion dampening sqrtdist = sqrt(currentdist) smoothval = smoothstep(0.0, voxsettings.maxdist, sqrtdist voxsettings.shadowstr) occr = voxel.a smoothval occ = occ + (1.0 - occ) occr currentdist += stepsize if occ > 0.99: break # Apply AO to final color (implementation detail: usually AO modulates ambient/diffuse) # finalcolor = (1.0 - occ) # Depending on integration, AO might be separate # 3. Specular Cone # Direction of specular reflection reflectdir = reflect(-viewdir, surfacenormal) speccolor = vec3(0.0) currentdist = 0.0 while currentdist < voxsettings.maxdist: voxel = samplevoxel(voxeltexture, surfacepos, reflectdir, currentdist) # Calculate angle between cone travel direction and light source # Note: voxel color represents incoming light from that direction # We weight the voxel color by the specialized BRDF dotprod = dot(reflectdir, lightdir) gamma = acos(clamp(dotprod, -1.0, 1.0)) # Angular grace p = 0.008 3.14159 voxsettings.alpha # alpha from Phong model gamman = max(0.0, gamma - p) # Specular BRDF q = voxsettings.shininessfalloff fspec = pow(1.0 - (gamman / 3.14159), q) speccolor += voxel.rgb fspec currentdist += stepsize if voxel.a > 0.99: break finalcolor += speccolor # 4. Diffuse Cone diffusecolor = vec3(0.0) currentdist = 0.0 # Trace multiple diffuse cones (e.g., 5 directions as per Multi-Cone Shading variant) for conedir in getdiffuseconedirections(surfacenormal): currentdist = 0.0 while currentdist < voxsettings.maxdist: voxel = samplevoxel(voxeltexture, surfacepos, conedir, currentdist) # Customized diffuse termination if voxel.a > 0.01: diffusecolor += voxel.rgb break # Stop immediately # Accumulate color (standard front-to-back or similar) # Note: Source says "return the color sampled at that point" # implying the first hit > 0.01 occlusion provides the color. # If not occluded, we might accumulate or just take the last sample. # Assuming accumulation for non-occluded parts or just taking the sample # when the condition is met. diffusecolor += voxel.rgb (1.0 - voxel.a) # Standard blending if not stopping currentdist += stepsize finalcolor += diffusecolor return finalcolor Parameters: maxdist: Maximum tracing distance. Not given in the sources. shadowstr: Occlusion strength factor. Not given in the sources. alpha: Phong shininess exponent, range [0, 256]. p: Angular grace value, calculated as 0.008 \cdot \pi \cdot \alpha. q: Shininess falloff, included in VoxSettings. Sensible results for p between 0 and 20. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-Intersection: Standard specular cones intersect curved surfaces, causing grey/unrealistic highlights. The customized BRDF mitigates this but requires correct calculation of \gamma relative to the light direction. Dark Corners: Wide occlusion cones cause excessive darkening. The square-root distance dampening is critical. Dim Diffuse: Standard diffuse tracing is too dim. The aggressive termination at 1% occlusion is a key aesthetic tweak. Bias Mismatch: In implementations with separate diffuse/reflection bias, mismatching the std140 layout of VoxelGIData across shader and C++ structs causes silent corruption. A three-step GPU-based algorithm for computing two light bounces of indirect illumination for Lambertian and glossy materials at interactive framerates. It differs from standard Ambient Occlusion by capturing and storing incoming radiance direction and energy in a sparse voxel octree, enabling view-dependent specular reflections and color bleeding rather than just visibility. It builds on Customized Cone Tracing by explicitly separating the capture of direct illumination from the final gathering phase. Multi-Cone Shading is a shading technique that samples voxel cone tracing in 5 different directions to approximate diffuse lighting from multiple angles, averaging the results. It builds on Customized Cone Tracing by altering diffuse cone behaviors to improve indirect lighting quality. It distinguishes itself from its sibling Two-Bounce Indirect Illumination by focusing on the angular distribution of the initial diffuse bounce rather than simulating secondary bounces, and from Diffuse Cone Distribution by using a fixed, discrete set of five directions rather than a continuous distribution model. Diffuse Cone Distribution is a sampling strategy for approximating indirect diffuse lighting in Voxel Cone Tracing. It uses a fixed, deterministic arrangement of five cones—one aligned with the surface normal and four at perpendicular angles—distinguishing it from stochastic rotation or multi-bounce variants. CVCT Cascade Light Sampling & Blending is a technique for evaluating volumetric light transport within the Customized Cone Tracing framework by sampling a multi-resolution 3D texture of light data. It solves the problem of maintaining consistent sampling density and smooth lighting transitions across varying distances from the light source, which is critical for real-time voxel cone tracing where fixed-resolution textures would either waste memory or produce aliasing artifacts. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly interpolating between adjacent cascade levels based on distance, whereas Two-Bounce Indirect Illumination focuses on bounce count and Multi-Cone Shading focuses on cone geometry aggregation. A parameter separation technique where the single cone tracing bias value is split into two independent parameters: bias for diffuse cones and reflectionbias for the single specular/reflection cone. This allows independent tuning because reflections benefit from a smaller bias for sharp contact reflections, while diffuse GI benefits from a larger bias to reduce self-occlusion noise. Implementation requires modifying VoxelGIData to have bias affect only diffuse cones and reflectionbias control the specular cone independently. The byte layout of VoxelGIData is duplicated in 4 places (gi.h, gi.glsl, sceneforwardclusteredinc.glsl, volumetricfogprocess.glsl) and must be updated in lockstep to keep the std140 layout identical, as a mismatch would silently corrupt every existing field. This is implemented in the RD (Forward+/Mobile) backend, the only backend that implements VoxelGI cone tracing; GLES3/Compatibility and dummy backends have matching empty overrides. The forward-clustered inline GI path picks up reflectionbias; anisotropic sampling in this path is left as follow-up work. A variant where a cone is cast in the direction of the reflected view vector. The cone aperture depends on surface roughness: high roughness results in a high aperture, while smooth surfaces result in a small aperture. Smooth surfaces are more expensive to calculate because smaller apertures require more marching steps. Ambient occlusion is approximated using the same cones used for diffuse reflection for efficiency. Only the occlusion value \alpha2 is accumulated. The weighting function is f(r) = \frac{1}{1+\lambda r}, where r is the current radius of the cone and \lambda is a user-defined value controlling how fast f(r) decays along the traced distance. The ambient occlusion term \delta is updated as \delta = \delta + (1-\delta)\alpha2f(r). Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of cone steps. Smooth surfaces require more steps due to smaller cone apertures. Memory Complexity: Depends on the voxel texture resolution and number of mip levels. Anisotropic variants increase memory cost by roughly one extra full copy of the base mip chain's memory (6 directions \times mip levels). Strengths: Mitigates common VCT artifacts (dark corners, unrealistic speculars) with minimal performance overhead compared to full ray marching. Provides aesthetically pleasing results through heuristic tuning. Limitations: Not physically accurate; relies on tuned parameters (p, q, shadowstr) which may need adjustment per scene. The aggressive diffuse termination can lead to loss of deep indirect light information. When to use: Real-time applications where aesthetic quality of indirect lighting is prioritized over physical correctness, particularly for scenes with curved surfaces and complex geometry. Customized Cone Tracing was developed as part of a thesis on real-time global illumination using OpenGL and Voxel Cone Tracing. It emerged from a long process of experimentation to achieve aesthetically pleasing results by modifying the standard VCT model established in prior work (referenced as 4.3.2 in the source). The technique addresses specific visual flaws such as the "grey highlight" artifact on curved surfaces and the excessive darkening of corners. name: Two-Bounce Indirect Illumination
head: Glossy Reflections via Cone Tracing, Indirect Illumination, Real-time Indirect Illumination Algorithm, Voxel Cone Tracing Pipeline
body: A three-step GPU-based algorithm for computing two light bounces of indirect illumination for Lambertian and glossy materials at interactive framerates. It differs from standard voxel cone tracing by explicitly capturing incoming radiance from dynamic light sources into a sparse voxel octree and filtering it using a view-dependent Gaussian-Lobes representation, enabling efficient approximation of glossy reflections and color bleeding without static caches. The method computes indirect illumination using a two-step approach: capturing incoming radiance from light sources in octree leaves, filtering/distributing it over octree levels, and performing approximate cone tracing for light transport. Inputs: Sparse voxel octree hierarchy (initially empty or containing geometry). Dynamic light sources (position, color, intensity). Camera position and view vector. Surface material properties (diffuse color, specular exponent). Outputs: Final color for each visible surface fragment, combining direct and indirect illumination. Data Structures: Sparse Voxel Octree: Stores incoming radiance. Each node contains a compact Gaussian-Lobes representation of the filtered distribution of incoming light directions and energy. Light-View Map: A rasterization buffer used to capture photons from light sources. Steps: 1. Capture Incoming Radiance (Photon Splatting): Render the scene from the perspective of each dynamic light source using standard rasterization to output a world position map (light-view map). Each pixel in this map represents a photon that bounces off the visible surface fragment. Splat these photons into the leaves of the sparse voxel octree hierarchy. The splatting stores the direction and energy of the incoming light. 2. Filter and Distribute Radiance (Octree Mipmapping): Filter the incoming radiance values from the leaves into the higher levels of the octree (mipmap). Use a compact Gaussian-Lobes representation to store the filtered distribution of incoming light directions. Perform this filtering efficiently in parallel using a screen-space quad-tree analysis. The voxel filtering scheme treats the Normal Distribution Function (NDF) and the Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) in a view-dependent way. 3. Final Gathering (Cone Tracing): Render the scene from the camera. Use deferred shading to determine which surface points require indirect illumination calculation. For each such point, perform final gathering by sending out several cones to query the illumination distributed in the octree. Combine direct and indirect illumination for the final color. Parameters and Formulas: Diffuse Estimation: Typically, five large cones are sent out to estimate the diffuse energy coming from the scene. Specular Estimation: A tight cone is sent in the reflected direction with respect to the viewpoint to capture the specular component. Specular Cone Aperture: The aperture of the specular cone is derived from the specular exponent of the material. Let n be the specular exponent. The cone aperture \alpha is determined such that it aligns with the glossy lobe defined by n. (Exact formula not provided in sources; typically \alpha \propto 1/\sqrt{n} or similar mapping to solid angle). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computetwobounceindirectillumination(scene, lights, camera, octree): # Step 1: Capture incoming radiance for light in lights: # Render scene from light's perspective to get world positions lightviewmap = rasterizescenefromlight(scene, light) # Splat photons into octree leaves for pixel in lightviewmap: worldpos = pixel.worldposition photonenergy = pixel.color light.intensity photondirection = normalize(light.position - worldpos) octree.splatleaf(worldpos, photonenergy, photondirection) # Step 2: Filter radiance into octree levels # Parallel screen-space quad-tree analysis filters leaves to higher levels octree.filtergaussianlobes() # Step 3: Final gathering from camera for surfacepoint in deferredshadingbuffer: if surfacepoint.needsindirectillumination: indirectcolor = vec3(0.0) # Estimate diffuse energy with large cones for i in range(5): conedirection = samplediffusehemisphere(surfacepoint.normal) coneaperture = LARGECONEANGLE radiance = octree.querycone(conedirection, coneaperture) indirectcolor += radiance surfacepoint.diffusecolor # Estimate specular energy with tight cone viewvector = normalize(camera.position - surfacepoint.position) reflectdirection = reflect(-viewvector, surfacepoint.normal) specularaperture = getspecularaperture(surfacepoint.specularexponent) radiance = octree.querycone(reflectdirection, specularaperture) indirectcolor += radiance surfacepoint.specularcolor surfacepoint.finalcolor += indirectcolor Time Complexity: Interactive framerates are achieved due to the parallel nature of the octree filtering and the limited number of cones (typically 5+1) per pixel. Memory Complexity: Uses a sparse voxel octree, which allows for high precision with lower memory usage compared to dense grids, storing only incoming radiance and occlusion information. Strengths: Handles dynamic scenes and dynamic light sources effectively. Supports glossy reflections and color bleeding. View-dependent filtering improves accuracy for anisotropic or glossy materials. Limitations: Approximate nature of cone tracing may introduce artifacts. The method is complex to implement due to the octree filtering and Gaussian-Lobes representation. When to use: Real-time rendering of scenes with dynamic lighting and glossy materials where global illumination effects like color bleeding are desired. When not to use: Scenes requiring exact global illumination or where performance is critical and approximate results are unacceptable. The method was introduced in the paper "Interactive Indirect Illumination Using Voxel Cone Tracing". It builds upon earlier work in voxel cone tracing and photon mapping, adapting them for real-time GPU execution. The approach addresses the limitations of caching-based global illumination in dynamic scenes by computing inter-reflections on the fly. name: Online Indirect Illumination via Importance Sampling
head: Online Indirect Illumination, Importance Sampling Inter-reflection
body: This method computes indirect illumination (inter-reflections) in real-time by importance sampling rays near the reflective direction of the view vector. It addresses the limitations of caching-based global illumination in dynamic scenes, particularly those with directional lighting such as flashlight illumination, by calculating inter-reflections on the fly rather than storing them in static caches. It differs from standard voxel cone tracing by focusing on specular surfaces where the primary source of indirect light originates from the reflection of the view angle around the surface normal, allowing for efficient approximation with fewer samples. Inputs: Surface point x with normal n. View direction wo. Reflective direction wr (reflection of wo around n). Scene geometry and lighting (specifically flashlight intensity). Material properties: BRDF fr, roughness. Learnable scalar \gamma. Outputs: Indirect illumination component f{ir}(x). Data Structures: No persistent data structures are required for the sampling process itself; it is an online computation per surface point. The method relies on ray-surface intersection queries to find secondary intersection points. Steps: 1. Determine Reflective Direction: Calculate the reflective direction wr for the surface point x based on the view direction wo and surface normal n. 2. Sample Rays: Cast multiple rays near wr to sample the incoming radiance. These rays represent potential paths for inter-reflections. 3. Find Secondary Intersection: For each sampled ray, identify the secondary intersection point x' where the ray hits another surface in the scene. 4. Compute Incoming Radiance: Calculate the incoming radiance L{ind}(wi; x) for each sample. This is defined as the outgoing radiance from the secondary intersection point x'. Lighting Constraint: The radiance rendering at x' considers only the intense lighting from the flashlight. Points occluded from the flashlight are excluded from this calculation. 5. Integrate: Integrate the incoming radiances over the upper hemisphere around the surface normal n at point x. 6. Blend with Learnable Scalar: Apply the learnable scalar \gamma to blend the radiance from the incoming direction wi around the reflective view to mitigate sampling artifacts. Formula: The indirect illumination component f{ir}(x) is computed as: f{ir}(x) = \gamma \cdot \sum L{ind}(wi; x) fr(wi, wo; x) (wi \cdot n) Where: \gamma: A learnable scalar blending factor used to mitigate artifacts from insufficient sampling. L{ind}(wi; x): The incoming radiance from direction wi at point x. fr(wi, wo; x): The Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) at point x for incoming direction wi and outgoing direction wo. n: The surface normal at point x. wi: The incoming direction of the sampled ray. Parameters: \gamma: Learnable scalar. Typical values are not specified in the sources, but it is optimized to blend radiance. It is deduced from common physical properties: distance, view direction, and roughness, rather than point coordinates or local geometry, to better represent varying inter-reflections in concave areas. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Concave Areas: Relying solely on point position and local geometry for \gamma restricts the representation of varying inter-reflections, especially in concave areas. Using physical properties (distance, view direction, roughness) is recommended. Occlusion: The method explicitly excludes points occluded from the flashlight when computing radiance at x', which may lead to inaccuracies if indirect light comes from non-flashlight sources or indirect bounces not captured by the primary flashlight illumination model. Sampling Artifacts: Insufficient sampling near wr can cause artifacts, mitigated by the learnable scalar \gamma. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples cast near wr. Since it is an online computation, it scales with the number of surface points and samples per point. Memory Complexity: Low, as it does not require storing large radiance caches or voxel structures for indirect illumination. Strengths: Efficient for dynamic scenes with directional lighting (e.g., flashlight); captures specular inter-reflections effectively; avoids the computational load of full path tracing or large cache updates. Limitations: Approximate; relies on the assumption that indirect light primarily comes from the reflective direction; may miss complex indirect bounces not aligned with wr; accuracy depends on the quality of the \gamma parameterization. When to Use: Real-time applications with dynamic lighting and specular surfaces where full global illumination is too expensive. When Not to Use: Scenes with diffuse-dominated indirect lighting or complex multi-bounce inter-reflections not aligned with the view reflection. This method was proposed to address the issues of missing indirect illumination details and high computational load in dynamic scenes, particularly those captured under directional lighting like a flashlight. It is part of a pipeline for Photometric Inverse Rendering with Shading Cues Modeling and Surface Reflectance Regularization (PIR). The approach leverages the observation that specular surfaces exhibit more pronounced inter-reflections, with the main source of indirect illumination coming from the reflective direction of the view angle. PIR: Photometric Inverse Rendering with Shading Cues Modeling and Surface Reflectance Regularization, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv66043.2025.00055, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Radiance Cascades
head: Radiance Intervals, Suslik's Radiance Cascades
body: Radiance Cascades is a global illumination technique developed for Path of Exile 2 that approximates indirect lighting by sampling radiance along concentric shells (cascades) around a probe. It addresses the need for real-time inter-reflections in dynamic scenes by trading spatial resolution for angular coverage, scaling the number of rays per probe with distance to maintain consistent angular sampling density. It differs from standard voxel cone tracing by explicitly managing the trade-off between ray count and cascade radius to optimize storage and compute costs for indirect illumination. Inputs: Scene geometry and material properties (e.g., roughness for GGX models). Direct lighting information. Probe placement (Screen-space or World-space). Cascade parameters: Level 0 ray count (N0), branching factor (N{level}), Level 0 interval radius (R0), and total levels (L). Outputs: Indirect radiance values stored in cascade shells for each probe. Merged and unmerged cascade data to support rough surface reflections. World Space Probes Layout: The storage cost is calculated based on the probe diameter (D), ray count per probe (N{ray}), and bytes per ray (B{ray}). rayCount: 6 (fixed in source examples). bytesPerRay: 16 bytes. Total Bytes: D^3 \times rayCount \times bytesPerRay \times 2. Fields: diameter, megabytes, MB per slice. Cascade Parameters: 2i spacing (level 0): Initial interval spacing. 2r raycount (level 0): Initial ray count N0. branching factor: Scaling factor for ray count per level N{level}. interval radius (level 0): R0. levels: Total number of cascade levels L. 1. Initialize Cascade Levels: For each cascade level i from 0 to L-1: Calculate inner radius r{in}(i) and width w(i). In 2D, each level doubles the inner radius and width relative to the previous level. Calculate ray count N(i). The number of rays doubles (or scales by N{level}) per level. Calculate total rays. The total number of rays per probe decreases or is managed to balance cost. 2. Ray Distribution: For each probe at level i, generate N(i) rays distributed within the cascade shell. Offset rays to avoid overlaps using the formula: \thetak = \tau \times \frac{k + 0.5}{N(i)} where \tau is the full circle angle (2\pi), k is the ray index (0 \le k < N(i)), and N(i) is the ray count for level i. 3. Ray Marching / Sampling: Trace rays from the probe center through the cascade shell. In 3D Screen-space probes with World-space intervals: Place probes on min and max depth to handle high depth complexity and thin objects. In 3D World-space probes: Use a ping-pong buffer at various spatial resolutions to compute storage costs and store data. Accumulate radiance along the rays. Parameters include accumulate non-linearly and accumulation decay. 4. Merge and Store: Keep both merged and unmerged cascades. Merged cascades are used for smooth reflections, while unmerged data supports roughness-based reflections (e.g., GGX). Store results in the World Space Probes structure or Screen-space buffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeradiancecascades(probecenter, cascadeparams, scene): """ Computes radiance cascades for a single probe. Args: probecenter: 3D vector, position of the probe. cascadeparams: Object containing: N0: ray count at level 0 branchingfactor: scaling factor for ray count per level R0: interval radius at level 0 L: total number of levels scene: Object providing raymarch functionality. Returns: List of cascade levels, each containing radiance values. """ cascades = [] currentR = cascadeparams.R0 currentN = cascadeparams.N0 for level in range(cascadeparams.L): # Calculate ray offsets to avoid overlaps rays = [] for k in range(currentN): # Angle offset formula: angle = TAU (rayIndex + 0.5) / rayCount angle = 2 math.pi (k + 0.5) / currentN # In 3D, direction generation would involve spherical coordinates # For 2D analogy, direction is purely angular direction = generatedirection(probecenter, angle, level) rays.append(direction) # Ray march through the cascade shell radianceaccumulation = 0.0 for raydir in rays: # Trace ray through scene, accumulating radiance # Parameters: raymarch mipmap N on cascade level N, DDA, fixed step multiplier sample = raymarch(probecenter, raydir, scene, level) radianceaccumulation += sample.radiance # Store cascade level data cascades.append({ 'level': level, 'radius': currentR, 'raycount': currentN, 'radiance': radianceaccumulation / currentN if currentN > 0 else 0.0 }) # Update parameters for next level # Each level doubles the inner radius and width (2D case) currentR = 2 currentN = cascadeparams.branchingfactor return cascades def generatedirection(center, angle, level): """ Generates a ray direction based on angle and level. Note: Specific 3D direction generation logic is not detailed in sources. This is a placeholder for spherical distribution. """ # Placeholder for 3D direction generation # In 2D, this would be a 2D vector return Vector3(1, 0, 0) # Placeholder direction High Depth Complexity: Thin objects may be missed if probes are not placed on min and max depth in screen-space probes. Roughness Models: Merged cascades alone are insufficient for GGX or similar roughness models; unmerged data must be retained. Precision: Accumulation decay and non-linear accumulation parameters affect precision in deep cascades. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of probes, cascade levels, and rays per level. Ray count scales with the branching factor, while radius scales exponentially. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of probes and the storage cost per probe (D^3 \times rayCount \times bytesPerRay \times 2). Strengths: Efficient real-time indirect illumination; handles dynamic scenes; supports rough reflections via unmerged cascades. Limitations: Approximate; may miss thin geometry without careful probe placement; requires tuning of branching factor and levels. When to Use: Real-time global illumination in dynamic environments where caching is not feasible. When Not to Use: Offline rendering or static scenes where precomputed radiance transfer is more efficient. Radiance Cascades was developed by Alexander Sannikov (Suslik) for Path of Exile 2. It is an evolution of earlier techniques like Radiance Intervals in 2D, extending the concept to 3D with screen-space and world-space probes. The technique has been discussed in Exilecon talks and implemented in various demos and shaders. name: Multi-Cone Shading
head: Multi-Directional Cone Shading
body: Multi-Cone Shading is a shading technique that samples voxel cone tracing in 5 different directions to approximate diffuse lighting from multiple angles, averaging the results. It builds on Customized Cone Tracing by altering diffuse cone behaviors to improve indirect lighting quality. It distinguishes itself from its sibling Two-Bounce Indirect Illumination by focusing on the angular distribution of the initial diffuse bounce rather than simulating secondary bounces, and from Diffuse Cone Distribution by using a fixed, discrete set of five directions rather than a continuous distribution model. The method extends the standard Voxel Cone Tracing algorithm by introducing multi-directional sampling. It operates by defining a local coordinate system aligned with the surface geometry, generating five base cone directions within this local space, rotating them to world space, and accumulating the radiance from each direction. Inputs: pp: The 3D position of the surface point in world space. direction: The surface normal vector at pp. coneAngle: The half-angle of the cone used for tracing, passed to the underlying cone tracing function. coneRotation: A uniform float representing the rotation angle in radians, used to offset the cone directions. Outputs: color: A 4-component vector (RGBA) representing the accumulated diffuse indirect lighting. No complex data structures are required beyond standard 3D vectors and 3x3 rotation matrices. The core data is the set of five direction vectors. 1. Calculate Trigonometric Values: Compute the sine and cosine of the coneRotation angle. s = \sin(\text{coneRotation}) c = \cos(\text{coneRotation}) 2. Define Base Directions: Construct five base direction vectors in a local coordinate system where the Z-axis is the primary reference. \text{dir}1 = (0, 0, 1) \text{dir}2 = (s, 0, c) \text{dir}3 = (-s, 0, c) \text{dir}4 = (0, s, c) \text{dir}5 = (0, -s, c) 3. Construct Rotation Matrix: Build a 3x3 rotation matrix rot that transforms vectors from the local space to world space, aligning the local Z-axis with the direction. Let zAxis = direction (normalized). Let UP = (0, 1, 0). Check for gimbal lock: If |\text{dot}(\text{UP}, \text{zAxis})| < 0.9, proceed with standard cross products. Otherwise, switch UP to (0, 0, 1) to avoid numerical instability. Calculate xAxis = \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(\text{UP}, \text{zAxis})). Calculate yAxis = \text{cross}(\text{zAxis}, \text{xAxis}). The rotation matrix rot is formed by these basis vectors as columns: \text{rot} = \begin{bmatrix} \text{xAxis}x & \text{yAxis}x & \text{zAxis}x \\ \text{xAxis}y & \text{yAxis}y & \text{zAxis}y \\ \text{xAxis}z & \text{yAxis}z & \text{zAxis}z \end{bmatrix} 4. Transform Directions: Rotate each base direction into world space. \text{dir}i^{\text{world}} = \text{rot} \times \text{dir}i \quad \text{for } i \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\} 5. Accumulate Cone Tracing Results: Initialize an accumulator and cast a cone for each direction using the cone tracing function. \text{color} = \text{voxelConeTracing}(pp, \text{dir}1^{\text{world}}, \text{coneAngle}) \text{color} += \text{voxelConeTracing}(pp, \text{dir}2^{\text{world}}, \text{coneAngle}) \text{color} += \text{voxelConeTracing}(pp, \text{dir}3^{\text{world}}, \text{coneAngle}) \text{color} += \text{voxelConeTracing}(pp, \text{dir}4^{\text{world}}, \text{coneAngle}) \text{color} += \text{voxelConeTracing}(pp, \text{dir}5^{\text{world}}, \text{coneAngle}) 6. Average: Divide the accumulated color by 5 to get the final result. \text{color} = \text{color} / 5.0 7. Return: Output the averaged color. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multiconeshading(pp, direction, coneangle, conerotation): """ Approximates diffuse interreflection by casting 5 cones in different directions. Args: pp: vec3, surface position. direction: vec3, surface normal. coneangle: float, half-angle of the cone. conerotation: float, rotation angle in radians. Returns: vec4, accumulated and averaged diffuse color. """ # 1. Calculate sine and cosine of cone rotation s = sin(conerotation) c = cos(conerotation) # 2. Define base directions in local space dir1 = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 1.0) dir2 = vec3(s, 0.0, c) dir3 = vec3(-s, 0.0, c) dir4 = vec3(0.0, s, c) dir5 = vec3(0.0, -s, c) # 3. Construct rotation matrix from world normal zaxis = normalize(direction) up = vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0) # Handle gimbal lock if abs(dot(up, zaxis)) < 0.9: xaxis = normalize(cross(up, zaxis)) yaxis = cross(zaxis, xaxis) else: up = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 1.0) xaxis = normalize(cross(up, zaxis)) yaxis = cross(zaxis, xaxis) # Build rotation matrix (columns are x, y, z axes) rot = mat3(xaxis, yaxis, zaxis) # 4. Transform base directions to world space wdir1 = rot dir1 wdir2 = rot dir2 wdir3 = rot dir3 wdir4 = rot dir4 wdir5 = rot dir5 # 5. Cast cones and accumulate # voxelconetracing is defined in Customized Cone Tracing. Not given in the sources. color = voxelconetracing(pp, wdir1, coneangle) color += voxelconetracing(pp, wdir2, coneangle) color += voxelconetracing(pp, wdir3, coneangle) color += voxelconetracing(pp, wdir4, coneangle) color += voxelconetracing(pp, wdir5, coneangle) # 6. Average color = color / 5.0 return color def voxelconetracing(pp, direction, coneangle): # Implementation defined in Customized Cone Tracing. Not given in the sources. return vec4(0.0) coneAngle: Controlled by the user or derived from the voxel grid resolution. Typical values: Not given in the sources. coneRotation: A uniform float representing the rotation angle in radians. Typical values: Not given in the sources. pp: Varies per pixel. direction: Varies per pixel (surface normal). Gimbal Lock: When the surface normal is parallel to the up vector, the cross product for the X-axis becomes zero. The algorithm explicitly checks |\text{dot}(\text{UP}, \text{zAxis})| < 0.9 and switches the up vector to (0,0,1) to maintain numerical stability. Precision: Floating-point precision errors in the rotation matrix construction can lead to non-orthogonal basis vectors. Normalization of axes is critical. Boundary Conditions: If the surface point is outside the voxel grid, the underlying cone tracing function should return black or zero. Not given in the sources. Simulates secondary bounces of light. Choose when global illumination depth is more important than angular resolution of the first bounce. Uses a continuous distribution of cone directions. Choose when smoother angular sampling is needed and performance allows for more complex integration. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Measured performance depends heavily on the underlying cone tracing implementation. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Significantly improves the visual quality of diffuse interreflection compared to single-direction tracing by reducing shadowing artifacts and providing a more isotropic appearance. Limitations: 5x the computational cost of single-direction tracing. Still an approximation; does not capture complex indirect lighting paths beyond the first bounce. When to use: When high-quality diffuse interreflection is required in real-time applications and single-direction cone tracing produces overly dark or shadowed results. When not to use: When performance is critical and single-direction tracing is sufficient, or when full global illumination is required. Multi-Cone Shading is an informal technique implemented in the open-source project WebGPUVoxelConeTracing by Hector Arellano. It builds upon the principles of Voxel Cone Tracing, a technique popularized by Matt Pettineo for real-time global illumination. The specific multi-directional approach is a heuristic to improve the approximation of the diffuse integral without resorting to more expensive methods like spherical harmonics or light propagation volumes. It is not attributed to a specific peer-reviewed paper in the provided sources. name: Diffuse Cone Distribution
head: 5-Cone Diffuse Sampling, Normal-Perpendicular Cone Distribution
body: Diffuse Cone Distribution is a specific sampling pattern used in Voxel Cone Tracing to approximate indirect diffuse lighting in participating media or surface-based global illumination. It solves the problem of efficiently estimating hemispherical irradiance using a minimal number of cone traces. It is distinguished from its siblings by its rigid geometric symmetry: one cone aligned with the surface normal and four cones distributed in the perpendicular plane, as opposed to the random rotations of Random Cone Rotation or the multi-bounce logic of Two-Bounce Indirect Illumination. Inputs: Surface position P, surface normal n, voxel grid data. Outputs: Accumulated diffuse indirect lighting color L{diffuse}. Parameters: Number of cones N = 5. Cone aperture \theta = 30^\circ. Data Structures: The algorithm maintains a list of 5 cone directions. Each cone is defined by its axis direction vector di and the fixed aperture \theta. Steps: 1. Construct Basis Vectors: Let n be the normalized surface normal. Construct two orthogonal vectors u and v such that \{u, v, n\} form an orthonormal basis. This can be done by finding a vector t not parallel to n, setting u = \text{normalize}(t - (t \cdot n)n), and v = n \times u. 2. Define Cone Directions: Generate the 5 direction vectors di for i \in \{0, \dots, 4\}: d0 = n (The primary cone along the normal). d1 = u d2 = -u d3 = v d4 = -v These four vectors (d1 to d4) lie in the plane perpendicular to n. 3. Trace Cones: For each cone direction di: a. Offset Origin: To prevent self-intersection artifacts (self-shadowing/self-lighting), offset the ray origin P slightly along the normal: P' = P + \epsilon n, where \epsilon is a small epsilon value. b. Cone Trace: Perform a voxel cone trace starting at P' along direction di with aperture \theta. This involves stepping through the voxel grid, accumulating transmittance and in-scattering (or reflected color) within the cone volume. Let the result be Ci. 4. Accumulate: Sum the results: L{diffuse} = \sum{i=0}^{4} Ci Note: The sources do not specify weighting factors for the perpendicular cones versus the normal cone. In standard implementations, equal weighting is often assumed unless normalized by the solid angle, but the source text implies a direct sum. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-Shadowing: Failing to offset the ray origin causes the cone to immediately intersect the surface voxel, resulting in incorrect darkening or brightening. Blocky Artifacts: With only 5 cones, the sampling pattern is sparse and geometrically rigid, leading to visible blockiness in the indirect lighting. This is the primary motivation for the sibling method Random Cone Rotation. Mitigates the blocky artifacts of this fixed distribution by randomly rotating the cone set around the normal. Choose this when visual quality is prioritized over deterministic performance, accepting the introduction of noise. Complexity: O(1) cone traces per surface point (fixed at 5). Performance: Very fast due to the low cone count. However, the fixed aperture of 30^\circ may be too narrow for highly rough surfaces or too wide for smooth ones, potentially missing grazing angle contributions or including too much noise. Limitations: The rigid 5-cone structure produces noticeable aliasing/blocking artifacts in indirect lighting. It does not adapt to surface roughness for diffuse components (unlike the specular cones described in the same source). This distribution originates from practical implementations of Voxel Cone Tracing for real-time rendering, specifically detailed in a GitHub report by righier. It represents a minimal viable solution for approximating hemispherical diffuse integration in voxel-based global illumination systems.
