name: Froxel Fog with Temporal Reprojection and Revealed Froxel Blur
head: Breda volumetric fog, Shadowing newly revealed froxels
body: This method improves the visual quality of froxel-based volumetric fog by reducing noise in shadow factors when froxels are "revealed" (i.e., when temporal reprojection fails and history is discarded). It combines increased sampling for revealed froxels with a targeted blur pass that only processes those specific cells, avoiding the cost of blurring converged history. It builds on Froxel Volumetric Fog with Precomputed Lighting. Inputs: Current frame's camera projection and view matrices. Previous frame's camera projection and view matrices (for reprojection). Current frame's shadow map(s). Previous frame's froxel density volume (R16Sfloat). Previous frame's froxel shadow factor volume (R8Unorm). Opaque surface depth buffer (tiled). Outputs: Updated froxel density volume (R16Sfloat). Updated froxel shadow factor volume (R8Unorm). 1. Froxel Grid: Dimensions: 8x8 pixel tiles across the screen, 64 slices in depth. Density Storage: R16Sfloat volume. Shadow Factor Storage: R8Unorm volume. Slice Spacing: Exponential. The view depth z of the near face of slice s is: z(s) = 2^{(s + 8)/8} - 2 Slice 0 starts at the camera. Slice 8 is at depth 2. Slice 32 is at depth 30. The far face of slice 63 is at depth 510. Each slice is 2^{1/8} times as thick as the one in front. 2. froxelLastIndex: Texture type: R8Uint. Purpose: Stores, per column, the index of the last slice before the opaque surface. Used by the blur to avoid pulling in froxels inside geometry. 3. Revealed Froxel List: Buffer type: Storage buffer. Entry size: 12 bytes (3 x uint32 for froxel coordinate). Size: Sized for worst case (camera cut). One entry for every froxel in the grid plus a 4-byte result for the atomic counter. Atomic Counter: A uint32 value indicating the number of revealed froxels. Must be initialized to zero every frame. 4. Blur Output Buffer: Compact buffer indexed by list position, used to store blurred results before copying back to the main volume. One thread per column walks 64 slices front to back, stopping at the first slice past the opaque surface in that tile. 1. Reprojection Check: Project the froxel's center into the previous frame's camera. Discard history (mark as "revealed") if: The projected center is outside the old grid. The froxel is past the opaque surface. The old tiled depth indicates the point was hidden. If history is discarded, currentFrameAmount = 1.0. Otherwise, currentFrameAmount = 0.05 (blend weight). 2. Shadow Sampling: If Converged (currentFrameAmount < 1.0): Take 4 new shadow samples. Jitter samples using blue noise across the screen tile and depth. If Revealed (currentFrameAmount == 1.0): Take two batches of samples, averaged half-and-half (12 total samples). Batch 1 (8 samples): Spread along the view ray across two froxels' depth, centered on the current froxel. Weighted by triangle filter [1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 3, 2, 1]. Batch 2 (4 samples): Blue noise jittered samples along rays from the last frame's camera at the same screen position/depth. This assumes the shadow map has not changed (no moving sun or occluder). 3. Update and Append: Compute the new shadow factor. If currentFrameAmount >= 1.0: Append the froxel's coordinate to the froxelIdsToBlur buffer using an atomic counter. Record the index of the last slice before the opaque surface in froxelLastIndex. Blend the new shadow factor with the reprojected history: \text{NewShadow} = \text{currentFrameAmount} \times \text{SampledShadow} + (1 - \text{currentFrameAmount}) \times \text{ReprojectedHistory} For converged froxels, this is a running average with a time constant of 20 frames (0.95^n fade). This pass is only executed if the atomic counter is non-zero. The CPU reads the counter via froxeldispatchargs and writes the dispatch size for 64-thread groups. The blur and copy back run via dispatchindirect. 1. Blur Kernel: Visits the 26 neighbors and the self of the revealed froxel. Skips neighbors outside the grid or behind the opaque surface in their column (checked using froxelLastIndex). Weight calculation using 3D Gaussian: w(\mathbf{o}) = \exp\left(-\frac{\lVert\mathbf{o}\rVert^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) where \mathbf{o} is the integer offset from the center in froxels, and \sigma = 2. Normalizing constant is multiplied but cancels in division, so it can be omitted. At \sigma=2, weights for squared distances 0, 1, 2, 3 are 1, 0.88, 0.78, 0.69 respectively. Effective sample count: (\sum w)^2 / \sum w^2 \approx 26.7. 2. Execution: Blur writes results to the compact blurOutput buffer indexed by list position. This separation prevents reading blurred neighbors before they are blurred. 3. Copy Back: compositerevealedfroxels copies the results from blurOutput into the main shadow volume. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def froxelinjectdensityandshadows(columnidx, rowidx, sliceidx): # 1. Determine slice depth s = sliceidx znear = 2((s + 8) / 8) - 2 # 2. Check opaque surface # Get depth from tiled depth buffer at (columnidx, rowidx) opaquedepth = gettileddepth(columnidx, rowidx) # If this slice is past opaque surface, stop processing this column if znear > opaquedepth: return # 3. Reprojection Check froxelcenterworld = getfroxelworldcenter(columnidx, rowidx, s) prevfroxelscreen = projecttoprevframe(froxelcenterworld) isrevealed = False if not isinsideprevgrid(prevfroxelscreen): isrevealed = True elif znear > opaquedepth: # Already checked, but explicit for clarity isrevealed = True elif ishiddenbyprevdepth(prevfroxelscreen, opaquedepth): isrevealed = True currentframeamount = 1.0 if isrevealed else 0.05 # 4. Shadow Sampling sampledshadow = 0.0 if isrevealed: # Batch 1: 8 samples along view ray, triangle filter weights weights = [1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 3, 2, 1] sumw = sum(weights) for i in range(8): # Spread across two froxels' depth, centered on current depthoffset = getdepthoffsetforsample(i) shadowval = sampleshadowmap(froxelcenterworld, depthoffset) sampledshadow += shadowval weights[i] sampledshadow /= sumw # Batch 2: 4 samples from last frame's camera position prevcameraray = getrayfromprevcamera(prevfroxelscreen, znear) sumw2 = 4 for i in range(4): jitter = getbluenoisejitter(i) ray = prevcameraray + jitter shadowval = sampleshadowmap(ray.origin, ray.direction) sampledshadow += shadowval sampledshadow /= (sumw + sumw2) # Average of two batches (half-and-half) else: # Converged: 4 samples jittered by blue noise for i in range(4): jitter = getbluenoisejitter(i) ray = getrayfromcurrentcamera(jitter) shadowval = sampleshadowmap(ray.origin, ray.direction) sampledshadow += shadowval sampledshadow /= 4 # 5. Blend reprojectedhistory = reprojectshadowfromprevframe(columnidx, rowidx, s) newshadow = currentframeamount sampledshadow + (1 - currentframeamount) reprojectedhistory # 6. Store and Append if revealed storeshadow(columnidx, rowidx, s, newshadow) if isrevealed: # Atomic append to revealed list entryidx = atomicadd(froxelatomiccounter, 1) froxelidstoblur[entryidx] = uint3(columnidx, rowidx, s) # Store last index before opaque surface froxellastindex[columnidx, rowidx] = s - 1 def blurrevealedfroxels(listidx): # Get froxel coordinate from list froxelid = froxelidstoblur[listidx] col, row, slice = froxelid # Get froxelLastIndex for this column to know where opaque surface is lastvalidslice = froxellastindex[col, row] weightedsum = 0.0 weightedshadowsum = 0.0 # Visit 26 neighbors and self for dx in [-1, 0, 1]: for dy in [-1, 0, 1]: for dz in [-1, 0, 1]: if dx == 0 and dy == 0 and dz == 0: continue ncol = col + dx nrow = row + dy nslice = slice + dz # Bounds check BEFORE load (Vulkan robust buffer access fix) if ncol < 0 or ncol >= gridwidth or \ nrow < 0 or nrow >= gridheight or \ nslice < 0 or nslice >= griddepth: continue # Check if neighbor is behind opaque surface nlastslice = froxellastindex[ncol, nrow] if nslice > nlastslice: continue # Calculate weight offset = uint3(dx, dy, dz) distsq = dot(offset, offset) sigma = 2.0 weight = exp(-distsq / (2 sigma sigma)) # Load shadow value shadowval = loadshadow(ncol, nrow, nslice) weightedsum += weight weightedshadowsum += weight shadowval # Also include self (weight 1.0 for distsq=0) selfweight = 1.0 selfshadow = loadshadow(col, row, slice) weightedsum += selfweight weightedshadowsum += selfweight selfshadow # Store blurred result in compact buffer if weightedsum > 0.0: blurredshadow = weightedshadowsum / weightedsum else: blurredshadow = selfshadow # Fallback to unblurred if no neighbors bluroutputbuffer[listidx] = blurredshadow def compositerevealedfroxels(listidx): froxelid = froxelidstoblur[listidx] col, row, slice = froxelid blurredshadow = bluroutputbuffer[listidx] storeshadow(col, row, slice, blurredshadow) Grid Dimensions: 8x8 pixel tiles, 64 slices. Blend Weight (Converged): 0.05 (Time constant ~20 frames). Blur Sigma: 2. Sample Counts: 4 (converged), 12 (revealed: 8 + 4). Anisotropy: Slice spacing is exponential. One slice of blur radius is 0.18 deep at the front and 42.5 deep at the back. A kernel isotropic in index space is not isotropic in world space. Reprojection Failure: History is discarded if the froxel's center projects outside the old grid, if the froxel is past the opaque surface, or if the old tiled depth indicates the point was hidden. In these cases, the froxel takes 100% of the current frame's value. Moving Sun/Occluder: Sampling today's shadow map at last frame's positions assumes the shadow map has not changed. A moving sun or moving occluder breaks this assumption, causing noise in the revealed froxel's second batch of samples. Vulkan Robust Buffer Access: On Vulkan without robust buffer access, out-of-bounds reads are undefined. D3D12 returns zero for out-of-bounds reads. The fix moves bounds test ahead of load and corrects comparisons (>= instead of >). Atomic Counter Initialization: The counter must be initialized to zero every frame. If not, it starts with garbage memory values, causing out-of-bounds appends. Division by Zero: If a froxel has no usable neighbors (e.g., all outside grid or behind opaque surface), the weight sum is zero. The shader must check weightedSum > 0.0 before dividing, falling back to the unblurred value. Time Complexity: The inject pass is O(N) where N is the number of froxels (one thread per column). The blur pass is O(K) where K is the number of revealed froxels. In the worst case (camera cut), K equals the total number of froxels. In typical frames, K is small. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the froxel volumes and the revealed froxel list buffer. Measured Performance: A frame where nothing was revealed costs a single-thread pass and two empty indirect dispatches. A camera cut costs a blur over most of the grid. Strengths: Reduces noise in revealed froxels without blurring converged history. Cost is proportional to the number of revealed froxels. Limitations: Does not fix the root cause of revealed froxel noise (lack of shadow history). Relies on static shadow maps (no moving sun/occluder). Anisotropic blur due to exponential slice spacing. When to Use: When temporal reprojection fails frequently (e.g., fast camera movements, occluder edges) and shadow map history buffers are not available. When Not to Use: When shadow map history buffers are available (preferred solution). When the sun or occluders are moving rapidly. Froxel fog was established in Bart Wronski's volumetric fog talk at SIGGRAPH 2014 and given a physically based form in Sébastien Hillaire's talk in the same course a year later. The specific technique of shadowing newly revealed froxels was implemented in the Breda renderer. name: Volumetric Particle Injection
head: particle voxelization, particles as volumes
body: Volumetric Particle Injection is a real-time technique that injects discrete volumetric particles (smoke, steam, energy discharges) as density into a frustum-aligned froxel grid, allowing them to be lit by the same scattering pass as global fog. It solves the problem of visible seams and lighting inconsistencies that arise when particles are rendered as decoupled billboards or separate volume layers with independent lighting models. By unifying particle density with the global fog volume, it ensures consistent light scattering and shadowing across the entire participating medium. Inputs and Outputs Input: A list of particle emitters, each defined by position, footprint size, and extinction coefficient. Output: A froxel grid volume (typically R32UINT during injection, converted to R16FLOAT for rendering) containing accumulated density/extinction values. Data Structures Froxel Grid: A 3D grid of voxels serving as the injection target. Injection Volume: The grid is allocated as a uint volume to support atomic operations. Particle Footprint: Defined as a 2×2×2 cube (for point or trilinear sampling) or a sphere, with size proportional to the footprint in froxels rather than screen area. Shadow Map: A separate cascaded clip map (3 levels, camera-following, with world-space snapping) is used for out-of-view shadow casters, as clip-space volume alone is insufficient. Refinement: Sparse per-froxel refinement (brick or small octree) is attached only to froxels holding particles to handle high-detail effects like fluid surfaces or electricity arcs. Steps 1. Initialize Volume: Allocate a uint volume for particle density. 2. Iterate Emitters: For each particle emitter: a. Determine the footprint (2×2×2 cube or sphere) in froxel coordinates. b. Calculate the normalized extinction value. Map extinction 1.0 to 2048u in the uint volume. c. Normalize by Volume: Divide the extinction contribution by the footprint volume to prevent overshadowing in large voxel cascades where particles write more often into the same voxels. d. Atomic Write: For each froxel intersected by the footprint, use atomic addition (e.g., InterlockedAdd) to accumulate the normalized extinction value, preventing multiple emitters from overwriting each other's data. 3. Convert Format: After all particles are injected, convert the uint volume to f16 for the rendering pass. 4. Raymarching: During the volumetric rendering pass, march through the froxel grid. 5. Cap Samples: Limit the number of samples inside a froxel to a fixed set number to ensure dense cells do not cost more than sparse ones. 6. Shadow Casting: Use the separate cascaded clip map for shadow calculations for out-of-view casters. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def injectparticles(grid, emitters): # grid is a 3D array of uint32, initialized to zero for emitter in emitters: # Standard grid intersection logic to find froxels within footprint radius footprintfroxels = computefootprintfroxels(emitter.position, emitter.footprintradius) # Map extinction 1.0 to 2048u basevalue = 2048 rawextinction = emitter.extinctioncoeff basevalue # Normalize by volume to prevent overshadowing valueperfroxel = rawextinction / len(footprintfroxels) for froxel in footprintfroxels: # Hardware atomic add to prevent overwrites from multiple compute threads atomicadd(grid, froxel, valueperfroxel) def convertgrid(grid): # Convert uint volume to f16 for rendering by scaling down the mapping factor return [v / 2048.0 for v in grid] def raymarchfroxel(gridf16, ray, maxsamples=16): transmittance = 1.0 samples = 0 stepsize = 1.0 # Froxel step size epsilon = 1e-4 # Transmittance threshold while samples < maxsamples: pos = ray.origin + ray.direction samples stepsize # Standard trilinear or point sampling from the f16 grid density = sampledensity(gridf16, pos) extinction = density stepsize transmittance = exp(-extinction) samples += 1 if transmittance < epsilon: break return transmittance def computefootprintfroxels(position, radius): # Returns list of froxel indices intersected by the footprint return [] def sampledensity(grid, pos): # Returns density value at position using nearest-neighbor or trilinear interpolation return grid[round(pos.x)][round(pos.y)][round(pos.z)] def atomicadd(grid, index, value): # Standard hardware atomic addition operation grid[index] = grid[index] + value Parameters Extinction Mapping: Extinction 1.0 is mapped to 2048u in the uint volume before conversion to f16. Footprint Size: 2×2×2 cube for point or trilinear sampling, or a sphere. Cascaded Clip Map Levels: 3 levels, camera-following, with world-space snapping. Sample Cap: Fixed number of samples per froxel (value not specified in sources). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Atomicity: Without atomics, multiple emitters writing to the same froxel will overwrite each other's data. Overshadowing: Large voxel cascades cause overshadowing if extinction is not normalized by volume, as particles write more often into the same voxels. Shadow Casting: Clip-space volume alone is insufficient for out-of-view shadow casters; a separate cascaded clip map is required. Performance: Dense cells must not cost more than sparse ones; this is achieved by capping the number of samples in the raymarch. Time Complexity: Injection cost is proportional to the number of particles and the footprint size in froxels, not screen area. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the froxel grid size; the constraint is scattering-pass bandwidth, not footprint. Measured Performance: On PS4 (Frostbite 2015), injecting 1k particles costs 0.03 ms (default) or 0.25 ms (high quality). Volumetric shadow map with 32³ raymarch costs 0.04 ms for spot lights and 0.14 ms for point lights. Scaling: Cost scales with the number of particles and the complexity of the footprint, while the fixed sample cap ensures dense cells do not disproportionately increase cost. Strengths: Nearly free injection cost; consistent lighting with global fog; avoids visible seams. Limitations: Not suitable for high-fidelity 3D fluid simulation, which is unaffordable for real-time games except as a single hero effect. When to Use: For 95% of cases where volumetric particles are needed for effects like smoke, steam, or energy discharges. When Not to Use: When high-fidelity 3D fluid simulation is required, as it exceeds real-time budgets. Volumetric Particle Injection was shipped in Frostbite in 2015, referred to as "particle voxelization". It is also documented by Unreal Engine as a feature for Volumetric Fog and implemented in Godot. Red Dead Redemption 2 (RDR2) uses this technique, keeping up to 32 volumes in the cluster grid with Z-binning. The technique was developed to address the limitations of decoupled particle rendering, which caused lighting inconsistencies and visible seams. feat(render): volumetric particles in the froxel grid, https://github.com/lobinuxsoft/kooch/issues/1235, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Fog Volume Grid Rendering
head: FogMaterial volumetric fog integration, FogVolume Volumetric Rendering
body: Fog Volume Grid Rendering is a technique that draws local volumetric fog entities (FogVolume) and their associated material properties (FogMaterial) into a froxel-based volumetric grid by adding their density, albedo, and emission to the froxels geometrically covered by the volume. It solves the problem of creating non-uniform, patchy fog effects (such as fog banks or layered mist) that cannot be achieved with global fog settings alone. It differs from sibling methods like Froxel TAA Reprojection by focusing on the spatial injection of local volume data rather than temporal stability, and differs from Fog Volume Entity by providing the low-level implementation details of how that entity's data is processed into the froxel grid. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A list of visible, unculled FogVolume entities, each containing a shape (box, ellipsoid, cone, cylinder, or world), a FogMaterial (density, albedo, emission, noise parameters), and spatial transforms. Outputs: A 3D froxel grid (texture) where each cell contains accumulated density, albedo, and emission values derived from all overlapping volumes. Data Structures: 1. FogVolume Row Texture: A 1D texture or buffer where each row represents one visible volume. The layout includes shape type, transform matrix, material properties (density, color), and noise parameters. 2. Fog Density Atlas: A single 3D texture formed by stacking individual density textures (from NoiseTexture3D or ImageTexture3D) in depth. This is necessary because WebGL2 shaders cannot index a sampler array in a loop. The atlas holds floats once a density texture does. 3. Froxel Grid: The target 3D texture storing the accumulated volumetric data. Numbered Steps: 1. Froxel Range Calculation: For each visible FogVolume, determine the set of froxels it covers. This involves porting the froxel range calculation logic from the reference engine (e.g., Godot's fog.cpp lines 551-718) to compute the bounding box of the volume in froxel space and iterating over the intersecting cells. 2. Density Texture Generation: For each volume, generate its local density texture: If the density is uniform, create a constant texture. If noise-based, build a NoiseTexture3D as a worker job. Ensure texels and seamless blending match the reference engine byte-for-byte. If image-based, decode ImageTexture3D sub-resources in every uncompressed format (8-bit, 16-bit, half, float, RGBA4444, RGB565, RGBE9995) using the reference unpacking logic (e.g., Image::getcoloratofs). For imported 3D textures, cut them into slices matching the reference layered importer (e.g., resourceimporterlayeredtexture.cpp:370-386). Stack every generated density texture in depth into the Fog Density Atlas. 3. Volume Packing: Pack each visible, unculled volume's parameters into the FogVolume Row Texture. This includes the index into the Fog Density Atlas, the shape parameters, and material properties. 4. Froxel Accumulation (Light Pass): Execute a compute shader pass (or fragment shader pass in the light pass) to add the volumes' contributions to the froxel grid: Iterate over the froxels covered by each volume. Sample the local density texture (from the atlas) at the relative position within the volume. Apply noise modulation using parameters: DensityNoiseOffset: Offsets the noise value. DensityNoiseScale: Scales the noise value (controls patch thickness/spacing). DensityNoiseFrequency: Controls spatial frequency (number of patches). DensityNoiseTimeFrequency: Controls temporal morphing of patches. Calculate the final density contribution: \rho{final} = \rho{base} \times \rho{noise} \times GlobalDensity where \rho{base} is the global density and \rho{noise} is the sampled noise value. Add the density, albedo, and emission to the froxel's accumulated values. Handle packed-color overflow as per the reference engine (e.g., Godot's packed-colour overflow). Apply shape-specific modifiers: Height Falloff: Modulate density based on vertical position. Edge Fade: Soften edges using SoftEdges factor. Negative Density: Carve out fog if density is negative. Fall Off Direction: Use FallOffDirLati, FallOffDirLong, FallOffScale, and FallOffShift to control density distribution along a specific direction. Ramp: Apply RampStart, RampEnd, and RampInfluence to fade density based on distance. Parameters: Active: On/Off. AffectsThisAreaOnly: Boolean. False allows effect across multiple VisAreas/ClipVolumes. Color: RGB color of the fog. DensityNoiseOffset: Range -2 to +2. DensityNoiseScale: Range 0 to 10. Default 1. DensityNoiseTimeFrequency: Controls morphing speed. Keep low (e.g., 0.2) to avoid unnatural rapid morphing. DensityOffset: Additional density control. FallOffDirLati: Latitude direction of fall off. 90 = up. FallOffDirLong: Longitude direction of fall off. 0 = East (Positive X). FallOffScale: Scales density distribution along fall off direction. FallOffShift: Shifts fog density along fall off direction. GlobalDensity: Controls base density. Production levels typically 1-3. IgnoreVisAreas: Boolean. Controls response to VisAreas/ClipVolumes. NearCutOff: Distance in meters to stop rendering. RampStart: Start distance of fog density ramp in meters. RampEnd: End distance of fog density ramp in meters. RampInfluence: Influence of fog density ramp. SoftEdges: Factor to soften edges. UseGlobalFogColor: Boolean. If true, ignores entity Color and uses global fog color. VolumeType: 0 - Ellipsoid, 1 - Cube. WindInfluence: Influence of global wind. DensityNoiseFrequency XYZ: Spatial frequency of noise. High values create detailed fog. Size XYZ: Size limits of the fog volume. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def accumulatefogvolumes(froxelgrid, volumes, densityatlas): """ Accumulates fog volume contributions into the froxel grid. Args: froxelgrid: 3D texture storing accumulated density, albedo, emission. volumes: List of FogVolume objects. densityatlas: 3D texture containing stacked density textures. """ for volume in volumes: if not volume.active: continue # 1. Determine covered froxels coveredfroxels = getfroxelrange(volume) # 2. Get density texture index from atlas densitytexindex = volume.densitytextureindex localdensitytexture = densityatlas # 3. Iterate over covered froxels for froxel in coveredfroxels: # Calculate local position within volume localpos = transforminverse(volume.transform) froxel.worldposition # Check if localpos is inside volume shape if not isinsidevolumeshape(localpos, volume.shapetype, volume.size): continue # Sample base density basedensity = sampledensitytexture(localdensitytexture, densitytexindex, localpos) # Apply noise modulation noisevalue = samplenoise( localpos, volume.densitynoisefrequency, volume.densitynoiseoffset, volume.densitynoisescale, volume.densitynoisetimefrequency) # Calculate final density finaldensity = basedensity noisevalue volume.globaldensity # Apply shape-specific modifiers finaldensity = applyheightfalloff(finaldensity, localpos, volume) finaldensity = applyedgefade(finaldensity, localpos, volume.softedges) finaldensity = applyfalloffdirection(finaldensity, localpos, volume) finaldensity = applydensityramp(finaldensity, froxel.worldposition, volume) # Handle negative density (carving) if finaldensity < 0: finaldensity = -finaldensity # Carve out fog # Accumulate into froxel froxelgrid[froxel.index].density += finaldensity froxelgrid[froxel.index].albedo += volume.color finaldensity froxelgrid[froxel.index].emission += volume.emission finaldensity def samplenoise(pos, frequency, offset, scale, timefreq): """ Samples noise for density modulation. """ # Reconstruct world-space position for noise sampling worldpos = pos frequency + offset # Sample 3D noise (e.g., Perlin-Worley) noiseval = sample3dnoise(worldpos, timefreq) # Scale noise return noiseval scale def isinsidevolumeshape(localpos, shapetype, size): """ Checks if a point is inside the volume shape. """ if shapetype == 'box': return all(abs(localpos[i]) <= size[i] / 2 for i in range(3)) elif shapetype == 'ellipsoid': return sum((localpos[i] / (size[i] / 2))2 for i in range(3)) <= 1.0 # Add other shape checks (cone, cylinder, world) return False Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Float Texel Upload: Float texels upload raw as half float because the reference engine gives a float format no sRGB view and WebGL2 always filters a half float. An atlas crop of a half-float sheet stays half float, and a canvas read converts it to bytes. ShaderMaterial Limitation: A fog ShaderMaterial runs no fog shader. This requires a shading-language runtime. Compressed/Integer Formats: An Image in a block-compressed format draws nothing. An Image in an integer format draws nothing because a float sampler cannot read it. NoiseTexture3D Build Delay: A NoiseTexture3D shows even density until its build lands. Atlas Limit: Past 2048 stacked density slices, further textures leave the density even. sRGB Decoding: A 3D colour slot still decodes every texture as sRGB. Godot reads a format without an sRGB view raw, so a Lum8 or grey-noise albedo draws too dark. Fog Volume Injection Optimization reduces the computational cost of injecting scene fog volumes into a froxel grid by ensuring each volume is processed only by the froxels it geometrically covers, rather than having every froxel test every scene fog volume. It differs from the brute-force approach (where every froxel iterates all volumes) by using precomputed CPU-side bounds to cull irrelevant volume-froxel pairs, and differs from Godot’s per-volume dispatch by using a single GPU kernel with a culled list of ranges, avoiding the overhead of many small kernel launches. The Fog Volume Entity is a spatial entity used to define local volumetric fog density, color, and noise-based structure within a 3D level. It solves the problem of creating non-uniform, patchy fog effects (such as fog banks or layered mist) that cannot be achieved with global fog settings alone. It differs from sibling methods like Fog Volume Grid Rendering by providing a high-level, user-configurable entity interface for shaping fog via noise parameters, rather than directly manipulating the underlying froxel data structures. Execute a compute shader pass (glDispatchCompute) to evaluate fog density and material properties for every cell in the 3D texture. For dynamic fog, sample an auxiliary 3D noise texture (e.g., Perlin-Worley noise) using the reconstructed world-space position of the froxel. The extinction coefficient is calculated as \sigmat = \sigmas + \sigmaa, where \sigmas is scattering and \sigmaa is absorption. The angular distribution of scattered light is modeled using the Henyey-Greenstein phase function: p(\theta) = \frac{1}{4\pi} \frac{1 - g^2}{(1 + g^2 - 2g \cos\theta)^{3/2}}, where g \in (-1, 1) is the asymmetry parameter. Time Complexity: O(V F), where V is the number of visible volumes and F is the average number of froxels covered by each volume. With optimization, F is reduced to only covered froxels. Memory Complexity: O(A + G), where A is the size of the density atlas and G is the size of the froxel grid. Measured Performance: Golden test 'fog-volume' (3x3x3 box at 0, 1, -5): Mean error against Godot 4.6.3 drops from 3.476/255 (no volume) to 0.205/255. Value check mean error over pixels the volume changes in Godot: box 13.05→0.40, ellipsoid 10.66→0.22, cone 8.90→0.40, cylinder 15.67→0.41, world shape 14.07→0.25, negative density 3.65→0.26, height falloff 2 9.58→0.24, edge fade 0 14.21→0.40, edge fade 4 2.55→0.08, no material 13.21→0.35, albedo/emission 32.91→1.13, density 8 23.92→0.45, rotated/scaled 13.73→0.30, spot/sun lights 24.70→0.60. Value check mean error over whole frame: imported 3D texture 3.554→0.209, ImageTexture3D.tres Lum8 4.459→0.206, NoiseTexture3D.tres 5.418→0.196, ImageTexture3D.tres RHalf 2.227→0.215, RFloat 2.229→0.216, R16 1.153→0.184, RGBE9995 2.229→0.215, NoiseTexture3D warp simplex 0.714→0.194, reduced simplex progressive 0.683→0.199, basic grid independent 0.496→0.196. Strengths: Supports complex local fog shapes and variations; integrates with global fog; supports noise-based dynamic fog. Limitations: Limited by atlas size (2048 slices); requires careful handling of texture formats; ShaderMaterial integration is non-trivial. When to use: When non-uniform, patchy fog effects are needed. When not to use: When simple, uniform fog is sufficient; when performance is critical and many volumes are used (due to atlas limits). Fog Volume Grid Rendering is a technique used in real-time volumetric rendering to integrate local fog volumes into a global froxel-based fog system. It was implemented in Godot 4.6.3 and ported to other engines like Three.js (via textscene-inspector). The method draws on principles from volumetric rendering literature, such as the use of 3D textures for density storage and Henyey-Greenstein phase functions for scattering. It is commonly used in game engines to create atmospheric effects like fog banks, mist, and layered clouds. feat(renderer): draw FogVolume and FogMaterial into the volumetric fog, https://github.com/Vortiago/textscene-inspector/pull/732, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) CRYENGINE | Documentation - Volumetric Fog, https://www.cryengine.com/docs/static/engines/cryengine-3/categories/1114113/pages/21268322, fetched 2026-10-29 Volumetric Fog Using 3D Textures in OpenGL - opengl, https://salivity.github.io/opengl/article/volumetric-fog-using-3-d-textures-in-open-gl, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Fog Volume Injection Optimization
head: Fog Volume Froxel Culling, Froxel-culled fog injection, Per-volume fog injection, Per-volume froxel bounds culling, SGL3D Fog Volume Injection Optimization, inject scene fog volumes only into the froxels they cover
body: Fog Volume Injection Optimization reduces the computational cost of injecting scene fog volumes into a froxel grid by ensuring each volume is processed only by the froxels it geometrically covers, rather than having every froxel test every scene fog volume. It differs from the brute-force approach (where every froxel iterates all volumes) by using precomputed CPU-side bounds to cull irrelevant volume-froxel pairs, and differs from Godot’s per-volume dispatch by using a single GPU kernel with a culled list of ranges, avoiding the overhead of many small kernel launches. Inputs: List of scene fog volumes, each defined by eight world-space corners and associated density, albedo, and emission parameters. Camera parameters: view matrix, projection matrix, near plane distance, and Fog::length (far clip). Froxel grid parameters: grid dimensions (Nx, Ny, Nz) and world-space origin/spacing. Outputs: Updated froxel storage buffers: density (fixed-point) and scattering (R11G11B10 packed). Data Structures: fogvolumefroxels: A storage buffer (group 1, binding 9) containing a list of structures. Each structure represents a volume's froxel range: first: u32, the first froxel index (linearized) covered by the volume. last: u32, the last froxel index covered. volume: u32, the index of the scene fog volume in the scene list. The list is sorted by volume index (scene order). Parameters: Density scaling factor: 1024. Density is multiplied by this factor and truncated to integer. Froxel bound widening: 0.01. Added to computed bounds to absorb floating-point rounding errors. Steps: 1. Frustum Culling: For each scene fog volume, determine if it intersects the visible frustum. Drop volumes that lie entirely behind the camera, entirely beyond Fog::length, or entirely beside the frame without crossing the camera plane. 2. Bounding Froxel Range Calculation: Transform the volume's eight world-space corners to view space. Handle volumes crossing the camera's near plane: If any corner is on or behind the camera's plane, expand the froxel range to cover the entire frame (all x, y) up to the slice of the farthest corner. For other volumes, compute the min and max froxel indices (i{min}, i{max}) occupied by the corners. Apply widening: i{min} \leftarrow \max(0, i{min} - \lceil 0.01 \times \text{grid\size} \rceil) and i{max} \leftarrow \min(\text{grid\size} - 1, i{max} + \lceil 0.01 \times \text{grid\size} \rceil). Linearize the 3D froxel indices to a 1D range [first, last] based on the grid dimensions. 3. Upload Range List: Construct the fogvolumefroxels list with entries (first, last, volume) for all surviving volumes. Sort the list by volume index. Upload this list to the fogvolumefroxels storage buffer every frame. 4. Injection Shader Execution: The GPU launches a compute shader for the froxel grid. Each workgroup/thread processes a specific froxel (or a tile of froxels). For the current froxel index F, iterate through the fogvolumefroxels list. For each entry (first, last, vol\idx), check if first \le F \le last. If the condition holds, evaluate the volume's density and scattering at the froxel's position and accumulate into the froxel's storage buffers using atomics. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computefroxelrange(volumecorners, cameraviewmatrix, froxelgrid): # Transform corners to view space viewcorners = [transform(c, cameraviewmatrix) for c in volumecorners] # Check if any corner is behind or on the near plane if any(c.z <= 0.0 for c in viewcorners): # Expand to whole frame up to farthest corner's slice maxz = max(c.z for c in viewcorners) farslice = froxelgrid.zindexatdepth(maxz) return (0, froxelgrid.totalxyfroxels() farslice, volume.index) # Compute min/max froxel indices for all corners minx = min(froxelgrid.xindexatview(c.x, c.z) for c in viewcorners) maxx = max(froxelgrid.xindexatview(c.x, c.z) for c in viewcorners) miny = min(froxelgrid.yindexatview(c.y, c.z) for c in viewcorners) maxy = max(froxelgrid.yindexatview(c.y, c.z) for c in viewcorners) minz = min(froxelgrid.zindexatdepth(c.z) for c in viewcorners) maxz = max(froxelgrid.zindexatdepth(c.z) for c in viewcorners) # Apply widening widen = ceil(0.01 froxelgrid.resolution) minx = max(0, minx - widen) maxx = min(froxelgrid.width - 1, maxx + widen) miny = max(0, miny - widen) maxy = min(froxelgrid.height - 1, maxy + widen) minz = max(0, minz - widen) maxz = min(froxelgrid.depth - 1, maxz + widen) # Linearize to 1D range first = froxelgrid.linearindex(minx, miny, minz) last = froxelgrid.linearindex(maxx, maxy, maxz) return (first, last, volume.index) @compute fn injectfog(froxelindex: u32, fogvolumefroxels: array<VolumeRange>, fogvolumes: array<FogVolume>, densitybuffer: atomic<u32>, scatteringbuffer: atomic<u32>) { for i in 0..fogvolumefroxels.length { let range = fogvolumefroxels[i]; if froxelindex >= range.first && froxelindex <= range.last { let volume = fogvolumes[range.volume]; // Evaluate density at froxel position let density = evaluatedensity(volume, froxelposition); // Accumulate density (scaled by 1024, truncated) let densityfixed = u32(density 1024.0); atomicAdd(&densitybuffer[froxelindex], densityfixed); // Accumulate scattering (albedo clamp(density, 0, 1), packed R11G11B10) let scatteringweight = clamp(density, 0.0, 1.0); let scatteringval = volume.albedo scatteringweight; let scatteringpacked = packr11g11b10(scatteringval); atomicAdd(&scatteringbuffer[froxelindex], scatteringpacked); } } } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Rounding Errors: Floating-point projection of corners can cause off-by-one froxel errors. The widening factor of 0.01 froxels absorbs this. Camera Plane Crossing: Volumes holding or crossing the camera plane must be handled carefully. Clamping corners behind the camera (as done in some implementations) can fail to bound boxes crossing the plane. Expanding the bound to the whole frame if any corner is on or behind the plane is safer. Determinism: The order of accumulation must remain consistent with the original brute-force method to ensure identical density and albedo sums where volumes overlap. Time Complexity: Reduces the fog injection loop from O(F \times V) to O(F \times V{in\view}) + O(V \times F{per\volume}), where F is total froxels, V is total volumes, V{in\view} is volumes in view, and F{per\volume} is froxels per volume. Measured Performance: In Hyperdrive (1920×1080, High, 32 tunnel volumes), brute-force volume loop was ~1.3–1.5 ms of 4.5 ms total fog injection. With the optimization (SGL main #42 fix), fog injection dropped from 1.72 ms to 1.25 ms (High/Low night), 4.74 ms to 3.55 ms (High/High night), and 4.96 ms to 3.97 ms (Ultra night). At High/Low day, it dropped from 0.91 ms to 0.31 ms; at Ultra day, from 4.14 ms to 2.15 ms. Strengths: Eliminates redundant volume tests; avoids overhead of many small kernel dispatches (compared to Godot's per-volume dispatch). Limitations: Requires CPU-side bounds calculation every frame; still iterates all volumes in view for each froxel (though fewer volumes pass the range test). When to Use: When the number of scene fog volumes is significant and many do not intersect the visible froxel grid. When Not to Use: When the number of volumes is very small, or when volumes are uniformly distributed across the entire grid, reducing the benefit of culling. The optimization was developed for the SGL3D rendering engine, following its rendering development rules (RD-1–RD-7) and architecture (AR rules). It was implemented in pull request #64, addressing issue #42, to improve performance in scenes with many fog volumes, such as the Hyperdrive test environment. It draws inspiration from Godot's per-volume froxel AABB computation and frustum culling. name: Fog Volume Entity
head: Fog Volume Entity Setup, FogVolume
body: The Fog Volume Entity is a spatial entity used to define local volumetric fog density, color, and noise-based structure within a 3D level. It solves the problem of creating non-uniform, patchy fog effects (such as fog banks or layered mist) that cannot be achieved with global fog settings alone. It differs from sibling methods like Fog Volume Grid Rendering by providing a high-level, user-configurable entity interface for shaping fog via noise parameters, rather than directly manipulating the underlying froxel data structures. The entity accepts spatial placement (position and scale) and parameter values. It outputs a modified fog field that contributes to the global volumetric lighting calculation. The entity exposes a set of scalar and boolean parameters. The specific ranges and defaults are defined below. Parameter Layout: Density: Float. Range: [0, 100]. Default: Not specified. Controls base fog density. DensityNoiseOffset: Float. Range: [-2, +2]. Default: Not specified. Offsets the noise value for density. DensityNoiseScale: Float. Range: [0, 10]. Default: 1. Scales the noise value for density. DensityNoiseFrequency: Vector3 (X, Y, Z). Default: Not specified. Defines the frequency of noise patches. DensityNoiseTimeFrequency: Float. Default: Not specified. Controls the speed of temporal morphing. WindInfluence: Float. Range: [0, 20]. Default: Not specified. Controls the influence of global wind. UseGlobalFogColor: Boolean. Default: Not specified. Overrides local color with global fog color. Enabled: Boolean. Default: True. Controls entity state. The entity generates a local fog field by combining a base density with a noise function. The exact noise function implementation is not provided in the sources. The following procedural steps describe the configuration and runtime behavior: 1. Initialization: Place the entity in the level. Define its spatial bounds (e.g., 50m \times 50m \times 50m). 2. Base Density Setup: Set Density to a high value (e.g., 100) for visibility during setup, or to a production value (typically 1-3) for subtle effects. 3. Noise Offset Application: Apply DensityNoiseOffset. A negative value (e.g., -1.2) breaks the solid volume into patches. 4. Noise Scaling: Apply DensityNoiseScale. This defines the thickness of individual fog patches (clouds) or the spacing between them. A value of 0.5 thins density and increases spacing. 5. Frequency Definition: Set DensityNoiseFrequency (X, Y, Z). Increasing Z (e.g., from 10 to 100) creates a layered effect. Higher X and Y values create more individual patches. Varying X, Y, Z values randomly breaks up patches into different sizes. 6. Temporal Morphing: Apply DensityNoiseTimeFrequency. A low value (e.g., 0.2) ensures natural morphing; higher values cause unnatural quick morphing. 7. Color Blending: If UseGlobalFogColor is enabled, the entity's local color is overridden by the global fog color, ensuring natural blending. 8. Wind Interaction: Apply WindInfluence to allow global wind to affect the fog volume's shape or movement. The following pseudocode represents the runtime update loop for a Fog Volume Entity, assuming a noise function Noise3D(x, y, z, time) is available. This is a reconstruction based on the parameter interactions described. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updatefogvolumeentity(entity, globalwind, timestep): # 1. Get parameters densitybase = entity.Density noiseoffset = entity.DensityNoiseOffset noisescale = entity.DensityNoiseScale freq = entity.DensityNoiseFrequency # Vector3 timefreq = entity.DensityNoiseTimeFrequency windinf = entity.WindInfluence useglobalcolor = entity.UseGlobalFogColor # 2. Calculate temporal offset for noise # The source mentions morphing patches over time timeoffset = time timefreq # 3. For each point P within the entity's bounding box: # Note: Exact shader integration is not provided # The following represents the logical contribution to density localwind = globalwind windinf # Calculate noise value at point P # Assuming P is relative to entity center noiseval = Noise3D( P.x freq.x, P.y freq.y, P.z freq.z, timeoffset) # Apply offset and scale # Source: Offset breaks solid shape, Scale defines thickness/spacing adjustednoise = (noiseval + noiseoffset) noisescale # Combine with base density # Source: Density controls overall density finaldensity = densitybase adjustednoise # 4. Determine color if useglobalcolor: finalcolor = globalfogcolor else: finalcolor = entity.localcolor return finaldensity, finalcolor High Density Values: Setting Density to 100 is intended for setup visibility only. Using this in production results in unnatural, opaque fog. Fast Morphing: High DensityNoiseTimeFrequency values cause unnatural, rapid morphing of fog patches. Parameter Coupling: DensityNoiseOffset and DensityNoiseScale work closely together; adjusting one often requires tweaking the other to maintain the desired patch structure. Color Clashing: Without UseGlobalFogColor enabled, local colors (e.g., red) may blend poorly with the scene. Performance: Performance impact depends on the number of active Fog Volume entities and their overlap with the view frustum. The entity is controlled via Flow Graph, allowing runtime modification of parameters. Memory: Memory usage is associated with the entity's transform and parameter storage. The underlying froxel data is handled by the Fog Volume Grid Rendering system. Strengths: Allows for complex, non-uniform fog structures (banks, layers) without manual texture painting or complex shader graphs. Limitations: Limited to the parameters exposed by the entity. Fine-grained control requires understanding the interaction between noise parameters. When to use: For creating localized fog effects like mist, fog banks, or layered clouds in specific areas of a level. When not to use: For uniform, global fog effects, which are better handled by global fog settings. The Fog Volume Entity is part of the CRYENGINE 5 Volumetric Fog system. It was introduced to provide artists with control over density noise, enabling the creation of interesting shapes within fog volumes. It is used in conjunction with the Flow Graph system for runtime control. name: Hardware Ray Tracing Global Illumination
body: Hardware Ray Tracing Global Illumination is a real-time, one-bounce diffuse global illumination technique that leverages hardware-accelerated ray tracing cores to compute indirect lighting. It approximates the indirect irradiance at a surface point by cosine-sampling the hemisphere around the surface normal, tracing short rays against a voxel grid, and gathering irradiance from hits or skylight when rays escape. It differs from sibling methods like Voxel Cone Tracing by performing explicit per-pixel ray queries rather than cone-based approximations, trading higher per-sample computational overhead for improved geometric accuracy. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Surface position o, surface normal n, camera direction v, and a precomputed voxel grid representing the scene geometry and lighting. Output: Accumulated indirect irradiance contribution to the pixel color. Data Structures: The method relies on a voxel grid where each voxel (or "brick") contains metadata. The specific internal layout of the voxel data is not detailed in the sources, but the access pattern involves querying for the first solid, non-transparent voxel along a ray. The system uses a RayQuery object (standard in DXR/Vulkan RT) to manage traversal state. Parameters: GIRAYS: Number of fresh samples per frame. Value: 1. GIDIST: Bounce ray reach in voxels. Value: 40.0. GISTRENGTH: Multiplier for GI intensity. Value: 1.0. GISKY: Soft skylight fill factor. Value: 0.32. Algorithm Steps: 1. Tangent Frame Construction: Construct a local tangent frame from the surface normal n to facilitate hemisphere sampling. Select an up vector: up = select(z, x, abs(n.z) > 0.9). Compute tangent: tang = normalize(cross(n, up)). Compute bitangent: bitan = cross(n, tang). 2. Ray Sampling Loop: For each ray k in GIRAYS: Generate two random numbers r1, r2 from a hash of the pixel position and a seed. Compute a cosine-weighted hemisphere direction d{local}: rr = \sqrt{r1} \phi = 2\pi r2 d{local} = (rr \cos \phi, rr \sin \phi, \sqrt{\max(0, 1 - r1)}) Transform to world space: dir = \text{normalize}(tang \cdot d{local}.x + bitan \cdot d{local}.y + n \cdot d{local}.z) 3. Ray Tracing (gitrace): Initialize a RayQuery with origin o, direction dir, and hit range [0.02, \text{GI\DIST}]. Iterate through ray query candidates. If a candidate is an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB), retrieve its brick index bi. Check if the brick is active using rtbrickactive(bi). If inactive, continue to the next candidate. Call resolvebrick with skiptransparent = true to find the first solid, non-transparent voxel within the brick. If a hit is found at distance t \ge 0, generate an intersection in the ray query: rayQueryGenerateIntersection(&rq, t). Update the best hit distance bestt if t < \text{best\t}. 4. Irradiance Accumulation (rtgatherindirect): If a hit is recorded with voxel hv, normal hn, and brick hbi: Retrieve the albedo or color of the hit voxel. Accumulate light: light += hitcolor GISTRENGTH. If no hit is recorded (ray escapes): Accumulate skylight: light += GISKY. The final contribution is typically scaled by the cosine of the angle between the ray direction and the surface normal, though the source notes imply the cosine-weighted sampling handles the distribution, and the accumulation sums the gathered values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math GIRAYS = 1 GIDIST = 40.0 GISTRENGTH = 1.0 GISKY = 0.32 def rtgatherindirect(o: vec3, n: vec3) -> vec3: # 1. Tangent frame construction up = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 1.0) if abs(n.z) > 0.9 else vec3(1.0, 0.0, 0.0) tang = normalize(cross(n, up)) bitan = cross(n, tang) totalirradiance = vec3(0.0) # 2. Ray sampling loop for k in range(GIRAYS): # Generate randoms from hash of position and seed r1, r2 = hashrandoms(o, k) # Cosine-weighted hemisphere direction rr = math.sqrt(r1) phi = 2.0 math.pi r2 dlx = rr math.cos(phi) dly = rr math.sin(phi) dlz = math.sqrt(max(0.0, 1.0 - r1)) dir = normalize(tang dlx + bitan dly + n dlz) # 3. Trace ray hit = gitrace(o, dir) # 4. Accumulate if hit is not None: totalirradiance += hit.color GISTRENGTH else: totalirradiance += vec3(GISKY) return totalirradiance def gitrace(o: vec3, dir: vec3) -> HitRecord | None: # Initialize ray query with origin, direction, and hit range [0.02, GIDIST] bestt = GIDIST besthit = None # Iterate through ray query candidates for candidate in rayquerycandidates(o, dir, mint=0.02, maxt=GIDIST): if candidate.isaabb(): bi = candidate.brickindex() if not rtbrickactive(bi): continue # Resolve brick for first solid, non-transparent voxel t = resolvebrick(bi, skiptransparent=True) if t >= 0 and t < bestt: bestt = t besthit = gethitinfo(candidate, t) return besthit def hashrandoms(position: vec3, seed: int) -> tuple[float, float]: # Returns two pseudo-random floats in 0, 1) derived from position and seed h = hash((position.x, position.y, position.z, seed)) return (h % 10000 / 10000.0, (h >> 16) % 10000 / 10000.0) def rayquerycandidates(o: vec3, dir: vec3, mint: float, maxt: float): # Yields intersection candidates from the hardware/software ray query engine # within the specified hit range. Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot R) where N is the number of pixels/samples and R is the number of rays per sample (typically 1). The cost is dominated by the hardware ray traversal. Memory Complexity: Depends on the voxel grid size. The method itself requires minimal per-pixel state, storing only the accumulated irradiance. Performance: Performance scales with the number of active bricks and the depth of the ray traversal. Hardware RT cores provide significant acceleration over software ray tracing. Strengths: High geometric accuracy for indirect lighting; handles complex occlusion and shadowing naturally via ray tracing; simple to implement on modern hardware. Limitations: Limited to one-bounce illumination (diffuse GI); noisy with low sample counts (mitigated by temporal accumulation); no specular reflections; performance can degrade with deep voxel grids or high GIDIST values. When to use: Real-time applications requiring accurate diffuse global illumination where hardware RT is available. When not to use: Applications requiring specular GI, multi-bounce lighting, or running on hardware without RT cores. name: Dynamic Diffuse Global Illumination (DDGI)
body: Dynamic Diffuse Global Illumination (DDGI) is a real-time global illumination technique that computes one-bounce diffuse indirect lighting by maintaining a 3D grid of low-resolution cubemap probes. It extends classic irradiance probes by blending hardware-accelerated ray tracing with rasterization to compactly encode the full irradiance field, specifically aiming to eliminate the light and shadow leak issues inherent in voxel-based methods like Voxel Cone Tracing (VCT). Unlike its parent Hardware Ray Tracing Global Illumination, which traces rays per-pixel, DDGI traces rays per-probe to build a spatially coherent lighting field, offering O(1) rendering complexity and significantly lower memory consumption at the cost of slightly lower visual quality compared to VCT. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scene geometry, active probe locations, ray tracing acceleration structure. Output: A probe atlas containing irradiance data and depth information for each probe, used during shading to interpolate indirect lighting. Data Structures: Probe Atlas: A 3D grid array of cubemaps. Each probe consists of two very low-resolution cubemaps (e.g., 4 \times 4 resolution). Irradiance Cubemap: Stores the accumulated indirect diffuse lighting. Depth Cubemap: Stores the distance to the nearest surface hit from the probe center, used to prevent light/shadow leaks. Surfel G-Buffer: A structure storing position and normal data for geometry hits intersected by probe rays. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Tracing and Surfel Generation: For each of the m active probes, generate and trace n rays into the scene. The rays can be generated via cone tracing (if hardware RT is unavailable) or hardware-accelerated ray tracing (RTX/DXR/RadeonRays). Store all geometry hits in a G-Buffer structure as surfels, recording their position and normal vectors. 2. Surfel Shading: Shade each surfel with direct and indirect illumination. 3. Probe Update (Blending): Update the texels in the active probes by blending in updated shading, distance, and square-distance results for each intersected surfel. This blending process allows the probe data to adapt to changes in scene geometry over time. 4. Interpolation: Interpolate probe depth information and irradiance data from the grid to the shading point to determine indirect illumination. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from dataclasses import dataclass import math @dataclass class Surfel: position: tuple normal: tuple shading: tuple distance: float distancesq: float def traceray(origin, direction, bvh): hit = bvh.intersect(origin, direction) if hit: directlight = (0.8, 0.8, 0.8) # Standard direct illumination calculation return Surfel( position=hit.point, normal=hit.normal, shading=directlight, distance=math.dist(origin, hit.point), distancesq=math.dist(origin, hit.point)2) return None def generateraydirection(normal): return (0.0, 1.0, 0.0) # Standard hemisphere sampling def worldtocubemap(direction): return 0, (0.5, 0.5) # Standard direction-to-face mapping def blend(current, new, weight): return current (1.0 - weight) + new weight def updateddgiprobes(probes, bvh, numraysperprobe): for probe in probes: hits = [] for in range(numraysperprobe): direction = generateraydirection(probe.normal) hit = traceray(probe.position, direction, bvh) if hit: hits.append(hit) for surfel in hits: face, uv = worldtocubemap(surfel.position - probe.position) weight = 1.0 / (1.0 + surfel.distancesq) probe.irradiancecubemap[face][uv] = blend( probe.irradiancecubemap[face][uv], surfel.shading, weight=weight) probe.depthcubemap[face][uv] = blend( probe.depthcubemap[face][uv], surfel.distance, weight=weight) def getsurroundingprobes(probegrid, point): return probegrid # Standard grid lookup def interpolatecubemaps(probes, point): return probes[0].irradiancecubemap[0][0] # Standard trilinear interpolation def interpolatedepths(probes, point): return probes[0].depthcubemap[0][0] # Standard trilinear interpolation def shadewithddgi(probegrid, shadingpoint): surrounding = getsurroundingprobes(probegrid, shadingpoint) irradiance = interpolatecubemaps(surrounding, shadingpoint) depth = interpolatedepths(surrounding, shadingpoint) return irradiance Parameters: Probe Resolution: Very low, e.g., 4 \times 4 per cubemap face. Active Probes: All probes in the grid are active by default; no heuristics are provided for selecting a subset, though heuristics could be implemented to reduce updates. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Light/Shadow Leaks: Mitigated by the second depth cubemap, which stores distance to the nearest surface to prevent light from leaking through geometry. Performance: Without heuristics for active probes, all probes are updated every frame, which can be computationally expensive if the grid is large. Diffuse Only: The method does not handle specular reflections. A probe-based technique that approximates indirect lighting using spherical harmonics coefficients in a 3D grid. It differs from DDGI by replacing depth-texture-based visibility with ray-traced visibility to eliminate aliasing and reduce memory overhead, while retaining the core structure of low-resolution cubemaps or spherical harmonics probes. Complexity: Rendering complexity is O(1), as shading requires only interpolation from the probe grid. Memory: Consumes far less memory than Voxel Cone Tracing (VCT) due to the use of very low-resolution cubemaps instead of a dense voxel grid. Performance: Ideal for real-time applications due to O(1) shading cost. Building probes can be accelerated significantly using hardware ray tracing (RTX/DXR) compared to rasterization or cone tracing. Quality: Handles only diffuse GI. Visual quality is slightly lower than diffuse VCT. Limitations: No specular reflections. Lack of heuristics for active probe selection may lead to unnecessary updates. DDGI was presented by McGuire et al.. It builds upon prior work by McGuire et al. [41] (referenced within) and extends classic irradiance probes to compactly encode the full irradiance field. The technique was developed to address performance issues with sparse octrees and light/shadow leaks in previous global illumination approaches. It is often implemented in two stages: first using Voxel Cone Tracing (VCT) to build probes (without hardware RT), and later migrating to hardware-accelerated ray tracing (RTX/DXR/RadeonRays) for faster and more accurate probe building. name: Probe-based Global Illumination (DDGI-like)
head: DDGI, DDGI implementation, Probe Grid, Probe-based Methods (DDGI Baseline)
body: A probe-based global illumination technique implemented for quantitative comparison with NIV, supporting visibility-based probe rejection using ray tracing. It differs from its parent Dynamic Diffuse Global Illumination (DDGI) by replacing depth-texture-based visibility with ray-traced visibility to eliminate aliasing and reduce memory overhead, while retaining the core structure of spherical harmonics probes. Inputs: Scene geometry (for ray tracing), camera position, shading point position, and shading normal. Outputs: Approximated indirect irradiance at the shading point. Probe Grid: A regular 3D grid of probes. Probe Storage Layout: Each probe stores directional indirect irradiance represented by second-order spherical harmonics (9 coefficients) [RH01]. The coefficients are quantized to half-precision after baking, resulting in 54 bytes per probe (9 \times 3 \times 2 bytes, representing RGB irradiance per coefficient). Alternative quantization to 28 bytes per probe is possible but has little influence on results. Visibility: Computed via ray tracing from the shading point to the probe locations. 1. Ray Traced Visibility: Compute visibility using ray tracing rather than depth textures. 2. Cosine Fall-off: Apply a cosine fall-off [Hoo16] such that probes behind the sampled normal do not contribute to trilinear interpolation. 3. Weight Clamping: Clamp interpolation weights to a small number (10^{-6}) to avoid no probes contributing to a shading point. 4. Re-normalization: Re-normalize interpolation weights after applying the heuristics (cosine fall-off and clamping). 5. Trilinear Interpolation: Perform trilinear interpolation of the SH coefficients from the surrounding probes in the grid based on the normalized weights. 6. SH Evaluation: Evaluate the interpolated SH coefficients to compute the indirect irradiance at the shading point. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeprobeillumination(shadingpoint, shadingnormal, probegrid): """ Computes indirect irradiance using a probe grid with ray-traced visibility. Args: shadingpoint: tuple(float, float, float), world position of the shading point. shadingnormal: tuple(float, float, float), normalized surface normal. probegrid: dict containing 'origin', 'spacing', 'dims', and 'probes' (list of 3D arrays). Returns: tuple(float, float, float), the computed indirect irradiance (RGB). """ origin = probegrid['origin'] spacing = probegrid['spacing'] dims = probegrid['dims'] probes = probegrid['probes'] # 1. Convert world position to grid coordinates gridcoords = [(shadingpoint[i] - origin[i]) / spacing[i] for i in range(3)] # 2. Determine the 8 surrounding integer grid cells and trilinear weights lower = [math.floor(c) for c in gridcoords] frac = [gridcoords[i] - lower[i] for i in range(3)] neighbors = [] weights = [] for dx in (0, 1): for dy in (0, 1): for dz in (0, 1): idx = [lower[i] + (dx if i == 0 else 0) + (dy if i == 1 else 0) + (dz if i == 2 else 0) for i in range(3)] # Clamp indices to grid bounds idx = [max(0, min(dims[i] - 1, idx[i])) for i in range(3)] w = 1.0 for i in range(3): w = (frac[i] if (idx[i] == lower[i] + 1) else (1.0 - frac[i])) neighbors.append((idx, w)) # 3. Apply visibility, cosine fall-off, and compute final weights finalweights = [] for idx, basew in neighbors: # Direction from shading point to probe center probepos = [origin[i] + (idx[i] + 0.5) spacing[i] for i in range(3)] direction = [probepos[i] - shadingpoint[i] for i in range(3)] length = math.sqrt(sum(dd for d in direction)) direction = [d / length for d in direction] # Ray trace visibility isvisible = not raytrace(shadingpoint, direction, length) # Cosine fall-off costheta = sum(shadingnormal[i] direction[i] for i in range(3)) weight = basew (costheta if (isvisible and costheta > 0) else 0.0) finalweights.append(weight) # 4. Clamping minweight = 1e-6 finalweights = [max(w, minweight) for w in finalweights] # 5. Re-normalization weightsum = sum(finalweights) normalizedweights = [w / weightsum for w in finalweights] # 6. Trilinear Interpolation of SH Coefficients # SH layout: 9 coefficients 3 RGB channels shinterp = [0.0] 27 for i, (idx,) in enumerate(neighbors): probesh = probes[idx[0]][idx[1]][idx[2]] for k in range(27): shinterp[k] += normalizedweights[i] probesh[k] # 7. SH Evaluation irradiance = evaluatesh(shinterp, shadingnormal) return irradiance def raytrace(origin, direction, maxdistance): """Returns True if geometry is hit, False if path is clear.""" # Standard ray-scene intersection test return False # Placeholder for scene-specific intersection logic def evaluatesh(shcoeffs, normal): """Evaluates second-order SH basis functions at the normal.""" # Standard SH irradiance projection for l=2 (9 coefficients, 3 channels) # Y0 = 1/(2sqrt(pi)) # Y1 = sqrt(3/(4pi)) n # Y2 = sqrt(15/(4pi)) (nxny, nynz, nz(2nz - nx - ny), nxnz, nxnx - nyny) # Irradiance = sum(shk Yk(normal)) pi = math.pi y = [0.0] 9 nx, ny, nz = normal y[0] = 1.0 / (2.0 math.sqrt(pi)) y[1] = math.sqrt(3.0 / (4.0 pi)) nx y[2] = math.sqrt(3.0 / (4.0 pi)) ny y[3] = math.sqrt(3.0 / (4.0 pi)) nz y[4] = math.sqrt(15.0 / (4.0 pi)) nx ny y[5] = math.sqrt(15.0 / (4.0 pi)) ny nz y[6] = math.sqrt(15.0 / (4.0 pi)) nz (2.0 nz - nx - ny) y[7] = math.sqrt(15.0 / (4.0 pi)) nx nz y[8] = math.sqrt(15.0 / (4.0 pi)) (nx nx - ny ny) irradiance = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for c in range(3): for k in range(9): irradiance[c] += shcoeffs[k 3 + c] y[k] return tuple(irradiance) Spherical Harmonics Order: Second-order (9 coefficients) [RH01]. Quantization: Half-precision (16-bit) for SH coefficients. Further quantization to 28 bytes per probe is possible but has little influence on results. Clamping Threshold: 10^{-6} for interpolation weights. Grid Size: Example: 22^3 probe grid for the Sponza scene, consuming 35.5 MB in standard DDGI. Light Leaks: Occur if ray-traced visibility is not employed and cosine fall-off is insufficient or incorrectly applied. Contact Shadows: Probe-based methods fail to capture contact shadows entirely due to the low resolution of the irradiance volume. Probe Placement Errors: Erroneous probe placement (e.g., inside geometry) combined with runtime updates can produce artifacts like dark smudges on surfaces. Memory Overhead: Standard DDGI uses 1168 bytes per probe, with 1024 bytes dedicated to depth buffers. Using ray-traced visibility reduces this to 54 bytes per probe for SH data. Time Complexity: Query time is dominated by simple trilinear interpolation of SH coefficients, which is highly competitive. Ray-traced visibility adds significant runtime cost compared to depth-texture lookups. Memory Complexity: Scales cubically with spatial discretization. For a 22^3 grid, it consumes 35.5 MB (standard DDGI) or significantly less if depth buffers are removed (54 bytes/probe). Performance: Simple probe-based methods have a performance edge over neural implicit methods (like NIV) if optimized, due to the simplicity of trilinear interpolation. NIV requires input encoding evaluation and matrix multiplications, incurring a cost of around 1 ms on an RTX 4090. Strengths: Simple implementation, predictable memory usage, fast query times if visibility is cheap. Limitations: Poor representation of high-frequency details (contact shadows), light leaks without careful visibility handling, cubic memory scaling. When to Use: When memory budget is fixed and scene geometry is static or slowly changing, and high-frequency shadow details are not critical. When Not to Use: When contact shadows are essential, or when adaptive resolution is needed to handle complex lighting details efficiently. Origin: Based on the Dynamic Diffuse Global Illumination (DDGI) method [MGNM19]. Development: Implemented as a baseline for comparison with Neural Irradiance Volumes (NIV). The specific variant described uses ray-traced visibility instead of depth textures to improve quality and reduce memory overhead. Usage: Used in real-time rendering systems for global illumination approximation, particularly in games and interactive applications where path tracing is too expensive.
