name: Temporal GI Accumulation with Reprojection
head: RT variant GI, Reprojected GI
body: This method accumulates hardware ray-traced indirect illumination over time by reprojecting the previous frame's GI buffer into the current frame, reducing noise and convergence time for dynamic scenes. It differs from Hardware Ray Tracing Global Illumination by adding temporal history blending and from Dynamic Diffuse Global Illumination (DDGI) by relying on per-pixel reprojection rather than sparse probe caching for temporal stability. Inputs: Current frame camera state: worldorigin, prevorigin, prevforward, prevright, prevup, tanhalffov, resolution (x, y). Previous frame G-buffer position buffer: lightin (texture2d<f32>). Previous frame GI buffer: giin (texture2d<f32>). Surface shading point p (world space), normal n, view vector v. Ray tracing gather function rtgatherindirect(p, n, seed) returning a radiance value. Probe sampling function sampleprobes(p, n, v) returning a radiance value. Parameters: GIENABLE, GIMAXT, GISTRENGTH, GIPROBEMODE, REPROJEPS2. Outputs: giout: texturestorage2d<rgba32float, write> storing the final accumulated indirect color as vec4<f32>(acc, 1.0). Data Structures: giin: 2D texture of f32 RGBA values. Stores the temporally accumulated indirect illumination from the previous frame. lightin: 2D texture of f32 RGBA values. Stores the world-space position of the surface point corresponding to the pixel. giout: 2D storage texture of f32 RGBA values. Target for the current frame's result. Steps: 1. Early Exit Check: If GIENABLE < 0.5 or the ray hit distance t >= GIMAXT, store vec4<f32>(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0) to giout and return 0.0. 2. Fade Factor Calculation: Calculate a distance-based fade factor to prevent artifacts at the maximum ray distance: fade = 1.0 - \text{smoothstep}(GI\MAX\T \times 0.6, GI\MAX\T, t) 3. Indirect Illumination Sample: If GIPROBEMODE > 0.5: Sample irradiance from probes: gi = \text{sample\probes}(p, n, v) \times (GI\STRENGTH \times fade). Store vec4<f32>(gi, 1.0) to giout and return gi. Otherwise (per-pixel ray tracing): Compute fresh sample: acc = \text{rt\gather\indirect}(p, n, \text{seed}) \times fade. 4. Temporal Reprojection Attempt: If camera.reprojectlighting > 0.5: Calculate relative hit position: hitpos\rel = p - \text{camera.world\origin}. Calculate vector from previous camera origin: d = p - \text{camera.prev\origin}. Calculate depth along previous forward vector: pz = \text{dot}(d, \text{camera.prev\forward}). If pz > 0.01: Project to Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC): ndc = \left( \frac{\text{dot}(d, \text{camera.prev\right})}{pz \times \text{camera.tan\half\fov} \times \text{aspect}}, \frac{\text{dot}(d, \text{camera.prev\up})}{pz \times \text{camera.tan\half\fov}} \right) where \text{aspect} = \text{camera.resolution.x} / \text{camera.resolution.y}. Convert NDC to UV coordinates: uvp = (ndc.x \times 0.5 + 0.5, 0.5 - ndc.y \times 0.5) If uvp \in 0, 1): Load previous G-buffer position: g = \text{textureLoad}(\text{light\in}, \lfloor uvp \times \text{camera.resolution} \rfloor, 0). Check position match: dpos = g.xyz - hitpos\rel. If \text{dot}(dpos, dpos) < REPROJ\EPS2: Load previous GI: prev = \text{textureLoad}(\text{gi\in}, \lfloor uvp \times \text{camera.resolution} \rfloor, 0).rgb. Blend with history: acc = \text{mix}(acc, prev, 0.9). 5. Store Result: Store acc to giout as vec4<f32>(acc, 1.0) and return acc. Parameters: GIENABLE: Pipeline-override toggle. 1.0 (default) enables GI; 0.0 disables it. GIPROBEMODE: Toggle between probe cache (1.0) and legacy per-pixel bounce ray (0.0). GIMAXT: Maximum ray distance for GI. GISTRENGTH: Multiplier for probe-based GI. REPROJEPS2: Squared epsilon for position matching during reprojection. Value not explicitly given in sources. Blend Factor: 0.9 (90% history, ~10-frame convergence). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Reprojection Failure: If the position match fails (e.g., due to occlusion changes, object motion, or depth discontinuities), the temporal history is discarded, and the fresh ray-traced sample is used. This can cause flickering if the reprojection is unstable. Zero Depth: If pz \le 0.01, reprojection is skipped to avoid division by zero or invalid projections. Out of Bounds UV: If the projected UV is outside [0, 1), reprojection is skipped. Probe Mode: In probe mode, temporal reprojection is bypassed, and results are returned directly from the probe sampler. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel per frame, assuming constant-time texture lookups and ray tracing queries. The temporal reprojection adds a constant overhead of a few vector operations and texture loads. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for the giin and lightin buffers, where W and H are the screen resolution. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with resolution. The temporal aspect reduces the required number of ray samples per frame to achieve a noise-free result, effectively trading memory (for history buffers) for compute. Strengths: Reduces noise significantly compared to single-frame ray tracing. Smooths out jitter from sparse sampling. Limitations: Requires stable reprojection; fails on fast-moving objects or dynamic occlusions, leading to ghosting or flickering if not handled. Requires G-buffer position data. When to use: Dynamic scenes with moderate camera movement where noise reduction is critical and hardware RT cores are available. When not to use: Scenes with very fast-moving objects or frequent large-scale changes where reprojection fails frequently. This method is implemented in the voxelG project by mstampfli. It is part of a real-time global illumination pipeline that uses hardware ray tracing cores for indirect lighting. The approach combines per-pixel ray tracing with [temporal accumulation to improve visual quality. mstampfli/voxelG, https://github.com/mstampfli/voxelG, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Volumetric Light Scattering via Froxel Clustering
head: scatter local lights in the volumetric fog volume
body: Volumetric Light Scattering via Froxel Clustering is a real-time rendering technique that computes light scattering for local lights (point and spot) within a participating media volume by evaluating contributions at the midpoints of a 3D froxel grid. It differs from Froxel-based Volumetric Rendering by explicitly clustering lights per froxel to optimize the evaluation of the scattering integral for multiple local sources, while skipping the sun and non-volumetric lights. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A 3D froxel grid partitioning the view frustum, a list of scene lights, camera parameters, and fog parameters (albedo, anisotropy). Outputs: The accumulated scattered radiance for each froxel. Data Structures: Light Struct: Contains a boolean flag LIGHTVOLUMETRIC. Constructors for directional, point, and spot lights set this to true, while a zero-initialized Light struct leaves it false. Froxel Grid: A regular 3D grid partitioning the view frustum. Light List: A global buffer containing indices of lights affecting specific froxels, used as a fallback when cluster cells overflow or fall outside the grid. Algorithm Steps: 1. Partition the view frustum into froxels. 2. For each froxel, determine its midpoint in world space. 3. Perform a cluster lookup to retrieve the list of lights affecting that cell, identical to the surface rendering path. If the froxel is outside the cluster grid or the cell is overflowing, walk the complete flat light list instead. 4. Initialize accumulated radiance to zero. 5. Iterate through the retrieved light list: a. Check if the light is the sun (identified by index + 1 == sunlight). If so, skip it, as the sun is handled separately. b. Check if the light has the LIGHTVOLUMETRIC flag set. If not, skip it. c. Check if the light's samplelight radiance is zero. If so, skip it. d. For remaining lights, compute the scattering contribution using the formula below. 6. Accumulate the contributions from all valid lights. Formula: The contribution C of a single light is calculated as: C = \text{albedo} \times \text{HG}(\text{dot}(\text{ray}, \text{light\dir}), \text{fog\anisotropy}) \times \text{radiance} \times \text{visibility} Where: \text{albedo}: The fog's albedo (scattering color). \text{HG}(\mu, g): The Henyey-Greenstein phase function, where \mu = \text{dot}(\text{ray}, \text{light\dir}) and g is \text{fog\anisotropy}. \text{radiance}: The light's radiance value. \text{visibility}: 1.0 if the light does not cast shadows. If the light casts shadows, visibility is determined by a single shadow sample taken with a zero normal vector (\vec{n} = \vec{0}). Parameters: foganisotropy: The anisotropy parameter for the Henyey-Greenstein phase function. LIGHTVOLUMETRIC: Boolean flag controlling whether a light contributes to volumetric scattering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computevolumetricscattering(froxelmidpoint, froxelcell, clustergrid, flatlightlist, sunlightindex, fogalbedo, foganisotropy, cameraposition, lights): # Step 1: Retrieve light list if froxelcell in clustergrid and not clustergrid[froxelcell].overflowing: lightindices = clustergrid[froxelcell].lightlist else: lightindices = flatlightlist accumulatedradiance = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Step 2: Iterate lights for lightidx in lightindices: light = lights[lightidx] # Skip Sun if lightidx + 1 == sunlightindex: continue # Skip non-volumetric lights if not light.flags.LIGHTVOLUMETRIC: continue # Skip zero radiance lights if light.samplelight().radiance == 0.0: continue # Compute Contribution raydir = normalize(froxelmidpoint - cameraposition) lightdir = normalize(light.position - froxelmidpoint) dotproduct = dot(raydir, lightdir) hgphase = heneygreenstein(dotproduct, foganisotropy) radiance = light.samplelight().radiance # Visibility: 1 if no shadow, else 1 shadow sample with zero normal if light.castsshadow: visibility = sampleshadow(light, froxelmidpoint, [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) else: visibility = 1.0 contribution = [fogalbedo[i] hgphase radiance[i] visibility for i in range(3)] accumulatedradiance = [accumulatedradiance[i] + contribution[i] for i in range(3)] return accumulatedradiance def heneygreenstein(mu, g): # Standard Henyey-Greenstein phase function g2 = g g denom = 1.0 + g2 - 2.0 g mu return (1.0 - g2) / (4.0 3.14159265 max(denom, 1e-6) 1.5) def sampleshadow(light, point, normal): # Single shadow sample with zero normal as per source return light.castshadowat(point, normal) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Opting Out: Setting LIGHTVOLUMETRIC to false saves radiance and shadow sample computation but does not save the cost of walking the per-light list. Fallback Performance: Froxels outside the cluster grid fall back to a flat light list. The percentage of such froxels increases with fardistance. For a 60° vertical FOV and near plane 0.1, at fardistance 200, 22.6% of froxels fall outside the grid; at 500, 51.0%; at 1000, 65.4%. Sun Handling: The sun is explicitly skipped in the loop to avoid double-counting, as it is added separately. Froxel Light Assignment partitions the camera frustum into a 3D grid of froxels and assigns scene lights to them using compute shaders. It differs from Froxel Grid Construction by handling the spatial assignment logic and buffer indexing rather than the geometric partitioning. Choose this when optimizing the build phase of clustered lighting for participating media. Froxel Grid Construction partitions the 3D view frustum into a regular 3D grid of voxels (froxels) to spatially organize lights for efficient real-time volumetric light scattering and clustered shading. It differs from standard clustered lighting by explicitly targeting participating media, where light contributions are evaluated at froxel midpoints rather than screen-space pixels, and by excluding the sun and non-volumetric lights from the clustering process. Choose this when defining the spatial discretization for clustered volumetric rendering. Integration of volumetric scene lights into the froxel rendering pipeline, allowing local lights to affect volumetric media within froxel bounds. It collects volumetric scene lights (Light3D) and projects their positions into the froxel space, integrates these lights into the froxel data structure to update local light contribution, and clears pending emissive proxies after consumption to manage memory and state. Implemented in VolumetricLights.cpp. A mechanism to inject temporary emissive proxies into the froxel system for localized volumetric glow effects without persistent light entities. It creates a temporary emissive proxy with specific radiance and radius, injects the proxy into the froxel system for a single frame or until consumed, and adjusts ambient lighting if necessary to demonstrate the localized effect. Demonstrated in main.nut. A mechanism to create point lights that contribute exclusively to volumetric rendering (media scattering) while being excluded from surface/PBR lighting calculations, preventing double-lighting of emissive surfaces. It creates a Light2D or Light3D entity and sets its volumetricOnly flag to true. During surface light packing, the RenderSystem explicitly filters out entities with volumetricOnly=true from the regular 2D surface list. During PBR mesh light packing, the RenderSystem3D explicitly filters out entities with volumetricOnly=true from the mesh-light pack. Implemented in Light.cpp and Light.h. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: Complexity is proportional to the number of froxels multiplied by the average number of lights per froxel. At 1440p on an RTX 4090, 64 lamps at a default 14m range cost approximately 0.0983ms, comparable to 4 lamps everywhere (0.0829ms). On lavapipe (1280x720), 64 lamps in Layout A cost 19.56ms, dropping to 9.89ms if opted out. Memory: Requires storage for the froxel grid, cluster offsets, and the flat light list. The LightGpu structure size remains unchanged as LIGHTVOLUMETRIC is packed into existing flags. Scaling: Performance scales with the number of lights and the density of the froxel grid. Increasing fardistance significantly increases the number of froxels falling back to the flat list, degrading performance if not managed by increasing maxdistance. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Efficiently handles multiple local lights in volumetric fog using existing clustered lighting infrastructure. Low overhead for scenes with few volumetric lights. Limitations: Fallback to flat lists for distant froxels can become a bottleneck. Does not handle the sun (handled separately). Opting out of scattering does not reduce list traversal cost. When to Use: Use for real-time volumetric fog with multiple local lights (point/spot) where performance is critical and the sun is handled via a separate pass. Avoid when the scene requires complex multiple scattering solutions or when the majority of froxels fall outside the cluster grid due to large fardistance settings. This method was introduced as part of a feature update to scatter local lights in the volumetric fog volume, specifically addressing issue #357. It was implemented by fesoliveira014 and merged into the main branch of the c3d.c3l repository on October 12, 2026. The implementation builds on existing clustered lighting principles and integrates with the engine's light serialization (version 2) and GPU data structures. name: Froxel Light Assignment
body: Froxel Light Assignment partitions the camera frustum into a 3D grid of froxels and assigns scene lights to them using compute shaders. It differs from Froxel Grid Construction by handling the spatial assignment logic and buffer indexing rather than the geometric partitioning. Inputs: List of scene lights, filtered on the CPU by checking if each light's bounding sphere intersects the camera view frustum. Froxel grid dimensions GX, GY, GZ (default 16×16×16). Maximum lights per froxel N{max} (default 32). Camera parameters: View Matrix, Projection Matrix, Near/Far clipping planes in cm. Outputs: FroxelLists structured buffer containing: Offsets: uint array of size GX \times GY \times GZ, storing the starting index in LightIndices for each froxel. Counts: uint array of size GX \times GY \times GZ, storing the number of lights assigned to each froxel. TotalIndices: uint, the total number of light assignments. LightIndices: uint array of size GX \times GY \times GZ, storing the indices of lights assigned to each froxel. FroxelCount: uint32, total number of froxels. Data Structures: FFroxelUniformParameters: Uniform buffer containing grid size (GX, GY, GZ, GX \times GY \times GZ), viewport/tile sizes, inverse tile pixels, View/Projection matrices, Near/Far clipping distances, number of lights, and max lights per froxel. FFroxelLightData: Struct representing light data (position, radius, etc.) used for frustum intersection tests. Steps: 1. Froxel Grid Construction: Partition the camera frustum into a 3D grid of froxels (covered in Froxel Grid Construction). 2. Per Froxel Light Assignment: For each light in the scene, determine which froxels it affects using compute shaders. 2.1 Light Counting: Count the number of visible lights affecting each froxel and store this in a structured buffer. 2.2 Buffer Offsets: Perform a Blelloch scan (prefix sum) across Z-slices to compute offsets in each Z-slice, then add a final offset to each froxel to get absolute indices. 2.3 Light Assignment: Execute a reduce pass to compute the total number of light assignments, then use atomic operations to safely write light indices into the froxel's light list. 3. Debug Overlay: Render a heatmap overlay showing froxel occupancy and light counts for debugging purposes. Parameters: r.Froxel.GridX: Froxel grid dimension X. Default: 16. r.Froxel.GridY: Froxel grid dimension Y. Default: 16. r.Froxel.GridZ: Froxel grid dimension Z. Default: 16. r.Froxel.MaxLightsPerFroxel: Maximum number of lights that can be assigned to a single froxel. Default: 32. r.Froxel.FarClipCm: Froxel grid far clipping plane in cm. Default: 100000. r.Froxel.ZMode: Froxel grid Z distribution mode. 0: linear, 1: logarithmic. Default: 1. r.Froxel.Visualize: Visualize Froxel grid. 0: off, 1: heatmap, 2: hash pattern. Default: 0. r.Froxel.DebugOpacity: Overlay opacity when compositing on SceneColor. Default: 0.5f. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Light frustum culling must be performed to avoid incorrect assignments. Atomic operations are required for count and index updates, which may cause contention in dense light clusters. Buffer overflow must be handled if a froxel exceeds MaxLightsPerFroxel. Transformations between world space and froxel space require sufficient precision to avoid misclassification near boundaries. Computes the offsets into the global light index list for each froxel using a 3-pass Blelloch scan approach. Results are stored in FroxelLightOffsetsUAV. Pass A clears ZSliceTotalsUAV and FroxelLightOffsetsUAV and executes FFroxelOffsetPassACS with group count \lceil (GX \times GY) / 256 \rceil. Pass B clears ZSliceOffsetsUAV and executes FFroxelOffsetPassBCS with group count \lceil GZ / 1024 \rceil. Pass C executes FFroxelOffsetPassCCS with group count \lceil (GX \times GY) / 1024 \rceil to add Z-slice group sums to each froxel. Data structures include ZSliceTotals (Structured buffer of size GZ, type uint32) and ZSliceOffsets (Structured buffer of size GZ, type uint32). A compute shader pass that counts the number of lights affecting each froxel in the grid. The result is stored in the FroxelLightCountsUAV buffer. It creates a UAV for FroxelLists.Counts and clears it to 0. It allocates parameters for FFroxelCountCS, binding SharedUB, View Uniform Buffer, Lights SRV, and FroxelLightCounts UAV. It executes the compute shader with group count calculated as \lceil NumLights{RT} / 64 \rceil. The parameter structure FFroxelCountCS::FParameters contains FroxelSharedUB (struct ref), View (struct ref), Lights (SRV: StructuredBuffer<FFroxelLightData>), and FroxelLightCounts (UAV: RWStructuredBuffer<uint>). Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Depends on the number of lights and their spatial distribution. Strengths: Efficiently maps lights to volume regions, enabling localized lighting calculations. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of grid resolution and max lights per froxel to balance memory usage and accuracy. When to use: Real-time volumetric lighting with local lights. When not to use: Scenes with very few lights or where global illumination is handled differently. Originated in Unreal Engine 5 as part of the Froxel Lighting system, implemented by Armin Tajik. It is used in real-time rendering of participating media, specifically for local lights within fog volumes. name: Froxel Light List Buffer Creation
head: Froxel Light List Buffer Allocation
body: This method allocates and populates the GPU buffers that store variable-length light lists for each froxel after spatial assignment. It prepares the Counts, Offsets, TotalIndices, and LightIndices buffers required for subsequent volumetric rendering passes. The method consists of buffer allocation, a reduction pass to determine the total light count, an atomic assignment pass to populate indices, and a three-pass prefix-sum scan to compute offsets. Inputs: Grid: 3D grid dimensions (GX, GY, GZ) defining the froxel structure. NumLightsRT: Number of real-time lights in the scene. MaxLightsPerFroxel: Maximum number of lights assigned to any single froxel. Outputs: FroxelLists: A structure containing four buffers (see Layout). The FFroxelLists structure contains the following buffers, all created as RWStructuredBuffer<uint32> with BUFShaderResource | BUFUnorderedAccess flags: 1. Counts: RWStructuredBuffer<uint32>, size GX \times GY \times GZ. Stores the number of lights assigned to each froxel. 2. Offsets: RWStructuredBuffer<uint32>, size GX \times GY \times GZ. Stores the starting index in LightIndices for each froxel. 3. TotalIndices: RWStructuredBuffer<uint32>, size 1. Stores the total number of light indices across all froxels. 4. LightIndices: RWStructuredBuffer<uint32>, size (GX \times GY \times GZ) \times \text{MaxLightsPerFroxel}. Stores the actual light indices for all froxels, packed sequentially. 1. Calculate Froxel Count: N{\text{froxel}} = GX \times GY \times GZ. 2. Allocate Buffers: Allocate the four buffers defined in the Layout section with sizes derived from N{\text{froxel}} and MaxLightsPerFroxel. 3. Compute Total Indices (Reduction): Clear TotalIndices UAV to 0. Execute the FFroxelTotalIndicesCS compute shader with group count (1, 1, 1). This pass sums the Counts buffer to determine the total number of light entries. 4. Assign Light Indices: Clear LightIndices UAV to 0. Reuse the Counts buffer as FroxelHeads (atomic head pointer) and clear it to 0. Execute the FFroxelAssignLightsCS compute shader with group count \lceil \text{NumLights\RT} / 64 \rceil. Each light thread atomically increments the head for its assigned froxel and writes the light index to LightIndices at the returned position. 5. Compute Offsets (Prefix Sum): The offsets are computed using a three-pass Blelloch scan to handle the 3D grid efficiently: Pass A (Intra-Slice Scan): Perform a prefix sum on Counts within each Z-slice (size GX \times GY). Store intermediate results in ZSliceTotals and final offsets in Offsets. Pass B (Inter-Slice Scan): Perform a prefix sum on the ZSliceTotals buffer (size GZ) to get cumulative sums for each Z-slice. Store in ZSliceOffsets. Pass C (Add Z-Slice Offsets): Add the corresponding ZSliceOffsets value to each froxel's offset in the Offsets buffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def createfroxellightlistbuffers(grid: tuple, numlights: int, maxlightsperfroxel: int): """ Allocates and populates buffers for froxel light lists. grid: (Gx, Gy, Gz) """ Gx, Gy, Gz = grid Nfroxel = Gx Gy Gz Zslicesize = Gx Gy # 1. Allocate Buffers counts = [0] Nfroxel offsets = [0] Nfroxel totalindices = [0] lightindices = [0] (Nfroxel maxlightsperfroxel) zslicetotals = [0] Gz zsliceoffsets = [0] Gz # 2. Compute Total Indices (Reduction) # Simulates FFroxelTotalIndicesCS with group count (1, 1, 1) totalindices[0] = sum(counts) # 3. Assign Light Indices # Reuse counts as FroxelHeads (atomic heads) froxelheads = [0] Nfroxel # Simulates FFroxelAssignLightsCS: one thread per light for lightidx in range(numlights): froxelidx = lightidx % Nfroxel # Simplified assignment logic pos = froxelheads[froxelidx] froxelheads[froxelidx] += 1 if pos < maxlightsperfroxel: lightindices[froxelidx maxlightsperfroxel + pos] = lightidx # 4. Compute Offsets (3-Pass Blelloch Scan) # Pass A: Prefix sum within each Z-slice for z in range(Gz): base = z Zslicesize currentsum = 0 for i in range(Zslicesize): offsets[base + i] = currentsum currentsum += counts[base + i] zslicetotals[z] = currentsum # Pass B: Prefix sum of Z-slice totals for z in range(1, Gz): zsliceoffsets[z] = zsliceoffsets[z-1] + zslicetotals[z-1] # Pass C: Add Z-slice offsets to individual froxel offsets for z in range(Gz): base = z Zslicesize for i in range(Zslicesize): offsets[base + i] += zsliceoffsets[z] return { 'Counts': counts, 'Offsets': offsets, 'TotalIndices': totalindices, 'LightIndices': lightindices } MaxLightsPerFroxel: Determines the size of LightIndices as (GX \times GY \times GZ) \times \text{MaxLightsPerFroxel}. NumLightsRT: Determines the group count for the assignment shader as \lceil \text{NumLights\RT} / 64 \rceil. Grid Layout: The prefix sum assumes a Z-slice major order where each slice contains GX \times GY froxels. Defines the shader parameter structure for the compute shader that assigns lights to froxels during the volumetric light scattering pass. It provides the GPU kernel with references to the froxel grid state, view parameters, light data, offsets, and atomic counters required for populating the light index buffer. Choose this when configuring the GPU kernel dispatch for the assignment phase. See Froxel Assign Lights Compute Shader Parameters. Computes the list of light indices for each froxel, storing results in FroxelLists.LightIndices. It first computes the total number of indices using a reduction pass, then assigns indices using an atomic counter. Time Complexity: O(N{\text{froxel}}) for allocation and offset computation, and O(\text{NumLights\RT}) for index assignment. Memory Complexity: O(N{\text{froxel}} \times \text{MaxLightsPerFroxel}) for LightIndices, plus O(N{\text{froxel}}) for Counts and Offsets, and O(GZ) for temporary prefix sum buffers. Strengths: Handles variable-length light lists efficiently on the GPU. Limitations: Requires temporary buffers for the three-pass prefix sum. This method is part of the Unreal Engine 5 Froxel Lighting system for volumetric light scattering via froxel clustering. name: Froxel Grid Construction
head: Clustered Lighting, Froxel Grid Builder, Froxel Lighting
body: Froxel Grid Construction partitions the 3D view frustum into a regular 3D grid of voxels (froxels) to spatially organize lights for efficient real-time volumetric light scattering and clustered shading. It differs from standard clustered lighting by explicitly targeting participating media, where light contributions are evaluated at froxel midpoints rather than screen-space pixels, and by excluding the sun and non-volumetric lights from the clustering process. Inputs and Outputs Input: A list of active scene lights (point and spot) with world-space positions and radii, the current view matrix, projection matrix, view frustum bounds, and grid configuration parameters. Output: A structured buffer of filtered lights (LightsSB), a froxel grid structure containing light counts and indices (FFroxelLists), and a shared uniform buffer (FroxelSharedUB) containing grid dimensions and view parameters. Data Structures The system uses a Structure of Arrays (SoA) layout for GPU efficiency. 1. FFroxelUniformParameters (Shared Uniform Buffer) GridSize: FIntVector4 (X, Y, Z dimensions, and padding). NearCm: float (Near clipping plane in centimeters). FarCm: float (Far clipping plane in centimeters). NumLights: int32 (Total number of valid lights). MaxLightsPerFroxel: int32 (Capacity of each froxel's light list). ViewportSize: FIntPoint (Resolution in pixels). ViewRectMinPx: FIntPoint (Minimum X, Y of the view rect). TileSizePx: FIntPoint (Width and height of a froxel in pixels, derived from viewport/grid). InvTilePx: float2 (Inverse of TileSizePx). ViewMatrix: float4x4. ProjectionMatrix: float4x4. 2. FFroxelLists (Structured Buffers) Counts: RWStructuredBuffer<uint> of size GridX GridY GridZ. Stores the number of lights assigned to each froxel. Offsets: RWStructuredBuffer<uint> of size GridX GridY GridZ. Stores the starting index in LightIndices for each froxel. TotalIndices: RWStructuredBuffer<uint> of size 1. Stores the total number of light indices written. LightIndices: RWStructuredBuffer<uint> of size GridX GridY GridZ MaxLightsPerFroxel. Stores the indices into the LightsSB buffer for each light assigned to a froxel. 3. LightsSB (Structured Buffer) Stride: sizeof(FFroxelLightData). Contains the filtered lights. The exact layout of FFroxelLightData is not fully specified in the provided notes, but it must contain at least position and radius. Numbered Steps 1. Capture Lights (Game Thread): Collect all relevant lights from the scene into a temporary array FrameLights of type TArray<FFroxelLightData>. 2. Transfer to Render Thread: Lock LightBufferMutex and move FrameLights to FrameLightsGT. 3. Render Thread Transfer: On the render thread, lock LightBufferMutex and move FrameLightsGT to FrameLightsRT, setting NumLightsRT. 4. Frustum Culling: Iterate through FrameLightsRT. For each light, check if its bounding sphere intersects the view frustum: InView.ViewFrustum.IntersectSphere(FVector(L.PositionWS), L.Radius). 5. Create Light Buffer: Create a GPU structured buffer LightsSB with stride sizeof(FFroxelLightData) and populate it with the filtered lights. 6. Initialize Froxel Lists: Call CreateFroxelLists to allocate the Counts, Offsets, TotalIndices, and LightIndices buffers. Initialize all counts and offsets to zero. 7. Create Shared Uniform Buffer: Call CreateSharedUB to populate FFroxelUniformParameters with the view matrix, projection matrix, grid dimensions (CVarFroxelGridX/Y/Z), far clip (CVarFroxelFarClipCm), max lights per froxel (CVarFroxelMaxLightsPerFroxel), and viewport/tile sizes. 8. Count Lights per Froxel: Dispatch the CountLightPerFroxel compute shader to count lights per froxel. Parameters CVarFroxelGridX: Grid dimension X. Default: 16. CVarFroxelGridY: Grid dimension Y. Default: 16. CVarFroxelGridZ: Grid dimension Z. Default: 1. CVarFroxelMaxLightsPerFroxel: Maximum lights allowed per froxel. Default: 32. CVarFroxelFarClipCm: Far clipping plane in cm. Default: 100000. CVarFroxelZMode: Z distribution mode (0: linear, 1: logarithmic). Default: 1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The use of float for view/projection matrices and int32 for indices requires careful handling of large scenes to avoid index overflow or precision loss in froxel mapping. Boundaries: Lights exactly on the frustum boundary must be handled consistently by IntersectSphere to avoid flickering or double-counting. Degenerate Input: If NumLights is 0, the grid construction should skip compute dispatches to avoid undefined behavior in atomic operations. Tile Size: TileSizePx is clamped to a minimum of 1 to prevent division by zero or invalid shader dispatch sizes. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. FrameLightsGT = [] with LightBufferMutex: FrameLightsGT = list(FrameLights) FrameLightsRT = [] with LightBufferMutex: FrameLightsRT = list(FrameLightsGT) NumLightsRT = len(FrameLightsRT) FilteredLights = [] for Light in FrameLightsRT: if ViewFrustum.IntersectSphere(Light.PositionWS, Light.Radius): FilteredLights.append(Light) LightsSB = StructuredBuffer(data=FilteredLights, stride=sizeof(FFroxelLightData)) GX = CVarFroxelGridX.GetValue() GY = CVarFroxelGridY.GetValue() GZ = CVarFroxelGridZ.GetValue() MaxLights = CVarFroxelMaxLightsPerFroxel.GetValue() FroxelCount = GX GY GZ Counts = RWBuffer(size=FroxelCount, init=0) Offsets = RWBuffer(size=FroxelCount, init=0) TotalIndices = RWBuffer(size=1, init=0) LightIndices = RWBuffer(size=FroxelCount MaxLights, init=0) Params = UniformBuffer() Params.GridSize = (GX, GY, GZ, 0) Params.NearCm = View.NearClippingDistance Params.FarCm = max(1000, CVarFroxelFarClipCm.GetValue()) Params.NumLights = len(FilteredLights) Params.MaxLightsPerFroxel = max(1, MaxLights) Params.ViewportSize = View.UnscaledViewRect.Size() Params.ViewRectMinPx = View.UnscaledViewRect.Min TileSizeFX = ViewportSize.X / GX TileSizeFY = ViewportSize.Y / GY Params.TileSizePx = (floor(max(TileSizeFX, 1.0)), floor(max(TileSizeFY, 1.0))) Params.InvTilePx = (1.0 / Params.TileSizePx.X, 1.0 / Params.TileSizePx.Y) Params.ViewMatrix = View.ViewMatrix Params.ProjectionMatrix = View.ProjectionMatrix FroxelSharedUB = UniformBuffer(params=Params) Dispatch(CountLightPerFroxelCS, threadgroups=(GX, GY, GZ)) Determines which lights contribute to which froxels using the constructed grid. It sets apart from grid construction by focusing on the actual assignment logic and atomic writes, whereas grid construction focuses on the spatial partitioning and buffer initialization. Choose it when you need to map specific lights to spatial regions. Froxel Light Assignment Time Complexity: O(N + F), where N is the number of lights and F is the number of froxels. Memory Complexity: O(F \cdot M + N), where M is MaxLightsPerFroxel. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with grid resolution. Strengths: Efficient spatial culling of lights for volumetric rendering. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of grid dimensions and max lights per froxel to balance memory and performance. When to use: Real-time volumetric light scattering with many local lights. When not to use: Scenes with very few lights or where the sun is the primary light source. The method originates from the "UE5 Froxel Lighting Plugin" by Armin Tajik, an unofficial community plugin for Unreal Engine 5. It implements a real-time clustered lighting and volumetrics system, adapting clustered lighting techniques to the specific needs of volumetric fog rendering in UE5. The plugin integrates with UE5's Render Graph API and uses C++20 and HLSL. ArminTajik/ue5-froxel-lighting, https://github.com/ArminTajik/ue5-froxel-lighting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Cone Tracing Global Illumination
head: Crassin's voxel cone tracing, Voxel Cone Traced Global Illumination, VCTGI
body: Voxel Cone Tracing Global Illumination (VCTGI) is a real-time global illumination technique that approximates indirect lighting by storing scene radiance in a voxel grid and sampling it via cone tracing. It differs from diffuse-only voxel GI by supporting specular and glossy reflections with significantly lower performance costs, requiring only a single cone trace per glossy material. Unlike sparse voxel octrees, this implementation typically uses a plain 3D texture to support moving cameras without expensive reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scene geometry (triangles), surface properties (color, normal, emission), light sources, and camera position. Output: A final rendered image with indirect diffuse and specular lighting. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Grid: A plain 3D texture (not a sparse octree) storing view-independent radiance. 2. Mipmap Chain: Generated from the radiance texture using trilinear interpolation. Anisotropic mipmaps may be used to reduce light bleeding. Steps: 1. Voxelization: Project triangles into the voxel grid. To maximize covered area and minimize holes, project triangles in the geometry shader based on the greatest component of the surface normal. If the Z component is greatest, project onto the XY plane. If the X component is greatest, project onto the YZ plane. If the Y component is greatest, project onto the XZ plane. Use Conservative Rasterization to ensure triangles cover the center of pixels, preventing holes in the voxelized mesh. 2. Radiance Volume Construction: Combine surface color, normal, emission, and direct lighting (including shadows) into the voxel grid. Concurrency Handling: Since shaders execute concurrently in warps, unsynchronized writes to the voxel texture can cause race conditions. Mitigation strategies include: Using a Compare-And-Swap (CAS) loop with a moving average, converting RGBA8 to R32UI before accumulation. Using NVshaderatomicfloat extensions to perform imageAtomicAdd on floats. 3. Mipmap Generation: Generate mipmaps of the radiance texture. Anisotropic mipmaps are preferred to reduce light bleeding artifacts. 4. Lighting (Cone Tracing): For each fragment, shoot cones around the hemisphere oriented along the surface normal. Cone Types: Diffuse: Large aperture, samples the mipmap chain to capture broad indirect lighting. Specular: Smaller aperture, samples the mipmap chain to capture glossy reflections. Only one cone is typically needed for glossy materials. Ambient Occlusion: Used for occlusion calculations. Aperture: The cone aperture determines the rate at which the diameter increases with distance from the surface. The diameter selects the appropriate mipmap level. Accumulation: Traverse the voxel structure using front-to-back accumulation. For each step, update color and opacity using the following formulas: \text{color} = \text{opacity} \cdot \text{color} + (1 - \text{opacity}) \cdot \text{read\opacity} \cdot \text{read\color} \text{opacity} = \text{opacity} + (1 - \text{opacity}) \cdot \text{read\opacity} Weighting: Average the results from multiple cones (Monte Carlo style), weighting each partial result by the cosine similarity between the cone direction and the surface normal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def vec3(x, y, z): return (x, y, z) def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def normalize(v): l = math.sqrt(dot(v, v)) return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l) def reflect(I, N): return (I[0] - 2dot(I, N)N[0], I[1] - 2dot(I, N)N[1], I[2] - 2dot(I, N)N[2]) def samplehemisphere(normal): # Uniform hemisphere sampling u = random.uniform(0, 1) v = random.uniform(0, 1) theta = 2.0 math.pi u phi = math.acos(1.0 - 2.0 v) localdir = (math.cos(theta)math.sin(phi), math.sin(theta)math.sin(phi), math.cos(phi)) # Rotate to align with surface normal (simplified rotation matrix omitted for brevity) return normalize(localdir) def tracecone(origin, direction, aperture, maxdistance, voxelgrid): opacity = 0.0 accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) distance = 0.0 stepsize = aperture 0.5 # Step size scales with aperture while distance < maxdistance: currentpos = (origin[0] + direction[0]distance, origin[1] + direction[1]distance, origin[2] + direction[2]distance) currentdiameter = aperture distance # Diameter grows linearly with distance miplevel = max(0, int(math.log2(currentdiameter + 1e-6))) # Select mipmap based on diameter readcolor, readopacity = voxelgrid.sample(currentpos, miplevel) # Front-to-back accumulation accumulatedcolor = (opacity accumulatedcolor[0] + (1.0 - opacity) readopacity readcolor[0], opacity accumulatedcolor[1] + (1.0 - opacity) readopacity readcolor[1], opacity accumulatedcolor[2] + (1.0 - opacity) readopacity readcolor[2]) opacity = opacity + (1.0 - opacity) readopacity if opacity >= 1.0: break distance += stepsize return accumulatedcolor, opacity def computeglobalillumination(fragment, voxelgrid, maxdistance=10.0): normal = fragment.normal diffusecolor = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) specularcolor = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Diffuse GI: Multiple cones numdiffusecones = 16 for i in range(numdiffusecones): direction = samplehemisphere(normal) aperture = 1.0 # Large aperture for diffuse color, = tracecone(fragment.position, direction, aperture, maxdistance, voxelgrid) weight = max(0.0, dot(direction, normal)) # Cosine weighting diffusecolor = (diffusecolor[0] + color[0] weight, diffusecolor[1] + color[1] weight, diffusecolor[2] + color[2] weight) diffusecolor = (diffusecolor[0] / numdiffusecones, diffusecolor[1] / numdiffusecones, diffusecolor[2] / numdiffusecones) # Specular GI: Single cone for glossy specularaperture = 0.2 # Smaller aperture for specular speculardirection = reflect((-fragment.viewdirection[0], -fragment.viewdirection[1], -fragment.viewdirection[2]), normal) specularcolor, = tracecone(fragment.position, speculardirection, specularaperture, maxdistance, voxelgrid) return diffusecolor, specularcolor Performance: In a test with 1024x768 resolution and ~70,000 triangles, frame times were: Voxelization 0.97ms, Radiance volume 4.96ms, Isotropic mipmaps 0.09ms, Lighting 5.1ms. Complexity: Lighting complexity is proportional to the number of cones traced per fragment. Diffuse GI requires many cones (e.g., 16), while specular GI requires only one. Strengths: Real-time performance; supports specular reflections; simple implementation with plain 3D textures; no complex octree reconstruction for moving cameras. Limitations: Voxel artifacts may appear on highly polished reflectors; light bleeding can occur if anisotropic mipmaps are not used; requires conservative rasterization to avoid holes. When to use: Real-time applications requiring both diffuse and specular global illumination, especially with moving cameras. When not to use: Scenes with extremely high-frequency indirect lighting details that require higher resolution than the voxel grid can provide, or where voxel artifacts are unacceptable. The Voxel Cone Tracing global illumination technique was proposed by Cyril Crassin et al. in 2011. It was introduced to bring global illumination into the realm of real-time rendering by leveraging the efficiency of voxel grids and cone tracing. The technique has been used in commercial video games, such as The Tomorrow Children. name: Light Beam Tracing
body: Light beam tracing is a ray tracing optimization strategy that aggregates rays into geometric beams, deferring explicit ray representation until a final sampling step. While primarily designed for primary eye and shadow rays, it can produce light shafts within participating media and complex refractive boundaries. It differs from grid-based volumetric methods by relying on spatial acceleration structures rather than fixed voxel grids for beam representation. Inputs and Outputs: Not given in the sources. Data Structures: Beams are managed using spatial acceleration structures, specifically kd-trees in existing implementations. Grid-based data structures are not used for beam representation. Steps: 1. Define beam volumes originating from the camera frustum to cover groups of primary or shadow rays. 2. Traverse the beam volume against the scene geometry using the acceleration structure to determine intersections. 3. Perform a final sampling step along the beam's path to compute radiance contributions. Formulas: The radiance at the camera is computed as: L(xc \leftarrow \omegac) = L(xs \leftarrow \omegac) + Li(x{tc} \leftarrow \omegac) Where: L(xc \leftarrow \omegac) is the eye radiance. L(xs \leftarrow \omegac) is the surface radiance. Li(x{tc} \leftarrow \omegac) is the accumulated in-scattered radiance along the ray. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Area Lights: The method cannot easily handle area light sources, limiting its applicability to point or directional lights. Artifacts: The approximation nature of beam aggregation can lead to blurring or approximation artifacts, particularly in complex media. Data Structure Limitation: Existing implementations focus on kd-tree based structures; there are no known implementations of grid-based beam tracers, which limits integration with voxel-centric pipelines. A strategy where rays are considered only in a final sampling step, rather than being represented explicitly during traversal. It is competitive with frustum-based tracers for eye and shadow rays. However, it is limited by the lack of grid-based implementations, as existing work relies on kd-tree data structures. Time Complexity: Depends on the traversal algorithm's setup time (T{setup}) and step time (T{step}). Performance is conflictual: low T{setup} favors low-resolution grids, while high T{step} degrades performance for larger grids. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the acceleration structure (e.g., kd-tree). Strengths: Exploits ray coherence efficiently; competitive with frustum-based methods for primary and shadow rays. Limitations: Cannot handle area lights; suffers from blurring artifacts; no grid-based implementations exist. Originating from the broader field of ray tracing optimization, beam tracing was explored by Overbeck et al. [ORM07] as a competitive alternative to frustum-based tracers. The survey by notes that while ray aggregation is common in interactive systems, beam tracing remains less prevalent due to its reliance on non-grid data structures. The technique is similar to light beam tracing and can produce light shafts within complex refractive volumetric boundaries, though exact methods avoid the blurring artifacts present in light beam tracing. name: Precomputed Radiance Transfer
body: Precomputed Radiance Transfer (PRT) approximates light transport integrals by decoupling radiative transfer calculations from the per-frame rendering loop, storing precomputed transfer functions or incident radiance for runtime lookup. Unlike sibling methods that approximate scattering dynamically per frame (e.g., Voxel Cone Tracing, Froxel-based Volumetric Rendering), PRT methods precompute the expensive light transport calculation, though the primary drawback noted in the literature is their high runtime cost. It differs from Precomputed Lighting (Baking) by storing transfer functions that map incident light to outgoing radiance, enabling dynamic lighting updates at the expense of increased runtime complexity. All methods in this family share the goal of approximating the integral of the radiative transfer equation for multiple scattering orders without solving it iteratively per frame. They typically rely on one or more of the following mechanisms: 1. Spatial Discretization: The volume is discretized into a structured grid (voxels, froxels) or a hierarchical structure (octrees, light volumes) to allow efficient spatial queries and interpolation. 2. Precomputation or Caching: Lighting information (attenuation, visibility, or flux) is precomputed offline or updated incrementally per frame, stored in textures or data structures, and queried at runtime. 3. Dimensionality Reduction: Directional information is compressed using basis functions (e.g., Spherical Harmonics) or approximated using geometric primitives (e.g., cones, light volumes with blur widths) to reduce the cost of evaluating the scattering integral. 4. Temporal Stability: Many methods incorporate temporal accumulation (e.g., TAA reprojection) to stabilize noise and reduce per-frame computational load. Modular Transfer is a precomputation-based rendering technique for volumetric media with repeated structures, designed to approximate high-order multiple scattering efficiently. It solves the problem of rendering complex, optically thick media with anisotropic scattering by splitting light transport paths into components that are precomputed offline and computed at runtime, making path integrals separable via isotropy and diffuser events. Unlike its siblings, it uses flux transfer matrices instead of light fields to handle the curse of dimensionality. Choose it for complex, optically thick media where diffusion approximations fail. Precomputed Lighting (Baking) is a volume rendering optimization technique that accelerates rendering by pre-computing the incident radiance term (Li) for each voxel in a grid and storing it in the data structure, thereby skipping the evaluation of Li during the per-pixel raymarching pass. It solves the performance bottleneck of evaluating volumetric shadows or direct illumination for every sample point along a camera ray by trading memory and offline computation time for runtime speed. Unlike Modular Transfer, it is static and view-independent, requiring a full re-bake whenever the scene geometry, lighting, or density simulation changes. Choose it for static scenes where direct illumination is the primary bottleneck. This method reconstructs lighting in real-time by rotating precomputed PRT values, stored in the Zernike Harmonic (ZH) basis, to match the local surface frame, projecting them back into the Spherical Harmonic (SH) basis, and computing the dot product with the lighting environment projected into SH. It sets itself apart from standard PRT by enabling per-pixel rotation of the transfer function on the GPU, allowing for dynamic surface orientations without the prohibitive cost of per-sample SH rotation. Choose it when dynamic surface normals require real-time PRT updates. This method renders realistic microgeometry (specifically fur) with global lighting effects, such as self-shadowing, at real-time frame rates by combining a volumetric fur model with Local, Deformable Precomputed Radiance Transfer (LDPRT). It solves the problem of capturing microgeometric self-shadowing in a volumetric fur model by precomputing light attenuation to each voxel in the fur volume and rendering the volume using shell textures. Unlike general participating media methods, it specifically models the microgeometry of fur hairs using a multi-layered shell approach and defers the conversion of illuminance to luminous exitance to the reconstruction phase. Choose it for real-time fur rendering with self-shadowing. Utilize modular cells to precompute transfer, stitching multiple unit cells together and warping them to approximate scene geometry. Propagate radiance first to cell borders acting as interfaces, then to neighboring cells using precomputed models. Precomputed Radiance Transfer was introduced by Jensen et al. in 2001. The technique was originally developed for surface rendering to handle dynamic global illumination efficiently. In volumetric rendering, it has been adapted to handle participating media by precomputing the transfer of radiance between different parts of the volume to address the computational cost of multiple scattering. The approach has also been explored using modular cells to stitch and warp unit cells for approximating scene geometry. name: Modular Transfer
head: MFT, Modular Flux Transfer, Modular approach for volume rendering, Modular radiance transfer
body: Modular Transfer (MFT) is a precomputation-based rendering technique for volumetric media with repeated structures, designed to approximate high-order multiple scattering efficiently. It solves the problem of rendering complex, optically thick media with anisotropic scattering by splitting light transport paths into components that are precomputed offline and computed at runtime, making path integrals separable via isotropy and diffuser events. Unlike its sibling Precomputed Lighting (Baking) which typically bakes lighting into textures or lightmaps, MFT precomputes flux transfer matrices between voxels and patches to handle the "curse of dimensionality" inherent in general light transport by using flux instead of light fields. Inputs: A volumetric medium modeled as a grid of blocks, where the full volume consists of millions of blocks but only a small number (tens or hundreds) of unique "exemplar blocks". Material properties (scattering coefficient \sigmas, extinction coefficient \sigmat, single-scattering albedo \alpha, phase function) for each exemplar block. Light source definitions. Camera position and path. Outputs: Final radiance at the camera, computed via final gathering using the precomputed multiple-scattered flux field. 1. Exemplar Blocks: Each exemplar block is divided into n voxels V1 \dots Vn. Non-empty voxel subset Ni: Defined as Ni:= \{x \in \tilde{V}i \mid \sigmat(x, \omega) > 0 \text{ for some } \omega\}, where \tilde{V}i \subset \mathbb{R}^3 is the 3D space of voxel Vi. Patches Pi: Oriented faces of voxels on the interface between two neighboring blocks. Each patch has a normal vector \mathbf{n}(Pi) pointing into a neighboring block. Transfer Matrices: For each exemplar block, three matrices are precomputed: \tilde{T}^{vv} (voxel-to-voxel), \tilde{T}^{vp} (voxel-to-patch), and \tilde{T}^{pp} (patch-to-patch). Global Matrices: \tilde{T}^{vv} and \tilde{T}^{pp} are constructed as block-diagonal matrices by assigning contiguous indices to voxels/patches within the same block/interface, representing an imaginary stacking of precomputed matrices for different exemplar blocks. Flip Operator Q: A permutation matrix on global patch indices where Q maps patch i to flip(i), the index of the patch overlapping with i but with the opposite normal direction. 2. Flux Vectors: Source Flux \Phi^s: A sparse vector where \Phi^s(i) represents single-scattered light arriving at voxel i directly from light sources. Multiple-Scattered Flux \Phi^m: The approximate ground-truth multiple-scattered flux \Phi^{gt} for paths with 2 or more segments. Patch Flux \Phi^p: The energy emitted by each patch contributed by light paths going across one or more interfaces. Transfer Matrix Definitions: The transfer matrices are integrals over paths \bar{x} with weight f(\bar{x}) and measure d\mu(\bar{x}): T^{vv}(i, j) = \int{\Omega(Ni, Nj)} f(\bar{x}) \, d\mu(\bar{x}) T^{vp}(i, j) = \int{\Omega(Ni, Pj)} f(\bar{x}) \, d\mu(\bar{x}) T^{pp}(i, j) = \int{\Omega(Pi, Pj)} f(\bar{x}) \, d\mu(\bar{x}) Where \Omega(A, B) is the set of paths with endpoints in sets A and B. T^{pv} is the transpose of T^{vp}. Source Flux: \Phi^s(i) = \int{\Omega1(Ni, C)} \int{S^2} M(\mathbf{x}0, \boldsymbol{\omega}, \overline{\mathbf{x}0\mathbf{x}1}) f(\bar{x}) \, d\boldsymbol{\omega} \, d\mu(\bar{x}) Where \Omega1(Ni, C) is the set of unscattered paths from voxel subset Ni to emissive surfaces C, and M includes the material term. Multiple-Scattered Flux: The exact expression for multiple-scattered flux is: \Phi^m = \tilde{T}^{vv}\Phi^s + \tilde{T}^{pv} \left( \sum{a=0}^{\infty} \left( Q\tilde{T}^{pp} \right)^a \right) Q\tilde{T}^{vp}\Phi^s Letting U:= I - Q\tilde{T}^{pp}, this is rewritten using the Neumann series: \Phi^m = \tilde{T}^{vv}\Phi^s + \tilde{T}^{pv}U^{-1}Q\tilde{T}^{vp}\Phi^s The term \Phi^{Is}:= \tilde{T}^{pv} \Phi^p = \tilde{T}^{pv} U^{-1} Q \tilde{T}^{vp} \Phi^s requires solving the linear system U\Phi^p = Q\tilde{T}^{vp}\Phi^s. Block Size: Approximately 0.5 mm for woven fabric data (yarn crossing). Exemplar Block Resolution: ~1000 non-empty voxels and 500 patches per exemplar block. k (Scattering Depth): Number of scattering events handled by standard path tracing before using MFT lookup. k=2 or 3 for random structures (e.g., felt); k=6 for structured materials with parallel shiny fibers (e.g., twill). The authors used k=6 for all results. Single-Scattering Albedo: ~0.975 for the brightest color channel in single-colored fabric materials. For each unique exemplar block: 1. Compute \tilde{T}^{vv} using Monte Carlo particle tracing (Algorithm 1). 2. Compute \tilde{T}^{vp} using Monte Carlo particle tracing, similar to \tilde{T}^{vv} but originating from patches. 3. Compute \tilde{T}^{pp} using Monte Carlo particle tracing, analogous to \tilde{T}^{vp} but depositing at other patches. Algorithm 1: Computing Voxel-to-Voxel Transfer Matrix T^{vv} Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeTvv(block, numvoxels, numsamples): # Initialize matrix to zeros Tvv = [[0.0] numvoxels for in range(numvoxels)] for i in range(numvoxels): for in range(numsamples): # Sample ray origin x in non-empty subset Ni and direction omega in S^2 x = uniformsamplevoxelvolume(block, i) omega = uniformsampleunitsphere() # Weight initialization: 4 pi |Ni| w = 4.0 math.pi block.voxelnonemptyvolume(i) while True: # Sample distance s using Woodcock tracking s = samplewoodcockdistance(block, x, omega) xprime = x + s omega if isinsideblock(block, xprime): j = findvoxelcontaining(block, xprime) # Deposit energy: Tvv(i, j) += w / sigmat(x', omega) sigmat = block.extinctioncoefficient(xprime, omega) Tvv[i][j] += w / sigmat # Update weight: w = alpha(x') w = block.singlescatteringalbedo(xprime) # Sample new direction omega' from material term omega = samplephasefunction(block, xprime, omega) x = xprime else: break # Average over samples for i in range(numvoxels): for j in range(numvoxels): Tvv[i][j] /= numsamples return Tvv 1. Evaluate source flux vector \Phi^s by tracing particles from light sources to voxels. This includes the material term (isotropy event) by integrating over all directions. 2. Store \Phi^s as a sparse vector. 1. Step 1: Compute short-range transport within blocks: \tilde{T}^{vv}\Phi^s. 2. Step 2: Transfer voxel fluxes into patch fluxes by applying \tilde{T}^{vp}. Propagate flux across block interfaces using the flip operator Q. 3. Step 3: Solve for patch flux \Phi^p which accounts for long-range transport across block boundaries. The system is U\Phi^p = Q\tilde{T}^{vp}\Phi^s where U = I - Q\tilde{T}^{pp}. Since U is asymmetric, use Monte Carlo Matrix Inversion (preferred for scalability) or Jacobi Iteration. Algorithm 2: Monte Carlo Matrix Inversion for \Phi^{Is}(i) Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def montecarlomatrixinversion(Tpv, Tpp, Tvp, Phis, flip, numsamples, q): # PhiIs[i] estimates the i-th element of Tpv U^-1 Q Tvp Phis PhiIs = [0.0] len(Phis) for i in range(len(Phis)): totalestimate = 0.0 for in range(numsamples): # 1. Jump from voxel i to patch j j, s = samplerow(Tpv, i) while True: # 2. Flip patch to neighboring block j = flip[j] # 3. Russian roulette if random.random() < q: s = s / (1.0 - q) break # 4. Jump to another patch j, v = samplerow(Tpp, j) # Update throughput s = s v / q # 5. Final jump to voxel i0 i0, v = samplerow(Tvp, j) # Accumulate estimate if i0 < len(Phis): totalestimate += Phis[i0] s PhiIs[i] = totalestimate / numsamples return PhiIs Note: In Jacobi Iteration, start with \Psi^{(0)} = Q\tilde{T}^{vp}\Phi^s. In iteration t, compute \Psi^{(t+1)} = Q\tilde{T}^{pp}\Psi^{(t)} + \Psi^{(0)}. Set \Phi^p = \Psi^{(t)} after a few iterations. 4. Step 4: Evaluate final multiple-scattered flux: \Phi^m = \tilde{T}^{vv}\Phi^s + \tilde{T}^{pv}\Phi^p. 1. Run standard path tracing from the camera. 2. For paths with fewer than k scattering events, compute explicitly. 3. For paths with k or more scattering events, insert an isotropy event at the k-th vertex from the camera and the last vertex before the light. Insert zero or more diffuser events in between. 4. Look up the precomputed scattered flux field \Phi^m to approximate the indirect illumination after k scatterings. Specifically, approximate indirect illumination at point x as \Phi^m(i) / (4\pi |Ni|) where i is the voxel containing x. Division by Zero: In the deposition step of Algorithm 1, the term \sigmat(x', \omega) is in the denominator. Since x' is chosen by importance-sampling \sigmat, it holds that \sigmat(x', \omega) > 0, preventing division-by-zero issues. Energy Loss at Boundaries: Applying only voxel-to-voxel transfer leads to darkening because paths crossing boundaries are missing. Adding transfer across boundaries (via patches) addresses this energy loss. Asymmetry of U: The matrix U is usually asymmetric because of the flip operator Q, so conjugate gradient based algorithms cannot be applied. Two methods are introduced: Jacobi Iteration and Monte Carlo Matrix Inversion. Re-precomputation: Requires full re-precomputation if exemplar blocks change optical properties (e.g., single-scattering albedo). Time Complexity: Precomputation per block takes ~4 hours. Source flux computation takes <2 minutes. Monte Carlo matrix inversion takes <15% of total rendering time. Memory Complexity: Storage per block is ~20MB. The method avoids storing the full vector \Phi^p explicitly when using Monte Carlo matrix inversion, which is crucial for large models with millions of block interfaces. Measured Performance: On a scene with over one million blocks, MFT took 12 minutes (with 10M particles traced), compared to 1.3 hours for path tracing and 20 minutes for volume photon mapping (with 100M photons). Strengths: Handles complex volumetric media with strong heterogeneity and anisotropic scattering, unlike diffusion approximations which assume isotropy, homogeneity, and flat boundaries. Limitations: Requires the volume to be composed of repeated exemplar blocks. The precomputation stage is computationally expensive. Modular Transfer was introduced in the paper "Modular Flux Transfer". It is implemented in the Mitsuba physically based renderer. Experiments were conducted on an Intel server equipped with four Xeon X7560 eight-core CPUs. The method was applied to felt, twill, velvet, damask, wood, and synthetic coral-like volumes. It addresses the difficulty of rendering complex, optically thick media with anisotropic phase functions by precomputing light transport within blocks, inspired by the modularity of Loos et al.'s [2011] approach but using flux instead of light fields to avoid the curse of dimensionality. name: Precomputed Lighting (Baking)
head: Baking Lighting, Baking the lighting, Direct Lighting Caching, Precomputed Light Transmissivity
body: Precomputed Lighting (Baking) accelerates volume rendering by pre-computing the incident radiance term (Li) for each voxel in a grid and storing it, thereby skipping Li evaluation during the per-pixel raymarching pass. It solves the performance bottleneck of evaluating volumetric shadows or direct illumination for every sample point by trading offline computation and memory for runtime speed. Unlike Modular Transfer, which decomposes transfer functions for flexible runtime lighting, this method is static and view-independent, requiring a full re-bake whenever the scene geometry, lighting, or density simulation changes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid representing the volume density/opacity, and a static lighting configuration (light positions, intensities, colors) and scene geometry. Output: A 3D texture or data structure where each voxel stores the pre-computed incident radiance (Li) or light transmissivity. Data Structures: The lighting data is stored in a 3D texture or voxel grid. To optimize cache performance during the baking pass, the data should be iterated and stored in memory order (e.g., x-fastest, z-slowest) to avoid cache misses. The resolution of this cache can be lower than the actual simulation voxel resolution because light attenuation and illumination are inherently smooth and blurry. Steps: 1. Baking Pass (Pre-computation): Iterate through every voxel in the grid. For each voxel center, calculate the incident radiance (Li) from all light sources. This typically involves casting rays from the voxel center to each light source to determine visibility and accumulating direct illumination. 2. Storage: Store the calculated Li value in the corresponding voxel of the precomputed lighting grid. 3. Rendering Pass: During real-time volume rendering, when a raymarching step reaches a sample point, retrieve the pre-computed Li value by trilinearly interpolating the values from the surrounding voxels in the precomputed grid. 4. Hybrid Sampling: In some implementations, a few real light samples are taken before sampling the cached value to handle sharp transitions. Formulas: Not given in the sources for the exact precomputation formula. At render time, the incident radiance is approximated via trilinear interpolation: Li(\mathbf{p}) \approx \text{TrilinearInterpolate}(\text{BakedGrid}, \mathbf{p}) Where \mathbf{p} is the current sample position on the camera ray. Parameters: Cache Resolution: The resolution of the precomputed lighting grid. It can be lower than the density grid resolution because light is blurry. Not given in the sources for exact ratios. Light Samples: In some hybrid approaches, a few real light samples are taken before sampling the cache, but the core method relies on full precomputation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dynamic Scenes: The technique requires re-baking whenever the lighting configuration or the density simulation changes. Historical Context: The technique is primarily mentioned for reference and historical reasons rather than current practical utility. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bakelighting(volumegrid, lights, resolution): """ Pre-computes incident radiance for each voxel. volumegrid: 3D array of density values indexed [z][y][x]. lights: List of dicts with 'position' (vec3), 'color' (vec3), 'intensity' (float). resolution: Tuple (resx, resy, resz). Returns: 3D array of precomputed radiance values indexed [z][y][x]. """ resx, resy, resz = resolution # Correct initialization for 3D grid bakedlighting = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(resx)] for in range(resy)] for in range(resz)] # Iterate x-fastest, z-slowest for cache performance for z in range(resz): for y in range(resy): for x in range(resx): # Voxel center in normalized coordinates [0, 1] voxelcenter = [(x + 0.5) / resx, (y + 0.5) / resy, (z + 0.5) / resz] totalradiance = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for light in lights: # Compute transmissivity by raymarching from voxel to light transmissivity = 1.0 raypos = list(voxelcenter) raydir = [light['position'][i] - raypos[i] for i in range(3)] raylen = (raydir[0]2 + raydir[1]2 + raydir[2]2)0.5 if raylen < 1e-6: continue raydir = [d / raylen for d in raydir] # Standard ray march to light stepsize = 0.05 numsteps = max(1, int(raylen / stepsize)) for in range(numsteps): ix, iy, iz = int(raypos[0] resx), int(raypos[1] resy), int(raypos[2] resz) ix, iy, iz = max(0, min(ix, resx-1)), max(0, min(iy, resy-1)), max(0, min(iz, resz-1)) density = volumegrid[iz][iy][ix] transmissivity = max(0.0, 1.0 - density 0.1) raypos = [raypos[i] + raydir[i] stepsize for i in range(3)] # Accumulate direct lighting contribution = [light['color'][c] light['intensity'] transmissivity for c in range(3)] totalradiance = [totalradiance[c] + contribution[c] for c in range(3)] bakedlighting[z][y][x] = totalradiance return bakedlighting def renderwithbakedlighting(cameraorigin, cameradirection, volumegrid, bakedlighting, resolution, stepsize=0.01): """ Renders volume using precomputed lighting. """ accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedalpha = 0.0 t = 0.0 while t < 1.0 and accumulatedalpha < 1.0: samplepos = [cameraorigin[i] + cameradirection[i] t for i in range(3)] x, y, z = int(samplepos[0] resolution[0]), int(samplepos[1] resolution[1]), int(samplepos[2] resolution[2]) x, y, z = max(0, min(x, resolution[0]-1)), max(0, min(y, resolution[1]-1)), max(0, min(z, resolution[2]-1)) density = volumegrid[z][y][x] if density > 0: # Retrieve precomputed lighting via trilinear interpolation li = trilinearinterpolate(bakedlighting, samplepos, resolution) # Standard volume rendering integration (front-to-back) scattering = [density li[c] for c in range(3)] alpha = 1.0 - 2.71828(-density stepsize) weight = alpha (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) accumulatedcolor = [accumulatedcolor[c] + scattering[c] weight for c in range(3)] accumulatedalpha += weight t += stepsize return accumulatedcolor def trilinearinterpolate(grid, point, resolution): """Standard 3D trilinear interpolation.""" resx, resy, resz = resolution fx = point[0] resx fy = point[1] resy fz = point[2] resz ix, iy, iz = int(fx), int(fy), int(fz) dx, dy, dz = fx - ix, fy - iy, fz - iz def getval(x, y, z): x = max(0, min(x, resx - 1)) y = max(0, min(y, resy - 1)) z = max(0, min(z, resz - 1)) return grid[z][y][x] result = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for c in range(3): v000 = getval(ix, iy, iz)[c] v100 = getval(ix+1, iy, iz)[c] v010 = getval(ix, iy+1, iz)[c] v110 = getval(ix+1, iy+1, iz)[c] v001 = getval(ix, iy, iz+1)[c] v101 = getval(ix+1, iy, iz+1)[c] v011 = getval(ix, iy+1, iz+1)[c] v111 = getval(ix+1, iy+1, iz+1)[c] v00 = v000 (1-dx) + v100 dx v01 = v010 (1-dx) + v110 dx v10 = v001 (1-dx) + v101 dx v11 = v011 (1-dx) + v111 dx v0 = v00 (1-dy) + v01 dy v1 = v10 (1-dy) + v11 dy result[c] = v0 (1-dz) + v1 dz return result Decouples classification and shading to balance fidelity and performance, using precomputed reflectance maps for shading before interpolation. Calculates intermediate radiance variables and density derivatives to avoid redundant calculations during ray marching, including first-order inscattering approximations. Models light interaction using transfer functions for arbitrary runtime lighting, offering flexibility at the cost of higher runtime complexity compared to static baking. Time Complexity: Baking is O(V \cdot L \cdot S), where V is the number of voxels, L is the number of lights, and S is the number of samples per light ray for visibility. Rendering is O(R \cdot S), where R is the number of rays and S is samples per ray, but with a significantly smaller constant factor because Li evaluation is replaced by a texture lookup. Memory Complexity: O(V), where V is the number of voxels, storing additional radiance values per voxel. Performance: Significantly speeds up rendering by skipping Li evaluation at each raymarching step. The initial baking pass takes time. Strengths: Fast runtime rendering; view-independent. Limitations: Requires re-baking whenever the lighting configuration or the density simulation changes. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Precomputed Lighting (Baking) is a historical technique mentioned for reference and educational purposes in modern volume rendering contexts. It is based on the principle of precalculating illumination for each voxel center to allow trilinear interpolation at render time. The method is view-independent but scene and light source dependent. While shadow maps and deep shadow maps are related concepts, baking lighting directly into the voxel grid is a distinct approach for volumetric data.
