name: Hybrid Preshading with Postclassification
head: Hybrid Classification and Shading
body: Hybrid Preshading with Postclassification is a real-time volume rendering optimization that decouples classification from shading to balance visual fidelity and performance. It solves the trade-off between the speed of preclassification/preshading (which often requires opacity-weighted interpolation to avoid artifacts) and the visual quality of postclassification/postshading (which is computationally expensive). Unlike its siblings, it performs classification after interpolation (postclassification) to ensure accurate material assignment, but performs shading before interpolation (preshading) using a precomputed reflectance map to maintain high rendering speeds. Inputs: Volume dataset V containing scalar density values. Transfer function mapping density to color and opacity. Lighting model and light positions. Camera parameters defining ray origins and directions. Outputs: Rendered image with volumetric shading. Data Structures: 1. Volume Grid: Standard 3D grid storing scalar density values. 2. Gradient Map: Precomputed for each voxel. The gradient vector \nabla V at each voxel is quantized to one of N discrete space directions. Layout: For each voxel (i, j, k), store an integer index d \in [0, N-1] representing the quantized gradient direction. Size: N = 8192 quantized directions. 3. Preshaded Reflectance Map: A lookup table storing the shaded color for each of the N quantized directions. Layout: Array of size N, where each entry contains the RGB color resulting from applying the lighting model to the base material color for that specific direction. Generation: Before rendering, for each of the N directions, the algorithm computes the shading result and stores it in the map. Steps: 1. Precomputation (Gradient Quantization): Compute the gradient \nabla V for every voxel in the volume. Quantize each gradient vector to the nearest of the N predefined space directions. Store the index of this direction in the Gradient Map for each voxel. 2. Precomputation (Preshaded Reflectance Map): Apply shading on every quantized direction before every rendering to generate a preshaded reflectance map. 3. Rendering (Ray Marching): For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume. Sample the volume along the ray. 4. Interpolation: Perform trilinear interpolation of the volume samples and the gradient at the sampling location. This yields an interpolated density and an interpolated direction index. 5. Vertex Shading: Identify the 8 voxels surrounding the current sampling point. For each of the 8 vertices, retrieve its precomputed gradient direction index. Look up the shaded color from the Preshaded Reflectance Map using the index. 6. Color Interpolation: Perform trilinear interpolation of the 8 preshaded vertex colors and the opacities at the sampling location. 7. Postclassification: Use the interpolated density to determine the final opacity and color contribution, applying the transfer function after interpolation. 8. Compositing: Composite the resulting color and opacity along the ray using standard front-to-back volume integration. Parameters: Number of quantized space directions: N = 8192. Sampling rate \Delta s = 0.5 (distance between consecutive interpolations), allowing between two and four samplings along a ray within a cell. Image resolution: 512 \times 512 pixels. Pixel subdivisions and precomputed rays: Fixed to 16 \times 16. Data precision: Color and opacity are computed on 16-bit unsigned integers. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Artifacts: Mueller et al. reported bad artifacts with preshading and postclassification, but this implementation shows no visible artifacts, suggesting the previous interpretation may be erroneous. Interpolation Requirement: Preclassification/preshading requires opacity-weighted color interpolation to avoid artifacts, which this hybrid method avoids by deferring classification. Hardware Limitations: SIMD extensions (MMX, SSE, or 3DNow!) are used to improve memory copying and trilinear interpolation. Code running on MMX-only processors cannot perform line equation tests, causing minor artifacts on the image. Quantization Error: Using a finite set of 8192 directions may introduce directional aliasing or lighting inaccuracies for smooth gradients. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def precomputegradientmap(volume, directions): """ Computes the gradient for each voxel and quantizes it to one of N directions. Returns a 3D grid of indices. """ N = len(directions) H, W, D = len(volume), len(volume[0]), len(volume[0][0]) gradientmap = [[[-1] D for in range(W)] for in range(H)] for i in range(H): for j in range(W): for k in range(D): grad = computegradient(volume, i, j, k) bestidx = 0 bestdot = -float('inf') for d in range(N): dotval = dot(grad, directions[d]) if dotval > bestdot: bestdot = dotval bestidx = d gradientmap[i][j][k] = bestidx return gradientmap def precomputereflectancemap(volume, transferfunction, directions): """ Generates a preshaded reflectance map for each quantized direction. """ N = len(directions) reflectancemap = [None] N basecolor = transferfunction.getcolor(0.5) for d in range(N): shadedcolor = applylighting(basecolor, directions[d]) reflectancemap[d] = shadedcolor return reflectancemap def rendervolume(volume, gradientmap, reflectancemap, camera, transferfunction): """ Renders the volume using hybrid preshading and postclassification. """ H, W = camera.height, camera.width image = [[(0, 0, 0) for in range(W)] for in range(H)] deltas = 0.5 for y in range(H): for x in range(W): ray = camera.getray(x, y) r, g, b = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 alpha = 0.0 t = ray.origin while t < ray.end: coords = getvoxelcoords(t) preshadedcolors = [] opacities = [] for v in coords: idx = gradientmap[v[0]][v[1]][v[2]] preshadedcolors.append(reflectancemap[idx]) density = volume[v[0]][v[1]][v[2]] opacities.append(transferfunction.getopacity(density)) interpcolor = trilinearinterpolate(preshadedcolors, t) interpopacity = trilinearinterpolate(opacities, t) alphac = interpopacity if alphac > 0: r += interpcolor[0] alphac (1.0 - alpha) g += interpcolor[1] alphac (1.0 - alpha) b += interpcolor[2] alphac (1.0 - alpha) alpha += alphac (1.0 - alpha) t += deltas image[y][x] = (int(r 255), int(g 255), int(b 255)) return image Fast Two-Pass Shading is a rendering optimization that avoids redundant per-fragment computations—specifically volume texture access, classification, and lighting—by sharing intermediate results between pixels covered by the same splat. It decouples the classification and illumination steps from the geometric filtering step by storing intermediate results in a render target (P-buffer). Congradient shading is a real-time volumetric shading acceleration technique that defines the surface orientation of a voxel as one of a finite set of local gradients, enabling a fast table-driven mechanism. It solves the performance bottleneck of per-voxel normal calculation and lighting integration by integrating shading into the projection pipeline, generating "congradient values" (concatenated color and gradient data) that serve as direct indices to a precomputed illumination look-up table. Unlike sibling methods that may perform shading in a separate post-processing stage or require complex normal quantization, congradient shading operates as a pipeline with the viewing process, accruing no additional time for shading because the congradient calculation time is much less than the projection time. Fake Phong Illumination via Normal Quantization is a real-time approximation technique for volume rendering that replaces per-voxel Phong lighting calculations with a pre-computed color lookup table indexed by quantized surface normals. It solves the performance bottleneck of interactive volumetric rendering by moving the computational cost of the Phong equation to a pre-processing stage, allowing rendering to proceed via simple texture mapping. Unlike real-time Phong illumination which calculates lighting dynamically for every sample, this method sacrifices image fidelity to achieve speed, specifically introducing directional aliasing artifacts due to the discrete nature of the normal vector quantization. A technique to compute gradient directions for lighting that adaptively align with post-classified density variations while using pre-computed gradient directions for sampling, avoiding the need for two-sided lighting. It differs from standard pre-classified gradients by flipping normals to ensure single-sided lighting correctly illuminates low-scalar-value regions (like dentin) without lighting back-facing surfaces. Time Complexity: The per-voxel shading cost is reduced to a table lookup during rendering, as shading is precomputed. The dominant cost is the trilinear interpolation of the preshaded colors and opacities. The precomputation phase is O(N \cdot V) where N is the number of directions and V is the number of voxels, but this is done once. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume data, the gradient map (1 integer per voxel), and the preshaded reflectance map (N colors). With N=8192, the reflectance map is small. Performance: Benchmarks were performed on platforms using MMX, SSE, or 3DNow! SIMD extensions for memory copying and trilinear interpolation. The method allows high-quality rendering on 512 \times 512 images with up to 4x zoom without visible noise. Strengths: Combines the speed of preshading with the visual quality of postclassification. Avoids the artifacts associated with preclassification/preshading (which requires opacity-weighted interpolation) and the slowness of postclassification/postshading. Limitations: Relies on quantization of gradient directions, which may introduce directional artifacts. The claim of "no artifacts" contradicts Mueller et al., suggesting potential sensitivity to specific volume characteristics or transfer functions. Described in, the method addresses the limitations of traditional preclassification/preshading and postclassification/postshading approaches by proposing a hybrid strategy. The authors argue against the interpretation by Mueller et al. that preshading and postclassification inherently produce bad artifacts, claiming their implementation shows no visible artifacts. The technique is part of a broader effort to optimize real-time volume rendering using SIMD instructions and precomputed data structures. name: Fast Two-Pass Shading
head: P-buffer shading, Two-pass shading
body: Fast Two-Pass Shading is a rendering optimization that avoids redundant per-fragment computations—specifically volume texture access, classification, and lighting—by sharing intermediate results between pixels covered by the same splat. It decouples the classification and illumination steps from the geometric filtering step by storing intermediate results in a render target (P-buffer). Inputs and Outputs: Input: A slice of voxels to be rendered as splats. Output: A composited image of the slice. Intermediate Data: A P-buffer (render target) storing intermediate results for each splat. Data Structures: The P-buffer stores one entry per splat. Each entry contains the results of volume texture access, voxel classification (via lookup table), and illumination computation. Numbered Steps: 1. First Pass (P-buffer Generation): Project each voxel of the current slice as a single-pixel point. For each point splat, compute volume texture access, voxel classification, and illumination. Store these intermediate results in the P-buffer (render target). 2. Second Pass (Splat Rendering): Project the full splat geometry (covering multiple pixels, e.g., 2×2 to 40×40 pixels depending on viewpoint). For each fragment covered by the splat, perform per-fragment lighting and EWA filtering while reusing the intermediate results from the P-buffer via lookup. 3. Final Composition: Composite all splats from the slice into the final image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fasttwopassshading(sliceofvoxels, viewmatrix, splatradius): # Initialize P-buffer render target as a dictionary mapping screen coords to intermediates pbuffer = {} # Pass 1: Compute intermediate results for each splat for voxel in sliceofvoxels: # Project voxel center to screen as a single-pixel point screenx, screeny = projecttoscreen(voxel.center, viewmatrix) key = (int(screenx), int(screeny)) # Compute intermediate results texturesample = samplevolume(voxel.position) classification = classifyvoxel(texturesample) illumination = computeillumination(classification, voxel.position) # Store in P-buffer pbuffer[key] = { 'texturesample': texturesample, 'classification': classification, 'illumination': illumination } # Pass 2: Render full splats with filtering finalimage = initializeimage() for voxel in sliceofvoxels: # Project full splat geometry splatcenterx, splatcentery = projecttoscreen(voxel.center, viewmatrix) radius = splatradius # Varies from 2 to 40 pixels depending on viewpoint # Render fragments covered by the splat for dy in range(-radius, radius + 1): for dx in range(-radius, radius + 1): fragx, fragy = splatcenterx + dx, splatcentery + dy if not inimagebounds(fragx, fragy, finalimage): continue # Lookup intermediate results from P-buffer pkey = (int(splatcenterx), int(splatcentery)) intermediate = pbuffer.get(pkey) if intermediate is None: continue # Apply per-fragment lighting and EWA filtering weight = computeewaweight(dx, dy, radius) finalcolor = applyewafiltering(intermediate, weight, fragx, fragy) # Composite into image compositeintoimage(finalcolor, fragx, fragy, finalimage) return finalimage def projecttoscreen(position, viewmatrix): # Standard perspective projection projected = transform(position, viewmatrix) return projected.x / projected.w, projected.y / projected.w def samplevolume(position): # Trilinear interpolation from volume texture return volumetexture.sample(position) def classifyvoxel(texturevalue): # Lookup table classification return classificationlut[texturevalue] def computeillumination(classification, position): # Standard lighting model using classification and position return lightingmodel(classification, position) def computeewaweight(dx, dy, radius): # Elliptical Weighted Average weight calculation return exp(-(dxdx + dydy) / (2 radius radius)) def applyewafiltering(intermediate, weight, fragx, fragy): # Reuse intermediate results with EWA weight return intermediate['illumination'] weight def compositeintoimage(color, x, y, image): # Alpha blending into final image image[y][x] = blend(image[y][x], color) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Context Switches: The additional rendering pass increases the number of context switches, which can offset some performance gains. Splat Size: Splat sizes vary from 2×2 to as many as 40×40 pixels depending on the viewpoint. Performance Improvement: 5%–10%. Hardware: Measured on a 2.4 GHz P4 system with 2 GB memory and an ATI 9800 Pro video card (256 MB local memory) using DirectX 9.0 SDK. Strengths: Reduces redundant computation for pixels covered by the same splat. Limitations: Increased context switches due to the extra pass. Origin: Proposed in "Hardware-Accelerated Adaptive EWA Volume Splatting" by Wei Chen et al.. History: Implemented with DirectX 9.0 SDK under Windows XP. Usage: Used in volume rendering for scientific visualization, specifically for EWA volume splatting. name: Congradient Shading
head: Gradient-Based Shading Lookup, Gradient-based Table-driven Shading, Table-driven congradient shading, real-time congradient shading
body:
Congradient shading is a real-time volumetric shading acceleration technique that defines the surface orientation of a voxel as one of a finite set of local gradients, enabling a fast table-driven mechanism. It solves the performance bottleneck of per-voxel normal calculation and lighting integration by integrating shading into the projection pipeline, generating "congradient values" (concatenated color and gradient data) that serve as direct indices to a precomputed illumination look-up table. Unlike sibling methods that may perform shading in a separate post-processing stage or require complex normal quantization, congradient shading operates as a pipeline with the viewing process, accruing no additional time for shading because the congradient calculation time is much less than the projection time. It builds on Hybrid Preshading with Postclassification by preshading volume gradients and associating a quantized space direction index with every voxel. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset with precomputed normals, opacities, and an octree structure. The light source location can be arbitrarily changed. Output: A shaded image where each pixel's color is determined by the congradient value derived from the voxel's local gradient and color. Data Structures: 1. Triple Shift Register: A hardware structure holding the depth and color values of the voxel being processed, the whole scan-line before it, and the whole scan-line after it. This makes the voxel's two horizontal and vertical neighbors readily available for gradient computation. 2. Congradient Value: A data unit holding concatenated values of color and local gradient. 3. Look-Up Table (LUT): A table containing color as a function of local voxel gradient. The indices are the congradient values, and the values are the shaded colors based on light source parameters. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Compute normals, opacities, and the octree as a preprocessing step. Define the surface orientation of a voxel as one of a finite set of local gradients. 2. Projection and Congradient Generation: The shading unit is an integral part of the projection process. Each projected pixel is pipelined through memory access, the projection unit, and the shading unit. 3. Gradient Computation: Using the triple shift register, compute the local gradient for the current voxel. Two approaches are implemented: Unidirectional Shading: The gradient is computed only from the depth of the horizontal neighbors. Bidirectional Shading: Both horizontal and vertical neighbors are employed. 4. Concatenation: Generate a congradient value by concatenating the voxel's color and the computed local gradient. The production time of a congradient value is interleaved with the projection time of the next pixel. 5. Lookup: The display stage uses standard hardware where the congradient values are used as indices to the look-up table. 6. Shading: The look-up table translates the congradient value to its shaded color based upon the light source parameters. Formulas: Unidirectional gradient: 
abla d = d{	ext{right}} - d{	ext{left}}. Bidirectional gradient: 
abla d = (d{	ext{right}} - d{	ext{left}}, d{	ext{bottom}} - d{	ext{top}}). Congradient value: C = 	ext{pack}(color, 	ext{quantize}(
abla d)). Parameters: Light Source Location: Can be arbitrarily changed, providing motion parallax. Gradient Set: A predefined set of surface gradients stored in the look-up table. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hardware Realization: The architecture is designed to be simple and suitable for hardware realization. Precision: The method relies on a finite set of local gradients, which may limit the accuracy of surface orientation representation compared to continuous normal fields. Positional Lights: Positional light sources cannot be supported accurately because they result in different light vectors for data samples with the same gradient due to different positions in the volume. Perspective View: Specular highlights are only accurate for orthographic viewing directions where the view vector does not vary based on sample position. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preprocess(volume): normals = computenormals(volume) opacities = computeopacities(volume) octree = buildoctree(volume) return normals, opacities, octree def initshiftregister(scanlines): return [scanlines[0], scanlines[1], scanlines[2]] def computegradienthorizontal(depthleft, depthright): return depthright - depthleft def computegradientbidirectional(depthleft, depthright, depthtop, depthbottom): dx = depthright - depthleft dy = depthbottom - depthtop return (dx, dy) def quantizegradient(gradientvector): # Standard nearest-neighbor lookup in predefined gradient set return 0 def concatenate(colorrgb, gradientindex): return (colorrgb[0] << 16) | (colorrgb[1] << 8) | colorrgb[2] | (gradientindex << 24) def runpipeline(shiftregister, lightparams, lut): shadedpixels = [] width = len(shiftregister[1]) for i in range(width): current = shiftregister[1][i] left = shiftregister[1][i - 1] if i > 0 else current right = shiftregister[1][i + 1] if i < width - 1 else current top = shiftregister[0][i] bottom = shiftregister[2][i] # Unidirectional or bidirectional approach gradient = computegradienthorizontal(left[0], right[0]) # gradient = computegradientbidirectional(left[0], right[0], top[0], bottom[0]) gradientindex = quantizegradient(gradient) congradientvalue = concatenate(current[1], gradientindex) shadedcolor = lut[congradientvalue] shadedpixels.append(shadedcolor) return shadedpixels A technique to accelerate rendering by precomputing illumination for each possible encoded gradient direction index, storing results in a table independent of color. It computes illumination once for each possible encoded index and stores results in an array where each scalar value may have separate entries for ambient, diffuse, and specular illumination. Positional light sources cannot be supported accurately because they result in different light vectors for data samples with the same gradient due to different positions in the volume; thus, positional lights are approximated as infinite lights, and a single view direction is used for specular highlights to prioritize fast rendering over accuracy. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: No additional time is accrued for shading because the congradient calculation time for each pixel is much less than its projection time. The total time for an arbitrary projection is O(n^2 \log n), allowing real-time arbitrary projection. Memory: Requires a look-up table for congradient values and a triple shift register for neighbor access. Measured Performance: Implemented on the Cube architecture, a VLSI-based volume visualization system. Tested on workstations such as Sun-S, Sun-4, Silicon Graphics IRIS, and HP Turbo SRX with resolutions of 128^3, 256^3, and 512^3. Scaling: The modular nature of the Cube architecture is well suited for VLSI implementation. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Faster than alternative techniques, simpler for hardware realization, supports arbitrary light source movement for motion parallax. Limitations: Accuracy of specular highlights is limited to orthographic viewing directions where the view vector does not vary based on sample position. Positional lights are approximated as infinite lights. When to Use: When real-time performance is critical and hardware implementation is feasible. When motion parallax is desired with arbitrary light source movement. When Not to Use: When high accuracy for positional lights or perspective specular highlights is required. Congradient shading was developed for the Cube architecture, emphasizing real-time performance. It capitalizes on the advantages of both gradient shading and contextual shading by defining the surface orientation of a voxel as one of a finite set of local gradients. The technique was developed as part of the Cube project, which aimed to build a full-scale VLSI-based volume visualization system. The first implementation, Cube-1, used a 16^3 resolution and verified basic concepts of skewed memory, parallel access, and parallel processing of an orthographic beam. name: Fake Phong Illumination via Normal Quantization
head: Color map Phong approximation, Normal Vector Quantization Lighting, Pre-computed Phong Lighting, Pre-computed Phong illumination
body: Fake Phong Illumination via Normal Quantization is a real-time approximation technique for volume rendering that replaces per-voxel Phong lighting calculations with a pre-computed color lookup table indexed by quantized surface normals. It solves the performance bottleneck of interactive volumetric rendering by moving the computational cost of the Phong equation to a pre-processing stage, allowing rendering to proceed via simple texture mapping. Unlike real-time Phong illumination which calculates lighting dynamically for every sample, this method sacrifices image fidelity to achieve speed, specifically introducing directional aliasing artifacts due to the discrete nature of the normal vector quantization. The method relies on the "infinite viewer and light" approximation, where the light direction (\mathbf{lightDir}) and view direction (\mathbf{viewDir}) are assumed constant for all points in the volume. Under this assumption, the Phong illumination equation depends only on the normal vector (\mathbf{normal}) at the point being lit (p). Input: Volumetric scalar field data; a static set of N pre-defined normal vector directions; Phong lighting parameters (ambient, diffuse, specular coefficients, shininess). Output: A rendered image where each voxel's color is determined by a lookup into a pre-computed color map based on the quantized normal index stored in the voxel data. 1. Normal Vector Table A static table containing N pre-defined normal vector directions. Size: N entries. Typical value is N=240. Content: Each entry is a 3D unit vector (x, y, z). Generation: In standard implementations, the unit sphere is tessellated by subdividing a regular dodecahedron into 60 triangles, and each triangle is further subdivided into 4 smaller triangles, yielding 240 almost equal-sized triangles. Each normal vector is quantized to the center of gravity of the respective triangle. 2. Voxel Data The volume data structure used for rendering. Layout: Instead of storing the full gradient vector or normal vector, each voxel stores a single integer index. Size: 1 integer per voxel. Content: The index points to an entry in the Normal Vector Table. 3. Color Map (Lookup Table) A pre-computed table mapping normal indices to colors. Size: N entries (typically 240). Constraint: Hardware typically supports color maps with 256 entries. Content: Each entry contains the RGB color result of the Phong equation evaluated for the corresponding normal vector in the Normal Vector Table. 1. Pre-processing: Gradient Calculation Calculate the gradient vector \nabla f for each voxel in the volume data. This gradient serves as the surface normal approximation. 2. Quantization Quantize each calculated gradient vector to one of the N pre-defined normal vector directions from the Normal Vector Table. For each gradient \mathbf{g}, find the index i in the Normal Vector Table such that the vector \mathbf{n}i minimizes the angular distance (or maximizes the dot product) with \mathbf{g}. Store the index i in the Voxel Data structure for that voxel, replacing the full vector. 3. Pre-rendering: Phong Evaluation Evaluate the Phong illumination equation for every normal vector \mathbf{n}i in the Normal Vector Table. The Phong equation factors are: position p, normal vector \mathbf{normal}, light direction \mathbf{lightDir}, and view direction \mathbf{viewDir}. Under the infinite viewer/light approximation, \mathbf{lightDir} and \mathbf{viewDir} are constant. Thus, the result depends only on \mathbf{n}i. Compute the color Ci for each \mathbf{n}i. 4. Color Map Construction Create the Color Map by storing the computed colors Ci at index i. 5. Rendering For each voxel during texture-mapping: Retrieve the stored index i from the Voxel Data. Look up the pre-computed Phong color Ci from the Color Map. Use this color for the voxel's contribution to the final image. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def fakephongnormalquantization(volumedata, phongparams): """ Implements Fake Phong Illumination via Normal Quantization. Args: volumedata: 3D array of scalar values. phongparams: Object containing ambient, diffuse, specular coefficients, shininess, lightDir, viewDir. Returns: quantizedvoxeldata: 3D array of integer indices. colormap: 1D array of RGB colors. """ N = 240 normaltable = generatedodecahedronnormals(N) quantizedvoxeldata = [[0] len(volumedata[0][0]) for in range(len(volumedata[0]))] for x in range(len(volumedata)): for y in range(len(volumedata[0])): for z in range(len(volumedata[0][0])): gradient = calculategradient(volumedata, x, y, z) bestindex = 0 maxdot = -float('inf') for i in range(N): dotproduct = dot(gradient, normaltable[i]) if dotproduct > maxdot: maxdot = dotproduct bestindex = i quantizedvoxeldata[x][y][z] = bestindex colormap = [None] N for i in range(N): normal = normaltable[i] color = evaluatephongequation( normal=normal, lightDir=phongparams.lightDir, viewDir=phongparams.viewDir, ambient=phongparams.ambient, diffuse=phongparams.diffuse, specular=phongparams.specular, shininess=phongparams.shininess) colormap[i] = color return quantizedvoxeldata, colormap def calculategradient(volumedata, x, y, z): """Central difference gradient approximation.""" gx = volumedata[x+1][y][z] - volumedata[x-1][y][z] if 0 < x < len(volumedata)-1 else 0.0 gy = volumedata[x][y+1][z] - volumedata[x][y-1][z] if 0 < y < len(volumedata[0])-1 else 0.0 gz = volumedata[x][y][z+1] - volumedata[x][y][z-1] if 0 < z < len(volumedata[0][0])-1 else 0.0 return [gx, gy, gz] def generatedodecahedronnormals(N): """Generates N normals by subdividing a regular dodecahedron. 1. Start with regular dodecahedron (60 faces). 2. Subdivide each face into 4 smaller triangles. 3. Total triangles = 60 4 = 240. 4. Return center of gravity for each triangle.""" if N != 240: raise ValueError("Standard implementation assumes N=240") # Standard geometric construction for dodecahedron subdivision # Returns 240 normalized 3D vectors normals = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(240)] # Actual dodecahedron subdivision geometry omitted; returns valid unit vectors return normals def evaluatephongequation(normal, lightDir, viewDir, ambient, diffuse, specular, shininess): n = normalize(normal) l = normalize(lightDir) v = normalize(viewDir) diff = max(dot(n, l), 0.0) r = [2 dot(n, l) n[k] - l[k] for k in range(3)] spec = pow(max(dot(r, v), 0.0), shininess) return [ambient + diffuse diff + specular spec] def dot(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def normalize(v): mag = math.sqrt(sum(x x for x in v)) return [x / mag for x in v] N: The number of pre-defined normal vector directions. Typical value is 240. Quantizer Type: Static (dodecahedron subdivision) is standard; data-dependent (Simulated Annealing) is mentioned as future work. Directional Aliasing: The major problem is image quality. Because gradients are quantized to a discrete set of directions (usually 240), the resulting image exhibits strong "directional aliasing" artifacts. Hardware Limits: Hardware typically supports color maps with 256 entries. If N exceeds this, the method may require extension or reduction of N. Quantization Error: The choice of quantizer significantly impacts image quality. A poor quantizer will exacerbate aliasing. Time Complexity: Rendering time is reduced to O(1) per voxel lookup, as the expensive Phong calculation is moved to pre-processing. Pre-processing is O(V \cdot N) where V is the number of voxels and N is the number of normals. Memory Complexity: Requires storing an index per voxel (1 integer) plus the Color Map (N colors) and Normal Table (N vectors). Performance: Evaluating the Phong equation for 240 vectors can be done in real-time without problems. Using a color map for texture-mapping is supported by current graphics hardware. Strengths: Enables interactive frame rates for volumetric data that would otherwise be too slow for per-voxel Phong lighting. Limitations: Significant loss of image quality due to directional aliasing. The approximation is only valid under the "infinite viewer and light" assumption. When to use: When interactive performance is required and the lighting setup allows for the infinite viewer/light approximation. Origin: The technique is described in the context of interactive volume rendering using 3D texture mapping. History: Current implementations use a static quantizer based on subdividing a regular dodecahedron. Future work involves data-dependent quantizers using Simulated Annealing to improve the distribution of normal vectors and allow for different numbers of vectors. Usage: Used in real-time volume rendering systems where Phong illumination is desired but per-voxel calculation is prohibitive. name: Hybrid Gradient Computation
head: Adaptive Gradient Flipping
body: A technique to compute gradient directions for lighting that adaptively align with post-classified density variations while using pre-computed gradient directions for sampling, avoiding the need for two-sided lighting. It differs from standard pre-classified gradients by flipping normals to ensure single-sided lighting correctly illuminates low-scalar-value regions (like dentin) without lighting back-facing surfaces. Inputs: Original scalar field V, post-classification transfer function (implicit in post-classified sample densities), and a 2D lookup table (LUT) for lighting transfer with an alpha channel reserved for gradient flip logic. Outputs: Adaptive gradient direction \mathbf{g}{hybrid} for each sample point. Data Structures: A 3D vector field storing the normalized pre-computed gradient direction \mathbf{n}{pre} at each voxel, and a 2D LUT texture where the alpha channel stores the pre-computed density difference for the flip decision. Steps: 1. Precompute the gradients of the original scalar field at all voxel centers and normalize them to form the pre-computed gradient direction field \mathbf{n}{pre}. 2. For every voxel (or representative sample point), perform the following offline to populate the LUT alpha channel: let \mathbf{n}{pre} be the normalized pre-computed gradient direction at position \mathbf{p}, read two additional scalar values along the linearly interpolated normalized direction, compute the difference between the post-classified sample densities at the start and end of the gradient step, and store the precomputed difference in the alpha channel of the 2D lookup table used for the lighting transfer function. 3. During volume rendering, for each sample point \mathbf{p}: retrieve the pre-computed gradient direction \mathbf{n}{pre} from the gradient field, retrieve the pre-computed difference from the alpha channel of the 2D LUT, and determine the adaptive direction \mathbf{g}{hybrid} using the formula: \mathbf{g}{hybrid} = \begin{cases} \mathbf{n}{pre} & \text{if the density difference sign matches the gradient direction} \\ -\mathbf{n}{pre} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} This adaptively flips the direction if the sign of the density difference indicates the pre-computed direction points opposite to the maximum variation in post-classified density. Use \mathbf{g}{hybrid} for lighting calculations. Pitfalls: Pre-classified and post-classified gradients are rarely parallel, so the resulting hybrid directions are not equivalent to true post-classified gradients. The method adds a constant-time lookup and conditional flip per sample during rendering, while the pre-computation step is performed once offline. Memory complexity requires storage for the pre-computed gradient field and an additional alpha channel in the 2D LUT for the pre-computed difference. Strengths include enabling single-sided lighting to correctly illuminate surfaces that would otherwise be back-facing or inward-facing due to pre-classified gradient orientation (e.g., dentin in tooth models), and avoiding the visual artifacts of two-sided lighting where back-facing surfaces are incorrectly illuminated. Limitations are that the hybrid directions are approximations and not true post-classified gradients. The technique originated in the context of volume rendering with lighting transfer functions, specifically addressing the issue where pre-classified gradients point opposite to the classified opacity distribution. It was introduced as a hybrid between pre-classified and post-classified gradient techniques. PDF Lighting Transfer Functions Using Gradient Aligned Sampling, https://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~ma/papers/lightingtf.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Pre-computation
body: Pre-computation is a method in volume rendering that calculates intermediate radiance variables and their density derivatives, storing them as voxels to avoid redundant calculations during the ray marching phase. It solves the problem of expensive volumetric illumination by pre-calculating terms such as incident radiance, absorption coefficients, and scattering sources, allowing the renderer to skip evaluating these complex integrals at each raymarching step. It is distinguished from full path-tracing methods by its reliance on precomputed segment data and from simple direct illumination by its inclusion of first-order inscattering approximations via a diffusion solver. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Diffusion radiance fields L{0d}, \vec{L}{1d} and their derivatives; scattering source S; extinction coefficient \kappa; absorption coefficient \kappaa; total extinction coefficient \kappat. Outputs: Precomputed radiance field L{ri} and its derivative \partial\pi L{ri}; diffusion radiance fields L{0d}, \vec{L}{1d} and their derivatives \partial\pi L{0d}, \partial\pi \vec{L}{1d}. Data Structures: The method stores fields as voxels, where each voxel at position v{xu} contains scalar or vector values for the computed variables. The specific bit-packing or memory layout is not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Iterate over each voxel position v{xu} in the volume in parallel. 2. Compute the incident radiance L{ri}(v{xu}, \boldsymbol{\omega}') and its density derivative \partial\pi L{ri}(v{xu}, \boldsymbol{\omega}') using Equations 31 and 41. 3. Compute the intermediate variable Q{0ri}(v{xu}) and its derivative \partial\pi Q{0ri}(v{xu}) using Equations 37 and 15. 4. Compute the intermediate variable \vec{Q}{1ri}(v{xu}) and its derivative \partial\pi \vec{Q}{1ri}(v{xu}) using Equations 38 and 16. 5. Compute the extinction coefficient \kappa(v{xu}) and its derivative \partial\pi \kappa(v{xu}) using Equations 35 and 12. 6. Compute the scattering source S(v{xu}) and its derivative \partial\pi S(v{xu}) using Equations 36 and 14. 7. Call DiffusionSolver to compute the diffusion radiance L{0d}, \vec{L}{1d} and their derivatives \partial\pi L{0d}, \partial\pi \vec{L}{1d} using the pre-computed S, \kappa, and \kappaa. 8. Return L{ri}, L{0d}, \vec{L}{1d} and their derivatives. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def Precomputation(L0d, L1d, S, kappa, kappaa, kappat): numvoxels = len(S) Lri = [None] numvoxels dLri = [None] numvoxels Q0ri = [None] numvoxels dQ0ri = [None] numvoxels Q1ri = [None] numvoxels dQ1ri = [None] numvoxels dkappa = [None] numvoxels dS = [None] numvoxels for vxu in range(numvoxels): # Compute incident radiance and derivative (Eq 31, 41) Lri[vxu], dLri[vxu] = computeLriandderivative(vxu) # Compute Q0ri and derivative (Eq 37, 15) Q0ri[vxu], dQ0ri[vxu] = computeQ0riandderivative(vxu) # Compute Q1ri and derivative (Eq 38, 16) Q1ri[vxu], dQ1ri[vxu] = computeQ1riandderivative(vxu) # Compute extinction and derivative (Eq 35, 12) kappa[vxu], dkappa[vxu] = computekappaandderivative(vxu) # Compute scattering source and derivative (Eq 36, 14) S[vxu], dS[vxu] = computeSandderivative(vxu) # Solve diffusion radiance and derivatives using Jacobi iteration # Standard Jacobi iteration for linear system is not detailed in sources. L0dout, dL0dout, L1dout, dL1dout = DiffusionSolver(L0d, L1d, S, kappa, kappaa) return Lri, L0dout, L1dout, dLri, dL0dout, dL1dout def computeLriandderivative(vxu): # Eq 31, 41 return 0.0, 0.0 def computeQ0riandderivative(vxu): # Eq 37, 15 return 0.0, 0.0 def computeQ1riandderivative(vxu): # Eq 38, 16 return 0.0, 0.0 def computekappaandderivative(vxu): # Eq 35, 12 return 0.0, 0.0 def computeSandderivative(vxu): # Eq 36, 14 return 0.0, 0.0 def DiffusionSolver(L0d, L1d, S, kappa, kappaa): # Jacobi iterative method details not provided in sources. return L0d, [0.0]len(L0d), L1d, [0.0]len(L1d) Parameters and Edge Cases: The Monte Carlo method estimates the solid angle integral over the unit sphere S^2 for L{ri}. The sample count is not given. The DiffusionSolver uses a Jacobi iterative method. The iteration count and convergence criteria are not given. Precision handling for density derivatives \partial\pi is not detailed. Approximates global light transport in participating media by decomposing the radiative transfer equation into convection (absorption) and diffusion (scattering) steps on a regular grid. It computes high-resolution local shadows via piecewise opacity segments and propagates light energy using a convection-diffusion solver, enabling real-time rendering via single texture lookups. Choose it when real-time volumetric rendering with accurate local shadows is required. Time and Memory Complexity: The pre-computation step requires iterating over all voxels in parallel, making it O(N) with respect to the number of voxels N. The DiffusionSolver involves iterative solving, the complexity of which depends on the convergence rate of the Jacobi method. Memory usage is proportional to the number of voxels, storing multiple fields (L{ri}, L{0d}, \vec{L}{1d}, and their derivatives). Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Eliminates redundant calculations during ray marching by storing intermediate variables as voxels. Allows for efficient reuse of precomputed values. Limitations: Requires significant memory to store multiple radiance fields and their derivatives. The accuracy depends on the pre-computation of incident radiance and the diffusion solver's convergence. When to Use: Use when rendering participating media where the lighting term is expensive to compute per-voxel during ray marching, and sufficient memory is available to store the precomputed fields. Origin: The method is described in "A Differential Diffusion Theory for Participating Media". History and Development: The method incorporates a pre-computation step to address challenges in rendering participating media and computing radiance derivatives. It builds on differential diffusion theory. A Differential Diffusion Theory for Participating Media, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14956, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Local Piecewise Integration for Light Propagation
head: Local Piecewise Integration
body:
Local Piecewise Integration for Light Propagation is a precomputation technique that approximates global light transport in participating media by decomposing the radiative transfer equation into convection (absorption) and diffusion (scattering) steps solved on a regular grid. It solves the problem of expensive volumetric illumination by computing high-resolution local shadows via piecewise opacity segments and propagating light energy through the volume using a convection-diffusion solver, allowing real-time rendering via single texture lookups. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volume dataset (resampled to grid), Transfer Function (TF), light source definitions (position, intensity, type), grid resolution \Delta x. Outputs: Final illumination volume L(x) (RGB 3D texture), piecewise opacity segments \alpha{lp}(sn). Data Structures: 1. Opacity Volume: 3D grid derived from the transfer function and resampled data volume. Resolution matches the light volume. Used to compute absorption coefficient \sigmaa(x). 2. Light Volume: 3D grid of energy density values ho{i,j,k}. Resolution Nx, Ny, Nz. Typically half the resolution of the original volume data. 3. Light Color Field: 3D grid of RGB vectors L(x), composed from individual light energy densities hok(x) and light colors Lk. 4. Piecewise Segments: Stored transparency values T{lp}(sn) or opacity \alpha{lp}(sn) for segments of length \Delta s. Parameters: \Delta x: Grid resolution. Can be lower than volume dataset for performance. c: Speed of light (used in CFL condition). Implementation uses c\Delta t = \Delta x/2. \sigmaa(x): Absorption coefficient, 0 \le \sigmaa \le 1. \sigmas: Scattering coefficient. Scalar for Eq. 13, vector \hat{\sigma}s for Eq. 23 (RGB channels). N: Number of samples along a local piecewise segment. \Delta s: Step length for global light integration, equal to segment length. Typically 8-16 voxels. I{bias}: Minimum lighting adjustment to prevent completely dark regions. R^\Omega: Scattering sphere radius; larger values result in less distinct shadows. Iterations per layer: Typically 4-5 iterations for the upwind scheme. Algorithm Steps: 1. Volume Discretization: Discretize the volume domain using a regular grid with resolution \Delta x. Energy density ho(x) is discretized as ho{i,j,k} = ho(x{i,j,k}) where x{i,j,k} = (i\Delta x, j\Delta x, k\Delta x). 2. Local Piecewise Integration (Shadowing): For each voxel location in the volume, cast rays in the direction of the light source. Compute the transparency T{lp}(sn) for segments starting at sn = n\Delta s, where s0 is the current voxel location. The intensity of direct light reaching position s is calculated as: I(s) = I0 	imes \prod{n=0}^k T{lp}(sn) where I0 is the light source intensity and T{lp}(sn) is the transparency of the n-th segment. The transparency of a single segment is defined as: T{lp}(sn) = e^{-\int{sn}^{sn+1} 	au(t) dt} where 	au(t) is the absorption coefficient. The segment opacity \alpha{lp}(sn) is discretized by sampling N points along the segment: \alpha{lp}(sn) = 1 - \prod{i=0}^N (1 - \alpha(ni)) where \alpha(ni) is the opacity of the i-th sample point in the current Transfer Function (TF) domain. Note: These segments must be recomputed whenever the TF changes or the volume moves relative to the light source. 3. Light Volume Initialization: Initialize the light volume grid ho{i,j,k}. Set boundary values according to light source type (Dirichlet/Neumann) and set interior values to zero, except for internal point lights. External Point Lights: If xP 
otin \Omega, use hybrid Dirichlet-Neumann boundary conditions. ho(x)|{\partial \Omega} = G(x, xP)hoP if n(x) \cdot (x - xP) < 0, else  rac{\partial ho(x)}{\partial n} = 0. G(x, xP) is a Gaussian falloff function. Internal Point Lights: If xP \in \Omega, set voxels within distance 2\Delta x from xP to the light intensity hoP. These voxels are treated as an internal boundary and not updated during simulation: ho(xP) = hoP. 4. Convection Step (Absorption): Solve the convection equation with absorption for each light source individually:  rac{\partial ho(x)}{\partial t} = -c u(x) \cdot 
abla ho(x) - \sigmaa(x)ho(x) where c is speed of light, u(x) is unit light direction, and \sigmaa(x) is absorption coefficient. Use a first-order upwind scheme. Update layer by layer along the light propagation direction. Repeat until steady state (-c u(x) \cdot 
abla ho(x) - \sigmaa(x)ho(x) = 0) is reached, typically 4-5 iterations per layer. The upwind gradient component x is computed as: ho{i,j,k}^x =  egin{cases}  rac{ho{i+1,j,k} - ho{i,j,k}}{\Delta x} & 	ext{if } u{i,j,k} < 0 \  rac{ho{i,j,k} - ho{i-1,j,k}}{\Delta x} & 	ext{if } u{i,j,k} > 0 \end{cases} (Similar formulas apply for y and z components based on v{i,j,k} and w{i,j,k}). The update rule is: ho{i,j,k}(t+\Delta t) = (1 - \sigmaa(x))ho{i,j,k}(t) -  rac{\Delta t}{\Delta x} \Delta ho{i,j,k}(t) with CFL condition C = c\Delta t/\Delta x \le 1. Implementation uses c\Delta t = \Delta x/2, so C=1/2. 5. Light Field Composition: Composite solutions from all light sources into a single light color field L(x): L(x) = \sum{k=1}^N (hok(x)Lk) where hok(x) is the solution for the k-th light source and Lk is its color. 6. Diffusion Step (Scattering): Solve the diffusion equation for scattering using Gauss-Seidel iteration on the combined light field L(x):  rac{\partial L(x)}{\partial t} = \hat{\sigma}s 
abla^2 L(x) where \hat{\sigma}s consists of three scattering coefficients for different color channels. Use the solution at t=1 as the final illumination volume. Solving this once for the combined field is significantly cheaper than solving for each light source separately. 7. Rendering: Render using volume ray casting. For each sample point, lookup illumination L(x) from the final volume and combine with Phong shading: L{final}(x) = L(x)(Ia(x) + Id(x) + Is(x)) where Ia, Id, Is are ambient, diffuse, and specular lighting intensities. Only one additional texture lookup is performed for each sample to apply the pre-computed light intensities. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def localpiecewiseintegration(volumedata, transferfunction, lights, gridresolution): # 1. Discretize and Initialize # Opacity volume derived from transfer function and resampled data volume opacityvolume = [[computeopacity(v, transferfunction) for v in row] for row in volumedata] # Light volume grid of energy density values lightvolume = [[[0.0 for in range(gridresolution.z)] for in range(gridresolution.y)] for in range(gridresolution.x)] # 2. Compute Local Piecewise Segments (Shadows) # Recompute if TF or volume-light relation changes piecewisesegments = [] for voxel in volumedata: segmentopacities = [] for n in range(gridresolution.z): # Assuming segments along z for simplicity, or use segment length # Sample ray in light direction for segment length # Sources do not specify exact sampling routine; assume raymarching over segment alphasegment = 1.0 for in range(numsamples): alphasegment = (1.0 - sampleopacityatraypoint(voxel, lightdirection, n)) segmentopacities.append(1.0 - alphasegment) piecewisesegments.append(segmentopacities) # 3. Solve Convection for each light for light in lights: currentenergy = [[[0.0 for in range(gridresolution.z)] for in range(gridresolution.y)] for in range(gridresolution.x)] # Initialize boundaries based on light type (Dirichlet/Neumann/Internal) # Sources do not specify exact boundary setup routine; implement logic inline for i, j, k in gridindices: if isboundary(i, j, k, light): currentenergy[i][j][k] = setboundaryvalue(light, i, j, k) elif isinternalpointlight(light, i, j, k): currentenergy[i][j][k] = light.intensity else: currentenergy[i][j][k] = 0.0 # Upwind Scheme Iteration for layer in layersalonglightdirection: for iteration in range(5): # 4-5 iterations for i, j, k in gridindices: # First-order upwind scheme # CFL condition: cdt = dx/2 gradx = upwindgradient(currentenergy, i, j, k, light.direction.x, gridresolution.x) grady = upwindgradient(currentenergy, i, j, k, light.direction.y, gridresolution.y) gradz = upwindgradient(currentenergy, i, j, k, light.direction.z, gridresolution.z) divergence = light.direction.x gradx + light.direction.y grady + light.direction.z gradz sigmaa = opacityvolume[i][j][k] currentenergy[i][j][k] = (1.0 - sigmaa) currentenergy[i][j][k] - 0.5 divergence accumulateenergy(lightvolume, currentenergy, light.color) # 4. Solve Diffusion for Scattering # Solve once on combined light field finalillumination = solvediffusiongaussseidel(lightvolume, scatteringcoefficient) return finalillumination, piecewisesegments def upwindgradient(energy, i, j, k, dircomponent, dimsize): if dircomponent < 0: return (energy[i][j][k] - energy[max(0, i-1)][j][k]) / 1.0 # dx=1 for simplicity else: return (energy[min(dimsize-1, i+1)][j][k] - energy[i][j][k]) / 1.0 def accumulateenergy(target, source, color): for i in range(len(target)): for j in range(len(target[0])): for k in range(len(target[0][0])): target[i][j][k] += source[i][j][k] color Piecewise Integration is a precomputation technique for real-time volume rendering that approximates global light transport by dividing light paths into discrete segments. It solves the problem of expensive volumetric illumination by storing transmittance data in a multiresolution 3D texture, allowing incoming radiance to be computed via a single texture lookup per sample. It is distinguished from full path-tracing methods by its reliance on precomputed segment data and from simple direct illumination by its inclusion of first-order inscattering approximations. A variant for handling external directional light Ll. It computes the multiple scattering source term q{ri}(x) for external directional light as q{ri}(x) = Ll \cdot \sigmas(x) \cdot T(x), where \sigmas is the scattering coefficient and T(x) is transmittance. This term is computed via raymarching and stored at the full resolution of the dataset extinction field. A propagation scheme using radial grids (topologically equivalent to rectilinear grids but cyclic in two angular dimensions) for local point lights, allowing approximate treatment of space as locally Euclidean. It extends the Principal-Ordinates Propagation (POP) method to local light sources by using spherical grids aligned with the initial principal directions of the point source. VPLs with large importance have high initial anisotropy, which is accounted for in the grid spacing. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: The whole volume data is stored in GPU memory, constraining maximum volume size by total available GPU memory. Time: Integration of light intensities without the local piecewise approximation is approximately 10 times slower. Global light integration updates in 284-552 ms (for 8 voxel segments) depending on Shadow Volume Representation (SVR) size; first order scattering incremental refinements take 62-233 ms. Light simulation time for a 128 	imes 128 	imes 128 light volume: Absorption takes 34ms, Scattering takes 18ms. Measured Performance: Hardware: Laptop with Intel 1.7GHz CPU and NVIDIA Geforce 460M GPU. Accuracy: Root Mean Square (RMS) error of 0.19 for \Delta E (CIE 1976 Luv color space), with 6% of pixels having \Delta E above 6. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Interactive frame rates (15-22 fps) once light calculations are updated; nearly physically correct scattering effects compared to blur-based methods like Kniss et al. [KPH03]; light source can be positioned anywhere, even within the volume; handles large scale volumes via multi-resolution data management. Limitations: Numerical dissipation from first-order upwind scheme causes soft shadows instead of hard shadows (though considered visually plausible); not as fast as precomputation-based techniques that do not require per-frame updates; block artifacts and banding effects appear if SVR resolution is too low. When to use: Real-time volume visualization where lighting changes (TF, light position) occur frequently, and precomputation is not feasible. When not to use: When hard shadows are required, or when the volume is extremely large and GPU memory is insufficient. The method was introduced by Cheng and Cheng in 2012 and further refined by Larsson et al. in 2008. It is based on solving the convection-diffusion equation to model light propagation, absorption, and scattering in optically thick media. The upwind scheme originates from Courant et al. (1952). The technique is implemented using NVIDIA CUDA for simulation and OpenGL for rendering, with the final light volume stored in an OpenGL 3D texture. name: Piecewise Integration
head: Piecewise Light Propagation, Segmented Light Transport
body: Piecewise Integration is a precomputation technique for real-time volume rendering that approximates global light transport by dividing light paths into discrete segments. It solves the problem of expensive volumetric illumination by storing transmittance data in a multiresolution 3D texture, allowing incoming radiance to be computed via a single texture lookup per sample. It is distinguished from full path-tracing methods by its reliance on precomputed segment data and from simple direct illumination by its inclusion of first-order inscattering approximations. Inputs: Volumetric dataset. Light source definition (position, radiance L0, type: directional or point). Transfer function. Number of segments k. Outputs: Final radiance 3D texture. Data Structures: 1. Piecewise Segment Texture: An intermediate 3D texture storing transmittance values between segment endpoints. It uses a multiresolution structure and a lower-resolution grid to reduce memory usage. 2. Final Radiance Texture: A 3D texture accumulating the progressive refinement results. 3. Auxiliary Textures: Three additional 3D textures are required for intermediate computations. Steps: 1. Segmentation: For each voxel in the volume, cast short rays towards the light source to determine piecewise segments. 2. Precomputation: Store the transmittance T(\tilde{x}n, \tilde{x}{n+1}) for each segment endpoint pair into the Piecewise Segment Texture. 3. Radiance Evaluation: For each voxel, send global rays towards the light source taking steps equal to the short ray size, sampling from the Piecewise Segment Texture. 4. Inscattering Approximation: Approximate first-order inscattering by treating scattering in the vicinity of the sample point as emission. 5. Progressive Refinement: To maintain interactivity, refine the final radiance by sending one ray at a time and blending the result into the Final Radiance Texture. Formula: The incoming radiance Li at a position \tilde{x} from direction \tilde{\omega}i is computed as: Li(\tilde{x}, \tilde{\omega}i) = L0 \cdot \prod{n=0}^{k} T(\tilde{x}n, \tilde{x}{n+1}) Where: L0 is the source radiance. k is the number of segments. T(\tilde{x}n, \tilde{x}{n+1}) is the transmittance between segment endpoints \tilde{x}n and \tilde{x}{n+1}. \tilde{x}n and \tilde{x}{n+1} are the endpoints of the n-th segment. Parameters: k: The number of segments into which rays are divided. Value not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Recomputation: If the light source position, type, or the transfer function changes, the radiance must be fully recomputed. Memory: Requires sufficient graphics memory for three additional 3D textures, though mitigated by multiresolution structures. Light Source Limitation: Supports only a single directional or point light source. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def normalize(v): mag = math.sqrt(sum(cc for c in v)) return tuple(c/mag for c in v) def isinside(pos, dims): return 0 <= pos[0] < dims[0] and 0 <= pos[1] < dims[1] and 0 <= pos[2] < dims[2] def piecewiseintegration(volumedims, lightpos, L0, k, stepsize, transferfunction): """ Computes volumetric illumination using piecewise integration. Args: volumedims: Tuple (Dx, Dy, Dz) of grid dimensions. lightpos: Tuple (x, y, z) of light source position. L0: Source radiance scalar. k: Number of segments. stepsize: Fixed step length for short and global rays. transferfunction: Callable mapping volume scalar to optical density. Returns: finalradiancetexture: Dict mapping (x,y,z) to radiance value. """ # 1. Precompute piecewise segments piecewisesegmenttexture = {} for x in range(volumedims[0]): for y in range(volumedims[1]): for z in range(volumedims[2]): voxelpos = (x, y, z) direction = normalize(tuple(lightpos[i] - voxelpos[i] for i in range(3))) currentpos = voxelpos accumulatedT = 1.0 for n in range(k + 1): density = transferfunction(volumedims, currentpos) segmentT = math.exp(-density stepsize) accumulatedT = segmentT piecewisesegmenttexture[currentpos] = accumulatedT currentpos = tuple(currentpos[i] + direction[i] stepsize for i in range(3)) if not isinside(currentpos, volumedims): break # 2. Progressive refinement finalradiancetexture = {} for x in range(volumedims[0]): for y in range(volumedims[1]): for z in range(volumedims[2]): voxelpos = (x, y, z) direction = normalize(tuple(lightpos[i] - voxelpos[i] for i in range(3))) currentpos = voxelpos incomingradiance = 0.0 accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 while isinside(currentpos, volumedims): segmentT = piecewisesegmenttexture.get(currentpos, 1.0) accumulatedtransmittance = segmentT density = transferfunction(volumedims, currentpos) emittedradiance = density L0 incomingradiance += emittedradiance accumulatedtransmittance currentpos = tuple(currentpos[i] + direction[i] stepsize for i in range(3)) finalradiancetexture[voxelpos] = incomingradiance return finalradiancetexture Time Complexity: Low rendering times due to the single extra lookup required to compute incoming radiance at the sample position. Memory Complexity: Requires three additional 3D textures for computations. Memory requirements are alleviated by using a multiresolution structure and a lower-resolution grid. Performance: Supports interactive frame rates, provided sufficient graphics memory is available. Strengths: Enables interactive progressive refinement; supports dynamic movement of a single light source. Limitations: Radiance must be recomputed if the light source or transfer function changes, which can be costly but is performed interactively and progressively. Limited to single directional or point light sources. Piecewise Integration was introduced by Habel et al. in 2008. It was developed for volume ray-casting but can be combined with other rendering paradigms. The technique is part of the broader effort to achieve interactive volume rendering with volumetric illumination, building on concepts like Summed Area Tables which were exploited by Diaz et al. for illumination effects. name: Shadow Volume Propagation
head: Ropinski et al
body: Shadow volume propagation is an illumination model for volume rendering that approximates light propagation direction to generate shadows and simulate scattering within volumetric datasets. It decouples shadow computation from scattering to achieve hard shadow borders, which improves depth perception. Unlike half-angle slicing, it specifically separates chromaticity and luminance processing. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volumetric dataset (density, absorption, scattering coefficients), light direction \vec{\omega}l, viewing direction \vec{\omega}o, cone apex angle \theta. Outputs: Final radiance L(x, \vec{\omega}o) for each sample point x along the viewing ray. Data Structures: Auxiliary Volume: A 3D volume storing precomputed luminance and scattering information. This volume is computed once per light direction and reused for all viewing rays. Formulas: The radiance L(x, \vec{\omega}o) at point x in viewing direction \vec{\omega}o is given by: L(x, \vec{\omega}o) = L(x0, \vec{\omega}o)\tau(x, x0) + \int{x0}^{x} \tau(x, x')Le(x', \vec{\omega}o)dx' + \int{x0}^{x} \tau(x, x')Li(x', \vec{\omega}o)dx' Where: x0 is the entry point of the viewing ray into the volume. \tau(x, x') is the transmittance between x and x'. Le is emitted radiance. Li is in-scattered radiance. The in-scattered radiance Li is approximated using the auxiliary volume: Li(x', \vec{\omega}o) = \lambda(Lb(x', \vec{\omega}l)) Where: Lb is the blurred incoming light. \lambda extracts luminance. \gamma extracts chromaticity (used in the blurring step). Blurring Model: The method assumes a cone phase function to limit incoming light directions to a cone with apex angle \theta centered on the light direction \vec{\omega}l: f(x, \vec{\omega}i, \vec{\omega}o) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2\pi(1-\cos(\theta))} & \text{if } \vec{\omega}i \cdot \vec{\omega}l < \cos(\theta) \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Algorithm Steps: 1. Precomputation: Compute the auxiliary volume storing luminance and scattering information for the given light direction. 2. Chromaticity-Luminance Split: Decompose the incoming light into luminance and chromaticity components. 3. Blurring: Apply blurring to the chromaticity part of the incoming light within the cone defined by \theta. Do not blur the luminance component. 4. Rendering: For each viewing ray: a. Sample the volume along the ray. b. Retrieve the precomputed luminance/scattering data from the auxiliary volume. c. Modulate the Phong shading at each sample using the retrieved data. d. Combine the unblurred luminance with the blurred chromaticity to compute final radiance. Parameters: \theta (cone apex angle): Not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Decoupling luminance and chromaticity is critical for maintaining hard shadow borders. Blurring luminance would soften shadows and reduce depth perception. Strengths: Produces hard shadow borders which improve depth perception. Decouples shadowing from scattering, allowing for efficient approximation of global illumination effects like scattering. Limitations: Approximates scattering using a cone model rather than full spherical integration, which may reduce accuracy for highly anisotropic scattering. Requires precomputation of an auxiliary volume. Performance: Not given in the sources. Shadow volume propagation was introduced by Ropinski et al. [85] as a technique to simulate global illumination effects like scattering in volume rendering. It is similar to half-angle slicing but differs in its decoupling of chromaticity and luminance. The method is used to enhance perception in volume visualization by providing realistic shadowing and scattering effects. name: Precomputed Radiance Transfer (PRT)
head: Directional surface prelighting, PRT with SH, Precomputed Radiance Transfer (PRT) with SH, SH PRT, SH-based global illumination
body: Precomputed Radiance Transfer (PRT) is a real-time global illumination technique that models light interaction with surfaces using transfer functions rather than operating on actual radiance values. It differs from Hybrid Preshading with Postclassification and Pre-computation by explicitly separating the geometry/material response from the lighting environment via transfer functions, and builds on Precomputed Lighting (Baking) by allowing arbitrary dynamic lighting setups at runtime, albeit with higher runtime computational costs. PRT leverages the linearity of light transport to separate the scene's response from the lighting environment. The method consists of three main phases: precomputing the transfer function, projecting the environment lighting into the same basis, and evaluating the final radiance via a dot product. Inputs: Geometry representation, chosen global illumination algorithm (e.g., radiosity, subsurface scattering) to determine the transfer function, and environment lighting (static or dynamic). Outputs: Per-vertex or per-voxel SH coefficients representing the light transfer function, and final radiance L(p) for each point p. Transfer Function: A vector of real numbers containing the precomputed response of the entity to each SH basis function. Environment Lighting: A vector of real numbers containing the SH coefficients of the incoming light field. Storage: Coefficients are stored per-vertex in a mesh or per-voxel in a grid, allowing interpolation across polygons or trilinear interpolation in volumes. 1. Precompute the Transfer Function: a. For each SH basis function Y{lm}, represent it as light approaching the entity from the infinite sphere. b. Because SH functions contain negative values, compute the lighting contribution twice: once with the positive light intensity and once with the opposite of the negative light intensity. c. Run the chosen global illumination algorithm for both cases. d. Subtract the result of the negative light calculation from the positive light calculation to obtain the net transfer response for that basis function. e. Store the resulting real numbers as the SH coefficients for the transfer function. 2. Project Environment Lighting into SH: a. For dynamic lighting, this step must be performed at least partly per-frame. b. Sample the incoming light function h(S) over the sphere S using n uniformly distributed random samples X = \{x1, x2,..., xn\}. c. Compute the SH coefficients \hat{c}^ml for the environment lighting using the approximate integration formula: \hat{c}^ml = \frac{4\pi}{n} \sum{i=1}^{n} h(xi) Y{lm}(xi) where Y{lm} is the SH basis function for degree l and order m. d. If multiple lights are present, project each separately and sum their coefficients in SH space, as addition is trivial in this basis. 3. Evaluate Outgoing Light: a. Compute the dot product between the precomputed transfer function SH coefficients and the environment lighting SH coefficients. b. This calculation is typically performed per-vertex in the model. c. Interpolate the resulting light values across each polygon. The final radiance L(p) for a point p is defined as the sum of the contributions of each light, leveraging the linearity of light transport: L(p) = \sumi Li(p) Wi Where: L(p) is the final radiance for point p. Li(p) is the precomputed unit contribution of light i (the transfer function response). Wi is the current brightness of light i. In the SH basis, this summation is equivalent to the dot product of the transfer vector and the environment lighting vector. SH Bands: The number of spherical harmonic bands determines the frequency detail captured. Sample Count (n): The number of samples used for projecting the environment lighting into SH. Negative Coefficients: SH basis functions have negative lobes, requiring the compute-positive-and-negative-separately-then-subtract approach to handle them correctly. Dynamic Lighting Cost: Projecting an arbitrary spherical environment into SH is expensive, requiring per-frame calculation for dynamic lights. Deformation: Standard PRT computes the transfer for an entire entity, which becomes inaccurate if geometry deforms significantly. Local PRT (LDPRT) computes transfer for local surface patches but cannot capture effects like shadows from distant parts of the model. Rotation Handling: For PRT, the transfer function cannot be easily rotated on the GPU; instead, rotate the lighting environment by the inverse model transform on the CPU. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Supports arbitrary dynamic lighting setups; captures complex global illumination effects (indirect lighting, soft shadows) in real-time. Limitations: Higher runtime cost than static full baking; expensive per-frame projection for dynamic environments; inaccurate for highly deformable geometry unless using LDPRT. When to Use: Real-time applications requiring dynamic global illumination. When Not to Use: Static scenes where full baking is sufficient. Precomputed Radiance Transfer was introduced by Sloan et al. in 2002. While originally formulated using Spherical Harmonics, the concept of using transfer functions is not limited to SH. A later extension, Local Deformable PRT (LDPRT), was introduced by Sloan et al. in 2005 to handle deformable geometry. name: Real-time PRT Reconstruction via ZH Rotation
head: Per-pixel PRT reconstruction, ZH to SH projection
body: This method reconstructs lighting in real-time by rotating precomputed Precomputed Radiance Transfer (PRT) values, stored in the Zernike Harmonic (ZH) basis, to match the local surface frame, projecting them back into the Spherical Harmonic (SH) basis, and computing the dot product with the lighting environment projected into SH. It sets itself apart from standard PRT by enabling per-pixel rotation of the transfer function on the GPU, allowing for dynamic surface orientations without the prohibitive cost of per-sample SH rotation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Precomputed PRT coefficients stored in ZH basis textures; lighting environment projected into SH basis; interpolated surface normal per pixel. Output: Final lit color (radiance) per pixel. Data Structures: ZH Coefficients: Stored in textures. The specific bit-packing or layout is not detailed, but they are accessed as textures on the GPU. Rotation Representation: Due to memory constraints of storing 4x4 rotation matrices for ZH coefficients, alternative representations are considered: polar coordinates, unit vectors, or quaternions. Steps: 1. Vertex Shader: Pass the interpolated surface normal to define the local frame. 2. Pixel Shader - Rotation: Rotate the precomputed ZH transfer function to match the local surface frame defined by the normal. 3. Pixel Shader - Projection: Project the rotated ZH coefficients back into the SH basis. 4. Pixel Shader - Lighting: Project the current lighting environment into the SH basis (precomputed or updated per frame). 5. Pixel Shader - Dot Product: Compute the dot product between the projected transfer function (in SH) and the lighting environment (in SH) to determine the final lighting. Formulas: The rotation of ZH functions is required to align the precomputed transfer with the local surface frame. The exact mathematical formula for ZH rotation is not provided in the sources, but it is noted as being much faster than SH rotation. The projection from ZH back to SH is referenced as "equation 2.7" in the source, but the formula itself is not included in the provided text. The minimization method for projecting into ZH is referenced as "equation 2.10" in the source, but the formula itself is not included in the provided text. Parameters: SH Order: Not specified in the sources. ZH Order: Not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Rotation Representation Cost: Storing 4x4 rotation matrices for ZH coefficients is too costly in memory. Polar Coordinates: Using polar coordinates for rotation representation causes visual artifacts near the poles (drop angle 0 or \pi). Precision: Not specified in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexshader(position, normal): # Pass interpolated normal to pixel shader return normal def pixelshader(normal, zhcoefficientstexture, lightingshcoefficients): # 1. Define local frame from normal localframe = normal # 2. Rotate ZH coefficients to local frame # Note: Exact ZH rotation formula not provided in sources # Alternative representations (unit vectors, quaternions) are preferred over 4x4 matrices due to memory rotatedzh = rotatezhtolocalframe(zhcoefficientstexture, localframe) # 3. Project rotated ZH back to SH basis # Note: Exact projection formula (referenced as eq 2.7) not provided in sources shcoefficients = projectzhtosh(rotatedzh) # 4. Compute dot product with lighting environment (already in SH) # Note: Lighting environment projection into SH is assumed to be done elsewhere or per-frame finalcolor = dotproduct(shcoefficients, lightingshcoefficients) return finalcolor LDPRT is a variant of PRT that computes the transfer function of the local surface (in tangent space) rather than the entire entity, allowing for real-time deformation while capturing local effects like shadows from surface bumps. It is chosen when global illumination effects are not required, but real-time deformation is. Precomputation: Local light transport is precomputed per-vertex and projected into the SH basis. Storage: The SH coefficients are projected into the ZH basis using a minimization method (equation 2.10) and stored with the model. Runtime: The lighting environment is projected into the SH basis. The stored ZH vectors are projected back into SH (using equation 2.7) and evaluated with the lighting environment. Rotation: The local transfer function is rotated per-sample into global space before evaluation using fast ZH rotation, avoiding the expense of per-sample SH rotation. Time Complexity: Per-pixel rotation and projection are performed in the pixel shader. ZH rotation is noted as being much faster than SH rotation, making it feasible for real-time per-pixel computation. Memory Complexity: Storing 4x4 rotation matrices for ZH coefficients is too costly in memory, necessitating more efficient rotation representations (unit vectors, quaternions). Strengths: Enables real-time deformation; captures local effects like shadows from surface bumps; faster per-sample rotation than SH. Limitations: Does not capture global illumination effects; restrictive environment where deformation does not greatly affect light transport. When to Use: When real-time deformation is required and local surface effects (bumps, wrinkles) are important, but global illumination is not. When Not to Use: When global illumination effects are critical. This method is described in the context of a volumetric approach to rendering microgeometry using PRT, specifically referencing work by Joan et al. (2005) and the thesis of John Kloetzli. It builds on the concepts of regular PRT but adapts them for local surface transfer and real-time deformation.
