name: TF Simplification
head: Error-tolerance window algorithm for TF, TF Line Segment Reduction, Transfer Function Simplification Method, Window-based TF Approximation
body: TF Simplification reduces the number of line segments in a hand-drawn Transfer Function (TF) by approximating consecutive segments using a sliding error-tolerance window, thereby reducing computational overhead for ambient occlusion calculations. It distinguishes itself from general curve fitting by enforcing strict geometric constraints where simplified segments must pass through defined error windows around original vertices, specifically targeting noise from hand-drawn inputs. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A hand-drawn TF represented as a sequence of vertices (xi, yi) connected by line segments. Output: A simplified TF with fewer line segments that approximates the original within the error tolerance. Data Structures: Vertices: A list of points P = [(x0, y0), (x1, y1), \dots, (xn, yn)]. Windows: For each vertex Pi, an error tolerance window Wi is defined. The source does not specify the exact geometric shape of the window, so it is implemented as a vertical band [yi - w, yi + w] where w is the window size parameter. Pre-processing: 1. Apply a pre-filtering average filter with kernel size 5 to the input TF vertices to remove noise caused by hand tremors. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the starting point s to the first vertex P0. 2. Define the error tolerance window W{next} for the next vertex P{next} (initially P1). 3. Connect s to the window W{next} to determine the initial slope range [m{min}, m{max}] of the potential line segment. 4. Iterate through subsequent vertices Pi: a. Update the slope range [m{min}, m{max}] such that the line segment from s to Pi passes through the window Wi. This involves intersecting the current valid slope range with the slopes required to hit Wi. b. If the current slope range becomes empty (i.e., no line from s can pass through both previous windows and the current window Wi): i. Finalize the current simplified segment from s to the previous vertex P{i-1}. ii. Set s = P{i-1}. iii. Reset the slope range based on the new starting point s and the window Wi. 5. Finalize the last segment from the final s to the last vertex Pn. Parameters: Window Size: Controls the trade-off between speed and quality; larger windows reduce the number of line segments more aggressively but degrade image quality. Filter Kernel Size: 5. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def simplifytf(vertices, windowsize): """ Simplifies a transfer function using the error-tolerance window algorithm. Args: vertices: List of (x, y) tuples representing the hand-drawn TF. windowsize: Float defining the vertical tolerance band width around each vertex. Returns: List of (x, y) tuples representing the simplified TF control points. """ # Pre-filtering: average filter with kernel size 5 def applyaveragefilter(pts, k=5): n = len(pts) if n < k: return pts out = [] half = k // 2 for i in range(n): ysum = 0.0 count = 0 for j in range(max(0, i-half), min(n, i+half+1)): ysum += pts[j][1] count += 1 out.append((pts[i][0], ysum / count)) return out filtered = applyaveragefilter(vertices) if len(filtered) < 2: return filtered simplified = [] s = filtered[0] slopemin = float('-inf') slopemax = float('inf') n = len(filtered) for i in range(1, n): # Calculate slope range to window at i ycenter = filtered[i][1] yminw = ycenter - windowsize ymaxw = ycenter + windowsize dx = filtered[i][0] - s[0] if dx == 0: newmin, newmax = float('-inf'), float('inf') else: newmin = (yminw - s[1]) / dx newmax = (ymaxw - s[1]) / dx if newmin > newmax: newmin, newmax = newmax, newmin # Intersect ranges slopemin = max(slopemin, newmin) slopemax = min(slopemax, newmax) if slopemin > slopemax: # Range invalid, finalize segment simplified.append(s) # New start is previous vertex s = filtered[i-1] # Reset range slopemin = float('-inf') slopemax = float('inf') # Recalculate for new start and current i ycenter = filtered[i][1] yminw = ycenter - windowsize ymaxw = ycenter + windowsize dx = filtered[i][0] - s[0] if dx == 0: slopemin, slopemax = float('-inf'), float('inf') else: slopemin = (yminw - s[1]) / dx slopemax = (ymaxw - s[1]) / dx if slopemin > slopemax: slopemin, slopemax = slopemax, slopemin simplified.append(filtered[-1]) return simplified Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Window Size Degradation: Increasing the window size sharply reduces the number of line segments (stabilizing around size 10) but continues to degrade image quality. Hand Tremor Noise: Without pre-filtering, hand-drawn TFs may have unintentionally sharp graphs that increase segment count and reduce speed. Time Complexity: The computational cost is proportional to the number of line segments in the TF. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: On a PC with Intel Q9550 CPU, 4 GB RAM, and GeForce GTX 1050 GPU, the method enables real-time rendering with ambient occlusion by reducing calculation iterations. Strengths: Reduces noise from hand-drawn inputs, improves rendering speed, and produces visually comparable images. Limitations: Image quality degrades as window size increases, and the method assumes CT values follow a normal distribution, which may cause lighting differences in binary images. The method is based on the error-tolerance window algorithm by Hadwiger et al.. It was developed to handle hand-drawn Transfer Functions in real-time computed tomography volume visualization with ambient occlusion. name: Blurring a Step Function
head: Step Function Blurring
body: Blurring a Step Function is an algorithm that convolves a step function with a rectangular pulse to yield a piecewise linear spline. It operates directly on input arrays x and y representing the domain and range values of the step function. Inputs: x: Array of N domain values. y: Array of N range values. r: Scalar half-width of the rectangular pulse. Outputs: xr: Array of 2N sorted domain values defining the breakpoints of the resulting spline. yr: Array of 2N range values defining the piecewise linear spline at xr. Data Structures: Dense arrays of length N for inputs and length 2N for outputs. Parameters: r: Half-width of the rectangular pulse. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps: 1. Concatenate arrays [x - r, x + r] and sort them to obtain xr and sortidx (the indices of the sorted elements). 2. Compute intermediate slopes y' by subtracting shifted y arrays and dividing by 2r: y' = ([y, 0] - [0, y]) / (2r). 3. Compute y'' by concatenating [y', -y'] and reordering according to sortidx excluding the last element: y'' = \text{concatenate}([y', -y'])[\text{sortidx}[:-1]]. 4. Compute output yr by taking the cumulative sum of the product of interval lengths (xr[1:] - xr[:-1]) and the cumulative sum of y'': yr = [0, cumsum((xr[1:] - xr[:-1]) cumsum(y''))]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def concatenate(a, b): return a + b def sortwithindices(arr): indices = sorted(range(len(arr)), key=lambda i: arr[i]) return [arr[i] for i in indices], indices def cumsum(arr): result = [] s = 0.0 for v in arr: s += v result.append(s) return result def blurstepfun(x, y, r): # Step 1: Compute breakpoints and sort indices xshifted = concatenate([x - r, x + r]) xr, sortidx = sortwithindices(xshifted) # Step 2: Compute slopes y' yappended = concatenate([y, [0]]) yprepended = concatenate([[0], y]) yprime = [(ya - yp) / (2 r) for ya, yp in zip(yappended, yprepended)] # Step 3: Compute y'' ydouble = concatenate([yprime, [-v for v in yprime]]) ydoubleprime = [ydouble[i] for i in sortidx[:-1]] # Step 4: Compute yr dx = [xr[i+1] - xr[i] for i in range(len(xr) - 1)] cumydoubleprime = cumsum(ydoubleprime) weightedcum = [d c for d, c in zip(dx, cumydoubleprime)] cumweighted = cumsum(weightedcum) yr = [0.0] + cumweighted return xr, yr Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The algorithm requires r > 0 to avoid division by zero. If x is not sorted, the sorting step reorders the domain, but the step function definition implies monotonic x. Manages the optimization of control points x and y. Use when adjusting the shape of the transfer function dynamically. Resamples a step function to a different domain resolution. Use when changing the discretization of the input domain. name: Step Function Resampling
head: Inner/Outer Measures
body: Step Function Resampling constructs inner and outer measures on a step function to resample values defined by endpoints into new intervals. It solves the problem of aggregating piecewise-constant data (such as transfer function weights or probability mass) over arbitrary query ranges, providing both the exact sum (outer measure) and the guaranteed contained mass (inner measure). It preserves the discontinuous nature of the source data rather than interpolating between control points, unlike Piecewise Linear Interpolation (Lookup Table), and provides exact bounds rather than smoothed approximations, unlike Blurring a Step Function. Inputs: Source step function defined by endpoints tp (sorted, length N) and values vp (length N). Query points t0 (length M) defining new intervals. Boolean flag useavg: if True, computes weighted average; if False, computes sum. Optional parameters: minval, maxval for interval sampling bounds; eps for numerical stability. Outputs: Resampled values y0 (length M-1) corresponding to intervals defined by t0. If useavg is True, returns the average value over each interval. If useavg is False, returns the sum of the step function over each interval. Data Structures: Arrays tp, vp, t0 are 1D tensors of floating-point numbers. Cumulative sum arrays are padded with a leading zero to align indices with interval boundaries. Steps: 1. Compute Cumulative Sum: Compute the cumulative sum of the source values vp with a leading zero: cv = [0, v{p,0}, v{p,0} + v{p,1}, \dots, \sum{i=0}^{N-1} v{p,i}]. Let cv have length N+1. 2. Find Insertion Indices: Determine the indices of the query points t0 within the source endpoints tp: \text{idx\lo}, \text{idx\hi} = \text{searchsorted}(tp, t0). 3. Gather Cumulative Values: Gather cumulative values at indices: c{v,\text{lo}} = cv[\text{idx\lo}] and c{v,\text{hi}} = cv[\text{idx\hi}]. 4. Compute Outer Measure (Sum): The outer measure for the interval [t{0,i}, t{0,i+1}] is the total mass of the source step function that overlaps with this interval: y{0,i}^{\text{outer}} = c{v,\text{hi}}[i+1] - c{v,\text{lo}}[i] for i = 0, \dots, M-2. 5. Compute Inner Measure: The inner measure sums only the source bins fully contained within the query interval: y{0,i}^{\text{inner}} = c{v,\text{lo}}[i+1] - c{v,\text{hi}}[i] if \text{idx\hi}[i] \le \text{idx\lo}[i+1], else 0. 6. Average Mode (if useavg is True): To compute the weighted average, resample the weighted values vp \cdot wp and the widths wp separately using the sum mode (steps 1–5), then divide. Compute wp = tp[1:] - tp[:-1]. Compute v{\text{numer}} = \text{Resample}(tp, vp \cdot wp, t0) and v{\text{denom}} = \text{Resample}(tp, wp, t0). Result: y0 = \frac{v{\text{numer}}}{\max(\epsilon, v{\text{denom}})}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def stepfunctionresampling(tp, vp, t0, useavg=False, eps=1e-8): """ Resample a step function defined by endpoints tp and values vp into intervals defined by query points t0. Args: tp: Tensor of shape (N,), sorted source endpoints. vp: Tensor of shape (N,), source values. t0: Tensor of shape (M,), query points defining intervals [t0[i], t0[i+1]]. useavg: If True, return weighted average. If False, return sum. eps: Small value to prevent division by zero. Returns: y0: Tensor of shape (M-1,), resampled values. """ # Step 1: Compute cumulative sum with leading zero cy1 = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(tp[...,:1]), torch.cumsum(vp, dim=-1)], dim=-1) # Step 2: Find insertion indices (left for lo, right for hi to match outer/inner measure logic) idxlo = torch.searchsorted(tp, t0, side='left') idxhi = torch.searchsorted(tp, t0, side='right') # Step 3: Gather cumulative values cy1lo = torch.takealongdim(cy1, idxlo.unsqueeze(-1), dim=-1).squeeze(-1) cy1hi = torch.takealongdim(cy1, idxhi.unsqueeze(-1), dim=-1).squeeze(-1) # Step 4: Compute outer measure (sum) y0outer = cy1hi[..., 1:] - cy1lo[...,:-1] # Step 5: Compute inner measure condition = idxhi[...,:-1] <= idxlo[..., 1:] y0inner = torch.where(condition, cy1lo[..., 1:] - cy1hi[...,:-1], torch.zeroslike(idxlo[..., 1:])) if useavg: # Compute widths of source intervals wp = tp[1:] - tp[:-1] # Resample weighted values and widths using sum mode (inlined for self-containment) def resamplesum(tp, vp, t0): cy1w = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(tp[...,:1]), torch.cumsum(vp, dim=-1)], dim=-1) idxlow = torch.searchsorted(tp, t0, side='left') idxhiw = torch.searchsorted(tp, t0, side='right') cy1low = torch.takealongdim(cy1w, idxlow.unsqueeze(-1), dim=-1).squeeze(-1) cy1hiw = torch.takealongdim(cy1w, idxhiw.unsqueeze(-1), dim=-1).squeeze(-1) return cy1hiw[..., 1:] - cy1low[...,:-1] vnumer = resamplesum(tp, vp wp, t0) vdenom = resamplesum(tp, wp, t0) y0 = vnumer / torch.clamp(vdenom, min=eps) else: y0 = y0outer return y0 Parameters: eps: Small value to prevent division by zero when useavg=True. Default is torch.finfo(t.dtype).eps. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If numsamples (length of t0) is less than 2, no intervals can be formed. If source endpoints tp are not sorted, searchsorted behavior is undefined. If query points t0 are not sorted, the interval logic breaks. Division by zero in average mode if the denominator (total width of source bins covering the query interval) is zero. Handled by eps. Max Dilation is a resampling technique that expands the support of a non-negative step function or weight distribution via max-pooling, effectively smoothing or widening the distribution. It sets itself apart from CDF Integration from Weights by preserving the peak values of the original distribution rather than integrating mass, which makes it suitable for maintaining sharp features while adapting sample density. Computes the cumulative distribution function (CDF) from a set of discrete weights that sum to 1, treating them as a step function. It preserves the integral mass of the distribution rather than finding local extrema, and serves as the inverse operation to Weight-PDF Conversion. Samples intervals (rather than points) from a step function by reflecting midpoints around sampled centers. Steps: 1. Sample centers using sample(..., deterministiccenter=True). 2. Compute midpoints between adjacent centers: mid = (centers[..., 1:] + centers[...,:-1]) / 2. 3. Compute first fencepost by reflecting first midpoint around first center, clamped to minval: first = (2 \cdot centers[...,:1] - mid[...,:1]).clamp\min(minval). 4. Compute last fencepost by reflecting last midpoint around last center, clamped to maxval: last = (2 \cdot centers[..., -1:] - mid[..., -1:]).clamp\max(maxval). 5. Concatenate first, mid, and last: t{samples} = \text{torch.cat}([first, mid, last], dim=-1). Pitfall: Raises ValueError if numsamples <= 1. Approximates the step function using smooth sigmoid functions for differentiable rendering. Formulas: Gaussian approximation: x \mapsto \frac{1}{2} \left( 1 + \text{erf} \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} \right). Laplace approximation: x \mapsto \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} \exp(x) & \text{if } x \le 0 \\ 1 - \frac{1}{2} \exp(-x) & \text{if } x \ge 0 \end{cases}. Logistic approximation: x \mapsto \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-x)}. Parameters: Training batch size: 64. Total training steps: 250,000. Learning rate schedule: 10^{-4} for steps 0–150,000; 3 \cdot 10^{-5} for steps 150,001–250,000. Temperature parameter \tau: decreased by a factor of 0.3 after step 150,000. Time Complexity: O(N \log M) for searchsorted operations, where N is the number of source endpoints and M is the number of query points. The cumulative sum is O(N). The final aggregation is O(M). Memory Complexity: O(N + M) for storing cumulative sums and indices. Performance: The method is efficient for GPU implementation using PyTorch tensor operations. It is used in the context of differentiable rendering and 3D reconstruction to handle transfer functions and weight distributions efficiently. The soft Heaviside approximations are discussed in the context of GenDR (Generalized Differentiable Renderer) for training neural rendering models. name: Max Dilation
head: Max-Dilation of Step Functions
body: Max Dilation resamples a non-negative step function or weight distribution by expanding its support intervals via max-pooling, effectively smoothing or widening the distribution. It builds on Step Function Resampling by providing a specific weight transformation logic that prioritizes peak preservation over mass integration. Inputs: Original interval boundaries t (sorted, shape [N]). Weights w associated with intervals (ti, t{i+1}) (shape [N-1]). Dilation amount d \ge 0. Domain bounds [t{min}, t{max}] (optional, for clipping). Outputs: Dilated interval boundaries t{dilate} (sorted, shape [M]). Dilated weights w{dilate} (shape [M-1]). Data Structures: t: 1D tensor of boundaries. w: 1D tensor of weights, where wi corresponds to interval [ti, t{i+1}]. t{dilate}: 1D tensor of new boundaries. w{dilate}: 1D tensor of new weights. Steps: 1. Compute Expanded Boundaries: Calculate the expanded interval boundaries by shifting the original boundaries outward by the dilation amount: t0 = t[:-1] - d and t1 = t[1:] + d. 2. Sort Combined Endpoints: Concatenate the original boundaries t, the left-shifted boundaries t0, and the right-shifted boundaries t1, then sort them along the last axis to form t{dilate}. 3. Clip to Domain: Clip the dilated boundaries to the valid domain [t{min}, t{max}] to prevent out-of-bounds values. 4. Compute Dilated Weights: For each new boundary in t{dilate}, find the maximum weight from original intervals that cover it using a boolean mask: w{dilate, j} = \maxi (wi \cdot \mathbb{I}(t0[i] \le t{dilate, j} < t1[i])), then take the interval weights as w{dilate} = w{points}[:-1]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def maxdilate(t: torch.Tensor, w: torch.Tensor, dilation: float, domain: tuple = None) -> tuple: """ Dilates a step function defined by boundaries t and weights w. Args: t: Sorted boundaries of shape (N,) or (B, N) w: Weights of shape (N-1,) or (B, N-1), corresponding to intervals [t[i], t[i+1]] dilation: Non-negative dilation amount domain: Optional tuple (min, max) for clipping Returns: tdilate: Sorted dilated boundaries wdilate: Dilated weights """ # Step 1: Compute expanded boundaries t0 = t[...,:-1] - dilation t1 = t[..., 1:] + dilation # Step 2: Sort combined endpoints tcombined = torch.cat([t, t0, t1], dim=-1) tdilate, = torch.sort(tcombined, dim=-1) # Step 3: Clip to domain if domain is not None: tdilate = torch.clip(tdilate, min=domain[0], max=domain[1]) # Step 4: Compute dilated weights # Create boolean mask: True if dilated point j is covered by original interval i # t0[..., None,:] <= tdilate[..., None] compares (..., N-1, 1) with (..., 1, M) mask = (t0[..., None,:] <= tdilate[..., None]) & (t1[..., None,:] > tdilate[..., None]) # Replace non-covering weights with 0 so max ignores them maskedw = torch.where(mask, w[..., None,:], torch.zeroslike(w[..., None,:])) # Take max over original intervals for each dilated point wpoints = torch.max(maskedw, dim=-2)[0] # Interval weights correspond to points[...,:-1] wdilate = wpoints[...,:-1] return tdilate, wdilate def maxdilateweights(t: torch.Tensor, w: torch.Tensor, dilation: float, renormalize: bool = False, eps: float = None) -> torch.Tensor: """ Variant: Convert weights to PDF, dilate, convert back to weights. Args: t: Boundaries w: Weights dilation: Dilation amount renormalize: Whether to renormalize weights to sum to 1 eps: Numerical stability constant Returns: wdilate: Dilated weights """ if eps is None: eps = torch.finfo(w.dtype).eps 2 # Convert weights to PDF totalw = torch.sum(w, dim=-1, keepdim=True) p = w / torch.maximum(eps, totalw) # Dilate the PDF tdilate, pdilate = maxdilate(t, p, dilation) # Convert back to weights wdilate = pdilate torch.maximum(eps, totalw) # Optional renormalization if renormalize: wdilate = wdilate / torch.maximum(eps, torch.sum(wdilate, dim=-1, keepdim=True)) return wdilate Parameters: dilation: Non-negative float controlling the width of the expansion. domain: Optional tuple (min, max) for clipping dilated boundaries. renormalize: Boolean flag to renormalize dilated weights to sum to 1 after dilation. eps: Numerical stability constant for renormalization, default \text{torch.finfo}(\text{torch.float16}).\text{eps}^2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: When using floating-point arithmetic, boundary comparisons (t0 \le t{dilate} < t1) may suffer from precision issues. Degenerate Input: If t has fewer than 2 points, the method is undefined. Empty Intervals: If dilation is 0, the output should match the input. Performs max pooling with Morton coordinates on a 3D density grid. It sets itself apart from the 1D step function dilation by operating on 3D grids using Morton ordering for cache efficiency. Choose it when working with 3D density grids in neural rendering. Definition: Dilates a 3D density grid using Morton coordinates. Steps: 1. Ensure the grid is a contiguous CUDA tensor. 2. Calculate H = \sqrt[3]{H^3} (where H^3 is the total number of voxels). 3. Call the backend CUDA kernel backend.morton3Ddilation(grid, C, H, griddilation). Parameters: grid: Density values, float tensor of shape [C, H \times H \times H], assuming H \% 2 == 0. Layout: griddilation: Float tensor of shape [C, H \times H \times H]. Blurpool Resampling is a differentiable resampling method used in neural volume rendering to generate new sample positions (t values) along rays based on a learned or estimated weight distribution [Brief]. It solves the problem of adapting sample density to scene complexity by treating the sampling process as a differentiable operation on a discrete probability distribution [Brief]. It sets itself apart from Max Dilation by using average pooling on max-pooled weights to create a smoother, blurrier distribution, whereas Max Dilation uses only max-pooling [Brief]. It builds on Step Function Resampling by providing the specific weight transformation logic required before sampling [Brief]. Strengths: Preserves peak values of the original distribution. Limitations: Can introduce artifacts if dilation is too large relative to interval size. Not suitable for preserving mass conservation without renormalization. When to use: When you need to smooth a weight distribution while preserving its peaks, such as in adaptive sampling for volume rendering. When not to use: When mass conservation is critical and renormalization is not desired, or when sharp boundaries must be preserved exactly. Max Dilation was introduced in the context of neural volume rendering to adapt sample density to scene complexity. It is used in methods like InstantSplat and ER-NeRF for efficient resampling of weights. name: Blurpool Resampling
head: Resampling Along Rays
body: Blurpool Resampling generates new sample positions (t values) along rays from a weight distribution. It differs from Max Dilation by applying average pooling to max-pooled weights before sampling. The method transforms input weights associated with initial sample positions into a new set of sample positions. It operates on a piecewise constant probability density function (PDF) derived from the weights. Input Weights: Tensor of shape [batchsize, numsamples] representing the importance or probability mass of each initial sample. Input Parameters: resamplepadding: Float value added to the weights before normalization. stopgrad: Boolean flag to prevent backpropagation through the sampling process. Output tsamples: Tensor of shape [batchsize, numsamples + 1] containing the new sampled t values. Output Points: Tensor of shape [batchsize, numsamples, 3] containing the 3D coordinates corresponding to the new samples, derived via ray casting. The core data structure is the weight tensor. The algorithm assumes the weights define a discrete distribution over the initial sample indices. The output tsamples defines the boundaries of the new intervals, implying numsamples + 1 boundaries for numsamples intervals. 1. Padding: Pad the input weights tensor weights along the last dimension by concatenating the first element, the original weights, and the last element: weightspad = cat([weights[...,:1], weights, weights[..., -1:]], dim=-1). 2. Max Pooling: Compute the element-wise maximum of adjacent elements in weightspad: weightsmax = maximum(weightspad[...,:-1], weightspad[..., 1:]). 3. Blurpool: Compute the element-wise average of adjacent elements in weightsmax: weightsblur = 0.5 (weightsmax[...,:-1] + weightsmax[..., 1:]). 4. Add Padding: Add the resamplepadding scalar to weightsblur: weightsfinal = weightsblur + resamplepadding. 5. Sampling: Sample new t values from the normalized distribution defined by weightsfinal using a sorted piecewise constant PDF sampler: newtvals = sortedpiecewiseconstantpdf(tvals, weightsfinal, tvals.shape[-1], randomized). 6. Gradient Control: If stopgrad is true, wrap steps 1–5 in a no-gradient context (e.g., torch.nograd() or jax.lax.stopgradient). 7. Ray Casting: Cast rays using the new t values, ray origins, directions, radii, and rayshape to compute the mean positions and covariances: means, covs = castrays(newtvals, origins, directions, radii, rayshape, a, f, l). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def blurpoolresampling(weights, tvals, origins, directions, radii, rayshape, resamplepadding=1e-6, stopgrad=False, randomized=True, a=None, f=None, l=None): """ Resamples t-values along rays based on weights using blurpool technique. Args: weights: Tensor [batchsize, numsamples] tvals: Tensor [batchsize, numsamples + 1] origins: Tensor [batchsize, 3] directions: Tensor [batchsize, 3] radii: Tensor [batchsize] or scalar rayshape: String defining ray geometry resamplepadding: Float added to weights stopgrad: Boolean, if True, disable gradients randomized: Boolean, if True, use randomized sampling a, f, l: Additional ray parameters (exact usage not specified in sources) Returns: newtvals: Tensor [batchsize, numsamples + 1] means: Tensor [batchsize, numsamples, 3] covs: Tensor [batchsize, numsamples, 3, 3] """ if stopgrad: with torch.nograd(): return blurpoolcore(weights, tvals, origins, directions, radii, rayshape, resamplepadding, randomized, a, f, l) return blurpoolcore(weights, tvals, origins, directions, radii, rayshape, resamplepadding, randomized, a, f, l) def blurpoolcore(weights, tvals, origins, directions, radii, rayshape, resamplepadding, randomized, a, f, l): # Step 1: Pad weights with first and last elements along the last dimension weightspad = torch.cat([weights[...,:1], weights, weights[..., -1:]], dim=-1) # Step 2: Max pooling of adjacent elements weightsmax = torch.maximum(weightspad[...,:-1], weightspad[..., 1:]) # Step 3: Blurpool (average pooling) of adjacent elements weightsblur = 0.5 (weightsmax[...,:-1] + weightsmax[..., 1:]) # Step 4: Add padding weightsfinal = weightsblur + resamplepadding # Step 5: Sample new t values newtvals = samplepiecewiseconstant(tvals, weightsfinal, tvals.shape[-1], randomized) # Step 6: Cast rays means, covs = castrays(newtvals, origins, directions, radii, rayshape, a, f, l) return newtvals, (means, covs) def samplepiecewiseconstant(tvals, weights, numsamples, randomized): # Normalize weights to form a probability distribution probs = weights / weights.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True) # Compute cumulative distribution function cdf = torch.cumsum(probs, dim=-1) # Generate uniform samples u = torch.randlike(probs) if randomized else torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, probs.shape[-1], device=probs.device) # Inverse CDF sampling indices = torch.searchsorted(cdf, u, right=True) - 1 indices = torch.clamp(indices, 0, probs.shape[-1] - 1) # Linear interpolation within intervals batchidx = torch.arange(tvals.shape[0])[:, None] tlow = tvals[batchidx, indices] thigh = tvals[batchidx, indices + 1] plow = cdf[batchidx, indices] phigh = cdf[batchidx, indices + 1] denom = phigh - plow denom = torch.where(denom == 0, 1.0, denom) tnew = tlow + (u - plow) / denom (thigh - tlow) # Return boundaries: prepend first t, append last t to match [B, N+1] shape return torch.cat([tvals[...,:1], tnew, tvals[..., -1:]], dim=-1) def castrays(tvals, origins, directions, radii, rayshape, a, f, l): # Compute mean positions along rays means = origins[..., None,:] + tvals[...,:, None] directions[..., None,:] # Compute covariance based on ray shape and radii # Exact covariance formula for parameters a, f, l is not specified in sources if rayshape == "gaussian": r2 = radii[..., None, None] 2 covs = torch.zeros(means.shape[0], means.shape[1], 3, 3, device=means.device) covs[:,:, 0, 0] = r2 covs[:,:, 1, 1] = r2 else: covs = torch.zeros(means.shape[0], means.shape[1], 3, 3, device=means.device) return means, covs Zero Weights: If all weights are zero, normalization fails. The resamplepadding parameter is added to weights before normalization. Precision: Floating-point precision issues in cumulative sum and inverse CDF sampling can lead to incorrect sample positions. Use stable CDF computation. Boundary Conditions: The padding step handles boundaries by repeating the first and last weights, which affects the max and blurpool operations at the edges. Time Complexity: O(N) per ray, where N is the number of samples. The operations are element-wise tensor operations. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing intermediate tensors (weightspad, weightsmax, weightsblur). Strengths: Differentiable, allowing gradient-based optimization of sample positions. Smooths the weight distribution, potentially leading to more stable sampling. Limitations: The blurpool operation may oversmooth sharp peaks in the weight distribution, leading to less accurate sampling in high-detail regions compared to non-smoothed methods. When to Use: When differentiable sampling is required and a smooth weight distribution is beneficial. When Not to Use: When sharp, precise sampling is needed and differentiability is not required. Blurpool Resampling is used in neural volume rendering frameworks, specifically in implementations like AlexSheldrick/densityboundedrayweights and CPREgroup/CaSE-NeRF. It adapts the "blurpool" concept from image processing to ray sampling. The method was introduced in unofficial repositories as part of efforts to improve the stability and quality of NeRF training by adapting sample densities. name: CDF Integration from Weights
head: Weight Integration
body: Computes the cumulative distribution function (CDF) from a set of discrete weights that sum to 1, treating them as a step function. It preserves the integral mass of the distribution rather than finding local extrema, and serves as the inverse operation to Weight-PDF Conversion. Inputs: w: Tensor of weights. Assumed to sum to 1 along the last axis. Outputs: cw0: Tensor where cw0[..., 0] = 0 and cw0[..., -1] = 1. The size on the last dimension is one greater than the input size. Data Structures: The output is a tensor with the same shape as the input, except the last dimension is expanded by 1. Steps: 1. Compute the cumulative sum of all weights except the last one along the last axis: cw = \text{cumsum}(w[...,:-1], \text{axis}=-1) 2. Clamp the cumulative sum to a maximum value of 1 to prevent numerical overflow: cw = \min(cw, 1) 3. Prepend a tensor of zeros and append a tensor of ones to ensure the CDF starts exactly at 0 and ends exactly at 1: cw0 = \text{concatenate}([0, cw, 1], \text{axis}=-1) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cdfintegrationfromweights(w): # w: 2D list of weights. Assumes each row sums to 1. cw0rows = [] for row in w: # Step 1: Cumulative sum of all weights except the last one cw = [] acc = 0.0 for i in range(len(row) - 1): acc += row[i] cw.append(acc) # Step 2: Clamp to 1 to prevent numerical overflow cw = [min(val, 1.0) for val in cw] # Step 3: Prepend zeros and append ones cw0 = [0.0] + cw + [1.0] cw0rows.append(cw0) return cw0rows Parameters: w: Input tensor of weights assumed to sum to 1 along the last axis. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The function silently breaks if the input weights do not sum to 1 along the last axis. name: Weight-PDF Conversion
body: Weight-PDF Conversion transforms a vector of discrete weights that sum to 1 into a probability density function (PDF) that integrates to 1 over given spatial or temporal intervals, and vice versa. This method serves as the inverse operation to CDF Integration from Weights, bridging the gap between discrete sampling weights and continuous density representations required for accurate volume rendering classification. It is distinct from simple normalization by accounting for the variable width of the intervals defined by the boundaries t. Inputs and Outputs: w: A tensor of discrete weights with shape (, N) that sums to 1 along the last dimension. p: A tensor of PDF values with shape (, N) that integrates to 1 over the intervals. t: A tensor of interval boundaries with shape (, N+1) defining the endpoints of each interval. Data Structures: All inputs and outputs are dense tensors. The last dimension stores the N discrete values, while preceding dimensions support batched or multi-ray evaluation. The boundary tensor t always contains one more element than the weight or PDF tensor along the last dimension to define N intervals [ti, t{i+1}). Numbered Steps: 1. Compute the width of each interval using the boundary tensor t. 2. For weight-to-PDF conversion, divide each weight by its corresponding interval width, clamped to a stability constant. 3. For PDF-to-weight conversion, multiply each PDF value by its corresponding interval width. Formulas: Weight to PDF: pi = \frac{wi}{\max(\epsilon, t{i+1} - ti)}, where pi is the PDF value, wi is the weight, ti and t{i+1} are interval boundaries, and \epsilon is a numerical stability constant. PDF to Weight: wi = pi \cdot (t{i+1} - ti), where wi is the weight, pi is the PDF value, and ti, t{i+1} are interval boundaries. Parameters: eps: Numerical stability constant to prevent division by zero. Typically set to torch.finfo(torch.float16).eps2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def weighttopdf(w: torch.Tensor, t: torch.Tensor, eps: float = 1e-12) -> torch.Tensor: """ Convert weights summing to 1 into a PDF integrating to 1. Args: w: Weights tensor of shape (, N). t: Boundaries tensor of shape (, N+1). eps: Numerical stability constant. Returns: p: PDF tensor of shape (, N). """ dt = t[..., 1:] - t[...,:-1] dtclamped = torch.clampmin(dt, eps) p = w / dtclamped return p def pdftoweight(p: torch.Tensor, t: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Convert a PDF integrating to 1 into weights summing to 1. Args: p: PDF tensor of shape (, N). t: Boundaries tensor of shape (, N+1). Returns: w: Weights tensor of shape (, N). """ dt = t[..., 1:] - t[...,:-1] w = p dt return w Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero-width intervals: If t{i+1} = ti, the interval width is zero. Direct division results in infinity or NaN. Clamping with eps prevents this. Precision: When using low-precision types (e.g., float16), eps should be scaled appropriately (e.g., eps2) to maintain stability. Boundary Consistency: The input t must have one more element than w or p along the last dimension. Mismatched shapes will cause broadcasting errors or incorrect interval calculations. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of intervals/elements. The operation involves a single pass over the data to compute differences and element-wise multiplication/division. This variant extends weight-PDF conversion to multivariate scenarios where variables are statistically dependent. It distinguishes between "guiding variables" (which define the interval of interest, such as cloud density) and "following variables" (which are only important when guiding variables fall within a specific interval, such as vertical velocity). For following variables, the weighting function is constructed using the conditional probability density function of the following variable given that the guiding variable lies within a specific interval [B0, B1]. This approach assigns increased weight where the conditional PDF is high, reducing the relative importance of values outside the guiding variable's interval of interest. Quality improves with narrower intervals, similar to univariate cases. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of intervals/elements. The operation involves a single pass over the data to compute differences and element-wise multiplication/division. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the interval widths and the output tensor. Strengths: Simple, differentiable, and numerically stable with proper clamping. It correctly handles non-uniform sampling intervals, which is critical for accurate volume rendering where ray step sizes vary. Limitations: Requires accurate boundary information t. If boundaries are incorrect or missing, the conversion yields biased densities. When to use: When converting between discrete weight-based accumulation (common in ray marching) and continuous density fields for transfer function evaluation or optimization. When not to use: When intervals are uniform and fixed, simple normalization may suffice, though this method remains valid. The concept of converting between discrete weights and continuous PDFs is fundamental in statistical sampling and volume rendering. The specific formulation using interval widths for stability is documented in implementations such as densityboundedrayweights. The application of conditional PDFs for multivariate weighting in volume rendering contexts, particularly for level-of-detail selection in climate data, was introduced in work on histogram spectra for multivariate time-varying volume LOD selection. name: Target Value Configuration
head: Isovalue selection
body: Target Value Configuration is a user-driven method for defining volume rendering appearance by specifying discrete data values of interest (isosurfaces) along with their associated visual properties. It solves the problem of manually mapping scalar field data to color and opacity by allowing users to select specific "target" data values and assign them distinct RGB colors, allowable deviation windows, and maximum opacity levels. It differs from general transfer function editing (e.g., Transfer Function) by focusing on explicit iso-surface definition rather than continuous curve manipulation. It differs from Cubic Spline Transfer Function by using discrete target points with defined tolerance windows rather than smooth polynomial interpolation across the entire domain. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar volume dataset; user-specified parameters for up to five target values. Output: A classification configuration consisting of target data values, RGB color triplets, deviation windows, and maximum opacity values, which drives the rendering pipeline. Data Structures: These parameters are stored as a record; a separate record is maintained for each target value selected. Each record contains: 1. targetvalue: The scalar data value of interest. 2. color: An RGB triplet (r, g, b) where r, g, b \in [0.0, 1.0]. 3. deviation: The maximum allowable deviation from the targetvalue. 4. maxopacity: The maximum surface opacity for this target, ranging from 0.0 to 1.0. Parameters: Number of Targets: Up to five target data values can be selected simultaneously. RGB Triplets: Expressed as three real numbers in the range [0.0, 1.0]. They must be distinct for each target to avoid color ambiguity. Deviation Window: Defines the range [target\value - deviation, target\value + deviation] of values rendered for that target. Max Opacity: A scalar in [0.0, 1.0] controlling the transparency of the rendered surface. Algorithm Steps: 1. User Selection: The user selects up to five scalar data values from the volume as targets. 2. Color Assignment: For each target, the user assigns a unique RGB color triplet. Care must be taken to ensure triplets are distinct enough to prevent "color crossover," where surface highlighting variations cause different surfaces to appear identical. 3. Deviation Definition: The user defines an allowable value deviation (window) for each target. Samples near the center of the window (the target value) are rendered with higher opacity than samples near the window edges. 4. Opacity Setting: The user sets the maximum opacity for each target. An opacity of 0.0 renders the surface invisible. 5. Rendering: The renderer identifies samples within the deviation windows of the target values. The opacity of a sample s for a target t is determined by its proximity to t within the window, capped by the maxopacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class TargetConfig: targetvalue: float colorr: float # 0.0 to 1.0 colorg: float # 0.0 to 1.0 colorb: float # 0.0 to 1.0 deviation: float maxopacity: float # 0.0 to 1.0 def computesamplergba(samplevalue: float, targets: list) -> tuple: """Returns (r, g, b, a) for a single sample value.""" bestr, bestg, bestb, besta = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 for t in targets: dist = abs(samplevalue - t.targetvalue) if dist <= t.deviation: # Linear falloff from center to edge if t.deviation == 0.0: alpha = t.maxopacity if dist == 0.0 else 0.0 else: alpha = t.maxopacity (1.0 - dist / t.deviation) if alpha > besta: besta = alpha bestr, bestg, bestb = t.colorr, t.colorg, t.colorb return bestr, bestg, bestb, besta def raycast(origin, direction, stepsize, volumedata, bounds, targets): """Front-to-back volume rendering accumulation.""" outr, outg, outb, outa = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 t = 0.0 # Volume sampling and bounds checking not given in the sources while bounds.contains(origin + direction t) and outa < 1.0: sampleval = volumedata.sample(origin + direction t) r, g, b, a = computesamplergba(sampleval, targets) # Front-to-back compositing not given in the sources weight = a (1.0 - outa) outr += r weight outg += g weight outb += b weight outa += weight t += stepsize return outr, outg, outb, outa Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Identical RGB Triplets: Using the same RGB triplet for different target values causes surfaces to appear with the same color, leading to visual ambiguity. Color Crossover: RGB triplets must be distinct enough that variations in surface highlighting do not cause surfaces with different initial colors to appear identical. Zero Opacity: An opacity of 0.0 renders the surface invisible. Zero Deviation: A deviation of 0.0 requires a guard to avoid division by zero during opacity calculation. A specific interaction technique for Target Value Configuration where the user manually draws transfer function shapes and intervals while simultaneously inspecting the volume. The user draws opacity curves with the left mouse button and sets intervals of influence with the right mouse button. Colors are assigned via a picker, with the interval painted using linear interpolation centered on the selected color. Opacities in the interval are scaled via keyboard. A dual-domain approach uses a clipping plane to sweep the volume, displaying the slice as a gray-level image. As the mouse moves, the voxel value is shown, and a marker appears on the transfer function plot; clicking increases the opacity for that voxel value. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides explicit control over specific isosurfaces; intuitive for users who know the data values of interest; direct visual feedback via dual-domain interaction. Limitations: Limited to up to five targets; requires careful color selection to avoid ambiguity; less flexible for complex, non-isosurface features compared to continuous transfer functions. When to use: When the user wants to highlight specific, known scalar values (e.g., specific tissue types, fluid boundaries) and wants explicit control over their appearance. When not to use: When the data features are not well-defined by single scalar values or when more than five distinct features need to be highlighted. It is part of a broader effort to make volume rendering more accessible through user-friendly interfaces, including manual specification and dual-domain interaction techniques. name: Smoothstep Interpolation
head: Cubic Hermite Spline Interpolation (Smoothstep), Perlin Smoothstep, smoothstep
body: Smoothstep interpolation clamps and interpolates a scalar input x between two bounds edge0 and edge1 using a cubic Hermite spline. The function clips the normalized input to [0, 1] and evaluates a cubic polynomial. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar value x, a lower bound edge0, and an upper bound edge1. Output: A scalar value y \in [0, 1]. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required; the method operates on standard floating-point scalars. Steps: 1. Compute t = \text{clamp}((x - edge0) / (edge1 - edge0), 0.0, 1.0). 2. Return t^2(3.0 - 2.0 t). Formula: Let t be the normalized input: t = \text{clamp}\left(\frac{x - edge0}{edge1 - edge0}, 0.0, 1.0\right) The output y is: y = t^2 (3.0 - 2.0 t) where \text{clamp}(v, min, max) returns min if v < min, max if v > max, and v otherwise. Parameters: edge0: The lower bound of the transition interval. edge1: The upper bound of the transition interval. Typical values: Not given in the sources; they are tuned per transfer function segment. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If edge0 = edge1, division by zero occurs; implementers must guard against this, typically returning 0.0 or 1.0 based on x relative to edge0. Inputs x < edge0 result in y = 0.0 due to clamping. Inputs x > edge1 result in y = 1.0 due to clamping. Precision issues near boundaries are handled by the clamping step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x): # Guard against division by zero if edge0 == edge1: return 0.0 if x < edge0 else 1.0 # Normalize and clamp t = (x - edge0) / (edge1 - edge0) t = max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) # Apply cubic Hermite spline return t t (3.0 - 2.0 t) Time Complexity: O(1) per sample. Memory Complexity: O(1). Performance: The calculation involves a few arithmetic operations and is extremely fast. Strengths: Simple to implement, computationally cheap, provides smooth derivatives (C^1 continuity), and avoids ringing artifacts. Limitations: Cannot represent sharp transitions or discontinuities; the fixed curve shape limits flexibility compared to splines with adjustable control points. When to use: Ideal for general-purpose transfer functions where smoothness is desired but complex curve fitting is unnecessary. When not to use: When sharp edges or specific curvature control is required, use Cubic Spline Transfer Function. The smoothstep function was popularized by Ken Perlin in the context of procedural noise generation. It is a standard component in graphics programming libraries. In volume rendering, it maps scalar values to transfer function properties with smooth derivatives. name: Lookup Table Implementation
head: Post-Interpolation Transfer Function Lookup Table, vzParameterLookupTable
body: Lookup Table Implementation is the mechanism for mapping scalar volume data values to RGBA color and opacity properties using a one-dimensional lookup table (LUT) applied after texture interpolation in the imaging pipeline. It solves the problem of efficient, hardware-accelerated classification by storing pre-computed or dynamically generated appearance properties in a contiguous array, allowing the GPU to sample visual attributes via standard texture fetches. What sets it apart from direct function evaluation is that it decouples the mathematical definition of the transfer function from the rendering loop, relying on a discrete, power-of-two sized table that can be updated dynamically or uploaded as a texture resource. The core mechanism involves storing a 1D array of 4-component vectors (R, G, B, \alpha) where each entry corresponds to a normalized scalar value in the domain [0, 1]. Data Structure and Constraints Format: Entries are typically stored as interleaved 4-component vectors. Common formats include float4 (32-bit floats per component) or 8-bit integers (uint8t[4]). Hardware-specific implementations may use non-standard widths, such as 36-bit entries (8-bit RGB, 12-bit alpha). Size: The number of entries N must be a power of two (e.g., 256, 1024, 4096, 65536) to support hardware texture sampling and indexing. Layout: A contiguous 1D array where index i maps to the normalized coordinate x = i / (N-1) or x = (i + 0.5) / N depending on the binning scheme. Normalization and Sampling The input scalar value v is normalized to the domain [0, 1] using window/level parameters (x{min}, x{max}): x = \frac{v - x{min}}{x{max} - x{min}} Values outside [x{min}, x{max}] are clamped to [0, 1]. Two primary sampling methods are used: 1. Hardware Interpolation: The LUT is uploaded as a 1D texture with LINEAR filter mode and CLAMPTOEDGE wrap mode. The hardware interpolates between adjacent entries based on the normalized coordinate x. 2. Direct Lookup: The integer index is computed for nearest-neighbor sampling: idx = \text{clamp}(\lfloor x \cdot (N-1) \rfloor, 0, N-1) The value at table[idx] is returned. Opacity Correction In hardware pipelines, opacities may require correction to account for non-unit sample spacing \Delta. The opacity entry \alpha0 is computed as: \alpha0 = 1 - e^{-map[Ci] \Delta0} If the distance changes to \Deltak, opacity values must be corrected accordingly. Resource Management Upload: The LUT is uploaded to GPU memory as a 1D texture (e.g., GLTEXTURE1D or GLTEXTURE2D with height 1) or a Shader Storage Buffer Object (SSBO). Binding: Uniforms such as tfsize, tfwindowleft, and tfwindowwidth are set to define the domain and resolution for the shader. Updates: Modifications to dataPtr, dataType, or dataFormat trigger a reload of the table. A method that maps a single scalar data value directly to a color and opacity tuple using a static, pre-defined 1D LUT. It solves the problem of visualizing scalar field data with minimal user interaction and computational resources. Unlike gradient-based or texture-based transfer functions, it cannot differentiate between samples with the same scalar value but different local structure. Manages the lifecycle of a 1D opacity transfer function on the GPU, handling memory allocation, data validation, and binding to shader resources. It differs from Hardcoded Transfer Function by supporting dynamic updates and from 1D Transfer Function Generation and Sampling by focusing on the GPU upload and validation step rather than mathematical generation. A key feature is its optional integration of a Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) correction to support Discrete Density Accumulation (DDA) optimizations. Maps scalar volume data values to RGBA properties using a 1D LUT constructed from user-defined control points. It solves the problem of quantitative data visualization by assigning visual appearance to numerical voxel intensities. Unlike Parametric Function Generation which computes values analytically, this method performs a deterministic, per-voxel assignment based on a pre-computed 1D LUT. It builds on Lookup Table Implementation by defining the specific algorithm for constructing the LUT from control points and sampling it during rendering. Generates the color and opacity entries for a 1D LUT by applying a shading model (e.g., Phong) to the scalar field values. It solves the problem of mapping raw scalar data to visually meaningful RGBA values that account for lighting, material properties, and view orientation, rather than using static, pre-shaded colors. It differs from Hardcoded Transfer Function by computing values dynamically based on current scene parameters, and from UpdateOpacityTransferFunction by encompassing the full color/opacity computation rather than just opacity adjustments. A helper procedure that generates a cosine-shaped ramp table for smoothly attenuating density values. It is used to fade out density contributions based on distance from the center of a volume slab. Steps: 1. Loop i from 0 to RAMPSIZE-1. 2. Compute normalized distance: dist = i / (RAMP\SIZE - 1.0). 3. Compute ramp value: ramp[i] = (\cos(dist \cdot \pi) + 1.0) / 2.0. A method to map a set of input values X to output values Y using dot products, allowing evaluation on encrypted data without revealing the input value, solving the inability to use comparison operators in probabilistic PHE. Formula: V \cdot \tilde{l} = \tilde{y} where V is a Vandermonde matrix with rows \tilde{v}i = (1, xi^1, \dots, xi^{n-1}), \tilde{l} is the lookup vector, and \tilde{y} is the result vector. f(xi) = (1, xi^1, xi^2, \dots, xi^{n-1}) \cdot \tilde{l} = yi Parameters: V: A Vandermonde matrix used to ensure linear independence of vectors \tilde{v}i. Pitfalls: It is not possible to calculate the vector \tilde{v}i from an encrypted [xi] because it requires multiplying two encrypted numbers, which Paillier does not support. Storing vectors \tilde{v}i instead of scalars xi increases storage by a factor of n (e.g., 256 for 8-bit voxels), leading to impractical sizes (16TB for a 512^3 volume). The concept of using lookup tables for volume rendering classification originated with early hardware-accelerated volume rendering systems. The vzParameterLookupTable class, part of the SGI OpenGL Volumizer toolkit, formalized the interface for specifying these tables as one-dimensional textures applied in the imaging pipeline after texture interpolation. The interface required specifying width (power of two), data pointer, data type, and external format, allowing for shallow copying of data pointers and dynamic reloading upon modification. This approach enabled efficient post-interpolation transfer function application, becoming a standard technique in volumizer-based rendering pipelines. Chapter 4. name: Hardcoded Transfer Function
head: Fixed RGBA Array, Static 1D Lookup Table, 1D Transfer Function, 1D data-based TF, 1D data-based transfer function, 1dTF
body: The Hardcoded Transfer Function (HTF) is a classification method that maps scalar volume data values directly to color and opacity using a static, pre-defined 1D lookup table (LUT). It solves the problem of visualizing scalar fields by assigning RGBA values based solely on intensity, without considering spatial context or gradients. Unlike gradient-based or texture-based transfer functions, the HTF relies exclusively on the scalar value x, making it the simplest and most computationally efficient classification method. Its primary limitation is the inability to distinguish between different features that share the same scalar value but differ in their local structure or context. Inputs and Outputs Input: A scalar data value v (typically normalized to [0, 1] or mapped via window/level parameters). Output: A 4-component vector (R, G, B, \alpha) representing the color and opacity of the sample. Data Structures The transfer function is stored as a static 1D array of 4-component vectors. Format: Entries are interleaved 4-component vectors. Common formats include float4 (32-bit floats per component) or 8-bit integers (uint8t[4]). Hardware-specific implementations may use non-standard widths, such as 36-bit entries (8-bit RGB, 12-bit alpha). Size: The number of entries N is typically a power of two (e.g., 256, 1024, 4096) to support hardware texture sampling. Specific implementations may use fixed sizes like 4096 entries. Layout: A contiguous 1D array where index i maps to the normalized coordinate x = i / (N-1) or x = (i + 0.5) / N depending on the binning scheme. Algorithm 1. Normalization: The input scalar value v is normalized to the domain [0, 1] using window/level parameters (x{min}, x{max}): x = \frac{v - x{min}}{x{max} - x{min}} Values outside [x{min}, x{max}] are clamped to [0, 1]. 2. Lookup: The RGBA value is retrieved from the LUT. Two primary sampling methods are used: Hardware Interpolation: The LUT is uploaded as a 1D texture with LINEAR filter mode and CLAMPTOEDGE wrap mode. The hardware interpolates between adjacent entries based on x. Direct Lookup: The integer index is computed for nearest-neighbor sampling: idx = \text{clamp}(\lfloor x \cdot (N-1) \rfloor, 0, N-1) The value at table[idx] is returned. 3. Opacity Correction (Optional): In some hardware pipelines, opacities may require correction to account for non-unit sample spacing \Delta. If gradient modulation is enabled (e.g., Gmom=1), the alpha is modulated by a gradient LUT: \alpha = \text{GmLUT}[\text{Gradient}] \cdot \text{opacityLUT}[\text{sampleValue}] If Gmom=0, \alpha = \text{opacityLUT}[\text{sampleValue}]. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hardcodedtransferfunction(v, xmin, xmax, table, N): # 1. Normalize if xmax == xmin: x = 0.0 else: x = (v - xmin) / (xmax - xmin) # Clamp to [0, 1] x = max(0.0, min(1.0, x)) # 2. Direct Lookup (Nearest Neighbor) # Index calculation based on binning scheme x = i / (N-1) idx = int(x (N - 1)) idx = max(0, min(N - 1, idx)) # 3. Return RGBA return table[idx] def hardcodedtransferfunctionlinear(v, xmin, xmax, table, N): # 1. Normalize if xmax == xmin: x = 0.0 else: x = (v - xmin) / (xmax - xmin) # Clamp to [0, 1] x = max(0.0, min(1.0, x)) # 2. Linear Interpolation # Compute float index floatidx = x (N - 1) i0 = int(floor(floatidx)) i1 = min(i0 + 1, N - 1) t = floatidx - i0 # Interpolate c0 = table[i0] c1 = table[i1] r = lerp(c0.r, c1.r, t) g = lerp(c0.g, c1.g, t) b = lerp(c0.b, c1.b, t) a = lerp(c0.a, c1.a, t) return (r, g, b, a) Parameters x{min}, x{max}: Window/level bounds defining the scalar range mapped to [0, 1]. Typical values depend on the dataset (e.g., Hounsfield units for CT). N: LUT size. Typical values: 256, 1024, 4096. Gmom: Boolean flag for gradient modulation. If true, alpha is modulated by gradient magnitude. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Opacity values in hardcoded tables are often sparse (e.g., mostly 0.0 or 0.1). This can lead to aliasing or loss of detail if the LUT resolution is too low. Ambiguity: Features with identical scalar values but different visual importance (e.g., different tissues with similar density) cannot be distinguished. Boundary Conditions: Values outside [x{min}, x{max}] must be clamped to avoid out-of-bounds access. 2D Transfer Function Volume Rendering extends the 1D Lookup Table with Interpolation method by mapping both the scalar data value f and the local gradient magnitude |\nabla f| to color and opacity. It solves the problem of overlapping data-value intervals in 1D transfer functions, where different materials or boundaries share similar scalar values but differ in their local structure. By using gradient magnitude as a second dimension, it uniquely isolates material boundaries and homogeneous regions, providing superior tissue differentiation and boundary visualization compared to Hardcoded Transfer Function. The Tent Alpha Transfer Function is a hardcoded 1D RGBA transfer texture generation method for fluorescence microscopy data that maps 8-bit scalar values to color and opacity using a tent-shaped alpha curve and gamma corrections. It provides a parametric opacity profile centered on a user-defined peak value. It builds on the Hardcoded Transfer Function by defining the color and opacity as a static float array generated from a closed-form mathematical profile rather than a manually edited lookup table. A piecewise linear color mapping function that maps a value in [0,1] to a gradient from gray to dark gray to red to orange to yellow. Clamp: Input d to [0.0, 1.0]. Interpolation: If x < 0.25: lerp(gray, darkgray, x \cdot 4.0) If 0.25 \le x < 0.5: lerp(darkgray, red, x \cdot 4.0 - 1.0) If 0.5 \le x < 0.75: lerp(red, orange, x \cdot 4.0 - 2.0) If x \ge 0.75: lerp(orange, yellow, x \cdot 4.0 - 3.0) Colors: gray=(0.4, 0.4, 0.4), darkgray=(0.2, 0.2, 0.2), red=(1.0, 0.0, 0.0), orange=(1.0, 0.6, 0.0), yellow=(1.7, 1.3, 1.0). Note: components can exceed 1.0. Maps volume intensity to color and alpha using an exponential function for alpha and linear interpolation for color. Colors: high=(1.0, 1.0, 1.0), low=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0). Alpha: \alpha = \frac{e^{intensity} - 1}{e^1 - 1}. Color: C = intensity \cdot high + (1.0 - intensity) \cdot low. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample. The lookup is a direct array access or texture fetch. Memory Complexity: O(N), where N is the LUT size. Typically 256–4096 entries. Performance: Lowest computation power and memory usage among transfer function types. Strengths: High safety against misinterpretation due to simplicity; low user interaction required; fast rendering. Limitations: Cannot differentiate features with identical scalar values but different contexts (e.g., boundaries, textures). When to Use: Simple scalar fields where intensity is the primary discriminant; real-time applications with strict resource constraints. When Not to Use: Multi-channel data; scenes requiring differentiation of structures with similar intensities. The Hardcoded Transfer Function is the foundational method for volume rendering classification, originating from early ray-casting systems. It was prominently used in hardware-accelerated systems like VolumePro, which employed a 4096-entry, 36-bit classification LUT. The method is described in foundational surveys as the "1D data-based TF" (1dTF). name: 2D Transfer Function Volume Rendering
head: 2D TF Volume Rendering, Intensity-Gradient Transfer Function, Joint histogram transfer function, TF based on value and gradient magnitude
body: 2D Transfer Function Volume Rendering extends the 1D Lookup Table with Interpolation method by mapping both the scalar data value f and the local gradient magnitude |\nabla f| to color and opacity. It solves the problem of overlapping data-value intervals in 1D transfer functions, where different materials or boundaries share similar scalar values but differ in their local structure. By using gradient magnitude as a second dimension, it uniquely isolates material boundaries and homogeneous regions, providing superior tissue differentiation and boundary visualization compared to Hardcoded Transfer Function. Input: A 3D scalar volume V (e.g., medical CT/MRI data). Output: A rendered image with color and opacity determined by the 2D transfer function. 1. 2D Transfer Function Texture The transfer function is stored in a 2D texture for efficient GPU lookup. Dimensions: W \times H \times 1, where W is the intensity resolution and H is the gradient magnitude resolution. Common resolutions: 256×256, or 1024×512 for the renderer texture and 512×256 for the histogram. X-axis maps to normalized gradient magnitude g \in [0, 1]. Y-axis maps to normalized scalar data value v \in [0, 1]. Format: 4 components per texel (RGBA). R, G, B: Color channels. A: Opacity (Alpha) channel. Data Type: Floating point (e.g., VTKFLOAT) or normalized unsigned integer (e.g., eR8G8B8A8Unorm). 2. Joint Histogram (Optional Pre-computation) A 2D histogram of intensity vs. gradient magnitude can be computed to visualize the data distribution and guide TF design. Axes: Intensity (bins NI) and Gradient Magnitude (bins NG). Default Bins: NI=512, NG=256 for histogram; NI=1024, NG=512 for renderer texture. 1. Preprocessing (Optional): Load and orient the volume data (e.g., to LPS coordinate system). Compute the gradient magnitude for each voxel. Standard gradient computation requires 6 texture look-ups per sample (3 for each axis). Alternatively, precompute the gradient magnitude volume to reduce runtime look-ups to 2 (data + precomputed gradient). Note: Precomputation requires additional GPU memory and may reduce illumination smoothness. 2. Histogram Computation (Optional): Compute the 2D joint histogram of intensity and gradient magnitude using the volume data and precomputed gradients. Identify homogeneous regions as low-gradient clusters at the bottom of the histogram. Identify material boundaries as high-gradient arches between clusters. 3. Transfer Function Definition: Define color RGB and opacity \alpha mappings in the 2D domain (v, g). This can be done by: Drawing Regions of Interest (ROIs) on the 2D histogram. Using parametric formulas (see Formulas below). Modulating a 1D transfer function with gradient magnitude. 4. Texture Population: Initialize the 2D transfer function texture with RGBA values (0, 0, 0, 0). For each texel (x, y) corresponding to value v and gradient g: Compute opacity \alpha(v, g) and color RGB(v, g) based on the defined TF. Store the values in the texture. 5. Rendering: For each ray cast through the volume: Sample the scalar value v from the volume texture. Sample the gradient magnitude g from the gradient texture (or compute it on-the-fly). Normalize v and g to [0, 1]. Lookup the color and opacity from the 2D transfer function texture using (v, g) as coordinates. Composite the sample using standard volume rendering integration. Parametric Opacity (Simple Model): If using a parametric approach, opacity is computed as the product of value-based and gradient-based opacity: a{\text{value}} = \text{clamp}\left(\frac{v - v0}{v1 - v0}, 0, 1\right) a{\text{gradient}} = \text{clamp}\left(\frac{g - g0}{g1 - g0}, 0, 1\right) a = a{\text{value}} \cdot a{\text{gradient}} Where: v: Sampled voxel value, normalized to [0, 1]. g: Gradient magnitude, normalized to [0, 1]. v0, v1: Parameters defining the voxel value range for opacity. g0, g1: Parameters defining the gradient magnitude range for opacity. If not specified, a{\text{gradient}} = 1 (1D TF). Gradient Modulation (1D to 2D Extension): Alternatively, a 1D base opacity a{base} is modulated by gradient magnitude g: a = a{base} \cdot ((1.0 - \alpha) + \alpha \cdot g) Where: a{base}: Opacity sampled from the 1D transfer function based on v. \alpha: Gradient emphasis parameter, range [0.0, 1.0]. g: Normalized gradient magnitude. Gradient Magnitude: f' = \|\nabla f\| Where f is the scalar function representing the data. Gradient Emphasis (\alpha): Controls the weight of gradient magnitude in opacity modulation. Default: 0.7. 0.0: Disables modulation (pure 1D TF). 1.0: Fully modulates opacity by gradient. Value Range Parameters (v0, v1): Define the voxel value range. Typical values for 'Present' image: 0.071 to 1.0. Gradient Range Parameters (g0, g1): Define the gradient magnitude range. Not specified in some sources, defaulting to 1D behavior. Texture Resolution: Intensity bins: Default 1024 in renderer, 512 in histogram. Gradient bins: Default 512 in renderer, 256 in histogram. Lighting Parameters (if shading is enabled): Ambient: 0.4 Diffuse: 0.6 Specular: 0.3 Specular Power: 10.0. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compute2dtransferfunction(volumedata, binsintensity=1024, binsgradient=512, grademphasis=0.7): """ Computes a 2D transfer function texture from volume data. Args: volumedata: 3D list of lists of lists of scalar values. binsintensity: Resolution of the intensity axis. binsgradient: Resolution of the gradient axis. grademphasis: Weight of gradient magnitude in opacity modulation (0.0 to 1.0). Returns: tftexture: 2D list of lists of 4 floats (RGBA). """ import math def clamp(val, lo, hi): return max(lo, min(hi, val)) def sqrt(x): return x 0.5 # 1. Compute gradient magnitude using central differences depth = len(volumedata) height = len(volumedata[0]) width = len(volumedata[0][0]) gradientmagnitude = [[[0.0 for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for in range(depth)] for z in range(1, depth - 1): for y in range(1, height - 1): for x in range(1, width - 1): gx = (volumedata[z][y][x+1] - volumedata[z][y][x-1]) / 2.0 gy = (volumedata[z][y+1][x] - volumedata[z][y-1][x]) / 2.0 gz = (volumedata[z+1][y][x] - volumedata[z-1][y][x]) / 2.0 gradientmagnitude[z][y][x] = sqrt(gx2 + gy2 + gz2) # 2. Normalize data to [0, 1] vmin = min(min(min(row) for row in vol) for vol in volumedata) vmax = max(max(max(row) for row in vol) for vol in volumedata) gmin = min(min(min(row) for row in grad) for grad in gradientmagnitude) gmax = max(max(max(row) for row in grad) for grad in gradientmagnitude) vnorm = [[[(vol[z][y][x] - vmin) / max(vmax - vmin, 1e-8) for x in range(width)] for y in range(height)] for z in range(depth)] gnorm = [[[(grad[z][y][x] - gmin) / max(gmax - gmin, 1e-8) for x in range(width)] for y in range(height)] for z in range(depth)] # 3. Define 1D base opacity (example: linear ramp) def get1dopacity(v): return clamp((v - 0.2) / 0.6, 0.0, 1.0) # 4. Populate 2D Transfer Function Texture # Dimensions: (binsintensity, binsgradient, 4) tftexture = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(binsgradient)] for in range(binsintensity)] for i in range(binsintensity): v = i / max(binsintensity - 1, 1) baseopacity = get1dopacity(v) for j in range(binsgradient): g = j / max(binsgradient - 1, 1) # Apply gradient modulation finalopacity = baseopacity ((1.0 - grademphasis) + grademphasis g) # Set color (grayscale proportional to opacity) tftexture[i][j][0] = finalopacity tftexture[i][j][1] = finalopacity tftexture[i][j][2] = finalopacity tftexture[i][j][3] = finalopacity return tftexture def renderwith2dtf(volumedata, gradientdata, tftexture, binsintensity, binsgradient): """ Renders a volume using a 2D transfer function. Args: volumedata: 3D list of lists of lists of scalar values. gradientdata: 3D list of lists of lists of gradient magnitudes. tftexture: 2D list of lists of 4 floats (RGBA). binsintensity: Resolution of the intensity axis. binsgradient: Resolution of the gradient axis. Returns: image: 2D list of lists of 3 floats (RGB). """ import math def clamp(val, lo, hi): return max(lo, min(hi, val)) depth = len(volumedata) height = len(volumedata[0]) width = len(volumedata[0][0]) vmin = min(min(min(row) for row in vol) for vol in volumedata) vmax = max(max(max(row) for row in vol) for vol in volumedata) gmin = min(min(min(row) for row in grad) for grad in gradientdata) gmax = max(max(max(row) for row in grad) for grad in gradientdata) vnorm = [[[(vol[z][y][x] - vmin) / max(vmax - vmin, 1e-8) for x in range(width)] for y in range(height)] for z in range(depth)] gnorm = [[[(grad[z][y][x] - gmin) / max(gmax - gmin, 1e-8) for x in range(width)] for y in range(height)] for z in range(depth)] image = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alphaaccum = 0.0 for z in range(depth): v = vnorm[z][y][x] g = gnorm[z][y][x] # Map to texture coordinates # X-axis = gradient, Y-axis = intensity per source comment tx = int(clamp(g (binsgradient - 1), 0, binsgradient - 1)) ty = int(clamp(v (binsintensity - 1), 0, binsintensity - 1)) # Lookup color and opacity rgba = tftexture[ty][tx] c = rgba[:3] a = rgba[3] # Composite weight = a (1.0 - alphaaccum) color[0] += weight c[0] color[1] += weight c[1] color[2] += weight c[2] alphaaccum += weight if alphaaccum > 0.99: break image[y][x] = color return image Noise Sensitivity: The gradient metric is highly error-prone to noise. In very blurry volumes (e.g., PET-scans), it provides only marginal additional information compared to 1D TFs. Precomputation Trade-off: Precomputing the gradient reduces texture look-ups to 2 but requires additional GPU memory and may reduce the smoothness of illumination. Normalization: Voxel values and gradients must be normalized between 0 and 1 from their underlying representation when sampled. Boundary Conditions: Gradient computation at volume boundaries requires handling edge cases (e.g., zero-padding or clamping). Overlapping Values: If g0 and g1 are not specified, the transfer function defaults to 1D behavior (a{\text{gradient}} = 1). A method to generate final volume renderings by simultaneously using selected intensity-based and gradient-based transfer functions. It constructs visualizations by combining three intensity-based TFs (e.g., one preserving all tissue information, one intermediate, one emphasizing calcifications) with three gradient-based TFs (e.g., linear ramp, triangular-shaped centered on peak 2, triangular-shaped centered on peak 3), producing 9 distinct final renderings. This approach allows automatic generation of opacity/color TFs based on scalar intensity and gradient magnitude histograms, improving visualization of complex structures like those in digital breast tomosynthesis data. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels sampled per frame. Real-time capability is Yes. Memory Complexity: O(V + W \cdot H) where V is the volume size, and W \cdot H is the 2D TF texture size. Texture Look-ups: 7 per sample (1 for data + 6 for gradient components, which are also needed for illumination). If gradient is precomputed, 2 look-ups (data + precomputed gradient). Strengths: Resolves overlaps in data-value intervals by adding gradient magnitude as a second dimension. Allows isolation of boundaries that share similar scalar values. Better tissue differentiation and more intuitive volume design compared to 1D TFs. Limitations: Risk of misinterpretation: Moderate. No additional information in blurry datasets compared to 1D TF. Gradient metric is highly error-prone to noise. Requires more user interaction (1-2 minutes) and technical prior knowledge. When to Use: When materials have similar scalar values but different boundaries (e.g., distinguishing dentin from background). Medical CT/MRI datasets to separate materials such as air, soft tissue, and bone. When Not to Use: Very blurry volumes (e.g., PET-scans) where gradient information is unreliable. When real-time performance is critical and precomputed gradients are not feasible. Origin: Introduced by Levoy [Lev88]. Development: Further developed by Kindlmann and Durkin [KD98] and Koth et al. [KKH02]. Usage: Applied to medical CT/MRI datasets, such as the Chapel Hill CT Head dataset, to separate materials like air, soft tissue, and bone.
