name: Gradient/Color Ramp Sampling
head: Color Ramp Sampling, Gradient Texture Sampling
body: Gradient/Color Ramp Sampling is a method for generating a 2D color map (texture) from a set of key-value pairs defining color and opacity gradients, which is then sampled to map scalar data to RGBA values. It differs from direct 1D LUT interpolation by explicitly constructing a 2D texture where one axis represents the scalar value (mapped to color via a gradient) and the other axis often represents a secondary parameter like opacity or intensity, allowing for more complex visual mappings than simple 1D lookup. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of gradient stops (key-value pairs) defining color and optionally opacity/intensity curves. For the specific implementation cited, this involves a "sim data" channel laid out horizontally along the X-axis (color gradient) and a vertical Y-axis mapping (opacity/intensity). Output: A 2D texture (GradientTexture2D) containing the sampled color ramp. Data Structures: Gradient Stops: Defined by position (offset) and RGBA values. GradientTexture2D: A 2D texture resource. If usehdr is enabled, it may store channels above 1.0. Steps: 1. Define Gradient Stops: Specify the color and opacity/intensity values at specific offsets (0.0 to 1.0). 2. Construct 2D Texture: Map the scalar value to the X-axis. The color gradient remaps the sim data to fire color horizontally. Map the opacity/intensity to the Y-axis. In "Use Own Opacity" mode, this maps to fire opacity; otherwise, it maps to fire intensity. 3. Sample the Texture: Read the luminance in float format. Truncate each channel for the color ramp, as done in Godot's NoiseTexture2D implementation (color.h:106-108, image.cpp:3577-3580). Run the Gradient sampler and channelToByte in float, as per Gradient::getcoloratoffset and Color::getr8 (gradient.h:151-235, color.h:228). 4. Handle HDR: If usehdr is true, ensure channels above 1.0 are preserved in the output texture (gradienttexture.cpp:239-270). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def samplegradientramp(scalarvalue, opacityvalue, gradientstops, usehdr=False): # 1. Map scalar to X, opacity to Y x = clamp(scalarvalue, 0.0, 1.0) y = clamp(opacityvalue, 0.0, 1.0) # 2. Sample the 2D gradient texture # Note: In the cited implementation, the color is mapped horizontally (X) # and opacity/intensity vertically (Y). color = sample2dtexture(x, y, gradientstops) # 3. Process channels # Read luminance in float and truncate each channel r = truncatetobyte(color.r) g = truncatetobyte(color.g) b = truncatetobyte(color.b) a = truncatetobyte(color.a) # 4. Handle HDR if usehdr: # Keep channels above 1.0 if HDR is enabled # This step implies no truncation for HDR, or different handling pass else: # Standard truncation as per Godot's channelToByte r = channeltobyte(r) g = channeltobyte(g) b = channeltobyte(b) a = channeltobyte(a) return (r, g, b, a) def truncatetobyte(value): # Truncate float to byte range [0, 255] return int(clamp(value, 0.0, 1.0) 255) def channeltobyte(value): # As per Color::getr8 return int(clamp(value, 0.0, 1.0) 255) Parameters: usehdr: Boolean. If true, preserves channels > 1.0. Default: False. gradientstops: List of (offset, color, opacity) tuples. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Truncation can introduce quantization errors. Godot-measured ramp bytes off by one drop from 1212 to 0 of 2244 after fixing the ramp implementation. HDR: If usehdr is enabled, channels above 1.0 must be handled correctly to avoid clipping or incorrect display. Boundary Conditions: Ensure scalar and opacity values are clamped to [0.0, 1.0] before sampling to avoid out-of-bounds access. Remaps grid simulation data to render data. Sim data channel is laid out horizontally along the X axis. Color gradient remaps sim data to fire color. Curve remaps sim data to fire opacity (in Use Own Opacity mode) or fire intensity (otherwise). Opacity/intensity is mapped vertically on the Y axis. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, assuming constant-time texture lookup. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the 2D texture, where N is the texture resolution. Performance: The cited implementation shows significant error reduction after fixing the ramp (mean error 0.776/255 → 0.735/255 for noisetexture2d). Strengths: Allows for complex 2D mappings (color and opacity/intensity) in a single texture lookup. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of the 2D texture. HDR handling adds complexity. This method is used in Godot's rendering engine, specifically in NoiseTexture2D and GradientTexture2D nodes, to provide flexible color mapping for procedural textures and volumetric effects. feat(renderer): draw FogVolume and FogMaterial into the volumetric fog, https://github.com/Vortiago/textscene-inspector/pull/732, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Fire Color and Opacity Curves
head: Color Gradient, Intensity/Opacity Curve
body: Fire Color and Opacity Curves remap grid simulation data channels (such as Temperature or Fuel) into render-ready color and opacity values for fire visualization. It distinguishes itself from generic transfer functions by explicitly separating the color mapping (via a gradient) from the intensity/opacity mapping (via a curve), with specific modes for handling opacity relative to smoke. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A grid simulation data channel (e.g., Temperature, Fuel) laid out horizontally along the X-axis. Output: Final fire color (RGB) and opacity (alpha) or intensity values used in rendering. Data Structures: The method uses two primary controls, both defined by a set of points (xi, yi): 1. Color Gradient: Maps simulation value (x) to color (y). The x-axis represents the selected source channel value. The y-axis represents the color component. 2. Intensity/Opacity Curve: Maps simulation value (x) to a scalar value (y). The x-axis represents the selected source channel value. The y-axis represents either luminance (intensity) or opacity, depending on the mode. Parameters: emRampColort, emRampColors, emRampColorv, emRampColorf: Control the color of the light as a function of the selected channel's value. These correspond to the color gradient points. epowert, epowers, epowerv, epowerf: Control the scalar value of the curve. If Opacity Mode is Use Smoke Opacity or Fully Visible, these determine the luminance (intensity) of the emitted light. If Opacity Mode is Use Own Opacity, these determine the opacity of the emitted light. emMult: General multiplier for the fire color's intensity. emAlphaMult: Multiplier for the fire's own opacity. Used only when Opacity Mode is Use Own Opacity. Numbered Steps and Formulas: 1. Select Source Channel: Identify the grid simulation channel (e.g., Temperature) to base the mapping on. 2. Sample Gradient: For a given simulation value v, sample the Color Gradient to get a base color C{base}. The gradient points define the mapping from v to RGB. 3. Sample Curve: For the same value v, sample the Intensity/Opacity Curve to get a scalar factor S. If Opacity Mode is Use Smoke Opacity or Fully Visible: S is the intensity multiplier. If Opacity Mode is Use Own Opacity: S is the base opacity. 4. Apply Color Multiplier: Calculate the final fire color C{final}: C{final} = C{base} \times emMult 5. Apply Opacity/Intensity: Case A: Use Smoke Opacity or Fully Visible The fire's opacity is determined by the smoke (external). The fire contributes color with intensity S. Color{render} = C{final} \times S Alpha{render} = Alpha{smoke} Case B: Use Own Opacity The fire's opacity is determined by the curve S. Alpha{final} = S \times emAlphaMult Color{render} = C{final} (Note: The final alpha is clamped to [0, 1]). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Data Range Highlight: The selected channel's data range is highlighted in light blue on the curve controls. Values outside this range may behave unpredictably if extrapolation is not defined. Mode Dependency: The interpretation of epower points changes based on the Opacity Mode. Using epower for intensity when "Use Own Opacity" is selected will incorrectly set opacity instead of brightness. Multiplier Interaction: emMult affects color intensity, while emAlphaMult affects opacity only in "Use Own Opacity" mode. A control that maps simulation values to RGB colors. It sets apart from the curve by outputting a vector (color) rather than a scalar. Choose it when you need to define the visual hue and brightness distribution of the fire based on simulation data. Gradient/Color Ramp Sampling A control that maps simulation values to a scalar. It differs from the gradient by outputting a single value used for either luminance or alpha. Choose it to control how "bright" or "transparent" the fire appears at different simulation densities. Gradient/Color Ramp Sampling Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use/not: Not given in the sources. This method originates from the Phoenix for Maya plugin by Chaos Group. It is part of the Voxel Shader system, specifically designed to bridge the gap between fluid/grid simulation data and the final rendered image. The terminology (emRampColor, epower) reflects the internal API of the Phoenix software. Voxel Shader - Phoenix for Maya, https://documentation.chaos.com/space/PHX4MAYA/125768009, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Color Blending
head: Linear Color Interpolation, Linear RGB Blending
body: Color Blending linearly interpolates between two RGBA color values based on a scalar ratio, handling the red, green, blue, and alpha channels separately. It serves as the atomic step for mapping scalar voxel data to visible colors in volume rendering, ensuring smooth transitions between material properties defined by transfer functions. Unlike advanced techniques that account for opacity weighting or physical density, this method treats color channels independently and linearly. Inputs and Outputs Input 1: Color C1 (RGBA), a 4-component vector. Input 2: Color C2 (RGBA), a 4-component vector. Input 3: Ratio r (float), a scalar in [0, 1] representing the interpolation weight. Output: Color C{result} (RGBA), a 4-component vector. Data Structures Colors are represented as 4-element arrays or vectors. In standard implementations, these are often stored as 8-bit unsigned integers per channel (0–255) or normalized floats (0.0–1.0). The algorithm assumes the input format matches the output format. Exact bit packing layouts are Not given in the sources. Steps 1. Extract the Red, Green, Blue, and Alpha components from C1 and C2. 2. For each color channel c \in \{R, G, B\}, compute the linear interpolation: c{result} = \text{round}(c1 \cdot (1 - r) + c2 \cdot r). 3. Set the Alpha component of the result directly from C1: \alpha{result} = \alpha1. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def colorblend(c1: tuple, c2: tuple, ratio: float) -> tuple: """ Linearly interpolates between two RGBA colors based on a scalar ratio. c1, c2: tuples of (R, G, B, A) values. ratio: float in [0.0, 1.0]. Returns: tuple (R, G, B, A). """ # Interpolate RGB channels using the standard formula rres = round(c1[0] (1.0 - ratio) + c2[0] ratio) gres = round(c1[1] (1.0 - ratio) + c2[1] ratio) bres = round(c1[2] (1.0 - ratio) + c2[2] ratio) # Alpha is taken directly from the first color ares = c1[3] return (rres, gres, bres, ares) Parameters Ratio (r): Typically determined by the fractional distance between the ray origin and the sample point within the voxel, or the interpolation weight between two transfer function keys. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: When using integer arithmetic, rounding errors can accumulate during repeated interpolations. Boundary Conditions: If r is outside [0, 1], the interpolation becomes extrapolation, which may produce colors outside the defined range if not clamped. SVT Animation Interpolation is a technique used to smooth the playback of animated Sparse Volume Textures (SVTs) by blending between two adjacent frames using a scalar alpha value. It applies the core color blending logic to temporal data, ensuring smooth transitions between discrete animation frames. Opacity Weighted Color Interpolation is a technique used during the resampling phase of volume rendering to calculate the material color at a specific point within a voxel. It solves the problem of "color bleeding" or interface confusion that occurs when color and opacity are interpolated independently, particularly at boundaries between materials with differing opacities. Unlike standard trilinear interpolation which treats color and opacity as separate vectors, this method multiplies each vertex's color by its opacity before interpolation, ensuring that transparent regions do not incorrectly influence the color of opaque neighbors. A mechanism to preserve sharpness when the average method causes object blur due to large differences between C1 and C2, by replacing the voxel's colour with that of a neighbouring voxel from a 'clear group'. Steps: 1. Set defined colours into a blur group if the difference of C1 and C2 is more than a particular threshold. 2. Set defined colours into a clear group if the difference of C1 and C2 is less than or equal the threshold. 3. Replace colour C{old} of the voxel in the blur group by colour of neighbouring voxel that has the closest value to C{old} and has to be in the clear group. An improvement to color blending where the blending function is based on the physical density of the medium integrated along the camera ray, rather than an empirical function of distance. Formula: The blending function b' is defined as the integral of density \varrho along the ray: b'(\mathbf{x}{2D}) = \int{\text{camera}}^{\text{pixel } \mathbf{x}} \varrho(\mathbf{x}') \, d\mathbf{x}'. Pitfall: The values of b' are not in [0, 1], so the equation must be normalized by a certain maximum density before use in the blending formula. Blends between multiple transfer functions by interpolating a floating-point index, wrapping around if it exceeds the number of functions. Steps: 1. Get current transfer function index from mapper. 2. Add step value. 3. If index \ge nrfunctions, wrap using index = index - floor(index). 4. Set new index as float. Parameter: blendperframe: Controls transition speed. Scaled as 0.01 \times \text{speed}. Applied per frame to index. Pitfall: Index wrapping uses floor() to handle fractional overshoot correctly, ensuring smooth cycling through functions. An optional constraint to preserve original primitive color while allowing learnable variation, controlled by hyperparameter \mu{blend}. Formula: \mathbf{c}i = \mu{\text{blend}} \mathbf{c}i^{\text{org}} + (1 - \mu{\text{blend}}) \mathbf{c}i^{\text{var}}. Where \mathbf{c}i^{\text{org}} is original color, \mathbf{c}i^{\text{var}} is learnable color, and \mu{\text{blend}} \in [0,1] is the hyperparameter. Parameter: \mu{\text{blend}}: ratio defining blend between original and learnable color. Default is 0. Value 1 uses original colors. Computes the selected transfer function color by interpolating between white, black, and a base color based on 2D picker coordinates. Steps: 1. Compute normalized picker coordinates: tw = \text{currentColorPickerPos.x} / \text{MAXWPC}, th = (\text{currentColorPickerPos.y} - \text{MINHPC}) / (\text{MAXHPC} - \text{MINHPC}). 2. Interpolate between white and the current color along the x-axis: \text{colorW} = \text{whiteColor} \cdot (1.0 - tw) + \text{copyCurrentColor} \cdot tw. 3. Interpolate between colorW and black along the y-axis: \text{colorList}[\text{pointSelected} - 1] = \text{colorW} \cdot (1.0 - th) + \text{blackColor} \cdot th. 4. Set alpha based on y-position: \alpha = 1.0 - ((\text{pointList}[\text{pointSelected} - 1].y - \text{MINH}) / (\text{MAXH} - \text{MINH})). Assign to \text{colorList}[\text{pointSelected} - 1].w. Parameter: \text{MAXWPC} = 360, \text{MINWPC} = 0, \text{MAXHPC} = 448, \text{MINHPC} = 241 (picker coordinate bounds). Parameter: \text{whiteColor} = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0), \text{blackColor} = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0). Time Complexity: O(1) per color blend operation. It involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations (multiplications, additions, rounding). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. Strengths: Extremely fast, simple to implement, and computationally inexpensive. It provides smooth visual transitions for continuous scalar fields. Limitations: Does not account for opacity interactions (leading to color bleeding at material boundaries) or physical light transport properties. It is purely a geometric interpolation of color values. When to use: Standard volume rendering with transfer functions where materials have similar opacities or where performance is critical and advanced blending is not required. When not to use: When rendering interfaces between materials with significantly different opacities (use Opacity Weighted Color Interpolation) or when physically accurate light transport is needed (use Density-based Blending). Color Blending is a foundational technique in computer graphics, originating from basic linear interpolation methods used in texture mapping and color theory. In the context of volume rendering, it is the standard method for sampling 1D transfer functions, which map scalar voxel values to RGBA colors. The specific implementation described here, which fixes alpha to the first color, is noted in open-source implementations such as the quadtree-raycast project. Variations such as density-based blending have been proposed to address the limitations of empirical blending functions in participating media. name: SVT Animation Interpolation
head: SVT Frame Interpolation
body: SVT Animation Interpolation is a technique used to smooth the playback of animated Sparse Volume Textures (SVTs) by blending between two adjacent frames using a scalar alpha value. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Two adjacent SVT frame textures (current and next), a scalar interpolation value \alpha \in [0, 1], and the SVT Controller instance. Outputs: A single blended SVT frame texture rendered in the material graph. Data Structures: The method relies on the Animated Sparse Volume Texture Controller exposed via the SVT Blueprint. The controller manages the internal state of the SVT, including frame indexing and timing. The material graph utilizes standard scalar parameters and texture sample parameters to interface with the controller. Steps: 1. Retrieve Frames and Alpha: Call the Get Current Frames For Interpolation function on the SVT Controller to retrieve the two closest frames and a scalar value \alpha between 0 and 1. 2. Setup Material Parameters: Create two SVT texture parameters in the material graph for the retrieved frames, and one scalar parameter for the interpolation alpha. 3. Interpolate: Use an Interpolation node in the Material Graph to blend between the two frame textures using the alpha value. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendersvtinterpolatedframe(controller, materialgraph): # Step 1: Retrieve the two adjacent frames and the interpolation alpha framecurrent, framenext, alpha = controller.getcurrentframesforinterpolation() # Step 2: Setup material parameters # Bind framecurrent to the first SVT texture parameter # Bind framenext to the second SVT texture parameter # Bind alpha to the scalar interpolation parameter # Step 3: Perform interpolation in the material graph # The Interpolation node computes the weighted average of the two frames blendedframe = materialgraph.interpolationnode( a=framecurrent, b=framenext, alpha=alpha) return blendedframe Parameters: Alpha (\alpha): A scalar value between 0 and 1, where 0 represents the current frame and 1 represents the next frame. Frame Rate: Configured via the Frame Rate property of the controller, with a default of 24 fps. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision and Streaming: Real-time playback performance depends heavily on resolution and sparseness; if data streaming is too slow, rendering falls back to coarser mip levels, causing visible fidelity drops. SVT Sequencer Control extends the animated SVT Blueprint to allow playback control via Unreal Engine Sequencer by exposing an animation alpha variable to cinematics. It is chosen when precise, keyframe-driven animation control is required in a cinematic context, rather than real-time event-driven playback. Steps: 1. Expose Variable: In the animated SVT Blueprint, add a Fraction node and promote its A input to a variable named Animation Alpha. 2. Connect to Controller: Get the Controller variable, add a Get Duration node, and connect Event Tick execution to Get Duration. 3. Set Time: Add a Set Time node (from the Animated Sparse Volume Texture Controller category) and connect the Controller to the Target pin. 4. Calculate Time: Multiply the Get Duration return value by the Animation Alpha variable, and connect the result to the Time input of the Set Time node. 5. Expose to Cinematics: In the Details panel for the Animation Alpha variable, check "Expose to Cinematics". 6. Sequencer Integration: Add a Track to Sequencer for the Blueprint and key the AnimationAlpha variable in the Sequencer panel to control playback. Time Complexity: Real-time playback performance is not strictly defined by algorithmic complexity but by I/O streaming performance, depending on resolution and sparseness. Memory/Streaming: If volume data takes too long to stream in, rendering falls back to coarser mip levels, causing a visible drop in fidelity. Optimization: Using a smaller pixel format when importing a VDB improves streaming performance. Strengths: Provides smooth temporal interpolation for animated volumes and integrates with Sequencer for cinematic control. Limitations: Performance is sensitive to data size and sparseness, with fallback to lower mip levels degrading visual quality. SVT Animation Interpolation is part of the Sparse Volume Textures feature set in Unreal Engine 5.8, developed by Epic Games. It builds upon the Animated Sparse Volume Texture Blueprint system, which allows for real-time playback of animated VDB data. The technique is analogous to skeletal mesh animation control via Sequencer, adapting that workflow for volumetric data. Sparse Volume Textures in Unreal Engine | Unreal Engine 5.8... - Epic Dev, https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/sparse-volume-textures-in-unreal-engine, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Opacity Weighted Color Interpolation
head: Color Calculation at Resampling Points, Opacity-Weighted Trilinear Color Interpolation, Opacity-weighted voxel color interpolation, Trilinear Opacity-Weighted Color Interpolation
body: Opacity Weighted Color Interpolation is a technique used during the resampling phase of volume rendering to calculate the material color at a specific point within a voxel. It solves the problem of "color bleeding" or interface confusion that occurs when color and opacity are interpolated independently, particularly at boundaries between materials with differing opacities. Unlike standard trilinear interpolation which treats color and opacity as separate vectors, this method multiplies each vertex's color by its opacity before interpolation, ensuring that transparent regions do not incorrectly influence the color of opaque neighbors. Inputs: Scalar field values at the 8 vertices of a voxel. Color Transfer Function (CTF) mapping scalar values to RGB colors. Opacity Transfer Function (OTF) mapping scalar values to opacity \alpha. Lighting model parameters (e.g., Blinn-Phong coefficients). Outputs: Weighted material color \tilde{C}m(S) at the resampling point S. Opacity \alpha(S) at the resampling point S (interpolated via standard trilinear interpolation of raw opacities). Data Structures: Voxel vertices: 8 points, each storing a scalar value vj (j=1..8). Vertex attributes: Material color Cm(S)j: RGB vector computed via CTF and lighting model. Opacity \alphaj: Scalar value computed via OTF. Trilinear interpolation weights: Determined by the resampling point's position within the voxel. Steps: 1. Vertex Color and Opacity Calculation: For each of the 8 voxel vertices j, compute the material color Cm(S)j and opacity \alphaj using the respective transfer functions and lighting model. The material color Cm(S)j is derived from the scalar value at vertex j using the CTF and a lighting model (e.g., Blinn-Phong). The opacity \alphaj is derived from the scalar value at vertex j using the OTF. 2. Opacity Weighting: For each vertex j, compute the weighted color \tilde{C}j by multiplying the material color by the opacity: \tilde{C}j = \alphaj Cm(S)j This step ensures that transparent vertices contribute less to the interpolated color, preventing "bleeding" from transparent regions into opaque ones. 3. Trilinear Interpolation: Compute the final weighted material color \tilde{C}m(S) at the resampling point S by performing trilinear interpolation on the weighted colors \tilde{C}j of the 8 vertices: \tilde{C}m(S) = f{\text{Trilinear}}(\alphaj Cm(S)j) where j=1..8. 4. Final Color Composition: The final color at the resampling point is typically composed using the interpolated opacity \alpha(S) and the weighted color \tilde{C}m(S) in the volume rendering equation (e.g., Eq. 11 in), often involving accumulation along the ray. The opacity \alpha(S) is computed via standard trilinear interpolation of the raw opacities \alphaj. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def opacityweightedcolorinterpolation(voxelvertices, scalarvalues, ctf, otf, lightingmodel, u, v, w): """ Calculate the weighted material color at a resampling point within a voxel. Args: voxelvertices: List of 8 3D coordinates defining the voxel corners. scalarvalues: List of 8 scalar values at the voxel corners. ctf: Function mapping scalar value to RGB color vector. otf: Function mapping scalar value to opacity scalar. lightingmodel: Function computing reflected light color given normal, view, light vectors, and base color. u, v, w: Fractional coordinates of the resampling point in [0, 1]. Returns: weightedcolor: RGB vector representing the opacity-weighted color at the resampling point. interpolatedopacity: Scalar opacity at the resampling point. """ # Step 1: Calculate vertex colors and opacities vertexcolors = [] vertexopacities = [] for i in range(8): s = scalarvalues[i] # Calculate material color using CTF and lighting model # Lighting model calculation (e.g., Blinn-Phong) depends on normal, view, and light vectors basecolor = ctf(s) materialcolor = lightingmodel(basecolor, normal, viewdir, lightdir) # Lighting specifics not provided in sources # Calculate opacity using OTF opacity = otf(s) vertexcolors.append(materialcolor) vertexopacities.append(opacity) # Step 2: Apply opacity weighting to vertex colors weightedvertexcolors = [] for i in range(8): # Multiply color by opacity weightedcolor = vertexopacities[i] vertexcolors[i] weightedvertexcolors.append(weightedcolor) # Step 3: Trilinear interpolation of weighted colors weightedcolor = trilinearinterpolate(weightedvertexcolors, u, v, w) # Step 4: Trilinear interpolation of raw opacities (for final compositing) interpolatedopacity = trilinearinterpolate(vertexopacities, u, v, w) return weightedcolor, interpolatedopacity def trilinearinterpolate(values, u, v, w): """ Perform trilinear interpolation on 8 values. values: List of 8 values (RGB vectors or scalars). u, v, w: Fractional coordinates in [0, 1]. """ # Interpolate along x-axis c000 = values[0] c100 = values[1] c010 = values[2] c110 = values[3] c001 = values[4] c101 = values[5] c011 = values[6] c111 = values[7] # Linear interpolation along x c00 = c000 (1 - u) + c100 u c01 = c010 (1 - u) + c110 u c10 = c001 (1 - u) + c101 u c11 = c011 (1 - u) + c111 u # Linear interpolation along y c0 = c00 (1 - v) + c01 v c1 = c10 (1 - v) + c11 v # Linear interpolation along z result = c0 (1 - w) + c1 w return result Parameters: Trilinear interpolation weights: Determined by the resampling point's position within the voxel. CTF/OTF: User-defined or automatically generated transfer functions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Color Bleeding: Independent interpolation of color and opacity causes color bleeding, where transparent regions incorrectly influence opaque neighbors (e.g., bone classified opaque white surrounded by transparent red flesh results in incorrect blended colors). Interface Confusion: Without opacity weighting, interfaces between materials with different colors and opacities can produce intermediate colors that do not correspond to any actual material (e.g., orange at a red/green interface). Darkening Artifacts: Independent interpolation can also lead to darkening artifacts in volumetric datasets. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method reduces image entropy, indicating a reduction in visual "chaos" and interface confusion. In tests, image entropy was reduced from 3.25 to 2.79 (14.15% reduction) in Group A (plate-like entities) and from 1.76 to 1.66 (5.68% reduction) in Group B (jet invasion). Strengths: Prevents color bleeding and interface confusion, leading to more physically plausible and visually clear results. Limitations: Requires accurate computation of vertex colors and opacities. The effectiveness depends on the quality of the transfer functions and lighting model. Opacity Weighted Color Interpolation was introduced to address limitations in standard volume rendering techniques where color and opacity are interpolated separately. It is based on the principle that color should be weighted by opacity before interpolation to prevent transparent regions from affecting the color of opaque regions. The technique has been applied to explosion field data visualization to improve material interface clarity. A volume rendering visualization method oriented to explosion field features, https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0226283, fetched 2026-10-26 Volume Visualization and Volume Rendering Techniques, https://www.cs.unh.edu/~cs880/visualization/Meissner-VolRenderingEGTutorial-rdb.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Parametric Function Generation
body: Parametric Function Generation constructs transfer functions by evaluating mathematical functions of a normalized scalar input to determine color and opacity values, rather than relying on piecewise linear interpolation between user-defined control points. It differs from sibling methods like Voxel Color Mapping and Color Specification by defining the mapping through continuous analytical formulas (e.g., Gaussians, sigmoids, or trigonometric functions) rather than explicit lookup table entries or discrete color specifications. The family shares the mechanism of mapping a normalized scalar input t \in [0, 1] to an RGBA output vector \mathbf{C} using a parametric equation. The input t is typically derived from the parent method 1D Transfer Function Generation and Sampling, which normalizes raw voxel values. The output is a 4-channel vector where the first three channels represent RGB color and the fourth represents alpha (opacity). The specific parametric form varies by child method, but the core operation is the evaluation of a function f(t) that yields \mathbf{C}. Cosine Palette Color Mapping generates smooth, perceptually uniform color gradients by evaluating a parametric cosine function with distinct phase offsets for each RGB channel. It differs from sibling methods like the Gaussian Transfer Function or Sigmoid Function with Jacobian by relying on trigonometric interference rather than probability distributions or logistic curves, producing vibrant, continuous transitions without explicit piecewise definitions. See Cosine Palette Color Mapping. The Gaussian Transfer Function is a parametric method for generating a 4-channel RGBA lookup table (LUT) using three additive Gaussian basis functions to control color and opacity based on normalized scalar input values. It constructs the LUT by evaluating Gaussian bumps at fixed Red, Green, and Blue color channels to highlight specific scalar ranges. See Gaussian Transfer Function. The Style Function Animation is a module that generates a time-varying coefficient S(t) to modify the rendering style of volume data based on user interaction events. It solves the problem of smoothly transitioning visualization parameters (such as opacity or projection type) in response to user engagement, such as zooming or rotating. Unlike static transfer functions, this method provides a dynamic factor that blends between different rendering styles (e.g., Direct Volume Rendering and Maximum Intensity Projection) based on the duration and spatial proximity of user interaction. See Style Function Animation. Computes the logistic sigmoid function \sigma(x) and its derivative \sigma'(x) simultaneously. It is used in volume rendering and differentiable rendering pipelines to map scalar inputs to probabilities or soft boundaries, enabling gradient-based optimization. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Gaussian Transfer Function by its S-shaped monotonicity and its explicit provision of the Jacobian (derivative) for backpropagation, which is critical for differentiable renderers. See Sigmoid Function with Jacobian. Definition: Generates a transfer function initialized with a 7-segment rainbow color map spanning [0, 1], with no Gaussian objects. Steps: 1. Create TF with given resolution. 2. Clear existing controls. 3. Add 7 ColorControls at positions 0/6, 1/6, 2/6, 3/6, 4/6, 5/6, 6/6. 4. Assign RGB values: (0, 0.364706, 1), (0, 1, 0.976471), (0, 1, 0.105882), (0.968627, 1, 0), (1, 0.490196, 0), (1, 0, 0), (0.662745, 0, 1). 5. Clear Gaussian objects. 6. Call updateColorMap(). Definition: Generates a random transfer function LUT. Steps: 1. Clear the LUT. 2. Iterate i from 0 to nbins - 1. If i == 0, push glm::vec4(0). Otherwise, push glm::vec4(randf(), randf(), randf(), randf()). 3. Call uploadgpu(). Parameters: nbins: Number of bins. Default value is 8. Definition: A function defined as a product of threshold functions, used to generalize the approach of defining materials via range selections in the histogram. Formula: \Theta(x) = \prodi \thetai(si(x)), where \thetai are threshold functions (typically trapezoids and ramps) with value range [0.0, 1.0], and si(x) is the value of variate i at position x. The concept of parametric transfer functions allows for smooth, continuous mapping of scalar data to visual properties, avoiding the jagged edges of piecewise linear interpolation. name: Cosine Palette Color Mapping
head: Inigo Quilez Palette
body: Cosine Palette Color Mapping generates a smooth color gradient from a scalar input using a cosine function with specific parameters, as described by Inigo Quilez. It maps a normalized scalar input t \in [0, 1] to an RGBA output vector \mathbf{C} using a parametric equation. Unlike sibling methods that rely on probability distributions or piecewise linear interpolation, this approach uses trigonometric periodicity to define color transitions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A normalized scalar value t \in [0, 1]. Output: An RGBA color vector \mathbf{C} where the RGB channels are computed via the cosine palette and the Alpha channel is set to 1.0 unless blended with other transfer function logic. Data Structures: vec3 a: Base color offset. vec3 b: Amplitude scaling. vec3 c: Frequency scaling. vec3 d: Phase shift. Formula: The color \mathbf{C}{\text{rgb}} is calculated as: \mathbf{C}{\text{rgb}} = \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b} \cdot \cos(2\pi \cdot (\mathbf{c} \cdot t + \mathbf{d})) Where: \mathbf{a} = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) \mathbf{b} = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) \mathbf{c} = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) \mathbf{d} = (0.00, 0.33, 0.67) \cos is applied component-wise. t is the scalar input. Parameters: The parameters \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{d} are fixed constants defined by Inigo Quilez. t must be clamped to [0, 1] to prevent out-of-bounds evaluation if raw values are not pre-normalized. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision errors in t may cause slight color banding if the output is quantized to 8-bit integers without dithering. Boundaries: If t exceeds [0, 1], the color will wrap around due to the periodic nature of the cosine function. Clamping t is essential for monotonic data mapping. Alpha: This method defines RGB only. Alpha must be handled separately, often by setting it to 1.0 or blending with opacity transfer functions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def cosinepalette(t: float) -> tuple[float, float, float, float]: # Clamp input to [0, 1] to prevent wrapping artifacts t = max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) # Define vector parameters a = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) b = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) c = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) d = (0.00, 0.33, 0.67) # Compute RGB using component-wise cosine r = a[0] + b[0] math.cos(2 math.pi (c[0] t + d[0])) g = a[1] + b[1] math.cos(2 math.pi (c[1] t + d[1])) blue = a[2] + b[2] math.cos(2 math.pi (c[2] t + d[2])) # Alpha is not defined by the palette formula; set to 1.0 alpha = 1.0 return (r, g, blue, alpha) The Blue-Red Colormap normalizes scalar depth values to the range [0, 1] and maps them to a piecewise linear color gradient ranging from blue at minimum depth to red at maximum depth. It solves the problem of interpreting 3D spatial structure from rendered depth buffers by providing a high-contrast continuous representation. Unlike the parent Cosine Palette Color Mapping which generates smooth gradients via trigonometric functions, this method uses explicit linear piecewise functions optimized for depth visualization. The Hue Transfer Function is a procedural method that maps a scalar input value to an RGB color by cycling through hue bands using smoothstep functions. It serves as a specific implementation of color mapping within volume rendering classification, distinct from parent Cosine Palette Color Mapping by using piecewise linear interpolation (smoothstep) rather than trigonometric functions to define color transitions. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(1) per voxel, involving a constant number of arithmetic operations and trigonometric evaluations. Memory: O(1), requiring only storage for the four vector parameters and the input scalar. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. name: Blue-Red Colormap
head: Depth Normalization & Blue-Red Colormap, Depth Visualization, Depth Visualization via Min-Max Normalization, Jet-like Colormap
body: The Blue-Red Colormap normalizes scalar depth values to the range [0, 1] and maps them to a piecewise linear color gradient ranging from blue at minimum depth to red at maximum depth. It solves the problem of interpreting 3D spatial structure from rendered depth buffers by providing a high-contrast continuous representation. Unlike the parent Cosine Palette Color Mapping which generates smooth gradients via trigonometric functions, this method uses explicit linear piecewise functions optimized for depth visualization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A depth buffer containing raw depth values d{i,j} for each pixel (i,j), and the global minimum (d{min}) and maximum (d{max}) depth values across the entire image. Output: An RGB image where each pixel is colored according to its normalized depth value. Data Structures: depth: A 2D array or flattened vector of shape (H, W) or (H \times W) containing raw depth values. renderbuffer: A 2D array of shape (H, W, 3) storing the final RGB output. minv, maxv: Scalar values representing the global minimum and maximum depth. Steps: 1. Compute Global Extents: Determine the minimum and maximum depth values across all pixels. Parallel implementations compute these using atomic operations across all rays. d{min} = \min{i,j} (d{i,j}) d{max} = \max{i,j} (d{i,j}) 2. Normalize Depth: For each pixel, normalize the raw depth value to the range [0, 1] using min-max normalization. A small epsilon (\epsilon = 10^{-8}) is added to the denominator to prevent division by zero in degenerate cases. x = \frac{d{i,j} - d{min}}{d{max} - d{min} + \epsilon} 3. Compute Color Channels: Calculate the Red (R), Green (G), and Blue (B) channels using piecewise linear functions of the normalized depth x: R = \text{clip}(2x - 1, 0, 1) G = \text{clip}(1 - |2x - 1|, 0, 1) B = \text{clip}(1 - 2x, 0, 1) When x=0 (near), R=0, G=0, B=1 (Blue). When x=0.5 (mid), R=0, G=1, B=0 (Green). When x=1 (far), R=1, G=0, B=0 (Red). 4. Finalize Output: Stack the channels into an RGB vector, scale to [0, 255], and cast to uint8 for storage or display. \text{Color}{i,j} = \text{uint8}([R, G, B] \times 255) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def blueredcolormap(depthbuffer): """ Applies Blue-Red colormap to a depth buffer. Args: depthbuffer: 2D list of shape (height, width) with raw depth values. Returns: rgbimage: 2D list of shape (height, width, 3) with uint8 RGB values. """ def clip(val, lo, hi): return lo if val < lo else (hi if val > hi else val) # Step 1: Compute global min and max minv = min(min(row) for row in depthbuffer) maxv = max(max(row) for row in depthbuffer) # Step 2: Normalize depth to [0, 1] epsilon = 1e-8 normalizeddepth = [[(depthbuffer[r][c] - minv) / (maxv - minv + epsilon) for c in range(len(depthbuffer[0]))] for r in range(len(depthbuffer))] # Step 3: Compute RGB channels height = len(normalizeddepth) width = len(normalizeddepth[0]) rgbimage = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for r in range(height): for c in range(width): x = normalizeddepth[r][c] # Red channel: increases linearly from 0.5 to 1.0 red = clip(2.0 x - 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) # Green channel: triangular shape, peak at 0.5 green = clip(1.0 - abs(2.0 x - 1.0), 0.0, 1.0) # Blue channel: decreases linearly from 1.0 to 0.0 blue = clip(1.0 - 2.0 x, 0.0, 1.0) rgbimage[r][c] = [red, green, blue] # Step 4: Stack and convert to uint8 finalimage = [[tuple(int(ch 255) for ch in rgbimage[r][c]) for c in range(width)] for r in range(height)] return finalimage Parameters: epsilon: Small constant for numerical stability, typically 10^{-8}. Tthreshold: Transparency threshold for ray marching termination, default 10^{-2}. maxsamplesforrendering: Maximum samples per ray, default 100. disttofocus: Distance to focus for Depth of Field, default 1.2. lendis: Lens size for Depth of Field, default 0.04. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Variance: If d{max} = d{min}, the denominator becomes zero. The epsilon term prevents division by zero. Out-of-Bounds Depth: Depth values outside the [d{min}, d{max}] range calculated from the buffer will be clipped to 0 or 1 by the clip function in the channel calculations, ensuring valid RGB output. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: High contrast between near and far objects; simple piecewise linear implementation. Limitations: Not perceptually uniform; the green band in the middle may obscure subtle depth variations in the mid-range. When to use: Visualizing depth maps where spatial structure needs to be quickly assessed. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method is implemented in open-source repositories for 3D vision and depth visualization, such as nerf-3d-vision and taichi-ngp-renderer. yashtmy/nerf-3d-vision, https://github.com/yashtmy/nerf-3d-vision, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Linyou/taichi-ngp-renderer, https://github.com/Linyou/taichi-ngp-renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Hue Transfer Function
head: Hue Cycle Transfer Function, Smoothstep Hue Mapping
body: The Hue Transfer Function is a procedural method that maps a scalar input value to an RGB color by cycling through hue bands using smoothstep functions. It serves as a specific implementation of color mapping within volume rendering classification, distinct from parent Cosine Palette Color Mapping by using piecewise linear interpolation (smoothstep) rather than trigonometric functions to define color transitions. Inputs and Outputs Input: A scalar value x (typically normalized to [0, 1]). Output: An RGBA color vector (R, G, B, A). Data Structures HUE: A constant float representing the width of one hue segment, defined as 1/6. Parameters HUE: 1/6 \approx 0.16666666666666. Algorithm The function calculates the red, green, and blue channels independently using the smoothstep function. The smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x) function returns 0 if x \le edge0, 1 if x \ge edge1, and performs smooth Hermite interpolation between 0 and 1 otherwise. 1. Calculate the Red channel r: r = \text{smoothstep}(HUE, 2HUE, x) - \text{smoothstep}(4HUE, 5HUE, x) 2. Calculate the Green channel g: g = \text{smoothstep}(0, HUE, x) - \text{smoothstep}(3HUE, 4HUE, x) 3. Calculate the Blue channel b: b = \text{smoothstep}(2HUE, 3HUE, x) - \text{smoothstep}(5HUE, 6HUE, x) 4. Return the final color: RGB = (1-r, g, b) A = 1.0 Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def huetransferfunction(x: float) -> tuple: # HUE is 1/6 h = 1.0 / 6.0 # Helper for smoothstep: returns 0 if x <= edge0, 1 if x >= edge1, else smooth interpolation def smoothstep(edge0: float, edge1: float, x: float) -> float: if x <= edge0: return 0.0 if x >= edge1: return 1.0 # Standard smoothstep interpolation t = (x - edge0) / (edge1 - edge0) return t t (3.0 - 2.0 t) # Calculate channels r = smoothstep(h, 2 h, x) - smoothstep(4 h, 5 h, x) g = smoothstep(0.0, h, x) - smoothstep(3 h, 4 h, x) b = smoothstep(2 h, 3 h, x) - smoothstep(5 h, 6 h, x) # Return inverted red, green, blue, and alpha 1.0 return (1.0 - r, g, b, 1.0) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision errors in floating-point arithmetic may cause discontinuities at the boundaries of the hue segments if not handled carefully. Maps scalar values to the hue channel of the HSV color model, keeping saturation and value constant. It allows lighting effects to modulate saturation and value without altering the semantic meaning of the hue, ensuring the mapping remains invertible even under illumination. It is distinct from RGB mapping, where lighting affects all channels, and from texture-based uncertainty visualization, which doubles polygon count. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, as it involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations and smoothstep evaluations. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring only a few scalar variables. Strengths: Simple to implement, computationally inexpensive, and produces smooth color transitions. Limitations: The color palette is fixed and may not be suitable for all data distributions. When to use: When a simple, smooth, cyclic color mapping is needed for scalar data visualization in volume rendering. When not to use: When specific color semantics or perceptual uniformity are critical, or when the data distribution requires a non-cyclic mapping. It is part of a family of procedural transfer functions that use mathematical functions to generate color maps without relying on predefined lookup tables. terier/vpt, https://github.com/terier/vpt, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: HSV Hue Color Mapping
body: HSV Hue Color Mapping maps scalar values to the hue channel of the HSV (Hue, Saturation, Value) color model, keeping saturation and value constant. This approach allows lighting effects to modulate saturation and value without altering the semantic meaning of the hue, ensuring the mapping remains invertible even under illumination. It is distinct from RGB mapping, where lighting affects all channels, and from texture-based uncertainty visualization, which doubles polygon count. Inputs: Scalar field values v in range [v{min}, v{max}]; target hue range [H{min}, H{max}]; optional emphasis value vd. Outputs: RGB color values. Data Structures: None required beyond standard scalar and color types. 1. Linear Mapping: Map input scalar v to hue H using a linear function: H(v) = H{min} + \frac{v - v{min}}{v{max} - v{min}} (H{max} - H{min}) where v \in [v{min}, v{max}]. 2. Emphasis Mapping (Optional): To emphasize a specific value vd, provide a wider colour spectrum for an interval close to vd. The source does not specify a precise mathematical formula for this expansion, only that a wider colour spectrum is provided near vd. 3. HSV to RGB Conversion: Convert the computed hue H (with constant saturation S and value V) to RGB. 4. Vector Field Application: For vector field visualization on isosurfaces, map streamline color to hues based on flow direction (inflow or outflow) and magnitude. Parameters: S, V: Constant saturation and value, kept for colour mapping to allow lighting effects. H{min}, H{max}: Hue range. Edge Cases: Division by zero if v{min} = v{max}. Hue wrapping: Ensure hue values are normalized to 0, 360) if using cyclic hue spaces. A technique for visualizing uncertainty in [isosurface rendering by mapping error magnitude to the hue channel of the HSL color space, keeping saturation and brightness constant. Low uncertainty maps to 144 degrees (green) and high uncertainty maps to 0 degrees (red). It is faster than texture-based error visualization because it does not double the number of polygons rendered. Performance on a dual processor 800MHz Mac OS X with GeForce 3 (64MB): 136.1 FPS for 32^3, 31.5 FPS for 64^3, 6.5 FPS for 128^3. Time Complexity: Not explicitly stated. Rendering performance is hardware-dependent. Memory Complexity: Not explicitly stated. Performance: On a dual processor 800MHz Mac OS X with GeForce 3 (64MB), hue-based uncertainty visualization achieves 136.1 FPS for 32^3, 31.5 FPS for 64^3, and 6.5 FPS for 128^3. Texture-based methods are roughly half as fast due to doubled polygon count. Scaling: Performance degrades with dataset size, dropping from 136.1 FPS at 32^3 to 6.5 FPS at 128^3. Strengths: Lighting effects do not corrupt the semantic hue mapping; invertible mapping. Faster than texture-based uncertainty visualization. Limitations: Requires constant saturation/value for lighting compatibility. When to use: When simultaneous visualization of scalar and vector fields is required, or when uncertainty must be visualized without increasing polygon count. When not to use: When lighting must dynamically alter the semantic color mapping or when precise non-linear emphasis formulas are required. Originated in adaptive multi-valued volume data visualization for regular and irregular tetrahedral meshes. Used for simultaneous visualization of scalar and vector fields, such as coloring streamlines on isosurfaces based on flow direction and magnitude. Also applied to uncertainty visualization in isosurface rendering of multiresolution data. name: Gaussian Transfer Function
head: 3-Gaussian Transfer Function, TransferFunctionWidget3
body: The Gaussian Transfer Function constructs a 4-channel RGBA lookup table using three Gaussian bumps to map scalar values to color and opacity. It differs from its siblings by explicitly normalizing RGB channels by their maximum sum to prevent overflow and by using fixed primary colors (red, green, blue) for the three respective bumps, whereas Cosine Palette Color Mapping uses a continuous palette and Sigmoid Function with Jacobian uses monotonic transitions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Three sets of parameters (levelj, opacityj, widthj) for j \in \{1, 2, 3\}. Output: A texture rgba of shape (1024, 4), where index i corresponds to normalized scalar t = i/1023. Data Structures: rgba: Array of shape (1024, 4). colors: Fixed list of RGB vectors: [ (1,0,0), (0,1,0), (0,0,1) ]. Steps: 1. Initialize rgba with zeros. 2. For each texel index i from 0 to 1023: a. Calculate position t = i / 1023.0. b. For each Gaussian j \in \{1, 2, 3\}: i. Calculate intensity: Ij = \exp\left(-\left(\frac{t - levelj}{widthj}\right)^2\right). ii. Add color contribution: rgba[i, 0:3] += colors[j-1] \times opacityj \times Ij. iii. Add opacity contribution: rgba[i, 3] += opacityj \times Ij. c. Normalize RGB: If rgba[i, 0:3].max() > 0, divide rgba[i, 0:3] by rgba[i, 0:3].max(). If max is 0, leave RGB as 0 to avoid NaN. d. Clamp: rgba[i] = clip(rgba[i], 0, 1). Formulas: Ij(t) = \exp\left(-\left(\frac{t - levelj}{widthj}\right)^2\right) \mathbf{C}{raw}[i] = \sum{j=1}^{3} \mathbf{c}j \cdot opacityj \cdot Ij(t) \alpha[i] = \sum{j=1}^{3} opacityj \cdot Ij(t) \mathbf{C}{final}[i] = \text{clip}\left( \frac{\mathbf{C}{raw}[i]}{\max(\mathbf{C}{raw}[i])}, 0, 1 \right) Parameters: levels: [0.1, 0.5, 0.8] (Default). opacities: [0.4, 0.1, 0.1] (Default). widths: [0.1, 0.1, 0.1] (Default). Pitfalls: Division by zero if all Gaussians contribute 0 intensity at a specific t. The source code clips to [0,1] after division, which may leave NaNs if not guarded. A guard if maxval > 0 is required. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generategaussiantf(levels, opacities, widths): N = 1024 rgba = np.zeros((N, 4)) colors = np.array([[1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]]) for i in range(N): t = i / 1023.0 rgbsum = np.zeros(3) alphasum = 0.0 for j in range(3): level = levels[j] opacity = opacities[j] width = widths[j] intensity = np.exp(-((t - level) / width) 2) rgbsum += colors[j] opacity intensity alphasum += opacity intensity maxrgb = np.max(rgbsum) if maxrgb > 0: rgbsum /= maxrgb rgba[i, 0:3] = rgbsum rgba[i, 3] = alphasum return np.clip(rgba, 0, 1) Pre-renders scalar data into multi-layered 2D images for interactive transparency/color modification without re-rendering 3D. Use when computational resources are limited. Time complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Originated in the ipyvolume library by Maarten Breddels. It is implemented as TransferFunctionWidget3 in the transferfunction module. https://github.com/maartenbreddels/ipyvolume/blob/master/ipyvolume/transferfunction.py, https://github.com/maartenbreddels/ipyvolume/blob/master/ipyvolume/transferfunction.py, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Explorable Image Representation
head: Image-based volume exploration, Multi-layer explorable images
body: Explorable Image Representation is a method for interactive volume visualization that pre-renders scalar data into a set of multi-layered 2D images, allowing users to modify layer transparency and color without re-rendering the 3D scene. It differs from standard ray-casting by decoupling interaction from the 3D data, enabling image-based exploration on devices with limited computational resources. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scalar volume data; user-defined ranges of interest; number of layers to explore. Output: A set of 2D explorable images; metadata describing layer order, approximate color, and opacity for each layer. Data Structures: Explorable Image: A 2D raster image (RGBA) containing superimposed layers. Layer Metadata: A list of objects, each containing: layerid: Identifier for the material/region. approxcolor: RGB estimate used for separation during generation. approxopacity: Initial opacity estimate. bounds: Information defining the spatial extent of the layer within the volume. Algorithm Steps: 1. Transfer Function Generation: Compute peaks in the transfer function to identify material boundaries (iso-values). Select peak centers to be as equally spaced as possible within the user-defined range. Construct a transfer function consisting of Gaussian curves centered on these peaks. The width, height, and number of peaks determine the granularity of the layers. Note: The initial transfer function is not optimized for final visualization because it serves as a basis for separable layer extraction. 2. Layer Separation and Image Generation: Assume a rough estimate of each layer’s color to ensure separability during rendering. Render the volume using the generated transfer function. Apply boundary blurring control if specified by the user; otherwise, use a default value. 3. Layer Combination Scheme: Generate a minimal set of images that allows reconstruction of any layer combination via compositing. Image 1: Contains the innermost and outermost layers. Image 2: Contains the innermost, outermost, and the middle layer. Subsequent Images: Follow the pattern where each new image adds the next intermediate layer, bounded by the previously established inner and outer layers. This allows data in between to be constructed from bounding layer information. 4. Interaction: Users modify transparency and color of individual layers by applying image-based operations (e.g., alpha blending, color multiplication) to the pre-rendered explorable images. No 3D data access or additional rendering passes are required during interaction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateexplorableimages(volumedata, userranges, numlayers): # Step 1: Generate Transfer Function # Compute peaks in the transfer function to find material boundaries peaks = computetransferfunctionpeaks(volumedata, userranges) # Select peaks to be equally spaced selectedpeaks = selectequallyspacedpeaks(peaks, numlayers) # Create Gaussian transfer function centered on selected peaks transferfunction = creategaussiantransferfunction(selectedpeaks) # Step 2: Render and Separate Layers # Assume rough color estimates for separation layercolors = estimatelayercolors(volumedata, selectedpeaks) # Render volume with boundary blurring (default if not specified) blurredvolume = applyboundaryblurring(volumedata, defaultblur) # Render using the transfer function to get initial composite # Note: The method implies extracting layers from the rendered result # or rendering layers separately and combining them according to the scheme. # Based on the text, we generate a set of multi-layered images. images = [] metadata = [] # Step 3: Layer Combination Scheme # Determine layer indices from innermost to outermost layerindices = getlayerindices(selectedpeaks) # Generate Image 1: Innermost and Outermost if len(layerindices) >= 2: inneridx = layerindices[0] outeridx = layerindices[-1] # Render or extract these specific layers img1 = renderlayers(blurredvolume, [inneridx, outeridx], layercolors) images.append(img1) # Store metadata metadata.append({ 'layers': [inneridx, outeridx], 'colors': [layercolors[inneridx], layercolors[outeridx]], 'bounds': getlayerbounds(volumedata, [inneridx, outeridx]) }) # Generate subsequent images adding intermediate layers for i in range(1, len(layerindices) - 1): mididx = layerindices[i] # Current image contains inner, outer, and mid currentlayers = [inneridx, mididx, outeridx] img = renderlayers(blurredvolume, currentlayers, layercolors) images.append(img) metadata.append({ 'layers': currentlayers, 'colors': [layercolors[l] for l in currentlayers], 'bounds': getlayerbounds(volumedata, currentlayers) }) return images, metadata def interactwithexplorableimage(image, metadata, usercolorchanges, useropacitychanges): # Image-based interaction # Apply user-defined color and opacity changes to the pre-rendered image # using the stored metadata to identify layers resultimage = image for layerid in metadata['layers']: if layerid in usercolorchanges: resultimage = applycolorchange(resultimage, layerid, usercolorchanges[layerid]) if layerid in useropacitychanges: resultimage = applyopacitychange(resultimage, layerid, useropacitychanges[layerid]) return resultimage Parameters: Boundary Blurring: Controls the amount of blurring at material boundaries. Default value is used if not specified. Number of Layers: Controls the number of generated input images. Users can select a range from a single image (entire data) to individual images for each layer. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Storage/Bandwidth Trade-off: There is a trade-off between storage space/bandwidth requirements and the ability to reproduce all possible interactions between layers. Initial Optimization: The initial transfer function is not optimized for visualization because it allows users to change color and opacity of individual layers. Color Approximation: The method assumes a rough estimate of each layer’s color for separating input images. If colors are too similar, separation may fail. Uses Gaussian bumps to define opacity and color based on scalar value position. Provides the basis for the transfer function generation in Explorable Image Representation. Gaussian Transfer Function Generates transfer functions using parametric curves (like Gaussians). Explorable Image Representation uses this to create the initial multi-layered transfer function. Parametric Function Generation Time Complexity: Pre-rendering time depends on the volume size and the number of layers. Interaction time is constant relative to the volume size, as it operates on 2D images. Memory Complexity: Storage requirements increase with the number of generated explorable images. The method trades off storage/bandwidth for interactive flexibility. Strengths: Enables image-based interaction without 3D data access or re-rendering passes. Suitable for mobile devices or client-server architectures with limited bandwidth. Limitations: Initial transfer function is not optimized for final visualization. Relies on color approximation for layer separation. Trade-off between storage and interaction fidelity. When to Use: When interactive exploration of layer properties is required on devices with limited rendering capabilities, or when bandwidth is constrained. When Not to Use: When high-fidelity, optimized visualization is the primary goal, or when the number of layers is very large, leading to excessive storage requirements. The Explorable Image Representation method was proposed by Tikhonova et al. in the context of volumetric medical images visualization on mobile devices. It addresses the challenge of interactive volume exploration on resource-constrained devices by pre-computing explorable images. The method is part of a broader effort to optimize volume rendering for mobile and web-based applications. name: Style Function Animation
head: Animation Module, Exponential Style Function, Time-varying coefficient, Time-varying coefficient function for style transitions
body: The Style Function Animation module generates a time-varying coefficient S(t) that modulates rendering styles based on user interaction events, such as zooming or rotation. It solves the problem of smoothly transitioning visualization parameters (e.g., between Direct Volume Rendering and Maximum Intensity Projection) in response to dynamic user engagement. Unlike static parametric functions, this method introduces temporal continuity, ensuring that style changes are perceptually smooth rather than abrupt. Inputs and Outputs Input: Current time t{current}, interaction start time t{start}, initial style value S(t{start}), and target style value S(t{dest}). Output: A floating-point value S(t{current}) \in [0, 1] representing the current style intensity. Contextual Data: Flags for extra features (e.g., cut-aways) and factors defining contributions of different rendering styles. Data Structures The module returns a structure containing: 1. Flags: Boolean or integer indicators for auxiliary features like cut-aways. 2. Factors: Floating-point values defining the weight of specific rendering styles (e.g., the value of S(t)). Parameters S(t{dest}): The target style value. It is 1 if the user starts interacting and 0 if the user stops interacting. S(t{start}): The style value immediately before the interaction event begins or ends. Output Range: [0, 1], where 0 indicates no interaction and 1 indicates prolonged interaction. Algorithm The core calculation uses an exponential interpolation function to blend between the previous state and the target state. 1. Calculate the elapsed time since the interaction event: \Delta t = t{current} - t{start}. 2. Compute the exponential decay factor: E = e^{-\Delta t}. 3. Calculate the current style value using the formula: S(t{current}) = S(t{start}) \cdot e^{-(t{current} - t{start})} + S(t{dest}) \cdot (1 - e^{-(t{current} - t{start})}). 4. Determine spatial adjustments if the interaction is zooming: If the interaction is rotation, S(t{current}) is uniform across the entire object. If the interaction is zooming, adjust the style parameters spatially. 5. Return the structure containing the computed S(t{current}) and relevant flags. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def stylefunctionanimation(tcurrent, tstart, sstart, sdest, interactiontype, voxelprojection, interactionpoint): """ Calculates the time-varying style coefficient S(t). Args: tcurrent (float): Current time. tstart (float): Time when interaction started or stopped. sstart (float): Style value before the interaction event. sdest (float): Target style value (1 if started, 0 if stopped). interactiontype (str): 'rotation' or 'zooming'. voxelprojection (float): Distance or metric of voxel projection to interaction point. interactionpoint (float): Reference point for spatial calculation. Returns: dict: Structure with 'stylevalue' (float) and 'flags' (dict). """ # Calculate elapsed time deltat = tcurrent - tstart # Guard for boundary condition tcurrent < tstart if deltat < 0: deltat = 0 # Compute exponential factor expfactor = math.exp(-deltat) # Core interpolation formula scurrent = sstart expfactor + sdest (1 - expfactor) # Spatial adjustment for zooming: not given in the sources. # The style function value increases as the projection of a voxel's position gets closer to the interaction point. # Flags for extra features like cut-aways are determined by other modules or defaults flags = { 'cutaway': False, 'interactionactive': sdest == 1 } return { 'stylevalue': scurrent, 'flags': flags } Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The exponential function e^{-\Delta t} can underflow for large \Delta t, resulting in 0. This is generally acceptable as it converges to S(t{dest}). Boundary Conditions: If t{current} < t{start}, the behavior is undefined in the sources. Implementation should clamp \Delta t to 0. Interaction Point Definition: For zooming, the "interaction point" is defined as the position of initial interaction on the object. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides smooth, perceptually pleasing transitions between rendering styles (e.g., DVR to MIP) based on user intent. It decouples interaction logic from rendering logic. Limitations: The exponential decay rate is fixed (implicit in the formula e^{-\Delta t}). Users cannot easily tune the speed of transition without modifying the source code or extending the parameter set. The spatial adjustment for zooming requires calculating voxel projections, which adds computational overhead compared to uniform rotation effects. When to use: When dynamic focus+context visualization is required, specifically for smooth transitions between different rendering techniques (DVR, MIP, etc.) driven by user interaction. When not to use: For static visualizations or when precise control over the transition curve shape (beyond exponential) is required. The Style Function Animation module was introduced in the context of Dynamic Focus+Context for Volume Rendering by Sikachev, Rautek, Bruckner, and Gröller. It addresses the need for visual representations that adapt to user engagement, such as rotation and zooming. The method builds on earlier work by Bruckner and Gröller regarding DVR-MIP interpolation. It is part of a larger system that includes an engagement estimation module and a rendering module. name: Sigmoid Function with Jacobian
head: Logistic Function, Logistic Sigmoid, Sigmoid Function, Sigmoid derivative
body: Computes the logistic sigmoid function \sigma(x) and its analytical derivative \sigma'(x) for a scalar input x. It serves as a differentiable activation function in volume rendering and differentiable rendering pipelines, mapping real-valued inputs to the (0, 1) interval while providing gradient information for optimization. Inputs and outputs: Input: A scalar value x \in \mathbb{R}. Output: A tuple (s, ds), where s = \sigma(x) \in (0, 1) is the sigmoid value, and ds = \sigma'(x) is the derivative with respect to x. Data structures: No complex data structures are required; the computation operates on scalar floating-point values. Steps: 1. Compute the exponential term e^{-x}. 2. Compute the sigmoid value s using the logistic formula. 3. Compute the derivative ds using the identity \sigma'(x) = s(1-s). Formulas: The logistic sigmoid function is defined as: s = \sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}} The derivative of the sigmoid function is: \frac{ds}{dx} = s(1 - s) Parameters: None. The function is standard and parameter-free. Edge cases and pitfalls: Numerical Stability: For large positive x, e^{-x} approaches 0 and s approaches 1. For large negative x, e^{-x} becomes very large, potentially causing overflow if computed naively as 1/(1+e^{-x}) without care, though standard IEEE 754 floating-point handles large exponents by saturating to infinity, resulting in s=0. Derivative at Extremes: As x \to \pm \infty, ds \to 0, which can lead to vanishing gradients in deep optimization problems. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sigmoidwithjacobian(x: float) -> tuple[float, float]: expnegx = math.exp(-x) s = 1.0 / (1.0 + expnegx) ds = s (1.0 - s) return s, ds Computes the inverse of the sigmoid function, mapping probability values in (0, 1) to the real line (-\infty, \infty). It serves as the canonical link function in logistic regression and is used in volume rendering to invert normalized transfer function outputs back to logit space for linear interpolation or gradient-based optimization. Unlike the parent Sigmoid Function with Jacobian which maps reals to probabilities, this method performs the reverse transformation. Time Complexity: O(1) per evaluation, requiring one exponential and a few arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary storage is needed. Strengths: Analytically differentiable, computationally inexpensive, and bounded output makes it suitable for probabilistic interpretations and soft thresholding in differentiable renderers. Limitations: Suffers from vanishing gradients for large |x|. When to use: When a smooth, monotonic transition between two states is required, or when aggregating probabilistic contributions in differentiable rendering. When not to use: When the inverse mapping is required (use Inverse Sigmoid Function). The logistic sigmoid function, also known as the FL function, corresponds to the logistic distribution. In the context of differentiable rendering, it is a popular choice for soft evaluation of geometric primitives (e.g., determining if a pixel lies inside a triangle) and for aggregating face contributions, where it provides a differentiable approximation of hard boolean operations. It is frequently referred to as "the" sigmoid in recent literature, distinguishing it from more general sigmoidal functions.
