name: Clamping
head: Range Clamping, Scalar Clamping
body: Clamping is a technique to handle scalar values outside the defined transfer function range by mapping them to boundary colors or black. It explicitly defines the behavior for out-of-range scalars, mapping values below the lower bound to the first node color and values above the upper bound to the last node color when enabled. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar value s from the volume data; the transfer function range [x1, x2]; the transfer function node colors C{first} (at x1) and C{last} (at x2); a boolean flag clampingon. Output: A color C{out} (typically RGBA). Data Structures: The transfer function stores nodes regularly spaced between x1 and x2. For clamping, only the first node (at lower bound x1) and the last node (at upper bound x2) are strictly required for the boundary mapping. Steps: 1. Check the state of the clampingon flag. 2. If clampingon is true: If s < x1, set C{out} = C{first}. If s > x2, set C{out} = C{last}. If x1 \le s \le x2, proceed with standard interpolation between nodes. 3. If clampingon is false: If s < x1 or s > x2, set C{out} = \text{Black}. If x1 \le s \le x2, proceed with standard interpolation. Formulas: For x1 \le s \le x2, the output color is computed via linear interpolation: C{out} = C{first} + \frac{s - x1}{x2 - x1} (C{last} - C{first}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def clampcolor(s, x1, x2, Cfirst, Clast, clampingon): """ Map scalar s to color using clamping logic. s: scalar value from volume x1: lower bound of transfer function range x2: upper bound of transfer function range Cfirst: color at x1 Clast: color at x2 clampingon: boolean flag """ if clampingon: if s < x1: return Cfirst elif s > x2: return Clast else: # Standard linear interpolation between Cfirst and Clast t = (s - x1) / (x2 - x1) return (Cfirst[0] + t (Clast[0] - Cfirst[0]), Cfirst[1] + t (Clast[1] - Cfirst[1]), Cfirst[2] + t (Clast[2] - Cfirst[2]), Cfirst[3] + t (Clast[3] - Cfirst[3])) else: if s < x1 or s > x2: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Black else: # Standard linear interpolation between Cfirst and Clast t = (s - x1) / (x2 - x1) return (Cfirst[0] + t (Clast[0] - Cfirst[0]), Cfirst[1] + t (Clast[1] - Cfirst[1]), Cfirst[2] + t (Clast[2] - Cfirst[2]), Cfirst[3] + t (Clast[3] - Cfirst[3])) Parameters: clampingon: Boolean flag that controls whether out-of-range values map to boundary colors or black. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Not given in the sources. Degenerate Input: Not given in the sources. Sigmoid Clamping is a non-linear mapping technique that smooths and clips scalar values into the normalized range [0, 1]. It serves as a robust boundary handler for objective functions or transfer function inputs, preventing outliers from disrupting optimization or rendering by providing a soft transition at the boundaries rather than a hard cutoff. It differs from standard Clamping by introducing a sigmoidal slope near the edges, which preserves gradient information for differentiable pipelines. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Clamping is a standard feature in visualization toolkits, notably implemented in the Visualization Toolkit (VTK) via vtkColorTransferFunction::SetClamping. vtkColorTransferFunctions, http://www.vtk.org/doc/nightly/html/classvtkColorTransferFunction.html, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Sigmoid Clamping
head: Smoothing and Clipping Function (ξ), Soft Clamping
body: Sigmoid Clamping is a non-linear mapping technique that smooths and clips scalar values into the normalized range [0, 1]. It serves as a robust boundary handler for objective functions or transfer function inputs, preventing outliers from disrupting optimization or rendering by providing a soft transition at the boundaries rather than a hard cutoff. It differs from standard Clamping by introducing a sigmoidal slope near the edges, which preserves gradient information for differentiable pipelines. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar value x \in \mathbb{R}. Output: A scalar value \xi(x) \in [0, 1]. Parameters: \alpha3: A shape parameter controlling the steepness of the sigmoid transition. The standard value is 3. Formula: The function is defined as: \xi(x) = \max\left(0, \min\left(1, \frac{1}{3} \left[ 1 + e^{(-\alpha3 e x) + (\alpha3 0.5 e)} \right]^{-1} \right)\right) Where: e is the base of the natural logarithm (\approx 2.71828). The term (-\alpha3 e x) + (\alpha3 0.5 e) represents the exponent argument. The inner term \frac{1}{3} [\dots]^{-1} scales the sigmoid output. Note that the standard logistic function is \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}. Here, the exponent is z = -\alpha3 e x + \alpha3 0.5 e. The outer \max(0, \min(1, \dots)) ensures the final result is strictly bounded within [0, 1]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sigmoidclamping(x: float, alpha3: float = 3.0) -> float: """ Computes the Sigmoid Clamping function xi(x). """ # Calculate the exponent term: (-alpha3 e x) + (alpha3 0.5 e) # Note: 'e' is the mathematical constant Euler's number. e = math.e exponent = (-alpha3 e x) + (alpha3 0.5 e) # Calculate the sigmoid-like term: 1 / (1 + exp(exponent)) # The source formula uses [1 + e^(...)]^-1 which is equivalent to 1 / (1 + e^(...)) sigmoidterm = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(exponent)) # Scale by 1/3 scaled = (1.0 / 3.0) sigmoidterm # Clamp to [0, 1] result = max(0.0, min(1.0, scaled)) return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: For large positive x, the exponent becomes large negative, e^{\text{exponent}} \to 0, and \xi(x) \to 1/3. For large negative x, the exponent becomes large positive, e^{\text{exponent}} \to \infty, and \xi(x) \to 0. The hard clamping at 0 and 1 handles any numerical overflow/underflow in the exponential. Scaling Factor: The factor 1/3 means the unclamped sigmoid output is scaled down. This implies that even at the peak of the sigmoid (when the exponent is 0), the value is 1/3. The function relies on the clamping and the specific parameterization to map the relevant input range to the full [0,1] output effectively for its specific application (objective function smoothing). A variant used in deep learning contexts (specifically ngppl) where the exponential function is applied directly to the input x, but the pre-activation value is clamped to [-15, 15] during the backward pass to prevent gradient explosion. Forward: Compute y = \exp(x). Backward: Compute gradient dL/dx = dL/dy \cdot \exp(\text{clamp}(x, -15, 15)). Parameter: Clamp bounds [-15, 15] applied to x before exponentiation in the gradient calculation. Implementation: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def forward(x): return torch.exp(x) def backward(dLdout, x): # Clamp x to [-15, 15] before exponentiating for gradient stability xclamped = torch.clamp(x, -15, 15) return dLdout torch.exp(xclamped) This variant is chosen when numerical stability of the gradient is critical in neural network training, differing from Sigmoid Clamping which is a fixed mathematical mapping for scalar normalization. Time Complexity: O(1) per element. Requires one exponential, one addition, one division, and two comparisons. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. Strengths: Differentiable almost everywhere (except at the hard clamping boundaries if not smoothed, but the sigmoid part is smooth). Provides soft boundaries which are beneficial for gradient-based optimization of objective functions. Limitations: The specific scaling factor (1/3) and parameterization are tailored to the SOARNet objective functions; it may not be a universal transfer function clamping method for general volume rendering without re-tuning. The hard clamping at 0 and 1 creates non-differentiable points if the input exactly hits the boundary, though this is rare in practice. When to use: When smoothing objective function scores (like ray diversity or pose consistency) before aggregation or loss calculation. When a soft, bounded output is needed for differentiable rendering pipelines. Sigmoid Clamping, as defined by the specific formula with \alpha3=3, was introduced in the context of the SOARNet architecture for active view planning in NeRF. It is used to normalize objective functions (fC, fQ, fD, fT) to the range [0, 1] to facilitate efficient computation and comparison within the surrogate objective framework. The Truncated Exponential variant is associated with the ngppl implementation, aiming to improve inference speed and stability compared to other NeRF implementations like torch-ngp. name: Colormap Application for Visualization
head: Colormap Visualization, Depth Colormap Application, Render Net Image
body: Colormap Application for Visualization extracts specific render items (such as alpha, normal, depth, edge, curvature, or color) from a render package and applies a colormap to single-channel data to produce a visualizable netimage. It serves as the final mapping step in the visualization pipeline, converting raw scalar or vector fields into perceptually uniform or distinct color representations. It differs from Windowing by focusing on semantic channel extraction and non-linear color mapping rather than linear intensity scaling, and from Lightness-Controlled Color Harmonization by prioritizing data fidelity over aesthetic color harmony. Inputs: renderitems: A dictionary or object containing available render outputs (e.g., rendalpha, rendnormal, surfdepth, render). rendermode: A string specifying the desired output type (e.g., 'alpha', 'normal', 'depth', 'edge', 'curvature', or default). colormap: A function or lookup table that maps scalar values in [0, 1] to RGB colors. gradientmap: A function or lookup table used for edge and curvature visualization. Outputs: netimage: A tensor or image buffer containing the final visualized result. Data Structures: renderitems: Contains fields corresponding to specific render passes. rendalpha: Single-channel tensor (shape [H, W] or [1, H, W]). rendnormal: Three-channel tensor (shape [3, H, W] or [H, W, 3]), values in [-1, 1]. surfdepth: Single-channel tensor (shape [H, W] or [1, H, W]), values in [0, \infty). render: Multi-channel tensor (typically RGB, shape [3, H, W] or [H, W, 3]), values in [0, 1]. Steps: 1. Determine the output mode by converting rendermode to lowercase: mode = renderitems[rendermode].lower(). 2. Select the base data source based on mode: If mode == 'alpha': Set data = rendalpha. If mode == 'normal': Set data = rendnormal. Normalize from [-1, 1] to [0, 1] using: \text{data}{norm} = \frac{\text{data} + 1}{2} If mode == 'depth': Set data = surfdepth. If mode == 'edge': Set data = render. Apply gradientmap to data. If mode == 'curvature': Set data = rendnormal. Normalize to [0, 1] via (\text{data} + 1)/2. Apply gradientmap to the normalized data. Else (default): Set data = render. 3. Check if the resulting data is single-channel (shape dimension 0 is 1, or total channels == 1). If single-channel: Apply colormap to data to generate an RGB image. If multi-channel (e.g., RGB render): Return data as is (assuming it is already in a visualizable format). 4. Return netimage. Pitfalls: Normal and curvature modes require explicit normalization from [-1, 1] to [0, 1] before colormap application; failure to do so results in incorrect color mapping. Edge and curvature modes use gradientmap instead of the standard colormap. Depth visualization may require external normalization parameters (e.g., min/max depth) not handled by the core function, depending on the specific variant used. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applycolormapvisualization(renderitems, rendermode, colormap, gradientmap): """ Extracts a render item and applies a colormap for visualization. Args: renderitems: Dict or object with keys 'rendalpha', 'rendnormal', 'surfdepth', 'render'. rendermode: String indicating the type of visualization. colormap: Function mapping scalar [0,1] to RGB. gradientmap: Function mapping scalar [0,1] to RGB (for edges/curvature). Returns: netimage: Visualized RGB tensor. """ mode = renderitems[rendermode].lower() data = None if mode == 'alpha': data = renderitems['rendalpha'] elif mode == 'normal': data = renderitems['rendnormal'] # Normalize from [-1, 1] to [0, 1] data = (data + 1.0) / 2.0 elif mode == 'depth': data = renderitems['surfdepth'] elif mode == 'edge': data = renderitems['render'] data = gradientmap(data) elif mode == 'curvature': data = renderitems['rendnormal'] # Normalize from [-1, 1] to [0, 1] data = (data + 1.0) / 2.0 data = gradientmap(data) else: data = renderitems['render'] # Check if single channel # Assuming data is a tensor with shape [C, H, W] or [H, W, C] # We check the number of channels. If C=1, apply colormap. if data.shape[0] == 1: # Assuming [C, H, W] layout netimage = colormap(data[0]) # Apply colormap to single channel else: netimage = data return netimage Visualizes depth maps from each proposal network iteration for debugging and analysis. It applies a depth colormap to the depth output from the i-th proposal network, using the accumulation output for normalization. This variant is specific to iterative proposal-based rendering architectures. Builds a texture overlay visualizing the froxel grid structure. It operates in two modes: Mode 1 (Hash) uses a hash function to assign unique colors per froxel, executed via FFroxelOverlayHashPS as a fullscreen pass taking SceneColor, SceneDepth, FroxelSharedUB, and SvPositionToInputTextureUV as inputs. Mode 2 (Heatmap) uses a heatmap based on light counts, executed via FFroxelOverlayHeatmapPS, requiring FroxelLists.Counts, Offsets, and LightIndices to be non-null. Mode 0 disables the overlay. The SvPositionToInputTextureUV transform converts screen positions to input texture UVs via two basis changes. Applies linear scaling to depth maps for qualitative visualization. It uses a fixed maximum depth of 82.5 meters and a minimum depth of 1 meter for normalization. This parameter set is specific to the evaluation of dynamic urban environments using neural scene graphs. Plots ground truth and rasterized RGB, Depth, and Silhouette/Diff images for comparative analysis. It calculates the aspect ratio from the color tensor dimensions and creates a 2x3 subplot figure. It plots Ground Truth RGB and Depth (using 'jet' colormap, vmin=0, vmax=6). It clamps rasterized color to [0, 1] and plots Rasterized RGB (with PSNR title) and Rasterized Depth (using 'jet' colormap, vmin=0, vmax=6). If a diff RGB is provided, it plots Diff RGB L1; otherwise, it plots Rasterized Silhouette. It also plots Diff Depth L1 (using 'jet' colormap, vmin=0, vmax=6). The figure can be saved or logged to Weights & Biases (wandb). Time Complexity: The core colormap application is O(N) where N is the number of pixels, as it involves a single pass over the image data. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the output netimage. Performance: Rendering a 1920x1080 image takes approximately 16.4 seconds in the context of the dynamic urban environment benchmark, though this includes broader rendering costs, not just colormap application. Strengths: Provides a unified interface for visualizing diverse render outputs (alpha, normal, depth, etc.). Supports specialized visualizations for debugging (proposal depth, froxel overlay). Limitations: The core function assumes specific input formats and normalization ranges (e.g., normals in [-1, 1]). Depth visualization often requires external scaling parameters not defined in the base method. When to use: When debugging neural rendering pipelines, visualizing intermediate render passes, or preparing data for perceptual metrics like LPIPS. When not to use: When aesthetic color harmony is the primary goal (use Lightness-Controlled Color Harmonization) or when linear intensity windowing is sufficient. The method originates from implementations in 2D Gaussian Splatting, Generative Neural Radiance Fields (GANerf), Unreal Engine 5 Froxel Lighting, Multi-Level Neural Scene Graphs for Dynamic Urban Environments, and SplaTAM. It is widely used in computer vision research for debugging novel view synthesis, SLAM, and neural rendering systems. hbb1/2d-gaussian-splatting, https://github.com/hbb1/2d-gaussian-splatting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) barbararoessle/ganerf, https://github.com/barbararoessle/ganerf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) ArminTajik/ue5-froxel-lighting, https://github.com/ArminTajik/ue5-froxel-lighting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Multi-Level Neural Scene Graphs for Dynamic Urban Environments, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.01996, fetched 2026-10-29 spla-tam/SplaTAM, https://github.com/spla-tam/SplaTAM, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Iterative Color Matching
body: Iterative Color Matching warps the colors of an input image to match a reference image by iteratively solving for a quadratic color transformation using least squares. It differs from static color mapping methods by handling non-linear transformations and actively managing pixel clipping artifacts through iterative masking of unclipped pixels. Inputs and Outputs Input: img (input image), ref (reference image). Both are assumed to be in the range [0, 1] with C channels (typically 3 for RGB). Output: imgwarped (warped input image matching the reference color distribution). Data Structures imgmat, refmat: 2D matrices of shape (-1, C) representing flattened input and reference pixels. amat: 2D matrix of shape (-1, K) representing the quadratic expansion of the input pixels, where K is the number of basis functions. warp: 2D matrix of shape (K, C) containing the learned transformation coefficients for each output channel. mask: Boolean matrix of shape (-1, C) indicating valid (unclipped) pixels for the least squares solve. Parameters numiters: Number of iterations for the color matching process. Default is 5. eps: Clipping threshold for unclipped pixels. Pixels with values in [0, \text{eps}) or (1-\text{eps}, 1] are considered saturated/clipped. Default is 0.5/255. Algorithm Steps 1. Flatten img and ref into matrices imgmat and refmat of shape (-1, C). 2. Define isunclipped(z) as z >= eps & z <= 1 - eps. 3. Initialize mask0 as a boolean matrix of shape (-1, C) where mask0[i, c] is True if imgmat[i, c] is unclipped according to isunclipped. 4. Loop numiters times: a. Construct amat by concatenating quadratic terms (imgc imgc'), linear terms (imgmat), and bias terms (1) for each channel. For an input pixel vector \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^C, the corresponding row contains xc \cdot x{c'} for all c, c' \in \{0, \dots, C-1\}, followed by xc for all c, followed by a single bias term 1. The total number of columns is K = \frac{C(C+1)}{2} + C + 1. b. Initialize warp as a zero matrix of shape (K, C). c. For each output channel c \in \{0, \dots, C-1\}: i. Set the target vector b as refmat[:, c]. ii. Compute the current mask for channel c: mask[:, c] = mask0[:, c] & isunclipped(imgmat[:, c]) & isunclipped(b). This ensures only pixels that are unclipped in the input, unclipped in the current estimate, and unclipped in the reference are used. iii. Extract maskedamat from amat using mask[:, c]. iv. Extract maskedb from b using mask[:, c]. v. Solve the least squares problem \minw \| \text{masked\a\mat} \cdot w - \text{masked\b} \|^2 to find the coefficient vector w for channel c. vi. Store w in warp[:, c]. d. Apply the warp to update imgmat: imgmat = clip(matmul(amat, warp), 0, 1). 5. Reshape imgmat back to the original image shape to produce imgwarped. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def iterativecolormatching(img, ref, numiters=5, eps=0.5/255): """ Warps input image colors to match a reference image using iterative least squares. Args: img: Input image array of shape (H, W, C) with values in [0, 1]. ref: Reference image array of shape (H, W, C) with values in [0, 1]. numiters: Number of iterations. eps: Clipping threshold. Returns: imgwarped: Warped image array of shape (H, W, C). """ # Flatten images imgmat = img.reshape(-1, img.shape[-1]) refmat = ref.reshape(-1, ref.shape[-1]) C = imgmat.shape[1] N = imgmat.shape[0] # Helper for unclipped check def isunclipped(z): return (z >= eps) & (z <= 1 - eps) # Initialize mask for unclipped pixels in input mask0 = isunclipped(imgmat) for in range(numiters): # Construct amat for current imgmat # Quadratic terms: xc xc' for c <= c' quadterms = [] for c1 in range(C): for c2 in range(c1, C): quadterms.append((imgmat[:, c1] imgmat[:, c2]).reshape(-1, 1)) # Linear terms linearterms = imgmat # Bias term biasterms = np.ones((N, 1)) # Concatenate amat = np.concatenate(quadterms + [linearterms, biasterms], axis=1) # Initialize warp coefficients warp = np.zeros((amat.shape[1], C)) for c in range(C): b = refmat[:, c] # Update mask: unclipped in input, unclipped in current img estimate, unclipped in ref currentimgunclipped = isunclipped(imgmat[:, c]) refunclipped = isunclipped(b) mask = mask0[:, c] & currentimgunclipped & refunclipped # Masked matrices maskeda = amat[mask] maskedb = b[mask] # Solve least squares # w = argmin || maskeda @ w - maskedb ||^2 w = np.linalg.lstsq(maskeda, maskedb, rcond=-1)[0] warp[:, c] = w # Apply warp imgmat = np.clip(amat @ warp, 0, 1) # Reshape back imgwarped = imgmat.reshape(img.shape) return imgwarped Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles non-linear color mappings effectively. Iterative masking reduces the impact of clipped pixels, which are common in HDR or high-contrast images. Limitations: Computationally expensive for large images due to the quadratic expansion. Sensitive to the choice of eps; too small a value may include noisy clipped pixels, too large a value may discard valid data. When to use: When static color correction fails to match complex non-linear color distributions between two images. When not to use: For real-time applications or very large images where performance is a concern. Iterative Color Matching is used in computer vision and graphics for color correction and initialization of splat colors. It is implemented in projects such as AnySplat and mrGSplat. The method relies on iterative least squares estimation to handle non-linearities and clipping, which are common challenges in image processing. name: Palette Remapping
head: Color Palette Remapping, Schematic Color Remapping
body: Palette Remapping replaces the colors of a source volume or image with colors from a target palette, ensuring the output strictly adheres to a limited set of allowed colors. It differs from Windowing and Colormap Application for Visualization by mapping discrete source colors to discrete target palette entries rather than interpolating continuous scalar values into a gradient. Inputs: A source schematic or volume containing a set of unique colors and a target palette. Outputs: A remapped schematic or volume where each voxel's color is replaced by the closest match in the target palette. Data Structures: 1. Source Colors List: A collection of unique colors found in the input. 2. Target Palette: An ordered list of colors, typically capped at 256 entries for 8-bit indexing. 3. Palette Dictionary: A hash map mapping source color identifiers (RGB tuples) to their corresponding index in the target palette. Steps: 1. Collect all unique colors used in the input schematic via schematic.UsedColors. 2. For each unique color, find its index in the target palette using ColorComparison.CompareColorRGB and store the mapping in paletteDictionary. 3. Iterate over all voxels in the schematic. 4. Replace each voxel's color with the remapped color from the target palette using the dictionary lookup. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Standard squared Euclidean distance is used for color comparison. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Target palette size is typically capped at 256 entries for 8-bit indexing. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If a color in the schematic is not found in the palette, the dictionary lookup may throw a KeyNotFoundException or return an invalid index, as the code assumes CompareColorRGB always succeeds. A fallback strategy (e.g., default color or nearest neighbor with tolerance) is required. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def remappalette(sourceschematic, targetpalette): # Step 1: Collect unique colors sourcecolors = set() if hasattr(sourceschematic, 'UsedColors'): sourcecolors = set(sourceschematic.UsedColors()) else: for voxel in sourceschematic.voxels: sourcecolors.add(voxel.color) # Step 2: Build mapping palettedictionary = {} for srccolor in sourcecolors: bestindex = 0 mindistance = float('inf') for idx, tgtcolor in enumerate(targetpalette): distance = comparecolorrgb(srccolor, tgtcolor) if distance < mindistance: mindistance = distance bestindex = idx palettedictionary[srccolor] = bestindex # Step 3: Remap voxels for voxel in sourceschematic.voxels: if voxel.color in palettedictionary: mappedindex = palettedictionary[voxel.color] voxel.color = targetpalette[mappedindex] else: voxel.color = targetpalette[0] # Fallback for missing colors return sourceschematic def comparecolorrgb(colora, colorb): rdiff = colora.r - colorb.r gdiff = colora.g - colorb.g bdiff = colora.b - colorb.b return rdiff2 + gdiff2 + bdiff2 A technique to find the best matching color from a palette by computing error in gamma-corrected space, optionally using a precomputed lookup table for performance. It precomputes a 16×16×16 lookup table (4096 entries) where each entry stores an unsigned int packing foreground (5 bits) and background (5 bits) indices as (bg << 5) | fg. For each input color, gamma correction (power 2.2) is applied to palette entries and the input color before computing error. The error metric is the squared Euclidean distance in gamma space, with an additional weight of 0.04 on the difference between foreground and background gamma values. The formula for error E between a target color C and a palette entry with foreground P{fg} and background P{bg} is: E = \sum{c \in \{r,g,b\}} (\gamma(P{bg,c}) - \gamma(Cc))^2 + 0.04 \sum{c \in \{r,g,b\}} (\gamma(P{bg,c}) - \gamma(P{fg,c}))^2 Parameters include a gamma exponent of 2.2 and an error weight of 0.04. This variant is chosen when perceptual accuracy is prioritized over raw RGB distance and performance constraints allow a 4096-entry LUT. A process to remove color palettes that do not contribute significantly to the stylization, reducing the number of base colors used. It initializes NP = 8 base colors according to a uniform distribution \hat{P} \sim U[0, 1). It samples 10 poses from the training dataset and evaluates the weight network. It derives a per-palette mean contribution, which is always between 0 and 1. Finally, it removes all color palettes with a mean contribution less than the threshold of 0.025. A user-controlled linear transformation of the learned weights \hat{w} using palette weights and biases to modify the importance of individual base colors. The transformation is applied as: \hat{w}{\text{new}} = \min(\hat{w}{\text{old}} \cdot \hat{w}P + \hat{b}P, 0) followed by normalization of \hat{w}{\text{new}} by its sum. Variables are \hat{w}{\text{old}} (original weight), \hat{w}P (palette weight), and \hat{b}P (palette bias). Parameters are palette weights \hat{w}P \in \mathbb{R}^{NP} and palette biases \hat{b}P \in [-1, 1]^{NP}. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M) for building the mapping where N is the number of unique source colors and M is the target palette size; the remapping step is O(V) where V is the number of voxels, assuming O(1) dictionary lookup. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the source colors and the dictionary. The gamma-corrected variant uses a fixed 4096-entry table. Strengths: Guarantees output colors are strictly from the target palette; fast lookup after initial mapping; simple to implement. Limitations: Discontinuous color transitions if source colors are not well-represented in the target palette; sensitive to the definition of "closest" color; potential for KeyNotFoundException if source colors are not found. When to use: Schematic visualization, voxel art conversion, or any scenario requiring a strict, limited color set. When not to use: When smooth gradients or continuous color mapping are required (use Colormap Application for Visualization instead). Palette Remapping is commonly used in voxel-based game engines and schematic tools to convert high-color-depth models into formats that support limited palettes, such as the Minecraft.schematic format or legacy 8-bit display modes. The technique is implemented in tools like FileToVox for converting.vox files to schematics. It is also adapted in neural radiance field stylization pipelines to manage and prune learned color palettes for efficient rendering. name: Color Composition
head: AWP Color Composition, Adaptive Weighted Color Composition
body: Color composition aggregates multiple color samples along a ray into a final pixel color using learned or adaptive weights. It solves the problem of combining contributions from different semantic or physical regions (e.g., rigid vs. non-rigid motion) into a single coherent visual output. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Windowing and Colormap Application for Visualization by explicitly modeling weighted blending of distinct color sources rather than simple thresholding or direct mapping. The method varies by variant. The primary implementation (AWP Color Composition) uses a neural network to predict weights. Inputs: \hat{C}{s;i}: Predicted or sampled colors for sample i along ray s. ms{;0,...,k}: Rigid weights. m^{p-rig}{s;i}: Adaptive non-rigid weights. \tilde{m}^{p}{s;0}: Adaptive weight for the primary component. Outputs: \hat{B}{sp}: Composed color for rigid components. \tilde{B}{sp}: Composed color for adaptive components. Weights: Scalars normalized such that \sum{i=0}^{k} ms{;i} = 1. Colors: RGB vectors. Before composition, all input colors are tone-mapped using a gamma function: g(c0) = c0^{\frac{1}{2.2}} where c0 is the predicted scene irradiance or color value. The final color is computed as a sum of tone-mapped colors weighted by rigid and adaptive factors: \hat{B}{sp} = ms{;0} g(\hat{C}{s;0}) + \sum{i=1}^{k} m^{p-rig}{s;i} g(\hat{C}{s;i}) \tilde{B}{sp} = \tilde{m}^{p}{s;0} g(\hat{C}{s;0}) + \sum{i=1}^{k} \tilde{m}^{p-rig}{s;i} g(\hat{C}{s;i}) Where: ms{;0,...,k} are rigid weights normalized along the motion axis k. m^{p-rig}{s;i} and \tilde{m}^{p-rig}{s;i} are adaptive weights derived from an Adaptive Weighted Prediction (AWP) module. k is a hyper-parameter controlling the number of rigid camera motions. Details for a CTF-specific blending variant are not given in the sources. k: Number of rigid camera motions (hyper-parameter). Normalization: Rigid weights ms{;0,...,k} must be normalized along the motion axis k to ensure \sum{i=0}^{k} ms{;i} = 1. Tone Mapping: Failure to tone-map predicted irradiance colors before composition can lead to incorrect visual results. Transparency: The transparency compositing formula (see Subtopics) is often omitted in basic raycasters, resulting in opaque images only. Lightness-Controlled Color Harmonization is a technique for volume visualization that transforms a transfer function’s color distribution to fit a specific harmonic template while strictly preserving the original lightness values. It solves the problem that standard hue-based harmonization alters lightness, thereby destroying the perceptual contrast and "pop-out" effects critical for highlighting density intervals. It sets itself apart from Windowing and Colormap Application for Visualization by operating in the perceptually uniform CIE LAB space to decouple hue shifts from lightness changes, ensuring that visual salience is maintained during colorization. Choose this when perceptual contrast must be preserved during colorization. Lightness-Controlled Color Harmonization Harmonized Color Change is a local feature enhancement technique for volume rendering that replaces the computed color of a sample with its harmonic (complementary) counterpart when the sample represents a significant local density peak. It solves the problem of subtle internal structures being lost in the global color palette by providing high-contrast visual cues for boundaries and high-density regions without altering the overall perceptual impression of the volume. It differs from Lightness-Controlled Color Harmonization by using hue complementarity rather than lightness adjustment, and from Iterative Color Matching by being a direct, non-iterative replacement based on local density gradients. Choose this for highlighting local density peaks without global palette shifts. Harmonized Color Change Details for this variant are not given in the sources. Choose this when semantic clustering is required alongside voxel data. CTF Color Blending Applies the standard alpha compositing formula recursively along the ray: C{out} = C{in} (1 - \alpha(Xi)) + C(Xi) \alpha(Xi) Where C(Xi) is shading from the local gradient, \alpha(Xi) is opacity from the CT value, C{out} is outgoing intensity, and C{in} is incoming intensity. The recursion stops when \alpha(Xi) = 0 (e.g., bone). Pitfall: Many implementations (including the one in) do not implement this formula, offering only opaque images. Complexity: Linear in the number of samples k and ray length. The AWP variant adds neural network inference cost for weight prediction. Performance: Dependent on the efficiency of the MLPs used for weight prediction in AWP. Strengths: Allows for physically plausible blending of motion-blurred or semantically distinct regions. Limitations: Requires careful normalization of weights. The transparency formula is often omitted in simple implementations. The AWP Color Composition method originates from DP-NeRF, which introduces adaptive weighted prediction for deblurring Neural Radiance Fields. The transparency compositing approach is a standard volume rendering technique, though specific implementations vary. name: Lightness-Controlled Color Harmonization
head: Lightness-Preserving Harmonic Colorization, Lightness-preserving color harmonization
body: Lightness-Controlled Color Harmonization is a technique for volume visualization that transforms a transfer function’s color distribution to fit a specific harmonic template while strictly preserving the original lightness values. It solves the problem that standard hue-based harmonization (e.g., Cohen et al.) alters lightness, thereby destroying the perceptual contrast and "pop-out" effects critical for highlighting density intervals. It sets itself apart from Windowing and Colormap Application for Visualization by operating in the perceptually uniform CIE LAB space to decouple hue shifts from lightness changes, ensuring that visual salience is maintained during colorization. The method maps RGB transfer function values through HSV to CIE LAB space to find a target hue that matches a harmonic template while retaining the source lightness. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An RGB transfer function (TF) defined over scalar density values; a target harmonic hue template (e.g., from the 8 Itten/Matsuda types). Output: A harmonized RGB transfer function where hues follow the template but lightness L^ is preserved from the input. Data Structures: Transfer Function: A set of N triples (ri, gi, bi) representing color at specific density intervals. Harmonic Template: One of 8 predefined hue distributions (I, V, L, I, T, Y, X, N). The N-type consists only of grey hues. Templates can be rotated by an arbitrary angle \theta but cannot be resized. Steps: 1. Convert to HSV: Transform each RGB triple (ri, gi, bi) of the transfer function into HSV coordinates (Hi, Si, Vi). 2. Map to CIE LAB: Map each HSV triple to CIE LAB space (L^i, a^i, b^i). 3. Locate Harmonized LAB Value: For each TF entry, locate the LAB triple (L^{new}, a^{new}, b^{new}) such that it has the target hue (from the harmonic template), the source saturation, and the source lightness. 4. Convert to RGB: Convert the resulting LAB triple back to RGB to obtain the harmonized transfer function. The algorithm must prioritize lightness preservation, potentially resulting in less saturated colors if the target hue demands higher lightness than the source. It addresses the limitation of hue-only harmonization by preserving existing lightness contrasts and salience, which are critical for highlighting and contrast enhancement. Unlike standard HSV manipulation, this method accounts for the non-perceptual nature of HSV by grounding color adjustments in the perceptually uniform CIE LAB space. Harmonic Color Harmonization is a method that transforms a given image with a non-harmonic hue distribution into one that fits a specific harmonic hue template, using optimization to re-colorize the image while preserving lightness. It accepts an image with a possibly non-harmonic hue distribution, finds the closest (rotated) harmonic hue template, and uses an optimization algorithm to re-colorize the image to have a hue distribution that fits the nearest harmonic template. Pixels with higher saturation receive more weight in the template matching procedure because their hue is perceptually more salient. The eight harmonic hue wheel templates (I, V, L, I, T, Y, X, N) define grey sectors where the hue histogram must occupy; the N-type is composed only of grey hues. Templates can be rotated by an arbitrary angle but cannot be resized. A limitation is that the base algorithm only considers hue, not saturation or lightness, which is a drawback for volume visualization where lightness preservation is critical. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of transfer function entries, as each entry undergoes a fixed sequence of color space conversions. Memory Complexity: Constant per entry, requiring storage for intermediate HSV and LAB values. Performance: The method preserves contrast and details significantly better than Cohen et al.'s method, as observed in volume renderings of the Buckyball and human silhouettes. Strengths: Maintains lightness channel to support the pop-out effect; preserves contrast relationships between density intervals; perceptually uniform adjustments via CIE LAB. Limitations: Monitor-specific mapping requires accurate sRGB conversion and white point adaptation; cannot always increase lightness without sacrificing saturation; N-type templates may result in desaturated outputs. When to use: When harmonic color schemes are desired but visual salience and density contrast must be preserved. When not to use: When monitor-independent color reproduction is critical without calibration; when the N-type (grey) template is used and chroma is needed. The method originates from the work of Wang and Mueller (2008) on "Harmonic Colormaps for Volume Visualization". It builds upon Itten’s color wheel and Matsuda’s 80 harmonic color schemes, which were the basis for Cohen et al.'s automated image color harmonization system. Cohen et al.'s method allowed users to transform ill-chosen scene colorizations into harmonious ones but only shifted hue in HSV space, changing lightness and destroying visual salience. Wang and Mueller extended this by introducing CIE LAB-based iso-lightness curves to preserve lightness during hue harmonization, addressing the specific needs of volume visualization where lightness contrasts guide the viewer. name: Iso-lightness Curve Mapping
body: Iso-lightness curve mapping is a technique that uses iso-lightness curves derived from the CIE LAB color space, mapped onto HSV hue slices, to determine the correct saturation/lightness trade-off when shifting hues in volume visualization. It addresses the limitation of hue-only harmonization by preserving existing lightness contrasts and salience, which are critical for highlighting and contrast enhancement. Unlike standard HSV manipulation, this method accounts for the non-perceptual nature of HSV by grounding color adjustments in the perceptually uniform CIE LAB space. The method maps transfer function parameters from HSV to CIE LAB to ensure that hue changes do not inadvertently alter the perceived lightness of the volume data. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A source HSV triple (Hs, Ss, Ls) representing a color in the transfer function; a target hue Ht for harmonization. Output: A target HSV triple (Ht, St, Lt) that maintains the source lightness Ls while adopting the target hue. Data Structures: Iso-lightness Curves: A set of pre-computed trajectories in CIE LAB space. Each curve corresponds to a specific hue slice in HSV space. For a given hue in HSV, the trajectory in CIE LAB space maintains constant lightness while varying chroma. Monitor Profile: Required for accurate sRGB conversion, specifically the monitor's white point. Steps: 1. Derive Iso-lightness Curves: Convert the monitor's sRGB color space to CIE XYZ using the monitor's specific white point. Convert CIE XYZ to CIE LAB. For a given hue in HSV, identify the trajectory in CIE LAB space that maintains constant lightness while varying chroma. These trajectories form the iso-lightness curves. Note that these curves are monitor-specific. 2. Map Source Color to LAB: Convert the source HSV triple to sRGB, then to CIE XYZ using the monitor's white point, and finally to CIE LAB (Ls, as, bs). 3. Locate Target Color: Determine the target hue Ht. In the CIE LAB space, locate the point that has the target hue and the source lightness Ls. This involves finding the intersection of the iso-lightness curve corresponding to the target hue with the lightness plane defined by Ls. 4. Handle Saturation/Lightness Trade-off: If the target hue's iso-lightness curve does not allow the desired saturation at the source lightness, the method identifies the closest valid point on the curve. The resulting LAB triple is converted back to HSV to yield the final harmonized color. Parameters: Monitor White Point: Essential for the sRGB to XYZ conversion. Tolerance Levels: CIE LAB is perceptually uniform within certain tolerance levels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Monitor Specificity: The iso-lightness curves are monitor-specific. Impossible Lightness: It is not always possible to increase lightness without sacrificing saturation. HSV Non-Perceptual Nature: HSV is not a perceptual color space. This variant uses equi-lightness curves to design color scales where vividness (chroma) changes from high to low while keeping lightness constant. By applying such a scale, specific features in volume data can be highlighted, drawing the observer's attention without altering the lightness-based contrast of other features. This leverages the "pop-out" effect of vivid colors while maintaining the structural integrity provided by lightness. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Preserves lightness contrasts, which are crucial for highlighting, contrast enhancement, and pop-out in volume visualization. Allows for harmonic colorization without losing salience. Limitations: Monitor-specific, requiring accurate white point calibration. CIE LAB is only perceptually uniform within certain tolerance levels. When to use: When harmonic colorization is desired but lightness-based features (like highlighting) must be preserved. When not to use: When monitor-specific calibration is unavailable. The method was introduced by Wang and Mueller in 2008 as part of their work on harmonic colormaps for volume visualization. It addresses a significant shortcoming of previous color harmonization frameworks, which did not preserve lightness. The technique builds on the observation that HSV is intuitive but inappropriate for lightness preservation, while CIE LAB is perceptually uniform. name: Harmonized Color Change
head: Harmonic color feature emphasis
body: Harmonized Color Change is a local feature enhancement technique for volume rendering that replaces a sample's computed color with its harmonic (complementary) counterpart when the sample represents a significant local density peak. It solves the problem of subtle internal structures being lost in the global color palette by providing high-contrast visual cues for boundaries and high-density regions without altering the overall perceptual impression of the volume. It differs from Lightness-Controlled Color Harmonization by using hue complementarity rather than lightness adjustment, and from Iterative Color Matching by being a direct, non-iterative replacement based on local density gradients. Inputs: Volume dataset V with scalar density values. Ray casting parameters (view direction, sample positions). Base color transfer function C{base}(d) mapping density d to RGB. Shading model (e.g., Phong) to compute initial sample color C{phong}. Neighborhood radius r for density averaging. Threshold factor \alpha for density comparison (Not given in the sources). Outputs: Final pixel color C{final}. Data Structures: Sample point p with position \mathbf{x}, density d(\mathbf{x}), and normal \mathbf{n} (if shading is used). Neighborhood set N(\mathbf{x}) = \{ \mathbf{x}i \mid \|\mathbf{x}i - \mathbf{x}\| \le r \}. Steps: 1. Compute Base Color: Calculate the initial color C{phong} for the sample at \mathbf{x} using the chosen shading model and the base transfer function. 2. Determine Harmonic Color: Convert C{phong} to a hue-based representation (e.g., HSV or HSL). Identify the complementary hue H{comp} by rotating the hue angle by 180^\circ on the color circle. Reconstruct the harmonic color C{harmonic} using H{comp} and the original saturation/value components. 3. Transform to CIELab: Convert C{harmonic} to CIELab color space. 4. Check Density Condition: Calculate the average density \bar{d} of the neighborhood N(\mathbf{x}). Check if the sample's density d(\mathbf{x}) is significantly larger than \bar{d}. Condition: d(\mathbf{x}) > \bar{d} + \alpha or d(\mathbf{x}) > k \cdot \bar{d} (exact formula not given in the sources). 5. Replace and Enhance: If the condition is met, replace C{phong} with C{harmonic}. Apply a lightening unsharp masking equation to emphasize the feature. Formula: C{final} = C{harmonic} + \beta (C{harmonic} - C{blurred}) (Equation 4.2 in, specific coefficients not given in the sources). If the condition is not met, C{final} = C{phong}. Parameters: Neighborhood radius r (Not given in the sources). Threshold factor \alpha (Not given in the sources). Lightening factor \beta (Not given in the sources). Multi-scale volume hierarchy levels (2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 16, 32) for applying lightening and darkening effects. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: At volume boundaries, the neighborhood N(\mathbf{x}) may be incomplete, affecting \bar{d} calculation. If the volume has uniform density, the condition d(\mathbf{x}) > \bar{d} will never be met, and no enhancement occurs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def harmonizedcolorchange(sample, neighborhood): # 1. Compute Phong color Cphong = computephongcolor(sample) # 2. Determine harmonic color H = rgbtohue(Cphong) Hcomp = (H + 180.0) % 360.0 Charmonic = huetorgb(Hcomp, sample.saturation, sample.value) # 3. Transform to CIELab Charmoniclab = rgbtocielab(Charmonic) # 4. Check density condition davg = meandensity(neighborhood) if sample.density > davg: # Condition met if significantly bigger # 5. Replace and enhance Cblurred = applyblur(Charmoniclab) Cfinallab = Charmoniclab + beta (Charmoniclab - Cblurred) return cielabtorgb(Cfinallab) else: return Cphong Contextual Color Ghosting is a variant used in focus+context rendering where the context (non-focus) data is rendered in grayscale to enhance the perception of the colored focus by contrast. It is chosen when the user wants to reduce visual clutter in the background while preserving color information in the region of interest. The color of the contextual cluster can be computed using structural coloring or, if the color ghosting flag is activated, set to grayscale by considering only the node's intensity rather than RGB values. The opacity of contextual clusters is modulated inversely proportional to the depth of the nodes in the hierarchy. Measured Performance: Tested on volume models up to 512 \times 512 \times 512 voxels. Strengths: Enhances local features without changing the overall color impression; effective for pollen grain and orange data sets. When to use: When local density peaks need to be highlighted without altering the global color scheme. The method was proposed in the context of enhancing local features in volume visualization using harmonic colors to stress important details. It was tested on various volume models, including pollen grains and orange data sets, demonstrating its effectiveness in emphasizing boundaries and high-density regions. The approach is part of a broader effort to improve the perceptual quality of volume rendering by leveraging color theory principles. name: Reference Image Guided Colorization
body: Reference Image Guided Colorization transfers color attributes from a semantically aligned reference image to a monochromatic target image or volume rendering. It solves the tedious trial-and-error process of manual transfer function design by automating color assignment. Unlike learning-based methods that require large-scale training datasets, it operates directly on pixel colors or deep features using a comparatively small set of reference images. The family shares the goal of mapping chromatic properties from a reference image R to a target image or volume T while preserving the structural content of T. The specific mechanism, parameters, and mathematical formulation vary by child method. Common steps include feature extraction, correspondence or statistical matching, and color transfer filtering. This method automates the colorization of monochromatic medical volume data (CT/MRI) by transferring visual attributes from a database of colored reference images (e.g., cryosections) using deep semantic correspondence. It distinguishes itself from traditional volume rendering by replacing user-defined color/opacity parameters with automatic color transfer and luminance-based opacity, and from learning-based colorization by requiring only a small set of reference images rather than large-scale training datasets. See Reference Based Color Transfer for Medical Volume Rendering. Color Transfer is a post-processing technique applied to improve the color match between final volume renderings and an input style image. It serves as a lightweight alternative to full neural style transfer by operating directly on pixel colors rather than deep feature spaces, ensuring the structural content of the target volume remains unchanged while adopting the chromatic properties of the reference. Args: targetrgb: numpy array of shape (H, W, 3) referencergb: numpy array of shape (H, W, 3) Returns: outputrgb: numpy array of shape (H, W, 3) """ import numpy as np # Convert RGB to Lab color space targetlab = rgb2lab(targetrgb) referencelab = rgb2lab(referencergb) # Extract luminance (L) and chrominance (a, b) channels LT = targetlab[:,:, 0] aT = targetlab[:,:, 1] bT = targetlab[:,:, 2] aR = referencelab[:,:, 1] bR = referencelab[:,:, 2] # Compute mean and standard deviation for chrominance channels muaT, sigmaaT = np.mean(aT), np.std(aT) mubT, sigmabT = np.mean(bT), np.std(bT) muaR, sigmaaR = np.mean(aR), np.std(aR) mubR, sigmabR = np.mean(bR), np.std(bR) # Guard against zero variance in target chrominance channels eps = 1e-8 sigmaaT = max(sigmaaT, eps) sigmabT = max(sigmabT, eps) # Normalize and scale chrominance channels to match reference statistics aprime = ((aT - muaT) / sigmaaT) sigmaaR + muaR bprime = ((bT - mubT) / sigmabT) sigmabR + mubR # Reconstruct image with original luminance and scaled chrominance outputlab = np.stack([LT, aprime, bprime], axis=-1) # Convert back to RGB outputrgb = lab2rgb(outputlab) return outputrgb def rgb2lab(rgb): """Standard RGB to Lab conversion.""" pass def lab2rgb(lab): """Standard Lab to RGB conversion.""" pass Trained Exposure Application is a post-processing step applied to rendered RGB images to normalize their appearance to match the exposure conditions present in the training dataset. It solves the problem of domain shift where test-time rendering conditions differ from the conditions the model was trained on. It differs from its sibling Reference Based Color Transfer for Medical Volume Rendering by using a fixed, data-driven affine transform rather than a learned style transfer, and from Color Transfer by operating on a per-image basis using stored metadata rather than global histogram matching. See Trained Exposure Application. The Appearance Optimization Module is a learnable neural network component designed to refine the colors of 3D Gaussian splats by predicting per-image color offsets based on viewing direction and scene context. It solves the problem of static, view-independent color assignment in Gaussian Splatting by introducing appearance variability that adapts to specific camera viewpoints and lighting conditions. Unlike standard Gaussian Splatting which uses fixed spherical harmonics for color, this module decouples structural color from appearance adjustments, allowing for more realistic rendering of dynamic lighting or material variations. See Appearance Optimization Module. A colorization technique applied after gamma encoding to transfer color from a reference image to a target image. Parameters: Radius r = 16, Regularization term \epsilon = 2. A colorization technique applied after gamma encoding to transfer color from a reference image to a target image. Parameters: Lambda \lambda = 32, Sigma range \sigmar = 200. Loss function for color editing, combining reconstruction loss against user-specified foreground/background colors and regularization loss to prevent large weight deviations. Optimize L{color} over latent color vector z(c) and F{rad} using Adam optimizer with learning rate 10^{-2}. Formula: L{color} = L{rec} + \lambda{reg} \cdot L{reg}, where L{reg} penalizes squared difference between original and updated model weights. Parameter: Regularization weight \lambda{reg} = 10. A practical alternative to manual painting where voxel colors are derived from an appearance source image aligned with the 3D object. Un-project the color of the pixels from the appearance source image directly onto the voxels. Project the centers of the voxels to the image using the camera parameters. Take the color for every voxel from the pixel it falls into. Input: An appearance source image A aligned with the 3D object. Requires aligned images with the 3D objects, though recent 2D-to-3D alignment advances can provide this automatically. Input consists of the rerendered image S (generated by splatting voxels onto the image plane) plus the light position as an additional channel. Output is the target image T. name: Reference Based Color Transfer for Medical Volume Rendering
head: Deep Semantic Color Transfer
body: This method automates the colorization of monochromatic medical volume data (CT/MRI) by transferring color attributes from a database of semantically similar colored reference images (e.g., cryosections). It eliminates the need for manual user interaction with transfer functions to define color mappings, addressing the tedious trial-and-error process of traditional volume rendering. Unlike learning-based methods requiring large-scale training datasets, this approach uses a comparatively smaller set of reference images. It builds on Reference Image Guided Colorization by integrating a semantic recommendation engine and applying the result to direct volume rendering. Inputs: 1. A stack of monochromatic medical images (Target T), such as CT scans or MRI slices. 2. A database of colored reference images (R), such as histological cryosections. Outputs: 1. A stack of colorized images with RGBA values. 2. A rendered 3D volume visualization. Data Structures: Feature Maps: Multi-level feature vectors extracted from a pre-trained CNN (VGG-19) for both T and R. Correspondence Map: A dense pixel-to-pixel mapping between T and R in the deep feature domain, computed via PatchMatch. Intermediate Image (T'): An image constructed via dense correspondence that contains the visual attributes of R. Colorized Image: The final output where RGB channels come from the filtered color transfer and the Alpha channel comes from the original target luminance. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Extract multi-level feature maps from the target image T and each candidate reference image R using a pre-trained VGG-19 network. 2. Reference Recommendation: Compute deep features for the target T and query the database to select the top-k semantically similar reference images. 3. Dense Correspondence (Deep Image Analogy): For each selected reference R, establish dense correspondence with T in the deep feature domain using the PatchMatch algorithm. This constructs an intermediate image T' that contains the visual attributes of R. 4. Color Isolation (Guided Image Filter): Apply a Guided Image Filter (GIF) to T' using the original target image T as the guidance image. This isolates the transferred color information while discarding texture and style artifacts from R. 5. Volumetric Mapping: Assign the RGB components from the colorized image to the volume voxels. Derive the Alpha (opacity) channel directly from the luminance values of the original monochromatic target data. 6. Volume Rendering: Perform direct volume rendering (ray casting) on the stack of colorized images using the derived RGBA values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def referencebasedcolortransfervolumerendering(targetstack, referencedb, vgg19model): """ Performs color transfer and volume rendering for a stack of medical images. Args: targetstack: List of monochromatic medical images (H, W) or (H, W, 1). referencedb: List of colored reference images (H, W, 3). vgg19model: Pre-trained VGG-19 network for feature extraction. Returns: renderedvolume: List of RGBA images (H, W, 4) ready for ray casting. """ colorizedstack = [] for targetimage in targetstack: # Step 1 & 2: Feature Extraction and Reference Recommendation targetfeatures = extractdeepfeatures(targetimage, vgg19model) selectedreferences = recommendreferences(targetfeatures, referencedb, vgg19model) # Step 3: Dense Correspondence and Step 4: Color Isolation bestreference = selectedreferences[0] intermediateimage = deepimageanalogy(targetimage, bestreference, vgg19model) colorizedimage = guidedimagefilter(intermediateimage, targetimage) # Step 5: Volumetric Mapping alphachannel = computeluminance(targetimage) rgbaimage = combinergba(colorizedimage, alphachannel) colorizedstack.append(rgbaimage) # Step 6: Volume Rendering renderedvolume = directvolumerender(colorizedstack) return renderedvolume def extractdeepfeatures(image, model): """Extracts multi-level feature maps using VGG-19.: Standard CNN forward pass.""" # Source does not specify exact layer indices return model.getfeatures(image) def recommendreferences(targetfeatures, referencedb, vgg19model): """Selects semantically similar reference images using deep features.""" similarities = [] for ref in referencedb: reffeatures = extractdeepfeatures(ref, vgg19model) sim = cosinesimilarity(targetfeatures, reffeatures) similarities.append((ref, sim)) similarities.sort(key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True) return [ref for ref, in similarities[:3]] def cosinesimilarity(a, b): """Computes cosine similarity between two flattened vectors.""" aflat = a.flatten() if hasattr(a, 'flatten') else np.array(a).flatten() bflat = b.flatten() if hasattr(b, 'flatten') else np.array(b).flatten() dot = np.dot(aflat, bflat) norma = np.linalg.norm(aflat) normb = np.linalg.norm(bflat) return dot / (norma normb + 1e-8) def deepimageanalogy(target, reference, vgg19model): """Constructs T' using Deep Image Analogy via PatchMatch in deep feature domain.""" tfeatures = extractdeepfeatures(target, vgg19model) rfeatures = extractdeepfeatures(reference, vgg19model) #: PatchMatch finds nearest neighbors in feature space # Source does not specify exact PatchMatch implementation details correspondence = findcorrespondence(tfeatures, rfeatures) # Reconstruct T' by transferring visual attributes tprime = reconstructimage(target, reference, correspondence) return tprime def findcorrespondence(tfeatures, rfeatures): """Finds dense correspondence map.""" # Simplified nearest-neighbor search for self-containment tflat = tfeatures.reshape(-1, tfeatures.shape[-1]) rflat = rfeatures.reshape(-1, rfeatures.shape[-1]) dists = np.linalg.norm(tflat[:, None,:] - rflat[None,:,:], axis=2) indices = np.argmin(dists, axis=1) return indices.reshape(tfeatures.shape[:2]) def reconstructimage(target, reference, correspondence): """Reconstructs T' by mapping reference colors via correspondence.""" h, w = target.shape[:2] tprime = np.zeros((h, w, 3), dtype=np.float32) for y in range(h): for x in range(w): idx = correspondence[y, x] tprime[y, x] = reference.reshape(-1, 3)[idx] return tprime def guidedimagefilter(source, guidance): """Applies Guided Image Filter to isolate color.""" #: Standard GIF implementation. Source does not specify parameters # Simplified to a 3x3 box filter for self-containment kernel = np.ones((3, 3), dtype=np.float32) / 9.0 filtered = np.zeroslike(source) for c in range(3): channel = source[:,:, c] padded = np.pad(channel, 1, mode='edge') out = np.zeroslike(channel) for dy in range(3): for dx in range(3): out += padded[dy:dy+channel.shape[0], dx:dx+channel.shape[1]] filtered[:,:, c] = out return filtered def computeluminance(image): """Computes luminance from a grayscale image.""" return image if image.ndim == 2 else np.mean(image, axis=2) def combinergba(color, alpha): """Combines RGB color and Alpha channel.""" return np.stack([color[:,:, 0], color[:,:, 1], color[:,:, 2], alpha], axis=-1) def directvolumerender(stack): """Performs ray casting on the RGBA stack.""" #: Standard direct volume rendering accumulation. Source does not specify ray casting details return stack Parameters: Feature Extractor: VGG-19. Opacity Mapping: Voxel luminance is mapped directly to the alpha channel. Reference Selection: Top-k semantically similar images (exact k not specified). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Opacity Determination: The method does not address the automatic determination of opacity parameters from a transfer function; it relies solely on voxel luminance for alpha. Texture/Style Leakage: Without the Guided Image Filter, the intermediate image T' may contain unwanted texture and style artifacts from the reference image. Reference Suitability: The quality of colorization depends on the semantic similarity between the target and the selected reference images. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Eliminates tedious user interaction with transfer functions; requires a comparatively smaller set of reference images than learning-based methods. Limitations: Does not automatically determine opacity parameters; relies on the availability of semantically similar colored reference images (e.g., cryosections). When to use: When manual transfer function tuning is prohibitive and high-quality colored reference data (like histology) is available for the anatomical region. When not to use: When opacity needs to be tuned based on specific diagnostic criteria not correlated with luminance, or when no suitable colored references exist. The method was proposed by Devkota et al. in 2020/2022. It extends the work of Liao et al. on Deep Image Analogy to the domain of medical imaging. The authors used the Visible Human Project dataset, including 33 MRI samples, 328 CT scans, and 696 color cryosections. The approach aims to enhance medical professionals' ability to extract valuable information by providing colored 3D representations without manual intervention. name: Color Transfer
head: Reference Image Color Transfer, Style Transfer (Color)
body: Color Transfer is a post-processing technique that improves the color match between final volume renderings and an input style image. It builds on Reference Image Guided Colorization by mapping the chromatic properties of a reference image onto a target rendering while preserving the target's structural content. It differs from sibling methods like Trained Exposure Application by applying a direct statistical color mapping rather than learned exposure adjustments. Inputs: Target image T (final volume rendering), Reference image R (style image). Outputs: Stylized image O. Data Structures: Images are represented as 2D arrays of pixel values. Each pixel is a vector (r, g, b). Steps: 1. Color Space Conversion: Convert T and R from RGB to a color space that separates luminance from chrominance, such as CIELAB. Let LT, aT, bT be the channels of T and LR, aR, bR be the channels of R. 2. Statistical Matching: Compute the mean (\mu) and standard deviation (\sigma) for the chrominance channels (a and b) of both images. For the target: \mu{aT}, \sigma{aT}, \mu{bT}, \sigma{bT} For the reference: \mu{aR}, \sigma{aR}, \mu{bR}, \sigma{bR} 3. Normalization and Scaling: Adjust the chrominance channels of the target image to match the reference's statistics. a'T = \frac{aT - \mu{aT}}{\sigma{aT}} \sigma{aR} + \mu{aR} b'T = \frac{bT - \mu{bT}}{\sigma{bT}} \sigma{bR} + \mu{bR} 4. Reconstruction: Combine the original luminance channel LT with the scaled chrominance channels a'T and b'T. 5. Conversion: Convert the resulting Lab image back to RGB to produce O. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def colortransferstatistical(targetrgb, referencergb): """ Transfers color statistics from reference to target in Lab color space. Args: targetrgb: numpy array of shape (H, W, 3) referencergb: numpy array of shape (H, W, 3) Returns: outputrgb: numpy array of shape (H, W, 3) """ import numpy as np # Convert RGB to Lab color space Standard sRGB to XYZ to Lab matrix conversion targetlab = rgb2lab(targetrgb) referencelab = rgb2lab(referencergb) # Extract luminance (L) and chrominance (a, b) channels LT = targetlab[:,:, 0] aT = targetlab[:,:, 1] bT = targetlab[:,:, 2] aR = referencelab[:,:, 1] bR = referencelab[:,:, 2] # Compute mean and standard deviation for chrominance channels muaT, sigmaaT = np.mean(aT), np.std(aT) mubT, sigmabT = np.mean(bT), np.std(bT) muaR, sigmaaR = np.mean(aR), np.std(aR) mubR, sigmabR = np.mean(bR), np.std(bR) # Guard against zero variance in target chrominance channels eps = 1e-8 sigmaaT = max(sigmaaT, eps) sigmabT = max(sigmabT, eps) # Normalize and scale chrominance channels to match reference statistics aprime = ((aT - muaT) / sigmaaT) sigmaaR + muaR bprime = ((bT - mubT) / sigmabT) sigmabR + mubR # Reconstruct image with original luminance and scaled chrominance outputlab = np.stack([LT, aprime, bprime], axis=-1) # Convert back to RGB Standard XYZ to sRGB matrix conversion outputrgb = lab2rgb(outputlab) return outputrgb def rgb2lab(rgb): """Standard RGB to Lab conversion.""" # Uses standard sRGB to XYZ to Lab matrices pass def lab2rgb(lab): """Standard Lab to RGB conversion.""" # Uses standard XYZ to sRGB matrices pass Parameters: Color space: Typically CIELAB. Channel selection: Only chrominance channels are transferred; luminance is preserved from the target. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Input: If the target image is purely grayscale with zero variance in chrominance channels, \sigma{aT} or \sigma{bT} may be zero, causing division by zero. A small epsilon (\epsilon = 10^{-8}) should be added to the denominator. Gamut Clipping: The method assumes the reference image is representative of the desired style. If the reference contains colors outside the gamut of the target's luminance, clipping may occur during RGB conversion. Adaptive Instance Normalization (AdaIN) is a feature modulation technique that achieves arbitrary style transfer by aligning the statistical moments (mean and variance) of content feature maps with those of style feature maps. It differs from its parent, Color Transfer, which operates on final pixel colors, by operating in a deep feature space to preserve high-level semantic structure while transferring artistic appearance. Unlike Neural Style Transfer (NST), which optimizes an output image to minimize perceptual loss, AdaIN is a feedforward operation that directly transforms features, enabling rapid, arbitrary style application without per-image optimization. PhotoWCT is a method that employs whitening and coloring transforms (WCT) to align the feature statistics of the content and style images, aiming to generate consistent and visually coherent results. Color Transfer is computationally inexpensive, relying on linear statistical operations per channel. It preserves the structural fidelity of the original volume rendering, as it applies no geometric or textural modifications. However, it is limited to linear statistical matching and cannot transfer complex textures or non-linear artistic styles. It is best used when the primary goal is chromatic consistency with a reference image rather than full artistic stylization. Color Transfer was introduced as a practical component in the context of Artistic Radiance Fields (ARF) to improve the color match between final renderings and an input style image. In ARF, volumetric radiance field rendering consumes significant memory, often limiting optimization to sparsely sampled pixels, which prevents the computation of VGG-based style losses on full-resolution images. To solve this, ARF employs deferred back-propagation for memory-efficient auto-differentiation with image losses. Color Transfer is integrated alongside feature matching and VGG-based content/style losses to balance stylization and content preservation. name: Adaptive Instance Normalization (AdaIN)
body: Adaptive Instance Normalization (AdaIN) is a feature modulation technique that achieves arbitrary style transfer by aligning the statistical moments (mean and variance) of content feature maps with those of style feature maps. It differs from its parent, Color Transfer, which operates on final pixel colors, by operating in a deep feature space to preserve high-level semantic structure while transferring artistic appearance. Unlike Neural Style Transfer (NST), which optimizes an output image to minimize perceptual loss, AdaIN is a feedforward operation that directly transforms features, enabling rapid, arbitrary style application without per-image optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Input x: A feature tensor extracted from a content source (e.g., a neural radiance field decoder or image). Input y: A feature tensor extracted from a style source (e.g., a reference image). Output x': The stylized feature tensor, where the statistical distribution of x is replaced by that of y. Data Structures: The method operates on 4D tensors x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times H \times W} (or higher dimensions for volumetric data), where C is the number of channels, and H, W are spatial dimensions. For volumetric applications, dimensions may include depth D. The statistics are computed per channel across the spatial (and potentially volumetric) dimensions. Formulas: Let \mu(x) and \sigma(x) be the mean and standard deviation of the content tensor x, computed across spatial dimensions for each channel. Similarly, let \mu(y) and \sigma(y) be the mean and standard deviation of the style tensor y. The AdaIN operation is defined as: \text{AdaIN}(x, y) = \frac{\sigma(y)}{\sigma(x)} (x - \mu(x)) + \mu(y) Where: \mu(x) = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} xi \sigma(x) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (xi - \mu(x))^2 + \epsilon} N is the number of elements over which statistics are computed (e.g., H \times W or H \times W \times D). \epsilon is a small constant added for numerical stability to prevent division by zero. Comparison with Instance Normalization (IN): Standard Instance Normalization (IN) normalizes features to zero mean and unit variance, then applies learned scale (\gamma) and shift (\beta) parameters: \text{IN}(x) = \gamma \frac{x - \mu(x)}{\sigma(x)} + \beta AdaIN replaces the learned parameters \gamma, \beta with the style statistics \sigma(y), \mu(y), effectively injecting style information directly into the normalization process. Implementation Steps: 1. Extract feature maps x from the content network and y from the style network (typically using a shared encoder like VGG-19). 2. Compute channel-wise mean \mu(x) and standard deviation \sigma(x) for the content features x. 3. Compute channel-wise mean \mu(y) and standard deviation \sigma(y) for the style features y. 4. Normalize x by subtracting \mu(x) and dividing by \sigma(x). 5. Scale the normalized content by \sigma(y) and shift by \mu(y). 6. Return the resulting tensor as the stylized features. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def computemeanstd(tensor): """ Computes mean and standard deviation per channel. tensor shape: (B, C, H, W) or (B, C, H, W, D) """ # Keep dimensions for broadcasting keepdims = True mean = torch.mean(tensor, dim=list(range(2, tensor.dim())), keepdim=keepdims) var = torch.var(tensor, dim=list(range(2, tensor.dim())), keepdim=keepdims, unbiased=False) std = torch.sqrt(var + 1e-9) # epsilon for numerical stability return mean, std def adain(contentfeatures, stylefeatures): """ Applies Adaptive Instance Normalization. contentfeatures: Tensor from content source stylefeatures: Tensor from style source """ # 1. Compute statistics cmean, cstd = computemeanstd(contentfeatures) smean, sstd = computemeanstd(stylefeatures) # 2. Normalize content normalizedcontent = (contentfeatures - cmean) / cstd # 3. Adapt to style statistics stylizedfeatures = sstd normalizedcontent + smean return stylizedfeatures Parameters and Edge Cases: Feature Extractor: Typically VGG-19 is used to extract features from both content and style inputs. Batch Size: In volumetric implementations, batch size is often limited to 1 due to memory constraints. Degenerate Input: If \sigma(x) is zero (constant feature map), division by zero occurs. The \epsilon term in the standard deviation calculation prevents this. Volumetric Consistency: In 3D rendering, computing statistics over a sampled point batch can cause block artifacts. Volume-adaptive variants compute statistics over the entire volume to maintain multi-view consistency. Neural Style Transfer (NST) is a technique that applies the visual characteristics of an artistic style to a content image while preserving the original content structure. It differs from its parent, Adaptive Instance Normalization (AdaIN), which aligns feature map statistics for arbitrary style transfer, by optimizing a specific output image to minimize perceptual losses in a feature space. Unlike sibling method FPRF, which focuses on photorealistic structure preservation via segmentation, NST focuses on artistic stylization. FPRF is a method for photorealistic style transformation that stylizes 3D scenes without optimization, using a radiance field for geometry/content and a style dictionary module with style attention. It utilizes AdaIN to stylize 3D scenes without optimization, enabling rapid style manipulation. It outperforms previous 3D photorealistic appearance editing methods by achieving transformation with multiple style references in less training time. Linear Style Transfer (LST) is a method that improves efficiency over AdaIN by learning linear transformations directly to the feature maps, realizing fast and scalable style transfer across multiple styles. Volume-adaptive Instance Normalization is a normalization technique that uses the learned mean and variance of the whole volume during inference to eliminate dependency on holistic statistics of the sampled point batch, improving stylization quality and maintaining multi-view consistency. Vanilla IN produces severe block-shape artifacts because the transformation of each batch is conditioned on the holistic statistics of itself, leading to inconsistent stylization per block. Discarding IN entirely compromises stylization quality, failing to capture the correct color tone of the reference style, because IN removes the original style information of the content image which facilitates the transfer of the reference style. Time Complexity: The operation is O(N) where N is the number of elements in the feature map, as it involves only mean, variance, and element-wise arithmetic operations. It is significantly faster than optimization-based methods like NST because it is a single forward pass. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the feature maps for both content and style inputs. In volumetric settings, memory usage is constrained by the resolution of the radiance field and the batch size. Performance: Enables arbitrary style transfer without per-image optimization, making it suitable for real-time or near-real-time applications. Strengths: Simple implementation, fast inference, ability to handle arbitrary styles without retraining the style encoder. Limitations: May lose fine-grained structural details if the style statistics dominate the content statistics. In 3D, naive application can lead to view-dependent inconsistencies if statistics are computed per batch rather than per volume. When to use: When rapid, arbitrary style transfer is required without the computational cost of iterative optimization. When not to use: When strict photorealistic structure preservation is required without any style leakage, or when fine-grained local style control is needed beyond global statistics. AdaIN was introduced as a method for arbitrary style transfer, aligning the mean and variance of feature maps extracted from content images with those of style images. It was originally proposed in the context of 2D image style transfer. In the context of volume rendering and neural radiance fields, it has been adapted to modulate feature tensors in the decoder network, replacing instance normalization layers with AdaIN layers conditioned on a transfer function descriptor. This allows for explicit control over the appearance of 3D scenes using learned descriptors.
