name: Machine Learning and Feature Extraction
body: This family applies machine learning algorithms and feature extraction techniques to determine the optical properties of volume data, moving beyond manual transfer function design. It solves the problem of classifying complex, high-dimensional volumetric structures automatically or semi-automatically by learning decision boundaries from training data or extracting statistical features. It differs from Data Feature-Based Classification by explicitly using learned models (e.g., SVMs, Neural Networks, Boosting) or statistical clustering (e.g., K-means) rather than static, user-defined heuristic functions. Builds on Data Feature-Based Classification, which evaluates a classification function C(\mathbf{x}) for each sample point \mathbf{x} in the volume to produce optical properties. K-means-based hybrid segmentation is an image processing approach that enhances ray casting object distinction by assigning object membership information (ID tags) to cubical vertices in the volume. It differs from standard clustering by combining Self-Organizing Maps (SOM) for robust initialization, K-means for preliminary grouping, and Fisher discriminant analysis for statistical optimization, specifically designed to generate binary, non-overlapping transfer functions for color and opacity assignment. AdaBoost Look Up Table (LUT) Classification is a machine learning method for volume rendering that accelerates multi-class segmentation by storing trained AdaBoost weak classifiers in a compact lookup structure. It solves the problem of interactive volume classification by replacing iterative model evaluation with fast table lookups, enabling real-time testing after an interactive training phase. It differs from AdaBoost Volume Classification by explicitly encoding the decision stumps into a 3-row LUT structure optimized for GPU parallel testing, and from K-means-based hybrid segmentation by using boosting-based binary dichotomizers within an Error Correcting Output Codes (ECOC) framework rather than centroid-based clustering. AdaBoost Volume Classification is an interactive, data-driven method for multi-class segmentation of volumetric data using a framework of Error Correcting Output Codes (ECOC) and Discrete AdaBoost classifiers. It solves the problem of classifying multiple regions of interest on demand without requiring preprocessing or complex optimization procedures. Unlike graph cuts or random walker methods, it avoids segmentation dependencies among neighboring voxels, making it suitable for real-time applications and handling thinned or complex structures. Two-stage k-means streamline clustering is a method for abstracting 3D vector fields by decomposing a large set of streamlines into coherent bundles and extracting representative streamlines for visualization. It solves the problem of visual clutter and high computational complexity associated with rendering raw streamline data by reducing the dataset to a concise set of representative paths. Unlike standard k-means which operates on high-dimensional point vectors, this method uses low-dimensional feature vectors (spatial coordinates and entropy metrics) to ensure efficiency and coherence in flow structure representation. This method suggests the optimal viewpoint for features of interest in a given input volume and transfer function by considering the similarity between input features and features in a collected image set. It sets itself apart from image-based viewpoint selection models by separating viewpoint estimation and similarity calculation into distinct stages solved by Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), rather than applying a single similarity measure to mix these stages. Definition: Saving a trained neural network or SVM configuration to apply it to new data sets with similar characteristics, reducing classification time. Step: Apply the saved classifier to the new data set. If misclassification occurs, the user can refine it by supplying additional training data. Parameter: Saved classifier size: under 30 kilobytes. Pitfall: Position information is specific to a given data set; using it reduces reusability because location changes between scans. It should be excluded if reusability is intended. Reused classifiers may misclassify materials if the new data set does not share similar characteristics (e.g., data value ranges or material locations). Number: SVM IoU on CT-ORG dataset with DINO features: 0.24 (liver), 0.36 (bones), 0.0 (other classes), mean 0.09. Fit time: 407s. Inference time: 2077s. Definition: A technique using Independent Component Analysis (ICA) to represent voxel signatures via linear transformation into a space where manual classification is simpler, often achievable using separator planes perpendicular to the new coordinate axes. ICA infers the linear transformation coefficients to simplify the signature representation. Step: 1. Apply ICA to voxel signatures. 2. Infer appropriate linear transformation coefficients. 3. Transform voxel signatures into the new space. 4. Perform manual classification using separator planes perpendicular to the new axes. The application of machine learning to volume rendering classification emerged in the early 2000s as a response to the complexity of high-dimensional data. Tzeng et al. introduced intelligent systems using Support Vector Machines (SVMs) and neural networks for higher-dimensional classification, demonstrating the reuse of classifiers across similar datasets. Concurrently, Takanashi et al. proposed using Independent Component Analysis (ICA) to simplify the classification space for multidimensional volumes. More recently, self-supervised vision transformers (e.g., DINO) have been leveraged for segmentation-based transfer function design, although computational costs remain a challenge. name: K-means-based hybrid segmentation
head: hybrid segmentation
body: K-means-based hybrid segmentation is an image processing approach that enhances ray casting object distinction by assigning object membership information (ID tags) to cubical vertices in the volume. It differs from standard clustering by combining Self-Organizing Maps (SOM) for robust initialization, K-means for preliminary grouping, and Fisher discriminant analysis for statistical optimization, specifically designed to generate binary, non-overlapping transfer functions for color and opacity assignment. Inputs: Volume data (typically RGB color bands, though gray levels are supported). Optional: Noise reduction filters and histogram equalization parameters. Outputs: Object membership ID tags assigned to cubical vertices. Optimum segments representing inherent color and formation characteristics. Data Structures: Neural Map: A 2D grid of nodes with dimensions mapwidth \times maplength. Each node stores a weight vector wv. Feature Vector: For K-means, features are limited to three color bands and a Diagonal Busyness Factor (DF). DF Calculation: Computed for each pixel using four diagonal neighbors xi and center C: DF = \sum{i=1}^4 |C - xi|. Parameters: SOM Learning Rate: Starts at 0.9, reduces to 0.1 in Stage 1; 0.01 in Stage 2. SOM Neighborhood Size: Starts at half map size, reduces to 1 in Stage 1; remains 1 in Stage 2. Feature Normalization: RGB values normalized from [0, 255] to [-1, 1]. Steps: 1. Pre-processing (Optional): Apply high pass/low pass filters and histogram equalization to remove noise and rectify intensity imbalance. 2. Neural Map Initialization: Calculate NumberofMapNodes = mapwidth \times maplength. Find SmallestAvailableColorValue = \min(R, G, B) and LargestAvailableColorValue = \max(R, G, B). Calculate Range = LargestAvailableColorValue - SmallestAvailableColorValue. Calculate Interval = Range / (NumberofMapNodes - 1). Initialize nodes by setting the first node to SmallestAvailableColorValue, then incrementing by Interval for each subsequent node. 3. SOM Training Stage 1: Randomly select pixels as input vectors D(t). Find Best Matching Unit (BMU) u for each input. Adjust BMU and neighborhood weights using: wv(s+1) = wv(s) + \theta(u,v,s)\alpha(s)(D(t) - wv(s)) where \alpha(s) is the monotonically decreasing learning coefficient and \theta(u,v,s) is the neighborhood function based on lattice distance. Reduce learning rate from 0.9 to 0.1 and neighborhood size from half map size to 1. 4. SOM Training Stage 2 (Refinement): Stabilize feature vectors with a learning rate of 0.01. Neighborhood size remains 1 (only BMU adjusted). 5. K-means Clustering: Use SOM output as initial cluster centers. Perform few rounds of K-means clustering using features: 3 color bands + DF. Identify preliminary groups/elementary clusters. 6. Statistical Optimization: Apply Fisher discriminant ratio to convert preliminary groups into optimum segments. Use edge detection to exempt important boundary/pattern information from irrelevant recombination. Apply recombination and epsilon tolerance factor for spatial tuning. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def kmeanshybridsegmentation(volumedata, mapwidth, maplength): # Phase 1.1: Optional Pre-processing processeddata = volumedata # Apply high pass/low pass filters and histogram equalization if needed # Phase 1.2: Neural Map Initialization numberofmapnodes = mapwidth maplength minval = min(processeddata.flatten()) maxval = max(processeddata.flatten()) rangeval = maxval - minval interval = rangeval / (numberofmapnodes - 1) nodes = [minval + i interval for i in range(numberofmapnodes)] # Helper: Normalize data to [-1, 1] def normalizetominusoneone(data): return (data / 255.0) 2 - 1 normalizeddata = normalizetominusoneone(processeddata) # Helper: Linear decay def decay(current, target, epoch, maxepoch): return current - (current - target) (epoch / maxepoch) # Helper: Lattice distance on 2D grid def latticedistance(idx1, idx2, width): r1, c1 = divmod(idx1, width) r2, c2 = divmod(idx2, width) return abs(r1 - r2) + abs(c1 - c2) # Helper: Neighborhood function (Gaussian) def neighborhoodfunction(dist, size): return math.exp(-(dist 2) / (2 (size / 2) 2)) # Helper: Find BMU def findbmu(pixel, nodes): dists = [np.linalg.norm(pixel - w) for w in nodes] return np.argmin(dists) # Phase 1.2: Training Stage 1 learningrate = 0.9 neighborhoodsize = mapwidth / 2 maxepochsstage1 = 100 # Not given in the sources for epoch in range(maxepochsstage1): for pixel in normalizeddata: bmuindex = findbmu(pixel, nodes) for i, node in enumerate(nodes): dist = latticedistance(i, bmuindex, mapwidth) theta = neighborhoodfunction(dist, neighborhoodsize) nodes[i] = node + theta learningrate (pixel - node) learningrate = decay(learningrate, 0.1, epoch, maxepochsstage1) neighborhoodsize = max(1, neighborhoodsize / 2) # Phase 1.2: Training Stage 2 learningrate = 0.01 neighborhoodsize = 1 maxepochsstage2 = 100 # Not given in the sources for epoch in range(maxepochsstage2): for pixel in normalizeddata: bmuindex = findbmu(pixel, nodes) nodes[bmuindex] = nodes[bmuindex] + learningrate (pixel - nodes[bmuindex]) # Phase 1.3: K-means Clustering # Features: 3 color bands + Diagonal Busyness Factor (DF) def extractfeatures(data): features = [] h, w, = data.shape for y in range(h): for x in range(w): c = data[y, x] df = 0.0 for dx, dy in [(-1, -1), (1, -1), (-1, 1), (1, 1)]: nx, ny = x + dx, y + dy if 0 <= nx < w and 0 <= ny < h: df += np.linalg.norm(c - data[ny, nx]) else: df += 0.0 features.append(np.concatenate([c, [df]])) return np.array(features) features = extractfeatures(processeddata) initialcenters = nodes # Not given in the sources: kmeansclustering(features, initialcenters, rounds=3) # Statistical Optimization # Not given in the sources: applyfisherdiscriminant(clusters) # Not given in the sources: applyedgedetectionandrecombination(optimumsegments) # Not given in the sources: assignidtags(optimumsegments) Time Complexity: Dominated by SOM training iterations and K-means convergence. The use of SOM for initialization reduces the risk of local optima, potentially reducing the number of K-means iterations required compared to random initialization. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the neural map nodes and feature vectors (color + DF) for each voxel. Strengths: Improves clustering accuracy by avoiding random initialization pitfalls; handles noise via pre-processing; generates binary transfer functions suitable for clear object distinction. Limitations: Requires tuning of SOM parameters (map size, learning rates); DF calculation adds computational overhead per pixel; limited to 3 color bands + DF for K-means features. The method was proposed by Azimzadeh & Pourgholi in 2020 to enhance ray casting object distinction by integrating image processing techniques with volume rendering. It addresses the issue of K-means converging to local optima when initialized randomly by using a Self-Organizing Map (SOM) to provide rational initial cluster centers. name: AdaBoost Look Up Table (LUT) Classification
head: Discrete AdaBoost with ECOC, Voxel-based AdaBoost Classification
body: AdaBoost Look Up Table (LUT) Classification is a machine learning method for volume rendering that accelerates multi-class segmentation by storing trained AdaBoost weak classifiers in a compact lookup structure. It solves the problem of interactive volume classification by replacing iterative model evaluation with fast table lookups, enabling real-time testing after an interactive training phase. It differs from AdaBoost Volume Classification by explicitly encoding the decision stumps into a 3-row LUT structure optimized for GPU parallel testing, and from K-means-based hybrid segmentation by using boosting-based binary dichotomizers within an Error Correcting Output Codes (ECOC) framework rather than centroid-based clustering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N classes (volume structures) and a training dataset T consisting of voxel samples (\rho, l(\rho)). Output: A Look Up Table (LUT) L containing the parameters for n dichotomizers, and a classification map assigning each voxel in the volume to one of the N classes. Data Structures: The core data structure is the LUT L, which stores the parameters for all weak classifiers across all dichotomizers. It is organized as a table with 3 rows and n \times M columns (where n is the number of dichotomizers and M is the number of stumps per dichotomizer): Row 1: Codifies the 8 sample features \rhos (s \in [1..8]) used for splitting. Row 2: Codifies the polarity (p) for each weak classifier. Row 3: Codifies the threshold (t) for each weak classifier. Numbered Steps: 1. Define Classes: Define N classes representing the volume structures to be segmented. 2. Form Dichotomizers: Create n binary partitions (dichotomizers) of the N classes using an ECOC design. 3. Train Dichotomizers: For each dichotomizer hi: a. Select a subset of training voxels T. b. Train an AdaBoost classifier using Decision Stumps as weak learners. c. Extract the polarity and threshold for each stump's selected feature. d. Populate the corresponding columns in the LUT L with the feature index (Row 1), polarity (Row 2), and threshold (Row 3). 4. Test (Classify): For each voxel in the volume: a. Compute the 8 features \rho for the voxel. b. For each dichotomizer i: i. Retrieve the feature index s, polarity p, and threshold t from LUT L. ii. Evaluate the decision stump: if p=1, check if \rhos > t; if p=-1, check if \rhos < t. c. Aggregate the binary outputs from all n dichotomizers using the ECOC decoding scheme to determine the final class label. Formulas: Training Cost: The total cost of sequential training for one dichotomizer is O(|T| \times M), where |T| is the cardinality of the training data set T and M is the number of iterations/stumps. Feature Vector: \rho = [x, y, z, gx, gy, gz, |g|, v]. Parameters: Features: 8 features per voxel. Weak Classifier: Decision Stumps. Number of Stumps: 30 per dichotomizer. Training Data Size: Small subset of voxels, ranging from 1,880 (first iteration) to 14,200 (last iteration) in simulations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Training Data Selection: The method relies on user-selected voxels. Serial Bottleneck: While dichotomizers are trained in parallel, the training of a single dichotomizer is serial due to dependencies between AdaBoost iterations. ECOC Design: The choice of ECOC design affects the number of dichotomizers n. For N classes using one-versus-one, n = N(N-1)/2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def trainadaboostlut(classes, trainingsamples, numstumps=30): nclasses = len(classes) # One-versus-one ECOC design dichotomizers = [] for i in range(nclasses): for j in range(i + 1, nclasses): dichotomizers.append((classes[i], classes[j])) ndichotomizers = len(dichotomizers) totalstumps = ndichotomizers numstumps # LUT structure: 3 rows, totalstumps columns # Row 0: Feature indices (0-7) # Row 1: Polarity (-1 or 1) # Row 2: Thresholds (float) lut = [[0.0] totalstumps for in range(3)] for didx, (classa, classb) in enumerate(dichotomizers): binfeatures = [] binlabels = [] for features, label in trainingsamples: if label == classa: binfeatures.append(features) binlabels.append(1) elif label == classb: binfeatures.append(features) binlabels.append(-1) if not binfeatures: continue weights = [1.0 / len(binlabels)] len(binlabels) stumps = [] for m in range(numstumps): stump = traindecisionstump(binfeatures, binlabels, weights) stumps.append(stump) errors = [] for i in range(len(binlabels)): pred = stump.evaluate(binfeatures[i]) errors.append(1 if pred != binlabels[i] else 0) errorrate = sum(w e for w, e in zip(weights, errors)) if errorrate >= 0.5: break alpha = 0.5 math.log((1.0 - errorrate) / max(errorrate, 1e-10)) for i in range(len(weights)): weights[i] = math.exp(-alpha binlabels[i] (1 if errors[i] == 0 else -1)) wsum = sum(weights) weights = [w / wsum for w in weights] for m, stump in enumerate(stumps): col = didx numstumps + m lut[0][col] = stump.featureindex lut[1][col] = stump.polarity lut[2][col] = stump.threshold return lut, dichotomizers def traindecisionstump(features, labels, weights): beststump = None minweightederror = float('inf') for fidx in range(8): values = [f[fidx] for f in features] thresholds = sorted(set(values)) for t in thresholds: for p in [1, -1]: weightederror = 0.0 for i in range(len(labels)): pred = p if values[i] > t else -p if pred != labels[i]: weightederror += weights[i] if weightederror < minweightederror: minweightederror = weightederror beststump = {'featureindex': fidx, 'threshold': t, 'polarity': p} return beststump def classifyvoxel(lut, voxelfeatures, dichotomizers, numstumps): ndichotomizers = len(dichotomizers) classvotes = {c: 0 for c in set(c for pair in dichotomizers for c in pair)} for didx in range(ndichotomizers): vote = 0 for k in range(numstumps): col = didx numstumps + k fidx = int(lut[0][col]) p = lut[1][col] t = lut[2][col] val = voxelfeatures[fidx] pred = p if val > t else -p vote += pred classa, classb = dichotomizers[didx] if vote > 0: classvotes[classa] += 1 else: classvotes[classb] += 1 return max(classvotes, key=classvotes.get) Time Complexity: Training one dichotomizer is O(|T| \times M). Total training time is interactive, with a worst-case bound of 5 seconds for the tested datasets. Testing is real-time. Memory Complexity: The LUT size is proportional to 3 \times n \times M entries, where n is the number of dichotomizers and M is the number of stumps per dichotomizer. For N classes using one-versus-one, n = N(N-1)/2. Performance: Mean accuracy exceeds 90% by the 5th iteration across datasets. Brain: 0.960 accuracy (Ref: 0.968). Foot: 0.989 accuracy (Ref: 1.000). Thorax: 0.922 accuracy (Ref: 0.922). Data Efficiency: High accuracy is achieved with very few training samples (0.1% to 4% of voxels). Strengths: Real-time testing, interactive training, high accuracy with minimal user input, GPU parallelization of dichotomizer training. Limitations: Training of individual dichotomizers is serial; accuracy depends on user-provided training samples; ECOC design complexity grows with number of classes. The method was proposed by S. Grau, A. Puig, S. Escalera, and M. Salamó in the paper "Intelligent Interactive Volume Classification" presented at Eurographics 2013. It builds on Discrete AdaBoost and ECOC frameworks for multi-class classification, adapting them for volume rendering by using decision stumps and a LUT for efficient evaluation. The approach addresses the need for interactive segmentation in volume visualization, where traditional machine learning methods are too slow for real-time feedback. Intelligent Interactive Volume Classification, https://doi.org/10.2312/pe.pg.pg2013short.023-028, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: AdaBoost Volume Classification
head: ECOC-AdaBoost Volume Classification, GPU-Parallelized AdaBoost Volume Classification, Intelligent Interactive Volume Classification
body: AdaBoost Volume Classification is an interactive, data-driven method for multi-class segmentation of volumetric data using a framework of Error Correcting Output Codes (ECOC) and Discrete AdaBoost classifiers. It solves the problem of classifying multiple regions of interest on demand without requiring preprocessing or complex optimization procedures. Unlike graph cuts or random walker methods, it avoids segmentation dependencies among neighboring voxels, making it suitable for real-time applications and handling thinned or complex structures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A voxel model V^M of size dimx \times dimy \times dimz and a set of k training samples labeled by the user. Each training sample consists of a feature vector \rho and a ground truth label l(\rho). Output: A classification for every voxel in the volume, determining its optical properties (opacity and color) for rendering. Data Structures: 1. Feature Vector (\rho): An 8-dimensional vector for each voxel containing: Coordinates: x, y, z Density: d Gradient components: gx, gy, gz Gradient magnitude: |g| 2. Look Up Table (LUT) (L): A matrix of size 3 \times (|\rho| \times Wc) used to store the trained weak classifiers for GPU parallelization. |\rho| = 8 (feature dimensionality). Wc is the number of weak classifiers. In a one-versus-one ECOC design for N classes, Wc = N(N-1)/2. Row 1: Stores the weight cm for each weak classifier. The position i in this row corresponds to the feature index mod(i, |\rho|). The next weight for the same feature is at i + |\rho|. Positions for features not considered by a specific stump are set to zero. Row 2: Stores the polarity Pm for each weak classifier at column i. Row 3: Stores the threshold Tm for each weak classifier at column i. Algorithm Steps: 1. Training Stage (Discrete AdaBoost): The system trains binary classifiers for each dichotomy in the ECOC framework. 1. Initialize weights wi = 1/k for i = 1 \dots k. 2. For m = 1 to M (number of weak classifiers): a. Fit a weak classifier fm(\rho) \in \{-1, 1\} using the current weights wi on the training data. The weak classifier is a Decision Stump, fitting a threshold Tm and polarity Pm on a selected feature. b. Compute the weighted error: errm = Ew[1(l(\rho) \neq fm(\rho))]. c. Compute the classifier weight: cm = \log((1 - errm) / errm). d. Update sample weights: wi \leftarrow wi \cdot \exp[cm \cdot 1(l(\rhoi) \neq fm(\rhoi))] for i = 1 \dots k. e. Normalize wi so that \sumi wi = 1. 3. Output the final classifier: \text{sign}[\sum{m=1}^M cm fm(\rho)]. 2. LUT Construction: For each trained weak classifier (Decision Stump), store Pm and Tm in rows 2 and 3 of L at the column corresponding to the feature index used by that stump. Store cm in row 1. Positions for features not considered by a specific stump are set to zero. 3. Testing Stage (Classification): Applied to all voxels in the volume. The authors parallelized the training stage using a GPU-based implementation for rapid interaction. 1. Initialize F(\rho) = 0. 2. For m = 1 to M: a. Let \rhom be the value of the feature selected by the m-th weak classifier for the test sample \rho. b. Retrieve Pm and Tm from the LUT. c. Update F(\rho) = F(\rho) + cm \cdot (Pm \cdot \rhom < Pm \cdot Tm). 3. Output the label: \text{sign}(F(\rho)). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def trainadaboost(trainingsamples, numclasses): """ trainingsamples: list of tuples (rho, label) rho: array of 8 floats [x, y, z, d, gx, gy, gz, |g|] label: integer class index numclasses: N """ k = len(trainingsamples) weights = [1.0 / k] k Wc = numclasses (numclasses - 1) // 2 weakclassifiers = [] M = 20 # Number of boosting rounds, not given in sources for m in range(M): bestfeatureidx, bestthreshold, bestpolarity, besterror = findbeststump(trainingsamples, weights) predictions = [] for rho, label in trainingsamples: val = rho[bestfeatureidx] if bestpolarity == 1: pred = 1 if val < bestthreshold else -1 else: pred = 1 if val >= bestthreshold else -1 predictions.append(pred) errm = sum(weights[i] for i in range(k) if predictions[i] != trainingsamples[i][1]) if errm <= 0 or errm >= 1: cm = 0.0 else: cm = math.log((1 - errm) / errm) weakclassifiers.append({ 'featureidx': bestfeatureidx, 'threshold': bestthreshold, 'polarity': bestpolarity, 'weight': cm }) for i in range(k): if predictions[i] != trainingsamples[i][1]: weights[i] = math.exp(cm) sumw = sum(weights) weights = [w / sumw for w in weights] return weakclassifiers def findbeststump(trainingsamples, weights): """Finds the decision stump (feature, threshold, polarity) minimizing weighted error.""" besterror = float('inf') bestfeatureidx = 0 bestthreshold = 0.0 bestpolarity = 1 for featidx in range(8): values = sorted(set(rho[featidx] for rho, in trainingsamples)) if len(values) < 2: continue thresholds = [(values[i] + values[i+1]) / 2.0 for i in range(len(values) - 1)] for thresh in thresholds: for pol in [1, -1]: error = 0.0 for i, (rho, label) in enumerate(trainingsamples): val = rho[featidx] pred = 1 if (pol val < pol thresh) else -1 if pred != label: error += weights[i] if error < besterror: besterror = error bestfeatureidx = featidx bestthreshold = thresh bestpolarity = pol return bestfeatureidx, bestthreshold, bestpolarity, besterror def classifyvolume(volumedata, weakclassifiers): """ volumedata: list of voxel objects with.features attribute (8 floats) weakclassifiers: list of dicts from training """ classifiedvolume = [] for voxel in volumedata: rho = voxel.features Frho = 0.0 for clf in weakclassifiers: Pm = clf['polarity'] Tm = clf['threshold'] cm = clf['weight'] rhom = rho[clf['featureidx']] condition = (Pm rhom < Pm Tm) contribution = cm condition Frho += contribution if Frho > 0: label = 1 elif Frho < 0: label = -1 else: label = 1 # Tie-breaking, not specified classifiedvolume.append(label) return classifiedvolume Parameters: Feature Vector \rho: 8 features (x, y, z, d, gx, gy, gz, |g|). Number of Weak Classifiers (Wc): Determined by the ECOC design. For N classes, Wc = N(N-1)/2 in one-versus-one design. Number of Boosting Rounds (M): Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Feature Indexing in LUT: The first row of L stores weights for features s \in [1..8]. Position i in row 1 corresponds to feature mod(i, |\rho|). The next weight for the same feature is at i + |\rho|. Precision: Floating point precision in the accumulation of F(\rho) may affect the sign decision in edge cases where F(\rho) \approx 0. Degenerate Input: If errm = 0 or errm = 1, the log term becomes undefined. The pseudocode handles this by setting cm = 0. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Standard AdaBoost training scales with O(M \cdot k \cdot |\rho|) per binary problem, and testing scales with O(M) per voxel. Memory Complexity: The LUT requires 3 \times |\rho| \times Wc storage. For N classes, Wc = N(N-1)/2. Performance: The authors parallelized the training stage using a GPU-based implementation for rapid interaction and classification. Strengths: No preprocessing required; interactive; handles thinned and complex structures better than probabilistic segmentation methods; no dependency on neighboring voxels. Limitations: Requires user-labeled training samples; performance depends on the quality and quantity of training data; multi-class extension relies on ECOC which increases the number of classifiers. When to use: Interactive volume visualization where users paint voxels on 2D slices to label samples. When not to use: When automatic, unsupervised segmentation is required; when real-time performance is critical and the number of classes is very large (increasing Wc). The method was proposed by S. Grau, A. Puig, S. Escalera, and M. Salamó from the Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya, Universitat de Barcelona, and Centre de Visió per Computador, Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona. It was published in 2013 as part of the Eurographics conference proceedings. The work extends previous data-driven and image-driven classification methods and addresses limitations of graph cuts and random walker methods which involve complex optimization and segmentation dependencies. Intelligent Interactive Volume Classification, https://doi.org/10.2312/pe.pg.pg2013short.023-028, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Two-stage k-means Streamline Clustering
head: Two-stage k-means Clustering
body: Two-stage k-means streamline clustering abstracts 3D vector fields by decomposing large streamline sets into coherent bundles and extracting representative paths for visualization. It solves visual clutter and high computational complexity by reducing raw streamline data to concise representative paths using low-dimensional feature vectors instead of full point clouds. Inputs: A set of generated streamlines from a 3D vector field. Outputs: A set of representative streamlines grouped into sub-bundles, ready for illustrative rendering (e.g., as streamtapes). Data Structures: Each streamline is mapped to a 1D feature vector. The method uses two distinct feature layouts: 1. Spatial Property Vector: A 9-component vector formed by concatenating the start, middle, and end points of the streamline. 2. Shape Property Vector: A 2-component vector containing Linear Entropy (EL) and Angular Entropy (EA). Feature Formulas: Shape properties quantify flow magnitude distribution and directional variation along the streamline. Linear Entropy (EL) measures information in flow magnitude: EL = - \frac{1}{\log2(m + 1)} \sum{j=1}^{m} \left( \frac{Dj}{LS} \right) \log2 \left( \frac{Dj}{LS} \right) Where: m is the number of streamline segments. Dj is the length of the j-th segment. LS = \sum{j=1}^{m} Dj is the total streamline length. Angular Entropy (EA) measures directional variation: EA = - \frac{1}{\log2(m)} \sum{j=1}^{m-1} \left( \frac{Aj}{LA} \right) \log2 \left( \frac{Aj}{LA} \right) Where: m is the number of streamline segments. Aj is the absolute angle at the j-th joint. LA = \sum{j=1}^{m-1} Aj is the total angular variation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Compute the 9D Spatial Property Vector and 2D Shape Property Vector for every input streamline. 2. Stage 1 Clustering: Partition all streamlines into p bundles using k-means with Lloyd’s algorithm on the Spatial Property Vectors. Each bundle contains streamlines with roughly coherent spatial layout. 3. Stage 2 Clustering: For each bundle i (i = 1 \dots p), partition it into qi sub-bundles using k-means on the Shape Property Vectors. The total cluster count is c = \sum{i=1}^{p} qi. 4. Representative Selection: Within each sub-bundle, compute the feature-space centroid, sort streamlines by Euclidean distance to the centroid, and select the closest streamline(s) as representatives. 5. Parameter Optimization (Optional): Determine optimal p and qi values using the elbow criterion, which identifies the cluster count where the percentage of variance explained (ratio of within-cluster variance to total variance) shows an abrupt change. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def norm(a): return math.sqrt(dot(a, a)) def dist(a, b): return norm([x - y for x, y in zip(a, b)]) def meanvec(vecs): return [sum(v[i] for v in vecs) / len(vecs) for i in range(len(vecs[0]))] def kmeanslloyd(data, k, maxiter=100): if k > len(data): k = len(data) centroids = data[:k] labels = [0] len(data) for in range(maxiter): newlabels = [] for d in data: bestc = min(range(k), key=lambda c: dist(d, centroids[c])) newlabels.append(bestc) if newlabels == labels: break labels = newlabels for c in range(k): clusterpoints = [data[i] for i in range(len(data)) if labels[i] == c] if clusterpoints: centroids[c] = meanvec(clusterpoints) return labels def computelinearentropy(segments): m = len(segments) if m == 0: return 0.0 LS = sum(segments) if LS == 0: return 0.0 entropy = sum((d / LS) math.log2(d / LS) for d in segments if d > 0) return - (1.0 / math.log2(m + 1)) entropy def computeangularentropy(angles): m = len(angles) if m == 0: return 0.0 LA = sum(angles) if LA == 0: return 0.0 entropy = sum((a / LA) math.log2(a / LA) for a in angles if a > 0) return - (1.0 / math.log2(m)) entropy def twostagekmeansclustering(streamlines, p, qlist=None): spatialfeats = [] shapefeats = [] for sl in streamlines: spatialfeats.append(sl.start + sl.middle + sl.end) shapefeats.append((computelinearentropy(sl.segments), computeangularentropy(sl.jointangles))) stage1labels = kmeanslloyd(spatialfeats, p) bundles = [[] for in range(p)] for idx, label in enumerate(stage1labels): bundles[label].append(idx) representatives = [] for i in range(p): bundleindices = bundles[i] bundleshape = [shapefeats[idx] for idx in bundleindices] qi = qlist[i] if qlist else 2 sublabels = kmeanslloyd(bundleshape, qi) for c in range(qi): subindices = [bundleindices[j] for j in range(len(bundleindices)) if sublabels[j] == c] if not subindices: continue centroid = meanvec([shapefeats[idx] for idx in subindices]) subindices.sort(key=lambda idx: dist(shapefeats[idx], centroid)) representatives.append(streamlines[subindices[0]]) return representatives Note: The sources do not provide the implementation details for the elbow criterion optimization. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Complexity: Standard k-means on line data has high complexity because lines are represented as vectors of original points. This method avoids that by using 5-component feature vectors (3 spatial points + 2 shape metrics). Degenerate Streamlines: If a streamline has zero length or zero angular variation, the logarithmic terms in entropy calculations may be undefined. Guard clauses (e.g., returning 0.0) are required. Parameter Selection: The choice of p and qi significantly affects the abstraction level. The elbow criterion is suggested but requires computing variance ratios for multiple cluster counts. Time Complexity: The complexity is determined by the number of streamlines N and the number of clusters. Since each streamline is reduced to a fixed-size feature vector (9 dimensions for Stage 1, 2 dimensions for Stage 2), the complexity is O(N \cdot K \cdot I) where K is the number of clusters and I is the number of iterations, rather than O(N \cdot L \cdot K \cdot I) where L is the number of points per streamline. Memory Complexity: Low, as it only stores the feature vectors and cluster assignments, not the full point clouds for all streamlines during clustering. Strengths: Efficiently decomposes large streamline sets into coherent bundles; reduces visual clutter; facilitates illustrative rendering (e.g., streamtapes). Limitations: Relies on the quality of the feature vectors; spatial clustering may group streamlines with different flow shapes if they share start/end points; shape clustering ignores spatial position. When to use: When visualizing complex 3D vector fields with many streamlines and needing a concise, illustrative representation. The method was introduced by Chen, Yan, Yu, Max, and Ma in 2011 in the paper "An Illustrative Visualization Framework for 3D Vector Fields". It was developed to address the limitations of existing vector field visualization techniques, which often assume no particular structure or require topological connectivity. The method builds on the concept of using entropy metrics (Linear and Angular Entropy) originally proposed by Furuya and Itoh. It is used in the context of illustrative visualization, specifically rendering streamlines as "streamtapes" to enhance depth perception and depict vicinity flow. An Illustrative Visualization Framework for 3D Vector Fields, http://vis.cs.ucdavis.edu/papers/pg2011paper.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: CNN-feature based viewpoint selection
head: weighted probability voting for viewpoint selection
body: This method suggests the optimal viewpoint for features of interest in a given input volume and transfer function by considering the similarity between input features and features in a collected image set. It sets itself apart from image-based viewpoint selection models [38] by separating viewpoint estimation and similarity calculation into distinct stages solved by Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), rather than applying a single similarity measure to mix these stages. Inputs: Input volume V. Transfer function T. Pre-trained category classification network (AlexNet-based). Pre-trained viewpoint estimation network. Collected image set C = \{I1, I2, \dots, In\} for the determined category, where n = |C| is the number of collected images. Outputs: Optimal viewpoint parameters (camera position, orientation, tilt, background). Data Structures: Feature vectors f(\cdot) \in \mathbb{R}^{4096} extracted from the last hidden layer of the category classification network. Rendered image set S = \{R1, R2, \dots, Rk\} with k=40. Steps: 1. Category Determination: Render several images randomly from the input volume V using the provided transfer function T. Classify these rendered images through the category classification network. The most voted category among these images is considered the category of the volume. 2. Retrieve Collected Images: Obtain the collected image set C = \{I1, I2, \dots, In\} corresponding to the determined category. 3. Estimate Viewpoints for Collected Images: For each collected image Ii \in C, estimate its viewpoint vi using the viewpoint estimation network. 4. Generate Rendered Image Set: Render the input volume V with the provided transfer function T under the estimated viewpoint vi for each Ii. This rendering considers different camera-tilt angles and background colors to generate a rendered image set S = \{R1, R2, \dots, Rk\} with k=40 images. 5. Calculate Similarity: Calculate the similarity wi between the collected image Ii and the input volume (with transfer function) using the cosine distance of features from the last hidden layer of the category classification network. The feature vectors f(Rj) and f(Ii) are in \mathbb{R}^{4096}. The similarity is defined as: wi = \max{Rj \in S} (\cos(f(Rj), f(Ii))) where \cos(a, b) denotes the cosine similarity between vectors a and b. 6. Compute Weighted Probability: Design an exponential similarity weight wi' by weighting the probability by its similarity with the input volume and transfer function: wi' = \exp\left((wi - 0.5) \cdot \frac{|C|}{10}\right) where |C| is the number of images in the collected image set. 7. Generate Voting Distribution: Sum up all weighted probability distributions (viewpoint probability distributions of Ii weighted by wi') to generate the voting probability distribution. 8. Select Optimal Viewpoint: Select the viewpoint with the largest probability from the summed distribution as the optimal viewpoint. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cnnfeatureviewpointselection(volume, transferfunction, categorynet, viewpointnet, collectedimagesC): """ volume: Input volume data transferfunction: Transfer function T categorynet: Pre-trained AlexNet-based category classification network viewpointnet: Pre-trained viewpoint estimation network collectedimagesC: List of collected images Ii for the determined category Returns: Optimal viewpoint parameters """ # Step 1: Determine category # Render several random images from volume using transferfunction randomrenderedimages = renderrandomimages(volume, transferfunction, count=5) # Count arbitrary, source says "several" # Classify these images categoryvotes = [] for img in randomrenderedimages: pred = categorynet.predict(img) categoryvotes.append(pred) # Most voted category is the volume's category volumecategory = getmostvotedcategory(categoryvotes) # Step 2: Retrieve collected images C (already provided as input for this category) # C = collectedimagesC # Step 3 & 4: For each collected image, estimate viewpoint and render variations renderedsetsS = [] # List of sets Si for each Ii estimatedviewpointsv = [] for Ii in collectedimagesC: # Estimate viewpoint vi vi = viewpointnet.estimateviewpoint(Ii) estimatedviewpointsv.append(vi) # Render volume under vi with different tilt angles and background colors # k=40 images Si = rendervariations(volume, transferfunction, vi, numimages=40) renderedsetsS.append(Si) # Step 5: Calculate similarity wi for each collected image similaritiesw = [] for idx, Ii in enumerate(collectedimagesC): Si = renderedsetsS[idx] # Get feature vector for collected image fIi = categorynet.extractfeatures(Ii) # From last hidden layer, R^4096 maxcossim = -1.0 for Rj in Si: fRj = categorynet.extractfeatures(Rj) # From last hidden layer, R^4096 cossim = cosinesimilarity(fRj, fIi) if cossim > maxcossim: maxcossim = cossim wi = maxcossim similaritiesw.append(wi) # Step 6: Compute weighted probability wi' n = len(collectedimagesC) weightedprobswprime = [] for wi in similaritiesw: wiprime = math.exp((wi - 0.5) (n / 10.0)) weightedprobswprime.append(wiprime) # Step 7: Generate voting distribution # Assume each collected image Ii has an associated viewpoint probability distribution P(v | Ii) # This distribution is derived from the viewpoint estimation network or stored data # Sum up weighted distributions votingdistribution = {} for idx, Ii in enumerate(collectedimagesC): # Get viewpoint probability distribution for Ii # This might be a histogram or set of probabilities over possible viewpoints # The source implies "viewpoint probability distribution of Ii" exists probdistIi = getviewpointprobabilitydistribution(Ii) wiprime = weightedprobswprime[idx] # Weight the distribution weighteddist = {} for viewpoint, prob in probdistIi.items(): weightedviewpoint = viewpoint # Viewpoint identity weightedprob = prob wiprime if weightedviewpoint not in votingdistribution: votingdistribution[weightedviewpoint] = 0.0 votingdistribution[weightedviewpoint] += weightedprob # Step 8: Select optimal viewpoint optimalviewpoint = max(votingdistribution, key=votingdistribution.get) return optimalviewpoint def cosinesimilarity(a, b): dotproduct = sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) norma = math.sqrt(sum(x x for x in a)) normb = math.sqrt(sum(x x for x in b)) if norma == 0 or normb == 0: return 0.0 return dotproduct / (norma normb) Parameters: k: Number of rendered images in set S, set to 40. Feature dimension: The features f(Rj) and f(Ii) are vectors in \mathbb{R}^{4096}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method relies on the availability of a pre-trained category classification network and viewpoint estimation network. The collected image set C must be representative of the determined category. The exponential weighting formula wi' = \exp((wi - 0.5) \cdot |C| / 10) assumes wi is in a range where this transformation is meaningful (cosine similarity is typically in [-1, 1]). Time Complexity: The method involves multiple CNN inferences (category classification, viewpoint estimation, feature extraction) and rendering operations. The complexity is dominated by the number of collected images |C| and the number of rendered variations k=40 per image. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the collected image set C, the rendered image sets S, and the feature vectors. Strengths: Separates viewpoint estimation and similarity calculation, allowing for more accurate similarity measurement based on CNN features. Considers the specific input volume and transfer function, unlike viewpoint preference analysis which suggests the same viewpoint for different features. Limitations: Requires pre-trained CNNs and a collected image set. Computationally expensive due to multiple renderings and CNN inferences. When to use: When an optimal viewpoint for specific features of interest in a volume is needed, and computational resources allow for CNN-based processing and multiple renderings. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and pre-computation is not feasible, or when no collected image set is available. Origin: Proposed in "CNNs Based Viewpoint Estimation for Volume Visualization". History: Inspired by similarity voting for viewpoint selection [38], this method improves upon it by separating viewpoint estimation and similarity calculation. Usage: Used in volume visualization to suggest optimal viewpoints for features of interest. CNNs Based Viewpoint Estimation for Volume Visualization, https://doi.org/10.1145/3309993, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Similarity-based Classification
body: Similarity-based classification methods determine optical properties by measuring the distance or agreement between a sample's feature vector and a reference set, rather than relying on absolute scalar thresholds. This family solves the problem of segmenting complex, high-dimensional, or semantically rich data where intensity alone is insufficient, by mapping spatial points to the "nearest" exemplar or by evaluating structural alignment. Unlike basic intensity-based methods, these techniques leverage geometric, spectral, or learned latent relationships to define classification boundaries. All methods in this family evaluate a classification function C(\mathbf{x}) for each sample point \mathbf{x} in the volume to produce optical properties. Input Domain: The input to the classification function is a feature vector \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}) associated with position \mathbf{x}. While basic methods use scalar intensity v = f(\mathbf{x}), this family extends the domain to include derived features such as gradient magnitude \|\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\|, curvature, shape descriptors, color components, or topological graph attributes. Output Range: The output is a set of optical properties, most commonly: Opacity (\alpha): A value in [0, 1] representing the probability of absorption or the inverse of transparency. \alpha=0 is fully transparent; \alpha=1 is fully opaque. Color (C): A vector (r, g, b) representing the emitted or reflected light color. Weight: In some emission-only models, a weight w is assigned to modulate the contribution of samples during accumulation. Classification Types: 1. Binary Classification: Uses hard thresholds to include or exclude data [6229-binary-and-soft-classification.md]. Values below a threshold are assigned \alpha=0, and values above are assigned \alpha=1 (or a constant high value). 2. Soft Classification: Uses smooth transitions (e.g., piecewise linear ramps, Gaussian bumps, or power functions) to assign intermediate opacity values. Evaluation Order: The timing of classification relative to sampling interpolation defines two main approaches: Pre-classification: The transfer function is applied to scalar values at the grid points (voxels) before sampling. Colors and opacities are interpolated during ray casting. Pre-classification produces blurred images when the image resolution is higher than the volume resolution, but prevents color bleeding if color interpolation is done with opacity-weighted colors. Post-classification: Scalar values are interpolated from the volume texture during ray casting, and the transfer function is applied to these continuous sample values. Post-classification produces images with defined edges but is prone to aliasing because high-frequency details may be missed. Implementation Structures: Transfer functions are commonly implemented as piecewise linear functions defined by user-specified keypoints, lookup tables (LUTs) stored as 1D, 2D, or 3D textures for fast GPU sampling, or shader functions evaluated dynamically during ray casting. Projects high-dimensional function samples into scalar fields based on distance to exemplar functions, preserving spatial layout unlike MDS. Choose when segmenting hyperspectral or time-varying data by functional similarity. Measures angular agreement between feature vectors, factoring out magnitude. Choose when semantic content depends on direction (e.g., gradients) rather than intensity scale. Evaluates the preservation of relational structure (manifold geometry) between latent spaces. Choose when verifying if a learned latent space captures the same representational organization as a reference. Retrieves transfer functions by matching high-level spatial semantics from co-planar images. Choose when differentiating segments with similar intensities but distinct shapes or textures. Definition: Computes a similarity volume SL by comparing annotated feature vectors against the full feature volume F using cosine similarity, enabling interactive feedback. Formula: SL^C = \max{a \in AC} \frac{1}{|F|} \sum{i \in F} \frac{Fa \cdot Fi}{\|Fa\|2 \|Fi\|2} where AC is the set of annotations for class C, Fa is the feature vector at annotation a, and Fi is the feature vector at voxel i. Resulting SL^C \in [0, 1]^{W' \times H' \times D'}. A proximity parameter P(x) = \max{a \in AC} e^{-10\tilde{p}|x-a|} scales the similarity based on distance to annotations, where \tilde{p} \in [0, 1]. Parameter: Proximity parameter \tilde{p} \in [0, 1]. Performance: Computation takes a few milliseconds on CPU or GPU. Step: Computes the probability of a query using thresholded cosine similarity instead of softmax with negative queries. Sets p = 1 if similarity exceeds a threshold, and p = 0 otherwise for hard decomposition. Definition: A discrete voxel classification technique for multidimensional signatures where users perform merge or bipartition operations on existing classes and define visual properties. Step: 1. Preprocessing: Automatically establish initial classification respecting voxel similarity criteria. 2. User performs merge or bipartition operations on classes. 3. User defines visual properties for each class. 4. Bipartition operations are executed rapidly, respecting similarity criteria. Definition: A self-supervised approach to spatiotemporal similarity learning using a Siamese neural network trained on a binary pretext task to predict spatial-temporal proximity, eliminating the need for labeled data. Step: 1. Train a Siamese neural network on a binary pretext task: predict if two spatiotemporal patches originate from nearby locations in space and time. 2. Use the resulting latent space for similarity queries. 3. Users supply example patches as a query; S4 ranks the rest of the ensemble by learned similarity. Definition: A clustering algorithm to select a representative subset of particle trajectories to display as arrows, based on similarity of pathlines over three time steps. Step: Select any pathline not already in a cluster to serve as the reference pathline. Examine all other pathlines not already in a cluster as candidates. If the similarity score between the reference pathline and the candidate pathline is less than a preset threshold, add the candidate to the cluster. After examining all candidates, output the reference pathline as the trajectory arrow for that cluster. Choose the next pathline not in a cluster and repeat the process. Filter out pathlines shorter than a preset threshold. Discard clusters that do not have a preset minimum number of pathlines. Formula: Similarity Metric: The sum of squared distances between particle positions at each time step in the three-time-step window. Parameter: Time Window: The number of time steps considered for trajectory similarity. Default: 3. Similarity Threshold: Determines cluster size. It is determined separately for each dataset based on distances between particles and can be changed interactively. Definition: A linear correlation coefficient across feature dimensions of latent vectors, probing per-dimension structure agreement. It measures stricter equivalence than cosine similarity by detecting poorly coordinated feature dimensions that high cosine similarity might miss. Formula: \rhoP = \frac{\sumk (z{render,k} - \bar{z}{render})(z{target,k} - \bar{z}{target})}{\sqrt{\sumk (z{render,k} - \bar{z}{render})^2} \sqrt{\sumk (z{target,k} - \bar{z}{target})^2}} where z{render,k} and z{target,k} are the k-th feature dimensions of the rendered and target latent vectors, and \bar{z} denotes their mean. Parameter: z{render}, z{target}: Latent vectors in \mathbb{R}^d. Comparison: Unlike cosine similarity which measures aggregate direction, Pearson correlation measures the coordination of individual feature dimensions. A gap between Pearson (\rhoP) and Spearman (\rhoS) indicates if mismatch is driven by outlier dimensions (large gap) or systematic non-linear warp (small gap). Definition: A rank-based correlation coefficient that captures monotonic (possibly non-linear) agreement between feature dimensions by computing the Pearson correlation on the ranks of the entries. Comparison: Unlike Pearson which measures linear correlation, Spearman measures rank agreement, making it robust to non-linear but order-preserving distortions. Similarity-based classification emerged from the need to handle multidimensional and semantically complex volume data where simple intensity thresholds fail. Early work focused on discrete classification of multidimensional signatures using voxel similarity criteria for rapid user interaction. The field expanded with self-supervised learning, such as S4, which uses Siamese networks to learn spatiotemporal proximity without labels. More recently, methods like those leveraging DINO vision transformers have enabled interactive similarity mapping based on annotated features. In the context of neural rendering, techniques like thresholded cosine similarity and Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) are used to decompose and probe latent spaces for editing and verification. name: Range-Space Segmentation
head: Function Field Visualization via Range-Space Segmentation, Function-space distance segmentation, Range-Space Segmentation Visualization
body: Range-Space Segmentation is a method for visualizing and analyzing function field data by projecting high-dimensional function samples into scalar fields based on their distance to a set of user-defined exemplar functions. It solves the problem of intelligently segmenting complex datasets (such as hyperspectral imagery or time-varying pollution data) by creating a classification field that assigns each spatial point to the nearest exemplar, thereby enabling feature-based visualization and surface extraction. Unlike multidimensional scaling (MDS) techniques which lose spatial layout, this method preserves the original spatial structure of the data while reducing the functional dimensionality to a scalar distance field and an integer label field. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A function field F defined over a spatial domain \mathbb{R}^n, where each point \mathbf{p} has an associated function f\mathbf{p}. A set of m exemplar functions M = (f1, f2, \dots, fm) selected by the user (via probes, analytic definitions, or statistics). A similarity metric \|\cdot\|. Output: Two scalar fields defined on \mathbb{R}^n: 1. A multi-function scalar distance field S^, where S^(\mathbf{p}) is the minimum distance from f\mathbf{p} to any exemplar in M. 2. An integer-valued classification field L, where L(\mathbf{p}) is the index i of the exemplar fi \in M that minimizes the distance. Data Structures: Distance Field (S^): A scalar grid of size N (number of spatial points). Each element stores a floating-point value representing the minimal function-space distance. Classification Field (L): An integer grid of size N. Each element stores an integer index i \in \{1, \dots, m\}. Exemplar Set (M): A list of m function samples. Each sample fi is typically represented as a discrete vector of k values (e.g., spectral bands). Similarity Metric: The distance between two functions f and g is computed using a weighted norm. For a function f defined over a closed interval I with weight function w(x): \|f\| = \left( \intI w(x) f(x)^2 dx \right)^{1/2} For discrete functions represented by a sequence of k points (f1, \dots, fk) with weights (w1, \dots, wk): \|f\| = \left( \sum{j=1}^k wj fj^2 \right)^{1/2} The distance between two functions f and g is \|f - g\|. If weights are constant, this corresponds to a Voronoi tessellation in range-space. Algorithm Steps: 1. Define Metric: Select the similarity metric \|\cdot\| (e.g., weighted Euclidean, Earth Mover’s Distance). 2. Select Exemplars: Define the ordered set M = (f1, \dots, fm). Exemplars can be user-probed points f\mathbf{p}, analytic functions, or derived statistics. 3. Compute Single-Function Distance Fields: For each exemplar fi \in M and for each spatial point \mathbf{p}, compute the scalar distance field S{fi}: S{fi}(\mathbf{p}) = \| fi - f\mathbf{p} \| 4. Compute Multi-Function Distance Field (S^): For each point \mathbf{p}, find the minimum distance across all exemplars: S^(\mathbf{p}) = \min{i \in \{1, \dots, m\}} S{fi}(\mathbf{p}) = \min{i \in \{1, \dots, m\}} \| fi - f\mathbf{p} \| 5. Compute Classification Field (L): For each point \mathbf{p}, store the index of the exemplar that achieved the minimum distance: L(\mathbf{p}) = \arg \min{i \in \{1, \dots, m\}} \| fi - f\mathbf{p} \| 6. Visualization: Single Exemplar (m=1): Map S^ directly to color/opacity using a 1D transfer function. Multiple Exemplars (m>1): Associate a transfer function ti with each exemplar fi. The color at \mathbf{p} is determined by applying the transfer function corresponding to the classification label: \text{color}(\mathbf{p}) = t{L(\mathbf{p})}(S^(\mathbf{p})) 7. Feature Segmentation (Optional): Extract surfaces separating features by isosurfacing the classification field L. For m=2, use an isovalue of 0.5 with Marching Cubes. For m>2, use multi-label segmentation algorithms (e.g., multi-label Marching Cubes, Dual Contouring). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rangespacesegmentation(volumefunctions, exemplars, metricfunc): """ volumefunctions: List of functions fp for each spatial point p. Each fp is a vector/array of values. exemplars: List of m exemplar functions M = [f1,..., fm]. metricfunc: Function that computes ||f - g||. Returns: Sstar: 2D array (numpoints, 1) of minimal distances. L: 2D array (numpoints, 1) of integer labels (0-indexed). """ numpoints = len(volumefunctions) numexemplars = len(exemplars) # Initialize fields Sstar = [None] numpoints L = [None] numpoints # Precompute distances for all exemplars to optimize min/argmin # Distances[i][p] = distance from exemplar i to point p distances = [[0.0] numpoints for in range(numexemplars)] for i in range(numexemplars): fi = exemplars[i] for p in range(numpoints): fp = volumefunctions[p] distances[i][p] = metricfunc(fi, fp) # Compute S and L for p in range(numpoints): mindist = float('inf') minidx = -1 for i in range(numexemplars): d = distances[i][p] if d < mindist: mindist = d minidx = i Sstar[p] = mindist L[p] = minidx return Sstar, L def visualizerangespace(Sstar, L, transferfunctions, numexemplars): """ Sstar: Minimal distance field. L: Classification field (integer labels). transferfunctions: List of m transfer functions [t0,..., t{m-1}]. """ resultcolors = [] for p in range(len(Sstar)): label = L[p] # Ensure label is within bounds if label < 0 or label >= numexemplars: label = 0 t = transferfunctions[label] distanceval = Sstar[p] color = t(distanceval) resultcolors.append(color) return resultcolors Parameters: m: Number of exemplar functions. Typically large, leading to tens or hundreds of samples per data point. Transfer Functions: 1D transfer functions are standard for volume rendering, but 2D, multidimensional, or local transfer functions may be applied to emphasize local structures. Probes: User-specified points in the data domain \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^n used to define exemplars f\mathbf{p}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Voronoi Tessellation: If the weight function/vector is constant, the segmentation corresponds to a Voronoi tessellation of the range-space. Interactive Latency: When modifying a single function sample (e.g., repositioning a probe), only one of the m distance fields changes. The remaining m-1 fields remain unchanged. The latency experienced is S + S^, where S is the time to compute one single-function distance field and S^ is the time to combine all fields. Metric Choice: The choice of distance metric (e.g., weighted Euclidean, Earth Mover’s Distance, Chang’s spectral distance) significantly affects segmentation results. Feature Query is a method for identifying spatial regions in a function fields where 1-dimensional functions are similar to a user-defined exemplar. It solves the problem of intelligently paring down large scientific datasets by identifying regions of interest based on user-specified selection queries, allowing for the analysis of smaller, more meaningful subsets rather than processing the entire dataset. Unlike traditional visualization which processes the whole dataset, this approach constrains computational complexity to the number of items returned by a query. Time Complexity: Computing the distance field for one exemplar takes time S. Combining m fields to produce S^ and L takes time S^. Total generation time is proportional to m \times S + S^. Memory Complexity: Requires storing m distance fields temporarily or computing them on the fly, plus the final S^ and L fields. Measured Performance: On an Apple MacBook Pro (2.33 GHz Intel Core 2 Duo, 2 GB memory, ATI Radeon X1600): Hyperspectral Imagery segmentation: 336 ms total (80 ms for S, 16 ms for S^). H2O Aerosol (National): 51 ms total (20 ms for S, 11 ms for S^). SO4 Aerosol (CRPAQS): 104 ms total (27 ms for S, 23 ms for S^). Strengths: Preserves original spatial layout (unlike MDS); allows interactive exploration via probes; supports time-varying fields by treating probes as points in \mathbb{R}^n \times T. Limitations: Performance scales with the number of exemplars m; requires careful selection of distance metric and exemplars. When to Use: Ideal for hyperspectral imagery and particulate pollution data where functional similarity is more important than spatial proximity. Range-Space Segmentation was introduced in the context of scientific visualization for function field data, specifically for hyperspectral imagery and time-varying particulate pollution data (CRPAQS). The method was developed to address the limitations of dimension reduction and clustering techniques that either lose spatial information or require fragile high-dimensional queries. It builds on the concept of function-space distance metrics and Voronoi tessellations in range-space. name: Feature Query
head: Function Field Feature Query, Range Query
body: Feature Query identifies spatial regions in a function field where 1-dimensional functions are similar. It pares down large scientific datasets by identifying regions of interest via user-specified selection queries, constraining computational complexity to the number of returned items rather than processing the whole dataset. Inputs and Outputs Input: A dataset containing m samples per function, where each spatial point p has an associated 1-dimensional function f^p. Output: A binary mask or subset of spatial points p that satisfy the query constraints. Data Structures The query is defined by a set of constraints over a closed interval I. The specific layout includes three modifiable curves: 1. Minimum Constraint Curve: Defines the lower bound for each sample index. 2. Maximum Constraint Curve: Defines the upper bound for each sample index. 3. Sample Weights Curve: Defines the importance of each sample index. Control points for these curves can be added, removed, and manipulated by the user. Algorithm Steps 1. Exploration: The user explores the function field using distance field renderings to identify potential features. 2. Constraint Definition: The user sketches a pair of curves to define the feature query's minimum and maximum constraints. Let Qi be the minimum-maximum interval constraint for sample index i, where i = 1, \dots, m. 3. Evaluation: For each point p in the dataset with function f^p, evaluate the condition: f^pi \in Qi \quad \forall i \in \{1, \dots, m\} A point p is part of the feature if and only if its function value at every sample index i falls within the corresponding interval Qi. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def featurequery(dataset, m, mincurve, maxcurve): """ dataset: List of point objects, each with a.function attribute (list of m floats). m: Number of samples per function. mincurve: Callable or list returning the lower bound Qmin[i] for sample index i. maxcurve: Callable or list returning the upper bound Qmax[i] for sample index i. Returns: List of point objects that satisfy the query constraints. """ matchingpoints = [] # Pre-calculate constraint intervals for all sample indices # Qi corresponds to the closed interval [Qmin[i], Qmax[i]] constraints = [] for i in range(m): qmin = mincurve(i) if callable(mincurve) else mincurve[i] qmax = maxcurve(i) if callable(maxcurve) else maxcurve[i] constraints.append((qmin, qmax)) for point in dataset: ismatch = True for i in range(m): fi = point.function[i] qmin, qmax = constraints[i] # Check if f^pi is within the closed interval Qi if not (qmin <= fi <= qmax): ismatch = False break if ismatch: matchingpoints.append(point) return matchingpoints Parameters m: The number of samples per function in the dataset. Qi: The minimum-maximum interval constraint for sample i. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The constraints are defined over closed intervals, so implementation must handle floating-point comparisons carefully to ensure boundary inclusion matches the mathematical definition f^pi \in Qi. Degenerate Input: If the minimum curve exceeds the maximum curve at any index i, the interval Qi is empty, and no points will match for that index. Time Complexity: The computational complexity is constrained to the number of items returned by the query, rather than the size of the entire dataset. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Tested on a 2.6 GHz Mobile Pentium 4-M laptop with 1.0 GB RAM and nVidia GeForce 4200 Go graphics card: Hyperspectral image query execution times were 320ms (Water), 218ms (Golf Courses), 257ms (Evaporation Ponds), and 23ms (High SO4 Concentration). Distance fields were generated at ~6 per second for hyperspectral images and ~25 per second for CRPAQS. Strengths: Allows for the extraction of reusable query constraints across multiple datasets and enables rapid identification and visualization of regions of interest. Limitations: Performance depends on the number of samples m and the dataset size during the initial exploration phase (distance field generation). When to use/not: Use when intelligently paring down large scientific datasets to analyze smaller, meaningful subsets is required; avoid when processing the entire dataset simultaneously is necessary. The concept of coupling visualization with high-performance query technology was first presented by Stockinger et al., who introduced the DEX software system utilizing the FastBit indexing infrastructure to identify regions of interest. Feature Query applies these Query-Driven Visualization (QDV) techniques specifically to extract features from function fields. The method was evaluated on datasets including AVIRIS hyperspectral images of Moffett Field and the San Francisco Bay area, and air quality simulations from the California Regional Particulate Air Quality Study (CRPAQS). name: Cosine Similarity
head: Cosine Similarity on Unit Hypersphere
body: Cosine similarity measures the angular agreement between two vectors by computing the inner product of their L2-normalized forms, effectively factoring out magnitude variations to focus on directional information. In volume rendering classification, this allows transfer functions to distinguish semantic content based on the orientation of feature vectors (e.g., gradients or latent codes) rather than their scalar intensity or norm, which may be affected by scale or activation statistics. It is distinct from magnitude-dependent methods and correlation-based methods like Pearson or Spearman, which assess linear or monotonic agreement across individual feature dimensions rather than global direction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two feature vectors \mathbf{z}{\text{render}}, \mathbf{z}{\text{target}} \in \mathbb{R}^d associated with a sample point \mathbf{x} in the volume. Output: A similarity score sim \in [-1, 1], representing the cosine of the angle between the vectors. Data Structures: Vectors \mathbf{z} are dense arrays of floating-point numbers of dimension d. No additional lookup tables or textures are required; the computation is algebraic. Steps: 1. Compute the squared L2 norm for each vector by summing the squares of its components. 2. Take the square root of the sum to obtain the L2 norm. 3. Divide each component of the original vectors by their respective L2 norm plus a stability constant \epsilon to obtain normalized vectors on the unit hypersphere. 4. Compute the dot product of the two normalized vectors. 5. Return the dot product as the similarity score. Formulas: L2 norm: \|\mathbf{z}\|2 = \sqrt{\sum{k=1}^d zk^2}. Normalization map: \hat{\mathbf{z}} = \phi(\mathbf{z}) = \frac{\mathbf{z}}{\|\mathbf{z}\|2 + \epsilon}, where \phi: \mathbb{R}^d \to S^{d-1} maps to the unit hypersphere. Similarity: sim = \hat{\mathbf{z}}{\text{render}}^\top \hat{\mathbf{z}}{\text{target}} = \cos \theta, where \theta is the angle between the original vectors. Parameters: \epsilon: A small positive constant added for numerical stability in the denominator. Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Vectors: If a feature vector is zero, the L2 norm is zero. The addition of \epsilon ensures the denominator is non-zero, resulting in a normalized vector of zeros, which yields a similarity of 0 against any other vector. Dimensionality: The method assumes vectors are in the same space \mathbb{R}^d. Mismatched dimensions are undefined. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cosinesimilarity(zrender, ztarget, eps): # Compute L2 norms normrender = sqrt(sum(z2 for z in zrender)) normtarget = sqrt(sum(z2 for z in ztarget)) # Normalize vectors zhatrender = [z / (normrender + eps) for z in zrender] zhattarget = [z / (normtarget + eps) for z in ztarget] # Compute dot product sim = sum(a b for a, b in zip(zhatrender, zhattarget)) return sim A pairwise cosine similarity metric normalized per query to remove encoder-specific global structure, averaged by class pair to summarize within-class and between-class affinity. It computes a query-wise normalized affinity a{ij} for every non-self pair using the mean \mu and standard deviation \sigma of the non-self gallery for each query, then averages a{ij} by class pair. The normalization formula is a{ij} = \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{s{ij} - \muj}{\sigmai} + \frac{s{ij} - \mui}{\sigmaj} \right). This normalization ensures that zero denotes the query-specific gallery average, not absolute similarity, revealing stronger class-relative organization in the feature space. Parameters include an embedding dimension of 768 and query-wise normalization using gallery statistics. Time Complexity: O(d) per pair, where d is the vector dimension. The normalization and dot product are linear in dimensionality. Memory Complexity: O(d) to store the vectors. No auxiliary structures like LUTs are needed for the core calculation. Strengths: Scale-invariant; robust to variations in vector magnitude caused by activation statistics or training dynamics. Focuses on directional semantic content. Limitations: Ignores magnitude information, which may be relevant in some physical contexts. Sensitive to the dimensionality d; high-dimensional spaces may suffer from the "curse of dimensionality" where distances become less discriminative. When to use: When feature vectors encode semantic content primarily through orientation (e.g., deep latent representations) rather than norm. When not to use: When magnitude carries critical information (e.g., density magnitude in some physical simulations) or when linear correlation across dimensions is more important than global direction (use Pearson/Spearman instead). The method is applied in probing vision models for 3D scene understanding using differentiable rendering. It is used to handle latent representations from deep networks where semantic content is encoded by vector orientation rather than norm, which can be affected by scale or training dynamics. The method maps vectors to S^{d-1} via L2-normalization and computes the inner product, which corresponds to \cos \theta. It is contrasted with Pearson and Spearman correlations, which assess agreement across individual feature dimensions rather than global direction.
