name: Continuous Indexed Points
head: Comparison with Traditional Multidimensional Transfer Functions
body: Continuous Indexed Points (CIP) is a visualization mapping technique that translates multidimensional data correlations into a continuous spatial representation within parallel coordinates, enabling the classification of volume rendering features through local fitting information rather than direct scalar thresholds. Unlike traditional multidimensional transfer functions that rely on selecting arches in scatterplots of scalar and gradient magnitude, CIP replicates this classification by mapping data attributes to continuous stripes in the image plane, allowing for the separation of features in noisy datasets where traditional methods fail. The method operates by computing indexed points from data attributes (e.g., scalar value and gradient magnitude) and transforming them into a bounded, symmetric representation to facilitate exploration and density estimation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Multivariate data attributes for each voxel, typically including scalar value v and gradient magnitude \|\nabla v\|. Output: A continuous density field in the parallel coordinates image plane, where specific regions (stripes) correspond to correlated data patterns, allowing users to define lassos for classification. Data Structures: Indexed Point Representation: Each data point is represented as an indexed point \eta in a 2D image plane associated with parallel axes. Homogeneous Coordinates: The 2D coordinates of the original image plane are rewritten in homogeneous coordinates [c1, c2, c3]. Orientation: The orientation \phi of the associated 2D Cartesian line is computed using point-line duality. Transformed Coordinates: New bounded 2D coordinates (u, v) are computed in the image plane. Steps: 1. Compute Indexed Points: For each voxel, compute the indexed point \eta based on the selected data attributes (e.g., scalar and gradient). 2. Angle-Uniform Transformation: Apply the angle-uniform transformation to map the unbounded, asymmetric indexed points to a bounded, symmetric representation. Rewrite the 2D coordinates of the original image plane in homogeneous coordinates [c1, c2, c3]. Compute the orientation \phi of the associated 2D Cartesian line using point-line duality. Map the tuple (c1, c2, c3, \phi) to new bounded 2D coordinates (u, v) in the image plane. Translate the transformed points to corresponding axes, bounding them in an area with the width of three adjacent vertical axes. 3. Density Estimation: Compute the density field of continuous indexed points using a forward-mapping of point samples to the image plane. 4. Classification: Users define lassos over the continuous stripes in the indexed point representation. Parts of an arch within parallel axes correspond to negatively correlated regions (downward going), while parts outside correspond to positively correlated regions (upward going). 5. Volume Rendering: Apply the classification defined by the lassos to the volume rendering, using the local fitting information of the attributes to determine optical properties. Formulas: Homogeneous coordinates: [c1, c2, c3]. Orientation computation: \phi computed via point-line duality. Transformation: (c1, c2, c3, \phi) \rightarrow (u, v). Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Standard indexed points are unbounded and asymmetric for positive and negative correlations, which forbids the visualization of all points in a limited image plane area. The angle-uniform transformation resolves this. Traditional 2D transfer functions may fail to classify clear boundaries in noisy data (e.g., MRI) due to the absence of visible arches in Cartesian histograms. A method to make Parallel Coordinates Plots (PCPs) continuous, providing a smooth and uncluttered representation. Heinrich and Weiskopf [41] demonstrated how PCPs can be made continuous to improve visualization quality. Transforms unbounded, asymmetric indexed points into a bounded, symmetric representation in the image plane to allow visualization of all points and facilitate exploration. It generalizes the method from 1-flats to 2-flats by computing indexed points in their original infinite image planes and transforming them to the bounded image plane with the same point transformation, then translating them to the corresponding axes. Strengths: Successfully classifies features in noisy datasets (e.g., MRI, DTI) where traditional multidimensional transfer functions fail to separate tissues or boundaries. It allows for the classification of complex features like tumor, corpus callosum, and brain tissues by revealing multiple branches of patterns. Limitations: The method relies on the computation of indexed points and their transformation, which may be computationally intensive for large datasets. The effectiveness depends on the ability to identify meaningful patterns in the continuous indexed point representation. Performance: Not given in the sources. When to use: When traditional multidimensional transfer functions fail to classify boundaries due to noise or lack of clear arches in scatterplots. When not to use: When simple scalar or gradient-based classification is sufficient and computational resources are limited. Continuous Indexed Points were introduced as a method for multivariate volume visualization, offering an alternative to traditional multidimensional transfer functions. The approach leverages local fitting information of data attributes to replicate classification tasks typically performed by selecting arches in scatterplots. The technique has been applied to benchmark datasets such as CT Tooth and Brain T1 MRI, as well as Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) data. name: Viewpoint Preference Analysis
body: Viewpoint Preference Analysis quantifies expert preferences in volume rendering by analyzing a database of existing rendered images. It recovers camera viewpoints from these images using category-specific Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and accumulates the resulting probability distributions to generate a viewing map. Unlike methods that optimize transfer functions or lighting parameters, this approach operates on the geometric configuration of the camera to identify regions of high expert consensus, such as side views for fish or front views for vessels. Inputs: A database of rendered volume images collected from visualization journals and conferences, categorized by object type (e.g., fish, vessel, tooth, engine, head). Pre-trained category-specific CNNs capable of estimating camera parameters from 2D images. Outputs: A viewing map: a 2D probability distribution over the sphere of possible viewpoints for a given volume category. Estimated viewpoint parameters (v\mu, v\sigma) for each input image. Data Structures: Viewpoint Distribution: Modeled as a bivariate Gaussian distribution N(v\mu, v\sigma^2), where v\mu is the mean viewpoint and v\sigma is the standard deviation representing uncertainty. Viewing Map: A grid or continuous function representing the accumulated probability density of viewpoints for a specific category. Steps: 1. Database Collection: Gather rendered images of volumes from expert sources (journals, conferences) and assign them to semantic categories. 2. Viewpoint Recovery: For each image in the database, pass it through the trained category-specific CNN to estimate the camera viewpoint. 3. Verification: Visually compare the rendered image generated from the recovered viewpoint against the original collected image to verify classification correctness. 4. Distribution Modeling: Model the estimated viewpoint for each image as a bivariate Gaussian N(v\mu, v\sigma^2). If the visual comparison indicates a correct classification, the distribution is considered reliable. If the image is misclassified (e.g., due to different projection types or non-uniform background colors), the standard deviation v\sigma will be very high, indicating low confidence in the mean v\mu. 5. Accumulation: Accumulate the Gaussian distributions of all images within a category to generate the final viewing map. The resulting map resembles a Gaussian mixture model. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def viewpointpreferenceanalysis(imagedatabase, cnnmodels): """ Analyzes viewpoint preferences for a category of volume renderings. Args: imagedatabase: List of tuples (image, category) cnnmodels: Dictionary mapping category to trained CNN model Returns: viewingmap: Accumulated probability distribution over viewpoints """ accumulateddistributions = [] for image, category in imagedatabase: # Step 2: Recover viewpoint using category-specific CNN # CNN inference step: recovers camera parameters from 2D image vmu, vsigma = cnnmodels[category].estimateviewpoint(image) # Step 3 & 4: Verification and Distribution Modeling # Visual verification is performed by humans. # Misclassified images naturally yield high vsigma. # Create the bivariate Gaussian distribution N(vmu, vsigma^2) distribution = BivariateGaussian(mean=vmu, std=vsigma) accumulateddistributions.append(distribution) # Step 5: Accumulate distributions to generate viewing map viewingmap = AccumulatedViewingMap(distributions=accumulateddistributions) return viewingmap class BivariateGaussian: def init(self, mean, std): self.mean = mean self.std = std def probabilitydensity(self, viewpoint): """ Calculate the probability density at a given viewpoint. Assumes viewpoints are 2D vectors (e.g., azimuth/elevation). """ distsq = sum((m - v) 2 for m, v in zip(self.mean, viewpoint)) return math.exp(-distsq / (2 self.std 2)) class AccumulatedViewingMap: def init(self, distributions): self.distributions = distributions def evaluate(self, viewpoint): """Sum of probability densities from all accumulated distributions.""" return sum(d.probabilitydensity(viewpoint) for d in self.distributions) Parameters: CNN Architecture: Category-specific models trained on the collected image database. Gaussian Model: Bivariate Gaussian is used to model viewpoint uncertainty. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Misclassification: Images may be misclassified due to different projection types (e.g., perspective vs. orthographic) or non-uniform background colors. High Uncertainty: Misclassified images exhibit very high v\sigma, which naturally limits their influence on the final viewing map due to the low probability density of the Gaussian tail. Unknown Ground Truth: Ground-truth viewpoints for collected images are often unknown, requiring visual verification rather than automated metrics. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in the paper "CNNs Based Viewpoint Estimation for Volume Visualization". It addresses how experts select viewpoints to maximize information or highlight features in volume renderings. The approach leverages deep learning to recover camera parameters from 2D images and was validated on categories such as fish, vessel, tooth, engine, and head, revealing specific preferences like side views for fish to avoid occlusion and front views for vessels to highlight aneurysms. name: Multi-field, vector and tensor volume visualization
body: This family encompasses techniques for visualizing multi-component data fields—specifically vector, tensor, and complex-valued fields—within a volume rendering context. It solves the problem of representing directional, anisotropic, or phase-dependent information that scalar volume rendering cannot convey. It sets itself apart from Classification and transfer functions by mapping non-scalar data attributes (direction, magnitude, phase) to visual properties, and from Illustrative and non-photorealistic volume rendering by focusing on geometric or color-based encoding of field structure rather than artistic style. All methods evaluate a mapping function M(\mathbf{x}) at sample points \mathbf{x} within the volume to produce visual attributes. The core mechanism involves sampling the multi-component data field at \mathbf{x}, decomposing or normalizing the value (e.g., extracting magnitude, direction, eigenvalues, or phase), and applying a transfer function or geometric construction to map these features to rendering parameters such as color, opacity, or primitive geometry. Domain Colouring maps complex numbers to colors using a cyclic colormap scaled by a degree parameter and brightness. It solves the problem of visualizing the phase and magnitude of complex-valued fields, such as spin orientation. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Line Glyphs by providing a dense, pixel-wise color field rather than discrete geometric primitives. Line Glyphs represent vector fields by line segments, with orientation matching the vector and length/color determined by magnitude. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Arrow Glyphs by its extreme computational efficiency and memory footprint, allowing for millions of glyphs, but suffers from ambiguity regarding vector direction and 3D orientation due to the lack of shading. Arrow glyphs resolve the direction ambiguity inherent in line-based vector field visualizations by using arrow-shaped primitives that explicitly encode flow direction. Unlike Line Glyphs for Vector Field Visualization, which suffer from orientation ambiguity, arrow glyphs use triangular faces to allow for 3D shading and clear directional cues. This method is implemented entirely on the GPU to avoid CPU-GPU data transfer, resulting in performance approximately 2x faster than line glyphs (about 10 ms for typical scenes) due to the larger visual size of arrows allowing for lower sampling density. A volume rendering method that visualizes diffusion tensor fields by correlating a random noise field anisotropically using the diffusion tensor, preserving high-frequency components in transversal directions while smearing noise in the direction of greater diffusivity. Visualization of vector fields by computing trajectories of mass-less particles (stream lines) seeded at specific locations, using an integrator to advance the particle position. An MRI based acquisition modality yielding 3x3 symmetric diffusion tensors as its native measurement quantity. Combines multiple field datasets (e.g., density, velocity, temperature) into a single visual representation for previewing and debugging simulation data. Solves verification of multi-component data without full rendering overhead. Choose for interactive simulation debugging. A visualization strategy combining volumetric scalar fields (object volume) with vector field geometry (glyphs and streamlines from optical flow) to convey both object location and motion status. An error metric for vector fields defined by a weighted sum of individual error metrics for parameters such as vector magnitude, gradient, curl, and divergence. A technique to analyze vector field topology based on critical point classification to capture global features of a flow field. Visualizing helicity, a scalar value calculated as the dot product of velocity and vorticity, to identify vortices. A vector space spanned by the three eigenvalues of a tensor, where tensor shape is represented by a point with coordinates called shape descriptors. A histogram analyzing the distribution of principal shear directions or eigenvectors projected onto a unit sphere. A direct multivariate volume rendering technique where voxels are mapped to a radial colormap based on the values of their multiple channels, allowing visualization of cross-channel interactions and phase/composite identification. Map each voxel to the radial colormap according to the values of its channels: a voxel high in channel A appears close to the node for A; a voxel high in channel B appears close to the node for B; a voxel containing a mixture of channels appears in between the respective nodes. Plot a subsampled distribution of voxels within the display to provide a general idea of the voxel distribution relative to the radial colormap. The radial colormap has distinct nodes corresponding to each channel (e.g., Ce, Gd) in the multivariate dataset. Used in the RadVolViz research application and the MultivariateView prototype for visualizing multivariate volume datasets such as the MIEC dataset and medical datasets (knee sarcoma). A single error metric for multivalued volume data (multiple scalar and/or vector fields) used for view-dependent visualization decisions. Defined as Em(T) = \sum{i=1}^{k} bi E{s,i}(T) + \sum{i=1}^{l} b{k+i} E{v,i}(T) where k is the number of scalar fields, l is the number of vector fields, E{s,i} is the error for the i-th scalar field, E{v,i} is the error for the i-th vector field, and bi are normalization coefficients. The coefficients are bi = \frac{1}{v{\delta,i}^2 \beta} where v{\delta,i} = |v{max,i} - v{min,i}| is the range of the i-th error component, and \beta is the power used in the function g. Coefficients bi act as normalization coefficients to make the influence of all scalar and vector fields equal. A two-field visualization technique where enstrophy defines the opacity and the Seed LIC texture of the vorticity field defines the color, creating vortex tube structures resembling 'candy canes'. Calculate the enstrophy field (\epsilon = |\omega|^2) from the vorticity field. Generate a Seed LIC texture for the vorticity field to convey directional structure. Map enstrophy values to opacity using a transfer function. Map the Seed LIC texture values to color. Render the volume using direct volume rendering with the defined transfer functions. A rendering approach that handles multiple data fields (e.g., temperature and density) simultaneously, often using multi-variate transfer functions. A representation of vector fields in polar coordinates (magnitude, azimuth, elevation) to map vector properties to visual parameters (opacity, hue, saturation). Designate the free stream velocity direction as the zero direction vector (axis). Calculate the azimuth (rotational) angle around the free stream vector. Map the azimuth angle to Hue. The alignment is arbitrary; the y-axis direction was used as zero in the implementation. Calculate the elevation (upstream to downstream) angle the field vector makes with the free stream vector. Map the elevation angle to Saturation. Vectors parallel to free stream are nearly gray (unsaturated); vectors 180 degrees to free stream are maximally saturated. Map the magnitude of the vector to Opacity. The free stream velocity direction is selected as the axis for zero direction. Visualizing specific components of the velocity field (e.g., x-component) to identify flow separation and reversal. Map the smallest x velocity values (including negative values) to cyan and high opacity. Map the largest x velocity components to yellow and near transparency. A technique to improve multivariate volume visualization by representing linear structures in parallel coordinates to encode local correlation of multivariate volume data using continuous indexed points. Perform local linear fitting in the spatial neighborhood of each volume sample using principal component analysis, accelerated by hierarchical spatial data structures. Visualize the local linear information as continuous indexed points in parallel coordinates, which is a density representation of indexed points in a continuous domain. Utilize both 1-flat and 2-flat indexed points to identify correlations between two variables and three variables, respectively. Apply an interactive occlusion shading model to facilitate good spatial perception of the volume rendering of volumetric correlation characteristics. Support interactive exploration using specifically designed multivariate transfer function widgets working in the image plane of parallel coordinates. A 2D plot depicting the relation between two scalar invariants, specifically principal stresses, to quantify normal and shear stresses. Sort the three principal stresses in descending order: σ1 ≥ σ2 ≥ σ3. Plot σ1 on the x-axis and σ3 on the y-axis, dividing the plot into four quadrants (A, B, C, D). Apply a sign-preserving logarithmic mapping to the eigenvalues: f(σi) = log(σi + 1) for σi ≥ 0, and f(σi) = −log(1 − σi) for σi < 0. Linearly map the results of the logarithmic mapping to the range [-1, 1]. Unlike standard logarithmic mappings that require positive domains, this method preserves signs to distinguish between positive (tensile) and negative (compressive) invariants. The visualization of vector and tensor fields is a fundamental problem in scientific visualization, arising in fluid dynamics, electromagnetism, and medical imaging (specifically Diffusion Tensor Imaging). Early methods relied on glyph-based approaches (arrows, lines) for their intuitive geometric representation. As computational power increased, GPU-based implementations allowed for dense glyph rendering. Color-based methods, such as domain coloring for complex fields, provide a dense alternative to glyphs. The integration of these techniques into volume rendering pipelines allows for the simultaneous visualization of scalar context and vector/tensor structure. name: Stream Lines
head: Integral Curve, Particle Tracer, Stream Lines and Ribbons Rendering
body: Stream lines are a local point tracking algorithm that visualizes vector fields by computing curves tangent to the field at every point, approximating the path of an infinitesimal massless particle. Unlike Glyph-based Vector/Tensor Visualization, which displays discrete vectors at fixed grid locations, stream lines reveal continuous flow topology and connectivity. They differ from Stream Surfaces by representing individual trajectories rather than surfaces formed by families of lines. Inputs: Vector field data \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}) defined on a 3D grid or texture. Seed points \mathbf{x}0 defining the starting locations of the lines. Integration parameters: step size \Delta t, maximum integration steps or length, and termination thresholds. Outputs: A set of polylines (sequences of vertices) representing the trajectories. Optional visual attributes: color mapped to velocity magnitude. Data Structures: Vector Field: Stored as a 3D texture or array. For GPU implementations, a cudaArray with cudaCreateChannelDesc<float4>() is bound to a 3D texture object with linear filtering and clamp addressing. The fourth component stores the vector magnitude for color mapping. Seeds: An array of 3D coordinates (float3). Output Buffers: outVertices: Array of float3 positions. Each streamline occupies maxSteps / geometrySampling + 1 vertices. outVertexColors: Array of float3 colors, aligned with vertices. outComputedSteps: Array of uint tracking the number of valid steps per seed. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: For each seed point i, initialize the current position \mathbf{p} in double precision for accuracy, and write the initial position to the output buffer. Set the integration step counter k=0. 2. Integration Loop: Iterate while k < \text{maxSteps}: a. Boundary Check: If \mathbf{p} is outside the volume bounds (e.g., x < 0 or x > \text{width}), terminate the streamline for this seed. b. Vector Lookup: Sample the vector field \mathbf{v} at \mathbf{p} using trilinear interpolation. c. Termination Check: If |\mathbf{v}| < \text{threshold} (e.g., minimum speed), terminate. d. Position Update: Compute the new position \mathbf{p}{new} using an integrator (Euler or RK4). e. Geometry Sampling: If the current integration step is a multiple of geometrySampling, write \mathbf{p}{new} to outVertices and the magnitude-based color to outVertexColors. This reduces memory usage by emitting fewer vertices than integration steps. f. Update: Set \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p}{new}, increment k. 3. Finalization: Store the total computed steps for each seed in outComputedSteps. Formulas: The fundamental ordinary differential equation for a streamline in a steady field is: \frac{d\mathbf{r}}{dt} = \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{r}(t)) With initial condition \mathbf{r}(t0) = \mathbf{x}0. Euler Integration (First-order, used for time-averaged fields like PCA data): \mathbf{r}(t + \Delta t) = \mathbf{r}(t) + \Delta t \cdot \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{r}(t)) The step \Delta t is typically chosen to match the minimum voxel dimension (e.g., 0.5–1 mm). Runge-Kutta 4th Order (RK4) (Higher accuracy, used in CUDA implementations): \mathbf{r}{new} = \mathbf{r} + \frac{\Delta t}{6} (k1 + 2k2 + 2k3 + k4) Where: k1 = \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{r}) k2 = \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{r} + \frac{\Delta t}{2} k1) k3 = \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{r} + \frac{\Delta t}{2} k2) k4 = \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{r} + \Delta t k3) RK4 requires four texture lookups per step. Trilinear Interpolation (Piecewise): For a point \mathbf{x}=(x,y,z) in a cell defined by corners (xi, yi, zi) to (xi+dx, yi+dy, zi+dz), the value is: \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{j=1}^{8} bj \mathbf{v}j The weights bj are calculated as: b1 = \frac{(xi+dx-x)(yi+dy-y)(zi+dz-z)}{dx \cdot dy \cdot dz} b2 = \frac{(x-xi)(yi+dy-y)(zi+dz-z)}{dx \cdot dy \cdot dz} b3 = \frac{(x-xi)(y-yi)(zi+dz-z)}{dx \cdot dy \cdot dz} b4 = \frac{(xi+dx-x)(y-yi)(zi+dz-z)}{dx \cdot dy \cdot dz} b5 = \frac{(xi+dx-x)(yi+dy-y)(z-zi)}{dx \cdot dy \cdot dz} b6 = \frac{(x-xi)(yi+dy-y)(z-zi)}{dx \cdot dy \cdot dz} b7 = \frac{(x-xi)(y-yi)(z-zi)}{dx \cdot dy \cdot dz} b8 = \frac{(xi+dx-x)(y-yi)(z-zi)}{dx \cdot dy \cdot dz} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computestreamlines(seeds, vectorfield, maxsteps, dt, geometrysampling, volumebounds, speedthreshold): """ seeds: list of (x, y, z) tuples vectorfield: callable returning (vx, vy, vz) at (x, y, z) volumebounds: (minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz) """ vertices = [] colors = [] stepscount = [] minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz = volumebounds for seed in seeds: # Initialize in double precision for accuracy x, y, z = float(seed[0]), float(seed[1]), float(seed[2]) # Write initial position vertices.append((x, y, z)) colors.append((1.0, 0.0, 0.0)) # Transfer function lookup based on magnitude currentsteps = 1 geometrystep = geometrysampling for step in range(1, maxsteps): # Boundary check if x < minx or x > maxx or y < miny or y > maxy or z < minz or z > maxz: break # Vector lookup via trilinear interpolation vx, vy, vz = vectorfield(x, y, z) mag = (vx2 + vy2 + vz2)0.5 # Termination check if mag < speedthreshold: break # Euler Integration xnew = x + dt vx ynew = y + dt vy znew = z + dt vz x, y, z = xnew, ynew, znew # Geometry sampling geometrystep -= 1 if geometrystep == 0: vertices.append((x, y, z)) colors.append((mag, 0.0, 0.0)) # Transfer function lookup currentsteps += 1 geometrystep = geometrysampling stepscount.append(currentsteps) return vertices, colors, stepscount Parameters: dt (Step size): Typically equal to the minimum voxel dimension (0.5–1 mm). maxSteps: Maximum number of integration steps. In ParaView, MaximumStreamlineLength is often set to 6\pi. geometrySampling: Integer specifying integration steps per output vertex. Default 1 (every step); higher values save GPU memory. SeedType: "Point Cloud" (spherical distribution, radius ~2.2, count ~300) or "Line Source" (high resolution line). TubeRadius: If rendered as tubes, typical value 0.03. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Integration should be performed in double precision to prevent drift, but results can be stored in single precision to save memory. Self-Intersection: In steady fields, streamlines do not cross except at cycles. Termination may occur if a streamline re-enters a previously visited cell. Distorted Coordinates: If the volume is distorted (e.g., horseshoe shape), the vector field must be transformed from computation space (C-space) to physical space (P-space) using the Jacobian of the coordinate transformation to ensure correct traces. Time-Varying Fields: Streamlines are defined for steady fields. For time-varying fields, these are technically pathlines, which may self-intersect and are not tangential to the instantaneous field. Adaptive Stream Line Seeding refines the density of stream lines in regions of high flow divergence (turbulence, vortices) while keeping them sparse in laminar areas. It iteratively subdivides neighboring stream lines when the distance between them exceeds a threshold, creating denser surface representations where complexity is highest. This method enhances standard 1D stream lines by overlaying an animated 1D texture (e.g., zebra pattern) that moves along the line in the direction of flow. This resolves the ambiguity of direction inherent in static lines. Stream surfaces stitch adjacent stream lines together to form a continuous geometric surface. This provides topological separation of the flow volume and helps ascertain overall flow direction in regions where lines curl around each other. HOT Lines visualize vector and tensor fields of arbitrary order by integrating trajectories that follow local extrema of a function on the unit sphere. This allows for multiple distinct trajectories per voxel, solving issues in fiber crossings where second-order tensors fail. A rendering approach for flow visualization using geometry bricks that hold range information of the visible region. Streamlines are stored in a single vertex buffer as a line strip, and arrows in an indexed buffer. Opaque geometry is rendered before the semi-transparent volume using depth testing to accurately mix geometry and volume information. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of seeds and S is the number of integration steps per streamline. RK4 is 4x more expensive per step than Euler due to multiple texture lookups. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot S / \text{geometrySampling}) for output buffers. GPU implementations use geometrySampling to trade precision for memory. Performance: Real-time visualization is achievable on GPUs using CUDA and texture lookups for interpolation. Strengths: Intuitive representation of flow direction and connectivity; effective for identifying vortices and stagnation points. Limitations: Sensitive to seed placement; may clutter the visualization if too dense; does not show flow magnitude as clearly as color-mapped glyphs without additional encoding. When to use: When tracking local flow paths and individual particle trajectories is required. When not to use: For time-varying fields (use pathlines); for fields with extremely high complexity where line density becomes unreadable (use stream surfaces or adaptive seeding). Stream lines were introduced as a fundamental technique for visualizing vector fields, originating from the mathematical definition of integral curves. They are widely used in fluid dynamics (blood flow, aerodynamics) and diffusion tensor imaging (neural connectivity). Modern implementations leverage GPU acceleration (CUDA) for real-time rendering of large datasets. name: Adaptive Stream Line Seeding
head: Adaptive Line Extension, Adaptive seeding of stream lines, Streamline Subdivision
body: Adaptive Stream Line Seeding is a GPU-based algorithm that dynamically increases streamline density in regions of high flow divergence (such as turbulent areas or vortices) while maintaining sparse sampling in laminar regions. It sets itself apart from static seeding methods by iteratively subdividing pairs of neighboring streamlines based on their spatial separation, using a control kernel to identify divergence and an evaluation kernel to generate the new trajectories. The method operates in an iterative loop controlled by the CPU, alternating between a Control Kernel (divergence detection and seed generation) and an Evaluation Kernel (actual streamline integration). The control kernel uses atomic operations to manage a pre-allocated static memory buffer as a dynamic array, allowing threads to append new seeds and line pairs without prior knowledge of the final count. Control Kernel Inputs: linePairs: uint2 array of pairs of line indices representing neighboring streamlines to be tested. linePairsCount: uint, number of pairs in linePairs. lineVertices: float3 array containing all vertices of all current streamlines. verticesPerLine: uint, number of vertices per streamline. verticesPerSample: uint, stride (step) between sampled points in lineVertices. lineLengths: uint, length (number of vertices) of each streamline. seeds: float3, array of seed positions for each streamline. maxAllowedLineDist: float, threshold for maximum distance between corresponding points before subdivision is triggered. Control Kernel Outputs: outLinePairs: uint2, updated array of neighboring line pairs (includes original pairs and new pairs linking new seeds). outPairsIndex: uint, atomic counter for the number of pairs written to outLinePairs. outLinesIndex: uint, atomic counter for the number of new lines/seeds written to seeds. linesMaxCount: uint, maximum capacity of the seeds and outLinePairs arrays. Line Pairs: Stored as uint2 (two 32-bit unsigned integers). x and y fields store indices into the seeds array. Line Vertices: Stored as float3 (three 32-bit floats). The buffer is flattened; the vertex at index k of line L is at lineVertices[L verticesPerLine + k verticesPerSample]. Seeds: Stored as float3. The seed for line L is at seeds[L]. 1. Initialization: The CPU allocates memory for a maximum number of lines (linesMaxCount) and initializes outLinesIndex and outPairsIndex to 0. The initial linePairs array is populated with the indices of the initial streamlines (typically starting with two lines or a small set). 2. Kernel Launch: The CPU launches the computeLineAdaptiveExtensionKernel with one thread per pair in linePairs. 3. Thread Execution (for each thread id): a. Boundary Check: Calculate global thread ID. If id >= linePairsCount, terminate. b. Pair Retrieval: Get the current pair indices: currPair = linePairs[id]. c. Length Check: Calculate count = min(lineLengths[currPair.x], lineLengths[currPair.y]). If count < 2, terminate (lines are too short to sample). d. Divergence Test: i. Initialize maxDist = 0. ii. Iterate i from 0 to count with step count / 32 (sampling 32 points evenly along the shorter line). iii. Get vertices: v1 = lineVertices[currPair.x verticesPerLine + i verticesPerSample] and v2 = lineVertices[currPair.y verticesPerLine + i verticesPerSample]. iv. Update maxDist = max(maxDist, length(v1 - v2)). e. Threshold Check: If maxDist < maxAllowedLineDist, terminate (no subdivision needed). f. Calculate New Lines: Compute the number of new seeds to insert: newLines = \lfloor \sqrt{\frac{maxDist}{maxAllowedLineDist}} \rfloor. g. Atomic Allocation: i. Atomically allocate space for new lines: outLineIndex = atomicAdd(outLinesIndex, newLines). ii. If outLineIndex + newLines >= linesMaxCount, rollback: atomicAdd(outLinesIndex, -newLines) and terminate (buffer full). h. Seed Generation: i. Calculate step vector: seedStep = (seeds[currPair.y] - seeds[currPair.x]) / (newLines + 1). ii. Loop i from 0 to newLines - 1: 1. Set new seed: seeds[outLineIndex + i] = seeds[currPair.x] + (i + 1) seedStep. 3. Atomically allocate space for new pair: outPairIndex = atomicAdd(outPairsIndex, 1). 4. Link previous pair end to new seed: outLinePairs[lastOutPairIndex].y = outLineIndex + i. 5. Link new seed to current pair end: outLinePairs[outPairIndex].x = outLineIndex + i, outLinePairs[outPairIndex].y = currPair.y. 6. Update lastOutPairIndex = outPairIndex. i. Preserve Original Pair: The original pair currPair is also written to outLinePairs at the index allocated at the start of the thread execution (before divergence check) to maintain the neighbor list structure for the next iteration. 4. Evaluation: The CPU launches the evaluation kernel using the updated seeds and linePairs to integrate the new streamlines. 5. Iteration: The CPU repeats steps 2-4 until a maximum number of adaptive steps is reached or no new lines are generated. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computelineadaptiveextension( maxallowedlinedist, linepairs, linepairscount, linevertices, verticesperline, verticespersample, linelengths, seeds, outlinepairs, outpairsindex, outlinesindex, linesmaxcount): # Global thread ID threadid = getglobalthreadid() if threadid >= linepairscount: return currpair = linepairs[threadid] # Allocate space for the original pair in output outpairindex = atomicadd(outpairsindex, 1) outlinepairs[outpairindex].x = currpair.x outlinepairs[outpairindex].y = currpair.y # Determine minimum length of the two lines count = min(linelengths[currpair.x], linelengths[currpair.y]) if count < 2: return # Lines too short # Test 32 samples for divergence maxdist = 0.0 step = count // 32 if step == 0: step = 1 for i in range(0, count, step): v1 = linevertices[currpair.x verticesperline + i verticespersample] v2 = linevertices[currpair.y verticesperline + i verticespersample] dist = length(v1 - v2) if dist > maxdist: maxdist = dist if maxdist < maxallowedlinedist: return # Lines do not diverge # Calculate number of new lines newlines = floor(sqrt(maxdist / maxallowedlinedist)) # Atomically allocate output line indices outlineindex = atomicadd(outlinesindex, newlines) if (outlineindex + newlines) >= linesmaxcount: atomicadd(outlinesindex, -newlines) # Rollback return # Not enough space # Calculate seed step seedstep = (seeds[currpair.y] - seeds[currpair.x]) / (newlines + 1) lastoutpairindex = outpairindex for i in range(newlines): # Set new seed seeds[outlineindex + i] = seeds[currpair.x] + (i + 1) seedstep # Insert new pair outpairindex = atomicadd(outpairsindex, 1) # Link previous pair end to new seed outlinepairs[lastoutpairindex].y = outlineindex + i # Link new seed to current pair end outlinepairs[outpairindex].x = outlineindex + i outlinepairs[outpairindex].y = currpair.y lastoutpairindex = outpairindex maxAllowedLineDist: The maximum distance between corresponding points of two lines before subdivision is triggered. Typical values depend on the scale of the vector field. verticesPerSample: Stride between sampled points in the lineVertices buffer. Set to verticesPerLine / 32 to ensure exactly 32 samples are taken. Buffer Overflow: If the pre-allocated linesMaxCount is insufficient, new seeds are discarded via atomic rollback. This can lead to incomplete adaptive refinement in highly turbulent regions. Short Lines: Lines with fewer than 2 vertices are skipped to prevent division by zero or invalid sampling. Performance: The algorithm is slower than non-adaptive versions due to the overhead of atomic operations and the iterative CPU-GPU synchronization. The number of new lines grows exponentially in the early iterations (2^n), which can cause initial slowdowns. Precision: Floating-point precision in maxDist calculation and seedStep interpolation can affect the accuracy of seed placement in highly curved flows. An iterative algorithm that generates streamlines by starting with a fixed number of seeds, extending them via CUDA kernels, and recursively adding new seeds based on the endpoints of previously generated lines until a maximum number of adaptive steps is reached or no new lines are generated. Multi-Seed Streamline Tracking is a method for visualizing vector and tensor fields by integrating streamlines from multiple simultaneous seed points. It solves the problem of sparse or ambiguous flow representation by seeding a neighborhood of voxels (e.g., a 26-neighbourhood) or a regular grid across the volume, rather than relying on single isolated seeds. It sets itself apart from Adaptive Stream Line Seeding by using fixed spatial intervals or local neighborhoods for seeding rather than dynamic subdivision based on flow divergence, and from Entropy-based Seeding by not using information-theoretic metrics to determine seed density. Entropy-based Seeding is a method for selecting streamline seed locations in 3D vector fields by using Shannon’s entropy to measure local information content. It places seeds proportionally to entropy values to quantitatively capture critical flow features, such as turbulent cores, ensuring important regions are densely sampled. It differs from sibling methods like Adaptive Stream Line Seeding by deriving seed density directly from an information-theoretic scalar field rather than geometric divergence or control kernels. Time Complexity: The control kernel runs in O(N) where N is the number of line pairs. Each iteration involves atomic operations which can cause contention. The number of lines grows exponentially in early iterations, leading to a potentially high total number of iterations before convergence. Memory Complexity: Requires pre-allocation of memory for the maximum possible number of lines (linesMaxCount). This can be significantly larger than the initial number of lines, leading to high memory usage. Performance: The algorithm is performance-costly due to thread communication overhead and atomic operations on GPU. The iterative CPU-GPU synchronization further reduces efficiency compared to non-adaptive versions. Strengths: Provides detailed visualization of complex flow features (turbulence, vortices) by concentrating samples where they are most needed. Regular vs. adaptive comparisons show that adaptive seeding reveals important features that regular seeding misses. Limitations: High memory consumption due to pre-allocation. Slower execution time. Complexity in implementation due to dynamic memory management on GPU. When to Use: When visualizing complex 3D vector fields where flow divergence is a key feature to highlight, and sufficient GPU memory is available. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and memory is constrained, or when the flow field is largely laminar and uniform. The method was developed by Marek Fiser and described in his blog post "Realtime visualization of 3D vector fields using CUDA". The implementation is also available in the GitHub repository "NightElfik/Vector-field-visualization-using-cuda". The approach addresses the challenge of implementing adaptive algorithms on GPU, where thread communication and dynamic memory management are difficult and performance-costly. name: Adaptive Streamline Generation
head: Adaptive Line Extension, Streamline Subdivision
body: An iterative algorithm to generate streamlines by starting with a fixed number of seeds, extending them via CUDA kernels, and recursively adding new seeds based on the endpoints of previously generated lines until a maximum number of adaptive steps is reached or no new lines are generated. Inputs: Vector field data, initial seed points (mstartPt, mendPt), maximum number of adaptive steps (mmaxAdaptiveSteps), maximum adaptive distance (mmaxAdaptiveDistance), time step (mdt), integration method flag (museRk4), maximum samples (mmaxSamples), line width (mlineWidth), tube rendering flag (museTubes), and tube radius (mtubeRadius). Outputs: A set of streamlines represented as vertex buffers. Data Structures: mhseeds: Host array of seed points. mdseeds: Device array of seed points. mhptCounts: Host array tracking the number of vertices per line. mdptCounts: Device array tracking the number of vertices per line. dinLinePairs: Device array of uint2 storing pairs of line indices to extend. Size: mlinesCount. doutLinePairs: Device array of uint2 storing new line pairs generated in the current step. Size: mlinesCount. dvertices: Device array of vertices for all lines. doutLinesIndex: Device pointer to the current index in the vertex buffer for new lines. doutLinePairsIndex: Device pointer to the current index in the line pair buffer for new pairs. Parameters: mmaxAdaptiveSteps: Maximum number of adaptive iterations allowed for streamline generation. mmaxAdaptiveDistance: Maximum distance parameter passed to the adaptive extension kernel. mdt: Time step for integration. museRk4: Boolean flag indicating whether to use Runge-Kutta 4th order integration. verticesPerSample: Number of vertices per sample point (e.g., for tube rendering). verticesPerLine: Total vertices per line. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize mhptCounts to zero for all lines. Set linesToGenerate to 2. Set mhseeds[0] to mstartPt and mhseeds[1] to mendPt. Copy these 2 seeds to device memory mdseeds. Set mlinePairsCount to 1. Create a uint2 line pair {0, 1} and copy to dinLinePairs. Set totalLinesCount to 0. 2. Call runKernel with nullptr seeds and linesToGenerate (2) at totalLinesCount (0). Increment totalLinesCount by linesToGenerate. 3. Loop for adaptiveSteps from 0 to mmaxAdaptiveSteps - 1: a. Copy totalLinesCount to doutLinesIndex and 0 to doutLinePairsIndex. b. Call runLineAdaptiveExtensionKernel with maxAdaptiveDistance, dinLinePairs, mlinePairsCount, dvertices, verticesPerLine, verticesPerSample, mdptCounts, mdseeds, doutLinePairs, doutLinePairsIndex, doutLinesIndex, and mlinesCount. c. Call runKernel with nullptr seeds and linesToGenerate at totalLinesCount. Increment totalLinesCount by linesToGenerate. d. Update dinLinePairs with doutLinePairs for the next iteration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivestreamlinegeneration(startpt, endpt, maxadaptivesteps, maxadaptivedistance, mlinescount): # Initialization mhptcounts = [0] mlinescount linestogenerate = 2 mhseeds = [startpt, endpt] mdseeds = list(mhseeds) # Host-to-device memory copy mlinepairscount = 1 dinlinepairs = [(0, 1)] # uint2 pair {0, 1} totallinescount = 0 dvertices = [] # Vertex buffer doutlinesindex = 0 doutlinepairsindex = 0 doutlinepairs = [] # New line pairs buffer verticespersample = 8 # Typical value verticesperline = 0 # Not given in sources # Initial generation runkernel(None, linestogenerate, totallinescount) totallinescount += linestogenerate # Adaptive loop for adaptivesteps in range(maxadaptivesteps): doutlinesindex = totallinescount doutlinepairsindex = 0 runlineadaptiveextensionkernel( maxadaptivedistance, dinlinepairs, mlinepairscount, dvertices, verticesperline, verticespersample, mhptcounts, mdseeds, doutlinepairs, doutlinepairsindex, doutlinesindex, mlinescount) runkernel(None, linestogenerate, totallinescount) totallinescount += linestogenerate # Update input line pairs for next iteration dinlinepairs = doutlinepairs def runkernel(seeds, count, offset): pass def runlineadaptiveextensionkernel(maxdist, inpairs, paircount, vertices, vpl, vps, ptcounts, seeds, outpairs, outpairidx, outlineidx, linescount): pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Curvature Field Line Tracing for Strokes is a method for generating hatching strokes in volume illustration by tracing paths from seed points along maximal curvature directions in object space. It differs from standard streamline tracing by following the principal direction of the scalar field's curvature rather than a velocity vector, and by employing an adaptive step size controlled by a deviation threshold to ensure strokes remain visually coherent and front-facing. name: Curvature Field Line Tracing for Strokes
head: Stroke generation via RK4(3)
body: Curvature Field Line Tracing for Strokes generates hatching strokes in volume illustration by tracing paths from seed points along maximal curvature directions in object space. It differs from standard streamline tracing by following the principal direction of the scalar field's curvature rather than a velocity vector, and by employing an adaptive step size controlled by a deviation threshold to ensure strokes remain visually coherent and front-facing. Inputs: Scalar field f(\mathbf{x}). A set of seed points \mathbf{x}0. A deviation threshold angle \theta{\max}. Outputs: A set of strokes, where each stroke is a line strip (sequence of points). Each point in a stroke stores: Vertex coordinates \mathbf{p}i. Gray-scale gradient \nabla f(\mathbf{p}i) interpolated from the scalar field. Texture coordinate ti, defined as the distance from the seed point relative to the total stroke length. Data Structures: Curvature Field: Derived from the scalar field. The direction of tracing is the "maximal curvature direction" in object space. The exact mathematical definition (e.g., Hessian eigenvector) is not explicitly detailed in the source, but it is treated as a vector field \mathbf{V}(\mathbf{x}). Stroke Point: A struct containing position, gradient, and texture coordinate. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: For each seed point \mathbf{x}0, determine the initial hatch direction \mathbf{d}0 as the maximal curvature direction at \mathbf{x}0. Initialize current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{x}0 and current direction \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{d}0. Initialize stroke point list S = [\mathbf{p}]. 2. Integration Loop: While the stroke is not terminated: a. Compute the curvature direction \mathbf{V}(\mathbf{p}) at the current position. b. Use RK4(3) integration with adaptive step size control to advance the position along \mathbf{V}(\mathbf{p}). The adaptive step size reduces the number of intermediate points when the field is smooth. Tri-linear interpolation is used for the curvature field. c. Let the new position be \mathbf{p}{\text{new}} and the new direction be \mathbf{d}{\text{new}} = \mathbf{V}(\mathbf{p}{\text{new}}). d. Termination Check: Calculate the angle \alpha between the current hatch direction \mathbf{d}{\text{new}} and the original hatch direction \mathbf{d}0. If \alpha > \theta{\max}, terminate the stroke. e. Lighting and Culling Prep: Interpolate the gray-scale gradient \nabla f(\mathbf{p}{\text{new}}) from the scalar field. f. Store Point: Add \mathbf{p}{\text{new}} to S. Compute texture coordinate t = \text{dist}(\mathbf{p}{\text{new}}, \mathbf{x}0) / \text{total\length}. g. Update \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p}{\text{new}} and \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{d}{\text{new}}. 3. Post-processing: Compute a cone of normals from the set of all gradients in the stroke to cull back-facing strokes. Render the stroke as a line strip using the stored points, gradients, and texture coordinates. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def mag(v): return math.sqrt(dot(v, v)) def dist(a, b): return mag([x - y for x, y in zip(a, b)]) def normalize(v): m = mag(v) return [x / m for x in v] if m > 0 else [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] def rk43step(field, p, h): # Standard RK4(3) step with adaptive error estimation. # Sources do not specify the exact coefficients or controller formula. k1 = field(p) k2 = field([p[i] + h k1[i] / 2.0 for i in range(3)]) k3 = field([p[i] + h k2[i] / 2.0 for i in range(3)]) k4 = field([p[i] + h k3[i] for i in range(3)]) return [p[i] + h (k1[i] + 2 k2[i] + 2 k3[i] + k4[i]) / 6.0 for i in range(3)] def generatestroke(seed, curvaturefield, scalarfield, thetamax): # 1. Initialization originaldir = normalize(curvaturefield(seed)) currentpos = list(seed) strokepoints = [] strokepoints.append({'pos': list(currentpos), 'grad': scalarfield.gradient(currentpos), 't': 0.0}) totallen = 0.0 prevpos = currentpos # 2. Integration Loop while True: # Adaptive step size control h = 0.1 # Initial step size; controller adjusts based on local error nextpos = rk43step(curvaturefield, currentpos, h) nextdir = normalize(curvaturefield(nextpos)) # Termination Check angle = math.acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, dot(nextdir, originaldir)))) if angle > thetamax: break # Lighting and Culling Prep grad = scalarfield.gradient(nextpos) # Update length seglen = dist(prevpos, nextpos) totallen += seglen # Store Point strokepoints.append({'pos': list(nextpos), 'grad': grad, 't': dist(seed, nextpos)}) prevpos = nextpos currentpos = nextpos # Normalize texture coordinates relative to total stroke length if totallen > 0: for pt in strokepoints: pt['t'] /= totallen return strokepoints Parameters: Deviation Threshold (\theta{\max}): A constant angle deviation from the original hatch direction that terminates the stroke. No specific value is given in the sources. Integration Method: RK4(3) with adaptive step size. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Curvature Variations: The deviation threshold prevents stepping into regions where the curvature field shows high variations, which could otherwise lead to erratic strokes. Back-facing Strokes: Strokes that turn away from the viewer may be back-facing; the method computes a cone of normals from gradients to cull these. Interpolation Accuracy: Although tri-linear interpolation is used for the curvature field, the RK4(3) method ensures high accuracy in field line computation. An integral surface is a geometric construct that generalizes streamlines and pathlines to two dimensions by sweeping a seeding curve through a vector field. It serves as a surface representation of flow, where the surface is generated by integrating the trajectories of all points along a one-dimensional seeding curve (also called a rake). It sets itself apart from single streamline tracing by providing a continuous surface topology that captures the collective behavior of a flow region, and from streaklines by tracking particles released simultaneously from the curve rather than continuously over time. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of seed points and the average stroke length. Adaptive step size reduces the number of intermediate points, improving performance in smooth regions. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the total number of points in all strokes. Each point stores position, gradient, and texture coordinate. Strengths: High accuracy in field line computation despite simple tri-linear interpolation. Efficient encoding of strokes using a small number of line segments due to adaptive step size. Effective culling of back-facing strokes using gradient-based normal cones. Limitations: Requires computation of curvature field, which may be more expensive than velocity field evaluation. Termination is based on deviation from the original direction, which may not be suitable for all visualization goals. When to Use: When generating hatching strokes for volume illustration that need to follow the structural curvature of the scalar field and maintain visual coherence. When Not to Use: When velocity-based flow visualization is required, or when the curvature field is noisy or ill-defined. The method was introduced in the context of interactive volume illustration. It is described in the paper "Interactive volume illustration". The approach leverages the fact that strokes placed entirely in front of a selected surface can effectively illustrate the volume's structure. The use of RK4(3) with adaptive step size is chosen to balance accuracy and performance, allowing for high-quality strokes with minimal computational overhead. name: Integral Surface
head: Path Surface, Rake, Stream Surface
body: An integral surface is a path surface in time-varying velocity fields or a stream surface in steady flow, generated by sweeping a univariate seeding curve (or rake) through the field. It generalizes single streamline tracing by capturing the collective behavior of a flow region along a continuous curve. Unlike streaklines, which track particles continuously emerging from a fixed point, integral surfaces integrate trajectories simultaneously from all points on the seeding curve. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A vector field v(\mathbf{x}, t), a univariate seeding curve c(s) mapping a parameter interval I \subseteq \mathbb{R} to \mathbb{R}^n, and a time interval [t0, t]. Output: A parametric surface S(s, t) defined over the domain I \times [t0, t]. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize: Sample the seeding curve c(s) at discrete intervals to obtain a set of seed points. 2. Integrate: For each seed point, solve the ordinary differential equation \frac{d\mathbf{x}}{d\tau} = v(\tau, \mathbf{x}) from \tau = t0 to \tau = t to compute the trajectory. 3. Assemble: Collect the integrated trajectories to form the parametric surface S(s, t). Formulas: For a time-varying velocity field v, the integral surface S(s, t) is defined by the integral equation: S(s, t) = c(s) + \int{t0}^{t} v(\tau, S(s, \tau)) \, d\tau Where: s is the parameter along the seeding curve c. t is the time parameter. c(s) is the initial position of the particle at time t0. v(\tau, \mathbf{x}) is the velocity vector at time \tau and position \mathbf{x}. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-Intersection: In time-varying fields, the resulting lines may no longer be tangential to the flow field and may self-intersect. Parameterization Distortion: Stretching and divergence of the surface can distort the parameterization, which is particularly problematic if texture mapping (e.g., stream arrows) is applied, resulting in very large or small visual elements. Higher Dimensions: The definition generalizes to higher-dimensional seeding geometry, creating path volumes and time surfaces, which increases computational complexity significantly. On-the-Fly Generation (Hultquist's Method): An alternative implementation, first investigated by Hultquist, propagates a front of particles through the flow field: 1. Front Propagation: Maintain a front of particles forming a surface segment. 2. Adaptive Integration: Integrate particle trajectories as needed during the propagation of the front. 3. Triangulation: Perform on-the-fly triangulation of the surface using a greedy approach to connect the integrated points into a mesh. 4. Resolution Control: Treat divergence and convergence of particles in the advancing front using a simple distance criterion. Insert new particles where the distance between existing front particles exceeds a threshold, and remove particles where the distance is too small, ensuring a balanced resolution of the surface. This method generates a synthetic dataset of Earth's magnetospheric magnetic field lines by tracing dipole field lines from ionospheric footpoints and magnetosheath draped lines, encoding field intensity to grayscale, and outputting the result as a compact JSON file. It serves as a data preparation step for volumetric visualization, distinct from general stream line tracing by its specific geometric constraints (ionospheric seeding, magnetopause boundaries) and reliance on an analytical dipole model rather than a grid-based vector field. It builds on Integral Surface by providing the discrete point-cloud input required for surface generation. Particle traces on 2D surfaces is a visualization technique that represents the magnitude and direction of a 3D vector field on arbitrary 2D surfaces (not necessarily contour surfaces) by drawing long, evenly spaced particle trace lines. Unlike random seed placement which does not guarantee coverage near every point, this method uses a hierarchical integer lattice to ensure some seed point is near every point on the surface, avoiding density issues where the visualization becomes too dense or too sparse. It sets itself apart from its parent Integral Surface by explicitly breaking traces into segments of contrasting color to resolve directional ambiguity in still images and by projecting the vector field onto the surface geometry rather than integrating within the volume. A method to compute integral surfaces by propagating a front of particles through a flow field, integrating trajectories as needed, and performing on-the-fly triangulation. It was first investigated by Hultquist. The algorithm integrates particle trajectories dynamically during front propagation and uses a greedy approach for triangulation. It handles particle divergence and convergence using a distance criterion to insert or remove particles, ensuring balanced surface resolution. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides a continuous surface representation of flow, useful for visualizing flow topology and transport. The on-the-fly method allows for adaptive resolution. Limitations: Susceptible to self-intersection in complex time-varying flows. Parameterization distortion can complicate texture mapping. When to use: When a continuous surface representation of a flow region is needed. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Integral surfaces were first investigated by Hultquist. Advanced visualization techniques, such as texture mapping arrows on stream surfaces (stream arrows) to convey local flow direction, were introduced by Löffelmann. This work addressed the challenge of conveying directionality on the surface but initially did not account for the distortion of the parameterization caused by surface stretching and divergence. Subsequent work by the same authors introduced regular, hierarchical tiling of texture space to adjust for these distortions. The concept is formally defined in the context of multi-field visualization, distinguishing between path surfaces (time-varying) and stream surfaces (steady). name: Magnetosphere Field Line Tracing
head: Earth Magnetosphere Dataset Generation Pipeline, Earth Magnetosphere Field Line Tracing, Earth data generation, dipole field line integration
body: This method generates a synthetic dataset of Earth's magnetospheric magnetic field lines by tracing dipole field lines from ionospheric footpoints and magnetosheath draped lines, encoding field intensity to grayscale, and outputting the result as a compact JSON file. It serves as a data preparation step for volumetric visualization, distinct from general stream line tracing by its specific geometric constraints (ionospheric seeding, magnetopause boundaries) and reliance on an analytical dipole model rather than a grid-based vector field. It builds on Integral Surface by providing the discrete point-cloud input required for surface generation. Inputs: rstart: Initial radial distance (default 3.0 RE). theta0: Co-latitude of the ionospheric footpoint (radians). phi0: Azimuth (longitude) of the footpoint (radians). npoints: Maximum number of sample points per field line. step: Fixed step size for Euler integration (value not given in sources; typical values for magnetospheric scales are 0.01-0.1 RE). NFIELDLINES, NPOINTSPERLINE, NSHEATHLINES, NPOINTSSHEATH: Global dataset parameters. MAXRECORDS: Hard cap on total output points (default 5000). RANDOMSEED: Seed for reproducibility. Outputs: A JSON array where the first record is metadata (source='meta') and subsequent records are field line points. Each point record contains: x, y, z (position in RE), Bx, By, Bz (field vector), intensity (field magnitude), source ('magnetosphere' or 'magnetosheath'), and gray (normalized grayscale intensity). Data Structures: Record: Dictionary with keys x, y, z, Bx, By, Bz, intensity, source, gray. All floats are rounded to a specified precision (e.g., 3 decimal places) for compression. Metadata: Dictionary with keys source ('meta'), sourcelabel, date, coordunits, fieldunits, planetaryref, domainscale, measured, datatype, mpmodel, bsmodel, Bmodel, notes. Algorithm: 1. Initialize Global State: Set random seed: random.seed(RANDOMSEED). Initialize allrecords list. 2. Trace Magnetospheric Dipole Field Lines: Define angular steps: phisteps = 8, thetasteps = NFIELDLINES // phisteps. Loop iphi from 0 to phisteps - 1: Calculate azimuth: phi = (iphi / phisteps) 2.0 math.pi. Loop ith from 0 to thetasteps - 1: Calculate co-latitude: theta = math.radians(25.0 + ith 30.0 / max(thetasteps - 1, 1)). Call tracedipolefieldline(theta, phi, NPOINTSPERLINE). Append returned points to allrecords. 3. Trace Magnetosheath Lines: Call generatemagnetosheathlines(NSHEATHLINES, NPOINTSSHEATH). Append returned points to allrecords. 4. Encode Intensity to Grayscale: Extract all intensities: intensities = [r['intensity'] for r in allrecords]. Calculate range: imin = min(intensities), imax = max(intensities). For each record r in allrecords: Normalize: norm = (r['intensity'] - imin) / max(imax - imin, 1e-9). Apply gamma correction: norm = max(0.0, min(1.0, norm)) 0.7. Compute gray value: r['gray'] = int(round(norm 255)). 5. Enforce Point Cap: If len(allrecords) > MAXRECORDS: truncate to allrecords[:MAXRECORDS]. 6. Create Metadata: Construct meta dictionary with standard keys (source='meta', etc.). 7. Output: Combine: output = [meta] + allrecords. Write to OUTPUTFILE as JSON with compact separators (no whitespace). tracedipolefieldline(theta0, phi0, npoints) Function: 1. Initialize Position: Calculate starting position at rstart = 3.0: x = rstart math.sin(theta0) math.cos(phi0) y = rstart math.sin(theta0) math.sin(phi0) z = rstart math.cos(theta0). 2. Iterate for npoints: Calculate radial distance: r = math.sqrt(x2 + y2 + z2). Check Ionosphere Boundary: If r < 1.1, break loop. Check Magnetopause Boundary: Calculate polar angle from sunward X axis: thetasun = math.atan2(math.sqrt(y2 + z2), max(x, -40.0)). Calculate magnetopause radius: mpr = magnetopauseradius(thetasun) (function not defined in sources; must be implemented based on a chosen magnetopause model, e.g., Shue et al.). If r > mpr, break loop. Evaluate Dipole Field: Calculate field components: Bx, By, Bz = dipolefield(x, y, z). Calculate magnitude: mag = math.sqrt(Bx2 + By2 + Bz2). Check Zero Field: If mag < 1e-9, break loop. Record Point: Append {'x': x, 'y': y, 'z': z, 'Bx': Bx, 'By': By, 'Bz': Bz, 'intensity': mag, 'source': 'magnetosphere'} to linepoints. Euler Step: Update position: x += step Bx / mag y += step By / mag z += step Bz / mag. 3. Return: linepoints. dipolefield(x, y, z) Function: The magnetic field of a centered dipole aligned with the Z-axis is given by: \mathbf{B} = \frac{\mu0 m}{4\pi r^5} \left( 3z x, 3z y, 3z^2 - r^2 \right) where r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2} and m is the dipole moment (standard physics formula; constant factors can be absorbed into step or ignored if only direction matters for tracing, but intensity requires magnitude). In normalized units (RE, arbitrary field units): Bx = \frac{3xz}{r^5}, \quad By = \frac{3yz}{r^5}, \quad Bz = \frac{3z^2 - r^2}{r^5} magnetopauseradius(thetasun) Function: Not given in the sources. Must be implemented using a standard model (e.g., Shue et al. 1998). Generates draped interplanetary magnetic field (IMF) line samples within the magnetosheath region, bounded by the bow shock and the magnetopause. Unlike the parent method which traces single lines from ionospheric footpoints, this method seeds lines randomly in the dayside magnetosheath to capture the draped topology of the solar wind magnetic field. It is distinct from general stream line tracing by its specific geometric constraints (dayside-only seeding) and reliance on external magnetosheath field models. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of field lines and points per line (O(N{lines} \times N{points})). Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the total number of output points, capped at MAXRECORDS. Measured Performance: At precision=3, a reduction of 8–15% in file size is observed relative to default 4–5 decimal place output, with negligible visual impact for scene-scale data. Scaling: The method is designed for offline dataset generation. The visualizer enforces a secondary cap of 5000 records if the generated dataset exceeds MAXRECORDS (default 5000). Strengths: Simple, fast generation of synthetic magnetospheric data; compact JSON output; handles boundary conditions (ionosphere, magnetopause) explicitly. Limitations: Relies on a simplified dipole model; does not account for time-varying solar wind conditions or realistic magnetohydrodynamic effects; requires external implementation of magnetopause and magnetosheath models. When to Use: When a synthetic, reproducible dataset of magnetospheric field lines is needed for testing visualization pipelines or educational purposes. This method originates from the AstroSplat-Browser project, which focuses on native volumetric visualization for astrophysical vector fields. The method uses a fixed-step Euler integration scheme, a common choice for its simplicity and low computational overhead in synthetic data generation. name: Magnetosheath Draped Field Line Generation
head: draped IMF field lines
body: Generates draped field line samples within the magnetosheath region, bounded by the bow shock and the magnetopause. Unlike the parent method which traces single lines from ionospheric footpoints, this method seeds lines randomly in the dayside magnetosheath to capture the draped topology of the solar wind magnetic field. It is distinct from general stream line tracing by its specific geometric constraints (dayside-only seeding) and reliance on external magnetosheath field models. Inputs: nlines: Number of field lines to generate. npts: Maximum number of sample points per field line. magnetopauseradius(theta): Callable returning the radial distance of the magnetopause surface for a given polar angle theta. bowshockradius(theta): Callable returning the radial distance of the bow shock surface for a given polar angle theta. magnetosheathfield(x, y, z): Callable returning the magnetic field vector (Bx, By, Bz) at position (x, y, z). Outputs: A flat list of dictionaries. Each record contains keys: x, y, z (float position coordinates), Bx, By, Bz (float magnetic field components), intensity (float magnitude |B|), and source (string 'magnetosheath'). Parameters: step: Fixed Euler integration step size, set to 0.20 Earth radii (RE). thetamax: Polar angle upper bound for seeding, set to 1.4 radians. cosclamp: Lower bound for \cos(\theta), set to -0.98. boundarymargin: Offset from surface boundaries for seeding, set to 0.3. Algorithm: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def generatemagnetosheathlines(nlines, npts, magnetopauseradius, bowshockradius, magnetosheathfield): records = [] for in range(nlines): # Seed selection phi = random.uniform(0.0, 2.0 math.pi) theta = random.uniform(0.0, 1.4) tcos = max(math.cos(theta), -0.98) mpr = magnetopauseradius(math.acos(tcos)) bsr = bowshockradius(math.acos(tcos)) rseed = random.uniform(mpr + 0.3, bsr - 0.3) if rseed <= mpr: continue # Initialization x = rseed math.sin(theta) math.cos(phi) y = rseed math.sin(theta) math.sin(phi) z = rseed math.cos(theta) step = 0.20 # Tracing loop for in range(npts): thetasun = math.atan2(math.sqrt(y2 + z2), max(x, -40.0)) mpr2 = magnetopauseradius(thetasun) bsr2 = bowshockradius(thetasun) r2 = math.sqrt(x2 + y2 + z2) if r2 < mpr2 or r2 > bsr2: break Bx, By, Bz = magnetosheathfield(x, y, z) mag = math.sqrt(Bx2 + By2 + Bz2) if mag < 1e-9: break records.append({ "x": x, "y": y, "z": z, "Bx": Bx, "By": By, "Bz": Bz, "intensity": mag, "source": "magnetosheath" }) x += step Bx / mag y += step By / mag z += step Bz / mag return records Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dayside Restriction: The method enforces a dayside-only generation by limiting \theta to [0, 1.4] radians and clamping \cos(\theta) to \ge -0.98. This prevents seeding in the nightside magnetosheath. Boundary Precision: The boundary check uses the current position's projected angle \theta{\text{sun}} to query surface radii. If the field line crosses the boundary between steps, it may be recorded outside the valid region before the next check breaks the loop. Zero Field: If the field magnitude drops below 10^{-9}, tracing stops to avoid division by zero. Seeding Gap: The seed radius is restricted to (r{mp} + 0.3, r{bs} - 0.3). If r{bs} - r{mp} \le 0.6, no valid seeds exist for that angle. The code checks if rseed <= mpr but relies on the uniform distribution to naturally fail if the interval is invalid or empty. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot P), where N is nlines and P is npts. Each step requires a field evaluation and boundary checks. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot P) to store the output records. The source implementation truncates the output to 5,000 records if the total count exceeds this limit. Strengths: Simple to implement; captures the general draped structure of the magnetosheath field; efficient random seeding avoids bias towards specific regions. Limitations: Does not trace lines back to their source (solar wind) or footpoints; relies on external functions for magnetopause/bow shock shapes and field values; fixed step size may lead to inaccuracies in high-gradient regions. This method is part of a pipeline for volumetric visualization of astrophysical vector fields, specifically focusing on Earth's magnetosphere. It builds on Magnetosphere Field Line Tracing by providing complementary data for the magnetosheath region, which is not covered by ionospheric footpoint tracing. name: Particle Traces on 2D Surfaces
head: Particle traces on surfaces, Surface particle traces, Trace lines on surfaces
body: Particle traces on 2D surfaces is a visualization technique that represents the magnitude and direction of a 3D vector field on arbitrary 2D surfaces (not necessarily contour surfaces) by drawing long, evenly spaced particle trace lines. Unlike random seed placement which does not guarantee coverage near every point, this method uses a hierarchical integer lattice to ensure some seed point is near every point on the surface, avoiding density issues where the visualization becomes too dense or too sparse. It sets itself apart from its parent Integral Surface by explicitly breaking traces into segments of contrasting color to resolve directional ambiguity in still images and by projecting the vector field onto the surface geometry rather than integrating within the volume. Inputs: A set of arbitrary 2D surfaces (represented as piecewise linear meshes). A 3D vector field defined over the domain containing the surfaces. A length threshold parameter L{thresh} (initially large, reduced gradually). A constant time interval \Delta t for segment length calculation. Outputs: A set of particle trace lines rendered on the surfaces, composed of colored segments. Data Structures: Octree: The surfaces are scan-converted into an octree. Each cell in the octree holds a plane equation (four numbers: Ax + By + Cz + D = 0). Only cells intersecting the surfaces are present. Surfaces are subdivided down to a constant size cell. Seed Lattice: An integer lattice used for seed point selection, organized spatially hierarchically. Trace Storage: A list of segments for each trace. Each segment stores its start and end points, color, and length. Cell History: For each octree cell, store the length of the longest erased trace that passed through it, to prevent extensive recalculation during backtracking. Steps: 1. Surface Representation: Scan convert the input surfaces into an octree. Subdivide surfaces until they fit into constant-size cells. Each cell stores a plane equation. 2. Seed Selection: Choose seed points on an integer lattice in a spatially hierarchical manner. This ensures the first particle traces start well away from each other. 3. Advection Loop: For each seed point: a. Initialize particle position P at the seed point. b. Advect the particle along the surface in both forward and backward directions using variable step size Euler's method. c. At each step, project the 3D vector field \vec{V} onto the surface to get the tangent direction \vec{T}. d. Calculate segment length L{seg} = \Delta t \cdot |\vec{V}|, where |\vec{V}| is the magnitude of the vector field. e. Create a segment from the previous position to the new position. Color the segment using a sawtooth-shaped color map to resolve directional ambiguity in still images. f. Check termination conditions: i. Particle reaches a stagnation zone (velocity approaches zero). ii. Particle reaches an edge of the surface. iii. Particle becomes too close to its own trace or another particle's trace. g. If the total trace length L{trace} is greater than the current length threshold L{thresh}, keep the trace. h. If L{trace} < L{thresh}, erase the trace. Preserve the length of the erased trace in the octree cells it passed through to prevent extensive recalculation while backtracking. 4. Threshold Reduction: After all seed points at the current resolution are tried, reduce the length threshold L{thresh} and repeat the process. Gradually reducing the threshold from maximum to minimum produces an aesthetically pleasing distribution but takes longer than using a single threshold value. 5. Rendering: Render the trace segments. Color table animation can be used to add motion, making the lines "flow" in the direction of the vector field with velocity proportional to the magnitude. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def magnitude(v): return math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def normalize(v): m = magnitude(v) return (v[0]/m, v[1]/m, v[2]/m) if m > 0 else (0, 0, 0) def projectvectorontosurface(v, normal): return (v[0] - dot(v, normal)normal[0], v[1] - dot(v, normal)normal[1], v[2] - dot(v, normal)normal[2]) def calculatesawtoothcolor(mag, period=1.0): return (mag % period) / period class Segment: def init(self, start, end, color, length): self.start = start self.end = end self.color = color self.length = length def scanconverttooctree(surfaces): # Scans surfaces into an octree where each cell holds a plane equation (A,B,C,D). # Only cells intersecting surfaces are stored. Subdivided to constant size. # Not given in the sources. return {} def generatehierarchicalintegerlattice(boundingbox, maxres=8): # Generates seed points on an integer lattice, starting coarse and doubling resolution. # Not given in the sources. return [] def getsurfacenormal(planeeq, point): A, B, C, D = planeeq return normalize((A, B, C)) def updatecellhistory(cellhistory, segment, length): # Not given in the sources: exact cell ID computation for octree traversal cellid = hash(segment.start) if cellid not in cellhistory or cellhistory[cellid] < length: cellhistory[cellid] = length def isedge(point, octree): # Not given in the sources: exact implementation for surface boundary check return False def istooclosetoothertrace(point, segments, threshold=0.01): # Not given in the sources: exact implementation for proximity check against own/other traces for seg in segments: if magnitude((point[0]-seg.start[0], point[1]-seg.start[1], point[2]-seg.start[2])) < threshold: return True return False def advectalongsurface(startpos, vectorfield, octree, deltat, cellhistory, direction=1): segments = [] currentpos = startpos prevpos = startpos epsilon = 1e-6 while True: v = vectorfield(currentpos) if magnitude(v) < epsilon: break #
