name: Seed Line Integral Convolution
head: Seed LIC, Volume LIC
body: Seed Line Integral Convolution (Seed LIC) is a volume rendering method for visualizing 3D vector fields that computes Line Integral Convolution (LIC) only along field lines originating from a sparse set of seed points, rather than covering every voxel in the output texture. It solves the problem of high computational cost associated with Fast LIC when applied to large 3D datasets by exploiting the sparsity of the input texture. Unlike its sibling Image Space Fabric Visualization which renders explicit geometric primitives, Seed LIC generates a sparse texture of field lines, setting it apart from Line Integral Convolution (LIC) by avoiding unnecessary computations in areas where field lines do not coincide with cells containing seed points. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D vector field \mathbf{V}, a scalar field for Region Of Interest (ROI) definition (e.g., vorticity magnitude), and a density factor \delta \in [0,1] controlling seed point sparsity. Output: A 3D scalar texture where voxel values represent the convolved intensity of field lines, normalized to the range [0, 255]. Data Structures: Input Texture (T): A 3D grid of the same resolution as the vector field (or an enlarged resolution for detail enlargement). Voxels are initialized to 0. Selected seed voxels are set to 255. Output Texture (I): A 3D grid of the same resolution as the input texture. Initialized to 0. Stores the convolution result. Hit Count Map (H): A 3D grid storing the number of field lines passing through each voxel, used for normalization. Parameters: Filter Kernel Length (2L): Typically set to 21 times the grid cell size. Field Line Length: Typically set to 51 times the grid cell size. Minimum Seed Distance: Points within 3 voxels of an existing seed are discarded to prevent merging. Threshold Value: Scalar value threshold for ROI inclusion. Density Factor (\delta): Probability threshold for seed placement. Steps: 1. Generate Sparse Input Texture: Initialize all voxels in T to 0. For each voxel v: If scalar value(v) > threshold value: Generate random number r \in [0,1]. If r > \delta: Set T(v) = 255. Enforce minimum distance: Discard any seed points that fall within 3 voxels of a previously inserted seed point. 2. Initialize Output: Initialize all voxels in I to 0. Initialize all voxels in H to 0. 3. Trace Field Lines and Compute Convolution: For each voxel v in the grid: If T(v) > 0: Set starting position x0 to the center of voxel v. Trace field line forward and backward from x0 using a fifth-order adaptive Runge-Kutta method with a fixed sample interval. Compute convolution integral for x0: I(x0) = \int{s0-L}^{s0+L} k(s-s0) T(\alpha(s)) ds where \alpha(s) is the curve parameterized by arc-length s, and k is the filter kernel of length 2L. Add I(x0) to I(v). Increment H(v) by 1. Iterate along the field line for m = 1 to M (where M corresponds to the field line length limit): Update positions xm and x{-m} along the field line. Compute convolution I(xm) and I(x{-m}) using the same integral formula. Add I(xm) to the voxel containing xm and increment its hit count. Add I(x{-m}) to the voxel containing x{-m} and increment its hit count [G: The source pseudocode implies adding to the voxel containing the point, but does not explicitly state the accumulation logic for intermediate points in the loop; standard LIC accumulates contributions]. 4. Normalize Output: For each voxel v: If H(v) > 0: I(v) = I(v) / H(v). Else: I(v) = 0 [G: Implicit from normalization logic]. Scale all voxel values in I so that the maximum value is 255. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def seedlic(vectorfield, scalarfield, densityfactor, threshold, kernellength, linelength): # 1. Generate Sparse Input Texture inputtexture = zeroslike(vectorfield) seedpoints = [] # Determine potential seeds based on ROI and density for v in allvoxels: if scalarfield[v] > threshold: if random() > densityfactor: seedpoints.append(v) # Enforce minimum distance between seeds validseeds = [] for v in seedpoints: if not any(distance(v, existing) < 3 for existing in validseeds): validseeds.append(v) inputtexture[v] = 255 # 2. Initialize Output and Hit Count outputtexture = zeroslike(vectorfield) hitcount = zeroslike(vectorfield) # 3. Trace Field Lines and Compute Convolution for v in validseeds: x0 = centerofvoxel(v) # Trace forward and backward forwardline = tracefieldline(vectorfield, x0, direction=1, length=linelength) backwardline = tracefieldline(vectorfield, x0, direction=-1, length=linelength) # Compute convolution for start point convstart = computeconvolutionintegral(forwardline, backwardline, inputtexture, kernellength) outputtexture[v] += convstart hitcount[v] += 1 # Compute convolution for intermediate points for m in range(1, linelength): xm = forwardline[m] xminusm = backwardline[m] convm = computeconvolutionintegral(forwardline, backwardline, inputtexture, kernellength, startindex=m) voxelxm = voxelcontainingpoint(xm) voxelxminusm = voxelcontainingpoint(xminusm) if voxelxm is not None: outputtexture[voxelxm] += convm hitcount[voxelxm] += 1 if voxelxminusm is not None: outputtexture[voxelxminusm] += convm hitcount[voxelxminusm] += 1 # 4. Normalize Output maxval = 0 for v in allvoxels: if hitcount[v] > 0: outputtexture[v] /= hitcount[v] if outputtexture[v] > maxval: maxval = outputtexture[v] if maxval > 0: outputtexture /= maxval outputtexture = 255 return outputtexture def computeconvolutionintegral(forwardline, backwardline, inputtexture, kernellength, startindex=0): # Simplified integration along the line segment defined by startindex # Sum of inputtexture values weighted by kernel total = 0 for s in range(-kernellength, kernellength + 1): idx = startindex + s if 0 <= idx < len(forwardline): pos = forwardline[idx] val = trilinearinterpolate(inputtexture, pos) total += val kernelweight(s) elif 0 <= -idx < len(backwardline): # Assuming symmetric backward line # Note: Source pseudocode is ambiguous on backward line indexing relative to forward # Assuming standard LIC where s goes from -L to L along the curve pass return total Direct Volume Rendering of LIC Textures is a visualization method that renders nerve fibre structures and other tissue types simultaneously by combining a Line Integral Convolution (LIC) texture with a probability map. It solves the problem of efficiently visualizing complex directional data in Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) without the computational overhead of ensuring uniform coverage across the entire volume. Unlike streamline-based techniques which render explicit geometric primitives, this method uses volume rendering to represent finer details via noise texture resolution and allows for semi-transparent or nearly opaque fibre tracts. It sets itself apart from its sibling Seed Line Integral Convolution by utilizing the generated LIC texture and hit-count probability map as dual inputs for transfer function definition, rather than just rendering the texture itself. Sparse Volume LIC is a variant of Seed LIC that emphasizes detail enlargement and aliasing reduction through specific parameter adjustments. It differs from standard Seed LIC by explicitly managing the relationship between input texture resolution and vector field resolution to maintain stroke accuracy. It is chosen when higher visual fidelity is required at the cost of increased computation due to smaller step sizes. Step: For each voxel v, if scalar value(v) > threshold, compute random number in [0,1]; if random number > density factor, set input texture value(v) = 255. To avoid aliasing during detail enlargement, reduce the step size between sample points when computing convolution integrals inversely proportional to the texture size increase. Parameter: Threshold value: scalar value threshold used to determine if a voxel contributes to the input texture. Density factor: a value in [0,1] controlling the sparsity of the input texture points. Comparison: Detail enlargement uses a smaller step size to ensure most voxels are covered by the field line when the input texture is larger than the vector field. Aliasing Reduction via 3x3x3 Convolution is a post-processing step for Seed LIC that reduces aliasing artifacts by smoothing the output texture. It sets itself apart by explicitly addressing the "stair-stepped" appearance of voxel-based field lines through isotropic filtering. It is chosen when the visual smoothness of field lines is prioritized over strict geometric accuracy. Definition: Reducing aliasing in Seed LIC textures by convolving the output texture with a 3x3x3 filter to smear field lines and create smoother strokes. Step: Convolve the output texture with the 3x3x3 filter to smear field lines. Parameter: Convolution filter A: a 3x3x3 filter where the center entry a{222} = 1 and the rest of the entries are set to 0.25. Pitfall: Convolution leads to thicker strokes; to preserve thickness, increase the resolution of input and output texture by a factor of three prior to convolution. Number: Convolution of the LIC texture took 206.19 seconds. Time Complexity: Significantly faster than Fast LIC for sparse textures. For a 256x256x256 texture with 17,341 seed points, Seed LIC took 70.9 seconds, compared to 752 seconds for Fast LIC. For a 128x128x128 texture, Fast LIC took 752 seconds while Seed LIC took 4.7 seconds. For a 398x298x798 texture, Fast LIC took about 25 hours, while Seed LIC took 26.86 seconds. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the input texture, output texture, and hit count map. The input texture is sparse, but stored as a dense grid. Measured Performance: On an SGI ONYX 3800 using a single 500 MHz R14000 processor, Seed LIC showed immense computational cost reduction compared to Fast LIC on synthetic vector fields. Strengths: Reduces computational cost immensely for sparse input textures; allows interactive exploration; ROI preprocessing aligns boundaries with flow direction. Limitations: More affected by aliasing than Fast LIC due to fewer calculated voxels, resulting in a less smooth appearance. Convolution can cause field lines to merge into bundles if seed points are too close. Rendering solid LIC textures as 2D slices via direct volume rendering loses inner details. When to Use: Large 3D datasets where Fast LIC is too slow; when sparse representation of flow is acceptable or desired; when ROI-based visualization is needed. When Not to Use: When smooth, continuous texture coverage is required without aliasing artifacts; when computational resources are not a constraint and Fast LIC is feasible. Seed LIC was proposed by Helgeland and Andreassen in 2004 as a method for effective volume visualization of three-dimensional vector fields. It builds on the Line Integral Convolution (LIC) algorithm by Stalling and Hege (Fast LIC) but optimizes it for sparsity. The method was developed to address the perceptual difficulties of dense 3D displays and the high computational cost of applying LIC to large volumes. It is used in scientific visualization, particularly for visualizing vorticity fields and nerve fibre structures in Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI). body: Direct Volume Rendering of LIC Textures is a visualization method that renders nerve fibre structures and other tissue types simultaneously by combining a Line Integral Convolution (LIC) texture with a probability map. It solves the problem of efficiently visualizing complex directional data in Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) without the computational overhead of ensuring uniform coverage across the entire volume. Unlike streamline-based techniques which render explicit geometric primitives, this method uses volume rendering to represent finer details via noise texture resolution and allows for semi-transparent or nearly opaque fibre tracts. It sets itself apart from its sibling Seed Line Integral Convolution by utilizing the generated LIC texture and hit-count probability map as dual inputs for transfer function definition, rather than just rendering the texture itself. Inputs: 1. A set of seed points distributed based on the probability of being within a Region of Interest (ROI). These seed points are identical to those used in a preceding streamline visualization. 2. A streamline generation algorithm (or pre-computed streamlines) that enforces physiological constraints for nerve fibre tracking. 3. A noise texture used for convolution. 4. Transfer functions (colour and transparency look-up tables). Outputs: A volume-rendered image representing the directional information of nerve fibre structures and other tissue types. Data Structures: 1. LIC Texture: A 2D or 3D texture encoding the direction information of nerve fibre structures. The resolution of this texture determines the level of fine detail visible. 2. Probability Map: A data set estimating the probability that a voxel lies within a nerve fibre structure. This is computed by counting the number of times each cell (voxel) is hit by field lines during the LIC texture generation process. Algorithm Steps: 1. Reuse Streamlines: Reuse the generation of streamlines performed for previous visualizations to ensure nerve fibre structures are tracked appropriately with physiological constraints. 2. Distribute Seeds: Distribute seed points based on the probability that a point is within the Region of Interest (ROI). 3. Generate LIC Texture: Compute the LIC texture using the seed points and streamlines, similar to the Seed LIC algorithm. This involves convolving the noise texture along the streamlines passing through the seed points. 4. Compute Probability Map: During the LIC generation, count the number of times each voxel is hit by the field lines. This count forms the probability map. 5. Define Transfer Functions: Use two data sets to define the transfer functions: The LIC texture, which encodes directional information. The probability map, which indicates the likelihood of a voxel belonging to the nerve fibre structure. 6. Volume Render: Perform direct volume rendering using the LIC texture and the probability map to define colour and transparency. The opacity transfer functions can be adjusted to represent fibre tracts as semi-transparent or nearly opaque. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def directvolumerenderingoflictextures( roiprobabilitygrid, streamlinegenerator, noisetexture, colourlut, opacitylut): """ Performs Direct Volume Rendering of LIC Textures. Args: roiprobabilitygrid: 3D grid of probabilities for ROI membership. streamlinegenerator: Function to generate streamlines from seed points. noisetexture: 2D or 3D noise texture for convolution. colourlut: Colour lookup table. opacitylut: Opacity lookup table. Returns: Rendered image. """ # Step 1: Reuse or generate streamlines based on ROI probabilities # Seed points are distributed based on the probability that a point is within the ROI seedpoints = [] for voxel in roiprobabilitygrid: if random() < voxel.probability: seedpoints.append(voxel.center) # Generate streamlines using the seed points # This reuses the generation logic from streamline visualization streamlines = streamlinegenerator(seedpoints) # Step 2: Generate LIC Texture and Probability Map # Initialize LIC texture and hit count map lictexture = createtexturelike(noisetexture) hitcountmap = zeroslike(roiprobabilitygrid) for streamline in streamlines: # Trace the streamline and convolve noise for point in streamline: # Convolve noise along the streamline direction at point # This is similar to Seed LIC algorithm convolvednoise = convolvenoisealongdirection( noisetexture, point, streamline.directionat(point)) # Store in LIC texture settexturevalue(lictexture, point, convolvednoise) # Increment hit count for probability map hitcountmap[point] += 1 # Normalize hit count map to get probability map probabilitymap = normalize(hitcountmap) # Step 3: Define Transfer Functions # Use LIC texture for directional info and probability map for structure likelihood # The specific mapping logic depends on the fuzzy classifier implementation # Assuming a standard volume rendering transfer function application def getcolourandopacity(licvalue, probvalue): # Map LIC value to colour based on direction c = colourlut(licvalue) # Map probability to opacity o = opacitylut(probvalue) return c, o # Step 4: Volume Render # Render the volume using the LIC texture and the computed transfer functions image = volumerender( lictexture, getcolourandopacity, opacitylut=opacitylut) return image Parameters: Noise Texture Resolution: Determines the fineness of details that can be represented. Opacity Transfer Functions: Control whether fibre tracts are represented as semi-transparent or nearly opaque. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Transparency: For high transparency values, the 3D arrangement of fibre tracts is not as clear as for streamline-based techniques. ROI Definition: The method relies on accurate ROI probability distribution to avoid overhead; incorrect distribution may lead to incomplete coverage or wasted computation. Time Complexity: Generation time is measured in seconds rather than hours, avoiding the overhead of Fast LIC and ensuring hits everywhere (even outside ROI). Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the LIC texture and the probability map (hit count map). Strengths: Efficient generation time; reuses streamline generation; represents finer details via noise texture resolution; allows interactive variation of opacity to improve 3D perception. Limitations: For high transparency values, the 3D arrangement of fibre tracts is less clear compared to streamline-based techniques. When to Use: When efficient visualization of directional nerve fibre structures is required, and interactive opacity adjustment is beneficial. When Not to Use: When clear 3D arrangement of fibre tracts at high transparency is critical. This method was developed for visualizing Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) data to view brain anatomy and nerve fibre tracking in vivo. It was presented by Burkhard Wünsche, Jarno van der Linden, and Nathan Holmberg in a preprint submitted to Elsevier Science in March 2005. The work is part of a broader effort in biomedical visualization and tensor field visualization. name: Image Space Fabric Visualization
head: Advection of eigenvector field, Fabric-Like Tensor Field Visualization on Surfaces, Iterative Eigenvector Field Advection, LIC-like advection, Surface Tensor LIC
body: Image Space Fabric Visualization is a method to visualize symmetric tensor fields on arbitrary non-self-intersecting surfaces by projecting tensor data into image space, advecting a noise texture along eigenvectors, and blending with lighting and edge information to create a fabric-like appearance. It differs from CPU-based or multi-pass geometry rendering methods by performing all intermediate calculations in GPU offscreen framebuffer objects (FBOs), leading to large speed gains and real-time performance. Inputs: 1. Geometry: A non-self-intersecting surface with smooth normals. 2. Tensor Field: Symmetric second-order tensors defined on the surface vertices. 3. Noise Texture: A scalar noise field (pre-calculated or stored in a file). 4. Camera parameters: For projection and lighting calculation. Outputs: 1. Final image: A visualization with a fabric-like texture modulated by lighting and edge information. Data Structures: Vertex Attributes: Position, normal, and two 3D texture coordinates for tensor information. If tensors are symmetric, 6 floating-point values per vertex are transferred. Textures: Intermediate textures for FBO passes. Due to hardware limits (e.g., NVIDIA GeForce 8800 GTS), a maximum of four bound textures per rendering pass and active FBO are used. Edge detection output texture layout: Green channel stores depth buffer value; Blue channel stores unprocessed input noise; Alpha channel stores noise mapped to geometry's surface. Steps: 1. Projection and Pre-computation (Vertex/Fragment Shaders): Render the geometry into an offscreen FBO. In the vertex shader, map the two main tensor directions to the surface described by the normal n at the current vertex. Calculate each vertex's position in one voxel of the noise texture using equations from Section 2.3 of the source. Pre-calculate Phong light intensity L(x,y) \in [0,1] at every fragment with coordinates x and y. In the fragment shader, perform eigenvalue decomposition and eigenvector calculation after interpolation to avoid sign flip artifacts. Project eigenvectors to image space. Normalize eigenvectors for texture storage. Scale eigenvectors v'{\lambda1} and v'{\lambda2} so values are in [0,1] for texture transportation. Determine the noise texture element for each fragment using the interpolated voxel position calculated in the vertex shader. 2. Edge Detection (Separate Pass): Apply an edge detection filter to the depth map using a discrete Laplacian filter kernel implemented in a separate offscreen rendering pass. Store results in the edge detection output texture as defined in the layout above. 3. Advection (Iterative Passes): Advect the previously mapped noise texture using the eigenvector color map from the projection step. The advection step grabs data directly from a single merged texture (depth buffer, edge detection texture, eigenvector color map, and last iteration's output) to reduce texture bindings. Transfer the unprocessed input noise to the advection texture to allow toggling between noise fields during advection, as near-planar geometry does not require complex geometry mapping. Iterate for i = 0, 1,... until value change exceeds a threshold (reached after a few iterations depending on k). 4. Final Output Processing: Blend both advected eigenvector fields with light information and geometry edges. Clip fragments using the depth buffer. Use the last output texture from advection, color map with lighting info, and edge detection output texture to create the final visualization. Optional modification: Blend in fractional anisotropy, \lambda2, and implicitly \lambda1 to emphasize additional tensor field features. Blend eigenvector fields with silhouettes and Phong luminance calculated in the projection step. Formulas: Phong Shading Normal: The normal n used for Phong shading to produce a tube-like effect is calculated as: n = (1-r)(0,0,1)^T + r b0 where r is a parameter describing the ratio between the normal completely on the plane (zero z-component) and the normal completely pointing towards the camera (z-component of one), and b0 is a base vector. Eigenvector Normalization: Since \lambda1 \ge \lambda2, normalize the vector (\lambda1, \lambda2) using the maximum norm. Transfer only the smaller \lambda2 because \lambda1 is always 1 after normalization. Advection Iteration: For each eigenvector field \lambda \in \{\lambda1, \lambda2\}, initialize input and output fields Pi^\lambda. Iterate: P{i+1}^\lambda = k \cdot \beta{x,y} + (1-k) \cdot \frac{f{Pi^\lambda}(x+v'{\lambdax}, y+v'{\lambday}) + f{Pi^\lambda}(x-v'{\lambdax}, y-v'{\lambday})}{2} where \beta{x,y} is the input noise, k is a scalar factor determining the mix ratio between original and advected noise, and v' are the scaled eigenvectors. Parameters: r: Parameter for Phong shading normal calculation. k: Scalar factor for advection mix ratio (e.g., 0.05 for smooth/blurred, 0.09 for coarse/contrast-rich). Texture limit: Maximum four bound textures per rendering pass and active framebuffer object (hardware-dependent, e.g., NVIDIA GeForce 8800 GTS). Pitfalls: Sign Flips: Eigenvectors are without orientation, causing sign flips between adjacent vertices. If decomposition happens before interpolation, these sign changes render interpolation useless. Solution: Perform eigenvalue decomposition and eigenvector calculation in the fragment shader after interpolation. Discontinuities: The local approach causes discontinuities along tubes and artifacts from blurry input fields where borders are unclear. These are less visible due to the high frequency of the fabric structure. Pseudocode: Unverified code. a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]) def normalize(v): mag = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) return (v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag) def computesurfacenormal(vertex): return normalize(crossproduct(vertex.edge1, vertex.edge2)) def maptonoisespace(position, noisetexture): return (position[0], position[1], position[2]) def eigendecompose(tensor): eigenvalues = [1.0, 0.5, 0.1] eigenvectors = [(1,0,0), (0,1,0), (0,0,1)] return eigenvalues, eigenvectors def scaleto01(vector): return ((vector[0]+1)/2, (vector[1]+1)/2, (vector[2]+1)/2) def samplenoise(texture, coords): return texture[coords] def interpolate(attributes): return attributes def computephonglighting(n, cameraparams): return 0.5 def createemptytexturelike(template): return {} class Framebuffer: def init(self): self.depthbuffer = {} self.alphachannel = {} self.fragments = [] class Texture: def init(self): self.green = {} self.blue = {} self.alpha = {} self.grid = [] def imagespacefabricvisualization(geometry, tensorfield, noisetexture, cameraparams): fbo1 = Framebuffer() fbo1.fragments = geometry.fragments for vertex in geometry.vertices: vertex.surfacenormal = computesurfacenormal(vertex) vertex.noisecoords = maptonoisespace(vertex.position, noisetexture) vertex.lightintensity = 0.0 for fragment in fbo1.fragments: interpolatednormal = interpolate(fragment.vertexnormals) interpolatednoisecoords = interpolate(fragment.vertexnoisecoords) tensor = interpolate(fragment.vertextensors) eigenvalues, eigenvectors = eigendecompose(tensor) lambda1, lambda2 = eigenvalues[0], eigenvalues[1] v1, v2 = eigenvectors[0], eigenvectors[1] normalizedlambda2 = lambda2 / max(lambda1, lambda2) v1scaled = scaleto01(v1) v2scaled = scaleto01(v2) noisevalue = samplenoise(noisetexture, interpolatednoisecoords) r = 0.5 b0 = (0, 0, 1) nphong = ((1-r)0 + rb0[0], (1-r)0 + rb0[1], (1-r)1 + rb0[2]) lightintensity = computephonglighting(nphong, cameraparams) fragment.data = { 'eigenvector1': v1scaled, 'eigenvector2': v2scaled, 'lambda2': normalizedlambda2, 'noisevalue': noisevalue, 'lightintensity': lightintensity, 'depth': fragment.depth } edgetexture = Texture() edgetexture.green = fbo1.depthbuffer edgetexture.blue = noisetexture edgetexture.alpha = fbo1.alphachannel advectednoise = fbo1.alphachannel k = 0.05 for i in range(10): newadvected = createemptytexturelike(advectednoise) for x, y in advectednoise.grid: posplus = (x + v2scaled[0], y + v2scaled[1]) posminus = (x - v2scaled[0], y - v2scaled[1]) sampleplus = samplenoise(advectednoise, posplus) sampleminus = samplenoise(advectednoise, posminus) beta = edgetexture.blue[x, y] newadvected[x, y] = k beta + (1 - k) (sampleplus + sampleminus) / 2 advectednoise = newadvected mergedtexture = Texture() mergedtexture.green = fbo1.depthbuffer mergedtexture.blue = edgetexture.blue mergedtexture.alpha = advectednoise advectednoise = mergedtexture.alpha finalimage = advectednoise fbo1.lightintensity finalimage = finalimage finalimage = finalimage return finalimage Time Complexity: The bottleneck is the hardware's ability to render large and triangle-rich geometry. All further steps (advection, blending) can be done in constant time per pixel, assuming fixed iteration counts for advection. Memory Complexity: Limited by GPU texture memory. On NVIDIA GeForce 8800 GTS, a maximum of four bound textures per rendering pass and active FBO are used. Data merging techniques are employed to reduce texture bindings. Measured Performance: Frame rates are high enough for real-time user interaction. Strengths: Real-time performance, ability to handle arbitrary non-self-intersecting surfaces, GPU-based implementation avoids CPU calculations and multiple geometry renders. Limitations: Local approach causes discontinuities along tubes and artifacts from blurry input fields. Sign flip artifacts must be handled by performing decomposition in the fragment shader. When to use: When visualizing tensor fields on surfaces derived from scalar metrics (e.g., fractional anisotropy), hyper-stream surfaces, wrapped streamlines, or domain-dependent dissection-like surfaces, especially in medical or mechanical datasets. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Fabric-Like Visualization of Tensor Field Data on Arbitrary Surfaces in Image Space". History and Development: It builds on ideas from [17] to transform the algorithm into image space, similar to the method introduced in [13]. Usage: Applied to medical diffusion tensor data sets to visualize fiber directions, modulating color coding based on fractional anisotropy (major direction in RGB, secondary in grayscale below primary). Also applied to mechanical datasets including earthquake simulations (concrete pile) and analytical strain tensor fields (single point load). name: Variable Convolution Length for Dye
head: Separate dye convolution length
body: Variable Convolution Length for Dye decouples the convolution length of the dye advection from the global Line Integral Convolution (LIC) texture. It solves the problem where extending the global convolution length to highlight long-range flow features degrades the contrast of the LIC texture and increases computational cost. By allowing a separate, longer convolution length for the dye, it enables long dye trails without compromising the efficiency or visual quality of the underlying LIC. Inputs: Vector field defining the flow, scalar noise field for LIC texture, global convolution length L, dye convolution length T, and standard LIC animation steps steps. Outputs: Final composite scalar field combining LIC texture and dye advection. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Numbered Steps: 1. Calculate the number of animation steps required for the dye advection. 2. For cells not affected by the dye, compute only steps steps of standard LIC output. 3. For dyed cells, compute the dye advection output D{out}(I,x,y) at animation step I \in [0, X-1] using a box filter along the streamline. 4. Combine the standard LIC output with the dye advection output. Formulas: Number of animation steps for dye: X = steps \times \frac{T}{L}. LIC formula for dyed advection: D{out}(I,x,y) = \frac{\sum{i=0}^{Z-1} D{in}(Pi) \cdot \mathbb{I}(Si)}{\sum{i=0}^{Z-1} \mathbb{I}(Si)}. Combine standard LIC and dye advection: Final{out}(I, x, y) = D{out}(I, x, y) \otimes F{out}(I \mod steps, x, y). Parameters: L (global convolution length), T (dye convolution length), steps (standard LIC steps), Z (number of samples in the filter), \Delta L (length of filter box), r (streamline position). Assumption: T is a multiple of L. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Requires T to be a multiple of L for the step calculation. Box filters can cause artifacts when boxes reenter the interval; solutions exist in cited literature. The LIC volume values consist primarily of noise signals for texture construction and lack physical meaning, requiring specific visualization techniques like volume rendering or isosurface extraction. The exact definition of the combination operator \otimes is not detailed in the source text. Time Complexity: Increases with the ratio T/L. The dye advection requires X = steps \times (T/L) steps, while standard LIC remains at steps steps for unaffected cells. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows long dye trails to highlight local flow features without degrading global LIC contrast or slowing down the standard LIC computation. Limitations: Requires careful handling of box filter artifacts. The combination operator is not detailed in the source text. This method was introduced in the context of visualizing vector fields using Line Integral Convolution and Dye Advection. It addresses the limitations of standard LIC, which uses a single global convolution length for all cells. The technique is part of a broader effort to enhance the clarity of flow visualization by separating the texture generation (LIC) from the feature highlighting (dye). name: Variable Step Euler LIC
head: CL-LIC, Cabral and Leedom LIC
body: Variable Step Euler LIC is a texture-based filtering technique that blurs an input texture locally along given vector field lines, causing voxel intensities to be highly correlated along the field lines but independent in directions perpendicular to them. It is a 2D Line Integral Convolution method where field lines are computed using a variable step Euler's method to approximate local vector field behavior. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly computing curved field line paths via numerical integration for each pixel, rather than using straight-line approximations (like DDA) or pre-computed streamline seeds, allowing it to capture small-scale structures like eddies and vortices that straight-line methods miss. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D scalar field (input texture) F{in}, a 2D vector field V, a convolution filter kernel k(w), and a convolution length parameter L. Output: A 2D scalar field (output texture) F{out}. Data Structures: F{in}: 2D array of pixel values. V: 2D array of 2D vectors (Vx, Vy). Pi: 2D coordinates (x, y) of the i-th point on the field line. \Delta si: Scalar arc length step size. Numbered Steps: 1. For each pixel at integer coordinates (x, y) in the output image: a. Set the start point P0 = (x + 0.5, y + 0.5). b. Compute the downstream field line points Pi for i = 1, \dots, l using variable step Euler integration: Pi = P{i-1} + \frac{V(P{i-1})}{||V(P{i-1})||} \Delta s{i-1} where V(P{i-1}) is the vector field value at P{i-1}, and \Delta s{i-1} is the arc length step. c. Compute the upstream field line points P'i for i = 1, \dots, l' using variable step Euler integration: P'i = P'{i-1} - \frac{V(P'{i-1})}{||V(P'{i-1})||} \Delta s'{i-1} starting from P'0 = P0. d. Calculate the integration weights hi and h'i for each step: hi = \int{si}^{si + \Delta si} k(w) dw h'i = \int{s'i}^{s'i + \Delta s'i} k(w) dw where k(w) is the convolution filter function. e. Compute the output intensity F{out}(x, y) by summing the weighted input texture values along the field lines and normalizing by the sum of weights: F{out}(x, y) = \frac{\sum{i=0}^{l} F{in}(Pi) hi + \sum{i=0}^{l'} F{in}(P'i) h'i}{\sum{i=0}^{l} hi + \sum{i=0}^{l'} h'i} where l and l' are the number of steps downstream and upstream, respectively. Formulas: Forward step: Pi = P{i-1} + \frac{V(P{i-1})}{||V(P{i-1})||} \Delta s{i-1} Backward step: P'i = P'{i-1} - \frac{V(P'{i-1})}{||V(P'{i-1})||} \Delta s'{i-1} Convolution output: F{out}(x, y) = \frac{\sum{i=0}^{l} F{in}(Pi) hi + \sum{i=0}^{l'} F{in}(P'i) h'i}{\sum{i=0}^{l} hi + \sum{i=0}^{l'} h'i} Weight: hi = \int{si}^{si + \Delta si} k(w) dw Parameters: Convolution length 2L: Determines the extent of blurring. Stalling and Hege found good results choosing 2L to be 1/10th of the image width. If L=0, the input texture is unchanged. l and l': The convolution distances (number of steps) along the positive and negative directions, respectively. k(w): The convolution filter function. Pitfalls: The algorithm is very compute intensive and slow due to the large number of arithmetic operations and the recomputation of field line parts for multiple pixels. Precision issues may arise if the vector field magnitude is near zero, causing division by zero in the normalization term ||V(P{i-1})||. A guard should check for small magnitudes. Boundary conditions: Points Pi may fall outside the image domain. Sampling F{in} at these points requires handling (e.g., clamping, wrapping, or zero-padding). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def variablestepeulerlic(Fin, V, L, imagewidth, imageheight, stepsize=0.5): """ Fin: 2D list of input texture values V: 2D list of 2D vectors (Vx, Vy) L: half-convolution length imagewidth, imageheight: dimensions of the image stepsize: arc length step deltas (variable step rule not specified in sources) """ Fout = [[0.0] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] def magnitude(vx, vy): return math.sqrt(vx vx + vy vy) def sample2d(grid, x, y): # Clamp coordinates to image boundaries x = max(0, min(imagewidth - 1, x)) y = max(0, min(imageheight - 1, y)) return grid[int(y)][int(x)] for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): currx = x + 0.5 curry = y + 0.5 # Downstream integration scurr = 0.0 weightedsumdown = 0.0 totalweightdown = 0.0 while scurr < L: vx = V[int(curry)][int(currx)][0] vy = V[int(curry)][int(currx)][1] mag = magnitude(vx, vy) if mag < 1e-6: break # Guard against division by zero nx = vx / mag ny = vy / mag deltas = stepsize # Variable step size rule not specified in sources hi = deltas # Uniform kernel assumption for weight calculation finval = sample2d(Fin, currx, curry) weightedsumdown += finval hi totalweightdown += hi currx += nx deltas curry += ny deltas scurr += deltas # Upstream integration currx = x + 0.5 curry = y + 0.5 scurr = 0.0 weightedsumup = 0.0 totalweightup = 0.0 while scurr < L: vx = V[int(curry)][int(currx)][0] vy = V[int(curry)][int(currx)][1] mag = magnitude(vx, vy) if mag < 1e-6: break nx = vx / mag ny = vy / mag deltas = stepsize hi = deltas finval = sample2d(Fin, currx, curry) weightedsumup += finval hi totalweightup += hi currx -= nx deltas curry -= ny deltas scurr += deltas totalweight = totalweightdown + totalweightup if totalweight > 0: Fout[y][x] = (weightedsumdown + weightedsumup) / totalweight else: Fout[y][x] = sample2d(Fin, x + 0.5, y + 0.5) return Fout Uses sparse seed points to generate streamlines, reducing computation compared to per-pixel integration. Choose when performance is critical and high-frequency detail is less important. A frequency-domain approach that avoids explicit integration. Choose for real-time applications or when integration is too expensive. Uses a box filter for convolution, which is simpler but less accurate than variable step Euler for curved fields. Choose for simplicity and speed. Adjusts convolution length based on local flow properties. Choose when varying detail levels are needed across the field. Time Complexity: The algorithm is very compute intensive and slow due to the large number of arithmetic operations and recomputation of field line parts for multiple pixels. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing input and output textures. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance degrades linearly with image resolution and convolution length. Strengths: Captures curved field lines and small-scale structures like eddies and vortices better than straight-line approximations (DDA). Limitations: Very slow due to per-pixel integration and recomputation of field lines. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Variable Step Euler LIC was introduced in 1993 by Cabral and Leedom. The specific algorithm using variable step Euler's method is referred to as CL-LIC. It is a foundational technique in scientific visualization for representing vector fields with high accuracy. name: Box Filter Dye Advection
head: Hanning filter replacement, Phase-shifted box filter
body: Box Filter Dye Advection is a variation of Line Integral Convolution (LIC) that replaces the standard Hanning windowed filter with a simple box filter to facilitate the visualization of dye advection in vector fields. While standard LIC produces static textures, this method introduces a phase-shift mechanism that allows the "dye" to move along streamlines over time, creating natural flow motion. It is distinguished from its parent method by its specific kernel choice and temporal animation capability, and from siblings like Variable Convolution Length by its focus on temporal phase shifting rather than spatial length variation. Inputs: A 2D vector field \mathbf{V}(x,y). A scalar noise field (dye texture). The current animation step l. The total number of animation steps \text{steps}. The filter box length \Delta L. Outputs: A rendered scalar field F{out}(l,x,y). Data Structures: The algorithm operates on pixel coordinates (x,y). Streamlines are computed by integrating the vector field. The filter box is defined by a start position L and length \Delta L along the streamline parameter s. Steps: 1. For each pixel (x,y), compute the streamline path through the vector field. 2. Determine the integration interval for the current frame using the start position L and length \Delta L. 3. Calculate the predicate T(I, si) for each sample point si along the streamline: T(I, si) = 1 if the sample point lies within the filter box range [L, L + \Delta L). T(I, si) = 0 otherwise. 4. Handle wrap-around: if L + \Delta L exceeds the streamline period or maximum length, apply modulo arithmetic to map the interval back into bounds. 5. Compute the output value using uniform weighting over the box interval. Formulas: Predicate: T(I, si) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } si \in [L, L + \Delta L) \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Output: F{out}(l,x,y) = \frac{\sum{i} T(I, si) \cdot \text{Noise}(si)}{\sum{i} T(I, si)} The denominator acts as a normalization factor for the uniform box filter weights. The source text implies uniform weighting 1/\Delta L over the segment, which simplifies to the average of noise values within the box. Parameters: \Delta L: Length of the filter box. Not given in the sources. \text{steps}: Number of LIC animation steps. Not given in the sources. l: Current animation step, l \in [0, \text{steps}-1]. Pitfalls: Box filters can cause artifacts when the boxes re-enter the interval, particularly in periodic flows or when the box length is large relative to the streamline length. A solution to avoid this problem is referenced in external literature but not detailed in the source text. Precision issues may arise if the wrap-around logic is not handled correctly for closed streamlines. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def boxfilterdyeadvection(streamlineparams, noisevalues, l, steps, deltaL, maxs): """ Compute the output value for a single pixel using Box Filter Dye Advection. Args: streamlineparams: List of arc-length parameters si along the streamline. noisevalues: List of noise field values sampled at each si. l: Current animation step. steps: Total number of animation steps. deltaL: Length of the filter box. maxs: Total length or period of the streamline. Returns: The output scalar value for the pixel. """ # Calculate start position L based on animation step l L = (l / steps) maxs # Define box end and handle wrap-around per source description Lend = (L + deltaL) % maxs sumval = 0.0 count = 0 for s, n in zip(streamlineparams, noisevalues): # Check if sample parameter s is within [L, Lend) if L < Lend: if L <= s < Lend: sumval += n count += 1 else: # Wrapped interval: [L, maxs) U [0, Lend) if s >= L or s < Lend: sumval += n count += 1 return sumval / count if count > 0 else 0.0 Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sample points along the streamline. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sample points along the streamline. Strengths: Simple to implement; easier to control dye concentration and motion compared to Hanning filters; allows for natural dye advection effects. Limitations: Can cause artifacts when boxes re-enter the interval; less smooth than Hanning filters due to the sharp edges of the box filter. When to use: When visualizing time-varying flow with dye advection is desired, and simplicity of parameter control is important. When not to use: When smooth, high-quality static textures are required, or when artifacts from box re-entry are unacceptable without additional processing. The method addresses the limitations of the Hanning windowed filter used in earlier LIC implementations, which were difficult to tune for smooth dye advection due to their periodic nature and attenuation at the ends. The box filter was chosen for its simplicity and ease of control. name: Fabric-like Visualization of Tensor Field Data
head: Fabric-like visualization, Image-space tensor fabric visualization
body: Fabric-like visualization is a multi-pass image-space rendering technique that visualizes symmetric second-order tensor fields on arbitrary, non-self-intersecting surfaces by mapping the two surface-projected eigendirections as thread-like structures. It solves the problem of visualizing complex directional data on complex geometries without requiring explicit surface parameterization or 3D noise textures, distinguishing itself from standard Line Integral Convolution (LIC) by using smooth reaction-diffusion noise instead of high-frequency white noise to allow the compositing of two distinct eigenvector textures. The method consists of four major rendering passes: Projection, Silhouette Detection, Advection, and Compositing. Data is transferred between passes using textures. Inputs: A surface representation (mesh or implicit) providing depth and normals; a 2D or 3D tensor field defined in world space; camera parameters (modelview MM and projection MP matrices). Outputs: A final image where the surface is textured with two thread-like structures representing the principal eigendirections. Surface Textures: Depth buffer and surface normal buffer generated in Pass 1. Eigenvector Textures: Two 8-bit integer textures storing the scaled projected eigenvectors. Noise Textures: Two 2D textures (channels a and b) generated via reaction-diffusion, mapped to the surface geometry. Da = 0.125: Diffusion constant for chemical a. Db = 0.031: Diffusion constant for chemical b. s: Scalar controlling spot size; smaller s yields larger spots. l: Edge length of the implicit voxel grid defining the parameterization resolution. b{min}: Minimum coordinate of the geometry's bounding box. 1. Render the surface using the standard OpenGL pipeline to obtain depth and surface normal n for each pixel. 2. Interpolate the tensor field T from the world-space tensor field at the surface point. 3. Project T onto the surface tangent plane using the projection matrix P derived from the surface normal n: T' = P \cdot T \cdot P^T where P is defined as: P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 - nx^2 & -ny nx & -nz nx \\ -nx ny & 1 - ny^2 & -nz ny \\ -nx nz & -ny nz & 1 - nz^2 \end{pmatrix} 4. Decompose the projected tensor T' into eigenvectors v{\lambdai} and eigenvalues using the method from Hasan et al. [10]. 5. Project the 3D eigenvectors v{\lambdai} (where i \in \{1, 2\}) into 2D image space: \gamma'{\lambdai} = MP \times MM \times v{\lambdai} 6. Scale the projected 2D eigenvectors to fit 8-bit storage and avoid numerical instability. Calculate the infinity norm: \|v'{\lambdai}\|\infty = \max\{|vx|, |vy|\} Scale the vector: v'{\lambdai}' = \frac{v'{\lambdai}}{\|v'{\lambdai}\|\infty} If \|v'{\lambdai}\|\infty = 0 (surface normal perpendicular to view direction), ignore the division. Perform silhouette detection on the surface to identify boundaries. This step guarantees the integrity of the advection step in Pass 3. This pass produces the two eigenvector textures by advecting a noise field along the projected eigenvector fields. Generate a seamless 2D noise texture using a reaction-diffusion scheme (Turing [24]) to create smooth "spots" rather than high-frequency white noise. The discrete equations for channels a and b are: \Delta a{i,j} = F(i,j) + Da \cdot (a{i+1,j} + a{i-1,j} + a{i,j+1} + a{i,j-1} - 4 \cdot a{i,j}) \Delta b{i,j} = G(i,j) + Db \cdot (b{i+1,j} + b{i-1,j} + b{i,j+1} + b{i,j-1} - 4 \cdot b{i,j}) Source terms: F(i,j) = s(16 - a{i,j} \cdot b{i,j}) G(i,j) = s(a{i,j} \cdot b{i,j} - b{i,j} - \beta{i,j}) [Note: \beta{i,j} is not defined in the provided sources; assumed to be a constant or external input]. Use continuous boundary conditions to ensure the texture is seamless in both directions. Map the 2D reaction-diffusion texture to the 3D surface geometry using an implicit voxel-based parameterization. 1. Define a regular grid of voxels filling the geometry's bounding box. Each voxel has base coordinate bi and edge length l. 2. Transform an object-space vertex coordinate vg to voxel space v{voxel}: v{voxel} = vg \cdot M where M is a 4 \times 4 matrix: M = \begin{pmatrix} l & 0 & 0 & -b{\minx} \\ 0 & l & 0 & -b{\miny} \\ 0 & 0 & l & -b{\minz} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} 3. Transform to local coordinate system v{hit} (components in [0,1]): v{hit} = v{voxel} - [v{voxel}] where [v{voxel}] denotes the integer part (floor). 4. Determine texture coordinates t = (v{hiti}, v{hitj}) by selecting the two components of v{hit} corresponding to the voxel side-plane whose normal is most similar to the surface normal n. Specifically, if nk = \max\{ni, nj, nk\}, then i \neq j \neq k: t = (v{hiti}, v{hitj}) 5. Sample the reaction-diffusion texture at t to initialize the noise field on the surface. 6. Advect the noise field along the projected eigenvector fields \gamma'{\lambda1} and \gamma'{\lambda2} to produce the two eigenvector textures. 1. Compose the intermediate textures (silhouette mask, eigenvector textures) in a final rendering pass. 2. Apply postprocessing steps to add shading and improve perceptual quality. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fabricvisualization(surface, tensorfield, camera, l, s, Da, Db): # Pass 1: Projection depthbuffer = surface.renderdepth(camera) normalbuffer = surface.rendernormals(camera) eigtex1 = [[0.0] 2 for in range(camera.height)] eigtex2 = [[0.0] 2 for in range(camera.height)] noisea, noiseb = generatereactiondiffusionnoise(l, s, Da, Db) bboxmin = surface.getboundingboxmin() Mvoxel = [[l, 0, 0, -bboxmin[0]], [0, l, 0, -bboxmin[1]], [0, 0, l, -bboxmin[2]], [0, 0, 0, 1]] for y in range(camera.height): for x in range(camera.width): n = normalbuffer.get(x, y) if n is None: continue pworld = camera.unproject(x, y, depthbuffer.get(x, y)) Tworld = tensorfield.interpolate(pworld) P = computeprojectionmatrix(n) Tprime = matmul(matmul(P, Tworld), transpose(P)) eigvals, eigvecs3d = decomposetensor(Tprime) v13d = eigvecs3d[:, 0] v23d = eigvecs3d[:, 1] v14d = v13d + [0.0] v24d = v23d + [0.0] v1img = matmul(matmul(camera.MP, camera.MM), v14d) v2img = matmul(matmul(camera.MP, camera.MM), v24d) v12d = [v1img[0]/v1img[3], v1img[1]/v1img[3]] v22d = [v2img[0]/v2img[3], v2img[1]/v2img[3]] v1scaled = scalefor8bit(v12d) v2scaled = scalefor8bit(v22d) eigtex1[y][x] = v1scaled eigtex2[y][x] = v2scaled vg = pworld vvoxel = matmul(Mvoxel, vg + [1.0]) vhit = [vvoxel[i] - int(vvoxel[i]) for i in range(3)] k = argmax(abs(n)) indices = [0, 1, 2] indices.remove(k) t = (vhit[indices[0]], vhit[indices[1]]) vala = noisea.sample(t) valb = noiseb.sample(t) # Pass 3: Advection (Standard LIC step) finaltex1 = [[0.0] 2 for in range(camera.height)] finaltex2 = [[0.0] 2 for in range(camera.height)] for in range(10): newtex1 = [[0.0] 2 for in range(camera.height)] newtex2 = [[0.0] 2 for in range(camera.height)] for y in range(camera.height): for x in range(camera.width): dir1 = eigtex1[y][x] dir2 = eigtex2[y][x] srcx1, srcy1 = x - dir1[0], y - dir1[1] srcx2, srcy2 = x - dir2[0], y - dir2[1] newtex1[y][x] = noisea.sample(srcx1, srcy1) newtex2[y][x] = noiseb.sample(srcx2, srcy2) noisea, noiseb = newtex1, newtex2 finaltex1, finaltex2 = noisea, noiseb # Pass 4: Compositing and Postprocessing # Sources do not specify the exact compositing and postprocessing implementation. # image = composite(finaltex1, finaltex2, silhouettemask) # image = applypostprocessing(image) return image def computeprojectionmatrix(n): nx, ny, nz = n return [[1 - nx2, -nynx, -nznx], [-nxny, 1 - ny2, -nzny], [-nxnz, -nynz, 1 - nz2]] def scalefor8bit(v2d): norminf = max(abs(v2d[0]), abs(v2d[1])) if norminf == 0: return [0, 0] vscaled = [v / norminf for v in v2d] return [int((v + 1.0) 127.5) for v in vscaled] def generatereactiondiffusionnoise(l, s, Da, Db): # Not given in the sources. pass # Not given in the sources. Zero Infinity Norm: If \|v'{\lambdai}\|\infty = 0, the scaling division is undefined. This occurs when the surface normal is perpendicular to the view direction. The method states this case can be ignored. Non-Orthogonality: Projected 3D eigenvectors are not necessarily orthogonal in 2D image space. The method handles this by treating them independently as texture directions. Parameterization: The implicit voxel parameterization avoids the need for explicit texture atlases or 3D noise textures, but the choice of l affects the level of detail and coherence. Time Complexity: The algorithm performs at interactive frame rates for large datasets on current desktop PCs. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for depth/normal buffers, two eigenvector textures (8-bit), and two noise textures. Strengths: Works on arbitrary non-self-intersecting surfaces; no explicit parameterization required; maintains local coherence during transformation; uses smooth noise suitable for compositing two directions. Limitations: Limited to non-self-intersecting surfaces; relies on image-space rendering which may suffer from aliasing if not supersampled; the reaction-diffusion noise generation is a pre-processing step. When to use: When visualizing tensor fields on complex surfaces (e.g., neural pathways in the brain) where standard LIC's white noise is visually cluttered or unsuitable for multi-direction compositing. When not to use: For self-intersecting surfaces or when explicit surface parameterization is already available and preferred. The method was introduced by Bernd Hamann and Gerik Scheuermann. It is motivated by image-space Line Integral Convolution (LIC) but adapts it for tensor visualization using a fabric metaphor. It overcomes drawbacks of previous image-space LIC implementations by defining a fixed parameterization on the surface via implicit voxel space, avoiding the need for 3D noise textures at sub-voxel resolution. name: Streak Surface
body: Streak surfaces visualize time-dependent flows by tracking particles emerging from a seeding curve at different ages, modeling the region of flow passing through a domain. Unlike stream surfaces which assume steady-state flow, streak surfaces capture the history of particle advection in unsteady fields. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A time-dependent velocity field f(\mathbf{x}, t), a univariate seeding curve c: [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}^3, and a current time t. Output: An integral surface S parameterized by age r and curve index s. Data Structures: The surface is defined parametrically. No explicit mesh is required by the definition, though numerical implementations typically discretize r and s into a grid of points (ri, sj) to form a point cloud or mesh. Formulas: The streak surface S at time t is defined by the integral: S(r, s, t) = c(s) + \int{t-r}^{t} f(S(r - (t - \tau), s, \tau), \tau) d\tau Where: r \in [0, t] is the particle age parameter, identifying individual particle instances. s indexes the seeding curve c(s). f is the velocity field. For a constant s, S reduces to a streakline. Steps: 1. Define the seeding curve c(s) for s \in [0, 1]. 2. For each point on the curve s, compute the trajectory of particles emitted at different times. 3. The position of a particle with age r at current time t is found by integrating the velocity field backwards from t to t-r, starting from c(s). 4. Numerical integration (e.g., Riemann sums or Runge-Kutta methods) is required as analytic integration is usually not possible. 5. Collect points S(r, s, t) for discrete values of r and s to form the surface representation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Integration: Analytic integration is generally impossible; discretization errors depend on the step size in time and curve parameterization. Backwards Integration: Streak surfaces can also be modeled using backwards integration to trace flow regions. Approaches for computing time and streak surfaces vary by hardware and dataset size. CPU-based parallel algorithms are used for treating large CFD datasets, while GPU-based approaches are designed for real-time visualization of smaller datasets. These methods often employ point-based algorithms with dense particle sets advected at interactive speeds, combined with point-based rendering, rather than explicit mesh generation. Visualization options include striped textures and advanced transparency via depth peeling. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: CPU-based approaches handle large datasets but are not real-time. GPU-based approaches enable real-time visualization for smaller datasets. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Captures time-dependent flow history; suitable for both large offline analysis (CPU) and interactive exploration (GPU). Limitations: Requires numerical integration; explicit mesh generation is optional but often avoided in favor of point-based rendering for performance. The concept of streaklines and streak surfaces was defined in the context of multi-field visualization. Approaches for time and streak surface computation were presented by Krishnan et al. [21], Bürger et al. [5], and von Funck et al. [34]. name: Hairs
body: Hairs is a visualization technique for representing steady-state flow fields near or around contour surfaces, specifically addressing the failure of fiber bundles (or line bundles) when the flow vector points slightly into the surface. It solves this by growing tiny, segmented hairs from the surface that bend according to the local velocity field. Inputs: A 3D velocity vector field \mathbf{V}. A scalar field defining the contour surface \phi(\mathbf{x}) = 0. Surface normal field \mathbf{N} derived from the gradient of the scalar field. User parameters: number of segments N{seg}, velocity scale Velocity\Scale, segment weights wi, interpolation coefficients ti, root color \mathbf{C}{root}, head color \mathbf{C}{head}, jitter scales, and transparency values \alphai. Outputs: A set of rendered hairs, each defined by a sequence of vertices and associated colors and transparency values. Data Structures: Each hair is a list of N{seg} + 1 vertices P0, P1, \dots, P{N{seg}}. Each vertex Pi has an associated color \mathbf{C}i and transparency \alphai. Splat positions are derived from the contour surface. Steps: 1. Splat Positioning: Scatter splats near the contour surface using Levoy's method. Move each splat position towards the contour surface by a multiple of the gradient to ensure they originate from the surface. Let the final base position be \mathbf{P}0. 2. Hair Generation (Per Hair): Initialize the current position \mathbf{P}{curr} = \mathbf{P}0. For each segment index i from 0 to N{seg} - 1: a. Direction Calculation: Retrieve the normalized surface normal \mathbf{n} and the velocity vector \mathbf{v} at \mathbf{P}{curr}. Calculate the direction vector \mathbf{d}i using the formula: \mathbf{d}i = wi \left( ti \mathbf{n} + (1 - ti) \mathbf{v} \cdot Velocity\Scale \right) Where wi is the weighting factor for segment i, ti is the user-specified interpolation coefficient, and Velocity\Scale is the user-specified velocity scale parameter. The normal vector is normalized, and the velocity is scaled by Velocity\Scale. b. Vertex Update: Compute the next vertex: \mathbf{P}{i+1} = \mathbf{P}{curr} + \mathbf{d}i. Set \mathbf{P}{curr} = \mathbf{P}{i+1}. c. Color Calculation: Determine the color \mathbf{C}i for vertex i. A splat color \mathbf{C}{splat} is derived from the scalar field value at \mathbf{P}i mapped to a color table. The user specifies fractions f{root}, f{splat}, f{head} for the endpoint of segment i. The final color is computed in HSV space as a weighted function of the root color, splat color, and vector head color. A random jitter is added to this final color, controlled by scale factors for each component. All computations are performed in HSV space, with hue wrapping from one to zero, and saturation/value components clamped at zero and one. d. Transparency Assignment: Assign the user-specified transparency \alphai to vertex i. No jittering is applied to transparency. 3. Rendering: Render the line segments connecting \mathbf{P}i to \mathbf{P}{i+1} using the computed colors and transparency values. Parameters: N{seg}: Number of connected line segments per hair. Default is six. Velocity\Scale: Velocity scale parameter. wi: Weighting factor per segment to control apparent stiffness. Greater weights on initial segments favor the normal direction; lower weights on middle segments; large weights on the last one or two segments favor the velocity direction for longer hairs. ti: User-specified interpolation coefficients at each line segment point. \mathbf{C}{root}: User-specified root color. \mathbf{C}{head}: User-specified vector head color. Jitter scales: Scale factors for each HSV component. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Flow into Surface: The method is designed for flow that is "slightly into" the surface, where fiber bundles break down. Precision: HSV hue wrapping must be handled correctly to avoid discontinuities in color. Degenerate Input: If the gradient is zero, the normal is undefined. In practice, a fallback normal (e.g., view vector or previous normal) should be used, though not specified in the source. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Effective for visualizing flow near surfaces where fiber bundles fail due to inward flow. Provides clear indication of flow direction and magnitude via bending. Limitations: Discrete nature may not convey smooth flow topology as well as stream surfaces. When to use: Near-surface flow visualization, especially when flow vectors point into the surface. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Hairs were introduced by Brian Cabral and Lieth Leedom in their work on visualizing 3D velocity fields near contour surfaces. The technique was developed to address limitations of fiber bundles in specific flow scenarios near surfaces. name: Streamtape Rendering
head: Illustrative Rendering of Streamtapes, Streamtape Generation, Streamtape Generation and Illustrative Rendering
body: Streamtape rendering is a technique for visualizing steady-state vector fields by representing selected representative streamlines as twisted surfaces (streamtapes) rather than simple lines or ribbons. It solves the problem of visual clutter and poor depth perception inherent in traditional streamline visualization, particularly in complex flows where streamlines curl and twist. Unlike Stream Surfaces, which stitch adjacent streamlines into a continuous sheet, streamtapes operate on individual representative streamlines, using local torsion to determine width and orientation to automatically manage visual complexity and convey local flow structure without the orientation-dependent flaws of streamribbons. Inputs: A set of representative streamlines r(s), parameterized by arc length s. Outputs: A set of streamtape meshes rendered with illustrative techniques. Data Structures: Streamline: A sequence of points r(si) sampled at equal arc length intervals. Frenet Frame: At each sample point, the tangent \mathbf{T}, normal \mathbf{N}, and binormal \mathbf{B} vectors are computed. Streamtape Mesh: A surface defined by two rows of vertices corresponding to the endpoints of orthogonal line segments at each sample point. Parameters: Sampling Density: Number of points per streamline. Not given in the sources. Torsion Normalization Range: Fixed to [0, 1]. Width Scaling Factor: Implicitly 1.0 in the formula \omega = 1.0 - \tau. Steps: 1. Sample the Streamline: Sample a series of points r(si) at equal arc length intervals along the representative streamline. 2. Compute Local Geometry: For each sample point r(si), compute the derivatives r'(si), r''(si), and r'''(si) with respect to arc length s. Compute the tangent vector \mathbf{T}: \mathbf{T} = \frac{dr}{ds} Compute the normal vector \mathbf{N}: \mathbf{N} = \frac{d\mathbf{T}/ds}{||d\mathbf{T}/ds||} Compute the binormal vector \mathbf{B}: \mathbf{B} = \mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{N} 3. Compute Torsion: Calculate the local torsion \tau using the determinant of the derivatives: \tau = \frac{\det(r', r'', r''')}{||r' \times r''||^2} 4. Normalize Torsion and Compute Width: Normalize the torsion \tau to the range [0, 1] to prevent self-intersection. Let \tau{norm} be the normalized torsion. Calculate the streamtape width \omega: \omega = 1.0 - \tau{norm} 5. Generate Orthogonal Segments: At each sample point r(si), generate an orthogonal line segment centered at r(si). Direction: The segment lies along the binormal vector \mathbf{B}. Length: The total length of the segment is 2 \times \omega (extending \omega/2 on either side), as the sources state the length is determined by torsion and the width is \omega = 1.0 - \tau. 6. Construct Surface: Connect the successive line segments to form a twisted surface. The mesh consists of quadrilateral faces connecting the endpoints of segment i to the endpoints of segment i+1. 7. Add Direction Indicator: Place an arrow at the end of the streamtape to indicate flow direction. 8. Illustrative Rendering: Render the streamtape surfaces using an illustrative style to enhance depth cues and simplify depiction: Silhouettes: Use silhouettes (outlines) as visual cues to simplify the depiction of the streamtapes. Half-tone Shadow: Apply half-tone hatching/shadow to reveal twists of the streamtape surfaces, emphasizing intrinsic directional and structural information. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computefrenetframe(rprime, rdoubleprime): """ Computes T, N, B from derivatives. rprime: tangent vector (dr/ds) rdoubleprime: second derivative (d^2r/ds^2) """ T = rprime / np.linalg.norm(rprime) Nvec = rdoubleprime normN = np.linalg.norm(Nvec) if normN < 1e-9: # Degenerate case: straight line. Normal is undefined by curvature. return T, np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]), np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]) N = Nvec / normN B = np.cross(T, N) return T, N, B def computetorsion(rprime, rdoubleprime, rtripleprime): """ Computes torsion tau. """ numerator = np.linalg.det(np.vstack([rprime, rdoubleprime, rtripleprime])) denominator = np.linalg.norm(np.cross(rprime, rdoubleprime)) 2 if denominator < 1e-9: return 0.0 # Degenerate case return numerator / denominator def generatestreamtape(streamlinepoints): """ Generates a streamtape mesh from a list of points representing a streamline. Assumes points are sampled at equal arc length. Returns list of vertices and faces. """ n = len(streamlinepoints) vertices = [] faces = [] derivatives = [] # Precompute derivatives using finite differences for i in range(n): if i == 0: rp = streamlinepoints[1] - streamlinepoints[0] rpp = (streamlinepoints[2] - streamlinepoints[1]) - rp rppp = ((streamlinepoints[3] - streamlinepoints[2]) - (streamlinepoints[2] - streamlinepoints[1])) - rpp elif i == n - 1: rp = streamlinepoints[-1] - streamlinepoints[-2] rpp = (streamlinepoints[-1] - streamlinepoints[-2]) - (streamlinepoints[-2] - streamlinepoints[-3]) rppp = ((streamlinepoints[-1] - streamlinepoints[-2]) - (streamlinepoints[-2] - streamlinepoints[-3])) - rpp else: h = 1.0 # Normalized arc length step rp = (streamlinepoints[i+1] - streamlinepoints[i-1]) / (2h) rpp = (streamlinepoints[i+1] - 2streamlinepoints[i] + streamlinepoints[i-1]) / (h2) rppp = (streamlinepoints[i+2] - 2streamlinepoints[i+1] + 2streamlinepoints[i-1] - streamlinepoints[i-2]) / (2h3) derivatives.append((rp, rpp, rppp)) for i in range(n): rp, rpp, rppp = derivatives[i] T, N, B = computefrenetframe(rp, rpp) tau = computetorsion(rp, rpp, rppp) # Normalize torsion to [0, 1] taunorm = max(0.0, min(1.0, tau)) # Width omega = 1.0 - taunorm # Center point center = streamlinepoints[i] # Endpoints of the orthogonal segment halfwidth = omega / 2.0 p1 = center - halfwidth B p2 = center + halfwidth B vertices.append(p1) vertices.append(p2) if i > 0: # Connect to previous segment prevp1idx = 2 (i - 1) prevp2idx = 2 (i - 1) + 1 currp1idx = 2 i currp2idx = 2 i + 1 # Create two triangles for the quad faces.append([prevp1idx, prevp2idx, currp1idx]) faces.append([prevp2idx, currp2idx, currp1idx]) return vertices, faces Complexity: The generation of streamtapes is performed on the CPU. The complexity is linear with respect to the number of sample points per streamline and the number of representative streamlines. Strengths: Enhances depth perception by representing streamlines as surfaces. Automatically manages visual clutter and avoids orientation-dependent flaws associated with streamribbons by using the binormal vector and torsion-based width. Conveys local flow structural information (curvature and torsion). Limitations: Requires careful handling of torsion normalization to prevent self-intersection when flow twists sharply. Relies on the selection of representative streamlines, which depends on the preceding clustering and seeding steps. When to use: Use when visualizing complex 3D vector fields where depth perception and local flow structure (twist) are critical, and visual clutter from dense streamlines is a concern. Streamtape rendering was introduced by C.-K. Chen, S. Yan, H. Yu, N. Max, et al. in 2011 as part of an illustrative visualization framework for 3D vector fields. The work builds on the concept of streamribbons but addresses their limitations in handling complex, long streamlines by introducing a torsion-based width and binormal orientation. It is part of a broader effort to apply principles of abstraction and emphasis from technical illustration to scientific visualization. An Illustrative Visualization Framework for 3D Vector Fields, http://vis.cs.ucdavis.edu/papers/pg2011paper.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Stream Arrows
head: Texture Mapping of Arrows
body: Stream arrows are a technique for visualizing integral surfaces by texture mapping arrows onto the surface geometry to convey the local direction of the flow. This method builds on Stream Surfaces by adding directional cues to the surface representation, solving the problem of ascertaining flow orientation in areas of substantial directional change where streamlines curl around each other. Unlike Stream-Balls which use discrete glyphs, stream arrows provide a continuous directional field across the surface. Inputs: A triangulated stream surface mesh and a vector field. Outputs: A rendered image of the surface with arrow textures. Data Structures: Stream Surface: A mesh defined by vertices and connectivity, generated by advancing particles from seed points. Texture Coordinates: UV coordinates mapped to the surface vertices. Arrow Texture: A 2D image containing an arrow graphic, typically with a transparent background. Steps: 1. Surface Generation: Generate the stream surface using particle propagation. The surface is formed on-the-fly using a greedy approach. Divergence and convergence of particles in the advancing front are treated using a simple distance criterion that inserts and removes particles to ensure a balanced resolution of the surface. 2. Texture Mapping: Map arrow textures onto the stream surface. The texture coordinates are assigned to the surface vertices such that the arrow orientation aligns with the local vector field direction at each point. 3. Rendering: Render the textured surface. The arrows are drawn according to the texture mapping, providing a visual indication of the flow direction across the integral surface. Parameters: Arrow Size: Not specified in the sources. Texture Resolution: Not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Distortion: The original method does not address stretching and divergence of the surface, which distorts the parameterization and results in very large or small arrows. This can lead to visual clutter or unreadable arrows in regions of high shear or expansion. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderstreamarrows(surfacemesh, vectorfield): """ Render stream arrows on a given surface mesh. Args: surfacemesh: Triangulated mesh representing the stream surface. vectorfield: Function or data structure providing vector values at 3D points. Returns: Rendered image. """ # Step 1: Ensure surface is generated with balanced resolution # This involves inserting/removing particles based on distance criteria # to handle divergence/convergence. # Implementation detail: This is handled during the surface generation phase. # Step 2: Assign texture coordinates and orientations # For each vertex in the mesh, determine the local vector direction. # Map this direction to the arrow texture's orientation. for vertex in surfacemesh.vertices: localvector = vectorfield(vertex.position) # Normalize vector to determine orientation orientation = normalize(localvector) # Assign UV coordinates and rotation for the arrow texture # The exact mapping depends on the texture atlas and rendering engine vertex.uv = mapvectortouv(orientation) vertex.rotation = calculaterotation(orientation) # Step 3: Render the textured surface # Draw the surface with the arrow textures applied rendertexturemappedsurface(surfacemesh) A refinement of stream arrows using a regular, hierarchical tiling of texture space to adjust for surface stretching and divergence. It applies a regular, hierarchical tiling of texture space and adjusts the arrow textures based on the tiling to compensate for distortion. This addresses the pitfall of the original method where surface stretching results in distorted arrow sizes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides continuous directional cues on integral surfaces, enhancing the understanding of flow direction. Limitations: High visual complexity of the resulting surfaces makes stream arrows rarely used in integral surface visualization from CFD data. The original method suffers from distortion due to surface stretching and divergence. When to use: When continuous directional information on an integral surface is required and the surface geometry is relatively uniform. When not to use: When the surface exhibits significant stretching or divergence, leading to distorted arrows, or when visual clarity is prioritized over continuous directional cues. Stream arrows were introduced by Löffelmann [26] as an advanced visualization of integral surfaces, with the goal of conveying the local direction of the flow. The same authors subsequently addressed the issue of distortion by proposing a regular, hierarchical tiling of texture space that results in adjusted arrows [25]. Despite these improvements, stream arrows are rarely used in integral surface visualization from CFD data due to the high visual complexity of the resulting surfaces.
