name: Higher Order Tensor (HOT) Lines
head: Generalized Tensor Lines, HOT-Lines, Higher Order Tensor Line Tracking, Major tensor lines, Median higher order tensor lines, Minor tensor lines, Tracking Lines in Higher Order Tensor Fields
body: Higher Order Tensor (HOT) Lines is a method for visualizing higher-order tensor fields by tracking lines that follow the local maxima of the tensor's spherical function. It solves the problem of detecting fiber crossings locally without reducing spatial resolution, which is a limitation of second-order tensor lines that follow only the major eigenvector. Unlike second-order tensor lines, which are separated by a separatrix that cannot be crossed, HOT-lines allow for the representation of multiple directions within a single volume element, enabling the visualization of complex fiber structures such as the corpus callosum and pyramidal tract crossing. Inputs and Outputs Input: A symmetric higher-order tensor field T of order r and dimension d=3, defined on a domain U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3. The tensor field is typically derived from MRI diffusion data. Output: A set of curves (HOT-lines) representing the trajectories of mass-less particles advected by the direction fields defined by the maxima (major), minima (minor), or saddle points (median) of the tensor function on the unit sphere. Data Structures The tensor field is represented either as a set of tensor components T{j1 \dots jr} or via a spherical harmonic expansion. Spherical Harmonic Representation: For symmetric tensors, the field is represented as: f\sigma(g) = \suml \summ al^m Yl^m(g) where only even orders l are used for symmetric tensors. This requires (l+1)(l+2)/2 real coefficients per voxel. Tensor Components: For a tensor of order r, the components are stored in an array of size corresponding to the number of independent components of a symmetric tensor of order r in 3D. Mathematical Foundation A tensor T of order r is a multilinear form mapping r vectors to a scalar: T: (\mathbb{R}^d)^r \to \mathbb{R}, \quad (v^{(1)}, \dots, v^{(r)}) \mapsto T{i1 \dots ir} v^{(1)}{i1} \dots v^{(r)}{ir} At each position p, the tensor is interpreted as a scalar function fT(p) on the unit sphere S^2 using a normalized direction vector g: fT(p)(g) = T{j1 \dots jr}(p) \cdot g{j1} \dots g{jr} Degeneracy Definition A position p is defined as degenerated if there exists a point (\theta, \phi) on S^2 where the spherical gradient is zero AND the determinant of the spherical Hessian is zero: \nabla{S^2} fT(p)(\theta, \phi) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \det |\nabla^2{S^2} fT(p)(\theta, \phi)| = 0 Pure order zero tensors (scalar fields, a{00}) are degenerate as they have no orientation. For second-order tensors, \lambda0 = \lambda1 is degenerate, but \lambda0 > \lambda1 = \lambda2 is not. Line Definitions Major HOT-Lines: Follow the maxima of fT. At a regular point q, there are M isolated maxima m1 \dots mM. Using the implicit function theorem, unique C^1 functions wm(p) = (\thetam(p), \phim(p)) parameterize these maxima in neighborhoods Um. The line xm(t) is defined by: \frac{\partial xm(t)}{\partial t} = wm(xm(t)), \quad xm(0) = q Minor HOT-Lines: Follow the minima of fT. This is equivalent to tracking streamlines on the negated tensor field for first-order tensors. Median HOT-Lines: Follow the saddle points of fT. Algorithm Steps 1. Tensor Reconstruction: Compute the higher-order tensor T from raw MRI signals s(n) and baseline s(0) using the signal equation: s(n) = s(0) e^{-b T{i1 \dots ir} \cdot g{i1} \dots g{ir}} where b is the diffusion weighting factor. Solve for T using least squares fitting. 2. Initialization: For each seed point p, identify all isolated maxima (for major lines) of fT(p) on S^2. 3. Tracking Loop: Maintain a set totrack containing tuples (position, direction, stepsize). While totrack is not empty, pop a triple (pos, dir, step). Call trackline(pos, dir, step). 4. Integration (trackline): Initialize stopped = false. While not stopped: While step not accepted or stopped: If stepsize is too small (below lower limit), stop (degenerated point reached). Calculate nextpos = pos + dir stepsize. Evaluate directions at nextpos. If there is a single direction close to dir: Accept step: pos = nextpos. If new direction is close enough, increase stepsize (adaptive control). Else if there are multiple directions close to dir: Append pos to a set of degenerated points. Stop tracking this line. Else (no direction close): Reduce stepsize and retry. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trackhotlines(tensorfield, seedpoints, bfactor, minstep, maxstep, directionthreshold): """ tensorfield: 3D array of tensors (represented as spherical harmonic coefficients or components) seedpoints: list of (x, y, z) coordinates bfactor: float, diffusion weighting factor minstep: float, minimum step size before stopping maxstep: float, maximum step size directionthreshold: float, angular tolerance for direction matching """ alllines = [] for seed in seedpoints: # 1. Get initial directions (maxima) at seed point initialdirections = getmaximaonsphere(tensorfield[seed]) # 2. Initialize tracking queue # Queue items: (position, directionvector, currentstepsize) totrack = [] for dirvec in initialdirections: totrack.append((seed, dirvec, initialstepsize)) # initialstepsize is a parameter # 3. Process queue while totrack: pos, direction, stepsize = totrack.pop(0) linepoints = [pos] stopped = False while not stopped: stepaccepted = False # Check for degeneracy via step size if stepsize < minstep: stopped = True break # Propose step nextpos = pos + direction stepsize # Check if nextpos is within grid bounds if not isinsidegrid(nextpos): stopped = True break # Get candidate directions at nextpos candidates = getmaximaonsphere(tensorfield[nextpos]) # Find closest candidate to current direction closestdir = None minangle = infinity for cand in candidates: angle = anglebetween(direction, cand) if angle < minangle: minangle = angle closestdir = cand # Decision logic based on source if closestdir is None: # No directions found (e.g., scalar field) stopped = True break if minangle < directionthreshold: # Single direction close enough stepaccepted = True pos = nextpos linepoints.append(pos) # Adaptive step size: increase if direction is very stable if minangle < (directionthreshold / 2): stepsize = min(stepsize 1.1, maxstep) else: stepsize = max(stepsize 0.9, minstep) # Slight reduction if not super stable # Update direction for next iteration direction = closestdir else: # No direction close enough, or multiple close (handled by angle check logic in source) # Source says: "if multiple directions close... stop". # We approximate "multiple close" by checking if the second closest is also within threshold. secondclosestangle = infinity countclose = 0 for cand in candidates: if anglebetween(direction, cand) < directionthreshold: countclose += 1 if countclose > 1: # Multiple directions close -> Degenerate/Crossing stopped = True # Optionally record this point as a branching/degenerate point else: # No single direction close, but not multiple close -> Reduce step stepsize = stepsize / 2.0 if linepoints: alllines.append(linepoints) return alllines def getmaximaonsphere(tensoratpoint): """ Finds the local maxima of the function f(g) = T. g^r on the unit sphere. For implementation, this typically involves optimizing f(g) over g in S^2. Using spherical harmonics, f(g) is evaluated analytically. Returns a list of unit vectors (directions). """ # Implementation detail: # The source states maxima are found using the implicit function theorem # for continuous tracking, but for discrete step integration, we find # the maxima of the spherical function at the current voxel. # A common approach is to evaluate f(g) on a fine grid of S^2 and find peaks, # or use gradient ascent on the sphere. # Since the source does not provide the exact numerical optimization algorithm, # we assume a standard spherical optimization routine is used. pass Parameters b-factor: Diffusion weighting factor, assumed constant. Step size limits: Lower and upper limits related to data smoothness. Direction accuracy: Depends on tracking accuracy and tensor order (higher orders produce closer maxima). Anisotropy Threshold (for switching variant): 0.2–0.3 depending on SNR. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Degenerate Points: Positions where the Hessian determinant is zero. Lines are not uniquely defined. Tracking stops or branches. Scalar Fields: Pure order zero tensors (a{00}) make tracking impossible. Multiple Directions: If multiple directions are close to the current direction during tracking, the point is considered degenerate and tracking stops. Precision: Higher-order tensors can produce many maxima close together, requiring high direction accuracy. A variant that improves speed by using simple second-order tensor tracking in areas with one dominant fiber direction and switching to higher-order tensor analysis when anisotropy is low or direction deviation is large. It monitors local anisotropy measurements and orientation change. If anisotropy is below a threshold (typically 0.2–0.3) or direction deviation is too large, it processes the next step with higher-order lines; otherwise, it accepts the second-order step. This leverages the similarity of HOT-lines with second-order tensor lines in dominant direction areas. Time Complexity: Tracking is O(N \cdot S) where N is the number of seeds and S is the average number of steps. Finding maxima on the sphere is a local optimization problem per step. The anisotropy-based switching variant reduces time in coherent regions by using faster second-order eigenvector extraction. Memory Complexity: O(V) for storing the tensor field, where V is the number of voxels. Each voxel stores (l+1)(l+2)/2 coefficients for order l. Performance: Applied to datasets of size 128 \times 128 \times 44 with voxel size 1.7 \times 1.7 \times 3.0 mm^3. Uses 36 gradient directions. Strengths: Detects crossings locally without reducing resolution; preserves high angular resolution; generalizes streamlines and tensor lines. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than second-order tensor lines; sensitive to noise and degenerate points; requires careful step-size control. When to use: When visualizing fiber crossings in diffusion MRI data where second-order tensors fail (e.g., corpus callosum/pyramidal tract crossing). When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and crossings are rare; or when data is purely scalar/isotropic. HOT-lines were introduced by Hlawitschka and Scheuermann. The method generalizes streamlines (first-order tensors) and tensor lines (second-order tensors) to arbitrary even-order symmetric tensors. It was applied to MRI data to solve the tractography problem, specifically to address the limitation of second-order tensors in representing fiber crossings. The approach uses spherical harmonic representation for efficiency and relies on the implicit function theorem to ensure C^1 continuity of the tracked lines. name: Speedlines
head: Motion Streaks, Streak Lines
body: Speedlines are an illustrative visualization technique used to indicate the motion and history of specific features within time-varying datasets. Unlike standard stream lines that trace particle trajectories through a vector field, speedlines superimpose geometric primitives (cones) along the receding bounding contour of a moving feature to provide intuitive visual cues of direction and velocity history. This method is distinct from its siblings, such as Adaptive Stream Line Seeding which focuses on density, and Directional Textured Tracelines which use texture, by explicitly modeling the "streak" effect of a moving object's silhouette. Inputs: Feature geometry f (typically a mesh or point set). Feature motion data: average velocity vector \mathbf{v}{avg} and angular velocity vector \boldsymbol{\omega}. User parameters: number of speedlines N, cone base radius r{base}, time-difference \Delta t, number of cone facets n{facets}, and color/intensity. Outputs: A mesh geometry containing cones representing the speedlines, colored according to user specifications. Data Structures: Bounding Contour (bc): A list of 3D points \{p1, p2, \dots, pm\} representing the smoothed boundary of the feature. Centroid (c): The 3D center of mass of the feature. Indices (i{min}, i{max}): Integer indices into the contour list identifying the start and end of the trailing portion. Algorithm Steps: 1. Obtain Bounding Contour: Compute the bounding contour bc for feature f. 2. Smooth Contour: Apply Gaussian smoothing to bc to reduce noise and ensure a smooth trailing edge. 3. Identify Trailing Edge: Initialize d{min} = \infty and d{max} = -\infty. Initialize indices i{min} = 0 and i{max} = 0. For each point pi in bc: Calculate the distance metric di using Equation 9: di = (pi - c) \cdot \mathbf{v}{avg} where c is the feature centroid and \mathbf{v}{avg} is the average feature velocity. If di < d{min}, set d{min} = di and i{min} = i. If di > d{max}, set d{max} = di and i{max} = i. Note: The sources define the trailing portion as the segment between the points that minimize and maximize this dot product, effectively capturing the "rear" of the feature relative to motion. 4. Extract Trailing Segment: Reduce bc to the subset of points lying between indices i{min} and i{max} along the contour path. 5. Distribute Seeds: Distribute N seed points evenly along the extracted trailing segment of bc. Let these seed points be sj for j=1 \dots N. 6. Calculate Local Velocity: For each seed point sj, calculate the local velocity vector \mathbf{v}{local} using Equation 10: \mathbf{v}{local} = \mathbf{v}{avg} + \boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{r}j where \mathbf{r}j = sj - c is the position vector of the seed point relative to the centroid, and \times denotes the cross product. 7. Construct Cones: For each seed point sj: Determine cone length Lj: Lj = \|\mathbf{v}{local}\| \cdot \Delta t Determine cone orientation: The central axis of the cone is oriented opposite to the estimated velocity vector (-\mathbf{v}{local}) to indicate the direction from which the feature came (the "streak" trailing behind). Generate a cone geometry with base radius r{base}, length Lj, and n{facets} sides, centered at sj and aligned with -\mathbf{v}{local}. 8. Render: Add the generated cones to the output mesh geometry and apply the user-specified color/intensity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatespeedlines(featuremesh, vavg, omega, N, rbase, deltat, nfacets, color): """ Generates speedlines for a moving feature. Args: featuremesh: Mesh or point cloud representing the feature. vavg: 3D vector, average velocity of the feature. omega: 3D vector, angular velocity of the feature. N: int, number of speedlines to generate. rbase: float, base radius of the cones. deltat: float, user-defined time-difference for length calculation. nfacets: int, number of facets for the cone geometry. color: tuple, RGB or RGBA color for the speedlines. Returns: list of Cone objects to be added to the scene graph. """ # Step 1: Obtain bounding contour # Note: Algorithm 3 is referenced for contour extraction. # Assuming a function getboundingcontour exists that returns a list of 3D points. bc = getboundingcontour(featuremesh) # Step 2: Apply Gaussian smoothing bc = gaussiansmooth(bc) # Step 3: Identify trailing edge centroid = computecentroid(featuremesh) dmin = float('inf') dmax = float('-inf') imin = 0 imax = 0 for i, pi in enumerate(bc): # Eqn 9: Distance function # Vector subtraction and dot product diff = vectorsub(pi, centroid) di = dotproduct(diff, vavg) if di < dmin: dmin = di imin = i if di > dmax: dmax = di imax = i # Step 4: Reduce contour to trailing portion # Assuming bc is ordered cyclically or linearly. # The sources imply a linear segment between imin and imax. # If the contour is a closed loop, we must determine the correct path. # Based on "Reduce bc to the points between imin and imax", we assume linear indexing. trailingbc = bc[imin: imax + 1] # Step 5: Distribute points evenly # Interpolate N points along the trailingbc path seedpoints = distributepointsevenly(trailingbc, N) speedlines = [] for sj in seedpoints: # Step 6: Calculate local velocity # Eqn 10: vlocal = vavg + omega x r rj = vectorsub(sj, centroid) crossterm = crossproduct(omega, rj) vlocal = vectoradd(vavg, crossterm) # Step 7: Construct cone # Eqn for length: L = vlocal deltat (interpreted as magnitude dt) vmag = vectorlength(vlocal) length = vmag deltat # Orientation: opposite to velocity axis = vectornegate(vlocal) if vectorlength(axis) < 1e-9: axis = [0, 0, 1] # Fallback for zero velocity # Generate cone geometry # Note: VTK cone generator is referenced. We implement a simple cone here. cone = generatecone( center=sj, axis=axis, length=length, radius=rbase, facets=nfacets) cone.color = color speedlines.append(cone) return speedlines def generatecone(center, axis, length, radius, facets): """ Generates a simple cone mesh. """ # Normalize axis axis = normalize(axis) # Create vertices vertices = [] indices = [] # Apex apex = vectoradd(center, vectorscale(axis, length)) vertices.append(apex) # Base center basecenter = center # Base vertices # Create a basis perpendicular to axis if abs(axis[0]) < 0.9: perp1 = normalize(crossproduct(axis, [1, 0, 0])) else: perp1 = normalize(crossproduct(axis, [0, 1, 0])) perp2 = crossproduct(axis, perp1) for i in range(facets): angle = 2 3.14159265 i / facets offset = vectoradd( vectorscale(perp1, radius cos(angle)), vectorscale(perp2, radius sin(angle))) basevertex = vectoradd(basecenter, offset) vertices.append(basevertex) # Indices: Apex connects to all base vertices for i in range(1, facets + 1): indices.append((0, i, (i % facets) + 1)) return Mesh(vertices=vertices, indices=indices) Parameters: \Delta t: User-defined time-difference. Controls the length of the streaks. N: Number of speedlines. r{base}: Cone base radius. n{facets}: Number of facets for the cone geometry. Color/Intensity: Visual styling parameters. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Velocity: If \mathbf{v}{avg} and \boldsymbol{\omega} are zero, \mathbf{v}{local} is zero, resulting in zero-length cones. A fallback axis is required. Contour Ordering: The algorithm assumes the bounding contour points are ordered such that the segment between i{min} and i{max} represents the trailing edge. If the contour is a closed loop, the "between" logic must handle wrap-around or select the shorter/longer arc appropriately. The sources do not specify how to handle closed loops explicitly, only "Reduce bc to the points between imin and imax". Angular Velocity: If \boldsymbol{\omega} is not available, it is assumed to be zero. Adjusts seed point density based on flow complexity. Choose when uniform distribution is insufficient. Link Uses texture mapping on lines to show direction. Choose for high-density flow visualization. Link Generates surfaces from stream lines. Choose for volumetric flow visualization. Link Visualizes tensor fields. Choose for diffusion or stress data. Link Time Complexity: O(M + N), where M is the number of points in the bounding contour and N is the number of speedlines. Contour extraction and smoothing dominate M, while cone generation is linear in N. Memory Complexity: O(M + N \cdot F), where F is the number of vertices per cone (proportional to n{facets}). Strengths: Intuitively conveys motion direction and history for discrete moving features. Simple to implement. Limitations: Only applicable to discrete features with defined centroids and motion vectors. Not suitable for general vector fields without feature segmentation. Performance degrades with very high N or n{facets}. When to use: When visualizing the trajectory of specific, identifiable objects (e.g., particles, blobs) in time-varying data. When not to use: For continuous vector fields without distinct features, or when precise trajectory integration is required. Speedlines were introduced by Joshi and Rheingans as part of a set of illustrative visualization techniques for time-varying datasets. The technique is motivated by the human perception of motion streaks, where moving objects leave a visual trace. It is often used in conjunction with other techniques like opacity modulation and strobe silhouettes to provide a comprehensive view of feature history. Generalized Framework and Algorithms for Illustrative Visualization of Time-Varying Data on Unstructured Meshes, https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc838861/?q=illustrative volume rendering, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) Visualization
head: DTI Visualization
body: Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) Visualization is a method for rendering 3x3 symmetric diffusion tensors acquired via MRI to visualize water diffusion patterns and structural neural connections in biological tissues. It solves the problem of interpreting complex, direction-dependent diffusion data by mapping tensor properties to visual attributes such as color, opacity, or geometric primitives. Unlike scalar volume rendering, it handles multi-component tensor fields, distinguishing itself from sibling methods like Domain Colouring by explicitly leveraging the geometric structure of the diffusion ellipsoid rather than just angular phase. Inputs: A 3D volume where each voxel contains a 3x3 symmetric diffusion tensor \mathbf{D}. Outputs: A rendered image or geometric representation (streamlines, glyphs) of the diffusion field. Data Structures: The diffusion tensor \mathbf{D} at position \mathbf{x} is stored as a symmetric 3x3 matrix: \mathbf{D} = \begin{bmatrix} D{xx} & D{xy} & D{xz} \\ D{xy} & D{yy} & D{yz} \\ D{xz} & D{yz} & D{zz} \end{bmatrix} Each tensor is typically stored as 6 floating-point values (D{xx}, D{yy}, D{zz}, D{xy}, D{xz}, D{yz}) due to symmetry. Steps: 1. Tensor Decomposition: For each voxel, compute the eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 and corresponding eigenvectors \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \mathbf{v}3 of \mathbf{D}, sorted such that \lambda1 \ge \lambda2 \ge \lambda3 \ge 0. 2. Geometric Interpretation: The tensor represents a diffusion ellipsoid where the eigenvectors define the principal axes and the eigenvalues define the squared lengths of the semi-axes. 3. Visualization Mapping: Apply one of the following strategies: Tractography: Extract and visualize fiber tract trajectories from DTI data. Tensor Lines: Visualize tensor lines for tractography. Direct Volume Rendering: Perform direct volume rendering of DTI data. Formulas: Orthogonality: Eigenvectors are orthogonal in Cartesian space: \langle \mathbf{v}{\lambda1}, \mathbf{v}{\lambda2} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{v}{\lambda2}, \mathbf{v}{\lambda3} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{v}{\lambda1}, \mathbf{v}{\lambda3} \rangle = 0. Cross Product Relation: \mathbf{v}{\lambda1} \times \mathbf{v}{\lambda2} = \mathbf{v}{\lambda3}. This relation can be used to reduce calculation effort if two eigenvectors are known. Parameters: Sorting order: \lambda1 \ge \lambda2 \ge \lambda3. Integration step size for tractography: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Critical Points: Occur when two eigenvalues are equal (\lambdai = \lambdaj). At these points, the corresponding eigenvectors are not uniquely defined, and anisotropy measures become zero. Orientation Ambiguity: Eigenvectors are orientationless (direction only, no sign). This causes interpolation problems if adjacent sample points have contrary orientations (e.g., \mathbf{v} vs -\mathbf{v}). Visualizes diffusion tensor fields by generating a scalar volume from an anisotropically correlated random noise field, preserving high-frequency components in transversal directions while smearing noise along the direction of greatest diffusivity. Unlike glyphs, streamlines, or line integral convolution, it is not sensitive to occlusion, does not depend on starting points, and provides a continuous scalar field representation that handles non-linear diffusion better. Choose when occlusion resistance and continuous scalar representation are required. Interprets the tensor as a distortion of a flat metric, transforming the tensor field into a metric tensor field visualized using a texture resembling fabric, where eigenvalues control texture density and eigenvectors control alignment. Unlike Domain Colouring or Glyph-based Vector/Tensor Visualization, which often suffer from clutter or local view limitations, this method provides a continuous, global representation that explicitly distinguishes between positive (expansion) and negative (compression) eigenvalues. Choose for global, continuous metric visualization. A scalar quantity describing the diffusion along a specific direction vector \mathbf{v}, derived directly from the diffusion tensor \mathbf{D}. Unlike rotationally invariant metrics such as Mean Diffusivity (MD) or Fractional Anisotropy (FA) that summarize the entire tensor, ADC is direction-dependent, quantifying diffusion intensity along a chosen axis. Choose when directional intensity mapping is required rather than global tensor shape analysis. The Diffusion Tensor is a 3x3 symmetric positive-definite matrix that serves as the native measurement quantity in Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI), modeling the local anisotropic diffusion of water molecules in biological tissue. It is defined by three orthogonal eigenvectors and their corresponding eigenvalues, which geometrically represent the principal axes and magnitudes of a diffusion ellipsoid. Choose when full second-order directional information is required for fiber tracking, distinct from scalar metrics like ADC or derived visualizations. Acquisition of 40 or more diffusion weighted volumes to calculate and visualize water diffusion and structural neural connections in the brain. Extends standard DTI by capturing more complex diffusion profiles, allowing for the visualization of crossing fibers which standard DTI cannot resolve. Choose when high angular resolution is needed to resolve crossing fibers. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance with hardware, resolution and scene: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use it and when not: Not given in the sources. Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) was introduced by Basser in 1994 as an MRI-based acquisition modality yielding 3x3 symmetric diffusion tensors as its native measurement quantity. In 1998, Basser and colleagues published the first work extracting and visualizing fiber tract trajectories from DTI data of the brain. By 2000, the visualization community had developed methods for tensor line tractography and direct volume rendering of DTI data. The method is primarily used in medical imaging for therapy planning and understanding structural neural networks. name: Diffusion Tensor Visualization using Random Field Correlation
head: Adaptive filtering of noise fields for DTI, Random field correlation volume rendering
body: This method visualizes diffusion tensor fields by generating a scalar volume from an anisotropically correlated random noise field, preserving high-frequency components in transversal directions while smearing noise along the direction of greatest diffusivity. Unlike glyphs, streamlines, or line integral convolution, it is not sensitive to occlusion, does not depend on starting points, and provides a continuous scalar field representation that handles non-linear diffusion better. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D diffusion tensor field D. Each voxel contains a 3 \times 3 symmetric positive-definite tensor. Output: A scalar volume N{out} and a color volume, suitable for standard volume rendering. Data Structures Diffusion Tensor Field: Stored as a 3D grid. Each voxel holds a 3 \times 3 matrix. Noise Field: A 3D grid of floating-point values. Spectral Decomposition: For each voxel, the tensor D is decomposed into eigenvalues \lambda1 \ge \lambda2 \ge \lambda3 \ge 0 and corresponding orthonormal eigenvectors \hat{\mathbf{e}}1, \hat{\mathbf{e}}2, \hat{\mathbf{e}}3. These form the matrix \mathbf{E} = [\hat{\mathbf{e}}1, \hat{\mathbf{e}}2, \hat{\mathbf{e}}3] and diagonal matrix \mathbf{\Sigma} = \text{diag}(\lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3) such that D = \mathbf{E}\mathbf{\Sigma}\mathbf{E}^T. Parameters Amplification factor (\alpha): Not given in the sources. Number of iterations (J): 20. Filter Directions: The six high-pass filter directions correspond to the vertices of an icosahedron. Algorithm Steps 1. Spectral Decomposition: For every voxel in the input tensor field, compute the eigenvalues \lambdai and eigenvectors \hat{\mathbf{e}}i of D. 2. Generate Initial Noise: Create three independent zero-mean Gaussian noise processes. Let \mathbf{x} be a vector containing realizations of these three processes at each voxel location. 3. Compute Correlated Noise Magnitude: Calculate the initial noise field magnitude N using the formula: N = \|\mathbf{y}\| = \|\mathbf{E}\mathbf{\Sigma}\mathbf{x}\| where \mathbf{E} is the matrix of eigenvectors, \mathbf{\Sigma} is the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues, and \mathbf{x} is the vector of independent Gaussian noise. This creates a spatially independent but not identically distributed noise field with greater power in areas of stronger diffusivity. 4. Decompose Noise Field: Decompose the noise field N into a low-pass version N{lp} and six high-pass components Nk using spherical separable filters. The directions of these six high-pass filters are defined by the vertices of an icosahedron. 5. Iterative Adaptive Filtering: Perform J iterations of filtering. In each iteration j (from 1 to J): a. Compute Control Tensor: For each voxel, compute the control tensor \mathbf{C}: \mathbf{C} = \sum{n=2}^3 \frac{\lambda3}{\lambdan} \hat{\mathbf{e}}n \hat{\mathbf{e}}n^T This tensor is intentionally degenerated to rank 2 to allow full smearing in the major diffusion direction given by \lambda1. b. Compute Linearity Coefficient: Calculate the linearity coefficient cl: cl = \frac{\lambda1 - \lambda2}{\lambda1} This accounts for the degree of linearity of the diffusion tensor. c. Compute Mapping Function: Calculate the weighting factor h: h(|\mathbf{D}|) = h(cl) = (\alpha cl + 1)^{\frac{1}{2}} where \alpha is an amplification factor. d. Filter Output: Compute the filtered output F for the current iteration using the input noise field from the previous iteration (or N for the first iteration): F = N{lp} + h(|\mathbf{D}|) \sumk \langle \mathbf{C}, \mathbf{M}k \rangle Nk Here, \langle \mathbf{C}, \mathbf{M}k \rangle is the inner product of the control tensor \mathbf{C} and the dual basis \mathbf{M}k associated with filter direction k, and Nk are the high-pass components of the input noise field. e. Update Input: Set the input noise field for the next iteration to F. The goal is to make the noise structure more continuous and sharper. 6. Final Visualization Data: After J iterations, the output is N{out} = F. 7. Opacity and Color Computation: a. Opacity: Set opacity to N{out} \cdot cl. This shows the structure only in areas containing fibers. b. Color: Compute the color vector (r, g, b)^t as: (r \ g \ b)^t = N{out} \frac{(1 \ 1 \ 1)^t + \hat{\mathbf{e}}1}{2} where \hat{\mathbf{e}}1 is the eigenvector corresponding to the largest eigenvalue \lambda1. This multiplies the computed color by N{out} to darken the edges of the structures. Pseudocode Unverified code. Returns: eigenvalues: (H, W, D, 3) array of lambda1, lambda2, lambda3 eigenvectors: (H, W, D, 3, 3) array where eigenvectors[:,:,:,:, i] is ei """ # Implementation depends on the specific tensor field storage. # Assumes tensorfield is (H, W, D, 3, 3) eigenvalues = np.zeros((H, W, D, 3)) eigenvectors = np.zeros((H, W, D, 3, 3)) for h in range(H): for w in range(W): for d in range(D): T = tensorfield[h, w, d] # T is 3x3 symmetric vals, vecs = np.linalg.eigh(T) # eigh returns sorted eigenvalues, but we need lambda1 >= lambda2 >= lambda3 # Sort in descending order idx = np.argsort(vals)[::-1] eigenvalues[h, w, d] = vals[idx] eigenvectors[h, w, d] = vecs[:, idx] return eigenvalues, eigenvectors def generategaussiannoise(shape): """Generates three independent zero-mean Gaussian noise processes.""" return np.random.normal(0, 1, (shape[0], shape[1], shape[2], 3)) def decomposenoisefield(noisefield, filterdirections): """ Decomposes noise field into low-pass and high-pass components. noisefield: (H, W, D) filterdirections: (6, 3) array of icosahedron vertices Returns: Nlp: (H, W, D) Nk: (H, W, D, 6) """ # Implementation of spherical separable filters is not detailed in sources. # This is a placeholder for the filtering operation. # Nlp is the low-pass version of noisefield. # Nk are the high-pass components along the 6 filter directions. Nlp = applylowpassfilter(noisefield) Nk = np.zeros((H, W, D, 6)) for k in range(6): Nk[:,:,:, k] = applyhighpassfilter(noisefield, filterdirections[k]) return Nlp, Nk def computecontroltensor(eigenvalues, eigenvectors): """ Computes the control tensor C for each voxel. eigenvalues: (H, W, D, 3) eigenvectors: (H, W, D, 3, 3) Returns: C: (H, W, D, 3, 3) """ lambda1 = eigenvalues[:,:,:, 0] lambda2 = eigenvalues[:,:,:, 1] lambda3 = eigenvalues[:,:,:, 2] e2 = eigenvectors[:,:,:,:, 1] # Shape (H, W, D, 3) e3 = eigenvectors[:,:,:,:, 2] # Shape (H, W, D, 3) # C = sum{n=2}^3 (lambda3 / lambdan) en en^T # Note: lambdan here refers to lambda2 and lambda3 for n=2,3 # So for n=2: term is (lambda3 / lambda2) e2 e2^T # For n=3: term is (lambda3 / lambda3) e3 e3^T = e3 e3^T # Compute outer products # e2outer: (H, W, D, 3, 3) e2outer = np.einsum('...i,...j->...ij', e2, e2) e3outer = np.einsum('...i,...j->...ij', e3, e3) # Weights w2 = lambda3 / lambda2 w3 = lambda3 / lambda3 # = 1 C = w2[:,:,:, np.newaxis, np.newaxis] e2outer + w3[:,:,:, np.newaxis, np.newaxis] e3outer return C def computedualbasisinnerproduct(C, Mk): """ Computes <C, Mk> for each voxel and each k. C: (H, W, D, 3, 3) Mk: (6, 3, 3) dual basis tensors Returns: weights: (H, W, D, 6) """ # Inner product of two matrices A, B is trace(A^T B) or sum(AB) for symmetric # Mk is precomputed for the 6 directions weights = np.zeros((H, W, D, 6)) for k in range(6): Mk = Mk[k] # (3, 3) # Element-wise multiplication and sum over last two dimensions weights[:,:,:, k] = np.sum(C Mk[np.newaxis, np.newaxis, np.newaxis,:,:], axis=(3, 4)) return weights def adaptivefilteriteration(Nlp, Nk, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, alpha, Mk): """ Performs one iteration of adaptive filtering. Nlp: (H, W, D) Nk: (H, W, D, 6) eigenvalues: (H, W, D, 3) eigenvectors: (H, W, D, 3, 3) alpha: scalar Mk: (6, 3, 3) Returns: F: (H, W, D) """ C = computecontroltensor(eigenvalues, eigenvectors) lambda1 = eigenvalues[:,:,:, 0] lambda2 = eigenvalues[:,:,:, 1] cl = (lambda1 - lambda2) / lambda1 h = np.sqrt(alpha cl + 1) weights = computedualbasisinnerproduct(C, Mk) # F = Nlp + h sumk (weightsk Nkk) # weights: (H, W, D, 6), Nk: (H, W, D, 6) weightedNk = weights Nk sumk = np.sum(weightedNk, axis=3) F = Nlp + h sumk return F def visualize(Nout, eigenvalues, eigenvectors): """ Computes opacity and color for volume rendering. Nout: (H, W, D) eigenvalues: (H, W, D, 3) eigenvectors: (H, W, D, 3, 3) Returns: opacity: (H, W, D) color: (H, W, D, 3) """ lambda1 = eigenvalues[:,:,:, 0] lambda2 = eigenvalues[:,:,:, 1] e1 = eigenvectors[:,:,:,:, 0] # (H, W, D, 3) cl = (lambda1 - lambda2) / lambda1 opacity = Nout cl # Color = Nout ( (1,1,1) + e1) / 2 ones = np.ones((H, W, D, 3)) color = Nout[:,:,:, np.newaxis] (ones + e1) / 2.0 return opacity, color tensorfield = loadtensorfield() # Shape (H, W, D, 3, 3) eigenvalues, eigenvectors = computeeigendecomposition(tensorfield) x = generategaussiannoise((H, W, D)) # (H, W, D, 3) Sigmax = eigenvalues x # (H, W, D, 3) y = np.einsum('...ij,...j->...i', eigenvectors, Sigmax) N = np.linalg.norm(y, axis=3) # (H, W, D) icosahedronvertices = geticosahedronvertices() # (6, 3) Nlp, Nk = decomposenoisefield(N, icosahedronvertices) Mk = computedualbasisforicosahedron(icosahedronvertices) # (6, 3, 3) alpha = 1.0 # Not given in sources, placeholder J = 20 currentNlp = Nlp currentNk = Nk for j in range(J): F = adaptivefilteriteration(currentNlp, currentNk, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, alpha, Mk) # Decompose F for next iteration # Note: The source says "using the output noise field from the previous iteration as input" # It implies we re-decompose F into low-pass and high-pass components currentNlp, currentNk = decomposenoisefield(F, icosahedronvertices) Nout = currentNlp + np.sum(currentNk, axis=3) # Final output is the filtered field, which is effectively the sum of components if we consider the full reconstruction, but the source defines F as the output. Nout = F opacity, color = visualize(Nout, eigenvalues, eigenvectors) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Degenerate Tensors: If \lambda1 = 0, the linearity coefficient cl is undefined (division by zero). The sources do not specify a guard for this case. Zero Eigenvalues: If \lambda2 = 0, the control tensor computation involves division by zero. The sources do not specify a guard for this case. Precision: The iterative filtering process may accumulate numerical errors. The sources do not specify precision requirements. Boundary Conditions: The spherical separable filters require handling of volume boundaries. The sources do not specify boundary conditions. Transforms tensors into scalar metrics (e.g., FA, MD) for visualization. Chosen when a single scalar value per voxel is sufficient to represent diffusion characteristics, rather than a full field correlation. Tensor-to-Metric Transformation Computes a scalar measure of diffusion magnitude. Chosen for quantifying overall diffusion intensity, ignoring directionality. Apparent Diffusion Coefficient (ADC) Reconstructs the diffusion orientation distribution function (ODF) using spherical harmonics. Chosen when high angular resolution is needed to resolve crossing fibers, rather than a simple anisotropic noise correlation. Diffusion Tensor Reconstruction via Spherical Harmonics Time Complexity: The method involves spectral decomposition per voxel (O(1) per voxel), noise generation (O(N)), and J iterations of filtering. Each filtering iteration involves decomposing the noise field into 7 components (1 low-pass, 6 high-pass) and computing inner products. The complexity is dominated by the filtering operations, which are convolution-like. With J iterations, the time complexity is O(J \cdot N \cdot K), where N is the number of voxels and K is the filter kernel size. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the tensor field, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, noise fields (N{lp}, Nk), and intermediate results. Memory usage is O(N) for the tensor field and O(N) for the noise fields. Measured Performance: The method was applied to a 128^3 voxel volume resampled from 3 Tesla DT-MRI data with original resolution 0.86 \times 5 \times 0.86 mm. The resulting volume was rendered in real time. Strengths: Not sensitive to occlusion, does not depend on starting points, provides a continuous scalar field representation, handles non-linear diffusion better than streamlines or LIC. Limitations: Requires iterative filtering which can be computationally expensive. The quality of the visualization depends on the choice of parameters (\alpha, J). The method assumes the diffusion tensor accurately represents the underlying tissue structure. When to Use: When a continuous, occlusion-resistant visualization of fiber tracts is needed, and computational resources allow for iterative filtering. When Not to Use: When real-time performance on very large datasets is critical and iterative filtering is too slow, or when directional information beyond the primary eigenvector is needed (e.g., crossing fibers). The method was proposed by researchers from Valladolid, Spain, and Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston. It builds on the concept of adaptive filtering [1, 3] and was previously used to visualize strain-rate tensors in cardiac studies [2]. The specific application to diffusion tensor visualization aims to overcome limitations of glyphs, streamlines, and line integral convolution, such as occlusion sensitivity and dependence on starting points. The work was funded by the Swedish Research Council, the Swedish Heart and Lung Foundation, NIH grant P41-RR13218, and CIMIT. name: Tensor-to-Metric Transformation
head: Metric Tensor Mapping, Metric Tensor Visualization, Tensor Field to Metric Mapping
body: Tensor-to-Metric Transformation is a global visualization method for symmetric second-order tensor fields (e.g., stress, strain, or symmetric gradient) that interprets the tensor as a distortion of a flat metric. It transforms the tensor field into a metric tensor field, which is then visualized using a texture resembling fabric, where eigenvalues control texture density (compression vs. expansion) and eigenvectors control alignment. Unlike traditional icon and hyperstreamline methods that focus on eigendirections and neglect eigenvalues, and unlike probe-based methods that reduce the tensor to a vector via inner product, this method explicitly integrates the sign of the eigenvalues to distinguish compression from expansion. Unlike isometric embedding which is restricted to 2D and local, this method provides a global representation using texture deformation. The method maps a symmetric tensor field T to a metric tensor field g and visualizes g using Line Integral Convolution (LIC). Input: A symmetric second-order tensor field T(\mathbf{x}) defined on a domain D \subset \mathbb{R}^3 (or \mathbb{R}^2). Output: A composite image representing the tensor field as a fabric-like texture. Tensor Field: Stored as a 3x3 symmetric matrix at each grid point, containing 6 independent components. Eigen Decomposition: At each point, T is decomposed into real eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 and an orthogonal eigenvector matrix U = [\mathbf{w}1, \mathbf{w}2, \mathbf{w}3]. Noise Texture: A sparse noise image (spots) with parameters: base density d0, base radius r0, and base convolution length l0. 1. Diagonalization: For each point \mathbf{P} \in D, compute the eigenvalues \lambdai and eigenvectors \mathbf{w}i of T(\mathbf{P}). Construct the orthogonal matrix U where columns are \mathbf{w}i. Compute the diagonal tensor T0: T0 = U \cdot T \cdot U^T = \text{diag}(\lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3) 2. Transformation and Scaling: Define a positive monotone function F: [-\lambda{\max}, \lambda{\max}] \to \mathbb{R}^+, where \lambda{\max} = \max{\mathbf{P} \in D, i} |\lambdai(\mathbf{P})|. Compute the diagonal metric g0 in the eigenvector basis: g0 = \text{diag}(F(\lambda1), F(\lambda2), F(\lambda3)) 3. Inverse Diagonalization: Transform g0 back to the original coordinate system to obtain the final metric tensor g: g = U^T \cdot g0 \cdot U 4. LIC Parameter Encoding: For each eigenvector field \mathbf{w}i, generate an LIC image. The eigenvalues \lambdaj (where j \neq i) and \lambdai control the texture parameters: Density (di): Controls spots per unit area. Compression orthogonal to fibers increases density. In 2D: di(\lambda) = d0 \cdot \frac{ci}{F(\lambdaj)}, where c1=1/2, c2=1 and j is the orthogonal index. In 3D: d{i,j}(\lambda) = d0 / F(\lambdaj) for direction \mathbf{w}j. Spot Size (r{i,j}): Controls fiber width. In 3D: r{i,j} = r0 / d{i,j}. Convolution Length (li): Controls fiber length along \mathbf{w}i. li = l0 \cdot F(\lambdai). Color Intensity (Ii): Enhances compression/stretching impression. Red for compression (smallest negative eigenvalues), white for zero eigenvalues, green for tension (positive eigenvalues). 5. Integration and Rendering: Integrate integral curves for each eigenvector field \mathbf{w}i using 4th-order Runge-Kutta. Compute the LIC image for each \mathbf{w}i using Fast-LIC, applying the encoded density, spot size, and convolution length. Overlay all resulting LIC images to produce the final fabric-like texture. Transformation Function F: F must ensure g is positive definite. Common forms: 1. Linear (Identity): F(\lambda) = a + \sigma \lambda. Valid if \sigma < a/\lambda{\max}. 2. Anti-symmetric Logarithmic: f(\lambda; c) = \log(c\lambda+1) for \lambda \ge 0, -\log(1-c\lambda) for \lambda < 0. F(\lambda) = a + \sigma f(\lambda). Valid if \sigma < a/\log(c\lambda{\max}+1). 3. Asymptotic Arc-tangent: f(\lambda; c) = \arctan(c\lambda). F(\lambda) = a + \sigma f(\lambda). Valid if \sigma < 2a/\pi (independent of \lambda{\max}). 4. Non-symmetric Exponential: F(\lambda) = a \cdot \exp(\sigma f(\lambda)) with f(-\lambda)=-f(\lambda) (e.g., f(\lambda)=\arctan(c\lambda)). Always positive definite; \sigma is unlimited. Parameters: a: Unit length constant, F(0)=a. \sigma: Scaling factor (\sigma \neq 0). c: Sharpness constant at \lambda=0. d0: Unit density. r0: Base spot radius. l0: Base convolution length. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def tensortometricvisualization(tensorfield, gridshape, params): """ tensorfield: 3x3xNxNyNz array of symmetric tensors gridshape: tuple (Nx, Ny, Nz) params: dict with a, sigma, c, d0, r0, l0 """ # 1. Compute lambdamax over the entire domain lambdamax = 0.0 for x in range(gridshape[0]): for y in range(gridshape[1]): for z in range(gridshape[2]): T = tensorfield[:,:, x, y, z] eigenvalues = np.linalg.eigvalsh(T) for lam in eigenvalues: if abs(lam) > lambdamax: lambdamax = abs(lam) # 2. Define transformation function F def F(lam): # Non-symmetric exponential transformation (always positive definite) flam = math.atan(params['c'] lam) return params['a'] math.exp(params['sigma'] flam) # 3. Precompute metric eigenvalues and eigenvector fields metricfield = np.zeros((3, gridshape[0], gridshape[1], gridshape[2])) eigenvectorfields = [np.zeros((3, gridshape[0], gridshape[1], gridshape[2])) for in range(3)] for x in range(gridshape[0]): for y in range(gridshape[1]): for z in range(gridshape[2]): T = tensorfield[:,:, x, y, z] eigenvalues, U = np.linalg.eigh(T) for i in range(3): eigenvectorfields[i][:, x, y, z] = U[:, i] metricfield[:, x, y, z] = np.array([F(lam) for lam in eigenvalues]) # 4. Generate and overlay LIC images for each eigenvector field outputimage = np.zeros(gridshape[:2]) for i in range(3): j = (i + 1) % 3 k = (i + 2) % 3 # Compute texture parameters per point densitymap = params['d0'] / metricfield[j,:,:,:] spotsizemap = params['r0'] / densitymap lengthmap = params['l0'] metricfield[i,:,:,:] # Generate LIC image along eigenvector field i licimage = np.zeros(gridshape[:2]) # Fast-LIC integration using 4th-order Runge-Kutta for x in range(gridshape[0]): for y in range(gridshape[1]): # Trace integral curve using RK4 with step size modulated by lengthmap[x, y] # Sample noise texture with density and spot size modulated by densitymap[x, y], spotsizemap[x, y] # Convolve noise along curve using standard Fast-LIC kernel (implementation not given in sources) pass outputimage += licimage return outputimage Positive Definiteness: The metric g must be positive definite. If using symmetric transformations (Linear, Log, Arctan), \sigma must be constrained relative to \lambda{\max} and a. Failure to do so results in invalid metrics. Cluttering in 3D: Extending the method to 3D can cause visual cluttering due to the overlay of three LIC images. Noise Type: Standard white noise lacks flexibility for eigenvalue encoding. Sparse noise (lower density, larger spots) is required, which reduces resolution. Sign Distinction: Unlike isometric embedding or standard LIC, this method distinguishes positive and negative eigenvalues. Ensure F is not even (e.g., F(\lambda) = \lambda^2) as this would map compression and expansion to the same metric value. A variant that explicitly maps eigenvalues to texture parameters (density, spot size, convolution length, color intensity) to represent compression/expansion, treating the tensor as a distortion of a flat metric. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Evaluated on real finite element data sets of stress fields from applying load combinations to a solid block (ten-by-ten-by-ten grid). Fast-LIC implementation ensures efficiency. Strengths: Global view, intuitive distinction of compression/expansion, preserves topology. Limitations: 3D cluttering, lower resolution due to sparse noise, requires careful tuning of \sigma for symmetric F. Origin: Introduced by Hotz et al. in 2004/2005. History: Builds on Line Integral Convolution (LIC) introduced by Cabral and Leedom in 1993. Fast-LIC was proposed by Stalling and Hege in 1995. Usage: Applied to geomechanics, solid state physics, and Earth science data. name: Eigenvalue-Driven Texture Parameterization for LIC
head: LIC with eigenvalue-dependent parameters, Metric-based LIC parameterization, Metric-based Texture Parameter Mapping for Tensor Field Visualization, Physical tensor visualization via metric distortion, Tensor field LIC with eigenvalue scaling
body: This method visualizes symmetric second-order tensor fields (e.g., stress, strain) by interpreting the tensor as a distortion of a flat metric, mapping eigenvalues to Line Integral Convolution (LIC) texture parameters. Unlike standard LIC which uses constant parameters, this approach varies density, spot size, and convolution length based on eigenvalues to encode physical compression and expansion, providing an intuitive representation similar to stress/strain fields. It builds on Tensor-to-Metric Transformation by defining specific parameter assignments for 2D and 3D eigenvector fields. Inputs: A symmetric second-order tensor field T(\mathbf{x}) defined on a grid. Outputs: A textured image or volume where texture properties (density, spot size, convolution length, color) vary according to the local eigenvalues of T. Data Structures: The tensor field is stored as a grid of symmetric 3 \times 3 matrices (3D) or 2 \times 2 matrices (2D). For each point, the eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2 (and \lambda3 for 3D) and corresponding eigenvectors are computed. The eigenvectors define the integral line directions for LIC. Steps: 1. Eigen Decomposition: At each grid point, calculate the eigenvalues \lambdai and eigenvectors \mathbf{v}i of the tensor field. 2. Base LIC Generation: Generate an initial LIC image using constant density, spot size, color intensity, and convolution length. 3. Parameter Mapping: Adjust the texture parameters for each eigenvector field i based on the eigenvalues using the assignments in Table 1 (2D) or Table 2 (3D). Spot Radius: The radius r{i,j} changes proportionally to eigenvalues. For 2D, circular spots are defined by radius ri. The formula is: r{i,j} = r0 \frac{d{i,j}}{di} where r0 is a base radius, d{i,j} is a distance parameter, and di is a normalization factor. Convolution Length: The filter length li is proportional to a function of the eigenvalue, representing stretching/compressing along integral lines. The formula is: li = l0 \times F(\bar{\lambda}i) where l0 is a base length and F is a mapping function. Color Intensity: To enforce the impression of stretching/compressing along fibers, color intensity Ii is modified. The formula is: Ii = I0 \cdot \frac{1}{\lambdai} where I0 is a base intensity. Color Mapping: A continuous color code is applied: Red for smallest negative eigenvalues (compression), White for zero eigenvalues (no change), and Green for positive eigenvalues (expansion/tension). 4. Animation (Optional): To intensify the impression of expansion or compression, scale a factor \sigma or use a time variable t to animate the parameter changes. Parameter Assignments: The following tables define the mapping of eigenvalues to texture parameters for 2D and 3D fields. Table 1: 2D Parameter Assignments | Eigenvector Field | Density d{i,j} | Color Intensity Ii | Convolution Length li | Spot Size r{i,j} | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | i=1 | 1/\lambda2 | 1/\lambda1 | 1/\lambda1 | 1/\lambda2 | | i=2 | 1/\lambda1 | 1/\lambda2 | 1/\lambda2 | 1/\lambda1 | Table 2: 3D Parameter Assignments | Eigenvector Field | Density d{i,j} | Density d{i,k} | Color Intensity Ii | Convolution Length li | Spot Size r{i,j} | Spot Size r{i,k} | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | i=1 | 1/\lambda2 | 1/\lambda2 | 1/\lambda1 | \lambda1/\lambda2 | 1/\lambda1 | 1/\lambda1 | | i=2 | \lambda1/\lambda2 | \lambda3/\lambda1 | 1/\lambda2 | \lambda2/\lambda3 | 1/\lambda2 | 1/\lambda3 | | i=3 | 1/\lambda1 | 1/\lambda1 | 1/\lambda3 | \lambda3/\lambda1 | 1/\lambda3 | 1/\lambda1 | Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: tensorfield: 3D array of symmetric tensors (or 2D for 2D case). baseradius: Initial spot radius r0. baselength: Initial convolution length l0. baseintensity: Initial color intensity I0. Returns: resultimage: The final textured image. """ dim = tensorfield.shape[-1] eigenvalues, eigenvectors = computesymmetriceigendecomposition(tensorfield) # Standard LIC generation with constant parameters baselic = standardlic(eigenvectors, density=1.0, spotradius=baseradius, convolutionlength=baselength, colorintensity=baseintensity) resultimage = baselic.copy() for i in range(dim): lam = eigenvalues[..., i] if dim == 2: if i == 0: densityfactor = 1.0 / eigenvalues[..., 1] spotfactor = 1.0 / eigenvalues[..., 1] convfactor = 1.0 / eigenvalues[..., 0] intensityfactor = 1.0 / eigenvalues[..., 0] else: densityfactor = 1.0 / eigenvalues[..., 0] spotfactor = 1.0 / eigenvalues[..., 0] convfactor = 1.0 / eigenvalues[..., 1] intensityfactor = 1.0 / eigenvalues[..., 1] else: if i == 0: densityfactorj = 1.0 / eigenvalues[..., 1] densityfactork = 1.0 / eigenvalues[..., 1] spotfactorj = 1.0 / eigenvalues[..., 0] spotfactork = 1.0 / eigenvalues[..., 0] convfactor = eigenvalues[..., 0] / eigenvalues[..., 1] intensityfactor = 1.0 / eigenvalues[..., 0] elif i == 1: densityfactorj = eigenvalues[..., 0] / eigenvalues[..., 1] densityfactork = eigenvalues[..., 2] / eigenvalues[..., 0] spotfactorj = 1.0 / eigenvalues[..., 1] spotfactork = 1.0 / eigenvalues[..., 2] convfactor = eigenvalues[..., 1] / eigenvalues[..., 2] intensityfactor = 1.0 / eigenvalues[..., 1] else: densityfactorj = 1.0 / eigenvalues[..., 0] densityfactork = 1.0 / eigenvalues[..., 0] spotfactorj = 1.0 / eigenvalues[..., 2] spotfactork = 1.0 / eigenvalues[..., 0] convfactor = eigenvalues[..., 2] / eigenvalues[..., 0] intensityfactor = 1.0 / eigenvalues[..., 2] currentradius = baseradius spotfactor currentlength = baselength convfactor currentintensity = baseintensity intensityfactor currentdensity = densityfactor # Standard LIC generation for single eigenvector field with modified parameters componentlic = standardlic(eigenvectors[..., i], currentdensity, currentradius, currentlength, currentintensity) resultimage = resultimage + componentlic # Map eigenvalues to colors: red for negative, white for zero, green for positive resultimage = applycolormapping(resultimage, eigenvalues) return resultimage def computesymmetriceigendecomposition(tensorfield): # Post-processing: assign RGB based on eigenvalue sign/magnitude pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Discontinuities: The tensor field resulting from finite element simulations is continuous inside cells but not on cell boundaries. name: Apparent Diffusion Coefficient (ADC)
body: The Apparent Diffusion Coefficient (ADC) is a scalar quantity describing the diffusion along a specific direction vector \mathbf{v}, derived directly from the diffusion tensor \mathbf{D}. Unlike rotationally invariant metrics such as Mean Diffusivity (MD) or Fractional Anisotropy (FA) that summarize the entire tensor, ADC is direction-dependent, quantifying diffusion intensity along a chosen axis. It provides a direct tensor-based scalar for directional analysis, distinct from shape-domain metrics like linear or planar certainty. Inputs: 1. \mathbf{D}: A 3 \times 3 symmetric diffusion tensor at a specific voxel location. 2. \mathbf{v}: A direction vector along which the diffusion is to be measured. Outputs: 1. a{\mathbf{v}}: A scalar value representing the Apparent Diffusion Coefficient along \mathbf{v}. Data Structures: The diffusion tensor \mathbf{D} is stored as a 3 \times 3 matrix. Due to symmetry, only 6 unique values are required, but the formula operates on the full matrix representation: \mathbf{D} = \begin{bmatrix} D{xx} & D{xy} & D{xz} \\ D{yx} & D{yy} & D{yz} \\ D{zx} & D{zy} & D{zz} \end{bmatrix} where D{ij} = D{ji}. The direction vector \mathbf{v} is a 3-element vector: \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} vx \\ vy \\ vz \end{bmatrix} Steps: 1. Normalize the direction vector \mathbf{v} to unit length. 2. Compute the quadratic form a{\mathbf{v}} = \mathbf{v}^T \mathbf{D} \mathbf{v}. Formula: The ADC along direction \mathbf{v} is defined as: a{\mathbf{v}} = \mathbf{v}^T \mathbf{D} \mathbf{v} Expanding this into component form: a{\mathbf{v}} = D{xx}vx^2 + D{yy}vy^2 + D{zz}vz^2 + 2D{xy}vxvy + 2D{xz}vxvz + 2D{yz}vyvz Parameters: \mathbf{v}: A normalized direction vector. \mathbf{D}: The diffusion tensor. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Critical Points: If the diffusion tensor \mathbf{D} has two equal eigenvalues, it is a critical point and the eigenvectors are not uniquely defined. The ADC calculation remains numerically stable, but the choice of \mathbf{v} becomes sensitive to noise if derived from eigenvectors at these points. Normalization: The formula assumes \mathbf{v} is a unit vector. If \mathbf{v} is not normalized, the result scales with the square of the vector's magnitude, leading to incorrect physical interpretations. Tensor Validity: The tensor \mathbf{D} must be positive semi-definite. In practice, noise in DTI acquisition can lead to non-positive-definite tensors, which may result in negative ADC values for certain directions. Clamping or tensor regularization may be required before computation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeadc(tensorD, directionv): # tensorD is a 3x3 matrix (list of lists or array) # directionv is a 3-element vector vx, vy, vz = directionv normsq = vxvx + vyvy + vzvz if normsq == 0.0: return 0.0 invnorm = 1.0 / (normsq 0.5) vx, vy, vz = vx invnorm, vy invnorm, vz invnorm Dxx, Dxy, Dxz = tensorD[0] Dyx, Dyy, Dyz = tensorD[1] Dzx, Dzy, Dzz = tensorD[2] return (Dxx vxvx + Dyy vyvy + Dzz vzvz + 2.0 Dxy vx vy + 2.0 Dxz vx vz + 2.0 Dyz vy vz) FA is a scalar metric quantifying the degree of anisotropy in a voxel based solely on the diffusion tensor's eigenvalues. It distinguishes directional structures from isotropic environments where Mean Diffusivity is insufficient. Unlike higher-order anisotropy measures, FA is rotationally invariant but ignores higher-order tensor components, making it noise-sensitive for single-tensor data. Choose FA when a single rotationally invariant scalar is needed to quantify anisotropy magnitude, rather than directional diffusion values. Not given in the sources. The Apparent Diffusion Coefficient (ADC) is defined directly from the diffusion tensor \mathbf{D}. Basser et al. [BP96] introduced several rotationally invariant anisotropy metrics, such as fractional anisotropy, which measure the degree of anisotropy in a given voxel. The diffusion tensor can be interpreted as an ellipsoid describing the shape to which water diffuses from a given point in a given time. name: Fractional Anisotropy (FA)
body: Fractional Anisotropy (FA) is a scalar metric that quantifies the degree of anisotropy in a voxel based solely on the eigenvalues of the diffusion tensor. It solves the problem of distinguishing directional diffusion structures from isotropic environments where Apparent Diffusion Coefficient (ADC) alone is insufficient. Unlike higher-order anisotropy measures, FA is rotationally invariant but ignores higher-order tensor components, making it sensitive to noise when only a single tensor is available. Inputs: D: A 3 \times 3 symmetric positive-definite diffusion tensor. \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3: The three eigenvalues of D. Outputs: FA: A scalar value in the range [0, 1]. Data Structures: The diffusion tensor D is stored as a 3 \times 3 symmetric matrix containing 6 unique components. Eigenvalues are computed via standard linear algebra routines (e.g., solving the characteristic polynomial or using the Jacobi eigenvalue algorithm for symmetric matrices). Steps: 1. Compute the Mean Diffusivity (MD) of the tensor: MD = \frac{1}{3} \sum{i=1}^3 \lambdai 2. Compute the sum of squared deviations from the mean: S{dev} = \sum{i=1}^3 (\lambdai - MD)^2 3. Compute the sum of squared eigenvalues: S{sq} = \sum{i=1}^3 \lambdai^2 4. Calculate FA using the following formula: FA = \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}} \sqrt{\frac{S{dev}}{S{sq}}} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computefractionalanisotropy(eigenvalues): """ Computes Fractional Anisotropy from the three eigenvalues of a diffusion tensor. Args: eigenvalues (list of float): [lambda1, lambda2, lambda3] Returns: float: FA value in [0, 1] """ # Ensure eigenvalues are non-negative (physical constraint for diffusion tensors) # Clamp negative eigenvalues to zero if numerical noise produces them, # as diffusion tensors must be positive semi-definite. lam = [max(0.0, l) for l in eigenvalues] # Step 1: Compute Mean Diffusivity (MD) md = sum(lam) / 3.0 # Step 2: Compute sum of squared deviations from mean sumsqdev = sum((l - md) 2 for l in lam) # Step 3: Compute sum of squared eigenvalues sumsqeig = sum(l 2 for l in lam) # Handle degenerate case where all eigenvalues are zero if sumsqeig == 0: return 0.0 # Step 4: Compute FA # Formula: sqrt(3/2) sqrt( sum((lambdai - MD)^2) / sum(lambdai^2)) fa = (3.0 / 2.0) 0.5 (sumsqdev / sumsqeig) 0.5 # Clamp to [0, 1] to handle floating point inaccuracies return max(0.0, min(1.0, fa)) Parameters: None. FA is a deterministic function of the tensor's eigenvalues. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noise Sensitivity: FA is calculated using only one tensor per voxel, making it prone to noise conditions. Isotropic Limit: If \lambda1 = \lambda2 = \lambda3, then FA = 0, representing perfect isotropic diffusion. Anisotropic Limit: If \lambda2 = \lambda3 = 0 and \lambda1 > 0, FA = 1, representing the hypothetical case of an infinite cylinder. Higher-Order Ignorance: FA does not reveal any information about higher-order components due to the orthogonality of tensors. Definition: A measure of anisotropy based on the ratio of energy in higher-order spherical harmonics to those of second order, used to indicate the influence of multiple directions in a voxel. Formula: FMI = \frac{\sum{l>2} \sum{m} |a^ml|^2}{\sum{m} |a^m2|^2} where a^ml are the spherical harmonic coefficients of order l and degree m. Pitfall: Instabilities occur when both tensor components of order two and higher orders are close to zero. This is handled by introducing a threshold on the overall energy for calculation. When to choose: Use FMI when analyzing voxels with complex fiber architectures (e.g., crossings) that cannot be captured by a single second-order tensor, unlike FA which assumes a single dominant direction. Time Complexity: O(1) per voxel, assuming eigenvalues are pre-computed. Eigenvalue decomposition of a 3 \times 3 symmetric matrix is constant time. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per voxel. Strengths: Rotationally invariant. Effective for distinguishing white matter (high FA) from cerebrospinal fluid (low FA, high MD). Limitations: Prone to noise. Cannot resolve multiple fiber orientations within a single voxel (partial volume effect). Does not capture higher-order diffusion structures. When to use: When visualizing or quantifying the integrity of coherent fiber bundles where a single dominant diffusion direction is assumed. When not to use: In regions with complex fiber crossings or when higher-order diffusion information is required. Fractional Anisotropy was introduced by Basser et al. [BP96] as a rotationally invariant anisotropy metric for diffusion tensor imaging. It is widely used in medical imaging and computer science to characterize tissue microstructure, particularly in the brain. The metric is derived from the eigenvalues of the diffusion tensor, which describes the magnitude and direction of water diffusion in biological tissues. name: Diffusion Tensor Definition
head: DTI Tensor
body: The Diffusion Tensor is a 3x3 symmetric positive-definite matrix that serves as the native measurement quantity in Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI), modeling the local anisotropic diffusion of water molecules in biological tissue. It is defined by three orthogonal eigenvectors and their corresponding eigenvalues, which geometrically represent the principal axes and magnitudes of a diffusion ellipsoid. This definition distinguishes the tensor from scalar metrics like the Apparent Diffusion Coefficient (ADC) or derived visualizations such as those using Random Field Correlation, by providing the full second-order directional information required for fiber tracking. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3x3 symmetric diffusion tensor D at a specific voxel location in Cartesian space. Output: Three eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 (where \lambda1 \ge \lambda2 \ge \lambda3 \ge 0) and three corresponding unit eigenvectors v{\lambda1}, v{\lambda2}, v{\lambda3}. Data Structures The tensor D is stored as a 3x3 matrix: D = \begin{bmatrix} D{xx} & D{xy} & D{xz} \\ D{xy} & D{yy} & D{yz} \\ D{xz} & D{yz} & D{zz} \end{bmatrix} Due to symmetry, only 6 unique values are stored. The eigenvalues and eigenvectors are typically stored as a vector of 3 floats for eigenvalues and a 3x3 matrix (or 3 vectors) for eigenvectors. Mathematical Definition and Properties The eigenvectors and eigenvalues are derived from the characteristic equation: \det(D - \lambda I) = 0 The resulting eigenvectors satisfy the following orthogonality conditions in Cartesian space: \langle v{\lambda1}, v{\lambda2} \rangle = \langle v{\lambda2}, v{\lambda3} \rangle = \langle v{\lambda1}, v{\lambda3} \rangle = 0 Additionally, the eigenvectors form a right-handed coordinate system, allowing the third eigenvector to be computed via the cross product of the first two: v{\lambda1} \times v{\lambda2} = v{\lambda3} This property reduces computational effort during reconstruction or visualization. Geometric Interpretation The tensor defines an ellipsoid where the eigenvectors represent the spanning radii and the eigenvalues represent the squared lengths of these radii, describing the shape to which water diffuses from a given point in a given time. Pitfalls and Edge Cases 1. Critical Points: A critical point occurs when two eigenvalues are equal (\lambdai = \lambdaj for i \neq j). At these points, the corresponding eigenvectors are not uniquely defined, and anisotropy measures (such as cl or cp) become zero. 2. Orientation Ambiguity: Eigenvectors are orientationless, meaning they define a direction but not a sign (i.e., v and -v are equivalent). This causes interpolation problems if adjacent voxels have contrary orientations, requiring sign-flipping algorithms to ensure continuity. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def decomposetensor(D): """ Decomposes a 3x3 symmetric diffusion tensor D into eigenvalues and eigenvectors. D is a list of lists or 2D array: [[Dxx, Dxy, Dxz], [Dxy, Dyy, Dyz], [Dxz, Dyz, Dzz]] """ # 1. Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors # Using a standard symmetric eigensolver (e.g., Jacobi method or QR algorithm) eigenvalues, eigenvectors = solvesymmetriceigen(D) # 2. Sort eigenvalues in descending order: lambda1 >= lambda2 >= lambda3 # Corresponding eigenvectors must be reordered to match indices = argsortdescending(eigenvalues) lambda1 = eigenvalues[indices[0]] lambda2 = eigenvalues[indices[1]] lambda3 = eigenvalues[indices[2]] v1 = eigenvectors[:, indices[0]] v2 = eigenvectors[:, indices[1]] v3 = eigenvectors[:, indices[2]] # 3. Enforce right-handed coordinate system using cross product # v1 x v2 should equal v3. If not, flip v3. crossproduct = cross(v1, v2) if dot(crossproduct, v3) < 0: v3 = negate(v3) # 4. Handle Critical Points # If lambda1 approx equals lambda2 or lambda2 approx equals lambda3, # the corresponding eigenvectors are not unique. # Implementation note: In practice, small perturbations or fallback # to principal axes of symmetry may be needed, but the definition # simply states they are not uniquely defined. return { "eigenvalues": [lambda1, lambda2, lambda3], "eigenvectors": [v1, v2, v3] } Tractography is the process of obtaining curves of neural pathways by extracting underlying continuous anatomical structures from diffusion tensor data. It uses streamlines, streamtubes, or surfsurfaces to trace paths through the tensor field, aligning the tracing direction with the principal eigenvector field (v{\lambda1}) to follow neural fibers. Complexity: Eigen decomposition of a 3x3 symmetric matrix is O(1) per voxel, but requires numerical stability checks for critical points. Strengths: Provides complete directional information; orthogonal eigenvectors simplify geometric interpretation and computation. Limitations: Ambiguity in eigenvector sign complicates interpolation and streamline integration; critical points (isotropy) break directional uniqueness. When to use: When full directional fiber architecture is required for visualization or tractography. When not to use: When only scalar diffusion magnitude is needed (use ADC) or when computational resources are extremely limited and only dominant direction is needed (though tensor is still small). Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) visualization relies on the mathematical definition of the diffusion tensor as a symmetric positive-definite matrix. The geometric interpretation of the tensor as an ellipsoid and the properties of its eigenvectors are foundational to scientific information visualization in medical imaging. The challenges of critical points and orientation ambiguity are well-documented in image-space tensor field visualization literature.
