name: Combined DTI/MRI Volume Rendering
head: Combined MRI and DTI Volume Rendering, Interactive Volume Rendering of Diffusion Tensor Data, Magic Lens Selection for DTI/MRI, Multi-modal volume rendering
body: Combined DTI/MRI Volume Rendering is a technique that integrates the visualization of conventional scalar-valued MRI (providing high-resolution gyral structure and blood vessels) with Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) data in a single volume rendering pass to aid surgical planning and navigation. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by restricting the diffusion tensor color map to the standard RGB model to avoid misleading color mixing, while using MRI data solely to highlight object boundaries via a grayscale transfer function. Unlike methods that apply different transfer functions to a single dataset, this approach selects different transfer functions on different modalities to build a combined image without distorting geometry. The method extends a standard GPU-based raycasting volume renderer to handle two distinct data modalities simultaneously. It relies on a single-pass rendering pipeline for interactive performance, utilizing a "magic lens" concept to allow interactive selection of the weighting between MRI context and DTI fiber data. Inputs: Scalar MRI volume data representing anatomical structures. DTI volume data representing diffusion tensors. A "magic lens" region (defined by position and size) that determines where DTI data is emphasized versus where MRI context is dominant. Outputs: A composite RGB image where DTI fibers are color-coded and MRI structures provide geometric context. The implementation uses a 3D texture-based approach for storing volume data. MRI Data: Stored as a 3D texture of scalar values. DTI Data: Stored as a 3D texture of tensor values. Transfer Functions: MRI Transfer Function: A 2D lookup table (LUT) mapping scalar value and gradient magnitude to opacity and grayscale color. DTI Transfer Function: Evaluated analytically on the GPU based on tensor properties (e.g., Fractional Anisotropy) and potentially MRI scalar values. Lighting Parameters: OpenGL light sources are repurposed to encode parameters for the transfer functions. Specifically, unused light sources (typically five or more in medical imaging where only one or two are used) provide global parameters like cut-off angle and exponent for smooth step functions. 1. Compute Stencil: Determine the spatial region of interest, often defined by the "magic lens" or clipping planes. 2. Compute Tensor Volume Rendering: Cast rays through the DTI volume, sample tensor values along the ray, compute color based on the principal eigenvector for directional coloring, and apply opacity based on FA. The tensor transfer function is evaluated analytically on the GPU to allow real-time manipulation without texture updates. 3. Compute Conventional MRI Overlay: Cast rays through the MRI volume, sample scalar values, apply a 2D grayscale transfer function based on value and gradient magnitude to highlight boundaries, and apply special material attributes and gradient-based shading to improve 3D perception of surfaces. 4. Composite: Combine the DTI rendering and MRI overlay in a single rendering pass. The magic lens allows the user to interactively adjust the weighting between the DTI fiber visualization and the MRI structural context. Tensor Color Mapping: The color C is derived from the principal eigenvector \vec{v} of the diffusion tensor \mathbf{D}. The specific mapping is restricted to the RGB model. Transfer Function Evaluation: MRI TF: T{MRI}(v, g) \rightarrow (r, g, b, \alpha), where v is scalar value and g is gradient magnitude. DTI TF: T{DTI}(tensor, v{MRI}) \rightarrow (r, g, b, \alpha). The sources note that 2D functions can be based on two scalar values, e.g., MRI signal and FA. Light Parameterization: Smooth step functions for transfer functions are parameterized using OpenGL light parameters: cut-off angle (\thetac) and exponent (e). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def generaterayfromcamera(pixel, cameraorigin, cameradirection, cameraup, cameraright, pixelspacing): """Generates a ray origin and direction for a given pixel.""" origin = cameraorigin direction = cameradirection + (pixel.x cameraright + pixel.y cameraup) pixelspacing return origin, direction / math.linalg.norm(direction) def sample3dtexture(volume, point): """Performs trilinear interpolation on a 3D texture.""" # Standard trilinear interpolation implementation return volume.interpolate(point) def computegradient(volume, point): """Computes gradient magnitude using central differences.""" # Standard central difference implementation dx = (sample3dtexture(volume, point + (1,0,0)) - sample3dtexture(volume, point - (1,0,0))) / 2 dy = (sample3dtexture(volume, point + (0,1,0)) - sample3dtexture(volume, point - (0,1,0))) / 2 dz = (sample3dtexture(volume, point + (0,0,1)) - sample3dtexture(volume, point - (0,0,1))) / 2 return math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) def computefractionalanisotropy(tensor): """Computes FA from a 3x3 symmetric tensor.""" # Standard FA formula using eigenvalues eigenvalues = math.linalg.eigvals(tensor) l1, l2, l3 = sorted(eigenvalues, reverse=True) numerator = math.sqrt(1.5) math.sqrt((l1-l2)2 + (l2-l3)2 + (l3-l1)2) denominator = math.sqrt(l12 + l22 + l32) return numerator / denominator if denominator > 1e-8 else 0.0 def getprincipaleigenvector(tensor): """Returns the eigenvector corresponding to the largest eigenvalue.""" # Standard eigenvector extraction eigenvalues, eigenvectors = math.linalg.eigh(tensor) return eigenvectors[:, math.argmax(eigenvalues)] def evaluatemritf(value, gradient): """Returns grayscale color and opacity based on 2D LUT lookup.""" # Standard 2D LUT mapping to grayscale (r=g=b) return (value, value, value, gradient) def evaluatedtitf(tensor, fa, lightparams): """Returns RGB color and opacity based on analytical evaluation.""" eigenvector = getprincipaleigenvector(tensor) color = (abs(eigenvector.x), abs(eigenvector.y), abs(eigenvector.z)) cutoff = lightparams['cutoffangle'] exponent = lightparams['exponent'] t = max(0.0, min(1.0, (fa - (1.0 - cutoff)) / cutoff)) opacity = t t (3 - 2 t) exponent return (color[0], color[1], color[2], opacity) def isinsidelens(point, lenscenter, lensradius): """Checks if a point is within the magic lens sphere.""" return math.linalg.norm(point - lenscenter) <= lensradius def fronttobackcomposite(acccolor, accalpha, newcolor, newalpha): """Performs standard front-to-back alpha compositing.""" outalpha = accalpha + newalpha (1.0 - accalpha) outcolor = ( acccolor[0] accalpha + newcolor[0] newalpha (1.0 - accalpha), acccolor[1] accalpha + newcolor[1] newalpha (1.0 - accalpha), acccolor[2] accalpha + newcolor[2] newalpha (1.0 - accalpha)) return outcolor, outalpha def rendercombineddtimri(mrivolume, dtivolume, lenscenter, lensradius, lightparams, cameraparams): """Renders a combined view of MRI and DTI data in a single pass.""" imagewidth, imageheight = 1920, 1080 image = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(imagewidth)] for in range(imageheight)] for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): rayorigin, raydirection = generaterayfromcamera((x, y), cameraparams) acccolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accalpha = 0.0 for t in range(0, 1000, 2): point = rayorigin + raydirection t if not mrivolume.contains(point): break mrival = sample3dtexture(mrivolume, point) mrigrad = computegradient(mrivolume, point) mritf = evaluatemritf(mrival, mrigrad) dtitensor = sample3dtexture(dtivolume, point) fa = computefractionalanisotropy(dtitensor) dtitf = evaluatedtitf(dtitensor, fa, lightparams) inlens = isinsidelens(point, lenscenter, lensradius) weightdti = 1.0 if inlens else 0.2 weightmri = 0.2 if inlens else 1.0 combinedcolor = ( mritf[0] weightmri + dtitf[0] weightdti, mritf[1] weightmri + dtitf[1] weightdti, mritf[2] weightmri + dtitf[2] weightdti) combinedalpha = (mritf[3] weightmri + dtitf[3] weightdti) 0.5 acccolor, accalpha = fronttobackcomposite(acccolor, accalpha, combinedcolor, combinedalpha) if accalpha > 0.99: break image[y][x] = (acccolor[0] / max(accalpha, 1e-8), acccolor[1] / max(accalpha, 1e-8), acccolor[2] / max(accalpha, 1e-8), accalpha) return image Gray/White Matter Interface: There is an area of approximately two to three millimeters in the outer gyri where streamline tracking algorithms fail due to ambiguity of tensor information at the interface between gray and white matter. Volume rendering combined with cortex extraction shows the limits of these algorithms. Misleading Line Structures: Pre-computed line structures (streamlines) can be misleading because they are often started and stopped based on parameters like FA, implying single lines with defined start and end points. Color Model Restriction: The diffusion tensor color map is restricted to the RGB model. Introducing additional colors from MRI would be misleading. Performance: The method provides interactive frame rates on a full-screen application. Scalability: The speed of the algorithm is independent of the size of the magic lens. No change in frame rate was experienced for different sizes of DTI and MRI data sets. Strengths: Context-preserving visualization: MRI provides gyral structure and blood vessels, while DTI provides fiber connectivity. Interactive: The magic lens allows real-time adjustment of the weighting between modalities. Single-pass rendering: Efficient compositing of both datasets. Limitations: MRI data is volume rendered only to highlight boundaries of objects using a standard 2D grayscale transfer function. Gradient computation can be performed either on the GPU or on the CPU, depending on the available graphics board or user choice. This method was developed to address the limitations of pseudo-colored slices and fiber tracking algorithms in neuro-surgery and brain connectivity research. It specifically targets the need to understand neural fiber connectivity in brain gyri while maintaining the anatomical context provided by conventional MRI. It was applied to study conditions like Deletion 22q Syndrome, characterized by increased FA and ADC in certain brain areas. The approach contrasts with earlier methods like Wang et al. [WZMK05] by using separate transfer functions for separate modalities rather than modifying a single dataset's transfer function. Interactive Volume Rendering of Diffusion Tensor Data, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-88378-48, fetched 2026-10-26 (book)

name: Scalarization of Vector Fields
head: Scalar Field Rendering from Vector Fields
body: Scalarization of Vector Fields converts multi-component vector data into single-component scalar fields to enable standard volume rendering or surface extraction techniques. It sets itself apart from direct vector visualization methods (like Stream Lines) by projecting the vector information onto a scalar metric, allowing the use of established transfer functions for opacity and color mapping. All methods in this family evaluate a mapping function M(\mathbf{x}) at sample points \mathbf{x} within the volume to produce visual attributes. The core mechanism involves sampling the multi-component data field at \mathbf{x}, decomposing or normalizing the value (e.g., extracting magnitude, direction, eigenvalues, or phase), and applying a transfer function or geometric construction to map these features to rendering parameters such as color, opacity, or primitive geometry. Helicity Visualization is a scalarization technique for vector fields that maps the dot product of velocity and vorticity to opacity and color to identify vortices. It sets itself apart from siblings like Metric Scalar Field Rendering from Vector Fields by explicitly leveraging the alignment between flow direction and local rotation (curl) to highlight swirling features, whereas metric methods often rely on magnitude or strain. See Helicity Visualization. Metric Scalar Field Rendering converts vector field data into scalar values to enable standard surface or volume rendering techniques. It solves the problem of visualizing vector fields, which lack a single intensity value, by calculating metrics such as velocity magnitude, vorticity, or divergence. It differs from Helicity Visualization by focusing on general magnitude-based scalarization rather than the specific alignment of curl and velocity. See Metric Scalar Field Rendering from Vector Fields. Definition: Visualizing specific components of the velocity field (e.g., x-component) to identify flow separation and reversal. Step: Map the smallest x velocity values (including negative values) to cyan and high opacity. Map the largest x velocity components to yellow and near transparency. The technique originated in early computational fluid dynamics (CFD) visualization research. Volume Rendering for Computational Fluid Dynamics: Initial Results (1991) demonstrated the use of scalarization to visualize perturbation velocity fields, specifically mapping negative x-components to cyan to highlight flow separation from surfaces. name: Helicity Visualization
head: Helicity Calculation
body: Helicity Visualization maps the scalar helicity field to color and opacity to identify vortices and their rotation direction in fluid flows. It sets itself apart from siblings like Metric Scalar Field Rendering from Vector Fields by explicitly utilizing the directional relationship between velocity and vorticity (via the dot product) rather than just magnitude or eigenvalues, allowing for the distinction of vortex chirality through signed color mapping. Inputs: Velocity field \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}) = (u, v, w) defined on a grid. Vorticity field \boldsymbol{\omega}(\mathbf{x}) = \nabla \times \mathbf{F}. Outputs: Color C(\mathbf{x}) and Opacity \alpha(\mathbf{x}) for each sample point. Data Structures: The helicity scalar field h(\mathbf{x}) is computed per voxel. Transfer function T(h) maps scalar value to (R, G, B, \alpha). Steps: 1. Compute Vorticity: Calculate the curl of the velocity field at each grid point \mathbf{x}: \boldsymbol{\omega}(\mathbf{x}) = \nabla \times \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}) 2. Compute Helicity: Calculate the dot product of the velocity and vorticity vectors: h(\mathbf{x}) = \boldsymbol{\omega}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}) This scalar represents the curl in the direction of the velocity. 3. Map Opacity: Map the magnitude of helicity |h(\mathbf{x})| to opacity \alpha: Large magnitude \rightarrow High opacity (opaque). Small magnitude \rightarrow Near transparency. 4. Map Color: Map the signed value of helicity h(\mathbf{x}) to color: Extreme negative values \rightarrow Cyan. Extreme positive values \rightarrow Magenta. Values near zero \rightarrow Yellow. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computehelicityvisualization(velocityfield): """ velocityfield: 3D array of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz, 3) containing (u, v, w) Returns: 4D array of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz, 4) containing (R, G, B, alpha) """ # 1. Compute Vorticity (Curl of Velocity) # Using central differences for gradient approximation # omega = (dw/dy - dv/dz, du/dz - dw/dx, dv/dx - du/dy) vorticity = computecurl(velocityfield) # 2. Compute Helicity (Dot Product) # h = omega. F # Element-wise dot product of velocity and vorticity arrays helicity = sum(v w for v, w in zip(velocityfield, vorticity)) # 3. Initialize Output Buffer output = np.zeroslike(helicity, dtype=float) output = np.append(output, np.zeros((helicity.shape[0], helicity.shape[1], helicity.shape[2], 1)), axis=3) # 4. Apply Transfer Function for x in range(helicity.shape[0]): for y in range(helicity.shape[1]): for z in range(helicity.shape[2]): hval = helicity[x, y, z] magh = abs(hval) # Map Opacity based on magnitude # Large magnitude -> opaque, small -> transparent # Assuming a linear or sigmoidal mapping not explicitly defined in sources # Standard practice: alpha = sigmoid(magh scale) or normalized linear alpha = normalizemagnitudetoopacity(magh) # Map Color based on sign if hval > thresholdpositive: color = [1.0, 0.0, 1.0] # Magenta elif hval < thresholdnegative: color = [0.0, 1.0, 1.0] # Cyan else: color = [1.0, 1.0, 0.0] # Yellow output[x, y, z, 0] = color[0] output[x, y, z, 1] = color[1] output[x, y, z, 2] = color[2] output[x, y, z, 3] = alpha return output def computecurl(field): # Placeholder for standard finite difference curl implementation # Implementation detail: Central differences for interior points, # forward/backward for boundaries. pass def normalizemagnitudetoopacity(mag): # Specific mapping function not provided in sources. # Typically involves normalization against max helicity in the domain. pass Parameters: Thresholds for "extreme" positive/negative and "near zero" are not explicitly defined in the sources. Scaling for opacity mapping is not specified. Edge Cases: Zero Velocity: If \mathbf{F} = 0, helicity is 0, resulting in yellow color and low opacity. Flow Reversal: Negative x-component values in velocity (flow reversal) are of particular interest as they indicate separation, which may result in negative helicity values mapped to cyan. Strengths: Effectively visualizes vortices and distinguishes their rotation direction (chirality) using color. It makes features like "lambda" shocks and vortex cores visible by mapping magnitude to opacity. Limitations: Requires accurate computation of both velocity and its curl (vorticity), which can be noisy in discrete data. The specific thresholds for color mapping are not standardized in the source material. Performance: Depends on the cost of computing the curl and the dot product per voxel. No specific hardware performance metrics are provided in the sources. Origin: The method is described in early CFD volume rendering work. History: Helicity is defined as the scalar function representing the curl in the direction of the velocity. It was used to visualize vortices generated by fins in flow fields, identifying features like the "lambda" shock. Usage: Used in Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) to isolate flow disturbances and identify vortices. name: Perturbation Velocity Visualization
head: Subtracting free stream velocity
body: Perturbation Velocity Visualization is a technique in Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) to isolate flow disturbances by making the bulk of irrelevant free stream flow invisible. It achieves this by mapping the magnitude of the perturbation velocity vector to opacity. This method sets itself apart from standard velocity visualization by explicitly removing the uniform background flow, thereby highlighting regions of interaction, such as wakes or boundary layers, which would otherwise be obscured by the high opacity of the free stream. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D velocity field \mathbf{V} and a constant free stream velocity vector \mathbf{V}{fs}. Output: A volume rendering where opacity is determined by the magnitude of the perturbation velocity. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Compute Perturbation Velocity: For every cell in the velocity field, subtract the free stream velocity vector from the local velocity vector to compute the perturbation velocity vector \mathbf{V}{pert}: \mathbf{V}{pert} = \mathbf{V} - \mathbf{V}{fs} 2. Calculate Magnitude: Compute the Euclidean norm (magnitude) of the resulting perturbation velocity vector: |\mathbf{V}{pert}| = \sqrt{u{pert}^2 + v{pert}^2 + w{pert}^2} 3. Map to Opacity: Map the calculated magnitude |\mathbf{V}{pert}| to the opacity value for volume rendering. Typically, a magnitude of zero (matching the free stream) results in zero opacity, making the free stream invisible, while non-zero magnitudes result in higher opacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeperturbationvelocityvisualization(velocityfield, freestreamvelocity): """ velocityfield: 3D array of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz, 3) containing (u, v, w) freestreamvelocity: tuple or array of length 3 (ufs, vfs, wfs) returns: 3D array of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz) containing opacity values """ # Step 1: Subtract free stream velocity upert = velocityfield[:,:,:, 0] - freestreamvelocity[0] vpert = velocityfield[:,:,:, 1] - freestreamvelocity[1] wpert = velocityfield[:,:,:, 2] - freestreamvelocity[2] # Step 2: Calculate magnitude magnitude = (upert2 + vpert2 + wpert2)0.5 # Step 3: Map magnitude to opacity # Sources do not specify the exact transfer function; typically maps magnitude to opacity. opacity = magnitude return opacity Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No-slip boundaries: At solid surfaces, the fluid velocity is zero relative to the surface due to viscosity. Consequently, the perturbation velocity at the boundary is equal to the negative of the free stream velocity (\mathbf{V}{pert} = -\mathbf{V}{fs}), resulting in a large magnitude. This requires separate treatment to avoid rendering the entire surface as highly opaque or distorting the visualization of the wake. This variant visualizes a specific component (typically the x-component) of the perturbation velocity field rather than its magnitude. Negative values of the perturbation velocity x-component indicate locations where the flow is slower than the free stream velocity. These negative values are mapped to cyan and high opacity, while positive values (faster than free stream) are mapped to yellow and near transparency. The transfer function uses the extreme values of the data field to set the scale and offset into the linear color space. This approach is useful for identifying flow reversal or regions of significant deceleration. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of cells in the volume, as it requires a single pass to compute the difference and magnitude. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the velocity field and the resulting opacity field. Strengths: Effectively removes the visual clutter of uniform free stream flow, allowing the viewer to focus on flow disturbances, wakes, and boundary layer interactions. Limitations: Requires accurate knowledge of the free stream velocity vector. It may obscure the absolute velocity magnitude, making it difficult to assess flow speed without the context of the free stream. When to use: When the primary interest is in flow structures caused by obstacles or interactions, rather than the absolute speed of the fluid. The method was introduced in the context of volume rendering for Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD). It was developed to address the challenge of visualizing vector fields where the dominant free stream flow obscures interesting features. The technique is part of a broader effort to apply volume rendering to CFD data, leveraging the ability to map scalar fields (like perturbation magnitude) to visual properties like opacity. name: Metric Scalar Field Rendering from Vector Fields
head: Vector Field Metric Extraction
body: Metric Scalar Field Rendering from Vector Fields solves the problem of visualizing vector field data (such as velocity or magnetic fields) using standard scalar rendering techniques like volume rendering or isosurface extraction, which inherently require single-value inputs. It differs from direct vector visualization methods (e.g., arrow glyphs or streamlines) by projecting the multi-component vector data into a scalar metric (e.g., magnitude, divergence, or curl) to leverage the perceptual depth and occlusion handling of volume rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A vector field \mathbf{F}(x,y,z) defined on a 3D grid, potentially time-dependent. Output: A scalar field S(x,y,z) derived from \mathbf{F}, used as input for a scalar renderer (volume raymarching or isosurface extraction). Data Structures: Vector Field Grid: A 3D array storing components (F1, F2, F3) at each voxel (i,j,k). Scalar Field Grid: A 3D array storing the computed metric value S at each voxel. Steps: 1. Metric Calculation: For each voxel (i,j,k), compute the desired scalar metric from the vector components. Common metrics include: Velocity Magnitude: |\mathbf{F}| = \sqrt{F1^2 + F2^2 + F3^2}. Divergence: \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = \frac{\partial F1}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial F2}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial F3}{\partial z}. Curl Magnitude: |\text{curl } \mathbf{F}|. 2. Temporal Interpolation (if time-dependent): If the data consists of discrete time slices, interpolate the vector values at the current time step t between the surrounding time slices t1 and t2 to support smooth animation. 3. Rendering: Pass the resulting scalar field to a standard scalar volume renderer or isosurface extractor. The renderer uses a transfer function to map scalar values to color and opacity. Formulas: Curl Vector: \text{curl } \mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial F3}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial F2}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial F1}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial F3}{\partial x} \\ \frac{\partial F2}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial F1}{\partial y} \end{pmatrix} Curl Magnitude: |\text{curl } \mathbf{F}(i,j,k)| = \sqrt{ \left(\frac{\partial F3}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial F2}{\partial z}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial F1}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial F3}{\partial x}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial F2}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial F1}{\partial y}\right)^2 } Parameters: Metric Type: Selection of magnitude, divergence, or curl. Interpolation Method: Linear or higher-order interpolation for time steps. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Derivatives required for curl and divergence are sensitive to grid boundaries. Not given in the sources how boundaries are handled. Loss of Directional Information: Scalarization discards the vector direction, which may be critical for interpreting flow topology. A specific metric extraction method that computes the magnitude of the curl of the vector field to highlight swirling features and vorticity (turbulent behavior). It is chosen when the visual goal is to identify regions of rotation or turbulence within the flow, distinguishing it from magnitude-based methods which show speed. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels, for the metric calculation. Rendering complexity depends on the underlying scalar renderer. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the derived scalar field. Strengths: Allows the use of mature scalar volume rendering techniques (e.g., raymarching) for vector data; provides immersive 3D views of internal structures. Limitations: Discards directional information; requires careful selection of the metric to avoid misleading representations; derivatives (curl/divergence) are noisy and sensitive to discretization. The method originates from interactive visual data analysis systems that needed to bridge the gap between vector field simulations and standard scalar rendering pipelines. It was developed to allow simultaneous visualization of scalar structures (like density) and vector-derived features (like vorticity). The curl magnitude metric is formally defined in the context of multi-dimensional transfer functions for 3D flow visualization. name: X13 Volume Rendering and Isosurface Plotting
head: 3D isosurface figures, GLMakie volume render
body: X13 is a post-processing script that generates 3D volume renders and isosurface plots of scalar fields derived from vector field data (specifically velocity components) using the GLMakie library in Julia. It solves the problem of visualizing 3D turbulent flow structures (such as streamwise vortices) that are lost when reducing simulation data to 2D slices. It is distinguished from its sibling method X12, which uses orthogonal cutting planes via matplotlib, by rendering through the volume using GPU raymarching, providing a more immersive view of internal structures at the cost of requiring an OpenGL context (hardware or software rasterized). Inputs and Outputs: Input: NetCDF or HDF5 files containing simulation snapshots. Fields include velocity components (u, v, w) and optional derived fields. Output: PNG images of 3D figures containing volume renders or isosurfaces. Data Structures: The script reads data into memory arrays. For HDF5 virtual datasets (from multi-GPU merges), the storage must be registered before reading to avoid KeyError. Grid data is assumed to be stored at cell centers for all velocity components, allowing direct gradient computation without staggered interpolation. Parameters: --field: Comma-separated list of fields to render. Single field layouts panels by mode (volume/isosurface); multiple fields layout by field. --mode: 'volume' or 'isosurface'. --overlay: Name of a reference field (e.g., 'b') to draw as contours on vertical bounding walls. --clim-percentile: Upper percentile for color range, default 99. --zlim: Z-cropping limit. Default 5 (wider than plotting scripts' 4) to allow centred differences. --cols: Number of columns in panel grid, default 3. --scale: Appends suffix to budget terms. Steps: 1. Initialization and Virtual Storage Handling: If the input file is an HDF5 virtual dataset, call allowvirtualstorage!() to register the storage code, preventing KeyError during read operations. 2. Data Loading and Cropping: Load the specified fields from the NetCDF/HDF5 file. Crop the z-dimension to the active layer defined by --zlim. Keep one cell of margin on each side of the cropped slab to maintain accuracy for centred differences. Note: Cropping before differentiation is critical to reduce memory usage. Cropping after differentiation causes memory peaks of 15–25 GB at Nz=1024. 3. Derivation of Scalar Fields: If the requested fields are not present in the file, derive them from the velocity components u, v, w. Common derived fields include: Q-criterion (Q): Second invariant of the velocity gradient tensor. Enstrophy: Magnitude squared of the vorticity vector. Speed: Magnitude of the velocity vector. Note: The file's own \omega is often only the spanwise component, which is insufficient for 3D structure analysis. All three velocities are at cell centers, so the gradient tensor is computed using centred differences on the single grid. 4. Gradient Computation: Compute the velocity gradient tensor \nabla \mathbf{u} using centred differences. In x and y (periodic boundaries): Use centred differences. In z (bounded boundaries): Use one-sided differences at the walls, matching the pipeline's treatment of the bounded axis. Formula for centred difference of a field f at index i: \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \approx \frac{f{i+1} - f{i-1}}{2 \Delta x} This requires the one-cell margin established in Step 2. 5. Isosurface Level Calculation: Set isosurface levels symmetrically around zero. For each desired magnitude level L, create a pair of levels [-L, L]. Log these levels for visibility (e.g., -0.0849, -0.0299, 0.0299, 0.0849). For positive-definite fields, clamp positive-field isosurface levels into the color range. The top level is set to the 0.995 quantile of the data, while the color range ends at the --clim-percentile (default 99) quantile to prevent saturation. 6. Figure Layout and Rendering: Panel Resolution: Set panel resolution to 820x560 per panel to accommodate the cropped domain aspect ratio (roughly 14:4.7:8). Camera Orientation: Set camera azimuth to 1.30\pi to orient the streamwise direction (x) across the frame width while keeping the spanwise direction (y) readable. Color Scaling: Use a fixed fraction of each panel's own range for isosurface levels: 0.18, 0.515, and 0.85. This ensures a surface means the same thing across panels. Use a symmetric:balance color scale for all panels, including positive-definite fields, leaving the lower half unused to indicate the quantity never changes sign. Overlay: If --overlay is specified, draw contours of the reference field on the two vertical bounding walls. This shows the location of flow structures (e.g., billows) relative to the isosurfaces. Do not use isosurfaces for the overlay, as transparency cannot separate interpenetrating isosurfaces in GLMakie (alpha is ignored on volume contours). 7. Batch Rendering Setup: For off-screen rendering on clusters without GPUs/displays, use Xvfb and Mesa software rasterizer (LIBGLALWAYSSOFTWARE=1). Start Xvfb on a free display, smoke-test the OpenGL context, render, and kill the server. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. function renderx13(inputfile, args): # 1. Handle HDF5 virtual datasets if ishdf5virtual(inputfile): allowvirtualstorage!() # 2. Load and crop data # Load u, v, w and requested fields data = loaddataset(inputfile, fields=args.field) # Crop z to active layer with margin for centred differences zlimit = args.zlim if args.zlim else 5 margin = 1 zstart = max(1, 1 + margin) zend = min(Nz, Nz - margin) # Crop before differentiation to save memory datacropped = cropz(data, zstart, zend) # 3. Derive fields if necessary if "Q" in args.field and "Q" not in datacropped: # Compute gradient tensor using centred differences # Periodic in x, y; one-sided at z walls gradu = computegradient(datacropped.u, datacropped.deltax, periodicx=True, periodicy=True, boundedz=True) gradv = computegradient(datacropped.v, datacropped.deltay, periodicx=True, periodicy=True, boundedz=True) gradw = computegradient(datacropped.w, datacropped.deltaz, periodicx=True, periodicy=True, boundedz=True) # Compute Q-criterion (example derivation) # Q = 0.5 (|omega|^2 - |S|^2) where omega is vorticity, S is strain rate vorticity = computevorticity(gradu, gradv, gradw) strain = computestrain(gradu, gradv, gradw) datacropped.Q = 0.5 (norm(vorticity)^2 - norm(strain)^2) # 4. Calculate isosurface levels levels = [] for magnitude in desiredmagnitudes: levels.append(-magnitude) levels.append(magnitude) # Clamp positive fields if ispositivedefinite(field): toplevelquantile = quantile(fielddata, 0.995) climpercentile = args.climpercentile # default 99 climlimit = quantile(fielddata, climpercentile / 100.0) # Ensure levels are within clim range levels = [l for l in levels if abs(l) <= climlimit] # 5. Render fig = Figure(resolution=(820 cols, 560 rows)) for panelindex, fieldname in enumerate(args.field): ax = Axis3(fig[panelindex]) # Set camera azimuth ax.camera.azimuth = 1.30 pi # Draw isosurfaces or volume if args.mode == "isosurface": # Use symmetric levels drawisosurfaces(ax, datacropped[fieldname], levels=levels, colorscale=:balance, symmetric=true) else: drawvolume(ax, datacropped[fieldname]) # Overlay reference field on walls if specified if args.overlay: overlayfield = datacropped[args.overlay] drawcontoursonwalls(ax, overlayfield, zboundaries=[zstart, zend]) # Set color limits clim = quantile(datacropped[fieldname], args.climpercentile / 100.0) setcolorlimits!(ax, clim=clim) # Save figure save("output.png", fig) Time Complexity: Rendering time is approximately 90 seconds per six-panel figure at Nz=1024 on a Casper compute node. A full 101-record set takes ~2.5 hours. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is significantly reduced by cropping the z-dimension before differentiation. A subsetter script can reduce file size from 2.15 GiB to 0.006 GiB (336x compression) for testing. Without cropping, memory peaks can reach 15–25 GB at Nz=1024. Hardware Requirements: Requires an OpenGL context. Can run on CPU-only clusters using Xvfb and Mesa software rasterizer. Does not require a dedicated GPU. Strengths: Provides immersive 3D visualization of internal flow structures (e.g., vortices) that 2D slices miss. Efficient batch rendering on CPU clusters. Limitations: Transparency cannot separate interpenetrating isosurfaces. Requires careful tuning of isosurface levels and color scales for multi-field figures. Not suitable for batch jobs without any display/OpenGL support (use X12 instead). X13 was developed as part of the tomchor/CoarseGrainedKHAPE repository for rendering 3D isosurfaces of turbulent flow simulations. It was introduced in October 2026 as a companion to X12, which used orthogonal cutting planes. X13 leverages GLMakie for GPU raymarching volume rendering, addressing the need to visualize 3D structures like streamwise vortices in Kelvin-Helmholtz (KH) runs. It runs on the Casper compute cluster using off-screen rendering techniques. 3D isosurface figures: X13, a batch render job, and a subsetter, https://github.com/tomchor/CoarseGrainedKHAPE/pull/78, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Domain Colouring
body: Domain Colouring maps complex numbers to colors using a cyclic colormap scaled by a degree parameter and brightness, allowing the phase (angle) and magnitude (brightness) of a complex field to be read orthogonally in a single image. It is distinct from standard scalar transfer functions by exploiting the two-dimensional nature of the complex plane, mapping the angular component to hue and the radial component to intensity. Inputs: realpart: Real component of the complex number z. imagpart: Imaginary component of the complex number z. cycliccolourmap: A 2D array of shape (N, 3) or (N, 4) representing N colors in the cyclic colormap. degree: An integer scaling factor for the angular resolution. Outputs: output: A color tensor with the same spatial dimensions as the input, where each pixel is a color vector. Data Structures: The complex number is represented as z = \text{real\part} + i \cdot \text{imag\part}. The colormap is an array of N entries, where N is the length of cycliccolourmap. Steps: 1. Calculate the argument (phase) of z using the two-argument arctangent: \theta = \arg(z) = \operatorname{atan2}(\text{imag\part}, \text{real\part}). The result is in the range (-\pi, \pi]. 2. Normalize the angle to the range [0, 1) by adding 0.5 to the normalized angle \frac{\theta}{2\pi}: u = \frac{\theta}{2\pi} + 0.5 3. Scale the normalized angle by the degree parameter and the colormap length N to determine the color index: \text{index} = \lfloor u \cdot \text{degree} \cdot N \rfloor \bmod N This maps the cyclic phase to an integer index in the colormap. 4. Retrieve the base color c from the colormap: c = \text{cyclic\colourmap}[\text{index}] 5. Calculate the brightness b as the magnitude of z: b = |z| = \sqrt{\text{real\part}^2 + \text{imag\part}^2} 6. Compute the final output color by scaling the base color by the brightness: \text{output} = b \cdot c Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import torch def domaincolouring(realpart, imagpart, cycliccolourmap, degree): """ Maps complex numbers to colors using domain colouring. Args: realpart: Tensor of real components. imagpart: Tensor of imaginary components. cycliccolourmap: Tensor of shape (N, 3) or (N, 4) representing the colormap. degree: Integer scaling factor for angular resolution. Returns: Tensor of output colors. """ # Step 1: Calculate argument theta = torch.atan2(imagpart, realpart) # Step 2: Normalize angle to [0, 1) # math.tau is 2pi u = theta.div(math.tau).add(0.5) # Step 3: Calculate index # Scale by degree and colormap length, floor, and modulo cmaplen = cycliccolourmap.shape[0] index = u.mul(degree).multiply(cmaplen).floor().long().remainder(cmaplen) # Step 4: Retrieve base color colours = cycliccolourmap[index,:] # Step 5: Calculate brightness (magnitude) # Stack real and imag parts, compute squared sum, then square root zstack = torch.stack([realpart, imagpart], dim=-1) magnitudesq = zstack.pow(2).sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True) brightness = magnitudesq.pow(1 / 2) # Step 6: Scale color by brightness output = brightness.mul(colours) return output Parameters: degree: Controls the number of color cycles across the 2\pi range. Higher values increase angular resolution. Typical values are not specified in the sources. cycliccolourmap: Must be seamless at \pm \pi (i.e., the first and last colors should match or blend smoothly) to avoid discontinuities in the phase mapping. Common colormaps include twilight, HSV, infinity, and grayscale. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Magnitude: If z=0, the argument is undefined. atan2(0, 0) typically returns 0. The brightness will be 0, resulting in a black pixel regardless of the colormap index. Discontinuities: If the colormap is not cyclic (i.e., the first and last colors do not match), a visible seam will appear at the negative real axis (\theta = \pm \pi). Precision: Floating-point precision in atan2 and subsequent floating-point arithmetic may cause slight variations in index selection near boundaries. Using floor and long conversion ensures integer indexing. Projects surface normals onto the plane perpendicular to the ray direction, rotates them to camera space, and applies domain colouring to the resulting 2D tangent vectors to visualize spin orientation. Definition: Surface normals \mathbf{n} are projected onto the tangent plane defined by the ray direction \mathbf{r}, then rotated to camera space. Formula: The tangent vector is calculated as \mathbf{t} = \mathbf{n} - (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{r})\mathbf{r}, which removes the component of the normal parallel to the ray. This vector is then rotated by the camera orientation conjugate. Domain colouring is applied to the x and y components of the resulting tangent vector \mathbf{t}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tangentshading(surfacenormals, raydirections, cameraorientationconj, cycliccolourmap, degree): """ Applies domain colouring to tangent vectors derived from surface normals. Args: surfacenormals: Tensor of surface normals. raydirections: Tensor of ray directions. cameraorientationconj: Quaternion or rotation matrix representing camera orientation conjugate. cycliccolourmap: Colormap tensor. degree: Degree parameter for domain colouring. Returns: Tensor of colors. """ # Project normals onto the plane perpendicular to ray direction # t = n - (n. r) r dotproduct = surfacenormals.multiply(raydirections).sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True) projectednormals = surfacenormals.add(dotproduct.multiply(raydirections).mul(-1.0)) # Rotate to camera space # Note: Actual rotation implementation depends on the representation of cameraorientationconj # Assuming a helper function 'rotate' exists for the specific rotation format rotatednormals = rotate(projectednormals, cameraorientationconj) # Apply domain colouring to the x and y components tangentimage = domaincolouring( rotatednormals[..., 0], rotatednormals[..., 1], cycliccolourmap, degree) return tangentimage When to choose: Use when visualizing spin orientation or vector field tangents on surfaces relative to the camera. Volumetric 3-D plotting of complex scalar fields f(x, y, z) \in \mathbb{C} sampled on a grid, where magnitude drives opacity and phase drives color. Definition: Implements direct volume ray-marching for complex fields, typically as a Vulkan compute pipeline. The magnitude |f| drives opacity, and the phase \arg(f) drives color through a cyclic colormap. Inputs: Complex field data std::complex<float|double> on a grid with x-fastest memory layout. Parameters: Magnitude Mapping: Opacity is driven by |f| using linear or logarithmic transfer functions, with a decade window for high-dynamic-range data. Phase Mapping: Color is driven by \arg(f) using a cyclic colormap (e.g., twilight, HSV, infinity, grayscale). Output: R8G8B8A8UNORM image. Features: Includes world-space bounding box, ticked/labeled axes, and a phase \times magnitude legend with thickness-corrected opacity ramp. Supports inline LaTeX-subset math for labels. When to choose: Use for rendering quantum-mechanical wavefunctions or other complex-valued volumetric data where both amplitude and phase information are critical. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: For Complex-field Direct Volume Rendering, performance is approximately 15 ms/frame (~65 FPS) for a 500³ complex field on the tested hardware. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Allows orthogonal reading of amplitude and phase in a single image. Cyclic colormaps provide seamless phase visualization. Tangent shading enables visualization of spin orientation. Limitations: Requires complex-valued data. Performance may degrade with higher resolutions or more complex transfer functions. Discontinuities in non-cyclic colormaps can cause visual artifacts. When to use it and when not: Use when visualizing complex-valued fields where phase and magnitude are both important. Use Tangent Shading for visualizing vector field orientations on surfaces. Do not use for purely real-valued scalar fields where standard transfer functions are more appropriate. Domain Colouring originates from the visualization of complex functions, mapping the complex plane to the color plane. It has been adapted for volume rendering to visualize complex scalar fields, such as quantum-mechanical wavefunctions. The technique is implemented in libraries such as raymarching for shader-based rendering and imaginaryVolumes for Vulkan-based direct volume rendering. kyle-rosa/raymarching, https://github.com/kyle-rosa/raymarching, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) steubengineer/imaginaryVolumes, https://github.com/steubengineer/imaginaryVolumes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Illustrative and non-photorealistic volume rendering
head: Volume illustration, NPR volume rendering
body: Illustrative and non-photorealistic volume rendering (NPR) augments physics-based illumination pipelines with artistic techniques to enhance the perception of structure, shape, orientation, and depth in volumetric data. It solves the problem of ambiguous internal structure in traditional physics-based or classification-based renderings by applying feature enhancement and depth cues derived from local volumetric properties rather than sample values alone. Unlike surface-based NPR where features are well-defined boundaries, volume illustration determines feature areas through continuous analysis of local gradients and properties, requiring less manual tuning of transfer functions than traditional direct volume rendering. The family shares the goal of enhancing volume visualization through stylized lighting and feature abstraction. All methods operate on fragment-level data, typically utilizing the volume sample gradient as a proxy for surface normal orientation. They decouple illumination from the physical light transport equation, instead using mathematical functions of the view direction, light direction, and scalar field properties to modulate color. Common inputs include the normalized gradient \nabla fn, light vectors L, and base colors derived from transfer functions. The output is a final color c that combines ambient/gaseous components with directed illumination effects. The framework utilizes four types of properties for enhancement: 1. Volume sample location and value. 2. Local volumetric properties, such as gradient and minimal change direction. 3. View direction. 4. Light information. Volumetric illustration differs from surface-based NPR in several important ways. In surface NPR, surfaces (features) are well-defined, whereas with volumes, feature areas within the volume must be determined through analysis of local volumetric properties because volumetric features vary continuously throughout three-dimensional space. Geometric Buffers (G-buffers) is a Non-Photorealistic Rendering (NPR) technique that decouples geometric analysis from shading by storing per-pixel geometric properties (e.g., depth, normals) in intermediate 2D images. It solves the problem of efficiently generating illustrative effects (such as line drawings and edge enhancement) for complex 3D volumes by leveraging fast 2D image processing algorithms instead of expensive 3D analytic computations. Unlike sibling methods that may compute shading or illumination directly in 3D space, G-buffers provide hidden surface elimination for free and allow NPR parameters to be tweaked interactively without re-traversing the volume. The base renderer used for volume illustration examples, implementing physics-based illumination of gaseous phenomena. It can be replaced by a Phong illumination and linear accumulation renderer. Orientation-Based Color Modification simulates medical illustration techniques by altering the color, saturation, value, and transparency of volume samples based on the angle between the volumetric gradient and the viewer. It addresses the lack of depth cues in translucent volume rendering by using HSV color space to desaturate features facing the viewer and darken/saturate receding surfaces, thereby enhancing spatial understanding. A technique to create halo effects in planes orthogonal to the view vector by making regions just outside features darker and more opaque, obscuring background elements to reinforce depth perception. Context-Preserving Volume Rendering (CPVR) is an illustrative volume rendering technique that selectively reduces opacity in less important data regions to visualize interior structures while preserving exterior context. It solves the problem of context loss inherent in conventional clipping techniques by modulating sample opacity based on shading intensity, gradient magnitude, distance to the eye point, and previously accumulated opacity. Unlike clipping planes which remove context information, CPVR retains it by making homogeneous areas (high lighting intensity) transparent, allowing users to inspect the interior of an object without hiding occluded objects. Volume illustration is a non-photorealistic volume rendering method that augments a physics-based illumination pipeline with artistic techniques to enhance the perception of structure, shape, orientation, and depth in volumetric data. It solves the problem of ambiguous internal structure in traditional physics-based or classification-based renderings by applying feature enhancement and depth cues derived from local volumetric properties rather than sample values alone. Unlike surface-based NPR where features are well-defined boundaries, volume illustration determines feature areas through continuous analysis of local gradients and properties, requiring less manual tuning of transfer functions than traditional direct volume rendering. A technique to create a sketch-like appearance by making non-volumetric silhouettes (areas not near silhouette edges) transparent and using a specific sketch color (e.g., white or black), with shadows calculated based on original volume opacity. Exact Projection Full Opacity is a non-photorealistic volume rendering technique that simplifies the visual output by identifying a single primary front object and optionally one significant background object, blending them based on density and distance thresholds rather than performing full front-to-back accumulation. It differs from standard front-to-back compositing by skipping the accumulation of intermediate samples, storing only the first significant object (primary) and potentially one background object, then blending them directly to create a stylized, illustrative result. Illumination and Tone Shading Models provide non-photorealistic lighting cues to enhance the visual clarity and artistic style of volume renderings. Unlike photometric models that simulate physical light transport, these methods map geometric or scalar properties to pre-defined color variations, prioritizing interpretability and aesthetic control over physical accuracy. They are distinct from Geometric Buffers by focusing on color modulation rather than depth/normal encoding, and from Base Gaseous Illumination Renderer by incorporating directed shading components. An interactive object-space technique for illustrating volumetric data by simulating free-hand line art (hatching) using hardware-assisted volume and line rendering, with data-driven seed point selection to minimize memory and generation time. Line and Edge Detection is a family of Non-Photorealistic Rendering (NPR) techniques designed to detect and render lines within volume data to communicate structure, shape, and boundaries. It solves the problem of visualizing complex geometry and internal structures in volumetric datasets where traditional photorealistic rendering may obscure topological details. What sets this family apart from its siblings is its specific focus on line-based abstraction rather than surface shading or contour outlines; it distinguishes itself from Face-based volume rendering with edge highlights by generating lines that represent intrinsic surface properties (like curvature) rather than just silhouette edges, and from Outline and Contour Generation by often utilizing vector-oriented or texture-based approaches that are viewpoint-independent or analytically derived, rather than purely image-space depth-difference extraction. An interactive direct volume illustration system that simulates traditional stipple drawing by generating point lists based on volume characteristics (gradient magnitude/direction) and applying feature enhancements (silhouette curves, varying point sizes, resolution adjustments) to convey tone, texture, and shape. A method to visualize inter-penetrating volumetric objects by decomposing a scalar field into three distinct logical objects: selection, ghost, and background, allowing independent control of appearance and spatial transformation. Efficient non-photorealistic rendering of 3D polygonal meshes in OpenGL for non-living subjects, using specific conventions different from scientific illustration. Supported effects include line weighted depth cueing, fast silhouettes, shading using cool-to-warm lighting methods, light and highlight motion, and a non-parametric method of representing metal. A system that attempts to predict what kind of illustration a viewer would like to see by using an intent-based approach borrowing from AI knowledge bases. Rules that describe communicative intent are defined, and stylistic decisions that reflect particular goals are used to generate the actual illustrations. A visualization technique to emphasize differences in information content between two rendered fields by storing voxel-wise color differences. It calculates the l2-norm of opacity-weighted color values for each voxel to store in the residual map, which is then rendered interactively from arbitrary perspectives. Procedural coloring for butterfly wings using polar coordinates in wing space to generate veins, margins, bands, and apex patterns. It converts wing coordinates to polar, calculates base field color, vein patterns using sine waves, and mixes colors for veins, margins, and bands. A visualization mode to reveal structural differences between a reference volume (rendered with Tr) and an optimized volume (rendered with To) by rendering the residual field between them. It applies transfer functions to both fields, computes the residual by subtracting per-voxel colors and computing the l2-norm of the RGB\alpha difference vector, and uses RGB colors pre-multiplied with \alpha to ensure transparent regions have less contribution. Visualizes level sets of large CT scans (e.g., 1024^3) using slicemaps, which are small enough to fit in GPU memory and can be created by one slicing pass on the GPU. It estimates normals to compensate for the lack of binary information and reflect surface appearance, keeping several level sets at the same time and blending them together for interactive display. This avoids texture transfer stalls associated with slicing and the infeasibility of Marching Cubes at 1024^3 resolution. Cutaways remove occluding objects to reveal structures of interest, using a simplified three-object setup (Background, Ghost, Selection) with static importance functions to skip costly importance compositing. Ghosting selectively reduces opacity of occluding regions to preserve edges and spatial location impression, controllable from no ghosting to full cutaway. The degree of ghosting is smoothly controllable from no ghosting (opacity not reduced) to full cutaway view (occluding structures completely suppressed). The term "illustration" in the context of volume rendering was introduced by Ebert in 2000. The field is primarily motivated by the attempt to create renditions that consider the perceptual capabilities of humans. Visualization primarily motivated by this attempt includes boundary enhancement based on gradient approximation and curvature-based transfer functions. The approach augments a physics-based rendering process with non-photorealistic rendering (NPR) techniques to enhance the expressiveness of the visualization. NPR draws inspiration from fields such as art and technical illustration to develop automatic methods to synthesize images with an illustrated look from geometric surface models. While NPR research had effectively addressed surface shape and 2D data, it had virtually ignored the rendering of volume models until this work. Early systems like SIV (Scientific Illustrator for Volumes) separated a 3D volume into segments using seeded region growing with thresholding, assigning interest labels to abstract groups of voxels, which were then rendered using NPR techniques. SIV used Saito and Takahashi's G-buffer idea extensively. In 2003, GPU raycasting was introduced by Krüger, making it feasible from a computational standpoint to apply illustrative visualization techniques in practice, overcoming previous performance constraints. name: Geometric Buffers (G-buffers)
head: 2D Image Processing for NPR, G-buffer approach, Intermediate geometric buffers, Pixel-Based Geometric Buffer Approach
body: Geometric Buffers (G-buffers) is a Non-Photorealistic Rendering (NPR) technique that decouples geometric analysis from shading by storing per-pixel geometric properties (e.g., depth, normals) in intermediate 2D images. It solves the problem of efficiently generating illustrative effects for complex 3D volumes by leveraging fast 2D image processing algorithms instead of expensive 3D analytic computations. Unlike sibling methods that may compute shading or illumination directly in 3D space, G-buffers provide hidden surface elimination for free and allow NPR parameters to be tweaked interactively without re-traversing the volume. Inputs: A 3D volume dataset, camera position, and camera orientation. Outputs: A final 2D NPR image. Data Structures: G-buffers: A set of 2D images (arrays) corresponding to the screen resolution. Each buffer stores a single geometric property for every pixel. Common buffers include: Depth Buffer: Stores the distance from the camera to the visible surface along the view ray. Normal Buffer: Stores the surface normal vector (nx, ny, nz) of the visible surface at each pixel. Steps: 1. Single Volume Traversal: Traverse the 3D volume once from the camera's perspective to project the geometric scene onto a viewplane. For each pixel, determine the visible surface intersection, implicitly removing hidden surfaces. 2. Buffer Construction: For each pixel where a surface is visible, compute and store the relevant geometric properties into the corresponding G-buffers. Depth: Store the ray-surface intersection distance. Normal: Store the surface normal vector encapsulated during the projection phase. 3. 2D Image Processing: Apply various 2D image processing techniques to the G-buffers to achieve different NPR effects. Edge/Profile Extraction: Extract features such as profiles and internal edges from the depth map using a first-order differential operator. 4. Compositing: Apply image processing operators to the G-buffers to obtain the final rendering. 5. Reuse: If NPR parameters change but the scene geometry and camera position do not change, skip the traversal and reuse the existing G-buffers to avoid re-traversal. Formulas: Edge Detection: A first-order differential operator D applied to the depth buffer D{buf} yields the edge map E: E = |D(D{buf})| Pixels where E exceeds a threshold are marked as edges. Parameters: Thresholds: Used for edge detection in G-buffers. Determining the most suitable combination of enhancement techniques depends on the scene, purpose, and viewer's preferences, requiring trial and error. Reconstruction Resolution: High-resolution illustrations communicate more information, but source volume models are often smaller than final 2D images, necessitating consideration of reconstruction and interpolation issues. Variable Gaussian blurring reduces visible artifacts from the Nyquist limit. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: Sharp surface borders may exhibit aliasing artifacts and digitization problems due to pixel discretization. Transparency/Reflection: The basic method assumes all objects are opaque and cannot natively enhance reflected or transparent images without extensions. Parameter Tuning: There is no automatic way to determine the optimal combination of enhancement techniques; it requires manual trial and error based on scene context and viewer preference. Resolution Mismatch: If the source volume is significantly smaller than the target image, reconstruction artifacts appear due to the discrete sampled nature of the original volume models. Addresses the mismatch between low-resolution volume data and high-resolution NPR output. It is chosen when source volumes are significantly smaller than the target image to mitigate Nyquist limit artifacts. See Reconstruction and Interpolation. Modifies the opaque assumption to handle semi-transparent or reflective surfaces. It is chosen when the scene requires rendering of non-opaque objects. Time Complexity: Dominated by the single 3D volume traversal. Subsequent NPR effect generation is fast since much of the processing is done in 2D rather than 3D. Memory Complexity: Scales with the number of pixels and geometric properties stored per pixel. Performance: Fast enough for interactive user experimentation. Pixel-based techniques handle large or complex datasets better than analytic alternatives. Strengths: Reusability: G-buffers can be reused without recalculation if scene geometry and camera position do not change. Hidden Surface Elimination: Provided automatically by the traversal and buffering process. Scalability: Handles large or complex datasets better than analytic alternatives. Limitations: Assumes opacity without extensions. Susceptible to aliasing and digitization artifacts. Subjective tuning required for comprehensibility. The G-buffer approach was proposed by Saito and Takahashi [ST90] to enable line generation and NPR effects. The authors claim these techniques help make hand-drawn illustrations more comprehensible, and apply them to various digital domains like edge enhancement, line drawing illustrations, topographical maps, medical imaging, and surface analysis. The method is a foundational technique in pixel-based NPR for volume visualization, allowing for interactive user experimentation by decoupling geometry from style. Volume Visualisation Via Variable-Detail Non-Photorealistic Illustration, https://uwspace.uwaterloo.ca/bitstream/10012/1104/1/jlmckinl2002.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Frequency Distribution-based Transfer Function
head: Frequency-based Transfer Function, GPU-based FFT Transfer Function Design, TF considering frequency distribution
body: This method designs transfer functions by analyzing the statistical frequency distribution of the volume's scalar field to map voxel values to colors and opacities. It specifically addresses the difficulty of visualizing subtle spatial differences in data with narrow distribution ranges, such as lake water quality models, where conventional methods fail to distinguish fine variations. It builds on Probabilistic and Statistical Modeling. Inputs: V: The input volume dataset, a 3D grid of scalar values. N: Total number of voxels in V. Outputs: TF: A mapping function that assigns color C(v) and opacity \alpha(v) to any scalar value v. Data Structures: Histogram H: A 1D array representing the frequency distribution of scalar values. Probability Map P: A 1D array where P[i] represents the coloring probability for the i-th bin. Steps: 1. Count Frequency Distribution: Count the frequency distribution of the scalar field across the volume. 2. Calculate Ratios and Probabilities: Calculate the voxel ratios and the coloring probabilities of the frequency ranges. The exact mathematical transformation from voxel ratios to coloring probabilities is not given in the sources. 3. Map to Optical Properties: Map the voxel values to colors and transparencies according to the coloring probabilities. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computefrequencytf(volume, numbins): # 1. Count frequency distribution histogram = [0] numbins minval, maxval = min(volume), max(volume) for v in volume: binidx = int((v - minval) / (maxval - minval) (numbins - 1)) histogram[binidx] += 1 # 2. Calculate voxel ratios and coloring probabilities totalvoxels = len(volume) ratios = [h / totalvoxels for h in histogram] # Coloring probability calculation from voxel ratios is not given in the sources # 3. Map values to colors and transparencies tf = {} for v in set(volume): binidx = int((v - minval) / (maxval - minval) (numbins - 1)) # Mapping bin probability to color and opacity is not given in the sources return tf Pitfalls: Narrow Distribution: Narrow distribution ranges and small spatial differences of the scalar field make perspective expression of subtle differences difficult. Extends the concept by using 2D histograms of feature pairs (e.g., intensity and gradient) to visualize joint distributions, allowing isolation of materials indistinguishable in 1D frequency histograms. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. GPU-based FFT acceleration is mentioned for interactive design support. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Effective for enhancing perspective expression of subtle differences in narrow-range data. Interactive design support via GPU acceleration. Limitations: Narrow distribution ranges and small spatial differences of the scalar field make perspective expression of subtle differences difficult. The method was proposed to improve the visualization of lake water quality models, where pollutant distribution and diffusion exhibit narrow scalar ranges and subtle spatial variations. It builds on the concept of using frequency distributions to guide transfer function design, with earlier work by Vucini et al. utilizing GPU-based FFT for interactive frequency-based transfer function design. MULTIVARIATE TRANSFER FUNCTION DESIGN, https://www.sci.utah.edu/~lzhou/dissertationfinalzhoul.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Holographic display method for volume data by volume rendering, https://www.researchgate.net/publication/330223296Holographicdisplaymethodforvolumedatabyvolumerendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Multi-dimensional Transfer Function
head: 2D Histogram Analysis for Transfer Functions, 2D Volume Histogram, 2D histogram transfer functions, Effect Control via Transfer Functions, Hierarchical Transfer Functions
body: Multi-dimensional transfer functions (MTFs) map voxel data to visual properties using more than one feature dimension, typically scalar density and gradient magnitude, to resolve ambiguities inherent in 1D transfer functions. Unlike standard methods that rely solely on scalar value, MTFs utilize 2D histograms to identify homogeneous materials as distinct spots and material boundaries as arcs, allowing for the interactive assignment of color, opacity, and illustrative effects (e.g., sketch, illumination) to specific materials. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset where each voxel has at least two feature values, typically scalar density (d) and gradient magnitude (g). Output: A visualization where voxels are colored and rendered with opacity and illustrative effects based on their position in the 2D feature space. Data Structures: 2D Histogram: A 2D array where the X-axis represents density (d) and the Y-axis represents gradient magnitude (g). Each entry (i, j) stores the count of voxels falling into the bin defined by density range i and gradient range j. The brightness or intensity of the histogram entry represents the sample frequency (voxel count). Transfer Function Map: A mapping from histogram bins (or continuous feature pairs) to RGBA values and effect parameters. Steps: 1. Feature Computation: Compute the feature space pairs for all voxels. For each voxel v, calculate the scalar density dv and the gradient magnitude gv = \|\nabla dv\|. 2. Histogram Construction: Construct the 2D histogram. For each voxel, increment the counter in the bin corresponding to its (dv, gv) pair. 3. Material Identification: Analyze the histogram to identify materials: Homogeneous Materials: Identified as dense spots (clusters) in the histogram where many voxels share similar density and gradient values. Material Boundaries: Identified as arcs or ridges in the histogram connecting different material spots, representing transitions between materials. Probing: Use a probe tool to sample specific points in the dataset and observe their location in the histogram to verify material identity. 4. Transfer Function Assignment: Interactively assign visual properties to histogram regions: Assign color and opacity to histogram entries interactively until the desired visualization is obtained. Assign illustrative effect parameters (e.g., sketch strength, illumination intensity) to specific materials. 5. Rendering: For each voxel, determine its feature pair (d, g), look up the corresponding transfer function values, and apply the assigned color, opacity, and effects during volume rendering. Formulas: Gradient Magnitude: g = \sqrt{\left(\frac{\partial d}{\partial x}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial d}{\partial y}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial d}{\partial z}\right)^2}. Histogram Bin Index: For a voxel with features (d, g), the bin indices (i, j) are determined by quantizing d and g into discrete ranges. Parameters: Feature Dimensions: 2 (e.g., intensity and gradient magnitude). Histogram Resolution: Not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Manual Tuning: Requires manual trial-and-error tuning by the user to assign color and opacity, which can be time-consuming. Ambiguity Resolution: While it resolves 1D ambiguities, overlapping spots in the 2D histogram may still require careful interpretation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computegradientmagnitude(volume): """Compute gradient magnitude for each voxel using central differences.""" dims = (len(volume), len(volume[0]), len(volume[0][0])) gradmag = [[[0.0] dims[2] for in range(dims[1])] for in range(dims[0])] for i in range(dims[0]): for j in range(dims[1]): for k in range(dims[2]): dx = 0.0 dy = 0.0 dz = 0.0 if i > 0: dx -= volume[i-1][j][k] if i < dims[0]-1: dx += volume[i+1][j][k] if j > 0: dy -= volume[i][j-1][k] if j < dims[1]-1: dy += volume[i][j+1][k] if k > 0: dz -= volume[i][j][k-1] if k < dims[2]-1: dz += volume[i][j][k+1] gradmag[i][j][k] = (dxdx + dydy + dzdz)0.5 return gradmag def build2dhistogram(volume, gradmag, numbinsd, numbinsg): """Construct a 2D histogram of density vs gradient magnitude.""" histogram = [[0] numbinsg for in range(numbinsd)] mind, maxd = float('inf'), float('-inf') ming, maxg = float('inf'), float('-inf') for i in range(len(volume)): for j in range(len(volume[0])): for k in range(len(volume[0][0])): d = volume[i][j][k] g = gradmag[i][j][k] if d < mind: mind = d if d > maxd: maxd = d if g < ming: ming = g if g > maxg: maxg = g if maxd == mind: maxd += 1e-6 if maxg == ming: maxg += 1e-6 for i in range(len(volume)): for j in range(len(volume[0])): for k in range(len(volume[0][0])): d = volume[i][j][k] g = gradmag[i][j][k] bind = int((d - mind) / (maxd - mind) (numbinsd - 1)) bing = int((g - ming) / (maxg - ming) (numbinsg - 1)) bind = max(0, min(bind, numbinsd - 1)) bing = max(0, min(bing, numbinsg - 1)) histogram[bind][bing] += 1 return histogram, mind, maxd, ming, maxg def assigntransferfunction(histogram, userinteractions): """ Assign color and opacity based on user interactions with the histogram. userinteractions: list of tuples (bind, bing, color, opacity, effectparams) """ tfmap = {} for bind, bing, color, opacity, effectparams in userinteractions: tfmap[(bind, bing)] = { 'color': color, 'opacity': opacity, 'effectparams': effectparams } return tfmap def rendervolume(volume, gradmag, tfmap, mind, maxd, ming, maxg, numbinsd, numbinsg): """Render volume using the multi-dimensional transfer function.""" rendered = [[[0.0] len(volume[0][0]) for in range(len(volume[0]))] for in range(len(volume))] for i in range(len(volume)): for j in range(len(volume[0])): for k in range(len(volume[0][0])): d = volume[i][j][k] g = gradmag[i][j][k] bind = int((d - mind) / (maxd - mind) (numbinsd - 1)) bing = int((g - ming) / (maxg - ming) (numbinsg - 1)) bind = max(0, min(bind, numbinsd - 1)) bing = max(0, min(bing, numbinsg - 1)) if (bind, bing) in tfmap: entry = tfmap[(bind, bing)] rendered[i][j][k] = entry['color'] entry['opacity'] # Apply illustrative effects based on entry['effectparams'] return rendered 2D Histogram Visualization is a precomputed visual aid used to convey the distribution of voxel counts across sparse regions of a two-dimensional feature space, such as scalar value pairs. It differs from continuous scatterplots by using discrete bins, which simplifies implementation and better highlights sparse data regions. It serves as an exploratory tool for designing transfer functions or analyzing multi-field correlations, distinct from sibling methods like Spatialized Transfer Functions which focus on spatial context [5387-spatialized-transfer-functions.md] or Gray-Gradient Mode Histogram Clustering which focuses on clustering [5459-gray-gradient-mode-histogram-clustering-transfer-function.md]. Spatialized Transfer Functions (STF) is a technique that performs segmentation on the domain of the transfer function (histogram) rather than the volume domain, using spatial information (feature radius) to group scalar values into uniquely colored regions corresponding to materials. It solves the problem that standard transfer functions cannot separate features with identical statistical properties but different spatial positions. Unlike explicit segmentation which is time-consuming and not suitable for quick first impressions, STF performs segmentation on the transfer function domain automatically and fast, allowing interactive exploration. This method automatically generates a volume rendering transfer function (TF) by embedding volume data attributes (gray value and gradient mode) into a two-dimensional histogram, performing hierarchical clustering to identify tissue boundaries, and mapping the results to color, opacity, and gradient-based opacity multipliers. It solves the problem of manual TF specification by distinguishing tissues based on gray ranges and enhancing boundary visibility through clustering analysis of the gray-gradient mode histogram. Unlike standard piecewise-linear interpolation which may cause blurring at tissue edges, this method assigns constant color and opacity within identified tissue ranges defined by histogram valleys, ensuring uniform appearance for specific tissues. It builds on the principles of Multi-dimensional Transfer Function by utilizing a 2D histogram, but differs from siblings like 2D Histogram Visualization by explicitly using hierarchical clustering to extract curve peaks for automatic TF generation rather than direct visual inspection. Time Complexity: Constructing the 2D histogram is O(N) where N is the number of voxels. Rendering is O(N) per frame. Memory Complexity: The histogram requires O(Bd \times Bg) memory where Bd and Bg are the number of bins in density and gradient dimensions, respectively. This is typically small compared to the volume data. Strengths: Resolves ambiguities present in 1D transfer functions by using additional feature dimensions. Allows for the control of illustrative effects beyond color and opacity. Limitations: Requires manual trial-and-error tuning by the user. Interactive exploration can be slow if the histogram is not precomputed or optimized. When to Use: When 1D transfer functions fail to separate materials with similar scalar values but different gradients, or when illustrative effects need to be applied selectively to different materials. When Not to Use: When automatic transfer function generation is required without user interaction, or when computational resources are extremely limited and precomputation is not feasible. Multi-dimensional transfer functions were introduced to address the limitations of 1D transfer functions in conveying complex features and boundaries in volume data. Early work by Kindlmann, Kniss, and Lum explored 2D histograms for feature space analysis. Maciejewski et al. proposed non-parametric clustering to automate the process. Roettger et al. introduced spatialized transfer functions as a variant. The method is widely used in medical illustration and visualization systems to enhance the clarity of anatomical structures.
