name: Non-Parametric Transfer Function Generation
head: Variable Kernel Density Estimation for TF Clustering
body: Non-Parametric Transfer Function Generation is a clustering method for 2D histograms (conventional or abstracted) that groups data based on neighborhood information using variable kernel density estimation. It provides users with a means to group data in the 2D histogram by areas of similar value. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of N data points \{X1, X2,..., XN\} representing voxels in a 2D feature space (e.g., Gray-Gradient Mode Histogram). Output: A probability density estimate \hat{f}h(x) over the feature space, which identifies clusters as local maxima in the density distribution. Data Structures Samples: An array of N points, where each point Xi is a vector in the 2D feature space. Parameters: N: Total number of samples (voxels). k: Index of the nearest neighbor used to scale the kernel radius. d{i,k}: Multi-dimensional smoothing parameter for point Xi. Steps 1. Calculate Smoothing Parameters: For each sample Xi, compute d{i,k}, the distance from Xi to its k-th nearest neighbor in the set of N-1 other data points. 2. Select Kernel: Use the Epanechnikov kernel K(u) for computational efficiency. 3. Compute Density Estimate: Calculate the probability density \hat{f}h(x) at any location x in the feature space using the variable kernel formula. 4. Identify Clusters: Locate local maxima in the resulting density surface \hat{f}h(x). Each local maximum represents a potential volumetric feature cluster. Formulas The probability density estimate \hat{f}h(x) at location x is: \hat{f}h(x) = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \frac{1}{d{i,k}} K\left(\frac{x - Xi}{d{i,k}}\right) Where: N is the total number of samples in the histogram feature space. d{i,k} is the multi-dimensional smoothing parameter, defined as the distance from the i-th sample Xi to its k-th nearest neighbor in the set of N-1 data points. K(u) is the kernel function. The Epanechnikov kernel is used to reduce calculation time: K(u) = \frac{3}{4}(1 - \|u\|^2) \quad \text{for } \|u\| \le 1, \text{ and } 0 \text{ otherwise} Parameters k: The index of the nearest neighbor. Set to k = \lfloor \sqrt{N} \rfloor as a rule of thumb approximation for optimal density estimation fitting. Pitfalls Sparse Regions: Data points in sparse regions require flatter kernels to maintain density estimation accuracy. This is handled by scaling the kernel width proportional to d{i,k} (distance to k-th nearest neighbor). Boundary Effects: The method assumes the feature space is bounded; points near the edge may have underestimated density due to truncated kernel support. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def epanechnikovkernel(usqnorm): """Epanechnikov kernel K(u) = 3/4 (1 - ||u||^2) if ||u|| <= 1, else 0.""" if usqnorm <= 1.0: return 0.75 (1.0 - usqnorm) return 0.0 def computedik(samples, k): """Compute di,k for all samples: distance to k-th nearest neighbor.""" N = len(samples) dik = [] for i in range(N): dists = [] for j in range(N): if i == j: continue dx = samples[i][0] - samples[j][0] dy = samples[i][1] - samples[j][1] dists.append(math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy)) dists.sort() # k is 1-indexed in the source; list is 0-indexed if k <= len(dists): dik.append(dists[k-1]) else: dik.append(dists[-1]) return dik def computedensityatpoint(samples, dik, querypoint): """Compute fhat(x) at a single query point x.""" N = len(samples) density = 0.0 for i in range(N): d = dik[i] if d == 0.0: continue dx = querypoint[0] - samples[i][0] dy = querypoint[1] - samples[i][1] usq = (dx/d)2 + (dy/d)2 density += (1.0 / d) epanechnikovkernel(usq) return density / N def generatedensitygrid(samples, k, resolution=100): """Evaluate density on a grid and return the grid and dik values.""" dik = computedik(samples, k) minvals = [min(p[dim] for p in samples) for dim in range(2)] maxvals = [max(p[dim] for p in samples) for dim in range(2)] grid = [] for i in range(resolution): row = [] for j in range(resolution): x = minvals[0] + i (maxvals[0] - minvals[0]) / (resolution - 1) y = minvals[1] + j (maxvals[1] - minvals[1]) / (resolution - 1) row.append(computedensityatpoint(samples, dik, [x, y])) grid.append(row) return grid, dik Topology-based Non-Parametric Clustering decomposes a 2D density plot feature space into non-overlapping valley cells separated by valley lines, where each cell contains a local maximum representing a potential volumetric feature. It differs from discrete histogram-based clustering by operating on continuous density plots, thereby avoiding spurious peaks/valleys and preserving the spatial relationships of neighboring data points. Unlike frequency binning methods that consider only density magnitude, this method incorporates position in feature space via topological information, preventing disjoint segments for the same density value. name: Topology-based Non-Parametric Clustering
head: Morse complex decomposition, Morse complex-based clustering, Valley Cell-Based Clustering
body: Topology-based Non-Parametric Clustering decomposes a 2D density plot feature space into non-overlapping valley cells separated by valley lines, where each cell contains a local maximum representing a potential volumetric feature. It differs from discrete histogram-based clustering by operating on continuous density plots, thereby avoiding spurious peaks and valleys while preserving the spatial relationships of neighboring data points. Unlike frequency binning methods that consider only density magnitude, this method incorporates position in feature space via topological information, preventing disjoint segments for the same density value. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 2D density plot f(x, y) defined over a feature space where the x-axis represents scalar value and the y-axis represents gradient magnitude. Output: A set of non-overlapping valley cells, each associated with a local maximum, and a hierarchical tree representing the merging of these cells based on boundary persistence. Data Structures 1. Triangular Mesh: A tessellation of the 2D feature space domain where the density function is approximated as piecewise linear over the triangles. 2. Vertex Classification: Each vertex v is classified based on its density value relative to its neighbors in its star: maximum (greater than all neighbors), minimum (smaller than all neighbors), or k-fold saddle (has k+1 wedges in its lower star, where a wedge is a contiguous section of the lower star; regular points have k=0). 3. Valley Lines: Paths connecting saddles to minima or other saddles, representing steepest descent directions. 4. Valley Cells: Regions bounded by valley lines and minima, containing exactly one local maximum. 5. Boundary Persistence: A scalar value associated with each boundary between two adjacent valley cells, defined as the minimal persistence of the saddles forming that boundary. Steps 1. Construct Density Function: Build a continuous density function for the 2D density plot using Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) or continuous scatterplots. 2. Tessellate: Discretize the feature space into a 2D triangular mesh to enforce a piecewise linear approximation of the density function. 3. Identify Critical Points: Identify maxima, minima, and saddles on the mesh vertices. 4. Trace Valley Lines: For every k-fold saddle, trace k+1 paths of steepest descent. Each path follows a sequence of steepest descent edges. Termination conditions are: (a) hitting another saddle, or (b) hitting a previously traced path at a regular point J (junction), which is treated as an artificial saddle to ensure every boundary has at least one saddle. 5. Construct Valley Cells: Use region growing (flood-fill) starting from each maximum. Recursively grow the region of neighboring triangles, stopping at valley lines or triangles whose vertices are minima. 6. Saddle Duplication (Degeneracy Handling): In degenerate cases, a single saddle may belong to more than two cells (associated with more than two maxima). If a saddle S has a connected maximum set of size k, duplicate k-1 saddles. The original saddle is replaced by k distinct saddles, each associated with one of the maxima. 7. Calculate Persistence: For each saddle, calculate its persistence p as the smaller difference between the saddle value and its connected maximum value: p = \min(|v{saddle} - v{max}|) where v{saddle} is the density value at the saddle and v{max} is the density value at the connected maximum. Calculate the Boundary Persistence p{boundary} for each boundary between two adjacent cells as the minimal persistence of its associated saddles: p{boundary} = \min(p{saddles}). 8. Simplify Cells (Hierarchical Merging): Sort all boundaries by their boundary persistence in ascending order. Iterate through the sorted boundaries. For each boundary, merge the two adjacent valley cells. Update the parent-child relationships in the hierarchical tree. The root of the tree corresponds to the cell with the largest local maximum. Stop when a persistence threshold is reached. Parameters Persistence Threshold: Determines when to stop merging cells. Typically 0.1% - 1.5% of the maximal persistence, with 0.5% used as a default. Pitfalls and Edge Cases Degenerate Cases: Piecewise linear discretization can cause multi-fold saddles and intersecting paths. Paths may terminate at another saddle or a previously traced path at a regular point. Saddle Belonging to Multiple Cells: As noted in Step 6, a saddle may be associated with more than two maxima in degenerate cases. This is resolved by saddle duplication. Junctions: When a path hits a regular point J that is the maximum vertex on a path separating regions, J is treated as an artificial saddle. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def topologybasedclustering(densityfunction, bounds, gridres): """ Performs topology-based non-parametric clustering on a 2D density plot. Args: densityfunction: Callable f(x, y) returning density values. bounds: Tuple (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax). gridres: Tuple (resx, resy) for mesh resolution. Returns: cells: List of valley cells. hierarchy: Tree structure representing merged cells. threshold: The persistence threshold used. """ # Step 1 & 2: Tessellate and Evaluate Density vertices, triangles = tessellategrid(bounds, gridres) for v in vertices: v.density = densityfunction(v.x, v.y) # Step 3: Identify Critical Points maxima, minima, saddles = [], [], [] for v in vertices: lowerneighbors = [u for tri in triangles if v in tri for u in tri if u != v and u.density < v.density] if not lowerneighbors: v.type = 'MAX' maxima.append(v) elif len(lowerneighbors) == len([u for tri in triangles if v in tri for u in tri if u != v]): v.type = 'MIN' minima.append(v) else: k = countconnectedlowerwedges(v, lowerneighbors, triangles) if k > 0: v.type = 'SADDLE' v.fold = k saddles.append(v) else: v.type = 'REGULAR' # Step 4: Trace Valley Lines valleylines = [] traced = set() for s in saddles: for in range(s.fold + 1): path = [s] curr = s while True: neighbors = [u for tri in triangles if curr in tri for u in tri if u != curr] if not neighbors: break nxt = min(neighbors, key=lambda n: n.density) if nxt.type == 'SADDLE': path.append(nxt) break if nxt in traced: nxt.type = 'ARTIFICIALSADDLE' path.append(nxt) break path.append(nxt) curr = nxt valleylines.append(path) for node in path: traced.add(node) # Step 5: Construct Valley Cells via Region Growing cells = [] visitedtris = set() for m in maxima: celltris = [] queue = [m] while queue: curr = queue.pop(0) for tri in triangles: if curr in tri.vertices and tri not in visitedtris: if any(v.type in ('SADDLE', 'ARTIFICIALSADDLE') for v in tri.vertices) or \ any(v.type == 'MIN' for v in tri.vertices): continue celltris.append(tri) visitedtris.add(tri) for v in tri.vertices: if v not in visitedtris: queue.append(v) cells.append({'max': m, 'triangles': celltris, 'id': len(cells)}) # Step 6: Saddle Duplication for Degenerate Cases # Map each cell boundary to a unique saddle instance cellsaddlemap = {c['id']: [] for c in cells} for tri in visitedtris: saddleontri = [v for v in tri.vertices if v.type in ('SADDLE', 'ARTIFICIALSADDLE')] if saddleontri: adjcells = [c for c in cells if tri in c['triangles']] for s in saddleontri: for c in adjcells: cellsaddlemap[c['id']].append(s) # Duplicate saddles if associated with >2 maxima saddleinstances = {} for c in cells: for s in cellsaddlemap[c['id']]: if s not in saddleinstances: saddleinstances[s] = [] saddleinstances[s].append(c['id']) for s, cids in saddleinstances.items(): if len(cids) > 2: # Create k-1 duplicates as per topological simplification rules for in range(len(cids) - 1): news = Vertex(s.x, s.y) news.type = 'SADDLE' news.fold = 1 saddleinstances[s].append(news) # Step 7: Calculate Persistence boundaries = [] for c in cells: for tri in c['triangles']: for v in tri.vertices: if v.type in ('SADDLE', 'ARTIFICIALSADDLE'): adj = [other for other in cells if other is not c and tri in other['triangles']] if adj: p = min(abs(v.density - m.density) for m in [c['max'], adj[0]['max']]) boundaries.append({'saddles': [v], 'persistence': p, 'cells': [c['id'], adj[0]['id']]}) # Deduplicate boundaries and take min persistence per boundary pair uniqueboundaries = {} for b in boundaries: key = tuple(sorted(b['cells'])) if key not in uniqueboundaries or b['persistence'] < uniqueboundaries[key]['persistence']: uniqueboundaries[key] = b boundaries = list(uniqueboundaries.values()) # Step 8: Simplify and Build Hierarchy boundaries.sort(key=lambda b: b['persistence']) maxp = max((b['persistence'] for b in boundaries), default=0.0) threshold = maxp 0.005 hierarchy = {'root': None, 'nodes': {}} for b in boundaries: if b['persistence'] > threshold: break c1id, c2id = b['cells'] # Merge adjacent cells and update parent-child relationships parent = {'cellids': [c1id, c2id], 'children': [c1id, c2id], 'persistence': b['persistence']} hierarchy['nodes'][c1id] = parent hierarchy['nodes'][c2id] = parent if hierarchy['root'] is None or c1id == hierarchy['root']: hierarchy['root'] = c1id # Note: In a full implementation, update maximum sets and boundary persistences of remaining boundaries here return cells, hierarchy, threshold class Vertex: def init(self, x, y): self.x, self.y = x, y self.density = 0.0 self.type = 'REGULAR' self.fold = 0 def tessellategrid(bounds, res): xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax = bounds verts = [] for i in range(res[0] + 1): for j in range(res[1] + 1): verts.append(Vertex(xmin + i(xmax-xmin)/res[0], ymin + j(ymax-ymin)/res[1])) tris = [] for i in range(res[0]): for j in range(res[1]): idx = i(res[1]+1) + j tris.append([verts[idx], verts[idx+1], verts[idx+res[1]+1]]) tris.append([verts[idx+1], verts[idx+res[1]+2], verts[idx+res[1]+1]]) return verts, tris def countconnectedlowerwedges(v, lowerneighbors, triangles): if not lowerneighbors: return 0 visited = set() wedges = 0 for start in lowerneighbors: if start in visited: continue wedges += 1 q = [start] while q: curr = q.pop(0) if curr in visited: continue visited.add(curr) for tri in triangles: if curr in tri: for u in tri: if u != curr and u.density < v.density and u not in visited: q.append(u) return wedges Time Complexity: The complexity is dominated by the tessellation, critical point identification, and region growing. The region growing can be carried out quickly using flood-fill. The merging process involves sorting boundaries, which is O(B \log B) where B is the number of boundaries. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the triangular mesh, critical points, valley lines, and the hierarchical tree. Measured Performance: The method was tested on the "Feet" data set. The default threshold of 0.5% of maximal persistence was found sufficient to automatically generate meaningful clusters. Strengths: Non-parametric: Does not assume the number or shape of clusters. Continuous: Avoids spurious peaks and valleys associated with discrete histograms. Topological: Preserves spatial relationships in feature space. Hierarchical: Provides a tree structure for multi-scale exploration. Limitations: Degenerate cases in piecewise linear discretization require special handling (saddle duplication). Noise in the original data can create a large number of small valley cells, requiring simplification. When to Use: Suitable for automatic transfer function design in volume rendering when the user is not familiar with the data and needs an intuitive, non-parametric clustering of the 2D feature space. When Not to Use: When the feature space is not 2D (value and gradient magnitude) or when a discrete histogram approach is preferred for simplicity. Origin: Introduced by Yunhai Wang, Jian Zhang, Dirk J. Lehmann, Holger Theisel, and Xuebin Chi in the Eurographics Conference on Visualization 2012. History: The method is based on the theory of Morse complex [Sma61] and is inspired by the Morse complex construction scheme in [EHZ03]. It differs from hierarchical watershed segmentation by determining separability intrinsically during region growing rather than through flooding and overflow detection. It addresses limitations of previous methods like [MWCE09] which only considered density value magnitude and ignored position in feature space. name: Sketch Rendering via Silhouette Transparency
head: Volume Sketching, Volumetric Sketch Lines
body:
This method creates a sketch-like appearance by rendering volume features as lines or edges, making non-silhouette regions transparent and applying shadows based on the original volume's opacity. It differs from standard illustrative rendering by aggressively modulating opacity based on silhouette strength to abstract continuous volumetric data into discrete, sketch-like outlines, rather than preserving the full volumetric density structure. Inputs: Volume scalar field and view direction V{dir}. Light direction L{dir}. Sketch color (e.g., white or black). Original volume opacity \alpha{orig} computed from the transfer function and scalar values. Parameters: k{sc} (silhouette center), k{ss} (silhouette spread), k{se} (silhouette exponent). Outputs: Final fragment color and opacity. Data Structures: Fragment shader state holding the normalized gradient 
abla fn (a 3D vector) derived from the volume sample. Original volume opacity \alpha{orig} (a scalar) stored per sample for shadow calculation. Steps: 1. Compute Silhouette Enhancement Factor (E{sil}): Calculate the alignment between the view direction and the volume gradient normal 
abla fn. Features facing the viewer have low silhouette strength. The exact formula for E{sil} is not explicitly provided in the sources, but the parameters k{sc}, k{ss}, k{se} suggest a Gaussian-like or power-law falloff centered on the silhouette edge. A standard implementation is: E{sil} = \exp\left( -k{ss} \cdot (\max(0, 
abla fn \cdot V{dir}) - k{sc})^2 ight)^{k{se}} 2. Determine Sketch Opacity: Map E{sil} to the final opacity \alpha{final}. Regions with high silhouette enhancement (edges) remain opaque, while non-silhouette regions (interiors) become transparent. \alpha{final} = E{sil} 3. Set Sketch Color: The base color of the fragment is set to the specified sketch color (e.g., white or black). 4. Calculate Shadows: Compute the shadow term S using the original volume opacity \alpha{orig}, not the sketch opacity. This typically involves ray marching or pre-integration of \alpha{orig} along the light direction. 5. Composite Final Color: Modulate the sketch color and opacity by the shadow term S. C{final} = C{sketch} \cdot S \alpha{final} = \alpha{final} \cdot S Parameters: k{sc} = 0.9 (Silhouette center). k{ss} = 50 (Silhouette spread). k{se} = 0.25 (Silhouette exponent). Edge Cases: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sketchrender(gradientnormal, viewdir, lightdir, alphaorig, ksc, kss, kse, sketchcolor): # 1. Compute silhouette enhancement factor dotproduct = max(0.0, dot(gradientnormal, viewdir)) Esil = exp(-kss (dotproduct - ksc)2)kse # 2. Determine sketch opacity alphafinal = Esil # 3. Calculate shadows based on original volume opacity # Shadow integration along light direction S = integrateopacity(alphaorig, lightdir) # 4. Composite final color and opacity Cfinal = sketchcolor S alphafinal = alphafinal S return Cfinal, alphafinal Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Effectively emphasizes feature orientation and creates clear, stylized outlines of complex internal structures, such as the liver honeycomb and kidney interior. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When a sketch-like appearance is desired by making non-volumetric silhouettes transparent and shading them based on original volume opacity. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The technique originates from research on non-photorealistic rendering of volume models. It was developed to visualize complex internal structures in medical volumes by abstracting them into sketch-like forms that highlight boundaries and orientation. name: Illumination and Tone Shading Models
head: Illustrative Lighting, NPR Illumination
body: Illumination and Tone Shading Models are non-photorealistic rendering techniques that enhance volume visualization by decoupling lighting from physical light transport, using mathematical functions of view direction, light direction, and scalar field properties to modulate color. They simulate artistic lighting styles, such as painterly effects, cel-shading, or warm-to-cool gradients, to solve the problem of missing depth cues and feature abstraction in translucent volume rendering. Unlike photometric models, these methods map normal vectors or scalar values directly to pre-computed artistic colors or discrete tone bands, providing view-dependent or orientation-dependent shading that rotates with the camera or adapts to local data structure. The family shares the goal of enhancing volume visualization through stylized lighting and feature abstraction. All methods operate on fragment-level data, typically utilizing the volume sample gradient as a proxy for surface normal orientation. They decouple illumination from the physical light transport equation, instead using mathematical functions of the view direction, light direction, and scalar field properties to modulate color. Common inputs include the normalized gradient \nabla fn, light vectors L, and base colors derived from transfer functions. The output is a final color c that combines ambient/gaseous components with directed illumination effects. The framework utilizes four types of properties for enhancement: 1. Volume sample location and value. 2. Local volumetric properties, such as gradient and minimal change direction. 3. View direction. 4. Light information. Volumetric illustration differs from surface-based NPR in several important ways. In surface NPR, surfaces (features) are well-defined, whereas with volumes, feature areas within the volume must be determined through analysis of local volumetric properties because volumetric features vary continuously throughout three-dimensional space. Maps eye-space normal vectors to a pre-computed sphere texture to capture artistic lighting styles. It provides view-dependent lighting that rotates with the camera, ignoring front/back face ambiguity. Adjusts HSV color components based on the angle between the gradient and view direction. It simulates painterly effects where facing surfaces are desaturated/bright and receding surfaces are darkened/saturated. Maps gradient orientation relative to a light source to a warm-to-cool color gradient. It uses a positive dot product threshold to ensure zero contribution at orthogonal orientations, matching diffuse illumination models. A post-processing effect that darkens image corners based on the cubic alignment between ray direction and pixel frame normal, simulating projection falloff. Applies Blinn-Phong lighting followed by aggressive quantization (posterization) of diffuse bands and binary thresholding of specular highlights. Applies cel-shading to volumetric data using a pre-computed 3D normal map and hardware texture combiners, operating directly on the voxel gradient field without mesh extraction. Enhances material boundaries by using two scalar samples along the gradient direction as inputs to a 2D lighting transfer function, dynamically adjusting lighting coefficients based on local data structure. Uses the illumination model for curves of Banks to provide a better sense of curvature in line bundle rendering. Line bundles can be more opaque in this variant. A non-photorealistic rendering method used to visualize important information in an abstract but coherent way. The parameter \theta determines the effect of surrounding features, with higher values causing more distant features to increase shading variation. Tested values include 50^\circ and 85^\circ. The concept of Tone Rendering as a non-photorealistic method for abstract visualization was introduced in the context of volume visualization methods, contrasting with Phong Illumination which guarantees higher realistic images. The Banks illumination model for curves was applied in flow visualization techniques to enhance the perception of curvature in vector fields. name: Lit Sphere Shading
head: Lit sphere map shading, Sphere map shading
body: Lit sphere shading is a non-photorealistic rendering technique that captures artistic lighting styles by using an image of a sphere, shaded in a desired style, as a lookup table. It represents the shading of an object as a function of eye-space normal orientation, allowing the sphere to act as a proxy object for illumination. Unlike physical illumination models, it decouples lighting from light transport equations and relies on view-dependent mapping. It is distinct from Blinn-Phong Toon Shading and Volumetric Toon Shading because it does not compute lighting analytically per fragment but rather samples a pre-rendered or extracted artistic style map. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A lit sphere map texture T (square image), the normalized eye-space gradient \mathbf{n} = (nx, ny, nz) derived from the volume sample. Output: The final fragment color c. Data Structures: Lit Sphere Map (T): A square texture. The valid data is contained within an inscribed disk centered at (0.5, 0.5) in texture coordinates. Texels outside this disk are unused. Steps: 1. Sphere Map Acquisition: Obtain or render an image of a sphere under orthographic projection, shaded in the target artistic style. This image serves as the lit sphere map T. The sphere provides coverage of the complete set of unit normals on one hemisphere. 2. Normal Computation: For each volume fragment, compute the normalized eye-space gradient \mathbf{n} = (nx, ny, nz). This vector serves as the proxy surface normal. 3. Coordinate Conversion: Convert the nx and ny components of \mathbf{n}, which are in the range [-1, 1], to texture coordinates (u, v) in the range [0, 1]. 4. Lookup: Sample the lit sphere map T at (u, v) to retrieve the stylized color. 5. Output: Assign the sampled color to the fragment. Formulas: The texture coordinates (u, v) are calculated from the eye-space normal \mathbf{n} = (nx, ny, nz) as follows: u = \frac{nx + 1}{2} v = \frac{ny + 1}{2} Where: nx, ny \in [-1, 1] are the x and y components of the normalized eye-space gradient. u, v \in [0, 1] are the resulting texture coordinates. Parameters: Light Source Position: The light source is treated as a "headlight," rotating with the camera (view-dependent lighting). This is considered the desired setup in volume visualization. Texture Resolution: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Z-Component Ignorance: The nz component of the normal is ignored during indexing. Consequently, lighting does not distinguish between front and back faces. This is intentional because the gradient direction in volume data (used as the normal) might be flipped depending on data values at a material boundary. Boundary Access: Texture coordinates must be clamped to [0, 1] to prevent out-of-bounds sampling if \mathbf{n} is not perfectly normalized or due to precision errors, though the sources state texels outside the disk are "never accessed" by design. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def litsphereshading(normaleyespace, litspheremap, mapheight, mapwidth): """ Shading method using a lit sphere map. Args: normaleyespace: Tuple (nx, ny, nz) of the normalized eye-space gradient. litspheremap: 2D array of shape (mapheight, mapwidth, 3) representing the lit sphere map. mapheight: Integer height of the texture. mapwidth: Integer width of the texture. Returns: Color value sampled from the lit sphere map. """ nx, ny, nz = normaleyespace # Convert eye-space normal components from [-1, 1] to [0, 1] # The nz component is intentionally ignored as per the method definition u = (nx + 1.0) / 2.0 v = (ny + 1.0) / 2.0 # Clamp coordinates to valid texture range u = max(0.0, min(1.0, u)) v = max(0.0, min(1.0, v)) # Map to array indices (assuming top-left origin for array indexing) # In practice, this step uses hardware texture sampling with interpolation colidx = int(u (mapwidth - 1)) rowidx = int(v (mapheight - 1)) # Sample the lit sphere map color = litspheremap[rowidx, colidx] return color Lit sphere shading is often used as a component of style transfer functions, where the sphere map defines the lighting style while other parameters modulate color based on scalar values. Lit sphere maps can be extracted from non-spherical regions in existing pieces of artwork using interactive tools, allowing for the rapid creation of style databases. Time Complexity: O(1) per fragment for the lookup, assuming constant-time texture sampling. Memory Complexity: O(R^2) for the lit sphere map texture, where R is the resolution. Strengths: Well-suited to represent the general shading style of an object; images are relatively easy to obtain; allows for a large database of styles with little effort; view-dependent lighting effects appear regular. Limitations: Fails to capture complex aspects of realistic illumination. Cannot distinguish front/back faces, which may be undesirable in some surface-based contexts but is accepted for volume gradients. When to use: When a stylized, artistic lighting appearance is desired that moves with the camera, and computational efficiency is prioritized over physical accuracy. When not to use: When physically accurate light transport or complex shadowing/occlusion effects are required. Lit sphere shading was originally presented by Sloan et al. [SMGG01] for non-photorealistic rendering of polygonal models. It was adapted for illustrative volume rendering in the paper [Style Transfer Functions for Illustrative Volume Rendering]. The technique leverages the fact that a sphere under orthographic projection covers the complete set of unit normals on one hemisphere, making it an ideal proxy for capturing normal-dependent shading variations. name: Orientation-Based Color Modification
head: HSV Color Orientation, HSV color modification, oriented fading
body:
Orientation-Based Color Modification is a non-photorealistic volume rendering technique that modulates the color, saturation, value, and transparency of volume samples based on the orientation of the local volumetric gradient relative to the viewer. It addresses the lack of depth cues in translucent volumes by simulating illustrative "oriented fading," where structures facing the viewer are desaturated and structures oriented away are darkened and saturated. It sets itself apart from general illumination models by operating directly in the HSV color space to decouple brightness from hue and saturation, enabling painterly effects that mimic traditional medical illustration techniques. Inputs: Volume sample color C{rgb} (from transfer function). Normalized volumetric gradient 
abla fn (proxy for surface normal). View direction V (normalized vector from sample to camera). Outputs: Modified color C'{rgb} and potentially modified opacity \alpha'. Data Structures: The method operates on per-fragment (or per-sample) data. No persistent global data structures are required beyond the volume grid and transfer function. Intermediate state uses HSV color space components: Hue (H), Saturation (S), Value (V). Steps: 1. Compute Orientation: Calculate the angle 	heta between the normalized gradient 
abla fn and the view direction V using the dot product: \cos 	heta = 
abla fn \cdot V. The angle 	heta ranges from 0 (gradient aligned with view, facing viewer) to \pi (gradient opposed to view, receding). 2. Convert to HSV: Convert the input RGB color C{rgb} to HSV space (H, S, V). 3. Modulate Value (Brightness): Decrease the Value component V as the angle 	heta increases, simulating "oriented fading". The modified value is computed as V' = V \cdot \max(0, \cos 	heta). 4. Modulate Saturation (Optional): Desaturate surfaces oriented toward the viewer (small 	heta) and saturate surfaces oriented away from the viewer (large 	heta). The modified saturation is computed as S' = S \cdot (1.0 - 0.5 \cdot \max(0, \cos 	heta)). 5. Modulate Transparency (Optional): Adjust opacity \alpha based on orientation to enhance depth cues. 6. Convert to RGB: Convert the modified HSV values (H, S', V') back to RGB space to obtain C'{rgb}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def orientationbasedcolormodification(rgbcolor, gradientnormalized, viewdirection): # 1. Compute orientation factor (cos theta) costheta = max(-1.0, min(1.0, gradientnormalized[0]viewdirection[0] + gradientnormalized[1]viewdirection[1] + gradientnormalized[2]viewdirection[2])) # 2. Convert RGB to HSV h, s, v = rgbtohsv(rgbcolor) # 3. Modulate Value: decrease as angle increases (costheta decreases) vmodified = v max(0.0, costheta) # 4. Modulate Saturation: desaturate facing, saturate receding smodified = s (1.0 - 0.5 max(0.0, costheta)) # 5. Convert back to RGB return hsvtorgb(h, smodified, vmodified) def rgbtohsv(rgb): r, g, b = rgb cmax = max(r, g, b) cmin = min(r, g, b) delta = cmax - cmin if delta == 0: h = 0.0 elif cmax == r: h = 60.0 (((g - b) / delta) % 6) elif cmax == g: h = 60.0 (((b - r) / delta) + 2) else: h = 60.0 (((r - g) / delta) + 4) s = 0.0 if cmax == 0 else delta / cmax v = cmax return h, s, v def hsvtorgb(h, s, v): c = v s x = c (1.0 - abs((h / 60.0) % 2 - 1.0)) m = v - c if h < 60: r, g, b = c, x, 0 elif h < 120: r, g, b = x, c, 0 elif h < 180: r, g, b = 0, c, x elif h < 240: r, g, b = 0, x, c elif h < 300: r, g, b = x, 0, c else: r, g, b = c, 0, x return (r + m, g + m, b + m) Oriented Color Modification is a technique that adjusts the color value (brightness) of volume samples based on the orientation of the surface gradient relative to the viewer, simulating illustrative "oriented fading". It sets itself apart from general illumination models by operating directly in the HSV color space to decouple brightness from hue and saturation, allowing for painterly effects where facing surfaces remain bright and edge-on surfaces fade. Choose this when aiming for medical illustration styles where depth is conveyed through color intensity changes rather than shadows. A method to avoid false color effects in volume rendering where semi-transparency causes hue changes during color mixing, by adjusting saturation and blending weights. It reduces the global or local (in the overlap region only) saturation and blending weight of the background object in the mixture to control hue. Choose this when blending semi-transparent volumes to maintain harmonic color scales and avoid non-harmonic hue shifts caused by color mixing. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample/fragment, as it involves a dot product, HSV conversion, and simple arithmetic. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per sample. Strengths: Provides strong depth cues in translucent volumes where traditional shadows are absent; operates directly in HSV space for intuitive control. Limitations: Relies on the quality of gradient estimation; the effect is stylized and not physically based. When to use: Medical visualization and scientific illustration requiring enhanced depth perception in translucent data without photorealism. The method originates from non-photorealistic rendering (NPR) techniques for volume visualization, specifically drawing inspiration from medical illustration practices where anatomical structures oriented toward the viewer are desaturated and those oriented away are darkened and saturated. It was formalized in the context of "Non-Photorealistic Rendering of Volume Models" presented at IEEE Visualization '00. The approach leverages the HSV color space to provide an intuitive framework for applying these illustrative rules. name: Oriented Color Modification
body: Oriented Color Modification is a technique that adjusts the color value (brightness) of volume samples based on the orientation of the surface gradient relative to the viewer, simulating illustrative "oriented fading". It sets itself apart from general illumination models by operating directly in the HSV color space to decouple brightness from hue and saturation, allowing for painterly effects where facing surfaces remain bright and edge-on surfaces fade. Inputs: Volume sample color C in RGB. Volume sample opacity \alpha. Gradient vector \mathbf{g} at the sample point. View direction vector \mathbf{v} (typically from sample to camera). Outputs: Modified color C' and opacity \alpha'. Data Structures: Vectors \mathbf{g} and \mathbf{v} are 3D floating-point vectors. Color is converted to HSV space for modification. Steps: 1. Compute the angle \theta between the gradient \mathbf{g} and the view direction \mathbf{v}. \cos \theta = \frac{\mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{g}\| \|\mathbf{v}\|} 2. Convert the sample color from RGB to HSV. Let the value component be V. 3. Decrease V as \theta increases (i.e., as the surface becomes more edge-on to the viewer). The exact mapping function is not specified in the primary source, but the trend is monotonic decrease with increasing angle. 4. Convert the modified HSV color back to RGB to obtain C'. 5. (Optional/Variant) Modulate opacity \alpha based on the same or similar orientation metrics. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def orientedcolormodification(rgbcolor, gradient, viewdirection): # Normalize vectors glen = (gradient[0]2 + gradient[1]2 + gradient[2]2)0.5 vlen = (viewdirection[0]2 + viewdirection[1]2 + viewdirection[2]2)0.5 gnorm = (gradient[0]/glen, gradient[1]/glen, gradient[2]/glen) vnorm = (viewdirection[0]/vlen, viewdirection[1]/vlen, viewdirection[2]/vlen) # Calculate cosine of the angle between gradient and view costheta = gnorm[0]vnorm[0] + gnorm[1]vnorm[1] + gnorm[2]vnorm[2] # Convert RGB to HSV hsvcolor = rgbtohsv(rgbcolor) h, s, v = hsvcolor # Decrease value V as angle increases (costheta decreases) # Note: Exact formula for V' vs theta is not provided in # Assuming a linear fade for implementation completeness: vmodified = v (0.5 + 0.5 costheta) # Clamp value to [0, 1] vmodified = max(0.0, min(1.0, vmodified)) # Convert back to RGB newrgb = hsvtorgb((h, s, vmodified)) return newrgb def rgbtohsv(rgb): # Standard RGB to HSV conversion r, g, b = rgb[0]/255.0, rgb[1]/255.0, rgb[2]/255.0 cmax = max(r, g, b) cmin = min(r, g, b) delta = cmax - cmin if delta == 0: h = 0 elif cmax == r: h = 60 (((g - b) / delta) % 6) elif cmax == g: h = 60 (((b - r) / delta) + 2) else: h = 60 (((r - g) / delta) + 4) s = 0 if cmax == 0 else delta / cmax v = cmax return (h, s, v) def hsvtorgb(hsv): # Standard HSV to RGB conversion h, s, v = hsv c = v s x = c (1 - abs((h / 60) % 2 - 1)) m = v - c if h < 60: r1, g1, b1 = c, x, 0 elif h < 120: r1, g1, b1 = x, c, 0 elif h < 180: r1, g1, b1 = 0, c, x elif h < 240: r1, g1, b1 = 0, x, c elif h < 300: r1, g1, b1 = x, 0, c else: r1, g1, b1 = c, 0, x return ((r1 + m) 255, (g1 + m) 255, (b1 + m) 255) Edge Cases: Zero Gradient: If \|\mathbf{g}\| = 0, the direction is undefined. Handle by preserving original color or using a default view-aligned value. Precision: Floating-point errors in dot product near boundaries. A specific implementation of oriented color modification within the Importance-Driven Volume Rendering (IDVR) framework. It modulates color by calculating a new specular intensity based on modified gradients along cut-away borders and modulates the opacity of the current sample point prior to adapted compositing. It is integrated into the IDVRMImPCompositingModelSW class. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, as it involves basic vector operations and color space conversion. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per sample. Strengths: Provides intuitive, painterly control over visual emphasis; decouples brightness from color identity. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Illustrative volume rendering, medical visualization where edge-on structures need to be deemphasized. Introduced within volume illustration for non-photorealistic rendering. It adapts traditional illustration techniques of oriented fading to 3D volume data, leveraging the HSV color space for intuitive control. name: Volume Illustration Tone Shading
head: Gooch tone shading for volumes, Modified Gooch tone shading for volume, Modified Gooch tone shading for volume models, Tone Shading, Tone illumination model, Volumetric tone shading
body:
Volume Illustration Tone Shading is a non-photorealistic illumination model that enhances the perception of 3D shape in volume rendering by modulating color temperature based on the orientation of volume samples relative to a light source. It assigns warm colors (yellows/reds) to regions facing the light and cool colors (blues) to receding regions, creating an illustrative effect suggestive of warm light sources like sunlight. Unlike standard Gooch shading which uses the full signed dot product for illumination, this method modifies the illuminated object contribution to be zero at orientations orthogonal to the light vector, matching familiar diffuse illumination models more closely. It builds on Illumination and Tone Shading Models by combining gaseous illumination with directed tone shading. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volume scalar field f. Transfer function T(v) mapping scalar value v to base color c{base} and opacity \alpha. Normalized volume sample gradient

Formulas: The final color c is a weighted sum of gaseous illumination and the total tone and directed shading from all light sources: c = k{ta} IG + \sum{i=1}^{NL} (It + k{td} Io) Where: k{ta} controls the amount of gaseous illumination IG included. NL is the number of light sources. k{td} controls the amount of directed illumination included. It is the tone contribution to volume sample color. Io is the illuminated object color contribution. Gooch Shading is a non-photorealistic illumination model for volume rendering that maps surface orientation relative to a light source to a warm-to-cool color gradient to convey shape. It is distinguished from standard Gooch shading by its specific integration with on-the-fly central difference normal estimation in rasterization pipelines, ensuring consistent visual output across different extraction methods (rasterization vs. ray-marching). Cool to warm shading is a non-photorealistic illumination model that enhances the perception of 3D shape by mapping surface orientation relative to the viewer or light source to a color gradient, assigning warmer colors to facing regions and cooler colors to receding regions. Unlike physically based models like Phong, which may obscure shape information in shadowed areas, this method ensures that orientation cues are preserved across the entire visible surface. It builds on Volume Illustration Tone Shading by replacing the signed dot product illumination term with a direct view/light-dependent color mapping. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of volume samples per ray and the number of light sources NL. Each sample requires gradient computation, dot products, and color interpolation. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume data, gradient field (if precomputed), and transfer function. Performance: The method is computationally efficient as it avoids complex light transport calculations, relying on simple dot products and color interpolation. Strengths: Enhances shape perception and depth cues effectively; preserves basic tissue colors while adding illustrative shading; works well with medical and scientific data. Limitations: Can produce confusing results with too many lights; relies on accurate gradient estimation; the illustrative style may not be suitable for all scientific visualization tasks requiring photorealism. When to Use: When enhancing 3D shape perception and depth relationships in volume data is prioritized over photorealism, particularly in medical or scientific visualization. When Not to Use: When photorealistic rendering is required or when the scene contains complex lighting interactions that cannot be approximated by simple directional lights. Volume Illustration Tone Shading is based on the Gooch tone shading model proposed by Gooch et al. in 1998. It was adapted for volume rendering by Wilson, Lum, and Ma in their work on "Volume Illustration: Non-Photorealistic Rendering of Volume Models" (2000/2001). The method was applied to medical volumes (liver/kidney CT) and scientific data (iron protein, tomato MRI) to demonstrate its effectiveness in revealing internal structures and enhancing 3D shape perception. name: Gooch Shading
head: Central Difference Normal Shading, Gooch Shading with Central Difference Normals, Gooch Tone Shading, Phong/Tone Shading
body: Gooch Shading is a non-photorealistic illumination model for volume rendering that maps surface orientation relative to a light source to a warm-to-cool color gradient to convey shape. It is distinguished from standard Gooch shading by its specific integration with on-the-fly central difference normal estimation in rasterization pipelines, ensuring consistent visual output across different extraction methods (rasterization vs. ray-marching). Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scalar volume data V(x,y,z), light direction vector \mathbf{L}, warm color Cw, cool color Cc, warm/cool ratios kw, kc, base ray sample color Ir, and opacity \alpha. Output: Final fragment color c. Data Structures: Vertex Normals: Computed on the fly using central differences on the scalar field. No pre-computed normal buffer is required for the rasterization approach. Steps: 1. Normal Estimation: For each vertex or sample point on the isosurface, compute the gradient \mathbf{G} using central differences: \mathbf{G} = [\frac{\partial V}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial V}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial V}{\partial z}], where \frac{\partial V}{\partial x} \approx \frac{V(x+1, y, z) - V(x-1, y, z)}{2}, and similarly for y and z. Normalize \mathbf{G} to unit length. 2. Pass to Fragment Shader: The computed normal \mathbf{G} and normalized light direction \mathbf{L} are passed to the fragment shader. 3. Dot Product Factor: Compute \kappa = \mathbf{G} \cdot \mathbf{L}. The illuminated contribution uses only the positive dot product, becoming zero at orthogonal orientations. 4. Tone Contribution: Calculate It by interpolating between Cw and Cc based on \kappa: It = \left(kw \frac{1.0 + \kappa}{2}\right) Cw + \left(kc \left(1 - \frac{1.0 + \kappa}{2}\right)\right) Cc. 5. Final Color: Combine the tone contribution with the base ray sample color Ir and opacity \alpha: c = It \alpha + Ir (1 - \alpha). For multiple light sources, sum over all NL lights: c = \sum{i=1}^{NL} (I{ti} \alpha + I{ri} (1 - \alpha)). Parameters: Warm Color (Cw): Typically yellow, defined as RGB (Rw, Gw, Bw). Cool Color (Cc): Typically blue, defined as RGB (Rc, Gc, Bc). Ratios (kw, kc): Weights for warm and cool color contribution to the final result. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Central difference requires neighboring voxels; boundary handling is not specified in the sources. Degenerate Normals: If the scalar field is flat (zero gradient), the normal is undefined. Orthogonal Orientations: The dot product \kappa naturally handles values between -1 and 1, but the illuminated contribution becomes zero at orthogonal orientations (\kappa = 0). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecentraldifferencenormal(volume, x, y, z): # Central difference gradient approximation dx = (volume[x + 1, y, z] - volume[x - 1, y, z]) / 2.0 dy = (volume[x, y + 1, z] - volume[x, y - 1, z]) / 2.0 dz = (volume[x, y, z + 1] - volume[x, y, z - 1]) / 2.0 length = (dxdx + dydy + dzdz) 0.5 if length == 0.0: return vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Degenerate case: flat field return vec3(dx / length, dy / length, dz / length) def goocheshadingfragment(G, L, Cw, Cc, kw, kc, alpha, Ir): # Compute dot product factor kappa, clamped to positive values per source kappa = max(0.0, dot(G, L)) # Calculate tone contribution interpolation factor t = (1.0 + kappa) / 2.0 # Interpolate between warm and cool colors It = (kw t) Cw + (kc (1.0 - t)) Cc # Blend tone contribution with base ray sample color using opacity c = It alpha + Ir (1.0 - alpha) return c Time Complexity: Normal computation is O(1) per vertex/sample. Shading is O(1) per fragment. Memory Complexity: No additional memory for normals if computed on the fly. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Consistent visual appearance across different rendering techniques (rasterization and ray-marching) due to identical fragment shader implementation. Limitations: Relies on central difference normal estimation, which requires neighboring voxels and may produce undefined normals in flat regions. Boundary handling is not specified in the sources. Gooch Shading was originally proposed by Gooch et al. in 1998. It is used in volume rendering to provide illustrative shading that enhances shape perception by mapping orientation to warm and cool tones. The specific application with central difference normals in rasterization is described in. name: Cool to Warm Shading
head: Tone-based shading, Warm-to-cool Shading
body: Cool to warm shading is a non-photorealistic illumination model that enhances the perception of 3D shape by mapping surface orientation relative to the viewer or light source to a color gradient, assigning warmer colors to facing regions and cooler colors to receding regions. Unlike physically based models like Phong, which may obscure shape information in shadowed areas, this method ensures that orientation cues are preserved across the entire visible surface. It builds on Volume Illustration Tone Shading by replacing the signed dot product illumination term with a direct view/light-dependent color mapping. Inputs: Volume scalar field data. Camera position and view direction. Light direction (if using light-relative shading) or view direction (if using view-relative shading). Two color endpoints: a "cool" color (C{cool}) and a "warm" color (C{warm}). Outputs: Rendered pixel color. Data Structures: Color vectors C{cool} and C{warm}, typically RGB triplets. Normal vector \mathbf{n} at the sample point, derived from the volume gradient. Direction vector \mathbf{d}, defined as the view direction (from sample to camera) or light direction (from sample to light), normalized. Steps: 1. Compute the surface normal \mathbf{n} at the current volume sample. 2. Determine the direction vector \mathbf{d}. Sources differ on whether this is relative to the viewer or the light source. describes it as relative to the light source ("regions facing away from the light"), while describes it as relative to the observer ("surfaces facing the observer"). The implementation should allow selection of the reference vector. 3. Calculate the dot product k = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}. 4. Map k to a blending factor \alpha. Since \mathbf{n} and \mathbf{d} are unit vectors, k \in [-1, 1]. To map this to [0, 1] for linear interpolation: \alpha = \frac{k + 1}{2} If k < -1, clamp \alpha to 0. If k > 1, clamp \alpha to 1. 5. Interpolate between the cool and warm colors: C{final} = (1 - \alpha) C{cool} + \alpha C{warm} 6. Combine C{final} with the volume's opacity and density information, typically by using C{final} as the base color in the standard volume rendering integration equation. Parameters: C{cool}: Typical values are blues or cyans (e.g., (0.0, 0.0, 1.0)). C{warm}: Typical values are reds, oranges, or yellows (e.g., (1.0, 0.5, 0.0)). Reference vector: View direction or Light direction. Edge Cases: Degenerate Normals: If the gradient is zero (flat region), \mathbf{n} is undefined. Default to a neutral color or the average scene color. Precision: Dot product precision may affect subtle shading gradients in smooth volumes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cooltowarmshading(normal, viewdir, lightdir, uselightrelative=True, colorcool, colorwarm): # Determine reference direction if uselightrelative: direction = lightdir else: direction = viewdir # Ensure vectors are normalized direction = normalize(direction) normal = normalize(normal) # Compute dot product dotproduct = dot(normal, direction) # Clamp to [-1, 1] to handle numerical errors dotproduct = clamp(dotproduct, -1.0, 1.0) # Map to [0, 1] alpha = (dotproduct + 1.0) / 2.0 # Interpolate colors finalcolor = lerp(colorcool, colorwarm, alpha) return finalcolor Uses the view direction as the reference. Best for emphasizing silhouette and depth perception independent of light position. Uses the light direction as the reference. Best for consistent shading relative to a fixed light source, similar to diffuse lighting but with color mapping. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, same as standard shading. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for color parameters. Strengths: Enhances shape perception in regions that would otherwise be dark or featureless in physically based shading. Simple to implement and tune. Limitations: Does not simulate physical light interaction. Color choice is subjective and may not suit all data types. When to use: When shape perception is critical and physical accuracy is not required. Often used with silhouette edges. The cool to warm shading model was proposed by Gooch et al. in 1998. It is part of the broader field of illustrative rendering, which aims to enhance visual communication rather than photorealism. The technique is often compared to Gooch shading [1670-gooch-shading.md], with which it shares the goal of using color to convey orientation. name: Vignette Shading
head: Cubic Vignette, Vignette, Vignette Effect
body: Vignette Shading is a post-processing technique applied to display images to darken the corners and edges, simulating the optical falloff of light intensity due to projection onto a flat plane. It enhances the visual focus on the center of the image by modulating brightness based on the distance from the focal point or the alignment of the view ray with the camera's optical axis. Inputs and Outputs: The method operates on the final rendered image (or fragment color) before tonemapping. Inputs include pixel coordinates (or UVs), the ray direction \mathbf{r}, and camera frame information. The output is a modulated color c{\text{final}} = c{\text{base}} \cdot V, where V is the vignette factor. Data Structures: No complex volumetric data structures are required. The method relies on screen-space UV coordinates or ray vectors. Formulas and Parameters: Two primary formulations exist in the sources: 1. Cubic Alignment Vignette: This variant calculates the factor based on the alignment between the ray direction and the camera's z-axis (the third component of the pixel frame). V = (\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{f}z)^3 Where: \mathbf{r} is the normalized ray direction. \mathbf{f}z is the third component (z-axis) of the pixel frame. The result is cubed to create a smooth falloff. Alternatively, expressed using geometric parameters: \text{Factor} = \frac{f^2}{f^2+rp^2}(\mathbf{v}p \cdot \mathbf{n}p) = (\cos \theta)^3 = (\mathbf{v}p \cdot \mathbf{n}p)^3 Where: f is the focal distance. rp is the radial distance between pixel p and the line of focus. \mathbf{n}p is the unit normal of pixel p. \mathbf{v}p is a unit vector from pixel p to the focal point. \theta is the angle between the view vector and the normal. 2. UV Coordinate Vignette Effect: This variant uses normalized UV coordinates to darken corners. V = 0.5 + 0.5 \cdot (16 \cdot u \cdot v \cdot (1-u) \cdot (1-v))^{0.25} Where: u, v are normalized UV coordinates ranging from 0 to 1. The term 16 \cdot u \cdot v \cdot (1-u) \cdot (1-v) peaks at the center (0.5, 0.5) and drops to 0 at the edges. Pseudocode: The following implementation combines the cubic alignment method and the UV method. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vignetteshadingcubic(raydirections, pixelframes): """ Applies cubic vignette shading based on ray alignment with camera z-axis. Args: raydirections: Tensor of shape (..., 3) containing normalized ray directions. pixelframes: Tensor of shape (..., 3, 3) containing camera frame vectors. The z-axis is at index 2. Returns: Tensor of vignette factors. """ # Extract the z-axis (third component) of the pixel frame cameraz = pixelframes[..., 2] # Calculate dot product between ray direction and camera z-axis dotproduct = (raydirections cameraz).sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True) # Cube the result to create the vignette falloff vignettefactor = dotproduct.pow(3) return vignettefactor def vignetteshadinguv(uvcoords): """ Applies vignette shading based on UV coordinates. Args: uvcoords: Tensor of shape (..., 2) containing normalized UV coordinates (u, v). Returns: Tensor of vignette factors. """ u = uvcoords[..., 0] v = uvcoords[..., 1] # Calculate the term inside the root term = 16.0 u v (1.0 - u) (1.0 - v) # Apply the formula: 0.5 + 0.5 (term)^0.25 vignettefactor = 0.5 + 0.5 term.pow(0.25) return vignettefactor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Direction Normalization: The cubic method requires \mathbf{r} to be normalized; otherwise, the dot product will scale with ray length, causing incorrect shading. Negative Dot Products: If the ray direction points away from the camera's forward axis, the dot product may be negative. Cubing a negative number preserves the sign, potentially leading to inverted or dark artifacts. Clamping the dot product to [0, 1] or using absolute values may be necessary depending on the desired visual effect. UV Coordinate Range: The UV method assumes u, v \in [0, 1]. Coordinates outside this range will produce unexpected results. A specific variant of vignette shading that relies solely on screen-space UV coordinates rather than ray geometry. It produces a symmetric darkening centered on the image midpoint. Time and Memory Complexity: The method is O(1) per pixel and requires minimal memory, as it only needs local pixel data (UVs or ray vectors). It is computationally inexpensive compared to volumetric illumination models. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The effect is applied per-pixel, with computational cost independent of resolution. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple to implement; effective at directing viewer attention; works well with both ray marching and rasterization. Limitations: It is a post-processing effect applied before tonemapping. When to Use: Use when a stylized, cinematic look is desired, or when the optical properties of the camera need to be simulated for illustrative purposes. When Not to Use: Avoid when physical accuracy is required, as the effect is not based on light transport physics. Vignette shading originates from photographic optics, where lenses naturally produce darker corners due to light falloff and sensor orientation. In computer graphics, it has been adopted as a stylized post-processing effect to enhance image composition. name: Vignette Effect
head: Post-processing Vignette, Vignetting Post-Processing
body: The Vignette Effect darkens the corners and edges of a rendered image relative to the center, simulating optical lens falloff or drawing attention to the focal point. It is applied as a post-processing step to the final color buffer, distinct from volumetric illumination models like Vignette Shading which modulate lighting based on ray alignment within the volume. Inputs and Outputs Input: Final rendered color buffer (RGB or RGBA), image dimensions (W \times H). Output: Vignette-modified color buffer. Data Structures UV Coordinates: Normalized coordinates (u, v) where u \in [0, 1] and v \in [0, 1], representing the pixel's position in the image plane. Steps 1. For each pixel, calculate normalized UV coordinates: u = \frac{x}{W}, \quad v = \frac{y}{H} where x and y are pixel coordinates. 2. Compute the vignette factor. Two common formulations exist in the sources: Formulation A (Polynomial/Root-based): \text{vignette\factor} = 0.5 + 0.5 \cdot \left( 16 \cdot u \cdot v \cdot (1-u) \cdot (1-v) \right)^{0.25} The final color is multiplied by this factor. Formulation B (Power-based with Fringe): Let pos{2d} be the 2D position vector from the image center, and fr be a fringe radius parameter. \text{vignetting} = \min\left(\frac{\|pos{2d}\|}{fr}, 1.0\right) \text{vignetting} = \left( 1.0 - \text{vignetting}^2 \right)^{20.0} The color is mixed with a background color weighted by this factor: \text{color}{out} = \text{mix}(\text{vignetting\background} \cdot \text{color}w, \text{color}{xyz}, \text{vignetting}) where \text{color}w is the alpha channel and \text{color}{xyz} is the RGB channels. Parameters fr: Fringe radius. Not given in the sources for Formulation A. For Formulation B, typical values are not specified, but it controls the onset of the darkening. Exponent (20.0 in Formulation B): Controls the steepness of the vignette. Not given in the sources for Formulation A. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The term u \cdot v \cdot (1-u) \cdot (1-v) in Formulation A is zero at the edges and center, potentially causing floating-point underflow or exact zero results if not handled, though the root operation is stable. Boundaries: Formulation A naturally goes to 0.5 at the corners (since u,v \to 0 or 1), while Formulation B can go to 0 depending on the exponent and fr. Degenerate Input: If W or H is 0, UV calculation fails. Ensure W, H > 0. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applyvignetteuv(colorbuffer, width, height, vignettebackground=(0,0,0)): """ Applies vignette effect using Formulation A and Formulation B. colorbuffer: Nx3 or Nx4 array of floats [0,1]. Returns: Modified color buffer. """ h, w, c = colorbuffer.shape # Generate UV coordinates u = np.arange(w) / width v = np.arange(h) / height U, V = np.meshgrid(u, v) # Formulation A # Term inside root: 16 u v (1-u) (1-v) terma = 16.0 U V (1.0 - U) (1.0 - V) # Clamp to avoid negative due to precision terma = np.maximum(terma, 0.0) vignettefactora = 0.5 + 0.5 np.power(terma, 0.25) # Apply Formulation A resulta = colorbuffer vignettefactora[:,:, np.newaxis] # Formulation B # Center coordinates cx, cy = width / 2.0, height / 2.0 # 2D position from center posx = (np.arange(w) - cx) / width # Normalize by width for consistency? Source uses imagecoords directly. posy = (np.arange(h) - cy) / height PX, PY = np.meshgrid(posx, posy) pos2d = np.sqrt(PX2 + PY2) # Fringe radius. Not given in sources. Using 1.0 as normalized max distance approx. fr = 1.0 vignetting = np.minimum(pos2d / fr, 1.0) vignetting = np.power(1.0 - np.power(vignetting, 2.0), 20.0) # Mix with background # Assuming RGBA input for alpha handling if c == 4: alpha = colorbuffer[:,:, 3] rgb = colorbuffer[:,:,:3] bgrgb = vignettebackground # mix(bg alpha, rgb, vignetting) # Note: Source mixes vignettingbackground color.w with color.xyz mixedrgb = np.where( vignetting[:,:, np.newaxis] > 0.5, # Simple threshold for mix? No, mix is linear. bgrgb alpha[:,:, np.newaxis], rgb) # Correct linear mix: vignettingexpanded = vignetting[:,:, np.newaxis] resultbrgb = vignettingexpanded (vignettebackground alpha[:,:, np.newaxis]) + (1.0 - vignettingexpanded) rgb resultb = np.concatenate([resultbrgb, alpha[:,:, np.newaxis]], axis=2) else: # If no alpha, just multiply? Source implies alpha usage. # Fallback to simple multiplication if alpha not present, though source specifies mix. resultb = colorbuffer vignetting[:,:, np.newaxis] return resulta, resultb def applyvignettesimple(colorbuffer, width, height): """ Simplified implementation of Formulation A. """ h, w, c = colorbuffer.shape u = np.arange(w) / width v = np.arange(h) / height U, V = np.meshgrid(u, v) term = 16.0 U V (1.0 - U) (1.0 - V) term = np.maximum(term, 0.0) factor = 0.5 + 0.5 np.power(term, 0.25) return colorbuffer factor[:,:, np.newaxis] Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H) per frame, as it requires a single pass over all pixels. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) for the output buffer. Strengths: Computationally inexpensive; easily implemented as a post-process; effective for artistic stylization. Limitations: Does not account for 3D scene geometry or depth; purely 2D effect. When to use: When a quick artistic darkening of edges is desired without modifying the rendering pipeline or lighting models. When not to use: When physically accurate lens simulation is required (requires more complex optical models) or when the effect needs to interact with volumetric density. The vignette effect is a common post-processing technique in computer graphics and photography. The specific polynomial formulation using 16 \cdot u \cdot v \cdot (1-u) \cdot (1-v) is cited from. The power-based formulation with a fringe radius is cited from. arguskern/lumina-graphics-lab, https://github.com/arguskern/lumina-graphics-lab, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) notlasandu/spirulae-splat, https://github.com/notlasandu/spirulae-splat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Blinn-Phong Toon Shading
head: Toon Blinn-Phong
body: Blinn-Phong Toon Shading is a non-photorealistic illumination model that applies posterization to the diffuse component and binary thresholding to the specular component of the standard Blinn-Phong lighting equation. It differs from its siblings by explicitly discretizing continuous lighting values into distinct bands. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Normalized light direction vector L, normalized normal N (derived from volume gradient), normalized view direction V, normalized half-vector H = \frac{L+V}{\|L+V\|}, base color C{base}, shininess exponent k, and diffuse thresholds A=0.1, B=0.3, C=0.6, D=1.0. Outputs: Final fragment color C{final}. Data Structures: The method operates on scalar values and vectors computed per fragment. Parameters: Shininess k: Not given in the sources. Diffuse Thresholds: A=0.1, B=0.3, C=0.6, D=1.0. Steps: 1. Compute the diffuse factor fd using the dot product of the light direction and normal: fd = \max(0, L \cdot N) 2. Compute the specular factor fs using the dot product of the half-vector and normal, raised to the shininess power: fs = \max(0, H \cdot N)^k 3. Posterize the diffuse factor fd into discrete levels: If fd < 0.1, set fd = 0.0. Else if fd < 0.3, set fd = 0.3. Else if fd < 0.6, set fd = 0.6. Else, set fd = 1.0. 4. Apply a harsh cut (binary threshold) to the specular factor fs: fs = \text{step}(0.2, fs) 5. Combine the components with an ambient term C{amb} and specular color C{spec}: C{final} = C{amb} + (C{base} \cdot fd) + (C{spec} \cdot fs) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def blinnphongtoonshading(L, N, V, Cbase, Cspec, k, Camb=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)): L = normalize(L) N = normalize(N) V = normalize(V) H = normalize(L + V) diffusefactor = max(0.0, dot(L, N)) specularfactor = pow(max(0.0, dot(H, N)), k) if diffusefactor < 0.1: diffusefactor = 0.0 elif diffusefactor < 0.3: diffusefactor = 0.3 elif diffusefactor < 0.6: diffusefactor = 0.6 else: diffusefactor = 1.0 specularfactor = 1.0 if specularfactor >= 0.2 else 0.0 return Camb + (Cbase diffusefactor) + (Cspec specularfactor) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. A shading mode that enhances edges by darkening pixels where the surface normal is nearly perpendicular to the view direction. It calculates dv = \text{dot}(V, N) and ev = \text{pow}(1.0 - |dv|, 0.3). If ev \ge 0.1, it mixes the color towards black using \text{mix}(color.rgb, \text{vec3}(0), \text{pow}((ev-0.1)/(1.0 - 0.1), 6)). The edge threshold et is 0.1. Not given in the sources. The method is a toon-shaded variant of the Blinn-Phong model. fargiolas/qvrc, https://github.com/fargiolas/qvrc, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Volumetric Toon Shading
head: Fragment Shader Toon-Shading for Volumes, Interactive volume cartoon shading, Toon-Shading for Volumes, Toon-shading via 3D normal map
body: Volumetric Toon Shading is a non-photorealistic rendering technique that simulates cel shading for volumetric datasets without requiring explicit surface vertices or mesh extraction. It differs from surface-based NPR methods by operating directly on fragment-level data using a 3D normal map, allowing for interactive rendering of stylized volumes where features are defined by local gradient properties rather than discrete geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar field (volume data), a parallel light direction vector L, and two user-specified tone registers. Output: A 2D image with discrete tonal shading. Data Structures: 1. 3D Normal Map: A 3D texture storing gray-scale gradients of the volume data in its RGB components. 2. Toon-Shading Texture: A 1D texture used for nearest-neighbor interpolation to create discontinuities between illuminated and shadowed points. Steps: 1. Render a three-dimensional normal map storing gray-scale gradients in the RGB components. 2. Issue the parallel light vector L as a constant color in the texture combiner stage. 3. For each fragment, look up the normal vector N from the 3D normal map and compute the dot product D = L \cdot N using per-fragment arithmetic. 4. Add an optional offset to D to enable arbitrary mapping of shades to tones. 5. Use the resulting dot product value to trigger a multiplexer in the texture combiner stage. 6. If the value is greater than 0.5, the multiplexer outputs the first register; otherwise, it outputs the second register. 7. Write user-specified tones to the two registers to define the final rendered shades. Parameters: Threshold: The multiplexer threshold is 0.5, separating illuminated points from shadow points. Offset: An additive offset applied to the dot product before the threshold comparison, allowing arbitrary mapping of shades to tones. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def samplenearest(tex, coord): # Standard nearest-neighbor lookup: clamp and index idx = max(0, min(len(tex) - 1, int(coord len(tex)))) return tex[idx] def volumetrictoonshading(fragmentpos, normalmap3d, lightdir, toonlut1d, tone1, tone2, threshold=0.5, offset=0.0): # 1. Look up normal from 3D normal map (gray-scale gradients in RGB) N = normalmap3d.sample(fragmentpos).rgb # 2. Compute dot product with light direction (issued as constant color) D = dot(N, lightdir) # 3. Apply offset Dadjusted = D + offset # 4. Trigger multiplexer based on threshold if Dadjusted > threshold: selectedtone = tone1 else: selectedtone = tone2 # 5. Alternative software path: use dot product as 1D texture coordinate # with nearest-neighbor interpolation to create discontinuity # color = samplenearest(toonlut1d, Dadjusted) return selectedtone Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 3D normal map (same resolution as volume data) and the 1D toon-shading texture. Strengths: Interactive performance due to hardware-accelerated fragment shading and texture combiners; avoids the need for explicit surface vertices. Limitations: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in "Interactive volume illustration". It adapts polygonal toon-shading techniques to volumetric data by replacing vertex-based normal interpolation with per-fragment gradient lookup via a 3D normal map. The approach integrates directly with direct volume rendering algorithms via 3D texture maps and can be combined with hatch-based rendering methods.
