name: Lighting Transfer Function with Gradient Aligned Sampling
head: Gradient Aligned Sampling, LTF, Lighting Transfer Functions for Direct Volume Rendering, Lum and Ma In-Rendering TF
body:
Lighting Transfer Function (LTF) with Gradient Aligned Sampling is a direct volume rendering technique that enhances material boundaries by decoupling illumination from opacity. Unlike methods that attenuate lighting based on gradient magnitude, this method uses a 2D transfer function indexed by two scalar samples taken along the normalized gradient direction (one in the gradient direction, one opposite) to modulate specular and diffuse lighting coefficients. This allows independent control of surface lighting and opacity, enabling the illustration of translucent material boundaries that would otherwise be obscured by uniform absorption. Inputs: Volume scalar field data V. Precomputed volume gradients 
abla V. 1D Color Transfer Function (ColorTF) mapping scalar values to base color and opacity. 2D Lighting Transfer Functions (LTFs): Three separate 2D lookup tables (textures) for ambient (LTF{ka}), diffuse (LTF{kd}), and specular (LTF{ks}) coefficients. Light direction vector L and view direction vector V{dir}. Light scaling factor S{light} (typically >1 for high dynamic range). Sample pair distance d (typically 1 voxel). Outputs: Final fragment color C and opacity \alpha. 1. 2D Lighting Transfer Function (LTF) Implemented as 2D texture lookups indexed by the pair of scalar values (S1, S2) sampled along the gradient. Three separate textures are used: LTF{ka}(S1, S2): Ambient coefficient. LTF{kd}(S1, S2): Diffuse coefficient. LTF{ks}(S1, S2): Specular coefficient. Hybrid Gradient Sign Storage: To handle gradient direction flipping, the alpha channel of the LTF texture (or a separate auxiliary texture) stores a precomputed sign value. This value indicates the sign of the difference between post-classified sample densities at the two sample points, used to determine if the gradient should be flipped to point toward maximum variation in post-classified density. Sample Pair Distance (d): The distance between the two supplemental scalar samples read along the gradient direction. Typical value: 1 voxel in each direction. Light Scaling Factor (S{light}): A multiplier passed to the fragment program that modulates all light intensities. Values >1 are required to accommodate high dynamic range lighting where RGB color exceeds alpha, as surfaces rendered with this method do not have enhanced opacity. Specular Exponent (n): Phong shading exponent. 1. Preprocessing: Precompute gradients 
abla V of the original scalar field. Precompute the hybrid gradient sign for the LTF lookup tables based on the sign of the difference between post-classified sample densities. 2. Per-Sample Rendering (Fragment Program): 1. Read the current sample's scalar value S and gradient 
abla V from the volume data. 2. Normalize the gradient to obtain the unit vector N =  rac{
abla V}{\|
abla V\|}. 3. Hybrid Gradient Flipping: Determine the sign of the difference between post-classified densities at the two potential sample locations. If the pre-classified gradient points opposite to the direction of maximum variation in post-classified density, flip N to -N. 4. Gradient Aligned Sampling: Calculate the positions for two additional samples: P1 = P + d \cdot N and P2 = P - d \cdot N. Linearly interpolate and read the scalar values S1 and S2 from the volume data at P1 and P2. 5. Color and Opacity Lookup: Use the center sample value S to lookup base color C{base} and opacity \alpha from the 1D ColorTF. 6. Lighting Coefficient Lookup: Use the pair (S1, S2) as texture indices to lookup coefficients from the 2D LTFs: ka = LTF{ka}(S1, S2) kd = LTF{kd}(S1, S2) ks = LTF{ks}(S1, S2) 7. Lighting Computation: Compute the reflection vector R based on N and V{dir}. Calculate the final color C using the Phong model modulated by the LTF coefficients: C = C{base} \cdot (ka + kd \max(N \cdot L, 0)) + ks \max((N \cdot R)^n, 0) Apply the light scaling factor: C = C \cdot S{light}. 8. Alpha Modulation: Perform alpha modulation of the source color in the fragment program (rather than framebuffer blending) to handle cases where RGB color exceeds alpha. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderfragment(S, gradV, L, Vdir, n, d, Slight, ColorTF, LTFka, LTFkd, LTFks, VolumeData, HybridSignTexture): """ Renders a single volume sample using Lighting Transfer Function with Gradient Aligned Sampling. Args: S: Scalar value at current sample point. gradV: Gradient vector at current sample point. L: Normalized light direction vector. Vdir: Normalized view direction vector. n: Specular exponent. d: Distance between sample pairs (e.g., 1.0 voxel). Slight: Light scaling factor (>1 for HDR). ColorTF: 1D texture for base color and opacity. LTFka, LTFkd, LTFks: 2D textures for lighting coefficients. VolumeData: Volume scalar field for interpolation. HybridSignTexture: Texture storing precomputed sign of density difference for gradient flipping. Returns: C: Final color vector. alpha: Final opacity. """ # 1. Normalize gradient N = normalize(gradV) # 2. Hybrid Gradient Flipping # Determine if gradient should be flipped based on post-classified density variation # Note: The sign is precomputed and stored in the LTF's alpha channel or auxiliary texture # based on the difference between post-classified densities at P+dN and P-dN. # If the sign indicates the pre-classified gradient points away from max variation, flip N. # For implementation simplicity, we assume a function shouldflipgradient exists # which queries the precomputed sign data. if shouldflipgradient(S, N, HybridSignTexture): N = -N # 3. Gradient Aligned Sampling # Sample points displaced along the normalized gradient P1 = samplepoint + d N P2 = samplepoint - d N # Read scalar values at displaced points (linear interpolation) S1 = VolumeData.interpolate(P1) S2 = VolumeData.interpolate(P2) # 4. Color and Opacity Lookup basecolor, alpha = ColorTF.lookup(S) # 5. Lighting Coefficient Lookup # Use S1 and S2 as indices into 2D LTFs ka = LTFka.lookup(S1, S2) kd = LTFkd.lookup(S1, S2) ks = LTFks.lookup(S1, S2) # 6. Lighting Computation (Phong Model) # Compute reflection vector R # R = 2 dot(N, -Vdir) N + Vdir (assuming Vdir points from eye to surface) # Or standard: R = reflect(-Vdir, N) R = reflect(-Vdir, N) diffuseterm = kd max(dot(N, L), 0.0) specularterm = ks pow(max(dot(R, L), 0.0), n) # Combine ambient and diffuse with base color, add specular C = basecolor (ka + diffuseterm) + specularterm # 7. Apply Light Scaling Factor for HDR C = C Slight return C, alpha Gradient Direction Mismatch: Pre-classified gradients may point opposite to the classified opacity distribution (e.g., dentin in tooth scans), causing surfaces to be unlit with single-sided lighting. The hybrid gradient technique solves this by flipping normals based on post-classified density differences. High Dynamic Range: Since opacity is not enhanced, the alpha-multiplied RGB color can exceed the alpha value. The light scaling factor must allow values >1, and alpha modulation must be done in the fragment program, not framebuffer blending. Boundary Thickness Sensitivity: The method is sensitive to the thickness of material boundaries. If the sample pair distance d is greater than the boundary thickness, the samples read from adjacent homogeneous regions, failing to detect the boundary. Two-Sided Lighting Artifacts: Using two-sided lighting without gradient flipping illuminates back-facing surfaces incorrectly. Time and Memory Complexity: Requires approximately twice as many texture reads as traditional opacity-based transfer function methods due to the two additional scalar samples along the gradient. Memory usage increases by the storage of three 2D LTF textures and the hybrid sign data. Measured Performance: Rendering a 256 	imes 256 	imes 256 volume to a 512 	imes 512 buffer on an Nvidia GeForce 6800 at rendered sample spacing equal to the original volume resolution: LTF with Gradient Aligned Sampling: ~7.3 fps. Uniform lighting baseline: ~13.5 fps. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Independent control of lighting and opacity; effectively illustrates material boundaries in translucent volumes; handles high dynamic range lighting. Limitations: Sensitive to boundary thickness; requires precomputation of gradients and hybrid signs; higher texture read count reduces frame rate compared to simple methods. When to Use: When illustrating material boundaries independent of opacity is required, such as in CT scans of engines, protein electron probability distributions, vortex flows, and fuel injection simulations. Origin: The method was introduced by Lum and Ma in their paper "Lighting Transfer Functions for Direct Volume Rendering". It builds upon earlier work by Drebin et al. [2] who attenuated lighting based on gradient magnitude of post-classified density, but differs by using a hybrid of pre-classified gradients and post-classified density differences for direction flipping. History and Development: The technique was implemented in graphics hardware using view-aligned textured polygons and fragment programs. It was designed to address the limitations of uniform lighting and simple gradient-based attenuation, providing a user interface for specifying 2D lighting transfer functions that emphasize edges. Usage: Used in scientific visualization for enhancing the perception of structure in volumetric data where traditional opacity-based methods fail to distinguish material boundaries. Lighting Transfer Functions for Direct Volume Rendering, https://escholarship.org/uc/item/71g7h4kx, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Lighting Transfer Functions Using Gradient Aligned Sampling, https://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~ma/papers/lightingtf.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 Especificação de funções de transferência unidimensionais e multidimensionais para visualização volumétrica direta, http://hdl.handle.net/10183/12077, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Hybrid Shading
head: Hybrid CVR, Mixture of gradient-based shading with volumetric shading
body: Hybrid Shading blends gradient-based shading, which captures local surface details, with volumetric shading, which provides global ambient occlusion, to balance an image's local and global features while reducing noise. It distinguishes itself from pure gradient-based methods by introducing a dynamic interpolation controlled by opacity and gradient magnitude, offering a softer appearance that is particularly effective for noisy data such as ultrasound. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: v: User-defined blending factor, a scalar in the range [0, 1]. g: Gradient magnitude at the current sample point. \alpha x': Opacity value at the current sample point. L{phong}: Incident light computed via Phong lighting model. L{vs}: Incident light computed via volumetric shadow lighting. Output: L{in}: Final incident light value for the fragment. Data Structures No specific complex data structures are required beyond standard fragment shader inputs (gradient, opacity, light vectors). The method operates on per-sample values. Steps 1. Calculate the gradient-based shading value (L{phong}) using standard Phong illumination. 2. Calculate the volumetric shading value (L{vs}) using volumetric shadow lighting. 3. Compute the blending coefficient c{blend} using the formula below. 4. Interpolate between the two lighting models using c{blend} to produce the final incident light. Formulas The blending coefficient c{blend} is calculated as: c{blend} = v \left( 1 - e^{|g|^{\frac{1}{\alpha x'}}} \right) Where: v is the user-defined blending factor (0 \le v \le 1). g is the gradient magnitude. \alpha x' is the opacity value. The final incident light L{in} is calculated as: L{in} = (1 - c{blend}) L{phong} + c{blend} L{vs} Where: L{phong} is the Phong lighting contribution. L{vs} is the volumetric shadow lighting contribution. Parameters VolumetricScatteringBlending (v): A user-defined coefficient controlling the interpolation weight. Typical values are not explicitly defined in the sources, but the range is [0, 1]. Pitfalls and Edge Cases Exponentiation Stability: The term |g|^{\frac{1}{\alpha x'}} involves exponentiation where the exponent depends on the inverse of opacity. If \alpha x' approaches zero, the exponent approaches infinity, potentially causing numerical instability or overflow if |g| > 1. If |g| < 1, the term approaches zero. Implementers should guard against division by zero or extreme values in the exponent. Noise Reduction vs. Detail Loss: Setting the method to favor volumetric shading (higher v or conditions where c{blend} is high) results in a softer appearance and reduces image noise, which is beneficial for ultrasound data. However, small features may be dampened, which can be undesirable if fine detail preservation is required. Stochasticity vs. Interpolation: The method uses deterministic interpolation rather than stochastic blending to reduce artifacts introduced by random sampling. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridshading(v, g, alphaxprime, Lphong, Lvs): """ Computes hybrid shading by interpolating between Phong and volumetric shading. Args: v (float): User-defined blending factor [0, 1]. g (float): Gradient magnitude. alphaxprime (float): Opacity value. Lphong (float): Phong lighting intensity. Lvs (float): Volumetric shadow lighting intensity. Returns: float: Final incident light Lin. """ # Guard against division by zero in exponent if alphaxprime <= 0.0: # Fallback behavior: if opacity is zero, no light contributes, # or handle as pure volumetric/gradient based on v. # Source implies dynamic calculation; assuming standard behavior # where zero opacity yields zero contribution or requires clamping. # For implementation safety, clamp alphaxprime to a small epsilon. alphaxprime = 1e-6 # Calculate exponent term: |g|^(1 / opacity) # Note: If g is 0, result is 0. If g > 1 and opacity is small, this grows large. # If g < 1, this decays to 0 as opacity decreases. exponent = 1.0 / alphaxprime # Compute base for exponentiation base = abs(g) # Calculate e^(base^exponent) # Using math.exp and math.pow expterm = math.exp(math.pow(base, exponent)) # Calculate blending coefficient # cblend = v (1 - expterm) # Note: If expterm > 1, cblend becomes negative. # The source formula is cblend = v(1 - e^(...)). # If e^(...) > 1, cblend < 0. # If e^(...) < 1, cblend > 0. # Typically, for small g and reasonable opacity, e^(...) might be < 1? # Let's strictly follow the formula provided. cblend = v (1.0 - expterm) # Clamp cblend to [0, 1] if necessary for stability, # though the source does not explicitly state clamping. # Given the formula, if expterm > 1, cblend is negative. # If expterm < 0 (impossible for real g), cblend > v. # We assume the source intends cblend to be a weight. # However, strictly implementing the formula: # Final incident light Lin = (1.0 - cblend) Lphong + cblend Lvs return Lin Uses a sphere texture to simulate lighting on volumetric primitives. Choose when spherical symmetry is appropriate. Lit Sphere Shading Modifies color based on the angle between the view direction and the gradient. Choose for edge highlighting. Orientation-Based Color Modification Applies tone shading techniques to volume data for illustrative effects. Choose for artistic rendering. Volume Illustration Tone Shading Darkens the edges of the volume to focus attention on the center. Choose for compositional emphasis. Vignette Shading Applies toon shading using the Blinn-Phong model. Choose for stylized, non-photorealistic surfaces. Blinn-Phong Toon Shading Extends toon shading to volumetric data. Choose for cartoon-like volume rendering. Volumetric Toon Shading Aligns sampling with gradients to improve lighting accuracy. Choose for high-fidelity lighting. Lighting Transfer Function with Gradient Aligned Sampling Enhances details using multi-scale unsharp masking. Choose for detail enhancement. Volumetric Unsharp Masking with Multi-scale Hierarchy Time Complexity: The method adds a constant number of mathematical operations (exponentiation, multiplication, addition) per sample. It does not increase the number of ray casts or lookups compared to standard CVR, unlike methods that require additional gradient lookups or ray tracing. Memory Complexity: No additional memory structures are required beyond standard volume data and fragment state. Performance: The method is designed for interactive, in-browser rendering, balancing quality and speed. It avoids the computational cost of stochastic blending by using deterministic interpolation. Strengths: Reduces noise in volumetric data (e.g., ultrasound) by favoring volumetric shading in noisy regions; balances local and global features. Limitations: May dampen small features if volumetric shading is favored too strongly. Numerical stability of the exponent term requires careful handling of low opacity values. Hybrid Shading was developed by the CVR team at Kitware as part of their Cinematic Volume Rendering work. It was theorized to balance local and global features by combining gradient-based and volumetric shading. The method was implemented and evaluated for interactive, in-browser cinematic volume rendering of medical images. The original formula was adopted and modified to increase speed and reduce speckle artifacts. name: Volumetric Unsharp Masking with Multi-scale Hierarchy
head: Darkening Shadowed Regions, Enhanced perception method, Feature enhancement technique, Lightening Salient Features, Volumetric Unsharp Masking, feature enhancement by unsharp masking
body: Volumetric Unsharp Masking with Multi-scale Hierarchy is a feature enhancement technique for volume rendering that improves the perception of local details (edges, superficial features) by increasing local contrast through lightening salient features and darkening shadowed regions. Unlike classical unsharp masking which requires storing full-resolution smoothed radiance volumes, this method reduces memory consumption by using one or two levels of a multi-scale volume hierarchy of the original data to compute the smoothed signals required for the unsharp masking operation. It differs from Lit Sphere Shading and Volume Illustration Tone Shading by explicitly decoupling feature enhancement from the base shading model, applying a post-shading contrast modification in the CIELab color space. The method operates on the radiance signal computed along viewing rays during ray casting. It enhances local contrast by modifying the shading of each sample using unsharp masking in the CIELab color space, utilizing a multi-scale hierarchy to approximate the smoothed background signal without storing full-resolution auxiliary volumes. Inputs: Original volume dataset V with resolution Dx \times Dy \times Dz. Transfer function TF mapping density to color and opacity. Lighting parameters (light direction L, view direction V, material properties for Phong shading). Hierarchy levels H = \{h2, h3, h4, h5, h6, h8, h{16}, h{32}\}, where hi represents the volume downsampled by factor i. Parameters: \gamma (lightening intensity), \lambda{dark} (darkening intensity, implicitly 1 in the final combination formula), level for lightening L{lev}, level for darkening D{lev}. Outputs: Enhanced final color C{final} for each sample along the ray. 1. Original Volume (V): 3D texture containing the scalar field. 2. Multi-scale Hierarchy (H): A set of 3D textures. Each level hi has dimensions \lceil Dx/i \rceil \times \lceil Dy/i \rceil \times \lceil Dz/i \rceil. The hierarchy is computed on the CPU and uploaded to the GPU. Only one or two levels are stored in memory at a time, significantly reducing memory usage compared to storing full-resolution smoothed radiance volumes. 3. Ray Casting State: Accumulated color and opacity. 1. Preprocessing (CPU): Compute the multi-scale volume hierarchy from the original data set V. For each level i \in \{2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 16, 32\}, generate a volume where dimensions are divided by i. This is done by averaging or filtering the original data over blocks of size i \times i \times i. Upload V and the selected hierarchy levels to GPU 3D textures. 2. Ray Casting Loop (GPU): For each sample point P along the viewing ray: 2.1. Compute Base Radiance: Query the density d at P from V. Compute the Phong shading color C{phong} using the local gradient \nabla f, light vector, and view vector. Transform C{phong} from RGB to CIELab, yielding [L, a, b]. 2.2. Compute Lightening Signal (S{light}): Query the density d{smooth} at P from the hierarchy level L{lev} using trilinear interpolation. Compute the Phong shading color C{smooth} for density d{smooth} using the same lighting model. Transform C{smooth} to CIELab, yielding [L{level}, a{level}, b{level}]. Edge Case: If the opacity assigned by TF to d{smooth} is zero, replace [L{level}, a{level}, b{level}] with a color having lower luminance than [L, a, b] to ensure the unsharp masking results in lightening. Calculate the unsharped CIELab color UCIELab(C): L{new} = L + \gamma(L - L{level}) k = \frac{L{new}}{L} a{new} = k \cdot a b{new} = k \cdot b UCIELab(C) = [L{new}, a{new}, b{new}] where \gamma is the user-defined scaling factor for lightening intensity. Compute the color C{tf} assigned by the transfer function for density d{tf}. Transform C{tf} to CIELab, yielding [L{tf}, a{tf}, b{tf}]. Darkening Level Selection: Using lower resolution levels (higher scaling factors) for darkening produces extra, unpleasant shadowed regions. Levels 2 or 3 are recommended. Isosurface Sampling: Applying unsharp masking only at the isosurface level produces poor results because the contribution of a single sample to the final color may be quite low, especially when semi-transparent materials are traversed before reaching the isosurface. Performance gain is only 2% to 10%. Performance with Different Levels: Using different levels for lightening and darkening reduces texture coherence, causing frame rates to decrease up to 50% compared to using the same level (which decreases up to 20%). Time Complexity: Hierarchy building is O(N) where N is the number of voxels, but the constant factor is low. Building times for various datasets range from 192ms (192x180x168) to 4559ms (512x512x512). Memory Complexity: The method stores the original volume and one or two levels of the hierarchy. In the worst case (using levels 2 and 3), memory consumption increases by less than a sixth of the original volume, compared to triple storage in Tao et al.'s method. Measured Performance: On an Intel Core2 DUO CPU at 3.0 GHz and nVidia GeForce GTX 280 GPU with 1GB RAM: Using the same level for lightening and darkening: Frame rates decrease up to 20% compared to standard Phong shading. Using different levels: Frame rates decrease up to 50% due to less texture coherence. This is an improvement over Tao et al.'s method, which saw up to 70% frame rate decay. Strengths: Significantly reduced memory requirements compared to full-resolution smoothed radiance volumes. Effective enhancement of local features in both opaque and semi-transparent volumes. User studies show 72% preference for this method over Phong and Tao's method. Limitations: Performance penalty when using different hierarchy levels for lightening and darkening. Requires careful selection of hierarchy levels based on feature size. Not suitable for real-time applications requiring very high frame rates on low-end hardware if different levels are used. The method was proposed to overcome the high memory consumption limitations of the volumetric unsharp masking technique by Tao et al. [105], which required storing two additional full-resolution volumes (radiance and smoothed radiance). The multi-scale volume hierarchy approach allows for non-power-of-two levels and sparse storage, making it more efficient. The technique was evaluated in a user study involving 252 participants, where it was preferred for feature perception. name: Anisotropic Line/Streamtube Shading
head: Anisotropic shading for lines and streamtubes
body: Anisotropic Line/Streamtube Shading illuminates 1D fiber representations (lines or streamtubes) to provide depth cues and shape perception that unshaded lines lack, without the polygonal overhead of explicit tube geometry. It distinguishes itself from surface-based NPR methods by treating the fiber as a cylinder with rotational symmetry, using an anisotropic parameter (often sheen) to model specular highlights along the tangent, thereby revealing coherent structure and local curvature. Inputs: Fiber geometry: A sequence of points defining the streamline or line segment. View direction V and Light direction L. Anisotropic parameter k (sheen roughness or sharpness). Base color or transfer function output. Data Structures: Streamline Representation: A polyline or parametric curve. For hardware implementation, this may be rasterized as a set of quads or triangles approximating a thin tube, or rendered as lines with a custom shader. Precomputed Texture (Optional): A 2D or 3D texture encoding illumination results for varying view angles, light directions, and streamline tangents. Steps: 1. Tangent Estimation: For each fragment on the line/streamtube, compute the local tangent vector T of the streamline. If using explicit geometry, T is derived from the edge direction of the tube mesh. 2. Normal Approximation: Since lines lack a unique surface normal, define a plane of possible normals orthogonal to T. The effective normal N for shading is often derived from the view vector V and tangent T. A common approach in anisotropic shading (like sheen) is to use the half-vector H = \frac{V+L}{|V+L|} and compute the dot product with a normal that lies in the plane orthogonal to T. 3. Anisotropic Highlight Calculation: Compute the specular term using an anisotropic BRDF model (e.g., sheen). The intensity depends on the alignment of the view direction with the tangent. Formula (Sheen-like): I{spec} = k \cdot (1 - (V \cdot T)^2)^{shininess} or similar, where the highlight is strongest when the view is perpendicular to the tangent. Alternatively, using the precomputed texture: Sample the texture using normalized coordinates derived from V, L, and T. 4. Color Composition: Combine the base color C{base} with the anisotropic highlight I{spec} and ambient term C{amb}: C{final} = C{base} \cdot C{amb} + I{spec} \cdot C{highlight}. Parameters: Sheen Roughness/Sharpness: Controls the spread of the anisotropic highlight. Higher values create sharper highlights along the fiber axis. Sheen Tint: Modulates the color of the specular reflection, allowing control over the perceived material properties. Edge Cases: Degenerate Tangents: At endpoints or singularities, the tangent may be undefined. Interpolation or fallback to a default normal is required. Dense Packing: When fibers are densely packed, individual shading may cause visual clutter or aliasing. Reducing density or using overlay techniques can mitigate this. A technique that illuminates streamlines using a Phong illumination model to provide depth cues missing in simple streamlines. It replaces missing surface normals with planes of possible normals orthogonal to the streamline. Implemented efficiently by precomputing a texture encoding illumination for different view points, light directions, and streamline tangents. Provides finer 3D details and better depth cues than simple non-illuminated streamlines, which perform poorly in complex fiber tract arrangements. Performance: Significantly faster than rendering high-quality polygonal tubes, which require many polygons to avoid aliasing and visual clutter. Hardware-accelerated via precomputed textures or efficient shader calculations. Visual Quality: Provides better shape and depth cues than unshaded lines. Avoids the "visual cluttering" and aliasing issues associated with dense streamtubes. Limitations: May still suffer from aliasing if the line width is not handled carefully. Interpretation by laymen may still be ambiguous compared to explicit geometry, though less so than unshaded lines. Originated in the context of medical imaging visualization, particularly for fiber tractography (e.g., DTI). Inspired by human hair rendering techniques, which also deal with many polyline-like objects with specific shapes and coherencies. Used in tools like Horizon to compare plain gray, anisotropic lighting, and interpolated colors. Earlier work by Stalling et al. (1997) and Mallo et al. (2005) explored illuminated lines for fiber bundles. name: Line and Edge Detection
body: Line and Edge Detection is a family of non-photorealistic volume rendering techniques that enhance perceptual clarity by explicitly detecting and rendering edges, silhouettes, or structural boundaries within volumetric data. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Line Illustration Detection by focusing on boundary emphasis and structural outlines rather than flow-aligned strokes, and from LOG-based Silhouette Detection by employing diverse detection mechanisms ranging from gradient-based particle tracing to user-defined interactive selection. The family shares the fundamental goal of enhancing perceptual clarity through non-photorealistic edge representation. Common mechanisms include: 1. Edge Detection: Identifying boundaries based on local volumetric properties (gradients, Laplacian of Gaussian) or image-space properties (depth, normal discontinuities). 2. Line Rendering: Converting detected edges into line primitives (strips, segments) or stylized strokes. Line Illustration Detection is a family of Non-Photorealistic Rendering (NPR) techniques designed to detect and render lines that communicate the shape, structure, and boundaries of volumetric data or isosurfaces. It solves the problem of visualizing complex geometry, such as medical models, where standard photorealistic rendering may obscure structural details. What sets this family apart from its siblings is its focus on line-based abstraction rather than silhouette outlines or edge highlights; it distinguishes between analytical approaches, which are vector-oriented and resolution-independent, and pixel-based methods, which are faster and simpler but rely on image-space buffers. This method renders volumetric data by treating individual cells (faces) as the primary sampling units, applying a scalar-based colormap for the volume body while simultaneously detecting and highlighting cell edges. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Line Illustration Detection and Outline and Contour Generation by computing edge highlights directly within the face fragment shader based on distance to cell vertices and edges, rather than relying on post-processing contours or separate line-detection passes. It solves the problem of visualizing internal structures and boundaries in 3D volumes by providing explicit edge cues that enhance depth perception and structural clarity without obscuring the underlying scalar data. Outline and Contour Generation is a family of non-photorealistic volume rendering techniques that enhance perceptual clarity by explicitly detecting and rendering edges, silhouettes, or topological boundaries within volumetric data. Unlike surface-based NPR, which relies on well-defined geometric surfaces, this family operates on continuous volumetric fields where feature areas must be determined through local property analysis. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Line Illustration Detection by focusing on boundary emphasis and structural outlines rather than flow-aligned strokes, and from LOG-based Silhouette Detection by employing diverse detection mechanisms ranging from gradient-based particle tracing to user-defined interactive selection. LOG-based Silhouette Detection is a volumetric edge detection technique used to identify silhouette voxels for rendering sketch-like curves, replacing a more exhaustive 3x3x3 subspace search to improve performance. It identifies boundaries based on local volumetric properties (gradient magnitude and Laplacian of Gaussian values) to highlight structures such as bones or internal features. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Line Illustration Detection by operating directly on volumetric scalar fields using a precomputed Laplacian of Gaussian operator rather than image-space depth discontinuities or surface normals. Step: Calculate entry point hp = org + dir \times t{cur}. Calculate local cell coordinates local = (hp - bmin) / cell. Extract 2D face coordinates f based on entry axis: if axis=0, f=fract(local.yz); if axis=1, f=fract(local.xz); if axis=2, f=fract(local.xy). Calculate edge distance edge = \min(\min(f.x, 1.0-f.x), \min(f.y, 1.0-f.y)). If edge < 0.06, highlight color is yellow (1.0, 0.85, 0.1); otherwise mix lit color with yellow at 0.35 weight. Definition: An approach by Li et al. to detect silhouettes in Hough space for edge sampling. Usage: Used in Li's edge sampling approach [22, 23]. Definition: A pre-computed shape enhancement cue based on object-space analysis using a sharpened filter (Laplacian-like) on a 3x3x3 unit volume to enhance edges and contours, solving the concave/convex inconsistency of local illumination. Step: Select a 3x3x3 point unit volume surrounding the sampling center in the data volume. Clamp the shape factor: if g(x, y, z) + c > 1, set it to 1. Formula: Calculate the sharpened filter value 52f as: 52f = [f(x+1, y, z) + f(x-1, y, z) + \dots + f(x+1, y+1, z+1)] - 26f(x, y, z), where f(x,y,z) is the intensity of the sampling point. Calculate the enhanced intensity g(x,y,z) as: g(x, y, z) = f(x, y, z) - 52f. Calculate the shape factor S{object} as: S{object} = g(x, y, z) + c, where c is a factor to adjust the effect of object space enhancement. Parameter: Factor c: A parameter to adjust the effect of object space enhancement. Pitfall: Local illumination alone cannot solve the display of concave parts; this cue makes up for that shortcoming. Complexity: The cue is pre-computed before ray casting, so it does not occupy rendering time, allowing real-time interactivity. Definition: Detects prominent edges in the volume using a Sobel filter and dynamically positions a magnification lens to center on the largest connected feature. Step: Apply Sobel filter to the volume: edges = ndimage.sobel(self.volumedata). Compute threshold as twice the mean edge magnitude: T = \text{mean}(E) \times 2. Create binary feature mask: M = E > T. Label connected components in the mask: labeled, numfeatures = ndimage.label(featuremask). Find bounding box of the largest feature: largestfeature = ndimage.findobjects(labeled)[0]. Compute center coordinates: Cy = (s{start} + s{stop}) / 2, Cx = (s{start} + s{stop}) / 2. Normalize center to [0,1] range and update lens position: self.lens['position'] = glm.vec2(center[1] / H, center[0] / W). Line and edge detection techniques in volume rendering utilize various strategies to highlight structural boundaries. Analytical and object-space approaches, such as Li et al.'s Hough space silhouette detection, operate on geometric properties, while image-space methods like Sobel filtering and LOG-based voxel detection identify edges through gradient analysis. Pre-computed cues, such as the 3x3x3 sharpened filter for object-space enhancement, are used to improve edge visibility without impacting real-time rendering performance. wlim33/vox-ocean, https://github.com/wlim33/vox-ocean, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Physics-based differentiable rendering, https://doi.org/10.1145/3388769.3407454, fetched 2026-10-29 Local Detail Enhancement for Volume Rendering under Global Illumination, https://doi.org/10.2312/pg.20161334, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) GitHub - priscilla100/medicalvolumerenderer, https://github.com/priscilla100/medicalvolumerenderer/, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Line Illustration Detection
head: Analytical and pixel-based line detection, Line detection in NPR
body: Line Illustration Detection identifies and renders lines within volumetric data to enhance perceptual clarity through non-photorealistic edge representation. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by focusing specifically on line primitives rather than silhouettes or face-based highlights, categorizing approaches into analytical (vector-oriented, resolution-independent) and pixel-based (image-space, G-buffer dependent) techniques. The family shares the fundamental goal of enhancing perceptual clarity through non-photorealistic edge representation. Common mechanisms include: 1. Edge Detection: Identifying boundaries based on local volumetric properties (gradients, Laplacian of Gaussian) or image-space properties (depth, normal discontinuities). 2. Line Rendering: Converting detected edges into line primitives (strips, segments) or stylized strokes. Analytical approaches are vector-oriented, resolution-independent, and transformable without artifacts, but require explicit analytical representations of the volume or isosurfaces. These methods are generally more general and flexible than pixel-based alternatives. Pixel-based methods, such as those utilizing G-buffers, are faster and simpler to implement than analytical methods, particularly when explicit analytical representations are not available. They rely on image-space processing operators and can reuse G-buffers without recalculation. A technique for visualizing volume isosurfaces by advecting particles along principal curvature directions to create line textures that communicate surface shape. It is based on the premise that lines in the principal directions of curvature communicate surface shape better than lines in other directions. Steps: 1. Calculate the set of principal directions and principal curvatures in the volume. 2. Place an evenly distributed set of tiny opaque particles on the isosurfaces of interest. 3. Advect the particles through the vector field defined by the principal directions. 4. Treat the paths of the particles defined by this advection as a 3D line texture. Parameters: Particle distribution: evenly distributed on isosurfaces. Pitfalls: Algorithmic efficiency and artistic line quality must be addressed for NPR applicability. Showing line direction alone is not necessarily sufficient for an aesthetically pleasing rendering. A technique simulating copper plate etching by intersecting a scene with closely-spaced, equidistant, parallel planes to detect surface curves. It modulates the final line style using G-buffers containing geometric properties such as colour and depth. Steps: 1. Intersect the scene with a set of closely-spaced, equidistant, parallel planes. 2. Use a modified ray tracer to detect the surface curves resulting from these intersections. 3. Use G-buffers containing geometric properties such as colour and depth to modulate the final line style. The concept of line illustration in volume visualization has roots in traditional printmaking, specifically copper plate etching, which was used for centuries in scientific publications before modern photographic reproduction. Leister simulated this process by intersecting scenes with parallel planes and using a modified ray tracer. In the context of digital volume visualization, Interrante introduced a novel line illustration technique for visualizing volume isosurfaces in 1997. This work focused on using principal directions and curvatures to advect particles, creating viewpoint-independent line textures that could visualize multiple isosurfaces simultaneously. The distinction between analytical and pixel-based methods is well-documented in surveys of NPR techniques. Analytical methods are noted for their flexibility and lack of resolution dependence, while pixel-based methods (like those by Saito and Takahashi) are favored for their speed and simplicity when analytical models are unavailable. Hertzmann provided a survey of image-space outline generation algorithms, noting that simple outlines can be generated by extracting edges from depth maps. name: Face-based volume rendering with edge highlights
head: Volume Color and Highlight Edges Rendering
body: Face-based volume rendering with edge highlights renders volumetric data by treating individual cells (faces) as the primary sampling unit, applying a scalar-based colormap for the body, and superimposing anti-aliased edge highlights to enhance structural clarity. It differs from silhouette-based methods by detecting edges locally within each cell based on vertex attribute discontinuities or importance factors, rather than relying on global view-dependent depth discontinuities. The method operates in a fragment shader context where each fragment corresponds to a specific location within a volumetric cell (typically a quad or tetrahedron face). The algorithm blends the volume color with edge highlights using a back-to-front alpha compositing model. Inputs: vFragmentPositionWorld: World-space position of the current fragment. vVertexPositions[4]: World-space positions of the four vertices of the current cell. vVertexAttributes[4]: Scalar values at the four vertices (e.g., density, temperature). vLineAttributes[4]: Float array used to determine edge importance; an edge is considered important if vLineAttributes[i] >= 1.0 - uImportantLineBoostFactor. vEdgeLodValues[4]: Pre-computed Level of Detail (LOD) values for the four edges. uCellScalarTex: Texture containing scalar values for the cell (1 texel per face). Uniforms: Camera parameters (uCameraPosition, uLookingDirection), focus context (uSphereCenter, uSphereRadius), rendering parameters (uLineWidth, uMaxLodValue, uSelectedLodValueFocus, uSelectedLodValueContext, uImportantLineBoostFactor), colors (uBackgroundColor, uForegroundColor, uEdgeColor), and scalar range (uScalarMin, uScalarMax). contextFactor, focusFactor, fragmentDistance: Depth cue and focus modulation factors. Outputs: Blended fragment color and alpha. Custom depth value for subsequent processing via gatherFragmentCustomDepth. The implementation relies on GPU textures for buffer management, specifically for the Parallel Prefix List List (PPLL) structure used to manage fragments, though the core edge highlight logic is computed per-fragment. Start Offset Buffer: R32UI texture of size W \times H (viewport dimensions). Initialized to 0xFFFFFFFF (-1 as unsigned int) to serve as an end-of-list sentinel. Fragment Buffer: RGBA32UI texture of size W \times H. Each pixel stores a fragment node containing color, depth, and a next pointer (initialized to 0). Cell Scalar Texture: RED FLOAT texture. One texel per face, used to retrieve the cell's scalar value. 1. Calculate Line Geometry: Compute the effective line width: eWidthPrime = uLineWidth \times (-distanceToFocusPointNormalized \times 0.3 + 1.0). Compute the line radius: lineRadius = eWidthPrime / 2.0. Note: distanceToFocusPointNormalized is the normalized distance from the fragment to the focus sphere center. 2. Compute Volume Color: Calculate the cell scalar average: cellScalar = 0.25 \times \sum{i=0}^{3} vVertexAttributes[i]. Normalize the scalar: t = \frac{cellScalar - uScalarMin}{\max(uScalarMax - uScalarMin, 10^{-6})}. Apply colormap: baseColor = colormap(t). Set volume color: volumeColor = vec4(baseColor, 1.0). Modulate alpha by context factor: volumeColor.a \times= contextFactor. 3. Initialize LOD and Distance Tracking: Set LOD\EPSILON = 0.001. Compute discrete LOD thresholds: discreteSelectedLodValueFocus = \max(uSelectedLodValueFocus \times uMaxLodValue, LOD\EPSILON). discreteSelectedLodValueContext = \max(uSelectedLodValueContext \times uMaxLodValue, LOD\EPSILON). Initialize variables: minDistance = 10^9, minDistanceIndex = 0, minDistanceAll = 10^9, minDistanceIndexAll = 0, isLineNear = false. 4. Iterate Over Cell Edges: For each edge i from 0 to 3: Calculate distance from fragment to the line segment defined by vertices i and (i+1)\%4: currentDistance = getDistanceToLineSegment(vFragmentPositionWorld, vVertexPositions[i], vVertexPositions[(i+1)\%4]). Determine if the edge is "important" based on vLineAttributes[i] and uImportantLineBoostFactor. Calculate focus LOD level: lodLevelFocus = \max\left(\left(vLineAttributes[i] < 1.0 - uImportantLineBoostFactor ? 0.0: 1.0\right) \times uMaxLodValue, discreteSelectedLodValueFocus\right). Calculate the edge's LOD value: lodLineValue = vEdgeLodValues[i] \times uMaxLodValue. Determine opacity factor based on LOD thresholds and focusFactor: lodLevelOpacityFactor = mix\left(\begin{aligned} &lodLineValue \le discreteSelectedLodValueContext + LOD\EPSILON ? 1.0: 0.0, \\ &lodLineValue \le discreteSelectedLodValueFocus + LOD\EPSILON ? 1.0: 0.0, \\ &focusFactor \end{aligned}\right). Determine if the line should be drawn: drawLine = (lodLevelOpacityFactor > 0.01). Update minimum distances: If currentDistance < minDistance and drawLine: minDistance = currentDistance, minDistanceIndex = i, isLineNear = true. If currentDistance < minDistanceAll: minDistanceAll = currentDistance, minDistanceIndexAll = i. 5. Compute Edge Highlight Color: If isLineNear and minDistance \le lineRadius: Calculate depth cue factor: depthCueFactor = \min(contextFactor, focusFactor). Retrieve LOD value for the nearest edge: lodLineValue = vEdgeLodValues[minDistanceIndex]. Recalculate opacity factor using original LOD values: lodLevelOpacityFactor = mix\left(\begin{aligned} &lodLineValue \le uSelectedLodValueContext + LOD\EPSILON ? 1.0: 0.0, \\ &lodLineValue \le uSelectedLodValueFocus + LOD\EPSILON ? 1.0: 0.0, \\ &focusFactor \end{aligned}\right). Determine base line color: lineBaseColor = uEdgeColor. lineBaseColorFocus = mix(lineBaseColor, uBackgroundColor, 0.3). lineBaseColorContext = mix(baseColor, uForegroundColor, 0.3). lineBaseColor = mix(lineBaseColorContext, lineBaseColorFocus, focusFactor). Calculate normalized line coordinates: lineCoordinates = \max(minDistance / lineRadius, 0.0). Calculate anti-aliasing factor: EPSILON = clamp(getAntialiasingFactor(fragmentDistance / lineRadius), 0.0, 0.49). Calculate coverage: coverage = 1.0 - smoothstep(1.0 - 2.0 \times EPSILON, 1.0, lineCoordinates). Set line color: lineColor = vec4(lineBaseColor, coverage \times lodLevelOpacityFactor). 6. Composite and Output: Perform back-to-front alpha blending: blendedColor.a = lineColor.a + volumeColor.a \times (1.0 - lineColor.a) blendedColor.rgb = lineColor.rgb \times lineColor.a + volumeColor.rgb \times volumeColor.a \times (1.0 - lineColor.a). If blendedColor.a > 10^{-4}, premultiply RGB: blendedColor.rgb /= blendedColor.a. Call gatherFragmentCustomDepth(blendedColor, fragmentDistance) to store depth and color for further processing. name: Outline and Contour Generation
body: Outline and Contour Generation is a family of non-photorealistic volume rendering techniques that enhance perceptual clarity by explicitly rendering edges, silhouettes, or topological boundaries as line primitives or stylized strokes. Unlike standard volume rendering which relies on opacity and color to imply form, these methods detect geometric or scalar discontinuities and render them as distinct visual cues to define object boundaries, internal structures, or topological relationships. This family is distinguished from its siblings by its focus on explicit edge extraction and rendering strategies, ranging from object-space silhouette extraction to image-space depth discontinuity detection and topological landscape mapping. The family shares the fundamental goal of enhancing perceptual clarity through non-photorealistic edge representation. Common mechanisms include: 1. Edge Detection: Identifying boundaries based on local volumetric properties (gradients, Laplacian of Gaussian) or image-space properties (depth, normal discontinuities). 2. Line Rendering: Converting detected edges into line primitives (strips, segments) or stylized strokes. Generates view-dependent line primitives demarcating areas where an object's surface turns away from the viewer, relying on gradient magnitude and viewing angle for real-time tracing. A post-processing technique detecting screen-space depth or normal discontinuities to define boundaries without analytical geometry processing. An interactive technique allowing users to manually define regions of interest to generate contour overlays, isolating complex structures lacking sharp boundaries. Regulates contour thickness based on normal curvature along the view direction to prevent uncontrolled variation in thickness inherent in standard dot-product silhouette methods. An object-space technique extracting significant edges (silhouettes and feature lines) from geometry, assembling them into strokes, and rendering them with stylization to enhance perceptual clarity. Maps the connectivity of a scalar field’s level sets onto a 3D terrain model using the contour tree, leveraging human intuition for reading physical terrain to interpret complex topological relationships. Identifies surface locations where radial curvature is zero but increasing towards the viewer, complementing standard object contours to reveal hidden or occluded geometry. Displays line contours of a reference scalar field on the vertical bounding walls of a 3D volume to provide spatial context without occluding primary data. Determines contour correspondence in time-varying fields by verifying overlap of associated upper and lower object sets, avoiding higher-dimensional interpolations. Ghosted views with contours combine segmentation and contour rendering to clarify internal structures obscured by context. The method pre-segments the most interesting internal structures (e.g., small internal organs). It identifies context information (e.g., the body) that obscures these structures. In areas of occlusion, the visual representation of the context object is reduced to contours, providing a clear view of the interesting internal organ. 2D Stroke to 3D Line Picking is a method that locates the intended location of a 2D stroke in 3D space by finding the 3D line that is a projection of the 2D stroke and fits contours in the data best, determined by the dot product of the normal vector of the extruded stroke and the gradient in the data. This method only works at contours of objects and segments objects whose contour best fits the stroke, which may not be the most visible objects, whereas WYSIWYP is applicable to any position in the rendering. The family of outline and contour generation techniques has evolved to address the limitations of photorealistic volume rendering in conveying shape, boundaries, and topological information. Early work in illustrative visualization for medicine and science highlighted the utility of expressive visualizations, such as ghosted views with contours, to clarify internal structures obscured by context. The development of non-photorealistic rendering (NPR) techniques allowed for the explicit rendering of edges and silhouettes to enhance perceptual clarity. Object-space silhouette rendering techniques were developed to extract significant edges from geometry and assemble them into stylized strokes. Image-space techniques emerged to provide faster, post-processing based outline generation by detecting depth and normal discontinuities. More advanced methods introduced curvature control to maintain consistent visual weight across varying surface geometries and suggestive contours to reveal hidden geometry. Topological landscape techniques mapped scalar field connectivity to 3D terrain models to aid in interpreting complex topological relationships. Interactive methods like lasso contour rendering and 2D stroke to 3D line picking were developed to allow users to explicitly select and highlight regions of interest. name: Object Contour NPR
head: Csébfalvi's contour method, GPU-based contour tracing, Geometry shader contour rendering, Gradient-based contour visualization, View-Dependent Contour Generation
body:
Object Contour NPR generates view-dependent line primitives that demarcate areas where an object's surface turns away from the viewer, conveying shape through boundary emphasis. Unlike hatches, which are recorded to a texture buffer, these contours are traced and rendered directly to the screen. It differs from direct volume rendering by relying solely on gradient magnitude and viewing angle rather than voxel intensity values, allowing for faster parameter tuning. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset V, a viewing direction vector \vec{v}, and a user-defined distance threshold d{thresh} defining the neighborhood around the contour. Output: A set of line strips rendered directly to the screen buffer. Data Structures: Particle Set: A collection of point primitives. Each particle Pi stores its 3D position (x, y, z) in the volume. Gradient Field: A 3D vector field 
abla V computed via 4D linear regression. Steps: 1. Gradient Estimation: Compute the gradient 
abla V at every voxel using 4D linear regression, as conventional central difference is insufficient due to its narrow voxel neighborhood reliance. 2. Particle Selection: Identify particles within the user-defined distance d{thresh} from the implicit contour surface. 3. Primitive Transformation: Treat selected particles as point primitives. 4. Contour Tracing: Pass points to a geometry shader to trace along the contour direction, transforming them into line-strips that resemble contour segments. The trace direction and constant-width measure are adopted from the VolumeFlies framework. 5. Rendering: Render the generated line-strips directly to the screen, not to a texture buffer. 6. Color/Opacity Assignment: Determine color and opacity for each voxel/pixel based only on the gradient magnitude |
abla V| and the angle 	heta between the viewing direction \vec{v} and the gradient vector 
abla V. Formulas: Contour Condition: The contour exists where the gradient magnitude is high and the surface normal turns away from the view. Viewing Angle: \cos 	heta =  rac{

abla V| |\vec{v}|}. VolumeFlies Measure: The original framework uses a curvature-dependent measure 	au with a threshold for constant-width contours. Parameters: d{thresh}: User-defined distance from the contour for selecting particles. Gradient estimation method: 4D linear regression. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Accuracy: Using conventional central difference leads to inaccurate contours because it only considers a narrow voxel neighborhood. Performance: Adding multiple particle sets for combined styles incurs a performance cost that may lead to loss of interactivity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Image Space Outline Generation
head: Edge extraction from depth/normal maps, Hertzmann's outline generation, Outline Post Processing
body: Image Space Outline Generation is a post-processing technique that renders non-photorealistic outlines by detecting discontinuities in screen-space depth or normal buffers. It solves the problem of defining object boundaries in volume rendering without the computational overhead of analytical geometry processing. Unlike sibling methods that compute contours from volumetric gradients or topological features, this method relies on simple pixel-wise comparisons of existing rasterization buffers, making it significantly faster and easier to implement. Inputs: Depth buffer containing the depth value d(x,y) for each pixel (x,y). Normal buffer (optional) containing the surface normal vector \mathbf{n}(x,y) for each pixel. Threshold parameters for edge detection. Outputs: Binary edge map or stylized outline image. Data Structures: The depth and normal buffers are stored as 2D arrays. Depth values are typically stored as floating-point numbers. Normal vectors are 3-component vectors. Steps: 1. Depth Edge Extraction: Iterate over each pixel (x,y) and its neighbors. Apply an edge detection mechanism, such as the Sobel filter, to the depth buffer. Depth differences are minimal between adjacent pixels of a single object and large between objects. Ed(x,y) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } |d(x,y) - d(x',y')| > \Delta d{th} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where (x',y') is a neighbor pixel and \Delta d{th} is the depth threshold. 2. Normal Edge Extraction (Optional): Apply the same edge detection mechanism to the normal buffer. Normals vary smoothly across a single surface but show a discontinuity between surfaces. En(x,y) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \mathbf{n}(x,y) \cdot \mathbf{n}(x',y') < \theta{th} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where \theta{th} is the cosine of the angle threshold. 3. Combination: Combine the detected depth and normal edges to yield all perceptually significant silhouettes. Depth edges reflect C0 discontinuities, while normal edges reflect C1 discontinuities. E{final}(x,y) = Ed(x,y) \lor En(x,y) 4. Analytical Curve Fitting (Optional): For further processing, such as modifying line qualities, calculate analytical curves from the detected edge pixel lists. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateoutlines(depthbuffer, normalbuffer=None, depththreshold=0.0, normalthreshold=0.0): """ Generate outlines from depth and normal buffers. Args: depthbuffer: 2D list of depth values. normalbuffer: 2D list of normal vectors (optional). depththreshold: Minimum depth difference to be considered an edge. normalthreshold: Cosine threshold for normal angle difference. Returns: edgemap: 2D list of booleans. """ height = len(depthbuffer) width = len(depthbuffer[0]) edgemap = [[False for in range(width)] for in range(height)] offsets = [(-1, 0), (1, 0), (0, -1), (0, 1)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): isedge = False # Check depth discontinuities (C0) for dy, dx in offsets: ny, nx = y + dy, x + dx if 0 <= ny < height and 0 <= nx < width: if abs(depthbuffer[y][x] - depthbuffer[ny][nx]) > depththreshold: isedge = True break # Check normal discontinuities (C1) if normal buffer is provided if not isedge and normalbuffer is not None: for dy, dx in offsets: ny, nx = y + dy, x + dx if 0 <= ny < height and 0 <= nx < width: curvec = normalbuffer[y][x] nxvec = normalbuffer[ny][nx] dotproduct = curvec[0]nxvec[0] + curvec[1]nxvec[1] + curvec[2]nxvec[2] if dotproduct < normalthreshold: isedge = True break edgemap[y][x] = isedge return edgemap Parameters: depththreshold: Not given in the sources. normalthreshold: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Precision: Depth buffer precision can cause false edges in distant scenes or true edges in close-up scenes. Use logarithmic depth buffers or higher precision formats if necessary. Boundaries: Pixels at the image border have fewer neighbors. Handle by ignoring out-of-bounds neighbors or padding the buffer. Noise: Depth and normal buffers may contain noise from rasterization or volume rendering. Filtering (e.g., Sobel, Gaussian) is recommended. A method to generate a Cumulative Gradient Depth Map (CGDM) for close-up images (defined as scenes with no or multiple vanishing points) by leveraging occlusion cues and local edge histograms. It distinguishes itself from Perspective View Depth Map Generation by relying on local edge density rather than global geometric convergence, and from Distant View Depth Map Generation by handling moderate-distance scenes with perspective distortion rather than infinite-distance horizons. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of pixels, as it involves a single pass over the buffer with constant-time neighbor checks. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the edge map, plus the cost of the depth and normal buffers. Performance: Very fast and simple to implement, suitable for real-time applications. Strengths: Simplicity, speed, independence from geometry complexity. Limitations: Quality depends on buffer resolution and precision; may produce jagged edges; does not provide analytical curve data for stylization without additional processing. When to use: Real-time NPR, simple outline effects, when performance is critical. When not to use: When depth/normal buffers are unavailable or unreliable. The method was surveyed by Hertzmann [Her99] and is based on the observation that depth and normal discontinuities correspond to perceptual edges. It is widely used in post-processing pipelines for NPR. name: Close-Up Image Depth Map Generation
head: Local Edge Histogram CGDM, Occlusion-based CGDM
body: A method to generate a Cumulative Gradient Depth Map (CGDM) for close-up images (defined as scenes with no or multiple vanishing points) by leveraging occlusion cues and local edge histograms. It determines spatial relationships by counting edge amounts, where regions with fewer edges are considered farther away. Inputs: A 2D image I. Outputs: An 8-bit CGDM Df of the same dimensions as I. Data Structures: E: Binary edge map (same size as I), where 1 indicates an edge, 0 otherwise. B{ij}: A grid of 5×5 pixel blocks covering I. N{ij}: Integer count of edge pixels in block B{ij}. N{av}: Average edge count per block across the grid. M: Total number of "main blocks" identified. Di: Circular depth gradient map for the i-th main block. N{i0}: Edge count of the i-th main block. Steps: 1. Extract edges from I using the Canny algorithm to produce binary map E. 2. Divide E into a grid of 5×5 pixel blocks. 3. Count the number of edge pixels N{ij} in each block B{ij}. 4. Compute the average edge count N{av} across all blocks. 5. Identify blocks where N{ij} > N{av} as "main blocks". Let the set of main blocks be indexed i=1 \dots M, with edge counts N{10}, N{20}, \dots, N{M0}. 6. For each main block i: Define a circular depth gradient map Di centered at the center of block B{ij}. Assign pixel value 255 at the center. Assign pixel value 0 at the circumference. Decrease pixel values evenly (linearly) from the center to the circumference. Determine the radius R. The source states an optimized radius is half the length (or width) of the image. 7. Fuse all Di maps into the final CGDM Df using the weighted sum formula: Df = \sum{i=1}^{M} \left( Di \times \frac{N{i0}}{\sum{j=1}^{M} N{j0}} \right) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatecloseupcgdm(image: list[list[int]]) -> list[list[int]]: H, W = len(image), len(image[0]) # 1. Edge Extraction: Apply standard Canny edge detection edges = [[0] W for in range(H)] # 2. Block Division and Counting BLOCKH, BLOCKW = 5, 5 gridh = H // BLOCKH gridw = W // BLOCKW blockcounts = [[0] gridw for in range(gridh)] for i in range(gridh): for j in range(gridw): count = 0 for y in range(i BLOCKH, (i + 1) BLOCKH): for x in range(j BLOCKW, (j + 1) BLOCKW): count += edges[y][x] blockcounts[i][j] = count # 3. Average and Main Block Identification totalblocks = gridh gridw Nav = sum(sum(row) for row in blockcounts) / totalblocks if totalblocks > 0 else 0 mainblocks = [] for i in range(gridh): for j in range(gridw): if blockcounts[i][j] > Nav: mainblocks.append((i, j, blockcounts[i][j])) M = len(mainblocks) if M == 0: return [[0] W for in range(H)] # 4. Generate Individual CGDMs and Sum R = min(H, W) / 2.0 totalmainedges = sum(nb[2] for nb in mainblocks) fusedd = [[0.0] W for in range(H)] for i, j, ni0 in mainblocks: cy = (i + 0.5) BLOCKH cx = (j + 0.5) BLOCKW weight = ni0 / totalmainedges for y in range(H): for x in range(W): dist = ((y - cy)2 + (x - cx)2)0.5 if dist <= R: val = 255.0 (1.0 - dist / R) fusedd[y][x] += val weight return [[int(min(max(val, 0), 255)) for val in row] for row in fusedd] Parameters: Block size: 5×5 pixels. Radius R: Half the length or width of the image. Center value: 255. Circumference value: 0. Gradient type: Linear/even decrease. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Image Dimensions: Not given in the sources. Implementation typically truncates to full blocks. No Main Blocks: Not given in the sources. If M=0, the formula is undefined; a fallback returning a zero map is required. Circle Boundary: Not given in the sources. The source states the CGDM is fused from these circles but does not specify if values outside radius R are zero; the pseudocode assumes zero outside R. Precision: The source uses 8-bit values (0–255). Intermediate calculations should use float to prevent quantization errors during fusion. Generates a CGDM for perspective view images by calculating separate horizontal and vertical depth gradients based on distance from a detected vanishing point. It is chosen when the scene exhibits a single clear convergence point, distinguishing it from this method which relies on local occlusion cues rather than global geometric convergence. Generates a CGDM for distant views with infinite-distance horizons. It is chosen when the scene represents a sky/land horizon at extreme distance, distinguishing it from this method which handles moderate-distance close-up scenes without global perspective distortion. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple, fast, relies on local occlusion cues which are robust for close-up scenes without global perspective. Limitations: Discrete block structure may cause artifacts at block boundaries. Radius is fixed relative to image size, not object size. Does not handle perspective distortion explicitly. When to Use: Close-up images with no or multiple vanishing points. When Not to Use: Perspective views with a single vanishing point or distant views with infinite-distance horizons. Originated in the context of holographic 3D display using depth maps generated by 2D-to-3D rendering. It builds on the observation that regions with fewer edges are generally farther away in close-up scenes. name: Perspective View Depth Map Generation
head: Perspective View CGDM Calculation, Vanishing Point Depth Map Generation
body: A method to generate a Cumulative Gradient Depth Map (CGDM) for perspective view images by calculating separate horizontal and vertical depth gradients based on the distance from a detected vanishing point. It distinguishes itself from Close-Up Image Depth Map Generation by relying on global geometric convergence rather than local occlusion cues, and from Distant View Depth Map Generation by handling moderate-distance scenes with obvious perspective distortion rather than infinite-distance sky/land horizons. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D RGB image I. Output: A CGDM D of the same dimensions as I, where pixel values represent depth gradients ranging from 0 (farthest) to 2^{BD}-1 (nearest). Data Structures: I: Input image, dimensions W \times H. D: Output depth map, dimensions W \times H, type unsigned integer with bit depth BD (typically 8, range 0–255). (x{vp}, y{vp}): Coordinates of the vanishing point. M, N: Number of pixels in the CGDM in the horizontal and vertical directions, respectively. Steps: 1. Image Expansion (Padding): To mitigate depth errors caused by non-central vanishing points, expand the original image I to twice its size by zero-padding. Let the padded image be I{pad} with dimensions 2W \times 2H. 2. Edge Extraction: Extract edges from the original image I using the Canny algorithm. 3. Line Detection: Detect straight lines from the extracted edges using the Hough transform. 4. Vanishing Point Identification: Identify the vanishing point (x{vp}, y{vp}) as the intersection of the detected straight lines. If the lines do not intersect at a single point, the image is not a perspective image. 5. Cropping for Calculation: To ensure the vanishing point is treated as the center for gradient calculation: a. Search for the vanishing point (x{vp}, y{vp}) in the padded image I{pad}. b. Calculate the maximum distance from (x{vp}, y{vp}) to any edge of I{pad}. c. Crop I{pad} using (x{vp}, y{vp}) as the center and the maximum length from the vanishing point to the edge of the image as the side length to form a cropped image I{crop}. 6. CGDM Calculation: Calculate the CGDM for I{crop} using separate gradients for horizontal and vertical planes. For content on the horizontal plane, assign depth gradient values from 0 to 2^{BD}-1 along the columns from the vanishing point to the edge. For content on the vertical plane, assign depth gradient values from 0 to 2^{BD}-1 along the rows from the vanishing point to the edge. The depth values are calculated using the following formulas: \text{depth}h(x, y) = (2^{BD} - 1) \frac{y - y{vp}}{N - y{vp}} \text{depth}v(x, y) = (2^{BD} - 1) \frac{x - x{vp}}{M - x{vp}} Where \text{depth}h and \text{depth}v are the depth gradients on the horizontal and vertical planes, respectively. The variables (x, y) are pixel coordinates, (x{vp}, y{vp}) is the vanishing point coordinate, M and N are the CGDM dimensions, and BD is the bit depth. The formulas assume y increases downwards and x increases rightwards, implying a linear gradient from 0 at y = y{vp} to 2^{BD}-1 at y = N. 7. Final Output: Obtain the CGDM of the original image by cutting the CGDM of the cropped image to match the original image dimensions. Parameters: BD: Bit depth of the CGDM (e.g., 8). M, N: Number of pixels in the CGDM in the horizontal and vertical directions. (x{vp}, y{vp}): Coordinate value of the vanishing point. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Central Vanishing Point: If the vanishing point is not in the central area, depth error occurs in holographic reconstruction. The padding and cropping steps are specifically designed to avoid this error. No Single Intersection: If straight lines do not intersect at one point, the method fails to identify a perspective view. Plane Ambiguity: The method assumes content belongs to either horizontal or vertical planes, distinguished by vanishing lines, but the algorithmic distinction is not detailed in the source. A method to generate a CGDM for distant view images (outdoor scenes with sky, land, water) by assuming the sky is infinitely far and depth increases linearly from the sky-land borderline to the bottom of the image. It is chosen when the proportion p of pixels satisfying specific HSI color ranges is greater than 0.5. The vanishing point is located on the sky-land borderline, and depth is calculated using a cumulative horizontal edge histogram, avoiding the need for vanishing point detection. Time and memory complexity, measured performance, and scaling behavior are not given in the sources. The method requires clear straight lines and a single vanishing point, and fails for close-up or distant view images. Originated in the context of holographic 3D display using depth maps generated by 2D-to-3D rendering approaches. The method is part of a broader framework that classifies 2D images into distant view, perspective view, and close-up types to generate appropriate CGDMs. Holographic 3D Display Using Depth Maps Generated by 2D-to-3D Rendering Approach, https://doi.org/10.3390/app11219889, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Lasso Contour Rendering
body: Lasso Contour Rendering is an interactive non-photorealistic volume rendering technique that allows users to manually define regions of interest using a free-form selection tool to generate contour overlays. It solves the problem of isolating complex volumetric structures by enabling user-driven contour generation. It differs from siblings like Object Contour NPR by relying on explicit user interaction to define the region of interest rather than automatic geometric or scalar-based detection. The method operates within a rendering pipeline that supports interactive overlay rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset, a user-defined lasso shape, and the current camera view. Not given in the sources. Output: A rendered image where the selected lasso region is highlighted with contour lines, composited over the underlying volume rendering. Not given in the sources. Data Structures: Lasso State: A boolean flag indicating if the user is actively defining the shape, accessed via gLassoInputHandler.isCurrentlyDrawing(). Render Pipeline: An object containing the shader programs and render passes for drawing the contour overlay, accessed via gLassoRenderPipeline. Steps: 1. Interaction Check: The system checks if the user is currently drawing a lasso by querying gLassoInputHandler.isCurrentlyDrawing(). 2. Pipeline Validation: The system verifies that the specific render pipeline for lasso contours exists (gLassoRenderPipeline). 3. Rendering: If the conditions are met, the active lasso contour is rendered using the offscreen render pass by calling gLassoRenderPipeline.render(). Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderlassocontour(inputhandler, renderpipeline, offscreenpass): """ Renders the lasso contour if the user is actively drawing. """ # Step 1: Check if user is currently drawing a lasso if not inputhandler.isCurrentlyDrawing(): return # Step 2: Check if the render pipeline exists if renderpipeline is None: return # Step 3: Render if conditions are met renderpipeline.render(offscreenpass) Flow Contours is a variant technique designed for visualizing flow data where high gradients are rare and boundaries are not the primary concern. It uses a transfer function widget based on a sine function to control the frequency and amplitude of the contours, allowing users to reveal flow structures like vortices, sinks, and sources. To reduce visual clutter, it often combines these contours with silhouettes (projected 2D gradients) to highlight major structures. It is chosen when the goal is to understand flow topology rather than sharp material boundaries. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides precise user control over which features are highlighted; effective for complex, ambiguous volumetric data. Not given in the sources. Limitations: Requires user interaction; not suitable for fully automatic or batch processing. Not given in the sources. When to use: Interactive exploration of medical or scientific volumes where the user knows what feature to look for. Not given in the sources. When not to use: When automatic feature detection is required or when the user does not know the location of the features of interest. Not given in the sources. The technique is associated with the work of Nikolai Svakhine, Yun Jang, David Ebert, and Kelly Gaither, presented in the context of volume illustration for medicine and flows. It builds on the principles of non-photorealistic rendering to enhance perceptual clarity in volumetric data.
