name: Curvature-Controlled Style Contours
head: Kindlmann Contours, Normal Curvature Contours
body: Curvature-Controlled Style Contours is a volume rendering technique that regulates contour thickness based on the normal curvature along the view direction to prevent the uncontrolled variation in thickness inherent in standard dot-product silhouette methods. While standard methods (v \cdot n \approx 0) produce contours that are too thick on flat surfaces and too thin on fine structures, this method uses curvature to maintain consistent visual weight across varying surface geometries. It builds on Outline and Contour Generation by integrating curvature-aware edge detection with style transfer functions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric dataset, view vector v, user-defined thickness parameter T. Output: Rendered image with stylized contours whose thickness is controlled by local curvature. Data Structures: Sample point: Position, normal vector n, previous normal vector n{prev} (from the previous sample along the ray). Geometry: No pre-computed Hessian or geometry tensor textures are required. Approximation of Normal Curvature (\kappav): Exact curvature requires the geometry tensor derived from the Hessian matrix, which is too expensive for fragment programs and requires two additional 3D textures for pre-computation. Instead, \kappav is approximated using the rate of change of the normal along the viewing ray. 1. During ray casting, store the normal n{prev} at the previous sample point. 2. Calculate the angle between the current normal n and n{prev}. 3. Divide this angle by the step size \Delta s between sample points: \kappav \approx \frac{\angle(n, n{prev})}{\Delta s} This approximation is coarse because the sampling occurs along the ray, not strictly along the iso-surface, but it is sufficient for finite-resolution volumes and introduces negligible computational cost. Contour Detection Condition: A sample is considered to be on a contour if the following condition is met: |n \cdot v| \le \sqrt{T \kappav (2 - T \kappav)} Where: n is the surface normal at the current sample. v is the view vector. T is the user-defined thickness value. \kappav is the approximated normal curvature. Style Integration (Lit Sphere Map): To integrate contours with style transfer functions (e.g., lit sphere maps), the normal projection coordinates are adjusted based on the curvature measure. 1. Let r = |n{x,y}| be the length of the eye-space normal projected onto the lit sphere map. 2. Calculate the adjustment factor \delta: \delta = 1 - \min\left(1, \frac{\sqrt{T \kappav (2 - T \kappav)} - |n \cdot v|}{\sqrt{T \kappav (2 - T \kappav)}}\right) 3. Adjust the projected radius to r': r' = \min(1, \delta r) This pushes the coordinates outwards along the radius if the sample falls below the contour threshold, allowing the contour color to vary based on the normal direction and curvature. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def curvaturecontrolledcontour(volume, origin, direction, T, stepsize, maxsteps): color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 nprev = None posprev = origin for i in range(maxsteps): pos = [origin[j] + direction[j] (i stepsize) for j in range(3)] if not volume.contains(pos): break n = volume.getnormal(pos) dist = math.sqrt(sum((pos[j] - posprev[j])2 for j in range(3))) if nprev is not None and dist > 1e-6: cosangle = max(-1.0, min(1.0, sum(n[j] nprev[j] for j in range(3)))) angle = math.acos(cosangle) kappav = angle / dist else: kappav = 0.0 nprev = n posprev = pos thresholdsq = T kappav (2.0 - T kappav) if thresholdsq < 0.0: thresholdsq = 0.0 threshold = math.sqrt(thresholdsq) dotnv = abs(sum(n[j] direction[j] for j in range(3))) iscontour = dotnv <= threshold if iscontour: r = math.sqrt(n[0]2 + n[1]2) denom = threshold if denom > 1e-6: ratio = (denom - dotnv) / denom delta = 1.0 - min(1.0, ratio) else: delta = 1.0 rprime = min(1.0, delta r) c = volume.lookupstyle(rprime) else: c = volume.lookupstyle(math.sqrt(n[0]2 + n[1]2)) alpha = volume.getopacity(pos) color = [color[j] + transmittance alpha c[j] for j in range(4)] transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) if transmittance < 1e-4: break return color Note: Standard front-to-back volume rendering accumulation is implemented to resolve the ray marching loop and color blending, as the source focuses on the contour/style logic. Parameters: T: User-defined thickness value for the contours. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If \kappav is zero, the threshold becomes zero and the condition |n \cdot v| \le 0 requires perfectly orthogonal normals to trigger a contour. The approximation of \kappav is not geometrically exact as it samples along the ray rather than the surface, but this is accepted as sufficient for the method's purpose. A technique using transfer functions based on surface curvature to render feature contours with roughly constant image-space thickness, specifically applied to clarify the shape and position of individual bones in small animal imaging. It combines curvature-based opacity with depth cueing to enhance structural clarity. Time Complexity: Low overhead compared to exact curvature methods. The approximation requires only storing the previous normal and computing an angle, avoiding expensive Hessian calculations or additional texture lookups. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory (one previous normal per ray or tile). No pre-computed 3D textures for geometry tensors are needed. Strengths: Provides consistent contour thickness across varying surface curvatures, addressing the "too thick on flat, too thin on fine" problem of standard dot-product contours. Interactive performance is maintained. Limitations: The curvature approximation is coarse and not geometrically exact. It relies on the step size of the ray casting; varying step sizes may affect the consistency of \kappav. When to use: When illustrative rendering requires consistent visual emphasis on edges regardless of local surface flatness or curvature, and interactive performance is required. When not to use: When exact geometric curvature is required for scientific measurement, or when pre-computed geometry tensors are already available and performance is not a constraint. The method was proposed by Brückner and Gröller in 2007 as an improvement over the original curvature-controlled contours introduced by Kindlmann et al. in 2003. Kindlmann et al. identified the thickness variation problem and proposed using the geometry tensor for exact curvature, but noted its high computational cost and memory requirements for volume rendering. Brückner and Gröller introduced the normal-angle approximation to make the method viable for direct volume rendering without pre-computation. The approach has been applied in scientific visualization, such as visualizing bone structures in small animal imaging. name: Silhouette Rendering
head: Object-space line rendering, Silhouette Rendering Pipeline, Stroke Pipeline
body: Silhouette rendering is an object-space line rendering technique that extracts significant edges (silhouettes and feature lines) from geometry, assembles them into strokes, and renders them with stylization to enhance perceptual clarity. It solves the problem of discriminating object classes or indicating context objects (e.g., bones) by rendering "interesting" features with silhouettes while leaving others without. Unlike image-space methods, it operates on pre-extracted geometric primitives, allowing for independent stylization and combination with surface or volume rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Segmented geometry data (meshes) with adjacency information; a classification of objects/regions as "interesting" (requiring silhouettes) or not. Output: Stylized line strokes (width, color, saturation, texture) composited over the final image. Data Structures: Adjacency Structure: Created during geometry data preparation to facilitate edge extraction. Stroke Data: Assembled from extracted edges (silhouettes and feature lines). Z-Buffer: Depth buffer used for hidden line removal. Steps: 1. Geometry Data Preparation: Create a geometry structure providing adjacency information for the mesh. 2. Line Extraction: Extract significant edges, specifically silhouettes and feature lines, from the mesh. 3. Stroke Assembly: Assemble the extracted edges into strokes. 4. Hidden Line Removal (HLR): a. Render the objects into the z-buffer only (frame buffer remains unchanged). b. For each stroke, scan-convert the line individually. c. Classify each line segment as hidden or visible by locally comparing the line's z-depths against the pre-generated z-buffer data. 5. Stroke Stylization: Apply stylization to the visible strokes, including changing width, saturation, color, and texture. 6. Compositing: Render surface objects into the final image prior to the lines if surface rendering is used. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def silhouetterendering(meshes, interestingmask, cameraviewdir, zbuffer): # Step 1: Geometry Data Preparation adjacency = buildadjacencystructure(meshes) # Step 2 & 3: Line Extraction and Stroke Assembly strokes = [] for mesh in meshes: if interestingmask[mesh.id]: edges = extractsignificantedges(mesh, adjacency[mesh.id], cameraviewdir) strokes.extend(assemblestrokes(edges)) # Step 4: Hidden Line Removal visiblestrokes = [] for stroke in strokes: isvisible = True for segment in stroke.segments: linez = getlinezdepth(segment, cameraviewdir) bufferz = zbuffer[segment.screencoords] if linez > bufferz: isvisible = False break if isvisible: visiblestrokes.append(stroke) # Step 5: Stroke Stylization stylizedstrokes = [] for stroke in visiblestrokes: stroke.width = applystylization(stroke.width, "width") stroke.saturation = applystylization(stroke.saturation, "saturation") stroke.color = applystylization(stroke.color, "color") stroke.texture = applystylization(stroke.texture, "texture") stylizedstrokes.append(stroke) # Step 6: Compositing finalimage = rendersurface(meshes) for stroke in stylizedstrokes: drawstroke(finalimage, stroke) return finalimage def buildadjacencystructure(meshes): return {mesh.id: {edge: faces for edge, faces in mesh.edges} for mesh in meshes} def extractsignificantedges(mesh, adjacency, viewdir): edges = [] for edge, faces in adjacency.items(): if len(faces) == 1: edges.append(edge) elif len(faces) == 2: n1, n2 = faces[0].normal, faces[1].normal if dot(n1, viewdir) dot(n2, viewdir) < 0: edges.append(edge) return edges def assemblestrokes(edges): return [LineSegment(start=e.v1, end=e.v2) for e in edges] def getlinezdepth(segment, viewdir): return dot(segment.midpoint, viewdir) def applystylization(value, param): return value 1.2 if param == "width" else value def rendersurface(meshes): return createcolorbuffer() def drawstroke(image, stroke): rasterizeline(image, stroke.start, stroke.end, stroke.color) Parameters and Edge Cases: Interestingness Criteria: Defined by user or application context (e.g., lymph nodes touching critical structures). Z-Buffer Precision: Local comparison of z-depths requires sufficient precision to avoid artifacts at discontinuities. Order of Rendering: Surface objects must be rendered into the final image prior to the lines if surface rendering is combined. Extracts silhouettes in image space using edge detection filters with optional perturbation, chosen for interactive frame rates with huge or animated datasets. Time Complexity: Depends on mesh complexity and number of strokes. HLR requires rendering the scene once and then processing each stroke segment. Memory Complexity: Requires storing adjacency structures, stroke data, and a z-buffer. Strengths: Allows independent stylization of edges; effective for discriminating object classes and indicating context; fast HLR method using z-buffer comparison. Limitations: Requires pre-segmented geometry and adjacency information. When to Use: When precise control over edge stylization is needed, or when combining silhouettes with surface/volume rendering in a scenegraph-based approach. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Originated in the context of medical visualization, specifically for surgery education and planning, to help users distinguish between lymph nodes and critical structures. Developed by Tietjen et al. as part of a pipeline combining silhouettes, surface, and volume rendering. name: Image-space silhouette extraction with perturbation
head: Image-Space Silhouette Detection, Image-space silhouette extraction
body: This method extracts surface silhouettes in image space using edge detection filters, optionally modified by a procedural perturbation function for artistic variation, and combines them with Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) for depth perception. It is chosen for interactive frame rates with huge or animated data sets, as it avoids the high computational effort required by object-space and hybrid algorithms that rely on processing large integral surface meshes. Inputs: 1. A volume dataset or pre-rendered DVR image. 2. An edge detection filter kernel (e.g., Sobel, Canny). 3. A procedural perturbation function definition. Outputs: 1. A final composite image containing the DVR result overlaid with extracted silhouettes/feature lines. Data Structures: Rendered Image: A 2D array of color values (RGBA) corresponding to the pixel grid. Edge Map: A 2D array of scalar values (or binary mask) representing edge strength or presence. Perturbation Field: A 2D array of scalar values representing the perturbation magnitude or direction at each pixel. Steps: 1. Render Volume: Render the volume using Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) to produce the base image I{dvr}(x, y). 2. Apply Edge Detection: Apply an image processing filter (edge detector) to I{dvr} to extract feature lines, hatching strokes, ridges, and valley lines. Let the output be the edge map E(x, y). Note: The specific edge detector is not defined in the sources, but standard implementations use gradient-based operators. 3. Apply Perturbation (Optional): Modify the edge map E(x, y) using a procedural perturbation function P(x, y) to obtain the perturbed edge map E'(x, y). Formula: E'(x, y) = \text{Modify}(E(x, y), P(x, y)). Note: The exact mathematical form of \text{Modify} and P is not given in the sources. A common implementation might involve displacing edge pixels or modulating edge strength based on noise fields. 4. Composite: Combine the extracted silhouettes/feature lines (E') with the DVR result (I{dvr}) to enhance main features while preserving contextual information. Formula: I{final}(x, y) = \text{Composite}(I{dvr}(x, y), E'(x, y)). Note: The specific compositing operator (e.g., alpha blending, max, overlay) is not defined in the sources. Typically, silhouettes are rendered with high opacity over the volume. Parameters: Edge detection threshold: Not given in the sources. Perturbation intensity: Not given in the sources. Filter kernel size: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Edge detection on noisy volume renderings may produce spurious edges. Boundaries: Silhouettes at the image border may be truncated. Degenerate Input: Uniform regions will yield no edges. Time Complexity: Dominated by the DVR rendering and the 2D image processing filters. Generally O(N) where N is the number of pixels, assuming fixed-size kernels. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the rendered image and edge maps. Measured Performance: Preferred for interactive frame rates with huge or animated data sets. Strengths: Avoids the high effort of processing large integral surface meshes required by object-space and hybrid algorithms. Suitable for huge or animated data sets. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial DVR rendering; silhouettes are only as good as the rendered image's contrast. When to use: When interactive frame rates are required for large/animated data, and artistic variation is desired. When not to use: When precise geometric accuracy of silhouettes is critical and object-space methods are feasible. The technique is part of the broader field of illustrative and non-photorealistic volume rendering. It builds on the idea of combining traditional illustration effects (like hatching or edge lines) with volume rendering to enhance the perception of salient features. The approach by Yuan and Chen is cited as behaving similarly, using feature lines, hatching strokes, ridges, and valley lines combined with visualization algorithms. Isenberg et al. recommend image-space techniques for interactive frame rates with huge or animated data sets, excluding object-space and hybrid algorithms due to the high effort required for large integral surface meshes. name: Topological Landscape
body: Topological Landscape is a visualization technique that maps the connectivity of a scalar field’s level sets onto a 3D terrain model using the contour tree. It solves the problem of interpreting complex topological relationships (merges and splits of contours) by leveraging human intuition for reading physical terrain. It sets itself apart from standard contour rendering by transforming abstract graph nodes into a spatial height map where peaks and valleys explicitly encode topological events, differing from Contour Tree by providing a geometric metaphor rather than just a hierarchical graph structure. Inputs: Not given in the sources. Outputs: Not given in the sources. Data Structures: The contour tree, which maps topological events to a tree structure where edges correspond to individual contour classes and vertices correspond to critical points. The landscape maps these elements to a 3D terrain model. Steps: 1. Compute Contour Tree: Generate the contour tree for the scalar field data. 2. Construct Terrain: Use the contour tree to build a 3D terrain model. 3. Layout Data: Apply established 2D visualization techniques to lay out the topological data within the terrain model. 4. Interpret Features: Identify peaks as locations where two or more contours merge, and valleys as locations where a contour splits into two or more parts. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Layout Technique: Established 2D visualization techniques are used for laying out the data; specific methods are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High-Dimensional Data: The method is applicable to contour trees of any number of dimensions, making it useful for exploring high-dimensional data sets. Topological Correctness: The generated topological structures must be verified as valid to ensure accurate landscape representation. The Contour Tree is a topological data structure that represents the connectivity of level sets of a scalar field as the isovalue varies. It sets itself apart from the Topological Landscape by providing the explicit graph structure rather than just a visual metaphor of peaks and valleys. It is chosen when an explicit hierarchical representation of contour evolution is required rather than a terrain-based visualization. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Harnesses human ability to understand terrain structure, providing an easier-to-understand model of underlying data topology. Effective for exploring high-dimensional datasets by reducing topological complexity to a visual terrain. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the 2D layout algorithm; specific layout constraints are not given in the sources. When to use: When exploring topological connectivity in high-dimensional data sets. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Topological Landscape was proposed by Weber et al. [45]. It was further expanded using different methods for laying out the data, primarily from established 2D visualization techniques [77]. The approach is part of the broader field of topological visualization techniques for volume multifield data. name: Contour Tree
head: Join Tree, Split Tree
body: The Contour Tree is a topological data structure that represents the connectivity of level sets (contours) of a scalar field as the isovalue varies. It solves the problem of tracking how contours are created, split, merged, and destroyed by mapping these events to a tree structure where edges correspond to individual contour classes and vertices correspond to critical points. It sets itself apart from the Reeb Graph by requiring a simply connected domain without loops, and from the Topological Landscape by providing the explicit graph structure rather than just a visual metaphor of peaks and valleys. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar field f defined on a simply connected domain (e.g., a grid or mesh). Output: A tree structure T = (V, E) where V is the set of critical points and E is the set of edges connecting them. Data Structures: The contour tree consists of two primary elements: 1. Vertices (Supernodes): Leaf Nodes: Represent local extrema. Local maxima: Where a contour is created (Join Tree context) or destroyed (Split Tree context). Local minima: Where a contour is destroyed (Join Tree context) or created (Split Tree context). Interior Nodes: Represent saddle points. Split saddles: Where one contour splits into two or more disjoint contours. Join saddles: Where two or more disjoint contours merge into one. 2. Edges (Superarcs): Represent a single continuous contour class between the supernode where it is created and the supernode where it is destroyed. A contour class is defined as a maximal set of continuous contours that do not contain critical points. Construction Algorithm: The contour tree is typically constructed by first building two auxiliary structures: the Join Tree (JT) and the Split Tree (ST), and then merging them. The Join Tree captures connected sub-level sets (regions below an isovalue), while the Split Tree captures connected super-level sets (regions above an isovalue). Join Tree (JT) Construction: 1. Start from the global maximum function value. 2. Continuously decrease the isovalue w. 3. Define the marked region X(w) = \{x | f(x) \ge w\}. 4. Identify connected components of X(w) as "upper objects". 5. Node Creation (Upper Leaf): When w passes a local maximum, a new connected component is created. Create a JT node for this upper leaf. 6. Merge Event: When w passes a join saddle point, two or more components merge into one. Create a new JT node for the saddle point and connect it to the node of the latest critical point belonging to the same object. 7. Termination: When w reaches the global minimum, create a final JT node and connect it to the node of the latest critical point. 8. Implementation Detail: Vertices in the domain mesh are marked in decreasing order based on function value. When a vertex is marked, it is connected to the lowest vertex of neighboring objects to form the JT. Split Tree (ST) Construction: Symmetric to JT construction, but starts from the global minimum and increases the isovalue, tracking super-level sets. Contour Tree (CT) Formation: 1. Augmented Contour Tree (ACT): Successively delete upper leaves of the JT and lower leaves of the ST, inserting adjacent edges to form the ACT. 2. Final CT: Successively delete regular (non-critical) vertices in the ACT to obtain the final Contour Tree. Optimizations and Variants: Sorting: Chiang et al. improve processing time by only sorting critical vertices during the merge tree construction stage, rather than sorting all elements. Multithreading: Gueunet et al. present a "contour forest" algorithm using a shared memory approach for multithreaded computation of the augmented contour tree. Seeds: To facilitate contour tracing, "seeds" are identified as vertices where contours can be built from. An entire contour for a specified isovalue is computed from the seed bounded by the two supernodes representing the critical points of that contour. Using seeds reduces the number of seeds required for representation but may increase overall storage size. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecontourtree(scalarfield, domainmesh): """ Computes the Contour Tree by constructing Join and Split Trees. scalarfield: function f(x) returning scalar value at point x. domainmesh: list of vertices with connectivity information. Returns: Contour Tree T = (V, E) """ # 1. Identify Critical Points # Note: Identifying critical points in 4D+ is difficult. criticalpoints = identifycriticalpoints(scalarfield, domainmesh) # 2. Construct Join Tree (JT) # Sort critical points by value in descending order sortedcriticalpoints = sort(criticalpoints, key=lambda p: scalarfield(p), reverse=True) jointreenodes = [] jointreeedges = [] componentmap = {} # Maps vertex to its current component root for vertex in sortedcriticalpoints: val = scalarfield(vertex) # Check neighbors to find connected components neighbors = getneighbors(vertex, domainmesh) neighborroots = [componentmap.get(n) for n in neighbors if n in componentmap] if not neighborroots: # New component created (Upper Leaf) nodeid = createnode(vertex, type='upperleaf') jointreenodes.append(nodeid) componentmap[vertex] = nodeid else: # Merge existing components # Connect to the lowest vertex of neighboring objects # In practice, union-find or similar structure tracks components root = mergecomponents(neighborroots, componentmap) # If topology changes (saddle), create a new node if len(neighborroots) > 1: saddlenode = createnode(vertex, type='joinsaddle') jointreenodes.append(saddlenode) for r in neighborroots: jointreeedges.append((saddlenode, r)) componentmap[vertex] = saddlenode else: componentmap[vertex] = root # Connect vertex to existing component if needed jointreeedges.append((vertex, root)) # Termination: Connect to global minimum node globalminnode = createnode(getglobalminimum(), type='globalmin') jointreenodes.append(globalminnode) # Connect to latest critical point jointreeedges.append((globalminnode, componentmap[getglobalminimum()])) # 3. Construct Split Tree (ST) symmetrically # (Code omitted for brevity, follows similar logic with ascending order) splittreenodes, splittreeedges = constructsplittree(scalarfield, domainmesh) # 4. Form Augmented Contour Tree (ACT) # Delete upper leaves of JT and lower leaves of ST, insert adjacent edges actnodes, actedges = mergejtst(jointreenodes, jointreeedges, splittreenodes, splittreeedges) # 5. Form Final Contour Tree # Delete regular vertices in ACT contourtreenodes, contourtreeedges = simplifyact(actnodes, actedges) return contourtreenodes, contourtreeedges Parameters: Neighborhood Definition: Changing the method of defining neighbors during split/merge tree computations can slightly alter the location of critical points, though the underlying structure (number of supernodes and superarcs) remains fixed. Genus Information: The contour tree typically does not contain information regarding changes in topological genus (loops); this must be added to the output separately if required. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Simply Connected Domains: The input domain must be simply connected and free of loops. The merge tree computation phase cannot correctly handle data without a boundary or with loops. For such cases, the Reeb Graph should be used. High Dimensionality: Critical vertices are difficult to identify in data with dimensionality of four or more. Load Imbalance: In multithreaded implementations (e.g., contour forest), speedup is limited by load imbalance and redundant computations. The Reeb graph is a topological data structure that generalizes the contour tree to compute the topology of scalar data on domains that are not simply connected (contain loops) or lack a boundary. It solves the problem of capturing global topology in complex geometries where standard contour trees fail. It sets itself apart from the Contour Tree by explicitly handling domains with loops or missing boundaries, and from the Joint Contour Net by operating on single-variable scalar fields rather than multivariate data. This method applies distinct transfer functions to different topological zones of a scalar field, determined by mapping sample points to arcs in a contour tree via monotone paths. It sets itself apart from global transfer functions by allowing topology-aware color and opacity mapping, and from simple gradient reversal or flattening by using dynamic tube sweeping to broaden connections between components, providing a smoother approximation of the scalar field. Contour-Tree-Defined Segmentation partitions a scalar volume into topological zones, where each zone corresponds to an arc in the contour tree of the underlying trilinear interpolant. It solves the problem of assigning independent transfer functions to distinct topological structures, allowing for the isolation of specific features based on their creation and destruction isovalue ranges. It builds on the concept of topological zones defined by Cox et al. and extends prior work by allowing independent transfer functions per zone and using trilinear interpolation over hexahedral cells. Stratified Morse Theory (SMT) for Euler Characteristic is a mathematical framework and verification pipeline used to compute the Euler characteristic (\chi) of isosurfaces generated from piecewise trilinear scalar fields, specifically handling non-smoothness at cell boundaries and surfaces with boundary components. It solves the problem of verifying the topological correctness of isosurface extraction algorithms (such as Marching Cubes) by comparing the Euler characteristic derived from critical point analysis against the Euler characteristic of the extracted mesh. Unlike its siblings, which often rely on smooth manifold assumptions or digital topology constraints, SMT explicitly stratifies the grid into vertices, edges, faces, and cells to apply Morse theory locally, making it robust for verifying algorithms that guarantee topological correctness in the presence of ambiguous configurations. Time-varying Contour Topology Tracking is a method for establishing temporal correspondence between isosurfaces in time-varying scalar fields by maintaining and intersecting labeled Join Trees (JT) and Separate Trees (ST) across consecutive timesteps. It solves the problem of tracking topological changes (merges, splits, collisions) in contour evolution by labeling the JT from time t with edge sets derived from time t+1, then intersecting these labels with those from the ST to determine precise contour mapping. Unlike static contour tree analysis, this method explicitly handles the dynamic intersection of upper and lower objects between timesteps to resolve topology changes. After determining high and low vertices, look up their corresponding high and low arcs in the contour tree. Walk from the high arc towards the low arc to find the arc containing the sampled value f. Use the branch decomposition (a rooted tree) instead of the contour tree (a free tree) to find the path between branches b and c. Walk up the parent link of the deeper of the two branches b and c simultaneously. If neither stopping condition is met, the walk terminates when both paths reach the common ancestor a, which is the desired branch. When walking towards increasing function value, stop if the next step goes past a saddle with a higher value than the sampled point. When walking towards decreasing function value, stop if the next step goes past a saddle with a lower value than the sample. Complexity: The construction of the contour tree involves sorting critical points and processing connectivity changes. Chiang et al. note that sorting only critical vertices improves processing time in very large datasets. Memory: Using seeds reduces the number of seeds required for representation significantly but often increases the overall storage size of the contour tree. Performance: Multithreaded approaches (e.g., contour forest) offer quicker computations, but speedup is limited by load imbalance and redundant computations. Limitations: The method is restricted to simply connected domains without loops. It does not inherently capture genus changes. Critical point identification becomes difficult in dimensions four or higher. Usage: Merge trees are often used as a computation step in the construction of more complex topological data structures such as the contour tree. Alternatively, they can be used directly for analysis and feature extraction in complex data sets. The contour tree was introduced by Boyell and Ruston. It uses concepts from Morse theory to capture changes in the topology of a scalar field at critical points. Carr et al. investigated the use of contour trees in higher dimensional data sets and introduced the concept of augmented contour trees. The structure is fundamental in computational topology for tracking connected level sets. name: Reeb Graph
body: The Reeb graph is a topological data structure that generalizes the contour tree to compute the topology of scalar data on domains that are not simply connected (contain loops) or lack a boundary. It solves the problem of capturing global topology in complex geometries where standard contour trees fail. It sets itself apart from the Contour Tree by explicitly handling domains with loops or missing boundaries, and from the Joint Contour Net by operating on single-variable scalar fields rather than multivariate data. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar field defined on a simplicial mesh. The algorithm uses the 2-skeleton of the input volume to define relationships between vertices, edges, and triangles, a restriction that applies to scalar fields in any dimension. Output: A graph representing the topology of the scalar field's level sets. Data Structures: The method relies on a simplicial mesh representation (vertices, edges, triangles). Algorithm Steps: Reeb graph algorithms are split into two groups: sweep-based methods and split-and-compute methods. 1. Sweep-based Methods: These methods require the maintenance of level sets as the scalar value sweeps through the domain. Doraiswamy and Natarajan proposed an approach that explicitly maintains level sets, eliminating the need for loop-surgery pre-processing and generalizing to higher-dimensional inputs. 2. Split-and-Compute Methods: These methods collapse the problem to a contour tree computation. Loop Surgery (Tierny et al.): Perform symbolic cuts during the merge tree step to break loops, then stitch them back together to retrieve a topologically correct Reeb graph. Optimized Split-and-Compute (Doraiswamy and Natarajan): Use the join tree to identify potential loops, segment the domain into multiple loop-free contour trees instead of a single one, and compute these regions in parallel. 3. Streaming Algorithm (Pascucci et al.): An online algorithm that processes data points as they arrive, continually updating the output. This limits peak memory usage but has higher time complexity. 4. Random Collapse (Harvey et al.): Randomly collapses triangles for arbitrary 2-skeletons to improve running time. Formulas and Definitions: Streaming algorithm complexity: O(n^2), where n is the number of triangles. Random collapse complexity: O(m \log m), where m is the number of triangles. Parameters: Input Representation: The input must be represented on a simplicial mesh. Dimension: Applicable to models of any dimension, provided the 2-skeleton restriction is met. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Genus Sensitivity: Computations are sensitive to the topological genus of the input domain (e.g., sphere vs. torus). The number of loops from the Morse function extends algorithm complexity. Critical Point Precision: Variations in neighbor definition can slightly alter critical vertex locations without changing the graph structure. Stability: Output remains fixed provided the simplicial subdivision does not change. The Joint Contour Net (JCN) is a discrete graph-based representation of the Reeb space for multivariate scalar data, approximating the topology of n variables defined over an m-dimensional domain. It solves the problem of visualizing and analyzing the topological relationships between multiple scalar fields by partitioning the domain into connected regions called joint contour slabs. Unlike the Reeb Graph, which handles single-variable topology, the JCN extends this to multivariate inputs; it differs from the Multi-Dimensional Reeb Graph by using a quantization-based slab construction rather than critical node extraction. The Multi-Dimensional Reeb Graph (MDRG) is a hierarchical data structure used to represent the topology of multivariate scalar fields by recursively storing joint contours. It solves the problem of capturing complex topological relationships in domains with multiple independent functions (e.g., pressure, temperature) where standard univariate methods fail. It sets itself apart from the Joint Contour Net by providing a recursive, tiered representation of the Reeb space, which serves as an intermediate structure for extracting the Jacobi structure and the Reeb skeleton. This method measures the geometric size of topological handles in a scalar field by computing two specific nonseparating loops: the Reeb loop and the cross loop. It solves the problem of quantifying handle prominence to guide topology simplification, ensuring that geometric changes to the volume are minimized. It differs from sibling methods like Joint Contour Net by explicitly constructing these minimal loops on the isosurface to define a handle size metric, rather than relying solely on multi-dimensional topological descriptors. Time Complexity: The streaming algorithm by Pascucci et al. has O(n^2) complexity, where n is the number of triangles. This is optimal for 2D inputs but performs less favorably for higher-dimensional inputs. Harvey et al. propose a method with O(m \log m) complexity for arbitrary 2-skeletons. Memory Complexity: The streaming nature of the Pascucci et al. algorithm limits peak memory usage. Strengths: Correctly handles non-simply connected domains and domains without boundaries, which the contour tree cannot. Supports online/streaming computation. Generalizes to higher dimensions. Limitations: Computation is sensitive to topological genus; more loops increase complexity. Requires a simplicial mesh representation. When to use: Use when the scalar field is defined on a domain with loops or no boundary, and single-variable topology is sufficient. Use when online/streaming computation is required. When not to use: Use the Contour Tree if the domain is simply connected with a boundary, as it is simpler. Use Joint Contour Net or Multi-Dimensional Reeb Graph if the data is multivariate. The Reeb graph was first used for encoding topological features for visualization purposes by Shinagawa and Kunii, who applied it to represent objects from computerized-tomography (CT) sources. The sensitivity of Reeb graph computations to the topological genus of the input domain was first demonstrated by McLaughlin. Pascucci et al. later provided an online streaming algorithm. Tierny et al. introduced the "loop-surgery" technique to address genus sensitivity. Doraiswamy and Natarajan proposed alternative approaches, including explicit level set maintenance and optimized split-and-compute techniques using join trees. The Reeb graph has also been used to assist in the design of transfer functions in volume visualization by assigning opacity based on how many objects were obscured by nested surfaces and their proximity to the edge of a scalar field. name: Joint Contour Net
head: Discrete Reeb space
body: The Joint Contour Net (JCN) is a discrete graph-based representation of the Reeb space for multivariate scalar data, approximating the topology of n variables defined over an m-dimensional domain. It solves the problem of visualizing and analyzing the topological relationships between multiple scalar fields by partitioning the domain into connected regions called joint contour slabs. Unlike the Reeb Graph, which handles single-variable topology, the JCN extends this to multivariate inputs; it differs from the Multi-Dimensional Reeb Graph by using a quantization-based slab construction rather than critical node extraction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: n scalar functions f1, \dots, fn defined on an m-dimensional domain \mathbb{R}^m. Output: An undirected graph G = (V, E). If n < m, the output is an approximation of the Reeb space. If n \ge m, the output is a subdivision of the input geometry over the n variables. Data Structures: Graph: Undirected graph. Vertices (V): Represent joint contour slabs. Each vertex stores the barycentric spatial coordinates of the slab. Edges (E): Represent adjacency between joint contour slabs. Algorithm Steps: 1. Quantization: Define quantization intervals for each of the n input scalar functions. 2. Overlay: Overlay the quantization intervals to construct the bivariate/multivariate field. This partitions the domain into regions where the isovalue tuples of all n functions remain constant within their respective intervals. 3. Slab Identification: Identify connected regions formed by the overlay. These regions are the joint contour slabs. Each slab is a connected component of the domain where the quantized values of all input functions are identical. 4. Vertex Placement: For each identified joint contour slab, compute its barycenter (centroid) in the spatial domain. Place a vertex in the graph at this coordinate. 5. Edge Construction: Mark adjacency between regions. If two joint contour slabs share a boundary in the domain, add an undirected edge between their corresponding vertices in the graph. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computejointcontournet(scalarfields, quantizationintervals): """ scalarfields: List of n scalar function arrays on a regular grid. quantizationintervals: List of n tuples (min, max, step) for each field. Returns: vertices list of dicts, edges list of tuples. """ n = len(scalarfields) gridshape = scalarfields[0].shape numvoxels = 1 for dim in gridshape: numvoxels = dim # Step 1 & 2: Quantize and Overlay quantizedfields = [] for i, field in enumerate(scalarfields): minval, maxval, step = quantizationintervals[i] numbins = int((maxval - minval) / step) + 1 quantized = [] for val in field.flat: idx = int((val - minval) / step) idx = max(0, min(idx, numbins - 2)) quantized.append(idx) quantizedfields.append(quantized) combinedkeys = [tuple(q[idx] for q in quantizedfields) for idx in range(numvoxels)] # Step 3: Identify connected slabs (connected components of identical keys) visited = set() slabs = [] for idx in range(numvoxels): if idx not in visited: key = combinedkeys[idx] component = [] queue = [idx] visited.add(idx) while queue: curr = queue.pop(0) component.append(curr) c = [] rem = curr for dim in reversed(gridshape): c.append(rem % dim); rem //= dim for d in range(len(gridshape)): for delta in [-1, 1]: nc = c[:]; nc[d] += delta if all(0 <= nc[d] < gridshape[d] for d in range(len(gridshape))): nidx = 0 for dim, val in zip(gridshape, nc): nidx = nidx dim + val if combinedkeys[nidx] == key and nidx not in visited: visited.add(nidx) queue.append(nidx) slabs.append((key, component)) vertices = [] edges = [] vertexmap = {} # Step 4: Vertex Placement for slabkey, voxelindices in slabs: coords = [] for vidx in voxelindices: c = [] rem = vidx for dim in reversed(gridshape): c.append(rem % dim); rem //= dim coords.append(c) barycenter = [sum(c) / len(coords) for c in zip(coords)] vertexindex = len(vertices) vertices.append({'barycenter': barycenter, 'slabkey': slabkey}) vertexmap[slabkey] = vertexindex # Step 5: Edge Construction edgeset = set() for slabkey, voxelindices in slabs: currentv = vertexmap[slabkey] for vidx in voxelindices: c = [] rem = vidx for dim in reversed(gridshape): c.append(rem % dim); rem //= dim for d in range(len(gridshape)): for delta in [-1, 1]: nc = c[:]; nc[d] += delta if all(0 <= nc[d] < gridshape[d] for d in range(len(gridshape))): nidx = 0 for dim, val in zip(gridshape, nc): nidx = nidx dim + val nkey = combinedkeys[nidx] if nkey != slabkey: nv = vertexmap[nkey] edge = (min(currentv, nv), max(currentv, nv)) if edge not in edgeset: edgeset.add(edge) edges.append(edge) return vertices, edges Parameters: Quantization Intervals: The choice of intervals affects the resolution of the JCN. Finer intervals yield more slabs and a more detailed graph, but increase computational cost. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parallelization Merge: In distributed memory implementations, multiple sub-JCNs are constructed in parallel. The merge step, which combines these sub-JCNs into a single output, is the limiting factor for speedup. High Dimensionality: When n \ge m, the output is not a Reeb space approximation but a geometric subdivision. The algorithm still computes, but the topological interpretation changes. An improvement over the Jacobi set that relates the Jacobi set directly to the Reeb space by capturing the exact location of topological change. It includes 'regular sheets' connecting critical nodes, allowing it to capture topological elements (e.g., forking in multi-field topology) that the standard Jacobi set cannot represent. It is extracted as the set of critical nodes in the Multi-Dimensional Reeb Graph (MDRG). An alternative approach for presenting the Reeb space of multiple scalar functions. It differs from the MDRG by working directly with Jacobi sets rather than the Jacobi structure (which includes regular sheets). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The JCN is better suited to parallelization than contour tree algorithms because each joint contour slab is constructed from smaller independent regions called fragments. Limitations: The merge step in parallel implementations is the limiting factor for speedup. When to Use: Suitable for visualizing and analyzing multivariate data where topological relationships between multiple scalar fields are of interest, such as in nuclear physics (scission datasets) or meteorology (hurricane data). When Not to Use: When a single-variable topological summary is sufficient (use Reeb Graph or Contour Tree). The Joint Contour Net was first presented as a discrete representation of the Reeb space by Carr et al. [53]. It has been used in nuclear physics to visualize and analyze scission datasets, identifying the splitting of atomic nuclei into multiple parts using proton and neutron density fields. It was also used to visually analyze data from Hurricane Isabel, mapping vertices to barycentric spatial coordinates to capture topological changes. name: Multi-Dimensional Reeb Graph
head: Hierarchical Reeb graph, Multi-Dimensional Reeb Graph (MDRG) [S1, unofficial]
body: The Multi-Dimensional Reeb Graph (MDRG) is a hierarchical structure that recursively stores the joint contours of multiple scalar functions to represent the topology of multivariate data. It solves the problem of capturing complex topological relationships in domains with multiple independent functions (e.g., pressure, temperature, wind speed) or temporal snapshots. It sets itself apart from the Joint Contour Net by explicitly organizing the Reeb space into a tiered hierarchy of restricted Reeb graphs, serving as an intermediate structure for extracting the Jacobi structure and the Reeb skeleton. The MDRG constructs a hierarchy of Reeb graphs, where each level restricts the topology of a new function to the contours established by previous functions. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of n scalar functions F = \{f1, f2, \dots, fn\} defined on a common domain. Output: A hierarchical structure where Level k is the Reeb graph of fk restricted to the contours of f1, \dots, f{k-1}. Data Structures The structure is a list of Reeb graphs, indexed by level k \in \{1, \dots, n\}. Level 1: The standard Reeb graph of f1. Level k (k > 1): A Reeb graph representing the topology of fk, computed only on the connected components (contours) defined by the previous levels f1, \dots, f{k-1}. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialize Level 1: Compute the standard Reeb graph for the first function f1. 2. Iterate for k = 2 to n: a. Identify the joint contours of f1, \dots, f{k-1}. b. Restrict the domain of fk to these joint contours. c. Compute the Reeb graph for fk within these restricted domains. d. Store this Reeb graph as Level k of the MDRG. 3. Completion: The full MDRG consists of the sequence of Reeb graphs from Level 1 to Level n. Parameters Function Order: The order of functions f1, \dots, fn affects the hierarchy. The sources do not specify a default ordering rule, but note that the structure allows extracting the Reeb graph of any individual function fi from the hierarchy. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Degenerate Inputs: If functions are identical or linearly dependent, the joint contours may collapse, leading to degenerate Reeb graphs. Complexity: The recursive restriction can lead to a large number of components if the joint contours are highly fragmented. Pseudocode Unverified code. Args: functions: List of scalar functions [f1, f2,..., fn]. Returns: mdrg: List of Reeb graphs, where mdrg[i] is the Reeb graph for level i+1. """ mdrg = [] # Level 1: Standard Reeb graph of the first function # The sources do not specify the implementation for this step. mdrg.append(computestandardreebgraph(functions[0])) # Recursive levels for k in range(1, len(functions)): # The sources do not specify the implementation for this step. # The sources do not specify the implementation for this step. # The sources do not specify the implementation for this step. mdrg.append(computerestrictedreebgraph(functions[k], functions[0:k])) return mdrg def computestandardreebgraph(f): # The sources do not specify the implementation for this step. pass def computerestrictedreebgraph(f, prevfunctions): # The sources do not specify the implementation for this step. # The sources do not specify the implementation for this step. # The sources do not specify the implementation for this step. pass The Reeb skeleton is a simplified graph structure derived from the MDRG and the Jacobi structure. It takes into account the size of connected components, allowing measures of persistence to be assigned to its arcs. It is generated as the dual graph of the singular and regular components captured in the Jacobi structure. The generation process follows these steps: 1. Use the Jacobi structure to separate the Reeb space (approximated by the Joint Contour Net) into singular and regular components. 2. Generate the Reeb skeleton as the dual graph of these components. 3. Translate the sheet-like form of the Jacobi structure into a simplified skeletal form. 4. Assign measures of persistence to arcs of the Reeb skeleton. 5. Apply lip pruning techniques to progressively remove noisy features in the multi-field. Persistence measures can be applied to the Joint Contour Net, such as the accumulated volume of joint contour slabs in a connected region. Unlike the Layered Reeb graph, which works directly with Jacobi sets, the Reeb skeleton uses the Jacobi structure to aid multivariate simplification. Unlike the MDRG, which stores Reeb space criticalities, the Reeb skeleton provides a simplified graph for assigning persistence measures. It is used by Chattopadhyay et al. for multivariate simplification. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The complexity depends on the computation of the Reeb graphs at each level and the extraction of joint contours. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The structure stores a Reeb graph for each function, restricted by previous functions, which can be memory-intensive for high-dimensional data. Strengths: It provides a convenient structure for extracting the Reeb graphs of each individual function making up the Reeb space. It serves as a foundation for extracting the Jacobi structure and Reeb skeleton, which are crucial for multivariate simplification and persistence analysis. Limitations: The recursive nature can be complex to implement. It serves as an intermediate structure for extracting the Jacobi structure and Reeb skeleton, rather than a final visualization tool. The MDRG was introduced by Carr et al. as an extension of the Joint Contour Net (JCN). It was designed to extract further topological structure from the Reeb space by evaluating an intermediate structure, the MDRG. The MDRG is part of a broader effort in topological visualization techniques for volume multifield data, aiming to handle multiple independent functions such as pressure, temperature, or wind speed. The related Jacobi structure and Reeb skeleton were further developed by Chattopadhyay et al. to address the need for multivariate simplification and persistence measures. name: Handle Size Measurement via Nonseparating Cuts
head: Reeb loop and cross loop measurement
body: This method measures the geometric size of topological handles in a scalar field by computing two specific nonseparating loops: the Reeb loop and the cross loop. It solves the problem of quantifying handle prominence to guide topology simplification, ensuring that geometric changes to the volume are minimized. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar field F(x), its isosurface mesh M at level set F(x)=c, and a Reeb cycle CR in the Reeb graph R corresponding to a handle. Output: A handle size metric (scalar value) and the geometric definitions of the Reeb loop and cross loop. Data Structures: Isosurface Mesh M: A weighted graph of vertices and edges representing the level set, with geometric coordinates for edge lengths. Reeb Cycle CR: A sequence of contours on M that form a cycle in R corresponding to the handle. Shortest-Path State: Distance maps and predecessor pointers initialized for Dijkstra's algorithm on the mesh graph. Steps: 1. Identify the Reeb Cycle: Locate the cycle CR in the Reeb graph R corresponding to the handle to be measured. 2. Construct the Reeb Loop (L{Reeb}): Select a contour \gamma within the Reeb cycle CR. This contour is a nonseparating curve on the isosurface. Cut the isosurface along \gamma, topologically transforming the handle region into a cylinder open at both ends with two boundary sets A and B. Compute the shortest path on the isosurface mesh M between any point in A and any point in B. Constraint: The search for the shortest path must be strictly restricted to the region of the isolated handle associated with the Reeb cycle. This guarantees the loop matches the specific Reeb cycle. Combine the computed shortest path with the segment of \gamma it connects to form the Reeb loop L{Reeb}. This loop is locally nearly minimal because it closes by traversing along the contour. 3. Construct the Cross Loop (L{Cross}): Identify the two sides S1 and S2 of the Reeb loop L{Reeb} on the isosurface. Compute shortest paths from all points in S1 to all points in S2 on the isosurface mesh M. Among all shortest paths that form cycles when combined with L{Reeb}, select the one with the minimum length as the cross loop L{Cross}. 4. Calculate Handle Size: Calculate the length of the Reeb loop, |L{Reeb}|, and the cross loop, |L{Cross}|. The length corresponds to the extent of the cut along the surface necessary for loop closure. The handle size H is defined as: H = \min(|L{Reeb}|, |L{Cross}|) Alternative Metric: The area of the spanning minimal surface bounded by the loop can be used instead of length if deemed more appropriate for the application. 5. User Control and Filtering (Optional): Ratio Preservation: To avoid removing long, skinny handles, preserve handles where the ratio |L{Reeb}| / |L{Cross}| is large. Material Orientation: Determine the orientation of any contour in the Reeb graph cycle to check if the ribbon cycle encloses a void (F(x) \ge 0) or encloses material (F(x) < 0). This allows users to specify material addition or subtraction only by changing nodes with F(x) < 0 or F(x) \ge 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computehandlesize(meshadj, reebcontour, handlemask, scalarfield): """ Computes the handle size for a given Reeb cycle. Args: meshadj: Adjacency list of the isosurface mesh graph. reebcontour: List of vertices forming the contour gamma in CR. handlemask: Boolean array indicating vertices in the isolated handle region. scalarfield: Function or grid for F(x) orientation checks. Returns: handlesize: Float, the minimum loop length. reebloop: List of edges forming the Reeb loop. crossloop: List of edges forming the cross loop. """ # Step 2: Construct Reeb Loop gamma = reebcontour # Cut mesh along gamma to create boundary sets A and B # (Implementation: duplicate gamma vertices to form two boundary sets) A = list(gamma) B = list(gamma) # Compute shortest path between A and B restricted to handle region pathreeb = dijkstra(meshadj, A, B, handlemask) # Reeb loop combines the shortest path and the gamma segment it connects # (Exact segment extraction not given in sources) reebloop = pathreeb + extractcontoursegment(gamma, pathreeb[0], pathreeb[-1]) lengthreeb = sum(edgelength(meshadj, e) for e in reebloop) # Step 3: Construct Cross Loop # Identify two sides S1 and S2 of the Reeb loop on the mesh # (Mesh splitting not given in sources) S1, S2 = splitmeshbyloop(meshadj, reebloop) # Compute shortest paths from S1 to S2 pathcross = dijkstra(meshadj, S1, S2, handlemask) # Cross loop combines the shortest path and the Reeb loop segment it connects crossloop = pathcross + extractloopsegment(reebloop, pathcross[0], pathcross[-1]) lengthcross = sum(edgelength(meshadj, e) for e in crossloop) # Step 4: Calculate Handle Size # Handle size is the smaller of the two loop lengths handlesize = min(lengthreeb, lengthcross) return handlesize, reebloop, crossloop def dijkstra(adj, sources, targets, mask): """Standard Dijkstra's algorithm on a mesh graph.""" dist = {v: float('inf') for v in adj} prev = {v: None for v in adj} dist.update({v: 0 for v in sources}) pq = [(0, v) for v in sources] while pq: d, u = pq.pop(0) if u in targets: path = [] curr = u while curr is not None: path.append(curr) curr = prev[curr] return path[::-1] if d > dist[u]: continue for v, w in adj[u]: if mask[v] and dist[u] + w < dist[v]: dist[v] = dist[u] + w prev[v] = u pq.append((dist[v], v)) return [] def edgelength(adj, edge): """Returns geometric length of edge.""" pass # For a mesh with V vertices and E edges, each shortest path computation is O(E + V \log V) using a binary heap. Two such computations are performed per handle. Memory Complexity: O(V + E) to store the mesh and distance maps. Strengths: Provides a tight geometric measure of handle size. The use of shortest paths ensures the loops are locally minimal. The method allows for user control over topology simplification based on geometric properties (length vs. area) and material orientation. Limitations: Computationally expensive for large meshes due to multiple shortest path computations. The quality of the measure depends on the resolution of the isosurface mesh. The method assumes the Reeb graph is already computed. When to use: When simplifying isosurfaces while preserving significant topological features (handles) and minimizing geometric distortion. Particularly useful when distinguishing between "long skinny" handles and "short fat" handles is important. When not to use: For real-time applications where performance is critical and approximate topology simplification is acceptable. If the scalar field is noisy, the Reeb graph may contain spurious cycles, leading to incorrect handle measurements. The method was introduced by in the context of removing excess topology from isosurfaces. It builds on the concept of Reeb graphs for non-simply connected domains. The key insight is that a handle can be characterized by two nonseparating loops: one that follows the cycle of the handle (Reeb loop) and one that crosses it (cross loop). The minimum of their lengths serves as a robust measure of the handle's "size" or "thickness". This approach allows for more informed decisions about which handles to remove during topology simplification, compared to methods that rely solely on topological persistence or arbitrary geometric thresholds. name: Topological Zone Transfer Function Application
head: Contour Tree Mapping, Contour tree-based volume rendering, GPU-based Topological Zone Look-up, Topological Zone-Based Volume Rendering, Topology-Controlled Volume Rendering, Zone-based Rendering, Zone-specific transfer functions
body: This method applies distinct transfer functions to different topological zones of a scalar field, determined by mapping sample points to arcs in a contour tree via monotone paths. It sets itself apart from global transfer functions by allowing topology-aware color and opacity mapping, and from simple gradient reversal or flattening by using dynamic tube sweeping to broaden connections between components, providing a smoother approximation of the scalar field. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar field defined on a grid (voxels) or mesh (tetrahedra/hexahedra), a precomputed contour tree, and a set of transfer functions associated with contour tree branches. Output: A rendered image where each sample point is colored and opaqued based on its topological zone. Data Structures: 1. Branch Records: Stored logically in a 1D array but physically wrapped in a 2D texture due to dimension limits. Each record contains: Reference to parent branch, Value at its saddle, Depth in the rooted branch decomposition, Reference to its transfer function, and Scale-and-bias pair for simplification scaling. 2. Transfer Functions: Stored in a logically 1D, physically 2D array. References are texture coordinates; a function value is added to the coordinate to offset and select the proper color. 3. Voxel-to-Branch Map: Stored as a 3D texture with nearest-neighbor interpolation. Output is references (texture coordinates) to the branch array. 4. Tube Lookup Table: Stores three values for each function value v: Position pt(v), Tube radius rt(v), Replacement function value ft(v). 5. Tube Reference Map: A 3D texture storing references to the closest tube in each voxel's topological zone, determined in preprocessing. Algorithm Steps: 1. Determine Monotone Path Endpoints: For a sample point p in a cell, identify the local maximum vertex (v{high}) and local minimum vertex (v{low}) of the monotone path passing through p. Tetrahedral Meshes (Linear Interpolation): The path is implicit. Use the path from the highest-valued vertex to the lowest-valued vertex of the tetrahedron. Hexahedral Meshes (Trilinear Interpolation): Construct an explicit monotone path using axis-parallel segments because saddles may occur inside cells. Use Algorithm 1 below to find v{high} and v{low}. 2. Map to Contour Tree Branch: Look up the high arc (corresponding to v{high}) and low arc (corresponding to v{low}) in the contour tree. Identify the common ancestor a of the branches b (high) and c (low) in the rooted branch decomposition. Walk up the parent links of the deeper of branches b and c simultaneously. Stopping Condition: If walking towards increasing value, stop if the next step goes past a saddle with a higher value than the sample. If walking towards decreasing value, stop if the next step goes past a saddle with a lower value than the sample. If neither condition is met, terminate when both paths reach the common ancestor a. The branch containing the sample is the one where the walk stopped. 3. Apply Transfer Function: Trace the monotone path Q in the contour tree corresponding to the field path. Find the unique point q on Q with the same isovalue as p. Apply the transfer function associated with the branch on which q lies. 4. Tube Sweeping (Simplification/Gradient Reversal): For each voxel, retrieve the reference to the closest tube in its topological zone from the Tube Reference Map. During rendering, look up tube parameters (pt(v), rt(v), ft(v)) from the Tube Lookup Table indexed by the sample's function value v. Compute the blending function b based on the distance from the sample location ps to the tube axis pt(v): b = \frac{rt(v) - \|ps - pt(v)\|}{rt(v)} Clamp b to [0, 1]. The parameter \beta controls the width of the tube's influence, and \beta > 1 ensures the interior volume of the tube is visible during rendering. Compute the final output value v{out} by linearly interpolating between the original value v{in} and the replacement value ft(v{in}), weighted by b: v{out} = \text{clamp}(1 - b) v{in} + \text{clamp}(b) ft(v{in}) where \text{clamp}(x) = 0 if x \le 0, x if 0 < x < 1, and 1 if x \ge 1. 5. Simplification Scaling: If a branch is pruned, a scaling transformation s is applied to all children by multiplying each child's scale-and-bias pair by s. If pruning is reversed, apply s^{-1}. Scaling is performed on interpolated fragments during rendering before tube blending. The replacement function value ft must reflect this scale and bias transformation. Pseudocode for Hexahedral Monotone Path (Algorithm 1): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def findmonotonepathendpoints(trilinearinterpolant, p): """ Input: trilinearinterpolant: Function t(x,y,z) returning scalar value. p: Sample position (x, y, z) inside the cell [0,1]^3. Output: plo: Position of the local minimum vertex. phi: Position of the local maximum vertex. """ # Initialize path to boundary faces plo = rounddown('x', p) phi = roundup('x', p) if trilinearinterpolant(plo) > trilinearinterpolant(phi): plo, phi = phi, plo # Complete descending path to mesh vertex (from plo) temp = roundup('y', plo) plo = rounddown('y', plo) if trilinearinterpolant(plo) > trilinearinterpolant(temp): plo, temp = temp, plo temp = roundup('z', plo) plo = rounddown('z', plo) if trilinearinterpolant(plo) > trilinearinterpolant(temp): plo, temp = temp, plo # Complete ascending path to mesh vertex (from phi) temp = roundup('y', phi) phi = rounddown('y', phi) if trilinearinterpolant(phi) < trilinearinterpolant(temp): phi, temp = temp, phi temp = roundup('z', phi) phi = rounddown('z', phi) if trilinearinterpolant(phi) < trilinearinterpolant(temp): phi, temp = temp, phi return plo, phi def rounddown(axis, p): """Replaces the component corresponding to axis with 0.""" if axis == 'x': return (0, p[1], p[2]) elif axis == 'y': return (p[0], 0, p[2]) elif axis == 'z': return (p[0], p[1], 0) def roundup(axis, p): """Replaces the component corresponding to axis with 1.""" if axis == 'x': return (1, p[1], p[2]) elif axis == 'y': return (p[0], 1, p[2]) elif axis == 'z': return (p[0], p[1], 1) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hexahedral Saddles: Trilinear interpolation allows saddles inside cells, requiring explicit path construction (Algorithm 1) rather than using vertex extrema directly. Scaling Composition: When multiple simplifications are applied, scaling transformations must be composed into a single scale-and-bias pair per zone to ensure correct rendering. Time Complexity: The branch lookup involves walking up the branch decomposition tree, which is logarithmic in the number of branches in the worst case, but typically small. The tube lookup is O(1) via texture access. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the contour tree, branch decomposition, voxel-to-branch map (32 bits/voxel), tube reference map, and transfer functions. Texture usage depends on the number of branches and transfer functions. Performance: Measured on an NVIDIA 7800 GPU. Frame rates for 512x512 images with approx. one sample per voxel per ray. The Fuel dataset (64x64x64) and Nucleon dataset (41x41x41) were used for testing. The Chest CT dataset (384x384x240) was also rendered. Strengths: Provides topology-aware visualization, allowing users to highlight specific structures (e.g., ribs in CT) while maintaining context. Tube sweeping offers a smoother approximation of the scalar field than gradient reversal or flattening, with gradual growth of simplified components. Limitations: Requires preprocessing to build the contour tree and branch decomposition. The method is complex to implement due to the need for GPU-based branch lookup and tube sweeping. This method was introduced by J. Weber, J. Tierny, H. Hagen, J. P. Burgess, and C. Gold in their paper "Topology-Controlled Volume Rendering". It builds on the concepts of the contour tree Contour Tree and extends them to volume rendering by mapping topological zones to transfer functions. The method addresses the limitation of global transfer functions by allowing distinct visualizations for different topological features. name: Contour-Tree-Defined Segmentation
head: Topological Zone Segmentation
body: Contour-Tree-Defined Segmentation partitions a scalar volume into topological zones, where each zone corresponds to an arc in the contour tree of the underlying trilinear interpolant. It solves the problem of assigning independent transfer functions to distinct topological structures, allowing for the isolation of specific features based on their creation and destruction isovalue ranges. It builds on the concept of topological zones defined by Cox et al. and extends prior work by allowing independent transfer functions per zone and using trilinear interpolation over hexahedral cells. Inputs: A scalar field defined on a regular grid of hexahedral cells, typically with trilinear interpolation. Outputs: A segmentation of the volume into topological zones, each associated with a specific transfer function, and the final rendered image. Data Structures: 1. Grid: Hexahedral cells with scalar values at vertices. 2. Widget: A local graph structure within each cube. Edges include the cube's mesh edges, plus augmented edges connecting body saddles, face saddles, and vertices. 3. Contour Tree: A graph where nodes represent critical points (minima, maxima, saddles) and arcs represent intervals between critical values. 4. Simplified Tree: The contour tree after simplification to remove noise (symbolic perturbation). 5. Branch Decomposition: A hierarchical representation of the simplified contour tree to manage complexity and avoid oversegmentation. 6. Transfer Functions: A mapping from each topological zone (arc in the simplified tree) to opacity/color parameters. Steps: 1. Compute the Contour Tree: Compute the contour tree of the trilinear interpolant using a variation of the method by Pascucci and Cole-McLaughlin. Construct the widget in each cube as described above. Apply the graph-theoretic algorithm to the union of cellwise join and split trees derived from these widgets. Any graph accurately representing the topology of the trilinear interpolant may be substituted. 2. Simplify the Contour Tree: Apply topological simplification to the computed contour tree to remove symbolic perturbation (noise). This step merges insignificant arcs, reducing the number of topological zones. 3. Assign Transfer Functions: Assign a specific transfer function to each remaining arc (topological zone) in the simplified contour tree. The hierarchy is stored using branch decomposition to allow coarse interactions and propagation of transfer function changes. Branch decomposition concatenates sequences of arcs into single units if their regions do not overlap in value range, preventing oversegmentation. 4. Volume Rendering with Zone-Specific Opacity: For each ray cast through the volume, determine which topological zone the current sample point belongs to. Look up the opacity directly from the transfer function assigned to that specific zone. Apply the trilinear interpolant over the hexahedral cells to determine the scalar value at the sample point. For cells spanning multiple topological zones, the method calculates the correct opacity by identifying the specific zone active at the sample point's scalar value, rather than interpolating opacities across tetrahedra. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def contourtreesegmentationrender(grid, simplifiedtree, transferfunctionsmap, rayorigin, raydirection, stepsize, maxsteps): accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 t = 0.0 while t < maxsteps stepsize: pos = [rayorigin[i] + t raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] scalarvalue = trilinearinterpolate(grid, pos) # Standard trilinear interpolation over the containing hexahedral cell zoneid = getzoneidforscalar(simplifiedtree, scalarvalue) tf = transferfunctionsmap[zoneid] opacity = tf.getopacity(scalarvalue) color = tf.getcolor(scalarvalue) alphacontribution = opacity (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedcolor = [accumulatedcolor[i] + color[i] alphacontribution for i in range(3)] accumulatedopacity += alphacontribution if accumulatedopacity >= 1.0: break t += stepsize return accumulatedcolor def getzoneidforscalar(tree, scalarvalue): # Each arc spans from a creation critical value to a destruction critical value for arc in tree.arcs: if arc.mincriticalvalue <= scalarvalue <= arc.maxcriticalvalue: return arc.zoneid return tree.defaultzoneid # Fallback for out-of-bounds values Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Symbolic Perturbation: Without simplification, noise creates excessive topological zones, leading to oversegmentation and performance issues. Cells Spanning Multiple Zones: If a hexahedral cell contains critical points, it spans multiple topological zones. The method must correctly identify which zone is active at the specific sample point's scalar value. Trilinear Interpolation: The method relies on the topology of the trilinear interpolant, not a tetrahedral decomposition. Using tetrahedral interpolation for opacity lookup is explicitly avoided as it causes artifacts. Uses user-drawn 2D contours to isolate volume portions before transfer function specification. It differs by replacing topological tree traversal with direct geometric separation via sketches. Complexity: The complexity is dominated by the contour tree construction and simplification. For large datasets, branch decomposition is used to manage the hierarchy, allowing coarse interactions. Performance: The method avoids the artifacts associated with tetrahedral interpolation of opacities. It allows independent transfer functions for individual zones, which can increase the complexity of the rendering pipeline but provides finer control. Strengths: Topologically distinct regions are segmented correctly. It handles the trilinear interpolant directly, avoiding tetrahedral artifacts. Branch decomposition helps manage complexity and prevents oversegmentation. Limitations: Requires computation of the contour tree, which can be expensive for very large datasets without simplification. When to use: When isolating specific topological features based on their creation and destruction isovalue ranges is required. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in "Topology-Controlled Volume Rendering". It builds on the concept of topological zones defined by Cox et al. and extends the work of Takeshima et al. by allowing independent transfer functions for individual zones and using trilinear interpolation over hexahedral cells. The contour tree computation uses variations of methods by Pascucci and Cole-McLaughlin, and the hierarchical representation uses branch decomposition by Pascucci et al.. body: This method uses user-drawn contours to separate portions of a volume before transfer function (FT) specification, allowing manual parameter definition on the isolated region. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by using direct geometric separation via 2D sketches rather than topological tree traversal or neural network training. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset, a 2D slice or projection view of the volume, and user-drawn 2D contours. Output: A transfer function (FT) defined for the region enclosed by the contours. Data Structures: Volume: 3D grid of scalar values. Contours: 2D closed curves defined on a specific slice or projection plane. FT: Mapping from scalar value to opacity and color. Steps: 1. User draws contours to separate portions of the volume. 2. The desired region is isolated. 3. User manually specifies the FT for the isolated region. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. x1) (py - y1) / (y2 - y1) + x1): intersections += 1 return intersections % 2 == 1 def extrudemasktovolume(mask2d, volume): # Extrude 2D mask along the slice normal (assumed z-axis) depth = len(volume[0][0]) height, width = len(mask2d), len(mask2d[0]) mask3d = [[[False] depth for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for z in range(depth): for y in range(height): for x in range(width): mask3d[y][x][z] = mask2d[y][x] return mask3d def multiplyvolumebymask(volume, mask): # Element-wise multiplication to zero out voxels outside the mask return [[[volume[y][x][z] if mask[y][x][z] else 0.0 for z in range(len(volume[0][0]))] for x in range(len(volume[0]))] for y in range(len(volume))] def manualftspecification(isolatedregion): # Interactive UI step where user adjusts opacity/color parameters for active voxels return {"opacity": 1.0, "color": [1.0, 1.0, 1.0]} A technique using a neural network to adjust the transfer function (FT) based on a sketch drawn on a volume visualization, training the network to emphasize marked regions. body: A technique using a neural network to adjust the transfer function based on a sketch drawn on a volume visualization, training the network to emphasize marked regions. It implements multidimensional transfer functions as back-propagation neural networks to decide voxel visibility, where training is supervised by user-selected voxels on 2D slices. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by using a learned mapping from visual sketches to multidimensional visibility decisions rather than manual parameter tuning or geometric contour separation.
