name: Importance-Driven Visualization Model
head: Importance-Driven Visualization
body: The Importance-Driven Visualization Model is a framework that dynamically adjusts visual representation based on computed feature importance to resolve occlusion and maximize perceptible information. It replaces viewpoint-independent classification with a pipeline of importance specification, compositing, and sparseness representation. It differs from siblings like Geometric Buffers (G-buffers) and Volume Illustration by focusing on a unified pipeline of importance specification, compositing, and sparseness representation rather than specific shading or edge-detection techniques. The framework operates on the principle that visual clarity is improved when less important features are made transparent or desaturated, while important features remain opaque and saturated. The core mechanism involves three stages: 1. Importance Specification: Computing a scalar importance value for each voxel or region. 2. Compositing: Integrating the importance values into the rendering pipeline to modulate the contribution of samples. 3. Sparseness Representation: Adjusting the visual density of the representation (e.g., opacity, color saturation) based on the importance level. The importance value is a scalar in the range [0, \text{max}]. Typical visualization levels use specific importance thresholds (e.g., 0, 0.1, 0.7, max) to define distinct layers of sparseness. The model supports automatic specification of importance based on feature classification or user-steered assignment to segmented objects. Saliency-based Opacity Modulation is an illustrative volume rendering technique that dynamically adjusts voxel opacity based on computed spatial importance (saliency) values to guide viewer attention toward salient features, such as boundaries, while suppressing less relevant internal structures. It differs from standard volume rendering by replacing fixed transfer functions with a data-driven modulation pipeline that enhances perceptible information through thresholding and scaling of opacity based on local intensity gradients. See Saliency-based Opacity Modulation. Semantic Shader Augmentation is a technique that automatically extends an input GPU shader program with rule-based rendering functionality, replacing static visualization mappings (such as fixed transfer functions) with dynamic mappings defined by semantic rules and fuzzy membership functions. It solves the problem of rigid, hard-coded semantic layers by allowing arbitrary existing shaders to be dynamically augmented with the capability to evaluate illustration rules, enabling domain experts to interactively explore semantic mappings without programming skills. Unlike the original semantic-layers approach where rule-based functionality is hard-coded a priori, or UberShader/SuperShader which combine pre-coded fragments, this method generates code fragments entirely on the fly, allowing minimal overhead and quick exploration of different semantic mappings for various visualization techniques. See Semantic Shader Augmentation. A system that attempts to predict what kind of illustration a viewer would like to see by using an intent-based approach borrowing from AI knowledge bases. It defines rules that describe communicative intent and uses stylistic decisions that reflect particular goals to generate the actual illustrations. A measure of regional importance for voxels, defined as the magnitude of the gradient of the obscurance field. It highlights edges, occlusion variations, and corners. The saliency S(p) for a voxel p is computed as: S(p) = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + C^2} where A, B, C are components of the obscurance gradient estimated by 4D linear regression: A = \sumk w(k)O(k)x(k), \quad B = \sumk w(k)O(k)y(k), \quad C = \sumk w(k)O(k)z(k) Here, k iterates over voxels in a 5^3 neighborhood centered at p, w(k) is the distance between p and k, O(k) is the obscurance of voxel k, and x(k), y(k), z(k) are the components of the vector from p to k. The resulting saliency is scaled to [0, 1]. It is used to select the best viewpoints by maximizing visible saliency and to enhance visualization by modifying the transfer function (opacity modulation) based on saliency. Regulation of dot density in stipple rendering based on the normalized absolute spatial importance map, where higher importance leads to denser dots or white regions. The density of the dots is modulated by the spatial importance map. Two user-defined parameters are used: a threshold t above which everything is rendered white, and a factor f that regulates the density scale. Additionally, a random value r(s) is generated for each sample s in the ray casting. The Importance-Driven Visualization Model was introduced by Ivan Viola and M. Eduard Gröller. It was implemented in the VolumeShop tool for interactive direct volume illustration, supporting multi-object rendering, 3D painting segmentation, stylized rendering, smart visibility, and labeling. The model addresses the problem of occlusion in 3D visualization, where important features are often hidden by less important ones. Traditional techniques classify features independently of the viewpoint, limiting the ability to reveal important structures. The model allows for automatic specification of importance based on feature classification or user-steered assignment. name: Saliency-based Opacity Modulation
head: Opacity Modulation via Spatial Importance, Saliency-guided Enhancement
body: Saliency-based Opacity Modulation is an automated technique that enhances volume visualization by modifying voxel opacity based on computed saliency values to guide viewer attention. It solves occlusion and visual clutter by making less important regions transparent while preserving or enhancing the visibility of salient parts. Unlike static transfer functions, this method is data-driven, relying on spatial importance maps to determine which features deserve visual prominence. It builds on the Importance-Driven Visualization Model by implementing the compositing stage where importance values directly modulate the optical density of samples. The method operates by computing a spatial importance map for the volume data and using these values to scale the original opacity of each voxel during rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Original volume dataset V, original opacity transfer function A(z), spatial importance map \Delta D(z), and modulation parameters (thresholds tl, th and factors kl, kh). S1 also supports a single binary threshold parameter. Output: Rendered image with modulated opacity A'(z). Data Structures: Spatial Importance Map: A 3D grid of the same dimensions as the volume data, where each voxel z stores a scalar value \Delta D(z) representing local intensity variation. The absolute value |\Delta D(z)| is normalized to the range [0, 1]. Parameters: tl: Low threshold for absolute spatial importance. th: High threshold for absolute spatial importance. kl: Factor regulating modulation for importance < tl. kh: Factor regulating modulation for importance > th. S1 uses a single saliency threshold of 0.2 to separate transparent voxels from preserved/enhanced ones. Steps: 1. Compute Spatial Importance: Calculate the spatial importance map \Delta D(z) for the volume, typically using an unsharp mask filter. 2. Normalize: Normalize |\Delta D(z)| to the range [0, 1]. 3. Modulate Opacity: For each voxel z, compute the new opacity A'(z) based on the original opacity A(z) and the importance value |\Delta D(z)| using the piecewise function from S2: A'(z) = \begin{cases} A(z) \cdot kl \cdot |\Delta D(z)| & \text{if } |\Delta D(z)| < tl \\ A(z) \cdot kh \cdot |\Delta D(z)| & \text{if } |\Delta D(z)| > th \\ A(z) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Alternatively, a simpler binary thresholding approach can be used: If |\Delta D(z)| < 0.2, set A'(z) = 0 (transparent). If |\Delta D(z)| \ge 0.2, set A'(z) = A(z) (preserve) or A'(z) = 2 \cdot A(z) (enhance). 4. Render: Perform standard volume raycasting using the modulated opacity values A'(z). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def clamp(val, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(maxval, val)) def boxblur3d(volume, radius=1): dimsx = len(volume) dimsy = len(volume[0]) dimsz = len(volume[0][0]) result = [[[0.0 for in range(dimsz)] for in range(dimsy)] for in range(dimsx)] for x in range(dimsx): for y in range(dimsy): for z in range(dimsz): sumval = 0.0 count = 0 for dx in range(-radius, radius + 1): for dy in range(-radius, radius + 1): for dz in range(-radius, radius + 1): nx = clamp(x + dx, 0, dimsx - 1) ny = clamp(y + dy, 0, dimsy - 1) nz = clamp(z + dz, 0, dimsz - 1) sumval += volume[nx][ny][nz] count += 1 result[x][y][z] = sumval / count return result def subtractarrays(a, b): dimsx = len(a) dimsy = len(a[0]) dimsz = len(a[0][0]) return [[[a[i][j][k] - b[i][j][k] for k in range(dimsz)] for j in range(dimsy)] for i in range(dimsx)] def absolutevalues(arr): dimsx = len(arr) dimsy = len(arr[0]) dimsz = len(arr[0][0]) return [[[abs(arr[i][j][k]) for k in range(dimsz)] for j in range(dimsy)] for i in range(dimsx)] def maxelement(arr): m = arr[0][0][0] for i in range(len(arr)): for j in range(len(arr[0])): for k in range(len(arr[0][0])): if arr[i][j][k] > m: m = arr[i][j][k] return m def dividearrays(arr, scalar): dimsx = len(arr) dimsy = len(arr[0]) dimsz = len(arr[0][0]) return [[[arr[i][j][k] / scalar for k in range(dimsz)] for j in range(dimsy)] for i in range(dimsx)] def createzeroslike(arr): dimsx = len(arr) dimsy = len(arr[0]) dimsz = len(arr[0][0]) return [[[0.0 for in range(dimsz)] for in range(dimsy)] for in range(dimsx)] def computemodulatedopacity(volumedata, originalopacity, tl, th, kl, kh): """ Computes modulated opacity based on spatial importance. Args: volumedata: 3D list of intensity values. originalopacity: 3D list of original opacity values. tl: Low threshold for importance. th: High threshold for importance. kl: Factor for low importance. kh: Factor for high importance. Returns: modulatedopacity: 3D list of new opacity values. """ # Step 1: Compute spatial importance (unsharp masking) blurredvolume = boxblur3d(volumedata, radius=1) diff = subtractarrays(volumedata, blurredvolume) absdiff = absolutevalues(diff) maxval = maxelement(absdiff) if maxval > 0: importancemap = dividearrays(absdiff, maxval) else: importancemap = absdiff # Step 2: Modulate opacity dimsx = len(volumedata) dimsy = len(volumedata[0]) dimsz = len(volumedata[0][0]) modulatedopacity = createzeroslike(volumedata) for x in range(dimsx): for y in range(dimsy): for z in range(dimsz): val = importancemap[x][y][z] if val < tl: modulatedopacity[x][y][z] = originalopacity[x][y][z] kl val elif val > th: modulatedopacity[x][y][z] = originalopacity[x][y][z] kh val else: modulatedopacity[x][y][z] = originalopacity[x][y][z] return modulatedopacity A dynamic focus+context technique that modulates voxel opacity based on the distance from a central reference point, inspired by the angular velocity of a viscous fluid rotating around its center. It solves the problem of occlusion in volume rendering by making voxels further from the center more transparent, thereby revealing inner structures during rotation or zooming interactions. Unlike static saliency methods, it adapts opacity in real-time to user interaction, specifically distinguishing between global rotation (center-based) and local zooming (focus-based). See Radial Opacity Change. This method computes a 3D spatial importance map by subtracting the original volume intensity values from a low-pass filtered (blurred) version of itself, effectively creating an unsharp mask. It captures salient boundary and separability information to modulate color and opacity in illustrative volume rendering, distinguishing itself from radiance-based saliency methods by relying solely on input intensity, which allows it to be computed as a preprocessing step independent of lighting and transfer functions. See Spatial Importance Map via Unsharp Masking. A technique to modify visual prominence by controlling optical properties (color and opacity) based on the level of sparseness. It sets itself apart from siblings like Spatial Importance Map via Unsharp Masking by directly altering the saturation and transparency of ray samples rather than just the opacity or spatial weighting, ensuring that sparse objects recede visually while dense objects remain prominent. See Sparseness-based Color and Opacity Modulation. Smart Visibility is a category of illustrative visualization techniques that extends traditional light-propagation-based visibility by incorporating high-level abstractions of human cognition, such as object relevance and viewer pre-knowledge. Unlike standard volume rendering which relies solely on optical depth and occlusion, Smart Visibility explicitly handles semantic importance to ensure relevant data remains visible even when geometrically occluded by less important structures. See Smart Visibility. Modulation of voxel color based on the spatial importance map to emphasize boundaries, using either raw importance values or absolute importance values. The color I' is computed as I' = I + \Delta D \cdot \lambda for raw values or I' = I + |\Delta D| \cdot \lambda for absolute values, where I is the original color, \Delta D is the importance value, and \lambda is a modulation factor. Typical \lambda values are -10, 0, 10, 20 for raw values and -5, 0, 5, 10 for absolute values. A pitfall is that with raw values and positive \lambda, the image becomes darker because most importance values are negative; with absolute values, darkening and brightening effects are reversed because all values are positive. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: In, the method was applied to CT head and body models. The modulation allows for interactive adjustment of parameters like kl and kh. Strengths: Effectively emphasizes boundaries and structural details. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the spatial importance map. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The concept of saliency-based modulation in volume rendering was introduced in the context of obscurance-based rendering frameworks. The specific implementation using spatial importance maps derived from intensity filtering was proposed by Ruiz, Boada, Feixas, and Sbert in 2010. The work builds on earlier ideas of importance-driven visualization and interactive volume illustration. name: Radial Opacity Change
head: Angular velocity metaphor opacity, Distance-based opacity modulation
body: Radial Opacity Change is an illustrative volume rendering technique that modulates voxel opacity based on the distance from a reference point (typically the object center or a user-defined focus point) to create a focus+context effect. It solves the problem of visual clutter and occlusion during user interaction (rotation, panning, zooming) by making peripheral or distant structures more transparent, thereby revealing inner details. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly modeling opacity decay as a function of radial distance, inspired by the physics of viscous rotation, whereas Spatial Importance Map via Unsharp Masking uses spatial frequency analysis and Sparseness-based Color and Opacity Modulation relies on local data density. The method modifies the base opacity \alpha{base} of a voxel using an exponential decay function driven by a style function S(t) and the Euclidean distance from the voxel to a reference center. Inputs: Voxel position \vec{P}{voxel} in world or object space. Reference center position \vec{P}{center} (usually the geometric center of the volume). Style function S(t), a scalar value derived from the interaction state (e.g., rotation speed or zoom intensity). Base opacity \alpha{base} (optional, often incorporated into S(t) or applied multiplicatively). Outputs: Modulated opacity \alpha{voxel} \in [0, 1]. Data Structures: No specific complex data structures are required beyond standard volume grid access. The method is computed per-voxel or per-sample during ray casting. Steps: 1. Calculate the Euclidean distance \rho between the current voxel position \vec{P}{voxel} and the reference center \vec{P}{center}. \rho(\vec{P}{voxel}, \vec{P}{center}) = \| \vec{P}{voxel} - \vec{P}{center} \| 2. Retrieve the style function value S(t), which represents the intensity of the interaction (e.g., angular velocity for rotation). 3. Compute the modulated opacity using the exponential decay formula. Formulas: For standard rotation or center-based modulation: \alpha{voxel} = e^{-S(t) \cdot \rho(\vec{P}{voxel}, \vec{P}{center})} For zooming interaction, where the transparency gradient shifts to a user-defined focus point \vec{P}{focus}: \alpha{voxel} = e^{-S(t) \cdot \max(0, \rho(\vec{P}{voxel}, \vec{P}{center}) - \rho(\vec{P}{voxel}, \vec{P}{focus}))} Parameters: S(t): Style function. In rotation scenarios, this is proportional to the angular velocity. In zooming, it controls the strength of the focus effect. \rho(\vec{P}{voxel}, \vec{P}{center}): Distance from voxel to center. \vec{P}{focus}: The initial point of interaction on the object for zooming semantics. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeradialopacity(voxelpos, centerpos, stylefunction, focuspos=None): """ Computes the modulated opacity for a voxel using Radial Opacity Change. Args: voxelpos (tuple): (x, y, z) coordinates of the voxel. centerpos (tuple): (x, y, z) coordinates of the reference center. stylefunction (float): S(t), the interaction intensity (e.g., angular velocity). focuspos (tuple, optional): (x, y, z) coordinates of the focus point for zooming. If None, uses standard radial decay from center. Returns: float: Modulated opacity alpha in [0, 1]. """ # Calculate distance from voxel to center dx = voxelpos[0] - centerpos[0] dy = voxelpos[1] - centerpos[1] dz = voxelpos[2] - centerpos[2] rhocenter = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) if focuspos is None: # Standard rotation/center-based modulation # alpha = exp(-S(t) rho) exponent = -stylefunction rhocenter alpha = math.exp(exponent) else: # Zooming interaction modulation # Calculate distance from voxel to focus point fx = voxelpos[0] - focuspos[0] fy = voxelpos[1] - focuspos[1] fz = voxelpos[2] - focuspos[2] rhofocus = math.sqrt(fxfx + fyfy + fzfz) # Formula: alpha = exp(-S(t) max(0, rhocenter - rhofocus)) # This makes voxels closer to focus (smaller rhofocus) have larger exponent magnitude # if they are far from center, effectively shifting transparency. distancediff = rhocenter - rhofocus if distancediff < 0: distancediff = 0 exponent = -stylefunction distancediff alpha = math.exp(exponent) return alpha Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: If S(t) is large and \rho is large, the exponent becomes very negative, potentially underflowing to 0. This is generally desired (opacity becomes 0), but ensure floating-point handling does not produce NaNs. Boundary Conditions: The formula assumes \vec{P}{center} is well-defined. For non-convex or disconnected volumes, the geometric center may be outside the data, leading to unintuitive transparency gradients. Zooming Logic: The zooming formula \max(0, \rho{center} - \rho{focus}) implies that voxels closer to the focus point than the center will have 0 exponent (opacity 1) if \rho{focus} \ge \rho{center}. This preserves context far from the focus while revealing inner parts near the focus. Radial Opacity Change (Zooming) is an illustrative volume rendering technique that reveals inner structures by modulating voxel opacity based on the distance from a user-defined focus point, rather than the distance from the volume center. Unlike its sibling Radial Opacity Change, which uses angular velocity and distance from the center to create a "tunnel" effect during rotation, this method shifts the transparency gradient to follow the user's interaction point, allowing for detailed inspection of specific regions while maintaining context elsewhere [14595-radial-opacity-change-zooming.md]. Depth Opacity-Modulation is a technique used to ensure visibility of voxels at the back of an atomic structure by modulating opacity based on depth, preventing self-occlusion from hiding rear features. It is distinct from the radial distance-based modulation of the parent method by using depth buffer values relative to the viewpoint. It is chosen when rendering complex atomic structures where rear features are frequently occluded by front features. Formula: \alphav = \begin{cases} Z(v), & \text{if } Z(v) \le 1 \\ 1, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where Z(v) = \alphas \cdot G(gv) \cdot r^{dv - d{min}(s)} Parameters: \alphav: Opacity of voxel v. \alphas: Seed opacity value for the atomic structure s, provided by a genetic algorithm. G(gv): Monotonically-increasing gradient magnitude opacity-modulation function mapping gradient magnitudes gv to opacity-modulation factors. dv: Depth value of voxel v. d{min}(s): Minimum depth of all voxels in the atomic structure s. r: Depth opacity-modulation rate, controlling the influence of voxel depth in modulation. Pitfalls: Voxels with high depth values (back side) are assigned high opacity to ensure visibility even if occluded by low depth voxels (front side). This can lead to visual artifacts if the occlusion is not handled correctly by the rendering pipeline, potentially showing "ghost" structures. Time Complexity: O(1) per voxel/sample, as it involves basic arithmetic operations (distance calculation, exponential). It adds minimal overhead to the ray casting loop. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per voxel, as no additional large data structures are required. Performance: The method is computationally inexpensive. The exponential function is the most expensive operation, but it is standard in graphics hardware. Strengths: Effective for focus+context visualization during interaction. It naturally reveals inner structures without complex preprocessing. Limitations: The "angular velocity" metaphor may not intuitively map to all types of user interactions (e.g., panning). The choice of center point can be arbitrary for complex shapes. When to use: When the goal is to dynamically reveal internal structures during rotation or zooming in a volume visualization. When not to use: When precise quantitative analysis of outer structures is required, as they are intentionally made transparent. The Radial Opacity Change technique was proposed by Sikachev, Rautek, Bruckner, and Gröller in 2010 as part of a dynamic focus+context framework for volume rendering. It is inspired by the metaphor of a viscous fluid rotating around its center, where particles at the border have the highest speed and are candidates to disappear. The method was designed to aid users in exploring data efficiently and detecting unknown features during interaction. It is often used in conjunction with DVR-MIP interpolation to enhance the visual feedback during user interaction. name: Radial Opacity Change (Zooming)
body: Radial Opacity Change (Zooming) is an illustrative volume rendering technique that reveals inner structures by modulating voxel opacity based on the distance from a user-defined focus point, rather than the distance from the volume center. Unlike its sibling Radial Opacity Change, which uses angular velocity and distance from the center to create a "tunnel" effect during rotation, this method shifts the transparency gradient to follow the user's interaction point, allowing for detailed inspection of specific regions while maintaining context elsewhere. Inputs and Outputs Input: Volume dataset V, camera parameters, user interaction point \vec{P}{focus} (initial point of interaction on the object), and a scaling factor S(t) that may vary with time or interaction intensity. Output: Rendered image with modulated opacity. Data Structures Volume Data: Standard 3D grid of scalar values. Focus Point: A 3D vector \vec{P}{focus} representing the location in world or object space where the user is focusing. Algorithm For each voxel \vec{P}{voxel} in the volume: 1. Calculate the Euclidean distance from the voxel to the volume center \vec{P}{center}: \rho(\vec{P}{voxel}, \vec{P}{center}) = \| \vec{P}{voxel} - \vec{P}{center} \| 2. Calculate the Euclidean distance from the voxel to the focus point \vec{P}{focus}: \rho(\vec{P}{voxel}, \vec{P}{focus}) = \| \vec{P}{voxel} - \vec{P}{focus} \| 3. Compute the radial opacity change factor using the maximum of zero and the difference between the distance to the center and the distance to the focus: \Delta \rho = \max(0, \rho(\vec{P}{voxel}, \vec{P}{center}) - \rho(\vec{P}{voxel}, \vec{P}{focus})) 4. Apply the exponential attenuation to determine the effective opacity \alpha{voxel}: \alpha{voxel} = e^{-S(t) \cdot \Delta \rho} Parameters \vec{P}{focus}: The initial point of interaction on the object. This point defines the center of the "zoom" effect. S(t): A scaling factor that controls the strength of the opacity modulation. It may be constant or vary with time/interaction. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls If \vec{P}{focus} is outside the volume, the distance calculations still hold, but the effect may be unintuitive. Precision issues may arise if \vec{P}{voxel} and \vec{P}{focus} are very close, leading to \Delta \rho \approx 0 and thus \alpha{voxel} \approx 1. The term \max(0, \dots) ensures that opacity is only reduced when the voxel is closer to the focus point than to the center, preventing unintended brightening of outer layers. This variant extends the Maximum Intensity Display (MIDA) technique by modulating only the opacity contribution based on importance measurements. Instead of using the maximum operator for both color and opacity, it accumulates colors and opacities along rays as in DVR but modulates opacity when a local maximum is found. The modulation is driven by importance measurements derived from gradient magnitudes, depth, intensity information, or a combination of these values. This approach aims to enhance depth perception and reveal the arrangement of rendered structures with minimum loss of information, addressing the main issue of information loss in MIP visualizations when adding color cues or modifying shading. Time and Memory Complexity Time: O(N) per frame, where N is the number of voxels or samples, as it requires computing distances for each voxel. Memory: O(1) additional memory per voxel for storing the focus point and intermediate distance calculations. Measured Performance Not given in the sources. Scaling The method scales linearly with the number of voxels. Performance may be impacted by the complexity of calculating distances for large volumes. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Allows for detailed inspection of specific regions without losing context. Effective for revealing inner structures near the focus point. Limitations: The loss of information is a key issue, as modifying opacity may conceal some information that is worth preserving. The effectiveness depends on the choice of \vec{P}{focus} and S(t). When to Use Use when the user needs to inspect specific inner structures of a volume while maintaining a sense of the overall context. Suitable for interactive exploration where the focus point changes frequently. When Not to Use Not suitable when preserving all information is critical, as opacity modulation may hide details. Less effective if the focus point is not well-defined or if the volume has no clear inner/outer structure. The Radial Opacity Change (Zooming) technique was introduced in the paper "Dynamic Focus + Context for Volume Rendering". It is part of a broader effort to enhance depth perception and reveal inner structures in volume visualization. The technique builds on the concept of radial opacity change but adapts it for zooming interactions, where the user focuses on a specific point and the opacity is modulated accordingly. The MIDA extension, described in "Enhanced perception in volume visualization", further refines this approach by integrating importance-based opacity modulation. name: Spatial Importance Map via Unsharp Masking
head: Gaussian Blur Difference Map, Intensity Filtering, Intensity-based Saliency Map, Spatial Importance Map Computation, Unsharp Masking for Volume
body: This method computes a 3D spatial importance map by subtracting the original volume intensity values from a low-pass filtered (blurred) version of itself, effectively creating an unsharp mask. It captures salient boundary and separability information to modulate color and opacity in illustrative volume rendering, distinguishing itself from radiance-based saliency methods by relying solely on input intensity, which allows it to be computed as a preprocessing step independent of lighting and transfer functions. Inputs and Outputs Input: A scalar volume model V: \mathbb{N}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}, where \mathbb{Z} represents the scalar intensity values of the voxels. Output: A spatial importance map \Delta D, a 3D volume of the same dimensions as V, containing signed values representing boundary saliency. Data Structures Volume Data: Stored as a 3D array of floating-point values for computation. Gaussian Kernel: A 1D array of normalized weights sampled from the Gaussian function, clamped to a specific radius. Parameters Radius (R): The spatial extent of the Gaussian kernel in voxels. Typical values used in implementations are 5 and 10. Standard Deviation (\sigma): Controls the spread of the Gaussian blur. It is defined as one-third of the radius: \sigma = R / 3. Formulas The spatial importance map is computed as: \Delta D = G V - V where G V is the Gaussian blur of the volume. The 1D Gaussian function is defined as: G(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} e^{-\frac{x^2}{2\sigma^2}} where x is the distance from the origin and \sigma is the standard deviation. In 3D, the Gaussian kernel G is the product of three 1D Gaussians, one for each axis. Steps 1. Preprocessing: Convert the input volume data V to floating-point values. 2. Kernel Generation: Determine the kernel radius R and calculate \sigma = R / 3. Clamp the Gaussian kernel at a distance of 3\sigma from the center, as values further than this are negligible. Sample the 1D Gaussian function at the center of each voxel within the radius, then normalize the weights so that they sum to 1. 3. Separable Filtering: Compute the blurred volume G V by exploiting the separability of the Gaussian function. This requires three consecutive 1D convolutions: convolve V with the 1D kernel along the X-axis, then convolve the result along the Y-axis, and finally convolve that result along the Z-axis. 4. Subtraction: Compute the spatial importance map \Delta D by subtracting the original volume from the blurred volume for each voxel: \Delta D[i, j, k] = (G V)[i, j, k] - V[i, j, k]. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computespatialimportancemap(volume: list[list[list[float]]], radius: int) -> list[list[list[float]]]: """ Computes the spatial importance map using unsharp masking via separable Gaussian filtering. Args: volume: 3D list of floats representing the input volume V. radius: Integer radius R for the Gaussian kernel. Returns: 3D list of floats representing the spatial importance map Delta D. """ # 1. Prepare volume data (assumed already float) # 2. Generate 1D Gaussian Kernel sigma = radius / 3.0 kernelsize = 2 radius + 1 kernel = [] sumweights = 0.0 for x in range(-radius, radius + 1): weight = (1.0 / math.sqrt(2.0 math.pi sigma sigma)) math.exp(-(x x) / (2.0 sigma sigma)) kernel.append(weight) sumweights += weight # Normalize kernel so it sums to 1 kernel = [w / sumweights for w in kernel] # 3. Separable Filtering dimx = len(volume) dimy = len(volume[0]) dimz = len(volume[0][0]) # Allocate intermediate volumes vxy = [[[0.0] dimz for in range(dimy)] for in range(dimx)] vxyz = [[[0.0] dimz for in range(dimy)] for in range(dimx)] vblur = [[[0.0] dimz for in range(dimy)] for in range(dimx)] # Convolve along X-axis for y in range(dimy): for z in range(dimz): for x in range(dimx): sumval = 0.0 for k in range(-radius, radius + 1): xneighbor = x + k if xneighbor < 0: xneighbor = 0 elif xneighbor >= dimx: xneighbor = dimx - 1 sumval += volume[xneighbor][y][z] kernel[k + radius] vxy[x][y][z] = sumval # Convolve along Y-axis for x in range(dimx): for z in range(dimz): for y in range(dimy): sumval = 0.0 for k in range(-radius, radius + 1): yneighbor = y + k if yneighbor < 0: yneighbor = 0 elif yneighbor >= dimy: yneighbor = dimy - 1 sumval += vxy[x][yneighbor][z] kernel[k + radius] vxyz[x][y][z] = sumval # Convolve along Z-axis for x in range(dimx): for y in range(dimy): for z in range(dimz): sumval = 0.0 for k in range(-radius, radius + 1): zneighbor = z + k if zneighbor < 0: zneighbor = 0 elif zneighbor >= dimz: zneighbor = dimz - 1 sumval += vxyz[x][y][zneighbor] kernel[k + radius] vblur[x][y][z] = sumval # 4. Subtraction deltad = [[[0.0] dimz for in range(dimy)] for in range(dimx)] for x in range(dimx): for y in range(dimy): for z in range(dimz): deltad[x][y][z] = vblur[x][y][z] - volume[x][y][z] return deltad Edge Cases and Pitfalls Boundary Voxels: Boundary voxels have non-zero importance values because the blurred volume smooths boundaries, creating intensity differences compared to the original. Implementation must handle boundary conditions (e.g., clamping) during convolution. Memory Usage: Using radiance instead of intensity would require significantly more memory. This method uses original intensity values to minimize memory requirements and remain independent of the transfer function and lighting. Sign Interpretation: Positive values in \Delta D indicate voxels near boundaries with higher density material (intensity increased in blur relative to original), while negative values indicate boundaries with lower density material (intensity decreased in blur relative to original). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: CT Body (256×256×415) with radius 5: Total time 335.05 ms (1D filter: 20.85 ms, Subtraction: 18.03 ms). CT Head (512×512×297) with radius 10: Total time 1570.10 ms. Salmon (336×173×511) with radius 10: Total time 617.24 ms. Strengths: Interactive rates achievable with GPU implementations (CUDA); independent of lighting and transfer functions; low memory footprint compared to radiance-based methods. Limitations: Relies on intensity values rather than radiance or gradient-based metrics. When to use: As a preprocessing step for illustrative volume rendering to modulate color and opacity based on boundary saliency. The method was proposed by Marc Ruiz, Imma Boada, Miquel Feixas, and Mateu Sbert from the Graphics and Imaging Laboratory, Universitat de Girona, Spain. It extends the spatial importance function \Delta D proposed by Luft [LCD06] to 3D volumes. The approach was presented in the context of interactive volume illustration, aiming to enhance perceptual quality and interpretation by modulating color and opacity based on boundary saliency. It contrasts with methods like Tao et al. [TLB09] that use radiance, arguing for the efficiency and preprocessing capability of using intensity. name: Sparseness-based Color and Opacity Modulation
head: Color an Opacity Modulation, Color and Opacity Modulation, Sparseness-guided Modulation
body: A technique to modify visual prominence by controlling optical properties (color and opacity) based on the level of sparseness. It sets itself apart from siblings like Spatial Importance Map via Unsharp Masking by directly altering the saturation and transparency of ray samples rather than just the opacity or spatial weighting, ensuring that sparse objects recede visually while dense objects remain prominent. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Pre-computed sparseness value s for each object/region (where low s indicates dense/important, high s indicates sparse/less important). Input: Initial color C{init} and opacity \alpha{init} for each ray sample, resulting from local rendering steps (shading and compositing). Output: Modulated color C{mod} and opacity \alpha{mod} used in global compositing. Data Structures: Sparseness value: Scalar float s \in [0, 1] (normalized). Color: RGB vector C = [R, G, B]. Opacity: Scalar float \alpha \in [0, 1]. Steps: 1. Convert Color to HSV: Convert the initial color C{init} from RGB to HSV (Hue, Saturation, Value) space to isolate saturation. 2. Modulate Saturation: Adjust the saturation component S based on sparseness s. Sparse objects (high s) receive low saturation (approaching gray), while dense objects (low s) maintain or amplify saturation. Formula: S{mod} = f(s, S{init}). Note: The exact function f is not specified in the sources. 3. Modulate Opacity: Adjust opacity \alpha based on sparseness s. Increasing sparseness makes the object more transparent to reveal underlying data. Formula: \alpha{mod} = g(s, \alpha{init}). Note: The exact function g is not specified in the sources. 4. Convert Back to RGB: Convert the modulated HSV color [H, S{mod}, V] back to RGB to get C{mod}. 5. Apply Smooth Transitions: Ensure smooth transitions between different levels of sparseness to prevent misinterpretations caused by abrupt visual changes within the same object. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def modulatecolorandopacity(Cinit, alphainit, sparseness): """ Modulates color and opacity based on sparseness. Args: Cinit: Initial color as RGB tuple (0.0-1.0) alphainit: Initial opacity (0.0-1.0) sparseness: Sparseness value (0.0=dense, 1.0=sparse) Returns: Cmod: Modulated color as RGB tuple alphamod: Modulated opacity """ # Step 1: Convert RGB to HSV H, Sinit, V = rgbtohsv(Cinit) # Step 2: Modulate Saturation # Sparse objects (high sparseness) get low saturation (gray) # Dense objects (low sparseness) maintain or amplify saturation # Note: Exact function f is not specified in sources # Implementation detail: Use a linear or sigmoidal decay Smod = Sinit (1.0 - sparseness) # Clamp to valid range Smod = max(0.0, min(1.0, Smod)) # Step 3: Modulate Opacity # Increasing sparseness makes object more transparent # Note: Exact function g is not specified in sources # Implementation detail: Linear decay alphamod = alphainit (1.0 - sparseness) # Clamp to valid range alphamod = max(0.0, min(1.0, alphamod)) # Step 4: Convert HSV back to RGB Cmod = hsvtorgb(H, Smod, V) # Step 5: Smooth transitions are handled by the continuous nature of sparseness # and the smooth functions f and g return Cmod, alphamod def rgbtohsv(rgb): """Standard RGB to HSV conversion.""" r, g, b = rgb maxc = max(r, g, b) minc = min(r, g, b) diff = maxc - minc if diff == 0: h = 0.0 elif maxc == r: h = 60.0 (((g - b) / diff) % 6) elif maxc == g: h = 60.0 (((b - r) / diff) + 2) else: h = 60.0 (((r - g) / diff) + 4) v = maxc s = diff / maxc if maxc != 0 else 0.0 return h, s, v def hsvtorgb(h, s, v): """Standard HSV to RGB conversion.""" c = v s x = c (1 - abs((h / 60.0) % 2 - 1)) m = v - c if h < 60: r, g, b = c, x, 0 elif h < 120: r, g, b = x, c, 0 elif h < 180: r, g, b = 0, c, x elif h < 240: r, g, b = 0, x, c elif h < 300: r, g, b = x, 0, c else: r, g, b = c, 0, x return (r + m, g + m, b + m) Parameters: Sparseness threshold: Not given in the sources. Saturation modulation function: Not given in the sources. Opacity modulation function: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Changing only saturation does not increase the visibility of occluded objects; color and opacity must be changed simultaneously. Different visual appearances within the same object can cause misinterpretations; smooth transitions between different levels of sparseness must be applied. Time Complexity: O(1) per ray sample, as it involves simple arithmetic operations and color space conversions. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Described as a "very simple and fast method". Strengths: Directly controls visual prominence; highly saturated colors attract focus more than gray colors. Limitations: Requires pre-computed sparseness values; smooth transitions are necessary to avoid misinterpretations. When to use: When the goal is to enhance visual prominence by making sparse objects less visible and dense objects more prominent. When not to use: When occlusion of important objects is a concern and only saturation is changed. Origin: Introduced in the context of Importance-Driven Volume Rendering (IDVR). History: Part of the IDVR framework developed by Thurner et al.. Usage: Used in volume visualization to guide viewer attention by modifying transfer functions based on sparseness. name: Smart Visibility
body: Smart Visibility is a category of illustrative visualization techniques that extends traditional light-propagation-based visibility by incorporating high-level abstractions of human cognition, such as object relevance and viewer pre-knowledge. Unlike standard volume rendering which relies solely on optical depth and occlusion, Smart Visibility explicitly handles semantic importance to ensure relevant data remains visible even when geometrically occluded by less important structures. Smart Visibility is not a single algorithm but a set of principles and techniques for modifying visual representations to emphasize relevant data. It operates by altering the visibility determination process to account for semantic relevance rather than just physical occlusion. Inputs: Volumetric dataset or polygonal mesh representing the scene. Viewer pre-knowledge or semantic importance map defining the relevance of individual objects or regions. Camera view parameters. Outputs: Modified visual representation where important objects are emphasized, potentially through artificial cuts, deformations, or transparency adjustments. Data Structures: Not specified in the sources. Implementation requires a mechanism to store object relevance/importance values, typically associated with voxels or mesh primitives. Steps: 1. Determine Relevance: Assign a relevance score to individual objects or data regions based on user intent, domain knowledge, or automated saliency metrics. 2. Apply Cognitive Rules: Modify the visibility calculation to override standard occlusion based on relevance. If an important object is occluded by a less important one, the occluding object is rendered with increased transparency or removed to allow the important object to shine through. 3. Exploit Pre-knowledge (Cut-aways/Deformations): For objects with known shapes, apply local modifications such as artificial cuts or spatial deformations to reveal inner structures. This relies on the viewer's mental model to complete the object from partial information, such as cut-aways along symmetry axes. 4. Enforce Illustration Rules: Apply specific rules for section views and cut-away views to maintain clarity: Distinguish inside and outside objects. Represent section views as the intersection of two half-spaces. Ensure cut-outs consist of a single hole in the outside object. Ensure interior objects are visible from any viewing angle. Apply transparency fall-off close to edges of transparent objects. Ensure faces of transparent objects never shine through other transparent objects. Ensure objects occluded by two transparent objects do not shine through. Parameters: Relevance threshold: Determines which objects are considered "important" enough to override occlusion. Not given in the sources. Cut-away extent: The depth or area of artificial cuts. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Simple Visibility Calculation: A common pitfall is relying solely on light propagation and occlusion, which hides important structures behind less important ones. Smart Visibility must explicitly handle relevance to avoid this. Ambiguity: Over-modification (e.g., excessive cut-aways) may lead to loss of spatial context or confusion about the object's overall shape. Volumetric Clipping: The source notes that algorithms for cut-away views were applied to polygonal data and are "generally applicable in computer graphics," but does not provide specific volumetric clipping algorithms. Implementation for volumes requires adapting these polygonal rules to voxel-based rendering, potentially via transfer function modulation or ray-marching modifications. A technique involving artificial cuts to reveal inner structures, relying on viewer pre-knowledge. Chosen when inner details of a symmetrical or complex object are critical. See Spatial Importance Map via Unsharp Masking for a related saliency-based approach. Represented by the intersection of half-spaces, used to inspect internal structures. Chosen for cross-sectional analysis. See Sparseness-based Color and Opacity Modulation for opacity modulation alternatives. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Depends on the complexity of the relevance calculation and the rendering technique used (e.g., ray marching with modified opacity). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storage for relevance/importance maps if not pre-computed. Strengths: Enhances interpretability by ensuring critical data is visible; leverages human cognitive strengths (pattern completion, attention guidance). Limitations: Requires semantic information or viewer pre-knowledge; may introduce artificial artifacts (cuts, deformations) that do not represent physical reality; primarily defined for polygonal data in the source, requiring adaptation for volumes. When to Use: When the goal is illustrative communication of specific features rather than photorealistic representation; when viewer attention needs to be guided to specific structures. When Not to Use: When physical accuracy of occlusion is required; when semantic relevance is unknown or ambiguous. Smart Visibility was introduced as part of illustrative visualization techniques in scientific visualization, particularly for medicine and science. It draws inspiration from technical illustrations (e.g., cut-aways, exploded views) and applies these high-level abstractions to computer graphics. The concept emphasizes that visibility should be determined not just by light propagation but by the relevance of objects and the viewer's cognitive abilities. The specific rules for cut-away and section views were developed for polygonal data but are considered generally applicable to computer graphics, including volumetric data. name: Voxel Saliency
head: Saliency map
body: Voxel Saliency is a feature importance metric for volume data defined as the magnitude of the gradient of the obscurance field. It identifies regions of high perceptual importance, such as edges, occlusion variations, and corners, by measuring how rapidly obscurance changes across a local neighborhood. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on direct intensity gradients or semantic labels, Voxel Saliency is derived from volumetric shadowing information (obscurance), making it particularly effective for highlighting structural boundaries in complex, self-occluding datasets. It serves as the core importance specification mechanism in the Importance-Driven Visualization Model, enabling viewpoint selection and transfer function modulation. Inputs: A 3D volume dataset V. The precomputed obscurance field O, where O(k) is the obscurance value for voxel k. Outputs: A scalar saliency map S, where S(p) \in [0, 1] for each voxel p. Data Structures: Obscurance Field: A 3D array of floating-point values, same dimensions as the input volume. Saliency Map: A 3D array of floating-point values, same dimensions as the input volume. Parameters: Neighborhood Size: A cubic neighborhood of 5^3 voxels centered at the query voxel p. (Note: A 3^3 neighborhood was used in [NCKG00], but 5^3 yields smoother results). Scaling: Linear scaling to [0, 1] per data volume. Algorithm: 1. Compute Obscurance: Calculate the obscurance O(k) for all voxels k in the volume. This step relies on a local volumetric shadowing method (e.g., [HLY07, RMSD08]). 2. Iterate Voxels: For each voxel p in the volume: a. Define the neighborhood \mathcal{N}p as the set of voxels k within a 5^3 cube centered at p. b. Initialize gradient components A = 0, B = 0, C = 0. c. For each voxel k \in \mathcal{N}p: i. Calculate the vector \vec{d}{pk} = (x(k), y(k), z(k)) from p to k. ii. Calculate the distance weight w(k). The source defines w(k) as "the distance between voxels p and k". In standard 4D linear regression for gradient estimation, weights are typically inverse-square or Gaussian based on distance to reduce boundary bias. We implement w(k) as the Euclidean distance |\vec{d}{pk}| as stated, though inverse distance is common in literature. iii. Accumulate components: A \leftarrow A + w(k) \cdot O(k) \cdot x(k) B \leftarrow B + w(k) \cdot O(k) \cdot y(k) C \leftarrow C + w(k) \cdot O(k) \cdot z(k) d. Compute the saliency magnitude: S(p) = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + C^2} 3. Normalize: For the specific volume dataset, find the global maximum saliency S{max} = \maxp S(p). Scale the map: S(p) \leftarrow S(p) / S{max}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computevoxelsaliency(obscurancefield: Volume3D, neighborhoodradius: int = 2) -> Volume3D: """ Computes voxel saliency as the magnitude of the obscurance gradient. obscurancefield: 3D array of obscurance values O(k). neighborhoodradius: Half-size of the cubic neighborhood. 5^3 total implies radius 2. Returns: 3D array of saliency values S(p) scaled to [0, 1]. """ dims = obscurancefield.shape saliencymap = Volume3D.zeros(dims) # Precompute neighborhood offsets to avoid repeated calculation offsets = [] for dx in range(-neighborhoodradius, neighborhoodradius + 1): for dy in range(-neighborhoodradius, neighborhoodradius + 1): for dz in range(-neighborhoodradius, neighborhoodradius + 1): offsets.append((dx, dy, dz)) # Compute raw saliency for p in voxelsinvolume(dims): A = 0.0 B = 0.0 C = 0.0 for dx, dy, dz in offsets: k = (p.x + dx, p.y + dy, p.z + dz) # Boundary check if not isvalidvoxel(k, dims): continue # Vector from p to k xk = dx yk = dy zk = dz # Obscurance at k Ok = obscurancefield[k] # Weight w(k) is defined as the distance between p and k # Note: Using Euclidean distance as per literal interpretation of "distance" wk = math.sqrt(xk2 + yk2 + zk2) # Accumulate gradient components # A = sumk w(k)O(k)x(k) A += wk Ok xk B += wk Ok yk C += wk Ok zk # S(p) = sqrt(A^2 + B^2 + C^2) saliencymap[p] = math.sqrt(A2 + B2 + C2) # Normalize to [0, 1] maxsaliency = 0.0 for p in voxelsinvolume(dims): if saliencymap[p] > maxsaliency: maxsaliency = saliencymap[p] if maxsaliency > 0: for p in voxelsinvolume(dims): saliencymap[p] /= maxsaliency return saliencymap The XS Map is a combined importance map used in perceptual rendering of participating media. It integrates the Saliency map (S) with an Extinction map (X) to guide selective rendering. The combination is defined as XS(wx, ws, op), where wx and ws are weighting coefficients and op is the combination operator. The default configuration uses equal weighting (wx=0.5, ws=0.5) and an additive operator (+) to preserve all weighted features. A key limitation is that the XS Map fails to identify areas of strong multiple scattering around light sources, leading to poor sampling and visible artifacts in those regions. Complexity: The computation is O(N \cdot K), where N is the number of voxels and K is the neighborhood size (5^3 = 125). This is constant per voxel but requires access to the obscurance field. Memory: Requires storage for the input obscurance field and the output saliency map. Both are single-channel 3D arrays of the same resolution as the volume data. Strengths: Effectively highlights structural edges and occlusion boundaries in volumetric data. It is scale-dependent, allowing adjustment via neighborhood size. Limitations: Computationally expensive if obscurance is not precomputed or cached. It does not account for light scattering artifacts around sources (addressed partially by combining with X maps, but not fully). Usage: Primarily used for automatic viewpoint selection (maximizing visible saliency) and for modulating transfer functions (opacity/color) to enhance salient features. Voxel Saliency was proposed in the Obscurance-based Volume Rendering Framework. It adapts the concept of mesh saliency [LVJ05] to volumetric data. The gradient estimation technique is based on the 4D linear regression method proposed in [NCKG00]. The method emphasizes that obscurance, representing occlusion information, varies perceptually at edges and corners, making its gradient a suitable saliency measure. name: Contour Rendering
head: Contour Lines Rendering, Gradient-based Contouring, Non-Photorealistic Volume Rendering for Contours, Object Contour Visualization
body:
Contour Rendering is a non-photorealistic volume rendering technique that visualizes object boundaries by leveraging gradient magnitude and viewing angle, rather than direct data values or transfer functions. It solves the problem of visual clutter in volumetric data by producing sparse images containing only significant contours, avoiding the need for complex iso-surface extraction or transfer function tuning. Unlike Line Illustration Detection which focuses on flow or texture lines, or Outline and Contour Generation which often relies on geometric primitives, Contour Rendering operates directly on volumetric gradient fields to highlight internal structures. Inputs: Volumetric data D, viewing direction V, gradient threshold tg, exponent n, and windowing parameters. Outputs: A 2D image where pixels represent contour intensities. Data Structures: Gradient Field: A 3D grid of vectors 
abla D, computed via 4D linear regression for high quality. Windowing Function g(|
abla|): A scalar field mapping gradient magnitudes to "surfaceness" values. Default implementation is a windowing function that selects a range of interest. Sample Points: Points along viewing rays with computed intensity I(P, V). Steps: 1. Gradient Estimation: Compute the gradient magnitude |
abla(P)| for each voxel P in the volume. High-quality reconstruction is achieved using 4D linear regression. 2. Thresholding: For each ray sample at position P, check if |
abla(P)| > tg. If not, discard the sample. 3. Surfaceness Calculation: Apply the windowing function g(|
abla(P)|) to the gradient magnitude. This function characterizes the "surfaceness" of the voxel, emphasizing regions with significant data value changes. 4. View-Dependent Weighting: Calculate the view-dependent weight s(P, V) using the formula: s(P, V) = (1 - |
abla(P) \cdot V|)^n where V is the normalized viewing direction vector and n is an exponent controlling contour sharpness. 5. Intensity Calculation: Compute the view-dependent intensity I(P, V) for valid samples: I(P, V) = g(|
abla(P)|) \cdot s(P, V) This results in a sparse volume where only voxels with significant contours contribute. 6. Compositing: Choose one of the following compositing strategies: Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP): Assign the highest sample intensity I(P, V) along the ray to the pixel. Depth-Cued MIP: Weight sample intensities by distance from the viewpoint to improve spatial impression. Local Maximum Intensity Projection (LMIP): Project the first local maximum intensity along the ray that exceeds a predefined threshold, preventing higher intensity contours from hiding weaker ones closer to the viewer. Alpha-Blending: Assign g(|
abla(P)|) as color and opacity, modulated by I(P, V), and perform alpha-blending. This emphasizes low-curvature surfaces and is suitable for data with many high-frequency regions. 7. Optional Extension (Level Lines): Select specific slices (e.g., every twentieth slice). Assign values of g as intensities to these slices and render them using MIP with a different color channel to distinguish from object contours. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def contourrendering(volume, gradientfield, viewdirection, tg, n, compositingmode='MIP'): """ Render contours from volumetric data using gradient magnitude and view direction. Args: volume: 3D array of voxel values. gradientfield: 3D array of gradient vectors (computed via 4D linear regression). viewdirection: Normalized 3D vector representing the camera view direction. tg: Gradient magnitude threshold. n: Exponent for view-dependent weighting. compositingmode: 'MIP', 'LMIP', or 'AlphaBlend'. Returns: 2D image array. """ height, width, depth = volume.shape image = np.zeros((height, width)) # Precompute gradient magnitudes if not provided gradmag = np.linalg.norm(gradientfield, axis=-1) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): # Generate ray parameters (simplified for 2D example) rayorigin, raydirection = getrayparameters(x, y, viewdirection) maxintensity = -np.inf localmaxintensity = -np.inf alphaaccumulated = 0.0 coloraccumulated = np.zeros(3) # Traverse ray through volume for t in range(raylength): P = rayorigin + t raydirection if not isinsidevolume(P): continue # Get gradient at P grad = interpolategradient(gradientfield, P) gradmagnitude = np.linalg.norm(grad) # Step 2: Thresholding if gradmagnitude <= tg: continue # Step 3: Surfaceness gval = windowingfunction(gradmagnitude) # Step 4: View-dependent weight # Note: V is viewdirection, but for surface normal approximation, # the source uses gradient direction. The formula is (1 - |grad(P). V|)^n # However, standard contour rendering often uses surface normal. # Source explicitly states: s(P, V) = (1 - |∇(P) · V|)^n # This implies the gradient vector is treated as the surface normal. dotproduct = np.abs(np.dot(grad, viewdirection)) sval = (1 - dotproduct) n # Step 5: Intensity intensity = gval sval # Depth cueing (optional, from source) # intensity = depthcue(t) # Step 6: Compositing if compositingmode == 'MIP': if intensity > maxintensity: maxintensity = intensity elif compositingmode == 'LMIP': # Find first local maximum above threshold # Simplified: track if intensity is increasing then decreasing if intensity > localmaxintensity: localmaxintensity = intensity elif compositingmode == 'AlphaBlend': alpha = gval # Opacity based on surfaceness color = gval # Color based on surfaceness # Standard alpha blending coloraccumulated = coloraccumulated (1 - alpha) + color alpha alphaaccumulated += alpha (1 - alphaaccumulated) if compositingmode == 'MIP': image[y, x] = maxintensity elif compositingmode == 'LMIP': image[y, x] = localmaxintensity elif compositingmode == 'AlphaBlend': image[y, x] = coloraccumulated return image def windowingfunction(gradmag): """ Default windowing function. Source describes it as determining the range of interest. Source uses a binary threshold w(|g|). We implement a smooth window as suggested by for 'surfaceness'. """ # Placeholder for specific window shape. # Source Figure 1 shows a window. # A common implementation is a Gaussian or trapezoidal window. # Since exact formula is not given, we return 1 for significant gradients. # This aligns with 's binary approach but allows for 's emphasis. return 1.0 if gradmag > 0 else 0.0 Parameters: tg: Gradient magnitude threshold. Determines which samples are considered contours. n: Exponent controlling the sharpness of the contour in the view-dependent function. Windowing parameters: Define the range of gradient magnitudes of interest. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Estimation: Poor gradient estimation leads to poor results. 4D linear regression is recommended over central differences. Depth Information: Simple MIP does not provide depth cues. Use depth cueing or LMIP to mitigate. Occlusion: In MIP, higher intensity contours can hide weaker contours closer to the viewer. LMIP handles this by projecting the first local maximum above a threshold. High-Frequency Data: Alpha-blending may hide fine details in data with many high-frequency regions, as it emphasizes low-curvature surfaces. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels along the ray, but significantly reduced due to sparsity (only voxels with significant gradients contribute). Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume and gradient field. Performance: Interactive frame rates can be achieved without specialized hardware due to the sparse nature of the contribution. Strengths: No need for transfer function tuning; highlights internal structures without visual overload; view-dependent. Limitations: No direct depth information in basic MIP; sensitive to gradient estimation quality; may hide fine details in high-frequency data with alpha-blending. Contour Rendering was introduced as a non-photorealistic rendering technique for volumetric data. It was developed to visualize 3D structures characterized by significant changes in data values without being obstructed by continuous regions. The method relies on high-quality gradient reconstruction, specifically using 4D linear regression. It is used in medical imaging and other fields where clear visualization of object boundaries is required without the complexity of iso-surface extraction. name: Ghosting and Cutaway Techniques
head: Cutaway views, Ghosting
body: Ghosting and Cutaway Techniques are illustrative volume rendering methods that resolve occlusion by selectively suppressing or removing foreground objects to reveal interior structures of interest. Unlike standard clipping which discards context, these methods maintain spatial awareness through opacity modulation (ghosting) or explicit visual cues. They distinguish themselves from Context-Preserving Volume Rendering by using discrete object separation (Selection, Ghost, Background) rather than continuous opacity modulation based on shading intensity. The family operates on a three-object logical model: Selection (the object of interest), Ghost (the original position of the selection, often moved), and Background (the occluding environment). 1. Object Decomposition: The volume is conceptually split into these three sets. 2. Occlusion Handling: Cutaways remove the Background partially or fully in regions occluding the Selection or Ghost. Ghosting reduces the Background opacity in occluding regions to preserve edge cues and spatial context. 3. Visual Conventions: Auxiliary geometry clarifies the relationship between Ghost and Selection: Boxes provide orientation cues, Arrows depict translation between positions, and Fans indicate alternative depictions. 4. Rendering Strategy: Efficient implementation avoids costly per-voxel importance compositing by using static importance functions. Feature Halos reinforces depth perception by darkening and increasing opacity in regions just outside strong volumetric features, obscuring background elements. It distinguishes itself by generating these effects directly during the illumination pass using local spatial properties (gradient orientation relative to view and neighbors), rather than relying on post-processing or explicit surface extraction. The method is inherently view-dependent, ensuring features do not cast halos on themselves. Context-Preserving Volume Rendering (CPVR) selectively reduces opacity in less important data regions to visualize interior structures while preserving exterior context. It solves the problem of context loss inherent in conventional clipping techniques by modulating sample opacity based on shading intensity, gradient magnitude, distance to the eye point, and previously accumulated opacity. Unlike clipping planes which remove context information, CPVR retains it by making homogeneous areas (high lighting intensity) transparent, allowing users to inspect the interior of an object without hiding occluded objects. Exact Projection Full Opacity is a non-photorealistic volume rendering technique that simplifies visual output by identifying a single primary front object and optionally one significant background object, blending them based on density and distance thresholds rather than performing full front-to-back accumulation. It differs from standard front-to-back compositing by skipping the accumulation of intermediate samples, storing only the first significant object (primary) and potentially one background object, then blending them directly to create a stylized, illustrative result. Multi-object volume rendering with ghosting is a technique for visualizing inter-penetrating volumetric objects by decomposing a scalar field into three distinct logical objects: selection, ghost, and background, allowing independent control of appearance and spatial transformation. It solves the problem of occlusion in complex scenes by selectively reducing opacity in occluding regions to preserve features such as edges, aiding mental reconstruction of structures and spatial location. Unlike Cutaways and Ghosting which may remove occluding regions completely, this method allows smooth control from no ghosting (opacity not reduced) to full cutaway (occluding structures completely suppressed). It sets itself apart from single-pass multi-object compositing by using three separate rendering passes to avoid computational overhead and dynamic branching penalties. Cutaways remove occluding objects to reveal structures of interest, using a simplified three-object setup (Background, Ghost, Selection) with static importance functions to skip costly importance compositing. Definition: A technique where the occluding object is cut out to reveal the structure of interest, determined by an importance function. Step: In VolumeShop's simplified three-object setup, the importance function is statically defined to skip costly importance compositing, allowing efficient implementation. Cutaways are performed only on the background and can be independently defined for ghost and selection. Definition: Boxes: 3D bounding boxes providing cues on position and orientation. Useful during design but distracting during presentation. Arrows: Depict translation between ghost and selection (original to current position). Used to suggest movement or insertion. Fans: A connected pair of shapes (rectangles or circles) indicating a more detailed or alternative depiction. Constructed by connecting screen-space bounding rectangles of ghost and selection. Step: Control arrow curvature using screen-space depth difference to avoid very short arrows when ghost and selection project to nearby positions, creating bent arrows. The concepts of cutaways and ghosting originate from illustrative practices in information visualization and technical drawing. Viola et al. introduced importance-driven volume rendering as a general framework for determining which objects to cut. VolumeShop later provided an interactive system for direct volume illustration, implementing these concepts with a simplified three-object model to enable efficient real-time interaction. The techniques are applied in contexts such as surgical procedures and assembly instructions to clarify spatial relationships. name: Feature Halos
head: Auxiliary volume halos, Feature Halos Effect, Halo Effects, Null Halos
body:
Feature Halos is an illustrative volume rendering technique that enhances depth perception by generating dark, opaque regions around structures of interest, thereby obscuring background elements that would otherwise cause visual clutter. Unlike standard photorealistic rendering, this method uses view-dependent darkening and opacity increases in planes orthogonal to the viewing direction to create a visual separation around features, making foreground structures stand out more clearly. The method operates during the illumination/compositing pass of volume rendering. It computes a halo intensity value for each voxel based on the spatial relationship between that voxel and its neighbors, specifically targeting empty regions adjacent to strong features. Input: Volume data V (scalar field). View direction vector V (normalized). Parameters: k{hpe} (halo potential exponent, typically 1.0), k{hse} (halo separation exponent, typically 2.0). Output: Modified color C' and opacity \alpha' for each voxel, where halos are darker and more opaque than the base volume rendering. Volume Grid: Standard 3D array of scalar values. Gradient Field: 3D array of 3D vectors, computed via finite differences. Halo Field: 3D array of floats, storing the computed halo influence h(i) for each voxel. 1. Compute Gradient Field: Calculate the gradient 
ablaf(P) at every voxel P in the volume. 2. Initialize Halo Field: Create a halo field H of the same dimensions as the volume, initialized to zero. 3. Compute Halo Influence: For each voxel i at position Pi: a. Initialize h(i) = 0. b. Iterate over a specified neighborhood of voxels n at positions Pn. c. For each neighbor n: i. Calculate the displacement vector D = Pi - Pn and distance d = \|D\|. ii. Calculate the normalized direction u = D / d. iii. Compute the halo potential hn for the neighbor: hn = \left( 
ablaf(Pn) \cdot u ight)^{k{hpe}} (1 - 
ablaf(Pn) \cdot V)^{k{hse}} iv. Add the distance-weighted influence to the current voxel's halo field: h(i) \leftarrow h(i) +  rac{hn}{d^2} d. Weight the accumulated halo influence by the complement of the current voxel's gradient magnitude to restrict halos to less interesting (low-gradient) regions: h(i) \leftarrow h(i) \cdot (1 - \|
ablaf(Pi)\|) 4. Apply Visual Appearance: For each voxel i, adjust the base color C and opacity \alpha computed from the volume transfer function: a. Decrease brightness: C' = C \cdot (1 - k{dark} \cdot h(i)), where k{dark} is a scalar controlling the darkness of the halo. b. Increase opacity: \alpha' = \min(1.0, \alpha + k{opaque} \cdot h(i)), where k{opaque} is a scalar controlling the opacity increase. 5. Composite: Perform standard volume compositing (e.g., front-to-back or back-to-front) using the modified C' and \alpha' values. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computefeaturehalos(volume, viewdirection, khpe=1.0, khse=2.0): """ Compute feature halos for volume rendering. Args: volume: 3D numpy array of scalar values. viewdirection: 3D numpy array, normalized view vector. khpe: Halo potential exponent. khse: Halo separation exponent. Returns: halofield: 3D numpy array of halo intensities. """ # Step 1: Compute gradient field grad = np.gradient(volume) # Returns tuple of 3 arrays (dz, dy, dx) gradientmagnitude = np.sqrt(sum(g2 for g in grad)) maxgrad = np.max(gradientmagnitude) normalizedgradmag = gradientmagnitude / maxgrad if maxgrad > 0 else gradientmagnitude # Step 2: Initialize halo field halofield = np.zeroslike(volume) # Neighborhood radius (specified neighborhood) radius = 1 neighborhoodindices = np.arange(-radius, radius + 1) vx, vy, vz = viewdirection # Step 3: Compute halo influence for z in range(volume.shape[0]): for y in range(volume.shape[1]): for x in range(volume.shape[2]): hi = 0.0 currentgradmag = normalizedgradmag[z, y, x] for dzoff in neighborhoodindices: for dyoff in neighborhoodindices: for dxoff in neighborhoodindices: if dzoff == 0 and dyoff == 0 and dxoff == 0: continue nz, ny, nx = z + dzoff, y + dyoff, x + dxoff if not (0 <= nz < volume.shape[0] and 0 <= ny < volume.shape[1] and 0 <= nx < volume.shape[2]): continue dxvec, dyvec, dzvec = dxoff, dyoff, dzoff distsq = dxvec2 + dyvec2 + dzvec2 dist = np.sqrt(distsq) ux, uy, uz = dxvec / dist, dyvec / dist, dzvec / dist gradnz, gradny, gradnx = grad[0][nz, ny, nx], grad[1][nz, ny, nx], grad[2][nz, ny, nx] dotproduct = gradnz ux + gradny uy + gradnx uz costheta = gradnz vx + gradny vy + gradnx vz # Halo potential formula from potential = max(0.0, dotproduct) khpe viewfactor = (1.0 - costheta) khse hn = potential viewfactor hi += hn / distsq halofield[z, y, x] = hi (1.0 - currentgradmag) return halofield def applyhalos(basecolor, baseopacity, halofield, kdark=0.5, kopaque=0.5): """ Apply halo effects to color and opacity. Args: basecolor: RGB array. baseopacity: Float. halofield: Float halo intensity. kdark: Scalar for brightness reduction. kopaque: Scalar for opacity increase. Returns: modifiedcolor, modifiedopacity """ modifiedcolor = basecolor (1.0 - kdark halofield) modifiedopacity = np.minimum(1.0, baseopacity + kopaque halofield) return modifiedcolor, modifiedopacity k{hpe}: Controls how directly the neighbor's gradient must be oriented toward the current location. Typical value: 1.0. k{hse}: Controls how tightly halos are kept in the plane orthogonal to the view direction. Typical value: 2.0. k{dark}: Scalar controlling the amount of brightness reduction in halo regions. Not given in the sources. k{opaque}: Scalar controlling the amount of opacity increase in halo regions. Not given in the sources. Self-Obscuration: Since halos are view-dependent and computed based on the relationship between neighbors and the current voxel, features do not cast halos on themselves. This avoids the self-obscuration issues present in other methods like Line Integral Convolution (LIC). Gradient Normalization: The gradient magnitude must be normalized to [0,1] before being used in the weighting term (1 - \|
ablaf(Pi)\|) to ensure consistent behavior across different datasets. Boundary Conditions: Neighbors outside the volume bounds must be handled, typically by ignoring them or padding with zeros. Performance: The naive implementation is O(N \cdot R^3) where N is the number of voxels and R is the neighborhood radius. Optimization via separable filters or GPU parallelization is recommended for large volumes. A variant that uses a dual-layer splat presentation: an inner core for the primary structure and an outer halo for softer support. The inner core is rendered as the primary measured structure, while the outer halo is rendered as a softer support shell. The intensity of the halo can be tuned using a "Halo Strength" slider, which can be reduced to zero. A technique that enhances depth perception by processing the volume model in view-aligned slices to generate halos around structures of interest, using hue changes rather than just brightening/darkening. The steps are: 1) Classify structures to highlight based on density, direction, and position, and place seeds around them; 2) Generate the halo region of influence by filtering the seeds; 3) Assign colors and opacities to the halo regions and composite them with the volume rendering. Unlike previous techniques that only brighten or darken color, this approach considers hue changes. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot R^3) for a naive implementation, where N is the number of voxels and R is the neighborhood radius. Can be optimized to O(N) with separable filters or GPU acceleration. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the gradient field and halo field. Measured Performance: In medical volume rendering (e.g., liver and kidneys), halos make foreground structures stand out more clearly. Strengths: Enhances depth perception, reduces visual clutter from background elements, view-dependent (no self-obscuration), applicable to any type of data. Limitations: View-dependent (halos change with camera angle), requires gradient computation, may obscure fine details if parameters are not tuned correctly. When to Use: When depth perception is critical and background clutter is a problem, especially in medical or scientific visualization. When Not to Use: When photorealism is required, or when performance is extremely constrained and gradient computation is prohibitive. Feature Halos were introduced in non-photorealistic rendering literature. The technique builds on earlier work by Interrante and Grosch who applied halos to flow visualization. It is part of the broader family of Ghosting and Cutaway Techniques [8497-ghosting-and-cutaway-techniques.md].
