name: Real-time shell space rendering
body: A technique for real-time rendering of arbitrary volumetric geometry into a polygonal mesh's shell space, which is a layer of variable thickness on top or below the polygonal mesh. It differs from its parent Shell Method for Volume Rendering by explicitly defining the shell volume via a pre-computed tetrahedra mesh and using a 3D distance map to optimize ray traversal, overcoming the high storage requirements of [Wang et al. 2004] and the mapping distortions of [Policarpo and Oliveira 2006]. Inputs: 1. A polygonal base mesh defining the surface geometry. 2. Arbitrary volumetric geometry to be rendered within the shell space. Outputs: 1. A rendered image of the volumetric geometry within the shell space, including local lighting effects. Data Structures: 1. Pre-computed Tetrahedra Mesh: A mesh where tetrahedra subdivide prisms extruded from the polygonal base mesh, defining the shell volume boundaries. 2. Geometry Volume Texture: A 3D texture representing the arbitrary volumetric geometry within the shell space. 3. 3D Distance Map: A 3D texture storing distance values to skip empty space in the shell volume during ray tracing. Exact layouts, field sizes, and bit packing: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Pre-computation: Generate the geometry volume texture and the corresponding 3D distance map from the polygonal mesh and the volumetric data. Construct the pre-computed tetrahedra mesh by extruding prisms from the polygonal base mesh and subdividing them into tetrahedra. 2. Vertex Shader Processing: For each vertex of the tetrahedra mesh, compute the distances to the tetrahedron face planes. Use these distances to generate per-pixel tetrahedron thickness via non-linear interpolation across the primitive. 3. Pixel Shader Processing (Ray Tracing): Compute view ray intersections with the shell geometry defined by the tetrahedra mesh in the pixel shader. Use the 3D distance map to skip empty space in the shell volume, minimizing the number of ray tracing steps. Sample the geometry volume texture along the ray to determine color and opacity. Include local lighting in the rendering process. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Shell thickness: Variable, determined by the extrusion and tetrahedra subdivision process. Ray step size: Adapted by the 3D distance map skips. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Shallow view angles: Rendering artifacts common to many related techniques are reduced by this method. Empty space: The 3D distance map is critical for performance; without it, ray tracing steps would be excessive. Applies specific texture sampling strategies to the shell space to simulate volumetric microgeometry (such as fur) rather than just solid volume. Time Complexity: Optimized by the 3D distance map which skips empty space, minimizing ray tracing steps. Memory Complexity: Uses a pre-computed tetrahedra mesh and 3D textures (volume texture and distance map). Strengths: Handles arbitrary volumetric geometry and height-field shell geometry; reduces artifacts at shallow view angles; includes local lighting. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of the tetrahedra mesh and 3D textures. Comparison: Overcomes high storage requirements and per-vertex computations of [Wang et al. 2004] and low shell geometry depth complexity and mapping distortions of [Policarpo and Oliveira 2006]. This technique was introduced to address shortcomings in previous shell space rendering approaches. It builds on the general shell idea but implements it via a tetrahedra-based volume definition and distance-map-accelerated ray tracing for real-time performance. Real-time shell space rendering of volumetric geometry, https://doi.org/10.1145/1174429.1174477, fetched 2026-10-26 (abstract only)

name: Shell Textures
head: Concentric Shells
body: Shell textures is a technique for rendering complex surface geometry in real-time using concentric 3D rings or shells around a model, where shells are transparent except at the intersection with the microgeometry. It builds on Real-time shell space rendering by applying specific texture sampling strategies to the shell space to simulate volumetric microgeometry (such as fur) rather than just solid volume. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A base polygonal mesh representing the macro-geometry; a precomputed volumetric texture (e.g., fur volume) containing microgeometry data; spherical harmonic coefficients for precomputed radiance transfer (PRT). Output: A rendered image with realistic microgeometry and global lighting effects at real-time frame rates. Data Structures: Shell Volume: A 3D texture or volume data structure where the radial distance from the surface corresponds to the depth within the microgeometry (e.g., hair length). PRT Textures: Textures storing the object’s spherical light transfer function in a spherical/zonal harmonic basis, allowing approximate illumination in arbitrary lighting environments. Steps: 1. Shell Generation: For each shell index i from 0 to N-1 (where N is the total number of shells): a. Perturb the vertices of the base model along their surface normals by an offset amount di, increasing linearly with the shell index. b. Render the perturbed model into a framebuffer. c. Sample the shell volume texture at the corresponding radial level for each fragment. d. Apply alpha blending to accumulate the transparent shells. 2. Lighting Reconstruction: For each rendered point: a. Rotate the precomputed transfer function from its local frame to the world frame using the surface normal and tangent space. b. Project the rotated transfer function back into the spherical harmonic (SH) basis. c. Project the current lighting environment into the SH basis. d. Compute the dot product between the lighting SH coefficients and the transfer SH coefficients to determine the final color. Parameters: Number of Shells (N): 16 shells are usually sufficient to create realistic fur. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Silhouette Gaps: Shells create gaps near the object silhouette because they overlap when viewed from above but separate at edges. This occurs because shells become parallel to the view direction at the silhouette, making gaps apparent. Remedy: The original Lengyel method remedies this by adding fins, which are quads perpendicular to the model generated by extruding edges outward, or by adding small textures rendered normal to the surface across all edges, both faded in as the edge approaches the silhouette. Some implementations omit fins for simplicity, accepting the gap artifact. A variant specifically for rendering fur by generating concentric shells around a model. Each shell is rendered with an alpha-blended texture sampled from the fur volume at the corresponding level. The offset between shells creates the impression of geometric fur movement relative to the camera. It uses a vertex shader to perturb vertices along the normal linearly for each shell draw call. It typically uses 16 shells. It suffers from silhouette gaps where shells become parallel to the view direction. Unlike the base Lengyel method, this implementation may omit fins to simplify the model, relying solely on the shell textures. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of shells N, as the model is drawn once per shell. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Capable of real-time frame rates for complex microgeometry. Strengths: Realistic appearance of volumetric microgeometry (fur); supports global lighting effects via PRT. Limitations: Silhouette gaps if fins are not used; lighting scheme may be limited to ambient/diffuse/specular if full self-shadowing is not implemented. The technique was developed by John Kloetzli, combining Lengyel’s shell/fin method [2001] with Precomputed Radiance Transfer (PRT) using spherical harmonics. It allows for real-time rendering of microgeometry with global lighting effects. The method is viewed as a real-time implementation of the Kajiya and Kay [1989] fur model, adapted for PRT. A Volumetric Approach to Rendering Microgeometry Using PRT, https://www.cs.umbc.edu/~ugrad/honors/theses/JohnKloetzli.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Strobe Silhouettes
head: Strobe silhouette effect
body: Strobe silhouettes is an illustrative visualization technique that provides visual cues of feature histories by offsetting receding sections of feature boundaries multiple times along the path of motion with reduced thickness and detail. It solves the problem of conveying the temporal history and deformation of a specific feature within a single static image, allowing the observer to view the approximate time-history of a feature without animation. It sets itself apart from sibling techniques like Speedlines (which use cones/lines) and Opacity Modulation (which uses transparency) by generating discrete, geometric tube-like silhouettes that represent the feature's past positions. The method operates on a vector field and a geometric feature f defined on an unstructured mesh. It constructs a series of offset contours representing the feature's motion history. Inputs: Feature geometry f (surface or boundary). Velocity data associated with the feature (instantaneous average velocity v{avg}). User parameters: N: Number of strobe silhouettes to generate. \Delta t: Time-difference (time step) for offset calculation. r{init}: Initial tube diameter. \alpha: Reduction factor for curve point count and tube diameter per step. k: User-specified portion of end points to remove per step. C{color}: Silhouette color/intensity. F{facets}: Number of facets per tube. Smoothing parameters for DCT and Gaussian filters. Outputs: A mesh geometry containing the original feature and a series of offset cylindrical silhouettes. Data Structures: Contour (bc): A sequence of 3D points representing the bounding contour of feature f. Receding Curve (s): A subsequence of points from bc representing the receding portion. Offset Curve (s{new}): A sequence of 3D points representing the shifted silhouette. Steps: 1. Boundary Identification: Obtain the bounding contour bc of feature f using a boundary extraction algorithm (e.g., Algorithm 3 from source). 2. Smoothing: Apply a Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) smoothing filter to bc to reduce noise. 3. Receding Portion Extraction: Reduce bc to the receding portion s. This is done by: a. Calculating the distance di for each point pi in bc relative to the direction of motion (see Formula). b. Identifying the minimum distance d{min} and maximum distance d{max} (if applicable) to define the range of receding points. c. Selecting points between the indices corresponding to d{min} and d{max}. 4. Initial Offset: Calculate the offset vector V = v{avg} \cdot \Delta t. Offset the curve s by V to create the first silhouette position. 5. Trimming Overlaps: To prevent the silhouette from overlapping with the current feature position: a. Scan points in the original bounding contour bc to find the minimum distance value d{min} using Equation 11. b. For each point i in the offset curve s, calculate its distance di using Equation 11. c. Remove all points i from s where di > d{min}. This ensures the silhouette starts at the rear-most edge of the feature relative to motion. 6. First Silhouette Generation: Extrude the trimmed curve s into cylinders (tubes) using a built-in mesh generation filter (e.g., VTK TubeFilter) with parameters r{init} and F{facets}. Add these cylinders to the output mesh with color C{color}. 7. Iterative Strobe Generation: Repeat the following loop N times: a. Offset: Offset the current curve s by V again. b. Trim Ends: Remove a user-specified portion k of the end points from the offset curve s to simulate fading or truncation. c. Smooth: Apply Gaussian smoothing to the resulting curve s. d. Generate: Extrude the new curve s into cylinders. Reduce the tube diameter by the reduction factor \alpha relative to the previous step. Add to the output mesh with color C{color} (potentially with reduced intensity/opacity if specified by user). Formula: The distance function used for trimming and identifying receding points is: di = (pi - c) \cdot v{avg} Where: pi is the position of point i on the contour. c is the centroid of the feature or contour. v{avg} is the average feature velocity vector. \cdot denotes the dot product. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def strobesilhouettes(featuref, velocityfield, params): """ featuref: Geometry object with method getboundingcontour() velocityfield: Provides average velocity vavg for the feature params: Dictionary containing N, dt, rinit, alpha, k, color, facets, smoothingparams """ # 1. Identify boundary bc = featuref.getboundingcontour() # 2. DCT Smoothing bc = dctsmooth(bc, params['dctparams']) # 3. Extract receding portion (s) # Assuming Algorithm 6 logic is encapsulated or available # This involves calculating di for all points in bc and selecting the receding segment s = extractrecedingportion(bc, velocityfield) # 4. Initial Offset vavg = featuref.getaveragevelocity(velocityfield) offsetvector = vavg params['dt'] s = offsetcurve(s, offsetvector) # 5. Trim overlaps # Find dmin from the original bounding contour bc centroid = featuref.getcentroid() dmin = min((p - centroid).dot(vavg) for p in bc) # Remove points in s where di > dmin s = [p for p in s if (p - centroid).dot(vavg) <= dmin] # 6. Generate first silhouette mesh = featuref.getmesh() tube1 = generatetubes(s, diameter=params['rinit'], facets=params['facets']) mesh.addgeometry(tube1, color=params['color']) # 7. Iterative generation currents = s currentdiameter = params['rinit'] for i in range(params['N']): # a. Offset currents = offsetcurve(currents, offsetvector) # b. Remove end points numtoremove = int(len(currents) params['k']) if numtoremove > 0: currents = currents[:-numtoremove] # c. Gaussian Smoothing currents = gaussiansmooth(currents, params['gaussianparams']) # d. Generate tube with reduced diameter currentdiameter = params['alpha'] tubenext = generatetubes(currents, diameter=currentdiameter, facets=params['facets']) mesh.addgeometry(tubenext, color=params['color']) # Intensity reduction handled by color alpha if needed return mesh Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of points in the bounding contour and the number of strobes N. The dominant costs are the contour extraction, smoothing (DCT/Gaussian), and tube generation per iteration. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of points in the contour multiplied by N (for the stored silhouette points) plus the mesh storage for the generated tubes. Strengths: Provides clear, discrete visual cues for motion history and deformation in a single image. It is computationally efficient compared to full temporal volume compositing. Limitations: Relies on the assumption of constant average velocity between steps. It only visualizes the "receding" portion, potentially ignoring leading-edge history. Accuracy depends heavily on the quality of the velocity field and contour extraction. When to use: When the user needs to understand the trajectory and deformation of a specific feature boundary over a short time interval in a static view. When not to use: When the velocity field is highly non-uniform or turbulent, or when the full volumetric history (not just the boundary) is required. The technique was developed by Joshi and Rheingans and is part of a generalized framework for illustrative visualization of time-varying data on unstructured meshes. It is motivated by earlier work in illustrative visualization. It is distinct from "Speedlines" (which use cones) and "Opacity Modulation" (which uses transparency) within the same family of techniques. Generalized Framework and Algorithms for Illustrative Visualization of Time-Varying Data on Unstructured Meshes, https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc838861/?q=illustrative volume rendering, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Boundary Enhancement Volume Style
body:
Boundary Enhancement Volume Style is a non-photorealistic rendering technique that highlights feature bounds and reduces visual noise in volumetric data. It operates as a composable style within a rendering graph, modifying the compositing pass to emphasize edges, distinct from sibling methods like Line Illustration Detection that convert edges into line primitives. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric scalar field, a transfer function mapping values to color and opacity, ray origin, ray direction, and step size. Output: A 2D image where feature boundaries are enhanced with high-contrast highlights and noise is suppressed. Data Structures: The style is implemented as a node (e.g., BoundaryEnhancementVolumeStyle) that can be listed in the renderStyle field of a ComposedVolumeStyle node. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Marching: Step along the ray through the volume using a specified step size. 2. Gradient Estimation: Compute the local gradient magnitude |
abla f| at the current sample point using central differences between adjacent voxels. 3. Edge Detection & Noise Suppression: Compare the gradient magnitude against a threshold 	au. Values below 	au are treated as zero to suppress noise. 4. Style Application: Modulate the sample's opacity and color based on the edge strength. High gradient locations receive increased opacity or a bright highlight. 5. Compositing: Blend the enhanced sample along the ray using standard front-to-back alpha blending. Formulas: Gradient magnitude: |
abla f| = \sqrt{( rac{\partial f}{\partial x})^2 + ( rac{\partial f}{\partial y})^2 + ( rac{\partial f}{\partial z})^2}. Edge strength: e = \max(0, |
abla f| - 	au). Enhanced opacity: \alpha' = \min(1, \alpha \cdot (1 + e)). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def boundaryenhancevolumestyle(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata, transferfunction, threshold, stepsize): color = vec3(0.0) alpha = 0.0 t = 0.0 # Standard ray-box intersection tmin, tmax = -float('inf'), float('inf') for i in range(3): if raydirection[i] == 0.0: if not (volumedata.bounds.min[i] <= rayorigin[i] <= volumedata.bounds.max[i]): return color else: t1 = (volumedata.bounds.min[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] t2 = (volumedata.bounds.max[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) maxdistance = tmax if tmax > tmin else 0.0 while t < maxdistance: pos = rayorigin + t raydirection # Trilinear interpolation value = volumedata.interpolate(pos) # Central differences for gradient magnitude gx = volumedata.interpolate(pos + vec3(0.5, 0.0, 0.0)) - volumedata.interpolate(pos - vec3(0.5, 0.0, 0.0)) gy = volumedata.interpolate(pos + vec3(0.0, 0.5, 0.0)) - volumedata.interpolate(pos - vec3(0.0, 0.5, 0.0)) gz = volumedata.interpolate(pos + vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.5)) - volumedata.interpolate(pos - vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.5)) gradmag = (gx2 + gy2 + gz2)0.5 edgestrength = max(0.0, gradmag - threshold) basecolor, basealpha = transferfunction(value) enhancedalpha = min(1.0, basealpha (1.0 + edgestrength)) enhancedcolor = basecolor + vec3(edgestrength 0.2) alphaout = alpha + (1.0 - alpha) enhancedalpha color = color + (1.0 - alpha) enhancedalpha enhancedcolor alpha = alphaout if alpha > 0.99: break t += stepsize return color Parameters: threshold (	au): Gradient magnitude cutoff for edge detection. Not given in the sources. stepsize: Distance between samples along the ray. Set via RayGenerationVolumeSettings. Edge Cases: Non-equidistant grids: If the volume data is not equidistant, the dimensions field is unused and gradient calculations must account for voxel spacing. Swapped data: 16-bit volumes may have swapped byte order; the swapped field acts as a simple helper to handle this. A non-composable render style used alternatively in the VolumeData node's renderStyle field. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(N) where N is the number of samples per ray. Gradient computation adds a constant factor overhead per sample. Memory: O(1) additional memory per ray for gradient and compositing state. Measured Performance: Performance depends on the GPU model and gradient calculation complexity. Using "interleaved" ray generation reduces wood artifacts and can improve cache coherence. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Effective at reducing noise while preserving structural clarity. Can be combined with other styles like ShadedVolumeStyle and OpacityMapVolumeStyle via ComposedVolumeStyle. Limitations: Requires accurate gradient estimation, which can be sensitive to raw data noise. Not composable if using non-composable styles like XRayVolumeStyle. When to Use: Use when the goal is to clarify internal structures in noisy volumetric data without losing the context of the surrounding volume. The method is part of the InstantReality 1.0 volume rendering framework, which provides a set of composable volume styles for non-photorealistic visualization. It builds on the general principles of edge detection in volume rendering, where local intensity changes are mapped to visual highlights. instantreality 1.0 - tutorial - Volume Rendering, https://doc.instantreality.org/tutorial/volume-rendering/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Polarity Rendering
head: Polarity-based volume rendering, Sign-based field visualization
body: Polarity rendering visualizes volumetric data by coloring voxels based on the sign (positive or negative) of a selected vector field component basis (Bx, By, or Bz). It solves the problem of distinguishing directional orientation in vector fields, such as magnetic fields, where magnitude alone is insufficient. Unlike Geometric Buffers (G-buffers) which rely on surface normals, or Volume Illustration which uses gradient magnitude for edge enhancement, polarity rendering explicitly maps the algebraic sign of a specific axis component to distinct colors. Inputs: 1. A volumetric vector field dataset V, where each voxel contains a vector \mathbf{B} = (Bx, By, Bz). 2. A selected component basis C \in \{Bx, By, Bz\}. 3. Two distinct colors: c{pos} for positive values and c{neg} for negative values. Outputs: A rendered image where each pixel color is determined by the sign of the selected component at the corresponding sample location. Data Structures: The input data is typically stored as a 3D array of vectors. For implementation, the scalar component C is extracted into a 3D scalar field S where S(x,y,z) = C(x,y,z). Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Replace any NaN or Inf values in the input vector field with zero to prevent rendering artifacts, particularly at array boundaries. 2. Component Selection: Extract the scalar field S corresponding to the chosen basis component C. 3. Sign Evaluation: For each sample point p in the volume, evaluate the sign of S(p): \text{sign}(S(p)) = \begin{cases} +1 & \text{if } S(p) > 0 \\ -1 & \text{if } S(p) < 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } S(p) = 0 \end{cases} 4. Color Mapping: Assign the output color c{out} based on the sign: c{out} = \begin{cases} c{pos} & \text{if } \text{sign}(S(p)) > 0 \\ c{neg} & \text{if } \text{sign}(S(p)) < 0 \\ c{zero} & \text{if } \text{sign}(S(p)) = 0 \end{cases} Where c{zero} is typically a neutral color (e.g., black or gray) or transparent, though specific handling of zero-crossings is not detailed in the primary source. Parameters: Component Basis: The specific axis (Bx, By, or Bz) to evaluate. Colors: c{pos} and c{neg} are user-defined to maximize contrast. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Crossings: The behavior at exactly zero is not explicitly defined in the primary source. Implementers should define a default color or transparency for S(p)=0. Incomplete Topology: Polarity rendering does not represent full magnetic topology, connectivity classes, or radial polarity unless additional modes are implemented. It only indicates the sign of the chosen component, not the full vector direction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def polarityrender(vectorfield, componentindex, colorpos, colorneg, colorzero): """ Renders a volume based on the sign of a specific vector component. Args: vectorfield: 3D numpy array of shape (D, H, W, 3) containing vector components. componentindex: Integer 0, 1, or 2 corresponding to x, y, or z. colorpos: RGB tuple for positive values. colorneg: RGB tuple for negative values. colorzero: RGB tuple for zero values. Returns: 3D numpy array of shape (D, H, W, 3) with colored voxels. """ # Extract the scalar field for the chosen component scalarfield = vectorfield[:,:,:, componentindex] # Initialize output buffer output = np.zeroslike(scalarfield) output = np.stack([output, output, output], axis=-1) # Create masks for positive, negative, and zero values maskpos = scalarfield > 0 maskneg = scalarfield < 0 maskzero = ~maskpos & ~maskneg # Assign colors based on sign output[maskpos] = colorpos output[maskneg] = colorneg output[maskzero] = colorzero return output This variant is used when the input data is not a native vector field but rather scalar data representing different polarities (e.g., Radar Cross Section data with Vertical, Horizontal, and Cross-pole polarities). Instead of evaluating the sign of a vector component, distinct scalar values are assigned to each polarity type. Vertical polarity (W) and Horizontal polarities (HH) are given unique values, while Cross-pole polarities (HV and VH) are assigned the same scalar weight. A spacing of 50 units between scalar values is recommended to ensure accurate representation and avoid bias. A key pitfall is that closely spaced scalar values or values close to zero significantly bias the final results, leading to inaccurate visualizations. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of voxels, as it involves a single pass to evaluate the sign of the selected component. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the scalar field and output buffer. Strengths: Simple to implement; effectively highlights directional asymmetry in vector fields; computationally inexpensive. Limitations: Does not convey full vector direction or topology; sensitive to the choice of component basis; zero-crossings require explicit handling. When to use: When the primary interest is distinguishing regions of positive vs. negative orientation along a specific axis (e.g., magnetic polarity). When not to use: When full vector direction, magnitude, or topological connectivity is required. Polarity rendering was introduced in the context of astrophysical vector field visualization, specifically for magnetograms. It was developed to provide a native volumetric visualization method that could quickly indicate magnetic polarity in solar physics data. The method is also applied in radar cross-section (RCS) data visualization, where distinct scalar values are assigned to different polarization states to facilitate 3D interpretation. VitorFigueiredoResearch/AstroSplat-Browser-native-volumetric-visualization-for-astrophysical-vector-fields, https://github.com/VitorFigueiredoResearch/AstroSplat-Browser-native-volumetric-visualization-for-astrophysical-vector-fields, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) DTIC ADA258905: Methods for Viewing Radar Cross Section Data in Three Dimensions, https://archive.org/details/DTICADA258905, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Bi-variate Volume Rendering
head: LIC texture on scalar regions, Primary/Secondary data blending
body: Bi-variate volume rendering is a non-photorealistic technique that visualizes vector flow fields by blending a primary scalar data set (defining opacity and geometric regions) with a secondary Line Integral Convolution (LIC) texture data set (defining color and flow direction). It solves the problem of visualizing vector fields within volumetric regions where standard LIC outputs are noise-like and lack physical meaning, allowing users to interactively track scalar features while simultaneously viewing vector flow patterns. It differs from standard volume rendering by decoupling the geometric definition (opacity) from the textural definition (color), and from surface-based LIC by rendering the texture volumetrically within scalar-defined regions. Inputs and Outputs: Primary Data: A scalar volume (e.g., velocity magnitude, pressure, or vorticity) with an associated opacity map. Secondary Data: A 3D LIC texture volume derived from the vector field. Output: A final 2D image where scalar geometry and vector texture are blended. Data Structures: Primary Volume: 3D grid of scalar values defining opacity via a transfer function. Secondary Volume: 3D grid storing LIC-derived color values. Parameters: \beta \in [0, 1]: User-specified blending weight between primary and secondary data. \beta=1 renders only the scalar volume; \beta=0 renders only the LIC volume. Algorithm Steps: 1. Voxel Color Mixture: For each sample point Vi along a ray, compute the mixed color C{vi} using the blending weight \beta: C{vi} = \beta C{vi(p)} + (1 - \beta) C{vi(s)} where C{vi(p)} is the color contribution from the primary data at Vi, and C{vi(s)} is the color contribution from the secondary LIC data at Vi. 2. Light Attenuation: Compute the light attenuation factor W(i) for the i-th sample point, which determines how much light reaches the current sample based on the opacity of preceding samples. The opacity \alpha(Vi) is defined by the primary data set's opacity map and the data value at Vi: W(i) = \alpha(Vi) \left[ 1 - \sum{j=0}^{i-1} W(j) \right] where the summation runs over all preceding sample indices j. 3. Front-to-Back Compositing: Render the final pixel color Cp using standard front-to-back compositing: Cp = \sum{i=1}^{N-1} W(i) C{vi} where N is the total number of sample points along the ray. 4. Decoupled Rendering: By substituting the mixture formula into the compositing equation, the rendering process separates into two independent passes due to linearity: Cp = \beta \sum{i=1}^{N-1} W(i) C{vi(p)} + (1 - \beta) \sum{i=1}^{N-1} W(i) C{vi(s)} This allows the primary scalar volume and secondary LIC volume to be rendered separately into intermediate buffers, then blended in 2D space using \beta. Pseudocode: The following pseudocode implements the single-pass mixture approach, which directly follows Equations 8 and 9 and avoids the indexing/step-size bugs present in earlier drafts. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderbivariate(primarygrid, secondarygrid, beta, rayorigin, raydirection, stepsize, numsamples, boundsmin, boundsmax): """ Renders a bi-variate volume using single-pass front-to-back compositing. Implements Equation 9 combined with Equation 8 from the source. """ finalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 for i in range(numsamples): # Calculate sample position with correct step size and midpoint offset pos = rayorigin + (i + 0.5) stepsize raydirection # Check volume bounds to prevent out-of-bounds sampling if not (boundsmin[0] <= pos[0] <= boundsmax[0] and boundsmin[1] <= pos[1] <= boundsmax[1] and boundsmin[2] <= pos[2] <= boundsmax[2]): continue # Sample primary data for opacity alphap = primarygrid.sampleopacity(pos) # Compute transmittance (1 - sum of previous W(j)) transmittance = 1.0 - accumulatedopacity # Compute light attenuation factor W(i) Wi = alphap transmittance # Early exit if ray is fully opaque if transmittance < 1e-6: break # Sample colors from both volumes colorp = primarygrid.samplecolor(pos) colors = secondarygrid.samplecolor(pos) # Voxel color mixture (Equation 8) Cv = [beta colorp[k] + (1.0 - beta) colors[k] for k in range(3)] # Front-to-back compositing (Equation 9) for k in range(3): finalcolor[k] += Wi Cv[k] accumulatedopacity += Wi return finalcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: LIC Noise Interpretation: The values in the LIC volume are primarily noise signals used to construct vector textures and do not have physical meaning, so standard isosurface extraction or volume rendering cannot be directly applied to the LIC output alone. Opacity Definition: The opacity for the secondary LIC data is not defined by its own transfer function but is derived entirely from the primary data set's opacity map. Precision and Boundaries: Rays starting outside the volume bounds or stepping through empty regions must be handled to avoid sampling errors. The transmittance check prevents over-compositing when the ray exits the volume. An extension of bi-variate rendering where the LIC volume (secondary data) contributes to the total opacity, allowing visualization of dye propagation through the volume, not just color blending. In this variant, the opacity at each sample point is calculated as the sum of the primary data opacity and the LIC volume (dye) opacity. The color contribution of the LIC voxel is then computed using this combined opacity. Additionally, the dye color can be determined by additional scalar variables to visualize flow direction and scalar distribution simultaneously. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot R), where N is the number of rays (pixels) and R is the number of samples per ray. The decoupled rendering approach allows two separate volume rendering passes followed by a constant-time 2D blend, effectively doubling the volume rendering cost but simplifying the final compositing. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for two 3D volumes (primary scalar and secondary LIC) plus intermediate buffers if using the decoupled 2D blend approach. Strengths: Allows interactive adjustment of the blending parameter \beta to track features from one variable and visualize the counterparts of the other. It effectively visualizes vector flow within scalar-defined regions. Limitations: The LIC volume values lack physical meaning, so they cannot be used for geometric isolation alone without the primary data. The method relies on the linearity of the compositing equation, which may not hold for non-linear transfer functions or lighting models. Bi-variate volume rendering was introduced in a 1997 NASA Technical Report titled "Visualizing Vector Fields Using Line Integral Convolution and Dye Advection". It was developed to address the limitations of applying standard visualization techniques to 3D LIC outputs, which consist of noise signals without physical meaning. The method enables the interactive tracking of scalar features while visualizing vector flow, a capability not directly supported by standard volume rendering or surface-based LIC. Visualizing Vector Fields Using Line Integral Convolution and Dye Advection, https://archive.org/details/NASANTRSArchive19970011183, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Virtual Magic Lantern
head: Magic Lantern metaphor
body: The Virtual Magic Lantern (VML) is an interaction metaphor for volumetric data inspection that uses a virtual right circular cone, guided by a 3D pointer device, to define a region of interest (ROI). Inside this cone, the volume is rendered using a secondary transfer function or shading style, while the exterior uses the primary style, allowing simultaneous visualization of the focal region and its context. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Virtual Magic Window by providing explicit contextual information at the boundary of the ROI, whereas VMW acts as a restricted implementation where the lantern aligns with the viewing direction. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D volumetric dataset (texture), primary transfer function (TF), secondary transfer function (TF), cone geometry (apex position, axis direction, aperture angle), and camera parameters. Outputs: Rendered image with dual-style visualization. Data Structures: Volume Texture: 3D texture storing voxel values. In the source implementation, resolution is 512 \times 512 \times 512. Cone Parameters: Apex: \mathbf{a} (vec3), position of the pointer device. Axis: \mathbf{d} (vec3), normalized direction vector of the pointer. Aperture: \alpha (float), half-angle of the cone in radians, adjustable via joystick. Algorithm Steps: The method modifies the fragment shader of a classical GPU ray casting algorithm. 1. Initialization: Pass the transfer functions and cone geometry (\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{d}, \alpha) to the GPU. Initialize ray origin and direction based on screen coordinates (e.g., glFragCoord). 2. Ray Casting Loop: For each sample point \mathbf{p} along the ray: a. Sample Volume: Retrieve scalar value v from the volume texture at \mathbf{p}. b. Inclusion Test: Determine if \mathbf{p} lies inside the inspection cone. c. Color Calculation: If inside: Calculate material color \mathbf{c}{in} using the secondary transfer function and shading style. If outside: Calculate material color \mathbf{c}{out} using the primary transfer function and shading style. d. Shading: Apply Phong shading to the selected material color \mathbf{c}. e. Compositing: Accumulate the color and opacity using front-to-back compositing. f. Update: Advance \mathbf{p} along the ray. Point-in-Cone Test: A point \mathbf{p} is inside the cone defined by apex \mathbf{a}, axis \mathbf{d}, and aperture \alpha if the angle between the vector \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a} and the axis \mathbf{d} is less than or equal to \alpha, and \mathbf{v} points in the general direction of \mathbf{d} (dot product positive). Mathematically: \frac{(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{d}}{\|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}\|} \ge \cos(\alpha) \quad \text{and} \quad (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{d} > 0 In practice, to avoid division by zero when \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{a} and improve performance, the test is implemented as: (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{d} \ge \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}\| \cos(\alpha) with a guard that \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}\| > \epsilon and (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{d} > 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderfragment(glfragcoord): # 1. Calculate Ray (standard raycasting setup) rayorigin, raydirection = calculaterayfromscreen(glfragcoord) # 2. Initialize Compositing acccolor = vec4(0.0) accopacity = 0.0 position = rayorigin # 3. Ray Casting Loop for in range(maxsteps): # Sample Volume v = samplevolume(volumetexture, position) # Inclusion Test vectopoint = position - a dotprod = dot(vectopoint, d) lensq = dot(vectopoint, vectopoint) if lensq > epsilon and dotprod > 0: cosangle = dotprod / sqrt(lensq) isinside = cosangle >= cos(alpha) else: isinside = False # 4. Determine Material Color if isinside: material = applytf(tfinside, v) else: material = applytf(tfoutside, v) # 5. Shading and Compositing shadedcolor = phongshading(material, position) alpha = material.opacity acccolor = acccolor + shadedcolor alpha (1.0 - accopacity) accopacity = accopacity + alpha (1.0 - accopacity) # 6. Update Position position = position + stepsize raydirection return acccolor Helper definitions (standard operations): calculaterayfromscreen generates ray origin/direction from pixel coordinates; samplevolume trilinearly interpolates the 3D texture; applytf maps scalar v to color/opacity via the transfer function; phongshading computes diffuse/specular lighting; vec4, dot, sqrt, cos are standard math/vector operations. Parameters: Aperture Angle: Adjustable via joystick on the Wanda device. Resolution: Tested on 512 \times 512 \times 512 voxel models. Window Size: 900 \times 900 pixels. Samples: Typically 1 sample per voxel for real-time performance, though 2 samples are supported. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Navigation Misalignment: When navigating through a model, the cone apex (device position) may not point exactly in front of the user, causing the entire volume to be rendered with the primary transfer function if the cone misses the view frustum or relevant data. Solution: Generate the inspection cone with the apex at the observer position while keeping the direction guided by the hand/device. Abrupt Region Changes: The pointed region may change more abruptly than expected if the geometry is closer than supposed. Solution: Place the apex of the cone at a fixed distance back from the device. Performance Penalty: The inclusion test adds a rendering penalty compared to classical ray casting, but real-time framerates are maintained on the tested hardware. A restricted implementation of VML where the virtual lantern aligns with the viewing direction, creating a window. It incurs no performance penalty compared to classical volume ray casting but provides less contextual information at the ROI boundary [11345-virtual-magic-window.md]. Time and Memory Complexity: The method adds a constant-time geometric inclusion test per sample point to the standard ray casting loop. Memory usage: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Tests were conducted on a 3.00 GHz Intel Core 2 Duo PC, 8GB RAM, GeForce 8800 GTX (768MB RAM) in a stereo PowerWall system with a 900 \times 900 window. | Model | Samples | RC (fps) | VML (fps) | VMW (fps) | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | Feet | 1 | 32 | 17 | 32 | | Feet | 2 | 18.5 | 9.8 | 18.5 | | Manix | 1 | 18 | 13 | 18 | | Manix | 2 | 10 | 6.5 | 10 | | Head | 1 | 28 | 15.3 | 28 | | Head | 2 | 15 | 10 | 15 | | Rips | 1 | 32 | 14.8 | 32 | | Rips | 2 | 18 | 8.4 | 18 | VML incurs a performance penalty compared to classical Ray Casting (RC) and Virtual Magic Window (VMW). VMW has no penalty compared to RC. Framerates drop roughly 40% if the volume covers the whole viewport (close inspection). Disabling stereo rendering doubles framerates. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Intuitive interaction, provides rich contextual information at the ROI boundary, maintains interactive framerates. Limitations: Performance penalty relative to RC, potential for abrupt region changes during navigation, requires 3D pointer device (Wanda) for optimal interaction. When to Use: Immersive stereo systems (PowerWall) for volumetric data inspection. Scenarios requiring simultaneous view of a focal region and its context (e.g., surgery planning, injury diagnosis). When Not to Use: When maximum performance is required and contextual boundary information is not needed, VMW or classical ray casting are preferred. When the hardware is significantly older than the tested GeForce 8800 GTX, as the penalty may become prohibitive. The Virtual Magic Lantern was presented by A. Andujar, M. Fairen, and F. Argelaguet in 2007. It is tailored to facilitate volumetric data inspection, particularly in Virtual Reality setups with large screens. The metaphor is inspired by the historical magic lantern, where a virtual illumination cone provides the focal region. The implementation builds on classical GPU ray casting. The virtual magic lantern, https://doi.org/10.1145/1643928.1643955, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Virtual Magic Window
head: Magic Window
body: The Virtual Magic Window (VMW) is a volume rendering inspection metaphor that allows users to view a specific region of interest (ROI) within a volumetric dataset through a virtual "window" defined by a 3D pointer device, while the rest of the volume is rendered using a different style or transfer function. It serves as an efficient, restricted implementation of the Virtual Magic Lantern (VML), where the virtual lantern is constrained to align with the viewing direction, effectively creating a window through which the volume is seen. Unlike VML, VMW does not provide contextual information on the boundary of the ROI, but it incurs no performance penalty compared to classical volume ray casting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric dataset, primary transfer function (TF), secondary TF, viewing parameters (camera position, direction), and 3D pointer device state (origin and direction). Output: Rendered image where the ROI is visualized with the secondary TF and the exterior with the primary TF. Data Structures: Ray Start Position Textures: Two textures store the starting positions for ray casting. Texture 1: Stores starting positions for rays inside the ROI. Texture 2: Stores starting positions for rays outside the ROI. Volume Bounding Box: Defines the spatial extent of the volume. Steps: 1. Define ROI: Construct a virtual cone using the origin and direction from the 3D pointer device (e.g., Wanda device). 2. Intersect: Intersect this cone with the volume's bounding box to determine the ROI. 3. Label Rays: Determine which rays cast from the observer pass through the ROI; rays passing through the intersection are labeled "inside", others "outside". 4. Split Ray Initialization: Initialize the input ray directions by splitting the texture storing ray starting positions into two: for rays inside the ROI, initialize starting positions for the outside rays as if they were outside the volume; vice versa for the other texture. 5. Render ROI (Secondary Pass): Perform a classical ray casting pass using the secondary TF for rays identified as lying inside the cone/ROI. 6. Render Exterior (Primary Pass): Perform a second classical ray casting pass using the primary TF for rays lying outside the cone/ROI. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def virtualmagicwindow(volume, primarytf, secondarytf, camera, pointer, bbox): # camera: {origin, direction, right, up, width, height} # pointer: {origin, direction} # bbox: {min: [x,y,z], max: [x,y,z]} # Step 1 & 2: Define ROI by intersecting virtual cone with volume bounding box # Precompute pixel coordinates that fall inside the ROI shape roipixels = set() for y in range(camera.height): for x in range(camera.width): raydir = normalize(camera.direction + (x - camera.width/2) camera.right + (y - camera.height/2) camera.up) if rayintersectsroi(camera.origin, raydir, pointer.origin, pointer.direction, bbox): roipixels.add((x, y)) # Step 3 & 4: Split ray initialization textures # Texture A: for secondary TF pass (inside ROI) # Texture B: for primary TF pass (outside ROI) # Rays not belonging to the current pass are initialized as "outside volume" to be skipped texa = [[None for in range(camera.width)] for in range(camera.height)] texb = [[None for in range(camera.width)] for in range(camera.height)] for y in range(camera.height): for x in range(camera.width): raydir = normalize(camera.direction + (x - camera.width/2) camera.right + (y - camera.height/2) camera.up) startpos = computeraystart(camera.origin, raydir, bbox) if (x, y) in roipixels: texa[y][x] = startpos texb[y][x] = None # Mark as outside volume to skip else: texa[y][x] = None # Mark as outside volume to skip texb[y][x] = startpos # Step 5: Render ROI with secondary TF imgroi = renderpass(volume, texa, secondarytf) # Step 6: Render Exterior with primary TF imgext = renderpass(volume, texb, primarytf) # Composite: ROI pixels overwrite exterior pixels where valid imgfinal = [[imgext[y][x] for x in range(camera.width)] for y in range(camera.height)] for y in range(camera.height): for x in range(camera.width): if imgroi[y][x] is not None: imgfinal[y][x] = imgroi[y][x] return imgfinal def rayintersectsroi(rayorigin, raydir, coneorigin, conedir, bbox): # Check if ray passes through the intersection of the cone and bounding box if not rayhitsbbox(rayorigin, raydir, bbox): return False dot = dotproduct(raydir, conedir) return dot > 0.9 # Threshold approximating cone alignment def rayhitsbbox(rayorigin, raydir, bbox): # Standard ray-AABB intersection test tmin, tmax = -float('inf'), float('inf') for i in range(3): if raydir[i] == 0: if rayorigin[i] < bbox.min[i] or rayorigin[i] > bbox.max[i]: return False else: t1 = (bbox.min[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] t2 = (bbox.max[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) return tmax >= 0 and tmin <= tmax def computeraystart(rayorigin, raydir, bbox): # Returns entry point of ray into bounding box; None if no intersection tmin, tmax = -float('inf'), float('inf') for i in range(3): if raydir[i] == 0: if rayorigin[i] < bbox.min[i] or rayorigin[i] > bbox.max[i]: return None else: t1 = (bbox.min[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] t2 = (bbox.max[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmax < 0 or tmin > tmax: return None return [rayorigin[i] + tmin raydir[i] for i in range(3)] def renderpass(volume, texture, tf): # Classical GPU ray casting pass using given texture and transfer function img = [[None for in range(len(texture[0]))] for in range(len(texture))] for y in range(len(texture)): for x in range(len(texture[0])): start = texture[y][x] if start is None: continue color = samplevolumealongray(volume, start, tf) img[y][x] = color return img Parameters: Primary TF: Transfer function for the background/exterior region. Secondary TF: Transfer function for the ROI. Pointer Device: Provides the origin and direction for the virtual cone. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Context: VMW does not provide contextual information on the boundary of the ROI, which can make it harder to understand the spatial relationship of the ROI to the rest of the volume compared to VML. Performance: While VMW incurs no performance penalty with respect to classical volume ray casting, the implementation requires managing two ray casting passes and splitting the ray initialization. Time Complexity: Two passes of classical volume ray casting. The complexity is O(N) where N is the number of pixels, assuming constant time per ray. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for two ray start position textures and two intermediate images (or a mechanism to composite on the fly). Measured Performance: The implementation runs in real time and incurs no performance penalty with respect to classical volume ray casting. Strengths: Efficient, simple implementation, intuitive interaction, flexible shading style and region shape without volume deformation. Limitations: Lack of contextual information at the ROI boundary compared to VML. When to Use: When comparing rendering motifs or inspecting a specific region with a different style, and performance is critical. When Not to Use: When contextual information at the boundary of the ROI is important. The Virtual Magic Window (VMW) was introduced as a collateral implementation of the Virtual Magic Lantern (VML) in the paper "The virtual magic lantern". It is based on the Magic Lens metaphor but adapted for volume rendering with a 3D pointer device (Wanda device). The method was designed to be efficient and easy to adapt to GPU ray casting algorithms. The virtual magic lantern, https://doi.org/10.1145/1643928.1643955, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Volume Illustration
head: Ebert and Rheingans volume illustration, Non-photorealistic Volume Rendering
body:
Volume Illustration is a method that augments a physics-based volume rendering pipeline with non-photorealistic rendering (NPR) techniques to enhance the perception of structure, shape, orientation, and depth relationships in volumetric data. It solves the problem of ambiguous structural interpretation in traditional physics-based renderings by applying stylized enhancements such as boundary detection, silhouettes, and tone shading. Unlike surface-based NPR, which relies on well-defined geometric surfaces, Volume Illustration determines features through the analysis of local volumetric properties that vary continuously throughout 3D space. It is distinguished from its siblings by its unified framework that decouples illumination from physical light transport, using mathematical functions of view, light, and scalar field properties to modulate color and opacity. The method operates by modifying the standard volume rendering pipeline. It begins with a base renderer that implements physics-based illumination (e.g., atmospheric or Phong illumination with linear accumulation). The core innovation lies in the transformation of voxel properties before compositing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar field V(x,y,z), a transfer function TF mapping scalar values to base color c{base} and opacity \alpha, view direction \vec{v}, and light direction \vec{l}. Output: A final 2D image where voxels contribute to the final color via standard volume compositing, but with modified color and opacity values derived from NPR transformations. Data Structures: For each voxel sample i along a ray, the renderer computes or accesses: 1. Scalar Value: si = V(xi, yi, zi). 2. Gradient: 
abla fi = ( rac{\partial f}{\partial x},  rac{\partial f}{\partial y},  rac{\partial f}{\partial z})i. This is normalized to 
abla f{n,i} to serve as a proxy for surface normal orientation. 3. Minimal Change Direction: The direction of least variation in the scalar field, often derived from the gradient's orthogonal complement or principal component analysis of local neighborhoods. 4. Base Color and Opacity: c{base,i} and \alphai obtained from the transfer function applied to si. Numbered Steps: 1. Classification: Apply the transfer function to the voxel's scalar value to obtain initial color c{base} and opacity \alpha. 2. Feature Analysis: Compute local volumetric properties for the voxel: Calculate the gradient 
abla f. Determine the minimal change direction. Retrieve view direction \vec{v} and light direction \vec{l}. 3. NPR Transformation: Apply transformation functions to c{base} and \alpha using the properties from Step 2. These transformations encapsulate specific illustration techniques (e.g., boundary enhancement, tone shading). Note: The specific mathematical forms of these transformations vary by technique (see Subtopics). Common parameters include sample location, value, gradient magnitude, view angle, and light angle. 4. Compositing: Perform standard front-to-back volume compositing using the transformed color and opacity. The compositing equation remains unchanged from physics-based rendering: C{out} = \sum{i=1}^{N} c{final,i} \cdot \alpha{final,i} \cdot \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha{final,j}) All voxels in the volume still contribute to the final image. Formulas and Parameters: Gradient Normalization: 
abla fn =  rac{
abla f}{\|
abla f\|}. Boundary Enhancement: Often triggered when \|
abla f\| exceeds a threshold, increasing opacity or altering color to highlight edges. Tone Shading: Modulates brightness based on the dot product 
abla fn \cdot \vec{l} and 
abla fn \cdot \vec{v}. Parameters: Tunable parameters include thresholds for gradient magnitude, intensity of halos, and color blending factors. These parameters are dataset-dependent. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumeillustrationrender(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata, transferfunction, lightdirection, cameraposition): """ Renders a single ray using the Volume Illustration framework. """ coloraccum = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alphaaccum = 0.0 # Iterate along the ray through the volume for sample in raysamples(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata): # 1. Classification scalarval = sample.value basecolor, basealpha = transferfunction(scalarval) # 2. Feature Analysis # Compute gradient at sample position using standard finite differences gradient = computegradient(sample.position, volumedata) # Guard against zero gradient to avoid division by zero gradmag = magnitude(gradient) if gradmag > 1e-6: gradientnorm = [g / gradmag for g in gradient] else: gradientnorm = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # View direction from sample to camera viewvec = [cameraposition[i] - sample.position[i] for i in range(3)] viewmag = magnitude(viewvec) if viewmag > 1e-6: viewdirection = [v / viewmag for v in viewvec] else: viewdirection = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # 3. NPR Transformation # Apply transformations based on local properties. # Sources do not specify exact mathematical forms for all techniques. # Example: Boundary enhancement increases opacity if gradient magnitude exceeds a threshold. boundarythreshold = 0.5 # Dataset-dependent parameter if gradmag > boundarythreshold: finalalpha = basealpha 1.5 # Example enhancement factor finalcolor = [c 0.8 for c in basecolor] # Example darkening for edges else: finalalpha = basealpha finalcolor = basecolor # Example: Tone shading modulates color based on light and view directions # Dot product for diffuse lighting lightdot = sum(gradientnorm[i] lightdirection[i] for i in range(3)) viewdot = sum(gradientnorm[i] viewdirection[i] for i in range(3)) ambientlight = 0.2 diffusecoeff = 0.8 lightingfactor = ambientlight + diffusecoeff max(0.0, lightdot) finalcolor = [c lightingfactor for c in finalcolor] # 4. Compositing # Standard front-to-back volume compositing alphaterm = finalalpha (1.0 - alphaaccum) coloraccum = [coloraccum[i] + finalcolor[i] alphaterm for i in range(3)] alphaaccum = alphaaccum + finalalpha (1.0 - alphaaccum) if alphaaccum > 0.99: break return coloraccum Note: The specific transformation logic in Step 3 is highly variable depending on the chosen NPR technique (e.g., stippling, hatching, halos). The pseudocode above illustrates the pipeline structure. For specific techniques, refer to the Subtopics. A flexible framework associating user-defined interest labels with rendering techniques to allow variable detail levels and artistic styles per segment. It solves programmatic bias by prioritizing communicative abstraction over physical accuracy. Choose when different volume regions require distinct illustrative styles. Simulates traditional pen-and-ink hatching styles interactively using local volumetric properties for stroke placement. Choose when a hand-drawn, sketch-like appearance is desired. Generates stipple drawing effects by varying dot density and size based on scalar values and gradients. Choose for textured, illustrative appearances mimicking pen-and-ink stippling. Extracts and enhances contours and edges from volume data using gradient analysis. Choose when emphasizing structural boundaries and sketch-like lines is the primary goal. Adds glowing or darkened outlines around features to enhance depth perception and separation. Choose when distinguishing overlapping structures or enhancing depth cues is needed. Uses intermediate buffers storing geometric information to guide NPR techniques, adapted for volumes by deriving normals from gradients. Choose when precise geometric guidance is required for stylization. Provides the underlying physics-based illumination model that Volume Illustration augments. Choose as the foundational lighting layer before applying NPR effects. Modifies colors based on gradient orientation relative to view and light directions. Choose when enhancing structural cues through directional shading is required. Maintains global context while applying local NPR enhancements, often using focus+context techniques. Choose when balancing detailed local illustration with overall scene context is necessary. Enhances silhouettes and sketch lines by modulating transparency and color along boundaries. Choose when a pen-and-ink silhouette effect is desired. Renders fully opaque features with precise boundaries, often used with NPR to define clear extents. Choose when crisp, unambiguous feature boundaries are critical. Defines mathematical models for lighting and shading, decoupling illumination from physical transport. Choose when custom lighting behaviors are needed for illustrative purposes. Renders multiple objects with ghosting effects to show internal structure while maintaining external context. Choose when visualizing overlapping or nested volumetric objects requires transparency and depth layering. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Standard volume rendering scales linearly with the number of samples per ray. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storage for the volume dataset and temporary per-sample buffers for gradients and transformed properties. Measured Performance: Tested on datasets such as 256 	imes 256 	imes 128 abdominal CT volumes. Scaling: Scales linearly with resolution and dataset size. Interactive frame rates are achievable with optimization techniques like adaptive sampling or GPU acceleration. Strengths: Enhances structural perception significantly more than physics-based rendering alone; requires less manual tuning of transfer functions than traditional methods; flexible framework allowing combination of multiple NPR techniques. Limitations: Local implementation requires significant parameter tuning dependent on exact voxel intensity values and dataset characteristics; features are not as well-defined as in surface rendering, leading to potential ambiguity in feature detection. When to Use: When the goal is to create illustrative, textbook-quality images that emphasize structure and depth; when traditional volume rendering fails to convey internal structure clearly. When Not to Use: When physical accuracy is required; when real-time performance is critical and computational resources are limited; when the dataset has low contrast or noisy gradients that make feature detection unreliable. Volume Illustration was introduced by Penny Rheingans and David Ebert in 2000 (Vis '00) and published in TVCG in July 2001. It combines the familiarity of physics-approximated illumination with the expressive power of NPR techniques. The method was developed to address the limitations of traditional volume rendering in conveying complex 3D structures, particularly in medical imaging and scientific visualization. Popular styles include stippling, hatching, and silhouettes, drawing inspiration from the pen-and-ink family of illustration. The framework allows for the augmentation of a physics-based renderer with various NPR techniques, providing a unified approach to enhancing volumetric data.
