name: Interest-Based NPR Toolkit
head: Non-Photorealistic Rendering (NPR) Toolkit, Variable-Detail NPR
body: The Interest-Based NPR Toolkit is a flexible framework within the Volume Illustration pipeline that generates 2D non-photorealistic illustrations by associating user-defined interest labels with subsets of rendering techniques. It solves the problem of programmatic bias in automated visualization by allowing variable detail levels per segment, where different labels trigger different artistic styles simultaneously. Unlike physics-based rendering, it prioritizes communicative abstraction and artistic vision over physical accuracy. The method operates on an enriched model consisting of a geometric model (identified segments) and a structural model (associated interest labels). Inputs: 1. Geometric Model: A set of segments derived from segmentation. 2. Structural Model: A mapping from segment IDs to interest labels. 3. NPR Technique Library: A set of implemented techniques (greyscale shading, simple outlines, copper plate lines, short hatching lines). Outputs: A single 2D illustration image where each segment is rendered according to the NPR techniques associated with its interest label. Data Structures: Segment Map: A shadow volume recording the segment associated with each voxel. Label Map: A mapping SegmentID -> InterestLabel (integer). Technique Map: A mapping InterestLabel -> Subset{NPRTechnique} representing a one-to-many association. Numbered Steps: 1. Segmentation: Identify segments in the volume data. The system assumes all voxels in a segment are equally interesting (Single Interest Volume assumption). 2. Enrichment: Assign an interest label to each segment to augment the geometric model with structural information, forming an enriched model. 3. Association: The user defines a one-to-many mapping where each interest label is associated with a subset of available NPR techniques to avoid programmatic biases. 4. Rendering: Render all NPR techniques associated with all interest labels simultaneously to generate the final 2D illustration. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Number of Interest Labels: Defaults to 5, an arbitrary decision generalizable to any number. Default Label: All segments default to label 3 if not explicitly assigned. Technique Properties: Techniques are customizable to portray silhouettes, surface geometry, value, light and shade, and a primitive form of texture. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Segmentation avoids the algorithmic deficiencies of isosurfacing, such as poor topological properties and the need for prior dataset knowledge. Automatic label allocation is impossible because the system cannot infer the user's artistic vision. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def createblankimage(width, height): """Initialize a 2D buffer with zero values.""" return [[0.0] width for in range(height)] def applynprtechnique(voxels, techniquename, imagebuffer): """ Applies a specific NPR technique to the geometry defined by voxels. The sources do not provide the mathematical implementation for the NPR techniques. Standard operations would compute gradients, lighting, or line projections per voxel. """ # Apply technique rendering logic to voxels in imagebuffer pass def renderinterestbasednpr(segmentmap, labelmap, techniquemap, width, height): """ segmentmap: Dict mapping SegmentID to list of Voxels labelmap: Dict mapping SegmentID to InterestLabel (int) techniquemap: Dict mapping InterestLabel to List of Technique Strings """ outputimage = createblankimage(width, height) for segmentid, voxels in segmentmap.items(): interestlabel = labelmap[segmentid] techniques = techniquemap.get(interestlabel, []) for technique in techniques: applynprtechnique(voxels, technique, outputimage) return outputimage A generalization of binary segmentation where the level of interest in each segment is quantified by assigning an interest label. The relationship between segments and labels is many-to-one. The user assigns one of five labels to each segment in a synchronized structural view. This supports variable detail levels without enforcing a specific hierarchy. Complexity: Rendering uses a fast, pixel-based, geometric buffer approach to maintain interactivity. Memory: Supports single-level undo; multiple-level undo is a future improvement requiring extra memory or computation. Strengths: High flexibility, avoidance of programmatic biases, and creative artistic control. Limitations: Requires manual label assignment and technique mapping, making it non-fully automatic. Originated in the 2002 thesis "Volume Visualisation Via Variable-Detail Non-Photorealistic Illustration" by J.L. McKinley. It builds on the concept of enriched models combining geometric and structural information. It follows the lead of Ebert and Rheingans in providing a flexible NPR toolkit. Volume Visualisation Via Variable-Detail Non-Photorealistic Illustration, https://uwspace.uwaterloo.ca/bitstream/10012/1104/1/jlmckinl2002.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Illustrative Rendering
head: Illustrative visualization, Streamtape illustrative rendering
body: Illustrative rendering is a non-photorealistic visualization technique that combines Phong shading, half-tone hatching shadows, and silhouette outlines to enhance the depth and structural perception of volumetric objects, specifically streamtapes in 3D vector fields. It differs from procedural texture-based methods (e.g., Hummel et al.) by avoiding complex line patterns on narrow objects, which would increase visual complexity, instead relying on stylized lighting and edge detection to clarify geometry. Inputs: 3D vector field data. Pre-computed streamtapes (narrow tubular surfaces representing flow). Camera position and light direction. Outputs: Final illustrative image combining Phong shading, hatched shadows, and silhouette outlines. Data Structures: Framebuffer Object (FBO) for storing luminance. Color buffer for storing normalized normal vectors (RGB) and clamped depth (Alpha). Discontinuity mask buffer for silhouette detection. Parameters: Torsion normalization: \tau is normalized to [0, 1]. Streamtape width formula: \omega = 1.0 - \tau. Discontinuity threshold: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Phong Shading Pass: Render the streamtapes using standard Phong shading. Record the resulting luminance into a framebuffer object. 2. Hatched Shadow Generation: Generate a hatched shadow image using half-tone rendering styles to incorporate lighting and display depth/rotation information. 3. Silhouette Extraction Pass: Render the scene again to obtain silhouettes. Write the normalized normal direction of each fragment to the RGB channels of the output color. Clamp the depth value to [0, 1] and write it to the alpha channel. 4. Silhouette Detection: Check for discontinuities in the up, down, left, and right directions in image space on the output from Step 3. Mark pixels with large discontinuities as silhouette pixels. 5. Composition: Compose the hatched shadow image and the silhouette image with the Phong shaded image. 6. Coloring: Color the streamtapes either by cluster ID using a predefined color table or by local features such as curvature. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def illustrativerender(streamtapes, camera, lightdir): # Step 1: Phong Shading Pass phongluminance = renderphongpass(streamtapes, camera, lightdir) # Step 2: Hatched Shadow Generation hatchedshadow = renderhatchedshadowpass(streamtapes, camera, lightdir) # Step 3: Silhouette Extraction Pass normaldepthbuffer = rendernormalsanddepthpass(streamtapes, camera) # Step 4: Silhouette Detection silhouettemask = detectsilhouettes(normaldepthbuffer) # Step 5: Composition finalimage = composeimages(phongluminance, hatchedshadow, silhouettemask) # Step 6: Coloring finalimage = applycoloring(finalimage, streamtapes) return finalimage def renderphongpass(streamtapes, camera, lightdir): buffer = createbuffer(streamtapes.width, streamtapes.height) for frag in streamtapes.fragments: diffuse = max(dot(frag.normal, lightdir), 0.0) specular = pow(max(dot(reflect(-lightdir, frag.normal), camera.viewdir), 0.0), 32.0) lum = frag.basecolor (0.5 + 0.5 diffuse + 0.2 specular) buffer.set(frag.u, frag.v, lum) return buffer def renderhatchedshadowpass(streamtapes, camera, lightdir): buffer = createbuffer(streamtapes.width, streamtapes.height) for frag in streamtapes.fragments: intensity = max(dot(frag.normal, lightdir), 0.0) # Half-tone hatching style based on lighting and depth buffer.set(frag.u, frag.v, intensity) return buffer def rendernormalsanddepthpass(streamtapes, camera): buffer = createbuffer(streamtapes.width, streamtapes.height) for frag in streamtapes.fragments: norm = normalize(frag.normal) depth = clamp(frag.depth, 0.0, 1.0) buffer.setrgb(frag.u, frag.v, norm) buffer.seta(frag.u, frag.v, depth) return buffer def detectsilhouettes(buffer): mask = createbuffer(buffer.width, buffer.height) for y in range(buffer.height): for x in range(buffer.width): pixel = buffer.get(x, y) up = buffer.get(x, min(y + 1, buffer.height - 1)) down = buffer.get(x, max(y - 1, 0)) right = buffer.get(min(x + 1, buffer.width - 1), y) left = buffer.get(max(x - 1, 0), y) # Mark pixels with large discontinuities as silhouette pixels if (absdiff(pixel, up) > 0.1 or absdiff(pixel, down) > 0.1 or absdiff(pixel, right) > 0.1 or absdiff(pixel, left) > 0.1): mask.set(x, y, 1.0) return mask def composeimages(phong, shadow, silhouette): result = createbuffer(phong.width, phong.height) for y in range(phong.height): for x in range(phong.width): # Compose hatched shadow and silhouette with Phong shaded image base = phong.get(x, y) shadowval = shadow.get(x, y) sil = silhouette.get(x, y) result.set(x, y, base shadowval + sil 0.8) return result def applycoloring(image, streamtapes): for frag in streamtapes.fragments: # Assign colors by cluster ID or local features like curvature if frag.colormode == 'cluster': color = clustercolortable[frag.clusterid] else: color = curvaturetocolor(frag.curvature) image.set(frag.u, frag.v, color) return image def createbuffer(w, h): return [[None]w for in range(h)] def absdiff(a, b): return sum(abs(a[i]-b[i]) for i in range(len(a))) clustercolortable = {0: [1,0,0], 1: [0,1,0], 2: [0,0,1]} def curvaturetocolor(curv): return [curv, curv, curv] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-Intersection: When local flow twists sharply, streamtape surfaces can self-intersect. This is addressed by normalizing torsion \tau to [0, 1] and setting width \omega = 1.0 - \tau. Visual Complexity: Procedural line stripes (e.g., Hummel et al.) are incompatible because streamtapes are narrow objects where complex patterns increase visual complexity. Time Complexity: Entropy field calculation and streamline generation are implemented on the GPU (CUDA) and complete within a few seconds for given flow datasets. K-means clustering and streamtape generation are implemented on the CPU. Memory: Requires 1.5GB of video memory for the GPU (tested on Geforce GTX 480) and 16GB system memory (tested on Xeon 5450). Strengths: Enhances depth and structural perception; reveals structural information via curvature-based coloring. Limitations: Not suitable for integral surfaces requiring adaptive line stripes; limited to narrow objects like streamtapes. The method was introduced in 2011 as part of an illustrative visualization framework for 3D vector fields. It was implemented on the GPU and used to visualize streamtapes generated from vector field data. The half-tone rendering style references the work of Freudenberg et al. [FMS01] for an overview of half-tone rendering techniques. An Illustrative Visualization Framework for 3D Vector Fields, http://vis.cs.ucdavis.edu/papers/pg2011paper.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Trajectory Arrow Rendering
head: speed lines, particle trajectory visualization
body: Trajectory Arrow Rendering is an illustrative technique that overlays directional arrows on volume renderings of time-varying particle systems to visualize feature movement and provide temporal context within a single static image. Unlike sequential volume renderings which make it difficult to track features visually, this method highlights flow properties such as separation, convergence, and recirculation by integrating pathline geometry into the volumetric depth buffer. It sets itself apart from standard volume rendering by explicitly decoupling the representation of particle trajectories from the scalar field density, using a multi-pass approach to ensure arrows are correctly occluded by and blended with the volume interior. Inputs: Time-varying particle system data (positions at current time step t and previous time step t-1, or velocity vectors). Volume rendering parameters (transfer function, lighting model). Camera view matrix V and projection matrix P. Arrow width parameter w. Minimum pathline length threshold L{min} and minimum cluster size N{min}. Outputs: Final composite image containing the volume rendering with trajectory arrows blended at correct depths. Data Structures: Pathlines: A list of line segments connecting particle positions across time steps. Arrow Geometry: Triangle strips representing the arrows. Each arrow consists of a shaft and a head, generated from the pathline vector. Frame Buffers: F{arrow}: Color buffer storing the rendered arrow image. D{arrow}: Depth buffer storing the depth of the arrow geometry. F{vol}: Final volume rendering buffer. Steps: 1. Pathline Filtering: Compute pathlines for particles based on temporal data. Discard any pathline with length less than L{min}. Discard clusters of pathlines that contain fewer than N{min} pathlines. 2. Pass 1: Arrow Geometry Rendering: Render the filtered arrow geometry to F{arrow} and D{arrow}. Arrows are rendered as triangle strips. Billboarding: In the vertex shader, expand the arrow width to ensure it always faces the viewer. Let v be the vector representing the particle trajectory (direction of motion). Let V be the view matrix. Rotate v by V to get the view-space direction v{view}. Compute a perpendicular vector p in the view plane. Expand the geometry by adding \pm \frac{w}{2} p to the vertices of the arrow shaft. 3. Pass 2: Background Composition: Render a full-screen quad containing the image from F{arrow} to a background buffer. This prepares the arrow layer for blending. 4. Pass 3: Volume Raycasting with Depth-Aware Blending: Perform standard volume raycasting for the current time step. Pass D{arrow} into the raycaster as a depth texture. For each sample position s along the ray at depth ds: Check the depth of the arrow geometry at the corresponding screen coordinates, d{arrow}. Termination Condition: If ds > d{arrow} (the sample is behind the arrow), stop the ray integration. Blending: Blend the accumulated volume color c{vol} with the arrow color c{arrow} from the background image. The exact blending equation is not specified, but standard alpha blending or depth-based compositing is implied to ensure arrows appear inside the volume. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendertrajectoryarrows(particles, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix, arrowwidth, minlength, minclustersize): # Step 1: Filter Pathlines pathlines = computepathlines(particles) validpathlines = [] for pathline in pathlines: if length(pathline) < minlength: continue validpathlines.append(pathline) # Cluster filtering (simplified) clusters = grouppathlines(validpathlines) validclusters = [c for c in clusters if len(c) >= minclustersize] validpathlines = [p for c in validclusters for p in c] # Step 2: Render Arrow Geometry arrowframebuffer = createframebuffer() arrowdepthbuffer = createdepthbuffer() for pathline in validpathlines: direction = pathline.end - pathline.start viewdirection = normalize(viewmatrix direction) # Compute perpendicular vector for billboarding # Assuming viewdirection is not parallel to up vector (0,1,0) up = vec3(0, 1, 0) perpendicular = normalize(cross(viewdirection, up)) # Generate triangle strip vertices # Shaft vertices expanded by arrowwidth halfwidth = arrowwidth / 2.0 vertices = generatearrowstrip(pathline.start, pathline.end, perpendicular, halfwidth) rendertrianglestrip(vertices, arrowframebuffer, arrowdepthbuffer) # Step 3: Render Full Screen Quad with Arrow Image backgroundimage = renderfullscreenquad(arrowframebuffer) # Step 4: Volume Raycasting finalimage = createframebuffer() for each pixel in finalimage: ray = generateray(pixel, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix) accumulatedcolor = vec3(0) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 for samplepos along ray: depthsample = length(samplepos - cameraorigin) deptharrow = sampledepthtexture(arrowdepthbuffer, pixelcoords(samplepos)) if depthsample > deptharrow: # Stop ray, blend with arrow arrowcolor = samplecolortexture(backgroundimage, pixelcoords(samplepos)) accumulatedcolor = blend(accumulatedcolor, arrowcolor, accumulatedalpha) break # Standard volume sampling density = samplevolume(samplepos) color = transferfunction(density) accumulatedcolor, accumulatedalpha = accumulate(accumulatedcolor, accumulatedalpha, color, density) finalimage[pixel] = accumulatedcolor return finalimage Time Complexity: Dominated by the volume raycasting pass. The arrow rendering is O(N) where N is the number of valid pathlines, which is typically negligible compared to volume sampling. Memory Complexity: Requires additional framebuffers for arrow depth and color (O(W \times H) per buffer). Strengths: Provides immediate temporal context in a single image; effectively visualizes flow features (separation, convergence) without requiring animation. Limitations: Requires pre-computed or real-time pathline generation; filtering parameters (L{min}, N{min}) are critical and may require tuning to avoid visual clutter or loss of detail. When to use: When analyzing time-varying particle systems or flow fields where static visualization of motion is needed. When not to use: When precise quantitative tracking of individual particles over time is required, or when the volume density itself is the primary focus without need for motion cues. Trajectory Arrow Rendering was introduced by J. Chandler, H. Obermaier, and K. I. Joy in 2013 as part of their work on illustrative rendering of particle systems. It addresses the limitation of standard volume rendering, which only provides information about a single time step, making it difficult to track features in time-varying data. The method was applied to datasets such as the von Karman vortex street and jet flow fields to demonstrate its ability to reveal internal flow structures. Illustrative Rendering of Particle Systems, https://doi.org/10.2312/pe.vmv.vmv13.177-185, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Interaction
body: Interaction in volume rendering refers to the mechanisms by which users manipulate visualization parameters, data subsets, or view geometry to guide the rendering process and explore the dataset. It solves the problem of static, pre-computed images by allowing real-time exploration of complex volumetric data. This family is distinct from Classification and transfer functions (which map data to visual properties) and Illustrative and non-photorealistic volume rendering (which stylize the output); instead, it focuses on the control loop between the user and the renderer. It differs from Multi-field, vector and tensor volume visualization by addressing the general interaction paradigm rather than specific data types. Interaction operates via a feedback loop where user input modifies parameters that influence the rendering pipeline. These parameters typically fall into three categories: 1. Geometric/View Parameters: Camera position, orientation, and clipping planes (e.g., cropping). 2. Data/Selection Parameters: Subsets of the volume to render or modify (e.g., selection, brushing). 3. Visual/Mapping Parameters: Transfer function values, deformation fields, or LOD levels. Mathematically, interaction is often modeled as a function I: \mathcal{U} \rightarrow \mathcal{P}, where \mathcal{U} is the user input space and \mathcal{P} is the parameter space of the renderer. The renderer then computes the image V = R(D, P), where D is the data and P is the current parameter set. A key challenge in implementation is maintaining consistency across multiple coordinated views (e.g., linking selection in a 2D overview to the 3D volume), which requires a shared state management system. Cropping restricts volume rendering to a specific region of interest by cutting off the volume along planes parallel to its faces. It solves visual clutter and performance overhead by allowing users to see inside a volume without altering data. Unlike Clipping plane for volume suppression, which uses arbitrary-angle planes, cropping is strictly axis-aligned relative to the volume's object coordinates. It differs from Clipping by defining a bounded region of visibility via slabs rather than a half-space relative to the camera. The 3D Cursor is a direct interaction method that specifies X, Y, and Z coordinates to select or explore features within a volume dataset. It serves as a spatial probe, allowing users to identify internal structures without altering the geometry, distinct from clipping or deformation methods. Unlike 2D cursors, it operates in three dimensions, often visualized as intersecting planes or lines, and can be used for both local selection and action-at-a-distance targeting. Focus+Context Visualization via Deformation is an interactive technique that magnifies regions of interest within a high-resolution volume dataset while shrinking less important regions to fit within the original volume boundary. It solves the problem of inspecting detailed features on low-resolution displays by leveraging color gradient magnitudes derived from the user-specified transfer function to determine importance. Unlike binary focus/context methods or explicit lens-based techniques, this method provides continuous, varying extents of magnification for entire features without requiring explicit feature specification. Frustum Culling for Hierarchical Navigation is an interaction technique that reduces visual clutter and aids data exploration by selectively rendering nodes based on their position relative to the 3D viewing frustum. It sets itself apart from standard geometric culling by simultaneously managing the visual state of coordinated 2D views (overview maps and treemaps), ensuring that culling in 3D triggers specific contextual updates in 2D rather than simple invisibility. A framework for dynamic focus+context visualization in volume rendering that uses user interaction to guide enhancements of the visualization via animation modules. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by dynamically adapting the view and rendering style based on estimated user engagement rather than relying on pre-defined regions or static deformation fields. A technique to decompose a volume into a high-quality 'focus' region and a lower-quality 'context' region using depth-based clipping and early-z rejection, implemented in four rendering passes to maximize fragment shader discard efficiency. This family covers techniques for identifying specific subsets of volumetric data or rendering primitives for modification, deletion, or annotation, and for manipulating the spatial relationship between the selection and the scene. It solves the problem of precise user intent translation in 3D space, where traditional 2D screen-space interactions must be mapped to complex 3D structures. It is distinguished from Cropping by its focus on discrete object or primitive-level targeting rather than global volume partitioning, and from 3D Cursor by its broader scope including occlusion-based and state-based selection modes. A visualization approach combining volume rendering with glyphs and tensorlines to separate focus and context regions in stress tensor datasets. Context is visualized by volume rendering of scalar invariants, while focus regions (selected via user interaction) display explicit geometrical tensor representations. A system that monitors user interaction with virtual text to infer viewer intent and generate supporting graphics dynamically. Monitor user interaction with virtual text to infer intent. Generate supporting graphics dynamically based on user interaction according to a set of heuristics. Render surface models and display with OpenGL (extendable to voxel models). A technique allowing users to select a subset of nodes from the current LOD for operations like join or split, with dynamic linking across three views (rendering window, overview map, treemap). Brushing in the overview map allows joining or splitting all nodes at particular levels in the tree hierarchy. Brushing in the treemap allows changing resolutions of blocks in a local vicinity according to error values. Users click a node or specify a rectangular region to select multiple nodes simultaneously. Brushing in the rendering window allows direct interaction with the data set. Users identify 3D blocks of interest and link selection forward to other views. Provide sliders in the rendering window to specify brush coverage in data space as a 1D point, a 2D plane, or a 3D box. Allow brushing by specifying coverage in color space using two sliders in range [0, 1] to set minimum and maximum color values. Select all nodes in the current LOD within this color (and error) range. Use color space brushing to select nodes from a certain error range in a fuzzy manner, allowing resolution changes without degrading image quality too much. A rendering approach combining volume rendering with glyphs and tensorlines, steered by a mask volume created from diagram view selections. Create and update a mask volume through user selections (brushing) in the diagram views. Evaluate the mask volume to map selected features to geometrical tensor representations (glyphs, tensorlines) for focus regions. Visualize context regions using volume rendering. The concept of interaction in volume rendering evolved from early direct volume visualization (DVV) systems in the late 1980s and early 1990s, which primarily focused on rendering algorithms like ray casting and texture mapping. Early interaction was limited to camera navigation and simple transfer function adjustment. As datasets grew larger and more complex, the need for advanced interaction techniques such as cropping, focus+context, and hierarchical navigation became apparent. The integration of interaction with non-photorealistic illustration (NPR) and multi-view coordinated interfaces (like brushing and linking) has been a significant area of research, particularly in medical and scientific visualization. Key developments include the introduction of direct selection methods for splat-based rendering and the use of deformation fields for focus+context visualization. name: Cropping
head: Axis-Aligned Bounding Box Cropping, Axis-Aligned Cropping, SetCroppingRegionPlanes, Slab Cropping, Slab-based cropping
body: Cropping is an interaction technique that restricts volume rendering to a specific region of interest (ROI) by defining axis-aligned cut-planes along each spatial dimension. It solves the problem of visual clutter and performance overhead by rendering only the voxels within a defined rectilinear slab, thereby revealing internal structures without altering the underlying data. Unlike Clipping plane for volume suppression, which uses arbitrarily oriented planes to cut away portions of the volume, cropping is strictly axis-aligned relative to the volume's object coordinates. It differs from Clipping in that it defines a sub-volume for rendering rather than just a near/far boundary for projection correctness, and from Dynamic Clipping in Volume Rendering by being a static geometric constraint that can be updated interactively but is fundamentally defined by the intersection of axis-aligned slabs. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The volume dataset D with dimensions (Nx, Ny, Nz) and origin O. User-defined cropping parameters: six coordinates (x{min}, x{max}, y{min}, y{max}, z{min}, z{max}) defining the region of visibility. Output: A rendered image containing only the voxels satisfying the cropping constraints. Data Structures: The cropping region is stored as six floating-point or integer values representing the bounds in the volume's local coordinate system (object space). In implementations like VTK, this is managed via a vtkVolume mapper with a cropping flag and a set of plane coordinates. Steps: 1. Define Cropping Region: The user or application sets the six bounding coordinates. These define three slabs: Sx = \{ (x, y, z) \mid x{min} \le x \le x{max} \} Sy = \{ (x, y, z) \mid y{min} \le y \le y{max} \} Sz = \{ (x, y, z) \mid z{min} \le z \le z{max} \} 2. Combine Slabs: The region of visibility R is defined by the intersection of these slabs (standard cropping): R = Sx \cap Sy \cap Sz Alternatively, unions or inverses can be used to create complex visibility masks, but the standard ROI is the intersection. 3. Transform to World/Texture Space: If the volume is partitioned or transformed, the cropping planes must be transformed from object coordinates to the rendering space. For a subvolume with index (i, j, k) and dimensions (Nx, Ny, Nz) with overlap, the subvolume origin Origin{Sub} is calculated as: Origin{Sub} = (i(Nx - overlap), j(Ny - overlap), k(Nz - overlap)) The distance vector D{subj} from the subvolume origin to the cut-plane position D with normal N is: D{subj} = (D - Origin{Sub}) \cdot N 4. Enable Cropping: The rendering pipeline enables the cropping mode. In VTK, this is done by setting the cropping flag and the region planes: python mapper->SetCropping(1) mapper->SetCroppingRegionPlanes(xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax) mapper->SetCroppingMode(VTKCROPSUBVOLUME) 5. Ray Casting with Clipping: During ray casting, for each sample point P along the ray: Check if P lies within R. If P \in R, compute color and opacity as usual. If P \notin R, set opacity to 0 (or skip sampling entirely if the renderer supports early exit). Note: Cropping planes may fall at arbitrary voxel positions, not just integer grid indices. 6. Depth Handling: When using cutting planes, the depth texture from the DVR prepass is used to maintain correct depth order, ensuring that the cut surfaces are rendered correctly relative to the remaining volume. Parameters: Cropping Bounds: (x{min}, x{max}, y{min}, y{max}, z{min}, z{max}). Typical values depend on the dataset size and the desired ROI. Cropping Mode: Flag VTKCROPSUBVOLUME restricts rendering to the defined region. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Order: When cutting planes are active, standard depth buffering may fail if the entry/exit points are not correctly tracked. A front-face depth texture is often required to maintain correct depth order. Arbitrary Positions: Cropping planes can be placed at non-integer coordinates. The renderer must handle fractional voxel sampling correctly via interpolation or nearest-neighbor lookup. Invalid Regions: If x{min} > x{max}, the region is empty. Implementations should clamp or skip such regions. Boundary Artifacts: At the cropping boundaries, discontinuities may occur. Standard boundary handling techniques are required to mitigate artifacts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendercroppedvolume(volumedata, volumeorigin, volumespacing, cropbounds, cameraorigin, cameradirections, imagewidth, imageheight, stepsize): """ Render a volume with axis-aligned cropping. Args: volumedata: 3D array of voxel values. volumeorigin: (ox, oy, oz) in object coordinates. volumespacing: (sx, sy, sz) in object coordinates per voxel. cropbounds: (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax) in object coordinates. cameraorigin: (cx, cy, cz) in world coordinates. cameradirections: 2D array of direction vectors in world coordinates. imagewidth, imageheight: Output resolution. stepsize: Distance between samples in world coordinates. Returns: 2D array of RGBA tuples. """ # 1. Transform crop bounds to world coordinates wxmin = volumeorigin[0] + cropbounds[0] volumespacing[0] wxmax = volumeorigin[0] + cropbounds[1] volumespacing[0] wymin = volumeorigin[1] + cropbounds[2] volumespacing[1] wymax = volumeorigin[1] + cropbounds[3] volumespacing[1] wzmin = volumeorigin[2] + cropbounds[4] volumespacing[2] wzmax = volumeorigin[2] + cropbounds[5] volumespacing[2] image = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(imagewidth)] for in range(imageheight)] for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): rayo = cameraorigin rayd = cameradirections[y][x] # Normalize direction lend = (rayd[0]2 + rayd[1]2 + rayd[2]2)0.5 rayd = (rayd[0]/lend, rayd[1]/lend, rayd[2]/lend) # 2. Intersect ray with volume bounding box (world space) volmin = volumeorigin volmax = (volumeorigin[0] + volumedata.shape[0]volumespacing[0], volumeorigin[1] + volumedata.shape[1]volumespacing[1], volumeorigin[2] + volumedata.shape[2]volumespacing[2]) tmin, tmax = intersectrayaabb(rayo, rayd, volmin, volmax) if tmin is None or tmax is None: continue # 3. Intersect ray with crop bounds (world space) tcropmin, tcropmax = intersectrayaabb(rayo, rayd, (wxmin, wymin, wzmin), (wxmax, wymax, wzmax)) if tcropmin is None: continue # Ray misses crop region entirely # Clip ray segment to crop region tstart = max(tmin, tcropmin) tend = min(tmax, tcropmax) if tstart >= tend: continue # 4. Ray casting loop within crop region t = tstart acccolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) while t < tend: pos = (rayo[0] + trayd[0], rayo[1] + trayd[1], rayo[2] + trayd[2]) # Convert pos to voxel indices ix = int((pos[0] - volumeorigin[0]) / volumespacing[0]) iy = int((pos[1] - volumeorigin[1]) / volumespacing[1]) iz = int((pos[2] - volumeorigin[2]) / volumespacing[2]) # Clamp indices to volume bounds ix = max(0, min(volumedata.shape[0]-1, ix)) iy = max(0, min(volumedata.shape[1]-1, iy)) iz = max(0, min(volumedata.shape[2]-1, iz)) value = volumedata[ix][iy][iz] color, opacity = applytransferfunction(value) acccolor = compositergba(acccolor, color, opacity) if acccolor[3] >= 1.0: break t += stepsize image[y][x] = acccolor return image def intersectrayaabb(rayo, rayd, aabbmin, aabbmax): t1 = (aabbmin[0] - rayo[0]) / rayd[0] if rayd[0] != 0 else float('-inf') t2 = (aabbmax[0] - rayo[0]) / rayd[0] if rayd[0] != 0 else float('inf') t3 = (aabbmin[1] - rayo[1]) / rayd[1] if rayd[1] != 0 else float('-inf') t4 = (aabbmax[1] - rayo[1]) / rayd[1] if rayd[1] != 0 else float('inf') t5 = (aabbmin[2] - rayo[2]) / rayd[2] if rayd[2] != 0 else float('-inf') t6 = (aabbmax[2] - rayo[2]) / rayd[2] if rayd[2] != 0 else float('inf') tenter = max(min(t1, t2), min(t3, t4), min(t5, t6)) texit = min(max(t1, t2), max(t3, t4), max(t5, t6)) if tenter > texit: return None, None return tenter, texit def applytransferfunction(value): # Standard linear mapping for demonstration return (value, value, value, min(value, 1.0)) def compositergba(acc, color, opacity): r = acc[0] + color[0] opacity (1.0 - acc[3]) g = acc[1] + color[1] opacity (1.0 - acc[3]) b = acc[2] + color[2] opacity (1.0 - acc[3]) a = acc[3] + opacity (1.0 - acc[3]) return (r, g, b, a) A clipping plane for volume suppression uses one or more arbitrarily oriented planes to cut away selected portions of a volume dataset, uncovering internal details. Unlike Cropping, which restricts visibility to a rectilinear slab defined by planes parallel to the volume axes, clipping planes operate at arbitrary angles and can define a planar slice of finite thickness. It is distinct from Clipping in its specific application to volumetric data nodes where the interior of the clipped region retains data, often requiring capping of intersected geometry in medical contexts. Clipping is a technique to enable correct perspective projection in sliced-based volume rendering by defining a near clipping boundary relative to the viewpoint. It solves the problem of incorrect depth impression in inside views, where parallel projection fails to provide accurate spatial cues. Unlike general cropping Cropping which cuts along volume faces, this method clips against the camera's near/far planes and active clipping planes to ensure only relevant slabs are processed. Variance clipping is a history rectification technique used in Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) for volumetric rendering that constructs a tight bounding box for valid color values based on the statistical mean and variance of a neighborhood of samples. It solves the problem of ghosting artifacts during rapid illumination changes by adapting the clipping region to the local signal distribution, allowing it to reconstruct signals faster than fixed-bound methods. It sets itself apart from AABB Clamping and AABB Clipping by using a statistically derived, typically smaller, clipping region that reacts more precisely to changes, though at the cost of higher temporal instability. Clipped Cropping Region Planes is a preprocessing step that clamps user-defined axis-aligned cropping planes to the volume's bounding box, ensuring the resulting clipping region is valid and contained within the data bounds. It sets apart from its parent method, Cropping, by enforcing geometric validity before rendering, preventing undefined behavior when planes fall outside the dataset. Dynamic Clipping in Volume Rendering restricts the visualization to a specific region of interest (ROI) by applying six axis-aligned clipping planes (X min/max, Y min/max, Z min/max) that are updated in response to user interaction. Unlike static cropping masks which are pre-defined, this method allows the clipping boundaries to be adjusted interactively via a widget, converting index-space constraints into world-space planes for the renderer. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Clipping plane for volume suppression by explicitly managing the geometric transformation of clipping boundaries relative to the volume's coordinate system, and from Variance Clipping by operating on spatial extent rather than statistical data properties. A method to handle artifacts at clip boundaries when using pre-integrated volume rendering with low sampling rates, by mapping an opaque texture onto the clip geometry. It sets apart from Clipping and Clipped Cropping Region Planes by explicitly computing the optical contribution of the gap between the clipping surface and the first volume slice, rather than relying solely on depth buffering or simple suppression. Clipping geometry makes parts of the volume transparent. At the boundary of this geometry, the surface normal of the clipping geometry is used for illumination instead of the volume's gradient. This technique, described in Weiskopf et al., TVCG 2003, enhances the visual clarity of cutaway views by providing consistent lighting cues at the newly exposed surfaces. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of voxels in the cropped region. Cropping reduces the effective N by excluding voxels outside the ROI, thus improving performance proportionally to the volume of the ROI relative to the full volume. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for storing the six plane coordinates. Specific depth texture memory requirements are not given in the sources. Measured Performance: In VolumePro, cropping is described as an "easy way of specifying a rectilinear region of interest for rendering". In VTK, enabling VTKCROPSUBVOLUME allows the mapper to skip sampling outside the region, significantly speeding up rendering for large datasets with small ROIs. Strengths: Simple to implement; effective for focusing on specific features; reduces computational load; axis-aligned nature allows for efficient spatial partitioning and culling. Limitations: Cannot handle arbitrarily oriented cuts (use Clipping plane for volume suppression for that); may introduce artifacts at boundaries if not handled carefully; requires depth texture management for correct ordering when planes cut through the volume. When to use: When the user needs to inspect internal structures by removing outer layers; when performance is critical and the ROI is small; when the ROI is naturally axis-aligned (e.g., a specific organ in a medical scan aligned with the scanner axes). When not to use: When the ROI is oriented at an arbitrary angle; when the user needs to see the relationship between the cropped region and the rest of the volume in a single view without deformation (use Focus+Context Visualization via Deformation instead). Cropping originated as a fundamental interaction technique in volume visualization to allow users to "see inside" volumetric datasets. The VolumePro real-time ray-casting system popularized the concept of defining cropping regions using six registers for axis-aligned slabs, allowing for complex visibility masks through set operations (intersection, union, inverse). The technique is widely implemented in visualization libraries such as VTK (via SetCroppingRegionPlanes and VTKCROPSUBVOLUME) and is a core feature in educational tools like VolumeVisual, where it is synchronized with transfer function editing to help users understand volume rendering concepts. The patent US 6,407,737 B1 describes a method for rendering shear-warped partitioned volumes where cropping is specified by object coordinates and characterized by "slab" thickness. Clipping geometry illumination, a related technique for improving the visual quality of cropped views, was introduced by Weiskopf et al. in TVCG 2003. name: Clipping plane for volume suppression
head: Clip Plane, Clipping Planes, Cropping Widget Planes, Cut Planes, Volume Cropping via Clipping Planes
body: Clipping plane for volume suppression is a technique that removes specific regions of a volume dataset to reveal interior structures or resolve occlusion, typically by defining one or more arbitrary planes. Unlike Cropping, which restricts visibility to a rectilinear slab using axis-aligned planes, clipping planes allow for arbitrary orientation and can define complex cutaway views or smooth transitions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume dataset V (scalar or vector field), clipping plane definition (normal vector \mathbf{n} = (A, B, C) and distance parameter D from the origin, or two parallel planes for thickness), and optionally a falloff parameter D{\text{fallo}}. Output: Rendered image where voxels on the suppressed side of the plane have zero opacity, and voxels in the transition region have modified opacity. Data Structures: Clipping Plane: Defined by a normal vector \mathbf{n} = (A, B, C) and a distance parameter D from the origin. For a single plane, the implicit equation is Ax + By + Cz - D = 0. For a thick cut plane, two parallel planes are defined: Ax + By + Cz - D{\min} = 0 and Ax + By + Cz - D{\max} = 0, where D{\min} \neq D{\max}. The thickness is D{\max} - D{\min}. Widget State: In interactive systems, a frame-type widget reports the plane's orientation and position to the volume renderer. The widget can also query positions via mouse clicks on its surface. Steps: 1. Define Plane Geometry: For a 2D screen-based clipper, the plane is defined by the point of view (POV) and two user-selected screen points. Calculate the plane coefficients (A, B, C, D) from these three points. Alternatively, for a 3D widget, extract the normal and position from the widget's transformation matrix. 2. Calculate Signed Distance: For each voxel center \mathbf{v} = (x, y, z), calculate the signed distance D{\text{voxel}} to the plane: D{\text{voxel}} = \text{dot}(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{n}) - D where \mathbf{n} = (A, B, C) and D is the plane offset. For a thick cut plane, calculate distances to both D{\min} and D{\max}. 3. Determine Visibility and Opacity: Binary Suppression: If D{\text{voxel}} < 0 (or outside the slab defined by D{\min} and D{\max}), set opacity \alpha = 0. Smooth Transition: If a falloff parameter D{\text{fallo}} is specified: Outside the cut plane (suppressed side): \alpha = 0. In the transition region (width D{\text{fallo}}): Multiply the shading-stage opacity \alpha{\text{shade}} by a correction factor f that increases linearly from 0 to 1. In the interior (visible side): \alpha = \alpha{\text{shade}}. 4. Render: Render the clipped volume using a standard volume rendering algorithm (e.g., ray casting). Render the 3D plane widget in a second pass to visualize the clipping boundary. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def clipvolume(volume, planenormal, planeoffset, falloffwidth=0.0): # planenormal: (A, B, C), planeoffset: D clippedvolume = emptylike(volume) for voxel in volume: dist = dot(voxel.coords, planenormal) - planeoffset if dist < 0: clippedvolume[voxel] = 0.0 elif falloffwidth > 0 and dist < falloffwidth: factor = dist / falloffwidth clippedvolume[voxel] = voxel.opacity factor else: clippedvolume[voxel] = voxel.opacity return clippedvolume Parameters: D{\text{fallo}}: Width of the transition region from full opacity to none. Typical value: 5 voxels. Single vs. Multiple Planes: Most systems support a single clipping plane as a compromise between flexibility and usability. VolumePro supports a single cut plane. SFP renderer supports up to 6 cutting planes simultaneously. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Capping Geometry: In complex scenarios involving both polygonal geometry and volume data, clipped volume data always contains data inside the clipped region, whereas clipped polygonal objects may be empty. Medical applications often expect intersected 3D geometry to be capped. Orientation Perception: Users may find it confusing to perceive volume orientation and clipping plane location without additional cues like bounding boxes or stippled lines. Coordinate Systems: Some implementations use normalized coordinates (0,0,0) to (1,1,1) with the volume box center at (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) rather than world-space coordinates. This method enables interactive, selective suppression of volume datasets using an axis-aligned Clipping Cube and an arbitrary Cutting Plane, implemented via client-side widgets controlling server-side RTVR clipping capabilities. It distinguishes itself from standard polygon clipping by supporting non-uniform cube resizing via corner spheres and rendering the context region outside the cube as non-photorealistic contours rather than transparent geometry. Virtual Resection is a technique for selectively suppressing portions of a volume dataset to resolve occlusion problems, particularly in medical imaging where internal structures (e.g., pulmonary nodules) are hidden by surrounding tissue (e.g., lung parenchyma). It generates a deformable clipping plane or mask from user-defined resection lines on the organ's surface, allowing the user to cut away specific regions while preserving the texture of the remaining surface. Unlike standard clipping planes that cut the entire volume uniformly, this method enables complex, arbitrary-shaped cutaways centered on regions of interest. Cuts the sample after it has been played for x ticks. An interaction mode where a clipping plane slice is textured with map coordinates to help users understand the relationship between spatial and TF domains. The user rotates and translates the volume and places a clipping plane. Voxels on the clipping plane are sampled, and their map coordinates are mapped to color channels (e.g., x,y to Red,Green for Kohonen maps; x,y,z to RGB for Spherical maps). The textured slice is blended with the rendered volume using user-controlled opacity. The user can click on the clipping plane to set the Gaussian TF peak to the map coordinates of the pointed voxel, with a white cross displayed in the map representation corresponding to the mouse position. A visualization technique for superimposed anatomical and physiological data, displaying physiological data only within a known region of interest (e.g., inside the lung) and on a user-controlled cutting plane surface. The steps are: 1. Identify the region of interest. 2. Display physiological data only within this region. 3. Render the data as grey-scale on the surface exposed by the user-controlled cutting plane. Applying clipping planes to Maximum Intensity Projection of a Head CT dataset to extract interesting features by slicing the volume. The volume is clipped in half by removing half the face with a vertical plane. This highlights regions of interest unable to be captured in the original visualization without clipping. A depth-based clipping approach analyzing depth information of the cutting geometry to decide which part of the volume to clip. A method allowing the user to modify the appearance of elements in the clipped region via a rigging system defining how the cutaway affects each structure. A feature allowing the user to cut the volume layer by layer, excluding internal parts from being cut. Virtual planes that cut away parts of the image to allow viewing inside the object. Up to 6 cutting planes can be added simultaneously, and each cutting plane can be placed in an arbitrary position and orientation. A visualization method for scalar fields that renders a 2D slice of the data at a user-specified position, represented by a mesh in a symbolic box. A visualization method where the user holds and moves a small rectangle plane in the CAVE room. The plane color shows the distribution of a selected scalar field on the slice. It follows wand motion. Steps: 1. User selects 'Orthoslicer' and presses wand button, causing a box-shaped object symbolizing the data space to appear. 2. A mesh inside the box designates the current slice position. 3. User moves the wand in the desired direction while pressing the button; the mesh moves in accord with the wand motion. 4. When the button is released, render the scalar data distribution at the specified slice position. Mode 1: The normal vector of the plane is always perpendicular to the wand direction. Mode 2: The normal vector of the plane is always perpendicular to a specified vector field. Pitfall: Near a 'hot spot' where vector and scalar fields change sharply, the plane exhibits dynamic motion as the user slowly moves the wand around it. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels or samples, as each sample must be tested against the plane equation. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for plane coefficients, plus storage for the volume dataset. Performance: Real-time performance is achievable on modern GPUs using fragment shaders for distance calculation and opacity masking. VolumePro supports real-time ray-casting with a single cut plane. Strengths: Supports smooth transitions for better visual integration. Limitations: Single plane limits complex cutaway shapes unless combined with other techniques; binary suppression can create harsh edges without falloff. When to Use: When the user needs to remove bulk tissue or outer structures to see embedded details (e.g., chest wall removal for injection site visualization). When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The VolumePro system, developed in the late 1990s, introduced a single cut plane with smooth falloff capabilities. The X3D standard has supported clipping planes for volumetric data since version 3.2, though it notes ambiguities in capping intersected geometry. Interactive systems like Simian introduced frame-type widgets for clipping plane manipulation, allowing users to query positions and blend slices. More recent approaches include depth-based clipping for cutaway views and spatial domain interactions for transfer function design. name: Clipping Cube and Cutting Plane Interaction
head: Focus-plus-context clipping
body: This method enables interactive, selective suppression of volume datasets using an axis-aligned Clipping Cube and an arbitrary Cutting Plane, implemented via client-side widgets controlling server-side RTVR clipping capabilities. It distinguishes itself from standard polygon clipping by supporting non-uniform cube resizing via corner spheres and rendering the context region outside the cube as non-photorealistic contours rather than transparent geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset, a 3D input device (pen and PIP pad), and a rendering engine supporting RTVR axis-aligned and oblique clipping planes. Output: A rendered view where the interior of the clipping cube (or correct side of the cutting plane) is rendered as a solid surface (focus) and the exterior is rendered as invisible, transparent, or NPR contours (context), or where a single cutting plane isolates a specific slice. Data Structures: 1. Clipping Cube Widget: Represented as a wireframe cube with spheres at its corners, remaining axis-aligned, with spheres serving as interaction handles. 2. Cutting Plane: Defined by an arbitrary alignment, acting like a single face of the clipping cube, rendered as a visual indicator during placement. Parameters: Clipping Mode: Determines the behavior of the volume outside the clipping cube, supporting "invisible" (hard clip), "transparent", or "NPR" (focus-plus-context). Interaction Mode: Switches the PIP pad between "moving object", "cutting plane", and "clipping cube" modes. Steps: 1. Initialize Clipping Cube: The system renders a wireframe cube with spheres at the corners, which light up when the pen enters their trigger volume. 2. Resize Clipping Cube: The user drags a lit sphere, causing the cube to resize non-uniformly while maintaining its axis-aligned orientation, updating the six face planes. 3. Place Cutting Plane: The user switches the PIP pad to "cutting" mode, where the pad itself acts as the cutting plane, moves the pad to position the plane through the volume, and presses the second pen button to freeze the plane in place. The primary pen button is reserved for moving the volume object, enabling two-handed interaction (one hand moves the plane via the pad, the other moves the object via the pen). 4. Render Focus and Context: The region inside the clipping cube (or on the correct side of the cutting plane) is rendered using standard surface shading, while the region outside is rendered using Non-Photorealistic Rendering (NPR) contours or other specified modes. Selected segmented objects can be excluded from the clipping effect, remaining shaded even when intersected by the clipping boundaries. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updateinteraction(pen, pad, cube, plane, mode): if mode == "CLIPPINGCUBE": for i, sphere in enumerate(cube.spheres): if distance(pen.position, sphere.center) <= sphere.radius: sphere.highlight = True if pen.isdragging(): cube.spheres[i].center = pen.position cube.updateaxisalignedbounds() else: sphere.highlight = False elif mode == "CUTTINGPLANE": plane.position = pad.position plane.normal = pad.normal if pen.secondbuttonpressed: mode = "CLIPPINGCUBE" return mode def computeclippingplanes(cube, plane): planes = [] for i in range(6): planes.append(cube.getfaceplane(i)) planes.append(plane) return planes def rendervolume(clippingplanes, outsidemode): # Apply clipping planes to volume data clippeddata = applyplanestovolume(clippingplanes) # Render inside region as surface rendersurface(clippeddata, region="inside") # Render outside region according to mode if outsidemode == "NPRCONTOURS": rendernprcontours(clippeddata, region="outside") elif outsidemode == "INVISIBLE": pass elif outsidemode == "TRANSPARENT": rendertransparent(clippeddata, region="outside") Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion: The combination of image-based rendering with polygon-based interaction widgets yields occlusion problems. Convoluted Objects: For complex structures like vessels, distinguishing cut parts from the context can be difficult, making the NPR context rendering particularly valuable for clarity. This variant specifically utilizes Non-Photorealistic Rendering (NPR) for the context region. It isolates a focus region using a clipping cube widget (rendered as a surface) while rendering the context outside the cube as non-photorealistic contours. This approach is chosen when the user needs to see the structural outline of the clipped volume without the visual clutter of full volume rendering. The clipping cube widget is resizable via corner dragging and defines the bounded region for clipping. Selected segmented objects can be excluded from clipping, remaining shaded even when covered by the clipping planes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows intuitive, direct manipulation of the clipping region. Two-handed interaction (pad for plane, pen for object) improves workflow. NPR context reduces visual clutter. Limitations: The clipping cube is axis-aligned, limiting its orientation flexibility. The cutting plane is single-sided. Stereoscopic occlusion can be problematic with image-based rendering and polygon widgets. When to use: When exploring internal structures of a volume while needing to see the surrounding context's shape. This method was developed for distributed software-based volume visualization in a virtual environment. It builds on earlier focus-plus-context work [FG98] and integrates with RTVR capabilities for axis-aligned and oblique clipping. The approach was presented at the Eurographics conference in 2005. name: Virtual Resection
head: Deformable Clipping Plane, Resection via Clipping Plane, Selective Volume Clipping, Selective Volume Clipping in Resection of Lung Cancer
body:
Virtual Resection is a technique for selectively suppressing portions of a volume dataset to resolve occlusion problems, particularly in medical imaging where internal structures (e.g., pulmonary nodules) are hidden by surrounding tissue (e.g., lung parenchyma). It generates a deformable clipping plane or mask from user-defined resection lines on the organ's surface, allowing the user to cut away specific regions while preserving the texture of the remaining surface. Unlike standard clipping planes that cut the entire volume uniformly, this method enables complex, arbitrary-shaped cutaways centered on regions of interest. The method operates in two distinct contexts found in the literature: a general deformable plane manipulation for anatomical models and a specific computational framework for lung nodule visualization. The implementation details below describe the framework, as it provides a complete algorithmic pipeline. Input: A 3D volume dataset V (e.g., chest CT images) containing scalar values f(x, y, z). Output: A volume rendering where voxels inside a user-defined closed curve (but outside the nodule) are suppressed, revealing internal structures. 1. Feature Space Histogram: A 2D histogram where the horizontal axis represents gray scale intensity and the vertical axis represents gradient magnitude 
abla f(x, y, z). 2. Voxel Set \PhiU: A set of voxels selected from the volume based on a region U in the feature space. 3. Stack H: A stack data structure used for connected component tracing. 4. Binary Mask Image: A 2D image with the same dimensions as the screen rendering window, representing the inside/outside status of the closed curve. The process involves segmentation, mask generation, and clipping. 1. Segment Lungs via 2D Feature Space: Define the 2D feature space with coordinates (g, 
abla g), where g is gray scale and 
abla g is gradient magnitude. Identify region R1 as homogeneous regions with low gray gradient, corresponding to lung tissue. Define the selection region U = R1. Determine the initial voxel set \PhiU using Equation 1 (not explicitly provided in sources, but defined as the set of voxels satisfying the condition for U). 2. Extract Connected Lung Volume: Mark all voxels in \PhiU as not-visited. Select a not-visited voxel from \PhiU as a seed. Mark it visited and push it onto stack H. While H is not empty: 1. Pop a voxel v from H. 2. Check all voxels in the 18-neighborhood of v. 3. For each neighbor n: If n 
otin \PhiU or n is already visited, skip. If n \in \PhiU and not-visited, push n to H and mark n as visited. The result is the extracted connected lung volume. 3. Segment Pulmonary Nodules: Apply a region growing method to segment nodules from the lung tissue. 4. Generate Deformable Clipping Mask: Project voxels from the volume coordinate system onto the screen frame. The user draws discontinuous points on the screen around the region of interest (e.g., the nodule). Fit these points using a B-Spline to generate a closed curve. Create a binary mask image of the same size as the screen window. Voxels inside the closed curve are marked as inside, and those outside are marked as outside. 5. Selective Clipping: For each voxel in the volume: Project the voxel to the screen. If the voxel is inside the closed curve AND is part of the lung tissue (not the nodule), suppress it (clip it). Otherwise, retain it for rendering. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def virtualresection(volumedata, screenwindowsize): """ volumedata: 3D array of scalar values f(x,y,z) screenwindowsize: tuple (width, height) of the rendering window """ # Step 1: Segment Lungs # Define 2D feature space: horizontal=gray scale, vertical=gradient magnitude # Identify region R1 (low gray gradient) # Determine voxel set PhiU based on region U = R1 PhiU = segmentlungs2dfeaturespace(volumedata) # Step 2: Extract Connected Lung Volume # Initialize visited status for all voxels in PhiU visited = {v: False for v in PhiU} stackH = [] # Select a seed voxel from PhiU (user interaction or default) seedvoxel = selectseedvoxel(PhiU) visited[seedvoxel] = True stackH.append(seedvoxel) while stackH: currentvoxel = stackH.pop() # Check 18-neighborhood neighbors = get18neighbors(currentvoxel) for neighbor in neighbors: if neighbor in PhiU and not visited[neighbor]: visited[neighbor] = True stackH.append(neighbor) connectedlungvolume = set(visited.keys()) # Step 3: Segment Nodules nodules = segmentnodulesregiongrowing(volumedata, connectedlungvolume) # Step 4: Generate Mask # User draws points on screen userpoints = getuserdrawnpoints() # Fit B-Spline to create closed curve closedcurve = fitbspline(userpoints) # Create binary mask binarymask = createbinarymask(closedcurve, screenwindowsize) # Step 5: Clip renderedvolume = [] for voxel in volumedata: screenpos = projecttoscreen(voxel) insidecurve = isinsidemask(screenpos, binarymask) islungtissue = voxel in connectedlungvolume isnodule = voxel in nodules # Clip lung tissue inside the curve, preserve nodules and outside tissue if insidecurve and islungtissue and not isnodule: continue # Suppress voxel else: renderedvolume.append(voxel) return renderedvolume B-Spline Fit: Requires a sufficient number of discontinuous points to form a stable closed curve. 18-Neighbor Connectivity: The tracing algorithm uses 18-connectivity, which is specific to 3D voxel grids. Occlusion: The primary edge case addressed is the occlusion of nodules by lung tissue, which semi-transparent visualization fails to resolve due to loss of surface texture. Strengths: Solves the occlusion problem in chest CT images while preserving the texture of the pulmonary tongue on the lung surface, which is lost in semi-transparent visualization. Allows selective cutting layer by layer, excluding internal parts from being cut. Limitations: Requires initial segmentation of lungs and nodules, which adds computational overhead. The deformable plane is manipulated via mouse interaction, which may be less precise than parametric clipping planes for complex geometries. Performance: Not given in the sources. When to use: When visualizing internal structures (like nodules) hidden within a larger organ (like lungs) where surface texture preservation is critical. Virtual Resection was introduced by Konrad-Verse et al.. It is also referred to as Selective Volume Clipping in the context of lung cancer resection visualization. The method addresses the limitations of standard clipping planes and semi-transparent rendering in medical visualization. name: Clipping
head: Front Clipping for Perspective Projection, Near-plane clipping, Viewpoint-relative slab clipping
body: Clipping is a technique to enable correct perspective projection in sliced-based volume rendering by defining a near clipping boundary relative to the viewpoint. It solves the problem of incorrect depth impression in inside views, where parallel projection fails to provide accurate spatial cues. Unlike general cropping Cropping which cuts along volume faces, this method clips against the camera's near/far planes and active clipping planes to ensure only relevant slabs are processed. Inputs and outputs: Inputs: ren: A vtkRenderer pointer providing camera and clipping plane state. worldBounds[6]: A double array containing the unclipped world-space bounding box coordinates. vol: A vtkVolume pointer providing volume transformation and clipping state. Outputs: A set of slabs/primitives that pass the clipping tests against the camera near/far planes and active clipping planes. Data structures: Bounding Box: Represented as worldBounds[6], a double array containing the unclipped world-space bounding box coordinates. Clipping Planes: Defined by the renderer's state (ren). Steps: 1. Retrieve the camera state and active clipping planes from ren, and the unclipped world-space bounding box from worldBounds[6]. 2. Clip the volume bounding box against all active clipping planes and the camera near/far planes. 3. The user specifies the distance from the viewpoint to the first slab to be processed. 4. Only slabs beyond this defined distance are rendered, ensuring correct depth impression for inside views. Formulas: Let d{\text{slab}} be the distance from the viewpoint to a slab. The slab is processed if d{\text{slab}} \ge d{\text{first}}, where d{\text{first}} is the user-specified distance to the first slab. Parameters: ren: vtkRenderer pointer. worldBounds[6]: Double array of unclipped world-space bounding box coordinates. vol: vtkVolume pointer. Edge cases and pitfalls: Inside Views: Without front clipping, perspective projection artifacts occur because slabs behind the viewpoint might be rendered or ordered incorrectly. Precision: Not given in the sources. Degenerate Input: Not given in the sources. Definition: A clipping operator that keeps or drops each Gaussian primitive entirely based on whether its center lies within the half-space defined by the clip plane. It adds no per-pixel attenuation factor. Steps: For each primitive, compute the dot product of the clip normal \mathbf{n} and the primitive mean \boldsymbol{\mu}. If \mathbf{n}^\top \boldsymbol{\mu} \le \tau, keep the primitive; otherwise, drop it. Pitfalls: Primitives straddling the clip plane either overshoot (if kept) or vanish (if dropped), producing a center-quantized boundary artifact as the plane sweeps. The decision is non-differentiable. Comparison: Unlike Moment-Matched (MM) and analytic operators, Hard Cull has no gradient through its binary decision and updates only kept primitives. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and limitations: Strengths: Enables correct perspective projection for inside views, which is mandatory for accurate depth impression. Limitations: Does not handle partial occlusion or attenuation at the clipping boundary, leading to artifacts if primitives straddle the plane. When to use it and when not: Use when correct perspective projection is required, especially for inside views. Do not use when smooth attenuation at the clipping boundary is needed, in which case Moment-Matched or analytic clipping is preferred. Origin: The concept of front clipping for perspective projection was introduced to address limitations in sliced-based volume rendering systems like VolumePro, which lacked perspective projection support. The term "Front Clipping" was used in the Shear-Warp Factorization Volume Rendering System to solve the problem of incorrect depth impression in inside views. History and development: Early volume rendering systems like VolumePro supported only parallel projection and back-to-front compositing. The SWF VRS improved this by introducing perspective projection and front clipping. Modern implementations, such as those in VTK, integrate clipping with camera and volume state to handle complex scenes. In the context of Gaussian Splatting, Hard Cull was isolated as a binary operator to analyze the effects of clipping without learned components. Where it is used: Medical volume rendering, where inside views are common. General volume rendering systems that support perspective projection. Gaussian Splatting for volume rendering, as a baseline clipping operator. name: Variance Clipping
head: Local Variance
body: Variance clipping is a history rectification technique used in temporal anti-aliasing for volumetric rendering that constructs a tight bounding box for valid history samples based on the statistical distribution (mean and variance) of colors in the current frame's neighborhood. It solves the problem of ghosting artifacts by discarding history samples that fall outside the statistically probable range of current-frame colors, adapting more quickly to sudden illumination changes than simple extent-based clipping. It extends the concept of clipping against the current frame color extent by relying on the statistical distribution of values in the neighborhood to produce a smaller clipping region. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N color samples \{ci\}{i=1}^N from the current frame's neighborhood. Input: A user-defined parameter \gamma (gamma) controlling the clipping strength. Output: A clipping interval [c{min}, c{max}] for each color component. Data Structures: ci: A vector of color values (e.g., RGB) for the i-th sample. N: The number of samples in the neighborhood. \mu: The sample mean vector. \sigma: The sample standard deviation vector. Steps: 1. Compute the first sample moment m1 by summing all color vectors component-wise: m1 = \sum{i=1}^N ci \quad (2.3) 2. Compute the second sample moment m2 by summing the squared color vectors component-wise: m2 = \sum{i=1}^N ci^2 \quad (2.4) 3. Calculate the sample mean \mu by dividing m1 by N component-wise: \mu = \frac{1}{N}m1 \quad (2.5) 4. Calculate the sample standard deviation \sigma component-wise: \sigma = \sqrt{\left| \frac{1}{N} m2 - \mu^2 \right|} \quad (2.6) The absolute value is taken to avoid negative values caused by floating-point inaccuracies. 5. Construct the min-max clipping interval using the user-defined parameter \gamma: c{min} = \mu - \gamma \sigma \quad (2.7) c{max} = \mu + \gamma \sigma \quad (2.8) Parameters: \gamma (gamma): A user-defined parameter that controls the size of the clipping box and therefore the strength of clipping. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Floating-point inaccuracies can lead to negative values under the square root in the standard deviation calculation; the absolute value operation mitigates this. Variance clipping exhibits the highest Temporal Instability (TI) relative to the baseline EMA among tested techniques, making it prone to flickering in static scenes. Performing history rectification directly in RGB color space can produce color-related artifacts because RGB channels are highly correlated, leading to poorly aligned bounding boxes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def varianceclipping(samples, gamma): """ Compute variance-based clipping bounds for a set of color samples. Args: samples: List of color vectors (e.g., [r, g, b]), shape (N, 3). gamma: User-defined parameter controlling clipping strength. Returns: cmin: Lower bound vector. cmax: Upper bound vector. """ N = len(samples) if N == 0: raise ValueError("No samples provided") # Step 1: First sample moment m1 = sum(ci) m1 = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for c in samples: for k in range(3): m1[k] += c[k] # Step 2: Second sample moment m2 = sum(ci^2) m2 = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for c in samples: for k in range(3): m2[k] += c[k] c[k] # Step 3: Sample mean mu = (1/N) m1 mu = [m1[k] / N for k in range(3)] # Step 4: Standard deviation sigma = sqrt(|(1/N) m2 - mu^2|) sigma = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for k in range(3): varianceterm = (m2[k] / N) - (mu[k] mu[k]) sigma[k] = (abs(varianceterm) 0.5) # Step 5: Clipping interval cmin = [mu[k] - gamma sigma[k] for k in range(3)] cmax = [mu[k] + gamma sigma[k] for k in range(3)] return cmin, cmax A variant that transforms reprojected historical color data into a luminance-chrominance color space (YCoCg or YCrCb) before applying bounding-box clipping. It sets itself apart by decoupling luminance and chrominance to reduce chroma-related ghosting, which is a known issue when applying variance clipping directly in RGB space. Choose this when color bleeding artifacts are prominent due to high channel correlation. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of samples in the neighborhood, as it requires a single pass to compute sums and squared sums. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space if computed incrementally, or O(N) if storing all samples. Measured Performance: In a step response scenario (sudden illumination change), variance clipping produced the lowest RMSE (0.002977) compared to AABB Clamp/Clip (0.003136) and Baseline EMA (0.009724), indicating it is the best at reconstructing the signal when light is quickly introduced. However, it exhibits the highest Temporal Instability (TI), with a 190.23% increase in TI P95 relative to the baseline. Strengths: Tighter bounds allow the algorithm to adapt to changes much more quickly and precisely than extent-based methods. It operates entirely on current-frame data, making it easier to implement than methods requiring historical data analysis. Limitations: High temporal instability can cause flickering. Direct application in RGB space leads to color artifacts due to channel correlation. When to use: When rapid adaptation to illumination changes is prioritized over stability, or when used in conjunction with color space transformations like YCoCg to mitigate color artifacts. When not to use: In static scenes where temporal stability is critical, or if RGB color space artifacts are unacceptable without rectification. Variance clipping was introduced as a history rectification technique for temporal anti-aliasing in volumetric rendering. It extends the concept of clipping against the current frame color extent by relying on the statistical distribution of values in the neighborhood. The method was evaluated in the context of real-time froxel-based volumetric rendering, where it was found to be effective at reducing ghosting artifacts during dynamic scenes. The term "Local Variance" is also used in the context of volume visualization to describe the variance in the neighborhood of a voxel, which is used to distinguish tissues based on spatial coherence, such as removing CT streaking artifacts by selecting high-variance voxels.
