name: YCoCg Color Space Rectification
head: Color Space Selection for History Rectification, YCrCb Rectification
body: YCoCg Color Space Rectification is a history rectification method used in temporal anti-aliasing (TAA) for volumetric rendering that transforms reprojected historical color data into a luminance-chrominance color space (specifically YCoCg or YCrCb) before applying bounding-box clipping. It solves the problem of temporal color bleeding artifacts caused by high correlation between RGB channels, which leads to poorly aligned bounding boxes and stale color information persisting across frames. It sets itself apart from its parent method, Variance Clipping, by operating on a fixed geometric bounding box oriented along the luminance axis rather than a statistical distribution, and from its sibling AABB Clamping by explicitly decoupling luminance and chrominance to reduce chroma-related ghosting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Reprojected historical color sample h{reprojected} (RGB vector), current frame neighborhood samples (RGB vectors). Output: Rectified historical color sample h{clipped} (RGB vector). Data Structures: Color vectors are 3-element arrays/tuples. YCoCg space: [Y, Co, Cg]^T. YCrCb space: [Y, Cr, Cb]^T. Steps: 1. Transform to Luminance-Chrominance Space: Convert the reprojected historical color h{reprojected} and the current frame neighborhood samples from RGB to the chosen color space (YCoCg or YCrCb). 2. Define Bounding Box: Determine the minimum and maximum values for each component (Y, Co, Cg or Y, Cr, Cb) across the current frame's neighborhood samples. This creates an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) in the transformed space. 3. Clamp History: Clamp each component of the transformed historical sample h{reprojected} to the corresponding min/max bounds of the AABB. 4. Transform Back to RGB: Convert the clamped historical sample back to RGB space to produce h{clipped}. Formulas: RGB to YCoCg Transform: \begin{bmatrix} Y \\ Co \\ Cg \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{4} & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{1}{2} & 0 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ -\frac{1}{4} & \frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{4} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} R \\ G \\ B \end{bmatrix} Inverse YCoCg to RGB Transform: \begin{bmatrix} R \\ G \\ B \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} Y \\ Co \\ Cg \end{bmatrix} RGB to YCrCb Transform: \begin{bmatrix} Y \\ Cr \\ Cb \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.299 & 0.587 & 0.114 \\ -0.5 & -0.4187 & 0.0813 \\ -0.1687 & -0.3313 & -0.5 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} R \\ G \\ B \end{bmatrix} Inverse YCrCb to RGB Transform: \begin{bmatrix} R \\ G \\ B \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1.402 & 0 \\ 1 & -0.714 & -0.344 \\ 1 & 0 & 1.772 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} Y \\ Cr \\ Cb \end{bmatrix} Parameters: Color Space Selection: YCoCg or YCrCb. YCoCg is preferred for better decorrelation of luminance and chrominance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Color-Related Artifacts in RGB: Performing history rectification directly in RGB space causes the AABB to be poorly aligned with the actual distribution of color samples because RGB channels are highly correlated, leading to ghosting artifacts. Temporal Color Bleeding: In RGB space, abrupt color changes (e.g., a light turning from red to yellow) cause stale color information to bleed into subsequent frames, taking many frames to converge. Luminance Artifacts: While YCoCg and YCrCb reduce chrominance bleeding, they can increase luminance artifacts. For example, when color shifts from green to blue, stale luminance information in the green channel may bleed into the next frame, causing excess luminance around the light source. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rectifyhistoryycocg(hreprojectedrgb, neighborhoodsamplesrgb): """ Rectifies historical color using YCoCg color space rectification. Args: hreprojectedrgb: Tuple (R, G, B) of the reprojected historical sample. neighborhoodsamplesrgb: List of tuples [(R, G, B),...] of current frame neighborhood samples. Returns: Tuple (R, G, B) of the rectified historical sample. """ # Step 1: Transform historical sample to YCoCg hy, hco, hcg = rgbtoycocg(hreprojectedrgb) # Step 2: Transform neighborhood samples to YCoCg and find bounds # Initialize bounds with extreme values ymin, ymax = float('inf'), float('-inf') comin, comax = float('inf'), float('-inf') cgmin, cgmax = float('inf'), float('-inf') for samplergb in neighborhoodsamplesrgb: y, co, cg = rgbtoycocg(samplergb) # Update bounds if y < ymin: ymin = y if y > ymax: ymax = y if co < comin: comin = co if co > comax: comax = co if cg < cgmin: cgmin = cg if cg > cgmax: cgmax = cg # Step 3: Clamp historical sample components to bounds yclamped = max(ymin, min(ymax, hy)) coclamped = max(comin, min(comax, hco)) cgclamped = max(cgmin, min(cgmax, hcg)) # Step 4: Transform back to RGB hclippedrgb = ycocgtorgb(yclamped, coclamped, cgclamped) return hclippedrgb def rgbtoycocg(rgb): r, g, b = rgb y = 0.25 r + 0.5 g + 0.25 b co = 0.5 r + 0.0 g - 0.5 b cg = -0.25 r + 0.5 g - 0.25 b return (y, co, cg) def ycocgtorgb(ycocg): y, co, cg = ycocg r = 1.0 y + 1.0 co - 1.0 cg g = 1.0 y + 0.0 co + 1.0 cg b = 1.0 y - 1.0 co - 1.0 cg return (r, g, b) AABB Clamping is a history rectification method that individually limits each channel of the reprojected historical color to the minimum and maximum values of the current frame's neighborhood samples. It builds on YCoCg Color Space Rectification, which transforms colors into a luminance-chrominance space before applying rectification. What sets it apart from its siblings and nearest alternatives is its use of a simple Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) approximation constructed from per-channel minimum and maximum values, whereas variants like Variance Clipping use statistical distributions to define bounds. Color Space Conversion for TAA is a variant that involves transforming volumetric samples into a specific color space (RGB, YCoCg, or YCrCb) before blending, then transforming back to RGB for storage. It is evaluated as a general approach to handling color space selection in TAA for volumetric rendering, with YCoCg and YCrCb shown to reduce chrominance artifacts compared to RGB. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of neighborhood samples, due to the linear transformation and min/max operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per sample for storing transformed values and bounds. Measured Performance: In tests involving abrupt color changes (e.g., spot light changing from red to yellow), YCoCg and YCrCb significantly reduced temporal color bleeding artifacts compared to RGB, as measured by SSIM scores over time. However, these color spaces introduced increased luminance artifacts during specific color transitions (e.g., green to blue). Strengths: Reduces color-related ghosting and chrominance bleeding by decoupling luminance and chrominance. YCoCg provides better decorrelation than YCrCb. Limitations: Can introduce luminance artifacts when chrominance changes rapidly. Requires additional transform operations. When to Use: When temporal color bleeding is a prominent issue, especially with high-contrast color changes. When Not to Use: When luminance stability is critical during rapid color shifts, or when computational overhead of color space transforms is prohibitive. YCoCg Color Space Rectification originated in the context of temporal anti-aliasing for real-time froxel-based volumetric rendering. It was explored as an improvement over RGB-space history rectification to mitigate color-related artifacts. The method leverages the properties of luminance-chrominance color spaces, specifically YCoCg and YCrCb, to align the history rectification bounding box with the direction of luma, which typically has high local contrast. The approach was evaluated in a study on advances in volumetric temporal anti-aliasing, comparing RGB, YCoCg, and YCrCb color spaces in terms of artifact reduction and convergence speed. name: AABB Clamping
head: AABB Clamping History Rectification
body: AABB Clamping is a history rectification method that individually limits each channel of the reprojected historical color to the minimum and maximum values of the current frame's neighborhood samples. It builds on YCoCg Color Space Rectification, which transforms colors into a luminance-chrominance space before applying rectification. What sets it apart from its siblings and nearest alternatives is its use of a simple Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) approximation constructed from per-channel minimum and maximum values, whereas variants like Variance Clipping use statistical distributions to define bounds. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The reprojected historical color ch, and a set of N current-frame neighborhood samples ci \in \mathbb{R}^k (where k is the number of channels, e.g., 3 or 4). Output: The rectified color cr. Data Structures: AABB Bounds: Two vectors, c{min} and c{max}, each of size k. c{min}[j] = \min{i=1..N}(ci[j]) for each channel j. c{max}[j] = \max{i=1..N}(ci[j]) for each channel j. Steps: 1. Construct AABB: Compute the component-wise minimum and maximum across all current-frame neighborhood samples to define the bounding box bounds c{min} and c{max}. 2. Clamp: For each channel j of the historical color ch, clamp the value between the corresponding bounds c{min}[j] and c{max}[j]. Formula: The rectified color cr is obtained by clamping ch component-wise: cr = \min(\max(ch, c{min}), c{max}) \quad (2.2) where \min, \max, and arithmetic operations are performed component-wise. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def aabbclamp(historicalcolor, neighborhoodsamples): """ Rectifies historical color by clamping it to the AABB defined by neighborhood samples. Args: historicalcolor: List/Array of floats, shape (k,) representing ch. neighborhoodsamples: List/Array of floats, shape (N, k) representing ci. Returns: List/Array of floats, shape (k,) representing cr. """ k = len(historicalcolor) N = len(neighborhoodsamples) # Step 1: Construct AABB bounds cmin = [0.0] k cmax = [0.0] k for j in range(k): cmin[j] = min(sample[j] for sample in neighborhoodsamples) cmax[j] = max(sample[j] for sample in neighborhoodsamples) # Step 2: Clamp historical color to bounds rectifiedcolor = [0.0] k for j in range(k): val = historicalcolor[j] if val < cmin[j]: val = cmin[j] elif val > cmax[j]: val = cmax[j] rectifiedcolor[j] = val return rectifiedcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Corner Accumulation: Because each channel is individually clamped, values tend to collect in the corners of the AABB. Color Artifacts: This corner accumulation can lead to strange color-related artifacts in scenes with significant color information, although it is generally not an issue for grayscale scenes. Accuracy: This method is a fast approximation of the tighter convex hull approach. It is less accurate but much cheaper to build and intersect against. History Rectification is a class of Temporal Anti-Aliasing techniques that correct historical color values before blending by restricting the reprojected history to a region defined by current-frame neighborhood samples. It solves the problem of temporal lag and ghosting during abrupt scene changes where a baseline Exponential Moving Average fails to react quickly enough. What sets it apart from its siblings and nearest alternatives is the use of a spatial neighborhood of current-frame samples to define a "color extent" or bound; if the historical value falls outside this extent, it is considered stale and is corrected prior to blending. This approach builds on AABB Clamping, which uses a simpler Axis-Aligned Bounding Box approximation, whereas History Rectification encompasses more sophisticated variants like Variance Clipping and AABB Clipping that better handle color information and statistical distributions. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot k) to compute min/max over N samples with k channels, followed by O(k) for clamping. It is computationally efficient compared to convex hull projection. Memory Complexity: O(k) to store the min and max bounds. Strengths: Fast approximation of history rectification; easy to implement and intersect against; ensures history remains within valid color extent. Limitations: Less accurate than convex hull methods; prone to color artifacts due to channel-wise clamping causing values to collect in AABB corners. When to use: When performance is critical and the scene is predominantly grayscale or has limited color variation. When not to use: In scenes with complex color information where color artifacts are noticeable, or when higher fidelity rectification (like AABB Clipping or Variance Clipping) is required. AABB Clamping is a history rectification method implemented and evaluated in the context of temporal anti-aliasing for real-time froxel-based volumetric rendering. It serves as a fast approximation to the computationally expensive convex hull projection, which is too costly for real-time rendering constraints. The method is part of a class of techniques that correct historical color values before blending by restricting them to a region defined by current-frame neighborhood samples. name: History Rectification
head: AABB Clipping
body: History rectification is a class of Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) techniques that correct historical color values before blending by restricting the reprojected history to a region defined by current-frame neighborhood samples. It solves the problem of temporal lag and ghosting during abrupt scene changes (such as light introduction or sudden movement) where a baseline Exponential Moving Average (EMA) fails to react quickly enough. What sets it apart from its siblings and nearest alternatives is the use of a spatial neighborhood of current-frame samples to define a "color extent" or bound; if the historical value falls outside this extent, it is considered stale and is corrected (clamped or clipped) prior to blending. This approach builds on AABB Clamping, which uses a simpler Axis-Aligned Bounding Box approximation, whereas History Rectification encompasses more sophisticated variants like Variance Clipping and AABB Clipping that better handle color information and statistical distributions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The reprojected history buffer value H for the current pixel, and a neighborhood of current-frame color samples C{neighbor} (typically a 3x3 grid of pixels surrounding the current pixel). Output: A rectified history value H{rect} ready for blending with the current frame. Data Structures: Neighborhood Samples: A set of color vectors \{c1, c2,..., cn\} representing the RGB(A) values of the neighboring pixels in the current frame. Bounds: A minimum vector min and a maximum vector max defining the rectification region. For AABB-based methods, these are component-wise min/max. For Variance Clipping, these are derived from statistical moments. Steps: 1. Sample Neighborhood: Gather the color values of the neighboring pixels in the current frame. The standard evaluation uses a 3x3 neighborhood to avoid averaging across depth slices, which would act as a spatial stabilizer and hide flicker artifacts. Alternatives like 3x3x3 or 6-tap neighborhoods smooth across depth but are not used in the primary evaluation context. 2. Define Bounds: Calculate the bounding region based on the chosen variant (see Subtopics). For AABB variants: min = \min(ci), max = \max(ci) for each color channel independently. For Variance Clipping: Bounds are expanded beyond min/max using the standard deviation of the neighborhood values to account for statistical distribution. 3. Rectify History: Compare the reprojected history value H against the defined bounds. If H is within the bounds, H{rect} = H. If H is outside the bounds, H{rect} is adjusted to the nearest boundary value (clamping) or projected onto the boundary (clipping). 4. Blend: Blend H{rect} with the current frame color C{current} using the temporal blend factor \alpha (typically \alpha = 0.05 for evaluation comparability). Formulas: For AABB Clamping/Clipping, the rectified value for a single channel is: H{rect} = \text{clamp}(H, min, max) Where \text{clamp}(v, a, b) returns a if v < a, b if v > b, and v otherwise. For Variance Clipping, the bounds are extended by a factor of the standard deviation \sigma: min{var} = \mu - k \cdot \sigma max{var} = \mu + k \cdot \sigma Where \mu is the mean of the neighborhood, \sigma is the standard deviation, and k is a scaling factor. The first and second sample moments used for variance clipping are defined as m1 = \sum{i=1}^N ci and m2 = \sum{i=1}^N ci^2, from which \mu = m1/N and \sigma^2 = m2/N - \mu^2 are derived. Parameters: Neighborhood Size: 3x3 is the standard for evaluation to preserve depth separation. Blend Factor (\alpha): 0.05 is used in the cited evaluations to match baseline EMA conditions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Static Extent: When the light turns off, the neighborhood extent becomes 0 (a single point). The history is clamped to this point, eliminating temporal lag instantly. Gradual Color Change: AABB clamping struggles with gradual color transitions (e.g., red to blue fade). It exhibits an especially big RMSE spike at frame 500 and takes around 50 frames for the error to converge back down to the level of AABB clipping. Temporal Instability (TI): Tighter bounds allow faster adaptation but increase TI, perceived as visual flicker. The distance between highest error peaks is exactly 16 frames, corresponding to the jitter sequence length. Grayscale Scenes: AABB clipping and clamping produce identical results in grayscale scenes because color rectification is irrelevant. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def historyrectification(historyvalue, currentframecolor, neighborhoodcolors, method='aabbclamp'): """ Rectifies the history value based on the current frame neighborhood. Args: historyvalue: list of 3 floats, the reprojected history color [R, G, B]. currentframecolor: list of 3 floats, the current frame's color. neighborhoodcolors: list of lists of 3 floats, colors of neighboring pixels. method: str, one of 'aabbclamp', 'aabbclip', 'varianceclip'. Returns: list of 3 floats, the rectified history value. """ # Step 1: Calculate bounds from neighborhood if method in ('aabbclamp', 'aabbclip'): # Component-wise min and max across the neighborhood minval = [min(c[i] for c in neighborhoodcolors) for i in range(3)] maxval = [max(c[i] for c in neighborhoodcolors) for i in range(3)] if method == 'aabbclamp': # Clamp history to AABB bounds per channel rectified = [max(minval[i], min(historyvalue[i], maxval[i])) for i in range(3)] else: # aabbclip # Project history onto AABB towards the current frame sample # The current frame sample is guaranteed to be inside the AABB dirvec = [currentframecolor[i] - historyvalue[i] for i in range(3)] tmin = 1.0 for i in range(3): if abs(dirvec[i]) > 1e-6: t1 = (minval[i] - historyvalue[i]) / dirvec[i] t2 = (maxval[i] - historyvalue[i]) / dirvec[i] tlo = min(t1, t2) thi = max(t1, t2) tmin = max(tmin, tlo) # Clamp t to [0, 1] to stay within the segment between history and target t = max(0.0, min(1.0, tmin)) rectified = [historyvalue[i] + t dirvec[i] for i in range(3)] elif method == 'varianceclip': # Calculate first and second sample moments per channel n = len(neighborhoodcolors) m1 = [sum(c[i] for c in neighborhoodcolors) for i in range(3)] m2 = [sum(c[i]2 for c in neighborhoodcolors) for i in range(3)] meanval = [m1[i] / n for i in range(3)] variance = [m2[i] / n - meanval[i]2 for i in range(3)] stddev = [max(0.0, v)0.5 for v in variance] # Guard against negative variance due to precision k = 1.0 # Scaling factor not specified in sources minval = [meanval[i] - k stddev[i] for i in range(3)] maxval = [meanval[i] + k stddev[i] for i in range(3)] rectified = [max(minval[i], min(historyvalue[i], maxval[i])) for i in range(3)] else: rectified = list(historyvalue) # Fallback to no rectification return rectified A history rectification method that uses the statistical distribution of values in the current frame neighborhood to create the bounds of the AABB used for clipping. It calculates the mean and standard deviation of the neighborhood colors to define a range that is typically tighter than the raw min/max but accounts for variance. It consistently introduces less bias than AABB-based methods during movement, reducing ghosting artifacts more effectively, but exhibits higher Temporal Instability (flicker). In step response scenarios, it achieves the lowest RMSE (0.002977) but the highest TI P (0.004217, +190.23% increase over baseline). A history rectification method that projects the history onto the AABB defined by the minimum and maximum values in each color channel of the current frame neighborhood. In grayscale scenes, it produces identical results to AABB Clamping because color rectification is not relevant. It performs better than EMA in abrupt change scenarios and has lower TI than Variance Clipping (TI P of 0.002373, +63.32% over baseline). However, it struggles with gradual color changes, showing a large RMSE spike when a light fades from red to blue. Clipping the historical value against the convex hull formed by neighboring color samples, representing the smallest convex region containing all neighboring colors. Constructing and projecting history onto the convex hull is too computationally expensive for real-time rendering performance constraints. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(N) where N is the number of neighbors in the sampling kernel (e.g., 9 for 3x3). The operations are simple min/max or mean/std calculations per pixel. Memory: O(1) auxiliary memory per pixel for storing neighborhood samples during the rectification pass. Measured Performance: Hardware/Resolution: Not given in the sources. Scene: Evaluated in step response (abrupt light on/off) and gradual change (moving/rotating light) scenarios. Metrics: Baseline EMA: RMSE 0.009724, TI P 0.001453. AABB Clamp/Clip: RMSE 0.003136, TI P 0.002373 (+63.32% TI). Variance Clip: RMSE 0.002977, TI P 0.004217 (+190.23% TI). Scaling: Performance scales with neighborhood size. Larger neighborhoods (3x3x3, 6-tap) smooth the signal across depth, reducing visible flicker but potentially blurring details. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Superior to EMA in abrupt change scenarios; immediately drops error to zero when intensity drops, eliminating temporal lag. Variance clipping produces the lowest error spike when reconstructing the signal during quick illumination introduction. Limitations: Higher Temporal Instability (flicker) compared to EMA, especially with Variance Clipping. AABB Clamping struggles with gradual color changes, taking ~50 frames to converge after a color fade. Jittering causes periodic error patterns (16-frame cycle) perceived as flicker. When to use/not use: Use: When rapid reaction to scene changes (light on/off, fast motion) is prioritized over absolute temporal stability, and ghosting must be minimized. Not Use: In scenes with gradual color transitions where AABB clamping is used, or when visual flicker is unacceptable and higher TI is a dealbreaker. History rectification techniques were developed as part of the broader effort to improve Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) for real-time rendering, specifically in the context of froxel-based volumetric rendering. The specific evaluation of these methods (Variance Clipping, AABB Clamping, AABB Clipping) is detailed in the work on "Advances in volumetric temporal anti-aliasing for real-time rendering of participating media". The mathematical definition for each method remains unchanged from their original pixel-space TAA counterparts. name: Clipped Cropping Region Planes
head: ClipCroppingRegionPlanes, Cropping Region Plane Clipping, Volume Bounding Box Clipping
body: Clipped Cropping Region Planes is a preprocessing step for volume rendering that constrains user-defined cropping planes to the physical bounds of the input volume dataset. It solves the problem of invalid or out-of-bounds clipping regions by computing the intersection of arbitrary user-specified planes with the volume's axis-aligned bounding box (AABB). Unlike its sibling Cropping, which defines the logical clipping region, this method ensures the region is geometrically valid and contained within the data before rendering proceeds. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The input volume dataset (typically vtkImageData), the user-defined cropping planes array CroppingRegionPlanes[6], and the volume's bounding box bounds volBounds[6]. Output: The clipped cropping planes array ClippedCroppingRegionPlanes[6]. Data Structures: volBounds[6]: An array of 6 doubles representing the AABB of the volume. Indices 0-1 correspond to the minimum and maximum X coordinates, 2-3 to Y, and 4-5 to Z. CroppingRegionPlanes[6]: An array of 6 doubles representing the user-defined clipping planes. Indices 0-1 define the min/max X planes, 2-3 for Y, and 4-5 for Z. ClippedCroppingRegionPlanes[6]: An array of 6 doubles storing the result. Steps: 1. Validate Input: Assert that the input volume exists. 2. Retrieve Bounds: Obtain the volume's bounding box into volBounds[6] using the dataset's GetBounds method. 3. Validate Cropping Order: Assert that cropping is enabled and the planes are ordered correctly: CroppingRegionPlanes[0] < CroppingRegionPlanes[1], CroppingRegionPlanes[2] < CroppingRegionPlanes[3], and CroppingRegionPlanes[4] < CroppingRegionPlanes[5]. 4. Clip Min Planes: For each axis i \in \{0, 2, 4\} (representing X, Y, Z minimums): If CroppingRegionPlanes[i] < volBounds[i], set ClippedCroppingRegionPlanes[i] = volBounds[i]. Otherwise, set ClippedCroppingRegionPlanes[i] = CroppingRegionPlanes[i]. 5. Clip Max Planes: For each axis i \in \{1, 3, 5\} (representing X, Y, Z maximums): If CroppingRegionPlanes[i] > volBounds[i], set ClippedCroppingRegionPlanes[i] = volBounds[i]. Otherwise, set ClippedCroppingRegionPlanes[i] = CroppingRegionPlanes[i]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def clipcroppingregionplanes(croppingregionplanes, volbounds): """ Clamps user-defined cropping planes to the volume's bounding box. Args: croppingregionplanes (list[float]): 6-element list [minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz]. volbounds (list[float]): 6-element list [minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz]. Returns: list[float]: Clipped cropping planes. """ # Precondition checks assert len(croppingregionplanes) == 6 assert len(volbounds) == 6 # Assert ordering: min < max for each axis assert croppingregionplanes[0] < croppingregionplanes[1], "X planes not ordered" assert croppingregionplanes[2] < croppingregionplanes[3], "Y planes not ordered" assert croppingregionplanes[4] < croppingregionplanes[5], "Z planes not ordered" clippedplanes = [0.0] 6 # Clip minimum planes (indices 0, 2, 4) for i in [0, 2, 4]: if croppingregionplanes[i] < volbounds[i]: clippedplanes[i] = volbounds[i] else: clippedplanes[i] = croppingregionplanes[i] # Clip maximum planes (indices 1, 3, 5) for i in [1, 3, 5]: if croppingregionplanes[i] > volbounds[i]: clippedplanes[i] = volbounds[i] else: clippedplanes[i] = croppingregionplanes[i] return clippedplanes Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Invalid Ordering: If the user-defined planes are not ordered (min > max), the method fails the precondition check. The parent Render() method may silently stop if this check is not enforced by the caller. Out-of-Bounds Input: If a user plane is outside the volume bounds, it is clamped to the nearest bound. This prevents rendering artifacts or crashes caused by accessing invalid memory or computing intersections with non-existent geometry. Empty Volume: If the volume bounds are degenerate (e.g., min == max), the clipping logic still applies, potentially resulting in a zero-thickness slab. Supports arbitrary convex or non-convex polygonal shapes in screen space, unlike the axis-aligned planar cuts of this method. Choose when free-form region selection is required. Time Complexity: O(1), as it performs a fixed number of comparisons (6 comparisons) regardless of volume size. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring only a small fixed-size array for the output. Strengths: Fast, deterministic, and prevents invalid clipping regions. Limitations: Only handles axis-aligned clipping. Cannot handle arbitrary planes or complex shapes. When to use: When using axis-aligned cropping and ensuring robustness against user input errors. When not to use: When non-axis-aligned or free-form cropping is needed. This method originates from the Visualization Toolkit (VTK) library, specifically within volume rendering mappers such as vtkGPUMultiVolumeRayCastMapper. It is part of the VTK volume rendering pipeline, ensuring that cropping operations are geometrically valid before being passed to the rendering engine. name: Polygon-based Cropping
head: CutLineInside, CutLineOutside, CutingImagedata, Voxel-wise 2D Polygon Clipping
body: Polygon-based cropping is a voxel-wise volume rendering technique that masks voxels based on a user-defined 2D polygon drawn in the display (screen) coordinate space. It solves the problem of interactive, free-form region-of-interest selection by converting screen-space constraints into volume-space visibility masks. It differs from planar clipping methods by supporting arbitrary convex or non-convex polygonal shapes rather than just axis-aligned or arbitrary planar cuts, and it operates by explicitly iterating over voxels to test their projected positions against the polygon boundary. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A vtkImageData object containing the volume scalar data, a vtkRenderer for coordinate transformation, a QPolygonF defining the 2D clipping boundary in screen coordinates, and an integer type flag determining the clipping mode. Output: The modified vtkImageData where voxels outside the valid region are set to zero (transparent), effectively cropping the volume. Data Structures: vtkImageData: Stores voxel data. The implementation assumes the scalar type is unsigned char. If the type differs, pointer casting must be adjusted. QPolygonF: A 2D polygon defined by a sequence of QPointF vertices. vtkCoordinate: Used to transform world coordinates to display coordinates. Steps: 1. Retrieve volume metadata: Get dimensions: imgdims = imagedata->GetDimensions() Get spacing: imgspacing = imagedata->GetSpacing() Get origin: imgorigian = imagedata->GetOrigin() 2. Iterate over all voxel coordinates (i, j, k) within the volume bounds. Note: Direct indexing is required; vtkImageIterator cannot retrieve spatial positions. 3. Compute the world position of the current voxel: \text{world\pos} = [i \cdot \text{img\spacing}[0] + \text{img\origian}[0], \quad j \cdot \text{img\spacing}[1] + \text{img\origian}[1], \quad k \cdot \text{img\spacing}[2] + \text{img\origian}[2]] 4. Transform the world position to display coordinates: Use coordinate->GetComputedDoubleDisplayValue(renderer) to obtain displaypos. 5. Check if displaypos lies inside the user-drawn polygon: Call polygon.containsPoint(QPointF(displaypos[0], displaypos[1]), Qt::OddEvenFill). 6. Apply clipping based on type: If type == RenderWidget::CutLineInside and the point is inside the polygon, keep the voxel value. If outside, set pPixel = 0. If type == RenderWidget::CutLineOutside and the point is outside the polygon, set pPixel = 0. If inside, keep the voxel value. 7. After modification, update the volume and re-add it to the renderer: volume->Update() renderer->RemoveVolume(volume) renderer->AddVolume(volume) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def polygonbasedcropping(imagedata, volume, renderer, polygon, cliptype): # Retrieve metadata imgdims = imagedata.GetDimensions() imgspacing = imagedata.GetSpacing() imgorigian = imagedata.GetOrigin() # Create coordinate converter coordinate = vtkCoordinate() coordinate.SetCoordinateSystemToWorld() coordinate.SetRenderer(renderer) # Iterate over all voxels for k in range(imgdims[2]): for j in range(imgdims[1]): for i in range(imgdims[0]): # Compute world position worldpos = [ i imgspacing[0] + imgorigian[0], j imgspacing[1] + imgorigian[1], k imgspacing[2] + imgorigian[2] ] # Transform to display coordinates # Note: GetComputedDoubleDisplayValue expects world coordinates coordinate.SetCoordinate(worldpos[0], worldpos[1], worldpos[2]) displaypos = coordinate.GetComputedDoubleDisplayValue(renderer) # Check if point is inside polygon # Qt::OddEvenFill is used for winding rule containspoint = polygon.containsPoint( QPointF(displaypos[0], displaypos[1]), Qt.OddEvenFill) # Get pointer to voxel data # Assumes unsigned char type pixelptr = imagedata.GetScalarPointer(i, j, k) # Apply clipping logic if cliptype == RenderWidget.CutLineInside: if not containspoint: pixelptr[0] = 0 elif cliptype == RenderWidget.CutLineOutside: if containspoint: pixelptr[0] = 0 # Update volume and renderer volume.Update() renderer.RemoveVolume(volume) renderer.AddVolume(volume) Parameters: cliptype: Enum or integer flag. CutLineInside (keep inside polygon), CutLineOutside (keep outside polygon). fillrule: Qt::OddEvenFill is used for point-in-polygon testing. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The implementation assumes the bounding box origin starts at (0,0,0). Production code must validate actual bounds. Do not use vtkImageIterator as it cannot retrieve spatial positions; direct indexing is required. The scalar type is assumed to be unsigned char. If the scalar type differs, the pointer cast and assignment must be adjusted. A CPU-based algorithm that intersects parallel sampling planes against a convex VOI using a Weighted Sweep Graph to exploit coherence between planes, reducing GPU load by transmitting only valid portions. Choose this for large volumes where reducing ray casting overhead is critical and the VOI is convex. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the total number of voxels in the volume, as every voxel is visited and transformed. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, as it modifies the volume in place. Performance: The method is CPU-bound due to the per-voxel coordinate transformation and polygon containment test. It is suitable for interactive editing but may be slow for very large volumes compared to GPU-based clipping. Strengths: Supports arbitrary 2D polygonal shapes in screen space, allowing for intuitive free-form cropping. Limitations: Requires full volume iteration; not suitable for real-time rendering of large datasets without optimization. Assumes specific data types and coordinate systems. When to use: Interactive volume editing where the user draws a custom 2D shape to define the region of interest. When not to use: Real-time rendering of large volumes where performance is critical; use GPU-based clipping or the Convex VOI Clipping method instead. The method is described in the open-source project kpengk/VolumeClipping. It is part of a larger system for interactive volume visualization using VTK and Qt. The approach leverages VTK's coordinate transformation capabilities and Qt's polygon geometry classes to implement a simple, voxel-wise clipping mechanism. kpengk/VolumeClipping, https://github.com/kpengk/VolumeClipping, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Convex VOI Clipping via Weighted Sweep Graph
head: Clipper, WSG-based clipping
body: This method is a CPU-based clipping algorithm that intersects a sequence of parallel sampling planes against a user-defined convex Volume of Interest (VOI) to reduce the computational load on the GPU. It solves the problem of unnecessary volume rendering computation in empty or irrelevant regions by transmitting only the clipped, valid portions of sampling planes to the GPU. It sets itself apart from general convex clipping algorithms by exploiting the coherence between parallel planes and using a Weighted Sweep Graph (WSG) to efficiently manage topological changes (vertex events) during the sweep, avoiding the recomputation of edge lists from scratch for every plane. Inputs: 1. A convex VOI defined by a set of cutting planes. Each cutting plane is defined by a normal vector \mathbf{n} and a point \mathbf{p} on the plane. 2. A sequence of parallel sampling planes. Each sampling plane is defined by a normal vector \mathbf{n}{sample} (parallel to the viewing direction) and a distance di from the VOI center (or a reference origin). Outputs: A sequence of convex polygons, one for each sampling plane that intersects the VOI. Each polygon is defined by an ordered list of vertices lying on the edges of the VOI. Data Structures: VOI Representation: The convex VOI is implicitly defined by the intersection of half-spaces created by the cutting planes. The geometry is tracked via its edges and vertices. Weighted Sweep Graph (WSG): A graph structure that encodes the topological structure of the convex volume. It maintains: The current list of edges intersected by the sweep plane, ordered to form the convex polygon. Vertex events, which indicate when the sweep plane passes through a vertex of the VOI. Connections between vertices and edges to facilitate updates. Algorithm Steps: 1. VOI Definition: The user defines the convex VOI starting from a basic convex shape (e.g., a cube). Cutting planes are added to slice the volume. Each cutting plane is specified by: A normal vector \mathbf{n}, controlled by dragging a line endpoint from the VOI center. A reference point, controlled by a slider specifying the distance from the VOI center. The resulting VOI is the intersection of the initial shape and all added half-spaces. 2. Initialization: Initialize the WSG with the topology of the initial convex shape (e.g., the cube). The WSG stores the edges and their connectivity. Identify the initial set of edges that intersect the first sampling plane (or the plane closest to the VOI center). 3. Sweep Preparation: Sort the sampling planes by their distance from the VOI center along the viewing direction. Sort the vertices of the VOI by their projection onto the viewing direction to identify the order of vertex events (sweep events). 4. Sweep Loop: For each sampling plane i in the sorted order: a. Check for Vertex Events: Determine if any vertex of the VOI lies between the current plane i and the previous plane i-1. This is done by comparing the signed distance of the vertex to the plane normal against the plane positions. b. Update Edge List (if Vertex Event): If a vertex v is encountered: i. Identify the edges incident to v in the WSG. ii. Remove edges that are no longer intersected by the sweep plane (those "behind" the vertex relative to the sweep direction). iii. Add edges that become intersected (those "in front" of the vertex). iv. Ensure the edge list remains ordered to form a convex polygon. The WSG maintains this order. c. Compute Polygon Vertices: i. For each edge e in the current ordered edge list, compute the intersection point P between the edge e and the current sampling plane i. ii. The edge e is defined by two vertices A and B. The intersection point P is calculated as: P = A + \frac{di - \mathbf{n}{sample} \cdot A}{\mathbf{n}{sample} \cdot (B - A)} (B - A) where di is the signed distance of the plane from the origin, and \mathbf{n}{sample} is the plane normal. Note: The denominator is the dot product of the plane normal and the edge direction vector. If the denominator is zero, the edge is parallel to the plane and does not intersect (or lies on it). iii. Collect all intersection points P. These points form the vertices of the convex polygon for plane i. d. Output: Send the resulting polygon (list of vertices) to the GPU for volume rendering. 5. Termination: Stop when all sampling planes have been processed. Parameters: VOI Center: The reference point for user interaction (normal vector direction and plane distance). Plane Normal: The viewing direction, which is parallel for all sampling planes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parallel Edges: If an edge is parallel to the sampling plane, the intersection formula yields a division by zero. Such edges do not contribute a unique intersection point and should be handled by checking if the edge lies on the plane (in which case it might be part of the polygon boundary) or is strictly outside. Vertex Coincidence: If a vertex lies exactly on a sampling plane, it is a vertex event. The edge list update must be handled carefully to ensure the polygon remains closed and convex. The WSG structure is designed to detect these events. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise when determining if a vertex is between two planes or if an intersection point lies exactly on an edge. Robust geometric predicates are recommended. Pseudocode: Unverified code. In practice, this requires a constructive # solid geometry (CSG) or incremental clipping step. # Step 2: Initialize WSG # WSG maintains the current list of edges intersected by the sweep plane # and their order. currentedges = getinitialintersectededges(voiedges, voivertices, samplingplanes[0]) # Sort currentedges to form a convex polygon currentedges = sortedgestopolygon(currentedges, voivertices) # Precompute vertex distances along the sweep direction (sampling plane normal) sweepnormal = samplingplanes[0][0] vertexdistances = [dot(v, sweepnormal) for v in voivertices] # Sort sampling planes by distance sortedplaneindices = sorted(range(len(samplingplanes)), key=lambda i: samplingplanes[i][1]) polygons = [] for idx in sortedplaneindices: planenormal, planedist = samplingplanes[idx] # Step 4a: Check for vertex events # Find vertices that lie between the previous plane and the current plane # For the first plane, there is no previous plane, so no events if idx != sortedplaneindices[0]: prevplanedist = samplingplanes[sortedplaneindices[sortedplaneindices.index(idx) - planedist) < 1e-9: # Edge is on the plane. Add both endpoints? # This is a degenerate case. Usually, vertices are added via adjacent edges. pass continue t = (planedist - dot(va, planenormal)) / denom # Clamp t to [0, 1] to ensure intersection is on the segment if 0 <= t <= 1: intersectionpoint = va + t (vb - va) polygonvertices.append(intersectionpoint) # Step 4d: Output # polygonvertices should be in order. If not, sort them. # The WSG update should maintain order, but numerical errors might occur. polygonvertices = sortpolygonvertices(polygonvertices) polygons.append(polygonvertices) return polygons def getinitialintersectededges(voiedges, voivertices, plane): """Find edges intersecting the first plane.""" planenormal, planedist = plane intersected = [] for edge in voiedges: vaidx, vbidx = edge va = voivertices[vaidx] vb = voivertices[vbidx] denom = dot(vb - va, planenormal) if abs(denom) < 1e-9: continue t = (planedist - dot(va, planenormal)) / denom if 0 <= t <= 1: intersected.append(edge) return intersected def updateedgelistforvertex(currentedges, vidx, voiedges, voivertices, planenormal): """ Update the current edge list when a vertex vidx is crossed. Remove edges incident to vidx that are no longer intersected, and add edges that become intersected. """ # Find edges incident to vidx incidentedges = [e for e in voiedges if vidx in e] # For each incident edge, determine if it should be in the current list # This depends on the sweep direction and the position of the vertex relative to the plane # The WSG structure helps identify which edges to add/remove. # Simplified logic: # Edges that were intersecting before the vertex and are now "behind" the vertex are removed. # Edges that were not intersecting before and are now "in front" are added. newedges = [] for edge in currentedges: if vidx not in edge: # Edge not incident to the vertex, keep it newedges.append(edge) else: # Edge incident to the vertex. Check if it should be kept. # This requires knowing the sweep direction and the vertex's position. # For a convex VOI, as the plane sweeps past a vertex, the set of intersected edges # changes by removing the edges that are "behind" the vertex and adding those "in front". # This logic is complex and depends on the specific topology. # The WSG is designed to handle this. Here, we assume the WSG provides the correct # set of edges to keep/add/remove. # For the purpose of this pseudocode, we assume the WSG update is a black box # that returns the new set of edges. pass # In a real implementation, the WSG would provide the new edge list directly. # Here, we simulate the update by recomputing the intersection for the current plane # using the new set of edges determined by the WSG. # Since we don't have the full WSG implementation, we assume the edge list is updated # by the WSG logic described in the source. # Re-compute intersection for the current plane with the updated edge list # This is a simplification. The WSG should maintain the edge list incrementally. return currentedges # Placeholder for WSG update logic def sortedgestopolygon(edges, vertices): """Sort edges to form a convex polygon.""" if not edges: return [] # Build adjacency list adj = {} for e in edges: v1, v2 = e if v1 not in adj: adj[v1] = [] if v2 not in adj: adj[v2] = [] adj[v1].append(v2) adj[v2].append(v1) # Start from an arbitrary edge startv = edges[0][0] path = [startv] currentv = startv visited = {startv} while len(path) < len(edges) + 1: # +1 to close the loop neighbors = adj.get(currentv, []) nextv = None for n in neighbors: if n not in visited: nextv = n break if nextv is None: # If no unvisited neighbor, we might be at the end of a chain or the loop is closed # Check if we can close the loop if path[0] in neighbors: nextv = path[0] else: break path.append(nextv) visited.add(nextv) currentv = nextv return path def sortpolygonvertices(vertices): """Sort vertices to form a convex polygon.""" if len(vertices) < 3: return vertices # Compute centroid centroid = sum(vertices) / len(vertices) # Sort by angle relative to centroid def angle(v): return atan2(v[1] - centroid[1], v[0] - centroid[0]) return sorted(vertices, key=angle) def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def sub(v1, v2): return (v1[0]-v2[0], v1[1]-v2[1], v1[2]-v2[2]) def add(v1, v2): return (v1[0]+v2[0], v1[1]+v2[1], v1[2]+v2[2]) def scale(v, s): return (v[0]s, v[1]s, v[2]s) def atan2(y, x): import math return math.atan2(y, x) Time Complexity: The complexity depends on the number of sampling planes N, the number of edges E in the VOI, and the number of vertex events V. For each plane, the edge list update is O(V) in the worst case (if many vertices are crossed), and the intersection computation is O(E). With coherence, the average case is much faster, as most planes only require O(1) updates. Memory Complexity: O(E + V) to store the WSG and the VOI topology. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces GPU computation by clipping empty regions. Exploits coherence between parallel planes. Interactive VOI definition. Limitations: CPU-based, so it adds CPU overhead. Limited to convex VOIs. When to use: When the VOI is convex and the user wants to interactively define the clipping region. When the GPU is the bottleneck and can benefit from reduced sampling. When not to use: When the VOI is non-convex. When the CPU is the bottleneck. The method was proposed in the paper "Real-time interactive visualization and manipulation of the volumetric data using GPU-based methods". It addresses the need for efficient clipping of volumetric data to improve rendering performance. The WSG is a novel data structure introduced in this work to manage the topological changes during the sweep. name: GPU-based Eraser and Digger Tools
head: Painting paradigm clipping, Sculpting tools
body: GPU-based eraser and digger tools are interactive visualization methods that allow users to selectively remove voxels from a volume rendering using a "painting" paradigm. They solve the problem of intuitive, real-time data manipulation by mapping 2D screen interactions to 3D voxel selection via line-of-sight projection. Unlike the parent Convex VOI Clipping via Weighted Sweep Graph, which defines a static convex boundary for the entire Volume of Interest (VOI), these tools define dynamic, user-controlled removal zones that persist across multiple interaction strokes. Inputs: ClippedImage: The resampled 3D volume data defined by the parent clipper. Sight-Reference-Point (SRP): A 2D point (u, v) on the screen selected by the user via mouse input. Circle-of-Interest Radius (R): A scalar parameter defining the extent of the selection area on the projection plane. Digging Depth (D{dig}): A scalar parameter (for Digger tool only) defining the maximum depth from the surface along the viewing direction. Outputs: SculptBuffer: A 3D texture buffer storing visibility/distance information. Final rendered image where selected voxels are invisible. SculptBuffer Type: 3D Texture Buffer. Layout: Scalar values. Content: Stores the minimum screen-coordinate distance between any previously set SRP and the voxel's projection on the screen. Initialization: All voxels initialized to the largest representable number (infinity), indicating all voxels are visible. Update Logic: For a new SRP, if the new projected distance d{new} for a voxel is less than the stored value d{old}, update d{old} \leftarrow d{new}. Otherwise, leave unchanged. This ensures the buffer tracks the closest SRP encountered for each voxel. ClippedImage Type: 3D Volume Texture. Content: The original 3D image resampled by the parent convex clipper. 2DSculptBuffer Type: 2D Texture Array / Side-by-side slices. Purpose: Intermediate representation used to bypass hardware limitations regarding 3D texture writes from fragment shaders. 1. SRP Acquisition: The user places a 2D point (SRP) on the screen. 2. Line-of-Sight Calculation: Apply the inverse viewing transformation to the SRP to obtain the line of projective equivalent points in 3D space. For perspective projection, this defines a cone. For parallel projection, this defines a cylinder. 3. Voxel Projection: For every voxel in the ClippedImage: Project the voxel center onto the 2D projection plane (screen). Compute the 2D Euclidean distance d between the projected voxel center and the SRP. 4. SculptBuffer Update: Calculate the new distance d{new} for the current SRP. If d{new} < \text{SculptBuffer}[voxel], update \text{SculptBuffer}[voxel] \leftarrow d{new}. 5. Visibility Determination (Eraser): A voxel is considered for removal if \text{SculptBuffer}[voxel] \le R. Voxels satisfying this condition are marked invisible in the final rendering. 6. Visibility Determination (Digger): First, identify voxels selected by the Eraser criteria (\text{SculptBuffer}[voxel] \le R). For these selected voxels, determine the depth along the viewing direction from the first point of intersection with the volume. If the depth is less than the Digging Depth (D{dig}), write a specific value to the SculptBuffer that forces the voxel to be invisible. Voxels with depth \ge D{dig} remain visible (or retain their previous visibility state based on the distance check). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updatesculptbuffer(sculptbuffer, voxelcenters, srp2d, radius, diggingdepth, isdiggermode, viewmatrixinv, projmatrix): # 1. Compute ray from SRP using inverse viewing transformation rayorigin = unproject2dto3d(srp2d, viewmatrixinv, projmatrix, 0.0) rayend = unproject2dto3d(srp2d, viewmatrixinv, projmatrix, 1.0) raydirection = [rayend[0] - rayorigin[0], rayend[1] - rayorigin[1], rayend[2] - rayorigin[2]] raydirection = normalize3d(raydirection) for i, center in enumerate(voxelcenters): # 2. Project voxel center to projection plane (screen) projectedcenter = project3dto2d(center, projmatrix) # 3. Compute 2D Euclidean distance to SRP dx = projectedcenter[0] - srp2d[0] dy = projectedcenter[1] - srp2d[1] dist2d = (dx dx + dy dy) 0.5 # 4. Update SculptBuffer with minimum distance if dist2d < sculptbuffer[i]: sculptbuffer[i] = dist2d # 5. Visibility Determination isincircle = dist2d <= radius if isdiggermode: # Digger Logic: Check depth along viewing direction depthtosurface = rayboxintersection(center, rayorigin, raydirection) # Note: Sources contradict on depth threshold logic. # Source states: "only those voxels that have depth greater than the digging depth are discarded" # but also: "For voxels that have depths smaller than the digger depth, a value is written... that forces it to be invisible". # Implementation follows the explicit invisibility instruction for depth < diggingdepth. if isincircle and depthtosurface < diggingdepth: sculptbuffer[i] = 0.0 # Value <= radius forces invisibility else: # Eraser Logic: Simple radius check if isincircle: sculptbuffer[i] = 0.0 # Value <= radius forces invisibility def render(clippedimage, sculptbuffer, radius): # Renders the volume using the SculptBuffer for visibility for i, voxel in enumerate(clippedimage.voxels): if sculptbuffer[i] <= radius: continue # Skip rendering (invisible) else: rendervoxel(voxel, clippedimage[i]) def generate2dsculptbuffer(sculptbuffer3d): # Generates a 2D representation of the 3D SculptBuffer to bypass hardware limitations on 3D texture writes width = sculptbuffer3d.width sculptbuffer3d.depth height = sculptbuffer3d.height buffer2d = [0.0] (height width) for z in range(sculptbuffer3d.depth): for y in range(sculptbuffer3d.height): for x in range(sculptbuffer3d.width): buffer2d[y width + x + z sculptbuffer3d.width] = sculptbuffer3d[x, y, z] return buffer2d def load3dsculptbuffer(buffer2d, sculptbuffer3d): # Reads back the 2D buffer to CPU and reconstructs the 3D buffer on GPU for z in range(sculptbuffer3d.depth): for y in range(sculptbuffer3d.height): for x in range(sculptbuffer3d.width): sculptbuffer3d[x, y, z] = buffer2d[y sculptbuffer3d.width sculptbuffer3d.depth + x + z sculptbuffer3d.width] def unproject2dto3d(screencoord, viewinv, proj, znear): # Standard inverse projection: maps 2D screen coords to 3D ray point at given depth clip = [screencoord[0], screencoord[1], znear, 1.0] return viewinv @ clip # Matrix-vector multiplication def project3dto2d(center, proj): # Standard projection: transforms 3D center to 2D screen coords clip = proj @ center return [clip[0] / clip[3], clip[1] / clip[3]] def normalize3d(v): length = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) 0.5 return [v[0]/length, v[1]/length, v[2]/length] def rayboxintersection(center, origin, direction): # Sources do not specify the exact intersection algorithm. # Standard slab method computes distance to first volume boundary hit. return 0.0 # Placeholder for standard ray-box intersection logic def rendervoxel(voxel, data): # Standard rasterization/shading step pass # Standard graphics operation SRP: 2D point (u, v) on the screen. Circle-of-Interest Radius (R): Controls the extents of the imaginary volume on the projection plane. Defined by a slider. Digging Depth (D{dig}): Specifies the depth from the first point of intersection with the volume along the viewing direction. Defined by a slider. Hardware Limitation: Current graphics hardware prevents 3D textures from being written as the output of fragment processing. Solution: Generate a 2D representation (2DSculptBuffer) using several slices stored side-by-side, read back to CPU, then pass pointer to GPU to create 3D SculptBuffer without further processing. Precision: The distance calculation is performed in screen coordinates (2D Euclidean distance). Degenerate Input: If the SRP is outside the volume bounds, no voxels may be selected depending on the projection geometry. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Real-time interactive performance is achieved by offloading the selection logic to the GPU. Strengths: Intuitive "painting" interaction; supports persistent selection (accumulation of SRPs) via the SculptBuffer. Limitations: Dependent on hardware capabilities for 3D texture writes, requiring a CPU-GPU round-trip workaround. The "Digger" tool requires additional depth calculations. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Real-time interactive visualization and manipulation of the volumetric data using GPU-based methods". Context: It is part of a suite of interactive tools for volumetric data, including a convex VOI clipper using Weighted Sweep Graphs (WSG). Usage: Used for real-time interactive visualization and manipulation of volumetric data. name: Clipping Geometry Illumination
head: Clipping Surface Shading
body:
Clipping Geometry Illumination is a shading technique used during volume rendering to provide realistic lighting at the boundaries of user-defined clipping geometry. While standard volume rendering relies on the volume's internal gradient for surface normals, this method substitutes the gradient with the geometric normal of the clipping boundary at the intersection point. This distinguishes it from sibling methods like Clipping plane for volume suppression which may suppress data entirely, or Pre-integrated Clipping Boundary Handling which focuses on integration artifacts; Clipping Geometry Illumination specifically addresses the visual discontinuity of lighting at the cut plane. Inputs: Volume dataset V with scalar values. Transfer function T mapping scalar values to color and opacity. Clipping geometry defined by a set of planes or surfaces. Light source position and direction. Camera position and view direction. Outputs: Final pixel color with correct illumination at clipping boundaries. Data Structures: Ray structure: origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, length L. Sample point structure: position \mathbf{p}, scalar value s, opacity \alpha, color \mathbf{c}. Normal vector \mathbf{n}: computed either from volume gradient 
abla V(\mathbf{p}) or from clipping geometry. Steps: 1. Ray Casting: For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume. 2. Sampling: Advance along the ray, sampling the volume at discrete intervals. 3. Boundary Detection: At each sample point \mathbf{p}, determine if the point lies on the boundary of the clipping geometry. If the point is inside the volume and not on a clipping boundary, compute the normal \mathbf{n} using the volume gradient 
abla V(\mathbf{p}). If the point is on the boundary of the clipping geometry, compute the normal \mathbf{n} using the geometric surface normal of the clipping geometry at \mathbf{p}. 4. Illumination Calculation: Compute the lighting model (e.g., Phong) using the determined normal \mathbf{n}, light direction \mathbf{l}, and view direction \mathbf{v}. Diffuse term: kd (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}) Specular term: ks (\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{v})^{\alpha{spec}} where \mathbf{r} is the reflection vector. 5. Compositing: Accumulate color and opacity using front-to-back or back-to-front compositing, applying the lighting result to the sampled color. Formulas: Gradient normal: \mathbf{n}{vol} =  rac{
abla V(\mathbf{p})}{\|
abla V(\mathbf{p})\|} Geometric normal: \mathbf{n}{clip} = 	ext{Normal of clipping geometry at } \mathbf{p} Final Normal: \mathbf{n} =  egin{cases} \mathbf{n}{vol} & 	ext{if not on clipping boundary} \ \mathbf{n}{clip} & 	ext{if on clipping boundary} \end{cases} Parameters: Clipping geometry definition: Typically defined by plane equations ax + by + cz + d = 0 or mesh surfaces. Lighting coefficients: kd, ks, \alpha{spec} as per standard Phong model. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Detecting exact boundary intersection requires careful tolerance handling to avoid gaps or overlaps between volume gradient normals and geometric normals. Degenerate Input: If the clipping geometry is not watertight or has self-intersections, normal computation may be ambiguous. Time Complexity: Same as standard volume rendering, O(N) where N is the number of samples per ray. The additional normal computation is negligible. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per ray for storing the clipping normal. Performance: No significant performance impact compared to standard gradient-based shading. Strengths: Provides visually consistent lighting at clipping boundaries, avoiding the "unlit" or "noisy" appearance that can occur with gradient estimation at sharp cuts. Limitations: Requires explicit definition of clipping geometry normals. Does not handle internal volume gradients at the boundary, which may appear discontinuous if the geometry normal does not align with the volume structure. Clipping Geometry Illumination was described by Weiskopf et al. in TVCG 2003. It is part of the broader field of direct volume rendering techniques aimed at improving visual quality during interactive exploration. The method addresses the specific problem of lighting discontinuities when parts of the volume are made transparent via clipping geometry. name: Emissive Clip Planes
head: emissive illumination for clip planes
body: Emissive Clip Planes is a volume rendering technique that eliminates visual artifacts at the boundary of clipped volume data by overriding standard Phong illumination with purely emissive coloring. It solves two specific problems inherent in gradient-based lighting: random, noisy lighting in homogeneous materials caused by estimated gradient noise, and dark, unlit back-facing surfaces revealed when the volume is cut. Unlike methods that modify gradient normals or ignore clipped voxels, this approach preserves the classified material appearance directly at the cut plane while maintaining specular reflections on the rest of the volume. Inputs: Volume dataset (scalar values). Clip plane definition (position and normal). Classification map (transfer function mapping scalar values to RGBA). Lighting parameters (light positions, material properties for Phong model). Outputs: Final image with emissive illumination at clip boundaries and standard illumination elsewhere. Data Structures: Volume Data: 3D grid of scalar values. Classification Map: Function C(v) \rightarrow (R, G, B, A) mapping scalar value v to color and opacity. Clip Plane: Defined by a point P0 and a normal vector \mathbf{n}. A sample at position \mathbf{x} is considered "adjacent" to the clip plane if it lies on the visible side of the plane and is within a small distance threshold \epsilon from the plane, or if it is the first sample encountered along a ray after crossing the plane boundary. Steps: 1. Ray Casting: For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume. 2. Clipping Check: Determine if the ray intersects the clip plane. If it does, samples on the "cut" side (where (\mathbf{x} - P0) \cdot \mathbf{n} < 0) are treated as transparent/ignored. 3. Sample Processing: For each sample \mathbf{x} along the ray: a. Classification: Retrieve the scalar value v at \mathbf{x} and compute the base color C{base} = C(v). b. Adjacency Test: Determine if \mathbf{x} is immediately adjacent to the clip plane boundary. This is typically the first sample on the visible side of the plane. c. Illumination Decision: If \mathbf{x} is adjacent to the clip plane: Apply Emissive Illumination. The final color contribution is C{final} = C{base} \cdot \alpha. No lighting model is applied. If \mathbf{x} is not adjacent: Apply Standard Phong Illumination. i. Estimate gradient \mathbf{g} at \mathbf{x} using central differences or similar method. ii. Compute normal \mathbf{N} = \mathbf{g} / \|\mathbf{g}\|. iii. Compute Phong lighting model L(\mathbf{N}, \mathbf{V}, \mathbf{L}) using view vector \mathbf{V} and light vector \mathbf{L}. iv. C{final} = C{base} \cdot L(\mathbf{N}, \mathbf{V}, \mathbf{L}) \cdot \alpha. 4. Compositing: Accumulate C{final} and \alpha along the ray using standard front-to-back or back-to-front compositing. Formulas: Emissive Color: C{emissive} = C(v). Phong Illumination: I = ka + kd (\mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{L}) + ks (\mathbf{R} \cdot \mathbf{V})^n, where \mathbf{R} is the reflection vector. Clip Plane Test: Sample \mathbf{x} is clipped if (\mathbf{x} - P0) \cdot \mathbf{n} < 0. Parameters: \epsilon: Distance threshold for "adjacent" samples. Not given in the sources. Phong coefficients (ka, kd, ks, n): Standard lighting parameters. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Random Lighting: In homogeneous materials, estimated gradients \mathbf{g} have random orientations due to noise in neighboring voxels, causing random lighting artifacts when used as normals in the Phong model. Emissive clip planes solve this by bypassing lighting at the cut plane where such noise is most visible. Dark Back-Facing Surfaces: Clipping reveals inner structures that may be back-facing relative to light sources, appearing as dark, unlit regions. Emissive illumination ensures these surfaces are visible with their classified color. Incorrect Materials via Interpolation: If clipping is done by setting voxel values to zero before classification, interpolation of zero values leads to incorrect material appearance. Emissive clip planes avoid this by classifying before clipping or by using emissive coloring directly on the classified result. Specular Reflections on Cut Plane: Customers disliked specular reflections on the cut plane itself, even though they wanted them on the volume. Emissive clip planes remove specular highlights at the boundary while preserving them elsewhere. Time Complexity: Same as standard volume rendering with gradient-based lighting, plus a simple adjacency check per sample. Memory Complexity: No additional memory required beyond standard volume rendering buffers. Performance: Implemented in hardware (TeraRecon VolumePro 1000), suggesting efficient execution. Strengths: Eliminates noisy lighting artifacts at clip boundaries; preserves material appearance; avoids dark back-facing surfaces; maintains specular highlights on the volume body. Limitations: Does not provide gradient-based shading on the cut plane itself; may appear less "realistic" if specular highlights are desired on the cut surface (though this was a customer preference). When to Use: When clipping volumes and visual artifacts (noise, darkness) at the cut plane are unacceptable, and specular highlights on the cut plane are undesirable. When Not to Use: When gradient-based shading (e.g., specular highlights) is required on the cut plane surface itself. Emissive Clip Planes were developed to address illumination issues in volume rendering, specifically in the context of the TeraRecon VolumePro 1000 hardware renderer. The technique was documented in an unofficial supplement to a paper on volume rendering, highlighting common problems in gradient-based lighting when clipping is applied. The approach leverages the concept of emissive illumination from OpenGL, where the color is taken directly from the classification without lighting modification. The problem of random lighting in homogeneous materials was also discussed by Kniss et al. in 2002, who proposed using gradient magnitude to interpolate between lit and unlit results, but this was deemed too expensive and visually unsatisfactory for cut planes due to unwanted specular reflections.
