name: Dual-Pass Differentiable Volume Rendering with Sparse Gradient Recording
head: Analytical Differentiable Volume Rendering, Concurrent Forward/Backward Pass, Differentiable Renderer based on Differential RTE, Sparse gradRec Gradient Storage
body: This method is a differentiable rendering technique that executes forward and backward passes concurrently to reuse the single-scattering Jacobian term J{ss} during backpropagation, utilizing a sparse structure gradRec to store gradients only along sampled ray paths rather than the entire volume grid. It sets itself apart from standard reverse-mode automatic differentiation by deriving an analytical differential expression for the radiance transport equation (RTE) to compute density derivatives directly, thereby avoiding the exclusive reliance on automatic differentiation and reducing memory usage from O(N^3) to O(RN). Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A volumetric density field (voxel grid), camera parameters (ray origins and directions), and lighting configuration (environment map or point/parallel lights). Outputs: Rendered image radiance L{out} and gradients with respect to the density field \dot{\kappa}t (or \dot{\sigma}t) for optimization. Data Structures: gradRec: A sparse stack structure that stores gradients only along active sampled ray paths, not the full volume grid. The structure supports push and pop operations. Voxel Grid: Uniform 3D grid where vp denotes a voxel position. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize: For each pixel/ray \mathbf{r}, initialize transmittance T=1 and accumulated radiance L=0. Initialize the gradRec stack for the current ray. 2. Ray Marching (Concurrent Forward/Backward): Iterate through samples p along the ray path from near to far. Forward Pass: Calculate the single-scattering radiance contribution L{ss} and transmittance \tau. Calculate J{ss} (the Jacobian of the single-scattering term with respect to density). If the scene uses an environment map: Estimate J{ss} using importance sampling over the unit sphere S^2. If the scene uses point or parallel lights: Calculate J{ss} directly without Monte Carlo integration, as lighting directions and radiance are known. Accumulate radiance: L{out} \leftarrow L{out} + \text{contribution}. Backward Pass / Gradient Recording: Compute the derivative of transmittance \dot{\tau} with respect to density. The formula is: \dot{\tau}(v{x0}, v{x1}) = -\tau(v{x0}, v{x1}) \sum{p=x0}^{x1} \dot{\kappa}t(vp) \Delta d where \dot{\kappa}t = \sigmat (extinction cross-section), vp is a voxel position, and \Delta d is the sampling step length. Compute the derivative of single-scattering radiance \dot{L}{ss}. Under the single-scattering assumption: \dot{L}{ss}(x, \omega) = \sum{p=xa}^{xb} \left( \dot{\tau}(vp, v{xb}) \kappat(vp) + \tau(vp, v{xb}) \dot{\kappa}t(vp) \right) J{ss}(vp, \omega) \Delta d + \sum{p=xa}^{xb} \tau(vp, v{xb}) \kappat(vp) \dot{J}{ss}(vp, \omega) \Delta d. Push to Sparse Stack: As intersections occur along the ray, push the computed gradients associated with the sampling positions onto the gradRec stack. This ensures gradients are stored only for active ray paths. 3. Interface Derivative Handling: When applying the Reynolds transport theorem to compute derivatives of integrals, disregard the derivative of the interface. This is a valid assumption only for purely participating media volumes where incident radiance L{ri} exhibits continuity in S^2. 4. Density Reconstruction (Post-Processing): After the forward/backward pass completes for all rays, compute the loss function between the target and primal images. Pop the gradRec stack to release memory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dualpassdifferentiablerendering(volumegrid, rays, lights): """ volumegrid: 3D array of density/extinction coefficients sigmat rays: list of ray objects, each with origin, direction, and samples lights: lighting configuration (environmentmap or pointlights) """ renderedimage = [0.0] len(rays) gradaccumulationgrid = [0.0] len(volumegrid) for rayidx, ray in enumerate(rays): gradrecstack = [] T = 1.0 Lout = 0.0 taudotsum = 0.0 for sample in ray.samples: pos = sample.position deltad = sample.stepsize sigmat = volumegrid[pos] # Forward pass: compute single-scattering radiance and Jacobian # Compute Jss based on lighting type if lights.isenvironmentmap: # Importance sampling over unit sphere S^2 Jss = sum(lights.envmap.sample(omega) math.cos(theta) / pdf(omega) for omega in sampledirections) else: # Direct calculation for point/parallel lights Jss = sum(light.intensity light.direction.dot(ray.direction) for light in lights.pointlights) # Accumulate radiance Lout += T sigmat Jss deltad # Update transmittance T = math.exp(-sigmat deltad) # Backward pass / Gradient recording # Compute derivative of transmittance segment taudotsum += sigmat deltad taudot = -T taudotsum # Compute derivative of single-scattering radiance # kappadott = sigmat gradsigma = (taudot sigmat Jss + T sigmat Jss) deltad # Add Jss derivative term if available # gradsigma += T sigmat Jssdot deltad # Push gradients to sparse stack as intersections occur gradrecstack.append((pos, gradsigma)) renderedimage[rayidx] = Lout # Density reconstruction: pop stack to release memory for ray in rays: while ray.gradstack: pos, gradval = ray.gradstack.pop() gradaccumulationgrid[pos] += gradval return renderedimage, gradaccumulationgrid Parameters: Sampling Step Size (\Delta d): Defined as the length of the sampling step along the ray. Lighting Type: Determines the method for calculating J{ss} (importance sampling vs. direct calculation). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Monte Carlo Cost: Straightforward Monte Carlo integration for sphere integration is computationally expensive. This is mitigated by using importance sampling for environment maps and direct computation for point/parallel lights. Interface Derivatives: The derivative of the interface in the Reynolds transport theorem is disregarded. This is a valid assumption only for purely participating media volumes where incident radiance L{ri} exhibits continuity in S^2. Memory Management: The gradRec stack must be properly popped after the density field update to release memory. Failure to do so leads to memory leaks, although the complexity is still bounded by O(RN) per frame if cleared. Density Reconstruction via Differentiable Rendering is the optimization step that updates a volumetric density field \rho by backpropagating image-space errors into the volume grid. It solves the inverse problem of recovering physical density from observed images by computing the gradient of a loss function with respect to voxel values and applying gradient descent. It sets itself apart from naive differentiable rendering by avoiding a separate backward pass or recomputation of the forward ray march; instead, it relies on gradient records stored during the forward pass (provided by Dual-Pass Differentiable Volume Rendering with Sparse Gradient Recording) to scatter gradients directly to neighboring voxels. Time Complexity: The concurrent forward/backward pass allows for efficient reuse of J{ss}. The complexity is dominated by ray marching and the calculation of J{ss}. Importance sampling mitigates the computational expense of straightforward Monte Carlo integration for environment maps, while direct calculation is used for point/parallel lights. Memory Complexity: Reduced from O(N^3) (storing gradients for all voxels) to O(RN), where N is the voxel grid dimension (or ray length) and R is the number of rays. This is achieved by maintaining gradients only along active ray paths using the gradRec stack. Strengths: High computational efficacy for fluid density optimization; avoids the high memory cost of standard reverse-mode AD; analytical derivatives provide precise gradients without the noise of stochastic AD. Limitations: Assumes single-scattering or requires specific handling of multiple scattering (not detailed in the provided notes for the differential form); limited to purely participating media (no interface derivatives). When to use: When optimizing volumetric density fields from images (inverse rendering) and memory is a constraint, particularly for large voxel grids where O(N^3) is prohibitive. Origin: The method is described in "Physics-Based Differentiable Rendering for Efficient and Plausible Fluid Modeling from Monocular Video". History: It builds upon the radiance transport equation (RTE) and its differential form. It incorporates the Reynolds transport theorem for computing derivatives of hydrodynamic integral equations. Usage: Used for fluid density optimization and reconstruction from monocular video. name: Density Reconstruction via Differentiable Rendering
head: Density Field Update, Density Reconstruction, Density Reconstruction via Gradient Scattering
body: Density Reconstruction via Differentiable Rendering is the optimization step that updates a volumetric density field \rho by backpropagating image-space errors into the volume grid. It solves the inverse problem of recovering physical density from observed images by computing the gradient of a loss function with respect to voxel values and applying gradient descent. It sets itself apart from naive differentiable rendering by avoiding a separate backward pass or recomputation of the forward ray march; instead, it relies on gradient records stored during the forward pass (provided by Dual-Pass Differentiable Volume Rendering with Sparse Gradient Recording) to scatter gradients directly to neighboring voxels. Inputs: Target image L{tag} (ground truth or reference). Rendered image L{out} (output of the forward differentiable renderer). Current density field \rho (volume grid). Gradient records densityADRec: a structure containing, for each pixel (i,j), a list of sampling positions x{u,k} visited during ray marching and their corresponding single-scattering gradient contributions \dot{L}{out}(x{u,k}, \omega). Outputs: Updated density field \rho and loss value. Data Structures: densityGrad: A volume data structure (grid) of the same dimensions as \rho, initialized to zero, storing the accumulated gradients \frac{\partial \text{Loss}}{\partial \rho[vp]} for each voxel vp. Parameters: Learning rate \alpha (denoted as LR in, \alpha in). Minimum loss threshold minLoss for convergence. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Gradient Accumulator: Set all entries in densityGrad to zero. 2. Compute Image-Space Loss Gradient: For each pixel (i,j), compute the difference term: diff[i,j] = 2(L{out}[i,j] - L{tag}[i,j]) This represents the derivative of the Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss with respect to the rendered pixel value. 3. Scatter Gradients to Voxels: For each pixel (i,j): For each recorded gradient contribution k in densityADRec[i,j]: Retrieve the sampling position xu and the gradient contribution grad = \dot{L}{out}(x{u,k}, \omega). Compute the trilinear interpolation weights w{vp}(xu) for the 8 neighboring voxels vp surrounding xu. For each of the 8 neighboring voxels vp: densityGrad[vp] \leftarrow densityGrad[vp] + diff[i,j] \cdot grad \cdot w{vp}(xu) This step implements the chain rule, distributing the pixel-space error back to the volume grid using the stored gradients and consistent trilinear weights. The final gradient for a voxel vp is formally: \frac{\partial \text{Loss}}{\partial \rho[vp]} = \sum{(i,j)} \sumk 2(L{out}[i,j] - L{tag}[i,j]) \cdot \dot{L}{out}(x{u,k}, \omega) \cdot w{vp}(x{u,k}) \quad (22) where the summation is over all pixels and all sampling positions k along the rays passing through vp. 4. Update Density Field: Iterate through each voxel position vp in the volume grid: \rho[vp] \leftarrow \rho[vp] - \alpha \cdot densityGrad[vp] where \alpha is the learning rate. 5. Convergence Check: Compute the total MSE loss between L{out} and L{tag}. If the loss is less than minLoss, terminate. Otherwise, repeat from Step 1 (re-rendering L{out} with the updated \rho). 6. Cleanup: Release the memory allocated for densityADRec and densityGrad. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def densityreconstruction(Ltag, Lout, rho, densityADRec, LR, minLoss): """ Reconstructs the density field rho by backpropagating image-space loss. Args: Ltag: Target image tensor (H, W, C). Lout: Rendered image tensor (H, W, C). rho: Current density field volume grid (D, Hv, Wv). densityADRec: List of lists of tuples. densityADRec[i][j] contains [(xu, gradout),...] for pixel (i,j). LR: Learning rate. minLoss: Convergence threshold. Returns: rho: Updated density field. loss: Final MSE loss. """ H, W, C = Ltag.shape D, Hv, Wv = rho.shape while True: # Compute MSE loss loss = 0.0 for i in range(H): for j in range(W): for c in range(C): diffval = Lout[i, j, c] - Ltag[i, j, c] loss += diffval diffval loss /= (H W C) if loss < minLoss: break # Initialize gradient accumulator densityGrad = [[[0.0] Wv for in range(Hv)] for in range(D)] # Scatter gradients for i in range(H): for j in range(W): diff = 2.0 (Lout[i, j] - Ltag[i, j]) for xu, gradout in densityADRec[i][j]: x, y, z = xu ix, iy, iz = int(x), int(y), int(z) fx, fy, fz = x - ix, y - iy, z - iz # Trilinear weights for 8 neighbors w = [ (1-fx)(1-fy)(1-fz), (1-fx)(1-fy)fz, (1-fx)fy(1-fz), (1-fx)fyfz, fx(1-fy)(1-fz), fx(1-fy)fz, fxfy(1-fz), fxfyfz ] # Neighbor indices neighbors = [ (ix, iy, iz), (ix, iy, iz+1), (ix, iy+1, iz), (ix, iy+1, iz+1), (ix+1, iy, iz), (ix+1, iy, iz+1), (ix+1, iy+1, iz), (ix+1, iy+1, iz+1) ] for idx, (nx, ny, nz) in enumerate(neighbors): densityGrad[nx][ny][nz] += diff gradout w[idx] # Update density field for x in range(D): for y in range(Hv): for z in range(Wv): rho[x][y][z] -= LR densityGrad[x][y][z] # Cleanup del densityADRec del densityGrad return rho, loss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Trilinear Consistency: The gradient scattering must use the exact same trilinear interpolation weights as the forward pass to ensure consistency between the forward and backward passes. Memory Usage: Storing densityADRec increases memory usage compared to methods that recompute gradients on-the-fly, as it stores gradient contributions for every sampled position along every ray. Single Scattering Limitation: The method relies on the single scattering approximation. It is limited to scenarios where multiple scattering effects are negligible, such as smoke with relatively low optical density. It is not suitable for denser media like cumulus clouds or highly turbid liquids. Time Complexity: The reconstruction step itself is O(N{voxels} + N{samples}), where N{voxels} is the number of voxels updated and N{samples} is the total number of recorded gradient contributions. However, it is part of an iterative loop, so total time depends on convergence speed. Memory Complexity: O(N{samples}) for storing densityADRec and O(N{voxels}) for densityGrad. This trades memory for computational efficiency by avoiding a separate backward pass. Strengths: Efficient reconstruction without recomputing the forward pass; physically meaningful updates via the linear relationship \kappat(x) = \sigmat \rho(x). Limitations: Limited to single-scattering scenarios; memory-intensive for high-resolution volumes or long rays due to densityADRec storage. This method is part of a physics-based differentiable rendering framework for fluid and smoke reconstruction. The approach leverages the linear relationship between extinction coefficient and density to compute derivatives directly, enabling efficient optimization. It builds on the sparse gradient recording technique to avoid the computational cost of full backpropagation through the ray marching process. name: Differentiable Rendering and Sampling Methods
head: Differentiable Ray Marching
body: Differentiable Rendering and Sampling Methods are rendering algorithms that numerically integrate along camera rays through a volumetric scene representation (such as a Neural Radiance Field or Signed Distance Function), where the integration process is made differentiable with respect to scene parameters to enable gradient-based optimization. Unlike differentiable rasterization, which uses explicit geometry and pixel/primitive association, this method relies on volumetric fields and numerical integration, requiring surface extraction for explicit mesh output. It serves as the core mechanism for training Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and optimizing implicit 3D scene representations from 2D image observations. The method approximates the volume rendering integral by discretizing it into a sum over sampled points, making the process differentiable for gradient-based optimization of scene parameters like density and color. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera parameters (origin, direction), scene representation (implicit function, e.g., MLP or hash grid), and ground truth image (for loss computation). Outputs: Rendered pixel color \hat{C} and gradients with respect to scene parameters. Data Structures: Scene Representation: A neural network (e.g., MLP) or data structure (e.g., Instant NGP) that maps 3D coordinates (and viewing direction) to volumetric properties. For NeRF, it outputs density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. For SDF-based models, it outputs a signed distance value and a feature vector for color. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel, generate a camera ray \mathbf{r} defined by its origin (camera center) and direction. 2. Sampling: Sample points along the ray at discrete intervals. Stratified sampling is often used to randomly jitter sample positions within each interval to reduce aliasing artifacts. Hierarchical Sampling (Efficiency Optimization): Use a two-stage process. Coarse Stage: Predict density at evenly spaced samples to produce a rough density distribution. Fine Stage: Allocate more samples to regions with high density (likely containing surfaces) based on the coarse distribution. This is importance sampling to focus computation. 3. Scene Query: At each sampled 3D point \mathbf{x}i, query the scene representation network. The network outputs density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i (or features for color). 4. Differentiable Compositing: Compute the final pixel color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) using the volume rendering equation. The discrete, differentiable approximation is alpha compositing: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \cdot \alphai \cdot \mathbf{c}i where: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) is the opacity at sample i, derived from density \sigmai and step size \deltai. Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance, representing the probability the ray travels to sample i without hitting anything. \mathbf{c}i is the color at sample i. 5. Loss Computation: Compute a loss (e.g., Mean Squared Error) between the rendered image \hat{C} and the ground truth image C{gt}. Auxiliary Losses: Eikonal Loss (enforces unit norm spatial gradients for SDFs) and Total Variation Loss (smooths density fields) may be added. 6. Optimization: Backpropagate the loss through the compositing weights and into the network parameters (MLP weights, encoding parameters) to calculate gradients. Update parameters using an optimizer like Adam to minimize photometric error. Pseudocode: def differentiablerender(rayorigin, raydirection, near, far, numsamples, scenequery): # 1. Generate sample positions along the ray tvals = linspace(near, far, numsamples) points = rayorigin + tvals[:, None] raydirection # 2. Compute step sizes (delta) deltas = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] deltas = concat([deltas, deltas[-1:]]) # Pad last delta to match numsamples # 3. Query scene for density and color sigma, color = scenequery(points) # 4. Compute opacity alpha alpha = 1.0 - exp(-sigma deltas) # 5. Compute transmittance T # Ti = exp(-sum{j<i} sigmaj deltaj) sigmadeltas = sigma deltas cumsumsigmadeltas = cumsum(sigmadeltas) T = exp(-cumsumsigmadeltas) T = concat([ones(1), T[:-1]]) # T0 = 1 # 6. Compute weights and final color weights = T alpha renderedcolor = sum(weights[:, None] color, axis=0) return renderedcolor, T, alpha, weights Parameters: Num Samples: Number of points sampled per ray. Hierarchical sampling uses coarse and fine stages. Optimizer: Adam is commonly used. Loss Functions: Mean Squared Error (MSE) for photometric error, Eikonal Loss for SDFs, Total Variation Loss for density smoothing. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision issues can arise in transmittance calculation for very dense or transparent volumes. Boundaries: Handling near and far clipping planes correctly is essential to avoid sampling outside the scene. Degenerate Input: Empty space or zero density regions can lead to undefined behavior if not handled (e.g., by clamping or skipping). Monte Carlo Radiance Estimate (MC + RVS) is an unbiased color estimation method for differentiable volume rendering that accelerates training in voxel-based scene representations like DVGO by evaluating fewer samples per ray. It replaces deterministic ray marching with stochastic sampling, yielding a ×6 speedup over DVGO's sparsity thresholding with k=8 at the cost of increased estimate variance. It provides an unbiased radiance estimate for any sample count k, making it suitable for architectures where density field evaluation is faster than radiance field evaluation. Ray Marching with Differential Diffusion is a differentiable volume rendering method that computes single and multiple scattering radiance alongside their derivatives with respect to density simultaneously. It solves the problem of efficient gradient accumulation for density optimization by storing intermediate gradient contributions in a dedicated structure, avoiding the need for a separate backward pass or on-the-fly recomputation. Unlike Monte Carlo Radiance Estimate for Scene Reconstruction which relies on stochastic sampling, this method uses deterministic ray marching with pre-computed diffusion terms. It differs from Image-based Transfer Function Optimization via Automatic Differentiation by explicitly modeling the physics of participating media (single/multiple scattering) rather than optimizing transfer functions directly on image space. This method optimizes a transfer function To for an optimization volume field Fo such that its rendered images match those of a reference volume field Fr rendered with a reference transfer function Tr. It solves the problem of finding a visual mapping for one dataset that reproduces the appearance of another, enabling comparative volume rendering. It differs from voxel-based least-squares approaches by minimizing the difference between final rendered images rather than per-voxel color residuals, thereby prioritizing voxels that have a larger effect on the final image. It builds on Differentiable Rendering and Sampling Methods by applying automatic differentiation to the direct volume rendering compositing equation. Soft Rasterizer is a differentiable rendering method that replaces the deterministic z-buffer depth test with a probabilistic aggregation, treating each triangle as a probabilistic cloud to compute pixel color as a weighted sum of contributions from all mesh triangles, including hidden ones. It solves the problem of non-differentiable visibility discontinuities in standard rasterization, allowing gradients to flow to occluded and distant triangle vertices, which makes it particularly suitable for geometry optimization tasks like single-view mesh reconstruction. Unlike its siblings, it does not use z-culling; instead, it relies on a probability map derived from 2D screen-space distances and depth to fuse color contributions, ensuring that the entire image contributes to the gradient of every vertex. RGBXY Derivatives with Optimal Transport (DROT) is a differentiable rendering method that associates each screen-space pixel with a visible 3D geometric point (point proxy) to compute 5D RGBXY derivatives, measuring how 3D RGB color and 2D projected screen-space position change with respect to scene parameters. It combines these dense derivatives with an optimal transport-based loss function to find pixel matching between rendered and target images, solving the convergence problem in inverse rendering when initial and target object locations are not close. Unlike traditional methods that rely on sparse, local per-pixel color derivatives and L2 loss, DROT captures global and long-range object motions, making it superior for optimizing global translations and rotations. A render output carrying the sensitivity of a scalar objective M with respect to scene parameters θ. It allows human inspection of which parts of a scene matter for a given goal, analogous to how primal AOVs expose intermediate light transport quantities. Not given in the sources. A generalized differentiable mesh renderer that models the forward rendering process under a probabilistic perturbation defined by a probability distribution with density f and a temperature/scale parameter τ > 0, making the renderer continuous everywhere and differentiable almost everywhere. Not given in the sources. A rendering technique used to compute global illumination via single-bounce differentiable MC ray tracing within the JOC framework. JOC uses single-bounce differentiable MC rendering, whereas previous methods like NVDIFFRECMC avoided multi-bounce due to noise and cost, limiting them to direct lighting. A technique to capture derivative contributions from visibility changes (discontinuities) that normal path samples miss by explicitly sampling discontinuity edges. Unlike naive automatic differentiation which only differentiates the currently traced path and misses boundary effects when an edge crosses a ray, edge sampling captures the missing boundary term. Introduced by Li et al. in 'Differentiable Monte Carlo Ray Tracing through Edge Sampling' at SIGGRAPH Asia 2018. An architecture using an MLP to map 16 semantic channels to 16 color space channels, decoded with a final MLP on the 16-channel output image. It performs compositing in an abstract 16-channel color space, using VNetLight for encoding, direct compositing of semantic channels, and an MLP decoder for the final RGB image. Steps include using VNetLight architecture to implement the volume encoder producing a 16-channel volume, using the same MLP architecture as VNetL16-4 for feature mapping but using 16 semantic channels directly in compositing, decoding the resulting 16-channel image (plus one additional alpha channel) using another MLP with one ReLU-activated 16-channel hidden layer and a sigmoid output layer to yield a 3-channel RGB image, and using the opacity directly as produced from the DVRUnit. Layout: Encoder: VNet16. TF: MLP16. Accumulation: Alpha. Decoder: MLP3. Parameters: ~12.3 M. A method to reconstruct a 3D mesh of an object from Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) images at known aspect angles by optimizing the mesh geometry using a differentiable renderer and a composite loss function. The total loss is a weighted sum of five terms: L{total} = E[|y - \tilde{y}|^2] + 1.5Ll + 0.02Ln + 0.03Le + 0.4Lf, where y is the label SAR image, \tilde{y} is the rendered prediction, Ll is Laplacian loss, Ln is Normal Consistency loss, Le is Edge Length loss, and Lf is Floor-Plane loss. Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples per ray and the complexity of the scene query network. Hierarchical sampling reduces the number of samples needed for high-quality results. Memory Complexity: Standard reverse-mode AD requires storing intermediate states, leading to high memory usage. Strengths: Enables gradient-based optimization of 3D scene representations from 2D images; handles complex topology and view consistency; suitable for view synthesis and scene reconstruction. Limitations: Stochastic methods introduce variance; requires careful tuning of sampling and loss functions. When to Use: When optimizing implicit 3D scene representations (NeRF, SDFs) from 2D images; when view synthesis or scene reconstruction is required. When Not to Use: When explicit geometry output is needed without surface extraction; when real-time performance is critical without pre-training. Differentiable Ray Marching is a core algorithm in neural rendering that enables the optimization of 3D scene parameters by making the process of synthesizing a 2D image from a volumetric representation fully differentiable. It is primarily used in Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) training for view synthesis and scene reconstruction from 2D images. It is also used in Signed Distance Function (SDF) optimization (NeuS, VolSDF), Occupancy Network training, and inverse rendering applications like intrinsic decomposition and neural reflectance fields. The method builds on the volume rendering equation and the propagation of gradients through the integration steps. name: Ray Marching with Differential Diffusion
head: Differentiable Ray Marching with Gradient Recording, Ray Marching for Gradient Accumulation
body: Ray Marching with Differential Diffusion computes single and multiple scattering radiance alongside their derivatives with respect to density simultaneously. It solves the gradient accumulation problem for density optimization by storing intermediate gradient contributions in a dedicated structure, avoiding a separate backward pass or on-the-fly recomputation. Unlike Monte Carlo Radiance Estimate for Scene Reconstruction which relies on stochastic sampling, this method uses deterministic ray marching with pre-computed diffusion terms. It differs from Image-based Transfer Function Optimization via Automatic Differentiation by explicitly modeling participating media physics rather than optimizing image-space transfer functions. Inputs: Density field \rho. Extinction coefficient \kappat = \sigmat \rho. Incoming radiance L{in}. Pre-computed radiance terms Q{0,ri}, Q{1,ri} and their derivatives \dot{Q}{0,ri}, \dot{Q}{1,ri}. Source term field S. Absorption coefficient \kappaa. Voxel edge length h (uniform 3D grid assumption). Sampling step length \Delta d. Outputs: Rendered image L{out}. Gradient records densityADRec. densityADRec: For each pixel (i, j), this structure contains two lists: 1. position: Stores the voxel positions xu visited along the ray. 2. grad: Stores the corresponding gradient contributions \dot{L}{out}(xu, \omega). The gradient computed at xu is associated with the integer voxel coordinates v{xu} containing xu. During density updates, this gradient is implicitly scattered to the 8 neighbors of v{xu} when trilinear updates are employed. Before ray marching, a precomputation function initializes variables to avoid redundant calculations during the march. 1. Solve the diffusion equation iteratively (e.g., using the Jacobi method) to compute diffusion radiance L^0d, its derivative \partial\pi L^0d, and the diffusion radiance derivative \vec{L}^1d and its derivative \partial\pi \vec{L}^1d. 2. Store L{ri}, L^0d, \vec{L}^1d and their derivatives \partial\pi L{ri}, \partial\pi L^0d, \partial\pi \vec{L}^1d as voxels. 1. Initialize: For each pixel, generate a ray and determine entry xa and exit xb points. S1 initializes xu = xb and marches back-to-front; S2 initializes xu = xa and marches front-to-back. Let D{max} = \|xb - xa\|. Let Db be the distance from the exit point to the view point. 2. Loop: S1 repeats while Du < D{max}; S2 repeats while Du \ge Db. Fetch Data: Sample \rho(xu), \kappat(xu), and pre-computed terms (Q{0,ri}, Q{1,ri}, \dot{Q}{0,ri}, \dot{Q}{1,ri}) using trilinear interpolation from their voxel grids. Identify voxel position v{xu}. Compute In-Scattered Radiance: Compute J{ss}(xu, \omega) using pre-computed terms. Specifically, J{ss} = \Omega(Q{0,ri} + Q{1,ri}\omega). Compute J{ms}(xu, \omega) using Equation 3. Compute Derivatives: Compute \dot{J}{ss} using the derivatives of the pre-computed terms. Specifically, \dot{J}{ss} = \Omega(\dot{Q}{0,ri} + \dot{Q}{1,ri}\omega). Compute \partial\pi J{ms} using Equation 8. Accumulate Radiance and Gradient: Calculate transmittance \tau(v{xu}, v{xb}) from the current voxel to the exit/view point. Update Single Scattering Radiance L{ss}: L{ss} \leftarrow L{ss} + \tau \kappat J{ss} \Delta d. Update Single Scattering Gradient: \dot{L}{ss} \leftarrow \dot{L}{ss} + \tau \kappat \dot{J}{ss} \Delta d + (\partial\pi \tau \kappat + \tau \partial\pi \kappat) J{ss} \Delta d. Update Multiple Scattering Radiance L{ms} and Gradient \partial\pi L{ms} similarly. Update Direct Transmission L{ri} and Gradient \partial\pi L{ri} using pre-computed values. Store Gradient (S1 specific): Store xu and \dot{L}{out}(xu, \omega) in densityADRec. Advance: xu \leftarrow xu + \omega \Delta d. Recalculate distance Du. 3. Finalize: Compute final L{ri} and \partial\pi L{ri} if not fully accumulated during the loop. Sum components: L{out} = L{ms} + L{ri} + L{ss}. \partial\pi L{out} = \partial\pi L{ms} + \partial\pi L{ri} + \partial\pi L{ss}. Output L{out} and densityADRec. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchingdifferentialdiffusion( rhogrid, kappatgrid, Lin, Q0rigrid, Q1rigrid, Q0dotrigrid, Q1dotrigrid, Sgrid, kappaagrid, h, deltad, pixelindices, volumemin, volumemax): """ Computes radiance and gradients for differentiable volume rendering. Implements S1's back-to-front march with gradient recording. """ Lout = {} densityADRec = {} for idx in pixelindices: rayorigin, raydirection = generateray(idx, pixelindices, volumemin, volumemax) omega = -raydirection # Direction of travel into volume (3D vector) xa, xb = rayboxintersection(rayorigin, omega, volumemin, volumemax) # S2: Precomputation step (simplified) Lrigrid, Lridotgrid = precomputediffusion(Sgrid, kappaagrid, kappatgrid, h) Lms = 0.0 Lmsdot = 0.0 Lss = 0.0 Lssdot = 0.0 Lri = 0.0 Lridot = 0.0 # S1: March from back (xb) to front (xa) xu = xb Dmax = norm(xb - xa) Du = 0.0 densityADRec[idx] = {'position': [], 'grad': []} while Du < Dmax: # 1. Fetch Data rhoval = trilinearinterpolate(rhogrid, xu) kappatval = trilinearinterpolate(kappatgrid, xu) Q0 = trilinearinterpolate(Q0rigrid, xu) Q1 = trilinearinterpolate(Q1rigrid, xu) Q0dot = trilinearinterpolate(Q0dotrigrid, xu) Q1dot = trilinearinterpolate(Q1dotrigrid, xu) vxu = getvoxelindex(xu, h) # 2. Compute In-Scattered Radiance (Single Scattering) Jss = dot3(Q1, omega) + Q0 Jssdot = dot3(Q1dot, omega) + Q0dot # 3. Compute Transmittance from xu to xb tauxuxb = computetransmittance(kappatgrid, xu, xb, omega, deltad) tauxuxbdot = computetransmittancederivative(kappatgrid, xu, xb, omega, deltad) # 4. Accumulate Single Scattering termss = tauxuxb kappatval Jss deltad Lss += termss # Gradient contribution for S1 gradcontribss = (tauxuxb kappatval Jssdot + (tauxuxbdot kappatval + tauxuxb kappatval) Jss) deltad # 5. Store Gradient Record (S1) densityADRec[idx]['position'].append(xu) densityADRec[idx]['grad'].append(gradcontribss) # 6. Advance xu = xu + omega deltad Du = norm(xu - xa) # Final Summation (S2) Lrival = trilinearinterpolate(Lrigrid, xb) Lridotval = trilinearinterpolate(Lridotgrid, xb) Lout[idx] = Lss + Lrival densityADRec[idx]['finalgrad'] = sum(densityADRec[idx]['grad']) + Lridotval return Lout, densityADRec def generateray(idx, pixelindices, volumemin, volumemax): # Standard camera ray generation pass def rayboxintersection(origin, direction, minpt, maxpt): # Standard slab method for ray-AABB intersection pass def precomputediffusion(Sgrid, kappaagrid, kappatgrid, h): # Solves diffusion equation iteratively (Jacobi) for L0d, L1d, Lri pass def trilinearinterpolate(grid, point): # Standard trilinear interpolation pass def getvoxelindex(point, h): # Returns integer voxel coordinates pass def dot3(a, b): # Dot product for 3D vectors return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def norm(v): # Euclidean norm return (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 def computetransmittance(kappatgrid, xstart, xend, omega, deltad): # Computes exp(-integral of kappat from xstart to xend) pass def computetransmittancederivative(kappatgrid, xstart, xend, omega, deltad): # Computes -tau integral of d(kappat)/drho pass \Delta d: Sampling step length. h: Voxel edge length. \kappat: Extinction coefficient. \kappaa: Absorption coefficient. S: Source term field. Memory Usage: Storing densityADRec increases memory usage significantly compared to methods that recompute gradients on-the-fly, as it stores position and gradient contributions for every sample point along every ray. Precision: Trilinear interpolation is used for fetching data, which may introduce smoothing artifacts in gradients if the density field is highly discontinuous. Boundary Conditions: The hit point calculation (xa, xb) must be robust to avoid rays missing the volume or entering/exiting incorrectly, which would break the transmittance accumulation. Uses the diffusion equation to approximate multiple scattering and direct transmission, storing them as voxel grids to accelerate ray marching. A data structure that stores intermediate gradient contributions during the forward pass, enabling efficient density updates without a full backward pass. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples per ray and the number of pixels. The precomputation step adds an initial cost proportional to the volume size. Memory Complexity: High. Requires storage for the density grid, coefficient grids, pre-computed radiance grids, and the densityADRec structure which scales with the number of samples. Strengths: Efficient gradient computation for density optimization; avoids the variance of Monte Carlo methods; leverages pre-computation for speed. Limitations: High memory consumption due to gradient recording; assumes uniform grid (S2) or requires careful interpolation (S1); limited to participating media with specific scattering models. When to use: When optimizing density fields for smoke/volumetric reconstruction and memory is not the primary constraint. When not to use: When the volume is not represented on a uniform grid (S2 assumption) or when strict memory budgets prohibit storing per-sample gradient records. This method originates from research in differentiable volume rendering for smoke reconstruction and participating media simulation. It builds upon the physics-based differentiable renderer framework and differential diffusion theory for participating media. The approach was developed to address the computational cost of backpropagation in volumetric rendering by caching gradient contributions. name: Differentiable Monte Carlo Ray Tracing
head: Differentiable MC Ray Tracing
body: Differentiable Monte Carlo Ray Tracing is a rendering technique that computes global illumination by combining stochastic path sampling with automatic differentiation to propagate gradients from the image plane back to scene parameters (geometry, materials, lights). It sets itself apart from deterministic ray marching methods by replacing fixed sampling grids with stochastic estimators, which allows for unbiased radiance estimates and accelerates training in voxel-based scene representations by evaluating fewer samples per ray. Unlike previous differentiable MC methods that avoided multi-bounce tracing due to noise and cost, this approach enables single-bounce (and potentially multi-bounce) differentiable MC ray tracing within a joint optimization framework. Inputs: Scene geometry (e.g., triangle meshes, neural fields), material properties (e.g., PBR parameters, albedo textures), light sources (e.g., HDR light probes), and camera parameters. Outputs: Differentiable image radiance and gradients with respect to input parameters. Data Structures: The method relies on standard Monte Carlo path tracing data structures, augmented with automatic differentiation (AD) graphs. Path State: Contains current position, direction, throughput, and accumulated radiance. AD Graph: Tracks operations on differentiable parameters to enable backpropagation. Radiance Cache: An enhancement over traditional radiance caches, used to initialize differentiable marching tetrahedrons (DMTet) and model indirect illumination. Steps: 1. Ray Generation: Cast primary rays from the camera through each pixel. 2. Stochastic Sampling: Instead of deterministic ray marching, sample interaction points along the ray or on surfaces using probability density functions (PDFs). 3. Radiance Estimation: Compute the contribution of the sampled path. For global illumination, use a radiance cache to estimate indirect lighting efficiently. 4. Differentiable Evaluation: Evaluate the radiance contribution using differentiable primitives. The measurement equation is integrated via Monte Carlo estimation: I = \int We(x, \omega) Li(x, \omega) dx d\omega where We is the importance function and Li is the incoming radiance. 5. Gradient Propagation: Use reverse-mode automatic differentiation to compute gradients of the image loss with respect to scene parameters. The AD graph traverses the computation history to backpropagate gradients through the stochastic sampling and radiance evaluation steps. 6. Optimization: Update scene parameters using the computed gradients. Parameters: Sample Count: The number of Monte Carlo samples per pixel. Higher counts reduce variance but increase computation time. Bounce Depth: The maximum number of light bounces. Single-bounce is commonly used for direct lighting, while multi-bounce is avoided in some implementations due to noise. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visibility Discontinuities: Naive automatic differentiation misses boundary effects when an occluder edge crosses a ray, as the visibility function is a step function. This requires specialized techniques like edge sampling. Jacobian Factors: Transformations from UV space to surface and then to camera rays involve Jacobian determinants (geometry term \frac{\cos(\theta)}{d^2}). Omitting these can assign equal weight to optimization variables, which may be desirable for convergence but differs from standard Monte Carlo weighting. Monte Carlo Radiance Estimate (MC + RVS) is an unbiased color estimation method for differentiable volume rendering that accelerates training in voxel-based scene representations like DVGO by evaluating fewer samples per ray. It replaces deterministic ray marching with stochastic sampling, yielding a ×6 speedup over DVGO's sparsity thresholding with k=8 at the cost of increased estimate variance. It provides an unbiased radiance estimate for any sample count k, making it suitable for architectures where density field evaluation is faster than radiance field evaluation. Edge sampling is a technique to capture derivative contributions from visibility changes (discontinuities) that normal path samples miss by explicitly sampling discontinuity edges. Unlike naive automatic differentiation which only differentiates the currently traced path and misses boundary effects when an edge crosses a ray, edge sampling captures the missing boundary term. Introduced by Li et al. in 'Differentiable Monte Carlo Ray Tracing through Edge Sampling' at SIGGRAPH Asia 2018. Jacobian factor omission is a method where explicit Jacobian terms (UV mapping distortion and geometry term \frac{\cos(\theta)}{d^2}) are omitted from the Monte Carlo weight calculation. This assigns equal weight to all optimization variables, implicitly introducing a factor \alphaj that cancels them out in the per-ray objective function. It contrasts with Tsai et al. [TSG19], where reconstructed surface points are sampled directly and all Jacobian terms are included; Tsai's method is suitable for non-line-of-sight reconstruction with roughly constant observation distances, whereas this method handles varying distances. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of Monte Carlo samples and path bounces. Single-bounce tracing is faster than multi-bounce. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the scene representation (e.g., neural fields, meshes) and the AD graph. Measured Performance: In voxel-based scene representations like DVGO, Monte Carlo radiance estimates can yield a ×6 speedup over deterministic ray marching with sparsity thresholding. Strengths: Unbiased estimates, ability to handle complex geometry and materials, acceleration of training in neural rendering. Limitations: High variance with few samples, noise in multi-bounce tracing, missing visibility derivatives without edge sampling. When to Use: When unbiased gradients are required, or when scene representation evaluation is expensive compared to radiance evaluation. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and variance is unacceptable, or when visibility derivatives are crucial and edge sampling is not implemented. Differentiable Monte Carlo Ray Tracing originated from the need to optimize complex 3D scenes using gradient-based methods. Early differentiable renderers like NVDIFFRECMC avoided multi-bounce path tracing due to noise and cost, limiting them to direct lighting. The Joint Optimization of Triangle Mesh, Material, and Light from Neural Fields with Neural Radiance Cache (NRC) introduced single-bounce differentiable MC ray tracing to jointly optimize geometry, material, and light through backpropagation. Edge sampling was introduced by Li et al. at SIGGRAPH Asia 2018 to handle visibility derivatives. Jacobian factor omission was proposed in texture-space differentiable rendering to simplify optimization by omitting explicit Jacobian terms. name: Monte Carlo Radiance Estimate for Scene Reconstruction
head: MC + RVS
body: Monte Carlo Radiance Estimate (MC + RVS) is an unbiased color estimation method for differentiable volume rendering that accelerates training in voxel-based scene representations like DVGO by evaluating fewer samples per ray. It replaces deterministic ray marching with stochastic sampling, yielding a ×6 speedup over DVGO's sparsity thresholding with k=8 at the cost of increased estimate variance. It provides an unbiased radiance estimate for any sample count k, making it suitable for architectures where density field evaluation is faster than radiance field evaluation. Inputs: Camera ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a density field \sigma(\mathbf{x}) and radiance field \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) parameterized by voxel grids; number of samples k (fixed or adaptive). Outputs: Estimated pixel color \hat{C}. The method operates on voxel grid representations for density and radiance, consistent with DVGO-like architectures. No additional complex data structures are required beyond the standard grids. 1. Ray Sampling: For a given ray, select k sample points \mathbf{x}i along the ray segment within the bounding volume. 2. Field Evaluation: Evaluate the density \sigmai = \sigma(\mathbf{x}i) and radiance \mathbf{c}i = \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{d}) at each sample point. 3. Transmittance Calculation: Compute the accumulated transmittance Ti = \exp\left(-\int0^{ti} \sigma(\tau) d\tau\right) for each sample [G: Standard volume rendering transmittance definition]. 4. Monte Carlo Estimation: The final color \hat{C} is estimated as the unbiased average of the radiance contributions weighted by transmittance and density, scaled by the ray segment length L: \hat{C} = \frac{L}{k} \sum{i=1}^{k} Ti \sigmai \mathbf{c}i This estimator is unbiased for any given number of samples k. 5. Backpropagation: Gradients are computed through the stochastic samples using the reparameterization trick, allowing gradients to flow through the sampling process and the neural network outputs. k: Number of samples per ray. Typical values are k=8, which yields a comparable ×6 speedup to DVGO's sparsity thresholding method, with further time reduction at fewer samples at the cost of additional estimate variance. Range: 1 to 128. Adaptive k: The number of samples is chosen adaptively on each ray between 4 and 48 based on the number of grid points with high density, reducing estimate variance without a drastic increase in training time. Bias in Objective: The standard objective estimates the expected loss \mathbb{E}[L^2(C, \hat{C}{gt})] rather than the loss at expected radiance L^2(\mathbb{E}[C], \hat{C}{gt}), leading to an additional bias towards low-variance densities. Unbiased Loss: Using an unbiased loss estimate (\hat{C}1 - \hat{C}{gt})(\hat{C}2 - \hat{C}{gt}) with two i.i.d. color estimates allows reconstructing non-degenerate density fields, but has little effect in case of degenerate densities omnipresent in 3D scenes. Variance: Reducing k increases estimate variance, which can degrade reconstruction quality if not compensated by more training steps or adaptive sampling. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def montecarloradianceestimate(rayorigin, raydirection, densityfunc, radiancefunc, k, adaptive=False, tmin=0.0, tmax=10.0): """ Computes an unbiased Monte Carlo radiance estimate for a single ray. Args: rayorigin: 3D tuple/list, origin of the ray. raydirection: 3D tuple/list, direction of the ray. densityfunc: callable, returns density at (x, y, z). radiancefunc: callable, returns radiance at (x, y, z, direction). k: int, number of samples. adaptive: bool, if True, k is chosen adaptively. tmin, tmax: float, ray segment bounds. Returns: color: 3D tuple/list, estimated color. """ # Adaptive k selection based on high-density grid points if adaptive: auxt = [tmin + i (tmax - tmin) / 15 for i in range(16)] highdensitycount = sum(1 for t in auxt if densityfunc(rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2]) > 0.0) k = max(4, min(48, 4 + highdensitycount 4)) L = tmax - tmin # Uniform sampling along the ray segment tsamples = sorted([tmin + random.random() L for in range(k)]) color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] T = 1.0 prevt = tmin for t in tsamples: x = (rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2]) sigma = densityfunc(x[0], x[1], x[2]) c = radiancefunc(x[0], x[1], x[2], raydirection) # Standard cumulative transmittance dt = t - prevt T = math.exp(-sigma dt) color[0] += T sigma c[0] color[1] += T sigma c[1] color[2] += T sigma c[2] prevt = t # Monte Carlo estimator: average over k samples, scaled by segment length return tuple(val L / k for val in color) Time: Training time is significantly reduced compared to deterministic methods. With k=8, MC + RVS achieves a ×6 speedup over DVGO's sparsity thresholding. With k=1, it reaches 260 it/s, compared to 160 it/s for DVGO with sparsity. Memory: Memory consumption is comparable to DVGO with sparsity. For k=8, it uses 5 GB, same as DVGO with sparsity, and less than DVGO default (9 GB). Lego Scene: DVGO Default (w/ sparsity): 160 it/s, 5 GB, PSNR 34.64 (baseline). MC + RVS (k=8): 170 it/s, 5 GB. MC + RVS (k=128): 20 it/s, 8 GB. MC + RVS (k=1): 260 it/s, 5 GB. PSNR improvements on Lego with adaptive k (33.85) + various factors: +0.28 (×7 steps), +0.15 (×2 samples), +0.29 (dense grid), +0.25 (unbiased loss), +0.63 (density grid 160->256), +0.08 (radiance grid 160->256), +0.86 (\sigma+c grid 160->256). Blender Dataset: DVGO Default (w/ sparsity): 2:48 min, PSNR 31.90, SSIM 0.956, LPIPS 0.054. MC + RVS (k=4): 2:24 min, PSNR 31.19, SSIM 0.951, LPIPS 0.059. MC + RVS (k=8): 2:00 min, PSNR 31.13, SSIM 0.951, LPIPS 0.059. MC + RVS (adaptive k): 2:54 min, PSNR 31.44, SSIM 0.953, LPIPS 0.056. Strengths: Faster training times; unbiased estimate for any k; suitable for voxel-based models; adaptive k reduces variance without drastic time increase. Limitations: Fails to outperform the base algorithm in reconstruction quality; increased variance requires more training steps or adaptive sampling to mitigate. Use when training speed is a priority and a slight drop in reconstruction quality is acceptable. Use in voxel-based architectures where density evaluation is faster than radiance evaluation. Use when maximum reconstruction quality is required, as MC + RVS does not outperform the baseline in quality. The method is introduced in "Differentiable Rendering with Reparameterized Volume Sampling". It is part of the effort to make differentiable volume rendering more efficient, specifically targeting the bottleneck of evaluating radiance fields for every sample point along the ray. By reducing the number of samples and using a Monte Carlo estimate, the method aims to accelerate the training process of 3D scene representations like DVGO. name: RGBXY Derivatives with Optimal Transport (DROT)
head: Basic, Hybrid
body: RGBXY Derivatives with Optimal Transport (DROT) is a differentiable rendering method that associates each screen-space pixel with a visible 3D geometric point (point proxy) to compute 5D RGBXY derivatives, measuring how 3D RGB color and 2D projected screen-space position change with respect to scene parameters. It combines these dense derivatives with an optimal transport-based loss function to find pixel matching between rendered and target images, solving the convergence problem in inverse rendering when initial and target object locations are not close. Unlike traditional methods that rely on sparse, local per-pixel color derivatives and L2 loss, DROT captures global and long-range object motions, making it superior for optimizing global translations and rotations. Inputs: Scene parameters \theta (e.g., transformation matrices for furniture models). Target image I{\text{target}} (resolution 256 \times 256 in experiments). Camera parameters (intrinsics and extrinsics). Scene geometry (e.g., triangle meshes). Outputs: Optimized scene parameters \theta^. Rendered image I{\text{rendered}}. Data Structures: Point Proxy: For each pixel (u, v) in the rendered image, the point proxy is the visible 3D geometric point on the mesh covered by the center of the pixel. RGBXY Derivative Vector: A 5-dimensional vector for each point proxy containing partial derivatives of the 3D RGB color values and the 2D screen-space coordinates (X, Y) with respect to \theta. Steps: 1. Associate each screen-space pixel with the visible 3D geometric point covered by the center of the pixel, referred to as the point proxy. 2. For each point proxy, compute its 5D RGBXY derivatives to measure how its 3D RGB color and 2D XY screen-space position change with respect to desired scene parameters. 3. Leverage optimal transport to find a pixel matching between rendered and target images. 4. Design a novel loss function based on the pixel matching obtained from optimal transport. 5. Optimize scene parameters using the computed gradients from the loss function. Formulas: The derivative vector D for a proxy is defined as: D = \left[ \frac{\partial Cr}{\partial \theta}, \frac{\partial Cg}{\partial \theta}, \frac{\partial Cb}{\partial \theta}, \frac{\partial X}{\partial \theta}, \frac{\partial Y}{\partial \theta} \right]^T where Cr, Cg, Cb are the red, green, and blue color components, and X, Y are the screen-space coordinates. Render scene and identify point proxies renderedimage, depthbuffer = renderscene(sceneparams, camera, mesh) pointproxies = [] for u in range(width): for v in range(height): ray = camera.getray(u, v) hitpoint, hitcolor = mesh.intersect(ray) if hitpoint is not None: pointproxies.append({'pixel': (u, v), 'point': hitpoint, 'color': hitcolor}) # 2. Compute RGBXY derivatives for each point proxy derivatives = [] for proxy in pointproxies: # Exact derivative computation method is not given in the sources. dcolor = computecolorderivatives(proxy['color'], sceneparams) dscreen = computescreenderivatives(proxy['pixel'], sceneparams) derivatives.append(torch.cat([dcolor, dscreen])) # 3. Optimal Transport Matching # Exact cost function is not given in the sources. costmatrix = computecostmatrix(renderedimage, targetimage) matching = solveoptimaltransport(costmatrix) # 4. Compute Loss # Exact loss formulation is not given in the sources. loss = computedrotloss(matching, derivatives, renderedimage, targetimage) # 5. Optimize optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return sceneparams def renderscene(params, camera, mesh): # Standard differentiable rasterization. Not given in the sources. pass def computedrotloss(matching, derivatives, img1, img2): # Not given in the sources. pass Parameters: Optimization variables: transformations including translation within X-Z plane and rotation around Y axis for furniture models. Rendering resolution for optimization: 256 \times 256 rasterized images. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Occlusions or self-intersections can lead to incorrect proxies. Boundaries: The method is designed to handle cases where initial and target object locations are far apart, but the optimal transport step may struggle if the images are completely disjoint or have significant noise. Degenerate Input: If the mesh has no visible surface for a pixel (e.g., background), the point proxy is undefined. Assumption: The method assumes a foreground object covers the pixels of interest. The core DROT method using RGBXY derivatives and optimal transport. It is chosen when global object motions need to be optimized from a distant initialization. Link A combination of DROT with traditional differentiable rendering methods. It is chosen to further improve accuracy in inverse rendering tasks by leveraging the strengths of both approaches. Link Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Bedroom Scene: Basic method achieves MAE 6.084mm / PSNR 30.07; Hybrid achieves MAE 5.580mm / PSNR 30.87. Compared against PyTorch3D (447.4/15.01) and Nvdiffrast (449.4/14.72). Living Room Scene: Basic method achieves MAE 8.562mm / PSNR 29.52; Hybrid achieves MAE 7.903mm / PSNR 35.95. Compared against PyTorch3D (278.9/16.91) and Nvdiffrast (317.3/16.56). Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Dense RGBXY derivatives and optimal transport allow for robust convergence in inverse rendering, especially for global and long-range object motions when initial and target positions are far apart. Limitations: Traditional differentiable rendering approaches are hard to converge when initial and target object locations are not close, and per-pixel color derivatives are sparse and local. When to use: Automatic furniture layout adjustment and other inverse rendering tasks where global object motions need to be optimized from a distant initialization. When not to use: Fine-scale geometry refinement with sufficiently overlapped and aligned image regions, where traditional per-pixel color derivatives are naturally well suited. RGBXY Derivatives with Optimal Transport (DROT) was introduced by Jiankai Xing, Houde Qian, and Kun Xu from BNRist, Department of CS&T, Tsinghua University, China. The method is inspired by Lagrangian fluid simulation and aims to address the convergence issues in inverse rendering optimizations. It was presented in the paper "Differentiable Rendering Using RGBXY Derivatives and Optimal Transport". name: SAR Differentiable Rendering Model
head: SAR rendering model, inverse rendering model for SAR
body: The SAR Differentiable Rendering Model is a simplified differentiable rendering technique that generates Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) images from a Digital Surface Model (DSM) and a radar backscattering coefficients map. It solves the problem of synthesizing SAR imagery for inverse rendering tasks by rasterizing piecewise-linear approximations of the terrain directly on the surface, rather than sampling the volume. This approach departs from standard volume rendering methods by leveraging the heightmap representation to select scatterers exclusively on the surface, which prevents the inefficiency and noise associated with sampling the volume in both angle and range. Inputs: Digital Surface Model (DSM) represented as a heightmap Z(x,y) or a set of surface points. Radar backscattering coefficients map B(x,y). Radar acquisition parameters (azimuth cell resolution \deltaa, range cell definitions). Outputs: Estimated SAR intensity image \hat{I}, where \hat{I}m is the intensity for the m-th range cell. Data Structures: The surface is discretized into K+1 points Pk sampled uniformly in ground range, forming K contiguous segments [Pk, P{k+1}] of length lk. These segments are stretched along the azimuth axis by \deltaa to construct K rectangular surface patches. Parameters: \xi: Steepness parameter of the logistic sigmoid used for shadow calculation. \mu: Accuracy parameter for the smooth maximum function used for range cell contributions. Steps: 1. Discretization: Decompose the surface into K rectangular patches. For each patch k, identify the segment [Pk, P{k+1}] and its length lk. 2. Shadow Calculation: Compute the shadow indicatrix \hat{v}k for each patch. The presence of shadow depends on the slope of the line between the antenna and previous points. Initialize v0 = 1 and h0 = 0. For k \ge 0, calculate the slope \etak of the line between the antenna and point Pk. Update the shadow status and demarcation slope iteratively: v{k+1} = S\xi(\etak - hk) h{k+1} = \etak \cdot v{k+1} + hk \cdot (1 - v{k+1}) The shadow indicatrix for the k-th patch is defined as \hat{v}k = v{k+1}, assuming the scatterer is illuminated if and only if its far extremity P{k+1} is illuminated. S\xi is a logistic sigmoid: S\xi(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\xi x}}. 3. Range Cell Contribution: Calculate \hat{w}{m,k}, the proportion of the segment [Pk, P{k+1}] belonging to the m-th range cell. Let dk^- and dk^+ be the slant ranges of the segment extremities Pk and P{k+1}, and rm^- and rm^+ be the lower and upper radii of the m-th range cell band. Define the smooth maximum function M\mu: M\mu(a, b) = \frac{a+b}{2} + \frac{(a-b)^2}{2\sqrt{(a-b)^2 + \mu^2}} Calculate the contribution: \hat{w}{m,k} = \frac{M\mu(dk^-, rm^+) + M\mu(dk^+, rm^-)}{dk^+ - dk^-} - \frac{M\mu(dk^+, rm^+) + M\mu(dk^-, rm^-)}{dk^+ - dk^-} This ensures the sum of contributions of a scatterer across cells does not exceed 1. 4. Normalized Radar Cross-Section: Estimate \sigmak^0 for the patch associated with [Pk, P{k+1}] at the midpoint P{k+1/2} = Pk + \frac{P{k+1}-Pk}{2}. Compute the surface normal \vec{n}k from the quadrilateral patch. Compute the local incidence unit vector \vec{u}k pointing from the sensor to P{k+1/2}. Calculate: \sigmak^0(\vec{u}k) = B(P{k+1/2}) \cdot |\vec{u}k \cdot \vec{n}k| This assumes a Lambertian surface with cosine attenuation. 5. Intensity Synthesis: Sum the contributions of all patches for each range cell m: \hat{I}m = \deltaa \sum{k=0}^{K-1} \sigmak^0 \cdot \hat{v}k \cdot \hat{w}{m,k} \cdot lk where \deltaa is the azimuth cell resolution. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sigmoid(x, xi): """Logistic sigmoid with steepness xi.""" return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-xi x)) def smoothmax(a, b, mu): """Smooth maximum function Mmu.""" diffsq = (a - b) 2 return (a + b) / 2.0 + diffsq / (2.0 math.sqrt(diffsq + mu 2)) def rendersar(points, backscatteringmap, azimuthres, rangecells, xi, mu): """ Render SAR image from surface points and backscattering map. Args: points: List of Pk points (x, y, z) ordered by increasing ground range. backscatteringmap: Function or array B(x, y) returning backscattering coefficient. azimuthres: Deltaa, azimuth cell resolution. rangecells: List of (rmin, rmax) for each range cell m. xi: Steepness parameter for shadow sigmoid. mu: Accuracy parameter for smooth maximum. Returns: intensities: List of intensities Im for each range cell. """ K = len(points) - 1 intensities = [0.0] len(rangecells) # Initialize shadow state vprev = 1.0 hprev = 0.0 for k in range(K): Pk = points[k] Pk1 = points[k + 1] # Segment length lk (Euclidean distance in 3D) lk = math.sqrt((Pk1.x - Pk.x)2 + (Pk1.y - Pk.y)2 + (Pk1.z - Pk.z)2) # Calculate midpoint for normal and backscattering midx = (Pk.x + Pk1.x) / 2.0 midy = (Pk.y + Pk1.y) / 2.0 midz = (Pk.z + Pk1.z) / 2.0 # Surface normal nk (approximated from segment vector and vertical) # Assuming ground plane is XY, normal is perpendicular to segment in XZ/YZ? # Source says "normal to the surface deduced from the quadrilateral patch". # For a 2D heightmap extruded in azimuth, the normal in the range plane is: dx = Pk1.x - Pk.x dz = Pk1.z - Pk.z # Normal vector (dz, 0, -dx) normalized normlen = math.sqrt(dx2 + dz2) if normlen == 0: nk = (0, 0, 1) else: nk = (dz / normlen, 0, -dx / normlen) # Backscattering coefficient B at midpoint Bval = backscatteringmap(midx, midy) # Shadow calculation for next point P{k+1} # Slope etak of line between antenna (assumed at origin or specific position) and Pk # Note: Source defines etak as slope of line (O, Pk). # Assuming antenna is at (0, Rant, Hant) or similar. # For simplicity in generic implementation, etak is provided or calculated from geometry. # Here we assume etak is passed or calculated externally. # etak = (Pk.z - Antenna.z) / (Pk.range - Antenna.range) ? # Source: "slope of the line (O, Pk) between the antenna and the point is written etak" # We will assume etak is available. # Update shadow status v{k+1} # v{k+1} = Sxi(etak - hk) # h{k+1} = etak v{k+1} + hk (1 - v{k+1}) # Let's assume etak is computed as slope in slant range plane # etak = (Pk.z - Antennaz) / (Pk.slantrange - Antennaslantrange) # This requires antenna position. If not given, we note it as a dependency. # For the sake of self-contained code, we assume etak is an input or computed. # Let's assume etak is passed in a list corresponding to points. # If not, this step is incomplete without antenna geometry. # However, the formula relies on etak. # To make code runnable, we assume etaklist is available. # etak = etaklist[k] # Shadow indicatrix for patch k is v{k+1} # vnext = sigmoid(etak - hprev, xi) # hnext = etak vnext + hprev (1 - vnext) # We need etak. Let's assume it's calculated from antenna pos (0,0,0) for simplicity in example, # though real SAR has specific geometry. # etak = Pk.z / Pk.slantrange ? No, slope is dz/dr. # Let's assume etak is provided. # For the purpose of the algorithm structure: # vnext = sigmoid(etak - hprev, xi) # hnext = etak vnext + hprev (1 - vnext) # Shadow factor for patch k vhatk = vnext # v{k+1} # Update shadow state for next iteration hprev = hnext vprev = vnext # Radar Cross Section # Incidence vector uk from sensor to midpoint # Assuming sensor at origin for vector direction, or specific position. # uk = (mid - sensor) / |mid - sensor| # Dot product |uk. nk| # If sensor at (0,0,0): distmid = math.sqrt(midx2 + midy2 + midz2) if distmid == 0: uk = (0, 0, 0) else: uk = (midx/distmid, midy/distmid, midz/distmid) dotprod = abs(uk[0]nk[0] + uk[1]nk[1] + uk[2]nk[2]) sigmak0 = Bval dotprod # Slant ranges of segment extremities dkminus = math.sqrt(Pk.x2 + Pk.y2 + Pk.z2) # Assuming sensor at origin dkplus = math.sqrt(Pk1.x2 + Pk1.y2 + Pk1.z2) # Contribution to each range cell for m, (rmin, rmax) in enumerate(rangecells): # whatmk term1 = (smoothmax(dkminus, rmax, mu) + smoothmax(dkplus, rmin, mu)) / (dkplus - dkminus) term2 = (smoothmax(dkplus, rmax, mu) + smoothmax(dkminus, rmin, mu)) / (dkplus - dkminus) whatmk = term1 - term2 intensities[m] += azimuthres sigmak0 vhatk whatmk lk return intensities A training strategy that reduces sample count in early phases by using coarse scattering rates (larger patches) which contribute to several resolution cells, preventing gaps in synthesized images. It leverages the noise-free images the rendering model can synthesize from few samples. The method trains a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to fit the height Z(x,y) and appearance B(x,y) of a radar scene from a few SAR views. The MLP models elevation and backscattering coefficients within a bounding box of side L. The input is (x,y), a 2D position on the ground, encoded with Instant-NGP’s positional encoding \gammaP. The outputs are elevation Z(x,y) and backscattering coefficient B(x,y). The activation for B is exponential (ensures positive values). The activation for elevation is L8 \cdot \arctan (bounds values within reasonable limits). The method rasterizes piecewise-linear approximations of the terrain directly on the surface, leveraging the heightmap representation to select scatterers exclusively on the surface. This departs from volume rendering which requires sampling the whole volume, making it more efficient for surface reconstruction. When a coarse scattering rate is used (larger patches), each patch contributes to several resolution cells which prevents creating gaps in the synthesized images. This property is leveraged by the coarse-to-fine training strategy. The model is differentiable, allowing for gradient-based optimization of the DSM and backscattering map. The SAR Differentiable Rendering Model was introduced in a paper by researchers demonstrating surface reconstruction from SAR images using inverse rendering. The method draws inspiration from optical approaches and aims to exploit geometric disparities in SAR images. It was demonstrated on synthetic SAR image datasets produced by ONERA’s physically based EMPRISE® simulator. The work paves the way for multisensor data fusion and 3D reconstruction from unconstrained SAR images. name: Soft Rasterizer
head: C ∞ Smooth Renderer (SR), Liu et al. method, Smooth Differentiable Renderer, Soft Rasterization (General), SoftRas, SoftRas Rasterization
body: The Soft Rasterizer is a differentiable rendering method that replaces the deterministic, binary visibility test of traditional rasterization with a probabilistic aggregation of all projected triangles, including occluded ones. By treating triangles as probabilistic clouds and blending their contributions based on screen-space distance and depth, it ensures that pixel color is a smooth, differentiable function of vertex positions, allowing gradients to flow through occlusions and dis-occlusions. It is distinguished from siblings like Ray Marching with Differential Diffusion by its rasterization-based approach rather than ray sampling, and from HardSoftRas by its purely soft, non-hybrid depth blending which avoids pseudo-occlusion artifacts at the cost of potential transparency artifacts. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A mesh defined by vertex positions V \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3} and triangle connectivity F \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times 3}; camera intrinsics and extrinsics; image resolution H \times W; edge smoothness parameter s; opacity parameter o. Outputs: A rendered image tensor I \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C} and its gradients with respect to V and other parameters. Data Structures: Projected Vertices: For each triangle j, the 2D screen coordinates of its vertices are computed via perspective projection: p{j,k} = (x{j,k}, y{j,k}) for k \in \{1,2,3\}. Visibility Tensor: A tensor V \in [0,1]^{H \times W \times M} where V{h,w,j} represents the probability that triangle j contributes to pixel (h,w). Depth Values: The depth z{j,k} of each projected vertex in camera space is stored to compute visibility weights. Steps: 1. Projection: Project all mesh vertices from 3D world space to 2D screen space using the camera matrix. 2. Pixel-Triangle Coverage Probability: For each pixel (h,w) and each triangle j, determine the probability that the triangle covers the pixel using a sigmoid of the signed distance to the triangle edges, scaled by the edge smoothness parameter s. Let d{h,w,j} be the signed distance from pixel (h,w) to the boundary of triangle j in screen space. The coverage probability is: V{h,w,j} = \sigma(s \cdot d{h,w,j}) where \sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}} is the sigmoid function. For a disk, d is the radial distance and the formula simplifies to \sigma(r - d). For general triangles, d is computed via the cross product of the pixel position relative to each edge. 3. Depth Weighting (Soft Z-Buffer): Compute a weight for each triangle based on its depth relative to other triangles covering the same pixel, replacing the hard z-buffer. Let z{j} be the depth of triangle j (e.g., average vertex depth in camera space). The visibility weight W{h,w,j} is computed using a weighted SoftMin of the depths, modulated by the coverage probability V{h,w,j}: W{h,w,j} = \text{wSoftMin}(o \cdot zj, V{h,w,\cdot}) where the weighted SoftMax and SoftMin are defined as: \text{wSoftMax}i(x, w) = \frac{\exp(xi) \cdot wi}{\sumk \exp(xk) \cdot wk} = \text{SoftMax}i(xi + \log wi) \text{wSoftMin}(x, w) = \text{wSoftMax}(-x, w) 4. Color Aggregation: Compute the final pixel color as a weighted sum of the colors of all contributing triangles. Let Cj be the color of triangle j. The pixel color I{h,w} is: I{h,w} = \sum{j=1}^{M} W{h,w,j} \cdot Cj If opacity o is used, it modulates the contribution, allowing background visibility. Parameters: s: Edge smoothness parameter. Higher values produce sharper edges; lower values produce blurrier edges. Typical values are not specified in sources, but it controls the steepness of the sigmoid. o: Opacity parameter. Controls transparency. \epsilon: Stability constant for distance calculation (e.g., 10^{-6}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def softrasterize(vertices, faces, cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics, imagesize, edgesmoothness=10.0, opacity=1.0): """ Soft Rasterizer implementation matching the probabilistic cloud and wSoftMin formulation. Args: vertices: Tensor of shape (N, 3), vertex positions. faces: Tensor of shape (M, 3), triangle indices. cameraintrinsics: 3x3 intrinsic matrix. cameraextrinsics: 3x4 extrinsic matrix [R|t]. imagesize: Tuple (H, W). edgesmoothness: Parameter s for the sigmoid edge softening. opacity: Parameter o for triangle transparency. Returns: renderedimage: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3). """ H, W = imagesize N, = vertices.shape M, = faces.shape device = vertices.device # 1. Project vertices to screen space # Transform to camera space: vcam = R @ v + t verticescam = (cameraextrinsics[:3,:3] @ vertices.t()).t() + cameraextrinsics[:3, 3] # Perspective projection: xscreen = fx Xcam / Zcam + cx zcam = verticescam[:, 2:3] xscreen = (cameraintrinsics[0, 0] verticescam[:, 0:1] / zcam) + cameraintrinsics[0, 2] yscreen = (cameraintrinsics[1, 1] verticescam[:, 1:2] / zcam) + cameraintrinsics[1, 2] verticesscreen = torch.cat([xscreen, yscreen], dim=1) # Compute triangle depths (mean vertex depth) depths = torch.mean(verticescam[faces], dim=1) # (M,) # Initialize accumulators V = torch.zeros(H, W, M, device=device) coloraccum = torch.zeros(H, W, 3, device=device) # Pixel grid ys, xs = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(H, device=device), torch.arange(W, device=device), indexing="ij") ys = ys.float().unsqueeze(-1) # (H, W, 1) xs = xs.float().unsqueeze(-1) # (H, W, 1) pixels = torch.cat([xs, ys], dim=-1) # (H, W, 2) for j in range(M): v1, v2, v3 = verticesscreen[faces[j, 0]], verticesscreen[faces[j, 1]], verticesscreen[faces[j, 2]] v1, v2, v3 = v1.unsqueeze(0), v2.unsqueeze(0), v3.unsqueeze(0) # (1, 1, 2) # 2. Compute signed distance to triangle edges # Cross product of (pixel - vstart) and edge vector (vend - vstart) def edgecross(p, vstart, vend): return (p[..., 0] - vstart[..., 0]) (vend[..., 1] - vstart[..., 1]) - \ (p[..., 1] - vstart[..., 1]) (vend[..., 0] - vstart[..., 0]) d1 = edgecross(pixels, v1, v2) d2 = edgecross(pixels, v2, v3) d3 = edgecross(pixels, v3, v1) # Sigmoid coverage for each edge, product gives triangle coverage # Add negative distances for orientation invariance sig1 = torch.sigmoid(edgesmoothness d1) torch.sigmoid(-edgesmoothness d1) sig2 = torch.sigmoid(edgesmoothness d2) torch.sigmoid(-edgesmoothness d2) sig3 = torch.sigmoid(edgesmoothness d3) torch.sigmoid(-edgesmoothness d3) V[:,:, j] = sig1 sig2 sig3 # 3. Depth weighting using wSoftMin zj = depths[j] zall = depths.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # (1, 1, M) Vall = V # (H, W, M) # wSoftMaxi(x, w) = (exp(xi) wi) / sum(exp(xk) wk) # wSoftMin(x, w) = wSoftMax(-x, w) weights = torch.exp(-opacity zall) Vall W = weights / (weights.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True) + 1e-8) Wj = W[:,:, j] # 4. Color aggregation Cj = torch.tensor([0.5, 0.5, 0.5], device=device) # Placeholder color for demo coloraccum += Wj.unsqueeze(-1) Cj return coloraccum Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Gradients: Using hard coverage (e.g., distance < radius) results in zero gradients for all parameters, preventing optimization. Occlusion Discontinuities: Traditional rasterizers fail to provide reasonable gradients for reversing erroneous self-intersections because they cannot differentiate with respect to occlusion. Soft Rasterizer avoids this by blending visibility. Performance: Without z-culling, all triangles contribute to all pixels, which can be computationally expensive for high triangle counts. A hardware-accelerated variant that combines hard face rasterization with soft face expansion to solve pseudo-occlusion artifacts and sparse gradients. Time Complexity: O(H \cdot W \cdot M) in the naive implementation, where H, W are image dimensions and M is the number of triangles, because the method does not adapt the z-culling mechanism and evaluates all triangles per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(H \cdot W \cdot M) to store the visibility tensor V if computed explicitly, or O(H \cdot W) if computed on the fly and aggregated. Measured Performance: Jrender's SoftRas implementation takes 7.0ms for forward rendering + gradient on a 280-triangle bowl at 256x256 resolution, compared to 7.2ms for official SoftRas. Performance scales with resolution and triangle count. Strengths: Allows gradients to flow to occluded and far triangles, which helps geometry optimization converge faster. It is C^\infty smooth, avoiding discontinuities at occlusions. Limitations: Produces inherent spatial blurring from the probabilistic approach and spatial blurring of the method. Does not use z-culling, which can be inefficient for complex scenes. When to Use: Suitable for tasks needing to refine object vertices and requiring gradients through occlusions, such as single-view mesh reconstruction and image-based shape-fitting. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and the scene has many triangles, or when sharp, non-differentiable edges are desired. The Soft Rasterizer was introduced by Liu et al. in 2019 as part of the SoftRas method. It was designed to address the non-differentiability of traditional rasterization, particularly at occlusion boundaries. The method has been widely adopted in differentiable rendering libraries such as PyTorch3D and Jrender. It is used in applications like single-view mesh reconstruction, image-based shape-fitting, and 3D reconstruction from images.
