name: HardSoftRas
head: Hard Soft Rasterization, Hardware Accelerated Soft Rasterizer
body: HardSoftRas is a hardware-accelerated differentiable rasterization method that propagates gradients from screen space to far-range vertex attributes by combining hard face rasterization with soft face expansion. It solves the problem of pseudo-occlusion artifacts and sparse, discontinuous gradients common in prior soft rasterizers (like SoftRas) and geometric anti-aliasing methods (like Nvdiffrast) when using a small number of depth peeling buffers. Unlike its siblings, it uses a hybrid hard/soft depth test and uniform edge pixel blending to ensure dense, smooth gradients for inverse rendering. HardSoftRas rasterizes geometry through K peeling planes, using a hybrid hard/soft depth test to handle silhouette edges, and blends the resulting shaded images using weights derived from edge distances. The rendering function is defined as: I(\Theta) = f{pp}(f{shade}(f{rasterize}(\thetaG, \thetaC), \thetaM, \thetaL, \thetaE)) where I(\Theta) is the rendered image, and \thetaG, \thetaC, \thetaM, \thetaL, \thetaE are geometric, camera, material, lighting, and environment parameters. Inputs: Vertex positions (vtx\pos), UVs (vtx\uv), and face indices (faces). Model, view, and projection matrices (model\mat, view\mat, prj\mat). Material properties (albedo, metallic, roughness, normal map) and environment map. Background color. Parameters: Blur radius r \in [0, 1], number of buffers K \ge 1, blending parameter \sigma = r/7, silhouette edge width \delta = r. Outputs: Blended shaded image (blended\shaded\img). Blended silhouette image (blended\silhouette\img). Final image: Vec4(blended\shaded\img, blended\silhouette\img). Vertex Buffer: Contains projected 3D positions. For enlarged triangles, original vertex indices are stored to allow attribute interpolation from the original geometry. G-Buffer: Stores per-pixel attributes including depth, world position, world normal, and UVs for deferred shading. Stencil Masks: Binary masks indicating which pixels belong to the hard face (inside original triangle) or soft face (enlarged region) for each peeling plane. 1. Initialization: Set prevprjdepth to 0. Create empty lists for shadedimgs, stencils, and edgedists. 2. Depth Peeling Loop: Iterate k from 0 to K-1: a. Enlarge: For each face fj, compute the enlarged face f'j using Enlarge(fj, r). b. Rasterize: Perform hardware rasterization on f'j to generate pixels. c. Compute Distances: For each pixel i on f'j, compute the signed distance dist{ij} from the original face fj using SignedDist. d. Interpolate Attributes: Compute screen-space barycentric coordinates and interpolate projected positions, world positions, world normals, and UVs using the original vertex indices. e. Shift Depth: Modify the depth value to prevent pseudo-occlusion using Shift(depth^0{ij}, dist{ij}). f. Set Fragment Depth: Set the fragment depth to the modified depth. g. Peel Depth: Call PeelDepth(prjdepth, prevprjdepth) to generate the stencil mask for the current plane. h. Shade: Apply deferred shading (e.g., physically-based shading) to generate the shaded image for this plane. i. Update: Store the stencil, shaded image, and edge distance. Update prevprjdepth to the current prjdepth. 3. Blend: Call BuildBlend with shadedimgs, stencils, edgedists, background, K, \sigma, and \delta to compute blendedshadedimg and blendedsilhouetteimg. 4. Edge Masking: a. Compute ishard as (0.f < edge\dists[0]). b. Compute hardshaded as shadedimgs[0] ishard. c. Compute edgemask using BuildEdgeMask(edgedists[0], delta). d. Mix hardshaded and blendedcol using edgemask. e. Mix ishard and blendedsil using edgemask. 5. Post-Processing: Apply tone mapping to blendedshadedimg and construct the final image. Enlarge(fj, r): Expands the triangle fj by radius r in screen space. For acute triangles (smallest angle \ge 30^\circ), stretch vertices in the opposite direction of the centroid. For obtuse triangles (smallest angle < 30^\circ), expand the bounding box to cover r and split into pairs of triangles to avoid shaggy boundaries and precision errors. Store original vertex indices. SignedDist(pi, fj): Computes the signed distance from pixel position pi to the edges of the original face fj. Positive if inside, negative if outside. Shift(depth, dist): Modifies the depth value of the soft face to prevent pseudo-occlusion. Ensures all hard faces are rasterized in front of all soft faces. Shift(depth, dist) = \begin{cases} 0.5 \times depth & \text{if } dist \ge 0 \\ 0.5 \times |dist| + 0.5 & \text{if } dist < 0 \end{cases} BuildBlend(shadedimgs, stencils, edgedists, background, K, sigma, delta): Blends the shaded images from all peeling planes. Compute weights: Dk = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-distk/\sigma}} \times stencilk. Compute color blend: Ic = I(I{ce}, I{cne}), where I{ce} = \frac{\sumk Dk Ck}{\sumk Dk} for edges, and I{cne} = SH C1 for non-edges. Compute silhouette blend: Is = I(I{se}, I{sne}), where I{se} = 1 - \prodk (1 - Dk) for edges, and I{sne} = SH for non-edges. SH is the stencil mask of hard faces in the frontal buffer, and C1 is the shaded color of the first buffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def HardSoftRas(vtxpos, faces, modelmat, viewmat, prjmat, albedo, metallic, roughness, normal, background, K, r, sigma, delta): """ HardSoftRas differentiable rasterization. Args: vtxpos: Vertex positions (N, 3) faces: Face indices (F, 3) modelmat, viewmat, prjmat: Transformation matrices albedo, metallic, roughness, normal: Material attributes background: Background color K: Number of peeling buffers r: Blur radius sigma: Blending parameter (typically r/7) delta: Silhouette edge width (typically r) Returns: renderedimg: Final image (H, W, 4) """ prevprjdepth = 0.0 shadedimgs = [] stencils = [] edgedists = [] # Precompute world positions and normals if not provided # Note: In a full implementation, these are interpolated per-pixel # Here we assume helper functions exist for matrix multiplication and interpolation for k in range(K): # 1. Enlarge triangles # Returns enlarged projected vertices and original vertex indices largeprj0, largeprj1, largeprj2, originalvtxidxs = \ BuildEnlarge(vtxpos, faces, r) # Stack enlarged vertices into a single buffer largeprjflat = np.concatenate([largeprj0, largeprj1, largeprj2], axis=0) # 2. Rasterize enlarged triangles # Returns screen-space vertex indices for each fragment screenvtxidxs = Rasterize(largeprjflat, originalvtxidxs) # 3. Compute signed distances to original edges edgedist = BuildEdgeDistance(vtxpos, faces, screenvtxidxs) # 4. Compute barycentric coordinates for original triangles barycoords = BuildBaryCoord(vtxpos, faces, screenvtxidxs) # 5. Interpolate attributes using original vertex indices # Interpolate projected positions for depth prjpos = Interpolate(vtxpos, faces, screenvtxidxs, barycoords) # Interpolate world positions, normals, UVs for shading worldpos = Interpolate(vtxpos, faces, screenvtxidxs, barycoords) worldnor = Interpolate(normal, faces, screenvtxidxs, barycoords) uv = Interpolate(vtxuv, faces, screenvtxidxs, barycoords) # 6. Shift depth to handle pseudo-occlusion prjdepthw = prjpos[:,:, 3] # Extract w component softdepth = edgedist 0.5 + 0.5 harddepth = prjdepthw 0.5 isinside = (edgedist > 0.0).astype(np.float32) prjdepth = np.where(isinside, harddepth, softdepth) # 7. Set fragment depth and peel # Note: In a real GPU pipeline, this sets glFragDepth # Here we simulate the stencil generation stencil = (prjdepth < prevprjdepth).astype(np.float32) # 8. Shade # Deferred shading with PBR shadedimg = PhysicallyBasedShading(worldpos, worldnor, uv, albedo, metallic, roughness) # Store results shadedimgs.append(shadedimg) stencils.append(stencil) edgedists.append(edgedist) # Update previous depth for next peeling plane prevprjdepth = prjdepth # 9. Blend blendedshadedimg, blendedsilhouetteimg = BuildBlend( shadedimgs, stencils, edgedists, background, K, sigma, delta) # 10. Edge Masking ishard = (edgedists[0] > 0.0).astype(np.float32) hardshaded = shadedimgs[0] ishard edgemask = BuildEdgeMask(edgedists[0], delta) blendedcol = np.where(edgemask, blendedshadedimg, hardshaded) blendedsil = np.where(edgemask, blendedsilhouetteimg, ishard) # 11. Post-processing blendedshadedimg = ToneMap(blendedcol) # Construct final image with silhouette as alpha renderedimg = np.stack([blendedshadedimg, blendedsil], axis=-1) return renderedimg def BuildEnlarge(vtxpos, faces, r): """ Enlarge triangles by radius r. Returns enlarged projected vertices and original vertex indices. """ # Project vertices to screen space # For each face, determine if acute or obtuse # Acute: Stretch vertices opposite to centroid # Obtuse (smallest angle < 30 deg): Expand bounding box # Return new vertex positions and mapping to original indices # Standard geometric expansion logic; exact vertex manipulation omitted for brevity pass def BuildEdgeDistance(vtxpos, faces, screenvtxidxs): """ Compute signed distance from pixel to original triangle edges. """ # Use barycentric coordinates or explicit edge distance formula # Standard signed distance to triangle edges pass def BuildBaryCoord(vtxpos, faces, screenvtxidxs): """ Compute screen-space barycentric coordinates for original triangles. """ # Standard barycentric coordinate computation from projected vertices pass def Interpolate(attr, faces, screenvtxidxs, barycoords): """ Interpolate attribute using barycentric coordinates and original vertex indices. """ # attr: (N, D) # faces: (F, 3) # screenvtxidxs: (H, W, 3) indices into faces # barycoords: (H, W, 3) # Standard barycentric interpolation pass def Rasterize(vertices, originalvtxidxs): """ Hardware rasterization of enlarged triangles. Returns screen-space vertex indices per fragment. """ # Standard GPU rasterization pipeline simulation pass def PhysicallyBasedShading(worldpos, worldnor, uv, albedo, metallic, roughness): """ Compute PBR color for each pixel. """ # Standard PBR shading (e.g., Cook-Torrance BRDF) pass def BuildBlend(shadedimgs, stencils, edgedists, background, K, sigma, delta): """ Blend shaded images from all peeling planes. """ weights = [] weightedcols = [] for k in range(K): # Sigmoid weight based on edge distance prob = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-edgedists[k] / sigma)) weight = prob stencils[k] weights.append(weight) weightedcols.append(weight shadedimgs[k]) # Color blending # Sum of weighted colors sumweightedcols = np.sum(weightedcols, axis=0) sumweights = np.sum(weights, axis=0) # Avoid division by zero sumweights = np.maximum(sumweights, 1e-6) blendedcolor = sumweightedcols / sumweights # Silhouette blending blendedsil = 1.0 for k in range(K): blendedsil = (1.0 - weights[k]) blendedsil = 1.0 - blendedsil return blendedcolor, blendedsil def BuildEdgeMask(edgedist, delta): """ Create a binary mask for edge pixels. """ # Mask is 1 where edgedist is within delta of 0 return ((edgedist > -delta) & (edgedist < delta)).astype(np.float32) def ToneMap(img): """ Apply tone mapping (e.g., Reinhard or ACES). """ # Standard tone mapping operator pass r (Blur radius): Defines the range of blurring in screen space [0, 1]^2. Typical values: 0.01, 0.1, or pixel-based (1-7 pixels). K (Number of buffers): Maximum number of depth peeling buffers. Set to a maximum of 5 to avoid pseudo-occlusion artifacts with few buffers. Typical value: 2. \sigma (Blending parameter): Computed as r/7. Controls the smoothness of the sigmoid weight function. \delta (Silhouette edge width): Width of the edge mask. Default value is r. Pseudo-occlusion: Expanding soft faces by interpolated depth values may cause them to occlude necessary hard faces. This is handled by Shift(), which pushes soft faces behind hard faces and assigns depth based on distance to hard faces. Shaggy boundaries: Using only acute triangle enlargement without the full strategy results in shaggy boundaries for soft faces. Obtuse triangles (smallest angle < 30^\circ) require bounding box expansion. Numerical instability: SoftRas uses a square for distance in sigmoid computation, causing instability. HardSoftRas removes the square. Triangle count change: Enlarging triangles changes the number of triangles. Original vertex indices must be preserved and passed through to avoid mismatched attribute lookups. Conventional geometric anti-aliasing: Methods like Nvdiffrast select a limited number of edge pixels, leading to sparse and discontinuous gradients. HardSoftRas blends all edge pixels, ensuring dense and smooth gradients. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of faces F and buffers K. The depth peeling loop runs K times, and each iteration rasterizes F enlarged triangles. Memory Complexity: Proportional to K \times H \times W for storing G-buffers and stencils. K is kept small (≤ 5) to minimize memory usage. Performance: Less computationally expensive and more robust than conservative rasterization [HAO05] by keeping triangle primitives small and avoiding floating-point precision errors in obtuse triangles. Strengths: Dense and smooth far-range gradients; robust optimization without shape collapse; hardware-accelerated; works with small K. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of r and K; blending weights depend on edge distance, which may not always align with semantic edges. When to use: Differentiable rendering with physically-based shading, especially for inverse rendering tasks requiring stable gradients. HardSoftRas was introduced in the Dressi renderer paper by Y. Takimoto et al. in 2022. It is designed to propagate gradients from screen space to far-range vertex attributes using hardware rasterizers, addressing limitations in prior soft rasterization methods like SoftRas and PyTorch3D. The method is used in the Dressi renderer for differentiable rendering with physically-based shading. name: Generalized Differentiable Renderer (GenDR)
head: GenDR (Generalized Differentiable Renderer)
body: GenDR is a generalized differentiable mesh renderer that models the forward rendering process under a probabilistic perturbation defined by a probability distribution with density f and a temperature/scale parameter \tau > 0, making the renderer continuous everywhere and differentiable almost everywhere. It computes pixel occupancy/coverage by aggregating face contributions using a sigmoid function (CDF of a probability distribution) and a T-conorm for aggregation. Unlike hard renderers which are discrete and non-differentiable, GenDR provides meaningful gradients for gradient-based optimization tasks such as shape optimization. It generalizes existing differentiable renderers like SoftRas and DIB-R by allowing an array of different smoothing distributions. Inputs: A set of faces T (typically triangles) representing the 3D mesh. A pixel coordinate p in the image space. A temperature/scale parameter \tau > 0. A probability distribution with cumulative distribution function (CDF) F. A T-conorm operator \perp. Outputs: Occupancy/coverage value AO(p, T) \in [0, 1] for each pixel p. Gradients \frac{\partial AO}{\partial \text{mesh parameters}} for optimization. Data Structures: Faces (T): A list of triangles. Each triangle is defined by its vertices in 3D space. Distance (d(p, t)): The distance from pixel p to face t, projected into image space. T-conorm (\perp): A binary operation satisfying associativity, commutativity, monotonicity, and having 0 as a neutral element. Numbered Steps: 1. Transform to Image Space: Transform all objects (mesh vertices) into image space via a sequence of affine transformations followed by camera projection. This step is inherently differentiable. 2. Differentiable Occlusion Test: For each pixel p, compute the set of faces covering it by evaluating a differentiable occlusion test for each face t \in T. This is done by computing the distance d(p, t) from the pixel to the face and applying the sigmoid function F normalized by the temperature \tau. Compute the normalized distance: x = d(p, t) / \tau. Apply the CDF: pt = F(x) = F(d(p, t)/\tau). 3. Aggregate Occupancy: Aggregate the occupancy probabilities pt of all faces for each pixel using a continuous T-conorm \perp. The final occupancy AO(p, T) is computed as: AO(p, T) = \perp{t \in T} F\left(\frac{d(p, t)}{\tau}\right) where \perp is applied iteratively over all faces t \in T. 4. Shading (Optional): Apply a differentiable shading model (e.g., Phong) to color the faces. If depth is required, use Gumbel depth perturbations (softmin) for continuity, or take the closest triangle. Formulas: Occupancy: AO(p, T) = \perp{t \in T} F\left(\frac{d(p, t)}{\tau}\right) T-conorm Definition: A binary operation \perp: [0, 1] \times [0, 1] \to [0, 1] satisfying: Associativity: \perp(a, \perp(b, c)) = \perp(\perp(a, b), c) Commutativity: \perp(a, b) = \perp(b, a) Monotonicity: (a \le c) \land (b \le d) \implies \perp(a, b) \le \perp(c, d) Neutral Element: \perp(a, 0) = a Probabilistic Sum (Common T-conorm): \perpP(a, b) = a + b - ab = 1 - (1-a)(1-b). Parameters: \tau (tau): Temperature or scale parameter for the sigmoid function. Typical values in experiments: \tau \in \{10^{-0.1 \cdot n} \mid n \in \mathbb{N}, 0 \le n \le 80\}. A fine-grained grid search over \tau is critical as behavior differs for each distribution. Distribution F: The CDF of the chosen probability distribution (e.g., Logistic, Gaussian, Uniform, Cauchy, Laplace). T-conorm \perp: The aggregation function (e.g., Probabilistic Sum, Maximum, Hamacher, Frank, Yager). Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Dirac Delta: The Dirac delta distribution corresponds to the Heaviside function, which yields a discrete, non-differentiable renderer and is unsuitable for gradient-based optimization. Discontinuous T-conorms: Discontinuous T-conorms (e.g., drastic T-conorm) are not suitable for differentiable renderers. Finite Support: Distributions with finite support (e.g., Uniform) only provide meaningful gradients in a limited proximity to each face. Squared Distributions: Regular distributions F typically perform better than their squared counterparts F^2, except for Cauchy and reciprocal sigmoid which have linear convergence rates. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sigmoidlogistic(x): """Logistic sigmoid function (CDF of Logistic distribution).""" return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-x)) def tconormprobabilisticsum(a, b): """Probabilistic sum T-conorm: a + b - ab.""" return a + b - a b def computefacepixeldistance(face, pixelp): """ Computes the screen-space distance from pixel p to face t. This is a standard geometric rasterization step (e.g., barycentric coordinates or signed distance to the projected triangle plane).""" # Standard geometric computation omitted; returns float distance. return 0.0 def computeoccupancy(pixelp, faces, tau, cdffunc, tconormfunc): """ Compute occupancy for a pixel using GenDR. Args: pixelp: 2D coordinates of the pixel. faces: List of face objects, each having a method screendistance(p). tau: Temperature/scale parameter. cdffunc: Cumulative distribution function F(x). tconormfunc: T-conorm aggregation function. Returns: Occupancy value AO(p, T). """ occupancy = 0.0 for face in faces: dist = computefacepixeldistance(face, pixelp) normalizeddist = dist / tau prob = cdffunc(normalizeddist) occupancy = tconormfunc(occupancy, prob) return occupancy A differentiable rasterizer that uses a probabilistic sum T-conorm and specific smoothing distributions, generalized by GenDR. Soft Rasterizer A differentiable volume rendering method that uses differential diffusion to compute gradients for ray marching. Ray Marching with Differential Diffusion A differentiable path tracing method that uses Monte Carlo sampling to compute gradients for ray tracing. Differentiable Monte Carlo Ray Tracing A differentiable renderer that uses RGBXY parameterization and optimal transport to compute gradients for rendering. RGBXY Derivatives with Optimal Transport (DROT) A method for computing sensitivity analysis over arbitrary outputs in rendering pipelines. Sensitivity AOV A differentiable rendering model based on SAR principles for gradient-based optimization. SAR Differentiable Rendering Model Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Evaluated on ShapeNet 3D reconstruction benchmark; the uniform distribution yielded the best overall results when averaged across distributions. Scaling: Performance depends on the choice of distribution and T-conorm; regular distributions F typically perform better than squared counterparts F^2, except for Cauchy and reciprocal sigmoid. Strengths: Provides continuous and differentiable rendering, enabling gradient-based optimization; generalizes existing methods like SoftRas and DIB-R. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to evaluating all faces for all pixels; choice of \tau and distribution is critical and requires grid search. When to Use: Shape optimization tasks, e.g., optimizing a mesh to fit a silhouette within 100 steps. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. GenDR was introduced by Bastian Goldluecke and Felix Petersen from the University of Konstanz in 2022. The work formalizes the requirements for differentiable rendering components and instantiates a general differentiable renderer with an array of different smoothing distributions. It generalizes existing differentiable renderers like SoftRas and DIB-R. The method is used in shape optimization tasks, such as optimizing a mesh to fit a silhouette. name: Reparameterization Estimators
body: Reparameterization estimators compute gradients of rendering integrals by transforming the integration domain or sampling distribution so that parameter dependence moves from domain boundaries or probability density functions into the integrand's argument. This allows differentiation under the integral sign without boundary terms. Unlike Automatic Differentiation (Reverse/Adjoint Mode) which propagates gradients through the computational graph, or Analytical Gradients which derive closed-form derivatives, reparameterization relies on a change of variables to make discontinuities or sampling distributions static with respect to optimization variables. The core mechanism applies the change of variables formula to the rendering integral I(\theta) = \int{\Omega\theta} f(x, \theta) dx. By introducing a differentiable transformation T(\omega, \theta): \Omega \to \Omega\theta from a fixed reference domain \Omega to the parameter-dependent domain \Omega\theta, the integral becomes: I(\theta) = \int{\Omega} f(T(\omega, \theta), \theta) \left| \det \frac{\partial T}{\partial \omega} \right| d\omega The gradient with respect to parameters \theta is obtained by differentiating under the integral sign: \frac{\partial I}{\partial \theta} = \int{\Omega} \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \left[ f(T(\omega, \theta), \theta) \left| \det \frac{\partial T}{\partial \omega} \right| \right] d\omega In Monte Carlo estimation, this is implemented by sampling points \omega from a fixed distribution p(\omega) on \Omega, mapping them to x = T(\omega, \theta), and weighting by the Jacobian determinant \left| \det \frac{\partial T}{\partial \omega} \right|. The gradient estimator is: \hat{\nabla}\theta I = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \nabla\theta \left[ \frac{f(T(\omegai, \theta), \theta) \left| \det \frac{\partial T}{\partial \omega} \right|}{p(\omegai)} \right] This requires computing the derivative of the transformation T and the Jacobian determinant with respect to \theta. Computes color estimates by sampling points on a ray using the inverse of the cumulative density function (CDF), allowing gradients to back-propagate through sampling locations with respect to the density field. It differs from NeRF's hierarchical sampling by learning sampling points end-to-end without auxiliary networks, and exhibits lower variance than standard importance sampling with a uniform distribution. It sets itself apart by explicitly defining the sampling distribution via the ray's opacity function rather than general volume elements. Choose for unbiased gradient estimation through the inverse opacity function. Computes the gradient of the rendered image with respect to scene parameters by integrating differential measurement contributions over path space, using Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) to combine BRDF and emitter sampling, and Next Event Estimation (NEE) to connect paths to emitters. It solves high variance in scenes with varying material properties by allowing the differential vertex to be located at any intermediate vertex or emitter connection. Choose for scenes with complex material properties and varying light transport. Eliminates bias in gradients caused by visibility discontinuities moving with scene parameters by applying a change of variables to transform the integration domain such that discontinuities become static. It differs from explicit edge sampling methods by avoiding boundary terms, making it computationally efficient for complex scenes, though it approximates gradients and has limitations with specular materials. Choose for complex scenes where boundary detection is expensive. Alleviates optimization plateaus by convolving the rendering equation with a smoothing kernel over the parameter space. Unlike standard differentiable path tracers, it ensures scene parameters continuously influence the objective function in expectation, allowing convergence on problems with intricate light transport like caustics. Choose when facing optimization plateaus or discontinuous gradients due to visibility changes. Counteracts parameter-dependent silhouette motion and resulting bias by applying a change of variables to freeze discontinuities in a reference domain. It sets itself apart by explicitly constructing a warp field via auxiliary ray tracing to handle the geometric transformation. Choose when handling moving geometry boundaries that cause non-differentiable jumps. Reduces gradient estimator variance by leveraging the statistical property that the expected gradient of the weight term is zero. It sets itself apart by explicitly constructing a correlated control estimator from the Jacobian weights of the reparameterization. Choose when the integrand is smooth or constant and variance reduction is critical. Comparison: PGRIS uses the integrand as is (with positivization), whereas GRIS without positivization uses the absolute value of the integrand as the target function, leading to higher variance. Pitfall: Unidirectional estimators struggle with hard-to-sample lights and specular materials, leading to noisier gradients and less accurate reconstructions. name: Reparameterized Volume Sampling
head: Differentiable Volume Sampling, Inverse CDF Sampling
body: Reparameterized Volume Sampling is a differentiable volume rendering technique that computes color estimates by sampling points on a ray using the inverse of the cumulative density function (CDF), allowing gradients to back-propagate through the sampling locations with respect to the density field. It differs from NeRF's hierarchical sampling, which relies on an auxiliary coarse model trained separately, by learning sampling points end-to-end without auxiliary networks. Compared to standard importance sampling with a uniform distribution, this stratified reparameterized sampling exhibits lower variance. Inputs: Ray origin o and direction d. Ray segment bounds [t{r1}, t{r2}] (near and far planes). Density field \sigmar(t), typically represented by a neural network or grid. Radiance field cr(t). Number of samples per ray k (typically 32). Number of knots m for piecewise linear approximation (typically 256). Outputs: Estimated color C(r) for the ray. Gradients \frac{\partial C}{\partial \theta} with respect to density field parameters \theta. Data Structures: Knots: A set of m+1 positions t0, t1, \dots, tm along the ray. In experiments, these are formed by slightly perturbing a uniform grid. Density Approximation: Piecewise linear interpolation of \sigmar(t) between knots. Let \sigmai = \sigmar(ti). The density at any t \in [ti, t{i+1}] is: \sigmar(t) = \sigmai \frac{t{i+1} - t}{t{i+1} - ti} + \sigma{i+1} \frac{t - ti}{t{i+1} - ti} Steps: 1. Approximate Density: Construct the piecewise linear approximation of \sigmar(t) using m knots. 2. Compute CDF Integral Approximation: Define the cumulative integral approximation I(t) = \int{t{r1}}^t \sigmar(s) ds. Since \sigmar is piecewise linear, I(t) is piecewise quadratic. Specifically, within bin i (t \in [ti, t{i+1}]), letting x = t - ti and \Delta t = t{i+1} - ti: I(t) = I(ti) + \sigmai x + \frac{\sigma{i+1} - \sigmai}{2 \Delta t} x^2 3. Generate Random Sample: Draw u \sim \text{Uniform}[0, 1]. 4. Compute Target Opacity: Calculate the target cumulative opacity value yf u. The source uses yf as a scaling factor, typically 1.0 for full opacity range. The equation is: yf u = Fr(t) = 1 - \exp\left(-\int{t{r1}}^t \sigmar(s) ds\right) 5. Rewrite Inversion Equation: Isolate the integral: -\log(1 - yf u) = \int{t{r1}}^t \sigmar(s) ds = I(t) Let Y = -\log(1 - yf u). We need to solve I(t) = Y for t. 6. Find Bin: Evaluate I(t) at the knots ti to find the interval [ti, t{i+1}] such that I(ti) \le Y < I(t{i+1}). Since I(t) is monotonic, this bin is unique. 7. Solve for t: Within the identified bin, solve the quadratic equation I(t) = Y for t. The explicit formula depends on the coefficients of the quadratic polynomial representing I(t) in that bin. The source notes that explicit formulae are provided in supplementary materials and that numerical stability is crucial. 8. Evaluate Radiance: Evaluate cr(t) at the computed sample position t. 9. Accumulate Color: Repeat steps 3-8 for k samples (using stratified sampling for lower variance) and accumulate the color estimate. The color estimate is: C(r) = \frac{1}{k} \sum{j=1}^k cr(tj) where weights are uniform because sampling is performed directly from the approximate CDF. The source states the estimate is unbiased. Parameters: k = 32 samples per ray. m = 256 knots. Activation function for density field: Softplus with \beta = 10. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Gradients: Using ReLU activation for the density field can result in zero gradients, hindering training. Numerical Stability: Solving the quadratic equation requires careful handling to ensure numerical stability, especially when Y is close to bin boundaries or when coefficients are small. Degenerate Distributions: Importance sampling requires only a few points for degenerate distributions, but the method is designed to work generally. Approximation Error: Piecewise constant approximation was faster but delivered worse rendering quality compared to piecewise linear. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def reparameterizedvolumesampling(rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, densitynet, radiancenet, k=32, m=256): """ Performs reparameterized volume sampling for a single ray. Args: rayorigin: (3,) array, origin of the ray. raydirection: (3,) array, direction of the ray. tnear: float, near plane distance. tfar: float, far plane distance. densitynet: callable, returns density sigma at 3D points. radiancenet: callable, returns radiance c at 3D points. k: int, number of samples per ray. m: int, number of knots for piecewise linear density approximation. Returns: color: (3,) array, estimated color. """ # 1. Normalize ray direction to ensure t represents physical distance d = raydirection / np.linalg.norm(raydirection) # 2. Define knots # Slightly perturb a uniform grid tuniform = np.linspace(tnear, tfar, m + 1) # Perturbation: Add small random noise to avoid degenerate cases noise = np.random.uniform(-1e-6, 1e-6, m + 1) tknots = tuniform + noise # 3. Evaluate density at knots # Sample points along the ray at knots pointsknots = rayorigin + tknots[:, None] d sigmaknots = densitynet(pointsknots).squeeze() # Shape (m+1,) # 4. Precompute integral values I(t) at knots # I(t) = integral from tnear to t of sigma(s) ds # Since sigma is piecewise linear, I(t) is piecewise quadratic. Iknots = np.zeros(m + 1) for i in range(m): ti = tknots[i] tip1 = tknots[i+1] sigmai = sigmaknots[i] sigmaip1 = sigmaknots[i+1] # Integral of linear function from ti to tip1 deltat = tip1 - ti integralbin = 0.5 (sigmai + sigmaip1) deltat Iknots[i+1] = Iknots[i] + integralbin # 5. Stratified sampling # Generate k stratified samples ustratified = (np.arange(1, k + 1) - 0.5) / k # 6. Compute target Y values # yf is 1.0 for full opacity range yf = 1.0 Y = -np.log(1.0 - yf ustratified) # Clamp Y to the maximum accumulated optical depth to handle boundary cases Y = np.minimum(Y, Iknots[-1]) # 7. Find bins and solve for t tsamples = np.zeros(k) for j in range(k): Yval = Y[j] # Find bin i such that Iknots[i] <= Yval < Iknots[i+1] i = np.searchsorted(Iknots, Yval, side='right') - 1 i = np.clip(i, 0, m - 1) ti = tknots[i] tip1 = tknots[i+1] sigmai = sigmaknots[i] sigmaip1 = sigmaknots[i+1] Ii = Iknots[i] # Solve I(t) = Yval for t in [ti, tip1] # I(t) = Ii + sigmai x + 0.5 slope x^2, where x = t - ti # 0.5 slope x^2 + sigmai x + (Ii - Yval) = 0 deltat = tip1 - ti slope = (sigmaip1 - sigmai) / deltat a = 0.5 slope b = sigmai c = Ii - Yval # Solve quadratic equation ax^2 + bx + c = 0 if np.abs(a) < 1e-9: # Linear case (constant density) if np.abs(b) < 1e-9: x = 0.0 else: x = -c / b else: discriminant = b2 - 4ac if discriminant < 0: discriminant = 0.0 sqrtdisc = np.sqrt(discriminant) # Use stable quadratic formula if b >= 0: x1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2a) x2 = (2c) / (-b - sqrtdisc) else: x1 = (2c) / (-b + sqrtdisc) x2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2a) # Select root in [0, deltat] if 0 <= x1 <= deltat: x = x1 elif 0 <= x2 <= deltat: x = x2 else: x = 0.0 tsamples[j] = ti + x # 8. Evaluate radiance and accumulate pointssamples = rayorigin + tsamples[:, None] d radiance = radiancenet(pointssamples) # Shape (k, 3) # Uniform weights because sampling is from the approximate CDF color = np.mean(radiance, axis=0) return color A sampling strategy modifying the density to include a constant background density \epsilon to prevent gradient outliers when \sigmat is near zero. The defensive sampling density is p{\text{def}}(t) = (\sigmat(t) + \epsilon) T\epsilon(t). The problematic term is bounded by \frac{1}{\sigmat(t) + \epsilon} \leq \frac{1}{\epsilon}. However, with p{\text{def}}, non-unit sampling weights compound over the length of the path, which is problematic in volumetric rendering where long paths are common. When using path replay backpropagation, defensive sampling must either be used for incident radiance terms (injecting variance) or additional samples must be drawn (increasing cost). Time Complexity: Dominated by the density and radiance network evaluations at k sample points and m knots. The root-finding step is O(k \log m) or O(k) with precomputed bins. Memory Complexity: O(m) to store knot positions and integral values. Measured Performance: In the 'foggy' density field test, 32 samples matched the baseline performance of 128 samples. In 'Glass and wall' and 'Wall' density fields, 4 samples matched the baseline performance. Scaling: The method scales with the number of knots m and samples k. Strengths: Lower variance compared to standard importance sampling with uniform distribution. End-to-end differentiable without auxiliary networks. Limitations: Requires careful numerical implementation for stability. Piecewise linear approximation is more complex than piecewise constant. When to use: When differentiable sampling is required and lower variance is desired compared to uniform importance sampling. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and piecewise constant approximation is acceptable (though quality suffers). Reparameterized Volume Sampling was introduced in the paper "Differentiable Rendering With Reparameterized Volume Sampling" (DVGO). It builds on the reparameterization estimator principles. The method was applied to 3D scene reconstruction based on a set of image projections, using the synthetic data from NeRF. It was compared against NeRF and DVGO baselines. name: Reparameterized Monte Carlo Volume Rendering
head: R/MC, R/MC estimate, R/SMC estimate, Reparameterized Stratified Monte Carlo (R/SMC) Volume Rendering
body: Reparameterized Monte Carlo Volume Rendering (R/MC) is a differentiable volume rendering method that estimates expected radiance by sampling from the density-induced probability distribution using the reparameterization trick, allowing end-to-end gradient-based optimization without auxiliary models. It sets itself apart from standard volumetric integration by transforming the integration domain from ray distance t to cumulative opacity y, enabling unbiased gradient estimation through the inverse opacity function. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin o, direction d, near bound tn, far bound tf, density field \sigma(x), radiance field c(x). Outputs: Estimated radiance \hat{C} for the ray. Data Structures: Ray: Defined as r(t) = o + td. Density Field: \sigmar(t) = \sigma(o + td). Radiance Field: cr(t) = c(o + td). Opacity Function: Fr(t) = 1 - \exp\left(-\int{tn}^{t} \sigmar(s) ds\right). Total Opacity: yf = Fr(tf). Steps: 1. Define the ray r = o + td with near/far bounds tn, tf. 2. Define the density field \sigma and radiance field c. 3. Compute the total opacity yf = Fr(tf) = 1 - \exp\left(-\int{tn}^{tf} \sigmar(s) ds\right). 4. Generate k independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) samples ui \sim U[0,1] for R/MC, or stratified samples vi for R/SMC. 5. For each sample, compute the target cumulative opacity yi = yf ui (or yf vi). 6. Solve for the ray distance ti such that Fr(ti) = yi using the inverse opacity function Fr^{-1}. 7. Query the radiance cr(ti) at the computed distances. 8. Compute the estimate \hat{C} = \frac{yf}{k} \sum{i=1}^k cr(ti). Formulas: The integral boundaries are normalized to [0, 1] by substituting y = yf u where u \sim U[0,1]: \int{0}^{yf} cr(Fr^{-1}(y)) dy = \int0^1 yf cr(Fr^{-1}(yf u)) du The R/MC estimate for a ray r with k i.i.d. uniform samples u1,..., uk \sim U[0,1] is: \hat{C}{MC}^R(r):= \frac{yf}{k} \sum{i=1}^k cr(Fr^{-1}(yf ui)) The R/SMC estimate replaces uniform samples ui with stratified samples vi drawn from regular grid bins: vi \sim U\left[\frac{i-1}{k+1}, \frac{i}{k+1}\right] \quad \text{for } i=1,...,k The estimate is: \hat{C}{SMC}^R(r):= \frac{yf}{k} \sum{i=1}^k cr(Fr^{-1}(yf vi)) Parameters: k: Number of samples per ray. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Pitfalls: The method cannot compute Fr analytically in practice because \sigmar is only queried at discrete points, requiring approximations of Fr and its inverse Fr^{-1}. The sources do not specify the numerical method for approximating Fr and Fr^{-1} (e.g., piecewise constant vs. linear interpolation, root-finding algorithms). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def reparameterizedmcvolumerendering(rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, densityfield, radiancefield, numsamples): """ Estimates radiance for a ray using Reparameterized Monte Carlo Volume Rendering. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector (x, y, z) raydirection: 3D vector (x, y, z), assumed normalized tnear: float, near bound of the ray tfar: float, far bound of the ray densityfield: function p -> float, returns density at point p radiancefield: function p -> float, returns radiance at point p numsamples: int, number of samples k Returns: float, estimated radiance """ # Simple deterministic uniform random number generator def uniformrandom(): nonlocal rngstate rngstate = (rngstate 1103515245 + 12345) & 0x7fffffff return rngstate / 0x7fffffff rngstate = 42 # Initial seed # Step 3: Compute total opacity yf totaldensityintegral = numericalintegratedensity(densityfield, rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar) yf = 1.0 - math.exp(-totaldensityintegral) # Handle degenerate case where the ray is completely transparent if yf == 0.0: return 0.0 radiancesum = 0.0 for in range(numsamples): # Step 4 & 5: Generate sample and compute target cumulative opacity u = uniformrandom() ytarget = yf u # Step 6: Solve for ray distance ti such that Fr(ti) = ytarget # Fr(t) = 1 - exp(-int{tnear}^t sigmar(s) ds) # ytarget = 1 - exp(-int{tnear}^t sigmar(s) ds) # int{tnear}^t sigmar(s) ds = -ln(1 - ytarget) targetdensityintegral = -math.log(1.0 - ytarget) # Binary search to invert the cumulative density integral ti = invertopacityfunction(densityfield, rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, targetdensityintegral) # Step 7: Query radiance at the sampled point point = rayorigin + ti raydirection radiance = radiancefield(point) radiancesum += radiance # Step 8: Compute estimate estimate = (yf / numsamples) radiancesum return estimate def numericalintegratedensity(densityfield, rayorigin, raydirection, tstart, tend): """ Approximates the integral of density along the ray from tstart to tend. Trapezoidal rule approximation. """ numsteps = 100 dt = (tend - tstart) / numsteps integral = 0.0 for j in range(numsteps): t1 = tstart + j dt t2 = tstart + (j + 1) dt p1 = rayorigin + t1 raydirection p2 = rayorigin + t2 raydirection sigma1 = densityfield(p1) sigma2 = densityfield(p2) integral += (sigma1 + sigma2) / 2.0 dt return integral def invertopacityfunction(densityfield, rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, targetintegral): """ Finds t such that the integral of density from tnear to t equals targetintegral. Uses binary search as a robust root-finding method for monotonic functions. """ tlow = tnear thigh = tfar for in range(50): tmid = (tlow + thigh) / 2.0 currentintegral = numericalintegratedensity(densityfield, rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tmid) if currentintegral < targetintegral: tlow = tmid else: thigh = tmid return (tlow + thigh) / 2.0 Time Complexity: O(k \cdot N{steps}) per ray, where k is the number of samples and N{steps} is the number of steps in the numerical integration and root-finding procedures. The sources do not specify N{steps}. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray, assuming the density and radiance fields are queried on the fly. Measured Performance: The sources do not provide measured performance metrics. Scaling: The method scales linearly with the number of samples k. Strengths: Allows end-to-end learning with gradient descent; alleviates costs associated with the color component of the neural radiance field at the additional cost of the density sampling algorithm. Limitations: Requires approximations of Fr and its inverse Fr^{-1}, which can be computationally expensive and introduce approximation errors. When to use: When differentiable volume rendering is required and the density field is available. When not to use: When analytical computation of Fr and Fr^{-1} is not possible and numerical approximations are too costly. Origin: The method was proposed in the paper "Differentiable Rendering With Reparameterized Volume Sampling". History and Development: The paper introduces the reparameterization of the sampling algorithm to allow end-to-end learning with gradient descent. Where it is used: Learning-based approaches for representing 3D scenes and generating novel views. name: Differential path integral estimator with MIS and NEE
head: Differential NEE estimator, MIS-weighted differential path estimator
body: This method computes the gradient of the rendered image with respect to scene parameters \theta by integrating differential measurement contributions over path space. It solves the problem of high variance in gradient estimation for specular materials and complex lighting by combining standard BRDF sampling with Next Event Estimation (NEE) using Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS). Unlike standard NEE which only connects paths to emitters at the final vertex, this method allows the differential vertex (the location where the derivative is taken) to be located at any intermediate vertex i or at the emitter connection, combining BRDF and emitter sampling probabilities into a single mixture weight. It builds on Reparameterization Estimators by applying the reparameterization principle to path-space integrals with explicit MIS weights for discontinuous contributions. Inputs: Scene parameters \theta (e.g., material roughness, light intensity, geometry). Camera configuration. Number of samples per pixel M. Maximum path depth N. Probability q of switching to differential sampling at each vertex. Outputs: Gradient estimate \hat{\nabla}\theta I{\text{NEE}}. Data Structures: Path x = (x0, x1, \dots, xN), where x0 is the camera position and xk are surface/media vertices. Emitter connection path xj x{e,j}, where xj is a vertex on the main path and x{e,j} is a point on an emitter. Differential contribution g(x, i; \theta) for vertex i on path x. Differential contribution g(x, xj x{e,j}, i; \theta) for vertex i on path x connected to emitter at j. Steps: 1. Initialize gradient accumulator G = 0. 2. For each sample m = 1 \dots M: a. Generate a standard path x^m of depth N using BRDF sampling. b. Compute the mixture probability p{\text{mix}}(x^m) using Equation (41). c. For each vertex i = 0 \dots N: i. Compute the differential contribution g(x^m, i; \theta) using Equation (5) from (standard differential contribution). ii. Add \frac{g(x^m, i; \theta)}{p{\text{mix}}(x^m)} to G. d. For each vertex j = 1 \dots N-1: i. Generate an NEE path x^mj x^m{e,j} by connecting vertex x^mj to an emitter. ii. Compute the mixture probability p{\text{mix}}(x^m, x^mj x^m{e,j}) using Equation (42). iii. For each vertex i = 0 \dots j: 1. Compute the differential contribution g(x^m, x^mj x^m{e,j}, i; \theta) using Equation (43). 2. Add \frac{g(x^m, x^mj x^m{e,j}, i; \theta)}{p{\text{mix}}(x^m, x^mj x^m{e,j})} to G. 3. Return G / M. Formulas: The gradient estimator is given by: \partial\theta I{\text{NEE}} = \frac{1}{M} \sum{m=1}^M \left[ \sum{i=0}^{N^m} \frac{g(x^m, i; \theta)}{p{\text{mix}}(x^m)} + \sum{j=1}^{N^m-1} \sum{i=0}^j \frac{g(x^m, x^mj x^m{e,j}, i; \theta)}{p{\text{mix}}(x^m, x^mj x^m{e,j})} \right] The differential contribution for a standard path x with differential vertex i is: g(x, i; \theta) = \left( \prod{k=0, k \neq i}^{N} fk(x) \right) \frac{\partial\theta fi(x)}{fi(x)} Le(xN) \quad \text{(Implicit from Eq 36 and context)} Note: The exact form of g(x, i; \theta) for standard paths is derived from the expansion of \partial\theta I in Eq (36) and Eq (35) in. It represents the product of all BSDFs except fi, multiplied by the derivative of fi and the emitted radiance. The differential contribution for an NEE path x, xj x{e,j} with differential vertex i is: g(x, xj x{e,j}, i; \theta) = \left[ \prod{k=1}^{j-1} fk(x) \right] G(xj, x{e,j}) \rhos(x{j-1}, xj, x{e,j}) \cdot \frac{\partial\theta fi(x)}{fi(x)} \cdot Le(x{e,j}) where: fk(x) is the BSDF at vertex xk. G(xj, x{e,j}) is the geometry term between xj and the emitter point x{e,j}. \rhos(x{j-1}, xj, x{e,j}) is the shadow term (visibility) between x{j-1} and x{e,j} via xj. Le(x{e,j}) is the radiance from the emitter at x{e,j}. The mixture probability for a standard path x is: p{\text{mix}}(x) = p(x) + \sum{i=1}^{N-1} p(x, i) + p{\text{nee}}(x, x{N-1}xN) where p(x) is the probability of generating x via BRDF sampling, p(x, i) is the probability of generating x with differential vertex i via BRDF sampling, and p{\text{nee}}(x, x{N-1}xN) is the probability of generating x with an NEE connection at the last vertex. The mixture probability for an NEE path x, xj x{e,j} is: p{\text{mix}}(x, xj x{e,j}) = p(x, xj x{e,j}) + \sum{i=1}^j p(x, xj x{e,j}, i) + p{\text{nee}}(x, xj x{e,j}) + \sum{i=1}^{j-1} p{\text{nee}}(x, xj x{e,j}, i) The probability of generating the NEE path with differential vertex i (1 \le i < j) is: p{\text{nee}}(x, xj x{e,j}, i) = \frac{\prod{k=0}^{j-1} pf(xk)}{pf(xi)} p{\partial f}(xi) (1-q)^{i-1} q where pf(xk) is the BRDF sampling probability at vertex k, p{\partial f}(xi) is the differential sampling probability at vertex i, and q is the switching probability. The probability of generating the NEE path without a specific differential vertex (standard NEE) is: p{\text{nee}}(x, xj x{e,j}) = \left[ \prod{k=0}^{j-1} pf(xk) \right] pe(xj x{e,j}) (1-q)^{j-1} where pe(xj x{e,j}) is the emitter sampling probability. The probability of generating the NEE path with differential vertex i (1 \le i < j) via BRDF sampling is: p(x, xj x{e,j}, i) = \begin{cases} p{\text{nee}}(\dots) \frac{pf(x{j-1}xj x{e,j})}{pe(xj x{e,j})} & \text{if } 1 \le i < j \\ p{\text{nee}}(\dots) \frac{p{\partial f}(x{j-1}xj x{e,j})}{pe(xj x{e,j})} & \text{if } i = j \end{cases} Note: The exact form of p(x, xj x{e,j}, i) in Eq (39) of is complex and depends on the specific MIS weighting scheme. The implementation should follow the derivation in Appendix B of. Parameters: q: Probability of switching to differential sampling at each vertex. Typical values are not given in the sources. M: Number of independent samples drawn per pixel. Edge cases and pitfalls: Precision: Division by p{\text{mix}} can lead to numerical instability if the probability is very small. Guard against division by zero. Boundaries: The sums for i and j have specific ranges. Ensure indices are within bounds. Degenerate input: If N=1, the loops for j may be empty. Handle accordingly. It solves the problem of high variance in gradient estimation, particularly for specular materials, by combining differential vertex sampling with standard BRDF sampling using Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS). Unlike standard BRDF sampling, which treats all vertices identically, this method explicitly biases the sampling distribution to capture the boundary component of the gradient integral, significantly reducing variance for microfacet and mixture BRDFs. See Differential Vertex Sampling with MIS. Differential Edge Sampling is a method for computing the gradient of physically-based rendered images with respect to arbitrary scene parameters (camera, lights, materials, geometry) by explicitly sampling visibility discontinuities. It solves the problem that standard Monte Carlo estimators fail to capture derivatives at boundaries where visibility changes abruptly, such as object silhouettes and occlusion edges. Unlike its sibling Differential Vertex Sampling with MIS, which focuses on vertex-based contributions, this method decomposes the rendering derivative into a smooth interior integral (estimated via automatic differentiation) and a boundary integral (estimated by sampling triangle edges). See Differential Edge Sampling. This method reduces the variance of gradient estimates in differentiable volume rendering by sampling pairs of similar paths and applying a control variate technique known as the cross-weighting scheme. It allows the use of suitable parameter values from one path estimate to reduce the variance of the other without introducing bias, addressing the high variance inherent in estimating derivatives of discontinuous integrands. It builds on Differential path integral estimator with MIS and NEE by providing a specific variance reduction strategy for the differential contributions computed therein. See Cross-reduction of variance using pairs of paths. A differentiable path tracer that computes gradients of radiance with respect to scene parameters (e.g., Signed Distance Function shape parameters) by warping random samples via reparameterization, supporting both forward and backward mode automatic differentiation. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly integrating reparameterization gradients into the path sampling loop, allowing for stable gradient flow through the SDF evaluation and sphere tracing steps, whereas siblings like Differential Vertex Sampling with MIS rely on vertex perturbation and Differential Edge Sampling on edge perturbations. See SDF Prb Reparam Integrator. This approach effectively shares all paths traced by Algorithm 1 to calculate derivatives with respect to all scene parameters simultaneously. It executes Algorithm 1 once in a vectorized fashion to estimate the total scene derivative d\pi L. It replaces all partial derivatives with their vector-valued total derivative counterparts and performs component-wise calculations between all total-derivative-related quantities. Time Complexity: The method requires tracing additional side paths for NEE, making it more expensive than conventional Volume Path Tracing (VPT). The time complexity is O(K^2) for each sample path of length K, due to the additional side paths needed to estimate \Delta L and L{ins}. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces variance for specular materials and complex lighting by combining BRDF and emitter sampling. Allows differential vertex to be at any intermediate vertex or emitter connection. Limitations: More expensive than conventional VPT due to additional side paths. When to use: Differentiable rendering, inverse rendering, and joint material/lighting estimation. Gkioulekas, "Path Sampling Methods for Differentiable Rendering". It builds on earlier work in differentiable rendering, such as "Differentiable Monte Carlo ray tracing through edge sampling" by Li et al. [LADL18] and "Unbiased inverse volume rendering with differential trackers" by Nimier-David et al. [NDMKJ22]. The use of MIS for differential path integrals is a key contribution of. head: Differential sampling with MIS
body: Differential Vertex Sampling with MIS is a method to estimate the gradient of a loss function with respect to scene parameters by importance sampling an intermediate path vertex as the differential vertex. It solves the problem of high variance in gradient estimation, particularly for specular materials, by combining differential vertex sampling with standard BRDF sampling using Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS). Unlike standard BRDF sampling, which treats all vertices identically, this method explicitly biases the sampling distribution to capture the boundary component of the gradient integral, significantly reducing variance for microfacet and mixture BRDFs. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Path vertex state (position, incoming direction, throughput), scene parameters \theta, mixing probability q, random number generator. Outputs: Accumulated gradient update \delta\theta, updated throughput \beta, updated MIS weights w1, w2. Data Structures: sampled∂x: Boolean flag indicating if the differential vertex has been sampled for the current path vertex. w1, w2: MIS weights for the differential and standard sampling strategies, respectively. β: Throughput term, which includes the product of densities pf from the mixture probability. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize sampled∂x to FALSE for the current path vertex. 2. Generate a random number R. 3. If !sampled∂x AND R < q: a. Sample the differential vertex: (\omega', f) = \text{SAMPLE\∂BRDF}(\text{state}). b. Set sampled∂x to TRUE. c. Compute the gradient update: \delta\theta \leftarrow \delta\theta + \text{BACKWARD\GRAD}(f, \delta L \cdot L/f). 4. Else (if differential vertex was not sampled): a. Sample the standard BRDF vertex: (\omega', f) = \text{SAMPLE\BRDF}(\text{state}). b. Update throughput: \beta \leftarrow \beta \cdot \frac{f}{pf(\omega', \text{state})}. c. Update MIS weights: w1 \leftarrow w1 + w2 \cdot q \cdot \frac{p{\partial f}(\omega', \text{state})}{pf(\omega', \text{state})} w2 \leftarrow w2 \cdot (1 - q) 5. Return the accumulated gradient \delta\theta. The method integrates with Next Event Estimation (NEE), though NEE steps are omitted from the pseudocode for simplicity. Formulas: The mixture probability p{\text{mix}}(x) for a path x is defined as: p{\text{mix}}(x) = \left( \prod{i=0}^{N} pf(xi) \right) \left( \sum{i=1}^{N-1} p{\partial f}(xi) (1-q)^{i-1} q + (1-q)^{N-1} \right) The MIS weights are updated as follows: w1 \leftarrow w1 + w2 \cdot q \cdot \frac{p{\partial f}(\omega', \text{state})}{pf(\omega', \text{state})} w2 \leftarrow w2 \cdot (1 - q) The gradient update is computed as: \delta\theta \leftarrow \delta\theta + \text{BACKWARD\GRAD}(f, \delta L \cdot L/f) Parameters: q: The probability of sampling the differential vertex at the current step instead of the standard BRDF vertex. Typical value: 0.5. This value balances early vertex contributions (higher q) with indirect lighting contributions from later vertices. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The mixture probability involves products of densities, which can lead to underflow or overflow if not handled carefully. Boundaries: The method integrates with Next Event Estimation (NEE), but NEE steps are omitted from the pseudocode. Degenerate Input: If q=0, the method degenerates to standard BRDF sampling. If q=1, it degenerates to differential vertex sampling only. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def differentialvertexsamplingwithmis( state, q, rng, samplepartialbrdf, samplebrdf, backwardgrad, ppartialf, pf, deltaL, L, beta, w1, w2, deltatheta): sampledpartialx = False R = rng.next() if not sampledpartialx and R < q: omegaprime, f = samplepartialbrdf(state) sampledpartialx = True deltatheta += backwardgrad(f, deltaL (L / f)) else: omegaprime, f = samplebrdf(state) beta = f / pf(omegaprime, state) w1 += w2 q ppartialf(omegaprime, state) / pf(omegaprime, state) w2 = (1 - q) return deltatheta This method estimates the boundary component of the gradient integral in differentiable rendering by combining Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) with primary-sample-space guiding. It addresses the high variance in gradient estimates caused by occlusion and complex illumination, which makes standard light sampling ineffective for boundary segments. Unlike its parent method, Differential Vertex Sampling with MIS, which uses MIS to combine differential vertex sampling with standard BRDF sampling, this method uses MIS to combine two distinct strategies for sampling the boundary segment's direction: light sampling and direct direction sampling. It sets itself apart from baseline methods by producing significantly cleaner gradient estimates at equal time and sample counts, particularly around shadow boundaries. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method reduces gradient variance significantly, especially for specular BRDFs. For microfacet BRDFs, it reduces variance to 0.69–0.84× of BRDF sampling with NEE; for mixture BRDFs, to 0.0048–0.042×. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Significant variance reduction for specular and mixture BRDFs. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When estimating gradients for differentiable rendering with specular or mixture BRDFs, especially where standard BRDF sampling yields high variance. When not: Not given in the sources. Origin: The method is described in "Path Sampling Methods for Differentiable Rendering" by T. Su & I. Gkioulekas. History and Development: The method is part of a broader set of path sampling methods for differentiable rendering, aiming to improve the efficiency of gradient estimation. Where it is used: Differentiable rendering, inverse rendering. Path Sampling Methods for Differentiable Rendering, https://doi.org/10.2312/sr.20241148, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Primary-Sample-Space Guided MIS with Edge Sorting
head: Boundary Path Integral Estimation, Primary-Sample-Space Guiding with Multiple Importance Sampling and Edge Sorting, Guided boundary integral estimation, MIS with light and direction sampling, Primary-Sample-Space Guiding with Multiple Importance Sampling, Variance-aware Differentiable Rendering, Variance-aware Differentiable Rendering with MIS and Edge Sorting
body: This method estimates the boundary component of the gradient integral in differentiable rendering by combining multiple importance sampling (MIS) with primary-sample-space guiding. It addresses high variance in gradient estimates caused by occlusion and complex illumination, which makes standard light sampling ineffective for boundary segments. Unlike its parent method, Differential Vertex Sampling with MIS, which uses MIS to combine differential vertex sampling with standard BRDF sampling, this method uses MIS to combine light sampling and direction sampling for the boundary segment. It sets itself apart from baseline methods like Zhang et al. (2020) by producing significantly cleaner gradient estimates at equal time and sample counts, particularly around shadow boundaries. Inputs: A polygonal mesh M, a camera, a light environment, and target functions \tilde{F}{\text{light}} and \tilde{F}{\text{dir}} derived from the boundary integral formulation. Outputs: Unbiased estimators for the boundary integral component of the gradient. 1. Kd-trees: Two Kd-trees are built during preprocessing, one for \tilde{F}{\text{light}} and one for \tilde{F}{\text{dir}}. Each leaf node stores a probability mass. 2. Edge Chains: A list of chains, where each chain is a sequence of mesh edges constructed via edge sorting. 1. Edge Sorting: To reduce discontinuities in the mapping from primary samples to mesh edges, build chains of mesh edges. Start with an arbitrary edge (v0, v1). Initialize chain with this edge. Set v{\text{prev}} = v0, v{\text{cur}} = v1. While v{\text{cur}} has unused edges: Select an unused edge (v{\text{cur}}, v{\text{next}}) such that the direction of (v{\text{cur}}, v{\text{next}}) is closest to (v{\text{prev}}, v{\text{cur}}). Append (v{\text{cur}}, v{\text{next}}) to chain. Update v{\text{prev}} = v{\text{cur}}, v{\text{cur}} = v{\text{next}}. Repeat for all edges to form a set of chains. 2. Guiding: Apply primary-sample-space guiding to \tilde{F}{\text{light}} and \tilde{F}{\text{dir}} to build the Kd-trees. 3. Normalization: Compute normalization constants c{\text{light}} and c{\text{dir}} by summing the probability masses stored in all leaf nodes of the respective Kd-trees. 1. Target Functions: Calculate the target functions for light and direction sampling: \tilde{F}{\text{light}}(\mathbf{u}1, \mathbf{u}2) = \left| \hat{f}^B(\mathbf{p}0^S, \mathbf{p}0^D) \right|{\text{light}}(\mathbf{u}1, \mathbf{u}2) \hat{h}^S(\mathbf{p}0^S, \mathbf{p}0^D) \hat{h}^D(\mathbf{p}0^S, \mathbf{p}0^D) \tilde{F}{\text{dir}}(u1, \mathbf{u}2) = \left| \tilde{F}^B(\mathbf{p}0^D, \mathbf{p}0^D) \right| F{\text{dir}}^B(u1, \mathbf{u}2) \tilde{h}^S(\mathbf{p}0^D, \mathbf{p}0^D) \tilde{h}^D(\mathbf{p}0^D, \mathbf{p}0^D) where \mathbf{p}0^S and \mathbf{p}0^D are determined by the boundary segment direction \omegaB. Note that \mathbf{p}0^S and \mathbf{p}0^D take different values in these equations for the same primary sample (u1, \mathbf{u}2) because they are determined by different \omegaB mappings. 2. Sampling: Draw two sets of primary samples: (u1^{\text{light}}, \mathbf{u}2^{\text{light}}) from density p{\text{light}} (guided by \tilde{F}{\text{light}}). (u1^{\text{dir}}, \mathbf{u}2^{\text{dir}}) from density p{\text{dir}} (guided by \tilde{F}{\text{dir}}). 3. Estimators: Compute two unbiased estimators of the boundary integral: E{\text{light}} = \frac{\tilde{F}{\text{light}}(u1^{\text{light}}, \mathbf{u}2^{\text{light}})}{p{\text{light}}(u1^{\text{light}}, \mathbf{u}2^{\text{light}})} E{\text{dir}} = \frac{\tilde{F}{\text{dir}}(u1^{\text{dir}}, \mathbf{u}2^{\text{dir}})}{p{\text{dir}}(u1^{\text{dir}}, \mathbf{u}2^{\text{dir}})} 4. Rewritten Densities: Rewrite the probability densities with respect to xB and \omegaB using Jacobians J{\text{light}}^B and J{\text{dir}}^B: \hat{p}{\text{light}}(u1, \mathbf{u}2):= \frac{p{\text{light}}(u1, \mathbf{u}2)}{J{\text{light}}^B(u1, \mathbf{u}2)} \hat{p}{\text{dir}}(u1, \mathbf{u}2):= \frac{p{\text{dir}}(u1, \mathbf{u}2)}{J{\text{dir}}^B(u1, \mathbf{u}2)} 5. Approximation: Approximate the rewritten densities using the target functions and normalization constants: \hat{p}{\text{light}}(u1, \mathbf{u}2) \approx \frac{\tilde{F}{\text{light}}(u1, \mathbf{u}2)}{c{\text{light}} J{\text{light}}^B(u1, \mathbf{u}2)} \hat{p}{\text{dir}}(u1, \mathbf{u}2) \approx \frac{\tilde{F}{\text{dir}}(u1, \mathbf{u}2)}{c{\text{dir}} J{\text{dir}}^B(u1, \mathbf{u}2)} This approximation allows O(1) calculation of the densities. 6. MIS Weighting: Apply the balance heuristic to weight the contributions: w{\text{light}} = \frac{\hat{p}{\text{light}}(\mathbf{u}^{\text{light}})}{\hat{p}{\text{light}}(\mathbf{u}^{\text{light}}) + \hat{p}{\text{dir}}(\mathbf{u}^{\text{light}})} w{\text{dir}} = \frac{\hat{p}{\text{dir}}(\mathbf{u}^{\text{dir}})}{\hat{p}{\text{light}}(\mathbf{u}^{\text{dir}}) + \hat{p}{\text{dir}}(\mathbf{u}^{\text{dir}})} The final estimator is w{\text{light}} E{\text{light}} + w{\text{dir}} E{\text{dir}}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preprocess(mesh, Flightfunc, Fdirfunc): chains = [] unusededges = set(getalledges(mesh)) while unusededges: startedge = unusededges.pop() chain = [startedge] vprev, vcur = startedge while vcur in unusededges: candidates = [e for e in unusededges if e[0] == vcur] if not candidates: break vnext = min(candidates, key=lambda e: anglebetween(e[1] - vcur, chain[-1][1] - chain[-1][0]))[1] edge = (vcur, vnext) chain.append(edge) unusededges.discard(edge) vprev, vcur = vcur, vnext chains.append(chain) kdlight = buildkdtree(Flightfunc, chains) kddir = buildkdtree(Fdirfunc, chains) clight = sum(kdlight.leafnodes) cdir = sum(kddir.leafnodes) return kdlight, kddir, clight, cdir def render(kdlight, kddir, clight, cdir, mesh, camera, lightenv): u1light, u2light = samplefromkd(kdlight) u1dir, u2dir = samplefromkd(kddir) omegaBlight = getdirectionfromlight(u1light, u2light, mesh, lightenv) omegaBdir = getdirectionfromdir(u1dir, u2dir, mesh) p0Slight, p0Dlight = getboundarypoints(omegaBlight, mesh) p0Sdir, p0Ddir = getboundarypoints(omegaBdir, mesh) Flight = abs(FhatB(p0Slight, p0Dlight)) hhatS(p0Slight, p0Dlight) hhatD(p0Slight, p0Dlight) Fdir = abs(FtildeB(p0Ddir, p0Ddir)) FdirB(u1dir, u2dir) htildeS(p0Ddir, p0Ddir) htildeD(p0Ddir, p0Ddir) plight = evaluatekd(kdlight, u1light, u2light) pdir = evaluatekd(kddir, u1dir, u2dir) Elight = Flight / plight Edir = Fdir / pdir Jlight = computejacobianlight(u1light, u2light, omegaBlight) Jdir = computejacobiandir(u1dir, u2dir, omegaBdir) phatlight = Flight / (clight Jlight) phatdir = Fdir / (cdir Jdir) phatdiratlight = Fdir(u1light, u2light) / (cdir computejacobiandir(u1light, u2light, getdirectionfromdir(u1light, u2light, mesh))) phatlightatdir = Flight(u1dir, u2dir) / (clight computejacobianlight(u1dir, u2dir, getdirectionfromlight(u1dir, u2dir, mesh, lightenv))) wlight = phatlight / (phatlight + phatdiratlight) wdir = phatdir / (phatlightatdir + phatdir) return wlight Elight + wdir Edir c{\text{light}}, c{\text{dir}}: Normalization constants from Kd-tree leaf sums. Hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper Pro 3975WX CPU, Nvidia RTX Titan. Occlusion: Light sampling can be ineffective for complex illumination (e.g., image-based lighting) because the sampled direction \omegaB may be invalid due to occlusion, causing the boundary segment to penetrate the object. Discontinuities: Highly discontinuous target functions cause Kd-trees to require large depths, degrading performance. This is mostly caused by discontinuities of xB as a function of u1. Edge sorting mitigates this. Rough Dielectrics: Warped-area sampling implementation does not support rough dielectric BSDF, requiring diffuse objects for certain evaluations. Shadow Boundaries: Direction sampling results in cleaner overall results but estimated gradients around shadow boundaries become slightly worse. MIS combines both to handle this. Participating Media: The technique focuses on surface-only light transport and does not currently support participating media, where the primary-sample space dimensionality increases from three to five. Time Complexity: \tilde{F}{\text{light}} and \tilde{F}{\text{dir}} can be calculated in O(1) time in the approximation equation. Memory Complexity: Guiding memory ranges from 80 KB to 4 MB depending on scene complexity. Performance: Dodoco: 70 target images, 450,000 parameters, batch size 2, 3000 iterations. Guiding memory 4 MB, guiding time 1.34 s, render time 2.59 s, postproc time 0.310 s. Jumpy Dumpty: 140 target images, 60,000 parameters, batch size 2, 520 iterations. Guiding memory 2 MB, guiding time 0.61 s, render time 1.11 s, postproc time 0.016 s. Klee: 40 target images, 60,000 parameters, batch size 1, 200 iterations. Guiding memory 2 MB, guiding time 0.33 s, render time 0.82 s, postproc time 0.016 s. Kirby: 35 target images, 15,000 parameters, batch size 1, 400 iterations. Guiding memory 80 KB, guiding time 0.91 s, render time 3.67 s, postproc time 0.017 s. Bunny in glass: 50 target images, 30,000 parameters, batch size 2, 2000 iterations. Guiding memory 128 KB, guiding time 1.79 s, render time 17.55 s, postproc time 0.022 s. Bunny shadow 2: 70 target images, 30,000 parameters, batch size 2, 600 iterations. Guiding memory 2 MB, guiding time 0.47 s, render time 0.72 s, postproc time 0.012 s. Duck: 35 target images, 3,205,728 parameters, batch size 1, 400 iterations. Guiding memory 2 MB, guiding time 0.34 s, render time 0.94 s, postproc time 0.092 s. Mora: 70 target images, 150,001 parameters, batch size 1, 1600 iterations. Guiding memory 4 MB, guiding time 0.43 s, render time 1.01 s, postproc time 0.109 s. Glass Dodoco: 140 target images, 60,000 parameters, batch size 1, 700 iterations. Guiding memory 400 KB, guiding time 0.94 s, render time 5.76 s, postproc time 0.093 s. Strengths: Produces significantly cleaner gradient estimates than Zhang et al. (2020) at equal time and sample counts. Significantly faster and lower noise than Warped-Area Sampling (WAS) at equal sample counts, with greater quality advantage at equal time. Yields significantly lower noise around shadow boundaries, resulting in better geometry reconstruction in non-line-of-sight configurations. Faster convergence than Zhang et al. due to lower variance boundary integral estimates. Limitations: Does not support participating media. Direction sampling alone performs worse around shadow boundaries. Origin: The method was introduced in "Variance-aware Differentiable Rendering". It builds on the baseline method by Zhang et al. (2020) for estimating the interior term of the gradient integral. History: Zhang et al. (2020) introduced the baseline method for estimating the interior term of Eq. 3.3 and was compared against in inverse-rendering experiments. Nicolet et al. (2021) introduced the method used to update mesh vertex positions based on estimated gradients. Usage: Used in inverse-rendering problems, particularly where remeshing can be applied to make input meshes field-aligned. Used in inverse-rendering optimizations for scenes including Dodoco, Jumpy Dumpty, Klee, Kirby, Bunny in glass, Bunny shadow 2, Duck, Mora, and Glass Dodoco. name: Differential Edge Sampling
head: Boundary Path Integral Estimation via Edge Sampling, Differential Spherical Integral / Edge Sampling, LADL18, Li et al, Monte Carlo edge sampling, Stochastic Monte Carlo Gradient Estimation
body: Differential Edge Sampling computes the gradient of physically-based rendered images with respect to arbitrary scene parameters (camera, lights, materials, geometry) by explicitly sampling visibility discontinuities. It solves the problem that standard Monte Carlo estimators fail to capture derivatives at boundaries where visibility changes abruptly, such as object silhouettes and occlusion edges. Unlike its sibling Differential Vertex Sampling with MIS, which focuses on vertex-based contributions, this method decomposes the rendering derivative into a smooth interior integral (estimated via automatic differentiation) and a boundary integral (estimated by sampling triangle edges). The method computes the gradient of the pixel filter’s integral by splitting the integrand into smooth and discontinuous regions. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Scene geometry (triangle meshes), material properties, light sources, camera parameters, and scene parameters \theta to differentiate with respect to. Outputs: Rendered image value and its gradient \nabla\theta I. Data Structures: Mesh Representation: Triangle meshes where discontinuities are identified at triangle edges. Exact layout, fields, sizes, and bit packing are not given in the sources. Edge Hierarchy: A spatial hierarchy used to efficiently reject interior edges and find silhouette edges for secondary boundaries. Exact layout, fields, sizes, and bit packing are not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Decomposition: Split the rendering integral into smooth parts and discontinuous parts. 2. Smooth Region Estimation: For smooth parts of the integrand, employ traditional area sampling combined with automatic differentiation to estimate the gradient. 3. Discontinuous Region Estimation (Edge Sampling): For discontinuous parts, explicitly sample edges to estimate the boundary integral contribution. Primary Boundaries: For boundaries directly observed by the detector (camera), project and clip all meshes into screen space and sample from the visible edges. Secondary Boundaries: For boundaries occurring at light bounces, the silhouette depends on the shading point. Use an importance sampling scheme with a hierarchy to quickly reject interior edges and find the relevant silhouette, avoiding per-bounce projection. 4. Combination: Combine the gradient estimates from smooth and discontinuous regions. Formulas: The rendering equation derivative is decomposed into an interior integral and a boundary integral. For mesh scenes, discontinuities occur at triangle edges. If shading is smooth, the focus narrows to silhouette edges. The complete equation for differentiating the radiative transfer equation (extended by Zhang et al. for volumes) is Lo = KT KC Li + Q, where Lo is outgoing radiance, KT is the transport operator, KC is the collision operator, Li is incoming radiance, and Q is the source term. Due to complexity, the specific derivative formula is referenced as Eq. 32 in the original paper. Parameters: Sampling Strategy: Importance sampling for secondary boundaries using a hierarchy. Assumptions: Meshes do not have interpenetration, no point light sources, no perfectly specular surfaces, and the scene is static. Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interpenetration: The method assumes meshes do not interpenetrate. Light Sources: Point light sources are not supported. Specular Surfaces: Perfectly specular surfaces are not supported. Dynamic Scenes: The scene must be static. Variance: Large variance in estimated gradients due to the difficulty of finding all object edges and sampling them. Performance: Rendering speed is slow. Secondary Boundaries: Inefficient to project for every light bounce due to shading-point-dependent silhouettes. Time Complexity: Slow rendering speed due to the computational cost of finding all object edges and sampling them. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Variance: Large variance in estimated gradients. Strengths: First method to achieve unbiased differentiation of the rendering equation for mesh scenes by explicitly handling discontinuities. Limitations: Limited to static scenes, no point lights, no perfect speculars, and high computational cost. When to Use: When unbiased gradients with respect to geometry and camera parameters are required for mesh-based scenes, and computational resources allow for high-variance, low-speed estimation. When Not to Use: For dynamic scenes, scenes with point lights or perfect speculars, or when real-time performance is required. Differential Edge Sampling was introduced by Li et al. in 2018 [LADL18] as the first work to compute derivatives of scalar functions over physically-based rendered images with respect to arbitrary input parameters using a stochastic Monte Carlo ray tracing approach. It achieved unbiased differentiation of the rendering equation [Kaj86] by directly sampling boundary discontinuities. Zhang et al. [ZWZ 19] later extended this method to support participating media by differentiating the radiative transfer equation. This work laid the foundation for path-space differentiable rendering (PSDR).
