name: Cross-reduction of variance using pairs of paths
head: Cross-weighting scheme, Variance cross-reduction
body: This method reduces the variance of gradient estimates in differentiable volume rendering by sampling pairs of similar paths and applying a control variate technique known as the cross-weighting scheme. It allows the use of suitable parameter values from one path estimate to reduce the variance of the other without introducing bias, addressing the high variance inherent in estimating derivatives of discontinuous integrands. It builds on Differential path integral estimator with MIS and NEE by providing a specific variance reduction strategy for the differential contributions computed therein. Inputs: Not given in the sources. Outputs: Not given in the sources. Data Structures: Path Pair: Two paths, P0 and P1, generated for each sample index i. Path Contribution Components: For each path i \in \{0, 1\} and each emitter contribution index l: f{i,l}(\theta): Product of emitted radiance and path throughput at vertex l. W{i,l}(\theta): Product of all associated weights w{i,l}(\theta) for the path segment up to emitter l. Note: \mathbb{E}[\partial W{i,l} / \partial \theta] = 0 because weights are independent of the gradients of other weights. Steps: 1. Sample Path Pairs: For each sample i, generate a pair of paths (P0, P1). The paths must be "similar" (see Partially correlated path generation below). 2. Compute Contributions: For each path i \in \{0, 1\}, compute the total contribution ri as a sum over all emitter contributions l: ri = \sum{l=0}^{\infty} f{i,l}(\theta) W{i,l}(\theta) \quad (27) 3. Apply Cross-Reduction: Combine the contributions r0 and r1 to form the reduced variance estimate r' using the cross-weighting formula: \begin{aligned} r' = & \frac{1}{2} \sum f{0,l}(\theta) W{0,l}(\theta) - f{1,l}(\theta) (W{0,l}(\theta) - W{0,l}(\theta0)) \\ & + \frac{1}{2} \sum f{1,l}(\theta) W{1,l}(\theta) - f{0,l}(\theta) (W{1,l}(\theta) - W{1,l}(\theta0)). \end{aligned} \quad (28) Here, W{i,l}(\theta0) represents the weights evaluated at the reference parameters \theta0. The term (W{0,l}(\theta) - W{0,l}(\theta0)) acts as the control variate correction. 4. Accumulate Gradient: The gradient is estimated by averaging the derivatives of r' over all sampled pairs. Parameters: Samples per Integral: 4 samples (ray intersection queries) are used to estimate changes of variables in each emitter, BSDF, and pixel integral. Beckmann Roughness Threshold: 0.15 (root mean square of slopes in the microgeometry). Convolutions are applied when roughness exceeds this value to handle integrands that violate the small angular support assumption. von Mises-Fisher Concentration: \kappa = 1000. Used for spherical convolution kernels. Pitfalls: Degenerate Light Sources: Point or directional lights containing Dirac delta terms are incompatible because visibility-related discontinuities cause the integrals to collapse. Area Light Discontinuities: Area lights introduce two types of discontinuities (light source silhouette and occluder silhouettes), violating the single-discontinuity assumption. This is handled by replacing standard area lights with continuous analogues (e.g., smooth emission profiles falling to zero at boundaries). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def crossreducevariance(path0, path1, theta, theta0): """ Computes the cross-reduced variance estimate for a pair of paths. Args: path0, path1: Path objects containing throughput, emittedradiance, and weights arrays. theta: Current scene parameters. theta0: Reference scene parameters for control variate. Returns: rprime: The variance-reduced contribution estimate. """ sum0 = 0.0 sum1 = 0.0 numconnections = len(path0.emitterconnections) for l in range(numconnections): f0l = computethroughputradiance(path0, l, theta) W0l = computeweightproduct(path0, l, theta) W0lref = computeweightproduct(path0, l, theta0) f1l = computethroughputradiance(path1, l, theta) W1l = computeweightproduct(path1, l, theta) W1lref = computeweightproduct(path1, l, theta0) term0 = 0.5 (f0l W0l - f1l (W0l - W0lref)) term1 = 0.5 (f1l W1l - f0l (W1l - W1lref)) sum0 += term0 sum1 += term1 return sum0 + sum1 def computethroughputradiance(path, l, theta): # Returns the product of emitted radiance and path throughput at vertex l return path.throughput[l] path.emittedradiance[l] def computeweightproduct(path, l, theta): # Returns the product of all associated weights w{i,l}(theta) up to l wprod = 1.0 for k in range(l + 1): wprod = path.weights[k] return wprod A method to generate path pairs that are highly correlated to maximize variance reduction while maintaining the statistical independence required to avoid bias. It reuses random numbers for all sampling steps except those affecting the weights W{i,l}, specifically the sampling of directions in re-parameterized integrals with small angular support. This ensures that f{0,l} is uncorrelated with \partial W{1,l}(\theta) / \partial \theta (and vice versa), which is a strict requirement for the unbiasedness of the cross-weighting scheme. Complexity: Adds overhead proportional to the number of path pairs and the cost of evaluating weights at \theta0. The number of ray intersection queries increases by a factor related to the samples per integral (4 samples). Performance: Forward rendering and backpropagation for 512x512 images with 32 path pairs and 3 bounces take less than one minute on an NVIDIA TITAN RTX. Ray-triangle intersections account for approximately 9% of the computation time. Strengths: Substantially reduces variance of gradients without adding bias, enabling more stable optimization in differentiable rendering. Limitations: Incompatible with degenerate light sources (point/directional) and requires careful handling of area lights. Performance is sensitive to the number of samples used for variable change estimation. The method is based on the "cross-weighting scheme" introduced by Rousselle et al. [2016] for image-space gradients. It was adapted for differentiable path tracing to handle nested integrals corresponding to scattering events. The implementation described in the primary source uses Mitsuba 2 with automatic differentiation and a JIT compiler for GPU kernel generation. name: SDF Prb Reparam Integrator
body: A differentiable path tracer that computes gradients of radiance with respect to scene parameters (e.g., Signed Distance Function shape parameters) by warping random samples via reparameterization, supporting both forward and backward mode automatic differentiation. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly integrating reparameterization gradients into the path sampling loop, allowing for stable gradient flow through the SDF evaluation and sphere tracing steps, whereas siblings like Differential Vertex Sampling with MIS rely on vertex perturbation and Differential Edge Sampling on edge perturbations. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Scene description containing an SDF field, camera parameters, random number generator state, and scene parameters \theta (e.g., SDF coefficients). Outputs: Primal radiance image L and gradient images \nabla\theta L (forward or backward). Data Structures: self.primalimage: Tensor storing the computed radiance. self.warpfield: Optional field defining the reparameterization warp. reparammaxdepth: Integer, maximum depth for reparameterization rays. shadegradientmaxdepth: Integer, maximum depth for shading gradients, set equal to reparammaxdepth if warpfield is not None. reparamrays: Integer, number of reparameterization rays (default 16). reparamkappa: Float, reparameterization parameter (default 10^5). reparamexp: Float, reparameterization exponent (default 3.0). rrdepth: Integer, Russian Roulette depth (default 5). useaovs: Boolean, Auxiliary Output Variables flag (default False). hideemitters: Boolean, hide emitters flag (default False). Core Algorithm: The integrator operates in three phases: Primal Setup, Forward Gradient, and Backward Gradient. It utilizes a "Path Replay Backpropagation" loop when reparameterization is active. 1. Primal Setup: Prepare the scene SDF via self.preparesdf(scene). Suspend gradients for primal setup using dr.suspendgrad() to avoid tracking gradients during static scene preparation. Prepare the sampler and generate primary rays. If self.warpfield is not None, apply reparameterization warping to the random samples. Compute primal radiance L by calling self.sample with mode=dr.ADMode.Primal. Store L in self.primalimage. 2. Forward-Mode Gradients: Resume gradients. Compute sample position derivatives if enabled. Compute forward-mode gradients by calling self.sample with mode=dr.ADMode.Forward. Accumulate the reparameterization result gradients into resultgrad. 3. Backward-Mode Gradients: Prepare the scene SDF via self.preparesdf(scene). Suspend gradients for primal setup using dr.suspendgrad(). Generate primary rays with reparameterization. Compute primal radiance L using self.sample with mode=dr.ADMode.Primal. Resume gradients and enable gradient tracking on L. Set the gradient of the image to gradin and enqueue the backward pass. Compute backward-mode gradients by calling self.sample with mode=dr.ADMode.Backward. Sampling Loop (self.sample): The sampling loop handles path construction and reparameterization integration. 1. Initialize loop state: depth=0, L=0 (or statein), \beta=1, \eta=1, misem=1. 2. Perform preliminary ray intersection to get picur. 3. If warpfield is not None: Update reparammaxdepth to maxreparamdepth if >= 0, else 100,000. Set shadegradientmaxdepth equal to reparammaxdepth. 4. If reparameterization requires DRJITSTRUCT, start a loop named 'Path Replay Backpropagation'. 5. Sphere Tracing Step (for SDF evaluation): Evaluate SDF value s = \text{SDF}(p) and gradient g = \nabla \text{SDF}(p). Compute silhouette weight w{sil}: w{sil} = \frac{1}{(10^{-7} + |s| + \text{SIL\WEIGHT\OFFSET} \cdot (n \cdot d)^2)^3} where n = g / \|g\|, d is the ray direction, and \text{SIL\WEIGHT\OFFSET} = 0.05. Compute segment length and update integrals for warp position estimation using the trapezoid rule: W{int} \leftarrow W{int} + 0.5 \cdot \Delta t \cdot (w{prev} + w{sil}) T{warp} \leftarrow T{warp} + 0.5 \cdot \Delta t \cdot (t{prev} \cdot w{prev} + t \cdot w{sil}) Update ray position: t \leftarrow t + s. Check for intersection (|s| < \epsilon) and boundary conditions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import drjit as dr import mitsuba as mi def renderforward(scene, params): # 1. Primal Setup with dr.suspendgrad(): sdf = preparesdf(scene) sampler = preparesampler() # Generate primary rays with reparameterization if warpfield is active rays = generateprimaryrays(sampler, warpfield=scene.warpfield) # Compute primal radiance primalimage = sample(scene, rays, mode=dr.ADMode.Primal, sdf=sdf) # 2. Forward Gradients dr.resumegrad() # Compute sample position derivatives if enabled # Ensure gradients are attached to params before calling sample # Compute forward-mode gradients gradimage = sample(scene, rays, mode=dr.ADMode.Forward, sdf=sdf) # Accumulate reparameterization result gradients resultgrad = accumulategradients(gradimage) return primalimage, resultgrad def renderbackward(scene, params, gradin): # 1. Primal Setup with dr.suspendgrad(): sdf = preparesdf(scene) sampler = preparesampler() # Generate primary rays with reparameterization rays = generateprimaryrays(sampler, warpfield=scene.warpfield) # Compute primal radiance primalimage = sample(scene, rays, mode=dr.ADMode.Primal, sdf=sdf) # 2. Backward Gradients dr.resumegrad() dr.enablegrad(primalimage) # Set gradient of image to gradin primalimage.grad = gradin # Enqueue backward pass and compute backward-mode gradients gradimage = sample(scene, rays, mode=dr.ADMode.Backward, sdf=sdf) return gradimage def sample(scene, rays, mode, sdf): """ Core sampling loop supporting Path Replay Backpropagation. """ depth = 0 L = 0.0 beta = 1.0 eta = 1.0 misem = 1.0 # Initialize reparameterization state if needed if scene.warpfield is not None: reparammaxdepth = scene.maxreparamdepth if scene.maxreparamdepth >= 0 else 100000 shadegradientmaxdepth = reparammaxdepth else: reparammaxdepth = 0 shadegradientmaxdepth = 0 # Path Replay Backpropagation Loop # This loop structure is specific to DRJIT/Adjoint mode handling # The loop continues until max depth or termination condition while depth < shadegradientmaxdepth: # Preliminary ray intersection picur = intersectrays(rays, scene) if picur.hit: # Sphere tracing step for SDF p = picur.position sdfval = sdf.eval(p) sdfgrad = sdf.evalgrad(p) # Compute silhouette weight n = sdfgrad / dr.norm(sdfgrad) ndotd = dr.dot(rays.d, n) silweightoffset = 0.05 wsil = 1.0 / (1e-7 + dr.abs(sdfval) + silweightoffset ndotd2)3 wsil = dr.maximum(wsil, 0.0) # Update reparameterization integrals (Trapezoid rule) # Assuming state variables for weightintegral and warptintegral are maintained # in the loop context or passed as state segmentlength = dr.maximum(prevsdfvalue, 0.0) prevt = t - prevsdfvalue weightintegral += 0.5 segmentlength (prevsilw + wsil) warptintegral += 0.5 segmentlength (prevt prevsilw + t wsil) # Update ray position t += sdfval prevsdfvalue = sdfval prevsilw = wsil depth += 1 # Check for termination if dr.abs(sdfval) < 1e-6: # Surface hit, compute BSDF contribution # Standard path tracing BSDF evaluation and MIS weighting L += beta computeradiance(scene, rays, sdfval, misem) break else: # No hit, terminate or continue break return L Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels and the maximum path depth. The reparameterization step adds overhead proportional to the number of reparameterization rays (reparamrays, default 16) and the cost of evaluating the SDF and its gradient at each step. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the image resolution and path depth. The "Path Replay Backpropagation" requires storing path history for the backward pass, increasing memory usage compared to primal-only rendering. Performance: Performance depends heavily on the complexity of the SDF evaluation. The use of reparamrays=16 provides a balance between gradient accuracy and computational cost. Strengths: Provides stable gradients for SDF-based shape optimization. Supports both forward and backward mode AD, allowing flexibility in optimization setups. Limitations: Requires the SDF to be differentiable. The reparameterization warping may introduce bias if the warp field is poorly conditioned. High reparamkappa (10^5) and reparamexp (3.0) are used to stabilize the warping but may require tuning for specific scenes. When to use: When optimizing SDF parameters for shape reconstruction or editing. When not to use: When the scene does not involve SDFs or when memory is extremely constrained (due to path replay storage). The method originates from the work on Differentiable Signed Distance Function Rendering, specifically the implementation in the Mitsuba 3 renderer. It builds on the differential path integral estimator framework, incorporating reparameterization techniques to handle the non-differentiable nature of ray-SDF intersections by warping the random samples. The "Path Replay Backpropagation" loop is a key innovation to efficiently compute gradients through the iterative sphere tracing process. name: Reparametrized Integral Gradients
head: Reparameterized Integral Gradients, Loubet et al. method, Reparameterization for Discontinuous Integrands
body: Reparametrized Integral Gradients is a technique for differentiable rendering that eliminates bias in gradients caused by visibility discontinuities moving with scene parameters. Unlike explicit edge sampling methods that require detecting and sampling geometric boundaries, this method applies a change of variables to transform the integration domain such that discontinuities become static (parameter-independent). This allows differentiation under the integral sign without boundary terms, making it computationally efficient for complex scenes, though it approximates gradients and has limitations with specular materials. The method addresses the rendering integral I(\theta) where the integrand f(x, \theta) contains discontinuities at positions dependent on parameters \theta. Naïve differentiation yields incorrect gradients because the domain of integration or the location of discontinuities shifts. Inputs: Scene parameters \theta (e.g., camera position, light source position, triangle mesh vertices). Integrals over domains \Omega\theta containing discontinuities dependent on \theta. Outputs: Gradient \frac{\partial I}{\partial \theta} estimated via Monte Carlo sampling on a fixed domain. Data Structures: Transformation function T(\omega, \theta): \Omega \to \Omega\theta mapping a fixed reference domain \Omega to the parameter-dependent domain. Jacobian determinant J(\omega, \theta) = \left| \det \frac{\partial T}{\partial \omega} \right|. Steps: 1. Identify Discontinuities: Locate points in the integrand where visibility or material properties change abruptly, and determine how these points move as \theta changes. 2. Construct Transformation: Define a differentiable transformation T(\omega, \theta) that "warps" the domain such that the discontinuity in the transformed integrand is stationary. Specifically, choose T such that it yields the identity map when \theta = \theta0 (the parameter value for which gradients are evaluated). 3. Reparameterize Integral: Apply the change of variables to move the integral from \Omega\theta to the fixed domain \Omega: I(\theta) = \int{\Omega} f(T(\omega, \theta), \theta) \left| \det \frac{\partial T}{\partial \omega} \right| d\omega The discontinuities in the new integrand g(\omega, \theta) = f(T(\omega, \theta), \theta) \left| \det \frac{\partial T}{\partial \omega} \right| are now at fixed locations. 4. Differentiate: Since the domain \Omega and discontinuity locations are static, differentiate under the integral sign: \frac{\partial I}{\partial \theta} = \int{\Omega} \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \left[ f(T(\omega, \theta), \theta) \left| \det \frac{\partial T}{\partial \omega} \right| \right] d\omega No boundary term arises from the Reynolds Transport Theorem. 5. Estimate: Use Monte Carlo sampling on \Omega to estimate the gradient: Draw samples yi from a probability density function p(y) that does not depend on \theta. Evaluate the transformed integrand, density, and Jacobian determinant. Compute the estimator E = \frac{1}{N} \sum \frac{f(T(yi, \theta), \theta) |\det JT|}{p(yi)}. Apply automatic differentiation to E with respect to \theta to obtain the gradient. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reparameterizedgradient(theta, theta0, samples, p, integrandfn): """ Estimate gradient of rendering integral using reparameterization. theta: Current scene parameters. theta0: Parameter value for which gradients are evaluated (identity point). samples: Array of points omega drawn from fixed reference distribution p(omega). p: PDF function for the reference distribution. integrandfn: Function evaluating f(x, theta). """ gradsum = 0.0 N = len(samples) for omega in samples: # 1. Map reference sample to parameter-dependent domain x = transform(omega, theta, theta0) # 2. Compute Jacobian determinant |det(dT/domega)| jacobiandet = computejacobiandeterminant(omega, theta, theta0) # 3. Evaluate integrand at transformed point fval = integrandfn(x, theta) # 4. Form the transformed integrand transformedval = fval abs(jacobiandet) # 5. Compute gradient of the transformed integrand w.r.t theta # Using automatic differentiation on the composition gradval = computegradientwrttheta(transformedval, theta) # 6. Accumulate gradient estimate weighted by inverse PDF gradsum += gradval / p(omega) return gradsum / N def transform(omega, theta, theta0): # Standard translation example: T(omega, theta) = omega + theta - theta0 # For spherical domains, this would be a rotation R(omega, theta) return omega + theta - theta0 def computejacobiandeterminant(omega, theta, theta0): # For translation T(omega, theta) = omega + theta - theta0, dT/domega = 1 # For spherical rotations on S^2, the Jacobian determinant is 1. return 1.0 def evaluateintegrand(x, theta): # Evaluates the rendering integrand f(x, theta) at point x with parameters theta return 1.0 def computegradientwrttheta(val, theta): # Computes gradient using reverse-mode automatic differentiation # on the computational graph of val with respect to theta. return 0.0 Parameters: Sample count: The method produces high-quality gradients at low sample counts, specifically demonstrated at 64 samples per pixel (spp). \theta0: The specific value of the scene parameter \theta for which gradients are evaluated; T must be identity at this value. Sampling density p: Must not depend on \theta, otherwise discontinuities are reintroduced. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Specular Materials: The method does not support perfectly specular materials because the discontinuities in specular reflections cannot be easily reparameterized with a simple continuous warp. Dirac Delta Lights: Degenerate light sources containing Dirac delta functions are not supported. Multiple Discontinuities: The method struggles if multiple discontinuities exist within the support of the integrand, as a single global warp may not stabilize all of them. Approximation Error: Gradients are approximated and may not always be accurate. Small Angular Support: The method assumes integrands have small angular support (e.g., due to narrow BSDFs or small lights), where discontinuities consist of the silhouette of a single object. Warped-Area Sampling (WAS) is an unbiased method for differentiable rendering that eliminates the need for explicit boundary sampling by reparameterizing boundary integrals into interior integrals using a continuous warp field. It builds on Reparametrized Integral Gradients but improves upon the biased spherical rotation approach of Loubet et al. by satisfying the strict continuity requirements of the divergence theorem. Spherical Rotation Reparameterization is a technique for differentiable volume rendering that eliminates discontinuities in gradient estimates by applying a spherical rotation to the integration domain. It solves the problem of non-differentiable integrals caused by scene parameters \theta shifting discontinuity points across the sphere. Unlike Warped-Area Sampling, which explicitly samples and integrates over discontinuity boundaries, this method makes the discontinuity point parameter-independent through a change of variables, thereby removing the need for explicit boundary sampling. Time Complexity: Comparable to standard path tracing, as it avoids the overhead of explicit edge detection and sampling. However, it requires computing the Jacobian and its derivative, which may add computational cost per sample. Memory Complexity: Low, similar to standard path tracing, as it does not require storing edge lists or complex data structures for discontinuity tracking. Performance: Computationally efficient for scenes with many moving discontinuities where edge sampling would be expensive. Strengths: Eliminates bias from moving discontinuities without explicit edge sampling; works well with automatic differentiation. Limitations: Does not support perfectly specular materials, Dirac delta lights, or multiple discontinuities in one integrand; gradients are approximate. When to Use: When scene parameters cause visibility changes (e.g., object translation) and explicit edge sampling is too costly or complex. When Not to Use: For scenes with specular reflections, point lights, or complex multi-discontinuity integrands. Reparametrized Integral Gradients was introduced by Loubet et al. in "Reparameterizing Discontinuous Integrands for Differentiable Rendering" at SIGGRAPH Asia 2019. Unlike previous work (e.g., Li et al. 2018) which requires explicit sampling of silhouette edges, this method avoids edge sampling entirely by using changes of variables. The open source implementation of the method is part of version 2 of the Mitsuba renderer. name: Warped-Area Sampling
head: Warped-area reparameterization
body:
Warped-Area Sampling (WAS) is an unbiased method for differentiable rendering that eliminates the need for explicit boundary sampling by reparameterizing boundary integrals into interior integrals using a continuous warp field. It builds on Reparametrized Integral Gradients but improves upon the biased spherical rotation approach of Loubet et al. by satisfying the strict continuity requirements of the divergence theorem. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scene parameters \pi, primal ray direction \omega, and the discontinuity boundary \Delta S^2 in the spherical domain S^2. Output: An unbiased estimator for the gradient  rac{\partial I}{\partial \pi} via a single interior integral over S^2. Data Structures: Warp Field \mathbf{V}: A vector field defined on S^2. It must be continuous everywhere and converge to the boundary velocity \mathbf{v}{\partial} as \omega approaches \Delta S^2. Discontinuous Warp Field \mathbf{V}{dis}: An intermediate field used to construct \mathbf{V}. It is discontinuous at \Delta S^2 because rays cast on different sides of the boundary typically intersect different objects, yielding different velocities. Smoothing Kernel w(\omega, \omega'): A convolution kernel used to smooth \mathbf{V}{dis} into \mathbf{V}. Steps: 1. Construct \mathbf{V}{dis}: Cast auxiliary rays around the primal sampled ray. For each auxiliary ray direction \omegap, if it intersects an object dependent on \pi, compute the velocity \mathbf{v}p:= \partial \omegap / \partial \pi by differentiating the ray intersection process. This ensures that as \omegap approaches the boundary \Delta S^2, \mathbf{v}p converges to \mathbf{v}{\partial}. 2. Smooth \mathbf{V}{dis}: Convolve \mathbf{V}{dis} with the kernel w to produce the continuous warp field \mathbf{V}. The kernel is defined as:  rac{1}{w(\omega, \omega')}:=  rac{1}{D(\omega, \omega') + B(\omega')} where D(\omega, \omega') is a distance function and B(\omega') is a boundary-test function that converges to 0 when \omega' 	o \Delta S^2. 3. Estimate Gradient: Apply the divergence theorem to reparameterize the boundary integral into an interior integral: \int{\partial S^2} (\Delta f \mathbf{v}) \cdot \mathbf{n} d\ell(\omegai) = \int{S^2} (
abla \cdot \Delta f \mathbf{V}) d\sigma(\omegai) The total gradient estimator is the reparameterized spherical integral:  rac{\partial I}{\partial \pi} = \int{S^2} \left[  rac{\partial f}{\partial \pi} + (
abla \cdot \Delta f \mathbf{V}) ight] d\sigma(\omegai) where f:= Li fs is the integrand. Parameters: Warp Field Requirements: (a) \mathbf{V} must be continuous; (b) \mathbf{V}(\omega) must converge to \mathbf{v}{\partial} as \omega 	o \Delta S^2. Kernel Parameters: D(\omega, \omega') is a distance function and B(\omega') is a boundary-test function that converges to 0 when \omega' 	o \Delta S^2. Pitfalls: Using only one auxiliary ray to approximate boundary motion (as in Loubet et al.) results in a biased estimator because the resulting warp field does not strictly satisfy the boundary requirement. Precision issues may arise if the smoothing kernel does not preserve the boundary velocity \mathbf{v}{\partial} correctly. An extension of WAS to differential path integrals by Xu et al. [XBLZ23], enabling multi-bounce light transport estimation without explicit boundary sampling in path space. It decomposes the boundary integral from PSDR into a sum of integrals over sub-spaces \partial \hat{\Omega}{N,K}: \int{\partial \hat{\Omega}} \Delta \hat{f}K( ar{p}) \mathbf{V}K(pK) d\mu'( ar{p}) = \sum{N=1}^{\infty} \sum{K=0}^{N-1} \int{\partial \hat{\Omega}{N,K}} \Delta \hat{f}K( ar{p}) \mathbf{V}K(pK) d\mu'( ar{p}) The reparameterized differential path integral is:  rac{\partial I}{\partial \pi} = \int{\hat{\Omega}} \left[  rac{\partial \hat{f}( ar{p})}{\partial \pi} + \sum{K=0}^{N-1} 
abla \cdot \Delta \hat{f}K \mathbf{V}K(pK) ight] d\mu( ar{p}) Compared to the reparameterized spherical integral, this path integral has a more generalized form depicting multi-bounce light transport, enabling advanced Monte Carlo strategies like bidirectional path tracing. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Unbiased estimation; avoids explicit boundary sampling; enables multi-bounce transport estimation (via the path integral variant). Limitations: Requires construction of a continuous warp field; the auxiliary ray approximation approach is biased if not handled correctly. When to use: When unbiased differentiable rendering is required and explicit boundary sampling is difficult or biased. When not to use: When biased estimators are acceptable and simpler methods (like spherical rotation) suffice. Warped-Area Sampling was proposed by Bangaru et al. [BLD20] as a refinement to the biased spherical rotation approach by Loubet et al. [LHJ19]. It draws inspiration from the divergence theorem to reparameterize boundary integrals into interior integrals. The method was later extended to differential path integrals by Xu et al. [XBLZ23] to support multi-bounce light transport. A Survey on Physics-based Differentiable Rendering - arXiv.org, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.01402, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Spherical Rotation Reparameterization
head: Discontinuity removal via rotation, Reparameterization with spherical rotations, Rotation-based change of variables
body: Spherical Rotation Reparameterization is a technique for differentiable volume rendering that eliminates discontinuities in gradient estimates by applying a spherical rotation to the integration domain. It solves the problem of non-differentiable integrals caused by scene parameters \theta shifting discontinuity points (e.g., object silhouettes) across the sphere. Unlike Warped-Area Sampling, which explicitly samples and integrates over discontinuity boundaries, this method makes the discontinuity point parameter-independent through a change of variables, thereby removing the need for explicit boundary sampling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An integrand f(\omega, \theta) defined on the unit sphere S^2, where \omega is a direction and \theta represents scene parameters (e.g., object position, camera pose). The integrand typically has discontinuities dependent on \theta. Output: A differentiable estimate of the integral I = \int{S^2} f(\omega, \theta) d\omega and its gradient with respect to \theta. Data Structures: Rotation R(\omega, \theta): A function mapping a direction \omega to a rotated direction \omega', parameterized by \theta. Sampling Distribution p(\omega, \theta0): The probability density function used to generate samples \omegai, using a fixed parameter \theta0 independent of the current \theta to ensure sample independence from the gradient path. Steps: 1. Identify Discontinuity Motion: Determine how the discontinuity point T(\theta) moves with respect to the parameter \theta. 2. Construct Rotation R: Choose a spherical rotation R(\omega, \theta) such that its derivative with respect to \theta matches the derivative of the discontinuity trajectory: \frac{\partial R}{\partial \theta} = \frac{\partial T}{\partial \theta} This ensures that the transformed discontinuity point \omega0, defined by R(\omega0, \theta) = T(\theta), is independent of \theta. 3. Reparameterize Integral: Apply the change of variables to the integral: I = \int{S^2} f(\omega, \theta) d\omega = \int{S^2} f(R(\omega, \theta), \theta) d\omega The Jacobian determinant of this spherical rotation is exactly 1. 4. Monte Carlo Estimation: Generate samples \omegai from a distribution p(\omega, \theta0) using a fixed parameter \theta0. Compute the estimate: E = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \frac{f(R(\omegai, \theta), \theta)}{p(\omegai, \theta0)} Using \theta0 instead of \theta in the sampling distribution removes the dependency of the samples on \theta, preventing discontinuous jumps in the sample set. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sphericalrotationreparameterization(f, theta, theta0, N, samplefunc, pdffunc): """Estimate integral of f(w, theta) using spherical rotation reparameterization.""" # Rotation R is constructed to approximate discontinuity motion def R(omega, theta): # Returns rotated direction omega' = R(omega, theta) # Implementation depends on scene geometry to satisfy dR/dtheta = dT/dtheta return rotateomega(omega, theta) total = 0.0 for i in range(N): omegai = samplefunc(theta0) omegarotated = R(omegai, theta) pdfval = pdffunc(omegai, theta0) total += f(omegarotated, theta) / pdfval return total / N def rotateomega(omega, theta): # Standard spherical rotation (e.g., Rodrigues' formula or quaternion) # Returns a unit vector omega' return omega # Simplified structure; actual rotation applied per def constructrotation(theta): # Returns a rotation function R(omega, theta) # Construction matches discontinuity motion T(theta) via dR/dtheta = dT/dtheta return lambda omega: rotateomega(omega, theta) def evaluatepdf(omega, theta0): # Evaluates the probability density function p(omega, theta0) # Typically the default sampling scheme of the underlying renderer return pdffunc(omega, theta0) Parameters: \theta0: The fixed parameter used for sampling. It is chosen to remove the dependency of the samples on \theta. Rotation Approximation: The rotation R must accurately approximate the displacement of discontinuities. If the approximation is poor, bias remains. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Large Support: The method assumes the integrand has small angular support (vanishes outside a small neighborhood). If the support is large, the rotation approximation produces significant bias because the discontinuity structure is too complex to be modeled by a single rotation. Precision: The Jacobian is exactly 1, so no scaling factor is needed. A method to handle integrands with large support by convolving the integrand f with a spherical kernel k, allowing the small-support rotation technique to be applied to the inner integral. It is chosen when the integrand's discontinuities are localized, making direct rotation effective. The integral identity used is \int{S^2} f(\omega) d\omega = \int{S^2} \int{S^2} f(\mu) k(\mu, \omega) d\mu d\omega, where k satisfies \int{S^2} k(\mu, \omega) d\mu = 1. The kernel k can be any smooth distribution, such as a von Mises-Fisher distribution, with a concentration parameter controlling the trade-off between bias and variance. Small kernels reduce bias (better rotation approximation) but increase variance (lower probability of hitting discontinuities). The final estimator samples \omegai for the outer integral and \mui \sim k(\cdot, \omegai) for the inner integral, yielding: I \approx E = \frac{1}{N} \sum \frac{f(Ri(\mui, \theta), \theta) k(Ri(\mui, \theta), \omegai(\theta), \theta)}{p(\omegai(\theta), \theta) pk(\mui)}. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Produces gradient images that closely match ground truth for scenes with small-support integrands. Performance degrades with large-support integrands due to bias. Strengths: Eliminates the need for explicit boundary sampling; simple to implement; Jacobian is 1. Limitations: High bias for large-support integrands; requires accurate estimation of discontinuity motion. When to Use: Suitable for differentiable rendering of scenes with sharp, localized discontinuities (e.g., specular highlights, small object silhouettes). When Not to Use: Unsuitable for diffuse shading or large-area lights where the integrand support is large. Spherical Rotation Reparameterization was introduced by Loubet et al. in 2019. It is part of the broader field of differentiable rendering, specifically addressing the challenge of differentiating through discontinuous integrals. The method builds on the idea of reparameterization estimators, which transform the integration domain to remove parameter dependency from discontinuities. It is used in differentiable volume rendering and path tracing to enable gradient-based optimization of scene parameters. name: Plateau-Reduced Differentiable Path Tracing
head: PR-DPT, Differentiable Path Tracing with Derivative-Kernel (Our∂κP), Convolutional Gradient Estimation, Our∂κP
body: Plateau-Reduced Differentiable Path Tracing (PR-DPT) is an inverse rendering technique that alleviates optimization plateaus (regions of zero gradient) by convolving the rendering equation with a smoothing kernel over the parameter space. Unlike standard differentiable path tracers that suffer from discontinuous gradients due to visibility changes, PR-DPT ensures that scene parameters continuously influence the objective function in expectation, allowing gradient-based optimizers to converge on problems with intricate light transport like caustics. It sets itself apart from siblings like Reparameterization Estimators by avoiding the need for a gradient tape, adjoint formulation, or special integrators for visibility discontinuities; instead, it relies on stochastic sampling of a blurred parameter space. Inputs: Scene function f(x, \theta): A forward renderer (path tracer) mapping light paths x \in \Omega and scene parameters \theta \in \Theta to pixel values. Current parameters \theta. Kernel standard deviation \sigma. Number of perturbation samples N (even integer). Outputs: Gradient estimate \hat{\nabla}\theta Q. Data Structures: \theta: Parameter vector, normalized to [0, 1] where possible (e.g., rotations). \tau: Parameter offset vector, sampled from the kernel distribution. Method: The method estimates the gradient of the plateau-reduced rendering equation Q(\theta), defined as the convolution of the original rendering equation P(\theta) with a symmetric, monotonous decreasing kernel \kappa(\tau): Q(\theta) = \int{\Theta} \int{\Omega} \kappa(\tau) f(x, \theta - \tau) \, dx \, d\tau The Monte Carlo estimator for Q(\theta) is: \hat{Q} \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \kappa(\taui) f(xi, \theta - \taui) To compute the gradient \frac{\partial Q}{\partial \theta}, PR-DPT offers two paths depending on renderer differentiability. The paper primarily uses Eq. 10 for computational efficiency, as it skips the renderer's gradient computation. The gradient is estimated by sampling the derivative of the kernel: \frac{\partial Q}{\partial \theta} \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \frac{\partial \kappa}{\partial \theta}(\taui) f(xi, \theta - \taui) For a Gaussian kernel \kappa(\tau) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left(-\frac{\tau^2}{2\sigma^2}\right), the derivative with respect to \theta (where \tau represents the offset \theta{\text{sample}} - \theta) is: \frac{\partial \kappa}{\partial \theta}(\tau) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\sigma^2 \pi}} \frac{-\tau}{\sigma^2} \exp\left(\frac{-\tau^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) Note that \frac{\partial \kappa}{\partial \theta} is negative for \tau > 0. To perform importance sampling, the method uses "positivization" by sampling proportional to the absolute value |\frac{\partial \kappa}{\partial \theta}(\tau)|. Sampling Procedure: 1. Positivization: The PDF for sampling is proportional to |\frac{\partial \kappa}{\partial \theta}(\tau)|. 2. CDF Inversion: The Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) for this PDF is: F(\tau) = 0.5 \, \text{sgn}(\tau) \exp\left(\frac{-\tau^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) + C where C=1 for \tau > 0 and C=0 otherwise. 3. Sample Generation: Inverting the CDF yields the sample generation formula: \tau = \sqrt{-2\sigma^2 \log(\xi)} where \xi \sim U(0,1). 4. Antithetic Sampling: To achieve a zero-variance estimator for the point-symmetric function, for every generated \tau, the algorithm also uses -\tau. Algorithm: The following pseudocode implements the gradient estimation for the non-differentiable case using antithetic sampling and importance sampling derived from the kernel gradient. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def estimategradient(P, theta, sigma, N): """ Estimates the gradient of the plateau-reduced rendering equation using the derivative-kernel method (Eq. 10 in). Args: P: Forward renderer function f(x, theta). theta: Current scene parameters. sigma: Standard deviation of the blur kernel. N: Total number of perturbation samples (must be even). Returns: Gradient estimate G. """ G = 0.0 # Loop runs for N/2 iterations to generate N samples via antithetic pairs for i in range(N // 2): # 1. Generate uniform random number xi = random.uniform(0, 1) # 2. Sample tau proportional to |dkappa/dtheta| using inverse CDF # Formula: tau = sqrt(-2 sigma^2 log(xi)) tau = math.sqrt(-2 (sigma 2) math.log(xi)) # 3. Evaluate renderer at perturbed parameters # Note: P returns the scalar pixel value (or integrated radiance) valplus = P(theta + tau) valminus = P(theta - tau) # 4. Accumulate difference # The term P(theta + tau) - P(theta - tau) effectively handles the # weighting by the signed kernel gradient and the positivization. # See Eq. 10 and Algorithm 1 in. G = G + (valplus - valminus) # 5. Normalize by N return G / N Parameters: \sigma: Standard deviation of the blur kernel. Controls the spread of perturbations. \sigma0: Initial value. Typical default: 0.5. The paper recommends setting \sigma0 to roughly 50% of the normalized parameter domain. \sigmam: Minimum value. Set to 0.01 to avoid numerical instabilities. N: Number of perturbations (samples) per optimization iteration. Typical values: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. N=2 (one sample + antithesis) is often sufficient for convergence. spp: Samples per pixel for the underlying path tracer. Not a hyperparameter of PR-DPT but must be set high enough so rendering noise is less than the optimization signal. LR: Optimizer learning rate (e.g., Adam). Values vary by task (0.125 to 0.800). Annealing Schedule: The bandwidth \sigma is decayed linearly to refine the solution: \sigma{t+1} = \sigma0 - t(\sigma0 - \sigmam) The schedule is warm-started after approximately 50% of the total optimization iterations have completed. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Small \sigma0 (< 0.2): Optimization fails to converge. As \sigma0 \to 0, the method approaches rigid optimization, and the loss landscape is not smoothed, causing stagnation. Large \sigma0 (\to 1): Perturbation samples may fall outside the view frustum. With small N, this produces noisy gradients causing divergence. Alleviated by enlarging the camera FOV (e.g., 40° to 60°). High Dimensions: Variance increases with parameter dimensionality. Mitigated by increasing N. Time Complexity: Runtime scales linearly with N. The bulk of time is spent evaluating the forward renderer f; sampling and gradient computation overhead is negligible. Memory Complexity: Low. Does not require storing a gradient tape or compute graph. Performance: On average 8× faster than differentiable rendering with Mitsuba. At N \approx 16, runtime equals Mitsuba's constant baseline (which uses re-parametrization/adjoint methods for 1 sample). Convergence: Convergence improves with N up to \sim 10, then stagnates. Final parameter MSE decreases slightly with higher N (9.5 \times 10^{-5} for N=2 vs 4.7 \times 10^{-6} for N=16), but N>2 yields no net benefit for the tested task due to offsetting runtime. Accuracy: Achieves parameter-space MSE errors as low as 10^{-7} on tested tasks. Strengths: Works with black-box/non-differentiable renderers; handles complex light transport (caustics, GI) where standard differentiable tracers fail; no gradient tape required. Limitations: Variance increases in high-dimensional spaces; requires careful tuning of \sigma0. PR-DPT was introduced by Fischer et al. in 2023. It addresses the issue of optimization plateaus in inverse rendering, where standard differentiable renderers fail to converge due to zero gradients in regions where scene parameter changes do not immediately affect the image (e.g., occlusion). The method connects variational optimization approaches with inverse rendering, interpreting the stochastic sampling as a Monte Carlo estimate of the gradient of a smoothed objective. name: Reparameterization
head: Ray Reparameterization, Silhouette Motion Compensation via Reparameterization
body: Reparameterization is a technique in differentiable rendering that counteracts parameter-dependent silhouette motion and the resulting bias in differentiated rendering. It solves the problem where changes in scene parameters cause discontinuities in the rendering integral to move across the sampling domain, violating standard differentiation assumptions. By applying a change of variables to freeze these discontinuities within spherical integrals, it enables unbiased gradient estimation. The method applies a change of variables to the rendering integral, mapping a parameter-dependent domain to a fixed reference domain. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray with direction d and scene parameters \theta. Output: A transformed ray direction d' and the Jacobian determinant \det = \left| \det \frac{\partial T}{\partial \omega} \right|. Data Structures: ray: Contains direction vector d. det: Scalar float representing the Jacobian determinant. Steps: 1. Primal Pass: The reparameterize() function is called. In primal computation, it returns the input ray direction unchanged and a Jacobian determinant of 1. 2. Differentiated Pass: When gradients are required, reparameterize() expands into intricate operations: a. Auxiliary Ray Tracing: Trace auxiliary rays to construct a warp field that counteracts silhouette motion. b. Jacobian Computation: Compute the determinant of the Jacobian of this warp field. c. Gradient Scattering: Use reverse-mode automatic differentiation on the warp field to scatter scene parameter gradients into the intersected geometry. This accounts for the dependence of the BSDF at adjacent vertices x{i-1} and x{i+1} on the reparameterized vertex position xi. Pseudocode: The implementation exposes reparameterizations through a CustomOp-based abstraction. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reparameterize(ray, differentiate=False): if not differentiate: # Primal pass: identity transformation return ray.d, 1.0 else: # Differentiated pass: trace auxiliary rays to construct warp field auxrays = traceauxiliaryrays(ray) # Compute Jacobian determinant of the change of variables det = computejacobian(auxrays) return ray.d, det def traceauxiliaryrays(ray): # Sample and trace rays to build the warp field return [] def computejacobian(auxrays): # Compute determinant from auxiliary intersection data return 1.0 def rayintersect(ray, scene): return scene.findintersection(ray) def scattergradients(si, det): # Use reverse-mode AD to scatter scene parameter gradients into geometry pass def render(scene, ray, det, differentiate=False): si = rayintersect(ray, scene) if differentiate: scattergradients(si, det) return scene.evaluate(si) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dielectric Interfaces: Derivatives are biased in scenes containing dielectric objects such as a glass of water. How to reparameterize through perfectly specular interfaces is an open research problem. Program Size: The introduction of reparameterizations and steps to evaluate derivatives of adjacent vertices leads to very large computational graphs compared to primal rendering. A variant of Path Replay Backpropagation (PRB) that integrates reparameterizations. It introduces steps needed to evaluate the derivatives of adjacent vertices, leading to significantly larger programs than primal or non-reparameterized methods. Polymorphism-related optimizations (dead code elimination, value numbering, constant propagation) produce a 6.6x speedup on the OptiX backend. Loop state optimizations yield modest runtime improvements (a few percent) but may be more effective in methods using attached Monte Carlo sampling where large sets of derivatives are exchanged between loop iterations. Complexity: The method increases computational complexity due to the need for auxiliary ray tracing and the expansion of the AD tape. The generated kernel subroutines and data exchanged through function inputs/outputs are significantly larger than in non-reparameterized methods. Performance: On the OptiX backend, polymorphism-related optimizations provide a 6.6x speedup for reparameterized PRB. Loop state optimizations provide smaller gains. Limitations: Biased gradients in scenes with dielectric/specular interfaces. High memory and compilation overhead due to large program size. When to use: When optimizing scene geometry parameters (e.g., vertex positions) in differentiable rendering to avoid silhouette motion bias. Reparameterization was introduced in the context of differentiable path tracing to handle parameter-dependent geometry. It builds on the change of variables formula. The specific implementation using auxiliary rays to construct a warp field references prior work on warp fields. The technique is implemented within the DR.JIT framework. name: Control Variates for Gradient Variance Reduction
head: Gradient control variates, Variance reduction via control variates
body: Control variates for gradient variance reduction is a technique that reduces the variance of gradient estimators in differentiable volume rendering by leveraging the statistical property that the expected gradient of the weight term is zero. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like shift maps by explicitly constructing a correlated control estimator from the Jacobian weights of the reparameterization, rather than relying solely on path correlation through random number reuse. It addresses the high variance inherent in the gradient of the weight term wi(\theta) when the integrand f is smooth or constant. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Scene parameters \theta, reference parameters \theta0 (typically the current parameters from the previous iteration or a fixed baseline), sampling points yi from a fixed reference domain, transformation T(yi, \theta), integrand f(T(yi, \theta), \theta), and probability density k. Outputs: An unbiased gradient estimator \frac{\partial E'}{\partial \theta} with reduced variance. Data Structures: Weights wi(\theta): A scalar value per sample i, defined as the ratio of the probability density at the transformed point under current parameters to that under reference parameters: wi(\theta) = \frac{k(T(yi, \theta), \theta)}{k(T(yi, \theta0), \theta0)} Control Variate Parameter \alpha: A scalar coefficient, typically approximated as the average value of f or a running average, which must be independent of the specific weights wi(\theta) of the current sample set to avoid bias. Numbered Steps: 1. Sample and Transform: For each sample i \in \{1, \dots, N\}, generate yi from the fixed reference distribution and compute the transformed position xi = T(yi, \theta). 2. Compute Weights: Calculate the weight wi(\theta) for the current parameters \theta and the reference weight wi(\theta0) (which is typically 1 if \theta0 is the primal state, but generally computed for consistency). 3. Evaluate Integrand: Compute fi = f(T(yi, \theta), \theta). 4. Construct Control Variate Estimator: Form the intermediate estimator E' using the control variate formula: E' = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \left[ fi wi(\theta) + \alpha(wi(\theta) - wi(\theta0)) \right] Note that \mathbb{E}[wi(\theta) - wi(\theta0)] = 0, so E' is unbiased. 5. Differentiate: Compute the gradient of E' with respect to \theta. Since wi(\theta0) is constant with respect to \theta, its derivative is zero: \frac{\partial E'}{\partial \theta} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \left[ fi wi(\theta) + \alpha wi(\theta) \right] \frac{\partial E'}{\partial \theta} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \left( \frac{\partial fi}{\partial \theta} wi(\theta) + fi \frac{\partial wi(\theta)}{\partial \theta} + \alpha \frac{\partial wi(\theta)}{\partial \theta} \right) \frac{\partial E'}{\partial \theta} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \left( \frac{\partial fi}{\partial \theta} wi(\theta) + (fi + \alpha) \frac{\partial wi(\theta)}{\partial \theta} \right) 6. Return Gradient: Return the computed sum as the gradient estimate. Formulas: Weight: wi(\theta) = \frac{k(T(yi, \theta), \theta)}{k(T(yi, \theta0), \theta0)}. Optimal \alpha: \alpha = -\frac{\text{Cov}(E, F)}{\text{Var}(F)}, where E is the original gradient estimator and F is the control variate estimator \frac{\partial F}{\partial \theta} = \frac{1}{N} \sum \frac{\partial wi(\theta)}{\partial \theta}. In practice, \alpha is approximated (e.g., as -c if f(x)=c, or as a running average of f). Gradient Estimator: \frac{\partial E'}{\partial \theta} = \frac{1}{N} \sum \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} [ f(T(yi, \theta), \theta) wi(\theta) + \alpha wi(\theta) ]. Parameters: \alpha: The control variate coefficient. Optimal value is -\frac{\text{Cov}(E, F)}{\text{Var}(F)}. Practical approximation: average of f or constant c if f is constant. \theta0: Reference parameters. Often set to \theta for the primal pass, but for gradient estimation, it serves as the baseline for the weight ratio. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bias from \alpha: The parameter \alpha must be independent of the weights wi(\theta) to avoid introducing bias in the gradient of E'. If \alpha is computed using the same samples wi(\theta), the estimator becomes biased. Cross-weighting schemes or using uncorrelated estimates are required to estimate \alpha without bias. Constant Integrand: If f(x) = c, the variance of the gradient can be completely eliminated if \alpha = -c. Smoothness: The variance reduction is most effective when f is a smooth function with small gradients with respect to \theta. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computegradientcontrolvariates(samples, theta, theta0, T, f, k, alpha): """ Compute gradient of rendering integral using control variates. Args: samples: List of N reference samples yi. theta: Current scene parameters. theta0: Reference scene parameters. T: Transformation function T(y, theta). f: Integrand function f(x, theta). k: Probability density function k(x, theta). alpha: Control variate coefficient (must be independent of current weights). Returns: Gradient estimate dE'/dtheta. """ N = len(samples) gradsum = Vector3(0, 0, 0) # Assuming 3D gradient for i in range(N): yi = samples[i] # 1. Transform xi = T(yi, theta) xiref = T(yi, theta0) # 2. Compute weights # k(x, theta) is the PDF at transformed point x with params theta kcurr = k(xi, theta) kref = k(xiref, theta0) # Avoid division by zero if kref == 0: wi = 0.0 wiref = 0.0 else: wi = kcurr / kref wiref = 1.0 # Typically wi(theta0) = 1 if theta0 is primal, # but generally computed as k(T(y, theta0), theta0)/k(T(y, theta0), theta0) = 1 # Note: The formula uses wi(theta) - wi(theta0). # If theta0 is fixed baseline, wi(theta0) is constant. # In many implementations, wi(theta0) is precomputed or 1. # Here we assume wiref is the weight at theta0. # If theta0 is the "primal" state, wi(theta0) = 1. # Let's stick to the general formula: wi(theta0) = k(T(yi, theta0), theta0) / k(T(yi, theta0), theta0) = 1. wiref = 1.0 # 3. Evaluate integrand fi = f(xi, theta) # 4. Compute derivatives # We need df/dtheta and dw/dtheta # These are provided by the automatic differentiation system or analytical derivatives dfdtheta = computegradientf(f, xi, theta) dwdtheta = computegradientw(wi, T, k, yi, theta, theta0) # 5. Accumulate gradient # dE'/dtheta = 1/N sum( df/dtheta w + (f + alpha) dw/dtheta) term1 = dfdtheta wi term2 = (fi + alpha) dwdtheta gradsum += term1 + term2 return gradsum / N def computegradientw(wi, T, k, yi, theta, theta0): """ Compute gradient of weight wi(theta) = k(T(yi, theta), theta) / k(T(yi, theta0), theta0) Since theta0 is constant, denominator is constant. wi(theta) = numerator / constant dw/dtheta = (1/constant) d(numerator)/dtheta """ xi = T(yi, theta) # Numerator is k(xi, theta) # Gradient of k(x, theta) w.r.t theta involves dk/dx dx/dtheta + dk/dtheta # This is a placeholder for the actual derivative computation which depends on k and T # In practice, this is handled by AD return computegradientkwrttheta(xi, theta, T, yi) A variant that reduces variance by tracing pairs of correlated paths that reuse certain random numbers and combining their estimates using control variates. It is similar to shift maps [Kettunen et al. 2015; Lehtinen et al. 2013] in sampling correlated paths, and similar to Rousselle et al. [2016] in applying control variates to gradient estimates. Time Complexity: Adds minimal overhead to the standard reparameterization estimator, primarily the computation of the additional term \alpha \frac{\partial wi}{\partial \theta} and the storage of \alpha. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the reference parameters \theta0 and potentially precomputed weights wi(\theta0) if not computed on the fly. Performance: Significant variance reduction is achieved with low performance overhead. For constant f, variance can be eliminated with optimal \alpha. Strengths: Effective for smooth integrands; reduces variance of the weight gradient term which is often the dominant source of variance in reparameterization estimators. Limitations: Requires careful choice of \alpha to avoid bias; \alpha must be independent of the current weights. Performance gain depends on the correlation between E and F. When to use: When gradient variance is high due to the Jacobian weight term, especially for smooth scenes or constant integrands. When not to use: When f has large gradients or discontinuities that break the smoothness assumption, or when computing \alpha without bias is too costly. Originated in the context of differentiable rendering, specifically in the paper "Reparameterizing discontinuous integrands for differentiable rendering". It builds on the general control variates method from statistics and applies it to the gradient of reparameterized rendering integrals. It is related to shift maps [Kettunen et al. 2015; Lehtinen et al. 2013] and Rousselle et al. [2016] who applied control variates to image-space gradients. name: Reynolds Transport Theorem for Differentiable Rendering
head: Differentiable Rendering Equation, Differentiable Rendering via Reynolds Transport Theorem, Differential Rendering Equation, Interior and Boundary Integral Decomposition, Material-form parameterization, Physics-based Differentiable Rendering (PSDR), Reynolds transport theorem for rendering
body: Reynolds Transport Theorem (RTT) for Differentiable Rendering provides a principled mathematical framework to compute the gradient of a rendering integral with respect to scene parameters by decomposing the derivative into an interior term (derivative of the continuous integrand) and a boundary term (integral over discontinuities). It sets itself apart from standard reverse-mode automatic differentiation by avoiding the storage of intermediate states for all parameters, and from rasterization-based approximations by explicitly handling visibility discontinuities via a boundary integral, supporting transparent surfaces and complex geometry without spatial analytical approximations. The method computes the derivative of the measurement contribution I with respect to scene parameters \pi. It relies on a material-form parameterization to handle the dependency of the integration domain on \pi. Inputs: Scene parameters \pi (e.g., vertex positions, material properties), primal scene geometry M, light sources, sensors. Outputs: Gradient \frac{\partial I}{\partial \pi}, decomposed into interior and boundary contributions. The method operates on light paths \bar{x} = (x0, \dots, xN) in the primal domain and material paths \bar{p} = (p0, \dots, pN) in the material domain. Material Path Space \hat{\Omega}: A union of reference surfaces B independent of \pi, mapped to object surfaces M via a differentiable one-to-one mapping X(\cdot, \pi). Boundary \partial \hat{\Omega}: The set of material light paths containing a boundary segment (p{K-1}, pK) residing on a visibility boundary. The measurement contribution in the material form is: \hat{f}(\bar{p}):= \prod{n=0}^{N} \hat{f}v(\bar{p}, n) \prod{n=1}^{N} G(x{n-1} \leftrightarrow xn) where \hat{f}v(\bar{p}, n):= fv(\bar{x}, n) J(pn) and J(pn):= \|dA(xn)/dA(pn)\| is the Jacobian determinant of the area transformation. The vertex function fv is defined as: fv(\bar{x}, n):= \begin{cases} Le(x0 \to x1), & n=0 \\ We(x{N-1} \to xN), & n=N \\ fs(x{n-1} \to xn \to x{n+1}), & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where Le is source emission, We is sensor importance, and fs is the BSDF. The geometric term is: G(x \leftrightarrow y):= V(x \leftrightarrow y) \frac{|\mathbf{n}(x) \cdot \overrightarrow{xy}| |\mathbf{n}(y) \cdot \overrightarrow{xy}|}{\|x - y\|^2} where V is mutual visibility, \mathbf{n} is surface normal, and \overrightarrow{xy} is the normalized direction. The derivative of the integral I is decomposed as: \frac{\partial I}{\partial \pi} = \int{\hat{\Omega}} \frac{\partial \hat{f}(\bar{p})}{\partial \pi} d\mu(\bar{p}) + \int{\partial \hat{\Omega}} \Delta \hat{f}K(\bar{p}) VK(pK) d\mu'(\bar{p}) where: Interior Term: \int{\hat{\Omega}} \frac{\partial \hat{f}(\bar{p})}{\partial \pi} d\mu(\bar{p}). This involves the derivative of the integrand with respect to \pi over the fixed domain \hat{\Omega}. Boundary Term: \int{\partial \hat{\Omega}} \Delta \hat{f}K(\bar{p}) VK(pK) d\mu'(\bar{p}). \Delta \hat{f}K(\bar{p}):= \hat{f}(\bar{p}) \frac{\Delta G(x{K-1} \leftrightarrow xK)}{G(x{K-1} \leftrightarrow xK)} is the material boundary contribution, where \Delta G = G^- - G^+ is the difference of the geometric term approaching the visibility boundary from two directions. VK(pK) = \mathbf{n}\partial \cdot \mathbf{v}\partial is the scalar normal velocity of the discontinuity point pK, where \mathbf{n}\partial is the boundary's normal direction and \mathbf{v}\partial is the boundary's velocity. d\mu'(\bar{p}):= d\ell(pK) \prod{n \neq K} dA(pn) is the measure associated with \partial \hat{\Omega}. 1. Material-Form Parameterization: Define a reference surface union B independent of \pi. Map points p \in B to primal points x \in M via X(p, \pi) such that X(p, \pi0) = p for the current parameters \pi0. 2. Interior Integral Estimation: Estimate \int{\hat{\Omega}} \frac{\partial \hat{f}(\bar{p})}{\partial \pi} d\mu(\bar{p}) using conventional path sampling (e.g., unidirectional path tracing). For the interior integral, use the same discretization strategy as normal rendering, such as randomly sampling inside the filter support or dividing the filter support into a grid and sampling the center at each grid. Compute \frac{\partial \hat{f}}{\partial \pi} by differentiating the material-form integrand. 3. Boundary Integral Estimation: Estimate \int{\partial \hat{\Omega}} \Delta \hat{f}K(\bar{p}) VK(pK) d\mu'(\bar{p}) using a specialized Monte Carlo estimator. The boundary integral can be rewritten in a multi-directional form: I = \int{\DeltaB} \int{E} \hat{f}^S \hat{f}B JB \hat{f}^D d\sigma(\omegaB) d\ell(xB) where E is the union of all mesh edges, JB is the Jacobian determinant of the change of variable from (p0^S, p0^D) to (xB, \omegaB), and \hat{f}B:= \Delta G(x0^S \leftrightarrow x0^D) V{\DeltaB}. Monte Carlo Estimator Steps: 1. Sample an edge within the scene (e.g., randomly pick an edge from the mesh). 2. Generate the boundary segment (p0^S, p0^D) from the edge. 3. Trace the path in both directions to reach the light source and sensor respectively, completing a boundary light path. 4. Rasterization Context Note: When estimating many pixel integrals simultaneously, gather all pixels whose filter support intersects the picked edge point, and scatter the derivative to the corresponding pixel integral discretization. \epsilon: A small value used to query f from two sides of the boundary to evaluate \Delta f. Nb: Number of samples for the boundary integral. Typically much smaller than the number of pixels Ni due to the sparsity of boundaries in image space. Transparent Surfaces: The theory supports transparent surfaces without modification, unlike methods assuming only one triangle per pixel. 2D/3D Boundary Movement: In 2D/3D, the boundary movement speed is projected to the normal direction to account for infinitesimal area changes, unlike the 1D case where the boundary is always aligned with the normal. Discontinuity Definition: \Gamma is defined as the set of points on all triangle edges. Points in continuous regions evaluate to \Delta f = 0. A framework for differentiating integrals over implicit surfaces that change shape, explicitly handling parameterization dependence of tangential velocity and providing a parameterization-independent "normal scene derivative" for implicit surfaces, building on Reynolds Transport Theorem for Differentiable Rendering. Complexity: The boundary integral can be computed with much fewer samples (Nb) than pixels (Ni) because the set of boundaries is sparse in image space, achieving low error with fewer samples. Strengths: Supports transparent surfaces and complex geometry without spatial analytical approximations; decouples interior and boundary estimation; provides a principled mathematical model for future approximations. Limitations: Requires a ray-tracing based visibility engine for efficient computation of the boundary integral, as it requires random queries to the pixel integrand. Performance gap with rasterization is closing due to hardware ray tracing support. When to use: When principled gradient computation for complex scenes with transparency and evolving geometry is required, and ray tracing infrastructure is available. When not to use: When rasterization-only pipelines are strictly required and approximations like OpenDR or Kato et al. are acceptable trade-offs for speed. The method originates from the application of Reynolds Transport Theorem to the rendering equation, leading to the "differential rendering equation". It was formalized as Physics-Based Differentiable Rendering (PSDR) by Zhao, Jakob, and Li. The material-form parameterization was introduced to handle the dependency of the integration domain on scene parameters, allowing the decomposition of the derivative into interior and boundary terms. name: Scene Derivatives for Evolving Surfaces
head: Material-Form Parameterization for Implicit Surfaces, Normal Scene Derivative, Reynolds transport relation for evolving surfaces, Scene Derivative, Surface Evolution and Scene Derivatives, Transport Relation for Differentiating Surface Integrals
body: Scene Derivatives for Evolving Surfaces is a mathematical framework for differentiating integrals over implicit surfaces that change shape with respect to scene parameters \pi. It solves the problem of computing the gradient of rendering path integrals where the geometry is defined as a zero-level set \phi(\mathbf{x}; \pi) = 0, by decomposing the derivative into an interior term (accounting for field changes and surface curvature) and a boundary term (accounting for discontinuities). It sets itself apart from standard Reynolds transport formulations by explicitly handling the parameterization dependence of tangential velocity and providing a parameterization-independent "normal scene derivative" for implicit surfaces, building on Reynolds Transport Theorem for Differentiable Rendering. Inputs: \pi: An abstract parameter controlling global scene geometry. \phi(\mathbf{x}; \pi): A scalar-valued function defining the evolving implicit surface M(\pi) = \{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3: \phi(\mathbf{x}; \pi) = 0\}. \varphi(\mathbf{x}, \pi): A scalar spatial field defined on the trajectory T of the surface. \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{x}, \pi): The unit normal field of M(\pi). \kappa(\mathbf{x}, \pi): The total curvature (sum of principal curvatures) of M(\pi). \DeltaM: The set of discontinuity curves on M(\pi) where \varphi is discontinuous. Outputs: \dot{\varphi}(\mathbf{x}, \pi): The scene derivative (parameterization-dependent). \square \varphi(\mathbf{x}, \pi): The normal scene derivative (parameterization-independent). \frac{d}{d\pi} \int{M(\pi)} \varphi \, dA: The derivative of the surface integral. The method relies on the following geometric and kinematic quantities: 1. Reference Surface B: A fixed surface B = M(0). 2. Deformation Map X(\mathbf{p}, \pi): Maps a material point \mathbf{p} \in B to a spatial point \mathbf{x} \in M(\pi). For implicit surfaces, this is often approximated as X(\mathbf{p}, \pi) = \mathbf{p} + t(\mathbf{p}, \pi)\mathbf{n}B(\mathbf{p}), where t is the distance along the normal \mathbf{n}B to the intersection with M(\pi). 3. Local Parameterization \hat{\mathbf{x}}(\boldsymbol{\xi}, \pi'): A local coordinate map from an open set \mathcal{O} \subset \mathbb{R}^2 to M(\pi') near a point \mathbf{x}. 4. Velocity Fields: \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}, \pi): Local velocity of the surface point. V = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n}: Scalar normal velocity (parameterization-independent). \mathbf{v}{tan} = \mathbf{v} - V\mathbf{n}: Local tangential velocity (parameterization-dependent). V{\DeltaM}: Scalar normal velocity of the discontinuity curve \DeltaM. 1. Define the Reference Configuration: Establish the reference surface B = \{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3: \phi(\mathbf{x}; 0) = 0\}. 2. Compute Local Velocity: For a point \mathbf{x} \in M(\pi), determine the local velocity \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}, \pi) using the local parameterization \hat{\mathbf{x}}(\boldsymbol{\xi}, \pi'): \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}, \pi) = \frac{\partial \hat{\mathbf{x}}(\boldsymbol{\xi}, \pi')}{\partial \pi'} \bigg|{\pi'=\pi} where \boldsymbol{\xi} are the local coordinates of \mathbf{x}. 3. Decompose Velocity: Calculate the scalar normal velocity V and tangential velocity \mathbf{v}{tan}: V = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n} \mathbf{v}{tan} = \mathbf{v} - V\mathbf{n} Note that V is independent of the parameterization, while \mathbf{v}{tan} depends on it. 4. Compute Scene Derivative: Calculate the parameterization-dependent scene derivative \dot{\varphi}: \dot{\varphi}(\mathbf{x}, \pi) = \frac{\partial}{\partial \pi'} \varphi(\hat{\mathbf{x}}(\boldsymbol{\xi}, \pi'), \pi') \bigg|{\pi'=\pi} This represents the rate of change of the field \varphi following the parameterization. 5. Compute Normal Scene Derivative: Calculate the parameterization-independent normal scene derivative \square \varphi: \square \varphi = \dot{\varphi} - \mathbf{v}{tan} \cdot \text{grad}M(\varphi) where \text{grad}M(\varphi) is the surface gradient of \varphi. 6. Evaluate Discontinuity Jump: For points on the discontinuity curve \DeltaM, compute the jump \Delta \varphi: \Delta \varphi(\mathbf{x}, \pi) = \varphi^-(\mathbf{x}, \pi) - \varphi^+(\mathbf{x}, \pi) where \varphi^- and \varphi^+ are the one-sided limits approaching \mathbf{x} from directions -\mathbf{n}{\DeltaM} and \mathbf{n}{\DeltaM} respectively. 7. Compute Integral Derivative: Apply the transport relation to find the derivative of the integral: \frac{d}{d\pi} \int{M(\pi)} \varphi \, dA = \int{M(\pi)} (\square \varphi - \varphi \kappa V) \, dA + \int{\partial M(\pi)} \Delta \varphi V{\partial M} \, d\ell where \partial M(\pi) denotes the boundary of the surface or discontinuity curves, dA is the area measure, and d\ell is the curve length measure. Evolving Surface: M(\pi) = \{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3: \phi(\mathbf{x}; \pi) = 0\}. Reference Surface: B = M(0). Deformation (Implicit Approximation): X(\mathbf{p}, \pi) = \mathbf{p} + t(\mathbf{p}, \pi)\mathbf{n}B(\mathbf{p}). Local Velocity: \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}, \pi) = \frac{\partial \hat{\mathbf{x}}(\boldsymbol{\xi}, \pi')}{\partial \pi'} \big|{\pi'=\pi}. Normal Velocity: V = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n}. Tangential Velocity: \mathbf{v}{tan} = \mathbf{v} - V\mathbf{n}. Scene Derivative: \dot{\varphi}(\mathbf{x}, \pi) = \frac{\partial}{\partial \pi'} \varphi(\hat{\mathbf{x}}(\boldsymbol{\xi}, \pi'), \pi') \big|{\pi'=\pi}. Normal Scene Derivative: \square \varphi = \dot{\varphi} - \mathbf{v}{tan} \cdot \text{grad}M(\varphi). Transport Relation: \frac{d}{d\pi} \int{M} \varphi dA = \int{M} (\square \varphi - \varphi \kappa V) dA + \int{\partial M} \Delta \varphi V{\partial M} d\ell. Static Surface Simplification: If V=0, \frac{d}{d\pi} \int{M} \varphi dA = \int{M} \dot{\varphi} dA + \int{\DeltaM} \Delta \varphi V{\DeltaM} d\ell. \pi: Abstract parameter controlling global scene geometry. In physics, this typically represents time. Zero Tangential Velocity: If the parameterization results in \mathbf{v}{tan} = 0, then \square \varphi = \dot{\varphi}. Static Surface with Moving Discontinuities: Even if the surface is static (V=0), the velocity of discontinuity curves V{\DeltaM} may be nonzero because the discontinuity curves themselves can depend on \pi. Parameterization Dependence: The scene derivative \dot{\varphi} depends on the choice of local parameterization \hat{\mathbf{x}}, whereas the normal scene derivative \square \varphi does not. Implicit Mapping Limitations: Defining a global one-to-one mapping X(\cdot, \pi) for all \pi for implicit surfaces is hard or impossible; the method often relies on local parameterizations or the specific normal-offset approximation X(\mathbf{p}, \pi) = \mathbf{p} + t(\mathbf{p}, \pi)\mathbf{n}B(\mathbf{p}) which is only one-to-one at \pi=0. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def normalize(v): """Standard vector normalization.""" mag = math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in v)) return [x / mag for x in v] def dot(a, b): """Standard dot product.""" return sum(ai bi for ai, bi in zip(a, b)) def computescenederivatives(phifunc, x, pi, localparamfunc, gradMfunc, eps=1e-5): """ Computes scene derivative and normal scene derivative for a scalar field on an evolving implicit surface. """ # 1. Map spatial point x to local coordinates xi xi = localparamfunc.inverse(x, pi) # 2. Compute local velocity v via finite difference of parameterization xplus = localparamfunc(xi, pi + eps) xminus = localparamfunc(xi, pi - eps) v = [(xp - xm) / (2 eps) for xp, xm in zip(xplus, xminus)] # 3. Compute unit normal n from phi gradient gradphi = phifunc.gradient(x, pi) n = normalize(gradphi) # 4. Decompose velocity into normal and tangential components V = dot(v, n) vtan = [v[i] - V n[i] for i in range(3)] # 5. Compute scene derivative dotphi via finite difference of field phiplus = phifunc(xplus, pi + eps) phiminus = phifunc(xminus, pi - eps) dotphi = (phiplus - phiminus) / (2 eps) # 6. Compute normal scene derivative squarephi gradMphi = gradMfunc(x, pi) squarephi = dotphi - dot(vtan, gradMphi) return dotphi, squarephi, v, vtan, V def computeintegralderivative(phifunc, pi, surfacepoints, surfaceareas, squarephifunc, kappafunc, Vfunc, discontinuitypoints, discontinuitylengths, deltaphifunc, Vdeltafunc): """ Computes the derivative of the integral of phi over M(pi) using the transport relation. """ # Interior term: integral over M of (squarephi - phi kappa V) dA interiorintegral = 0.0 for point, area in zip(surfacepoints, surfaceareas): phival = phifunc(point, pi) sqphi = squarephifunc(point, pi) k = kappafunc(point, pi) V = Vfunc(point, pi) interiorintegral += (sqphi - phival k V) area # Boundary term: integral over discontinuity curves of deltaphi Vdelta dL boundaryintegral = 0.0 for point, length in zip(discontinuitypoints, discontinuitylengths): deltaphi = deltaphifunc(point, pi) Vdelta = Vdeltafunc(point, pi) boundaryintegral += deltaphi Vdelta length return interiorintegral + boundaryintegral The parent method that decomposes the derivative of a rendering integral into interior and boundary terms. Scene Derivatives provide the specific kinematic definitions for implicit surfaces within this framework. Reynolds Transport Theorem for Differentiable Rendering The broader context of differentiating path integrals directly. Scene Derivatives are a key component for handling geometry changes in this approach. Path-Space Differentiable Rendering Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides a rigorous, parameterization-independent normal scene derivative for implicit surfaces and handles discontinuities explicitly. Limitations: Requires a local parameterization or deformation map, which can be difficult to define globally for complex implicit surfaces. The tangential velocity component is parameterization-dependent. When to Use: When differentiating rendering integrals over implicit surfaces that evolve with parameters, especially when discontinuities are present. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from the application of continuum mechanics concepts, specifically the Reynolds transport theorem for evolving surfaces, to differentiable rendering. It builds on the work of Cermelli et al. [2005] in fluid mechanics and Zhang et al. [2020] in differentiable rendering of implicit surfaces. The parameter \pi is analogous to time in physics but represents abstract scene parameters in rendering. The approach was formalized in the context of path-space differentiable rendering to handle the differentiation of surface integrals over evolving implicit geometries.
