name: Projective Spatial Transformer (ProST)
body: ProST is a differentiable volume rendering module that generalizes spatial transformers to projective geometry, enabling volumetric rendering of transmission images that are differentiable with respect to both the input volume and the pose parameters. It solves the problem of performing end-to-end differentiable projection of voxelized data onto 2D planes, which is essential for tasks like 2D/3D registration where gradients must flow from a 2D similarity metric back through the projection to the 3D pose. Unlike mesh-based differentiable renderers, ProST operates directly on voxel grids using a cone-beam ray casting approach, making it suitable for medical imaging applications. Inputs: Input volume V \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times W \times H} with voxel sizes vD, vW, vH. Camera intrinsic matrix K \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} defining the projection geometry. Pose parameters \theta \in SE(3) defining the transformation of the volume relative to the source and detector. Grid dimensions: M \times N rays, K control points per ray. Outputs: Rendered 2D image I \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N}. Data Structures: Spatial Grid G: A matrix of shape \mathbb{R}^{4 \times (M \cdot N \cdot K)} where each column represents a control point in homogeneous coordinates. Transformed Grid GT: The grid G transformed by the pose \theta. Sampled Values GS: A tensor of shape \mathbb{R}^{M \times N \times K} containing interpolated volume values at the transformed control points. Steps: 1. Coordinate Normalization: Map the input volume V to normalized coordinates (d, w, h) \in [-1, 1]^3 using the dimensions and voxel sizes. The reference frame Fr origin is placed at the center of V. 2. Grid Construction: Define the source point in Fr as (0, 0, src). Construct M \times N rays originating from the source point. Cut the grid point cloud to a cone-shape structure that covers the exact volume space V. Place K control points uniformly spaced within the volume V on each ray. Store these points in the spatial grid G \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times (M \cdot N \cdot K)} in homogeneous coordinates. 3. Pose Transformation: Compute the affine transformation matrix T(\theta) from the pose parameters \theta. Transform the control points using GT = T(\theta) \cdot G. Transform the source point to T(\theta) \cdot (0, 0, src, 1) and the detection plane center to T(\theta) \cdot (0, 0, det, 1). 4. Grid Sampling (Interpolation): Interpolate the volume values V at the transformed control points GT. The interpolation function yields GS \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N \times K} via GS = \text{interp}(V, GT). The specific interpolation kernel is not specified in the sources. 5. Projection (Integration): Collapse the k dimension of GS by summing along the rays to produce the 2D image I. The projection is computed as I^{(m,n)} = \sum{k=1}^K GS^{(m,n,k)}. The detection plane is centered on (0, 0, det) and perpendicular to the z-axis, with its upper-right corner at (p{MM} vW W, p{NN} vH H, det). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def projectivespatialtransformer(V, Kmat, theta, M, N, Kpts, src, det): """ V: Volume tensor of shape (D, W, H) in normalized coordinates [-1, 1]^3 Kmat: Camera intrinsic matrix (3, 3) theta: Pose parameters (6,) representing SE(3) transformation M, N: Grid dimensions for the output image Kpts: Number of control points per ray src, det: Distances along the z-axis """ # 1. Generate detection plane grid points u = torch.linspace(-1, 1, M) v = torch.linspace(-1, 1, N) ugrid, vgrid = torch.meshgrid(u, v, indexing='ij') uv = torch.stack([ugrid.flatten(), vgrid.flatten()], dim=-1) # (MN, 2) # Map to detection plane at z = det using normalized coordinates detx = uv[:, 0] det dety = uv[:, 1] det detz = torch.fulllike(detx, det) detpoints = torch.stack([detx, dety, detz], dim=-1) # (MN, 3) # 2. Construct cone grid G source = torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, src], device=V.device) # (3,) directions = detpoints - source # (MN, 3) directions = directions / torch.norm(directions, dim=1, keepdim=True) # Volume bounds in normalized space: [-1, 1]^3 boundsmin = torch.tensor([-1.0, -1.0, -1.0], device=V.device) boundsmax = torch.tensor([1.0, 1.0, 1.0], device=V.device) # Per-ray ray-box intersection to find t range inside volume t1 = (boundsmin - source.unsqueeze(0)) / directions t2 = (boundsmax - source.unsqueeze(0)) / directions tmin = torch.max(torch.min(t1, t2), dim=1).values # (MN,) tmax = torch.min(torch.max(t1, t2), dim=1).values # (MN,) tmin = torch.clamp(tmin, min=0.0) tmax = torch.clamp(tmax, max=1e6) # Handle rays that miss the volume valid = tmin < tmax tmin = torch.where(valid, tmin, tmax) # Sample Kpts uniformly along valid t range tvals = torch.linspace(0, 1, Kpts, device=V.device) # (Kpts,) # Broadcast to (MN, Kpts) tsamples = tmin.unsqueeze(1) + tvals.unsqueeze(0) (tmax.unsqueeze(1) - tmin.unsqueeze(1)) # Compute control points: P = source + t direction Gcart = source.unsqueeze(0) + tsamples.unsqueeze(2) directions.unsqueeze(1) # (MN, Kpts, 3) # Convert to homogeneous coordinates and reshape to (4, MNKpts) ones = torch.ones(M N Kpts, 1, device=V.device) Gcartflat = Gcart.view(-1, 3) Ghom = torch.cat([Gcartflat, ones], dim=1).T # (4, MNKpts) # 3. Pose transformation Ttheta = se3tomatrix(theta, V.device) # GT = Ttheta @ Ghom # (4, MNKpts) # 4. Interpolation # Convert homogeneous to Cartesian GTcart = GT[:3,:] / GT[3,:] # (3, MNKpts) GTcart = GTcart.view(3, M, N, Kpts).permute(1, 2, 3, 0) # (M, N, Kpts, 3) # Ensure V has batch/channel dim for gridsample: (1, 1, D, W, H) if V.dim() == 3: V = V.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # gridsample expects grid in [-1, 1] GS = F.gridsample(V, GTcart.unsqueeze(0), mode='nearest', paddingmode='zeros', aligncorners=True) # (1, 1, M, N, Kpts) # 5. Integration I = GS.squeeze().sum(dim=-1) # (M, N) return I def se3tomatrix(theta, device): """Converts 6D SE(3) parameters to a 4x4 transformation matrix.""" rx, ry, rz, tx, ty, tz = theta cx, sx = torch.cos(rx), torch.sin(rx) cy, sy = torch.cos(ry), torch.sin(ry) cz, sz = torch.cos(rz), torch.sin(rz) R = torch.stack([ czcy, czsysx - szcx, czsycx + szsx, szcy, szsysx + czcx, szsycx - czsx, -sy, cysx, cycx ]).view(3, 3, device=device) T = torch.eye(4, device=device) T[:3,:3] = R T[:3, 3] = torch.tensor([tx, ty, tz], device=device) return T Parameters: M, N: Number of rays in the x and y directions, determining the resolution of the output image. K: Number of control points per ray, determining the sampling density along the ray. src: Distance from the volume center to the source point along the z-axis. det: Distance from the volume center to the detection plane along the z-axis. K{mat}: 3x3 camera intrinsic matrix. p{MM}, p{NN}: Scaling factors for the detection plane upper-right corner coordinates. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Regions: Control points in regions where no CT voxels exist do not contribute to the line integral. The grid is explicitly cut to a cone-shape to cover only the volume space to avoid sampling empty space unnecessarily. Precision: The implementation uses C++ and CUDA extensions for grid generation to ensure efficiency and precision, embedding the projection as a PyTorch layer for analytical gradient flow. This method trains a deep neural network to approximate the geodesic gradient in SE(3), enabling end-to-end learning of a convex similarity metric for 2D/3D registration. It differs from standard supervised registration by optimizing the network parameters \phi such that the gradient of the learned loss LN with respect to pose \theta aligns directionally with the true geodesic gradient \partial LG / \partial \theta, rather than minimizing pixel-wise error directly. This approach extends the capture range of initialization compared to traditional image-based methods like Grad-NCC. Time Complexity: The projection operation is embedded as a PyTorch layer with tensor variables, taking advantage of the spatial transformer grid to reduce the projection to a series of linear transformations. The intermediate variables are reasonably sized for modern computational graphics cards. Memory Complexity: The spatial grid G has size 4 \times M \times N \times K and the sampled tensor GS has size M \times N \times K, both loaded as tensor variables in memory. Strengths: Enables end-to-end learning of an image processing and projection model that approximates an image similarity function convex with respect to pose parameters, allowing effective optimization using conventional gradient descent. No learning parameters are required for the projection itself, allowing registration with PyTorch's built-in optimizers on large-scale volume representations. Limitations: The method is specific to volumetric data (voxelized models) and may not be directly applicable to mesh-based representations without modification. When to use: When performing 2D/3D registration between radiographs and CT scans, or any task requiring differentiable projection of 3D volumes to 2D images with respect to pose. ProST was proposed in the paper "Generalizing Spatial Transformers to Projective Geometry with Applications to 2D/3D Registration". It addresses the limitation of previous differentiable rendering approaches that focused on mesh-based representations, which are inappropriate for medical applications using volumetric, voxelized models. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first time spatial transformers have been described for projective geometry. The method is implemented using C++ and CUDA extensions of the PyTorch framework. Generalizing Spatial Transformers to Projective Geometry with Applications to 2D/3D Registration, https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.10987v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Geodesic Loss Approximation for 2D/3D Registration
head: Geodesic Loss, ProST Geodesic Loss
body: This method trains a deep neural network to approximate the geodesic gradient in SE(3), enabling end-to-end learning of a convex similarity metric for 2D/3D registration. It differs from standard supervised registration by optimizing the network parameters \phi such that the gradient of the learned loss LN with respect to pose \theta aligns directionally with the true geodesic gradient \partial LG / \partial \theta, rather than minimizing pixel-wise error directly. This approach extends the capture range of initialization compared to traditional image-based methods like Grad-NCC. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D volume V, pose parameter \theta \in SE(3), fixed target image If, target pose \thetat (for geodesic calculation), and network parameters \phi. Outputs: Network parameters \phi (trained), pose parameter \theta (optimized during application). Data Structures: Pose \theta: Represented in SE(3). The gradient \partial L / \partial \theta is decomposed into translation part v^t and rotation part v^r. The rotation vector is transformed into Rodrigues angle-axis representation. Gradients: \frac{\partial LN}{\partial \theta} and \frac{\partial LG}{\partial \theta} are 6-dimensional vectors (3 translation, 3 rotation). Numbered Steps: 1. Geodesic Gradient Calculation: Compute the geodesic gradient \frac{\partial LG(\theta, \thetat)}{\partial \theta} using the implementation from [10] (cited in), where LG is the square of the geodesic distance in SE(3). 2. Forward Pass (Network): Pass V, \theta, and If through the deep neural network (ProST-based architecture) to obtain embedded features em (from volume) and ef (from target image). 3. Network Loss Calculation: Compute the network loss LN as the mean squared error between embedded features: LN = \|em - ef\|^2 4. Network Gradient Calculation: Compute the gradient of the network loss with respect to pose \theta using back-propagation through the differentiable volume rendering layer (ProST): \frac{\partial LN}{\partial \theta} = \frac{\partial LN}{\partial Im} \cdot \frac{\partial Im}{\partial GS} \cdot \frac{\partial GS}{\partial GT} \cdot \frac{\partial GT}{\partial T(\theta)} \cdot \frac{\partial T(\theta)}{\partial \theta} 5. Directional Distance Calculation: Decompose \frac{\partial LN}{\partial \theta} and \frac{\partial LG}{\partial \theta} into translation (v1^t, v2^t) and rotation (v1^r, v2^r) components. Compute the directional distance metric M{dist}: M{dist}^{trans} = \left\| \frac{v1^t}{\|v1^t\|} - \frac{v2^t}{\|v2^t\|} \right\|^2 M{dist}^{rot} = \left\| \frac{v1^r}{\|v1^r\|} - \frac{v2^r}{\|v2^r\|} \right\|^2 M{dist} = M{dist}^{trans} + M{dist}^{rot} 6. Double Backward Pass: Perform a second back-propagation pass to compute \frac{\partial M{dist}}{\partial \phi} for updating network parameters \phi. 7. Network Update: Update \phi using gradient descent on M{dist}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def computegeodesicgradient(theta, thetat): # The sources do not provide the implementation for the geodesic gradient in SE(3). # This function must calculate the gradient of the squared geodesic distance # in SE(3) between current pose theta and target pose thetat. return torch.zeros(6, requiresgrad=True) def computenetworkgradient(theta, V, If, network): # Forward pass em, ef = network(V, theta, If, network.parameters()) LN = torch.mean((em - ef)2) # Compute gradient w.r.t theta while retaining graph for double backward gradN = torch.autograd.grad(LN, theta, retaingraph=True, creategraph=True)[0] return gradN, LN def computedirectionaldistance(gradN, gradG): v1t, v1r = gradN[:3], gradN[3:] v2t, v2r = gradG[:3], gradG[3:] eps = 1e-8 # Prevent division by zero v1tnorm = v1t / (torch.norm(v1t) + eps) v2tnorm = v2t / (torch.norm(v2t) + eps) v1rnorm = v1r / (torch.norm(v1r) + eps) v2rnorm = v2r / (torch.norm(v2r) + eps) Mtrans = torch.norm(v1tnorm - v2tnorm)2 Mrot = torch.norm(v1rnorm - v2rnorm)2 return Mtrans + Mrot def trainstep(V, If, theta, thetat, network, lrphi): gradG = computegeodesicgradient(theta, thetat) gradN, LN = computenetworkgradient(theta, V, If, network) Mdist = computedirectionaldistance(gradN, gradG) Mdist.backward() with torch.nograd(): for param in network.parameters(): if param.grad is not None: param -= lrphi param.grad param.grad.zero() return Mdist, LN def register(V, If, thetainit, network, lrtheta, lrncc, maxiter, windowsize=10): theta = thetainit.clone().requiresgrad(True) LNhistory = [] for i in range(maxiter): em, ef = network(V, theta, If, network.parameters()) LN = torch.mean((em - ef)2) gradN = torch.autograd.grad(LN, theta, retaingraph=True)[0] with torch.nograd(): theta -= lrtheta gradN LNhistory.append(LN.item()) if len(LNhistory) > windowsize: stdLN = torch.std(torch.tensor(LNhistory[-windowsize:])) if stdLN < 1e-4: # Convergence threshold # Switch to Grad-NCC optimization # LGNCC = computegradnccloss(Im, If) # LGNCC.backward() # with torch.nograd(): theta -= lrncc theta.grad pass return theta Parameters: Learning Rate \phi: Not given in the sources. Typical values for deep learning optimization (e.g., 0.001). Learning Rate \theta: Not given in the sources. Typical values for optimization (e.g., 0.01). Target Pose \thetat: Used for geodesic gradient calculation. Not given in the sources. Typically a random perturbation or ground truth during training. NCC Switch Iteration: Not given in the sources. Determined by monitoring STD of LN. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Gradients: If \|v1^t\| or \|v1^r\| is zero, normalization fails. Add epsilon to denominator. Precision: Rodrigues angle-axis representation must be consistent between geodesic gradient calculation and network gradient decomposition. Convergence Detection: Monitoring STD of LN is used to switch from network-based optimization to Grad-NCC. What it is: The square of the geodesic distance in SE(3), used as a target for convexity in registration. Differentiation: Provides a convex similarity metric with a large capture range. When to choose: When initialization is far from ground truth and traditional methods fail. Link: Geodesic Loss What it is: Gradient-based Normalized Cross Correlation, implemented as a PyTorch loss function. Differentiation: More sensitive to local textures than the network-based metric. When to choose: For fine-tuning after the network-based optimization has converged. Link: Grad-NCC Time Complexity: Training requires double backward passes, increasing computational cost per iteration. Application phase is similar to standard back-propagation through the network. Memory Complexity: Requires storing intermediate gradients for the double backward pass. Measured Performance: Tested on 1536x1536 images (downsampled to 128x128) with isotropic pixel spacing of 0.194 mm/pixel and source-to-detector distance of 1020 mm. Trained on 17 full body CT scans. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Extends capture range of initialization, less sensitive to local textures than traditional methods. Limitations: Requires training phase with geodesic gradient calculation. When to use: 2D/3D registration with large initial pose errors. When not: When computational resources for training are unavailable. Origin: Proposed in "Generalizing Spatial Transformers to Projective Geometry with Applications to 2D/3D Registration". History: Builds on geodesic loss for registration [13, 9] and geodesic gradient implementation [10]. Usage: 2D/3D registration in medical imaging (CT to DRR). name: C++/CUDA Implementation of Moment Bounds
head: Custom CUDA implementation, Primal/Adjoint C++ implementation
body: A hand-written C++/CUDA implementation of the primal (forward) and adjoint (backward) algorithms for computing moment bounds, designed to avoid the overhead of automatic differentiation (AD) graph traversal and JIT compilation limitations. Unlike AD-based approaches, it generates highly optimized code by knowing the floating-point type and moment order n at compile time. Inputs and Outputs: Primal Kernel: Input: density field, view direction, moment order n, floating-point type (32-bit float or 64-bit double). Output: moment bounds values. Adjoint Kernel: Input: upstream gradients, primal outputs (or retained roots), density field, view direction, n. Output: gradients with respect to density. Data Structures: Intermediate values are kept in registers to minimize global memory accesses, which are the primary bottleneck on GPUs. The implementation depends only on a small subset of the C++ standard library. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compile-time Configuration: The floating-point type and moment order n are defined as template parameters or compile-time constants, enabling the compiler to generate specialized, optimized code. 2. Primal Computation: All operations of the primal algorithm are compiled into a single CUDA kernel. This computes the moment bounds for the given scene parameters. 3. Adjoint Computation: A separate single CUDA kernel is compiled for the adjoint algorithm. It computes gradients by backpropagating through the primal operations. 4. Root Handling (Default): In the default variant, roots required for the adjoint phase are recomputed by re-running the primal algorithm. 5. Root Handling (Retained Roots Variant): For n > 2, root finding is iterative and can dominate adjoint runtime. This variant stores the roots of the kernel polynomial computed during the forward pass and reuses them in the backward pass, avoiding redundant iterative root finding. Formulas: Not given in the sources. The implementation relies on the algorithms defined in Section 5.1 of the source paper. Parameters: n: Moment order, tested for n = 1, \dots, 5. Floating-point type: 32-bit float or 64-bit double. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: For n > 2, root finding is an iterative procedure. Without the retained roots variant, this becomes the dominating operation during the adjoint phase. Some operations (e.g., finding eigenvalues of a matrix) are currently unsupported by the AD compiler, making hand-written implementations necessary for these cases. A variant of the C++/CUDA implementation that stores the roots of the kernel polynomial computed during the forward pass and reuses them in the backward pass to avoid redundant iterative root finding. It has similar computation time for the primal part but a considerably lower runtime for the adjoint part for n > 2. Memory complexity increases compared to the default variant (primal output array size is N, adjoint requires storage for retained roots plus adjoints), but remains significantly lower than AD. Time Complexity: For n > 2, the default variant's adjoint runtime is dominated by iterative root finding. The Retained Roots variant significantly reduces this runtime. Memory Complexity: The retained roots variant increases memory usage compared to the default, but it is still significantly lower than AD. Performance: On GPUs, global memory accesses are the bottleneck. The implementation mitigates this by keeping intermediate values in registers. Benchmarks show C++/CUDA implementations outperforming PyTorch AD, especially for n > 2 where AD suffers from JIT compilation limitations and unsupported operations. Strengths: Highly optimized code generation due to compile-time knowledge of types and n. Avoids AD graph traversal overhead. Limitations: Requires manual implementation of primal and adjoint algorithms. Less flexible than AD for changing algorithms. Originated from the paper "Moment Bounds are Differentiable: Efficiently Approximating Measures in Inverse Rendering". The authors found that PyTorch 2.x’s compile feature provided negligible improvements or worse runtime for n > 2 due to unsupported operations like matrix eigenvalue finding. Consequently, they implemented the primal and adjoint algorithms entirely in C++ with CUDA targeting. Moment Bounds are Differentiable: Efficiently Approximating Measures in Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1145/3730899, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Alpha-to-Weight Computation (Backward)
head: Alpha to Weight Conversion (Backward)
body: Computes the gradient of the rendering loss with respect to the per-sample alpha values, given the gradients flowing back from the rendered weights and the final transmittance. It is the backward pass counterpart to the Alpha-to-Weight computation, enabling differentiable volume rendering via the Adjoint Method [Parent]. It uses reverse accumulation to propagate gradients backwards through the ray samples. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: alpha: 1D tensor of size N{pts}, containing alpha values for all samples across all rays. weight: 1D tensor of size N{pts}, containing the rendered weights for all samples. T: 1D tensor of size N{pts}, containing the transmittance values just before each sample. alphainvlast: 1D tensor of size N{rays}, containing the final transmittance (alpha inverse) for each ray. istart: 1D tensor of size N{rays}, start indices of samples for each ray. iend: 1D tensor of size N{rays}, end indices of samples for each ray. gradweights: 1D tensor of size N{pts}, gradients of the loss with respect to the weights. gradlast: 1D tensor of size N{rays}, gradients of the loss with respect to the final transmittance. Output: grad: 1D tensor of size N{pts}, gradients of the loss with respect to the alpha values. All input and output layouts are specified in. Data Structures: The ray boundaries are defined by istart and iend. Algorithm: For each ray r from 0 to N{rays}-1: 1. Initialize a backward cumulative gradient variable backcum using the gradient from the final transmittance and the final transmittance value itself: \text{back\cum} = \text{grad\last}[r] \times \text{alphainv\last}[r] 2. Iterate backwards through the samples of the ray from index i = i\end[r] - 1 down to i\start[r]: a. Compute the gradient for the current alpha sample: \text{grad}[i] = \text{grad\weights}[i] \times T[i] - \frac{\text{back\cum}}{1.0 - \alpha[i] + \epsilon} where \epsilon = 10^{-10} is a numerical stability constant. b. Update the backward cumulative gradient: \text{back\cum} = \text{back\cum} + \text{grad\weights}[i] \times \text{weight}[i] Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def alpha2weightbackward(alpha, weight, T, alphainvlast, istart, iend, gradweights, gradlast, nrays): npts = len(alpha) grad = [0.0] npts epsilon = 1e-10 for r in range(nrays): is = istart[r] ie = iend[r] backcum = gradlast[r] alphainvlast[r] for i in range(ie - 1, is - 1, -1): grad[i] = gradweights[i] T[i] - backcum / (1.0 - alpha[i] + epsilon) backcum += gradweights[i] weight[i] return grad Parameters: epsilon: 10^{-10}. Added to the denominator to prevent division by zero when \alpha[i] is close to 1.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If \alpha[i] is exactly 1.0, the term (1 - \alpha[i]) becomes zero. The epsilon term prevents this. An alternative method to compute gradients by inverting the rendering equation, avoiding the explicit backward pass through samples. It is chosen when memory constraints prevent storing intermediate transmittance values. A technique to manage memory usage during the backward pass by accumulating gradients in chunks. It is chosen for high-resolution scenes where full gradient tensors exceed VRAM limits. A PyTorch wrapper that integrates the backward pass into the autograd engine. It is chosen when using standard deep learning frameworks without custom CUDA kernels. A sampling strategy that uses gradient information to adaptively select samples, potentially reducing the number of samples needed for accurate gradients. It is chosen when computational budget is limited and noise reduction is prioritized. A method that replays the forward pass during the backward pass to reconstruct intermediate variables, avoiding the need to store all activations in memory. It is chosen when VRAM is insufficient to cache forward pass tensors. Not given in the sources. The method is implemented in the DirectVoxGO repository and its reference implementation. The backward pass allows the gradients to flow back from the rendered image to the per-sample alpha values, which are then used to update the underlying neural network parameters. The specific implementation details, including the use of epsilon for stability, are documented in these repositories. sunset1995/DirectVoxGO, https://github.com/sunset1995/DirectVoxGO, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) gkouros/ref-dvgo, https://github.com/gkouros/ref-dvgo, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Variance-aware Adaptive Pixel Sampling
head: Adaptive pixel sampling for inverse rendering, Image-Space Adaptive Sampling, Pixel-level mini-batching, Variance-minimizing pixel sampling
body: Variance-aware adaptive pixel sampling accelerates gradient-based inverse rendering by dynamically allocating a fixed per-iteration pixel sampling budget based on the estimated variance of loss gradient contributions. Unlike uniform mini-batching or sampling proportional only to loss gradient magnitude, this method accounts for the variance of the differentiable rendering derivative, minimizing the total variance of the gradient estimator. It acts as a form of pixel-level mini-batching, rendering only a subset of pixels per iteration while maintaining low gradient noise. The method operates within an inverse rendering pipeline where the goal is to minimize a loss \mathcal{L} with respect to scene parameters \boldsymbol{\theta}. It assumes the availability of an adjoint method or equivalent mechanism to compute the derivative of the loss with respect to the image, \partial{\mathbf{I}} \mathcal{L}, and the derivative of the image with respect to parameters, d\mathbf{I}/d\boldsymbol{\theta}. Scene parameters \boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^{m\theta}. Target image \mathbf{I}^{\text{target}}. Per-iteration sampling budget N{\text{pix}} (number of pixels to render per iteration). Current estimate of pixel sampling probabilities pj (initialized uniformly or from previous iteration). Updated scene parameters \boldsymbol{\theta} (via gradient descent step). Updated sampling probabilities pj for the next iteration. Pixel Grid: A 2D array of size H \times W (image resolution). Sampling Weights: A 2D array of size H \times W storing the unnormalized weights wj for each pixel. Probability Map: A 2D array of size H \times W storing normalized probabilities pj. Gradient Estimators: Buffers to store \langle (\partial{\mathbf{I}} \mathcal{L})j \rangle and \langle dIj/d\theta \rangle (or their squared second moments) for variance estimation. 1. Primal Pass (Image Rendering): Render the current scene parameters \boldsymbol{\theta} to obtain the current image \mathbf{I}(\boldsymbol{\theta}). This pass may use a higher sample budget per pixel to ensure accurate image values for loss computation and weight estimation. 2. Compute Loss Gradient Derivatives: Compute the derivative of the loss with respect to the image, \partial{\mathbf{I}} \mathcal{L}, for all pixels. 3. Estimate Rendering Gradient Variance: Estimate the second moment of the rendering derivative, p{j2}, for each pixel by rendering the gradient dIj/d\theta (or its components) for a subset of pixels. For scalar \theta: p{j2} \approx \mathbb{E}[\langle dIj/d\theta \rangle^2]. For vector \boldsymbol{\theta}: p{j2} \approx \sum{k=1}^{m\theta} \mathbb{E}[\langle \partial Ij / \partial \thetak \rangle^2]. 4. Compute Sampling Weights: Calculate the unnormalized weight wj for each pixel j using the formula: wj = \sqrt{p{j1} p{j2}}. Here, p{j1} = \mathbb{E}[\langle (\partial{\mathbf{I}} \mathcal{L})j \rangle^2] is the second moment of the loss derivative estimator. 5. Normalize Probabilities: Normalize the weights to obtain sampling probabilities: pj = \frac{wj}{\sum{k=1}^{mI} wk}, where mI is the total number of pixels. 6. Sample Pixels: Randomly select N{\text{pix}} pixels according to the probability distribution pj. This forms the "mini-batch" of pixels to render in this iteration. 7. Adjoint/Gradient Pass: For each sampled pixel j, render the gradient dIj/d\theta (or compute it via the adjoint method) to obtain the estimator \langle dIj/d\theta \rangle. 8. Estimate Gradient: Compute the unbiased gradient estimator for the selected pixels using the single-sample Monte Carlo formula: \left\langle \frac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\boldsymbol{\theta}} \right\rangle = \sum{j \in \text{sampled}} \frac{\langle (\partial{\mathbf{I}} \mathcal{L})j \rangle}{pj} \left\langle \frac{dIj}{d\boldsymbol{\theta}} \right\rangle. 9. Update Parameters: Use the estimated gradient to update \boldsymbol{\theta} via a gradient descent step. 10. Update Variance Estimates: Update the running estimates of p{j1} and p{j2} to adapt to changes in the scene parameters. Loss Minimization: \boldsymbol{\theta}^ = \arg \min{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{L} \left( \mathbf{I}(\boldsymbol{\theta}); \mathbf{I}^{\text{target}} \right) \quad (4.1) Chain Rule: \frac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\boldsymbol{\theta}} = \sum{j=1}^{mI} (\partial{\mathbf{I}} \mathcal{L})j \frac{dIj}{d\boldsymbol{\theta}} \quad (4.2) Monte Carlo Estimator: \left\langle \frac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\boldsymbol{\theta}} \right\rangle = \frac{\langle (\partial{\mathbf{I}} \mathcal{L})j \rangle}{pj} \left\langle \frac{dIj}{d\boldsymbol{\theta}} \right\rangle \quad (4.4) Optimal Probability (Scalar Case): pj \propto \sqrt{p{j1} p{j2}} \quad (4.8) where p{j1}:= \mathbb{E}[\langle (\partial{\mathbf{I}} \mathcal{L})j \rangle^2] and p{j2}:= \mathbb{E}[\langle dIj/d\theta \rangle^2]. Optimal Probability (Vector Case): pj \propto \sqrt{p{j1} p{j2}} \quad (4.12) where p{j1}:= \mathbb{E}[\langle (\partial{\mathbf{I}} \mathcal{L})j \rangle^2] and p{j2}:= \sum{k=1}^{m\theta} \mathbb{E}[\langle \partial Ij / \partial \thetak \rangle^2]. Sampling Budget (N{\text{pix}}): The number of pixels sampled per iteration. This is fixed per iteration. Primal:Adjoint Sample Ratio: The optimal ratio found in practice is 3:1 (75% of samples for primal rendering, 25% for adjoint/gradient rendering). Independence Assumption: The derivation assumes that the loss derivative estimator \langle (\partial{\mathbf{I}} \mathcal{L})j \rangle and the rendering derivative estimator \langle dIj/d\theta \rangle are independent. If they are correlated, the variance minimization derivation does not hold directly. Negative Adjoint Radiance: The adjoint radiance \partialI \mathcal{L} can have negative values. Sampling proportional to its absolute value |\partialI \mathcal{L}| introduces sign variance. While positivization (sampling positive and negative components separately) removes this variance, it was found to have little effect on overall estimation variance in practice, so the simpler absolute value method is used. High Variance with Uniform Sampling: Naively reducing the sampling budget by uniformly sampling pixels results in high gradient variance, degrading performance. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def varianceawareadaptivesampling( theta, Itarget, renderfunc, rendergradfunc, lossfunc, lossgradfunc, Npix, maxiter=1000, lr=0.01): """ Variance-aware adaptive pixel sampling for inverse rendering. Args: theta: Initial scene parameters. Itarget: Target image. renderfunc: Function to render image I(theta). rendergradfunc: Function to render squared gradient magnitude for all pixels. lossfunc: Function to compute loss L(I, Itarget). lossgradfunc: Function to compute gradient dL/dI. Npix: Number of pixels to sample per iteration. maxiter: Maximum number of iterations. lr: Learning rate. Returns: theta: Optimized scene parameters. """ H, W = Itarget.shape[:2] mI = H W # Initialize variance estimates pj1 and pj2 pj1 = np.ones((H, W)) pj2 = np.ones((H, W)) # Initialize probabilities uniformly p = np.ones((H, W)) / mI for iteration in range(maxiter): # Step 1: Primal Pass Icurr = renderfunc(theta) dLdI = lossgradfunc(Icurr, Itarget) # Step 2 & 3: Estimate second moments # pj1:= E[<dL/dIj>^2] pj1 = dLdI 2 # pj2:= E[<dIj/dtheta>^2] (scalar or sum over params) pj2 = rendergradfunc(theta) # Step 4: Compute Sampling Weights weights = np.sqrt(pj1 pj2) weights = np.maximum(weights, 1e-8) # Step 5: Normalize Probabilities p = weights / np.sum(weights) # Step 6: Sample Pixels pflat = p.flatten() pixelindices = np.random.choice(mI, size=Npix, replace=False, p=pflat) # Step 7 & 8: Adjoint/Gradient Pass & Estimate Gradient gradestimates = np.zeroslike(theta) for idx in pixelindices: y, x = np.unravelindex(idx, (H, W)) dLdIj = dLdI[y, x] dIdthetaj = rendergradfuncpixel(theta, y, x) pj = p[y, x] gradest = (dLdIj / pj) dIdthetaj gradestimates += gradest # Step 9: Update Parameters theta -= lr gradestimates return theta def rendergradfuncpixel(theta, y, x): """Computes the rendering derivative dIj/dtheta for pixel (y, x).""" # Standard operation: evaluate differentiable renderer gradient at pixel (y, x) return np.zeroslike(theta) Time Complexity: O(N{\text{pix}} \cdot C{\text{render}}) per iteration, where C{\text{render}} is the cost of rendering a single pixel. This is significantly faster than full-image rendering O(mI \cdot C{\text{render}}) when N{\text{pix}} \ll mI. Memory Complexity: O(mI) to store the probability map and variance estimates. Measured Performance: Reduces loss gradient variance by 1–2 orders of magnitude compared to uniform sampling or BRDF-only sampling. Outperforms uniform mini-batching by allowing faster convergence at equal time. Strengths: Accelerates inverse rendering by reducing sampling budget without sacrificing performance. Lowers gradient variance by accounting for rendering derivative variance. Limitations: Requires estimation of rendering derivative variance, which can be costly if not approximated. Assumes independence between loss and rendering derivative estimators. When to Use: Inverse rendering pipelines for SVBRDF reconstruction, shape optimization, and inverse volume rendering where computational cost is a bottleneck. When Not to Use: When the independence assumption is strongly violated, or when the cost of estimating p{j2} outweighs the benefits of adaptive sampling. The method was introduced in the context of differentiable rendering and inverse rendering to address the high computational cost of rendering all pixels during optimization. It builds on the concept of mini-batching in gradient-based optimization and applies it to the image space. The theoretical foundation for optimal sampling probabilities is derived from minimizing the variance of the Monte Carlo estimator for the loss gradient. The technique has been applied to various inverse rendering problems, including SVBRDF reconstruction and shape optimization. Variance-aware Differentiable Rendering, https://core.ac.uk/works/337282320, fetched 2026-11-02 (unofficial) Path Sampling Methods for Differentiable Rendering, https://doi.org/10.2312/sr.20241148, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Path Replay Backpropagation
head: Reverse-mode differentiation benchmark
body: Path Replay Backpropagation (PRB) is an adjoint-based differentiable rendering method that computes gradients of a scalar loss function with respect to scene parameters without storing the full Monte Carlo computation graph. It solves the quadratic runtime complexity of its sibling, Radiative Backpropagation (RB), by using a two-pass approach: a primal pass to generate samples and store state, followed by an adjoint pass that replays the path using the same random seed to recover incident radiance. Unlike RB, which requires an intertwined simulation of adjoint and primal radiance leading to quadratic complexity, PRB achieves linear time complexity in path length. PRB transforms the derivative of a light transport simulation into an equivalent simulation of differential radiation, leveraging physical reciprocity and pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) replay to avoid explicit storage of the computational graph. Inputs: Scene parameters \pi (e.g., density, albedo, BRDF parameters), camera parameters, loss function L(I), and a random seed \bar{\boldsymbol{p}}. Outputs: Gradient \frac{\partial L}{\partial \pi}. The method is decomposed into three self-contained megakernels: 1. Megakernel #1 (Primal Path Tracer): Generates Monte Carlo samples. Implicitly depends on scene parameters. Outputs a primal rendering I and stores per-ray information (vertex positions, directions, BSDF evaluations) in a state array. 2. Megakernel #2 (Replay Sampler): Regenerates the same set of samples using the same random seed but a different pseudorandom sequence. Outputs a per-sample state array containing the specific random numbers used for each path segment. 3. Megakernel #3 (Adjoint Megakernel): Contains adjoint versions of all rendering steps. Takes the state array from Megakernel #2 and the primal rendering from Megakernel #1. Accumulates scene parameter gradients. 1. Primal Pass (Megakernel #1): Trace rays from the camera. For each ray, generate a path \bar{\boldsymbol{p}} using a PRNG. Store the path estimate \hat{f}(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}}) and per-ray information (vertices, directions, BSDF values). Compute the image I and the loss L(I). 2. Replay Pass (Megakernel #2): Regenerate the path \bar{\boldsymbol{p}} using the same initial random seed to ensure the same sequence of vertices and intersections is visited. Store the specific random numbers used for each segment n. 3. Adjoint Pass (Megakernel #3): Compute the adjoint radiance in image space: \frac{\partial L}{\partial I}. Emit this signed radiation from the camera into the scene. For each path segment n, replay the path using the stored random numbers to compute the segment weight gn(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}}). Compute the derivative of the segment weight \frac{\partial gn(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}})}{\partial \pi} using automatic differentiation on the specific segment n. Combine using the product rule to compute the gradient contribution. At every intersection, absorb the accumulated differential light by backpropagating to the scene parameters \pi. 4. Optimization Step: Compute one further decorrelated primal rendering to provide to the image loss function, resulting in three integration steps total. The gradient of the loss L with respect to parameters \pi is derived using the chain rule and the material form parameterization: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \pi} = \int{\hat{\Omega}} \frac{\partial L}{\partial I} \frac{\partial \hat{f}(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}})}{\partial I} \frac{\partial I}{\partial \pi} d\mu(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}}) This avoids explicitly computing or storing \frac{\partial I}{\partial \pi}. The path estimator \hat{f}(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}}) is decomposed into segment weights gn(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}}): gn(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}}) = \begin{cases} fv(\bar{x}, n) J(pn), & 0 \le n \le N \\ G(x{n-N-1} \leftrightarrow x{n-N}), & N < n \le 2N \end{cases} where N is the path length, fv is the volume scattering term, J is the Jacobian, and G is the geometry term. The derivative of the path estimator is computed via the product rule: \frac{\partial \hat{f}(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}})}{\partial \pi} = \sumn \frac{\partial gn(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}})}{\partial \pi} \prod{n' \ne n} g{n'}(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}}) = \sumn \frac{\partial gn(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}})}{\partial \pi} \frac{\hat{f}(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}})}{gn(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}})} Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pathreplaybackpropagation(scene, camera, params, lossfn, seed): """ Implements Path Replay Backpropagation (PRB). scene: Scene representation with differentiable parameters. camera: Camera configuration. params: Scene parameters pi to optimize. lossfn: Scalar loss function L(I). seed: Random seed for path generation. """ # Pass 1: Primal Path Tracing (Megakernel #1) # Generate paths and store per-ray information paths, pathestimates, rayinfo = traceprimalpaths(scene, camera, params, seed) # Compute image and loss image = reconstructimage(paths, pathestimates) loss = lossfn(image) # Pass 2: Replay Sampling (Megakernel #2) # Regenerate paths with same seed to get specific random numbers used # This ensures we visit the same vertices but can access the RNG state replayrngstates = replayrngstates(seed, rayinfo) # Pass 3: Adjoint Path Tracing (Megakernel #3) # Initialize gradient accumulator gradparams = zeroslike(params) # Compute adjoint radiance at the sensor adjointradiance = computeadjointradiance(loss, image) for pathidx in range(numpaths): # Replay the path using stored RNG states to get segment weights # and the specific random numbers used for each segment segments = [] for n in range(pathlength): rngstate = replayrngstates[pathidx][n] # Re-evaluate segment n using the same random numbers # This allows computing gn and its derivative d(gn)/d(pi) segmentweight, segmentderiv = computesegmentandderiv( scene, camera, params, pathidx, n, rngstate) segments.append((segmentweight, segmentderiv)) # Compute total path estimate for normalization totalestimate = pathestimates[pathidx] # Accumulate gradients using the product rule formula # d(L)/d(pi) = sumn ( d(gn)/d(pi) (totalestimate / gn)) for n in range(pathlength): gn, dgndpi = segments[n] if gn != 0: # Contribution from segment n contribution = dgndpi (totalestimate / gn) # Backpropagate to parameters gradparams += contribution return gradparams Quadratic Complexity: The sibling method RB suffers from quadratic complexity because it computes incident primal radiance at every intersection by building another complete light path integral. PRB avoids this by replaying the path. Visibility Discontinuities: When differentiated parameters affect visibility, derivatives can be severely biased, breaking shape reconstruction. Special precautions are needed. Memory: PRB uses minimal GPU memory compared to storing full computation graphs, which is critical for large scene representations like 3D volumes. Polymorphic Calls: The reverse-mode derivative of polymorphic calls (e.g., BSDF evaluation with large intersection records) creates redundancies. Global dead code elimination, constant propagation, and value numbering are required for efficiency. Time Complexity: Linear in path length. RB is quadratic. Memory Complexity: Constant memory complexity, avoiding the storage of per-bounce data required by standard AD. Performance: In the Veach Door scene (480x270, 16 spp primal, 4 spp adjoint), PRB peak memory was 3.00 GiB and gradient computation time was 2.46s, compared to RB's 3.51 GiB and 2.52s. On CPU, megakernel-style evaluation provides speedups reaching ~166x compared to baseline. GPU speedups from redundancy elimination reach 3.3x. Strengths: Unbiased gradients, low memory usage, linear complexity. Limitations: Requires careful handling of visibility discontinuities. The method is write-heavy, accumulating gradients rather than querying scene representation. PRB was introduced by Vicini et al. [2021] as an improvement over Radiative Backpropagation (RB) [Nimier-David et al. 2020]. It is used as a baseline in inverse rendering optimization experiments, such as optimizing BRDF material properties in the Veach door scene. The method is implemented in the Dr.Jit differentiable rendering framework. name: Checkpointing for Reverse-Mode Memory Optimization
head: Checkpointing, Griewank checkpointing, Logarithmic checkpointing, re-evaluation from checkpoints
body: Checkpointing is an optimization for reverse-mode automatic differentiation (AD) that reduces memory complexity by storing only a sparse subset of intermediate variables and recomputing loop segments during the backward pass. It addresses the scalability issue of exhaustive storage, where memory usage is proportional to the number of instructions, by trading increased time complexity for logarithmic memory usage. Unlike Inversion Trick or Path Replay Backpropagation, which exploit problem-specific structures to avoid differentiation entirely, checkpointing is a general-purpose mechanism applicable to any traced computation. Inputs: A primal computation consisting of N sequential operations (or a loop of length N). Outputs: Gradients of a scalar loss with respect to the input parameters. Data Structures: 1. Checkpoint Storage: A dictionary or array storing the full state at specific indices. The size is O(\log N). 2. Primal State: The current state of variables during recomputation. Algorithm: The method divides the sequence of N operations into segments. During the forward pass, the state is saved at predefined checkpoint indices. During the backward pass, the algorithm iterates backwards through the segments. For each segment, it restores the state from the nearest preceding checkpoint and re-executes the forward operations to reconstruct intermediate values required for gradient computation. 1. Forward Pass with Checkpointing: Initialize the primal state x0. Iterate i from 0 to N-1. Compute x{i+1} = fi(xi). If i is a checkpoint index, save xi to the Checkpoint Storage. Note: The optimal strategy for selecting checkpoint indices to minimize total recomputation time while maintaining O(\log N) memory is to use a recursive doubling or tree strategy. 2. Backward Pass with Recomputation: Initialize gradient accumulator \bar{x}N (typically \partial L / \partial xN). Iterate backwards through the segments defined by the checkpoints. Let the checkpoints be at indices c0, c1, \dots, ck where c0 = 0 and ck = N. For each segment from cj to c{j+1}: Restore the primal state x{cj} from the Checkpoint Storage. Recompute the forward operations for indices i from cj to c{j+1}-1: x{i+1} = fi(xi). Compute gradients for this segment in reverse order (i from c{j+1}-1 down to cj): \bar{x}i = \bar{x}{i+1} \cdot \frac{\partial fi}{\partial xi}. Accumulate \bar{x}i into the global gradient accumulator. Note: If the computation involves recursive function calls, a tree structure may be used instead of a stack to store intermediate results. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def checkpointedbackward(N, f, fprime, checkpoints, x0, gradout): savedstates = {} state = x0 # Forward pass: save state before update to enable correct segment restoration for i in range(N): if i in checkpoints: savedstates[i] = state state = f(state) grad = gradout # Sort checkpoint boundaries in descending order to process segments backwards segmentends = sorted(checkpoints + [N], reverse=True) for j in range(len(segmentends) - 1): endidx = segmentends[j] startidx = segmentends[j+1] # Restore primal state at segment start; default to x0 if startidx is 0 currentstate = savedstates.get(startidx, x0) forwardstates = [currentstate] tempstate = currentstate # Recompute forward operations for the segment for i in range(startidx, endidx): tempstate = f(tempstate) forwardstates.append(tempstate) # Compute gradients in reverse order for the segment for i in range(endidx - 1, startidx - 1, -1): xi = forwardstates[i - startidx] xnext = forwardstates[i - startidx + 1] # Standard reverse-mode adjoint update: xbari = xbarnext f'(xi) grad = fprime(xi, xnext, grad) return grad Parameters: Checkpoint Frequency: The number of checkpoints K. To achieve O(\log N) memory, K \approx \log2 N. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Recursive Calls: If the function f calls itself, the checkpointing strategy must handle the call stack correctly, potentially using a tree structure instead of a linear stack. Memory vs. Time Trade-off: While memory is reduced to O(\log N), time complexity increases to O(N \log N). Differentiation techniques that exploit problem-specific traits to reduce storage and reevaluation overheads, generally preferable to checkpointing when available. For Newton's method, the implicit function theorem provides the answer directly from the iteration's fixed point instead of differentiating through all steps. For ordinary differential equations, reverse time integration provides an efficient adjoint. A checkpointing mechanism that arises naturally from the combined AD/JIT system without intentional implementation effort. The JIT layer recomputes intermediate steps and temporaries from the last evaluation point. In systems like Dr.Jit, calling dr.backward(data) causes the AD layer to reference intermediate steps produced by f, which the JIT layer recomputes from the last dr.eval checkpoint. Checkpointing is not ideal for Path Replay Backpropagation (PBDR) workloads due to the large size of even a small number of checkpoints. Time Complexity: O(N \log N), where N is the number of operations or loop length. Memory Complexity: O(\log N), where N is the number of operations. Scaling: Reduces memory complexity to O(\log N), addressing scalability issues where exhaustive storage generates terabytes of intermediate state. Strengths: General applicability to any traced computation; significant memory savings for long sequences of operations. Limitations: Increased computational overhead due to recomputation; not ideal for workloads with large checkpoint sizes (e.g., PBDR). When to Use: When memory is the bottleneck and the computation is too large for exhaustive storage, and no custom adjoint is available. When Not to Use: When custom adjoints are available (e.g., Inversion Trick, Path Replay Backpropagation). Checkpointing for reverse-mode automatic differentiation was introduced by Andreas Griewank in 1992. The technique addresses the "age-old question" of how to manage intermediate state in reversed program references, where exhaustive storage does not scale due to the volume of data generated by modern processors. The concept of storing state at sparse checkpoints and recovering it via reevaluation was previously noted by Volin and Ostrovskii in 1985. Automatic recursive usage of this pattern was further analyzed by Siskind and Pearlmutter in 2018, formalizing the O(\log t) overhead for a program with t operations. In the context of differentiable rendering, checkpointing is a key component of general-purpose AD systems like Dr.Jit, enabling the differentiation of complex rendering programs without requiring custom adjoints for every operation. name: Forward-Mode Automatic Differentiation
head: Forward Differentiation, Forward mode differentiation, Tangent Mode AD, Tape-based Automatic Differentiation, Tracing (Automatic Differentiation), Wengert tape, computation graph
body: Forward-mode automatic differentiation (AD) computes derivatives by recursively applying the chain rule to elementary operations, propagating derivative information from input variables to output variables simultaneously with the forward simulation pass. It solves the problem of computing exact gradients without symbolic manipulation or finite differences by replacing every variable with a tuple of the original value and its derivative with respect to a parameter. Unlike reverse-mode AD, which traverses the graph from output to input, forward-mode traverses from input to output, making it efficient when the input dimension is low and the output dimension is high, but typically less suitable for optimization in high-dimensional scenes because each parameter requires a separate rendering pass or significant memory overhead. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A primal computational graph representing the rendering function f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m, where n is the number of input parameters (scene variables, camera parameters, etc.) and m is the number of output variables (pixel colors). Outputs: The primal values (rendered image) and the Jacobian-vector products (gradients) of the outputs with respect to the specified input parameters. Data Structures: The core data structure is the forward variable (often called fvar or dual number), which wraps a scalar value and its derivative information. 1. Dual Number / Forward Variable (fvar): Layout: A struct containing: value: The primal scalar value (T). derivatives: An array or vector of size p storing the partial derivatives with respect to p input parameters (T[p]). Bit Packing: Not given in the sources. Fields: value: Stores x. derivatives[i]: Stores \frac{\partial x}{\partial wi} for i \in \{0, \dots, p-1\}. 2. Computation Graph / Tape (Optional for Tracing-based AD): If using a tracing approach (Wengert tape), the graph records the sequence of operations. The trace ignores control flow constructs and stores unrolled versions of all loops and taken branches. Each edge carries a weight indicating sensitivity. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize constant variables with zero derivative: \tilde{x}{\text{const}} = \langle x{\text{const}}, 0 \rangle. Initialize parameters of interest with unit derivative: \tilde{w}i = \langle wi, ei \rangle, where ei is a vector with 1 at index i and 0 elsewhere. If computing derivatives for multiple parameters, extend the derivatives array to size p. 2. Forward Propagation (Primal and Tangent): Traverse the computational graph from inputs to outputs. For each operation c = f(a, b), compute the primal value and the derivative using the chain rule: \tilde{c} = \tilde{f}(\tilde{a}, \tilde{b}) = \left\langle f(a, b), \frac{\partial f}{\partial a} \frac{da}{dw} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial b} \frac{db}{dw} \right\rangle Apply operator overloading for elementary arithmetic operations: Addition: value += rhs.value; grad += rhs.grad; Multiplication: grad = value rhs.grad + rhs.value grad; value = rhs.value; Division: grad = (grad rhs.value - value rhs.grad) / (rhs.value rhs.value); value /= rhs.value; Elementary Functions (e.g., \sin, \cos, \sqrt{}): \sin(\tilde{a}): value = sin(d.value); grad = d.grad cos(d.value); \cos(\tilde{a}): value = cos(d.value); grad = -d.grad sin(d.value); \sqrt{\tilde{a}}: value = sqrt(d.value); grad = value 0.5 d.grad / d.value; |\tilde{a}|: returns -d if value < 0, else d 3. Accumulation: Derivatives are accumulated forward in time using the chain rule. If using a tracing-based approach with latent variables, ensure gradients are kept in all variables during traversal to handle dependencies between scene parameters (e.g., using a ClearEdges flag). 4. Output Retrieval: Extract the derivatives component from the output variables (e.g., the rendered image). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class fvar: def init(self, value, derivatives): self.value = value self.derivatives = derivatives # List or array of size p def add(self, other): # Addition: c = a + b newvalue = self.value + other.value newderivs = [self.derivatives[i] + other.derivatives[i] for i in range(len(self.derivatives))] return fvar(newvalue, newderivs) def mul(self, other): # Multiplication: c = a b newvalue = self.value other.value newderivs = [self.value other.derivatives[i] + other.value self.derivatives[i] for i in range(len(self.derivatives))] return fvar(newvalue, newderivs) def truediv(self, other): # Division: c = a / b denom = other.value other.value newvalue = self.value / other.value newderivs = [(other.value self.derivatives[i] - self.value other.derivatives[i]) / denom for i in range(len(self.derivatives))] return fvar(newvalue, newderivs) def sin(self): # sin(a) newvalue = math.sin(self.value) newderivs = [math.cos(self.value) self.derivatives[i] for i in range(len(self.derivatives))] return fvar(newvalue, newderivs) def computeforwardmode(): # 1. Initialize parameters # Parameter w with derivative 1 w.r.t itself w = fvar(value=2.0, derivatives=[1.0]) # Constant c with derivative 0 c = fvar(value=3.0, derivatives=[0.0]) # 2. Forward propagation # Example operation: y = w c + sin(w) temp1 = w c # temp1.value = 6.0, temp1.derivatives = [3.0] temp2 = w.sin() # temp2.value = sin(2.0), temp2.derivatives = [cos(2.0)] y = temp1 + temp2 # y.value = 6.0 + sin(2.0), y.derivatives = [3.0 + cos(2.0)] return y def computeforwardmodemulti(): # Parameters w0, w1 # w0 derivative vector: [1, 0] w0 = fvar(value=2.0, derivatives=[1.0, 0.0]) # w1 derivative vector: [0, 1] w1 = fvar(value=3.0, derivatives=[0.0, 1.0]) # Operation: y = w0 w1 y = w0 w1 # y.value = 6.0 # y.derivatives[0] = w0.val w1.deriv[0] + w1.val w0.deriv[0] = 20 + 31 = 3 # y.derivatives[1] = w0.val w1.deriv[1] + w1.val w0.deriv[1] = 21 + 30 = 2 return y Parameters: p: The number of parameters to differentiate with respect to. The derivatives array size is p. Typical values: p is small (e.g., 2 for camera viewpoint) for efficient use; large p (e.g., thousands for Transfer Functions) makes it inefficient. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Dimensionality: Forward differentiation becomes unfeasible for high-dimensional input data (like Transfer Functions or 3D volumetric fields) because the number of parameters p is large, requiring the process to be repeated for each parameter or extending the derivatives array significantly. Latent Variables: If gradients of latent variables are not propagated to scene parameters before rendering, the loop tracing may destroy the part of the computational graph outside the loop, resulting in incorrect gradients. Visualization: Gradient values are not necessarily within [0, 1]. Directly displaying them as RGB floats will clip or distort the visualization; use a colormap and clamp the display range. Control Flow: Differentiating long-running loops can be challenging in tracing-based implementations due to overheads from repeated tracing and unrolling. Computes exact gradients of scalar fields using dual numbers, primarily for computing vertex normals for implicit surfaces. Chosen when exact gradients are needed for geometric primitives, avoiding finite difference errors. Combines tracing (Wengert tape) with dynamic compilation to reduce overhead in dynamic dispatch scenarios. Chosen when runtime performance and compilation time are critical for complex, dynamic rendering code. Time Complexity: O(d) times the time complexity of the original algorithm, where d is the number of input variables (parameters). Scales linearly with the number of parameters p. Memory Complexity: O(np), where n is the size of intermediate results (e.g., image dimensions) and p is the number of parameters. Only the current state needs to be stored, unlike reverse mode which may require caching all states. Measured Performance: Efficient for functions with few input variables (e.g., viewpoint selection with 2 parameters). Inefficient for functions with thousands or millions of input variables (e.g., volume density fields). Strengths: Simpler implementation than source transformation; easier to incorporate into existing code; efficient for low-dimensional inputs; computes derivatives for arbitrary number of outputs in one pass. Limitations: Unfeasible for high-dimensional inputs; requires separate pass per parameter if p is large; runtime overheads dominate in scalar programs. When to Use: When the number of input parameters is small (e.g., camera pose optimization) and the number of outputs is large. When Not to Use: When the number of input parameters is large (e.g., optimizing a high-resolution Transfer Function or volume density field). Forward-mode automatic differentiation computes derivatives by replacing variables with tuples of values and derivatives, propagating them from inputs to outputs in the computation graph. It is historically used in optimal control (linear quadratic regulators, trajectory optimization) and robotics toolboxes. In the context of differentiable rendering, it is used to visualize the effect of individual scene parameters on the rendered image, such as how changes in a wall's color affect global illumination. Forward mode is typically less suitable for optimization than reverse-mode (backpropagation) because each parameter requires a separate rendering pass.
