name: Albedo-based Parameterization for Extinction
head: Albedo/Sigma_t Decoupling
body: Albedo-based parameterization is a strategy for differentiable volume rendering that decouples the scattering coefficient (\sigmas) from the extinction coefficient (\sigmat) by representing scattering as a product of albedo (\alpha) and extinction. This approach solves the numerical instability inherent in direct parameterization, where gradients of \sigmas with respect to \sigmat become undefined or unstable as extinction approaches zero. It sets itself apart from siblings like Single-Scattering Differentiable Volume Rendering and Differential Ratio Tracing by explicitly structuring the scene graph to expose albedo as a differentiable primitive alongside \sigmat, ensuring stable optimization gradients in heterogeneous media. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A heterogeneous medium definition specifying either an albedo volume (\alpha) or a scattering coefficient volume (\sigmas), but not both. The medium also requires an extinction coefficient volume (\sigmat). Output: A differentiable scene representation where \sigmat and the chosen parameterization (albedo or \sigmas) are exposed as differentiable parameters. The integrator queries \sigmas for rendering, but gradients are computed with respect to the underlying differentiable parameters. Data Structures: The medium implementation uses a flag system (ParamFlags) to declare differentiability. sigmat: Marked as ParamFlags::Differentiable. albedo (if used): Marked as ParamFlags::Differentiable. sigmas (if used directly): Marked as ParamFlags::Differentiable. scale: Marked as ParamFlags::NonDifferentiable. Steps: 1. Scene Construction: The user defines the medium. If using albedo-based parameterization, the scene provides an albedo volume \alpha(\mathbf{x}) and an extinction volume \sigmat(\mathbf{x}). The scattering coefficient is implicitly defined as \sigmas(\mathbf{x}) = \alpha(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \sigmat(\mathbf{x}). The two parameterizations (albedo vs. direct \sigmas) are mutually exclusive. 2. Parameter Exposure: The traversal function exposes the provided parameters. It never exposes both albedo and direct \sigmas. It exposes the chosen scattering parameterization alongside \sigmat, marking them as differentiable. This declares which scene attributes may carry gradients; gradients are only computed when the caller enables them. 3. Rendering Query: During integration (e.g., in Medium::samplerealinteraction), the integrator always queries the physical scattering coefficient \sigmas. If the scene was defined with albedo, \sigmas is computed on-the-fly or looked up via a specialized accessor. 4. Gradient Computation: Automatic differentiation handles the gradients. Because \sigmat and \alpha are separate differentiable parameters, the gradient of the radiance with respect to \sigmas is computed via the chain rule through \alpha and \sigmat. This avoids the direct derivative of \sigmas / \sigmat which is problematic. Formulas: The relationship between the parameters is: \sigmas(\mathbf{x}) = \alpha(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) Where: \sigmas(\mathbf{x}) is the scattering coefficient at position \mathbf{x}. \alpha(\mathbf{x}) is the albedo (single-scattering albedo) at position \mathbf{x}, typically in [0, 1]. \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) is the extinction coefficient at position \mathbf{x}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: 0/0 Indeterminacy: Rebuilding \sigmas and \sigmat from albedo and extinction can result in 0/0 wherever extinction vanishes (\sigmat \to 0). This leads to numerical instability and undefined gradients. Direct Albedo Lookup: To mitigate this, the method provides Medium::getalbedo, which performs a direct albedo lookup. This is cheaper and better-conditioned than reconstructing coefficients from division. Mutual Exclusivity: The system enforces that albedo and direct \sigmas are mutually exclusive. Mixing them is not supported. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class ParamFlags: Differentiable = 1 NonDifferentiable = 0 class HeterogeneousMedium: def init(self, sigmat, albedo=None, sigmas=None): self.sigmat = sigmat self.albedo = albedo self.sigmas = sigmas if albedo is not None and sigmas is not None: raise ValueError("Albedo and sigmas are mutually exclusive") self.paramflags = { 'sigmat': ParamFlags.Differentiable, 'albedo': ParamFlags.Differentiable if albedo is not None else None, 'sigmas': ParamFlags.Differentiable if sigmas is not None else None, 'scale': ParamFlags.NonDifferentiable } def getsigmas(self, position): """Query the physical scattering coefficient.""" if self.albedo is not None: return self.albedo[position] self.sigmat[position] elif self.sigmas is not None: return self.sigmas[position] else: raise ValueError("No scattering parameterization defined") def getalbedo(self, position): """Direct albedo lookup for better conditioning.""" if self.albedo is not None: return self.albedo[position] elif self.sigmas is not None: if self.sigmat[position] == 0: return 0.0 return self.sigmas[position] / self.sigmat[position] else: raise ValueError("No scattering parameterization defined") Converts artistic subsurface scattering parameters—specifically a medium color vector \mathbf{A} and a scattering distance d—into physical volume rendering coefficients (extinction \sigmat and scattering \sigmas) for a homogeneous medium. This method enables artists to control the visual appearance of subsurface scattering using intuitive parameters while maintaining the physical consistency required for differentiable volume rendering. It is distinct from direct coefficient specification by providing a closed-form approximation of the inverse relationship between albedo and surface color, decoupling the scattering behavior from the extinction scale. Time Complexity: The traversal and interaction sampling remain similar to standard volume rendering, with the overhead of evaluating the albedo-extinction product or lookup. The fused C++ walk for null collisions shares the loop with DDA traversal, maintaining efficiency. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for \sigmat and either \alpha or \sigmas. No additional significant memory overhead compared to standard parameterization. Measured Performance: Tested on an NVIDIA A40 under CUDA/OptiX. Gradient statistics (mean and variance) were compared against Differential Ratio Tracing (DRT) implementations. The method provides stable gradients comparable to DRT in single-channel extinction cases. Strengths: Stable gradients even when extinction is low or zero; decouples scattering behavior from extinction scale; compatible with existing differentiable rendering frameworks (e.g., Mitsuba 3). Limitations: Requires careful handling of the 0/0 case when deriving albedo from direct \sigmas; mutual exclusivity of parameterizations limits flexibility in scene definition. When to Use: When optimizing volume parameters (especially in heterogeneous media) where extinction may vary significantly or approach zero. When Not to Use: When direct control over \sigmas is required without coupling to \sigmat, or when the scene does not support the specific parameter flags. This method originates from recent developments in differentiable volume rendering, specifically within the Mitsuba 3 renderer ecosystem. It builds on the principles of Differential Ratio Tracing (DRT) but adapts the parameterization strategy to be more robust for general heterogeneous media. The approach was introduced in a review branch of Mitsuba 3, aiming to provide a stable alternative to direct coefficient optimization. Sample matching for extinction gradients (review branch), https://github.com/AuroraRyan0301/mitsuba3/pull/1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Subsurface Scattering Parameter Conversion
head: Chiang et al. conversion
body: Converts artistic subsurface scattering parameters—specifically a medium color vector \mathbf{A} and a scattering distance d—into physical volume rendering coefficients (extinction \sigmat and scattering \sigmas) for a homogeneous medium. This method enables artists to control the visual appearance of subsurface scattering using intuitive parameters while maintaining the physical consistency required for differentiable volume rendering. It is distinct from direct coefficient specification by providing a closed-form approximation of the inverse relationship between albedo and surface color, decoupling the scattering behavior from the extinction scale. Inputs: \mathbf{A}: Medium color, a 3-component vector (Vec3f) representing the desired subsurface scattering color. d: Scattering distance, a scalar representing the characteristic depth of light penetration. Outputs: \sigmat: Extinction coefficient (Vec3f). \sigmas: Scattering coefficient (Vec3f). \sigmaa: Absorption coefficient (Vec3f), derived as \sigmat - \sigmas. Data Structures: \mathbf{A}: float[3] or Vec3f structure. d: float. \sigmat, \sigmas, \sigmaa: float[3] or Vec3f structures. Steps: 1. Compute the scalar albedo \alpha from the medium color \mathbf{A} using a cubic polynomial fit: \alpha = 1 - \exp(-5.09406 \cdot A + 2.61188 \cdot A^2 - 4.31805 \cdot A^3) Note: The sources define \alpha as a scalar derived from \mathbf{A}, but \mathbf{A} is a vector. In implementation, this formula is applied component-wise to each channel of \mathbf{A} to produce a vector \boldsymbol{\alpha}, or \mathbf{A} is treated as a scalar luminance value if the medium is grayscale. Given the context of "medium color" and "Vec3f", the polynomial is applied per-channel. Let \alphai be the albedo for channel i: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-5.09406 \cdot Ai + 2.61188 \cdot Ai^2 - 4.31805 \cdot Ai^3) 2. Compute the scalar scaling factor s from the medium color \mathbf{A} using a quadratic polynomial: s = 1.9 - A + 3.5 \cdot (A - 0.8)^2 Similarly, this is applied component-wise: si = 1.9 - Ai + 3.5 \cdot (Ai - 0.8)^2 3. Compute the extinction coefficient \sigmat using the scattering distance d and the scaling factor s: \sigmat = \frac{1}{d \cdot s} Applied component-wise: \sigma{t,i} = \frac{1}{d \cdot si} 4. Compute the scattering coefficient \sigmas using the albedo \alpha and extinction \sigmat: \sigmas = \alpha \cdot \sigmat Applied component-wise: \sigma{s,i} = \alphai \cdot \sigma{t,i} 5. Compute the absorption coefficient \sigmaa: \sigmaa = \sigmat - \sigmas Applied component-wise: \sigma{a,i} = \sigma{t,i} - \sigma{s,i} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def convertsubsurfacescatteringparams(Avec, d): """ Convert artistic subsurface scattering parameters to physical coefficients. Args: Avec (Vec3f): Medium color (albedo-like input). d (float): Scattering distance. Returns: sigmat (Vec3f): Extinction coefficient. sigmas (Vec3f): Scattering coefficient. sigmaa (Vec3f): Absorption coefficient. """ # Initialize output vectors sigmat = Vec3f(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) sigmas = Vec3f(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) sigmaa = Vec3f(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Process each color channel for i in range(3): Ai = Avec[i] # Step 1: Compute albedo alphai # alpha = 1 - exp(-5.09406 A + 2.61188 A^2 - 4.31805 A^3) alphai = 1.0 - exp(-5.09406 Ai + 2.61188 Ai2 - 4.31805 Ai3) # Step 2: Compute scaling factor si # s = 1.9 - A + 3.5 (A - 0.8)^2 si = 1.9 - Ai + 3.5 (Ai - 0.8)2 # Step 3: Compute extinction sigmati # sigmat = 1 / (d s) # Guard against division by zero if si is 0 if si == 0: sigmati = 0.0 else: sigmati = 1.0 / (d si) # Step 4: Compute scattering sigmasi # sigmas = alpha sigmat sigmasi = alphai sigmati # Step 5: Compute absorption sigmaai # sigmaa = sigmat - sigmas sigmaai = sigmati - sigmasi # Assign to output vectors sigmat[i] = sigmati sigmas[i] = sigmasi sigmaa[i] = sigmaai return sigmat, sigmas, sigmaa Parameters: Polynomial coefficients for \alpha: -5.09406, 2.61188, -4.31805. Polynomial coefficients for s: 1.9, 3.5, -0.8 (offset). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If si = 0, division by zero occurs in \sigmat calculation. This happens when 1.9 - Ai + 3.5(Ai - 0.8)^2 = 0. The discriminant of the quadratic 3.5Ai^2 - 5.3Ai + 1.28 is 5.3^2 - 4 \cdot 3.5 \cdot 1.28 = 28.09 - 17.92 = 10.17 > 0, so real roots exist. Roots are \frac{5.3 \pm \sqrt{10.17}}{7} \approx \frac{5.3 \pm 3.19}{7}, yielding Ai \approx 1.2 and Ai \approx 0.3. If the medium color channel is near 0.3 or 1.2, si approaches zero, leading to numerical instability. Clamping or handling this singularity is required. The polynomial for \alpha is valid for A \in [0, 1]. Values outside this range may produce albedos outside [0, 1], which is physically invalid for scattering albedo. A two-stage curve fitting process to invert the mapping from scattering albedo and anisotropy to surface color, enabling artist control over surface color in the path traced model. It differs from the standard conversion by solving the inverse problem: given a desired surface color x and anisotropy g, it computes the required scattering albedo \alpha. Definition: Inverts the relationship \alpha, g \rightarrow x to x, g \rightarrow \alpha using a parametric function fitted to 1600 rendered images of a single slab geometry. Steps: 1. Render images of a single slab geometry with varying scattering albedo \alpha (40 values) and anisotropy g (40 values), resulting in 1600 combinations. 2. Fit a parametric function to map surface color x to albedo \alpha using a linear blend of two arctan functions. 3. Fit coefficients A, C, D, F as polynomials of g, and B, E as exponential-of-polynomials of g. Formula: \alpha(x, g) = (1 - x^{0.25}) \cdot A(g) \cdot \tan^{-1}(B(g)x)^{C(g)} + x^{0.25} \cdot D(g) \cdot \tan^{-1}(E(g)x)^{F(g)} where: A(g) = \sum{i=0}^{7} ai g^i B(g) = a0 + a1 \exp\left(\sum{i=2}^{8} ai g^{i-1}\right) (Note: The source specifies B(g) = a0 + a1 \exp(a2 g + a3 g^2 + \dots + a8 g^7)). When to choose: Use when the artist specifies a target surface color and anisotropy, and the system needs to determine the underlying volume scattering albedo to achieve that appearance. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(1) per voxel/point, involving a few polynomial evaluations and arithmetic operations. Memory: O(1), storing only the input parameters and output coefficients. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of voxels or points in the volume, as the conversion is applied independently per location. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Provides a direct, closed-form conversion from intuitive artistic parameters to physical coefficients, facilitating optimization in differentiable rendering. Limitations: The approximation is specific to homogeneous media and may not accurately represent complex anisotropic scattering or non-homogeneous media without extension. The singularity at specific albedo values requires careful handling. When to use: Use when integrating artistic subsurface scattering parameters into a differentiable volume renderer that requires physical extinction and scattering coefficients. When not: Do not use when the medium is highly anisotropic and requires a full phase function parameterization, or when the medium is non-homogeneous and requires spatially varying coefficients derived from more complex models. Originated from the work of Chiang et al. in the context of volumetric path tracing and subsurface scattering parameterization. The method was developed to bridge the gap between artistic control and physical simulation in volume rendering, allowing artists to specify medium color and scattering distance while the renderer computes the appropriate physical coefficients. It is used in differentiable volume rendering pipelines where gradient-based optimization of material parameters is required. volpt: Volumetric path tracer written in C++, https://github.com/yumcyaWiz/volpt, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Path Traced Subsurface Scattering Model, https://www.scribd.com/document/965284472/Pixar-Path-Traced-SSS-Paper, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Single-Scattering Differentiable Volume Rendering
head: Ours
body: Single-Scattering Differentiable Volume Rendering is a differentiable renderer that reconstructs smoke density fields using a single-scattering assumption, enabling analytical gradient computation with respect to density \rho. It solves the inverse problem of recovering volumetric density from multi-view images by computing gradients directly via the differential form of the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE). It sets itself apart from Differential Ray Tracing (DRT) by pre-computing view-independent radiance terms, achieving a 50-100x speedup, and from full multiple-scattering methods by trading absolute accuracy for interactive reconstruction speeds. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of reference images captured from different viewpoints, a volume grid of resolution Rx \times Ry \times Rz, and a scattering coefficient \sigmat. Output: A reconstructed density field \rho(x) and its analytical gradients \frac{\partial L{out}}{\partial \rho} with respect to the rendered image loss. Data Structures: Density Field: A 3D grid of floating-point values representing \rho(x) at voxel centers, accessed via trilinear interpolation during ray marching. Pre-computed Radiance: A set of radiance values computed for Nd directional samples, stored as view-independent terms to accelerate the inverse pass. Parameters: Learning Rate (\alpha): 0.01 for gradient descent optimization. Directional Samples (Nd): 30, determined as the optimal balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. Iterations: 200 iterations for reconstruction experiments. Scattering Coefficient (\sigmat): Constant, relating optical thickness to density via \kappat(x) = \sigmat \rho(x). Algorithm Steps: 1. Pre-computation: For each of the Nd directional light samples, compute the radiance contribution assuming single scattering and store these terms. This step scales linearly with Nd because radiance is computed for each sample direction independently. 2. Primal Rendering (Forward Pass): For each pixel in each view, cast a ray through the volume, perform ray marching using trilinear interpolation to sample \rho(x), and compute the transmitted radiance using the single-scattering approximation and the pre-computed directional terms. 3. Gradient Computation (Inverse Pass): Compute the loss L between the rendered image L{out} and the reference image, then compute the analytical gradient \frac{\partial L{out}}{\partial \rho} using the differential form of the RTE. The density directly influences optical properties through \kappat(x) = \sigmat \rho(x), allowing the gradient to be expressed analytically. 4. Optimization: Update the density field \rho using gradient descent: \rho{new} = \rho{old} - \alpha \frac{\partial L}{\partial \rho}. Repeat for the specified number of iterations (e.g., 200). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def singlescatteringdifferentiablerendering(referenceimages, volumeresolution, sigmat, numdirectionalsamples=30, learningrate=0.01, numiterations=200): # Initialize density field rho = [[[0.0 for in range(volumeresolution[2])] for in range(volumeresolution[1])] for in range(volumeresolution[0])] # Step 1: Pre-computation of radiance terms # Pre-computation scales linearly with directional samples precomputedradiance = [] for i in range(numdirectionalsamples): direction = computedirection(i, numdirectionalsamples) radiancei = computesinglescatteringradiance(rho, volumeresolution, sigmat, direction) precomputedradiance.append(radiancei) # Step 2 & 3: Optimization Loop for iteration in range(numiterations): totalloss = 0.0 totalgradient = [[[0.0 for in range(volumeresolution[2])] for in range(volumeresolution[1])] for in range(volumeresolution[0])] for viewidx, refimage in enumerate(referenceimages): # Primal Rendering renderedimage = renderview(rho, precomputedradiance, viewidx, volumeresolution, sigmat) # Compute Loss loss = computeloss(renderedimage, refimage) totalloss += loss # Inverse Rendering: Compute Gradient gradient = computegradient(renderedimage, refimage, rho, precomputedradiance, viewidx, volumeresolution, sigmat) for x in range(volumeresolution[0]): for y in range(volumeresolution[1]): for z in range(volumeresolution[2]): totalgradient[x][y][z] += gradient[x][y][z] # Update Density for x in range(volumeresolution[0]): for y in range(volumeresolution[1]): for z in range(volumeresolution[2]): rho[x][y][z] -= learningrate totalgradient[x][y][z] return rho def computedirection(index, total): # Generate uniformly distributed directions angle = index 2.399963229728653 return (math.sin(angle), math.cos(angle), 0.0) def computesinglescatteringradiance(rho, resolution, sigmat, direction): # The sources do not provide the exact physics implementation for single-scattering radiance calculation. return 0.0 def trilinearinterpolate(rho, x, y, z, resolution): # Gradient standard deviations are 0.000269 for this method vs. 0.000175 (FD) and 0.000202 (DRT). Spatial Bias: Reconstruction fidelity is higher in outer volume regions (e.g., z=84) than in inner regions (e.g., z=76) because image-based reconstruction provides stronger constraints for regions directly influencing pixel appearances. Grid Artifacts: Regular patterns may appear due to the discrete voxel representation combined with trilinear interpolation. The gradient scattering process preserves the voxel-grid structure rather than promoting smooth transitions. Flat Density Regions: Optically thin areas may exhibit unnaturally flat density distributions due to insufficient gradient information from the single-scattering model (where multiple scattering would contribute detail) and the under-constrained nature of the inverse problem. Primal Rendering: Scales favorably with resolution; consistently fast (21-28 ms for 256³ resolution) regardless of directional sampling count. Inverse Rendering: Stable time (91-95 ms for 256³ resolution) due to direct gradient computation. Memory: Reasonable usage even for high-resolution volumes (e.g., 2.73 GB for 256³ resolution). Measured Performance: Hardware: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti. Resolution: Experiments conducted at 128³ and 256³ resolutions. Speedup: 6x speedup over DRT for single-view at 512 samples per pixel, and 27x for multi-view. Overall 50-100x speedup compared to DRT. Accuracy: MSE ranges from 3.1 to 8.88 (pixel intensities 0-255). SSIM values are above 0.8 for all views, with some close to 0.95. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: High computational efficiency, enabling interactive reconstruction workflows. Suitable for moderately dense smoke and scenarios prioritizing speed over absolute accuracy. Limitations: Decreased absolute accuracy compared to full multiple-scattering methods. Susceptible to grid artifacts and spatial bias. When to Use: Moderately dense smoke reconstruction. Scenarios prioritizing reconstruction speed over absolute accuracy. Applications where approximate density distributions are sufficient for downstream processing. When Not to Use: Scenarios requiring high-fidelity reconstruction of optically thick or highly scattering media where multiple scattering effects are significant. Applications where grid artifacts are unacceptable. Origin: The method is described in "A High-Efficiency Physics-Based Differentiable Renderer for Smoke Reconstruction". It is based on the differential form of the RTE derived in Section 3.2 of the source. History and Development: The method validates its gradient computation approach against Finite Difference and Differential Ray Tracing. It is compared against Laplacian Projection, a physics-based tomographic reconstruction method. Usage: The method is used for smoke reconstruction using the ScalarFlow dataset. Reconstructed density fields are relit using a standard volumetric path tracker to demonstrate adaptability across diverse lighting conditions. name: Differential Ratio Tracing
head: Differential Ratio Tracking, Mitsuba 3's Differential Ratio Tracing, volpathsimple-drt
body: Differential Ratio Tracing (DRT) is a sampling strategy for estimating gradients of the radiative transfer equation with respect to medium density in differentiable volume rendering. It solves the problem of biased and high-variance gradients produced by standard volumetric free-flight sampling (e.g., delta tracking) by sampling distances proportional to the unweighted transmittance rather than extinction-weighted transmittance. Unlike Single-Scattering Differentiable Volume Rendering, which relies on pre-computed view-independent terms, DRT is a Monte Carlo estimator that must recompute gradients for each view. It is designed for physically-based scattering and absorbing volumes, as opposed to NeRF-style emissive volumes. DRT is an online algorithm that samples a distance t proportional to transmittance T(t) and returns a weight w estimating C = \int0^{ts} T(s) ds, by combining ratio tracking with weighted reservoir sampling to avoid storing all segments. Inputs: t{max}: The maximum distance to sample along the ray (typically the exit distance of the volume or the ray length). \bar{\sigma}: The majorant extinction coefficient, assumed constant for the homogenized medium sampling. \sigmat(t): The function returning the actual extinction coefficient at distance t. rng(): A function returning a uniform random number u \sim U0,1). Outputs: t: The sampled distance, where 0 \le t \le t{max}. w{acc}: The total accumulated weight, an unbiased estimate of the integral of transmittance. Reservoir: A tuple (tr, dr) storing the start distance tr and length dr of the currently selected segment. Initialized as empty or null. Accumulators: Tr: Transmittance estimate, initialized to 1.0. t{run}: Current run distance, initialized to 0.0. w{acc}: Accumulated weight, initialized to 0.0. The method proceeds in a loop until the ray is fully traversed or the maximum distance is reached: 1. Sample Step: Sample a step size dt from the homogenized medium with majorant \bar{\sigma}: dt = -\ln(1 - u) / \bar{\sigma} where u \sim U[0,1). 2. Clamp Step: Clamp dt to the remaining distance: dt = \min(dt, t{max} - t{run}). 3. Calculate Segment Weight: Calculate the weight of the current segment, representing the area under the transmittance curve for this step: w{step} = Tr \cdot dt. 4. Accumulate Weight: Add the segment weight to the total accumulated weight: w{acc} = w{acc} + w{step}. 5. Reservoir Update: Perform weighted reservoir sampling to select a segment proportional to its weight w{step} relative to the total weight w{acc}: Generate a random number u \sim U[0,1). If u \cdot w{acc} < w{step}, update the reservoir to the current segment: \text{reservoir} = (t{run}, dt). Note: The reservoir is updated at least once because w{acc} starts at 0 and the first segment always satisfies the condition if handled correctly (or via a specific first-segment logic implied by "happens at least once" in the source code comment). 6. Update Transmittance Estimate: Update the transmittance estimate for the next step based on the probability of interacting with a real particle: Tr = Tr \cdot \left(1 - \frac{\sigmat(t{run})}{\bar{\sigma}}\right). The tracking function f{RT}(t) is piecewise constant: f{RT}(t) = \prod{ti \leq \min(t, ts)} \left(1 - \frac{\sigmat(ti)}{\bar{\sigma}}\right). 7. Advance Distance: t{run} = t{run} + dt. 8. Loop Termination: Repeat steps 1-7 while t{run} < t{max}. 9. Final Sampling: After the loop, retrieve the selected segment (tr, dr) from the reservoir. Sample the final distance t uniformly within this segment: t = tr + u \cdot dr where u \sim U[0,1). 10. Return: Return the sampled distance t and the total accumulated weight w{acc}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def drtsample(tmax, sigmatfunc, majorantsigma, rng): """ Samples a distance t proportional to transmittance T(t) and returns the accumulated weight wacc estimating the integral of T(t). Args: tmax: Maximum distance along the ray. sigmatfunc: Function returning extinction coefficient sigmat(t). majorantsigma: Majorant extinction coefficient sigmabar. rng: Function returning uniform random number in [0, 1). Returns: t: Sampled distance. wacc: Accumulated weight. """ Tr = 1.0 trun = 0.0 wacc = 0.0 reservoir = None while trun < tmax: # Sample from the homogenized medium dt = -math.log(1.0 - rng()) / majorantsigma dt = min(dt, tmax - trun) # Propose current constant segment with weight equal to area under the curve wstep = Tr dt wacc += wstep # Update reservoir (happens at least once) if reservoir is None or (rng() wacc) < wstep: reservoir = (trun, dt) # Update transmittance estimate sigmatatcurrent = sigmatfunc(trun) Tr = 1.0 - (sigmatatcurrent / majorantsigma) # Advance the run distance trun = trun + dt # Final uniform sampling over the chosen segment tr, dr = reservoir t = tr + rng() dr assert t <= tmax return t, wacc usedrt: A boolean parameter that enables the Differential Ratio Tracking method. If false, the free-flight sampling-based baseline is used. usedrtmis: A boolean parameter that combines the gradients estimated with DRT and the baseline using [Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS). usedrtsubsampling: A boolean parameter that reduces the usage of the DRT sampling method to once per path rather than once at every path vertex, reducing overall runtime from O(n^2) to O(n). Zero Density Regions: Standard free-flight sampling places samples proportional to the product of transmittance and density (extinction-weighted). In empty or low-density regions, this leads to high variance for gradients because samples are rarely placed there, yet gradients may have non-trivial magnitude (e.g., to reconstruct an object where there was previously just air). DRT mitigates this by sampling proportional to just transmittance. Local Minima: Optimization of scattering parameters can get stuck in local minima. This can be alleviated by bootstrapping the optimization from nonphysical emissive volumes (similar to voxel-based radiance fields). Majorant Selection: The majorant \bar{\sigma} must be greater than or equal to the maximum extinction coefficient \sigmat(t) along the ray to ensure valid sampling from the homogenized medium. Time Complexity: Runs in linear time with respect to the number of steps. When integrated with path replay backpropagation, it uses constant memory. However, if usedrtsubsampling is false, the runtime can be O(n^2) where n is the number of path vertices, because DRT is applied at every vertex. With subsampling enabled, it reduces to O(n). Memory Complexity: Constant memory when integrated with path replay backpropagation, as it uses a reservoir to store only one segment. Performance: DRT's Monte Carlo estimation becomes more expensive with higher sample counts (SPP), leading to increasing speedup advantages for pre-computed methods like Single-Scattering Differentiable Volume Rendering at higher SPP. For example, at 512 SPP, the single-scattering method shows a 6.3x speedup over DRT. Strengths: Unbiased, yields low-variance gradients, and handles empty/low-density regions better than standard free-flight sampling. Limitations: Must recompute gradients for each view, unlike pre-computed methods. More expensive than single-scattering methods at high sample counts. When to Use: When using physically-based scattering and absorbing volumes and when gradient variance in low-density regions is a concern. When using Single-Scattering Differentiable Volume Rendering is not feasible due to multiple scattering or complex geometry. When Not to Use: When high sample counts are required and pre-computed methods are applicable, as DRT's cost scales with SPP. When using NeRF-style emissive volumes, as DRT is designed for scattering/absorbing volumes. Differential Ratio Tracing was introduced in the paper "Unbiased inverse volume rendering with differential trackers". It was implemented as a baseline in Mitsuba 3. The method addresses the limitations of standard differentiable volume rendering techniques that use free-flight sampling, which can produce biased and high-variance gradients. It is part of the family of differentiable rendering methods that use automatic differentiation in reverse/adjoint mode [Parent]. name: RAN Training Procedure
head: Pix2Vex training, Reconstruction Adversarial Network training
body: The RAN (Reconstruction Adversarial Network) training procedure is an unsupervised method for reconstructing 3D geometry from 2D images by finding an internal representation that minimizes content-wise changes while translating between image spaces. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Single-Scattering Differentiable Volume Rendering by relying on adversarial learning and cycle-consistency across multiple image domains rather than direct physical scattering models. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sets of 2D images (e.g., from synthetic ShapeNet meshes or camera-captured objects) rendered from multiple viewpoints. Outputs: A reconstructed 3D mesh (internal representation) and associated material/lighting parameters that minimize reconstruction error. Data Structures: Mesh: Defined by vertices and faces. A uniform sphere base model with 162 vertices and 320 faces is used in standard experiments. Image Space: Images are typically 128x128 or 64x64 pixels. Network Modules: Includes image-to-image translators (pix2pix) and a geometry translator (pix2vex). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the network weights. Use Float32 precision. Clamp extreme values for logarithmic and exponential functions to ensure stability. 2. Training Order: If training multiple modules simultaneously, split the training into two steps to avoid mode collapse: Train the module adjacent to the discriminator first (e.g., b \to a). Train the module adjacent to the input second (e.g., a \to b). 3. Loss Calculation: Discriminator Loss: Apply binary cross-entropy loss for the discriminator D. Reconstruction Loss: Apply L1 loss between any two images belonging to the same image space. 4. Weighting: Weight the sub-RANs based on relevance. For example, the path containing the pix2vex module carries more weight than the cycle of two image translators. 5. Iteration: Update weights using gradient descent. Maintain a low learning rate due to competing alternating losses. 6. Duration: Train for 1–3 weeks on a single GTX Titan Xp. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainran(imagesa, imagesb, mesh, discriminator, generatora2b, generatorb2a, generatorpix2vex): # Constants learningrate = 0.0002 # Low rate for stability batchsize = 1 precision = "float32" # Preprocessing: Clamp extreme values for log/exp functions imagesa = clampextremevalues(imagesa) imagesb = clampextremevalues(imagesb) for epoch in range(epochs): for batcha, batchb in zip(imagesa, imagesb): # Step 1: Train discriminator first (or module next to it) # Use binary cross-entropy loss lossd = computebinarycrossentropy(discriminator, batcha, batchb) updateweights(discriminator, lossd) # Step 2: Train generators # Generate fake images fakeb = generatora2b(batcha) fakea = generatorb2a(batcha) reconstructedmesh = generatorpix2vex(batcha) # Compute L1 loss between images of the same space # Cycle consistency: a -> b -> a losscyclea = l1loss(batcha, generatorb2a(fakeb)) # Cycle consistency: b -> a -> b losscycleb = l1loss(batchb, generatora2b(fakea)) # Adversarial loss for generators lossadva = computeadversarialloss(discriminator, fakea) lossadvb = computeadversarialloss(discriminator, fakeb) # Weighted combination of losses # pix2vex path carries more weight than image translator cycle totalloss = ( weightpix2vex computegeometryloss(reconstructedmesh, groundtruthmeshifavailable) + weightcycle (losscyclea + losscycleb) + weightadv (lossadva + lossadvb)) updateweights(generatora2b, totalloss) updateweights(generatorb2a, totalloss) updateweights(generatorpix2vex, totalloss) Parameters: Learning Rate: Must be kept low. Cannot be significantly increased even with huge batch sizes. Precision: Float32. Float16 causes worse instability. Float64 is numerically beneficial but inefficient on most GPUs. Training Duration: 1–3 weeks on a single GTX Titan Xp. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dissociating Vertices: Occurs when processing low-resolution images (64x64) with high mesh resolution (e.g., 642 vertices, 1280 faces), causing sub-pixel faces. Vertices dissociate from the mesh when invisible. This is worse if the smooth visibility test only considers distance to faces instead of directed distance to all edges. Silhouette Loss Instability: Using silhouette losses can drop accuracy because the RAN's internal representation lacks silhouette consistency due to shifts or small scaling factors between images of spaces A and B. Time Complexity: 4 seconds per iteration on a single GTX Titan Xp (batch size 1). 5.2 seconds on two GTX Titan Xp GPUs (batch size 2). 2 minutes per iteration on an i9-7920X CPU @ 2.90GHz with 12 threads. Memory Complexity: ~2GB per image in a batch at 128x128 resolution and 320 faces. Four-view training with batch size 1 requires 6.5GB VRAM. Scaling: Reducing image resolution to 64x64 pixels yields approximately four times faster training and a smaller memory footprint. Strengths: Unsupervised; robust to randomized azimuth, light source position, and class mixing; works on real-world camera-captured images. Limitations: High VRAM usage; slow training time; sensitive to learning rate; prone to vertex dissociation at low resolutions. When to Use: When ground truth 3D models are unavailable and multiple views of an object are accessible. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is required or when silhouette consistency is critical and cannot be handled by the internal representation. The RAN training procedure was introduced in the paper "Pix2Vex: Image-to-Geometry Reconstruction using a Smooth Differentiable Renderer". It was developed to reconstruct 3D geometry from 2D data without requiring ground truth 3D models or prior knowledge of materials and lighting conditions. The method leverages a globally differentiable renderer and adversarial learning to align 2D image spaces with 3D geometry. It has been evaluated on synthetic ShapeNet dataset meshes and camera-captured single-view shoe images. name: Automatic Differentiation for Rendering
head: Autograd-based Differentiable Rendering, Differentiable Rendering via Computational Graphs
body: Automatic Differentiation (AD) for rendering computes the derivatives of interior rendering integrands by applying reverse-mode automatic differentiation directly to the rendering program. It solves the problem of efficiently obtaining gradients for optimization-based inverse rendering by leveraging the fact that discretization commutes with differentiation for smooth interior integrands. Unlike the Adjoint Method, which derives custom adjoint equations for specific rendering paths, AD treats the renderer as a black-box computational graph, allowing the use of existing AD frameworks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A forward rendering program F that maps scene parameters \theta (e.g., material properties, geometry) to pixel values I. Output: The gradient \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta} of a loss function L (typically a function of I) with respect to \theta. Data Structures: The method relies on the computational graph representation provided by the deep learning framework. Forward Tape/Graph: A record of operations performed during the forward pass. Gradient Accumulators: Memory buffers storing partial derivatives \frac{\partial L}{\partial x} for each variable x in the graph. Steps: 1. Forward Pass: Execute the rendering program F(\theta) using tensor operations. 2. Loss Computation: Compute the scalar loss L from the rendered image I. 3. Backward Pass (Reverse AD): Traverse the recorded computational graph in reverse order. For each operation y = f(x), compute the local gradient \frac{\partial y}{\partial x} and propagate the upstream gradient \frac{\partial L}{\partial y} to \frac{\partial L}{\partial x} using the chain rule: \frac{\partial L}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial y} \cdot \frac{\partial y}{\partial x} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Tape: def init(self): self.operations = [] def record(self, backwardfn, inputs, outputs): self.operations.append((backwardfn, inputs, outputs)) def backward(self, upstreamgrad): grad = upstreamgrad for backwardfn, inputs, outputs in reversed(self.operations): grad = backwardfn(grad, inputs, outputs) return grad def renderforward(sceneparams): tape = Tape() # Example forward rendering steps rays = [sceneparams.camera.origin + t sceneparams.camera.direction for t in range(10)] tape.record(lambda g, i, o: [x g for x in i], [sceneparams.camera.direction], [rays]) hits = [ray + 1.0 for ray in rays] tape.record(lambda g, i, o: [x + g for x in i], [rays], [hits]) color = [hit sceneparams.materials.diffuse for hit in hits] tape.record(lambda g, i, o: [x g for x in i], [hits], [color]) return color, tape def computeloss(renderedimage, targetimage): return sum((r - t) 2 for r, t in zip(renderedimage, targetimage)) / len(renderedimage) def optimizescene(sceneparams, targetimage, numiterations): for in range(numiterations): renderedimage, tape = renderforward(sceneparams) loss = computeloss(renderedimage, targetimage) gradloss = 1.0 gradparams = tape.backward(gradloss) sceneparams.update(gradparams) return sceneparams Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Usage: The computational graph for rendering is extremely large (millions of operations) and unstructured. Storing the forward tape for reverse AD can consume excessive memory, leading to out-of-memory errors. Arithmetic Intensity: Rendering operations often have low arithmetic intensity (e.g., many additions, few multiplications). This causes excessive memory traffic when data are repeatedly stored to and read back from memory buffers, making it significantly slower than high-intensity neural network operations. Discontinuities: AD applies to interior integrands where discretization commutes with differentiation. Discontinuities in the rendering integrand (e.g., visibility changes, shadow boundaries) require separate handling, as the derivative is undefined or zero almost everywhere at the discontinuity. The Source Transformation Approach is an automatic differentiation (AD) strategy that converts the source code of a program into its derivative at compile-time, treating differentiation as a one-time compilation step rather than a runtime operation. It solves the problem of runtime overhead and optimization inhibition inherent in tracing-based AD by generating optimized, standalone derivative code. Unlike tracing approaches, it preserves the original control flow, allowing generated programs to function correctly regardless of loop iteration counts or dynamic branching. Dressi-AD is a hardware-agnostic automatic differentiation library for differentiable rendering (DR) built on the Vulkan API. It solves the problem of integrating reverse-mode AD into a graphics pipeline by using 2D images as primitive data structures instead of multi-dimensional tensors, maintaining compatibility with hardware rasterizers. Unlike general-purpose AD libraries that rely on multi-dimensional tensors, Dressi-AD aligns with graphics pipeline constraints and differentiable rendering workflows by utilizing fragment shaders with dummy vertex shaders for computation. Time Complexity: The backward pass is proportional to the forward pass. However, due to low arithmetic intensity, the constant factor is high due to memory bandwidth limitations. Memory Complexity: Requires storing intermediate values from the forward pass for the backward pass. This is a major bottleneck for large scenes. Measured Performance: Implementing rendering pipelines directly in frameworks like PyTorch or TensorFlow is extremely inefficient compared to specialized AD compilers or adjoint methods due to the unstructured nature of rendering graphs and the overhead of tensor management. Strengths: Easy to implement if the rendering primitives are already differentiable; leverages existing AD infrastructure; no need to manually derive adjoint equations. Limitations: High memory consumption; poor performance on GPUs due to low arithmetic intensity. When to Use: Suitable for small-scale differentiable rendering tasks or when rapid prototyping is prioritized over performance. Not recommended for production-scale inverse rendering with large scenes. The technique is based on the principle that for interior rendering integrands, discretization commutes with differentiation, allowing standard automatic differentiation techniques to be applied directly to the rendering program. Widely used deep learning frameworks such as PyTorch and TensorFlow provide built-in automatic differentiation interfaces. However, these frameworks were designed for linear algebra and neural networks, which have high arithmetic intensity and structured graphs, unlike rendering algorithms which produce large, unstructured graphs with low arithmetic intensity. This mismatch necessitates specialized AD compilers for efficient differentiable rendering. Physics-based differentiable rendering, https://doi.org/10.1145/3388769.3407454, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Source Transformation Approach
head: Enzyme, Stalin∇, Static compilation approach, Tapenade
body: The Source Transformation Approach is an automatic differentiation (AD) strategy that converts the source code of a program into its derivative at compile-time, treating differentiation as a one-time compilation step rather than a runtime operation. It solves the problem of runtime overhead and optimization inhibition inherent in tracing-based AD by generating optimized, standalone derivative code. Unlike tracing approaches, it preserves the original control flow, allowing generated programs to function correctly regardless of loop iteration counts or dynamic branching. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Source code of a primal program (e.g., C, Fortran, Julia, or LLVM IR) and a specification of the differentiation mode (Forward/JVP or Reverse/VJP). Output: Source code of the derivative program (JVP or VJP). Data Structures: Control Flow Graph (CFG): Used for activity analysis to determine which variables require derivative computation. Stack: Required in Reverse-mode (VJP) for loops to store intermediate primal states for later consumption during the backward pass. Steps: 1. Parse and Analyze: The tool parses the source code into an intermediate representation (IR) or abstract syntax tree. 2. Activity Analysis: To avoid unnecessary adjoint evaluations for variables that do not affect the final gradient, the tool performs a data-flow analysis. This analysis conservatively propagates "derivative liveness" through the control flow graph until a fixed point is reached. 3. Transformation: The source code is transformed into derivative code. Forward Mode (JVP): Each primal operation is paired with its derivative operation. Reverse Mode (VJP): The code is traversed to generate a backward pass. For loops, the forward pass records intermediate states into a stack, and a reversed loop consumes this stack to compute gradients. 4. Optimization: The generated code is optimized by the underlying compiler (e.g., LLVM). Pseudocode (VJP for Integer Power): The following Python-like pseudocode illustrates the VJP generation for an integer power function pow(x, n), as generated by tools like Tapenade. Note that this requires a stack to store intermediate states for the reverse loop. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def powvjp(x: float, n: int, dy: float): """ Computes the gradient of pow(x, n) with respect to x. x: primal input n: integer exponent (constant for differentiation purposes) dy: upstream gradient (d/dy of loss w.r.t output) Returns: dx, the gradient of the loss w.r.t x """ y = 1.0 dx = 0.0 stack = [] # Forward pass: record intermediate states for i in range(n): stack.append(y) y = y x # Reverse pass: consume stack to compute gradients for i in reversed(range(n)): y = stack.pop() # Chain rule: dx += (doutput/dycurrent) y # Here, doutput/dycurrent is dy (accumulated from downstream) # The local derivative of ynew = yold x w.r.t x is yold dx = dx + y dy # Update dy for the previous step: dloss/dyold = dloss/dynew x dy = dy x return dx Parameters: Differentiation Mode: Forward (JVP) or Reverse (VJP). Target Language/IR: C, Fortran, Julia, or LLVM IR. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Loops in Reverse Mode: Loops require two passes: one to record state and one to reverse it. This poses difficulties for massively parallel architectures like GPUs because stack or shadow memory must be provisioned for all threads running in parallel, handling worst-case requirements. Complex Control Flow: While source transformation preserves control flow, handling recursion and complex dynamic branching can be difficult to implement correctly. Subset of Language: The approach usually can only handle a subset of a general-purpose language, as the transformation must be statically analyzable. Performance: Generally offers better performance than tracing approaches because the derivative code is compiled once and optimized statically. Tracing approaches re-compile derivatives on every function evaluation, causing overhead. Implementation Complexity: Much more difficult to implement than tracing approaches. Language Support: Usually handles only a subset of a general-purpose language, as it requires static analysis capabilities. Control Flow: Preserves control flow, allowing generated programs to work regardless of loop iteration counts, unlike unrolled traces. Memory: Reverse-mode implementations may require significant memory for stack provisioning in parallel architectures (e.g., GPUs) due to the need to store intermediate states for all threads. The Source Transformation Approach is one of the two main ends of the spectrum for automatic differentiation, the other being the Tracing/Taping approach. Notable implementations include Tapenade [Hascoet and Pascual 2013], Stalin∇ [Pearlmutter and Siskind 2008], Zygote [Innes 2019], and Enzyme [Moses and Churavy 2020; Moses et al. 2021]. TensorFlow 1.0 is cited as a popular example of this approach in the context of machine learning frameworks. name: Dressi-AD
head: Vulkan-Based AD Library for DR
body: Dressi-AD is a hardware-agnostic automatic differentiation library for differentiable rendering (DR) built on the Vulkan API. It solves the problem of integrating reverse-mode AD into a graphics pipeline by using 2D images as primitive data structures instead of multi-dimensional tensors, maintaining compatibility with hardware rasterizers. Unlike general-purpose AD libraries that rely on multi-dimensional tensors, Dressi-AD aligns with graphics pipeline constraints and differentiable rendering workflows by utilizing fragment shaders with dummy vertex shaders for computation. Inputs and Outputs: Developers write mathematical problems using provided APIs. The system outputs a computational graph executed on GPUs. Data Structures: Variable Objects: Represent inputs and outputs of functions. They are converted into VkImage structures. VkImage handles 2D arrays and can store textures, vertex buffers, blend weight matrices, or higher-dimensional tensors represented as stacked 2D arrays. Function Objects: Each forward function object contains a GLSL representation compatible with a fragment shader and includes a method to generate corresponding backward function objects. Numbered Steps: 1. Instantiation: Developers write mathematical problems using provided APIs. Dressi-AD instantiates forward function objects and variable objects. 2. Graph Construction: The system builds a computational graph from the instantiated objects. 3. GLSL Code Generation: Forward function objects are converted into GLSL code. This generation step roughly follows the approach used in TensorFlow.js. 4. Backward Function Generation: Each forward function object generates its corresponding backward function object. 5. Stage Packing: A Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation technique maps multiple subpasses to a render pass. Shader codes on the computational graph are automatically packed into optimal GPU execution units, considering hardware constraints. A reactive cache is integrated to skip redundant computation. 6. Execution: The graph is executed on GPUs using a define-and-run scheme. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Some differentiable rendering function objects cannot be defined using built-in GLSL functions, requiring custom backward implementations (e.g., texture sampling). Standard hardware texture samplers (texture()) do not support automatic differentiation, necessitating the Inverse UV backward function. Fragment shaders with dummy vertex shaders are preferred for computation. Vertex shaders are avoided because they cannot export intermediate variables, and compute shaders are avoided because they are not well optimized for graphics purposes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Variable: def init(self, data): # Convert data into VkImage structure (2D array handling) self.vkimage = data class ForwardFunction: def init(self, glslcode): self.glslcode = glslcode self.backwardfunc = None def generatebackward(self): # Generate corresponding backward function object # For texture sampling, returns InverseUV backward function return BackwardFunction(self.glslcode, mode="backward") class BackwardFunction: def init(self, glslcode, mode="backward"): self.glslcode = glslcode self.mode = mode class DressiAD: def init(self): self.computationalgraph = [] def define(self, userprogram): # Instantiate function and variable objects from user APIs variables = [] functions = [] for operation in userprogram.operations: if operation.type == 'forward': func = ForwardFunction(glslcode=operation.glslrepresentation) functions.append(func) func.backwardfunc = func.generatebackward() elif operation.type == 'variable': var = Variable(data=operation.data) variables.append(var) self.computationalgraph = (variables, functions) def stagepack(self): # JIT compilation technique mapping multiple subpasses to a render pass # Pack shader codes into optimal GPU execution units considering hardware constraints # Integrate reactive cache to skip redundant computation packedstages = [] for var, funcs in self.computationalgraph: for func in funcs: packedstages.append({ 'forward': func.glslcode, 'backward': func.backwardfunc.glslcode }) return packedstages def execute(self): # Execute on GPU using Vulkan define-and-run scheme # Use fragment shaders with dummy vertex shaders packedstages = self.stagepack() for stage in packedstages: # Forward pass: compile and dispatch fragment shader with dummy vertex shader # Backward pass: compile and dispatch generated backward fragment shader # Reactive cache checks skip redundant computation if outputs unchanged # Exact Vulkan dispatch logic is hardware-specific and not detailed in sources. pass Hardware Support: Supports NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, Arm, and other hardware via the Vulkan API. Performance: Uses low-level Vulkan APIs to increase rendering speed compared to more abstract APIs like OpenGL. Optimization: Includes a reactive cache to skip redundant computation. Limitations: Relies on the graphics pipeline, which imposes limitations compared to general-purpose compute shaders. Some operations require custom backward implementations because they cannot be defined using built-in GLSL functions. Dressi-AD was proposed as part of the Dressi renderer system. The design choices were motivated by the limitations of other graphics APIs: OpenGL is too abstract to exploit modern hardware performance, and OpenCL/compute shaders may not be well-supported on mobile devices or lack correspondence to Vulkan’s subpasses. The system was published in 2022. Dressi: A Hardware‐Agnostic Differentiable Renderer with Reactive Shader Packing and Soft Rasterization, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14455, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Custom Adjoint Interface
head: dr.CustomOp
body: The Custom Adjoint Interface is a mechanism in differentiable programming systems that allows users to define custom forward and reverse-mode derivatives for functions, extending standard automatic differentiation (AD) by tracking implicit inputs and outputs (dependencies on global state) in addition to explicit function arguments and return values. It sets itself apart from standard AD interfaces by explicitly monitoring variable accesses during primal evaluation to automatically register implicit dependencies, ensuring correct gradient flow for operations involving global state such as scene parameters or texture lookups. Inputs include explicit function arguments (tensors/arrays) and implicit dependencies (global state accessed during execution). Outputs include explicit return values and implicit updates to global state, such as scene parameter gradients. The core data structure is the dr.CustomOp interface, which encapsulates a forward callback that computes the primal output from primal inputs, a backward callback that computes input derivatives from output derivatives or vice versa, and an implicit dependency tracker that monitors variable accesses during primal evaluation to automatically register implicit variable dependences with the AD system. 1. Registration: The user defines a dr.CustomOp subclass implementing the forward and backward callbacks. 2. Primal Execution: When the function is called, the primal computation runs while the AD system monitors variable accesses to detect implicit dependencies on global state. 3. Implicit Dependency Registration: Any variable accessed during the primal execution that is not an explicit argument is registered as an implicit input or output, ensuring the global flow of derivatives is correctly represented. 4. Backward Invocation: When dr.backward() is called, the AD system traverses the computational tape and invokes the backward() callback upon encountering a CustomOp. 5. Gradient Propagation: The backward() callback converts output derivatives into input derivatives, and for methods with implicit reads, the system issues atomic scatter-reductions to update scene parameter gradients. The following pseudocode illustrates the structure of a dr.CustomOp and its usage in Dr.Jit. It assumes a standard AD framework with gradient tracking and backward propagation operations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class MyCustomOp: def forward(self, x, y): result = x y return result def backward(self, gradout, x, y): gradx = gradout y grady = gradout x return gradx, grady x = [1.0, 2.0] y = [3.0, 4.0] op = MyCustomOp() result = op.forward(x, y) resultgrad = [1.0, 1.0] gradx, grady = op.backward(resultgrad, x, y) Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. Implicit reads of global state (e.g., scene parameters) require atomic scatter-reductions to update gradients during reverse-mode differentiation. Differentiating polymorphic method calls requires dynamic generation of Vector-Jacobian Product (VJP) functions, wrapped in a dr.CustomOp. If a return value does not carry derivatives, the system devirtualizes the zero-valued derivative and propagates zero-valued input derivatives to simplify call targets using constant propagation. Precision and boundary conditions are not discussed in the sources. GradBlock (also known as AD Tape Surgery) is a technique to attach derivative tracking to specific factors within an expression without recomputing the entire primal value, avoiding unnecessary extra computation in both primal and adjoint programs. It solves the problem of efficiently differentiating parts of a computation graph that were originally computed with detached or non-differentiable operations (e.g., GPU texture lookups or importance sampling strategies). It sets itself apart from naive substitution methods by combining the primal value of one variable with the AD trace of another, thereby bypassing redundant forward and backward passes. A technique to differentiate polymorphic method calls by dynamically generating Vector-Jacobian Product (VJP) functions for each method, wrapped in a dr.CustomOp. It sets itself apart by handling dynamic dispatch in differentiable code, allowing polymorphic calls to be differentiated without static knowledge of all possible targets. It is chosen when differentiating code with dynamic method resolution (e.g., obj.func() where obj is an array of instances). 1. Wrap the polymorphic method call (e.g., out = obj.func(arg1, arg2, arg3)) into a dynamically generated dr.CustomOp. 2. When CustomOp.backward() is invoked, dynamically define a VJP per method as a placeholder that calls the original function a second time with recursive AD usage. 3. Issue a polymorphic method call to the newly defined VJP functions. 4. The JIT layer traces each possible target, running all VJP placeholder functions to materialize the differentiation into ordinary traced computation. 5. If a return value does not carry derivatives, devirtualize the zero-valued derivative and propagate zero-valued input derivatives to simplify call targets using constant propagation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def funcvjp(gradout, arg1, arg2, arg3): arg1.requiresgrad = True arg2.requiresgrad = True arg3.requiresgrad = True result = func(arg1, arg2, arg3) result.grad = gradout result.backward() return arg1.grad, arg2.grad, arg3.grad This VJP function is dynamically generated for each method in the polymorphic call. Time complexity depends on the complexity of the forward and backward callbacks, with dynamic VJP generation for polymorphism adding overhead during JIT tracing but simplifying execution via constant propagation for zero-valued derivatives. Memory complexity requires storing the computational graph and intermediate values for reverse-mode AD. Strengths include correctly handling global state and implicit dependencies, which is crucial for differentiable rendering with scene parameters, and supporting polymorphism through dynamic VJP generation. Limitations require careful implementation of forward and backward callbacks to avoid incorrect gradient flow. It is used when differentiating functions with global state dependencies or polymorphic calls that standard AD systems cannot handle efficiently. The Custom Adjoint Interface is part of the Dr.Jit differentiable rendering framework, introduced in the paper "Dr.Jit: A Just-In-Time Compiler for Differentiable Rendering". It addresses the limitations of standard AD systems in handling implicit dependencies and polymorphism, which are common in rendering code. name: GradBlock with Automatic Differentiation
head: AD Tape Surgery, GradBlock
body: GradBlock (also known as AD Tape Surgery) is a technique to attach derivative tracking to specific factors within an expression without recomputing the entire primal value, avoiding unnecessary extra computation in both primal and adjoint programs. It solves the problem of efficiently differentiating parts of a computation graph that were originally computed with detached or non-differentiable operations, such as GPU texture mapping unit (TMU) lookups or importance sampling strategies. It sets itself apart from naive substitution methods by combining the primal value of one variable with the AD trace of another, thereby bypassing redundant forward and backward passes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two variables, a (primal value) and b (differential value/trace). Output: A new variable that carries the primal value of a but is linked to the AD tape via b. Data Structures: The implementation relies on the underlying AD tape structure of the framework. The function dr.replacegrad manipulates the tape to replace the dependency of a node on its original parent with a dependency on b, while retaining the computed value of a. Steps: 1. Compute the primal value a and a differentiable counterpart b that holds the same numerical value. 2. Call dr.replacegrad(a, b) to combine the primal value of a with the AD trace of b. 3. Use the resulting variable in subsequent computations to enable gradient flow through b without recomputing a. Formulas: The operation can be conceptually described as: c = \text{dr.replace\grad}(a, b) Where: val(c) = val(a) Gradients flow back through the tape associated with b. In the context of rescaling gradients (e.g., for BSDF values), the sources show usage like: Lr \leftarrow Lr \times \text{dr.replace\grad}\left(1, \frac{\text{bsdf\value\diff}}{\text{bsdf\value}}\right) Here, \text{bsdf\value} and \text{bsdf\value\diff} have the same value, but \text{bsdf\value\diff} is attached to the AD graph. Parameters: a: The primal value variable. b: The variable with the desired AD trace. Pitfalls: Naively changing a factor in the expression (e.g., Lr = bsdfvaluediff / bsdfvalue) introduces unnecessary extra computation in both primal and adjoint programs. Precision issues may arise if \text{bsdf\value} is near zero when dividing. The method assumes the framework supports tape manipulation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applygradblockexample(): # Primal value computed once bsdfvalue = 0.5 # Example primal value # Differentiable counterpart with same value bsdfvaluediff = bsdfvalue.clone().requiresgrad(True) # Efficient approach: attach AD trace of bsdfvaluediff to primal 1 # This avoids recomputing bsdfvalue in the adjoint pass Lr = Lr replacegrad(1, bsdfvaluediff / bsdfvalue) # Example: GPU texture lookup to differentiable software lookup # Standard array lookup simulating hardware TMU behavior texval = texturearray[texcoords] # Differentiable software interpolation softval = softwareinterpolate(texturearray, texcoords) # Combine primal value of texval with AD trace of softval difftexval = replacegrad(texval, softval) return difftexval def replacegrad(a, b): # Returns a tensor with the value of a, but gradients flow through b # Implementation detail: attaches the AD tape of b to the value of a result = a.detach().clone() result.requiresgrad(True) # In a real AD framework, this manipulates the tape to link result to b return result A mechanism to restrain the process of derivative propagation. Only edges within and just across the isolation boundary may be traversed; others are postponed until the scope is destructed. Used to ensure correct generation of a differential megakernel embedded within a larger differential calculation. Time Complexity: Avoids recomputing the primal value, thus saving forward pass time. Performance: Benchmarks show reduced time overhead compared to naive substitution. For example, in the "Staircase" scene, it contributed to a 0.71× speedup in kernel execution time compared to a baseline. Strengths: Efficiently enables differentiation of detached operations without redundant computation. Limitations: Requires framework support for tape manipulation. Not applicable to operations that cannot be represented in the AD tape. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The technique originates from the Dr.Jit paper. It is used in differentiable rendering to handle cases where importance sampling or texture lookups are not naturally differentiable. The technique allows for the generation of nonzero derivatives in scenarios like reflected radiance calculations with detached BSDF sampling strategies.
