It is designed to stabilize gradient-based optimization in volume rendering or rasterization-based novel view synthesis by ensuring that the rendering integrand is sufficiently smooth to allow Leibniz's rule to exchange differentiation and integration. newDINO/voxelraydemo, https://github.com/newDINO/voxelraydemo, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) yzslab/gaussian-splatting-lightning, https://github.com/yzslab/gaussian-splatting-lightning, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: À-trous Cross-Bilateral Filtering
head: Cross-Bilateral Filter, spatiotemporal gradient filtering
body:
À-trous cross-bilateral filtering is a spatial filtering technique applied to gradients and their associated first and second moment buffers in inverse rendering, implemented as a sequence of à-trous filters to enable fast optimization on regular 2D or 3D grids. It differs from standard bilateral filters by using parameter values 	heta rather than gradient values for the data term, which prevents over-smoothing across edges while leveraging the lower noise and dynamic range of parameters. Unlike Smooth Gradient Estimation via Convolution which uses fixed convolution kernels, this method adapts weights based on parameter similarity, and unlike Non-local Approximated Gradients which approximates gradients via differential filters, it explicitly smooths the optimization state variables. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Gradient 
abla	heta ft at iteration t, first moment buffer mt, second moment buffer vt, parameter values 	heta, and hyperparameters F, \sigmas, \sigmad,  eta1,  eta2. Output: Filtered gradient \widetilde{
abla	heta ft}, filtered moments 	ilde{m}t, 	ilde{v}t. Data Structures: 	heta, mt, vt, 
abla	heta ft: Stored on regular 2D or 3D grids. Grid dimensions depend on the scene (e.g., 512^2 for 2D texture, 64^3 for 3D volume). Formulas: The cross-bilateral filter for a function h is defined as: 	ilde{h}(x) =  rac{1}{z(x)} \int{\Omega} h(y) ws(x,y) wd(	heta(y),	heta(x)) dy where: \Omega is the spatial domain. ws(x,y) = \exp(-||x-y||/\sigmas) is the spatial isotropic low-pass filter weight. wd(	hetax,	hetay) = \exp(-||	hetax-	hetay||/\sigmad) is the data term weight. z(x) = \int{\Omega} ws(x,y) wd(	heta(y),	heta(x)) dy is the normalization term. \sigmas controls the scale of the spatial weight. \sigmad controls the scale of the data weight. Parameters: F: Number of à-trous filters in the sequence. Typical values: F=5 for texture recovery, F=3 for volume recovery and Laplacian smoothing. \sigmad: Data term scale. Typical values: 0.1 for texture recovery, 0.001 for albedo ho, and 0.2 for density \sigmat in volume recovery.  eta1: Temporal filtering coefficient for mt. Typical value: 0.2. Range: (0.2, 0.5).  eta2: Temporal filtering coefficient for vt. Set such that 1- eta1 = 1- eta2. \alpha: Learning rate. Typical values: 0.1 (non-Adam), 0.01 (Adam) for texture; 0.008 (Adam), 0.02 (others) for volume. Algorithm Steps: 1. Temporal Update: Update first and second moment buffers using exponential moving averages: mt =  eta1 m{t-1} + (1- eta1) 
abla	heta ft vt =  eta2 v{t-1} + (1- eta2) (
abla	heta ft)^2 Note: The source specifies  eta2 is set satisfying 1- eta1=1- eta2, implying  eta1 =  eta2. 2. Spatial Filtering (Pre-filtering): Apply a sequence of F à-trous cross-bilateral filters to the gradient 
abla	heta ft. At each step k \in \{1, \dots, F\}, use a dilated filter kernel. For 2D: Use a dilated 3 	imes 3 filter. For 3D: Use a dilated 3 	imes 3 	imes 3 filter. The dilation factor increases with each step to expand the support while keeping the number of non-zero elements fixed. The spatial standard deviation \sigmas is indirectly specified by F. 3. Spatial Filtering (Post-filtering): Apply the same cross-bilateral filter (same parameters 	heta, \sigmas, \sigmad) to both the first moment buffer mt and the second moment buffer vt. This ensures the ratio |	ilde{m}t|/	ilde{v}t < 1 is bounded, preventing instability. 4. Parameter Update: Compute the update step using the filtered moments and learning rate \alpha: 	heta{new} = 	heta{old} - \alpha  rac{	ilde{m}t}{\sqrt{	ilde{v}t} + \epsilon} Note: Standard Adam epsilon is assumed if not specified, though the source emphasizes the bounded ratio property. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def atrouscrossbilateralfilter(h, theta, sigmas, sigmad, F): """ Applies F steps of à-trous cross-bilateral filtering to h. h: array of values to filter (gradient or moment) theta: array of parameter values (used for data term) sigmas: spatial scale sigmad: data scale F: number of filter passes """ currenth = h for step in range(F): # Determine dilation for current step # Standard à-trous dilation: 1, 2, 4, 8,... dilation = 2 step # Initialize output array filteredh = zeroslike(currenth) normalization = zeroslike(currenth) # Define kernel offsets based on dilation # For 2D: offsets = [(-d, -d), (-d, 0), (-d, d), (0, -d), (0, 0), (0, d), (d, -d), (d, 0), (d, d)] # For 3D: 3x3x3 grid with stride dilation offsets = getkerneloffsets(dilation, dimension=currenth.ndim) for dx, dy, dz in offsets: # Sample neighbor coordinates with boundary handling (e.g., clamp or reflect) ycoords = shiftcoordinates(currenth.shape, (dx, dy, dz), dilation) # Compute spatial weight dist = computedistance(currenth.shape, (dx, dy, dz), dilation) ws = exp(-dist / sigmas) # Compute data weight using parameter values thetay = sampleat(currenth, ycoords) # Sample theta at neighbor location thetax = currenth # Current location theta (assuming theta is aligned with h's grid) # Note: In implementation, theta is a separate buffer. # wd depends on theta(y) and theta(x). wd = exp(-abs(thetay - theta) / sigmad) # Accumulate weighted sum and normalization hy = sampleat(currenth, ycoords) filteredh += hy ws wd normalization += ws wd # Normalize currenth = filteredh / (normalization + 1e-8) return currenth def updateparameters(theta, grad, m, v, alpha, beta1, beta2, sigmas, sigmad, F): """ Performs one step of optimization using à-trous cross-bilateral filtering. """ # 1. Temporal Update m = beta1 m + (1 - beta1) grad v = beta2 v + (1 - beta2) (grad 2) # 2. Spatial Filtering of Gradient filteredgrad = atrouscrossbilateralfilter(grad, theta, sigmas, sigmad, F) # 3. Spatial Filtering of Moments (Post-filtering) # Must use same theta, sigmas, sigmad filteredm = atrouscrossbilateralfilter(m, theta, sigmas, sigmad, F) filteredv = atrouscrossbilateralfilter(v, theta, sigmas, sigmad, F) # 4. Parameter Update # Bounded step size ensured by filtering both m and v with same weights update = alpha filteredm / (sqrt(filteredv) + 1e-8) theta = theta - update return theta, m, v Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Filtering only one of mt or vt violates the bound |	ilde{m}t|/	ilde{v}t < 1, resulting in much larger step sizes that significantly worsen recovery. Using different parameters 	heta for the data term in different filtering operations significantly degrades recovery and causes instability. Lower values of  eta1,  eta2 reduce temporal bias but increase noise; higher values increase bias and slow convergence. This method implements the cross-bilateral filter on regular 2D or 3D grids to enable real-time spatial filtering of gradients and associated buffers in inverse rendering. It differs from standard bilateral filters by decomposing the operation into a series of à-trous filters, which allows for fast optimization with a fixed number of non-zero elements per filter pass. It builds on À-trous Cross-Bilateral Filtering. A configuration where temporal filtering is turned off by setting  eta1 =  eta2 = 0, making the optimizer memoryless and eliminating the need to maintain buffers mt and vt. This results in a 2/3rd reduction in memory usage compared to methods maintaining these buffers. Unlike Adam which makes constant sized steps, purely spatial filtering allows postfiltering to dynamically adjust learning rates, resulting in faster convergence. Time Complexity: The method introduces little overhead (<4%) for both 2D and 3D filtering compared to standard optimizers, as the à-trous decomposition allows fixed-size kernels with increasing dilation. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for gradients, first moment mt, and second moment vt, same as Adam. Purely spatial variant reduces memory by 2/3. Performance: Tested on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 GPU using Mitsuba 3 and PyTorch with custom CUDA kernels. Strengths: Recovers fine details better than Laplacian smoothing and standard bilateral filtering; less noisy than Adam in texture recovery; bounded step sizes prevent instability. Limitations: Requires tuning of \sigmad and F per application (texture vs. volume); sensitive to violating the constraint of using the same 	heta for data terms. When to use: Inverse rendering of textures and volumes where gradient noise is high and edge preservation is critical. When not to use: When memory is extremely constrained and purely spatial filtering is insufficient, or when the parameter space does not have clear discontinuities that benefit from cross-bilateral weighting. Originated in the work on spatiotemporal bilateral gradient filtering for inverse rendering. The method builds on the cross-bilateral filter concept introduced by Eisemann and Durand [2004] and Petschnigg et al. [2004], adapting it for gradient preconditioning in optimization. It was specifically designed to address the noise in gradients during inverse rendering, leveraging the fact that parameter values are less noisy and have a lower dynamic range than gradients. Spatiotemporal Bilateral Gradient Filtering for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1145/3680528.3687606, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Grid-based Implementation of Cross-Bilateral Filter
head: Cross-Bilateral Filter
body: This method implements the cross-bilateral filter on regular 2D or 3D grids to enable real-time spatial filtering of gradients and associated buffers in inverse rendering. It differs from standard bilateral filters by decomposing the operation into a series of à-trous filters, which allows for fast optimization with a fixed number of non-zero elements per filter pass. It builds on À-trous Cross-Bilateral Filtering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Gradient \nabla\theta ft and associated buffers mt, vt defined on a regular 2D or 3D grid. Output: Filtered gradient and buffers. Data Structures: The data is stored on a regular grid matching the spatial resolution of the rendered views or volume. The grid layout follows standard row-major or column-major memory ordering. Steps: 1. Initialize the gradient \nabla\theta ft and buffers mt, vt on the grid. 2. Apply a sequence of à-trous cross-bilateral filters. 3. Each filter in the sequence uses an increasing spatial support but maintains a fixed number of non-zero elements per pass. 4. The filtering follows the implementation strategy of Dammertz et al.. Formulas: The filter computes a weighted average over neighbors at the current à-trous stride 2^k. The cross-bilateral weight between cell i and neighbor j is w{ij} = \exp(-\|pi - pj\|^2 / 2\sigmas^2) \cdot \exp(-\|bi - bj\|^2 / 2\sigmac^2), where p denotes spatial coordinates, b denotes the buffer value used for guidance, and \sigmas, \sigmac are spatial and cross-bilateral standard deviations. The filtered value at i is \hat{v}i = \frac{\sumj w{ij} vj}{\sumj w{ij}}. Parameters: Number of filter passes: Not given in the sources. Support size: Increases with each pass. Number of non-zero elements: Fixed per filter pass. \sigmas, \sigmac: Standard deviations for spatial and cross-bilateral terms. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Accumulators should use double precision to avoid normalization artifacts. Boundaries: Neighbors outside the grid are clamped or mirrored to prevent boundary bias. Degenerate input: Zero denominators in normalization are guarded with a small epsilon. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def gridbasedcrossbilateralfilter(gridgradient, gridbuffers, numpasses, supportradii, sigmas, sigmac): """ Applies a series of à-trous cross-bilateral filters to grid data. Args: gridgradient: 2D or 3D array of gradients. gridbuffers: 2D or 3D array of buffers (mt, vt). numpasses: Number of filter passes. supportradii: List of spatial support radii (strides) for each pass. sigmas: Spatial standard deviation. sigmac: Cross-bilateral standard deviation. Returns: Filtered gradient and buffers. """ filteredgradient = gridgradient.copy() filteredbuffers = gridbuffers.copy() for k in range(numpasses): stride = supportradii[k] accgrad = np.zeroslike(filteredgradient) accbuf = np.zeroslike(filteredbuffers) accweight = np.zeroslike(filteredgradient) for i in np.ndindex(filteredgradient.shape): spatialdistsq = 0.0 featurediffsq = 0.0 w = 0.0 # Accumulate contributions from neighbors at current stride for di in range(-stride, stride + 1, stride): for dj in range(-stride, stride + 1, stride): # Handle 3D case by extending loop or using ndenumerate ni = i[0] + di nj = i[1] + dj if len(i) > 2: dk = i[2] nk = ni + dk # Simplified for 2D/3D generalization else: nk = 0 if 0 <= ni < filteredgradient.shape[0] and 0 <= nj < filteredgradient.shape[1]: spatialdistsq = di2 + dj2 featurediffsq = (filteredbuffers[ni, nj] - filteredbuffers[i])2 w = np.exp(-spatialdistsq / (2 sigmas2)) np.exp(-featurediffsq / (2 sigmac2)) accgrad[i] += w filteredgradient[ni, nj] accbuf[i] += w filteredbuffers[ni, nj] accweight[i] += w # Normalize with guard accweight = np.maximum(accweight, 1e-8) filteredgradient[i] = accgrad[i] / accweight[i] filteredbuffers[i] = accbuf[i] / accweight[i] return filteredgradient, filteredbuffers The Bilateral Grid constructs a sparse 5D grid in spatial-luminance-chrominance space to facilitate efficient bilateral filtering via splatting and slicing. It differs from standard bilateral filters by discretizing the feature space into a grid, allowing the filter to be implemented as a sequence of sparse matrix-vector multiplications, which is significantly faster for large kernels. It builds on the Grid-based Implementation of Cross-Bilateral Filter [13144-grid-based-implementation-of-cross-bilateral-filter.md]. Computes diagonal matrices Dn and Dm to bistochastize a bilateral grid, ensuring row and column sums are equal. 1. Initialize m = \text{grid.splat}(\text{np.ones}(\text{grid.npixels})) and n = \text{np.ones}(\text{grid.nvertices}). 2. Iterate \text{maxiter} times: n = \sqrt{n \cdot m / (\text{grid.blur}(n) + 10^{-10})}. 3. Correct m: m = n \cdot \text{grid.blur}(n). 4. Create diagonal matrices Dn = \text{diags}(n, 0) and Dm = \text{diags}(m, 0). A filtering algorithm to remove invalid color values produced by the bilateral solver in isolated patches ('edge islands') within the masked region, preventing them from being used for supervision. 1. Dilate the reference mask Mr with kernel size 5 to obtain the dilated mask M{r{\text{dilated}}}. 2. Find the maximum absolute residual value inside M{r{\text{dilated}}} and outside Mr: res{\max,t} = \max |rest| over M{r{\text{dilated}}} \cap (1 - Mr). 3. Define a mask for out-of-distribution values for view t, M{r,t}^{ei}, as pixels in Mr with absolute values higher than res{\max,t} \times c{ei}, where c{ei} \ge 1 is the filtering threshold. 4. The edge island mask is the union of out-of-distribution masks across all target views: Mr^{ei} = \bigcupt M{r,t}^{ei}. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method enables real-time performance and faster optimization with low sample budgets. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Fast optimization, real-time performance, low sample budgets. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Inverse rendering applications requiring fast spatial filtering of gradients and buffers. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in "Spatiotemporal Bilateral Gradient Filtering for Inverse Rendering". It leverages previous work in real-time denoising. Spatiotemporal Bilateral Gradient Filtering for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1145/3680528.3687606, fetched 2026-10-29 weiyithu/NerfingMVS, https://github.com/weiyithu/NerfingMVS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Reference-guided Controllable Inpainting of Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/ICCV51070.2023.01633, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Bilateral Grid
head: Bilateral Space Grid
body: The Bilateral Grid constructs a sparse 5D grid in spatial-luminance-chrominance space to facilitate efficient bilateral filtering via splatting and slicing. It differs from standard bilateral filters by discretizing the feature space into a grid, allowing the filter to be implemented as a sequence of sparse matrix-vector multiplications, which decouples kernel size from spatial resolution. It builds on the Grid-based Implementation of Cross-Bilateral Filter [13144-grid-based-implementation-of-cross-bilateral-filter.md]. Inputs: An input image I (RGB), spatial sigma \sigmas, luma sigma \sigmal, and chroma sigma \sigmac. Outputs: A filtered image I{\text{out}}. Data Structures: 1. Grid Coordinates: A set of 5D coordinates for each pixel, computed from spatial position and YUV color values. 2. Splat Matrix (S): A sparse matrix mapping pixel values to grid vertices. 3. Blur Matrices (Bd): Sparse matrices representing 1D connections along each grid dimension. Steps: 1. Color Conversion: Convert the input RGB image I to YUV color space. I{\text{yuv}} = \text{rgb2yuv}(I) Let Y be the luma channel and U, V be the chroma channels. 2. Coordinate Computation: Compute 5D coordinates for each pixel (x, y) in the image grid. Spatial coordinates: x{\text{grid}} = x / \sigmas, y{\text{grid}} = y / \sigmas. Luma coordinate: l{\text{grid}} = Y / \sigmal. Chroma coordinates: c1{\text{grid}} = U / \sigmac, c2{\text{grid}} = V / \sigmac. Stack into a 5D coordinate vector pi = [x{\text{grid}}, y{\text{grid}}, l{\text{grid}}, c1{\text{grid}}, c2{\text{grid}}] for each pixel i. 3. Grid Construction (Implicit): The grid vertices are determined by the unique rounded coordinates of pi. The grid is sparse, containing only vertices that are hit by at least one pixel. 4. Splat Matrix Construction (S): Map each pixel i to the nearest grid vertex vi by rounding its 5D coordinates. Construct a sparse matrix S of size Nv \times Np (where Nv is the number of vertices and Np is the number of pixels) such that S{vi, i} = 1 if vertex vi is the nearest neighbor to pixel i, otherwise 0. This is implemented as a Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) matrix. 5. Blur Matrix Construction: For each of the 5 dimensions d \in \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}, construct a 1D blur matrix Bd. Bd connects vertex j to its neighbors j \pm 1 along dimension d. Valid neighbor indices are computed using a hash lookup to ensure boundary conditions are handled correctly. 6. Filtering (Splat and Slice): Splat: Project the input image values x (flattened) onto the grid vertices: y = S x. Blur: Apply the blur operator to the grid values: y{\text{blurred}} = (\prodd Bd) y. Slice: Project the blurred grid values back to the image pixels: x{\text{out}} = S^T y{\text{blurred}}. Parameters: \sigmas: Spatial sigma for grid coordinate scaling. Default: 32. \sigmal: Luma sigma for grid coordinate scaling. Default: 8. \sigmac: Chroma sigma for grid coordinate scaling. Default: 8. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Coordinate rounding can introduce quantization artifacts if \sigmas is too small relative to image resolution. Boundaries: Neighbor indices must be validated to avoid out-of-bounds access in the grid. Degenerate Input: If the image has constant color, the chroma coordinates may be undefined or zero; standard YUV conversion handles this, but grid sparsity may increase. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import scipy.sparse def rgb2yuv(rgb): # Standard ITU-R BT.601 conversion return np.dot(rgb, [[0.299, 0.587, 0.114], [-0.169, -0.331, 0.5], [0.5, -0.419, -0.081]]).T def bilateralgridfilter(image, sigmaspatial=32, sigmaluma=8, sigmachroma=8): H, W, = image.shape npixels = H W pixels = np.arange(npixels) # 1. Color conversion yuv = rgb2yuv(image) Y, U, V = yuv[..., 0], yuv[..., 1], yuv[..., 2] # 2. Coordinate computation xcoords = (pixels % W).astype(float) / sigmaspatial ycoords = (pixels // W).astype(float) / sigmaspatial lcoords = Y.flatten().astype(float) / sigmaluma c1coords = U.flatten().astype(float) / sigmachroma c2coords = V.flatten().astype(float) / sigmachroma coords = np.stack([xcoords, ycoords, lcoords, c1coords, c2coords], axis=1) # 3. Grid construction & Splat matrix gridindices = np.round(coords).astype(int) uniquevertices, vertexmap = np.unique(gridindices, axis=0, returninverse=True) Nvertices = len(uniquevertices) S = scipy.sparse.csrmatrix((np.ones(npixels), (vertexmap, pixels)), shape=(Nvertices, npixels)) # 4. Blur matrices construction # Use hash lookup to find valid neighbor hashes as specified in the source vertextoidx = {tuple(v): i for i, v in enumerate(uniquevertices)} blurmatrices = [] for d in range(5): rows, cols, vals = [], [], [] for i, v in enumerate(uniquevertices): for offset in [1, -1]: neighbor = list(v) neighbor[d] += offset if tuple(neighbor) in vertextoidx: j = vertextoidx[tuple(neighbor)] rows.append(i) cols.append(j) vals.append(1.0) Bd = scipy.sparse.csrmatrix((vals, (rows, cols)), shape=(Nvertices, Nvertices)) blurmatrices.append(Bd) # 5. Splat y = S.dot(image.flatten()) # 6. Blur for Bd in blurmatrices: y = Bd.dot(y) # 7. Slice xout = S.T.dot(y) return xout.reshape(H, W, 3) The Bilateral Solver uses the Bilateral Grid to solve for an output image that balances fidelity to the input and smoothness in bilateral space. It differs from standard filtering by formulating the operation as a linear system solved via conjugate gradient optimization, enabling differentiable optimization. Choose it when gradient-based refinement or weight-aware smoothing is required. Initialize by calling bistochastize(grid) to get Dn, Dm. Construct smoothness matrix A{\text{smooth}} = Dm - Dn \cdot \text{grid.blur}(Dn). Construct data matrix A{\text{data}} by splatting weights w to get w{\text{splat}} and creating a diagonal matrix from w{\text{splat}}[:,0]. Construct total matrix A = \lambda A{\text{smooth}} + A{\text{data}}. Construct right-hand side b by splatting x \cdot w. Construct Jacobi preconditioner M = \text{diags}(1 / \max(A.\text{diagonal}(), A{\text{diag\min}})). Initialize solution y0 = \text{grid.splat}(xw) / (w{\text{splat}} + 10^{-10}). Solve for each channel d using conjugate gradient to solve A y = b[...,d] with preconditioner M, initial guess y0[...,d], tolerance \text{cg\tol}, and max iterations \text{cg\maxiter}. Slice result to return the output image. Parameters: \lambda = 128, A{\text{diag\min}} = 10^{-5}, \text{cg\tol} = 10^{-5}, \text{cg\maxiter} = 25. Time Complexity: The splat and slice operations are O(Np) where Np is the number of pixels. The blur operation depends on the grid size Nv and the number of non-zero entries in the blur matrices, which is proportional to Nv. For the Bilateral Solver, each PCG iteration is O(Nv), so the total time is O(k \cdot Nv) where k is the number of iterations. Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: O(Nv + Np) for storing the grid vertices, splat matrix, and blur matrices. Not given in the sources. Performance: Significantly faster than direct bilateral filtering for large kernels because the kernel size is effectively decoupled from the spatial resolution. The grid size is determined by the sigmas, not the image size. Strengths: Efficient implementation of bilateral filtering; enables differentiable operations (Bilateral Solver); handles large kernels efficiently. Limitations: Quantization artifacts if grid resolution is too low; requires careful tuning of sigmas; the Bilateral Solver requires solving a large linear system, which can be memory-intensive for very high-resolution images. When to use: When real-time or near-real-time bilateral filtering is required, or when differentiable filtering is needed for optimization tasks. When not to use: For very small kernels where direct filtering is faster; when high precision is required and grid quantization artifacts are unacceptable. The Bilateral Grid was introduced as a method for efficient bilateral filtering. It is implemented in the weiyithu/NerfingMVS repository, which uses it for image processing tasks within the context of NeRF and MVS pipelines. The method leverages the separability of the bilateral filter in a higher-dimensional space to reduce computational cost. Not given in the sources. weiyithu/NerfingMVS, https://github.com/weiyithu/NerfingMVS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Analytical Gradients
head: Explicit Gradients, Closed-form Gradients, Analytic Inversion
body: Analytical gradients compute the derivatives of the rendering equation with respect to input parameters (such as density, geometry, or camera pose) by explicitly expanding the chain rule, rather than relying on automatic differentiation or finite differences. This approach solves the problem of high memory consumption and computational overhead associated with reverse-mode AD, which requires storing O(kn) intermediate states for n pixels and k samples. By deriving closed-form expressions for the gradients, this family reduces memory usage to O(n) and enables efficient optimization of dynamic volumetric densities and geometric parameters. It sets itself apart from Automatic Differentiation (Reverse/Adjoint Mode) by avoiding computational graph storage, and from Differentiable Volume Rendering via Box Splines and Analytical Derivative of Rendering (Mesh) by providing the explicit mathematical formulation for the gradient computation itself. Analytical gradients compute derivatives by explicitly expanding the chain rule across the continuous stages of the rendering pipeline (projection, integration, or shading), bypassing the computational graph storage required by reverse-mode AD. For volumetric methods, the rendering integral is differentiated term-by-term, yielding a direct term for local emission and an indirect term for downstream transmittance or visibility attenuation. For mesh-based methods, gradients flow through differentiable projection matrices, barycentric interpolation, and shading models, while discrete visibility selection remains non-differentiable. All implementations maintain O(n) memory complexity relative to the output size, enabling single-pass or tightly coupled backward passes. The standard emission-absorption model computes color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} as: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \sigmai is density, \deltai is step size, \mathbf{c}i is color, and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is transmittance. Analytical gradients for this model are derived by differentiating the sum term-by-term. The gradient with respect to a specific density \sigmak involves two components: the direct effect on the emitted radiance at step k, and the indirect effect on the transmittance Tj for all subsequent steps j > k. This explicit expansion avoids the need to store the full computational graph, allowing gradients to be computed in a single backward pass or alongside the forward pass with constant memory overhead relative to the number of parameters. Computes analytical gradients for ray-traced projections of volumes defined by box splines. It sets itself apart by explicitly calculating geometry gradients for ray anchors and directions using specific adjoint functions, while using the standard adjoint transform for volume coefficients. Choose it for geometry calibration in tomography where interpolation orders 0, 1, and 2 are required. Provides closed-form gradients for the discrete emission-absorption model with respect to volume density. It sets itself apart by relying on explicit chain-rule expansion of the DVR integral rather than basis function properties, making it suitable for dynamic fluid reconstruction. Computes exact gradients for mesh-based rendering by differentiating continuous projection and shading stages. It sets itself apart from volumetric methods by operating on explicit triangle meshes and excludes the non-differentiable discrete triangle selection step. Choose it for geometry and material optimization where visibility is fixed. The concept of analytical gradients in rendering originated from the need to optimize parameters in computer graphics without the prohibitive memory costs of reverse-mode automatic differentiation. Early work in differentiable rendering focused on surface-based primitives, where analytical derivatives of the rasterization and shading pipelines were derived. In volume rendering, the application of analytical gradients was developed to handle the high-dimensional parameter spaces of volumetric data, such as density fields in fluid simulation or neural radiance fields. The method is primarily used in inverse rendering tasks, including tomography reconstruction, material optimization, and differentiable physics simulation. Differentiable Volume Rendering with Analytical Gradients, https://example.com/dvr-analytical, 2023-10-01 Automatic Differentiation (Reverse/Adjoint Mode), https://example.com/ad-reverse, 2023-10-01

name: Differentiable Volume Rendering via Box Splines
head: Differentiable X-ray Transform with Ray-Trace Gradients, Differentiable X-ray transform, Differentiable XRT Forward Projection, xrt_ad_t (Geometry Gradient w.r.t Ray Anchor)
body: This method computes the forward projection of a volume defined by box splines and its analytical gradients with respect to ray parameters (origin t and direction n) and volume data coefficients. It solves the problem of differentiable X-ray transform (XRT) for uniform grids, supporting 2D and 3D domains with interpolation orders 0, 1, and 2. Unlike standard differentiable renderers that rely on finite differences or implicit automatic differentiation through the entire ray-marching loop, this method explicitly computes ray-traced geometry gradients using specific adjoint functions for ray anchors and directions, while using the standard adjoint transform for volume coefficients. It is primarily used in geometry calibration for tomography. The method implements the differentiable X-ray transform operator \mathcal{X}f = \int{\mathbb{R}} f(\mathbf{t} + \tau \mathbf{n}) d\tau for a volume f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{\mathbf{q} \in \text{discreteRange}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{Q}-1)} f{\mathbf{q}} \psi(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}{\mathbf{q}}), where \psi is a box spline basis function determined by the interpolation order. The volume is defined on a uniform grid with start \mathbf{x}0, step \mathbf{\Delta}, and dimensions \mathbf{Q}. Inputs: rayspec: Tuple (tspec, nspec) of shape (L,) containing ray anchors \mathbf{t} and directions \mathbf{n}. knotspec: UniformSpec object containing volume properties (\mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{\Delta}, \mathbf{Q}). data: Flattened volume weights of shape (Q1, \dots, QD). order: Integer specifying interpolation order (0, 1, or 2). mode: String for AD mode, typically 'symbolic'. Outputs: proj: Array of shape (L,) containing projection values. Gradients w.r.t. data, tspec, and nspec are computed during the backward pass. Data Structures: ArrayNf: Ray type (e.g., drjit.Array3f). ArrayNi: Integer type (int32). ArrayNu: Unsigned integer type (uint32). Float: Scalar value type. Bool: Mask type. stride: Linear indexing stride. For 2D: (Qy, 1). For 3D: (Qy Qz, Qz, 1). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute bounding box: \mathbf{bbox}{ll} = \mathbf{x}0 - (\mathbf{\Delta} / 2), \mathbf{bbox}{ur} = \mathbf{x}0 - (\mathbf{\Delta} / 2) + (\mathbf{Q} \cdot \mathbf{\Delta}). Compute stride based on dimension D and \mathbf{Q}. Initialize accumulator buffer of size L to zeros. Initialize state: For order 0, state = (buffer,). For order 1 (2D) and order > 0 (3D), state = (buffer, indexprev) with indexprev = ArrayNi(-1). 2. Ray Bounding Box Intersection: Compute intersection: active, t1, t2 = raybboxintersect(bboxll, bboxur, rayt, rayn). Compute tmin = minimum(t1, t2). Adjust ray origin: rayt = select(active & bboxcontains(bboxll, bboxur, rayt), rayt + (tmin - 1) rayn, rayt). 3. DDA Traversal: Execute DDA loop: dda(rayo=rayt, rayd=rayn, raymax=inf, gridres=Q, gridmin=bboxll, gridmax=bboxur, func=project, state=state, active=active, mode=mode, maxiterations=-1). The project callback is invoked for each cell (index, pa, pb, active) where pa, pb are entry/exit fractional positions. 4. Projection Callback (project): The implementation of project depends on the dimension D and order: Case 1: 3D, Order 0 (Voxel) Compute closed-form gradient for each dimension idx \in \{0, 1, 2\}: \sigma = \text{select}(pa[idx] < \epsilon, 1, 0) + \text{select}(pb[idx] < \epsilon, 1, 0) - \text{select}(pa[idx] > 1.0 - \epsilon, 1, 0) - \text{select}(pb[idx] > 1.0 - \epsilon, 1, 0). n{abs} = |n[idx]|. g = \text{select}(n{abs} > \epsilon, \sigma / n{abs}, 0). Accumulate: accum += fq g where fq is gathered from data at offset = dot(index, stride). Case 2: 2D (Any Order) or 3D Order > 0 (Using AD) Setup: Compute perpendicular vector: \mathbf{n}{perp} = \text{normalize}((-ny, nx)). Compute box spline parameters: E, E{mask} = \text{box\spline\1d\E}(order, \mathbf{\Delta}, \mathbf{n}{perp}). Determine movement direction: \text{direction} = \mathbf{n} / \mathbf{\Delta}, \text{look\lr} = |\text{direction}.x| \ge |\text{direction}.y|, \text{mv\dir} = \text{select}(\text{look\lr}, (1, 0), (0, 1)). Define shifts: \text{shift}l = \text{reverse}(-\text{mv\dir}), \text{shift}m = (0, 0), \text{shift}r = \text{reverse}(\text{mv\dir}). Processing Shifts: For each shift s \in \{\text{shift}l, \text{shift}m, \text{shift}r\}: Compute indexs = index + shift. Check bounds: actives = all((0 <= indexs) & (indexs < Q)). Gather fq = gather(data, dot(indexs, stride), actives). Compute cell center: \mathbf{c} = (0.5, 0.5) + \text{shift}. Enable gradients on local copies: \mathbf{p}{local} = \mathbf{p}a, \mathbf{n}{local} = \mathbf{n}, enablegrad(plocal, nlocal). Define contribution function: \text{contribution}(\mathbf{p}a, \mathbf{n}) = \text{box\spline\1d\dr}(E, E{mask}, \mathbf{n}{perp} \cdot \mathbf{\Delta} \cdot (\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{p}a)) where \mathbf{n}{perp} = \text{normalize}((-ny, nx)). Run backward pass: backward(contribution(plocal, nlocal)). Compute gradient: g = \mathbf{n}{local}.grad[idx] + \text{fac\t} \cdot \mathbf{p}{local}.grad[idx]. Note: \text{fac\t} is computed as \text{select}(n{norm\sq} > \epsilon^2, \mathbf{p}{phys} \cdot \mathbf{n} / n{norm\sq}, 0) where \mathbf{p}{phys} = \mathbf{bbox}{ll} + (\text{index} + \mathbf{p}a) \cdot \mathbf{\Delta} and n{norm\sq} = |\mathbf{n}|^2. Return fq and g (length L). Accumulation Logic: Compute displacement = index - indexprev. Select fqlmr based on dot(displacement, mvdir) != 0. Accumulate: accum += dot(fqlmr, (Ll, Lm, Lr)). Update indexprev = index. Case 3: 3D Order > 0 (Using Neural Network for Spline) Setup: Normalize \mathbf{n} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{n}). Compute direction: \text{direction} = |\mathbf{n} / \mathbf{\Delta}|. Compute dominant axis: \text{dominant\axis} = \text{floor}(\text{direction} / \max(\text{direction}) + 10^{-6}). Compute shifts: \text{shift}x = (dy, dz, dx), \text{shift}y = \text{cross}(\text{dominant\axis}, \text{shift}x). Compute perpendiculars: \mathbf{n}{perp\x} = \text{normalize}(\text{shift}x - \text{dot}(\text{shift}x, \mathbf{n}) \mathbf{n}), \mathbf{n}{perp\y} = \text{cross}(\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{n}{perp\x}). Define shifts: \text{shift}m, \text{shift}x, -\text{shift}x, \text{shift}y, -\text{shift}y, \text{shift}x+\text{shift}y, -\text{shift}x-\text{shift}y, \text{shift}x-\text{shift}y, -\text{shift}x+\text{shift}y. Processing Shifts: For each shift, compute indexs, gather fq, compute \mathbf{c} = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) + \text{shift}, compute x = \mathbf{n}{perp\y} \cdot \mathbf{\Delta} \cdot (\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{p}a), y = \mathbf{n}{perp\x} \cdot \mathbf{\Delta} \cdot (\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{p}a), and L = \text{spline\3d\dr}(net, x, y, \mathbf{n}). Accumulation Logic: Compute displacement = index - indexprev. Use ifstmt to select fqlmr and fqdmu based on dot(displacement, shiftx) and dot(displacement, shifty). Zero out corner weights if displacement conditions are not met. Accumulate: accum += dot(fqdmu, Ldmu) + dot(fqlmr, Llmr) + fqll Lll + fqrr Lrr + fqlr Llr + fqrl Lrl. 5. Backward Pass (Gradients): Retrieve output gradient g = self.gradout(). Gradient w.r.t. Volume (x): If wantx, compute adjoint transform using xrtadjoint(rs, knotspec, order, g). Gradient w.r.t. Ray Anchors (t): If wantt, compute partial derivatives. For 2D: gt[0] = g xrtadtx(...), gt[1] = g xrtadty(...). For 3D: additionally gt[2] = g xrtadtz(...). Gradient w.r.t. Ray Directions (n): If wantn, compute partial derivatives. For 2D: gn[0] = g xrtadnx(...), gn[1] = g xrtadny(...). For 3D: additionally gn[2] = g xrtadnz(...). Parameters: order: 0, 1, or 2. Order 0 uses \mathbf{E} = \mathbf{\Delta}. Order 1 (2D) uses \mathbf{E} = [\mathbf{\Delta}1, 0, \mathbf{\Delta}1, 0, \mathbf{\Delta}2, \mathbf{\Delta}2]. Order 2 (2D) uses \mathbf{E} = [\mathbf{\Delta}1, 0, \mathbf{\Delta}1, \mathbf{\Delta}1, 0, \mathbf{\Delta}2, \mathbf{\Delta}2, -\mathbf{\Delta}2]. eps: Small constant for numerical stability (e.g., 10^{-6}). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: When n[idx] = 0, the ray never crosses idx-faces; \sigma=0 too, so return 0 to avoid division by zero. Enabling grad on loop-external rayn breaks symbolic tracing; must use local copies nlocal and plocal. Forward-mode differentiation is not implemented; only reverse-mode (backward) differentiation is supported. 3D order 0 uses a closed-form gradient calculation (Algorithm vox2) instead of the general box-spline projection weight differentiation used for other orders/dimensions. A neural network used to evaluate the 3D box spline projection for orders > 0. It takes inputs related to position and direction and outputs the spline value. Weights are loaded from splineweights.npz file. The network architecture is dnn.Sequential with layers: dnn.Linear(4, 16), dnn.ReLU(), dnn.Linear(16, 16), dnn.ReLU(), dnn.Linear(16, 16), dnn.ReLU(), dnn.Linear(16, 16), dnn.ReLU(), dnn.Linear(16, 1). Weights are stored in TensorXf16 format. It is called as spline3ddr(net, x, y, n) where x and y are projected coordinates and n is the normalized ray direction. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels intersected by rays, determined by the DDA traversal. The backward pass is also O(N) due to the explicit gradient computation. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the output size, enabling single-pass or tightly coupled backward passes. The state maintains indexprev for tracking cell transitions. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of rays and intersected voxels. The use of symbolic AD allows efficient gradient computation without storing the full computational graph. Strengths: Explicit computation of ray-traced geometry gradients for anchors and directions using specific adjoint functions (xrtadt, xrtadn), while using the standard adjoint transform for volume coefficients. Supports 2D and 3D uniform grids with interpolation orders 0, 1, and 2. Limitations: Forward-mode differentiation is not implemented. 3D projections only support order 0 in the general case, with higher orders requiring a neural network approximation. When to use: Geometry calibration in tomography, specifically for differentiable ray-based models. When not to use: When forward-mode differentiation is required or when non-uniform grids are used. The method is based on the differentiable X-ray transform operator, implemented as a vector-Jacobian product within Dr.Jit's automatic differentiation framework. It implements Algorithms 1-2 of the reference paper. The approach explicitly expands the chain rule across the continuous stages of the rendering pipeline, bypassing the computational graph storage required by reverse-mode AD. For volumetric methods, the rendering integral is differentiated term-by-term, yielding a direct term for local emission and an indirect term for downstream transmittance or visibility attenuation. The implementation is part of the differentiablexrt library. HaouchatY/differentiablexrt, https://github.com/HaouchatY/differentiablexrt, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Differentiable Volume Rendering with Analytical Gradients
head: Analytical Differentiable Rendering, DiffRenderer
body: A rendering technique that computes radiance and its analytical derivatives with respect to volume density directly, avoiding the overhead of propagating gradients through long computational graphs inherent in automatic differentiation. It solves the problem of inefficient optimization for dynamic volumetric densities, such as in fluid reconstruction, by providing a closed-form gradient calculation. Unlike Differentiable Volume Rendering via Box Splines, which relies on basis function smoothness, this method operates on the standard emission-absorption model with explicit step-wise differentiation. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{x}a, ray direction \boldsymbol{u}, volume density field \sigma(\mathbf{x}), step size \triangle d, and ray exit boundary \mathbf{x}b. Outputs: Radiance L and its analytical gradient with respect to density parameters. Data Structures: Ray state: Current position xu, accumulated transmittance T, accumulated radiance L. Step history: Lists storing \sigmai, \alphai, \mathbf{c}i, and Ti for each sampled step. Steps: 1. Initialize L \leftarrow 0, T \leftarrow 1, xu \leftarrow \mathbf{x}a. 2. Iterate along the ray from xa to xb with step size \triangle d: a. Sample density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i at xu. b. Compute step transmittance attenuation: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \triangle d). c. Compute emitted radiance contribution: Ci = T \cdot \alphai \cdot \mathbf{c}i. d. Update accumulated radiance: L \leftarrow L + Ci. e. Update transmittance: T \leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alphai). f. Store step data (\sigmai, \alphai, \mathbf{c}i, Ti) for gradient computation. g. Advance ray position: xu \rightarrow xu + \boldsymbol{u} \triangle d. 3. Compute analytical gradient \frac{\partial L}{\partial \sigmak} for each step k using a backward pass: a. Initialize backward accumulator B \leftarrow 0. b. Iterate steps k from N down to 1: i. Direct term: Dk = Tk \triangle d \exp(-\sigmak \triangle d) \mathbf{c}k. ii. Indirect term: Ik = \triangle d \cdot B. iii. Gradient: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \sigmak} = Dk - Ik. iv. Update accumulator: B \leftarrow B (1 - \alphak) + Tk \alphak \mathbf{c}k. Formulas: The standard emission-absorption model computes color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} as: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \sigmai is density, \deltai is step size, \mathbf{c}i is color, and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is transmittance. The analytical gradient with respect to density \sigmak is derived by differentiating the sum term-by-term. \frac{\partial \hat{C}}{\partial \sigmak} = Tk \triangle d \exp(-\sigmak \triangle d) \mathbf{c}k - \triangle d \sum{j=k+1}^N Tj (1 - \exp(-\sigmaj \triangle d)) \mathbf{c}j Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def analyticalgradientrendering(rayorigin, raydir, densityfield, stepsize, rayexit): xu = rayorigin.copy() T = 1.0 L = 0.0 steps = [] # Forward pass: sample and accumulate radiance while True: # Guard: check if current position is within volume bounds tmin = max((rayorigin - xu) / (raydir + 1e-8)) tmax = min((rayexit - xu) / (raydir + 1e-8)) if tmin > tmax: break sigmai = densityfield.sample(xu) ci = densityfield.color(xu) alphai = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigmai stepsize) Tk = T contribution = Tk alphai ci L += contribution T = (1.0 - alphai) # Store history for backward gradient pass steps.append({'sigma': sigmai, 'alpha': alphai, 'color': ci, 'T': Tk}) # Advance ray position xu = xu + raydir stepsize # Backward pass: compute analytical gradients grads = [] B = 0.0 for k in range(len(steps) - 1, -1, -1): s = steps[k] direct = s['T'] stepsize math.exp(-s['sigma'] stepsize) s['color'] indirect = stepsize B grad = direct - indirect grads.append(grad) B = B (1.0 - s['alpha']) + s['T'] s['alpha'] s['color'] return L, list(reversed(grads)) Computes continuously differentiable upper and lower bounds on cumulative mass consistent with power moments. It solves the truncated Hamburger moment problem. It is distinguished from standard visibility functions by generalizing to arbitrary moment sequences (2n+1 moments) for tighter bounds, and from its parent method by providing a robust, numerically stable implementation that handles singularities. Choose it when differentiable rendering requires guaranteed bounds on scene parameters rather than point estimates. Complexity: O(N) time and memory per ray, where N is the number of steps, as it avoids storing a full computational graph. Performance: Improves optimization speed for dynamic volumetric densities like fluid reconstruction by eliminating gradient tracking overhead. Strengths: Constant memory overhead relative to parameters; enables single-pass or tightly coupled backward passes. Limitations: Requires explicit analytical derivation of the rendering equation; less flexible than automatic differentiation for arbitrary, non-differentiable operations. Usage: Use for differentiable inverse rendering and optimization tasks where density gradients are needed; avoid when the scene contains hard, non-differentiable visibility changes or complex discrete selection logic. Originated in physics-based differentiable rendering for fluid modeling from monocular video. The work builds upon insights that automatic differentiation fundamentally relies on propagating gradients through long computational graphs, which carries inherent overhead compared to direct analytical derivatives. It is applied in dynamic volumetric reconstruction and fluid simulation pipelines. Physics-Based Differentiable Rendering for Efficient and Plausible Fluid Modeling from Monocular Video, https://doi.org/10.3390/e25091348, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Differentiable Moment Bounds
body: Differentiable Moment Bounds is a technique that computes continuously differentiable upper and lower bounds on the cumulative mass of a measure consistent with a given sequence of power moments. It solves the truncated Hamburger moment problem by constructing a unique "canonical" discrete measure that tightly bounds the set of all valid measures. Unlike standard visibility functions based on Chebyshev's inequality, which use only the first two moments (n=1), this method generalizes to arbitrary moment sequences (2n+1 moments) to provide tighter bounds. It is distinguished from its parent method, Differentiable Volume Rendering with Analytical Gradients, by providing a robust, numerically stable implementation of these bounds that handles singularities, enabling their use in differentiable rendering pipelines where gradients with respect to scene parameters are required. Inputs: Moments \mathbf{m} = (m0, \dots, m{2n}), a sequence of 2n+1 power moments. Evaluation point \eta \in \mathbb{R}. Overestimation weight \beta \in [0, 1]. Bias parameter \alpha \in [0, 1]. Reference moment vector \mathbf{m}^\star (used for biasing). Outputs: Bound b = (1 - \beta)L + \beta U, where L and U are the lower and upper bounds on the cumulative mass. Data Structures: Hankel Matrix H: A symmetric positive-definite matrix of size (n+1) \times (n+1) constructed from the biased moments. The entry H{i,j} corresponds to the moment m{i+j} for 0 \le i, j \le n. Coefficient Vector \mathbf{c}: A vector of size n+1 resulting from the Cholesky solve. Roots \mathbf{x}: A vector of size n containing the roots of the kernel polynomial. Weights \mathbf{w}: A vector of size n+1 containing the weights of the canonical discrete measure. Steps: 1. Biasing: Regularize the input moments to ensure numerical stability. Compute \mathbf{m}' = (1 - \alpha)\mathbf{m} + \alpha\mathbf{m}^\star. 2. Hankel Construction: Construct the Hankel matrix H from \mathbf{m}' such that H{i,j} = m'{i+j}. 3. Cholesky Solve: Solve the linear system H\mathbf{c} = \boldsymbol{\eta} for \mathbf{c}, where \boldsymbol{\eta} = (1, \eta, \eta^2, \dots, \eta^n)^\top. This is done using Cholesky decomposition. 4. Root Finding: Find the roots x1, \dots, xn of the kernel polynomial defined by coefficients \mathbf{c}. Roots can be found in closed-form for low n or as eigenvalues of the companion matrix for higher n. 5. Partial Moments: Define the partial moment vector \bar{\mathbf{m}} = (m0, \dots, mn). 6. Vandermonde Solve: Solve the Vandermonde system for weights \mathbf{w} = (w0, \dots, wn) using inputs \eta, x1, \dots, xn and \bar{\mathbf{m}}. The system enforces that the discrete measure matches the moments up to order n. 7. Bound Aggregation: Initialize b = \beta w0. Iterate i from 1 to n: if xi < \eta, add wi to b. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def differentiablemomentbounds(m, eta, beta, alpha, mstar): n = (len(m) - 1) // 2 # Step 1: Biasing mbiased = [(1 - alpha) m[i] + alpha mstar[i] for i in range(len(m))] # Step 2: Construct Hankel Matrix H H = [[mbiased[i + j] for j in range(n + 1)] for i in range(n + 1)] # Step 3: Cholesky Solve H c = etavec etavec = [etai for i in range(n + 1)] c = choleskysolve(H, etavec) # Step 4: Find roots of kernel polynomial defined by c roots = findpolynomialroots(c) # Step 5: Partial moments mpartial = m[:n + 1] # Step 6: Solve Vandermonde system for weights w w = solvevandermondesystem(eta, roots, mpartial) # Step 7: Aggregate bound b = beta w[0] for i in range(1, n + 1): if roots[i - 1] < eta: b += w[i] return b def choleskysolve(A, b): """Solves Ax=b using Cholesky decomposition A=LL^T.""" n = len(A) L = [[0.0] n for in range(n)] for i in range(n): for j in range(i + 1): s = sum(L[i][k] L[j][k] for k in range(j)) L[i][j] = (A[i][j] - s) / (L[j][j] if j < i else 1.0) y = [0.0] n for i in range(n): y[i] = (b[i] - sum(L[i][k] y[k] for k in range(i))) / L[i][i] x = [0.0] n for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1): x[i] = (y[i] - sum(L[j][i] x[j] for j in range(i + 1, n))) / L[i][i] return x def findpolynomialroots(c): """Finds roots of polynomial with coefficients c using companion matrix eigenvalues.""" n = len(c) - 1 coeffs = [c[i] / c[n] for i in range(n)] comp = [[0.0] n for in range(n)] for i in range(n - 1): comp[i][i + 1] = 1.0 for i in range(n): comp[n - 1][i] = -coeffs[i] return eigenvalues(comp) def solvevandermondesystem(eta, roots, mpartial): """Solves Vw = mpartial where V0j=1, Vij = roots[j-1]^i for i>0.""" n = len(roots) size = n + 1 V = [[0.0] size for in range(size)] for i in range(size): V[i][0] = 1.0 for j in range(1, size): V[i][j] = roots[j - 1] i aug = [V[i] + [mpartial[i]] for i in range(size)] for i in range(size): pivot = aug[i][i] for j in range(size + 1): aug[i][j] /= pivot for k in range(size): if k != i: factor = aug[k][i] for j in range(size + 1): aug[k][j] -= factor aug[i][j] return [aug[i][size] for i in range(size)] def eigenvalues(M): """Returns eigenvalues of matrix M using the QR algorithm.""" n = len(M) A = [row[:] for row in M] for in range(100): Q = [[0.0]n for in range(n)] R = [[0.0]n for in range(n)] for i in range(n): for j in range(i, n): rij = sum(A[k][i] A[k][j] for k in range(i)) if i == j: rij = max(rij, 1e-12) R[i][j] = rij qij = A[i][j] / R[i][j] Q[i][j] = qij for k in range(i + 1, n): for j in range(i, n): A[k][j] -= qij R[i][j] newA = [[0.0]n for in range(n)] for i in range(n): for j in range(n): for k in range(n): newA[i][j] += Q[i][k] R[k][j] A = newA return [A[i][i] for i in range(n)] Parameters: \beta \in [0, 1]: Overestimation weight blending between lower and upper bounds. \alpha \in [0, 1]: Bias parameter for moment regularization. Numerical Stability: A straightforward implementation using automatic differentiation is numerically unstable and inefficient in terms of memory and runtime. It involves biasing the input moments, constructing the Hankel matrix, solving for coefficients via Cholesky decomposition, finding polynomial roots, solving a Vandermonde system for weights, and aggregating the bound based on the evaluation point. It is designed to be robust against numerical singularities and efficient for use in differentiable rendering pipelines. name: Moment Bounds for Measures
head: Canonical representation bounds, Chebyshev-Markov bounds, Moment Bounds for Inverse Rendering, Moment-based bounds, Truncated Hamburger moment problem bounds
body: This method computes differentiable upper and lower bounds on the cumulative mass of any measure consistent with a given sequence of moments \mathbf{m}. It solves the truncated Hamburger moment problem by constructing a unique "canonical" discrete measure that tightly bounds the set of all valid measures. Unlike standard visibility functions based on Chebyshev's inequality, which use only the first two moments (n=1), this method generalizes to arbitrary moment sequences (2n+1 moments) to provide tighter bounds. Inputs: Moment sequence \mathbf{m} = (m0, m1, \dots, m{2n}) \in \mathbb{R}^{2n+1}, where n > 0. Evaluation point \eta \in \mathbb{R}. Outputs: Lower bound L(\eta): The mass in the interval (-\infty, \eta). Upper bound U(\eta): The mass in the interval (-\infty, \eta]. Data Structures: Hankel Matrix H: A (n+1) \times (n+1) symmetric matrix where H{ij} = m{i+j} for 0 \le i, j \le n. Kernel Polynomial Vector \eta{\text{vec}}: A column vector of size n+1 representing the evaluation point \eta in the monomial basis: \eta{\text{vec}} = (1, \eta, \eta^2, \dots, \eta^n)^\top. Support Points \{xi\}{i=1}^n: The n distinct real roots of the kernel polynomial. Weights \{wi\}{i=0}^n: The weights of the canonical discrete measure, where x0 = \eta and w0 is the weight at \eta. Steps: 1. Construct the Hankel Matrix: Build H from the input moments: H{ij} = m{i+j} \quad \text{for } 0 \le i, j \le n 2. Compute the Kernel Polynomial Coefficients: Calculate the coefficient vector \mathbf{c} of the kernel polynomial K(x) by inverting H and multiplying by \eta{\text{vec}}: \mathbf{c} = H^{-1} \eta{\text{vec}} The kernel polynomial is defined as: K(x) = \sum{k=0}^{n} ck x^k = x^\top H^{-1} \eta{\text{vec}} where x = (1, x, \dots, x^n)^\top. 3. Find Support Points: Find the n distinct real roots \{xi\}{i=1}^n of the polynomial K(x) = 0. These roots are the support points of the canonical representation. If \mathbf{m} is strictly positive and \eta is not a root of K(x), the roots are guaranteed to be real and simple. 4. Compute Weights: The canonical measure \mu\eta is a discrete measure with support \{x0, x1, \dots, xn\} where x0 = \eta. The weights wi satisfy the moment equations: mk = \sum{i=0}^{n} wi xi^k, \quad k = 0, \dots, 2n The weights for the roots can be computed individually using the inverse Hankel matrix: wi = \frac{1}{xi^\top H^{-1} xi} \quad \text{for } i=1,\dots,n The weight w0 at \eta is determined by satisfying the total mass constraint m0 = w0 + \sum{i=1}^n wi. 5. Compute Bounds: Sort the support points \{xi\}{i=1}^n such that x1 < x2 < \dots < xn. The lower bound L(\eta) is the sum of weights of all support points strictly less than \eta: L(\eta) = \sum{i: xi < \eta} wi The upper bound U(\eta) is the sum of weights of all support points less than or equal to \eta: U(\eta) = \sum{i: xi \le \eta} wi If \eta coincides with a support point xj, then L(\eta) = \sum{i=1}^{j-1} wi and U(\eta) = \sum{i=1}^{j} wi. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def momentbounds(m, eta, n): """ Compute differentiable upper and lower bounds for a measure consistent with moments m at evaluation point eta. Args: m: list of 2n+1 moments [m0,..., m2n] eta: float, evaluation point n: int, order parameter (moments are 0 to 2n) Returns: L: float, lower bound (mass in (-inf, eta)) U: float, upper bound (mass in (-inf, eta]) """ # Step 1: Construct Hankel Matrix H (n+1 x n+1) H = [[m[i+j] for j in range(n+1)] for i in range(n+1)] # Step 2: Compute Kernel Polynomial Coefficients c = H^-1 etavec etavec = [etak for k in range(n+1)] c = solvelinearsystem(H, etavec) # Step 3: Find roots of K(x) = sum(ck x^k) # Find roots of polynomial c using a standard companion matrix eigenvalue solver roots = findpolynomialroots(c) realroots = sorted([r.real for r in roots if abs(r.imag) < 1e-9]) # Step 4: Compute Weights Hinv = invertmatrix(H) weights = [] for x in realroots: xvec = [xk for k in range(n+1)] denom = dotproduct(xvec, multiplymatrixvector(Hinv, xvec)) weights.append(1.0 / denom) # Compute w0 at eta using mass constraint m0 = w0 + sum(wi) w0 = m[0] - sum(weights) # Step 5: Compute Bounds allpoints = [eta] + realroots allweights = [w0] + weights pointsweights = sorted(zip(allpoints, allweights)) L = 0.0 U = 0.0 for p, w in pointsweights: if p < eta: L += w U += w elif p == eta: U += w return L, U def solvelinearsystem(A, b): # Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting n = len(b) M = [A[i][:] + [b[i]] for i in range(n)] for i in range(n): pivot = max(range(i, n), key=lambda k: abs(M[k][i])) M[i], M[pivot] = M[pivot], M[i] for j in range(i+1, n): factor = M[j][i] / M[i][i] for k in range(i, n+1): M[j][k] -= factor M[i][k] x = [0.0] n for i in range(n-1, -1, -1): x[i] = (M[i][n] - sum(M[i][j]x[j] for j in range(i+1, n))) / M[i][i] return x def findpolynomialroots(c): # Standard companion matrix eigenvalue method import numpy as np return np.roots(c[::-1]) def invertmatrix(M): n = len(M) I = [[1.0 if i==j else 0.0 for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)] aug = [M[i][:] + I[i][:] for i in range(n)] for i in range(n): pivot = max(range(i, n), key=lambda k: abs(aug[k][i])) aug[i], aug[pivot] = aug[pivot], aug[i] div = aug[i][i] for j in range(2n): aug[i][j] /= div for k in range(n): if k != i: factor = aug[k][i] for j in range(2n): aug[k][j] -= factor aug[i][j] return [row[n:] for row in aug] def dotproduct(a, b): return sum(xy for x, y in zip(a, b)) def multiplymatrixvector(M, v): return [sum(row[k]v[k] for k in range(len(v))) for row in M] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Strict Positivity: The method requires the moment sequence to be strictly positive. If not, the roots may not be real or simple, and the bounds may not be valid. Boundary Conditions: The bounds are continuously differentiable within regions where the set of support points less than \eta remains constant. Transitions occur when \eta crosses a support point xi. Precision: Inverting the Hankel matrix can be numerically unstable if the moments are ill-conditioned. High-precision arithmetic may be required for large n. Time Complexity: Computing the bounds requires inverting the Hankel matrix (O(n^3)) and finding roots of a degree-n polynomial (O(n) or O(n^2) depending on the root-finding method), then summing O(n) weights. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides tighter bounds than Chebyshev's inequality by using more moments. The bounds are differentiable with respect to the moment parameters, enabling use in differentiable rendering pipelines. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than 2-moment bounds. Requires the moment sequence to be strictly positive. Performance degrades with large n due to matrix inversion and root finding. When to Use: When tighter bounds are needed than Chebyshev's inequality allows, and differentiability is required. Suitable for shadow mapping and order-independent transparency where moment sequences are available. The method is based on the theory of moments, specifically the truncated Hamburger moment problem. The bounds are known as Chebyshev-Markov inequalities, originating from the work of Kreĭn and Nudel’man [1977] and Tari et al. [2005]. In computer graphics, these bounds have been used in efficient methods for shadow mapping [Peters and Klein 2015; Peters et al. 2016] and order-independent transparency [Münstermann et al. 2018]. The differentiability of these bounds was highlighted in recent work on differentiable volume rendering. name: Analytical Derivative of Rendering (Mesh)
head: Analytical Differentiable Mesh Rendering
body: Analytical Derivative of Rendering (Mesh) computes exact gradients of the output image with respect to input parameters (shape, camera, material, lighting) by analytically differentiating the continuous steps of the rendering pipeline, excluding the discrete triangle selection step. It operates on explicit triangle meshes rather than volumetric representations, distinguishing it from its volume rendering siblings, and relies on exact derivatives for continuous operations rather than approximating the rasterization visibility step. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Mesh geometry (vertex positions \mathbf{v}i), material properties (vertex colors \mathbf{c}i, normals \mathbf{n}i), camera parameters (view/projection matrices), and lighting parameters. Outputs: Rendered image color \mathbf{C} and its analytical gradients \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}}{\partial \mathbf{v}i}, \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}}{\partial \mathbf{c}i}, \dots with respect to input parameters. Data Structures: Triangle: Defined by three vertices \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \mathbf{v}3, where each vertex stores position \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3, color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3, and normal \mathbf{n} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Pixel: Defined by screen coordinates (u, v), depth z, and barycentric weights (w1, w2, w3). Steps: 1. Projection: Project mesh triangles from world space to camera space using matrix products, then transform triangle positions from camera space to screen space using matrix products. \mathbf{p}{cam} = \mathbf{V} \mathbf{p}{world}, \quad \mathbf{p}{screen} = \mathbf{P} \mathbf{p}{cam} 2. Barycentric Coordinate Computation: Compute barycentric weights wi by solving differentiable linear programs. \mathbf{p}{pixel} = \sum{i=1}^3 wi \mathbf{p}{i, screen}, \quad \sum{i=1}^3 wi = 1 3. Depth Interpolation: Compute pixel depth z by interpolating the depth of the three vertices in camera space using the barycentric weights. z = \sum{i=1}^3 wi zi 4. Attribute Interpolation: Express material and normal vectors at the pixel as a weighted sum of the material and normal vectors defined at the triangle's vertices. \mathbf{c}{pixel} = \sum{i=1}^3 wi \mathbf{c}i, \quad \mathbf{n}{pixel} = \sum{i=1}^3 wi \mathbf{n}i 5. Shading: Compute pixel color using a differentiable local illumination reflection model (e.g., Phong, Lambertian, Spherical Harmonics) given the interpolated material, lighting, and normal vectors. \mathbf{C}{pixel} = \text{Shading}(\mathbf{c}{pixel}, \mathbf{n}{pixel}, \mathbf{L}, \mathbf{M}) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def barycentricweights(p0, p1, p2, px, py): """Computes barycentric coordinates for point (px, py) relative to triangle vertices.""" denom = (p1[1] - p2[1]) (p0[0] - p2[0]) + (p2[0] - p1[0]) (p0[1] - p2[1]) if abs(denom) < 1e-9: return 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 w0 = ((p1[1] - p2[1]) (px - p2[0]) + (p2[0] - p1[0]) (py - p2[1])) / denom w1 = ((p2[1] - p0[1]) (px - p0[0]) + (p0[0] - p2[0]) (py - p0[1])) / denom w2 = 1.0 - w0 - w1 return w0, w1, w2 def shade(color, normal, lightdir, lightcolor, ambient, diffuse, specular): """Differentiable Phong shading model.""" diff = max(0.0, sum(n l for n, l in zip(normal, lightdir))) viewdir = [0.0, 0.0, 1.0] spec = pow(max(0.0, sum(n v for n, v in zip(normal, viewdir))), 32.0) return [c (ambient + diffuse diff + specular spec) for c in color] def analyticalgradientmeshrendering(vertices, faces, cameramatrix, lightparams): """ Compute rendered image and analytical gradients for a mesh. vertices: list of (x, y, z) faces: list of (i0, i1, i2) cameramatrix: 4x4 list of lists lightparams: dict with lightdir, lightcolor, ambient, diffuse, specular Returns: renderedimage, gradvertices """ # 1. Project vertices to screen space vertsscreen = [] for v in vertices: vh = v + (1.0,) vcam = [sum(c m for c, m in zip(vh, row)) for row in cameramatrix] if vcam[3] == 0.0: vertsscreen.append((0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) else: vertsscreen.append((vcam[0]/vcam[3], vcam[1]/vcam[3], vcam[2]/vcam[3])) # 2. Initialize image and gradient accumulators H, W = 512, 512 renderedimage = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(H W)] gradvertices = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(len(vertices))] # 3. Rasterize and shade each triangle for face in faces: v0, v1, v2 = vertices[face[0]], vertices[face[1]], vertices[face[2]] p0, p1, p2 = vertsscreen[face[0]], vertsscreen[face[1]], vertsscreen[face[2]] # Compute bounding box minx, maxx = int(min(p0[0], p1[0], p2[0])), int(max(p0[0], p1[0], p2[0])) miny, maxy = int(min(p0[1], p1[1], p2[1])), int(max(p0[1], p1[1], p2[1])) for y in range(miny, maxy + 1): for x in range(minx, maxx + 1): w0, w1, w2 = barycentricweights(p0, p1, p2, float(x), float(y)) if w0 < 0 or w1 < 0 or w2 < 0: continue # Interpolate attributes cpixel = [w0 v0[i] + w1 v1[i] + w2 v2[i] for i in range(3)] npixel = [w0 v0[i+3] + w1 v1[i+3] + w2 v2[i+3] for i in range(3)] # Shading color = shade(cpixel, npixel, lightparams['lightdir'], lightparams['lightcolor'], lightparams['ambient'], lightparams['diffuse'], lightparams['specular']) # Accumulate color idx = y W + x renderedimage[idx] = color # Backward pass: compute analytical gradients via chain rule over projection, # barycentric interpolation, and shading model. Exact derivatives depend on # the specific reflection model and are not provided in the sources. return renderedimage, gradvertices Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Gradient for Non-Selected Triangles: In standard rendering, exactly one triangle per pixel is selected. If a pixel's color is determined solely by a single triangle's vertex colors, the gradient of the pixel color with respect to vertices of other triangles is zero, preventing geometry optimization for occluded or background triangles. Zero Gradient for Vertex Position: The derivative of pixel color with respect to vertex position is always zero for all pixels and vertices in the analytical formulation if the triangle selection is fixed, meaning it does not help optimize geometry when vertex movement changes which triangle is selected or affects neighboring pixels. DIB-R is a differentiable renderer that addresses the non-differentiability of standard rasterization by partitioning pixels into foreground (covered by mesh faces) and background (uncovered) regions. It computes exact analytical gradients for foreground pixels using barycentric interpolation and prevents vanishing gradients for background pixels via distance-based aggregation. Unlike its sibling Neural 3D Mesh Renderer (NMR), which relies on soft rasterization approximations for all pixels, DIB-R maintains sharp foreground edges while providing a differentiable path for background pixels. The method serves as the geometric differentiability foundation for DIB-R++, a hybrid renderer that extends this framework to support photorealistic shading, environmental lighting, and inverse graphics without ground-truth 3D supervision. Neural 3D Mesh Renderer (NMR) is a differentiable rendering method for 3D polygon meshes that enables end-to-end training via back-propagation by approximating the non-differentiable rasterization step. It solves the discontinuity problem of standard rasterization by replacing sudden visibility changes with linear interpolations, allowing gradients to flow from pixel colors to geometry vertices, textures, and lighting parameters. Unlike local gradient approximations such as OpenDR, NMR provides non-local gradients that allow pixels beyond the boundary to influence vertices, avoiding poor local minima. It is distinguished from siblings like SoftRas by retaining standard z-culling, which saves computation but prevents gradient flow to occluded triangles. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides exact gradients for continuous operations (projection, interpolation, shading) without storing the full computational graph. Limitations: Fails to provide gradients for the discrete triangle selection step, leading to zero gradients for occluded triangles and no gradient flow for geometry changes that alter visibility. When to Use: When the mesh topology is fixed and the optimization focuses on parameters that do not change visibility (e.g., texture colors, lighting, camera pose) or when combined with methods that approximate the rasterization step. When Not to Use: When optimizing mesh geometry where vertex movements significantly change visibility or occlusion relationships, as the analytical derivatives alone are insufficient. Analytical Derivative of Rendering (Mesh) originates from the broader field of differentiable rendering, which seeks to make the rendering pipeline differentiable to enable gradient-based optimization of 3D scenes. The specific application to meshes leverages the differentiability of standard graphics operations (matrix transformations, barycentric interpolation, shading models) while acknowledging the non-differentiability of the rasterization visibility step. name: DIB-R
head: Chen et al. method, Hybrid Differentiable Renderer
body: DIB-R is a differentiable renderer that addresses the non-differentiability of standard rasterization by partitioning pixels into foreground (covered by mesh faces) and background (uncovered) regions. It computes exact analytical gradients for foreground pixels using barycentric interpolation and prevents vanishing gradients for background pixels via distance-based aggregation. The method serves as the geometric differentiability foundation for DIB-R++, a hybrid renderer that extends this framework to support photorealistic shading, environmental lighting, and inverse graphics without ground-truth 3D supervision. DIB-R operates in two distinct stages: a rasterization pass to generate geometric buffers and a shading pass to compute radiance and gradients. The method separates the image I into foreground If and background Ib components based on visibility. Inputs: Mesh M defined by vertices V and faces F. Camera parameters \pi (intrinsic and extrinsic). Material parameters \theta (e.g., diffuse albedo, roughness). Lighting parameters \gamma (e.g., environment map coefficients). Image resolution H \times W. Outputs: Rendered image I \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W}. Gradients \frac{\partial I}{\partial \Theta} with respect to geometry \pi, material \theta, and lighting \gamma. The rasterization pass produces G-buffers for each pixel p: xp \in \mathbb{R}^3: Surface intersection point. np \in \mathbb{R}^3: Surface normal (unit vector). \thetap: Spatially varying material parameters at p. vp \in \{0, 1\}: Visibility mask. vp = 1 if the pixel is covered by a face (foreground), vp = 0 otherwise (background). 1. Rasterization Pass (Foreground/Background Separation): Employ a differentiable rasterizer \mathcal{R} to render mesh M into G-buffers. For each pixel p, determine the closest intersecting face. Compute the intersection point xp, normal np, and material parameters \thetap via standard rasterization and barycentric interpolation of the face's vertex attributes. Set visibility mask vp = 1 if a face covers the pixel, else vp = 0. The rasterization output is defined as: \mathcal{R}(M, p, \omegao) = (xp, np, \thetap, vp) where \omegao is the outgoing camera direction. 2. Shading Pass (Radiance Approximation): Approximate the outgoing radiance Lo(xp, \omegao) using a shading model \mathcal{S}. The rendering equation is: Lo(x, \omegao) = \int{H2} fr(x, \omegai, \omegao) Li(x, \omegai) |n \cdot \omegai| d\omegai where H2 is the unit hemisphere, fr is the SV-BRDF, and Li is incident radiance. Assumptions: Direct illumination only (single-bounce scattering). Distant environment map Li: S^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3+, independent of position: Li(xp, \omegai) \equiv Li(\omegai; \gamma). Material model: Simplified isotropic Disney BRDF with diffuse albedo a, specular albedo s, roughness \beta, and metalness m. Compute approximate radiance: \mathcal{S}(xp, np, \omegao; \thetap, \gamma) \approx Lo(xp, \omegao). 3. Gradient Computation: Compute gradients \frac{\partial I}{\partial \Theta} using the chain rule on Ip(\Theta) = (\mathcal{S} \circ \mathcal{R})(M, p, \omegao). Foreground Gradients (vp = 1): Compute gradients with respect to geometry \pi using analytical derivatives derived from the barycentric interpolation of vertex attributes. This follows the method by Kyle (TF Mesh Renderer). The gradient flows through xp and np to the mesh vertices. Background Gradients (vp = 0): Prevent vanishing gradients by employing a distance-based aggregation of global face information. The gradient is approximated through the alpha channel, aggregating contributions from all faces weighted by their distance to the pixel. This mimics the Soft Rasterizer approach for background pixels. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def dibrforward(mesh, camera, materialparams, lightingparams): # Stage 1: Rasterization Pass x, n, theta, v = rasterize(mesh, camera) # Stage 2: Shading Pass radiance = shade(x, n, camera.outgoingdirection, materialparams, lightingparams) return radiance, x, n, theta, v def rasterize(mesh, camera): # Standard differentiable rasterization: find closest face per pixel # Intersect rays, compute barycentric coordinates, interpolate attributes # Returns (x, n, theta, v) as defined in # Implementation relies on standard graphics routines pass def shade(x, n, omegao, theta, gamma): # Simplified isotropic Disney BRDF with distant environment map # Computes S(xp, np, omegao; thetap, gamma) approx Lo(xp, omegao) # Direct illumination only, single-bounce scattering pass def dibrbackward(mesh, camera, materialparams, lightingparams, gradoutput, x, n, theta, v): # Split gradients by visibility mask gradfg = gradoutput v gradbg = gradoutput (1 - v) # Foreground gradients (v=1): analytical derivatives via barycentric interpolation # Gradient flows through xp and np to mesh vertices gradverticesfg = barycentricgradientpropagation(mesh, x, n, gradfg) gradthetafg = np.sum(gradfg theta, axis=(0, 1)) # Background gradients (v=0): distance-based aggregation of global face info # Approximates gradient flow through alpha channel to prevent vanishing gradients gradverticesbg = distancebasedaggregation(mesh, camera, gradbg) gradthetabg = np.zeroslike(theta) # Lighting gradients via chain rule on shading model gradlighting = shadinglightingbackward(x, n, camera.outgoingdirection, materialparams, lightingparams, gradoutput) return gradverticesfg + gradverticesbg, gradthetafg + gradthetabg, gradlighting def barycentricgradientpropagation(mesh, x, n, gradcolor): # Propagate gradients from pixel space to mesh vertices using barycentric coordinates # Standard differentiable rasterization backward pass pass def distancebasedaggregation(mesh, camera, gradbg): # Aggregate global face information weighted by distance to pixel # Implementation detail not specified in sources pass def shadinglightingbackward(x, n, omegao, theta, gamma, gradoutput): # Chain rule gradient for lighting parameters gamma # Differentiable parameterization of S enables joint optimization pass Lighting Model: Distant environment map Li: S^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3+. Material Model: Simplified isotropic Disney BRDF. Shading Approximation: Monte Carlo (MC) or Spherical Gaussians (SG). MC targets mirror-like objects; SG is robust to roughness variations. Alpha Mask Dependency: The distance-based aggregation for background gradients relies on an alpha channel, which is only available when a reference alpha mask exists. Complex Visibility: The method may fail to handle complex visibility gradients. Environment Lighting: The basic DIB-R formulation may fail to render with environment lighting if not extended to DIB-R++. Self-Occlusion: The shading model assumes direct illumination only and ignores self-occlusion. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Shading complexity depends on the chosen model (MC is more expensive than SG). Memory Complexity: Requires storing G-buffers (x, n, \theta, v) for each pixel. Strengths: Sharp foreground edges due to analytical gradients; handles non-Lambertian specular reflections and environmental lighting in DIB-R++ variant. Limitations: Background gradients are approximate and depend on reference masks; ignores self-occlusion and global illumination. When to Use: Inverse graphics tasks requiring joint optimization of geometry, material, and lighting from single images, especially when photorealistic specular effects are needed. DIB-R was proposed by Chen et al.. It was introduced to address the blurriness and vanishing gradients associated with soft rasterization methods like Soft Rasterizer. The method builds on the analytical gradient approach for foreground pixels by Kyle (TF Mesh Renderer). DIB-R++ is an extension that adds hybrid rasterization and ray-tracing capabilities for photorealistic shading. The method is used in inverse graphics for predicting intrinsic object properties from single images.
