name: Neural 3D Mesh Renderer (NMR)
head: Differentiable Mesh Renderer, Kato et al, NMR (Neural 3D Mesh Renderer) Rasterization, Neural 3D Mesh Renderer Rasterization, Neural Renderer
body: Neural 3D Mesh Renderer (NMR) is a differentiable rendering method for 3D polygon meshes that enables end-to-end training via back-propagation by approximating the non-differentiable rasterization step. It solves the discontinuity problem of standard rasterization by replacing sudden visibility changes with linear interpolations, allowing gradients to flow from pixel colors to geometry vertices, textures, and lighting parameters. Unlike local gradient approximations such as OpenDR, NMR provides non-local gradients that allow pixels beyond the boundary to influence vertices, avoiding poor local minima. It is distinguished from siblings like SoftRas by retaining standard z-culling, which saves computation but prevents gradient flow to occluded triangles. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D mesh defined by object-space vertices V^o = \{v1^o, \dots, v{Nv}^o\} where vi^o \in \mathbb{R}^3, and faces F = \{f1, \dots, f{Nf}\} where fj \in \mathbb{R}^3 represents the three vertex indices of the j-th triangle. Camera parameters (view/projection matrices) and lighting parameters (l^a, l^d, \boldsymbol{n}^d). Output: A rendered image I \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C} and gradients \frac{\partial L}{\partial vi^o}, \frac{\partial L}{\partial \text{texture}}, \frac{\partial L}{\partial \text{light}}. Data Structures: Mesh: List of vertices and face connectivity. In reconstruction applications, a template mesh (e.g., an isotropic sphere with 642 vertices) is deformed by adding local bias vectors \boldsymbol{b}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a global bias vector \boldsymbol{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 to each vertex: vi = vi^o + \boldsymbol{b}i + \boldsymbol{c}. Texture: Each face can hold a texture image of size st \times st \times C. Steps: 1. Transformation: Transform object-space vertices V^o to screen-space vertices V^s = \{v1^s, \dots, v{Nv}^s\} where vi^s \in \mathbb{R}^2 using a composition of differentiable transformations (projection and viewport). 2. Rasterization (Forward Pass): For each pixel Pj in the image, determine if its center lies inside a face fk. If multiple faces overlap, draw only the front-most face (z-culling). Assign the color I{kj} of the overlapping face to the pixel color Ij. Note: This step is discrete. Standard gradients \frac{\partial Ij}{\partial vi} are zero almost everywhere because the assignment is binary. 3. Shading: Compute pixel color Ij^l based on lighting and texture. Define ambient light intensity l^a and directional light intensity l^d with direction unit vector \boldsymbol{n}^d. For face j with normal \boldsymbol{n}j, the color is: Ij^l = (l^a + (\boldsymbol{n}^d \cdot \boldsymbol{n}j) l^d) Ij where Ij is the base color (possibly from texture sampling). Gradients flow to l^a, l^d, and \boldsymbol{n}^d. Texture sampling uses bilinear interpolation based on barycentric coordinates. 4. Gradient Approximation (Backward Pass): Replace the sudden change in visibility with linear interpolation to allow gradients to flow. For a vertex vi moving by \deltai^x in screen space, causing a color change \deltaj^I at pixel Pj: Let \deltaj^P be the gradient of the loss L with respect to pixel Pj (backpropagated from the loss function). The gradient \frac{\partial Ij}{\partial vi} is defined based on the sign agreement between the loss gradient and the color change direction: \frac{\partial Ij}{\partial vi} = \begin{cases} \frac{\deltaj^I}{\deltai^x} & \text{if } \deltaj^P \cdot \deltaj^I < 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } \deltaj^P \cdot \deltaj^I > 0 \end{cases} If \deltaj^P > 0 (loss increases if pixel brightens) and \deltaj^I > 0 (vertex movement brightens pixel), the product is positive, and gradient is 0 (movement does not help minimize loss). If \deltaj^P > 0 and \deltaj^I < 0 (movement darkens pixel, helping minimize loss), the product is negative, and gradient flows. If the vertex is inside the face, compute gradients for movements in both directions (left/right, up/down) and sum them. Z-culling Limitation: Only the closest triangle affects pixel color. Gradients do not flow to occluded triangles. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nmrforward(verticesscreen, faces, H, W): """Forward rasterization: returns pixelfacemap and barycentriccoords.""" pixelfacemap = [[-1 for in range(W)] for in range(H)] barycentriccoords = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(W)] for in range(H)] for fidx, (v0, v1, v2) in enumerate(faces): for y in range(H): for x in range(W): p = [float(x), float(y)] w = computebarycentric(p, v0, v1, v2) if w[0] >= 0 and w[1] >= 0 and w[2] >= 0: if pixelfacemap[y][x] == -1: pixelfacemap[y][x] = fidx barycentriccoords[y][x] = w return pixelfacemap, barycentriccoords def computebarycentric(p, v0, v1, v2): v0v1 = [v1[0]-v0[0], v1[1]-v0[1]] v0v2 = [v2[0]-v0[0], v2[1]-v0[1]] v0p = [p[0]-v0[0], p[1]-v0[1]] dot00 = v0v1[0]v0v1[0] + v0v1[1]v0v1[1] dot01 = v0v1[0]v0v2[0] + v0v1[1]v0v2[1] dot02 = v0v1[0]v0p[0] + v0v1[1]v0p[1] dot11 = v0v2[0]v0v2[0] + v0v2[1]v0v2[1] dot12 = v0v2[0]v0p[0] + v0v2[1]v0p[1] inv = 1.0 / (dot00 dot11 - dot01 dot01) u = (dot11 dot02 - dot01 dot12) inv v = (dot00 dot12 - dot01 dot02) inv w = 1.0 - u - v return [w, u, v] def nmrbackward(verticesscreen, faces, pixelfacemap, barycentriccoords, pixellossgradients, facecolors, H, W): """Compute gradients for screen-space vertices.""" Nv = len(verticesscreen) vertexgradients = [[0.0, 0.0] for in range(Nv)] for y in range(H): for x in range(W): fidx = pixelfacemap[y][x] if fidx == -1: continue lossgrad = pixellossgradients[y][x] facecolor = facecolors[fidx] w = barycentriccoords[y][x] v0, v1, v2 = faces[fidx] verts = [v0, v1, v2] for k in range(3): v = verts[k] # deltaI: color change if vertex moves to uncover pixel deltaI = -facecolor # Objective-aware gate: gradient flows only if movement helps minimize loss gate = 1.0 if lossgrad deltaI < 0 else 0.0 # Approximate gradient magnitude using barycentric coordinate as distance proxy # NMR uses linear interpolation: grad = deltaI / deltav dxgrad = gate deltaI w[k] dygrad = gate deltaI w[k] vertexgradients[verts[k]][0] += dxgrad vertexgradients[verts[k]][1] += dygrad return vertexgradients Parameters: Lighting: Ambient intensity l^a = 0.5, directional intensity l^d = 0.5. Direction \boldsymbol{n}^d can be random or optimized. Optimizer: Adam (\alpha=0.0001, \beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.999) for reconstruction; \alpha=2.5e-4 for vertices and 5e-2 for textures in style transfer. Resolution: 128x128 for reconstruction, 448x448 for style transfer. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Z-culling: Gradients do not flow to occluded triangles. This saves computation but may hinder geometry optimization if occluded geometry is relevant. Gradient Gating: The gradient is strictly zero if the product of the loss gradient and the color change direction is positive, meaning vertex movement does not help minimize the loss. Precision: Linear interpolation approximation may introduce artifacts near boundaries if not carefully implemented. A differentiable rendering technique for meshes that computes exact gradients of the output image with respect to input parameters by analytically differentiating the rendering pipeline steps, excluding the discrete triangle selection step. It sets itself apart by focusing on analytical derivatives for mesh parameters and is chosen when precise gradient computation for shape, camera, material, and lighting is required. DIB-R Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels and faces. Jrender's optimized implementation is ~10x faster than the official implementation. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to mesh size and image resolution. Performance: On a 280-triangle bowl at 256x256 resolution, Jrender's NMR takes 7.5ms (forward + gradient) vs 8.1ms for official NMR. Strengths: Supports fragment shading (textures, complex lighting); non-local gradients avoid local minima; efficient z-culling. Limitations: Cannot optimize occluded geometry; approximation may be inaccurate for complex mutual occlusions compared to SoftRas. When to use: General-purpose differentiable mesh rendering, single-image 3D reconstruction, style transfer. When not to use: When gradients to occluded geometry are critical (use SoftRas). Origin: Introduced by Kato et al. in 2017 (arXiv:1711.07566) and published at CVPR 2018. History: Developed to overcome limitations of OpenDR, specifically localness and lack of objective awareness. It integrates 3D mesh rendering into neural networks for tasks like 3D reconstruction and editing. Usage: Single-image 3D reconstruction, 3D mesh style editing, 3D Deep Dream. name: GAN-based Volume Rendering
head: Generative Model for Volume Rendering, Volume Rendering as GAN
body: This method treats volume rendering as a purely computational process that maps viewpoint and transfer function (TF) parameters directly to a color image, bypassing the explicit use of the volumetric scalar field. It distinguishes itself from traditional differentiable volume rendering by learning a data-driven mapping from visualization parameters to images using a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), rather than differentiating through the physical emission-absorption equation. Unlike Hybrid Differentiable Rendering Method which combines rasterization with neural networks, or Generative NeRF-to-NeRF Translation which translates between implicit representations, this approach synthesizes the final pixel values directly from parameter vectors. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A visualization parameter vector w containing viewpoint parameters v and sampled transfer function values \tau (opacity) and tc (color). Output: A color image I \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times w \times h} of fixed resolution w \times h. Data Structures: The visualization parameters w are constructed as a concatenation of: 1. Viewpoint vector v \in \mathbb{R}^{nv}, where nv = 5. The five parameters correspond to azimuth, elevation, in-plane rotation, and distance to the camera. The azimuth angle is separated into its cosine and sine components to handle the wrap-around discontinuity at 0 and 2\pi. 2. Opacity TF sampled vector \tau \in \mathbb{R}^{nt}, where nt = 256. 3. Color TF sampled vector tc \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times nt}, where nt = 256. Thus, w = [v, \tau, tc]. Network Architectures: The method employs a Generator G and a Discriminator D. Generator (G): Transforms the low-dimensional vector w into an image. It uses a DCGAN-style architecture interleaving upsampling and 2D convolutional layers. Viewpoint components are processed using Fully Connected (FC) layers because they lack spatial correlation. TF components are processed using 1D Convolutional layers because they are 1D signals with spatial dependencies. Nonlinearity: Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU), h(x) = \max(0, x). Batch Normalization is used in 2D convolutional layers to stabilize training. Discriminator (D): Takes w and an image I as input and produces a score in [0, 1] indicating if the image is real or fake. It transforms the image into a low-dimensional vector through 2D convolutions with stride 2. It fuses image features with input parameter features. Nonlinearity: Leaky ReLU, h(x) = \max(0, x) + \alpha \min(0, x). 1D Convolution Formula: For processing TFs, the 1D convolution is defined as: Z{a,b} = \sum{k=1}^{ci} \sum{l=1}^{w} X{sd \cdot a + l, k} W{l, b, k} where X is the input, W are filter weights, sd is the stride, a is the output position, b is the output channel, k is the input channel, and l is the filter width. Training Procedure: The networks are optimized via a min-max game using the adversarial loss: L{adv}(G, D) = \mathbb{E}{I,w \sim p{data}} [\log(D(w, I))] + \mathbb{E}{w \sim p{vis}} [\log(D(w, G(w)))] where I is a real volume-rendered image, w represents visualization parameters, G is the generator, and D is the discriminator. The first expectation is over the joint distribution of real images and parameters p{data}, and the second is over the distribution of visualization parameters p{vis}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def compute1dconvolution(X, W, stride=1): """ Computes 1D convolution as defined in. X: Input tensor of shape (N, Cin) where N is signal length, Cin is channels. W: Filter weights of shape (filterwidth, Cout, Cin). stride: Integer stride. Returns: Z of shape (Nout, Cout). """ filterwidth = W.shape[0] Cin = W.shape[2] Cout = W.shape[1] N = X.shape[0] # Calculate output length Nout = (N - filterwidth) // stride + 1 Z = np.zeros((Nout, Cout)) for a in range(Nout): for b in range(Cout): val = 0.0 for k in range(Cin): for l in range(filterwidth): inputidx = stride a + l # Guard against boundary if not padded, though sources imply valid convolution if 0 <= inputidx < N: val += X[inputidx, k] W[l, b, k] Z[a, b] = val return Z def generatorforward(w, params): """ Generator G forward pass. w: Visualization parameter vector [v, tau, tc]. v: Viewpoint vector (cos/sin azimuth, elevation, rotation, distance). tau: Opacity TF samples. tc: Color TF samples. """ # Split w v = w[:5] # nv = 5 tau = w[5:5+256] # nt = 256 tc = w[5+256:5+256+3256] # Process Viewpoint with Fully Connected Layers # zv = h(Wv @ v + bv) zv = applyfclayers(v) # Placeholder for specific FC layer definitions not in source # Process TFs with 1D Convolutions # ztau = compute1dconvolution(tau, Wtau) ztau = compute1dconvolution(tau, params['Wtau']) # ztc = compute1dconvolution(tc, Wtc) ztc = compute1dconvolution(tc, params['Wtc']) # Combine and upsample to image # Interleave upsampling and 2D convolution combined = concatenate(zv, ztau, ztc) image = applyupsamplingandconvlayers(combined) # Placeholder for DCGAN-style upsampling return image def discriminatorforward(w, image, params): """ Discriminator D forward pass. """ # Process image with 2D convolutions (stride 2) imgfeatures = apply2dconvlayers(image, params['Wimg']) # Placeholder # Process parameters w # Viewpoint via FC, TFs via 1D Conv v = w[:5] tau = w[5:5+256] tc = w[5+256:5+256+3256] zv = applyfclayers(v) ztau = compute1dconvolution(tau, params['Wtaudisc']) ztc = compute1dconvolution(tc, params['Wtcdisc']) paramfeatures = concatenate(zv, ztau, ztc) # Fuse image and parameter features fused = fusefeatures(imgfeatures, paramfeatures) # Placeholder for fusion mechanism # Produce score [0, 1] score = sigmoid(applyfinalfc(fused)) return score def trainstep(G, D, realimages, wreal, wfake, params): """ One step of the min-max game. """ # Generate fake images fakeimages = generatorforward(wfake, params) # Update Discriminator # Maximize D: Real images -> 1, Fake images -> 0 lossDreal = -np.mean(np.log(discriminatorforward(wreal, realimages, params) + 1e-8)) lossDfake = -np.mean(np.log(1 - discriminatorforward(wfake, fakeimages, params) + 1e-8)) lossD = lossDreal + lossDfake # Update Generator # Minimize G: Fake images -> 1 (trick D into thinking they are real) # Ladv(G, D) term for G is E[log(D(w, G(w)))] # To minimize G, we maximize log(D(w, G(w))), so we minimize -log(D(w, G(w))) lossG = -np.mean(np.log(discriminatorforward(wfake, fakeimages, params) + 1e-8)) return lossD, lossG This method performs spatial super-resolution on volumetric data by decomposing the 3D reconstruction problem into orthogonal 2D slice passes, avoiding the memory costs of full 3D convolutions. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D GANs by integrating physics-informed constraints directly into the training objective to ensure physically consistent reconstructions, rather than relying solely on statistical error minimization. Generative Adversarial Networks train a generator against a discriminator to produce perceptually realistic outputs rather than merely minimizing pixelwise error. This perceptual advantage makes GANs well-suited for volume super-resolution, where Mean Squared Error (MSE)-optimized outputs tend toward oversmoothing. The method solves the problem of generating high-fidelity volumetric visualizations by replacing explicit volume data with a computational process that maps viewpoints and transfer functions directly to images [Parent]. This is the first learned volume rendering system employing a two-stage conditional GAN architecture. It learns end-to-end mappings from volumetric data and parameters to rendered images, bypassing explicit transfer function specification by encoding opacity transfer functions into a latent space. Process: It encodes opacity transfer functions into an 8-dimensional latent space via 1D convolutions. The first GAN generates 64×64 opacity images conditioned on viewpoint and TF parameters. The second GAN translates these opacity images to 256×256 color renderings using color TF conditioning and skip connections. Parameters: Trained on 200,000 procedurally generated samples per volume. Performance: Achieved RMSE of 0.046–0.116 across six datasets. Inference time is 7ms for interactive TF sensitivity analysis. Limitations: Requires per-volume training with no cross-volume generalization. Limited to 256×256 output resolution and 1D transfer functions. Complexity: The method avoids the O(kn) memory usage of reverse-mode AD associated with storing intermediate states for differentiable volume rendering. Instead, memory usage is determined by the neural network parameters. Performance: Inference is extremely fast (e.g., 7ms for the two-stage variant), enabling interactive exploration. Strengths: Bypasses the need for explicit volume data storage during inference; handles complex mappings between parameters and images; perceptually superior to MSE-based methods. Limitations: Requires large datasets for training; may struggle with high-resolution synthesis (256x256) without architectural modifications like the two-stage approach; the two-stage variant lacks cross-volume generalization. When to use: When interactive exploration of viewpoint and TF space is required, and explicit volume data is either unavailable or too large to store/process in real-time. When not to use: When exact physical accuracy is required over perceptual quality, or when cross-volume generalization is needed without retraining. The method was introduced in "A Generative Model for Volume Rendering". It frames volume rendering not as a physical simulation but as a learned mapping from visualization parameters to images. This approach addresses the difficulty of exploring the high-dimensional space of viewpoints and transfer functions by using a GAN to synthesize images directly. The two-stage conditional GAN variant was later introduced as the first learned volume rendering system of its kind. name: Multi-pass GAN for Volumetric Super-Resolution
head: Multi-pass GAN (Werhahn et al.), Physics-informed Multi-pass GAN
body: This method performs spatial super-resolution on volumetric data by decomposing the 3D reconstruction problem into orthogonal 2D slice passes, thereby avoiding the memory costs associated with full 3D convolutions. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D GANs by integrating physics-informed constraints directly into the training objective to ensure physically consistent reconstructions, rather than relying solely on statistical error minimization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Low-resolution volumetric data, typically scalar fields such as density or velocity at 64^3 resolution. Output: High-resolution volumetric data at 512^3 resolution. Data Structures: Generators: Two distinct generator networks, G{XY} and G{YZ}. G{XY}: Processes 2D slices in the XY-plane. G{YZ}: Processes 2D slices in the YZ-plane. Discriminator: Architecture details are not specified in the sources. Method Steps: 1. Decomposition: The volumetric super-resolution task is decomposed into orthogonal 2D passes. 2. First Pass (G{XY}): The first generator upscales the input volume by processing it as a sequence of XY-plane slices. 3. Second Pass (G{YZ}): The second generator refines the output from the first pass by processing it as a sequence of YZ-plane slices. 4. Physics-Informed Training: The training objective incorporates constraints derived from governing equations directly into the loss function. 5. Progressive Growing: The network is trained using progressive growing with curriculum learning to handle the high resolution. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Upscaling Factor: 8× per dimension (e.g., 64^3 \rightarrow 512^3). Training Time: Approximately 60 seconds for the reported 64^3 \rightarrow 512^3 case. Pitfalls: Evaluation Limitations: The method was evaluated only on synthetic buoyant smoke data. Metrics: No quantitative reconstruction metrics (such as PSNR or SSIM) were reported in the source. Generalizability: Performance on non-synthetic or non-smoke data is not documented. SSRTVD is a GAN designed for spatial super-resolution of time-varying volumetric data, specifically targeting fluid flow density fields. It sets itself apart from single-volume GANs by introducing a temporal discriminator that operates on triplets of consecutive volumes to enforce frame-to-frame coherence, which prevents motion distortion. Choose it when spatial upscaling of fluid flows requires temporal smoothness without altering timestep resolution. SSRTVD STNet is an end-to-end GAN framework that extends super-resolution to joint spatial and temporal dimensions. It sets itself apart by performing feature-space temporal interpolation followed by voxel-shuffle spatial upscaling, optimizing PSNR-oriented losses rather than purely spatial metrics. Choose it when both spatial resolution and temporal consistency must be improved simultaneously. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory usage is reduced by decomposing 3D SR into 2D slice passes, avoiding the cost of full 3D convolutions. Training time is approximately 60 seconds for the reported 64^3 \rightarrow 512^3 case. Measured Performance: Produces detailed turbulent structures at 512^3 resolution from 64^3 inputs on synthetic buoyant smoke. Scaling: Handles 8× upscaling per dimension via progressive growing and curriculum learning. Strengths and Limitations: Competitive with direct numerical simulation (DNS) in visual fidelity, but lacks quantitative metrics and is untested on non-synthetic data. Usage Guidance: Use for physics-consistent spatial upscaling of synthetic fluid flows where memory constraints prohibit 3D convolutions; avoid for production pipelines requiring validated quantitative error bounds or non-smoke data. The method was proposed by Werhahn et al.. It belongs to the broader category of physics-informed super-resolution, which seeks physically consistent reconstructions by incorporating governing equation constraints into the training objective. This approach contrasts with purely statistical reconstruction error minimization. It is primarily used in scientific visualization for smoke and fluid flow simulations. name: SSRTVD
head: SSR-TVD, tempoGAN
body: SSRTVD is the first GAN-based spatial super-resolution method for time-varying volumetric data, designed to resolve frame-to-frame inconsistency that arises when spatial SR is applied independently to each timestep. It distinguishes itself from single-volume GANs by employing a temporal discriminator on triplets of consecutive volumes to enforce temporal coherence, and differs from temporal interpolation methods like TSR-TVD by focusing on spatial upscaling with advection-aligned constraints. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of coarse volumetric density fields \{Vt\}{t=1}^T representing time-varying fluid flow. Output: A sequence of high-resolution volumetric density fields \{\hat{V}t\}{t=1}^T upscaled by a factor of 4 in each spatial dimension (64× volumetric increase). Data Structures: Volumetric Grid: 3D tensor of shape (D, H, W) for each timestep, tested up to 256^3. Advection-Aligned Frames: Frames aligned according to the fluid velocity field to account for motion between timesteps. Network Architecture: 1. Generator (G): A densely connected convolutional network mapping coarse volumes to high-resolution volumes. 2. Spatial Discriminator (D{spatial}): Evaluates the realism of individual high-resolution volumes \hat{V}t. 3. Temporal Discriminator (D{temporal}): Processes triplets of consecutive volumes (\hat{V}{t-1}, \hat{V}t, \hat{V}{t+1}) to enforce temporal coherence. Training Steps: 1. Advection Alignment: Apply a differentiable semi-Lagrangian advection layer to align consecutive coarse volumes (V{t-1}, Vt, V{t+1}) with Vt based on the velocity field, producing advection-aligned frames. 2. Generator Forward Pass: Pass the aligned coarse frames through G to produce high-resolution predictions \hat{V}{t-1}, \hat{V}t, \hat{V}{t+1}. 3. Spatial Discrimination: Compute the spatial adversarial loss by comparing \hat{V}t against real high-resolution ground truth using D{spatial}. 4. Temporal Discrimination: Pass the triplet (\hat{V}{t-1}, \hat{V}t, \hat{V}{t+1}) through D{temporal}. 5. Gradient Propagation: Pass gradients from D{temporal} back through the differentiable semi-Lagrangian advection layer, allowing G to learn temporal smoothness constraints directly. 6. Loss & Optimization: The exact loss formulation weights and optimization algorithm are not given in the sources. Parameters: Upscaling Factor: 4× spatial (64× volumetric). Resolution: Tested up to 256^3. Dataset: Computer graphics smoke simulation data. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Per-Dataset Training: Requires training a separate model for each dataset, limiting generalization. Inference Time: Inference takes up to eight hours for large volumes due to sub-volume GPU processing constraints. Evaluation Limitations: Initial evaluation was qualitative with no PSNR or SSIM reported. A recurrent generative network that adapts the temporal discriminator concept to temporal interpolation rather than spatial super-resolution. It synthesizes intermediate timesteps using a generator combining ConvLSTM for temporal modeling with a voxel shuffle layer for feature-space upscaling, making forward and backward predictions blended with learned weights. It could only synthesize intermediate volumes at integer time positions. It achieved 23–27 dB PSNR across combustion, supernova, and vortex datasets, outperforming linear interpolation on both PSNR and isosurface similarity. Refines the GAN paradigm by incorporating self-attention into the generator encoder to capture global spatial dependencies beyond the local convolutional receptive field. It achieved improved perceptual scores at scale factors up to 8× on ionization and hurricane data. The evaluation reports SSIM improvement without quantifying absolute PSNR relative to SSR-TVD on matched splits, and the maximum tested volume (240 \times 240 \times 48) is smaller than prior GAN baselines. Time Complexity: Inference is computationally expensive, taking up to eight hours for large volumes (256^3) due to sub-volume GPU processing. Memory Complexity: Requires sufficient GPU memory for sub-volume processing; specific memory footprint is not given. Performance: At 4× upscaling, achieved 34–41 dB PSNR across combustion, ionization, and vortex datasets. Outperformed interpolation baselines on both PSNR and isosurface similarity. Strengths: Enforces temporal coherence in spatial SR, recovering fine-grained structures absent from coarse simulations. Limitations: Requires per-dataset training; initial evaluation lacked quantitative metrics; inference is slow. When to Use: Spatial SR of time-varying fluid data where temporal consistency is critical and per-dataset training is acceptable. When Not to Use: Real-time inference is required, or generalization across multiple datasets without retraining is needed. Introduced by Xie et al. as the first GAN-based spatial SR method for time-varying data. Originally developed for computer graphics smoke simulation. Established the temporal discriminator as a mechanism for enforcing coherence across timesteps using advection-aligned frames and a differentiable semi-Lagrangian advection layer. Cited in the context of scientific volume rendering and deep learning methods for scientific data. name: GAN Training Procedure
head: Min-Max Game Training
body: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) train a generator against a discriminator to produce perceptually realistic outputs rather than merely minimizing pixelwise error. This perceptual advantage makes GANs well-suited for volume super-resolution, where Mean Squared Error (MSE)-optimized outputs tend toward oversmoothing. The method solves the problem of generating high-fidelity volumetric visualizations by replacing explicit volume data with a computational process that maps viewpoints and transfer functions directly to images [Parent]. The procedure consists of two neural networks: a generator that produces increasingly realistic images and a discriminator that distinguishes real images from generated ones, trained in a competitive framework. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Real images (ground truth), visualization parameters (e.g., viewpoint, transfer function), and optionally an opacity image (for translation GANs). Outputs: Synthesized images from the generator; real/fake classification probabilities from the discriminator. Data Structures Generator (G): Neural network mapping visualization parameters to image space. Discriminator (D): Neural network mapping image space to scalar probability of being real. Training Data: Generated by performing volume rendering over a wide range of viewpoints and transfer functions (TFs). For each instance, the viewpoint is randomly generated, and the opacity TF is generated by sampling from a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM). The GMM samples 1 to 5 modes, each with a random mean, standard deviation, and amplitude relative to the scalar field range. Algorithm Steps The GAN is trained to optimize the min-max game using minibatch stochastic gradient descent. The parameters are updated using the ADAM optimizer. The training loop alternates gradient descent steps for the discriminator and the generator: 1. Discriminator Update (Real): Update discriminator parameters using a batch of real images and visualization parameters to minimize binary cross-entropy loss, encouraging the discriminator to predict these images as real. 2. Synthesis: Pass visualization parameters (and opacity image, if applicable) through the generator to synthesize images. 3. Discriminator Update (Fake): Update the discriminator to encourage a prediction of false for the synthesized images. 4. Generator Update: Update the generator’s parameters by tricking the discriminator, encouraging it to predict the synthesized images as being real. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traingan(generator, discriminator, realimages, vizparams, opacityimages, numepochs, batchsize, lr, beta1, beta2, epsilon): """ Trains a GAN using alternating gradient descent. Args: generator: The generator network G. discriminator: The discriminator network D. realimages: Tensor of ground truth images. vizparams: Tensor of visualization parameters (viewpoint, TF). opacityimages: Tensor of opacity images (optional, for translation GAN). numepochs: Total number of training epochs. batchsize: Number of samples per minibatch. lr: Learning rate for ADAM optimizer. beta1: Beta1 hyperparameter for ADAM. beta2: Beta2 hyperparameter for ADAM. epsilon: Epsilon hyperparameter for ADAM. """ # Initialize optimizers for both networks optG = Adam(generator.parameters(), lr=lr, betas=(beta1, beta2), eps=epsilon) optD = Adam(discriminator.parameters(), lr=lr, betas=(beta1, beta2), eps=epsilon) for epoch in range(numepochs): for batchrealimages, batchvizparams, batchopacity in zip(realimages, vizparams, opacityimages): # --- Discriminator Update --- optD.zerograd() # 1. Train on real images # Minimize binary cross-entropy loss encouraging D to predict 1 for real images predreal = discriminator(batchrealimages) lossDreal = binarycrossentropy(predreal, target=1.0) lossDreal.backward() # 2. Synthesize fake images # Pass visualization parameters through generator if batchopacity is not None: fakeimages = generator(batchvizparams, batchopacity) else: fakeimages = generator(batchvizparams) # 3. Train on fake images # Minimize binary cross-entropy loss encouraging D to predict 0 for fake images predfake = discriminator(fakeimages.detach()) # Detach to stop gradient flow to G lossDfake = binarycrossentropy(predfake, target=0.0) lossDfake.backward() optD.step() # --- Generator Update --- optG.zerograd() # 4. Update generator by tricking discriminator # Encourage D to predict 1 for fake images # Re-run generator to get fresh predictions (or use cached) if batchopacity is not None: fakeimages = generator(batchvizparams, batchopacity) else: fakeimages = generator(batchvizparams) predfakeforG = discriminator(fakeimages) lossG = binarycrossentropy(predfakeforG, target=1.0) lossG.backward() optG.step() Parameters Optimizer: ADAM. ADAM Hyperparameters: \epsilon = 10^{-8}, \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.999. L1 Loss Weight (\lambda): In practice, \lambda = 150 preserves color and stabilizes training without overly blurring generated images. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Oversmoothing: Standard MSE-optimized outputs tend toward oversmoothing, which GANs mitigate via perceptual loss. Training Instability: High-resolution GANs can be unstable; progressive training strategies may be required. Degenerate Input: Randomly generated TFs from GMMs must cover the relevant scalar field range to ensure generalization. A convolutional discriminator that grows progressively in resolution to stabilize training and allow larger batch sizes at lower resolutions. It solves the instability inherent in training high-resolution GANs by starting with coarse shapes and gradually introducing fine details. Unlike standard ProgressiveGAN where the generator architecture grows, this variant keeps the generator fixed, increasing resolution by sampling rays more densely from the same implicit representation. Uses spatial discriminators for normal and roughness maps, and temporal discriminators for temporal coherence, to enforce that inferred data spatial distribution is similar to real data. The overall loss is defined as: L{Total} = \alpha L{Image} + \beta1 L{Dn} + \beta2 L{Dr} + \gamma1 L{Dtn} + \gamma2 L{Dtr} where \alpha, \beta1, \beta2, \gamma1, \gamma2 are weights, and L{Dn}, L{Dr}, L{Dtn}, L{Dtr} are the losses of the corresponding discriminators. Training involves alternating training of the four auxiliary discriminators and the generator, as typically done for GAN training. Sub-net1 and sub-net2 are trained together using L{Total} for 200 epochs. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Demonstrated effectiveness for super-resolution, style transfer, and image-to-image translation. Hardware: Experiments conducted on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 SUPER GPU. Strengths: Produces perceptually realistic outputs, avoiding the oversmoothing typical of MSE-based methods. Limitations: Training can be unstable, particularly at high resolutions, requiring techniques like progressive growing. GANs [81] and diffusion models [82] have emerged as pivotal techniques for generating and modifying high-quality images. GANs consist of two neural networks trained in a competitive framework. They have demonstrated effectiveness for a variety of tasks, including super-resolution, style transfer, and image-to-image translation. In the context of volume rendering, GANs are used to bypass explicit volume data, mapping viewpoints and transfer functions directly to images [Parent]. name: Progressive GAN Discriminator
head: Progressive Growing Discriminator
body: A convolutional discriminator that grows progressively in resolution to stabilize training and allow larger batch sizes at lower resolutions. It solves the instability inherent in training high-resolution GANs by starting with coarse shapes and gradually introducing fine details. Unlike standard ProgressiveGAN where the generator architecture grows, this variant keeps the generator fixed, increasing resolution by sampling rays more densely from the same implicit representation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Real or generated image patches (RGB, optionally RGB-D) at the current training resolution. Output: A scalar score indicating the probability that the input is real. Data Structures: The discriminator is a convolutional neural network. It utilizes residual blocks and a minibatch standard deviation layer. If depth is included, it is normalized to [0, 1]. Steps: 1. Initialization: Begin training at a low resolution (e.g., 32 \times 32) with a large batch size. 2. Progressive Growth: Double the resolution twice during training, up to 128 \times 128. 3. Layer Addition: Add new layers to the discriminator to handle higher resolutions and discriminate fine details as resolution increases. 4. Final Rendering: Final results are rendered by sampling 512 \times 512 pixels, though training occurs at lower resolutions. 5. Discriminator Forward Pass (Standard): Input RGB-D. Normalize depth to [0, 1]. Apply Conv(3 \times 3). Pass through Residual Blocks. Apply Minibatch standard deviation. Apply Conv(3 \times 3). Flatten features. Apply two Linear layers. Output: 1. 6. Discriminator Forward Pass (With Decoder/Refinement): Input: 4 \times 4 feature maps from the discriminator (before minibatch standard deviation). Apply successive transposed convolutions with stride 2 and bilinear filtering to upsample. Apply Conv(3 \times 3). Apply activation. Output: 4 \times 64 \times 64. Parameters: Initial Resolution: 32 \times 32. Final Training Resolution: 128 \times 128. Final Rendering Resolution: 512 \times 512. Depth Normalization: [0, 1]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Resolution Mismatch: If the radiance field network is sampled at a lower resolution than the final output, generated depth maps will have lower resolution than real examples. Mitigation: To prevent the discriminator from exploiting this detail difference, downsample all real depth maps to match the generated depth map resolution, then upsample both back to full resolution. Progressive Patch Scaling is a training strategy for 3D GAN discriminators that operates on image patches of varying scales rather than full-resolution images, allowing the model to learn multi-scale features progressively. It solves the instability and diversity issues inherent in training 3D GANs from limited 2D observations by gradually reducing the scale of image patches used for training, starting from large sub-regions to smaller ones. Unlike methods that apply super-resolution modules to rendered values, this approach directly discriminates RGB color images or patches, relying on the progressive reduction of patch scale to stabilize training and promote diversity. The discriminator evaluates real vs. fake samples using residual blocks and minibatch standard deviation. The decoder upsamples feature maps to original resolution. The discriminator input is RGB-D, with depth normalized to [0, 1]. The process involves a Conv(3 \times 3), Residual Blocks, Minibatch stdev, Conv(3 \times 3), Flatten, and two Linear layers, outputting a single scalar. The decoder takes 4 \times 4 feature maps, applies successive transposed convolutions with stride 2 and bilinear filtering, a Conv(3 \times 3), and an activation, outputting 4 \times 64 \times 64. A key pitfall is that if the radiance field is sampled at lower resolution than the output, generated depth maps lack detail compared to real ones; this is mitigated by downsampling real depth maps to match generated resolution before upsampling both back to full resolution. Stability: Allows larger batch sizes at the beginning of training, which helps to stabilize and speed training. Resolution Scaling: Training resolution is limited to 128 \times 128 in standard experiments, while final rendering uses 512 \times 512. Generator Independence: The generator architecture does not grow; resolution is increased by sampling rays more densely from the same implicit representation. Originated from ProgressiveGAN [25] (cited in), this method was adapted for 3D-aware image synthesis in pi-GAN and unconstrained scene generation. It addresses the difficulty of training GANs at high resolutions by progressively introducing detail. pi-GAN: Periodic Implicit Generative Adversarial Networks for 3D-Aware Image Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr46437.2021.00574, fetched 2026-10-26 Unconstrained Scene Generation with Locally Conditioned Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv48922.2021.01404, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Progressive Patch Scaling
body: Progressive Patch Scaling is a training strategy for 3D GAN discriminators that operates on image patches of varying scales rather than full-resolution images, allowing the model to learn multi-scale features progressively. It solves the instability and diversity issues inherent in training 3D GANs from limited 2D observations by gradually reducing the scale of image patches used for training, starting from large sub-regions to smaller ones. Unlike methods that apply super-resolution modules to rendered values, this approach directly discriminates RGB color images or patches, relying on the progressive reduction of patch scale to stabilize training and promote diversity. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Generator \mathbf{G}, Discriminator \mathbf{D}, camera poses \tau, latent codes \mathbf{z}, and a time-varying scale schedule. Outputs: Discriminator scores for real and generated patches. Data Structures Patch Scale s: A scalar value sampled from a uniform distribution. Implementation-wise, this scalar is repeated to match the patch resolution if used as a channel or feature, though primarily it dictates the spatial coverage. Patch \rho: A spatial region of the image defined by the scale s. The sampled patch \rho is a function of the sampled scale s. Image Resolution: Input images have resolution H' \times H' (e.g., 512 \times 512). Fixed Patch Size: The discriminator processes patches of fixed size H \times H (e.g., 64 \times 64). Parameters Learning Rate: 2 \times 10^{-3}, used with the ADAM optimizer. Samples per Ray: 96 samples are used per ray during volume rendering. Batch Size: 1,000 samples per epoch. Scale Range Initialization: At epoch t=0, s{min}(0) = 0.6 and s{max}(0) = 0.8. Scale Range Finalization: At epoch t=100, s{min}(100) = 0.25 and s{max}(100) = 0.55. Rotation Augmentation: Gradually introduced up to 15^\circ for later training epochs where patch scale s decreases. Formulas The final training objective combines adversarial loss, R1 gradient penalty, and discriminator reconstruction loss: \mathcal{E}(\mathbf{G}, \mathbf{D}, \mathcal{T}) = \mathbb{E}{\mathbf{z},\tau \sim \mathcal{T},s,\rho} [f(\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{G}(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\rho, \mathbf{z}))) ] + \mathbb{E}{I,s,\rho} [f(-\mathbf{D}(\rho, s)) + \lambda1 |\nabla\rho \mathbf{D}(\rho, s)|^2 ] + \lambda2 \mathcal{E}R(\mathbf{D}) Where: f(a) = -\log(1 + \exp(-a)) is the adversarial loss function. \lambda1 and \lambda2 are balancing parameters for the R1 gradient penalty and reconstruction loss, respectively. \boldsymbol{\Gamma}\rho represents the volume rendering of the patch region. \rho is the sampled patch, which is a function of the sampled scale s. Numbered Steps 1. Initialize Scale Schedule: Define the linear interpolation of s{min}(t) and s{max}(t) over the first 100 epochs. s{min}(t) = 0.6 + (0.25 - 0.6) \times \frac{t}{100} s{max}(t) = 0.8 + (0.55 - 0.8) \times \frac{t}{100} For t > 100, fix s{min} and s{max} to the values at t=100. 2. Sample Scale: For each image instance in a batch, independently sample a scale factor s from the time-varying uniform distribution: s \sim U(s{min}(t), s{max}(t)) where t is the current epoch index. 3. Apply Augmentation: Apply data augmentation, including rotational augmentation. Start without rotational augmentation and gradually increase it up to 15^\circ in later epochs where s is smaller. 4. Extract Patches: Extract patches \rho from the input images I and generated images based on the sampled scale s. The text notes that when s=1, the 64 \times 64 patch covers the entire image, implying s acts as a scaling factor for the effective coverage or resolution relative to the fixed patch size. Implementation-wise, the scale value s is simply repeated to match the patch resolution if required by the discriminator architecture. 5. Compute Loss: Calculate the objective \mathcal{E} using the formula above. The generator produces patches \mathbf{G}(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\rho, \mathbf{z}), and the discriminator evaluates both real patches \rho and generated patches. 6. Optimize: Minimize the objective using the ADAM optimizer with a learning rate of 2 \times 10^{-3}. 7. Fix Scale: After epoch 100, stop updating s{min} and s{max} and keep them constant for the remainder of the training. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def progressivepatchscalingtraining(generator, discriminator, dataloader, numepochs=400): """ Implements Progressive Patch Scaling for 3D GAN training. Args: generator: The 3D GAN generator. discriminator: The convolutional discriminator. dataloader: Iterator yielding batches of (images, poses). numepochs: Total number of training epochs. """ optimizer = Adam(generator.parameters() + discriminator.parameters(), lr=2e-3) # Scale schedule parameters startepoch = 0 endscheduleepoch = 100 # Initial scale ranges smininit = 0.6 smaxinit = 0.8 # Final scale ranges sminfinal = 0.25 smaxfinal = 0.55 # Fixed patch size H = 64 Hprime = 512 # Augmentation max angle maxrotationangle = 15.0 for t in range(numepochs): # 1. Determine current scale range if t <= endscheduleepoch: progress = t / endscheduleepoch smint = smininit + (sminfinal - smininit) progress smaxt = smaxinit + (smaxfinal - smaxinit) progress else: smint = sminfinal smaxt = smaxfinal # 2. Determine current rotation augmentation strength # Linearly increase rotation augmentation up to 15 degrees # The paper states it is introduced and increased for later epochs where s decreases. # We assume linear increase over the first 100 epochs for simplicity, # or potentially mapped to the scale reduction. if t <= endscheduleepoch: currentmaxangle = maxrotationangle (t / endscheduleepoch) else: currentmaxangle = maxrotationangle for images, poses in dataloader: # 3. Sample scale for each image in the batch batchsize = images.shape[0] scales = np.random.uniform(smint, smaxt, size=batchsize) # 4. Apply augmentations and extract patches # Note: The exact implementation of extracting patches based on 's' # where s=1 covers the entire image is abstracted here. # In practice, this involves cropping or resizing logic. realpatches = [] generatedpatches = [] for i in range(batchsize): img = images[i] pose = poses[i] s = scales[i] # Apply rotational augmentation # Angle sampled uniformly from [-currentmaxangle, currentmaxangle] angle = np.random.uniform(-currentmaxangle, currentmaxangle) imgaug = applyrotation(img, angle) poseaug = applyrotationtopose(pose, angle) # Extract patch based on scale s # The paper implies s scales the effective coverage. # When s=1, 64x64 covers 512x512 (conceptually). # This likely means the patch is upsampled or the region is defined relative to s. # For implementation, we assume a helper function handles this mapping. patchreal = extractpatch(imgaug, s, H, Hprime) # Generate corresponding patch # Volume rendering with 96 samples per ray z = samplelatent() genpatch = generator.renderpatch(poseaug, z, samplesperray=96) realpatches.append(patchreal) generatedpatches.append(genpatch) realpatches = torch.stack(realpatches) generatedpatches = torch.stack(generatedpatches) # 5. Compute Loss # Adversarial loss for generated patches genscores = discriminator(generatedpatches) advlossgen = -torch.mean(torch.log(1 + torch.exp(-genscores))) # f(a) = -log(1+exp(-a)) # Adversarial loss for real patches realscores = discriminator(realpatches) advlossreal = torch.mean(torch.log(1 + torch.exp(realscores))) # f(-a) = -log(1+exp(a)) -> wait, f(-a) = -log(1+exp(a)) is not standard. # The formula is f(-D) = -log(1+exp(-(-D))) = -log(1+exp(D)). # Let's stick to the formula: f(a) = -log(1+exp(-a)). # So f(-D) = -log(1+exp(-(-D))) = -log(1+exp(D)). advlossreal = -torch.mean(torch.log(1 + torch.exp(realscores))) # R1 Gradient Penalty # Compute gradient of D with respect to real patches realscores.requiresgrad(True) gradreal = torch.autograd.grad( realscores.sum(), realpatches, creategraph=True)[0] r1penalty = torch.mean(torch.norm(gradreal.view(gradreal.size(0), -1), dim=1) 2) # Reconstruction Loss (placeholder for specific implementation) reconloss = computereconstructionloss(discriminator) # Total Loss lambda1 = 10.0 # Typical value for R1, not given in sources, marked as lambda2 = 1.0 # Typical value for recon, not given in sources, marked as totalloss = advlossgen + advlossreal + lambda1 r1penalty + lambda2 reconloss # 6. Optimize optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return generator, discriminator def extractpatch(image, scales, patchsizeh, imagesizehprime): """ Extracts a patch from the image based on the scale factor s. When s=1, the patch covers the entire image. When s=0.25, the effective resolution is higher relative to the patch. This function abstracts the specific cropping/resizing logic described in. """ # Implementation detail: The paper states "Implementation-wise, we simply repeat # the scale value to match the patch resolution." This suggests s might be # concatenated as a channel or used to modulate the patch. # The spatial extraction logic is not explicitly detailed beyond "s is a function of scale". # We assume standard cropping or resizing based on s. pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls Super-resolution: The method does not apply a super-resolution module on the rendered values; it directly outputs RGB color images or patches. Precision: The scale s is sampled from a continuous uniform distribution, requiring careful handling of floating-point precision when mapping to discrete pixel coordinates for patch extraction. Degenerate Input: The method assumes valid 2D observations. If input images are of poor quality or lack sufficient texture, the discriminator may struggle to learn multi-scale features. A convolutional discriminator that grows progressively in resolution to stabilize training and allow larger batch sizes at lower resolutions. It provides the architectural foundation upon which Progressive Patch Scaling operates. Progressive GAN Discriminator Uses GANs to generate 3D scenes from 2D images. Progressive Patch Scaling is a specific training procedure within this framework to improve discriminator stability. GAN-based Volume Rendering Time Complexity: Training typically exhibits the best KID score around 300 to 400 epochs. The progressive reduction of patch scale over the first 100 epochs adds computational overhead due to dynamic patch extraction and augmentation. Memory Complexity: The fixed patch size (64 \times 64) keeps memory usage constant regardless of the input image resolution (512 \times 512), allowing for larger batch sizes (1,000 samples) compared to full-resolution training. Measured Performance: Tested on Replica and Matterport3D datasets. The method achieves realistic 3D scene variations and view-consistent representations. Strengths: Promotes diversity and stability in 3D GAN training by forcing the discriminator to learn from multi-scale features. Allows the use of large batch sizes by processing small patches. Limitations: Does not apply super-resolution, which may limit the sharpness of generated details compared to methods that explicitly upsample. When to Use: Suitable for 3D GAN training from limited 2D observations where stability and diversity are critical. When Not to Use: When super-resolution is required for high-fidelity output, or when computational resources are extremely limited for the initial 100 epochs of dynamic scaling. Progressive Patch Scaling was introduced in the SinGRAF paper (2023) by. It is designed to address the challenges of training 3D GANs from a limited set of 2D observations. The method builds on the concept of progressive training in GANs, adapting it to the patch-based discrimination of 3D rendered views. It is used in the context of learning a 3D Generative Radiance Field for a single scene, specifically for indoor scenes from the Replica and Matterport3D datasets. name: Volumetric Sensor for Differentiable Rendering
head: DeltaVolumetricSensor
body: The Volumetric Sensor (DeltaVolumetricSensor) is a differentiable rendering component that accumulates radiance contributions into a volumetric film using delta tracking or similar path tracing logic, supporting both forward and reverse-mode automatic differentiation. It distinguishes itself from standard differentiable volume rendering by explicitly managing the gradient propagation through the scattering and extinction coefficients within the sensor's accumulation step, rather than relying solely on the integrator's path tracing loop. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray parameters (origin, direction, time t), volume density field (\sigmat), scattering coefficient (\sigmas), emitted radiance (em), and an active ray mask. Outputs: Accumulated radiance in the film buffer and gradients for \sigmat, \sigmas, and em. Data Structures: Film Buffer: Stores accumulated radiance. In primal mode, this is the final output. In forward-mode AD, contributions are scattered into a gradient buffer (δL.array). Gradient Buffers: gem, gst, gss initialized to zeros, storing gradients for emitted radiance, total extinction, and scattering coefficients respectively. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize gradient buffers gem, gst, gss to zeros. 2. Ray Validation: Determine active rays using active = mi.Bool(active & mei.isvalid()). 3. Position and Voxel Lookup: Compute ray position pos = ray(mei.t). Determine the current voxel index currentvoxel and its flat index currentvoxelflat. Check if the position is inside the grid bounds isinsidegrid. 4. Index Selection: Select the accumulation index. If surface-aware, use 2currentvoxelflat for inside and 2currentvoxelflat+1 for outside. Otherwise, use currentvoxelflat. 5. Gradient Setup: Detach primal values for emitted, sigmas, and sigmat to break the computational graph where necessary. Enable gradients for these variables and set initial gradients using dr.setgrad. 6. Forward-Mode AD Propagation: If operating in forward-mode AD, propagate gradients from sigmat to sigmas if sigmat has a gradient; otherwise, propagate from sigmas. Set gradients for ss and st accordingly. 7. Contribution Calculation: Compute the radiance contribution using the formulas below. 8. Accumulation: Primal Mode: Write the contribution to the film: self.mfilm.write(contrib, idx, active & isinsidegrid). Forward Mode (Non-Primal): Scatter and reduce the contribution into the gradient buffer δL.array. Formulas: The core accumulation relies on delta tracking statistics: Scattering Coefficient: sa = \sigmat - \sigmas Transmittance: tr = e^{-\sigmat t} Transmittance PDF: tr{pdf} = tr \cdot \sigmat Inverse PDF: inv{pdf} = \text{select}(tr{pdf} \neq 0, \text{detach}(1/tr{pdf}), 0) Throughput: throughput = \text{detach}(attenuation \cdot e^{\sigmat t{prev}}) \cdot e^{-\sigmat t{prev}} \cdot \text{select}(\sigmas \neq 0, \sigmas^{n{scat}} / \text{detach}(\sigmas^{n{scat}}), 1) Contribution: contrib = \text{select}(active, throughput \cdot sa \cdot tr \cdot inv{pdf} \cdot em, 0) Parameters: nscat: Number of scattering events considered in the throughput term. Not given in the sources. attenuation: Pre-computed attenuation factor. Not given in the sources. tprev: Previous time/distance step. Not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Inverse PDF Calculation: The calculation of invpdf is noted as potentially incorrect if free-flight distances are not sampled proportional to transmittance. Implementers must ensure the sampling strategy matches the PDF definition to avoid biased gradients. Gradient Detachment: Care must be taken when using detach() in the throughput and inverse PDF calculations to prevent gradient flow through terms that should remain constant during the specific AD mode. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import drjit as dr import mitsuba as mi def volumetricsensorstep(ray, mei, sigmat, sigmas, em, active, isinsidegrid, currentvoxelflat, surfaceaware=False, mode='primal', t=1.0, attenuation=1.0, tprev=0.0, nscat=1): """ Computes radiance contribution and handles gradient accumulation for the Volumetric Sensor. Args: ray: Ray object providing position and time. mei: Microstate or execution context. sigmat: Total extinction coefficient tensor. sigmas: Scattering coefficient tensor. em: Emitted radiance tensor. active: Boolean tensor of active rays. isinsidegrid: Boolean tensor indicating if ray is inside volume bounds. currentvoxelflat: Flat index of the current voxel. surfaceaware: Boolean flag for surface-aware accumulation indexing. mode: 'primal' or 'forward'. t: Step size/distance. Not given in the sources. attenuation: Pre-computed attenuation factor. Not given in the sources. tprev: Previous time/distance step. Not given in the sources. nscat: Number of scattering events. Not given in the sources. Returns: contrib: Radiance contribution tensor. gem, gst, gss: Gradient buffers. """ # 1. Initialize gradients to zeros gem = dr.zeroslike(em) gst = dr.zeroslike(sigmat) gss = dr.zeroslike(sigmas) # 2. Determine active rays active = mi.Bool(active & mei.isvalid()) # 3. Compute ray position and voxel index pos = ray(mei.t) # currentvoxelflat and isinsidegrid are provided by the traversal logic # 4. Select index for accumulation if surfaceaware: idx = dr.select(isinsidegrid, 2 currentvoxelflat, 2 currentvoxelflat + 1) else: idx = currentvoxelflat # 5. Detach and enable gradients emdetached = dr.detach(em) sigmasdetached = dr.detach(sigmas) sigmatdetached = dr.detach(sigmat) # 6. Forward-mode AD propagation if mode == 'forward': if dr.hasgrad(sigmat): # Propagate gradients from sigmat to sigmas pass elif dr.hasgrad(sigmas): # Propagate gradients from sigmas pass # Set gradients for ss and st pass # 7. Compute physics terms sa = sigmat - sigmas tr = dr.exp(-sigmatdetached t) trpdf = tr sigmatdetached invpdf = dr.select(trpdf != 0, dr.detach(1.0 / trpdf), 0.0) term1 = dr.detach(attenuation dr.exp(sigmatdetached tprev)) term2 = dr.exp(-sigmatdetached tprev) term3 = dr.select(sigmas != 0, sigmas nscat / dr.detach(sigmas nscat), 1.0) throughput = term1 term2 term3 # 8. Contribution contrib = dr.select(active, throughput sa tr invpdf emdetached, 0.0) # 9. Accumulation if mode == 'primal': # self.mfilm.write(contrib, idx, active & isinsidegrid) pass else: # Scatter reduce contribution into δL.array pass return contrib, gem, gst, gss A variant of the volumetric sensor that uses a majorant for ratio tracking or similar variance reduction techniques in volumetric rendering. It requires a majorant property during initialization, which represents the maximum extinction coefficient used to bound the sampling probability. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of active rays and samples per ray, dominated by the exponential and selection operations in the contribution formula. Memory Complexity: O(n) for the film buffer and gradient buffers, where n is the number of voxels or pixels, depending on the accumulation target. Strengths: Supports both forward and reverse-mode AD, allowing flexibility in optimization strategies. Limitations: The inverse PDF calculation is sensitive to sampling strategies; incorrect sampling proportional to transmittance leads to biased gradients. Requires specific Mitsuba variants (cudaadmono, llvmadmono, metaladmono) to function. The Volumetric Sensor originates from the drtvam repository, an inverse rendering framework for tomographic volumetric additive manufacturing. It leverages the Dr.Jit library for differentiable programming and is tied to specific Mitsuba renderer variants that support automatic differentiation. name: Parameter-space ReSTIR
head: GRIS for derivatives, PGRIS, Parameter-Space Differentiable Rendering, Parameter-centric reservoirs
body: Parameter-space ReSTIR is a differentiable rendering formulation that computes gradients with respect to scene parameters directly in parameter space rather than image space. It solves the memory bottleneck of standard reservoir-based differentiable rendering by reformulating the derivative estimation as a single integral over the parameter space. This allows the method to store only one reservoir per parameter (texel), accumulating derivative estimates from all relevant pixels, thereby reducing storage complexity from O(\text{pixels} \times \text{parameters}) to O(\text{parameters}). It builds on Differentiable volume rendering by enabling efficient sample reuse across optimization iterations. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Scene parameters (e.g., texture maps defining density \sigma or color \mathbf{c}), camera rays, and a loss function L dependent on the rendered image \hat{C}. Outputs: Gradient estimates \nabla\theta L with respect to the scene parameters \theta. Data Structures: The core data structure is the Parameter-space Reservoir, which stores a single selected sample and its associated weights. Reservoir Layout: The Reservoir struct contains five fields: 1. x: The selected sample (e.g., a path or sample index). 2. wsum: The sum of weights, calculated as \sum (q/p), where q is the target distribution and p is the source distribution. 3. M: The number of candidates or confidence weight. 4. W: The unbiased contribution weight. 5. lock: A synchronization lock to handle concurrent updates from multiple pixels. Algorithm Steps: 1. Candidate Generation: Generate paths from the camera, restricted to visible texels to avoid wasted computation on invisible parameters. 2. Reservoir Update: For each pixel, compute the derivative contribution of each candidate sample with respect to the texels it intersects, and update the corresponding texel's reservoir. The update uses the reservoir resampling rule: a new candidate xs with weight ws replaces the current reservoir sample x with probability ws / w{sum}. 3. Reuse Across Iterations: At optimization iteration v+1, if a newly drawn sample is occluded or poor, the algorithm reuses the sample stored in the reservoir from iteration v. This allows obtaining unoccluded samples by leveraging previous iterations' results. 4. Gradient Estimation: Use the final selected sample from each texel's reservoir to compute the derivative of the loss L with respect to the parameter. The weight w characterizes how the change in parameter affects the radiance carried by the path and how this change affects the loss L. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import threading import random class Reservoir: def init(self): self.x = 0 # Selected sample self.wsum = 0.0 # Sum of weights self.M = 0 # Number of candidates self.W = 0.0 # Unbiased contribution weight self.lock = threading.Lock() def update(self, xs, ws): with self.lock: self.wsum += ws if random.random() < (ws / self.wsum): self.x = xs self.M += 1 self.W = self.W + ws - (self.W ws / self.wsum) def parameterspacerestir(sceneparams, rays, lossfn, numiterations): reservoirs = {t: Reservoir() for t in sceneparams.texels} for v in range(numiterations): paths = [generatepath(ray, sceneparams) for ray in rays] for path in paths: for t in path.intersectedtexels: ws = computederivativeweight(path, t, lossfn) reservoirs[t].update(path.sampleid, ws) gradients = {t: evaluategradient(reservoirs[t].x, t, lossfn) for t in sceneparams.texels} sceneparams.update(gradients) def generatepath(ray, sceneparams): # Standard path generation from camera ray return Path(ray.origin, ray.direction, sceneparams) def computederivativeweight(path, t, lossfn): # Standard AD step to compute derivative weight return lossfn.derivative(path, t) def evaluategradient(sample, t, lossfn): # Standard gradient evaluation from selected sample return lossfn.evaluate(sample, t) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Invisible Texels: Generating candidates for texels not visible from the camera is wasteful as their contribution to the loss is zero. Visibility culling is required. Concurrency: Multiple pixels may update the same texel's reservoir simultaneously, requiring synchronization locks. Precision: Accumulating weights in wsum can lead to precision issues if weights vary significantly in magnitude. A data structure for storing a single selected sample and its associated weights to support reservoir resampling in parameter space. It allows for efficient merging and updating of candidate samples across iterations. It is chosen when memory usage must be minimized by sharing derivative estimates across pixels for a single parameter. See Parameter-space Reservoir. Memory Complexity: O(\text{parameters}) or O(\text{texels}), compared to O(\text{pixels} \times \text{parameters}) for per-pixel reservoirs. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of paths and texels, with candidate generation limited to visible texels. Strengths: Significant memory reduction for inverse rendering with many parameters; enables sample reuse across optimization iterations. Limitations: Requires synchronization for concurrent updates; visibility culling is necessary to avoid wasted computation. When to use: Inverse rendering problems with large texture maps or parameter sets where memory is a bottleneck. Parameter-space ReSTIR was introduced by Chang, Sivaram, Nowrouzezahrai, Hachisuka, Ramamoorthi, and Li. It extends Generalized Resampled Importance Sampling (GRIS) [Lin et al. 2022] to differentiable rendering. It builds on the principles of ReSTIR [Talbot et al. 2005] and applies them to the estimation of derivatives in inverse rendering. name: Parameter-space Reservoir
head: Parameter-space ReSTIR Reservoir
body: A data structure for storing a single selected sample and its associated weights to support reservoir resampling in parameter space, allowing for efficient merging and updating of candidate samples across iterations. It serves as the core storage mechanism for Parameter-space ReSTIR, enabling the reuse of samples across optimization iterations by storing one reservoir per parameter (texel) rather than per pixel. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A candidate sample xs and its associated weight ws (typically the ratio q/p). Output: An updated reservoir state containing the new selected sample, updated weight sums, and confidence metrics. Data Structures: The Reservoir struct contains five fields: 1. x: The currently selected sample. 2. wsum: The sum of weights, calculated as q/p. 3. M: The number of candidates or confidence weight. 4. W: The unbiased contribution weight. 5. lock: A synchronization lock to ensure thread-safe updates. Algorithm: The reservoir is updated using weighted reservoir sampling. When a new candidate (xs, ws) arrives, the reservoir state is updated as follows: 1. Acquire the reservoir lock. 2. Update the sum of weights: wsum \leftarrow wsum + ws. 3. Generate a random number r \in 0, 1). 4. If r < \frac{ws}{wsum}, update the selected sample: x \leftarrow xs. 5. Release the reservoir lock. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Reservoir: def init(self): self.x = 0 # Selected sample self.wsum = 0 # Sum of weights (q / p) self.M = 0 # Number of candidates / confidence weight self.W = 0 # Unbiased contribution weight self.lock = 0 # Lock to synchronize the reservoir update def update(self, xs, ws): # Acquire lock to prevent race conditions during concurrent updates acquirelock(self.lock) self.wsum = self.wsum + ws # Weighted reservoir sampling: select new sample with probability proportional to weight if random() < (ws / self.wsum): self.x = xs releaselock(self.lock) Parameters and Edge Cases: The weight ws represents the importance sampling ratio q/p. The lock mechanism is critical for parallel implementations where multiple threads may update the same texel's reservoir simultaneously. If wsum is zero initially, the first update sets x = xs with probability 1. This variant is used in [unbiased inverse volume rendering to estimate gradients with respect to heterogeneous medium parameters. Instead of computing the full O(n^2) gradient cost by tracing recursive paths at every bounce, this method selects only a single bounce of the original path to spawn a recursive path for gradient estimation. Steps: 1. As the path is traversed, update a reservoir using weighted reservoir sampling. 2. The weight for each segment is proportional to the throughput \text{Tr}(d) of that path segment. 3. Record the segment index and the necessary state to spawn the recursive path in the reservoir. 4. After the path is complete, spawn a single recursive path from the selected segment to estimate the gradient. Formula: The final estimate is weighted by w = \sum{d=0}^n \text{Tr}(d), where n is the path length and \text{Tr}(d) is the throughput of the path segment. This weight represents the unnormalized inverse probability of being selected. Parameters: n: The length of the path (number of segments). \text{Tr}(d): The throughput of the corresponding path segment d. Comparison: This method increases gradient variance compared to the O(n^2) full estimation but remains well below the variance of delta tracking. It reduces the computational cost from O(n^2) to O(n). Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: O(1) per texel, as only one reservoir is stored per parameter location. Time: The update operation is O(1) per candidate. In the gradient estimation variant, the cost is reduced from O(n^2) to O(n) by selecting only a single bounce. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Enables efficient sample reuse across optimization iterations. Reduces gradient estimation cost significantly compared to full path tracing. Limitations: The single-bounce gradient estimation variant increases gradient variance compared to the full O(n^2) estimator. Requires synchronization locks for parallel updates, which may introduce contention. When to Use: Use for differentiable volume rendering where sample reuse across iterations is beneficial. Use for inverse volume rendering when computational cost of full gradient estimation is prohibitive, accepting higher variance for lower cost. The Parameter-space Reservoir was introduced by Chang, Sivaram, Nowrouzezahrai, Hachisuka, Ramamoorthi, and Li in 2022 as part of the Parameter-space ReSTIR framework for differentiable and inverse rendering. The weighted reservoir sampling variant for gradient estimation was proposed by Lin et al. in 2023 in the context of unbiased inverse volume rendering with differential trackers. name: Differentiable Direct Volume Rendering (DVR)
head: Differentiable Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) family
body: Differentiable Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) enables the optimization of 3D scene parameters (such as neural network weights, transfer functions, or camera poses) by computing gradients of a rendering loss with respect to input variables. It solves the problem of optimizing visualization parameters using only 2D image supervision, eliminating the need for 3D ground truth data. It differs from voxel-based differentiable renderers by avoiding the storage of intermediate volumetric data, thereby achieving a memory footprint independent of sampling resolution. Unlike mesh-based methods, it represents geometry continuously as an isosurface of a neural network, allowing for arbitrary resolution extraction. The core mechanism is the evaluation of the volume rendering equation and the propagation of gradients through the integration steps. The standard emission-absorption model computes the color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} as: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\kappai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \kappai is the absorption coefficient, \deltai is the step size, \mathbf{c}i is the color, and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \kappaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance. Differentiation strategies fall into three main categories: 1. Reverse-Mode Automatic Differentiation (AD): Standard backpropagation through the computational graph. 2. Adjoint Method: Computes gradients by propagating adjoint variables backward through the rendering algorithm, evaluating the chain rule from output to input. 3. Analytic Inversion / Explicit Gradients: Uses a-priori knowledge of the DVR operations to invert the order of operations or derive closed-form gradients, reducing memory consumption by avoiding the storage of intermediate results. Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR) is a method for training implicit neural representations of 3D shape and texture using only 2D RGB image supervision, eliminating the need for 3D ground truth data. It differs from voxel-based differentiable renderers by avoiding the storage of intermediate volumetric data, thereby achieving a memory footprint independent of sampling resolution. Unlike mesh-based methods, it represents geometry continuously as an isosurface of a neural network, allowing for arbitrary resolution extraction. DiffDVR is an image-based optimization method that uses differentiable direct volume rendering to optimize transfer functions and other continuous parameters by minimizing residuals between rendered images and a reference. It sets itself apart from standard reverse-mode automatic differentiation by using analytic inversion of the blending functions to recompute intermediate results, thereby reducing memory consumption from O(kn) to O(n) without storing the computational graph. Unlike least-squares voxel-based solvers, DiffDVR accounts for ray-based integration effects like occlusion and attenuation, emphasizing structural differences in residual maps. It builds on the emission-absorption model shared by Differentiable Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) and differs from Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR) and Differentiable DRR Generation via Vectorized GPU Siddon's Method in its explicit analytic inversion of light accumulation along view rays. This method generates Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs (DRRs) that are fully differentiable with respect to 7 geometric imaging parameters by reformulating Siddon's ray-tracing algorithm as a series of vectorized tensor operations within PyTorch. It solves the problem of slow gradient-based optimization in intraoperative imaging by leveraging automatic differentiation, avoiding the high memory costs of standard reverse-mode AD and the complexity of adjoint methods. Unlike iterative ray-tracing implementations, it computes all plane intersections in parallel using GPU tensor algebra, trading memory efficiency for speed and compatibility with deep learning frameworks. Definition: A differentiable formulation of DVR that generalizes the emission-absorption model to arbitrary feature spaces and color channels, allowing replaceable functions for feature extraction, TFs, composition, and decoding. Step: The pipeline consists of three parts: (1) Feature extraction E(\mathbf{I}), (2) Deep volume rendering (sampling and accumulation), (3) Image decoding D(\mathbf{C}). Formula: Feature extraction transforms scalar input volume \mathbf{I} to nF-dimensional feature space: \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}) = E(\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{x})). Samples (\mathbf{C}i, \mathbf{A}i) are combined with an accumulation function \mathcal{A} to a final ray color: \mathbf{C}'\infty = \mathcal{A}(\{(\mathbf{C}i, \mathbf{A}i)|i\}). The image decoder transforms rendered features back to RGB: \mathbf{C}^{RGB} = D(\mathbf{C}'\infty). The concept of differentiable volume rendering has evolved to support inverse rendering and neural implicit representations. More recently, methods like Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR) have enabled the training of neural networks for 3D reconstruction from 2D images. The generalized formulation allows for flexible integration of deep learning components into the rendering pipeline.
