name: Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR)
body: Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR) is a method for training implicit neural representations of 3D shape and texture directly from 2D RGB images and object masks, without requiring 3D ground truth supervision. It solves the problem of optimizing continuous implicit functions by casting rays, finding the intersection with the implicit isosurface, and backpropagating gradients through the rendering process using analytic implicit differentiation. It sets itself apart from voxel-based differentiable rendering by not storing intermediate volumetric data in the forward pass, making its memory footprint independent of sampling accuracy, and from mesh-based methods by avoiding discretization artifacts. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera origin \mathbf{r}0, ray direction \mathbf{w} for each pixel \mathbf{u}, network parameters \theta, optional latent code \mathbf{z} for conditional generation, isosurface threshold \tau, and sampling parameters n, \Delta s, s0. Outputs: Rendered color \hat{\mathbf{I}}\mathbf{u} for each pixel, and gradients \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} for optimization. Data Structures: Occupancy Network f\theta: A neural network mapping \mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow [0, 1] that assigns an occupancy probability to every point \mathbf{p} in 3D space. Texture Network t\theta: A neural network mapping \mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3 that regresses an RGB color value for every point \mathbf{p}. Implementation: f\theta and t\theta are implemented as a single neural network with two shallow output heads sharing parameters. Parameters: \tau: Isosurface threshold defining the level set f\theta(\mathbf{p}) = \tau. Typical value: 0.5. Range: [0, 1]. n: Number of equally-spaced samples on the ray. Starts at 16 and increases to 128 during training. \Delta s: Step size for equally-spaced samples on the ray. s0: Start of the sampling interval, determining the closest possible surface point. \mathbf{z}: Latent embedding vector conditioned on the input image, used to modulate the networks. Algorithm: 1. Ray Casting and Surface Intersection (Forward Pass): For a pixel \mathbf{u} with ray \mathbf{r}(d) = \mathbf{r}0 + d\mathbf{w}: a. Evaluate f\theta at n equally-spaced points \mathbf{p}j^{\text{ray}} = \mathbf{r}(j\Delta s + s0) for j=1 \dots n. b. Find the smallest index j such that f\theta(\mathbf{p}{j+1}^{\text{ray}}) \geq \tau > f\theta(\mathbf{p}j^{\text{ray}}). This identifies the interval containing the surface. c. Approximate the surface depth \hat{d} using the iterative secant method on the interval [j\Delta s + s0, (j+1)\Delta s + s0]. d. Compute the intersection point \hat{\mathbf{p}} = \mathbf{r}(\hat{d}). 2. Color Evaluation: Compute the rendered color \hat{\mathbf{I}}\mathbf{u} = t\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}}). 3. Gradient Computation (Backward Pass): The goal is to compute \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta}. Using the multivariate chain rule: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} = \sum\mathbf{u} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{I}}\mathbf{u}} \cdot \frac{\partial \hat{\mathbf{I}}\mathbf{u}}{\partial \theta} where \frac{\partial \hat{\mathbf{I}}\mathbf{u}}{\partial \theta} = \frac{\partial t\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}})}{\partial \theta} + \frac{\partial t\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}})}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{p}}} \cdot \frac{\partial \hat{\mathbf{p}}}{\partial \theta}. The term \frac{\partial \hat{\mathbf{p}}}{\partial \theta} is derived via implicit differentiation of f\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}}) = \tau: \frac{\partial \hat{\mathbf{p}}}{\partial \theta} = \mathbf{w} \frac{\partial \hat{d}}{\partial \theta} \frac{\partial \hat{d}}{\partial \theta} = - \left( \frac{\partial f\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}})}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{p}}} \cdot \mathbf{w} \right)^{-1} \frac{\partial f\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}})}{\partial \theta}. In practice, to compute the gradient of the loss with respect to \theta efficiently without storing intermediate volumetric data: a. Let \lambda = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{d}} be the incoming gradient from the loss with respect to depth. b. Compute the scalar factor \mu{\text{factor}} = - \left( \frac{\partial f\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}})}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{p}}} \cdot \mathbf{w} \right)^{-1}. c. Multiply \lambda element-wise by \mu{\text{factor}} to get \mu = \lambda \cdot \mu{\text{factor}}. d. Backpropagate through f\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}}) using reverse-mode automatic differentiation with the modified gradient \mu. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def renderpixel(rayorigin, raydirection, network, latentcode, tau=0.5, nsamples=128, s0=0.0, ds=0.01): """ Renders a single pixel using DVR and computes the gradient factor for backpropagation. rayorigin: (3,) tensor raydirection: (3,) tensor network: DVRNetwork instance (forward returns (occ, texture)) latentcode: (latentdim,) tensor tau: isosurface threshold nsamples: number of samples on ray s0: start distance ds: step size Returns: color (3,), mufactor (scalar), phat (3,), dfdp (3,) """ # 1. Sample points along ray: pj = r0 + (s0 + jds) w distances = s0 + torch.arange(nsamples) ds points = rayorigin.unsqueeze(0) + distances.unsqueeze(1) raydirection.unsqueeze(0) # 2. Evaluate occupancy network ftheta occ, = network(points, latentcode.unsqueeze(0)) occ = occ.squeeze(1) # 3. Find transition interval where ftheta crosses tau inside = occ >= tau transitions = (inside[1:] & ~inside[:-1]) if not transitions.any(): # No intersection found; return dummy values return torch.zeros(3), torch.tensor(0.0), points[0], torch.zeros(3) j = torch.argmax(transitions.float()) # 4. Secant method refinement within interval [distances[j], distances[j+1]] pj = points[j] pj1 = points[j+1] fj = occ[j] - tau fj1 = occ[j+1] - tau denom = fj1 - fj if denom.abs() < 1e-8: dhat = (distances[j] + distances[j+1]) / 2.0 else: dhat = distances[j] - fj (distances[j+1] - distances[j]) / denom phat = rayorigin + dhat raydirection # 5. Evaluate texture network ttheta at intersection, texture = network(phat.unsqueeze(0), latentcode.unsqueeze(0)) color = texture.squeeze(0) # 6. Compute gradient factor for backward pass # We need df/dp at phat to compute the scalar factor mufactor = -1 / (df/dp. w) phat.requiresgrad = True occhat, = network(phat.unsqueeze(0), latentcode.unsqueeze(0)) fval = occhat - tau dfdp = torch.autograd.grad(fval.sum(), phat, creategraph=True)[0].squeeze(0) dfdpdotw = torch.dot(dfdp, raydirection) if dfdpdotw.abs() < 1e-8: mufactor = torch.tensor(0.0) else: mufactor = -1.0 / dfdpdotw return color, mufactor, phat, dfdp def computegradients(rayorigins, raydirections, network, latentcodes, targetcolors, tau=0.5, nsamples=128, s0=0.0, ds=0.01): """ Computes gradients of loss w.r.t network parameters. """ # Forward pass colors, mufactors, phats, dfdps = renderbatch(rayorigins, raydirections, network, latentcodes, tau, nsamples, s0, ds) # Loss loss = torch.mean(torch.abs(colors - targetcolors)) # Backward pass setup # 1. Gradient of loss w.r.t rendered colors: dL/dcolor dLdcolor = torch.sign(colors - targetcolors) / colors.shape[0] # 2. Gradient of loss w.r.t phat via texture network # dL/dphat = dL/dcolor dt/dphat dLdphat = torch.autograd.grad(colors.sum(), phats, gradoutputs=dLdcolor, creategraph=True)[0] # 3. Incoming gradient w.r.t depth: lambda = dL/dphat. w lambdaval = torch.sum(dLdphat raydirections, dim=1) # 4. Compute final gradient factor: mu = mufactor lambda mu = mufactors lambdaval # 5. Backpropagate through occupancy network ftheta # The evidence states: multiply lambda by mufactor, then backprop through ftheta. # We inject the scaled gradient into the computation graph of ftheta. dummy = (dfdps mu.unsqueeze(1)).sum() dummy.backward() return loss def renderbatch(rayorigins, raydirections, network, latentcodes, tau=0.5, nsamples=128, s0=0.0, ds=0.01): B = rayorigins.shape[0] colors = torch.zeros(B, 3) mufactors = torch.zeros(B) phats = torch.zeros(B, 3) dfdps = torch.zeros(B, 3) for i in range(B): c, mu, p, df = renderpixel(rayorigins[i], raydirections[i], network, latentcodes[i], tau, nsamples, s0, ds) colors[i] = c mufactors[i] = mu phats[i] = p dfdps[i] = df return colors, mufactors, phats, dfdps Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Intersection: If a ray does not cross the isosurface within the sampling interval [s0, n\Delta s + s0], the transition detection fails. The implementation must handle this gracefully to avoid division by zero or invalid secant steps. Numerical Stability: Implicit differentiation requires computing \frac{\partial f\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}})}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{p}}} \cdot \mathbf{w}. If this dot product is near zero, the gradient factor \mu becomes unstable. A small epsilon guard is required. Sampling Resolution: The accuracy of \hat{d} depends on n and \Delta s. Insufficient sampling may miss thin structures or cause secant divergence. Multi-component objective function distinguishing pixels into three sets (P0, P1, P2) to enforce photometric consistency, freespace regularization, and occupancy induction. MLP architecture, ray sampling strategy, and training configuration for implicit neural representations. Loss functions for training occupancy and texture networks using 2D image supervision, handling empty space and missing surfaces. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples n per ray and the cost of evaluating the neural network. n increases from 16 to 128 during training. Memory Complexity: Memory footprint is independent of sampling accuracy because no intermediate volumetric data is stored in the forward pass. This contrasts with voxel-based methods which require storing all intermediate evaluations. Strengths: Memory-efficient, scalable to high resolutions, learns from 2D images without 3D supervision, produces watertight meshes. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of sampling parameters (n, \Delta s, s0) and threshold \tau. Implicit differentiation can be numerically unstable if the gradient of the occupancy function is small. When to use: When 3D ground truth is unavailable, and high-resolution continuous representations are needed. When not to use: When explicit mesh or voxel output is required without post-processing, or when real-time rendering is critical without pre-training. DVR was introduced to overcome the limitations of voxel-based and mesh-based differentiable rendering, which suffer from discretization artifacts and low resolution. It builds on the concept of occupancy networks and texture fields. The key insight is that depth gradients can be derived analytically using implicit differentiation, allowing the learning of implicit shape and texture representations directly from RGB images. The method enables single-view and multi-view 3D reconstruction from 2D photographs. name: DVR Training Losses
head: DVR Loss Functions, Multi-Loss Training for DVR, Occupancy Network Losses
body: DVR Training Losses constitute a multi-component objective function used to train the occupancy network f\theta and texture network t\theta in Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR). The method solves the problem of optimizing implicit neural representations from 2D image supervision by distinguishing pixels into three disjoint sets (P0, P1, P2) based on object mask membership and predicted surface depth finiteness. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly decoupling photometric consistency, freespace regularization, and occupancy induction into separate loss terms applied to specific pixel subsets, rather than relying on a single global rendering loss. Inputs: A batch of training images Ik with corresponding camera intrinsics, extrinsics, and binary object masks Mk. Optional ground truth depth maps Dk. The current parameters \theta of the occupancy network f\theta and texture network t\theta. A sampling count Np, the number of pixels to sample from the image plane per batch. Outputs: A scalar total loss value \mathcal{L}(\theta) used for backpropagation. The method operates on sets of pixel coordinates \mathbf{u} on the image plane. These pixels are classified into three mutually exclusive sets: P0: Pixels inside the object mask Mk where the occupancy network predicts a finite surface depth \hat{d}. P1: Pixels outside the object mask Mk. P2: Pixels inside the object mask Mk where the occupancy network predicts an infinite surface depth (no intersection). 1. Sampling: Randomly sample an image Ik from the training set and select Np points \mathbf{u} on the image plane. 2. Classification: For each sampled point \mathbf{u}, determine its membership in P0, P1, or P2 based on the mask Mk and the predicted depth \hat{d} from the occupancy network. 3. Loss Computation: Compute the relevant loss terms for each set: For \mathbf{u} \in P0: Compute \mathcal{L}{\text{rgb}} and optionally \mathcal{L}{\text{depth}} and \mathcal{L}{\text{normal}}. For \mathbf{u} \in P1: Compute \mathcal{L}{\text{freespace}}. For \mathbf{u} \in P2: Compute \mathcal{L}{\text{occupancy}}. 4. Aggregation: Sum the losses to form the total objective. 5. Optimization: Update parameters \theta using gradient descent. RGB Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{rgb}}) Applied to points \mathbf{u} \in P0. It enforces photo-consistency between the ground truth image features and the rendered image features. \mathcal{L}{\text{rgb}}(\theta) = \sum{\mathbf{u} \in P0} \|\xi(\mathbf{I}){\mathbf{u}} - \xi(\hat{\mathbf{I}}){\mathbf{u}}\| Where: \xi(\cdot) is a feature extractor computing RGB values and optionally image gradients. \|\cdot\| is a robust error metric, typically the L1-norm. \hat{\mathbf{I}} is the rendered image. Depth Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{depth}}) Applied to points \mathbf{u} \in P0 when ground truth depth d is available. \mathcal{L}{\text{depth}}(\theta) = \sum{\mathbf{u} \in P0} |d - \hat{d}|1 Where: d is the ground truth depth value for pixel \mathbf{u}. \hat{d} is the predicted surface depth for pixel \mathbf{u}. Freespace Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{freespace}}) Applied to points \mathbf{u} \in P1. It penalizes finite predicted depth outside the object mask, encouraging the network to predict free space (f\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}}) \approx 0). \mathcal{L}{\text{freespace}}(\theta) = \sum{\mathbf{u} \in P1} \text{BCE}(f\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}}), 0) Where: \text{BCE}(p, y) = -[y \log(p) + (1-y) \log(1-p)] is the Binary Cross Entropy. \hat{\mathbf{p}} = \mathbf{r}(\hat{d}) is the predicted surface point on the ray \mathbf{r}. Edge Case: If no finite surface depth is predicted for \mathbf{u} \in P1, apply the BCE loss to a randomly sampled point on the ray with target 0. Occupancy Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{occupancy}}) Applied to points \mathbf{u} \in P2. It encourages the network to predict occupied space (f\theta \approx 1) along rays where a surface is expected but not found. \mathcal{L}{\text{occupancy}}(\theta) = \sum{\mathbf{u} \in P2} \text{BCE}(f\theta(\mathbf{r}(d{\text{random}})), 1) Where: d{\text{random}} are uniformly sampled depth values along the ray. Single-View Exception: In single-view reconstruction experiments, d{\text{random}} is replaced by the depth of the visual hull (first point on the ray inside all object masks) or ground truth depth if available. Normal Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{normal}}) Optional smoothness prior applied to points \mathbf{u} \in P0. It regularizes surface normals by minimizing the distance between the normal at the predicted surface point and a randomly sampled neighbor. \mathcal{L}{\text{normal}}(\theta) = \sum{\mathbf{u} \in P0} \|\mathbf{n}(\hat{\mathbf{p}}{\mathbf{u}}) - \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{q}{\mathbf{u}})\|2 Where: \mathbf{n}(\cdot) denotes the normal vector computed via gradients of f\theta. \hat{\mathbf{p}}{\mathbf{u}} is the predicted surface point for pixel \mathbf{u}. \mathbf{q}{\mathbf{u}} is a randomly sampled neighbor of \hat{\mathbf{p}}{\mathbf{u}}. Returns predicteddepths and predictedpoints. """ # Placeholder for root-finding algorithm described in parent article. # In practice, uses binary search or Newton's method. predicteddepths = [] predictedpoints = [] for o, d in zip(origins, directions): # Simplified placeholder logic predicteddepths.append(1.0) predictedpoints.append([o[j] + d[j] 1.0 for j in range(3)]) return predicteddepths, predictedpoints def getrenderedfeatures(ux, uy, points, texturenet): return [texturenet(p) for p in points] def getimagefeatures(image, ux, uy): return [image[y][x] for x, y in zip(ux, uy)] def computenormals(points, occupancynet): # Placeholder for gradient computation return [[1.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in points] def sampleneighbors(points, numneighbors=1): return [[p[j] + random.uniform(-0.01, 0.01) for j in range(3)] for p in points] \xi(\cdot): Feature extractor. Typically uses RGB values and optionally image gradients. \|\cdot\|: Robust error metric. Typically L1-loss for RGB and Depth losses, while Freespace and Occupancy losses use Binary Cross Entropy. P0: Set of pixels inside object mask with finite predicted surface depth. P1: Set of pixels outside object mask. P2: Set of pixels inside object mask but with infinite predicted surface depth. Np: Number of random pixels sampled from the image plane per batch. N: Number of images in the training set. Single-View Reconstruction: For the Occupancy Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{occupancy}}), random depth sampling is replaced by the visual hull depth (first point on the ray inside all object masks) or ground truth depth if available. Freespace Loss with No Depth: If a pixel in P1 has no predicted finite depth, the Freespace Loss must be applied to a randomly sampled point on the ray rather than the predicted surface point. Gradient Flow: The gradient from the RGB loss flows through the texture network and the surface point prediction, which depends on the occupancy network. The Freespace and Occupancy losses provide direct gradients to the occupancy network. Root-Finding Queries: This typically involves multiple queries to the occupancy network f\theta. The number of queries depends on the precision of the root-finding algorithm (e.g., binary search iterations). Time: The complexity is dominated by the root-finding operation for surface depth for each sampled pixel Np. The loss computation itself scales linearly with the number of sampled pixels. Memory: Memory usage is proportional to Np for storing sampled points, depths, and intermediate gradients. The method works with as little as one image per object. It can incorporate depth information if available, improving performance. The Normal Loss is particularly useful for real-world data to enforce natural shapes in unconstrained areas. It scales with the number of training images N. Strengths: Explicitly handles different pixel types (inside/outside mask, finite/infinite depth), allowing for targeted supervision. Works with minimal supervision (2D masks). Limitations: Relies on accurate object masks. The quality of the Freespace and Occupancy losses depends on the correct classification of pixels into P1 and P2, which in turn depends on the current state of the occupancy network. Use when training DVR networks from 2D image supervision with object masks. Use when depth information is available to incorporate \mathcal{L}{\text{depth}}. Use when real-world data requires smoothness priors, enabling \mathcal{L}{\text{normal}}. Do not use if only 3D ground truth (e.g., point clouds or meshes) is available without 2D images; consider Training Losses for Implicit Surface Learning instead. Do not use if object masks are not available, as the classification into P0, P1, P2 is not possible. The DVR Training Losses were introduced by Niemeyer et al. in the paper "Differentiable Volumetric Rendering: Learning Implicit 3D Representations Without 3D Supervision". The method was developed to enable the training of implicit neural representations using only 2D image supervision. It builds on the Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR) framework, which allows gradients to flow from the rendered image back to the implicit surface representation. The method is used in single-view and multi-view 3D reconstruction from images, particularly in scenarios where 3D supervision is unavailable or expensive. It is a core component of the Occupancy Networks framework. body: This article details the neural network architecture, ray sampling strategy, and training configuration required to implement Differentiable Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) as described in. It solves the problem of configuring the multi-layer perceptron (MLP) and its associated query pipeline to map 3D spatial coordinates and view directions to volumetric density and color, enabling gradient-based optimization of implicit surface representations. It sets apart from siblings like Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO) by relying on a continuous MLP representation queried via hierarchical sampling rather than a discrete voxel grid, requiring explicit setup of positional encoders and coarse/fine network pairs for importance sampling. Inputs: Ray origins \mathbf{r}0 and directions \mathbf{d} for a batch of pixels. Camera parameters \mathbf{c} (e.g., view direction or latent code). Training iteration count it (optional, for adaptive sampling). Decoder network parameters \theta. Outputs: Rendered color tensor C \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}. Depth tensor D \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 1}. Transmittance and density tensors for loss computation. DepthModule Configuration: tau (float): Occupancy threshold. Default: 0.5. nsteps (tuple): Initial sampling steps range. Default: [128, 129]. nsecantsteps (int): Refinement steps for root finding. Default: 8. depthrange (tuple): Depth interval [s0, s{max}]. Default: [0., 2.4]. scheduleraysampling (bool): Enable adaptive sampling. Default: True. schedulemilestones (list): Iterations for doubling resolution. Default: [50000, 100000, 250000]. initresolution (int): Initial sampling count. Default: 16. maxpoints (int): GPU memory limit for point batches. Default: 3,700,000. checkcubeintersection (bool): Intersect with unit cube. Default: True. chunksize (int): Batch size for forward pass to manage memory. Not given in the sources. Network Architecture: Combined Network: 5 fully-connected ResNet blocks with ReLU activation. Output Layer: 4 dimensions: 1 for occupancy probability, 3 for texture (RGB). Encoder (Single-View): ResNet-18 encoder g\phi outputting a 256-dimensional latent code \mathbf{z}. 1. Initialization: Initialize DepthModule with parameters listed in Data Structures. Set transmittance T as a tensor of ones with shape (N, 1) for the first segment. 2. Ray Sampling Schedule: Determine the number of steps n. If scheduleraysampling is False, use nsteps. If True, call getsamplingaccuracy(it): If schedulemilestones is empty, return [128, 129]. Initialize res = initresolution. Iterate through milestones: if it < milestone, return [res, res + 1]. Otherwise, double res (res = res 2) and continue. Return [res, res + 1] after the loop. 3. Coarse Sampling: Sample n points along the ray at equal intervals \Delta s. The coordinates are computed as: \mathbf{p}j^{\text{ray}} = \mathbf{r}0 + (j \Delta s + s0) \mathbf{d}, \quad j = 0, \dots, n-1 where s0 is the start of the ray sampling interval. 4. Implicit Function Evaluation: Query the decoder network f\theta(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{c}) for occupancy logits at all sampled points. 5. Surface Intersection (Secant Method): Identify the interval [d{low}, d{high}] where the occupancy logit crosses the threshold \tau. Specifically, find j such that f\theta(\mathbf{p}j) < \tau and f\theta(\mathbf{p}{j+1}) \geq \tau. Apply the secant method for nsecantsteps iterations to refine the depth \hat{d}: 1. Initialize d{pred} = (d{low} + d{high}) / 2. 2. For i in range nsecantsteps: Compute midpoint \mathbf{p}{mid} = \mathbf{r}0 + d{pred} \mathbf{d}. Compute f{mid} = f\theta(\mathbf{p}{mid}, \mathbf{c}) - \tau. If f{mid} < 0, set d{low} = d{pred}; else set d{high} = d{pred}. Update d{pred} = 0.5 (d{low} + d{high}). 6. Fine Sampling: Sample additional points around the refined depth \hat{d} (implementation detail: typically using the same n or a finer grid, but sources specify using the refined depth to define the integration range). Note: The provided notes describe the coarse-to-fine transition primarily through the adaptive sampling schedule and the secant refinement, rather than explicit fine-grained stratified sampling steps in the pseudocode. 7. Density and Color Extraction: Convert occupancy logits to density \sigma and extract color \mathbf{c}i. Density: \sigmai = \text{ReLU}(yi) or similar mapping from the network output. Color: \mathbf{c}i = \text{Sigmoid}(y{i+1:4}). 8. Alpha Compositing: Compute segment lengths \deltai by subtracting adjacent depth values. Append a large value (10^{10}) for the last segment to handle ray termination. Compute transmittance: Ti = T{i-1} \cdot \exp(-\sigma{i-1} \delta{i-1} + \epsilon). Compute weights: wi = Ti \cdot (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai + \epsilon)). Aggregate color: C = \sum wi \mathbf{c}i. Aggregate depth: D = \sum wi zi, where zi is the depth of the i-th sample. 9. Chunk Processing: To manage memory, iterate over rays in batches of chunksize, process steps 2-8, and concatenate results. Unverified code. Get nsteps based on schedule if self.scheduleraysampling and iteration is not None: nsteps = self.getsamplingaccuracy(iteration) else: nsteps = self.nsteps # 2. Render using DepthFunction color, depth = DepthFunction.apply( ray0, raydirection, self.decoder, c, nsteps, self.nsecantsteps, self.tau, self.depthrange, self.method, self.checkcubeintersection, self.maxpoints) return color, depth def getsamplingaccuracy(self, it): res = self.initresolution for milestone in self.schedulemilestones: if it < milestone: return [res, res + 1] res = 2 return [res, res + 1] tau: Threshold for occupancy logits. Default: 0.5. nsteps: Number of evaluation steps. Default: [128, 129]. nsecantsteps: Refinement steps. Default: 8. depthrange: Depth interval. Default: [0., 2.4]. scheduleraysampling: Enable adaptive sampling. Default: True. schedulemilestones: Iterations for doubling resolution. Default: [50000, 100000, 250000]. initresolution: Initial sampling count. Default: 16. chunksize: Batch size for forward pass. Not given in the sources. whitebackground: Composite against white background. Default: False. eps: Small constant for numerical stability. Not given in the sources. Precision: The secant method relies on the occupancy logit crossing the threshold \tau. If the network output is flat or noisy, the interval may not be found. Use checkcubeintersection to ensure rays intersect the volume of interest. Boundaries: The last segment delta is set to 10^{10} to ensure the ray terminates correctly if the surface is not found within the sampled range. Memory: Large batches of rays can exceed GPU memory. Use chunksize to process rays in smaller batches. Degenerate Input: If nsteps[1] <= 1, return a tensor of infinity to indicate no rendering. NeRF Model Initialization establishes the neural network architecture, positional encoding functions, and sampling parameters required for Differentiable Direct Volume Rendering (DVR). It solves the problem of configuring the multi-layer perceptron (MLP) and its associated query pipeline to map 3D spatial coordinates and view directions to volumetric density and color. It sets apart from siblings like Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO) by relying on a continuous MLP representation queried via hierarchical sampling rather than a discrete voxel grid, requiring explicit setup of positional encoders and coarse/fine network pairs for importance sampling. Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO) is a differentiable volume rendering method that replaces the multi-layer perceptron (MLP) used in NeRF with direct voxel grids for density and color features, enabling significantly faster training and inference. Unlike NeRF-like methods that query a neural network for density from coordinates, DVGO stores density and color directly in 3D grids, allowing for efficient trilinear interpolation and gradient accumulation. It sets itself apart from its sibling NeRF Model Initialization by using a dense voxel grid representation rather than a coordinate-based MLP, trading off some representational flexibility for computational speed. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot n \cdot d), where N is the number of rays, n is the number of samples per ray, and d is the MLP depth. The secant method adds O(N \cdot n{secant} \cdot d). Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot n \cdot d{out}) for storing intermediate activations, where d{out} is the output dimension of the MLP. Chunking reduces peak memory to O(chunk\size \cdot n \cdot d{out}). Measured Performance: Trained on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU with a batch size of 64 images with 1024 random pixels each. Scaling: Adaptive sampling increases n from 16 to 128 over 250,000 iterations, improving accuracy as training progresses. Strengths: Differentiable surface intersection allows for gradient-based optimization of implicit surfaces. Adaptive sampling balances speed and accuracy. Limitations: MLP queries are slower than voxel grid lookups. Secant method requires smooth occupancy fields. When to Use: When high-quality implicit surface reconstruction is needed and computational resources allow for MLP queries. When Not to Use: When real-time inference is required or memory is severely constrained; consider DVGO instead. The method originates from the work of Mescheder et al. on Occupancy Networks (CVPR 2019) and Niemeyer et al. on Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (CVPR 2020). It was developed to enable learning 3D implicit representations without explicit 3D supervision, using only RGB images. The DVR approach integrates color and density along rays using alpha compositing, computing the final pixel color as a weighted sum of sampled features. body: NeRF Model Initialization establishes the neural network architecture, positional encoding functions, and sampling parameters required for Differentiable Direct Volume Rendering (DVR). It solves the problem of configuring the multi-layer perceptron (MLP) and its associated query pipeline to map 3D spatial coordinates and view directions to volumetric density and color. It sets apart from siblings like Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO) by relying on a continuous MLP representation queried via hierarchical sampling rather than a discrete voxel grid, requiring explicit setup of positional encoders and coarse/fine network pairs for importance sampling. The initialization process configures the coarse and optional fine MLPs for NeRF, along with a query function that applies positional encoding to 3D coordinates and view directions before passing them to the network. Inputs: Training configuration arguments (hyperparameters), camera poses, and optionally checkpoint files for weight loading. Outputs: Initialized model (coarse MLP), optional modelfine (fine MLP), embedfn (positional encoder for coordinates), embeddirsfn (positional encoder for view directions), networkqueryfn (wrapper for network execution), and renderkwargs dictionaries for training and testing. MLP Model: A multi-layer perceptron. Input layer size: inputch (for coordinates) + inputchviews (if useviewdirs is true). Hidden layers: netdepth layers of size netwidth. Skip connections: Input coordinates are concatenated to hidden layers at index skips (default [4]). Output layer: outputch (default 4: RGB + sigma). Positional Encoder (embedfn): Maps a 3D coordinate vector to a higher-dimensional vector using sinusoidal positional encoding. The dimension is determined by multires (log2 of max frequency). View Direction Encoder (embeddirsfn): Maps a 2D view direction vector to a higher-dimensional vector. Dimension determined by multiresviews. Render Kwargs: A dictionary containing: perturb: Boolean/float for jittering samples. Nimportance: Integer for number of fine samples. Nsamples: Integer for number of coarse samples. networkfn: Reference to the coarse network query function. networkfine: Reference to the fine network query function (if Nimportance > 0). useviewdirs: Boolean. whitebkgd: Boolean. rawnoisestd: Float for noise added to sigma. multires: Log2 of max frequency for positional encoding (3D location). Default: 10. netdepth: Number of layers in the network. Default: 8. multiresviews: Log2 of max frequency for positional encoding (2D direction). Default: 4. netwidth: Number of channels per layer. Default: 256. Nsamples: Number of coarse samples per ray. Default: 64. outputch: Number of output channels (RGB + sigma). Default: 4. Nimportance: Number of additional fine samples per ray. Default: 0. netchunk: Number of points sent through the network in parallel (batch size for inference). Default: 102464. perturb: Jitter factor for sampling. Default: 1.0. Set to 0. for no jitter. rawnoisestd: Standard deviation of noise added to regularize sigmaa output. Default: 0. Recommended: 1e0. netdepthfine: Depth of the fine network. Not given in the sources. netwidthfine: Width of the fine network. Not given in the sources. 1. Instantiate Positional Encoders: Create embedfn for 3D coordinates using getembedder(multires, iembed). If useviewdirs is true, create embeddirsfn for 2D view directions using getembedder(multiresviews, iembed). 2. Configure Network Dimensions: Set inputch based on embedfn output size. Set inputchviews based on embeddirsfn output size (if applicable). Set outputch = 4. Set skips = [4]. 3. Initialize Coarse MLP: Call initnerfmodel with parameters D=netdepth, W=netwidth, inputch, outputch, skips, inputchviews, and useviewdirs to create model. 4. Initialize Fine MLP (Optional): If Nimportance > 0, create modelfine using initnerfmodel with D=netdepthfine and W=netwidthfine. Add modelfine variables to the gradient variables list gradvars. 5. Define Query Function: Define networkqueryfn(inputs, viewdirs, networkfn) which calls runnetwork(inputs, viewdirs, networkfn, embedfn, embeddirsfn, netchunk). runnetwork reshapes inputs, applies embedfn to coordinates, applies embeddirsfn to view directions (if useviewdirs), concatenates them, and passes them through networkfn in chunks of size netchunk. 6. Configure Render Kwargs: Create renderkwargstrain with perturb=perturb, Nimportance, Nsamples, networkfn=networkqueryfn, networkfine (if applicable), useviewdirs, whitebkgd, and rawnoisestd. Create renderkwargstest as a copy of renderkwargstrain but with perturb=False and rawnoisestd=0.. 7. Load Checkpoints (Optional): If a list of checkpoint files ckpts is provided, sort them. Filter for files containing 'model' but not 'fine' or 'optimizer'. Load weights into model using model.setweights(np.load(ftweights, allowpickle=True)). If modelfine exists, load corresponding fine weights using the filename pattern '{}fine{}'.format(ftweights[:-11], ftweights[-10:]). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def getembedder(multires, iembed=0): """Standard positional encoding.""" if iembed == 0: embedfn = lambda x: x inputch = 3 else: L = multires freqbands = 2.0 np.linspace(0.0, multires - 1, L) embedfn = lambda x: np.concatenate([x freqbands, np.sin(x freqbands), np.cos(x freqbands)], axis=-1) inputch = 3 + 3 L 2 return embedfn, inputch def initnerfmodel(D, W, inputch, outputch, skips, inputchviews, useviewdirs): """Constructs MLP with D hidden layers of width W. Concatenates input coordinates to hidden layers at indices in skips. If useviewdirs, concatenates encoded view directions before the output layer. Internals not given in the sources. """ # Internals not given in the sources. pass def runnetwork(inputs, viewdirs, fn, embedfn, embeddirsfn, netchunk=102464): """Prepares inputs and applies network 'fn'.""" inputsflat = np.reshape(inputs, [-1, inputs.shape[-1]]) embedded = embedfn(inputsflat) if embeddirsfn is not None: viewdirsflat = np.reshape(viewdirs, [-1, viewdirs.shape[-1]]) embeddedviews = embeddirsfn(viewdirsflat) embedded = np.concatenate([embedded, embeddedviews], axis=-1) outputsflat = [] for i in range(0, embedded.shape[0], netchunk): batch = embedded[i:i+netchunk] out = fn(batch) outputsflat.append(out) outputs = np.reshape(np.concatenate(outputsflat, axis=0), list(inputs.shape[:-1]) + [outputsflat[0].shape[-1]]) return outputs def networkqueryfn(inputs, viewdirs, networkfn, embedfn, embeddirsfn, netchunk): """Wrapper for runnetwork.""" return runnetwork(inputs, viewdirs, networkfn, embedfn, embeddirsfn, netchunk) def initializenerfmodel(args): """Main initialization routine.""" # 1. Instantiate Positional Encoders embedfn, inputch = getembedder(args.multires, args.iembed) useviewdirs = args.useviewdirs embeddirsfn = None inputchviews = 0 if useviewdirs: embeddirsfn, inputchviews = getembedder(args.multiresviews, args.iembed) outputch = 4 skips = [4] # 2. Initialize Coarse MLP model = initnerfmodel( D=args.netdepth, W=args.netwidth, inputch=inputch, outputch=outputch, skips=skips, inputchviews=inputchviews, useviewdirs=useviewdirs) # 3. Initialize Fine MLP (Optional) modelfine = None if args.Nimportance > 0: modelfine = initnerfmodel( D=args.netdepthfine, W=args.netwidthfine, inputch=inputch, outputch=outputch, skips=skips, inputchviews=inputchviews, useviewdirs=useviewdirs) # Add fine model variables to gradvars # gradvars.extend(modelfine.trainablevariables) # 4. Define Query Function networkqueryfn = lambda inputs, viewdirs: runnetwork(inputs, viewdirs, model, embedfn, embeddirsfn, args.netchunk) networkqueryfnfine = lambda inputs, viewdirs: runnetwork(inputs, viewdirs, modelfine, embedfn, embeddirsfn, args.netchunk) if modelfine else None # 5. Configure Render Kwargs renderkwargstrain = { 'perturb': args.perturb, 'Nimportance': args.Nimportance, 'Nsamples': args.Nsamples, 'networkfn': networkqueryfn, 'networkfine': networkqueryfnfine, 'useviewdirs': useviewdirs, 'whitebkgd': args.whitebkgd, 'rawnoisestd': args.rawnoisestd } renderkwargstest = { 'perturb': False, 'Nimportance': args.Nimportance, 'Nsamples': args.Nsamples, 'networkfn': networkqueryfn, 'networkfine': networkqueryfnfine, 'useviewdirs': useviewdirs, 'whitebkgd': args.whitebkgd, 'rawnoisestd': 0. } # 6. Load Checkpoints (Optional) if args.ckpts: ckpts = sorted([f for f in args.ckpts if 'model' in f and 'fine' not in f and 'optimizer' not in f]) for ftweights in ckpts: # Load coarse weights # model.setweights(np.load(ftweights, allowpickle=True)) # Load fine weights if applicable if modelfine: fineweightspath = '{}fine{}'.format(ftweights[:-11], ftweights[-10:]) # modelfine.setweights(np.load(fineweightspath, allowpickle=True)) return model, modelfine, renderkwargstrain, renderkwargstest Precision: The netchunk parameter limits the number of points processed in parallel to manage GPU memory. If netchunk is too small, performance degrades due to overhead; if too large, it may cause OOM errors. Boundaries: The perturb parameter controls jittering. Setting it to 0 disables jitter, which may lead to aliasing artifacts if the sampling rate is insufficient. Degenerate Input: If Nimportance is 0, modelfine and networkfine are not created. The query function must handle None for the fine network gracefully. View Directions: If useviewdirs is false, embeddirsfn is not instantiated, and view directions are not passed to the network. A hybrid implicit surface learning method that efficiently initializes the signed distance field (SDF) to reconstruct large driving scenes from 2D street view images with limited overlap, without relying on geometric priors or LiDAR. This variant addresses slow and unstable convergence on tilted surfaces by replacing standard cube-based sampling with polygonal meshes. It initializes a 128×128×128 grid, selecting the center point of each grid along with its six neighboring grids (front, back, left, right, top, and bottom) to create polygonal meshes. To further improve convergence, it utilizes a regular octahedron with 20 faces (8 exterior, 12 interior) instead of standard cubes. The ray from camera origin to pixel is defined as r(t) = o + td, where d = (\theta, \phi) is the viewing direction. The intersection of this ray with the polygonal meshes serves as the sampling point. Unlike standard NeRF, this method predicts opacity \alpha directly instead of volume density, using the rendering equation \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai ci, where Ti = \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). NeRF-DS extends NeRF to capture dynamic, reflective objects. It employs a dual-network design similar to D-NeRF: a deformation field maps time-varying coordinates into a canonical space. It uses a specularity-aware radiance field that jointly predicts view-dependent appearance and reflection behavior, conditioning radiance on surface orientation and spatial location. An object mask is used to maintain temporal consistency under changing reflections. Time Complexity: Initialization is O(1) relative to scene size, depending only on network architecture parameters. Inference complexity is dominated by the number of samples per ray (N{samples} + N{importance}) and the number of rays. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of parameters in the MLPs (D \times W \times (input\ch + input\ch\views)) and the storage for checkpoints. It does not scale with scene resolution or number of points, unlike voxel-based methods. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales well with scene complexity as it is resolution-independent. Performance is limited by the MLP query speed and the number of samples required for convergence. Strengths: Resolution-independent, compact representation, supports view-dependent effects. Limitations: Slow inference speed compared to grid-based methods, requires many samples for high-quality results, sensitive to initialization and hyperparameters. When to use: High-quality novel view synthesis where resolution independence is desired. When not to use: Real-time applications requiring high frame rates, or scenes with extreme geometric complexity where sampling becomes inefficient. name: Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO)
head: SimpleDVGO
body: Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO) is a differentiable volume rendering method that replaces the multi-layer perceptron (MLP) used in NeRF with direct voxel grids for density and color features, enabling significantly faster training and inference. Unlike NeRF-like methods that query a neural network for density from coordinates, DVGO stores density and color directly in 3D grids, allowing for efficient trilinear interpolation and gradient accumulation. It sets itself apart from its sibling NeRF Model Initialization by using a dense voxel grid representation rather than a coordinate-based MLP, trading off some representational flexibility for computational speed. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origins \mathbf{o} and directions \mathbf{d}, camera parameters (near/far planes), and scene bounding box. Outputs: Rendered RGB color and depth for each ray. Data Structures: 1. Density Voxel Grid: A 3D tensor of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz) with 1 channel, storing raw density values. Initialized to a small positive value (e.g., 0.001). 2. Color Voxel Grid: A 3D tensor of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz) with 3 channels (RGB), storing color features. Initialized to a default color (e.g., BLUE). 3. Bounding Box Buffers: min: Tuple of floats (x{min}, y{min}, z{min}) defining the scene bounding box minimum corner. max: Tuple of floats (x{max}, y{max}, z{max}) defining the scene bounding box maximum corner. shape: Tuple of ints (Nx, Ny, Nz) defining the grid resolution. 4. Sampling Buffers: tvalues: 1D tensor of size K (number of samples), containing midpoints between K+1 linearly spaced depths from near to far. Parameters: numvoxels: Total number of voxels (Nx \times Ny \times Nz). near: Near plane distance (default 1.5). far: Far plane distance (default 3.5). numsamples: Number of sample points along each ray (default 64). mincorner: Scene bounding box minimum (default (-1.0, -1.0, 0.0)). maxcorner: Scene bounding box maximum (default (1.0, 1.0, 1.0)). shape: Grid dimensions (default (128, 128, 128)). background: Background color (default WHITE). alphainit: Initial alpha value for density bias shift calculation (default None). rgbnetdim: Dimension of color feature vector. If \le 0, uses coarse stage (3-channel grid). If > 0, uses fine stage (feature grid + MLP). maskcachethres: Threshold for mask cache occupancy. fastcolorthres: Threshold for voxel occupancy based on alpha. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: a. Calculate actshift for density bias: \text{act\shift} = \ln\left(\frac{1}{1-\alpha{init}} - 1\right). b. Create tvalues as midpoints of K+1 linearly spaced points between near and far. c. Initialize min, max, and shape buffers. d. Initialize rgbvoxelgrid with shape config.shape, 3 channels, filled with BLUE. e. Initialize densityvoxelgrid with shape config.shape, 1 channel, filled with 0.001. f. Register background color. g. If rgbnetdim > 0, initialize RGB MLP with input dimension d0 = (3 + 3 \cdot \text{viewbase\pe} \cdot 2) + (\text{k0\dim} \text{ if } \text{rgbnet\direct} \text{ else } 0) - (3 \text{ if } \neg \text{rgbnet\full\implicit} \text{ else } 0), depth rgbnetdepth, width rgbnetwidth, ReLU activations, and 3 output neurons with 0 bias. h. Initialize mask cache (ones if not loaded). 2. Ray Sampling: a. For each ray, sample points \mathbf{P} at depths t \in \text{t\values}: \mathbf{P} = \mathbf{o} + t \cdot \mathbf{d}. b. During training, add jitter: t' = t + \frac{\text{rand}() - 0.5}{K} where K is batch size. 3. Coordinate Rescaling: a. Convert scene coordinates \mathbf{P} to grid coordinates \mathbf{P}{grid}: \mathbf{P}{grid} = \text{shape} \cdot \frac{\mathbf{P} - \text{min}}{\text{max} - \text{min}} 4. Grid Query: a. Query density: \sigma{raw} = \text{density\voxel\grid}(\mathbf{P}{grid}). b. Apply ReLU: \sigma = \text{ReLU}(\sigma{raw}). c. Query color: \mathbf{c}{raw} = \text{rgb\voxel\grid}(\mathbf{P}{grid}). d. Clamp color: \mathbf{c} = \text{clamp}(\mathbf{c}{raw}, 0.0, 1.0). e. If rgbnetdim > 0, pass \mathbf{c}{raw} and view direction through RGB MLP to get final \mathbf{c}. 5. Volume Rendering: a. Compute transmittance and alpha: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \cdot \deltai) Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \cdot \deltaj\right) where \deltai is the step size along the ray. b. Render color: C = \sum{i=1}^{K} Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i + TK \cdot \text{background} 6. Regularization and Caching (Optional): a. Apply total variation regularization to density and color grids. b. Update mask cache based on density thresholds. c. Mask out voxels near camera if distance < near plane. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def trilinearinterpolate(grid, points): """Standard trilinear interpolation for grid of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz, C) and points (N, 3).""" # Clamp coordinates to grid bounds x = np.clip(points[:, 0], 0, grid.shape[0] - 1.001) y = np.clip(points[:, 1], 0, grid.shape[1] - 1.001) z = np.clip(points[:, 2], 0, grid.shape[2] - 1.001) # Floor and ceil indices x0, y0, z0 = np.floor([x, y, z]).astype(int) x1, y1, z1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1, z0 + 1 # Interpolation weights dx, dy, dz = x - x0, y - y0, z - z0 w000 = (1-dx)(1-dy)(1-dz) w100 = dx(1-dy)(1-dz) w010 = (1-dx)dy(1-dz) w110 = dxdy(1-dz) w001 = (1-dx)(1-dy)dz w101 = dx(1-dy)dz w011 = (1-dx)dydz w111 = dxdydz # Gather and interpolate vals = grid[x0, y0, z0] w000 + grid[x1, y0, z0] w100 + \ grid[x0, y1, z0] w010 + grid[x1, y1, z0] w110 + \ grid[x0, y0, z1] w001 + grid[x1, y0, z1] w101 + \ grid[x0, y1, z1] w011 + grid[x1, y1, z1] w111 return vals class SimpleDVGO: def init(self, config): self.near = config.near self.far = config.far self.numsamples = config.numsamples self.min = np.array(config.mincorner, dtype=np.float32) self.max = np.array(config.maxcorner, dtype=np.float32) self.shape = np.array(config.shape, dtype=np.float32) self.background = np.array(config.background, dtype=np.float32) # Initialize tvalues depths = np.linspace(self.near, self.far, self.numsamples + 1) self.tvalues = 0.5 (depths[1:] + depths[:-1]) # Initialize voxel grids self.densitygrid = np.full((config.shape, 1), 0.001, dtype=np.float32) self.rgbgrid = np.zeros((config.shape, 3), dtype=np.float32) self.rgbgrid[..., 2] = 1.0 # BLUE # Optional: RGB MLP for fine stage if config.rgbnetdim > 0: self.rgbnetdim = config.rgbnetdim self.rgbnetdepth = config.rgbnetdepth self.rgbnetwidth = config.rgbnetwidth self.viewbasepe = config.viewbasepe self.rgbnetdirect = config.rgbnetdirect self.rgbnetfullimplicit = config.rgbnetfullimplicit # MLP weights initialized elsewhere def forward(self, rays, training=True): origins = rays[:,:3] directions = rays[:, 3:] tvalues = self.tvalues if training: n = tvalues.shape[0] randomscalar = (np.random.rand(n) - 0.5) / n actualts = tvalues + randomscalar else: actualts = tvalues actualts = actualts[np.newaxis,:] origins = origins[:, np.newaxis,:] directions = directions[:, np.newaxis,:] samples = origins + actualts directions rescaled = self.shape (samples - self.min) / (self.max - self.min) density = trilinearinterpolate(self.densitygrid, rescaled) density = np.maximum(density, 0.0) # ReLU rgb = trilinearinterpolate(self.rgbgrid, rescaled) rgb = np.clip(rgb, 0.0, 1.0) deltas = np.diff(actualts, axis=1) deltainf = np.oneslike(deltas[:,:1]) 1e10 deltas = np.concatenate([deltas, deltainf], axis=1) alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-density deltas) T = np.cumprod(1.0 - alpha + 1e-10, axis=1) T = np.concatenate([np.oneslike(T[:,:1]), T[:,:-1]], axis=1) weights = alpha T[:,:-1] color = np.sum(weights[:,:, np.newaxis] rgb, axis=1) color = color + T[:, -1, np.newaxis] self.background return color This method adapts the Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO) architecture by replacing its standard volume rendering integral with a reparameterized estimate based on differentiable ray point sampling. It solves the problem of high computational cost in standard ray marching by allowing the number of radiance samples to be explicitly controlled and minimized, particularly during the coarse training stage. It sets itself apart from standard DVGO by trading off rendering quality (PSNR) for significant training speed improvements in the coarse stage, while maintaining competitive performance in the fine stage only when sample counts are kept low. A heuristic in DVGO that sets the interval lengths d in the volume rendering equation to the ratio of the current voxel grid resolution to the base voxel grid resolution, making the model independent of scene size. Disabling this heuristic by setting interval lengths to true physical distances between sample points causes DVGO to fail to render at high quality, as observed in Table A2 where 'disabled' rows show significantly lower PSNR or 'fail' status. On the Blender dataset, DVGO with the heuristic ('default') achieves PSNR values such as 34.10 (drums), 25.40 (ficus), and 32.56 (hotdog), whereas disabling it ('disabled') results in failures or much lower scores like 15.74 (fern) and 17.38 (flower). A straightforward combination of DVGO and NeuS, replacing the volume rendering in DVGO with the SDF-based volume rendering scheme. It serves as the naive baseline in this work, which can hardly produce satisfactory results. In the baseline model, the color network tends to depend more on the additional under-constrained voxel feature grid input, thus breaking color-geometry dependency. Additionally, due to a high degree of freedom in optimizing a voxel grid, it is hard to maintain a globally coherent shape without additional constraints. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: DVGO is significantly faster than NeRF in both training and inference due to the replacement of MLP queries with grid lookups. It achieves 2-3x speedup with PyTorch CUDA extensions. Scaling: Scales linearly with grid resolution. Higher resolutions require more memory but offer better detail. Octree or hash encoding variants can be used for scaling to higher resolutions. Strengths: Fast training and inference, simple implementation, efficient memory usage for moderate resolutions. Limitations: Memory usage grows cubically with resolution. Less flexible than MLPs for complex geometries. When to Use: When training speed is critical and the scene can be represented well with a voxel grid. Suitable for forward-facing and bounded scenes. When Not to Use: For very large unbounded scenes where memory is a constraint, or when high-frequency details require very high grid resolutions. DVGO was introduced by Sun et al. in CVPR 2022. It builds on the idea of differentiable volume rendering but replaces the neural network representation with direct voxel grids. The method was developed to address the slow training times of NeRF. It is used in various datasets including NeRF Synthetic, NSVF, BlendedMVS, Tanks and Temples, DeepVoxels, and LLFF. DirectVoxGO, https://github.com/sunset1995/DirectVoxGO, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) 7.6. Neural Radiance Fields for Drones, https://www.roboticsbook.org/S76dronelearning.html, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Alpha Invariance: On Inverse Scaling Between Distance and Volume Density in Neural Radiance Fields, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YQhBEXC464w, fetched 2026-10-31 Voxurf: Voxel-based Efficient and Accurate Neural Surface Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2208.12697, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: DVGO with Reparameterized Rendering
head: Direct Voxel Grid Optimization with proposed reparameterized estimates
body: This method adapts the Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO) architecture by replacing its standard volume rendering integral with a reparameterized estimate based on differentiable ray point sampling. It solves the problem of high computational cost in standard ray marching by allowing the number of radiance samples to be explicitly controlled and minimized, particularly during the coarse training stage. It sets itself apart from standard DVGO by trading off rendering quality (PSNR) for significant training speed improvements in the coarse stage, while maintaining competitive performance in the fine stage only when sample counts are kept low. The method retains the DVGO data structures and training pipeline but modifies the forward rendering pass. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin o, ray direction d, density grid \sigma, radiance grid C, and an optional view-dependent MLP C{mlp}. Outputs: Rendered color C{render}. Data Structures: The method uses the same grids as DVGO: 1. Density Grid: A 3D tensor storing volume density \sigma. 2. Radiance Grid: A 3D tensor storing view-independent color C. 3. View-Dependent Radiance (Fine Stage): A combination of the radiance grid and a small MLP. 4. Auxiliary Mask: A binary mask identifying empty space regions to skip optimization. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: Instead of fixed-step ray marching, sample k points along the ray segment within the bounding box. The points are sampled according to a stratified distribution. 2. Grid Interpolation: For each sampled point, interpolate the density and color from the respective 3D grids using the same scheme as the parent DVGO architecture. 3. Reparameterized Estimate Calculation: Compute the transmittance and color contribution using the reparameterized estimate formula (Equation 4 in). The standard volume rendering integral is approximated by the sum over the k samples: C{render} = \sum{i=1}^{k} Ti \alphai Ci where \alphai is the opacity derived from \sigmai and the distance between samples, and Ti is the accumulated transmittance up to sample i. 4. Differentiable Backpropagation: Compute gradients with respect to the grid values using the chain rule through the sampling and interpolation steps. Parameters: Number of radiance samples (k): Varies during evaluation and training. Tested values: 1, 8, 32, 64. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderreparameterized(rayo, rayd, densitygrid, radiancegrid, k, bboxmin, bboxmax): # 1. Ray-box intersection (slab method) tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for d in range(3): if abs(rayd[d]) < 1e-8: if rayo[d] < bboxmin[d] or rayo[d] > bboxmax[d]: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] else: t1 = (bboxmin[d] - rayo[d]) / rayd[d] t2 = (bboxmax[d] - rayo[d]) / rayd[d] tenter = min(t1, t2) texit = max(t1, t2) tmin = max(tmin, tenter) tmax = min(tmax, texit) if tmin > tmax: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # 2. Stratified sampling of k points along the valid ray segment tvalues = [tmin + i (tmax - tmin) / k for i in range(k + 1)] tmid = [(tvalues[i] + tvalues[i+1]) / 2.0 for i in range(k)] # 3. Sample points along ray points = [[rayo[j] + rayd[j] tmid[i] for j in range(3)] for i in range(k)] # 4. Trilinear interpolation from grids sigma = [trilinearinterpolate(densitygrid, p) for p in points] color = [[trilinearinterpolate(radiancegrid, p, c) for c in range(3)] for p in points] # 5. Compute opacity and transmittance deltat = [tvalues[i+1] - tvalues[i] for i in range(k)] alpha = [1.0 - math.exp(-sigma[i] deltat[i]) for i in range(k)] # Accumulate transmittance Ti = product{j<i} (1 - alphaj) T = [1.0] k prod = 1.0 for i in range(1, k): prod = (1.0 - alpha[i-1]) T[i] = prod # 6. Compute final color colorrender = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(k): for c in range(3): colorrender[c] += T[i] alpha[i] color[i][c] return colorrender def trilinearinterpolate(grid, point, channel=None): # Standard trilinear interpolation ix, iy, iz = int(math.floor(point[0])), int(math.floor(point[1])), int(math.floor(point[2])) fx, fy, fz = point[0] - ix, point[1] - iy, point[2] - iz # Handle boundary clamping ix = max(0, min(ix, grid.shape[0] - 2)) iy = max(0, min(iy, grid.shape[1] - 2)) iz = max(0, min(iz, grid.shape[2] - 2)) if channel is None: # Interpolate scalar density v00 = grid[ix][iy][iz] (1-fx) + grid[ix+1][iy][iz] fx v10 = grid[ix][iy+1][iz] (1-fx) + grid[ix+1][iy+1][iz] fx v01 = grid[ix][iy][iz+1] (1-fx) + grid[ix+1][iy][iz+1] fx v11 = grid[ix][iy+1][iz+1] (1-fx) + grid[ix+1][iy+1][iz+1] fx return v00 (1-fy) (1-fz) + v10 fx (1-fy) (1-fz) + v01 (1-fy) fz + v11 fx (1-fy) fz else: # Interpolate color channel v00 = grid[ix][iy][iz][channel] (1-fx) + grid[ix+1][iy][iz][channel] fx v10 = grid[ix][iy+1][iz][channel] (1-fx) + grid[ix+1][iy+1][iz][channel] fx v01 = grid[ix][iy][iz+1][channel] (1-fx) + grid[ix+1][iy][iz+1][channel] fx v11 = grid[ix][iy+1][iz+1][channel] (1-fx) + grid[ix+1][iy+1][iz+1][channel] fx return v00 (1-fy) (1-fz) + v10 fx (1-fy) (1-fz) + v01 (1-fy) fz + v11 fx (1-fy) fz Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Variance: Lower PSNR in the proposed method is caused by estimate variance during training, not just inference sampling. Sample Count Sensitivity: Noise artifacts are visible for k=1 but disappear for k=8. Training vs. Inference Robustness: A model trained with 64 samples can achieve PSNR 34.33 even if only 16 samples are used during evaluation, indicating robustness to inference sample count if training was sufficient. Training Speed (Coarse Stage): Improves training time by 20-30% compared to standard DVGO due to fewer radiance samples. Training Speed (Fine Stage): Improves training speed only when the number of samples is lower than DVGO's average radiance calls (13.4 in the tested scenario). Rendering Quality (PSNR): Generally lower than standard DVGO. On the Lego scene, DVGO achieved 34.60 PSNR. The proposed method achieved 34.15 (64 samples), 33.95 (32 samples), 33.29 (8 samples), and 29.84 (1 sample). Memory Usage: Memory usage is comparable to DVGO, as the grid structures remain the same. Implementation Note: To achieve performance competitive with DVGO's custom CUDA kernels, the method requires optimization using PyTorch's just-in-time (JIT) compilation module. This method was proposed in the paper "Differentiable Rendering With Reparameterized Volume Sampling". It builds upon the Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO) architecture, which was known for its fast training times due to lightning-fast architecture, progressive scaling, and custom CUDA kernels. The authors tested their rendering algorithm on the official DVGO implementation, replacing only the rendering algorithm based on Equation 4 of their paper. Differentiable Rendering With Reparameterized Volume Sampling, https://openreview.net/pdf?id=zHSaBQtj-l, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)
