name: Training Losses for Implicit Surface Learning
head: Photometric and Occupancy Losses
body: This method defines a set of loss functions to train an occupancy network f\theta and a texture network t\theta using 2D image supervision, categorizing pixels into three distinct sets: P0 (inside the object mask with finite predicted depth), P1 (outside the object mask), and P2 (inside the object mask but with infinite predicted depth). It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly handling the ambiguity of empty space and missing geometry through specialized freespace and occupancy penalties, rather than relying solely on photometric consistency. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A single image Ik with corresponding camera intrinsics/extrinsics, an object mask Mk, and optionally ground truth depth Dk. Outputs: Gradients for \theta (occupancy network parameters) and texture parameters. Data Structures: Point Set \mathcal{P}0: Pixels \mathbf{u} inside Mk where the predicted depth \hat{d} is finite. Point Set \mathcal{P}1: Pixels \mathbf{u} outside Mk. Point Set \mathcal{P}2: Pixels \mathbf{u} inside Mk where the predicted depth \hat{d} is infinite. Ray \mathbf{r}(d): The ray originating from the camera center through pixel \mathbf{u} at depth d. Surface Point \hat{\mathbf{p}}: The point \mathbf{r}(\hat{d}) on the predicted surface. Parameters: Np: Number of random pixels sampled on the image plane per training step. \xi(\cdot): Feature extractor for RGB loss. Uses RGB values and optionally image gradients. \|\cdot\|: Robust error metric. Uses L1 loss in practice. Steps: 1. Randomly sample an image Ik and Np points \mathbf{u} on the image plane. 2. Classify each \mathbf{u} into sets \mathcal{P}0, \mathcal{P}1, or \mathcal{P}2 based on the mask Mk and the predicted surface depth \hat{d}. 3. Compute the respective losses for each set (formulas below). 4. Sum the losses and backpropagate. Formulas: RGB Loss (for \mathcal{P}0): Photo-consistency loss using the feature extractor \xi and robust metric \|\cdot\|: \mathcal{L}{\text{rgb}}(\theta) = \sum{\mathbf{u} \in \mathcal{P}0} \|\xi(\mathbf{I}){\mathbf{u}} - \xi(\hat{\mathbf{I}}){\mathbf{u}}\| In practice, \xi returns RGB values and optional gradients, and \|\cdot\| is the L1 norm. Depth Loss (for \mathcal{P}0, if depth Dk is available): L1 loss on predicted vs. ground truth depth: \mathcal{L}{\text{depth}}(\theta) = \sum{\mathbf{u} \in \mathcal{P}0} |d - \hat{d}|1 where d is the ground truth depth and \hat{d} is the predicted depth. Freespace Loss (for \mathcal{P}1): Binary Cross Entropy (BCE) penalizing occupancy where the surface should not exist. If a finite surface depth \hat{d} is predicted for a point outside the mask, the network falsely predicts a surface point \hat{\mathbf{p}} = \mathbf{r}(\hat{d}). The loss is: \mathcal{L}{\text{freespace}}(\theta) = \sum{\mathbf{u} \in \mathcal{P}1} \text{BCE}(f\theta(\hat{\mathbf{p}}), 0) If no surface depth is predicted (infinite \hat{d}), the freespace loss is applied to a randomly sampled point on the ray. Occupancy Loss (for \mathcal{P}2): BCE encouraging occupancy along rays where a surface is expected but not found. Uniformly sample depth values d{\text{random}}: \mathcal{L}{\text{occupancy}}(\theta) = \sum{\mathbf{u} \in \mathcal{P}2} \text{BCE}(f{\theta}(\mathbf{r}(d{\text{random}})), 1) In single-view experiments, d{\text{random}} is replaced by the visual hull depth (first point inside all object masks) or ground truth depth if available. Normal Loss (optional, for \mathcal{P}0): Smoothness prior regularizing surface normals: \mathcal{L}{\text{normal}}(\theta) = \sum{\mathbf{u} \in \mathcal{P}0} \|\mathbf{n}(\mathbf{p}{\mathbf{u}}) - \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{q}{\mathbf{u}})\|2 where \mathbf{n}(\cdot) is the normal vector, \hat{\mathbf{p}}{\mathbf{u}} is the predicted surface point, and \mathbf{q}{\mathbf{u}} is a randomly sampled neighbor of \hat{\mathbf{p}}{\mathbf{u}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computetrainingloss(image, mask, depthgt, cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics, occupancynet, texturenet, Np): """ Computes the total training loss for implicit surface learning. Args: image: Input image Ik. mask: Object mask Mk. depthgt: Ground truth depth Dk (optional). cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics: Camera parameters. occupancynet: Network ftheta predicting occupancy. texturenet: Network ttheta predicting texture. Np: Number of pixels to sample. Returns: totalloss: Scalar loss value. """ # 1. Sample Np points on the image plane usamples = samplerandompixels(Np) # 2. Classify points into P0, P1, P2 P0 = [] P1 = [] P2 = [] for u in usamples: # Project u to 3D ray r ray = getrayfrompixel(u, cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics) # Predict surface depth dhat along the ray # Note: Implementation detail - typically involves marching or root finding dhat = predictsurfacedepth(ray, occupancynet) if isinsidemask(u, mask): if isfinite(dhat): P0.append(u) else: P2.append(u) else: P1.append(u) totalloss = 0.0 # 3. Compute RGB Loss for P0 if P0: # Predict image Ihat for points in P0 Ihat = predictimageforpoints(P0, occupancynet, texturenet, cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics) # Feature extraction: RGB + optional gradients featuresgt = extractfeatures(image, P0) featurespred = extractfeatures(Ihat, P0) # L1 loss lrgb = sum(l1norm(fgt - fpred) for fgt, fpred in zip(featuresgt, featurespred)) totalloss += lrgb # 4. Compute Depth Loss for P0 (if depthgt available) if depthgt is not None: dgt = getdepthatpixels(depthgt, P0) dhatlist = [dhat for u in P0] # dhat was computed in step 2 ldepth = sum(abs(d - dh) for d, dh in zip(dgt, dhatlist)) totalloss += ldepth # 5. Compute Normal Loss for P0 (optional) # Implementation detail: Compute normals from occupancy gradient or geometry # lnormal = sum(normdist(pnormal, qnormal) for p, q in neighbors) # totalloss += lnormal # 6. Compute Freespace Loss for P1 if P1: lfreespace = 0.0 for u in P1: ray = getrayfrompixel(u, cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics) # Check if finite depth was predicted (false positive) dhat = predictsurfacedepth(ray, occupancynet) if isfinite(dhat): phat = ray.pointat(dhat) occval = occupancynet(phat) lfreespace += bce(occval, 0) else: # No surface predicted, sample random point on ray drand = randomdepth() prand = ray.pointat(drand) occval = occupancynet(prand) lfreespace += bce(occval, 0) totalloss += lfreespace # 7. Compute Occupancy Loss for P2 if P2: loccupancy = 0.0 for u in P2: ray = getrayfrompixel(u, cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics) # Sample random depth or use visual hull/ground truth if singleviewexperiment: dsample = getvisualhulldepth(ray, mask) # or ground truth if available else: dsample = randomdepth() psample = ray.pointat(dsample) occval = occupancynet(psample) loccupancy += bce(occval, 1) totalloss += loccupancy return totalloss A method focused on novel view synthesis of objects without background, using 3D bounding boxes and object masks to define Normalized Object Coordinate Spaces for per-object volume rendering. It sets itself apart by refining shape codes, appearance codes, and bounding boxes at test time using an occupancy loss. The occupancy loss is defined as \mathcal{L}{\text{occ}} = \frac{1}{|W{\text{occ}}|} \sum{\mathbf{u} \in W{\text{occ}}} \log(Y{\mathbf{u}} (1/2 - \alpha) + 1/2), where Y is the object mask and W{\text{occ}} is either the set of foreground or background pixels. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sampled pixels Np and the number of points in each set |\mathcal{P}0|, |\mathcal{P}1|, |\mathcal{P}2|. Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage of the occupancy and texture networks and the intermediate gradients for the sampled points. Strengths: Works with as little as one image per object. Can incorporate depth information if available. The normal loss is useful for real-world data to enforce natural shapes in unconstrained areas. Limitations: Relies on accurate object masks. The freespace and occupancy losses depend on the correct classification of pixels, which can be sensitive to depth prediction errors. When to use: When training implicit neural representations with 2D image supervision, especially in single-view or sparse-view settings. When not to use: When 3D ground truth geometry is available and can be used directly for supervision, as 2D-only supervision may lead to ambiguities. This method originates from the work on learning implicit 3D representations without 3D supervision. It was developed to address the challenge of training occupancy networks and texture networks using only 2D image data, masks, and optionally depth. The approach builds on the differentiable volumetric rendering framework Parent. Differentiable Volumetric Rendering: Learning Implicit 3D Representations without 3D Supervision, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lcub1KH-mmk, fetched 2026-10-27 Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Differentiable Direct Volume Rendering (DiffDVR)
body: DiffDVR is an image-based optimization method that uses differentiable direct volume rendering to optimize transfer functions and other continuous parameters by minimizing residuals between rendered images and a reference. It sets itself apart from standard reverse-mode automatic differentiation by using analytic inversion of the blending functions to recompute intermediate results, thereby reducing memory consumption from O(kn) to O(n) without storing the computational graph. Unlike least-squares voxel-based solvers, DiffDVR accounts for ray-based integration effects like occlusion and attenuation, emphasizing structural differences in residual maps. It builds on the emission-absorption model shared by Differentiable Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) and differs from Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR) and Differentiable DRR Generation via Vectorized GPU Siddon's Method in its explicit analytic inversion of light accumulation along view rays. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar volume V: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow [0,1] defined on a rectangular grid, a camera pose, a transfer function mapping density v to absorption \tau(v) and self-emission/color C(v), and a reference image. Output: A rendered image \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and gradients of a problem-specific loss function with respect to the transfer function parameters, camera pose, or volume densities. Data Structures: Volume: Scalar density field accessed via trilinear interpolation. Transfer Function: Functions \tau(v) and C(v) mapping density to optical properties. Ray: Arc-length parameterized ray \mathbf{r}(t). Rendering Model: The method uses the emission-absorption model without multiple scattering. The continuous light intensity L(a, b) reaching the eye from ray segment [a, b] is: L(a, b) = \inta^b g(V(\mathbf{r}(t))) e^{-\inta^t \tau(V(\mathbf{r}(u))) du} dt where g(v) = \tau(v)C(v) is the emission. In discrete form for N samples along a ray with step size \deltai: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \sigmai = \tau(Vi), \mathbf{c}i = C(Vi), and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance. Algorithm Steps: 1. Forward Pass: Render the image using standard DVR. For each ray, compute transmittance Ti and color contribution iteratively. 2. Loss Computation: Calculate the difference between the rendered image and the reference image using a loss function (e.g., L1 or L2 norm). 3. Gradient Computation (Analytic Inversion): Instead of recording operations for reverse-mode AD, DiffDVR uses a custom computation kernel that inverts the order of operations. It derives gradients by analytically inverting the light accumulation along view rays. The gradient with respect to a sample's density depends on the transmittance after that sample (backwards in ray order) and the accumulated color before that sample (forwards in ray order). This allows recomputing necessary intermediate states on the fly during the backward pass, avoiding storage. 4. Parameter Update: Use the computed gradients to update the optimization variables (transfer function, camera, etc.) via gradient descent. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trilinearinterpolate(volume, pos): """Standard 3D grid sampling operation.""" return volume.sample(pos) def diffdvrforward(volume, rayorigin, raydirection, transferfunc, numsamples, stepsize): alphas = [] Ts = [] colors = [] currentT = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(numsamples): t = i stepsize pos = rayorigin + t raydirection density = trilinearinterpolate(volume, pos) tau, color = transferfunc(density) alpha = 1.0 - exp(-tau stepsize) accumulatedcolor += currentT alpha color currentT = (1.0 - alpha) alphas.append(alpha) Ts.append(currentT) colors.append(color) return accumulatedcolor, Ts, alphas, colors def diffdvrbackward(renderedcolor, referencecolor, Ts, alphas, colors, volume, rayorigin, raydirection, transferfunc, numsamples, stepsize): dLdC = 2.0 (renderedcolor - referencecolor) # L2 loss gradient dLdT = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Gradient w.r.t transmittance entering the ray tfgradients = {} for i in range(numsamples - 1, -1, -1): t = i stepsize pos = rayorigin + t raydirection density = trilinearinterpolate(volume, pos) tau, color = transferfunc(density) alpha = alphas[i] Ti = Ts[i] # Gradient w.r.t color contribution at sample i dLdcolor = dLdC Ti alpha # Gradient w.r.t alpha at sample i dLdalpha = dLdC Ti color - dLdT Ti # Update gradient w.r.t transmittance for the next (previous) sample dLdT = dLdC (1.0 - alpha) # Chain rule to accumulate gradients for transfer function parameters # dL/dp = dLdtau dtau/dp + dLdcolor dcolor/dp # where dLdtau = dLdalpha d(alpha)/d(tau) # Exact derivatives depend on the specific TF parameterization accumulatetfgradients(tfgradients, density, tau, color, dLdcolor, dLdalpha, stepsize) return tfgradients def accumulatetfgradients(tfgradients, density, tau, color, dLdcolor, dLdalpha, stepsize): """Accumulates gradients for transfer function parameters via chain rule.""" dLdtau = dLdalpha (-stepsize exp(-tau stepsize)) # Example accumulation for a generic parameter p: # tfgradients[p] += dLdtau dtau/density d(density)/dp + dLdcolor dcolor/density d(density)/dp pass Parameters: Loss Function: L1 or L2 norm. L2 penalizes larger residuals more strongly; L1 tolerates outliers. Step Size: Fixed or adaptive, affects accuracy and performance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Convexity: The optimization problem is not convex, risking local minima. Ambiguity: Slightly different transfer functions may generate nearly identical images, making perfect reconstruction impossible. Small-Scale Structures: Standard DiffDVR may fail to faithfully optimize for small-scale structures; follow-up works limit differentiability to densities/colors to address this. Corrects gradient computation in DRR pipelines by explicitly handling non-linear, pose-dependent boundary conditions (min-max normalization, clinical inversion) that flip gradient signs and scale magnitudes incorrectly. Time Complexity: Slower than least-squares voxel-based approaches due to ray-based integration and gradient computation. Memory Complexity: O(n), where n is the number of pixels, independent of the number of samples k per ray. This is a significant improvement over reverse-mode AD which requires O(kn). Performance: Implemented in C++ and CUDA with PyTorch interoperability. Strengths: Accounts for occlusion and attenuation; better image similarity metrics for structural differences; low memory footprint. Limitations: Non-convex optimization; potential for local minima; ambiguity in transfer function reconstruction; struggles with small-scale structures without modifications. When to Use: When optimizing transfer functions or camera poses for image-based registration or comparative volume rendering where structural fidelity is key. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and structural fidelity is not required, or when optimizing small-scale structures without modifications. DiffDVR was introduced by Sebastian Weiss and Thomas Westermann. It addresses the limitations of reverse-mode automatic differentiation in volume rendering, which suffers from high memory usage. The method is part of the broader field of differentiable rendering, which has been applied to geometry, material, and lighting optimization. It is used for transfer function optimization, camera pose estimation, and tomographic reconstruction. Transfer Function Optimization for Comparative Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2306.05885, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Differentiable Direct Volume Rendering, https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12672v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Differentiable DRR with Post-Processing Normalization and Inversion
head: DRR VJP normalization fix, SlangDiffDRRFunction gradient correction
body: This method corrects the gradient computation in differentiable Digital Radiograph Reconstruction (DRR) pipelines where post-rendering normalization and inversion are applied outside the automatic differentiation graph. It solves the problem of anti-convergence in 2D/3D registration caused by omitted Jacobians for min-max normalization and clinical inversion, which flip gradient signs and scale magnitudes incorrectly. It sets itself apart from standard differentiable volume rendering by explicitly handling the non-linear, pose-dependent boundary conditions introduced by global image statistics (\min and \max) at the Python/CUDA interface. The method computes the Vector-Jacobian Product (VJP) of the post-processing functions at the boundary between the differentiable renderer and the Python framework. This ensures that gradients flowing back to the raw Beer-Lambert intensities correctly account for the normalization and inversion transforms. Inputs: 1. r: Raw rendered image tensor of shape (H, W), output of the differentiable DRR kernel. 2. g: Upstream gradient tensor of shape (H, W) representing \partial L / \partial f, where f is the processed image. 3. \text{cfg}: Configuration object containing normalize (bool, default True), invert (bool, default True), and \varepsilon (float stability constant). Outputs: 1. \tilde{g}: Corrected gradient tensor of shape (H, W) representing \partial L / \partial r, ready for the backward kernel. Raw Image r: Float32 tensor of shape (H, W) representing Beer-Lambert intensity I = i0 \exp(-\int \mu ds). Gradient g: Float32 tensor of shape (H, W) with the same layout as r. Statistics: r{\min} = \min(r), r{\max} = \max(r), \Delta = r{\max} - r{\min}, and D = \Delta + \varepsilon. The post-processing function f(r) is defined as: f(r) = 1 - \frac{r - r{\min}}{D} where D = \max(r) - \min(r) + \varepsilon and \varepsilon is a small stability constant to prevent division by zero. The goal is to compute \nablar L = \frac{\partial L}{\partial r} using the chain rule \nablar L = \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial r} \right)^{\mathsf T} g. The derivative \frac{\partial fi}{\partial rj} contains a direct term and indirect terms through r{\min} and r{\max}. Applying the quotient rule yields: \frac{\partial fi}{\partial rj} = -\frac{\delta{ij}}{D} - \frac{1}{D}\frac{\partial r{\min}}{\partial rj} + \frac{ri - r{\min}}{D^2}\left(\frac{\partial r{\max}}{\partial rj} - \frac{\partial r{\min}}{\partial rj}\right) The derivatives of the extrema are indicator functions: \frac{\partial r{\min}}{\partial rj} = \mathbb{I}(rj = r{\min}) and \frac{\partial r{\max}}{\partial rj} = \mathbb{I}(rj = r{\max}). Summing over j with weights gj gives the corrected gradient for pixel i: \tilde{g}i = -\frac{gi}{D} - \frac{S{\min}}{D}\mathbb{I}(ri = r{\min}) + \frac{ri - r{\min}}{D^2}\left(S{\max}\mathbb{I}(ri = r{\max}) - S{\min}\mathbb{I}(ri = r{\min})\right) where S{\min} = \sum{j: rj = r{\min}} gj and S{\max} = \sum{j: rj = r{\max}} gj. If invert is True, the total forward pass applies 1 - f(r), so the final gradient is negated: \tilde{g}{\text{total}} = -\tilde{g}. 1. Receive raw image r and upstream gradient g. 2. Compute r{\min} = \min(r), r{\max} = \max(r), \Delta = r{\max} - r{\min}, and D = \Delta + \varepsilon. 3. Identify masks M{\min} = (r == r{\min}) and M{\max} = (r == r{\max}). 4. Compute sums S{\min} = \sumj gj M{\min}[j] and S{\max} = \sumj gj M{\max}[j]. 5. Compute base gradient \tilde{g}{\text{base}} = -g / D. 6. Add min-term correction: \tilde{g} = \tilde{g}{\text{base}} - (S{\min} / D) M{\min}. 7. Add max-term correction: \tilde{g} = \tilde{g} + ((r - r{\min}) / D^2) (S{\max} M{\max} - S{\min} M{\min}). 8. If invert is True, negate \tilde{g}: \tilde{g} = -\tilde{g}. 9. Return \tilde{g}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def postprocessvjp(rawimage: torch.Tensor, gradoutput: torch.Tensor, cfg: dict) -> torch.Tensor: """ Computes the VJP of the post-processing (normalize + invert) for DRR. Args: rawimage: Tensor of shape (H, W), raw Beer-Lambert intensities. gradoutput: Tensor of shape (H, W), gradient w.r.t processed image. cfg: Dict with 'normalize' (bool), 'invert' (bool), 'eps' (float). Returns: Tensor of shape (H, W), gradient w.r.t rawimage. """ eps = cfg.get('eps', 1e-6) donormalize = cfg.get('normalize', True) doinvert = cfg.get('invert', True) if not donormalize: return -gradoutput if doinvert else gradoutput rmin = torch.amin(rawimage) rmax = torch.amax(rawimage) D = (rmax - rmin) + eps maskmin = (rawimage == rmin) maskmax = (rawimage == rmax) smin = torch.sum(gradoutput maskmin) smax = torch.sum(gradoutput maskmax) gradraw = -gradoutput / D gradraw -= (smin / D) maskmin gradraw += ((rawimage - rmin) / (D D)) (smax maskmax - smin maskmin) if doinvert: gradraw = -gradraw return gradraw normalize (bool, default True): Applies min-max normalization to the raw image. invert (bool, default True): Inverts the normalized image to clinical convention. \varepsilon (float): Stability constant added to the normalization denominator to prevent division by zero. Gradient Sign Flip: Applying post-processing outside the autograd graph omits its Jacobian, flipping the gradient sign and scaling magnitude by 1/(\Delta + \varepsilon), which causes anti-convergence. Tied Extrema: Multiple pixels sharing the minimum or maximum value require sharing gradients across them to match torch.amin and torch.amax behavior. Pose-Dependent Extrema: Switching extremal pixels with pose makes \min(r) and \max(r) pose-dependent, causing a piecewise smooth objective and decorrelating gradient components. Invert-Only Case: If only inversion is applied, the returned gradient is exactly the negative of the true one. Time Complexity: O(HW) for computing extrema, masks, sums, and applying the VJP. Memory Complexity: O(HW) for storing masks and intermediate tensors. Performance: Correcting the gradient restores convergence, reducing pose error from growing to 137.6 mm/118.1 deg to converging to 0.0005 mm/0.0009 deg within 200 Adam iterations on a chest CT. Strengths: Fixes critical convergence issues in differentiable registration workflows while preserving existing API outputs. Limitations: Requires explicit handling of tied extrema and pose-dependent min/max terms. When to Use: When using differentiable DRR with post-render normalization and inversion for 2D/3D registration workflows. When Not to Use: When raw Beer-Lambert intensities are used directly without post-processing, or when post-processing is kept inside the autograd graph. This method addresses a bug in the i4h-sensor-simulation package where the backward pass ignored post-render normalization and inversion, leading to wrong pose gradients. The omission was identified in the package's issue tracker, highlighting that the documented 2D/3D registration workflow anti-converged due to this omission. The fix applies the VJP at the Python/CUDA boundary, ensuring that gradients are correctly propagated to the raw intensity space before being used by the differentiable renderer's backward kernel. It is used in 2D/3D registration workflows for medical imaging, specifically for differentiable DRR generation with clinical normalization conventions. fix(fluoro): backward pass ignores post-render normalisation and inversion, so pose gradients are wrong and the documented 2D/3D registration workflow anti-converges, https://github.com/isaac-for-healthcare/i4h-sensor-simulation/issues/68, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Differentiable DRR Generation via Vectorized GPU Siddon's Method
head: Auto-Differentiable DRR, Auto-differentiable DRR Generation via Vectorized GPU Siddon's Method, DiffDRR, VGS, Vectorized GPU Siddon's method, Vectorized Siddon's Method for DRR Generation
body: This method generates Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs (DRRs) that are fully differentiable with respect to 7 geometric imaging parameters by reformulating Siddon's ray-tracing algorithm as a series of vectorized tensor operations within PyTorch. It solves the problem of slow gradient-based optimization in intraoperative imaging by leveraging automatic differentiation, avoiding the high memory costs of standard reverse-mode AD and the complexity of adjoint methods. Unlike iterative ray-tracing implementations, it computes all plane intersections in parallel using GPU tensor algebra, trading memory efficiency for speed and compatibility with deep learning frameworks. Inputs: \mathbf{V}: A discrete 3D CT volume (tensor). \eta = (\rho, \theta, \phi, \gamma, bx, by, bz): Imaging parameters. \rho: Radius (half source-to-detector distance). \theta, \phi: Azimuthal and polar angles of the X-ray source \mathbf{s}. \gamma: Rotation of the detector plane about the x-axis. bx, by, bz: Translation of the source and detector plane relative to the volume center. H, W: Desired DRR dimensions. nx, ny, nz: Dimensions of the CT volume \mathbf{V}. \Delta X, \Delta Y, \Delta Z: Voxel sizes of \mathbf{V}. Outputs: \mathbf{I} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W}: The DRR intensity image. Gradients \nabla\eta \mathbf{I}: Automatically computed by the framework. Data Structures: \mathbf{P} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}: Tensor of 3D coordinates for each pixel on the detector plane. \mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times (nx + ny + nz)}: Tensor containing intersection parameters \alpha for all x, y, and z planes for all pixels. \alpha{\min}, \alpha{\max} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W}: Entry and exit bounds for each ray. Steps: 1. Define Ray Geometry: The ray \mathbf{R}(\alpha) originates from the source \mathbf{s} and passes through pixel \mathbf{p} on the detector: \mathbf{R}(\alpha) = \mathbf{s} + \alpha(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s}) where \alpha=0 at the source and \alpha=1 at the detector. 2. Compute Intersection Parameters: Calculate the intersection parameters \alpha for all pixels with all orthogonal planes of the volume in parallel using tensor operations: \mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} bx \\ by \\ bz \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} i \\ j \\ k \end{pmatrix} \otimes \begin{pmatrix} \Delta X \\ \Delta Y \\ \Delta Z \end{pmatrix} - \mathbf{s} \oslash (\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{s}) where (i, j, k) are voxel indices, \otimes is the Hadamard (element-wise) product, and \oslash denotes element-wise division. In standard Siddon's, \alpha = (x{\text{plane}} - xs) / (xp - xs). 3. Determine Entry and Exit Bounds: Calculate the minimum and maximum \alpha values corresponding to the ray entering and exiting the volume bounds for each pixel: \alpha{\min} = \max \{ \min\{\alphax(0), \alphax(nx)\}, \min\{\alphay(0), \alphay(ny)\}, \min\{\alphaz(0), \alphaz(nz)\} \} \alpha{\max} = \min \{ \max\{\alphax(0), \alphax(nx)\}, \max\{\alphay(0), \alphay(ny)\}, \max\{\alphaz(0), \alphaz(nz)\} \} where \alphax(0), \alphax(nx) etc. are the \alpha values for the planes at index 0 and nx (and similarly for y, z). 4. Filter and Sort Intersections: Filter tensor \mathbf{A} to include only values in the range [\alpha{\min}, \alpha{\max}]. Sort each row \mathbf{A}(h, w, \cdot) for h \in \{1, \dots, H\}, w \in \{1, \dots, W\} to obtain the ordered sequence of plane intersections. 5. Evaluate Intensity: Compute the intensity for each pixel using the discrete summation formula: E(R) = \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s}\|2 \sum{m=1}^{M-1} (\alpha{m+1} - \alpham) \mathbf{V} \left[ \mathbf{s} + \frac{\alpha{m+1} + \alpham}{2} (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s}) \right] where \alpham are the sorted intersection parameters and M is the number of intersections. The term \mathbf{V}[\dots] samples the volume at the midpoint of the ray segment between intersections. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def generatediffdrr(V, eta, H, W, nx, ny, nz, dX, dY, dZ): """ V: Volume tensor (nx, ny, nz) eta: Parameters (rho, theta, phi, gamma, bx, by, bz) H, W: Output dimensions nx, ny, nz: Volume dimensions dX, dY, dZ: Voxel sizes """ # 1. Extract parameters rho, theta, phi, gamma, bx, by, bz = eta # 2. Compute Source Position s (Cartesian) sx = rho torch.sin(theta) torch.cos(phi) sy = rho torch.sin(theta) torch.sin(phi) sz = rho torch.cos(theta) s = torch.tensor([sx, sy, sz], device=V.device) + torch.tensor([bx, by, bz], device=V.device) # 3. Define Detector Plane Pixels P # Detector is tangent to sphere of radius rho at point -s. # Normal n = -s / rho. n = -s / rho # Create local detector grid at z = -rho, normal (0,0,-1) ycoords = torch.linspace(-W/2, W/2, W, device=V.device) xcoords = torch.linspace(-H/2, H/2, H, device=V.device) xx, yy = torch.meshgrid(xcoords, ycoords, indexing='ij') zz = -rho torch.oneslike(xx) Plocal = torch.stack([xx, yy, zz], dim=-1) # (H, W, 3) # Rotation to align (0,0,-1) to n ref = torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, -1.0], device=V.device) u = torch.cross(ref, n) if torch.norm(u) < 1e-6: u = torch.tensor([1.0, 0.0, 0.0], device=V.device) u = u / torch.norm(u) v = torch.cross(n, u) # Rotation matrix R such that R @ [0,0,-1]^T = n R = torch.stack([u, v, n], dim=-1) # (3, 3) # Apply rotation gamma about x-axis in the detector's local frame cosg = torch.cos(gamma) sing = torch.sin(gamma) Rx = torch.tensor([[1, 0, 0], [0, cosg, -sing], [0, sing, cosg]], device=V.device) Plocalrot = torch.einsum('ij,hwj->hwi', Rx, Plocal) Pworld = torch.einsum('ij,hwj->hwi', R, Plocalrot) - s.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # 4. Compute Intersection Parameters A iidx = torch.arange(nx, device=V.device).float() jidx = torch.arange(ny, device=V.device).float() kidx = torch.arange(nz, device=V.device).float() # Denominators (ray direction components) dxray = Pworld[..., 0] - s[0] dyray = Pworld[..., 1] - s[1] dzray = Pworld[..., 2] - s[2] # Guard against division by zero dxray = torch.where(dxray.abs() < 1e-9, 1e-9 torch.sign(dxray), dxray) dyray = torch.where(dyray.abs() < 1e-9, 1e-9 torch.sign(dyray), dyray) dzray = torch.where(dzray.abs() < 1e-9, 1e-9 torch.sign(dzray), dzray) # Alpha values for planes alphax = (iidx dX + bx - s[0]) / dxray.unsqueeze(0) alphay = (jidx dY + by - s[1]) / dyray.unsqueeze(0) alphaz = (kidx dZ + bz - s[2]) / dzray.unsqueeze(0) # Permute to (H, W, N) and concatenate alphax = alphax.permute(1, 2, 0) alphay = alphay.permute(1, 2, 0) alphaz = alphaz.permute(1, 2, 0) A = torch.cat([alphax, alphay, alphaz], dim=-1) # 5. Determine Bounds ax0, axn = alphax[..., 0], alphax[..., -1] ay0, ayn = alphay[..., 0], alphay[..., -1] az0, azn = alphaz[..., 0], alphaz[..., -1] minx, maxx = torch.min(ax0, axn), torch.max(ax0, axn) miny, maxy = torch.min(ay0, ayn), torch.max(ay0, ayn) minz, maxz = torch.min(az0, azn), torch.max(az0, azn) alphamin = torch.max(torch.max(minx, miny), minz) alphamax = torch.min(torch.min(maxx, maxy), maxz) # 6. Filter and Sort mask = (A >= alphamin.unsqueeze(-1)) & (A <= alphamax.unsqueeze(-1)) Asort = A.clone() Asort[~mask] = float('inf') Asorted, = torch.sort(Asort, dim=-1) # 7. Evaluate Intensity raydir = Pworld - s # (H, W, 3) raylen = torch.norm(raydir, dim=-1) # (H, W) # Handle variable number of intersections by masking valid = Asorted != float('inf') # Shift to get next alpha Anext = torch.roll(Asorted, shifts=-1, dims=-1) Anext[~valid] = 0.0 # Mask invalid # Segment validity: both current and next must be valid segvalid = valid & torch.roll(valid, shifts=1, dims=-1) # Mask the last column which wraps around segvalid[:,:, -1] = False dalpha = Anext - Asorted alphamid = (Anext + Asorted) / 2.0 # Sample volume at midpoints # Convert world coords to voxel indices midpos = s[None, None,:] + alphamid[:,:,:, None] raydir[:,:, None,:] vx = (midpos[..., 0] - bx) / dX vy = (midpos[..., 1] - by) / dY vz = (midpos[..., 2] - bz) / dZ # Trilinear interpolation x0, x1 = torch.floor(vx).long(), torch.ceil(vx).long() y0, y1 = torch.floor(vy).long(), torch.ceil(vy).long() z0, z1 = torch.floor(vz).long(), torch.ceil(vz).long() dx, dy, dz = vx - x0.float(), vy - y0.float(), vz - z0.float() v000 = V[x0, y0, z0] v100 = V[x1, y0, z0] v010 = V[x0, y1, z0] v110 = V[x1, y1, z0] v001 = V[x0, y0, z1] v101 = V[x1, y0, z1] v011 = V[x0, y1, z1] v111 = V[x1, y1, z1] v00 = v000 + dx (v100 - v000) v01 = v001 + dx (v101 - v001) v10 = v010 + dx (v110 - v010) v11 = v011 + dx (v111 - v011) v0 = v00 + dy (v10 - v00) v1 = v01 + dy (v11 - v01) Vsample = v0 + dz (v1 - v0) # Weighted sum intensity = raylen torch.sum(segvalid dalpha Vsample, dim=-1) return intensity Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Usage: The method requires storing the full intersection tensor \mathbf{A} of size H \times W \times (nx + ny + nz), leading to high memory requirements, especially for large volumes or high-resolution DRRs. This impacts performance for small image sizes compared to VGSJ. Division by Zero: If a ray is parallel to an axis (e.g., Px = sx), the denominator in the intersection calculation becomes zero. A guard value (e.g., 10^{-9}) should be used. Degenerate Input: Rays that do not intersect the volume should be handled by the filtering step, resulting in zero intensity. Time Complexity: The method performs vectorized tensor operations, which are highly parallelized on the GPU. The dominant costs are the computation of intersections, sorting, and volume sampling. Memory Complexity: O(H \cdot W \cdot (nx + ny + nz)) due to the storage of the intersection tensor \mathbf{A}. Performance: On an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti, VGS generates a 200 \times 200 DRR in 72.7 \pm 10 \mu s. For H=100, time is 17.6 \pm 0.05 ms; for H=500, time is 453 \pm 41.2 ms. Accuracy: Average RMSE of (8.3 \pm 1.9) \times 10^{-4} compared to CPU Plastimatch (CP) for normalized images. Gradient accuracy is within 0.05 \pm 0.01 of Forward Finite Differences (FFD). Gradient Efficiency: Gradient generation takes 35.1 ms \pm 73.3 \mu s, which is an order of magnitude faster than FFD (400.5 ms \pm 821.4 \mu s). Comparison: VGS is faster than CPU Plastimatch and faster than Vectorized GPU Siddon-Jacobs (VGSJ) for H < 500. At H=500, VGS and VGSJ have roughly equivalent run times. Strengths: Fast, differentiable, compatible with deep learning frameworks, GPU-accelerated. Limitations: High memory usage for large volumes or high-resolution DRRs. The method was introduced in the paper "Fast Auto-Differentiable Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs for Solving Inverse Problems in Intraoperative Imaging". It addresses the need for differentiable DRR generators in gradient-based optimization tasks, such as slice-to-volume registration in intraoperative imaging. The method builds on Siddon's ray-tracing algorithm, reformulating it for vectorized tensor computation in PyTorch. name: Inverse Rendering and Optimization
body: Inverse rendering and optimization recovers scene parameters (geometry, materials, lighting, or transfer functions) from observed images by minimizing a loss between rendered and target views. Unlike forward rendering, which computes images from known parameters, this family solves an optimization problem where the rendering integral is differentiated with respect to scene variables. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Plenoxel Data Structure by its focus on parameter recovery rather than data representation, and from Differentiable Depth Rendering by its primary output being semantic or physical scene properties rather than geometric depth maps. Builds on Differentiable volume rendering, which covers the core rendering equation and gradient propagation strategies. Optimizes transfer function parameters for a fixed scalar field to match natural language prompts. It sets itself apart by using a contrastive loss with negative prompts and a transmittance prior to ensure dense, realistic renderings, unlike naive CLIP maximization which yields transparent outputs. Choose it when semantic text guidance is required for visualization. Maps visualization parameters directly to images using a GAN, bypassing explicit physical integration. It is distinguished from Text-to-Transfer Function by its direct parameter-to-image synthesis and from Hybrid Differentiable Rendering Method by its reliance on adversarial loss rather than differentiable physics. Choose it for rapid synthesis of novel viewpoints and transfer functions without re-integrating the volume. Reconstructs 3D geometry and PBR materials from multi-view images by combining approximate rendering for geometry and physically-based rendering for reflectance. It addresses the trade-off between computational efficiency and visual fidelity, outperforming pure approximate or pure physically-based methods. Choose it when high-quality material reconstruction is needed from unstructured multi-view captures. Uses a genetic algorithm where the TF lookup table is the chromosome. It differs from vector-based genetic approaches by encoding the entire lookup table, enabling direct integration with other 1D design techniques and user-guided evolution. Choose it for interactive, user-in-the-loop transfer function design. Reconstructs scene appearance using voxel grids for opacity, normal, and reflectance parameters optimized against images from collocated point lighting. It learns global scene opacity for accurate shadows and pervoxel reflectance for complex materials, unlike methods that learn single color per voxel. Choose it for reconstructing spatially-varying reflectance and hard shadows from unstructured images. Trains a pipeline to predict silhouettes and keypoint heatmaps, learns pose/shape priors, and optimizes a differentiable renderer for mesh-to-image consistency. Train a CNN to predict silhouettes and heatmaps for predefined keypoints. Use predictions to learn pose and shape priors. Feed priors into a body mesh generator based on SMPL, trained to be consistent with learned distributions. Optimize a differentiable renderer for consistency between mesh-to-image projection and 2D annotations. A technique to recover physical parameters (sigma, q) from observed intensity data using a constant intensity model, likely for volume rendering calibration or inverse rendering. Constant intensity model: I = \text{constant\intensity}(I0, \sigma, q, s). The function signature is double constantintensity(double I0, double sigma, double q, double s) where I0 is initial intensity, \sigma is absorption coefficient, q is scattering parameter, and s is path length. RMSE calculation: rmseconstantmodel(intensity, ds, sigma, q) computes the Root Mean Square Error between the observed intensity vector and the model prediction given parameters \sigma and q, with step size ds. GridSearchResult struct: Contains double sigma, q, loss; int sigmacount, qcount; std::vector<double> lossmap; bool valid. Used to store results of a parameter search. InverseEstimate struct: Contains double sigma, q, a, b; double transitionrmse, reconstructionrmse; bool valid. Used to store the final recovered parameters and error metrics. Inverse rendering in volume visualization has evolved from manual transfer function design to automated, data-driven optimization. The advent of differentiable rendering allowed gradients to flow from image loss to scene parameters, enabling end-to-end learning. Pavlakos et al. [10] demonstrated the use of differentiable renderers for human body mesh reconstruction from 2D annotations, predicting silhouettes and keypoints to learn pose and shape priors. name: Hybrid Differentiable Rendering Method
head: Analysis-by-synthesis inverse rendering with SfM/MVS/Poisson initialization
body: The Hybrid Differentiable Rendering Method is an analysis-by-synthesis inverse rendering technique that reconstructs 3D geometry and physically-based reflectance (PBR) materials from multi-view 2D images captured by conventional hand-held cameras under uncontrolled lighting. It solves the trade-off between efficiency and visual fidelity by combining approximate differentiable rendering for geometry optimization with physically-based differentiable rendering for reflectance optimization. Unlike pure approximate methods that yield poor visual effects due to simple material models, or pure physically-based methods that incur high computational costs, this hybrid approach achieves high-quality PBR reconstructions efficiently. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of RGB images captured from multiple viewpoints using conventional hand-held cameras. No additional information (e.g., depth maps) is required. Output: Optimized 3D geometry (mesh) and physically-based reflectance parameters (material properties and environment map). Data Structures: Geometry: A triangular mesh with vertex positions and vertex colors. Lighting: An environment map representing the lighting source, stored as a learnable parameter. Scene Parameters (\Theta): Includes geometry parameters and reflection parameters. Initialization Phase: The method begins by generating a rough initial reconstruction using traditional computer vision techniques: 1. Sparse Reconstruction: Use Structure-from-Motion (SfM) to generate sparse feature points in each image and match them across images to reconstruct a sparse point cloud and a rough mesh. 2. Dense Matching: Use Multi-View Stereo (MVS) to generate dense pixel-level matching from the sparse point cloud/rough mesh. 3. Mesh Generation: Apply Poisson surface reconstruction to the dense matching to obtain a dense mesh with vertex colors derived from the input images. 4. Lighting Initialization: Initialize the environment map (lighting source) with white light, setting the three channels to (0.5, 0.5, 0.5). The environment map resolution is 512 \times 128. Optimization Phase: The optimization follows an analysis-by-synthesis formulation: \Theta^ = \arg \min{\Theta} L(I(\Theta), \Theta; \tilde{I}) where \Theta represents the scene parameters (geometry and reflection), L is the loss function, \tilde{I} is the ground truth image, and I(\Theta) is the image rendered by the hybrid method using the same camera parameters as \tilde{I}. The optimization is split into two sequential steps: 1. Geometry Optimization: Optimize the geometry first using an approximate differentiable rendering method. This method uses simplified rendering processes for efficiency. 2. Reflectance Optimization: Optimize the reflectance (and environment map) afterward using a physically-based differentiable rendering method. This method uses path tracing to reconstruct high-quality PBR materials. Both steps iteratively minimize the loss between rendered images and ground truth images for the same camera pose. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridinverserendering(inputimages, cameraposes): # Initialization Phase # Step 1: SfM for sparse reconstruction sparsecloud, roughmesh = structurefrommotion(inputimages, cameraposes) # Step 2: MVS for dense matching densematching = multiviewstereo(sparsecloud, inputimages, cameraposes) # Step 3: Poisson Surface Reconstruction for dense mesh mesh = poissonsurfacereconstruction(densematching) # Initialize lighting environmentmap = initializeenvironmentmap(resolution=(512, 128), value=(0.5, 0.5, 0.5)) # Optimization Phase # Step 4: Optimize Geometry # Use approximate differentiable renderer mesh = optimizegeometry(mesh, inputimages, cameraposes, renderer=approximatedifferentiablerenderer, lossfunction=loss) # Step 5: Optimize Reflectance and Lighting # Use physically-based differentiable renderer mesh, environmentmap = optimizereflectance(mesh, environmentmap, inputimages, cameraposes, renderer=physicallybaseddifferentiablerenderer, lossfunction=loss) return mesh, environmentmap Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method assumes the input images are captured by conventional hand-held cameras and do not contain additional information like depth. The initialization relies on the success of SfM and MVS; failure in feature matching or dense reconstruction will propagate errors. The environment map is a learnable parameter, so its initialization affects the convergence of the reflectance optimization. Efficiency: The hybrid approach combines the efficiency of approximate methods with the quality of physically-based methods. Approximate methods are efficient but have simple material models, while physically-based methods are high-quality but computationally expensive. Quality: The method produces reconstructions with similar or higher quality than state-of-the-art methods. Computational Cost: While more efficient than pure physically-based methods, it is still resource-consuming compared to pure approximate methods. Use Cases: Virtual reality, augmented reality, novel view synthesis, and relighting. Inverse rendering, which recovers 3D geometry, reflection properties, and illumination from 2D images, is a long-standing and challenging problem in computer graphics and vision. The development of multi-view inverse rendering tasks using triangular meshes as geometry representation has been promoted by the ability to back-propagate image loss along the rendering pipeline. Previous methods include approximate differentiable rendering methods [Loper and Black, 2014; Kato et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2019] and physically-based differentiable rendering methods [Li et al., 2018a; Li et al., 2021]. The hybrid method was introduced to address the limitations of both approaches. Efficient Multi-View Inverse Rendering Using a Hybrid Differentiable Rendering Method, https://doi.org/10.24963/ijcai.2023/205, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Stochastic Evolutive TF Design
head: Genetic Algorithm TF Design, Genetic Algorithm for TF Design, He et al. Genetic Algorithms, Stochastic Evolutive Transfer Function Design
body: Stochastic Evolutive TF Design is an interactive, genetic algorithm-based method for generating one-dimensional transfer functions (TFs) for volume rendering. It solves the problem of manual TF specification by allowing users to evolve a population of TFs through selection, crossover, and mutation, guided by visual feedback in the form of thumbnails. It differs from gradient-based inverse rendering methods by relying on user-driven selection rather than differentiable loss minimization, and from purely algorithmic TF generation by incorporating explicit genetic operators that manipulate the TF structure directly. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset, an initial population of TFs, and user selections of preferred TFs from rendered thumbnails. Output: An evolved TF (or set of TFs) that reveals desired structures in the volume. Data Structures: The method supports two encoding schemes for the TF chromosome: 1. Lookup Table (LUT) Encoding: The TF is represented as a fixed-size array of entries, where each entry corresponds to a scalar value bin. Each entry contains color and opacity values. This is the implementation described in as the primary method, allowing combination with other 1D TF design methods. 2. Control Point Encoding: The TF is represented as an ordered sequence of control points. Each point is defined by a scalar value and respective color and opacity. The TF used for rendering is obtained by interpolating between these control points. This is the original approach by He et al.. Note: The following steps describe the LUT-based implementation detailed in, as it provides specific operator definitions. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Generate an initial population of P TFs. Each TF is a lookup table of size N (number of scalar bins). For each TF, populate the entries with random color and opacity values, ensuring the scalar values are ordered. 2. Rendering: For each TF in the current population, render a thumbnail of the volume dataset. 3. Selection: The user inspects the thumbnails and selects the best ones to serve as parents for the next generation. The selected TFs are preserved in the selection pool. 4. Reproduction: Generate a new population of descendants from the selected parents using crossover and mutation operators. Crossover: 1. Randomly select two parent TFs. 2. Randomly determine two cutting points, c1 and c2, within the range [0, N-1], such that c1 < c2. 3. Create two offspring. For the first offspring, take the interval [c1, c2] from Parent A and the outer intervals [0, c1) and [c2, N-1] from Parent B. For the second offspring, take the interval [c1, c2] from Parent B and the outer intervals from Parent A. Mutation: Apply one or more of the following mutation operators to a TF: M1 (Triangular): Define a mutation region [m1, m2]. Define a center mc within this region. Define a target opacity o{center} for mc. Apply linear interpolation between o{center} and the opacity values at m1 and m2. M2 (Random): Define a mutation center mc and a range. Randomly set the opacities for the voxel values (bins) around mc. M3 (Rectangular): Randomly select a center and range for the mutation. Randomly set the colors and opacities for the bins within this range, constrained by limited intervals. M4 (Global Scale): Apply a random global scale factor to all opacity values in the TF. 5. Iteration: Render thumbnails for the new population. Repeat steps 3-4 until the user is satisfied with the visualization. High-resolution rendering can be used for detailed inspection if thumbnail quality is insufficient. Formulas: Rendering: The thumbnails are rendered using Engel's pre-integrated volume rendering method to handle high-frequency features introduced by genetic operators. The standard emission-absorption model is used for the final high-resolution rendering if needed. Interpolation (Control Point Variant): If using control points, the TF value T(v) for a scalar value v is obtained by interpolating between adjacent control points (vi, ci, oi) and (v{i+1}, c{i+1}, o{i+1}). Parameters: Population size: Not given in the sources. Mutation rate: Not given in the sources. Crossover rate: Not given in the sources. LUT size (N): Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High-Frequency Artifacts: Genetic operators can produce high-frequency features in the TF domain, which might cause artifacts in the resulting images. This is mitigated by using Engel's pre-integrated volume rendering method, which handles high frequencies well. Low-Resolution Evaluation: Thumbnail quality may be insufficient for proper evaluation. The method provides a second level of interaction for high-resolution inspection of specific TFs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random class TransferFunction: def init(self, size, numbins): self.size = size self.numbins = numbins # Initialize with random color and opacity for each bin self.colors = [[random.random(), random.random(), random.random()] for in range(numbins)] self.opacities = [random.random() for in range(numbins)] def crossover(self, other): """ Crossover operator: randomly takes two TFs and cuts them at two points. The interval between the two points of one TF is combined with the two outer intervals of the other TF. """ c1 = random.randint(0, self.numbins - 2) c2 = random.randint(c1 + 1, self.numbins - 1) # Offspring 1: Interval from self, outer from other child1colors = self.colors.copy() child1colors[c1:c2+1] = other.colors[c1:c2+1] child1opacities = self.opacities.copy() child1opacities[c1:c2+1] = other.opacities[c1:c2+1] # Offspring 2: Interval from other, outer from self child2colors = other.colors.copy() child2colors[c1:c2+1] = self.colors[c1:c2+1] child2opacities = other.opacities.copy() child2opacities[c1:c2+1] = self.opacities[c1:c2+1] return [TransferFunction(self.size, self.numbins) for in range(2)] # Placeholder for actual object creation def mutatetriangular(self): """ M1: Triangular mutation. Define an opacity value for the center of the mutation region and apply linear interpolation between the central opacity value and the opacity values at each border of the mutation. """ m1 = random.randint(0, self.numbins - 2) m2 = random.randint(m1 + 1, self.numbins - 1) mc = random.randint(m1, m2) ocenter = random.random() # Interpolate from m1 to mc for i in range(m1, mc + 1): t = (i - m1) / (mc - m1) if mc != m1 else 0 self.opacities[i] = self.opacities[m1] (1 - t) + ocenter t # Interpolate from mc to m2 for i in range(mc, m2 + 1): t = (i - mc) / (m2 - mc) if m2 != mc else 0 self.opacities[i] = ocenter (1 - t) + self.opacities[m2] t def mutaterandom(self): """ M2: Random mutation. Randomly set the opacities for the voxel values around the mutation center. """ mc = random.randint(0, self.numbins - 1) rangesize = random.randint(1, self.numbins // 2) start = max(0, mc - rangesize) end = min(self.numbins - 1, mc + rangesize) for i in range(start, end + 1): self.opacities[i] = random.random() def mutaterectangular(self): """ M3: Rectangular mutation. Randomly set the center and range of the mutation, as well as the colors and opacities, between limited intervals. """ center = random.randint(0, self.numbins - 1) rangesize = random.randint(1, self.numbins // 2) start = max(0, center - rangesize) end = min(self.numbins - 1, center + rangesize) for i in range(start, end + 1): self.opacities[i] = random.random() self.colors[i] = [random.random(), random.random(), random.random()] def mutateglobalscale(self): """ M4: Global Scale. Apply a random global scale to all opacity values. """ scale = random.random() for i in range(self.numbins): self.opacities[i] = min(1.0, self.opacities[i] scale) def evolvetf(volumedata, initialpopulation, numgenerations): """ Main evolution loop. """ population = initialpopulation for gen in range(numgenerations): # Render thumbnails for current population thumbnails = [renderthumbnail(tf, volumedata) for tf in population] # User selects parents (simulated here by selecting top K based on some metric) # In practice, this is an interactive step selectedparents = selectparentsinteractively(thumbnails) newpopulation = [] while len(newpopulation) < len(population): # Crossover if random.random() < 0.8: # Crossover rate p1, p2 = random.sample(selectedparents, 2) children = p1.crossover(p2) newpopulation.extend(children) # Mutation if len(newpopulation) < len(population): parent = random.choice(selectedparents) child = TransferFunction(parent.size, parent.numbins) child.colors = parent.colors.copy() child.opacities = parent.opacities.copy() # Apply random mutation mutationtype = random.choice(['triangular', 'random', 'rectangular', 'globalscale']) if mutationtype == 'triangular': child.mutatetriangular() elif mutationtype == 'random': child.mutaterandom() elif mutationtype == 'rectangular': child.mutaterectangular() elif mutationtype == 'globalscale': child.mutateglobalscale() newpopulation.append(child) population = newpopulation return population An alternative encoding where TFs are sequences of control points interpolated for rendering. It is more compact but requires interpolation logic. Choose when memory is constrained or smooth TFs are preferred. A complementary method where users draw directly on the TF plot. It offers precise control but lacks the stochastic exploration of genetic algorithms. Choose when a specific TF shape is known. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of generations, population size, and rendering time per thumbnail. Rendering thumbnails is the dominant cost. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the population size and TF size (LUT or control points). Strengths: Intuitive user interface; allows exploration of diverse TFs; handles high-frequency TF features via pre-integrated rendering. Limitations: Requires user interaction; not fully automated; performance depends on rendering speed. When to use: When the user has a vague idea of the desired visualization and wants to explore the space of possible TFs. When not to use: When a fully automated, gradient-based optimization is required, or when real-time feedback is critical and rendering is slow. The method is based on the work of He et al. [HE 96], who proposed a genetic algorithm-based technique for specifying 1D TFs directed at images. The implementation described in is a more flexible version that uses the TF lookup table itself as the chromosome, allowing combination with other 1D TF design methods. The method was developed to provide a more intuitive domain for TF specification, where the distance to the edge is mapped to optical attributes. name: Deep Reflectance Volumes
head: DRV, DRV rendering, Deep Reflectance Volume Rendering, discretized differentiable volume rendering
body: Deep Reflectance Volumes (DRV) is a differentiable volume rendering method that reconstructs scene appearance from unstructured images captured under collocated point lighting by optimizing a volumetric representation of opacity, surface normal, and reflectance parameters. It distinguishes itself from standard volume rendering by learning a global opacity field that accumulates along both view and light directions, enabling the synthesis of accurate hard shadows and complex specular reflections under novel lighting conditions, which standard alpha-compositing methods typically fail to model. Inputs: A set of K captured images \{Ik\}{k=1}^K with known camera poses and collocated light positions. Outputs: A learned volumetric scene representation consisting of voxel grids for opacity, normal, and reflectance, optimized to minimize the difference between rendered and captured images. The scene is represented in a "warped" latent space before being mapped to world space for rendering. The core data structure is an 8-channel tensor of resolution 128 \times 128 \times 128: Channel 0: Opacity \alphaw (scalar). Channels 1–3: Surface normal \mathbf{n}w (3D vector, typically normalized). Channels 4–6: Diffuse albedo (3D vector, RGB). Channel 7: Specular roughness (scalar). Additionally, the warping function requires: Global Affine Matrix: Wg (4 \times 4 matrix). Basis Affine Matrices: \{Wj\}{j=1}^{16} (16 matrices, each 4 \times 4). Weight Volume: B (32 \times 32 \times 32 tensor, 16 channels). Bj(\mathbf{x}) denotes the j-th channel value at position \mathbf{x}. To increase effective resolution, world-space positions \mathbf{x} are warped to a transformed space \mathbf{x}w using a learned affine-based warping function: W(\mathbf{x}) = \left[ \sum{j=1}^{16} Bj(\mathbf{x}) Wj \right]^{-1} Wg \mathbf{x} The volume is decoded into this warped space. During ray marching, points are sampled in world space, but the network queries the volume at the warped coordinates W(\mathbf{x}). The rendering module is a differentiable volume ray marcher based on classical alpha compositing. It computes reflected radiance by accumulating contributions from sampled points, modeling single-bounce light transport. 1. Ray Sampling: For a camera at position \mathbf{c} and direction -\boldsymbol{\omega}o, points are sampled along the ray with a fixed step size \Delta x: \mathbf{x}s = \mathbf{x}{s-1} - \boldsymbol{\omega}o \Delta x = \mathbf{c} - s \boldsymbol{\omega}o \Delta x Sampling continues until the ray exits the volume bounds (defined as a cube [-1, 1]^3). 2. Opacity Accumulation: Unlike standard volume rendering which only accumulates opacity along the view direction, DRV accumulates opacity from both the camera and the light source to model shadows. Camera Opacity: \alpha{c \to s} accumulates occlusion along the view ray. Light Opacity: \alpha{l \to t} accumulates occlusion along the ray from the sample point to the light source \mathbf{l}. During training with collocated camera and light, \alpha{l \to t} = \alpha{c \to s}, allowing a single-pass accumulation. For novel lighting, two-pass accumulation is required. 3. Radiance Compositing: At each sample point \mathbf{x}s, the local normal \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{x}s) and reflectance parameters R(\mathbf{x}s) (albedo and roughness) are queried from the volume. The reflected radiance L(\mathbf{x}s) is computed using a simplified Disney BRDF model: L(\mathbf{x}s) = fr(\boldsymbol{\omega}o, \boldsymbol{\omega}i, \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{x}s), R(\mathbf{x}s)) Ll(\mathbf{x}s, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) where \boldsymbol{\omega}i is the direction from \mathbf{x}s to the light \mathbf{l}, and Ll is the light radiance. The final accumulated radiance Ls and camera opacity \alpha{c \to s} are updated recursively: Ls = L{s-1} + [1 - \alpha{c \to (s-1)}][1 - \alpha{l \to (t-1)}]\alpha(\mathbf{x}s)L(\mathbf{x}s) \alpha{c \to s} = \alpha{c \to (s-1)} + [1 - \alpha{c \to (s-1)}] \alpha(\mathbf{x}s) \alpha{l \to t} = \alpha{l \to (t-1)} + [1 - \alpha{l \to (t-1)}] \alpha(\mathbf{x}t) The rendered color for the pixel is L{final} when the ray exits the volume. The network parameters (encoding vector, transposed convolutional layers for upsampling) and the volume values are optimized per scene using gradient descent. The loss function combines rendering error and regularization terms: \mathcal{L} = \sumk \| Lk - \tilde{L}k \|^2 + \beta1 \sumk \left[ \log(\alpha{ck \to s'}) + \log(1 - \alpha{ck \to s'}) \right] + \beta2 \sum \| \nabla{\mathbf{x}} \log \alpha(\mathbf{x}) \| Rendering Loss: Mean squared error between rendered image Lk and captured image \tilde{L}k. Opacity Regularization: Encourages accumulated opacity to be binary (0 or 1) to reduce artifacts. Sparsity Regularization: Encourages spatial sparsity of the volume opacity. Volume Bounds: Cube [-1, 1]^3. Ray Marching Step Size (\Delta x): 1/64 during training. Note that the voxel opacity \alpha is dependent on this step size, representing one minus the transmission over segment \Delta x. Training Batch: 128×128 pixels sampled from 8 captured images. Regularization Weights: Initial \beta1 = 0.01, \beta2 = 0.01. After 300,000 iterations, increased to \beta1 = 1.0, \beta2 = 0.1 to sharpen boundaries. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import numpy as np class DeepReflectanceVolume: def init(self, volumesize=128, warpinggridsize=32, numbasis=16): # Initialize learnable parameters # 8-channel volume: 1 alpha, 3 normal, 3 albedo, 1 roughness self.volume = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(8, volumesize, volumesize, volumesize)) # Warping parameters self.Wg = nn.Parameter(torch.eye(4)) # Global affine self.Wbases = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(numbasis, 4, 4)) # 16 basis matrices self.Bweights = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(16, warpinggridsize, warpinggridsize, warpinggridsize)) # 16-channel weight volume # Hyperparameters self.stepsize = 1.0 / 64.0 self.volumeboundsmin = -1.0 self.volumeboundsmax = 1.0 # Reflectance model parameters (simplified Disney BRDF) # Note: Actual BRDF implementation is complex; here we assume a callable self.brdf = SimplifiedDisneyBRDF() def warp(self, xworld): """ Warp world-space position x to transformed space. xworld: (N, 3) tensor Returns: (N, 3) tensor in warped space """ # Convert to homogeneous coordinates (N, 4) xhomo = torch.cat([xworld, torch.ones(xworld.shape[0], 1, device=xworld.device)], dim=1) # Compute spatially varying basis matrix sum # Bweights is (16, 32, 32, 32). We need to interpolate B at xworld. # Assuming xworld is normalized to [0,1] for grid lookup or scaled appropriately. # For implementation, we assume a helper function 'trilinearsample' exists. Bvals = trilinearsample(self.Bweights, xworld) # Shape: (N, 16) # Sum of Bj Wj # Wbases is (16, 4, 4) # Result is (N, 4, 4) Mspatial = torch.einsum('nj,jkl->nkl', Bvals, self.Wbases) # Inverse of the spatial matrix # Add small epsilon for stability Minv = torch.inverse(Mspatial + 1e-6 torch.eye(4).unsqueeze(0).repeat(Mspatial.shape[0], 1, 1)) # Apply global warp and inverse spatial warp # W(x) = [Sum Bj Wj]^-1 Wg x xwarpedhomo = torch.bmm(Minv, torch.bmm(self.Wg.unsqueeze(0).repeat(Mspatial.shape[0], 1, 1), xhomo.unsqueeze(2)).squeeze(2)) # Convert back to 3D xwarped = xwarpedhomo[:,:3] / xwarpedhomo[:, 3:4] return xwarped def queryvolume(self, xwarped): """ Query the 8-channel volume at warped coordinates. xwarped: (N, 3) tensor, coordinates in [0, 1] range relative to volume grid Returns: (N, 8) tensor """ # Normalize coordinates to [-1, 1] for trilinear interpolation if needed, # or scale to [0, 1] depending on PyTorch gridsample convention. # Assuming gridsample expects normalized coordinates [-1, 1] coords = 2.0 xwarped - 1.0 coords = coords.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # (1, 1, N, 3) # gridsample expects (N, C, H, W) or (N, C, D, H, W) # We need to permute volume to (1, 8, D, H, W) vol = self.volume.unsqueeze(0) # (1, 8, 128, 128, 128) # Sample # gridsample output shape: (1, 8, 1, N) samples = torch.nn.functional.gridsample(vol, coords, aligncorners=True) return samples.squeeze(2).squeeze(0).T # (N, 8) def renderray(self, camerapos, raydir, lightpos): """ Render a single ray using DRV. """ # Determine ray bounds intersection with [-1, 1]^3 # Simplified: assume ray starts inside or we clip. # For robustness, compute tmin and tmax. # Omitting detailed AABB intersection for brevity, assuming valid samples. numsamples = 100 # Example tvalues = torch.linspace(0, 1, numsamples, device=camerapos.device) 10.0 # Arbitrary max depth # Sample points in world space xworld = camerapos.unsqueeze(0) + raydir.unsqueeze(0) tvalues.unsqueeze(1) # Warp points xwarped = self.warp(xworld) # Query volume # Volume values: alpha, normal, albedo, roughness voldata = self.queryvolume(xwarped) # (N, 8) alpha = voldata[:, 0].sigmoid() # Ensure alpha in [0,1] normal = torch.nn.functional.normalize(voldata[:, 1:4], dim=1) albedo = voldata[:, 4:7] roughness = voldata[:, 7].sigmoid() # Initialize accumulators Lacc = torch.zeroslike(alpha[0]) alphac = torch.zeroslike(alpha[0]) # Camera opacity alphal = torch.zeroslike(alpha[0]) # Light opacity for s in range(numsamples): # Check if ray exited volume (opacity reached 1) if alphac[s] >= 1.0: break # Compute light direction lightdir = lightpos - xworld[s] lightdir = torch.nn.functional.normalize(lightdir, dim=0) # Compute light opacity (occlusion from light to point) # In collocated training, alphal == alphac. # For general case, we need to march towards light. # Simplified: assume alphal is computed via a separate pass or approximation. # Here we use the accumulated camera opacity as a proxy for shadow if collocated, # or compute it explicitly. The source says for non-collocated, two-pass is needed. # For this pseudocode, we assume a helper computelightopacity exists. alphals = computelightopacity(self, xworld[s], lightpos) # Compute reflected radiance # View direction is -raydir viewdir = -raydir radiance = self.brdf(normal[s], viewdir, lightdir, albedo[s], roughness[s]) # Compositing # Ls = L{s-1} + [1 - alphac][1 - alphal] alpha L contribution = (1.0 - alphac[s]) (1.0 - alphals) alpha[s] radiance Lacc = Lacc + contribution # Update camera opacity alphacnext = alphac[s] + (1.0 - alphac[s]) alpha[s] alphac = torch.cat([alphac, alphacnext.unsqueeze(0)]) return Lacc[-1] def forward(self, camerapos, raydir, lightpos): return self.renderray(camerapos, raydir, lightpos) def computelightopacity(drv, point, lightpos): """ Helper to compute light opacity. In practice, this requires marching from point to light. For collocated training, this equals camera opacity. """ # Placeholder for the second ray march towards light # Returns accumulated opacity along the light ray return 0.0 # Simplified for collocated case where alphal = alphac Step Size Dependency: The voxel opacity \alpha is dependent on the ray marching step size \Delta x. Changing \Delta x without retraining or adjusting the volume values will alter the appearance. Lighting Configuration: During training with collocated camera and light, light opacity is equivalent to camera opacity, allowing single-pass accumulation. Re-rendering under non-collocated lighting requires a two-pass accumulation (one for view, one for light) to compute accurate shadows. Multiple Scattering: The method simplifies the radiative transfer equation to single scattering. Fully computing multiple scattering is computationally expensive and unsuitable for this deep learning framework. Time Complexity: Rendering is O(N \cdot S) per pixel, where N is the number of samples per ray and S is the number of rays (pixels). The warping function adds overhead for coordinate transformation and volume interpolation. Memory Complexity: The volume representation requires memory proportional to the resolution of the voxel grids. For a 128^3 volume with 8 channels, this is significant but manageable. The warping grid adds 32^3 \times 16 channels. Strengths: Handles complex materials (high glossiness) and accurate hard shadows under novel lighting, which mesh-based methods and standard volume rendering struggle with. Editable reflectance volumes allow material editing. Limitations: Limited to single-bounce light transport. Performance is sensitive to the step size \Delta x and the learned warping function. Requires per-scene optimization, making it slower than feed-forward methods. Deep Reflectance Volumes was introduced by Kriegman et al. from UC San Diego and Adobe Research. It addresses the limitations of previous view synthesis methods that only accumulated opacity along view directions and learned single colors per voxel, failing to model complex reflectance and shadows. The method builds on differentiable volume rendering principles and physically-based shading models.
