name: Generative NeRF-to-NeRF Translation
head: Generative NeRF2NeRF Translation
body: Generative NeRF-to-NeRF Translation (GenN2N) is a unified framework that lifts 2D image edits to 3D by modeling the distribution of edited Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) via a conditional generative model. Unlike task-specific editing methods, it employs a plug-and-play 2D image-to-image translator to generate edited views, then learns a latent distribution of 3D edits to ensure multi-view consistency. It is distinguished from siblings like Text-to-Transfer Function by operating in the NeRF latent space rather than directly modifying transfer functions, and from GAN-based Volume Rendering by explicitly decoupling 2D editing from 3D consistency modeling via a VAE-GAN structure. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N multi-view images \{Ii\}{i=0}^{N-1} of a scene. Output: A translated NeRF model capable of rendering multi-view consistent 3D scenes corresponding to a user-defined edit (e.g., text, style, super-resolution). Data Structures: Edit Code Vector (z{ji}): A 64-dimensional real-valued vector (z{ji} \in \mathbb{R}^{64}) characterizing the specific edit for a translated image. Translated Image Set: A set of M edited images per view, denoted as \{S{ji}\}{j=0}^{M-1} for each view i \in [0, N-1]. Latent Distill Module: A tiny Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) network that maps features from a fixed pre-trained VAE encoder (from Stable Diffusion) to the edit code z{ji}. Parameters: N: Number of source views. M: Number of edited images generated per view. Steps: 1. Original NeRF Training: Train an original NeRF on the input multi-view images \{Ii\}{i=0}^{N-1} using Nerfstudio. 2. 2D Image Editing: Use a plug-and-play 2D image-to-image translator (e.g., InstructPix2Pix) to edit each source image Ii. Generate M distinct edited images S{ji} for each view i by varying initial noise or prompts, forming the translated image set \{S{ji}\}. 3. Latent Distillation: Map each translated image S{ji} to an edit code vector z{ji}. This is done by passing S{ji} through a fixed pre-trained VAE encoder (from Stable Diffusion) to extract latent features, then passing these features through the trainable tiny MLP to produce z{ji} \in \mathbb{R}^{64}. 4. Distribution Constraint: Constrain the distribution of all edit code vectors \{z{ji}\} to a standard Gaussian distribution \mathcal{N}(0, I) using a Kullback-Leibler (KL) loss, denoted as \mathcal{L}{KL}. 5. NeRF Translation and Rendering: Conditioned on the edit code z{ji}, render multi-view images \{Ci\}{i=0}^{N-1} from the translated NeRF. The NeRF architecture incorporates the latent code z to modulate its appearance/geometry. 6. Optimization: Optimize the translated NeRF parameters and the MLP parameters in the Latent Distill Module using three loss functions: Reconstruction Loss (\mathcal{L}{recon}): Ensures the rendered images match the edited 2D images. Adversarial Loss (\mathcal{L}{adv}): Improves the visual quality and realism of the rendered NeRF. Contrastive Loss (\mathcal{L}{contr}): Enforces 3D consistency. It operates by: Rendering multiple views C{ji} and C{jl} from the same NeRF using the same edit code z{ji} (different poses). These are passed back to the Latent Distill Module to get z{ji} and z{jl}. The loss minimizes the distance between these codes to ensure the same edit code yields consistent 3D semantics across views. For images S{ki} with different editing styles from S{ji}, the loss increases the distance between their respective edit codes to disentangle different edits. 7. Inference: Sample a latent vector z from the learned Gaussian distribution \mathcal{N}(0, I). Render the translated NeRF conditioned on z to generate a multi-view consistent 3D scene with the desired edit. Formulas: Edit Code Mapping: z{ji} = \text{MLP}(\text{Encoder}{\text{SD}}(S{ji})) where \text{Encoder}{\text{SD}} is the fixed VAE encoder from Stable Diffusion and MLP is the trainable network. KL Loss: \mathcal{L}{KL} = \text{KL}(q(z|S) || \mathcal{N}(0, I)) Constraining the aggregate distribution of z{ji} to a standard normal distribution. Total Loss: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{recon} + \mathcal{L}{adv} + \mathcal{L}{contr} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{KL} where \lambda is a weighting factor (value not specified in sources). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: 2D Inconsistency: The 2D translator may generate inconsistent content across views if different initial noises are used. The generative model mitigates this by learning a unified 3D distribution, but the quality depends on the diversity of the M generated images. Precision: The edit code is a continuous 64-dimensional vector. Discretization or quantization is not mentioned. Time Complexity: Training requires optimizing the NeRF, the MLP, and potentially the 2D translator (if not frozen). The use of a pre-trained VAE encoder keeps the distillation step lightweight. The contrastive loss adds computational overhead due to multiple forward passes for distance calculations. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the original NeRF, the translated NeRF, the MLP parameters, and the latent codes for the training set. The VAE encoder is frozen and off-the-shelf. Strengths: Universal framework supporting text-driven editing, colorization, super-resolution, and inpainting. Ensures 3D consistency through the generative model. Plug-and-play with 2D editors. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the 2D image-to-image translator. The Gaussian assumption for the edit code distribution may not capture complex, multi-modal edit distributions perfectly. When to use: When a unified solution for multiple NeRF editing tasks is needed, or when 3D consistency is critical and 2D edits are prone to view-dependent artifacts. When not to use: When specific, high-fidelity control over a single edit type is required and a specialized method might outperform the general framework. GenN2N was introduced in 2024 by Liu et al. in the paper "GenN2N: Generative NeRF2NeRF Translation". It addresses the limitation of previous NeRF editing methods that were designed for individual tasks (e.g., only text editing or only colorization) and often failed to maintain 3D consistency when lifting 2D edits. The method builds on the principles of Inverse Rendering and Optimization by optimizing NeRF parameters through differentiable rendering, but introduces a generative latent space to handle the ambiguity of 2D-to-3D lifting. It is used for various editing tasks including text-driven editing, colorization, super-resolution, and inpainting of human, item, indoor, and outdoor scenes. GenN2N: Generative NeRF2NeRF Translation, https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR52733.2024.00488, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Adversarial Cycle-Consistent Mesh Reconstruction
head: Adversarial Cycle-Consistent Mesh Reconstruction Loss, Pix2Vex Training Loss and Optimization
body: Adversarial Cycle-Consistent Mesh Reconstruction is an optimization framework for single-view image-to-geometry reconstruction that jointly trains a network to predict a mesh from an image (p2v), a network to predict a volume/voxel representation from an image (a2b), a network to render an image from a mesh (b2a), and a discriminator (D). It distinguishes itself from standard differentiable rendering approaches by incorporating cycle consistency between the mesh and volume domains and explicit mesh regularization to ensure topological and geometric validity. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a single input image a \in A (where A is the space of input images) and outputs a reconstructed mesh b^{00} \in B (where B is the space of 3D meshes/voxels) and an intermediate volume representation b^0 \in B. The networks p2v (image to mesh), a2b (image to volume), and b2a (mesh to image) are trained to minimize a combined loss function involving adversarial, cycle-consistency, and regularization terms. Data Structures and Network Architectures: The implementation relies on specific network topologies defined by convolutional blocks Ck and fully connected layers. Convolution-LeakyReLU Layer (Ck): A convolutional layer with k filters of size 4 \times 4 and stride 2, followed by a LeakyReLU activation with a negative slope of 0.2. From the fifth convolutional layer onwards, a dropout rate of 50% is applied. Discriminator (D): Architecture: C{64}-C{128}-C{256}-C{512}-C{1} followed by a sigmoid function. Image-to-Image Translation (a2b, b2a): These use Pix2Pix networks. The architecture consists of the first two or more residual layers of the symmetric residual network, followed by a sigmoid function. Image-to-Mesh (p2v / Pix2Vex): Based on the Pix2Pix network. The first half consists of symmetric residual network blocks: C{64}-C{128}-C{256}-C{512}-C{512}-C{512}-C{512}. This is followed by two fully connected layers: 1. Input size n^2/2 \rightarrow Output size n^2/2 + 3 \cdot v 2. Input size n^2/2 + 3 \cdot v \rightarrow Output size 3 \cdot v The output is passed through a sigmoid function. Here, n is the image resolution dimension and v is the number of vertices. Variables and Intermediate States: Given an input image a \in A: b^0 = a2b(a): The volume representation predicted directly from the image. b^{00} = SR \circ p2v(a): The mesh predicted by p2v and rendered by the Soft Rasterizer (SR). Note: In the loss definitions, b^{00} refers to the mesh representation itself in the context of the discriminator, while SR is used to generate images for comparison. The notation b^{00} in the discriminator inputs refers to the mesh generated by p2v. a^0 = b2a(b^0): The image reconstructed from the volume representation b^0. a^{00} = b2a(b^{00}): The image reconstructed from the mesh representation b^{00}. Loss Functions: The total loss is defined as: L = \min{p2v} \min{a2b} \min{b2a} \max{D} \sum{i=1}^{5} (\alphai \cdot Li) + L{reg} where \alphai \in [0, 1] are weights, Li are the five specific loss components, and L{reg} is the regularization loss. The five loss components are: L1 = E{a\sim A} [\log D(a, b^{00})] + E{a\sim A} [\log(1 - D(a, b^0))] + E{a\sim A} [\|b^{00} - b^0\|1] L2 = E{a\sim A} [\log D(a, b^{00})] + E{a\sim A} [\log(1 - D(a^{00}, b^{00}))] + E{a\sim A} [\|a^{00} - a\|1] L3 = E{a\sim A} [\log D(a, b^0)] + E{a\sim A} [\log(1 - D(a^{00}, b^0))] + E{a\sim A} [\|a^0 - a\|1] + E{a\sim A} [\|b^{00} - b^0\|1] L4 = E{a\sim A} [\log D(a, b^{00})] + E{a\sim A} [\log(1 - D(a^0, b^{00}))] + E{a\sim A} [\|a^0 - a\|1] + E{a\sim A} [\|b^{00} - b^0\|1] L5 = E{a\sim A} [\log D(a, b^0)] + E{a\sim A} [\log(1 - D(a^0, b^0))] + E{a\sim A} [\|a^0 - a\|1] Note: The source text lists the losses in a specific order that maps to specific training objectives. L1 and L3 involve cycle consistency between mesh and volume domains. L2 and L4 involve adversarial and cycle consistency for the mesh path. L5 involves adversarial and cycle consistency for the volume path. The exact mapping of indices to specific training steps is defined by the alternating training procedure below. Regularization Loss (L{reg}): Applied to the reconstructed mesh to enforce regularity and reduce curvature. It consists of three terms: 1. Normal Angle Similarity: L2 norm of the difference between normals of adjacent faces. 2. Edge Length Similarity: L1 norm of the difference between edge lengths. 3. Vertex Regularity: L1 norm of the distance from each vertex to the mean position of its adjacent vertices. Training Procedure: The training alternates in the following order: 1. Train discriminator D. 2. Train translation from B to A (b2a). 3. Train components performing translation from A to B (p2v+SR, a2b). For each section, the five losses Li are trained separately using the Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of 10^{-6}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Normal angle similarity (L2 norm) 2. Edge length similarity (L1 norm) 3. Train p2v and a2b trainp2va2b(p2v, a2b, SR, a, b0, b00, a0, a00) Stabilization of Smooth Z-Buffer: The smooth z-buffer used in the Soft Rasterizer can cause pixels not covered by any triangle to appear as if they have visible triangles because low weights close to zero can cause high values in the weighted SoftMin. To stabilize this, two triangles covering the background are added, and the visibility value is reduced with increasing distance from triangles. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Experiments were conducted with an image resolution of n \times n = 128 \times 128 and a number of vertices v = 162. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Combines adversarial training for realism, cycle consistency for domain alignment, and mesh regularization for geometric validity. Limitations: The smooth z-buffer requires stabilization tricks (background triangles) to handle uncovered pixels. The method relies on a fixed number of vertices (v=162 in experiments), which may limit the complexity of reconstructed geometries. When to Use: Use when single-view image-to-geometry reconstruction is required and the output needs to be a valid, regular mesh rather than just a volume or point cloud. The method was introduced in the paper "Pix2Vex: Image-to-Geometry Reconstruction using a Smooth Differentiable Renderer". It builds upon differentiable rendering techniques and adversarial training frameworks like Pix2Pix. The smooth z-buffer technique is related to work on blurred depth tests for non-photorealistic rendering. name: Implicit Surface Differentiable Rendering
head: Differentiable Isocontour Rendering
body: Implicit Surface Differentiable Rendering renders surfaces defined as isocontours of a scalar field f\theta: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R} by parameterizing the isosurface via the Marching Cubes algorithm. It solves the problem of differentiating through implicit surface geometry without storing or backpropagating through the complex, discrete topology of the resulting mesh. Unlike explicit mesh rendering or spline-based methods, this approach hides the non-differentiable topological decisions of Marching Cubes in a sampling function, allowing gradients to flow only through the continuous evaluation of the implicit function. Inputs: A scalar field function f\theta(\mathbf{x}) parameterized by \theta. Camera parameters defining rays \mathbf{r}. An isovalue \tau defining the surface (f\theta(\mathbf{x}) = \tau). Outputs: Rendered color buffers \mathbf{C}. Gradients \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}}{\partial \theta} with respect to the implicit function parameters. Data Structures: Sampling Parameters (Uk): A 9-dimensional vector per pixel/patch. 6 lattice indices \mathbf{v}1, \dots, \mathbf{v}6 identifying the 3 grid edges that cross the isosurface. 3 barycentric coordinates \beta1, \beta2, \beta3 defining the position of the surface point within the generated triangle. G-Buffer (Gk): Contains surface attributes. For implicit surfaces, this contains only the 3D world-space position \mathbf{x} of the surface point. Algorithm Steps: 1. Non-Differentiable Sampling (U): For each pixel, determine the intersection with the isosurface. This step identifies the 3 edges of the grid cell crossed by the isosurface and the barycentric coordinates of the intersection point. Pitfall Handling: The Marching Cubes algorithm is non-differentiable at singularities where neighboring grid values are nearly identical. To ensure well-defined derivatives, the sampling function U removes samples from grid cells where the scalar values are nearly identical, evaluating the surface only where the derivative is stable. Output: Uk = [\mathbf{v}1, \dots, \mathbf{v}6, \beta1, \beta2, \beta3]. 2. Differentiable Evaluation (G): Compute the surface point \mathbf{x} and its attributes using the parameters from Uk. This step is fully differentiable with respect to \theta. Evaluate f\theta at the 6 lattice vertices \mathbf{v}1, \dots, \mathbf{v}6. If f is grid-based, perform a lookup. Interpolate along the 3 crossing edges to find the coefficients \alpha1, \alpha2, \alpha3 that define the triangle vertices. The interpolation along an edge between vertices with values fa and fb to reach the isovalue \tau is linear: \alpha = \frac{\tau - fa}{fb - fa} The triangle vertices \mathbf{p}1, \mathbf{p}2, \mathbf{p}3 are computed as: \mathbf{p}i = (1 - \alphai) \mathbf{v}{start, i} + \alphai \mathbf{v}{end, i} Interpolate the final surface point \mathbf{x} using the barycentric coordinates \beta1, \beta2, \beta3: \mathbf{x} = \beta1 \mathbf{p}1 + \beta2 \mathbf{p}2 + \beta3 \mathbf{p}3 Store \mathbf{x} in the G-Buffer Gk. 3. Shading: Apply a shading function \mathcal{C} to the attributes in Gk to produce the final color \mathbf{C}k. For implicit surfaces, Gk contains only 3D world-space positions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def implicitsurfacerendering(ftheta, camera, isovalue, grid): # 1. Non-differentiable sampling U pixelsdata = [] for u, v in camera.pixelgrid(): ray = camera.rayforpixel(u, v) cell = rayboxintersect(ray, grid.origin, grid.cellsize) # vals = [ftheta(grid.vertex(cell, i)) for i in range(8)] if max(vals) - min(vals) < 1e-6: # singularity guard continue edges = marchingcubesedges(cell, vals, isovalue) # if len(edges) != 3: continue beta = raytriangleintersect(ray, edges, isovalue) # vindices = [e.v1 for e in edges] + [e.v2 for e in edges] pixelsdata.append((u, v, vindices, beta)) # 2. Differentiable evaluation G gbuffers = [] for u, v, vindices, beta in pixelsdata: vertexvals = [ftheta(grid.vertex(cell, idx)) for idx in vindices] trianglevertices = [] for i in range(3): vstart = grid.vertex(cell, vindices[2i]) vend = grid.vertex(cell, vindices[2i+1]) fstart = vertexvals[2i] fend = vertexvals[2i+1] alpha = (isovalue - fstart) / (fend - fstart) pedge = vstart + alpha (vend - vstart) trianglevertices.append(pedge) x = beta[0] trianglevertices[0] + beta[1] trianglevertices[1] + beta[2] trianglevertices[2] gbuffers.append({'position': x, 'u': u, 'v': v}) # 3. Shading colors = [] for g in gbuffers: color = shadingfunction(g['position']) # colors.append(color) return colors Parameters: Isovalue (\tau): The scalar value defining the surface. Typical values depend on the normalization of f\theta. Grid Resolution: Determines the granularity of the Marching Cubes triangulation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularities: Marching Cubes is non-differentiable when neighboring grid values are nearly identical, causing topological changes or degenerate triangles. The method handles this by discarding samples from such cells in the sampling function U. Topology Changes: As \theta changes, the isosurface topology may change (e.g., merging or splitting). The method avoids differentiating through these discrete changes by relying on the continuous evaluation G and filtering out unstable samples. Memory: Avoids storing the full mesh topology, reducing memory overhead compared to explicit mesh rendering. Memory usage is dominated by the storage of the scalar field f\theta and the G-buffers. Time Complexity: The sampling step U is non-differentiable. The evaluation step G is differentiable and scales with the number of pixels and the cost of evaluating f\theta. Strengths: Handles complex, evolving topologies naturally; no need to manage mesh connectivity or UVs; differentiable with respect to the implicit function parameters. Limitations: Cannot differentiate through topological changes (handled by filtering); requires evaluation of f\theta at multiple points per pixel; performance depends on the efficiency of the implicit function evaluation. When to use: When the surface geometry is defined by a continuous field (e.g., neural implicit surfaces, signed distance fields) and topology changes are expected or complex. When not to use: When the surface is static and well-represented by a mesh, or when the cost of evaluating f\theta is prohibitive. Implicit Surface Differentiable Rendering was introduced in "Differentiable Surface Rendering via Non-Differentiable Sampling" (2021). It renders implicit surfaces as isocontours of a function f\theta: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R} using a parameterization derived from Marching Cubes triangulation, allowing differentiable evaluation without storing full mesh topology. The key insight is to separate the non-differentiable topological decisions (sampling) from the differentiable geometric evaluation (interpolation). This approach builds on earlier work in differentiable rendering and implicit surface rendering. It is particularly relevant in the context of neural rendering and inverse rendering, where optimizing the parameters of an implicit surface is required. name: Sensitivity AOV
head: Adjoint Pass, Sensitivity as an Arbitrary Output Variable, Sensitivity AOVs via Reverse-Mode Differentiation, Sensitivity Buffer
body: Sensitivity AOV is a differentiable rendering technique that outputs scene parameter sensitivities as arbitrary output variables (AOVs) by computing a single adjoint pass per objective, which is then re-projected for multiple inspection viewpoints. It solves the problem of human interpretability in inverse rendering by exposing which parts of a scene matter for a given goal, analogous to how primal AOVs expose intermediate light transport quantities. Unlike forward-mode derivatives which answer "what a single parameter does to the image," sensitivity AOVs answer "which parameters matter for this objective" by being dense in parameters but sparse in objectives, and unlike transport views, placement views can re-project a finished buffer rather than accumulating contributions during the adjoint sweep. The method separates the fixed camera that defines the scalar objective from the free camera used to inspect the result. The method relies on a reverse-mode differentiation pass to populate a sensitivity buffer, from which various views (object-level, parameter-type, per-texel) are derived without recomputing gradients. Inputs: 1. Scene Parameters (\theta): A hierarchical set of parameters (e.g., floor.bsdf.reflectance) where leaves are individual parameters and interior nodes are materials or objects. 2. Objective Camera: The fixed camera defining the scalar objective M. 3. Inspection Camera: A free camera used only for viewing the sensitivity AOVs. 4. Scalar Objective (M): A function evaluated on the primal image I. Outputs: 1. Primal Image (I): I = R(\theta), where R is the renderer. 2. Sensitivity Buffer: A tree structure mirroring the scene's parameter hierarchy, storing the sensitivity g = \frac{\partial M}{\partial \theta} for every parameter component. 3. Sensitivity AOVs: Render outputs derived from the buffer via selection, aggregation, and binding. Sensitivity Buffer: A tree structure where: Leaves: Individual scene parameters (e.g., a single scalar reflectance value or a specific texel in a texture). Interior Nodes: Materials or objects grouping their parameters. Values: Scalar sensitivities \frac{\partial M}{\partial \thetai} for each leaf. Primary Visibility Data: For binding uniform parameters, a one-sample-per-pixel primary-visibility pass yields: Object Identity: The ID of the object hit by the ray. UV Coordinates: Texture coordinates for spatially varying parameters. 1. Evaluate Primal Image: Render the scene using the objective camera to obtain the primal image I = R(\theta). 2. Evaluate Objective: Compute the scalar objective value M(I). 3. Compute Adjoint Seed: Calculate the gradient of the objective with respect to the image, \frac{\partial M}{\partial I}. 4. Reverse-Mode Pass (Adjoint Sweep): Perform a single reverse-mode differentiation pass propagating \frac{\partial M}{\partial I} back through the light transport simulation. This yields the sensitivity vector g for every scene parameter \theta: g = \frac{\partial M(R(\theta))}{\partial \theta} = \frac{\partial M}{\partial I} \frac{\partial I}{\partial \theta} This step populates the Sensitivity Buffer. The cost is largely independent of the number of parameters. 5. Primary Visibility Pass (for Placement Views): Trace one ray per pixel from the inspection camera to identify the hit object and retrieve UV coordinates. This pass carries no gradient computation. 6. Selection and Aggregation: Query the sensitivity buffer to select a subtree (e.g., all parameters of one object, or all reflectance parameters across the scene). Aggregate the selected sensitivities into a single scalar per group. The standard aggregation uses the \ell2 norm of the value-weighted gradients: \text{norm} = \left\| \theta \frac{\partial M}{\partial \theta} \right\|2 This measures the total response to perturbing the whole group proportionally. For spatially varying parameters, per-texel gradients are carried to the surface via UVs. To suppress fireflies and fill gaps caused by independent sampling of gradients and visible texels, the per-texel field is pooled before projection. 7. Binding: Uniform Parameters: Bind the aggregated scalar to pixels using the object identity from the primary visibility pass. Paint the sensitivity of the hit object. Spatially Varying Parameters: Bind per-texel gradients to the surface using the hit UV coordinates. 8. Encoding: Apply tone mapping and normalization. A critical choice is whether to use raw gradients \frac{\partial M}{\partial \theta} or value-weighted gradients \theta \frac{\partial M}{\partial \theta}. The encoding must be recorded with the channel. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computesensitivityaov(scene, objectivecamera, inspectioncamera, objectivefunc): # Step 1: Evaluate Primal Image I = pathtrace(scene, objectivecamera) # Step 2: Evaluate Objective Mval = objectivefunc(I) # Step 3: Compute Adjoint Seed dMdI = autogradgradient(objectivefunc, I) # Step 4: Reverse-Mode Pass sensitivitybuffer = adjointsweep(scene, dMdI) # Step 5: Primary Visibility Pass visibilitydata = traceprimaryvisibility(scene, inspectioncamera) # Step 6 & 7: Selection, Aggregation, and Binding aovimage = Image(inspectioncamera.height, inspectioncamera.width, channels=1) for y in range(inspectioncamera.height): for x in range(inspectioncamera.width): ray = inspectioncamera.rayat(x, y) hit = scene.intersect(ray) if hit is not None: objid = hit.objectid uv = hit.uv objparams = sensitivitybuffer.selectsubtree(objid) weightedgrads = [] for param in objparams: thetaval = param.value gval = param.sensitivity weightedgrads.append(thetaval gval) if weightedgrads: aggregated = mathl2norm(weightedgrads) else: aggregated = 0.0 aovimage.setpixel(x, y, encodesensitivity(aggregated)) else: aovimage.setpixel(x, y, 0.0) return sensitivitybuffer, aovimage def traceprimaryvisibility(scene, camera): visibilitydata = {} for y in range(camera.height): for x in range(camera.width): ray = camera.rayat(x, y) hit = scene.intersect(ray) if hit: visibilitydata[(x, y)] = (hit.objectid, hit.uv) else: visibilitydata[(x, y)] = (None, None) return visibilitydata def mathl2norm(values): return math.sqrt(sum(v2 for v in values)) def encodesensitivity(value): # Encoding choice (raw vs weighted) must be recorded with the channel return value def pathtrace(scene, camera): # Standard differentiable path tracing to compute I = R(theta) pass def autogradgradient(func, x): # Standard reverse-mode automatic differentiation to compute dM/dx pass def adjointsweep(scene, dMdI): # Standard adjoint pass propagating dM/dI back to scene parameters pass Primary-visibility pass sample count: One sample per pixel. Objective Camera: Fixed camera defining M. Inspection Camera: Free camera for viewing. Encoding Weight: Parameters can be weighted by their value (\theta \frac{\partial M}{\partial \theta}) to report response to proportional perturbation. Visibility Discontinuities: Placement views read interior gradients and do not treat visibility discontinuities, making boundary-correct geometric sensitivity out of scope. Parameter Interactions: Sensitivities are local first-order quantities and do not capture interactions between parameters. Monte Carlo Variance: Derivatives inherit path-tracing variance. Buffers at low sample counts may need denoising, but denoising for faithful inspection without reordering dominant parameters is an unstudied problem. Comparability: Two sensitivity maps are only comparable if they share the same encoding (e.g., both weighted by parameter value). Comparing sensitivities across different parameter types (e.g., scalar reflectance vs. million-texel texture) requires careful normalization because their scales differ. Storage: Multiple objectives require separate adjoint propagation and buffers unless the renderer carries several adjoint channels through one sweep; storage grows linearly with the number of objectives. Time Complexity: The sensitivity buffer is computed at the cost of one backward pass, largely independent of the number of scene parameters. Generating placement views requires only a primary visibility pass, which is cheap compared to the adjoint sweep. Memory Complexity: Storage grows linearly with the number of scene parameters (for the buffer) and linearly with the number of objectives if multiple buffers are kept. Strengths: Allows human inspection of which parts of a scene matter for a given goal. One adjoint pass supports many inspection viewpoints (deferred shading analogy). Dense in parameters, sparse in objectives. Limitations: Does not capture parameter interactions. Placement views do not handle visibility discontinuities. Transport views (painting where influence lands) are not supported in the current implementation and require accumulation during the adjoint sweep. Denoising for human inspection is an open problem. When to use: When you need to understand which scene parameters drive a specific objective for a fixed camera, and you want to inspect these sensitivities from multiple viewpoints without re-differentiating. When not to use: When you need to see where a parameter's influence lands (transport view), or when you need to analyze interactions between parameters. Sensitivity AOV was introduced by Linas Beresna and Eugene Fiume in 2026. It builds on the concept of Arbitrary Output Variables (AOVs) used in rendering to decompose and inspect intermediate quantities. The method is implemented on a physically based path tracer using Dr.Jit and Path Replay Backpropagation. It positions reverse-mode attribution against its forward-mode dual, arguing that sensitivity AOVs deserve first-class output status alongside the primal image. name: Recursive Control Variates for Inverse Rendering
head: CV-PS, CV-PSS, RCV, Recursive Control Variates
body: Recursive Control Variates (RCV) is a gradient estimation technique for physically based differentiable inverse rendering that reduces variance and bias by leveraging information from previous optimization steps. It exploits the high correlation between consecutive renderings in gradient descent, where scene parameters change minimally, to recursively compound variance reduction across the optimization sequence. Unlike SAGA and SVRG which maintain a running approximation of the full gradient for machine learning pipelines, RCV handles variance from numerical integration over continuous domains, and unlike the optimal strategy of using all previous renderings as individual control variates, RCV uses only the immediate previous estimate to avoid growing covariance matrices. It effectively mitigates bias introduced by differentiating non-linear loss functions with respect to noisy inputs, preventing optimization drift. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current scene parameters \thetan, reference image I{ref}, previous control variate estimate \langle F{\theta} \rangle{CV}^{n-1}, and running statistics (mean, variance, covariance) estimated via exponentially weighted Welford’s algorithm. Outputs: Gradient estimate \langle \partial\theta L(F\theta, I{ref}) \rangle and updated control variate estimate \langle F{\theta} \rangle{CV}^{n}. Data Structures: Running Statistics: Per color channel: exponentially weighted mean Mn, variance numerator Sn, and covariance numerator Cn. The variance of the control variate \text{Var}[\langle F{\theta} \rangle{CV}] is tracked via a recurrence relation rather than direct estimation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: For n=0, set \langle F{\theta} \rangle{CV}^{0}:= \langle F{\theta} \rangle{0} and initialize running statistics. 2. Primal Rendering: Render with \thetan using sample set \mathcal{S}n to obtain \langle F{\theta} \rangle{n}. 3. Re-evaluation: Evaluate previous parameters \theta{n-1} using \mathcal{S}n to obtain \langle F{\theta} \rangle{n}^{prev}. This uses either CV-PSS (reset RNG state to match previous iteration's second pass) or CV-PS (reuse light paths with BSDF adapters and a majorant for media). 4. Compute Control Weight: Calculate \alphan = \text{Cov}[\langle F{\theta} \rangle{n}, \langle F{\theta} \rangle{n}^{prev}] / (\text{Var}[\langle F{\theta} \rangle{n}^{prev}] + \text{Var}[\langle F{\theta} \rangle{CV}^{n-1}]). Clamp \alphan \in [0, 1]. 5. Compute Control Variate: \langle F{\theta} \rangle{CV}^{n} = \langle F{\theta} \rangle{n} + \alphan (\langle F{\theta} \rangle{CV}^{n-1} - \langle F{\theta} \rangle{n}^{prev}). 6. Update Statistics: Update running statistics using \langle F{\theta} \rangle{n} and \langle F{\theta} \rangle{n}^{prev} after computing \langle F{\theta} \rangle{CV}^{n} to ensure \alphan is statistically independent of \langle F{\theta} \rangle{n-1}^{n-1}, mitigating bias. Track \text{Var}[\langle F{\theta} \rangle{CV}^{n}] via recurrence. 7. Gradient Estimation: Compute \langle \partial\theta L(F\theta, I{ref}) \rangle = \langle \partial\theta F\theta \rangle{PRB} \cdot \partial L(\langle F{\theta} \rangle{CV}^{n}, I{ref}). PRB estimates the forward gradient to maintain independence from the control variate term. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def recursivecontrolvariatesstep(paramsprev, paramscurr, cvprev, stats, refimg, lossfn, rngstate, majorant): # 1. Primal rendering with current parameters thetan # Standard path tracing evaluation using sample set Sn primalcurr = render(paramscurr, rngstate) # 2. Re-evaluate previous parameters theta{n-1} with current samples Sn # CV-PSS: reset RNG state; CV-PS: reuse paths with BSDF adapters & majorant primalprevoncurr = render(paramsprev, rngstate, reusepaths=True, majorant=majorant) # 3. Compute control weight alphan cov = stats['cov'] varprevprimal = stats['varprevprimal'] varprevcv = stats['varprevcv'] denom = varprevprimal + varprevcv alpha = cov / denom if denom > 1e-8 else 0.0 alpha = max(0.0, min(1.0, alpha)) # Clamp to [0, 1] # 4. Compute control variate estimate <F>CV^n cvcurr = primalcurr + alpha (cvprev - primalprevoncurr) # 5. Update statistics (after computing cvcurr to avoid bias) # Exponentially weighted Welford update for mean and variance/covariance numerators lambdaw = 0.99 # Exponential decay factor meanprev = stats['mean'] meancurr = lambdaw meanprev + (1 - lambdaw) primalcurr stats['mean'] = meancurr diffcurr = primalcurr - meanprev diffprev = primalprevoncurr - meanprev stats['varprevprimal'] = lambdaw stats['varprevprimal'] + (1 - lambdaw) diffcurr2 stats['cov'] = lambdaw stats['cov'] + (1 - lambdaw) diffcurr diffprev # Recurrence for CV variance: Var[<F>CV^n] = Var[<F>n] + alpha^2Var[<F>{n-1}^prev] - 2alphaCov + alpha^2Var[<F>CV^{n-1}] varcurrcv = stats['varprevprimal'] + alpha2 stats['varprevprimal'] - 2 alpha stats['cov'] + alpha2 varprevcv stats['varprevcv'] = varcurrcv # 6. Gradient estimation # PRB gradient computation of forward rendering function gradforward = computegradientprb(paramscurr, rngstate) lossderiv = lossfn(cvcurr, refimg) gradient = gradforward lossderiv return gradient, cvcurr, stats Parameters: Sample count per pixel: The method allows using only a few samples per pixel in the primal rendering phase, as the control variate reduces the resulting noise. Prior work often required tens to hundreds of samples to alleviate bias. Control weight \alphan: Clamped to the range [0, 1] to prevent negative correlation exploitation and aid convergence at the start of optimization. Color channels: Control weights are constructed separately per color channel. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bias from Correlated Weight: The weight \alphan is correlated with previous estimates, introducing bias. To mitigate this, update the running statistics after evaluating \langle F{\theta} \rangle{CV}. Bias from Non-linear Loss: For non-L2 losses, E[f(X)] \neq f(E[X]) causes bias in the loss derivative. L2 loss is the only loss function that leads to unbiased derivative estimates in this context. Bias from Multiplication: The product in the gradient estimator is only unbiased if both factors are independent estimators. This is handled by estimating the first factor using PRB and the second using the control variate. Geometric Optimization: Moving or deforming surfaces are not supported. CV-PSS would lose correlation; CV-PS would require 'shift mappings' to keep path vertices valid. Denoising: Applying a denoiser to primal images adds bias that impedes optimization. Denoising the control variate estimator instead reduces bias and yields the best results. A method for dynamically adjusting the influence of previous control variates to minimize bias and variance in gradient estimates. It addresses the trade-off between reusing historical rendering information and maintaining statistical independence from the current optimization step. It sets itself apart from static weighting schemes by adapting \alphan based on running (co-)variance statistics, though it requires careful ordering of updates to avoid introducing bias. Time Complexity: The method adds a re-evaluation step per iteration. CV-PSS doubles the primal rendering cost (approximately 1/3 of the total PRB step cost). CV-PS reduces primal rendering overheads from 2× to 1.6× and allows fusing computation into a single GPU kernel. Memory Complexity: Constant memory overhead, storing only the previous control variate estimate and running statistics per channel. This avoids the ever-growing covariance matrix required by the optimal strategy of using all previous renderings. Measured Performance: Primal rendering efficiency improves by a factor of up to 10 compared to prior work, leading to either significant speedup at equal reconstruction quality or higher quality after equal time. Scaling: When optimization reaches steady state, the recursive control variate becomes equivalent to rendering with a correspondingly larger sample count, implying unbounded noise reduction potential without proportional linear cost increase. Strengths: Reduces variance and bias; allows low sample counts; works with non-L2 losses by reducing bias; compatible with PRB for textured surfaces/homogeneous volumes and DRT for heterogeneous volumes. Limitations: Does not support geometric optimization; CV-PSS suffers from loss of correlation when parameters affect path geometry (roughness, IOR, extinction); bias remains due to correlation between weight and previous CV. When to use: Inverse rendering with textured surfaces and homogeneous/heterogeneous volumes where scene parameters change slowly between iterations. When not to use: Geometric optimization with deforming surfaces; scenarios where high correlation between steps is not present. Introduced by Baptiste Nicolet et al. in 2023. It builds on the theory of control variates [Fieller and Hartley 1954] and previous work on variance reduction in rendering [Lafortune and Willems 1995a,b; Rousselle et al. 2016]. Implemented in Mitsuba 3, combined with PRB for textured surfaces/homogeneous volumes and DRT for heterogeneous volumes. It addresses the issue of noisy gradients in differentiable rendering, which often leads to drift in optimization, by exploiting the redundancy in consecutive gradient descent steps. Recursive Control Variates for Inverse Rendering, https://research.nvidia.com/labs/rtr/publication/nicolet2023recursive/, fetched 2026-11-08

name: Heuristic Control Weights for Recursive Control Variates
head: alpha_n heuristics
body: Heuristic Control Weights for Recursive Control Variates dynamically adjusts the influence of previous control variates in differentiable volume rendering to minimize bias and variance in gradient estimates. It addresses the trade-off between reusing historical rendering information and maintaining statistical independence from the current optimization step. It sets itself apart from static weighting schemes by adapting \alphan based on running (co-)variance statistics, requiring careful ordering of updates to avoid introducing bias. The method computes a control variate estimate \langle F^n \rangle{CV} using a weight \alphan derived from historical data. The core challenge is ensuring that \alphan is not correlated with the current rendering noise, which would introduce bias. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current scene parameters, previous control variate estimate \langle F^{n-1} \rangle{CV}, running (co-)variance statistics. Output: Updated control variate estimate \langle F^n \rangle{CV}, updated statistics, new weight \alpha{n+1}. Data Structures: Running mean \mun and variance \sigma^2n of the control variate estimates. Running covariance \gamman between consecutive estimates. Weight parameter \alphan \in [0, 1]. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Control Variate Estimate: Calculate \langle F^n \rangle{CV} using the current weight \alphan and the previous control variate \langle F^{n-1} \rangle{CV}. 2. Update Statistics: Update the running (co-)variance statistics using the newly computed \langle F^n \rangle{CV} and \langle F^{n-1} \rangle{CV}. This step must occur after the evaluation of \langle F^n \rangle{CV} to ensure statistical independence between \alpha{n+1} and the current rendering noise. 3. Compute Next Weight: Calculate \alpha{n+1} based on the updated statistics. Formulas: The weight \alphan is derived from the ratio of covariance to variance. The running statistics are updated online: \mun = \mu{n-1} + \frac{\langle F^n \rangle{CV} - \mu{n-1}}{n} \sigma^2n = \sigma^2{n-1} + (\langle F^n \rangle{CV} - \mu{n-1})(\langle F^n \rangle{CV} - \mun) \gamman = \gamma{n-1} + (\langle F^n \rangle{CV} - \mu{n-1})(\langle F^{n-1} \rangle{CV} - \mu{n-1}) where n is the iteration count. The weight \alphan is then computed as \alphan = \gamma{n-1} / (\sigma^2{n-1} + \epsilon). Parameters: \alphan: The control variate weight. Typical values are determined by the optimization trajectory. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Setting \alphan = 1 causes unbounded variance because the previous control variate is never down-weighted while independent random variation continues to be added. Setting \alphan = n/(n+1) results in a uniform combination over all prior control variates regardless of how similar each one is to the current scene. Updating statistics before evaluation correlates the weight with the current image, adding significant bias. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updatecontrolvariate(prevcv, prevmean, prevvar, prevcov, currentrendering, n): # Step 1: Compute control variate estimate using current weight alphan # alphan is derived from running (co-)variance statistics; exact formula in parent article EPSILON = 1e-8 # Numerical stability constant alphan = prevcov / (prevvar + EPSILON) currentcv = alphan currentrendering + (1 - alphan) prevcv # Step 2: Update running (co-)variance statistics after evaluation # This ensures alpha{n+1} is statistically independent of current rendering noise newmean = prevmean + (currentcv - prevmean) / (n + 1) newvar = prevvar + (currentcv - prevmean) (currentcv - newmean) newcov = prevcov + (currentcv - prevmean) (prevcv - prevmean) return currentcv, newmean, newvar, newcov, n + 1 This variant focuses on the timing of the statistics update. Updating the running (co-)variance estimates after evaluating \langle F^n \rangle{CV} ensures that \alphan and \langle F^{n-1} \rangle{n-1} are statistically independent, removing the bias introduced by correlating the weight with the current image. A small amount of bias remains because \alphan is still correlated with \langle F^{n-1} \rangle{CV}, but this trade-off significantly reduces bias in the loss function gradient. Time Complexity: Adds overhead for computing and updating statistics, but reduces the number of samples needed for convergence. Memory Complexity: Requires storing running statistics (mean, variance, covariance). Strengths: Significantly reduces bias in gradient estimates, leading to higher effective sample counts (e.g., 1024 vs. 16 samples per pixel) at a fraction of the cost. Limitations: Requires careful implementation to avoid bias from correlated weights. Failure modes include unbounded variance if \alphan is not properly bounded. When to Use: When differentiable volume rendering is used for inverse rendering with iterative optimization, and bias in gradient estimates is a concern. Originated in the paper "Recursive Control Variates for Inverse Rendering" by Nicolet et al. (2023). The method addresses the issue of bias in control variate estimators when used in iterative optimization schemes for differentiable rendering. Recursive Control Variates for Inverse Rendering, https://research.nvidia.com/labs/rtr/publication/nicolet2023recursive/, fetched 2026-11-08

name: Straight-Through Estimator (STE) for Gradient Extension
head: Identity STE, Straight-Through Estimator (STE) for Codec Round-Trip, Surrogate Gradient
body: The Straight-Through Estimator (STE) is a gradient surrogate technique that enables backpropagation through non-differentiable operations, such as codec round-trips or hard windowing, by treating the operation as a black box. It solves the problem of zero gradients in regions where the forward pass involves discrete choices or irreversible transformations. Unlike standard reverse-mode automatic differentiation, which fails on non-differentiable nodes, STE decouples the forward and backward passes: the forward pass uses the actual non-differentiable function, while the backward pass applies an identity mapping (or a smooth surrogate) to extend gradients into previously inaccessible regions. It is distinct from modified variants like mSTE, which attempt to correct bias, and from analytic inversion methods that derive closed-form gradients for specific rendering integrals. The method operates in two distinct phases: a forward pass that computes the output using the non-differentiable operation, and a backward pass that propagates gradients using a surrogate rule. Input: Pre-operation values P (e.g., feature planes, primitive parameters). Output: Post-operation values \hat{P} (e.g., quantized features, rendered pixels with hard cutoffs). Gradient Input: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \hat{P}}, the gradient of the loss L with respect to the post-operation output. Gradient Output: \frac{\partial L}{\partial P}, the gradient with respect to the pre-operation input. The implementation relies on standard tensor structures for P and \hat{P}. No special bit-packing is required for the STE mechanism itself, as it operates on the computational graph level. The surrogate function, if used (as in), requires hyperparameters \beta and \gamma. 1. Forward Pass: Compute the output \hat{P} by applying the non-differentiable operation \mathcal{C} (e.g., codec encoding/decoding or hard windowing) to the input P. \hat{P} = \mathcal{C}(P) 2. Loss Computation: Compute the scalar loss L from \hat{P} using the standard differentiable loss function (e.g., \ell2 or photometric loss). 3. Backward Pass (Gradient Calculation): Compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the output \hat{P}: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \hat{P}} 4. Gradient Extension (Surrogate Rule): Assign the gradient to the input P using the identity mapping: \frac{\partial L}{\partial P} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \hat{P}} This effectively ignores the internal non-differentiable operations of \mathcal{C} during backpropagation. In contexts involving hard boundaries (e.g., primitive visibility windows), the identity mapping is replaced by a smooth surrogate function \tilde{w}(x) to allow gradients to flow across the boundary. Formula: The smooth surrogate for the hard window w(x) is defined as: \tilde{w}(x) = \operatorname{sigmoid}(\beta x) \cdot \left(\frac{\operatorname{softplus}(\beta x)}{\beta}\right)^{\sigmai} + \gamma \cdot \operatorname{sigmoid}(\beta x) where: x = (ri(\thetaj) - \rhoj)/ri(\thetaj) is the unclamped normalized distance (x > 0 inside, x < 0 outside). \sigmai is the density of the primitive. \beta and \gamma are fixed hyperparameters controlling the smoothness and extent of the gradient flow. Application: The gradient is computed through \tilde{w}(x) instead of the hard window. For exterior pixels (where x < 0), the gradient is restricted to Fourier coefficients c{i,k}, while position and orientation gradients are computed from interior pixels where the photometric loss is well-defined. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def straightthroughestimator(inputtensor, nondifferentiableop, lossfn): """ Implements the Straight-Through Estimator for gradient extension. Args: inputtensor (Tensor): The pre-operation values P. nondifferentiableop (Callable): The non-differentiable function C (e.g., codec, hard window). lossfn (Callable): The differentiable loss function L. Returns: Tensor: The gradient with respect to inputtensor. """ # 1. Forward Pass: Apply non-differentiable operation # This step is tracked by the autograd engine but contains the non-diff op outputtensor = nondifferentiableop(inputtensor) # 2. Compute Loss loss = lossfn(outputtensor) # 3. Backward Pass: Compute gradients # Standard autograd computes dL/doutputtensor loss.backward() # 4. Gradient Extension (Surrogate) # The gradient dL/dinputtensor is already set to dL/doutputtensor # by the autograd engine if the nondifferentiableop is implemented # with a custom backward pass that returns the identity. # If using a custom autograd Function: # class STEFunction(Function): # @staticmethod # def forward(ctx, x): # ctx.saveforbackward(x) # return nondifferentiableop(x) # @staticmethod # def backward(ctx, gradoutput): # return gradoutput, None # Identity mapping for x, None for op params # # outputtensor = STEFunction.apply(inputtensor) return inputtensor.grad def smoothsteforwardbackward(inputparams, hardwindowfunc, surrogatefunc, lossfn): """ Implements STE with a smooth surrogate for hard windows (e.g., Fourier Splatting). Args: inputparams (Tensor): Primitive parameters (e.g., Fourier coefficients, position). hardwindowfunc (Callable): The hard window function w(x) for forward pass. surrogatefunc (Callable): The smooth surrogate function wtilde(x) for backward pass. lossfn (Callable): The photometric loss function. Returns: Tensor: The gradient with respect to inputparams. """ # 1. Forward Pass: Use hard window # This creates a "dead zone" outside the boundary where gradients are zero renderedimage = hardwindowfunc(inputparams) loss = lossfn(renderedimage) # 2. Backward Pass: Use smooth surrogate # We must manually handle the backward pass to swap the window function # This requires a custom autograd Function or manual gradient computation # Compute gradient w.r.t rendered image gradrendered = lossfn.backward(renderedimage) # dL/drendered # Propagate through the smooth surrogate # The surrogate allows gradients to flow to parameters even for pixels outside the boundary # For exterior pixels, restrict gradient to Fourier coefficients # For interior pixels, compute position/orientation gradients normally # Pseudocode for the custom backward logic: # gradparams = torch.zeroslike(inputparams) # for pixel in pixels: # if pixel is interior: # gradparams += surrogatefunc.gradient(inputparams) gradrendered[pixel] # elif pixel is exterior: # # Only update Fourier coefficients, not position/orientation # gradparams.fouriercoeffs += surrogatefunc.gradient(inputparams.fouriercoeffs) gradrendered[pixel] # Note: In practice, this is often implemented via a custom autograd Function # where the forward pass uses hardwindowfunc and the backward pass # computes gradients using surrogatefunc. return inputparams.grad \beta (Smoothness): Controls the steepness of the sigmoid in the surrogate. Higher values make the surrogate closer to the hard window but may lead to numerical instability. Not given in the sources for specific values, but described as a fixed hyperparameter. \gamma (Exterior Gradient Weight): Scales the gradient contribution from exterior pixels. Not given in the sources for specific values, but described as a fixed hyperparameter. \sigmai (Density): The density of the primitive, used in the exponent of the surrogate function. Bias: The identity STE is biased because it ignores the non-linear distortions introduced by codecs (quantization, transforms, entropy coding). This can cause gradient mismatch and potential training instability. However, empirical evidence suggests it remains robust, particularly in low-bitrate regimes. Dead Zones: Without STE, hard windows create regions with zero gradient (dead zones) outside the primitive boundary, preventing optimization of parameters that affect those regions. Exterior Pixel Gradients: In the smooth surrogate variant, gradients for exterior pixels are restricted to Fourier coefficients to avoid unstable updates to position and orientation, which are better optimized using interior pixel gradients. A training framework that inserts standard, non-differentiable codecs directly into the neural radiance field training loop using a straight-through estimator (STE) to pass gradients. A variant of STE that rescales the detached codec error using the standard deviation of the quantization error to modulate the backward signal. Time Complexity: The forward pass complexity is dominated by the non-differentiable operation (e.g., codec encoding/decoding). The backward pass is O(1) relative to the operation's internal complexity, as it only involves an identity mapping or a simple surrogate function evaluation. Memory Complexity: No additional memory is required for intermediate states of the non-differentiable operation, unlike reverse-mode AD which may require storing all intermediate values. Performance: In ablation studies, vanilla STE achieved PSNR 33.56, SSIM 0.969, LPIPS 0.182, and training time 1h 14m at high-rate, and PSNR 31.91, SSIM 0.957, LPIPS 0.267, and training time 1h 9m at low-rate. It provides the most robust optimization, particularly in low-bitrate regimes where codec-induced distortions are strongest. Strengths: Simple to implement; enables training with standard, non-differentiable codecs; robust in practice despite theoretical bias. Limitations: Biased gradients; potential for training instability if the bias is severe; not suitable for applications requiring precise gradient accuracy (e.g., scientific simulation). When to Use: When integrating standard, non-differentiable codecs into differentiable rendering pipelines; when hard boundaries prevent gradient flow. When Not to Use: When precise gradient information is critical; when the non-differentiable operation has a known analytic gradient (use Analytical Gradients instead). The Straight-Through Estimator was introduced as a technique to address zero-gradient regions in differentiable rendering and optimization. It has been applied in various contexts, including differentiable volume rendering with codecs (CATRF) and Fourier Splatting for scalable radiance fields. The method is particularly relevant in the context of differentiable volume rendering, where non-differentiable operations like quantization or hard visibility masks are common. CATRF: Codec-Adaptive TriPlane Radiance Fields for Volumetric Content Delivery, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvprf71909.2026.00048, fetched 2026-10-30 Fourier Splatting: Generalized Fourier encoded primitives for scalable radiance fields, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2603.19834, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Standard-Codec-in-the-Loop (SCL)
head: Codec-in-the-Loop with STE
body: Standard-Codec-in-the-Loop (SCL) is a training framework that inserts standard, non-differentiable codecs (such as JPEG, HEVC, or AV1) directly into the neural radiance field (NeRF) training loop. It solves the problem of optimizing scene representations under realistic compression constraints by using a straight-through estimator (STE) to bypass the codec during backpropagation. Unlike prior codec-in-the-loop methods that rely on differentiable proxies or learned entropy models, SCL allows the use of arbitrary, off-the-shelf codecs. It builds on Straight-Through Estimator (STE) for Gradient Extension by applying the STE mechanism specifically to the quantization and packing steps of feature planes and density grids. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Pre-codec feature planes P^{ax} for each axis ax \in \{xy, xz, yz\}; pre-codec density grid D; camera parameters \pi; network weights \phi. Outputs: Rendered image I; updated parameters (P, D, \phi). Data Structures: P^{ax}: Feature planes for each spatial axis. D: Density grid. Q(\cdot): Quantization function mapping continuous values to discrete indices. \text{pack}(\cdot): Bit-packing function converting quantized data into a bitstream. Cq(\cdot): The standard codec encoder, taking packed bits and returning reconstructed bits \hat{Y} and bit count. \text{unpack}(\cdot): Bit-unpacking function converting reconstructed bits back to quantized indices. Q^{-1}(\cdot): Dequantization function mapping indices back to continuous values. \text{detach}(\cdot): A stop-gradient operator that returns the input in the forward pass but blocks gradients in the backward pass. Formulas: The STE overrides for the reconstructed feature planes \widetilde{P}^{ax} and density grid \widetilde{D} are defined as: \widetilde{P}^{ax} = \widehat{P}^{ax} + \left( P^{ax} - \texttt{detach}(P^{ax}) \right) \widetilde{D} = \widehat{D} + \left( D - \texttt{detach}(D) \right) where \widehat{P}^{ax} and \widehat{D} are the values obtained after the full codec round-trip (quantize, pack, encode, decode, unpack, dequantize). The gradient flow through these overrides is: \frac{\partial \widetilde{P}^{ax}}{\partial P^{ax}} = \mathbf{I}, \quad \frac{\partial \widetilde{D}}{\partial D} = \mathbf{I} This ensures gradients bypass the non-differentiable codec operations and flow directly to the pre-codec features P^{ax} and D. Parameters: Gradient-surrogate choice: The method supports vanilla STE, modified STE, and hybrid STE+SPSA. Vanilla STE is reported to provide the best robustness. Loss weights: \lambda{\text{rec}} for image reconstruction loss and \lambda{\text{tv}} for total variation regularization on P. Pseudocode: The training step for SCL is implemented as follows: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def scltrainingstep(P, D, pi, phi): # 1. Process feature planes for each axis Ptilde = {} for ax in ['xy', 'xz', 'yz']: # (a) Quantize and pack X01 = quantize(P[ax]) Y = pack(X01) # (b) Encode and decode using standard codec Yhat, bits = codecencode(Y) Phatax = dequantize(unpack(Yhat)) # (c) Apply STE override # Ptilde[ax] = Phatax + (P[ax] - detach(P[ax])) Ptilde[ax] = Phatax + P[ax] - detach(P[ax]) # 2. Process density # Quantize and mono tiling are applied to D before encoding # Assuming similar codec round-trip for density Dhat = codecroundtripdensity(D) # Apply STE override for density Dtilde = Dhat + D - detach(D) # 3. Render and Update # Render using the STE-override values I = render(Ptilde, Dtilde, pi, phi) # Compute loss (e.g., L1 reconstruction + TV regularization) L = computeloss(I, groundtruth, P) # Update parameters (P, D, phi) using gradients from L updateparameters(P, D, phi, L) return I, L Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on the assumption that the pre-codec values P^{ax} and D are differentiable. If the quantization or packing introduces numerical instability, gradients may be affected, though the STE bypasses the codec's internal non-differentiability. Codec Compatibility: The method is designed to work with any standard codec that accepts packed bitstreams and returns reconstructed bitstreams. The specific implementation of codecencode and codecroundtripdensity must match the codec's API. Reduces computational cost by caching decoded feature planes and density volumes, refreshing them only when necessary. Combines vanilla STE with SPSA to reduce gradient bias during cache updates, at the cost of higher variance and training time. Time Complexity: The forward pass involves a full codec round-trip for each feature plane and the density grid, which is computationally expensive. The backward pass is efficient as it bypasses the codec via STE. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the pre-codec features, density grid, and the codec's internal state during encoding/decoding. Performance: SCL enables training with standard codecs, which are widely available and optimized. It provides robust gradient flow compared to other surrogate methods. Strengths: No need for differentiable codec proxies; compatible with any standard codec; robust gradient estimation. Limitations: High computational cost during training due to codec invocation; potential for gradient bias if the codec's distortion is significant. When to use: When the goal is to optimize NeRFs for delivery over networks using standard compression codecs. When not to use: When real-time training is required or when differentiable compression models are available and sufficient. SCL was introduced in the CATRF (Codec-Adaptive TriPlane Radiance Fields) paper. It addresses the limitations of prior codec-in-the-loop frameworks that relied on differentiable proxies or learned codecs. By using STE, SCL allows the direct insertion of standard, non-differentiable codecs into the training loop, enabling more realistic optimization for volumetric content delivery. CATRF: Codec-Adaptive TriPlane Radiance Fields for Volumetric Content Delivery, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvprf71909.2026.00048, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Caching for SCL Training
head: Standard-Codec-in-the-Loop (SCL) caching
body: This method reduces the computational cost of invoking a standard codec round trip on every mini-batch during Standard-Codec-in-the-Loop (SCL) training, particularly for dynamic scenes where video codecs operate on sequences of frames. It maintains a per-frame cache of decoded feature planes and density volumes, refreshing them only when necessary based on time or parameter drift. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current global training step g, cached last refresh step g{cache}, current unquantized TriPlane features P^{ax}t for each axis ax \in \{xy, xz, yz\}, current unquantized density grid Dt, and a frame index t with associated rays \{(o, d)\} and camera pose \pi. Outputs: Updated cached decoded planes \widehat{P}^{ax}t, cached decoded density \widehat{D}t, and the rendered image I. Data Structures: Cache: Stores the decoded TriPlane \widehat{P}^{ax}t and a snapshot of the raw plane P^{ax}t at the time of refresh for each axis ax \in \{xy, xz, yz\}. Cache: Stores the decoded density grid \widehat{D}t and a snapshot of the raw density Dt at the time of refresh. Scalar: g{cache}, the global step at which the last cache refresh occurred. Parameters: M: The maximum interval between step-based refreshes. Typical value: M=128. \epsilon: Threshold for relative change (drift) to trigger change-based refresh. Measured by normalized \ell2 difference. Value not given in the sources. Algorithm: 1. Sample a frame index t, rays \{(o, d)\}, and camera pose \pi. 2. Determine if a refresh is required: Step-based refresh: If the cache is empty or g - g{cache} \ge M, mark refresh as true. Change-based refresh: Calculate the relative change between the current (P^{ax}t, Dt) and their cached snapshots. If this relative change exceeds \epsilon (measured by normalized \ell2 difference), mark refresh as true, even if g - g{cache} < M. 3. If refresh is true: Run the encode–decode codec round trip for the video segment to update the cache. Update g{cache} \leftarrow g. 4. Perform Straight-Through Estimator (STE) substitution using cached reconstructions: For each axis ax \in \{xy, xz, yz\}: \widehat{P}^{ax}t \leftarrow \text{cached decoded plane} \widetilde{P}^{ax}t \leftarrow \widehat{P}^{ax}t + (P^{ax}t - \texttt{detach}(P^{ax}t)) For density: \widehat{D}t \leftarrow \text{cached decoded density} \widetilde{D}t \leftarrow \widehat{D}t + (Dt - \texttt{detach}(Dt)) Here, \widehat{P} and \widehat{D} are the quantized/cached values, \widetilde{P} and \widetilde{D} are the values used for rendering/loss, and P and D are the current unquantized values. 5. Render and compute losses: I \leftarrow \mathcal{R}(\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}t, \widetilde{D}t, \pi; \phi) where \mathcal{R} is the rendering function and \phi represents the network parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def scltrainingstepwithcaching( globalstep: int, frameindex: int, rays: List[Tuple[Vector3, Vector3]], camerapose: CameraPose, currentplanes: Dict[str, Tensor], # Keys: 'xy', 'xz', 'yz' currentdensity: Tensor, cacheddecodedplanes: Dict[str, Tensor], cachedrawplanes: Dict[str, Tensor], cacheddecodeddensity: Tensor, cachedrawdensity: Tensor, lastrefreshstep: int, refreshinterval: int = 128, driftthreshold: float = 0.01 # Example value, not specified in source) -> Tuple[Tensor, int, Dict[str, Tensor], Tensor, Dict[str, Tensor], Tensor]: """ Performs one step of SCL training with caching. Returns: renderedimage: The rendered image tensor. newlastrefreshstep: Updated last refresh step. newcacheddecodedplanes: Updated cached decoded planes. newcachedrawplanes: Updated cached raw planes. newcacheddecodeddensity: Updated cached decoded density. newcachedrawdensity: Updated cached raw density. """ # Step 1: Determine if refresh is needed refreshneeded = False # Step-based refresh if lastrefreshstep == -1 or (globalstep - lastrefreshstep) >= refreshinterval: refreshneeded = True # Change-based refresh if not refreshneeded: # Calculate relative change for planes planedrift = 0.0 for ax in ['xy', 'xz', 'yz']: currentp = currentplanes[ax] cachedp = cachedrawplanes[ax] # Normalized L2 difference diff = currentp - cachedp normdiff = torch.norm(diff) normcurrent = torch.norm(currentp) if normcurrent > 0: planedrift += normdiff / normcurrent # Calculate relative change for density densitydrift = 0.0 currentd = currentdensity cachedd = cachedrawdensity diffd = currentd - cachedd normdiffd = torch.norm(diffd) normcurrentd = torch.norm(currentd) if normcurrentd > 0: densitydrift = normdiffd / normcurrentd # Combine drifts (simple sum, exact combination method not specified) totaldrift = planedrift + densitydrift if totaldrift > driftthreshold: refreshneeded = True # Step 2: Perform refresh if needed if refreshneeded: # Run encode-decode codec round trip for the video segment # This updates the cache with decoded values # Note: The exact implementation of the codec round trip is external # We assume it returns the decoded planes and density newdecodedplanes, newdecodeddensity = runcodecroundtrip( frameindex, currentplanes, currentdensity) # Update cached decoded values cacheddecodedplanes = newdecodedplanes cacheddecodeddensity = newdecodeddensity # Update cached raw snapshots (the unquantized values at refresh time) cachedrawplanes = {ax: currentplanes[ax].clone().detach() for ax in currentplanes} cachedrawdensity = currentdensity.clone().detach() # Update last refresh step lastrefreshstep = globalstep else: # No refresh, use existing cache pass # Step 3: STE Substitution # For planes renderedplanes = {} for ax in ['xy', 'xz', 'yz']: cacheddecodedp = cacheddecodedplanes[ax] currentp = currentplanes[ax] # STE: Use cached decoded value, add gradient from current unquantized value # detach(currentp) ensures gradient flows only through the difference term # effectively passing the gradient of the unquantized value to the cached value renderedplanes[ax] = cacheddecodedp + (currentp - currentp.detach()) # For density cacheddecodedd = cacheddecodeddensity currentd = currentdensity rendereddensity = cacheddecodedd + (currentd - currentd.detach()) # Step 4: Render # Render using the substituted (rendered) planes and density renderedimage = rendervolume(renderedplanes, rendereddensity, rays, camerapose) return renderedimage, lastrefreshstep, cacheddecodedplanes, cachedrawplanes, cacheddecodeddensity, cachedrawdensity Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The STE substitution relies on the difference between the current unquantized value and its detached version. If the quantization error is large, this difference may be significant, potentially affecting gradient stability. Boundaries: The change-based refresh depends on the normalized \ell2 difference. If the current planes or density are near zero, the normalization factor becomes small, potentially leading to numerical instability or false triggers. The source does not specify a minimum norm threshold. Degenerate Input: If the cache is empty, a refresh is always triggered. This is handled by the step-based refresh condition (g{cache} == -1 or similar). Time Complexity: The cost of the codec round trip is amortized over M training steps. With M=128, the overhead is manageable while capturing most of the SCL training benefit. Memory Complexity: Requires storing additional cached decoded planes and density grids, as well as snapshots of the raw planes and density at the time of refresh. The size is proportional to the number of axes (3 for TriPlanes) and the resolution of the density grid. Measured Performance: Tab. 4 in shows that increasing M yields a favorable trade-off between accuracy and training efficiency. M=128 captures most of the benefit of SCL training. Strengths: Reduces training time significantly for dynamic scenes by avoiding frequent codec invocations. The change-based refresh ensures responsiveness to rapid parameter changes early in training. Limitations: The cache may lag behind rapid parameter changes if the drift threshold \epsilon is not set appropriately. The step-based refresh alone may not be sufficient for early training stages. When to use: When training SCL models on dynamic scenes where codec round trips are computationally expensive. When not to use: When the scene is static and the codec overhead is negligible, or when real-time inference latency is critical and cache updates cannot be deferred. This caching mechanism was introduced in the CATRF (Codec-Adaptive TriPlane Radiance Fields) paper. It addresses the computational bottleneck of invoking standard codecs in the training loop, which is particularly problematic for dynamic scenes. name: Hybrid STE+SPSA Gradient Estimation
head: STE+SPSA
body: Hybrid STE+SPSA is a gradient estimation strategy for differentiable volume rendering that combines vanilla Straight-Through Estimator (STE) with Simultaneous Perturbation Stochastic Approximation (SPSA) to handle non-differentiable codecs within a training loop. It addresses the trade-off between gradient bias and computational cost by using vanilla STE during cached inference steps and switching to SPSA only when the codec cache is refreshed. Unlike vanilla STE, which provides biased but stable gradients, this hybrid approach attempts to reduce bias during cache updates, though it incurs significantly higher variance and training time. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current parameter vector \mathbf{P} (e.g., feature planes), codec cache state, perturbation scale \epsilon, and objective function \mathcal{C}q (e.g., reconstruction loss). Output: Gradient estimate \hat{g}(\mathbf{P}) for the optimizer. Data Structures: Codec Cache: Stores the output of the non-differentiable codec for the current parameters to avoid redundant encoding/decoding. Perturbation Vector \Delta: A vector of the same dimension as \mathbf{P}, where each element \Deltai is sampled independently from a symmetric Bernoulli distribution: \Deltai \in \{-1, 1\} with probability 0.5. Steps: 1. Check Cache Status: Determine if the codec cache is active (valid for current \mathbf{P}) or needs refresh. 2. If Cache is Active: Use vanilla STE. The gradient is computed by backpropagating through the decoder as if the codec were the identity function. The gradient is copied directly to the pre-codec feature plane. 3. If Cache is Refreshed: Sample a random perturbation vector \Delta where \Deltai = \pm 1 with probability 0.5. Compute the perturbed parameters: \mathbf{P}^+ = \mathbf{P} + \epsilon \Delta and \mathbf{P}^- = \mathbf{P} - \epsilon \Delta. Evaluate the objective function \mathcal{C}q for both perturbed states. This requires running the full codec pipeline (encoding and decoding) for both \mathbf{P}^+ and \mathbf{P}^-, updating the cache in the process. Compute the SPSA gradient estimate for each component i: \hat{g}i(\mathbf{P}) = \frac{\mathcal{C}q(\mathbf{P} + \epsilon \Delta) - \mathcal{C}q(\mathbf{P} - \epsilon \Delta)}{2 \epsilon \Deltai} Use this estimate for the optimizer step. Parameters: \epsilon (Perturbation Scale): A small scalar value. The exact value is not specified in the sources. \Deltai: Random variable, \pm 1 with p=0.5. Pitfalls: Computational Cost: Applying SPSA at every step is prohibitively expensive because it requires two additional full codec round trips (encoding/decoding) per iteration. Gradient Quality: SPSA yields the worst reconstruction quality and highest training time among tested methods. This is attributed to the high variance of zeroth-order estimates and poor signal-to-noise ratio caused by the severe non-linearity of the codec. Alignment: Although SPSA is less biased in principle, its gradient estimates can be substantially noisier for complex black-box codec round-trips, making them less aligned with the descent direction needed for radiance-field optimization compared to vanilla STE. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computegradienthybridstespsa(P, cache, epsilon, objectivefn): """ Compute gradient using Hybrid STE+SPSA. Args: P: Current parameter vector (e.g., feature planes). cache: Codec cache object. epsilon: Perturbation scale. objectivefn: Function computing loss Cq, handling codec encoding/decoding. Returns: gradient: Estimated gradient vector. """ # Check if cache is valid for current P if cache.isvalid(P): # Step 1: Use vanilla STE for cached steps # Vanilla STE: Backpropagate through decoder assuming identity codec # Gradient is copied directly to pre-codec features with torch.enablegrad(): P.requiresgrad = True # Forward pass using cached codec output or re-encoding if needed for identity assumption # In practice, this often means detaching the codec and passing gradient through loss = objectivefn(P, usecache=True) loss.backward() gradient = P.grad return gradient else: # Step 2: Cache needs refresh, use SPSA # Sample random perturbation vector Delta # Deltai = +/- 1 with probability 0.5 Delta = torch.randint(low=-1, high=2, size=P.shape).float() # Compute perturbed parameters Pplus = P + epsilon Delta Pminus = P - epsilon Delta # Evaluate objective function for both perturbed states # This triggers codec encoding/decoding, updating the cache Cplus = objectivefn(Pplus, usecache=False) Cminus = objectivefn(Pminus, usecache=False) # Compute SPSA gradient estimate # gi = (C(P + eDelta) - C(P - eDelta)) / (2 e Deltai) numerator = Cplus - Cminus denominator = 2 epsilon Delta # Handle division by zero if Deltai is 0 (though Bernoulli +/-1 avoids this) # In this specific Bernoulli case, Deltai is never 0. gradient = numerator / denominator return gradient The training framework that inserts standard, non-differentiable codecs directly into the neural radiance field training loop using a straight-through estimator (STE) to pass gradients. SCL A technique to optimize SCL training by caching codec outputs to avoid redundant computations. Caching Time Complexity: Significantly higher than vanilla STE. When the cache is refreshed, SPSA requires two additional full codec round trips per iteration. Applying SPSA at every step is described as "prohibitively expensive". Memory Complexity: Requires storing the codec cache and the perturbation vector \Delta. No additional major memory overhead compared to standard SCL with caching. Measured Performance: High-Rate: PSNR 29.63, SSIM 0.930, LPIPS 0.459, Training Time 3h 18m. Low-Rate: PSNR 27.94, SSIM 0.909, LPIPS 0.650, Training Time 3h 18m. Note: Training time is reported as identical for high and low rates in the source, which may indicate a fixed number of iterations or cache refresh frequency independent of rate. Strengths: Reduces gradient bias compared to vanilla STE during cache updates by using a zeroth-order estimator that does not rely on the identity surrogate. Limitations: Worst reconstruction quality and highest training time among compared methods (vanilla STE, mSTE, STE+SPSA) due to high variance and poor signal-to-noise ratio from codec non-linearity. When to Use: Only when cache refreshes are infrequent enough that the computational cost of SPSA is manageable, and when reducing bias during updates is critical. However, the source notes that vanilla STE is more robust and provides better overall quality, especially in low-bitrate regimes. When Not to Use: When computational efficiency is a priority, or when codec non-linearity introduces too much noise for zeroth-order estimates to be effective. Vanilla STE is preferred as the default due to robustness. The Hybrid STE+SPSA method was introduced in the context of Codec-Adaptive TriPlane Radiance Fields (CATRF) for volumetric content delivery. It was proposed as a way to improve upon vanilla STE by incorporating insights from black-box gradient approximation methods, specifically SPSA. The method was evaluated in ablation studies comparing it against vanilla STE and modified STE (mSTE). The authors found that while SPSA is less biased in principle, its practical performance was inferior due to the specific challenges of differentiating through non-linear codecs.
