name: Radiance-field optimization
head: Differentiable radiance field optimization, Inverse radiance field rendering
body: Radiance-field optimization is the family of inverse rendering methods that reconstruct a 3D scene representation by minimizing the photometric error between rendered images and ground-truth observations. It solves the problem of novel view synthesis by training a neural network to directly learn color and opacity (or density) values using the discrete volume rendering equation. Unlike explicit mesh-based reconstruction, radiance-field optimization relies on the differentiability of the forward volume rendering operator to propagate gradients from pixel space to the scene representation. Radiance-field optimization Optimizes explicit 3D voxel grids to reconstruct radiance fields, solving the computational bottleneck of implicit neural networks by replacing them with direct data access and interpolation. Chosen when memory efficiency and direct grid manipulation are prioritized over implicit representations. Represents a scene as a collection of anisotropic 3D Gaussian primitives defined by mean position, covariance, opacity, and spherical harmonics. Chosen for real-time rendering and high-fidelity novel view synthesis, setting itself apart by using explicit differentiable primitives instead of implicit MLPs or dense grids. Models the plenoptic transient field using an MLP to predict transient arrival times from sparse SPAD measurements for Non-Line-of-Sight imaging. Chosen for NLOS scenarios where sparse temporal data is available, differing from standard NeRF by operating on transient fields rather than static radiance. Represents a 3D scene as a continuous volumetric function parameterized by a neural network, mapping 3D coordinates and viewing directions to RGB color and density. Chosen as the foundational implicit representation for novel view synthesis, setting itself apart by enabling photorealistic rendering of complex scenes with view-dependent effects. Reduces NeRF computational cost by decomposing the radiance field into density, diffuse RGB, and feature vectors, using deferred shading to limit MLP evaluations. Chosen when inference speed is critical, differing from standard NeRF by caching geometry and using a small network for view-dependent effects. Jointly optimizes camera parameters (intrinsics and 6DoF poses) and the scene representation from sparse forward-facing RGB images. Chosen when camera poses are unknown, setting itself apart by eliminating the need for pre-computed SfM parameters. Trains deep neural architectures end-to-end to optimize volume rendering parameters for clinical data with high inter-patient variations. Chosen for medical imaging applications, differing from manual transfer functions by learning consistent visual outputs across subjects. Defines iterative procedures that minimize photometric loss by updating scene parameters. Chosen to manage training dynamics, ray sampling, and hyperparameter scheduling, addressing the ill-posed nature of inverse volume rendering. A regularization framework for sparse-input radiance fields that constrains the main model to learn simpler solutions by supervising it with depth estimates from lower-capacity versions. Chosen for sparse-view reconstruction, setting itself apart from methods like 3DGS by using self-supervision for regularization. Trains NeRFs for better geometry under non-Lambertian surfaces and dynamic lighting by normalizing view-dependence through self-distillation. Chosen to resolve shape-radiance ambiguity, differing from standard NeRF by encoding invariant information. Mitigates high computational cost by spatially decomposing a scene into multiple parts, each represented by a smaller neural network. Chosen for large scenes requiring near-constant inference time, setting itself apart by using differentiable spatial partitioning. A differentiable technique that jointly optimizes scene parameters by minimizing a combined loss from volumetric emission-absorption and surface reflectance models. Chosen for scenes requiring both volumetric and surface modeling, differing by using a dual rendering equation. A NeRF variant that jointly models planar reflectors and explicitly casts reflected rays to capture high-frequency reflections. Chosen for indoor scenes with windows/mirrors, setting itself apart by preventing false geometry along primary rays. Replaces uniform voxel grids or sparse point clouds with a dense set of non-overlapping tetrahedra from Delaunay triangulation. Chosen to solve empty regions in sparse methods and fixed resolution limits, differing by using a tetrahedral mesh. Synthesizes novel views by leveraging dense sampling of light rays from multiple viewpoints, either through explicit discretization or implicit neural representations. Chosen for light-field based rendering, differing from global implicit fields by focusing on ray sampling. Not given in the sources. Implicitly represents and renders 3D scenes by learning local features for each pixel in 2D images and projecting them to 3D space. Chosen for general 3D representation and rendering, setting itself apart by constructing an internal representation for every 3D point. Computes the color field solely from a given density field and posed training images in closed form. Chosen to decouple shape and radiance, reducing shape-radiance ambiguity inherent in NeRF. Reconstructs 3D geometry and appearance by modeling the scene as a continuous implicit surface defined by a Signed Distance Function (SDF). Chosen to disentangle geometry from appearance, enabling high-fidelity surface reconstruction. Represents 3D ambient illumination as a continuous volumetric radiance field, treating each sample as a light emitter. Chosen for fully differentiable illumination modeling, differing by integrating volumetric radiance along specular lobes. Distributes NeRF parameters across multiple GPUs by allocating them to disjoint spatial regions and training them jointly. Chosen for arbitrarily large capacity without redundancy, setting itself apart from independent training methods. Extends standard optimization by incorporating physical laws (e.g., ray refraction) or material properties (e.g., BRDFs) into the pipeline. Chosen for physically-based rendering, differing by enforcing physical constraints. A differentiable framework for novel LiDAR view synthesis that jointly learns geometry and 3D point attributes without explicit reconstruction. Chosen for LiDAR-based scene representation, differing by handling distance, intensity, and ray-drop probability. Extends static optimization to model scenes that change over time or undergo non-rigid deformation. Chosen for dynamic scenes, setting itself apart by introducing temporal or deformation components. Recovers a high dynamic range radiance field from low dynamic range views with different exposures. Chosen for HDR synthesis, differing by enabling generation of novel HDR and LDR views under arbitrary exposures. A differentiable framework for fast human radiance field optimization that replaces implicit MLPs with explicit neural voxel grids. Chosen to accelerate training from hours to minutes, setting itself apart by maintaining two separate voxel grids. Converts textured mesh models into NeRFs by generating a ground-truth point-based radiance field from mesh geometry and texture. Chosen for mesh-to-NeRF conversion, differing by eliminating the need for multi-view image rendering. Reconstructs high-quality radiance fields from blurry images by incorporating 3D scene context into blur modeling and using efficient importance sampling. Chosen for deblurring applications, differing by modeling blur with scene context. Reconstructs reasonable 3D geometry from a single reference view by propagating depth information to unseen views through image warping. Chosen to prevent overfitting and collapse in single-view reconstruction, differing by using pseudo ground truth labels. Encodes the 3D density field of a static object using a NeRF, trained on rich projection data to serve as a prior for dynamic reconstruction. Chosen for X-ray tomography, differing by using a canonical volume prior. Addresses high memory consumption and overfitting in dense voxel-based fields by modeling the scene as a factorized 4D tensor. Chosen for compact modeling, differing by using low-rank tensor decomposition. Not given in the sources. Optimizes scene parameters stored in discrete 3D grids or hierarchical structures, avoiding implicit MLP parameterization. Chosen for direct data access and interpolation, differing by optimizing explicit grids directly. Generates compact neural representations of dynamic scenes from RGB video by sequentially optimizing explicit feature, motion, and residual grids. Chosen for dynamic scene compression, differing by using sequential grid optimization. Optimizes a 3D neural volume with shape and SVBRDF while also optimizing per-image illuminations. Chosen for varying illumination and viewpoints, differing by decomposing volume, shape, and lighting. Synthesizes large-scale NeRF scenes from a smaller exemplar by controlling lighting effects using shading vectors. Chosen for large-scale synthesis without decoupling geometry, material, and lighting, differing by using shading vectors. Nerflets achieves efficient structure-aware 3D scene representation with only 2D supervision by representing a scene as a set of local neural radiance fields (Nerflets), each with orientation, spatial position, and range. For a sampled point, N small MLPs generate N densities and colors, one for each Nerflet. The final color and density of the sampled point are obtained through weighted averaging based on the influence weights of each Nerflet. On KITTI-360 and ScanNet datasets, PSNR is more than one point higher. General Radiance Field Rendering via MLP is an MLP that predicts RGB values and volumetric density for a 3D point using its aggregated feature vector and viewing direction, forming a general radiance field. The steps are: Render an image pixel RGB by casting a ray from the camera center and estimating the integral using volume rendering equations with numerical quadrature. Estimate the integrals with numerical quadrature using a hierarchical sampling strategy, strictly following NeRF. All 3D locations and RGB values are processed by the positional encoding proposed by NeRF. Optimization uses L2 loss between rendered RGBs and ground truth. Unlike original NeRF which uses point position xyz as input, this method uses the aggregated point features \bar{F}p as input to the MLP. Semantic Pseudo Label with Global Structure Prior uses a global structure prior using a pre-trained Vision Transformer (ViT) to enforce semantic consistency between unseen views and the reference view, robust to pixel-wise misalignment. Unlike DietNeRF which uses projected image embeddings, directly extract the [CLS] token from DINO-ViT’s output as it serves as a representation of an entire image. Calculate L2 distance between extracted features: \mathcal{L}{\text{cls}} = ||f{\text{vit}}(A) - f{\text{vit}}(B) ||^2, where f{vit}(\cdot) refers to the extracted [CLS] tokens, and A and B are patches from the reference view and an unseen view, respectively. The method adopts DINO-ViT [4], a self-supervised vision transformer trained on ImageNet [8] dataset. iVR-GS is a method for real-time editing of transfer functions and lighting during neural volume rendering using editable and composable 3DGS primitives, overcoming the limitation of baked visual parameters. Steps: 1. Compose multiple basic models trained on disjoint transfer function ranges. 2. Extend Gaussian primitives with normals and shading coefficients. 3. Incorporate Blinn-Phong reflection. 4. Enable real-time editing of color, opacity, and lighting at inference. 5. Perform automatic optimization to approximate reference images. Pitfalls: Model size scales linearly with the number of basic scenes, reaching gigabyte-level for hundreds of transfer functions. Uses uniform viewpoint sampling which may be suboptimal. Requires redesigning lighting representation for models beyond Blinn-Phong. Reconstruction quality: PSNR approximately 32–34 dB for novel view synthesis, 30–33 dB for relighting. Compression: Vector quantization achieved 7.2× compression (6.2 MB vs. 44.8 MB) while maintaining accuracy within 0.06 dB. R2L is a method distilling neural radiance fields into neural light fields via a deep residual MLP to improve rendering efficiency. Train by distilling from a pre-trained NeRF. Achieves 26–35× reduction in FLOPs. Achieves 28–31× speedup in wall-clock time. EG3D is a GAN framework using a novel hybrid tri-plane representation for neural rendering, achieving state-of-the-art results on FFHQ. Radiance-Driven Fluid Simulation is a joint training framework where the fluid simulator is learned from video supervision by backpropagating the error between rendered images and ground-truth video frames through the differentiable renderer to the simulator. Steps: Advect the volume field Vt using the velocity field ut inferred by the simulator to get the updated volume field V{t+1}. Assign the updated volume field V{t+1} into the scene space to render image \hat{I}{t+1}. Supervise the rendered image \hat{I}{t+1} with the ground-truth image I{t+1} to update simulator parameters. Pre-train the radiance field network with the initial volume field of all training sequences (volume of first frames) before joint training. Formulas: V{t+1} = \text{advect}(ut, \Delta t, Vt). L = \sumr \|\hat{C}(r) - C(r)\|2^2 + \beta \|\nabla \cdot u\|2^2, where \beta controls regularization strength. Parameter: \beta: Regularization strength for divergence penalty, set to 1e-6. Online Learning for Irradiance Volumes updates a learned irradiance cache at runtime, extending surface-based neural caching to full volumetric scene representations. Steps: Initialize online learning from a previously learned NIV to significantly improve convergence compared to learning from scratch. To achieve real-time updates, restrict sampling to the camera's view frustum and/or employ loss-driven sampling [DPD22]. Pitfall: Inherently slower to learn than surface methods due to a larger input domain (entire scene volume vs. surface subset) and the requirement for a low-bias representation to avoid deferring queries. 3DGS Radiance Caching is a caching technique for path-traced volume rendering that uses 3DGS primitives to store attenuated radiance at multiple path lengths, optimizing exponentially subsampled Gaussians from noisy path samples to achieve real-time frame rates. Parameter: Memory footprint: 28 MB for the cache, compared to 272 MB for neural radiance caching. Pitfall: Introduces bias with no guaranteed error bounds and requires re-initialization when transfer functions change. Performance on six scientific datasets at 720p: real-time frame rates achieved with 38–186ms total time. Radiance-field optimization emerged as a dominant paradigm for novel view synthesis following the introduction of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by Mildenhall et al. in 2020. Prior to this, image-based rendering relied on light-field sampling or explicit geometry reconstruction. NeRF demonstrated that a continuous volumetric function, optimized via gradient descent to minimize photometric error, could synthesize photorealistic images from sparse views. name: Image-based Transfer Function Optimization via Automatic Differentiation
head: DiffDVR, DiffDVR optimization, Gradient-based Transfer Function Optimization, Image-based Transfer Function Optimization via DiffDVR, Image-based solution
body: This method optimizes a transfer function To for an optimization volume field Fo such that rendered images of Fo visually match rendered images of a reference volume field Fr. It solves the problem of finding a transfer function mapping that minimizes the pixel-wise difference between two volume renderings, enabling comparative analysis of scalar fields. Unlike voxel-based least-squares approaches that operate on per-voxel residuals, this method operates directly on the final image space, prioritizing differences that have a larger effect on the rendered output. It is distinguished from other radiance-field optimizations by focusing specifically on the transfer function parameters of existing volume fields rather than learning the field representation itself. The method formulates transfer function optimization as a least-squares problem solved via automatic differentiation of the differentiable direct volume rendering (DiffDVR) pipeline. It builds on Radiance-field optimization principles but applies them to the post-shading stage of volume rendering. Inputs: Reference volume field Fr (scalar voxel data). Optimization volume field Fo (scalar voxel data). Initial transfer function To (mapping density values to color and opacity). Reference transfer function Tr (used to render the reference images). Camera poses (sampled randomly per iteration). Outputs: Optimized transfer function To that minimizes the difference between rendered images Io and Ir. The transfer function T is represented as a lookup table or parametric function mapping density values to color \mathbf{C} and opacity \alpha. The optimization adjusts the stored color entries of the transfer function. The volume fields Fr and Fo are accessed via trilinear interpolation during ray marching. Direct volume rendering composites samples along a view ray. For a ray with N samples, the final pixel color C{pixel} is computed as: C{pixel} = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where: Ci is the color of the i-th sample, determined by applying the transfer function to the density value Di of the volume field. \alphai is the opacity of the i-th sample, determined by the transfer function. The term \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) represents the transmittance from previous samples. 1. Forward Pass (Rendering): Sample random camera poses. For each camera pose, render an image Ir from the reference field Fr using the reference transfer function Tr. Render an image Io from the optimization field Fo using the current transfer function To. Resolution is fixed at 512 \times 512 pixels per image per iteration. Store intermediate compositing results (transmittance and accumulated color) for the backward pass. 2. Loss Computation: Compute the loss L as the difference between Io and Ir. The optimization minimizes the pixel-wise difference. Common metrics include Mean Squared Error (MSE), though the source notes that various image-based difference measures like RMSE, PSNR, SSIM, or LPIPS can be used for evaluation. 3. Backward Pass (Gradient Propagation): Use automatic differentiation in reverse mode to compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the transfer function parameters (the color/opacity entries in To). Inversion Trick: To overcome the memory scalability limitations of standard reverse-mode AD, the method exploits the invertibility of the compositing operation. The forward pass stores intermediate colors and transmittance values. The backward pass traverses the samples along the view rays in the opposite order (from back to front). Derivatives are propagated by reusing the intermediate values stored in the forward pass, significantly reducing memory requirements compared to storing the entire computation graph. The chain rule is applied to obtain the final derivative from the individual derivatives of each compositing operation along the view ray. 4. Optimization Step: Update the transfer function To using the computed gradients (e.g., via SGD or Adam) to minimize the loss. Repeat until convergence. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizetransferfunction(Fr, Fo, To, Tr, numiterations, learningrate): # To is a lookup table mapping density values to (color, opacity) for iteration in range(numiterations): # 1. Sample random camera poses cameraposes = [generaterandompose() for in range(4)] totalloss = 0.0 gradTo = createzeroarraylike(To) for pose in cameraposes: # 2. Forward Pass: Render Reference Image Ir Ir = rendervolume(Fr, Tr, pose, resolution=512) # Render Optimization Image Io with current To # Stores intermediate compositing states for the inversion trick Io, intermediates = rendervolumediff(Fo, To, pose, resolution=512) # 3. Compute Loss loss = computemse(Io, Ir) totalloss += loss # 4. Backward Pass: Compute Gradients w.r.t To # Uses reverse-mode AD with the inversion trick gradTo = accumulategradients(loss, intermediates, To, gradTo) # 5. Update Transfer Function To = applygradientdescent(To, gradTo, learningrate, len(cameraposes)) return To def generaterandompose(): # Returns a camera pose (position and orientation) return {"position": [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], "orientation": [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]} def createzeroarraylike(T): # Returns an array of zeros with the same shape as T return [0.0] len(T) def rendervolume(V, T, pose, resolution): # Standard non-differentiable render for reference image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(resolution resolution)] for y in range(resolution): for x in range(resolution): ray = castray(pose, x, y, resolution) image[y resolution + x] = compositeray(V, T, ray) return image def rendervolumediff(V, T, pose, resolution): # Differentiable render storing intermediates image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(resolution resolution)] intermediates = [] for y in range(resolution): for x in range(resolution): ray = castray(pose, x, y, resolution) acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] acctrans = 1.0 sampledata = [] for i in range(len(ray.samples)): Di = ray.samples[i].density Ci, alphai = T.lookup(Di) acccolor = [acccolor[c] (1.0 - alphai) + Ci[c] alphai for c in range(3)] acctrans = (1.0 - alphai) sampledata.append({"Ci": Ci, "alphai": alphai, "acccolorbefore": acccolor}) image[y resolution + x] = acccolor intermediates.append({"samples": sampledata, "acctrans": acctrans}) return image, intermediates def computemse(Io, Ir): # Mean squared error between two images total = 0.0 count = 0 for po, pr in zip(Io, Ir): for c in range(3): total += (po[c] - pr[c]) 2 count += 1 return total / count def accumulategradients(loss, intermediates, To, gradTo): # Initialize gradient of loss w.r.t final pixel colors dLdCfinal = [2.0 / len(intermediates) (Io[p] - Ir[p]) for p in range(len(intermediates))] for rayidx, inter in enumerate(intermediates): dLdC = dLdCfinal[rayidx] # Traverse samples in reverse order (back to front) for i in range(len(inter["samples"]) - 1, -1, -1): s = inter["samples"][i] Ci = s["Ci"] alphai = s["alphai"] acccolorbefore = s["acccolorbefore"] # Derivative propagation using stored intermediates dLdCprev = [dLdC[c] (1.0 - alphai) for c in range(3)] dLdalpha = sum(dLdC[c] Ci[c] - dLdCprev[c] alphai for c in range(3)) dLdCi = [dLdC[c] alphai for c in range(3)] # Accumulate gradients into transfer function entries # Assuming density is quantized to bins for the lookup table densitybin = int(s["Di"] 100) % len(To) gradTo[densitybin] += dLdalpha + sum(dLdCi) return gradTo def applygradientdescent(T, gradT, lr, numsamples): for i in range(len(T)): T[i] -= lr gradT[i] / numsamples return T def castray(pose, x, y, resolution): # Returns a ray object with samples return {"samples": [{"density": 0.5} for in range(10)]} def compositeray(V, T, ray): acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] acctrans = 1.0 for s in ray.samples: Di = s.density Ci, alphai = T.lookup(Di) acccolor = [acccolor[c] (1.0 - alphai) + Ci[c] alphai for c in range(3)] acctrans = (1.0 - alphai) return acccolor Rendering Resolution: 512 \times 512 pixels per image per iteration. Learning Rate: Not given in the sources. Optimizer: Not given in the sources. Structural Differences: If the two fields Fr and Fo have fundamentally different structural distributions, an optimized transfer function may not exist that produces visually similar images, or the result may be misleading. Memory Usage: Standard reverse-mode AD requires storing all intermediate operations, which is memory-intensive for volume rendering. The "inversion trick" overcomes scalability limitations and significantly reduces memory requirements by reusing intermediate values. Local Minima: The optimization is non-convex; the initial choice of To and the complexity of the fields may lead to local minima. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of iterations, camera poses, and ray marching steps. Each iteration requires rendering two images (Ir and Io) and a backward pass. Memory Complexity: Reduced significantly by the "inversion trick" compared to standard reverse-mode AD, as it avoids storing the full computation graph and reuses intermediate values. Strengths: Directly optimizes for visual similarity in image space. Prioritizes differences that affect the final rendered image more than voxel-based methods. Applicable to comparing different correlation measures or physical parameters in ensemble simulations. Limitations: Requires differentiable volume rendering implementation. May fail to find a matching transfer function if fields are structurally dissimilar. Computationally expensive due to iterative rendering and AD. When to Use: When comparing two volume fields and wanting to find a transfer function for one that makes it visually match the other, or when analyzing the impact of transfer function changes on image similarity. When Not to Use: When the goal is to optimize the volume field representation itself (use Neural Radiance Fields or similar) or when voxel-level accuracy is required rather than image-level similarity. The method is built upon DiffDVR, introduced by Weiss and Westermann [WW22], which uses automatic differentiation to optimize external parameters of the rendering process, such as viewpoint, transfer function, and integration stepsize. The specific application to optimizing a transfer function for a single field to reproduce reference images was demonstrated by Weiss and Westermann [WW22]. The approach described here extends this to optimize a transfer function for an optimization field Fo to match images of a reference field Fr. It is applied in the context of comparative volume rendering for numerical fluid simulation, where it helps compare different correlation measures in ensemble simulations or different physical parameters from a single simulation run. name: Neural Transient Fields (NeTF)
body: Neural Transient Fields (NeTF) is a differentiable volume rendering method for Non-Line-of-Sight (NLOS) imaging that models the plenoptic transient field using a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). It reconstructs hidden 3D scenes from sparse Time-Correlated Single-Photon Counting (TCSPC) measurements captured by a Single-Photon Avalanche Diode (SPAD) array. Unlike NeRF, which relies on dense, high-resolution RGB images to mitigate occlusion artifacts, NeTF operates on sparse spot measurements where occluded points may be visible from very few viewpoints, making occlusion handling and sampling bias critical challenges. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Sparse SPAD measurements of transient signals \taum(x', y', t) on a relay wall, where (x', y') are the 2D coordinates of the detection spots and t is time. Output: A continuous function \tau(x', y', t) representing the transient arrival time at the relay wall spots (x', y') and time t. Data Structures: MLP: Takes 3D Cartesian coordinates of hidden scene points as input. Network Output: Predicts the transient arrival time \tau. Algorithm Steps: 1. Coordinate Transformation: Convert hidden scene points to Cartesian coordinates (x, y, z). 2. MLP Forward Pass: Feed (x, y, z) into the MLP to predict \tau(x', y', t). 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the L2 norm loss between predicted \tau and measured \taum at SPAD spots. 4. Optimization: Minimize loss via gradient descent. 5. Two-Stage Training: Stage 1 trains on all samples to obtain an initial reconstruction. Stage 2 calculates the loss at every measurement spot, resamples the dataset to balance the distribution (over-sampling minority classes with high loss), and retrains to reduce artifacts. Formulas: The optimization objective is defined by the L2 loss function: L = \sum{x', y', t} (\taum(x', y', t) - \tau(x', y', t))^2 \quad (14) Where: L is the total loss. \taum(x', y', t) is the measured transient at spot (x', y') and time t. \tau(x', y', t) is the predicted transient at the same location and time. Parameters: Loss Function: L2 norm difference. Sampling: 2D hemispherical sampling is used for the SPAD spots, differing from NeRF's 1D ray sampling. Pitfalls: Occlusion Artifacts: Because SPAD captures sparse spots, occluded points may be captured from very few viewpoints. If not handled, this leads to strong reconstruction artifacts. Sampling Bias: The sparse nature of the data creates a long-tailed distribution of visibility, similar to long-tailed classification problems in machine learning. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np class MLP: def init(self, inputdim=3, hiddendim=256, outputdim=1): self.W = [np.random.randn(inputdim, hiddendim), np.random.randn(hiddendim, hiddendim), np.random.randn(hiddendim, hiddendim), np.random.randn(hiddendim, outputdim)] self.b = [np.zeros(hiddendim), np.zeros(hiddendim), np.zeros(hiddendim), np.zeros(outputdim)] def forward(self, x): h = x for w, bias in zip(self.W, self.b): h = np.maximum(0, h @ w + bias) # ReLU activation return h def trainnetf(measuredxyz, measuredtau, numepochs=1000, lr=0.001): model = MLP() # Stage 1: Initial training with all samples for epoch in range(numepochs // 2): predictedtau = model.forward(measuredxyz) loss = np.sum((predictedtau - measuredtau) 2) # Standard backpropagation to compute gradients and update parameters updateparameters(model, predictedtau, measuredtau, lr) # Stage 2: Resampling based on loss predictedtaustage1 = model.forward(measuredxyz) losses = (predictedtaustage1 - measuredtau) 2 probs = losses / np.sum(losses) indices = np.random.choice(len(measuredxyz), len(measuredxyz), p=probs, replace=True) xyzresampled = measuredxyz[indices] tauresampled = measuredtau[indices] # Retrain with resampled data for epoch in range(numepochs // 2, numepochs): predictedtau = model.forward(xyzresampled) loss = np.sum((predictedtau - tauresampled) 2) updateparameters(model, predictedtau, tauresampled, lr) return model Formulates the transient signal for non-confocal NLOS setups where illumination and detection spots are distinct, using ellipsoidal coordinates. It differs from the confocal formulation by handling asymmetric optical paths via a double integral over ellipsoidal surface parameters, and is chosen when the NLOS setup lacks a shared illumination-detection axis. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Can model the plenoptic transient field using an MLP, allowing for the minimization of arbitrary differentiable losses. The two-stage training strategy effectively addresses sampling bias and occlusion artifacts inherent in sparse SPAD data. Limitations: Requires careful handling of occlusions due to sparse viewpoint coverage. The sparse nature of the input data makes it more sensitive to sampling bias than dense-image methods like NeRF. When to use: Non-Line-of-Sight imaging scenarios with sparse SPAD measurements where occlusion is a significant factor. When not to use: Dense viewpoint settings where occlusion is less significant, or when high-resolution RGB images are available (prefer NeRF). Neural Transient Fields (NeTF) was introduced in the paper "Non-line-of-Sight Imaging via Neural Transient Fields". It adapts the neural radiance field concept to the domain of NLOS imaging, addressing the unique challenges of sparse, time-resolved photon data. The method builds on the principles of Radiance-field optimization but modifies the sampling and loss strategies to handle the sparsity and occlusion issues specific to SPAD-based NLOS systems. name: Non-confocal Neural Transient Field (NeTF) Formulation
head: Ellipsoidal NeTF, Non-confocal NeTF
body:
This method formulates the transient signal in Non-Line-of-Sight (NLOS) imaging for non-confocal setups, where the illumination spot P and detection spot P' are distinct. It models the received energy by integrating over semi-ellipsoids defined by foci at P and P' on the relay wall. It differs from the confocal NeTF formulation by using ellipsoidal coordinates to handle the asymmetric optical paths, allowing the transient to be computed as a double integral over the ellipsoidal surface parameters. Inputs: Illumination spot position P and detection spot position P' on the relay wall. Time t of the transient measurement. Scene density \sigma and reflectance ho represented as functions of ellipsoidal coordinates (\mu, 
u, \varphi). Outputs: Transient signal 	au(P, P', t) received at P' from P. Data Structures: Ellipsoidal coordinates (\mu, 
u, \varphi) parameterizing the semi-ellipsoid. Geometric constants: semi-major axis \alpha, focal length \gamma, eccentricity e. Parameters: \alpha = ct/2: Semi-major axis of the ellipsoid, where c is the speed of light. \gamma = |\vec{OP} - \vec{OP'}|: Focal length, distance from the origin to each focus (assuming origin O is the midpoint between P and P'). e = \gamma/\alpha: Eccentricity. \Gamma0: Constant system factor derived from illumination power, aperture, and detection parameters (simplified from \Gamma = A a r2^0 Ep / \pi). Steps: 1. Define Geometric Constants: Calculate the semi-major axis \alpha = ct/2 and the focal length \gamma based on the positions of P and P'. Compute eccentricity e = \gamma/\alpha. Pitfall: If e \ge 1, the geometry is degenerate (hyperbolic or planar), which is invalid for the standard ellipsoidal formulation. This occurs if ct < \gamma, i.e., the time of flight is less than the direct distance between P and P'. 2. Determine Coordinate \mu: For a fixed time t, the coordinate \mu is constrained by the Dirac delta function in the integral. The non-zero contribution occurs when: \mu = 	ext{arccosh}\left( rac{ct}{2\gamma}ight) If ct < 2\gamma, the transient is zero. 3. Compute Jacobian J: The Jacobian for the transformation from Cartesian to ellipsoidal coordinates is: J = \gamma^3 \sinh \mu \sin 
u (\sinh^2 \mu + \sin^2 
u) 4. Compute Distances r1 and r2: r1 is the distance from P to the scene point Q, and r2 is the distance from Q to P'. In the local coordinate system where P and P' are symmetric about the origin and parallel to the y-axis (P=(0,-\gamma,0), P'=(0,\gamma,0)), the Cartesian coordinates of Q are derived from the spherical-to-ellipsoidal transformation: x = \gamma \sinh \mu \sin 
u \cos \varphi y = \gamma \cosh \mu \cos 
u z = \gamma \sinh \mu \sin 
u \sin \varphi The distances are then computed as r1 = \sqrt{x^2 + (y+\gamma)^2 + z^2} and r2 = \sqrt{x^2 + (y-\gamma)^2 + z^2}. 5. Evaluate Integrand: The simplified transient equation (discarding attenuation) is: 	au(P, P', t) = \Gamma0 \iintE  rac{J}{r1^2 r2^2} \sigma(\mu, 
u, \varphi) ho(\mu, 
u, \varphi, P, P') \, d
u \, d\varphi Where \mu is fixed as calculated in Step 2. 6. Integrate: Perform the double integral over 
u \in [0, \pi] and \varphi \in [0, 2\pi]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computenonconfocalnetftransient(P, Pprime, t, sigmafunc, rhofunc, numsamplesnu, numsamplesphi, gammaval, Gamma0=1.0): """ Computes the transient signal for non-confocal NeTF using the simplified ellipsoidal formulation. Args: P: Array-like, position of illumination spot (unused in local frame calculation). Pprime: Array-like, position of detection spot (unused in local frame calculation). t: Float, time of flight. sigmafunc: Function, returns scene density given ellipsoidal coords (mu, nu, phi). rhofunc: Function, returns reflectance given ellipsoidal coords and spots. numsamplesnu: Int, number of samples for nu. numsamplesphi: Int, number of samples for phi. gammaval: Float, half the distance between P and P'. Gamma0: Float, constant system factor. Returns: Float, transient signal tau. """ c = 299792458.0 # Speed of light in m/s # Step 1 & 2: Geometric Constants and mu # mu = arccosh(ct / 2gamma) arg = (c t) / (2.0 gammaval) if arg < 1.0: return 0.0 mu = np.arccosh(arg) # Step 6: Discretize integration domain nus = np.linspace(0, np.pi, numsamplesnu) phis = np.linspace(0, 2 np.pi, numsamplesphi) # Create meshgrid NU, PHI = np.meshgrid(nus, phis, indexing='ij') # Step 3 & 4: Compute local Cartesian coordinates and Jacobian sinhmu = np.sinh(mu) coshmu = np.cosh(mu) sinnu = np.sin(NU) cosnu = np.cos(NU) Xlocal = gammaval sinhmu sinnu np.cos(PHI) Ylocal = gammaval coshmu cosnu Zlocal = gammaval sinhmu sinnu np.sin(PHI) # Step 4: Compute distances r1 and r2 # P is at (0, -gamma, 0), P' is at (0, gamma, 0) r1 = np.sqrt(Xlocal2 + (Ylocal + gammaval)2 + Zlocal2) r2 = np.sqrt(Xlocal2 + (Ylocal - gammaval)2 + Zlocal2) # Step 3: Compute Jacobian J J = (gammaval3) sinhmu sinnu (sinhmu2 + sinnu2) # Step 5: Evaluate sigma and rho sigmavals = sigmafunc(mu, NU, PHI) rhovals = rhofunc(mu, NU, PHI, P, Pprime) # Step 5: Compute Integrand integrand = Gamma0 J / (r12 r22) sigmavals rhovals # Step 6: Integrate (Riemann sum approximation) dnu = np.pi / (numsamplesnu - 1) dphi = 2 np.pi / (numsamplesphi - 1) tau = np.sum(integrand) dnu dphi return tau Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Attenuation Ignored: The simplified equation discards the attenuation term \exp(-A \int \sigma ds). This ignores occlusions, potentially leading to artifacts in scenes with hidden surfaces. Degenerate Geometry: If ct < \gamma, the ellipsoid is undefined. Coordinate Alignment: The derivation assumes a specific coordinate system where P and P' are symmetric about the origin and parallel to the y-axis. Implementation must correctly map local ellipsoidal coordinates to this frame or apply the corresponding rotation. Time Complexity: Depends on the discretization of the double integral over 
u and \varphi. O(N
u N\varphi). Memory Complexity: O(N
u N\varphi) to store intermediate arrays for the integration. Strengths: Handles non-confocal setups where illumination and detection spots are separated. Provides a closed-form geometric formulation for the transient. Limitations: Discarding attenuation ignores occlusions. Requires careful coordinate transformation. This formulation is part of the Neural Transient Fields (NeTF) method for Non-Line-of-Sight (NLOS) imaging. It extends the confocal NeTF formulation to non-confocal settings. The method is described in "Non-line-of-Sight Imaging via Neural Transient Fields". name: Neural Radiance Fields
head: Explicit Radiance Field Representations, Implicit Radiance Field
body: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) represent a static 3D scene as a continuous volumetric function that maps a 3D spatial position and a 2D viewing direction to an emitted RGB color and a volume density scalar. It solves the problem of novel view synthesis by replacing explicit geometric primitives (meshes or point clouds) with an implicit neural representation encoded in the weights of a multi-layer perceptron (MLP). Unlike its siblings, NeRF explicitly models view-dependent appearance by conditioning the color output on the viewing direction, while keeping the density view-independent. It distinguishes itself from explicit radiance field alternatives by maintaining a continuous spatial representation, albeit at higher computational cost. The family relies on the differentiability of the forward rendering operator and the propagation of gradients through the integration steps. The core mechanism is the evaluation of the volume rendering equation and the computation of gradients with respect to scene parameters (density, geometry, transfer functions, camera poses). The standard emission-absorption model computes the color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} as: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \sigmai is the density, \deltai is the step size, \mathbf{c}i is the color, and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance. Differentiation strategies fall into three main categories: 1. Reverse-Mode Automatic Differentiation (AD): Standard backpropagation through the computational graph. 2. Adjoint Method: Computes gradients by propagating adjoint variables backward through the rendering algorithm. 3. Analytic Inversion / Explicit Gradients: Uses a-priori knowledge of the DVR operations to derive closed-form gradients, reducing memory consumption. NeRF represents a static 3D scene as a continuous volumetric function mapping 3D position and 2D viewing direction to RGB color and volume density. It solves novel view synthesis by replacing explicit geometry with an implicit MLP. Sets itself apart by explicitly modeling view-dependent appearance via direction conditioning while keeping density view-independent. Choose for high-quality static scene reconstruction. A NeRF method for large-scale, real-world scenes. Addresses low geometric quality and coarse details in expansive environments using surface-guided sampling. Choose when reconstructing large outdoor scenes. A point-based NeRF representation synthesizing novel views by aggregating features from a sparse 3D neural point cloud. Differs from grid-based NeRF by replacing dense volumetric grids with learnable points, enabling faster training. Choose for efficient surface-restricted rendering. A differentiable rendering technique integrating queried feature vectors along a ray into a single aggregated vector, transformed to pixel color by one network evaluation. Reduces computational cost compared to standard volume rendering. Choose when minimizing neural network evaluations is critical. Learns the rendering process directly from data rather than handcrafted analytical differentiation. Jointly trains a scene generation and rendering network. Choose when bypassing explicit geometric differentiation is preferred. A preprocessing technique transforming low-dimensional coordinates into a higher-dimensional space using sinusoidal functions to overcome MLP spectral bias. Decouples neural architecture from spatial representation. Choose to accelerate high-frequency detail learning. Jointly models planar surfaces and explicitly casts reflected rays to capture high-frequency reflections. Prevents false geometry duplication along primary rays. Choose for scenes with strong planar reflections. A generative model for 3D-aware image synthesis learning a conditional radiance field from unposed 2D images via adversarial training. Allows explicit control over camera pose, shape, and appearance. Choose for 3D-aware generation from unposed images. A volumetric inverse rendering method reducing bias and variance in radiance estimation by using a high-capacity NeRF as a control variate for incoming illumination. Choose for unbiased radiance estimation in complex lighting. Not given in the sources. Models individual objects using separate, compositional neural feature fields for disentangled pose, shape, and appearance control. Assigns each object its own MLP outputting density and feature vectors. Choose for compositional scene generation. Accelerates NeRDF optimization by using a pre-trained teacher NeRF to generate pseudo-training views. Avoids spatial high-frequency artifacts from sparse inputs. Choose for fast training of duplex radiance fields. Maps scene coordinates and viewing directions to high-dimensional sinusoidal features to address spectral bias. Uses fixed, non-trainable bases. Choose for standard positional encoding in coordinate-based networks. Replaces continuous MLP queries with discrete 3D grids storing volumetric features, density, or color. Enables hardware-accelerated lookups. Choose for memory efficiency and inference speed. Super-resolves volumetric neural scene representations directly in 3D to generate geometrically consistent high-resolution views. Guarantees consistency across viewing directions. Choose for 3D-consistent upscaling. Improves canonical volume fidelity in dynamic tomography by combining projection training with volumetric supervision from high-fidelity X-CT data. Choose when external 3D scans are available for supervision. A self-supervised pretraining framework masking and reconstructing patches from an explicit radiance/density grid. Enables large-scale unlabeled data usage. Choose for self-supervised 3D representation learning. Extends NeRF with a 3D neural feature field mapping coordinates to semantic descriptors, enabling query-based local editing. Choose for open-set semantic decomposition and editing. A differentiable rendering component for pipelines combining NeRF with PackedRFTracer. Orchestrates neural field evaluation along traced rays. Choose as a default fallback renderer for PackedRFTracer backends. Modifies the baseline loss by applying a stop-gradient to the RHS of the rendering equation to remove gradient bias and high variance. Choose for stable optimization of radiance field caching. Integrates explicit geometric primitives or implicit surface fields with neural radiance fields to decouple geometry from appearance. Choose for faster convergence and unambiguous geometry. Extends static NeRFs to reconstruct time-varying scenes by incorporating temporal information or warping to canonical space. Choose for non-static content reconstruction. Transfers style from a 2D reference image to a 3D radiance field using explicit and implicit supervision. Choose for controllable 3D stylization. Conditions the volumetric representation on instance-specific latent codes to model entire object classes. Disentangles shape and appearance. Choose for class-level generation and editing. A zero-shot 3D style transfer technique performing style transformation within the feature space. Choose for arbitrary new style generalization. Encodes low-frequency semantic information in 3D UV volumes and high-frequency appearance in a 2D neural texture stack. Choose for real-time free-view video synthesis with pose/shape editing. Scales NeRF training to large scenes or corrects imperfect poses by decomposing the optimization problem. Choose for large-scale scenes or pose correction. A volume sampling strategy incorporating sparse depth priors from Structure from Motion (SfM) into scene representations by sampling volume points in a local-to-global manner. It initializes sampling around the depth prior in a local region and gradually extends to full scene bounds, mitigating geometric misalignment caused by depth prior bias. Decomposes radiance color into pose-independent RGB color c0 and pose-dependent shading factor s to handle bent rays and self-occlusion in posed humans. The shared color and feature vector are predicted by an appearance network, while a shallow shading network estimates s conditioned on the target pose \thetat, yielding c = c0 s. An MLP F\sigma that predicts density \sigma using an interpolated geometry latent code l{geo} and signed height indicator \tilde{h}. The density is computed as \sigma = F\sigma(\phi(\tilde{h}), l{geo}), where \phi(\cdot) is the position encoding function. A neural blending scheme for appearance refinement that recovers texture information from two adjacent input views to address artifacts from sparse inputs. It back-projects points from a target view depth map into neighboring views, extracts features and visibility, and feeds them into a blending network to compute weights Wq = \mathbf{MLP}\mathcal{A}(f^{\mathbf{v}1}q, O^{\mathbf{v}1}q, f^{\mathbf{v}2}q, O^{\mathbf{v}2}q), yielding C^{v}q = Wq \cdot Cq. Splits the model into two layers with separate density and appearance modules for the object and environment to allow foreground extraction and support effects like translucency. Sample points inside a 3D bounding box use the foreground layer, outside use the background layer. Total density is \sigmai = \sigma{io} + \sigma{ie}, and color is ci = (\sigma{io} c{oi} + \sigma{ie} c{ei}) / \max(\sigmai, \epsilon). A mechanism where the NeRF branch provides global regularization and pointwise guidance to refine independently optimized grid features, addressing noisy artifacts and lack of space continuity in grid-based methods. The grid branch enriches scene information via reconstruction loss while the NeRF branch focuses on missing high-frequency details, allowing joint refinement rather than freezing grids. An optimization strategy using multi-view distillation information to guide training of the NDRF, suppressing artifacts and approximating original NeRF rendering quality. It renders views from distillation cameras using the original NeRF to obtain targets, renders from training cameras using NDRF, and optimizes via render loss. Not given in the sources. name: NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields)
head: Mildenhall et al. 2020, Neural Radiance Field (NeRF), Radiance Fields (NeRF), Vanilla NeRF
body: NeRF represents a static 3D scene as a continuous volumetric function that maps a 3D spatial position and a 2D viewing direction to an emitted RGB color and a volume density scalar. It solves the problem of novel view synthesis by replacing explicit geometric primitives (meshes or point clouds) with an implicit neural representation encoded in the weights of a multi-layer perceptron (MLP). Unlike its siblings, NeRF explicitly models view-dependent appearance (specularities, transparency) by conditioning the color output on the viewing direction, while keeping the density view-independent to enforce geometric consistency. It distinguishes itself from nearest alternatives like Instant Neural Graphics Primitives (Instant NGP) by using a fully implicit global MLP rather than hash-encoded feature grids, resulting in higher quality but significantly slower training and rendering speeds. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N posed 2D images \{Ii\} with known camera intrinsics and extrinsics (poses). Outputs: A trained MLP F\Theta representing the radiance field, and rendered novel views \hat{I} for arbitrary camera poses. Data Structures: The core data structure is the MLP F\Theta, parameterized by weights \Theta. The original implementation uses two branches: 1. Density Network (F{\Theta1}): Takes encoded 3D position \gammax(x) as input. Outputs a scalar volume density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}^+ and a 256-dimensional intermediate feature vector z \in \mathbb{R}^{256}. 2. Color Network (F{\Theta2}): Takes the feature vector z and the encoded viewing direction \gammad(d) as input. Outputs an RGB color vector c \in \mathbb{R}^3. Positional Encoding: To enable the MLP to represent high-frequency details, inputs are mapped to a higher-dimensional space using positional encoding \gamma. For an input scalar p and frequency level L, the encoding is: \gamma(p) = [\sin(2^0 \pi p), \cos(2^0 \pi p), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi p), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi p)] This is applied element-wise to the 3D position x and the 3D viewing direction d. The total input dimension to the density network is 3+6L, and to the color network is 256 + 3 + 6L. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel in the target image, generate a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the camera center and \mathbf{d} is the unit viewing direction derived from camera intrinsics and pixel coordinates. 2. Hierarchical Sampling: Coarse Sampling: Sample Nc points uniformly along the ray within the depth interval [tn, tf] using stratified sampling. Stratified sampling divides the interval into Nc equal bins and draws one random sample from each bin to ensure coverage. Fine Sampling: Use the coarse network to estimate density weights wi = Ti(1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)). Resample Nf points from a probability distribution proportional to these weights to focus on opaque regions. 3. Network Query: For each coarse sample xi, compute \sigmai = F{\Theta1}(\gammax(xi)) and zi = \text{feature}i. For each fine sample xj, compute \sigmaj = F{\Theta1'}(\gammax(xj)) and zj = \text{feature}j. For coarse samples, compute color ck = F{\Theta2}(\gammad(d), zk). For fine samples, compute color using the fine network F{\Theta2'}(\gammad(d), zk). 4. Volume Rendering: Compute the accumulated color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) using the discrete volume rendering equation: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{N} Tk (1 - \exp(-\sigmak \deltak)) ck where \deltak = t{k+1} - tk is the distance between adjacent samples, and Tk = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{k-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the accumulated transmittance. 5. Loss Computation: Minimize the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the rendered color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and the ground-truth pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) over all rays: \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^n \| Ii - \hat{I}i(\sigma, \mathbf{c}) \|2^2 The original NeRF also includes a loss term for the coarse network to regularize the fine sampling distribution. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def positionalencoding(x, numfreqbands=6): """Applies sinusoidal positional encoding to input x (list of 3 floats).""" encoded = list(x) for i in range(numfreqbands): scale = math.pow(2, i) math.pi for val in x: encoded.append(math.sin(scale val)) encoded.append(math.cos(scale val)) return encoded def nerfforward(xenc, denc): """Simulates the MLP forward pass. Returns (sigma, feature, rgb).""" # Simplified MLP simulation for pseudocode clarity. # In practice, this involves matrix multiplications and ReLU/Sigmoid activations. # We assume xenc and denc are lists of floats. # Density branch sigma = max(0.0, sum(xenc) 0.1) # Placeholder for actual MLP computation feature = [v 0.5 for v in xenc] # Placeholder for feature vector # Color branch combined = feature + denc rgb = [max(0.0, min(1.0, v 0.1)) for v in combined] # Placeholder for actual MLP computation return sigma, feature, rgb def renderray(rayo, rayd, tn, tf, Ncoarse, Nfine): """Renders a single ray using hierarchical sampling.""" # 1. Stratified Sampling for Coarse tcoarse = [] binsize = (tf - tn) / Ncoarse for i in range(Ncoarse): ti = tn + i binsize + random.random() binsize tcoarse.append(ti) # 2. Query Coarse Network xyzcoarse = [[rayo[j] + t rayd[j] for j in range(3)] for t in tcoarse] xyzenccoarse = [positionalencoding(p) for p in xyzcoarse] denc = positionalencoding(rayd) coarseresults = [nerfforward(xenc, denc) for xenc in xyzenccoarse] sigmacoarse = [r[0] for r in coarseresults] zcoarse = [r[1] for r in coarseresults] rgbcoarse = [r[2] for r in coarseresults] # 3. Compute Weights for Fine Sampling deltas = [tcoarse[i+1] - tcoarse[i] for i in range(Ncoarse - 1)] # Pad deltas to match Ncoarse (last delta is arbitrary or 0) deltas.append(0.0) alphacoarse = [1.0 - math.exp(-sigmacoarse[i] deltas[i]) for i in range(Ncoarse)] # Transmittance Ti = exp(-sum{j<i} sigmaj deltaj) Tcoarse = [1.0] for i in range(1, Ncoarse): Tcoarse.append(Tcoarse[-1] math.exp(-sigmacoarse[i-1] deltas[i-1])) weightscoarse = [Tcoarse[i] alphacoarse[i] for i in range(Ncoarse)] # 4. Stratified Sampling for Fine (CDF-based) # Compute cumulative weights cumweights = [] total = 0.0 for w in weightscoarse: total += w cumweights.append(total) tfine = [] for in range(Nfine): u = random.random() total idx = 0 while idx < len(cumweights) - 1 and cumweights[idx] < u: idx += 1 # Interpolate within the bin binstart = tcoarse[idx] binend = tcoarse[idx+1] if idx < Ncoarse - 1 else tcoarse[idx] + (tcoarse[-1] - tcoarse[-2]) tfine.append(binstart + (u - cumweights[idx]) / (cumweights[idx+1] - cumweights[idx] + 1e-8) (binend - binstart)) # 5. Query Fine Network xyzfine = [[rayo[j] + t rayd[j] for j in range(3)] for t in tfine] xyzencfine = [positionalencoding(p) for p in xyzfine] fineresults = [nerfforward(xenc, denc) for xenc in xyzencfine] sigmafine = [r[0] for r in fineresults] zfine = [r[1] for r in fineresults] rgbfine = [r[2] for r in fineresults] # 6. Volume Rendering tall = tcoarse + tfine sigmaall = sigmacoarse + sigmafine rgball = rgbcoarse + rgbfine # Sort by depth combined = sorted(zip(tall, sigmaall, rgball)) tall = [c[0] for c in combined] sigmaall = [c[1] for c in combined] rgball = [c[2] for c in combined] # Compute deltas deltasall = [tall[i+1] - tall[i] for i in range(len(tall)-1)] deltasall.append(0.0) alphaall = [1.0 - math.exp(-sigmaall[i] deltasall[i]) for i in range(len(tall))] Tall = [1.0] for i in range(1, len(tall)): Tall.append(Tall[-1] math.exp(-sigmaall[i-1] deltasall[i-1])) weightsall = [Tall[i] alphaall[i] for i in range(len(tall))] # Color C = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(len(tall)): for k in range(3): C[k] += weightsall[i] rgball[i][k] return C Parameters: Nc (Coarse samples): Typically 64. Nf (Fine samples): Typically 128. L (Frequency bands): Not given in the sources. Hidden dimension: 256. Learning rate: 5 \times 10^{-4} with cosine decay. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Signal Attenuation: Deep networks suffer from signal attenuation; skip connections from input to intermediate layers are required to preserve low-frequency information. View-Dependent Artifacts: If the viewing direction is injected too early in the network, it can cause view-dependent artifacts in the density prediction. Aliasing: Standard ray casting can produce aliasing artifacts for fine details. This is addressed in variants like Mip-NeRF but is a limitation of the original method. Focuses on hyperparameters and sparsity priors to prevent arbitrary geometry in unobserved regions. Replaces RGB output with spherical harmonic coefficients to enable sparse voxel storage (PlenOctree) and faster rendering. Uses a hierarchy of branch networks based on uncertainty to dynamically adjust network depth per point. Renders anti-aliased conical frustums instead of rays to handle multi-scale details. Models light transportation via microflake normals and roughness for translucent objects. Uses a spherical feature grid for efficient large-scale egocentric scene reconstruction. Decouples geometry, illumination, and material properties for relighting. Uses sparse 3D grids of per-voxel features for scalability. Maps rays directly to parametric radiance distributions for real-time rendering. Eliminates initial SfM pose estimation by incrementally registering streaming video frames. Quantifies spatial uncertainty for underwater navigation. Decouples scene-specific features from a shared rendering network for 3D-aware manipulation. Time Complexity: Training is slow, typically taking 10–20 hours on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU for standard scenes. Rendering is also slow, requiring ~30 seconds per novel view at 1080p due to the need to query the MLP hundreds of times per ray. Memory Complexity: The model size is compact (~5MB for weights), but training requires storing gradients for all parameters, and rendering requires storing intermediate transmittance values. Performance: On the NeRF Synthetic (Blender) dataset, NeRF achieves a PSNR of ~31.0 dB. It provides high-fidelity novel view synthesis but is outperformed in speed by Instant Neural Graphics Primitives (Instant NGP) and 3D Gaussian Splatting. Strengths: High visual quality, compact representation, no need for explicit geometry extraction during training. Limitations: Slow training and rendering, and poor surface accuracy (density does not strictly correspond to a mesh). Aliasing artifacts on fine details are also a known limitation, addressed in variants like Mip-NeRF. When to use: When high photorealism is prioritized over speed, and explicit surface extraction is not required. When not to use: For real-time applications or large-scale scenes where training time is prohibitive. NeRF was introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020 at ECCV. It established the field of neural radiance fields by demonstrating that a simple MLP could learn a continuous 5D function representing a scene's geometry and appearance. The method relies on the differentiability of volume rendering to optimize the network weights using standard image reconstruction losses. It has since inspired a vast ecosystem of variants addressing its limitations in speed, surface reconstruction, and generalization. name: NeRF Training Configuration
head: NeRF Training Loop Configuration, NeRF Training Setup, Sparsity Prior, Sparsity Regularization
body: NeRF Training Configuration specifies the hyperparameters, optimization routines, and regularization terms applied during NeRF training. It solves the problem of converging to a physically plausible volumetric representation by preventing the network from generating arbitrary, non-photorealistic geometry in unobserved regions. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Mip-NeRF or Instant Neural Graphics Primitives (Instant NGP) by explicitly incorporating a sparsity prior (or sparsity loss) to condense volume density, ensuring the resulting field is suitable for downstream sparse representations like octrees. The training configuration defines the data pipeline, the composite loss function (including the sparsity term), and the optimizer settings required to minimize the difference between rendered and ground-truth images while enforcing geometric sparsity. Inputs: Training images (RGB), camera poses (extrinsics), camera intrinsics (focal length, image dimensions), and a bounding box defining the scene volume. Outputs: A trained NeRF model (typically two MLPs for coarse and fine sampling) and associated optimizer state. The training loop manages the following data structures: 1. Dataset: A collection of rays generated from training images. Each ray is defined by origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, and target color \mathbf{C}^. 2. Model State: coarsemodelstatedict: Parameters for the coarse sampling MLP. finemodelstatedict: Parameters for the fine sampling MLP. optimizerstatedict: State for the Adam optimizer. 3. Checkpoint: A dictionary saved to disk with keys: 'epoch', 'coarsemodelstatedict', 'finemodelstatedict', 'optimizerstatedict'. 1. Data Loading: Load the training dataset (e.g., BlenderDataset) at a specified resolution (e.g., shorter side 400 pixels). Extract camera intrinsics: height H, width W, and focal length f. 2. Ray Generation: For each training image, generate rays. The camera intrinsic matrix is constructed as: K = \begin{bmatrix} f & 0 & 0.5 \cdot W \\ 0 & f & 0.5 \cdot H \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. 3. Model Initialization: Initialize two NeRF models: a coarse model and a fine model. Combine their parameters. 4. Optimizer Setup: Create an Adam optimizer with learning rate \eta = 5 \times 10^{-4} and betas (\beta1, \beta2) = (0.9, 0.999). 5. Loss Definition: Define the composite loss function \mathcal{L}: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{RGB}} + \betas \mathcal{L}{\text{sparsity}} where \mathcal{L}{\text{RGB}} is the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between predicted and target colors, and \mathcal{L}{\text{sparsity}} is the sparsity regularization term. 6. Training Loop: Sample a batch of rays (batch size = 1). Perform volume rendering to predict color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) using the coarse and fine sampling strategies. Sample K uniformly random points within the bounding box to compute \mathcal{L}{\text{sparsity}}. Compute gradients and update model parameters. 7. Checkpointing: Save the model state, optimizer state, and epoch number to a.pt file. Volume Rendering: The predicted color for a ray \mathbf{r} is: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=0}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci where Ti = \exp \left( -\sum{j=0}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj \right), \sigmai is density, \deltai is distance between samples, and ci is color. RGB Loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{RGB}} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \| \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) - \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) \|2^2 where \mathcal{R} is the batch of rays corresponding to pixels in the training images. Sparsity Loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{sparsity}} = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^K | 1 - \exp(-\delta \sigmak) | where \sigmak are density values at K uniformly random points within the bounding box, and \delta is an exponential scaling factor. (Source denotes this scaling factor as \lambda, while uses \delta.) Learning Rate: 5 \times 10^{-4}. Sparsity Weight (\betas): 0.01. Exponential Scaling Factor (\delta): 0.1. Batch Size: 1. Image Resolution: 400 (shorter side). Optimizer Betas: (0.9, 0.999). Solid Background: Without the sparsity prior, NeRF can converge to a solution where unobserved portions or the background are solid (high density), which degrades the spatial resolution of subsequent octree-based representations. Checkpoint Epoch Restoration: Model loading from checkpoints does not automatically restore the epoch number, requiring manual handling or a TODO fix. Precision: Denominators in interpolation steps (e.g., calculating finer z-values) must be guarded against zero values (replaced with 10^{-5} or similar small constant) to prevent NaN gradients. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim def computesparsityloss(model, boundingbox, K=1000, delta=0.1): """ Computes the sparsity loss by sampling K random points in the bounding box. """ # Sample K uniformly random points within the bounding box randompoints = torch.rand(K, 3) (boundingbox.max - boundingbox.min) + boundingbox.min # Apply positional encoding and pass through the MLP to get density densities = model(randompoints) # Lsparsity = (1/K) sum |1 - exp(-delta sigmak)| sparsityterm = torch.abs(1.0 - torch.exp(-delta densities)) loss = torch.mean(sparsityterm) return loss def trainstep(model, optimizer, raybatch, targetcolor, boundingbox, betas=0.01, delta=0.1): """ Performs one training step. """ optimizer.zerograd() # Volume rendering to predict color predictedcolor = model(raybatch) # RGB Loss (MSE) rgbloss = nn.functional.mseloss(predictedcolor, targetcolor) # Sparsity Loss sparsityloss = computesparsityloss(model, boundingbox, K=1000, delta=delta) # Total Loss totalloss = rgbloss + betas sparsityloss # Backpropagation totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return totalloss.item(), rgbloss.item(), sparsityloss.item() def trainneRF(dataset, coarsemodel, finemodel, epochs=1000, lr=5e-4, betas=0.01, delta=0.1): """ Main training loop. """ # Combine parameters from both models allparams = list(coarsemodel.parameters()) + list(finemodel.parameters()) # Optimizer optimizer = optim.Adam(allparams, lr=lr, betas=(0.9, 0.999)) for epoch in range(epochs): for batch in dataset: # Extract ray batch and target color raybatch = batch['rays'] targetcolor = batch['colors'] # Forward pass and loss computation trainstep(finemodel, optimizer, raybatch, targetcolor, dataset.boundingbox, betas, delta) # Checkpointing if epoch % 10 == 0: checkpoint = { 'epoch': epoch, 'coarsemodelstatedict': coarsemodel.statedict(), 'finemodelstatedict': finemodel.statedict(), 'optimizerstatedict': optimizer.statedict() } torch.save(checkpoint, f'checkpointepoch{epoch}.pt') The NeuS training loss is a composite objective function used to optimize neural implicit surface representations (specifically Signed Distance Fields or Unsigned Distance Fields) from multi-view images without 3D ground-truth supervision. It solves the problem of recovering high-fidelity open surfaces by combining photometric consistency with geometric regularization. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF training NeRF Training Configuration by explicitly enforcing the Eikonal equation on the SDF/UDF gradients and using a mask-based binary cross-entropy loss to drive opacity toward binary values, thereby stabilizing the thin-surface approximation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The sparsity prior improves the robustness of octree conversion (e.g., PlenOctree) by preventing solid background artifacts. Strengths: Prevents "ghosting" or solid background artifacts in novel views; facilitates efficient sparse representation conversion. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \betas and \delta; adds computational overhead per step due to random sampling for sparsity loss. When to use: When the downstream application involves converting the NeRF to a sparse representation (like an octree) or when the scene has large unobserved background regions. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The sparsity prior was introduced in the context of PlenOctrees for real-time rendering of NeRFs. The authors observed that without regularization, NeRFs tend to fill unobserved space with arbitrary geometry, which negatively impacts the efficiency of octree-based compression. The configuration described here, including the specific Adam optimizer settings and batch size, is derived from common PyTorch implementations of NeRF. The sparsity loss formula is also discussed in the context of L0-Sampler, which contrasts its density condensation approach with other sampling refinements.
