name: EgoNeRF
body: EgoNeRF is an efficient adaptation of NeRF [1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md] for large-scale scenes with casual input, utilizing a balanced spherical feature grid and maintaining uniform ray hit rates for individual cells for scenes captured with a short video of omnidirectional cameras. It addresses the inefficiency and artifact issues of Cartesian grids in wide-field-of-view settings by employing a spherical coordinate system that matches egocentric capture geometry. Unlike Mip-NeRF which relies on a proposal MLP for resampling, EgoNeRF shares a single density grid for coarse and fine sampling, enabling faster convergence and superior preservation of fine structures. EgoNeRF represents the scene using a continuous volumetric field parameterized by a balanced spherical feature grid and a lightweight MLP, optimized via differentiable volume rendering. Inputs: Multi-view equirectangular images from an omnidirectional camera; camera poses estimated via Structure-from-Motion (SfM). Outputs: A neural volume representation allowing synthesis of novel views; rendered images with high fidelity to ground truth. The core data structure is the Balanced Spherical Feature Grid. Unlike Cartesian grids (e.g., DVGO or TensoRF), this grid is defined in spherical coordinates (r, \theta, \phi) to match the geometry of egocentric capture. 1. Radial Partition: Uniformly spaced concentric shells. 2. Angular Partition: Uses a Yin-Yang grid combined with a uniform radial partition to minimize valence variations at the poles. 3. Feature Storage: Each grid cell stores feature vectors, which are processed via vector-matrix factorization. 4. Density Grid (G\sigma): A shared grid used to query volume density for both coarse and fine sampling stages. Hardware: Experiments conducted on a single RTX-3090 GPU. Ray Batch Size: Same as baseline methods (DVGO, TensoRF) for fair comparison. Grid Resolution: Same number of feature grids as DVGO and TensoRF. Training Steps: High performance achieved at 5,000 steps. 1. Pose Estimation: Obtain camera poses from input video frames using the OpenMVG SfM library. 2. Grid Initialization: Initialize the balanced spherical feature grid with uniform radial partitions and Yin-Yang angular partitions. 3. Ray Sampling: Cast rays from the camera through each pixel. Sample points along the ray. Query the shared density grid G\sigma for volume density at these points. 4. Resampling: Employ resampling techniques to refine sample distribution based on the shared density grid G\sigma, rather than relying on a separate proposal MLP. 5. Feature Aggregation: Retrieve features from the spherical grid for each sample point. Apply vector-matrix factorization to combine features. 6. Rendering: Compute color and density for each sample. Perform volume rendering (compositing) to produce the final pixel color. 7. Optimization: Minimize the difference between rendered images and ground truth images. Update grid features and MLP parameters via gradient descent. 8. Environment Map: Include an environment map component to handle infinitely far regions, particularly in outdoor scenes. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def volumerenderray(rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax, gridsigma, gridspherical, envmap, numsamples=128): """ Renders a single ray using the shared density grid and spherical feature grid. Implements standard volume rendering compositing: C(r) = sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai deltai)) ci Ti = exp(-sum{j=1}^{i-1} sigmaj deltaj) """ # 1. Coarse sampling along the ray coarsets = [tmin + i (tmax - tmin) / (numsamples - 1) for i in range(numsamples)] coarsepoints = [rayorigin + raydirection t for t in coarsets] # 2. Query density from shared grid for coarse samples coarsesigmas = [gridsigma.query(p) for p in coarsepoints] # 3. Resampling based on density (importance sampling) # Generate fine samples weighted by coarse density finets = [] fineweights = [1.0 - math.exp(-s (tmax - tmin) / (numsamples - 1)) for s in coarsesigmas] fineweights = [w / sum(fineweights) for w in fineweights] # Simple stratified resampling for implementation clarity for i in range(numsamples): t = tmin + (i + 0.5) (tmax - tmin) / numsamples finets.append(t) finepoints = [rayorigin + raydirection t for t in finets] # 4. Fine rendering loop T = 1.0 coloraccum = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] deltat = (tmax - tmin) / (numsamples - 1) for i, point in enumerate(finepoints): sigma = gridsigma.query(point) alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma deltat) weight = alpha T # Query spherical grid and apply vector-matrix factorization r = math.sqrt(point[0]2 + point[1]2 + point[2]2) theta = math.atan2(math.sqrt(point[0]2 + point[1]2), point[2]) phi = math.atan2(point[1], point[0]) features = gridspherical.sample(r, theta, phi) color = [sum(f w for f, w in zip(features, [1.0, 0.5, 0.25])) for in range(3)] # Placeholder factorization coloraccum = [coloraccum[j] + weight color[j] for j in range(3)] T = (1.0 - alpha) if T < 1e-4: break # 5. Background accumulation for unbounded scenes background = envmap.query(raydirection) finalcolor = [coloraccum[j] + T background[j] for j in range(3)] return finalcolor, T def trainstep(images, poses, gridsigma, gridspherical, envmap, lr=0.01): """ One step of optimization. Computes loss and updates parameters. """ totalloss = 0.0 for image, pose in zip(images, poses): for u, v in image.pixels: rayorigin = pose.cameracenter raydirection = pose.getraydirection(u, v) renderedcolor, = volumerenderray(rayorigin, raydirection, pose.tmin, pose.tmax, gridsigma, gridspherical, envmap) targetcolor = image.getpixel(u, v) # MSE loss loss = sum((r - t)2 for r, t in zip(renderedcolor, targetcolor)) / 3.0 totalloss += loss # Gradient descent update gradients = computegradients(totalloss, [gridsigma, gridspherical, envmap]) updateparameters(gradients, lr) return totalloss Camera Pose Errors: Erroneous pose estimates cause rays to hit neighboring cells in the feature grid. This results in spotty artifacts in EgoNeRF, whereas MLP-based methods (like standard NeRF) tend to produce blurry rendering in the same scenario. Pole Distortion: Equirectangular images have distortion near poles. The authors additionally measure weighted-to-spherically uniform PSNR and SSIM (PSNRWS, SSIMWS) to account for this distortion during evaluation. Missing Components: Removing the balanced spherical grid components (uniform radial partition, Yin-Yang grid) degrades performance. Removing both radial and angular balanced grids (using uniform spherical grids) causes the biggest drop in performance, except for PSNR in indoor scenes. Not employing resampling techniques and using a double number of ray samples reduces performance. Removing the environment map in outdoor scenes shows blurry artifacts in infinitely far regions and reduces performance. Speed: EgoNeRF achieves high performance very quickly. It reaches competitive results at 5,000 training steps, taking only 10 minutes of wall-clock time. In contrast, Mip-NeRF requires approximately 8 hours to outperform EgoNeRF's 5k-step results. Accuracy: On the OmniBlender dataset, EgoNeRF (full) achieves: Indoor: PSNR 33.11, LPIPS 0.142, SSIM 0.902. Outdoor: PSNR 30.56, LPIPS 0.087, SSIM 0.904. Strengths: Efficient for large-scale, unbounded scenes captured with omnidirectional cameras. Preserves fine structures (e.g., thin wires, street lamps) better than Mip-NeRF, which often misses them due to reliance on the proposal MLP's initial guess. Avoids the "wasted cells" and low-resolution center issues of Cartesian grids (TensoRF, DVGO) in large scenes. Limitations: Sensitive to camera pose errors, leading to spotty artifacts. Performance degrades if the balanced spherical grid structure is simplified to uniform spherical grids. When to Use: Ideal for egocentric, large-scale scene reconstruction from casual omnidirectional video where fast training and high fidelity to fine details are required. When Not to Use: If camera poses are highly inaccurate and spotty artifacts are unacceptable, or if the scene is small and bounded where Cartesian grids might suffice. EgoNeRF is a variant of NeRF [1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md] introduced to address the limitations of standard NeRF and its variants in large-scale, egocentric settings. While Mip-NeRF adapts to unbounded scenes by warping space, EgoNeRF focuses on the geometric suitability of the feature grid for spherical capture. It was developed to enable efficient synthesis of novel views from short videos captured with omnidirectional cameras, leveraging a balanced spherical feature grid to maintain uniform ray hit rates. Balanced Spherical Grid for Egocentric View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.01592, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Intrinsic NeRF
head: Intrinsic Image Decomposition in NeRF, Intrinsic NeRF Decomposition, Intrinsic NeRF Model
body: Intrinsic NeRF is a variant of Neural Radiance Fields that decouples geometry, illumination, and material properties by decomposing the rendered color into reflectance and shading components, solving the ill-posed inverse rendering problem without supervision. It differs from standard NeRF by explicitly outputting physical scene attributes (density, reflectance, shading) rather than just radiance, enabling downstream tasks like relighting and material analysis. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D location \mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and view direction \mathbf{D} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (normalized). Output: A tuple (\sigma, \mathbf{R}, S) where \sigma \in \mathbb{R} is volume density, \mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is reflectance (albedo), and S \in \mathbb{R} is shading (incident illumination intensity). Data Structures: Two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) are used: 1. Reflectance MLP (fR): Takes \mathbf{X} as input. Outputs \mathbf{R}. 2. Shading MLP (fS): Takes \mathbf{X} and \mathbf{D} as inputs. Outputs S. 3. Density MLP (f\sigma): (Implicitly part of the standard NeRF architecture or a separate head) Takes \mathbf{X} as input. Outputs \sigma. Formulas: The rendered color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} is computed via volume rendering integration from near plane tn to far plane tf: \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigma(t) (\mathbf{S}(t) \cdot \mathbf{R}(t)) dt where: T(t) = \exp\left(-\int{tn}^{t} \sigma(s) ds\right) is the transmittance. \mathbf{S}(t) is the shading scalar at t. \mathbf{R}(t) is the reflectance vector at t. The dot product \mathbf{S}(t) \cdot \mathbf{R}(t) effectively scales the reflectance by the shading intensity. Training: The model is trained using only RGB images from the input dataset, with no additional lighting or material labels. The loss function is the mean squared error between the rendered color and the ground truth RGB: \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \|\hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r})\|2^2 where \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) is the ground truth color and \mathcal{R} is the set of camera rays in a batch. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def intrinsicnerfforward(xyz, viewdir, densitymlp, reflectancemlp, shadingmlp): """ Computes density, reflectance, and shading for a batch of points. Args: xyz: Tensor of shape (N, 3), 3D coordinates. viewdir: Tensor of shape (N, 3), normalized view directions. densitymlp: MLP taking xyz -> sigma (scalar). reflectancemlp: MLP taking xyz -> R (vector, 3). shadingmlp: MLP taking xyz, viewdir -> S (scalar). Returns: sigma: Tensor of shape (N, 1), density. R: Tensor of shape (N, 3), reflectance. S: Tensor of shape (N, 1), shading. """ # Compute density from location only sigma = densitymlp(xyz) # Compute reflectance from location only R = reflectancemlp(xyz) # Compute shading from location and view direction S = shadingmlp(xyz, viewdir) return sigma, R, S def renderintrinsicray(rayso, raysd, tn, tf, numsamples, densitymlp, reflectancemlp, shadingmlp): """ Renders a single ray using volume rendering with intrinsic decomposition. Args: rayso: Origin of the ray (3,). raysd: Direction of the ray (3,). tn: Near plane distance. tf: Far plane distance. numsamples: Number of samples along the ray. Returns: Chat: Rendered color (3,). """ # Sample points along the ray tvals = torch.linspace(tn, tf, numsamples) xyz = rayso.unsqueeze(0) + tvals.unsqueeze(1) raysd.unsqueeze(0) # Shape: (numsamples, 3) # Get view direction (constant for the ray) viewdir = raysd.unsqueeze(0).expandas(xyz) # Query networks sigma, R, S = intrinsicnerfforward(xyz, viewdir, densitymlp, reflectancemlp, shadingmlp) # Compute transmittance # alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma deltat) # T(t) = product(1 - alpha) # Standard volume rendering accumulation deltas = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] # Add infinite delta for the last segment to handle transparency correctly deltas = torch.cat([deltas, torch.tensor([1e10], device=deltas.device)]) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) T = torch.cumprod(torch.cat([torch.oneslike(alpha[:,:1]), 1.0 - alpha + 1e-10], dim=1)[:,:-1], dim=1) # Weighted sum of color # Color contribution = T(t) alpha(t) S(t) R(t) weights = T alpha colorcontribution = weights.unsqueeze(-1) S R Chat = torch.sum(colorcontribution, dim=0) return Chat def trainstep(batch, densitymlp, reflectancemlp, shadingmlp, optimizer): """ Single training step. """ optimizer.zerograd() # batch contains rayso, raysd, and ground truth colors C Chat = renderintrinsicray(...) # Implementation details for batched rays omitted for brevity # Loss calculation loss = torch.mean((Chat - batch.Cgt) 2) loss.backward() optimizer.step() return loss.item() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ill-posedness: Without supervision on shading or reflectance, the decomposition is ambiguous. The model relies on the inductive bias that reflectance is view-independent and shading is view-dependent. View Direction Normalization: View directions must be normalized before input to the shading MLP to ensure consistent lighting estimation. Density Independence: The density field \sigma is typically shared or derived from the same location-based network as in standard NeRF, but the color composition explicitly separates it from the material/illumination split. Enhances geometric consistency by computing differentiable normal maps from the volume density field and applying depth-dependent regularization loss. It solves noisy geometry issues by enforcing surface smoothness weighted by physical area. Time Complexity: Similar to standard NeRF training, dominated by MLP evaluations for density, reflectance, and shading per sample. The additional shading MLP adds computational overhead proportional to the number of samples. Memory Complexity: Requires storing parameters for three MLPs (density, reflectance, shading) instead of one or two. Strengths: Enables inverse rendering tasks such as relighting and material analysis without explicit supervision. Limitations: The decomposition is inherently ill-posed; results depend heavily on the network architecture's inductive biases. When to use: When the goal is to extract physical scene properties (albedo, lighting) for relighting or editing, rather than just novel view synthesis. Intrinsic NeRF was introduced to address the ill-posed problem of inverse rendering 3D scenes without supervision by utilizing a simplified intrinsic image decomposition model. It builds on the NeRF framework by adding explicit outputs for reflectance and shading. Relighting Scenes With Object Insertions in Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/TCSVT.2025.3535599, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Geometry Decomposition and Normal Regularization
head: Depth-Dependent Normal Regularization, Normal Map Computation
body:
This method enhances the geometric consistency of Intrinsic NeRF by computing differentiable normal maps from the volume density field and applying a depth-dependent regularization loss. It solves the problem of noisy, inconsistent geometry in complex scenes, which degrades subsequent reflectance and shading decomposition. Unlike standard NeRF variants that optimize only for RGB consistency, this approach explicitly enforces surface smoothness weighted by physical area, ensuring that background pixels (covering larger physical areas) are regularized more strongly than foreground pixels. The method operates on the volume density field \sigma and its gradient 
abla \sigma to derive geometric attributes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera rays \mathcal{R}, near/far bounds tn, tf, and the trained density field \sigma(\mathbf{x}). Output: Depth map \mathbf{D}, Normal map \mathbf{N}, and the regularization loss \mathcal{L}d. Data Structures: Density Field: A neural network or voxel grid mapping 3D coordinates \mathbf{x} to scalar density \sigma. Ray Structure: Each ray \mathbf{r} is defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Adjacency Map: A set of neighboring pixel indices for each pixel \mathbf{r} in the image plane. Formulas: 1. Transmittance: T(t) = \exp\left(-\int{tn}^{t} \sigma(s) dsight). 2. Depth Map: The expected depth along ray \mathbf{r}: \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigma(t) t dt 3. Normal Map: The expected surface normal along ray \mathbf{r}, derived from the negative gradient of density: \mathbf{N}(\mathbf{r}) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigma(t) (-
abla \sigma(\mathbf{x}(t))) dt where \mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. 4. Depth-Dependent Normal Regularization Loss: Encourages consistency between adjacent pixels, weighted by the inverse square of depth: \mathcal{L}d =  rac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \left( 1 -  rac{\mathbf{N}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \mathbf{N}(\mathbf{r}{adj})}{|\mathbf{N}(\mathbf{r})| |\mathbf{N}(\mathbf{r}{adj})|} ight)  rac{1}{\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{r})^2} where \mathbf{r}{adj} represents the set of adjacent pixels to \mathbf{r}. Parameters: Sampling Steps: Number of samples per ray for integration. Not given in the sources. Adjacency Window: Typically immediate 4- or 8-neighbors in the image grid. Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computegeometryloss(rays, densitynet, tn, tf, numsamples): """ Computes depth, normal maps, and the depth-dependent normal regularization loss. Args: rays: List of Ray objects, each with origin o and direction d. densitynet: Neural network returning (sigma, gradsigma) at point x. tn: Near plane distance. tf: Far plane distance. numsamples: Number of integration steps per ray. Returns: Ld: Scalar regularization loss. """ totalloss = 0.0 count = 0 # Pre-compute normals for all rays to access neighbors # In practice, this is done via batched differentiable rendering normals = [] depths = [] for ray in rays: # Sample points along the ray tvals = torch.linspace(tn, tf, numsamples) points = ray.o + tvals.unsqueeze(1) ray.d.unsqueeze(0) # Shape: [numsamples, 3] # Query density and gradient # densitynet returns sigma and dsigma/dx, dsigma/dy, dsigma/dz sigma, gradsigma = densitynet(points) # Compute transmittance # T(ti) = exp(-sum{j=0}^{i-1} sigmaj deltat) deltas = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) T = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha + 1e-10, dim=0) T = torch.cat([torch.ones(1, device=T.device), T[:-1]], dim=0) # Compute Depth # D(r) = sum(T(ti) sigma(ti) ti deltat) weights = T alpha depth = torch.sum(weights tvals) # Compute Normal # N(r) = sum(T(ti) sigma(ti) (-gradsigma(ti)) deltat) # Note: gradsigma is already the gradient of sigma normal = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(1) (-gradsigma) deltas.unsqueeze(1), dim=0) normals.append(normal) depths.append(depth) normals = torch.stack(normals) depths = torch.stack(depths) # Compute Loss # For each ray r, compare with adjacent rays radj # Assuming rays are ordered in image raster scan for adjacency # This is a simplified representation; actual implementation requires # reshaping to image grid to access neighbors efficiently. # Reshape to image grid (H, W) # H, W = imageheight, imagewidth # normalsgrid = normals.view(H, W, 3) # depthsgrid = depths.view(H, W) # Iterate over pixels (conceptually) for i in range(H): for j in range(W): r = rays[i W + j] nr = normalsgrid[i, j] dr = depthsgrid[i, j] # Get adjacent pixels (e.g., 4-neighbor) neighbors = getneighbors(i, j, H, W) for ni, nj in neighbors: nadj = normalsgrid[ni, nj] # Cosine similarity cossim = torch.dot(nr, nadj) / (torch.norm(nr) torch.norm(nadj) + 1e-8) # Depth-dependent weight # Avoid division by zero weight = 1.0 / (dr2 + 1e-8) # Loss term: (1 - cossim) weight totalloss += (1.0 - cossim) weight count += 1 return totalloss / count Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noise: Without this regularization, normal maps exhibit significantly more noise, particularly in complex scenes. Background Weighting: A pixel in the background corresponds to a larger physical area. The 1/\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{r})^2 weight guides regularization to account for this, preventing over-smoothing of foreground details while ensuring background consistency. Gradient Estimation: The normal map relies on 
abla \sigma. If the density field is not smooth, the gradient will be noisy, leading to unstable normals. Regularizes reflectance estimation by distilling DINO features from 2D images to 3D surfaces. It minimizes the distance between learnable DINO features on the surface and pre-trained ViT features. Steps: 1. Distill DINO feature to the initial geometry field. 2. Minimize the loss function by comparing learnable surface features with 2D image features. 3. Incorporate distilled DINO features into networks for specular albedo and roughness to enhance material decomposition accuracy. Parameter: Images are upsampled by a scaling factor of two to extract higher resolution DINO features for finer material decoupling. Time Complexity: Adds overhead for computing gradients of density 
abla \sigma and integrating normal maps. The adjacency comparison is O(|\mathcal{R}|) per batch. Memory Complexity: Requires storing normal maps for the current batch. Strengths: Significantly reduces noise in normal maps, leading to smoother geometry and better material decomposition. Limitations: Requires differentiable density field to compute 
abla \sigma. Sensitive to the choice of adjacency window and depth weighting. When to use: When high-quality geometry is required for subsequent intrinsic decomposition tasks, especially in complex scenes. Originated in the context of Intrinsic NeRF to address the ill-posed nature of inverse rendering. The depth-dependent normal regularization was introduced to improve geometric consistency by leveraging the pinhole camera model's property that background pixels cover larger physical areas. DINO feature regularization was later introduced to further constrain reflectance estimation using self-supervised 2D features. Relighting Scenes With Object Insertions in Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/TCSVT.2025.3535599, fetched 2026-10-29 PIR: Photometric Inverse Rendering with Shading Cues Modeling and Surface Reflectance Regularization, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv66043.2025.00055, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Sparse Neural Volume Representation
head: Sparse Neural Volume Radiance Field, Sparse Volume for Radiance Fields
body: Sparse Neural Volume Representation models a radiance field using a sparse 3D grid of per-voxel neural features that approximately cover the scene surface, enabling scalable reconstruction for large scenes. Unlike standard NeRF which relies on a global MLP without intermediate spatial structure, this method uses explicit voxel features to improve scalability for large scenes and generalization across scenes. Inputs: A sequence of RGB images with known camera poses (obtained via SLAM or SfM). Outputs: A sparse neural volume V containing per-voxel features, and a shared MLP decoder R. Data Structures: Sparse Neural Volume (V): A 3D grid structure where only voxels covering the scene surface contain data. It consists of two components: Local Volume (Vt): Reconstructed for each input frame t in the canonical world space. Global Volume (Vg): Reconstructed for the entire sequence in the canonical world space. MLP Decoder (R): A neural network shared across all volumes and scenes. Evaluation Steps: To evaluate the radiance field at a 3D location x for a viewing direction d: 1. Tri-linear Interpolation: Sample a feature vector \mathcal{V}(x) from the sparse volume V at location x using tri-linear interpolation. 2. MLP Regression: Input the feature vector \mathcal{V}(x), the 3D location x, and the viewing direction d into the MLP network R. 3. Output: The network R regresses the volume density \sigma and view-dependent radiance c. Formula: The relationship is defined as: \sigma, c = R(x, d, \mathcal{V}(x)) Where: \sigma: Volume density. c: View-dependent radiance. x: 3D location in the canonical world space. d: Viewing direction. R: The MLP decoder network. \mathcal{V}(x): The trilinearly interpolated feature vector from the sparse volume at x. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def evaluateradiancefield(x, d, sparsevolume, mlpdecoder): """ Evaluates density and radiance at point x for direction d. Args: x: 3D location (float32, shape [3]) d: Viewing direction (float32, shape [3]) sparsevolume: Sparse 3D grid/dict containing per-voxel features mlpdecoder: MLP network R Returns: sigma: Volume density (float32) c: View-dependent radiance (float32, shape [3]) """ # Step 1: Tri-linearly sample feature vector from sparse volume ix, iy, iz = x x0, y0, z0 = math.floor(ix), math.floor(iy), math.floor(iz) x1, y1, z1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1, z0 + 1 # Fetch 8 corner features (default to zero vector if voxel is empty) f000 = sparsevolume.get((x0, y0, z0), np.zeros(3)) f100 = sparsevolume.get((x1, y0, z0), np.zeros(3)) f010 = sparsevolume.get((x0, y1, z0), np.zeros(3)) f110 = sparsevolume.get((x1, y1, z0), np.zeros(3)) f001 = sparsevolume.get((x0, y0, z1), np.zeros(3)) f101 = sparsevolume.get((x1, y0, z1), np.zeros(3)) f011 = sparsevolume.get((x0, y1, z1), np.zeros(3)) f111 = sparsevolume.get((x1, y1, z1), np.zeros(3)) dx, dy, dz = ix - x0, iy - y0, iz - z0 # Tri-linear interpolation c00 = f000 (1 - dx) + f100 dx c10 = f010 (1 - dx) + f110 dx c01 = f001 (1 - dx) + f101 dx c11 = f011 (1 - dx) + f111 dx c0 = c00 (1 - dy) + c10 dy c1 = c01 (1 - dy) + c11 dy featurevector = c0 (1 - dz) + c1 dz # Step 2: Pass feature vector, location, and direction into MLP densityandradiance = mlpdecoder(x, d, featurevector) # Step 3: Extract density and radiance sigma = densityandradiance.density c = densityandradiance.radiance return sigma, c Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Voxels: Since the volume is sparse, querying a location outside the covered surface region may return undefined or zero features. The method assumes x lies within the approximate surface coverage. Regresses a local neural volume Vt for each input frame using the current image and neighboring views. Fuses local volumes into a global volume Vg for the entire sequence, inspired by TSDF fusion workflows. Leverages neural networks trained across multiple scenes to predict neural volumes, bypassing per-scene optimization. Scalability: Improves scalability for large scenes compared to global MLP-based NeRF by using a sparse volume grid. Speed: Enables fast radiance field reconstruction through direct network inference, bypassing slow per-scene optimization. Quality: Can be fine-tuned to boost quality, but initial reconstruction is achieved via inference. Comparison: Unlike Neural Sparse Voxel Fields which relies on per-scene optimization, this method generalizes across scenes. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in "NeRFusion: Fusing Radiance Fields for Large-Scale Scene Reconstruction". It builds on the classical TSDF (Truncated Signed Distance Function) fusion workflow, starting from per-view geometry and fusing reconstructions across key frames. It addresses the limitations of previous methods that required slow per-scene optimization by proposing a deep neural network trained across scenes. NeRFusion: Fusing Radiance Fields for Large-Scale Scene Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.00537, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Neural Radiance Distribution Field
head: NeRDF (Neural Radiance Distribution Field)
body: Neural Radiance Distribution Field (NeRDF) is a method for efficient novel view synthesis that combines the 3D prior consistency of NeRF with the single-evaluation rendering speed of NeLF. Unlike NeRF, which requires multiple network queries per ray, NeRDF maps a camera ray directly to a parametric radiance distribution (opacity and color coefficients) using a small neural network, enabling real-time rendering with low memory cost. NeRDF takes a camera ray \mathbf{r} as input and outputs the coefficients for a trigonometric approximation of the opacity and color distributions along that ray. These distributions are then integrated via volume rendering to produce the final pixel color. Input: A camera ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, defined by origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, and distance parameter t. Output: A synthesized RGB color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for the pixel corresponding to the ray. The network input is constructed by encoding the ray origin, direction, and sampled points along the ray path. 1. Ray Origin (\mathbf{o}): Encoded using frequency-based positional encoding with 10 frequencies. 2. Ray Direction (\mathbf{d}): Encoded using spherical harmonic (SH) embedding with 8 degrees, resulting in a 64-dimensional vector. 3. Path Points: N points are sampled along the ray \mathbf{r} using stratified sampling to capture path information. These N points form a 3N-dimensional vector, which is embedded using the same frequency-based positional encoding (10 frequencies) as the origin. 4. Concatenation: The encoded origin, encoded direction, and encoded path points are concatenated to form the final input vector to the MLP. The core model is an 8-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with a width of 384 and skip connections between neighboring layers. The network maps the encoded ray input to two sets of coefficients: \mathbf{w}^\sigma: Coefficients for the opacity distribution. \mathbf{w}^C: Coefficients for the color distribution. The total output channels of the MLP is 8K, where K is the number of frequencies in the Fourier approximation. The opacity \sigma(t) and color C(t) along the ray distance t are parameterized using a Fourier series with 2K coefficients each and trigonometric basis functions \mathcal{T}i(t): \sigma(t) = \sum{i=0}^{2K-1} wi^\sigma \cdot \mathcal{T}i(t) C(t) = \sum{i=0}^{2K-1} wi^C \cdot \mathcal{T}i(t) The basis functions \mathcal{T}i(t) are defined based on the ray length T and index i: \mathcal{T}i(t) = \begin{cases} \cos\left(\frac{i\pi}{T}t\right) & \text{for even } i \\ \sin\left(\frac{(i+1)\pi}{T}t\right) & \text{for odd } i \end{cases} The final pixel color is computed via volume rendering integration using the predicted distributions. 1. Sampling: Sample M points along the ray \mathbf{r} to obtain distance stamps tm (typically M=64 uniform samples). 2. Evaluation: Evaluate \sigma(tm) and C(tm) at each sampled point using the Fourier series formulas above. 3. Integration: Compute the final pixel color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) using standard volume rendering integration: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{m=1}^{M} Tm \left(1 - e^{-\sigma(tm)\deltam}\right) C(tm) where \deltam is the distance between adjacent samples and Tm = e^{-\sum{j=1}^{m-1} \sigma(tj)\deltaj} is the accumulated transmittance. NeRDF is trained using a knowledge distillation framework where a teacher NeRF synthesizes pseudo-data. Online View Sampling (OVS): Instead of pre-computing pseudo-data, camera poses are randomly sampled during training. A batch consists of 1 view origin and 2,048 directions. Loss Function: The primary loss is the L2 norm between the synthesized color and the ground truth (or teacher pseudo-data) color: L{render} = \sum{\mathbf{r}} \|\hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) - C(\mathbf{r})\|2^2 Volume Density Constraint (VDC): To ensure multi-view consistency and valid 3D priors, a VDC loss minimizes the L2 distance between the normalized volume density predicted by NeRDF (\hat{\sigma}1(t)) and the teacher NeRF (\hat{\sigma}2(\mathbf{r}(t))): M{vdc} = \lambda \sum{\mathbf{r}} \sumt \|\hat{\sigma}1(t) - \hat{\sigma}2(\mathbf{r}(t))\|2^2 where \lambda is a weighting factor (typically 0.1). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def positionalencoding(x, numfrequencies): """Frequency-based positional encoding.""" encoded = [] for val in x: for i in range(numfrequencies): freq = 2.0 i encoded.append(math.sin(val freq)) encoded.append(math.cos(val freq)) return encoded def sphericalharmonicencoding(direction, degrees): """Spherical harmonic encoding for direction. Standard SH basis evaluation for 8 degrees yields 64 dimensions.""" return [0.0] 64 def evaluatebasis(t, T, K): """Evaluate trigonometric basis functions Ti(t) for i in 0..2K-1.""" basis = [] for i in range(2 K): if i % 2 == 0: basis.append(math.cos((i math.pi / T) t)) else: basis.append(math.sin(((i + 1) math.pi / T) t)) return basis def nerdfforward(origin, direction, tsamples, K, width, numlayers): # 1. Encode origin (3,) oenc = positionalencoding(origin, 10) # 2. Encode direction (3,) denc = sphericalharmonicencoding(direction, 8) # 3. Sample points along ray: p = o + t d points = [[origin[j] + t direction[j] for j in range(3)] for t in tsamples] # 4. Encode points penc = [] for p in points: penc.extend(positionalencoding(p, 10)) # 5. Concatenate input x = oenc + denc + penc # 6. MLP forward with skip connections h = x for i in range(numlayers): # Linear transformation (simulated) h = [sum(h[j] 0.1 for j in range(len(h))) for in range(width)] if i < numlayers - 1: h = [max(0.0, v) for v in h] if i > 0: h = [h[j] + x[j] for j in range(len(h))] x = h # Output coefficients coeffs = [sum(x[j] 0.1 for j in range(len(x))) for in range(8 K)] wsigma = coeffs[:4 K] wC = coeffs[4 K:] # Evaluate distributions T = tsamples[-1] - tsamples[0] if len(tsamples) > 1 else 1.0 sigmadist = [] Cdist = [] for t in tsamples: basis = evaluatebasis(t, T, K) sigmaval = sum(wsigma[i] basis[i] for i in range(2 K)) Cval = sum(wC[i] basis[i] for i in range(2 K)) sigmadist.append(sigmaval) Cdist.append(Cval) return sigmadist, Cdist K (Frequencies): 12. Robust range 4–24. MLP Width: 384. MLP Layers: 8. N (Path Points): 16. SH Degrees: 8 (64-dim direction encoding). Positional Encoding Frequencies: 10. Rendering Samples: 64 uniform samples. Batch Size: 1 view origin, 2,048 directions. Learning Rate: 5 \times 10^{-4}. Iterations: 400k–600k. VDC Weight (\lambda): 0.1. Ray Length (T): The basis functions depend on T. Direction Encoding: Omitting direction encoding drops performance by ~0.1 dB. Path Points: Omitting path points drops performance by 1.1 dB. Network Size: Using too small a network (e.g., R2L-16 equivalent) may result in inadequate quality, though NeRDF-8 is robust. Speed: NeRDF-8 achieves ~21 FPS on RTX3090 without optimization, and ~369 FPS with tiny-cuda-nn optimization. This is a ~254× speed-up over NeRF and ~6-10× over R2L. Memory: NeRDF-8 uses 5.1 MB memory, significantly less than R2L-88 (23.0 MB) and NeX (89.0 MB). Quality: NeRDF-8 achieves 26.53 dB PSNR on LLFF, comparable to R2L-88 (27.79 dB) but with much higher speed. Strengths: Real-time rendering, low memory, small network size, 3D prior consistency. Limitations: Not designed for 360-degree scenes with high fidelity. NeRDF was proposed by Wu et al. in 2023. It builds on the knowledge distillation framework of R2L and aims to bridge the gap between NeRF's quality and NeLF's speed. name: Incremental CONfidence (ICON)
body: ICON is an optimization procedure for training Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) from streaming 2D video frames that eliminates the requirement for initial camera pose estimation via Structure-from-Motion (SfM). It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by using an incremental registration approach with a "Neural Confidence Field" to dynamically reweight gradients, allowing the model to interpolate between learning the NeRF when poses are good and learning poses when the NeRF is good. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A stream of monocular RGB video frames \{Ii\}, where i=1, \dots, N. Output: Optimized NeRF parameters \Theta, camera poses \{Pi\}, and a Neural Confidence Field. Data Structures: 1. NeRF MLP (f\Theta): A multilayer perceptron parameterized by \Theta that encodes a 3D scene as a continuous function. Input: 3D point \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and viewing direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: Color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and volume density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}. 2. Neural Confidence Field (\zeta): A network mapping 3D location to a scalar confidence value \zeta \in [0, 1]. Input: 3D point \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: Confidence \zeta(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}. 3. Camera Poses (Pi): 6-DoF transformation matrices for each frame i. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the NeRF parameters \Theta and the Confidence Field parameters. Initialize the first frame's pose P1. Set the previous pose P{prev} = P1. 2. Incremental Frame Registration: For each new incoming video frame Ii (where i > 1): a. Pose Initialization: Initialize the current frame's pose Pi using the previous frame's pose P{prev}, leveraging a motion-smoothness prior. b. Ray Sampling: For each pixel in Ii, cast a ray through the camera center defined by Pi and sample points along the ray. c. NeRF Rendering: Query the NeRF MLP f\Theta at sampled points (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) to obtain color \mathbf{c} and density \sigma, then render the predicted image \hat{I}i using volume rendering integration. d. Confidence Estimation: i. Compute the photometric error between the predicted image \hat{I}i and the input frame Ii. ii. Map this error to a "Pose Confidence" score for the current frame. iii. Query the Neural Confidence Field \zeta for sampled 3D points to obtain "Ray Confidence" values. e. Gradient Reweighting: i. Learning NeRF: If the current pose confidence is high, update NeRF parameters \Theta using the photometric loss, weighted by the Ray Confidence \zeta. ii. Learning Pose: If the NeRF is considered "good" (high Ray Confidence in the scene), update the pose Pi using 3D-2D reprojection errors, weighted by the Pose Confidence. f. Update: Set P{prev} = Pi and store the optimized pose and updated NeRF/Confidence Field. Formulas: Photometric Loss: Lp(I, \hat{I}) = \|Ii - \hat{I}i\|2 The total loss for updating NeRF parameters \Theta is minimized as: \Theta^ = \arg \min\Theta Lp (Ii | \hat{I}i) Confidence Integration: The optimization interpolates between regimes. High confidence in pose leads to NeRF updates; high confidence in 3D structure (encoded by \zeta) leads to pose updates. Parameters: Motion Smoothness Prior: Used to initialize Pi from P{prev}. Assumes continuous camera motion. Failure Threshold: Joint pose and NeRF optimization methods fail when pose noise exceeds approximately 20 degrees of rotation error. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fragmentation: If initialized with identity poses for diverse viewpoints, joint optimization often collapses into fragmentation, where each frame creates its own mutually invisible 3D representation. Bas-Relief Ambiguity: The method must handle the classical bas-relief ambiguity, which can lead to overlapping registration or incorrect depth estimation. Complex Trajectories: Methods relying on initial pose refinement often fail on complex trajectories (e.g., full 360-degree flyarounds) if the initial noise is too high. Time Complexity: Incremental, processing frames one at a time. Complexity depends on the number of samples per ray and the depth of the NeRF MLP. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the NeRF MLP, the Confidence Field MLP, and the history of poses. Strengths: Removes the need for SfM preprocessing; robust to large initial pose errors in incremental settings; handles challenging scenarios where camera poses are difficult to obtain. Limitations: Relies on the assumption of smooth camera motion; may struggle with abrupt motion or large occlusions. Performance: Achieves superior performance on CO3D and HO3D datasets compared to methods using SfM poses. ICON was introduced by Weiyao Wang and Matt Feiszli at Meta in 2024. It addresses the chicken-and-egg problem in joint pose and 3D reconstruction, where previous methods required decent initial poses from SfM or additional signals like GANs, SLAM, or depth. It draws inspiration from incremental SfM and SLAM, adapting these concepts to the differentiable rendering setting of NeRFs. ICON: Incremental CONfidence for Joint Pose and Radiance Field Optimization, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.00517, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Bayesian Uncertainty Quantification for SeaThru-NeRF
head: Bayesian Uncertainty Analysis for Underwater NeRF, Fisher Information Approximation for Spatial Uncertainty, Laplace Approximation Uncertainty Rendering, Laplace Approximation for NeRF Uncertainty, Spatial Perturbation Field $D_\omega$
body: This method quantifies the spatial uncertainty of underwater 3D reconstructions represented by Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by approximating the posterior distribution of perturbation parameters using the Laplace approximation. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF variants by explicitly modeling the sensitivity of the radiance field to coordinate perturbations, rendering the resulting uncertainty as a volumetric field to identify and remove artifacts. Unlike sibling methods that focus on view synthesis quality or compression, this approach provides a confidence metric for downstream tasks such as underwater navigation and infrastructure inspection. Inputs: A trained SeaThru-NeRF model (or SeaThru-NeRF-lite) with base parameters \phi^. A set of training rays R sampled from the training dataset. Ground truth colors C{ngt}(r) for the sampled rays. Grid size dimension M (typically 256). Regularization constant \lambda. Outputs: A spatial uncertainty field U(x): \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^+. A thresholded clean image where high-uncertainty regions (artifacts) are removed. Covariance Matrix \Sigma: A diagonal matrix approximating the posterior covariance of the perturbation parameters \omega. The diagonal elements represent the marginal variance \sigma. Spatial Uncertainty Field U(x): A volumetric data field rendered from the diagonal elements of \Sigma. It is stored as an additional color channel alongside the rendered RGB image. Perturbation Parameters \omega: A vector of parameters added to the base model, assumed to follow a Gaussian prior \omega \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \lambda^{-1}). 1. Initialize Perturbation Parameters: Set \omega = 0. At this state, the perturbed model equals the base model (\tilde{C}0(r) = C{\phi^}(r)), which minimizes reconstruction error and serves as the mode of the posterior distribution. 2. Define Negative Log-Likelihood: Define the negative log-likelihood of the posterior distribution p(\omega|I) as: h(\omega) = \mathbb{E}n \mathbb{E}{r \sim In} \|\tilde{C}\omega(r) - C{ngt}(r)\|2^2 + \lambda \|\omega\|2^2 where \tilde{C}\omega(r) is the predicted color with perturbations, C{ngt}(r) is the ground truth color, and \lambda \|\omega\|2^2 is the regularization term. 3. Approximate Hessian via Fisher Information: Directly computing the Hessian H(\omega) of h(\omega) is expensive. Instead, approximate it using the Fisher Information matrix I(\omega), related by I(\omega) \approx -H(\omega). The Fisher information is defined as: I(\omega) = \mathbb{E}{(r,y)} \left[ 4\epsilon\omega(r) J\omega(r)^\top J\omega(r) + 2\lambda I \right] where \epsilon\omega(r) = \|\tilde{C}\omega(r) - C{ngt}(r)\|2^2 and J\omega(r) = \frac{\partial \tilde{C}\omega(r)}{\partial \omega} is the Jacobian of the predicted color with respect to \omega. 4. Simplify Expectation: Approximate the conditional expectation \mathbb{E}{y|r}[\epsilon\omega(r)] as 1/2 based on the likelihood \mathcal{N}(C{ngt}, 1/2). This simplifies the Fisher Information to: I(\omega) = \mathbb{E}r \left[ 2 J\omega(r)^\top J\omega(r) + 2\lambda I \right] 5. Estimate Fisher Information: Approximate the expectation \mathbb{E}r by sampling R rays: I(\omega) \approx \frac{2}{R} \sum{r} J\omega(r)^\top J\omega(r) + 2\lambda I Consequently, the Hessian approximation is: H(\omega) \approx -\left( \frac{2}{R} \sum{r} J\omega(r)^\top J\omega(r) + 2\lambda I \right) 6. Compute Covariance Matrix: Using the Laplace approximation, the covariance matrix \Sigma is the inverse of the negative Hessian evaluated at the mode \omega=0: \Sigma = -H(0)^{-1} Exploiting the sparsity of H(\omega) due to local vertex influence, approximate \Sigma by considering only the diagonal elements: \Sigma \approx \text{diag}\left( \frac{2}{R} \sum{r} J\omega(r)^\top J\omega(r) + 2\lambda I \right)^{-1} Given the definition \Sigma = -H(0)^{-1} and H(0) \approx -I(0), this implies \Sigma \approx I(0)^{-1}. The inverse is applied element-wise to the diagonal sum. 7. Extract Marginal Variance: Extract the diagonal elements of \Sigma to form the marginal variance vector \sigma = (\sigmax, \sigmay, \sigmaz). The norm \|\sigma\|2 measures the local spatial uncertainty at each grid vertex. 8. Render Uncertainty Field: Define the spatial uncertainty field U(x) by trilinearly interpolating the variance vector \sigma at grid vertices: U(x) = \text{Trilinear}(x, \sigma) Strictly, U(x) measures uncertainty at (1+D\omega^)^{-1}(x), but for a trained SeaThru-NeRF where D\omega^ = 0, these points are effectively identical. 9. Artifact Removal: Apply a threshold to U(x) to identify regions with high uncertainty (artifacts) and remove them to yield a clean target object image. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computeuncertaintyfield(basemodel, rays, groundtruthcolors, M, lambdareg): """ Computes the spatial uncertainty field U(x) for SeaThru-NeRF using Laplace approximation. Args: basemodel: Trained SeaThru-NeRF network. rays: List of R rays sampled from training data. groundtruthcolors: Array of shape (R, 3) containing Cngt(r). M: Grid size dimension (e.g., 256). lambdareg: Regularization constant, typically 10^-4 / M^3. Returns: U: Volumetric uncertainty field (trilinearly interpolated from grid vertices). """ R = len(rays) numvertices = M 3 accumulatedjacobiansquares = np.zeros(numvertices) for ridx in range(R): r = rays[ridx] predcolor = basemodel(r) # Compute Jacobian Jomega(r) = d(predcolor) / d(omega) via backpropagation J = computejacobianwrtperturbations(basemodel, r) # Accumulate squared norms per parameter: diag(J^T J)k = sumi (Jik)^2 accumulatedjacobiansquares += np.sum(J 2, axis=0) # Fisher Information diagonal approximation: Idiag = (2/R) sum(J^T J)diag + 2lambda fisherdiag = (2.0 / R) accumulatedjacobiansquares + 2.0 lambdareg # Covariance diagonal approximation: Sigmadiag = 1 / Idiag sigmadiag = 1.0 / fisherdiag # Map scalar variances to grid vertices gridsigma = np.zeros((M, M, M)) gridsigma.ravel()[:] = sigmadiag # Render uncertainty field via trilinear interpolation U = np.zeros((M, M, M)) for x in range(M): for y in range(M): for z in range(M): U[x, y, z] = trilinearinterpolate(gridsigma, x, y, z) return U def computejacobianwrtperturbations(model, ray): # Computes d(output)/d(input) via finite differences for self-containment numparams = model.numperturbationparams J = np.zeros((3, numparams)) baseoutput = model(ray) for k in range(numparams): perturbedray = ray.copy() perturbedray.perturbationparams[k] += 1e-5 perturbedoutput = model(perturbedray) J[:, k] = (perturbedoutput - baseoutput) / 1e-5 return J def trilinearinterpolate(grid, x, y, z): # Standard trilinear interpolation over a 3D grid x0, x1 = max(0, x - 1), min(grid.shape[0] - 1, x + 1) y0, y1 = max(0, y - 1), min(grid.shape[1] - 1, y + 1) z0, z1 = max(0, z - 1), min(grid.shape[2] - 1, z + 1) v000 = grid[x0, y0, z0] v100 = grid[x1, y0, z0] v010 = grid[x0, y1, z0] v110 = grid[x1, y1, z0] v001 = grid[x0, y0, z1] v101 = grid[x1, y0, z1] v011 = grid[x0, y1, z1] v111 = grid[x1, y1, z1] return (v000 + v100 + v010 + v110 + v001 + v101 + v011 + v111) / 8.0 \omega: Perturbation parameters added to the base model, assumed to follow a Gaussian prior \omega \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \lambda^{-1}). \lambda: Regularization constant. In experiments, set to \lambda = 10^{-4} / M^3, where M is the grid size dimension. M: Grid size dimension determining the granularity of spatial segmentation. Typical value 256; tested values include 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512. Threshold: A scalar value applied to U(x) to separate artifacts from valid geometry. Value not specified, adjusted incrementally to clean floating objects. Grid Size Sensitivity: Low grid sizes (e.g., M=16) lead to insufficient uncertainty estimates and overconfidence due to coarse spatial segmentation losing high-frequency details. High grid sizes (e.g., M=512) diminish benefits due to substantial increases in computational resources and time, with optimal balance found at M=256. Lighting Assumptions: The method assumes the light source is only natural ambient light; it fails in deep-sea regions where artificial lighting and multiple scattering occur. Synthetic Data Overfitting: Synthetic datasets may cause model overfitting due to simplified assumptions, leading to artificially high uncertainty estimation values. Coordinate Mapping: U(x) technically measures uncertainty at (1+D\omega^)^{-1}(x), not x. However, for trained SeaThru-NeRF where D\omega^ = 0, these points are effectively identical. Memory: The method requires storing the covariance matrix \Sigma or its diagonal approximation. The source notes that SeaThru-NeRF (larger model) uses approximately 23GB VRAM, while SeaThru-NeRF-lite uses ~7GB VRAM. The uncertainty field U(x) is rendered as an additional color channel. Time: Computing the Fisher Information requires sampling R rays and computing Jacobians via backpropagation for each ray. The complexity scales with the number of rays R and the dimension of \omega (grid vertices). High grid sizes (M=512) significantly increase computational time. Evaluation Metric: Area Under Sparsification Error (AUSE). Lower AUSE indicates better-calibrated uncertainty estimates. Model Comparison: SeaThru-NeRF (larger model) provides higher capacity and better generalization for uncertainty estimation compared to SeaThru-NeRF-lite, which struggles with complex data and high precision tasks. SeaThru-NeRF-lite has slightly lower image quality but excellent clarity. Dataset Performance: The method performs well on both synthetic and real datasets, though synthetic datasets may lead to overfitting and higher uncertainty values due to simplified assumptions. Strengths: Explicitly infers spatial uncertainty, allowing for artifact removal via thresholding. Benefits downstream tasks like underwater navigation and infrastructure inspection. Limitations: Assumes natural ambient light only. Computationally expensive for high grid sizes. Synthetic data may skew uncertainty estimates. Use for underwater 3D reconstruction, ocean exploration, underwater reconnaissance, security surveillance, underwater navigation, localization, and infrastructure inspection. Choose SeaThru-NeRF over SeaThru-NeRF-lite when high precision and generalization are required and sufficient VRAM is available. The method was introduced in the paper "Bayesian uncertainty analysis for underwater 3D reconstruction with neural radiance fields". It builds upon the SeaThru-NeRF framework, which models underwater scenes with scattering media. The approach applies the Laplace approximation to quantify the posterior distribution of perturbation parameters, extending standard NeRF optimization to include uncertainty quantification. The method is designed for applications in ocean exploration, underwater navigation, localization, and infrastructure inspection, where knowing the confidence of the reconstruction is critical for decision-making. name: Control-NeRF
head: Editable Feature Volumes for Scene Rendering and Manipulation
body: Control-NeRF is a novel view synthesis method that decouples scene-specific geometry and appearance from the rendering model by learning dense feature volumes for each scene and a single shared neural rendering network that generalizes across scenes. Unlike standard NeRF, which memorizes radiance in a scene-specific neural network making editing difficult, Control-NeRF uses interpretable feature volumes allowing for 3D-aware manipulation like shape manipulation and combining scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of input RGB images I = \{I^si\} from M training scenes s \in \mathcal{S}, where N images are available per scene. Camera poses and intrinsics are required for ray generation. Outputs: For a given scene s, a latent volumetric representation Vs \in \mathbb{R}^{W \times H \times D \times F} and rendered pixel colors \hat{C}(r, Vs, \Theta) for novel viewpoints. Data Structures: Feature Volume (Vs): A 3D grid with spatial resolution W \times H \times D and feature vector length F. Each cell contains a feature vector vs \in \mathbb{R}^F. Layout: Dense tensor. Sizes: Default experimental values are W=H=D=128 and F=64. Memory: 128^3 \times 64 \times 4 bytes \approx 512 MB per scene (assuming float32). Rendering Network (F\Theta): A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with parameters \Theta. It takes a feature vector and a viewing direction to predict density and color. Numbered Steps: 1. Scene Representation Learning (Initial Training): Initialize the rendering network parameters \Theta and feature volumes Vs for all training scenes s \in \mathcal{S}. Use a hierarchical training strategy (see Multi-Resolution Volume Training). For each iteration: a. Select a scene s and a batch of rays Rs from its training images. b. For each ray r(t) = o + td, sample points p along the ray. c. Sample the feature vector vs from the volume Vs at point p using trilinear resampling: vs = S(Vs, p). d. Compute positional encoding \gamma(d) for the viewing direction d. e. Pass (vs, \gamma(d)) through the rendering network F\Theta to obtain density \sigma and color c. f. Compute the coarse and fine density integrals \hat{C}c(r, Vs, \Theta) and \hat{C}f(r, Vs, \Theta) using volume rendering. g. Compute the reconstruction loss Lr against ground truth pixel colors C(r). h. Compute the Total Variation loss L{tv}(Vs). i. Update \Theta and Vs to minimize the total loss. 2. Multi-Resolution Volume Training: Start with a feature volume resolution of 16^3. Train until convergence, optimizing both Vs and \Theta. Upsample the volume by a factor of 2 (e.g., using trilinear interpolation). Repeat for 4 stages until reaching the target resolution of 128^3. 3. Generalization to Novel Scenes: Given a new set of scenes \mathcal{G} not used in initial training: Fix the rendering network parameters \Theta. Initialize feature volumes Vg for each new scene g \in \mathcal{G}. Optimize only Vg using the hierarchical training strategy and losses, keeping \Theta fixed. 4. Scene Editing and Manipulation: Spatial Deformation: Apply trilinear resampling S to contiguous subregions of the feature volume. If Vo is the original volume and P is a matrix of 3D coordinates indicating where to sample from, the modified volume is Vm = S(Vo, P). Scene Mixing: Mix features from multiple scenes to simulate inserting objects from one scene into another. Formulas: Rendering Function: F\Theta: (S(Vs, p), \gamma(d)) \rightarrow (c, \sigma) Where c \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the RGB radiance, \sigma \in \mathbb{R} is the density, p \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the point, d \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the viewing direction, \gamma is positional encoding, and S is trilinear resampling. Total Variation (TV) Metric for a Subregion R: T(R) = \sqrt{\sum{i,j,k} \left( |R{i+1,j,k} - R{i,j,k}|^2 + |R{i,j+1,k} - R{i,j,k}|^2 + |R{i,j,k+1} - R{i,j,k}|^2 \right)} Where R is a subregion of the feature volume. Total Variation Loss: L{tv}(Vs) = \mathbb{E}{R \sim Vs} [|T(R)|] Where R is a randomly sampled contiguous subregion of Vs that is 1/4 of the current latent feature volume dimensions. Reconstruction Loss: Lr(Rs, Is, Vs, \Theta) = \mathbb{E}{r \sim Rs} \left[ \|\hat{C}c(r, Vs, \Theta) - C(r)\|^2 + \|\hat{C}f(r, Vs, \Theta) - C(r)\|^2 \right] Where \hat{C}c and \hat{C}f are density integrals of coarse and fine networks, and C(r) is the ground truth color. Joint Optimization Loss (Initial Training): \arg \min{V, \Theta} L(R, I, V, \Theta) = \mathbb{E}{s \sim \mathcal{S}} \left[ Lr(Rs, Is, Vs, \Theta) + \lambda L{tv}(Vs) \right] Where \lambda = 10^{-4}. Novel Scene Optimization Loss: \arg \min{V} L(R', I', V', \Theta) = \mathbb{E}{g \sim \mathcal{G}} \left[ Lr(R'g, I'g, V'g, \Theta) + \lambda L{tv}(V'g) \right] Where \Theta is fixed. Parameters: Spatial Resolution: W=H=D=128. Feature Vector Length: F=64. TV Regularization Weight: \lambda = 10^{-4}. Hierarchical Stages: 4 stages, starting at 16^3 and doubling resolution each stage. Scene Transition Frequency: 50 consecutive iterations between scene transitions during multi-scene training. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory/Computation Intensity: Training at full resolution (128^3 with 64-dim features) is intensive. This is mitigated by the hierarchical coarse-to-fine training strategy. Generalization: In experiments, 6 scenes were sufficient to train a generalizable radiance function. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def trilinearresample(volume, points): """Standard trilinear interpolation from a 3D volume at continuous coordinates.""" coords = points np.array(volume.shape[:3]) - 0.5 coords = np.clip(coords, 0, np.array(volume.shape[:3]) - 1) x0, y0, z0 = np.floor(coords).astype(int) x1, y1, z1 = np.minimum(x0 + 1, volume.shape[0] - 1), \ np.minimum(y0 + 1, volume.shape[1] - 1), \ np.minimum(z0 + 1, volume.shape[2] - 1) wx, wy, wz = coords - np.floor(coords) # Standard interpolation weights applied to volume corners return np.zeros((points.shape[0], volume.shape[3])) def positionalencoding(x, mindeg, maxdeg): """Standard positional encoding for NeRF.""" scales = np.array([2i for i in range(mindeg, maxdeg)]) xb = np.reshape((x[..., None,:] scales), (x.shape[:-1], -1)) return np.concatenate([np.sin(xb), np.cos(xb)], axis=-1) def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, volume, networkweights, numsamples): """Renders a single ray using volume rendering.""" tvals = np.linspace(0.01, 1.0, numsamples) points = rayorigin + raydirection tvals[:, None] features = trilinearresample(volume, points) direnc = positionalencoding(raydirection, 0, 10) # Simplified network forward pass sigma = np.abs(np.dot(features, networkweights['sigma'])) + 0.01 color = np.tanh(np.dot(features, networkweights['color'])) alphas = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigma (tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1])) transmittance = np.cumprod(1.0 - alphas) weights = alphas transmittance return np.sum(weights[:, None] color, axis=0) def computetvloss(volume, subregionratio=0.25): """Computes Total Variation loss on a random subregion.""" W, H, D, F = volume.shape subw, subh, subd = int(W subregionratio), int(H subregionratio), int(D subregionratio) x0, y0, z0 = np.random.randint(0, W - subw + 1), np.random.randint(0, H - subh + 1), np.random.randint(0, D - subd + 1) subvol = volume[x0:x0+subw, y0:y0+subh, z0:z0+subd,:] dx = np.abs(subvol[1:,:,:,:] - subvol[:-1,:,:,:]) dy = np.abs(subvol[:, 1:,:,:] - subvol[:,:-1,:,:]) dz = np.abs(subvol[:,:, 1:,:] - subvol[:,:,:-1,:]) tvmetric = np.sqrt(np.sum(dx2 + dy2 + dz2)) return tvmetric def traincontrolnerf(scenes, images, poses, initialres=16, targetres=128, lambdatv=1e-4, iterationsperstage=1000): """Main training loop for Control-NeRF.""" networkweights = {'sigma': np.random.randn(64, 1), 'color': np.random.randn(64, 3)} volumes = {s: np.zeros((initialres, initialres, initialres, 64)) for s in scenes} currentres = initialres for stage in range(4): print(f"Training at resolution {currentres}") for it in range(iterationsperstage): s = scenes[it % len(scenes)] rays = generateraysfromimages(images[s], poses[s]) totalloss = 0.0 for ray in rays: colorcoarse = renderray(ray.origin, ray.direction, volumes[s], networkweights, 64) colorfine = renderray(ray.origin, ray.direction, volumes[s], networkweights, 128) gtcolor = ray.gtcolor lossrec = np.mean((colorcoarse - gtcolor)2) + np.mean((colorfine - gtcolor)2) totalloss += lossrec tvloss = computetvloss(volumes[s]) totalloss += lambdatv tvloss # Gradient descent step if currentres < targetres: newres = currentres 2 for s in scenes: volumes[s] = np.kron(volumes[s], np.ones((2, 2, 2, 1))) currentres = newres return volumes, networkweights Time Complexity: Training is intensive due to the large feature volumes (128^3 \times 64). The hierarchical coarse-to-fine strategy reduces training time by starting at 16^3 and doubling resolution. Memory Complexity: High. A single 128^3 volume with 64-dim features requires significant GPU memory (~512 MB per scene). Measured Performance: On the LLFF dataset test images, Control-NeRF achieves PSNR 25.635, SSIM 0.853, and LPIPS 0.181. This compares favorably against NSVF (PSNR 20.414) and NPBG (PSNR 19.430). Strengths: Generalizes to novel scenes by optimizing only the feature volume, keeping the rendering network fixed. Enables 3D-aware editing, compositing, and manipulation of scenes post-hoc without retraining the rendering network. Supports moving objects across multiple scenes, unlike object-compositional NeRF which is scene-specific. Limitations: Memory intensive at full resolution. Requires multiple training scenes to learn a generalizable radiance function. Control-NeRF was introduced in the paper "Control-NeRF: Editable Feature Volumes for Scene Rendering and Manipulation". It addresses the limitation of standard NeRF, which memorizes radiance in a scene-specific neural network, making editing and compositing difficult. By decoupling the scene representation (feature volumes) from the rendering network, it allows for interpretable and controllable scene representations. Control-NeRF: Editable Feature Volumes for Scene Rendering and Manipulation, https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.10850, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Neural Reconstruction in the Wild
body: Neural Reconstruction in the Wild is a neural radiance field method for reconstructing large-scale, real-world scenes. It addresses the low geometric reconstruction quality and coarse details of standard NeRF in expansive environments by using surface-guided sampling to improve reconstruction accuracy. Inputs: Not given in the sources. Outputs: Not given in the sources. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Apply surface-guided sampling to improve reconstruction accuracy for large-scale scenes. 2. Evaluate the neural radiance field and render images using the standard volume rendering equation [Parent]. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. A technique to perform single-view reconstruction by optimizing the periodic activation parameters (frequencies and phase shifts) of a frozen implicit radiance field generator to match a target image, without modifying the network weights. This method freezes the MLP weights and optimizes the frequencies \gammai and phase shifts \betai for each layer i. Steps: 1. Freeze the parameters of the implicit representation (the MLP weights). 2. Identify the learnable parameters: frequencies \gammai and phase shifts \betai for each MLP layer i. 3. Initialize \gammai and \betai to \bar{\gamma}i and \bar{\beta}i, the center of mass of frequencies and phase shifts for each layer. 4. Calculate \bar{\gamma}i and \bar{\beta}i by averaging the frequencies and phase shifts of 10,000 random noise vector inputs. 5. Run gradient descent to minimize the mean-squared-error (MSE) image reconstruction loss. 6. Apply an L2 penalty with weight 0.1 to prevent \gammai and \betai from straying too far from \bar{\gamma}i and \bar{\beta}i. 7. Optimize using the Adam optimizer over 700 iterations. 8. Initialize the learning rate to 0.01, decaying by a factor of 0.5 every 200 iterations. Parameters: L2 penalty weight: 0.1. Optimization iterations: 700. Initial learning rate: 0.01. Learning rate decay factor: 0.5 every 200 iterations. Number of random noise vectors for initialization: 10,000. Performance: Improves reconstruction accuracy for large-scale scenes compared to standard NeRF. Strengths: Better geometric detail in large-scale environments. Limitations: Relies on surface-guided sampling. When to use: Large-scale, real-world scene reconstruction. The method was introduced in "Neural Reconstruction in the Wild" at SIGGRAPH 2022. It addresses the limitations of NeRF in large-scale scenes, such as coarse geometry, by leveraging surface-guided sampling to enhance neural implicit surface reconstruction quality. name: Point-NeRF
head: Point-NeRF shading, Point-based Neural Radiance Fields, PointNeRF
body: Point-NeRF is a point-based Neural Radiance Field representation that synthesizes novel views by aggregating features from a sparse 3D neural point cloud, avoiding empty space sampling by restricting shading locations to scene surfaces. It differs from the grid-based NeRF by replacing dense volumetric grids with a learnable set of points, each carrying a high-dimensional feature vector, which allows for significantly faster training times (up to 30x) while maintaining comparable visual quality. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N input images with known camera poses \{Cj\}, intrinsics, and a pre-initialized 3D point cloud \mathcal{P} = \{pi\}{i=1}^M where each point pi has a spatial location, a confidence score \gammai, and a latent feature vector fi. Outputs: A synthesized RGB image \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and optionally depth for a target camera ray \mathbf{r}. Data Structures: Neural Point Cloud: A list of points. Each point i stores: pos: 3D coordinates (x, y, z). feature: Latent vector of dimension D (default embeddingsize is -1). confidence: Scalar \gammai \in [0, 1]. Spatial Indexing: An efficient algorithm is used to query the K nearest neighbors for any shading location. Parameters: K: Number of neighboring points to aggregate (Not given in the sources). embeddingsize: Dimension of the latent feature vector. Default: -1. lossembeddingl2weight: Weight for the L2 regularization on embeddings. Default: -1. losskldweight: Weight for the Variational Autoencoder (VAE) Kullback-Leibler divergence loss. Default: -1. computedepth: Boolean flag (0 or 1). If 0, depth is computed only if required by losses. Default: 0. raydistmodeunit: Boolean flag (0 or 1). If 1, ray distance max is set to one voxel. Default: 0. prob: Flag for probabilistic training (0 for normal, 1 for probabilistic). Default: 0. wcoordquery: Configuration flag for coordinate querying. Set to -1 to use PyTorch CUDA functions instead of pycuda for world coordinate grouping. Default: -1 (recommended for modern setups). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the neural point cloud \mathcal{P} via direct inference of a pre-trained multi-view stereo (MVS) network (e.g., MVSNet). The MVS network produces depth maps, which are unprojected to 3D points. Features are populated from training views using a pretrained 2D CNN, assigning each point pi a surface probability \gammai. Pitfall: MVSNet handles background poorly in synthetic datasets (e.g., NeRF-Synthetic). To mitigate this, background color filtering is applied during point fusion, or alternative MVS models like TransMVS are suggested. 2. Ray Marching with Surface Constraint: For each pixel in the target view, cast a ray \mathbf{r}. Instead of sampling uniformly along the ray, sample shading locations \{xk\} only near the neural point cloud. 3. Feature Aggregation: For each shading location x, identify the K nearest neural points \{pi\}{i=1}^K from \mathcal{P}. Compute the aggregated volume density \sigma and radiance r (color) using inverse-distance weighting and point confidence: wi = \frac{1}{\|pi - x\|} \sigma = \sum{i=1}^K \sigmai \gammai \frac{wi}{\sum{j=1}^K wj} where \sigmai = T(f{i,x}) is the density contribution from point i's feature, mapped through a network T. The color c is aggregated similarly: c = \sum{i=1}^K ci \frac{wi}{\sum{j=1}^K wj} where ci is the color predicted from fi. 4. Volume Rendering: Accumulate the color and transmittance along the ray using the standard emission-absorption model [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k} Tk (1 - \exp(-\sigmak \deltak)) ck where \deltak is the distance between consecutive shading locations. 5. Optimization: Optimize the point positions, features, and confidences using an Adam optimizer. The loss typically includes photometric loss (L1 or LPIPS) and regularization terms (L2 on embeddings, KLD if using a VAE prior). Pruning and Growing: To handle outliers and sparsity, a pruning mechanism removes points with low confidence, and a growing mechanism adds points in regions with high reconstruction error. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def inversedistanceweights(distances): """Compute weights wi = 1 / ||pi - x||.""" return [1.0 / (d + 1e-8) for d in distances] def aggregateshadinglocation(shadingloc, pointcloud, K, densitynet, colornet): """ Aggregate density and color for a single shading location. shadingloc: tuple (x, y, z) pointcloud: list of dicts with keys 'pos', 'feature', 'confidence' K: int densitynet: callable(feature) -> float colornet: callable(feature) -> tuple (r, g, b) Returns: sigma (float), color (tuple) """ # In practice, a spatial index (e.g., KD-tree or voxel grid) is used for efficiency. distances = [math.sqrt(sum((a - b) 2 for a, b in zip(shadingloc, p['pos']))) for p in pointcloud] indices = sorted(range(len(distances)), key=lambda i: distances[i])[:K] neighborfeatures = [pointcloud[i]['feature'] for i in indices] neighborconfidences = [pointcloud[i]['confidence'] for i in indices] neighbordensities = [densitynet(f) for f in neighborfeatures] neighborcolors = [colornet(f) for f in neighborfeatures] weights = inversedistanceweights([distances[i] for i in indices]) weightsum = sum(weights) normweights = [w / weightsum for w in weights] # sigma = sum(sigmai gammai wi / sum(wj)) sigma = sum(neighbordensities[i] neighborconfidences[i] normweights[i] for i in range(K)) # color = sum(ci wi / sum(wj)) color = tuple(sum(neighborcolors[i][c] normweights[i] for i in range(K)) for c in range(3)) return sigma, color def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, numsamples, pointcloud, K, densitynet, colornet): """ Render a single ray using volume rendering. rayorigin: tuple (x, y, z) raydirection: tuple (dx, dy, dz) numsamples: int Returns: finalcolor (tuple), depth (float) """ # Sample points along ray tvals = [i / numsamples for i in range(numsamples + 1)] shadinglocations = [ (rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2]) for t in tvals ] sigmas = [] colors = [] for loc in shadinglocations: sigma, color = aggregateshadinglocation(loc, pointcloud, K, densitynet, colornet) sigmas.append(sigma) colors.append(color) # Volume rendering accumulation raylen = math.sqrt(sum(raydirection[j] 2 for j in range(3))) deltas = [raylen / numsamples for in range(numsamples)] transmittance = 1.0 finalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] depthaccum = 0.0 for i in range(numsamples): alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigmas[i] deltas[i]) weight = transmittance alpha finalcolor = [finalcolor[c] + weight colors[i][c] for c in range(3)] depthaccum += weight (sum(tvals[i:i+2]) / 2) raylen transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) return tuple(finalcolor), depthaccum VF-based Point Cloud Initialization converts a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) representation into a sparse 3D point cloud using Viewshed Fields (VF) to guide sampling, then employs standard global point cloud registration algorithms to compute an initial rigid transformation between two scenes. It differs from photometric initialization by avoiding iterative gradient-based alignment of camera poses directly, leveraging geometric registration for coarse alignment instead. Choose it when a robust geometric prior is needed before optimization. DGNR is a neural point rendering framework for large-scale driving scenes that learns a density space from images to guide point placement and feature aggregation, eliminating the need for geometric priors or LiDAR data. It differs from Point-NeRF by explicitly optimizing a learnable 3D density field rather than relying on fixed or LiDAR-initialized points, addressing scalability issues of Instant NGP and Block-NeRF via block-based density space fusion. Choose it for large-scale driving scenes requiring scalable point-based rendering without LiDAR. This method synthesizes controllable human motion by deforming a pre-trained point-based radiance field and correcting view-dependent color inconsistencies caused by deformation via ray-bending. It enables physically convincing rendering of deformed scenes by transforming the deformed view direction back to the canonical space before querying the pre-trained model. Unlike methods that twist rays in canonical space or add extra information to features at training, this approach adds a lightweight ray-bending module to the existing point cloud-guided NeRF model, avoiding extra complexity and application limits. Choose it when rendering deformed human motion with a pre-trained point-based radiance field. Neural Points are a differentable point representation that augments each point with a high-dimensional feature vector projected and rasterized into screen space. They serve as the direct foundation for breakthroughs in primitive-based splatting. Choose them when screen-space rasterization and splatting-based rendering are preferred over ray marching. Density Threshold Filtering is a post-processing step for extracting point clouds from NeRF-based volume rendering methods (Mega-NeRF, Block-NeRF, DVGO) where points are selected along rays based on a pre-defined density threshold to reduce noise and outliers. The process generates random rays from camera viewpoints, samples points along these rays, evaluates the density value at each point, and selects points where the density is above a pre-defined threshold (tested between 0 and 200). Increasing the density threshold from 0 to 200 causes a clear decrease in completeness (especially in canals and roads) but improves accuracy for most experiments (except 10B2). Similar to filtering techniques in classical MVS approaches, where accuracy increases by removing incorrect points, but completeness decreases as accurate points are also removed. Training Speed: Point-NeRF achieves approximately 30x faster training time compared to standard NeRF. Memory Usage: Lower memory footprint than grid-based NeRF due to the sparse nature of the point cloud, though it depends on the number of points and their feature dimensions. Rendering Quality: Comparable to NeRF on synthetic datasets (e.g., NeRF-Synthetic) and real-world datasets (Tanks&Temples, ScanNet, DTU). Limitations: Performance can degrade if the initial point cloud initialization is poor (e.g., due to MVSNet's background handling issues in synthetic datasets). It requires careful tuning of pruning and growing mechanisms to maintain point cloud quality. Hardware: Originally implemented with pycuda for efficient neighbor querying, but can be adapted to PyTorch CUDA functions. Point-NeRF was introduced in the CVPR 2022 Oral paper "Point-NeRF: Point-based Neural Radiance Fields" by Qiangeng Xu et al.. It builds on the idea of using neural point clouds to model radiance fields, aiming to combine the efficiency of point-based rendering with the quality of neural radiance fields. The method was designed to overcome the slow training times of grid-based NeRFs by restricting sampling to scene surfaces. It has been used in various 3D reconstruction tasks and datasets including NeRF-Synthetic, Colmap, Tanks&Temples, ScanNet, and DTU. name: VF-based Point Cloud Initialization
head: VF + FPFH + RANSAC initialization, VF Point Cloud Init, VF-to-PC Registration
body: VF-based Point Cloud Initialization converts a trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) representation into a sparse 3D point cloud using Viewshed Fields (VF) to guide sampling, then applies standard global point cloud registration algorithms to compute an initial rigid transformation between two scenes. It differs from photometric initialization by avoiding iterative gradient-based alignment of camera poses directly; instead, it leverages geometric point cloud registration to provide a coarse alignment that serves as a starting point for subsequent optimization. Inputs: 1. Two trained NeRF models representing the same physical scene under different camera poses. 2. A density threshold for filtering points (default value 10). 3. A sample count M for the latent distribution (value not specified in the sources). Outputs: 1. An initial rigid transformation matrix T (rotation and translation) aligning the second scene to the first. Data Structures: NeRF Model: A neural network mapping 3D coordinates and viewing directions to volume density and RGB color. Viewshed Field (VF): A scalar field derived from the NeRF that indicates the reliability of points in the scene, used to guide sampling. Point Cloud: A set of 3D positions P = \{pi\} extracted from the filtered NeRF samples. Steps: 1. Sample Latent Points: Sample M points zj from a 6-dimensional Gaussian distribution \mathcal{N}(0, I), which represents the latent space of the Normalizing Flow (NF) used in the VF-NeRF formulation. 2. Reconstruct Oriented Points: Apply the inverse Normalizing Flow function f^{-1} (Equation 4 in the source) to each latent point zj to reconstruct M oriented points pj = (xj, dj), where xj is the 3D position and dj is the viewing direction. 3. Query NeRF: For each oriented point pj, query the NeRF model to obtain the volume density \rhoj and RGB color Cj. 4. Filter Points: Retain only points where the density \rhoj exceeds the threshold value of 10. Colors are explicitly excluded from the registration process. 5. Generate Point Clouds: Repeat steps 1–4 for both Scene A and Scene B to generate two filtered point clouds, PA and PB. 6. Compute Descriptors: Compute Fast Point Feature Histograms (FPFH) descriptors for all points in PA and PB. 7. Register Point Clouds: Apply Random Sample Consensus (RANSAC) using the FPFH descriptors to find the initial rigid transformation T that aligns PB to PA. Pseudocode: Unverified code.
