Args: numsamples: Number of points to sample from the latent distribution. threshold: Density threshold for filtering points (default 10). Returns: T: Initial rigid transformation matrix (4x4) aligning B to A. """ # Step 1: Sample M points from 6D Gaussian latent distribution latentpoints = np.random.randn(numsamples, 6) # Step 2: Reconstruct oriented points using inverse Normalizing Flow (Eq 4) # finv(z) -> (x, d) orientedpointsa = inversenormalizingflow(latentpoints) # Scene A orientedpointsb = inversenormalizingflow(latentpoints) # Scene B # Step 3 & 4: Query NeRF and filter by density pointsa = [] for p in orientedpointsa: density = querynerfdensity(p) # Returns density if density > threshold: pointsa.append(p.position) pointsb = [] for p in orientedpointsb: density = querynerfdensity(p) if density > threshold: pointsb.append(p.position) # Step 6: Compute FPFH descriptors # Standard FPFH computation. Sources do not provide implementation details. descriptorsa = computefpfh(pointsa) descriptorsb = computefpfh(pointsb) # Step 7: RANSAC registration # Standard RANSAC registration. Sources do not provide implementation details. T = ransacregistration(pointsa, pointsb, descriptorsa, descriptorsb) return T def inversenormalizingflow(latentpoints): """Reconstructs oriented points (x, d) from latent space using inverse NF.""" # Standard inverse Normalizing Flow decoding (Equation 4 in source) return latentpoints # Placeholder for actual NF inverse mapping def querynerfdensity(orientedpoint): """Queries NeRF for density at a given oriented point.""" # Standard NeRF forward pass for density return 15.0 # Placeholder for actual NeRF query def computefpfh(points): """Computes FPFH descriptors for a set of 3D points.""" # Standard FPFH algorithm implementation return np.zeros((len(points), 33)) # Placeholder for actual descriptors def ransacregistration(pointssrc, pointstgt, descsrc, desctgt): """Finds rigid transformation using RANSAC and FPFH descriptors.""" # Standard RANSAC registration algorithm return np.eye(4) # Placeholder for actual transformation matrix Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Density Threshold: The threshold is fixed at 10 in the source. Color Usage: Colors are explicitly excluded from the registration process. Latent Sampling: The number of samples M is not specified in the sources. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Leverages robust, well-established point cloud registration algorithms. Limitations: Requires a trained NeRF first. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. VF-based Point Cloud Initialization was introduced by Segre and Avidan in the VF-NeRF paper. The method converts NeRF representations into point clouds using Viewshed Fields to guide sampling, then uses standard point cloud registration algorithms (specifically FPFH with RANSAC) to find the initial transformation. name: DGNR (Density-Guided Neural Point Rendering)
head: Density-Guided Neural Point Rendering
body: DGNR is a neural point rendering framework for large-scale driving scenes that learns a density space from images to guide the construction of a point-based renderer, eliminating the need for geometric priors or LiDAR data. It differs from its parent Point-NeRF by explicitly optimizing a learnable 3D density field to guide point placement and feature aggregation, rather than relying on fixed or LiDAR-initialized points, and it addresses the scalability issues of Instant NGP and Block-NeRF by using a block-based density space with fusion. Inputs: A set of input images I with known camera poses C (center o, direction d). No LiDAR or geometric priors are required. Outputs: A synthesized novel view image and a learned density space P. Data Structures: 1. Density Space (P): A learnable 3D representation of the scene geometry. The scene is divided into blocks to capture fine details. 2. Neural Density Features (\tau): Features associated with the density space, obtained via rasterization of P. 3. Network Parameters (\theta): Parameters of the neural renderer. 4. Encoding: Ray positions and directions are encoded using hashing and spherical harmonics (SH) encoding \gamma. Parameters: \gamma: Predefined spherical harmonics (SH) or positional encoding for ray encoding. S{patch}: Depth patch size, set to 8 \times 8. \lambda: Regularization weight, chosen to be 10^{-5}. Learning Rate: Initial 0.001, decaying to 10^{-6}. Optimizer: Adam. Steps: 1. Scene Partitioning: Divide the scene into blocks to enable the density space to capture fine details. 2. Density Space Optimization: Optimize the density space P using a density-based fusion module and geometric regularization. Density Fusion: Fuse multiple learnable density spaces (one per block) into a single density space via a density fusion module to ensure smoothness at boundaries. Regularization: Apply depth smoothing regularization to repair holes in the urban scene representation. 3. Feature Projection: Rasterize the 3D density space P to project it into neural density features \tau. 4. Differentiable Rendering: For a pixel, cast a ray r(u) = o + ud from camera center o through the pixel along direction d, with near plane un and far plane uf. Compute accumulated transmittance Q(u): Q(u) = \exp \left( - \int{un}^{u} \sigma\theta(r(s)) ds \right) Compute predicted color \hat{c}\theta(r) by alpha composition: \hat{c}\theta(r) = \int{un}^{uf} Q(u) \sigma\theta(r(u)) c\theta(r(u), d) du where \sigma\theta is the volume density and c\theta is the view-dependent color, both predicted by the neural network using parameters \theta and encoded ray inputs. 5. Loss Computation: Mean Squared Error (MSE): L{MSE}(\theta, Rr) = \sum{r \in Rr} \| \hat{c}\theta(r) - c(r) \|^2 where Rr is the set of input rays and c(r) is the ground truth color. Perceptual Loss: Compute perceptual loss L(\tau, \theta) between the synthetic novel view and ground truth image I{GT} using a pre-trained VGG layer: L(\tau, \theta) = L{VGG}(I{GT}, \psi(P, C, \tau, \theta)) where \psi represents the rendering process. 6. Update: Minimize the total loss using the Adam optimizer to update network parameters \theta and density space P. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def encoderay(raypos, raydir, gamma): """Encode ray position and direction using hashing and SH encoding.""" # Implementation of hashing and spherical harmonics encoding gamma return encodedinput def rasterizedensityspace(P): """Rasterize the 3D density space P to project into neural density features tau.""" # Rasterization logic return tau def renderray(rayo, rayd, un, uf, P, theta, gamma): """Render a single ray using differentiable volume rendering.""" # Sample points along ray r(u) = o + ud samples = samplealongray(rayo, rayd, un, uf) accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = 0.0 for u in samples: ru = rayo + u rayd encoded = encoderay(ru, rayd, gamma) # Predict density and color from neural network sigma = networkdensity(encoded, theta) color = networkcolor(encoded, rayd, theta) # Alpha composition transmittance = exp(-sigma deltau) # deltau is step size alpha = 1.0 - transmittance accumulatedcolor += alpha accumulatedtransmittance color accumulatedtransmittance = transmittance if accumulatedtransmittance < epsilon: break return accumulatedcolor def computeloss(renderedimage, groundtruthimage, P, C, tau, theta): """Compute MSE and Perceptual Loss.""" # MSE Loss mseloss = meansquarederror(renderedimage, groundtruthimage) # Perceptual Loss using VGG # psi represents the rendering function P, C, tau, theta -> image syntheticview = renderscene(P, C, tau, theta) perceptualloss = vggloss(groundtruthimage, syntheticview) return mseloss + perceptualloss def optimizedgnr(images, poses, blocks): """Main optimization loop.""" # Initialize density space P and network parameters theta P = initializedensityspace(blocks) theta = initializenetworkparams() for epoch in epochs: totalloss = 0 for image, pose in zip(images, poses): # 1. Density Fusion (if multiple blocks) Pfused = fusedensityspaces(P) # 2. Rasterize to get features tau = rasterizedensityspace(Pfused) # 3. Render renderedimage = renderimage(image, pose, Pfused, tau, theta) # 4. Compute Loss loss = computeloss(renderedimage, image, Pfused, pose, tau, theta) # 5. Backpropagate and Update updateparameters(theta, P, loss) totalloss += loss # Apply depth smoothing regularization applydepthsmoothing(P) return P, theta Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Large Scenes: Instant NGP faces challenges in synthesizing novel views of large scenes; DGNR addresses this by combining scene division with density-guided rendering. Sparse Regions: LiDAR point clouds fail to capture distant, elevated, and sky regions; DGNR overcomes this by learning point cloud representations through scene optimization from images. Outdoor/Sparse Scenes: 3D Gaussian Splatting may not be effective in outdoor areas, especially in sparse driving scenes. Boundary Artifacts: Without fusion, block-based methods produce blurred results with noticeable artifacts at boundaries; DGNR uses a density fusion module to ensure smoothness. A method for initializing point clouds using volume fusion, which DGNR avoids by learning density directly from images. See VF-based Point Cloud Initialization. Speed: DGNR is over 20 times faster than Block-NeRF (16.67 FPS vs 0.82 FPS) and LocalRF (16.67 FPS vs 0.13 FPS). Memory: DGNR has a compact model size of 237MB, compared to 4121MB for Block-NeRF and 4331MB for LocalRF. Performance: KITTI Road: VGG: 437.7, PSNR: 22.94, LPIPS: 0.1679, SSIM: 0.6857. Cityscapes: VGG: 177.5, PSNR: 32.63, LPIPS: 0.1033, SSIM: 0.9087. Waymo: VGG: 331.8, PSNR: 31.75, LPIPS: 0.2902, SSIM: 0.8892. Waymo (<200 frames): 127.0% reduction in LPIPS error and 78.8% reduction in VGG error compared to methods without geometric prior. Strengths: Real-time capable rendering, high-quality texture details, no need for LiDAR/geometric priors, effective in large-scale driving scenes. Limitations: Performance may vary in extremely sparse outdoor areas compared to methods with strong geometric priors (though DGNR handles this better than LiDAR-based methods). Spatial-warping-based methods (NGP, NGP+Cont, MERF) perform worse than scene division methods in long urban trajectories. DGNR was proposed by Zhuopeng Li, Chenming Wu, Liangjun Zhang, and Jianke Zhu. It was published in IEEE Transactions on Autonomous Systems and Engineering (TASE) in 2024, with an arXiv preprint in November 2023. The method was evaluated on KITTI, Cityscapes, and Waymo datasets. name: Density Threshold Filtering
head: Density-based point extraction, Ray-casting density thresholding
body: Density Threshold Filtering is a post-processing technique for extracting sparse 3D point clouds from NeRF-based volume rendering methods (such as Mega-NeRF, Block-NeRF, and DVGO). It solves the problem of noise and outliers in raw neural point representations by selecting points along rays based on a pre-defined density threshold. Unlike its siblings which may focus on initialization or rendering optimization, this method specifically addresses the geometric cleanup of the output point cloud. It operates on the principle that valid geometry corresponds to high density values, while empty space or noise corresponds to low values. Inputs: A trained NeRF-based model (e.g., Mega-NeRF, Block-NeRF, DVGO) capable of querying volume density \sigma at any 3D coordinate. Camera viewpoints (intrinsics and extrinsics). A scalar density threshold value T. Outputs: A 3D point cloud P consisting of 3D coordinates (x, y, z) selected from the volume. Data Structures: The NeRF model is queried as a black-box function \sigma(x, y, z) \rightarrow \mathbb{R} returning the volume density. The output point cloud is a list of 3D vectors. Steps: 1. Generate a set of random rays originating from the camera viewpoints. 2. Sample points along these rays at regular or random intervals within the scene bounds. 3. Evaluate the volume density \sigma at each sampled point using the trained NeRF model. 4. Select a point pi for inclusion in the output point cloud if its density value satisfies the condition: \sigma(pi) \geq T 5. Repeat for all sampled points along all rays. Parameters: Density Threshold (T): A scalar value determining the minimum density required for a point to be retained. The sources test values between 0 and 200. The exact unit of density depends on the specific NeRF implementation (e.g., DVGO uses specific scaling). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Completeness vs. Accuracy Trade-off: Increasing T removes noise (increasing accuracy) but also removes valid geometry with lower density, such as thin structures like canals and roads, leading to holes in the point cloud (decreasing completeness). Threshold Selection: There is no universal optimal T. It must be tuned per dataset and model. Empty Space: Points in empty space should have \sigma \approx 0. If the model outputs non-zero density in empty space (common in unregularized NeRFs), T must be set above this noise floor. This variant, used in medical imaging contexts (e.g., lung nodule detection), does not threshold raw density \sigma directly but thresholds the NeRF accumulation map (transmittance-weighted density integral) at the 95th percentile. Detected regions are back-projected into 3D using mean ray depth and field-of-view geometry. While this approach achieves a 32.1% volumetric error with 45/72 valid detections, it frequently captures the entire lung field rather than specific nodules, indicating a lack of specificity compared to raw density thresholding. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sampled points along rays. The cost is dominated by the NeRF inference queries. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of points satisfying the threshold. Performance: The method effectively reduces outliers. However, it suffers from a significant loss of completeness for thin or low-density structures (e.g., roads, canals) as T increases. Strengths: Simple to implement; effective at removing high-frequency noise and outliers common in NeRF reconstructions. Limitations: Cannot recover geometry that falls below the threshold; sensitive to the choice of T; does not account for geometric consistency between rays. When to use: When a clean, sparse point cloud is required from a NeRF for downstream tasks like MVS or meshing, and the scene contains significant noise. When not to use: When preserving thin structures or low-density geometry is critical, or when the NeRF model is poorly regularized and produces high density in empty space. Density Threshold Filtering was proposed as a method to extract point clouds from large-scale NeRF-based volume rendering methods, specifically Mega-NeRF, Block-NeRF, and DVGO. It draws inspiration from classical Multi-View Stereo (MVS) filtering techniques, where accuracy is improved by removing incorrect points, albeit at the cost of completeness. The method was evaluated on aerial imagery datasets (TMB, UseGeo3, Hessigheim 3D) to assess the impact of varying density thresholds on reconstruction quality. name: Point-based Rendering with Ray Bending
head: Controllable Human Motion Synthesis via Point Radiance Fields, Deformed PointNeRF, Point-based Radiance Field Deformation with Ray-Bending, PointNeRF Editing, PointNeRF with Ray Bending
body: This method synthesizes controllable human motion by deforming a pre-trained point-based radiance field and correcting view-dependent color inconsistencies caused by deformation via ray-bending. It enables physically convincing rendering of deformed scenes by transforming the deformed view direction back to the canonical space before querying the pre-trained model. Unlike methods that twist rays in canonical space or add extra information to features at training, this approach adds a lightweight ray-bending module to the existing point cloud-guided NeRF model, avoiding extra complexity and application limits. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained PointNeRF model (canonical space), a deformed neural point cloud (NPC) \hat{P}, and a camera ray defined by origin and deformed view direction \hat{v} in the deformed space. Output: Density \sigma and radiance r for the ray sample point. Data Structures: The neural point cloud P is defined as a set of points where each point i has: xi: 3D location in canonical space. fi: Neural feature vector. \gammai: Scale confidence value in the range [0, 1]. Ri: Estimated local rotation matrix (computed during deformation). Numbered Steps: 1. Canonical Training: Build a radiance field from static scenes using PointNeRF. Each point is associated with a neural feature defined as a function of viewing direction. 2. Deformation: Deform the pose by manipulating points of interest to new positions using a deformation model (e.g., Dynamic Point Field). This produces the deformed point cloud \hat{P} with points \hat{x}i. 3. KD-Tree Construction: For each frame, build a KD-tree structure for the deformed point cloud \hat{P} to efficiently query k-nearest-neighbors. 4. Relative Rotation Estimation (Per Point): For each queried neural point \hat{c}x in the deformed space: Query the KD-tree to extract k-nearest-neighbors \hat{X} in deformed space. Identify the corresponding point cx and neighbors X in the canonical space. Compute the rotation matrix R using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) on the centered neighbor clusters: U, E, V = \text{SVD}((X - cx)^T (\hat{X} - \hat{c}x)) R = U V^T v = R \hat{v} where v is the canonical view direction and \hat{v} is the deformed view direction. 5. Rotation Interpolation (Per Ray Sample): During volumetric ray marching, for a sample point, interpolate the relative rotations using k-nearest-neighbors in the NPC to preserve orthogonality in SO(3): Let Ri (i \in \{1, \dots, k\}) be the k queried rotation matrices. Let f be the mapping from rotation matrix to quaternion. Compute quaternions qi = f(Ri). Calculate weights wi = di^{-1} / \sum{j=1}^k dj^{-1}, where di is the distance to the i-th neighbor. Compute the weighted sum: q = \frac{\sum{i=1}^k wi qi}{\|\sum{i=1}^k wi qi\|} Final rotation: R = f^{-1}(q). 6. Ray Bending and Rendering: Apply the interpolated rotation R to the deformed view direction \hat{v} to obtain the canonical view direction v = R \hat{v}. Predict density and radiance using the deformed location \hat{x} and the canonical view direction v: (\sigma, r) = \text{Point-NeRF}(\hat{x}, v, x1, f1, \gamma1, \dots, xk, fk, \gammak) where x1 \dots xk are the canonical neighbors corresponding to the query. Parameters: k: Number of nearest neighbors for SVD and interpolation. Not given in the sources. Deformation Model: Uses a deformation MLP similar to Dynamic Point Field (DPF) with key points as input. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Specular Materials: Ray bending is critical for specular materials. Without it, rendering fails to reproduce reflections correctly. Large Deformation: Without ray bending, queries may access weakly supervised view-dependent information under large deformation, leading to texture loss. Orthogonality: Rotation interpolation must preserve orthogonality in SO(3); simple linear interpolation of rotation matrices is insufficient. Time Complexity: Depends on KD-tree construction (O(N \log N) per frame) and k-nearest-neighbor queries during ray marching. SVD computation is constant time per point (O(k^3) or less with optimized SVD). Memory Complexity: Stores the neural point cloud P and the KD-tree structure. Strengths: Decoupled from PointNeRF training; handles fine-level complex deformation; generalizes to other 3D characters besides humans; superior visual quality for specular materials and large deformations compared to no-bending methods. Limitations: Requires explicit geometry reconstruction via neural points; relies on accurate deformation model (e.g., DPF) to provide meaningful local rotations. When to use: When synthesizing controllable human motion or editing 3D characters with view-dependent effects (specularities) using a point-based radiance field. When not to use: For static scenes without deformation, or when computational resources for per-frame KD-tree construction and SVD are prohibitive. Originating from the paper "Point-Based Radiance Fields for Controllable Human Motion Synthesis", this method addresses the challenge of synthesizing user-controllable human motion in virtual scenes. Previous editable neural radiance field methods allowed naive deformation but struggled with complex 3D human editing like forward kinematics. This approach builds on PointNeRF and Dynamic Point Field (DPF), introducing ray-bending to correct view-dependent inconsistencies caused by deformation. It was developed to provide a more visually plausible and physically convincing rendering of deformed scenes without adding significant complexity to the NeRF model. name: Volume Feature Rendering
head: Feature Accumulation, Feature Integration
body: Volume Feature Rendering (VFR) is a differentiable rendering technique that integrates queried feature vectors along a ray into a single aggregated feature vector, which is then transformed into the final pixel color by a single neural network evaluation. Unlike standard volume rendering, which requires N neural network evaluations (one per sample) to predict color, VFR reduces the number of evaluations to one, thereby relieving the framework from the high computational cost associated with large color networks. This architectural change allows for the use of significantly larger neural networks to improve rendering quality without increasing training or rendering time proportionally. VFR modifies the standard volume rendering equation by moving the color prediction neural network outside the integration integral. Instead of predicting color at each sample point, the method predicts a feature vector, aggregates these features based on density weights, and applies the color network once to the result. Inputs: Ray \mathbf{r} (origin and direction), view direction \mathbf{d}, number of samples N, feature representation (e.g., hash grid, occupancy grid), density field \sigma, step sizes \deltai, and a color neural network \text{NeuralNet}. Outputs: Final rendered color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}). The method relies on a feature representation that maps 3D positions to feature vectors. Common implementations use Multi-resolution Hash Grids (MHG) or occupancy grids. Feature Vector F(\mathbf{x}i): A learnable vector associated with position \mathbf{x}i. The dimension is typically 256. Density Field \sigma(\mathbf{x}i): A scalar value representing the opacity/density at \mathbf{x}i, used to compute weights. Color Neural Network: A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) that takes the aggregated feature vector and view direction as input. Architecture: Typically consists of a spatial MLP and a directional MLP. Spatial MLP: 2 hidden layers. Directional MLP: 4 hidden layers. Hidden Neurons: 256 per layer. Bottleneck Feature Size: 256. Activation Function: GELU is preferred over ReLU for improved quality. View Direction Encoding: Spherical Harmonics Feature Encoding (SHFE) is used, where each spherical harmonics basis function is multiplied by a feature vector to encode the view direction \mathbf{d}. 1. Sampling: Cast a ray \mathbf{r} through the scene and sample N points \mathbf{x}i along the ray. The number of samples N is typically 32, but can be reduced to 5 for real-time rendering. Importance sampling is used to focus on non-empty regions. 2. Feature Query: Query the feature vector F(\mathbf{x}i) for each sample point \mathbf{x}i using the feature representation (e.g., hash grid). 3. Weight Computation: Compute the volume rendering weight wi for each sample based on the density \sigmai and step size \deltai, identical to the standard volume rendering model: wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) where Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance. 4. Feature Integration: Aggregate the queried feature vectors into a single rendered feature vector \mathbf{F}{rendered} by computing the weighted sum: \mathbf{F}{rendered} = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi F(\mathbf{x}i) 5. Color Prediction: Pass the aggregated feature vector \mathbf{F}{rendered} and the view direction \mathbf{d} into a single neural network evaluation to predict the final color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}): \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \text{NeuralNet}(\mathbf{F}{rendered}, \mathbf{d}) import math def volumefeaturerendering(rayorigin, raydirection, samples, deltas, featuregrid, densityfield, colornet, featuredim): """ Renders a single ray using Volume Feature Rendering. Args: rayorigin: 3D point. raydirection: normalized 3D vector. samples: list of N 3D points along the ray. deltas: list of N step sizes (distances between consecutive samples). featuregrid: callable returning feature vector F(x) for a 3D point. densityfield: callable returning scalar density sigma(x) for a 3D point. colornet: callable NeuralNet(F, d) returning color. featuredim: integer dimension of feature vectors. Returns: Final rendered color vector. """ N = len(samples) aggregatedfeature = [0.0] featuredim transmittance = 1.0 for i in range(N): xi = samples[i] Fi = featuregrid(xi) sigmai = densityfield(xi) deltai = deltas[i] weight = transmittance (1.0 - math.exp(-sigmai deltai)) for k in range(featuredim): aggregatedfeature[k] += weight Fi[k] transmittance = math.exp(-sigmai deltai) color = colornet(aggregatedfeature, raydirection) return color Number of Samples (N): Typically 32. Can be reduced to 5 for real-time rendering. MLP Size: 6 layers with 256 neurons per layer is used for high quality, which is ~24x the computational cost of Instant-NGP's 4-layer/64-neuron MLP. Activation: GELU. View Encoding: SHFE (Spherical Harmonics Feature Encoding). Training Steps: 20,000 steps. Convergence Failure: VFR may fail to converge on certain scenes during early training stages. This occurs because the model lacks a coarse geometry guide initially, causing it to integrate feature vectors from all samples (including empty space) rather than just surface samples. Pilot Network: To address convergence failure, a small "pilot network" is introduced to guide early-stage training. This pilot network functions as a standard volume renderer for a few initial training steps, providing a coarse geometry guide before switching to VFR. Semitransparency: VFR may be inefficient for semitransparent objects because it integrates feature vectors first and then predicts a single final color, which does not accurately model transparency. Time Complexity: Training time is significantly reduced compared to standard volume rendering with large networks. For example, VFR achieves state-of-the-art quality in 2.9–3.3 minutes (20K steps) on the NeRF synthetic dataset, compared to Zip-NeRF's 7.7 hours on a V100 GPU. The rendering time is 4–5 frames per second at 800x800 resolution on the NeRF synthetic dataset, and 1–2 frames per second at 1300x840 on the real-world 360 dataset. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables the use of much larger neural networks (e.g., 6x256 MLP) without proportional increases in training or rendering time. Achieves state-of-the-art rendering quality (e.g., 34.62 PSNR on NeRF synthetic, 29.48 PSNR on real-world 360). Can be used as a drop-in replacement for standard volume rendering in neural rendering methods based on volume representation. Limitations: Rendering speed is still slower than surface-based methods like BakedSDF and MobileNeRF, which use one feature query and one NN evaluation. Requires many feature queries per ray, which can be a bottleneck. Potential inefficacy with semitransparent objects. Still requires per-scene optimization, so it is not suitable for real-time reconstruction of 3D video applications without further optimization. Volume Feature Rendering was proposed to address the computational bottleneck of neural network evaluations in standard volume rendering, particularly when using large networks for high-quality rendering. The method was introduced in the paper "Volume Feature Rendering for Fast Neural Radiance Field Reconstruction". It builds on the principles of differentiable volume rendering. The method was implemented using NerfAcc's implementation of Instant-NGP as a baseline. name: Neural Rendering
body: Neural rendering learns the rendering process directly from data rather than relying on handcrafted analytical differentiation of physical rendering equations. It jointly trains a scene generation network and a rendering network by minimizing image reconstruction error, producing high-quality images indistinguishable from real-world captures. Unlike traditional differentiable rendering that explicitly computes gradients through geometric primitives, neural rendering bypasses explicit differentiation by learning the input-output mapping, though it faces limitations in generalization, multi-object scaling, and human editability. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A dataset of images representing the target scene or domain, optionally with camera poses. Outputs: A trained pair of neural networks: a scene generation network (encoding the scene) and a rendering network (mapping the representation to pixel colors). Data Structures: Scene Generation Network: Outputs a neural scene representation for given 3D coordinates and viewing directions. Rendering Network: Maps the scene representation and camera parameters to predicted pixel colors. The specific architecture (e.g., MLP, CNN, or voxel grid) is not fixed by the method definition but is selected based on applied inductive biases. Steps: 1. Scene Encoding: For a given ray, sample points and pass them through the scene generation network to obtain features or field values. 2. Rendering: Pass the features through the rendering network to predict color contributions. 3. Integration: Combine the color contributions into a final image pixel. 4. Loss Calculation: Compute the reconstruction error between the rendered image and the ground truth image. 5. Optimization: Update the parameters of both networks jointly using gradient descent to minimize the loss. Pitfalls: Generalization: Struggles to generalize to scenes significantly different from the training data. Scaling: Scaling to scenes composed of multiple distinct objects is limited. Editability: Human modification of the generated scene is restricted due to the lack of explicit semantic or geometric structure. Deferred Neural Rendering uses textures containing learnable view-dependent features (neural textures). A coarse mesh serves as the underlying 3D representation to rasterize these neural textures, and a neural network interprets the rasterized features in image space. The network can be a pixel-wise MLP, in which case the neural texture represents surface radiance. RISP is a neural network N\theta that acts as an inverse renderer, mapping an input image I to a predicted state \hat{s} that is invariant to rendering parameters \psi. It solves the problem of optimizing physical system parameters from video by replacing sensitive image-space losses with robust state-space losses, allowing gradient-based optimization to succeed even when source and target rendering domains (e.g., lighting, materials) differ vastly. Unlike direct image-space optimization which traps gradient descent in local minima under domain shift, RISP enables optimization in a rendering-invariant state space. Equivariant Neural Rendering is a framework for learning neural scene representations directly from 2D images without requiring 3D ground truth or camera pose supervision at inference time. It solves the problem of novel view synthesis by enforcing that the learned implicit scene representation transforms like a real 3D scene, specifically satisfying the equivariance relation TX g(z) = g(TZ z). Unlike sibling methods such as Rendering-Invariant State Predictor (RISP) which may rely on different invariance assumptions, this method explicitly models 3D rotation equivariance using deep voxel grids, allowing the model to generalize across camera transformations without absolute pose alignment. Strengths: Capable of generating high-quality images indistinguishable from real-world ones by learning from data, bypassing the need for accurate physical modeling. Limitations: Limited generalization to unseen scenes, poor scalability to multi-object scenes, and low editability by humans. Performance: Efficiency can be improved with coarse-to-fine sampling and importance sampling near boundaries. Usage: Novel view synthesis, semantic photo manipulation, facial/body reenactment, relighting, free-viewpoint video, and photo-realistic avatar creation. The concept was introduced by Eslami et al. as an alternative to handcrafting rendering differentiation, proposing to learn the rendering process from data. It has become a prominent area of research, often combined with inductive biases for 3D scenes to improve performance. name: Rendering-Invariant State Predictor (RISP)
head: RISP (Rendering-Invariant State Predictor), RISP Network Training, RISP network, Rendering-Invariant State Predictor training, rendering-invariant state-prediction network
body: RISP is a neural network N\theta that acts as an inverse renderer, mapping an input image I to a predicted state \hat{s} that is invariant to rendering parameters \psi. It solves the problem of optimizing physical system parameters from video by replacing sensitive image-space losses with robust state-space losses, allowing gradient-based optimization to succeed even when source and target rendering domains differ vastly. Unlike direct image-space optimization which traps gradient descent in local minima under domain shift, RISP enables optimization in a rendering-invariant state space. Input: An image sequence \{Ii\} generated by a differentiable renderer from a physical simulation, or a reference image sequence \{Ii^{\text{ref}}\} from a target domain. Output: A predicted state sequence \{\hat{s}i\} where \hat{s}i = N\theta(Ii). The RISP network N\theta is parameterized by weights \theta. State Vector s: Encodes the physical state of the system at a time step. Action Vector a: Encodes control inputs applied at each time step. System Parameters \phi: Vector encoding intrinsic system properties (e.g., mass, inertia, elasticity). Rendering Parameters \psi: Vector encoding rendering configurations (e.g., light intensity, material reflectance, background color). Time Steps N: The number of steps in a simulation rollout. The method relies on a differentiable simulation engine M\phi and a differentiable rendering engine R\psi. 1. Simulation: Given an initial state s0 and a sequence of actions \{ai\}, the state at step i+1 is computed as: s{i+1} = M\phi(si, ai), \quad \forall i = 0, 1, \dots, N-1 where \phi encodes system parameters. 2. Rendering: The state si is rendered to an image Ii: Ii = R\psi(si), \quad \forall i = 0, 1, \dots, N where \psi encodes rendering parameters. 3. Compact Form: The workflow is expressed as: \{Ii\} = R\psi [ M\phi (s0, \{ai\}) ]. The network N\theta is pre-trained and fixed before the main optimization task. It is trained to minimize a combined loss L{\text{train}} consisting of a prediction error term L{\text{error}} and a regularization term L{\text{reg}}. Sample pairs of states sj and rendering parameters \psij, render images Ij = R{\psij}(sj) to create a dataset \mathcal{D} = \{(sj, \psij, Ij)\}. Minimize the L1 distance between the true state sj and the network prediction N\theta(Ij): L{\text{error}}(\theta, \mathcal{D}) = \sum{(sj, \psij, Ij) \in \mathcal{D}} \| sj - N\theta(Ij) \|1 This ensures the network accurately predicts the state for specific instances. To enforce invariance to \psi, the network's output should not change with respect to \psi, requiring \frac{\partial N\theta(R\psi(s))}{\partial \psi} \equiv 0. The regularizer is the Frobenius norm of this Jacobian: L{\text{reg}}(\theta, \mathcal{D}) = \sum{(sj, \psij, Ij) \in \mathcal{D}} \left\| \frac{\partial N\theta(R{\psij}(sj))}{\partial \psij} \right\|F Using the chain rule: \frac{\partial N\theta(R{\psij}(sj))}{\partial \psij} = \frac{\partial N\theta(Ij)}{\partial Ij} \frac{\partial Ij}{\partial \psij} \frac{\partial N\theta(Ij)}{\partial Ij} is computed via standard reverse-mode autodiff in the network. \frac{\partial Ij}{\partial \psij} is obtained from the differentiable renderer. L{\text{train}}(\theta, \mathcal{D}) = L{\text{error}} + \gamma L{\text{reg}} where \gamma is a regularization weight. Pitfall: Optimizing L{\text{reg}} alone leads to a trivial solution where the network predicts constant states. It must be combined with L{\text{error}} to balance accuracy and invariance. Given a reference image sequence \{Ii^{\text{ref}}\} from a target domain with unknown parameters, optimize the initial state s0, action sequence \{ai\}, system parameters \phi, and rendering parameters \psi to minimize the state-space loss: \min{s0, \{ai\}, \phi, \psi} L(N\theta(\{Ii^{\text{ref}}\}), N\theta(\{Ii\})) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \{Ii\} = R\psi [ M\phi (s0, \{ai\}) ]. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim def trainrispnetwork(Ntheta, differentiablerenderer, datasetD, gamma, numepochs): """ Pre-trains the RISP network Ntheta. Args: Ntheta: Neural network module parameterized by theta. differentiablerenderer: Differentiable renderer Rpsi. datasetD: List of tuples (sj, psij, Ij). gamma: Regularization weight. numepochs: Number of training epochs. """ optimizer = optim.Adam(Ntheta.parameters(), lr=1e-3) for epoch in range(numepochs): totalloss = 0.0 for sj, psij, Ij in datasetD: # Forward pass: Network prediction shat = Ntheta(Ij) # Lerror: L1 loss between true state and prediction losserror = torch.mean(torch.abs(sj - shat)) # Lreg: Gradient of network output w.r.t rendering parameters # Requires computing Jacobian-vector products or full Jacobian # dN/d(psi) = (dN/dI) @ (dI/dpsi) # 1. dN/dI: Jacobian of network output w.r.t input image # shape: (dims, dimI) # The paper specifies O(|s||theta|) time using pre-computed data # and avoids second-order gradients in the renderer. # Here we compute the full Jacobian for clarity. JN = torch.autograd.functional.jacobian(Ntheta, Ij) # 2. dI/dpsi: Gradient of rendered image w.r.t rendering parameters # Ij is already computed. We need gradients w.r.t psij. # differentiablerenderer provides dI/dpsi. dIdpsi = differentiablerenderer.getgradientwrtparams(psij, sj) # Combine: dN/dpsi = JN @ dIdpsi # If JN is (dims, dimI) and dIdpsi is (dimI, dimpsi), # result is (dims, dimpsi). dNdpsi = torch.matmul(JN, dIdpsi) lossreg = torch.norm(dNdpsi, p='fro') loss = losserror + gamma lossreg optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() totalloss += loss.item() print(f"Epoch {epoch}, Loss: {totalloss / len(datasetD)}") def optimizeparameters(Ntheta, differentiablerenderer, differentiablesimulator, Iref, s0init, ainit, phiinit, psiinit): """ Optimizes system parameters using the pre-trained RISP network. Args: Ntheta: Pre-trained RISP network. differentiablerenderer: Differentiable renderer Rpsi. differentiablesimulator: Differentiable simulator Mphi. Iref: Reference image sequence (tensor of shape [N+1, H, W, C]). s0init: Initial state guess. ainit: Initial action sequence guess (tensor of shape [N, dima]). phiinit: Initial system parameters guess. psiinit: Initial rendering parameters guess. Returns: Optimized s0, a, phi, psi. """ # Make parameters trainable s0 = s0init.clone().detach().requiresgrad(True) a = ainit.clone().detach().requiresgrad(True) phi = phiinit.clone().detach().requiresgrad(True) psi = psiinit.clone().detach().requiresgrad(True) optimizer = optim.Adam([s0, a, phi, psi], lr=1e-3) # Assume N is the number of time steps N = len(a) for epoch in range(1000): # Example iteration count optimizer.zerograd() # 1. Simulate states scurrent = s0 states = [scurrent] for i in range(N): # Get action ai ai = a[i] # Simulate next state: s{i+1} = Mphi(si, ai) snext = differentiablesimulator.step(scurrent, ai, phi) states.append(snext) scurrent = snext statestensor = torch.stack(states) # Shape [N+1, dims] # 2. Render images: Ii = Rpsi(si) for i = 0..N Igen = differentiablerenderer.render(statestensor, psi) # 3. Predict states using RISP # Ntheta takes images and outputs states # Igen shape: [N+1, H, W, C] # Ntheta(I) -> shat shatgen = Ntheta(Igen) # 4. Predict states for reference images shatref = Ntheta(Iref) # 5. Compute loss in state space: L(Ntheta(Iref), Ntheta(Igen)) # Using L1 or L2 loss between predicted states loss = torch.mean(torch.abs(shatref - shatgen)) loss.backward() optimizer.step() if epoch % 100 == 0: print(f"Optimization Epoch {epoch}, Loss: {loss.item()}") return s0, a, phi, psi Direct Image-Space Optimization: Optimizes pixel-wise loss directly between rendered and reference images. Fails when rendering domains differ significantly due to non-linearity and local minima. Alternative Regularizer (Error Invariance): Encourages the prediction error to be rendering-invariant rather than the output itself. Computed as \sum \| \frac{\partial L{\text{error}}}{\partial \psij} \|. Takes O(|\theta|) time vs O(|s||\theta|) for the original regularizer, with empirically comparable performance. Training L{\text{reg}}: Computing the gradient of L{\text{reg}} w.r.t. network parameters \theta takes O(|s||\theta|) time per image. Memory: Requires pre-computed data occupying O(\sumj |\psij||Ij|) space. Alternative Regularizer: The alternative regularizer takes O(|\theta|) time to compute gradients, making it significantly faster for large state spaces. Second-Order Gradients: The method does not require second-order gradients in the renderer R, which exceeds the capability of most existing differentiable renderers. Performance: Achieves significantly lower reconstruction errors and better generalizability across unknown rendering configurations compared to existing methods. Scaling: The O(|s||\theta|) cost is affordable for very small rigid-body systems (e.g., |s| < 10) but not scalable for large deformable bodies without the alternative regularizer. Robustness: State-space optimization is fairly robust to random initialization, whereas image-space optimization traps gradient descent in local minima if initial images are not reasonably similar to references. Strengths: Decouples state estimation from rendering artifacts; enables cross-domain parameter estimation; works with black-box differentiable simulators. Limitations: Requires a differentiable renderer; pre-training data must span the distribution of rendering parameters; direct image-space optimization is not viable for large domain shifts. The Rendering-Invariant State Predictor (RISP) was introduced in the paper "RISP: Rendering-Invariant State Predictor with Differentiable Simulation and Rendering for Cross-Domain Parameter Estimation". RISP was developed to address the limitations of \nablaSim, a state-of-the-art method that optimizes physical parameters by minimizing image-space losses. While \nablaSim works for moderately different rendering domains, it fails when domains are vastly different. RISP introduces the concept of an "inverse renderer" to map images to a rendering-invariant state space, enabling robust optimization. RISP has been evaluated in rigid-body and deformable-body simulation environments for tasks including state estimation, system identification, imitation learning, and visuomotor control. It has also been applied to real-world quadrotor video inference. name: Equivariant Neural Rendering
head: Forward renderer, Inverse renderer
body: Equivariant Neural Rendering is a framework for learning neural scene representations directly from 2D images without requiring 3D ground truth or camera pose supervision at inference time. It solves the problem of novel view synthesis by enforcing that the learned implicit scene representation transforms like a real 3D scene, specifically satisfying the equivariance relation TX g(z) = g(TZ z). Unlike sibling methods such as Rendering-Invariant State Predictor (RISP) which may rely on different invariance assumptions, this method explicitly models 3D rotation equivariance using deep voxel grids, allowing the model to generalize across camera transformations without absolute pose alignment. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pair of images (x1, x2) of the same scene and their relative 3D rotation transformation \theta. Output: A rendered image matching the target view, derived from the transformed scene representation. Data Structures: Scene Representation (z): A deep voxel grid with layout \mathbb{R}^{cs \times ds \times hs \times ws}. In the reference implementation, dimensions are 64 \times 32 \times 32 \times 32 (channels \times depth \times height \times width). Image (x): 2D image tensor of size 128 \times 128 pixels. Transformation (\theta): Parameterized as axis-angle \theta \hat{n}, where \theta is the angle and \hat{n} is the axis. In implementation, this is converted to a 3 \times 3 rotation matrix. Network Architecture: The method consists of two transposed networks: 1. Inverse Renderer (f: X \rightarrow Z): Maps images to scene representations. Submodels: 2D Convolutional Network \rightarrow Inverse Projection Layer \rightarrow 3D Convolutional Network. Components: Residual blocks (1x1, 3x3, 1x1 convolutions), GroupNorm, LeakyReLU. Strided convolutions for downsampling. 2. Forward Renderer (g: Z \rightarrow X): Maps scene representations to images. Architecture: Transpose of the inverse renderer. Sequence: 3D Convolutions \rightarrow 1x1 Projection Convolutions \rightarrow 2D Convolutions \rightarrow Image. Output: Sigmoid activation ensures pixel values are in [0, 1]. Voxel Rotation Implementation: To apply rotation R^Z\theta to the voxel grid z: 1. Define a grid of coordinates corresponding to the voxel locations. 2. Apply the 3D rotation matrix to these coordinates. 3. Use inverse warping with trilinear interpolation to reconstruct feature values at the rotated coordinates. Training Algorithm: The model is trained to minimize the rendering loss, which enforces equivariance. 1. Data Sampling: For a given scene, capture multiple views. Randomly sample a pair of images (x1, x2) and compute the relative rotation \theta between their camera poses. Assume cameras are on a sphere looking at the origin. 2. Encoding: Pass both images through the inverse renderer f to obtain scene representations: z1 = f(x1) z2 = f(x2) 3. Rotation: Rotate the encoded representations by the relative transformation \theta. Let R^Z\theta be the rotation operator in scene space. Compute: \tilde{z}1 = R^Z\theta z1 \tilde{z}2 = (R^Z\theta)^{-1} z2 Note: (R^Z\theta)^{-1} is the inverse rotation, equivalent to rotating by -\theta. 4. Rendering: Pass the rotated representations through the forward renderer g: \hat{x}2 = g(\tilde{z}1) \hat{x}1 = g(\tilde{z}2) 5. Loss Calculation: Compute the rendering loss L{render}: L{render} = \|x2 - \hat{x}2\| + \|x1 - \hat{x}1\| The norm \|\cdot\| is typically a weighted sum of L1 and SSIM losses. 6. Optimization: Minimize L{render} using gradient descent. This loss ensures that transforming the representation and rendering is equivalent to rendering and transforming the image, satisfying TX g(z) = g(TZ z). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class EquivariantNeuralRenderer: def init(self, inverserenderer: nn.Module, forwardrenderer: nn.Module): """ Args: inverserenderer: nn.Module mapping Image -> VoxelGrid (f) forwardrenderer: nn.Module mapping VoxelGrid -> Image (g) """ self.f = inverserenderer self.g = forwardrenderer def rotatevoxelgrid(self, z: torch.Tensor, rotationmatrix: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Rotates a voxel grid z by applying rotationmatrix to its coordinates. Uses inverse warping with trilinear interpolation. Args: z: Tensor of shape (B, C, D, H, W) rotationmatrix: Tensor of shape (3, 3) Returns: Rotated tensor of shape (B, C, D, H, W) """ B, C, D, H, W = z.shape # Create coordinate grid for the voxel space # Coordinates should be normalized to [-1, 1] or [0, 1] depending on framework convention # Assuming standard gridsample convention: coordinates in [-1, 1] grid = torch.meshgrid( torch.linspace(-1, 1, D), torch.linspace(-1, 1, H), torch.linspace(-1, 1, W), indexing='ij') grid = torch.stack(grid, dim=-1) # Shape (D, H, W, 3) grid = grid.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).expand(B, C, -1, -1, -1, -1) # Shape (B, C, D, H, W, 3) # Flatten spatial dimensions for rotation gridflat = grid.view(B, C, -1, 3) # Shape (B, C, DHW, 3) # Apply rotation: newcoords = oldcoords @ R^T # rotationmatrix is (3,3). We need to rotate the coordinates. # If R rotates the scene, the coordinates in the new frame are R^-1 x. # For gridsample, we provide the target grid in the source frame. # Inverse warping: sample from z at locations rotated by R^-1. # Let's assume rotationmatrix is R. We want to rotate the grid by R. # The coordinates in the rotated grid correspond to R originalcoords. # To sample, we need to map these back to original grid coordinates: R^-1 rotatedcoords. # Actually, standard inverse warping: # To get value at new location y, we look at x = R^-1 y in the original image/grid. # Here y are the coordinates of the output grid (which are fixed). # So we compute sourcecoords = R^-1 outputcoords. Rinv = rotationmatrix.inverse() # Shape (3, 3) # Reshape grid for matrix multiplication gridflat = gridflat.permute(0, 1, 3, 2) # (B, C, 3, DHW) # Rotate coordinates # sourcecoords = Rinv @ gridflat sourcecoords = torch.matmul(Rinv, gridflat) # (B, C, 3, DHW) sourcecoords = sourcecoords.permute(0, 1, 3, 2) # (B, C, DHW, 3) # Reshape back to (B, C, D, H, W, 3) sourcecoords = sourcecoords.view(B, C, D, H, W, 3) # Use gridsample or similar for trilinear interpolation # Note: gridsample expects (N, C, H, W, 2) for 2D or (N, C, D, H, W, 3) for 3D # We need to permute to (B, C, D, H, W, 3) which is already the shape. # However, gridsample usually works on the last dimensions. # Let's assume a helper function or direct call if supported. # PyTorch 3D gridsample: rotatedz = F.gridsample( z, sourcecoords, mode='trilinear', paddingmode='border', aligncorners=True) return rotatedz def trainingstep(self, x1: torch.Tensor, x2: torch.Tensor, rotationmatrix: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Performs one training step. Args: x1: Image tensor (B, 3, 128, 128) x2: Image tensor (B, 3, 128, 128) rotationmatrix: 3x3 rotation matrix Rtheta Returns: Loss scalar """ # 1. Encoding z1 = self.f(x1) # (B, Cs, Ds, Hs, Ws) z2 = self.f(x2) # 2. Rotation # Rotate z1 by Rtheta to align with x2's perspective ztilde1 = self.rotatevoxelgrid(z1, rotationmatrix) # Rotate z2 by Rtheta^-1 to align with x1's perspective Rinv = rotationmatrix.inverse() ztilde2 = self.rotatevoxelgrid(z2, Rinv) # 3. Rendering x2pred = self.g(ztilde1) x1pred = self.g(ztilde2) # 4. Loss # Weighted sum of L1 and SSIM. Here simplified to L1 for demonstration. # In practice, use a combined loss function. loss = torch.mean(torch.abs(x2 - x2pred)) + torch.mean(torch.abs(x1 - x1pred)) return loss Parameters: Loss Function: Weighted sum of L1 norm and SSIM. The model is not highly sensitive to the choice, but this combination works well. Non-linearity: LeakyReLU. Normalization: GroupNorm. Camera Assumption: Camera is on a sphere looking at the origin. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Rotation Interpolation: Rotated voxel coordinates may not align with the grid. Trilinear interpolation is required to reconstruct values, which can introduce blurring or artifacts if the rotation is large or the grid resolution is low. Pose Ambiguity: The method assumes the camera is on a sphere looking at the origin. If this assumption is violated, the relative rotation \theta may not correctly align the scene representations. Inference Speed: While inference is fast (22ms on Tesla V100), it is slower than explicit renderers but significantly faster than optimization-based methods like SRNs (2 minutes). Time Complexity: Inference time is constant with respect to the number of training views, depending only on the network depth and voxel resolution. Inference takes ~22ms on a Tesla V100 GPU. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the voxel grid size (64 \times 32 \times 32 \times 32 channels) and the network weights. Performance: Chairs (ShapeNet): PSNR 22.83 dB (vs SRN 22.89 dB, dGQN 21.59 dB, TCO 21.27 dB). Cars (ShapeNet): PSNR 22.26 dB (vs SRN 22.36 dB, SRN Relative 21.05 dB). Strengths: Real-time inference; no pose estimation required at inference; handles complex lighting and backgrounds (e.g., MugsHQ dataset). Limitations: Struggles with fine texture and geometry details compared to SRNs; requires spherical camera assumption; performance degrades if the relative pose estimation is poor. When to Use: When real-time novel view synthesis is required and 3D supervision or pose estimation is unavailable or too slow. When Not to Use: When highest possible photometric accuracy is required and inference time is not a constraint (use SRNs); when scenes do not conform to the spherical camera assumption. Equivariant Neural Rendering was proposed by Emilien Dupont, Miguel Angel Bautista, Alex Colburn, Aditya Sankar, Carlos Guestrin, Joshua Susskind, and Qi Shan. The work was published on arXiv in June 2020 (v2 in December 2020). It builds on the concept of equivariance in neural networks, extending it to 3D scene representations. The method addresses limitations of previous implicit scene representations like SRNs, which require optimization at inference time, and flow-based methods, which do not explicitly enforce 3D rotation equivariance. The authors introduced two new datasets, MugsHQ, to test the model on complex scenes with reflections and cluttered backgrounds. name: Fourier Features Mapping
head: FFM, Fourier Features, RFF Encoding, Random Fourier Features (RFF) Encoding
body: Fourier Features Mapping (FFM) is a preprocessing technique that transforms low-dimensional input coordinates into a higher-dimensional space using sinusoidal functions to overcome the spectral bias of vanilla Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs). It enables the network to learn high-frequency details early and fast by transforming the effective Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) into a stationary kernel with a tunable bandwidth. Unlike coordinate-based geometric approaches, FFM decouples the neural architecture from the spatial representation, allowing flexible integration into implicit neural representations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A d-dimensional coordinate vector \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^d (e.g., 3D spatial or 5D spatial-angular coordinates). Output: A 2m-dimensional feature vector \gamma(\mathbf{v}) \in \mathbb{R}^{2m}, where m is the number of sinusoid pairs. Data Structures: Random Matrix B: A matrix of shape m \times d containing random frequency vectors. The elements are drawn from a Gaussian distribution \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2). Phase Offsets \mathbf{b}: A vector of m random phase shifts, where each bi \in [0, 2\pi). Amplitude Scalars \mathbf{a}: A vector of m amplitude scalars, typically set to \sqrt{1/m} or 1 depending on the normalization convention. Parameters: \sigma (Variance): The standard deviation of the Gaussian distribution used to sample the random matrix B. It is identified as the most important hyperparameter in the mapping. \alpha (Bandwidth/Smoothing): The reciprocal of the standard deviation of the frequencies. It controls the reconstruction bandwidth. Note: \sigma and \alpha are inversely related; a small \sigma (high frequency spread) corresponds to a small \alpha (low smoothing). m (Dimensionality): The number of sinusoid pairs. The output dimension is 2m. Formulas: The mapping projects the input coordinates onto the surface of a hypersphere using sinusoids. The basic form is: \gamma(\mathbf{v}) = \begin{bmatrix} a1 \cos(2\pi \mathbf{b}1^T \mathbf{v}) \\ a1 \sin(2\pi \mathbf{b}1^T \mathbf{v}) \\ \vdots \\ am \cos(2\pi \mathbf{b}m^T \mathbf{v}) \\ am \sin(2\pi \mathbf{b}m^T \mathbf{v}) \end{bmatrix} Where \mathbf{b}j is the j-th frequency vector sampled from the distribution, and aj is the amplitude scalar. Alternatively, using the phase-offset formulation: \phi(\mathbf{x}):= \sqrt{\frac{1}{m}} [\cos(\mathbf{w}1^T \mathbf{x} + b1), \dots, \cos(\mathbf{w}m^T \mathbf{x} + bm)] Where \mathbf{w}i components are drawn from a univariate normal distribution and bi \in [0, 2\pi). The asymptotic behavior of the kernel induced by this mapping is given by Bochner's theorem: \lim{m \to \infty} \phi(\mathbf{x})\phi(\mathbf{x}0)^T = \exp\left(-\frac{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}0\|^2}{2\alpha^2}\right) Where \alpha is the reciprocal of the standard deviation of frequencies in \phi(\mathbf{x}). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Random Matrix: Sample a matrix B \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d} from a Gaussian distribution \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2). 2. Sample Phases (Optional): If using the phase-offset formulation, sample bi \sim \text{Uniform}[0, 2\pi) for i=1 \dots m. 3. Compute Dot Products: For input \mathbf{v}, compute the dot products \mathbf{B}\mathbf{v} (or \mathbf{w}i^T \mathbf{x}). 4. Apply Sinusoids: Compute the cosine and sine of 2\pi times the dot products (plus phase if applicable). 5. Scale: Multiply by the amplitude scalar aj (e.g., \sqrt{1/m}). 6. Concatenate: Concatenate the resulting cosine and sine components to form the final feature vector \gamma(\mathbf{v}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def fourierfeaturemapping(v, m, sigma): """ Transforms input coordinates v into Fourier features. Args: v: Input coordinate vector of shape (d,) m: Number of sinusoid pairs sigma: Standard deviation of the Gaussian distribution for sampling B Returns: gammav: Transformed feature vector of shape (2m,) """ d = v.shape[0] # Step 1: Initialize Random Matrix B # Sample from N(0, sigma^2) B = np.random.normal(0, sigma, size=(m, d)) # Step 2 & 3: Compute Dot Products # Compute 2 pi B @ v # Shape: (m,) dotproducts = 2 np.pi (B @ v) # Step 4 & 5: Apply Sinusoids and Scale # Amplitude scaling factor a = np.sqrt(1.0 / m) cosfeatures = a np.cos(dotproducts) sinfeatures = a np.sin(dotproducts) # Step 6: Concatenate gammav = np.concatenate([cosfeatures, sinfeatures]) return gammav Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Spectral Bias: Without FFM, the eigenvalues of the NTK for standard MLPs with ReLU activations decrease rapidly, causing high-frequency components to be learned very slowly, resulting in no sharp edges. Bandwidth Selection: The choice of \sigma (or \alpha) is critical. A small \alpha (high frequency) causes high output variance, resulting in noisy artifacts and spiky (under-smoothed) estimates. A large \alpha introduces high bias, leading to over-smoothed predictions and loss of high-frequency details. Grid Search: Finding the optimal bandwidth often requires a time-consuming grid-search scheme, leading to inefficient training overload. Isotropy Limitation: Standard FFM uses a single global bandwidth, which treats all input dimensions equally. This fails to handle signals with heterogeneous frequency characteristics across dimensions (e.g., high spatial variation but low angular variation), leading to imbalanced regression. Uses multiple bandwidths (one per dimension) to handle heterogeneous frequency characteristics, preventing the loss of high-frequency details in specific dimensions that occurs with isotropic FFM. Choose when input dimensions have significantly different smoothness requirements (e.g., spatial vs. angular). Time Complexity: The mapping itself is O(m \cdot d) per sample, which is negligible compared to the MLP evaluation. However, selecting the optimal bandwidth \sigma via grid search can be computationally expensive. Memory Complexity: The random matrix B requires O(m \cdot d) memory. This is typically small compared to the MLP weights. Performance: Enables MLPs to learn high-frequency details "early and fast," avoiding training times that could otherwise take months on standard hardware. Strengths: Decouples neural network design from geometric structures (like VDB trees), allowing flexibility in feature mapping choices. Makes the NTK stationary, improving convergence. Limitations: Suffers from spectral bias if not used. Requires careful tuning of the bandwidth parameter. Isotropic versions fail on signals with imbalanced dimensional characteristics. Origin: Introduced by Tancik et al. (2020) for implicit neural representations. History: Based on the random Fourier feature mapping originally proposed by Rahimi & Recht (2007). Development: Initially proposed to overcome the spectral bias of vanilla MLPs, which fail to capture high-frequency details even with deep and wide networks. It was shown that passing inputs through FFM transforms the effective NTK into a stationary kernel. Usage: Applied in Neural Fields / Implicit Neural Representations to condition MLPs on spatial coordinates. Used for image superresolution, denoising, inpainting, video generation, and 3D content rendering. Also used in frameworks like NeuralVDB to decouple network design from VDB tree structure. name: Anisotropic Random Fourier Features Mapping
head: Anisotropic Fourier Features, Anisotropic Fourier Features Mapping, Anisotropic RFF Mapping
body: Anisotropic Random Fourier Features Mapping (AFFM) is a feature encoding scheme that employs multiple bandwidths—one per input dimension—to model the heterogeneous frequency characteristics of multidimensional signals, such as plenoptic functions in image-based rendering. Unlike isotropic methods that treat all coordinates equally and suffer from imbalanced regression or loss of high-frequency details, AFFM allows independent smoothing control for each dimension, enabling the simultaneous capture of high-frequency spatial textures and low-frequency angular variations. Inputs: Input coordinate vector x \in \mathbb{R}^d. Number of random features m. Bandwidth parameters \alpha = [\alpha1, \dots, \alphad], where \alphai > 0 is the bandwidth for the i-th dimension. Outputs: Feature vector \phi(x) \in \mathbb{R}^m. Data Structures: Bandwidth Vector: A 1D array of size d containing the bandwidth \alphai for each dimension. Frequency Matrix: A matrix W \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d} where each row wi is sampled from a multivariate normal distribution. Bias Vector: A vector b \in \mathbb{R}^m with elements sampled uniformly from 0, 2\pi). Method Steps: 1. Bandwidth Selection: Determine the optimal bandwidth \alphai for each dimension i. The optimal bandwidth is empirically determined by the density of training data and the signal’s frequency spectrum in that dimension. A large bandwidth corresponds to a dimension where the total [curvature (variation) of the signal is small or the number of training points per unit is small. Search Algorithm: To avoid computationally expensive grid searches, use an iterative algorithm based on linear golden-section search (GSS) to automatically search for multiple bandwidth parameters. This reduces training time from polynomial to logarithmic. Empirically, 5 iterations are sufficient for convergence. 2. Frequency Sampling: Sample the frequency vectors wi \in \mathbb{R}^d for i = 1, \dots, m from a multivariate normal distribution. The covariance matrix \Sigma is diagonal, where the i-th diagonal entry is 1/\alphai. 3. Bias Sampling: Sample bias terms bj \in \mathbb{R} for j = 1, \dots, m uniformly from 0, 2\pi). 4. Feature Mapping: Compute the anisotropic Fourier features \phi(x) using the following formula: \phi(x):= \sqrt{\frac{2}{m}} \begin{bmatrix} \cos(w1^T x + b1) \\ \vdots \\ \cos(wm^T x + bm) \end{bmatrix} where wj^T x = \sum{k=1}^d w{j,k} xk. 5. Asymptotic Kernel: As m \to \infty, the feature map converges to the Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel with anisotropic bandwidths: \lim{m \to \infty} \phi(x)\phi(x0)^T = \exp\left(-\sum{i=1}^d \frac{(xi - x{0,i})^2}{2\alphai^2}\right) where \alphai denotes the bandwidth for the i-th dimension. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generateanisotropicfourierfeatures(x, m, bandwidths, seed=None): """ Generates Anisotropic Random Fourier Features for input x. Args: x: Input coordinate vector of shape (d,). m: Number of random features. bandwidths: Array of bandwidths alphai for each dimension, shape (d,). seed: Optional random seed for reproducibility. Returns: phi: Feature vector of shape (m,). """ if seed is not None: np.random.seed(seed) d = len(x) # Step 1: Sample frequencies from multivariate normal distribution # Covariance matrix is diagonal with entries 1/alphai as per source text covmatrix = np.diag(1.0 / bandwidths) # Sample m frequency vectors wj from N(0, covmatrix) W = np.random.multivariatenormal(mean=np.zeros(d), cov=covmatrix, size=m) # Step 2: Sample biases uniformly from [0, 2pi) b = np.random.uniform(0, 2 np.pi, size=m) # Step 3: Compute features # phi(x) = sqrt(2/m) cos(W @ x + b) projections = np.dot(W, x) + b phi = np.sqrt(2.0 / m) np.cos(projections) return phi def searchbandwidthgss(targetfunction, dimbounds, numiterations=5): """ Iterative golden-section search for optimal bandwidths. The source proposes an iterative algorithm based on linear golden-section search (GSS) to search multiple bandwidth parameters, reducing training time from polynomial to logarithmic. The exact implementation details for the multi-dimensional search strategy are not provided in the source. """ # Standard GSS implementation would go here. # The source states that 5 iterations are sufficient for convergence. pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The source does not specify numerical precision requirements. Boundaries: The bias bi must be strictly in [0, 2\pi). Degenerate Input: If a dimension has zero variance in the training data, the optimal bandwidth for that dimension should be large to ensure smoothness. What it is: A specific instantiation of AFFM using two bandwidths for Surface Light Field (SLF) rendering. Difference: It assigns one bandwidth to the spatial domain (high-frequency texture) and another to the angular domain (low color variation). When to choose: Use when rendering surfaces where spatial texture varies rapidly but color changes smoothly with viewing angle. Link: [Two-Bandwidth Gaussian Kernel What it is: A specific instantiation of AFFM for image-based relighting tasks. Difference: It leverages the fact that BRDF reflectance shows more data coherence in the angular domain than in the spatial domain. When to choose: Use when regressing continuous reflectance functions R(\omega, p) from discrete images. Link: Two-Bandwidth Gaussian Kernel for Relighting Time Complexity: The feature mapping itself is O(m \cdot d). The bandwidth search using golden-section search reduces the complexity from polynomial time (brute-force grid search) to logarithmic time. Memory Complexity: O(m \cdot d) to store the frequency matrix W and biases b. Measured Performance: The method significantly outperforms isotropic Fourier features mapping (IFFM) in preserving fine texture details and smooth view transitions, especially when angular and spatial samples are highly imbalanced. It achieves visually lossless reconstruction and higher PSNR on strip-like pattern regression tests. Strengths: Handles heterogeneity of plenoptic functions across dimensions; avoids over-smoothing or under-smoothing in specific dimensions; efficient bandwidth search. Limitations: Requires careful selection or search of bandwidth parameters per dimension; more complex than isotropic methods. When to use: Neural image-based rendering and relighting tasks where input dimensions (e.g., spatial vs. angular) have different frequency characteristics. When not to use: When the signal is isotropic (similar frequency characteristics across all dimensions) or when computational resources for bandwidth search are extremely limited. Origin: Proposed in the paper "Anisotropic Fourier Features for Neural Image-Based Rendering and Relighting". History: The method addresses limitations of Isotropic Fourier Features Mapping (IFFM) introduced by Tancik et al. (2020). IFFM uses a single bandwidth, leading to imbalanced regression for multidimensional signals like plenoptic functions. The authors analyze the influence of bandwidth via the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) and Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel composition. Usage: Applied to neural surface light-field rendering and image-based relighting. name: Reflection-aware NeRF
head: RA-NeRF
body: Reflection-aware NeRF is a neural rendering method that jointly models planar surfaces and explicitly casts reflected rays to capture the source of high-frequency reflections, preventing false geometry duplication along the primary ray. It differs from methods like NeRFReN and MS-NeRF, which decompose the scene into independent components and may cause false geometries, by using a single radiance field and ensuring that if an actual object is observed along the reflected ray, no false duplicate is created along the primary ray at the same depth. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Multi-view images of a scene containing planar reflections. Output: A radiance field model (InstantNGP-based) capable of rendering reflection-aware images and accurate geometry. Data Structures: Plane Parameterization: Each planar surface is defined by s = (p, n, u, w, h). p: Plane center (3D point). n: Plane normal (unit vector). u: Normalized up vector defining the y-axis direction of the plane. w, h: Dimensions of the plane. Radiance Field: Uses the InstantNGP architecture (hash grid + MLP) to predict volume density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Attenuation Field: A separate NGP predicts an attenuation factor to model Fresnel effects and compositing. Algorithm Steps: 1. Plane Annotation and Parameterization: Train an initial InstantNGP model and render depth maps for the input views. Use Segment Anything (SAM) to segment planar regions (e.g., windows) in 2D images. Unproject the four dilated corners of the segmented regions into 3D space using the rendered depth maps. Perform a least-squares fit to these 3D points to initialize the plane parameters s = (p, n, u, w, h). If multiple planes intersect a ray, select the intersection with the nearest plane. 2. Ray Casting and Reflection Handling: For a primary ray \mathbf{r} = (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}), check for intersection with any annotated plane. If an intersection occurs at point \mathbf{x} with normal \mathbf{n}: Calculate the reflected direction \mathbf{d}': \mathbf{d}' = \mathbf{d} - 2(\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{n}) \mathbf{n} Define the reflected ray \mathbf{r}' = (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}'). Query the same NeRF model along \mathbf{r}' to obtain the volume density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} for the source of the reflection. Perform volume rendering along \mathbf{r}' to obtain the reflection color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}'). If no intersection occurs, standard volume rendering proceeds along the primary ray. 3. Color Composition: The final color is composed of the primary rendering \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) and the reflected rendering \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}') modulated by an attenuation field. The attenuation field is optimized to compensate for non-linear RGB space (post-tone mapping), which invalidates direct application of Fresnel equations. Let \alpha be the attenuation factor predicted by the attenuation NGP. The composed color \mathbf{C}{comp}(\mathbf{r}) is calculated as: \mathbf{C}{comp}(\mathbf{r}) = (1 - \alpha) \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) + \alpha \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}') The loss function uses \mathbf{C}{comp}. 4. Training Schedule: Phase 1 (0–50K iterations): Jointly optimize plane geometry s, the radiance field, and the attenuation field using photometric loss: \mathcal{L}{photo} = \| \mathbf{C}{comp}(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{C}{gt}(\mathbf{r}) \|^2 Phase 2 (50K–100K iterations): Fix s. Add sparse edge regularization loss \mathcal{L}{edge} with weight 0.5: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{photo} + 0.5 \mathcal{L}{edge} Phase 3 (100K–200K iterations): Fix the attenuation field. Gradually decay the weight of \mathcal{L}{edge} to restore detail. Parameters: Hardware: Single NVIDIA V100 GPU. Network: InstantNGP (hash grid + MLP) for density/color; additional NGP for attenuation. Scene Parameterization: Contraction parameterization. Iterations: 150K total iterations (50K joint optimization + 50K regularization + 100K decay). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-linear Color Space: Fresnel equations cannot be directly applied because RGB values are in non-linear space after tone mapping. The method solves this by optimizing an adaptable attenuation field instead of using physical Fresnel equations. False Geometry: Without explicit reflection handling, reflections are often modeled as solid objects at the wrong depth (e.g., a shelf reflected in a window appearing as a real shelf). This method prevents that by explaining the reflection via the reflected ray. Time Complexity: The method adds approximately 2 hours to the 5 hours required for vanilla InstantNGP to complete 150K iterations on a single V100 GPU. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Eliminates false geometry duplication caused by reflections; handles non-linear color spaces via learned attenuation; uses a single radiance field for simplicity. Limitations: Requires plane annotation (via SAM and depth unprojection); performance depends on the accuracy of plane detection; may require significant training time for joint optimization. When to use: Scenes with prominent planar reflections (windows, mirrors) where standard NeRF methods produce false geometry. Origin: Introduced in "Planar Reflection-Aware Neural Radiance Fields" by Chen Gao, Yipeng Wang, Changil Kim, Jia-Bin Huang, and Johannes Kopf. History: The method addresses limitations in self-supervised decomposition methods like NeRFReN and MS-NeRF, which can lead to suboptimal decomposition and persistent false geometries. It builds on InstantNGP and SAM for plane detection. Usage: Evaluated on the "Office" dataset, a real-world 360-degree dataset containing pronounced reflections. name: GRAF
head: GRAF (Generative Radiance Fields), Generative Radiance Fields
body:
GRAF is a generative model for 3D-aware image synthesis that learns a conditional radiance field from a collection of unposed 2D images using an adversarial framework. It allows explicit control over camera rotation, translation, shape, and appearance by mapping latent codes and camera parameters to image patches via differentiable volume rendering. Unlike voxel-based approaches (e.g., HoloGAN, PLATONIC GAN) which suffer from memory limitations and discretization artifacts, GRAF uses a continuous representation that scales well with image resolution and incorporates 3D consistency by design without learned projections. Inputs and Outputs: Generator Input: Camera matrix K, camera pose \xi = [R|t], 2D sampling pattern 
u = (u, s), shape code zs \in \mathbb{R}^{Ms}, appearance code za \in \mathbb{R}^{Ma}. Generator Output: A predicted image patch P0 of size K 	imes K pixels. Discriminator Input: A real image patch P extracted from a real image I and the predicted patch P0. Discriminator Output: A scalar score indicating realness. Data Structures: 1. Generate Patch predpatch = generator(K, xi, (ux, uy, s), zs, za) # 3. Sample Real Patch realpatch = extractpatchbilinear(realimage, ux, uy, s, K, W, H) # 4. Discriminator Forward scoregen = discriminator(predpatch) scorereal = discriminator(realpatch) # 5. Compute Losses # Non-saturating GAN loss: f(t) = -log(1 + exp(-t)) lossgen = -math.log(1 + math.exp(-scoregen)) lossdiscreal = -math.log(1 + math.exp(-scorereal)) # R1 Regularization: lambda || grad D(I) ||^2 # Compute gradient of discriminator output w.r.t real patch (simplified) gradreal = [random.uniform(-1, 1) for in range(len(realpatch))] r1reg = lambdar1 sum(gg for g in gradreal) lossdisc = lossdiscreal + r1reg # 6. Chosen such that the principal point is in the center of the image. S: Maximum scale for the virtual patch, S = \min(W, H)/K. N: Number of 3D points sampled along each ray for numerical integration. \lambda: Strength of the R1 regularization term. Learning Rate: 0.0005 for the generator, 0.0001 for the discriminator. Batch Size: 8. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Training Cost: Predicting one color value per pixel is too expensive at training time. The solution is to predict a fixed K 	imes K patch randomly scaled and rotated to provide gradients for the entire field. Continuous Coordinates: The patch coordinates P(u, s) are continuous real numbers, not discrete integers, allowing continuous evaluation of the radiance field. Discriminator Scale: The discriminator is similar to PatchGAN but allows continuous displacements u and scales s. It does not downsample the real image I based on s, but queries sparse locations to retain high-frequency details. Time and Memory Complexity: The continuous representation scales well with image resolution and memory consumption compared to voxel-based methods. Training uses a fixed patch size K 	imes K regardless of the target image resolution, reducing computational cost. Measured Performance: FID scores on Cars dataset at 64^2 resolution: 34 (GRAF) vs 199 (PLATONIC GAN), 59 (HoloGAN), 59 (2D GAN). FID scores on Faces dataset at 512^2 resolution: 25 (GRAF) vs 134 (HoloGAN), 321 (PLATONIC GAN), 66 (2D GAN). Reconstruction Accuracy (MMD-CD) on Cars: 0.044 (GRAF) vs 0.109 (HoloGAN). Strengths: Continuous representation avoids discretization artifacts and memory limitations of voxel-based methods. Incorporates 3D consistency by design through differentiable volume rendering, avoiding entangled latents common in learned projection methods. Allows explicit control over camera rotation, translation, shape, and appearance. Limitations: Requires adversarial training which can be unstable. Relies on the quality of the conditional radiance field representation. When to Use: Suitable for 3D-aware image synthesis from unposed 2D images where explicit control over camera and appearance is desired, and high resolution is needed. When Not to Use: When posed images of a single scene are available (use standard NeRF), or when computational resources for adversarial training are limited. GRAF (Generative Radiance Fields) was introduced in the paper "GRAF: Generative Radiance Fields for 3D-Aware Image Synthesis". It builds on the principles of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). The method addresses the problem of 3D-aware image synthesis from unposed 2D images, a setting where traditional NeRF cannot be directly applied due to the lack of camera poses and the need for a generative model. It was evaluated on synthetic datasets (Chairs, Cars) and real-world datasets (Faces, Cats, Birds).
