name: Flash Cache
head: Fast Cache, Fast Cache approximation
body: Flash Cache is a volumetric inverse rendering method that reduces bias and variance in radiance estimation by using a high-capacity Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) as a control variate for incoming illumination. Unlike prior radiance caches that use low-capacity models, which fail to capture high-frequency and near-field illumination, Flash Cache uses a high-capacity cache. Unlike methods that use a NeRF as a cache but render at only a single evaluation point, which causes bias, Flash Cache uses the cache as a control variate for unbiased estimation. It achieves this by replacing the recursive incoming radiance term with a NeRF-based cache output, evaluated via importance sampling, while maintaining computational tractability through a "Fast Cache" approximation. Flash Cache combines volumetric rendering with physically-based Monte Carlo light transport to optimize scene parameters \Phi (geometry, materials, lighting). The method avoids the recursive evaluation cost of standard path tracing by approximating the volume rendering integral with a single sample point per ray and using a NeRF as a radiance cache for incoming light. Inputs: A set of input images I(\mathbf{o}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o), where \mathbf{o} is the camera origin and \boldsymbol{\omega}o is the viewing direction. Scene representation parameters \Phi. Outputs: Optimized parameters \Phi that minimize the difference between measured images and rendered incident radiance. NeRF Radiance Cache: A neural network (MLP or grid-based) that maps a 3D position \mathbf{x} and direction \boldsymbol{\omega}i to outgoing radiance L{\text{cache}}(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i). This cache acts as a proxy for incoming radiance Li. Mixture of von-Mises Fisher (vMF) Distributions: A spatially-varying probability distribution used to importance-sample incoming directions \boldsymbol{\omega}i based on the expected distribution of incoming radiance. 1. Ray Sampling: For each camera ray (\mathbf{o}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o), sample a single point \mathbf{x}(tk) along the ray. This approximates the volume rendering integral with one sample. 2. Weight Calculation: Compute the quadrature weight wk for the sample point using the density \sigma along the ray: wk = \left(1 - e^{-\sigma(\mathbf{x}(tk)) (t{k+1} - tk)}\right) \exp \left( - \sum{j=1}^{k-1} \sigma(\mathbf{x}(tj))(t{j+1} - tj) \right) where tk is the distance along the ray, and t{k+1} - tk is the step size. 3. Importance Sampling: At the sample point \mathbf{x}(tk), use the spatially-varying mixture of vMF distributions to sample M incoming directions \boldsymbol{\omega}i^{(j)}. The distribution p(\boldsymbol{\omega}i) is parameterized by the vMF mixture to capture spatially-varying illumination effects like occlusion and interreflections. 4. Radiance Cache Query: For each sampled direction \boldsymbol{\omega}i^{(j)}, query the NeRF radiance cache to obtain the estimated incoming radiance L{\text{cache}}(\mathbf{x}(tk), \boldsymbol{\omega}i^{(j)}). This replaces the recursive evaluation of Li. 5. Outgoing Radiance Estimation: Compute the unbiased estimator for outgoing radiance \hat{L}o(\mathbf{x}(tk), \boldsymbol{\omega}o) using the BRDF f, the cache output, and the sampling distribution: \hat{L}o(\mathbf{x}(tk), \boldsymbol{\omega}o) = \frac{1}{M} \sum{j=1}^{M} f(\mathbf{x}(tk), \boldsymbol{\omega}i^{(j)}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) L{\text{cache}}(\mathbf{x}(tk), \boldsymbol{\omega}i^{(j)}) \frac{(\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}i^{(j)})}{p(\boldsymbol{\omega}i^{(j)})} where \mathbf{n} is the surface normal at \mathbf{x}(tk). 6. Incident Radiance Approximation: Approximate the incident radiance Li(\mathbf{o}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) for the camera ray using the single sample and its weight: \hat{L}i(\mathbf{o}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) = wk \hat{L}o(\mathbf{x}(tk), \boldsymbol{\omega}o) The source describes approximating the volume rendering integral with a single sample point. The full integral is \int Lo T \sigma dt, approximated here as wk Lo. 7. Optimization: Minimize the loss function with respect to \Phi: \min{\Phi} \sum{\mathbf{o}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o} \| I(\mathbf{o}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) - Li(\mathbf{o}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o; \Phi) \|^2 + \mathcal{L}{\text{reg}}(\Phi) where Li is the estimated incident radiance. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def flashcacherender(rayorigin, raydirection, tk, deltat, nerfcache, vmfmixture, brdf): """ Renders a single ray using Flash Cache approximation. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, camera origin o. raydirection: 3D vector, camera direction omegao. tk: float, distance to the single sample point along the ray. deltat: float, step size for quadrature weight calculation. nerfcache: Neural Radiance Field function providing density, normal, and radiance. vmfmixture: Spatially-varying mixture of vMFs for sampling omegai. brdf: Physically-based BRDF function f(x, omegai, omegao). Returns: incidentradiance: Scalar, estimated Li(o, omegao). """ # Sample point position xt = rayorigin + tk raydirection # Query NeRF cache for density and normal sigma = nerfcache.getdensity(xt) normal = nerfcache.getnormal(xt) # Compute transmittance T(o, x(tk)) = exp(-int0^{tk} sigma(x(s)) ds) # Approximated by numerical integration along the ray accumulatedsigma = 0.0 steps = 10 dt = tk / steps for s in range(steps): pos = rayorigin + (s dt) raydirection accumulatedsigma += nerfcache.getdensity(pos) dt transmittance = exp(-accumulatedsigma) # Compute quadrature weight wk # wk = (1 - exp(-sigma deltat)) exp(-sum{j=1}^{k-1} sigmaj deltatj) # The exponential term corresponds to the transmittance to the sample point weightk = (1 - exp(-sigma deltat)) transmittance # Importance sample M incoming directions from the vMF mixture M = 10 incomingdirections = vmfmixture.sample(M, xt) outgoingradiancesum = 0.0 for omegai in incomingdirections: # Query cache for incoming radiance Lcache(xt, omegai) lcache = nerfcache.query(xt, omegai) # Evaluate BRDF fval = brdf.evaluate(xt, omegai, raydirection) # Cosine term costheta = dot(normal, omegai) # Evaluate PDF pval = vmfmixture.pdf(omegai, xt) if pval < 1e-8: pval = 1e-8 # Accumulate estimator term outgoingradiancesum += fval lcache costheta / pval outgoingradiance = outgoingradiancesum / M incidentradiance = weightk outgoingradiance return incidentradiance M: Number of Monte Carlo samples for incoming directions. Not given in the sources. \Phi: Scene representation parameters (geometry, materials, lighting). Optimized via gradient descent. \mathcal{L}{\text{reg}}: Regularization term. Not given in the sources. Recursive Evaluation: Naïve use of the rendering equation requires recursive evaluation of Li, leading to high computational cost. Flash Cache avoids this by using the cache as a control variate. Bias: Using low-capacity caches or single-point NeRF evaluation introduces bias. Flash Cache uses a high-capacity cache and control variate to avoid this. Precision: Division by p(\boldsymbol{\omega}i) requires care to avoid numerical instability when the PDF is near zero. A neural field that approximates incoming radiance Li to avoid recursive path tracing. It is cheaper to evaluate than full volume rendering. A variance reduction technique where the NeRF cache output is used to reduce the variance of the Monte Carlo estimator without introducing bias. A spatially-varying distribution used for importance sampling incoming directions, capturing effects like occlusion and interreflections. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples M and the cost of querying the NeRF cache. It is cheaper than recursive path tracing but more expensive than single-point NeRF evaluation. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the NeRF cache parameters and the vMF distribution parameters. Strengths: Reduces bias and variance in inverse rendering. Captures high-frequency and near-field illumination. Preserves thin structures via volumetric representation. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than low-capacity cache methods. Requires careful tuning of the vMF distribution. When to Use: When unbiased estimation of complex lighting effects (interreflections, specularities) is required in volumetric inverse rendering. When Not to Use: When computational resources are extremely limited and bias is acceptable. Flash Cache was introduced by Attal et al. in the paper "Flash Cache: Reducing Bias in Radiance Cache Based Inverse Rendering". It addresses limitations in prior radiance cache methods, which either introduced bias through low-capacity models or single-point evaluations. The method builds on the principles of Neural Radiance Fields and physically-based Monte Carlo rendering. name: C-ToF Gaussian Splatting Image Formation
head: C-ToF GS phasor formation model, C-ToF GS raw image formation model
body: This method defines the forward rendering equations for continuous-wave time-of-flight (C-ToF) cameras within a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework, enabling the reconstruction of dynamic scenes from monocular raw sensor samples. It extends standard Gaussian splatting by modeling the complex physics of modulated light propagation, specifically addressing the under-constrained nature of depth optimization in single-camera dynamic settings where the measured signal (phasor or raw quad) is not the property of interest (depth). Unlike neural volumetric approaches, this primitive-based method achieves 100× faster optimization and rendering while maintaining similar or better accuracy, and it avoids the need for additional constraints like camera motion or RGB integration required by prior works such as ToRF. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{Gk\}{k=1}^N. Camera parameters: modulation frequency f, speed of light c, and intrinsic/extrinsic matrices. For the raw image model: a temporal offset t for each raw frame in the quartet. Outputs: Phasor Model: A complex-valued phasor image \mathbf{p}(\mathbf{x}) at pixel coordinates \mathbf{x}. Raw Image Model: A vector of four raw intensity values \mathbf{q}(\mathbf{x}) corresponding to the phase offsets \phi \in \{0, \pi/2, \pi, 3\pi/2\}. Mean Depth: A scalar depth map d(\mathbf{x}) derived from the Gaussian distribution (computed separately, see below). Each Gaussian Gk stores the following properties: 1. Center: \mathbf{x}k \in \mathbb{R}^3. 2. Covariance: \Sigmak \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, describing 3D scale and rotation. 3. Opacity: ok \in [0, 1]. 4. Reflectivity: rk \in [0, 1], view-dependent, parameterized by 16 spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients. 5. Distance: dk, the distance from the camera center to the Gaussian center \mathbf{x}k. 6. Source Intensity: sk (or constant s), representing emitted signal intensity. Note: View-dependent color \mathbf{c}k is used in standard RGB splatting but is replaced by reflectivity rk and source intensity s in the C-ToF models. 1. Standard C-ToF Physics (Reference) The standard derivation of depth d{\text{ToF}} from raw frames Q\phi assumes simultaneous capture and opaque Lambertian surfaces: d{\text{ToF}} = \frac{c}{4\pi f} \psi, \quad \text{where} \quad \psi = \arctan\left(\frac{Q0 - Q\pi}{Q{\pi/2} - Q{3\pi/2}}\right) The complex phasor representation of the C-ToF signal is: a \cdot W(d{\text{path}}) = a \cdot \exp\left(i \frac{2\pi d{\text{path}} f}{c}\right) = (Q0 - Q\pi) + i(Q{\pi/2} - Q{3\pi/2}) where a = 2A, d{\text{path}} = 2d{\text{ToF}}, phase \psi = \angle W(d{\text{path}}), and amplitude A = |a \cdot W(d{\text{path}})| / 2. 2. C-ToF GS Phasor Formation Model This model renders the complex phasor \mathbf{p}(\mathbf{x}) at pixel \mathbf{x}: \mathbf{p}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{p}^{\text{bg}} TN + \sum{k=1}^N \frac{2s \cdot rk}{dk^2} W(dk) ok \mathcal{G}k^{2\text{D}}(\mathbf{x}) Tk^2 Definitions: \mathbf{p}^{\text{bg}}: Background phasor intensity. TN = \prod{l=1}^N (1 - ol \mathcal{G}l^{2\text{D}}(\mathbf{x})): Final transmittance. Tk = \prod{l=1}^{k-1} (1 - ol \mathcal{G}l^{2\text{D}}(\mathbf{x})): Transmittance before Gaussian k. \mathcal{G}k^{2\text{D}}(\mathbf{x}): 2D Gaussian projection of Gk at pixel \mathbf{x}. W(dk) = \exp(i \psik): Phase weighting function, where \psik = \frac{4\pi dk f}{c}. The term Tk^2 accounts for the round-trip light travel (transmission squared). rk is the view-dependent surface reflectivity. 3. C-ToF GS Raw Image Formation Model This model renders the four raw intensity samples \mathbf{q}(\mathbf{x}) for dynamic scenes, allowing arbitrary time t: \mathbf{q}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{q}^{\text{bg}} TN + \sum{k=1}^N \frac{sk \cdot TN}{dk^2} \phi(dk) ok \mathcal{G}k^{2\text{D}}(\mathbf{x}) Tk^2 Definitions: \mathbf{q}^{\text{bg}}: Background raw intensity vector. \phi(dk): Modulated raw sample quad vector replacing the phasor: \phi(dk) = \begin{bmatrix} \sin(\psik) \\ \cos(\psik) \\ -\sin(\psik) \\ -\cos(\psik) \end{bmatrix} where \psik = \frac{4\pi dk f}{c}. sk \cdot TN: Source intensity modulated by final transmittance (strictly follows source notation sk^{TN}). 4. Mean Gaussian Depth The depth property of interest is computed as the weighted mean of Gaussian distances: d(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{k=1}^N dk ok \mathcal{G}k^{\text{D}}(\mathbf{x}) Tk Note: \mathcal{G}k^{\text{D}}(\mathbf{x}) refers to the 1D depth projection or the contribution of the Gaussian to the depth integral along the ray. Modulation Frequency (f): The frequency of the sinusoidal light modulation. Typical values result in an unambiguous depth range du of 5–10 m. Speed of Light (c): Physical constant. Unambiguous Depth Range (du): du = \frac{c}{2f}. Depths exceeding this range wrap around to [0, du]. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def evaluatesh(shcoeffs, viewdir): """Evaluates 16 spherical harmonic coefficients for a view direction.""" x, y, z = viewdir xx, yy, zz = xx, yy, zz xy, yz, xz = xy, yz, xz # Standard degree-3 SH basis (16 coefficients) basis = np.array([ 0.282095, -0.325742 y, 0.325742 x, -0.325742 z, 0.543139 xy, -1.092287 yz, 0.315392 (3zz - 1), -1.092287 xz, 0.543139 (xx - yy), -0.590044 y (3xx - yy), 2.890611 x y z, -0.457894 z (5zz - 1), 1.445306 z (xx - yy), -0.373175 (7zzzz - 3zz + 2) ]) return np.dot(shcoeffs, basis) # Returns 3-channel vector def projectgaussian(center, cov3d, viewmatrix, projmatrix, imgsize): """Projects 3D Gaussian to 2D screen space.""" # Extract camera pose and intrinsics campos = np.linalg.inv(viewmatrix)[:3, 3] # Transform center to camera space centercam = viewmatrix[:3,:3] @ center + viewmatrix[:3, 3] # Project to 2D center2d = projmatrix[:3,:3] @ centercam center2d /= center2d[2] # Compute 2D covariance (Jacobian approximation) T = np.eye(4) T[:3,:3] = viewmatrix[:3,:3] T[:3, 3] = viewmatrix[:3, 3] J = projmatrix[:3,:3] @ T[:3,:3] W = J @ cov3d @ J.T # Apply perspective division to covariance W[0, 0] /= center2d[2]2 W[1, 1] /= center2d[2]2 W[0, 1] /= center2d[2]2 W[1, 0] /= center2d[2]2 # Clip and extract 2x2 W2d = W[:2,:2] # Ensure positive definite if np.linalg.det(W2d) < 0.01: W2d = np.eye(2) 0.1 return center2d[:2], W2d def renderctofphasor(gaussians, camera, pixelcoords): """Renders the C-ToF phasor image using the phasor formation model.""" H, W = pixelcoords.shape[:2] phasorimage = np.zeros((H, W), dtype=np.complex128) c = 299792458.0 f = camera.modulationfrequency T = np.ones((H, W)) # Running transmittance Tk for k in range(len(gaussians)): g = gaussians[k] # 1. Project Gaussian to 2D mu2d, Sigma2d = projectgaussian(g.center, g.cov3d, camera.viewmatrix, camera.projmatrix, (H, W)) # 2. Evaluate 2D Gaussian at pixel coordinates diff = pixelcoords - mu2d # (H, W, 2) invSigma = np.linalg.inv(Sigma2d) distsq = np.sum((diff @ invSigma) diff, axis=2) # (H, W) G2D = np.exp(-0.5 distsq) # 3. Compute Transmittance Tk and update T Tk = T.copy() T = T (1.0 - g.opacity G2D) # 4. Compute Phase Weighting W(dk) camcenter = camera.viewmatrix[:3, 3] dk = np.linalg.norm(camcenter - g.center) psik = 4 np.pi dk f / c Wdk = np.exp(1j psik) # 5. Compute Reflectivity rk viewdir = camcenter - g.center viewdir = viewdir / np.linalg.norm(viewdir) rk = evaluatesh(g.reflectivitysh, viewdir) # 6. Accumulate contribution term = (2 g.sourceintensity rk / (dk2)) Wdk g.opacity G2D[:,:, np.newaxis] (Tk2)[:,:, np.newaxis] phasorimage += term # Add background phasorimage += camera.backgroundphasor T[:,:, np.newaxis] return phasorimage def renderctofraw(gaussians, camera, pixelcoords): """Renders the C-ToF raw image quartet using the raw image formation model.""" H, W = pixelcoords.shape[:2] rawimage = np.zeros((H, W, 4)) c = 299792458.0 f = camera.modulationfrequency T = np.ones((H, W)) for k in range(len(gaussians)): g = gaussians[k] mu2d, Sigma2d = projectgaussian(g.center, g.cov3d, camera.viewmatrix, camera.projmatrix, (H, W)) diff = pixelcoords - mu2d invSigma = np.linalg.inv(Sigma2d) distsq = np.sum((diff @ invSigma) diff, axis=2) G2D = np.exp(-0.5 distsq) Tk = T.copy() T = T (1.0 - g.opacity G2D) camcenter = camera.viewmatrix[:3, 3] dk = np.linalg.norm(camcenter - g.center) psik = 4 np.pi dk f / c viewdir = camcenter - g.center viewdir = viewdir / np.linalg.norm(viewdir) rk = evaluatesh(g.reflectivitysh, viewdir) phivec = np.array([np.sin(psik), np.cos(psik), -np.sin(psik), -np.cos(psik)]) term = (g.sourceintensity T / (dk2)) phivec g.opacity G2D[:,:, np.newaxis] (Tk2)[:,:, np.newaxis] rawimage += term rawimage += camera.backgroundraw T[:,:, np.newaxis] return rawimage def computemeandepth(gaussians, camera, pixelcoords): """Computes the mean Gaussian depth.""" H, W = pixelcoords.shape[:2] depthmap = np.zeros((H, W)) T = np.ones((H, W)) for k in range(len(gaussians)): g = gaussians[k] mu2d, Sigma2d = projectgaussian(g.center, g.cov3d, camera.viewmatrix, camera.projmatrix, (H, W)) diff = pixelcoords - mu2d invSigma = np.linalg.inv(Sigma2d) distsq = np.sum((diff @ invSigma) diff, axis=2) G2D = np.exp(-0.5 distsq) Tk = T.copy() T = T (1.0 - g.opacity G2D) camcenter = camera.viewmatrix[:3, 3] dk = np.linalg.norm(camcenter - g.center) depthmap += dk g.opacity G2D Tk return depthmap 1. Depth-Phasor Mismatch: Fitting C-ToF raw quads or phasors volumetrically does not guarantee consistency with the rendered mean depth. This discrepancy arises because sine/cosine functions oscillate between convex/concave regions, violating Jensen's inequality equality unless all Gaussians are clustered at the same z-position along each ray. 2. Motion Blur in Quartets: Capturing four frames for C-ToF requires 120 Hz raw capture for 30 Hz depth. If the scene moves within the quartet, depth errors occur because light arrives from different world points. The raw image model allows rendering at arbitrary time t, but correspondence across time must be resolved during optimization. 3. Unambiguous Depth Range: C-ToF cameras can only measure depth unambiguously up to du = c / 2f. Depths over this range map back to [0, du] due to sinusoidal periodicity. Typical du is 5–10 m. 4. Initialization Sensitivity: Optimization is sensitive to initialization and hyperparameters. Unlike ToRF, this method does not require moving the camera, making it suitable for static cameras but potentially brittle without good initialization. Time Complexity: The method achieves 100× faster optimization and rendering compared to neural volumetric approaches. This is due to the use of fast primitive-based scene representation (3D Gaussian Splatting) rather than neural networks. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians N. Each Gaussian stores center, covariance, opacity, and SH coefficients for reflectivity (16 coefficients). Strengths: Fast optimization and rendering. Suitable for static cameras (unlike ToRF which requires camera motion). More stable optimization for dynamic scenes with a single camera compared to F-ToRF. Handles dynamic scenes by rendering raw quads at arbitrary time t. Limitations: Under-constrained depth optimization in single-camera dynamic settings. Depth-Phasor mismatch can lead to geometric inaccuracies if not addressed with heuristics. Sensitive to motion blur within the 4-frame quartet. Limited by the unambiguous depth range of the C-ToF sensor. When to Use: When high-fidelity dynamic 3D reconstruction from a single viewpoint is needed quickly, and the scene is within the unambiguous depth range of the C-ToF camera. When Not to Use: When the scene contains large motions within the 4-frame capture window, or when the scene depth exceeds the unambiguous range of the camera. The method was introduced by Runfeng Li, Mikhail Okunev, Zixuan Guo, Anh Ha Duong, Christian Richardt, Matthew O'Toole, and James Tompkin in the paper "Time of the Flight of the Gaussians: Optimizing Depth Indirectly in Dynamic Radiance Fields". It builds upon 3D Gaussian Splatting and C-ToF imaging principles. The work addresses the challenge of reconstructing dynamic scenes from monocular C-ToF cameras, where depth is not directly measured but derived from raw sensor samples. Previous works like ToRF required additional constraints (camera motion, RGB integration), while F-ToRF struggled with stability in dynamic single-camera settings. This method leverages the speed of Gaussian splatting to achieve faster optimization while incorporating C-ToF physics. name: Generative Neural Feature Fields (GIRAFFE)
head: GIRAFFE Object Representation, Neural Feature Fields
body: Generative Neural Feature Fields (GIRAFFE) is a scene representation framework that models individual objects within a scene using separate, compositional neural feature fields, enabling disentangled control over pose, shape, and appearance. Unlike its siblings NeRF and GRAF, which represent the entire scene with a single monolithic model, GIRAFFE assigns each object its own MLP that outputs a scalar density and a deep feature vector, composing the final scene via a density-weighted sum. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of object-specific latent codes \mathbf{z}s (shape) and \mathbf{z}a (appearance), sampled from a standard normal distribution \mathcal{N}(0, I). Object transformation parameters \mathbf{T} = \{\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{t}, \mathbf{R}\}, where \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is scale, \mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is translation, and \mathbf{R} \in SO(3) is rotation. A 3D query point \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d}. Outputs: A rendered 2D image. Internally, each object field outputs a scalar density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}^+ and a feature vector \mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{R}^{Mf}. Data Structures: Object Field MLP (h\theta): A shared architecture and weights across all objects. It maps encoded inputs to (\sigma, \mathbf{f}). Latent Codes: \mathbf{z}s \in \mathbb{R}^{Ms}, \mathbf{z}a \in \mathbb{R}^{Ma}. Transformation Parameters: \mathbf{T} containing \mathbf{s}, \mathbf{t}, \mathbf{R}. Upsampling CNN: A 2D convolutional network that upsamples the rendered feature map to image resolution. Discriminator: A 2D CNN discriminator for adversarial training. Positional Encoding: Input components t (from \mathbf{x} or \mathbf{d}) are mapped to higher-dimensional features using positional encoding with L frequency octaves: \gamma(t, L) = (\sin(2^0 t\pi), \cos(2^0 t\pi), \dots, \sin(2^L t\pi), \cos(2^L t\pi)) This is applied element-wise to each component of \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{d}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Object Transformation: For each object k, transform the query point \mathbf{x} from object space to scene space using the affine transformation \mathbf{T}: k(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{R} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} s1 & & & \\ & s2 & & \\ & & s3 & \\ & & & s3 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{t} The source formula contains a typographical repetition of s3 in the diagonal matrix. Standard 3D implementation uses a 3 \times 3 scaling matrix \text{diag}(s1, s2, s3). 2. Feature Field Evaluation: For each object, evaluate its specific MLP h\theta using the transformed point k(\mathbf{x}), direction \mathbf{d}, and object-specific latent codes \mathbf{z}s, \mathbf{z}a: (\sigmak, \mathbf{f}k) = h\theta(\gamma(k(\mathbf{x})), \gamma(\mathbf{d}), \mathbf{z}s, \mathbf{z}a) where Mf is the dimensionality of the feature vector \mathbf{f}. 3. Scene Composition: Compose the scene's volume feature field by performing a density-weighted sum of the features from all objects. This is typically done during volume rendering by accumulating density-weighted features along the ray, similar to the standard emission-absorption model but accumulating \mathbf{f} instead of \mathbf{c}. \hat{\mathbf{F}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{f}i where \hat{\mathbf{F}} is the accumulated feature vector for ray \mathbf{r}, and Ti is the transmittance. 4. Image Synthesis: Render a small 2D feature map from the 3D volume feature field using volume rendering. Feed this 2D feature map into an upsampling CNN to produce the final image. 5. Adversarial Training: Train the model using adversarial loss. The synthesized image is compared against real images using a 2D CNN discriminator. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn def positionalencoding(t, L): """ Applies positional encoding element-wise to input t. t: tensor of shape (..., 1) L: number of frequency octaves Returns: tensor of shape (..., 2L) """ freqbands = 2.0 torch.arange(L, device=t.device).float() return torch.cat([torch.sin(freqbands t torch.pi), torch.cos(freqbands t torch.pi)], dim=-1) class ObjectFieldMLP(nn.Module): """ The neural feature field MLP htheta. Shared architecture and weights across objects. """ def init(self, dimx, dimd, dims, dima, dimf): super().init() self.net = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(dimx + dimd + dims + dima, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 1 + dimf)) def forward(self, gammax, gammad, zs, za): x = torch.cat([gammax, gammad, zs, za], dim=-1) out = self.net(x) return torch.relu(out[:, 0:1]), out[:, 1:] class GIRAFFE: def init(self, numobjects, dimf, dims, dima, octavesx, octavesd): self.numobjects = numobjects self.dimf = dimf self.octavesx = octavesx self.octavesd = octavesd # Shared MLP across all objects self.objectfield = ObjectFieldMLP(2octavesx, 2octavesd, dims, dima, dimf) # Upsampling CNN self.upsampler = nn.Sequential( nn.ConvTranspose2d(dimf, 64, 4, 2, 1), nn.ReLU(), nn.ConvTranspose2d(64, 3, 4, 2, 1), nn.Tanh()) # Discriminator self.discriminator = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(3, 64, 4, 2, 1), nn.LeakyReLU(0.2), nn.Conv2d(64, 128, 4, 2, 1), nn.BatchNorm2d(128), nn.LeakyReLU(0.2), nn.Conv2d(128, 1, 4, 1, 0), nn.Sigmoid()) def transformpoint(self, x, s, t, R): """ Transforms point x from object space to scene space. x: (N, 3), s: (3,), t: (3,), R: (3, 3) """ # Source formula uses a 4x4 matrix with repeated s3, which is a typo for 3D scaling. # We implement standard 3D scaling: R diag(s) x + t S = torch.diag(s) return torch.matmul(torch.matmul(R, S), x.t()).t() + t def render(self, rayorigins, raydirections, objectparams, zs, za, numsamples): """ rayorigins: (H, W, 3), raydirections: (H, W, 3) objectparams: list of dicts with 's', 't', 'R' zs: (numobjects, dims), za: (numobjects, dima) """ H, W = rayorigins.shape[:2] rayoriginsflat = rayorigins.reshape(-1, 3) raydirectionsflat = raydirections.reshape(-1, 3) numrays = rayoriginsflat.shape[0] # Sample points along rays tvals = torch.linspace(0, 1, numsamples, device=rayorigins.device) xsamples = rayoriginsflat[:, None,:] + raydirectionsflat[:, None,:] tvals[None,:, None] # Initialize accumulation totalfeature = torch.zeros(numrays, self.dimf, device=rayorigins.device) transmittance = torch.ones(numrays, device=rayorigins.device) for i, obj in enumerate(objectparams): # Transform points to object space xobj = self.transformpoint(xsamples, obj['s'], obj['t'], obj['R']) # Positional encoding gammax = torch.cat([positionalencoding(xobj[..., j:j+1], self.octavesx) for j in range(3)], dim=-1) gammad = torch.cat([positionalencoding(raydirectionsflat[:, j:j+1], self.octavesd) for j in range(3)], dim=-1) # Get latent codes for this object zsobj = zs[i:i+1].expand(numrays, -1) zaobj = za[i:i+1].expand(numrays, -1) # Evaluate MLP sigma, f = self.objectfield(gammax, gammad, zsobj, zaobj) # Volume rendering step deltat = tvals[1] - tvals[0] alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltat) weight = transmittance[:, None] alpha totalfeature += weight f transmittance = (1.0 - alpha).mean(dim=1) # Reshape to feature map (H, W, dimf) featuremap = totalfeature.reshape(H, W, self.dimf).permute(2, 0, 1) # Upsample to image image = self.upsampler(featuremap) image = image.permute(1, 2, 0) return image def computeloss(self, predimage, realimage): l1loss = nn.functional.l1loss(predimage, realimage) preddisc = self.discriminator(predimage.permute(0, 3, 1, 2)) realdisc = self.discriminator(realimage.permute(0, 3, 1, 2)) advloss = nn.functional.binarycrossentropy(preddisc, torch.oneslike(preddisc)) + \ nn.functional.binarycrossentropy(realdisc, torch.zeroslike(realdisc)) return l1loss + advloss Performance: GIRAFFE enables disentangled control over scene elements, allowing for fine-grained manipulation of pose, shape, and appearance. This comes at the cost of increased model complexity compared to single-NeRF approaches, as each object requires its own set of parameters and latent codes. Strengths: Disentangled representation, compositional scene modeling, and generative capabilities. Limitations: Requires explicit object segmentation or detection to assign latent codes and transformations to objects, which is not inherent to the method. The density-weighted sum composition assumes objects are opaque or semi-opaque and can be ordered or blended appropriately. GIRAFFE was introduced as an extension of GRAF (Generative RADiance Fields). While GRAF represents the entire scene with a single generative model, GIRAFFE assigns each object its own neural feature field, allowing for compositional scene modeling. The framework builds on the differentiable volume rendering principles established in prior radiance field optimization methods [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28 GIRAFFE: Representing Scenes as Compositional Generative Neural Feature Fields, https://github.com/chaerinkong/paper-reviews/issues/63, fetched 2026-10-28

name: NeRDF Learning via Knowledge Distillation
head: Multi-View Distillation, NeRDF Distillation, Teacher-Student NeRF Distillation
body: NeRDF Learning via Knowledge Distillation is a training framework that accelerates the optimization of Neural Radiance Distribution Fields (NeRDF) by using a pre-trained teacher NeRF to generate dense, diverse pseudo-training views. Unlike standard NeRF optimization which relies solely on sparse input camera poses, this method synthesizes interpolated viewpoints to guide the student model, thereby avoiding the spatial high-frequency artifacts that occur when training a duplex field from scratch. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) by decoupling the geometry/radiance learning phase from the sparse input data constraint, enabling faster convergence and higher efficiency. The method trains a student NeRDF to mimic the radiance distribution of a teacher NeRF. The process involves generating synthetic views, encoding rays, and minimizing losses that match both pixel colors and volume density distributions. Inputs: Sparse set of training images with known camera poses. A pre-trained teacher NeRF model (e.g., TensoRF). Spherical coordinate ranges (r{min}, r{max}), (\theta{min}, \theta{max}), (\phi{min}, \phi{max}) derived from the training camera poses. Outputs: A trained student NeRDF model capable of real-time view synthesis. Distillation View: Defined by spherical coordinates (rs, \thetas, \phis) relative to the scene origin, converted to Cartesian coordinates for ray generation. Ray Encoding: A method capturing rich ray information, including position and direction, used as input to the student network. Volume Density Distribution: The scalar field \sigma predicted by the student and teacher networks, used for density matching. 1. Teacher Preparation: Train or load a pre-trained teacher NeRF model (e.g., TensoRF) on the sparse input images. 2. Pose Alignment and Coordinate Conversion: Align the view directions of all training cameras with the scene origin. Convert camera poses into spherical coordinates (r, \theta, \phi) relative to the origin. 3. Online View Sampling: Randomly sample radius rs \sim U(r{min}, r{max}), angle \thetas \sim U(\theta{min}, \theta{max}), and \phis \sim U(\phi{min}, \phi{max}). Convert sampled spherical coordinates to Cartesian coordinates to generate interpolated camera poses. Repeat to generate N{distill} distillation views (typically 1,000). 4. Synthesis of Pseudo-Training Data: Render images and volume density fields from the teacher NeRF using the sampled distillation viewpoints. 5. Student Training (Distillation Phase): Train the student NeRDF on the distilled views for the first half of the optimization iterations. Compute the color loss between student and teacher rendered colors. Compute the volume density constraint loss, matching the student's volume density distribution to the teacher's. 6. Fine-Tuning: Fine-tune the student NeRDF on the original sparse training images for the second half of the optimization iterations to sharpen appearance. The rendering equation for a ray \mathbf{r} remains the standard emission-absorption model [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \sigmai is the density, \deltai is the step size, \mathbf{c}i is the color, and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance. The total loss \mathcal{L} for the student network includes: 1. Color Loss (\mathcal{L}{color}): Mean Squared Error (MSE) between student and teacher rendered colors. 2. Density Loss (\mathcal{L}{density}): Matching loss between the volume density distribution of the student NeRDF and the teacher NeRF. \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{color} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{density} where \lambda is a weighting factor. Number of distillation views: 1,000. Teacher Model: TensoRF. Learning Rate: 10^{-3} initially, decaying exponentially to 10^{-5}. Training Split: 50% of iterations on distilled views, 50% on original training images. Spatial Artifacts: Training a neural duplex radiance field from scratch without distillation fails to match the high fidelity of original NeRFs and produces spatial high-frequency artifacts. Camera Pose Subspace: For real-world captures, camera poses may occupy a small subspace; the spherical sampling strategy ensures meaningful interpolated viewpoints even in this case. Training Time: The distillation process increases training time compared to standard NeRF due to the generation of pseudo-data and two-phase optimization. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainnerdfwithdistillation(sparseimages, sparseposes, teachernerf, numdistillviews=1000, totaliterations=10000): """ Train a student NeRDF using knowledge distillation from a teacher NeRF. """ studentnerdf = initializestudentnerdf() # Step 2: Align poses and convert to spherical coordinates origin = getsceneorigin(sparseposes) sphericalranges = converttosphericalranges(sparseposes, origin) rmin, rmax = sphericalranges['r'] thetamin, thetamax = sphericalranges['theta'] phimin, phimax = sphericalranges['phi'] # Step 3 & 4: Generate distillation views and teacher renderings distillationviews = [] teachertargets = [] for in range(numdistillviews): # Random sampling in spherical coordinates rs = uniformsample(rmin, rmax) thetas = uniformsample(thetamin, thetamax) phis = uniformsample(phimin, phimax) # Convert to Cartesian for camera pose campos = sphericaltocartesian(rs, thetas, phis, origin) campose = generatecamerapose(campos, origin) # Render from teacher teachercolor, teacherdensity = teachernerf.render(campose) distillationviews.append(campose) teachertargets.append((teachercolor, teacherdensity)) # Step 5: Distillation Phase (First half of iterations) halfiter = totaliterations // 2 for i in range(halfiter): # Sample a distillation view idx = randomindex(len(distillationviews)) pose = distillationviews[idx] targetcolor, targetdensity = teachertargets[idx] # Student forward pass studentcolor, studentdensity = studentnerdf.render(pose) # Compute losses losscolor = mse(studentcolor, targetcolor) lossdensity = mse(studentdensity, targetdensity) # Total loss with weighting factor lambda loss = losscolor + 1.0 lossdensity # Backpropagate and update student studentnerdf.update(loss) # Step 6: Fine-Tuning Phase (Second half of iterations) for i in range(halfiter, totaliterations): # Sample from original sparse training images idx = randomindex(len(sparseimages)) pose = sparseposes[idx] targetcolor = sparseimages[idx] # Student forward pass studentcolor, studentdensity = studentnerdf.render(pose) # Compute color loss only (standard supervision) loss = mse(studentcolor, targetcolor) # Backpropagate and update student studentnerdf.update(loss) return studentnerdf A variant where the input data is augmented with synthetic renderings generated by a fully trained teacher model (e.g., NeRF) to improve quantitative metrics. It uses a 10x10 grid of renderings from the teacher. On the Real Forward-Facing dataset, this variant outperforms NeRF quantitatively in PSNR (e.g., Fern: 26.06 vs 26.92, Flower: 28.90 vs 28.57, Fortress: 32.60 vs 32.94) but requires increased training time. Time Complexity: Training time is increased compared to standard NeRF due to the two-phase optimization and teacher rendering. Inference speed is comparable to NeLF (~21 FPS) and ~100x faster than original NeRF. Memory Complexity: The student model uses an 8-layer MLP, comparable to NeRF. GPU memory consumption is quantified for WebGL applications. Strengths: Avoids spatial artifacts from scratch training; leverages dense teacher knowledge; fast inference. Limitations: Increased training time; requires a pre-trained teacher model. When to use: When high-fidelity view synthesis is required with limited input views and fast inference is desired. When not to use: When training time is a critical constraint and standard NeRF performance is acceptable. The method is based on knowledge distillation principles. It was proposed to address the limitations of training neural duplex radiance fields from scratch, which suffer from spatial artifacts. The approach extends the R2L method [41] by incorporating volume density matching. The teacher model TensoRF was chosen for its high efficiency in reconstruction and synthesis. name: Fourier Feature Encoding
head: Fourier Feature Mapping, Fourier Feature Positional Encoding, Fourier Features, NeRF Positional Encoding, Positional Encoding (NeRF), Sinusoidal Positional Encoding
body: Fourier Feature Encoding is a preprocessing technique applied to scene coordinates and viewing directions to address the spectral bias of neural networks, which naturally favor low-frequency functions. By mapping input vectors into a high-dimensional space via sinusoidal functions, it provides high-frequency features directly to the network, greatly improving fine detail reconstruction in rendered views. It sets itself apart from standard positional encodings (like those in Transformers) by using fixed, non-trainable sinusoidal bases rather than learned embeddings, and from learnable frequency mappings by relying on a deterministic geometric progression of frequencies. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A vector \mathbf{v} representing either a 3D scene coordinate \mathbf{x} or a viewing direction \mathbf{d}. Output: A higher-dimensional vector \gamma(\mathbf{v}) containing sinusoidal features. Data Structures: The encoding is a static transformation applied element-wise or vector-wise. No persistent data structures are required beyond the input vector and the output vector. Parameters: L (or N): The number of frequency bands (or encoding dimensionality parameter). The output dimension is 2L. Typical values: In the original NeRF implementation, N=10 for coordinates \mathbf{x} and N=4 for directions \mathbf{d}. Formulas: The positional encoding function \gamma maps a vector \mathbf{v} to a vector of sines and cosines with exponentially increasing frequencies: \gamma(\mathbf{v}) = \left( \sin(2^0 \pi \mathbf{v}), \cos(2^0 \pi \mathbf{v}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{v}), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{v}) \right) The neural radiance field F{\Theta} is reformulated as a composition F{\Theta} = F^{\prime}{\Theta} \circ \gamma, where F^{\prime}{\Theta} is the MLP that takes the encoded features: (\mathbf{c}, \sigma) = F^{\prime}{\Theta}(\gamma(\mathbf{x}), \gamma(\mathbf{d})) Numbered Steps: 1. Normalize the input coordinate \mathbf{x} and direction \mathbf{d} to the range [-1, 1]. 2. For each component v of the input vector: a. Initialize an empty list of features. b. For b from 0 to L-1: i. Calculate frequency \omega = 2^b \pi. ii. Append \sin(\omega v) to the list. iii. Append \cos(\omega v) to the list. 3. Concatenate the features for all components of the input vector to form the final encoded vector. 4. Pass the encoded vector into the MLP F^{\prime}{\Theta}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def fourierfeatureencoding(v, numbands): """ Encodes a vector v using Fourier features. Args: v: A list or array of floats (coordinates or direction components), expected to be in range [-1, 1]. numbands: Integer L, the number of frequency bands. Returns: A list of floats representing the encoded features. """ features = [] for val in v: for b in range(numbands): # Frequency is 2^b pi freq = (2 b) math.pi features.append(math.sin(freq val)) features.append(math.cos(freq val)) return features def nerfforward(x, d, xbands, dbands, mlp): """ Simulates the forward pass of a NeRF with Fourier Feature Encoding. Args: x: 3D coordinate vector [x, y, z]. d: Viewing direction vector [dx, dy, dz]. xbands: Number of bands for coordinates (e.g., 10). dbands: Number of bands for directions (e.g., 4). mlp: A function representing the MLP F'Theta. Returns: Color c and density sigma. """ # Encode inputs xencoded = fourierfeatureencoding(x, xbands) dencoded = fourierfeatureencoding(d, dbands) # Concatenate encoded inputs inputfeatures = xencoded + dencoded # Pass through MLP c, sigma = mlp(inputfeatures) return c, sigma Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: High-frequency bands (2^{L-1}) can lead to numerical instability if inputs are not strictly normalized to [-1, 1]. Values outside this range may cause oscillations that the network cannot resolve or gradients that vanish/explode. Boundary Conditions: The encoding is periodic. If the scene geometry extends beyond the normalized bounding box, the encoding wraps around, potentially causing artifacts. Degenerate Input: If the input vector is zero, the encoding results in zeros for sines and ones for cosines, which is valid but provides no directional information for that component. Time Complexity: The encoding itself is O(L \cdot D), where D is the input dimension (3 for coordinates/directions). This is negligible compared to the MLP evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(L \cdot D) to store the encoded vector. No additional memory is required for the encoding process itself. Strengths: Significantly improves the reconstruction of high-frequency details (textures, sharp edges) compared to unencoded MLPs. It is simple to implement and requires no additional training parameters for the encoder. Limitations: The fixed frequency spectrum may not be optimal for all scenes. Very high frequencies can lead to aliasing or optimization difficulties if the sampling rate along rays is insufficient. When to use: Standard for NeRF-like implicit radiance fields where high-frequency detail is desired. When not to use: If the scene is inherently low-frequency or if computational resources are extremely constrained and the overhead of encoding is non-trivial (though it usually is not). Fixed sinusoidal positional encoding was introduced in the seminal paper "NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis" by Mildenhall et al. in 2020. It was motivated by the observation that standard MLPs struggle to learn high-frequency functions due to spectral bias. The technique was later analyzed theoretically using Neural Tangent Kernels. Modern variants include trainable parametric encodings, integral encodings, and hierarchical variants. name: Voxel-based Representation
head: Voxel Grids, 3D Grids, Discrete Radiance Fields
body: Voxel-based representations use discrete 3D grids to store volumetric features, density, or color. This approach trades spatial continuity for memory efficiency and inference speed, with resolution limits imposed by grid size. The family builds on the differentiability of the forward rendering operator and the propagation of gradients through the integration steps. The core mechanism is the evaluation of the volume rendering equation and the computation of gradients with respect to scene parameters (density, geometry, transfer functions, camera poses). The standard emission-absorption model computes the color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} as: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \sigmai is the density, \deltai is the step size, \mathbf{c}i is the color, and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance. FastNeRF is a neural rendering method that accelerates inference by factorizing the view-dependent radiance field into position-dependent and direction-dependent components, enabling efficient caching of intermediate network outputs. It solves the problem of high computational cost in standard NeRF by avoiding MLP evaluations at inference time, instead relying on hardware-accelerated ray tracing and grid lookups to achieve interactive frame rates (200Hz) on consumer hardware. It differs from its siblings, such as C-NeRF and V4D, by using a low-rank inner-product factorization to decouple spatial and directional information, whereas other methods may use spherical harmonics or explicit voxel grids for density only. C-NeRF is a voxel-based radiance field representation that uses a 3D convolutional neural network (CNN) to generate feature volumes, which are then decoded by a NeRF-like multi-layer perceptron (MLP) to predict density and color. C-NeRF serves as a baseline for dynamic scene representation. When decomposing 4D volumes into a weighted summation of shared 3D volumes, this factorization is referred to as Volume Basis. V4D is a voxel-based architecture for 4D novel view synthesis in dynamic scenes that models the 4D neural radiance field directly without requiring a canonical space. It distinguishes itself from continuous neural radiance fields and other voxel-based methods by using separate 3D voxel grids for density and texture, combined with a conditional positional encoding (CPE) module and a look-up table (LUT) refinement module to mitigate the over-smoothing effects of total variation regularization. Unlike its sibling TiNeuVox which uses a canonical space and position offsets, V4D relies on temporal concatenation and total variation loss to enforce temporal consistency, resulting in longer training times but faster inference. RenderNet is a differentiable rendering convolutional neural network that generates 2D images from 3D voxel grids by jointly learning visibility computation and pixel color calculation (shading). Unlike traditional rasterization or ray tracing which rely on discrete, non-differentiable operations like z-buffering, RenderNet uses a CNN to encode spatial occlusion and shading automatically. It is distinguished from sibling methods like FastNeRF and VoxGRAF by its explicit use of a "Projection Unit" that collapses the 3D depth dimension into 2D feature maps while learning visibility, rather than relying on continuous volume rendering equations or sparse voxel structures. It handles low-resolution or noisy voxel inputs more robustly than mesh-based differentiable renderers. ExBluRF is a novel view synthesis method designed to reconstruct sharp 3D scenes from extreme motion-blurred images by jointly optimizing voxel-based radiance fields and 6-DOF camera trajectories. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like FastNeRF and C-NeRF, which focus on static scene acceleration, by addressing the ill-posed problem of deblurring through a trajectory-based blur model and memory-efficient voxel representations, unlike DeblurNeRF which relies on spatially varying 2D kernels and MLPs. Part-based MHE-augmented NeRF is a method for learning neural volumetric videos of dynamic humans from sparse view videos in minutes with competitive visual quality. It addresses the slow convergence of per-scene optimization methods by decomposing the canonical human body into multiple anatomical parts, assigning each part its own Multiresolution Hash Encoding (MHE)-augmented NeRF network with varying resolutions to efficiently distribute representational power. Unlike single-resolution voxelized representations or continuous implicit functions that treat the entire body uniformly, this method leverages a 2D motion parameterization scheme on a parametric mesh (SMPL) to accelerate deformation field learning. Object-NeRF is a composition model that separates and edits objects within a scene using a hybrid voxel-based approach with jointly optimized voxel grid features and MLP parameters. It differs from its siblings by explicitly partitioning the scene into a background "scene branch" and foreground "object branch," allowing for the shifting, addition, or removal of specific objects without retraining the entire radiance field. VoxGRAF is a 3D-aware Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) that replaces the coordinate-based Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) scene representation with a sparse voxel grid generator. It solves the problem of slow rendering and viewpoint/content entanglement inherent in previous 3D-aware GANs by enabling fast, 3D-consistent image synthesis with a single forward pass. Unlike its siblings FastNeRF, C-NeRF, V4D, RenderNet, and Object-NeRF which often rely on dense coordinate-based queries or hybrid rendering, VoxGRAF generates the entire 3D radiance field on a sparse voxel grid using 3D convolutions, allowing for efficient rendering via alpha composition without reducing sample counts. Voxel-based Gaussian Splatting (VoxGS) is a volume representation that places isometric 3D Gaussians at the fixed centroids of a regular 3D voxel grid to enable efficient Computed Tomography (CT) volume extraction and differentiable X-ray rendering. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) which optimizes primitive positions and uses spherical harmonics for view-dependent color, VoxGS fixes positions and removes color coefficients, retaining only opacity, scale, and rotation to support isotropic density modeling. This design solves the instability and inaccurate volume extraction issues associated with applying original 3DGS directly to CT data. Gaussian Voxel Kernel Functions (GVKF) is a method for efficient 3D surface reconstruction in open scenes that establishes a continuous scene representation based on discrete 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) through kernel regression. It differs from explicit 3DGS by using implicit continuous representation via kernel regression instead of explicit discrete summation, reducing memory consumption and improving surface continuity. Unlike standard volume rendering which relies on continuous sampling, GVKF integrates fast 3DGS rasterization with implicit scene representations to achieve high-fidelity open scene surface reconstruction without computationally intensive volume rendering. This method converts OpenVDB volumetric datasets into a set of non-overlapping 3D Gaussian particles to enable memory-efficient, lossy representation with Level of Detail (LOD) support, rendered via forward ray marching using NVIDIA OptiX. It differs from standard voxel-based representations by replacing the discrete grid sampling with continuous Gaussian primitives, allowing for hardware-accelerated bounding box intersections and real-time performance with millions of particles, while maintaining compatibility with traditional volume rendering transfer functions. Global Scene Generator (GSN) is a generative model that synthesizes unconstrained 3D scenes by decomposing them into local regions using a global generator and a locally conditioned radiance field. Unlike dictionary-based memory models that limit unseen viewpoints, GSN uses a learned scene prior to allow extrapolation beyond given observations. It sets itself apart from sibling voxel-based methods by explicitly generating a 2D latent "floorplan" grid to condition multiple local radiance fields, rather than storing static features in a 3D voxel grid. Definition: A framework that synthesizes realistic images given object voxels as input, providing editing functionalities for illumination, object geometry, and appearance. Parameters: Initial voxel resolution is 100^3. Scene volume is V \in 128^3 \times 4. Environment map resolution (realism variant) is 32 \times 32, processed by convolutional layers to extract a latent code supplied to NVR+. Performance: At 25^3 voxel resolution, performance decreases gracefully but still produces plausible outputs. Comparison: NVR captures color and structure but smooths fine texture details. NVR+ accurately renders geometry and texture, realistically synthesizing shadows, specular reflections, and highlights. Usage: Trained on ShapeNet chair category. Tested on Pix3D and Ikea datasets for sofas, tables, and miscellaneous objects. Not given in the sources. Neural Voxel Renderer: Learning an Accurate and Controllable Rendering Tool, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr42600.2020.00546, fetched 2026-10-26

name: FastNeRF
head: Factorized NeRF, Factorized Neural Radiance Fields
body: FastNeRF is a neural rendering method that accelerates the inference of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by factorizing the view-dependent color function into position-dependent and direction-dependent components, enabling efficient caching of intermediate radiance values. It solves the problem of high computational cost in standard NeRF, which requires hundreds of MLP evaluations per pixel, by reducing inference to memory-bound cache lookups and dot products, achieving speeds over 3000 times faster than the original NeRF. It differs from its siblings, such as C-NeRF and VoxGRAF, by explicitly separating the 5D radiance field into two independent low-dimensional manifolds (position and direction) to allow for compact, sparse caching of a "deep radiance map" rather than caching the full 5D function or using smaller local MLPs. FastNeRF builds on Voxel-based Representation by replacing the single monolithic MLP with two factorized networks and caching their outputs. Inputs: A set of training images with known camera poses; a bounding box V enclosing the scene. Outputs: A trained position-dependent network \mathcal{F}{\text{pos}}, a direction-dependent network \mathcal{F}{\text{dir}}, and optionally, cached grids for inference. 1. Position Cache: A sparse 3D grid storing outputs of \mathcal{F}{\text{pos}}. Fields: Density \sigma (scalar) and a deep radiance map components (\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}) (each D-dimensional vectors). Layout: Stored as dense 16-bit floating point values in a grid of size k^3 (or sparse subset thereof). 2. Direction Cache: A sparse 2D grid storing outputs of \mathcal{F}{\text{dir}}. Fields: Weight vector \boldsymbol{\beta} (D-dimensional). Layout: Stored as dense 16-bit floating point values in a grid of size l^2 (parameterized by spherical coordinates \theta, \phi). 3. Collision Mesh: A triangle mesh derived from the density volume \sigma using Marching Cubes, used for hardware-accelerated ray tracing to skip empty space. \mathcal{F}{\text{pos}}: An 8-layer MLP with 384 hidden units (256 for LLFF scenes). Input: 3D position \mathbf{p}. Output: \{\sigma, (\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w})\}. \mathcal{F}{\text{dir}}: A 4-layer MLP with 128 hidden units. Input: 2D viewing direction \mathbf{d} (parameterized as a unit vector or spherical coordinates). Output: \boldsymbol{\beta}. Positional Encoding: Applied to inputs of both MLPs, as in standard NeRF. 1. Define bounding box V for the scene. 2. Sample k uniform values for x, y, z within V and l uniform values for \theta \in [0, \pi], \phi \in [0, 2\pi]. 3. Compute \mathcal{F}{\text{pos}} for all position combinations and \mathcal{F}{\text{dir}} for all direction combinations to initialize caches (optional, primarily for initialization or analysis; training typically optimizes the MLPs directly on rendered images). 4. Train \mathcal{F}{\text{pos}} and \mathcal{F}{\text{dir}} jointly using the standard NeRF loss (MSE between rendered and ground truth colors). 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel, generate a ray \mathbf{r} defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. 2. Empty Space Skipping: Intersect \mathbf{r} with the collision mesh. Start integration only after the first hit. 3. Sampling: Uniformly sample N points \mathbf{p}i along the ray within the mesh bounds. 4. Cache Lookup: For each \mathbf{p}i, lookup \sigmai and (\mathbf{u}i, \mathbf{v}i, \mathbf{w}i) from the Position Cache using nearest-neighbor interpolation. For the ray direction \mathbf{d}, lookup \boldsymbol{\beta} from the Direction Cache using trilinear sampling (on the \theta, \phi grid). 5. Color Computation: Compute color \mathbf{c}i for each sample point: \mathbf{c}i = \boldsymbol{\beta}^T \cdot (\mathbf{u}i, \mathbf{v}i, \mathbf{w}i) = \sum{j=1}^D \betaj (u{i,j}, v{i,j}, w{i,j}) where D is the number of components (typically 8 for Synthetic 360, 6 for LLFF). 6. Volume Rendering: Integrate color and density along the ray using the standard NeRF volume rendering equation [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) and \deltai is the distance between samples. 7. Termination: Terminate ray integration once transmittance Ti drops below a threshold (saturation). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def fastnerfinfer(rayorigin, raydirection, poscache, dircache, D, k, l): """ Renders a single pixel using FastNeRF caches. Args: rayorigin: (3,) array, camera origin. raydirection: (3,) array, normalized ray direction. poscache: Sparse 3D grid storing {sigma, u, v, w}. Access via nearest neighbor interpolation. dircache: Sparse 2D grid storing beta. Access via trilinear interpolation on theta/phi. D: Number of components (e.g., 8). k: Grid resolution for position (x,y,z). l: Grid resolution for direction (theta, phi). Returns: color: (3,) array, RGB color. """ # 1. Empty Space Skipping using Collision Mesh # Note: Collision mesh is pre-computed from density volume via Marching Cubes. hitpoint, tnear, tfar = intersectraywithmesh(rayorigin, raydirection) if hitpoint is None: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Background color # 2. Sample points along the ray within the mesh bounds numsamples = 1024 # Typical value, can vary samples = [] for i in range(numsamples): t = tnear + (tfar - tnear) (i + 0.5) / numsamples p = rayorigin + raydirection t samples.append(p) # 3. Lookup from Caches # Pre-fetch direction weights once per ray # Convert raydirection to spherical coordinates (theta, phi) theta = math.acos(raydirection[2]) # Assuming z-up or standard convention phi = math.atan2(raydirection[1], raydirection[0]) beta = dircache.trilinearsample(theta, phi) # Shape: (D,) # 4. Compute Color and Density for each sample sigmas = [] colors = [] for p in samples: # Lookup position cache sigma, u, v, w = poscache.nearestneighborsample(p) sigmas.append(sigma) # Compute color via inner product # c = beta. (u, v, w) # u, v, w are each D-dimensional vectors color = dotproduct(beta, u, v, w, D) colors.append(color) # 5. Volume Rendering Integration totalcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) transmittance = 1.0 # Calculate step size delta delta = (tfar - tnear) / numsamples for i in range(numsamples): sigma = sigmas[i] c = colors[i] # Alpha for this segment alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma delta) # Weight for this segment weight = transmittance alpha # Accumulate color totalcolor += weight c # Update transmittance transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) # Early termination if transmittance is negligible if transmittance < 1e-4: break return totalcolor def dotproduct(beta, u, v, w, D): """ Computes the inner product of beta with the deep radiance map (u, v, w). """ r = 0.0 g = 0.0 b = 0.0 for i in range(D): r += beta[i] u[i] g += beta[i] v[i] b += beta[i] w[i] return (r, g, b) D (Components): Dimensionality of the deep radiance map and direction weights. Typical values: 8 for NeRF Synthetic 360 scenes, 6 for LLFF scenes. k (Position Grid Size): Number of uniform samples for each worldspace coordinate (x, y, z) in the position cache bounding box. Typical values: 512, 768, 1024. l (Direction Grid Size): Number of uniform samples for each ray direction coordinate (\theta, \phi). Typical values: 256, 512. Grid Resolution: Number of divisions of the longest side of the bounding volume. Typical values: 256^3, 384^3, 512^3, 768^3, 1024^3. Aliasing: Caching the model to a grid after training can introduce aliasing artifacts, leading to a decrease in metrics as a function of grid resolution. Memory Limits: Discretizing the full 5D space with 512 bins per dimension would require ~176 TB, which is infeasible. FastNeRF reduces this to ~54 GB (dense) or ~3 GB (sparse). Mesh Complexity: For density volumes larger than 512^3, the collision mesh must be downsampled by a factor of two to reduce complexity. Uncached Performance: Without caching, FastNeRF is slower than standard NeRF due to larger MLPs (384 hidden units vs 256). Provides analytical formulas to calculate the memory footprint of the position-dependent and direction-dependent caches, solving the problem of determining if a configuration fits in hardware memory. Time Complexity: Inference is O(N) where N is the number of samples per ray, dominated by cache lookups and dot products, avoiding MLP evaluations. Memory Complexity: Caching standard NeRF is O(k^3 l^2). FastNeRF reduces this to O(k^3 (1 + 3D) + l^2 D). For k=l=1024, D=8, dense cache size is ~54 GB, compared to ~5600 TB for standard NeRF. Sparse cache size is ~3 GB. Performance: Renders high-fidelity photorealistic images at 200Hz on high-end consumer GPUs. It is on average more than 3000x faster than NeRF. On Nvidia Tesla V100, it renders 300x300 pixel images of a face at 30 fps in telepresence scenarios, ~50x faster than NeRF. Strengths: Extremely fast inference; compatible with hardware-accelerated ray tracing; maintains visual quality comparable to NeRF. Limitations: High memory usage for caches (several GBs); aliasing artifacts at lower resolutions; slower than NeRF when not cached. When to use: Scenarios requiring interactive rates on consumer hardware, such as mobile devices, mixed reality, and telepresence. When not to use: Memory-constrained embedded systems without large caches; scenarios where training speed is the primary bottleneck (FastNeRF does not address training speed). FastNeRF was proposed by Garbin et al. in March 2021. It was motivated by the need for real-time neural rendering on mobile and mixed reality devices. The method draws inspiration from real-time computer graphics techniques for approximating the rendering equation, such as spherical harmonics, by factorizing the 5D radiance field into position and direction components. It is a key development in the evolution of NeRF acceleration, preceding methods like KiloNeRF and PlenOctrees. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28 Recent Advances and Trends in Learning‐Based 3D Representations, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70530, fetched 2026-10-26 SqueezeNeRF: Further factorized FastNeRF for memory-efficient inference, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvprw56347.2022.00307, fetched 2026-10-26 FastNeRF by Garbin et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.10380, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: FastNeRF Cache Size Estimation
head: FastNeRF memory estimation, FastNeRF cache size formula
body: FastNeRF Cache Size Estimation provides analytical formulas to calculate the memory footprint of the position-dependent and direction-dependent caches in the FastNeRF architecture. It solves the problem of determining whether a specific configuration of cache dimensions and data types fits within available hardware memory, addressing the impracticality of standard NeRF caches which can exceed 60TB even for sparse volumes. It differs from standard NeRF cache estimation by accounting for the factorized representation (low-rank decomposition) of the direction-dependent cache, resulting in significantly smaller memory requirements. The method calculates the total memory size M in bits for the two distinct cache structures used in FastNeRF: the position-dependent cache and the direction-dependent cache. Inputs: \alpha \in 0, 1): Inverse volume sparsity. \alpha = 1 indicates a dense volume; lower values indicate sparser occupancy. k: Number of bins per dimension in the position-dependent cache. l: Number of bins per dimension in the direction-dependent cache. D: Number of components or factors in the direction cache decomposition. s\sigma: Size in bits of the stored transparency (density) value. s{rgb}: Size in bits of the stored RGB color value. s{uvw}: Size in bits of the stored (ui, vi, wi) coordinate values. s{\beta}: Size in bits of the stored weights \betai. Outputs: M{NeRF}: Estimated memory size for a standard NeRF cache. M{FastNeRF}: Estimated memory size for the FastNeRF cache. Formulas: 1. Standard NeRF Cache Size: M{NeRF} = \alpha(s\sigma + s{rgb})k^3l^2 This formula assumes a dense lookup table for direction-dependent colors, requiring storage of full RGB vectors for every direction bin. 2. FastNeRF Cache Size: M{FastNeRF} = \alpha \left( (D \cdot s{uvw} + s{\sigma})k^3 \right) + D \cdot s{\beta}l^2 This formula accounts for the factorized representation. The position cache stores D coordinate factors and transparency. The direction cache stores D weight factors. Parameters and Typical Values: Standard implementation uses k = l = 1024. Number of factors D = 8. Color channels (r, g, b) stored as individual bytes (s{rgb} = 24 bits per color, or 8 bits per channel). Coordinate and weight values stored as half-precision floats (s{uvw} = 16 bits, s{\beta} = 16 bits). Transparency s\sigma size is not explicitly defined in bits in the provided notes, but is included in the formula. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Memory Usage: Even for highly sparse volumes with \alpha = 0.01, the standard NeRF cache size is nearly 60TB, which exceeds the memory capacity of consumer-grade hardware. Dense Volume: If \alpha = 1, the memory requirements are maximized. Data Type Sensitivity: The choice of storage size (s{uvw}, s{\beta}, s{rgb}) significantly impacts the total memory. Using half-precision floats instead of single-precision reduces size by half. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculateneRFcachesize(alpha, ssigma, srgb, k, l): """ Calculate memory size for standard NeRF cache. Args: alpha (float): Inverse volume sparsity [0, 1). ssigma (int): Size in bits of transparency value. srgb (int): Size in bits of RGB color value. k (int): Number of bins per dimension in position cache. l (int): Number of bins per dimension in direction cache. Returns: int: Total memory size in bits. """ return alpha (ssigma + srgb) (k 3) (l 2) def calculatefastNeRFcachesize(alpha, D, suvw, ssigma, sbeta, k, l): """ Calculate memory size for FastNeRF cache. Args: alpha (float): Inverse volume sparsity [0, 1). D (int): Number of components/factors. suvw (int): Size in bits of stored (u, v, w) values. ssigma (int): Size in bits of stored transparency. sbeta (int): Size in bits of stored weights betai. k (int): Number of bins per dimension in position cache. l (int): Number of bins per dimension in direction cache. Returns: int: Total memory size in bits. """ positioncachesize = alpha ((D suvw) + ssigma) (k 3) directioncachesize = D sbeta (l 2) return positioncachesize + directioncachesize Time Complexity: The calculation is O(1) as it involves basic arithmetic operations with constant number of inputs. Memory Complexity: The estimated memory scales linearly with \alpha, k^3, and l^2 for standard NeRF, and linearly with \alpha, k^3, and l^2 for FastNeRF, but with a much smaller coefficient due to factorization. Measured Performance: For k=l=1024, D=8, with (r,g,b) as bytes and other values as half-precision floats, the [NeRF cache size is approximately \alpha \cdot 5.6 PB. For FastNeRF, it is approximately \alpha \cdot 54 GB (specifically \alpha \cdot 53,687,091,200 + 16,777,216). Strengths: Provides a quick, analytical way to estimate memory requirements without training or running the network. Highlights the significant memory savings of FastNeRF over standard NeRF. Limitations: Does not account for overhead from the sparse spatial structure (e.g., voxel grid vertices, hash tables) or the MLP parameters themselves. Assumes uniform sparsity \alpha across the entire volume. When to Use: During the configuration search phase to filter out infeasible cache sizes before training. When Not to Use: When precise memory usage including system overhead or non-uniform sparsity is required. The FastNeRF Cache Size Estimation method originates from the FastNeRF paper by Garbin et al.. It was developed to address the high memory requirements of standard NeRF architectures, which store full RGB vectors for every direction bin. The factorized representation in FastNeRF reduces this footprint, making it feasible for consumer-grade hardware. The formulas are derived from the structure of the position-dependent and direction-dependent caches in the FastNeRF architecture. name: Lightweight Profiling
head: Mesh-assisted NeRF Profiling Model, Polynomial-based Size and Quality Prediction
body: Lightweight Profiling is a white-box model that predicts the representation data size and rendering quality of mesh-assisted Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) for specific configurations without training the network. It solves the problem of high computational cost in configuration search by providing an analytical approximation of performance metrics, avoiding the significant time and resource costs associated with full network training. It differs from black-box profiling models (e.g., neural networks) by using explicit polynomial functions derived from rendering knowledge, and it differs from its parent FastNeRF Cache Size Estimation by focusing on mesh-assisted NeRFs (like mobile-NeRF) where geometry and texture knobs are decoupled from the MLP. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Two configuration knobs: g: Number of voxel grids allocated for each axis in the 3D voxel grid representation (geometry knob). p: One-dimensional size of the texture image allocated for each quad face (texture knob, p \times p pixels). Outputs: S: Total data size (memory load). Q: Rendering quality metric, specifically SSIM (Structural Similarity Index Measure). Data Structures: The model consists of two polynomial functions, fs and fq, parameterized by a set of coefficients \theta = \{k, m, a, b, k', a', b'\}. These coefficients are determined via curve fitting. Formulas: The size S and quality Q are calculated as follows: S = fs(g, p) = \frac{m}{3}(g + a)^3 \cdot (p + b)^2 Q = fq(g, p) = k \cdot (g + a')^3 \cdot (p + b')^2 Where: m, k, a, b, a', b' are constants determined by curve fitting. The exponent 3 on the geometry term (g+a) reflects the 3D nature of the voxel grid. The exponent 2 on the texture term (p+b) reflects the 2D nature of the texture image. The MLP size is excluded from S as it is negligible (a few KB) and has poor compatibility with commercial rendering engines when quantized. Parameters and Typical Values: Quality Metric Q: SSIM, evaluating luminance, contrast, and structure. Size Metric S: Total data size in bytes or KB. Knob g: Integer, number of voxels per axis. Knob p: Integer, texture resolution per face. Coefficients: Not given in the sources. They are determined by curve fitting on sampled data. Sampling Strategy for Curve Fitting: To minimize the number of sampling points required to fit the coefficients \theta, a variable step-size searching strategy is used: 1. Select g values using a step size of 2 \cdot g', where g' is the value of the previous sample point. 2. For each selected g, select three distinct p values: the maximum, minimum, and midpoint of the valid patch size range. 3. Pair each g with these three p values to generate sample points. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fitprofilingmodels(samplepoints): """ Fits the coefficients for the size and quality polynomial models. Args: samplepoints: List of tuples (g, p, Strue, Qtrue) obtained from actual rendering/training of mesh-assisted NeRFs. Returns: thetas: Coefficients (m, a, b) for the size model. thetaq: Coefficients (k, aprime, bprime) for the quality model. """ # Extract data gvals = [pt[0] for pt in samplepoints] pvals = [pt[1] for pt in samplepoints] Svals = [pt[2] for pt in samplepoints] Qvals = [pt[3] for pt in samplepoints] # Fit Size Model: S = (m/3) (g + a)^3 (p + b)^2 # This is a non-linear least squares problem. # We define the residual function and solve for thetas = [m, a, b] def sizeresidual(theta, g, p, S): m, a, b = theta predicted = (m / 3.0) (g + a)3 (p + b)2 return predicted - S # Initial guess for size coefficients [G: Placeholder values, # actual values depend on the specific dataset and range of g, p] initialguesss = [1000.0, 0.0, 0.0] thetas = optimizenonlinearleastsquares(sizeresidual, initialguesss, gvals, pvals, Svals) # Fit Quality Model: Q = k (g + a')^3 (p + b')^2 def qualityresidual(theta, g, p, Q): k, aprime, bprime = theta predicted = k (g + aprime)3 (p + bprime)2 return predicted - Q # Initial guess for quality coefficients [G: Placeholder values] initialguessq = [0.5, 0.0, 0.0] thetaq = optimizenonlinearleastsquares(qualityresidual, initialguessq, gvals, pvals, Qvals) return thetas, thetaq def predictsizeandquality(g, p, thetas, thetaq): """ Predicts size and quality for a given configuration. Args: g: Geometry knob (voxels per axis). p: Texture knob (texture size per face). thetas: Coefficients (m, a, b) for size. thetaq: Coefficients (k, aprime, bprime) for quality. Returns: S: Predicted size. Q: Predicted quality (SSIM). """ m, a, b = thetas k, aprime, bprime = thetaq S = (m / 3.0) (g + a)3 (p + b)2 Q = k (g + aprime)3 (p + bprime)2 return S, Q def generatesamplepoints(gmin, gmax, pmin, pmax, numgsamples=5): """ Generates sample points using the variable step-size strategy. Args: gmin: Minimum geometry knob value. gmax: Maximum geometry knob value. pmin: Minimum texture knob value. pmax: Maximum texture knob value. numgsamples: Number of g values to sample. Returns: points: List of (g, p) tuples. """ points = [] # Variable step-size for g: step = 2 previousg # This implies an exponential growth in g values. # Start with a small g value.
