name: C-NeRF
head: Neural Volumes follow-up
body: C-NeRF is a voxel-based radiance field optimization method that replaces the coordinate-based MLP of standard NeRF with a 3D convolutional neural network to produce feature volumes, which are then decoded by a NeRF-like MLP to predict radiance fields. It is designed to improve upon the blurry results of its predecessor, Neural Volumes, by leveraging the inductive bias of 3D convolutions for volumetric data. Unlike coordinate-based methods that suffer from high-frequency detail loss due to single shared MLP structures, C-NeRF operates on a discrete voxel grid, enabling faster training and inference for volumetric video representation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of multi-view images (or a single view for reconstruction) and camera poses. Output: A differentiable radiance field representation consisting of a 3D feature volume and a decoding MLP, allowing for novel view synthesis and volume rendering. Data Structures: 1. 3D Feature Volume: A 3D grid of tensors. Each voxel contains a feature vector (dimension not explicitly specified in sources, but implied to be fixed per voxel). The resolution is determined by the scene bounding box and chosen grid size. 2. Decoding MLP: A Multi-Layer Perceptron that takes spatial coordinates and the sampled feature vector from the 3D volume as input, and outputs density (\sigma) and color (\mathbf{c}). Method Steps: 1. 3D CNN Encoding: A 3D Convolutional Neural Network processes the input data (or a cost volume derived from multi-view stereo) to produce a 3D feature volume. This step replaces the implicit coordinate mapping of standard NeRF with an explicit volumetric representation. 2. Ray Sampling: For each ray \mathbf{r}, sample N points along the ray within the scene bounding box. 3. Feature Interpolation: For each sample point, trilinearly interpolate the feature vector from the 3D feature volume based on the point's spatial coordinates. 4. Radiance Field Prediction: Pass the spatial coordinates and the interpolated feature vector into the NeRF-like MLP. The MLP outputs the density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i for each sample point i. 5. Volume Rendering: Compute the final pixel color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) using the standard differentiable volume rendering equation [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance, and \deltai is the distance between sample points. 6. Optimization: Minimize the photometric loss between rendered images and ground truth images using gradient descent. Gradients are backpropagated through the rendering equation and the MLP. The 3D CNN parameters are also updated if the network is trained end-to-end from raw inputs. Parameters: Voxel Resolution: Not given in the sources. CNN Architecture: Not given in the sources. MLP Architecture: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High-Frequency Detail Loss: C-NeRF tends to lose details in high-frequency regions of the image compared to more advanced methods, attributed to the limitations of its single shared MLP model structure combined with the voxel resolution. Memory Usage: Storing a 3D feature volume requires significant memory, scaling with the cube of the resolution. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Dominated by the storage of the 3D feature volume and the CNN/MLP parameters. The volume size scales with R^3 where R is the resolution. Time: Training time is significantly faster than coordinate-based NeRF due to the efficiency of 3D convolutions and parallelizable voxel access. However, specific complexity formulas are not provided. Measured Performance: C-NeRF is evaluated on the D-NeRF dataset. It achieves higher PSNR and SSIM than Neural Volumes but lower than some newer factorization methods like HexPlane. Qualitative results show it produces sharper images than Neural Volumes but still suffers from blurring in high-frequency regions compared to methods using dynamic representations. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Faster training than MLP-only NeRF; better detail preservation than Neural Volumes; explicit volumetric representation allows for efficient 3D operations. Limitations: Loses high-frequency details; memory intensive for high resolutions; less flexible than implicit representations for complex geometries. When to Use: When faster training than standard NeRF is required and the scene has moderate complexity. When an explicit volumetric representation is preferred for downstream 3D processing. When Not to Use: When high-frequency detail preservation is critical. When memory is constrained and high resolution is needed. C-NeRF was introduced as a follow-up work to Neural Volumes. It was proposed to address the blurriness and lack of detail in Neural Volumes by adopting a 3D CNN to produce feature volumes, which are then decoded by a NeRF-like MLP. The method is part of the evolution of voxel-based radiance field representations, aiming to balance the efficiency of voxel grids with the expressive power of neural networks. It is used in the context of volumetric video representation and novel view synthesis. name: MVSNeRF
head: MVS-NeRF
body: MVSNeRF is a method for fast, generalizable radiance field reconstruction from multi-view stereo that learns a data prior to bypass per-scene optimization. It extracts 2D image features using a pretrained CNN, maps them to a 3D voxelized cost volume through plane sweeping with a variance-based cost, and uses a pretrained 3D CNN to produce a 3D neural encoding volume. Inputs: A set of multi-view images \{It\} with known camera parameters. Outputs: A rendered image \hat{I}. Data Structures: 1. 2D Feature Volume: Extracted from input images using a pretrained CNN. 2. 3D Cost Volume: A voxelized grid constructed via plane sweeping. 3. 3D Neural Encoding Volume (V): A 3D tensor produced by a pretrained 3D CNN, storing latent codes for spatial points. 4. NeRF MLP: A multi-layer perceptron taking latent codes, coordinates, and viewing directions as input. Steps: 1. 2D Feature Extraction: Extract 2D features from each input image It using a pretrained CNN. 2. Cost Volume Construction: Map the 2D features to a 3D voxelized cost volume through plane sweeping using a variance-based cost metric. 3. 3D Neural Encoding: Pass the cost volume through a pretrained 3D CNN to produce the 3D neural encoding volume V. 4. Latent Code Interpolation: For any 3D point p, retrieve its latent code zp by interpolating values from V. 5. Radiance Field Prediction: Input zp, the 3D point coordinates p, and the viewing direction d into the NeRF MLP to predict density \sigma and color c. 6. Volume Rendering: Render the image by integrating predicted density and color along camera rays. 7. Joint Optimization: During training, jointly optimize the 3D feature volume (via the 3D CNN) and the NeRF MLP parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def interpolate(volume, point): # Standard trilinear interpolation from 3D tensor return volume[point] def mvsnerfrender(rayorigin, raydirection, V, nerfmlp, near, far, numsamples): renderedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 for i in range(numsamples): t = near + (far - near) (i + 0.5) / numsamples p = [rayorigin[j] + raydirection[j] t for j in range(3)] zp = interpolate(V, p) sigma, color = nerfmlp(zp, p, raydirection) delta = (far - near) / numsamples alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma delta) weight = accumulatedtransmittance alpha renderedcolor = [renderedcolor[j] + weight color[j] for j in range(3)] accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - alpha) return renderedcolor def trainmvsnerf(images, gtimages, nerfmlp, optimizer): # Joint optimization of 3D feature volume and NeRF MLP rendered = mvsnerfrender(rayorigin, raydirection, V, nerfmlp, near, far, numsamples) loss = sum((r - g)2 for r, g in zip(rendered, gtimages)) / len(gtimages) loss.backward() optimizer.step() Parameters: Plane sweeping depth range: Not given in the sources. Variance-based cost threshold: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Precision: Interpolation from the 3D neural encoding volume requires careful handling of grid boundaries. Regresses a local neural volume for each input frame using neighboring images. It solves per-frame radiance field estimation by aggregating multi-view features in a canonical world coordinate frame. Unlike MVSNeRF, which builds perspective frustum volumes for small-baseline rendering, this method constructs volumes directly in canonical space to facilitate global fusion. Time Complexity: Training is significantly faster than baseline NeRF; on the DTU dataset, MVSNeRF reached results comparable to hours of baseline NeRF training within 15 minutes. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the 3D neural encoding volume and the cost volume. Strengths: Fast generalizable reconstruction. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Fast reconstruction from multi-view images where per-scene optimization is too slow. When not to use: Not given in the sources. MVSNeRF was introduced in March 2021. It differs from General Radiance Field (GRF) by taking a slightly different approach, whereas GRF operated in canonical space as opposed to view-space for pixelNeRF. It builds on the idea of using multi-view stereo to initialize or guide the radiance field representation. name: Local Sparse Volume Reconstruction
head: Local Radiance Field Reconstruction, Per-frame Local Radiance Field, Reconstructing Local Volumes
body: Local Sparse Volume Reconstruction regresses a local neural volume Vt for each input frame t using its image It and K-1 neighboring images. It solves per-frame radiance field estimation by aggregating multi-view features in a canonical world coordinate frame, ensuring alignment with a global volume for large-scale reconstruction. Unlike MVS-NeRF, which builds perspective frustum volumes for small-baseline rendering, this method constructs volumes directly in canonical space to facilitate global fusion. Inputs: A sequence of RGB images I1, \dots, IN with known camera parameters \Phi1, \dots, \PhiN. For each frame t, a set of K neighboring viewpoints \mathcal{N}t (typically temporal neighbors in monocular video). Outputs: A local sparse neural volume \mathcal{V}t representing the local radiance field for frame t in canonical world space. Data Structures: 1. 2D Feature Map Ft: A standard 2D tensor (height, width, channels) extracted for each image It using a deep 2D CNN. 2. Sparse Voxel Set: A set of 3D voxel centers \{v\} within an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) covering the frustums of all K neighboring viewpoints in the world coordinate frame, with voxels invisible to all views masked out. 3. 3D Feature Volume \mathcal{U}i: For each neighboring view i \in \mathcal{N}t, a 3D feature volume where each visible voxel v stores a concatenated feature vector. 4. Local Volume \mathcal{V}t: The output volume with the same spatial layout as \mathcal{U}i, containing the regressed local radiance field features. Parameters: K: Number of neighboring viewpoints used for reconstruction. Not given in the sources. G: MLP for computing direction features. Architecture details not given in the sources. J: Deep neural network for regressing the local volume from aggregated statistics. Architecture details not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Extract 2D Image Features: For each input image It in the sequence, pass it through a deep 2D convolutional neural network to extract a 2D feature map Ft. 2. Define Bounding Box and Sparse Voxels: Define an axis-aligned bounding box in the canonical world coordinate frame that encompasses the viewing frustums of all K neighboring viewpoints in \mathcal{N}t. Identify the set of voxels within this box and mask out any voxel that is not visible to at least one of the K neighboring views, resulting in a sparse set of active voxels. 3. Build 3D Feature Volumes (\mathcal{U}i): For each neighboring viewpoint i \in \mathcal{N}t and its corresponding feature map Fi, iterate over each visible voxel v in the sparse set. Compute the 2D projection ui of the voxel center v onto the image plane of view i. Fetch the 2D image feature Fi(ui) from the feature map at location ui. Compute the viewing direction di from viewpoint i to voxel v in world coordinates. Pass di through an MLP G to get direction features G(di). Concatenate the image and direction features to form the per-view feature at voxel v: \mathcal{U}i(v) = [Fi(ui), G(di)], where [\cdot, \cdot] denotes concatenation. 4. Aggregate and Regress Local Volume (\mathcal{V}t): For each visible voxel v, compute the element-wise mean and variance of the features \mathcal{U}i(v) across all K neighboring viewpoints i \in \mathcal{N}t: \text{Mean}v = \text{Mean}{i \in \mathcal{N}t} \mathcal{U}i(v) and \text{Var}v = \text{Var}{i \in \mathcal{N}t} \mathcal{U}i(v). These operations are invariant to the number and order of inputs, naturally handling voxels with varying numbers of visible viewpoints. Concatenate the mean and variance features: [\text{Mean}v, \text{Var}v]. Pass this concatenated vector through a deep neural network J to regress the local volume feature at voxel v: \mathcal{V}t(v) = J([\text{Mean}{i \in \mathcal{N}t} \mathcal{U}i(v), \text{Var}{i \in \mathcal{N}t} \mathcal{U}i(v)]). The result \mathcal{V}t is the local neural volume for frame t. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def reconstructlocalvolume(images, neighbors, K, cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics, featureextractor, directionmlp, regressor, voxelgrid): # Step 1: Extract 2D features for all K views featuremaps = [featureextractor(img) for img in images] # Step 2: voxelgrid contains 3D points v visible to at least one neighbor voxelstats = {} # v -> [sumfeatures, sumsqfeatures, count] for i in range(K): Fi = featuremaps[i] camintr = cameraintrinsics[i] camextr = cameraextrinsics[i] for v in voxelgrid: # Project voxel v to 2D image plane of view i ui = project2d(v, camintr, camextr) # Fetch 2D feature via bilinear interpolation feat2d = samplefeature(Fi, ui) # Compute viewing direction di from camera center to v camcenter = getcameracenter(camextr) di = normalize(v - camcenter) # Encode direction featdir = directionmlp(di) # Concatenate image and direction features Uiv = concatenate(feat2d, featdir) # Accumulate for mean/var if v not in voxelstats: voxelstats[v] = [zeroslike(Uiv), zeroslike(Uiv), 0] stats = voxelstats[v] stats[0] = [a + b for a, b in zip(stats[0], Uiv)] stats[1] = [a + b b for a, b in zip(stats[1], Uiv)] stats[2] += 1 localvolume = {} for v, stats in voxelstats.items(): sumfeat, sumsqfeat, count = stats meanfeat = [s / count for s in sumfeat] varfeat = [s / count - m m for s, m in zip(sumsqfeat, meanfeat)] inputtoJ = concatenate(meanfeat, varfeat) localvolume[v] = regressor(inputtoJ) return localvolume def project2d(v, intr, extr): vh = v + (1.0,) camcoord = [sum(extr[i][j] vh[j] for j in range(4)) for i in range(4)] u = [sum(intr[i][j] camcoord[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] return (u[0] / u[2], u[1] / u[2]) def samplefeature(F, u): # Bilinear interpolation assumed return F[u[1], u[0]] def getcameracenter(extr): R = extr[:3,:3] t = extr[:3, 3] return tuple(-sum(r ti for r, ti in zip(R[:, j], t)) for j in range(3)) def normalize(v): norm = math.sqrt(sum(c c for c in v)) return tuple(c / (norm + 1e-8) for c in v) def concatenate(a, b): return a + b def zeroslike(t): return [0.0] len(t) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Varying Visibility: Voxels have different numbers of visible viewpoints across the K neighbors. The mean and variance operations are invariant to the number and order of inputs, naturally handling this variation without requiring explicit masking or padding. Coordinate Frame: Volumes are built in the canonical world coordinate frame, not the view's perspective coordinate. This is crucial for aligning with the global volume Vg. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Depends on the number of voxels, K, and the depth of networks G and J. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Depends on the size of the bounding box and the sparsity of visible voxels. Strengths: Builds volumes in canonical space, facilitating global large-scale reconstruction and fusion. Uses mean and variance aggregation, which is robust to varying visibility and order of inputs. Incorporates viewing direction information to account for view-dependent effects. Limitations: Requires a sparse voxel grid and visibility checks, which may be computationally intensive to set up. Limited to local reconstruction per frame; requires a subsequent fusion step (e.g., GRU) for global consistency. When to use: For large-scale scene reconstruction from monocular video where global consistency is required, and when leveraging multi-view cues per frame is beneficial. When not to use: For small-baseline rendering where perspective frustum volumes (like MVS-NeRF) are sufficient and simpler. Local Sparse Volume Reconstruction was introduced in the paper "NeRFusion: Fusing Radiance Fields for Large-Scale Scene Reconstruction". It is part of the NeRFusion framework, which aims to fuse radiance fields for large-scale scene reconstruction. The method was developed to address the limitations of previous approaches like MVS-NeRF, which built perspective frustum volumes for small-baseline rendering, by constructing volumes in canonical space for global reconstruction. The technique leverages mean and variance aggregation, a strategy widely used in MVS-based cost volumes, to fuse per-view appearance and geometry cues. name: V4D (Voxel for 4D Novel View Synthesis)
body: V4D is a voxel-based architecture for 4D novel view synthesis in dynamic scenes that models the 4D neural radiance field directly without requiring a canonical space. It addresses the limitations of MLP-only representations by using separate 3D voxel grids for density and texture, combined with a conditional positional encoding module and a look-up table (LUT) refinement module to preserve high-frequency details and prevent over-smoothing. Unlike continuous neural radiance fields that require per-pixel optimization, V4D pre-computes a shared volumetric representation, offering competitive reconstruction quality with faster inference times than MLP-based dynamic baselines. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single-view video sequence (providing spatial coordinates \mathbf{x}=(x,y,z), time index t, and view direction (\theta, \phi)) and ground-truth RGB images for supervision. Output: Rendered RGB images \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for novel viewpoints and time steps. Data Structures: 1. Density Volume: A 3D voxel grid initialized with dimensions 160 \times 160 \times 160 \times 12. It stores features F{den}. 2. Texture Volume: A 3D voxel grid initialized with dimensions 160 \times 160 \times 160 \times 12. It stores features F{tex}. 3. Basic LUTs: M=5 learnable 3D look-up tables, each with resolution 33 \times 33 \times 33. One is initialized as the identity LUT, and the remaining M-1 are initialized to zero. 4. MLPs: Density MLP: 5 layers. Texture MLP: 5 layers. Weight Prediction MLP: 10 layers. Numbered Steps: 1. Voxel Sampling: For a ray \mathbf{r} sampled at N points along its path, retrieve the feature vectors F{den} and F{tex} from the density and texture volumes at the 3D spatial location (x, y, z) using trilinear interpolation. 2. Conditional Positional Encoding (CPE): Apply CPE to the sampled texture features F{tex} to recover high-frequency details lost by regularization. The encoding is defined as: \gamma(pv) = \left( \sin\left(2^\pi pv + \frac{2\pi}{L-1}t\right), \cos\left(2^\pi pv + \frac{2\pi}{L-1}t\right) \right) where pv is the sampled feature vector, L=5 is the frequency order, and t is the time index. Pitfall: CPE is not applied to the density features F{den}. The density volume must be initialized to zero for correct initial volume rendering; applying CPE to density features breaks this initialization and causes learning collapse. Let the encoded texture feature be \hat{F}{tex}. The density feature remains F{den}. 3. Feature Concatenation: Concatenate the time index t, the 3D location (x, y, z), the view direction (\theta, \phi), and the features (F{den} for density, \hat{F}{tex} for texture) into a single vector. 4. Field Estimation: Feed the concatenated vector into the 5-layer Density MLP to predict volume density \sigma. Feed the concatenated vector into the 5-layer Texture MLP to predict RGB color \mathbf{c}. 5. Volume Rendering: Compute the coarse RGB color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for the ray using the standard emission-absorption model: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance, \deltai = t{i+1} - ti is the step size, and N is the number of sampled points. 6. Pseudo-Surface Depth Estimation: Compute the expected depth \hat{d} for the ray to guide the refinement module: \hat{d} = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ti where ti represents the depth coordinate of the i-th sample point. 7. LUT Refinement (Pixel-Level): Treat the coarse RGB value \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) as a spatial coordinate in the RGB space. Perform trilinear interpolation on each of the M=5 basic LUTs using this coordinate to obtain interpolated RGB values \mathbf{r}m for m=1 \dots M. Use the pseudo-surface depth \hat{d} (and potentially spatial coordinates) as input to the 10-layer Weight Prediction MLP to predict spatial-aware weights wm for each basic LUT. Combine the interpolated values using the predicted weights to produce the refined RGB color. This process is repeated for Z=3 recurrent iterations. Loss Function: The total loss is a weighted sum of four components: Loss = w1 L{rgb} + w2 L{pt\rgb} + w3 L{bg} + w4 L{TV} RGB Loss (L{rgb}): Mean squared error between rendered and ground truth colors. L{rgb} = \frac{1}{R} \sum{r \in R} |\hat{C}(r) - C(r)|^2 where R is the set of training rays. Point-wise RGB Loss (L{pt\rgb}): Encourages consistency at sampled points. L{pt\rgb} = \frac{1}{R} \sum{r \in R} \sum{i=1}^{K} (Ti ai \hat{C}(r) - C(r))^2 where K is the number of queried points in the texture volume, Ti is accumulated transmittance, and ai is the probability of termination at point i. Background Loss (L{bg}): Encourages foreground/background separation by penalizing intermediate transmittance values. L{bg} = -T{K+1} \log(T{K+1}) - (1 - T{K+1}) \log(1 - T{K+1}) where T{K+1} is the transmittance after the last sample. Total Variation Loss (L{TV}): Applied directly to the voxel grids of the density and texture volumes to prevent over-fitting and maintain geometry. It is not applied to the LUTs. Parameters: Voxel Resolution: 160 \times 160 \times 160. Feature Dimension: 12. MLP Layers: 5 for density/texture fields, 10 for weight prediction. CPE Frequency Order (L): 5. Basic LUTs (M): 5. LUT Resolution: 33 \times 33 \times 33. Recurrent Iterations (Z): 3. Learning Rates: Voxel grids (density/texture): 0.1. Density/Texture MLPs: 1 \times 10^{-3}. LUTs refinement MLPs and voxels: 1 \times 10^{-4}. Optimizer: Adam. Batch Size: 8,196 rays (first stage), 4,196 rays (second stage). Loss Weights: w1=1.0, w2=0.01, w3=0.001, w4=0.1. TV Loss Decay: Exponential decay factor of 0.005 applied to w4 during training to alleviate over-smoothing. Training Iterations: 250k for synthetic datasets, 100k for real scene datasets. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Over-smoothing: Total variation loss causes blurring and loss of high-frequency details. This is mitigated by the CPE module and the LUT refinement module. Initialization Collapse: Applying CPE to density features breaks the zero-initialization rule required for stable volume rendering at the start of training. CPE must only be applied to texture features. Spatial Awareness: Using low-resolution images to predict LUT weights loses 3D spatial awareness. Using pseudo-surface depth via an MLP preserves this awareness. MAV3D synthesizes time-varying 3D scenes directly from text prompts by optimizing a 4D neural radiance field (4D-NeRF) under the guidance of a pretrained text-to-video diffusion model. It is distinguished from its parent V4D by its data-free supervision strategy, which relies solely on text and video priors rather than multi-view video inputs, and from its sibling Explicit Neural View Synthesis by its use of a hexplane-based hybrid representation for efficient spacetime encoding. Explicit Neural View Synthesis (ENR) is a novel view synthesis method that explicitly encodes sparse source observations into a volumetric representation (RGB\alpha volume) to enable amortized rendering, avoiding per-pixel ray sampling and scene-specific optimization. Unlike continuous neural radiance fields such as NeRF [26], which require independent ray integrals for each pixel and prevent amortization across views, ENR pre-computes a shared RGB\alpha volume that can be rendered for any target view via geometric transformations. This approach offers rendering speeds over 400x faster than continuous baselines while maintaining comparable or superior reconstruction quality. Performance: V4D achieves state-of-the-art performance on synthetic dynamic scenes (e.g., PSNR 33.72, SSIM 0.98 on [23] datasets) and competitive performance on real dynamic scenes. It outperforms D-NeRF, NDVG, and TiNeuVox in PSNR/SSIM. Training Time: Training requires 250k iterations for synthetic data and 100k for real data. It has a longer training time than canonical-space methods (like D-NeRF) because it lacks canonical space adaptation and relies on TV loss to propagate temporal information, requiring more iterations. Inference Time: V4D has shorter inference time than TiNeuVox (0.48s vs 1.42s on A100) because it does not use an MLP-based sub-network to predict position offsets for each moment. Memory: Uses two 160^3 \times 12 voxel grids and five 33^3 LUTs. This is more memory-intensive than compact MLP representations but allows for faster inference compared to methods requiring per-frame offset prediction. Strengths: No canonical space required; plug-and-play LUT refinement; high-quality dynamic novel view synthesis from single-view video. Limitations: Longer training time compared to canonical-space methods; potential for over-smoothing if TV loss is not balanced with CPE/LUT refinement. V4D was proposed to address the limitations of MLP-based neural radiance fields in dynamic scenes, specifically the lack of multi-view constraints and the computational burden of global MLP optimization. It builds on the principles of differentiable volume rendering [44-radiance-field-optimization.md] and extends 3D voxel-based representations to 4D by modeling density and texture fields separately. The method was evaluated on 8 synthetic dynamic scene datasets and 4 real scene datasets, demonstrating superiority over existing single-view dynamic novel view synthesis methods. V4D: Voxel for 4D Novel View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2023.3312127, fetched 2026-10-26

name: MAV3D
head: Text-to-4D via HexPlane
body: MAV3D synthesizes time-varying 3D scenes directly from text prompts by optimizing a 4D neural radiance field (4D-NeRF) under the guidance of a pretrained text-to-video diffusion model. It is distinguished from its parent V4D by its data-free supervision strategy, which relies solely on text and video priors rather than multi-view video inputs, and from its sibling Explicit Neural View Synthesis by its use of a hexplane-based hybrid representation for efficient spacetime encoding. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A text prompt describing the desired dynamic scene. Output: A 4D neural radiance field parameterized by a hexplane representation, capable of rendering novel views of the dynamic scene at arbitrary timestamps. Data Structures: The core representation is the HexPlane, a hybrid 4D structure that decomposes the 4D spacetime volume into a set of 2D planes. Layout: For a 4D coordinate (x, y, z, t), the representation consists of six 2D planes: Three spatial planes: P{xy}, P{yz}, P{xz} encoding static geometry. Three temporal-spatial planes: P{xt}, P{yt}, P{zt} encoding dynamic deformation over time. Encoding: Each plane is a learnable tensor of size H \times W (or H \times T for temporal planes). The feature vector for a point is computed by bilinearly sampling the corresponding locations on these six planes and concatenating or summing the results. This avoids the memory explosion of a full 4D voxel grid. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the HexPlane tensors with random values. Initialize the MLP that maps the aggregated plane features to density and color. 2. Multi-stage Static-to-Dynamic Training: Stage 1 (Static): Freeze temporal planes (P{xt}, P{yt}, P{zt}) and optimize only spatial planes (P{xy}, P{yz}, P{xz}) and the MLP using a static prior or a single frame from the generated video. This establishes a coherent 3D geometry. Stage 2 (Dynamic): Unfreeze temporal planes. Optimize the full HexPlane using temporal regularization to ensure smooth motion across frames. 3. Data-Free Supervision: Since no 4D dataset is used, supervision is derived from a pretrained text-to-video diffusion model (e.g., Stable Video Diffusion). Render a video sequence from the current 4D-NeRF estimate. Compute a loss between the rendered video and the video generated by the diffusion model from the input text prompt. This typically involves a score distillation sampling (SDS) or similar gradient-based loss that leverages the diffusion model's denoising prior to guide the rendering towards the text description. 4. Temporal Regularization: Apply a loss term that penalizes large, unphysical changes in the HexPlane features between adjacent time steps to enforce temporal coherence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainmav3d(textprompt, numsteps, learningrate): # Initialize HexPlane representation # Pxy, Pyz, Pxz: spatial planes (H, W, C) # Pxt, Pyt, Pzt: temporal planes (H, T, C) hexplane = HexPlane() mlp = MLP() # Diffusion model for supervision diffusionmodel = loadpretrainedtexttovideodiffusion() for step in range(numsteps): # 1. Sample a random time t and camera pose t = sampletime() camera = samplecamera() # 2. Render from 4D-NeRF # Query hexplane for point p at time t features = hexplane.query(p, t) density, color = mlp(features) renderedimage = volumerendering(camera, density, color) # 3. Generate target video frame from text # The diffusion model generates a video sequence consistent with textprompt targetvideo = diffusionmodel.generate(textprompt) targetframe = targetvideo[t] # 4. Compute Loss # Data-free loss using diffusion prior (e.g., SDS) lossdata = computediffusionloss(renderedimage, targetframe, diffusionmodel) # Temporal regularization losstemporal = computetemporalsmoothness(hexplane) totalloss = lossdata + lambdatemp losstemporal # 5. Update if step < staticsteps: # Stage 1: Optimize only spatial planes optimize(hexplane.spatialplanes, mlp, totalloss) else: # Stage 2: Optimize all planes optimize(hexplane, mlp, totalloss) Parameters: Temporal Regularization Weight (\lambda{temp}): Not given in the sources. HexPlane Resolution (H, W, T): Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Temporal Incoherence: Without sufficient regularization, the dynamic planes may produce flickering or jittering artifacts. The multi-stage training helps mitigate this by establishing a stable static base first. Text-Video Mismatch: The quality of the output is heavily dependent on the alignment between the text prompt and the diffusion model's generation. 4DGen is a video-to-4D generation method that utilizes HexPlane as the dynamic representation. It differs from MAV3D by using video input instead of text. It constructs point clouds using generated multi-view images as pseudo ground truth for 3D deformation, leveraging SyncDreamer to generate these multi-view images from input frames. Time Complexity: Training is iterative and depends on the number of optimization steps and the cost of querying the diffusion model for supervision. The hexplane representation offers significant speedup compared to fully implicit NeRF baselines and compression compared to 4D voxel-based representations. Memory Complexity: The hexplane representation is memory-efficient, scaling with the number of planes rather than the full 4D volume. Strengths: Data-free (no 4D datasets required); efficient spacetime encoding; capable of generating dynamic 3D content from text. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the pretrained text-to-video diffusion model; potential for temporal inconsistencies if regularization is insufficient. When to use: When generating dynamic 3D scenes from text descriptions is required, and no 4D video data is available. When not to use: When high-fidelity, temporally consistent 4D data is already available (e.g., use V4D or 4DGen). MAV3D was introduced in January 2023. It addresses the challenge of synthesizing time-varying 3D scenes from text without requiring large-scale 4D datasets. It builds on the concept of neural radiance fields and extends it to 4D using a hybrid hexplane representation for efficiency. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28 PDF Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting - Springer, https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s41095-024-0436-y.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Explicit Neural View Synthesis (Voxel-based Neural Rendering)
head: Fast and Explicit Neural View Synthesis, explicit voxel-like scene representation, our model
body: Explicit Neural View Synthesis (ENR) is a novel view synthesis method that explicitly encodes sparse source observations into a volumetric representation (RGBα volume) to enable amortized rendering, avoiding per-pixel ray sampling and scene-specific optimization. Unlike continuous neural radiance fields such as NeRF [26], which require independent ray integrals for each pixel and prevent amortization across views, ENR pre-computes a shared RGBα volume that can be rendered for any target view via geometric transformations. This approach offers rendering speeds over 400x faster than continuous baselines while maintaining comparable or superior reconstruction quality. The method consists of four main stages: 2D feature encoding, inverse projection (back-projection), 3D feature decoding, and amortized rendering. Input: Source image(s) Is \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times h \times w} and camera intrinsic parameters K (assumed constant). For multi-view, multiple source images are aggregated into a single latent volume. Output: Target image \hat{I}t \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times h \times w} rendered from a target camera pose Pt. 1. 2D Feature Map (Fs): Layout: \mathbb{R}^{32 \times h \times w}. Spatial resolution matches the input image. Channels: 32. 2. Latent Volumetric Tensor (Zs): Layout: \mathbb{R}^{c \times ds \times hs \times ws}. ds, hs, ws are depth, height, and width of the volumetric representation. Spatial height and width are halved with respect to the input feature map (hs = h/2, ws = w/2). Depth ds corresponds to the depth of the voxel grid. 3. RGBα Volume (Vs): Layout: \mathbb{R}^{4 \times ds \times h \times w}. Channels: 4 (R, G, B, α). Spatial resolution matches the input image (h, w). Produced by a final 3D convolution and sigmoid activation. 1. 2D Feature Encoding: Process the source image Is through a 2D U-Net encoder with a ResNet-18 backbone. Downsampling: Intermediate feature channels are 64, 128, 256, 512 at each spatial resolution level. Upsampling: Perform deconvolution and fuse resulting features with skip encoder features at the same level through concatenation followed by two consecutive convolution blocks. Output: A 32-channel feature map Fs \in \mathbb{R}^{32 \times h \times w} preserving the spatial resolution of Is. 2. Inverse Projection (Back-projection): Back-project Fs into a latent volumetric tensor Zs \in \mathbb{R}^{c \times ds \times hs \times ws}. Tiling: Tile the 2D features into a 3D cube to prepare for sampling. Homography: Leverage camera intrinsic parameters K to compute the homography matrix mapping the cube to the viewing frustum. Grid Mapping: Obtain the grid mapping function by multiplying the homography matrix with individual points from a fixed voxel mesh grid set. Sampling: Apply the gridsample function to perform the inverse projection. This step is critical to preserve 3D geometry and texture information, which is lost if 2D feature maps are reshaped directly into 3D volumes. 3. 3D Feature Decoding: Process the latent volume Zs with a 3D U-Net model to predict the final RGBα volume Vs. Architecture: 3D U-Net with ResNet-3D blocks. Channel Scaling: When spatial resolution is downscaled by 2 times, double the channel numbers. Output Feature Map: 16 channels with the same spatial resolution as the input image. Final Layer: Apply one 3D convolution to transform the tensor map into 4 channels. Activation: Apply sigmoid activation to produce the RGBα volume Vs \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times ds \times h \times w}. 4. Amortized Rendering: Render the transformed RGBα volume Vt into the target image \hat{I}t. Pose Transformation: Compute the relative rigid transformation P{st} = Pt Ps^{-1} between source pose Ps and target pose Pt. Apply this transformation to Vs to obtain Vt = T(P{st}, Vs), aligning the volume with the target view. This combines rotation (transferring volume from source to target view) and perspective deformation (mapping viewing frustum to output cube) via left matrix multiplication. Perspective Deformation: Apply inverse warping and trilinear sampling to the transformed volume. Similar to inverse projection, use mesh grid multiplication and gridsample to obtain the voxel volume aligned with the target camera. Alpha Blending: Calculate the expected color \hat{C}{i,j} for each pixel (i,j) using accumulated transmittance: \hat{C}{i,j} = \sum{k=1}^{ds} T{i,j}^k \alpha{i,j}^k \mathbf{c}{i,j}^k where: \mathbf{c}{i,j}^k is the color value (first 3 channels) of the voxel at depth k. \alpha{i,j}^k is the alpha value (4th channel) of the voxel at depth k. T{i,j}^k is the accumulated transmittance, calculated using the cumprod method: T{i,j}^k = \prod{m=1}^{k-1} (1-\alpha{i,j}^m) The product is over the depth dimension k=1 \dots ds. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class ExplicitNeuralViewSynthesis(nn.Module): def init(self, intrinsicparams, voxeldepth=16, voxelheight=64, voxelwidth=64): super().init() self.K = intrinsicparams self.ds = voxeldepth self.hs = voxelheight self.ws = voxelwidth self.encoder2d = UNet2D(channelsin=3, channelsout=32) self.decoder3d = UNet3D(channelsin=32, channelsout=4) # Fixed voxel mesh grid for inverse projection and rendering # Shape: (1, ds, hs, ws, 3) normalized to [-1, 1] self.voxelgrid = self.createvoxelgrid() def createvoxelgrid(self): z = torch.linspace(-1, 1, self.ds) y = torch.linspace(-1, 1, self.hs) x = torch.linspace(-1, 1, self.ws) z, y, x = torch.meshgrid(z, y, x, indexing='ij') return torch.stack([x, y, z], dim=-1).unsqueeze(0) def inverseprojection(self, Fs): B, C, h, w = Fs.shape hs, ws = self.hs, self.ws # Tile 2D features into a 3D cube (B, C, ds, h, w) Ftiled = Fs.unsqueeze(2).repeat(1, 1, self.ds, 1, 1) # Implementation detail: Compute homography matrix from K and map voxel centers to image pixels. # Returns grid of shape (B, ds, hs, ws, 3) in normalized [-1, 1] coordinates. samplinggrid = self.getinverseprojectiongrid(Fs) # Perform inverse projection using gridsample on 4D tensor Zs = F.gridsample(Ftiled, samplinggrid, aligncorners=True) return Zs def getinverseprojectiongrid(self, Fs): # Not given in the sources. Computes homography and maps voxel centers to image pixels. pass def forward(self, Is, Pt, Ps): Fs = self.encoder2d(Is) Zs = self.inverseprojection(Fs) Vs = self.decoder3d(Zs) return self.render(Vs, Pt, Ps) def render(self, Vs, Pt, Ps): B, C, ds, h, w = Vs.shape Pst = Pt @ torch.linalg.inv(Ps) # Apply rigid transformation to volume # Not given in the sources. Uses gridsample with a grid generated from Pst to rotate/translate the voxel grid. Vt = self.transformvolume(Vs, Pst) Ct = Vt[:,:3,:,:,:] Alphat = Vt[:, 3:4,:,:,:] oneminusalpha = 1.0 - Alphat cumprod = torch.cumprod(oneminusalpha, dim=2) ones = torch.oneslike(cumprod[:,:, 0:1,:,:]) T = torch.cat([ones, cumprod[:,:,:-1,:,:]], dim=2) weightedcolor = T Alphat Ct return torch.sum(weightedcolor, dim=2) def transformvolume(self, Vs, Pst): # Not given in the sources. Uses gridsample with a grid generated from Pst to rotate/translate the voxel grid. pass class UNet2D(nn.Module): def init(self, channelsin, channelsout): super().init() # Not given in the sources. 2D U-Net with ResNet-18 backbone. pass class UNet3D(nn.Module): def init(self, channelsin, channelsout): super().init() # Not given in the sources. 3D U-Net with ResNet-3D blocks. pass Learning Rate: 0.0016 (fixed throughout training). SSIM Loss Weight: 0.05. Training Epochs: 150. Nonlinearity: ReLU used throughout the model for each nonlinear transformation. Normalization: GroupNorm [54] used throughout the model for each nonlinear transformation. Data Normalization: ImageNet statistics applied only at the preprocessing stage. Intrinsic Camera Parameters: Used for inverse projection and perspective deformation; assumed constant. Geometry Preservation: Reshaping 2D feature maps directly into 3D volumes loses 3D geometry and texture information. The inverse projection step is essential to preserve this. Resolution Limits: The resolution of rendered images is capped by the explicit voxel-like scene representation. Continuous representations are resolution-free but slower. Future work plans to use octrees, mixture of volumetric primitives, or scene graphs to increase capacity for complex regions while minimizing resources for empty regions, and to enhance with super-resolution methods. View-Dependent Lighting: The current model cannot produce view-dependent lighting effects. It assumes a Lambertian RGBA model. Future work plans to incorporate physically based rendering with view direction, light sources, material properties (roughness, metalness), and surface information (normals, displacement maps), potentially using spherical harmonics or learned MLPs for specular effects. Rendering Speed: Over 400x faster than continuous baselines like NeRF. Complexity: Rendering is amortized across views because the RGBα volume is shared. The cost is dominated by the initial encoding and decoding, which are fixed per scene. Memory: Memory usage is determined by the size of the 3D voxel grid (ds \times h \times w). The source does not specify exact memory consumption in MB, but notes that resolution is capped by the explicit representation. Performance: On unseen-category view synthesis (Table 8 in), the two-view model achieves mean PSNR 24.80, SSIM 0.893, LPIPS 0.107, outperforming the ENR baseline (PSNR 23.16, SSIM 0.807, LPIPS 0.190). The single-view model achieves the same mean metrics (PSNR 24.80, SSIM 0.893, LPIPS 0.107). Strengths: Fast rendering, no per-pixel ray sampling, no scene-specific optimization, category-agnostic training. Limitations: Resolution capped by voxel grid, no view-dependent lighting effects. Explicit Neural View Synthesis was proposed by Pengsheng Guo et al. from Apple. It challenges the trend of continuous and implicit radiance field representations by proposing a simple, explicit volumetric approach that achieves comparable or better quality with significantly faster rendering speeds. Fast and Explicit Neural View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/wacv51458.2022.00009, fetched 2026-10-30

name: RenderNet
head: RenderNet: A deep convolutional network for differentiable rendering from 3D shapes
body: RenderNet is a differentiable rendering convolutional neural network that generates 2D images from 3D voxel grids by jointly learning visibility computation and pixel color calculation (shading). Unlike traditional rasterization or ray tracing which rely on discrete, non-differentiable operations like z-buffering, RenderNet uses a CNN to implicitly handle occlusion and complex shading, enabling inverse rendering tasks such as shape, pose, and texture estimation from single images. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by learning the projection and shading via a dedicated "Projection Unit" rather than using surrogate gradients for discrete operations or approximate rasterization, allowing it to robustly handle low-resolution or noisy voxel inputs that would fail in mesh-based differentiable renderers. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D voxel grid V with dimensions HV \times WV \times DV \times CV (height, width, depth, channel). Typical input resolution is 64 \times 64 \times 64 \times 1. Parameters: Camera pose (azimuth \theta, elevation \eta, distance R), light position \tilde{l}, and optionally texture coefficients \phi. Output: A 2D RGB image I with dimensions HI \times WI \times CI (height, width, channel). Typical output resolution is 512 \times 512 \times 3. Data Structures The core data structure is the voxel grid tensor. The network processes this through a "Projection Unit" which reshapes the 4D tensor into a 3D squeezed tensor V' with dimensions W \times H \times (D \cdot C). Steps 1. Coordinate Transformation: Apply a rigid-body transformation to the input voxel grid V to convert from world coordinates to camera coordinates. The camera is assumed axis-aligned, looking along the negative z-axis. The transformation is parameterized by rotation around the y-axis (azimuth), rotation around the z-axis (elevation), and a distance R (scaling factor). 2. Resampling: Trilinearly sample the transformed input voxel grid to handle the coordinate change and ensure the object is not cut off (the input is embedded in a larger grid to accommodate rotation). 3. Geometry Encoding: Pass the sampled input through a sequence of 3D convolutions and PReLU activations to encode geometry. The specific sequence is: Conv3d, PReLU, Conv3d, PReLU, PReLU, Down-conv3d. 4. Projection and Visibility (Projection Unit): Reshaping: Collapse the depth dimension with the feature maps to map the incoming 4D tensor to a 3D squeezed tensor V' with dimension W \times H \times (D \cdot C). MLP/1x1 Convolution: Apply a Multilayer Perceptron (implemented as a 1x1 convolution) on each (D \cdot C) vector of the squeezed tensor to produce a 3D tensor with K channels. This allows the network to learn visibility along the depth axis, unlike max pooling which only creates a silhouette. The operation is defined as: I'{i,j,k} = \sum{dc} w{k,dc} \cdot V'{i,j,dc} + bk where i, j are pixel coordinates, k is the image channel, dc is the squeezed depth channel (combining original depth d and channel c), and w, b are the weights and biases of the 1x1 convolution. The Projection Unit outputs intermediate representations including a Normal Map and a Final Output (depth/visibility). 5. Shading and Rendering: Apply 2D convolutions and PReLU activations to the projected features to generate the final RGB image. The sequence is: Conv2d, PReLU, Conv2d, PReLU, Up-conv2d, PReLU, PReLU, Up-conv2d. Phong Illumination Extension: If rendering Phong shading, the network outputs a Normal Map and an Albedo Map. The shaded color S is calculated as S = \max(0, \tilde{l} \cdot \tilde{n} + a), where \tilde{l} is the light direction, \tilde{n} is the normal vector (from the Normal Map RGB channels), and a is an ambient constant. The final image is I = A \cdot S, where A is the Albedo Map. Texture Mapping: For texture, a separate network maps 1D texture vectors (e.g., PCA coefficients) to a 3D texture representation, which is concatenated with the input shape before rendering. An additional output branch renders the Normal Map. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendernet(voxelgrid, cameraparams, lightparams=None, textureparams=None): """ Renders a 2D image from a 3D voxel grid using RenderNet. Args: voxelgrid: Tensor of shape (Hv, Wv, Dv, Cv) cameraparams: Dict containing 'azimuth', 'elevation', 'distance' lightparams: Dict containing 'lightdirection' (optional) textureparams: Tensor of texture coefficients (optional) Returns: image: Tensor of shape (Hi, Wi, 3) """ # 1. Coordinate Transformation # Transform voxel grid from world to camera space # Camera is axis-aligned, looking along negative z-axis # Parameters: azimuth (y-rot), elevation (z-rot), distance R (scale) transformedgrid = rigidbodytransform( voxelgrid, azimuth=cameraparams['azimuth'], elevation=cameraparams['elevation'], distance=cameraparams['distance']) # 2. Resampling # Trilinearly sample the transformed grid sampledgrid = trilinearsample(transformedgrid) # 3. Geometry Encoding (3D CNN) # Sequence: Conv3d, PReLU, Conv3d, PReLU, PReLU, Down-conv3d encodedfeatures = conv3dblock(sampledgrid) # 4. Projection Unit # Reshape: Collapse depth and channels # Input shape: (H, W, D, C) -> Output shape: (H, W, DC) squeezedtensor = reshapedepthchannels(encodedfeatures) # MLP / 1x1 Convolution to determine visibility and project # Computes: I'{i,j,k} = sum{dc} w{k,dc} V'{i,j,dc} + bk projectedfeatures = apply1x1conv(squeezedtensor) # Output intermediate maps: Normal Map, Final Output normalmap, finaloutput = extractintermediates(projectedfeatures) # 5. Shading and Rendering (2D CNN) # Sequence: Conv2d, PReLU, Conv2d, PReLU, Up-conv2d, PReLU, PReLU, Up-conv2d # If texture is provided, concatenate with input before projection # (Handled in geometry encoding step if texture network is integrated) # Render Albedo and Normal maps via 2D convolutions albedomap = renderalbedo(finaloutput) # If Phong shading is enabled if lightparams is not None: lightdir = lightparams['lightdirection'] # Calculate shading: S = max(0, l~. n~ + a) # n~ is from normalmap RGB channels shading = phongshading(normalmap, lightdir, ambientconstant=0.1) # Final image: I = A S image = albedomap shading else: # Direct RGB output from the 2D convolutions image = renderrgb(finaloutput) return image def rigidbodytransform(grid, azimuth, elevation, distance): """ Applies rotation and scaling to the voxel grid. Assumes grid is embedded in a larger volume to prevent clipping. """ # Create rotation matrices for Y-axis (azimuth) and Z-axis (elevation) Ry = rotationmatrixy(azimuth) Rz = rotationmatrixz(elevation) R = Rz @ Ry # Scale by distance R (inverse scaling to move camera/object) # Note: The paper describes R as a scaling factor determining how close the object is scalematrix = scalingmatrix(distance) # Apply transformation to voxel coordinates # This requires generating a grid of coordinates and applying the affine transform coords = generatevoxelcoordinates(grid.shape) transformedcoords = applyaffine(coords, R, scalematrix) # Trilinear interpolation to resample the grid at new coordinates # Standard trilinear interpolation implementation resampled = trilinearinterpolation(grid, transformedcoords) return resampled def conv3dblock(tensor): """ Applies the 3D convolution sequence: Conv3d, PReLU, Conv3d, PReLU, PReLU, Down-conv3d """ x = conv3d(tensor) x = prelu(x) x = conv3d(x) x = prelu(x) x = prelu(x) x = downconv3d(x) # Down-conv3d likely implies strided or pooled convolution return x def reshapedepthchannels(tensor): """ Collapses depth and channel dimensions. Input: (H, W, D, C) Output: (H, W, DC) """ H, W, D, C = tensor.shape return tensor.view(H, W, D C) def apply1x1conv(tensor): """ Applies 1x1 convolution (MLP) on each (DC) vector. Input: (H, W, DC) Output: (H, W, K) where K is the number of output channels """ # 1x1 convolution is equivalent to a linear layer applied per spatial location # In PyTorch, this is F.conv2d with kernelsize=1 return conv2d1x1(tensor) def phongshading(normalmap, lightdirection, ambientconstant=0.1): """ Calculates Phong shading. S = max(0, l~. n~ + a) """ # Normalize normal map vectors (RGB channels) normals = normalize(normalmap) light = normalize(lightdirection) # Dot product dotproduct = sum(normals light, axis=-1) # Apply formula shading = torch.clamp(dotproduct + ambientconstant, min=0) return shading Parameters Optimizer: Adam with learning rate 0.00001. Loss Function: Mean Squared Error (MSE) for colored images; Binary Cross Entropy for grayscale images. Training Strategy: Patch training. Random spatially cropped samples (width/height) are used, keeping depth/channel intact. Patch size starts at 1/8 of the full grid and increases to 1/2 at the end of training. Full-sized grid is used only during inference. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Noisy/Low-Resolution Input: RenderNet handles erroneous or low-resolution voxel inputs robustly, unlike mesh renderers which require clean, high-quality meshes. Inverse Rendering Instability: Directly minimizing reconstruction loss for shape/pose/texture estimation leads to noisy, unstable results. This is mitigated by using a shape prior (a pre-trained 3D auto-encoder) to regularize the optimization. Instead of optimizing the shape z directly, the latent representation z' of the auto-encoder is optimized: \min{z', \theta, \phi', \eta} \| I - f(g(z'), \theta, h(\phi'), \eta) \|^2, where g is the decoder. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: On the Phong-shaded chair dataset, RenderNet achieved a PSNR of 25.39, compared to 22.37 for EC and 27.43 for EC-Deep. For Contour shading, RenderNet scored 24.21, while EC-Deep scored 27.43 (Note: Source lists 27.43 for EC-Deep Phong, and 24.21 for RenderNet Contour; exact comparison for Contour between EC variants is not explicitly detailed in the text snippet, but RenderNet is shown to generalize well). Strengths: Handles occlusion and complex shaders (ambient occlusion, cartoon shading) without explicit geometric visibility tests. Generalizes well to unseen categories and corrupted/low-resolution inputs. Differentiable end-to-end, enabling inverse rendering (shape, pose, texture, lighting estimation). Limitations: Requires voxel grid input, which can be memory inefficient for high-resolution scenes compared to sparse representations (though the paper notes recent work addresses this with octrees). Performance depends on the quality of the training data for the specific shader style. When to use: When differentiable rendering from voxel data is required, especially for inverse rendering tasks involving complex shading or noisy inputs. When not to use: When high-resolution mesh-based rendering is preferred, or when explicit geometric visibility control is required rather than learned visibility. RenderNet was introduced by Thu Nguyen-Phuoc, Chuan Li, Stephen Balaban, and Yong-Liang Yang from the University of Bath and Lambda Labs. The paper "RenderNet: A deep convolutional network for differentiable rendering from 3D shapes" was published on arXiv in April 2019. It addresses the challenge of non-differentiable operations in traditional rendering pipelines (rasterization and ray tracing) which hinder inverse graphics tasks. By framing rendering as a feed-forward CNN, it allows the network to learn visibility and shading jointly. It is used for novel-view synthesis, pose prediction, and image-based 3D shape reconstruction. RenderNet: A deep convolutional network for differentiable rendering from 3D shapes, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.1806.06575, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: ExBluRF
head: Efficient Radiance Fields for Extreme Motion Blurred Images
body: ExBluRF is a novel view synthesis method designed to reconstruct sharp 3D scenes from extreme motion-blurred images by jointly optimizing voxel-based radiance fields and 6-DOF camera trajectories. It differs from sibling methods like FastNeRF or C-NeRF which focus on static scene acceleration, and from DeblurNeRF (a sibling in the broader deblurring context, though not listed in the immediate sibling tree, it is the primary comparison in) which uses 2D pixel-wise blur kernels, by formulating motion blur as a trajectory-based accumulation of rays along a Bézier curve. This approach allows ExBluRF to handle extreme blur with significantly lower memory and computational costs compared to MLP-based deblurring methods, as its memory complexity remains constant relative to the number of blur samples. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of M extremely motion-blurred images \{Im\}{m=1}^M with known or estimated initial camera poses. Outputs: A sharp voxel-based radiance field (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}) and the optimized 6-DOF camera trajectory parameters for each input image. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Grid: Replaces the MLP f{NeRF} used in standard NeRF. It stores volumetric densities \sigma and colors \mathbf{c} at voxel centers. Direct trilinear interpolation is used to query \sigma and \mathbf{c} at any 3D point \mathbf{X}. 2. Bézier Curve Control Points: The camera trajectory for each view is parameterized by control points \{\hat{\mathbf{p}}j\}{j=0}^M in the Lie algebra \mathfrak{se}(3), where M is the order of the Bézier curve. Parameters: N: Number of sampling points (intermediate sub-frames) along the camera trajectory to approximate the motion blur integral. Typical values range from 5 to 31. P: Number of sample points on a single ray during volume rendering. M: Order of the Bézier curve. Typical values are 1 (linear) or 3. B: Number of rays processed in a batch. Algorithm Steps: 1. Trajectory Reparameterization: For each input image, define the initial pose P{\tauo} and final pose P{\tauc}. Reparameterize the 6-DOF motion trajectory using a Bézier curve of order M in the Lie algebra \mathfrak{se}(3). The pose at normalized time \tau'i is computed as: \mathbf{p}{\taui} = \sum{j=0}^{M} \binom{M}{j} (1-\tau'i)^{M-j} (\tau'i)^j \cdot \hat{\mathbf{p}}j where \tau'i = \frac{\taui - \tauo}{\tauc - \tauo} and \hat{\mathbf{p}}j are the learnable control points. The actual camera pose P{\taui} is obtained by exponentiating \mathbf{p}{\taui}. 2. Ray Generation: For each training iteration and each blurry input image: a. Define the camera intrinsic matrix \mathbf{K} and extrinsic matrix \mathbf{R} (derived from P{\taui}). b. For each pixel x in the image, compute the ray direction \mathbf{d}{\taui} at each of the N intermediate shutter times \taui: \mathbf{d}{\taui} = \mathbf{R}{\taui} \cdot \mathbf{K}^{-1} [\mathbf{x}]+ where [\mathbf{x}]+ is the homogeneous coordinate of pixel x. c. The ray origin is the camera center corresponding to P{\taui}. 3. Volume Rendering (Per Ray): For each generated ray \mathbf{r}{\taui}, compute the color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}{\taui}) using the standard volume rendering equation with the voxel-based radiance field: \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}{\taui}) = \sum{k=1}^{P} Tk (1 - \exp(-\sigmak \deltak)) \mathbf{c}k where \sigmak and \mathbf{c}k are the density and color sampled from the voxel grid at the k-th sample point along the ray, \deltak is the distance between sample points, and Tk = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{k-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance. 4. Blur Accumulation: Compute the blurred color \hat{\mathbf{C}}B(\mathbf{x}) for pixel x by averaging the rendered colors from the N intermediate rays: \hat{\mathbf{C}}B(\mathbf{x}) \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}{\taui}(\mathbf{x})) This approximates the integral of ray colors accumulated while the shutter is open. 5. Optimization: Compute the photo-consistency loss (e.g., L1 or L2) between the estimated blurred image \hat{\mathbf{C}}B and the input blurry image I{blur}. Backpropagate the loss to optimize both the voxel grid parameters (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) and the Bézier control points \{\hat{\mathbf{p}}j\}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def beziercurve(controlpoints, t): """ Compute pose in Lie algebra se(3) using Bézier curve. controlpoints: list of M+1 vectors in se(3) (6D each). t: normalized time in [0, 1]. Returns: vector in se(3). """ M = len(controlpoints) - 1 result = np.zeros(6) for j in range(M + 1): coeff = comb(M, j) ((1 - t) (M - j)) (t j) result += coeff controlpoints[j] return result def raymarchvoxel(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelgrid, numsamples): """ Render a single ray using voxel-based radiance field. voxelgrid: function query(x, y, z) -> (sigma, color) """ totaltransmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = np.zeros(3) # Sample points along the ray # Assuming fixed step size or near/far bounds defined elsewhere # For simplicity, assume we have pre-computed sample depths sk for k in range(numsamples): # Sample point Xk = origin + sk direction # In a real implementation, sk would be generated based on near/far planes # Here we assume a helper getsamplepoint exists or is implicit Xk = rayorigin + raydirection getsampledepth(k) sigma, color = voxelgrid.query(Xk) # Alpha and transmittance alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigma getstepsize(k)) weight = totaltransmittance alpha accumulatedcolor += weight color totaltransmittance = (1.0 - alpha) return accumulatedcolor def exblurfoptimize(blurryimages, initialposes, voxelgrid, beziercontrolpoints): """ Main optimization loop. """ Nsamplestrajectory = 21 # Example value Nsamplesray = 128 # Example value for iteration in range(maxiterations): totalloss = 0.0 for imageidx, blurryimage in enumerate(blurryimages): # 1. Get initial and final poses for this view Pstart = initialposes[imageidx][0] Pend = initialposes[imageidx][1] # 2. Generate N intermediate poses along Bézier curve intermediateposes = [] for i in range(1, Nsamplestrajectory + 1): t = i / (Nsamplestrajectory + 1) # Interpolate in Lie Algebra ptau = beziercurve(beziercontrolpoints[imageidx], t) # Convert Lie Algebra to SE(3) pose (exponential map) # Implementation detail: expmap(ptau) converts se(3) to SE(3) posetau = expmap(ptau) intermediateposes.append(posetau) # 3. Render blurred image renderedblurredimage = np.zeroslike(blurryimage) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): pixelcoloraccum = np.zeros(3) for pose in intermediateposes: # Get camera extrinsic R and intrinsic K R = pose.rotationmatrix # K is assumed constant or known # Ray direction # [x]+ is homogeneous coordinate raydir = R @ np.linalg.inv(K) @ np.array([x, y, 1]) raydir = raydir / np.linalg.norm(raydir) # Ray origin is camera center rayorigin = pose.translation # Render single ray color = raymarchvoxel(rayorigin, raydir, voxelgrid, Nsamplesray) pixelcoloraccum += color # Average over N samples renderedblurredimage[y, x] = pixelcoloraccum / Nsamplestrajectory # 4. Compute Loss loss = np.mean(np.abs(renderedblurredimage - blurryimage)) totalloss += loss # 5. Backpropagate # Standard AD through the voxel grid query and Bézier curve # Update voxelgrid parameters and beziercontrolpoints[imageidx] pass # Update global optimizer step pass Time Complexity: Training time is significantly reduced compared to MLP-based methods. On the 'Camellia' dataset, ExBluRF achieves 10x less training time than DeblurNeRF (4.41 hrs vs 27.48 hrs). Memory Complexity: The memory complexity per ray is O(1) because ray marching evaluates sample points sequentially. In contrast, DeblurNeRF requires O(P \cdot L) memory per ray due to synchronous feed-forwarding of P points through L MLP layers. ExBluRF's total memory usage is constant with respect to the number of trajectory samples N. Performance: On the 'Camellia' scene, ExBluRF achieves a PSNR of 28.83 with 4.31 GB GPU memory, compared to DeblurNeRF's 27.76 PSNR with 13.89 GB memory. Strengths: Handles extreme motion blur efficiently; allows large N (e.g., 31 samples) without memory explosion; jointly optimizes geometry and camera pose. Limitations: Requires per-scene optimization; sensitive to the order of the Bézier curve (higher orders may overfit, lower orders may underfit complex motion). When to use: When dealing with extreme motion blur where 2D kernel methods fail or are too memory-intensive, and ground truth sharp images are unavailable for supervised pre-training. ExBluRF was introduced by Dongwoo Lee, Sunghyun Cho, Joon-Young Lee, Kyoung Mu Lee, et al. in 2023. It addresses the limitations of previous NeRF-based deblurring methods like DeblurNeRF and BAD-NeRF, which struggled with extreme blur due to high computational costs or inability to model complex 6-DOF trajectories. The method builds on the principles of differentiable volume rendering [44-radiance-field-optimization.md] and voxel-based representations [10852-voxel-based-representation.md]. It was validated on the newly proposed ExBlur dataset, which contains multi-view extremely blurred images with ground truth sharp pairs and trajectories.
