name: Part-based MHE-augmented NeRF
head: Instant NVR, Learning Neural Volumetric Representations of Dynamic Humans in Minutes, Part-based voxelized human representation
body: Part-based MHE-augmented NeRF is a method for learning neural volumetric videos of dynamic humans from sparse view videos in minutes with competitive visual quality. It addresses the challenge of quickly reconstructing free-viewpoint videos of dynamic humans by decomposing the canonical human body into multiple anatomical parts, assigning each part its own Multiresolution Hash Encoding (MHE)-augmented NeRF network. This approach efficiently distributes representational power to handle varying shape and texture complexity across different body parts (e.g., face vs. torso) and accelerates training convergence compared to a single unified NeRF. It builds on Voxel-based Representation by using a structured set of voxelized NeRF networks rather than a single global field. Inputs: Sparse multi-view video frames of a dynamic human. SMPL parameters for each frame: pose \rho, shape \beta, and camera extrinsics/intrinsics. For each query point \mathbf{x} at frame t, the method requires finding the nearest surface point on the posed SMPL mesh. Outputs: Density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} for any query point \mathbf{x} in space and time t. Rendered novel view images via volume rendering. Data Structures: 1. SMPL Model: Parametric human model M=(V, E) with vertices V and edges E. Contains blend weights wi for each vertex vi and UV coordinates (ui, vi) for the template mesh. 2. Part Decomposition: The body is divided into K parts. For each part k, a subset of bones \Omegak is defined. The mesh for part k is Mk = (Vk, Ek), where Vk = \{vi \mid \arg\max wi \in \Omegak\}. 3. MHE Tables: Each part k has its own multiresolution hash table with size Tk adapted to the local complexity of that part. 4. Networks: Density Network MLP{\sigmak}: Takes encoded canonical point \psik(\mathbf{x}{can}) as input. Outputs density \sigmak and feature vector \mathbf{z}. Color Network MLP{ck}: Takes feature vector \mathbf{z}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and latent embedding \mathbf{l}t as input. Outputs color \mathbf{c}k. Residual Deformation MLP: Takes hash-encoded (u, v, t) as input. Outputs residual translation \Delta \mathbf{x}. 5. Latent Embeddings: A latent vector \mathbf{l}t for each frame t to model temporally-varying appearance. Numbered Steps: 1. Part Decomposition: Manually divide the human body into K parts based on the SMPL model's blend weights. Define \Omegak as the set of bones for part k. 2. Query Processing (Per Part): For a query point \mathbf{x} at frame t: a. Find the nearest surface point \mathbf{p}k on each part Mk of the posed SMPL mesh. b. Obtain the blend weight wk and UV coordinate (uk, vk) of surface point \mathbf{p}k from the SMPL model. 3. Motion Parameterization (Canonical Space Mapping): a. Inverse LBS: Transform the query point \mathbf{x} to the unposed space using inverse Linear Blend Skinning (LBS). Given pose \rho, blend weight wk, and query point \mathbf{x}, the transformed point \mathbf{x}0 is calculated as: \mathbf{x}0 = \Phi{LBS}(\mathbf{x}, wk, \rho) = \left( \sum{j=1}^{J} w{k,j} Gj \right)^{-1} \mathbf{x} where \rho denotes the human pose, \{Gj\}{j=1}^J are the transformation matrices for the bones, and w{k,j} is the weight of bone j for the part. b. Residual Deformation: Apply Multiresolution Hash Encoding (MHE) \psi{res} to the 2D UV coordinates and time (uk, vk, t). Feed the encoded point to the residual deformation MLP to regress the residual translation \Delta \mathbf{x}. c. Canonical Point: Add the residual translation to the inverse LBS output to obtain the canonical point \mathbf{x}{can}: \mathbf{x}{can} = \mathbf{x}0 + \Delta \mathbf{x} 4. Density and Color Prediction (Per Part): a. Predefine the MHE function \psik for part k. Apply \psik to the canonical point \mathbf{x}{can} to get the encoded point. b. Feed \psik(\mathbf{x}{can}) to the density network MLP{\sigmak} to predict density \sigmak and feature vector \mathbf{z}: (\sigmak, \mathbf{z}) = MLP{\sigmak}(\psik(\mathbf{x}{can})) c. Feed \mathbf{z}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and latent embedding \mathbf{l}t to the color network MLP{ck} to predict color \mathbf{c}k: \mathbf{c}k = MLP{ck}(\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{d}, \mathbf{l}t) 5. Final Selection: From the set of predictions \{(\sigmak, \mathbf{c}k)\}{k=1}^K for all K parts, select the one with the maximum density as the final density and color for the query point: (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) = (\sigma{k^}, \mathbf{c}{k^}), \quad \text{where } k^ = \arg\maxk \sigmak 6. Rendering: Use the standard volume rendering equation [44-radiance-field-optimization.md] to compute the pixel color from the sampled points along the ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class PartBasedMHENeRF: def init(self, numparts, smplmodel, hashtablesizes, mheconfig): """ Initialize the part-based MHE-augmented NeRF. Args: numparts (int): Number of anatomical parts (K). smplmodel: SMPL model instance providing mesh, blend weights, and UVs. hashtablesizes (list): List of hash table sizes Tk for each part. mheconfig: Configuration for Multiresolution Hash Encoding. """ self.K = numparts self.smpl = smplmodel self.parts = [] # Initialize part-specific networks and MHE tables for k in range(self.K): # Create MHE table for part k with specific size mhetable = createmhetable(size=hashtablesizes[k], config=mheconfig) # Density network: Input -> Density + Feature Vector densitynet = nn.Sequential( #... layers taking MHE output... nn.Linear(mheoutputdim, 1), # Density nn.Linear(mheoutputdim, 256) # Feature vector z) # Color network: Feature Vector + View Dir + Latent -> Color colornet = nn.Sequential( #... layers taking z, d, lt... nn.Linear(256 + 3 + 32, 3) # Color RGB) # Residual deformation network: UV + Time -> Delta X resmhetable = createmhetable(size=hashtablesizes[k], config=mheconfig) resnet = nn.Sequential( #... layers taking resmhe output... nn.Linear(mheoutputdim, 3) # Residual translation) self.parts.append({ 'mhe': mhetable, 'densitynet': densitynet, 'colornet': colornet, 'resmhe': resmhetable, 'resnet': resnet }) # Latent embeddings for each frame self.latentembeddings = nn.Embedding(numframes, 32) def getnearestsurfacepoint(self, querypoint, partmesh): """ Find the nearest surface point on a specific part's mesh. Returns: surfacepoint, blendweight, uvcoords """ # Implementation depends on nearest neighbor search on mesh # Using SMPL model's precomputed data or efficient spatial search pass def inverselbs(self, querypoint, blendweight, pose): """ Compute inverse LBS transformation. x0 = (sum(wj Gj))^-1 x """ # Get bone transformation matrices Gj from pose # Compute weighted sum of matrices # Invert the matrix # Apply to querypoint pass def forward(self, querypoints, frameindices, poses, viewdirections): """ Forward pass for a batch of query points. Args: querypoints: Tensor of shape (N, 3) frameindices: Tensor of shape (N,) indicating frame t for each point poses: Tensor of shape (N, posedim) viewdirections: Tensor of shape (N, 3) Returns: densities: Tensor of shape (N,) colors: Tensor of shape (N, 3) """ densities = [] colors = [] for k in range(self.K): part = self.parts[k] # 1. Find nearest surface point on part k's mesh # Note: In practice, this is done efficiently for all points # For simplicity, assuming we have precomputed nearest points for this part # surfacepoints, blendweights, uvs = self.getnearestsurfacepointforpart(querypoints, k) # 2. Inverse LBS # x0 = inverselbs(querypoints, blendweights, poses) # 3. Residual Deformation # Encode (u, v, t) # tcoords = frameindices to time values # resencoded = part'resmhe' # deltax = part'resnet' # 4. Canonical Point # xcan = x0 + deltax # 5. Density Prediction # encodedx = part'mhe' # densityout, z = part'densitynet' # densitiesk = densityout # 6. Color Prediction # latent = self.latentembeddings(frameindices) # colorsk = part'colornet' # Store results for selection # densities.append(densitiesk) # colors.append(colorsk) # Placeholder for actual implementation logic # densities.append(torch.zeroslike(querypoints[:, 0])) # colors.append(torch.zeroslike(querypoints)) pass # 7. Select max density # densitiesstack = torch.stack(densities, dim=1) # (N, K) # maxdensityindices = torch.argmax(densitiesstack, dim=1) # (N,) # finaldensities = densitiesstack.gather(1, maxdensityindices.unsqueeze(1)).squeeze(1) # colorsstack = torch.stack(colors, dim=1) # (N, K, 3) # finalcolors = colorsstack.gather(1, maxdensityindices.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(2).expand(-1, -1, 3)).squeeze(1) return finaldensities, finalcolors Parameters: Hash Table Size: Adapted per part based on complexity. Uniformly large tables (e.g., 2^{20}) increase memory and training time without quality gains. Learning Rate: 5 \times 10^{-4} (Adam optimizer). Training Time: Approximately 5 minutes on a single RTX 3090 GPU for a 512x512 video with 100 frames. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Uniform Hash Table Size: Using a uniformly large hash table across all parts increases memory consumption and per-iteration training time without guaranteed quality gains. Equal Complexity Assumption: Treating all parts as equally complex wastes representational power on simple regions and degrades PSNR (e.g., by 1.98dB). Motion Parameterization: Human motion occurs around a surface; points near the surface projected to neighboring regions on a parametric model have similar motion behavior. Ignoring this 2D structure (e.g., using 3D coordinates) reduces convergence rate. Time Complexity: Training time is significantly reduced compared to prior methods. It is approximately 100 times faster than Neural Body [58], which typically requires more than 10 hours of training. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is optimized by adapting hash table sizes per part. Uniformly large tables increase memory consumption. Measured Performance: On the ZJU-MoCap dataset, the method achieves competitive PSNR. Ablation studies show that the part-based approach (286M params) yields higher PSNR than a single MHE-augmented NeRF (302M params). Removing the UV-based residual deformation reduces PSNR from 32.09dB to 31.40dB. Strengths: Fast convergence (minutes vs. hours), efficient distribution of representational power, competitive visual quality. Limitations: Requires SMPL parameters and sparse multi-view videos. Performance may degrade if the human model is not well-aligned with the SMPL template. Origin: Proposed by Zhen Xu, Hujun Bao, and Xiaowei Zhou from Zhejiang University. Paper: "Learning Neural Volumetric Representations of Dynamic Humans in Minutes" (CVPR 2023). History: Addresses the limitation of per-scene optimization methods that require hours of training. Builds on Neural Body [58] and generalizable NeRF models [34, 99] but focuses on rapid per-scene optimization without sacrificing fidelity. Usage: Used for creating volumetric videos of human performers for immersive telepresence, video games, and movie production. Learning Neural Volumetric Representations of Dynamic Humans in Minutes, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00846, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Object-NeRF
head: ObjectNeRF
body: Object-NeRF is a composition model that separates and edits objects within a scene using a hybrid voxel-based approach with jointly optimized voxel grid features and MLP parameters. It differs from standard volume rendering by explicitly partitioning the radiance field into distinct scene and object branches, enabling the shifting or addition of objects within the scene without requiring explicit objectness priors during training. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view RGB images, corresponding camera poses, and instance segmentation labels for each in-scene object. Outputs: A decomposed radiance field consisting of separate scene and object components, allowing for per-object editing and re-rendering. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Grid: A 3D grid of features that is jointly optimized with MLP parameters. The grid stores latent features used to condition the neural networks. 2. Scene Branch: A neural network (MLP) conditioned on interpolated voxel features to encode scene geometry and appearance. 3. Object Branch: A neural network (MLP) conditioned on interpolated voxel features and object activation latent codes to encode object geometry and appearance. 4. Object Activation Latent Codes: A set of latent codes specific to each object instance, conditioning the object branch. Method Steps: 1. Voxel Feature Optimization: Create a voxel grid of features and jointly optimize these features with the MLP parameters. 2. Branch Definition: Introduce two separate neural network branches: A scene branch for encoding the global scene geometry and appearance. An object branch for encoding individual object geometry and appearance. 3. Conditioning: Both the scene and object branches are conditioned on features interpolated from the voxel grid. The object branch is further conditioned on a set of object activation latent codes. 4. Rendering: Use the two different NeRFs (one for objects, one for the scene) to compute radiance values. 5. Training Loss: Incorporate segmentation labels with a mask loss term to identify each in-scene object. Use photometric losses for both foreground (objects) and background (scene). Formulas: The rendering process involves two separate radiance fields. Let \mathbf{r} be a ray. The final pixel value is a composition of the scene and object contributions. While the exact compositional formula is not explicitly detailed in the provided notes, the method relies on separating the radiance field into components. The object NeRF is conditioned on latent codes \mathbf{z}o: \text{Object Branch} = f{\text{obj}}(\text{VoxelFeatures}(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{z}o) The scene branch is conditioned only on voxel features: \text{Scene Branch} = f{\text{scene}}(\text{VoxelFeatures}(\mathbf{x})) The training objective includes a mask loss \mathcal{L}{mask} derived from segmentation labels and photometric losses \mathcal{L}{photo} for foreground and background. Parameters: Voxel Grid Resolution: Not given in the sources. MLP Architecture: Not given in the sources. Latent Code Dimension: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Segmentation Dependency: The method requires instance segmentation labels for training. Object Identification: The mask loss term is critical for identifying each in-scene object. This method decomposes a composite radiance field into individual object layers and distinct background layers (near and far) to enable per-object editing and re-rendering. It differs from standard volume rendering by explicitly partitioning the ray integration domain based on 3D bounding boxes, allowing objects to be isolated from the background without requiring explicit objectness priors during training. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Trained and evaluated on ScanNet [31] and an in-house ToyDesk dataset. Strengths: Enables shifting or addition of objects within the scene. Achieves good results for amodal segmentation and object interpolation. Limitations: Requires instance segmentation labels. When to use: When object-based modeling and editing are required. When not to use: When segmentation labels are unavailable. Object-NeRF was created by Yang et al. in September 2021. It is a composition model that can separate and edit objects within the scene. The method utilizes a hybrid voxel-based approach [39] and was trained and evaluated on ScanNet [31] as well as an in-house ToyDesk dataset with instance segmentation labels. It incorporates segmentation labels with a mask loss term, identifying each in-scene object. name: Scene Editing and Decomposition
head: Object Re-rendering, Object-NeRF Scene Decomposition, Scene Decomposition
body: This method decomposes a composite radiance field into individual object layers and distinct background layers (near and far) to enable per-object editing and re-rendering. It differs from standard volume rendering by explicitly partitioning the ray integration domain based on 3D bounding boxes, allowing objects to be isolated from the background without requiring explicit objectness priors during training. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A trained hybrid voxel-MLP model (from Object-NeRF), 3D bounding boxes for each object in the scene (obtained from a detector), and camera ray parameters (\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}). Outputs: Decomposed color \mathbf{c} and opacity \alpha for individual objects, near background, and far background. Data Structures Triplanar Feature Grid (\mathbf{S}): Stores features for bilinear interpolation at query locations. 3D Bounding Boxes: Axis-aligned or oriented boxes defining the spatial extent of each object i. Parameters Negative Density Threshold: \sigma{\text{neg}} = -1 \times 10^{-5}, used to prune rays inside object bounding boxes for near-background calculation. Steps 1. Ray Partitioning: For a given ray, determine which segments intersect the 3D bounding boxes of the objects. 2. Far Background Rendering: For ray segments outside all object bounding boxes, query the standard scene MLP to retrieve color \mathbf{c}^bi and density \sigma^bi. These values are unchanged from the original rendering formulation. 3. Near Background Rendering: To isolate the near background, prune rays inside the object bounding boxes. This is achieved by setting the density \sigma^{nb}i to a large negative value (-1 \times 10^{-5}) before volumetric rendering. Query the MLP for color \mathbf{c}^{nb}i and this modified density. 4. Object Rendering: For each object i, restrict sampling to the interior of its 3D bounding box. Sample the foreground MLP (using features from grid \mathbf{S}) to retrieve object color \mathbf{c}^oi and density \sigma^oi. 5. Compositing: Aggregate the contributions from far background (b), near background (nb), and objects (o) using alpha compositing weights w. Formula The composited color \mathbf{c} is calculated as: \mathbf{c} = \sumi w^bi \mathbf{c}^bi + \sumi w^{nb}i \mathbf{c}^{nb}i + \sumi w^oi \mathbf{c}^oi Where w^bi, w^{nb}i, w^oi are the accumulated weights for the far background, near background, and object i respectively along the ray. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderdecomposed(rayorigin, raydirection, objectboxes, scenemlp, featuregrid): """ Renders a ray decomposed into far background, near background, and objects. """ # 1. Calculate intersection intervals for all object boxes objectintervals = [] for box in objectboxes: intervals = rayboxintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, box) if intervals: objectintervals.append((box.id, intervals)) # Sort intervals by tstart objectintervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[1][0]) # 2. Define background intervals (outside all boxes) backgroundintervals = getcomplementintervals( rayorigin, raydirection, objectintervals) # Initialize accumulators colorfar = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alphafar = 0.0 colornear = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alphanear = 0.0 objectcolors = {} # id -> color objectalphas = {} # id -> alpha weightsfar = [] weightsnear = [] weightsobjects = [] currentt = rayorigin.tmin # Start of ray # Helper to accumulate color/alpha for a segment def accumulatesegment(tstart, tend, queryfn): nonlocal currentt, colorfar, alphafar, colornear, alphanear if tend <= tstart: return # Sample points along segment numsamples = 128 ts = linspace(tstart, tend, numsamples) for t in ts: pos = rayorigin + t raydirection color, density = queryfn(pos) # Alpha compositing step alpha = 1.0 - exp(-density (tend - tstart) / numsamples) # Approximation weight = alpha exp(-sum(alphassofar)) # This is a simplified accumulation logic; standard NeRF uses cumulative alpha # For decomposition, we separate the contributions based on the segment type pass # Note: Full implementation requires standard volumetric integration loop # Here we conceptualize the separation logic described in pass # 3. Render Far Background for interval in backgroundintervals: # Standard MLP query color, density = scenemlp.query(interval.start, interval.end) # Accumulate to far background buffers accumulatefar(interval, color, density) # 4. Render Near Background # Prune by setting density to negative high value inside object boxes # This effectively makes the object boxes transparent/invisible to the near background pass for interval in backgroundintervals: # Standard MLP query color, density = scenemlp.query(interval.start, interval.end) accumulatenear(interval, color, density) for boxid, intervals in objectintervals: for interval in intervals: # Query MLP but force density to negative value pos = rayorigin + interval.start raydirection color, = scenemlp.query(pos) density = -1e-5 # Pruning value accumulatenear(interval, color, density) # 5. Render Objects for boxid, intervals in objectintervals: for interval in intervals: # Sample inside foreground MLP / feature grid pos = rayorigin + interval.start raydirection color, density = objectmlp.query(pos, featuregrid) accumulateobject(boxid, interval, color, density) # 6. Composite # Combine far, near, and object contributions finalcolor = composite(weightsfar, colorfar, weightsnear, colornear, weightsobjects, objectcolors) return finalcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls No Objectness Prior: The decomposition is purely learned from multi-view image-based rendering. No explicit objectness prior is enforced during training, which may lead to artifacts if the detector provides inaccurate bounding boxes. Pruning Value: The specific negative density value (-1 \times 10^{-5}) must be consistent to ensure rays are correctly pruned for the near-background pass without causing numerical instability. The parent method that provides the hybrid voxel-MLP representation and jointly optimized features required for this decomposition. Object-NeRF The underlying integration technique used to compute the weights and colors for each segment. Volumetric Rendering Time Complexity: Depends on the number of objects and the resolution of the feature grid. Requires additional ray-box intersection tests and separate integration passes for far background, near background, and each object. Memory Complexity: Requires storing 3D bounding boxes for all objects. The feature grid size is determined by the parent Object-NeRF model. Performance: On the NeRDS 360 dataset with 3-view input, NeO 360 achieves a PSNR of 19.35 and SSIM of 0.59, outperforming baselines like mipNeRF360 (PSNR 13.25, SSIM 0.31) and PixelNeRF (PSNR 13.25, SSIM 0.31). Strengths: Enables accurate object re-rendering and editing from very few input views. Provides full control over object editability. Limitations: Relies on accurate 3D bounding boxes from a detector. Artifacts may appear in regions with no overlap in sparse views. No explicit objectness prior ensures decomposition is data-driven, which may fail on ambiguous scenes. The method was introduced in "NeO 360: Neural Fields for Sparse View Synthesis of Outdoor Scenes" (ICCV 2023). It builds upon the Object-NeRF framework to address few-shot novel view synthesis and scene decomposition tasks. The approach was evaluated on the NeRDS 360 dataset, demonstrating superior performance in both full scene synthesis and object-level decomposition compared to generalizable NeRF baselines like PixelNeRF and MVSNeRF. name: VoxGRAF
head: Sparse Voxel Grid GAN, VoxGRAF Sparse Voxel Grid Generation
body: VoxGRAF is a 3D-aware Generative Adversarial Network that replaces the coordinate-based Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) scene representation with a sparse voxel grid generator. It solves the problem of slow rendering and viewpoint/content entanglement inherent in previous 3D-aware GANs by enabling fast, 3D-consistent image synthesis via a single forward pass to generate the entire 3D scene. Unlike siblings that query an MLP per sample or use hybrid neural rendering, VoxGRAF generates high-resolution geometry directly on a sparse grid, allowing efficient rendering from arbitrary viewpoints without reducing sample size. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Latent code z \in \mathbb{R}^M sampled from \mathcal{N}(0,1); Camera pose \xi (extrinsics); Camera intrinsics K; Optional background latent code. Outputs: Rendered RGB image \hat{I}; Alpha mask \hat{a}. Data Structures: Sparse Voxel Grid: A 3D grid of resolution RG \times RG \times RG. Fields: Color c \in \mathbb{R}^3 and Density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}^+ at each voxel vertex. Layout: Stored as a sparse structure (e.g., using coordinate lists or hash maps) to exclude empty/occluded voxels. The generator outputs dense tensors of shape \mathbb{R}^{3 \times RG \times RG \times RG} and \mathbb{R}^{1 \times RG \times RG \times RG}, which are then pruned. Sampling Points: N points along each camera ray \mathbf{r}, denoted \{xi^{\mathbf{r}}\}{i=1}^N. Parameters: RG: Grid resolution. Typical values: 32, 64, 128. N: Number of sampling points per ray. Typical value: 48. \tauT: Transmittance pruning threshold. \tau\sigma: Density pruning threshold. \tau: Depth variance loss threshold (hyperparameter defining surface thickness). \lambda{DV}: Weight for Depth Variance Loss. \lambda: R1 regularization strength. Learning Rates: Generator 0.0025, Discriminator 0.002. Batch Size: 64. Numbered Steps: 1. Foreground Generation: The foreground generator G{f,\theta{fg}} takes z and \xi as input. It produces dense color values c \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times RG \times RG \times RG} and densities \sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times RG \times RG \times RG} on a voxel grid of resolution RG. 2. Pruning: To enforce sparsity, voxels are discarded based on rendering visibility. For each ray \mathbf{r}, let V{\mathbf{r}} be the set of voxels intersecting the ray. The pruning operator \rho retains voxels i \in V{\mathbf{r}} if: V{\mathbf{r}}^p = \{ i \in V{\mathbf{r}} \mid (Ti > \tauT) \land (\sigmai > \tau\sigma) \} where Ti is the transmittance and \sigmai is the density. 3. Upsampling (Progressive Growing): After pruning, kept voxels are upsampled via sparse transposed convolutions to increase resolution. 4. Ray Sampling: For each pixel in the target image, cast a camera ray \mathbf{r} defined by K and \xi. Sample N points xi^{\mathbf{r}} along the ray. 5. Interpolation: Compute color ci^{\mathbf{r}} and density \sigmai^{\mathbf{r}} at each sampling point xi^{\mathbf{r}} by trilinearly interpolating the values stored at the nearest eight vertices of the voxel grid. 6. Alpha Composition: Compute the transmittance Ti^{\mathbf{r}} and alpha \alphai^{\mathbf{r}} for each sample: \alphai^{\mathbf{r}} = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai^{\mathbf{r}} \deltai^{\mathbf{r}}) Ti^{\mathbf{r}} = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj^{\mathbf{r}}) where \deltai^{\mathbf{r}} = \|x{i+1}^{\mathbf{r}} - xi^{\mathbf{r}}\|2 is the distance between neighboring sample points. 7. Foreground Rendering: Compute the foreground color c{\mathbf{r}} and alpha a{\mathbf{r}}: c{\mathbf{r}} = \sum{i=1}^N Ti^{\mathbf{r}} \alphai^{\mathbf{r}} ci^{\mathbf{r}} a{\mathbf{r}} = \sum{i=1}^N Ti^{\mathbf{r}} \alphai^{\mathbf{r}}. 8. Background Generation: Generate a background image using a separate 2D GAN G{bg,\thetab} conditioned on the pose. 9. Composition: Combine foreground and background using alpha composition to produce the final image \hat{I}. 10. Refinement (Optional): Refine the rendered image with a shallow 2D CNN (2 hidden layers, dimension 16, kernel size 3) operating on 3 channels at full resolution to model dataset biases (e.g., eye direction). 11. Discrimination: The discriminator D{\phi} compares the generated image \hat{I} to the real image I{real}, conditioned on the camera pose. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class VoxGRAF: def init(self, RG, Nsamples, tauT, tausigma, taudepthvar): self.RG = RG self.Nsamples = Nsamples self.tauT = tauT self.tausigma = tausigma self.taudepthvar = taudepthvar # Generators self.Gfg = ForegroundGenerator(RG) # Outputs dense c, sigma self.Gbg = BackgroundGenerator() # Outputs background image self.RefineNet = RefineCNN() # Optional 2D CNN # Discriminator self.D = Discriminator() # Optimizers self.optG = torch.optim.Adam(list(self.Gfg.parameters()) + list(self.Gbg.parameters()) + list(self.RefineNet.parameters()), lr=0.0025) self.optD = torch.optim.Adam(self.D.parameters(), lr=0.002) def prunegrid(self, cdense, sigmadense, rays, K, pose): """ Prunes the dense voxel grid based on transmittance and density thresholds. Returns sparse coordinates and values. """ # 1. Render a proxy view to determine visibility # Sample points along rays points = samplepointsalongrays(rays, self.Nsamples) # Interpolate dense grid at points cinterp, sigmainterp = trilinearinterpolate(cdense, sigmadense, points) # Compute alpha and transmittance for proxy rendering deltas = computedeltas(points) alphas = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmainterp deltas) transmittances = computetransmittance(alphas) # Pruning logic: discard if T < tauT OR sigma < tausigma # Note: In practice, this is done via CUDA kernels on the grid structure # Here we simulate the mask creation for retained voxels validmask = (transmittances > self.tauT) & (sigmainterp > self.tausigma) # Identify unique voxels intersecting valid rays # This step typically involves mapping ray samples back to voxel indices # and aggregating. For implementation clarity, we assume a sparse structure # is built from the valid voxels. sparsecoords, sparsec, sparsesigma = buildsparsestructure( cdense, sigmadense, validmask, self.RG) return sparsecoords, sparsec, sparsesigma def renderray(self, sparsecoords, sparsec, sparsesigma, rayorigin, raydirection, K): """ Renders a single ray using the sparse voxel grid. """ # 1. Sample N points along the ray tvals = torch.linspace(0, 1, self.Nsamples) points = rayorigin + raydirection.unsqueeze(1) tvals.unsqueeze(0) # 2. Trilinear interpolation on sparse grid # Map continuous points to grid coordinates gridcoords = pointstogridcoords(points, self.RG) # Interpolate color and density cvals = sparsetrilinearinterpolate(sparsecoords, sparsec, gridcoords) sigmavals = sparsetrilinearinterpolate(sparsecoords, sparsesigma, gridcoords) # 3. Compute alpha and transmittance # Assuming uniform spacing or pre-computed deltas deltas = computedeltasfrompoints(points) alphas = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmavals deltas) # Cumulative product for transmittance # Ti = prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - alphaj) oneminusalpha = 1.0 - alphas T = torch.cumprod(oneminusalpha, dim=0) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[0:1]), T[:-1]], dim=0) # Shift for T1 = 1 # 4. Alpha composition weights = T alphas color = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) cvals, dim=0) alphamask = torch.sum(weights, dim=0) return color, alphamask def forward(self, z, pose, K, backgroundz=None): # 1. Generate dense foreground grid cdense, sigmadense = self.Gfg(z, pose) # 2. Prune grid # In training, we prune based on the current pose rays = generaterays(K, pose, imageresolution=128) sparsecoords, sparsec, sparsesigma = self.prunegrid( cdense, sigmadense, rays, K, pose) # 3. Render foreground # Render all rays in parallel foregroundcolors, foregroundalphas = [], [] for rayo, rayd in rays: c, a = self.renderray(sparsecoords, sparsec, sparsesigma, rayo, rayd, K) foregroundcolors.append(c) foregroundalphas.append(a) foregroundcolors = torch.stack(foregroundcolors) foregroundalphas = torch.stack(foregroundalphas) # 4. Generate background if backgroundz is None: backgroundz = torch.randnlike(z) backgroundimg = self.Gbg(backgroundz, pose) # 5. Composite # backgroundimg is RGB, foregroundalphas is single channel # Combine: I = F A + B (1 - A) foregroundcolors = foregroundcolors.permute(1, 2, 0) # H, W, C foregroundalphas = foregroundalphas.unsqueeze(-1) composite = foregroundcolors foregroundalphas + backgroundimg (1 - foregroundalphas) # 6. Refine (Optional) if self.RefineNet is not None: composite = self.RefineNet(composite) return composite def computeloss(self, generatedimg, realimg, pose, z): # GAN Loss with R1 Regularization # f(t) = -log(1 + exp(-t)) # V = E[f(-D(G(z))) + f(D(I)) - lambda ||grad D(I)||^2] # Generator loss (non-saturating) Dgen = self.D(generatedimg, pose) Lgen = -torch.mean(torch.log(1 + torch.exp(-Dgen))) # Discriminator loss Dreal = self.D(realimg, pose) Dgendetached = self.D(generatedimg.detach(), pose) # R1 Regularization on real images realimg.requiresgrad = True Drealval = self.D(realimg, pose) gradreal = torch.autograd.grad( outputs=Drealval.sum(), inputs=realimg, creategraph=True)[0] gradpenalty = torch.sum(gradreal2) gradpenalty = gradpenalty 10.0 # lambda for R1 Ldisc = torch.mean(torch.log(1 + torch.exp(-Dgendetached))) + \ torch.mean(torch.log(1 + torch.exp(Dreal))) + \ gradpenalty # Depth Variance Loss for Generator # Encourages sharp surfaces # Var(zhat) = E[zhat^2] - E[zhat]^2 # zhat = sum(Ti alphai zi) / sum(Ti alphai) # This requires access to the rendering internals (zi positions) # Simplified placeholder for the loss term LDV LDV = computedepthvarianceloss(self.Gfg, z, pose, K, self.taudepthvar) # Total Generator Loss LtotalG = Lgen + LDV return LtotalG, Ldisc def step(self, batch): realimg, pose, K, z = batch # Update Generator self.optG.zerograd() generatedimg = self.forward(z, pose, K) LG, = self.computeloss(generatedimg, realimg, pose, z) LG.backward() self.optG.step() # Update Discriminator self.optD.zerograd(), LD = self.computeloss(generatedimg, realimg, pose, z) LD.backward() self.optD.step() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Foreground: Without regularization, the generator may produce empty scenes. The Depth Variance Loss L{DV} with threshold \tau prevents this by encouraging a single sharp surface. Viewpoint/Content Entanglement: Changing camera pose might alter geometry if not properly conditioned. VoxGRAF conditions on pose \xi (per-image) rather than view direction (per-ray) to mitigate this, though a 2D refinement CNN is often needed for strong dataset biases (e.g., eyes looking at camera). Sparsity vs. Runtime: Sparse convolutions reduce memory but increase runtime due to coordinate management overhead. VoxGRAF prioritizes faster training by using dense convolutions with zeroed pruned voxels, accepting higher memory usage for speed. Pruning Thresholds: Choosing \tauT and \tau\sigma is critical. Too high, and the scene becomes too sparse/incomplete; too low, and sparsity benefits are lost. Time Complexity: Rendering time is dominated by the single forward pass of the generator. Once generated, rendering takes milliseconds. For a 256x256 image with 48 samples, standard MLP-based methods require ~3M queries, whereas VoxGRAF uses fast trilinear interpolation. Memory Complexity: Scales with the number of active voxels. Sparsity reduces memory significantly compared to dense grids. On FFHQ (RG=128), memory usage is 0.9 GB with Depth Variance Loss (95% sparsity) vs 1.4 GB without (74% sparsity). Performance: On FFHQ (RG=128, RI=128), generation time is 198 ms and rendering time is 4 ms with L{DV}. Without L{DV}, generation is 229 ms and rendering is 7 ms. Using dense convolutions with zeroed voxels reduces generation time to 58 ms but increases memory. Strengths: Fast inference (milliseconds per view after generation), 3D consistency, high resolution via sparse grids. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of pruning thresholds and regularization. 2D refinement is needed for certain dataset biases. Training is computationally expensive (3-7 days on 8 V100s). VoxGRAF was introduced by as a method to combine the benefits of sparse voxel grids (fast rendering, high resolution) with the generative capabilities of 3D-aware GANs. It addresses the limitations of coordinate-based MLPs (slow rendering, entanglement) and hybrid rendering approaches (viewpoint/content entanglement). The method builds on prior work in sparse voxel novel view synthesis (Plenoxels, DVGO) and 3D-aware GANs (GRAF). name: Voxel-based Gaussian Splatting
head: VoxGS
body: VoxGS is a volume representation for Computed Tomography (CT) that places isometric 3D Gaussians at the centers of a regular 3D voxel grid, enabling efficient CT volume extraction and differentiable X-ray rendering. It sets itself apart from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by fixing Gaussian positions to voxel centroids and removing view-dependent spherical harmonic (SH) color coefficients, which solves the inaccurate volume extraction and unstable optimization issues associated with applying original 3DGS to CT data. Unlike discrete 3D voxels, VoxGS supports differentiable rendering, allowing gradients from X-ray projection losses to propagate back to the Gaussian attributes during training. Inputs: A set of K X-ray projection images. Camera projection matrices \mathbf{P}k \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 4} for each view k=1 \dots K. A regular 3D voxel grid V of dimensions M \times N \times L. View-specific feature maps \mathbf{F}k \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C} extracted from the X-ray projections via a Transformer encoder (e.g., ViT). Outputs: A set of Np 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{gi\}{i=1}^{Np}, where Np = M \times N \times L. A CT density volume V \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N \times L}. Data Structures: Each Gaussian gi is defined by the following attributes: Position \boldsymbol{\mu}i: Fixed at the centroid of the voxel grid. \boldsymbol{\mu}i = (x, y, z)^T, where x \in [1, M], y \in [1, N], z \in [1, L]. This is not a learnable parameter but a structural index. Opacity \alphai: A scalar float representing the density/attenuation coefficient. Learnable. Scale \mathbf{s}i: A 3D vector (sx, sy, sz) controlling the isotropic spread. Learnable. Rotation \mathbf{r}i: A 4D quaternion (w, x, y, z) controlling orientation. Learnable. Color: No SH coefficients or view-dependent color are stored. The representation assumes isotropic density for X-ray attenuation. Numbered Steps: 1. Position Initialization: Assign each Gaussian gi a fixed position \boldsymbol{\mu}i corresponding to the integer coordinates of the voxel grid. There are Np = M \times N \times L Gaussians. 2. Feature Querying: For each Gaussian gi and each view k=1 \dots K: Project the fixed 3D position \boldsymbol{\mu}i to 2D image coordinates using the view's projection matrix: \mathbf{p}{i,k} = \mathbf{P}k \boldsymbol{\mu}i. Query the view-specific feature map \mathbf{F}k at \mathbf{p}{i,k} using bilinear interpolation: \mathbf{F}{i,k} = \text{Interp}(\mathbf{F}k, \mathbf{p}{i,k}) \in \mathbb{R}^C where \text{Interp}(\cdot) denotes bilinear interpolation. 3. Feature Aggregation: Aggregate the K queried features for Gaussian gi using MaxPooling to obtain a view-invariant feature vector: \mathbf{F}{max}^i = \text{MaxPool}(\mathbf{F}{i,1}, \mathbf{F}{i,2}, \dots, \mathbf{F}{i,K}) \in \mathbb{R}^C This step selects the most salient feature across all views. 4. Attribute Regression: Pass the aggregated feature \mathbf{F}{max}^i through a prediction Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), denoted as MLPS, to predict the Gaussian attributes: [\alphai, \mathbf{s}i, \mathbf{r}i] = MLPS(\mathbf{F}{max}^i) \in \mathbb{R}^{1+3+4} The MLP outputs: Opacity \alphai (1 float). Scale \mathbf{s}i (3 floats). Rotation \mathbf{r}i (4 floats, quaternion). 5. Volume Extraction: To extract the final CT density volume V \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N \times L}, directly index the opacity of the Gaussian at the corresponding voxel position: V(x, y, z) = \alphai \quad \text{where} \quad \boldsymbol{\mu}i = (x, y, z)^T This allows for O(1) extraction without trilinear interpolation. 6. Differentiable X-ray Rendering: Render X-ray projections from the Gaussian set \mathcal{G} using a differentiable rasterizer (e.g., based on [75] in the source) to compute the loss against input X-ray projections. The rendering process integrates the Gaussian densities along rays, leveraging the fixed positions for efficient computation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class VoxGS: def init(self, M, N, L, C, K): """ Initialize VoxGS representation. M, N, L: Voxel grid dimensions. C: Feature dimension from transformer. K: Number of views. """ self.M, self.N, self.L = M, N, L self.K = K self.C = C self.numgaussians = M N L # Fixed positions: shape (Np, 3) # Coordinates are 1-based in source, converted to 0-based for indexing if needed, # but projection matrices handle the coordinate system. x = torch.arange(1, M + 1).float().view(-1, 1, 1) y = torch.arange(1, N + 1).float().view(1, -1, 1) z = torch.arange(1, L + 1).float().view(1, 1, -1) self.mu = torch.stack([x, y, z], dim=-1).reshape(-1, 3) # Shape (Np, 3) # Learnable attributes initialized randomly or via prior self.alpha = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(self.numgaussians, 1) 0.1) self.scale = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(self.numgaussians, 3)) self.rotation = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(self.numgaussians, 4)) # Prediction MLP self.mlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(C, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 1 + 3 + 4) # alpha, s, r) def queryfeatures(self, Fklist, Pklist): """ Fklist: List of K tensors, each (H, W, C) Pklist: List of K tensors, each (3, 4) projection matrix Returns: Fmax (Np, C) """ allfeatures = [] for k in range(self.K): Fk = Fklist[k] # (H, W, C) Pk = Pklist[k] # (3, 4) # Project positions: mu is (Np, 3). Pk is (3, 4). # Homogeneous coordinates: (Np, 4) muh = torch.cat([self.mu, torch.ones(self.numgaussians, 1, device=self.mu.device)], dim=1) p2dh = torch.matmul(muh, Pk.t()) # (Np, 3) p2d = p2dh[:,:2] / p2dh[:, 2:3] # (Np, 2) normalized coordinates? # Note: Source uses Interp(Fk, Pk(mui)). # Assuming Pk outputs coordinates in the range of Fk's spatial dimensions. # Standard bilinear interpolation expects coordinates in [-1, 1] or [0, H/W]. # We assume Pk maps to valid 2D coordinates for Fk. # Reshape for gridsample: (N, C, H, W) -> (N, C, 1, 1) for point sampling # gridsample expects grid of shape (N, Hout, Wout, 2) # Here we sample Np points. grid = p2d.view(1, 1, self.numgaussians, 2) Fkperm = Fk.permute(2, 0, 1).unsqueeze(0) # (1, C, H, W) # Sample features Fsampled = F.gridsample(Fkperm, grid, aligncorners=False) # (1, C, 1, Np) Fki = Fsampled.squeeze(0).squeeze(2).permute(1, 0) # (Np, C) allfeatures.append(Fki) # MaxPool across views: shape (Np, C) featuresstack = torch.stack(allfeatures, dim=0) # (K, Np, C) Fmax = torch.max(featuresstack, dim=0).values # (Np, C) return Fmax def predictattributes(self, Fmax): """ Fmax: (Np, C) Returns: alpha, scale, rotation """ out = self.mlp(Fmax) # (Np, 8) alpha = out[:, 0:1] scale = out[:, 1:4] rotation = out[:, 4:8] return alpha, scale, rotation def extractvolume(self): """ Returns CT volume V of shape (M, N, L) """ V = self.alpha.view(self.M, self.N, self.L) return V def renderxray(self, Pk, Fk): """ Placeholder for differentiable X-ray rendering using the Gaussian set. Uses a rasterizer similar to [75] in source. """ # Implementation depends on the specific differentiable rasterizer used. # The key is that gradients flow from the rendered projection to alpha, scale, rotation. pass Parameters: M, N, L: Voxel grid dimensions. Typical values depend on the CT scan resolution (e.g., 256^3, 512^3). K: Number of X-ray views. Sparse-view scenarios (e.g., K=12, 20) are common in the source context. C: Feature dimension from the Transformer encoder. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Direct 3DGS Application: Using standard 3DGS with optimized positions and SH coefficients for CT leads to inaccurate volume extraction and unstable optimization in feed-forward frameworks. VoxGS avoids this by fixing positions and removing SH. Isotropic Assumption: The removal of SH coefficients assumes isotropic density for X-ray attenuation. If view-dependent effects are significant, this simplification may limit accuracy. Projection Coordinate Mapping: The bilinear interpolation requires accurate mapping of 3D voxel centroids to 2D image coordinates via \mathbf{P}k. Incorrect calibration will lead to misaligned feature queries. Time Complexity: Volume extraction is O(1) per voxel due to direct indexing. Feature querying is O(Np \cdot K) for bilinear interpolation. Attribute regression is O(Np) via MLP. Memory Complexity: Stores Np Gaussians with 8 floats each (1 opacity, 3 scale, 4 rotation) plus fixed positions. Total memory is proportional to Np. This is comparable to storing a dense volume but with additional overhead for scale/rotation. Performance: X-GRM using VoxGS reconstructs CT volumes within one second for sparse X-ray inputs, significantly outperforming SOTA methods in inference speed and reconstruction quality. Strengths: Enables differentiable X-ray rendering, allowing gradient-based optimization from X-ray projections. Fast volume extraction. Stable optimization for feed-forward models. Limitations: Assumes isotropic density (no SH). Fixed positions limit flexibility in representing complex geometries compared to optimized 3DGS. VoxGS was introduced in the paper "X-GRM: Large Gaussian Reconstruction Model for Sparse-view X-rays to Computed Tomography". It addresses the limitations of applying standard 3D Gaussian Splatting to CT reconstruction, specifically the instability and inaccuracy in volume extraction. By fixing Gaussian positions to voxel centroids and removing view-dependent color, it creates a representation tailored for X-ray attenuation modeling while retaining the differentiable rendering benefits of 3DGS. name: Gaussian Voxel Kernel Functions (GVKF)
body:
Gaussian Voxel Kernel Functions (GVKF) is a method for efficient 3D surface reconstruction in open scenes that establishes a continuous scene representation based on discrete 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) through kernel regression. It integrates fast 3DGS rasterization with implicit scene representations to achieve high-fidelity surface reconstruction while significantly reducing memory consumption compared to explicit Gaussian primitives. Unlike standard 3DGS which relies on discrete summation of explicit splats, GVKF replaces discrete opacity values with Gaussian kernel functions decoded from a feature vector, enabling direct mesh extraction and continuous surface representation. GVKF builds on Voxel-based Representation by using a sparse voxel grid to manage Gaussian primitives implicitly. The method replaces the explicit optimization of Gaussian attributes with a neural decoding process, allowing for dynamic generation and pruning of Gaussians based on gradient accumulation. Inputs: Downsampled Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point clouds for initialization; camera poses and image observations for training; a feature vector F \in \mathbb{R}^d stored in voxels. Outputs: A continuous scene opacity density field; a reconstructed 3D mesh surface. Sparse Voxel Grid: A hierarchical grid structure initialized from SfM points. Each voxel stores a feature vector F. Feature Vector (F): Stored in each voxel, F \in \mathbb{R}^d. It contains relative coordinates of Gaussians to the parent voxel center and serves as input to Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) to decode Gaussian attributes. Gradient Accumulator (
abla): A scalar value stored per voxel, accumulating gradients from 3DGS rendering after each iteration. m: The maximum number of Gaussian primitives allowed per sparse grid voxel. 
abla{thresh}: The threshold value for accumulated gradient used to trigger voxel subdivision. d: The dimensionality of the feature vector F. Max Depth: The maximum subdivision depth for the voxel grid. The Gaussian kernel function G(\mathbf{x}) is defined as: G(\mathbf{x}) = \alpha \cdot \exp\left(- rac{1}{2} (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{p})^T \mathbf{P}^{-1} (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{p})ight) where: \mathbf{x} is the query point in 3D space. \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the position of the Gaussian. \alpha \in \mathbb{R} is the opacity. \mathbf{P} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 	imes 3} is the covariance matrix, defined as \mathbf{P} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^T \mathbf{R}^T. \mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 	imes 3} is the rotation matrix. \mathbf{S} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the scaling vector. name: 3D Gaussian Particle Approximation of VDB Datasets
head: Gaussian Particle Approximation, Gaussian Particle Rendering, VDB to Gaussian Conversion
body: This method converts OpenVDB volumetric datasets into a set of non-overlapping 3D Gaussian particles to enable memory-efficient, lossy representation with Level of Detail (LOD) support. It solves the problem of rendering large sparse volumetric datasets in real-time by replacing dense voxel grids with hardware-accelerated ray tracing of Gaussian primitives. Unlike standard Gaussian Splatting which often uses overlapping primitives for photorealism, this approach strictly maintains non-overlapping Gaussians derived from OpenVDB's non-overlapping leaf nodes, limiting the model to specific refinement levels but ensuring compatibility with traditional volume rendering pipelines via transfer functions. Inputs: An OpenVDB grid containing volumetric or level-set data. Camera parameters (origin, direction). Rendering parameters: LOD level (Low, Medium, High), maximum recursion depth, step size. Outputs: A rendered image with accumulated color and transmittance. Device-side buffers containing Gaussian properties (position, covariance, opacity). GaussianModel A parent class containing device-side pointers to contiguous arrays for each Gaussian property: opacity: Scalar array. For volumes, this reflects the average scalar value of the voxel region. For level sets, opacity is uniform and may not require per-particle storage. worldposition: 3D vector array. The center in world space, derived from the centroid of the voxel region or its bounding box. covariance: 3D vector array (for ellipsoids) or scalar array (for spheres). Represents the diagonal of the 3x3 covariance matrix, defining spatial extent along axes. Acceleration Structures Geometry Acceleration Structure (GAS): Built on the GPU using a CUDA device-side array of Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes (AABBs). Each AABB encloses a single Gaussian particle, defined by its minimum and maximum coordinates in OpenVDB Index Space. Build Flags: OPTIXBUILDFLAGALLOWCOMPACTION, OPTIXBUILDINPUTTYPECUSTOMPRIMITIVES. Instance Acceleration Structure (IAS): Stores the GAS instance with the OpenVDB Grid transform. Sets visibility masks for all Gaussians to visible for primary and continuation rays. HitGroupRecord A structure initialized for Gaussian particles rendering that specifies the shaders associated with the Gaussian primitive. It contains a pointer to the GaussianModel object. 1. Data Generation (CPU): Retrieve all leaf nodes from the OpenVDB Grid Tree using the OpenVDB API. Apply LOD logic to determine Gaussian properties for each leaf node or cluster: Low LOD: Each leaf node is represented by a single Gaussian reflecting the distribution of active voxels. Medium LOD: Dense leaf nodes are merged into 4x4x4 groups; sparse nodes into 2x2x2 groups. Remaining voxels become individual Gaussians. High LOD: Sparse leaf nodes contribute one Gaussian per active voxel; dense leaf nodes are merged into 2x2x2 blocks. For each Gaussian, compute: Position \mu: Centroid of the voxel region/bounding box. Opacity \alpha: Average scalar value of the region. Covariance \Sigma: Diagonal vector of the 3x3 matrix (axis-aligned). Note: Tiled leaf nodes (homogeneous regions) are excluded from Gaussian creation as their value is stored in the parent node's value mask. 2. Data Transfer (CPU to GPU): Allocate contiguous device-side buffers using cudaMalloc for opacity, world position, and covariance. Copy data using cudaMemcpy. Store device pointers in a GaussianModel object added to the OptiX Shader Binding Table (SBT). 3. Acceleration Structure Build (GPU): Build the GAS using the CUDA device-side array of AABBs derived from Gaussian extents in Index Space. Build the IAS with the OpenVDB Grid transform. 4. Ray Generation: Shoot primary rays from the camera using the raygen program. 5. Intersection Test (intersection): Use the primitive index to retrieve the Gaussian AABB. Perform ray-box intersection with the world AABB. If intersected: Retrieve Gaussian center \mu and inverse covariance \Sigma^{-1}. Transform the ray into the Gaussian's local space using \Sigma^{-1}. Solve the quadratic equation for the ellipsoid/sphere intersection to find entry (t0) and exit (t1) distances. Store t0 and t1 in the payload and exit the intersection shader early. 6. Ray Marching and Density Evaluation: Step along the ray within the interval [t0, t1] using a predefined step size \Delta t based on the distance between entry and exit points. For each sample point xk: Compute difference \delta = xk - \mu. Compute squared Mahalanobis distance D^2 = \delta^\top \Sigma^{-1} \delta. Evaluate density \rhok = \exp(-D^2/2). 7. Absorption and Transmittance Update: Compute volume factor: Vf = 1/\det(\Sigma). Calculate absorption: Ak = \rhok \cdot \Delta t \cdot Vf. Update color: C \leftarrow C + Tk \cdot c(\sigmak) \cdot Ak, where c(\sigmak) is the scattering color derived from opacity via a transfer function. Update transmittance: T{k+1} = Tk \cdot \exp(-Ak). 8. Ray Continuation: Advance the ray origin: o{new} = o + d \cdot (t1 - t0), where o is the current origin, d is the direction, and t0/t1 are entry/exit points. Recursively trace the next Gaussian using optixTrace with RAYTYPERADIANCE. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computegaussiandensity(samplepoint, gaussiancenter, inversecovariance): """ Computes the density of a Gaussian at a specific point. """ delta = samplepoint - gaussiancenter # Mahalanobis distance squared dsquared = dot(delta, multiplymatrixvector(inversecovariance, delta)) density = exp(-dsquared / 2.0) return density def rayintersectgaussian(rayorigin, raydirection, gaussiancenter, inversecovariance): """ Solves for entry (t0) and exit (t1) distances of a ray intersecting a Gaussian ellipsoid. Transforms ray into Gaussian local space. """ # Transform ray origin and direction into local space defined by inverse covariance # Note: The source describes transforming the ray using the inverse covariance matrix. # In standard ellipsoid intersection, this typically involves scaling the ray by the inverse of the square root of covariance, # but we follow the source's description of using inverse covariance for transformation. localorigin = multiplymatrixvector(inversecovariance, rayorigin - gaussiancenter) localdirection = multiplymatrixvector(inversecovariance, raydirection) # Solve quadratic equation for unit sphere intersection in local space: # |localorigin + t localdirection|^2 = 1 a = dot(localdirection, localdirection) b = 2.0 dot(localorigin, localdirection) c = dot(localorigin, localorigin) - 1.0 discriminant = bb - 4ac if discriminant < 0: return None, None sqrtdisc = sqrt(discriminant) t0 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2.0 a) t1 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2.0 a) return t0, t1 def rendergaussianparticles(rayorigin, raydirection, gaussianmodel, maxdepth, currentdepth=0): """ Recursive ray marching through Gaussian particles. """ if currentdepth >= maxdepth: return backgroundcolor, 1.0 accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0) transmittance = 1.0 # 1. Intersect with World AABB (GAS/IAS structure) tmin, tmax = intersectworldaabb(rayorigin, raydirection) if tmin is None: return backgroundcolor, transmittance # 2. Iterate through Gaussians in the AABB # Note: In OptiX, this is handled by the intersection/closest-hit programs. # Here we simulate the logic described in the recursive loop. # Find the closest Gaussian intersection within [tmin, tmax] closestt0 = None closestt1 = None closestgaussianidx = None for i in range(gaussianmodel.numgaussians): center = gaussianmodel.position[i] invcov = inverse(gaussianmodel.covariance[i]) # Assuming 3x3 matrix construction from diagonal t0, t1 = rayintersectgaussian(rayorigin, raydirection, center, invcov) if t0 is not None and t0 >= tmin and t0 < tmax: if closestt0 is None or t0 < closestt0: closestt0 = t0 closestt1 = t1 closestgaussianidx = i if closestt0 is None: return backgroundcolor, transmittance # 3. March within the Gaussian gaussian = gaussianmodel.gaussians[closestgaussianidx] stepsize = (closestt1 - closestt0) / numsamples # Predefined step size logic for k in range(numsamples): tsample = closestt0 + k stepsize samplepoint = rayorigin + raydirection tsample density = computegaussiandensity(samplepoint, gaussian.center, gaussian.inversecovariance) # Volume factor volumefactor = 1.0 / determinant(gaussian.covariancematrix) # Absorption absorption = density stepsize volumefactor # Color accumulation (using transfer function for scattering color) scatteringcolor = transferfunction(gaussian.opacity) accumulatedcolor += transmittance scatteringcolor absorption # Transmittance update transmittance = exp(-absorption) if transmittance < epsilon: break # 4. Ray Continuation and Recursion # Advance ray origin to exit point of current Gaussian newrayorigin = rayorigin + raydirection closestt1 # Recursive trace for next Gaussian nextcolor, nexttransmittance = rendergaussianparticles( newrayorigin, raydirection, gaussianmodel, maxdepth, currentdepth + 1) finalcolor = accumulatedcolor + transmittance nextcolor return finalcolor, transmittance Grid Layout Variant: The '5-4-3' variant is used for all explanations and rendering samples. Top-level ('5-level') nodes: 2^5 \times 2^5 \times 2^5 resolution (32,768 children). Intermediate-level ('4-level') nodes: 2^4 \times 2^4 \times 2^4 resolution (4,096 children). Leaf-level ('3-level') nodes: 2^3 \times 2^3 \times 2^3 resolution (512 voxels). Build Flags: OPTIXBUILDFLAGALLOWCOMPACTION, OPTIXBUILDINPUTTYPECUSTOMPRIMITIVES. Ray Type: RAYTYPERADIANCE for all optixTrace calls, indicating a purely forward-ray-marching approach. Non-overlapping Constraint: The implementation uses non-overlapping Gaussians because OpenVDB leaf nodes are strictly non-overlapping cubic regions. This limits the model to three overarching refinement levels and introduces lossiness. NanoVDB Limitation: NanoVDB does not support device-side traversal of the Grid Tree or device-side iterators/accessors. This creates a bottleneck for random access required in ray-BVH or ray-particle intersections. Therefore, NanoVDB cannot be used for 3D Gaussian generation or rendering in this pipeline; OpenVDB must be used for generation. NanoVDB HDDA Incompatibility: NanoVDB's built-in HDDA transmittance algorithm only works with regular float grid volumes. It is invalid for overlapping and variable-size particle data with custom ray tracing pipelines. OptiX Register Constraint: Propagating state via recursive optixTrace calls is limited by OptiX’s 8-payload register constraint, causing sub-optimal accumulation and inconsistent resetting of payload values. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory footprint depends on LOD and dataset sparsity. For the 'dragon' dataset: High LOD: 546MB, 23.3M Gaussians. Low LOD: 174.4MB, 7.4M Gaussians. Time complexity is driven by the number of Gaussians and the ray tracing overhead. The use of AABB acceleration structures reduces intersection tests. Measured Performance: The renderer consistently provides above 150 FPS for all tested datasets (bunnycloud, explosion, fire, utahteapot, venusstatue, dragon) across all LODs, even with millions of Gaussians. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Real-time performance via hardware-accelerated ray tracing (OptiX); memory efficiency through sparse VDB representation and LOD; support for transfer functions (unlike baked-color Gaussian Splatting). Limitations: Lossy representation due to non-overlapping constraint; limited to specific refinement levels; dependency on OpenVDB for generation (NanoVDB unsupported); register constraints in recursive tracing. When to Use: Scientific visualization (SciVis) applications requiring real-time rendering of large sparse volumetric datasets with transfer function support. When Not to Use: Photorealistic rendering requiring overlapping Gaussian mixtures for soft shadows and complex light transport. Scenarios where NanoVDB is the only available format for data generation. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "3D Gaussian Particle Approximation of VDB Datasets: A Study for Scientific Visualization". It explores the integration of OpenVDB and NVIDIA OptiX to leverage memory compaction and hardware acceleration. History and Development: Gaussian approximation and mixture models have a history in Scientific Visualization, with prior work by Jang et al.. This work builds on the popularity of Gaussian Splatting (Kerbl et al. [12]) but adapts it for VDB datasets and SciVis pipelines rather than stereoscopic image-to-3D conversion. Usage: Used in NVIDIA OptiX-based rendering engines for forward ray marching through Gaussian particles. 3D Gaussian Particle Approximation of VDB Datasets: A Study for Scientific Visualization, https://www.emergentmind.com/papers/2504.04857, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Global Scene Generator (GSN)
body: Global Scene Generator (GSN) is a generative model that synthesizes unconstrained 3D scenes by decomposing them into local regions using a global latent code and a locally conditioned radiance field. It solves the scalability problem of single-network radiance fields (like standard NeRF or GRAF) by distributing scene representation across a 2D grid of local latent codes, allowing the model to handle large, densely populated environments. Unlike dictionary-based memory models that are limited to viewing angles present in training data, GSN learns a scene prior that enables extrapolation to unseen viewpoints. Inputs: Global latent code z \sim pz sampled from a prior distribution. Camera pose T = [R, t] \in SE(3) sampled from an empirical pose distribution pT. Camera intrinsics K \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}. Outputs: Rendered image \hat{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times w \times h}. Data Structures: 1. Global Generator Output (W): A 2D grid of local latent codes W \in \mathbb{R}^{c \times s \times s}. This acts as a "latent floorplan" for the scene. 2. Radiance Field Input: A concatenated vector [p0, d] \in \mathbb{R}^5 and a local latent code w{ij} \in \mathbb{R}^c. 3. Radiance Field Architecture: A network f where the local latent code w{ij} modulates linear layers (similar to CIPS). Numbered Steps: 1. Generate Local Latent Grid: Sample z \sim pz and feed it to the global generator g (implemented using StyleGAN2 architecture). The generator outputs the 2D grid of local latent codes W \in \mathbb{R}^{c \times s \times s}. 2. Determine Local Context: For a 3D point p in the global coordinate system, determine its projection onto the zx-plane (assuming the y-axis points up). This projection yields discrete grid indices (i, j). 3. Sample Local Latent Code: Sample the local latent code w{ij} \in \mathbb{R}^c from the grid W at indices (i, j) using bi-linear sampling. 4. Transform Coordinates: Transform the global point p into a local point p0 relative to the local coordinate system defined by w{ij}. This decomposition prevents the radiance field f from relying on absolute global coordinates, enabling spatial sharing of latent codes. 5. Prepare Radiance Field Input: Apply positional encoding to p0 and concatenate it with the camera direction d to form the input vector [p0, d] \in \mathbb{R}^5. 6. Evaluate Radiance Field: Evaluate the locally conditioned radiance field f using inputs [p0, d] and modulation by w{ij}. The network outputs occupancy \sigma \in [0, \infty] and appearance a \in \mathbb{R}^3. 7. Volumetric Rendering: Render the image by evaluating f along rays \mathbf{r}. The color c(\mathbf{r}) for a ray is obtained by approximating the integral in Eq. 1: c(\mathbf{r}, W) = \int{un}^{uf} T{\mathbf{r}}(u) \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(u, w{ij}) a{\mathbf{r}}(u, d, w{ij}) \, du where the transmittance T{\mathbf{r}}(u) is defined as: T{\mathbf{r}}(u) = \exp \left( - \int{un}^{u} \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(v, w{ij}) \, dv \right) Here, un and uf are the near and far clipping planes, and w{ij} is the local latent code associated with the spatial location of the point on the ray. 8. Refinement: The rendering step produces a feature map at a lower resolution. This feature map is upsampled using a small convolutional refinement network to achieve the final output resolution \hat{X}. Parameters: c: Dimension of the latent codes. s: Spatial resolution of the grid W. T: Camera extrinsic parameters. K: Camera intrinsic parameters. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Invalid Camera Poses: Sampling camera poses inside walls or solid objects is a risk. GSN handles this by performing stochastic weighted sampling over a set of candidate poses. The weights are derived from the occupancy \sigma predicted by the generator at those locations, normalized via a softmin function to create a multinomial distribution. Coordinate System Dependency: If the global coordinate system is not decomposed into local coordinate systems for each w{ij}, the radiance field f will rely on absolute coordinates, breaking the spatial sharing property and preventing the model from generalizing across different grid positions. Dimensionality: The method uses a 2D grid for efficiency. While it can be extended to a 3D grid, the 2D approach is the standard implementation for computational efficiency. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class GlobalSceneGenerator: def init(self, latentdim, gridsize, featuredim): """ latentdim: dimension of global latent code z gridsize: s, spatial dimension of the local latent grid W featuredim: c, dimension of local latent codes wij """ super().init() # Global generator g using StyleGAN2-like architecture self.globalgenerator = StyleGAN2Generator(latentdim, featuredim, gridsize) # Locally conditioned radiance field f self.radiancefield = LocallyConditionedRadianceField(featuredim) # Convolutional refinement network for upsampling self.refinementnet = ConvRefinementNetwork() def forward(self, z, camerapose, cameraintrinsics, raydirections): """ z: Global latent code [B, latentdim] camerapose: Camera pose T = [R, t] [B, 3, 4] or [B, 6] cameraintrinsics: K [B, 3, 3] raydirections: Directions for each pixel [B, H, W, 3] Returns: renderedimage: Final rendered image [B, 3, Hout, Wout] """ # Step 1: Generate local latent grid W # W shape: [B, featuredim, gridsize, gridsize] W = self.globalgenerator(z) # Step 2-6: Evaluate radiance field along rays # For each ray, we need to sample points and query f # This is typically done via volumetric rendering loop # Pre-compute ray origins and directions in global coordinates rayorigins = computerayorigins(camerapose, cameraintrinsics) # Render feature map at lower resolution # The actual volumetric integration is handled by the renderer # which queries f with local conditioning featuremap = self.volumetricrender( W=W, rayorigins=rayorigins, raydirections=raydirections, radiancefield=self.radiancefield) # Step 8: Refine and upsample renderedimage = self.refinementnet(featuremap) return renderedimage def volumetricrender(self, W, rayorigins, raydirections, radiancefield): """ Implements the integration in Eq. 1 """ # Sample points along rays # un to uf are near/far planes pointsglobal = samplepointsalongrays(rayorigins, raydirections, un, uf) # For each point, determine local context # Project point to zx-plane to get (i, j) # Note: Implementation details for projection depend on coordinate system convention # Assuming y is up, project to zx plane projectedpoints = pointsglobal[:, [0, 2]] # x, z # Map projected points to grid indices (i, j) # This requires normalizing coordinates to grid space gridindices = maptogridindices(projectedpoints, gridsize=W.shape[-1]) # Sample local latent codes wij using bi-linear sampling # W shape: [B, C, S, S] # gridindices shape: [B, N, 2] where N is number of samples wij = bilinearsamplegrid(W, gridindices) # Transform global points to local coordinates p0 # This involves subtracting the local origin and rotating # The local origin and rotation are implicitly defined by the grid position # For simplicity, assuming a fixed local frame per grid cell pointslocal = transformtolocalcoordinates(pointsglobal, gridindices) # Apply positional encoding to p0 pointslocalencoded = positionalencoding(pointslocal) # Get camera directions d for each sample # Directions are constant along the ray directions = raydirections[gridindices[:, 0, 0]] # Broadcast direction to samples # Concatenate [p0, d] # p0 is encoded, so dimension is higher, plus d (3) # The paper states input is R^5, implying p0 is 2D or encoded to 2D? # Standard NeRF uses 3D pos + 3D dir = 6D. # Paper says [p0, d] in R^5. This implies p0 might be 2D (x,z) or encoded differently. # Given "positional encoding" is applied, and input to f is R^5, # it is likely p0 is the 2D local coordinate (x,z) in the local frame, # and d is 3D direction. Or p0 is 3D but d is 2D? # Re-reading: "p0 which results from expressing p relative to the local coordinate system... # and applying positional encoding". # If input is R^5, and d is 3D, p0 must be 2D. # Since projection is on zx-plane, local coordinates might be (xlocal, zlocal). # Let's assume p0 is 2D local coordinate (x, z) in the local frame # and d is 3D direction. # However, standard volumetric rendering requires 3D position for density. # The paper says "f: R^5 x R^c -> [0,1] x R^3". # It is most likely that p0 is the 2D coordinate in the local plane, # and the depth is handled by the ray parameter u? # No, radiance fields usually take 3D position. # Let's stick to the text: "input [p0, d] in R^5". # If d is 3D, p0 is 2D. # Construct input tensor # p0local2d = pointslocal[:, [0, 2]] # x, z in local frame # d = raydirections # inputtof = torch.cat([p0local2d, d], dim=-1) # [B, N, 5] # Evaluate f # sigma, a = radiancefield(inputtof, wij) # Compute transmittance and color using Eq. 1 # Ti = exp(-sum(sigmaj deltaj)) # C = sum(Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai deltai)) ai) # Return feature map pass class LocallyConditionedRadianceField(nn.Module): def init(self, latentdim): super().init() # Modulated linear layers similar to CIPS self.modulation = ModulatedLinear(latentdim) def forward(self, x, wij): """ x: [B, N, 5] -> [p0, d] wij: [B, N, c] """ # Modulate weights of linear layers using wij # This is similar to AdaIN or StyleGAN modulation out = self.modulation(x, wij) return out class StyleGAN2Generator(nn.Module): def init(self, latentdim, featuredim, gridsize): super().init() # Mapping network, modulated conv blocks, learned constant pass class ConvRefinementNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # Small convolutional network for upsampling pass Complexity: The method uses a 2D grid for computational efficiency, though it can be extended to 3D. The memory usage is determined by the size of the grid W (c \times s \times s) and the radiance field network parameters. Strengths: It scales effectively to large, densely populated scenes where single-network radiance fields show diminishing returns. It allows for explicit control over viewpoint and field of view via camera parameters. Limitations: The 2D grid assumption may not capture vertical variations as well as a 3D grid, although the paper notes the framework can be extended. Sampling invalid camera poses (e.g., inside walls) requires a specific stochastic weighted sampling strategy to mitigate. When to use: Use GSN when generating unconstrained, large-scale scenes with diverse viewpoints, particularly when single-network approaches fail to scale. When not to use: Avoid if the scene is small and simple, where a single radiance field (like NeRF or GRAF) would be more efficient and sufficient. GSN was introduced in the paper "Unconstrained Scene Generation with Locally Conditioned Radiance Fields". It builds upon the concept of locally conditioned radiance fields [34] and StyleGAN2 [25]. The method addresses the limitations of 1D global latent codes used in models like GRAF [49] and \pi-GAN [3], which do not scale well to large scenes. It also contrasts with dictionary-based memory models that rely on stored observations and cannot extrapolate to unseen viewpoints.
