name: Dynamic and Deformation Modeling
body: Dynamic and Deformation Modeling extends static Neural Radiance Fields to reconstruct time-varying scenes from multi-view video or sparse image collections, solving the problem of novel view synthesis for non-static content. It sets itself apart from static NeRF variants by explicitly incorporating temporal information, either through direct time-conditioned radiance fields or by warping spatial coordinates to a canonical space, allowing for the coherent reconstruction of moving objects that would otherwise appear inconsistent in a static model. Builds on Neural Radiance Fields. All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward rendering operator and the propagation of gradients through the integration steps. The core mechanism is the evaluation of the volume rendering equation and the computation of gradients with respect to scene parameters (density, geometry, transfer functions, camera poses). Deformation Field Parametrization methods map 3D spatial coordinates from a dynamic, time-varying state to a static canonical space (or vice versa) to enable the rendering of dynamic scenes using static neural radiance fields. This approach solves the problem of modeling non-rigid, time-varying geometry without requiring a separate radiance field for every time step. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by the specific mathematical representation of the deformation field: while some use cubic B-splines for sparse data efficiency, others use MLPs guided by parametric models like 3DMMs or inverse Linear Blend Skinning with neural residuals. Choose this when explicit geometric warping is preferred over direct temporal conditioning. Dynamic Scene Representation methods extend static radiance fields to model temporal variations, enabling novel view synthesis of non-static scenes. Unlike static methods, these approaches incorporate time or scene variables as inputs to the neural field or deformation operators to predict density and color for specific moments. They differ from sibling methods like Deformation Field Parametrization by explicitly handling the evolution of geometry and appearance over time, often through shared networks, explicit temporal interpolation, or deformation fields. Choose this when direct temporal conditioning or shared network architectures are sufficient for the scene's dynamics. Deformable Neural Radiance Fields (Nerfies) reconstructs non-rigidly deforming scenes by decomposing the scene into a static canonical template volume (a standard NeRF) and a per-observation continuous deformation field that maps observation-space coordinates to canonical-space coordinates. Unlike methods that condition deformation on time or define it on discrete meshes/voxels, Nerfies conditions the deformation on a learned per-frame latent code and models the deformation as a continuous function using an MLP. It distinguishes itself from siblings by introducing elastic regularization to resolve ambiguities between motion and scaling, and a coarse-to-fine optimization strategy to avoid local minima. Choose this for high-quality reconstruction of non-rigid human deformation or elastic objects. JointRF is a compact residual feature grid representation for dynamic Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) that handles large motions and long sequences by decomposing the radiance field into a long-reference basis feature grid and a coefficient feature grid. Unlike canonical space methods that warp features back to a static canonical space—making them fragile to large motions and topological changes—JointRF uses residual grids to capture temporal variations, thereby diminishing temporal redundancy and improving compression efficiency. Choose this when dealing with long sequences or large motions where canonical warping fails. D-TensoRF is a dynamic radiance field model that maps 3D location, viewing direction, and time instant to emitted color and volume density using factorized 4D/5D tensor grids. It extends TensoRF by incorporating a time dimension and applying Matrix-Matrix decomposition to reduce memory complexity. Unlike Deformable Neural Radiance Fields (Nerfies), which rely on explicit deformation fields to warp static coordinates, D-TensoRF models temporal dynamics directly within the tensor structure, augmented by smoothing regularization to enforce temporal dependency. Choose this when memory efficiency and direct temporal modeling in tensor grids are prioritized over explicit deformation fields. The SE(3) Deformation Field encodes scene deformation as a rigid transformation (rotation and translation) per point using a screw axis representation. It replaces per-point translation fields to simplify optimization by requiring a single rotation parameter across space, rather than distinct translation vectors for each point. This method is primarily used in dynamic scene reconstruction to handle rotational motion more efficiently than pure translation-based deformation fields. Choose this when scenes exhibit significant rigid rotational motion and a simpler optimization landscape is desired. The extension of NeRF to dynamic scenes originated with the recognition that static radiance fields cannot represent temporal changes. Early approaches focused on direct time-conditioning, where the temporal variable is concatenated with spatial coordinates to predict density and color. Subsequent work introduced deformation fields to handle non-rigid motion, mapping points from observation space to a canonical space to leverage static NeRF priors. These methods are primarily used in novel view synthesis for video, 4D reconstruction, and dynamic scene analysis. Radiance Field Optimization, URL, date fetched

name: Deformation Field Parametrization
head: Dynamic Coordinate Mapping, Canonical Space Deformation
body: Deformation Field Parametrization methods map 3D spatial coordinates from a dynamic, time-varying state to a static canonical space (or vice versa) to enable the rendering of dynamic scenes using static neural radiance fields. This approach solves the problem of modeling non-rigid, time-varying geometry without requiring a separate radiance field for every time step. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by the specific mathematical representation of the deformation field: while some use cubic B-splines for sparse data efficiency [11457-spline-based-deformation-field.md], others use MLPs guided by parametric models like 3DMMs [12044-deformation-guided-neural-fields.md] or inverse Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) with neural residuals [12724-neural-deformation-field.md]. All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward rendering operator and the propagation of gradients through the integration steps [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. The core mechanism is the evaluation of the volume rendering equation and the computation of gradients with respect to scene parameters (density, geometry, transfer functions, camera poses) [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. The standard emission-absorption model computes the color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} as [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \sigmai is the density, \deltai is the step size, \mathbf{c}i is the color, and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. Differentiation strategies fall into three main categories [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]: 1. Reverse-Mode Automatic Differentiation (AD): Standard backpropagation through the computational graph. This requires storing O(kn) intermediate states (where n is pixels and k is samples), leading to high memory usage [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. 2. Adjoint Method: Computes gradients by propagating adjoint variables backward through the rendering algorithm, evaluating the chain rule from output to input. This has computational complexity largely constant in the number of parameters, making it preferable for optimizing many parameters like the transfer function [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. 3. Analytic Inversion / Explicit Gradients: Uses a-priori knowledge of the DVR operations to invert the order of operations or derive closed-form gradients, reducing memory consumption to O(n) by avoiding the storage of intermediate results [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. This method parametrizes the deformation field using cubic B-splines with time-modulated weights to map spatial coordinates (x, y, z) at time t to canonical coordinates (x0, y0, z0) [11457-spline-based-deformation-field.md]. It enables the reconstruction of dynamic scenes from sparse projection data by combining a pre-trained canonical volume with the learned deformation field [11457-spline-based-deformation-field.md]. Unlike Neural Deformation Fields which rely on MLPs and complex regularization, this approach allows reconstruction from as few as two projections due to the efficient encoding provided by B-splines [11457-spline-based-deformation-field.md]. Deformation-Guided Neural Fields address the problem of modeling dynamic, articulated subjects (specifically human faces) in neural radiance fields by decoupling identity from pose and expression [12044-deformation-guided-neural-fields.md]. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly guiding the deformation field MLP with a parametric 3D morphable model (3DMM), ensuring that the learned deformations adhere to anatomical priors rather than relying solely on unconstrained neural predictions [12044-deformation-guided-neural-fields.md]. The Neural Deformation Field (NDF) is a method for modeling non-rigid, time-varying deformations in neural radiance fields by predicting per-point displacements in a canonical space [12724-neural-deformation-field.md]. It solves the problem of animating static neural representations without relying on rigid body assumptions or human-specific priors like SMPL [12724-neural-deformation-field.md]. Unlike cage-based or linear blend skinning methods, NDF generalizes to arbitrary objects and enables fine-level complex deformation through user-defined or algorithmically extracted key points [12724-neural-deformation-field.md]. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Deformation-Guided Neural Fields by explicitly decoupling the rigid skeletal transformation (LBS) from the residual non-rigid displacement predicted by a neural network [12724-neural-deformation-field.md]. Local Rotation Estimation via SVD is a technique used in dynamic neural radiance fields to correct view-dependent rendering artifacts caused by large rigid-body rotations during deformation [14864-local-rotation-estimation-via-svd.md]. It estimates the local rotation for each point in a deformed point cloud using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), inspired by As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) mesh deformation [14864-local-rotation-estimation-via-svd.md]. This estimated rotation is then interpolated to query view directions to "bend" rays, ensuring consistency between the deformed space and the canonical space representation [14864-local-rotation-estimation-via-svd.md]. It differs from sibling methods like Neural Deformation Field by explicitly modeling rotational components of the deformation field rather than relying solely on translation or dense deformation vectors, thereby handling complex fine-level deformations without introducing extra complexity into the radiance field model itself [14864-local-rotation-estimation-via-svd.md]. Not given in the sources.

name: Spline-based Deformation Field
head: Cubic B-spline deformation, Time-modulated spline deformation
body: This method parametrizes the deformation field in dynamic volume rendering using cubic B-splines with time-modulated weights to map spatial coordinates (x, y, z) at time t to canonical coordinates (x0, y0, z0). It enables the reconstruction of dynamic scenes from sparse projection data by combining a pre-trained canonical volume with the learned deformation field. Unlike Neural Deformation Fields which rely on MLPs and complex regularization, this approach allows reconstruction from as few as two projections due to the efficient encoding provided by B-splines. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sparse few-projection data recorded at intermediate times t during a dynamic experiment; a pre-trained canonical volume (obtained from rich many-projection data via traditional CT). Outputs: A deformation field \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{x}, t) that maps dynamic coordinates to canonical space, and full spatio-temporal volumetric information. Data Structures: The deformation field is represented by a 3D grid of cubic B-spline control points. The temporal evolution is handled by time-modulated weights associated with these control points. The exact bit-packing or grid resolution is not specified in the sources. Steps: 1. Pre-training (Canonical Volume): Reconstruct a static canonical volume using traditional computed tomography from rich, many-projection data acquired at a reference state (e.g., t=0 or a static phase). 2. Deformation Field Calculation: For each time step t where sparse data is available, calculate the deformation field parameters. This involves optimizing the B-spline control points and time-modulated weights to align the canonical volume with the sparse projections at time t. 3. Spatio-Temporal Reconstruction: Combine the canonical volume and the calculated deformation field to obtain full field spatio-temporal information. For any point \mathbf{x} at time t, the canonical coordinate is computed as \mathbf{x}0 = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{x}, t) (or similar mapping depending on convention), and the density/color is queried from the canonical volume at \mathbf{x}0. Formulas: The sources describe the parametrization conceptually but do not provide the explicit mathematical formula for the cubic B-spline basis functions or the time-modulation weights. The general mapping is described as: \mathbf{x}0 = f(\mathbf{x}, t; \text{B-spline parameters}) where \mathbf{x}0 is the canonical coordinate. Parameters: Number of Projections: As few as two. B-spline Order: Cubic (degree 3). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Topology Changes: Deformation fields based on canonical models fail when the scene topology changes over time, as they assume topology-preserving motion. Sparse Data: While effective for sparse data, the quality depends on the pre-training of the canonical volume. If the canonical volume is inaccurate, the deformation field cannot correct for static errors. Fully-differentiable variable-knot splines used as measurement representations. They allow optimization of spline control points and control point weights via automatic differentiation. This variant is faster to fit and simpler to interpret than implicit neural networks, while performing equally well in reconstruction quality. It is used in contexts such as uncalibrated imaging where measurement coordinates are uncertain. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. However, splines are noted to be faster to fit than implicit neural networks. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables reconstruction from very sparse data (as few as two projections). Simpler to interpret than neural fields. Limitations: Fails for scenes with topological changes over time. Requires a pre-trained canonical volume from dense data. When to use: Dynamic tomography with sparse projections where topology is preserved. When not to use: Scenes with significant topological changes. Originated in the context of dynamic X-ray computed tomography (X-CT). The method combines traditional CT in data-rich regimes with neural rendering in data-sparse regimes. It addresses the trade-off between detail and acquisition time in tomography by allowing efficient encoding of tomographic data. name: Deformation-Guided Neural Fields
head: Deformation Field NeRF, Morphable Model Guided NeRF, RigNeRF
body: Deformation-Guided Neural Fields address the problem of modeling dynamic, articulated subjects (specifically human faces) in neural radiance fields by decoupling identity from pose and expression. Unlike static NeRFs, this method constructs a fully 3D face portrait where geometry and appearance are controllable via pose and expression parameters. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly guiding the deformation field MLP with a parametric 3D morphable model (3DMM), ensuring that the learned deformations adhere to anatomical priors rather than relying solely on unconstrained neural predictions. The method operates by mapping 3D spatial coordinates from the canonical (neutral) space to the deformed (current pose/expression) space using a deformation field, which is then queried by a standard appearance field. Inputs: Training images with known camera poses and 3DMM parameters (pose, expression coefficients). A pre-trained 3D Morphable Model (3DMM) providing the mean face geometry and basis vectors for shape and expression variations. Outputs: A trained neural field capable of rendering novel views of the face with arbitrary pose and expression. Controllable 3D face portrait. Data Structures: 1. 3DMM Model: Defines the canonical mesh \mathbf{V}{canon} and basis shapes \mathbf{S}{shape} and expressions \mathbf{S}{exp}. 2. Deformation Field MLP (\mathcal{M}{def}): A neural network that takes canonical coordinates and expression/pose parameters as input and outputs a displacement vector. 3. Appearance Field MLP (\mathcal{M}{app}): A standard NeRF MLP that takes deformed 3D coordinates and viewing direction as input and outputs density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Steps: 1. Canonical Space Definition: Define the canonical space as the neutral expression state of the subject. The 3DMM provides the mean shape \mathbf{V}{mean}. 2. Deformation Field Evaluation: For a query point \mathbf{x}{canon} in canonical space, compute the deformation \Delta \mathbf{x} using the deformation field MLP \mathcal{M}{def}. The input to \mathcal{M}{def} includes \mathbf{x}{canon} and the current expression/pose parameters \theta derived from the 3DMM fit. \Delta \mathbf{x} = \mathcal{M}{def}(\mathbf{x}{canon}, \theta) 3. Coordinate Transformation: Map the canonical coordinate to the deformed space \mathbf{x}{def}: \mathbf{x}{def} = \mathbf{x}{canon} + \Delta \mathbf{x} 4. Appearance Query: Query the appearance field \mathcal{M}{app} with the deformed coordinate \mathbf{x}{def} and the viewing direction \mathbf{d} to obtain density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}: (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) = \mathcal{M}{app}(\mathbf{x}{def}, \mathbf{d}) 5. Volume Rendering: Render the image using the standard emission-absorption model (see 44-radiance-field-optimization.md) with the sampled (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) values along rays. 6. Optimization: Minimize the photometric loss between rendered and ground-truth images. The 3DMM guidance ensures that the deformation field \mathcal{M}{def} learns physically plausible facial movements. Parameters: 3DMM coefficients (pose, expression): Typically 3DMM-specific dimensions (e.g., 100-300 coefficients). MLP hidden layers: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fitting Errors: If the 3DMM fit to the input images is inaccurate, the canonical space definition may be misaligned, leading to artifacts. A common mitigation is to include a mask supervision loss to ensure the rendered alpha channel aligns with the subject's silhouette. Degenerate Input: Extreme expressions outside the 3DMM basis may cause extrapolation errors in the deformation field. Canonical Face Space Transformation normalizes world coordinates to a canonical face space using a rigid transform to address face shape variations between training data and real-world inputs, making the NeRF robust to geometry and pose variations. It sets itself apart from methods that rely on detailed mesh priors or non-rigid deformation fields by using only a rigid alignment derived from a mean geometry, avoiding the need for mesh details during view synthesis. Mesh-anchored Hash Table Blendshapes is a 3D neural avatar system achieving real-time rendering with high fidelity and fine-grained control through mesh-anchored hash table blendshapes. Each vertex of a 3DMM mesh is linked to a local hash table, allowing for expression-dependent embeddings and localized facial deformations. Local blendshapes are combined using per-vertex weights predicted in UV space from driving signals. It uses a hash encoding with decoding MLP in a hybrid neural implicit field to predict color and density from 3D queries using volume rendering. HiDe-NeRF is a neural radiation field technique for detailed, unobstructed dynamic head synthesis. It depicts a three-dimensional dynamic environment as a standard appearance field encompassing the standard source face, and a subtle deformation field that mimics the primary pose and expression. HiDe-NeRF is equipped with a multi-scale generalized appearance module (MGA) and a streamlined expression-aware deformation module (LED) to enhance expression precision while preserving identity data. Time Complexity: Rendering time is dominated by the evaluation of two MLPs (deformation and appearance) per sample point, plus the 3DMM projection if computed per sample. This is generally slower than static NeRFs but comparable to other deformation-based methods like Neural Body. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the parameters for both the deformation and appearance MLPs, plus the 3DMM model data. The 3DMM itself is lightweight compared to the neural fields. Strengths: Provides explicit control over pose and expression; robust to identity variations; leverages strong anatomical priors from the 3DMM. Limitations: Dependent on the quality of the 3DMM fit; may struggle with non-facial regions or occlusions not covered by the face model; limited to the expression range of the 3DMM basis. When to use: When controllable, high-fidelity 3D face avatars are required from video or image collections. When not to use: For non-rigid, non-anatomical dynamic scenes or when 3DMM fitting is unreliable (e.g., heavy occlusion, extreme angles). Deformation-Guided Neural Fields emerged as a solution to the limitations of standard NeRFs in handling moving subjects. While standard NeRFs struggle with moving bodies, mesh deformation approaches like Neural Body demonstrated the ability to interpolate between frames and poses. RigNeRF, introduced in June 2022, innovated on this topic by using deformation field MLPs guided by a morphable 3D face model, creating a fully 3D face portrait with controllable pose and expression. This approach built upon the popular paradigm of animating articulated bodies using a baseline skeleton equipped with an MLP-based deformation field, a paradigm established by works such as A-NeRF (Feb 2021) and Animatable NeRF (May 2021). name: Canonical Face Space Transformation
head: Canonical face coordinate, Rigid transform
body: Canonical Face Space Transformation normalizes world coordinates to a canonical face space using a rigid transform to address face shape variations between training data and real-world inputs, making the NeRF robust to geometry and pose variations. It addresses the challenge of rendering novel views of faces from a single frontal image by normalizing geometric variations across different subjects into a shared canonical space, allowing a single pre-trained NeRF model to be fine-tuned for individual subjects. It sets itself apart from methods that rely on detailed mesh priors or non-rigid deformation fields by using only a rigid alignment derived from a mean geometry, avoiding the need for mesh details during view synthesis. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A point x in the subject’s world coordinate system; viewing direction \tilde{d} in world coordinates. Output: A point x0 in the face canonical space; color and occlusion values retrieved from the MLP f\theta. Parameters: Optimized scale sm, rotation Rm, and translation tm for subject m. Data Structures: Facial Geometry (Fm): Approximate 3D facial mesh for subject m, obtained from frontal image using a 3D morphable model and image-based landmark fitting. Mean Geometry (F): Average of all facial geometries in the training dataset. Rigid Transform: Tuple (sm, Rm, tm) where sm is a scalar, Rm is a 3 \times 3 rotation matrix, and tm is a 3 \times 1 translation vector. Steps: 1. Compute Subject Geometry: For each subject m in the training data, compute approximate facial geometry Fm from the frontal image using a 3D morphable model and image-based landmark fitting. 2. Compute Mean Geometry: Calculate the mean geometry F by averaging all facial geometries Fm in the dataset. 3. Optimize Rigid Transform: Optimize the rigid transform (sm, Rm, tm) by minimizing the L2 loss between corresponding vertices of Fm and F using SVD decomposition on vertex correspondences. 4. Warp Coordinates: During prediction, warp the input coordinate x from world space to canonical space using the optimized transform: x0 = sm Rm x + tm where x is the point in the subject's world coordinate and x0 is the point in the face canonical space. 5. Query MLP: Feed the warped coordinate x0 and the original viewing direction \tilde{d} (kept in world coordinates) to the MLP network f\theta to retrieve color and occlusion. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def canonicalfacespacetransform(xworld, viewingdirection, subjectid, subjecttransforms): """ Transforms world coordinates to canonical face space for a specific subject. Args: xworld: numpy array, shape (3,), point in subject's world coordinate. viewingdirection: numpy array, shape (3,), viewing direction in world coordinate. subjectid: int, identifier for the subject. subjecttransforms: dict mapping subjectid to (sm, Rm, tm). Returns: xcanonical: numpy array, shape (3,), point in face canonical space. viewingdirection: numpy array, shape (3,), unchanged viewing direction. """ # Retrieve pre-optimized rigid transform for the subject # sm: scalar scale factor # Rm: 3x3 rotation matrix # tm: 3x1 translation vector sm, Rm, tm = subjecttransforms[subjectid] # Apply rigid transform: x0 = sm Rm x + tm xcanonical = sm (Rm @ xworld) + tm # Viewing direction remains in world coordinates return xcanonical, viewingdirection Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The 3D mesh models are used only to obtain the rigid transform; mesh details and priors are not required or used in the view synthesis process itself. The viewing direction \tilde{d} is kept in the world coordinate and is not warped to canonical space. The parent method that uses deformation fields MLP guided by a morphable 3D face model. Canonical Face Space Transformation is a specific rigid alignment technique within this family. Deformation-Guided Neural Fields Performance: Using canonical coordinates yields better quality (higher PSNR/SSIM, lower LPIPS) than using world coordinates, particularly on chin and eyes. World Coordinate: PSNR 24.80, SSIM 0.8167, LPIPS 0.172 Canonical Coordinate: PSNR 24.98, SSIM 0.8178, LPIPS 0.156 Strengths: Robust to variation in face geometry and poses in training and testing inputs. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the initial 3D morphable model and landmark fitting to derive the mean geometry and subject geometries. Canonical Face Space Transformation was introduced in "Portrait Neural Radiance Fields from a Single Image". It addresses the challenge of rendering novel views of faces from a single frontal image by normalizing geometric variations across different subjects into a shared canonical space, allowing a single pre-trained NeRF model to be fine-tuned for individual subjects. name: Neural Deformation Field
head: non-rigid deformation network
body: The Neural Deformation Field (NDF) is a method for modeling non-rigid, time-varying deformations in neural radiance fields by predicting per-point displacements in a canonical space. It solves the problem of animating static neural representations without relying on rigid body assumptions or human-specific priors like SMPL. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Deformation-Guided Neural Fields by explicitly decoupling the rigid skeletal transformation (LBS) from the residual non-rigid displacement predicted by a neural network. Builds on Deformation Field Parametrization. The method operates by mapping points from a target deformed space to a canonical space using a combination of inverse Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) and a neural displacement field. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A point in the target deformed space \mathbf{x}t, the target pose \thetat, and the 2D UV coordinates [u, v] of the point on the underlying mesh surface. Output: The corresponding point \mathbf{x}c in the canonical space. Data Structures: Signed Height Indicator (\tilde{h}): A vector encoding the geometric relationship of the point to the mesh surface. It is defined as \tilde{h} = [u, v, \bar{d}], where [u, v] are the 2D UV coordinates and \bar{d} is the signed distance. Neural Network (F\Delta): An MLP that takes the position-encoded signed height indicator and the target pose as input to predict the displacement \Delta. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Project to Mesh Surface: Given a target point \mathbf{x}t, project it onto the mesh surface to find the nearest surface point \mathbf{x}0. 2. Calculate Signed Distance (\bar{d}): Compute the direction vector from the surface point to the target point: \tilde{\mathbf{r}} = \mathbf{x}t - \mathbf{x}0. Obtain the surface normal \tilde{\mathbf{n}} at \mathbf{x}0. Calculate the signed distance: \bar{d} = \text{sign}(\tilde{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \tilde{\mathbf{n}}) \|\tilde{\mathbf{r}}\|2 3. Construct Signed Height Indicator: Combine the UV coordinates and signed distance: \tilde{h} = [u, v, \bar{d}] 4. Predict Displacement (\Delta): Pass the position-encoded signed height indicator \phi(\tilde{h}) and the target pose \thetat through the neural deformation network F\Delta: \Delta = F\Delta(\phi(\tilde{h}), \thetat) 5. Compute Canonical Point (\mathbf{x}c): Apply the inverse LBS transformation to the target point and add the predicted displacement: \mathbf{x}c = LBS^{-1}(\mathbf{x}t) + \Delta Parameters: \phi(\cdot): Position encoding function. LBS^{-1}: Inverse Linear Blend Skinning transformation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Static Background: If a point's nearest SMPL vertex exceeds a certain threshold, it is classified as a static background point. In this case, the bone weight is set to zero, the background weight to one, and no non-rigid deformation is applied. Precision: The calculation of \bar{d} relies on the accuracy of the surface normal \tilde{\mathbf{n}} and the projection \mathbf{x}0. Dynamic Point Field Deformation (DPF) models non-rigid, time-varying deformations in point-based radiance fields by predicting translations between canonical and deformed space point clouds using a neural network. It animates static neural point clouds without rigid body assumptions or human-specific priors like SMPL. Unlike cage-based or linear blend skinning methods, DPF generalizes to arbitrary objects and enables fine-level complex deformation through user-defined or algorithmically extracted key points. This variant addresses the consistency of learnable signed distances when deforming a neural implicit field by deforming the mesh scaffold. To maintain local consistency, the rotation of the surface normal is compensated in the learnable signed indicator \tilde{h}(x). The compensated signed indicator is calculated as: \tilde{h}'(x) = \tilde{h}(x) + \delta hx where \delta hx is the relative difference of the vertex normal (averaged from nearby surface normals) from the original mesh to the deformed mesh. This ensures that the interpolated signed distance of locally deformed or rotated regions remains consistent. Not given in the sources. The Neural Deformation Field was introduced in the context of unified volumetric avatars for view synthesis, pose rendering, and geometry editing. It was proposed to address the limitations of previous methods that relied on baking polygon meshes from pre-trained neural fields, which required manual parameter tuning. The method jointly optimizes the geometry field with other components from scratch. name: Dynamic Point Field Deformation
body: Dynamic Point Field Deformation (DPF) is a method for modeling non-rigid, time-varying deformations in point-based radiance fields by predicting the translation between a canonical space point cloud and a deformed space point cloud using a neural network. It solves the problem of animating static neural point clouds without relying on rigid body assumptions or human-specific priors like SMPL. Unlike cage-based or linear blend skinning methods, DPF generalizes to arbitrary objects and enables fine-level complex deformation through user-defined or algorithmically extracted key points. Inputs and Outputs: Canonical Space Point Cloud: A static neural point cloud X = \{(xi, fi, \gammai) | i = 1, \dots, N\}, where xi \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the position, fi is the neural feature, and \gammai \in [0, 1] is the scale confidence. Key Points: A sparse subset \{\hat{x}i\}{i=1}^{n} of size n extracted from the canonical space. Target Pose Key Points: A set of T frames of target key points \{xi^{(t)}\}{i=1}^{n} \subseteq X^{(t)} for t=1, \dots, T, which have fine correspondence with the source key points \{\hat{x}i\}. Output: A series of deformation networks \{g{\theta}^{(t)}\}{t=1}^{T} and the deformed point cloud positions. Data Structures: Key Points: Stored as a list or tensor of shape (n, 3) containing 3D coordinates. The number of key points N{kp} is a hyperparameter; experiments tested N{kp} \in \{20, 200, 2000\}. Deformation MLP (g{\theta}^{(t)}): A Multi-Layer Perceptron mapping \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3. It takes a canonical point as input and outputs a displacement vector. Steps: 1. Extract Key Points: Identify a sparse set of key points \{\hat{x}i\} from the canonical neural point cloud X. These can be user-defined or derived from a mesh (e.g., SMPL vertices). 2. Define Target Poses: For each time step t, provide the corresponding target key point positions \{xi^{(t)}\}. 3. Train Deformation Network: Train the MLP g{\theta}^{(t)} to predict the translation such that the deformed key point matches the target. The loss minimizes the difference between the predicted deformed key point and the target key point. 4. Compute Deformation: For any point p in the canonical space, compute its deformed position p^{(t)} using the trained network: p^{(t)} = p + g{\theta}^{(t)}(p) Specifically for key points: xi^{(t)} = \hat{x}i + g{\theta}^{(t)}(\hat{x}i) 5. Ray Bending (Rendering): To render the deformed scene, rays cast from the camera are bent along the volumetric marching path. The deformation induces an absolute transformation (translation and rotation) that maps the query point in deformed space back to the canonical space for feature query. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class DeformationMLP(nn.Module): """ MLP that predicts displacement vector for a given canonical point. Input: (N, 3) canonical points Output: (N, 3) displacement vectors """ def init(self, hiddendim=256, numlayers=4): super().init() layers = [] layers.append(nn.Linear(3, hiddendim)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) for in range(numlayers - 2): layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddendim, 3)) self.network = nn.Sequential(layers) def forward(self, x): return self.network(x) def traindeformationnetwork(canonicalkeypoints, targetkeypoints, numepochs=1000): """ Trains the deformation MLP to map canonical keypoints to target keypoints. Args: canonicalkeypoints: Tensor of shape (n, 3) targetkeypoints: Tensor of shape (n, 3) Returns: trainedmodel: The trained DeformationMLP """ model = DeformationMLP() optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3) for epoch in range(numepochs): # Forward pass: predict displacement displacement = model(canonicalkeypoints) # Predicted deformed positions predicteddeformed = canonicalkeypoints + displacement # Compute loss (e.g., MSE) loss = nn.functional.mseloss(predicteddeformed, targetkeypoints) # Backward pass optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return model def deformpointcloud(canonicalpointcloud, trainedmodel): """ Deforms the entire canonical point cloud using the trained model. Args: canonicalpointcloud: Tensor of shape (N, 3) trainedmodel: The trained DeformationMLP Returns: deformedpointcloud: Tensor of shape (N, 3) """ displacement = trainedmodel(canonicalpointcloud) return canonicalpointcloud + displacement Parameters: Number of Key Points (N{kp}): The density of key points affects deformation quality. Experiments showed results for N{kp}=20, 200, 2000. MLP Architecture: Not explicitly defined in the notes, but standard MLPs are used. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Inconsistent Rendering: Direct rendering of deformed points without ray bending can lead to inconsistent results if the deformation causes gaps or overlaps. Generalization: Unlike SMPL-based methods, DPF does not require a human prior, allowing it to handle non-human objects. A neural network approach that uses key points (user-defined or SMPL-derived) as input to predict point cloud deformations, avoiding restrictions to linear blend skinning. It generalizes to all kinds of objects, enabling fine-level complex deformation, unlike cage/tetrahedron-based barycentric methods or SMPL-prior methods which are limited to humans or coarse deformation. Complexity: The method relies on an MLP for deformation prediction, which is computationally attractive compared to complex skeletal rigs. Performance: The method demonstrates superior deformation and rendering quality for fine-level user editing compared to simple local deformation methods. Limitations: The quality depends on the selection and number of key points. Insufficient key points may lead to poor deformation fidelity. Hardware: Not specified in the sources. Dynamic Point Field Deformation was introduced in the context of point-based radiance fields, specifically building upon PointNeRF. It was proposed to allow efficient editing of point clouds and the synthesis of human motion without relying on linear blend skinning or human-specific priors like SMPL. The method was demonstrated on datasets generated using Blender NeRF and multi-view stereo algorithms. Point-Based Radiance Fields for Controllable Human Motion Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2310.03375, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Local Rotation Estimation via SVD
head: SVD-based Rotation Estimation
body: Local Rotation Estimation via SVD is a technique used in dynamic neural radiance fields to correct view-dependent rendering artifacts caused by large rigid-body rotations during deformation. It estimates the local rotation for each point in a deformed point cloud using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), inspired by As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) mesh deformation. This estimated rotation is then interpolated to query view directions to "bend" rays, ensuring consistency between the deformed space and the canonical space representation. It differs from sibling methods like Neural Deformation Field by explicitly modeling rotational components of the deformation field rather than relying solely on translation or dense deformation vectors, thereby handling complex fine-level deformations without introducing extra complexity into the radiance field model itself. Inputs: 1. A set of canonical space points P{can} = \{(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{f}i, \gammai)\}{i=1}^N, where \mathbf{x}i is position, \mathbf{f}i is neural feature, and \gammai is scale confidence. 2. A deformed space point cloud P{def}, obtained by applying a deformation MLP to predict translations from canonical to deformed space. 3. A pre-trained static radiance field model (e.g., PointNeRF) that predicts density \sigma and radiance \mathbf{r} given a query location and view direction. 4. A query ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{v} in camera space. Outputs: 1. Corrected ray direction \mathbf{v}' in canonical space for accurate sampling. 2. Rendered color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) consistent with the deformed pose. Data Structures: Point Cloud: List of tuples (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{f}, \gamma). Rotation Matrix: 3 \times 3 orthogonal matrix R with determinant +1. Algorithm Steps: 1. Deformation Translation: For each canonical point \mathbf{x}i, compute its deformed position \mathbf{x}'i using a deformation MLP D: \mathbf{x}'i = \mathbf{x}i + D(\mathbf{x}i) 2. Local Rotation Estimation via SVD: For each point \mathbf{x}i, estimate the local rotation Ri that best aligns the local neighborhood in the canonical space to the deformed space. Let \mathcal{N}i be the set of k nearest neighbors of \mathbf{x}i in the canonical space. Construct two matrices A and B of size 3 \times k: Columns of A are vectors from \mathbf{x}i to its neighbors: \mathbf{a}j = \mathbf{x}{nj} - \mathbf{x}i for nj \in \mathcal{N}i. Columns of B are vectors from \mathbf{x}'i to the corresponding deformed neighbors: \mathbf{b}j = \mathbf{x}'{nj} - \mathbf{x}'i. Compute the cross-covariance matrix H: H = A B^T = \sum{j=1}^k (\mathbf{x}{nj} - \mathbf{x}i)(\mathbf{x}'{nj} - \mathbf{x}'i)^T Perform Singular Value Decomposition on H: H = U \Sigma V^T Compute the rotation matrix Ri: Ri = V U^T Correction for Reflection: If \det(Ri) = -1, the decomposition yields a reflection. Correct it by setting the last column of V to -V{last} before computing Ri (i.e., Ri = V \text{diag}(1, 1, -1) U^T). This ensures Ri is a proper rotation matrix (\det(Ri)=1). 3. Interpolation to Query Direction: Given a query ray with direction \mathbf{v} in camera space, determine the corresponding direction \mathbf{v}{can} in canonical space. First, find the intersection point \mathbf{x}{hit} of the ray with the deformed point cloud or use the nearest deformed point \mathbf{x}'k to the ray. Interpolate the rotation R{query} from the estimated local rotations Ri of nearby points. A common approach is inverse-distance weighting based on the distance from the query ray to the canonical points \mathbf{x}i: R{query} = \frac{\sum{i \in \mathcal{K}} wi Ri}{\|\sum{i \in \mathcal{K}} wi Ri\|{F}} where \mathcal{K} is a set of m nearest canonical points to the query ray, and wi = 1 / \|\mathbf{x}{hit} - \mathbf{x}i\|^2 + \epsilon. The Frobenius norm normalization ensures the result is a valid rotation matrix. 4. Ray Bending: Rotate the query view direction \mathbf{v} using the interpolated rotation R{query} to obtain the canonical view direction \mathbf{v}{can}: \mathbf{v}{can} = R{query} \mathbf{v} 5. Rendering: Use the canonical radiance field to sample density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} at points along the ray using \mathbf{v}{can} and the canonical positions. Compute the final color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) using the standard volume rendering equation [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. Parameters: k: Number of neighbors for SVD estimation. Typical value: 6-10. m: Number of neighbors for rotation interpolation. Typical value: 6-10. \epsilon: Small constant for numerical stability. Typical value: 10^{-6}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Neighbors: If neighbors are collinear or coplanar, H may be rank-deficient, leading to unstable SVD. Add a small regularization term to H or increase k. Reflection: As noted, SVD can produce reflections. The determinant check is mandatory. Boundary Points: Points on the boundary of the deformed object may have sparse neighbors. Use a larger search radius or fallback to identity rotation. ARAP Mesh Deformation is a technique for deforming a triangular mesh while preserving local rigidity, minimizing distortion energy by approximating local rotations. It solves the problem of transferring user-specified boundary edits to the interior of a mesh without excessive stretching or shearing. It differs from global rigid transformations by allowing local rotation estimation per vertex, and from linear blend skinning by avoiding skeletal dependencies, relying instead on the mesh connectivity and cotangent weights. Time Complexity: The SVD step is O(k) per point for covariance matrix construction and O(1) for 3 \times 3 SVD. Interpolation is O(m). Overall, it adds a small constant overhead per ray query compared to pure translation-based deformation. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the deformation MLP and the point cloud. No additional large structures are needed beyond the point features. Strengths: Handles large rotations effectively without modifying the core radiance field architecture. Improves visual consistency for complex deformations (e.g., human motion). Limitations: Requires a well-defined point cloud structure. Performance degrades if the point cloud is sparse or noisy. The interpolation step can introduce artifacts if the rotation field is not smooth. When to Use: When deforming scenes with significant rigid-body motion (e.g., articulated characters) where translation-only deformation causes view-dependent artifacts. When Not to Use: For small deformations where translation is sufficient, or for scenes without a clear point cloud representation. This method was introduced in "Point-Based Radiance Fields for Controllable Human Motion Synthesis" by Zhang et al. (2023). It builds on the observation that direct rendering of deformed point clouds leads to inconsistencies due to changed viewing directions. By borrowing the SVD-based rotation estimation from ARAP mesh deformation, the method provides a simple yet effective "ray-bending" module. It is particularly relevant for dynamic NeRF applications involving digital humans and other 3D characters. Point-Based Radiance Fields for Controllable Human Motion Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2310.03375, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: ARAP Mesh Deformation
head: ARAP energy minimization, As-Rigid-As-Possible deformation
body: ARAP Mesh Deformation is a technique for deforming a triangular mesh while preserving local rigidity, minimizing distortion energy by approximating local rotations. It solves the problem of transferring user-specified boundary edits to the interior of a mesh without excessive stretching or shearing. It differs from global rigid transformations by allowing local rotation estimation per vertex, and from linear blend skinning by avoiding skeletal dependencies, relying instead on the mesh connectivity and cotangent weights. Inputs: Original mesh S with vertex positions vi \in \mathbb{R}^3 for i=1 \dots n. Connectivity information (adjacency list N(i) for each vertex). Boundary conditions: deformed positions v'i for a subset of vertices (user edits). Outputs: Deformed mesh S' with vertex positions v'i for all i. Data Structures: Adjacency list: N(i) contains indices of vertices adjacent to i. Cotangent weights: w{ij} stored for each edge (i,j). Rotation matrices: Ri \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} for each vertex i. Formulas: The ARAP energy is defined as: E(S') = \sum{i=1}^{n} \sum{j \in N(i)} w{ij} \| (v'i - v'j) - Ri(vi - vj) \|^2 where: w{ij} = \frac{1}{2}(\cot \alpha{ij} + \cot \beta{ij}) is the cotangent weight for edge (i,j). \alpha{ij}, \beta{ij} are the angles opposite to edge (i,j) in the two triangles sharing it. Ri is the local rotation matrix at vertex i. Steps: 1. Precompute Weights: Calculate w{ij} for all edges using the original mesh geometry. 2. Initialize: Set initial rotations Ri = I (identity) for all i. Fix boundary vertices v'i to user-specified positions. 3. Optimize Rotations: For each vertex i, compute the optimal rotation Ri that minimizes the energy term involving i and its neighbors, given current v'j. This typically involves a Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of a covariance matrix constructed from vectors (vi - vj) and (v'i - v'j) [S1, Note: SVD step implied by parent article context and standard ARAP literature, but specific matrix construction not detailed in S1 text. We assume standard ARAP rotation update]. 4. Optimize Positions: Solve for v'i for all free vertices by setting the gradient of E(S') with respect to v'i to zero. This results in a linear system A v' = b, where A is a sparse matrix derived from the cotangent weights and Ri, and b incorporates boundary conditions and rotation terms. 5. Iterate: Repeat steps 3 and 4 until convergence (change in energy or positions below a threshold). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def arapdeformation(mesh, boundaryvertices, boundarypositions, maxiter=100, tol=1e-6): """ mesh: object with vertices V (n x 3), faces, and adjacency list N boundaryvertices: list of vertex indices fixed to boundarypositions boundarypositions: list of 3D positions for boundary vertices """ n = len(mesh.V) Vprime = mesh.V.copy() # Initialize rotations to identity R = [np.eye(3) for in range(n)] # Precompute cotangent weights weights = computecotangentweights(mesh) for iteration in range(maxiter): # Step 1: Optimize Rotations for i in range(n): # Construct covariance matrix Mi = sum{j in N(i)} wij (V[i] - V[j]) (Vprime[i] - Vprime[j]).T Mi = np.zeros((3, 3)) for j in mesh.N[i]: difforig = mesh.V[i] - mesh.V[j] diffdeformed = Vprime[i] - Vprime[j] Mi += weights[(i,j)] np.outer(difforig, diffdeformed) # SVD to find optimal rotation Ri U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Mi) R[i] = Vt.T @ U.T # Handle reflection case if necessary (det(R[i]) < 0) if np.linalg.det(R[i]) < 0: Vt[-1,:] = -1 R[i] = Vt.T @ U.T # Step 2: Optimize Positions # Solve linear system A Vprime = b # A is constructed from weights and R, b from boundary conditions and R A, b = buildlinearsystem(mesh, weights, R, boundaryvertices, boundarypositions) Vprimeflat = np.linalg.solve(A, b) Vprime = Vprimeflat.reshape(n, 3) # Check convergence if np.linalg.norm(Vprime - mesh.V) < tol: break return Vprime def computecotangentweights(mesh): weights = {} for face in mesh.faces: i, j, k = face # Calculate angles opposite to edges (i,j), (j,k), (k,i) # This requires a helper to get opposite vertices and angles # Simplified: assume helper function exists weights[(i,j)] = 0.5 (cot(angleoppositetoij) + cot(angleoppositetoijothertriangle)) weights[(j,k)] =... weights[(k,i)] =... return weights def buildlinearsystem(mesh, weights, R, boundaryvertices, boundarypositions): # Construct sparse matrix A and vector b # For each free vertex i: # sum{j in N(i)} wij (v'i - v'j) = sum{j in N(i)} wij Ri (vi - vj) # Rearrange to form linear equations # This is a standard ARAP linear solve step # Not fully detailed in S1, but implied by "efficiently solved" pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Incorrectly fixing boundary vertices can lead to unrealistic deformations. Degenerate Triangles: Cotangent weights become undefined for degenerate triangles (zero area). Handle by skipping or smoothing weights. Reflections: SVD may produce a reflection (det(R) = -1). Ensure proper handling to maintain orientation. Extends ARAP deformation from triangular meshes to tetrahedral meshes. It deforms the tetrahedral mesh T under constraints from the surface mesh deformation. The optimization problem is \min E(T') subject to A t' = v', where A is the barycentric weight matrix and t' are deformed tetrahedron vertices. It involves finding which tetrahedron each triangular mesh vertex is located in and calculating barycentric coordinates. The problem is converted to linear equations using Lagrangian multipliers. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of iterations and the cost of solving the linear system. Each iteration involves SVD for rotations and a sparse linear solve for positions. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of vertices and edges for storing weights, rotations, and the linear system matrix. Strengths: Preserves local rigidity well, handles complex deformations, no need for skeletons. Limitations: Can be slow for large meshes due to iterative optimization. Sensitive to boundary conditions. When to Use: When rigid deformation is desired without skeletal animation, or for transferring deformations from a surface mesh to a volume representation. ARAP mesh deformation was introduced in the context of NeRF editing, specifically in the paper "NeRF-Editing: Geometry Editing of Neural Radiance Fields". It is used to transfer user edits from a triangular mesh to an implicit volume representation, enabling geometry editing of neural radiance fields. name: Embedded Deformation (Stage I)
head: ARAP Deformation, Deformation Graph
body: Embedded Deformation (Stage I) applies As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) geometric deformation to 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations using a deformation graph of control nodes. It differs from direct Gaussian displacement by estimating per-Gaussian affine transformations via endpoint sampling to mitigate visual artifacts caused by the mismatch between deformed geometry and the radiance field. Inputs: Set of 3D Gaussians, each defined by center pi, covariance \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients Hi. User-defined constraints ql for specific control points. Outputs: Deformed Gaussian centers \tilde{p}i. Deformed covariance matrices \tilde{\Sigma}i (via rotation r and scaling s). Rotated spherical harmonics. Data Structures: Deformation Graph: A graph where vertices are control points gj and edges connect neighbors. Control Point Affine Transform: Each node j stores a 3 \times 3 matrix Aj and a 3 \times 1 translation vector tj. Gaussian Endpoints: For each Gaussian, 6 endpoints Q = [q1, \dots, q6] \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 6} located at \pm 2\sigma along the three principal axes. Steps: 1. Construct Deformation Graph: Select control points from the set of Gaussian centers using Furthest Point Sampling (FPS). Construct edge connections between control points using the K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) algorithm. 2. Define Energies: Minimize the total energy E{geo} to find optimal Aj and tj: E{geo} = \sumj \left( w{rot} E{rot}(Aj) + w{reg} E{reg}(Aj) \right) + w{con} E{con} where: E{rot}(A) measures deviation from rigid rotation. Let c1, c2, c3 \in \mathbb{R}^3 be the column vectors of A: E{rot}(A) = (c1 \cdot c2)^2 + (c1 \cdot c3)^2 + (c2 \cdot c3)^2 + (c1 \cdot c1 - 1)^2 + (c2 \cdot c2 - 1)^2 + (c3 \cdot c3 - 1)^2 E{reg}(A) penalizes sharp translational changes between adjacent control nodes k: E{reg}(A) = \sumk \| A(gk - g) + g + t - (gk + tk) \|^2 Here, g and t are the translation and matrix of the current node, and gk, tk are those of neighbor k. E{con} enforces user constraints ql for deformed control point positions \tilde{g}l: E{con} = \suml \| \tilde{g}l - ql \|^2 3. Optimize Transformations: Solve for Aj and tj that minimize E{geo}. 4. Displace Embedded Geometries: Compute the deformed position \tilde{v}i for any embedded geometry point vi (e.g., Gaussian center or endpoint) using weights wj(vi) inherited from control node j: \tilde{v}i = \sumj wj(vi) \left( Aj (vi - gj) + gj + tj \right) where gj is the original position of control node j. 5. Reconstruct Gaussians: For each Gaussian, select 6 endpoints along the three axes at twice the standard deviation from the center. Displace these endpoints using the Embedded Deformation formula above. Let P \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 6} be the matrix of original endpoints and \tilde{P} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 6} be the matrix of deformed endpoints. Estimate the local deformation matrix M: M = \tilde{P} Q^\top (Q Q^\top)^{-1} where Q is the matrix of original endpoint positions. Perform polar decomposition on M to obtain rotation r and scaling s. Update the Gaussian's covariance matrix using r and s. Rotate the spherical harmonics coefficients corresponding to the new rotation r. Parameters: w{rot} = 1 w{reg} = 10 w{con} = 100 Pitfalls: Direct geometric deformation causes visual artifacts under large deformations due to the mismatch between deformed Gaussians and the deformed radiance field. This method addresses the geometry but requires Stage II to align with the radiance field. Complexity: Depends on the number of control points, their neighbors (KNN), and the number of Gaussians. Optimization of E{geo} is typically solved via least squares or iterative solvers. Strengths: Provides physically plausible, rigid-like deformation for point clouds and meshes; avoids the need for explicit mesh topology in Gaussian Splatting. Limitations: Does not fully correct radiance field misalignment artifacts on its own; requires a second stage for full consistency. Embedded deformation was originally introduced for meshes and point clouds. In the context of 3DGS, it is adapted to handle the particle-like nature of Gaussians. This method is part of a two-stage pipeline for ARAP deformation of Gaussian Radiance Fields. name: Polynomial Motion Field
head: Hierarchical motion model, Parametric Motion Field, Polynomial warp field
body: The Polynomial Motion Field is a parametric deformation model used in dynamic volume rendering to represent temporal motion as a continuous function of time. It solves the problem of reconstructing 4D (3D space + time) scenes from sparse or limited view measurements by warping a static template volume to arbitrary time points using polynomial coefficients. Unlike neural deformation fields that map (x, y, z, t) to displacement via a network, this method explicitly parameterizes the motion trajectory at each voxel as a polynomial, allowing for efficient optimization and arbitrary temporal upsampling. It differs from spline-based methods by using global polynomial bases rather than piecewise continuous splines, and from neural fields by avoiding the computational overhead of network inference during rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N sparse or limited-view 2D projections (sinograms) sampled at discrete time points t{i=0 \dots N-1}. A static template volume \hat{\sigma} (or an initial estimate). Output: A Motion Coefficient Tensor C and the reconstructed dynamic volume \sigma(x, y, z, t) for any t \in [0, 1]. Data Structures: Motion Coefficient Tensor C: A tensor of shape \mathbb{R}^{\beta^3 \times k \times 3}. \beta^3: The spatial resolution of the scene (number of voxels). k: The polynomial order (degree). 3: The three spatial dimensions (x, y, z). Each voxel stores k coefficients for each of the 3 spatial displacement components. Time Samples: N time points ti linearly spaced in [0, 1]. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the Motion Coefficient Tensor C. To mitigate poor motion reconstruction at full resolution, initialize C at a base spatial resolution \alpha (where \alpha < \beta), resulting in C\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^{\alpha^3 \times k \times 3}. 2. Hierarchical Upsampling (Coarse-to-Fine): Iteratively increase the spatial resolution \alpha (e.g., 2^3 \to 4^3 \to 8^3 \to 16^3). At each step, upsample the current coefficient tensor C{\alphai} to the next resolution C{\alpha{i+1}} using linear upsampling U: C{\alpha{i+1}} = U(C{\alphai}) where U: \mathbb{R}^{\alphai^3} \to \mathbb{R}^{\alpha{i+1}^3}. 3. Warp Field Computation: For a specific time ti, compute the 3D displacement vector W(C, ti) for all voxels using the polynomial expansion: W(C, ti) = \sum{j=0}^{k} C{:, j,:} ti^j where W(C, ti) \in \mathbb{R}^{\beta^3 \times 3} is the warp field at time ti, and C{:, j,:} denotes the slice of coefficients for the j-th polynomial order across all voxels and spatial dimensions. 4. Differentiable Grid Sampling: Warp the template volume \hat{\sigma} using the computed displacement field. The volume at time ti is obtained via a differentiable grid sampling function fn: \sigma(x, y, z, ti) = fn(W(C, ti), \hat{\sigma}) This function interpolates the template values at the displaced coordinates. 5. Optimization: Minimize the reconstruction error between the rendered projections of \sigma(x, y, z, ti) and the measured sinograms. The optimization encourages the polynomial coefficients to fit a continuous representation of motion, allowing the model to be evaluated at arbitrary time points t not present in the training set. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def computewarpfield(C, timet): """ Compute the displacement field W for a given time t. C: Tensor of shape (numvoxels, k, 3) timet: Scalar or Tensor of time values in [0, 1] Returns: W of shape (numvoxels, 3) """ # C[:, j,:] are the coefficients for order j # We compute sum(C[:, j,:] t^j for j in 0..k) W = torch.zeroslike(C[:, 0,:]) # Shape (numvoxels, 3) tpower = torch.oneslike(timet) # t^0 = 1 # Ensure timet is broadcastable to (numvoxels, 1) if needed # Assuming timet is a scalar or 1D tensor matching the batch/time dimension # For a single time point evaluation: tval = timet if isinstance(timet, float) else timet.item() for j in range(C.shape[1]): # Iterate over polynomial order k if j > 0: tpower = tpower tval # Add C[:, j,:] t^j to W # C[:, j,:] is (numvoxels, 3) W = W + C[:, j,:] tpower return W def hierarchicalupsample(Calpha, targetalpha): """ Upsample the coefficient tensor from resolution alpha to targetalpha. Calpha: Tensor of shape (alpha^3, k, 3) targetalpha: Integer target resolution Returns: Tensor of shape (targetalpha^3, k, 3) """ # Reshape to 3D grid for interpolation # alpha^3 voxels -> reshape to (alpha, alpha, alpha, k, 3) # Note: The source specifies linear upsampling U. # In practice, this involves reshaping, interpolating the spatial dims, # and reshaping back. alpha = int(Calpha.shape[0] (1/3)) k = Calpha.shape[1] # Reshape to (alpha, alpha, alpha, k, 3) Cgrid = Calpha.view(alpha, alpha, alpha, k, 3) # Interpolate spatial dimensions (alpha -> targetalpha) # Using trilinear interpolation on the first 3 dims # PyTorch gridsample or F.interpolate can be used. # F.interpolate expects (N, C, D, H, W) or similar. # Here we treat k3 as channels. Cinterp = F.interpolate( Cgrid.permute(0, 1, 2, 4, 3).contiguous().view(1, 1, alpha, alpha, alpha, k3), # Hacky reshape for interp size=(targetalpha, targetalpha, targetalpha), mode='trilinear', aligncorners=False) # Reshape back to (targetalpha^3, k, 3) # This step is conceptual; exact tensor manipulation depends on framework # The source states: "constrained to simple trilinear interpolation" # We assume a helper trilinearupsample exists for the tensor structure Cnew = trilinearupsampletensor(Cgrid, targetalpha) return Cnew def trilinearupsampletensor(Cgrid, targetalpha): """ Helper to perform trilinear interpolation on the spatial dimensions of Cgrid. Cgrid: (alpha, alpha, alpha, k, 3) """ # Reshape to (alpha, alpha, alpha, k3) Cflat = Cgrid.view(Cgrid.shape[0], Cgrid.shape[1], Cgrid.shape[2], -1) # Add batch and channel dims for F.interpolate C4d = Cflat.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # (1, 1, alpha, alpha, alpha, k3) -> needs correct dim order # Correct dim order for F.interpolate in 3D: (N, C, D, H, W) # Cflat is (alpha, alpha, alpha, k3). Transpose to (k3, alpha, alpha, alpha) Ctrans = Cflat.permute(3, 0, 1, 2) # (k3, alpha, alpha, alpha) Cbatch = Ctrans.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # (1, 1, k3, alpha, alpha, alpha) - wait, F.interpolate 3D is (N, C, D, H, W) # Actually, F.interpolate for 3D takes (N, C, D, H, W). # So Ctrans should be (k3, alpha, alpha, alpha). # Let's use gridsample or a simpler view. # For simplicity, assuming a standard library call for 3D trilinear upsample of the spatial grid # while keeping k and 3 dimensions intact. # Re-evaluating based on "simple trilinear interpolation for upsampling the field itself" # The field is C. We upsample the spatial grid. # We can view C as a volume of vectors. # Reshape to (alpha, alpha, alpha, k3) # Interpolate the first 3 dims. # Using F.interpolate on (N, C, D, H, W) # We treat k3 as the channel dimension C. # Shape: (1, k3, alpha, alpha, alpha) Cview = Cflat.permute(3, 0, 1, 2).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # (1, 1, k3, alpha, alpha, alpha) -> Wrong. # F.interpolate 3D: (N, C, D, H, W) # Cflat is (alpha, alpha, alpha, k3). # Permute to (k3, alpha, alpha, alpha). # Add N, C dims: (1, k3, alpha, alpha, alpha). Cinterp4d = F.interpolate( Cflat.permute(3, 0, 1, 2).unsqueeze(0), # (1, k3, alpha, alpha, alpha) size=(targetalpha, targetalpha, targetalpha), mode='trilinear', aligncorners=False) # Remove N, C dims -> (k3, target, target, target) Cinterpflat = Cinterp4d.squeeze(0).squeeze(0) # Reshape to (target, target, target, k, 3) Cinterpgrid = Cinterpflat.view(targetalpha, targetalpha, targetalpha, k, 3) # Flatten spatial dims to (target^3, k, 3) return Cinterpgrid.view(-1, k, 3) def renderdynamicvolume(C, templatesigma, timet, resolutionbeta): """ Render the volume at time t. C: (beta^3, k, 3) templatesigma: (beta^3,) or (beta, beta, beta) timet: float resolutionbeta: int """ # 1. Compute Warp W = computewarpfield(C, timet) # (beta^3, 3) # 2. Reshape W to grid coordinates # W is displacement. We need source coordinates. # Assuming templatesigma is defined on a grid. # We need to sample templatesigma at (gridcoords + W). # Create grid coordinates for resolutionbeta # This part depends on the specific differentiable grid sampling implementation # Typically involves creating a meshgrid and adding W. # Placeholder for the specific fn implementation from [34] # fn(W, sigma) = sigma(x + Wx, y + Wy, z + Wz) # For the purpose of this article, we assume fn handles the grid sampling. # The key is that W is computed from C and t. # Return the warped volume # In a real implementation, this would return the 3D tensor pass Parameters: Polynomial Order k: The degree of the polynomial. Typically k=5 is sufficient for deformable and periodic motion. Base Resolution \alpha: The initial resolution for coarse-to-fine optimization. Examples include 2^3, 4^3, 8^3, 16^3. Target Resolution \beta: The final spatial resolution of the scene. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Upsampling Accuracy: The parametric representation constrains the upsampling of the motion field itself to simple trilinear interpolation. This may limit accuracy compared to other interpolation methods, especially for high-frequency motion details. Resolution Scaling: Attempting to estimate the warp field directly at the full resolution \beta^3 without hierarchical initialization results in poor motion reconstruction. Memory Complexity: The memory usage is dominated by the Motion Coefficient Tensor C, which scales as O(\beta^3 \cdot k \cdot 3). This is significantly lower than storing explicit displacement fields for every time step. The method allows optimizing on low-resolution measurements (e.g., 80^3) and upsampling to high resolutions (e.g., 256^3) post-optimization, bypassing substantial GPU memory requirements. Time Complexity: The warp field computation is O(\beta^3 \cdot k) per time point. Rendering involves grid sampling, which is typically O(\beta^3). The hierarchical optimization adds overhead but improves convergence. Strengths: Arbitrary Temporal Resolution: The polynomial representation allows evaluation at any time t \in [0, 1], enabling arbitrary frame rate upsampling (e.g., from 10 to 90 frames). Memory Efficiency: Parametric representation reduces memory footprint compared to storing discrete time steps. Differentiability: The method is fully differentiable, allowing gradient-based optimization of the coefficients. Limitations: Interpolation Constraint: Trilinear interpolation for upsampling the field itself may not capture complex motion details as well as learned upsamplers. Polynomial Order: High-order polynomials may oscillate (Runge's phenomenon) if not regularized, though k=5 is found sufficient for typical dynamic scenes. When to Use: Suitable for dynamic CT reconstruction from sparse/limited views where temporal continuity is expected and memory is a constraint. When Not to Use: When motion is highly discontinuous or non-polynomial in nature, or when extremely high-fidelity temporal upsampling is required without the interpolation limitations. The Polynomial Motion Field was introduced in the context of dynamic CT reconstruction from limited views. It leverages implicit neural representations and parametric motion fields to warp a template volume to different time values. The method was proposed to address the challenges of reconstructing objects from limited views, which is traditionally more challenging than from sparse views. It assumes only that the scene is sparse view sampled, without requiring specialized sampling schemes or phase information. The hierarchical coarse-to-fine estimation strategy was introduced to overcome poor motion reconstruction at full resolution. The approach builds on differentiable grid sampling functions.
