name: Dynamic Scene Representation
body: Dynamic Scene Representation methods extend static radiance fields to model temporal variations, enabling novel view synthesis of non-static scenes. Unlike static methods, these approaches incorporate time or scene variables as inputs to the neural field or deformation operators to predict density and color for specific moments [12734-neural-rendering-of-variable-scenes.md][7274-dynerf.md]. They differ from sibling methods like Deformation Field Parametrization by explicitly handling the evolution of geometry and appearance over time, often through shared networks, explicit temporal interpolation, or deformation fields. All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward rendering operator and the propagation of gradients through the integration steps [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. The core mechanism is the evaluation of the volume rendering equation and the computation of gradients with respect to scene parameters (density, geometry, transfer functions, camera poses) [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. The standard emission-absorption model computes the color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} as [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \sigmai is the density, \deltai is the step size, \mathbf{c}i is the color, and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. Differentiation strategies fall into three main categories [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]: 1. Reverse-Mode Automatic Differentiation (AD): Standard backpropagation through the computational graph. This requires storing O(kn) intermediate states (where n is pixels and k is samples), leading to high memory usage [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. 2. Adjoint Method: Computes gradients by propagating adjoint variables backward through the rendering algorithm, evaluating the chain rule from output to input. This has computational complexity largely constant in the number of parameters, making it preferable for optimizing many parameters like the transfer function [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. 3. Analytic Inversion / Explicit Gradients: Uses a-priori knowledge of the DVR operations to invert the order of operations or derive closed-form gradients, reducing memory consumption to O(n) by avoiding the storage of intermediate results [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. DyNeRF represents volumetric videos using a single shared Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) that takes spatial coordinates and a temporal embedding as input to predict the radiance field for a specific video frame. It sets itself apart from Neural Rendering of Variable Scenes by using a monolithic shared network structure rather than decomposing the scene into static and dynamic components or using explicit voxel structures. While simple to implement, this single shared MLP structure tends to lose details in high-frequency regions of the image. This method explicitly incorporates scene variation into the training phase by encoding predefined ranges of dynamic scene elements into a structured vector representation. Unlike methods that constrain learning to a single static manifold, these approaches learn a surface radiance field capable of handling all possible permutations of the specified scene variables. This distinguishes them from sibling methods like DyNeRF, which typically model deformation or motion through explicit geometric transformations or temporal bases, whereas variable scene methods treat dynamic parameters as direct inputs to the neural field to capture higher-order interactions between moving objects and the static environment. Explicit 4D Gaussian Splatting (Ex4DGS) achieves memory efficiency and rendering speed by separating scene primitives into static and dynamic categories and explicitly interpolating their attributes over time. Unlike implicit deformation fields or continuous trajectory models, Ex4DGS stores sparse keyframe data for dynamic Gaussians and uses specific interpolators to reconstruct continuous motion, handling complex phenomena like self-occlusion and object disappearance without requiring auxiliary masks or supervision. It builds on Dynamic Scene Representation by introducing a fully explicit temporal domain where attributes are sampled at discrete timestamps and interpolated. GauFRe augments 3D Gaussian Splatting with a time-conditioned forward-warping deformation field to enable real-time novel view synthesis of dynamic scenes. Unlike NeRF-based methods that use backward warps to query canonical space, GauFRe stores Gaussians in a canonical space and uses a neural network to output deformed attributes (position, rotation, scale) for each time step t. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly separating the scene into static and deformable Gaussian sets, preventing capacity waste and noise in static regions, and by modeling non-rigid deformations (scaling) in addition to rigid motion. Light-weight 4D Gaussian Splatting (LGS) is a memory-efficient method for reconstructing and rendering dynamic scenes, specifically designed for surgical endoscopy. It addresses the high memory consumption and computational cost of standard 4D Gaussian Splatting by combining three compression techniques: Deformation-Aware Pruning (DAP), Gaussian-Attribute Pruning (GAP), and Feature Field Condensation (FFC). Unlike Explicit 4D Gaussian Splatting which stores full attributes, or Gaussian Deformation Field (GauFRe) which uses a deformation network, LGS achieves compression by pruning redundant Gaussians and condensing the feature field resolution, maintaining real-time rendering speeds with significantly smaller model sizes. A neural radiance field that takes transformed 3D location, view direction, and aggregated features as input to predict volume density and color. The concept of representing dynamic scenes using neural radiance fields emerged with the need to extend static NeRF capabilities to video and dynamic content. Early works like DyNeRF established the baseline of using temporal embeddings in shared MLPs. Subsequent research focused on efficiency and explicit modeling, leading to methods like Ex4DGS and GauFRe which leverage Gaussian Splatting for faster rendering and explicit temporal control. The field continues to evolve with compression techniques like LGS to handle resource-constrained environments. HumanNeRF: Efficiently Generated Human Radiance Field from Sparse Inputs, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.00759, fetched 2026-10-26

name: DyNeRF
body: DyNeRF is a baseline method for representing volumetric videos by employing a single NeRF-like Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) that takes spatial coordinates and a temporal embedding as input to predict the radiance field for a specific video frame. This single shared MLP structure tends to lose details in high-frequency regions of the image. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D spatial coordinate \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z) and a scalar time value t. Output: Volume density \sigma and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}. Data Structures: MLP: A standard feedforward neural network. The exact architecture (number of layers, hidden dimensions, activation functions) is not given in the sources. Standard NeRF implementations typically use 8 layers with 256 hidden units and ReLU activations, with positional encoding applied to \mathbf{x}. Steps: 1. Temporal Embedding: Convert the continuous time value t into a fixed-dimensional embedding vector \mathbf{e}t. This is typically done using sinusoidal positional encoding similar to the spatial coordinates, or a simple learned lookup table if the number of frames is small. 2. Concatenation: Concatenate the spatial coordinate \mathbf{x} (potentially positional encoded) and the temporal embedding \mathbf{e}t to form the input vector \mathbf{v} = [\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{e}t]. 3. MLP Evaluation: Pass \mathbf{v} and the ray direction \mathbf{d} through the shared MLP to predict the density \sigma and the view-dependent color \mathbf{c} for the ray passing through \mathbf{x} at time t. 4. Rendering: Use the standard volume rendering equation (as defined in [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]) to integrate \sigma and \mathbf{c} along the ray to produce the final pixel color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def dynerfforward(mlp, x, t, direction, timeembeddings): """ mlp: The shared neural network function f(x, t, d) -> (sigma, color) x: Spatial coordinates [N, 3] t: Time values [N] direction: View directions [N, 3] timeembeddings: Pre-computed embeddings for time t [N, Dt] """ # 1. Prepare inputs: concatenate spatial coordinates and time embedding inputvectors = np.concatenate([x, timeembeddings], axis=1) # 2. Evaluate MLP: predict density and color based on position, time, and direction sigma, color = mlp(inputvectors, direction) # 3. Return values for standard volume rendering integration return sigma, color Parameters: Time Embedding Dimension: Not given in the sources. Typically matches the positional encoding dimension of the spatial coordinates or is a small learned vector. MLP Architecture: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High-Frequency Detail Loss: The single shared MLP structure struggles to capture high-frequency details in dynamic scenes, leading to blurry or artifact-prone results in complex motion regions. Decomposed Spatiotemporal Representation is a method for modeling dynamic volumetric scenes by categorizing spatial regions into static, deforming, and new content, assigning each category a specialized neural field to optimize temporal consistency and computational efficiency. It sets itself apart from the parent DyNeRF method by replacing a single monolithic MLP with a mixture of specialized fields (stationary, deformation, and newness) weighted by a learned decomposition probability, rather than relying on a single temporal embedding. FDRF is a method that uses time-aware voxel features to represent scenes and simulates rough motion trajectories with a small coordinate deformation network. It enhances time information in the radiation network and significantly accelerates the optimization of dynamic radiation fields while maintaining high rendering quality. Complexity: The method relies on a single MLP, making the per-sample evaluation cost comparable to standard NeRF, but the need to model temporal dynamics within the same network can increase the required capacity and training time compared to static NeRF. Performance: Quantitative results on the T-REX dataset show DyNeRF achieves a PSNR of 30.87, SSIM of 0.943, and LPIPS of 0.118, with a rendering time of 5195 milliseconds and storage of 239 MB. This is inferior to the proposed "Dynamic MLP Maps" method (PSNR 32.20, SSIM 0.953, Rendering time 33 ms, Storage 239 MB) and comparable to or worse than D-NeRF (PSNR 31.32, SSIM 0.949) in some metrics, while being significantly slower than Neural Volumes (73 ms). Strengths: Simple implementation; baseline for comparison. Limitations: Loses details in high-frequency regions due to the single shared MLP structure. DyNeRF was introduced as a baseline method for representing volumetric videos using a NeRF-like MLP that takes spatial coordinates and temporal embeddings as input. It is cited in comparative studies against other dynamic NeRF variants such as Neural Volumes, C-NeRF, and D-NeRF. The code for DyNeRF was not released by its original authors, requiring re-implementation for comparison in subsequent works. name: Decomposed Spatiotemporal Representation
head: NeRFPlayer Decomposition
body: Decomposed Spatiotemporal Representation is a method for modeling dynamic volumetric scenes by categorizing spatial regions into static, deforming, and new content, assigning each category a specialized neural field to optimize temporal consistency and computational efficiency. It sets itself apart from the parent DyNeRF method by replacing a single monolithic MLP with a mixture of specialized fields (stationary, deformation, and newness) weighted by a learned decomposition probability, rather than relying on a single temporal embedding. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D spatial coordinate p \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a scalar time t \in \mathbb{R}. Output: A density \sigma \in \mathbb{R} and a view-dependent color c \in \mathbb{R}^3. Data Structures: 1. Decomposition Field (f): Maps (p, t) to a probability distribution over three categories. Implemented as an explicitly cached feature volume Vf and a small MLP decoder Df. Output: Probabilities P{static}, P{deform}, P{new} such that \sum P = 1. 2. Stationary Field (s): Maps p to a feature vector v{static}. Used for static geometry and low-frequency appearance. Implementation: Explicitly cached features Vs and a tiny MLP. 3. Deformation Field (d): Maps (p, t) to a displacement vector \Delta p. Implementation: A small MLP. 4. Newness Field (n): Maps (p, t) to a feature vector v{new}. Implementation: Explicitly cached features and a tiny MLP. 5. View-Conditioned Network (Decoder): Maps the aggregated feature vector v and view direction dv to density and color. Numbered Steps: 1. Query Decomposition: For a query point p at time t, compute the decomposition probabilities P{static}(p,t), P{deform}(p,t), and P{new}(p,t) using the decomposition field f(p,t). 2. Compute Expected Feature Vector: Retrieve v{static} from the stationary field s(p). Retrieve \Delta p from the deformation field d(p,t). Compute the deformed position p' = p + \Delta p. Query v{deform} from the stationary field s(p') in canonical space. Retrieve v{new} from the newness field n(p,t). Compute the aggregated feature vector: v = \sum{ \in \{static, deform, new\}} P v. 3. Thresholding (Optimization): If any probability P < \tau (default \tau = 0.001), set the corresponding feature vector v = \mathbf{0} and skip the field query to save computation. 4. Decode Radiance: Pass the aggregated feature vector v and the view direction dv to the lightweight view-conditioned network to predict density \sigma and color c. Formulas: Aggregation: v = \sum{ \in \{static, deform, new\}} P v. Regularization Loss: To encourage static background and penalize new content (assuming most points are static or deforming): L{reg} = \alpha P{deform} + P{new}. Here, P = \frac{1}{|Rp|} \sum{p \in Rp} P(p) is the average probability over the batch Rp, and \alpha weights the ratio of deforming to new. Total Loss: L = L{rec} + \lambda L{reg}. Here, L{rec} is the reconstruction loss and \lambda is a balancing hyper-parameter. Parameters: \tau: Threshold for skipping fields. Default: 0.001. \alpha: Weight for deformation probability in regularization. Value not given in the sources. \lambda: Weight for regularization loss. Value not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The sum of probabilities must be normalized to 1. If the decomposition field outputs unnormalized logits, a softmax is required. Deformation Query: The deformation field outputs \Delta p, which is added to p before querying the static field for the deforming component's feature, implying the deforming component's appearance is anchored to the canonical static geometry. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def zeros(n): return [0.0] n def decomposedspatiotemporalrender(p, t, viewdir, model): """ p: (3,) spatial coordinate t: scalar time viewdir: (3,) view direction model: object containing fields f, s, d, n, and decoder """ # 1. Decomposition probabilities probs = model.f(p, t) # Returns [Pstatic, Pdeform, Pnew] Pstatic, Pdeform, Pnew = probs # 2. Feature aggregation vstatic = model.s(p) # Deformation: query canonical space deltap = model.d(p, t) pdeformed = [p[i] + deltap[i] for i in range(3)] vdeform = model.s(pdeformed) # Newness vnew = model.n(p, t) # 3. Thresholding tau = 0.001 if Pstatic < tau: vstatic = zeros(len(vstatic)) if Pdeform < tau: vdeform = zeros(len(vdeform)) if Pnew < tau: vnew = zeros(len(vnew)) # 4. Weighted sum v = [Pstatic vstatic[i] + Pdeform vdeform[i] + Pnew vnew[i] for i in range(len(vstatic))] # 5. Decode sigma, color = model.decoder(v, viewdir) return sigma, color A technique that explicitly linearly interpolates opacity and premultiplied radiance terms based on learned blending weights, rather than aggregating feature vectors before decoding. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by avoiding separate volume rendering integrals or hard segmentation masks. Choose it when adaptive mixing of static and dynamic radiance is preferred over feature-space blending. A method that separates 'stuff' (background static objects) from 'things' (moving objects), representing stuff with a single radiance field MLP and each dynamic thing with its own radiance field inside a dynamic bounding box. It sets itself apart from the Decomposed Spatiotemporal Representation family by assigning individual MLPs to each dynamic instance within bounding boxes rather than using a unified decomposition field. Choose it when instance-level semantic segmentation and editing of moving objects are required. Time Complexity: Rendering time depends on the number of active fields. With thresholding, fields with low probability are skipped, reducing computation for static backgrounds. Memory Complexity: Uses explicit feature volumes for static and new fields, which can increase model size compared to pure MLPs. However, it allows for smaller MLPs for deformation and newness due to specialized representation. Strengths: Maintains temporal consistency by separating static, deforming, and new content. Saves computation by not modeling static areas with time-dependent fields. Handles rigid and non-rigid motion. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of regularization parameters (\alpha, \lambda). Assumes static background exists. New content must be modeled explicitly, which may be inefficient for highly dynamic scenes with no static parts. When to use: Dynamic scenes with significant static background and distinct deforming objects. When not to use: Scenes with no static elements or highly chaotic dynamics where decomposition is unstable. The method was introduced in as a streamable dynamic scene representation that decomposes the scene into static, deforming, and new areas to maintain temporal consistency and reduce computation. It builds on the DyNeRF baseline [7274-dynerf.md] by addressing its limitation of using a single MLP for all temporal variations, which can lead to temporal inconsistency and high computational cost for static regions. NeRFPlayer: A Streamable Dynamic Scene Representation with Decomposed Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2023.3247082, fetched 2026-10-26 Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Dynamic Field Blending
body: Dynamic Field Blending is a technique for modeling dynamic scenes by blending static and dynamic neural network predictions for opacity and radiance, evaluated via quadrature to compute the final RGB radiance. It addresses the problem of rendering time-varying scenes by decomposing the scene representation into static and dynamic components, allowing the renderer to adaptively mix these components based on a learned blending weight. It sets itself apart from sibling methods in the Decomposed Spatiotemporal Representation family by explicitly linearly interpolating the opacity and premultiplied radiance terms rather than using separate volume rendering integrals or hard segmentation masks. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera position \mathbf{x}, view direction \boldsymbol{\omega}0, time \tau, number of samples N, sample positions \mathbf{x}k, step size \Delta \mathbf{x}k, static network outputs (\sigma^{\text{stat}}, Ls^{\text{stat}}), dynamic network outputs (\sigma^{\text{dyn}}, Ls^{\text{dyn}}), and blending weights b(\mathbf{x}k, \tau). Output: Final RGB radiance I{\text{RGB}}(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}0, \tau). Data Structures: The method relies on the outputs of two neural networks (static and dynamic) and a blending weight field. Static Network Output: Volume density \sigma^{\text{stat}}(\mathbf{x}) and scattered radiance Ls^{\text{stat}}(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}0). Dynamic Network Output: Volume density \sigma^{\text{dyn}}(\mathbf{x}, \tau) and scattered radiance Ls^{\text{dyn}}(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}0, \tau). Blending Weight Field: b(\mathbf{x}, \tau), a scalar value indicating the contribution of the dynamic component. Numbered Steps: 1. For each sample point \mathbf{x}k along the ray (where \mathbf{x}k = \mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\omega}0 k for k=0 \dots N): a. Query the static network for \sigma^{\text{stat}}(\mathbf{x}k) and Ls^{\text{stat}}(\mathbf{x}k, \boldsymbol{\omega}0). b. Query the dynamic network for \sigma^{\text{dyn}}(\mathbf{x}k, \tau) and Ls^{\text{dyn}}(\mathbf{x}k, \boldsymbol{\omega}0, \tau). c. Query the blending weight field for b(\mathbf{x}k, \tau). d. Compute static opacity \alpha^{\text{stat}}(\mathbf{x}k) using Equation (13). e. Compute dynamic opacity \alpha^{\text{dyn}}(\mathbf{x}k, \tau) using Equation (14). f. Compute blended opacity \alpha^{\text{blend}}(\mathbf{x}k, \tau) using Equation (15). g. Compute blended premultiplied radiance \alpha^{\text{blend}}(\mathbf{x}k, \tau) Ls^{\text{blend}}(\mathbf{x}k, \boldsymbol{\omega}0, \tau) using Equations (16) and (17). 2. Compute blended transmittance \hat{T}^{\text{blend}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}k, \tau) for each sample using Equation (12). 3. Sum the contributions of all samples to compute the final radiance using Equation (11). Formulas: Blended Transmittance: \hat{T}^{\text{blend}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}k, \tau) = \prod{j=0}^{k-1} \left(1 - \alpha^{\text{blend}}(\mathbf{x}j, \tau)\right) \quad (12) where \hat{T}^{\text{blend}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}0, \tau) = 1. Static Opacity: \alpha^{\text{stat}}(\mathbf{x}k) = 1 - \exp(-\sigma^{\text{stat}}(\mathbf{x}k) \Delta \mathbf{x}k) \quad (13) Dynamic Opacity: \alpha^{\text{dyn}}(\mathbf{x}k, \tau) = 1 - \exp(-\sigma^{\text{dyn}}(\mathbf{x}k, \tau) \Delta \mathbf{x}k) \quad (14) Blended Opacity: \alpha^{\text{blend}}(\mathbf{x}k, \tau) = (1 - b(\mathbf{x}k, \tau)) \cdot \alpha^{\text{stat}}(\mathbf{x}k) + b(\mathbf{x}k, \tau) \cdot \alpha^{\text{dyn}}(\mathbf{x}k, \tau) \quad (15) Blended Premultiplied Radiance: \alpha^{\text{blend}}(\mathbf{x}k, \tau) Ls^{\text{blend}}(\mathbf{x}k, \boldsymbol{\omega}0, \tau) = (1 - b(\mathbf{x}k, \tau)) \cdot \alpha^{\text{stat}}(\mathbf{x}k, \tau) Ls^{\text{stat}}(\mathbf{x}k, \boldsymbol{\omega}0) + b(\mathbf{x}k, \tau) \cdot \alpha^{\text{dyn}}(\mathbf{x}k, \tau) Ls^{\text{dyn}}(\mathbf{x}k, \boldsymbol{\omega}0, \tau) \quad (16, 17) The source explicitly writes \alpha^{\text{stat}}(\mathbf{x}k, \tau) in Equation (16) despite defining \alpha^{\text{stat}} without time dependence in Equation (13). Final Radiance: I{\text{RGB}}(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}0, \tau) = \sum{k=0}^N \hat{T}^{\text{blend}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}k, \tau) \alpha^{\text{blend}}(\mathbf{x}k, \tau) Ls^{\text{blend}}(\mathbf{x}k, \boldsymbol{\omega}0, \tau) \quad (11) Parameters: b(\mathbf{x}k, \tau): The blending weight at position \mathbf{x}k and time \tau, used to linearly interpolate between static and dynamic opacity and radiance terms. N: Number of samples along the ray. Not given in the sources. \Delta \mathbf{x}k: Step size between samples. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The product in the transmittance calculation (Eq 12) can underflow to zero if the scene is dense, leading to numerical instability. Standard volume rendering techniques (e.g., using log-space accumulation) should be applied. Blending Weight Boundaries: If b(\mathbf{x}k, \tau) is not constrained to [0, 1], the blending may produce invalid opacity values (e.g., >1 or <0). The blending weight network should use a sigmoid activation or similar constraint. Temporal Consistency: The blending weight b(\mathbf{x}k, \tau) must vary smoothly with time to avoid flickering artifacts. This is typically enforced via temporal regularization during training. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dynamicfieldblending(rayorigin, raydirection, time, numsamples, stepsize, staticnet, dynamicnet, blendingnet): """ Renders a single ray using Dynamic Field Blending. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, camera position x. raydirection: 3D vector, view direction omega0. time: float, time tau. numsamples: int, N. stepsize: float, Delta xk. staticnet: Function returning (sigmastat, Lstat) for a given position. dynamicnet: Function returning (sigmadyn, Ldyn) for a given position and time. blendingnet: Function returning blending weight b for a given position and time. Returns: RGB radiance value. """ totalradiance = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 for k in range(numsamples + 1): # Sample position as defined in the source xk = rayorigin - raydirection k # Query networks sigmastat, Lstat = staticnet(xk) sigmadyn, Ldyn = dynamicnet(xk, time) b = blendingnet(xk, time) # Compute opacities alphastat = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigmastat stepsize) alphadyn = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigmadyn stepsize) # Compute blended opacity alphablend = (1.0 - b) alphastat + b alphadyn # Compute blended premultiplied radiance # Source explicitly writes alphastat(xk, tau) in Eq 16 premultipliedradiance = ((1.0 - b) alphastat Lstat + b alphadyn Ldyn) # Accumulate radiance totalradiance += transmittance premultipliedradiance # Update transmittance for next sample transmittance = (1.0 - alphablend) return totalradiance Separates the scene into static and dynamic components. It is chosen when the scene contains both static background and dynamic foreground elements. Determines the contribution of static versus dynamic components via a learned scalar field. It is chosen when smooth transitions between static and dynamic regions are required. Time Complexity: O(N) per ray, where N is the number of samples. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the static, dynamic, and blending networks. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of samples and the complexity of the neural networks. Strengths: Allows for smooth blending between static and dynamic components, avoiding hard edges. Limitations: Requires training three networks (static, dynamic, blending) and learning the blending weight. When to Use: When rendering dynamic scenes with significant static background. When Not to Use: When the scene is entirely static or entirely dynamic. Dynamic Field Blending was introduced in the TöRF (Time-of--Flight Radiance Fields) paper. It is part of the DyNeRF family of methods for dynamic scene view synthesis. The method builds on the idea of decomposing the scene into static and dynamic components and blending their contributions. TöRF: Time-of-Flight Radiance Fields for Dynamic Scene View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2109.15271, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Neural Rendering of Variable Scenes
head: Variable Scene Methods
body: Neural rendering of variable scenes is a method that explicitly incorporates scene variation into the training phase by encoding predefined ranges of dynamic scene elements into a structured vector representation. Unlike methods that constrain learning to a single static manifold, these approaches learn a surface radiance field capable of handling all possible permutations of the specified scene variables. This distinguishes them from sibling methods like DyNeRF, which typically model deformation or motion through explicit geometric transformations or temporal bases, whereas variable scene methods treat dynamic parameters as direct inputs to the neural field to capture higher-order interactions between moving objects and the static environment. The method operates by mapping a set of dynamic scene parameters to radiance values, allowing the neural network to generalize across different configurations of the scene without retraining for every specific instance. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A ray \mathbf{r} (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}) and a vector of scene variables \mathbf{v} representing the current state of dynamic elements (e.g., object positions, light angles). Outputs: The estimated color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and optionally density \sigma for volume rendering or surface shading. Data Structures Scene Variable Vector (\mathbf{v}): A structured representation encoding the predefined range of each variable scene element. The dimensionality of \mathbf{v} corresponds to the number of dynamic parameters being modeled. Neural Radiance Field Model: A neural network (e.g., MLP or hash-based encoding) that takes the ray coordinates and the encoded scene variables as input. Steps 1. Encode Scene Variables: The dynamic scene parameters are encoded into a vector \mathbf{v}. This can be done directly or processed through a learned encoding scheme. 2. Construct Input Tensor: Combine the ray sampling position (or surface point) with the encoded scene variables \mathbf{v} to form the input to the neural network. 3. Evaluate Radiance Field: The neural network predicts the outgoing radiance (and density, if applicable) for the given ray and scene configuration. 4. Render: Compute the final pixel color using the standard volume rendering equation or surface shading model, integrating the predicted radiance along the ray. Formulas The core prediction is a function f parameterized by weights \theta: (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) = f\theta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}) where \mathbf{x} is the spatial coordinate along the ray, and \mathbf{v} is the scene variable vector. The final color is computed via the volume rendering equation defined in the parent article [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. Parameters Number of Variables: Typically limited to 1-2 variables to maintain performance and avoid visible reconstruction error at fixed representational capacity. Encoding Method: Frequency encoding is often used for parameter changes to add little inference overhead. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Retraining Requirement: The model requires retraining if the set of scene parameters changes (e.g., objects are added, removed, or modified). Performance Scaling: Inference time scales with the number of dynamic objects, limiting the use of primitives with many variables like animated meshes. Capacity Limits: Scaling to more than two scene variables at the same representational capacity causes visible reconstruction error. Extends a pre-computed neural irradiance volume by adding inputs for known runtime-changing scene parameters (e.g., emitter positions) to avoid real-time representation updates and temporal artifacts. It trains the irradiance field while randomly sampling the variable scene parameter during the training phase. This approach is suitable for simulating phenomena like time-of-day cycles with rotating directional lights or moving occluders. To ensure artifact-free results, the hash table size encoding scene position may need to be doubled (e.g., to ~10MB). However, scaling to more than two scene variables at the same capacity causes visible error, which might be resolved with learned encodings but introduces other disadvantages. Time Complexity: Inference times exceed 100 ms in reported experiments, failing to achieve real-time performance. The inference time scales with the number of dynamic objects present in the scene. Memory Complexity: Not explicitly given, but hash table sizes may need to be increased (e.g., ~10MB) to handle variable parameters artifact-free. Strengths: Can produce shading effects resembling path-traced global illumination, including higher-order interactions between variable parameters and the scene, potentially dropping below the theoretical lower bound of irradiance volumes as capacity grows. Limitations: Requires retraining for changes in the set of scene parameters; poor real-time performance; scaling issues with many dynamic objects. Comparison: For a fixed model size, Neural Irradiance Volumes (NIV) often achieve comparable or lower rendering error than variable-scene methods as the number of scene variables increases, because variable-scene methods must devote capacity to learning interactions on top of outgoing radiance. This method is discussed in the context of comparing different approaches to dynamic scene rendering, specifically contrasting with Neural Irradiance Volumes (NIV). The work highlights the trade-offs between explicit variable encoding and implicit generalization via irradiance volumes. Real-time Rendering with a Neural Irradiance Volume, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2602.12949, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Explicit 4D Gaussian Splatting
head: Dynamic 3DGS with Keyframe Interpolation, Fully Explicit Dynamic Gaussian Splatting
body: Explicit 4D Gaussian Splatting (Ex4DGS) is a method for dynamic novel view synthesis that achieves memory efficiency and rendering speed by separating scene primitives into static and dynamic categories and explicitly interpolating their attributes over time. Unlike implicit deformation fields or continuous trajectory models, Ex4DGS stores sparse keyframe data for dynamic Gaussians and uses specific interpolators to reconstruct continuous motion, handling complex phenomena like self-occlusion and object disappearance without requiring auxiliary masks or supervision. It builds on Dynamic Scene Representation by introducing a fully explicit temporal domain where attributes are sampled at discrete timestamps and interpolated. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of input images (video frames) and initial 3D points (e.g., from COLMAP on the first frame). Output: A set of learnable Gaussian primitives defined over time t \in [0, T], capable of rendering novel views at any timestamp within the interval. Data Structures: The scene consists of N Gaussians. Each Gaussian i is classified as either Static (Gs) or Dynamic (Gd). 1. Static Gaussian (Gs): Fields: Pivot position x \in \mathbb{R}^3, translation vector d \in \mathbb{R}^3, scale S, rotation R (constant), density \sigma, color c (view-dependent via spherical harmonics). Layout: x and d define the linear motion. S, R, \sigma, c are constant over time. 2. Dynamic Gaussian (Gd): Fields: A sequence of keyframes K = \{t | t = nI, n \in \mathbb{Z}, t \in T\}, where I is the time interval. Keyframe Data: For each keyframe n, store position pn \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation rn (quaternion), and opacity parameters. Opacity Parameters: Two Gaussians g{so}, g{fo} with means a{so}, a{of} and variances b{so}, b{fo}. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize all N Gaussian points as Static (Gs), assuming linear motion. The initial position is the 3D point from the first frame. The translation vector d is initialized based on the initial estimate of motion. 2. Static Motion Model: For a static Gaussian, the position \mu(t) at time t is calculated using normalized time t' = t/l, where l is the scene duration: \mu(t) = x + t' d, \quad t' = \frac{t}{l} \in [0, 1] where x is the pivot position and d is the translation vector. 3. Dynamic Classification (Motion-Based Trigger): During training, measure the motion of each static Gaussian. Calculate the normalized translation magnitude: \frac{\|d\|}{\|\lambda\|^2}, where \lambda is the distance between the point and the camera at the last timestamp. Sort all Gaussians by this metric. Convert the top-\eta percent of points (empirically \eta = 2) into Dynamic Gaussians (Gd). Initialization of Converted Gd: Estimate position pn at each keyframe using x and d. Set rotation rn to the same value for all keyframes. Initialize opacity to be visible in all keyframes. 4. Progressive Training: Start training with a short initial duration (e.g., 10 frames). Increment the duration by the interval I every specific step (e.g., every 400 iterations). When the number of keyframes increases, estimate the position and rotation of the Gaussian by linear regression using the last \rho frames to share motion information with the next keyframe. 5. Temporal Interpolation (Rendering): Position: Use Cubic Hermite Interpolation (CHip) for position. Compute tangents mn, m{n+1} from neighbor keyframe positions: mn = \frac{p{n+1} - p{n-1}}{2I}, \quad m{n+1} = \frac{p{n+2} - pn}{2I} For t in interval [nI, (n+1)I], let t' = \frac{t - nI}{I} and n = \lfloor t/I \rfloor. Then: \mu(t) = CHip(pn, mn, p{n+1}, m{n+1}; t') where CHip(p0, m0, p1, m1; t) = (2t^3 - 3t^2 + 1)p0 + (t^3 - 2t^2 + t)m0 + (-2t^3 + 3t^2)p1 + (t^3 - t^2)m1. Rotation: Use Spherical Linear Interpolation (Slerp) for rotation quaternions rn, r{n+1}: q(t) = Slerp(rn, r{n+1}; t') where Slerp(x0, x1; t) = \frac{\sin[(t)\Omega]}{\sin \Omega}x0 + \frac{\sin[(1 - t)\Omega]}{\sin \Omega}x1 and \cos \Omega = x0 \cdot x1. Opacity: Use a simplified Gaussian mixture model. Temporal opacity \sigmat(t) is: \sigmat(t) = \begin{cases} e^{-\frac{(t-a{so})^2}{b{so}}} & t < a{so} \\ 1 & a{so} \le t \le a{of} \\ e^{-\frac{(t-a{of})^2}{b{fo}}} & t > a{of} \end{cases} where a{so}, a{of} are means and b{so}, b{fo} are variances of the two Gaussians. 6. Rendering: Compute the 3D covariance \Sigma from scale S and rotation R: \Sigma = R S S^\top R^\top. Project to 2D: \Sigma' = J W \Sigma W^\top J^\top, where J is the Jacobian of the affine approximation of perspective projection and W is the viewing transformation. Render color C via alpha blending: C = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai })ci, \quad Ti = e^{-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj} where \deltai is the interval along the ray, and i,j are depth-ordered visible Gaussians. 7. Optimization and Pruning: Losses: Use L1 loss and SSIM loss between rendered and ground truth images. Regularization: Minimize \|d\| for static points and \|p{n+1} - pn\| for dynamic points (parameter 0.0001). Point Backtracking: Calculate error E for pixel k: E = \frac{\sum{i} \sigmai \times \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \sigmaj) \times qk}{\sum{i} \sigmai \times \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \sigmaj)} where qk is the measured error (L1/SSIM) at pixel k, and i,j are depth-ordered visible Gaussians. Calculate accumulated error E{total} = \sum{v \in D} \frac{Ev}{|D|} over training views D. Prune points with error > E{total} at pre-defined steps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.spatial.transform import Rotation def cubichermite(p0, m0, p1, m1, t): """ Cubic Hermite Interpolation for position. p0, p1: positions (np.array, shape (3,)) m0, m1: tangents (np.array, shape (3,)) t: normalized time in [0, 1] """ t2 = t t t3 = t2 t h00 = 2 t3 - 3 t2 + 1 h10 = t3 - 2 t2 + t h01 = -2 t3 + 3 t2 h11 = t3 - t2 return h00 p0 + h10 m0 + h01 p1 + h11 m1 def slerp(q0, q1, t): """ Spherical Linear Interpolation for quaternions. q0, q1: quaternions (np.array, shape (4,)) t: normalized time in [0, 1] """ # Normalize quaternions q0 = q0 / np.linalg.norm(q0) q1 = q1 / np.linalg.norm(q1) dot = np.dot(q0, q1) # If dot product is negative, slerp won't take the shorter path, # so negate one quaternion. if dot < 0: q1 = -q1 dot = -dot # Clamp dot = np.clip(dot, -1.0, 1.0) omega = np.arccos(dot) sinomega = np.sin(omega) if sinomega < 1e-6: return q0 # Linear interpolation if close ratio0 = np.sin((1 - t) omega) / sinomega ratio1 = np.sin(t omega) / sinomega return ratio0 q0 + ratio1 q1 def gettemporalopacity(t, aso, aof, bso, bfo): """ Simplified Gaussian mixture model for opacity. """ if t < aso: return np.exp(-((t - aso)2) / bso) elif t > aof: return np.exp(-((t - aof)2) / bfo) else: return 1.0 def rendergaussian(gaussian, cameraparams, timet, intervalI, durationl): """ Renders a single Gaussian at time t. gaussian: dict with type ('static' or 'dynamic'), attributes cameraparams: dict with projection matrix, view matrix, etc. timet: current timestamp intervalI: keyframe interval durationl: scene duration """ if gaussian['type'] == 'static': # Static motion model tprime = timet / durationl mu = gaussian['pivot'] + tprime gaussian['translation'] R = gaussian['rotation'] # Constant S = gaussian['scale'] sigma = gaussian['density'] c = gaussian['color'] elif gaussian['type'] == 'dynamic': # Dynamic interpolation n = int(timet // intervalI) tprime = (timet - n intervalI) / intervalI # Position via CHip pn = gaussian['keyframes'][n]['pos'] pn1 = gaussian['keyframes'][n+1]['pos'] # Tangents from neighbors pn1prev = gaussian['keyframes'][n-1]['pos'] if n > 0 else pn pn2 = gaussian['keyframes'][n+2]['pos'] if n+2 < len(gaussian['keyframes']) else pn1 mn = (pn1 - pn1prev) / (2 intervalI) mn1 = (pn2 - pn) / (2 intervalI) mu = cubichermite(pn, mn, pn1, mn1, tprime) # Rotation via Slerp rn = gaussian['keyframes'][n]['rot'] rn1 = gaussian['keyframes'][n+1]['rot'] q = slerp(rn, rn1, tprime) R = Rotation.fromquat(q).asmatrix() S = gaussian['scale'] # Assuming scale is constant or interpolated similarly if needed # Opacity sigma = gettemporalopacity( timet, gaussian['opacityparams']['aso'], gaussian['opacityparams']['aof'], gaussian['opacityparams']['bso'], gaussian['opacityparams']['bfo']) c = gaussian['color'] # Project to 2D # Sigma = R S S^T R^T Smat = np.diag(S) Sigma = R @ Smat @ Smat.T @ R.T # Camera projection (simplified) # J is Jacobian of affine approximation, W is viewing transform # In practice, this involves camera extrinsics/intrinsics # Sigmaprime = J @ W @ Sigma @ W.T @ J.T # For implementation, use standard 3DGS projection routine Sigmaprime = projectto2d(Sigma, cameraparams) return { 'mu2d': projectmean(mu, cameraparams), 'Sigmaprime': Sigmaprime, 'sigma': sigma, 'color': c } def trainex4dgs(frames, initialpoints): """ Main training loop. """ # 1. Initialize all as static gaussians = [] for p in initialpoints: gaussians.append({ 'type': 'static', 'pivot': p.pos, 'translation': np.zeros(3), # Initial estimate 'rotation': np.eye(3), 'scale': np.ones(3), 'density': 1.0, 'color': p.color }) durationl = 10 # Initial duration intervalI = 10 iteration = 0 while iteration < maxiterations: # 2. Progressive Training: Extend duration if iteration % 400 == 0 and iteration > 0: durationl += intervalI # Re-estimate positions/rotations for new keyframes using linear regression # on last rho frames (implementation detail omitted for brevity) # 3. Classification: Convert top 2% dynamic if iteration % 1000 == 0: # Check periodically motions = [] for g in gaussians: if g['type'] == 'static': # Measure motion in image space # lambda is distance to camera at last timestamp lambdadist = getcameradistance(g['pivot'], lastcameraparams) motionmetric = np.linalg.norm(g['translation']) / (lambdadist2) motions.append((motionmetric, g)) motions.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True) numdynamic = int(len(motions) 0.02) for i in range(numdynamic): g = motions[i][1] # Convert to dynamic g['type'] = 'dynamic' # Initialize keyframes # Estimate pos at each keyframe using x and d # Set rotation same in all keyframes # Initialize opacity visible g['keyframes'] = createkeyframes(g['pivot'], g['translation'], durationl, intervalI) g['opacityparams'] = {'aso': 0, 'aof': durationl, 'bso': 1, 'bfo': 1} # 4. Render and Loss loss = 0 for frame in frames: rendered = renderscene(gaussians, frame.cameraparams, frame.time) gt = frame.image loss += l1loss(rendered, gt) + ssimloss(rendered, gt) # 5. Backprop and Update loss.backward() optimizer.step() # 6. Pruning if iteration % prunestep == 0: prunegaussians(gaussians, threshold=Etotal) iteration += 1 Parameters: Time Interval (I): 10 frames. Initial Duration: 10 frames. Duration Increment Step: Every 400 iterations. Dynamic Point Conversion Threshold (\eta): 2 percent. Regularization Parameters: 0.0001 for both static (\|d\|) and dynamic (\|p{n+1} - pn\|). Optimizer: RAdam. Pitfalls: Disappearing/Reappearing Objects: Self-occlusion can cause objects to disappear and reappear. Previous methods require multiple Gaussians for this, increasing memory. Ex4DGS handles this via the simplified Gaussian mixture model for opacity and point-backtracking to prune redundant points. Rotation Bias: Linear interpolation of rotation angles causes bias. Slerp is required. Overfitting/Over-smoothing: Linear interpolation for position may not capture complex movements. CHip is used to avoid this without additional storage. Time Complexity: Rendering speed is comparable to static 3DGS because interpolation is computed per Gaussian during rasterization, but the number of Gaussians is reduced by separating static/dynamic and pruning. Measured at 62 fps on a single NVIDIA 2080Ti GPU for 300-frame scenes with 1352×1014 resolution. Memory Complexity: Memory efficient. Static Gaussians store only linear motion parameters (x, d). Dynamic Gaussians store sparse keyframes. No auxiliary encoding modules are needed. Strengths: Handles sparse initial point clouds well via progressive training. No need for auxiliary masks or supervision for static/dynamic separation. Handles complex motions and occlusions effectively. Limitations: Requires uniform keyframe intervals for simplicity. Performance depends on the accuracy of the initial point cloud (COLMAP). Explicit 4D Gaussian Splatting (Ex4DGS) was introduced to address the limitations of existing dynamic novel view synthesis methods, which often suffer from slow rendering speeds due to reliance on neural networks or high memory costs due to continuous trajectory models. The method builds on the static 3D Gaussian Splatting framework [13] and extends it with explicit temporal interpolation. It was validated on the Neural 3D Video dataset and the Technicolor dataset. Fully Explicit Dynamic Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.52202/079017-0174, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Gaussian Deformation Field (GauFRe)
head: Dynamic Gaussian Splatting with static component, Forward-warping deformation field
body: GauFRe is a dynamic scene representation that augments 3D Gaussian Splatting with a time-conditioned forward-warping deformation field to enable real-time novel view synthesis of dynamic scenes. Unlike NeRF-based methods that use backward warps to query canonical space, GauFRe stores Gaussians in a canonical space and uses a neural network to output deformed attributes (position, rotation, scale) for each time step t. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly separating the scene into static and deformable Gaussian sets, preventing capacity waste and noise in static regions, and by modeling non-rigid deformations (scaling) in addition to rigid motion. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N canonical 3D Gaussians \{Gi\}, each defined by position xi, rotation qi, scale si, opacity \sigmai, and color ci. A query time t. Camera parameters (view and projection matrices). Output: A rendered 2D image at time t. Data Structures: 1. Deformable Gaussians \{Gi\}: Stored in canonical space. Parameters: xi \in \mathbb{R}^3, qi \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion), si \in \mathbb{R}^3 (log-scale), \sigmai \in \mathbb{R}, ci \in \mathbb{R}^3. 2. Static Gaussians \{Gj\}: Stored in world space. Parameters: xj \in \mathbb{R}^3, qj \in \mathbb{R}^4, sj \in \mathbb{R}^3, \sigmaj \in \mathbb{R}, cj \in \mathbb{R}^3. These are not deformed. 3. Deformation Field Network \Phi: An MLP with 6 hidden layers and 256 width. Inputs are positional encodings of xi and t. Outputs \delta x{ti}, \delta q{ti}, \delta s{ti}. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize static Gaussians \{Gj\} using a Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point cloud. Initialize deformable Gaussians \{Gi\} with uniform random samples within the scene bounding box. Initialize \Phi with random weights. 2. Positional Encoding: Compute positional encoding \gamma(x) for position x and \gamma(t) for time t using base L=10: \gamma(v) = (\sin(2^0 v), \cos(2^0 v), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} v), \cos(2^{L-1} v)) Concatenate \gamma(xi) and \gamma(t) to form the input vector for \Phi. 3. Deformation Field Evaluation: Pass the encoded input through \Phi to obtain deltas: (\delta x{ti}, \delta q{ti}, \delta s{ti}) = \Phi(\gamma(xi), \gamma(t)) Note: \Phi maps \mathbb{R}^{2Lx + 2Lt} \to \mathbb{R}^{10} (3 for pos, 4 for rot, 3 for scale). 4. Attribute Update (Forward Warp): Update position: x{ti} = xi + \delta x{ti} \quad (4) Update scale (pre-exponentiation): \text{Exp}(s{ti}) = \text{Exp}(si + \delta s{ti}) \quad (5) Pre-exponentiation is used because it is a log-linear estimation problem, simpler than exponential, and allows handling negative changes. Update rotation (quaternion multiplication): q{ti} = qi \cdot \delta q{ti} \quad (6) Quaternion multiplication is used instead of addition to maintain geometric bounds. The resulting quaternion must be normalized. Opacity \sigmai and color ci are not deformed; they remain constant in canonical space. 5. Concatenation: Combine deformed Gaussians \{G{ti}\} and static Gaussians \{Gj\} into a single set for rendering. 6. Rendering: Project the 3D covariance \Sigma{ti} (derived from q{ti}, s{ti}) to 2D using the standard Jacobian J [Parent]. Rasterize using standard back-to-front alpha blending [Parent]. 7. Optimization: Compute loss \mathcal{L}(I, I{gt}) between rendered image I and ground truth I{gt}. For iterations itr \le 20,000, use L2 loss. For itr > 20,000, switch to L1 loss. Loss function: \mathcal{L}(I, I{gt}) = \begin{cases} (1 - \lambda{ssim})\mathcal{L}2(I, I{gt}) + \lambda{ssim}(1 - \text{SSIM}(I, I{gt})) & \text{if } itr \le 20,000 \\ (1 - \lambda{ssim})\mathcal{L}1(I, I{gt}) + \lambda{ssim}(1 - \text{SSIM}(I, I{gt})) & \text{if } itr > 20,000 \end{cases} Optimize Gaussians and \Phi using Adam (\beta=(0.9, 0.999), \epsilon=10^{-15}). Densify and prune both static and deformable sets separately until 20,000 iterations. Continue optimizing until 40,000 iterations. Deformation Field Learning Rate: 0.001, with exponential scheduling shrinking to 0.001 \times original rate until 30,000 iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class PositionalEncoding(nn.Module): def init(self, base=10): super().init() self.base = base def forward(self, x): # x shape: (..., 1) # Output shape: (..., 2 base) freqbands = 2.0 torch.arange(self.base, device=x.device).float() # sin(2^0 x), cos(2^0 x),... out = torch.cat([ torch.sin(x freqbands), torch.cos(x freqbands) ], dim=-1) return out class DeformationField(nn.Module): def init(self, posbase=10, timebase=10, hiddendim=256, numlayers=6): super().init() self.posenc = PositionalEncoding(posbase) self.timeenc = PositionalEncoding(timebase) inputdim = 2 posbase + 2 timebase # 20 + 20 = 40 self.mlp = nn.Sequential() layers = [] for i in range(numlayers): indim = inputdim if i == 0 else hiddendim outdim = hiddendim layers.append(nn.Linear(indim, outdim)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddendim, 10)) # 3 pos, 4 rot, 3 scale self.mlp = nn.Sequential(layers) def forward(self, x, t): # x: (N, 3), t: (N,) or (N, 1) # Encode position and time xenc = self.posenc(x) # (N, 20) tenc = self.timeenc(t.unsqueeze(-1)) # (N, 20) inputvec = torch.cat([xenc, tenc], dim=-1) # (N, 40) deltas = self.mlp(inputvec) # (N, 10) deltax = deltas[:,:3] deltaq = deltas[:, 3:7] deltas = deltas[:, 7:10] return deltax, deltaq, deltas def normalizequaternion(q): return F.normalize(q, p=2, dim=-1) def updategaussians(xi, qi, si, deltax, deltaq, deltas): # Position update xt = xi + deltax # Scale update (pre-exponentiation) # si is log-scale. deltas is added in log-space. st = si + deltas # Rotation update (quaternion multiplication) # qi and deltaq are unit quaternions qt = quaternionmultiply(qi, deltaq) qt = normalizequaternion(qt) return xt, qt, st def quaternionmultiply(q1, q2): # q = [w, x, y, z] w1, x1, y1, z1 = q1[..., 0], q1[..., 1], q1[..., 2], q1[..., 3] w2, x2, y2, z2 = q2[..., 0], q2[..., 1], q2[..., 2], q2[..., 3] w = w1w2 - x1x2 - y1y2 - z1z2 x = w1x2 + x1w2 + y1z2 - z1y2 y = w1y2 - x1z2 + y1w2 + z1x2 z = w1z2 + x1y2 - y1x2 + z1w2 return torch.stack([w, x, y, z], dim=-1) def rendergaussians(gaussians, cameraparams): # Standard 3DGS rasterization # 1. Project 3D covariance to 2D # 2. Rasterize and alpha composite pass def trainstep(gaussians, staticgaussians, cameraparams, gtimage, time, itr, optimizer, phi): # 1. Get deformable Gaussians deltax, deltaq, deltas = phi(gaussians.x, time) xt, qt, st = updategaussians(gaussians.x, gaussians.q, gaussians.s, deltax, deltaq, deltas) # 2. Create deformed set deformedgaussians = Gaussians(x=xt, q=qt, s=st, sigma=gaussians.sigma, color=gaussians.color) # 3. Concatenate with static allgaussians = concatenate(deformedgaussians, staticgaussians) # 4. Render renderedimage = rendergaussians(allgaussians, cameraparams) # 5. Compute Loss if itr <= 20000: l1loss = F.mseloss(renderedimage, gtimage) ssimloss = 1 - ssim(renderedimage, gtimage) loss = (1 - lambdassim) l1loss + lambdassim ssimloss else: l1loss = F.l1loss(renderedimage, gtimage) ssimloss = 1 - ssim(renderedimage, gtimage) loss = (1 - lambdassim) l1loss + lambdassim ssimloss # 6. Backprop optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return loss Parameters: Positional Encoding Base for Position (Lx): 10. Positional Encoding Base for Time (Lt): 10. Network Architecture: MLP, 6 hidden layers, 256 width. Optimizer: Adam, \beta=(0.9, 0.999), \epsilon=10^{-15}. Deformation Field Learning Rate: 0.001, exponential decay to 0.001 \times original until 30,000 iterations. Densification/Pruning: Until 20,000 iterations. Total Optimization: Until 40,000 iterations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Quaternion Addition: Using addition for rotation deformation causes artifacts at novel viewpoints and timesteps because the result is not geometrically bound. Normalization after deformation is required. Deforming Opacity/Color: Deforming \sigmai and ci causes severe overfitting on training sets and artifacts in novel views. These are optimized in canonical space only. Initialization Conflict: Initializing both static and deformable sets with SfM or both with random samples causes them to "fight" over scene occupancy, leading to worse reconstruction. Static must be SfM, deformable must be random. Time Complexity: Training takes 10–20 minutes on D-NeRF and NeRF-DS datasets. This is significantly faster than MLP-based NeRF representations. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: D-NeRF: 34.5 PSNR, 0.01s rendering time (100 FPS) on NVIDIA 3090. NeRF-DS: 23.9 PSNR, 0.01s rendering time. HyperNeRF: 24.1 PSNR, 0.06s rendering time. Strengths: Real-time rendering speeds, fast training, handles non-rigid deformations (scaling), separates static/dynamic regions for efficiency. Limitations: Requires careful initialization to avoid conflicts between static and deformable sets. Deforming opacity/color is detrimental. When to use: Dynamic scenes with significant static regions, requiring real-time rendering and fast training. When not to use: Scenes where opacity/color change significantly over time (GauFRe does not model this). GauFRe was introduced in the paper "GauFRe: Gaussian Deformation Fields for Real-Time Dynamic Novel View Synthesis". It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting [Parent] and addresses the limitations of backward-warping NeRF methods and other dynamic Gaussian methods that either only model rigid motion or struggle with static regions. GauFRe: Gaussian Deformation Fields for Real-Time Dynamic Novel View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/wacv61041.2025.00262, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Light-weight 4D Gaussian Splatting (LGS)
body: Light-weight 4D Gaussian Splatting (LGS) is a memory-efficient method for reconstructing and rendering dynamic scenes, specifically designed for surgical endoscopy. It addresses the high memory consumption and computational cost of standard 4D Gaussian Splatting by combining three compression techniques: Deformation-Aware Pruning (DAP), Gaussian-Attribute Pruning (GAP), and Feature Field Condensation (FFC). Unlike Explicit 4D Gaussian Splatting which stores full attributes, or Gaussian Deformation Field (GauFRe) which uses a deformation network, LGS achieves compression by pruning redundant Gaussians and condensing the feature field resolution, maintaining real-time rendering speeds with significantly smaller model sizes. LGS operates on a set of N 3D Gaussians where attributes evolve over time t \in [0, T] [14584-explicit-4d-gaussian-splatting.md][15458-gaussian-deformation-field-gaufre.md]. The method reduces memory usage through three sequential pruning/condensation steps, followed by a knowledge distillation optimization phase. Inputs: A set of initialized 3D Gaussians with temporal attributes (position \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients C, and feature field data). Ground truth images I{gt}(t) for a set of training timestamps t. A pre-trained, uncompressed "teacher" model. Outputs: A compressed set of Gaussians and a condensed feature field capable of rendering high-quality dynamic scenes. The core data structure remains the 3D Gaussian primitive, but its attribute storage is modified: 1. Gaussian Attributes: Standard parameters (\mu, \Sigma, \alpha) plus spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients. GAP reduces the dimensionality of SH coefficients in non-crucial areas. 2. Feature Field: A 4D voxel grid representing spatial-temporal features. FFC reduces the resolution of this grid. Default resolution: [16, 16, 16, 25] for axes (x, y, z, t). 3. Deformation MLP: A tiny Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) F used to preserve deformation calculation ability after feature field condensation. 1. Deformation-Aware Pruning (DAP): Prunes Gaussians based on their contribution to deformation. Gaussians with low impact on the scene's dynamic structure are removed to minimize redundancy. Parameters: Threshold h = 0.5, weight \beta = 0.1. 2. Gaussian-Attribute Pruning (GAP): Prunes the dimensions of Gaussian attributes (specifically spherical harmonics) to simplify texture and lighting representation in non-crucial areas. Parameter: Threshold h{sh} = 2. Note: Without GAP, model size increases significantly (e.g., to 26.30MB on ENDONERF) and FPS drops (e.g., to 187.9), indicating GAP reduces Gaussian parameters by ~40%. 3. Feature Field Condensation (FFC): Reduces the resolution of the spatial-temporal feature field to tackle high-resolution redundancy. This is achieved via 3D adaptive pooling on each 4D voxel plane. The condensation preserves deformation calculation ability using a tiny MLP F. The compressed feature value E{\Phi'} at indices (i, j) is calculated from the original feature field E{\Phi} using Eq. 5: E{\Phi'}(i, j) = \frac{1}{r{\Phi1} r{\Phi2}} \sum{i'=i \cdot r{\Phi1}}^{(i+1) \cdot r{\Phi1}} \sum{j'=j \cdot r{\Phi2}}^{(j+1) \cdot r{\Phi2}} E{\Phi}(i', j') where \Phi \in \{(x, y), (x, z), (y, z), (x, t), (y, t), (z, t)\} denotes the subplanes of the spatial-temporal feature field, and r{\Phi i} represents the compression rate on the \Phi i axis. 4. Knowledge Distillation Optimization: The compressed "student" model is optimized to match the output of the uncompressed "teacher" model. The total loss L is the sum of distillation loss Ld and rendering loss Lr: L = Ld + Lr Distillation Loss Ld: Mean squared error between teacher rendered image \hat{I}{tch}(t) and student rendered image \hat{I}{stu}(t): Ld = \frac{1}{T} \sum{t} \| \hat{I}{tch}(t) - \hat{I}{stu}(t) \|^2 Rendering Loss Lr: Mean squared error between ground truth image I{gt}(t) and student rendered image \hat{I}{stu}(t): Lr = \frac{1}{T} \sum{t} \| I{gt}(t) - \hat{I}{stu}(t) \|^2 T is the number of training timestamps. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lgstraining(initialgaussians, groundtruthimages, teachermodel, timestamps): """ Implements the LGS training pipeline. """ # Step 1: Deformation-Aware Pruning (DAP) # Prunes Gaussians based on deformation contribution # Parameters: h=0.5, beta=0.1 gaussiansdap = deformationawarepruning(initialgaussians, h=0.5, beta=0.1) # Step 2: Gaussian-Attribute Pruning (GAP) # Prunes SH dimensions to simplify texture/lighting # Parameter: hsh=2 gaussianspruned = gaussianattributepruning(gaussiansdap, hsh=2) # Step 3: Feature Field Condensation (FFC) # Condenses the 4D feature field resolution # Default resolution: [16, 16, 16, 25] featurefield = createfeaturefield(gaussianspruned, resolution=[16, 16, 16, 25]) # Apply 3D adaptive pooling to condense the field # Preserves deformation via tiny MLP F condensedfield = featurefieldcondensation(featurefield) # Initialize student model with pruned Gaussians and condensed field studentmodel = StudentModel(gaussianspruned, condensedfield) # Step 4: Knowledge Distillation Optimization optimizer = Adam(studentmodel.parameters()) for epoch in range(maxepochs): totalloss = 0 for t in timestamps: # Render student image imgstu = studentmodel.render(t) # Render teacher image (using pre-trained teacher) imgtch = teachermodel.render(t) # Get ground truth imggt = groundtruthimages[t] # Calculate Losses # Ld = MSE(imgtch, imgstu) lossd = mseloss(imgtch, imgstu) # Lr = MSE(imggt, imgstu) lossr = mseloss(imggt, imgstu) # L = Ld + Lr loss = lossd + lossr totalloss += loss # Backpropagate optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return studentmodel Performance Degradation without GAP: Removing GAP leads to a significant increase in model size (e.g., 26.30MB vs 25.00MB on ENDONERF) and a drop in FPS (187.9 vs 188.3), demonstrating that GAP is critical for reducing Gaussian parameters by ~40% and handling repetitive textures. Feature Field Resolution: The resolution of the feature field must be carefully chosen. The default [16, 16, 16, 25] is used to balance memory and quality. Distillation Dependency: The method relies on a well-trained uncompressed teacher model. If the teacher is not well-trained, the student will inherit poor quality. Memory Efficiency: LGS achieves significant compression compared to baseline 4D GS methods. On the ENDONERF dataset, it achieves a model size of 25.00MB, which is 15x smaller than EndoGaussian (334.5MB). On the SCARED dataset, it achieves 20.40MB, 9x smaller than EndoGaussian (184.0MB). Rendering Speed: LGS maintains real-time rendering speeds. On ENDONERF, it achieves 188.3 FPS. On SCARED, it achieves 194.66 FPS. It is faster than EndoGaussian (by 21.8 FPS on ENDONERF) and EndoGS (by 87.9 FPS on ENDONERF). Rendering Quality: LGS maintains high quality with minimal loss. On ENDONERF, it achieves SSIM 0.963, PSNR 37.48, and LPIPS 0.068. The quality difference compared to GS-based methods is negligible (0.3 lower PSNR and 0.05 lower SSIM on ENDONERF). On SCARED, it achieves SSIM 0.826, PSNR 27.05, and LPIPS 0.297. Strengths: High memory efficiency (comparable to NeRF-based methods) while retaining the speed of Gaussian Splatting. Effective for dynamic surgical scenes with repetitive textures. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained teacher model for distillation. Performance is evaluated on specific surgical datasets (ENDONERF, SCARED); generalization to other dynamic scenes is not explicitly detailed in the sources. LGS was proposed by Liu et al. in the paper "LGS: A Light-Weight 4D Gaussian Splatting for Efficient Surgical Scene Reconstruction". It was developed to address the challenges of rendering efficiency and memory efficiency in endoscopic surgical scene reconstruction. The method builds upon the principles of 4D Gaussian Splatting, extending them with specific compression techniques tailored for the constraints of surgical imaging. LGS: A Light-Weight 4D Gaussian Splatting for Efficient Surgical Scene Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72384-162, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Deformable Neural Radiance Fields (Nerfies)
head: Deformable NeRF, Nerfies
body: Deformable Neural Radiance Fields (Nerfies) reconstructs non-rigidly deforming scenes by decomposing the scene into a static canonical template volume (a standard NeRF) and a per-observation continuous deformation field that maps observation-space coordinates to canonical-space coordinates. Unlike methods that condition deformation on time or define it on discrete meshes/voxels, Nerfies conditions the deformation on a learned per-frame latent code and models the deformation as a continuous function using an MLP. It distinguishes itself from siblings by introducing elastic regularization to resolve ambiguities between motion and scaling, and a coarse-to-fine optimization strategy to avoid local minima. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of n images \{Ii\}{i=1}^n of a non-rigidly deforming scene, along with their camera poses. Outputs: A canonical NeRF F (representing the template) and a deformation field T (parameterized by an MLP), along with per-frame latent codes \omegai (deformation) and \psii (appearance). The system renders novel views of the deforming subject. Data Structures: 1. Canonical NeRF F: An MLP mapping (x', d, \psii) \to (\sigma, c), where x' is a canonical 3D coordinate, d is a viewing direction, \sigma is density, and c is color. 2. Deformation MLP W: An MLP mapping (x, \omegai) \to (r, v) \in \mathbb{R}^6, where x is an observation-space 3D coordinate and \omegai is the deformation latent code. The output (r, v) parameterizes an SE(3) transformation. 3. Latent Codes: \omegai \in \mathbb{R}^8: Per-frame learned latent deformation code encoding the scene state. \psii \in \mathbb{R}^8: Per-frame learned latent appearance code modulating color output to handle exposure/white balance variations. 4. Positional Encoding: Input coordinates x are encoded using \gamma\alpha(x), which applies frequency-dependent weights wk(\alpha) to sinusoidal basis functions. Parameters: Network Architecture: Deformation network depth 6, hidden size 128, skip connection at the 4th layer. Samples: 256 coarse and 256 fine ray samples per ray for full HD (1920x1080). Annealing: 6 frequency bands; \alpha annealed from 0 to 6 over 80K iterations. Loss Weights: \lambda = \mu = 10^{-3} for elastic and background regularization. Robust Loss Hyperparameter: c = 0.03 for the Geman-McClure function. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Initialization: Initialize the weights of the last layer of the deformation MLP W from a uniform distribution U(-10^{-5}, 10^{-5}). This ensures the deformation starts near the identity, as the exponential map e^S is the identity when S=0. Initialize latent codes \omegai and \psii via embedding layers. 2. Ray Casting and Sampling: For a target view, cast rays \mathbf{r} through the camera. Sample N points xi along each ray in the observation space. 3. Deformation (Observation to Canonical): For each sample point xi and frame i, retrieve the deformation latent code \omegai. Encode xi using the positional encoding \gamma\alpha(xi), where \alpha is the current annealing parameter. Pass (\gamma\alpha(xi), \omegai) through the deformation MLP W to obtain (r, v) \in \mathbb{R}^6. Compute the SE(3) transformation e^S from the screw axis S = (r; v): Compute rotation angle \theta = \|r\| and axis \hat{r} = r/\|r\|. Compute rotation matrix e^r using Rodrigues' formula: e^r = I + \frac{\sin \theta}{\theta}[r]\times + \frac{1 - \cos \theta}{\theta^2}[r]\times^2 where [r]\times is the cross-product matrix of r. Compute translation p using the matrix G: G = I + \frac{1 - \cos \theta}{\theta^2}[r]\times + \frac{\theta - \sin \theta}{\theta^3}[r]\times^2 p = Gv Transform the point to canonical space: x'i = e^r xi + p. 4. Radiance Field Evaluation: Query the canonical NeRF F with the transformed point x'i, viewing direction d, and appearance code \psii to obtain density \sigmai and color ci. 5. Volume Rendering: Compute the rendered color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) using the standard emission-absorption model: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance and \deltai is the step size. 6. Loss Computation and Regularization: Photometric Loss: Compute MSE between \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and the ground truth image color. Elastic Regularization: Compute the Jacobian JT(x) of the deformation field with respect to x using automatic differentiation. Compute the singular values \Sigma of JT(x). Apply the robust elastic loss: L{\text{elastic-r}}(x) = \rho(\|\log \Sigma\|F, c) where \rho(x, c) = \frac{2(x/c)^2}{(x/c)^2 + 4} is the Geman-McClure robust error function with c=0.03. Weight this loss by the sample's contribution to the rendered view wi to allow free deformation in empty space. Background Regularization (Optional): If static 3D points \{xk\}{k=1}^K are known, penalize their movement: L{\text{bg}} = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^K \|T(xk) - xk\|^2 Total Loss: L{\text{total}} = L{\text{rgb}} + \lambda L{\text{elastic-r}} + \mu L{\text{bg}}. 7. Optimization: Optimize the parameters of F, W, \omegai, and \psii using Adam. Anneal the positional encoding bandwidth parameter \alpha(t) linearly: \alpha(t) = m \cdot \frac{t}{N}, where t is the current iteration, N is the total iterations for \alpha to reach m, and m is the max number of frequency bands (e.g., 6). This implements coarse-to-fine optimization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. """ return m (t / N) Coarse-to-Fine Optimization is a training strategy for deformable neural radiance fields that stabilizes convergence by gradually increasing the model's capacity to represent high-frequency details. It addresses the difficulty of simultaneously optimizing complex geometry, texture, and non-rigid deformation from scratch by annealing the frequency components of the positional encoding used by the deformation network. It starts with low-frequency bands to learn smooth, large-scale motions, then introduces higher frequencies to capture fine details, preventing local minima. TFS-NeRF is a template-free 3D semantic NeRF method for reconstructing dynamic scenes from sparse or single-view RGB videos, specifically handling interactions between two or more entities (rigid, non-rigid, or deformable). It distinguishes itself from Nerfies by explicitly disentangling the motions of interacting entities and from LBS-based approaches like TAVA by using an Invertible Neural Network (INN) to predict Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) weights directly, thereby bypassing computationally expensive root-finding optimizations. This enables time-efficient training and semantically separable geometry reconstruction without relying on pre-defined template models (e.g., SMPL) or latent codes. Time Complexity: Training is computationally intensive. Full HD models require training on 8 V100 GPUs for a week, while half-resolution models take 16 hours. The deformation field evaluation adds overhead to each ray sample compared to static NeRF. Memory Complexity: High memory usage due to storing latent codes for each frame and the large MLPs for both the canonical NeRF and deformation field. The use of automatic differentiation for elastic regularization also requires storing intermediate states for the Jacobian computation. Performance: Capable of photorealistic rendering of non-rigidly deforming scenes (e.g., human faces, bodies) from casually captured mobile phone videos. Strengths: Continuous deformation field allows for smooth, high-quality reconstructions without discretization artifacts. Elastic regularization resolves ambiguities between motion and scaling. Coarse-to-fine optimization improves robustness. Limitations: Prone to local minima without coarse-to-fine optimization. Requires careful tuning of regularization weights. Performance degrades if the scene has significant non-rigid deformations that violate the "as-rigid-as-possible" prior (e.g., extreme stretching). When to use: When reconstructing non-rigidly deforming scenes (like humans) from casual video, especially when a template is not available or when continuous deformation is preferred over discrete mesh-based methods. When not to use: For static scenes (use standard NeRF), or for scenes with severe non-rigid deformations that break the local rigidity assumption (e.g., fluid-like motions). Deformable Neural Radiance Fields (Nerfies) was introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2021. It builds on the original NeRF paper [39] by adding a continuous volumetric deformation field conditioned on per-frame latent codes. The method was motivated by the challenge of capturing people with hand-held cameras, where non-rigidity and camera motion make reconstruction difficult. It draws inspiration from geometry processing and physical simulation, specifically elastic energy formulations, to regularize the deformation field. The method was evaluated on data captured using a rig of two synchronized mobile phones. Nerfies: Deformable Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv48922.2021.00581, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Coarse-to-Fine Optimization
head: Exponential Loss Weighting Strategy, Exponential Weight Decay for Coarse-to-Fine, Frequency Annealing for Deformation Fields
body: Coarse-to-Fine Optimization is a training strategy for deformable neural radiance fields that stabilizes convergence by gradually increasing the model's capacity to represent high-frequency details. It addresses the difficulty of simultaneously optimizing complex geometry, texture, and non-rigid deformation from scratch by either decaying the weight of a coarse reconstruction loss relative to a fine-grained loss or by annealing the frequency components of the positional encoding used by the deformation network. Inputs: Training images, camera poses, latent codes for deformation conditioning, and hyperparameters (\lambdas, \lambdae, ec, ef for loss weighting; frequency cutoff schedule for encoding). Outputs: Updated network weights (deformation field, radiance field) and optimized scene representation. Positional Encoding Vector: A vector \phi(\mathbf{x}) constructed by applying sinusoidal functions at multiple frequencies to input coordinates \mathbf{x}. Loss Weights: A scalar \lambda that varies per training iteration. Method 1: Exponential Loss Weighting (DP-NeRF) 1. Define hyperparameters \lambdas, \lambdae, ec, ef, and current epoch ei. 2. Compute the exponential decay rate \alpha. 3. Calculate the current coarse loss weight \lambda for epoch ei. 4. Combine the RBK (coarse) and AWP (fine) reconstruction losses using \lambda. 5. Backpropagate through the combined loss to update network weights. Method 2: Frequency Annealing (Nerfies) 1. Construct the standard positional encoding \phi(\mathbf{x}) for input coordinates \mathbf{x} (typically 3D spatial coordinates plus time or latent code). 2. At the start of optimization, zero out the components of \phi(\mathbf{x}) corresponding to high frequencies. 3. As optimization proceeds, gradually introduce higher frequency components into the positional encoding. 4. Backpropagate to update network weights, allowing the effective capacity of the deformation field to increase over time. All symbols are defined in the steps above. The exponential decay rate \alpha is computed as: \alpha = -\frac{\log(\lambdas / \lambdae)}{ef - ec} The current weight \lambda for the coarse loss at epoch ei is: \lambda = \lambdas \exp(\alpha (ec - ei)) The total loss \mathcal{L}{total} balances the RBK and AWP losses using the decaying weight \lambda: \mathcal{L}{total} = \lambda \mathcal{L}{RBK} + \mathcal{L}{AWP} \lambdas: Initial weight for the coarse loss (typically > 1). \lambdae: Final weight for the coarse loss (typically < 1). ec: Start epoch for decay. ef: End epoch for decay. Frequency cutoff schedule: Not specified in the sources; implementers typically use a linear or stepwise ramp. \lambdas and \lambdae must be chosen such that \lambdas > \lambdae for decay to occur. Frequency cutoff indices must be integers aligned with the positional encoding vector dimensions. Floating point precision in exponential calculations should be sufficient to avoid underflow for large epoch differences. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computecoarsetofineweight(currentepoch, startepoch, endepoch, lambdastart, lambdaend): if currentepoch < startepoch: return lambdastart if currentepoch > endepoch: return lambdaend alpha = -math.log(lambdastart / lambdaend) / (endepoch - startepoch) lambdacurrent = lambdastart math.exp(alpha (startepoch - currentepoch)) return lambdacurrent def trainstep(lossrbk, lossawp, currentepoch, startepoch, endepoch, lambdastart, lambdaend): lambdaweight = computecoarsetofineweight(currentepoch, startepoch, endepoch, lambdastart, lambdaend) totalloss = lambdaweight lossrbk + lossawp return totalloss Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def getpositionalencoding(x, maxfreqindex, currentfreqindex): encoded = [] for i in range(maxfreqindex): if i < currentfreqindex: encoded.append(math.sin(2i math.pi x)) else: encoded.append(0.0) return encoded def annealfrequencyschedule(currentepoch, totalepochs, minfreq, maxfreq): # Schedule not specified in sources; linear interpolation shown as example progress = currentepoch / totalepochs currentfreq = minfreq + progress (maxfreq - minfreq) return int(currentfreq) Time complexity adds negligible overhead to standard NeRF training. Memory complexity requires no additional memory beyond standard buffers. Strengths include preventing oscillation and local minima in high-frequency deformation fields. Limitations include requiring careful tuning of hyperparameters and potentially slowing convergence if decay is too slow. Use when training deformable NeRFs (Nerfies) or deblurred NeRFs (DP-NeRF) from scratch. Coarse-to-Fine Optimization was introduced in two key papers: Nerfies (Park et al., 2021) proposed frequency annealing of positional encodings to regularize the deformation field, preventing it from overfitting to high-frequency noise early in training. DP-NeRF (Zhang et al., 2022) proposed exponential decay of the weight between a coarse rigid background loss and a fine adaptive weighting prior loss to stabilize training for deblurred scene reconstruction. Both methods address the instability of optimizing high-capacity neural networks for complex 3D representations from scratch.
