name: Template-Free NeRF (TFS-NeRF)
head: TFS-NeRF
body: TFS-NeRF is a template-free 3D semantic NeRF method for reconstructing dynamic scenes from sparse or single-view RGB videos, specifically handling interactions between two or more entities (rigid, non-rigid, or deformable). It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Nerfies by explicitly disentangling the motions of interacting entities and from LBS-based approaches like TAVA by using an Invertible Neural Network (INN) to predict Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) weights directly, thereby bypassing computationally expensive root-finding optimizations. This enables time-efficient training and semantically separable geometry reconstruction without relying on pre-defined template models (e.g., SMPL) or latent codes. Inputs: Sparse or single-view RGB video frames and corresponding 2D semantic segmentation masks. Outputs: A composite scene rendering and semantically separable Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) for deformable and non-deformable entities. Data Structures: Canonical Space: A static reference frame where geometry is defined independently of time and pose. Deformed/View Space: The coordinate system of the observed frame at a specific timestamp. Bone Transformation Matrices (B): A set of nb rigid transformation matrices representing the bones of the deformable entity. Skining Weights (w(xc)): A function mapping a canonical point xc to a weight vector, predicted by the INN. SDF Networks (F{c \to \Omega}^{(\theta)}): Two independent neural networks (MLPs) parameterized by \theta, one for deformable entities (j=d) and one for non-deformable entities (j=nd), predicting canonical SDFs. Formulas: The forward Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) computes the deformed point xv in view space from a canonical point xc using skinning weights w(xc) and bone transformation matrices B: xv = \text{LBS}(w(xc), B, xc) = \sum{b=1}^{nb} w(xc)b \cdot Bb \cdot xc where nb is the total number of bones. Steps: 1. Semantic-Aware Ray Sampling: Given a 2D semantic segmentation mask for the current frame, shoot two distinct sets of rays from the camera: One set samples 3D points \{xd^v\} corresponding to deformable entities. Another set samples 3D points \{xv\} corresponding to non-deformable entities. 2. Inverse Warping to Canonical Space: Transform the sampled points from the deformed/view space to their respective canonical spaces. This is achieved by inverting the forward LBS mapping. Since TFS-NeRF uses an INN to predict the forward LBS weights w(xc), the inverse warping is enabled by the invertibility of the INN, avoiding the iterative root-finding procedures used in prior work. 3. Individual Geometry Prediction: At the canonical space, use two independent SDF prediction networks F{c \to \Omega}^{(\theta)} to predict the Signed Distance Fields: F{c \to \Omega}^{(\theta, d)} predicts the SDF for the deformable entity. F{c \to \Omega}^{(\theta, nd)} predicts the SDF for the non-deformable entity. 4. Joint Optimization: Optimize both branches (deformable and non-deformable) jointly. The optimization minimizes the RGB reconstruction loss between the rendered composite image and the ground truth image, while simultaneously learning the per-entity skinning weights and SDFs. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tfsnerfforward(framergb, semanticmask, cameraparams, innmodel, sdfnetdeform, sdfnetnondeform, bones): """ Performs one forward pass of TFS-NeRF. Args: framergb: RGB image of the current frame. semanticmask: 2D semantic segmentation mask for the current frame. cameraparams: Intrinsics and extrinsics for the current view. innmodel: Invertible Neural Network predicting LBS weights w(xc). sdfnetdeform: MLP predicting SDF for deformable entities. sdfnetnondeform: MLP predicting SDF for non-deformable entities. bones: List of bone transformation matrices Bb. Returns: renderedcolor: Rendered RGB color. loss: Reconstruction loss. """ # 1. Semantic-Aware Ray Sampling # Shoot rays based on semantic mask to separate deformable and non-deformable regions raysdeform, raysnondeform = semanticraysampling(semanticmask, cameraparams) # Sample 3D points along these rays in the deformed/view space # Note: Depth sampling strategy (e.g., uniform or importance sampling) is not specified in sources pointsdeformv = samplepointsalongrays(raysdeform) pointsnondeformv = samplepointsalongrays(raysnondeform) # 2. Inverse Warping to Canonical Space # Predict LBS weights w(xc) using INN. # The INN takes canonical points as input and outputs weights. # However, we have deformed points. The INN is used to bypass root-finding. # The source states: "inverse warping enabled by the learned forward LBS". # This implies the INN allows direct computation or efficient inversion. # We assume the INN predicts weights for canonical points, and we need to find xc such that LBS(w(xc), B, xc) = xv. # TFS-NeRF uses INN to predict LBS directly. The source contrasts with TAVA which uses root-finding. # Implementation detail: The INN likely maps xc -> w. To go xv -> xc, we might need an inverse INN or # the INN is structured to allow direct inversion. Given "INN for LBS prediction", we assume: # w = innmodel(xc). # To find xc from xv, we solve xv = sum(w(xc)b Bb xc). # The key contribution is that this is solved efficiently via INN, avoiding iterative root-finding. # For the purpose of the algorithm, we denote the inverse mapping as: pointsdeformc = inversewarpdeform(pointsdeformv, innmodel, bones) pointsnondeformc = inversewarpnondeform(pointsnondeformv) # Non-deformable may not need LBS inversion if static, # but source says "transform... to respective canonical spaces" # 3. Individual Geometry Prediction # Predict SDFs at canonical points sdfdeform = sdfnetdeform(pointsdeformc) sdfnondeform = sdfnetnondeform(pointsnondeformc) # 4. Volume Rendering # Render the composite scene from the SDFs # Standard volume rendering from SDF (e.g., using marching cubes or differentiable ray marching) is implied renderedcolor = volumerendersdf(sdfdeform, sdfnondeform, raysdeform, raysnondeform) # 5. Loss Calculation loss = rgbloss(renderedcolor, framergb) return renderedcolor, loss def inversewarpdeform(pointsv, innmodel, bones): """ Maps deformed points to canonical space using INN-predicted LBS. Avoids iterative root-finding by leveraging INN properties. """ # The source does not provide the exact mathematical inversion formula, # only that INN bypasses root-finding. # A common approach with INN is that the network is bijective. # If INN predicts w from xc, we need xc from xv. # This step is the core efficiency gain. # Placeholder for the specific INN inversion logic not detailed in source return innmodel.inverse(pointsv) Parameters: Number of Bones (nb): Total number of bones in the deformable entity. Not given in the sources. Semantic Mask: Required input for ray sampling. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusions: Complex interactions between entities can cause occlusions, which the method handles by disentangling motions. Topological Variations: The method is designed for dynamic scenes but does not explicitly handle topological changes within a frame (unlike Tensor4D which also lacks this). Precision: The use of INN avoids the numerical instability and convergence issues associated with Broyden’s method used in prior LBS-based NeRFs. A technique where an Invertible Neural Network predicts skinning weights directly, replacing iterative root-finding. It sets itself apart by offering time-efficient training compared to methods like TAVA. Choose this when training speed is critical and the scene involves deformable entities with known bone structures. Link to TFS-NeRF. A sampling strategy that uses 2D semantic masks to separate rays into deformable and non-deformable categories. It sets itself apart by enabling independent optimization of interacting entities. Choose this when semantic separation of dynamic and static parts is required. Link to TFS-NeRF. Time Efficiency: TFS-NeRF is significantly more time-efficient than LBS-based approaches like TAVA [28] because it bypasses the computationally demanding root-finding optimization (e.g., Broyden’s method) for LBS inversion. Memory: Not given in the sources. Performance: Produces high-quality reconstructions of both deformable and non-deformable objects in complex interactions (e.g., human-object, hand-object). Strengths: Template-free (no need for SMPL or similar priors), semantically separable, handles interactions between multiple entities, efficient training. Limitations: Requires 2D semantic segmentation masks as input. Relies on LBS, which assumes a skeletal structure for deformable entities. Scaling: Not given in the sources. TFS-NeRF was introduced in the paper "TFS-NeRF: Template-Free NeRF for Semantic 3D Reconstruction of Dynamic Scene". It builds upon prior work such as TAVA [28], which used computationally expensive root-finding for LBS, and addresses the challenge of reconstructing dynamic scenes with interacting entities without relying on template models like SMPL. The method was developed to handle sparse or single-view RGB videos, extending the capabilities of NeRFies [Parent] by adding semantic separation and efficient LBS prediction via INN. name: JointRF Representation
head: JointRF, Joint Optimization for Dynamic Neural Radiance Field Representation and Compression
body: JointRF is a compact residual feature grid representation for dynamic Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) that handles large motions and long sequences by decomposing the radiance field into a long-reference basis feature grid and a coefficient feature grid. Unlike canonical space methods that warp features back to a static canonical space—making them fragile to large motions and topological changes—JointRF uses residual grids to capture temporal variations, thereby diminishing temporal redundancy and improving compression efficiency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of dynamic radiance fields over time, represented as a set of frames. Output: A compressed representation consisting of a keyframe basis grid, a keyframe coefficient grid, and a sequence of residual grids and coefficient grids for subsequent frames. Data Structures: The representation is organized into Groups of Feature grids (GOF). Each GOF G = \{ft\}{t=1}^N contains: 1. Keyframe (t=1): B1: Long-reference basis feature grid. Captures signal commonality across the sequence. C1: Coefficient feature grid. Depicts spatial variations for the keyframe. 2. Subsequent Frames (1 < t \le N): Rt: Compact residual feature grid. Represents the compensation for errors and newly observed regions between the keyframe's basis grid and the current frame's basis grid. Ct: Coefficient feature grid for frame t. Formulas: The radiance field for any frame is reconstructed using a tiny Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) \Phi: (c, \sigma) = \Phi(\text{interp}(x, C) \circ \text{interp}(x, B), d) where: x is the 3D spatial coordinate. d is the viewing direction. \text{interp}(\cdot) is the interpolation function on the grids (e.g., trilinear interpolation). \circ denotes the Hadamard (element-wise) product. c is the color and \sigma is the density. For t > 1, the basis grid Bt is calculated as: Bt = B1 + Rt The coefficient grid Ct is learned directly for frame t, but the sources note that learning residuals for Ct holds no physical significance; only the basis grid residuals are modeled. Numbered Steps: 1. Divide the long sequence of dynamic radiance fields into multiple continuous Groups of Feature grids (GOF). 2. For the first frame (keyframe) of each GOF, initialize a long-reference basis feature grid B1 and a coefficient feature grid C1. 3. For each subsequent frame t (1 < t \le N) in the GOF: a. Learn a compact residual feature grid Rt. b. Learn a coefficient feature grid Ct. c. Compute the current frame's basis grid: Bt = B1 + Rt. 4. To render a ray \mathbf{r} at frame t: a. Sample points along the ray. b. For each sample point xi, retrieve features from Bt and Ct using interpolation: f{B} = \text{interp}(xi, Bt) and f{C} = \text{interp}(xi, Ct). c. Compute the combined feature vector: fi = f{C} \circ f{B}. d. Pass fi and the viewing direction di through the MLP \Phi to obtain density \sigmai and color ci. 5. Compute the final color \hat{c}(\mathbf{r}) using the standard volume rendering equation: \hat{c}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj), \deltai is the distance between adjacent samples, ci is color, and \sigmai is density. Parameters: GOF Size: Not given in the sources. Grid Resolution: Not given in the sources. MLP Architecture: Described as a "tiny MLP". Specific layer sizes are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Large Motions: Canonical space warping methods fail under large motions; JointRF handles them by using residual grids. Coefficient Residuals: Learning residuals for the coefficient grid Ct is physically insignificant and should not be done; only basis grid residuals Rt are modeled. Temporal Redundancy: The method is designed to minimize redundancy by leveraging the commonality in the basis grid. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def jointrfrender(rayorigin, raydirection, timeindex, gofdata): """ Renders a single ray for a specific time index using JointRF representation. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, origin of the ray. raydirection: 3D vector, direction of the ray. timeindex: int, index of the frame within the GOF (0-based). gofdata: dict containing: 'B1': Tensor, long-reference basis feature grid for the keyframe. 'C1': Tensor, coefficient feature grid for the keyframe. 'R': List of Tensors, residual grids for frames 1 to N-1. 'C': List of Tensors, coefficient grids for frames 1 to N-1. 'mlp': Function, the tiny MLP Phi. 'interp': Function, interpolation on grids. Returns: color: 3D vector, rendered color. """ # 1. Determine the basis and coefficient grids for the current time index if timeindex == 0: # Keyframe Bt = gofdata['B1'] Ct = gofdata['C1'] else: # Subsequent frame # Bt = B1 + Rt Rt = gofdata['R'][timeindex - 1] Bt = gofdata['B1'] + Rt Ct = gofdata['C'][timeindex - 1] # 2. Sample points along the ray # Assume Nsamples is a predefined constant tvals = linspace(0, maxdist, Nsamples) points = rayorigin + outer(tvals, raydirection) # Shape: (Nsamples, 3) # 3. Interpolate features from grids # interp(grid, points) returns features for each point featuresB = gofdata'interp' # Shape: (Nsamples, featuredim) featuresC = gofdata'interp' # Shape: (Nsamples, featuredim) # 4. Hadamard product combinedfeatures = featuresC featuresB # Element-wise multiplication # 5. MLP to get density and color # directions repeated for each sample directions = repeat(raydirection, Nsamples) # Phi(combinedfeatures, directions) -> (sigma, color) # Assuming mlp returns a tuple or concatenated tensor output = gofdata'mlp' # Extract sigma and color based on MLP output structure # Note: Exact MLP output structure is not specified, assuming standard NeRF output sigma = output[:, 0] # Assuming first channel is density color = output[:, 1:4] # Assuming next 3 channels are color # 6. Volume Rendering # Compute transmittance # deltat is the distance between adjacent samples deltat = tvals[1] - tvals[0] # Alpha values alpha = 1.0 - exp(-sigma deltat) # Transmittance Ti = exp(-sum{j=1}^{i-1} sigmaj deltaj) # We can compute this iteratively or using cumulative sum # T0 = 1.0 # Ti = T{i-1} (1 - alpha{i-1}) transmittance = ones(Nsamples) for i in range(1, Nsamples): transmittance[i] = transmittance[i-1] (1.0 - alpha[i-1]) # Weighted sum weights = transmittance alpha renderedcolor = sum(weights color, axis=0) return renderedcolor Time Complexity: Rendering complexity is similar to standard NeRF, O(N \cdot S) where N is the number of rays and S is the number of samples per ray, plus the cost of grid interpolation. The representation allows simultaneous rendering of multiple non-keyframes because it relies on only one keyframe during rendering, facilitating parallel computation. Memory Complexity: The representation is compact. It stores one long-reference basis grid B1 and one coefficient grid C1 for the keyframe, plus residual grids Rt and coefficient grids Ct for subsequent frames. The residual grids are compact, reducing memory usage compared to storing full feature grids for every frame. Strengths: Handles large motions without compromising quality; diminishes temporal redundancy; supports streamable dynamic and long-sequence radiance fields; enables efficient sequential feature modeling. Limitations: Learning residuals for the coefficient grid Ct is physically insignificant and should be avoided. The method requires a sequential feature compression subnetwork for optimal compression, which adds complexity to the training pipeline. When to use: When representing dynamic scenes with large motions and long durations where canonical space warping methods fail. When not to use: For static scenes or scenes with very small motions where simpler representations might suffice. JointRF was proposed in 2024 by authors from Shanghai Jiao Tong University, supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China and STCSM. It addresses the challenges of storing and transmitting volumetric video using NeRF, particularly for sequences involving arbitrary motions and long durations. The method builds on the idea of residual radiance field techniques, similar to ReRF, but introduces a joint optimization scheme for representation and compression. It decomposes the static scene radiance field into coefficient and basis feature grids via basis expansion, extending this to dynamic scenes by using residual grids for temporal variations. name: D-TensoRF
head: Dynamic Tensorial Radiance Fields
body: D-TensoRF is a dynamic radiance field model that maps 3D location \mathbf{x}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and time instant t to emitted color \mathbf{c} and volume density \sigma using factorized 4D/5D tensor grids. It extends TensoRF by incorporating a time dimension and applying Matrix-Matrix (MM) decomposition to reduce memory complexity from O(n^4) to O(n^2) compared to naive 4D grid representations. Unlike Deformable Neural Radiance Fields (Nerfies), which rely on explicit deformation fields to warp static coordinates, D-TensoRF models temporal dynamics directly within the tensor structure, augmented by smoothing regularization to enforce temporal dependency. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z), viewing direction \mathbf{d} = (\theta, \phi), and time instant t. Outputs: Volume density \sigma and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}. Data Structures: The model utilizes two primary grids, factorized via MM decomposition: 1. Geometry Grid (G\sigma): A 4D tensor with dimensions I \times J \times K \times N, where I, J, K are spatial resolutions (X, Y, Z) and N is the time axis resolution. 2. Appearance Grid (Gc): A 5D tensor with dimensions I \times J \times K \times N \times P, where P is the number of feature channels. MM Decomposition Layout: For a 4D tensor T \in \mathbb{R}^{I \times J \times K \times N}, MM decomposition expresses T as a summation of outer products of matrix factors corresponding to pairs of modes: T = \sum{r=1}^{R1} M{r,1,2} \circ M{r,3,4} + \sum{r=1}^{R2} M{r,1,3} \circ M{r,2,4} + \sum{r=1}^{R3} M{r,2,3} \circ M{r,1,4} where M{r,i,j} \in \mathbb{R}^{di \times dj} is a matrix factor for modes i and j, and \circ denotes the outer product of the scalar values resulting from the interaction of the two matrices at specific indices. Parameters: Components: R\sigma for geometry, Rc for appearance. Rc is typically set to 3 \times R\sigma. Time Resolution (Nt): Set to 0.25 \times (\text{number of training images}). Initial Grid Resolution: 64^3 \times Nt. Converting Function S: A small MLP with two fully-connected layers and 128-channel hidden layers. Smoothing Regularization: Window size S=3, smoothing degree \sigma=0.5. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Grids: Initialize geometry grid G\sigma and appearance grid Gc with random values for their matrix and vector factors. Set initial spatial resolution to 64^3 and time resolution Nt = 0.25 \times N{images}. 2. Compute Density (\sigma): Evaluate G\sigma(\mathbf{x}, t) using MM decomposition. For each component r, compute the scalar value by multiplying the corresponding entries from the matrix factors (e.g., M{\sigma,r,X,Y}(x,y) \times M{\sigma,r,Z,T}(z,t)). Sum these products across all components. \sigma = \sum{r=1}^{R\sigma} \left( M{\sigma,r,X,Y} \circ M{\sigma,r,Z,T} + M{\sigma,r,X,Z} \circ M{\sigma,r,Y,T} + M{\sigma,r,Y,Z} \circ M{\sigma,r,X,T} \right) The result is the volume density \sigma at (\mathbf{x}, t). 3. Compute Appearance Features (Gc): Evaluate Gc(\mathbf{x}, t) using MM decomposition. This involves matrix factors for appearance (M{c}) and geometry (M{\sigma}). The decomposition for Gc is defined as: Gc = \sum{r=1}^{Rc} \left( M{c,r,X,Y} \circ M{c,r,Z,T} \circ \mathbf{b}{3r-2} + M{c,r,X,Z} \circ M{c,r,Y,T} \circ \mathbf{b}{3r-1} + M{\sigma,r,Y,Z} \circ M{c,r,X,T} \circ \mathbf{b}{3r} \right) Here, \mathbf{b} represents vector factors. The term M{c,r,X,Y} \circ M{c,r,Z,T} produces a scalar value for the spatial-temporal interaction, which is then multiplied by the vector \mathbf{b}. 4. Compute Color (\mathbf{c}): Pass the appearance features Gc(\mathbf{x}, t) and viewing direction \mathbf{d} through the converting function S: \mathbf{c} = S(Gc(\mathbf{x}, t), \mathbf{d}) S is implemented as a 2-layer MLP with 128 hidden units. 5. Render: Use differentiable volume rendering (standard emission-absorption model) to compute the pixel color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) from \sigma and \mathbf{c} along ray \mathbf{r}. 6. Regularization: Apply smoothing regularization L{smooth} to enforce temporal dependency on time-related factors (vectors \mathbf{b} and matrices involving the time axis T). For a feature value ev{it} (or em{l,it} for matrices) at time index it: L{smooth} = \sum{r=1}^{R} \sum{it=0}^{N} \left\| ev{it} - \sum{iw \in \text{window}(it,S)} w(it, iw) ev{iw} \right\|^2 The weight w(it, iw) is a Gaussian kernel: w(it, iw) = \frac{K(it, iw)}{\sum{i'w \in \text{window}(it,S)} K(it, i'w)}, \quad K(it, iw) = \exp\left(-\frac{(it - iw)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) where \sigma=0.5 and window size S=3. Apply L1 regularization on all vector and matrix factors to prevent overfitting. 7. Optimization: Minimize L2 rendering loss against 2D image supervision using gradient descent. 8. Upsampling: Upsample vector and matrix factors linearly and bilinearly at training steps 2000, 3000, 4000, 5500, and 7000. Do not upsample the feature grid along the time axis. 9. Bounding Box Refinement: At training step 2000, calculate a binary occupancy mask grid to create a more accurate bounding box, preventing unnecessary computation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class DTensoRF: def init(self, I, J, K, N, Rsigma, Rc, P=128): """ Initialize D-TensoRF model. I, J, K: Spatial resolutions N: Time resolution Rsigma: Number of components for geometry Rc: Number of components for appearance P: Feature channels (hidden size for MLP) """ self.I, self.J, self.K, self.N = I, J, K, N self.Rsigma = Rsigma self.Rc = Rc # Initialize Geometry Grid Factors (MM Decomposition) # MsigmarXY, MsigmarZT, etc. self.MsigmaXY = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rsigma, I, J)) self.MsigmaZT = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rsigma, K, N)) self.MsigmaXZ = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rsigma, I, K)) self.MsigmaYT = nnParameter(torch.randn(Rsigma, J, N)) self.MsigmaYZ = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rsigma, J, K)) self.MsigmaXT = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rsigma, I, N)) # Initialize Appearance Grid Factors # McrXY, McrZT, etc. self.McXY = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rc, I, J)) self.McZT = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rc, K, N)) self.McXZ = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rc, I, K)) self.McYT = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rc, J, N)) # Vector factors b for appearance # b3r-2, b3r-1, b3r self.b = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(3 Rc, P)) # Converting Function S (MLP) self.S = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(P, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 3) # Output RGB) def getsigma(self, x, y, z, t): """Compute density sigma using MM decomposition.""" # Normalize coordinates to [0, I-1], etc. for indexing # In practice, use gridsample or manual interpolation # Here we assume discrete indices for clarity, # but implementation should use quadrilinear interpolation # Term 1: MXY(x,y) MZT(z,t) term1 = torch.einsum('rxy, rzT -> r', self.MsigmaXY[x, y], self.MsigmaZT[z, t]) # Term 2: MXZ(x,z) MYT(y,t) term2 = torch.einsum('rxz, ryT -> r', self.MsigmaXZ[x, z], self.MsigmaYT[y, t]) # Term 3: MYZ(y,z) MXT(x,t) term3 = torch.einsum('ryz, rxt -> r', self.MsigmaYZ[y, z], self.MsigmaXT[x, t]) sigma = torch.sum(term1 + term2 + term3, dim=0) return sigma def getcolor(self, x, y, z, t, d): """Compute color c using MM decomposition and MLP S.""" # Compute appearance features Gc(x,t) # Term 1: McXY(x,y) McZT(z,t) b3r-2 feat1 = torch.einsum('rxy, rzT -> r', self.McXY[x, y], self.McZT[z, t]) self.b[0::3] # Term 2: McXZ(x,z) McYT(y,t) b3r-1 feat2 = torch.einsum('rxz, ryT -> r', self.McXZ[x, z], self.McYT[y, t]) self.b[1::3] # Term 3: MsigmaYZ(y,z) McXT(x,t) b3r # Note: Uses geometry matrix MsigmaYZ and appearance matrix McXT feat3 = torch.einsum('ryz, rxt -> r', self.MsigmaYZ[y, z], self.McXT[x, t]) self.b[2::3] features = torch.sum(feat1 + feat2 + feat3, dim=0) # Shape: [P] # Pass through MLP S with viewing direction d # d is typically encoded or concatenated color = self.S(features) return color def smoothnessloss(self, factors, timeaxisidx): """ Compute smoothing regularization loss. factors: tensor of shape [R,..., N,...] timeaxisidx: index of the time dimension in the tensor """ loss = 0 Swindow = 3 sigmasmooth = 0.5 # Iterate over components and other dimensions # This is a simplified representation; actual implementation # requires iterating over all relevant factors (vectors and matrices) # involving the time axis. # Example for a matrix factor M[..., N] # M shape: [R, D1, N] # We need to smooth along N # Construct Gaussian weights # Window size S=3 means indices it-1, it, it+1 # w(it, iw) = exp(-(it-iw)^2 / 2sigma^2) / sum(...) # For implementation, one would gather neighbors and apply weights # This function returns the scalar loss value return loss # Placeholder for complex tensor operations def forward(self, rays): """ rays: tensor of shape [Nrays, 6] containing (x, y, z, theta, phi, t) """ x, y, z, theta, phi, t = rays.split(1, dim=1) d = torch.cat([torch.sin(theta)torch.cos(phi), torch.sin(theta)torch.sin(phi), torch.cos(theta)], dim=1) sigma = self.getsigma(x, y, z, t) color = self.getcolor(x, y, z, t, d) return sigma, color Memory Complexity: MM decomposition reduces memory complexity from O(n^4) to O(n^2) compared to a naive 4D grid representation. Performance: The MLP converting function S consistently shows better results than Spherical Harmonics (SH). Hardware: Evaluated on a single GeForce RTX 3090 GPU. Strengths: Compact representation for dynamic scenes; effective handling of temporal dependencies via smoothing regularization; efficient memory usage compared to dense 4D grids. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of upsampling schedule; smoothing regularization parameters (S, \sigma) are fixed and not learned; does not model explicit deformations, which may limit accuracy for highly non-rigid or large-displacement motions compared to deformation-based methods. When to use: Suitable for dynamic scenes with continuous motion where memory efficiency is critical and explicit deformation fields are not preferred or available. When not to use: Scenes with large, discontinuous motions or where explicit geometric deformation is more appropriate. D-TensoRF was introduced in the paper "D-TensoRF: Tensorial Radiance Fields for Dynamic Scenes". It extends the TensoRF method, which uses tensor decomposition for static scenes, to handle dynamic content by adding a time dimension. The method was developed to address the limitations of existing dynamic radiance field models in terms of memory efficiency and representation capacity. It builds on the principles of differentiable volume rendering and tensor factorization. name: SE(3) Deformation Field
head: 6-DOF SE(3) field, Rigid transformation field, Screw axis deformation
body: The SE(3) Deformation Field encodes scene deformation as a rigid transformation (rotation and translation) per point using a screw axis representation. It replaces per-point translation fields to simplify optimization by requiring a single rotation parameter across space, rather than distinct translation vectors for each point. This method is primarily used in dynamic scene reconstruction to handle rotational motion more efficiently than pure translation-based deformation fields. Inputs: Spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and temporal coordinate t \in \mathbb{R} (or a latent code representing time). A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) trained to predict deformation parameters. Outputs: A deformed 3D point \mathbf{x}' \in \mathbb{R}^3. The homogeneous transformation matrix \mathbf{e}^{\hat{S}} \in SE(3). Data Structures: Screw Axis Parameters (\hat{S}): A 6-dimensional vector \hat{S} = (\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{v}) \in \mathbb{R}^6, where \mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{R}^3 defines the rotation axis and angle, and \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^3 defines the translation component. Skew-Symmetric Matrix ([\mathbf{x}]\times): A 3 \times 3 matrix constructed from a vector \mathbf{x} = [x1, x2, x3]^T: [\mathbf{x}]\times = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -x3 & x2 \\ x3 & 0 & -x1 \\ -x2 & x1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} This matrix satisfies [\mathbf{a}]\times \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}. Steps: 1. Prediction: The MLP takes the input (\mathbf{x}, t) and predicts the screw axis parameters \hat{S} = (\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{v}) \in \mathbb{R}^6. 2. Angle Calculation: Compute the rotation angle \theta as the magnitude of the rotation vector \mathbf{r}: \theta = \|\mathbf{r}\|. 3. Rotation Matrix Construction: Compute the rotation matrix \mathbf{R} using Rodrigues' formula: \mathbf{R} = \mathbf{I} + \frac{\sin \theta}{\theta} [\mathbf{r}]\times + \frac{1 - \cos \theta}{\theta^2} [\mathbf{r}]\times^2 where \mathbf{I} is the 3 \times 3 identity matrix. 4. Translation Matrix Construction: Compute the matrix \mathbf{G} used to derive the translation from the screw axis vector \mathbf{v}: \mathbf{G} = \mathbf{I} + \frac{1 - \cos \theta}{\theta^2} [\mathbf{r}]\times + \frac{\theta - \sin \theta}{\theta^3} [\mathbf{r}]\times^2. 5. Translation Vector Calculation: Compute the translation vector \mathbf{p}: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{G}\mathbf{v}. 6. Homogeneous Transform: Form the homogeneous transformation matrix \mathbf{e}^{\hat{S}} \in SE(3): \mathbf{e}^{\hat{S}} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{R} & \mathbf{p} \\ \mathbf{0} & 1 \end{pmatrix}. 7. Deformation: Apply the transformation to the input point \mathbf{x} (treated as a homogeneous vector [\mathbf{x}, 1]^T) to obtain the deformed point \mathbf{x}': \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{e}^{\hat{S}} \mathbf{x}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def skewsymmetric(v): """ Constructs the skew-symmetric cross-product matrix for vector v. """ return np.array([ [0, -v[2], v[1]], [v[2], 0, -v[0]], [-v[1], v[0], 0] ]) def se3deformation(mlppredict, x, t): """ Applies the SE(3) deformation field to a point x at time t. Args: mlppredict: A function that takes (x, t) and returns screw axis params (r, v). x: Input 3D point (numpy array of shape (3,)). t: Time coordinate (scalar or numpy array). Returns: xprime: Deformed 3D point. """ # Step 1: Predict screw axis parameters # mlppredict returns r (3,) and v (3,) r, v = mlppredict(x, t) # Step 2: Compute rotation angle theta = np.linalg.norm(r) # Handle singularity when theta is close to 0 # Standard limit for Rodrigues' formula as theta -> 0 if theta < 1e-8: R = np.eye(3) G = np.eye(3) else: # Step 3: Construct skew-symmetric matrix [r]x rcross = skewsymmetric(r) # Step 4: Compute rotation matrix R using Rodrigues' formula # R = I + (sin(theta)/theta) [r]x + ((1 - cos(theta))/theta^2) [r]x^2 sintheta = np.sin(theta) costheta = np.cos(theta) R = np.eye(3) + (sintheta / theta) rcross + ((1 - costheta) / (theta2)) np.dot(rcross, rcross) # Step 5: Compute matrix G for translation # G = I + ((1 - cos(theta))/theta^2) [r]x + ((theta - sin(theta))/theta^3) [r]x^2 G = np.eye(3) + ((1 - costheta) / (theta2)) rcross + ((theta - sintheta) / (theta3)) np.dot(rcross, rcross) # Step 6: Compute translation vector p = G v p = np.dot(G, v) # Step 7: Apply transformation x' = R x + p xprime = np.dot(R, x) + p return xprime Parameters: Elastic Regularization (\lambda): Used in conjunction with the SE(3) field to improve results for dynamic scenes. A stronger regularization (\lambda = 0.01) is recommended for dynamic scenes, while \lambda = 0.001 suffices for quasi-static scenes. Coarse-to-Fine Optimization: Implemented by windowing the frequency bands of the positional encoding. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity at \theta = 0: When the rotation angle is zero, the division by \theta in Rodrigues' formula and \mathbf{G} calculation becomes undefined. The limit as \theta \to 0 is the identity matrix. Topological Changes: The method fails in the presence of topological changes in the scene, as it assumes a rigid transformation structure. Gauge Ambiguity: Slight misalignments may result from gauge ambiguity, affecting PSNR metrics, though LPIPS may remain robust. What it is: A general category of methods defining how deformation fields are represented (e.g., translation fields, rotation fields, SE(3) fields). Differentiation: SE(3) specifically uses screw axis theory to combine rotation and translation into a single rigid body motion, whereas other parametrizations might use separate translation vectors or simpler rotation encodings. When to choose: Choose SE(3) when the scene deformation is predominantly rigid rotation, as it simplifies optimization by requiring a single rotation parameter across space. Link: Deformation Field Parametrization What it is: Methods that represent scenes changing over time, often involving temporal encoding or latent codes. Differentiation: SE(3) is a specific deformation mechanism applied within a dynamic scene representation to handle rigid body motions. When to choose: Use SE(3) within a dynamic scene representation when the primary motion is rotational and rigid. Link: Dynamic Scene Representation What it is: The foundational method that introduced the use of deformation fields for dynamic NeRFs. Differentiation: SE(3) is a specific refinement or alternative deformation technique inspired by Nerfies, focusing on rigid transformations via screw axes. When to choose: Use SE(3) if you are building upon Nerfies and need to handle rigid rotations more efficiently than the original translation-based deformation. Link: Deformable Neural Radiance Fields (Nerfies) What it is: A representation that jointly optimizes radiance fields and deformation fields. Differentiation: SE(3) can be used as the deformation field component within a JointRF framework. When to choose: Use SE(3) as the deformation model in JointRF when rigid body motion is dominant. Link: JointRF Representation What it is: A tensor-based factorization of NeRFs for dynamic scenes. Differentiation: SE(3) provides a specific rigid transformation model that can be integrated into the deformation component of D-TensoRF. When to choose: Use SE(3) in D-TensoRF for efficient handling of rigid rotations. Link: D-TensoRF Time Complexity: The SE(3) field increases training time by approximately 50% compared to methods without this specific deformation field. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Rendering Performance: The additional computational overhead results in about a 20% decrease in FPS during rendering. Strengths: Simplifies optimization by requiring a single rotation parameter across space, making it easier to optimize than per-point translation fields for rotational motion. Limitations: Diminishes quality on complex real-world datasets (e.g., NeRF-DS) compared to simpler methods like direct addition. Fails in the presence of topological changes. When to use: Use when the scene deformation is primarily rigid rotation and computational resources allow for the increased training time. When not to use: Avoid for complex real-world scenes with non-rigid deformations or topological changes, or when rendering FPS is critical. Origin: The SE(3) deformation field was introduced in the paper "Nerfies: Deformable Neural Radiance Fields" by Park et al.. It draws inspiration from screw axis theory in rigid body kinematics. History: The method was proposed to address the inefficiency of translation-based deformation fields in encoding rotational motion. By using a screw axis, it allows a single rotation parameter to encode rotation for all points, simplifying the optimization process. Usage: It is used in dynamic scene reconstruction, particularly in datasets like D-NeRF, where it offers minor improvements over baseline methods. It has also been applied to 3D Gaussian Splatting for dynamic scenes. name: Reference-Based Non-Photorealistic Radiance Fields
head: Ref-NPR
body: Ref-NPR is a controllable scene stylization method that transfers the style of a single 2D reference image to a 3D scene represented by a radiance field, ensuring semantic consistency across novel views. Unlike standard NeRF optimization which minimizes photometric error against ground-truth photos, Ref-NPR optimizes a non-photorealistic (NP) radiance field using explicit supervision from a stylized reference view and implicit supervision for occluded regions. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Neural Reconstruction in the Wild by explicitly mapping 2D stylized pixels to 3D space via ray registration to establish semantic correspondence, rather than relying solely on global style loss or 2D warping. Ref-NPR builds on the differentiable volume rendering principles of Neural Radiance Fields. It optimizes a new NP radiance field \omega{NP} using a pre-trained photorealistic radiance field \omegaP as a geometric prior. Inputs: 1. Pre-trained photorealistic radiance field \omegaP (parameters \sigma, \mathbf{c}). 2. Set of training camera poses \Phi = \{\phi1, \dots, \phiK\} and their corresponding content images IT. 3. A specific reference camera pose \phiR \in \Phi (or arbitrary) and its content image IR. 4. A stylized version of the reference image SR, obtained via 2D stylization (e.g., Gatys [11] or AdaIN [20]) or manual editing. Outputs: 1. Optimized non-photorealistic radiance field \omega{NP}. 2. Stylized renderings ST for arbitrary target camera poses \phiT. Data Structures: Radiance Field \omega: A neural network mapping 3D position \mathbf{x} and view direction \mathbf{d} to density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Reference Dictionary \mathcal{D}: A collection of rays from the reference camera \phiR, each associated with a 3D intersection point and a stylized color. Pseudo-Ray Supervision \GammaR: A set of rays from training views \Phi mapped to the reference dictionary, carrying stylized color targets. Algorithm Steps: 1. Render Reference View: Render the content image IR from camera \phiR using \omegaP to obtain the reference view. 2. Stylize Reference: Apply a 2D stylization algorithm to IR to generate the stylized reference view SR. 3. Estimate Pseudo-Depth: For each ray r in the reference view, estimate the depth l(r) where the ray intersects the scene geometry. The intersection point is defined as: x(r) = o + l(r)\mathbf{d} where o is the camera origin, \mathbf{d} is the ray direction, and l(r) is the depth at which the accumulated transmittance drops below a threshold \sigmaz: l(r) = \min \left\{ ti \mid \sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj (t{j+1} - tj) \ge \sigmaz \right\}. 4. Build Reference Dictionary: Construct a dictionary \mathcal{D} for SR by storing the mapping from pixel coordinates (x,y,z) to the stylized color \hat{C}R(r) and the ray direction. 5. Reference Ray Registration (R3): For each training ray rj from poses \Phi \setminus \{\phiR\}, find a corresponding ray \hat{r}j in the reference dictionary \mathcal{D} (associated with \phiR) that minimizes the Euclidean distance between their 3D intersection points. The registration constraint requires that the intersection point of rj falls into the same voxel D(x,y,z) as the reference ray, and the angle between their directions \mathbf{d}{ri} and \mathbf{d}{rj} is less than a threshold \theta: \hat{r}j = \arg \min{r \in \mathcal{D}} \| x(rj) - x(r) \|2 \quad \text{subject to} \quad \angle(\mathbf{d}{ri}, \mathbf{d}{rj}) < \theta. 6. Construct Pseudo-Ray Supervision: Create the supervision set \GammaR by assigning the stylized color \hat{C}R(\hat{r}j) from the reference dictionary to the registered training ray rj. 7. Template-based Correspondence Module (TCM): For regions in the reference view that are occluded in the training views (or vice versa), use TCM to propagate style implicitly. This module uses feature matching to fill occluded regions with perceptually similar styles, ensuring consistency where direct ray registration is impossible. 8. Optimize NP Radiance Field: Train \omega{NP} by minimizing a composite loss function \mathcal{L}{NP} that includes: Explicit Supervision: Photometric loss between the rendered color \hat{C}{NP}(rj) and the stylized color from \GammaR for registered rays. Feature Loss: Style loss (e.g., Gram matrix distance) between features of the rendered image and SR. Implicit Supervision: Loss terms derived from TCM for occluded regions. \mathcal{L}{NP} = \mathcal{L}{ref} + \mathcal{L}{feat} + \mathcal{L}{color}. 9. Inference: Render stylized images ST from arbitrary target poses \phiT using the optimized \omega{NP}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def refnproptimize(omegaP, phiR, IR, SR, Phi, sigmaz, theta): """ Optimizes a non-photorealistic radiance field using reference-based stylization. Args: omegaP: Pre-trained photorealistic radiance field. phiR: Reference camera pose. IR: Content image for reference view. SR: Stylized reference image. Phi: Set of training camera poses. sigmaz: Depth threshold for pseudo-depth estimation. theta: Maximum angle threshold for ray registration. Returns: omegaNP: Optimized non-photorealistic radiance field. """ # Step 1 & 2: Reference view is already stylized to SR # Step 3 & 4: Build Reference Dictionary # Sample rays from phiR refrays = samplerays(phiR) referencedict = {} for ray in refrays: # Estimate pseudo-depth l(r) # This requires querying omegaP for density along the ray lr = estimatepseudodepth(ray, omegaP, sigmaz) # Calculate intersection point x(r) = o + l(r)d xr = ray.origin + lr ray.direction # Store in dictionary mapped by voxel coordinates (x,y,z) voxelcoords = quantizetovoxel(xr) referencedict[voxelcoords] = { 'ray': ray, 'color': getpixelcolor(SR, ray.pixelcoords), 'direction': ray.direction } # Step 5 & 6: Reference Ray Registration (R3) pseudoraysupervision = [] for phi in Phi: if phi == phiR: continue trainrays = samplerays(phi) for rayj in trainrays: # Estimate intersection for training ray lj = estimatepseudodepth(rayj, omegaP, sigmaz) xj = rayj.origin + lj rayj.direction voxelcoordsj = quantizetovoxel(xj) # Find best match in reference dictionary bestmatch = None mindist = infinity if voxelcoordsj in referencedict: refentry = referencedict[voxelcoordsj] refray = refentry['ray'] # Check angle constraint angle = anglebetween(rayj.direction, refray.direction) if angle < theta: dist = euclideandistance(xj, refray.origin + lref refray.direction) # Note: lref is implicitly handled by the voxel match if dist < mindist: mindist = dist bestmatch = refentry if bestmatch is not None: # Assign stylized color from reference to training ray pseudoraysupervision.append({ 'ray': rayj, 'targetcolor': bestmatch['color'] }) # Step 7: TCM for occluded regions (Implicit Supervision) # This module handles regions where direct registration fails # Implementation details depend on specific feature matching library tcmloss = computeimplicitstyleloss(SR, omegaP, phiR, Phi) # Step 8: Optimize NP Radiance Field omegaNP = initializeradiancefield() for iteration in range(numiterations): # Sample rays from training poses batchrays = samplebatchrays(Phi) # Render colors using omegaNP renderedcolors = rendervolume(batchrays, omegaNP) # Compute explicit loss for registered rays explicitloss = 0 for sup in pseudoraysupervision: # Find corresponding rendered color for sup['ray'] # In practice, this is done via batch rendering renderedc = getrenderedcolorforray(renderedcolors, sup['ray']) targetc = sup['targetcolor'] explicitloss += mseloss(renderedc, targetc) # Compute feature loss (style loss) featureloss = computestyleloss(renderedcolors, SR) # Total loss totalloss = explicitloss + featureloss + tcmloss # Backpropagate and update omegaNP updateweights(omegaNP, totalloss) return omegaNP def estimatepseudodepth(ray, omegaP, sigmaz): """ Estimates depth l(r) where accumulated transmittance drops below sigmaz. """ # Sample points along ray tvalues = linspace(ray.origin, ray.origin + ray.direction maxdist, Nsamples) accumulatedsigma = 0 lr = maxdist for i, t in enumerate(tvalues): sigma = omegaP.querydensity(t, ray.direction) deltat = tvalues[i+1] - t if i < len(tvalues)-1 else 0 accumulatedsigma += sigma deltat if accumulatedsigma >= sigmaz: lr = t break return lr Parameters: \sigmaz: Depth threshold for pseudo-depth estimation. Not given in the sources. \theta: Angle threshold for ray registration. Not given in the sources. N: Number of samples per ray. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Occlusions: Rays from training views may not intersect the same 3D points as reference rays due to occlusion. R3 handles explicit supervision for visible regions, while TCM handles implicit supervision for occluded regions. Over-matching: Rays with similar intersection points but vastly different directions may be incorrectly matched. The angle constraint \theta prevents this. Precision: Depth estimation relies on the accuracy of \omegaP. Errors in \omegaP propagate to the pseudo-depth and thus the ray registration. A sub-method for establishing semantic consistency by mapping stylized reference pixels to 3D space via pseudo-depth and voxel-based matching. It provides explicit supervision for visible regions. Choose it when semantic correspondence is critical and a pre-trained geometric model is available. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of training views, samples per ray, and the size of the reference dictionary. Ray registration requires searching the dictionary for each training ray, which can be optimized with spatial hashing (voxels). Memory Complexity: Requires storing the reference dictionary and the optimized NP radiance field. The dictionary size is proportional to the resolution of the reference view. Strengths: Preserves semantic correspondence better than global style transfer methods; handles occlusions via TCM; controllable via single reference image. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the pre-trained photorealistic radiance field \omegaP for geometry; may struggle with large viewpoint changes where ray registration fails; requires 2D stylization quality. When to use: When stylizing a known 3D scene with a specific artistic style from a single reference image while maintaining object identity and structure. When not to use: When no pre-trained NeRF is available; when the reference view is significantly different from the training views (large baseline); when real-time performance is required without optimization. Ref-NPR was introduced in 2023 by the authors of "Ref-NPR: Reference-Based Non-Photorealistic Radiance Fields for Controllable Scene Stylization". It addresses the limitation of existing 3D scene stylization methods that lack meaningful semantic correspondences between the reference and novel views. The method builds on the differentiable rendering of NeRF and incorporates techniques from 2D style transfer (Gatys, AdaIN) and 3D geometry estimation. name: Reference Ray Registration (R3)
body: Reference Ray Registration (R3) is a method for establishing semantic consistency between a stylized reference view and novel views in non-photorealistic radiance field optimization. It solves the problem of propagating style from a single 2D reference image to 3D novel views by creating a reference dictionary of rays and assigning stylized colors to registered novel view rays. Unlike methods that rely solely on 2D warping or implicit feature matching, R3 explicitly maps pixels in the stylized reference view to 3D space using pseudo-depth information to create a supervision signal for novel views. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A pre-trained photorealistic radiance field \omegaP (typically Plenoxels), a stylized reference view SR with camera pose \phiR, a set of accessible camera poses \Phi for novel views, and a foreground mask for the reference view. Outputs: A reference-dependent pseudo-ray supervision set \GammaR, which contains registered rays from novel views and their assigned stylized colors. Data Structures Reference Dictionary D: A 3D grid (cube) containing 256^3 voxels. Each entry D(x,y,z) stores a list of rays. Maximum number of rays stored per entry: 8. Supervision Set \GammaR: A collection of tuples (rj, \hat{C}R(\hat{r}j)) where rj is a registered ray and \hat{C}R(\hat{r}j) is the assigned stylized color. Steps 1. Estimate Pseudo-Depth: Estimate pseudo-depth information for the radiance field \omegaP using the depth rendering property. Let l(ri) be the ray length (pseudo-depth) for a ray ri. 2. Map Reference Pixels to 3D: For each pixel in the stylized reference view SR, estimate the 3D intersection point x(ri) of the corresponding ray ri \in \phiR using the pseudo-depth l(ri). 3. Construct Reference Dictionary: Split 3D space into discrete voxels. For each ray ri in the reference camera set \phiR, compute its intersection point x(ri) and map it to a voxel index (x,y,z) using a quantization operator Q(\cdot). The dictionary is defined as: D(x,y,z) = \{ ri \in \phiR \mid Q(x(ri)) = (x, y, z) \} 4. Register Novel View Rays: For each ray rj from the accessible camera poses \Phi (or \phiR), find a ray \hat{r}j in the reference dictionary D(x,y,z) such that \hat{r}j intersects the same voxel and the angle between their directions d{ri} and d{rj} is within a threshold \theta. The registration finds the ray minimizing the distance in the voxel: \arg \min \| x(ri) - x(rj) \|^2, \quad \text{subject to } ri \in D(x,y,z) \text{ and } \angle(d{ri}, d{rj}) < \theta 5. Assign Colors: Construct the reference-dependent pseudo-ray supervision set \GammaR by collecting each validated, registered ray rj and assigning its color \hat{C}R(\hat{r}j) according to the corresponding reference ray \hat{r}j. The set is defined as: \GammaR = \{ (rj, \hat{C}R(\hat{r}j)) \mid rj \in \Phi \cup \phiR, \hat{r}j \neq \emptyset \} Parameters Dictionary Size: 256^3 voxels. Max Rays per Voxel: 8. Angle Constraint: \cos(\theta) > 0.6. Sample Size: |Ns| = 10^6 pseudo-ray samples per training step, with half from \phiR and half from registered rays in correlated views. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Mask Boundary Overflow: To avoid the stylized view overflowing onto the background at the mask boundary, apply a 2D morphological erosion on the foreground mask in R3. Dictionary Compactness: In the Tanks and Temples (T&T) dataset, register only rays in Plenoxels’s foreground model (apart from the reference view) to make the dictionary more compact. Occlusion: R3 struggles to register reference rays to occluded regions under the reference camera, especially in 360° scenes. This is addressed by the Template-Based Correspondence Module (TCM). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def referencerayregistration(omegaP, SR, phiR, Phi, foregroundmask): """ omegaP: Pre-trained radiance field for depth estimation SR: Stylized reference view phiR: Camera pose of the reference view Phi: Set of accessible camera poses for novel views foregroundmask: Binary mask for the reference view """ # 1. Erode foreground mask to prevent boundary overflow erodedmask = morphologicalerosion(foregroundmask) # 2. Estimate pseudo-depths for reference rays # Rays from reference camera refrays = getraysfrompose(phiR, SR.resolution) pseudodepths = estimatedepth(omegaP, refrays) # 3. Construct Reference Dictionary D # D is a 3D array of size 256^3, each entry is a list of rays D = initializedictionary(size=256) quantizationop = QuantizationOperator(gridsize=256) for ray in refrays: if not isinmask(ray, erodedmask): continue # Estimate 3D intersection point from pseudo-depth xray = ray.origin + ray.direction pseudodepths[ray.id] # Map to voxel index voxelidx = quantizationop(xray) # Add to dictionary if space available (max 8 rays) if len(D[voxelidx]) < 8: D[voxelidx].append(ray) # 4. Register novel view rays and build supervision set GammaR GammaR = [] anglethresholdcos = 0.6 # Combine reference rays and novel view rays for registration allcandidaterays = list(Phi.rays) + list(refrays) for rj in allcandidaterays: xj = rj.origin + rj.direction estimatedepth(omegaP, rj) voxelidxj = quantizationop(xj) bestmatch = None mindist = infinity bestmatchray = None # Search for a ray in the same voxel with similar direction for ri in D[voxelidxj]: xi = ri.origin + ri.direction pseudodepths[ri.id] # Check angle constraint cosangle = dotproduct(normalize(ri.direction), normalize(rj.direction)) if cosangle < anglethresholdcos: continue # Check distance in voxel space dist = squareddistance(xi, xj) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist bestmatch = ri bestmatchray = ri if bestmatch is not None: # Assign stylized color from the matched reference ray # CR denotes the stylized color according to SR assignedcolor = getstylizedcolor(SR, bestmatch) GammaR.append((rj, assignedcolor)) return GammaR A module that leverages semantic correspondence consistency to broadcast reference style to novel views with semantically similar content, overcoming occlusion issues in 360° scenes where R3 fails to register reference rays. It uses a content-style mapping template established from the stylized reference view and source content to provide implicit feature-level supervision. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: The reference dictionary D consumes memory proportional to 256^3 voxels, with up to 8 rays per voxel. Measured Performance: Evaluated on Tanks and Temples (T&T), LLFF, and Synthetic datasets. Trained on one NVIDIA 3090 GPU for 10 epochs. Strengths: Establishes explicit semantic consistency between stylized reference and novel views using 3D information. Limitations: Struggles with occluded regions in 360° scenes without the TCM module. When to use: When stylizing a 3D scene with a single 2D reference view and maintaining semantic consistency across novel views is required. When not to use: When the scene has significant occlusions relative to the reference view and TCM is not available or applicable. Reference Ray Registration (R3) is part of the Ref-NPR (Reference-Based Non-Photorealistic Radiance Fields) method, introduced in 2023. It builds on the idea that precise 3D positions and camera parameters enable pixel-wise correspondence between views, utilizing pseudo-depth from a radiance field to create supervision signals. Ref-NPR is based on the ARF codebase and uses Plenoxels as the radiance field representation. name: Template-Based Correspondence Module
body: The Template-Based Correspondence Module (TCM) is a method for non-photorealistic radiance field optimization that broadcasts style from a reference view to novel views by enforcing semantic correspondence consistency. It addresses the limitation of Reference Ray Registration (R3), which fails to register reference rays to occluded regions in 360° scenes, by using a content-style mapping template to guide stylization across the entire scene. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: \omegaP: Photorealistic radiance field. \omega{NP}: Non-photorealistic radiance field (to be optimized). IR: Content reference image. SR: Style reference image. \phi: Camera pose for a content domain view. \phiR: Reference camera pose. Outputs: Optimized \omega{NP}. Stylized novel views rendered from \omega{NP}. Data Structures: Feature Maps: High-level semantic feature maps FI, F{IR}, F{SR}, FG, and \hat{F}S. These are 2D arrays of feature vectors. The specific extractor is VGG16. Features used for loss calculation are concatenated from stages 3 and 4 (relu 3, relu 4). Color Patches: Average color \bar{C} for patches at feature-level indices. Parameters: \lambda0: Balancing factor for feature loss, typically 5 \times 10^{-3}. \lambdac: Balancing factor for color loss, typically 5. \lambdar, \lambdaf: Balancing factors for reference and feature terms in the total objective, typically 1. dist(a, b): Distance metric between feature vectors, implemented as cosine distance. Steps: 1. Extract Reference Features: Compute semantic feature maps F{IR} from content reference IR and F{SR} from style reference SR using a pre-trained VGG16 extractor. 2. Render and Extract Content Features: For a content domain view I rendered from \omegaP under camera pose \phi, compute its semantic feature map FI using the same VGG16 extractor. 3. Construct Guidance Feature (FG): Perform a search-and-replace process to map the reference style to the current content view. For each 2D position (i, j) in FI: Find the index (i^, j^) in FI that minimizes the distance to the reference feature F{IR} at (i, j): (i^, j^) = \arg \min{i0, j0} dist(FI(i0, j0), F{IR}(i, j)) Set the guidance feature at (i, j) to the style reference feature at the matched index: FG(i, j) = F{SR}(i^, j^) 4. Render Stylized View: Render a stylized view S from the non-photorealistic radiance field \omega{NP} under the same camera pose \phi. 5. Extract Stylized Features: Compute the semantic feature map \hat{F}S for the stylized view S using the VGG16 extractor. 6. Compute Feature Loss (L{feat}): Enforce implicit feature-level supervision by forcing \hat{F}S to imitate FG and match the content structure FI: L{feat} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i,j} dist(FG(i, j), \hat{F}S(i, j)) + \lambda0 \| FI(i, j) - \hat{F}S(i, j) \|2^2 where N is the number of pixels/elements. 7. Compute Color Loss (L{color}): Address color mismatches that cosine distance optimization cannot eliminate by transferring average color in patches. For each position (i, j), let \bar{C}{NP} be the average color of the patch in the stylized view at (i, j), and \bar{C}R(i^, j^) be the average color of the reference patch matched by the feature distance minimization in Step 3: L{color} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i,j} \| \bar{C}{NP}(i, j) - \bar{C}R(i^, j^) \|2^2 8. Optimize: Minimize the total objective L{NP} = \lambdaf L{feat} + \lambdar L{ref} + \lambdac L{color} to update \omega{NP}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def templatebasedcorrespondencemodule( omegaP, omegaNP, IR, SR, phi, phiR, lambda0=5e-3, lambdac=5, lambdaf=1, lambdar=1): # 1. Extract Reference Features FIR = vgg16extract(IR) FSR = vgg16extract(SR) # 2. Render and Extract Content Features I = render(omegaP, phi) FI = vgg16extract(I) # 3. Construct Guidance Feature FG H, W, C = FI.shape FG = zeroslike(FI) # Precompute distances to find matches for all (i,j) # dist is cosine distance for i in range(H): for j in range(W): target = FIR[i, j] # Find (i, j) minimizing distance to FIR[i,j] within FI mindist = infinity bestidx = (0, 0) for i0 in range(H): for j0 in range(W): d = cosinedistance(FI[i0, j0], target) if d < mindist: mindist = d bestidx = (i0, j0) istar, jstar = bestidx FG[i, j] = FSR[istar, jstar] # 4. Render Stylized View S = render(omegaNP, phi) # 5. Extract Stylized Features FShat = vgg16extract(S) # 6. Compute Feature Loss # dist(FG, FShat) is cosine distance # ||FI - FShat||2^2 is MSE featdist = cosinedistance(FG, FShat) contentdist = squaredL2norm(FI - FShat) Lfeat = mean(featdist) + lambda0 mean(contentdist) # 7. Compute Color Loss # Get average color for patches at (i,j) and matched (i,j) # Note: In implementation, patches are defined by the feature grid resolution CNP = getpatchaveragecolor(S, FI.shape) CR = getpatchaveragecolorfromreference(IR, SR, FI, FIR, FSR) # CR[i,j] corresponds to the color at the matched index (i, j) Lcolor = mean(squaredL2norm(CNP - CR)) # 8. Total Loss and Optimization # Lref is assumed to be computed separately by R3 module Lref = computereferenceloss(omegaNP, phiR) # Placeholder for R3 specific loss Ltotal = lambdaf Lfeat + lambdar Lref + lambdac Lcolor # Update omegaNP using gradient descent on Ltotal # Note: Optimize patch-wise following gradient cache strategy to save memory return omegaNP, Ltotal Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Limitation: Semantic features are extracted at the image level, which can cause memory overflow during back-propagation. The optimization of \omega{NP} should be performed patch-wise following the gradient cache strategy. Color Mismatch: Cosine distance optimization alone cannot eliminate color mismatches. The coarse color-matching loss L{color} is required to address this. Occlusion: TCM is specifically designed to handle occluded regions in 360° scenes where R3 fails, by leveraging semantic consistency across the entire scene. Time Complexity: The search-and-replace process involves finding the nearest neighbor in the feature map for each pixel, which is O(H \cdot W \cdot H \cdot W) if naive, or O(H \cdot W \log(H \cdot W)) with optimized spatial indexing. The feature extraction and loss computation are linear in the number of pixels N. Memory Complexity: High, due to storing feature maps for multiple views and the need for gradient caching during patch-wise optimization. Strengths: Overcomes occlusion issues in 360° scenes by broadcasting style based on semantic correspondence rather than just geometric ray registration. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that semantic correspondence is consistent before and after stylization, which may not hold for all scenes or styles. Computationally expensive due to feature matching and VGG16 extraction. When to use: When stylizing 360° scenes with significant occlusions where reference-based ray registration fails to cover all regions. When not to use: For scenes where semantic consistency is not a valid assumption or when computational resources are severely limited. The Template-Based Correspondence Module was introduced in the Ref-NPR paper. It builds on the Reference Ray Registration (R3) method, addressing its inability to handle occluded regions in 360° scenes. The method leverages the common assumption in scene stylization that semantic correspondence remains consistent across stylization. It uses VGG16 as the semantic feature extractor, following practices in prior work. The implementation is based on the ARF codebase and uses Plenoxels for scene representation. name: Conditional Radiance Field Architecture
head: Conditional NeRF, Shape-Color Disentangled NeRF
body: Conditional Radiance Field Architecture extends the standard Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) by conditioning the volumetric representation on instance-specific latent codes, enabling the modeling of an entire class of objects (e.g., "chairs") rather than a single static scene. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF by disentangling shape and appearance into separate latent codes (z^{(s)} and z^{(c)}) and modifying the network topology to support efficient editing of these attributes. Unlike global conditioning methods, it allows for specific components of the network to be updated during editing tasks, balancing computational efficiency with reconstruction accuracy. The architecture maps a 3D position \mathbf{x}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and instance-specific latent codes to density \sigma and radiance \mathbf{c}. The rendering process follows the standard differentiable volume rendering equation [44-radiance-field-optimization.md], but the network inputs and internal structure are modified to support conditional generation and editing. Inputs: 3D position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Viewing direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Shape code z^{(s)} \in \mathbb{R}^{ds}: Instance-specific latent vector controlling geometry. Color code z^{(c)} \in \mathbb{R}^{dc}: Instance-specific latent vector controlling appearance. Outputs: Density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}. Radiance \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3. The network is composed of modular parts to disentangle shape and color. It builds on the standard NeRF architecture [4972-neural-radiance-fields.md] with the following specific modifications: 1. Skip Connections: The shape code z^{(s)} and the embedded input points (position \mathbf{x} and direction \mathbf{d}) are fed into two places: The "fusion shape network" (the initial layers processing geometry). The very beginning of the network (standard NeRF skip connection). 2. Code Injection: When injecting a shape code z^{(s)} or color code z^{(c)} into a specific layer l: The code is passed through a linear layer Wl followed by a ReLU nonlinearity. The output is concatenated with the layer's input features. Formula for injection at layer l: \text{input}l' = \text{concat}(\text{input}l, \text{ReLU}(Wl z^{(k)})) where k \in \{s, c\}. 3. Bottleneck: A bottleneck layer is introduced in the architecture to reduce dimensionality, making feature caching computationally feasible during editing. 4. Color Branch Input: The input to the color branch is an 8-dimensional vector. This vector is cached during color editing to avoid recomputation. 1. Embedding: Embed position \mathbf{x} and direction \mathbf{d} using positional encoding (as in standard NeRF). 2. Shape Processing: Concatenate embedded \mathbf{x}, embedded \mathbf{d}, and shape code z^{(s)}. Pass through the initial layers (fusion shape network). Inject z^{(s)} into subsequent layers via the linear+ReLU+concat mechanism. 3. Color Processing: Extract the 8-dimensional bottleneck feature vector. Inject color code z^{(c)} into the later layers of the network via the linear+ReLU+concat mechanism. 4. Output Prediction: The network outputs density \sigma and radiance \mathbf{c}. Density \sigma is typically passed through a softplus or ReLU to ensure non-negativity (implementation detail inferred from and standard practice, though does not explicitly specify the activation for \sigma in the base architecture, it relies on the standard NeRF formulation). 5. Rendering: Sample points along rays. Evaluate \sigma and \mathbf{c} for each point using the conditional network. Compute transmittance Ti and accumulated color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) using the standard volume rendering equation [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right). Shape Code Dimension (ds): Not given in the sources. Color Code Dimension (dc): Not given in the sources. Bottleneck Dimension: 8 dimensions for the color branch input. Linear Layer Channels: Not specified for the base conditional architecture. View Direction Dependence: Using only one training view per instance can cause color inconsistency across rendered views. This is addressed by regularizing the view dependence of radiance \mathbf{c} with a self-consistency loss. Editing Stability: Updating all network weights is slow; updating only latent codes yields low quality. The hybrid update strategy (updating specific layers and codes) is required for efficient editing. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def conditionalnerfforward(x, d, zs, zc): """ Forward pass for Conditional Radiance Field. Args: x: 3D position, shape (..., 3) d: Viewing direction, shape (..., 3) zs: Shape code, shape (..., ds) zc: Color code, shape (..., dc) Returns: sigma: Density, shape (..., 1) c: Radiance, shape (..., 3) """ # 1. Embedding (Standard NeRF positional encoding) xembed = positionalencoding(x) dembed = positionalencoding(d) # 2. Initial Fusion Shape Network # Concatenate embedded inputs and shape code initialinput = concat(xembed, dembed, zs) # Process through initial layers # Note: Exact layer definitions are not provided in, # assuming a standard MLP structure with skip connections. h = initialmlp(initialinput) # 3. Inject Shape Code into Intermediate Layers # The shape code is injected into the "fusion shape network" and # potentially other layers as per the modular design. # For each layer l where shape code is injected: for l in shapeinjectionlayers: zsprojected = relu(linearlayer(l, zs)) h = concat(h, zsprojected) h = layerforward(h) # 4. Bottleneck and Color Branch # Extract 8-dimensional bottleneck vector bottleneckvec = getbottleneck(h) # Shape (..., 8) # Inject Color Code into Later Layers # The color code is injected into the later layers of the network for l in colorinjectionlayers: zcprojected = relu(linearlayer(l, zc)) h = concat(h, zcprojected) h = layerforward(h) # 5. Output Prediction sigma = outputsigma(h) c = outputcolor(h) return sigma, c def volumerendering(rays, conditionalnerf, zs, zc): """ Standard differentiable volume rendering. """ # Sample points along rays points = samplepointsalongrays(rays) # Evaluate network sigma, c = conditionalnerfforward(points, rays.direction, zs, zc) # Compute transmittance and accumulated color # Ti = exp(-sum{j=1}^{i-1} sigmaj deltaj) # C = sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai deltai)) ci accumulatedcolor = standardvolumerendering(points, sigma, c, rays.delta) return accumulatedcolor Hybrid Updates for Editing is a strategy that targets specific network components for updates to balance efficiency and accuracy during user interaction in conditional radiance fields. It updates only specific layers of the network and latent codes to achieve both accuracy and efficiency, avoiding the slowness of updating all weights and the low quality of updating only latent codes. Unlike updating the entire network or only codes, this method updates only a subset of components (later layers) to achieve significant computational speed-up. Not given in the sources. A neural radiance field network that maps 3D coordinates and view directions to appearance a and occupancy \sigma, conditioned on local latent codes w{ij} to represent multiple distinct radiance fields. It improves performance over global conditioning by decomposing the scene into many independent locally conditioned radiance fields. Definition: A modular network architecture for conditional radiance fields that includes a shape branch shared across object instances to capture part semantics. The shape branch provides an inductive bias to encode a shared representation whenever possible, improving shape reconstruction accuracy. Layout: The network weights are updated during color and shape editing, while codes remain static in the "Network with Shared Branch" variant. In the "Hybrid Update" variant, the shape code is updated during shape editing, network weights are updated during color editing, and network weights are updated during shape editing. Comparison: Sampling higher resolution feature maps directly from the radiance field yields higher quality results than sampling at low resolution and applying many refinement blocks, but incurs significantly higher computational cost. GSN uses locally conditioned radiance fields, where the scene is decomposed into many independent locally conditioned radiance fields, improving performance over global conditioning. Time Complexity: The base architecture has similar time complexity to standard NeRF per ray evaluation, but the modular design and code injection add minor overhead. Hybrid updates reduce training time for editing tasks by limiting the number of parameters updated. Memory Complexity: The bottleneck layer (8-dimensional input to color branch) allows for feature caching, reducing memory usage during editing. Standard NeRF memory usage applies to the forward pass. Performance: The architecture enables effective user edits with significant computational speed-up compared to updating the entire network. It handles complex edits without explicit spatial or boundary constraints, and edits appear consistently across viewpoints. Strengths: Disentangles shape and appearance; supports editing of entire object classes; efficient editing via hybrid updates. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of injection layers and code dimensions; view dependence can cause inconsistencies if not regularized. Conditional Radiance Field Architecture was introduced in "Editing Conditional Radiance Fields". It builds on the original NeRF representation [4972-neural-radiance-fields.md] to enable editing over an entire shape class (e.g., "chairs") rather than a single static scene. The work investigates which parts of the network affect different editing tasks, showing that shape and color edits can effectively take place in the later layers of the network. It also introduces a shape branch shared across object instances to implicitly bias the network to encode a shared representation.
