name: Hybrid Updates for Editing
head: Hybrid Network Update Strategy, Selective Layer Finetuning
body: Hybrid Updates for Editing is a strategy that targets specific network components for updates to balance efficiency and accuracy during user interaction in conditional radiance fields. It updates only specific layers of the network and latent codes to achieve both accuracy and efficiency, avoiding the slowness of updating all weights and the low quality of updating only latent codes. Unlike updating the entire network or only codes, this method updates only a subset of components (later layers) to achieve significant computational speed-up. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A pre-trained conditional radiance field model F consisting of shared shape network F{share}, instance-specific shape network F{inst}, fusion shape network F{fuse}, output density network F{dens}, and output radiance network F{rad}. User constraints (e.g., target colors or shape modifications). Outputs: Updated network weights for the selected layers and updated latent codes (z^{(s)} for shape, z^{(c)} for color). Data Structures: Shape Code (z^{(s)}): 32-dimensional vector. Color Code (z^{(c)}): 32-dimensional vector. Network Components: F{share}: Operates on positional encoding \gamma(x). F{inst}: Conditioned on z^{(s)} and \gamma(x). F{fuse}: Fuses representations from F{share} and F{inst}. F{dens}: Linear layer taking output of F{fuse} to predict density \sigma. F{rad}: Takes concatenated output of F{fuse}, z^{(c)}, and viewing direction encoding \gamma(d) to predict radiance c. Parameters: Learning Rate: 10^{-2} for editing optimization steps. (Note: Initial training uses 10^{-4}). Optimizer: Adam. Ray Sampling: Color editing: Randomly sample 64 rays. Shape editing: Randomly sample 8,192 rays. Algorithm Steps: The method distinguishes between shape editing and color editing, updating different subsets of the network. 1. Initialize Optimization: Load pre-trained conditional radiance field F. Initialize latent codes z^{(s)} and z^{(c)} if not already present or if joint optimization is required. Set learning rate \eta = 10^{-2}. 2. Determine Edit Type and Target Components: If Color Editing: Target components: Output radiance network F{rad} and color code z^{(c)}. Note: The source states "potentially network weights" generally, but specifies for color editing: "Update only F{rad} and z^{(c)}". If Shape Editing: Target components: Fusion shape network F{fuse} and output density network F{dens}. Also update shape code z^{(s)}. 3. Apply Feature Caching (Optional but Recommended): Identify network components that remain unchanged during the specific edit. For Color Editing: Since only F{rad} is optimized, its input features are unchanged. Cache the outputs of F{share}, F{inst}, and F{fuse} (specifically the input to F{rad}) for the views being rendered/optimized. For Shape Editing: Cache outputs of components not in \{F{fuse}, F{dens}\} if applicable, though the primary speedup comes from gradient computation reduction. Implementation Note: During optimization, skip forward passes for cached components and use stored values. 4. Optimization Loop: Sample rays based on edit type (64 for color, 8,192 for shape). Perform forward pass through the network: Compute features using cached values where applicable. Compute gradients only for the target components (F{rad}, z^{(c)} for color; F{fuse}, F{dens}, z^{(s)} for shape). Compute loss (e.g., reconstruction loss L{rec} based on user constraints). Update target parameters using Adam optimizer with \eta = 10^{-2}. Repeat until convergence or user satisfaction. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusions: The basic method assumes desired object parts do not occlude other parts. Additional slower methods are required for occluded edits (see appendix of source). Precision: Standard floating-point precision is assumed; no specific bit-packing is mentioned for the codes or weights in the context of the update strategy itself. Boundary Conditions: The method relies on the conditional radiance field architecture being properly trained first. Updating only later layers assumes the earlier layers (shared shape) provide a sufficient base representation. Feature caching is an optimization technique that caches network outputs that remain unchanged during editing to avoid unnecessary computation. During color editing optimization, since only F{rad} is optimized, its input features (outputs of F{share}, F{inst}, F{fuse}) are cached. This reduces rendering time for a 256x256 image from 6.2 to under 0.8 seconds (7.8x speedup). It also accelerates color edit optimization by 3.2x and shape edit optimization by 1.9x. Time and Memory Complexity: Optimization Time: Overall training optimization time is reduced by 3.2x (from 1,081 to 342 seconds) using hybrid updates compared to updating the entire network. Color editing optimization time is reduced from 972 to 260 seconds (3.7x speedup) compared to optimizing the whole network. Shape editing optimization time is reduced by 1.9x. Rendering Time: Rendering time for a 256x256 image is reduced from 6.2 to under 0.8 seconds (7.8x speedup) with feature caching during color edits. Subsampling Impact: Subsampling user constraints provides additional speedups: 24x for color edits and 2.9x for shape edits. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significant computational speed-up while maintaining edit accuracy. Avoids unwanted changes in unedited regions that can occur when updating the entire network. Efficiently propagates edits to unseen views. Limitations: Requires identifying the correct network components for specific edits (shape vs. color). May not handle complex occlusions as effectively as full network updates without additional methods. When to Use: Use when user interaction requires real-time or near-real-time feedback for color or shape edits in a conditional radiance field. Use when computational resources are limited but high-quality editing is required. When Not to Use: Use full network updates if the edit requires changes to the shared shape representation or if the specific layer mapping is unknown. Use if the scene has complex occlusions that require global re-optimization (unless the slower occlusion-handling method is employed). Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Editing Conditional Radiance Fields". History and Development: The approach builds upon neural radiance fields (NeRF) and adapts them to a 3D neural editing setting for object classes (e.g., "chairs"). It addresses the limitations of prior neural editing approaches by proposing a hybrid update strategy that targets specific network components. The authors observed that shape and color edits can effectively take place in the later layers of the network, motivating the selective update strategy. Usage: Demonstrated on various editing tasks over three shape datasets, showing effectiveness for object view synthesis, color editing, and shape editing. Also applied to editing the appearance and shape of real photographs, with edits propagating to extrapolated novel views. name: Conditional Radiance Field Editing
head: Editing Fine Network Only
body: Conditional Radiance Field Editing modifies a trained conditional radiance field to alter its appearance or geometry without retraining the entire model from scratch. It solves the problem of efficient, targeted scene manipulation by freezing the coarse network and optimizing only the fine network's parameters and associated latent codes. Unlike Hybrid Updates for Editing, which may involve more complex update strategies, this method relies on a strict separation of coarse and fine networks to isolate the editing domain. The method operates on a conditional radiance field architecture that consists of a coarse network F{coarse} and a fine network F{fine}, along with latent codes. The editing process targets only the fine network components. Inputs: A pre-trained conditional radiance field model (F{coarse}, F{fine}, and associated codes). A target edited view or scene configuration. Training rays sampled from the target configuration. Outputs: Updated parameters for F{fine} and its associated latent codes. The coarse network F{coarse} remains unchanged. Data Structures: The color branch of the fine network accepts an 8-dimensional vector input, which is cached during editing to improve computational feasibility. Latent codes (shape and color codes) are optimized alongside network weights. Steps: 1. Freeze Coarse Network: Set all parameters in F{coarse} to non-trainable (gradient disabled). 2. Initialize Optimizer: Configure an Adam optimizer for the trainable parameters of F{fine} and the latent codes. Learning rate: \eta = 10^{-2}. Beta parameters: \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.999. Epsilon: \epsilon = 10^{-8}. 3. Sample Training Rays: Randomly select an edited view of the instance. Randomly sample batches of rays from a subsampled set of foreground and background rays corresponding to this view. 4. Optimize: Iterate for 100 iterations. Forward pass through F{fine} using the sampled rays and current latent codes. Compute loss against the target rendered image or view. Backpropagate gradients to update F{fine} parameters and latent codes. Keep F{coarse} parameters constant. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def editconditionalradiancefield(model, targetview, iterations=100, lr=1e-2): """ Edit a conditional radiance field by optimizing only the fine network. Args: model: Object containing Fcoarse, Ffine, and latent codes. targetview: The desired edited view configuration. iterations: Number of optimization steps (default 100). lr: Learning rate (default 1e-2). """ # 1. Freeze coarse network model.Fcoarse.requiresgrad(False) # 2. Initialize optimizer for fine network and codes # Parameters include Ffine weights and latent codes trainableparams = list(model.Ffine.parameters()) + model.latentcodes optimizer = Adam(trainableparams, lr=lr, betas=(0.9, 0.999), eps=1e-8) # 3. Pre-calculate or cache 8-dim vector for color branch if applicable # This is handled internally by the model's forward pass structure for i in range(iterations): # 4. Sample training rays # Randomly select an edited view view = targetview # Randomly sample batches of rays from subsampled foreground/background rays = samplerays(view) # 5. Forward pass # Render using Ffine and current codes # Fcoarse is used but gradients are not computed for it renderedimage = model.render(rays) # 6. Compute loss # Loss function is not specified in the provided notes [G: Assume standard L1/L2 pixel loss] loss = computeloss(renderedimage, targetimage) # 7. Backpropagate and update optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return model Parameters: Learning rate: 10^{-2}. Iterations: 100. Optimizer: Adam with \beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.999, \epsilon=10^{-8}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method assumes the coarse network provides a stable base; if the coarse network is poorly trained, editing the fine network may not yield satisfactory results. Precision issues may arise if the latent codes are not properly initialized or if the learning rate is too high for the specific scene complexity, though 10^{-2} is empirically set for this method. This variant involves modifying the local latent grid W directly to alter the generated scene, allowing manual control over synthesis beyond random sampling. It enables high-level modifications like mirroring or rearrangement. The process involves: 1. Obtaining the latent code grid W from a single scene (via inversion or sampling); 2. Manipulating W (e.g., mirroring along the horizontal axis); 3. Rendering the modified W to produce the edited scene. A key pitfall is that the low resolution of W in current models limits editing to high-level modifications; fine-grained control (e.g., furniture rearrangement) requires training with larger local latent grids. Additionally, editing results are most convincing when inputs are well-aligned in appearance and geometry; combining multiple scenes requires them to be similar enough. Time Complexity: The editing process is significantly faster than full training because the coarse network is frozen and only the fine network is optimized for a fixed number of iterations (100). Memory Complexity: Memory usage is comparable to standard training but reduced by the caching of the 8-dimensional vector in the color branch, which makes feature caching computationally feasible. Performance: The method achieves convergence in a small number of iterations (100) compared to the ~1M iterations required for initial training. Strengths: Efficient, targeted editing without retraining the entire model; allows for manual control via latent manipulation. Limitations: Limited to high-level edits due to latent grid resolution; requires well-aligned inputs for convincing results when combining scenes. When to use: When a user wants to quickly modify a specific aspect of a scene (e.g., rotation, mirroring) without retraining the entire radiance field. When not to use: When fine-grained structural changes are required that exceed the resolution of the latent grid. The method originates from the work on Conditional Radiance Fields, specifically detailed in "Editing Conditional Radiance Fields". It builds upon the original NeRF architecture and introduces a bottleneck for feature caching. The concept of editing via latent manipulation is further explored in "Unconstrained Scene Generation with Locally Conditioned Radiance Fields", which highlights the properties of local latent grids for scene synthesis. name: GSN Model Architecture Components
head: Locally Conditioned Radiance Fields
body: GSN (Generative Scene Network) decomposes a scene into many independent locally conditioned radiance fields to improve generative performance over global conditioning methods like GRAF. It distinguishes itself by using modulated linear layers in the generator and a local latent code representation W \in \mathbb{R}^{c \times s \times s}, whereas GRAF uses global conditioning with standard linear layers and \pi-GAN uses modulated sine layers. The core mechanism of GSN is the decomposition of the scene representation into a grid of local radiance fields, each conditioned by a local latent code. Local Latent Code Representation Instead of a single global latent vector w \in \mathbb{R}^c that conditions the entire radiance field f\theta, GSN uses a local latent grid W \in \mathbb{R}^{c \times s \times s}. This decomposition allows the scene to be modeled as many independent locally conditioned radiance fields, which drastically improves generative performance (e.g., reducing FID from 68.42 to 41.75 and SwAV-FID from 6.14 to 4.14 in ablation studies). Local Coordinate System and Feature Sharing Each local radiance field operates within its own local coordinate system. This design enables feature sharing: a latent code w{ij} at grid position (i, j) can represent the same semantic scene part regardless of its absolute position in the global grid. This robustness is validated by rigidly rearranging latent codes via 2D rotation; models with local coordinate systems maintain lower FID scores under rearrangement compared to global coordinate systems. Camera Pose Normalization Camera poses are normalized relative to the middle frame of a sub-sequence during training. This enforces an egocentric coordinate system with the origin at the center of the scene, ensuring consistent spatial relationships across different viewpoints. Generator Network Architecture The radiance field generator in GSN utilizes modulated linear layers. This contrasts with GRAF, which uses standard linear layers, and \pi-GAN, which employs modulated sine layers. All compared models use the same base architecture and training pipeline to ensure fair comparison. GSN was introduced in the paper "Unconstrained Scene Generation with Locally Conditioned Radiance Fields". The method was developed to address limitations in global conditioning approaches for generative modeling of radiance fields. It was evaluated on unconstrained scene generation tasks where an interactive agent explores scenes, collecting RGB, depth, and camera pose data. Performance was measured using Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and SwAV-FID metrics, sampling 5,000 real and 5,000 generated images for evaluation. name: Hierarchical and Distributed Optimization
body: Hierarchical and Distributed Optimization refers to strategies for scaling Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) training to large-scale scenes or correcting imperfect camera poses by decomposing the optimization problem. It addresses the limitations of standard single-stage optimization, which fails with large initial pose errors [8223-cascaded-bundle-adjusting-neural-radiance-fields-cbarf.md] or suffers from memory bottlenecks and blending artifacts when scaling to arbitrarily large scenes [10947-nerf-xl-joint-training.md]. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like BlockNeRF or MegaNeRF by either using a cascaded coarse-to-fine pose refinement strategy [8223-cascaded-bundle-adjusting-neural-radiance-fields-cbarf.md] or by enforcing 0% overlap with joint training of global embeddings to eliminate train-test discrepancies [10947-nerf-xl-joint-training.md]. The family relies on the differentiability of the forward rendering operator and the propagation of gradients through the integration steps [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. The core mechanism is the evaluation of the volume rendering equation and the computation of gradients with respect to scene parameters (density, geometry, transfer functions, camera poses) [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. The standard emission-absorption model computes the color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} as [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \sigmai is the density, \deltai is the step size, \mathbf{c}i is the color, and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. Differentiation strategies fall into three main categories [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]: 1. Reverse-Mode Automatic Differentiation (AD): Standard backpropagation through the computational graph. This requires storing O(kn) intermediate states (where n is pixels and k is samples), leading to high memory usage [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. 2. Adjoint Method: Computes gradients by propagating adjoint variables backward through the rendering algorithm, evaluating the chain rule from output to input. This has computational complexity largely constant in the number of parameters, making it preferable for optimizing many parameters like the transfer function [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. 3. Analytic Inversion / Explicit Gradients: Uses a-priori knowledge of the DVR operations to invert the order of operations or derive closed-form gradients, reducing memory consumption to O(n) by avoiding the storage of intermediate results [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. CBARF is a 3D reconstruction framework that simultaneously optimizes camera poses and scene representation from input images with imperfect or partially unknown camera poses [8223-cascaded-bundle-adjusting-neural-radiance-fields-cbarf.md]. It addresses the limitation where standard NeRF and single-stage Bundle Adjustment (BA) methods fail or over-fit when initial pose deviations are large [8223-cascaded-bundle-adjusting-neural-radiance-fields-cbarf.md]. Unlike single-stage BA which quickly falls into sub-optimal solutions, CBARF uses a coarse-to-fine multi-stage approach with cascaded compact BA modules to progressively refine poses, avoiding the learning of incorrect scene representations [8223-cascaded-bundle-adjusting-neural-radiance-fields-cbarf.md]. NeRF-XL is a method for distributing Neural Radiance Fields across multiple GPUs by allocating NeRF parameters across a disjoint set of spatial regions and training them jointly, enabling arbitrarily large capacity without the redundancy and blending artifacts of independent training [10947-nerf-xl-joint-training.md]. Unlike sibling methods such as BlockNeRF and MegaNeRF which rely on overlapping regions and post-hoc blending, NeRF-XL uses 0% overlap and a single unified optimization process, eliminating train-test discrepancies and per-camera embedding inconsistencies [10947-nerf-xl-joint-training.md]. An optimization step where the simplified NeRF weights are finetuned under a low-rank constraint using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to prepare for Tensor Train decomposition. Not given in the sources.

name: Cascaded Bundle-Adjusting Neural Radiance Fields (CBARF)
head: Cascaded BA, Compact BA, Compact BA Module
body: CBARF is a 3D reconstruction framework that simultaneously optimizes camera poses and scene representation from input images with imperfect or partially unknown camera poses. It addresses the limitation where standard Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and single-stage Bundle Adjustment (BA) methods fail or over-fit when initial pose deviations are large. Unlike single-stage BA which quickly falls into sub-optimal solutions, CBARF uses a coarse-to-fine multi-stage approach with cascaded compact BA modules to progressively refine poses, avoiding the learning of incorrect scene representations. CBARF operates in three phases: Coarse, Recursive, and Fine stages. The core mechanism is the iterative refinement of camera poses using compact BA modules, interspersed with a neighbor-replacement strategy to correct persistent errors, before final scene reconstruction via a density voxel grid. Inputs: Set of input images \{Ik\}{k=1}^K. Initial camera poses \{Pk^{(0)}\}{k=1}^K, which may contain significant errors. Initial scene representation (implicitly handled by the BA module's internal NeRF/MLP structure, though the final output uses a voxel grid). Outputs: Refined camera poses \{Pk^{final}\}{k=1}^K. High-quality 3D scene reconstruction using a density voxel grid. 1. Camera Pose: A 6-DoF vector or 4 \times 4 transformation matrix Pk for each view k. 2. Compact BA Module: A modified BA module based on BARF, but with reduced training iterations and adjusted learning rates. It internally maintains a neural representation (MLP) for rendering during the optimization phase. 3. Density Voxel Grid: The final scene representation used for high-quality reconstruction after pose refinement. Phase 1: Coarse Stage 1. Initialize the process with the provided imperfect poses P^{(0)}. 2. Apply the first Compact BA module to coarsely eliminate cumulative errors. The Compact BA module performs a limited number of optimization iterations to prevent over-fitting and reduce computational cost. The learning rate is adjusted to match the coarse training stage, as high-quality reconstruction is not essential at this point. Phase 2: Recursive Stage (Cascaded Optimization) This stage iteratively refines poses using a variable number of cascaded Compact BA modules. 1. Loop Detection: Determine the number of cascades adaptively using a loop detection technique to assess optimization effectiveness and avoid insufficient or excessive rounds. 2. Iteration Loop: For each cascade m = 1, 2, \dots, M: a. Compact BA Optimization: Use the pose estimates from the previous stage (or initial poses for m=1) as initialization. Run the Compact BA module for a limited number of iterations. Update poses P^{(m)} based on the optimization result. b. Neighbor-Replacement Strategy: Identification: Identify poorly estimated poses that remain inaccurate after BA optimization. Render images using the current poses and the internal neural representation. Evaluate the quality of rendered images to identify potentially inaccurate poses. Use a novel criterion based on rendered image quality to detect erroneous poses arising from over-fitting. Apply non-maxima suppression to enhance the identification of inaccurate poses. Replacement: For each identified inaccurate pose Pk, find the nearest pose from all other views in the dataset. Replace Pk with this nearest neighbor's pose. Update: Feed the updated poses into the next cascade stage. Phase 3: Fine Stage and Reconstruction 1. Final Check: After the recursive stage, check the optimized poses again to remove any remaining incorrect poses. 2. Reconstruction: Input the final refined poses \{Pk^{final}\} into a density voxel grid for high-quality scene reconstruction. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math COARSEITERATIONS = 100 COARSELR = 1e-3 RECURSIVEITERATIONS = 50 RECURSIVELR = 5e-4 QUALITYTHRESHOLD = 0.5 class SimpleMLP: """Internal neural representation (MLP) used during BA optimization.""" def init(self): self.weights = [0.1] def sample(self, pose): # Returns (sigma, c, delta) tuples for volume rendering return [(0.5, 1.0, 0.1)] def rendervolume(nerfmodel, poses, images): """Standard volume rendering equation from parent article.""" rendered = [] for pose, img in zip(poses, images): samples = nerfmodel.sample(pose) color = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 for sigma, c, delta in samples: alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma delta) color += transmittance alpha c transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) rendered.append(color) return rendered def computemseloss(rendered, target): return sum((r - t)2 for r, t in zip(rendered, target)) / len(rendered) def backpropagate(loss, poses, nerfmodel): """Standard reverse-mode automatic differentiation.""" return [0.0] len(poses), 0.0 def gradientdescentstep(poses, nerfmodel, gradients, lr): for i in range(len(poses)): poses[i] -= lr gradients[i] return poses def nonmaximasuppression(indices): """Standard NMS to remove overlapping detections.""" return sorted(indices) def loopdetection(poses, images): """Adaptive determination based on optimization effectiveness.""" # Checks convergence of pose updates to avoid insufficient/excessive rounds return 3 def CBARF(inputimages, initialposes): currentposes = [list(p) for p in initialposes] # Phase 1: Coarse Stage currentposes = compactbamodule(currentposes, inputimages, COARSEITERATIONS, COARSELR) # Phase 2: Recursive Stage numcascades = loopdetection(currentposes, inputimages) for m in range(1, numcascades + 1): currentposes = compactbamodule(currentposes, inputimages, RECURSIVEITERATIONS, RECURSIVELR) inaccurateindices = identifyinaccurateposes(currentposes, inputimages) for idx in inaccurateindices: nearestidx = findnearestposeindex(idx, currentposes) currentposes[idx] = list(currentposes[nearestidx]) # Phase 3: Fine Stage and Reconstruction finalposes = finalposecheck(currentposes) voxelgrid = densityvoxelgridreconstruction(finalposes, inputimages) return finalposes, voxelgrid def compactbamodule(poses, images, iterations, lr): nerfmodel = SimpleMLP() for i in range(iterations): renderedimages = rendervolume(nerfmodel, poses, images) loss = computemseloss(renderedimages, images) gradients = backpropagate(loss, poses, nerfmodel) poses = gradientdescentstep(poses, nerfmodel, gradients, lr) return poses def identifyinaccurateposes(poses, images): inaccurateindices = [] for i, pose in enumerate(poses): rendered = rendersingleview(pose, images[i]) qualityscore = evaluaterenderquality(rendered, images[i]) if qualityscore < QUALITYTHRESHOLD: inaccurateindices.append(i) return nonmaximasuppression(inaccurateindices) def rendersingleview(pose, targetimage): return pose def evaluaterenderquality(rendered, target): return 1.0 def findnearestposeindex(idx, poses): mindist = float('inf') nearestidx = -1 for j, pose in enumerate(poses): if j == idx: continue dist = math.sqrt(sum((a-b)2 for a, b in zip(poses[idx], pose))) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist nearestidx = j return nearestidx def finalposecheck(poses): return poses def densityvoxelgridreconstruction(poses, images): """Initialize density voxel grid and render with refined poses.""" return {} Iterations: The Compact BA module uses a reduced number of iterations compared to standard BARF. Exact values are not given in the sources. Learning Rate: Adjusted to match different training stages (coarse, recursive, fine). Exact values are not given in the sources. Number of Cascades: Adaptive, determined by loop detection. Not fixed. Large Initial Pose Deviations: Single-stage BA may over-fit or fail if initial poses have significant errors. CBARF addresses this by cascading modules. Over-fitting: Excessive iterations in BA can lead to over-fitting of the neural radiance field network, learning incorrect scene representations. The Compact BA module mitigates this by limiting iterations. Sub-optimal Solutions: Single-stage BA can quickly fall into sub-optimal solutions. Cascaded BA exhibits fluctuations at cascaded nodes, leading to better final results. Time Complexity: The method involves multiple stages of BA optimization. The Compact BA module reduces computational cost by limiting iterations. The number of cascades is adaptive, which may vary based on dataset characteristics. Memory Complexity: Not explicitly given in the sources. Performance: Multi-stage BA rectifies inaccurate poses more efficiently than single-stage BA within the same training time. Cascaded BA with neighbor-replacement demonstrates a more significant reduction in pose noise compared to single-stage BA and cascaded BA without neighbor-replacement. Strengths: Handles imperfect camera poses effectively. Prevents over-fitting and learning incorrect scene representations. Adaptive number of cascades avoids insufficient or excessive optimization. Neighbor-replacement strategy enhances performance by correcting persistent errors. Limitations: Relies on the quality of initial poses to some extent, though less than single-stage BA. Computational cost is higher than single-stage BA due to multiple stages, but optimized by Compact BA. When to Use: When input camera poses are imperfect or partially unknown, and single-stage BA methods fail or over-fit. CBARF was proposed in a paper titled "CBARF: Cascaded Bundle-Adjusting Neural Radiance Fields From Imperfect Camera Poses". It builds upon the BARF (Bundle-Adjusting NeRF) method, which uses an MLP and alternates between optimizing camera poses and the neural representation. CBARF addresses the limitations of BARF, such as over-fitting and failure with large pose deviations, by introducing a multi-stage cascaded BA approach. The framework was published in IEEE Transactions on Multimedia. name: NeRF-XL Joint Training
head: Distributed NeRF, Multi-GPU NeRF, NeRF-XL
body: NeRF-XL is a method for distributing Neural Radiance Fields across multiple GPUs by allocating NeRF parameters across a disjoint set of spatial regions and training them jointly, enabling arbitrarily large capacity without the redundancy and blending artifacts of independent training. Unlike sibling methods such as BlockNeRF and MegaNeRF which rely on overlapping regions and post-hoc blending, NeRF-XL uses 0% overlap and a single unified optimization process, eliminating train-test discrepancies and per-camera embedding inconsistencies. Inputs: N training images with known camera poses and intrinsics. A scene bounding box partitioned into K disjoint spatial regions, one per GPU. A NeRF architecture (MLP) with parameters \thetak assigned to region k. Outputs: Optimized NeRF parameters \{\theta1, \dots, \thetaK\} for each region. A single set of per-camera embeddings (appearance/pose) optimized jointly. Data Structures: Region Assignment: A mapping from 3D coordinates to GPU ID based on disjoint bounding boxes. Each GPU k stores parameters \thetak for its tile. Per-Camera Embeddings: A global list of embeddings, one per training image, shared across all GPUs. Sample Buffer: For each ray, a list of samples (ti, \mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{c}i, \sigmai, Ti) along the ray segment within the scene bounding box. Numbered Steps: 1. Partitioning: Divide the 3D scene bounding box into K disjoint, non-overlapping spatial regions. Assign each region to a distinct GPU k \in \{1, \dots, K\}. 2. Forward Pass (Local Evaluation): For a given training image and its corresponding ray: determine the intersection of the ray with the global bounding box and sample points \mathbf{x}i along the ray. For each sample \mathbf{x}i, identify the GPU k responsible for the region containing \mathbf{x}i. On GPU k, evaluate the local NeRF \thetak at \mathbf{x}i using the global per-camera embedding for the current image to obtain local color \mathbf{c}i and density \sigmai. 3. Broadcast: Collect the (\mathbf{c}i, \sigmai) pairs from all GPUs. Broadcast these sample values to all GPUs so that every GPU possesses the complete set of samples for the ray. 4. Global Volume Rendering: On each GPU, perform standard front-to-back volume rendering using the global set of samples to compute the final pixel color \mathbf{C} and transmittance. The rendering equation is: C(tn \rightarrow tf) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(tn \rightarrow t) \sigma(t) c(t) dt, \quad T(tn \rightarrow t) = \exp\left(-\int{tn}^t \sigma(s) ds\right) where T is transmittance, \sigma is density, and c is color. (Discrete approximation is standard.) 5. Loss Computation: Compute the photometric loss and the distortion loss \mathcal{L}{dist} on each GPU. The distortion loss is calculated as: \mathcal{L}{dist}(tn \rightarrow tf) = \int{tn}^{tf} w(ti)w(tj) |ti - tj| \, dti \, dtj where w(t) = T(tn \rightarrow t)\sigma(t) is the volume rendering weight. 6. Backward Pass (Local Gradient): Compute gradients for the local NeRF parameters \thetak and the global per-camera embeddings locally on each GPU. No gradient synchronization is required between GPUs during the backward pass. 7. Parameter Update: Update the local parameters \thetak locally on each GPU. Update the shared per-camera embeddings using standard distributed optimization techniques. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math numgpus = K cameraembeddings = [Embedding() for in range(numimages)] nerfparams = [MLP() for in range(numgpus)] regionbounds = [Box(mini, maxi) for i in range(numgpus)] lr = 0.001 def sampleray(origin, direction, numsamples): tvals = [i / numsamples for i in range(numsamples)] return [Point(t=t, x=origin + direction t) for t in tvals] def getgpuforpoint(point, regionbounds): for k, box in enumerate(regionbounds): if box.contains(point.x): return k return 0 def volumerender(samples): T = 1.0 color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] prevt = samples[0].t for sample in samples: delta = max(1e-6, sample.t - name: SNeRG
head: Deferred Shading NeRF, SNeRG (Deferred Shading NeRF), Sparse Neural Radiance Fields with View-dependent Effects
body: SNeRG reduces the computational cost of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by decomposing the radiance field into a deferred shading model, limiting Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) evaluations to one per ray. Unlike standard NeRF which queries view-dependent color for every sample, SNeRG caches diffuse colors and uses a small network for view-dependent effects, enabling real-time rendering. Inputs: Camera poses, intrinsics, and training images. Outputs: Rendered images and an optimized scene representation. Data Structures: 1. Sparse 3D Grid: Stores density (\sigma) and diffuse color (cd) at voxel centers, using a hash map or sparse array for memory efficiency. 2. 3D Texture Atlas: Caches baked diffuse colors for fast lookup. 3. Feature Vectors (f): Stored per voxel or interpolated, used to modulate view-dependent effects. 4. Small Network: A lightweight MLP that takes spatial and directional inputs to output view-dependent color. Steps: 1. Ray Marching: For each pixel, cast a ray through the scene and use the sparse 3D grid to quickly locate surface boundaries and skip empty space. 2. Sample Query: For each sample point x along the ray, query its eight neighbors on a low-resolution 3D grid and project x onto three axis-aligned planes to query four neighbors on each high-resolution 2D grid. Trilinearly interpolate density \sigma, diffuse color cd, and feature vectors f from these neighbors. 3. Deferred Shading: Compute transmittance T and accumulated density using standard volume rendering integration. The base color is the interpolated diffuse color cd. Pass position x, features f, and view direction v to the small network to compute the final view-dependent color c. 4. Rendering: Composite the final pixel color using the accumulated transmittance and the view-dependent color c. 5. Optimization: Minimize the difference between rendered and ground truth images. Apply a sparsity loss to reduce the VRAM usage of sparse voxels. Formulas: The radiance field is decomposed into density \sigma, diffuse color cd, and features f. The final color C(r) for a ray r is: C(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai}) ci where Ti = e^{-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj}, \deltai = x{i+1} - xi is the distance between adjacent samples, and ci is the view-dependent color computed by the small network. Parameters: Grid resolution: Low-resolution 3D grid for density/color, high-resolution 2D projections for spatial queries. Network size: Small MLP for view-dependent effects. Edge Cases: Sparse grid boundaries require careful handling to avoid artifacts. Uses hierarchical structures for adaptive resolution; chosen when scene complexity varies significantly across space. Uses explicit Gaussians instead of implicit fields; chosen for rasterization-based real-time rendering. Handles dynamic scenes; chosen when temporal coherence and motion are required. Extends to general light transport; chosen for complex material and lighting interactions. Training strategies; chosen to improve convergence and stability. Simplified radiance field representations; chosen for lightweight deployment. View-dependent networks; chosen when explicit view modulation is preferred. Decomposes fields for efficiency; chosen for memory-constrained pipelines. Optimizes both forward and inverse problems; chosen for inverse graphics tasks. Handles reflections; chosen for scenes with glossy or mirror surfaces. Uses tetrahedral meshes; chosen for structured domain decomposition. Sampling-based approaches; chosen for dense camera array inputs. Zero-shot generalization; chosen for few-shot or unseen scene synthesis. Unified representation; chosen for multi-modal scene modeling. Analytical solutions; chosen for fast, non-iterative color prediction. Uses signed distance functions; chosen for sharp surface reconstruction. Models lighting separately; chosen for relighting and material editing. Large-scale training; chosen for city-scale or massive datasets. Incorporates physical properties; chosen for physically plausible synthesis. Uses LiDAR data; chosen for metrically accurate reconstruction. Handles motion; chosen for non-rigid scene capture. High dynamic range; chosen for scenes with extreme lighting variations. GPU-optimized voxels; chosen for high-throughput voxel rendering. Combines meshes and NeRF; chosen for hybrid geometry-texture pipelines. Handles motion blur; chosen for dynamic capture with camera shake. Uses warping for geometry; chosen for self-supervised depth estimation. X-ray specific; chosen for medical or industrial volumetric imaging. Compresses fields; chosen for storage-constrained applications. Combines explicit and implicit; chosen for balancing speed and detail. Grid-based methods; chosen for deterministic memory allocation. Models residuals; chosen for incremental scene updates. Decomposes volumes; chosen for modular scene editing. Uses shading for guidance; chosen for improved surface normal accuracy. Time complexity is reduced compared to standard NeRF due to fewer MLP evaluations. Memory complexity is reduced via sparse voxels and caching. Enables real-time view synthesis. Strengths include fast rendering and memory efficiency. When to use: real-time applications and large scenes. When not to use: high-fidelity offline rendering where maximum detail is required. name: NeRF++
body: NeRF++ generates novel views for unbounded scenes by separating the scene into a foreground (inside a unit sphere) and a background (outside the sphere) using two separate Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) models. It solves the parameterization failure of standard NeRF, which assumes the entire scene fits within a bounded volume, leading to missing background elements or loss of detail due to limited sampling resolution in large-scale scenes. It sets itself apart from its parent Radiance-field optimization by explicitly handling infinite depth via radial inversion. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N RGB images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N with known camera poses and intrinsics. Outputs: Two NeRF models: F{in} for the interior volume and F{out} for the exterior volume, enabling novel view synthesis. Data Structures: 1. Scene Partitioning: The 3D space is divided by a unit sphere centered at the origin. Interior: Points \mathbf{x} where \|\mathbf{x}\| \le 1. Exterior: Points \mathbf{x} where \|\mathbf{x}\| > 1. 2. NeRF Models: F{in}: \mathbb{R}^3 \times S^2 \to \mathbb{R}^4: Maps 3D position \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} to volume density \sigma{in} and color \mathbf{c}{in}. F{out}: \mathbb{R}^3 \times S^2 \to \mathbb{R}^4: Maps 3D position \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} to volume density \sigma{out} and color \mathbf{c}{out}. Note that F{out} operates on the inverted coordinates of the exterior points. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Definition: For a pixel p in image Ii, define the camera ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the camera center and \mathbf{d} is the unit direction vector. 2. Sampling: Sample N points \{tn\}{n=1}^N along the ray within near tn and far tf bounds. Uniform random sampling is used: ti \sim U \left[ tn + \frac{i-1}{N} (tf - tn), tn + \frac{i}{N} (tf - tn) \right]. 3. Point Classification: For each sample point \mathbf{x}n = \mathbf{r}(tn), classify as Interior if \|\mathbf{x}n\| \le 1, or Exterior if \|\mathbf{x}n\| > 1. 4. Coordinate Transformation (Radial Inversion): For Exterior points, apply radial inversion to map them into the unit sphere. Let r = \|\mathbf{x}n\|. The inverted coordinate is \mathbf{x}'n = \mathbf{x}n / r^2. This allows the exterior MLP to be trained on a bounded domain. 5. NeRF Query: Query F{in}(\mathbf{x}n, \mathbf{d}) for Interior points and F{out}(\mathbf{x}'n, \mathbf{d}) for Exterior points to obtain (\sigman, \mathbf{c}n). 6. Volume Rendering Integration: Evaluate the ray integral in two parts: the segment inside the sphere and the segment outside the sphere. Let t' be the intersection distance of the ray with the unit sphere (the smaller positive root of \|\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}\|^2 = 1). The total color C(\mathbf{r}) accounts for transmittance accumulation across the boundary: C(\mathbf{r}) = \int{tn}^{t'} T(t) \sigma{in}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \mathbf{c}{in}(\mathbf{r}(t), \mathbf{d}) dt + \int{t'}^{tf} T(t) \sigma{out}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \mathbf{c}{out}(\mathbf{r}(t), \mathbf{d}) dt where T(t) = \exp\left(-\int{tn}^t \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s)) ds\right) is the accumulated transmittance. In discrete form: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i \in \text{In}} Ti (1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai}) \mathbf{c}i + T(t') \sum{j \in \text{Out}} T'j (1 - e^{-\sigmaj \deltaj}) \mathbf{c}j where T(t') is the transmittance at the sphere boundary and T'j is the transmittance relative to the start of the exterior segment. 7. Loss Calculation: Minimize the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the rendered image \hat{I} and the ground truth image I: \mathcal{L}{MSE} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \| C(\mathbf{r}) - \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) \|2^2 Pseudocode: Unverified code. tvals[:,:-1] deltas = torch.cat([deltas, torch.tensor([1e10], device=points.device).expandas(deltas[:,:1])], dim=-1) sigmaall = torch.where(isexterior, sigmaout, sigmain) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmaall deltas) T = torch.cumprod(torch.exp(-sigmaall deltas), dim=1) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[:,:1]), T[:,:-1]], dim=-1) weights = alpha T color = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) torch.where(isexterior, colorout, colorin), dim=1) return color def trainstep(self, rayo, rayd, gtcolor): predcolor = self.forward(rayo, rayd) loss = torch.mean((predcolor - gtcolor) 2) self.optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() self.optimizer.step() return loss.item() Parameters: N: Number of samples per ray. Not given in the sources. tn, tf: Near and far bounds. Not given in the sources. Sphere Radius: 1.0 (unit sphere). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision at Boundary: Sampling points exactly on the sphere boundary (\|\mathbf{x}\|=1) can cause ambiguity in which MLP to query. It is recommended to use a small epsilon or consistently assign boundary points to one domain (e.g., interior). Inversion Singularity: Points at the origin (\mathbf{x}=0) cannot be inverted. However, the origin is inside the sphere, so it is handled by F{in}. Exterior points are strictly >1 distance, so inversion is safe. Inverted Sphere Parameterization is a spatial parameterization scheme that allows Neural Radiance Fields to model 360° captures of unbounded scenes by separately representing foreground and background content. It solves the parameterization failure of standard NeRF, which assumes the entire scene fits within a bounded volume, leading to missing background elements or loss of detail due to limited sampling resolution in large-scale scenes. It sets itself apart from its parent NeRF++ by providing the specific mathematical mapping for the outer volume. Choose it when modeling 360° unbounded captures requiring precise outer volume parameterization. DoubleNeRF is a method for synthesizing dynamic scenes by representing them as the superposition of two or more static neural radiance fields, specifically separating a static background from a moving object with a static shape. Unlike NeRF++, which separates scenes using a spherical boundary, DoubleNeRF separates content semantically (background vs. foreground object) without spherical constraints, and unlike D-NeRF, it does not use time as an input or map canonical space to deformed space, assuming instead that the object's appearance is independent of its position relative to the background. Choose it for dynamic scenes with static-shaped foreground objects. This method recovers surface materials (albedo, roughness, metallic) and environment lighting from multi-view images by integrating Sur2f with differentiable rendering and a split-sum approximation of the rendering equation. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by decoupling geometry and appearance, allowing seamless transfer of different appearances to different geometries by exchanging the shading network, whereas other methods often couple them. Choose it when physically based material and lighting recovery is required. This method enables volume rendering of scenes with unbounded or complex backgrounds by mapping points outside a unit sphere into its interior, thereby eliminating the need for foreground masks during optimization. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Inverted Sphere Parameterization by explicitly using a separate density voxel grid and shallow MLP for the inverted background, rather than relying on a single continuous field or point-based representations. Choose it when avoiding foreground masks is necessary for unbounded backgrounds. SNeRF is a neural radiance field method designed for novel view synthesis in large-scale, unbounded street-view scenes collected by self-driving cars, jointly reconstructing static backgrounds and foreground moving vehicles. Unlike sibling methods such as Block-NeRF or Urban-NeRF which require heavy camera overlap or dense LiDAR depth, SNeRF operates effectively with sparse, noisy LiDAR points and minimal camera overlap by employing implicit pose refinement and a robust confidence metric. Choose it for large-scale street-view reconstruction with sparse sensor data. NDJIR is an inverse rendering method that jointly decomposes geometry (signed distance function), lighting (environment and implicit), and materials (base color, roughness, specular reflectance) by directly addressing the integrals of the rendering equation using a volume rendering framework. It sets itself apart from siblings like DoubleNeRF or SNeRF by avoiding approximations such as Spherical Gaussians, split-sum, or pre-integrated lights, instead computing the physically-based rendering integral directly within the volume rendering pipeline. Choose it when direct physical decomposition without lighting approximations is required. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S) per pixel, where N is the number of rays (pixels) and S is the number of samples per ray. The dual-MLP query adds a constant factor overhead compared to single-MLP NeRF. Memory Complexity: O(M), where M is the number of parameters in the two MLPs. No additional large data structures are required beyond the MLP weights. Measured Performance: NeRF++ enables high-quality novel view synthesis for unbounded scenes, which standard NeRF fails to do without masking or truncation. Strengths: Handles infinite background; no need for manual masking or background removal; maintains view-dependent effects in the background. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the sphere radius; performance degrades if the scene geometry does not align well with the spherical partition. When to use: Unbounded scenes (e.g., outdoor environments, cityscapes) where the background extends to infinity. When not to use: Bounded indoor scenes where standard NeRF suffices; scenes with strong occlusions that cross the sphere boundary in complex ways. NeRF++ was introduced by Zhang et al. in October 2020. It was developed to address the limitations of the original NeRF, which exhibited large computation requirements, difficulty modeling details of objects within a large scene, and vulnerability to variable illumination and transient occluders. The method was adapted to generate novel views for unbounded scenes by separating the scene using a sphere, with the inside containing foreground objects and the outside containing the background, which was reparameterized with radial inversion. It is a foundational method for unbounded NeRF variants. name: DoubleNeRF
head: Double NERF
body: DoubleNeRF is a method for synthesizing dynamic scenes by representing them as the superposition of two or more static neural radiance fields, specifically separating a static background from a moving object with a static shape. Unlike NeRF++, which separates scenes using a spherical boundary, DoubleNeRF separates content semantically (background vs. foreground object) without spherical constraints, and unlike D-NeRF, it does not use time as an input or map canonical space to deformed space, assuming instead that the object's appearance is independent of its position relative to the background. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Two sets of oriented images: Ab (background images, excluding the dynamic object) and Ao (object images, with background masked out using alpha channels). Outputs: A dynamic radiance field nd capable of rendering novel views of the dynamic scene. Data Structures and Coordinate Systems: The method relies on two distinct coordinate systems. 1. Background Scene Coordinate System (Ob Xb Yb Zb): Origin: Center of mass of the scene 3D model on the ground level. Xb axis: Directed collinear to the projection of the optical axis of the first camera in set Ab. Zb axis: Normal to the surface of the ground. Yb axis: Completes the right-handed coordinate system. 2. Object Coordinate System (Oo Xo Yo Zo): Origin: Located on the projection of the center of mass of the object to the ground plane. Xo axis: Directed toward the positive direction of the construction axis of the object (e.g., forward motion). Zo axis: Normal to the surface of the ground. Yo axis: Completes the right-handed coordinate system. Method Steps: 1. Estimate Background Field: Train a neural radiance field nb using the image set Ab. This field operates in the background coordinate system Ob Xb Yb Zb. 2. Estimate Object Field: Train a neural radiance field no using the image set Ao. The training data for no uses alpha channels to mask the background. A critical constraint is applied: for any point in no not located on the object, the volume density is equal to 0. This field operates in the object coordinate system Oo Xo Yo Zo. 3. Define Transformation: Define the rigid body transformation from the background coordinate system to the object coordinate system using a rotation matrix R{bo} and a translation vector T{bo}. 4. Superposition: Compute the dynamic radiance field nd by summing the background field and the transformed object field. Formulas: The dynamic radiance field nd at a scene point (x, y, z) is defined as: nd(x, y, z, \Theta, \phi) = nb(x, y, z, \Theta, \phi) + no(x'o, y'o, z'o, \Theta, \phi) where (x'o, y'o, z'o) are the object coordinates transformed from the scene coordinates (x, y, z). The transformation is given by: X'o = R{bo} \cdot Xo + T{bo} where Xo = [x, y, z]^T is the point in the background coordinate system, R{bo} is the rotation matrix, and T{bo} is the translation vector. Assumptions and Constraints: The surface brightness and reflections of the moving object are independent of the location of the object with respect to the background scene. The object has a static shape. The object field no contributes zero density outside the object's geometry. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def doublenerfrender(camerapose, scenepoint, Rbo, Tbo): """ Renders a single point in the scene using the DoubleNeRF superposition. Args: camerapose: Camera extrinsics and intrinsics for the target view. scenepoint: 3D point (x, y, z) in the background coordinate system. Rbo: 3x3 rotation matrix transforming background coordinates to object coordinates. Tbo: 3x1 translation vector transforming background coordinates to object coordinates. Returns: color: RGB color at the scene point. density: Volume density at the scene point. """ # 1. Evaluate Background Field # nb takes scene coordinates directly bgcolor, bgdensity = standardnerfquery(scenepoint, camerapose) # Standard NeRF forward pass # 2. Transform Scene Point to Object Coordinates # Xo is the scene point in background coordinates Xo = [float(scenepoint[0]), float(scenepoint[1]), float(scenepoint[2])] # Apply rigid transformation from background to object frame Xprimeo = [ Rbo[0][0]Xo[0] + Rbo[0][1]Xo[1] + Rbo[0][2]Xo[2] + Tbo[0], Rbo[1][0]Xo[0] + Rbo[1][1]Xo[1] + Rbo[1][2]Xo[2] + Tbo[1], Rbo[2][0]Xo[0] + Rbo[2][1]Xo[1] + Rbo[2][2]Xo[2] + Tbo[2] ] # 3. Evaluate Object Field # no takes transformed coordinates objcolor, objdensity = standardnerfquery(Xprimeo, camerapose) # Standard NeRF forward pass # 4. Superposition # The dynamic field is the sum of the two fields totaldensity = bgdensity + objdensity totalcolor = [bgcolor[0] + objcolor[0], bgcolor[1] + objcolor[1], bgcolor[2] + objcolor[2]] return totalcolor, totaldensity Complexity: The rendering complexity is effectively doubled compared to a single NeRF, as two neural network forward passes are required per sample (one for background, one for object). Performance: Evaluated on the SematicVoxels dataset using city scenes as background and cars as foreground dynamic objects. The method achieves and surpasses state-of-the-art results in dynamic scene synthesis metrics including PSNR, SSIM, LPIPs, and FID. Strengths: Handles dynamic scenes with static-shape objects without requiring time as an input. Avoids the spherical boundary artifacts and limitations of NeRF++. Separates background and foreground cleanly, allowing independent optimization. Limitations: Limited to scenes with a static background and objects with static shapes (no non-rigid deformation). Requires separate training data for background and object, with the object data needing background masking. Assumes object appearance is invariant to its position relative to the background, which may not hold for complex lighting interactions (e.g., shadows cast by the object on the background). DoubleNeRF was proposed in 2023 by authors associated with the ISPRS Archives. It was implemented using the TensorFlow library. The method was developed to address the limitation of standard NeRF, which cannot synthesize dynamic scenes. It builds on the concept of NeRF++ but diverges by using semantic separation rather than geometric (spherical) separation. It is distinct from D-NeRF, which uses time and canonical space deformation. name: Physically Based Inverse Rendering with Split-Sum Approximation
head: NVDIFFREC-based PBR, Sur2f PBR
body: This method recovers surface materials (albedo, roughness, metallic) and environment lighting from multi-view images by integrating Sur2f with differentiable rendering and a split-sum approximation of the rendering equation. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by decoupling geometry and appearance, allowing seamless transfer of different appearances to different geometries by exchanging the shading network, whereas other methods often couple them. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view RGB images, camera poses, and an initial geometry representation (from Sur2f). Outputs: Learnable environment map E, base color \mathbf{k}d, metallic value km, and surface roughness kr. Data Structures: 1. Environment Map (E): A learnable texture representing incident illumination. 2. Environment BRDF Lookup Texture (\mathbf{K}): A 2D texture storing the pre-calculated specular integral. 3. Pre-Filtered Environment Map (\mathbf{I}s): A texture obtained by convolving E with a multi-level GGX distribution. 4. Diffuse Irradiance (\mathbf{I}d): A texture/vector representing the integration of the upper hemisphere of E. Parameters: Base color \mathbf{k}d \in [0, 1]^3: View-independent diffuse term parameter. Metallic value km \in [0, 1]: View-independent diffuse term parameter. Surface roughness kr \in [0, 1]: Conditions the microfacet distribution function (D), Fresnel reflection (F), and geometric shadowing factor (G). Formulas: The BRDF B(\mathbf{l}, -\boldsymbol{\omega}) is modeled as a sum of Lambertian diffuse and Cook-Torrance specular terms: B(\mathbf{l}, -\boldsymbol{\omega}) = (1 - km) \frac{\mathbf{k}d}{\pi} + \frac{DFG}{4 \langle \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l} \rangle \langle \mathbf{n} \cdot -\boldsymbol{\omega} \rangle} where \mathbf{n} is the surface normal, \mathbf{l} is the light direction, and \boldsymbol{\omega} is the view direction. The rendering equation is split into diffuse and specular components: L(\mathbf{x}S, \boldsymbol{\omega}) = L{\text{diffuse}}(\mathbf{x}S) + L{\text{specular}}(\mathbf{x}S, \boldsymbol{\omega}) 1. Diffuse Component: Approximated using the environment map E: L{\text{diffuse}}(\mathbf{x}S) \approx (1 - km) \frac{\mathbf{k}d}{\pi} \mathbf{I}d where \mathbf{I}d is the diffuse irradiance obtained by integrating the upper hemisphere of E. 2. Specular Component: Uses split-sum approximation to handle the intractable integral: L{\text{specular}}(\mathbf{x}S, \boldsymbol{\omega}) \approx \mathbf{K} \mathbf{I}s where \mathbf{K} is the Environment BRDF stored in a 2D look-up texture searchable by kr and \langle \mathbf{n} \cdot -\boldsymbol{\omega} \rangle, and \mathbf{I}s is the Pre-Filtered Environment Map obtained by convolving E with multi-level GGX distribution. The final rendered color \mathbf{C}{\text{pbr}}(\mathbf{r}) for ray \mathbf{r} is obtained via linear-to-sRGB tone mapping: \mathbf{C}{\text{pbr}}(\mathbf{r}) = \text{ToneMap}(L(\mathbf{x}S, \boldsymbol{\omega})) Optimization: The method minimizes the L1 loss between the predicted color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) and the PBR rendered color \mathbf{C}{\text{pbr}}(\mathbf{r}): \mathcal{L}{\text{pbr}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \mathbb{L}1 \left( \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}), \mathbf{C}{\text{pbr}}(\mathbf{r}) \right) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computepbrcolor(surfacepoint, normal, viewdirection, roughness, metallic, basecolor, envmap, envbrdflut): # 1. Diffuse irradiance Id: integrate upper hemisphere of E Id = integratediffuseirradiance(envmap, normal) # 2. Diffuse term diffuseterm = (1.0 - metallic) (basecolor / math.pi) Id # 3. Specular term via split-sum # Is: convolve E with GGX distribution D based on roughness Is = prefilterenvmap(envmap, normal, roughness) # K: lookup Environment BRDF by roughness and <n. -omega> dotnv = dot(normal, -viewdirection) K = envbrdflut[roughness, dotnv] specularterm = K Is # 4. Combine and tone map L = diffuseterm + specularterm return lineartosrgb(L) def trainstep(images, poses, surfacepoints, normals, envmap, materials, envbrdflut): # Integrate Id and Is from envmap E at start of each step Id = integratediffuseirradiance(envmap, normals) Is = prefilterenvmap(envmap, normals, materials.roughness) # Render viewdirections = computeviewdirections(poses, surfacepoints) Cpbr = computepbrcolor(surfacepoints, normals, viewdirections, materials.roughness, materials.metallic, materials.basecolor, envmap, envbrdflut) # Loss loss = meanl1loss(images, Cpbr) loss.backward() def integratediffuseirradiance(envmap, normal): # Approximates integral of envmap over upper hemisphere weighted by max(0, n.l) return shevaluate(envmap, normal) def prefilterenvmap(envmap, normal, roughness): # Convolves envmap with GGX distribution D based on roughness return ggxconvolution(envmap, normal, roughness) def lineartosrgb(c): # Standard linear-to-sRGB tone mapping return [12.92 x if x <= 0.0031308 else 1.055 math.pow(x, 1.0/2.4) - 0.055 for x in c] def dot(a, b): return sum(ai bi for ai, bi in zip(a, b)) def computeviewdirections(poses, surfacepoints): return [normalize(p - pose.camerapos) for p, pose in zip(surfacepoints, poses)] def meanl1loss(images, Cpbr): return sum(abs(i - c) for i, c in zip(images, Cpbr)) / len(images) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Intractable Integral: The specular integral is intractable analytically; the split-sum approximation is required to make it computationally feasible. Lookup Texture Indexing: The Environment BRDF \mathbf{K} must be correctly indexed by roughness kr and \langle \mathbf{n} \cdot -\boldsymbol{\omega} \rangle. Tone Mapping: The final color must undergo linear-to-sRGB tone mapping to match the input image space. A hybrid representation for high-quality and efficient surface reconstruction from multi-view images. It provides the geometry and appearance disentanglement foundation for this PBR method. A differentiable rendering framework used to integrate the PBR shading model into the optimization loop. Time Complexity: Depends on the cost of integrating the environment map (\mathbf{I}d and \mathbf{I}s) at each training step. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the environment map E, the pre-filtered environment map \mathbf{I}s, and the Environment BRDF lookup texture \mathbf{K}. Strengths: Enables disentanglement of geometry and appearance, allowing seamless transfer of different appearances to different geometries. Suitable for editing and relighting tasks. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the split-sum approximation. The intractable specular integral is approximated, which may introduce errors in complex lighting scenarios. When to use: Physically based inverse rendering tasks, including editing and relighting, on NeRF synthetic datasets and DTU datasets. The method was introduced in the paper "Sur2f: A Hybrid Representation for High-Quality and Efficient Surface Reconstruction from Multi-view Images". It builds on the Sur2f representation and integrates it with NVDIFFREC for differentiable rendering. The split-sum approximation technique is based on the work cited as [16] in the source, which pre-calculates the Environment BRDF and Pre-Filtered Environment Map. Sur2f: A Hybrid Representation for High-Quality and Efficient Surface Reconstruction from Multi-view Images, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-73027-61, fetched 2026-10-26

name: SNeRF
head: Neural Radiance Fields for Street Views, S-NeRF
body: SNeRF is a neural radiance field method designed for novel view synthesis in large-scale, unbounded street-view scenes collected by self-driving cars, jointly reconstructing static backgrounds and foreground moving vehicles. Unlike sibling methods such as Block-NeRF or Urban-NeRF which require heavy camera overlap or dense LiDAR depth, SNeRF operates effectively with sparse, noisy LiDAR points and minimal camera overlap by employing implicit pose refinement and a robust confidence metric. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sparse and noisy LiDAR point clouds, multi-view RGB images from self-driving car cameras, initial camera poses derived from sensor-fusion SLAM and IMU, and viewing directions. Outputs: Synthesized novel-view RGB images and depth maps for both static background and dynamic foreground objects. Data Structures: NeRF MLPs: Two successive Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) implement the mapping function f. Input: 3D position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and viewing direction \boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: Color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and differential density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}. Pose Refinement Offsets: A learnable pair \Delta P = (\Delta R, \Delta T) where \Delta R is a rotation offset and \Delta T \in \mathbb{R}^3 is a translation offset, added to initial poses P = [R, T]. Confidence Map: A scalar value per depth sample derived from geometry and reprojection consistency, used to weight depth losses. Numbered Steps: 1. Initial Pose Estimation: Obtain initial camera poses P using sensor-fusion SLAM and IMU data from the self-driving vehicle. 2. Pose Refinement (Static Background): For static background scenes, a learning-based network implicitly learns refinement offsets \Delta P to correct SLAM errors and reduce inconsistency between multi-camera views. The refined pose is P' = P + \Delta P. 3. Virtual Camera Transformation (Moving Vehicles): For foreground moving vehicles, compute the relative position \hat{P} between the camera and the target object center. Apply a virtual camera transformation to handle the complex motion of both the ego-vehicle and the target object, enabling reconstruction of dynamic entities. 4. Depth Completion and Confidence Estimation: Propagate sparse LiDAR depths using a depth completion network (e.g., Park et al., 2020). Compute a robust confidence metric based on geometry consistency and reprojection consistency to identify and handle outliers in the sparse LiDAR data. 5. Volume Rendering: For each ray r(t) = o + td, sample N points along the ray between near and far bounds. Render the color \hat{I}(r) using the volume rendering equation: \hat{I}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai}) ci where Ti = \exp \left( -\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj \right), \deltaj = t{j+1} - tj, and ci, \sigmai are the color and density at sample ti. 6. Loss Computation: Calculate RGB loss between rendered and ground truth images, and depth loss between rendered depth and LiDAR-derived depth, weighted by the confidence metric. 7. Optimization: Train the NeRF MLPs, pose refinement network, and confidence estimator using the combined losses. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random import math def confidencenet(completeddepth, rendereddepth): """External confidence estimator per.""" return 1.0 # Placeholder for external network def depthcompletionnetwork(lidardepths): """External depth completion network per.""" return lidardepths # Placeholder for external network def snerfrender(rayorigin, raydirection, nerfmlp, poserefinementnet, initialpose, lidardepths, confidencenetfn): """Renders a single ray using SNeRF components.""" # 1. Refine Camera Pose deltaR, deltaT = poserefinementnet(initialpose) Rrefined = initialpose.R @ deltaR Trefined = initialpose.T + deltaT rayorigincam = (Rrefined.T @ (rayorigin - Trefined)) raydirectioncam = Rrefined.T @ raydirection # 2. Sample Points along Ray near, far = 0.0, 100.0 # Not given in the sources. tvals = [near + (far - near) (i + random.uniform(0, 1)) / N for i in range(N)] # 3. Query NeRF MLP colors, densities = nerfmlp(tvals, raydirectioncam) # 4. Volume Rendering deltas = [tvals[i] - tvals[i-1] for i in range(1, N)] transmittances = [1.0] for i in range(1, N): transmittances.append(transmittances[-1] math.exp(-densities[i-1] deltas[i-1])) alphas = [1.0 - math.exp(-densities[i] deltas[i]) for i in range(N-1)] alphas.append(1.0) weights = [alphas[i] transmittances[i] for i in range(N)] renderedcolor = sum(weights[i] colors[i] for i in range(N)) rendereddepth = sum(weights[i] tvals[i] for i in range(N)) # 5. Depth and Confidence completeddepth = depthcompletionnetwork(lidardepths) confidence = confidencenetfn(completeddepth, rendereddepth) return renderedcolor, rendereddepth, confidence def trainsnerf(dataset, nerfmlp, posenet, confidencenetfn, optimizer): """Alternating training loop for SNeRF.""" for epoch in range(numepochs): renderedimages = [] for view in dataset.views: ray = generateray(view.camera, view.pixelcoords) color, depth, conf = snerfrender(ray, nerfmlp, posenet, view.initialpose, view.lidar, confidencenetfn) renderedimages.append(color) # Stylization extension per stylizedimages = imagestylizationmodule(renderedimages) rgbloss = computergbloss(stylizedimages, dataset.gtimages) depthloss = computedepthloss(rendereddepths, dataset.lidardepths, confidence) totalloss = rgbloss + depthloss optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() Parameters: Number of samples (N): Not given in the sources. Learning Rate: Not given in the sources. Near/Far Bounds: Determined by the scene scale and camera frustum; specific values not given. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse LiDAR Outliers: Standard depth supervision fails with noisy and sparse LiDAR, which SNeRF addresses by learning a confidence metric based on reprojection and geometry consistency. Moving Objects: Conventional NeRFs fail on moving vehicles, so SNeRF uses a virtual camera transformation to handle dynamic foregrounds. Memory Limitations: The alternating training approach (stylize then train) allows hardware capacity to be allocated separately, addressing memory constraints. Implicitly learns rotation and translation offsets to correct SLAM errors. Choose when initial poses are noisy. Link: Pose Refinement. Handles dynamic foregrounds by computing relative positions. Choose for scenes with moving objects. Link: Virtual Camera Transform. Uses reprojection and geometry consistency to weight depth errors. Choose when LiDAR is sparse or noisy. Link: Confidence Metric. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On large-scale driving datasets (nuScenes and Waymo), SNeRF reduces mean-squared error by 7–40% compared to state-of-the-art rivals. It achieves a 45% PSNR gain for moving vehicles rendering compared to conventional NeRFs or mesh-based methods. Strengths: Works with panoramic settings where rays barely intersect and overlaps are small; handles noisy/sparse LiDAR; reconstructs moving vehicles. Limitations: Requires SLAM/IMU data for initial poses; relies on external depth completion network. When to use: Large-scale street-view synthesis with sparse LiDAR and low camera overlap. When not to use: Object-centric scenes with high overlap (use standard NeRF); scenes with dense, accurate LiDAR (Urban-NeRF may be simpler). SNeRF was published as a conference paper at ICLR 2023 by Ziyang Xie, Junge Zhang, Wenye Li, Feihu Zhang, and Li Zhang from Fudan University and the University of Oxford. It addresses the limitations of original NeRF, which is designed for object-centric scenes with heavy camera overlap, and fails on unbounded outdoor street-view data collected by self-driving cars.
