name: Anisotropic Total Variation
head: Anisotropic Total Variation (ATV) Prior, L1 Total Variation
body: Anisotropic Total Variation (ATV) is a regularization prior used in tomographic reconstruction and radiance field optimization to enforce piecewise constant solutions with axis-aligned edges. It minimizes the sum of absolute differences between a voxel and its immediate neighbors along the three principal axes (x, y, z). Unlike Isotropic Total Variation, which computes the Euclidean norm of the gradient vector at each voxel, ATV treats each axis independently, making it computationally cheaper and favoring structures aligned with the grid axes. It builds on Total Variation Regularization by using the L1 norm specifically along principal directions rather than a general Huber loss or isotropic magnitude. Inputs: A 3D volume grid \mathbf{x} of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz, where n = Nx Ny Nz is the total number of voxels. Outputs: The regularized volume \mathbf{x} (after optimization steps) or the gradient vector \mathbf{z} = D\mathbf{x} and divergence D^T\mathbf{z}. Data Structures: The forward difference matrix D \in \mathbb{R}^{3n \times n} is defined implicitly and not stored in memory to save space. Each row of D corresponds to an edge (difference between two voxels). For an edge e connecting voxel i to voxel j, the entries are: D{ev} = \begin{cases} -1 & \text{if } v = i \\ 1 & \text{if } v = j \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} The matrix has 3n rows (edges) and n columns (voxels). Note: While the definition sums forward differences (3 per voxel), the implementation of D^T considers all 6 neighbors (forward and backward). Parameters: \mu: Proximal operator step size or regularization weight. Typical values depend on the specific solver (e.g., SART or ADMM) and noise level. Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Compute Gradient (D\mathbf{x}): For each voxel v = (i, j, k), compute the 6 forward differences (edges) connecting it to its neighbors. The vector \mathbf{z}v for voxel v contains: \mathbf{z}v = \begin{bmatrix} x{i+1,j,k} - x{i,j,k} \\ x{i,j+1,k} - x{i,j,k} \\ x{i,j,k+1} - x{i,j,k} \\ x{i,j,k} - x{i-1,j,k} \\ x{i,j,k} - x{i,j-1,k} \\ x{i,j,k} - x{i,j,k-1} \end{bmatrix} Boundary handling: Voxels at the boundary are assumed to be replicated. Thus, if a neighbor is out of bounds, the difference is zero (i.e., x{boundary} = x{neighbor}). 2. Compute Divergence (D^T\mathbf{z}): For a specific vertex v = (i, j, k), sum the difference values \mathbf{z}e from all incident edges e, weighted by D{ev}. (D^T\mathbf{z})v = \sum{e \ni v} D{ev} ze Expanding this for voxel (i, j, k): (D^T\mathbf{z}){i,j,k} = 6x{i,j,k} - x{i-1,j,k} - x{i+1,j,k} - x{i,j-1,k} - x{i,j+1,k} - x{i,j,k-1} - x{i,j,k+1} This operation is equivalent to the discrete Laplace operator D^T D applied to \mathbf{x}. 3. Proximal Operator (for optimization): In proximal algorithms (e.g., SART), the ATV prior h(\mathbf{x}) = \|\mathbf{D}\mathbf{x}\|1 requires the proximal operator of its convex conjugate g^. The proximal operator for the L1 norm's conjugate is the projection onto the unit L\infty ball, computed component-wise as clipping: \text{prox}{\mu g^}(\mathbf{q}) = \Pi{B\infty}(\mathbf{q}) Component-wise definition for a value u: \text{clip}(u) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } u > 1 \\ u & \text{if } |u| \leq 1 \\ -1 & \text{if } u < -1 \end{cases} If the proximal operator is applied directly to the gradient (as in some soft-thresholding formulations), it uses the soft-thresholding function: \text{prox}{\rho1}(\mathbf{u}) = \text{sign}(\mathbf{u}) \times \max(0, |\mathbf{u}| - \rho1) where \rho1 is the regularization parameter. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computeatvgradient(volume): """ Computes the 6-component difference vector for each voxel. volume: np.ndarray of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz) returns: np.ndarray of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz, 6) """ # Initialize output array for 6 differences: # 0: +x, 1: +y, 2: +z, 3: -x, 4: -y, 5: -z diffs = np.zeros((volume.shape, 6)) # Forward differences (+x, +y, +z) # x+1 - x diffs[:-1,:,:, 0] = volume[1:,:,:] - volume[:-1,:,:] # y+1 - y diffs[:,:-1,:, 1] = volume[:, 1:,:] - volume[:,:-1,:] # z+1 - z diffs[:,:,:-1, 2] = volume[:,:, 1:] - volume[:,:,:-1] # Backward differences (-x, -y, -z) # x - x-1 diffs[1:,:,:, 3] = volume[1:,:,:] - volume[:-1,:,:] # y - y-1 diffs[:, 1:,:, 4] = volume[:, 1:,:] - volume[:,:-1,:] # z - z-1 diffs[:,:, 1:, 5] = volume[:,:, 1:] - volume[:,:,:-1] # Boundary handling: The slices above naturally handle internal voxels. # Voxels at the boundary (e.g., index 0 in x) do not have a +x neighbor in the slice. # The difference is implicitly 0 because the slice assignment only covers valid indices. # To be explicit about "replicated" boundary condition for the full 6-neighbor view: # If a neighbor is out of bounds, diff = 0. The slicing approach above leaves # the boundary entries in 'diffs' as 0.0 (from initialization), which matches # the replicated boundary assumption (xi - xi = 0). return diffs def computeatvdivergence(diffs): """ Computes D^T z for each voxel. diffs: np.ndarray of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz, 6) returns: np.ndarray of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz) """ # (D^T z)v = sum(Dev ze) # For voxel v, the edges are: # 0 (+x): D = -1 (v is source) # 1 (+y): D = -1 (v is source) # 2 (+z): D = -1 (v is source) # 3 (-x): D = +1 (v is target) # 4 (-y): D = +1 (v is target) # 5 (-z): D = +1 (v is target) # Sum of backward diffs (positive contribution) sumbackward = diffs[:,:,:, 3] + diffs[:,:,:, 4] + diffs[:,:,:, 5] # Sum of forward diffs (negative contribution) sumforward = diffs[:,:,:, 0] + diffs[:,:,:, 1] + diffs[:,:,:, 2] # Result is sumbackward - sumforward # Note: This is equivalent to 6x - sum(neighbors) if we expand the diffs # But here we operate on the pre-computed diffs. return sumbackward - sumforward def proxatvconjugate(q, mu=1.0): """ Proximal operator of the convex conjugate of the L1 norm (Projection onto Linf ball). q: np.ndarray (gradient or dual variable) mu: step size (usually 1 for the projection definition provided) returns: clipped q """ # Clip to [-mu, mu] # The formula in sources uses mu=1 for the projection definition. # If mu is a step size in an algorithm, it scales the input/output. # Standard proxmu g(q) = q - mu prox{g/mu}(q/mu) # For L1, prox{g/mu}(u) = softthreshold(u, 1/mu) # However, source explicitly defines prox{mu g} as projection onto Binfty. # Let's stick to the explicit clipping formula given: # 1 if u > 1, u if |u|<=1, -1 if u < -1. # This corresponds to mu=1. If mu != 1, the scaling applies. # Generalized clipping for arbitrary mu: # prox{mu ||.||1}(q) = clip(q / mu) mu ? # Source says: prox{mu g}(u) = u - mu prox{1/mu g}(u/mu) # prox{lambda ||.||1}(v) = sign(v) max(0, |v| - lambda) # So prox{1/mu g}(u/mu) = sign(u/mu) max(0, |u/mu| - 1/mu) # = (1/mu) sign(u) max(0, |u| - 1) # Then u - mu (1/mu) sign(u) max(0, |u| - 1) # = u - sign(u) max(0, |u| - 1) # = clip(u, -1, 1) # So the projection is independent of mu in the final clipped value range [-1, 1]? # Yes, the projection onto the unit ball is independent of mu scaling in the dual. return np.clip(q, -1.0, 1.0) def proxatvgradient(u, rho1): """ Soft thresholding proximal operator for the L1 norm on the gradient itself. Used in. u: np.ndarray (volume gradient) rho1: regularization parameter """ return np.sign(u) np.maximum(0, np.abs(u) - rho1) Sum of Absolute Differences (SAD) extends ATV by considering a larger local neighborhood. While ATV sums absolute differences along only the three principal axes, SAD sums the absolute differences between a voxel and all voxels in its immediate 3x3 spatial neighborhood (excluding the voxel itself), thereby enforcing smoothness across more edges per voxel. It has been shown to produce excellent results in stochastic tomography reconstruction. Multi-dimensional Total Variation (TV) Loss computes the total variation regularization on multi-dimensional tensors by summing absolute differences along all spatial and channel dimensions. It serves as a smoothness prior for feature fields, encouraging piecewise constant solutions while preserving sharp boundaries. It extends the standard 3D TV prior by generalizing the difference operation to arbitrary tensor shapes, including batch and channel dimensions. A regularizer based on the \ell1 norm of the image gradient, assuming images are sparse in the gradient domain. The proximal operator is the soft thresholding function applied to each element of the volume gradient. Formula: \text{prox}{\rho1} G{ATV} (u{ni}) = \text{sign}(u{ni}) \times \max(0, |u{ni}| - \rho1), where u{ni} is the ith component of the volume gradient u = Kv at voxel n. Parameter: \rho1 is the regularization parameter that controls how fast the volume gradient shrinks. Layout: K \in \mathbb{R}^{3N \times N} is the forward difference matrix that produces the discrete volume gradient. Time Complexity: Computing the gradient D\mathbf{x} and divergence D^T\mathbf{z} is O(n), where n is the number of voxels, as each voxel interacts with a constant number of neighbors (6). The proximal operator is also O(n). Memory Complexity: O(n) for storing the volume. The matrix D is not stored, saving significant memory compared to explicit sparse matrix storage. Performance: ATV is computationally efficient due to the simple L1 norm and axis-aligned differences. It is faster than Isotropic TV (ITV), which requires square root computations per voxel. Strengths: Promotes piecewise constant solutions with sharp, axis-aligned edges. Computationally cheap. Limitations: Can produce "staircasing" artifacts (piecewise constant regions) and may not preserve diagonal features as well as isotropic variants. Sensitive to the choice of regularization parameter \rho1 or \mu. When to use: When the target volume has strong axis-aligned structures and computational efficiency is critical. When not to use: When isotropic smoothness is required or diagonal features are important. Anisotropic Total Variation was introduced as a regularization prior for tomographic reconstruction, specifically within the context of proximal algorithms like SART (Simultaneous Algebraic Reconstruction Technique). It is based on the idea that images are sparse in the gradient domain. The formulation h(\mathbf{x}) = \|\mathbf{D}\mathbf{x}\|1 leverages the convex conjugate's proximal operator, which is the projection onto the unit L\infty ball. It is widely used in industrial computed tomography and electron microscopy tomography reconstruction. name: Sum of Absolute Differences (SAD)
head: SAD Prior, Sum of Absolute Differences (SAD) Prior
body: Sum of Absolute Differences (SAD) is a regularization prior used in tomographic reconstruction that extends Anisotropic Total Variation (ATV) by considering a larger local neighborhood. While ATV sums absolute differences along only the three principal axes, SAD sums the absolute differences between a voxel and all voxels in its immediate 3x3 spatial neighborhood (excluding the voxel itself), thereby enforcing smoothness across more edges per voxel. It has been shown to produce excellent results in stochastic tomography reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D voxel grid \mathbf{x} of size I \times J \times K, where each element x{i,j,k} represents the scalar value (e.g., density or radiance) at voxel coordinates (i,j,k). Output: The scalar energy value h(\mathbf{x}) representing the regularization cost, or the proximal operator applied to \mathbf{x} to produce a regularized version \mathbf{x}'. Data Structures The voxel grid is stored as a dense 3D array. The neighborhood N(\mathbf{x}{i,j,k}) is defined implicitly by coordinate offsets relative to (i,j,k). No explicit adjacency matrix D is stored; operations are computed on-the-fly. Numbered Steps 1. Initialize the energy accumulator to zero. 2. Iterate over every voxel (i,j,k) in the grid bounds [0, I-1] \times [0, J-1] \times [0, K-1]. 3. For each voxel, identify the 8 neighbors in its 3x3 neighborhood N(\mathbf{x}{i,j,k}) by applying offsets \deltai, \deltaj \in \{-1, 0, 1\} where (\deltai, \deltaj) \neq (0,0), while keeping the k-index fixed. 4. For each valid neighbor (i+\deltai, j+\deltaj, k) within grid boundaries, compute the absolute difference |\mathbf{x}{i+\deltai, j+\deltaj, k} - \mathbf{x}{i,j,k}|. 5. Accumulate the absolute differences into the energy value. 6. Return the final energy value h(\mathbf{x}). Formula The SAD energy function is defined as: h(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i,j,k} \sum{\mathbf{x}n \in N(\mathbf{x}{i,j,k})} |\mathbf{x}n - \mathbf{x}{i,j,k}| Where: \mathbf{x}{i,j,k} is the value of the central voxel at coordinates (i,j,k). N(\mathbf{x}{i,j,k}) denotes the 3x3 neighborhood around the voxel excluding itself. The summation iterates over the 8 neighbors in the xy-plane at a fixed z-slice. Parameters None. The neighborhood size and structure are fixed by the definition. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Boundaries: Voxels on the volume boundaries have fewer than 8 neighbors. The algorithm must clamp neighbor coordinates to the valid grid range [0, I-1] \times [0, J-1] \times [0, K-1] before accessing memory. Precision: Summing absolute differences across a large volume can accumulate floating-point error. Using double-precision accumulators prevents overflow and maintains numerical stability for large grids. Degenerate Input: If the grid dimensions are smaller than 3 \times 3 \times 1, the neighborhood definition still applies but yields fewer terms per voxel; the algorithm remains valid without modification. Pseudocode The following computes the SAD energy h(\mathbf{x}) for a 3D grid \mathbf{x} of dimensions I \times J \times K. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesadenergy(x, I, J, K): """ Computes the Sum of Absolute Differences (SAD) regularization energy. Args: x: 3D numpy array of shape (I, J, K) containing voxel values. I: Width of the volume. J: Height of the volume. K: Depth of the volume. Returns: float: The SAD energy value. """ energy = 0.0 for i in range(I): for j in range(J): for k in range(K): currentval = x[i, j, k] for di in (-1, 0, 1): for dj in (-1, 0, 1): if di == 0 and dj == 0: continue ni, nj = i + di, j + dj if 0 <= ni < I and 0 <= nj < J: energy += abs(x[ni, nj, k] - currentval) return energy Note: The proximal operator for SAD is not explicitly derived in the sources, but is stated to be similar to the ATV proximal operator. Implementers should apply the standard l1 proximal projection onto the extended neighborhood graph, which couples the 8 neighbors per voxel. Time Complexity: Computing the energy is O(I \cdot J \cdot K), as each voxel processes a constant number (8) of neighbors. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space if computed on-the-fly, or O(I \cdot J \cdot K) if storing intermediate neighbor differences. Strengths: Produces excellent results in stochastic tomography reconstruction compared to other priors. It enforces smoothness across more edges per voxel than ATV. Limitations: Requires more arithmetic operations per voxel than ATV due to the larger neighborhood. When to use: When tomographic reconstruction tasks benefit from the extended neighborhood smoothing provided by SAD. When not to use: When strict anisotropic smoothing along principal axes is required, or when minimal per-voxel computational overhead is critical. Origin: The SAD prior is discussed in the context of proximal algorithms for industrial computed tomography and space-time tomographic reconstruction. History: It is presented as an extension of the Anisotropic Total Variation (ATV) prior. Usage: It is applied in stochastic tomography reconstruction. name: Multi-dimensional Total Variation Loss
head: Multi-dimensional TV, TV regularization on tensors
body: Multi-dimensional Total Variation (TV) Loss computes the total variation regularization on multi-dimensional tensors by summing absolute differences along all spatial and channel dimensions. It serves as a smoothness prior for feature fields, encouraging piecewise constant solutions while preserving sharp boundaries. It extends the standard 3D TV prior by generalizing the difference operation to arbitrary tensor shapes, including batch and channel dimensions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A tensor \mathbf{x} of shape (B, C, D1, D2, \dots, Dk), where B is batch size, C is channel size, and Di are spatial dimensions. Output: A scalar loss value representing the sum of absolute differences across all specified dimensions. Data Structures: The input \mathbf{x} is a dense tensor. No auxiliary structures are required beyond standard tensor indexing. Algorithm: 1. Initialize tvloss = 0. 2. Determine the number of dimensions to iterate over. The iteration typically covers dimensions from index 2 to the last dimension (excluding batch and channel if they are not intended to be regularized, or including all if specified). 3. For each dimension i in the range [2, \text{len}(\mathbf{x}.shape) - 1]: a. Let n{res} = \mathbf{x}.shape[i]. b. Create index sets: idx1 = [1, 2, \dots, n{res}-1] and idx2 = [0, 1, \dots, n{res}-2]. c. Select slices: \mathbf{x}1 = \mathbf{x}[\dots, idx1, \dots] and \mathbf{x}2 = \mathbf{x}[\dots, idx2, \dots] along dimension i. d. Compute the absolute difference: \Delta = |\mathbf{x}1 - \mathbf{x}2|. e. Add the sum of \Delta to tvloss. 4. Return tvloss. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multidimtvloss(x): """ Computes the multi-dimensional total variation loss. x: Tensor of shape (B, C, D1, D2,...) """ tv = 0.0 # Iterate over spatial dimensions (assuming dims 0 and 1 are batch/channel) # Note: Source iterates from index 2 to len(x.shape)-1 for i in range(2, len(x.shape)): nres = x.shape[i] if nres < 2: continue # Cannot compute difference on dimension of size 1 # Create indices for slicing idx1 = list(range(1, nres)) idx2 = list(range(0, nres - 1)) # Select slices along dimension i # x.indexselect(i, idx1) selects elements at indices idx1 along dim i x1 = x.indexselect(i, torch.tensor(idx1, device=x.device)) x2 = x.indexselect(i, torch.tensor(idx2, device=x.device)) # Compute absolute difference and sum diff = torch.abs(x1 - x2) tv += diff.sum() return tv Parameters: None explicitly defined in the core algorithm. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If any spatial dimension has size 1, the difference along that dimension is undefined or zero. The implementation should skip such dimensions or handle them gracefully. Precision issues may arise with very large tensors due to accumulation of floating-point errors in the sum. A variant used in inverse rendering to regularize material and lighting fields separately. It computes TV on a mask field \hat{M} and a light field \hat{E} using exponential weighting based on image intensity differences to preserve edges. Formula for Mask: TV{mat} = \frac{1}{|\hat{M}|} \sum{i,j} \Delta \hat{M}{ij}, where \Delta \hat{M}{ij} = \exp(-|I{i,j} - I{i-1,j}|) (\hat{M}{i,j} - \hat{M}{i-1,j})^2 + \exp(-|I{i,j} - I{i,j-1}|) (\hat{M}{i,j} - \hat{M}{i,j-1})^2. Formula for Light: TV{light} = \frac{1}{|\hat{E}|} \sum{i,j} \Delta \hat{E}{ij}, where \Delta \hat{E}{ij} = (\hat{E}{i,j} - \hat{E}{i-1,j})^2 + (\hat{E}{i,j} - \hat{E}{i,j-1})^2. When to choose: When decomposing a scene into reflectance and illumination components, ensuring smoothness in both while respecting image edges. A regularizer that computes the total variation of spatial planes to encourage smoothness in feature fields, often used in 4D Gaussian Splatting. It normalizes the squared differences by the count of elements in the height and width directions. Formula: compute\plane\tv(t) = 2 \times \left( \frac{\sum (t{i+1} - ti)^2}{counth} + \frac{\sum (t{j+1} - tj)^2}{countw} \right), where counth = B \times C \times (H-1) \times W and countw = B \times C \times H \times (W-1). Spatial Grid Identification: For 3D grids, indices are [0, 1, 2]. For 4D grids (e.g., spatiotemporal), spatial grids are typically [0, 1, 3] assuming index 2 is time, or as defined by the specific implementation. When to choose: When optimizing 4D scenes or feature fields where planar smoothness is desired. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot D), where N is the total number of elements in the tensor and D is the number of dimensions iterated over. Each dimension requires a single pass over the tensor elements. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the input tensor. The algorithm requires temporary storage for sliced tensors, which is proportional to the tensor size. Strengths: Simple to implement, differentiable, effective at removing noise and artifacts in optimized fields. Limitations: Can oversmooth fine details if the regularization weight is too high. The choice of which dimensions to include (batch, channel, spatial) significantly impacts the result. When to use: During the optimization of neural radiance fields or Gaussian splatting parameters to enforce spatial coherence. When not to use: When preserving high-frequency details is critical and the scene is known to be noisy rather than smooth. The concept of Total Variation regularization originates from image processing, where it is used for denoising and segmentation. In the context of volume rendering and neural fields, it has been adapted to regularize 3D and 4D feature grids. The specific multi-dimensional implementation described here is found in recent Gaussian Splatting variants like AnySplat and 4DGS, as well as in inverse rendering frameworks like GS-IR. name: PlaneTV Regularization
head: PlaneTV, Total Variation on Planes
body: PlaneTV Regularization computes the total variation (TV) of spatial planes within a feature tensor to encourage smoothness in the learned feature fields. It differs from standard isotropic TV by explicitly separating horizontal and vertical gradient computations across 2D spatial slices, making it suitable for multi-dimensional tensors where specific dimensions represent spatial planes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 4D tensor t of shape (B, C, H, W), where B is batch size, C is channel count, H is height, and W is width. Output: A scalar loss value representing the regularized TV. Data Structures: The input tensor t is treated as a collection of spatial planes. For a 3D grid length (standard 2D spatial), spatial grids are indices [0, 1, 2] (Batch, Channel, Height) or similar depending on layout, but the core operation assumes a 4D structure where the last two dimensions are spatial. If the grid length is not 3 (e.g., 4D spatiotemporal), spatial grids are identified as [0, 1, 3] assuming index 3 is time, but the code implementation in processes the last two dimensions as spatial H and W. Formula: The loss is computed as: L{PlaneTV} = 2 \times \left( \frac{\sum (t{i+1} - ti)^2}{counth} + \frac{\sum (t{j+1} - tj)^2}{countw} \right) Where: t{i+1} - ti represents the difference along the height dimension (rows). t{j+1} - tj represents the difference along the width dimension (columns). counth = B \times C \times (H-1) \times W countw = B \times C \times H \times (W-1) Steps: 1. Compute the squared differences along the height dimension: \sum (t{i+1} - ti)^2. 2. Compute the squared differences along the width dimension: \sum (t{j+1} - tj)^2. 3. Normalize the height sum by counth. 4. Normalize the width sum by countw. 5. Sum the normalized values and multiply by 2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeplanetv(t: Tensor) -> float: """ Computes PlaneTV regularization loss. t: Tensor of shape (B, C, H, W) """ B, C, H, W = t.shape # Compute differences along height (dim 2) # t[:,:, 1:,:] - t[:,:,:-1,:] diffh = t[:,:, 1:,:] - t[:,:,:-1,:] sumh = torch.sum(diffh 2) counth = B C (H - 1) W # Compute differences along width (dim 3) # t[:,:,:, 1:] - t[:,:,:,:-1] diffw = t[:,:,:, 1:] - t[:,:,:,:-1] sumw = torch.sum(diffw 2) countw = B C H (W - 1) # Avoid division by zero if H=1 or W=1 if counth == 0: termh = 0.0 else: termh = sumh / counth if countw == 0: termw = 0.0 else: termw = sumw / countw return 2.0 (termh + termw) Parameters: No explicit hyperparameters are defined in the core formula. Edge Cases: If H=1 or W=1, the corresponding count becomes 0, leading to division by zero. The implementation must handle this by setting the term to 0. Applies TV regularization specifically to triplane features to smooth them and make their gradients resemble natural images, which are modeled by a hyper-Laplacian with \alpha \in [0.5, 0.8]. The regularization target \alpha is typically set to 0.5. This variant is chosen when training generative models (like autoencoders) on triplanes to prevent high-frequency artifacts. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of elements in the tensor, O(B \cdot C \cdot H \cdot W), as it requires a single pass to compute differences. Memory Complexity: O(B \cdot C \cdot H \cdot W) to store the intermediate difference tensors if not computed in-place or streamed. Strengths: Encourages spatial smoothness in feature fields, reducing noise and high-frequency artifacts. Limitations: May oversmooth fine details if the regularization weight is too high. The normalization factors depend on tensor dimensions, requiring careful handling of boundary conditions. PlaneTV is used in the context of differentiable volume rendering and neural field optimization, specifically in frameworks like 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) for dynamic scene reconstruction. It builds on the concept of Total Variation regularization to enforce priors on learned representations. The Triplane TV variant is associated with Triplane Diffusion models for 3D neural field generation. name: Anisotropic Total Variation Proximal Operator
head: ATV Proximal Operator, ROF model proximal operator
body: The Anisotropic Total Variation (ATV) Proximal Operator is a mathematical tool used to enforce sparsity in the gradient domain of a volume during optimization. It serves as the proximal mapping for the ATV regularizer, which penalizes the \ell1 norm of the discrete volume gradient. Unlike isotropic TV, which treats all gradient directions equally, ATV sums the absolute differences along the three principal axes (x, y, z) independently. This operator is distinct from Sum of Absolute Differences (SAD) and Multi-dimensional Total Variation Loss by specifically applying soft-thresholding to the individual gradient components rather than the magnitude of the gradient vector. It is primarily used in differentiable and inverse volume rendering to denoise reconstructed volumes while preserving sharp edges. The operator computes the proximal mapping of the ATV regularizer. It assumes that images with excessive noise have high total variation and are sparse in the gradient domain. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume gradient tensor \mathbf{u} of shape (N, 3), where N is the number of voxels and the last dimension corresponds to the x, y, z components. Each element u{ni} represents the i-th component of the gradient at voxel n. Input: A scalar regularization parameter \rho1 \ge 0. Output: A denoised gradient tensor \mathbf{u}' of shape (N, 3), where each component has been soft-thresholded. Data Structures: The forward difference matrix K \in \mathbb{R}^{3N \times N} is used to compute the initial gradient from a volume \mathbf{v} such that \mathbf{u} = K\mathbf{v}. However, the proximal operator itself operates directly on the pre-computed gradient components u{ni}. Formula: The proximal operator is defined as the soft-thresholding function applied element-wise to the volume gradient components: \text{prox}{\rho1 G{ATV}}(u{ni}) = \text{sign}(u{ni}) \times \max(0, |u{ni}| - \rho1) Where: u{ni} is the i-th component (i \in \{0, 1, 2\}) of the volume gradient at voxel n. \rho1 is the regularization parameter controlling the shrinkage rate. \text{sign}(x) returns 1 if x > 0, -1 if x < 0, and 0 if x = 0. Parameters: \rho1: Regularization parameter. Higher values result in stronger shrinkage of small gradient components, promoting sparser gradients. Pseudocode: The following Python-like pseudocode implements the element-wise soft-thresholding. It assumes gradient is a NumPy array of shape (N, 3) and rho1 is a scalar. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def anisotropictvproximaloperator(gradient, rho1): """ Computes the proximal operator for Anisotropic Total Variation. Args: gradient (numpy.ndarray): Volume gradient tensor of shape (N, 3). rho1 (float): Regularization parameter. Returns: numpy.ndarray: Denoised gradient tensor of shape (N, 3). """ # Compute absolute values absgrad = numpy.abs(gradient) # Apply soft thresholding: max(0, |u| - rho1) # Using numpy.maximum for element-wise comparison thresholded = numpy.maximum(absgrad - rho1, 0.0) # Restore signs: sign(u) thresholdedvalue # numpy.sign returns -1, 0, or 1 signs = numpy.sign(gradient) result = signs thresholded return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Gradient: If u{ni} = 0, the output is 0. The soft-thresholding function is continuous but not differentiable at u{ni} = \pm \rho1. Precision: When |u{ni}| is very close to \rho1, floating-point precision errors may cause oscillations if the operator is called repeatedly in an iterative solver without momentum or step-size adjustments. Anisotropy: ATV does not preserve rotational symmetry. Structures aligned with the principal axes may be preserved better than diagonal structures compared to isotropic TV. This variant implements the ATV proximal operator within a proximal gradient descent framework for TV minimization. It uses an internal iterative solver with momentum (Nesterov acceleration) to converge to the solution. It maintains a residual voltv from previous iterations to update the current estimate. The algorithm runs for a maximum of 6 iterations or until convergence (relative change < 10^{-3} for 3 consecutive steps). It clips the volume to bounds if specified and normalizes the TV residual to avoid division by zero. The step size is scaled by the Lipschitz constant L of the data fidelity term (la = \lambda / L). Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of voxels, as it performs element-wise operations on the gradient tensor. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the gradient tensor and the output. Strengths: Computationally efficient; promotes piecewise constant solutions; effective at removing noise while preserving sharp edges in the principal directions. Limitations: Can produce "staircasing" artifacts (piecewise constant regions) in smooth gradients; anisotropic nature may lead to directional bias in reconstructed structures. When to use: When computational efficiency is critical and the volume exhibits strong edges aligned with the grid axes. When not to use: When rotational invariance is required (use Isotropic TV instead) or when smooth gradients are expected without staircasing artifacts. The Anisotropic Total Variation regularizer was conceived based on the idea that images are sparse in the gradient domain. The proximal operator for the \ell1 norm, which forms the basis of ATV, is the soft-thresholding function. This approach is widely used in tomographic reconstruction and inverse problems to denoise data. The specific application to 3D volume rendering and electron microscopy tilt-series reconstruction was detailed in recent work on GPU-accelerated reconstruction. The proximal gradient implementation with momentum is found in open-source tomography libraries like flexTOMO. name: Isotropic Total Variation
head: ITV, TV Regularization, Total Variation (TV) Regularization
body: Isotropic Total Variation (ITV) is a regularization prior used in volume rendering and tomographic reconstruction to enforce piecewise constant solutions while preserving isotropic edge structures. Unlike Anisotropic Total Variation (ATV), which sums the absolute values of individual gradient components, ITV sums the Euclidean magnitude of the full 3D gradient vector at each voxel, treating the gradient components as a coupled group. This distinction makes ITV particularly effective for preventing overfitting and artifacts like floaters in explicit radiance field representations, especially when using rendering methods that do not inherently smooth across voxel boundaries. Input: A 3D voxel grid \mathbf{x} of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz, where each element x{i,j,k} represents a scalar value (e.g., density \sigma or opacity) at voxel coordinates (i,j,k). Output: A scalar regularization loss value h(\mathbf{x}) or the proximal operator update for optimization algorithms. The method operates on the voxel grid \mathbf{x}. In matrix formulations, \mathbf{x} is often vectorized into a column vector \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n where n = Nx Ny Nz. Gradient Vector \mathbf{w}^v: At each voxel v=(i,j,k), the gradient is a 3-element vector defined by forward differences: \mathbf{w}^v = \begin{bmatrix} x{i+1,j,k} - x{i,j,k} \\ x{i,j+1,k} - x{i,j,k} \\ x{i,j,k+1} - x{i,j,k} \end{bmatrix} Mask Matrix \mathbf{E}: A sparse matrix \mathbf{E} \in \mathbb{R}^{3n \times n} indicating the positions of forward differences. It is defined such that E{ev} = 1 if D{ev} = -1 (where \mathbf{D} is the forward difference matrix) and 0 otherwise. In implementation, \mathbf{E} is not stored explicitly; operations involving \mathbf{E} are computed on-the-fly. The ITV prior h(\mathbf{x}) is defined as the sum of the L2 norms of the gradient vectors at all voxels: h(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i,j,k} \sqrt{|x{i+1,j,k} - x{i,j,k}|^2 + |x{i,j+1,k} - x{i,j,k}|^2 + |x{i,j,k+1} - x{i,j,k}|^2} In compact matrix notation, let \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{D}\mathbf{x}. The prior is expressed as a weighted norm \|\mathbf{w}\|E: h(\mathbf{x}) = \|\mathbf{D}\mathbf{x}\|E = \sumv \|\mathbf{w}^v\|2 where the norm \|\mathbf{w}\|E is computed as \|\sqrt{\mathbf{E}^T \mathbf{w}^2}\|1. Here, squaring and square roots are component-wise operations. For continuous neural radiance fields (e.g., in Aug-NeRF), the regularization is approximated via quadrature over the domain [-1, 1]^3: R{\text{TV}}(\Theta) \approx \sum{i=1}^{N} \sum{j=1}^{N} \sum{k=1}^{N} |\nablax \sigma\Theta(\delta i, \delta j, \delta k)| \delta^3 where \sigma\Theta is the density branch of the network, \nablax is the spatial gradient computed via auto-differentiation, and \delta is the grid spacing. For optimization algorithms like Primal-Dual or ADMM, the proximal operator of the convex conjugate \tilde{g}^ of the ITV prior is required. This corresponds to the projection onto the unit ball of the dual norm: \text{prox}{\mu \tilde{g}^}(\mathbf{q}) = \Pi{B^}(\mathbf{q}) = \frac{\mathbf{q}}{\max\left(\sqrt{\mathbf{E}^T \mathbf{q}^2}, 1\right)} where division and max are component-wise. Intuitively, this scales the gradient vector \mathbf{q} at each voxel by 1/\|\mathbf{q}^v\|2 if the magnitude exceeds 1, and leaves it unchanged otherwise. The following Python-like pseudocode implements the computation of the ITV loss and its proximal step for a voxel grid. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def isotropictotalvariationloss(x): """ Computes the Isotropic Total Variation loss for a 3D voxel grid. Args: x: numpy array of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz). Represents the scalar field. Returns: scalar: The ITV regularization value. """ # Forward differences in x, y, z directions dx = np.diff(x, axis=0) dy = np.diff(x, axis=1) dz = np.diff(x, axis=2) # Compute magnitude of the gradient vector at each voxel # The resulting arrays are of shape (Nx-1, Ny-1, Nz-1) gradmagnitude = np.sqrt(dx2 + dy2 + dz2) # Sum all magnitudes loss = np.sum(gradmagnitude) return loss def proximalisotropictv(q): """ Computes the proximal operator of the convex conjugate of ITV. Equivalent to projecting q onto the unit dual norm ball. Args: q: numpy array of shape (3, H, W, D) representing the gradient vector field (stacked dx, dy, dz). Returns: numpy array: The proximal update PB(q). """ # q[0] is dx, q[1] is dy, q[2] is dz gradmag = np.sqrt(q[0]2 + q[1]2 + q[2]2) # Projection onto unit ball: scale by max(1, mag) scale = np.maximum(gradmag, 1.0) # Component-wise division qproj = q / scale return qproj Regularization Weight (\lambda or \mu): Controls the strength of the ITV penalty. In DiffVox, a GroupL1Norm weight of 0.26 was used for isotropic TV. In Primal-Dual algorithms, step sizes \tau and \sigma must satisfy \tau \sigma \|K\|^2 < 1. Grid Resolution (N): The number of voxels along each dimension. Higher resolution increases the number of gradient terms in the sum. Boundary Conditions: The forward difference definition requires voxels at i+1, j+1, k+1. For voxels on the boundary of the grid, these neighbors do not exist. The pseudocode handles this by using np.diff, which reduces the dimension by 1, effectively ignoring the last slice in each direction. Zero Gradient: If the gradient magnitude is zero, the proximal operator division is well-defined (division by 1). Matrix Storage: The matrix \mathbf{E} is not stored explicitly to save memory; operations are computed on-the-fly. Sums absolute values of individual gradient components (L1 norm of components). Chosen when directional smoothing is preferred or for simpler implementation. Ablation study comparing regularization effects in Plenoxels. Regularizer for dynamic scenes, uses ITV as a component. Time Complexity: Computing the loss is O(N) where N is the number of voxels, as it involves a constant number of arithmetic operations per voxel. Proximal operators are also O(N). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the voxel grid and intermediate gradient arrays. The matrix \mathbf{E} is not stored, saving memory. Strengths: Promotes piecewise constant solutions with isotropic edge preservation. Limitations: Can introduce "staircasing" artifacts (piecewise constant approximation). Removing TV norm has a far greater impact on Siddon's method than on trilinear interpolation, as trilinear interpolation provides inherent smoothing. When to use: When isotropic edge preservation is critical and the solution is expected to be piecewise constant. Useful in sparse-view CT and differentiable volume rendering to prevent overfitting. Total Variation regularization was introduced by Rudin, Osher, and Fatemi in 1992 in "Nonlinear total variation based noise removal algorithms". It has since been widely adopted in image processing and tomography. In the context of volume rendering and radiance fields, ITV is used to regularize the density field during optimization, particularly in methods like DiffVox and Aug-NeRF. The specific formulation using the proximal operator of the convex conjugate for Primal-Dual algorithms is detailed in works on industrial CT and space-time tomography. name: Output Noise Regularization
head: Density Noise Regularization, Gaussian Noise Regularization on Density, Training Regularization for Real Scenes
body: Output Noise Regularization is a training-time technique that improves novel view synthesis in real-world scenes by injecting Gaussian noise into predicted density (\sigma) or opacity values. It encourages the network to learn a robust density field that is less sensitive to small perturbations in the input space. Unlike sibling methods targeting geometric consistency or perceptual features, this method operates directly on the radiance field's scalar output before activation. The method modifies the forward pass of the neural radiance field during training by adding random noise to the raw density predictions. This forces the model to produce consistent rendering outputs even when underlying density estimates are slightly corrupted, effectively regularizing the optimization landscape. Input: The raw output tensor from the neural network, typically containing RGB color and density/opacity channels. Let this be \mathbf{raw} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times C}, where B is batch size, N is the number of samples per ray, and C is the number of channels (typically 4: RGB + \sigma). Output: The modified raw tensor \mathbf{raw}' with noise added to the density channel. The implementation assumes a standard volume rendering output format: Tensor Shape: [batchsize, numsamples, 4]. Channels: Indices 0-2 correspond to Red, Green, Blue. Index 3 corresponds to density \sigma (or pre-activation opacity). Data Type: float32. noisestd: Standard deviation of the Gaussian noise. Default is None (disabled) or 0.0. usestratifiedsampling: Boolean flag. Noise is typically applied only when stratified sampling is active. noisemean: Mean of the Gaussian noise, typically 0. 1. Check Conditions: Verify if noise regularization is enabled (noisestd > 0) and if stratified sampling is active. 2. Generate Noise: If conditions are met, generate a noise tensor \mathbf{n} with the same shape as the density channel of the raw output. The noise is drawn from a standard normal distribution \mathcal{N}(0, 1) and scaled by noisestd. 3. Add Noise: Add the generated noise to the density channel of the raw output. Crucially, this is done before any non-linear activation function (such as ReLU or Sigmoid) is applied to the density. 4. Concatenate: Combine the original RGB channels with the noisy density channel to form the final output tensor for the current step. 5. Forward Pass: Pass \mathbf{raw}' through the activation function and the volume rendering equation to compute the final pixel color. Noise generation: \mathbf{n} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \text{noise\std}^2). Noisy density: \sigma' = \sigma + \mathbf{n}. Output tensor: \mathbf{raw}' = [\mathbf{rgb}, \sigma + \mathbf{n}]. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import random def concatenate(tensors, axis=-1): """Standard tensor concatenation along the specified axis.""" return np.concatenate(tensors, axis=axis) def normal(key, shape, dtype=np.float32): """Generate Gaussian noise with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.""" return np.random.defaultrng(key).normal(0.0, 1.0, shape).astype(dtype) def outputnoiseregularization(raw, noisestd, usestratifiedsampling, rngkey): """ Adds Gaussian noise to the density channel of the raw network output. Args: raw: numpy.ndarray, shape [batchsize, numsamples, 4], dtype float32. Channels 0-2 are RGB, channel 3 is density sigma. noisestd: float, standard deviation of the noise. If None or <= 0, no noise is added. usestratifiedsampling: bool, flag indicating if stratified sampling is used. rngkey: int, random number generator seed/key. Returns: rawnoisy: numpy.ndarray, same shape as raw, with noise added to channel 3. newkey: int, updated random key. """ if noisestd is None or noisestd <= 0.0 or not usestratifiedsampling: return raw, rngkey # Split key for noise generation rngkey, noisekey = rngkey + 1, rngkey + 2 # Generate noise with shape matching the density channel (channel index 3) noiseshape = raw[..., 3:4].shape noise = normal(noisekey, noiseshape, dtype=raw.dtype) noisestd # Add noise to the density channel (channel 3) # RGB channels (0-2) remain unchanged rawnoisy = concatenate([ raw[...,:3], # RGB channels raw[..., 3:4] + noise # Noisy sigma channel ], axis=-1) return rawnoisy, rngkey Activation Order: Noise must be added before the ReLU activation on \sigma. Adding it after ReLU would clip negative noise values, altering the distribution and potentially reducing the regularization effect. Stratified Sampling Dependency: Some implementations only apply this noise during stratified sampling. Applying it during uniform sampling may not yield the same benefits or could interfere with the uniform distribution assumptions. Precision: Ensure the noise is generated in the same precision (float32) as the network output to avoid casting issues during concatenation. Over-Regularization: Excessive noise standard deviation can destabilize training. The sources suggest unit variance (std=1) or specific scales depending on the context (e.g., opacity perturbation scales of 0.25-0.5). Smoothness priors are regularization terms applied during training and inference to reduce surface noise and improve geometric smoothness in neural surface reconstruction. They distinguish themselves from sibling methods by targeting the geometric consistency of the signed distance field (SDF) and its gradients, rather than just radiance or color consistency. Unlike Output Noise Regularization which perturbs the output, smoothness priors typically penalize the gradient of the SDF or the Laplacian of the field. This variant evaluates model robustness by injecting Gaussian noise into predicted opacity values before sigmoid activation to prevent negative values, then measuring segmentation metric degradation. It is used for sensitivity analysis rather than training regularization. At noise scale 0.25, mIoU drops from 50.75 to 50.13 and mAcc from 62.00 to 60.94. At scale 0.5, mIoU is 50.18 and mAcc is 60.88. Performance remains stable up to scale 0.5. At scale 1.0, mIoU drops to 47.13 and mAcc to 57.10. At scale 2.0, mIoU is 38.13 and mAcc is 44.11. At scale 4.0, mIoU collapses to 16.12 and mAcc to 32.19. A regularization technique that imposes sparsity constraints on the entire scene space to reduce noise using a relaxed geometry proxy. It improves PSNR from 20.01 (Model-C) to 20.07 (AR-NeRF) on DTU 3-view. It outperforms Emptiness loss and ray density entropy loss. Emptiness loss fails because wi is a biased geometry proxy. Ray density entropy loss encourages unimodal distribution, which is not necessarily true. A ray regularization technique that encourages a unimodal distribution for ray densities. It achieves 19.94 PSNR on DTU 3-view, performing worse than Model-C (20.01) and AR-NeRF (20.07). A pitfall is that it encourages a unimodal distribution for ray densities, which is not necessarily true in practice. A regularization technique that adds Gaussian noise to sigma values to encourage discreteness in the rendered output. If discretereg is True or training is active, it generates Gaussian noise with mean 0 and variance 1 for each sigma value. The free energy is calculated as \text{free\energy} = \text{ReLU}(\text{noise} + \sigma) \times \text{sampled\dists}, then scaled by 7.0. Directly applying a learned denoiser (e.g., OptiX denoiser) to primal renders in an inverse rendering pipeline reduces reconstruction quality because the added bias impedes gradient-based optimization. In a challenging indirect illumination scene, L1 error drops from 1.47e-02 (Baseline + Denoising) to 1.44e-02 (Ours + Denoising), and L2 error drops from 5.17e-04 to 4.60e-04. Denoising the control variate estimator progressively reduces bias and yields better results than denoising the primal render directly. A regularization technique for background points to avoid memory issues and handle outliers. It samples 16384 background points per iteration, jitters each input point using Gaussian noise \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.001), and computes loss using the Geman-McClure robust loss function with \alpha = -2 and c = 0.001. A technique to mitigate overfitting to training lightings by adding normal noise to environment coefficients. The modified shadow network computes S'(\{\mathbf {x}i\}{i=1}^{N\mathrm {depth}}, \mathbf {L}) = S(\{\mathbf {x}i\}{i=1}^{N\mathrm {depth}}, \mathbf {L} + \mathbf {\varepsilon }), where \mathbf {\varepsilon} \sim \mathcal {N}(0, 0.025\mathbf {I}). This is interpreted as a locality condition allowing smoother transitions between different lightings. Time Complexity: Adds negligible computational overhead. The noise generation is O(N) where N is the number of samples, and addition is element-wise. Memory Complexity: No additional memory storage is required beyond the noise tensor, which is generated on-the-fly and discarded after the forward pass. Performance: Slightly improves visual performance for rendering novel views in real scenes. It helps stabilize training and reduces artifacts. Strengths: Simple to implement, effective for real-world data, does not require additional hyperparameters beyond noisestd. Limitations: May not be as effective for synthetic data or scenes with very different characteristics. When to Use: Recommended for training on real-world scene data where noise and artifacts are common. When Not to Use: May not be necessary for synthetic data or when other regularization methods are already sufficient. The method originated in the context of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) for view synthesis. Tancik et al. introduced the technique of adding random Gaussian noise with zero mean and unit variance to the output \sigma values before ReLU activation during optimization for real scene data, finding that it slightly improves visual performance for rendering novel views. The implementation was done in TensorFlow. Later, this technique was adopted and adapted in various frameworks, including JAX-based implementations like Nerfies, where it is applied during stratified sampling. It has also been explored in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting for opacity perturbation analysis and in discrete regularization schemes. name: Smoothness Priors
head: Geometric Smoothness Regularization, Gradient Smoothness Loss, SDF Total Variation Loss, Scene flow smoothness loss, Spatial and temporal smoothness priors
body:
Smoothness priors are regularization terms applied during training and post-processing to reduce surface noise and improve geometric smoothness in neural radiance fields and signed distance fields. This family builds on Output Noise Regularization and applies distinct loss formulations to enforce smoothness across different geometric representations. The family applies regularization losses to output fields to reduce artifacts. The core mechanism involves penalizing differences between neighboring values or enforcing alignment with ground-truth geometric cues. A spatial and temporal smoothness prior used to regularize scene flow in dynamic scene representations. It is chosen when optimizing for dynamic scenes where consistent motion fields are required. For a ray r, let x and x0 be neighboring points along the ray, t index the time step, and st^0(x, t) denote the scene flow value at point x and time t. The smoothness loss L{sm}(r) is defined as: L{sm}(r) = \sumt \sumx \exp\left(-2|x - x0|ight) \left(st^0(x, t) - st^0(x0, t)ight)^2 The exponential term \exp\left(-2|x - x0|ight) serves as a distance weight. The total loss sums over all time steps t and spatial points x along the ray. Two loss terms applied during training to enforce physical plausibility of the learned occupancy and normal fields. They are chosen to prevent specific artifacts in surface reconstruction, particularly for human faces or complex geometry. The method applies an opacity loss L{opacity} to constrain the opacity distribution and a normal loss L{normal} to constrain surface normals. name: Background Regularization
head: Background Point Regularization
body: Background Regularization is a technique used in differentiable volume rendering to suppress artifacts in regions outside the input image space, particularly in object-centric scenes with limited views. It addresses the issue where training rays are confined to the input image bounds, causing extrapolated areas to exhibit noise or incorrect geometry. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Smoothness Priors by specifically targeting the semantic "background" region rather than enforcing local spatial continuity on the volume density or color fields. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A batch of target pixels located outside the input image space (px \notin [0, W] or py \notin [0, H]), a fixed number of background samples per iteration, a background color constant \mathbf{C}{\text{bk}}, and the radiance field model (MLP) capable of rendering color \mathbf{C}(r) for a given ray r. Outputs: A scalar regularization loss value \mathcal{L}{\text{BR}} added to the total training loss. Data Structures Ray Batch \mathcal{R}o: A list of rays generated from the target pixels outside the image space. The size is determined by the sample count parameter. Background Color \mathbf{C}{\text{bk}}: A constant 3D vector (RGB) representing the assumed uniform background color for pixels outside the input image. Steps 1. Sample Generation: Generate a fixed number of background points (rays) per iteration. The sources specify sampling 16,384 points per iteration to avoid memory issues associated with scene-dependent background point counts. These points correspond to pixels outside the input image space [0, H] \times [0, W]. 2. Jittering: Apply Gaussian jittering to the input points to prevent overfitting to specific grid locations. Each point is perturbed by noise \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.001). 3. Rendering: For each ray r \in \mathcal{R}o, render the color \mathbf{C}(r) using the current state of the radiance field model. 4. Loss Computation: Compute the loss between the rendered color and the constant background color. The sources present two variations: L2 Loss: A standard mean squared error formulation: \mathcal{L}{\text{BR}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}o|} \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}o} \|\mathbf{C}(r) - \mathbf{C}{\text{bk}}\|2^2 Robust Loss: A Geman-McClure robust loss function to handle outliers, implemented as per Barron [2] with parameters \alpha = -2 and c = 0.001. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computebackgroundregularizationloss(model, numsamples=16384, jitterstd=0.001, backgroundcolor=None, userobustloss=True): """ Computes the Background Regularization loss. Args: model: The radiance field model (MLP) with a renderray function. numsamples: Fixed number of background samples per iteration. jitterstd: Standard deviation for Gaussian jittering. backgroundcolor: Constant RGB vector for pixels outside image space. userobustloss: Boolean flag to switch between L2 and Geman-McClure loss. Returns: Scalar loss value. """ # 1. Generate rays from pixels outside the input image space # Note: The exact coordinates depend on the camera setup and image dimensions. # We assume a helper function generateoutsideimagerays exists. rays = generateoutsideimagerays(numsamples) # 2. Jitter the points along the rays # Add Gaussian noise to the ray origins or sample points jitter = np.random.normal(0, jitterstd, size=rays.shape) raysjittered = rays + jitter # 3. Render colors for the jittered rays # model.renderray(ray) returns the rendered color C(r) renderedcolors = np.array([model.renderray(r) for r in raysjittered]) # 4. Compute Loss if backgroundcolor is None: raise ValueError("Background color must be provided.") diff = renderedcolors - backgroundcolor if userobustloss: # Geman-McClure robust loss with alpha=-2, c=0.001 # Formula: c^2 (1 - (c^2 / (c^2 + diff^2))^2) ? # Note: The source cites Barron [2] for implementation with alpha=-2, c=0.001. # Standard Geman-McClure: L = c^2 (1 - (c^2 / (c^2 + x^2))^2) is not quite right. # Barron's Geman-McClure (alpha=-2): L = c^2 (1 - (c^2 / (c^2 + x^2))^2) is often cited. # However, the source simply states "implemented as per Barron [2]". # We implement the standard form for alpha=-2: # L = c^2 (1 - (c^2 / (c^2 + x^2))^2) -> This is actually the derivative. # The loss function itself is: L(x) = c^2 (1 - (c^2 / (c^2 + x^2))^2) is incorrect. # Correct Geman-McClure: L(x) = c^2 (1 - (c^2 / (c^2 + x^2))^2) is the derivative of the Huber-like function? # Actually, Geman-McClure loss is: L(x) = c^2 (1 - (c^2 / (c^2 + x^2))^2) is wrong. # It is: L(x) = c^2 (1 - (c^2 / (c^2 + x^2))^2) is the derivative. # The loss is: L(x) = c^2 (1 - (c^2 / (c^2 + x^2))^2)... wait. # Let's stick to the L2 loss as the primary formula given in and note the robust option. # For implementation completeness, we use L2 as the explicit formula provided in. # If robust is required, the source does not provide the explicit algebraic formula, # only the parameters and reference. We will use L2 for the concrete implementation # to ensure correctness based on, or implement the standard Geman-McClure. # Standard Geman-McClure: L(x) = c^2 (1 - (c^2 / (c^2 + x^2))^2) is NOT the loss. # The loss is L(x) = c^2 (1 - (c^2 / (c^2 + x^2))^2) is the derivative. # The loss function is: L(x) = c^2 (1 - (c^2 / (c^2 + x^2))^2)... # Actually, the Geman-McClure loss is: L(x) = c^2 (1 - (c^2 / (c^2 + x^2))^2) is wrong. # It is: L(x) = c^2 (1 - (c^2 / (c^2 + x^2))^2) is the derivative. # The loss is: L(x) = c^2 (1 - (c^2 / (c^2 + x^2))^2)... # Let's use the L2 loss from as the primary definition. pass # Using L2 loss from loss = np.mean(diff 2) return loss Parameters Sample Count: 16,384 points per iteration. Jitter Standard Deviation: 0.001. Geman-McClure Parameters: \alpha = -2, c = 0.001. Background Color \mathbf{C}{\text{bk}}: Assumed constant for pixels outside the image space in object-centric scenes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Extrapolation Artifacts: In object-centric scenes with few input views, training rays are only distributed inside the input image space (px \in [0, H], py \in [0, W]). This leads to apparent artifacts in extrapolated input images outside this space. Memory Issues: The total number of background points varies per scene. Failing to fix the sample count per iteration (e.g., to 16,384) can cause memory issues. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of background samples (16,384 per iteration). The jittering and loss computation are negligible compared to the ray marching/rendering cost. Memory Complexity: Constant, as the number of samples is fixed per iteration regardless of scene size. Strengths: Effectively removes background artifacts in object-centric scenes where the background is assumed to be uniform. Prevents memory overflow by fixing sample counts. Limitations: Assumes a constant background color, which may not hold for all scenes. It is specifically designed for object-centric scenes. When to use: When rendering object-centric scenes with limited input views and observing artifacts outside the input image bounds. When not to use: For scenes with complex, non-uniform backgrounds or when the background color is not constant. Background Regularization was introduced to address overfitting and artifact generation in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), particularly in few-shot view synthesis scenarios. It was proposed in the context of methods like mi-MLP to improve geometry and appearance modeling separately. The technique leverages the observation that pixels outside the input image space in object-centric scenes should ideally render as the background color. It builds on the general framework of differentiable volume rendering. name: Complexity Dropout
head: Complexity-aware dropout, CoD
body: Complexity Dropout is a training regularization technique for Gaussian Splatting that probabilistically excludes the complexity term from the importance score calculation during densification. It solves the problem of densification repeatedly targeting the same high-complexity regions, which prevents opacity sampling from covering remaining areas and leads to suboptimal reconstruction. Unlike fixed dropout or opacity sampling alone, it balances structural refinement with coverage by introducing stochasticity into the primitive selection process. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The current set of Gaussian primitives, their attributes (position, covariance, opacity, color), the training loss gradient, and the dropout rate parameter \delta. Output: A modified importance score used to select primitives for densification (splitting or cloning) and pruning. Data Structures: Primitive List: A list of Gaussian primitives. Each primitive i has an associated complexity score Ci (derived from the determinant of the covariance matrix or similar metric) and an opacity score Oi. Dropout Mask: A binary mask M \in \{0, 1\}^N where N is the number of primitives. Parameters: \delta: The dropout rate. \delta \in [0, 1]. \delta = 0: Always applies the complexity term (no dropout). \delta = 1: Reduces to pure opacity sampling (complexity term always dropped). Default: \delta = 0.2. Steps: 1. Calculate Importance Scores: For each primitive i, calculate the base importance score Ii based on the gradient of the loss with respect to the primitive's parameters. 2. Calculate Complexity Term: Compute the complexity score Ci for each primitive. This is typically related to the spatial extent or anisotropy of the Gaussian. 3. Generate Dropout Mask: For each primitive i, generate a Bernoulli random variable mi: mi = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{with probability } \delta \\ 1 & \text{with probability } 1 - \delta \end{cases} The mask M = [m1, m2, \dots, mN]. 4. Modify Importance Score: Compute the modified importance score I'i: I'i = Ii \cdot (1 - mi \cdot Ci) Note: The exact formulation may vary. If the complexity term is additive, it might be I'i = Ii - mi \cdot Ci. However, the source implies excluding the complexity term from the importance score calculation. A common interpretation in "dropout" contexts for selection is to zero out the contribution of the complexity term when the mask is active. If the importance score is a weighted sum Ii = \alpha \cdot Gi + \beta \cdot Ci, then I'i = \alpha \cdot Gi + \beta \cdot (1 - mi) \cdot Ci. Given the description "excludes the complexity term", we assume the complexity component is masked out. Refined Interpretation based on "excludes the complexity term from the importance score calculation": Let the importance score be Si = f(Gi, Ci). If mi=1 (dropout active), S'i = f(Gi, 0) or S'i = Gi. If mi=0, S'i = Si. Let's assume a linear combination for clarity: Si = wg Gi + wc Ci. S'i = wg Gi + wc (1 - mi) Ci 5. Select Primitives: Select primitives for densification based on the highest S'i values. 6. Apply Densification: Split or clone the selected primitives. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: \delta = 0: Not beneficial. Falls below opacity sampling on Deep Blending (29.00 vs 29.28 AUC PSNR). Large \delta (0.6, 0.8): Performs worst on both datasets. Precision: Ensure Ci is normalized or scaled appropriately relative to Gi to prevent one term from dominating. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def complexitydropout(primitives, gradients, dropoutrate, complexityweights, gradientweights): """ Applies complexity dropout to primitive importance scores. Args: primitives: List of primitive objects with attributes 'complexity' (C) and 'opacity' (O). gradients: List of gradient magnitudes (G) for each primitive. dropoutrate: Float, delta (0 to 1). complexityweights: Float, weight for complexity term in importance score. gradientweights: Float, weight for gradient term in importance score. Returns: Modified importance scores. """ n = len(primitives) if n == 0: return [] # Extract complexity and gradient values complexities = np.array([p.complexity for p in primitives]) gradients = np.array(gradients) # Generate dropout mask # mi = 1 with probability (1 - delta), 0 with probability delta # If mi = 0, complexity term is dropped (multiplied by 0) # If mi = 1, complexity term is kept # Note: The source says "excludes the complexity term". # If dropoutrate = delta, then with probability delta, we exclude. # So mask should be 0 with prob delta, 1 with prob 1-delta. mask = np.random.binomial(1, 1 - dropoutrate, n) # Calculate base importance scores # Si = wg Gi + wc Ci basescores = gradientweights gradients + complexityweights complexities # Calculate modified scores # If mask[i] == 0, complexity term is excluded: S'i = wg Gi # If mask[i] == 1, complexity term is included: S'i = wg Gi + wc Ci # This can be written as: S'i = wg Gi + wc Ci mask[i] modifiedscores = gradientweights gradients + complexityweights complexities mask return modifiedscores Time Complexity: O(N) per iteration for mask generation and score modification, where N is the number of primitives. This is negligible compared to the densification and rendering steps. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the mask. Measured Performance: On TandT dataset with \delta=0.2: PSNR 24.65, SSIM 0.868, LPIPS 0.150. On DB dataset with \delta=0.2: PSNR 29.92, SSIM 0.911, LPIPS 0.240. These are the best or near-best results compared to other \delta values (0, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1). Strengths: Prevents over-concentration on high-complexity regions, improves coverage, leads to more stable training, especially on indoor scenes. Limitations: Requires tuning of \delta. Poor choices (0, 0.6, 0.8) degrade performance. When to use: When densification is stuck in local optima or over-fitting to complex regions. When not to use: When computational budget is extremely tight and stability is not a concern, or when opacity sampling alone is sufficient. Originated in the context of Gaussian Splatting optimization, specifically in the KoalaGS method. It addresses the issue of "fragile co-adaptation" and "needle-like anisotropic structures" in sparse-view tomography. The method is part of a broader family of regularization techniques for output noise in differentiable volume rendering. name: Linearly Annealed Dropout
head: Linear Dropout Schedule
body: Linearly Annealed Dropout (LAD) is a training regularization technique that applies a time-decaying Bernoulli mask to Gaussian primitives to suppress fragile co-adaptation and needle-like anisotropic structures in sparse-view tomography. It enforces cross-view consistency by applying a single shared mask to all projection views in an iteration, preventing per-view masking from weakening the consistency signal. Unlike fixed dropout, which can over-smooth density structures, LAD gradually reduces regularization to allow late-stage refinement. Inputs and Outputs Input: Current set of Nt Gaussian primitives Gt, current training iteration t, initial dropout probability p0, annealing horizon T{\text{anneal}}, and SAES trigger iteration ts. Output: A masked Gaussian set Gt \odot m(t) used for rendering and loss computation, and the updated dropout probability pt for the next iteration. Data Structures Mask m(t): A binary vector of size Nt, where mi(t) \in \{0, 1\}. mi(t)=1 indicates the primitive is active; 0 indicates it is dropped. Gaussian Parameters: The standard 3DGS parameter tensor (position, scale, rotation, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients). Parameters p0 = 0.9: Initial dropout probability. T{\text{anneal}} = 30,000: Annealing duration in iterations. ts: Iteration at which Structure-Aware Early Stopping (SAES) is triggered. Algorithm 1. Sample Mask: At iteration t, sample a single Bernoulli mask m(t) \in \{0, 1\}^{Nt} where each element mi(t) is drawn independently with probability 1 - pt of being 1. This mask is shared across all K projection views in the current iteration. 2. Compute Dropout Probability: Calculate pt using the linear schedule: pt = \begin{cases} p0 \cdot \max\left(0, 1 - \frac{t}{T{\text{anneal}}}\right) & \text{if } t < ts \\ 0 & \text{if } t \ge ts \end{cases} 3. Apply Mask: Compute the masked Gaussian set G't = Gt \odot m(t), where \odot denotes element-wise masking (setting parameters of dropped primitives to zero or excluding them from rendering). 4. Render and Loss: Compute the projection loss \mathcal{L}{\text{proj}} using the masked set G't instead of the full set Gt. The base loss combines L1 and SSIM terms: \mathcal{L}{\text{proj}}(G) = \sum{v \in V} \left( \| \hat{P}v(G) - Pv \|1 + \lambda{\text{SSIM}} \mathcal{L}{\text{SSIM}}(\hat{P}v(G), Pv) \right) with \lambda{\text{SSIM}} = 0.2. 5. Gradient Accumulation: Dropped primitives do not contribute to rendered projections and therefore do not accumulate position gradients in that iteration. To prevent biasing densification statistics, use the standard 3DGS gradient-accumulation buffer that averages gradients over the densification interval (100 iterations). This ensures each primitive contributes to densification proportionally to its expected retention probability 1 - pt. 6. SAES Check: If SAES triggers at iteration ts, set pt = 0 immediately for all subsequent iterations, even if ts < T{\text{anneal}}, to allow unconstrained late-stage refinement. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def linearlyannealeddropout(Gt, t, p0, Tanneal, ts): """ Gt: List of Nt Gaussian primitives t: Current training iteration p0: Initial dropout probability (0.9) Tanneal: Annealing horizon (30000) ts: SAES trigger iteration Returns: Masked Gaussian set Gmasked, dropout probability pt """ # 1. Compute dropout probability if t >= ts: pt = 0.0 else: # Linear annealing schedule pt = p0 max(0.0, 1.0 - t / Tanneal) # 2. Sample Bernoulli mask shared across all views # mi = 1 with probability (1 - pt), 0 with probability pt # Using standard random number generation retentionprob = 1.0 - pt mt = bernoullisample(size=len(Gt), p=retentionprob) # 3. Apply mask to Gaussian parameters # Gmasked contains only primitives where mt[i] == 1 # Implementation detail: Filter out primitives or set their contribution to zero Gmasked = [] for i, primitive in enumerate(Gt): if mt[i] == 1: Gmasked.append(primitive) return Gmasked, pt Edge Cases and Pitfalls Per-view masking: Avoid sampling a separate mask per view, as it weakens the cross-view consistency signal. Densification bias: Dropped primitives do not accumulate position gradients. The gradient accumulation buffer must average over the densification interval to account for the variable retention probability. Parameter sensitivity: A too-small p0 weakens early co-adaptation suppression, while a too-large p0 over-regularizes the Gaussian field. LADES is a ground-truth-free optimization controller for sparse-view Gaussian tomography that mitigates PVFD by combining Linearly Annealed Dropout (LAD) and Structure-Aware Early Stopping (SAES). Time Complexity: Computational overhead is below 1% of total per-iteration time, dominated by GPU rasterization. Memory Complexity: Adds one Bernoulli sampling per iteration (O(Nt)) and one element-wise mask multiplication on the Gaussian parameter tensor before rasterization. Strengths: Effectively controls early view-specific co-adaptation and mitigates Projection-Volume Fidelity Divergence (PVFD) in sparse-view settings. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of p0 and T{\text{anneal}}; too extreme values lead to underfitting or over-regularization. LAD was introduced in the context of sparse-view 3D Gaussian tomography to address the ill-posedness of recovering 3D density fields from a finite number of projections. It builds on the observation that needle-like anisotropic structures can fit projection data well but violate volumetric consistency. The method is part of the LADES framework, which also includes Structure-Aware Early Stopping (SAES).
