name: LADES
head: Linearly Annealed Dropout and Structure-Aware Early Stopping, Linearly Annealed Dropout with Structure-Aware Early Stopping
body: LADES is a ground-truth-free optimization controller for sparse-view 3D Gaussian tomography that mitigates Projection-Volume Fidelity Divergence (PVFD) by combining Linearly Annealed Dropout (LAD) and Structure-Aware Early Stopping (SAES). It addresses the problem where improved projection fitting coincides with deteriorating volumetric fidelity due to structural degeneration, such as needle-like anisotropic primitives and fragile co-adaptation. Unlike fixed dropout or validation-based stopping, LADES disrupts premature co-adaptation via time-decaying stochastic masking and terminates densification based on intrinsic Gaussian population dynamics rather than external metrics. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sparse-view X-ray projections Pv, a set of Gaussian primitives Gt (initialized via R2-GS or similar), and hyperparameters p0, T{anneal}, t{min}, \tau, W, \gamma{cool}. Outputs: A final set of Gaussian primitives G{final} and their parameters (position, scale, opacity, color) optimized for volumetric fidelity. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitive i: Contains position \mathbf{x}i, scale \mathbf{s}i, opacity \alphai, and color coefficients. Mask m^{(t)}: A binary vector where mi^{(t)} \in \{0, 1\} indicates if primitive i is active at iteration t. Population Counter Nj: The number of active Gaussians at monitoring step j. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussian primitives G0. Set iteration counter t=0. Set monitoring step counter j=0. Initialize Adam optimizer moments for position and scaling parameters. 2. Dropout Probability Calculation: Compute the current dropout probability pt: pt = \begin{cases} p0 \max\left(0, 1 - \frac{t}{T{anneal}}\right), & t < ts \\ 0, & t \ge ts \end{cases} where p0 is the initial dropout probability, T{anneal} is the annealing horizon, and ts is the SAES trigger iteration (initially undefined or \infty). 3. Mask Sampling: For each Gaussian primitive i, sample a Bernoulli mask mi^{(t)} with retention probability 1 - pt: mi^{(t)} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(1 - pt) mi^{(t)} = 1 means the primitive is retained for the forward and backward pass. 4. Loss Computation: Compute the projection loss using the masked Gaussian set Gt \odot m^{(t)}: L{LAD}^{(t)} = \sum{v \in V} \left\| \hat{P}v(Gt \odot m^{(t)}) - Pv \right\|^2 + \lambda{SSIM} L{SSIM}(\hat{P}v(Gt \odot m^{(t)}), Pv) where \hat{P}v is the rendered projection, Pv is the ground truth projection, and L{SSIM} is the SSIM loss. 5. Optimization Step: Perform gradient descent using the Adam optimizer to update Gaussian parameters based on L{LAD}^{(t)}. 6. Densification (Conditional): If t < ts, perform standard densification operations (clone, split, prune) according to the R2-GS densification rule. If t \ge ts, disable all topology-changing operations. 7. Monitoring (SAES): Every \Delta iterations, increment j and monitor the Gaussian population: Let Nj be the number of active Gaussians at step j. Compute the normalized population growth rate gj: gj = \frac{Nj - N{j-1}}{\max(N{j-1}, 1)} Compute the averaged growth rate \bar{g}j over a sliding window of size W: \bar{g}j = \frac{1}{W-1} \sum{q=j-W+2}^{j} gq Check for SAES trigger: If tj \ge t{min} and \bar{g}j < \tau, set ts = tj. 8. Transition to Fixed-Topology Refinement: Once ts is triggered (or if ts was never triggered, after T{anneal} or a max iteration limit): Set final training iteration T{final} = 2ts. Disable dropout (pt = 0). Cool down learning rates for geometry (\eta{xyz}) and scaling (\eta{scale}) parameters by factor \gamma{cool}: \eta{xyz} \leftarrow \gamma{cool} \eta{xyz}, \quad \eta{scale} \leftarrow \gamma{cool} \eta{scale} Reset the first- and second-order Adam moments for position and scaling parameters to remove optimization inertia. Continue optimization until T{final}. Parameters: p0: Initial dropout probability. Default: 0.9. T{anneal}: Annealing horizon. Default: 30,000 iterations. t{min}: Minimum iteration count before SAES can trigger. Default: 2,000. \tau: Growth threshold for SAES. Default: 10^{-3}. W: Sliding window size for SAES. Default: 5. \gamma{cool}: Learning rate cooling factor. Default: 0.2. \Delta: Monitoring interval. Default: 100 iterations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Over-regularization: If p0 is too large, the model may underfit volumetrically, dropping 3D PSNR significantly (e.g., from 35.45 dB to 30.62 dB). Under-suppression: If p0 is too small, early co-adaptation is not sufficiently disrupted. Premature Stopping: If t{min} is too low, SAES may trigger before structural saturation, leading to incomplete reconstruction. Ground-Truth Dependency: SAES must not access ground-truth volumes or 3D PSNR during training; doing so violates the ground-truth-free design and may lead to overfitting to validation metrics. A regularization technique that applies strong stochastic masking in early training to disrupt premature primitive co-adaptation, then linearly decays the dropout probability to zero to restore full capacity for structural consolidation. Choose when early view-specific co-adaptation is a primary concern. See Linearly Annealed Dropout. A stopping criterion that monitors Gaussian population growth momentum to detect structural saturation and terminates densification without ground-truth metrics. Choose when volumetric fidelity degradation due to redundant late-stage densification is observed. See Structure-Aware Early Stopping. Time Complexity: Training time is reduced compared to fixed-budget training because SAES terminates densification early, though the final refinement phase extends training to 2ts. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is determined by the number of active Gaussians, which is controlled by SAES to prevent excessive growth. Performance: On sparse-view CT reconstruction (e.g., 25-view FIPS dataset), LADES improves volumetric fidelity, suppresses structural degeneration, and maintains competitive projection accuracy (PSNR ~36.33 dB, SSIM ~0.853). Strengths: Ground-truth-free; mitigates PVFD; reduces training time; robust to hyperparameter variations. Limitations: Evaluated primarily on sparse-view CT with Gaussian-based backbones; generalization to other scanner geometries, noise levels, and clinical protocols requires further validation. When to Use: Sparse-view 3D Gaussian tomography where volumetric fidelity is critical and ground-truth volumes are unavailable during training. When Not to Use: Dense-view reconstruction where PVFD is less severe; non-Gaussian representations; scenarios where ground-truth validation metrics are available and preferred. LADES was introduced in the paper "Projection-Volume Fidelity Divergence: Diagnosing and Controlling Optimization Drift in Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Tomography". The authors identified PVFD as a failure mode in sparse-view 3DGS-CT where projection fitting improves while volumetric fidelity deteriorates due to structural degeneration (needle-like primitives, fragile co-adaptation). LADES combines LAD and SAES to address this, using diagnostics like Geometric Anisotropy Index (GAI) and Volumetric Co-adaptation Score (VCS) to characterize the problem. The method was evaluated on real X-ray CT data from the Finnish Inverse Problems Society (FIPS) dataset. Projection-Volume Fidelity Divergence: Diagnosing and Controlling Optimization Drift in Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Tomography, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2606.22525, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Perceptual Loss Training
head: PIPS Loss, Perceptual Loss for 3DGS, Perceptual loss for dynamic NeRF
body: Perceptual Loss Training is an optimization strategy that incorporates a perceptual loss term to improve the visual fidelity of rendered images, addressing the smoothness and texture distortion issues inherent in pixel-wise losses like L1 or L2. It sets itself apart from its siblings by leveraging features from pre-trained convolutional neural networks (typically VGG) to enforce high-level structural consistency, whereas methods like Total Variation Regularization operate directly on spatial gradients of the output or scene parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rendered image \hat{I} (prediction), ground truth image Ig, pre-trained feature extractor network \Phi (e.g., VGG-19), and loss weights \lambdal or w{\cdot}. Output: Scalar loss value \mathcal{L}{\text{perc}} used for backpropagation. Data Structures: Feature Maps: Intermediate activations from the pre-trained network. For VGG-19, these are typically extracted from specific convolutional layers. Weights: Scalars \lambdal balancing the contribution of each layer's feature distance. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Pass both the rendered image \hat{I} and the ground truth image Ig through the pre-trained network \Phi. Extract feature maps from a set of layers L. \mathbf{F}{\hat{I}}^l = \Phil(\hat{I}), \quad \mathbf{F}{Ig}^l = \Phil(Ig) \quad \forall l \in L 2. Distance Calculation: Compute the distance between the feature maps of the prediction and the ground truth. The L1 norm is commonly used. D^l = \| \mathbf{F}{\hat{I}}^l - \mathbf{F}{Ig}^l \|1 3. Aggregation: Sum the distances weighted by layer-specific coefficients \lambdal. \mathcal{L}{\text{perc}} = \sum{l \in L} \lambdal D^l Formulas: The general perceptual loss is defined as: L(Pf, \theta) = \suml \lambdal \| \Phil(Ig) - \Phil(f(Pf; \theta)) \|1 where Pf represents the scene parameters (e.g., point features), \theta are the network parameters, f is the rendering function, and \Phil are the VGG-19 layers. In the context of Gaussian Splatting (PIPS), the total loss combines L1, SSIM, and Perceptual (PIPS) terms: \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda1 - \lambda2)\mathcal{L}1 + \lambda1\mathcal{L}{\text{SSIM}} + \lambda2\mathcal{L}{\text{PIPS}} where \mathcal{L}{\text{PIPS}} is the perceptual loss term. Parameters: VGG-19 Layers: Commonly used layers include 'input', 'conv1-2', 'conv2-2', 'conv3-2', 'conv4-2', and 'conv5-2'. Weights (\lambdal): Balancing weights for each layer. Specific values are not provided in the sources, but they follow the scheme in Chen et al.. Weights (\lambda1, \lambda2): In the PIPS formulation, \lambda1 weights the SSIM term and \lambda2 weights the perceptual term. Exact values are not given. Optimization: Adam optimizer is typically used. Learning rate initialized at 0.01, decreased every 7 epochs: 0.01 \to 0.005 \to 0.001. Learning rate 10^{-4}. Pitfalls: Computational Overhead: CNN-based perceptual loss computation is expensive. It is recommended to compute it every 20 training iterations to alleviate overhead without significantly impacting quality. Color Shifts: Perceptual loss can introduce color shifts in the rendered output. This may require auxiliary terms like Anti-Bias Loss to correct. Visual Quality Degradation: Omitting perceptual loss increases LPIPS distance, indicating degraded visual quality even if pixel-wise metrics (PSNR/SSIM) remain acceptable. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeperceptualloss(renderedimage, groundtruth, vggmodel, layers, weights): """ Computes the perceptual loss using VGG features. Args: renderedimage (Tensor): Rendered image tensor, shape (H, W, 3). groundtruth (Tensor): Ground truth image tensor, shape (H, W, 3). vggmodel (nn.Module): Pre-trained VGG-19 model. layers (List[str]): List of layer names to extract features from. weights (Dict[str, float]): Weights for each layer's loss contribution. Returns: Tensor: Scalar perceptual loss. """ # Ensure inputs are normalized similarly to VGG training (e.g., mean/std of ImageNet) # Standard VGG preprocessing: normalize by ImageNet mean and std. # Extract features featurespred = {} featuresgt = {} # Forward pass through VGG to get intermediate features # Assuming vggmodel returns a dict of features for requested layers # or we hook into the model. Here we assume a helper function. featurespred = vggmodel.extractfeatures(renderedimage, layers) featuresgt = vggmodel.extractfeatures(groundtruth, layers) loss = 0.0 for layer in layers: featp = featurespred[layer] featg = featuresgt[layer] # Compute L1 distance between feature maps # torch.nn.functional.l1loss computes mean over all elements layerloss = torch.nn.functional.l1loss(featp, featg) # Weight the layer loss if layer in weights: layerloss = weights[layer] loss += layerloss return loss def computepipsloss(renderedimage, groundtruth, vggmodel, lambda1, lambda2): """ Computes the PIPS loss as part of the total loss for Gaussian Splatting. Args: renderedimage (Tensor): Rendered image. groundtruth (Tensor): Ground truth image. vggmodel (nn.Module): Pre-trained VGG-19. lambda1 (float): Weight for SSIM loss. lambda2 (float): Weight for Perceptual loss. Returns: Tensor: Total loss scalar. """ # 1. L1 Loss l1loss = torch.nn.functional.l1loss(renderedimage, groundtruth) # 2. SSIM Loss # Assuming a standard SSIM implementation ssimloss = 1.0 - computessim(renderedimage, groundtruth) # 3. Perceptual (PIPS) Loss # Use specific layers as per S2: 'input', 'conv1-2', etc. layers = ['input', 'conv1-2', 'conv2-2', 'conv3-2', 'conv4-2', 'conv5-2'] # Weights for VGG layers as per Chen et al. vggweights = { 'input': 1.0, 'conv1-2': 1.0, 'conv2-2': 1.0, 'conv3-2': 1.0, 'conv4-2': 1.0, 'conv5-2': 1.0 } pipsloss = computeperceptualloss(renderedimage, groundtruth, vggmodel, layers, vggweights) # Total Loss Formula from S1 # L = (1 - lambda1 - lambda2)L1 + lambda1LSSIM + lambda2LPIPS totalloss = (1 - lambda1 - lambda2) l1loss + lambda1 ssimloss + lambda2 pipsloss return totalloss Stable View Synthesis (SVS) is a view synthesis method that blends training images together to render novel views, relying on proxy geometry from an external system. It is distinguished from its siblings by its explicit dependence on external proxy geometry (typically piecewise planar meshes) and access to all training images, whereas High-Frequency Aware Loss and WD-Regularized Loss operate within different optimization frameworks without this specific blending-and-proxy requirement. High-Frequency Aware Loss (LHF) is a perceptual regularization term designed to recover high-frequency details in rendered images while avoiding the texture distortion common in deeper perceptual losses. It sets itself apart from standard VGG-based perceptual losses by restricting feature extraction to the first block of the network, before any max-pooling operations, thereby preserving fine-grained spatial information. It builds on Perceptual Loss Training by specifically targeting the loss of high-frequency content that occurs when using pixel-wise losses on misaligned data. A training objective that augments the Wasserstein Distance (WD) perceptual loss with a lightly weighted version of the original 3DGS pixel-level loss to avoid artifacts in regions with constrained splat counts or small numbers of training views. An l1 loss applied to downsampled versions of prediction and ground truth to eliminate color shifts introduced by perceptual loss while remaining robust against minor misalignments. Formula: Calculate Lab as the l1 distance between k-fold downsampled ground truth patch P and predicted patch \hat{P}: L{ab} = \| DSk(P) - DSk(\hat{P}) \|1 where DSk(\cdot) denotes k-fold downsampling. The full objective function is: L = w{l1} \cdot L{l1} + w{vgg} \cdot L{vgg} + w{ab} \cdot L{ab} where L{l1} is pixel-wise l1 distance, L{vgg} is perceptual loss, and w{\cdot} are weights. Time Complexity: High. Perceptual loss requires forward passes through a deep CNN (VGG-19) for both the rendered and ground truth images. notes that computing it every 20 iterations is necessary to alleviate this overhead. reports training taking on average 41.5 hours per scene on one GeForce 1080 Ti. Memory Complexity: Moderate to High. Requires storing intermediate feature maps from the VGG network for the backpropagation step. Performance: Improves perceptual quality (LPIPS) significantly compared to pixel-wise losses. However, it may introduce color shifts if not regularized (e.g., with Anti-Bias Loss). Strengths: Better visual fidelity, recovers high-frequency details, reduces structural artifacts. Limitations: Computationally expensive, prone to color shifts, requires careful tuning of weights. When to use: When visual quality is prioritized over training speed, and when pixel-wise losses result in overly smooth or blurry outputs. When not to use: When real-time training is required, or when color accuracy is critical and auxiliary bias correction is not feasible. Perceptual loss was originally introduced for image generation tasks. In the context of volume rendering and radiance fields, it has been adopted to address the "smoothness" problem of L1/L2 losses, which often produce blurry results. It is used in various NeRF and Gaussian Splatting optimizations to enhance high-frequency details and structural consistency. name: Stable View Synthesis (SVS) Baseline
head: SVS Baseline, SVS*, Stable View Synthesis (SVS)
body: Stable View Synthesis (SVS) is a view synthesis method that blends training images together to render novel views, relying on proxy geometry from an external system. It is distinguished from its siblings by its explicit dependence on external proxy geometry (typically piecewise planar meshes) and access to all training images, whereas High-Frequency Aware Loss and WD-Regularized Loss operate within different optimization frameworks without this specific blending-and-proxy requirement. SVS is trained using a perceptual loss. The method operates by blending training images together to render novel views. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of training images; proxy geometry produced by an external system. Outputs: Rendered novel views. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Obtain proxy geometry from an external system. 2. Train the model using a perceptual loss. 3. Render novel views by blending training images together. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: SVS may fail when the external proxy geometry is incorrect. It struggles particularly with distant or unobserved content, such as trees, where the proxy geometry reconstruction (e.g., via COLMAP) is poor. Pseudocode: Not given in the sources. Improves perceptual quality by targeting high-frequency details. Choose when SVS fails on natural content due to proxy geometry errors. See High-Frequency Aware Loss. Uses weight decay regularization for stability. Choose when SVS's reliance on external geometry is unavailable. See WD-Regularized Loss. SVS requires multiple large CNNs and access to all training images to render novel views. It is better suited to large piecewise planar objects (e.g., vehicles) due to its reliance on piecewise planar mesh proxy geometry, whereas it performs poorly on scenes with natural content (trees, grass, flowers). Stable View Synthesis was introduced by Riegler and Koltun in CVPR 2021. name: High-Frequency Aware Loss
head: LHF, Shallow VGG Loss
body: High-Frequency Aware Loss (LHF) is a perceptual regularization term designed to recover high-frequency details in rendered images while avoiding the texture distortion common in deeper perceptual losses. It sets itself apart from standard VGG-based perceptual losses by restricting feature extraction to the first block of the network, thereby preserving fine structural details without enforcing semantic texture consistency that may conflict with the ground truth. It builds on Perceptual Loss Training by providing a differentiable proxy for high-frequency similarity. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Gi (ground truth image patch after alignment), R (rendered image patch). Output: Scalar loss value L{HF}. Data Structures: Feature Extractor (F): The first block of a pre-trained VGG-19 model. This block consists of convolutional layers followed by ReLU activations, but explicitly excludes the max-pooling layer that typically follows this block in the standard VGG-19 architecture. Feature Maps: The output of F is a tensor of dimensions C \times W \times H, where C is the number of channels, and W, H are the width and height of the feature map. Parameters: w: Weight for the LHF term in the total loss function (value not specified in sources). F: Pre-trained VGG-19 weights (frozen). Steps: 1. Extract features from the ground truth patch Gi using the shallow VGG block: F(Gi). 2. Extract features from the rendered patch R using the same block: F(R). 3. Compute the squared Euclidean distance between the feature maps. 4. Normalize by the total number of elements in the feature map (C \times W \times H) and divide by 2. Formula: L{HF}(Gi, R) = \frac{1}{2CW H} \|F(Gi) - F(R)\|2^2 Where: \| \cdot \|2^2 denotes the squared L2 norm (sum of squared differences). C, W, H are the dimensions of the extracted feature maps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def highfrequencyawareloss(groundtruthpatch, renderedpatch, vggblock): """ Computes the High-Frequency Aware Loss using the first block of VGG-19. Args: groundtruthpatch (Tensor): Ground truth image patch Gi. renderedpatch (Tensor): Rendered image patch R. vggblock (Module): The first block of a pre-trained VGG-19 model (convolutions + ReLUs, no max-pooling). Returns: Tensor: Scalar loss value LHF. """ # Extract features using the shallow VGG block # F(Gi) and F(R) are tensors of shape (C, W, H) featuresgt = vggblock(groundtruthpatch) featuresrendered = vggblock(renderedpatch) # Compute squared L2 distance between feature maps diff = featuresgt - featuresrendered squareddiff = diff 2 # Sum over all elements (C, W, H) sumsquareddiff = torch.sum(squareddiff) # Normalize by 2 C W H # Note: C, W, H are derived from the shape of featuresgt c, w, h = featuresgt.shape[1], featuresgt.shape[2], featuresgt.shape[3] normalizationfactor = 2.0 c w h loss = sumsquareddiff / normalizationfactor return loss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Misalignment: The loss assumes Gi and R are aligned. Misalignment prevents the recovery of high-frequency details, as the feature comparison will penalize structural shifts rather than texture errors. Texture Distortion: Using deeper VGG blocks can distort actual textures; restricting to the first block mitigates this. Noise Sensitivity: Like other perceptual losses, it may suffer from loss-induced bias if rendered images contain noise. Time Complexity: Dominated by the forward pass through the first block of VGG-19, which is lightweight compared to the full network. Memory Complexity: Requires storing intermediate feature maps from the first VGG block for the gradient computation. Strengths: Improves high-frequency details while preserving real textures, addressing the smoothness issues of pixel-wise MSE losses. Limitations: Sensitive to misalignment between ground truth and rendered patches. When to use: When optimizing radiance fields or images where high-frequency detail recovery is critical and standard MSE loss results in overly smooth outputs. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited or when the input images are heavily misaligned without prior alignment correction. The High-Frequency Aware Loss was introduced in the AligNeRF paper. It modifies the original perceptual loss proposed by Johnson et al. ] by using only the output of the first block of a pre-trained VGG-19 model, before the max-pooling layer. This modification was motivated by observations in image restoration tasks where deeper perceptual losses distorted actual textures. The loss is typically combined with a patch-based MSE loss to handle misalignment, replacing the standard per-pixel MSE loss. name: VGG Loss for Image Patches
head: Perceptual Loss (VGG), VGG Loss, VGG feature distance
body: A perceptual loss computed on image patches using a VGG network, encouraging the generated patches to have similar high-level features as the real patches. It serves as a differentiable proxy for perceptual similarity that truncates the VGG network and computes the Euclidean distance between high-level features produced during model evaluation. Unlike traditional pixel-wise losses, VGG loss measures perceptual similarity but suffers from loss-induced bias when rendered images contain noise. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Real image patches, generated (fake) image patches, a pre-trained VGG network (typically VGG-19), and a loss multiplier parameter. Outputs: A scalar loss value representing the perceptual distance between the patches. Data Structures: Patches: 2D image arrays (e.g., height H, width W, channels C). VGG Features: Activation maps from a specific layer of the VGG network. The parent method High-Frequency Aware Loss specifies using only the first block of VGG-19 (before max-pooling) to preserve high-frequency details. Steps: 1. Extract real and fake patches from the outputs and batch. 2. Slice the patches to include only the first numpatches if batch processing is used. 3. Pass both real and fake patches through the truncated VGG network to obtain high-level feature representations. 4. Compute the Euclidean distance (L2 norm) between the feature maps of the real and fake patches. 5. Multiply the computed distance by the vgglossmult parameter to scale the contribution to the total loss. Formula: Let x{real} and x{fake} be the real and fake patches. Let \Phi(x) be the feature extraction function of the truncated VGG network. The VGG loss L{VGG} is: L{VGG} = \| \Phi(x{real}) - \Phi(x{fake}) \|2^2 The final loss term added to the optimization objective is: L{final} = \text{vgg\loss\mult} \times L{VGG} Parameters: vgglossmult: The multiplier for the VGG loss in the total loss computation. Value not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noise Sensitivity: High-level feature propagation makes the loss highly sensitive to noise, which can bias optimization towards suboptimal solutions. This is particularly problematic in inverse rendering where rendered images may contain Monte Carlo noise. Boundary Conditions: When slicing patches, ensure indices do not exceed batch dimensions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computevgglossforpatches(realpatches, fakepatches, vggmodel, vgglossmult): """ Computes the VGG perceptual loss for a batch of image patches. Args: realpatches: Tensor of shape (B, C, H, W) containing real image patches. fakepatches: Tensor of shape (B, C, H, W) containing generated image patches. vggmodel: A pre-trained VGG-19 model, truncated to the first block (before max-pooling). vgglossmult: Scalar multiplier for the loss. Returns: Scalar loss value. """ # 1. Extract features from real and fake patches using the truncated VGG model # The parent method specifies using only the first block of VGG-19 featuresreal = vggmodel(realpatches) featuresfake = vggmodel(fakepatches) # 2. Compute Euclidean distance (L2 norm) between feature maps # This is the core definition of VGG loss as a differentiable proxy for perceptual similarity diff = featuresreal - featuresfake loss = torch.sum(diff 2) # 3. Apply multiplier finalloss = vgglossmult loss return finalloss A variant that uses the LPIPS (Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity) metric for patch supervision. In each training step, it randomly renders a 300 × 300 image patch and compares it with the ground-truth image patch to compute the LPIPS loss. The total training loss is L = L{reg} + \lambda{LPIPS} L{LPIPS}, where L{reg} = \lambda{color} L{color} + \lambda{density} L{density} is the regularization loss. The weight \lambda{LPIPS} is set to 0.025. Unlike NeRF, which requires multiple network evaluations per ray or small 32×32 patches, this method renders a large 300×300 patch in a single step, enabling efficient large-patch LPIPS supervision. On the light change dataset, ProLiF with large-patch LPIPS achieves higher SSIM and lower LPIPS than NeRF with 32×32 patch supervision or 256×256 up-sampled patch supervision. Time Complexity: Depends on the VGG network inference time and the number of patches. Large patches (e.g., 300×300) increase memory usage but reduce the number of forward passes compared to small patches. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the patch size and batch size. Large patches require more VRAM. Measured Performance: On the light change dataset, large-patch LPIPS supervision achieves better quality than small-patch (32×32) or up-sampled (256×256) supervision in terms of SSIM and LPIPS. Strengths: Measures perceptual similarity, robust to noise, intensity changes, and distortions. Preserves high-frequency details when using shallow VGG blocks. Limitations: Highly sensitive to noise in rendered images, leading to loss-induced bias. Not compatible with PSNR in varying light conditions. When to use: When perceptual quality is more important than pixel-wise accuracy, and the rendering pipeline can handle the computational cost of VGG inference. When not to use: When the rendered images contain significant noise that biases the optimization. VGG loss was introduced by Johnson et al. [2016] as a way to measure perceptual similarity by truncating the VGG-19 network [Simonyan and Zisserman 2015] and computing the Euclidean distance between high-level features. It has been widely used in image synthesis and optimization tasks. In the context of volume rendering, it is used as a regularization loss to improve perceptual quality. The specific application to image patches in large-scale rendering is explored in methods like ProLiF. barbararoessle/ganerf, https://github.com/barbararoessle/ganerf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Recursive Control Variates for Inverse Rendering, https://research.nvidia.com/labs/rtr/publication/nicolet2023recursive/, fetched 2026-11-08 Progressively-connected Light Field Network for Efficient View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2207.04465, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: WD-Regularized Loss
head: WD with original loss regularizer, WD-R, WD-R Objective, WD-Regularized, Wasserstein Distortion (WD) Loss Optimization
body: WD-Regularized Loss (WD-R) is a training objective for 3D Gaussian Splatting that combines the Wasserstein Distance (WD) perceptual loss with a lightly weighted version of the original pixel-level loss. It solves the problem of visual artifacts that occur in regions with constrained Gaussian splat counts or limited training views, where the pure WD loss may fail to enforce sufficient pixel fidelity. Unlike its sibling Stable View Synthesis (SVS) Baseline which focuses on gradient stability, or High-Frequency Aware Loss which targets high-frequency details, WD-R specifically balances perceptual fidelity against raw pixel error to maintain compact representations without sacrificing sharpness. The method augments the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization by introducing a composite loss function. The core mechanism relies on computing the Wasserstein Distance between VGG feature pyramids of the rendered and ground-truth images, while adding a scaled original loss term to regularize the optimization. Inputs: Current 3D Gaussian parameters (means, covariances, opacities, colors, spherical harmonics). Camera poses and intrinsics for the current training view. Ground-truth image for the current view. Pre-computed ground-truth VGG features and pyramid statistics (if caching is enabled). Outputs: Rendered image. Scalar loss value L{WD-R}. Gradients with respect to Gaussian parameters. VGG Feature Pyramid: A stack of feature maps extracted from a pre-trained VGG network. The implementation uses 96 pyramid levels. Pyramid Weights: A scalar weight for each pyramid level i, computed as \text{ReLU}(1 - |\log2 \sigma - i|). Cached Statistics: Ground-truth VGG features and their corresponding pyramid statistics (mean and variance) are cached to avoid recomputation. The total loss is defined as: L{WD-R} = \gamma (d{WD} + \beta L{orig}) Where: L{WD-R} is the WD-Regularized loss. \gamma is a dataset-specific global scale factor. It modulates the magnitude of positional gradients to control the number of generated Gaussian splats, ensuring fair comparison with baselines under similar representation budgets. d{WD} is the Wasserstein Distance distortion metric computed in VGG feature space. \beta is the weighting factor for the original loss. It is chosen such that L{orig} acts as a mild pixel fidelity regularizer without overwhelming the WD term. L{orig} is the original 3DGS pixel-level loss (typically a combination of L1 and SSIM). The pure WD loss is defined as: L{WD} = \gamma d{WD} The per-level pyramid weight is calculated as: wi = \text{ReLU}(1 - |\log2 \sigma - i|) Where: \sigma = 4 is a constant. i is the pyramid level index. \beta: Set to 0.09 for all scenes. This value ensures that the gradient from the original loss is moderate; empirical analysis shows the gradient ratio \frac{\|\nabla d{WD}\|}{\|\nabla (\beta L{orig})\|} has a mean of \sim 1.6\times across training iterations, confirming WD remains the dominant signal. \gamma: A dataset-specific global scale. It is tuned per scene to align Gaussian counts across methods. Exact values are scene-dependent and not provided as a single constant. \sigma: Constant set to 4. 1. Warm-up Phase: Optimize the model using the standard 3DGS loss (L{orig}) for 3,000–5,000 iterations. 2. Perceptual Phase: For the remaining iterations (up to 30,000 total), switch to the WD-R objective. 3. Feature Extraction: Render the current view to obtain the predicted image. Extract VGG features from the predicted image. If caching is enabled, retrieve pre-computed VGG features and pyramid statistics for the ground-truth image. If caching is not enabled, extract VGG features from the ground-truth image and compute pyramid statistics. 4. Pyramid Weighting: Compute the weight wi for each pyramid level i using \sigma = 4. 5. Pruning: Identify pyramid levels where wi = 0. These levels do not contribute to the loss and can be skipped during computation. In the standard setup, only 20 of 96 pyramid levels contribute. 6. Loss Computation: Compute d{WD} using the weighted VGG feature differences. Compute L{orig} (L1 + SSIM). Calculate L{WD-R} = \gamma (d{WD} + \beta L{orig}). 7. Backpropagation: Compute gradients with respect to Gaussian parameters and update them. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computewdregularizedloss(gaussians, camera, gtimage, cachedgtfeatures, cachedgtstats, gamma, beta, sigma=4): """ Computes the WD-Regularized loss for a single training step. Args: gaussians: Current 3D Gaussian parameters. camera: Camera pose and intrinsics. gtimage: Ground-truth image tensor. cachedgtfeatures: Cached VGG features for gtimage (if available). cachedgtstats: Cached pyramid statistics for gtimage (if available). gamma: Dataset-specific global scale. beta: Weight for original loss (0.09). sigma: Pyramid weighting constant (4). Returns: loss: Scalar loss value. grads: Gradients for gaussians. """ # Step 1: Render current view renderedimage = render3dgs(gaussians, camera) # Step 2: Extract VGG features # Note: VGG feature extraction is assumed to be a standard function predfeatures = extractvggfeatures(renderedimage) if cachedgtfeatures is not None: gtfeatures = cachedgtfeatures gtstats = cachedgtstats else: gtfeatures = extractvggfeatures(gtimage) gtstats = computepyramidstatistics(gtfeatures) # Cache these for future iterations # Step 3: Compute Pyramid Weights # Only levels with non-zero weight contribute numlevels = 96 weights = [] activelevels = [] for i in range(numlevels): # wi = ReLU(1 - |log2(sigma) - i|) log2sigma = math.log2(sigma) weight = max(0.0, 1.0 - abs(log2sigma - i)) weights.append(weight) if weight > 0: activelevels.append(i) # Step 4: Compute WD Distortion (dWD) # dWD is computed over the active pyramid levels using the weights # The exact formula for dWD involves statistical distance (e.g., Wasserstein-2) # between the feature distributions at each level. dWD = 0.0 for i in activelevels: predfeatlevel = predfeatures[i] gtfeatlevel = gtfeatures[i] # Compute mean and variance for predicted features at level i predmean = mean(predfeatlevel) predvar = variance(predfeatlevel) # Use cached stats for ground truth gtmean = gtstats['mean'][i] gtvar = gtstats['var'][i] # Compute weighted Wasserstein distance for this level # Assuming standard Wasserstein-2 distance between Gaussians leveldist = wasserstein2(predmean, predvar, gtmean, gtvar) dWD += weights[i] leveldist # Step 5: Compute Original Loss (Lorig) # Typically L1 + SSIM Lorig = computel1ssimloss(renderedimage, gtimage) # Step 6: Combine Losses loss = gamma (dWD + beta Lorig) # Step 7: Backpropagate grads = backwardpass(loss, gaussians) return loss, grads Gradient Dominance: Although \beta=0.09 appears large, the WD gradient consistently exceeds the scaled original loss gradient (mean ratio \sim 1.6\times), preventing the original loss from overwhelming the perceptual signal. Pyramid Pruning: With \sigma=4, most of the 96 pyramid levels have zero weight. Ignoring these levels is critical for performance but must be handled correctly to ensure bit-exact gradients. Global Scale Tuning: \gamma must be tuned per dataset to ensure fair comparison of Gaussian counts. Incorrect tuning can lead to either too many or too few splats, invalidating the compactness benefits. Warm-up Requirement: Skipping the warm-up phase with the original loss may lead to instability or artifacts, as the perceptual objective requires a stable initial representation. This variant refers to the specific optimizations applied to the WD loss computation to reduce overhead. It involves caching ground-truth VGG features and their pyramid statistics since the ground-truth view is constant across iterations, and pruning zero-weight VGG pyramid levels (only 20 of 96 levels contribute with \sigma=4). These optimizations reduce the per-iteration time by approximately 48%, lowering the relative training overhead from \approx 4.5\times to \approx 2.8\times over the original 3DGS. Time Complexity: The WD loss introduces significant computational overhead due to VGG feature extraction and statistical computation. At 1063 × 1600 resolution with 4.79M Gaussians, the forward/backward pass takes 273.9 ms/iteration compared to 61.1 ms for L1+SSIM, a 4.5× overhead. With caching and pruning optimizations, this is reduced to \approx 2.8\times overhead. Memory Complexity: Requires storing VGG features for the ground-truth image and potentially cached statistics. The VGG feature stack consists of 96 levels. Performance: WD-R consistently outperforms Original Loss and Perceptual-GS in perceptual metrics while maintaining compact representations (e.g., reducing Gaussian count on BungeNeRF from 6.92M to 4.89M). It trades higher training time for improved visual quality and fewer splats, which can partially offset rendering costs. Strengths: High perceptual fidelity, compact Gaussian representations, robust against artifacts in sparse-view regions. Limitations: High training time overhead (2.8×–4.5× slower than baseline), requires careful tuning of \gamma per dataset. When to Use: When perceptual quality and compactness are prioritized over training speed, and when artifacts from pure WD loss are observed in constrained regions. When Not to Use: When real-time training speed is critical, or when the scene has abundant training views and no constraint on Gaussian count. WD-Regularized Loss was introduced by Özyılkan and Chen et al. in the paper "Drop-In Perceptual Optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It builds upon the Wasserstein Distance (WD) perceptual loss for 3D Gaussian Splatting. The method addresses the limitations of pure WD loss by adding a regularizer to handle regions with constrained splat counts or small numbers of training views. It is part of the broader effort to improve perceptual quality in differentiable volume rendering and 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization. name: Second-Order Chamfer Distance
head: Second-Order CD
body: Second-Order Chamfer Distance is a supervised geometric loss that measures the discrepancy between a predicted mesh vertex and a ground truth surface by incorporating local surface curvature. It applies a quadratic approximation of the point-to-point distance to penalize deviations along the principal curvature directions and surface normal. It serves as a supervised baseline for meshing implicit functions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A predicted mesh vertex \mathbf{x} (output of network h\phi) and a ground truth mesh. Output: A scalar loss value \mathcal{L} representing the second-order distance error. Data Structures: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3: The 3D coordinates of the query point (predicted vertex). \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^3: The closest point on the reference (ground truth) surface to \mathbf{x}. \vec{n} \in \mathbb{R}^3: The unit surface normal at \mathbf{y}. \vec{e}1, \vec{e}2 \in \mathbb{R}^3: The orthonormal principal curvature directions at \mathbf{y}. \hat{\delta}1, \hat{\delta}2 \in \mathbb{R}: The magnitudes of the principal curvatures at \mathbf{y}. Steps: 1. Find Closest Point: For each predicted vertex \mathbf{x}, find the closest point \mathbf{y} on the ground truth mesh. 2. Compute Geometric Properties: At the reference point \mathbf{y}, compute the surface normal \vec{n}, the principal curvature directions \vec{e}1, \vec{e}2, and their magnitudes \hat{\delta}1, \hat{\delta}2. 3. Compute Displacement Vector: Calculate the vector \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}. 4. Project Displacement: Project \mathbf{d} onto the normal and the two principal curvature directions: dn = \vec{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}, d{e1} = \vec{e}1 \cdot \mathbf{d}, d{e2} = \vec{e}2 \cdot \mathbf{d}. 5. Calculate Loss: Compute the loss using the quadratic approximation formula: \mathcal{L} = \hat{\delta}1 (d{e1})^2 + \hat{\delta}2 (d{e2})^2 + (dn)^2 Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def secondorderchamferdistance(predictedvertices, groundtruthmesh): totalloss = 0.0 npoints = len(predictedvertices) for i in range(npoints): x = predictedvertices[i] y = groundtruthmesh.findclosestpoint(x) n = groundtruthmesh.getnormal(y) e1, e2 = groundtruthmesh.getprincipaldirections(y) delta1, delta2 = groundtruthmesh.getprincipalcurvatures(y) d = [x[j] - y[j] for j in range(3)] dotn = n[0]d[0] + n[1]d[1] + n[2]d[2] dote1 = e1[0]d[0] + e1[1]d[1] + e1[2]d[2] dote2 = e2[0]d[0] + e2[1]d[1] + e2[2]d[2] lossi = (delta1 dote12) + (delta2 dote22) + (dotn2) totalloss += lossi return totalloss / npoints Parameters: \mathbf{x}: The mesh vertex predicted by the network h\phi. \mathbf{y}: The closest point on the ground truth mesh from the training dataset (ABC dataset). \hat{\delta}1, \hat{\delta}2: Magnitude of principal curvatures at \mathbf{y}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Approximate Level Set Discrepancy (LSD-A) is a metric used to quantify the geometric discrepancy between a generated mesh and a ground truth mesh, specifically designed for scenarios where the ground truth is non-watertight or an analytic Signed Distance Field (SDF) is ill-defined. Unlike the Precise Level Set Discrepancy (LSD-P), which evaluates distance errors on a fixed grid near the surface, LSD-A measures the point-to-face distance from points sampled directly on the ground truth mesh to the generated mesh. It serves as a robust alternative to standard Chamfer Distance when strict watertightness cannot be guaranteed. Not given in the sources. The method is a supervised baseline for meshing implicit functions that uses a quadratic approximation of point-point distance proposed in [51] (cited in). It was applied in "Self-Supervised Dual Contouring" to measure distance between a query point and a reference surface using local surface curvature. name: Approximate Level Set Discrepancy
head: LSD-A
body: Approximate Level Set Discrepancy (LSD-A) is a metric used to quantify the geometric discrepancy between a generated mesh and a ground truth mesh, specifically designed for scenarios where the ground truth is non-watertight or an analytic Signed Distance Field (SDF) is ill-defined. Unlike the Precise Level Set Discrepancy (LSD-P), which evaluates distance errors on a fixed grid near the surface, LSD-A measures the point-to-face distance from points sampled directly on the ground truth mesh to the generated mesh. It serves as a robust alternative to standard Chamfer Distance when strict watertightness cannot be guaranteed. Inputs: \mathcal{M}^: The ground truth mesh. \mathcal{M}: The generated (reconstructed) mesh. N: The number of points to sample on \mathcal{M}^. Outputs: A scalar value representing the average point-to-face distance. Data Structures: Points q: A set of N points sampled on the surface of \mathcal{M}^. Mesh \mathcal{M}: Represented as a collection of vertices and faces supporting point-to-face distance queries. Steps: 1. Sample N points q distributed over the surface of the ground truth mesh \mathcal{M}^. 2. For each point q \in \mathcal{M}^, compute the Euclidean distance to the closest point on the generated mesh \mathcal{M}. This distance is denoted as d^p(q, \mathcal{M}). 3. Sum these distances and divide by N to obtain the mean. Formula: \text{LSD-A} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{q \in \mathcal{M}^} d^p(q, \mathcal{M}) Where: \mathcal{M}^ is the ground truth mesh. \mathcal{M} is the generated mesh. q are points sampled on \mathcal{M}^. d^p(q, \mathcal{M}) is the point-to-face distance from point q to the generated mesh \mathcal{M}. N is the number of sampled points. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def approximatelevelsetdiscrepancy(groundtruthmesh, generatedmesh, numsamples): """ Computes the Approximate Level Set Discrepancy (LSD-A). Args: groundtruthmesh: Mesh object representing M. generatedmesh: Mesh object representing M. numsamples: Integer N, number of points to sample on M. Returns: float: The LSD-A score. """ # Step 1: Sample points on the ground truth mesh sampledpoints = samplepointsuniformly(groundtruthmesh, numsamples) totaldistance = 0.0 # Step 2 & 3: Compute point-to-face distance and average for q in sampledpoints: dist = pointtofacedistance(q, generatedmesh) totaldistance += dist return totaldistance / numsamples def samplepointsuniformly(mesh, numsamples): # Standard area-weighted uniform sampling on a triangle mesh faces = mesh.faces areas = [trianglearea(f.v0, f.v1, f.v2) for f in faces] totalarea = sum(areas) cumareas = [] acc = 0.0 for a in areas: acc += a cumareas.append(acc) points = [] for in range(numsamples): r = random.uniform(0, totalarea) idx = 0 for i, ca in enumerate(cumareas): if r <= ca: idx = i break v0, v1, v2 = faces[idx].v0, faces[idx].v1, faces[idx].v2 s, t = random.random(), random.random() if s + t > 1: s, t = 1 - s, 1 - t points.append(vectoradd(v0, vectoradd(vectormul(s, vectorsub(v1, v0)), vectormul(t, vectorsub(v2, v0))))) return points def trianglearea(v0, v1, v2): return 0.5 vectornorm(vectorcross(vectorsub(v1, v0), vectorsub(v2, v0))) def pointtofacedistance(point, mesh): mindist = float('inf') for face in mesh.faces: dist = distancepointtotriangle(point, face.v0, face.v1, face.v2) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist return mindist def distancepointtotriangle(point, v0, v1, v2): # Standard point-to-triangle distance closest = computeclosestpointontriangle(point, v0, v1, v2) return vectornorm(vectorsub(point, closest)) def computeclosestpointontriangle(point, v0, v1, v2): # Standard barycentric projection v0v1 = vectorsub(v1, v0) v0v2 = vectorsub(v2, v0) v0p = vectorsub(point, v0) d1 = vectordot(v0v1, v0v1) d2 = vectordot(v0v2, v0v2) d3 = vectordot(v0v1, v0v2) d = d1 d2 - d3 d3 u = (d2 vectordot(v0v1, v0p) - d3 vectordot(v0v2, v0p)) / d v = (d1 vectordot(v0v2, v0p) - d3 vectordot(v0v1, v0p)) / d if u <= 0 and v <= 0: return v0 if u > 1 and v <= 0: return v1 if v > 1 and u <= 0: return v2 if u + v > 1: e = vectorsub(v2, v1) w = vectorsub(point, v1) denom = vectordot(e, e) t = max(0, min(1, vectordot(w, e) / denom)) return vectoradd(v1, vectormul(t, e)) return vectoradd(v0, vectoradd(vectormul(u, v0v1), vectormul(v, v0v2))) Parameters: N: The number of points sampled on the ground truth mesh \mathcal{M}^. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-watertight Ground Truth: LSD-A is specifically intended for cases where the ground truth mesh is non-watertight, making analytic SDF computation ill-defined. Distance Definition: The metric uses point-to-face distance, not point-to-vertex distance, ensuring that the entire surface area contributes to the error measurement. Precision: Floating-point comparisons in barycentric projection require epsilon guards to avoid degenerate edge cases. Precise Level Set Discrepancy (LSD-P) gauges the discrepancy in signed distance values between a reconstructed mesh and the ground truth mesh at fixed points sampled on a regular grid close to the ground truth surface. It is defined as \text{LSD-P} = \sum{g \in \tilde{\mathcal{G}}} \|\text{abs}(\mathbf{d}^p(\mathcal{M}^, g)) - \text{abs}(\mathbf{d}^p(\mathcal{M}, g))\|2, where \tilde{\mathcal{G}} is the grid of points and \mathbf{d}^p is the distance from a query point to its closest point on the surface. LSD-P is chosen when a fixed spatial grid is preferred over surface sampling, whereas LSD-A is preferred for non-watertight meshes where surface sampling is more robust. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Robust to non-watertight ground truth meshes; does not require an analytic SDF; directly measures surface proximity. Limitations: Requires sampling on the ground truth mesh; sensitive to the number of samples N; does not account for signed distance errors in the same way LSD-P does. When to Use: Use LSD-A when evaluating generated meshes against non-watertight ground truth meshes (e.g., ShapeNet dataset) where analytic SDF is ill-defined. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Approximate Level Set Discrepancy (LSD-A) was introduced in the context of self-supervised dual contouring for 3D mesh reconstruction. It was specifically designed to handle the challenges posed by datasets like ShapeNet, which contain non-watertight meshes, making traditional SDF-based metrics unreliable. The metric was used in experiments to evaluate the quality of reconstructed meshes against ground truth in these challenging scenarios. name: Color-Corrected Error Metrics
head: Per-image polynomial color correction, Photometric variation mitigation metrics
body: Color-Corrected Error Metrics are evaluation procedures designed to mitigate the impact of photometric variations—such as autoexposure shifts, white balance changes, and RGB clipping—in "in the wild" datasets. They solve the problem of ill-posed view synthesis evaluation where the ground truth image's photometric conditions may not match the model's neutral rendering. Unlike standard metrics that penalize brightness or color shifts as errors, these metrics first align the rendered image to the ground truth via a per-image least-squares fit, allowing for quantitative comparison of geometry and texture independent of lighting conditions. Inputs: Rendered image \hat{I} (RGB values). Ground truth image I (RGB values). Mask M of saturated/clipped pixels in I (pixels to ignore). Outputs: Corrected error metric value (e.g., PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) computed on the aligned images. Data Structures: No specific complex data structures required; standard image buffers suffice. Steps: 1. Identify Saturated Pixels: Determine the set of pixels in the ground truth image I that are clipped (e.g., at 0 or 1, or sensor saturation limits). These pixels are excluded from the fitting process. 2. Fit Polynomial Expansion: Solve a per-image least-squares problem to find coefficients for a quadratic polynomial expansion that maps the rendered RGB values \hat{I} to the ground truth I. This step accounts for non-linear photometric variations. Let the mapping be f(\hat{I}). The coefficients are chosen to minimize the error between f(\hat{I}) and I over non-saturated pixels. 3. Apply Correction: Transform the rendered image using the fitted polynomial: I{corr} = f(\hat{I}). 4. Compute Metric: Calculate the desired error metric (PSNR, SSIM, etc.) between I{corr} and I. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def colorcorrectederror(renderedimg, gtimg, saturatedmask): """ renderedimg: np.array, shape (H, W, 3), float32 gtimg: np.array, shape (H, W, 3), float32 saturatedmask: np.array, shape (H, W, 3), bool (True if pixel is saturated/clipped) """ # 1. Filter out saturated pixels validpixels = ~saturatedmask # 2. Solve least squares for quadratic polynomial expansion # This step maps rendered values to ground truth values. # A quadratic expansion implies fitting terms like 1, r, g, b, r^2, g^2, b^2, rg, rb, gb. # The sources specify "quadratic polynomial expansion" but do not provide the exact # basis functions or solver implementation details. # Implementation note: Construct design matrix X from renderedimg[validpixels] # and target vector y from gtimg[validpixels]. Solve for coefficients beta # using least squares (e.g., numpy.linalg.lstsq). # 3. Apply the fitted transformation to the entire rendered image # Icorr = f(renderedimg) # Apply the learned polynomial coefficients to all pixels of renderedimg. # 4. Compute standard metric (e.g., PSNR) between Icorr and gtimg # Note: The sources do not specify if the metric is computed on all pixels or only valid ones. # Standard practice usually includes all pixels for the final metric report. error = computepsnr(Icorr, gtimg) return error Parameters: Polynomial degree: Quadratic (2nd order). Saturated pixel threshold: Not given in the sources. Typically defined by the camera's dynamic range limits (e.g., 0.0 or 1.0 in normalized space). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Saturated Pixels: Ignoring saturated pixels is critical; including them would bias the polynomial fit towards the clipped values, which do not contain valid scene information. Ill-posedness: Without this correction, metrics become ill-posed because the model cannot be expected to replicate arbitrary autoexposure or white balance settings. The Textural Complexity Objective (T) is a metric used in active view planning for radiance-field optimization to identify camera poses that capture regions with high photometric variation. Unlike geometric metrics that analyze 3D mesh structure, T operates on 2D image projections, leveraging the fact that textural characteristics are readily discernible in 2D even if 3D geometry is ambiguous. It serves as a component of Color-Corrected Error Metrics, helping to mitigate photometric variations such as autoexposure shifts or white balance changes in "in the wild" datasets by prioritizing views with rich texture. A post-processing white balance technique using Bradford chromatic adaptation to map from a Planck/CIE-daylight illuminant to D65. It applies the Bradford chromatic adaptation transform, differing from simple gray-world or white-patch algorithms. For synthetic data, explicitly computes a 3-channel rescale factor for base color by taking the median value of all pixel-wise ratios between the model's prediction and ground truth. For real captures, omits the rescale procedure and presents only qualitative results as no ground truth on base color is provided. The PBR rendering pipeline operates in linear (HDR) space, and the final result is clipped to [0, 1] and mapped to SRGB just before calculating photometric loss or evaluation. A data augmentation technique simulating variable lighting and exposure by applying random affine transformations to RGB pixel values across training images. For each training image Ii \in [0, 1]^{800 \times 800 \times 3}, scale s{ij} and offset b{ij} are sampled uniformly. The transformation is applied to each channel j: \tilde{I}{ij} = \min(1, \max(0, s{ij} I{ij} + b{ij})) where s{ij} \sim \mathcal{U}(0.8, 1.2) and b{ij} \sim \mathcal{U}(-0.2, 0.2). Perturbations are applied to all training images except the first, which serves as the reference view. On the Lego dataset, this perturbation alone decreases NeRF's PSNR by approximately 10 dB on average compared to the original unperturbed dataset. Time and Memory Complexity: The fitting step involves solving a least-squares problem per image. The complexity depends on the number of polynomial terms (quadratic implies ~10 terms for RGB) and the number of valid pixels. It is generally fast relative to the rendering process itself. Memory usage is minimal, requiring only storage for the image buffers and the small set of polynomial coefficients. Measured Performance: On the Tanks and Temples dataset, using these color-corrected metrics allows for quantitative comparison between models like Stable View Synthesis (SVS) and models with Global Lighting Optimization (GLO), which would otherwise be incomparable due to photometric shifts. The correction makes SVS and the GLO model variant quantitatively comparable. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Mitigates the impact of autoexposure and white balance variations in "in the wild" datasets. Allows for fair evaluation of geometric and textural accuracy independent of lighting. Limitations: Does not solve the underlying issue of photometric variation during training; it is an evaluation procedure. Requires identification of saturated pixels, which may be ambiguous in some datasets. When to Use: Use when evaluating view synthesis on datasets with uncontrolled lighting or camera settings (e.g., Tanks and Temples, Phototourism). Use when comparing models that handle photometric variation differently (e.g., explicit appearance embeddings vs. neutral rendering). When Not to Use: Do not use for synthetic datasets with controlled, known lighting conditions where photometric consistency is expected and required. Do not use if the goal is to evaluate the model's ability to replicate specific lighting conditions (e.g., relighting tasks). Originating from the challenges of evaluating neural radiance fields on "in the wild" datasets, this method addresses the issue where camera autoexposure and white balance vary between images, making standard error metrics misleading. The approach was highlighted in the context of the Mip-NeRF 360 paper, which constructed a dataset with fixed photometric conditions to avoid these issues, but acknowledged the need for such metrics for existing uncontrolled datasets like Tanks and Temples. The concept of mitigating photometric variation is also related to NeRF in the Wild (NeRF-W), which uses appearance embeddings to isolate tinting, but Color-Corrected Error Metrics specifically refer to the post-hoc evaluation correction. name: Textural Complexity Objective
body: The Textural Complexity Objective (T) is a metric used in active view planning for radiance-field optimization to identify camera poses that capture regions with high photometric variation. Unlike geometric metrics that analyze 3D mesh structure, T operates on 2D image projections, leveraging the fact that textural characteristics are readily discernible in 2D even if 3D geometry is ambiguous. It serves as a component of Color-Corrected Error Metrics, helping to mitigate photometric variations such as autoexposure shifts or white balance changes in "in the wild" datasets by prioritizing views with rich texture. The method computes a complexity score for an image captured at a specific camera pose. The core idea is that images with higher textural complexity (more unique local patterns) provide more information for reconstruction. The final score is derived from the distribution of Local Binary Patterns (LBP) in the Hue and Saturation channels of the image. Inputs: mk: The rendered or captured image at camera pose ck. rT: Filter radius for LBP (default: 3). pT: Number of circularly symmetric local neighborhood points for LBP (default: 3). dT: Discount factor to prevent overfitting to previously seen textures. Outputs: fT: The normalized textural complexity score for the image. Data Structures: Histogram array: A 1D array representing the frequency of LBP codes. The size depends on the number of possible LBP codes for the given pT. Steps: 1. Channel Selection: Extract the Hue (H) and Saturation (S) channels from the image mk. 2. LBP Computation: For each channel separately, compute the Local Binary Pattern descriptor. For each pixel, compare its intensity to its pT neighbors arranged in a circle of radius rT. Generate a binary code based on whether neighbors are greater than or equal to the center pixel. Aggregate these codes into a histogram Hist(\cdot). 3. Histogram Normalization: Let f'T be the histogram of LBP codes. The source defines f'T = Hist(LBP(mk; rT, pT)). 4. Complexity Calculation: Compute the complexity score for the channel using the last bin of the histogram. Let b be the index of the last bin in the histogram. Calculate fT = 1 - f'T[b]. Maximizing this equation selects images with the highest textural complexity. 5. Channel Averaging: Compute the final score by averaging the fT values obtained from the Hue and Saturation channels. 6. Discounting: Apply a discount factor dT to the T values of views that overlap with previously planned trajectories to prevent the planner from overfitting to specific textures already seen. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rgbtohsv(r, g, b): """Converts a single RGB pixel to HSV.""" maxc = max(r, g, b) minc = min(r, g, b) diff = maxc - minc if maxc == 0: h, s = 0.0, 0.0 else: s = diff / maxc if maxc == r: h = 60.0 (((g - b) / diff) % 6) elif maxc == g: h = 60.0 (((b - r) / diff) + 2) else: h = 60.0 (((r - g) / diff) + 4) return h, s, maxc def interpolate(image, x, y): """Bilinear interpolation for floating point coordinates.""" x0 = int(math.floor(x)) y0 = int(math.floor(y)) x1 = x0 + 1 y1 = y0 + 1 height = len(image) width = len(image[0]) # Clamp coordinates to image bounds x0 = max(0, min(x0, width - 1)) y0 = max(0, min(y0, height - 1)) x1 = max(0, min(x1, width - 1)) y1 = max(0, min(y1, height - 1)) val00 = image[y0][x0] val01 = image[y0][x1] val10 = image[y1][x0] val11 = image[y1][x1] dx = x - x0 dy = y - y0 return (1 - dx) (1 - dy) val00 + dx (1 - dy) val01 + (1 - dx) dy val10 + dx dy val11 def computetexturalcomplexity(image, rT=3, pT=3, dT=0.0): """ Computes the Textural Complexity Objective for an image. Args: image: 2D list of RGB tuples or 3D array-like (H, W, 3). rT: LBP filter radius. pT: Number of LBP neighborhood points. dT: Discount factor for previously seen views. Returns: fT: Normalized textural complexity score. """ # Step 1: Extract Hue and Saturation channels height = len(image) width = len(image[0]) huechannel = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] satchannel = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): r, g, b = image[y][x] h, s, = rgbtohsv(r, g, b) huechannel[y][x] = h satchannel[y][x] = s # Step 2 & 3: Compute LBP Histogram for each channel numbins = 2 pT histhue = [0.0] numbins histsat = [0.0] numbins for channel, hist in [(huechannel, histhue), (satchannel, histsat)]: for y in range(1, height - 1): for x in range(1, width - 1): centerval = channel[y][x] code = 0 for i in range(pT): angle = 2 math.pi i / pT nx = x + rT math.cos(angle) ny = y - rT math.sin(angle) neighborval = interpolate(channel, nx, ny) if neighborval >= centerval: code |= (1 << i) hist[code] += 1 # Normalize histograms to sum to 1 (standard practice for probability distributions) sumhue = sum(histhue) sumsat = sum(histsat) if sumhue > 0: histhue = [h / sumhue for h in histhue] if sumsat > 0: histsat = [h / sumsat for h in histsat] # Step 4: Calculate complexity for each channel b = numbins - 1 fThue = 1.0 - histhue[b] fTsat = 1.0 - histsat[b] # Step 5: Average the scores fTraw = (fThue + fTsat) / 2.0 # Step 6: Apply discount factor if needed # The source mentions applying dT towards T values seen during planning. # This is typically done at the trajectory planning level, not per-image. # Here we return the raw score. return fTraw Parameters: rT = 3: Filter radius for LBP. pT = 3: Number of circularly symmetric local neighborhood points. Pitfalls: Overfitting: The planner may overfit to specific textures if it repeatedly selects views of the same complex region. This is mitigated by the discount factor dT. A surrogate objective corresponding to the variability of mesh faces' configurations, quantified via mesh normals to identify regions requiring varied views. It is computed using mesh normals \hat{n}j. The objective function Q quantifies the variability of mesh faces' configurations to identify geometrically complex regions (e.g., pillars, domes) that require varied views. Formula: The per-face geometric complexity is defined as: f'Q = |LoG(\hat{n}j; \sigmaQ)|^{\betaQ} V{jk} + 1 where LoG(\cdot) is the Laplacian of Gaussian filter, \sigmaQ is the standard deviation of the Gaussian filter, \betaQ is a scaling factor, f'Q is the per-face geometric complexity, and V{jk} is an indicator function corresponding to the visibility of face j from the k-th camera-pose. The absolute value is taken because the directionality of normal variations does not matter. The normalized total complexity is: fQ = \frac{1}{J} \sum{j=1}^{J} f'Q where J is the total number of faces. Maximization of fQ encourages the selection of camera-poses with higher geometric complexity. Pitfalls: Local Maxima: Over-emphasis on local regions with unusually high geometric complexity can trap the planner in a local maxima. This is handled by applying a scaling discount factor dQ towards the Q values of overlapping faces seen during trajectory planning. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Effective at identifying regions with rich texture that are crucial for high-fidelity reconstruction. Robust to some lighting variations by using Hue/Saturation. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than simple photometric error metrics. Relies on accurate camera poses and rendered images. When to use: When optimizing for "in the wild" datasets with varying lighting and texture, such as Tanks and Temples. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The Textural Complexity Objective was introduced in the context of active view planning for NeRF (SO-NeRF). It is part of a family of surrogate objectives (including Geometric Complexity and Ray Diversity) designed to guide camera trajectory planning for better 3D reconstruction. The method builds on the observation that textural characteristics are discernible in 2D projections, unlike some geometric features. SO-NeRF: Active View Planning for NeRF using Surrogate Objectives, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2312.03266, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Distortion Loss
head: distloss
body: Distortion Loss is a regularization term for differentiable volume rendering that prevents "floaters" (disconnected volumetric artifacts) and "background collapse" (distant surfaces modeled as semi-transparent clouds near the camera) by encouraging the rendering weights to be compact along the ray. It minimizes the expected distance between two independent samples drawn from the weight distribution, effectively penalizing spread-out density. Unlike sibling methods such as Total Variation Regularization which smooths spatial gradients, Distortion Loss operates on the 1D depth distribution along rays. It sets itself apart from Variance Loss by explicitly modeling the pairwise distances between all samples rather than just the variance around the mean depth, providing a more robust constraint against multi-modal depth distributions. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: \mathbf{s}: Array of normalized ray distances (sample positions) with shape (B, N+1), where B is batch size and N is number of intervals. Values are in [0, 1], derived from non-linear normalization of near-far clipping distances to prevent upweighting distant intervals. \mathbf{w}: Array of ray weights (opacity contributions) with shape (B, N). Outputs: \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}: Scalar distortion loss value, averaged over the batch. Data Structures: s: Float tensor, shape (B, N+1). si is the start of interval i, s{i+1} is the end. w: Float tensor, shape (B, N). m: Float tensor, shape (B, N), storing interval midpoints mi = (si + s{i+1})/2. prefixw: Float tensor, shape (B, N+1), prefix sums of w. prefixwm: Float tensor, shape (B, N+1), prefix sums of w \odot m. suffixw: Float tensor, shape (B, N+1), suffix sums of w. suffixwm: Float tensor, shape (B, N+1), suffix sums of w \odot m. Steps: 1. Compute Midpoints: Calculate the center of each interval i: mi = \frac{si + s{i+1}}{2} 2. Compute Intra-Interval Loss: Calculate the second term of the distortion loss, which penalizes the width of individual intervals: \mathcal{L}{\text{intra}} = \frac{1}{3} \sum{i=0}^{N-1} wi^2 (s{i+1} - si) 3. Compute Inter-Interval Loss (Efficient O(N)): The first term involves a double sum over all pairs. To achieve O(N) complexity, eliminate the diagonal (i=j) and split the sum into j < i and j > i cases. Since mi < m{i+1}, |mi - mj| = mi - mj for j < i. \mathcal{L}{\text{inter}} = 2 \sum{i=1}^{N-1} wi mi \left( \sum{j=0}^{i-1} wj \right) - 2 \sum{i=1}^{N-1} wi \left( \sum{j=0}^{i-1} wj mj \right) This is computed using prefix sums: Let Pw[i] = \sum{j=0}^{i-1} wj and P{wm}[i] = \sum{j=0}^{i-1} wj mj. \mathcal{L}{\text{inter}} = 2 \sum{i=1}^{N-1} wi mi Pw[i] - 2 \sum{i=1}^{N-1} wi P{wm}[i]. 4. Combine: \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}} = \mathcal{L}{\text{inter}} + \mathcal{L}{\text{intra}} 5. Average: Average \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}} over the batch dimension B. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computedistortionloss(s, w): """ s: (B, N+1) normalized ray distances w: (B, N) ray weights Returns: (B,) distortion loss per ray """ B, N = w.shape # 1. Compute midpoints m = (s[:,:-1] + s[:, 1:]) / 2.0 # (B, N) # 2. Intra-interval loss: 1/3 sum(w^2 intervallength) intervallengths = s[:, 1:] - s[:,:-1] # (B, N) lossintra = (w 2 intervallengths).sum(dim=1) / 3.0 # (B,) # 3. Inter-interval loss: O(N) implementation # Prefix sums of w and wm # pad with 0 at the beginning for prefix sum logic wpadded = torch.cat([torch.zeros(B, 1, device=w.device), w], dim=1) # (B, N+1) wmpadded = torch.cat([torch.zeros(B, 1, device=w.device), w m], dim=1) # (B, N+1) prefixw = torch.cumsum(wpadded, dim=1)[:,:-1] # (B, N), sum{j=0}^{i-1} wj prefixwm = torch.cumsum(wmpadded, dim=1)[:,:-1] # (B, N), sum{j=0}^{i-1} wj mj # Term 1: 2 sumi (wi mi prefixw[i]) term1 = 2.0 (w m prefixw).sum(dim=1) # Term 2: 2 sumi (wi prefixwm[i]) term2 = 2.0 (w prefixwm).sum(dim=1) lossinter = term1 - term2 # (B,) return lossinter + lossintra Parameters: \lambda{\text{dist}}: Weight for the distortion loss in the total loss function. Typical value: 0.01. N: Number of sampled points per ray. The efficient implementation supports uneven N across rays. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normalization: Using unnormalized ray distances t instead of normalized s significantly upweights distant intervals, causing nearby intervals to be ignored. Memory: A naive O(N^2) implementation consumes excessive GPU memory (e.g., >3GB for a batch of 4,096 rays with >256 samples). The prefix-sum method reduces this to O(N) memory and compute. Diagonal Term: The derivation explicitly eliminates the diagonal term (i=j) because |mi - mi| = 0, which is consistent with the integral definition. The 2D-GS Loss Configuration is a variant applied to 3D Gaussian Splatting that decomposes the penalty into a uniform term (penalizing weight magnitude) and a bi-directional term (penalizing variance of depth distribution). It balances uniformity and bi-directional consistency to stabilize training, differing from the standard Distortion Loss which focuses purely on compactness around true depth. A variant used in Gaussian Splatting that computes the sum of squared distances between depths of all Gaussian pairs, weighted by their contribution \omegak \omegal. It implicitly assumes an opaque surface, which can reduce the ability to model complex light transport and lead to oversmoothed depth reconstructions. A heuristic adjustment rather than a direct loss term, used in conjunction with distortion-like constraints. It decreases the learning rate for scene reflectivity by 10× compared to position/opacity, encouraging the optimizer to fit data by varying occupancy (structure) rather than reflectivity. This avoids forcing Gaussians to be artificially close to each other as in the standard Depth Distortion Loss. A loss term \mathcal{L}u = \mathcal{D}{sq} - \mathcal{D}^2 that minimizes depth uncertainty (\mathcal{D}{sq} = \sum wi di^2, \mathcal{D} is mean depth) to drive Gaussian points to the object surface. It assumes the object possesses an accurate surface and aims to reduce geometric uncertainty. Time Complexity: O(N) per ray using the prefix/suffix sum optimization, where N is the number of samples. The naive implementation is O(N^2). Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing prefix/suffix sums, compared to O(N^2) for the pairwise distance matrix in the naive approach. Performance: Significantly reduces artifacts like floaters and background collapse without degrading reconstruction quality, outperforming noise-injection regularizers. Strengths: Effective at enforcing compact depth distributions; differentiable; works well with both MLP-based NeRFs and point-based queries. Limitations: Implicitly assumes opaque surfaces when used with Gaussian variants; may oversmooth depth in complex light transport scenarios. When to use: When training unbounded or forward-facing scenes where background collapse is prevalent; when floaters appear in novel views. When not to use: When modeling transparent or complex light transport scenes where opaque assumptions are invalid. Distortion Loss was introduced in Mip-NeRF 360 (2022) as a regularizer to improve the quality of neural radiance fields in unbounded scenes. It was motivated by the observation that standard NeRF training often produces "floaters" and "background collapse". The efficient O(N) implementation was later popularized by DirectVoxGO (2022) to handle point-based queries with high sample counts. It has since been adopted in various Gaussian Splatting variants and differentiable rendering pipelines.
