name: Depth Consistency Check / Depth Outlier Removal
head: Geometric Consistency Masking, Reprojection-based Depth Filtering
body: This method filters noisy depth data by unprojecting depth maps to 3D space and reprojecting them into nearby views to verify geometric consistency. It solves the problem of incorrect depth supervision caused by moving objects, ill-posed views, and occlusions in street view scenarios. It sets itself apart from Depth Supervision Loss (Laug) by using explicit geometric reprojection checks rather than direct loss minimization, and from Multi-view Consistency Depth Filtering by focusing on pairwise reprojection error thresholds rather than complex multi-view voting or probabilistic models. Inputs: Depth map Di for source frame i. Camera extrinsics and intrinsics for source frame i and target frame j. Pixel coordinates \mathbf{u}i for frame i. Thresholds: \sigma (absolute error), \delta (image space), \varepsilon (relative depth), N{geo} (min views). Outputs: Geometric consistency mask Md (binary or boolean array same size as Di). Filtered depth values (where Md is true). Data Structures: Di: 2D array of depth values. Md: 2D boolean array. \mathbf{u}i: 2D array of pixel coordinates (u, v). Steps: 1. Unproject: Convert the depth map Di of frame i into 3D points using the inverse projection matrix \pii^{-1}. For each pixel \mathbf{u}i, compute the 3D point \mathbf{X}i = \pii^{-1}(\mathbf{u}i, Di(\mathbf{u}i)). 2. Reproject: Project the 3D points \mathbf{X}i into the coordinate system of a nearby view j using the projection matrix \pij. This yields the projected pixel coordinates and the projected depth D{i \to j}. Formula: D{i \to j} = Dj(\pij \pii^{-1}(\mathbf{u}i)). Note: Dj is sampled at the projected pixel location. 3. Compare: Calculate the absolute difference between the reprojected depth D{i \to j} and the actual depth Dj at the corresponding pixel in view j. 4. Filter: Apply the consistency check. A pixel is considered consistent if the error is below the threshold. Formulas: The primary consistency mask Md is defined as: Md = |D{i \to j} - Dj| < \sigma where: D{i \to j} is the reprojected depth from frame i to frame j. Dj is the ground truth or estimated depth in frame j at the projected location. \sigma is the empirical threshold for absolute relative error. Parameters: \sigma = 0.2 m: Empirical threshold for the absolute error in depth reprojection. \delta = 1: Image space consistency threshold (pixel distance). \varepsilon = 0.01: Depth consistency threshold (relative error). N{geo}: Minimum number of source views required for consistency acceptance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusions: If a point is occluded in view j but visible in view i, the reprojection will land on a different surface or background, causing a large error. This method filters such outliers. Moving Objects: Dynamic objects cause inconsistencies between frames. The reprojection check identifies these as outliers. Interpolation: When retrieving depth di or d{reproj}, interpolation is required if projected coordinates are non-integer. This introduces small errors. Precision: Floating-point precision in matrix multiplications for reprojection can accumulate errors. Using a 3D statistical filter (e.g., Open3D) on unprojected point clouds can remove clear floaters before reprojection. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def depthconsistencycheck(Di, Dj, Ki, Kj, sigma=0.2, delta=1.0, epsilon=0.01, Ngeo=1): """ Perform depth consistency check between frame i and frame j. Supports both simple absolute error check (S1) and multi-view geometric filtering (S2). """ # 1. Unproject Di to 3D # Xi is a 3D point cloud corresponding to pixels in Di Xi = unprojectdepth(Di, Ki) # 2. Reproject Xi to frame j # Get projected pixel coordinates and depth in frame j uproj, vproj, Dreproj = projectpoints(Xi, Kj, Ki) # 3. Sample Dj at projected locations # Handle boundary checks and interpolation Djsampled = sampledepth(Dj, uproj, vproj) # 4. Calculate errors abserror = abs(Dreproj - Djsampled) # 5. Apply threshold (S1 method) masksimple = abserror < sigma # 6. Apply geometric filtering (S2 method) # Calculate image space distance # Note: uproj, vproj are floats; need to compare with integer pixel p # For simplicity, assume p is the integer coordinate of the original pixel in i # But S2 describes projecting p from reference to source, then back. # Here we are doing i -> j. Let's adapt S2 logic for pairwise i->j. # S2 Logic: # p is pixel in reference (i). pi is pixel in source (j). # Here i is reference, j is source. # Project p (from i) to pi (in j). # Retrieve depth di in source (j) -> this is Djsampled. # Re-project pi back to reference (i) -> this is Dreproj. # Check |preproj - p| < delta and |dreproj - d0|/d0 < epsilon. # Calculate image space distance between original pixel and reprojected pixel # We need the original pixel coordinates in i pixelcoordsi = getpixelcoordinates(Di) imagedist = sqrt((uproj - pixelcoordsi[:, 0])2 + (vproj - pixelcoordsi[:, 1])2) # Calculate relative depth error relativedeptherror = abserror / Di # Apply S2 thresholds maskgeo = (imagedist < delta) & (relativedeptherror < epsilon) # Combine masks or choose one. S1 uses masksimple. S2 uses maskgeo and Ngeo. # For this function, we return both for flexibility. return masksimple, maskgeo def multiviewgeometricfilter(Dref, Dsources, Kref, Ksources, delta=1.0, epsilon=0.01, Ngeo=1): """ Accept estimations as reliable if consistent in at least Ngeo source views (S2). """ totalviews = len(Dsources) consistencycounts = np.zeroslike(Dref, dtype=int) for i in range(totalviews): Dsrc = Dsources[i] Ksrc = Ksources[i] # Unproject reference depth Xref = unprojectdepth(Dref, Kref) # Reproject to source view uproj, vproj, Dreproj = projectpoints(Xref, Ksrc, Kref) # Sample source depth Dsrcsampled = sampledepth(Dsrc, uproj, vproj) # Calculate errors abserror = abs(Dreproj - Dsrcsampled) relativeerror = abserror / Dref # Image space distance pixelcoordsref = getpixelcoordinates(Dref) imagedist = sqrt((uproj - pixelcoordsref[:, 0])2 + (vproj - pixelcoordsref[:, 1])2) # Check consistency isconsistent = (imagedist < delta) & (relativeerror < epsilon) # Count consistent views consistencycounts += isconsistent.astype(int) # Final mask finalmask = consistencycounts >= Ngeo return finalmask Probabilistic Depth Testing determines which input view's reprojection contains the correct geometric information for a novel view pixel by calculating the probability that its depth is closer than all other views' depths. It differs from hard visibility tests by using a mixture model with triangular distributions to perform soft depth resolution, which is necessary because point splatting lacks mesh connectivity and soft rasterization introduces uncertainty from noisy Multi-View Stereo (MVS) data. See Probabilistic Depth Testing. Reprojection Confidence Measurement is a method to measure depth accuracy and locate outliers by warping pixels from source images to target images and comparing similarities. It addresses the problem of wrong depth supervisions caused by moving objects, ill-posed views, and occlusions in street view scenarios. It sets itself apart from siblings like Probabilistic Depth Testing by using deterministic geometric warping and multi-level similarity metrics (RGB, SSIM, VGG, flow) rather than probabilistic distributions. See Reprojection Confidence Measurement. Geometric Consistency Filtering measures the consistency of depth estimates among multiple views. For each pixel p in the reference view with depth d0, it projects to a pixel pi in the i-th source view, retrieves depth di, and reprojects back to get d{reproj} at p{reproj}. It accepts the estimation as reliable if |p{reproj} - p| < \delta and |d{reproj} - d0|/d0 < \varepsilon. It requires consistency in at least N{geo} source views. Parameters: \delta = 1, \varepsilon = 0.01, N{geo} varies. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot V), where N is the number of pixels and V is the number of source views checked. Each pixel requires unprojection, reprojection, and sampling. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing depth maps and masks. Unprojected 3D points require O(N) additional memory. Measured Performance: In, the method is used to remove noisy depth data and clear floaters in unprojected point clouds. It uses a 3D statistical filter (Open3D) with 20 neighbors and a standard deviation ratio of 2.0 to further clean the data. Strengths: Effective at removing outliers caused by occlusions, moving objects, and MVS noise. Simple to implement and understand. Limitations: Relies on accurate camera calibration. Fails in textureless regions where depth estimation is inherently noisy. The threshold \sigma is empirical and may need tuning for different scenes. When to use: When using monocular depth estimators or MVS outputs that contain significant noise or outliers, especially in dynamic scenes. When not to use: When high precision is required in textureless regions or when computational resources are extremely limited and simple thresholding is insufficient. The method originates from the need to clean depth data for volume-based Gaussian Splatting and multi-view reconstruction. introduces the basic reprojection consistency check for EVolSplat, an efficient volume-based Gaussian Splatting method for urban view synthesis. adapts and expands this concept for VolRecon, using geometric consistency filtering for generalizable multi-view reconstruction. The approach builds on traditional multi-view stereo techniques. EVolSplat: Efficient Volume-based Gaussian Splatting for Urban View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR52734.2025.01054, fetched 2026-11-03 VolRecon: Volume Rendering of Signed Ray Distance Functions for Generalizable Multi-View Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.01601, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Probabilistic Depth Testing
head: Probabilistic Depth Weight Calculation, Probabilistic Per-View Depth Testing, Probabilistic visibility, Soft Depth Resolution, Soft depth test
body:
Probabilistic Depth Testing determines which input view's reprojection contains the correct geometric information for a novel view pixel by calculating the probability that its depth is closer than all other views' depths. It differs from hard visibility tests by using a mixture model with triangular distributions to perform soft depth resolution, which is necessary because point splatting lacks mesh connectivity and soft rasterization introduces uncertainty from noisy Multi-View Stereo (MVS) data. Inputs: Set of input views N{views}. For each view n, a set of reprojected points Nn on the novel view pixel. For each point i \in Nn: depth d{n,i} and opacity \alpha{n,i}. Support parameter \sigma for the triangular distribution. Number of samples S. Outputs: Probability P(Dn < \min{m 
eq n} Dm) for each view n, representing the likelihood that view n is the front-most (correct) view. Data Structures: Points are stored as a list of tuples/objects containing (d{n,i}, \alpha{n,i}). No complex spatial structures are required; the method operates on the set of points projected to a single pixel. Steps: 1. Compute Visibility Weights ( eta): For each view n, sort points i \in Nn by depth (front to back). Compute the weight  eta{n,i} for each point, representing the probability that point i is visible (not occluded by preceding points in the same view):  eta{n,i} = \alpha{n,i} \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha{n,j}) If i=1, the product is defined as 1. 2. Define Sample Positions: Generate S sample positions s(t) within the support of the triangular distribution centered at the point's depth: s(t) = d{n,i} - \sigma +  rac{t}{S+1} \quad 	ext{for } t = 1, \dots, S The source provides this exact linear sampling formula without additional scaling factors. 3. Define Distributions: Triangular Distribution T: A symmetrical triangular distribution with support 2\sigma centered at d{m,j}. It is chosen for its finite support and computational efficiency compared to Gaussians. Density Function fi: The density function associated with the depth distribution of point i in view n. In the mixture model, this represents the likelihood of the depth s(t) given point i. 4. Compute Probability: Calculate the probability that view n is closer than all other views m 
eq n. The derivation rewrites the joint probability as a product of pairwise comparisons using a mixture model: P(Dn < \min{m 
eq n} Dm) \approx \sum{i \in Nn}  eta{n,i} \prod{t=1}^{S} \left[ fi(s(t), d{n,i}) \prod{m 
eq n} \left( \sum{j \in Nm}  eta{m,j} T(s(t), d{m,j}, \sigma) ight) ight] The product over m 
eq n computes the probability that all other views are not closer than the sample location. The inner sum computes the mixture density for view m at s(t). The term fi(s(t), d{n,i}) acts as a weighting for the current view's point i. 5. Parallel Execution: The computation is performed in parallel for each pixel using CUDA. Parameters: S: Number of samples. Typical value: 1. \sigma: Support of the symmetrical triangular distribution. Controls the softness and accounts for depth uncertainty. Pitfalls: Inaccurate Geometry: Point splats lack connectivity, making it hard to determine correct information when geometry is inaccurate. The probabilistic approach is necessary to handle this noise rather than discarding data via hard visibility. Precision: The quadratic complexity can become expensive if many points are projected to a single pixel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def triangularpdf(x, center, sigma): """PDF of a symmetrical triangular distribution with support 2sigma centered at 'center'.""" if abs(x - center) >= sigma: return 0.0 return (1.0 - abs(x - center) / sigma) / sigma def probabilisticdepthtesting(pointsperview, sigma, S=1): """ pointsperview: dict mapping viewid -> list of dicts { 'd': depth, 'alpha': opacity } sigma: support of triangular distribution S: number of samples Returns: dict mapping viewid -> probability that this view is the front-most """ viewids = list(pointsperview.keys()) probabilities = {} # Precompute sorted points and beta weights for all views viewdata = {} for n in viewids: pts = sorted(pointsperview[n], key=lambda p: p['d']) betas = [] prodoccluded = 1.0 for p in pts: beta = p['alpha'] prodoccluded betas.append(beta) prodoccluded = (1.0 - p['alpha']) viewdata[n] = (pts, betas) for n in viewids: ptsn, betasn = viewdata[n] probn = 0.0 for i, pi in enumerate(ptsn): betai = betasn[i] dni = pi['d'] viewfactor = 1.0 for t in range(1, S + 1): st = dni - sigma + t / (S + 1) fi = triangularpdf(st, dni, sigma) otherviewsprod = 1.0 for m in viewids: if m == n: continue ptsm, betasm = viewdata[m] summ = 0.0 for j, pj in enumerate(ptsm): summ += betasm[j] triangularpdf(st, pj['d'], sigma) otherviewsprod = summ viewfactor = fi otherviewsprod probn += betai viewfactor probabilities[n] = probn return probabilities Time Complexity: Quadratic with respect to the number of points reprojected on the pixel (O(|Nn| \cdot |Nm| \cdot S)). Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of points, as it requires storing  eta weights and point attributes. Performance: Computation is performed in parallel per pixel using CUDA. Strengths: Handles noisy MVS data gracefully by using soft visibility; finite support of triangular distribution simplifies and speeds up computation compared to Gaussians. Limitations: Computationally expensive for pixels with many overlapping points; relies on the accuracy of the initial MVS depth estimates. When to use: When using point-based rendering with soft splatting and noisy depth maps where hard visibility would discard valuable information. Probabilistic Depth Testing was introduced by Kopanas, Philip, Leimkühler, and Drettakis in their 2021 paper "Point-Based Neural Rendering with Per-View Optimization". It addresses the challenge of resolving uncertain depth in Image-Based Rendering (IBR) when using point splats, which lack the connectivity of meshes. The method builds on earlier work in soft rasterization and probabilistic visibility. It is used in temporally consistent neural rendering frameworks for multi-view imaging tasks such as free-viewpoint IBR, multi-view harmonization, and stylization. name: Reprojection Confidence Measurement
head: Warping-based confidence
body: Reprojection Confidence Measurement evaluates the geometric consistency of depth estimates by warping pixels from a source view to a target view and comparing the reconstructed appearance against the actual target image. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Probabilistic Depth Testing by explicitly constructing confidence maps at multiple semantic levels (pixel, patch, and feature) to identify outliers caused by moving objects, ill-posed regions, and occlusions. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Source image Is, source depth map Ds, target image It, source camera parameters Ps, target camera parameters Pt. Outputs: Confidence maps C{rgb}, C{ssim}, C{vgg}. Data Structures: Pixel coordinates X = (x, y, d), where (x,y) are 2D image coordinates and d is the depth value. Camera parameters P containing intrinsic and extrinsic matrices. Steps: 1. Unproject: Convert source pixel Xs = (xs, ys, ds) to 3D world coordinates using the inverse warping function \psi^{-1} and source camera parameters Ps. 2. Reproject: Project the 3D point to the target image plane using the warping function \psi and target camera parameters Pt to obtain target pixel coordinates Xt = (xt, yt, dt): Xt = \psi(\psi^{-1}(Xs, Ps), Pt) 3. Warp Image: Sample the target image It at the reprojected coordinates Xt to generate the warped source image \hat{I}s: \hat{I}s = It(Xt) 4. Compute RGB Confidence: Calculate the pixel-wise absolute difference between the original source image Is and the warped image \hat{I}s: C{rgb} = 1 - |Is - \hat{I}s| 5. Compute SSIM Confidence: Calculate the Structural Similarity Index Measure between Is and \hat{I}s to measure patch structure similarity: C{ssim} = \text{SSIM}(Is, \hat{I}s) 6. Compute VGG Confidence: Extract features Fs from Is and \hat{F}s from \hat{I}s using a pre-trained VGG network Ft, then compute the feature-level similarity: C{vgg} = 1 - ||Fs - \hat{F}s|| where \hat{F}s = Ft(Xt). Parameters: VGG Network: Pre-trained VGG feature extractor (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2015). SSIM Window: Standard SSIM calculation (Wang et al., 2004). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusions: Pixels occluded in the target view will result in incorrect warping, leading to low confidence scores. Moving Objects: Dynamic objects violate the static scene assumption, causing reprojection errors. Ill-posed Regions: Areas with insufficient texture or depth ambiguity may produce unreliable depth ds, leading to erroneous reprojection. Precision: The warping process relies heavily on the accuracy of Ds; depth outliers directly propagate to confidence errors. Time and Memory Complexity: Time complexity is dominated by the warping operation and feature extraction, scaling with the number of pixels and the complexity of the VGG network. Memory complexity requires storing intermediate warped images and feature maps. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: The receptive fields of the confidence maps expand from pixels to local patches and non-local regions, constructing robust measurements. Limitations: Relies on accurate depth maps for unprojection; sensitive to dynamic scenes and occlusions. When to Use: Use when jointly optimizing neural radiance fields (e.g., S-NeRF) and needing to filter noisy depth supervisions. When Not to Use: Not suitable for scenes with significant non-rigid motion without additional flow constraints (see Geometry Confidence Measurement). Origin: Introduced in S-NeRF: Neural Radiance Fields for Street Views. History and Development: The method was designed to address the quantity of outliers due to moving objects, ill-posed regions, and occlusions in street view data. Usage: Used in the training of S-NeRF to provide robust confidence measurements for depth supervision. S-NeRF: Neural Radiance Fields for Street Views, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2303.00749, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Geometry Confidence Measurement
head: Depth and flow consistency
body: A method to measure geometry consistency of depths and flows across different views to identify outliers in multi-view stereo and neural rendering pipelines. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly combining geometric reprojection errors with optical flow consistency, rather than relying solely on photometric or feature similarity. It builds on Reprojection Confidence Measurement by adding a flow-based constraint to detect motion inconsistencies that reprojection alone might miss. Inputs: Source depth image Ds and source image Is. Set of target views, each with depth image Dt and image It. Camera poses for source and target views. Threshold \tau for outlier identification. Outputs: Depth consistency map C{depth}. Flow consistency map C{flow}. Combined geometry confidence (optional, via learnable weights). Data Structures: Pixel coordinates: Xs = (xs, ys, ds), Xt = (xt, yt, dt). Depth values: ds (source), dt (reprojected), \hat{d}t (target ground truth/reconstruction). Flow vectors: f{s \to t} (computed optical flow), \Delta{x,y} (reprojection displacement). Steps: 1. Reprojection: For each pixel Xs = (xs, ys, ds) in the source depth image Ds, project it into the coordinate system of each adjacent target view using the known camera poses. This yields the projected pixel coordinates Xt = (xt, yt) and the reprojected depth dt. Note: The specific projection equation is referenced as "equation 4" in the source. Implementers must use standard perspective projection: Xt = Kt (Rt Rs^T (Xs - ts) + tt), where K is the intrinsic matrix, R and t are rotation and translation. 2. Optical Flow Computation: Compute the pixel motion (optical flow) from the source image to the adjacent target views, denoted as f{s \to t}(xs, ys), using an optical flow method. The source cites Zhang et al. (2021) as the reference implementation. 3. Depth Consistency Calculation: Compute the depth consistency C{depth} for each pixel by comparing the reprojected depth dt with the original target view's depth \hat{d}t = Dt(xt, yt). Formula: C{depth} = \gamma\left(\frac{|dt - \hat{d}t|}{ds}\right) Where \gamma(x) is a clamping function: \gamma(x) = \begin{cases} 1 - \frac{x}{\tau} & \text{if } x < \tau \\ 0 & \text{if } x \ge \tau \end{cases} Here, \tau is a threshold parameter used to identify outliers. The error is normalized by the source depth ds. 4. Flow Consistency Calculation: Compute the flow consistency C{flow} by comparing the computed optical flow f{s \to t} with the geometric displacement derived from reprojection \Delta{x,y}. Define displacement: \Delta{x,y} = (xt - xs, yt - ys). Formula: C{flow} = \gamma\left(\frac{\|\Delta{x,y} - f{s \to t}(xs, ys)\|}{\|\Delta{x,y}\|}\right) This measures the relative difference between the expected geometric motion and the observed photometric motion. 5. Confidence Combination (Optional): The final confidence map can be learned by combining multiple metrics (e.g., RGB, SSIM, VGG, Depth, Flow) with learnable weights \omegai: \hat{C} = \sumi \omegai Ci, \quad \text{where } \sumi \omegai = 1 The weights \omega are optimized jointly during training to automatically focus on correct confidence metrics. Parameters: \tau: Threshold for outlier identification. Value not explicitly given in sources, but described as a threshold to identify outliers. Optical Flow Method: Zhang et al. (2021). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: In C{depth}, if ds = 0, the normalization fails. Guard against zero or near-zero source depths. Zero Displacement: In C{flow}, if \|\Delta{x,y}\| = 0 (pixel does not move between views), the denominator is zero. This typically occurs for pixels at infinity or static background. Handle by setting C{flow} = 1 (perfect consistency) or ignoring such pixels. Occlusions: Reprojection into occluded regions will yield incorrect dt or \hat{d}t. The flow consistency helps detect these, but extreme occlusions may still produce misleading confidence. A variant that assigns geometric labels to points independently of predicted opacity values, using ground-truth depth as the reference. It excludes samples located at depth edges from the analysis. A point is classified as geometrically inconsistent if it violates GT-observed free space in at least two views AND agrees with no observed surface depth. A point is surface-consistent if it agrees with at least two views AND has no free-space violations. All remaining points are classified as uncertain. The depth tolerance threshold is \max(0.03 \text{ m}, 0.01d), where d is the depth value. On held-out Hypersim validation scenes, this procedure identifies 36,125 inconsistent points. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of target views and the cost of the optical flow method. Optical flow is typically O(W \cdot H) per view pair. Memory Complexity: Requires storing depth maps, flow fields, and confidence maps for all views. Strengths: Explicitly models geometric and photometric consistency, robust to outliers through the \gamma function. Learnable combination allows adaptation to different scene types. Limitations: Requires accurate camera poses and reliable optical flow. Sensitive to the threshold \tau. Does not account for textureless regions where flow is unreliable. When to Use: Multi-view stereo, neural rendering, and depth estimation pipelines where outlier removal is critical. When Not to Use: Single-view reconstruction, scenes with significant non-rigid motion (unless flow is robust), or real-time applications where optical flow is too expensive. Originated in the context of street view neural radiance fields, specifically S-NeRF. The method leverages the redundancy of multi-view observations to enforce geometric consistency. The geometric consistency analysis variant was further developed in InfiniSplat v2 for feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting. S-NeRF: Neural Radiance Fields for Street Views, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2303.00749, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) InfiniSplat v2: Analyzing and Improving Feed-Forward 3DGS from Any Views, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20341, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Depth-free motion evidence (Epipolar Residual)
head: Epipolar Line Distance for Motion Evidence, Epipolar Residual, Epipolar Residual for Depth-Free Motion Evidence
body: A method to detect motion without requiring correct depth, by measuring the distance of measured correspondences to their epipolar lines in the target frame. It measures motion evidence by calculating the distance from each measured correspondence to its epipolar line in pixels, using no correct depth, only camera pose, making it robust against noisy monocular depth that defeats rigid-flow residuals. This approach serves as a geometry confidence metric within the broader framework of Geometry Confidence Measurement, distinguishing true motion from depth estimation errors by leveraging the geometric constraint that static points must lie on their epipolar lines regardless of depth. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Measured optical flow field \mathbf{F} of shape (H, W, 2), where H and W are height and width. Camera poses for source frame i and target frame j: Rotation matrices Ri, Rj \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} and translation vectors Ci, Cj \in \mathbb{R}^3. Camera intrinsics: focal lengths fx, fy and principal point (cx, cy). Outputs: A confidence map (or residual map) D \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W} representing the point-to-line distance in pixels for each pixel. Data Structures Pixel coordinate grids Xs, Ys \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W} containing the x and y coordinates of each pixel in the source frame. Arbitrary depth values zl (near) and zf (far) used to construct the epipolar line. Typical values are zl = 0.85 and zf = 0.15. Steps 1. Construct Source Pixel Grids: Create grids of pixel coordinates (xs, ys) for the source frame i with dimensions H \times W. 2. Define Arbitrary Depths: Select two arbitrary depth values, zl and zf, to define the epipolar line. These values do not need to correspond to actual scene depths. 3. Reproject to Target Frame: For each pixel (xs, ys), convert to normalized camera coordinates and then to 3D points at depths zl and zf in frame i. Transform these 3D points into frame j using the relative pose (Rj Ri^T, Cj - Rj Ri^T Ci). Project these 3D points back to the image plane of frame j using intrinsics to obtain two 2D points: (u1, v1) corresponding to zl and (u2, v2) corresponding to zf. 4. Compute Line Geometry: Calculate the direction vector \mathbf{d} = (u2 - u1, v2 - v1) and its norm \|\mathbf{d}\|. Identify valid pixels where both projections are finite and \|\mathbf{d}\| > \epsilon (e.g., \epsilon = 10^{-3}) to avoid degeneracy at the epipole. 5. Compute Line Normal: For valid pixels, compute the unit normal vector \mathbf{n} = (nx, ny) to the epipolar line. This is typically (-dy, dx) / \|\mathbf{d}\| or (dy, -dx) / \|\mathbf{d}\| depending on coordinate system orientation. 6. Determine Correspondence: Calculate the measured correspondence in frame j by adding the measured flow to the original pixel coordinates: (xc, yc) = (xs + Fx, ys + Fy). 7. Compute Point-to-Line Distance: Calculate the distance from the correspondence (xc, yc) to the epipolar line defined by point (u1, v1) and normal \mathbf{n}. The distance is given by the absolute dot product: D = |nx(xc - u1) + ny(yc - v1)|. Reshape the result to image dimensions H \times W. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computeepipolarresidual( flow: np.ndarray, # Shape (H, W, 2) posei: np.ndarray, # 4x4 transformation matrix from world to frame i posej: np.ndarray, # 4x4 transformation matrix from world to frame j intrinsics: np.ndarray, # [fx, fy, cx, cy] znear: float = 0.85, zfar: float = 0.15, eps: float = 1e-3) -> np.ndarray: """ Compute depth-free motion evidence using epipolar residuals. Args: flow: Measured optical flow (H, W, 2). posei: 4x4 pose matrix of source frame. posej: 4x4 pose matrix of target frame. intrinsics: [fx, fy, cx, cy]. znear, zfar: Arbitrary depths for epipolar line construction. eps: Minimum norm for line direction to avoid degeneracy. Returns: residual: Point-to-line distance map (H, W). """ H, W = flow.shape[:2] fx, fy, cx, cy = intrinsics # 1. Create pixel coordinate grids xs, ys = np.meshgrid(np.arange(W), np.arange(H)) # 2. Convert to homogeneous coordinates in camera frame i # xcam = (x - cx) / fx, ycam = (y - cy) / fy xcam = (xs - cx) / fx ycam = (ys - cy) / fy # 3. Construct 3D points at two arbitrary depths in frame i # Point = [xcam z, ycam z, z, 1] ptsneari = np.stack([xcam znear, ycam znear, znear, np.oneslike(xs)], axis=-1) ptsfari = np.stack([xcam zfar, ycam zfar, zfar, np.oneslike(xs)], axis=-1) # 4. Transform to world coordinates # Pworld = posei^{-1} @ Pcam (assuming posei is world-to-camera) # Note: Standard convention varies. If posei is Tworldfromcam, then Pcam = posei @ Pworld. # So Pworld = inv(posei) @ Pcam. invposei = np.linalg.inv(posei) ptsnearworld = (invposei @ ptsneari.T).T ptsfarworld = (invposei @ ptsfari.T).T # 5. Transform to frame j coordinates # Pcamj = posej @ Pworld ptsnearj = (posej @ ptsnearworld.T).T ptsfarj = (posej @ ptsfarworld.T).T # 6. Project to image plane j # u = x/z fx + cx, v = y/z fy + cy # Handle division by zero or negative z def project(pts): z = pts[:,:, 2] x = pts[:,:, 0] y = pts[:,:, 1] # Avoid division by zero validz = np.abs(z) > eps u = np.zeroslike(z) v = np.zeroslike(z) u[validz] = (x[validz] / z[validz]) fx + cx v[validz] = (y[validz] / z[validz]) fy + cy return u, v, validz u1, v1, valid1 = project(ptsnearj) u2, v2, valid2 = project(ptsfarj) # 7. Identify valid pixels valid = valid1 & valid2 dx = u2 - u1 dy = v2 - v1 norm = np.sqrt(dx2 + dy2) valid = valid & (norm > eps) # 8. Compute line normal # Normal is perpendicular to direction (dx, dy). n = (-dy, dx) / norm nx = np.zeroslike(dx) ny = np.zeroslike(dy) nx[valid] = -dy[valid] / norm[valid] ny[valid] = dx[valid] / norm[valid] # 9. Compute correspondence in frame j # Correspondence = (xs + flowx, ys + flowy) flowx = flow[:,:, 0] flowy = flow[:,:, 1] xc = xs + flowx yc = ys + flowy # 10. Compute point-to-line distance # Distance = |n. (Pcorr - Pline)| # Pline can be (u1, v1) dist = np.abs(nx (xc - u1) + ny (yc - v1)) # Set invalid pixels to 0 or NaN depending on usage. # For confidence, 0 might mean "on line" (static), but invalid projections are uncertain. # Here we keep the calculated distance for valid pixels and 0 for invalid. dist[~valid] = 0.0 return dist Parameters zl, zf: Arbitrary depths. Values 0.85 and 0.15 are used in the source implementation. \epsilon: Threshold for line norm, typically 10^{-3}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Epipole Degeneracy: If the pixel is near the epipole, the direction vector norm approaches zero. The method explicitly checks for \|\mathbf{d}\| > \epsilon to avoid numerical instability. Noisy Monocular Depth: This method survives noisy monocular depth that defeats rigid-flow residuals because it does not rely on correct depth estimates. Invalid Projections: Pixels where reprojected points have invalid or negative depth are masked out. Time Complexity: O(HW) per frame pair, as it involves per-pixel operations. Memory Complexity: O(HW) for storing coordinate grids and intermediate projections. Strengths: Robust to inaccurate depth estimates; leverages fundamental epipolar geometry constraints. Limitations: Requires accurate camera poses and intrinsics; fails if poses are significantly incorrect. When to Use: When monocular depth estimates are unreliable or noisy, and camera poses are known. When Not to Use: When camera poses are unknown or highly inaccurate. This method is part of the Geometry Confidence Measurement pipeline, which aims to identify outliers in depth and flow consistency across views. It is implemented in the context of volumetric video processing and 4D Gaussian Splatting optimization, specifically in the devarshh/volumetric-video-4dgs repository. The approach exploits the property that static points lie on their epipolar lines regardless of their depth, allowing motion detection without depth priors. devarshh/volumetric-video-4dgs, https://github.com/devarshh/volumetric-video-4dgs, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Multi-view Consistency Depth Filtering
head: Confidence Modeling, Multi-view consistency depth masking, Ray confidence filtering, Self-training confidence
body: Multi-view Consistency Depth Filtering is a mechanism to verify the accuracy and reliability of monocular depth estimates before distilling them into a radiance field. It generates a binary confidence map by measuring the consistency between scaled monocular depth predictions and rendered NeRF depth across multiple viewpoints, filtering out inaccurate rays. Inputs: Input image Ii from a seen viewpoint i. Initial Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) depth map Di^(p) for pixel p. Camera intrinsic matrix K. Rotation matrix R{i \to l} representing the viewpoint difference from seen view i to target view l. Rendered depth map \bar{D}l(p') from the NeRF at target viewpoint l. Threshold parameter \tau. Outputs: Binary confidence mask Mi(p) indicating valid depth values. Masked MDE depth map used for loss computation. Data Structures: Di^(p): 2D array of depth values, same resolution as input image. \bar{D}l(p'): 2D array of depth values, same resolution as target view. Mi(p): 2D binary array (0 or 1) of same resolution. Steps: 1. Predict Initial Depth: Predict the initial MDE depth map Di^(p) from the input image Ii. 2. Scale and Shift Adjustment: Fit Di^ to the absolute scale of the NeRF depth \bar{D}i at the same viewpoint i by computing scale wi and shift qi parameters using least squares. The adjusted depth is wi Di^(p) + qi. 3. Reprojection: Transform pixel p in the seen viewpoint i to pixel p' in the target viewpoint l. The homogeneous coordinates are transformed as follows: p' \sim K R{i \to l} Di^(p) K^{-1} p Note: Di^(p) is treated as a depth value to unproject p to 3D, then project to view l.. 4. Consistency Check: Measure the distance between the scaled MDE depth from the seen viewpoint and the rendered NeRF depth at the reprojected pixel p' in the target view. 5. Generate Confidence Mask: Generate the binary confidence map Mi(p) using the Iverson bracket notation: Mi(p) = \left[ \left\| (wi Di^(p) + qi) - \bar{D}l(p') \right\| < \tau \right] Where [\cdot] is 1 if the condition is true, and 0 otherwise. 6. Filtering: Apply Mi(p) to filter the MDE depth values. Only pixels where Mi(p)=1 are used in the distillation loss. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def multiviewconsistencyfiltering( inputimage, mdenetwork, nerfmodel, cameraintrinsicsK, rotationmatrixRitol, thresholdtau, viewpointi, viewpointl): """ Generates a confidence mask for monocular depth based on multi-view consistency. Args: inputimage: Input RGB image from seen viewpoint i. mdenetwork: Pre-trained Monocular Depth Estimation network. nerfmodel: Current NeRF model. cameraintrinsicsK: 3x3 camera intrinsic matrix. rotationmatrixRitol: 3x3 rotation matrix from view i to view l. thresholdtau: Scalar threshold for consistency check. viewpointi: Identifier for the seen viewpoint. viewpointl: Identifier for the target viewpoint. Returns: confidencemask: 2D binary array (H, W). scaledmdedepth: 2D array of scaled monocular depth. """ # Step 1: Predict initial MDE depth Distar = mdenetwork.predict(inputimage) # Shape (H, W) # Step 2: Scale and Shift Adjustment # Get NeRF rendered depth at the SAME viewpoint i for calibration Dbari = nerfmodel.renderdepth(viewpoint=viewpointi) # Shape (H, W) # Compute scale wi and shift qi via least squares between Distar and Dbari # Flatten arrays for linear regression: y = wx + q y = Dbari.flatten().astype(np.float64) x = Distar.flatten().astype(np.float64) # Solve for w and q using closed-form least squares: minimize ||wx + q - y||^2 meanx = np.mean(x) meany = np.mean(y) wi = np.sum((x - meanx) (y - meany)) / np.sum((x - meanx)2) qi = meany - wi meanx # Compute scaled MDE depth scaledmdedepth = wi Distar + qi # Step 3 & 4: Reprojection and Consistency Check # Get NeRF rendered depth at target viewpoint l Dbarl = nerfmodel.renderdepth(viewpoint=viewpointl) # Shape (Hl, Wl) H, W = Distar.shape confidencemask = np.zeros((H, W), dtype=bool) # Precompute inverse intrinsics Kinv = np.linalg.inv(cameraintrinsicsK) for py in range(H): for px in range(W): # Get pixel coordinates in homogeneous form for view i phomogeneous = np.array([px, py, 1.0]) # Get depth value at p depthval = Distar[py, px] # 1. Unproject to normalized camera coordinates xnorm = Kinv @ phomogeneous # 2. Scale by depth X3Dcam = xnorm depthval # 3. Rotate to target view l X3Dtarget = rotationmatrixRitol @ X3Dcam # 4. Project to target view pixel coordinates pprimehomogeneous = cameraintrinsicsK @ X3Dcam # Normalize homogeneous coordinates pprimex = pprimehomogeneous[0] / pprimehomogeneous[2] pprimey = pprimehomogeneous[1] / pprimehomogeneous[2] # Check if p' is within bounds of target image if 0 <= pprimex < Dbarl.shape[1] and 0 <= pprimey < Dbarl.shape[0]: # Get depth at reprojected pixel in target view depthtarget = bilinearinterpolate(Dbarl, pprimex, pprimey) # Get scaled MDE depth at original pixel depthsource = scaledmdedepth[py, px] # Step 5: Generate Confidence Mask # Check if absolute difference is less than tau if abs(depthsource - depthtarget) < thresholdtau: confidencemask[py, px] = True else: confidencemask[py, px] = False else: # Out of bounds, mark as invalid (0) confidencemask[py, px] = False return confidencemask, scaledmdedepth def bilinearinterpolate(depthmap, x, y): """Standard bilinear interpolation for depth map.""" x0, x1 = int(np.floor(x)), int(np.ceil(x)) y0, y1 = int(np.floor(y)), int(np.ceil(y)) # Clip to bounds x0 = max(0, min(x0, depthmap.shape[1] - 1)) x1 = max(0, min(x1, depthmap.shape[1] - 1)) y0 = max(0, min(y0, depthmap.shape[0] - 1)) y1 = max(0, min(y1, depthmap.shape[0] - 1)) q11 = depthmap[y0, x0] q12 = depthmap[y0, x1] q21 = depthmap[y1, x0] q22 = depthmap[y1, x1] wx = x - x0 wy = y - y0 return (1 - wx) (1 - wy) q11 + wx (1 - wy) q12 + (1 - wx) wy q21 + wx wy q22 Parameters: \tau: Threshold parameter for the confidence map. wi, qi: Scale and shift parameters obtained by least squares between Di^ and \bar{D}i. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Reprojection Bounds: If p' falls outside the image boundaries of the target view, the consistency check cannot be performed. The method marks these as invalid (0). Occlusions: Multi-view consistency may fail at occlusion boundaries where the NeRF depth and MDE depth disagree due to different geometric interpretations. The threshold \tau must be tuned to handle these discrepancies. NeRF Accuracy: The method relies on the NeRF depth \bar{D}l being reasonably accurate. If the NeRF is poorly trained, the confidence mask may incorrectly filter valid MDE depth or retain invalid depth. Uses augmented monocular depth for supervision. Focuses on loss formulation rather than filtering. Choose when direct depth supervision is preferred over consistency masking. Link General term for removing outliers. This method specifically uses NeRF-rendered depth as the consistency reference. Choose when geometric consistency with a learned radiance field is available. Link Strengths: Effectively eliminates inaccurate information from both NeRF and MDE networks by leveraging multi-view consistency. Limitations: Depends on the quality of the initial NeRF depth. If NeRF is inaccurate, the mask may be misleading. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. When to use: When distilling monocular depth into sparse-view NeRF and MDE errors are significant. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and NeRF rendering is too slow. Originated in the DaRF paper (2023) by. It is inspired by self-training approaches. It addresses the propagation of errors from both few-shot NeRF and estimated monocular depths during the distillation process. name: Pseudo-depth Supervised Loss
head: Depth Loss, Pseudo-Depth Supervision, SFM Depth Loss
body: Pseudo-depth Supervised Loss enforces geometric consistency in neural radiance fields by comparing rendered depth against pseudo-depth targets derived from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) data. Unlike standard photometric losses that only constrain color, this method explicitly constrains the density distribution along rays. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Reliable Depth Estimation via Reprojection by relying on sparse SfM point clouds rather than dense multi-view stereo consistency, making it suitable for scenarios where dense depth priors are unavailable but camera poses are known. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rendered RGB color \tilde{c}(p) and depth \tilde{d}(p) for pixel p; target color C(p); pseudo-depth D(p); confidence score U(p) for pixel p. Outputs: Scalar loss value L used for gradient backpropagation. Data Structures: Sparse Point Cloud: A set of 3D points \{Pj\} with coordinates (xj, yj, zj) generated by SfM solvers (e.g., COLMAP). Ray Batch: A set of rays R (or pixels p) sampled for the current training step. Confidence Map: A per-pixel scalar U(p) \in [0, 1] indicating the reliability of the depth estimate. Step-by-Step Procedure: 1. Generate Pseudo-Depth (if not provided): Estimate camera poses using an SfM solver (e.g., COLMAP) to obtain a sparse point cloud. Align the camera coordinate system with the point cloud coordinate system. For a ray r originating at camera center C with direction \mathbf{v}, find the intersection with the nearest point P \in \text{PointCloud} along the ray. Calculate pseudo-depth D(r) = \| P - C \|2. Note: SfM struggles in texture-less regions, leading to sparse or missing depth data. 2. Render Depth and Color: For each ray r in the batch, sample points ti along the ray. Compute opacity \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \Deltai), where \sigmai is volume density and \Deltai = t{i+1} - ti. Render color \tilde{c}(r) = \sumi \alphai ci \prod{j<i} (1-\alphaj) and depth \tilde{d}(r) = \frac{\sumi \alphai ti \prod{j<i} (1-\alphaj)}{\sumi \alphai \prod{j<i} (1-\alphaj)}. 3. Filter by Confidence: Calculate a confidence score U(p) for each pixel p. Define an indicator function \mathbb{I}(U(p) > \delta) which returns 1 if the confidence exceeds threshold \delta, and 0 otherwise. Typical threshold \delta = 0.5. 4. Compute Loss Components: Photometric Loss: L{color} = \sum{r \in R} \| \tilde{c}(r) - C(r) \|^2. Depth Loss (Ray-wise, MSE): L{depth} = \sum{r \in R} \| \hat{D}(r) - D(r) \|^2. Depth Loss (Pixel-wise, L1 with confidence mask): L{render} = \sum{p \in I} \left( \lambda1 \|\tilde{c}(p) - I(p)\|^2 + \lambda2 \mathbb{I}(U(p) > \delta) |\tilde{d}(p) - D(p)| \right). 5. Aggregate Total Loss: Standard combination: L = \lambda{color} L{color} + \lambda{depth} L{depth} Multi-level combination (if applicable): L = \sum{l=1}^{3} L{render}^l + \lambda3 L{mvs} Parameters: \lambda{color}: Weight for photometric loss. Typical value: 1.0. \lambda{depth}: Weight for depth loss. Grows linearly from 1e-4 to 1e-2 over training steps. \delta: Confidence threshold. Typical value: 0.5. \lambda3: Weight for multi-view stereo loss. Typical value: 1.0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pseudodepthsupervisedloss(renderedcolor, rendereddepth, targetcolor, pseudodepth, confidencemap, lambdacolor=1.0, lambdadepth=0.01, delta=0.5): """ Computes the pseudo-depth supervised loss. Args: renderedcolor: List of arrays of shape (3,), rendered RGB colors per pixel. rendereddepth: List of floats, rendered depths per pixel. targetcolor: List of arrays of shape (3,), ground truth/target colors per pixel. pseudodepth: List of floats, pseudo-depth from SfM per pixel. confidencemap: List of floats, confidence scores U(p) per pixel. lambdacolor: Weight for color loss. lambdadepth: Weight for depth loss. delta: Confidence threshold. Returns: Scalar loss value. """ # 1. Create mask for reliable pixels # Indicator function: 1 if confidence > delta and pseudodepth > 0, else 0 reliablemask = [] for p in range(len(confidencemap)): reliablemask.append(1.0 if (confidencemap[p] > delta and pseudodepth[p] > 0) else 0.0) # 2. Compute Photometric Loss (MSE) colordiffsq = [] for i in range(len(renderedcolor)): diff = [renderedcolor[i][k] - targetcolor[i][k] for k in range(3)] colordiffsq.append(sum(d2 for d in diff) reliablemask[i]) colorloss = sum(colordiffsq) / max(len(colordiffsq), 1) # 3. Compute Depth Loss (L2/MSE as per) depthdiffsq = [] for i in range(len(rendereddepth)): diff = rendereddepth[i] - pseudodepth[i] depthdiffsq.append(diff2 reliablemask[i]) depthloss = sum(depthdiffsq) / max(len(depthdiffsq), 1) # 4. Combine totalloss = lambdacolor colorloss + lambdadepth depthloss return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Texture-less Regions: SfM fails to generate points in uniform areas (walls, ceilings), leading to missing pseudo-depth. The confidence filter \delta mitigates this by excluding low-confidence predictions. Coordinate Alignment: Camera and point cloud must be aligned in the same coordinate system before calculating distances. Moving Objects: Dynamic objects cause inconsistencies in depth maps; semantic segmentation masks may be required to exclude them. Uses multi-view consistency and reprojection errors to refine depth, avoiding reliance on sparse SfM points. Choose when dense geometric consistency is available and SfM is sparse. Link Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Online training cost is dominated by the rendering pass. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storing the sparse point cloud and the confidence map. Strengths: Effective at removing floating artifacts and improving geometric accuracy in indoor scenes. Provides explicit geometric supervision where photometric loss is ambiguous. Limitations: Relies on the quality of SfM reconstruction; fails in texture-less regions without confidence filtering. Requires accurate camera poses. When to Use: Indoor scenes with known camera poses (e.g., from COLMAP) where geometric consistency is critical. When Not to Use: Scenes with no distinctive features for SfM, or where camera poses are unknown/unreliable. The method originates from the need to improve geometric consistency in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), particularly in indoor environments where photometric loss alone leads to floating artifacts. It leverages Structure-from-Motion (SfM) techniques, specifically COLMAP, which are standard for estimating camera poses and generating sparse point clouds. The concept of using pseudo-depth from SfM as a supervision signal was introduced to address the lack of ground truth depth in real-world scenarios. Confidence filtering was later introduced to handle the unreliability of depth predictions in texture-less regions. name: Self-Supervised Depth Losses
body: Self-supervised depth losses constrain the estimated depth and confidence intervals using monocular depth estimates and image gradients to address the difficulty of obtaining ground truth depth. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rendered depth map \hat{D}, monocular depth estimate \tilde{D}{mono}, aligned RGB image I, and image dimensions H, W. Outputs: Scalar loss value \mathcal{L}{smooth}. Data Structures: \hat{D}: Array of shape (H, W) containing per-pixel depth values. \tilde{D}{mono}: Array of shape (H, W) containing per-pixel monocular depth/disparity values. I: Array of shape (H, W, 3) containing RGB pixel values. Steps: 1. Compute spatial gradients of \hat{D}, I, and \tilde{D}{mono} in horizontal (x) and vertical (y) directions. 2. Compute exponential weights from the gradient magnitudes of I and \tilde{D}{mono}. 3. Weight the gradient magnitudes of \hat{D} by the computed weights and sum over all pixels. Formula: The smoothness loss \mathcal{L}{smooth} is defined as: \mathcal{L}{smooth} = \frac{1}{HW} \sum{r} \left( \|\partialx \hat{D}(r)\| (e^{-|\partialx I(r)|} + e^{-|\partialx \tilde{D}{mono}(r)|}) + \|\partialy \hat{D}(r)\| (e^{-|\partialy I(r)|} + e^{-|\partialy \tilde{D}{mono}(r)|}) \right) Where: r iterates over all pixels (x, y). \|\cdot\| denotes the magnitude of the gradient. e^{-|\cdot|} acts as a weight that suppresses the loss at edges (high gradient magnitude) in the RGB image or monocular depth map. H, W are the height and width of the image. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Gradients near zero are handled naturally by the exponential decay. Boundaries: Gradient computation at image borders requires padding or boundary handling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computesmoothnessloss(rendereddepth, monodepth, rgbimage): H = len(rendereddepth) W = len(rendereddepth[0]) totalloss = 0.0 for y in range(H): for x in range(W): dxd = rendereddepth[y][x + 1] - rendereddepth[y][x] if x < W - 1 else 0.0 dyd = rendereddepth[y + 1][x] - rendereddepth[y][x] if y < H - 1 else 0.0 dxi = math.sqrt(sum((rgbimage[y][x + 1][c] - rgbimage[y][x][c]) 2 for c in range(3))) if x < W - 1 else 0.0 dyi = math.sqrt(sum((rgbimage[y + 1][x][c] - rgbimage[y][x][c]) 2 for c in range(3))) if y < H - 1 else 0.0 dxm = monodepth[y][x + 1] - monodepth[y][x] if x < W - 1 else 0.0 dym = monodepth[y + 1][x] - monodepth[y][x] if y < H - 1 else 0.0 totalloss += abs(dxd) (math.exp(-dxi) + math.exp(-dxm)) + abs(dyd) (math.exp(-dyi) + math.exp(-dym)) return totalloss / (H W) A loss function that combines RGB image gradient weighting with L1 loss between rendered depth \hat{D} and ground truth depth D to regularize depth estimation. It is set apart by its use of an L1 norm and explicit ground truth supervision rather than smoothness priors on monocular estimates. Formula: \mathcal{L}{\hat{D}} = g{\text{rgb}} \frac{1}{|\hat{D}|} \sum \log(1+\|\hat{D}-D\|1), where g{\text{rgb}} = \exp(-\nabla I) and |\hat{D}| is the total number of pixels. Time and Memory Complexity: Linear in the number of pixels HW for gradient computation and summation. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with image resolution. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Self-supervised, does not require ground truth depth. Limitations: Relies on the quality of monocular depth estimates. When to Use: Use when ground truth depth is unavailable and monocular depth estimates are reliable. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Originated in NeRF-SDP (GRF, MVSNeRF, ENeRF, IBRNet) presented at MMAsia ’23. Developed to efficiently generalize neural radiance fields with scene depth perception without ground truth. Also used in DN-Splatter for Gaussian Splatting and Meshing. name: Depth Prior Loss
body: Depth Prior Loss is a regularization term that constrains the geometry of a radiance field by enforcing consistency between rendered depth and monocular depth priors. It is typically combined with cross-scale geometric adaptation losses (e.g., L{geo}) to leverage their complementarity. Inputs and Outputs: Rendered depth map Dr and monocular depth prior Dm for a given view, producing a scalar loss Ld. Data Structures: Dr and Dm are 2D tensors of shape (H, W) representing depth along each ray. Steps: 1. Alignment: Compute scale s and shift t parameters that minimize the least-squares error between Dr and Dm using a closed-form solution. 2. Transformation: Align the monocular prior to the rendered depth scale: \hat{D}m = s \cdot Dm + t. 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the mean squared error between the rendered depth and the aligned prior: Ld = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i,j} (Dr(i,j) - \hat{D}m(i,j))^2, where N is the number of valid pixels. Formulas: The closed-form least-squares alignment computes the means \bar{D}r and \bar{D}m over valid pixels, then s = \frac{\sum (Dr - \bar{D}r)(Dm - \bar{D}m)}{\sum (Dm - \bar{D}m)^2} and t = \bar{D}r - s \bar{D}m. Parameters: Scale and shift are computed per image or per batch to handle scale ambiguity. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Using Ld in isolation initially offers good performance but later suffers from higher error due to scale mismatches between the depth prior and voxel resolutions. A regularization term that aligns rendered depth with monocular or MVS depth priors using a relative formulation (D{mvs}/Dr), which exhibits high sensitivity to errors at closer depths. It is distinguished from its parent by rejecting erroneous MVS values via thresholding and weighting by rendering certainty. Choose it when relative geometric structure is more critical than absolute scale. Strengths: Initially offers good performance due to strong geometric constraints. Limitations: Suffers from higher error in later training stages due to scale mismatches between the depth prior and voxel resolutions when used in isolation. Performance: Combining Ld with L{geo} yields better PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS scores than using either loss alone, with comparable model size and training time (~10 minutes for FrugalNeRF). When to use: Use as part of a combined regularization strategy with cross-scale geometric adaptation losses to leverage fast initial convergence while mitigating long-term scale drift. It is used in few-shot NeRF methods, specifically FrugalNeRF, to constrain geometry during training using monocular depth priors. The method addresses high-quality novel view synthesis with limited training views by providing an initial geometric constraint that complements cross-scale geometric adaptation. FrugalNeRF: Fast Convergence for Extreme Few-shot Novel View Synthesis without Learned Priors, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52734.2025.01049, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Relative Depth Loss
head: Lrel, Single-view relative depth loss
body: Relative Depth Loss is a regularization term that constrains the geometry of a radiance field by aligning rendered depth with monocular or Multi-View Stereo (MVS) depth priors. It differs from absolute depth consistency losses by using a relative formulation (D{mvs}/Dr), which exhibits high sensitivity to errors at closer depths. It is distinguished from its parent Depth Prior Loss by its specific mechanism of rejecting erroneous MVS values via thresholding and weighting by rendering certainty. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: MVS depth map D{mvs}, rendered depth map Dr, rendering certainty U, thresholding hyperparameter s. Output: Scalar loss value L{rel}. Data Structures D{mvs}: 2D array of depth values from an external MVS estimator or monocular depth network. Dr: 2D array of rendered depth values, computed per-pixel. U: 2D array of rendering certainty, computed per-pixel. \omegai: Blending weight of the i-th Gaussian. ti: Depth of the i-th Gaussian. Ti: Accumulated transmittance up to the i-th Gaussian. Formulas The rendered depth Dr is computed as the median depth, defined as the largest depth value ti considered visible: Dr = \max\{ti \mid Ti > 0.5\} where Ti is the accumulated transmittance. Rendering certainty U is defined as the sum of blending weights: U = \sumi \omegai. The loss is calculated as: L{rel} = 1 - \frac{D{mvs}}{Dr} \cdot U \cdot I(|Dr - D{mvs}| < s \cdot Dr) where: D{mvs} is the MVS depth. Dr is the rendered depth. s is the thresholding tolerance hyperparameter. I(\cdot) is the indicator function, yielding 1 if the condition holds and 0 otherwise. Parameters s: Thresholding tolerance. Typically annealed from a less restrictive to a more restrictive value during optimization. Pitfalls and Edge Cases Mean Depth Artifacts: Using mean depth (\sum \omegai ti / \sum \omegai) leads to inaccurate estimates for semi-transparent or transparent objects and introduces "flying pixel" artifacts near boundaries of opaque objects. Weight Instability: Reliance on mean depth calculated using potentially unstable weights \omegai during optimization can harm reconstruction quality. Sensitivity: The relative formulation is highly sensitive to errors at closer depths. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computerelativedepthloss(Dmvs, Dr, U, s): """ Computes the Relative Depth Loss (Lrel) per pixel. Args: Dmvs: 2D array, MVS depth map. Dr: 2D array, rendered median depth map. U: 2D array, rendering certainty (sum of blending weights). s: float, thresholding tolerance hyperparameter. Returns: 2D array, per-pixel loss values. """ epsilon = 1e-6 # Guard against division by zero if Dr is 0 ratio = Dmvs / (Dr + epsilon) indicator = (abs(Dr - Dmvs) < s Dr).astype(float) return 1.0 - ratio U indicator def computerendereddepth(Gaussians): """ Computes rendered depth Dr as the median depth. Args: Gaussians: List of Gaussian objects contributing to a pixel, sorted by depth. Each Gaussian has attributes: t: depth T: accumulated transmittance (pre-computed or computed during rasterization) Returns: float, the median depth Dr. """ visiblegaussians = [g for g in Gaussians if g.T > 0.5] if not visiblegaussians: return 0.0 # Fallback for empty pixel return max(g.t for g in visiblegaussians) def computerenderingcertainty(Gaussians): """ Computes rendering certainty U as the sum of blending weights. Args: Gaussians: List of Gaussian objects contributing to a pixel. Each Gaussian has attribute: omega: blending weight Returns: float, the rendering certainty U. """ return sum(g.omega for g in Gaussians) Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Mitigates artifacts associated with mean depth (flying pixels, transparency issues) by using median depth. High sensitivity to close-depth errors improves geometric fidelity. Limitations: Single-view application may not regularize all scene regions effectively, as gradients primarily affect Gaussians contributing to the median depth in that specific view. When to use: When high geometric fidelity is required, especially for close-range objects, and MVS priors are available. Suitable for scenes where mean depth fails due to transparency or boundary artifacts. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Relative Depth Loss was introduced in the context of Multiview Geometric Regularization of Gaussian Splatting for Accurate Radiance Fields. It addresses limitations of mean depth computation in 3D Gaussian Splatting, such as "flying pixel" artifacts and inaccuracies with transparent objects. The method builds on the observation that median depth provides a more robust estimate of surface location. Multiview Geometric Regularization of Gaussian Splatting for Accurate Radiance Fields, https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13508v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Patch-level Scale-Shift Alignment
head: Patch-level fitting, Patch-wise scale-shift fitting, Patch-wise scale-shift invariant loss
body: Patch-level Scale-Shift Alignment is a regularization technique that adapts monocular depth estimation (MDE) outputs to a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) scene by optimizing scale and shift parameters locally per image patch rather than globally per image. It solves the problem of local misalignment errors that arise when a single global transformation fails to account for depth inconsistencies among different objects within the same scene. Unlike its sibling Monocular Depth Consistency Loss, which computes a single scale-shift pair for the entire batch or image, this method partitions the depth map into non-overlapping patches to minimize local alignment errors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: S: The set of images in the scene. D^i(p): The predicted depth value at pixel p for image i \in S (rendered or estimated). \bar{D}i(p): The target depth value at pixel p for image i \in S (monocular depth prior or ground truth). P: The set of pixels belonging to a specific non-overlapping patch. Outputs: wi: The scale parameter for the patch. qi: The shift parameter for the patch. L: The total alignment loss. Data Structures: The depth map is partitioned into a grid of non-overlapping patches. Standard implementation uses a patch resolution of 80 \times 80 pixels. Parameters: Patch Resolution: 80 \times 80 pixels. This size balances local adaptability against computational overhead. Steps: 1. Partition the depth map of each image i \in S into non-overlapping patches of size 80 \times 80 pixels. 2. For each patch P in each image i, define the optimization objective to find scale wi and shift qi that minimize the alignment error between the predicted depth D^i(p) and the target depth \bar{D}i(p). 3. Solve for the optimal parameters (wi, qi) using a closed-form least-squares solution. 4. Compute the loss contribution for the patch using the aligned parameters. 5. Sum the loss contributions across all patches and all images in the set S to obtain the total loss L. Formulas: The total loss is defined as: L = \sum{Ii \in S} \sum{p \in P} \| (wi D^i(p) + qi) - \bar{D}i(p) \| where wi and qi are the patch-specific scale and shift, D^i(p) is the predicted depth, and \bar{D}i(p) is the target depth. The parameters (wi, qi) are determined by minimizing the sum of squared errors within the patch: (wi, qi) = \arg \min{wi, qi} \sum{p \in P} \| (wi D^i(p) + qi) - \bar{D}i(p) \| This can be rewritten in matrix form. Let hi = [wi, qi]^T and \vec{D}i(p) = [D^i(p), 1]^T. The optimal hi is given by: hi^{opt} = \left( \sum{p \in P} \vec{D}i(p) \vec{D}i(p)^T \right)^{-1} \left( \sum{p \in P} \vec{D}i(p) \bar{D}i(p) \right) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def patchlevelscaleshiftalignment(predicteddepth, targetdepth, patchsize=80): """ Computes the patch-level scale-shift alignment loss. Args: predicteddepth (np.ndarray): 2D array of shape (H, W), predicted depth D. targetdepth (np.ndarray): 2D array of shape (H, W), target depth Dbar. patchsize (int): Size of the square patches (default 80). Returns: float: Total loss L. """ H, W = predicteddepth.shape totalloss = 0.0 # Iterate over non-overlapping patches for y in range(0, H, patchsize): for x in range(0, W, patchsize): # Define patch boundaries yend = min(y + patchsize, H) xend = min(x + patchsize, W) # Extract patch data ppred = predicteddepth[y:yend, x:xend] ptarget = targetdepth[y:yend, x:xend] # Flatten patches to 1D arrays predflat = ppred.flatten() targetflat = ptarget.flatten() # Number of pixels in the current patch N = len(predflat) # If patch is empty, skip if N == 0: continue # Construct design matrix A where each row is [D, 1] # A shape: (N, 2) A = np.columnstack((predflat, np.ones(N))) # Solve least squares: min || A @ h - targetflat ||^2 # h = [w, q]^T # Using numpy's linear algebra solver for stability # hopt = (A^T A)^-1 A^T target try: hopt, residuals, rank, s = np.linalg.lstsq(A, targetflat, rcond=None) w, q = hopt # Compute aligned prediction alignedpred = w predflat + q # Compute L1 loss for this patch (as per formula definition using norm) # Note: The formula uses ||...|| which typically implies L1 or L2. # The optimization uses least-squares (L2), but the loss summation # in the source text uses ||...||. We follow the source's explicit # summation formula which uses the norm. # Standard interpretation of ||x|| in loss contexts without square # often implies L1, but given the optimization is L2, we compute # the residual magnitude. To be precise to the source formula # L = sum ||...||, we sum the absolute differences (L1) or # squared differences? The source writes ||...|| in the loss # but minimizes squared error. # Re-reading source: "L = sum || (w D + q) - Dbar ||" # Usually, if optimization is L2, the loss is L2. # However, the text explicitly writes the norm without square in L. # We will compute the L2 norm of the residual vector for the patch # or sum of absolute errors? # Let's look at Eq 1: L = sum ||...||. Eq 2 minimizes sum ||...||^2. # It is common to use the same norm for loss and optimization. # Given Eq 3 uses squared error (D - Dbar)^2, the optimization is L2. # The loss L in Eq 1 likely represents the L2 norm (Euclidean distance) # of the residual vector, or the sum of absolute errors. # Given "least-square alignment", we assume the loss is the sum of # squared errors or the L2 norm. # Let's stick to the explicit formula: sum of norms. # If ||x|| is Euclidean norm, then it is sqrt(sum(res^2)). # If ||x|| is L1 norm, it is sum(|res|). # In computer vision depth consistency, L1 is very common. # However, the optimization is strictly L2. # We will compute the L2 norm of the residual vector for the patch # to match the "norm" notation, or simply sum the squared errors # if the notation was loose. # Let's assume the standard L2 loss (sum of squares) for consistency # with the least-squares optimization, as is typical in such papers. # But the source text says: L = sum ||...||. # Let's implement the L2 norm of the residual vector for the patch. residual = alignedpred - targetflat patchloss = np.linalg.norm(residual) # L2 norm of the vector totalloss += patchloss except np.linalg.LinAlgError: # Fallback if matrix is singular (e.g., all depths are constant) # If the patch has zero variance in predicted depth, # the least squares solution is undefined. # We treat the loss as 0 or skip. pass return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singular Matrices: If the predicted depth within a patch is constant (zero variance), the matrix \sum \vec{D}i(p) \vec{D}i(p)^T may be singular or ill-conditioned, making the least-squares solution unstable. A guard should check for variance or use a pseudo-inverse. Boundary Conditions: Patches at the image boundaries may be smaller than 80 \times 80 if the image dimensions are not multiples of the patch size. The algorithm must handle these partial patches correctly by adjusting N in the summations. Depth Inconsistency: The method assumes that within a local patch, a linear scale-shift transformation is sufficient to align the depths. If local depth structures are highly non-linear or contain significant noise, the local fit may introduce artifacts. A regularization loss that encourages rendered depth maps to align with monocular depth priors by maximizing the Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC) between corresponding image patches, thereby enforcing local structural consistency without requiring global scale/shift alignment. It differs from Patch-level Scale-Shift Alignment by avoiding explicit parameter estimation for scale and shift, which can introduce unwanted distortion if the transformation is not constant across pixels, and instead relies on rank-order similarity within local neighborhoods. Time Complexity: The complexity is linear with respect to the number of pixels in the depth map, O(H \times W), as each pixel is processed exactly once within its respective patch. The per-patch least-squares solution involves a fixed-size 2 \times 2 matrix inversion, which is O(1) per patch. Memory Complexity: O(H \times W) to store the depth maps. The additional memory for patch processing is minimal, requiring storage for the 2 \times 2 matrix and vectors of size N (patch pixel count) during the solve step. Strengths: Significantly reduces misalignment errors in rendered depth maps compared to image-level fitting, especially in scenes with depth inconsistencies among different objects. It adapts locally to the depth structure. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than global fitting due to the repeated matrix operations. It may overfit to noise in the monocular depth prior if the patches are too small or the prior is unreliable. When to use: Use when monocular depth priors exhibit local scale/shift variations that a global fit cannot correct, such as in sparse-view NeRF training where MDE outputs may have inconsistent absolute scales across different regions. When not to use: Avoid if computational resources are extremely limited and global alignment is sufficient, or if the depth prior is known to be globally consistent. Patch-level Scale-Shift Alignment was introduced in the context of boosting radiance fields from sparse inputs using monocular depth adaptation. It is a core component of the DaRF (Depth-aware Radiance Fields) method. The technique builds upon the concept of scale-shift invariant loss [39] and least-square alignment [53], adapting them to a patch-wise granularity to handle the limitations of global fitting in complex scenes. It is applied in DaRF to refine MDE depth maps during sparse-view NeRF training.
