name: NTS Training Objective
head: UV Volumes Training Loss
body: The NTS Training Objective is a composite loss function designed to optimize UV volumes and neural texture stack parameters for real-time rendering of human performances. It solves the problem of training differentiable radiance fields by combining photometric, perceptual, semantic, UV-metric, and silhouette losses. Unlike methods that sample image patches during training, this objective renders entire images, leveraging a memory-saving framework that disentangles appearance and geometry. The method optimizes the model parameters by minimizing a weighted sum of five distinct loss terms. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Ground-truth image \mathcal{I}, ground-truth binary human mask \mathcal{S}, DensePose outputs (semantic probability \mathcal{P}k, UV coordinates \mathcal{U}k, \mathcal{V}k for k=1 \dots Nk), and rendered image \hat{\mathcal{I}}. Outputs: Scalar loss value \mathcal{L} used for gradient descent. Data Structures Rendered Image \hat{\mathcal{I}}: Tensor of shape H \times W \times 3. Ground-truth Image \mathcal{I}: Tensor of shape H \times W \times 3. Binary Mask \mathcal{S}: Tensor of shape H \times W. \mathcal{S}(\mathbf{r}) = 0 for foreground (human), \mathcal{S}(\mathbf{r}) = 1 for background. DensePose Outputs: \mathcal{P}k: Semantic probability for body part k. \mathcal{U}k, \mathcal{V}k: UV coordinates for body part k. Nk: Number of body parts. Predicted UV Outputs: \hat{\mathcal{P}}k, \hat{\mathcal{U}}k, \hat{\mathcal{V}}k: Predicted semantic probability and UV coordinates for body part k. Parameters \lambda{\text{vgg}}, \lambda{\text{p}}, \lambda{\text{uv}}, \lambdas: Weighting coefficients for perceptual, semantic, UV-metric, and silhouette losses respectively. \psi(\cdot): Pretrained fixed VGG network used for feature extraction. Formulas 1. Photometric Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{rgb}}): \mathcal{L}{\text{rgb}} = \left\| \hat{\mathcal{I}} - \mathcal{I} \right\|2^2 2. Perceptual Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{vgg}}): \mathcal{L}{\text{vgg}} = \left\| \psi(\hat{\mathcal{I}}) - \psi(\mathcal{I}) \right\|1 3. Semantic Loss (\mathcal{L}p): \mathcal{L}p = \sum{k=1}^{Nk} \mathcal{P}k \log(\hat{\mathcal{P}}k) 4. UV-Metric Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{uv}}): \mathcal{L}{\text{uv}} = \sum{k=1}^{Nk} \mathcal{P}k \left( \left\| \hat{\mathcal{U}}k - \mathcal{U}k \right\|2^2 + \left\| \hat{\mathcal{V}}k - \mathcal{V}k \right\|2^2 \right) 5. Silhouette Loss (\mathcal{L}s): First, compute accumulated transmittance T(\mathbf{r}) for ray \mathbf{r}: T(\mathbf{r}) = \exp \left( - \sum{j=1}^{Ni-1} \sigma(\mathbf{x}j) \deltaj \right) where \sigma(\mathbf{x}j) is density and \deltaj is step size. Then: \mathcal{L}s = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \left( \mathcal{S}(\mathbf{r})(1 - T(\mathbf{r})) + (1 - \mathcal{S}(\mathbf{r}))T(\mathbf{r}) \right) 6. Total Loss (\mathcal{L}): \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{rgb}} + \lambda{\text{vgg}} \mathcal{L}{\text{vgg}} + \lambda{\text{p}} \mathcal{L}p + \lambda{\text{uv}} \mathcal{L}{\text{uv}} + \lambdas \mathcal{L}s Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ntstrainingobjective(renderedimage, groundtruthimage, binarymask, denseposesemantics, denseposeuvs, predictedsemantics, predicteduvs, vggnetwork, transmittancemap, lambdavgg, lambdap, lambdauv, lambdas): """ Compute the NTS Training Objective. Args: renderedimage: Tensor (H, W, 3), predicted image. groundtruthimage: Tensor (H, W, 3), ground truth image. binarymask: Tensor (H, W), 0 for foreground, 1 for background. denseposesemantics: Tensor (H, W, Nk), semantic probabilities from DensePose. denseposeuvs: Tuple of Tensors (H, W, Nk), (U, V) coordinates from DensePose. predictedsemantics: Tensor (H, W, Nk), predicted semantic probabilities. predicteduvs: Tuple of Tensors (H, W, Nk), predicted (U, V) coordinates. vggnetwork: Pretrained fixed VGG network. transmittancemap: Tensor (H, W), accumulated transmittance T(r). lambdavgg, lambdap, lambdauv, lambdas: Float weights. Returns: Total loss scalar. """ # 1. Photometric Loss Lrgb lrgb = torch.sum((renderedimage - groundtruthimage) 2) # 2. Perceptual Loss Lvgg # Extract features using pretrained VGG featurespred = vggnetwork(renderedimage) featuresgt = vggnetwork(groundtruthimage) # L1 norm between feature maps lvgg = torch.sum(torch.abs(featurespred - featuresgt)) # 3. Semantic Loss Lp # Sum over body parts k=1 to Nk # Note: Source uses log(hatPk). Implementation assumes standard cross-entropy-like form # or log-likelihood as defined. # denseposesemantics is Pk, predictedsemantics is hatPk lp = torch.sum(denseposesemantics torch.log(predictedsemantics + 1e-8)) # 4. UV-Metric Loss Luv denseposeu, denseposev = denseposeuvs predu, predv = predicteduvs # Weighted L2 loss between DensePose UVs and predicted UVs # Sum over k, weighted by Pk uvdiff = ((predu - denseposeu) 2 + (predv - denseposev) 2) luv = torch.sum(denseposesemantics uvdiff) # 5. Silhouette Loss Ls # T(r) is transmittancemap # S(r) is binarymask # Ls = sum( S(r)(1-T(r)) + (1-S(r))T(r)) ls = torch.sum(binarymask (1 - transmittancemap) + (1 - binarymask) transmittancemap) # 6. Total Loss totalloss = lrgb + lambdavgg lvgg + lambdap lp + lambdauv luv + lambdas ls return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls Noisy DensePose Supervision: DensePose outputs may contain incorrect semantic and UV labels. The method relies on the intrinsic multi-view constraint of the RGB loss to recover proper UV volumes despite this noise. Mask Definition: The binary mask \mathcal{S} must strictly follow the convention: 0 for foreground (human) and 1 for background. Inverting this leads to incorrect silhouette loss gradients. Memory Efficiency: The method renders entire images during training rather than sampling patches, which is enabled by the memory-saving framework that disentangles appearance and geometry. Performance: The method achieves real-time rendering capabilities (FPS reported in experiments) and high-fidelity novel view synthesis. Strengths: Joint optimization of photometric, perceptual, and geometric (UV/mask) constraints allows for robust training even with noisy pseudo-supervision from DensePose. Limitations: Reliance on DensePose introduces potential noise, though mitigated by the RGB loss constraint. The NTS Training Objective was introduced in the paper "UV Volumes for Real-time Rendering of Editable Free-view Human Performance". It is part of a framework for real-time rendering of human performances, utilizing UV volumes to store appearance and geometry information. The method was developed to address the limitations of patch-based training and to leverage pseudo-supervision from pre-trained models like DensePose to regularize the solution space of UV volumes. name: Recovery-stage optimization objective
head: Quantization recovery objective, Recovery loss
body: The recovery-stage optimization objective is a composite loss function designed to restore rendering quality and minimize artifacts introduced by feature and attribute quantization in differentiable volume rendering pipelines. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly combining image-space reconstruction, teacher-student feature distillation, and explicit constraints on geometric offsets and scaling factors, rather than relying solely on perceptual or standard L2 losses. Inputs: I^{Stu}: The rendered image from the student (quantized) model. I^{GT}: Ground truth reference image. I^{Tea}: Reference image rendered by the teacher (pre-quantization) model. \mathbf{f}i^{Tea}: Teacher anchor features for anchor i. \widehat{\mathbf{f}}i^{Stu}: Recovered student anchor features for anchor i. \tilde{\mathbf{O}}i, \tilde{\mathbf{S}}i^{\text{pos}}, \tilde{\mathbf{s}}i^{\text{anchor}}: Quantized offsets and scaling factors. \hat{\mathbf{O}}i, \hat{\mathbf{s}}i^{\text{anchor}}: Adapted (corrected) offsets and scaling factors produced by the Attribute Adapter. \mathcal{A}{\text{vis}}: Set of anchors visible in the current view. Na: Total number of anchors. K: Number of stages in the Residual Vector Quantization (RVQ). Outputs: Scalar loss value \mathcal{L} used for gradient backpropagation. The method operates on the following internal states, which are maintained during the optimization stages: RVQ Codebooks: Three codebooks initialized via residual K-means. Each contains 1,024 entries. Context Refiner: A lightweight Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) shared across anchors, used to recover features from quantized states. Attribute Adapter: A lightweight MLP shared across anchors, used to refine offsets and scaling. Anchor Features: Vectors of dimension Df = 50. Local Offsets: 10 offsets per anchor. The optimization proceeds in four distinct stages: 1. RVQ Codebook Initialization: Initialize the three RVQ codebooks using residual K-means. Optimize them to reconstruct teacher anchor features. 2. Context Refiner Training: Train the Context Refiner using quantized anchor features. Sample different RVQ depths during training to allow the refiner to recover features from various reconstruction states. 3. Attribute Adapter Optimization: Freeze the Context Refiner. Optimize the Attribute Adapter to refine the quantized offsets and scaling based on the features recovered by the Context Refiner. 4. Joint Fine-tuning: Fix the nearest-neighbor RVQ indices. Jointly fine-tune the RVQ codebooks, Context Refiner, and Attribute Adapter using the total objective function \mathcal{L} defined below. After the recovery stage, the RVQ codebooks, Context Refiner, and Attribute Adapter are frozen. Subsequent steps involve fitting a contextual entropy model and performing index search/calibration, which are outside the scope of the optimization objective itself. The total objective \mathcal{L} is a weighted sum of five terms: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{render}} \left( I^{Stu}, I^{GT} \right) + \lambdaf^{\text{train}} \mathcal{L}f + \mathcal{L}{Os} + \lambda{\text{distill}} \mathcal{L}{\text{render}} \left( I^{Stu}, I^{Tea} \right) + \lambdaA \mathcal{L}{\text{adapter}} 1. Rendering Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{render}}): Combines Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Structural Similarity (SSIM): \mathcal{L}{\text{render}}(I, I^{\text{ref}}) = (1 - \gamma{\text{SSIM}}) \text{MAE}(I, I^{\text{ref}}) + \gamma{\text{SSIM}} [1 - \text{SSIM}(I, I^{\text{ref}})] Where I^{\text{ref}} is either I^{GT} or I^{Tea}, and \gamma{\text{SSIM}} controls the SSIM weight. 2. Feature Recovery Loss (\mathcal{L}f): Average L1 loss between teacher and student anchor features: \mathcal{L}f = \frac{1}{Na} \sum{i=1}^{Na} \left\| \mathbf{f}i^{Tea} - \widehat{\mathbf{f}}i^{Stu} \right\|1 3. Explicit-Attribute Loss (\mathcal{L}{Os}): Constrains offsets (Ei^O) and scaling (Ei^s) errors for visible anchors: \mathcal{L}{Os} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}{\text{vis}}|} \sum{i \in \mathcal{A}{\text{vis}}} (\lambdaO Ei^O + \lambdas Ei^s) Note: Ei^O and Ei^s are defined in external equations (17 and 18 of the source) evaluated at the current quantized state. 4. Adapter Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{adapter}}): Penalizes large corrections from the Attribute Adapter, normalizing offset corrections by positional scale and constraining relative anchor scaling changes: \mathcal{L}{\text{adapter}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}{\text{vis}}|} \sum{i \in \mathcal{A}{\text{vis}}} \left[ \frac{1}{3K} \left\| (\hat{\mathbf{O}}i - \tilde{\mathbf{O}}i) \otimes (\tilde{\mathbf{S}}i^{\text{pos}} + \epsilon) \right\|1 + \frac{1}{6} \left\| (\hat{\mathbf{s}}i^{\text{anchor}} - \tilde{\mathbf{s}}i^{\text{anchor}}) \otimes (\tilde{\mathbf{s}}i^{\text{anchor}} + \epsilon) \right\|1 \right] Where \otimes denotes element-wise multiplication, and \epsilon is a small constant for numerical stability. Typical values from the source experiments: \gamma{\text{SSIM}} = 0.2: Weight for SSIM in rendering loss. \lambdaf^{\text{train}} = 1/Df = 0.02: Weight for feature recovery loss (Df=50). \lambdaO = 1, \lambdas = 1: Weights for offset and scaling errors in \mathcal{L}{Os}. \lambda{\text{distill}} = 0.1: Weight for teacher-student rendering distillation. \lambdaA = 10^{-3}: Weight for adapter regularization. \etao = 0.1, \etas = 0.05: Adaptation rates for offset and scaling (used in attribute refinement, context for \mathcal{L}{Os}). Visible Anchor Set: The losses \mathcal{L}{Os} and \mathcal{L}{\text{adapter}} are averaged only over \mathcal{A}{\text{vis}}. If no anchors are visible, these terms are undefined or zero; implementation must handle empty sets gracefully. Numerical Stability: The term (\tilde{\mathbf{S}}i^{\text{pos}} + \epsilon) and (\tilde{\mathbf{s}}i^{\text{anchor}} + \epsilon) in \mathcal{L}{\text{adapter}} requires \epsilon > 0 to prevent division by zero or instability if scales are near zero. Fixed Indices: During joint fine-tuning (Stage 4), RVQ indices are fixed. Gradients do not flow through the discrete index selection, only through the codebook values and adapter/refiner parameters. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computerecoveryloss( Istu, Igt, Itea, ftea, fstuhat, Otilde, Spostilde, sanchortilde, Ohat, sanchorhat, Avis, Na, K, gammassim=0.2, lambdaftrain=0.02, lambdaO=1.0, lambdas=1.0, lambdadistill=0.1, lambdaA=1e-3, epsilon=1e-8): """ Computes the total recovery-stage optimization objective. Args: Istu: Rendered student image tensor. Igt: Ground truth image tensor. Avis: Set of indices of visible anchors. Na: Total number of anchors. K: Number of RVQ stages. Returns: Total loss scalar. """ # 1. Rendering Loss against Ground Truth # MAE and SSIM are assumed to be available functions lrendergt = (1 - gammassim) mae(Istu, Igt) + gammassim (1 - ssim(Istu, Igt)) # 2. Feature Recovery Loss (L1) # Average over all anchors featurediff = torch.abs(ftea - fstuhat) lf = torch.mean(featurediff) # 3. Explicit-Attribute Loss # Note: EO and ES are external errors defined in source Eqs 17/18. # Assuming helper functions getoffseterror and getscalingerror exist. # We iterate only over visible anchors. if len(Avis) == 0: los = torch.tensor(0.0) else: errorso = [] errorss = [] for i in Avis: errorso.append(getoffseterror(Otilde[i], Ohat[i])) # Placeholder for Eq 17 logic errorss.append(getscalingerror(Spostilde[i], sanchortilde[i])) # Placeholder for Eq 18 logic # Average error per visible anchor avgeo = torch.mean(torch.tensor(errorso)) avges = torch.mean(torch.tensor(errorss)) los = lambdaO avgeo + lambdas avges # 4. Rendering Distillation Loss (Teacher) lrendertea = (1 - gammassim) mae(Istu, Itea) + gammassim (1 - ssim(Istu, Itea)) # 5. Adapter Loss if len(Avis) == 0: ladapter = torch.tensor(0.0) else: adapterlosses = [] for i in Avis: # Term 1: Offset correction normalized by positional scale # Element-wise multiplication (tensor) offsetcorr = Ohat[i] - Otilde[i] scalenorm = Spostilde[i] + epsilon term1 = torch.norm(offsetcorr scalenorm, p=1) / (3 K) # Term 2: Anchor scaling change normalized scorr = sanchorhat[i] - sanchortilde[i] snorm = sanchortilde[i] + epsilon term2 = torch.norm(scorr snorm, p=1) / 6.0 adapterlosses.append(term1 + term2) ladapter = torch.mean(torch.tensor(adapterlosses)) # Total Loss ltotal = lrendergt + lambdaftrain lf + los + lambdadistill lrendertea + lambdaA ladapter return ltotal A sibling loss function focusing on specific radiance field properties. SRF-Loss A sibling objective utilizing different training strategies. NTS Training Objective Complexity: The loss computation involves standard tensor operations (MAE, SSIM, L1 norms) over anchors and pixels. The complexity is linear with respect to the number of visible anchors |\mathcal{A}{\text{vis}}| and the number of anchors Na for the feature loss. Performance: The method was evaluated on Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks and Temples, and Deep Blending datasets. Hardware: Implemented in PyTorch, running on a single NVIDIA RTX 4080 GPU. Strengths: Explicitly addresses quantization errors in both features and geometric attributes (offsets/scaling), preserving high-frequency details better than generic reconstruction losses. Limitations: Requires access to a pre-trained teacher model for distillation (I^{Tea}) and feature supervision (\mathbf{f}^{Tea}). The multi-stage optimization (initialization, refiner training, adapter optimization, joint fine-tuning) increases training time compared to single-stage objectives. The recovery-stage optimization objective was introduced in the context of compressing 3D Gaussian Splatting representations using Adaptive Residual Quantization and Error Compensation. name: Composite Photometric and Regularization Loss
head: Combined Loss Function, L_recon + λ_TV L_TV + λ_smooth L_smooth, Model Optimization with Loss Functions, Optimization Loss, Optimization Loss Functions, Training Losses, Training Objective and Regularization
body: This method defines the composite objective function used to optimize neural radiance fields and related representations by balancing image fidelity with geometric and structural regularization. It addresses the ill-posed nature of inverse rendering by combining photometric reconstruction errors with auxiliary terms such as total variation, smoothness, and compactness priors. It differs from its sibling Composite Image Loss with Visibility Weighting by explicitly integrating diverse regularization strategies (e.g., opacity concentration, distortion penalties, and scale compactness) rather than focusing primarily on visibility-aware weighting of the photometric term. The method computes a scalar loss \mathcal{L} as a weighted sum of a photometric reconstruction term and one or more regularization terms. The specific components depend on the representation (voxels, Gaussians, or implicit fields) and the scene dynamics. Inputs: Rendered color images (or patches) \hat{C} (or \tilde{I}P), ground-truth images I{gt} (or IP), sampled rays \mathcal{R}, and representation parameters (e.g., voxel opacities \sigma, spherical harmonic coefficients, Gaussian scales si, opacities \alphai). Outputs: Scalar loss value \mathcal{L} and gradients for optimization. The data structures vary by variant: Voxel/Grid: Opacity \sigma and color features (e.g., SH coefficients) stored in a 3D grid. Gaussians: A set of primitives G, each with position, scale si \in \mathbb{R}^3, opacity \alphai, and color. Rays: A batch of rays \mathcal{R} sampled from camera views. The general structure is \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{photo} + \sumk \lambdak \mathcal{L}{reg, k}. The core term minimizes the difference between rendered and ground-truth colors. Variant A: Standard MSE/SSIM \mathcal{L}{photo} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \| \hat{C}(r) - C{gt}(r) \|2^2 Or combined with perceptual loss: L{rgb} = \| \tilde{I}P - IP \|2^2 + \| F{vgg} (\tilde{I}P) - F{vgg} (IP) \|2^2 Where F{vgg} is a VGG feature extractor. Variant B: Saturation-Masked LDR Loss For HDR/LDR pipelines, saturation masks Mi(r) exclude overexposed pixels: \mathcal{L}{recon} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} Mi(r) \| Ii(\Pii(r)) - T(\hat{C}(r)) \|2^2 Where \Pii is the camera projection, T is tone mapping, and Mi(r) = \text{mask}(Ii(\Pii(r))). Variant C: Dual-Grid Photometric Loss \mathcal{L}{photo} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \| C{Inp}(r) - C{gt}(r) \|2^2 + \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \| C{Up}(r) - C{gt}(r) \|2^2 Where C{Inp} is rendered from an inpainted grid and C{Up} from an up-sampled grid. Various regularizers are applied depending on the representation. Total Variation (TV) Loss Encourages spatial smoothness. For voxels: \mathcal{L}{TV} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|} \sum{v \in \mathcal{V}, d \in [D]} \sqrt{\Deltax^2(v,d) + \Deltay^2(v,d) + \Deltaz^2(v,d) + \epsilon} Where \Delta are differences between successive voxels along axes. Applied to opacity \sigma and SH coefficients separately. Smoothness Loss (CRF) For Camera Response Functions (CRF) gi(e): \mathcal{L}{smooth} = \sum{i=1}^N \sum{e \in [0,1]} gi''(e)^2 Where gi''(e) is the second-order derivative. Opacity and Distortion Losses Opacity loss \mathcal{L}0. Distortion loss \mathcal{L}d. Normal consistency loss \mathcal{L}n. Size Regularization Encourages larger triangles in triangle splatting: \mathcal{L}s = 2 \| (v1 - v0) \times (v2 - v0) \|^{-1} Where v0, v1, v2 are vertices of a triangle. Compactness Terms for Gaussians Volume term: \frac{1}{|G|} \sumi \prod{j=1}^3 s{i,j} Opacity term: \frac{1}{|G|} \sumi \alphai Scaling Regularization Prevents Gaussians from becoming long and thin: \mathcal{L}{scaling}(i) = \begin{cases} |\hat{s}i|, & \hat{s}i > \max(Ts, Tr \tilde{s}i) \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Where \hat{s}i is max scaling, \tilde{s}i is min scaling, Ts is length threshold, Tr is thinness ratio. Background Mixing A random background color is generated every iteration to mix with rendered image I and ground truth I{gt} to provide silhouette cues. Point Color Supervision \mathcal{L}{ptc} Directly supervises the color of sampled points, weighted by their contribution to the rendered color (following DVGO [44]). Background Entropy Loss \mathcal{L}{bg} Encourages densities to concentrate on either foreground or background. Flow Regularization \mathcal{L}{flow} = \| V^{flow}t \|1 Encourages most 3D points in canonical space to be static. Inpaint Network Loss \mathcal{L}{vdiff} = \| V^{R{Inp}}t - V^{R{Up}}t \|1 L1 norm of the difference between input and output of the inpaint network. Depth Total Variation \mathcal{L}{tv}(D) Minimizes total variations of rendered depths D. \lambda{TV, SH}: TV weighting for SH coefficients. Typical value: 1 \times 10^{-2}. \lambda{TV, \sigma}: TV weighting for opacity. Typical value: 5 \times 10^{-4}. \lambda{smooth}: Smoothness weighting. Typical value: 1 \times 10^{-3}. \lambdaD: Weight for D-SSIM term. Default: 0.2. \lambdas, \lambdao: Compactness weights for scale volume and opacity. Default: 0.01. \lambdal, \lambdas: Weights for LPIPS and Scaling regularization. w1 \sim w7: Weights balancing components in dynamic scene loss. Ts, Tr: Thresholds for scaling regularization length and thinness. Saturation: In LDR/HDR pipelines, failing to mask saturated pixels leads to incorrect gradients. Degenerate Gaussians: Without compactness or scaling regularization, Gaussians may grow excessively large or thin, causing artifacts. Precision: The square root in TV loss requires a small \epsilon to avoid division by zero or NaN gradients. Background Ambiguity: In monocular settings, background/foreground separation is ill-posed; background mixing or entropy loss helps disambiguate. This method defines the composite objective function used to optimize neural Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) and physically-based rendering (PBR) material parameters from multi-view photometric images. It addresses the ill-posed nature of inverse rendering by combining image fidelity, structural similarity, geometric validity constraints, and material smoothness priors. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly integrating SDF entropy regularization for geometry cleanup and light regularization for shadow disentanglement, often in conjunction with Gaussian Splatting or neural SDF representations. The MPF Training Objective is a composite loss function designed to optimize the parameters of a Metric-Phase Field (MPF) network for multi-view image reconstruction. It combines standard photometric supervision with geometric regularizers that exploit rendering weights as soft indicators for near-surface and free-space regions, addressing the lack of ground-truth 3D geometry in this setting. Unlike the original MPF formulation which relies on explicit point cloud supervision, this method adapts the metric-phase decomposition constraints to be implicit and differentiable through the rendering process. This variant focuses on preventing degenerate Gaussian shapes in monocular or limited-view settings. It introduces a scaling regularization term that penalizes Gaussians that are both long (exceeding threshold Ts) and thin (max scaling > Tr \times min scaling). Additionally, it employs background mixing, where a random background color is generated each iteration and composited with the rendered and ground-truth images to provide silhouette cues for better boundary learning. This variant augments the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting photometric loss with two lightweight compactness terms: a volume term (product of scale axes) and an opacity term (L1 on opacity). The volume term penalizes oversized primitives more sharply than their sum, discouraging large Gaussians, while the opacity term drives redundant Gaussians below the prune threshold, producing a more compact set. It replaces the L1 penalty on scale axes used in 3D-GS-MCMC with this product-based volume term. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of sampled rays |\mathcal{R}| and primitives/voxels. TV and smoothness losses add overhead proportional to the number of voxels/primitives and their neighbors. Memory Complexity: Requires storing gradients for all representation parameters and intermediate values for regularization terms (e.g., neighbors for TV). Performance: Balances photometric accuracy with geometric regularity. Over-regularization can blur details; under-regularization leads to noise or artifacts (e.g., floating geometry, degenerate Gaussians). Strengths: Robust to noise and incomplete data; prevents overfitting to photometric errors; handles dynamic scenes and limited views better than pure photometric loss. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of multiple hyperparameters (\lambda weights); can be computationally more expensive due to additional loss terms. The concept of combining photometric loss with regularization terms is fundamental to differentiable rendering and inverse graphics. Early works like NeRF [21] used L1/L2 photometric loss. Subsequent works introduced regularization to improve geometry and training stability: Total Variation: Used in early volumetric methods to enforce smoothness. Opacity/Distortion Losses: Introduced in 3D Gaussian Splatting variants and triangle splatting to improve rendering quality and geometry. Compactness: Developed to address the unbounded growth of Gaussians in 3DGS. Background Mixing: Proposed for monocular avatar reconstruction to handle silhouette ambiguity. Inverse Rendering Losses: Extended to SDFs and PBR materials, adding geometric and material priors [10241-inverse-rendering-loss-function.md]. This method defines the composite objective function used to optimize neural Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) and physically-based rendering (PBR) material parameters from multi-view photometric images. It addresses the ill-posed nature of inverse rendering by combining image fidelity, structural similarity, geometric validity constraints, and material smoothness priors. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly integrating SDF entropy regularization for geometry cleanup and light regularization for shadow disentanglement, often in conjunction with Gaussian Splatting or neural SDF representations. Inputs: Ground truth multi-view images I{gt} and masks M{gt}. Predicted images \hat{I} and masks \hat{M} from the differentiable renderer. Neural SDF field S(\mathbf{x}) or scalar field \zeta(\mathbf{x}). Material attributes: diffuse albedo  eta, roughness \alpha, metalness \kappa (or similar parameterizations). Lighting components: diffuse lighting Ld, specular lighting Ls. Camera parameters and light positions (often co-located with camera). Outputs: Scalar loss value L for backpropagation. The method operates on standard tensor structures: Images: H 	imes W 	imes 3 (RGB) or H 	imes W 	imes 4 (RGBA). SDF: Scalar field, typically stored in a grid (e.g., VDB, Tetrahedral mesh) or queried via a neural network MLP. Materials: Per-vertex or per-Gaussian attributes. The total loss is a weighted sum of photometric, geometric, and material/lighting terms. Two primary formulations exist in the literature, detailed below. Used in, this formulation focuses on neural SDF validity and roughness constraints. L = L{img} + \lambda1 L{eikonal} + \lambda2 L{roughness} 1. Image Loss (L{img}): Combines multi-scale pixel error and structural similarity. L{img} = L2(	ext{pyramid}(\hat{I}), 	ext{pyramid}(I)) + (1 - 	ext{SSIM}(\hat{I}, I)) 	ext{pyramid}(\cdot) denotes a Gaussian pyramid. L2 is the mean squared error between the predicted and ground truth pyramid levels. 	ext{SSIM} is the Structural Similarity Index. 2. Eikonal Loss (L{eikonal}): Enforces the SDF property that the gradient magnitude is 1. L{eikonal} = \|
ablax S - 1\|2^2 S is the neural SDF value at position \mathbf{x}. 
ablax S is the gradient of the SDF with respect to spatial coordinates. 3. Roughness Range Loss (L{roughness}): Encourages estimated roughness to stay below 0.5. Specific formula not provided in, referred to as Eq. 13. Typically implemented as a clamp or penalty if \alpha > 0.5. Used in, this formulation includes entropy regularization for geometry and light regularization for appearance. L = L{photo} + \lambda{sdf} L{sdf} + \lambda{smooth} L{smooth} + \lambda{light} L{light} 1. Photometric Loss (L{photo}): L{photo} = \|I{gt} - \hat{I}\|1 + \lambda{ssim} 	ext{SSIM}(I{gt}, \hat{I}) + \lambda{mask} \|\hat{M} - M{gt}\|2^2 \lambda{ssim} = 0.2. \lambda{mask} = 5.0. 2. SDF Entropy Regularization (L{sdf}): Penalizes internal geometry and floaters by encouraging consistent signs of the SDF across edges. L{sdf} = \sum{(vi, vj) \in \mathcal{E}, 	ext{sgn}(S(vi)) 
eq 	ext{sgn}(S(vj))} \left[ \mathcal{H}(S(vi), 	ext{sgn}(S(vj))) + \mathcal{H}(S(vj), 	ext{sgn}(S(vi))) ight] \mathcal{E} is the set of edges in the underlying mesh/tetrahedral structure. \mathcal{H}(a, b) is the binary cross-entropy loss. 	ext{sgn}(\cdot) returns the sign of the SDF value. 3. Smoothness Regularization (L{smooth}): Prevents high-frequency variations in material attributes. L{smooth} = \| eta -  eta'\|1 + \|\alpha - \alpha'\|1 + \|\kappa - \kappa'\|1  eta, \alpha, \kappa are albedo, roughness, and metalness at position \mathbf{p}.  eta', \alpha', \kappa' are the same attributes sampled at \mathbf{p} + \Delta \mathbf{p}, where \Delta \mathbf{p} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2) and \sigma = 0.01. 4. Light Regularization (L{light}): Disentangles shadows by assuming demodulated lighting is monochrome. L{light} = \|Y(Ld + Ls) - V(I{gt})\| Y(\mathbf{x}) = (xr + xg + xb)/3 is the luminance operator. V(\mathbf{x}) = \max(xr, xg, xb) is the HSV value component. IRON: \lambda1, \lambda2 are loss weights. Values not explicitly given in the provided text. GeoSplatting: \lambda{ssim} = 0.2 \lambda{mask} = 5.0 \lambda{smooth} = 0.03 \lambda{light} = 0.15 \lambda{sdf}: Starts at 0.2, linearly decreases to 0.01 by the midpoint of training. \sigma = 0.01 for smoothness sampling. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeinverserenderingloss( Igt, Mgt, Ipred, Mpred, sdffield, materialfield, Ld, Ls, config): """ Computes the composite inverse rendering loss. Supports both IRON-style and GeoSplatting-style formulations. """ lambdassim = config.get('lambdassim', 0.2) lambdamask = config.get('lambdamask', 5.0) lambdasmooth = config.get('lambdasmooth', 0.03) lambdalight = config.get('lambdalight', 0.15) lambdasdf = config.get('lambdasdf', 0.2) # Should be decayed by epoch sigma = config.get('sigma', 0.01) # 1. Photometric Loss l1loss = meanabsoluteerror(Igt, Ipred) ssimloss = 1.0 - structuralsimilarity(Igt, Ipred) maskloss = meansquarederror(Mgt, Mpred) Lphoto = l1loss + lambdassim ssimloss + lambdamask maskloss # 2. SDF Entropy Regularization (GeoSplatting style) # Requires access to mesh edges or tetrahedral connectivity Lsdf = 0.0 edges = getedges(sdffield) # e.g., from FlexiCubes or mesh for vi, vj in edges: si = sdffield.query(vi) sj = sdffield.query(vj) # Only compute if signs differ if sign(si) != sign(sj): # Binary cross entropy approximation for SDF values # H(p, q) = - [q log(p) + (1-q) log(1-p)] # Here, target is sign(sj) which is 1 or -1. # Map to [0,1] for BCE: target = (sign + 1) / 2 targetj = (sign(sj) + 1) / 2 targeti = (sign(si) + 1) / 2 # Clamp SDF values to [0,1] for log stability if treating as probability # Or use sigmoid output if SDF is normalized. # Note: Standard SDF is not probability. # implies using H(S(v), sgn(S(v))). # Implementation detail: Often S(v) is passed through sigmoid or # treated as logit. Assuming S(v) is raw SDF, we might need # a sigmoid activation for the BCE input. probi = sigmoid(si) probj = sigmoid(sj) Lsdf += binarycrossentropy(probi, targetj) Lsdf += binarycrossentropy(probj, targeti) # 3. Smoothness Regularization # Sample neighbors with Gaussian noise positions = getmaterialpositions(materialfield) deltas = randomgaussian(positions.shape, sigma) posnoisy = positions + deltas beta, alpha, kappa = materialfield.query(positions) betan, alphan, kappan = materialfield.query(posnoisy) Lsmooth = meanabsoluteerror(beta, betan) + \ meanabsoluteerror(alpha, alphan) + \ meanabsoluteerror(kappa, kappan) # 4. Light Regularization # Y(x) = mean(x), V(x) = max(x) lightingsum = Ld + Ls luminancelight = mean(lightingsum, axis=-1) # (H, W) valuegt = max(Igt, axis=-1) # (H, W) # Reshape for broadcasting if necessary Llight = meanabsoluteerror(luminancelight, valuegt) # 5. Total Loss Ltotal = Lphoto + lambdasdf Lsdf + lambdasmooth Lsmooth + lambdalight Llight return Ltotal SDF Sign Ambiguity: The entropy loss requires consistent sign interpretation. If the SDF is not properly initialized or regularized, signs may flip arbitrarily, leading to unstable gradients. Light Regularization Assumption: The light regularization assumes demodulated lighting is monochrome. This may fail for scenes with strong colored shadows or non-Lambertian lighting effects. Smoothness Noise: The smoothness term relies on random perturbations. If \sigma is too large, it may oversmooth fine details; if too small, it may not regularize high-frequency noise effectively. Mask Loss: The mask loss weight \lambda{mask}=5.0 is high, indicating that accurate alpha blending is critical for the photometric term. Photometric Loss: O(N) where N is the number of pixels. SSIM adds overhead due to local window computations. SDF Entropy: O(E) where E is the number of edges in the geometric representation. Smoothness: O(V) where V is the number of material points (Gaussians or vertices). Requires two additional field queries per point. Light Regularization: O(N) for luminance/value computation. Specific performance metrics (FPS, convergence time) are not provided in the sources. The method is designed for offline optimization or slow training stages, as it involves multiple differentiable passes (SDF gradient, material sampling, light computation). Strengths: Combines multiple constraints to stabilize the ill-posed inverse rendering problem. Entropy regularization effectively removes floaters and internal geometry. Light regularization helps disentangle shadows from albedo. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of loss weights (\lambda values). The SDF entropy term requires access to geometric connectivity (edges), which may not be available in all neural SDF implementations (e.g., pure grid-based without mesh extraction). The roughness range loss formula is not explicitly defined in, potentially leading to implementation ambiguity. Use when optimizing neural SDFs or Gaussian Splatting attributes for physically-based inverse rendering. Use when floaters or internal geometry artifacts are prevalent. Use when shadow disentanglement is required. Use MPF Training Objective if the focus is purely on multi-view photometric consistency without explicit SDF/material regularization. Use simpler L2/SSIM losses if computational resources are extremely limited and geometry/material priors are not needed. IRON: Introduced in "IRON: Inverse Rendering by Optimizing Neural SDFs and Materials from Photometric Images" (CVPR 2022). It combines neural SDFs with PBR materials and uses Eikonal and roughness losses. GeoSplatting: Introduced in "GeoSplatting: Towards Geometry Guided Gaussian Splatting for Physically-Based Inverse Rendering" (ICCV 2025). It extends Gaussian Splatting with geometry guidance and introduces entropy, smoothness, and light regularization. Inverse rendering has evolved from mesh-based methods to neural representations (NeRF, SDFs) and now to Gaussian Splatting. The composite loss function reflects the trend of combining multiple regularization terms to handle the ambiguities of inverse rendering, such as the separation of albedo, shading, and geometry. head: OMeGa Loss
body: The Total Training Objective is a composite loss function used to optimize neural radiance fields and explicit mesh representations by combining photometric reconstruction with geometric regularization. It solves the problem of producing high-fidelity, geometrically consistent 3D structures from sparse or noisy input views by penalizing deviations in surface smoothness, normal consistency, and monocular geometry priors. It is distinguished from its parent, the MPF Training Objective, by its specific inclusion of Laplacian smooth, normal consistency, and monocular normal losses rather than near-surface or free-space regularizers. The method minimizes a weighted sum of four distinct loss terms. The inputs are the rendered images, the predicted mesh geometry (normals and positions), and monocular depth/normal estimates. The output is the scalar loss value used for gradient-based optimization of network parameters. The total loss L is defined as: L = L{img} + \lambda{lap} L{lap} + \lambda{nc} L{nc} + \lambdan Ln Where: L{img} is the photometric loss measuring pixel-wise color difference between rendered and target views. L{lap} is the Laplacian smooth loss, encouraging surface smoothness. L{nc} is the normal consistency loss, ensuring normals are consistent across different views. Ln is the monocular normal loss, aligning predicted normals with estimates from monocular foundational models. \lambda{lap}, \lambda{nc}, \lambdan are scalar hyperparameters controlling the weight of each geometric regularizer. Monocular Normal Loss (Ln) Details: The monocular normal loss uses a margin-based hinge formulation to handle inconsistencies inherent in monocular predictions. It is calculated as: Ln = \sum \max(\| \mathbf{N} - \hat{\mathbf{N}} \| - m, 0) Where: \mathbf{N} is the predicted surface normal. \hat{\mathbf{N}} is the monocular estimated normal. m is a small margin hyperparameter that tolerates minor inconsistencies between views. Implementation Steps: 1. Render images and surface normals from the current network state. 2. Compute photometric loss L{img} against ground truth target views. 3. Compute Laplacian smooth loss L{lap} on the mesh geometry. 4. Compute normal consistency loss L{nc} by comparing normals of corresponding points across multiple views. 5. Compute monocular normal loss Ln by comparing predicted normals \mathbf{N} with monocular estimates \hat{\mathbf{N}} using the margin m. 6. Combine losses using weights \lambda{lap}, \lambda{nc}, \lambdan to form L. 7. Backpropagate L to update network parameters. Parameters: \lambda{lap}, \lambda{nc}, \lambdan: Weights for geometric regularizers. Specific values are not given in the sources. m: Margin for monocular normal loss. Described as "small" but no exact value is provided. Edge Cases: Monocular normal inconsistency: The margin m in Ln is specifically designed to handle inherent normal inconsistencies across different views produced by monocular foundational models. A variant of the total training objective used in MAC-Splat, combining photometric reconstruction with Multi-Attribute Consistency (MAC) loss to train Gaussian prediction heads and residual fusion modules. The formula is L{total} = L{photo} + \lambda{MAC} L{MAC}. L{photo} is a weighted sum of an \ell2 reconstruction term and an LPIPS term applied to rendered target views. The MASt3R correspondence loss weight is set to zero in reported results. This variant is chosen when using Gaussian Splatting with multi-attribute consistency constraints rather than explicit mesh regularization. The method requires computing multiple geometric regularizers (Laplacian, normal consistency, monocular) in addition to standard photometric loss, increasing computational overhead per iteration compared to photometric-only training. The sources do not provide specific time or memory complexity metrics, hardware performance data, or resolution scaling characteristics. The Total Training Objective, also known as the OMeGa Loss, originates from the OMeGa framework for joint optimization of explicit meshes and Gaussian splats for robust scene-level surface reconstruction. It was developed to address suboptimal mesh density and geometric artifacts in sparse-view reconstructions by introducing specific geometric regularizers. name: Composite RGB and Entropy Loss
head: L_rgb + L_entropy
body: This method defines the total training loss for differentiable volume rendering (specifically Gaussian Splatting) by combining a composite photometric fidelity term with an entropy regularization term. It solves the problem of ensuring high-fidelity image reconstruction while preventing the learned scene representation from becoming overly transparent or sparse, which can lead to artifacts and poor generalization. It sets itself apart from pure photometric losses by explicitly penalizing uncertainty in the foreground alpha accumulation, and from simple L1/SSIM losses by weighting the SSIM component and adding the entropy constraint. The method computes a scalar loss \mathcal{L} as a weighted sum of the RGB composite loss and the entropy loss. Inputs: Rendered image \hat{C} (or Ir). Ground-truth image C (or I{gt}). Foreground accumulated alpha value per pixel \mathbf{O}{\text{fg}}. Outputs: Scalar loss value \mathcal{L}. Data Structures: \mathbf{O}{\text{fg}}: A 2D tensor (H x W) containing the accumulated alpha values for the foreground component of the volume rendering equation for each pixel. Formulas: 1. RGB Composite Loss: \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{rgb}} = (1 - \lambdar) \mathcal{L}1 + \lambdar \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{ssim}} Where: \mathcal{L}1 is the L1 loss between \hat{C} and C. \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{ssim}} is the SSIM loss between \hat{C} and C. \lambdar is the weight for the SSIM component. 2. Entropy Loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{entropy}} = -\sum \left( \mathbf{O}{\text{fg}} \log \mathbf{O}{\text{fg}} + (1 - \mathbf{O}{\text{fg}}) \log (1 - \mathbf{O}{\text{fg}}) \right) Where the sum is over all pixels. This term is the binary cross-entropy (or negative entropy) of the foreground alpha, encouraging \mathbf{O}{\text{fg}} to be close to 0 or 1 (opaque/clear) rather than intermediate values. 3. Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambdar) \mathcal{L}1 + \lambdar \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{ssim}} + \lambdae \mathcal{L}{\text{entropy}} Where \lambdae is the weight for the entropy loss. Parameters: \lambdar: Weight for SSIM in RGB loss. Typical value: 0.2. \lambdae: Weight for entropy loss. Typical value: 0.1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compositergbandentropyloss(renderedimage, groundtruth, foregroundalpha, lambdar=0.2, lambdae=0.1): """ Computes the composite RGB and Entropy loss. Args: renderedimage (Tensor): Rendered color image [H, W, 3]. groundtruth (Tensor): Ground truth color image [H, W, 3]. foregroundalpha (Tensor): Accumulated foreground alpha [H, W]. lambdar (float): Weight for SSIM component. lambdae (float): Weight for entropy component. Returns: Tensor: Scalar loss value. """ # 1. Compute L1 Loss # Note: Standard L1 loss is mean absolute error l1loss = torch.mean(torch.abs(renderedimage - groundtruth)) # 2. Compute SSIM Loss # Note: SSIM is typically computed on luminance or per channel, # then averaged. We assume a standard SSIM implementation that returns # a value between 0 and 1, where 1 is identical. # Loss is usually 1 - SSIM. ssimvalue = computessim(renderedimage, groundtruth) ssimloss = 1.0 - ssimvalue # 3. Compute RGB Composite Loss rgbloss = (1.0 - lambdar) l1loss + lambdar ssimloss # 4. Compute Entropy Loss # Clamp alpha to avoid log(0) eps = 1e-7 alphaclamped = torch.clamp(foregroundalpha, min=eps, max=1.0 - eps) # Binary cross-entropy term: -(plog(p) + (1-p)log(1-p)) # Sum over all pixels entropyterm = -(alphaclamped torch.log(alphaclamped) + (1.0 - alphaclamped) torch.log(1.0 - alphaclamped)) entropyloss = torch.sum(entropyterm) # 5. Total Loss totalloss = rgbloss + lambdae entropyloss return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Logarithm Domain: The entropy loss involves \log(\mathbf{O}{\text{fg}}) and \log(1-\mathbf{O}{\text{fg}}). If \mathbf{O}{\text{fg}} is exactly 0 or 1, the log is undefined. Implementation must clamp \mathbf{O}{\text{fg}} to [\epsilon, 1-\epsilon]. Gradient Scale: The entropy loss sums over all pixels. In high-resolution images, this sum can become large, potentially dominating the L1/SSIM terms if \lambdae is not scaled appropriately relative to image size. Foreground vs Background: The entropy term specifically targets foreground alpha. If the rendering pipeline does not explicitly separate foreground and background components (e.g., using a hemisphere background model as in), this term may need adjustment or may not be applicable. A variant used in 3D Gaussian Splatting compression contexts that balances reconstruction fidelity with bit consumption. It incorporates a binary mask m to weight the bit cost of color attributes based on whether they are processed through a Masked Entropy Module (MEM) or directly quantized. The loss is defined as: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{fidelity}}(I, \hat{I}) + \lambdag \sum{i=1}^{Ng} \frac{1}{N \times 56} \left( \text{bit}i^{\text{geo}} + mi \text{bit}i^{\text{col}}|{mi=1} + (1 - mi) \text{bit}i^{\text{col}}|{mi=0} \right) Where: Ng is the amount of Gaussians. 56 is the dimension of the Gaussian attribute parameters f{\text{gau}}. \text{bit}i^{\text{geo}} and \text{bit}i^{\text{col}} are the bit consumptions for geometry and color attributes of Gaussian i. mi is a binary mask for Gaussian i's color attributes (mi=1 if processed via MEM, 0 if directly quantized). \lambdag controls the trade-off between fidelity and entropy. \mathcal{L}{\text{fidelity}} includes both MSE and SSIM metrics. This variant allows gradients to backpropagate through both encoding paths by using the mask m to compute a weighted sum of bit outputs. Time Complexity: The computation is dominated by the SSIM calculation (typically O(H \cdot W \cdot K^2) where K is the kernel size) and the element-wise operations for L1 and Entropy (O(H \cdot W)). The entropy term is very cheap. Memory Complexity: O(H \cdot W) to store the foreground alpha tensor and intermediate loss tensors. Strengths: Encourages crisp, opaque foregrounds which improves visual quality and reduces "floaters" or transparent artifacts common in early-stage Gaussian Splatting training. The combination of L1 and SSIM provides robust photometric supervision. Limitations: The entropy loss is specific to representations that produce a distinct foreground alpha component. It may not be directly applicable to standard NeRF volume rendering without modification. The choice of \lambdae is critical; too high may force opacity at the cost of detail, too low may fail to regularize transparency. When to use: When training 3D Gaussian Splatting or similar differentiable volume representations where foreground/background separation is explicit and transparency artifacts are a concern. The composite RGB loss (L1 + SSIM) is a standard practice in differentiable rendering and image synthesis. The addition of entropy regularization on foreground alpha was introduced in the context of efficient volume-based Gaussian Splatting for urban view synthesis (EVolSplat). The masked entropy variant for compression was introduced in the context of fast feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting compression. name: Numerical Gradient Eikonal Loss
head: Numerical Gradient Computation, Numerical gradients for higher-order derivatives
body:
Numerical Gradient Eikonal Loss is a regularization technique used in differentiable volume rendering with hash-encoded Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) to enforce the eikonal equation \|
abla f(\mathbf{x})\|2 = 1. It addresses the locality problem inherent in analytical gradients of hash encodings, where non-differentiable rounding operations restrict back-propagation updates to only the local hash grid cells involved in trilinear interpolation. By computing surface normals via numerical finite differences, the method distributes optimization updates beyond the immediate local grid cell, acting as a smoothed gradient that ensures non-local smoothness and consistent surface reconstruction without requiring auxiliary networks. Inputs: \mathbf{x}i: A 3D point in canonical space, \mathbf{x}i = (xi, yi, zi). f(\cdot): The neural network function predicting the SDF value, which internally uses a hash encoding \gamma. \epsilon: The step size for numerical differentiation. N: The total number of sampled points in the batch. Outputs: \mathcal{L}{	ext{eik}}: The scalar eikonal loss value. Gradients  rac{\partial \mathcal{L}{	ext{eik}}}{\partial 	ext{hash\params}}: Back-propagated gradients that update the hash grid entries. The method operates on the standard hash encoding structure used in neural surface reconstruction. Hash Grid: A collection of learnable feature vectors indexed by spatial coordinates. SDF Prediction: The output of the network f(\mathbf{x}), computed via trilinear interpolation of features from the hash grid at location \mathbf{x}. 1. Initialize Step Size: Set the numerical gradient step size \epsilon. In practice, \epsilon is initialized to the coarsest hash grid size and is exponentially decreased to match different hash grid sizes throughout optimization. 2. Sample Perturbed Points: For each input point \mathbf{x}i, compute six additional points by perturbing \mathbf{x}i along the positive and negative directions of the x, y, and z axes by \epsilon. \mathbf{x}{i, x+} = \mathbf{x}i + [\epsilon, 0, 0] \mathbf{x}{i, x-} = \mathbf{x}i - [\epsilon, 0, 0] \mathbf{x}{i, y+} = \mathbf{x}i + [0, \epsilon, 0] \mathbf{x}{i, y-} = \mathbf{x}i - [0, \epsilon, 0] \mathbf{x}{i, z+} = \mathbf{x}i + [0, 0, \epsilon] \mathbf{x}{i, z-} = \mathbf{x}i - [0, 0, \epsilon] 3. Evaluate SDF: Compute the SDF values for the original point and all six perturbed points using the hash encoding and network f. v0 = f(\mathbf{x}i) v{x+} = f(\mathbf{x}{i, x+}), v{x-} = f(\mathbf{x}{i, x-}) v{y+} = f(\mathbf{x}{i, y+}), v{y-} = f(\mathbf{x}{i, y-}) v{z+} = f(\mathbf{x}{i, z+}), v{z-} = f(\mathbf{x}{i, z-}) 4. Compute Numerical Gradient: Calculate the components of the gradient 
abla f(\mathbf{x}i) using central finite differences: 
ablax f(\mathbf{x}i) =  rac{v{x+} - v{x-}}{2\epsilon} 
ablay f(\mathbf{x}i) =  rac{v{y+} - v{y-}}{2\epsilon} 
ablaz f(\mathbf{x}i) =  rac{v{z+} - v{z-}}{2\epsilon} Let \mathbf{g}i = [
ablax f(\mathbf{x}i), 
ablay f(\mathbf{x}i), 
ablaz f(\mathbf{x}i)]^T. 5. Compute Eikonal Loss: Calculate the loss for the batch based on the deviation of the gradient norm from 1: \mathcal{L}{	ext{eik}} =  rac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N (\|\mathbf{g}i\|2 - 1)^2 where \|\mathbf{g}i\|2 = \sqrt{
ablax f(\mathbf{x}i)^2 + 
ablay f(\mathbf{x}i)^2 + 
ablaz f(\mathbf{x}i)^2}. 6. Back-Propagation: Perform a double backward pass (second-order derivative) on \mathcal{L}{	ext{eik}} with respect to the hash encoding parameters. This propagates gradients to the hash entries accessed by \mathbf{x}i and its six neighbors, effectively smoothing the update across the local neighborhood. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def numericalgradienteikonalloss(f, xbatch, epsilon): """ Computes the Eikonal loss using numerical gradients for a batch of points. Args: f: Neural network function (SDF predictor with hash encoding). xbatch: Array of shape (N, 3) containing sampled 3D points. epsilon: Float, step size for numerical differentiation. Returns: loss: Scalar, the computed eikonal loss. """ N = xbatch.shape[0] # Define perturbation vectors epsx = [epsilon, 0.0, 0.0] epsy = [0.0, epsilon, 0.0] epsz = [0.0, 0.0, epsilon] # Sample perturbed points (standard array broadcasting) xplusx = xbatch + epsx xminusx = xbatch - epsx xplusy = xbatch + epsy xminusy = xbatch - epsy xplusz = xbatch + epsz xminusz = xbatch - epsz # Evaluate SDF for all points forig = f(xbatch) fplusx = f(xplusx) fminusx = f(xminusx) fplusy = f(xplusy) fminusy = f(xminusy) fplusz = f(xplusz) fminusz = f(xminusz) # Compute numerical gradient components gradx = (fplusx - fminusx) / (2.0 epsilon) grady = (fplusy - fminusy) / (2.0 epsilon) gradz = (fplusz - fminusz) / (2.0 epsilon) # Compute gradient norm (element-wise square root) gradnorm = sqrt(gradx2 + grady2 + gradz2) # Compute Eikonal loss: mean squared error of (norm - 1) loss = sum((gradnorm - 1.0)2) / N return loss \epsilon (Step Size): Controls the resolution and amount of recovered details. It determines the spatial extent over which the gradient is evaluated; a larger \epsilon enforces consistency at a coarser scale, while a smaller \epsilon affects a smaller region to preserve details. Typical Value/Strategy: Initialized to the size of the coarsest hash grid cell. It is exponentially decreased throughout the optimization process to match the activation of finer hash grid resolutions. Locality of Analytical Gradients: Analytical gradients of hash encoding with trilinear interpolation are discontinuous across space because the rounding operations \lfloor \cdot floor and \lceil \cdot ceil used to find voxel grid corners are non-differentiable. This limits back-propagation to only the locally sampled hash entries, preventing non-local smoothness. Numerical gradients distribute back-propagation updates beyond the local hash grid cell, acting as a smoothed version of analytical gradients. Detail Loss with Large \epsilon: If \epsilon is too large relative to the current hash grid resolution, geometric details may be smoothed out or lost. Convergence Issues: If all hash grids are activated from the start, fine grids may need to "unlearn" coarse optimization patterns. If optimization converges prematurely with a large \epsilon, details may be lost. Progressive activation of hash grids is recommended alongside the decreasing \epsilon schedule. Computational Cost: Requires six additional SDF evaluations per point. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Solves the locality problem of hash encoding gradients, ensuring updates propagate to non-local hash cells. Acts as a smoothed version of analytical gradients, improving surface continuity. Does not require additional networks or teacher-student curriculum approaches. Limitations: Requires six additional SDF evaluations per point. Requires careful scheduling of \epsilon to balance smoothness and detail preservation. When to Use: Use when optimizing hash-encoded SDFs where surface normal consistency and non-local smoothness are critical, and analytical gradients result in noisy or discontinuous surfaces due to hash grid locality. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Neuralangelo: High-Fidelity Neural Surface Reconstruction". Context: It was developed to address specific limitations of hash encoding in neural surface reconstruction, particularly the discontinuity of analytical gradients caused by trilinear interpolation and non-differentiable rounding operations. Development: Prior approaches, such as teacher-student curriculum methods, attempted to smooth normals but still suffered from the locality issue of analytical gradients in hash encodings. Numerical gradients provided a simpler, network-free solution to distribute back-propagation updates. Usage: It is a key component in high-fidelity neural surface reconstruction pipelines that use hash-based neural fields, such as Neuralangelo. Neuralangelo: High-Fidelity Neural Surface Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00817, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Opacity Loss
head: Binary Cross Entropy Opacity Loss, Object Mask Constraint
body: The Opacity Loss is a regularization term used in differentiable volume rendering to enforce geometric consistency when a binary object mask is available. It forces the rendered opacity of rays passing through the object region to align with the mask distribution, typically resulting in an opaque surface. It operates directly on the alpha compositing output rather than pixel color, distinguishing it from photometric losses. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: M: Binary object mask tensor of shape (H, W), where H and W are image dimensions. Values are 0 or 1. O: Rendered opacity tensor of shape (H, W), computed via alpha compositing. w: Scalar weight for the loss term. Outputs: \mathcal{L}O: Scalar loss value. Data Structures Mask (M): A binary array/tensor. Values must be strictly 0 (background) or 1 (object). Opacity (O): The accumulated opacity along the ray, defined as O = \sum{i \in N} Ti \alphai, where N is the set of samples along the ray, Ti is the transmittance up to sample i, and \alphai is the opacity of sample i. Formulas The primary formulation uses Binary Cross Entropy (BCE): \mathcal{L}{O} = -M\log {O} - (1-M)\log {(1-O)} where M is the object mask and O is the rendered opacity. An alternative formulation, used in specific implementations, uses a mean absolute error on transmittance T within the mask region: L = w \cdot \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} mi \cdot |Ti - 1| where L is the loss, w is the weight, N is the number of samples along the ray, mi \in \{0, 1\} is the binary mask value, and Ti is the throughput (transmittance) value. Parameters masks: Binary mask array/tensor indicating regions where objects should be opaque. Values should be 0 or 1. weight: Float scalar multiplying the loss term. Default/typical value: 1.0. Pseudocode The following implementation uses the BCE formulation, which is the standard definition in the literature. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def opacityloss(renderedopacity, objectmask, weight=1.0): eps = 1e-7 # Clip opacity to avoid log(0) singularities clippedopacity = [max(eps, min(1.0 - eps, o)) for o in renderedopacity] mask = objectmask # Compute BCE per pixel: -Mlog(O) - (1-M)log(1-O) bceperpixel = [-m math.log(o) - (1 - m) math.log(1 - o) for m, o in zip(mask, clippedopacity)] # Average over all pixels loss = sum(bceperpixel) / len(renderedopacity) return weight loss Edge Cases and Pitfalls Logarithm of Zero: If rendered opacity O is exactly 0 or 1, \log(O) or \log(1-O) becomes undefined. Clipping O to [\epsilon, 1-\epsilon] is required. Mask Precision: The mask M must be strictly binary (0 or 1). Gradient Flow: The loss encourages opacity to be 1 where M=1 and 0 where M=0. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Effectively enforces hard surface boundaries when ground-truth masks are available, preventing "floaters" or translucent artifacts in object regions. Limitations: Requires a binary object mask, which may not be available for all scenes or objects. It does not enforce geometric correctness directly, only opacity consistency. When to use: When training differentiable volume rendering (e.g., NeRF, 3D Gaussians) with access to segmentation masks or object boundaries. When not to use: When no mask is available, or when the object is transparent/translucent and should not be forced to be opaque. The Opacity Loss, also known as the Object Mask Constraint, was introduced in the context of Relightable 3D Gaussians. It leverages Binary Cross Entropy loss [43] to constrain the optimization of Gaussian points to align with an object mask, thereby improving geometric reconstruction by driving points to the object surface. It is used as part of the total loss function in differentiable rendering pipelines. Relightable 3D Gaussians: Realistic Point Cloud Relighting with BRDF Decomposition and Ray Tracing, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72995-95, fetched 2026-10-26 JackZhouSz/tlir, https://github.com/JackZhouSz/tlir, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Sparse Depth Consistency Loss
head: Overall Loss Function, Sparse Depth Loss
body: The Sparse Depth Consistency Loss enforces geometric consistency between rendered depth maps and sparse, structure-from-motion (SfM) derived depth estimates in radiance field optimization. It distinguishes itself from photometric losses by directly penalizing depth discrepancies, thereby mitigating floaters and depth discontinuities common in sparse-input scenarios. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: zm (depth map from the main radiance field model), za (depth map from the augmented radiance field model), and \hat{z} (sparse depth map from the SfM model). Output: Scalar loss value L{sd}. Data Structures Depth maps are per-pixel values aligned with the image resolution. Not given in the sources. Steps 1. Render depth maps zm and za from the main and augmented radiance field models at the current camera pose. 2. Retrieve sparse depth values \hat{z} from the SfM model for corresponding pixel locations. 3. Compute the L2 norm difference between each rendered depth map and the sparse depth map. 4. Sum the two differences to obtain L{sd}. Formula L{sd} = ||zm - \hat{z}||2 + ||za - \hat{z}||2 Where: ||\cdot||2 denotes the L2 norm applied to the flattened vector of valid pixel differences. zm is the depth from the main model. za is the depth from the augmented model. \hat{z} is the sparse depth from SfM. Parameters The loss is weighted by a hyperparameter \lambda{sd} in the total loss function: L = \lambdam Lm + \lambdaa La + \lambda{sd} L{sd} + \lambda{aug} L{aug} + \lambda{cfc} L{cfc} + \lambda{mc} L{mc}. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Sparse Coverage: Since \hat{z} is sparse, the loss is only computed where SfM provides valid depth estimates. Precision: Standard floating-point arithmetic is used for the L2 norm computation. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sparsedepthconsistencyloss(zm, za, zsparse): # zm, za, zsparse: 2D arrays of shape (H, W) # zsparse contains valid depth values where SfM provides estimates, and 0 elsewhere validmask = zsparse > 0 if not validmask.any(): return 0.0 diffm = zm[validmask] - zsparse[validmask] diffa = za[validmask] - zsparse[validmask] normm = (sum(d2 for d in diffm) 0.5) norma = (sum(d2 for d in diffa) 0.5) return normm + norma EndoGaussian Optimization is a training procedure for dynamic endoscopic scene reconstruction using 3D Gaussians, designed to handle non-rigid tissue deformation and tool occlusion in real-time. It distinguishes itself from standard Gaussian Splatting by incorporating binocular and monocular depth constraints alongside spatiotemporal Total Variation (TV) regularization, specifically tailored for endoscopic video sequences where absolute depth consistency is challenging but structural coherence is critical. Unlike static splatting methods, it employs a warmup phase for canonical Gaussians followed by joint optimization of the full deformable framework. Choose it when optimizing endoscopic video sequences with non-rigid deformation and tool occlusion. Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of valid pixels in the sparse depth map. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the sparse depth map and the rendered depth maps, proportional to image resolution. Strengths: Provides strong geometric regularization in sparse input settings, reducing floaters and improving depth accuracy. Limitations: Relies on the quality and coverage of the SfM sparse depth. When to use: Sparse input radiance field optimization where geometric consistency is critical and photometric loss alone is insufficient. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The Sparse Depth Consistency Loss was introduced in "Simple-RF: Regularizing Sparse Input Radiance Fields with Simpler Solutions". It addresses the challenge of optimizing radiance fields from very few input views by leveraging sparse geometric priors from Structure-from-Motion (SfM). The method combines this loss with photometric and regularization losses to stabilize training. Simple-RF: Regularizing Sparse Input Radiance Fields with Simpler Solutions, https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.19015v5, fetched 2026-10-27 Improved Neural Radiance Fields Using Pseudo-depth and Fusion, https://core.ac.uk/download/577699041.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: EndoGaussian Optimization
body: EndoGaussian Optimization is a training procedure for dynamic endoscopic scene reconstruction using 3D Gaussians, designed to handle non-rigid tissue deformation and tool occlusion in real-time. It distinguishes itself from standard Gaussian Splatting by incorporating binocular and monocular depth constraints alongside spatiotemporal Total Variation (TV) regularization, specifically tailored for endoscopic video sequences where absolute depth consistency is challenging but structural coherence is critical. The method employs a warmup phase for canonical Gaussians followed by joint optimization of the full deformable framework. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A sequence of endoscopic images (RGB and depth, if available), binary tool masks \mathbf{M}, and camera poses. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian parameters (position, rotation, scale, opacity) that minimize the total loss \mathcal{L}. Data Structures The method operates on a set of 3D Gaussians. Each Gaussian i is defined by position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion), scale \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, opacity \alphai \in [0, 1], and spherical harmonic coefficients for color \mathbf{c}i. The source explicitly notes that deformation of SH coefficients is not modeled, as position, rotation, scaling, and opacity are sufficient to capture tissue movement and shape variations. Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: Randomly sample 0.1% of the initial point cloud points to reduce redundancy and computational load. 2. Warmup: Optimize the Canonical Gaussians (static representation) for 1,000 iterations. 3. Main Optimization: Optimize the entire framework (including deformation fields and all Gaussian parameters) for 3,000 iterations using the Adam optimizer. Formulas The total loss \mathcal{L} is a weighted sum of rendering constraints and spatiotemporal smoothness constraints: \mathcal{L} = (\lambda1 \mathcal{L}{color} + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{depth}^{-1} / \mathcal{L}{depth}^{-1}) + (\lambda3 \mathcal{L}{spatial} + \lambda4 \mathcal{L}{temporal}) Where \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3, \lambda4 are balancing weights. The notation \mathcal{L}{depth}^{-1} / \mathcal{L}{depth}^{-1} in the source denotes the combined binocular and monocular depth loss terms. Rendering Constraints: Color Loss: Minimizes the difference between predicted and real colors, masked by tool occlusion: \mathcal{L}{color} = \sum{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{I}} \|\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{x})(\hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x}))\|1 Binocular Depth Loss: Uses reciprocal depth for stability, masked by tool occlusion: \mathcal{L}{depth}^B = \sum{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{I}} \|\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{x})(\hat{\mathbf{D}}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbf{D}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}))\|1 Monocular Depth Loss: Uses correlation to align structure despite absolute depth inconsistencies, masked by tool occlusion: \mathcal{L}{depth}^M = 1 - \frac{Cov(\mathbf{M} \odot \hat{\mathbf{D}}, \mathbf{M} \odot \mathbf{D})}{\sqrt{Var(\mathbf{M} \odot \hat{\mathbf{D}})Var(\mathbf{M} \odot \mathbf{D})}} Depth Term in Total Loss: The source notation \mathcal{L}{depth}^{-1} / \mathcal{L}{depth}^{-1} appears to be a typographical error in the source text for a combined depth loss term (likely \mathcal{L}{depth}^B + \mathcal{L}{depth}^M or similar). Given the context of "binocular/monocular input image sequence," the implementation should combine the binocular and monocular depth losses. Regularization Constraints: Spatial TV Loss: Enforces smoothness in predicted color and reciprocal depth to avoid black/white holes in tool-occluded regions: \mathcal{L}{spatial} = TV(\hat{\mathbf{C}}) + TV(\hat{\mathbf{D}}^{-1}) Temporal TV Loss: Constrains encoding voxels over time to ensure temporal smoothness. Parameters Optimizer: Adam. Initial Learning Rate: 1.6 \times 10^{-3}. Warmup Iterations: 1,000. Main Optimization Iterations: 3,000. Balancing Weights (\lambdai): Not given in the sources. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def endogaussianoptimization(initialpoints, images, masks, poses, binoculardepths, monoculardepths, numwarmup=1000, nummain=3000, lr=1.6e-3, lam1=1.0, lam2=1.0, lam3=1.0, lam4=1.0): # Step 1: Initialization # Randomly sample 0.1% of points to reduce redundancy samplecount = max(1, int(len(initialpoints) 0.001)) sampledpoints = random.sample(initialpoints, samplecount) gaussians = initializegaussians(sampledpoints) # Sources do not provide the Gaussian rasterization or initialization routines; # these follow standard 3D Gaussian Splatting implementations. optimizer = AdamOptimizer(gaussians.parameters(), lr=lr) prevrendereddepthinv = None # Step 2: Warmup # Optimize Canonical Gaussians for 1k iterations for in range(numwarmup): optimizer.zerograd() renderedcolor, rendereddepthinv = rendercanonical(gaussians, poses) loss = computecolorloss(renderedcolor, images, masks) loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Step 3: Main Optimization # Optimize the whole framework for 3k iterations for in range(nummain): optimizer.zerograd() totalloss = 0.0 for img, mask, pose, bdepth, mdepth in zip(images, masks, poses, binoculardepths, monoculardepths): # Render current frame with deformation renderedcolor, rendereddepth, rendereddepthinv = renderdeformable(gaussians, pose) # Rendering Constraints # Color Loss lcolor = suml1norm(mask (renderedcolor - img)) # Binocular Depth Loss (using reciprocal depth) ldepthb = suml1norm(mask (rendereddepthinv - bdepth)) # Monocular Depth Loss (using correlation) maskedpred = mask rendereddepth maskedreal = mask mdepth cov = covariance(maskedpred, maskedreal) varpred = variance(maskedpred) varreal = variance(maskedreal) ldepthm = 1.0 - cov / math.sqrt(varpred varreal) # Combine depth losses (correcting source notation typo) ldepth = ldepthb + ldepthm # Regularization Constraints # Spatial TV Loss lspatial = totalvariation(renderedcolor) + totalvariation(rendereddepthinv) # Temporal TV Loss if prevrendereddepthinv is not None: ltemporal = totalvariationtemporal(rendereddepthinv, prevrendereddepthinv) else: ltemporal = 0.0 # Total Loss for this frame frameloss = (lam1 lcolor + lam2 ldepth + lam3 lspatial + lam4 ltemporal) totalloss += frameloss totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() prevrendereddepthinv = rendereddepthinv return gaussians class AdamOptimizer: def init(self, params, lr, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, eps=1e-8): self.params = params self.lr = lr self.beta1 = beta1 self.beta2 = beta2 self.eps = eps self.state = {} def zerograd(self): for p in self.params: if p.grad is not None: p.grad.detach() p.grad.zero() def step(self): for p in self.params: if p.grad is None: continue g = p.grad if p not in self.state: self.state[p] = {'m': [0.0]len(p), 'v': [0.0]len(p), 't': 0} state = self.state[p] state['t'] += 1 for i in range(len(p)): state['m'][i] = self.beta1 state['m'][i] + (1 - self.beta1) g[i] state['v'][i] = self.beta2 state['v'][i] + (1 - self.beta2) g[i]2 mhat = state['m'][i] / (1 - self.beta1state['t']) vhat = state['v'][i] / (1 - self.beta2state['t']) p[i] -= self.lr mhat / (math.sqrt(vhat) + self.eps) def initializegaussians(points): pass def rendercanonical(gaussians, poses): pass def renderdeformable(gaussians, pose): pass def computecolorloss(rendered, targets, masks): return suml1norm(masks (rendered - targets)) def suml1norm(tensor): return sum(abs(x) for x in tensor) def covariance(a, b): meana = sum(a) / len(a) meanb = sum(b) / len(b) return sum((a[i] - meana) (b[i] - meanb) for i in range(len(a))) / len(a) def variance(tensor): mean = sum(tensor) / len(tensor) return sum((x - mean) 2 for x in tensor) / len(tensor) def totalvariation(tensor): return sum(abs(tensor[i+1] - tensor[i]) for i in range(len(tensor)-1)) def totalvariationtemporal(curr, prev): return sum(abs(curr[i] - prev[i]) for i in range(len(curr))) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Tool Occlusion: The binary tool mask \mathbf{M} is critical. Failure to correctly mask tool regions leads to artifacts in color and depth, as the model tries to fit non-existent tissue behind the tool. Depth Scale Ambiguity: Monocular depth loss uses correlation, which is invariant to scale and shift. This is necessary because absolute depth from monocular cues is inconsistent. However, this means the method cannot recover absolute metric depth from monocular data alone. Reciprocal Depth Stability: Binocular depth loss uses reciprocal depth (\mathbf{D}^{-1}) for stability. Implementers must ensure numerical stability when computing reciprocals for near-zero depth values. Deformation Modeling: The method does not model deformation of SH coefficients, assuming position, rotation, scale, and opacity are sufficient for tissue movement. This simplification may limit high-frequency appearance changes. Time Complexity: The method is optimized for real-time performance. Training takes approximately 4,000 iterations (1k warmup + 3k main). Memory Complexity: Uses a single RTX 4090 GPU for training. Performance: Achieves real-time inference speeds (FPS) comparable to or better than previous SOTA methods like EndoNeRF and EndoSurf, which require hours for optimization. Strengths: Handles non-rigid deformation and tool occlusion effectively. Real-time capability. Limitations: Relies on accurate tool masks. Monocular depth is relative. EndoGaussian Optimization was introduced in the paper "EndoGaussian: Real-time Gaussian Splatting for Dynamic Endoscopic Scene Reconstruction". The method was evaluated on the ENDONERF and SCARED datasets, which contain in-vivo prostatectomy data and porcine cadaver abdominal anatomies, respectively.
