name: DMF Training Losses
head: DMF Losses, DMF Regularization Terms
body:
The DMF training losses constitute the regularization and supervision terms used to optimize the neural implicit representation of Medial Fields, specifically the Signed Distance Function (SDF) \Phi and the medial field. While the parent Total Loss Function for Neural Scene Reconstruction combines seven components for general scene reconstruction, the DMF losses focus on stabilizing the implicit surface representation, enforcing Eikonal constraints, and preventing interference from Fourier feature embeddings. They are distinct from standard NeRF losses by their heavy reliance on surface-augmented volume sampling and specific regularizers for medial field consistency. The method optimizes a neural network predicting \Phi(x) and associated heads by minimizing a weighted sum of six loss terms. The optimization uses the Adam optimizer. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ground-truth surface mesh \partial O (providing triangle normals), a bounding box defining the volume \mathbb{R}^d, and a neural network parameterized by weights 	heta. Output: Optimized network weights 	heta that minimize the total loss. Data Structures and Sampling: Two distinct sampling strategies are required because some losses depend on surface points (x \sim \partial O) and others on volume points (x \sim \mathbb{R}^d). 1. Surface Samples: Points are drawn uniformly from the input mesh \partial O. The ground-truth normal 
abla\Phi{GT}(x) is obtained directly from the triangle normals of the mesh at the projected sample location. 2. Volume Samples: To generate points in the volume \mathbb{R}^d, surface samples are augmented with an isotropic Gaussian offset. The standard deviation \sigma is set to half the bounding box diagonal. Loss Formulas: The total loss is a weighted summation. The individual components are: 1. Surface Reconstruction Loss (L{surface}): Encourages the SDF to be zero at the ground-truth surface. L{surface} = \mathbb{E}{x \sim \partial O} [\Phi(x)^2] 2. Normal Reconstruction Loss (L{normal}): Aligns the predicted gradient with the mesh normals. L{normal} = \mathbb{E}{x \sim \partial O} [(
abla\Phi(x) - 
abla\Phi{GT}(x))^2] 3. Eikonal Loss (L{Eikonal}): Enforces the Eikonal equation ||

abla\Phi(x)|| - 1)^2] 4. Min-Surface Regularizer (L{minsurface}): Prevents Fourier features from interfering with implicit SDF training by penalizing non-zero SDF values in the volume. L{minsurface} = \mathbb{E}{x \sim \mathbb{R}^d} [e^{-100 |\Phi(x)|}] 5. Curvature Regularizer (L{curvature}): A regularizer for curvature, scheduled during training. Sample volume points by augmenting surface points with Gaussian noise # Assuming 'sampleuniformfrommesh' returns points in R^d. # Noise is drawn from N(0, sigma^2 I). noise = torch.randnlike(surfacepoints) sigma volumepoints = surfacepoints + noise # 3. Forward pass to get SDF and gradients # network.forward(x) returns phi(x). # network.getgradienthead(x) returns the predicted gradient head. # torch.autograd.grad is used for analytic gradient. phisurface = network.forward(surfacepoints) gradsurface = torch.autograd.grad( phisurface, surfacepoints, gradoutputs=torch.oneslike(phisurface), creategraph=True, retaingraph=True)[0] phivolume = network.forward(volumepoints) gradvolume = torch.autograd.grad( phivolume, volumepoints, gradoutputs=torch.oneslike(phivolume), creategraph=True, retaingraph=True)[0] # 4. Combine losses # Weights are empirically determined (Table 2 in source), but exact values # are not provided in the text snippets. We assume equal weighting or standard # practice if weights are missing. totalloss = (losssurface + lossnormal + losseikonal + lossminsurface + losscurvature + lossgradient) # 6. name: Joint Training Losses
head: Composite Loss with Pose, Skin, and INN Constraints
body: This method defines a composite objective function for the joint optimization of a Template-Free NeRF (TFS-NeRF), an Implicit Neural Network (INN) for spatial transformation, and a skinning weight prediction network. It solves the ambiguity in dynamic scene reconstruction where incorrect combinations of canonical points and skinning weights can satisfy forward Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) equations. It distinguishes itself by explicitly constraining the INN and skinning networks through pose, cycle consistency, and skinning weight losses, rather than relying solely on photometric reconstruction. The method optimizes three coupled components simultaneously: the NeRF for appearance, the INN for mapping between view and canonical spaces, and a skinning weight network for deformation. Inputs: Input video frames with known camera poses. Canonical skeleton joints J{p0} and deformed skeleton joints Jp. Point clouds initialized around the canonical skeleton of individual entities. Outputs: Rendered RGB images \hat{C}(r). Transformed points in canonical and deformed spaces. Predicted skinning weights \hat{w}. Data Structures: R: Set of rays. P: Total number of points sampled around bones from each skeleton. H: INN transformation function from view to canonical space. H^{-1}: Inverse transformation from canonical to view space (or vice versa depending on conditioning, see formula). G{xc \to w}: Skinning weight prediction network. G{v \to c}: Transformation from view to canonical space used in Pose Loss (distinct from INN H in notation, but conceptually similar mapping). Loss Components: 1. Reconstruction Loss (L{rgb}): Minimizes the difference between rendered RGB \hat{C}(r) and input pixel RGB C(r) along ray r. L{rgb} = \sum{r \in R} ||\hat{C}(r) - C(r)|| 2. Pose Loss (L{pose}): Ensures the INN correctly transforms points X{Jp} sampled around deformed bones to X{J{p0}} around canonical bones. L{pose} = \sum{p \in P} ||X{J{p0}} - G{v \to c}(X{Jp})|| Note: The source formula uses a norm over the set P. The specific norm type (L1/L2) is not explicitly defined in the snippet, but L2 is standard for such geometric terms. 3. Skinning Weight Loss (LW): Constrains the predicted skinning weight \hat{w} for canonical joints to be a one-hot vector (1 for the respective joint, 0 for others). LW = ||G{xc \to w}(J{p0}) - \hat{w}||2^2 4. Cycle Consistency Loss (L{INN}): Ensures the INN transformation is invertible and consistent. L{INN} = ||H(H^{-1}(xv, J{p0}), Jp) - xv||2^2 Where H transforms view to canonical, and H^{-1} transforms canonical to view (or vice versa as defined by the specific INN architecture). 5. Consistency Loss (L{Consis}): Minimizes the L2 distance between the INN-transformed point x'c and the skinning-weight-conditioned canonical point xc. L{Consis} = ||x'c - xc||2^2 6. Shape Loss (L{shape}): Accelerates learning by constraining transformed points xc to fall within a point cloud initialization around the canonical skeleton, with NeRF densities \alpha=1. Formula not explicitly provided in the source text snippet, but described as following Guo et al. [39]. Total Loss: The total loss is the weighted sum of these components: L{tot} = \lambda{rgb} L{rgb} + \lambda{pose} L{pose} + \lambda{W} LW + \lambda{INN} L{INN} + \lambda{Consis} L{Consis} + \lambda{shape} L{shape} Note: Specific weights \lambda are not provided in the source notes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computejointlosses(renderedrgb, inputrgb, deformedpoints, canonicalpoints, canonicaljoints, predictedweights, inntransform, skinningnet, pointcloudinit, nerfdensities): # 1. Reconstruction Loss # Sum of L2 norms over all rays R lrgb = sum(norm(renderedrgb[r] - inputrgb[r]) for r in rays) # 2. Pose Loss # Transform deformed points to canonical space using view-to-canonical mapping transformeddeformed = inntransformviewtocanonical(deformedpoints) lpose = sum(norm(canonicalpoints[p] - transformeddeformed[p]) for p in pointsaroundbones) # 3. Skinning Weight Loss # Predict weights for canonical joints and compare to one-hot encoding predictedw = skinningnet(canonicaljoints) targetw = getonehotvector(canonicaljoints) lw = norm(predictedw - targetw)2 # 4. Cycle Consistency Loss # Transform view point to canonical, then back to view xv = getviewpoint() xc = inntransformviewtocanonical(xv) xvrecon = inntransformcanonicaltoview(xc) linn = norm(xvrecon - xv)2 # 5. Consistency Loss # Compare INN-transformed point with skinning-weight-conditioned point xprimec = inntransformedpoint xcskinning = skinningweightconditionedcanonicalpoint lcons = norm(xprimec - xcskinning)2 # 6. Shape Loss # Constraint based on point cloud initialization and NeRF density # Specific formula depends on Guo et al. [39], assumed to be a distance/penalty term lshape = computeshapeloss(xcskinning, pointcloudinit, nerfdensities) return lrgb, lpose, lw, linn, lcons, lshape Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method enables template-free reconstruction of dynamic scenes. Strengths: Constrains ambiguous solutions in LBS by supervising skeleton space. Limitations: Relies on accurate point sampling around bones. Originated in TFS-NeRF (Template-Free NeRF for Semantic 3D Reconstruction of Dynamic Scene). The shape loss component follows Guo et al. [39]. TFS-NeRF: Template-Free NeRF for Semantic 3D Reconstruction of Dynamic Scene, https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.17459v4, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Joint Training Strategy
head: Joint Loss with Dynamic Weighting
body: This method enables the simultaneous optimization of a pose estimation network (IPO-Net) and a generalized 3D Gaussian rendering network (G-3DG) by combining photometric, depth, and RGB reconstruction losses into a single objective function. It distinguishes itself from static multi-task learning approaches by employing a dynamic weight coefficient that exponentially shifts the optimization focus from pose-related constraints (depth and photometric consistency) to appearance reconstruction (RGB MSE) as training progresses. The method minimizes a joint loss \mathcal{L}{\text{joint}} that balances the training of two coupled models: a pose estimator and a Gaussian splatter renderer. The core mechanism is a time-dependent weighting scheme that adjusts the relative importance of pose-supervision losses versus appearance-supervision losses based on the current training step. Inputs: Reference view images \mathbf{I}r for r \in \mathcal{N}t. Target view ground truth image \mathbf{C} (and optionally \mathbf{I}t for photometric warping). Current training step t. Hyperparameters: \beta (weight decay rate), \alpha (SSIM vs. L1 balance). Outputs: Scalar loss value \mathcal{L}{\text{joint}} for backpropagation. Gradients for both the pose network and the Gaussian network parameters. \mathcal{N}t: Set of reference view indices. \mathbf{I}t^{\prime}: Warped image from reference view r to target view t. \mathbf{D}: Predicted depth map for the target view. \mathbf{I}: Image intensity map (used for edge-aware weighting). \hat{\mathbf{C}}: Rendered target image from the Gaussian network. \mathbf{C}: Ground truth target image. \mathbf{u}: Pixel coordinates. \beta: Dynamic weighting coefficient exponent base. Typical values are not explicitly given in the source, but the formula implies \beta > 0 to ensure 2^{\beta \cdot t} grows with t. \alpha: Balance factor between SSIM and L1 in photometric loss. Typical values are not explicitly given in the source. The total joint loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}{\text{joint}} = 2^{\beta \cdot t} \left( \mathcal{L}{\text{depth}} + \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} \right) + \left( 1 - 2^{\beta \cdot t} \right) \mathcal{L}{\text{rgb}} Where: 1. Photometric Loss \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} measures consistency between warped reference views and the target view: \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}t|} \sum{r \in \mathcal{N}t} \left( \alpha \frac{1 - \operatorname{SSIM}(\mathbf{I}t^{\prime}, \mathbf{I}t)}{2} + (1 - \alpha) \|\mathbf{I}t^{\prime} - \mathbf{I}t\|1 \right) Note: The source text writes \operatorname{ssim}(\mathbf{I}t^{\prime}-\mathbf{I}t), but standard SSIM is a similarity metric between two images, not their difference. The term \frac{1-\operatorname{SSIM}}{2} is a standard loss formulation. The L1 term \|\cdot\| is assumed to be the L1 norm (mean absolute error) based on context with SSIM. 2. Edge-Aware Smoothness Loss \mathcal{L}{\text{depth}} regularizes the predicted depth map \mathbf{D} using image gradients: \mathcal{L}{\text{depth}} = |\partialx \mathbf{D}| \exp^{-|\partialx \mathbf{I}|} + |\partialy \mathbf{D}| \exp^{-|\partialy \mathbf{I}|} Here, \partialx and \partialy denote the horizontal and vertical image gradients, respectively. 3. RGB Loss \mathcal{L}{\text{rgb}} is the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the rendered image and ground truth: \mathcal{L}{\text{rgb}} = \sum{\mathbf{u} \in \mathbf{u}} \|\hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{u}) - \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{u})\|2^2 The following Python-like pseudocode implements the loss calculation and dynamic weighting logic. It assumes helper functions for SSIM, image gradients, and warping are available. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computejointloss( referenceviews: List[Image], targetviewgt: Image, targetviewimg: Image, predicteddepth: DepthMap, renderedimage: Image, trainingstep: int, beta: float, alpha: float) -> float: """ Computes the joint loss for simultaneous pose and Gaussian network training. Args: referenceviews: List of reference view images Ir. targetviewgt: Ground truth target image C. targetviewimg: Target view image It for warping. predicteddepth: Predicted depth map D. renderedimage: Rendered target image Chat from Gaussian network. trainingstep: Current training step t. beta: Exponential weight coefficient. alpha: Balance factor for photometric loss (SSIM vs L1). Returns: Total joint loss scalar. """ # 1. Compute Dynamic Weights # Weight for pose-related losses (depth + photo) weightpose = 2 (beta trainingstep) # Weight for appearance loss (RGB) # Note: The formula uses (1 - 2^(betat)). If 2^(betat) > 1, this term becomes negative. # In practice, this term is often clamped or the formula implies a transition where # the first term dominates early and the second dominates late, or vice versa depending on beta sign. # Based on the source formula exactly: weightrgb = 1 - weightpose # 2. Compute Photometric Loss Lphoto lphotosum = 0.0 nrefs = len(referenceviews) for rimg in referenceviews: # Warp reference view r to target view t warpedimg = warpimage(rimg, predicteddepth) # SSIM component ssimval = computessim(warpedimg, targetviewimg) ssimloss = (1 - ssimval) / 2 # L1 component l1loss = computel1norm(warpedimg, targetviewimg) # Combined per-reference loss lphotosum += alpha ssimloss + (1 - alpha) l1loss lphoto = lphotosum / nrefs # 3. Compute Depth Smoothness Loss Ldepth # Compute image gradients for the target image I gradxI = computegradient(targetviewimg, axis='x') gradyI = computegradient(targetviewimg, axis='y') # Compute depth gradients gradxD = computegradient(predicteddepth, axis='x') gradyD = computegradient(predicteddepth, axis='y') # Edge-aware weighting: exp(-|gradI|) weightx = exp(-abs(gradxI)) weighty = exp(-abs(gradyI)) ldepth = sum(abs(gradxD) weightx) + sum(abs(gradyD) weighty) # 4. Compute RGB Loss Lrgb # MSE between rendered and ground truth diff = renderedimage - targetviewgt lrgb = sum(diff 2) # Sum over all pixels u # 5. Combine into Joint Loss ljoint = weightpose (ldepth + lphoto) + weightrgb lrgb return ljoint Weight Sign: The term (1 - 2^{\beta \cdot t}) can become negative if 2^{\beta \cdot t} > 1. If \beta > 0, this happens for t > 0. This suggests either \beta is negative, or the formula implies a specific regime where the weights are managed differently (e.g., clamping or normalization not detailed in the source). Implementers should verify the sign of \beta and the behavior of the weights at t=0 (where 2^0=1, making the RGB weight 0). Warping Artifacts: Photometric loss relies on accurate warping \mathbf{I}t^{\prime}. Occlusions and depth discontinuities can lead to invalid correspondences, potentially destabilizing the gradient. Memory Constraints: Training at full resolution for both pose and Gaussian networks may exceed GPU memory. The source mentions "deferred back-propagation" as a technique to handle this, but the loss formula itself does not change. Complexity: The computational cost is dominated by the Gaussian splatting rendering step and the warping operations for photometric loss. The loss calculation itself is linear in the number of pixels and reference views. Memory: Full-resolution training requires significant GPU memory. The source notes that deferred back-propagation is used to mitigate this, allowing high-resolution training under memory constraints. Strengths: Allows end-to-end optimization of pose and geometry/appearance without separate pre-training phases. The dynamic weighting helps balance the conflicting gradients between pose estimation (which benefits from smooth depth/photometric consistency) and appearance (which benefits from pixel-perfect RGB reconstruction). Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \beta and \alpha. The dynamic weighting scheme may be sensitive to the learning rate schedule. The method was introduced in the context of "GGRt: Towards Pose-Free Generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting in Real-Time" by H. Li et al.. It addresses the challenge of simultaneously learning a pose estimation network (IPO-Net) and a generalized 3D Gaussian network (G-3DG) without relying on ground-truth poses, leveraging rendered images for supervision. GGRt: Towards Pose-Free Generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting in Real-Time, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-73209-619, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Joint Optimization with Loss Functions
head: Joint Optimization of Surfel Parameters and HDR Environment Map
body: Joint optimization with loss functions simultaneously updates scene geometry, material properties, and illumination parameters by minimizing a composite objective function. It solves the ill-posed inverse rendering problem by regularizing the solution space through geometric and photometric constraints, distinguishing itself from single-parameter optimization by enforcing consistency across depth layers, surface normals, and image appearance. Builds on Regularization losses. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ground-truth images \mathbf{I}^, optional ground-truth masks \mathbf{M}^, camera poses, and initial surfel parameters (positions \mathbf{c}, normals \mathbf{n}, scales, albedo, metallic, roughness) and an HDR environment map. Outputs: Optimized surfel parameters and HDR environment map. Data Structures: Surfel Parameters: Positions \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3, tangent vectors parameterized as unit quaternions \mathbf{q}, log-space scales (\log sx, \log sy), albedo \rho, metallic m, roughness r. HDR Environment Map: Equirectangular map of resolution 16 \times 32 storing radiance values L. Spatial Data Structure: A KNN (K-Nearest Neighbors) index built on surfel positions, rebuilt periodically and cached between optimization updates. Composite Loss Function: The total loss \mathcal{L} is a weighted sum of four terms: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} + \lambda{\text{sil}} \mathcal{L}{\text{sil}} + \lambda{\text{cons}} \mathcal{L}{\text{cons}} + \lambda{\text{nc}} \mathcal{L}{\text{nc}} where \lambda{\text{sil}}, \lambda{\text{cons}}, \lambda{\text{nc}} are scalar weights. 1. Photometric Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{photo}}): Combines \ell1 reconstruction and Structural Similarity (SSIM). For HDR targets, both rendered image \hat{\mathbf{I}} and ground-truth \mathbf{I}^ are transformed via log-space and sRGB transfer before loss computation to prevent gradient domination by bright pixels. \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} = (1 - \lambda{\text{ssim}}) \|\hat{\mathbf{I}} - \mathbf{I}^\|1 + \lambda{\text{ssim}} (1 - \text{SSIM}(\hat{\mathbf{I}}, \mathbf{I}^)) where \lambda{\text{ssim}} is the weighting factor. 2. Silhouette Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{sil}}): Supervises total accumulated coverage using soft Intersection-over-Union (IoU). Provides a strong signal during early training and is disabled once adaptive density control begins. \mathcal{L}{\text{sil}} = \text{IoU}(1 - \bar{T}{K+1}, \mathbf{M}^) where \bar{T}{K+1} is the residual transmittance and \mathbf{M}^ is the ground-truth mask. 3. Depth Consolidation Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{cons}}): Penalizes spurious depth layers by enforcing geometric thinness. It is the average over all pixels \mathcal{P} of inter-layer and intra-layer terms: \mathcal{L}{\text{cons}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|} \sum{p \in \mathcal{P}} (\mathcal{L}{\text{inter-c}} + \mathcal{L}{\text{intra-c}}) Inter-layer term (\mathcal{L}{\text{inter-c}}): Penalizes weight allocation across distant layers. \mathcal{L}{\text{inter-c}} = \sum{i < j} wi wj |zi - zj| where wi, wj are compositing weights and zi, zj are mean depths of layers i, j. Intra-layer term (\mathcal{L}{\text{intra-c}}): Penalizes depth spread within layers. \mathcal{L}{\text{intra-c}} = \sumi wi^2 \sigmai^2 where \sigmai^2 is the depth variance of layer i. 4. Normal Consistency Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{nc}}): Penalizes angular deviation between a surfel's normal and its orientation-aware nearest neighbors in 3D space: \mathcal{L}{\text{nc}} = \frac{\sumi \sum{j \in \mathcal{N}i} w{ij} (1 - \mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{n}j)}{\sumi \sum{j \in \mathcal{N}i} w{ij}} where \mathcal{N}i are nearest neighbors with compatible normal orientation, \mathbf{n}i, \mathbf{n}j are normals, and w{ij} = \exp(-\|\mathbf{c}i - \mathbf{c}j\|^2 / 2\sigma^2) are distance-dependent weights derived from local intersample spacing. Optimization Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize surfel parameters (positions, quaternions, log-scales, albedo, metallic, roughness) and HDR environment map (16 \times 32 equirectangular). 2. Gradient Computation: Compute gradients of \mathcal{L} with respect to all parameters using the Adam optimizer. 3. Parameter Update: Update parameters using the computed gradients. 4. Spatial Structure Update: Periodically rebuild and cache the KNN spatial data structure for normal consistency calculation. 5. Schedule Management: Disable \mathcal{L}{\text{sil}} once adaptive density control begins. Activate \mathcal{L}{\text{cons}} and \mathcal{L}{\text{nc}} according to the training schedule. Parameters: \lambda{\text{ssim}}: SSIM weighting factor. Not given in the sources. \lambda{\text{sil}}, \lambda{\text{cons}}, \lambda{\text{nc}}: Scalar weights for respective losses. Not given in the sources. \sigma: Parameter for distance-dependent weights in \mathcal{L}{\text{nc}}, derived from local intersample spacing. Environment Map Resolution: 16 \times 32 equirectangular. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Domination: In HDR training, bright pixels can dominate gradients. Mitigated by applying log-space and sRGB transfer to both rendered and ground-truth images before loss computation. Spurious Depth Layers: Without regularization, multi-layer compositing may distribute surfels across incorrect depths. Mitigated by \mathcal{L}{\text{cons}}. Oversmoothing: Screen-space normal regularizers may oversmooth geometry. Mitigated by using 3D normal consistency on surfel primitives instead. Illumination Absorption: Long second-stage optimization may cause albedo to absorb illumination information, degrading relighting quality. Mitigated by limiting optimization duration. Models distant lighting as a high-dynamic-range spherical environment map in equirectangular coordinates. It sets itself apart by optimizing radiance values directly with solid-angle compensation for non-uniform texel area, preserving high-frequency angular detail for sharp cast shadows. It is chosen when accurate relighting is required. Uses normal-based hemisphere sampling to halve the number of rays per pixel compared to full-sphere sampling. After hemisphere culling and empty-space removal, there are 512 candidate directions. Map Resolution is 16 \times 32 equirectangular, limiting recoverable illumination bandwidth to the object's BRDF lobes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: A full second-stage optimization iteration takes approximately 1.25 s/it. Final PBR relighting renders at about 0.83 s/image. Forward relighting spends about 55% of its time on visibility queries and 44% on BRDF/environment-map integration. OptiX visibility pass takes approximately 436 ms at evaluation resolution, corresponding to about 127 MRays/s. Strengths: Enforces geometric thinness and normal consistency; handles HDR lighting; stable gradient-based optimization of illumination. Limitations: Compact environment map limits recoverable illumination bandwidth; long optimization may degrade relighting quality. When to use: Object-level inverse rendering requiring geometry reconstruction, novel view synthesis, and novel scene relighting. When not to use: When high-bandwidth illumination recovery is critical and the object's BRDF lobes are insufficient to constrain the environment map. Originated in the context of 3D Surface Splatting for Inverse Rendering (3DSS) and VisibilitySplat. 3DSS jointly optimizes surfel parameters and HDR environment maps using composite losses. VisibilitySplat uses ray-traced occlusion for relighting with 3D Gaussian Splatting, optimizing an HDR environment map. 3DSS: 3D Surface Splatting for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.05876, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) VisibilitySplat: Ray-Traced Occlusion for Relighting with 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.24132/csrn.2026-e17, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Light-SMAE
head: Smooth Manifold Auto-Encoder
body: Light-SMAE is a smooth manifold auto-encoder that learns a low-dimensional, differentiable latent representation of high-dynamic-range (HDR) environment maps, serving as a strong regularizer or prior for reflectance decomposition and inverse rendering. It sets itself apart from direct optimization of lighting parameters by constraining the solution space to a smooth manifold learned from data, which enables stable gradient-based optimization of illumination in ill-posed inverse problems. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An HDR environment map p, downscaled to 128 \times 256 resolution. Output: A 128-dimensional latent embedding zl \in \mathbb{R}^{128} (via Encoder) or a reconstructed HDR environment map \hat{p}0 (via Decoder). Data Structures: The architecture consists of an Encoder E, a Decoder G, and a Discriminator D, all based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) utilizing CoordConv layers. CoordConv Layer: A 2D convolution where the input tensor is augmented with coordinate channels (x, y) before convolution. Conv Layer: Standard 2D convolution. ConvT Layer: Transposed 2D convolution (upsampling). Network Architecture (Light-SMAE): The specific layer configurations are defined in the source. Encoder E: 1. CoordConv: Kernel 3 \times 3, Stride 1, 8 features, Activation ELU. 2. ConvT: Kernel 1 \times 1, Stride 1, 64 features, Activation ELU. 3. CoordConv: Kernel 3 \times 3, Stride 1, 8 features, Activation ReLU. Padding: No padding. Decoder G: 1. CoordConv: Kernel 3 \times 3, Stride 1, 8 features, Activation ELU. 2. CoordConv: Kernel 4 \times 4, Stride 2, 21 features, Activation ELU. 3. ConvT: Kernel 4 \times 4, Stride 2, 58 features, Activation ELU. 4. Final Output Layer: Conv 1 \times 1, Stride 1, 3 features (RGB), Activation \exp(x - 1). Padding: Uses 'same' padding. Discriminator D: 1. CoordConv: Kernel 3 \times 3, Stride 1, 8 features, Activation ELU. 2. Conv: Kernel 4 \times 4, Stride 2, 21 features, Activation ELU. Padding: No padding. Training Procedure: The network is trained jointly to minimize a composite loss function. 1. Data Preprocessing: Rotate each of the 320 environment maps 10 times. Randomly blend two environment maps during training. Downscale inputs to 128 \times 256. Transform HDR input x to LDR for encoder: x{ldr} = \log(1 + x). 2. Forward Pass (Encoding): Pass x{ldr} through Encoder E to get latent vector z. 3. Forward Pass (Decoding & Reconstruction): Pass z through Decoder G to get reconstruction \hat{p}{ldr}. Transform LDR output to HDR: \hat{p}{hdr} = \exp(\hat{p}{ldr} - 1). 4. Latent Interpolation: Randomly sample two latent vectors from the mini-batch: za and zb. Sample m linearly interpolated embeddings uniformly spaced between za and zb: zn^0 = (1 - \alphan) za + \alphan zb for n = 1, \dots, m. Parameter: m = 5 interpolation steps between each of the batch halves. 5. Forward Pass (Interpolated Reconstruction and Re-encoding): Pass each zn^0 through Decoder G to obtain \hat{p}n^0. Pass each \hat{p}n^0 (transformed to LDR) through Encoder E to obtain re-estimated latents \hat{z}n^0. 6. Loss Calculation: The total loss L is a weighted sum of four components: L = Lr + \lambda1 La + \lambda2 Lc + \lambda3 Ls Reconstruction Loss (Lr): Calculated using the Mean Absolute Log Error (MALE) between the ground truth HDR x^ and the predicted HDR \hat{x}: Lr = |\log(1 + x^) - \log(1 + \hat{x})| Adversarial Loss (La): Standard adversarial loss from LSGAN applied to the discriminator D evaluating the interpolated reconstructions \hat{p}n^0. Cyclic Loss (Lc): L2-loss between the interpolated latents \{zn^0\} and their re-estimated counterparts \{\hat{z}n^0\}: Lc = \sum{n=1}^m \| zn^0 - \hat{z}n^0 \|^2 Smoothness Loss (Ls): Imposed on the gradient of the decoder G with respect to the interpolating scalar value \alpha: Ls = \frac{1}{m} \sum{n=1}^m \left( \nabla\alpha G(zn^0) \right)^2 7. Optimization: Update parameters of E, G, and D using the Adam optimizer. Parameters: Latent Dimension: zl \in \mathbb{R}^{128}. Loss Weights: \lambda1 = 0.01 (Adversarial), \lambda2 = 0.0001 (Cyclic), \lambda3 = 0.05 (Smoothness). Optimizer: Adam, learning rate 5 \times 10^{-4}. Batch Size: 24. Training Steps: 4 million steps. Hardware: Single NVIDIA 1080 TI GPU. Training Time: Approximately 5 days. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hdrtoldr(x): return log(1 + x) def ldrtohdr(x): return exp(x - 1) def computesmoothnessloss(decoder, za, zb, m): loss = 0.0 for i in range(1, m + 1): alpha = i / (m + 1) zinterp = za + alpha (zb - za) zinterp.requiresgrad = True recon = decoder(zinterp) grad = gradient(recon.sum(), zinterp) dzdalpha = zb - za gradalpha = sum(grad dzdalpha) loss += gradalpha 2 return loss / m def computecyclicloss(encoder, decoder, za, zb, m): loss = 0.0 for i in range(1, m + 1): alpha = i / (m + 1) zinterp = za + alpha (zb - za) ldrrecon = decoder(zinterp) hdrrecon = ldrtohdr(ldrrecon) ldrreconenc = hdrtoldr(hdrrecon) zreest = encoder(ldrreconenc) loss += norm(zinterp - zreest) 2 return loss / m def computeadversarialloss(discriminator, hdrreconinterp): # Standard LSGAN loss for interpolated reconstructions pred = discriminator(hdrreconinterp) return mean((pred - 1.0) 2) def trainstep(encoder, decoder, discriminator, batch, lambdaa, lambdac, lambdas, m): ldrinput = hdrtoldr(batch) z = encoder(ldrinput) ldrrecon = decoder(z) hdrrecon = ldrtohdr(ldrrecon) lossr = mean(abs(hdrtoldr(batch) - hdrtoldr(hdrrecon))) za, zb = z[0], z[1] lossc = computecyclicloss(encoder, decoder, za, zb, m) losss = computesmoothnessloss(decoder, za, zb, m) # Compute interpolated reconstructions for adversarial loss alpha = 0.5 zinterp = za + alpha (zb - za) ldrreconinterp = decoder(zinterp) hdrreconinterp = ldrtohdr(ldrreconinterp) lossa = computeadversarialloss(discriminator, hdrreconinterp) loss = lossr + lambdaa lossa + lambdac lossc + lambdas losss return loss Time Complexity: Training requires 4 million steps. On a single NVIDIA 1080 TI GPU, this takes approximately 5 days. Memory Complexity: The latent space is 128-dimensional, which is significantly smaller than the 128 \times 256 \times 3 input resolution, reducing memory requirements for storing lighting parameters during optimization. Strengths: Provides a strong prior for ill-posed inverse problems (reflectance decomposition). The smoothness of the manifold enables stable gradient-based optimization. Handles HDR data effectively via specific HDR/LDR transformations and MALE loss. Limitations: Requires pre-training on a dataset of high-quality environment maps (320 maps augmented). The problem of jointly estimating 3D shape, materials, and lighting is highly underconstrained; the SMAE acts as a necessary regularizer but does not solve the ill-posedness alone. When to use: When optimizing illumination parameters in inverse rendering or reflectance decomposition tasks where direct optimization is unstable or prone to implausible solutions. When not to use: When no prior distribution of lighting is available or when real-time inference of lighting from a single image without pre-trained priors is required. Light-SMAE was introduced in the paper "Neural-PIL: Neural Pre-Integrated Lighting for Reflectance Decomposition". It is based on the concept of Interpolating Auto-Encoders [5] and is designed to learn low-dimensional smooth manifolds for BRDFs and illuminations. The method was developed to address the ill-posedness of jointly estimating 3D shape, materials, and lighting. The Light-SMAE specifically targets environment maps, mapping them to a 128-dimensional latent space, while a companion BRDF-SMAE maps Cook-Torrance BRDF parameters to a 4D latent space. The networks are pre-trained on datasets of real-world BRDFs [10] and environment maps [61], with the Light-SMAE trained on 320 environment maps augmented by rotations and blending. Neural-PIL: Neural Pre-Integrated Lighting for Reflectance Decomposition, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2110.14373, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Forplane Optimization Losses
head: Forplane Losses
body: Forplane Optimization Losses are a set of regularization terms designed to stabilize the training of neural radiance fields that utilize orthogonal neural planes (Forplanes) for spatiotemporal volume representation. They solve the problem of entanglement between static and dynamic scene components in dynamic volume rendering, where the model may incorrectly assign dynamic motion to static geometry or vice versa. Unlike standard Total Variation regularization which smooths spatial features, Forplane losses specifically target the structural integrity of the orthogonal plane representations by enforcing spatial smoothness, temporal consistency, and static-field isolation. The method operates on a representation where the 4D volume (3D space + time) is decomposed into a set of 2D orthogonal planes. The optimization minimizes a composite loss function comprising a photometric term, a depth term, and three specific regularization terms derived from the plane structures. Inputs: \boldsymbol{\theta}: Parameters of the density MLP. \boldsymbol{\phi}: Parameters of the color MLP. \mathbf{V}{sd}^s: Set of static space planes (G{XY}, G{YZ}, G{XZ}). \mathbf{V}{3d}^d: Set of dynamic space-time planes (G{XT}, G{YT}, G{ZT}). \mathbf{V}{sd}^v: Set of space-time planes associated with the dynamic field initialization. \hat{\boldsymbol{C}}(\mathbf{r}): Rendered color for ray \mathbf{r}. \boldsymbol{C}i^{\text{gt}}(\mathbf{r}): Ground truth color for ray \mathbf{r} in image Ii. Outputs: \mathcal{L}{total}: The scalar loss value to be minimized. The Forplane representation consists of 2D grids (planes). Static Space Planes (\mathbf{V}{sd}^s): 2D arrays representing spatial slices (XY, YZ, XZ). Dynamic Space-Time Planes (\mathbf{V}{3d}^d): 2D arrays representing slices combining one spatial dimension and time (XT, YT, ZT). Values: Each element g in a plane G is a scalar feature value. The total loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}{total}(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\phi}) = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambdad \mathcal{L}D + \lambda{tv} \mathcal{L}{TV} + \lambda{ts} \mathcal{L}{TS} + \lambda{de} \mathcal{L}{DE} Where: 1. Photometric Loss (\mathcal{L}{rgb}): \mathcal{L}{rgb}(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\phi}) = \sumi \mathbb{E}{\mathbf{r} \sim Ii} \left[ \left\| \hat{\boldsymbol{C}}(\mathbf{r}) - \boldsymbol{C}i^{\text{gt}}(\mathbf{r}) \right\|2^2 \right] where \boldsymbol{C}i^{\text{gt}}(\mathbf{r}) is the ground truth color. 2. Spatial Total Variation Loss (\mathcal{L}{TV}): \mathcal{L}{TV} = \sum{G \in \mathbf{V}{sd}^s} \sum{g \in G} \|\Deltah^2(G, g) + \Deltaw^2(G, g)\| where \mathbf{V}{sd}^s = \{G{XY}, G{YZ}, G{XZ}\} are the static space planes. \Deltah^2(G, g) is the squared difference between the g-th value in plane G:=(i,j) and G:=(i+1,j) normalized by resolution. 3. Temporal Smoothness Loss (\mathcal{L}{TS}): \mathcal{L}{TS} = \sum{G \in \mathbf{V}{3d}^d} \sum{g \in G} \|\Deltat^2(G, g)\| where \mathbf{V}{3d}^d = \{G{XT}, G{YT}, G{ZT}\} are the space-time planes. \Deltat^2(G, g) represents the squared difference along the time axis. 4. Disentangle Loss (\mathcal{L}{DE}): \mathcal{L}{DE} = \sum{G \in \mathbf{V}{sd}^v} \sum{g \in G} \|1 - g\| where \mathbf{V}{sd}^v refers to the space-time planes associated with the dynamic field initialization. This loss encourages features to remain at the initial value of 1. \lambdad: Weight for depth loss \mathcal{L}D. Default: 1. \lambda{tv}: Weight for spatial TV loss. Default: 0.001. \lambda{ts}: Weight for temporal smoothness loss. Default: 0.05. \lambda{de}: Weight for disentangle loss. Default: 0.001. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeforplanelosses(renderedcolors, groundtruthcolors, staticspaceplanes, dynamicspacetimeplanes, dynamicfieldspacetimeplanes, lambdad=1.0, lambdatv=0.001, lambdats=0.05, lambdade=0.001): # 1. Photometric Loss (Lrgb) lrgb = sum((c - gt) 2 for c, gt in zip(renderedcolors, groundtruthcolors)) / len(renderedcolors) # LD (depth loss) is not defined in the provided source notes. ld = 0.0 # 2. Spatial Total Variation Loss (LTV) ltv = 0.0 for plane in staticspaceplanes: # Deltah^2: squared difference between (i, j) and (i+1, j) hdiff = [(plane[i][j] - plane[i+1][j]) 2 for i in range(len(plane)-1) for j in range(len(plane[0]))] # Deltaw^2: squared difference between (i, j) and (i, j+1) wdiff = [(plane[i][j] - plane[i][j+1]) 2 for i in range(len(plane)) for j in range(len(plane[0])-1)] ltv += sum(hdiff) + sum(wdiff) # 3. Temporal Smoothness Loss (LTS) lts = 0.0 for plane in dynamicspacetimeplanes: # Deltat^2: squared difference along the time axis (assumed axis 1) tdiff = [(plane[i][j] - plane[i][j+1]) 2 for i in range(len(plane)) for j in range(len(plane[0])-1)] lts += sum(tdiff) # 4. Disentangle Loss (LDE) lde = 0.0 for plane in dynamicfieldspacetimeplanes: lde += sum(abs(1.0 - val) for row in plane for val in row) # Total Loss totalloss = lrgb + (lambdad ld) + (lambdatv ltv) + (lambdats lts) + (lambdade lde) return totalloss Initialization: The dynamic field planes \mathbf{V}{3d}^d are initialized to 1 to ensure they do not influence the static field features during element-wise multiplication in the rendering procedure. Failure to initialize correctly may cause immediate entanglement. Boundary Conditions: The definition of \Deltah^2 and \Deltaw^2 involves differences between adjacent grid cells. Boundary handling (e.g., zero-padding vs. wrapping) is not explicitly detailed in the source notes. Standard practice suggests zero-padding or ignoring boundary terms to avoid artifacts. Monocular Input: In endoscopic procedures with monocular cameras, the reliance on stereo depth can be limiting. The Forplane method is designed to work with monocular inputs, but the depth loss \mathcal{L}D may need adaptation or removal if depth supervision is unavailable. Apply SVD plane regularization exclusively to semantic classes expected to exhibit flat surfaces, such as roads and sidewalks. Group semantic classes that share the same physical plane into a single semantic group. Apply the regularization loss only when a single semantic group is detected within the current patch. Pitfalls: Multiple semantic classes within one patch likely indicate multiple distinct planes; skip regularization to avoid violating the single-plane assumption. Multiple semantic classes may belong to the same physical plane (e.g., road and lane markings); group them together and apply regularization. Time Complexity: The regularization losses are computed directly on the plane tensors. \mathcal{L}{TV} and \mathcal{L}{TS} involve simple finite difference operations on the planes, which is O(N{planes} \times N{cells}). Memory Complexity: No additional memory is required beyond the plane tensors themselves. Strengths: Enforces spatial smoothness, temporal consistency, and static-field isolation. The disentangle loss specifically prevents the dynamic field from learning static structures. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of hyperparameters (\lambda{tv}, \lambda{ts}, \lambda{de}). The method assumes a specific orthogonal plane structure; it is not directly applicable to other volume representations like voxels or Gaussian splats without modification. Forplane Optimization Losses were introduced in the context of "Efficient Deformable Tissue Reconstruction via Orthogonal Neural Plane". The method builds upon the concept of Neural Fields and specifically the use of orthogonal planes (Forplanes) to represent 3D and 4D volumes efficiently. The specific losses (\mathcal{L}{TV}, \mathcal{L}{TS}, \mathcal{L}{DE}) were proposed to address the challenges of reconstructing dynamic, deformable tissues (such as in endoscopic surgery) where static and dynamic elements coexist and must be separated for accurate modeling. Efficient Deformable Tissue Reconstruction via Orthogonal Neural Plane, https://doi.org/10.1109/tmi.2024.3388559, fetched 2026-10-26 PlaNeRF: SVD Unsupervised 3D Plane Regularization for NeRF Large-Scale Urban Scene Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv62453.2024.00114, fetched 2026-11-04

name: Geometric and Normal Alignment Losses
head: Geometric regularization, Normal alignment, Curvature regularization
body: Geometric and Normal Alignment Losses are a family of regularization techniques used in differentiable volume rendering to enforce physical plausibility and structural coherence in reconstructed scenes. They solve the ambiguity inherent in inverse rendering problems—particularly in sparse-view or ill-posed scenarios—by penalizing geometric inconsistencies, noisy surface normals, and high-frequency oscillations in the underlying scalar fields [13295-normal-consistency-and-alignment.md][2911-curvature-loss.md]. This family sets itself apart from sibling methods like Total Variation Regularization or Distortion Loss by explicitly targeting the orientation, curvature, and spatial consistency of the geometry and material fields rather than just the photometric output or density distribution [13295-normal-consistency-and-alignment.md][2911-curvature-loss.md]. All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward rendering operator and the propagation of gradients through the integration steps [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. The core mechanism is the evaluation of the volume rendering equation and the computation of gradients with respect to scene parameters (density, geometry, transfer functions, camera poses) [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. The standard emission-absorption model computes the color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} as [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \sigmai is the density, \deltai is the step size, \mathbf{c}i is the color, and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. Differentiation strategies fall into three main categories [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]: 1. Reverse-Mode Automatic Differentiation (AD): Standard backpropagation through the computational graph. This requires storing O(kn) intermediate states (where n is pixels and k is samples), leading to high memory usage [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. 2. Adjoint Method: Computes gradients by propagating adjoint variables backward through the rendering algorithm, evaluating the chain rule from output to input. This has computational complexity largely constant in the number of parameters, making it preferable for optimizing many parameters like the transfer function [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. 3. Analytic Inversion / Explicit Gradients: Uses a-priori knowledge of the DVR operations to invert the order of operations or derive closed-form gradients, reducing memory consumption to O(n) by avoiding the storage of intermediate results [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. Curvature Loss is a geometric regularization term used in differentiable volume rendering and neural implicit surface optimization to penalize high-frequency oscillations in the predicted scalar field [2911-curvature-loss.md]. It solves the problem of noisy, jagged, or topologically incorrect geometry by enforcing smoothness in the second-order derivatives of the model output [2911-curvature-loss.md]. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Normal Consistency and Alignment by operating on the curvature (second derivative) of the field rather than the alignment of first-order normals, and from Surface Curvature Regularization by serving as the foundational mechanism that those methods build upon [2911-curvature-loss.md]. 2D Planar Image Alignment is a simplified joint optimization problem that aligns overlapping 2D image patches with learned content [6845-2d-planar-image-alignment.md]. It reconstructs a ground truth image from transformed patches by simultaneously optimizing the image content representation and the geometric transformation parameters [6845-2d-planar-image-alignment.md]. It differs from other geometric losses by operating in 2D patch space using homography parameters and low-rank tensor decompositions, rather than directly constraining 3D geometry or normals [6845-2d-planar-image-alignment.md]. Material Smoothness Loss is a regularization term applied to material fields to enforce spatial smoothness by penalizing differences in material parameters between neighboring surface points [7299-material-smoothness-loss.md]. A specific variant, the BRDF Smoothness Loss, enforces smoothness of BRDF parameters using a normalized difference weighted by pseudo-albedo gradients [7299-material-smoothness-loss.md]. It differs from standard smoothness losses by incorporating a bilateral weight derived from rendered color and irradiance to modulate the penalty, ensuring smoothness is preserved across material boundaries [7299-material-smoothness-loss.md]. This family enforces geometric plausibility in differentiable volume rendering by constraining predicted surface normals against ray directions, ground truth data, or density gradients [13295-normal-consistency-and-alignment.md]. It solves the ambiguity of implicit surfaces in radiance fields, particularly in sparse-view or ill-posed reconstruction scenarios, by stabilizing optimization and improving surface quality [13295-normal-consistency-and-alignment.md]. Unlike sibling methods that focus on curvature or material smoothness, these losses specifically target the orientation and consistency of the normal field [13295-normal-consistency-and-alignment.md]. Geometry Consistency Loss is a regularization technique used in differentiable volume rendering, specifically within style transfer frameworks like INS, to enforce view-consistent scene geometry. It addresses the problem of geometric distortions and inconsistencies that arise when applying style transformations to radiance fields by ensuring that the underlying 3D structure remains stable across different viewpoints. Unlike sibling methods such as Curvature Loss or Normal Consistency which focus on local surface properties or alignment with external normals, this method relies on self-distillation to maintain global geometric coherence without requiring explicit depth supervision [14883-geometry-consistency-loss.md]. Definition: A loss function that accounts for spatial misalignment between rendered and ground truth images by searching for the best-matching subpatch in the ground truth set, regularized by coordinate distance. Formula: L{PM}(G, R) = \min{i=1,...,N} (D(Gi, R) + \lambda \cdot D{coord}(Gi, R)). Here, D(Gi, R) = \|Gi - R\|2^2 and D{coord}(Gi, R) = \sqrt{\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2}, where \Delta x and \Delta y are the horizontal and vertical offsets between the ground truth subpatch Gi and the rendered patch R. Parameters: \lambda is the regularization weight for the coordinate distance penalty, typically set to 0.01. The ground truth patch size (G) is sampled at 48 \times 48 pixels, and the rendered patch size (R) is 32 \times 32 pixels. Comparison: Unlike standard losses defined on single pixels, this loss is defined on patches, allowing alignment vectors (\Delta x, \Delta y) to be estimated more robustly. Definition: A depth loss function that enforces constraints on planar boundaries by directly addressing sample weights, effectively reducing ambiguity during the volume rendering procedure. Formula: L{bound} = \sum{r \in R} \sum{i} \left( wi - e^{-\frac{(ti - D(r))^2}{2\sigma^2}} \right)^2, where L{bound} is the boundary loss, wi is the weight, ti is the distance of the sample from the ray origin, D(r) is ground truth depth, and \sigma is a sigma parameter. Parameters: \delta is set to 1 mm as a tolerance/threshold parameter for boundary enforcement. D(r) is the ground truth depth of ray r, wi is the weight corresponding to a point sampled on ray r at distance ti from the ray origin. Pitfall: In open space, transmittance Ti remains high and opacity \alphai remains low, producing low weights and minimal interaction to indicate boundaries. At boundary surfaces, opacity \alphai rises due to increasing material density, causing weights to peak. Comparison: Produces fewer artifacts and cleaner renderings than MSE loss by directly addressing the weights of samples, effectively reducing ambiguity during volume rendering. Definition: A comparison of various ray-based regularization losses used during NeRF/DVGO training to evaluate their sensitivity to false geometry. The CF loss is noted as being more sensitive to false geometry than others. Data: On DTU scan 40 with false geometry, the percentage of loss value in the false geometry region (normalized [0,1]) for various losses: Background entropy loss (11.0%), Photometric loss (11.1%), Per-point RGB loss (12.4%), CF loss (6.5%), Ray-entropy loss (4.7%), Distortion loss (28.0%). Definition: A two-stage pipeline addressing the vector field counterpart to STNet, combining U-Net-based motion estimation with deformable alignment. These objectives reflect the additional fidelity constraints that vector data imposes. Steps: Introduces domain-motivated objectives including cosine direction loss and a Jacobian loss for capturing divergence and curl. Definition: Three regularization/alignment losses used in DP-GES: Ls enforces geometric alignment with ground-truth colors, Lt prevents background leakage from overlapping semi-transparent regions, and L{scale} regularizes surfel scaling for spatial uniformity. Steps: Apply Ls during optimization to align surfel geometry with ground-truth colors, preventing missing geometry. Apply Lt during optimization to prevent background leakage caused by stacks of overlapping semi-transparent regions. Apply L{scale} during optimization to regularize surfel scaling distribution, reducing color leakage from chaotic scaling. Pitfall: Stopping transmittance-mediated gradients (w/o trans. grad) leads to blurrier details and prominent small surfels, similar to GES artifacts. Data: Ablation PSNR (MipNeRF360 1080p): Ours (full) 28.11, Ours (base) 27.72, w/ 2 layers 27.02, w/ 4 layers 28.10, w/o trans. grad 27.82, w/o Ls 28.05, w/o L{scale} 28.07, w/o Lt 27.86. Definition: A variant of direct alignment that replaces the RGB alignment loss with feature and gradient alignment losses to mitigate artifacts from photo-consistency violations. Steps: Replace the RGB alignment loss with an alignment loss computed on DINO features and image gradients. Pitfall: Mitigates ghosting artifacts and structural inaccuracies, allowing recovery of semi-transparent objects such as glass supports. The concept of using geometric constraints to regularize neural radiance fields emerged as a response to the "floaters" and noisy geometry artifacts common in sparse-view reconstruction. Early works like NeRF [44-radiance-field-optimization.md] relied primarily on photometric loss, which often led to ambiguous geometry. Subsequent research introduced curvature regularization [2911-curvature-loss.md] and normal consistency losses [13295-normal-consistency-and-alignment.md] to enforce smoothness and plausibility. The alignment-aware patch matching loss was introduced to handle misalignments in high-frequency details, while boundary losses specifically targeted architectural surfaces. More recent approaches have extended these principles to material fields [7299-material-smoothness-loss.md] and style transfer contexts [14883-geometry-consistency-loss.md], demonstrating the versatility of geometric regularization in differentiable rendering. AligNeRF: High-Fidelity Neural Radiance Fields via Alignment-Aware Training, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00013, fetched 2026-10-26 Improving Geometric Consistency for 360-Degree Neural Radiance Fields in Indoor Scenarios, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13710v1, fetched 2026-10-27 Reducing Shape-Radiance Ambiguity in Radiance Fields with a Closed-Form Color Estimation Method, https://doi.org/10.52202/075280-2570, fetched 2026-10-26 PDF Deep Learning Methods and Neural Representations for Scientific Volume..., https://www.cs.uoregon.edu/Reports/AREA-202603-Mathai.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Depth Peeling for High-Fidelity Gaussian-Enhanced Surfel Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2605.25345, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) ACCV 2024 Open Access Repository, https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/ACCV2024/html/GargDirectAlignmentforRobustNeRFLearningACCV2024paper.html, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Curvature Loss
head: Curvature Regularization, Geometric Curvature Penalty
body: Curvature Loss is a geometric regularization term used in differentiable volume rendering and neural implicit surface optimization to penalize high-frequency oscillations in the predicted scalar field (typically a Signed Distance Function or density field). It solves the problem of noisy, jagged, or topologically incorrect geometry by enforcing smoothness in the differential properties of the surface. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Normal Consistency and Alignment by operating on the second-order derivatives (curvature) of the implicit function rather than first-order derivatives (normals) or pixel-space alignment. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The predicted scalar field values (e.g., SDF values \phi) at query points \mathbf{x}, typically obtained from a neural network or grid-based representation. Output: A scalar loss value L{curv} representing the magnitude of curvature at the queried points. Data Structures: The scalar field is represented as a continuous function \phi(\mathbf{x}; \theta) parameterized by \theta (neural weights or grid values). Query points \mathbf{x} are sampled from the surface vicinity or volume. Method: 1. Query Field: Evaluate the scalar field \phi(\mathbf{x}) and its derivatives at the query points \mathbf{x}. 2. Compute Curvature Operator: Apply a curvature operator C to the field. The operator C typically computes the Laplacian \nabla^2 \phi or the sum of principal curvatures (Mean Curvature) or the product of principal curvatures (Gaussian Curvature). In the context of, the operator self.C is applied directly to the model output. 3. Compute Loss: Calculate the loss as the norm (e.g., L2 or L1) of the curvature values. 4. Weight: Multiply the computed curvature loss by a weighting factor \lambda{curvature}. Formula: L{curv} = \lambda{curvature} \cdot \| C(\phi(\mathbf{x})) \| where: \lambda{curvature} is the curvature loss weight. C(\cdot) is the curvature operator. \phi(\mathbf{x}) is the scalar field value at point \mathbf{x}. Parameters: \lambda{curvature}: The weight for the curvature loss term. Retrieved from configuration (e.g., self.config.system.loss.lambdacurvature). Typical values are not specified in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecurvatureloss(model, querypoints, lambdacurvature): """ Computes the curvature regularization loss for a neural implicit model. Args: model: The neural network or implicit function representing the scalar field. querypoints: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing query points x. lambdacurvature: Float weight for the curvature loss. Returns: Scalar loss value. """ # 1. Evaluate the scalar field and its derivatives at query points # The model must support differentiation to compute curvature (second derivatives) phi = model(querypoints) # 2. Apply curvature operator C # The operator C computes the curvature (e.g., Laplacian or Mean Curvature) # This requires computing second-order derivatives of phi with respect to x # Note: The exact implementation of self.C depends on the specific framework # but generally involves automatic differentiation of the first derivatives. curvaturevalues = model.curvatureoperator(querypoints) # 3. Compute the norm of the curvature values # Using L2 norm as a common default, though L1 is also possible curvatureloss = torch.mean(curvaturevalues 2) # 4. Weight the loss totalloss = lambdacurvature curvatureloss return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Computing second-order derivatives can be numerically unstable, especially if the network output is not smooth. Ensure the network architecture supports stable gradient computation (e.g., using smooth activation functions). Boundaries: Curvature is undefined or ill-behaved at boundaries of the domain. Exclude points near the boundary of the query volume or use appropriate padding. Degenerate Input: If the scalar field is constant, curvature is zero, and the loss provides no gradient. This is generally not a problem for optimization but worth noting for debugging. Focuses on sign changes at mesh edges, enforcing zero-crossing consistency for specific representations like FlexiCubes. Penalizes discontinuities in surface normals (first-order derivatives) along viewing rays, enforcing spatial smoothness. Computes and penalizes Gaussian and Mean curvatures directly on the implicit function, enabling direct surface regularization. A dynamic weighting strategy that scales down curvature regularization strength as optimization progresses to preserve high-frequency details. Time Complexity: Computing curvature requires second-order derivatives, which is more expensive than first-order derivatives (normals) or zeroth-order (values). The cost depends on the method used for derivative computation (e.g., automatic differentiation adds overhead). Typically O(N) where N is the number of query points, but with a higher constant factor than normal consistency. Memory Complexity: Requires storing intermediate gradients for backpropagation. Similar to other differentiable losses, memory usage scales with the number of query points and the depth of the computational graph for derivatives. Strengths: Enforces geometric smoothness, reduces noise, and helps in recovering clean surfaces from noisy predictions. Limitations: May oversmooth fine details if the weight \lambda{curvature} is too high. Computationally more expensive than simpler regularization terms. When to Use: When the target geometry is expected to be smooth or when the initial reconstruction is noisy. When Not to Use: When preserving high-frequency details is critical and the curvature weight is not decayed appropriately. Curvature Loss originates from the broader field of geometric regularization in computer vision and graphics, where penalizing high-order derivatives is a standard technique for denoising and smoothing. name: SDF Edge Regularization Loss
body: A loss function that penalizes Signed Distance Function (SDF) values at mesh edges where the sign changes, encouraging sharp features or correct topology at boundaries. It differs from general curvature penalties by focusing specifically on the discrete edge connectivity of the underlying representation (e.g., FlexiCubes) to enforce zero-crossing consistency. Inputs: sdf: Tensor of SDF values at vertices. Shape depends on the mesh representation (e.g., [V] or [B, V]). alledges: Tensor of edge indices. Shape [E, 2] or [B, E, 2], where E is the number of edges. Outputs: loss: Scalar tensor representing the regularization loss. Data Structures: sdff1x6x2: Intermediate tensor storing SDF values at edge endpoints. mask: Boolean tensor identifying edges with sign changes. Steps: 1. Gather SDF values at edge endpoints: \text{sdf}{\text{edges}} = \text{sdf}[\text{all\edges}] Reshape to [E, 2] (or [B, E, 2] for batched). 2. Create a mask for edges where signs differ: \text{mask} = \text{sign}(\text{sdf}{\text{edges}}[:, 0]) \neq \text{sign}(\text{sdf}{\text{edges}}[:, 1]) Note: \text{sign}(0) is typically treated as positive or handled via strict inequality. 3. Filter SDF values to only those edges with sign changes: \text{sdf}{\text{filtered}} = \text{sdf}{\text{edges}}[\text{mask}] 4. Compute binary cross-entropy loss between the first endpoint and the boolean second endpoint, and vice versa. Specifically, treat one endpoint's sign as the target and the other's value (normalized or raw) as the prediction, or use a hinge-like penalty. The source describes computing BCE between the first endpoint and boolean second endpoint, and vice versa. 5. Return the computed loss. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: sdf: Tensor of shape [V] or [B, V] containing SDF values at vertices. alledges: Tensor of shape [E, 2] or [B, E, 2] containing edge indices. Returns: loss: Scalar tensor. """ # Gather SDF values at edge endpoints # Handle batched or unbatched case if sdf.dim() == 1: sdfedges = sdf[alledges] # Shape [E, 2] else: # Assuming alledges is broadcastable or batched sdfedges = sdf[alledges] # Shape [B, E, 2] # Determine sign of SDF values # sign(0) is usually 1 or 0; here we assume standard sign function signs = torch.sign(sdfedges) # Shape [E, 2] or [B, E, 2] # Create mask for edges where signs differ # Using != to detect sign changes (e.g., +1 vs -1) mask = signs[:, 0] != signs[:, 1] # Shape [E] or [B, E] # Filter SDF values to only those edges with sign changes sdffiltered = sdfedges[mask] # Shape [K, 2] where K is number of crossing edges if sdffiltered.numel() == 0: return torch.tensor(0.0, device=sdf.device) # Compute binary cross-entropy loss # Treat first endpoint as target, second as prediction (and vice versa) # Note: BCE expects probabilities in [0, 1]. # The source implies a direct BCE between "first endpoint" and "boolean second endpoint". # This likely means converting signs to 0/1 targets and using raw SDF values or normalized values as logits/probs. # However, standard BCE on raw SDF values is unstable. # A common interpretation in this context (FlexiCubes) is to penalize the magnitude of SDF at the crossing # or ensure the signs are consistent with a binary classification. # Given the source description "binary cross-entropy loss between first endpoint and boolean second endpoint", # we interpret this as: # Target: sign(sdf[:, 0]) mapped to {0, 1} # Prediction: sigmoid(sdf[:, 1]) or similar, OR simply using the sign of the second as the target and the value as the loss? # Re-reading: "Compute binary cross-entropy loss between first endpoint and boolean second endpoint, and vice versa." # This phrasing is ambiguous. A more robust interpretation for SDF regularization is to minimize the SDF value at the zero crossing. # However, we must follow the source. Let's assume the source implies a classification loss on the signs. # Let's map signs to 0/1. target0 = (signs[:, 0] > 0).float() # Shape [E] or [B, E] target1 = (signs[:, 1] > 0).float() # Use the SDF values themselves as logits for BCE? Or normalized? # Without explicit normalization in source, we use raw values passed through sigmoid if treating as logits, # or just the values if the source implies a specific formulation. # Given "binary cross-entropy", we need probabilities. # Let's assume the source uses the SDF values directly in a BCE formulation, which is non-standard. # A safer implementation of "BCE between first and boolean second" might be: # Loss = BCE(target=sign(sdf0), input=sdf1) ? A regularization term to prevent density from growing from background into foreground by enforcing the SDF decision boundary using low-resolution SDF values. It minimizes the SDF likelihood under a Laplacian distribution using low-resolution probe values. name: Normal Smoothness Loss
head: Normal Continuity Loss, Normal Smoothness
body: Normal Smoothness Loss is a regularization term for differentiable volume rendering that encourages geometric consistency by penalizing discontinuities in surface normals along a viewing ray. It differs from sibling methods like Surface Curvature Regularization by operating directly on the dot product of consecutive normals rather than higher-order differential operators, and from Normal Regularization Loss by relying solely on internal spatial coherence rather than external monocular depth/normal estimates. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of surface normals \mathbf{n}i computed at sample points along a ray, and a scalar weight w. Outputs: A scalar loss value L representing the smoothness penalty. Data Structures: Normals Array: A list or tensor of 3D vectors \mathbf{n}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, where each vector is normalized (\|\mathbf{n}i\| = 1). The order corresponds to the sampling order along the ray (e.g., from near to far). Steps: 1. Iterate through the sequence of normals along the ray. 2. For each sample point i (where i > 0), compute the dot product between the current normal \mathbf{n}i and the previous normal \mathbf{n}{i-1}. 3. Calculate the per-pair loss as 1.0 - (\mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{n}{i-1}). 4. Aggregate the loss by summing over all pairs along the ray. 5. Scale the aggregated loss by the weight w. Formula: L = w \cdot (1 - \mathbf{n}p \cdot \mathbf{n}{prev}) Where: L is the loss contribution for a pair of adjacent samples. w is the weight scalar. \mathbf{n}p is the normal at the current sample point. \mathbf{n}{prev} is the normal at the previous sample point along the ray. Parameters: Weight (w): Float scalar multiplying the loss term. Typical value: 1.0. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Ray Tracking: The method requires tracking adjacent sample normals along a ray. This is not natively supported by all standard volume renderers, which may process samples independently or in parallel batches without maintaining ray-wise history. Implementation Status: In some codebases, this is currently a placeholder for future implementation due to the difficulty of integrating ray-wise state into the integrator. Normalization: Normals must be normalized before computing the dot product to ensure the metric accurately reflects angular difference. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def normalsmoothnessloss(normals: list, weight: float = 1.0) -> float: """ Computes the Normal Smoothness Loss for a single ray. Args: normals: List of normalized 3D vectors representing surface normals at consecutive sample points along the ray, ordered from near to far. weight: Scalar weight for the loss term. Returns: Scalar loss value. """ if len(normals) < 2: return 0.0 totalloss = 0.0 for i in range(1, len(normals)): np = normals[i] nprev = normals[i-1] # Compute dot product dotproduct = sum(a b for a, b in zip(np, nprev)) # Clamp to [-1, 1] to handle floating point errors dotproduct = max(-1.0, min(1.0, dotproduct)) # Calculate loss for this pair: 1.0 - dotproduct pairloss = 1.0 - dotproduct totalloss += pairloss # Scale the aggregated loss by the weight return weight totalloss A regularization term that uses the Jacobian of the map of normals to regularize scene geometry, derived from differential geometry principles. It differs from the basic smoothness loss by considering the spatial variation of the normal field across the image plane (or ray bundle) rather than just along a single ray. It is significantly slower to compute, processing approximately 1100 rays/s compared to ~5000 rays/s for depth regularization on an NVIDIA V100. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(N) where N is the number of samples per ray. The Jacobian-based variant is much slower than depth regularization, with measured performance of ~1100 rays/s vs ~5000 rays/s on NVIDIA V100. Memory: Requires storing normals for adjacent samples along the ray, or recomputing them. The basic implementation requires minimal extra memory beyond the normal field itself. Measured Performance: On NVIDIA V100, normals regularization (Jacobian-based) processes ~1100 rays/s, while depth regularization processes ~5000 rays/s. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Encourages geometric smoothness by penalizing normal discontinuities. Limitations: Requires ray-wise state tracking which may not be supported by all integrators; slower than depth-based regularization if using Jacobian variants; may oversmooth fine geometric details if weight is too high. When to Use: Use when normal consistency is critical and computational budget allows for ray-wise processing. Avoid when high throughput is required and depth regularization suffices. The concept of normal smoothness as a regularization term in differentiable rendering is discussed in the context of Total Light Inverse Rendering (TLIR). The specific formula L = w \cdot (1 - \mathbf{n}p \cdot \mathbf{n}{prev}) is documented in the TLIR codebase. Differential geometry-based normal regularization, including Jacobian approaches, is detailed in "Regularization of NeRFs using differential geometry". Normal Regularization Loss enforces geometric consistency in differentiable volume rendering and Gaussian splatting by combining monocular normal supervision with a total variation smoothness prior on predicted normals. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Normal Smoothness Loss by explicitly incorporating external monocular normal estimates to anchor the geometry, rather than relying solely on internal spatial coherence. The method minimizes a composite loss \mathcal{L}{	ext{normal}} defined as the sum of a monocular normal loss \mathcal{L}{\hat{N}} and a smoothness prior \mathcal{L}{	ext{smooth}}. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Predicted normal map \hat{ oldsymbol{N}} \in \mathbb{R}^{H 	imes W 	imes 3}, monocular normal estimates  oldsymbol{N}{	ext{mono}}, and scaling parameters  oldsymbol{s}i for each Gaussian primitive i. Outputs: Scalar loss value \mathcal{L}{	ext{normal}}. Data Structures: \hat{ oldsymbol{N}}{i,j}: The predicted normal vector at pixel coordinates (i, j).  oldsymbol{s}i: A 3D vector representing the scaling axes of the i-th Gaussian. Formulas: 1. Monocular Normal Loss (\mathcal{L}{\hat{N}}): An L1 loss between the predicted normals and monocular estimates. \mathcal{L}{\hat{N}} = \sum{i,j} \| \hat{ oldsymbol{N}}{i,j} -  oldsymbol{N}{	ext{mono}, i,j} \|1 2. Smoothness Loss (\mathcal{L}{	ext{smooth}}): Encourages spatial smoothness using finite differences. \mathcal{L}{	ext{smooth}} = \sum{i,j} \left( |
ablai \hat{ oldsymbol{N}}{i,j}| + |
ablaj \hat{ oldsymbol{N}}{i,j}| ight) Where 
abla is the finite difference operator convolving with [-1, 1] for the i-axis and [-1, 1]^	op for the j-axis. 3. Scale Loss (\mathcal{L}{	ext{scale}}): Applied to force Gaussians to become disc-like surfels, aiding normal estimation convergence. \mathcal{L}{	ext{scale}} = \sumi \|\arg\min( oldsymbol{s}i)\|1 The normal \hat{ oldsymbol{n}}i is derived from the scaling axes via a rotation matrix R and a one-hot encoding of the minimum axis index: \hat{ oldsymbol{n}}i = R \cdot 	ext{OneHot}(\arg\min( oldsymbol{s}i)) The rotation matrix R is constructed from quaternion q = (w, x, y, z)^	op: R =  egin{bmatrix} 1 - 2(y^2 + z^2) & 2(xy - wz) & 2(xz + wy) \ 2(xy + wz) & 1 - 2(x^2 + z^2) & 2(yz - wx) \ 2(xz - wy) & 2(yz + wx) & 1 - 2(x^2 + y^2) \end{bmatrix} 4. Total Loss: \mathcal{L}{	ext{normal}} = \mathcal{L}{\hat{N}} + \mathcal{L}{	ext{smooth}}. Parameters: Weight for smoothness prior: Not given in the sources. Monocular Normal Loss (L1) lmono = 0.0 for i in range(H): for j in range(W): for k in range(3): lmono += abs(predictednormals[i, j, k] - monocularnormals[i, j, k]) # 2. Smoothness Loss (Total Variation) lsmooth = 0.0 for i in range(H): for j in range(W): # i-axis difference (row direction) if i < H - 1: diffi = [predictednormals[i+1, j, k] - predictednormals[i, j, k] for k in range(3)] lsmooth += sum(abs(d) for d in diffi) # j-axis difference (column direction) if j < W - 1: diffj = [predictednormals[i, j+1, k] - predictednormals[i, j, k] for k in range(3)] lsmooth += sum(abs(d) for d in diffj) # 3. Scale Loss (auxiliary, not included in Lnormal per source formula) lscale = 0.0 for i in range(N): minidx = 0 for k in range(1, 3): if scales[i, k] < scales[i, minidx]: minidx = k lscale += minidx # ||argmin(si)||1 for a scalar index is the index itself return lmono + lsmooth Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Not given in the sources. It differs from the standard smoothness loss by using image intensity gradients as edge-aware weights.
