name: MSE Loss and PSNR Conversion
head: Loss Function for Constant Model, MSE Loss, Mean Squared Error, Mean Squared Error Loss, Pixel-wise RGB Mean Squared Error (MSE)
body: MSE Loss and PSNR Conversion computes the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between predicted and target RGB values (or volumes) and converts this error into Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) for logging and evaluation. It serves as the primary photometric consistency loss for training differentiable volume rendering models, minimizing the pixel-wise intensity difference between rendered images and ground truth. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Predicted image/volume \hat{I} (or \hat{C}), Target image/volume I (or C), and optionally a binary mask M indicating valid voxels/pixels. Outputs: Scalar MSE loss value, PSNR value (for logging), and optionally masked statistics. Data Structures: Predicted/Target Arrays: 3D arrays (H, W, 3) for images or 3D grids (D, H, W) for volumes, containing floating-point color/intensity values. Mask (Optional): Boolean array of same spatial dimensions as input, where True indicates valid regions. Steps: 1. Input Validation: Check that inputs are not empty and have compatible shapes. If using a mask, ensure it is not entirely false. 2. Compute Difference: Calculate the element-wise difference between predicted and target values: D = \hat{I} - I. 3. Square Difference: Square the difference element-wise: S = D^2. 4. Masking (Optional): If a mask M is provided, apply it to the squared errors. Let N be the number of elements where M is true. 5. Compute MSE: Average the squared errors over the valid elements: \text{MSE} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i \in \text{valid}} (\hat{I}i - Ii)^2 For a constant intensity model parameterized by density \sigma and step size q, the predicted intensity is computed via a lookup function, and the loss is half the sum of squared residuals. 6. Compute PSNR: Convert MSE to PSNR in decibels (dB): \text{PSNR} = -10 \cdot \log{10}(\text{MSE}) Alternatively, using the signal-to-noise ratio form where the maximum signal value is 1 (for normalized RGB): \text{PSNR} = 20 \cdot \log{10}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\text{MSE}}}\right) If MSE is 0, PSNR is defined as infinity. Parameters: Mask Threshold (Optional): A relative threshold maskthresholdrel (default 0.01) applied to the normalized mask volume to create the boolean mask. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Mask: If the boolean mask has no true values, raise a RuntimeError. Zero MSE: If MSE is exactly 0.0, PSNR remains infinity to avoid division by zero in the log10 calculation. Precision: Ensure inputs are in linear color space (no gamma compression) for accurate photometric loss, especially when handling under/over-exposed values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def computemseandpsnr(predicted: np.ndarray, target: np.ndarray, mask: np.ndarray = None) -> dict: """ Computes MSE and PSNR between predicted and target arrays. Args: predicted: Array of predicted values (H, W, C) or (D, H, W). target: Array of target values with same shape as predicted. mask: Optional boolean array of same spatial dimensions. Returns: Dictionary with 'mse', 'psnr', 'maskedvoxelcount', 'volumeshape'. """ # Validate inputs if predicted.shape != target.shape: raise ValueError("Predicted and target must have the same shape.") if mask is not None: # Apply mask threshold if mask is not boolean if not mask.dtype == bool: threshold = 0.01 np.max(mask) mask = mask > threshold if not np.any(mask): raise RuntimeError("Mask has no true values.") # Flatten spatial dimensions for masking predictedflat = predicted.flatten() targetflat = target.flatten() maskflat = mask.flatten() # Apply mask validpred = predictedflat[maskflat] validtarget = targetflat[maskflat] nvalid = len(validpred) else: validpred = predicted.flatten() validtarget = target.flatten() nvalid = len(validpred) # Compute squared differences squareddiff = (validpred - validtarget) 2 # Compute MSE mse = np.mean(squareddiff) # Compute PSNR if mse == 0.0: psnr = float('inf') else: psnr = 20.0 math.log10(1.0 / math.sqrt(mse)) return { 'mse': float(mse), 'psnr': psnr, 'maskedvoxelcount': int(nvalid) if mask is not None else int(nvalid), 'volumeshape': list(predicted.shape) } Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) is a standard benchmark metric used to evaluate the photometric fidelity of reconstructed images or volumes in novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction. It quantifies the error between a predicted image and a ground-truth reference by converting the Mean Squared Error (MSE) into a logarithmic decibel (dB) scale, where higher values indicate better quality. Unlike structural metrics such as SSIM, PSNR focuses strictly on pixel-wise intensity accuracy, making it sensitive to large smooth regions while largely ignoring small, high-frequency features like specular highlights. SSIM is a full-reference quality assessment metric that evaluates image fidelity by measuring perceptual similarity through local comparisons of luminance, contrast, and structure. Unlike pixel-wise error metrics such as MSE or PSNR, which often correlate poorly with human perception, SSIM captures structural information changes to approximate perceived distortion. It is widely used as a standard benchmark for image quality in 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis. The Normal-L2 Score computes the mean squared error between predicted surface normals and ground-truth normals to evaluate geometric fidelity in radiance-field optimization. It differs from sibling metrics like PSNR Metric Calculation by focusing on shading-critical surface orientation rather than color intensity, and from IoU Loss by measuring local geometric accuracy rather than global silhouette alignment. Minkowski's Metric (also known as the Lp norm or Lgamma loss) is a family of photometric consistency losses used in radiance-field optimization to quantify the dissimilarity between a rendered image and a ground-truth reference. It generalizes the Mean Squared Error (MSE) by allowing the exponent \gamma to vary, enabling a trade-off between sensitivity to large errors and robustness to outliers. Unlike MSE, which penalizes large deviations quadratically, Minkowski's Metric with \gamma < 2 (e.g., L1) is less sensitive to outliers, while \gamma > 2 increases sensitivity to large errors. IoU Loss is a binary segmentation metric that computes the ratio of overlapping voxels above a threshold to the total union of predicted and target voxels. The perceptually-motivated variance metric quantifies the error between an 8-bit ambient occlusion (AO) approximation T and a high-fidelity ray-traced reference R. It differs from raw pixel Mean Squared Error (MSE) by operating on log-transformed values and spatial gradients, thereby aligning with human visual sensitivity to radiance and its changes. This metric is specifically designed for evaluating AO approximations where reflected ambient radiance is linear in accessibility. Depth Accuracy Metrics evaluate the geometric fidelity of predicted depth maps against ground truth data in radiance field optimization pipelines. They quantify scale- and translation-invariant errors on valid depth pixels. They are used to evaluate depth prior quality and monocular depth estimation outputs in NeRF pipelines. The Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) Loss is a regularization term for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that minimizes the difference between the frequency representations of rendered and ground-truth images by decomposing them into sub-bands. It addresses high-frequency overfitting in few-shot NeRF training by explicitly prioritizing low-frequency learning during early stages. Unlike its sibling MSE Loss and PSNR Conversion, which compares pixel-wise values globally, the DW loss operates on local structures using patch-based sampling to supervise low and mid-frequency components. Calculates the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) between observed intensity values and a predicted constant intensity model parameterized by density (\sigma) and step size (q). It serves as a photometric consistency loss in differentiable volume rendering, specifically fitting a constant radiance assumption along a ray. Unlike the parent MSE Loss and PSNR Conversion which operates on raw RGB predictions, this method explicitly models the physical integration of a constant source over a ray segment. Computes a normalized L1 loss between a reconstructed image and an original image, scaling the loss to the [0, 1] range. It is used in sparse pixel sampling optimization pipelines to provide an error metric for adaptive Gaussian densification and pruning. Masked and Weighted Losses is a family of techniques that modify the standard photometric error computation in differentiable volume rendering by applying spatial masks or per-pixel weights to the loss function. It solves the problem of training instability and evaluation bias caused by invalid background regions, sensor artifacts, multiscale resolution disparities, or structural inconsistencies. It sets itself apart from its sibling MSE Loss and PSNR Conversion by introducing selective suppression or amplification of error terms rather than computing a global average, and from Masked Volume Metrics by focusing on training-time gradient correction rather than evaluation-time metric definition. The Restricted Mean Error Metric is a loss function designed to optimize scalar weight factors for pre-computed scattering lobe shapes in volume rendering, specifically addressing parameter heterogeneity across voxel clusters. Unlike standard Mean Squared Error (MSE) which treats all pixels equally or global mean metrics that obscure local errors, this method computes the average intensity only for pixels "directly" visible to specific voxel clusters, allowing the optimizer to identify which clusters cause rendering artifacts (such as seams) and correcting them individually. It is primarily used in the context of optimizing SGGX lobe weights via Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). Silhouette Loss provides boundary supervision for differentiable volume rendering by penalizing discrepancies between predicted surface probabilities and ground-truth image masks. It ensures that the rendered alpha channel aligns with the object's silhouette, preventing geometric artifacts and providing warm-start supervision for fine-grained geometry. It is distinct from photometric losses (e.g., MSE) by operating on the alpha channel rather than RGB values, and from depth losses by focusing on binary boundary presence rather than metric distance. Treating the TAA algorithm as a biased estimator to analyze correctness using Mean Squared Error (MSE), decomposed into variance and bias squared. The formula is \text{MSE}[F] = \mathbb{E}[(F - G)^2] = V[F] + \beta[F]^2, where F is the output of the estimator, G is the true value (ground truth), V[F] is the variance of the estimator, and \beta[F] is its bias. A fast assignment strategy used during Phase 1 to compute the L2 matching loss between heuristic samples and learnt proposals. For each heuristic sample, find the closest proposal from the learnt proposer set. Optimal matching (Hungarian algorithm) or strict 1-1 greedy matching significantly slows training. Calculates Mean Squared Logarithmic Error between two RGB colors, optionally weighted by luminance. The formula is \text{MSLE} = \sumc (\log2(\frac{bc + 1.0}{ac + 1.0}))^2 \cdot wc where wc is 1.0 or luminance weight. L2 loss between the simulated blurry image and the input blurry image. The parameter B(x) is the input blurry image at pixel x. A pixel-wise mean squared loss operating in linear color space (no gamma compression) that handles under-exposed and over-exposed values using a one-sided difference based on clipping thresholds. The parameters are v{min} (lower clipping threshold) and v{max} (upper clipping threshold). Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of pixels or voxels, as it involves a single pass to compute differences and averages. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the squared differences, though this can be computed on-the-fly to reduce memory to O(1) if streaming. Measured Performance: Standard metric for NeRF training, often used in conjunction with Adam optimizer. Scaling: Scales linearly with resolution and batch size. Strengths: Simple to implement, differentiable, and widely understood. Provides a direct measure of pixel-wise error. Limitations: Does not correlate well with human perception for high-frequency details. Sensitive to outliers. When to use: Standard training loss for photometric consistency. When not to use: When perceptual quality is more important than pixel-wise accuracy (use SSIM or LPIPS). MSE Loss is a fundamental metric in image processing and computer vision, originating from statistical error analysis. It is widely used in 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis to evaluate the quality of reconstructed volumes and rendered views. name: PSNR Metric Calculation
head: PSNR Calculation, PSNR Metric, Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio
body: Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) is a standard benchmark metric used to evaluate the photometric fidelity of reconstructed images or volumes in novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction. It quantifies the error between a predicted image and a ground-truth reference by converting the Mean Squared Error (MSE) into a logarithmic decibel (dB) scale, where higher values indicate better quality. Unlike structural metrics such as SSIM, PSNR focuses strictly on pixel-wise intensity accuracy, making it sensitive to large smooth regions while largely ignoring small, high-frequency features like specular highlights. Inputs and Outputs Input x: Ground-truth image or volume. Input y: Predicted/reconstructed image or volume. Parameter MAX: The maximum possible representable pixel value (e.g., 1.0 for normalized float, 255 for 8-bit integer). Parameter eps: A small constant (typically 10^{-10}) added to MSE to prevent \log(0). Output: A scalar float representing the PSNR in decibels (dB). Data Structures The inputs are dense arrays or tensors containing pixel/voxel values. The computation aggregates errors over all elements in the array. Steps 1. Validation: Ensure x and y have identical dimensions; if not, return an error or maximum float value. 2. Compute Squared Error: Calculate the element-wise squared difference between x and y. 3. Compute MSE: Calculate the mean of the squared differences over all pixels/voxels. 4. Compute PSNR: Apply the logarithmic conversion using MAX and eps. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def calculatepsnr(x: list, y: list, maxval: float = 1.0, eps: float = 1e-10) -> float: """Calculate Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio between two images/volumes x and y.""" if len(x) != len(y): raise ValueError("Input arrays must have identical dimensions") n = len(x) if n == 0: return 0.0 errorsum = 0.0 for i in range(n): diff = x[i] - y[i] errorsum += diff diff mse = errorsum / n psnr = 10.0 math.log10((maxval 2) / (mse + eps)) return psnr Parameters and Typical Values maxval: Default is 1.0 for normalized floating-point images. eps: Default is 10^{-10}. Interpretation: A difference of 3 dB corresponds to a halving of the squared error; a 6 dB difference corresponds to a quartering. Target PSNR for NeRF Blender scenes is typically 31–33 dB. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Zero MSE: If the prediction is perfect (MSE = 0), PSNR is infinite. The eps term prevents this from causing a runtime error but results in a very large finite number. Smooth Region Bias: PSNR averages over every pixel, weighting large smooth regions heavily and ignoring small bright features like specular highlights or grass blades. Noise Floor: In scientific volumes, if the noise level is zero (signal-limited), MAD estimators may return exactly zero, bounding nothing. 3D Evaluation Metrics quantify the fidelity of reconstructed volumetric or radiance-field representations against ground-truth references, addressing the problem of assessing both geometric accuracy and photometric consistency in 3D reconstruction. Unlike sibling methods that focus on specific aspects like mesh topology Mesh Reconstruction Evaluation or surface orientation Normal Consistency, this category encompasses a suite of metrics including PSNR, SSIM, and mIoU to provide a comprehensive assessment of reconstruction quality. It distinguishes itself from PSNR Metric Calculation by extending the evaluation to 3D volumes and multi-view consistency, and from Benchmark Performance Numbers by providing the specific algorithmic definitions of the scores rather than just reporting aggregated results. Benchmark Performance Numbers provide standardized quantitative baselines for evaluating radiance field optimization methods, primarily using the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset metrics (average PSNR and LPIPS). They serve as a reference point to compare the reconstruction quality of different variants (e.g., 3DGS, Mip-Splatting) against established baselines. Unlike raw metric calculation, these numbers aggregate results across a specific scene set to highlight trade-offs between visual fidelity, geometric accuracy, and resource efficiency. The PSNR Difference Metric for Ablation quantifies the performance degradation caused by removing a specific component from a rendering pipeline by comparing the Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) of the ablated configuration against the full method. It isolates the error ratio independent of the bit depth (MAX), as MAX cancels out in the logarithmic difference, providing a scale-invariant measure of quality loss. Noise Floor Estimation via MAD estimates the noise standard deviation \sigma in volumetric data to determine the theoretical maximum achievable PSNR (noise floor). It uses Median Absolute Deviation (MAD) estimators: (1) Laplacian MAD applies the D-dimensional discrete Laplacian and scales the MAD of the response by 1/(0.6745 \sqrt{2D(2D+1)}); (2) Haar finite-difference MAD uses per-slice diagonal second differences d = I(y,x) - I(y,x+1) - I(y+1,x) + I(y+1,x+1), scaling MAD by 1/(0.6745 \sqrt{2}). The noise floor PSNR is then 10 \log{10}(1/\sigma^2). A pitfall is that MAD estimators may return exactly zero for signal-limited volumes (e.g., Mouse heart nuclei), bounding nothing. PSNR Loss computes the Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio between predicted and target images, used as a regression metric during training. It is defined as \text{PSNR} = 20 \log{10}\left(\frac{\text{max\val}}{\sqrt{\text{MSE}}}\right). Unlike the standard PSNR metric which is used for evaluation, this variant is often used as a differentiable loss function (or its negative) during optimization, with maxval defaulting to 1.0. Color PSNR (YUV) computes color degradation by converting RGB to YUV and combining per-component PSNR values. Points in the distorted content are associated to reference points using a nearest neighbor algorithm, and RGB values are converted to YUV per ITU-R BT.709-3. PSNR is computed for Y, U, and V components separately, then combined using a weighted average: PSNRYUV = \frac{6 \cdot PSNRY + PSNRU + PSNRV}{8}. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple to implement, computationally inexpensive, and widely understood as a standard benchmark for image quality. Limitations: Does not correlate well with human perception for structural details or textures; heavily biased towards smooth regions; sensitive to global brightness shifts. When to Use: Standard reporting for novel view synthesis benchmarks (e.g., Mip-NeRF 360, Blender scenes) where photometric accuracy is the primary concern. When Not to Use: When structural similarity or perceptual quality is more important than pixel-wise accuracy; in such cases, SSIM or LPIPS should be used alongside or instead. In the context of volume rendering and neural radiance fields (NeRF), PSNR became a standard metric for evaluating novel view synthesis quality, with early benchmarks targeting 31–33 dB on Blender scenes. It is frequently reported alongside SSIM and LPIPS to provide a more complete picture of reconstruction fidelity, as PSNR alone fails to capture perceptual similarities in complex scenes. name: 3D Evaluation Metrics
body: 3D Evaluation Metrics quantify the fidelity of reconstructed volumetric or radiance-field representations against ground-truth references, addressing the problem of assessing both geometric accuracy and photometric consistency in 3D reconstruction. Unlike sibling methods that focus on specific aspects like mesh topology Mesh Reconstruction Evaluation or surface orientation Normal Consistency, this category encompasses a suite of metrics including PSNR, SSIM, and mIoU to provide a comprehensive assessment of reconstruction quality. It distinguishes itself from PSNR Metric Calculation by extending the evaluation to 3D volumes and multi-view consistency, and from Benchmark Performance Numbers by providing the specific algorithmic definitions of the scores rather than just reporting aggregated results. The evaluation process varies depending on the specific metric (photometric vs. geometric) and the representation type (voxel volume vs. splat-based radiance field). The following steps cover the standard procedures for computing PSNR/SSIM on volumes and mIoU for occupancy grids. Inputs: Reconstructed volume V{pred} (normalized to [0, 1] or binarized occupancy). Ground-truth volume V{gt} (normalized to [0, 1] or binary occupancy). Camera poses (for novel view synthesis evaluation). Rendering engine (differentiable renderer for splats or direct volume access for voxels). Outputs: PSNR (dB), SSIM (0–1), and/or mIoU (0–100%). Volume: A 3D tensor of shape (D, H, W) or (N, D, H, W) for multiple views/channels. Occupancy Grid: A binary 3D tensor where 1 indicates occupied space and 0 indicates empty space. Splats: A list of Gaussian parameters (\mu, \Sigma, c, \alpha) used for rendering. 1. Normalization: Ensure V{pred} and V{gt} are normalized to the range [0, 1]. 2. View Selection: Iterate over axial, coronal, and sagittal slices, or render novel views from held-out camera poses. 3. MSE Calculation: Compute the Mean Squared Error (MSE) averaged over all voxels, including background: MSE = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (V{pred}[i] - V{gt}[i])^2 where N is the total number of voxels. 4. PSNR Calculation: Compute PSNR using the normalized maximum value MAX=1: PSNR = 10 \log{10} \left( \frac{1}{MSE} \right). 5. SSIM Calculation: Compute Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) using a window size of 11 and Gaussian weighting with \sigma = 1.5. 6. Aggregation: Print or return the mean PSNR and SSIM across all views or slices. 1. Alpha Extraction: Extract the predicted \alpha volume, which corresponds to the last channel of the predicted volume Vs. 2. Binarization: Binarize the predicted \alpha volume using a fixed threshold \tau = 0.05: V{pred\bin}[i] = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } V{pred}[i] \ge \tau \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 3. The primary metric is the Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), which quantifies pixel-wise reconstruction error in decibels by comparing rendered images against ground-truth references. While PSNR is the standard baseline due to its computational cheapness, it is widely recognized as insensitive to perceptual quality, often necessitating companion metrics like SSIM or LPIPS for a complete evaluation. Evaluates 3D geometry learned in a self-supervised manner by minimizing a novel view synthesis objective, using mean intersection-over-union (mIoU) between predicted and ground truth volumes. The predicted \alpha volume (last channel of Vs) is binarized using a threshold \tau = 0.05 and compared against the ground truth occupancy volume. The mIoU is averaged across categories. Evaluation requires holding out photos never trained on, rendering the trained splat from those poses, and comparing against real photos. Standard scores are PSNR (higher is better), SSIM (closer to 1 is better), and LPIPS (lower is better, correlates with human perception). A key pitfall is that low training-view error but high held-out error indicates overfitting, usually caused by insufficient scene coverage. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the volumes and intermediate buffers for SSIM. Limitations: PSNR is insensitive to perceptual quality. SSIM parameters (window size, sigma) must be chosen carefully. mIoU requires a threshold, which can be sensitive to the choice of \tau. name: Mesh Reconstruction Evaluation
body: Mesh Reconstruction Evaluation quantifies the geometric fidelity of a reconstructed triangular mesh against a ground-truth reference mesh. It solves the problem of assessing how well a surface reconstruction method captures the true shape, topology, and detail of the underlying scene. Unlike radiance-field metrics that evaluate visual appearance, this method focuses strictly on spatial accuracy, distinguishing it from PSNR Metric Calculation which measures pixel-level photometric error. The evaluation computes statistical distances between the vertices of the reconstructed mesh and the ground-truth surface. The primary metrics are Chamfer Distance and F-Score. Inputs: Reconstructed mesh \mathcal{M}{rec} and ground-truth mesh \mathcal{M}{gt}, typically represented as sets of vertices and faces. Outputs: Scalar scores for Chamfer Distance and F-Score. Data Structures: Point clouds or vertex sets for distance queries; KD-trees or spatial hashing for efficient nearest-neighbor search. Steps: 1. Sample points uniformly from the surface of \mathcal{M}{rec} and \mathcal{M}{gt} to obtain point sets P{rec} and P{gt}. 2. Compute the Chamfer Distance (CD) as the sum of squared nearest-neighbor distances in both directions: CD(P{rec}, P{gt}) = \frac{1}{|P{rec}|} \sum{p \in P{rec}} \min{q \in P{gt}} \|p - q\|^2 + \frac{1}{|P{gt}|} \sum{q \in P{gt}} \min{p \in P{rec}} \|p - q\|^2. 3. Compute the F-Score at a threshold distance \tau by calculating precision (fraction of P{rec} within \tau of P{gt}) and recall (fraction of P{gt} within \tau of P{rec}), then taking the harmonic mean: F(\tau) = \frac{2 \cdot \text{precision} \cdot \text{recall}}{\text{precision} + \text{recall}}. Parameters: Threshold \tau for F-Score, typically 0.01 to 0.02 of the bounding box diagonal. Number of sampled points per mesh, typically 10^4 to 10^5. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Over-explanation: The method focuses heavily on geometric details, which can cause over-explanation of texture on flat surfaces with complex geometry, leading to visible artifacts. Metric Discrepancy: Quantitative mesh metrics (F-score, Chamfer distance) are good, but visualizations show apparent artifacts compared to ground truth. Evaluators should always inspect visual results alongside metrics. A mesh regularization term that encourages geometric flatness by minimizing the smallest eigenvalue of the vertex normal covariance matrix, weighted by vertex area. It distinguishes itself from smoothness-based regularizers like Laplacian smoothing by explicitly penalizing curvature to promote planar patches. Choose it when differentiable surface reconstruction requires explicit flatness constraints. It builds on Mesh Reconstruction Evaluation. name: Developability Regularizer
head: Stein et al. regularizer
body:
The Developability Regularizer is a mesh regularization term that encourages geometric flatness (developability) by minimizing the smallest eigenvalue of the vertex normal covariance matrix, weighted by vertex area. It penalizes non-planar local geometry during differentiable surface reconstruction. The method computes a per-vertex contribution to the loss based on the local geometry of incident triangles. It aggregates normal covariances and areas, then computes the minimum eigenvalue as a measure of non-developability. Inputs: tripos: Tensor of shape (T, 3, 3), containing the 3D positions of the three vertices for each of the T triangles. tris: Tensor of shape (T, 3), containing the vertex indices for each triangle. V: Number of unique vertices in the mesh. Outputs: loss: Tensor of shape (V,) containing per-vertex developability penalties. Data Structures: vertnormalcovariancesum: Tensor of shape (V, 9), initialized to zeros. Stores the flattened 3 	imes 3 normal covariance matrix for each vertex. vertarea: Tensor of shape (V), initialized to zeros. Stores the weighted area contribution for each vertex. vertdegree: Tensor of shape (V), initialized to zeros (int32). Stores the number of triangles incident to each vertex. Parameters: RELEPS: 1 	imes 10^{-6}. Added to the covariance matrix to ensure numerical stability during eigenvalue decomposition. POSEPS: 1 	imes 10^{-6}. Used in normalization denominators to prevent division by zero. Steps: 1. Initialize Accumulators: Set vertnormalcovariancesum, vertarea, and vertdegree to zero tensors of the specified shapes. 2. Iterate Over Triangle Corners: For each triangle t in the mesh, and for each corner index iC \in \{0, 1, 2\}: a. Gather Vertices: Let p{Root} = 	ext{tri\pos}[t, iC], pA = 	ext{tri\pos}[t, (iC + 1)  mod 3], and pB = 	ext{tri\pos}[t, (iC + 2)  mod 3]. b. Compute Edge Vectors: vA = pA - p{Root}, vB = pB - p{Root}, and normalize them to v{An} and v{Bn}. c. Compute Face Geometry: area
ormal = vA 	imes vB, face\area = 0.5 	imes \|area
ormal\|, and normal =  rac{area
ormal}{\|area
ormal\|}. d. Compute Corner Angle: corner\angle = \arccos(	ext{clamp}(	ext{dot}(v{An}, v{Bn}), -1, 1)). e. Compute Normal Outer Product: outer = normal \otimes normal (Resulting in a 3 	imes 3 matrix), then flatten to a vector of length 9. f. Scatter Updates: Let idx = 	ext{tris}[t, iC]. Accumulate outer to 	ext{vert
ormal\covariance\sum}[idx], add  rac{face\area}{3} to 	ext{vert\area}[idx], and add 1 to 	ext{vert\degree}[idx]. 3. Process Covariance Matrices: Reshape vertnormalcovariancesum to (V, 3, 3) and add 	ext{REL\EPS} 	imes I to each matrix, where I is the identity matrix. 4. Compute Minimum Eigenvalues: Compute the eigenvalues for each vertex's covariance matrix and take the minimum absolute value: 	ext{min\eigvals}[v] = \min(|\lambda1|, |\lambda2|, |\lambda3|). 5. Mask Degree-3 Vertices: Set 	ext{vert\area}[v] = 0 where 	ext{vert\degree}[v] == 3. 6. Normalize Area: Normalize 	ext{vert\area} by scaling it: 	ext{vert\area} \leftarrow 	ext{vert\area} 	imes  rac{V}{\sum 	ext{vert\area}}. 7. Compute Loss: Return the element-wise product 	ext{vert\area} 	imes 	ext{min\eigvals}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: POSEPS prevents division by zero during edge/normal normalization and area scaling. Boundaries: Vertices with exactly three incident triangles (degree-3) are masked out to avoid degenerate covariance contributions. Degenerate Input: Zero-length edges or collinear vertices produce zero-area faces; the POSEPS guard and eigenvalue absolute value handling prevent NaN propagation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def computedevelopabilityregularizer(tripos, tris, V, releps=1e-6, poseps=1e-6): """ Compute the Developability Regularizer loss. Args: tripos: Tensor (T, 3, 3) - Vertex positions for each triangle. tris: Tensor (T, 3) - Vertex indices for each triangle. V: int - Number of vertices. releps: float - Regularization epsilon for eigenvalues. poseps: float - Epsilon for normalization. Returns: loss: Tensor (V,) - Per-vertex loss values. """ T = tripos.shape[0] # Initialize accumulators vertnormalcovariancesum = torch.zeros((V, 9), device=tripos.device) vertarea = torch.zeros((V), device=tripos.device) vertdegree = torch.zeros((V), dtype=torch.int32, device=tripos.device) # Loop over triangles and corners for iC in range(3): # Gather vertices proot = tripos[:, iC] pa = tripos[:, (iC + 1) % 3] pb = tripos[:, (iC + 2) % 3] # Edge vectors va = pa - proot vb = pb - proot # Normalize edges normva = torch.norm(va, dim=1, keepdim=True) normvb = torch.norm(vb, dim=1, keepdim=True) van = va / (normva + poseps) vbn = vb / (normvb + poseps) # Face area and normal areanormal = torch.cross(va, vb, dim=1) facearea = 0.5 torch.norm(areanormal, dim=1) normal = areanormal / (torch.norm(areanormal, dim=1, keepdim=True) + poseps) # Compute corner angle (computed per source, but unused in final loss) cornerangle = torch.acos(torch.clamp(torch.sum(van vbn, dim=1), -1.0, 1.0)) # Outer product of normal (3x3 matrix) outer = torch.einsum('ti,tj->tij', normal, normal) outerflat = outer.reshape(T, 9) # Scatter updates indices = tris[:, iC] vertnormalcovariancesum.scatteradd(0, indices.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, 9), outerflat) vertarea.scatteradd(0, indices, facearea / 3.0) vertdegree.scatteradd(0, indices, torch.ones(T, dtype=torch.int32, device=tripos.device)) # Reshape covariance to (V, 3, 3) covmatrix = vertnormalcovariancesum.reshape(V, 3, 3) # Add regularization covmatrix = covmatrix + releps torch.eye(3, device=tripos.device) # Compute eigenvalues eigvals = torch.linalg.eigvalsh(covmatrix) # Minimum absolute eigenvalue mineigvals = torch.min(torch.abs(eigvals), dim=1).values # Mask out degree-3 vertices maskdegree3 = (vertdegree == 3) vertarea = vertarea.clone() vertarea[maskdegree3] = 0.0 # Normalize area totalarea = vertarea.sum() vertarea = vertarea (V / (totalarea + poseps)) # Final loss loss = vertarea mineigvals return loss Not given in the sources. Implemented in the FlexiCubes framework. It is used as a regularization term in differentiable surface reconstruction to encourage mesh flatness. name: Normal Consistency
body: Normal Consistency (NC) is a metric for 3D surface reconstruction that measures the angular deviation between estimated surface normals and ground truth normals. It quantifies how well the orientation of the reconstructed surface aligns with the underlying geometry, serving as a complementary measure to distance-based metrics like Chamfer Distance. Unlike distance metrics that assess positional accuracy, NC specifically evaluates surface orientation fidelity. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N points on the estimated surface, their corresponding estimated surface normals \{Ni\}{i=1}^N, and the ground truth surface normals \{Ni^\}{i=1}^N at the corresponding locations. Output: A scalar percentage value representing the average normal consistency error. Data Structures: Ni: Estimated surface normal vector for the i-th point. Ni^: Ground truth surface normal vector for the i-th point. N: Total number of points on the surface. Steps: 1. For each point i from 1 to N, compute the cosine similarity between the estimated normal Ni and the ground truth normal Ni^: \cos(Ni, Ni^) = Ni \cdot Ni^ (assuming Ni and Ni^ are unit vectors). 2. Compute the error term for each point: 1 - \cos(Ni, Ni^). 3. Sum the error terms for all N points and divide by N to obtain the mean error. 4. Multiply the mean error by 100 to express the result as a percentage. Formula: \text{NC} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N (1 - \cos(Ni, Ni^)) \times 100\% Parameters: Ni, Ni^: Estimated and ground truth surface normals for the i-th point. N: Number of points on the surface. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The normalization term \frac{1}{N} ensures the metric is independent of the number of points on the surface. If normals are not normalized to unit length, the cosine similarity calculation must explicitly divide by the magnitudes of the vectors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def normalconsistency(estimatednormals, groundtruthnormals): n = len(estimatednormals) totalerror = 0.0 for i in range(n): dot = estimatednormals[i][0] groundtruthnormals[i][0] + \ estimatednormals[i][1] groundtruthnormals[i][1] + \ estimatednormals[i][2] groundtruthnormals[i][2] error = 1.0 - dot totalerror += error meanerror = totalerror / n return meanerror 100.0 Measures surface orientation accuracy by comparing ground truth mesh normals with network-computed SDF gradients (normalized) at sampled surface points. It computes the angular difference in degrees. Formula: \theta = \arccos( | \mathbf{n}{mesh} \cdot \mathbf{n}{net} |) \times \frac{180}{\pi} where \mathbf{n}{mesh} and \mathbf{n}{net} are normalized mesh and network normals. Parameters: n\samples: 2097152 (default number of surface points); batch\size: 16384 (processing chunk size). Steps: Sample points and get face normals. Scale points by trainingdata.R. Batch process with batchsize = 16384: enable gradients, compute SDF, compute normals via net.normal(batchpoints), normalize gradients. Concatenate normals. Normalize mesh normals. Compute dot products, clamp to [-1, 1], apply acos(abs(dot)), convert to degrees. Compute MAE, Std, Max, Median. Code: python import math def angularnormalerror(meshnormals, netnormals): angulardifferencesdeg = [] for n1, n2 in zip(meshnormals, netnormals): dot = n1[0]n2[0] + n1[1]n2[1] + n1[2]n2[2] dot = max(-1.0, min(1.0, dot)) rad = math.acos(abs(dot)) deg = rad (180.0 / math.pi) angulardifferencesdeg.append(deg) return angulardifferencesdeg Pitfall: Dot products may exceed [-1, 1] due to floating point precision. Clamped to [-1.0, 1.0] before acos to avoid NaNs. Not given in the sources. Normal Consistency was introduced as a standard metric for evaluating 3D surface reconstruction tasks. name: Standard Rendering Metrics
head: LinearQuantizer.psnr, PSNR (Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio), PSNR Calculation, PSNR Evaluation, PSNR computation, Peak Signal to Noise Ratio
body: Standard Rendering Metrics provide an objective, numerical assessment of image fidelity for 3D reconstructions and novel view synthesis. The primary metric is the Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), which quantifies pixel-wise reconstruction error in decibels by comparing rendered images against ground-truth references. While PSNR is the standard baseline due to its computational cheapness, it is widely recognized as insensitive to perceptual quality, often necessitating companion metrics like SSIM or LPIPS for a complete evaluation. The calculation of PSNR involves computing the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the predicted (rendered) image and the target (ground-truth) image, followed by a logarithmic transformation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Rendered image tensor \hat{I} and Ground-truth image tensor I. Both must be of identical dimensions H \times W \times C (typically C=3 for RGB). Output: A scalar float representing the PSNR in decibels (dB). Data Structures: Images are typically stored as floating-point tensors. If the source data is integer-based (e.g., 8-bit), it must be normalized to a range where the peak signal is defined (commonly [0, 1] or [0, 255]). Steps: 1. Normalization: Ensure both \hat{I} and I are normalized to the same range. If using the formula with MAXI=1.0, values should be in [0, 1]. If using MAXI=255, values should be in [0, 255]. 2. MSE Calculation: Compute the Mean Squared Error between the two images. MSE = \frac{1}{N} \sum{k=1}^{N} (\hat{I}k - Ik)^2 Where N is the total number of pixels (H \times W \times C) and \hat{I}k, Ik are the pixel values at index k. 3. Clamping: Clamp the MSE to a minimum value (e.g., 10^{-12}) to prevent numerical instability (logarithm of zero or negative numbers). 4. PSNR Calculation: Compute the PSNR using the clamped MSE. PSNR = -10 \log{10}(\max(MSE, \epsilon)) Alternatively, using the peak intensity MAXI: PSNR = 10 \log{10} \left( \frac{(MAXI)^2}{MSE} \right) Where \epsilon is the stability floor (e.g., 10^{-12}). Parameters: \epsilon (MSE clamp min): 10^{-12} is a common value for numerical stability. MAXI: The maximum possible intensity value. For normalized [0,1] data, this is 1.0. For 8-bit integer data, this is 255. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-finite Values: If the MSE is zero (identical images) or negative (due to numerical error), the logarithm is undefined. Clamping prevents \log(0), resulting in a very high but finite PSNR. If the result is NaN or Inf, it should trigger an error or be handled specifically. Range Mismatch: Calculating MSE between images with different normalization ranges (e.g., one in [0,1] and one in [0,255]) will yield incorrect results. Perceptual Irrelevance: High PSNR does not guarantee high perceptual quality. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def calculatepsnr(rendered: list, groundtruth: list, maxval: float = 1.0, mseclampmin: float = 1e-12) -> float: """ Calculate PSNR between rendered and ground truth images. Args: rendered: Flattened list or array of pixel values (predicted). groundtruth: Flattened list or array of pixel values (target). maxval: The maximum possible pixel value (e.g., 1.0 for [0,1], 255 for [0,255]). mseclampmin: Minimum value for MSE to prevent log(0). Returns: PSNR value in dB. """ if len(rendered) != len(groundtruth): raise ValueError("Rendered and ground truth images must have the same number of elements.") n = len(rendered) msesum = 0.0 for i in range(n): diff = rendered[i] - groundtruth[i] msesum += diff diff mse = msesum / n # Clamp MSE to prevent log(0) mse = max(mse, mseclampmin) # Calculate PSNR # Formula: 10 log10((maxval^2) / MSE) # Equivalent to: 20 log10(maxval / sqrt(MSE)) # Or: -10 log10(MSE) if maxval is 1.0 if maxval == 1.0: psnr = -10.0 math.log10(mse) else: psnr = 10.0 math.log10((maxval 2) / mse) return psnr This method provides an objective, numerical metric for estimating sampling artifacts in Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) by treating rendered images as noisy signals. Unlike traditional assessment which relies on subjective human visual judgment, it quantifies the dispersion of pixel colors across multiple renders with different stochastic jitter seeds to produce a Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) value. It is distinct from standard PSNR calculations for image compression because it measures the variance of the rendering algorithm itself rather than the error between a rendered image and a ground-truth reference. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of pixels. It is extremely cheap to compute compared to perceptual metrics like LPIPS which require neural network inference. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the images during comparison, or O(1) if computed in a streaming fashion. Strengths: Simple to implement and fast to compute. Limitations: Insensitive to perceptual quality; correlates poorly with human judgment compared to SSIM or LPIPS. When to use: As a baseline metric for rapid iteration and comparison of reconstruction accuracy. When not to use: When perceptual fidelity is the primary goal; in such cases, LPIPS or SSIM should be used alongside or instead of PSNR. PSNR originated in signal processing and image compression as a measure of reconstruction quality. In the context of 3D rendering, it has become a standard metric for evaluating novel view synthesis. It is often reported alongside SSIM and LPIPS to provide a more comprehensive evaluation. The metric is widely used in benchmarks such as Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, and NeRF Synthetic. name: PSNR-based Quality Estimation for Ray Casting
head: Noise-based quality estimation, PSNR for DVR quality
body: This method provides an objective, numerical metric for estimating sampling artifacts in Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) by treating rendered images as noisy signals. Unlike traditional assessment which relies on subjective human visual judgment, it quantifies the dispersion of pixel colors across multiple renders with different stochastic jitter seeds to produce a Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) value. It is distinct from standard PSNR calculations for image compression because it measures the variance of the rendering algorithm itself rather than the error between a rendered image and a ground-truth reference. Inputs: 1. A volumetric dataset. 2. A fixed camera viewpoint and transfer function. 3. A set of K rendered images of the same scene, generated using the same ray casting algorithm but with different random seeds for stochastic jittering of ray starting positions. 4. A binary mask or logic to identify background pixels (pixels with null dispersion). Outputs: 1. A global PSNR value (in dB) representing the overall rendering quality. 2. Optionally, a per-pixel quality map showing local sampling artifact intensity. Data Structures: Rendered Images: A list of K images, each of dimensions n \times m (width \times height). Each pixel contains a color vector C. Color Space: The color values are converted to the YPbPr color space before calculation. Background Mask: A boolean grid of size n \times m indicating which pixels are background (null dispersion). Parameters: n, m: Image width and height. K: Number of rendered images with different jitter seeds. MAXC: Maximum possible length of the color vector. Set to 1 in the source implementation. N: Number of non-background pixels in the image. Steps: 1. Render: Generate K images of the volumetric dataset from the same viewpoint using the same transfer function and visualization settings, varying only the random seed for stochastic jittering of ray starting positions. 2. Convert: Convert the color values of all K rendered images to the YPbPr color space. 3. Calculate Per-Pixel Error: For each pixel (i, j), calculate the dispersion (error) of the color vector. Let Ck(i, j) be the color vector of pixel (i, j) in the k-th rendered image. Calculate the average color M(i, j) across all K images: M(i, j) = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^{K} Ck(i, j) Calculate the error (dispersion) D(i, j) for pixel (i, j): D(i, j) = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^{K} \| M(i, j) - Ck(i, j) \|^2 Note: The source formula is written as M(M(C(i, j)) - C(i, j))^2. In the context of dispersion of a random variable, this represents the variance. The outer M denotes the mean operator applied to the squared difference. The norm \| \cdot \| is applied to the color vector difference. 4. Calculate MSE: Compute the Mean-Square Error (MSE) over all non-background pixels. Identify the set of indices \Omega for all pixels (i, j) that are not background (i.e., have non-null dispersion). Calculate N = |\Omega|. Calculate MSE: MSE = \frac{1}{N} \sum{(i, j) \in \Omega} D(i, j) Pitfall: Background pixels have null dispersion. Including them in the sum would artificially inflate the quality score (overstatement). 5. Calculate PSNR: Compute the global PSNR in decibels: PSNR = 10 \log{10} \left( \frac{MAXC^2}{MSE} \right) With MAXC = 1. Interpretation: A PSNR > 40 dB indicates no noticeable noise, corresponding to a mean error of less than 1\%. A PSNR < 30 dB indicates rather noticeable noise. The desired quality range for RC algorithms is between 30 dB and 40 dB. 6. Optional Quality Map: To visualize local quality, calculate the PSNR for each single pixel individually using the local dispersion D(i, j): PSNR(i, j) = 10 \log{10} \left( \frac{MAXC^2}{D(i, j)} \right) (Handle division by zero if D(i, j) = 0 by assigning infinite PSNR or a maximum value). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def calculatepsnrquality(renderedimages: list[np.ndarray], backgroundmask: np.ndarray) -> float: """ Calculate PSNR-based quality estimation for ray casting. Args: renderedimages: List of K numpy arrays, each of shape (n, m, 3) in YPbPr space. backgroundmask: Boolean numpy array of shape (n, m), True for background pixels. Returns: Global PSNR in dB. """ if not renderedimages: return 0.0 # Stack images into a single array of shape (K, n, m, 3) images = np.stack(renderedimages, axis=0) K, n, m, = images.shape # Calculate mean color across the K renders for each pixel # Mean color M(i,j) shape: (n, m, 3) meancolor = np.mean(images, axis=0) # Calculate dispersion (variance) for each pixel # D(i,j) = mean(||M - Ck||^2) # Difference shape: (K, n, m, 3) diff = meancolor - images # Squared Euclidean norm for each pixel across the K samples # Sum over color channels (axis=-1) then average over K (axis=0) squareddiff = np.square(diff) dispersion = np.mean(np.sum(squareddiff, axis=-1), axis=0) # Shape: (n, m) # Identify non-background pixels # backgroundmask is True for background. We want False (non-background). nonbgmask = ~backgroundmask # Extract dispersion values for non-background pixels dispersionflat = dispersion.flatten() nonbgmaskflat = nonbgmask.flatten() nonbgdispersion = dispersionflat[nonbgmaskflat] N = len(nonbgdispersion) if N == 0: # No non-background pixels, quality is undefined or infinite return float('inf') # Calculate MSE mse = np.mean(nonbgdispersion) # Calculate PSNR MAXC = 1.0 if mse == 0: return float('inf') psnr = 10 np.log10((MAXC 2) / mse) return psnr Time Complexity: O(K \cdot n \cdot m), where K is the number of renders, and n, m are image dimensions. The method requires rendering the scene K times, which is the dominant cost. The post-processing calculation is linear in the number of pixels and renders. Memory Complexity: O(K \cdot n \cdot m) to store the K rendered images. Strengths: Provides an objective, numerical metric that correlates with perceptual noise levels. It allows for automated comparison of different Ray Casting (RC) algorithms and sampling rates without human intervention. It generates quality maps to identify specific areas of high/low rendering quality. Limitations: It is insensitive to perceptual quality aspects other than noise (e.g., color accuracy, structural fidelity). It requires multiple renders with different jitter seeds, increasing computational cost. It assumes that sampling artifacts manifest as noise, which may not hold for all types of rendering errors. When to use: When comparing different RC algorithms (e.g., unoptimized vs. pre-integrated) or tuning sampling rates to achieve a desired quality-performance trade-off. When not to use: When a ground-truth reference image is available (standard PSNR against reference is more appropriate) or when perceptual quality metrics (SSIM, LPIPS) are required. The method was proposed by N. Gavrilov and N. Gavrilov in 2013. It addresses the lack of numerical quality estimation approaches for images obtained by visualization of medical and scientific volumetric datasets. Prior to this, researchers primarily relied on subjective human visual judgment, placing images side-by-side for comparison. The method leverages the fact that sampling artifacts in DVR, caused by uniform sampling missing thin features, can be converted to noise via stochastic jittering. It adapts the PSNR metric, traditionally used for image compression error measurement, to quantify the noise introduced by the rendering algorithm itself. name: Benchmark Performance Numbers
head: Average PSNR/LPIPS, M360 Metrics
body: Benchmark Performance Numbers provide standardized quantitative baselines for evaluating radiance field optimization methods, primarily using metrics from the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset. They serve as a reference point to compare the reconstruction quality of different variants (e.g., 3DGS, Mip-Splatting) against established baselines. Unlike raw metric calculation, these numbers aggregate results across a specific scene set to highlight trade-offs between visual fidelity, geometric accuracy, and resource efficiency. Inputs: Standardized evaluation datasets (e.g., Mip-NeRF 360 room-scale scenes) and trained model checkpoints. Outputs: Scalar metrics (average PSNR, LPIPS) and comparative statistics (primitive count, training time, inference speed). Data Structures: Metric Record: A tuple or object containing: methodname: String identifier. psnr: Float (dB). lpips: Float (0-1 range, lower is better). ssim: Float (0-1 range, optional). trainingtime: Float (minutes). inferencefps: Float (frames per second). primitivecount: Integer or relative ratio. Steps: 1. Load the trained model for the method being evaluated. 2. Render images for the held-out test views of the benchmark dataset (e.g., Mip-NeRF 360). 3. Compute PSNR and LPIPS scores for each rendered image against ground truth. 4. Average PSNR and LPIPS across all test scenes in the benchmark set. 5. Record auxiliary metrics: training time and inference speed, and primitive count or relative ratios. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Dataset: Mip-NeRF 360 (room-scale) is the primary reference for these specific numbers. Metric Weights: Not specified; standard averaging is used. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting: Train PSNR is easy to overfit and does not reflect generalization; test PSNR on held-out trajectories is the critical metric. Metric Disagreement: LPIPS often disagrees with PSNR; a model may have lower PSNR but better perceptual quality (lower LPIPS). Cherry-picking: Beware of metrics that ignore inference speed, memory footprint, or primitive count inflation. Failure Modes: Floaters, popping, aliasing, and over-smoothing can distort these numbers if not properly handled by the method. Applies regularization during training to mitigate artifacts introduced by compressing multilevel hash encodings and MLP architectures. It uses a strong Laplacian regularizer and a lower learning rate to improve reconstruction quality under compression constraints. A regularization term applied during training to force the radiance field representation to be sparser, accelerating rendering speed by reducing the number of active voxels/features evaluated during ray marching. It uses an occupancy grid bitmap (binary mask: 0 for empty, 1 for non-empty) to visualize and enforce sparsity. Adopting this loss can accelerate rendering speed (e.g., 23% for Ours-B8) with minor decreases in PSNR (e.g., 33.60 to 33.59) and unchanged SSIM. Time and Memory Complexity: Training Time: Varies by method and sparsity. For example, Ours-B8 training time decreased from 14.7 min to 13.9 min with sparsity loss. Inference Speed: Can be significantly improved by sparsity. Ours-B8 inference speed increased from 2.2 fps to 2.7 fps (23% acceleration) with sparsity loss. Memory/Size: Compression regularization reduces storage size. For example, binary feature encoding reduces TiNeuVox-B size from 47.51 MB to 3.88 MB. Measured Performance (Mip-NeRF 360, Room Scale): Vanilla 3DGS: 27.4 PSNR / 0.18 LPIPS. Mip-Splatting: 27.7 PSNR / 0.17 LPIPS. Scaffold-GS: 27.9 PSNR / 0.18 LPIPS. 2DGS: ~27.0 PSNR / similar LPIPS (but better geometry). GES: Comparable PSNR with ~30% fewer primitives. Hierarchical 3DGS: Comparable performance with LoD streaming. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Provides a common ground for comparing diverse methods (Gaussian Splatting, NeRF, Hash-based). Highlights trade-offs between quality and efficiency (FPS, size). Limitations: Metrics can be misleading if cherry-picked; PSNR may not correlate with perceptual quality (LPIPS). Benchmarks may not cover all failure modes (e.g., dynamic scenes, glossy materials). When to Use: Use for initial comparison of new radiance field methods against SOTA baselines. Use to evaluate the impact of regularization techniques (sparsity, compression) on efficiency and quality. When Not to Use: Do not rely solely on PSNR for perceptual quality assessment; always check LPIPS and visual inspection. Do not use for dynamic/deformable scenes unless the benchmark specifically supports it (e.g., D-NeRF, HyperNeRF). Origin: The specific numbers for Mip-NeRF 360 room-scale scenes are compiled from various SOTA Gaussian Splatting and radiance field papers, summarized in an unofficial cheat sheet. The concept of using PSNR/LPIPS benchmarks for NeRF/3DGS is standard in the field. Sparsity loss and compression regularization are techniques developed to improve efficiency and reduce artifacts in hash-based and voxel-based radiance fields. History and Development: Synthetic-NeRF is used as a benchmark dataset for ablation studies on feature grid design and sparsity loss. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and its variants (Mip-Splatting, Scaffold-GS, 2DGS, GES, Hierarchical 3DGS) established new baselines for real-time rendering and quality. Techniques like Sparsity Loss and Compression Regularization were introduced to address the high memory and computational costs of dense radiance fields. Where it is Used: Academic research for comparing new radiance field optimization methods. Game development and real-time rendering applications where efficiency and quality trade-offs are critical. name: PSNR Difference Metric for Ablation
head: Delta PSNR
body: The PSNR Difference Metric for Ablation quantifies the performance degradation caused by removing a specific component from a rendering pipeline by comparing the Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) of the ablated configuration against the full method. It isolates the error ratio independent of the bit depth (MAX), as MAX cancels out in the logarithmic difference, providing a scale-invariant measure of quality loss. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: \text{MSE}{\text{full}} (Mean Squared Error of the full method), \text{MSE}{\text{config}} (Mean Squared Error of the ablated configuration). Output: \Delta (The PSNR difference in decibels). Data Structures No specific data structures are required; the metric operates on scalar MSE values derived from image comparisons. Steps 1. Compute the PSNR difference \Delta directly from the MSE ratio, which avoids calculating individual PSNRs and explicitly cancels the \text{MAX}^2 term: \Delta = 10 \log{10} \frac{\text{MSE}{\text{full}}}{\text{MSE}{\text{config}}} 2. To recover the error ratio from the difference, apply the inverse relation: \frac{\text{MSE}{\text{config}}}{\text{MSE}{\text{full}}} = 10^{-\Delta/10} Parameters MAX: The maximum possible pixel value (e.g., 255 for 8-bit images). This parameter is implicit in the cancellation and does not appear in the final difference formula. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Division by Zero: If \text{MSE}{\text{config}} is zero, the logarithm is undefined. This implies the ablated method produces an identical result to the ground truth, which is rare in ablation studies involving component removal. Sign Interpretation: A negative \Delta indicates the ablated method has higher error (worse quality) than the full method. A positive \Delta indicates the ablated method has lower error (better quality), which may suggest the removed component was detrimental or the full method was overfitting. Fixed Gaps: A difference of 3 dB corresponds to exactly a factor of two in error, and 6 dB to a factor of four, independent of the absolute PSNR values. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def psnrdifference(msefull: float, mseconfig: float) -> float: """ Calculate the PSNR difference between a full method and an ablated configuration. Args: msefull: Mean Squared Error of the full method. mseconfig: Mean Squared Error of the ablated configuration. Returns: Delta PSNR in decibels. """ if mseconfig == 0: raise ValueError("MSE of config cannot be zero (logarithm undefined).") if msefull == 0: # If full MSE is 0, the full method is perfect. # Any non-zero config MSE results in infinite loss. if mseconfig > 0: return float('inf') return 0.0 # Formula: Delta = 10 log10(MSEfull / MSEconfig) # This cancels out MAX^2 from the individual PSNR definitions. ratio = msefull / mseconfig delta = 10 math.log10(ratio) return delta def mseratiofromdelta(delta: float) -> float: """ Recover the MSE ratio from the PSNR difference. Args: delta: The PSNR difference in decibels. Returns: The ratio MSEconfig / MSEfull. """ return 10 (-delta / 10) Calculates the average quality (BD-PSNR) or bit-rate (BD-BR) difference between two rate-distortion curves. Provides a single scalar for objective compression comparison, avoiding full curve plotting. Chosen when comparing multiple compression techniques across varying bitrates. Time Complexity: O(1) for the calculation itself, assuming MSE values are precomputed. Memory Complexity: O(1). Strengths: It isolates the error ratio independent of the bit depth of the image format. Limitations: It only measures the difference relative to a specific baseline (the full method) and does not provide an absolute quality metric. It assumes the MSE values are computed on the same pixel grid and color space. The metric is derived from the properties of the logarithmic scale used in PSNR calculations. It is used in ablation studies to isolate the error ratio caused by removing a specific component from a rendering pipeline, such as in 3D Gaussian Splatting. The cancellation of the MAX term is a key property that makes the metric robust across different image formats. An Architectural Review of the 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering Pipeline, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21739653, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Bjøntegaard Delta PSNR (BD-PSNR) and BD-BR
head: BD-BR, BD-PSNR, Bjøntegaard Delta
body: BD-PSNR and BD-BR are metrics used to evaluate lossy compression performance by calculating the average difference in quality (BD-PSNR) or bit-rate (BD-BR) between two rate-distortion (RD) curves. They set themselves apart from point-wise comparisons by integrating the area between two continuous RD curves, providing a single value that facilitates objective comparison of compression techniques. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Two sets of rate-distortion data points. Each set consists of pairs (Ri, Di), where R is the bit-rate (or size) and D is the distortion metric (e.g., MSE, PSNR). Let the reference method be R{ref}, D{ref} and the test method be R{test}, D{test}. Outputs: A single BD-PSNR value (in dB) representing the average quality difference, or a single BD-BR value (in %) representing the average bit-rate difference. Data Structures: Two lists of tuples: [(rate, distortion),...] for the reference and test methods. The number of points should be sufficient to model the curve (typically 4 or more points per curve are recommended in standard implementations, though the source notes do not specify a minimum). Steps: 1. Logarithmic Transformation: Convert the bit-rate values R to natural logarithms \ln(R) for both reference and test curves. The distortion values (PSNR or MSE) are used directly or transformed depending on the specific variant (PSNR vs BR). For BD-PSNR, the distortion is typically PSNR. For BD-BR, the distortion is often PSNR, and the rate is the variable of integration. 2. Cubic Spline Interpolation: Fit a cubic spline through the data points of the reference curve (\ln(R{ref}), D{ref}) and the test curve (\ln(R{test}), D{test}). This creates continuous functions D{ref}(\ln R) and D{test}(\ln R). 3. Integration: Calculate the area between the two interpolated curves over the range of common bit-rates. For BD-PSNR: Integrate the difference in distortion (PSNR) with respect to \ln(R). The result is the average difference in PSNR. For BD-BR: Integrate the difference in bit-rate with respect to the distortion metric (usually PSNR). The result is normalized to a percentage. 4. Normalization: BD-PSNR is expressed in dB. A positive value indicates the test method is better (higher PSNR) than the reference. BD-BR is expressed as a percentage. A negative value indicates the test method uses less bitrate for the same quality. Formulas: Let y{ref}(x) and y{test}(x) be the cubic spline interpolations of the reference and test curves, where x = \ln(R). The BD-PSNR is calculated as: \Delta \bar{P} = \frac{1}{x2 - x1} \int{x1}^{x2} (y{test}(x) - y{ref}(x)) \, dx where x1 and x2 are the minimum and maximum \ln(R) values common to both curves. The BD-BR is calculated as: \Delta \bar{R} = \frac{\int{y1}^{y2} (x{test}(y) - x{ref}(y)) \, dy}{\int{y1}^{y2} x{ref}(y) \, dy} \times 100\% where y1 and y2 are the minimum and maximum distortion values common to both curves. Parameters: Spline type: Cubic spline. Integration limits: The overlapping range of the two curves. Edge cases and pitfalls: Non-overlapping ranges: If the rate-distortion curves do not overlap in their operational range, the integration limits are undefined. The source notes do not specify how to handle this. Monotonicity: RD curves should be monotonic. Non-monotonic data may require smoothing or filtering before interpolation. Precision: The accuracy depends on the number of data points used to define the curves. Sparse data leads to inaccurate spline interpolation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.interpolate import CubicSpline def calculatebdpsnr(refrates, refpsnrs, testrates, testpsnrs): """ Calculates BD-PSNR between two rate-distortion curves. refrates, testrates: array-like of bit-rates (R) refpsnrs, testpsnrs: array-like of PSNR values (D) """ # 1. Log-transform rates xref = np.log(refrates) xtest = np.log(testrates) # 2. Determine common range xmin = max(np.min(xref), np.min(xtest)) xmax = min(np.max(xref), np.max(xtest)) if xmin >= xmax: return 0.0 # Or raise error # 3. Interpolate # Create a dense set of x values within the common range xdense = np.linspace(xmin, xmax, 1000) csref = CubicSpline(xref, refpsnrs) cstest = CubicSpline(xtest, testpsnrs) yref = csref(xdense) ytest = cstest(xdense) # 4. Integrate difference # Using trapezoidal rule for numerical integration integral = np.trapz(ytest - yref, xdense) # 5. Normalize by range bdpsnr = integral / (xmax - xmin) return bdpsnr def calculatebdbr(refrates, refpsnrs, testrates, testpsnrs): """ Calculates BD-BR between two rate-distortion curves. """ # Note: Standard BD-BR integrates rate difference w.r.t distortion # This requires inverting the spline or interpolating R as a function of D # 1. Determine common PSNR range ymin = max(np.min(refpsnrs), np.min(testpsnrs)) ymax = min(np.max(refpsnrs), np.max(testpsnrs)) if ymin >= ymax: return 0.0 # 2. Interpolate Rate as a function of PSNR ydense = np.linspace(ymin, ymax, 1000) # CubicSpline requires x to be monotonic. PSNR is typically monotonic with Rate. # However, if PSNR is not strictly monotonic in the input data, this may fail. try: csrefr = CubicSpline(refpsnrs, np.log(refrates)) cstestr = CubicSpline(testpsnrs, np.log(testrates)) except ValueError: # Fallback or error handling for non-monotonic data return 0.0 xreflog = csrefr(ydense) xtestlog = cstestr(ydense) # 3. Integrate difference in log-rate integraldiff = np.trapz(xtestlog - xreflog, ydense) integralref = np.trapz(xreflog, ydense) # 4. Calculate percentage # BD-BR is often defined as exp(integral) - 1 or similar depending on log usage # The source describes it as "average relative difference in bit-rate" # Standard VCEG implementation uses: bdbr = (np.exp(integraldiff) - 1) 100.0 return bdbr BD-Rate is a metric for fair comparison of overall rate-distortion (RD) performance that calculates the average bit-rate saving at a given quality level between two methods. It sets itself apart from point-wise comparisons by integrating the area between two continuous RD curves, providing a single percentage value representing efficiency gains. It builds on the concept of BD-PSNR but inverts the perspective to measure bitrate reduction [7176-bj-ntegaard-delta-psnr-bd-psnr-and-bd-br.md]. Time Complexity: Dominated by cubic spline interpolation and numerical integration. For N points, spline construction is O(N) and integration is O(M) where M is the number of integration steps. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the data points and spline coefficients. Strengths: Provides a single, robust metric for comparing compression algorithms that accounts for the entire RD curve, not just specific operating points. It is widely accepted in video coding standards. Limitations: Requires multiple RD points per method. Sensitive to the number and distribution of data points. Assumes the RD curve can be accurately modeled by a cubic spline. When to use: When comparing two or more compression methodologies where a single scalar metric summarizing the RD performance is needed. When not to use: When only a single operating point is available, or when the RD curves do not overlap significantly. The Bjøntegaard Delta metrics were originally designed within the Video Coding Experts Group (VCEG) – ITU SG 16 – for the comparison of various video coding techniques. They were developed to address the impracticality of providing full rate-distortion curves in publications, allowing researchers to summarize performance differences in a single value. Wavelet based volumetric medical image compression, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.image.2014.12.007, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Bjøntegaard Delta-Rate (BD-Rate)
head: BD-R, BD-Rate, Piecewise cubic Bjøntegaard Delta-Rate (BD-Rate) metric
body: BD-Rate is a metric for fair comparison of overall rate-distortion (RD) performance that calculates the average bit-rate saving at a given quality level between two methods. It sets itself apart from point-wise comparisons by integrating the area between two continuous RD curves, providing a single percentage value representing efficiency gains. It builds on the concept of BD-PSNR but inverts the perspective to measure bitrate reduction [7176-bj-ntegaard-delta-psnr-bd-psnr-and-bd-br.md]. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Two sets of RD points for Method A and Method B. Each set consists of pairs (Ri, Di), where R is the bitrate (e.g., bits per pixel) and D is the distortion metric (e.g., PSNR in dB). Output: A single percentage value representing the average bitrate saving. A negative value indicates Method A uses less bitrate than Method B for the same quality. Data Structures: Two lists of tuples: pointsA = [(R1, D1), (R2, D2),...] and pointsB = [(R1, D1), (R2, D2),...]. Points must be sorted by Distortion (D) in ascending order. Steps: 1. Log-Transform: Convert bitrate values to natural logarithms. Let x = \ln(R) and y = D. This linearizes the typically exponential relationship between bitrate and quality. 2. Piecewise Cubic Interpolation: Fit a continuous cubic spline curve through the (x, y) points for each method. The spline ensures C^2 continuity (continuous first and second derivatives). 3. Integration: Calculate the area between the two interpolated curves over the range of distortion values covered by both methods. The integral is computed as: \Delta R = \int{y{min}}^{y{max}} (xA(y) - xB(y)) \, dy where xA(y) and xB(y) are the interpolated log-bitrate functions for Method A and Method B, respectively, and [y{min}, y{max}] is the intersection of their distortion ranges. 4. Normalization: Divide the integrated area by the range of distortion (y{max} - y{min}) to get the average difference in log-bitrate. 5. Exponentiation: Convert the average log-bitrate difference back to a linear scale to obtain the BD-Rate percentage: BD\text{-}Rate = 100 \times (e^{\Delta R / \Delta y} - 1) where \Delta y = y{max} - y{min}. Parameters: Interpolation Method: Piecewise cubic spline. Standard cubic splines may oscillate; piecewise cubic ensures stability across the RD curve. Distortion Metric: Typically PSNR (dB). Rate Metric: Bits per pixel (bpp) or model size in MB. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-overlapping Ranges: If the two methods do not cover the same range of distortion, the integration limits are restricted to the intersection of their D ranges. Extrapolation is not performed. Precision: Log-transforming small bitrate values can lead to numerical instability if R \le 0. Ensure R > 0. Monotonicity: RD curves should be monotonic. If a method produces non-monotonic RD points (e.g., higher bitrate for lower quality), the interpolation may produce artifacts. Pre-processing to remove non-Pareto-optimal points is recommended. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.interpolate import CubicSpline def calculatebjontegaarddeltarate(pointsa, pointsb): """ Calculate BD-Rate between two rate-distortion curves. Args: pointsa: List of tuples (bitrate, psnr) for method A. pointsb: List of tuples (bitrate, psnr) for method B. Returns: float: BD-Rate percentage. """ # 1. Sort by PSNR (distortion) pointsa = sorted(pointsa, key=lambda p: p[1]) pointsb = sorted(pointsb, key=lambda p: p[1]) # 2. Extract arrays ra, da = zip(pointsa) rb, db = zip(pointsb) # 3. Log-transform bitrate xa = np.log(ra) xb = np.log(rb) # 4. Determine integration range (intersection of PSNR ranges) dmin = max(min(da), min(db)) dmax = min(max(da), max(db)) if dmin >= dmax: return 0.0 # No overlap # 5. Create cubic splines # Note: CubicSpline requires at least 4 points for full cubic, # but scipy handles fewer with 'not-a-knot' or similar boundary conditions. # For robustness, ensure sufficient points. csa = CubicSpline(da, xa) csb = CubicSpline(db, xb) # 6. Integrate the difference between curves # We integrate from dmin to dmax # Using numerical integration (trapezoidal rule) for simplicity and robustness numpoints = 1000 dint = np.linspace(dmin, dmax, numpoints) xdiff = csa(dint) - csb(dint) # Area under the curve of the difference area = np.trapz(xdiff, dint) # 7. Calculate average log-bitrate difference deltay = dmax - dmin avglogdiff = area / deltay # 8. Convert to percentage bdrate = 100.0 (np.exp(avglogdiff) - 1.0) return bdrate This is the primary application context for BD-Rate. It is used to compare compression algorithms (e.g., SPC-NeRF vs. VQRF) by evaluating their overall efficiency across multiple quality levels. It is chosen when a single scalar metric is needed to summarize the trade-off between model size/bitrate and rendering quality (PSNR). Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(N \log N) for sorting, where N is the number of RD points. Spline fitting and integration are O(N) or O(N \log N) depending on the implementation. Memory: O(N) to store the RD points and spline coefficients. Measured Performance: In comparisons of SPC-NeRF against VQRF on the Synthetic-NeRF dataset, BD-Rate showed a 28% bit saving for the base configuration and 32% for the HR configuration. BD-Rate is sensitive to the range of distortion covered. If one method significantly outperforms another only at very high or very low bitrates, the BD-Rate may not reflect the practical utility if the operating range is limited. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Provides a single, comparable metric for overall RD performance. Accounts for the entire curve, not just a single operating point. Limitations: Assumes a smooth, continuous RD curve. Discrete, sparse RD points can lead to inaccurate interpolation. It does not indicate where the gains occur (e.g., low bitrate vs. high bitrate). When to Use: Use when comparing two compression methods across a wide range of bitrates and quality levels. Use when a single percentage metric is required for ablation studies or final reporting. When Not to Use: Do not use if the RD curves do not overlap significantly in distortion range. Do not use if the RD points are too sparse to form a reliable cubic spline. BD-Rate was introduced by Bjøntegaard in the context of video compression standards. It has been adapted for evaluating neural radiance field compression methods, such as SPC-NeRF, to provide a fair comparison against prior works like VQRF. The metric relies on piecewise cubic interpolation to estimate the continuous RD curve from discrete experimental points.
