name: Perceptually-motivated variance metric
head: AO estimation error metric, log-mean and log-gradient MSE metric
body: The perceptually-motivated variance metric quantifies the error between an 8-bit ambient occlusion (AO) approximation T and a high-fidelity ray-traced reference R. It differs from raw pixel Mean Squared Error (MSE) by operating on log-transformed values and spatial gradients, thereby aligning with human visual sensitivity to radiance and its changes. This metric is specifically designed for evaluating AO approximations where reflected ambient radiance is linear in accessibility. Inputs and Outputs Input T: An 8-bit "test" accessibility approximation image, where each pixel value T{x,y} satisfies 0 < T{x,y} < 255. Input R: A ray-traced reference image used as ground truth, typically computed with 5000 samples per pixel to ensure high accuracy. Output E[T]: A scalar value representing the total perceptual error. Data Structures Images are treated as 2D arrays of floating-point values derived from 8-bit integers. Gradients are computed as 2D arrays of the same dimensions as the input images. Mathematical Definitions 1. Modified Logarithm (\log^\dagger): To handle values near zero and preserve sign, the metric uses a modified logarithm defined as: \log^\dagger x = \text{sign}(x) \cdot \log(|x| + 1) This function avoids the singularity at x=0 by adding 1 to the absolute value before taking the natural logarithm. 2. Mean Squared Error (MSE): \text{MSE}[A] computes the variance (mean squared deviation from the mean) of the values in array A across all pixels. Algorithm Steps 1. Compute the log-transformed test values: L{test} = \log^\dagger T. 2. Compute the log-transformed reference values: L{ref} = \log^\dagger R. 3. Calculate the variance of the log-transformed test image: \text{MSE}{mean} = \text{MSE}[L{test}]. 4. Compute the horizontal spatial gradient of T, denoted \frac{\partial T}{\partial x}, and the vertical spatial gradient of T, denoted \frac{\partial T}{\partial y}. 5. Apply \log^\dagger to each gradient component for both test and reference: G{test, x} = \log^\dagger \frac{\partial T}{\partial x} G{test, y} = \log^\dagger \frac{\partial T}{\partial y} G{ref, x} = \log^\dagger \frac{\partial R}{\partial x} G{ref, y} = \log^\dagger \frac{\partial R}{\partial y} 6. Calculate the variance for the horizontal gradients: \text{MSE}{x} = \text{MSE}[G{test, x}]. 7. Calculate the variance for the vertical gradients: \text{MSE}{y} = \text{MSE}[G{test, y}]. 8. Combine the errors using the following formula: E[T] = \text{MSE}{mean} + \frac{1}{2} \left( \text{MSE}{x} + \text{MSE}{y} \right) Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def logdag(x: float) -> float: """Modified logarithm that preserves sign and avoids singularity at 0.""" return math.copysign(1.0, x) math.log(abs(x) + 1.0) def mse(values: list[float]) -> float: """Computes the variance (mean squared deviation from the mean) of a list of values.""" n = len(values) if n == 0: return 0.0 meanval = sum(values) / n return sum((v - meanval) 2 for v in values) / n def computegradients(img: list[list[float]]) -> tuple[list[list[float]], list[list[float]]]: """Computes horizontal and vertical gradients using forward differences.""" height = len(img) width = len(img[0]) gradx = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] grady = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] for i in range(height): for j in range(width - 1): gradx[i][j] = img[i][j+1] - img[i][j] gradx[i][width-1] = img[i][width-2] - img[i][width-1] if width > 1 else 0.0 for i in range(height - 1): for j in range(width): grady[i][j] = img[i+1][j] - img[i][j] for j in range(width): grady[height-1][j] = img[height-2][j] - img[height-1][j] if height > 1 else 0.0 return gradx, grady def computeperceptualerror(T: list[list[float]], R: list[list[float]]) -> float: """Computes the perceptually-motivated variance metric.""" height = len(T) width = len(T[0]) # Step 1 & 2: Log-transform test and reference Ltest = [[logdag(T[i][j]) for j in range(width)] for i in range(height)] Lref = [[logdag(R[i][j]) for j in range(width)] for i in range(height)] # Step 3: Variance of log-transformed test image msemean = mse([Ltest[i][j] for i in range(height) for j in range(width)]) # Step 4: Compute gradients Tgradx, Tgrady = computegradients(T) Rgradx, Rgrady = computegradients(R) # Step 5: Log-transform gradients Tgradxlog = [[logdag(Tgradx[i][j]) for j in range(width)] for i in range(height)] Tgradylog = [[logdag(Tgrady[i][j]) for j in range(width)] for i in range(height)] Rgradxlog = [[logdag(Rgradx[i][j]) for j in range(width)] for i in range(height)] Rgradylog = [[logdag(Rgrady[i][j]) for j in range(width)] for i in range(height)] # Step 6 & 7: Variance of log-transformed gradients msex = mse([Tgradxlog[i][j] for i in range(height) for j in range(width)]) msey = mse([Tgradylog[i][j] for i in range(height) for j in range(width)]) # Step 8: Combine errors return msemean + 0.5 (msex + msey) Parameters Reference Sampling: The reference image R should be computed using 5000 samples per pixel to ensure high accuracy. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Zero Values: The logarithmic transformation is undefined at 0. The metric uses \log^\dagger, which adds 1 inside the log and preserves the original sign, preventing numerical singularities when T or gradients approach 0. Gradient Boundaries: The sources do not specify boundary conditions for gradient computation. Implementers must define how to handle pixels at the image edges (e.g., clamping, replication, or exclusion). Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of pixels, as it involves a constant number of passes over the image data (log, gradient, MSE). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store intermediate gradient and log-transformed images. Strengths: Aligns with human visual perception by tracking both absolute radiance and spatial changes with decreasing marginal sensitivity. It is particularly appropriate for reflected ambient radiance which is linear in accessibility. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than raw pixel MSE due to gradient calculation and logarithmic transformations. It is specific to AO approximation evaluation and may not generalize to other rendering metrics without modification. When to Use: When evaluating the perceptual quality of ambient occlusion approximations against a high-quality reference. When Not to Use: When computational efficiency is paramount and perceptual accuracy is secondary, or when evaluating metrics other than AO. The metric was introduced in the context of Ambient Occlusion Volumes (AOV). It was designed to provide a quantitative measure of error that correlates better with human visual perception than standard pixel-wise MSE, specifically for evaluating AO approximation algorithms. The method is detailed in the paper "Ambient Occlusion Volumes". name: Depth Accuracy Metrics
head: AbsRel, RMSE
body: Depth Accuracy Metrics evaluate the geometric fidelity of predicted depth maps against ground truth data in radiance field optimization pipelines. They quantify scale- and translation-invariant errors on valid depth pixels. They are used to evaluate depth prior quality and monocular depth estimation outputs in NeRF pipelines. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ground truth depth map d, predicted depth map \hat{d}, and a binary validity mask identifying pixels k=1,...,K with valid ground truth depth. Outputs: Scalar error values for RMSE, RMSE log, AbsRel, and SqRel. Data Structures: Depth maps are represented as 2D arrays of floating-point values. The validity mask is a boolean array of the same dimensions, where True indicates a pixel with valid ground truth. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Normalize depth to a consistent range if required by the dataset (e.g., [0, 1] for H3DS). 2. Masking: Filter to pixels k=1,...,K with valid ground truth depth. For specific datasets, mask both output and ground truth to the non-empty region predicted by the baseline. 3. Computation: Calculate the selected metric using the formulas below for all K valid pixels. Formulas: Let K be the number of pixels with valid ground truth depth. 1. Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE): RMSE(d, \hat{d}) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1,...,K} (dk - \hat{d}k)^2} 2. Log RMSE (RMSE log): RMSE{log}(d, \hat{d}) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1,...,K} (\log dk - \log \hat{d}k)^2} 3. Absolute Relative Error (AbsRel): AbsRel(d, \hat{d}) = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1,...,K} \frac{|dk - \hat{d}k|}{dk} 4. Squared Relative Error (SqRel): SqRel(d, \hat{d}) = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1,...,K} \frac{(dk - \hat{d}k)^2}{dk} Parameters: K: Number of pixels with valid ground truth depth. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometry Collapse: In methods like HeadNeRF, geometry may collapse to a plane in front of the subject, requiring careful mask handling to avoid misleading error scores. Invalid Pixels: Errors must only be computed on valid depth pixels to avoid skewing results. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computedepthmetrics(gtdepth: np.ndarray, preddepth: np.ndarray, validmask: np.ndarray) -> dict: """ Compute depth accuracy metrics for valid pixels. Args: gtdepth: Ground truth depth map (H, W). preddepth: Predicted depth map (H, W). validmask: Boolean mask of valid pixels (H, W). Returns: Dictionary containing RMSE, RMSElog, AbsRel, SqRel. """ # Extract valid pixels gtvalid = gtdepth[validmask] predvalid = preddepth[validmask] K = len(gtvalid) if K == 0: return {"RMSE": np.nan, "RMSElog": np.nan, "AbsRel": np.nan, "SqRel": np.nan} # RMSE rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean((gtvalid - predvalid) 2)) # RMSE log rmselog = np.sqrt(np.mean((np.log(gtvalid) - np.log(predvalid)) 2)) # AbsRel absrel = np.mean(np.abs(gtvalid - predvalid) / gtvalid) # SqRel sqrel = np.mean((gtvalid - predvalid) 2 / gtvalid) return { "RMSE": rmse, "RMSElog": rmselog, "AbsRel": absrel, "SqRel": sqrel } A set of quantitative metrics used to evaluate the accuracy of predicted depth maps against ground truth, plus a consistency metric for multi-view alignment. These metrics assess the fidelity of monocular depth estimation (MDE) modules within radiance field optimization pipelines, distinguishing between per-image accuracy and global scene consistency. Time Complexity: O(K), where K is the number of valid pixels. Memory Complexity: O(K) to store valid pixel values during computation. Strengths: RMSE provides a direct measure of geometric error magnitude. SqRel emphasizes errors relative to ground truth depth. Limitations: Metrics are sensitive to outliers in depth predictions. SqRel heavily penalizes errors in regions with small ground truth depth values. Originating from evaluations in neural radiance field (NeRF) research, these metrics were adopted to assess the geometric quality of depth priors and monocular depth estimation modules. The H3DS dataset introduced specific protocols for scale- and translation-invariant evaluation. The metrics are used in works such as DäRF and studies on outdoor NeRFs. name: MDE evaluation metrics
head: Depth consistency metrics, Monocular Depth Estimation metrics
body: A set of quantitative metrics used to evaluate the accuracy of predicted depth maps against ground truth, plus a consistency metric for multi-view alignment. These metrics assess the fidelity of monocular depth estimation modules within radiance field optimization pipelines, distinguishing between per-image accuracy and global scene consistency. The evaluation framework relies on comparing a predicted depth map \bar{D} against a ground truth depth map D^{GT} at each pixel coordinate p. The metrics are computed over the set of valid pixels in an image I. For multi-view consistency, a scene-level scaling factor s is computed to align predicted depths with ground truth without per-frame fitting. This factor is derived from the median ratio of ground truth to predicted depth across all images in a scene. Let S be the set of images belonging to a single scene, and N = |S| be the total number of images in S. The scaling factor s is defined as: s = \frac{1}{N} \sum{Ii \in S} \text{median}\left(\frac{Di^{GT}}{\bar{D}i}\right) where Di^{GT} and \bar{D}i are the ground truth and predicted depth maps for image Ii. This metric evaluates view consistency by applying a single scale factor to the entire scene rather than optimizing per-frame. Measures the mean absolute relative difference between predicted and ground truth depth. \text{AbsRel} = \frac{1}{|I|} \sum{p \in I} \frac{|\bar{D}(p) - D^{GT}(p)|}{D^{GT}(p)} Computes the mean of the squared relative differences. \text{SqRel} = \frac{1}{|I|} \sum{p \in I} \frac{|\bar{D}(p) - D^{GT}(p)|^2}{D^{GT}(p)} The square root of the mean squared error between predicted and ground truth depths. \text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{|I|} \sum{p \in I} |\bar{D}(p) - D^{GT}(p)|^2} Computes the RMSE on the logarithmic scale of depths. \text{RMSE log} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{|I|} \sum{p \in I} |\log \bar{D}(p) - \log D^{GT}(p)|^2} These metrics are used to evaluate monocular depth estimation modules within radiance field optimization pipelines. The specific formulation for the scene-level consistency scaling factor s follows prior work cited as [64] in the source. The implementation details, such as the use of the median for consistency evaluation, were adopted to ensure fair comparison with relevant prior work. name: Discrete Wavelet Transform Loss
head: DW loss, Discrete Wavelet Loss, LDW
body: The Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) Loss is a regularization term for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that minimizes the difference between the frequency representations of rendered and ground-truth images by decomposing them into sub-bands. It addresses high-frequency overfitting in few-shot NeRF training by explicitly prioritizing low-frequency learning during early stages. Unlike its sibling MSE Loss and PSNR Conversion, which compares pixel-wise values globally, the DW loss operates on local structures using patch-based sampling to supervise low and mid-frequency components. The method decomposes rendered images into frequency sub-bands using the Discrete Wavelet Transform and calculates a weighted sum of squared errors between the rendered and ground-truth coefficients, with higher weights assigned to low-frequency sub-bands. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: I: Rendered image (RGB) from a batch of adjacently sampled rays. I{gt}: Ground-truth image corresponding to the same camera pose. \lambda{sb}: Weighting factors for each sub-band sb \in \{LL, LH, HL, HH\}. K{DW}: Iteration interval for computing the loss. T{DW}: Maximum iteration after which the loss is disabled. Outputs: L{DW}: Scalar loss value. Data Structures Wavelet Filters: 1D low-pass filter \ell and high-pass filter h. Common types are Haar (n=1) or Daubechies (dbN, e.g., db2, db3). 2D Matrices: L: Low-pass 2D matrix constructed by shifting rows of \ell. H: High-pass 2D matrix. If \ell is orthogonal, h is derived from \ell, and H is derived from L. Sub-bands: Four 2D arrays of size \frac{H}{2} \times \frac{W}{2} (quarter the size of the original image): I{LL}: Low frequencies in both directions. I{LH}: Low horizontal, high vertical frequencies. I{HL}: High horizontal, low vertical frequencies. I{HH}: High frequencies in both directions. Numbered Steps 1. Ray Sampling: Sample rays in patches to form a 2D image I. This ensures rays are adjacent, forming a square grid compatible with 2D DWT. Use random ray sampling for the standard MSE loss to capture global structure. 2. Filter Construction: Construct the 2D low-pass matrix L by shifting rows of the 1D low-pass wavelet filter \ell. Construct the high-pass matrix H similarly using \ell (if orthogonal) or derived h. 3. DWT Decomposition: Apply the DWT to I and I{gt} using L and H to obtain the four sub-bands: I{LL} = L I L^T, \quad I{LH} = H I L^T I{HL} = L I H^T, \quad I{HH} = H I H^T (Note: The source notation I{LL} = L I L^T implies convolution/transform operations; standard DWT implementation involves filtering and downsampling). 4. Loss Calculation: Compute the squared Euclidean distance between corresponding sub-bands of I and I{gt}, weighted by \lambda{sb}. 5. Lazy Regularization: Calculate L{DW} only every K{DW} iterations. Stop calculating it entirely after iteration T{DW} to facilitate high-frequency learning in later stages. 6. Combination: Combine L{DW} with the photometric MSE loss L{MSE} and other regularizations. Formula The total Discrete Wavelet Loss is defined as: L{DW} = \sum{sb \in \{LL,LH,HL,HH\}} \lambda{sb} ||I{sb} - I{sb}^{gt}||^22 Where: I{sb} and I{sb}^{gt} are the sub-band images for the rendered and ground-truth views, respectively. ||\cdot||^22 denotes the squared L2 norm (sum of squared differences) over all pixels in the sub-band. \lambda{sb} is the weight for sub-band sb. The source notes initially included a term \frac{\sum{r \in R} ||c(r) - c{gt}(r)||^22}{|R|}, but this is the definition of L{MSE}, not L{DW}. The formula above represents the specific DW component as described in the text. Parameters Sub-band Weights (\lambda{sb}): \lambda{LL}: Typically 0.4 for LLFF dataset, 0.04 for NeRF-Synthetic dataset. \lambda{LH}, \lambda{HL}, \lambda{HH}: Typically 0.2 for LLFF dataset, 0.02 for NeRF-Synthetic dataset. \lambda{LL} > \lambda{other} to prioritize low-frequency learning. Lazy Regularization: K{DW}: 10 iterations for LLFF, 150 iterations for NeRF-Synthetic. T{DW}: 5000 iterations. Wavelet Type: Haar (n=1) or Daubechies (db2, db3). Higher-order wavelets provide finer decomposition details but show no significant performance difference in final metrics. Patch Size: 192 \times 192 square patches (requiring 36864 rays). Sub-band Size: Sub-bands are quarter the size of the original image. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computedwtloss(renderedimage, gtimage, wavelettype='haar', lambdall=0.4, lambdaother=0.2, currentiter=0, tdw=5000, kdw=10): # Lazy Regularization: Skip if not at interval or past max iteration if currentiter % kdw != 0 or currentiter > tdw: return 0.0 # 1. Get 1D wavelet filters if wavelettype == 'haar': l = [1.0 / 20.5, 1.0 / 20.5] h = [1.0 / 20.5, -1.0 / 20.5] elif wavelettype == 'db2': l = [0.4829629131445341, 0.836516303737469, 0.2241438680420134, -0.1294095225509214] h = [-0.1294095225509214, -0.2241438680420134, 0.836516303737469, -0.4829629131445341] else: raise ValueError("Unsupported wavelet type") # 2. Decompose images into sub-bands Ill, Ilh, Ihl, Ihh = apply2ddwt(renderedimage, l, h) gtll, gtlh, gthl, gthh = apply2ddwt(gtimage, l, h) # 3. Calculate weighted squared error lossll = sum((Ill[r][c][ch] - gtll[r][c][ch])2 for r in range(len(Ill)) for c in range(len(Ill[0])) for ch in range(3)) losslh = sum((Ilh[r][c][ch] - gtlh[r][c][ch])2 for r in range(len(Ilh)) for c in range(len(Ilh[0])) for ch in range(3)) losshl = sum((Ihl[r][c][ch] - gthl[r][c][ch])2 for r in range(len(Ihl)) for c in range(len(Ihl[0])) for ch in range(3)) losshh = sum((Ihh[r][c][ch] - gthh[r][c][ch])2 for r in range(len(Ihh)) for c in range(len(Ihh[0])) for ch in range(3)) loss = (lambdall lossll) + (lambdaother losslh) + (lambdaother losshl) + (lambdaother losshh) return loss def apply2ddwt(image, l, h): # image is H x W x 3 H, W, C = len(image), len(image[0]), len(image[0][0]) # Filter rows rowll = convolve1d(image, l, axis=1) rowlh = convolve1d(image, h, axis=1) # Downsample rows rowllds = rowll[::2,:,:] rowlhds = rowlh[::2,:,:] # Filter columns ll = convolve1d(rowllds, l, axis=0) lh = convolve1d(rowlhds, l, axis=0) hl = convolve1d(rowllds, h, axis=0) hh = convolve1d(rowlhds, h, axis=0) # Downsample columns llds = ll[::2,:,:] lhds = lh[::2,:,:] hlds = hl[::2,:,:] hhds = hh[::2,:,:] return llds, lhds, hlds, hhds def convolve1d(data, kernel, axis): # 1D convolution with zero-padding # axis=0: rows, axis=1: columns if axis == 1: # Convolve along columns H, W, C = len(data), len(data[0]), len(data[0][0]) out = [[[0.0]C for in range(W)] for in range(H)] klen = len(kernel) pad = klen // 2 for r in range(H): for c in range(W): for ch in range(C): val = 0.0 for k in range(klen): idx = c - pad + k if 0 <= idx < W: val += data[r][idx][ch] kernel[k] else: pass # Zero-padding at boundaries out[r][c][ch] = val return out else: # Convolve along rows H, W, C = len(data), len(data[0]), len(data[0][0]) out = [[[0.0]C for in range(W)] for in range(H)] klen = len(kernel) pad = klen // 2 for r in range(H): for c in range(W): for ch in range(C): val = 0.0 for k in range(klen): idx = r - pad + k if 0 <= idx < H: val += data[idx][c][ch] kernel[k] else: pass # Zero-padding at boundaries out[r][c][ch] = val return out Edge Cases and Pitfalls Sub-band Size: Sub-bands are quarter the size of the original image. If the rendered image I is too small, sub-bands become too coarse and visually meaningless. This requires large images, incurring heavy computational overhead (N^2 rays for an N-sized square patch). High-Frequency Content: DWT high-frequency components include not just fine structural details but also specularity and light-dependent effects, which are not disentangled by the transform. Auxiliary Nature: The DW loss does not eliminate high-frequency overfitting because it is auxiliary to the photometric MSE loss, which compares pixel-wise differences regardless of frequency. Time Complexity: The DWT computation is O(N^2) for an N \times N image patch. Due to the large number of rays required for a meaningful patch (192 \times 192 = 36864 rays), it incurs significant overhead. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the rendered image, ground-truth image, and intermediate sub-bands. The lazy regularization (computing every K{DW} iterations) mitigates memory and time costs. Performance: On the 3-shot LLFF benchmark, DWTNeRF with DW loss/DB2 achieved PSNR 20.23, SSIM 0.678, LPIPS 0.193, compared to CombiNeRF baseline PSNR 20.12, SSIM 0.676, LPIPS 0.197. Strengths: Explicitly prioritizes low-frequency learning, which is crucial for few-shot NeRF convergence. Combines global (random ray sampling for MSE) and local (patch-based for DW) structure supervision. Limitations: Does not disentangle high-frequency components like specularity. High-frequency overfitting may still occur due to the presence of MSE loss. Sub-bands are quarter the size of the original image; if the rendered image is too small, sub-bands become too coarse, requiring large images that incur heavy computational overhead (N^2 rays for an N-sized square patch). When to Use: Few-shot NeRF training where low-frequency convergence is slow or unstable. When Not to Use: When computational resources are limited and patch-based sampling is too expensive, or when high-frequency details (specularity) are the primary focus and need to be preserved without interference from low-frequency bias. The Discrete Wavelet Transform Loss was introduced in the DWTNeRF paper to boost few-shot Neural Radiance Fields. It builds on the CombiNeRF framework, which combines regularization and model-based approaches. The method leverages the Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) to decompose images into frequency sub-bands, allowing for explicit supervision of low frequencies during early training stages. The paper evaluates the method on the LLFF and NeRF-Synthetic datasets under few-shot conditions. name: RMSE Loss for Constant Model
head: RMSE for Constant Model
body: Calculates the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) between observed intensity values and a predicted constant intensity model parameterized by density (\sigma) and step size (q). It serves as a photometric consistency loss in differentiable volume rendering, specifically fitting a constant radiance assumption along a ray. Unlike the parent MSE Loss and PSNR Conversion which operates on raw RGB predictions, this method explicitly models the physical integration of a constant source over a ray segment. Inputs: intensity: A list or array of observed intensity values Ik for k=0 \dots N-1. sigma: The volume density \sigma (scalar). q: The step size or integration parameter q (scalar). ds: The distance step between samples (scalar). Outputs: rmse: The Root Mean Squared Error (scalar). Data Structures: intensity: Array of floats. squared: Accumulator for squared errors (float). Steps: 1. Validation: Check if intensity is empty or ds <= 0. If invalid, return infinity. 2. Initialization: Set squared = 0. 3. Iteration: For each sample index k from 0 to intensity.size() - 1: a. Calculate the predicted intensity for the constant model. The source notes imply a function constantintensity(intensity.front(), sigma, q, k ds). In a standard constant volume rendering model with density \sigma and step size ds, the transmittance at distance t is T(t) = e^{-\sigma t}. The expected intensity at sample k (distance tk = k \cdot ds) given a constant source intensity I0 (here taken as intensity.front()) is: I{pred}(k) = I0 \cdot (1 - e^{-\sigma \cdot ds}) \cdot \sum{j=0}^{k-1} e^{-\sigma \cdot j \cdot ds} + I0 \cdot e^{-\sigma \cdot k \cdot ds} However, the source notes specifically reference constantintensity(intensity.front(), sigma, q, k ds). Without the explicit formula for constantintensity in the provided text, we assume it computes the theoretical constant-radiance accumulation. A common simplification for constant \sigma and constant radiance c is I(t) = c(1 - e^{-\sigma t}). If q represents the total length or a scaling factor, the implementation must follow the specific constantintensity logic. Given the ambiguity, the pseudocode below uses a placeholder comment for the specific physics model, but the structure is strictly as defined in. b. Calculate error: error = I{pred} - intensity[k]. c. Update accumulator: squared += error^2. 4. Finalize: Return \sqrt{\frac{squared}{N}}, where N is intensity.size(). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rmselossconstantmodel(intensity, sigma, q, ds): """ Calculates RMSE between observed intensities and a constant intensity model. Args: intensity (list[float]): Observed intensity values. sigma (float): Volume density. q (float): Integration parameter/step scaling. ds (float): Distance step between samples. Returns: float: RMSE value. """ # Step 1: Validate inputs if not intensity or ds <= 0: return float('inf') n = len(intensity) squared = 0.0 # Step 2 & 3: Iterate and accumulate squared errors for k in range(n): # Calculate predicted intensity for the constant model. # The source specifies: constantintensity(intensity.front(), sigma, q, k ds) # intensity.front() is intensity[0]. # Note: The exact mathematical definition of constantintensity is not provided in the source text. # Assuming a standard constant radiance c along a ray with density sigma: # Ipred(t) = c (1 - exp(-sigma t)) where t = k ds. # However, 'q' is passed. If q is a step count or scaling, it must be incorporated. # Given the note "constantintensity(intensity.front(), sigma, q, k ds)", # we implement a generic call that must be defined by the specific physics model. # For the purpose of this article, we assume the function exists or is defined as: # Ipred = intensity[0] (1 - math.exp(-sigma (k ds))) # if q is not used in the exponent. If q is the step size, ds might be redundant or q=ds. # We stick to the structure: t = k ds # Placeholder for the specific constantintensity implementation referenced in. # In many constant-volume contexts, if the source is constant I0, the accumulated intensity # at depth t is I0 (1 - exp(-sigma t)). predicted = intensity[0] (1 - math.exp(-sigma t)) error = predicted - intensity[k] squared += error error # Step 4: Return RMSE return math.sqrt(squared / n) Parameters: sigma: Volume density. Typical values depend on the scene scale. q: Integration parameter. Value not explicitly defined in the source notes beyond being passed to the model function. ds: Distance step. Must be > 0. Edge Cases: Empty intensity list: Returns infinity. Non-positive ds: Returns infinity. Computes the error between rasterized depth and ground truth depth, optionally masking by silhouette and valid depth masks depending on training state. It is used in Gaussian Splatting-based SLAM/NeRF optimization (SplaTAM). Definition: Calculates RMSE and L1 error for depth maps, applying masks for silhouette presence and valid depth ranges. Steps: 1. Compute squared difference between rasterized depth D{rast} and ground truth depth D{gt}, multiplied by presence silhouette mask M{sil}. 2. Multiply result by valid depth mask M{valid} to exclude invalid pixels (e.g., depth \le 0). 3. Compute RMSE by summing the masked squared differences and dividing by the sum of the valid depth mask. 4. Compute L1 error similarly using absolute difference. Formula: For the case where mappingiters==0 and not addnewgaussians: rmse = \frac{\sum{i,j} \sqrt{((D{rast} - D{gt}) \cdot M{sil})^2} \cdot M{valid}}{\sum{i,j} M{valid}} Where: D{rast}: Rasterized depth. D{gt}: Ground truth depth. M{sil}: Presence silhouette mask. M{valid}: Valid depth mask, defined as (curr\data['depth'] > 0). Parameters: mappingiters: Number of mapping iterations. If 0, silhouette mask is applied to depth error. addnewgaussians: Boolean flag. If false, silhouette mask is applied to depth error. Pitfalls: Invalid depth values (\le 0) are excluded by multiplying by validdepthmask. Failure to apply this mask leads to incorrect error calculations for pixels with no valid depth observation. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of intensity samples. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, excluding input storage. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides a direct metric for constant-radiance assumption validity. Limitations: Assumes constant radiance along the ray, which may not hold for complex scenes. Sensitive to invalid depth or empty inputs. When to use: When optimizing for scenes or ray segments where constant radiance is a valid approximation, or as a baseline loss component. When not to use: For scenes with high dynamic range or complex lighting variations where constant intensity is a poor model. name: Depth RMSE and L1 Calculation
head: 2D Depth Map Evaluation, Depth Error Metrics, Depth RMSE/L1
body: Computes the error between rasterized depth and ground truth depth, optionally masking by silhouette and valid depth masks depending on training state. It provides accuracy and completeness metrics between two depth maps, supporting absolute, relative, and log-squared error variants. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rasterized depth map D{rast}, ground truth depth map D{gt}, presence silhouette mask M{sil}, valid depth mask M{valid}, and training state flags mappingiters and addnewgaussians. Outputs: RMSE value, L1 error value. Data Structures: D{rast}: Float tensor of shape (H, W), values > 0 for valid depth. D{gt}: Float tensor of shape (H, W), values > 0 for valid depth. M{sil}: Boolean/Float tensor of shape (H, W), 1 where silhouette is present, 0 otherwise. M{valid}: Boolean/Float tensor of shape (H, W), 1 where depth is valid, 0 otherwise. Steps: 1. Determine if silhouette masking is active. If mappingiters == 0 and not addnewgaussians, apply M{sil} to the depth error calculation. 2. Create a validity mask M{valid} where D{rast} > 0 and 0 < D{gt} < 10. Note: Some implementations define M{valid} simply as (D{gt} > 0) to exclude invalid depth values (\le 0). 3. Apply masks to the depth maps. Multiply the difference by M{sil} (if active) and M{valid}. 4. Compute RMSE by summing the masked squared differences and dividing by the sum of the valid depth mask. 5. Compute L1 error similarly using absolute difference. Formulas: For the case where mappingiters==0 and not addnewgaussians: rmse = \frac{\sum{i,j} \sqrt{((D{rast} - D{gt}) \cdot M{sil})^2} \cdot M{valid}}{\sum{i,j} M{valid}} where D{rast} is rasterized depth, D{gt} is ground truth depth, M{sil} is presence silhouette mask, and M{valid} is valid depth mask. General RMSE: RMSE = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum (dp - dt)^2} where dp is predicted depth, dt is target depth, and N is the number of valid pixels. L1 Error: L1 = \frac{1}{N}\sum |dp - dt| Other variants mentioned: Absolute difference: |dp - dt|. Relative difference: |dp - dt| / dt. Squared relative: (dp - dt)^2 / dt. Log squared difference: (\log dp - \log dt)^2. LogRMSE: \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum (\log dp - \log dt)^2}. Accuracy threshold ratio: r = \max(dt/dp, dp/dt). Compute ratios r < 1.25, r < 1.25^2, r < 1.25^3. Parameters: mappingiters: Number of mapping iterations. If 0, silhouette mask is applied to depth error. addnewgaussians: Boolean flag. If false, silhouette mask is applied to depth error. Pitfalls: Invalid depth values (\le 0) are excluded by multiplying by validdepthmask, which is defined as (curr\data['depth'] > 0). Ensure M{valid} handles the boundary condition 0 < D{gt} < 10 if specified by the source, or just D{gt} > 0 if following the other source. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computedepthmetrics(drast, dgt, msil, mappingiters, addnewgaussians): """ Compute RMSE and L1 error between rasterized and ground truth depth. Args: drast: Tensor (H, W), rasterized depth. dgt: Tensor (H, W), ground truth depth. msil: Tensor (H, W), silhouette mask (1 if present, 0 otherwise). mappingiters: int, number of mapping iterations. addnewgaussians: bool, whether new Gaussians are being added. Returns: rmse: float, Root Mean Squared Error. l1: float, L1 Error. """ # Step 1: Determine if silhouette masking is active usesilmask = (mappingiters == 0) and (not addnewgaussians) # Step 2: Create validity mask # Source suggests 0 < dgt < 10, Source suggests dgt > 0 # We use the more restrictive one from if available, otherwise # Note: The exact threshold 10 might be dataset-specific. # Here we follow for simplicity as it's more common in SLAM contexts, # but note the discrepancy. mvalid = (dgt > 0) & (drast > 0) # Step 3: Apply masks if usesilmask: # Multiply difference by silhouette mask diff = (drast - dgt) msil else: diff = drast - dgt # Multiply by valid mask to exclude invalid pixels maskeddiff = diff mvalid # Step 4: Compute RMSE # Sum of squared differences sumsqdiff = torch.sum(maskeddiff 2) # Sum of valid mask (number of valid pixels) sumvalid = torch.sum(mvalid) # Avoid division by zero if sumvalid == 0: return 0.0, 0.0 rmse = torch.sqrt(sumsqdiff / sumvalid) # Step 5: Compute L1 error sumabsdiff = torch.sum(torch.abs(maskeddiff)) l1 = sumabsdiff / sumvalid return rmse.item(), l1.item() Not given in the sources. name: Normalized L1 Loss
head: L1 Loss, Sparse Loss Calculation, normalized L1
body: Computes a normalized L1 loss between a reconstructed image and an original image, scaling the loss to the [0, 1] range. It is used in sparse pixel sampling optimization pipelines to provide an error metric for adaptive Gaussian densification and pruning. Inputs: reconstructedimage: Tensor of predicted RGB values. originalimage: Tensor of ground truth RGB values. Outputs: l1lossnorm: Tensor of normalized L1 error per pixel. Steps: 1. Compute the absolute difference between the reconstructed and original images: \Delta = |\text{reconstructed\image} - \text{original\image}|. 2. Compute the mean absolute error along the channel dimension: \text{l1\loss} = \text{mean}(\Delta, \text{dim}=0). The result is detached from the computation graph. 3. Compute the minimum and maximum values of l1loss across all spatial elements: \text{min\val} = \min(\text{l1\loss}), \text{max\val} = \max(\text{l1\loss}). 4. Normalize the loss using min-max scaling: \text{l1\loss\norm} = (\text{l1\loss} - \text{min\val}) / (\text{max\val} - \text{min\val}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def normalizedl1loss(reconstructedimage, originalimage): diff = abs(reconstructedimage - originalimage) l1loss = mean(diff, dim=0) # Detach from computation graph minval = min(l1loss) maxval = max(l1loss) if maxval == minval: return l1loss 0 l1lossnorm = (l1loss - minval) / (maxval - minval) return l1lossnorm Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: If all pixel errors are identical, the denominator becomes zero and the result is undefined. The normalization is global per image. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. name: Masked and Weighted Losses
head: Area Loss Scaling, Density-based Loss for Shape Addition, Bayer Masking for Loss Supervision, Edge Loss Regularization
body: Masked and Weighted Losses is a family of techniques that modify the standard photometric error computation in differentiable volume rendering by applying spatial masks or per-pixel weights to the loss function. It solves the problem of training instability and evaluation bias caused by invalid background regions, sensor artifacts, multiscale resolution disparities, or structural inconsistencies. It sets itself apart from its sibling MSE Loss and PSNR Conversion by introducing selective suppression or amplification of error terms rather than computing a global average, and from Masked Volume Metrics by focusing on training-time gradient correction rather than evaluation-time metric definition. The core mechanism involves computing a base loss L{base} (typically MSE or Huber) between the rendered prediction P and the ground truth G, then applying a mask M or weight W before aggregation. For masking, the loss is computed as: L = \frac{1}{N{valid}} \sum{i} Mi \cdot L{base}(Pi, Gi) where Mi \in \{0, 1\} is a binary mask indicating whether ray i or froxel i contributes to the loss, and N{valid} is the count of valid elements (where Mi=1). For weighting, the loss is computed as: L = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i} Wi \cdot L{base}(Pi, Gi) where Wi is a scalar weight for element i. Common masking strategies include: 1. Validity Masks: Excluding rays that do not intersect scene geometry or froxels that are empty in both the rendered volume and ground truth. 2. Sensor Masks: Applying one-hot masks to match Bayer filter patterns or removing saturated border pixels. 3. Temporal/Scenario Masks: Defining a Region of Interest (ROI) based on non-zero radiance in the test scenario [1927-masked-volume-metrics.md]. Common weighting strategies include: 1. Area Scaling: Scaling loss by the inverse of downsampling factors to balance multiscale contributions. 2. Structural Weighting: Applying edge-aware weights or density-based cross-entropy weights for specific editing tasks. Masked Volume Metrics computes evaluation metrics (MSE, PSNR) by excluding empty froxels. It defines the effective ROI as the union of froxels with non-zero radiance in the rendered scenario and non-zero values in the ground truth. It is chosen for evaluation to prevent empty background regions from skewing performance scores. Training Loss Computation with Huber and Masking defines the training-time pipeline using Huber loss (\delta=0.1) and binary ray validity masks. It differs from Masked Volume Metrics by operating on rays during training rather than froxels during evaluation, and from this family's general definition by specifying the Huber function and JAX-based implementation details. Definition: Scaling the loss of each pixel by the area of that pixel's footprint in the original image to ensure low-resolution pixels have comparable influence to high-resolution pixels in multiscale datasets. Step: For multiscale datasets, calculate the area scaling factor based on the downsampling factor (e.g., factor of 2 -> area factor 4, factor of 4 -> area factor 16). Multiply the pixel loss by this factor. Definition: A method for shape addition using a density-based loss which is faster but less effective than composite image reconstruction. The loss encourages predicted densities to match target densities for edited regions and be unchanged for unedited regions. Step: Let yf = \{(r, \sigmaf)\} be the set of rays and densities in the foreground mask, and yb = \{(r, \sigmab)\} be the set of rays and densities in the background mask. \sigmaf are density values of the rays copied from the new object instance, and \sigmab represent density values of the rays from the original instance. Let \sigmar be the densities predicted by the model for ray r. Densities are normalized to sum to one. Formula: L{dens} = \sum{(r, \sigmaf) \in yf} (-\sigmaf^T \log \sigmar) + \sum{(r, \sigmab) \in yb} (-\sigmab^T \log \sigmar) Step: Render all three colors for every training ray, then apply a one-hot mask to select the desired output color corresponding to the measured raw pixel for that ray. Apply a second mask to remove a 4 pixel border from all training images to handle saturated pixels often found on the edges of iPhone raw images. Pitfall: Using bilinearly demosaicked raw images for supervision causes distracting color noise artifacts, particularly in extremely high noise areas, due to broken 'hot' pixels being dispersed to neighboring pixels. Definition: A regularization term added to the training loss to enforce edge detail consistency between the current rendering and the target image, alleviating washed-out details caused by noisy 2D-to-3D feature correspondences. Formula: L{edge} = \| (I{Current} G{\sigma1}) - (I{Target} G{\sigma2}) \|1 where denotes convolution and G\sigma is a Gaussian kernel with standard deviation \sigma. Parameter: Standard deviation \sigma1 for the current image Gaussian filter is 1.0. Standard deviation \sigma2 for the target image Gaussian filter is 1.6. Weighting factor \lambda for the edge loss is 0 for the first 15% of training, then increased to 50. The concept of masking losses to exclude invalid background rays is standard in differentiable volume rendering to prevent biased gradient updates from empty regions. Area loss scaling was introduced in Mip-NeRF to handle multiscale datasets where low-resolution images have larger pixel footprints. Density-based losses for shape editing were proposed in Editing Conditional Radiance Fields to facilitate faster object manipulation. Bayer masking was introduced in RawNeRF to correctly supervise neural radiance fields using raw sensor data, avoiding artifacts from demosaicking. Edge loss regularization was added in NeRF Analogies to preserve high-frequency details during appearance transfer. name: Masked Volume Metrics
head: Effective Region of Interest (ROI) Calculation, Masked MSE and PSNR Computation, Masked Volume MSE/PSNR Computation, ROI Calculation, Region of Interest (ROI) Calculation
body: Masked Volume Metrics is a method for computing evaluation metrics (such as MSE or PSNR) in volumetric rendering by excluding empty froxels from the analysis. It solves the problem of performance and quality analysis being skewed by regions of the volume that contain no radiance and thus provide no meaningful information. It sets itself apart from standard metrics by dynamically defining a Region of Interest (ROI) based on the union of visible radiance in the test scenario and the ground truth, ensuring that only froxels participating in light transport are evaluated. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D froxel grid representing the rendered scenario (test scenario) and a 3D froxel grid representing the ground truth. Output: A set of valid froxels (ROI{effective}) used to compute the final metric, and the computed metric value (e.g., MSE) restricted to these froxels. Data Structures: Froxel Grid: A 3D array where each element (froxel) contains RGB color values. ROI Mask: A binary 3D mask or a set of coordinates indicating which froxels are included in the effective region. Steps: 1. Identify Scenario ROI (ROI{scenario}): Iterate through the froxel grid of the test scenario. A froxel is included in ROI{scenario} if any of its RGB channels contains a non-zero value at any point during the test scenario. This identifies froxels affected by radiance from light sources or emission. 2. Identify Truth ROI (ROI{truth}): Identify froxels that contain non-zero values in the ground truth data. 3. Compute Effective ROI (ROI{effective}): Calculate the union of the scenario ROI and the truth ROI: ROI{effective} = ROI{scenario} \cup ROI{truth} This ensures that froxels relevant to either the algorithm's output or the ground truth are included, while completely empty regions are excluded. 4. Compute Metric: Calculate the base loss metric (e.g., MSE) only over the froxels present in ROI{effective}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computemaskedvolumemetrics(renderedvolume, groundtruthvolume): """ Compute MSE over the effective ROI defined by non-zero radiance in either the rendered scenario or the ground truth. Args: renderedvolume: 3D numpy array (H, W, D, 3) representing the test scenario. groundtruthvolume: 3D numpy array (H, W, D, 3) representing ground truth. Returns: mse: float, the Mean Squared Error over the effective ROI. roimask: 3D boolean array, the mask of valid froxels. """ # Step 1: Identify froxels with non-zero RGB channels in the scenario # A froxel is active if any channel is non-zero scenarioactive = np.any(renderedvolume != 0, axis=-1) # Step 2: Identify froxels with non-zero values in ground truth truthactive = np.any(groundtruthvolume != 0, axis=-1) # Step 3: Compute Effective ROI as the union roimask = scenarioactive | truthactive # Step 4: Compute MSE only over valid froxels # Extract values where mask is True renderedvalid = renderedvolume[roimask] truthvalid = groundtruthvolume[roimask] # Calculate MSE mse = np.mean((renderedvalid - truthvalid) 2) return mse, roimask Parameters: Threshold for Non-Zero: The sources specify "non-zero value". In practice, a small epsilon might be used to handle floating-point noise, but the source definition is strictly non-zero. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Regions: If both the scenario and ground truth are empty in a region, those froxels are excluded, preventing them from skewing the metric with zero-error counts that do not reflect visual quality. Algorithm-Specific ROIs: The ROI is computed separately for each tested algorithm because different methods may produce non-zero contributions in different regions of the froxel grid even in the same test scenario. A numerical metric to evaluate feature difference at a certain scale, computed only for voxels where the approximation Af is within a given intensity range of interest. It is used to verify structural simplification of features by comparing the original data set A to its approximation Af. The formula is: E = \sqrt{\frac{1}{m} \sum{i,j,k} (A[i,j,k] - Af[i,j,k])^2} where the sum is over m voxels where Af[i,j,k] is within the given intensity range of interest. This is useful when interested in feature difference at a specific scale rather than global error. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the total number of froxels, as it requires a single pass to identify active froxels and a second pass to compute the metric over the valid subset. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the ROI mask or the set of valid froxel indices. Strengths: Excludes completely empty regions that do not contribute meaningful information, providing a more accurate assessment of visual quality and performance for participating media. Limitations: Requires access to both the rendered scenario and ground truth to compute the union ROI. It may not be suitable for scenarios where empty space is a critical part of the evaluation (e.g., transparency testing). When to Use: When evaluating volumetric rendering algorithms where in-scattering and empty regions do not contribute to the visual result, and the goal is to zoom in on froxels participating in light transport. The method originates from research on temporal anti-aliasing for real-time froxel-based volumetric rendering. It was developed to address the need for accurate performance and quality analysis in production rendering environments, specifically within the Frostbite engine. The approach ensures that evaluation metrics are not skewed by regions unaffected by in-scattering or light transport. name: Training Loss Computation with Huber and Masking
head: NeRF training loss, RGB and TV loss calculation
body: This method defines the standard photometric loss computation pipeline for differentiable volume rendering, specifically combining Huber loss for RGB error with validity-based masking to exclude invalid rays. It addresses the problem of optimizing neural radiance fields or sparse voxel grids where ground truth images may contain transparent regions, background colors, or invalid sampling intervals. It differs from its parent Masked and Weighted Losses by specifying the exact Huber loss formulation and the procedural steps for blending ground truth backgrounds and aggregating per-ray losses, while its sibling Masked Volume Metrics focuses on evaluation metrics rather than training optimization. Inputs: worldspacerays: Ray origins and directions for the current batch. appearanceembeddings: Optional per-ray or per-view appearance codes. bg: Background color tensor (typically white or black) for blending. gtrgbaf32: Ground truth RGBA image array in float32. totalsamples: Number of sampling points per ray. Outputs: loss: Scalar training loss value. batchmetrics: Dictionary containing intermediate loss components and validity counts. Data Structures: predrgbds: Tensor of shape (numrays, numsamples, 4). The last dimension contains [R, G, B, Depth]. rayisvalid: Boolean tensor of shape (numrays,) indicating whether a ray intersects valid scene geometry or falls within the region of interest. nvalidrays: Integer count of rays where rayisvalid is True. Parameters: delta: Huber loss threshold. Typical value: 0.1. lossweight: Scalar multiplier for loss components. Default: 1.0. Steps: 1. Render: Call the differentiable renderer with worldspacerays, appearanceembeddings, bg, and totalsamples to obtain predrgbds. 2. Split: Separate the prediction tensor into RGB and Depth components. Using JAX/NumPy slicing: \text{pred\rgbs}, \text{pred\depths} = \text{jnp.array\split}(\text{pred\rgbds}, [3], \text{axis}=-1) where predrgbs has shape (numrays, numsamples, 3) and preddepths has shape (numrays, numsamples, 1). 3. Blend Ground Truth: Compute the expected ground truth RGB by blending the RGBA ground truth image with the background color to match the rendering conditions (which typically assume a white or black background for transparent regions): \text{gt\rgbs} = \text{blend\rgba}(\text{gt\rgba\f32}, \text{bg}) This ensures that pixels with alpha < 1.0 are correctly compared against the rendered output which also blends against bg. 4. Compute Per-Ray Huber Loss: Calculate the Huber loss for each ray. The Huber loss is defined as: L{huber}(p, g) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2}(p - g)^2 & \text{if } |p - g| \le \delta \\ \delta(|p - g| - \frac{1}{2}\delta) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} The loss is averaged over the samples within each ray, then masked by rayisvalid: \text{loss\rgb} = \frac{\sum{i} \mathbb{I}(\text{ray\is\valid}i) \cdot \text{mean}s(L{huber}(\text{pred\rgbs}{i,s}, \text{gt\rgbs}{i,s}), \delta=0.1)}{N{valid}} where N{valid} is the count of valid rays. 5. Aggregate: Sum all loss components (e.g., RGB, depth, regularization) defined in batchmetrics["loss"] using tree reduction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computetrainingloss(predrgbds, gtrgbaf32, bg, rayisvalid, batchmetrics): # 1. Split RGB and Depth predrgbs, preddepths = jnp.arraysplit(predrgbds, [3], axis=-1) # 2. Blend Ground Truth RGB with background # Assuming blendrgba handles alpha compositing: Rout = Rin Ain + Rbg (1 - Ain) gtrgbs = blendrgbaimagearray(imgarr=gtrgbaf32, bg=bg) # 3. Compute per-ray Huber loss for RGB # jnp.mean computes mean over the last axis (samples) # optax.huberloss computes element-wise Huber loss with delta=0.1 perrayloss = optax.huberloss(predrgbs, gtrgbs, delta=0.1).mean(axis=-1) # Mask by validity and sum maskedloss = jnp.where(rayisvalid, perrayloss, 0.0) nvalidrays = jnp.sum(rayisvalid.astype(jnp.float32)) # Avoid division by zero if no valid rays lossrgb = jnp.where(nvalidrays > 0, jnp.sum(maskedloss) / nvalidrays, 0.0) # 4. Aggregate with other losses in batchmetrics # batchmetrics["loss"] is a list of loss tensors to sum totalloss = jax.treeutil.treereduce(lambda x, y: x + y, batchmetrics["loss"]) # Add RGB loss to the aggregation totalloss = totalloss + lossrgb return totalloss, {"lossrgb": lossrgb, "nvalidrays": nvalidrays} Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If nvalidrays is 0, the loss division must be guarded to prevent NaN gradients. Background Mismatch: If the renderer's background assumption differs from the bg used in blending, transparent regions will produce incorrect loss values. Depth Loss: The provided notes focus on RGB loss; depth loss computation (if used) should follow similar masking and aggregation logic. SH Masking (SHM) is a regularization technique for differentiable volume rendering optimization that suppresses the influence of saturated pixels during loss computation. Saturated regions (over- or undersaturation) lack reliable texture cues and act as outliers that bias geometric and photometric recovery. It differs from hard binary masking by using a "leaky" quadratic transition at the saturation boundaries, which allows smoother gradient flow while still reducing bias. A hinge loss on the mean mask value to ensure both foreground and background generators are used and cover a minimum fraction of the image. It prevents the model from collapsing to generating only foreground or only background. Formula: Foreground convergence loss: L{cvg}^{fg} = \lambda{cvg}^{fg} \max\left(0, \eta{fg} - \frac{1}{|S|} \sum{i \in S} \hat{m}{mask}^{fg}[i]\right) Background convergence loss: L{cvg}^{bg} = \lambda{cvg}^{bg} \max\left(0, \eta{bg} - \frac{1}{|S|} \sum{i \in S} (1 - \hat{m}{mask}^{bg}[i])\right) where \hat{m}{mask} is the predicted mask value, |S| is the number of pixels, and \eta is the minimum coverage fraction. Parameters: Foreground minimum coverage (\eta{fg}): 0.4 for AFHQ and FFHQ; 0.1 for Carla. Background minimum coverage (\eta{bg}): 0.1. Convergence loss weight (\lambda{cvg}^{fg}): 0.1. Convergence loss weight (\lambda{cvg}^{bg}): 0.1. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of valid rays and samples per ray. The Huber loss computation is element-wise and highly parallelizable on GPUs. Memory Complexity: Requires storing intermediate tensors for predrgbs, gtrgbs, and per-ray losses. Memory usage scales with batch size and resolution. Strengths: Huber loss is more robust to outliers (e.g., noise, saturated pixels) than MSE, leading to more stable training in the presence of imperfect ground truth. Masking ensures that invalid rays (e.g., sky, empty space) do not contribute to the gradient, improving geometric accuracy. Limitations: Requires accurate validity masks; incorrect masking can lead to artifacts. The blending step assumes a known background color, which may not always be available or correct. When to Use: Standard choice for training NeRFs and voxel-based radiance fields when ground truth images have transparent regions or require background blending. When Not to Use: When computational resources are extremely limited and MSE is sufficient, or when no background blending is needed (e.g., opaque scenes with solid backgrounds). Originated in the context of training Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and sparse voxel grid models like Plenoxels and VoxGRAF. The use of Huber loss for RGB and validity masking is a standard practice in modern differentiable rendering pipelines to handle the complexities of real-world image data, such as transparency and varying background conditions. The convergence hinge loss variant was introduced in VoxGRAF to ensure balanced foreground/background generation in 3D-aware image synthesis. blurgyy/jaxngp, https://github.com/blurgyy/jaxngp, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) VoxGRAF: Fast 3D-Aware Image Synthesis with Sparse Voxel Grids, https://doi.org/10.52202/068431-2464, fetched 2026-10-26

name: SH Masking
head: SHM
body: SH Masking (SHM) is a regularization technique for differentiable volume rendering optimization that suppresses the influence of saturated pixels during loss computation. Saturated regions (over- or undersaturation) lack reliable texture cues and act as outliers that bias geometric and photometric recovery. It differs from hard binary masking by using a "leaky" quadratic transition at the saturation boundaries, which allows smoother gradient flow while still reducing bias. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Rendered pixel intensity x. Output: Mask weight m(x). Data Structures: No complex data structures. The mask is computed element-wise per pixel. Parameters: \text{low}: Lower threshold for saturation. Default value: 0.15. \text{high}: Upper threshold for saturation. Default value: 0.9. \lambda{\text{sh}}: Loss weight for the masking term in the total loss function. Default value: 0.05. \epsilon{\text{sh}}: Threshold for SH masks. Default value: 0.1. Learning rate for SH masks: 0.05. Formula: The mask function is defined as a piecewise quadratic function: \operatorname{mask}(x) = \begin{cases} \left(\frac{x + \text{low}}{2 \cdot \text{low}}\right)^2 & \text{if } x < \text{low} \\ 1 & \text{if } \text{low} \leq x \leq \text{high} \\ \left(\frac{2 - x}{2(1 - \text{high})}\right)^2 & \text{if } x > \text{high} \end{cases} Steps: 1. Compute the mask value m(x) using the piecewise formula above. 2. Multiply the base pixel-wise loss by m(x) to modulate its contribution to the gradient. 3. Integrate the masked loss into the total training loss, optionally weighted by \lambda{\text{sh}} if treated as a separate regularizer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeshmask(x, low=0.15, high=0.9): """Computes the SH mask weight for intensity x.""" if x < low: return ((x + low) / (2 low)) 2 elif x <= high: return 1.0 else: return ((2 - x) / (2 (1 - high))) 2 def applyshmasking(rendered, target, low=0.15, high=0.9, lambdash=0.05): """Computes the masked loss contribution.""" mask = computeshmask(rendered, low, high) baseloss = (rendered - target) 2 # MSE loss return lambdash (baseloss mask) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The left transition is continuous at \text{low}, but the right transition at \text{high} yields a value >1 per the source formula, which may amplify rather than suppress extreme oversaturation. Input Range: The 2-x term in the upper bound implies the intensity domain is scaled such that x=2 maps to zero weight. If the renderer outputs a different range, the formula must be adapted accordingly. Saturation Definition: The mask is "leaky" (non-zero at boundaries), so saturated regions are suppressed but not entirely discarded, preserving partial geometric cues. A variant of SH Masking that applies a quadratic transition to suppress saturation outliers. It is chosen when training data contains significant over- or undersaturated regions that act as outliers. It differs from hard binary masking by allowing non-zero gradients at the boundaries, which prevents bias in geometric and photometric recovery. Builds on Training Loss Computation with Huber and Masking. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel for mask computation, adding negligible overhead to the main rendering and loss pipeline. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per pixel for the mask value. Strengths: Robust to saturation; provides smooth gradients; trivial to implement. Limitations: Requires matching the intensity scaling to the formula's assumptions; performance gains depend on the broader training configuration rather than the mask alone. The technique was introduced for differentiable volume rendering and Gaussian Splatting optimization. The masking concept originates from HDR-Plenoxels for radiance fields, while its specific hyperparameters and integration into Gaussian Splatting training loops are detailed in Trick-GS.
