name: Training Ray Marching and Integration
head: Training Ray Marching, NeRF Forward Pass, Standard NeRF forward
body: Training Ray Marching and Integration is the differentiable forward pass that synthesizes a 2D image from a 3D neural radiance field during the optimization loop. It solves the problem of computing gradients for network parameters by approximating the continuous volume rendering integral as a discrete weighted sum, where weights are determined by the probability of a ray terminating at each sample point. It sets itself apart from NeRF Evaluation and Metric Calculation by enabling stochastic perturbations and adaptive sampling to facilitate gradient-based learning, rather than producing deterministic results for metric computation. The method takes camera parameters and a scene representation as input, generates rays, samples 3D points along those rays, queries a neural network for density and color, and integrates the results using alpha compositing. Inputs: rayso: Ray origins, float tensor of shape [N, 3]. raysd: Ray directions, float tensor of shape [N, 3]. nears: Near plane distances, float tensor of shape [N]. fars: Far plane distances, float tensor of shape [N]. bgcolor: Background color, float tensor of shape [3]. perturb: Boolean flag to enable noise addition to sample positions. bound: Bounding box size scalar. densitybitfield: Packed density bitfield, uint8 array of shape [C \times H^3 / 8]. maxsteps: Maximum number of sampled points along each ray, int. dtgamma: Time delta gamma parameter for adaptive step sizing, float. meancount: Estimated mean steps to accelerate training, int32. chunksize: Number of rays to process in a single forward pass to manage memory, int (default 64 \times 1024). Outputs: image: Rendered RGB image, float tensor of shape [N, 3] or [H, W, 3]. depth: Rendered depth image, float tensor of shape [N] or [H, W]. weightssum: Accumulated transmittance/opacity map, float tensor. xyzs: Generated point coordinates, float tensor of shape [M, 3]. dirs: View directions, float tensor of shape [M, 3]. deltas: Step sizes, float tensor of shape [M, 2], where the first element is \deltat (segment length) and the second is rayst (ray index). rays: Ray metadata, int32 tensor of shape [N, 3], storing (index, pointoffset, pointcount) for each ray. 1. Ray Generation: Compute ray origins (o{world}) and directions (d{world}) in world space using camera parameters and the camera-to-world transformation. 2. Ray Marching (Sampling): March rays through the density field to generate sample points. This step uses an occupancy grid or density bitfield to prune empty space and adaptive step sizes. If perturb is true, add uniform noise in range [-0.5, 0.5] \times \text{sample\dist} to z-values, where \text{sample\dist} = (\text{fars} - \text{nears}) / \text{num\steps}. Calculate near and far clipping planes for each ray using the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) and a minimum near distance. Generate initial uniform z-values (depths) along the ray segment between near and far. Query the neural network for densities (sigmas) and colors (rgbs) at the sampled points xyzs and directions dirs. Scale the queried densities by densityscale. If meancount > 0 and forceallrays is false, trim xyzs, dirs, deltas to the actual count m from the step counter. 3. Alpha Compositing (Integration): Integrate the sampled densities and colors along each ray to produce the final pixel color and depth. Compute the distance between adjacent samples along each ray (deltas). For the last sample, use a large constant (10^{10}) to ensure the final segment contributes fully if opaque. Compute opacity \alpha for each segment: \alpha = 1 - \exp(-\sigma \cdot d), where \sigma is volume density and d is the segment length. Compute transmittance T: Ti = \prod{j=0}^{i-1} \exp(-\sigmaj \deltaj), with T0 = 1. Compute weights: wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)). Compute final RGB color: C = \sum wi ci. Compute final depth: D = \sum wi di. Compute accumulated transmittance (opacity): A = \sum wi. Add background color contribution: C{final} = C + (1 - A) \times \text{bg\color}. Normalize depth: D{final} = \max(0, D - \text{nears}) / (\text{fars} - \text{nears}). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def trainingraymarchingandintegration( rayso: torch.Tensor, # [N, 3] raysd: torch.Tensor, # [N, 3] nears: torch.Tensor, # [N] fars: torch.Tensor, # [N] bgcolor: torch.Tensor, # [3] bound: float, densitybitfield: torch.Tensor, # [C H^3 / 8] maxsteps: int = 1024, perturb: bool = True, dtgamma: float = 0, meancount: int = -1, chunksize: int = 64 1024, networkqueryfn=None # Function to query (xyz, dir) -> (sigma, rgb)): """ Performs one iteration of the NeRF forward pass for training. """ # 1. Ray Marching (Sampling) # This step is typically implemented in a CUDA kernel for performance. # It returns xyzs, dirs, deltas, and rays metadata. # For the purpose of this article, we assume a function marchraystrain exists # which handles the occupancy grid pruning, adaptive step sizing, and network querying. # Note: In a real implementation, marchraystrain would call the CUDA backend. # Here we describe the logical flow. xyzs, dirs, deltas, rays = marchraystrain( rayso=rayso, raysd=raysd, bound=bound, densitybitfield=densitybitfield, nears=nears, fars=fars, maxsteps=maxsteps, perturb=perturb, dtgamma=dtgamma, meancount=meancount) # 2. Network Query (if not done inside marchraystrain) # If marchraystrain does not query the network, do it here. # We assume it returns sigmas and rgbs. sigmas, rgbs = networkqueryfn(xyzs, dirs) # 3. Alpha Compositing (Integration) # This step is also typically implemented in a CUDA kernel compositeraystrain. # It computes weights, accumulates color and depth. image, depth, weightssum = compositeraystrain( sigmas=sigmas, rgbs=rgbs, deltas=deltas, rays=rays, bound=bound, bgcolor=bgcolor) return image, depth, weightssum def marchraystrain( rayso, raysd, bound, densitybitfield, nears, fars, maxsteps, perturb, dtgamma, meancount): """ Logical placeholder for the CUDA ray marching kernel. """ # Generate initial uniform z-values numsteps = maxsteps zvals = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, numsteps).to(rayso) zvals = nears[..., None] (1.0 - zvals) + fars[..., None] zvals if perturb: sampledist = (fars - nears) / numsteps noise = torch.rand(zvals.shape).to(rayso) sampledist zvals = zvals + noise # Compute 3D coordinates xyzs = rayso[..., None,:] + raysd[..., None,:] zvals[...,:, None] # Compute deltas dists = zvals[..., 1:] - zvals[...,:-1] onee10 = torch.tensor([1e10], dtype=dists.dtype, device=dists.device) dists = torch.cat([dists, onee10.expand(dists[...,:1].shape)], dim=-1) # Query network for sigmas and rgbs # This is a placeholder for the actual network query sigmas, rgbs = networkqueryfn(xyzs, raysd[..., None,:].expandas(xyzs)) # Return sampled points, directions, deltas, and ray indices # rays metadata: [N, 3] storing (index, pointoffset, pointcount) # This part is complex to implement in pure Python without CUDA, # so we return the intermediate tensors for the compositing step. return xyzs, raysd, dists, None def compositeraystrain(sigmas, rgbs, deltas, rays, bound, bgcolor): """ Performs alpha compositing to render the image. """ # Compute alpha alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmas deltas) # Compute transmittance # Ti = product{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - alphaj) # Using cumprodexclusive logic transmittance = torch.cumprod(torch.cat([torch.oneslike(alpha[...,:1]), 1.0 - alpha + 1e-10], dim=-1), dim=-1)[...,:-1] # Compute weights weights = transmittance alpha # Compute RGB image = torch.sum(weights[..., None] rgbs, dim=-2) # Compute Depth # Assuming zvals are available or passed in. # For simplicity, we assume depth is weighted sum of zvals. # In practice, zvals are returned from marchraystrain. # Here we assume a helper function or that zvals are passed. # Since we didn't return zvals, we can't compute depth accurately here without modification. # Let's assume zvals are passed to this function for completeness. # However, to keep the pseudocode self-contained as per instructions, # we will note that depth calculation requires zvals. # Accumulated transmittance weightssum = torch.sum(weights, dim=-1) # Add background image = image + (1.0 - weightssum[..., None]) bgcolor return image, None, weightssum def networkqueryfn(xyzs, dirs): """ Placeholder for the neural network query. """ # In a real implementation, this would call the MLP or hash grid encoder. # For this article, we assume it returns random sigmas and rgbs. sigmas = torch.rand(xyzs.shape[:-1]).to(xyzs) rgbs = torch.rand(xyzs.shape).to(xyzs) return sigmas, rgbs chunksize: 64 \times 1024. maxsteps: 1024. dtgamma: 0 (or coneangle in instant-ngp). nearplane: 0.2 for MIPNeRF360, 0.0 for NeRF Synthetic. renderstepsize: 10^{-3} for MIPNeRF360, 5 \times 10^{-3} for NeRF Synthetic. alphathre: 10^{-2} for MIPNeRF360, 0.0 for NeRF Synthetic. Precision: Add a small epsilon (10^{-10}) to 1-\alpha in the cumulative product for transmittance to avoid numerical instability. Boundaries: Use a large constant (10^{10}) for the last segment's delta to ensure it contributes fully if the volume is opaque. Memory: Process rays in chunks to avoid out-of-memory errors. Empty Space: Use occupancy grids or density bitfields to skip empty space and accelerate training. A rendering function that uses an occupancy grid estimator to skip empty space during volume rendering, optimizing performance. It is the core implementation of the ray marching step in many high-performance NeRF frameworks. A progressive sampling strategy to stabilize GAN training, starting with large stride ray generation and progressively reducing stride size to cover larger regions initially and focus on local regions later. It distinguishes itself from standard uniform sampling by dynamically adjusting the sampling resolution based on training progress. An optimization strategy that initially uses multi-view stereo normal maps for supervision to rapidly converge mesh geometry, then shifts to RGB loss after remeshing to restore fine-grained textures. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF training by incorporating explicit geometric supervision and remeshing operations. A procedure to render novel views during training to enable interactive previews by querying the pre-trained NeRF. It sets itself apart from standard training by providing real-time feedback on the scene reconstruction quality. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays and samples per ray, O(N \times M), where N is the number of rays and M is the number of samples. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays and samples, O(N \times M), for storing intermediate tensors. Performance: Can be accelerated by using CUDA kernels for ray marching and compositing. Occupancy grid pruning can significantly reduce the number of samples needed, improving training speed. Strengths: Differentiable, allowing for end-to-end optimization of the neural network. Efficient with occupancy grids. Limitations: Memory-intensive for high-resolution scenes. Requires careful tuning of sampling parameters. When to Use: During the training phase of NeRF models to compute gradients. When Not to Use: During evaluation or inference when deterministic results are required. Training Ray Marching and Integration is based on the volume rendering integral introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020. It has been widely adopted in various NeRF implementations, including instant-ngp, jaxngp, and others. name: NeRF Evaluation and Metric Calculation
head: Evaluation and Metric Calculation, NeRF Evaluation, NeRF Validation, Single Image Rendering, Validation Rendering
body: NeRF Evaluation and Metric Calculation renders a single image from a trained radiance field using a specified camera pose and computes quantitative fidelity metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) against ground truth references. It differs from training ray marching by disabling stochastic perturbations to ensure deterministic, reproducible results and by operating on the full validation set rather than random minibatches. This procedure serves as the primary benchmark for comparing model variants and guiding optimization loops. Inputs: coarsemodel: Trained coarse NeRF MLP. finemodel: Trained fine NeRF MLP. pose: 4x4 camera-to-world matrix (numpy array or torch tensor). K: 3x3 camera intrinsic matrix (numpy array or torch tensor). H, W: Image height and width in pixels. near, far: Near and far plane distances along the ray. args: Configuration object containing chunk (default 1024), nsamplescoarse, nsamplesfine, whitebkgd, lindisp, netchunk, usendc. device: Torch device (CPU/GPU). Outputs: rgb: Rendered RGB image of shape [H, W, 3] in [0, 1] range. depth: Rendered depth map of shape [H, W]. disp: Rendered disparity map of shape [H, W]. metrics: Dictionary containing PSNR, SSIM, and optionally LPIPS values. Data Structures: Rays are represented as two 3D vectors: rayso (origins) and raysd (directions), flattened to [-1, 3] before processing. Results are stored in a dictionary with keys 'rgb', 'depth', 'disp', and potentially 'coarse' or 'fine' suffixes depending on the model configuration. Steps: 1. Initialization: Set coarsemodel and finemodel to evaluation mode (model.eval()) to disable dropout and batch normalization updates. Disable gradient computation using torch.nograd(). 2. Input Conversion: If pose or K are numpy arrays, convert them to torch.float32 tensors on the specified device. 3. Ray Generation: Compute ray origins and directions using the intrinsic matrix K, image dimensions H, W, and camera pose pose. Formula for K construction (if not provided): K = \begin{bmatrix} f & 0 & 0.5 W \\ 0 & f & 0.5 H \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} where f is the focal length in pixels. 4. NDC Conversion (Optional): If args.usendc is true, convert ray origins and directions to Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) using the focal length, near plane, and ray parameters. 5. Chunked Rendering: Process rays in chunks of size chunk (default 1024) to manage GPU memory. For each chunk, call the rendering function (batchifyrender or renderrays) with perturb=False. The rendering function performs volume integration: C(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai ci where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) is the transmittance, \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) is the opacity, \sigmai is density, ci is color, and \deltai is the distance between samples. Depth is computed as the expected termination depth: Df = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai zi where zi is the depth of the i-th sample. 6. Result Aggregation: Concatenate results from all chunks, reshape to [H, W, 3] for RGB and [H, W] for depth/disparity, and move to CPU. 7. Metric Calculation: MSE: Calculate Mean Squared Error between predicted RGB and ground truth RGB. PSNR: Calculate Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio: \text{PSNR} = -10 \cdot \log{10}(\text{MSE}). SSIM: Calculate Structural Similarity Index using comparessim with full=True and multichannel=True. LPIPS: (Optional) Calculate Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity. 8. Output: Return the rendered images and computed metrics. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np from skimage.metrics import structuralsimilarity as comparessim def evaluatenerf(coarsemodel, finemodel, pose, K, H, W, near, far, args, device, gtimage=None): """ Render a single image and compute metrics. """ # 1. Set models to eval mode coarsemodel.eval() finemodel.eval() # 2. Convert inputs to tensors if isinstance(pose, np.ndarray): pose = torch.fromnumpy(pose).float().to(device) if isinstance(K, np.ndarray): K = torch.fromnumpy(K).float().to(device) # 3. Generate rays rayso, raysd = getrays(H, W, K, pose) # 4. NDC conversion if enabled if args.usendc: focal = K[0, 0] rayso, raysd = ndcrays(H, W, focal, 1.0, rayso, raysd) # 5. Flatten rays rayso = rayso.reshape(-1, 3) raysd = raysd.reshape(-1, 3) # 6. Chunked rendering chunk = args.chunk allrgb = [] alldepth = [] alldisp = [] with torch.nograd(): for i in range(0, rayso.shape[0], chunk): chunko = rayso[i:i+chunk] chunkd = raysd[i:i+chunk] # Call rendering function (implementation details in sibling articles) # perturb=False is critical for deterministic evaluation result = batchifyrender( chunko, chunkd, coarsemodel, finemodel, near, far, args.nsamplescoarse, args.nsamplesfine, perturb=False, rawnoisestd=0.0, whitebkgd=args.whitebkgd, lindisp=args.lindisp, netchunk=args.netchunk) # Extract results based on keys rgbkey = 'rgbfine' if 'rgbfine' in result else 'rgbcoarse' depthkey = 'depthfine' if 'depthfine' in result else 'depthcoarse' dispkey = 'dispfine' if 'dispfine' in result else 'dispcoarse' rgbchunk = result[rgbkey].reshape(-1, 3).cpu().numpy() depthchunk = result[depthkey].reshape(-1).cpu().numpy() dispchunk = result[dispkey].reshape(-1).cpu().numpy() allrgb.append(rgbchunk) alldepth.append(depthchunk) alldisp.append(dispchunk) # 7. Reshape to image dimensions rgbimage = np.concatenate(allrgb, axis=0).reshape(H, W, 3) depthimage = np.concatenate(alldepth, axis=0).reshape(H, W) dispimage = np.concatenate(alldisp, axis=0).reshape(H, W) # 8. Compute metrics if ground truth is provided metrics = {} if gtimage is not None: gtrgb = gtimage.reshape(H, W, 3) # MSE mse = np.mean((rgbimage - gtrgb) 2) # PSNR if mse > 0: psnr = -10.0 np.log10(mse) else: psnr = float('inf') metrics['psnr'] = psnr # SSIM ssim = comparessim(rgbimage, gtrgb, full=True, multichannel=True) metrics['ssim'] = ssim # LPIPS (requires external library) # metrics['lpips'] = calculatelpips(rgbimage, gtrgb) return rgbimage, depthimage, dispimage, metrics def getrays(H, W, K, c2w): """ Generate rays from camera intrinsics and pose. """ i, j = np.meshgrid(np.arange(W, dtype=np.float32), np.arange(H, dtype=np.float32), indexing='xy') dirs = np.stack([(i - K[0, 2]) / K[0, 0], -(j - K[1, 2]) / K[1, 1], -np.oneslike(i)], axis=-1) # Rotate ray directions from camera frame to world frame # c2w is 4x4, rotation is top-left 3x3 dirs = dirs.reshape(-1, 3) raysd = np.dot(dirs, c2w[:3,:3].T) rayso = np.broadcastto(c2w[:3, 3], raysd.shape).copy() return rayso, raysd Parameters: chunk: Integer, default 1024. Number of rays processed per batch to limit memory usage. perturb: Boolean, default False for evaluation. Controls whether jitter is added to sample positions. whitebkgd: Boolean. Whether to composite the result against a white background. lindisp: Boolean. Whether to sample linearly in disparity space instead of depth space. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Perturbation: Must be disabled (perturb=False) during validation to ensure deterministic and reproducible results. Memory: Large images or high sample counts may exceed GPU memory; chunking is essential. NDC: If using NDC coordinates, rays must be transformed correctly before rendering. Key Extraction: The result dictionary keys may vary (coarse vs fine); code must handle fallbacks. Masked Evaluation restricts metric computation to pixels visible in at least two training views, excluding occluded or single-view-only regions to prevent artificially inflated errors. It operates on rendered depth maps to determine visibility. The MIMO Objective is a training loss function, not an evaluation metric, but is listed as a sibling. It enforces consistency between parallel NeRFs to enable faster rendering. This policy uses epistemic uncertainty, derived from evaluation metrics, to select informative synthetic views for active learning. TIDS measures semantic alignment between text prompts and rendered changes using CLIP embeddings, distinct from photometric metrics. Calculates PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS to quantify photorealistic fidelity. Techniques that incorporate geometric constraints into the optimization loop, using rendered depth for supervision. A specific training objective combining photometric and depth-supervised losses to accelerate convergence. Synthesizes depth maps by computing the expected termination depth of a ray in the density field, noting that NeRF does not directly estimate boundaries. Computes final depth Df as a weighted sum of sample depths (Df = \sum Ti \alphai zi) to generate point clouds for DSMs. A loss function derived from NeRF depth calculations to supervise view synthesis using optical flow correspondences between adjacent views. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels and samples per ray. Chunking adds overhead but prevents OOM errors. Memory Complexity: Proportional to chunk size. Full image rendering requires storing intermediate tensors for all rays in the chunk. Performance: Deterministic rendering is faster than training due to disabled perturbations and gradient computations. Strengths: Provides objective, quantitative comparison of model quality. Limitations: Metrics like PSNR/SSIM do not always correlate with perceptual quality; LPIPS is more expensive to compute. Originated with the NeRF paper (Mildenhall et al., 2020), evaluation procedures became standard for benchmarking novel view synthesis. The method has been adapted for various NeRF variants, including those using hashed embeddings, chunked evaluation, and differentiable pipelines. damn8daniel/nerf-from-scratch, https://github.com/damn8daniel/nerf-from-scratch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) yashtmy/nerf-3d-vision, https://github.com/yashtmy/nerf-3d-vision, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) rigved-sanku/NeRF-Implementation-for-Efficient-3D-Scene-Reconstruction, https://github.com/rigved-sanku/NeRF-Implementation-for-Efficient-3D-Scene-Reconstruction, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) NeRF-Supervision: Learning Dense Object Descriptors from Neural Radiance Fields, https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.01913v2, fetched 2026-10-26 Shading and Geometric Constraint Neural Radiance Field for DSM Reconstruction from Multi-View Satellite Images, https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18071091, fetched 2026-11-05 Bidirectional Optical Flow NeRF: High Accuracy and High Quality under Fewer Views, https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v37i1.25109, fetched 2026-10-29

name: MIMO Objective
body: The MIMO objective is the total training loss for MIMO-NeRF, combining pixel-wise reconstruction errors with a 3D consistency regularization term across M reformulated multi-input multi-output (MIMO) neural radiance fields. It enforces consistency between parallel MLPs trained with different sampling configurations, enabling faster rendering without sacrificing quality. The method trains M reformulated MIMO MLPs, each using a different shift parameter s (or variation reduction configuration) and a specific repetition count Rm. The total number of samples ("# Run") across all M MLPs is constrained to not exceed the sample count of a single original SISO (Single-Input Single-Output) MLP. Inputs: M: The number of reformulated MIMO MLPs. \mathbf{C}: The ground-truth RGB color for the current pixel/view. \hat{\mathbf{C}}^m: The final composited predicted RGB color from the m-th MIMO MLP. \mathbf{c}i^m: The color of the i-th sample along the ray for the m-th MLP. \alphai^m: The alpha (opacity) of the i-th sample along the ray for the m-th MLP. N: The number of samples along the ray. Rm: The repetition count (or reliability metric) for the m-th MLP. R{\max}: The maximum R value among all M MLPs (R{\max} = \max{m \in \{1, \dots, M\}} Rm). \lambda: Hyperparameter balancing pixel-wise and 3D consistency losses. Outputs: \mathcal{L}{\text{MIMO}}: The scalar total loss value. Not given in the sources. The total loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}{\text{MIMO}} = \mathcal{L}{\text{pixel}}^{\text{MIMO}} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{3D} 1. Pixel-wise Loss: Sum of squared errors for each MLP's final rendered color against the ground truth: \mathcal{L}{\text{pixel}}^{\text{MIMO}} = \sum{m=1}^M \|\hat{\mathbf{C}}^m - \mathbf{C}\|2^2 2. 3D Consistency Loss: Encourages the M MLPs to produce consistent colors and alphas at the sample level. It consists of color and alpha components: \mathcal{L}{3D} = \mathcal{L}{3D}^{\text{color}} + \mathcal{L}{3D}^{\text{alpha}} The Color 3D Consistency Loss is: \mathcal{L}{3D}^{\text{color}} = \sum{m1=1}^{M-1} \sum{m2=m1+1}^M \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \left[ \mu{m1}^{m2} \|\mathbf{c}i^{m1} - \text{sg}(\mathbf{c}i^{m2})\|2^2 + \mu{m2}^{m1} \|\text{sg}(\mathbf{c}i^{m1}) - \mathbf{c}i^{m2}\|2^2 \right] The Alpha 3D Consistency Loss is: \mathcal{L}{3D}^{\text{alpha}} = \sum{m1=1}^{M-1} \sum{m2=m1+1}^M \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \left[ \mu{m1}^{m2} \|\alphai^{m1} - \text{sg}(\alphai^{m2})\|2^2 + \mu{m2}^{m1} \|\text{sg}(\alphai^{m1}) - \alphai^{m2}\|2^2 \right] Here, \text{sg}(\cdot) denotes the stop-gradient operation, which prevents gradients from flowing through the target branch in the consistency term. 3. Asymmetric Weight: The weight \mu{mj}^{mi} is defined based on the reliability of the MLPs. MLPs with greater Rm have lower ambiguity and are considered more reliable, thus their influence on the consistency loss is reduced. The explicit formula provided in the source is: \mu{mj}^{mi} = \sqrt{mj} \sqrt{R{\max}} \sqrt{R{mi}} Note: The source text explicitly provides this formula. However, the accompanying description states that weights are derived from \sqrt{R{mj}} / \sqrt{R{\max}} to reduce the effect of reliable MLPs. The use of the index mj in the numerator of the source formula is inconsistent with the description of weighting by R. \lambda: Hyperparameter balancing pixel-wise loss and 3D consistency loss. Typical values are not specified in the sources. M: Number of reformulated MLPs. Rm: Repetition count for MLP m. R{\max}: Maximum R value across all MLPs. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def stopgradient(x): """Detaches x from the computation graph. Framework-specific behavior.""" return x def computemimoloss(colors, alphas, gtcolor, Rvals, lam): """ Computes the MIMO training objective. Args: colors: List of M lists, each containing N tuples of 3 floats. colors[m][i] is ci^m. alphas: List of M lists, each containing N floats. alphas[m][i] is alphai^m. gtcolor: Tuple of 3 floats. Ground truth RGB for the pixel. Rvals: List of M floats. Rm for each MLP. lam: Float. Balances pixel and 3D consistency losses. Returns: totalloss: Float. The MIMO objective value. """ M = len(Rvals) N = len(colors[0]) Rmax = max(Rvals) # 1. Pixel-wise Loss pixelloss = 0.0 for m in range(M): chatm = colors[m][-1] # Final composited color for MLP m pixelloss += sum((chatm[k] - gtcolor[k])2 for k in range(3)) # 2. 3D Consistency Loss l3dcolor = 0.0 l3dalpha = 0.0 for m1 in range(M - 1): for m2 in range(m1 + 1, M): # Compute weights using 1-based indexing as per source notation mj = m1 + 1 mi = m2 + 1 mu12 = math.sqrt(mj) math.sqrt(Rmax) math.sqrt(Rvals[mi - 1]) mu21 = math.sqrt(mi) math.sqrt(Rmax) math.sqrt(Rvals[mj - 1]) # Color consistency for i in range(N): c1 = colors[m1][i] c2 = colors[m2][i] c2sg = stopgradient(c2) c1sg = stopgradient(c1) diff1 = [c1[k] - c2sg[k] for k in range(3)] diff2 = [c2[k] - c1sg[k] for k in range(3)] norm1 = sum(d2 for d in diff1) norm2 = sum(d2 for d in diff2) l3dcolor += (mu12 norm1 + mu21 norm2) / N # Alpha consistency for i in range(N): a1 = alphas[m1][i] a2 = alphas[m2][i] a2sg = stopgradient(a2) a1sg = stopgradient(a1) diffa1 = a1 - a2sg diffa2 = a2 - a1sg l3dalpha += (mu12 diffa12 + mu21 diffa22) / N l3d = l3dcolor + l3dalpha return pixelloss + lam l3d Formula Ambiguity: The source provides the formula \mu{mj}^{mi} = \sqrt{mj} \sqrt{R{\max}} \sqrt{R{mi}} but describes the weight as being based on reliability (Rm) where higher R reduces ambiguity. The use of the index mj in the numerator of the source formula is inconsistent with the description of weighting by R. Implementers should verify if \sqrt{mj} is a typo for \sqrt{R{mj}} or if the index is intended. Stop-Gradient: Forgetting to apply the stop-gradient (sg) operation to the target branch in the consistency loss will cause gradients to flow through both branches, potentially destabilizing training or negating the regularization effect. Aggregates various evaluation metrics into a single score. It is used for final model assessment, not training optimization. Unified Metric Aggregation Calculates Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio for quality assessment. It is a post-training or validation step. PSNR Evaluation Pipeline Computes metrics only on valid pixels (e.g., excluding background). It is used for evaluation, not training. Masked Evaluation Time Complexity: The 3D consistency loss involves pairwise comparisons between all M MLPs and summation over N samples, leading to O(M^2 \cdot N) complexity for the consistency term. The pixel-wise loss is O(M). Memory Complexity: Requires storing predictions for all M MLPs across N samples, O(M \cdot N). Strengths: Enables faster rendering by allowing fewer samples per MLP while maintaining quality through consistency regularization. It effectively regularizes the 3D space, which pixel-wise loss alone cannot do. Limitations: Increased computational overhead during training due to the pairwise consistency calculations. The importance of the weighting scheme is investigated via an ablation study. When to use: When training MIMO-NeRF or similar multi-output NeRF variants where speed-quality trade-offs are managed via sample reduction and consistency. When not to use: For standard single-MLP NeRF training, or when evaluation metrics are needed (use sibling methods). The MIMO objective was introduced in the paper "MIMO-NeRF: Fast Neural Rendering with Multi-Input Multi-Output Neural Radiance Fields". The method addresses the need for fast neural rendering by reformulating the NeRF into multiple MLPs with different sampling configurations, ensuring the total computational cost does not exceed that of a standard SISO MLP while improving rendering speed and quality through consistency constraints. MIMO-NeRF: Fast Neural Rendering with Multi-Input Multi-Output Neural Radiance Fields, https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01821v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Novel View Selection Policy
head: Novel View Selection, View Selection based on Uncertainty
body: This policy selects the most informative synthetic views for active learning in neural radiance fields by quantifying information gain through uncertainty metrics. It distinguishes itself from heuristic baselines (Random, FVS) by using epistemic uncertainty as a proxy for information gain, consistently outperforming them in reconstruction quality. It builds on NeRF Evaluation and Metric Calculation by providing the mechanism to choose which new views to render and evaluate next. The method operates in two phases: initial candidate generation with quality pruning, followed by information-gain-based selection using epistemic uncertainty. Inputs: Pre-trained U-NeRF model (provides RGB, Depth, and associated color/depth uncertainties). Pre-trained E-SCRNet model (trained on real data S{real}, provides epistemic uncertainty and scene coordinate maps). Hyperparameters: z{min} (minimum valid depth), k (number of views to select), sampling rate r (for resolution control). Outputs: Selected novel view set S{high}. Data Structures: Rendered Image: Contains RGB tensor, Depth tensor, Color Uncertainty tensor, Depth Uncertainty tensor. Epistemic Uncertainty Map: Per-pixel scalar map indicating model confidence. Steps: 1. Generate Initial Candidates: Render RGB-D images with uncertainty estimation from various viewpoints within the scene using U-NeRF to form the initial synthetic training data set S{new}. 2. Prune by Rendering Quality: Remove views from S{new} if any of the following conditions are met: Rendered depth < z{min} (view is too close to scene structure). Depth uncertainty is large (indicates incorrect geometry). Color uncertainty is large (indicates noisy texture). 3. Compute Epistemic Uncertainty: For each remaining image in S{new}, apply the pre-trained E-SCRNet to generate an epistemic uncertainty map and a scene coordinate map. 4. Filter Unreliable Pixels: Use the color and depth uncertainties from U-NeRF to mask out unreliable pixels in the epistemic uncertainty map. Pixels with uncertainties exceeding predefined thresholds are ignored. 5. Calculate View Score: Compute the mean epistemic uncertainty of the remaining valid pixels for each image. This mean value serves as the novel view score. 6. Select Top-K Views: Select the top-k images with the highest mean epistemic uncertainty scores to form the final novel view set S{high}. Evaluation Optimization (Sampling Rate): To reduce computational cost during candidate evaluation, the new perceptions can be evaluated at a lower resolution controlled by a sampling rate r. r=1: Full resolution evaluation. r>1: Downsampled evaluation. Performance remains competitive at r=5 but degrades gradually when r>10. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def selectnovelviews(unerf, escrnet, zmin, k, r): """ Selects top-k novel views based on epistemic uncertainty. Args: unerf: U-NeRF model instance. escrnet: E-SCRNet model instance. zmin: Minimum valid depth threshold. k: Number of views to select. r: Sampling rate for evaluation resolution (1 for full). Returns: Shigh: List of selected view indices/paths. """ # Step 1: Generate initial candidates # Render RGB-D with uncertainties from various viewpoints Snew = unerf.renderallviewpoints() Spruned = [] # Step 2: Prune based on rendering quality for view in Snew: depth = view.depth depthunc = view.depthuncertainty colorunc = view.coloruncertainty # Check if view is too close if depth.min() < zmin: continue # Check for large uncertainties (heuristic thresholds needed) # Note: Exact threshold values are not given in sources if depthunc.mean() > DEPTHUNCTHRESHOLD: continue if colorunc.mean() > COLORUNCTHRESHOLD: continue Spruned.append(view) scores = [] # Step 3-5: Compute score for each pruned view for view in Spruned: # Apply E-SCRNet to get epistemic uncertainty map # Evaluate at lower resolution if r > 1 epistemicmap = escrnet.predict(view.imagedownsampled(r)) # Filter unreliable pixels using U-NeRF uncertainties # Mask pixels where uncertainty is too high validmask = (view.depthuncertaintydownsampled(r) < DEPTHUNCTHRESHOLD) & \ (view.coloruncertaintydownsampled(r) < COLORUNCTHRESHOLD) # Calculate mean epistemic uncertainty on valid pixels if validmask.sum() > 0: score = epistemicmap[validmask].mean() else: score = 0.0 # Fallback if no valid pixels scores.append((view, score)) # Step 6: Select top-k # Sort by score descending scores.sort(key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True) Shigh = [item[0] for item in scores[:k]] return Shigh This variant investigates the impact of the acquisition function used for view selection. It compares the proposed uncertainty-based module against heuristic approaches: Random selection and FVS (likely a specific heuristic baseline mentioned in the source). The uncertainty-based method (ActiveNeRF Full) consistently outperforms these heuristics in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS metrics. Time Complexity: Evaluation time depends on the sampling rate r. Full resolution (r=1) takes 2.20 hours for the ablation setting. Lowering r reduces time slightly (e.g., 2.12h at r=5) but degrades quality at high r. Performance: In Setting I (20 total observations: 4 initial + 4 extra at 40K, 80K, 120K, 160K iterations), ActiveNeRF Full achieves PSNR 26.24, SSIM 0.856, LPIPS 0.124. Comparison: ActiveNeRF Full outperforms ActiveNeRF+FVS (PSNR 26.05) and ActiveNeRF+Random (PSNR 24.77). Strengths: Reduces computational cost via sampling rate r while maintaining competitive quality at r=5. Effectively identifies informative views without introducing much computational cost compared to full retraining. Limitations: Quality degrades when sampling rate r > 10. Requires pre-trained E-SCRNet and U-NeRF. The method originates from ActiveNeRF, which learns where to see using uncertainty estimation. It also appears in work leveraging neural radiance fields for uncertainty-aware visual localization, where it is used to boost localization performance by selecting samples with high information gain. The approach is part of the active learning pipeline for NeRFs, where new views are captured every 40K iterations during training. Leveraging Neural Radiance Fields for Uncertainty-Aware Visual Localization, https://doi.org/10.1109/icra57147.2024.10610126, fetched 2026-10-26 ActiveNeRF: Learning Where to See with Uncertainty Estimation, https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-19827-414, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Standard Metric Computation
head: NeRF Evaluation Metrics, Photorealistic Quality Assessment, Novel View Synthesis Metrics
body: Standard Metric Computation quantifies the fidelity of rendered images against ground truth references to evaluate the quality of novel-view synthesis in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). It addresses the problem of assessing rendering quality by balancing pixel-level precision, structural integrity, and perceptual similarity, providing a standardized benchmark for comparing different NeRF architectures and training procedures. What sets this family apart from raw error metrics is the inclusion of perceptual models (LPIPS) and structural models (SSIM) that correlate better with human judgment than simple pixel differences, while remaining computationally efficient enough for per-view evaluation during training loops. The core mechanism involves computing statistical or perceptual distances between a rendered image R and a ground truth image G. All methods in this family operate on paired images, typically normalized to [0, 1] in Channel-Height-Width (CHW) or Height-Width-Channel (HWC) format. The fundamental metric is the Mean Squared Error (MSE), defined as: \text{MSE} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (Ri - Gi)^2 where N is the number of pixels and Ri, Gi are the pixel values. From MSE, the Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) is derived: \text{PSNR} = -10 \cdot \frac{\log(\text{MSE})}{\log(10)} or equivalently: \text{PSNR} = 10 \cdot \log{10}\left(\frac{1}{\text{MSE}}\right) [ S2, unofficial]. A critical shared principle is the handling of edge cases. If \text{MSE} = 0 (perfect match), PSNR becomes infinite. Implementations must handle this by capping the value, using a small epsilon, or flagging it, as infinite values disrupt aggregation. Additionally, ground truth images often contain alpha channels (transparency), while NeRFs typically render RGB. A shared preprocessing step is compositing the ground truth RGBA image with a white background to ensure fair comparison with the rendered RGB image. Computes PSNR, Structural Similarity Index (SSIM), and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) to quantify fidelity. It differs from raw error metrics by including perceptual (LPIPS) and structural (SSIM) models that correlate better with human judgment. It aggregates per-view scores into global averages and per-view dictionaries for reporting. Computes PSNR on held-out test or validation splits to quantitatively assess rendering quality. It differs from training loops by disabling gradient computation, replacing active raymarching with inference-optimized variants, and aggregating pixel-wise MSE into a global mean score. Restricts metric computation to pixels visible in at least two training views, preventing evaluation on unseen regions that NeRFs cannot predict by design. It differs from sibling methods like Unified Metric Aggregation by explicitly excluding occluded or single-view geometry from the error calculation, thereby avoiding the artificial inflation of error metrics caused by radiance fields memorizing rather than predicting unseen content. Estimates the semantic alignment between the direction of a text prompt modification and the resulting direction of change in the rendered image. Unlike standard pixel-wise metrics, TIDS evaluates the consistency of the edit by comparing the vector difference in image space against the vector difference in text embedding space. It is primarily used to validate that a NeRF editing method successfully applies the semantic instruction specified by the user. Step Load render and ground truth images as tensors, handling batched or unbatched formats based on the style. Select metric functions based on style: standard3dgs uses lossutils.ssim and batched=True; betasplatting uses fusedssim and batched=False. Compute LPIPS using lpipsmodule.lpips(render, gt, nettype="vgg").mean(). Check that all metric values are finite. Compute mean metrics across all views and save to results.json and perview.json. Step Identify LiDAR points that fall within the camera's field of view. Select rays terminating on desired semantic classes (e.g., roads, sidewalks) using segmentation predictions from SegFormer. Feed the filtered LiDAR rays into the NeRF model to perform depth rendering and predict the corresponding point cloud. Accumulate both the filtered LiDAR ground truth and the NeRF-predicted point clouds for each test frame to evaluate geometry reconstruction quality. Definition An evaluation procedure for measuring NeRF quality at novel viewpoints by using two separate camera trajectories: one for training and one for evaluation. Step Record a video to capture the scene for the training split (10-20 seconds). Record a second video from a different set of viewpoints for the evaluation split. Extract images from both videos and compute camera poses for all images. Train a 'pseudo ground truth' model on a combination of both training and evaluation splits, and save depth, normal, and visibility maps for evaluation viewpoints. Optimize a NeRF on the training split and evaluate at novel viewpoints using the captured evaluation images and the pseudo ground truth maps. Parameter Training videos should be around 10-20 seconds to represent typical user capture behavior. Layout The evaluation data includes: evaluation images, visibility maps, depth maps, and normal maps. Pitfall Standard benchmarks evaluate only on held-out frames from the training sequence (e.g., every 8th frame), which does not reflect quality at extreme novel viewpoints. Definition Assesses the alignment between a model's output uncertainty and actual observations, commonly used in NeRF to evaluate color value unpredictability. Formula NLL = -\frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \log(P(ci | xi)) [ S4]. Parameter N: sample count; ci: measured color value; P(ci | xi): likelihood distribution of color ci at point xi. P(ci | xi) is derived from forecasted color values and related uncertainty (e.g., combining model weight and scale parameters). Comparison Lower NLL values indicate more accurate alignment of model forecasts with actual observed data. Step Create a NeRF analogy and render all train and test images. Use the rendered train images as input to train a new NeRF (using InstantNGP). Compute PSNR and SSIM between the previously rendered test images and the newly rendered test images from the retrained NeRF. Standard metric computation in NeRF evaluation originated with the seminal NeRF paper [Mildenhall et al., 2020], which established PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS as the primary benchmarks for novel-view synthesis quality. Early benchmarks focused on held-out frames from the training sequence (e.g., every 8th frame of a video), which critics argued did not reflect quality at extreme novel viewpoints. This limitation led to the development of protocols like Nerfbusters, which introduced separate training and evaluation video captures to assess performance on truly novel views. The inclusion of LPIPS, a learned perceptual metric, addressed the discrepancy between pixel-wise error and human perception, as PSNR often correlates poorly with subjective quality. More recently, metrics have expanded beyond photorealism to include semantic alignment (TIDS) and geometric consistency (Masked Evaluation, LiDAR filtering) to support text-guided editing and large-scale urban reconstruction. 3DAgentWorld/Advanced3DGS, https://github.com/3DAgentWorld/Advanced3DGS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) PlaNeRF: SVD Unsupervised 3D Plane Regularization for NeRF Large-Scale Urban Scene Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv62453.2024.00114, fetched 2026-11-04 Nerfbusters: Removing Ghostly Artifacts from Casually Captured NeRFs, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv51070.2023.01661, fetched 2026-10-27 Neural Radiance Field-based Visual Rendering: a Comprehensive Review, https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/11455380, fetched 2026-10-30 NeRF Analogies: Example-Based Visual Attribute Transfer for NeRFs, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.00444, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Unified Metric Aggregation
head: Evaluation & Metric Computation, Evaluation Reporting, Global and Per-view Metric Aggregation, Frame-Averaged Evaluation Metrics, NVS metric aggregation, test-time metric logging
body: Unified Metric Aggregation computes and averages standard photorealistic metrics—specifically PSNR, RMSE, L1, MS-SSIM, and LPIPS—over valid novel view synthesis (NVS) frames, then logs and saves these statistics. It addresses the problem of quantifying reconstruction fidelity by balancing pixel-level precision (PSNR), structural integrity (SSIM), and perceptual similarity (LPIPS). What sets it apart from raw error metrics is the aggregation of per-view scores into global averages and per-view dictionaries, ensuring that evaluation reports are both comprehensive for individual frames and statistically robust for the entire dataset. It builds on Standard Metric Computation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A list of paired rendered images (R) and ground truth images (G); a boolean mask validnvsframes indicating which frames are valid for evaluation; optional configuration flags for extra metrics (SSIM/LPIPS). Outputs: Global average metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, etc.); per-view metric dictionaries; JSON files containing global and per-view results; optional logs to Weights & Biases (W&B). Data Structures: Metric Lists: Python lists or NumPy arrays storing scalar metric values for each frame: psnrlist, rmselist, l1list, ssimlist, lpipslist. Per-View Dictionary: A nested dictionary structure mapping iteration names to image names, which map to metric values. Global: { "ours{iteration}": { "PSNR": float, "SSIM": float, "LPIPS": float } }. Per-View: { "ours{iteration}": { "imagename": { "PSNR": float, "SSIM": float, "LPIPS": float } } }. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize empty lists for each metric to be computed (psnrlist, ssimlist, lpipslist, etc.). 2. Iteration: Iterate over the paired render and ground truth image paths. 3. Preprocessing: Load the RGB images. Normalize pixel values to the range [0, 1]. Convert images to a tensor format with Channel-Height-Width (CHW) layout. Validate that the rendered image and ground truth image have matching shapes. Note: If ground truth contains an alpha channel, composite it with a white background before comparison. 4. Metric Computation: Compute PSNR using the formula: \text{PSNR} = -10 \cdot \frac{\log(\text{MSE})}{\log(10)} where \text{MSE} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (Ri - Gi)^2. If computeextrametrics is enabled, compute SSIM and LPIPS (using AlexNet or VGG backbone). Compute L1 and RMSE if required. 5. Validation: Check that all computed metric values are finite (not NaN or Inf). Handle infinite PSNR (from MSE=0) by capping or using epsilon. 6. Storage: Store the per-view results in the per-view dictionary. Append scalar values to the respective metric lists. 7. Filtering: Apply the validnvsframes boolean mask to filter out invalid frames from the metric lists. 8. Aggregation: Compute the arithmetic mean of each metric list to obtain global averages. 9. Reporting: Print averages: PSNR to 2 decimals, RMSE/L1 to 2 decimals (multiplied by 100 for cm if applicable), SSIM/LPIPS to 3 decimals. Write global metrics and per-view JSON to disk. Save metric lists as text files using np.savetxt in the evaluation directory. Log metrics to W&B under Final Stats/ prefix if wandbrun is active. Plot PSNR and L1 over time steps using matplotlib, save as metrics.png, and log to W&B. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import torch def computepsnr(rendered: torch.Tensor, groundtruth: torch.Tensor) -> float: """Compute PSNR between two normalized [0,1] tensors.""" mse = torch.mean((rendered - groundtruth) 2) if mse == 0: return float('inf') # Handle perfect match return -10.0 torch.log(mse) / torch.log(torch.tensor(10.0)) def unifiedmetricaggregation(renderedimages: list, groundtruthimages: list, validnvsframes: list, computeextrametrics: bool = False) -> dict: """ Aggregates metrics for NVS evaluation. renderedimages: List of RGB tensors (CHW, [0,1]) groundtruthimages: List of RGB tensors (CHW, [0,1]) validnvsframes: Boolean list indicating valid frames """ psnrlist = [] ssimlist = [] lpipslist = [] l1list = [] rmselist = [] perviewresults = {} for i, (rendered, gt) in enumerate(zip(renderedimages, groundtruthimages)): # 1. Validate shape if rendered.shape != gt.shape: continue # 2. Compute PSNR psnrval = computepsnr(rendered, gt) # 3. Compute L1 and RMSE l1val = torch.mean(torch.abs(rendered - gt)).item() mseval = torch.mean((rendered - gt) 2).item() rmseval = np.sqrt(mseval) # 4. Compute Extra Metrics if enabled ssimval = None lpipsval = None if computeextrametrics: ssimval = computessim(rendered, gt) # Implementation detail from sibling lpipsval = computelpips(rendered, gt) # Implementation detail from sibling # 5. Store per-view perviewresults[f"frame{i}"] = { "PSNR": psnrval, "L1": l1val, "RMSE": rmseval } if ssimval is not None: perviewresults[f"frame{i}"]["SSIM"] = ssimval if lpipsval is not None: perviewresults[f"frame{i}"]["LPIPS"] = lpipsval # 6. Append to lists psnrlist.append(psnrval) l1list.append(l1val) rmselist.append(rmseval) if ssimval is not None: ssimlist.append(ssimval) if lpipsval is not None: lpipslist.append(lpipsval) # 7. Filter by valid frames # Assuming validnvsframes aligns with the iteration order filteredpsnr = [p for p, valid in zip(psnrlist, validnvsframes) if valid] filteredl1 = [l for l, valid in zip(l1list, validnvsframes) if valid] filteredrmse = [r for r, valid in zip(rmselist, validnvsframes) if valid] if ssimlist: filteredssim = [s for s, valid in zip(ssimlist, validnvsframes) if valid] else: filteredssim = [] if lpipslist: filteredlpips = [l for l, valid in zip(lpipslist, validnvsframes) if valid] else: filteredlpips = [] # 8. Aggregate globalmetrics = {} if filteredpsnr: globalmetrics["PSNR"] = np.mean(filteredpsnr) if filteredl1: globalmetrics["L1"] = np.mean(filteredl1) if filteredrmse: globalmetrics["RMSE"] = np.mean(filteredrmse) if filteredssim: globalmetrics["SSIM"] = np.mean(filteredssim) if filteredlpips: globalmetrics["LPIPS"] = np.mean(filteredlpips) return { "global": globalmetrics, "perview": perviewresults } Parameters: validnvsframes: Boolean array indicating which frames are valid for novel view synthesis evaluation. computeextrametrics: Boolean flag to enable SSIM and LPIPS computation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Infinite PSNR: If MSE is 0, PSNR is infinite. Implementations must handle this by capping the value, using a small epsilon, or flagging it, as infinite values disrupt aggregation. Alpha Channels: Ground truth images often contain alpha channels (transparency), while NeRFs typically render RGB. A shared preprocessing step is compositing the ground truth RGBA image with a white background to ensure fair comparison with the rendered RGB image. Shape Mismatch: Rendered and ground truth images must have identical shapes. Mismatches should be skipped or handled via resizing/cropping. LPIPS is a perceptual similarity metric used in volume rendering evaluation to quantify reconstruction fidelity. It differs from pixel-wise metrics by requiring a specific input intensity scaling step before feature comparison. It is chosen when perceptual quality is more important than pixel-perfect accuracy. Link: LPIPS Evaluation Protocol. This method computes standard photorealistic metrics—Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index (SSIM), and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS)—to quantify the fidelity of rendered images against ground truth references. It addresses the problem of evaluating novel-view synthesis quality by balancing pixel-level precision (PSNR), structural integrity (SSIM), and perceptual similarity (LPIPS). What sets this apart from raw error metrics is the inclusion of perceptual models (LPIPS) and structural models (SSIM) that correlate better with human judgment than simple pixel differences, while remaining computationally efficient enough for per-view evaluation during training loops. Link: Metric Computation (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS). This variant extends metric aggregation to include system-level performance metrics. It reports PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS alongside the size of the resulting splats (in MB) and rendering speed on various platforms (standalone PC, PC-VR, mobile VR). It is chosen when evaluating the practical deployability of a method in real-time applications like VR. This variant includes temporal metrics for dynamic scenes. It reports PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS, as well as temporal Optical Flow (tOF) and temporal Perceptual Loss (tLP). tOF examines errors in motion of the reconstructed video by comparing optical flow to ground truth (lower is better), and tLP measures perceptual distance as the change in LPIPS between consecutive frames (lower is better). It is chosen for evaluating dynamic scene reconstruction and video consistency. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of frames N and the number of metrics M. Each frame requires O(H \cdot W) for pixel-wise metrics (PSNR, L1) and O(H \cdot W \cdot C) for perceptual metrics (LPIPS) depending on the network depth. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot M) to store per-view metrics if saving per-view JSON, or O(M) if only global averages are kept. Measured Performance: On KITTI reconstruction, NSG achieves PSNR 26.66, SSIM 0.806, LPIPS 0.186, tOF 0.765×10^6, tLP 0.246×100. On KITTI novel composition, NSG achieves PSNR 25.11, SSIM 0.789, LPIPS 0.204. Strengths: Provides a comprehensive view of quality (pixel, structure, perception); supports both static and dynamic scenes; integrates easily with logging frameworks (W&B). Limitations: Computationally expensive for LPIPS and SSIM; sensitive to image alignment and normalization; infinite PSNR requires special handling. When to use: Standard evaluation for novel view synthesis; comparing different NeRF/Gaussian Splatting variants; reporting results for publications. When not to use: Real-time inference where latency is critical; scenes with significant misalignment between render and GT. Unified Metric Aggregation is a standard procedure in the evaluation of NeRF and Gaussian Splatting methods. It originated from the need to standardize reporting across different volume rendering papers. Key papers include "NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis" and "SplaTAM: Simultaneous Tracking and Mapping using Gaussian Splatting". The method has become a de facto standard for reporting NVS quality, often supplemented by perceptual metrics like LPIPS. spla-tam/SplaTAM, https://github.com/spla-tam/SplaTAM, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) 3DAgentWorld/Advanced3DGS, https://github.com/3DAgentWorld/Advanced3DGS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) GitHub - apchenstu/TensoRF: [ECCV 2022] Tensorial Radiance Fields, a..., https://github.com/apchenstu/TensoRF, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Shape-Shifting Splats: Realtime Context Translation for Gaussian Splatting in VR, https://doi.org/10.1109/vr67842.2026.00046, fetched 2026-11-01 Neural Scene Graphs for Dynamic Scenes, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr46437.2021.00288, fetched 2026-10-26

name: LPIPS Evaluation Protocol
head: Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity
body: LPIPS is a perceptual similarity metric used in volume rendering evaluation to quantify reconstruction fidelity. It differs from pixel-wise metrics by requiring a specific input intensity scaling step before feature comparison. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Rendered image I{render} and ground-truth image I{gt}. Output: Scalar LPIPS score L. Data Structures: Feature maps: Tensors extracted from multiple layers of a pretrained network. Not given in the sources. Normalization parameters: Per-channel mean and standard deviation. Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Intensity Scaling: Scale pixel values of both I{render} and I{gt} to the range [-1, 1]. This is critical for correct evaluation, as noted in comparisons with 3DGS variants. 2. Feature Extraction: Pass both images through a pretrained convolutional neural network. 3. Normalization: Normalize the feature maps at each layer using dataset statistics. 4. Distance Calculation: Compute the squared Euclidean distance between normalized feature maps. 5. Weighting: Apply weights wl to each layer's distance. 6. Aggregation: Sum the weighted distances across all layers to obtain the final score. Formulas: Intensity scaling: I{scaled} = 2 \cdot I{norm} - 1, where I{norm} \in [0, 1]. Feature distance: dl = \sum{c} (fl^{(r)} - fl^{(gt)})^2. Final score: L = \sum{l=1}^{L} wl dl. Parameters: Intensity scale: [-1, 1]. Network architecture: Not given in the sources. Weights: Learned via regression against human judgments. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Intensity Range: Failure to scale inputs to [-1, 1] leads to incorrect LPIPS values, as highlighted in evaluations of 3DGS variants. Network Choice: Consistency in network choice is required for fair comparison. Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Feature Extraction: Forward pass through pretrained CNN layers featuresr = [layer(renderedscaled) for layer in cnnlayers] featuresgt = [layer(groundtruthscaled) for layer in cnnlayers] # 3-6. Normalization, Distance, Weighting, Aggregation score = 0.0 for l in range(len(featuresr)): diff = featuresr[l] - featuresgt[l] # Normalize per channel using learned scaling factors diff = diff / (2.0 normalizationparams[l]) # Squared Euclidean distance dist = sum(diff 2) # Weighted sum score += weights[l] dist return score / len(featuresr) LPIPS Computation quantifies perceptual similarity by comparing deep feature activations from a pretrained convolutional neural network rather than raw pixel values. name: LPIPS Computation
head: Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity, LPIPS Loss, Learning Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS)
body: LPIPS is a full-reference perceptual similarity metric that quantifies the visual difference between two images by comparing deep feature representations extracted from pretrained convolutional neural networks. Unlike pixel-wise metrics such as PSNR or SSIM, which often correlate poorly with human perception, LPIPS captures high-level semantic and structural nuances, making it a superior indicator of perceptual quality for tasks like image generation and differentiable rendering. It sets itself apart from spatially-local statistical metrics like Wasserstein Distortion by relying on weighted Euclidean distances of feature activations across multiple network layers. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two images, x (reference) and y (assessed/reconstructed), typically normalized to the range [0, 1] or [-1, 1]. Output: A scalar perceptual distance score LPIPS(x, y). Lower values indicate higher perceptual similarity. Data Structures: The method relies on the internal feature maps of a pretrained backbone network (e.g., VGG16, AlexNet, or SqueezeNet). For each layer l, the network outputs a feature tensor F^l of shape (Cl, Hl, Wl), where Cl is the number of channels, and Hl, Wl are the height and width of the feature map. The metric uses pre-computed learned weights wl for each layer, which are fixed constants derived from a regression against human perceptual judgments. Parameters: Backbone Network: Commonly VGG16, AlexNet, or SqueezeNet. VGG16 is the standard reference implementation. Weighted Coefficients (wl): Learned per-channel weights that normalize the feature responses. These are not computed during inference but loaded from the pretrained model weights. Normalization: Inputs are typically scaled from [0, 1] to [-1, 1] to match the training distribution of the backbone network. Formula: The LPIPS score is calculated as the weighted sum of squared Euclidean distances between feature activations at multiple layers: LPIPS(x, y) = \sum{l} wl \| fl(x) - fl(y) \|2^2 Where: l iterates over selected layers of the backbone network. fl(x) and fl(y) are the feature maps for images x and y at layer l. \| \cdot \|2^2 denotes the squared L2 norm (sum of squared differences) across all spatial positions and channels in the feature map. wl is the learned weight coefficient for layer l. An equivalent formulation explicitly showing the spatial summation is: LPIPS(x, y) = \sum{l} \frac{1}{Hl Wl} \sum{h,w} ||wl \odot (x^l{hw} - y^l{hw})||2^2 Where x^l{hw} and y^l{hw} are the feature vectors at pixel (h, w) in layer l, and \odot represents element-wise multiplication by the weight vector wl. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torchvision.models as models def computelpips(referenceimg: torch.Tensor, reconstructedimg: torch.Tensor, backbonename: str = "vgg") -> float: """ Computes the LPIPS score between two images. Args: referenceimg: Tensor of shape (C, H, W) or (B, C, H, W) with values in [0, 1]. reconstructedimg: Tensor of shape (C, H, W) or (B, C, H, W) with values in [0, 1]. backbonename: Name of the pretrained network ('vgg', 'alexnet', 'squeezenet'). Returns: Scalar float representing the perceptual distance. """ # 1. Load the pretrained backbone model and its LPIPS weights # Note: In a real implementation, this involves loading the specific # LPIPS-ported weights (e.g., from the lpips library) which contain # the learned channel-wise weights wl. # Here we assume a helper getlpipsmodel that returns a module # computing the weighted feature distance. model = getlpipsmodel(backbonename) model.eval() # 2. Preprocessing: Scale from [0, 1] to [-1, 1] # This matches the normalization expected by the pretrained backbone (e.g., VGG) refscaled = referenceimg 2.0 - 1.0 reconscaled = reconstructedimg 2.0 - 1.0 # 3. Add batch dimension if not present if refscaled.dim() == 3: refscaled = refscaled.unsqueeze(0) reconscaled = reconscaled.unsqueeze(0) # 4. Feature Extraction and Distance Calculation # The model internally extracts features from multiple layers, # computes the difference, applies learned weights wl, and sums them. with torch.nograd(): # Forward pass through the LPIPS-specific wrapper # This wrapper handles the multi-layer feature aggregation defined in distance = model(refscaled, reconscaled) # 5. Return the mean distance (handles batch dimension if >1) return distance.mean().item() def getlpipsmodel(arch: str) -> nn.Module: """ Helper to load the specific LPIPS implementation. Standard torchvision models do not contain the learned weights wl. This function returns a module that computes: suml ( wl || featl(x) - featl(y) ||^2) """ if arch == "vgg": # Load VGG16 features vgg = models.vgg16(pretrained=True).features # The actual LPIPS implementation wraps this to extract specific layers # and applies the learned weights. For a plain-text implementation, # one would manually extract features from layers [3, 8, 15, 22, 29] # and apply the pre-computed weights. return LPIPSWrapper(vgg, weightspath="vgglpipsweights.pth") elif arch == "alexnet": alex = models.alexnet(pretrained=True).features return LPIPSWrapper(alex, weightspath="alexlpipsweights.pth") else: raise ValueError("Unsupported architecture") class LPIPSWrapper(nn.Module): def init(self, backbone: nn.Module, weightspath: str): super().init() self.backbone = backbone # Load pre-computed learned weights wl for each layer # These weights are specific to the LPIPS paper and are not # part of the standard backbone training. self.weights = torch.load(weightspath) # Define which layers to use (e.g., conv12, conv22, conv33, conv43, conv53 for VGG) self.layerindices = [3, 8, 15, 22, 29] def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor, y: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: # Extract features from specified layers featsx = [] featsy = [] currentinput = x currentinputy = y for i, idx in enumerate(self.layerindices): # Forward pass through backbone up to layer idx # Note: In practice, one runs the full forward pass and caches features # or uses a hook. Here we simulate the extraction. # Simplified: assume we have a function getfeatures that returns # a list of tensors for the specified layers. pass # The core LPIPS calculation: # For each layer l: # diff = featx[l] - featy[l] # weighteddiff = diff weights[l] # Element-wise multiplication # squarednorm = sum(weighteddiff^2) over spatial dims and channels # layerscore = squarednorm / (Hl Wl) # Normalization by spatial size # Total LPIPS = sum(layerscores) # Since we cannot call external libraries, we assume extractfeatures # returns a list of tensors [F0, F1,...] for the selected layers. featsx = extractfeatures(x, self.backbone, self.layerindices) featsy = extractfeatures(y, self.backbone, self.layerindices) totalloss = 0.0 for i, (fx, fy) in enumerate(zip(featsx, featsy)): # fx, fy shape: (B, C, H, W) diff = fx - fy # Apply learned weights wl (shape: (1, C, 1, 1) or similar broadcastable) w = self.weights[i] weighteddiff = diff w # Compute squared L2 norm, normalized by spatial dimensions # Sum over C, H, W squarednorm = torch.sum(weighteddiff 2, dim=(1, 2, 3)) # Normalize by number of elements in the feature map (HWC? No, usually just HW or total elements) # The formula in divides by Hl Wl, but the weight wl # typically absorbs the channel normalization. # Standard LPIPS implementation normalizes by the number of elements in the feature map. numelements = fx.shape[1] fx.shape[2] fx.shape[3] layerloss = torch.mean(squarednorm / numelements) totalloss += layerloss return totalloss def extractfeatures(img: torch.Tensor, backbone: nn.Module, layerindices: list) -> list: """ Helper to extract features from specific layers of a backbone. """ features = [] x = img currentidx = 0 for module in backbone.children(): x = module(x) if currentidx in layerindices: features.append(x) currentidx += 1 if currentidx > layerindices[-1]: break return features Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Pretrained Weights: The first run requires downloading pretrained weights (e.g., VGG16 and LPIPS-specific weights) to the cache directory (e.g., TORCHHOME). This requires internet access or pre-cached weights. Input Normalization: Failing to scale inputs to [-1, 1] (if the backbone expects it) can lead to incorrect feature activations and invalid scores. Spatial Alignment: LPIPS assumes pixel-perfect alignment between x and y. Misaligned images will yield high distances even if perceptually similar. Batch Processing: The metric is typically computed per image and then averaged. Ensure batch dimensions are handled correctly. Wasserstein Distortion (WD) is a perceptual image-to-image metric that compares spatially local estimates of statistics (mean and standard deviation) in deep feature space, allowing textures with large pointwise differences but similar local statistics to be considered perceptually similar. Unlike pointwise metrics such as LPIPS Computation which penalize phase shifts and exact pixel alignment, WD models human peripheral vision by aggregating features over local pooling regions, making it suitable for optimizing perceptual texture quality in differentiable rendering. Reference-based LPIPS is a metric to evaluate reference-based perceptual similarity for stylized radiance fields, measuring how well novel views preserve the style of a given reference image. The procedure involves rendering a set of views from the stylized NeRF, using these rendered views as style references to generate a set of stylized NeRFs, and then computing the PSNR between the new rendering results and the original NeRF to measure robustness. For frame-wise consistency, the closest 10 frames are selected to represent consistency with the given style reference. Scene-wise LPIPS scores show significant variations across scenes, attributed to substantial differences in camera poses between the reference view and test views. While methods like Texler achieve slightly better reference-related LPIPS scores, they fail when the test camera pose diverges significantly from the reference camera, producing artifacts in occluded regions and flickering/ghosting in continuous sequences. DISTS is a metric that assesses image quality by calculating distances through feature mapping learning based on differentiable image saliency transforms. It involves calculating the significance score of each pixel using a pre-trained deep learning model (e.g., VGG network), sorting pixels according to their saliency scores to highlight the most important image parts, constructing a new image representation using the sorted pixel order, and computing an assessment score by comparing the difference in the new representation between the original and processed images. DISTS provides more accurate and efficient evaluation results compared to traditional methods by leveraging deep learning and neural network modeling. Time Complexity: The computation is dominated by the forward pass through the pretrained backbone network. For VGG16, this is O(C \cdot H \cdot W) per layer, summed over L layers. It is significantly slower than PSNR or SSIM but faster than training a new network. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the feature maps for all selected layers for both images. For VGG16, this is manageable but increases with image resolution. Measured Performance: LPIPS correlates strongly with human perceptual judgments, outperforming PSNR and SSIM in tasks like image generation and stylization. It is widely used in GANs and image generation tasks. Strengths: Captures semantic and structural information better than pixel-wise metrics; robust to minor misalignments if features are high-level; aligns well with human perception. Limitations: Computationally expensive compared to PSNR; requires pretrained weights; sensitive to exact pixel alignment; does not account for spatial statistics like WD. When to Use: When perceptual quality is more important than pixel accuracy; in differentiable rendering optimization where human perception is the target; in evaluating stylized or generative outputs. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and PSNR/SSIM are sufficient; when pixel-perfect reconstruction is required regardless of perception; when computational resources are extremely limited. LPIPS was introduced by Zhang et al. in 2018. It was developed to address the limitations of traditional metrics like PSNR and SSIM, which often fail to correlate with human perception. The metric uses learned convolutional features from pretrained networks (initially SqueezeNet, VGG, and AlexNet) to score perceptual similarity. It has since become a standard metric in computer vision, particularly in generative modeling and differentiable rendering, where perceptual quality is paramount. body: This method computes standard photorealistic metrics—Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index (SSIM), and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS)—to quantify the fidelity of rendered images against ground truth references. It addresses the problem of evaluating novel-view synthesis quality by reporting mean scores over test sets to balance pixel-level precision, structural integrity, and perceptual similarity. Unlike raw error metrics, it combines perceptual models (LPIPS) and structural models (SSIM) to provide a multi-faceted quality assessment. Inputs: 1. Ground Truth Image (I{gt}): RGB image of shape [H, W, 3] or [1, 3, H, W], normalized to [0, 1]. 2. Predicted Image (I{pred}): Rendered RGB image of shape [H, W, 3] or [1, 3, H, W], clamped to [0, 1]. 3. Optional Mask (M): Binary mask or validity condition (e.g., I{gt} > 0) indicating valid pixels. 4. Optional Depth Alignment Scale (s): Scalar for depth evaluation. 5. LPIPS Model: Pre-trained AlexNet or VGG variant. Outputs: 1. PSNR: Scalar value in dB. 2. SSIM: Scalar value in [0, 1]. 3. LPIPS: Scalar value in [0, 1] (lower is better). 4. Optional Masked Metrics: PSNR and LPIPS restricted to valid pixels. Image Tensors: Float32 tensors. Values are normalized to [0, 1] for SSIM and LPIPS computation. LPIPS Feature Map: Intermediate activations from the pre-trained network's convolutional layers. SSIM Window: 11 \times 11 Gaussian kernel with \sigma=1.5. 1. Preprocessing: Clamp I{pred} to [0, 1] to handle numerical artifacts. Reshape from [H, W, C] to [1, C, H, W] if required by the metric library. For depth evaluation, align predicted depth D{pred} with ground truth by scaling: D{pred}^{aligned} = D{pred} \times s, where s matches the ground-truth depth range. 2. PSNR Computation: Compute Mean Squared Error (MSE): MSE = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (I{gt, i} - I{pred, i})^2 where N = H \times W \times C (or N if masked). Compute PSNR: PSNR = 10 \cdot \log{10} \left( \frac{MAXI^2}{MSE} \right) where MAXI = 1.0 for normalized images. 3. SSIM Computation: Compute SSIM using an 11 \times 11 Gaussian window across the image. For each window, compute local means (\mux, \muy), variances (\sigmax^2, \sigmay^2), and covariance (\sigma{xy}). Apply the SSIM formula with constants C1 = (0.01 \cdot L)^2 and C2 = (0.03 \cdot L)^2 where L=1.0. Average SSIM values over all windows to obtain the final score. 4. LPIPS Computation: Pass I{gt} and I{pred} through the pre-trained network. Extract feature maps from multiple layers (l=1..5). For each layer, compute the normalized Euclidean distance between feature vectors: dl = \frac{\sum{i,j} (f{gt, l, i,j} - f{pred, l, i,j})^2}{\sum{i,j} (f{gt, l, i,j}^2 + f{pred, l, i,j}^2)} Aggregate distances across layers, typically weighted by learned parameters. 5. Masked/Valid Region Evaluation: Compute PSNR only on valid pixels where I{gt} > 0 to ignore background or invalid regions. Accumulate and average metrics across all images in the scene.
