The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def computepsnr(gt: torch.Tensor, pred: torch.Tensor) -> float: """Compute PSNR between ground truth and predicted images. Inputs: [1, C, H, W], values in [0, 1].""" mse = torch.mean((gt - pred) 2) if mse == 0: return float('inf') psnr = 10 torch.log10(1.0 / mse) return psnr.item() def computessim(gt: torch.Tensor, pred: torch.Tensor) -> float: """Compute SSIM between ground truth and predicted images. Inputs: [1, C, H, W], values in [0, 1].""" # Create 11x11 Gaussian kernel with sigma=1.5 kernelsize = 11 sigma = 1.5 kernel = torch.ones(1, 1, kernelsize, kernelsize) # Apply Gaussian blur for local statistics mux = F.conv2d(gt, kernel, padding=kernelsize//2) muy = F.conv2d(pred, kernel, padding=kernelsize//2) muxx = F.conv2d(gt gt, kernel, padding=kernelsize//2) muyy = F.conv2d(pred pred, kernel, padding=kernelsize//2) muxy = F.conv2d(gt pred, kernel, padding=kernelsize//2) varx = muxx - mux mux vary = muyy - muy muy covxy = muxy - mux muy C1 = (0.01 1.0) 2 C2 = (0.03 1.0) 2 ssimmap = ((2 mux muy + C1) (2 covxy + C2)) / \ ((mux2 + muy2 + C1) (varx + vary + C2)) return torch.mean(ssimmap).item() def computelpips(gt: torch.Tensor, pred: torch.Tensor, net: torch.nn.Module) -> float: """Compute LPIPS using AlexNet/VGG features. Inputs: [1, C, H, W], values in [0, 1].""" net.eval() with torch.nograd(): featuresgt = [] featurespred = [] # Forward pass collecting conv layer outputs x = gt for module in net.modules(): if isinstance(module, torch.nn.Conv2d): x = module(x) featuresgt.append(x) if isinstance(module, torch.nn.ReLU): pass # ReLU applied in forward pass x = pred for module in net.modules(): if isinstance(module, torch.nn.Conv2d): x = module(x) featurespred.append(x) dist = 0.0 for fgt, fpred in zip(featuresgt, featurespred): fgtnorm = F.normalize(fgt, p=2, dim=1) fprednorm = F.normalize(fpred, p=2, dim=1) dist += torch.mean((fgtnorm - fprednorm) 2) return dist.item() def evaluatemetrics(gt: torch.Tensor, pred: torch.Tensor, mask: torch.Tensor = None, lpipsnet: torch.nn.Module = None) -> dict: """Main evaluation function.""" pred = torch.clamp(pred, 0.0, 1.0) if gt.dim() == 3: gt = gt.permute(2, 0, 1).unsqueeze(0) if pred.dim() == 3: pred = pred.permute(2, 0, 1).unsqueeze(0) metrics = {} metrics['psnr'] = computepsnr(gt, pred) metrics['ssim'] = computessim(gt, pred) if lpipsnet is not None: metrics['lpips'] = computelpips(gt, pred, lpipsnet) else: metrics['lpips'] = 0.0 # Not given in the sources if no net provided. if mask is not None: gtmasked = gt mask predmasked = pred mask metrics['psnrmasked'] = computepsnr(gtmasked, predmasked) if lpipsnet is not None: metrics['lpipsmasked'] = computelpips(gtmasked, predmasked, lpipsnet) return metrics LPIPS Network: AlexNet or VGG variant. LPIPS Weights: Learned weights from the original LPIPS paper. SSIM Window Size: 11 \times 11 Gaussian kernel with \sigma=1.5. Depth Scale (s): Computed via alignment to match ground-truth depth range. Evaluation Interval: Every 300 iterations. Information Leakage: In appearance-aware NeRFs, optimizing appearance embeddings on held-out pixels causes metrics to fail by memorizing the image rather than generalizing. Use split-image evaluation to prevent this. Zero/Mean Embeddings: Setting appearance embeddings to zeros or mean values results in structurally accurate but appearance-mismatched renderings, causing perceptual metrics to fail. Depth Alignment: Predicted depth must be scaled to match ground-truth range before computing depth errors. Clamping: Predicted RGB values must be clamped to [0, 1] before LPIPS computation. FID Resampling: FID is sensitive to resizing; use antialiased (area) interpolation at 128×128 resolution. An evaluation protocol for appearance-aware NeRF models that optimizes the appearance embedding on a subset of pixels to adapt scene appearance without directly optimizing held-out pixels, preventing information leakage while measuring perceptual similarity. It splits a ground-truth test image into left and right halves, optimizes the appearance embedding using only the left half, renders the right half, and calculates perceptual metrics on the rendered right half against the ground truth right half. Unlike the NRW baseline which encodes the entirety of a held-out image with an appearance encoder, this scheme isolates geometry from appearance and limits information leakage. Pitfall: Setting the appearance embedding to zeros or the mean of optimized embeddings results in plausible but structurally accurate renderings that fail to match ground truth appearance, causing perceptual metrics to fail. A metric reporting protocol that computes PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS on both the full image and the valid-masked region to isolate visible reconstruction quality. It computes standard metrics over all pixels and then recomputes PSNR restricted to pixels inside the validity mask (I{gt} > 0), reporting these values alongside global metrics. Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) evaluates how well the method captures the appearance distribution of images. It is computed on an empty background (value=0, gray) at 128×128 resolution, using antialiased resampling if resizing is needed, as FID is sensitive to this aspect. Reports SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS, and storage size for specific benchmark scenes. On Mip-NeRF360 scenes (bicycle, garden, stump, room, counter, kitchen, bonsai), SSIM scores are 0.705, 0.842, 0.784, 0.925, 0.914, 0.928, 0.946 respectively. PSNR scores are 24.50, 27.17, 26.27, 31.93, 29.34, 31.30, 32.70 respectively. LPIPS scores are 0.306, 0.146, 0.284, 0.202, 0.191, 0.126, 0.185 respectively. Storage sizes are 248, 271, 493, 133, 194, 173, 258 MB respectively. On Tanks&Temples/Deep Blending scenes (Truck, Train, Dr Johnson, Playroom), SSIM scores are 0.879, 0.857, 0.779, 0.774 respectively. Time Complexity: PSNR and SSIM are O(N) where N is the number of pixels. LPIPS is dominated by the forward pass through the feature extractor. Memory Complexity: LPIPS requires storing intermediate feature maps for all layers, which scales with image resolution. Performance: Evaluated every 300 iterations during training. On KITTI reconstruction, NSG achieves PSNR 26.66, SSIM 0.806, LPIPS 0.186. Strengths: PSNR provides pixel-level precision. SSIM captures structural information. LPIPS captures perceptual similarity. Limitations: PSNR is sensitive to pixel-level errors. SSIM can be sensitive to misalignment. LPIPS depends on a pre-trained network. When to Use: Use PSNR and SSIM for quick checks and standard comparison. Use LPIPS for perceptual quality assessment, especially in appearance-aware NeRFs. PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS are standard metrics in computer vision and image processing. They were adopted for NeRF evaluation to provide a multi-faceted view of rendering accuracy, balancing pixel-level precision with structural and perceptual similarity. The use of LPIPS in NeRF evaluation was popularized by works like BARF and NeRF-W. The split-image evaluation protocol was introduced to address the issue of information leakage in appearance-aware NeRFs. name: Masked Metrics Evaluation
head: Loss-masked Metric Reporting, Masked PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, Object-crop image quality metrics
body: Masked Metrics Evaluation is a protocol for computing quantitative image quality metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FLIP) restricted to a specific region of interest defined by a ground-truth mask. It isolates visible reconstruction quality by excluding background or irrelevant pixels from the error calculation, enabling fair comparison between object-centric and scene-level renders. Unlike standard metric computation which averages over the entire image, this method reports two values: the global metric and the masked metric (typically in parentheses). Inputs and Outputs Inputs: I{pred}: Rendered image of size H \times W \times C. I{gt}: Ground truth image of size H \times W \times C. M: Binary loss mask of size H \times W, where M{i,j} = 1 if pixel (i,j) is inside the region of interest, and 0 otherwise. Outputs: Metric{global}: Metric value computed over all pixels. Metric{masked}: Metric value computed only over pixels where M{i,j} = 1. Data Structures The mask M is a binary tensor. In implementation, it is often derived from segmentation or depth-based cropping. Images are normalized to [0, 1] or [-1, 1] depending on the metric implementation, consistent with the parent Quantitative Evaluation Metrics. Steps 1. Compute Global Metrics: Calculate PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS using all pixels in I{pred} and I{gt}. 2. Apply Mask: Create masked images I{pred}^{mask} and I{gt}^{mask} by zeroing out pixels where M{i,j} = 0. Alternatively, filter pixel coordinates to indices where M{i,j} = 1. 3. Compute Masked Metrics: Recalculate PSNR and LPIPS (and optionally SSIM/FLIP) using only the pixels in the masked region. 4. Report: Report the global metric as the primary value and the masked metric in parentheses. Formulas PSNR (Masked): PSNR{mask} = 10 \cdot \log{10} \left( \frac{MAXI^2}{MSE{mask}} \right) Where MAXI is the maximum possible pixel value (e.g., 1.0), and MSE{mask} is the mean squared error computed only over pixels where M{i,j} = 1: MSE{mask} = \frac{1}{N{mask}} \sum{i,j: M{i,j}=1} (I{pred}(i,j) - I{gt}(i,j))^2 And N{mask} is the count of pixels where M{i,j} = 1. SSIM (Masked): SSIM{mask} = \frac{1}{N{mask}} \sum{i,j: M{i,j}=1} SSIM(I{pred}(i,j), I{gt}(i,j)) Where SSIM(\cdot) is the local structural similarity index for a window centered at (i,j). LPIPS (Masked): LPIPS{mask} = \frac{1}{N{mask}} \sum{i,j: M{i,j}=1} LPIPS(I{pred}(i,j), I{gt}(i,j)) Where LPIPS(\cdot) is the learned perceptual image patch similarity. Parameters Mask Generation: Not specified in the method definition itself, but typically derived from ground truth depth or semantic segmentation. Window Size: For SSIM, standard window sizes (e.g., 11 \times 11) apply. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Empty Mask: If N{mask} = 0, metrics are undefined. Implementation should handle this by returning NaN or skipping the masked report. Boundary Effects: For SSIM, pixels near the mask boundary may have incomplete windows. Standard SSIM implementations handle this by padding or reducing window size. Precision: Ensure mask alignment with image resolution. Misalignment leads to incorrect pixel sampling. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def maskedmetricsevaluation(Ipred, Igt, M): """ Ipred: Tensor (H, W, C) Igt: Tensor (H, W, C) M: Tensor (H, W) binary mask (1 for valid, 0 for invalid) """ # 1. Global Metrics psnrglobal = computepsnr(Ipred, Igt) ssimglobal = computessim(Ipred, Igt) lpipsglobal = computelpips(Ipred, Igt) # 2. Masked Pixels maskindices = torch.where(M > 0.5) Ipredmasked = Ipred[maskindices] Igtmasked = Igt[maskindices] # 3. Masked Metrics # Handle case where no pixels are in mask if Ipredmasked.numel() == 0: return { 'psnrglobal': psnrglobal, 'ssimglobal': ssimglobal, 'lpipsglobal': lpipsglobal, 'psnrmasked': float('nan'), 'ssimmasked': float('nan'), 'lpipsmasked': float('nan') } psnrmasked = computepsnr(Ipredmasked, Igtmasked) ssimmasked = computessim(Ipredmasked, Igtmasked) lpipsmasked = computelpips(Ipredmasked, Igtmasked) return { 'psnrglobal': psnrglobal, 'ssimglobal': ssimglobal, 'lpipsglobal': lpipsglobal, 'psnrmasked': psnrmasked, 'ssimmasked': ssimmasked, 'lpipsmasked': lpipsmasked } def computepsnr(I1, I2): mse = torch.mean((I1 - I2) 2) if mse == 0: return float('inf') return 10 torch.log10(1.0 / mse) def computessim(I1, I2): # Placeholder for standard SSIM implementation # Returns mean SSIM over provided pixels return 0.9 # Placeholder for actual SSIM logic def computelpips(I1, I2): # Placeholder for standard LPIPS implementation # Returns mean LPIPS over provided pixels return 0.1 # Placeholder for actual LPIPS logic A specific application of masked metrics where the mask corresponds to an object crop, allowing comparison of object-level renders against scene-level renders. The practice of reporting masked metrics in parentheses alongside global metrics to highlight reconstruction quality in the presence of occlusions or background variations. Time Complexity: O(H \cdot W) for global metrics; O(N{mask}) for masked metrics, where N{mask} is the number of pixels in the mask. Since N{mask} \le H \cdot W, masked computation is faster or equal to global. Memory Complexity: O(H \cdot W) to store the mask and intermediate masked images. Strengths: Isolates reconstruction quality from background artifacts; enables fair comparison between methods with different background handling (e.g., randomized backgrounds vs. ground truth). Limitations: Requires a reliable ground-truth mask; does not penalize errors in the background, which may be visually significant. When to Use: When evaluating object-centric reconstruction or when background variations are irrelevant or randomized. When Not to Use: When background fidelity is a key evaluation criterion. The protocol originates from NeRS [38] and is used to evaluate object-level renders against scene-level renders by restricting pixel comparison to the ground-truth mask region. It is employed in works like Splatt3R and CADSplat to report metrics on masked regions, particularly in datasets with object-centric focus. name: PSNR Evaluation Pipeline
head: NeRF validation loop, PSNR calculation, Quantitative Evaluation, Test Set PSNR, Validation and PSNR Evaluation Pipeline
body: The PSNR Evaluation Pipeline computes the Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) on held-out test or validation splits to quantitatively assess the rendering quality of a trained NeRF model. It differs from training metrics by using inference-optimized rendering paths and strictly handling ground truth transparency via white-background compositing to ensure fair comparison with the rendered RGB output. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Trained model state (coarse and/or fine MLPs), dataset split identifier ("test" or "val"), and optional resolution flag (halfres). Outputs: Per-frame PSNR values, mean PSNR, standard deviation, and optionally side-by-side visual comparisons of ground truth, rendered RGB, and depth. Data Structures Evaluation State: A model configuration object where the standard training raymarch and render functions are replaced with inference variants (e.g., stateeval = state.replace(raymarch=args.raymarcheval, render=args.rendereval)). Image Arrays: Ground truth images are stored as RGBA (uint8 or float32) and rendered images as RGB (float32). Steps 1. Load Data: Load the camera poses and images for the specified split. If halfres is true, images are loaded at half resolution (e.g., 200 \times 200 for Blender datasets). 2. Prepare State: Instantiate the evaluation state using inference-specific rendering functions to optimize for speed during validation. 3. Composite Ground Truth: For each ground truth image in the split, composite the RGBA image against a white background. This step is critical because NeRFs typically render opaque RGB images, while ground truth may contain transparent regions. Formula: I{composite} = I{rgba} \cdot \alpha + (1 - \alpha) \cdot I{white}, where I{white} is white (1, 1, 1). 4. Render: Iterate over each validation view. For each view, extract the camera transform and render the image using the inference state. Chunked rendering is often used to manage memory. Output: Rendered RGB, background, and depth maps. 5. Compute MSE: Calculate the Mean Squared Error between the composite ground truth RGB and the rendered RGB. Formula: \text{MSE} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (Ri - Gi)^2, where Ri is the rendered pixel and Gi is the composite ground truth pixel. 6. Compute PSNR: Convert MSE to PSNR. Formula: \text{PSNR} = -10 \cdot \log{10}(\text{MSE}). Edge Case: If \text{MSE} = 0, PSNR is infinite. Implementations must cap this value or use a small epsilon to prevent aggregation errors. 7. Aggregate: Accumulate PSNR values across all frames in the split. Compute the mean and standard deviation. 8. Visualize (Optional): Concatenate ground truth, rendered RGB, and depth maps side-by-side for qualitative inspection. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatepsnr(modelstate, dataset, split="test", halfres=False): # 1. Load data images, poses = loadblenderdata(dataset, split=split, halfres=halfres) # 2. Prepare evaluation state evalstate = modelstate.replace( raymarch=modelstate.raymarcheval, render=modelstate.rendereval) psnrvalues = [] # 3. Iterate over views for i, (imagergba, transform) in enumerate(zip(images, poses)): # 4. Composite ground truth with white background # imagergba is (H, W, 4), alpha is channel 3 alpha = imagergba[..., 3:4] / 255.0 rgbgt = imagergba[...,:3] / 255.0 whitebg = np.oneslike(rgbgt) gtrgbcomposite = rgbgt alpha + whitebg (1 - alpha) # 5. Render # renderimageinference returns bg, rgb, depth rendered = renderimageinference( key=i, transform=transform, state=evalstate) renderedrgb = rendered.rgb # 6. Compute MSE # Ensure shapes match and handle potential dtype differences mse = np.mean((renderedrgb - gtrgbcomposite) 2) # 7. Compute PSNR if mse == 0: psnr = float('inf') # Handle perfect match else: psnr = -10.0 np.log10(mse) psnrvalues.append(psnr) # 8. Aggregate meanpsnr = np.mean(psnrvalues) stdpsnr = np.std(psnrvalues) return meanpsnr, stdpsnr, psnrvalues Parameters split: Dataset split to evaluate ("test" or "val"). halfres: Boolean flag to load images at half resolution for faster evaluation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Infinite PSNR: Occurs when MSE is exactly zero. Must be handled to avoid NaNs in mean/std calculations. Alpha Handling: Failing to composite ground truth RGBA with a white background leads to incorrect MSE calculations against opaque RGB renders. Resolution Mismatch: Ensure rendered resolution matches ground truth resolution before computing MSE. A variant of the evaluation pipeline that focuses on comparing PSNR values across different methods (e.g., NeRF vs. SDF-based methods) on standard datasets like NeRFsynthetic. It highlights that NeRF often achieves higher PSNR than geometric regularization-based methods because it prioritizes color reproduction over strict geometric fidelity. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels and number of test views. Rendering is the dominant cost, optimized by using inference-specific raymarching. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to image resolution. Chunked rendering is used to limit peak memory usage during ray marching. Strengths: Standard, interpretable metric for image fidelity; easy to implement and compare across papers. Limitations: PSNR correlates poorly with perceptual quality; sensitive to alpha channel handling; does not measure geometric accuracy. When to Use: Standard validation for novel view synthesis tasks where photometric accuracy is the primary goal. The PSNR evaluation pipeline is a standard component of NeRF training and validation workflows, originating from the original NeRF paper and widely adopted in subsequent works. It is used to benchmark rendering quality on datasets like NeRFsynthetic (Blender) and DTU. The specific handling of alpha compositing and inference state replacement is detailed in community implementations and forks. yashtmy/nerf-3d-vision, https://github.com/yashtmy/nerf-3d-vision, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) blurgyy/jaxngp, https://github.com/blurgyy/jaxngp, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) PET-NeuS: Positional Encoding Tri-Planes for Neural Surfaces, http://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05594v1, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Masked Evaluation
head: Depth reprojection masking, Evaluation Visibility Mask Generation
body: Masked Evaluation restricts radiance field metric computation to pixels visible in at least two training views, preventing metric degradation from evaluating regions that NeRFs cannot predict by design. Unlike sibling methods like Unified Metric Aggregation which may aggregate errors across all pixels, or PSNR Evaluation Pipeline which computes standard metrics on full images, this method explicitly excludes occluded or single-view-only geometry to ensure fair comparison of geometric consistency. It differs from View-Consistency Metric (Ewarp) by serving as a preprocessing step for standard metrics (like PSNR) rather than a self-supervised regularizer, using depth reprojection to define the valid evaluation domain. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Set of training views V{train} = \{v1,..., vN\} with associated camera poses Pi and intrinsics Ki. Predicted depth maps Di for each training view vi, generated by a Dense-NeRF model. Test view v{test} with camera pose P{test} and intrinsics K{test}. Predicted depth map D{test} for the test view, generated by the same Dense-NeRF model. Threshold parameter \tau. Outputs: Binary visibility mask M{test} of the same spatial dimensions as v{test}, where M{test}(x,y) = 1 if the pixel is visible in at least two training views, and 0 otherwise. Data Structures: Depth maps are 2D arrays of floating-point values representing distance from the camera center. The mask is a 2D binary array (uint8 or bool). Steps: 1. Initialize Visibility Counter: Create a zero-initialized integer array C{test} with the same height and width as D{test}. This array will count how many training views consider each pixel visible. 2. Iterate Training Views: For each training view vi \in V{train}: a. Reprojection: Warp the depth map Di from the coordinate system of vi to the coordinate system of v{test} using the relative camera pose Pi^{-1} P{test} and intrinsics Ki, K{test}. Let the warped depth map be D{i \to test}. b. Depth Comparison: For each pixel (x,y) in v{test}: i. Retrieve the predicted depth from the test view: d{test} = D{test}(x,y). ii. Retrieve the warped depth from the training view: d{warped} = D{i \to test}(x,y). iii. Compute the absolute depth difference: \Delta d = |d{test} - d{warped}|. iv. Thresholding: If \Delta d < \tau, mark the pixel as visible in view vi by incrementing the counter: C{test}(x,y) \leftarrow C{test}(x,y) + 1. 3. Final Mask Generation: For each pixel (x,y) in v{test}: a. If C{test}(x,y) \ge 2, set M{test}(x,y) = 1. b. Otherwise, set M{test}(x,y) = 0. Parameters: Depth Difference Threshold (\tau): Set to 0.05 \times \max(D{train}), where \max(D{train}) is the maximum depth value in the training view's depth map. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatemaskedevaluationmask( trainviews: List[View], testview: View, densenerf: DenseNeRFModel, thresholdfactor: float = 0.05) -> np.ndarray: """ Generates a binary visibility mask for a test view based on depth consistency with at least two training views. Args: trainviews: List of training view objects containing camera pose, intrinsics, and associated depth map from Dense-NeRF. testview: Test view object containing camera pose, intrinsics, and associated depth map from Dense-NeRF. densenerf: Model used to predict depth maps (assumed to provide depth maps for all views passed). thresholdfactor: Factor to multiply max depth by for thresholding. Returns: Binary mask (numpy array) where 1 indicates visibility in >= 2 training views. """ # Get depth maps from Dense-NeRF # Note: In practice, these are pre-computed or passed as inputs. # Here we assume densenerf.predictdepth(view) returns the depth map. traindepths = {v.id: densenerf.predictdepth(v) for v in trainviews} testdepth = densenerf.predictdepth(testview) # Initialize visibility counter h, w = testdepth.shape visibilitycount = np.zeros((h, w), dtype=np.int32) # Threshold calculation # Use max depth of the current training view being processed or a global max? # Sources say "maximum depth of the train view" (singular), implying per-view or global. # We use the max depth of the specific training view for consistency with "train view" singular in source. # However, standard practice often uses a global scene max. # Source says "0.05 times the maximum depth of the train view". # We will use the max depth of the specific training view i for the threshold. for trainview in trainviews: dtrain = traindepths[trainview.id] dtest = testdepth # Warp depth from trainview to testview # This function handles the projection: # 1. Unproject dtrain to 3D points in trainview frame # 2. Transform 3D points to testview frame using relative pose # 3. Project 3D points to testview image plane to get dwarped dwarped = warpdepth(dtrain, trainview, testview) # Calculate max depth for threshold for this specific training view maxdepthtrain = np.max(dtrain) threshold = thresholdfactor maxdepthtrain # Compute absolute difference # Handle invalid depths (e.g., 0 or infinity) if necessary # Assuming valid depths are positive. diff = np.abs(dtest - dwarped) # Check visibility condition # Note: dwarped might have invalid values where warping fails (occlusion in source view). # We should only count if dwarped is valid. validwarped = (dwarped > 0) & (np.isfinite(dwarped)) validtest = (dtest > 0) & (np.isfinite(dtest)) valid = validwarped & validtest visibleintrain = (diff < threshold) & valid # Increment counter for visible pixels visibilitycount += visiblewarped.astype(np.int32) # Generate final mask: visible in at least 2 views mask = (visibilitycount >= 2).astype(np.uint8) return mask def warpdepth(depthmap: np.ndarray, srcview: View, dstview: View) -> np.ndarray: """ Warps a depth map from source view to destination view. Args: depthmap: 2D array of depth values in srcview. srcview: Source view with camera matrix Ksrc and pose Psrc. dstview: Destination view with camera matrix Kdst and pose Pdst. Returns: 2D array of depth values in dstview coordinate system. """ # 1. Get image dimensions h, w = depthmap.shape # 2. Create 2D grid of pixel coordinates in source view y, x = np.meshgrid(np.arange(h), np.arange(w), indexing='ij') # 3. Unproject to 3D points in source camera frame # Inverse intrinsic matrix Kinvsrc = np.linalg.inv(srcview.K) # Homogeneous coordinates in image plane # Shape: (3, HW) imgcoords = np.vstack([x.flatten(), y.flatten(), np.ones(hw)]) # Ray directions in camera frame (assuming normalized device coordinates or similar) # Actually, we need to convert pixel coords to 3D points given depth. # Point = Kinv [x, y, 1] depth rays = Kinvsrc @ imgcoords # Shape: (3, HW) # Scale rays by depth to get 3D points in source camera frame # depthmap is (H, W). Flatten to (HW,) depthsflat = depthmap.flatten() # 3D points in source camera frame pointssrccam = rays depthsflat[np.newaxis,:] # Shape: (3, HW) # 4. Transform 3D points to world frame # Psrc is usually [R|t]. We assume Psrc transforms world to camera? # Or camera to world? Standard NeRF conventions vary. # Let's assume Psrc is the transformation from World to Camera (view matrix). # So pointsworld = Psrc^{-1} @ pointscam # Or if Psrc is World->Camera, then pointscam = Psrc @ pointsworld. # Let's assume standard: P is World->Camera. # We need points in World frame to transform to dstview. # pointsworld = Psrc^{-1} @ [pointscam; 1] # Construct homogeneous points in src camera frame pointssrccamh = np.vstack([pointssrccam, np.ones(hw)]) # Inverse of view matrix to get World coordinates # Assuming srcview.P is 4x4 World->Camera matrix Psrcinv = np.linalg.inv(srcview.P) pointsworldh = Psrcinv @ pointssrccamh # Extract 3D points pointsworld = pointsworldh[:3,:] # 5. Transform 3D points to destination camera frame # Pdst is World->Camera pointsdstcamh = dstview.P @ pointsworldh # Extract 3D points in dst camera frame pointsdstcam = pointsdstcamh[:3,:] # 6. Project to destination image plane # Kdst @ pointsdstcam projectedh = dstview.K @ pointsdstcam # Normalize by z z = projectedh[2,:] xdst = projectedh[0,:] / z ydst = projectedh[1,:] / z # 7. Interpolate depth from original depth map? # No, we are warping the depth map itself. # The depth in dst view is the z-coordinate of the point in dst camera frame. # But we need to map this back to the dst image grid. # We have xdst, ydst for every pixel in src. # We need to create a dst image where each pixel (xdst, ydst) gets the depth z. # Create output depth map dstdepth = np.zeros((h, w)) # Round coordinates to nearest integer xdstint = np.round(xdst).astype(np.int32) ydstint = np.round(ydst).astype(np.int32) # Filter valid pixels (within dst image bounds) validmask = (xdstint >= 0) & (xdstint < w) & \ (ydstint >= 0) & (ydstint < h) & \ (z > 0) # Valid depth xdstvalid = xdstint[validmask] ydstvalid = ydstint[validmask] zvalid = z[validmask] # Assign depths dstdepth[ydstvalid, xdstvalid] = zvalid return dstdepth Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Accuracy Dependency: Mask accuracy is entirely dependent on the accuracy of the Dense-NeRF depth estimation. Incorrect Dense-NeRF depths produce incorrect masks. Specular Surfaces: Using depth-based reprojection is robust to specular objects, whereas color-based reprojection fails on such surfaces. Unseen Regions: Unmasked evaluation includes regions not visible in training views, which radiance fields memorize rather than predict, artificially inflating error metrics. Invalid Depths: Warping may produce invalid depths (e.g., from occlusions in the source view). These should be handled by ignoring pixels where d{warped} is invalid or zero. Generates a binary visibility mask to identify pixels in a reference view that are occluded (invisible) when observed from a new camera pose. It solves the problem of evaluating or inpainting regions that have no geometric correspondence in other views, which often leads to artifacts or incorrect depth predictions in radiance field optimization. It differs from sibling methods like View-Consistency Metric by explicitly using depth warping errors to detect occlusion rather than relying solely on photometric color differences or optical flow consistency. The View-Consistency Metric (Ewarp) evaluates the geometric and photometric consistency of a radiance field by measuring the reconstruction error between a rendered view and a neighboring view warped into the target viewpoint. It serves as a self-supervised regularizer or evaluation metric that penalizes inconsistencies arising from incorrect depth or color predictions, leveraging optical flow and occlusion masks to isolate valid correspondences. It differs from standard PSNR or LPIPS by explicitly accounting for viewpoint changes and occlusions, ensuring that errors are only measured where scene content is visible in both views. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot H \cdot W), where N is the number of training views, and H, W are the image dimensions. Each training view requires warping and comparison for every pixel. Memory Complexity: O(H \cdot W) for storing the visibility counter and mask, plus O(H \cdot W) for intermediate warped depth maps if processed sequentially. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of training views. Strengths: Robust to specular objects; prevents metric degradation from evaluating unseen geometry; ensures fair comparison of geometric consistency. Limitations: Highly dependent on the accuracy of the Dense-NeRF depth estimation; incorrect depths lead to incorrect masks. When to Use: When evaluating radiance fields trained on sparse input views, particularly when comparing models that may memorize unseen regions. When Not to Use: When depth estimation is unreliable or when evaluating full-image fidelity including unseen regions is desired. Masked Evaluation was introduced in the context of regularizing sparse input Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) to prevent them from being evaluated on regions they cannot predict by design. Radiance fields are designed to memorize a scene and are ill-equipped to predict unseen regions or the depth of objects seen in only one input view. The method was proposed to address the issue that unmasked evaluation artificially inflates error metrics by including these unpredictable regions. It relies on depth-based reprojection techniques similar to those described by Cho et al. [2017] and Kanchana et al. [2022]. The approach was implemented and released alongside the SimpleNeRF and Simple-RF models. name: Masked Evaluation (Depth-based Visibility Mask Generation)
head: Depth reprojection masking, Invisible Mask Computation, Invisible Region Detection via Depth Warping
body: This method generates a binary visibility mask to identify pixels in a reference view that are occluded (invisible) when observed from a new camera pose. It solves the problem of evaluating or inpainting regions that have no geometric correspondence in other views, which often leads to artifacts or incorrect depth predictions in radiance field optimization. It differs from sibling methods like View-Consistency Metric by explicitly using depth warping errors to detect occlusion rather than relying solely on photometric color differences or optical flow consistency. Inputs: A reference view with RGB image I{rgb} and depth map Id. A new (source) view with RGB image I'{rgb} and depth map I'd. Camera intrinsics and extrinsics for both views. A trained NeRF or depth estimation model to provide initial depth values if not given directly. Outputs: A final binary mask m of the same spatial dimensions as the reference view, where m{ij}=1 indicates an invisible (occluded) pixel and m{ij}=0 indicates a visible pixel. Masked RGB image \bar{I}{rgb} and masked depth map \bar{I}d for subsequent processing (e.g., inpainting). Data Structures: Id, I'd: 2D arrays of floating-point depth values. m, m': 2D binary arrays (uint8 or bool). v{ij}: Depth value at pixel (i,j) in the reference view. v'{ij}: Warped depth value at pixel (i,j) from the new view. Steps: 1. Depth Warping: For each pixel (i,j) in the reference view, project the corresponding 3D point from the new view's depth map I'd into the reference view's coordinate system using the relative camera pose. Let the resulting depth value be v'{ij}. 2. Per-View Invisible Mask Generation: Compute the intermediate mask m' for the current new view using the indicator function: m'{ij} = \mathbb{I}(v'{ij} - v{ij} > \varepsilon) where \mathbb{I}(\cdot) is the indicator function (1 if true, 0 otherwise). If the warped depth v'{ij} is significantly larger than the reference depth v{ij}, the point is considered occluded in the reference view because the surface seen in the new view is "behind" the surface seen in the reference view. 3. Final Mask Aggregation: If multiple new views are used, compute m' for each. The final mask m is the logical AND of all intermediate masks: m = \bigwedge{k} m'k A pixel is marked invisible only if it is occluded in all compared new views. 4. Masking Inputs: Apply the final mask to the reference RGB and depth images: \bar{I}{rgb} = I{rgb} \otimes (1 - m) \bar{I}d = Id \otimes (1 - m) where \otimes denotes element-wise multiplication. Parameters: \varepsilon: A small positive threshold value to allow for minor warping errors or depth estimation noise. Typical values are not specified in the source but should be small relative to the scene scale. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Depth values must be consistent in units and coordinate systems. Misalignment in camera poses will cause false occlusions. Degenerate Input: If Id or I'd contains invalid values (e.g., infinity or zero), they must be handled or filtered out before warping. Boundary Conditions: Pixels at the image border may not have valid correspondences in the new view. These should be treated as invisible or masked out. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatevisibilitymask(referencedepth, newdepth, refintrinsics, newintrinsics, refpose, newpose, epsilon): """ Generates an invisible mask for a reference view based on depth warping from a new view. Args: referencedepth (np.ndarray): 2D array of depth values for the reference view. newdepth (np.ndarray): 2D array of depth values for the new view. refintrinsics (np.ndarray): 3x3 camera intrinsic matrix for the reference view. newintrinsics (np.ndarray): 3x3 camera intrinsic matrix for the new view. refpose (np.ndarray): 4x4 camera pose matrix for the reference view. newpose (np.ndarray): 4x4 camera pose matrix for the new view. epsilon (float): Threshold for depth difference. Returns: np.ndarray: Binary mask where 1 indicates invisible (occluded) pixels. """ # Get image dimensions height, width = referencedepth.shape # Create grid of pixel coordinates y, x = np.meshgrid(np.arange(height), np.arange(width), indexing='ij') # Convert pixel coordinates to homogeneous coordinates in reference view refpixels = np.stack([x, y, np.oneslike(x)], axis=-1).astype(np.float32) # Unproject reference pixels to 3D points using reference depth and intrinsics # Pref = Kref^-1 [x, y, 1]^T dref refintrinsicsinv = np.linalg.inv(refintrinsics) refhomogeneous = refpixels @ refintrinsicsinv.T # Shape: (H, W, 3) ref3dpoints = refhomogeneous referencedepth[:,:, np.newaxis] # Shape: (H, W, 3) # Transform 3D points to new view's coordinate system # Pnew = R Pref + t, where [R|t] is the relative pose from ref to new # Relative pose: newpose @ inv(refpose) relpose = newpose @ np.linalg.inv(refpose) R = relpose[:3,:3] t = relpose[:3, 3] # Apply rotation and translation # Note: ref3dpoints is (H, W, 3), need to handle batched operation rotatedpoints = ref3dpoints @ R.T transformedpoints = rotatedpoints + t[np.newaxis, np.newaxis,:] # Project transformed 3D points to new view's image plane # pnew = Knew Pnew newhomogeneous = transformedpoints @ refintrinsicsinv.T # Wait, should use newintrinsics # Correction: Project to new view newhomogeneous = transformedpoints @ newintrinsics.T newu = newhomogeneous[:,:, 0] / newhomogeneous[:,:, 2] newv = newhomogeneous[:,:, 1] / newhomogeneous[:,:, 2] newz = newhomogeneous[:,:, 2] # Check if projected points are within image bounds validmask = (newu >= 0) & (newu < width) & (newv >= 0) & (newv < height) & (newz > 0) # Interpolate depth from newdepth at (newu, newv) # Using bilinear interpolation warpeddepth = interpolatedepth(newdepth, newu, newv) # Handle invalid projections warpeddepth[~validmask] = np.inf # Compute depth difference depthdiff = warpeddepth - referencedepth # Generate mask: 1 if warped depth is significantly larger (occluded) invisiblemask = (depthdiff > epsilon).astype(np.float32) return invisiblemask def interpolatedepth(depthmap, u, v): """ Bilinear interpolation of depth map at sub-pixel coordinates. """ # Clamp coordinates to valid range uclamped = np.clip(u, 0, depthmap.shape[1] - 1) vclamped = np.clip(v, 0, depthmap.shape[0] - 1) # Get integer coordinates u0 = np.floor(uclamped).astype(int) v0 = np.floor(vclamped).astype(int) u1 = u0 + 1 v1 = v0 + 1 # Handle boundary conditions u1 = np.clip(u1, 0, depthmap.shape[1] - 1) v1 = np.clip(v1, 0, depthmap.shape[0] - 1) # Get depth values at corners d00 = depthmap[v0, u0] d01 = depthmap[v0, u1] d10 = depthmap[v1, u0] d11 = depthmap[v1, u1] # Interpolate du = uclamped - u0 dv = vclamped - v0 d0 = d00 (1 - du) + d01 du d1 = d10 (1 - du) + d11 du d = d0 (1 - dv) + d1 dv return d Generates a consistency mask Ml to identify pixels with geometric inconsistencies during feature-level regularization. It distinguishes itself by explicitly comparing rendered depth maps between views to detect warping errors, rather than relying solely on photometric color differences or optical flow consistency. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels in the reference view and the number of new views used for comparison. Depth warping and interpolation are the dominant operations. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels, storing depth maps and masks. Strengths: Explicitly handles occlusions by leveraging geometric consistency. Effective for identifying regions that lack multi-view support. Limitations: Relies on accurate depth estimation or rendering. Sensitive to camera pose errors and depth noise. Does not account for textureless regions where depth estimation might be unreliable. When to Use: When inpainting or regularizing radiance fields in regions that are occluded in some views but visible in others. When Not to Use: When depth information is unavailable or highly unreliable. When computational resources are extremely limited and a simpler photometric consistency check suffices. The method originates from the PERF (Panoramic Neural Radiance Field) paper, which addresses the challenge of completing large-size occlusions in complex 3D panoramic scenes using collaborative RGBD inpainting. It was developed to overcome the limitations of adversarial learning and high-level semantic constraints, which fail to fill large invisible regions effectively. PERF: Panoramic Neural Radiance Field From a Single Panorama, https://doi.org/10.1109/tpami.2024.3387307, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Occlusion-Aware Masking
head: Depth-based Visibility Mask Generation, Invisible Mask Computation, Invisible Region Detection via Depth Warping
body: Occlusion-Aware Masking generates a consistency mask Ml to identify and ignore pixels with geometric inconsistencies, such as artifacts or self-occlusion, during feature-level regularization in NeRF training. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly comparing rendered depth maps between a target view and a source view to detect warping errors, rather than relying solely on photometric color differences or optical flow consistency. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rendered depth map of the target (unseen) view Dj, rendered depth map of the source (seen) view Di, camera intrinsics K, relative rotation R{j \to i} between views, and a depth threshold \tau. Outputs: A binary consistency mask Ml aligned with the dimensions of the l-th layer feature map. Data Structures: Dj, Di: 2D arrays of floating-point depth values, size H \times W. Ml: 2D binary array (0 or 1), size Hl \times Wl, where Hl, Wl are the spatial dimensions of the feature map at layer l. Steps: 1. Reprojection: For each pixel pj in the target view image Ij, compute its corresponding coordinate p{j \to i} in the source view image Ii. This is done by transforming the 3D point defined by Dj(pj) back to the source camera frame using R{j \to i} and K, then projecting it. The coordinate is calculated as: p{j \to i} \sim K R{j \to i} Dj(pj) K^{-1} pj where \sim indicates approximate equality due to continuous coordinate values. 2. Depth Sampling: Sample the depth value Di(p{j \to i}) from the source depth map at the reprojected coordinate p{j \to i} using a differentiable sampler. 3. Mask Generation: Compute the binary mask M(pj) for each pixel in the target view by comparing the depth difference against the threshold \tau: M(pj) = [ || Dj(pj) - Di(p{j \to i}) || < \tau ] where [\cdot] is the Iverson bracket (1 if true, 0 if false). If the distance between the two depth points exceeds \tau, the rays are considered to render separate surfaces (occlusion or artifact), and the pixel is masked out. 4. Resizing: Apply nearest-neighbor downsampling to the generated mask M to match the spatial dimensions of the l-th layer feature map outputs, resulting in Ml. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateocclusionmask(Dj, Di, K, Rjtoi, tau): """ Generate occlusion-aware mask by comparing depth maps. Args: Dj: Depth map of target view (H, W) Di: Depth map of source view (H, W) K: Camera intrinsic matrix (3, 3) Rjtoi: Rotation matrix from target to source view (3, 3) tau: Depth difference threshold Returns: M: Binary mask (H, W) """ H, W = Dj.shape M = np.zeros((H, W), dtype=float) # Precompute inverse intrinsic for projection Kinv = np.linalg.inv(K) for j in range(H): for i in range(W): # 1. Get 3D point in target camera frame # Assuming homogeneous coordinates for pj pjhom = np.array([i, j, 1.0]) depthval = Dj[j, i] # 2. Project to 3D in target frame # x = Kinv [u, v, 1] depth pt3dtarget = Kinv @ pjhom depthval # 3. Transform to source camera frame pt3dsource = Rjtoi @ pt3dtarget # 4. Project to source image plane pihom = K @ pt3dsource pihom = pihom / pihom[2] # Normalize by z ui, vi = pihom[0], pihom[1] # 5. Check bounds and sample depth # Note: In practice, use bilinear/nearest sampling for continuous coords if 0 <= ui < W and 0 <= vi < H: # Sample Di at (ui, vi) # Using nearest neighbor for simplicity in this basic implementation # In production, use a differentiable sampler as noted in disample = Di[int(round(vi)), int(round(ui))] # 6. Compare depths diff = abs(Dj[j, i] - disample) if diff < tau: M[j, i] = 1.0 else: M[j, i] = 0.0 else: M[j, i] = 0.0 return M def applymasktofeatures(M, featuremapl): """ Resize mask and apply to feature map. Args: M: Binary mask (H, W) featuremapl: Feature map at layer l (Hl, Wl, Cl) Returns: Ml: Resized mask (Hl, Wl) """ Hl, Wl = featuremapl.shape[0], featuremapl.shape[1] # Nearest-neighbor downsampling Ml = resizenearestneighbor(M, (Hl, Wl)) return Ml Parameters: \tau: Threshold determining if two rays render depths of separate surfaces. If the distance between depth points is greater than \tau, the pixel is masked out. Value not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Continuous Coordinates: The reprojected coordinate p{j \to i} is a continuous value. A differentiable sampler is required to extract color/depth values accurately. Boundary Conditions: Pixels reprojected outside the source image bounds should be masked out (set to 0). Precision: Depth values must be rendered consistently between views to ensure valid comparison. A process to distinguish between valid and invalid optical flow areas to handle occlusion and lighting errors. It computes forward and backward optical flow coordinates, calculates the absolute difference between the predicted flow point and the target ground-truth image, and sets the mask to 1 if the difference is below a threshold \theta and the point is within image bounds, else 0. Parameter \theta is the threshold between optical flow prediction and ground truth. Time Complexity: O(H \times W) per view pair for mask generation, where H, W are image dimensions. Memory Complexity: O(H \times W) for storing the depth maps and the mask. Strengths: Prevents imperfect and distorted warpings caused by erroneous geometry from influencing the model, degrading reconstruction quality. Specifically handles artifacts and self-occlusion. Limitations: Requires accurate depth rendering from both views. Performance depends heavily on the choice of threshold \tau. When to use: When training NeRFs with few shots or in scenes with significant occlusions and geometric artifacts. Originated in GeCoNeRF (Geometric Consistency NeRF) for few-shot neural radiance fields. The method addresses the issue of geometric inconsistencies in feature-level regularization by constructing a consistency mask Ml. name: Optical Flow Masking
head: Flow-based Occlusion Masking, Optical Flow Validity Masking
body: Optical Flow Masking distinguishes between valid and invalid optical flow areas to handle occlusion and lighting errors during NeRF optimization. It sets aside regions where geometric inconsistencies or artifacts would corrupt feature-level regularization, building on Occlusion-Aware Masking by using pixel-space flow consistency rather than just depth-based visibility. Inputs: Two adjacent RGB images (source Ia, target Ib), forward optical flow field f{a \to b}, backward optical flow field f{b \to a}, image dimensions H \times W, and a threshold \theta. Outputs: A binary validity mask M{a \to b} of size H \times W. Data Structures: f{a \to b}(r, c): 2D vector (u, v) representing flow at pixel (r, c). M{a \to b}: Binary matrix, M{a \to b}(r, c) \in \{0, 1\}. Steps: 1. Compute forward corresponding point coordinates F{a \to b}(r, c) for all r \in [0, H], c \in [0, W]: F{a \to b}(r, c) = (r, c) + f{a \to b}(r, c) Similarly for backward flow F{b \to a}(r, c) = (r, c) + f{b \to a}(r, c). 2. Calculate the absolute difference d between the target ground-truth image True{rgb} and the source image warped by the flow: d = |Flow{rgb} - True{rgb}| Where Flow{rgb} is the pixel value at F{a \to b}(r, c) sampled from Ia, and True{rgb} is the pixel value at (r, c) in Ib. 3. Set the mask value M{a \to b}(r, c): M{a \to b}(r, c) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } d \le \theta \text{ and } F{a \to b}(r, c) \in [W, H] \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} The condition F{a \to b}(r, c) \in [W, H] checks if the corresponding point lies within the image bounds. Parameters: \theta: Threshold between optical flow prediction and ground truth. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: If F{a \to b}(r, c) falls outside image bounds, the mask is 0. Lighting changes or occlusions cause large d, resulting in mask 0. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeopticalflowmask(Ia, Ib, fatob, H, W, theta): """ Ia: Source image (H, W, 3) Ib: Target image (H, W, 3) fatob: Forward flow field (H, W, 2) H, W: Image height and width theta: Consistency threshold """ mask = np.zeros((H, W), dtype=np.float32) # Get coordinates rows, cols = np.meshgrid(np.arange(H), np.arange(W), indexing='ij') # Compute corresponding points # fatob contains (dx, dy) fx = cols + fatob[:,:, 0] fy = rows + fatob[:,:, 1] # Check bounds validbounds = (fx >= 0) & (fx < W) & (fy >= 0) & (fy < H) # Sample warped source image # Clamp coordinates for sampling to avoid index errors, though validbounds handles logic fxclamped = np.clip(fx, 0, W - 1).astype(np.int32) fyclamped = np.clip(fy, 0, H - 1).astype(np.int32) # Get RGB values from source image at corresponding points # Note: Ia shape is (H, W, 3) flowrgb = Ia[fyclamped, fxclamped] # Calculate absolute difference d = np.abs(flowrgb.astype(np.float32) - Ib.astype(np.float32)) # Sum differences across channels (or use mean, source says "absolute difference") # Source implies scalar d, likely sum or max of channel diffs dscalar = np.sum(d, axis=2) # Apply threshold and bounds validflow = dscalar <= theta mask = (validbounds & validflow).astype(np.float32) return mask Creates a soft [0,1] dynamism mask by comparing measured flow against rigid flow predicted by depth. Used in synthetic tests; real data uses the depth-free epipolar residual. Generates per-frame soft dynamism masks for a moving-camera clip by measuring dense flow to a neighbor, subtracting rigid flow predicted by recovered pose, and thresholding the residual. 1. Check for OpenCV availability and sufficient frames/poses; return empty masks if unavailable or insufficient. 2. Initialize DISOpticalFlow with PRESETMEDIUM and finest scale 0. 3. Convert RGB frames to grayscale. 4. For each frame i, determine neighbor j (i+1, or i-1 for last frame). 5. Calculate measured flow between frames i and j. 6. Compute rigid flow prediction and validity mask from depth and camera poses. 7. Calculate the residual as the L2 norm of the difference between measured flow and predicted flow, masked by validity. 8. Compute epipolar residual using measured flow and camera poses. 9. Apply the robust thresholding function to the residual. 10. Clean and threshold the residual to get the mask, then append to list. 11. Update statistics with the mean dynamic fraction (m > 0.5). Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and limitations: Handles occlusion and lighting errors effectively. Limitations include sensitivity to lighting changes and occlusions which generate invalid flow areas. When to use it: When using optical flow to guide view synthesis or feature regularization in NeRF, specifically to ignore invalid flow regions. When not: When high-quality depth and pose information is available for rigid flow subtraction (use Per-Frame Soft Dynamism Masks instead). Origin: Introduced in "Bidirectional Optical Flow NeRF: High Accuracy and High Quality under Fewer Views". History and development: Used to preprocess optical flow graphs before NeRF optimization to ensure correct and photorealistic novel views under fewer input views. Where it is used: In NeRF training loops that incorporate bidirectional optical flow constraints. name: View-Consistency Metric (E_warp)
head: Warped View Consistency Metric
body: The View-Consistency Metric (Ewarp) evaluates the geometric and photometric consistency of a radiance field by measuring the reconstruction error between a rendered view and a neighboring view warped into the target viewpoint. It serves as a self-supervised regularizer or evaluation metric that penalizes inconsistencies arising from incorrect depth or color predictions, leveraging optical flow and occlusion masks to isolate valid correspondences. It differs from standard PSNR or LPIPS by explicitly accounting for viewpoint changes and occlusions, ensuring that errors are only measured where scene content is visible in both views. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of rendered images V from a pre-trained NeRF at camera poses i and i+\delta; an occlusion detection method; an optical flow estimator. Outputs: A scalar consistency error E{\text{warp}}. Data Structures: V{i+\delta}: Rendered image at pose i+\delta (target view). \bar{V}{i+\delta}: Warped image at pose i+\delta (source view Vi warped to i+\delta). O: Binary occlusion mask of the same spatial dimensions as the images, where O(x,y)=1 if the pixel is visible in both views, 0 otherwise. |O|: The number of pixels where O(x,y)=1. Steps: 1. Render Sequence: Render images Vi and V{i+\delta} from the NeRF at camera poses separated by a temporal or spatial offset \delta. 2. Estimate Optical Flow: Compute the optical flow field from Vi to V{i+\delta} using a pre-trained optical flow network (e.g., RAFT). 3. Derive Occlusion Mask: Generate the occlusion mask O using an occlusion detection algorithm (e.g., Ruder et al. [35]) based on the estimated flow and image consistency. 4. Warp Source View: Use the optical flow to warp Vi into the coordinate system of V{i+\delta}, producing \bar{V}{i+\delta}. 5. Compute Error: Calculate the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the warped view and the target view, restricted to the valid pixels in O. Formula: E{\text{warp}}(V{i+\delta}, \bar{V}{i+\delta}) = \frac{1}{|O|} \left\| \bar{V}{i+\delta} - V{i+\delta} \right\|2^2 Where: V{i+\delta} is the rendered view at pose i+\delta. \bar{V}{i+\delta} is the warped view from pose i to i+\delta. O is the occlusion mask. \| \cdot \|2^2 denotes the squared L2 norm (sum of squared differences). Parameters: \delta: The offset between viewpoints. Short-range consistency: \delta = 1. Long-range consistency: \delta = 7. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion Handling: Pixels occluded in one view but visible in the other must be masked out (O=0) to prevent the metric from penalizing valid geometric changes as errors. Flow Accuracy: The quality of the warp depends heavily on the accuracy of the optical flow estimator. Large displacements or textureless regions may lead to incorrect flow, causing false errors. Pre-trained Requirement: The optical flow must be estimated on a video sequence rendered from a pre-trained NeRF to ensure the flow corresponds to the scene geometry rather than training artifacts. A variant of the view-consistency metric that uses Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) instead of MSE to assess consistency. It is defined as E{\text{warp}}(Iv, I{v'}) = \text{LPIPS}(M{v,v'} \cdot Iv, W(I{v'})), where Iv and I{v'} are renders from nearby viewpoints v and v', W(\cdot) is the warping function, and M{v,v'} is the warping mask. The warping process involves backprojecting pixels from I{v'} to a point cloud in world space using predicted depths, then rasterizing this point cloud into viewpoint v to produce W(I{v'}). The LPIPS score is computed between the target image Iv and the warped image W(I{v'}) over the masked regions. In experiments, v' is selected as the 3rd nearest test pose from v. This metric is used as a no-reference evaluator for super-resolution quality. Time Complexity: Dominated by the rendering of the NeRF views and the inference of the optical flow network (e.g., RAFT) and occlusion detector. The warping and MSE/LPIPS computation are linear in the number of pixels. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the rendered images and the optical flow field. The occlusion mask is typically binary and compact. Strengths: Provides a geometrically aware consistency check that is robust to lighting changes if the flow is accurate. It does not require ground truth multi-view data, making it suitable for self-supervised training or evaluation of unstructured captures. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of external models (RAFT, occlusion detector). Fails in textureless regions or areas with large occlusions where flow estimation is ambiguous. Long-range consistency (\delta=7) may suffer from accumulated warping errors. When to use: Evaluating the geometric coherence of NeRFs, particularly in video stylization or super-resolution tasks where temporal or spatial consistency is critical. When not to use: When ground truth multi-view data is available and direct photometric error is preferred, or when the scene contains significant non-rigid motion that violates the optical flow assumption. The metric is based on the view-consistency evaluation introduced in SNeRF [31], which generalized the approach from Lai et al. [22] to the NeRF setting. It was adopted in LAENeRF for evaluating 3D-aware stylization and recoloring consistency, using short-range (\delta=1) and long-range (\delta=7) offsets. It was also employed in DiSR-NeRF as a no-reference evaluator for super-resolution, utilizing a point-cloud-based warping strategy and LPIPS. name: Warped LPIPS Metric
head: E_warp (LPIPS variant), Warped LPIPS Consistency Metric, Warped View Consistency with LPIPS
body: The Warped LPIPS Metric is a no-reference evaluation method used to assess geometric and photometric consistency across viewpoints in novel view synthesis, particularly for stylized or super-resolved NeRFs. It quantifies consistency by computing the Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) between a target rendered view and a source view warped into the target's coordinate system using estimated depth. Unlike standard metrics that require ground truth, it measures how well the underlying 3D structure supports consistent appearance from nearby angles. It distinguishes itself from the base View-Consistency Metric (Ewarp) by using LPIPS instead of MSE, making it more sensitive to perceptual artifacts and texture consistency. Inputs: Iv: Rendered image from target viewpoint v. I{v'}: Rendered image from source viewpoint v' (a nearby viewpoint). D{v'}: Predicted depth map corresponding to I{v'}. Kv, K{v'}: Intrinsic camera matrices for viewpoints v and v'. T{v \to v'}: Extrinsic transformation matrix from v to v'. M{v,v'}: Warping mask indicating valid pixels (occlusion-free regions). Outputs: E{warp}: Scalar LPIPS score representing inconsistency. Lower values indicate higher consistency. Data Structures: Depth map D{v'}: 2D array of floats, shape (H, W), where each element represents the distance from the camera center to the surface along the ray. Warping mask M{v,v'}: 2D binary array, shape (H, W), where 1 indicates a valid pixel and 0 indicates an occluded or invalid region. Steps: 1. Select Source Viewpoint: Select v' as the 3rd nearest test pose from v. For short-range consistency, pairs with a gap of 5 indices (Oi, O{i+5}) are used; for long-range, a gap of 15 (Oi, O{i+15}) is used. 2. Backproject to World Space: For each pixel (u, v) in I{v'} with depth d = D{v'}[u, v]: Convert pixel coordinates to normalized device coordinates (NDC) or camera coordinates using K{v'}. Unproject to world space coordinates P{world} using the inverse of the extrinsic matrix T{v \to v'} and depth d. This creates a point cloud in world space. 3. Reproject to Target View: Project the world space points P{world} onto the image plane of viewpoint v using Kv and the extrinsic matrix of v. This yields warped coordinates (u', v') in the target image space. 4. Render Warped Image W(I{v'}): Use a point cloud rasterizer to render the warped image W(I{v'}) at viewpoint v. The rasterizer samples the color from I{v'} at the backprojected locations and interpolates to fill the target grid. Handle floating-point inaccuracies by clamping projected coordinates to image bounds and discarding points with negative depth relative to v. 5. Compute Warping Mask M{v,v'}: Identify pixels in the target view v that correspond to valid, non-occluded regions in v'. Common implementation: Cast rays from v through each pixel. If the ray intersects the surface defined by D{v'} (warped back to v's space) at a distance closer than the depth rendered by Iv, mark as occluded (0). Otherwise, mark as valid (1). The mask ensures LPIPS is only computed on geometrically consistent regions. 6. Compute LPIPS Score: Calculate the LPIPS score between the masked target image M{v,v'} \cdot Iv and the warped image W(I{v'}). Formula: E{warp}(Iv, I{v'}) = \text{LPIPS}(M{v,v'} \cdot Iv, W(I{v'})) Only pixels where M{v,v'} = 1 contribute to the LPIPS calculation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computewarpedlpips(Iv, Ivprime, Dvprime, Kv, Kvprime, Tvtovprime, Tv): """ Compute the Warped LPIPS metric between view v and v'. Args: Iv: Target rendered image (H, W, 3) Ivprime: Source rendered image (H, W, 3) Dvprime: Depth map for source view (H, W) Kv, Kvprime: Camera intrinsics Tvtovprime: Extrinsics from v to v' Tv: Extrinsics for view v Returns: Ewarp: Scalar LPIPS score """ H, W = Iv.shape[:2] # 1. Backproject source pixels to world space # Create grid of pixel coordinates u, v = np.meshgrid(np.arange(W), np.arange(H)) # Convert to camera coordinates in v' # Assuming pinhole model: x = (u - cx)/fx, y = (v - cy)/fy fx, fy = Kvprime[0, 0], Kvprime[1, 1] cx, cy = Kvprime[0, 2], Kvprime[1, 2] xcam = (u - cx) / fx ycam = (v - cy) / fy # Unproject to world space using depth # Pworld = Tvtovprime^-1 [xcam d, ycam d, d, 1]^T # Note: Tvtovprime transforms v to v'. We need points in v' space to transform to v. # Actually, we have points in v' camera space. We need to transform them to world, then to v. # Let's assume Tvtovprime is the transform from v to v'. # So inverse transforms v' to v? No, usually T is world-to-camera or camera-to-world. # Standard: Pworld = Tworldtocam^-1 Pcam. # If Tvtovprime is v -> v', then Pvprime = Tvtovprime Pv. # We have Pvprime (from depth). We want Pv. # Pv = Tvtovprime^-1 Pvprime. # Construct homogeneous coordinates in v' camera space Z = Dvprime X = xcam Z Y = ycam Z # Stack to (4, H, W) Pvprimehomo = np.stack([X, Y, Z, np.oneslike(Z)], axis=0) # Transform to v camera space # Tinv is the inverse of Tvtovprime Tinv = np.linalg.inv(Tvtovprime) # Apply transformation Pvhomo = Tinv @ Pvprimehomo # (4, H, W) Xv = Pvhomo[0] / Pvhomo[2] Yv = Pvhomo[1] / Pvhomo[2] Zv = Pvhomo[2] # 2. Project to target image coordinates fxv, fyv = Kv[0, 0], Kv[1, 1] cxv, cyv = Kv[0, 2], Kv[1, 2] uwarped = Xv fxv + cxv vwarped = Yv fyv + cyv # 3. Create Warped Image W(Ivprime) # Use bilinear interpolation to sample Ivprime at (uwarped, vwarped) # Clip coordinates to image bounds uwarpedclipped = np.clip(uwarped, 0, W - 1) vwarpedclipped = np.clip(vwarped, 0, H - 1) # Sample colors # Note: Ivprime is (H, W, 3). Need to index carefully. # Using scipy.ndimage.mapcoordinates or similar for bilinear interpolation coords = np.stack([vwarpedclipped, uwarpedclipped], axis=-1) WIvprime = mapcoordinates(Ivprime, coords, mode='nearest') # 4. Compute Warping Mask Mv,v' # Mask is 1 if the point is valid (positive depth in v) and not occluded. # Occlusion check: Compare depth of warped point Zv with depth of Iv at (uwarped, vwarped). # If Zv > DepthIv, then the warped point is behind the surface, so it's occluded. # Get depth of Iv (assumed available or estimated) # For simplicity, assume we have Dv (depth of target view) # If Dv is not available, this step cannot be completed without estimation. # The source mentions "predicted depths", implying Dv is also available. # Let's assume Dv is passed or estimated similarly. # Check bounds validbounds = (uwarped >= 0) & (uwarped < W) & (vwarped >= 0) & (vwarped < H) validdepth = Zv > 0 # Occlusion check (requires Dv) # Interpolate Dv at warped coordinates coordsd = np.stack([vwarpedclipped, uwarpedclipped], axis=-1) Dvsampled = mapcoordinates(Dv, coordsd, mode='nearest') # Valid if warped depth is closer than target depth (not occluded) # Note: In camera coordinates, smaller Z is closer. # So if Zv < Dvsampled, it is in front (not occluded). # If Zv > Dvsampled, it is behind (occluded). notoccluded = Zv < Dvsampled Mvvprime = (validbounds & validdepth & notoccluded).astype(float) # 5. Compute LPIPS # Apply mask Ivmasked = Iv Mvvprime[..., np.newaxis] # Compute LPIPS between Ivmasked and WIvprime # LPIPS function takes two images and returns a scalar Ewarp = lpipsscore(Ivmasked, WIvprime) return Ewarp Parameters: View Selection: v' is the 3rd nearest test pose. Consistency Range: Short-range uses view pairs with a gap of 5; long-range uses a gap of 15. LPIPS Model: Standard LPIPS network (typically VGG or AlexNet based). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusions: The warping mask must correctly identify occluded regions. Incorrect masking leads to high LPIPS scores due to comparing background with foreground. Depth Errors: Inaccurate depth predictions in D{v'} cause misalignment in warping, increasing LPIPS even if the view is consistent. Boundary Conditions: Pixels near image borders may not have valid correspondences, requiring careful handling of the mask. Measures consistency between very close viewpoints (gap of 5). Sensitive to high-frequency details and local geometry. Use when evaluating fine-grained texture consistency. Measures consistency between viewpoints further apart (gap of 15). Sensitive to global structure and large-scale geometry. Use when evaluating overall 3D coherence. Time Complexity: Dominated by the backprojection and rasterization steps, which are O(H \times W) per view pair. LPIPS computation is also O(H \times W) but involves neural network inference. Memory Complexity: O(H \times W) for storing depth maps, warped images, and masks. Measured Performance: On the LLFF dataset, the metric shows low scores for high-consistency methods. For short-range consistency, scores range from 0.0018 (Trex) to 0.0037 (Orchids) for the best method. For long-range, scores range from 0.0049 (Fern) to 0.0140 (Trex). Strengths: No-reference; perceptually relevant (LPIPS); sensitive to both geometric and photometric inconsistencies. Limitations: Requires predicted depth maps; sensitive to depth estimation errors; computationally more expensive than MSE-based metrics. When to Use: Evaluating novel view synthesis methods where ground truth is unavailable, especially for stylized or super-resolved NeRFs. When Not to Use: When ground truth is available (use PSNR/SSIM); when depth estimation is unreliable. The Warped LPIPS Metric was introduced as a no-reference evaluator for assessing view consistency in NeRF-based super-resolution and stylization tasks. It builds on the concept of warping views using depth to detect inconsistencies, adapting the LPIPS metric for perceptual quality assessment. It is used in evaluating methods like DiSR-NeRF and Instant Photorealistic Neural Radiance Fields Stylization. name: Text-Image Direction Score
head: TIDS
body: The Text-Image Direction Score (TIDS) is a quantitative metric used in text-guided NeRF editing to estimate the semantic alignment between the direction of a text prompt change and the resulting change in the rendered image. Unlike pixel-level metrics such as MSE or PSNR, which measure visual fidelity, TIDS evaluates whether the edit performed by the model corresponds to the semantic intent of the instruction. It sets itself apart from sibling metrics like R-Precision by focusing on the directionality of the edit in embedding space rather than the retrieval accuracy of a single view against a caption. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: oIi: The original rendered image for view i. eIi: The edited rendered image for view i. oTi: The text caption/prompt describing the original scene. eTi: The text caption/prompt describing the edited scene. \mathbf{C}I: The CLIP image encoder. \mathbf{C}T: The CLIP text encoder. Output: A scalar value representing the cosine similarity between the image edit vector and the text edit vector. Data Structures: Embeddings are vectors of fixed dimensionality (e.g., 512 or 768 depending on the CLIP variant). Images are typically normalized to [0, 1] or [-1, 1] as required by the specific CLIP implementation. Steps: 1. Encode the original rendered image oIi using the image encoder to obtain \mathbf{C}I(oIi). 2. Encode the edited rendered image eIi using the image encoder to obtain \mathbf{C}I(eIi). 3. Encode the original text prompt oTi using the text encoder to obtain \mathbf{C}T(oTi). 4. Encode the edited text prompt eTi using the text encoder to obtain \mathbf{C}T(eTi). 5. Compute the image direction vector: \Delta \mathbf{V}I = \mathbf{C}I(eIi) - \mathbf{C}I(oIi). 6. Compute the text direction vector: \Delta \mathbf{V}T = \mathbf{C}T(eTi) - \mathbf{C}T(oTi). 7. Calculate the cosine similarity between \Delta \mathbf{V}I and \Delta \mathbf{V}T. Formula: \text{TIDS} = \cos(\mathbf{C}I(eIi) - \mathbf{C}I(oIi), \mathbf{C}T(eTi) - \mathbf{C}T(oTi)) \text{TIDS} = \frac{(\mathbf{C}I(eIi) - \mathbf{C}I(oIi)) \cdot (\mathbf{C}T(eTi) - \mathbf{C}T(oTi))}{\|\mathbf{C}I(eIi) - \mathbf{C}I(oIi)\| \|\mathbf{C}T(eTi) - \mathbf{C}T(oTi)\|} where \cos denotes cosine similarity. Parameters: CLIP Model: The standard CLIP model is used for both \mathbf{C}I and \mathbf{C}T. Views: The score is typically computed per view i and averaged across the evaluation set. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Vectors: If the image or text embeddings do not change (i.e., \Delta \mathbf{V}I = \mathbf{0} or \Delta \mathbf{V}T = \mathbf{0}), the denominator becomes zero. Implementations must handle this by returning 0 or skipping the view, as the direction is undefined. Prompt Specificity: The metric assumes that oTi and eTi accurately reflect the semantic difference intended by the user. Ambiguous prompts may yield low scores even if the visual edit is correct. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def textimagedirectionscore(clipimageencoder, cliptextencoder, originalimage, editedimage, originaltext, editedtext): """ Computes the Text-Image Direction Score (TIDS). Args: clipimageencoder: Function/Model to encode images to CLIP embeddings. cliptextencoder: Function/Model to encode text to CLIP embeddings. originalimage: Tensor of shape (C, H, W) or (B, C, H, W). editedimage: Tensor of shape (C, H, W) or (B, C, H, W). originaltext: String or list of strings. editedtext: String or list of strings. Returns: float: The cosine similarity score. """ # 1. Encode images emboimg = clipimageencoder(originalimage) embeimg = clipimageencoder(editedimage) # 2. Encode text embotxt = cliptextencoder(originaltext) embetxt = cliptextencoder(editedtext) # 3. Compute direction vectors # Ensure embeddings are normalized if the encoder doesn't do it automatically # CLIP embeddings are typically L2-normalized, but the difference vector is not. imgdirection = embeimg - emboimg txtdirection = embetxt - embotxt # 4. Compute cosine similarity # Dot product dotproduct = torch.sum(imgdirection txtdirection, dim=-1) # Norms imgnorm = torch.norm(imgdirection, dim=-1) txtnorm = torch.norm(txtdirection, dim=-1) # Denominator denominator = imgnorm txtnorm # Handle zero division # If either norm is zero, the direction is undefined. # A common convention is to return 0.0 or NaN. # Here we return 0.0 for safety in aggregation. mask = denominator > 0 score = torch.where(mask, dotproduct / denominator, torch.zeroslike(dotproduct)) return score.item() R-Precision measures how well a rendered view of a synthesis object aligns with the text caption used to generate it, rather than the direction of an edit. It computes the precision of rendered views over a group of text captions using a retrieval model. The procedure involves collecting an object-centric captions dataset (e.g., from COCO) and sampling captions for training. For evaluation, it computes the precision of rendered views per synthesis object over a set of captions (e.g., 153 captions). Unlike TIDS, which compares an edit pair, R-Precision assesses the alignment of a single generated view against a pool of captions. It may use CLIP or BLIP2 as the language-image model backbone. Time Complexity: Dominated by the inference time of the CLIP image and text encoders. For a single view, it is O(1) relative to the number of pixels but depends on the encoder's depth. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the CLIP model weights and the embeddings for the original and edited images/text. Performance: In simple settings (e.g., 5 edits on NeRF-Art face scene), TIDS scores for methods like Instruct-NeRF2NeRF are around 0.1477, while ViCA-NeRF achieves 0.1545. The metric is sensitive to the quality of the text prompts and the semantic consistency of the edit. Strengths: Directly measures semantic alignment with the text instruction, which is the primary goal of text-guided editing. Limitations: Does not measure visual fidelity or photorealism. It relies entirely on the CLIP embedding space, which may not perfectly correlate with human perception of "edit correctness" for all types of changes. The Text-Image Direction Score was introduced in the context of evaluating text-guided NeRF editing methods. It was adopted from prior work on image editing evaluation [38] (cited in) to quantify how well the visual changes in a NeRF correspond to the textual instructions provided. It is used alongside consistency scores to evaluate methods like ViCA-NeRF and Instruct-NeRF2NeRF.
