name: Depth Supervision and Pseudo-Depth
body: This family of techniques incorporates geometric constraints into the radiance field optimization loop to improve reconstruction quality, particularly in low-data regimes or when explicit geometry is required for downstream tasks. While standard NeRF optimization relies solely on photometric RGB losses, these methods introduce depth-related penalties or sampling strategies. Depth Supervision explicitly minimizes the difference between rendered depth and ground-truth depth (derived from SfM keypoints or stereo), whereas Pseudo-Depth approximates surface geometry via weighted averaging of sampled points to guide feature distillation or segmentation without requiring explicit depth labels. This family builds on NeRF Evaluation and Metric Calculation by extending metric calculation with geometric losses. All methods in this family operate within the differentiable volume rendering framework. The core mechanism involves computing a depth estimate \hat{D}(r) for a ray r during the forward pass of the renderer and incorporating this value into the loss function or sampling strategy. The predicted depth \hat{D}(r) is computed as the expected depth along the ray, weighted by the transmittance and density at each sample point ti: \hat{D}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) where \sigmai is the volume density, \deltai = t{i+1} - ti is the interval between adjacent samples, and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the accumulated transmittance up to sample i. This formulation ensures that depth contributions are proportional to the opacity of the surface encountered at that depth. This variant applies explicit depth supervision to the TensoRF architecture to enhance performance in low-data scenarios. It differs from standard NeRF depth supervision by leveraging TensoRF's tensor decomposition for efficiency, while using COLMAP keypoints to generate sparse ground-truth depth labels. Definition TensoRF is augmented with a depth supervision term derived from COLMAP keypoints to improve low-data performance. Procedure 1. Extract 3D point locations and their corresponding 2D pixel coordinates from the COLMAP keypoints stored in the dataset. 2. Using the coordinate information and the camera matrix for the ground truth image, calculate the ray r(t) = o + td and the ground-truth depth D from the projection origin. 3. Sample the TensoRF model along these rays to calculate the model-estimated depths \hat{D}. Loss Function The depth loss is calculated using Mean Squared Error (MSE): L{\hat{D}} = \mathbb{E}{r \in R(P)} ||\hat{D}(r) - D(r)||2^2 where \hat{D}(r) is the predicted depth and D(r) is the ground-truth depth. The total loss combines this with the color loss LC and a weighting hyperparameter \lambdai: L{tot} = LC + \lambdai L{\hat{D}} Parameters and Context Dataset: LLFF dataset, consisting of 20-30 images of household/office environments captured with a smartphone in a grid pattern. Rationale: The LLFF dataset was chosen due to the small variance of angles, making it more suitable for this approach than 360-degree view datasets. Loss Choice: MSE loss was implemented as a baseline. Although the DS-NeRF paper reported slightly better results with KL loss, the improvements were of similar magnitude. Architecture: TensoRF was selected over standard NeRF due to faster training times and lower space complexity, fitting limited GPU and RAM resources. This technique approximates surface geometry without explicit depth labels. It is primarily used in feature field distillation (e.g., for CLIPNeRF) to enable efficient sampling around the "surface" for feature extraction. Procedure 1. Compute the pseudo depth of the surface as a weighted average of the depth of each sampled point during volume rendering. 2. Use this pseudo-surface point to compute features by sampling a small neighborhood (e.g., five points) around it with small perturbations during training and inference. Context This method is employed for computational efficiency in feature rendering, avoiding the complete process of volume rendering for features. It allows gradients to be backpropagated only to rays selected by specific semantic masks (e.g., "apple") during optimization. This method generates ground-truth depth for novel panoramic views by projecting 2D pixel coordinates onto a uniform sphere centered at the camera position. It enables the extraction of depth priors for 360-degree scenes. Definition A method to extract depth ground truths for novel panoramic views by projecting 2D pixel coordinates to a uniform sphere centered at the camera position. Procedure 1. For a pixel (x, y) on a panorama of height H and width W, calculate the vertical viewing angle \theta = \pi y / H and horizontal viewing angle \phi = 2\pi x / W. 2. Define the ray origin as the camera position (coordinate center) and the ray direction as the unit vector from the center to the sphere point defined by \theta and \phi. 3. Determine visibility for a novel view by moving the camera to a new position and checking which parts of the ground truth sphere are visible to the emitted rays from the new origin. Optimization The network parameters \theta are optimized using RGB-D frames. The geometric loss is the absolute difference between predicted and true depths, normalized by the depth variance. Depth supervision in NeRF-like models originated from the observation that photometric loss alone often leads to ambiguous geometry, especially in textureless regions or with sparse inputs. The DS-NeRF paper introduced depth supervision using KL divergence to align predicted depth distributions with ground truth. TensoRF-DS adapted this to tensor-decomposed fields for efficiency. Pseudo-depth techniques emerged in the context of feature distillation, where explicit depth is unavailable but surface proximity is needed for feature sampling. Panoramic depth extraction extends these concepts to 360-degree scenes using spherical projections. name: Ray-Based Volumetric Uncertainty Estimator
head: NeRF Uncertainty via Weight PDF, NeRF uncertainty estimator, Ray-Based Volumetric Uncertainty Estimation, Weight Distribution Entropy, entropy of weight distribution
body: The Ray-Based Volumetric Uncertainty Estimator computes the uncertainty of the underlying 3D geometry in a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) by calculating the entropy of the weight distribution of color samples along each ray. It treats the opacity function as a cumulative distribution function (CDF) and its derivative as a probability density function (PDF), allowing the weight distribution to serve as a proxy for geometric certainty. Unlike explicit 3D representations or RGB-D fusion methods, this approach leverages the implicit neural shape representation to estimate information gain without relying on structure-from-motion or depth sensors. It is distinct from methods like S-NeRF or NeRF-W as it requires no model modification or additional training, functioning as a post-hoc analysis plug-in. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A trained NeRF model (MLP parameters \Theta), a camera pose (origin o, direction d), and the number of samples N per ray. Outputs: A scalar uncertainty value (entropy H) for each ray, and optionally a mean entropy value for the entire image. Data Structures Ray Samples: An array of N positions ti along the ray r(t) = o + td. NeRF Query: For each sample point r(ti), the MLP returns volume density \sigmai and color ci. Weights: An array of N weights wi representing the contribution of each sample to the final color. Numbered Steps 1. Ray Sampling: For each ray r emanating from camera position o in direction d, sample N points along the ray at positions r(ti) for i = 1 \dots N. 2. NeRF Query: Query the NeRF MLP for volume density \sigmai and color ci at each sample point r(ti). 3. Transmittance Calculation: Calculate the transmittance factor pi for each sample using the volume density and the distance to the next sample: pi = \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) where \deltai = t{i+1} - ti is the distance between adjacent samples. 4. Weight Calculation: Calculate the weight wi for each sample using the accumulated transmittance from previous samples: wi = (1 - pi) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} pj This weight represents the probability that the ray is occluded at sample i. 5. Normalization: Normalize the weights wi to form a valid probability distribution P(xi) such that \sum{i=1}^N P(xi) = 1. The normalized probability for the i-th sample is: P(xi) = \frac{wi}{\sum{k=1}^N wk}. Note: In standard volume rendering, \sum wi \approx 1 for rays hitting an object, but normalization ensures a valid PDF for entropy calculation. 6. Entropy Calculation: Calculate the Shannon entropy H for each pixel (ray) using the normalized weights: H = -\sum{i=1}^N P(xi) \log P(xi). High entropy indicates a spread-out weight distribution (low certainty/incomplete geometry), while low entropy indicates a concentrated weight distribution (high certainty/concentrated surface). 7. Aggregation (Optional): Compute the mean entropy across all pixels in the image to serve as the uncertainty metric for that view. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def computerayuncertainty(nerfmodel, rayorigin, raydirection, numsamples): """ Computes the volumetric uncertainty (entropy of weight distribution) for a single ray. Args: nerfmodel: A callable that takes (points, directions) and returns (sigma, color). rayorigin: 3D vector (ox, oy, oz). raydirection: 3D vector (dx, dy, dz), assumed normalized. numsamples: Integer N, number of samples along the ray. Returns: float: Shannon entropy H of the weight distribution. """ # Step 1: Sample points along the ray # Assuming uniform spacing for simplicity, though hierarchical sampling may be used in practice. # t values range from near to far clipping planes. tvals = np.linspace(tnear, tfar, numsamples + 1) # Sample points at midpoints or endpoints depending on convention. # Standard NeRF often uses ti as the start of the segment. # Let's assume ti are the sample positions. tsamples = tvals[:-1] # N samples # Calculate deltai = t{i+1} - ti deltas = np.diff(tvals) # Step 2: Query NeRF # Points are rayorigin + tsamples raydirection points = rayorigin + np.outer(tsamples, raydirection) # NeRF typically takes points and view directions. # Assuming nerfmodel returns (sigma, color) for batched inputs. sigma, color = nerfmodel(points, raydirection) # Step 3 & 4: Calculate weights # pi = exp(-sigmai deltai) p = np.exp(-sigma deltas) # wi = (1 - pi) product(pj for j < i) # Cumulative product of p, shifted. # prodj=1^{i-1} pj is the accumulated transmittance Ti # T1 = 1 (empty product) # Ti = T{i-1} p{i-1} # Calculate accumulated transmittance Ti for each sample i # T[i] = exp(-sum{j=0}^{i-1} sigma[j] delta[j]) # This is equivalent to the cumulative product of p, starting with 1. accumulatedtransmittance = np.ones(numsamples) for i in range(1, numsamples): accumulatedtransmittance[i] = accumulatedtransmittance[i-1] p[i-1] weights = (1 - p) accumulatedtransmittance # Step 5: Normalize weights to form probability distribution # Sum of weights should be close to 1 if the ray hits an object. # However, for entropy calculation, we normalize to ensure sum(P) = 1. weightsum = np.sum(weights) if weightsum == 0: # If no weight is accumulated (ray misses object or empty space), # entropy is undefined or zero. # In practice, this might be handled by masking or returning 0. return 0.0 probabilities = weights / weightsum # Step 6: Calculate Shannon Entropy # H = - sum(P(x) log(P(x))) # Handle log(0) by ignoring zero probabilities entropy = 0.0 for prob in probabilities: if prob > 0: entropy -= prob math.log(prob) return entropy def computeimageuncertainty(nerfmodel, camerapose, imagewidth, imageheight, numsamples, downsamplefactor=4): """ Computes the mean entropy for an entire image. """ # Downsample for speed h, w = imageheight // downsamplefactor, imagewidth // downsamplefactor totalentropy = 0.0 count = 0 # Generate rays for downsampled grid for y in range(0, imageheight, downsamplefactor): for x in range(0, imagewidth, downsamplefactor): # Convert pixel (x,y) to ray direction # This depends on the camera intrinsics. # Assuming standard pinhole camera model. # u = (x - cx) / fx, v = (y - cy) / fy # direction = normalize([u, v, -1]) rotated by camera orientation raydir = getraydirection(x, y, camerapose, intrinsics) hval = computerayuncertainty(nerfmodel, camerapose.origin, raydir, numsamples) totalentropy += hval count += 1 return totalentropy / count if count > 0 else 0.0 Parameters Number of samples (N): 64 for the 'coarse' network and 128 for the 'fine' network. Downsampling factor: Images are downsampled by a factor of 4 during entropy evaluation to speed up computation. \sigmai: The volume density predicted by the NeRF MLP at the i-th sample point. ci: The color (r,g,b) predicted by the NeRF MLP at the i-th sample point. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Transparency: The method is restricted to non-transparent objects with solid surfaces. It fails for transparent objects (e.g., glass) because Marching Cubes removes low density regions (noise) and transparent surfaces do not produce a clear single peak in weight distribution. Empty Space: If a ray does not hit any object, the weights will be near zero, leading to potential division by zero or undefined entropy. The pseudocode handles this by returning 0.0. Precision: The calculation of accumulated transmittance involves products of values less than 1, which can lead to underflow for very long rays or high densities. Log-space computation is recommended for stability in implementation. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot P) per image, where N is the number of samples per ray and P is the number of pixels. The method requires a forward pass through the NeRF MLP for every sample point. Memory Complexity: O(N) per ray to store weights and transmittance values. Performance: The method is computationally expensive due to the need to query the MLP for every sample point on every ray. Downsampling by a factor of 4 is used to mitigate this. Strengths: It provides a direct measure of geometric uncertainty from the implicit representation without requiring explicit mesh extraction or additional training. It is applicable to any NeRF-based approach. Limitations: It is not suitable for transparent objects or scenes with significant transparency. It assumes that the weight distribution concentration correlates with geometric certainty, which may not hold for all scene types. When to use: Active robotic 3D reconstruction to determine the next best view for effective 3D reconstruction of an object. When not to use: Scenes with transparent objects or when explicit geometric meshes are required directly from the NeRF without further processing. The Ray-Based Volumetric Uncertainty Estimator was introduced in the paper "Uncertainty Guided Policy for Active Robotic 3D Reconstruction Using Neural Radiance Fields". The authors leveraged the popular neural radiance fields-based object representation to solve the next-best-view selection problem for dense 3D reconstruction. The key insight is that the weight distribution in NeRF, which is the derivative of the opacity function, can be treated as a probability density function. By computing the entropy of this distribution, the method provides a proxy for the uncertainty of the underlying 3D geometry. This approach distinguishes itself from explicit 3D representations and RGB-D fusion methods by using the implicit neural shape representation to estimate information gain without relying on structure-from-motion or depth sensors. It is also distinct from Bayesian NeRF variants like S-NeRF as it requires no model modification. name: Depth-Supervised EndoNeRF Loss
head: Depth-Supervised Loss, EndoNeRF Loss
body: A training objective that combines photometric color loss with a depth-supervised loss using estimated stereo depth to accelerate convergence and remove the need for a depth refinement module. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF losses by explicitly constraining the rendered depth to match external stereo-matching estimates, thereby reducing training time compared to methods like STTR that require iterative depth refinement. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: \mathcal{R}: The set of camera rays \textbf{r}(z). t \in [0,1]: The time parameter for dynamic scenes. \hat{\textbf{C}}(\textbf{r}(z), t): The rendered color for ray \textbf{r}(z) at time t. \textbf{C}(\textbf{r}(z), t): The ground truth pixel color for ray \textbf{r}(z) at time t. \hat{\textbf{D}}(\textbf{r}(z), t): The rendered depth for ray \textbf{r}(z) at time t. \textbf{D}(\textbf{r}(z), t): The estimated stereo depth for ray \textbf{r}(z) at time t, obtained via stereo-matching feature correspondence of robotic surgery videos using Unimatch. \lambdad: The weight coefficient for the depth loss term. Output: \mathcal{L}: The total loss value. Data Structures Rays: Represented as \textbf{r}(z), where zj is the distance of the j-th sample along the ray. Depth Maps: \textbf{D} is a 2D map (or per-ray value) derived from Unimatch. No specific bit-packing is defined in the sources; it is treated as a dense depth estimate. Steps 1. Estimate Stereo Depth: Compute the estimated stereo depth \textbf{D}(\textbf{r}(z),t) by performing stereo-matching on feature correspondence of the robotic surgery videos using the Unimatch algorithm. 2. Render Color and Depth: For each ray \textbf{r}(z) \in \mathcal{R} and time t \in [0,1], compute the rendered color \hat{\textbf{C}}(\textbf{r}(z), t) and rendered depth \hat{\textbf{D}}(\textbf{r}(z), t) from the current radiance field representation. 3. Compute Photometric Loss: Calculate the L2 norm squared between the rendered color and the ground truth color: \left\| \hat{\textbf{C}}(\textbf{r}(z), t) - \textbf{C}(\textbf{r}(z), t) \right\| 2^2. 4. Compute Depth Loss: Calculate the Huber loss between the rendered depth and the estimated stereo depth: {\text {Huber}}\left( \hat{\textbf{D}}(\textbf{r}(z), t), \textbf{D}(\textbf{r}(z), t) \right). 5. Aggregate Loss: Sum the photometric and weighted depth losses over all rays and time steps to obtain \mathcal{L}. Formulas The total loss function is defined as: \mathcal {L}= \sum {\textbf{r}(z) \in \mathcal {R}, t\in [0,1]} \left\| \hat{\textbf{C}}(\textbf{r}(z), t) - \textbf{C}(\textbf{r}(z), t) \right\| 2^2 + \lambda d {\text {Huber}}\left( \hat{\textbf{D}}(\textbf{r}(z), t), \textbf{D}(\textbf{r}(z), t) \right) Where: \textbf{r}(z) is the camera ray. zj is the distance of the j-th sample along the ray. t \in [0,1] is the time. \hat{\textbf{C}} is the rendered color. \textbf{C} is the ground truth pixel color. \hat{\textbf{D}} is the rendered depth. \textbf{D} is the estimated stereo depth from Unimatch. \lambdad is the weight for the depth loss. Parameters \lambdad: The weight coefficient for the Huber depth loss term. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Pitfalls Outliers: The Huber loss is adopted for the depth term because it is more stable to outliers than L2 loss. Using L2 for depth may lead to instability if the stereo estimates contain noise or errors. Stereo Quality: The effectiveness of the depth supervision depends on the quality of the stereo-matching provided by Unimatch. Poor stereo correspondence may lead to suboptimal convergence. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def depthsupervisedendonerfloss( rays: List[Ray], timesteps: List[float], renderedcolors: Tensor, # Shape: (numrays, numtimesteps, 3) groundtruthcolors: Tensor, # Shape: (numrays, numtimesteps, 3) rendereddepths: Tensor, # Shape: (numrays, numtimesteps) stereodepths: Tensor, # Shape: (numrays, numtimesteps) lambdad: float) -> Tensor: """ Computes the Depth-Supervised EndoNeRF Loss. Args: rays: List of camera rays. timesteps: List of time values t in [0, 1]. renderedcolors: Predicted RGB values from the radiance field. groundtruthcolors: Ground truth RGB values from the input images. rendereddepths: Predicted depth values from the radiance field. stereodepths: Estimated stereo depth values from Unimatch. lambdad: Weight for the depth loss term. Returns: Total loss value. """ # 1. Photometric Color Loss (L2) # Calculate element-wise squared difference between rendered and ground truth colors colordiff = renderedcolors - groundtruthcolors colorloss = torch.sum(colordiff 2) # 2. Depth Loss (Huber) # Calculate Huber loss between rendered and stereo depth depthdiff = rendereddepths - stereodepths # Huber loss implementation: # If |diff| <= delta: 0.5 diff^2 # Else: delta (|diff| - 0.5 delta) # Note: The specific delta value for Huber loss is not given in sources. # Using a standard default delta of 1.0 if not specified. delta = 1.0 absdiff = torch.abs(depthdiff) quadratic = torch.clamp(absdiff, max=delta) linear = absdiff - quadratic depthloss = torch.sum(0.5 quadratic 2 + delta linear) # 3. Total Loss totalloss = colorloss + lambdad depthloss return totalloss Uses external depth estimates to guide training. Sets itself apart by using stereo-matching (Unimatch) rather than pseudo-depth from other NeRF variants. Choose when stereo data is available and training speed is critical. Link Focuses on multi-modal inputs. Sets itself apart by incorporating additional modalities beyond RGB and depth. Choose when multi-sensor data is available. Link Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Supervising with Unimatch depth maps decreases training time compared to STTR. This is because the depth refinement module proposed in EndoNeRF (which requires depth rendering of all training images) is no longer needed. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Accelerates convergence; removes the need for a computationally expensive depth refinement module; robust to outliers via Huber loss. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the external stereo-matching algorithm (Unimatch); requires stereo-capable input data or pre-computed stereo depths. When to use: When training dynamic radiance fields for robotic surgery videos where stereo depth estimates are available and training efficiency is a priority. When not: When stereo depth estimates are unreliable or unavailable; when computational resources for external stereo matching are prohibitive. The method originates from the Efficient EndoNeRF paper, which focuses on reconstruction and data-driven surgical simulation. It was developed to address the computational overhead of depth refinement in previous EndoNeRF variants. The approach leverages Unimatch for stereo depth estimation. Efficient EndoNeRF reconstruction and its application for data-driven surgical simulation., https://doi.org/10.1007/s11548-024-03114-1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: NeRF Network Query with Hashed Embeddings
head: HashNeRF query, Instant-NGP NeRF, NeRF with Hash Encoding, NeRF with Multiresolution Hash Encoding, Neural Radiance and Density Fields (NeRF) with Multiresolution Hash Encoding
body: This method queries a neural radiance field by mapping 3D spatial coordinates and 2D view directions into high-dimensional feature vectors using a multiresolution hash encoding, which are then processed by concatenated Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) to predict volume density and view-dependent color. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF [Mildenhall et al. 2020] by replacing expensive positional encoding with a learnable, sparse hash grid that enables significantly faster training convergence and real-time rendering performance on consumer hardware. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A batch of 3D positions \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3} and view directions \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}. Outputs: Volume density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{N} and RGB color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}. Data Structures Hash Grid: A collection of L resolution levels. Each level l consists of a hash table mapping integer coordinates to feature vectors. Hash Table: A flat array of size 2^{22} (or similar capacity) storing F-dimensional feature vectors. The hash function maps 3D grid coordinates to table indices. Feature Vector: A vector of size F (typically F=2) stored in the hash table. MLP Weights: Density MLP: 1 hidden layer, 64 neurons. Color MLP: 2 hidden layers, 64 neurons. Numbered Steps 1. Reshape Inputs: Flatten the input positions to shape [-1, 3]. 2. Position Embedding: Apply the multiresolution hash encoding function embedfn to the positions. This involves: For each resolution level l, discretizing the position into grid coordinates. Hashing these coordinates to find indices in the level-l hash table. Trilinearly interpolating the F-dimensional features from the four nearest neighbors in the hash table. Concatenating the interpolated features from all L levels along the last dimension to form the position embedding \mathbf{y}. Generate a validity mask keepmask to identify valid points (e.g., within bounds). 3. Direction Embedding: If view directions are provided: Expand directions to match the input batch shape and reshape to flat [-1, 3]. Project the view direction onto the first 16 coefficients of the spherical harmonics basis (up to degree 4). Apply direction embedding embeddirsfn (which may include additional hashing or fixed encoding). 4. Concatenate Embeddings: Concatenate the position embedding \mathbf{y} and the direction embedding along the last dimension to form the full input vector for the network. 5. Batched Network Evaluation: Apply the network function fn in batches of size netchunk (default 102464) to avoid Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors. Density MLP: Input is \mathbf{y}. Output is 16 values. The first value is treated as log-space density \log(\sigma). Color MLP: Input is the concatenation of the 16 density MLP outputs and the spherical harmonics projected view direction. Color Output: Apply Sigmoid activation for low dynamic-range (sRGB) data or Exponential activation for high dynamic range (linear HDR) data. 6. Mask Invalid Points: Set density \sigma to 0 for points where ~keepmask is true. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class HashNeRFQuery: def init(self, hashtablesize, numlevels, leveldim, hiddendim=64): """ Initialize the HashNeRF query module.:param hashtablesize: Size of the hash table (e.g., 2^22):param numlevels: Number of resolution levels (L):param leveldim: Dimension of features per level (F, typically 2):param hiddendim: Number of neurons in MLP hidden layers """ self.numlevels = numlevels self.leveldim = leveldim self.hashtablesize = hashtablesize # Initialize hash tables for each level # Each table maps grid coords to F-dimensional features self.embeddings = nn.ModuleList([ nn.Embedding(hashtablesize, leveldim) for in range(numlevels) ]) # Initialize MLPs # Density MLP: 1 hidden layer, 64 neurons # Input dim: L F # Output dim: 16 inputdim = numlevels leveldim self.densitymlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(inputdim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 16)) # Color MLP: 2 hidden layers, 64 neurons # Input dim: 16 (from density MLP) + 16 (SH directions) # Output dim: 3 (RGB) self.colormlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(16 + 16, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 3)) # Activation for HDR or LDR self.coloractivation = nn.Sigmoid() # Or nn.Softplus/Exp for HDR def hashencode(self, x): """ Multiresolution hash encoding for 3D positions.:param x: Tensor of shape [N, 3]:return: Concatenated features from all levels [N, LF] """ features = [] for l in range(self.numlevels): # Discretize position to grid coordinates for level l # This step depends on the specific grid resolution for level l # Assuming a helper function getgridcoords exists gridcoords = getgridcoords(x, level=l) # Hash coordinates to indices indices = hashfunction(gridcoords, self.hashtablesize) # Gather features from hash table # Note: In practice, trilinear interpolation is used. # For simplicity, we assume direct lookup or a placeholder for interpolation # Trilinear interpolation requires fetching 8 neighbors and weights. # Here we use direct lookup for brevity, but real implementation interpolates. feat = self.embeddingsl features.append(feat) # Concatenate features from all levels return torch.cat(features, dim=-1) def directionalencoding(self, d): """ Spherical Harmonics encoding for view directions.:param d: Tensor of shape [N, 3]:return: Tensor of shape [N, 16] """ # Project direction onto first 16 coefficients of SH basis (degree 4) # This involves computing SH basis functions for the direction vector. shcoeffs = computesphericalharmonics(d, degree=4) return shcoeffs[:,:16] def forward(self, x, d): """ Forward pass for NeRF query.:param x: Positions [N, 3]:param d: View directions [N, 3]:return: Density [N], Color [N, 3] """ # 1. Position Embedding posfeat = self.hashencode(x) # 2. Direction Embedding dirfeat = self.directionalencoding(d) # 3. Concatenate inputfeat = torch.cat([posfeat, dirfeat], dim=-1) # 4. Density MLP densityout = self.densitymlp(inputfeat) logdensity = densityout[:, 0] density = torch.exp(logdensity) # 5. Color MLP # Input: 16 density outputs + 16 SH directions colorinput = torch.cat([densityout, dirfeat], dim=-1) colorout = self.colormlp(colorinput) color = self.coloractivation(colorout) return density, color Parameters Density MLP: 1 hidden layer, 64 neurons. Color MLP: 2 hidden layers, 64 neurons. View Direction Encoding: First 16 coefficients of spherical harmonics (degree 4). Color Activation: Sigmoid for sRGB, Exponential for linear HDR. Batch Size (netchunk): Default 102464. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Hash Collisions: Cause "grainy" microstructure artifacts, especially visible in learned signed distance functions. The MLP cannot fully compensate for this. Concatenation vs. Reduction: Concatenating F-dimensional features from each resolution is preferred over reduction (e.g., summing) because reduction may result in dimensionality L \times F being too small to encode useful information. Linear Replacement: Replacing the MLP with a single linear matrix multiplication compromises quality significantly, failing to capture specular effects and resolve hash collisions, despite being cheaper. HybridNeRF is a neural radiance field architecture that combines dense multi-resolution 3D feature grids with multi-resolution triplanes to efficiently featurize 3D sample locations. It solves the trade-off between the high memory cost of pure 3D grids and the limited geometric expressiveness of pure 2D triplanes by using a hybrid representation. It sets itself apart from its sibling MVS Network Query by explicitly summing features across resolution levels rather than concatenating them, and from SqueezeNeRF by utilizing a spatially adaptive surfaceness field for density estimation. MVS Network Query prepares inputs for a neural network by embedding points and view directions, then applies the network in batches. It differs from standard NeRF network queries by explicitly handling multi-view geometric consistency through the generation of angle and point features derived from camera poses and depth candidates. It builds on NeRF Network Query with Hashed Embeddings and relates to HybridNeRF Model Architecture, Simple-ZipNeRF, VoxNeRF, Deformation Field Integration for Telepresence, and Multi-resolution Hash Encoding. SqueezeNeRF is a memory-efficient neural rendering method that further factorizes the position-dependent Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) of FastNeRF into three separate 2D networks operating on coordinate pairs (x,y), (y,z), and (z,x) to reduce cache size complexity from O(n^3) to O(n^2). It builds on NeRF Network Query with Hashed Embeddings by replacing the dense 3D position cache with a set of 2D position caches and a 2D direction cache, enabling real-time inference with significantly lower memory overhead than FastNeRF or NeRF-SH while maintaining high rendering speeds. VoxNeRF is a neural rendering method that integrates explicit scene geometry priors (mesh, point cloud, or depth map) with implicit radiance field representation to improve sampling efficiency and reconstruction accuracy. It addresses the ill-posed nature of recovering 3D geometry from 2D images by using a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) to model geometric uncertainty, which guides a hybrid sampling strategy. Unlike standard NeRF methods that sample uniformly or via stratified noise, VoxNeRF concentrates samples near the estimated surface while maintaining coverage of free space, reducing computational waste in empty regions. This method extends the FastNeRF architecture to support dynamic, expression-driven head avatars for telepresence by integrating a learnable deformation field network (F{deform}) and a non-trainable skeletal deformation field (F{bone}) into the ray marching process. It solves the problem of rendering animatable 3D heads from static multi-view images by warping sample positions based on an expression vector before querying the radiance field. It is distinguished from static NeRF variants by its explicit handling of temporal expression parameters and from other dynamic NeRF methods by its specific integration with the FastNeRF caching infrastructure and grid-based pruning. HDR-HexPlane is an end-to-end neural radiance field framework for dynamic scenes that learns 3D scene representations from dynamic 2D images captured with various exposures, allowing for novel view synthesis with adjustable exposure levels. It explicitly separates the modeling of dynamic scene geometry/radiance from the learning of scene illumination (exposure), addressing color inconsistency caused by objects moving between dark and bright regions. Unlike static HDR-NeRF methods, HDR-HexPlane handles dynamic scenes by incorporating temporal information (timestamp t) into the HexPlane representation. Multi-scale PointNeRF++ is a method for obtaining radiance (\rhoq) and density (\sigmaq) for a query point q by operating on a sparse, hierarchical point cloud representation at multiple granularity levels. It solves the problem of rendering in empty regions without relying on failure-prone region-growing heuristics. Unlike its sibling PointNeRF, this method naturally fills empty regions by averaging feature embeddings over valid scale levels where neighbors exist. It builds on NeRF Network Query with Hashed Embeddings by replacing hash grids with a multi-scale point cloud hierarchy. FourieRF is a few-shot Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) estimation method that prevents high-frequency artifacts and catastrophic overfitting by parameterizing grid-based features with a Fourier Transform prior. Unlike sibling methods that rely on external data priors or complex occlusion regularization, FourieRF uses an explicit curriculum training procedure to progressively increase the maximum learnable Fourier frequency, ensuring stable convergence on sparse data. It builds on NeRF Network Query with Hashed Embeddings by applying frequency control to the feature grids of grid-based NeRFs (specifically TensoRF) rather than MLP positional encodings. This family encompasses techniques that modify the hash-grid encoding mechanism in neural radiance fields to mitigate artifacts such as high-frequency aliasing and sparse-view floaters. It differs from standard hash-grid encoding by introducing either capacity constraints (smaller hash tables) to enforce feature sharing and geometric consistency, or statistical down-weighting factors to suppress high-frequency noise during rendering. NeRF-W extends Neural Radiance Fields to handle unconstrained internet photo collections by modeling temporal modifications, specifically variable illuminations and transient objects (people, cars, occlusions). It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF by introducing per-image appearance embeddings to handle photometric variations and a secondary transient MLP head to model dynamic content, allowing the rendering of static geometry while accounting for scene changes. A geometry estimator and appearance model using UniSDF, a state-of-the-art volume rendering approach based on a signed distance function (SDF), which decouples geometry from appearance and allows mesh extraction for radiance cue computation. A method that modifies Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) to reconstruct scenes in linear HDR color space by supervising directly on noisy raw input images, rather than postprocessed low dynamic range (LDR) images. A radiance field representation that uses two geometric proxy meshes (inner and outer) to define a ray segment. Instead of dense volumetric sampling, it learns to map the two endpoints of the ray segment (intersections with the inner and outer meshes) and the view direction to the final pixel color, reducing the number of sampled points per ray to two. A method to resample points along a ray based on the importance (weight) of previous samples, improving detail in high-density regions. It normalizes bin weights by adding epsilon (1e-5) and dividing by sum to create a PDF, computes the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) by cumsumming the PDF and padding with zeros at the start, generates uniform random values u in [0, 1] (or deterministic midpoints if det=True), finds indices in the CDF where u falls using searchsorted, identifies lower and upper bin indices for interpolation, and interpolates the final sample position within the bin using linear interpolation based on u's position in the CDF interval. A sparse neural rendering method that explicitly conditions the color prediction network on local features extracted from a pretrained network to improve color and feature consistency. It extracts local features F{gt}(r) from a pretrained VGG network's Relu1-1 layer for each ray r, concatenates bottleneck feature bi, prior feature fi, and view direction d, and predicts color ci = Mc(bi, fi, d). The loss function is L = Lc + \lambda Lf, where Lf = || F(r) - F^{gt}(r) ||2. It is trained at low resolution for 44K iterations with a batch size of 1024 due to memory limitations, and frequency regulation ends at 40K iterations. Using deeper VGG layers introduces interpolation artifacts because their output size differs from the input image; Relu1-1 is used because it is the same size as the input image. A post-training optimization step to ensure consistent appearance across adjacent Block-NeRFs by matching an appearance latent code from a target Block-NeRF to its neighbors. It selects a 3D matching location between pairs of adjacent Block-NeRFs where visibility prediction is high for both blocks, freezes the Block-NeRF network weights, and optimizes only the appearance code of the adjacent Block-NeRF to match the target appearance. Without appearance matching, randomly initialized appearance codes lead to different appearances in different blocks, causing inconsistencies during compositing. A rendering model that computes NeRF-based color by combining albedo, a shading scalar, and ambient color, replacing the standard transmittance/opacity accumulation with a shadow-aware irradiance formulation to handle illumination inconsistency. The rendered color is I{p1} = \rho(P) \times (s(P, w) + (1 - s(P, w)) \times a(w)), where \rho(P) is the albedo of surface point P, s(P, w) is the shading scalar (values 0 to 1), and a(w) is the ambient color indicating shadowed areas. The NeRF-based rendering color is C(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti oi s{vi}, where C(r) is the rendered color, oi is opacity, Ti is transmittance, and s{vi} is the shadow value at the i-th sampled point. Opacity is oi = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), where \sigmai is the density value at the sampled point and \deltai is the distance between adjacent sampled points along the ray. Transmittance is Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - oj). Time Complexity: Training time is significantly reduced compared to standard NeRF. For example, accumulating 128 samples at 1080p on a single RTX 3090 GPU takes approximately 5 seconds for a modular synthesizer scene. Memory Complexity: The hash grid memory usage is determined by the hash table size and the number of levels. It is generally more memory-efficient than dense 3D grids for large scenes but can still be substantial depending on the number of levels and feature dimensions. Measured Performance: Rendering performance can reach 10 frames per second on an RTX 3090 GPU for a large natural 360 scene. Scaling: Performance scales well with hardware acceleration due to the efficient implementation of the hash encoding and MLPs. Strengths: Fast training convergence, real-time rendering capabilities, ability to handle large scenes with occupancy grid pruning. Limitations: Hash collisions can cause grainy artifacts. The quality is significantly compromised if the MLP is replaced with a simple linear lookup. When to Use: When real-time rendering or fast training is required, and the scene can benefit from sparse representations. When Not to Use: When high-fidelity specular details are critical and hardware constraints prevent the use of the MLP component, or when the scene is very small and the overhead of hash encoding is not justified. The method originates from the "Instant Neural Graphics Primitives with a Multiresolution Hash Encoding" paper by Müller et al.. It builds on the original NeRF architecture by Mildenhall et al., which uses positional encoding and concatenated MLPs. The key innovation is the introduction of a learnable multiresolution hash encoding that maps 3D coordinates to feature vectors, enabling efficient training and rendering. The method has been widely adopted in various NeRF variants and extensions, such as HybridNeRF, SqueezeNeRF, and VoxNeRF. yashbhalgat/HashNeRF-pytorch, https://github.com/yashbhalgat/HashNeRF-pytorch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Instant Neural Graphics Primitives with a Multiresolution..., https://www.cs.jhu.edu/~misha/ReadingSeminar/Papers/Mueller22.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 NeRF-Factory/IDDR-NGP, https://github.com/NeRF-Factory/IDDR-NGP, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) AIM 2024 Sparse Neural Rendering Challenge: Methods and Results, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-91856-82, fetched 2026-10-27 Block-NeRF: Scalable Large Scene Neural View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.00807, fetched 2026-10-26 Shading and Geometric Constraint Neural Radiance Field for DSM Reconstruction from Multi-View Satellite Images, https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18071091, fetched 2026-11-05

name: HybridNeRF Model Architecture
head: HybridNeRF
body: HybridNeRF is a neural radiance field architecture that combines 3D feature grids with 2D triplanes to efficiently represent complex scenes. It solves the trade-off between the high memory cost of pure 3D voxel representations and the limited geometric expressiveness of pure 2D plane-based methods by using a hybrid query mechanism. Unlike its sibling MVS Network Query which relies on multi-view stereo consistency, or VoxNeRF which uses pure voxel grids, HybridNeRF explicitly separates geometric and appearance features into distinct multi-resolution structures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D point coordinate \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a viewing direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: Color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and volume density \sigma \in \mathbb{R} (or signed distance, depending on the specific variant, but standard HybridNeRF predicts density). Data Structures: 1. 3D Feature Grids: A set of 3D voxel grids at 3 resolution levels: 128^3, 256^3, and 512^3. 2. Triplanes: A set of 2D feature planes at 7 resolution levels, ranging from 128^2 to 8,192^2. 3. MLP: A Multi-Layer Perceptron that takes the aggregated features and viewing direction to predict color and density. Algorithm: For a given query point \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d}: 1. Fetch 3D Features: For each of the 3 resolution levels l \in \{1, 2, 3\}: Retrieve K=4 feature vectors from the 3D grid at level l using trilinear interpolation at position \mathbf{x}. Let F{3D}^{(l)} be the concatenated features from this level. 2. Fetch Triplane Features: For each of the 7 resolution levels l \in \{1, \dots, 7\}: Retrieve K=4 feature vectors from the triplanes at level l using bilinear interpolation at the projection of \mathbf{x} onto the planes. Let F{2D}^{(l)} be the concatenated features from this level. 3. Aggregate Features: Sum the features across all 3D levels: F{3D} = \sum{l=1}^{3} F{3D}^{(l)}. Sum the features across all triplane levels: F{2D} = \sum{l=1}^{7} F{2D}^{(l)}. Note: The method uses summation instead of concatenation for levels within the same structure to reduce dimensionality before combining structures. 4. Combine Structures: Concatenate the summed 3D features and summed 2D features: F{total} = \text{Concat}(F{3D}, F{2D}). The resulting input dimension to the MLP is 4K = 16 (since K=4 features per level are summed, and the sum preserves the feature dimensionality, but the text specifies the final MLP input is 16-dimensional, implying the feature dimension per level is 4, or the sum results in a 16-dim vector. Given "K=4 features per level" and "4K=16", it implies the feature vector size per level is 4, and summing them results in a vector of size 4? No, if K=4 features are fetched, and they are summed, the dimension remains the feature dimension. If the final input is 16, and there are two sources (3D and 2D), each contributes 8? The text says "concatenate the summed features... to obtain a 4K=16-dimensional MLP input". With K=4, 4K=16. This implies the summed feature vector from 3D grids is 8-dim and from triplanes is 8-dim? Or perhaps K refers to the number of features per level being summed into a single vector? Let's stick to the explicit output dimension: 16. 5. Encode Viewing Direction: Encode the viewing direction \mathbf{d} using spherical harmonics up to the 4th degree. Let \mathbf{d}{SH} be the resulting directional encoding vector. 6. MLP Prediction: Concatenate F{total} and \mathbf{d}{SH} (or pass them through separate branches as per standard NeRF, but HybridNeRF typically feeds the spatial features into the MLP and direction as auxiliary input). Pass through the MLP to predict color \mathbf{c} and density \sigma. Pitfalls: Aliasing: Due to the multi-resolution feature grid, aliasing artifacts can occur. This is handled similarly to VR-NeRF. A variant for inserting objects into scenes. It transforms sampling points from scene coordinates to object coordinates using the object's insertion position (translation and rotation). It composites density as the normalized sum of densities from the scene and object at the same position, and composites reflectance as a weighted sum of reflectance values weighted by voxel particle densities. A rendering pipeline that mixes a neural proxy sampler Sp for animated objects and a neural scene sampler Sc for static elements. It separates particles into a proxy set Xp and scene set Xc. For each ray, it finds the convex set bounded by intersections with the proxy mesh using triangle intersection methods to determine Barycentric coordinates, then samples the neural texture locally. Learns sharp neural 3D representations from blurred images and event data by combining bio-inspired event camera and standard RGB camera inputs. It introduces blur rendering loss and event rendering loss to guide the network. Jointly estimates camera pose and scene representation by synchronizing locally unlocalized NeRFs using a local-to-global learning framework. Enhances new view creation from limited inputs in indoor settings by integrating structural indicators into self-guided depth estimation and applying planar coherence loss. A generalizable human NeRF model for recovering animatable 3D humans from a single input image, using conditional implicit maximum likelihood estimation (cIMLE) to address depth estimation uncertainty. A NeRF training method without camera poses that improves robustness by introducing implicit pose regularization via a scene codebook. Synthesizes new views from finite perspectives by extracting depth priors from pre-trained depth models or rough depth maps, introducing local depth ordering and spatial continuity constraints. Memory: Uses a hybrid of 3D grids and 2D triplanes. The 3D grids are at 3 levels (128^3, 256^3, 512^3) and triplanes at 7 levels (128^2 to 8,192^2). Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient representation by leveraging the compactness of 2D planes for appearance and 3D grids for geometry, reducing memory compared to pure 3D methods. Limitations: Requires careful handling of aliasing due to multi-resolution grids. HybridNeRF was introduced in 2024 by the authors of "HybridNeRF: Efficient Neural Rendering via Adaptive Volumetric Surfaces". It builds on the concept of hybrid representations to balance efficiency and quality in neural radiance fields. name: SeaThru-NeRF
head: SeaThru
body: SeaThru-NeRF is a neural radiance field method designed for visualizing and reconstructing scenes within dispersed scattering media, such as fog, haze, and subaquatic environments. It extends the standard NeRF formulation by treating the scattering medium as a semi-transparent entity with distinct color and density parameters, separate from opaque objects. This allows the model to distinguish between unblemished (directly illuminated) and backscattered segments of the scene, enabling the restoration of scene hue and 3D configuration in far-off areas that are typically obscured. It builds on HybridNeRF Model Architecture by incorporating specific scattering physics into the volume rendering integral. SeaThru-NeRF modifies the standard volume rendering equation to account for the additive density and color contributions of a scattering medium. It assumes that the total density at any point along a ray is the sum of the object density and the medium density. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera ray r, scene geometry and appearance data (learned via MLPs). Output: Rendered color C(r), potentially decomposed into object-only and medium-only components. Data Structures: The method utilizes the standard NeRF MLP architecture but outputs two sets of parameters for each sampled point t along the ray: 1. Object density \sigma{obj}(t) and object color c{obj}(t). 2. Medium density \sigma{med}(t) and medium color c{med}(t). Rendering Formulas: The rendered color C(r) is computed by integrating the accumulated color along the ray segment from tn to tf: C(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \left[ \sigma{obj}(t)c{obj}(t) + \sigma{med}(t)c{med}(t) \right] dt \quad (8) where T(t) is the transmittance, representing the probability that light travels from the camera to point t without being absorbed or scattered: T(t) = \exp \left( - \int{tn}^{t} \left[ \sigma{obj}(s) + \sigma{med}(s) \right] ds \right) \quad (9) Here, c{obj}(t) and c{med}(t) are the colors of the object and medium at t, respectively. Training: The model parameters are optimized by minimizing the squared distance between the expected color \hat{C}(r) and the ground truth color C{gt}(r). Pseudocode: The following pseudocode illustrates the rendering step for a single ray, assuming the MLPs queryobject and querymedium are defined elsewhere. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderseathruray(rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, numsamples, queryobject, querymedium): """ Renders a single ray using the SeaThru-NeRF scattering model. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, camera origin. raydirection: 3D vector, normalized ray direction. tnear: float, near plane distance. tfar: float, far plane distance. numsamples: int, number of sample points along the ray. queryobject: function, returns (sigmaobj, cobj) for a 3D point. querymedium: function, returns (sigmamed, cmed) for a 3D point. Returns: color: float, rendered color value. """ # Discretize the ray into sample points tvals = linspace(tnear, tfar, numsamples) accumulatedtransmittance = 0.0 accumulatedcolor = 0.0 # Calculate delta distances between samples # Note: In practice, tvals are often sampled adaptively or uniformly. # Here we assume uniform sampling for simplicity. deltat = (tfar - tnear) / (numsamples - 1) for i in range(numsamples): t = tvals[i] point = rayorigin + t raydirection # Query object properties sigmaobj, cobj = queryobject(point) # Query medium properties sigmamed, cmed = querymedium(point) # Total density at this point sigmatotal = sigmaobj + sigmamed # Calculate transmittance up to this point # T(t) = exp(-integral from tnear to t of sigmatotal(s) ds) # Approximating integral as sum of previous deltas if i == 0: transmittance = 1.0 else: # Accumulate opacity from previous steps # This is a simplified Euler integration of the transmittance # A more robust implementation would maintain running transmittance pass # Calculate weight for this sample # Weight = T(t) (1 - exp(-sigmatotal deltat)) # However, the standard NeRF formulation uses: # Weighti = Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai deltat)) # where Ti = exp(-sum{j<i} sigmaj deltat) # Let's implement the standard discrete volume rendering accumulation pass # Re-implementing the standard accumulation loop for clarity accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = 0.0 for i in range(numsamples): t = tvals[i] point = rayorigin + t raydirection sigmaobj, cobj = queryobject(point) sigmamed, cmed = querymedium(point) sigmatotal = sigmaobj + sigmamed # Calculate opacity for this segment # alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma deltat) alpha = 1.0 - exp(-sigmatotal deltat) # Weight = accumulatedtransmittance alpha weight = accumulatedtransmittance alpha # Add contribution to color # The color contribution is the sum of object and medium colors weighted by their densities # ctotal = (sigmaobj cobj + sigmamed cmed) / sigmatotal # But the integral form (Eq 8) suggests: # contribution = T(t) (sigmaobj cobj + sigmamed cmed) deltat # In discrete form: weight ctotal is not quite right if we use the alpha formulation. # The standard NeRF discrete form is: # C = sumi Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai deltat)) ci # Where ci is the color emitted by the volume element. # In SeaThru, the "emitted" color is the sum of object and medium emissions. ctotal = (sigmaobj cobj + sigmamed cmed) / (sigmatotal + 1e-6) accumulatedcolor += weight ctotal # Update transmittance for next step accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - alpha) return accumulatedcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Input: If the medium density is zero everywhere, the model reduces to standard NeRF. If object density is zero, it renders only the medium. Precision: The exponential function in transmittance calculation can lead to underflow for very dense media. Clamping or using log-space arithmetic may be necessary. Boundary Conditions: The integration limits tn and tf must be carefully chosen to include all relevant scattering and object contributions. Focuses on modifying shading for relighting, not scattering media. Link Uses hybrid representations for multi-space scenes, not specifically scattering. Link Hybrid representation for large-scale scenes, not scattering. Link Panoramic NeRF, not scattering. Link Fast super-resolution NeRF, not scattering. Link Compression for NeRF, not scattering. Link Depth estimation with ambiguity, not scattering. Link Dynamic scenes, not scattering. Link Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples per ray and the depth of the MLPs. Similar to standard NeRF but with double the output channels (object and medium). Memory Complexity: Requires storing two sets of density and color parameters per point, effectively doubling the output size of the MLPs compared to standard NeRF. Strengths: Capable of restoring scene hue and 3D configuration in far-off areas obscured by scattering media. Can produce lifelike new-view composites while maintaining or eliminating the medium effect. Limitations: Performance in highly complex reflective and refractive scenes may require more subspaces, similar to MS-NeRF. Not given in the sources for specific hardware performance metrics. When to use: Underwater, fog, or haze visualization and reconstruction. When not to use: Clear air scenes where standard NeRF is sufficient and more efficient. SeaThru-NeRF was introduced in 2023. It is inspired by the SeaThru method. It extends the capability of NeRFs to handle scattering media such as underwater environments. The method showcases proficiency in depicting scenes in both simulated and actual settings, resulting in cutting-edge, realistic new-view composites. name: FastSR-NeRF
head: NeRF + SR pipeline, Simple NeRF+SR Pipeline
body: FastSR-NeRF is a method that improves the rendering efficiency of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) on consumer-grade hardware by combining a lightweight NeRF model with a CNN-based super-resolution (SR) module. It solves the problem of high computational cost and long training times associated with high-resolution NeRF rendering by training the NeRF to produce low-resolution (LR) 3D-consistent features and upscaling them to high-resolution (HR) outputs. Unlike prior NeRF+SR methods that rely on complex training procedures, knowledge distillation, or high-resolution reference images, FastSR-NeRF requires no architectural changes to the NeRF backbone and uses a simple end-to-end training pipeline. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N{img} input images (typically 20-200 per scene) at resolution 800 \times 800; a pretrained SR model S (e.g., EDSR); a hybrid NeRF backbone (e.g., TensoRF). Outputs: High-resolution rendered images H. Data Structures: Hybrid NeRF Model: Consists of grid-based feature decompositions \mathcal{G}{\sigma} and \mathcal{G}{c}, and two small MLPs \mathcal{F}{\sigma} and \mathcal{F}{c}. \mathcal{G}{\sigma}(\mathbf{x}): Fetches density features from a grid at position \mathbf{x}. \mathcal{G}{c}(\mathbf{x}): Fetches color features from a grid at position \mathbf{x}. \mathcal{F}{\sigma}: MLP mapping density features to scalar density \sigma. \mathcal{F}{c}: MLP mapping color features and viewing direction \mathbf{d} to color c. SR Module S: A CNN-based upsampling network (e.g., EDSR) that takes LR RGB images and outputs HR RGB images. Ray Patches: R{LR}^P: A contiguous 2D patch of rays sampled at low resolution. R{HR}^P: The corresponding high-resolution patch of rays, obtained by upsampling R{LR}^P using bilinear interpolation. Numbered Steps: 1. Warm-up: Train the backbone NeRF model (e.g., TensoRF) at low resolution (LR) using its default hyperparameters for 5,000 iterations. 2. Pipeline Construction: Plug a pretrained SR model S with the desired upscaling ratio (2× or 4×) into the pipeline. 3. Random Patch Sampling: For each training iteration, randomly sample a contiguous 2D patch of rays R{LR}^P from the scene's ray space. This differs from standard stochastic ray sampling. 4. Volume Rendering: For each ray \mathbf{r}{LR} \in R{LR}^P, compute the color \widehat{C}(\mathbf{r}{LR}) using the hybrid NeRF model. 5. Super-Resolution: Upsample the low-resolution output image generated from R{LR}^P using the SR module S to generate the final high-resolution output H. 6. Loss Computation: Compute the Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss between the ground-truth high-resolution image C(\mathbf{r}{HR}) and the upscaled NeRF output S(\widehat{C}(\mathbf{r}{LR})). 7. Optimization: Update all parameters (NeRF and SR) end-to-end using the Adam optimizer. Formulas: Volume Rendering Equation: \widehat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} T{i} \cdot (1 - \exp (-\sigma{i} \delta{i})) \cdot c{i} Where: N: Number of sampling points along the ray. \deltai: Distance between sampling points t{i-1} and ti. Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} \exp(-\sigmaj \deltaj): Accumulated transmittance up to point i. \sigmai: Density at position x. ci: Color at position x. Hybrid NeRF Feature Fetching: \sigma{i} = \mathcal{F}{\sigma} (\mathcal{G}{\sigma}(\mathbf{x})) c{i} = \mathcal{F}{c}(\mathcal{G}{c}(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{d}) Where \mathbf{x} is the 3D position and \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction. End-to-End Training Loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{MSE}} = \sum{\mathbf{r}{\text{HR}}, \mathbf{r}{\text{LR}}} \big\| C(\mathbf{r}{\text{HR}}) - S(\widehat{C}(\mathbf{r}{\text{LR}};\mathcal{F};\mathcal{G})) \big\|{2}^{2} Where C is the ground-truth color, S is the SR module, and \mathbf{r}{HR} is the high-resolution counterpart of \mathbf{r}{LR}. Parameters: Upscaling Ratio: 2× or 4×. Learning Rate: 0.0001. Patch Size: 256 pixels for SR-2×; 128 pixels for SR-4×. Optimizer: Adam. Training Duration: 150 epochs. Iterations per Epoch: One patch per iteration. Warm-up Iterations: 5,000 iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainfastsrnerf(inputimages, srmodel, nerfbackbone, lr=0.0001, epochs=150, patchsize=256, srratio=2): """ Trains the FastSR-NeRF pipeline end-to-end. Args: inputimages: List of ground-truth HR images. srmodel: Pretrained SR CNN (e.g., EDSR). nerfbackbone: Hybrid NeRF model (e.g., TensoRF). lr: Learning rate. epochs: Number of training epochs. patchsize: Size of the random patch in pixels. srratio: Upscaling factor (2 or 4). """ optimizer = Adam(list(nerfbackbone.parameters()) + list(srmodel.parameters()), lr=lr) # Step 1: Warm-up NeRF at LR print("Warming up NeRF for 5000 iterations...") for i in range(5000): # Standard stochastic ray sampling for warm-up rayslr, rayshr, gtcolors = samplestochasticrays(inputimages, resolutionfactor=1.0/srratio) predcolorslr = volumerender(nerfbackbone, rayslr) # Simple MSE on LR during warm-up (standard NeRF training) loss = mseloss(predcolorslr, gtcolors) loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() # Step 2 & 3: End-to-End Training with Random Patch Sampling print("Starting end-to-end training...") for epoch in range(epochs): # Randomly select a patch from the scene rayslrpatch, rayshrpatch, gtpatch = randompatchsampling(inputimages, patchsize, srratio) # Step 4: Volume Rendering on LR rays predcolorslrpatch = volumerender(nerfbackbone, rayslrpatch) # Step 5: Super-Resolution # predcolorslrpatch is an image tensor of shape (Hlr, Wlr, 3) # srmodel upsamples it to (Hhr, Whr, 3) predcolorshrpatch = srmodel(predcolorslrpatch) # Step 6: Loss Computation # gtpatch is the HR ground truth corresponding to the patch loss = mseloss(predcolorshrpatch, gtpatch) # Step 7: Optimization loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() def volumerender(nerfmodel, rays): """ Performs volume rendering for a batch of rays using the hybrid NeRF. """ colors = [] for ray in rays: # Sample points along the ray points, deltas = samplepointsalongray(ray) densities = [] colorspoint = [] for x, d in zip(points, ray.direction): # Fetch features from grids featsigma = nerfmodel.gridsigma(x) featcolor = nerfmodel.gridcolor(x) # Compute density and color via MLPs sigma = nerfmodel.mlpsigma(featsigma) c = nerfmodel.mlpcolor(featcolor, d) densities.append(sigma) colorspoint.append(c) # Apply volume rendering equation # Ti = product(exp(-sigmaj deltaj)) # C = sum(Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai deltai)) ci) transmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = 0.0 for i in range(len(points)): alpha = 1.0 - exp(-densities[i] deltas[i]) accumulatedcolor += transmittance alpha colorspoint[i] transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) colors.append(accumulatedcolor) return stack(colors) def randompatchsampling(images, patchsize, srratio): """ Samples a random contiguous 2D patch of rays and corresponding ground truth. """ # Randomly select top-left corner (x, y) within valid bounds h, w = images[0].shape[:2] ystart = random.randint(0, h - patchsize) xstart = random.randint(0, w - patchsize) # Extract HR patch from ground truth gthr = images[0][ystart:ystart+patchsize, xstart:xstart+patchsize] # Downsample to get LR patch for ray generation # Bilinear interpolation as per source gtlr = bilinearinterpolatedownsample(gthr, srratio) # Generate rays corresponding to the LR patch pixels rayslr = generateraysfrompatch(gtlr) # Generate rays corresponding to the HR patch pixels (upsampled ray space) rayshr = generateraysfrompatch(gthr) return rayslr, rayshr, gthr Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sampling Strategy: Standard NeRF training uses stochastic sampling of individual rays. The NeRF+SR pipeline requires contiguous 2D patches to match the SR module's input structure. Using standard stochastic sampling will break the SR module's convolutional kernels. Grid-based vs. Random Patch Sampling: Grid-based patch sampling cuts ray space with rigid grid lines, causing variations between grid boundaries to be unseen by convolutional kernels, leading to lower PSNR (e.g., 31.84 vs 32.53 on NeRF-Synthetic SR-2×). Random patch sampling avoids this by shuffling regions. Hardware Support: Apple Metal Performance Shader (MPS) support in PyTorch may not fully run NeRF and SR operators on MPS devices, forcing experiments to run on CPUs, which is significantly slower than expected GPU performance. High Upscaling Ratios: At 8× upscaling, quality degrades significantly (e.g., PSNR drops to 27.27 on NeRF-Synthetic). Time Complexity: Training time is significantly reduced compared to high-resolution NeRF training. For example, on NeRF-Synthetic, SR-2× takes 1.5 hours and SR-4× takes 30 minutes, compared to TensoRF's 18 minutes (but TensoRF renders at full resolution). On an M1 Pro MacBook, SR-2× training takes 22.5 hours, compared to MobileNeRF's >375 hours. Memory Complexity: The hybrid NeRF model size is smaller than vanilla NeRF due to smaller MLPs and grid features. Model sizes are 20 MB for SR-2× and 13 MB for SR-4× on NeRF-Synthetic, compared to 71.8 MB for TensoRF. Measured Performance: NeRF-Synthetic (SR-2×): 32.53 PSNR, 0.961 SSIM, 0.309s render time. NeRF-Synthetic (SR-4×): 30.47 PSNR, 0.944 SSIM, 0.077s render time. LLFF (SR-4×): 25.41 PSNR, 0.784 SSIM, 0.165s render time. M1 Pro MacBook (SR-2×): 15.9s render time. Scaling: Rendering speed increases by up to 18× on NVIDIA V100 and 12.8× on M1 Pro chip compared to full-resolution rendering. Strengths: Simple implementation, model-agnostic (can use any pretrained SR model), suitable for consumer-grade hardware, no need for high-resolution reference images or distillation. Limitations: Quality degrades at high upscaling ratios (8×). Training on Apple Silicon may be slow due to MPS support limitations. Not real-time on all consumer devices (e.g., 15.9s on M1 Pro for SR-2×). FastSR-NeRF was introduced in December 2023. It addresses the need for efficient NeRF rendering on consumer devices, where training with 8 server-class GPUs (as required by MobileNeRF) is not feasible. The method builds on the HybridNeRF Model Architecture [4842-hybridnerf-model-architecture.md], which uses grid-based decompositions for efficiency. It contrasts with methods like MobileR2L, which uses expensive distillation, and RefSR-NeRF, which requires high-resolution reference images. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28 FastSR-NeRF: Improving NeRF Efficiency on Consumer Devices with A Simple Super-Resolution Pipeline, https://doi.org/10.1109/wacv57701.2024.00593, fetched 2026-10-26
