name: NeRFCodec
head: Neural Feature Compression Meets Neural Radiance Fields for Memory-Efficient Scene Representation
body: NeRFCodec is an end-to-end compression framework for plane-based hybrid Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that integrates non-linear transform, quantization, and entropy coding to achieve memory-efficient scene representation. It solves the high storage footprint of hybrid NeRF representations by compressing feature planes using a pre-trained 2D neural image codec backbone, adapted with content-specific parameters. Unlike raw parameter counting or generic image codecs, NeRFCodec exploits inter-channel information in feature planes through a specialized encoder-decoder adaptation, achieving superior rate-distortion performance compared to methods like Masked Wavelet NeRF and VQ-TensoRF. It enables high-quality novel view synthesis within a strict memory budget of approximately 0.5 MB per scene. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained hybrid NeRF model (specifically plane-based variants like TensoRF-VM or HexPlane) for a specific scene, consisting of orthogonal feature planes and a small attribute regression MLP. Output: A compressed bitstream containing quantized latent codes, quantized hyperprior latent codes, content-specific decoder head parameters, feature residual vectors, tiny MLP parameters, and metadata. Data Structures: The framework modifies a pre-trained 2D neural image codec (backbone: Cheng et al. [10], implementation: CompressAI [4]). Encoder Head (E{\phi1}): The first layer of the 2D codec, modified to accept the channel dimension of the NeRF feature planes. Frozen Decoder Body: The intermediate layers of the pre-trained 2D decoder remain frozen. Decoder Head (D{\phi2}): The last layer of the 2D codec, modified to output the target channel dimension. This head contains content-specific learnable parameters. Feature Planes (x): Orthogonal feature planes extracted from the pre-trained hybrid NeRF. Tiny MLP (f): The small MLP used for attribute regression (color/density) in the renderer. Bitstream Components: 1. Quantized latent code \hat{y}. 2. Quantized hyperprior latent code \hat{z}. 3. Feature decoder head parameters D{\phi2}. 4. Feature residual vectors v{\Delta x}. 5. Tiny MLP parameters f. 6. Metadata. Training Procedure: The training occurs in three phases: 1. Pre-training: Pre-train the hybrid NeRF on the target scene for 100,000 iterations to obtain feature planes x and tiny MLP f. 2. Warm-up: Perform a warm-up of the neural feature codec using only the feature plane reconstruction loss to establish a better starting point. 3. Joint Training: Jointly train the neural feature codec and the neural radiance field for 100,000 iterations. The loss function L{total} combines rendering loss and entropy loss. During this phase, the full encoder and the decoder head are adapted to fit the specific scene, while the remaining parts of the decoder are frozen. 4. Quantization-Aware Training (QAT): Perform QAT on the network parameters to be transmitted (decoder head and MLP in renderer) for 10,000 iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainnerfcodec(scenedata, pretrainedneurf, pretrained2dcodec): """ Trains the NeRFCodec framework for a specific scene. """ # 1. Pre-train Hybrid NeRF # Obtain feature planes x and tiny MLP f nerfmodel = pretrainedneurf for i in range(100000): renderloss = computerenderingloss(nerfmodel, scenedata) renderloss.backward() optimizerneurf.step() featureplanes = nerfmodel.getfeatureplanes() tinymlp = nerfmodel.getmlp() # 2. Initialize Neural Feature Codec # Modify encoder and decoder heads of pre-trained 2D codec codec = pretrained2dcodec codec.encoderhead = modifylayer(codec.encoderhead, targetchannels=featureplanes.shape[1]) codec.decoderhead = modifylayer(codec.decoderhead, targetchannels=featureplanes.shape[1]) # Freeze intermediate decoder layers for param in codec.decoderbody.parameters(): param.requiresgrad = False # 3. Warm-up Phase # Optimize codec only with feature plane reconstruction loss optimizercodec = torch.optim.Adam(codec.parameters()) for i in range(warmupiterations): # Iteration count not specified in sources latent = codec.encode(featureplanes) reconstructedplanes = codec.decode(latent) recloss = mseloss(reconstructedplanes, featureplanes) recloss.backward() optimizercodec.step() # 4. Joint Training Phase # Supervised by rendering loss and entropy loss optimizerjoint = torch.optim.Adam(list(codec.parameters()) + list(tinymlp.parameters())) for i in range(100000): # Encode feature planes latent = codec.encode(featureplanes) # Decode feature planes reconstructedplanes = codec.decode(latent) # Render image using reconstructed planes and tiny MLP renderedimage = renderscene(reconstructedplanes, tinymlp, scenedata) # Compute losses renderingloss = computerenderingloss(renderedimage, scenedata.gtimage) entropyloss = computeentropyloss(latent, codec.probabilitymodel) Ltotal = renderingloss + entropyloss Ltotal.backward() optimizerjoint.step() # 5. Quantization-Aware Training Phase # Quantize parameters to be transmitted: decoder head and MLP optimizerqat = torch.optim.Adam(list(codec.decoderhead.parameters()) + list(tinymlp.parameters())) for i in range(10000): latent = codec.encode(featureplanes) reconstructedplanes = codec.decode(latent) renderedimage = renderscene(reconstructedplanes, tinymlp, scenedata) renderingloss = computerenderingloss(renderedimage, scenedata.gtimage) entropyloss = computeentropyloss(latent, codec.probabilitymodel) Ltotal = renderingloss + entropyloss Ltotal.backward() optimizerqat.step() return codec, tinymlp def encodescene(codec, tinymlp, featureplanes): """ Encodes the scene into a bitstream at test time. """ bitstreams = [] # 1. Encode Feature Planes # Orthogonal feature planes are fed into the codec one by one for plane in featureplanes: latent = codec.encode(plane) quantizedlatent = quantize(latent) bitstreamlatent = entropyencode(quantizedlatent) bitstreams.append(bitstreamlatent) # Encode hyperprior if applicable hyperprior = codec.gethyperprior(latent) quantizedhyperprior = quantize(hyperprior) bitstreamhyperprior = entropyencode(quantizedhyperprior) bitstreams.append(bitstreamhyperprior) # 2. Encode Content-Specific Parameters # Compress decoder head parameters quantizeddecoderhead = quantize(codec.decoderhead.parameters()) bitstreamdecoderhead = entropyencode(quantizeddecoderhead) bitstreams.append(bitstreamdecoderhead) # Compress feature residual vectors (if used) # Note: Sources mention residual vectors vdeltax in bitstream # Assuming these are derived or stored separately bitstreams.append(encoderesiduals()) # 3. Encode Tiny MLP quantizedmlp = quantize(tinymlp.parameters()) bitstreammlp = entropyencode(quantizedmlp) bitstreams.append(bitstreammlp) # 4. Multiplex totalbitstream = multiplex(bitstreams) return totalbitstream def decodescene(codec, tinymlp, totalbitstream): """ Decodes the bitstream and reconstructs the scene for rendering. """ # 1. Demultiplex substreams = demultiplex(totalbitstream) # 2. Decode Feature Planes # Reconstruct feature planes once reconstructedfeatureplanes = [] for i, planesubstream in enumerate(substreams['latentstreams']): quantizedlatent = entropydecode(planesubstream) # Decode using the adapted decoder head # Note: The decoder head parameters must also be decoded first reconstructedplane = codec.decode(quantizedlatent) reconstructedfeatureplanes.append(reconstructedplane) # 3. Decode Parameters quantizeddecoderhead = entropydecode(substreams['decoderheadstream']) codec.decoderhead.setparameters(quantizeddecoderhead) quantizedmlp = entropydecode(substreams['mlpstream']) tinymlp.setparameters(quantizedmlp) # 4. Render # Subsequent querying operations are executed on the reconstructed planes renderedimage = renderscene(reconstructedfeatureplanes, tinymlp, querypoints) return renderedimage Parameters: Memory Budget: 0.5 MB per scene. Joint Training Iterations: 100,000. Quantization-Aware Training Iterations: 10,000. Pre-training Iterations: 100,000. Implementation Base: CompressAI library [4]. Backbone: Neural image codec proposed by Cheng et al. [10]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Architecture Modification: Using a pre-trained 2D neural image codec without modifying the encoder/decoder heads (e.g., splitting planes into three channels and normalizing) results in significantly higher bitrate consumption because it fails to fully exploit inter-channel information. Generalization: A neural feature codec trained on a small-scale feature dataset (e.g., 8 scenes from NeRF-Synthetic) fails to generalize to unseen objects from other datasets (e.g., NSVF-Synthetic) without test-time optimization, producing unreasonable rendering results. Training Time: Training the non-linear transform is time-consuming. Scene Specificity: A specialized neural feature codec must be trained for each scene individually. Feature Reconstruction Loss: Adding a feature plane reconstruction loss during joint training degrades performance (PSNR 32.81 dB vs 35.08 dB) compared to relying solely on rendering loss. This method estimates the compressed bitrate budget for the decoder-side parameters of the NeRFCodec framework, which must be transmitted alongside encoded Neural Radiance Fields. It differs from raw parameter counting by applying per-tensor quantization and entropy estimation to approximate the actual payload size in a streaming application. It serves as a proxy for memory footprint when NeRFCodec is used as a 3D representation for content delivery. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: NeRFCodec achieves a total compressed size of 0.453 MB for the TensoRF-VM variant, compared to an original size of 72.342 MB (compression ratio x159.7). Compressed Feature planes: 0.052 MB (Original 69.953 MB, Ratio x1345.3). Compressed Decoder head: 0.269 MB (Original 1.761 MB, Ratio x6.5). Compressed MLP in renderer: 0.042 MB (Original 0.160 MB, Ratio x3.8). Feature vectors: 0.049 MB (Original 0.234 MB, Ratio x4.8). Residual vectors: 0.041 MB (Original 0.234 MB, Ratio x5.7). Compression Ratio: The non-linear transform allows for a compression ratio over 1000 times for feature planes. Measured Performance: NeRF-Synthetic Dataset: 36.60 dB PSNR at 0.91 MB. 36.21 dB PSNR at 0.46 MB. Ablation (Chair Scene, NeRF-Synthetic): Auto-encoder Size: 0.453 MB, PSNR: 35.08 dB, SSIM: 0.981. Auto-decoder Size: 0.461 MB, PSNR: 34.41 dB, SSIM: 0.973. Without Entropy Loss: Size 0.701 MB, PSNR 34.98 dB, SSIM 0.980. With Feature Reconstruction Loss: Size 0.479 MB, PSNR 32.81 dB, SSIM 0.965. Re-using unmodified Image Codec: Size 1.786 MB, PSNR 29.96 dB, SSIM 0.923. Re-using Tuned Image Codec: Size 1.150 MB, PSNR 33.25 dB, SSIM 0.961. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Superior rate-distortion performance compared to Masked Wavelet NeRF, Binary Radiance Fields, and VQ-TensoRF across three datasets (NeRF-Synthetic, NSVF-Synthetic, Tanks and Temples). The use of a non-linear transform instead of a wavelet transform improves upon Masked Wavelet NeRF. Compatible with different plane-based NeRF approaches (validated on TensoRF-VM and HexPlane). Limitations: Training the non-linear transform is time-consuming. Requires training a specialized neural feature codec for each scene individually. Does not generalize well to unseen objects without test-time optimization if trained on limited data. When to Use: Use when high-quality novel view synthesis is required with a strict memory budget (e.g., < 0.5 MB per scene). Use when compressing plane-based hybrid NeRF representations. When Not to Use: Do not use if real-time training of a generalized codec for unseen objects is required without per-scene adaptation. Do not use if computational resources for the time-consuming non-linear transform training are limited. NeRFCodec was proposed by researchers from Zhejiang University, published in CVPR 2024. It addresses the significant storage requirements of hybrid NeRF representations, which combine feature grids and small MLPs for high reconstruction quality and fast training. The method leverages advances in neural compression and neural field representation, specifically reusing pre-trained neural 2D image codecs (such as the one by Cheng et al.) by adapting their encoder and decoder heads to the specific channel dimensions of NeRF feature planes. It was validated on the NeRF-Synthetic, NSVF-Synthetic, and Tanks and Temples datasets. name: NeRFCodec Decoder Payload Estimation
head: NeRFCodec Bitrate Budget Estimation
body: This method estimates the compressed bitrate budget for the decoder-side parameters of the NeRFCodec framework, which must be transmitted alongside encoded Neural Radiance Fields. It differs from raw parameter counting by applying per-tensor quantization and entropy estimation to approximate the actual payload size in a streaming application. It serves as a proxy for memory footprint when NeRFCodec is used as a 3D representation for content delivery. The procedure estimates the bit cost for each tensor in the decoder-side model (density and appearance codecs) by simulating quantization and calculating the theoretical entropy bound plus header overhead. Input: A tensor x of floating-point values (typically 32-bit float) representing decoder-side parameters. Output: The estimated total bit cost for the tensor. Tensor x: A multi-dimensional array of values. Histogram: An array of size L = 2^{qbits} storing counts of each quantized level. PMF: An array of size L storing empirical probabilities pi. 1. Per-tensor Quantization: Compute the minimum and maximum values of the tensor: x{\min} = \min(x), \quad x{\max} = \max(x) Determine the number of quantization bits qbits (typically 8). Calculate the number of levels L: L = 2^{qbits} Compute the scale factor: \mathrm{scale} = \frac{x{\max} - x{\min}}{L - 1} Map each element xj to an integer level qj: qj = \mathrm{round}\left(\frac{xj - x{\min}}{\mathrm{scale}}\right) Clamp qj to the range [0, L - 1]. 2. Entropy Estimate: Compute a histogram of the quantized levels qj. Derive the empirical probability mass function (PMF) pi for each level i \in \{0, \dots, L-1\}: pi = \frac{\text{count}(i)}{N} where N is the total number of elements in the tensor. Calculate the Shannon entropy bound (idealized bit cost) H{\text{bits}} by summing over non-zero probabilities: H{\text{bits}} = N \sum{i: pi > 0} -pi \log2 pi 3. Per-tensor Header: Calculate the overhead bits required to transmit side information (x{\min}, x{\max}, qbits, and tensor shape). The header size depends on the number of dimensions d of the tensor: \mathrm{header\bits} = 2 \cdot 32 + 8 + 32 \cdot d This assumes 32-bit floats for x{\min} and x{\max}, 8 bits for qbits, and 32 bits per dimension for the shape. 4. Total Bits: Sum the entropy cost and header overhead: \mathrm{bits} = H{\text{bits}} + \mathrm{header\bits} Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def estimatetensorbits(x, qbits=8): """ Estimate the bit cost for a single tensor x. Args: x: numpy-like array of floating point values. qbits: Number of bits for quantization (default 8). Returns: Total estimated bits for the tensor. """ # 1. Per-tensor Quantization xmin = min(x) xmax = max(x) L = 2 qbits # Avoid division by zero if all elements are identical if xmax == xmin: scale = 1.0 else: scale = (xmax - xmin) / (L - 1) # Map to integer levels and clamp # Note: In practice, this involves rounding and clamping quantizedlevels = [] for val in x.flat: q = round((val - xmin) / scale) q = max(0, min(L - 1, q)) quantizedlevels.append(q) N = len(quantizedlevels) # 2. Entropy Estimate # Compute histogram histogram = [0] L for q in quantizedlevels: histogram[q] += 1 # Calculate Shannon entropy Hbits = 0.0 for count in histogram: if count > 0: pi = count / N Hbits -= pi math.log2(pi) Hbits = N # 3. Per-tensor Header # d is the number of dimensions of the tensor d = x.ndim headerbits = 2 32 + 8 + 32 d # 4. Total Bits totalbits = Hbits + headerbits return totalbits def estimatenerfcodecpayload(tensors): """ Estimate total payload for NeRFCodec decoder parameters. Args: tensors: List of tensors (density and appearance codec parameters). Returns: Total estimated bits. """ totalbits = 0 for tensor in tensors: totalbits += estimatetensorbits(tensor) return totalbits qbits: Number of bits for quantization. Typically set to 8 in experiments. Zero Range: If x{\max} = x{\min}, the scale becomes zero. The pseudocode handles this by setting scale to 1.0, resulting in all values mapping to level 0. Empty Tensor: If N=0, the entropy calculation should return 0. Dimensionality: The header cost scales linearly with the number of dimensions d. High-dimensional tensors incur higher overhead. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of elements N for quantization and histogram computation. Entropy calculation is constant time with respect to N (depends on L=2^{qbits}). Memory Complexity: Linear in N for storing the tensor and histogram. Measured Performance: The raw decoder payload for NeRFCodec is roughly 24 MB (11.9 MB for density codec, 12.8 MB for appearance codec). After compression, this reduces to about 1.6 MB. Strengths: Provides a more realistic estimate of streaming payload than raw parameter size. Simple to implement. Limitations: Uses Shannon entropy bound, which assumes ideal entropy coding. Actual bitrates may vary depending on the specific entropy coder used. Does not account for encoder-side parameters, which are excluded from the budget. This estimation procedure is described in the context of evaluating NeRFCodec's efficiency for volumetric content delivery. The NeRFCodec framework integrates non-linear transform, quantization, and entropy coding for memory-efficient scene representation of plane-based hybrid NeRF. The estimation method is applied to decoder-side parameters to determine the bitrate budget required for transmission. The authors of NeRFCodec do not release their bitrate budget estimation code, so this procedure is used as a proxy. name: Space-time Neural Irradiance Fields
head: ST-NIF, Space-time Neural Irradiance Fields for Free-Viewpoint Video
body: Space-time Neural Irradiance Fields (ST-NIF) is a differentiable volume rendering method that represents a dynamic scene as a 4D implicit function mapping spatiotemporal coordinates (x,t) to color and volume density. It solves the problem of free-viewpoint video synthesis from a single moving camera by regularizing the inherently under-constrained geometry of dynamic scenes. Unlike static NeRF variants, ST-NIF introduces empty-space and static-scene losses to prevent haze-like artifacts and disocclusion errors, respectively. Inputs: A stream of Nf RGB-D images It: u \rightarrow (c, d) at discrete time steps t \in \mathcal{T} = \{1, \dots, Nf\}, where u=(u,v) are 2D pixel coordinates. Camera calibrations Pt for each frame. Near and far clipping planes sn and sf. Outputs: A neural network F that approximates the irradiance field: F: (x,t) \rightarrow (c, \sigma), where c is color and \sigma is volume density. Rendered RGB images for novel viewpoints and time steps. Neural Network: An MLP with the same architecture as the original NeRF, except the first 8 layers use 1024 activations instead of 256. Positional Encoding: Applied to spatial coordinates with 4 frequency bands. Time Normalization: Time t is normalized to the range [-1, 1]. Sample Pool: A set of 3D points \mathcal{X} derived from the union of sampling locations along all rays of all frames, excluding points closer than \epsilon to observed surfaces. Batch Size: Nr = 1024 rays randomly drawn from an input frame It without replacement. Empty-space margin: \epsilon = 0.05 \cdot (sf - sn). Loss Weights: \alpha, \beta, \gamma for depth, empty-space, and static losses respectively. Training Iterations: 800,000. A ray r at time t is determined by a pixel location u and camera calibration Pt. The ray is parameterized such that the parameter s denotes scene depth. This is achieved by setting the directional vector d such that its projection onto the principal ray has a unit norm in the camera space. 1. Hierarchical Sampling: Use hierarchical volume sampling as in the original NeRF to generate coarse and fine samples along each ray. 2. Static Scene Sample Pool Construction: Take the union of all sampling locations along all rays of all frames to form a sample pool \mathcal{X}. Exclude all points closer to any observed surfaces than threshold \epsilon. 3. Static Loss Sampling: Randomly draw a fixed number of sampling locations from \mathcal{X} at each training iteration. Add small random jitters to each sampling location. Randomly choose a time t' for each sample location x, ensuring (x, t') is not close to any scene surfaces. 4. Forward Pass: Query the network F for color and density at sampled points. 5. Volume Rendering: Compute rendered color \hat{C}(r,t) using numerical quadrature (Eq. 1). 6. Loss Computation: Calculate L{color}, L{depth}, L{empty}, and L{static}. 7. Optimization: Minimize total loss L. Volume Rendering: \hat{C}(r) = \int{sn}^{sf} T(s) \sigma(r(s)) c(r(s), d) ds T(s) = \exp \left( -\int{sn}^{s} \sigma(r(p)) dp \right) Color Reconstruction Loss: L{color} = \sum{(r,t) \in \mathcal{R}} \| \hat{C}(r,t) - C(r,t) \|^2 where \mathcal{R} is a batch of rays associated with time t, and C(r,t) is the ground truth color. Depth Reconstruction Loss: L{depth} = \sum{(r,t) \in \mathcal{R}} \left\| \frac{1}{\hat{D}(r,t)} - \frac{1}{D(r,t)} \right\|^2 where D(r,t) is the input depth, and \hat{D}(r,t) is the integrated sample depth: \hat{D}(r,t) = \int{sn}^{sf} T(s,t) \sigma(r(s),t) s \, ds Empty-Space Loss: L{empty} = \sum{(r,t) \in \mathcal{R}} \int{sn}^{dt(u) - \epsilon} \sigma(r(s),t) \, ds where dt(u) is the scene depth for pixel u at time t, and \epsilon = 0.05 \cdot (sf - sn). Static Scene Loss: Measured on the jittered samples from pool \mathcal{X} at random times t'. The specific formula is not provided in the sources, but it constrains spaces surrounding surface regions to handle disocclusions. Total Loss: L = L{color} + \alpha L{depth} + \beta L{empty} + \gamma L{static} Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainstnif(frames, cameras, sn, sf, numiterations=800000): """ frames: List of RGB-D images It with associated camera calibrations Pt. sn, sf: Near and far clipping distances. """ # Initialize MLP F with NeRF architecture (1024 units for first 8 layers) # Initialize positional encoder with 4 frequency bands # Normalize time to [-1, 1] # Precompute static sample pool X samplepool = [] for t in range(len(frames)): rays = generaterays(frames[t], cameras[t]) for r in rays: # Hierarchical sampling along ray r coarsesamples = hierarchicalsample(r, sn, sf) finesamples = hierarchicalsample(r, sn, sf) allsamples = coarsesamples + finesamples # Filter points closer than epsilon to observed surface depth = frames[t].depth for x in allsamples: if distancetosurface(x, depth, cameras[t]) > epsilon: samplepool.append(x) for iteration in range(numiterations): # 1. Sample Rays for Color/Depth/Empty Losses batchrays = randomsamplerays(frames, cameras, Nr=1024) totalloss = 0 lcolor = 0 ldepth = 0 lempty = 0 for r, t in batchrays: # Hierarchical sampling coarsepts, finepts = hierarchicalvolumesampling(r, sn, sf) # Query Network # Coarse pass ccoarse, sigmacoarse = querynetwork(coarsepts, t) # Fine pass cfine, sigmafine = querynetwork(finepts, t) # Volume Rendering crendered = volumerender(cfine, sigmafine, r) # Ground Truth cgt = frames[t].color[r.pixel] dgt = frames[t].depth[r.pixel] # Color Loss lcolor += normsq(crendered - cgt) # Depth Loss dpred = integratedepth(sigmafine, coarsepts, r) ldepth += normsq(1/dpred - 1/dgt) # Empty Space Loss # Integrate sigma from sn to dgt - epsilon emptysigma = integratesigmaupto(sigmafine, coarsepts, r, dgt - epsilon) lempty += emptysigma # 2. Sample for Static Loss staticsamples = randomsamplefrompool(samplepool, count=1024) lstatic = 0 for x in staticsamples: # Random time t' ensuring (x, t') is not close to surface tprime = randomtimenotnearsurface(x, frames, cameras, epsilon) sigmastatic, = querynetwork(x, tprime) # Static loss constrains spaces surrounding surface regions # Formula not explicitly given, but implies penalizing density in unconstrained regions lstatic += computestaticloss(sigmastatic, x, tprime) # Total Loss loss = lcolor + alpha ldepth + beta lempty + gamma lstatic # Backpropagate and update optimize(loss) Motion-Appearance Ambiguity: In dynamic scenes, a single video provides only one observation per time step, making geometry estimation severely under-constrained. Incorrect geometry leads to artifacts when deviating from the original camera trajectory. Haze-like Artifacts: Predicted depth is a weighted sum of depth values along the ray, leading to haze-like visual artifacts at novel views. Addressed by the empty-space loss. Disocclusion Artifacts: Unconstrained spaces hidden from input viewpoints are prone to artifacts when disoccluded due to viewpoint changes. Addressed by the static scene loss. Time Complexity: Training takes approximately 48 hours for a network with about 100 video frames. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles dynamic scenes from a single moving camera; produces geometrically correct novel view synthesis when combined with depth and empty-space constraints. Limitations: Relies on input depth maps; prone to artifacts in disoccluded regions if static loss is insufficient; computationally expensive training. When to use: Free-viewpoint video synthesis from a single moving camera with RGB-D input. When not to use: Static scenes (use standard NeRF); scenes with no depth information; real-time rendering (requires offline training). Origin: Proposed in "Space-time Neural Irradiance Fields for Free-Viewpoint Video". History: Builds on the original NeRF framework. Usage: Free-viewpoint video synthesis. name: LU-NeRF
head: LU-NeRF-1, Local Unposed NeRF, Locally Unlocalized NeRF
body: LU-NeRF is a method for few-shot local unposed NeRF that jointly estimates camera poses and scene representation from a small subset of images (mini-scene) without requiring accurate pose initialization or priors, specifically designed to handle mirror symmetry ambiguities. It employs a local-to-global learning framework that first optimizes overlapping mini-scenes using lightweight models and then synchronizes them into a global reference frame. Unlike BARF, LU-NeRF does not require coarse pose initialization close to the true poses and does not use positional encoding or view dependency, making it lighter and faster for rough local estimation. Inputs: A set of images from a scene. Outputs: Global camera poses and a global radiance field representation. Data Structures: Mini-scene: An overlapping subset of images, typically containing 3 to 5 images. LU-NeRF-1 Model: A lightweight NeRF model consisting of small Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs). Network Architecture: Small MLPs. Positional encoding is eliminated. View dependency is eliminated. Parameters: \theta represents the model parameters (weights of the MLPs) and camera poses. Camera Poses: Represented as relative parameters. One camera pose in the mini-scene is frozen to the identity matrix to resolve global translation/rotation ambiguity. All other poses are optimized as relative parameters. Ray Samples: R is a set of ray samples. Depth Rendering: d\theta(r) is the depth rendering function for a ray r. Steps: 1. Partitioning: Partition the scene into overlapping subsets of images called mini-scenes, typically containing three to five images. 2. Initialization: For each mini-scene, initialize all camera poses close to the identity matrix, leveraging the assumption that images in a mini-scene are spatially close. Freeze one camera pose in the mini-scene to the identity matrix. 3. Local Optimization: For each mini-scene, optimize the neural scene representation and camera poses jointly using the lightweight LU-NeRF-1 model. The optimization minimizes a loss function comprising the photometric \ell2 loss and a total variation regularization term on predicted depths. The total variation loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}{TV} = \frac{1}{|R|} \sum{r \in R} \sum{i,j=1}^{K} \left( \| d\theta(r{i,j}) - d\theta(r{i,j+1}) \|2^2 + \| d\theta(r{i,j}) - d\theta(r{i+1,j}) \|2^2 \right) where R is the set of ray samples, d\theta(r) is the depth rendering function for ray r, \theta are the model parameters and camera poses, K is the patch size, and (i, j) is the pixel index. Strong regularization is applied to the radiance field optimization. 4. Global Synchronization: Bring the poses of these mini-scenes into a global reference frame through a robust pose synchronization step. 5. Global Refinement: Perform fine-grained optimization of the global poses and scenes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lunerftraining(images): # Step 1: Partition scene into overlapping mini-scenes # Each mini-scene contains 3-5 images miniscenes = partitionintominiscenes(images, size=5) localposes = {} localmodels = {} # Step 2 & 3: Local Optimization for each mini-scene for miniscene in miniscenes: # Initialize poses close to identity poses = initializeposesidentity(miniscene) # Freeze one pose to identity to resolve ambiguity poses[0] = IdentityMatrix() # Initialize lightweight NeRF model (small MLPs, no positional encoding) model = initlightweightnerf() # Jointly optimize poses and scene representation # Loss = Photometric L2 + Total Variation of Depth for iteration in range(numiterations): rays = generaterays(miniscene, poses) colors, depths = model.forward(rays) # Photometric L2 loss lossphotometric = l2loss(colors, miniscene.images) # Total Variation loss on depth # K is patch size, (i,j) is pixel index losstv = 0 for r in rays: for i, j in range(K): dcurr = depths[r][i, j] dright = depths[r][i, j+1] ddown = depths[r][i+1, j] losstv += l2norm(dcurr - dright)2 + l2norm(dcurr - ddown)2 losstv = losstv / len(rays) totalloss = lossphotometric + losstv gradients = computegradients(totalloss, model.parameters, poses) updateparameters(model.parameters, poses, gradients) # Store results localposes[miniscene.id] = poses localmodels[miniscene.id] = model # Step 4: Global Synchronization globalposes = synchronizeposes(localposes) # Step 5: Global Refinement globalmodel = initglobalnerf() for iteration in range(numglobaliterations): rays = generaterays(images, globalposes) colors, = globalmodel.forward(rays) loss = l2loss(colors, images) gradients = computegradients(loss, globalmodel.parameters, globalposes) updateparameters(globalmodel.parameters, globalposes, gradients) return globalposes, globalmodel Parameters: Mini-scene size: Typically 3 to 5 images. Patch size (K): Used in the total variation loss calculation. Not given in the sources. Regularization: Strong regularization is applied, specifically photometric \ell2 loss and total variation of predicted depths. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Mirror Symmetry Ambiguity: Two distinct 3D scenes and camera configurations produce similar images under affine projection. The model must reconcile this ambiguity inherent in the local unposed setting. Initialization: The method relies on initializing poses close to the identity matrix, assuming images in a mini-scene are spatially close. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Experimental results show that LU-NeRF outperforms previous techniques on the tasks of camera pose estimation and new view synthesis. Evaluation on the LLFF dataset shows higher scores in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS metrics compared to methods like BARF. Scaling: The local-to-global framework allows handling large scenes by breaking them into manageable mini-scenes. Strengths: Does not require coarse pose initialization close to the true poses. Does not use positional encoding or view dependency, making it lighter and faster for rough local estimation. Succeeds even in the absence of a priori knowledge of the pose distribution. Limitations: Jointly optimizing camera poses and scene representation over a full scene is difficult and underconstrained. When to use: When accurate pose initialization is not available and computational resources are limited. When not to use: When high-precision global pose estimation is required without subsequent refinement steps. LU-NeRF was introduced in 2023. It addresses the challenges of few-shot novel view synthesis and optimizing unknown poses in a combined setting. The method builds on the idea of breaking up a large scene into mini-scenes to overcome the non-convexity of global pose optimization without accurate initialization. It is related to methods like BARF, which also optimizes camera poses but requires coarse initialization and uses positional encoding. name: Knowledge NeRF
body: Knowledge NeRF is a few-shot novel view synthesis method for dynamic articulated objects that reconstructs a current state S1 using sparse inputs (typically 5 images) by leveraging a pretrained NeRF model of a previous state S0 as a knowledge base. It differs from previous dynamic NeRF methods that learn deformation from monocular videos by considering two frames at a time: a frozen pretrained base and the current state, using a lightweight projection module to map points from the current state to the knowledge base. This approach achieves clarity comparable to NeRF trained with abundant images, avoiding the limited clarity often suffered by methods relying solely on monocular video deformation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A pretrained NeRF model representing the knowledge base state S0; 5 input images of the object in a new state S1; 3D positions X1 of points in S1 (derived from the 5 images via standard NeRF ray marching or depth estimation). Outputs: Color (r, g, b) and opacity (\sigma) for points in S1, enabling novel view synthesis for the dynamic state. Data Structures: 1. Pretrained NeRF (S0): A frozen neural network taking 3D position (x0, y0, z0) and viewing angles (\theta0, \phi0) as input, outputting color and density. This structure is not modified during the training of S1. 2. Projection Module (FP): A lightweight neural network composed of 4 fully connected layers. Input: 3D position vector X1 = (x1, y1, z1) from the current state S1. Output: 3D position vector X0 = (x0, y0, z0) in the knowledge base S0. Numbered Steps: 1. Knowledge Base Construction: Pretrain a standard NeRF model on a set of images of the articulated object in a specific initial pose S0. This model serves as the frozen knowledge base. 2. Data Acquisition: Capture 5 input images of the object in a new state S1. 3. Projection Module Training: Train the projection module FP end-to-end. The module is placed before the frozen NeRF. The training minimizes the Mean-Squared Error (MSE) loss between the projected point X0 = FP(X1) and the true corresponding point in S0 (if ground truth is available) or implicitly learns the correspondence through the reconstruction loss of the rendered images from S1 using the frozen NeRF. 4. Rendering Query: For a point X1 in the current state S1: a. Query FP to obtain the corresponding position X0 in S0: X0 = FP(X1). b. Assume viewing angles are approximately equal: (\theta1, \phi1) \approx (\theta0, \phi0), based on the assumption that most points are not reflective and look the same from all directions. c. Query the frozen pretrained NeRF with (X0, \theta0, \phi0) to retrieve color (r, g, b) and opacity (\sigma). Formulas: The projection function FP maps a point X1 in the current state to X0 in the knowledge base: X0 = FP(X1) = \begin{cases} X1, & \text{if } X1 \text{ is in a static part}, \\ T(X1), & \text{if } X1 \text{ is in a moving part}. \end{cases} Where T represents rotation, translation, scaling, or the introduction of new contents. Parameters: Input images per state: 5. Viewing angle assumption: (\theta1, \phi1) \approx (\theta0, \phi0). Projection Module Architecture: 4 fully connected layers. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Air Particles: Air particles in S1 may not have a correspondence to S0. However, this is handled because their transparency makes them irrelevant to the reconstruction. Reflective Surfaces: The assumption that viewing angles are equal (\theta1, \phi1) \approx (\theta0, \phi0) may fail for highly reflective surfaces, as the appearance would change significantly with viewing angle. New Contents: The introduction of new parts in S1 that were not present in S0 must be handled by the projection module T(X1), which implicitly learns these changes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class ProjectionModule(nn.Module): """ Lightweight projection module FP with 4 fully connected layers. Maps X1 (current state) to X0 (knowledge base state). """ def init(self, inputdim=3, outputdim=3): super(ProjectionModule, self).init() # 4 fully connected layers as per source self.fc1 = nn.Linear(inputdim, 64) self.fc2 = nn.Linear(64, 64) self.fc3 = nn.Linear(64, 64) self.fc4 = nn.Linear(64, outputdim) def forward(self, X1): # X1 shape: (N, 3) x = F.relu(self.fc1(X1)) x = F.relu(self.fc2(x)) x = F.relu(self.fc3(x)) X0 = self.fc4(x) return X0 class KnowledgeNeRF: def init(self, pretrainednerf, projectionmodule): """ pretrainednerf: Frozen NeRF model for state S0. projectionmodule: Trainable ProjectionModule FP. """ self.pretrainednerf = pretrainednerf self.pretrainednerf.eval() # Freeze self.projectionmodule = projectionmodule def query(self, X1, theta1, phi1): """ Query color and opacity for a point X1 in state S1. """ # Step 1: Project X1 to X0 in knowledge base S0 X0 = self.projectionmodule(X1) # Step 2: Assume viewing angles are approximately equal # assumes (theta1, phi1) approx (theta0, phi0) theta0 = theta1 phi0 = phi1 # Step 3: Query frozen pretrained NeRF with X0 and assumed angles # Note: Standard NeRF query usually takes (x, y, z, theta, phi) # The frozen NeRF outputs color (r, g, b) and density (sigma) with torch.nograd(): color, sigma = self.pretrainednerf(X0, theta0, phi0) return color, sigma def trainstep(self, imagesS1, raysS1, optimizer): """ Train the projection module using 5 images from state S1. """ optimizer.zerograd() # Render images from S1 using the projection module and frozen NeRF renderedimages = [] for ray in raysS1: X1 = ray.origin + ray.direction ray.t # Example ray marching color, sigma = self.query(X1, ray.theta, ray.phi) # Standard volume rendering integration would happen here # Assuming standard NeRF volume rendering integration renderedpixel = integratevolumerendering(color, sigma, ray.t) renderedimages.append(renderedpixel) renderedimages = torch.stack(renderedimages) # Compute MSE loss against ground truth images from S1 loss = F.mseloss(renderedimages, imagesS1) # Backpropagate only through projection module loss.backward() optimizer.step() return loss.item() The parent architecture that Knowledge NeRF builds upon, integrating hashed embeddings and other components. HybridNeRF Model Architecture A sibling method that also deals with dynamic scenes but focuses on relighting capabilities. Shading Replacement for Relighting A sibling method for underwater scenes, handling light absorption and scattering. SeaThru-NeRF A sibling method for panoramic view synthesis. Pano-NeRF A sibling method focusing on fast super-resolution for NeRFs. FastSR-NeRF A sibling method for compressing NeRF representations. NeRFCodec A sibling method that addresses depth ambiguity in NeRF training. Ambiguity-Aware Depth Estimates A sibling method for dynamic scenes with time-varying lighting. Space-time Neural Irradiance Fields A sibling method for interpolating between views. NeRF-based View Morphing A sibling method that uses information theory to improve NeRF training. InfoNeRF Time Complexity: Training is efficient as only the lightweight projection module (4 fully connected layers) is trained, while the main NeRF is frozen. Memory Complexity: Low memory overhead for the projection module. The frozen NeRF must be stored in memory, but no additional large structures are required. Measured Performance: Achieves clarity comparable to NeRF trained with abundant images using only 5 input images per state. Scaling: The method scales to dynamic articulated objects by considering two frames at a time (pretrained base + current state). Strengths: Few-shot capability (5 images), high clarity, efficient training (lightweight module), handles rigid motion and new contents. Limitations: Assumes viewing angles are approximately equal, which may not hold for reflective surfaces. Requires a pretrained NeRF for the initial state. When to use: When reconstructing dynamic articulated objects from sparse views, especially when a pretrained model of the object in a previous state is available. When not to use: When the object is highly reflective, or when no initial state is available to train the knowledge base. Knowledge NeRF was proposed by Wang et al. in 2024. It addresses the challenge of reconstructing dynamic 3D scenes from sparse views, which is difficult for previous dynamic NeRF methods that learn deformation from monocular videos and suffer from limited clarity. The method leverages the idea of considering two frames at a time: a pretrained knowledge base and the current state, to achieve high-quality novel view synthesis. The data and implementation are publicly available at https://github.com/RussRobin/KnowledgeNeRF. Knowledge NeRF: Few-shot Novel View Synthesis for Dynamic Articulated Objects, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2404.00674, fetched 2026-10-29

name: InfoNeRF
head: Ray Entropy Minimization for Few-Shot Neural Volume Rendering
body: InfoNeRF is an information-theoretic regularization technique for few-shot novel view synthesis that minimizes reconstruction inconsistency by imposing an entropy constraint on the density distribution along individual rays. It addresses two primary failures in few-shot neural rendering: noise and artifacts caused by insufficient viewpoints, and degenerate overfitting to seen views when training images are redundant. Unlike methods that rely on external data structures (voxels, meshes) or pretrained encoders, InfoNeRF is a generic plug-in regularizer that enforces scene compactness along rays and spatial smoothness across neighboring viewpoints without adding learnable parameters. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A neural implicit scene representation (e.g., an MLP mapping 3D coordinates and viewing directions to density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}), a set of training rays \mathcal{R}s from known viewpoints, and a set of unseen rays \mathcal{R}u sampled from random camera poses. Outputs: Optimized neural network parameters that minimize the total loss, producing rendered RGB images and depth maps for novel views. Data Structures Ray Samples: For each ray \mathbf{r}, a set of N 3D points \{\mathbf{r}1, \dots, \mathbf{r}N\} is sampled. Sample Attributes: Each sample i stores: \sigmai: Volume density (scalar). \deltai: Distance to the adjacent sample along the ray (scalar). \alphai: Opacity, computed as 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) (scalar). \mathbf{c}i: Emitted RGB color (vector of size 3). Ray Sets: \mathcal{R}s: Set of rays from training images (size |\mathcal{R}s|). \mathcal{R}u: Set of rays from randomly sampled unseen images (size |\mathcal{R}u|). Numbered Steps 1. Ray Sampling: For each ray \mathbf{r}, sample N points in a two-stage manner: first uniformly along the ray segment, then stratified according to the opacity distribution. 2. Network Query: Query the neural network at each sample point \mathbf{r}i to obtain density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i. 3. Compute Normalized Ray Density: Calculate the normalized density p(\mathbf{r}i) for each sample, which represents the probability mass of the i-th sample along the ray: p(\mathbf{r}i) = \frac{\alphai}{\sum{j=1}^{N} \alphaj} = \frac{1-\exp(-\sigmai \deltai)}{\sum{j=1}^{N} 1-\exp(-\sigmaj \deltaj)} where \alphai is the opacity of the i-th sample. 4. Compute Ray Mask: Determine if the ray hits any objects by calculating the cumulative ray density Q(\mathbf{r}): Q(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} 1-\exp(-\sigmai \deltai) Define the mask M(\mathbf{r}) using a threshold \epsilon (typically small, e.g., 10^{-5}, though exact value not specified in sources): M(\mathbf{r}) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } Q(\mathbf{r}) > \epsilon \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} This prevents entropy minimization on rays that do not intersect the scene. 5. Compute Ray Entropy: Calculate the Shannon entropy H(\mathbf{r}) for the ray's density distribution: H(\mathbf{r}) = -\sum{i=1}^{N} p(\mathbf{r}i) \log p(\mathbf{r}i). 6. Compute Ray Entropy Loss: Aggregate entropy over both seen and unseen rays, applying the mask to ignore non-hitting rays: \mathcal{L}{\text{entropy}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}s| + |\mathcal{R}u|} \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}s \cup \mathcal{R}u} M(\mathbf{r}) \cdot H(\mathbf{r}) where \cdot denotes element-wise multiplication (or scalar multiplication if M is scalar per ray). 7. Generate Neighboring Ray: For each ray \mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}s, generate a neighboring ray \tilde{\mathbf{r}} by slightly perturbing the camera pose of \mathbf{r} within a range of -5^\circ to 5^\circ. 8. Compute Information Gain Reduction Loss: Calculate the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the normalized density distributions of the original ray \mathbf{r} and its neighbor \tilde{\mathbf{r}}: \mathcal{L}{\text{KL}} = D{\text{KL}}(P(\mathbf{r}) || P(\tilde{\mathbf{r}})) = \sum{i=1}^{N} p(\mathbf{r}i) \log \frac{p(\mathbf{r}i)}{p(\tilde{\mathbf{r}}i)}. Note: p(\tilde{\mathbf{r}}i) is computed using the samples from \tilde{\mathbf{r}}. 9. Compute RGB Loss: Calculate the mean squared error between the rendered color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and the ground truth C(\mathbf{r}) for seen rays: \mathcal{L}{\text{RGB}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}s|} \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}s} \| C(\mathbf{r}) - \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) \|2^2. 10. Compute Total Loss: Combine the terms: \mathcal{L}{\text{total}} = \mathcal{L}{\text{RGB}} + \lambda1 \mathcal{L}{\text{entropy}} + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{\text{KL}}. 11. Optimization: Update the neural network parameters using gradient descent. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import math def computeraydensityprobabilities(sigma, delta): """ Computes normalized ray density probabilities p(ri). Args: sigma: Tensor of shape (N,), volume densities. delta: Tensor of shape (N,), distances between adjacent samples. Returns: p: Tensor of shape (N,), normalized probabilities. alpha: Tensor of shape (N,), opacities. """ # Opacity alphai = 1 - exp(-sigmai deltai) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma delta) # Sum of opacities for normalization sumalpha = torch.sum(alpha) # Avoid division by zero sumalpha = torch.clamp(sumalpha, min=1e-8) # Normalized probability p = alpha / sumalpha return p, alpha def computerayentropy(p): """ Computes Shannon entropy H(r) = - sum(p log(p)). Args: p: Tensor of shape (N,), probabilities. Returns: H: Scalar, entropy value. """ # Clamp p to avoid log(0) pclamped = torch.clamp(p, min=1e-8) H = -torch.sum(pclamped torch.log(pclamped)) return H def computekldivergence(pr, prtilde): """ Computes KL divergence DKL(P(r) || P(rtilde)). Args: pr: Tensor of shape (N,), probabilities for ray r. prtilde: Tensor of shape (N,), probabilities for neighbor ray rtilde. Returns: kl: Scalar, KL divergence value. """ # Clamp probabilities to avoid log(0) or div/0 prclamped = torch.clamp(pr, min=1e-8) prtildeclamped = torch.clamp(prtilde, min=1e-8) kl = torch.sum(prclamped torch.log(prclamped / prtildeclamped)) return kl def infonerfstep( network, rayss, # List of Ray objects for seen views raysu, # List of Ray objects for unseen views Nsamples, # Number of samples per ray lambda1, # Weight for entropy loss lambda2, # Weight for KL loss epsilon=1e-5 # Threshold for ray mask): """ Performs one training step for InfoNeRF. Args: network: Neural implicit model returning (sigma, color). rayss: List of Ray objects from training images. raysu: List of Ray objects from random unseen poses. Nsamples: Number of samples along each ray. lambda1: Balancing term for Lentropy. lambda2: Balancing term for LKL. epsilon: Threshold for cumulative density mask. Returns: totalloss: Scalar loss value. """ totalloss = 0.0 lrgb = 0.0 lentropy = 0.0 lkl = 0.0 # 1. Process Seen Rays (for RGB loss and KL loss) for ray in rayss: # Sample points along ray (two-stage: uniform then opacity-based) # Implementation detail: Standard NeRF sampling strategy points, delta = ray.sample(Nsamples) # Query network sigma, color = network(points, ray.direction) # Compute rendered color for RGB loss alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma delta) transmittance = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha + 1e-10, dim=0) # Ti # Standard volume rendering equation: sum Ti alphai ci renderedcolor = torch.sum(transmittance alpha color, dim=0) # RGB Loss gtcolor = ray.getgroundtruthcolor() lrgb += torch.mean((renderedcolor - gtcolor) 2) # Compute Probabilities for Entropy and KL p, = computeraydensityprobabilities(sigma, delta) # Ray Mask cumulativedensity = torch.sum(1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma delta)) mask = 1.0 if cumulativedensity > epsilon else 0.0 # Entropy Loss component H = computerayentropy(p) lentropy += mask H # KL Loss component (Information Gain Reduction) # Generate neighbor ray by perturbing camera pose (-5 to 5 degrees) neighborray = ray.perturbpose(anglerangedeg=5.0) # Sample neighbor ray pointstilde, deltatilde = neighborray.sample(Nsamples) sigmatilde, = network(pointstilde, neighborray.direction) ptilde, = computeraydensityprobabilities(sigmatilde, deltatilde) # KL Divergence kl = computekldivergence(p, ptilde) lkl += kl # 2. Process Unseen Rays (for Entropy Loss only) for ray in raysu: points, delta = ray.sample(Nsamples) sigma, = network(points, ray.direction) p, = computeraydensityprobabilities(sigma, delta) # Ray Mask cumulativedensity = torch.sum(1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma delta)) mask = 1.0 if cumulativedensity > epsilon else 0.0 # Entropy Loss component H = computerayentropy(p) lentropy += mask H # Normalize losses # Note: |Rs| and |Ru| are the counts of rays in the batches counts = len(rayss) countu = len(raysu) if counts > 0: lrgb = lrgb / counts lkl = lkl / counts if counts + countu > 0: lentropy = lentropy / (counts + countu) # Total Loss totalloss = lrgb + lambda1 lentropy + lambda2 lkl return totalloss Parameters N: Number of samples along a ray. Not given in the sources. \lambda1: Balancing term for \mathcal{L}{\text{entropy}}. Not given in the sources. \lambda2: Balancing term for \mathcal{L}{\text{KL}}. Decayed by a factor of 2 at every 5,000 iterations. Learning Rate: Initial value 5 \times 10^{-4}, decays exponentially by a factor of 10 at every 250,000 iterations. |\mathcal{R}s|: Number of rays from seen views. Set to 1024. |\mathcal{R}u|: Number of rays from unobserved views. Set to 1024. Pose Perturbation Range: -5^\circ to 5^\circ. \epsilon: Threshold for ray mask M(\mathbf{r}). Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Non-hitting Rays: Rays that do not intersect any objects in the scene can artificially drive entropy to zero if not masked, leading to artifacts. The mask M(\mathbf{r}) based on cumulative density Q(\mathbf{r}) prevents this. Overfitting to Redundant Views: If training images are from similar viewpoints, the model may overfit, causing degenerate solutions where slight viewpoint changes result in completely different renderings. The KL loss \mathcal{L}{\text{KL}} mitigates this by enforcing smoothness between neighboring rays. Noise in Few-Shot Settings: Insufficient viewpoints lead to noisy 3D depth estimation and rendering. The entropy minimization encourages sparsity, reducing noise. Time Complexity: The method adds negligible computational cost because \sigma and \delta are already computed for volume rendering. Ray entropy is 1D, avoiding the heavy cost of 3D volume entropy methods that require large numbers of samples to estimate occupancy maps. Memory Complexity: Does not require external data structures (voxels, meshes) or additional learnable parameters, avoiding memory bounds associated with explicit representations. Performance: Evaluated on Realistic Synthetic 360° (Lego, Materials, Ficus) in 4-view settings, DTU in 3-view settings, and ZJU-MoCap. Achieves improved PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FID, and KID metrics compared to baselines like PixelNeRF. Strengths: Generic applicability to various NeRF-based algorithms; no need for scene priors or pretrained encoders; effective for few-shot scenarios. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the underlying neural implicit representation; performance depends on the effectiveness of the regularization weights (\lambda1, \lambda2). InfoNeRF was introduced by Mijeong Kim, Seonguk Seo, and Bohyung Han from Seoul National University in 2022. It addresses the limitations of existing few-shot novel view synthesis methods, such as PixelNeRF [38] and class-specific methods [14, 24], which rely on features from seen images or semantic priors. InfoNeRF is distinct from explicit representation methods like octree sparsity [37] or voxel grid total variation [17] by being fully implicit and generic. It builds on the NeRF framework [21] and classical volume rendering theory [19]. InfoNeRF: Ray Entropy Minimization for Few-Shot Neural Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.01257, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Relighting and Shading
head: Irradiance Fields, Shading Replacement
body: Relighting and Shading techniques address the problem of lighting inconsistency when compositing objects into neural radiance field (NeRF) scenes or synthesizing novel views under varying illumination conditions. Unlike standard radiance field methods that treat radiance as a static view-dependent signal, this family explicitly models lighting interactions, inter-reflections, or shading correlations to enable physically plausible relighting and HDR synthesis. It sets itself apart from direct relighting methods by either replacing object shading based on scene correlations Shading Replacement for Relighting or integrating surface rendering principles into the volume rendering framework to model irradiance Pano-NeRF. The core mechanism involves decoupling or explicitly modeling the illumination component of the radiance field. In standard NeRF, radiance c(x, \mathbf{d}) is a direct output of the network. In this family, the representation is extended to account for how light interacts with geometry. 1. Irradiance-Radiance Coupling: Radiance is treated as both a signal conveying lighting information and a light source illuminating other pixels. This increases observation counts for geometry and leverages irradiance-radiance attenuation for High Dynamic Range (HDR) reconstruction. 2. Surface-Volume Integration: Methods may integrate surface rendering principles (BRDF, normals) into the volumetric framework. For instance, outgoing radiance Ci(x) is computed by integrating irradiance from incoming light directions \omegai over a sphere \Omega centered at x Pano-NeRF: Ci(x) = \int{\omegai \in \Omega} fr(x, \omegao, \omegai) \cdot \max(\omegai \cdot \mathbf{n}, 0) \cdot ci(x, \omegai) \, d\omegai where fr is the BRDF, \mathbf{n} is the surface normal, and ci(x, \omegai) is the incoming radiance computed via volume rendering Pano-NeRF. 3. Shading Correlation: In object insertion tasks, shading is inferred by correlating surface normals and shading values between the inserted object and the existing scene, avoiding explicit light source estimation Shading Replacement for Relighting. Shading Replacement for Relighting is a technique for object insertion that avoids inferring scene illumination by replacing the inserted object's shading with shading from existing scene points Shading Replacement for Relighting. It solves the problem of lighting inconsistency when compositing objects into NeRF scenes, where naive composition leads to unrealistic results due to varying illumination Shading Replacement for Relighting. It sets itself apart from direct relighting methods by not requiring explicit light source estimation, instead relying on the correlation between surface normals and shading in Lambertian scenes Shading Replacement for Relighting. Choose this method when inserting objects into a scene where the lighting environment is complex and unknown, but surface normals are available or estimable. Pano-NeRF is a method for geometry recovery and High Dynamic Range (HDR) novel view synthesis from sparse Low Dynamic Range (LDR) panoramic images Pano-NeRF. It models the scene using irradiance fields, which treat radiance as both a signal conveying lighting information and a light source illuminating other pixels, thereby increasing observation counts for geometry and leveraging irradiance-radiance attenuation for HDR reconstruction Pano-NeRF. It differs from standard radiance field methods by integrating surface rendering principles into the volume rendering framework to explicitly model inter-reflection and lighting interactions Pano-NeRF. Choose this method when working with sparse panoramic inputs and requiring HDR output or improved geometry recovery through inter-reflection modeling. CI-NeRF utilizes NeRF for volumetric rendering to deduce essential scene characteristics like diffuse albedo, surface normals, shadows, and lighting settings. It employs a CNN for forecasting interpretable and modifiable lighting parameters from an individual image. This allows for the physical interpretation of outdoor scene relighting through a unified image inference process, enhancing both the quality and realism of the relighting. The concept of integrating lighting and shading into neural radiance fields has evolved to address limitations in standard NeRF regarding physical plausibility and dynamic lighting. CI-NeRF (2023) was introduced to allow physical interpretation of outdoor scene relighting through a unified image inference process, surpassing current methods in inherent image breakdown and real-world landmark scene relighting. Pano-NeRF and Shading Replacement for Relighting further extend this by explicitly handling irradiance fields and shading correlations, respectively, to solve issues in sparse view synthesis and object compositing. These methods build on the foundational NeRF architecture but modify the query and rendering process to include lighting-aware representations. name: Shading Replacement for Relighting
head: Normal-Based Shading Transfer, Shading Replacement
body: Shading Replacement for Relighting is a technique for object insertion that avoids inferring scene illumination by replacing the inserted object's shading with shading from existing scene points. It solves the problem of lighting inconsistency when compositing objects into neural radiance field (NeRF) scenes, where naive composition leads to unrealistic results due to varying illumination. It sets itself apart from direct relighting methods by not requiring explicit light source estimation, instead relying on the correlation between surface normals and shading in Lambertian scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Object points O: List of tuples (\mathbf{p}o, \mathbf{n}o, So) representing positions, normals, and initial shading values. Scene points V: List of tuples (\mathbf{p}v, \mathbf{n}v, Sv) representing positions, normals, and shading values from the scene NeRF. Parameters: p (integer count of top-ranked pairs to select), \beta{avg,r} (average brightness of scene reflectance), \beta{o,avg,r} (average brightness of object reflectance). Output: Updated shading values S{updated} for each object point. Data Structures: Scene points V: List of tuples (\mathbf{p}v, \mathbf{n}v, Sv). Object points O: List of tuples (\mathbf{p}o, \mathbf{n}o, So). Candidate pairs: List of tuples containing a scene point and a scalar score. Steps: 1. Pair Formation: For each object point o \in O, find all scene points v \in V that share similar normal vectors to form candidate pairs (o, v). 2. Scoring: Rank candidate pairs for each object point based on a score combining normal similarity and distance. Solely relying on normal similarity results in global shading (too broad), while solely relying on distance fails to align with physical interpretations; combining both allows querying shading within a localized range. 3. Selection: Select the top p pairs for each object point based on the ranking. 4. Mean Shading Calculation: Compute the mean shading value S{mean} of the selected p scene points. This is preferred over maximum shading (which is not plausible) or normal-similarity-only shading (which is noisy). 5. Reflectance Compensation: Adjust the mean shading to account for differences in the average brightness of the object and scene reflectance. 6. Update: Assign the final updated shading S{updated} to the object point. Formulas: The updated shading S{updated} is calculated as: S{updated} = S{mean} \frac{\beta{avg,r}}{\beta{o,avg,r}} where S{mean} is the average shading of the top p selected scene points, \beta{avg,r} is the average brightness of the scene reflectance, and \beta{o,avg,r} is the average brightness of the object reflectance. Parameters: p: Integer count of top-ranked pairs to select. Typical value not given in the sources. \beta{avg,r}: Average brightness of scene reflectance. \beta{o,avg,r}: Average brightness of object reflectance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normal similarity only results in global shading, which is too broad and noisy. Distance only fails to align with physical interpretations of lighting. Maximum shading generates implausible results. Naive composition without lighting consistency leads to unrealistic results due to varying illumination. Direct composition can lead to missing areas of the object in rendered images. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def shadingreplacement(objectpoints, scenepoints, p, betaavgr, betaoavgr): """ objectpoints: list of dicts with keys 'pos', 'normal', 'shading' scenepoints: list of dicts with keys 'pos', 'normal', 'shading' p: int, number of top-ranked pairs to select betaavgr: float, average brightness of scene reflectance betaoavgr: float, average brightness of object reflectance Returns: list of updated shading values for object points """ updatedshadings = [] epsilon = 1e-8 for obj in objectpoints: candidates = [] for scene in scenepoints: # Normalize normals nobj = [x / math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in obj['normal'])) for x in obj['normal']] nscene = [x / math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in scene['normal'])) for x in scene['normal']] # Normal similarity (dot product) normalsim = sum(a b for a, b in zip(nobj, nscene)) # Euclidean distance dist = math.sqrt(sum((a - b)2 for a, b in zip(obj['pos'], scene['pos']))) # Distance score (inverse distance) distancescore = 1.0 / (dist + epsilon) # Score is the product of normal similarity and distance score score = normalsim distancescore candidates.append({'scene': scene, 'score': score}) # Rank pairs according to scores (descending) candidates.sort(key=lambda x: x['score'], reverse=True) # Select top p pairs toppcandidates = candidates[:p] # Compute mean shading of selected points if len(toppcandidates) > 0: smean = sum(c['scene']['shading'] for c in toppcandidates) / len(toppcandidates) else: # Fallback to original shading if no candidates found, as sources do not specify smean = obj['shading'] # Apply reflectance compensation supdated = smean (betaavgr / betaoavgr) updatedshadings.append(supdated) return updatedshadings Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Depends on the number of object points, scene points, and the efficiency of finding similar normals and distances. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storing scene points and their shading values. Strengths: Avoids inferring scene illumination; handles lighting variations between object and scene; produces plausible shading by averaging; works well for Lambertian scenes. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that points with similar normals have similar shading (Lambertian assumption); requires scene points to be available; performance depends on the density of scene points. When to use: When inserting objects into NeRF scenes and lighting consistency is crucial, but explicit light estimation is difficult or unavailable. When not to use: For non-Lambertian scenes where normal-shading correlation is weak; when high-frequency lighting details are critical and scene point density is low. Originated in the paper "Relighting Scenes With Object Insertions in Neural Radiance Fields". The method addresses the challenge of integrating objects into neural radiance field scenes with consistent lighting. It builds on the observation that for Lambertian scenes, surface normals are correlated with shading. The method is part of a larger pipeline that includes hybrid parametric lighting models (Spherical Harmonics and Spherical Gaussians) for scene representation. name: Pano-NeRF
head: irradiance fields
body: Pano-NeRF is a method for geometry recovery and High Dynamic Range (HDR) novel view synthesis from sparse Low Dynamic Range (LDR) panoramic images. It models the scene using irradiance fields, which treat radiance as both a signal conveying lighting information and a light source illuminating other pixels, thereby increasing observation counts for geometry and leveraging irradiance-radiance attenuation for HDR reconstruction. It differs from standard NeRF by integrating surface rendering principles into the volumetric framework to explicitly model inter-reflection, and it differs from sibling methods like Shading Replacement for Relighting by deriving shading through volumetric irradiance integration rather than explicit light source estimation or normal correlation [S1, 6346-shading-replacement-for-relighting.md]. Inputs: Sparse LDR panoramic images; initial scene geometry or implicit representation parameters. Outputs: HDR radiance field, geometry (density \sigma), and spatially varying lighting estimates. Data Structures: The method extends the standard NeRF representation. 1. Radiance Field: Standard MLP or grid-based representation outputting density \sigma(x) and outgoing radiance cr(x, \mathbf{d}) for a viewing direction \mathbf{d}. 2. Irradiance Field: Implicitly defined by the integration of incoming radiance over the sphere. No separate storage is required; it is computed on-the-fly during the shading step. Numbered Steps: 1. Scene Representation: Model the scene as a combination of volumetric particles (for standard NeRF rendering) and surface pieces with reflection effects. The scene is represented by an irradiance field integrated into the existing radiance field framework. 2. Incoming Radiance Calculation (ci): For a point x on a surface, consider incoming light directions \omegai distributed on a sphere \Omega centered at x. For each direction \omegai, calculate the incoming radiance ci(x, \omegai). This value is equal to the outgoing radiance Cr of the incident ray traveling in direction -\omegai, computed via standard volume rendering along that ray. Standard volume rendering formula for Cr: Cr = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigma(t) cr(t, \mathbf{d}) dt where T(t) = \exp(-\int{tn}^t \sigma(s) ds) is the transmittance. 3. Outgoing Radiance Calculation (Ci): Compute the outgoing radiance Ci(x) at position x through surface rendering by integrating irradiance from incoming light directions \omegai. The formula is: Ci(x) = \int{\omegai \in \Omega} fr(x, \omegao, \omegai) \cdot \max(\omegai \cdot \mathbf{n}, 0) \cdot ci(x, \omegai) \, d\omegai where: fr(x, \omegao, \omegai) is the Bidirectional Reflection Distribution Function (BRDF). \mathbf{n} is the surface normal at point x. \omegao is the outgoing viewing direction. \max(\omegai \cdot \mathbf{n}, 0) handles back-face culling, replacing the dot product \omegai \cdot \mathbf{n} when it is negative. 4. Joint Optimization: Integrate the irradiance fields into the existing radiance fields framework and perform joint optimization to recover geometry and HDR radiance. Although ci is not directly supervised, its integral is constrained through the training error between the observed ground-truth radiance C{gt} and the computed outgoing radiance Ci. This facilitates the optimization of density \sigma and radiance cr. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeoutgoingradiance(x, normal, viewdirection, brdf, nerfmodel): """ Computes outgoing radiance Ci(x) using irradiance field integration. Args: x: 3D position vector. normal: Surface normal vector n at x. viewdirection: Outgoing viewing direction omegao. brdf: Function fr(x, omegao, omegai). nerfmodel: The NeRF model capable of volume rendering. Returns: Ci: Scalar outgoing radiance. """ # Sample incoming directions omegai on the unit sphere Omega # In practice, this is approximated via Monte Carlo integration numsamples = 1024 # Typical value for Monte Carlo estimation omegaisamples = samplesphereuniform(numsamples) totalirradiance = 0.0 for omegai in omegaisamples: # 1. Calculate incoming radiance ci(x, omegai) # This is the radiance Cr of the incident ray traveling in direction -omegai # Computed via standard volume rendering along that ray rayorigin = x raydirection = -omegai # Perform volume rendering to get Cr # Standard NeRF volume rendering: # T(t) = exp(-integral(sigma)) # Cr = integral(T(t) sigma(t) cr(t, direction)) ci = nerfmodel.volumerender(rayorigin, raydirection) # 2. Calculate BRDF term # fr(x, omegao, omegai) fr = brdf(x, viewdirection, omegai) # 3. Calculate cosine term with back-face culling # max(omegai. n, 0) dotproduct = dot(omegai, normal) cosineterm = max(dotproduct, 0.0) # 4. Accumulate contribution # Integrand: fr max(omegai. n, 0) ci contribution = fr cosineterm ci # Monte Carlo integration: sum / N 4pi (if uniform sampling on sphere) # Or simply average if normalized weights are used totalirradiance += contribution # Average over samples Ci = totalirradiance / numsamples return Ci def trainingstep(panoimages, nerfmodel, brdf, geometryparams): """ Joint optimization step. """ # For each pixel in panoramic image: # 1. Cast ray to get x and normal n. # 2. Compute Ci(x) using computeoutgoingradiance. # 3. Compare Ci with ground truth Cgt from LDR image. # 4. Compute loss = ||Ci - Cgt||^2. # 5. Backpropagate to update nerfmodel (sigma, cr) and geometryparams. pass Parameters: Number of Monte Carlo samples: Not given in the sources. BRDF: Not specified; assumed to be a standard model (e.g., Lambertian or Phong). Sphere Sampling: Uniform distribution on \Omega. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Back-facing surfaces: The dot product \omegai \cdot \mathbf{n} can be negative for back-facing surfaces. This is handled by replacing \omegai \cdot \mathbf{n} with \max(\omegai \cdot \mathbf{n}, 0) in the implementation. Sparse Inputs: Sparse inputs bring a small number of observation counts, which might cause unconstrained geometry. The irradiance fields mitigate this by increasing observation counts through inter-reflection between irradiance and outgoing radiance. LDR to HDR: The method leverages irradiance-radiance attenuation to reconstruct HDR radiance from LDR inputs. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: The method requires additional volume rendering passes for each incoming direction \omegai during the shading step. If N samples are used for the sphere integration, the shading cost is O(N \cdot R), where R is the number of ray marching steps. This is significantly more expensive than standard NeRF which is O(R) per pixel. Memory: Memory usage is similar to standard NeRF, as the irradiance field is not stored explicitly but computed on-the-fly. Measured Performance: The method outperforms state-of-the-art methods on both geometry recovery and HDR reconstruction. It achieves faithful geometry recovery even with sparse inputs. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Increases observation counts for geometry recovery; leverages irradiance-radiance attenuation for HDR reconstruction; provides spatially varying lighting estimation as a byproduct. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to the integration over the sphere and multiple volume rendering passes; relies on sparse LDR inputs which may limit the quality of the initial geometry. When to Use: Use when reconstructing HDR novel views and geometry from sparse LDR panoramic images. Use when explicit light source estimation is not desired, but spatially varying lighting is needed. When Not to Use: Use standard NeRF if inputs are dense and HDR is not required. Use Shading Replacement for Relighting if the task is object insertion and shading correlation is sufficient. Pano-NeRF was proposed by Lu Zhan et al. in 2023. It addresses the problem of geometry recovery and HDR novel view synthesis from sparse LDR panoramic images. The method builds on the concept of irradiance fields, observing that radiance from each pixel in panoramic images can be modeled as both a signal to convey scene lighting information and a light source to illuminate other pixels. This approach increases observation counts for faithful geometry recovery and leverages irradiance-radiance attenuation for HDR reconstruction. The code is available at https://github.com/Lu-Zhan/Pano-NeRF. Pano-NeRF: Synthesizing High Dynamic Range Novel Views with Geometry from Sparse Low Dynamic Range Panoramic Images, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2312.15942, fetched 2026-10-29

name: NeRF-based View Morphing
head: VM-NeRF
body: NeRF-based View Morphing (VM-NeRF) is a data augmentation technique that synthesizes intermediate training views from sparse input camera pairs using geometric constraints and disparity-based warping. It addresses the challenge of sparse training data in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by generating photometrically consistent intermediate views, thereby improving reconstruction quality compared to semantic-based augmentation methods like DietNeRF. VM-NeRF generates a set of morphed views M = \{M{(k,k'),\alpha}\} from a pair of input views k and k' with a mixing parameter \alpha. The process consists of rectification, disparity computation, image morphing, and coalescence, followed by a training loop integration. Inputs: Two input views k and k', each consisting of an image I, a predicted depth map D, and a camera pose P (containing rotation R and translation t). Camera intrinsics include focal lengths fk, f{k'} and principal points ok, o{k'}. Outputs: A set of morphed images \hat{I}{k,\alpha} and \hat{I}{k',\alpha} which are fused into a single new training view. Camera Pose: P = [R, t], where R is a 3 \times 3 rotation matrix and t is a 3 \times 1 translation vector. Rectification Matrix: \tilde{R} = [ax, ay, az], a 3 \times 3 rotation matrix representing the common coplanar image plane. Disparity Map: E, a 2D array of the same spatial dimensions as the input image, storing disparity values. Baseline Direction: \tilde{\beta}k, a 3D vector. \gamma: Threshold for discarding camera pairs. Pairs with distance > \gamma are discarded to prevent morphing across invisible regions. Typical value: 6. \sigma: Standard deviation for the Gaussian distribution sampling \alpha. Chosen such that 3\sigma reaches the optic center positions. Typical value: 0.2. M: Number of new views regenerated every \eta iterations for each valid camera pair. Typical value: 1. \eta: Interval in training iterations after warm-up to regenerate VM-NeRF views. Typical value: 5. \lambda: Number of iterations NeRF warms up on known views before synthesizing VM-NeRF views. Typical value: 500. 1. Rectification: Rotate known camera poses Pk and P{k'} around their optical centers until their image planes become coplanar. Compute the common image plane rotation matrix \tilde{R} = [ax, ay, az] using a stereo rectification algorithm. Apply \tilde{R} to the original images \{Ik, I{k'}\} and depth maps \{Dk, D{k'}\} to generate rectified images \{\tilde{I}k, \tilde{I}{k'}\} and rectified depth maps \{\tilde{D}k, \tilde{D}{k'}\}. Pitfall: Conventional rectification assumes horizontal alignment. If the angle between az and the z-component of the original view poses Pk, P{k'} is greater than 45°, rotate the warping matrices and poses by 90° or 180° to mitigate rectification error. 2. Disparity Computation: Compute disparity maps Ek and E{k'} as functions of the rectified estimated depths. Compute the baseline direction \tilde{\beta}k: \tilde{\beta}k = az \times ((ok - o{k'}) \times az) where \times denotes the cross product. Compute disparity maps: Ek = \frac{fk}{\tilde{D}k} \frac{1}{\|\tilde{\beta}k\|} E{k'} = \frac{f{k'}}{\tilde{D}{k'}} \frac{1}{\|\tilde{\beta}k\|} where fk, f{k'} are focal lengths and \tilde{D}k, \tilde{D}{k'} are rectified depths. Image Morphing: Compute the position of each pixel on the morphed camera using warp functions to obtain \hat{I}{k,\alpha} and \hat{I}{k',\alpha}. Use the rectified depth maps \{\tilde{D}k, \tilde{D}{k'}\} to determine the distance of the points. 6. View Sampling: Randomly sample new views for training. Args: az: 3D vector, z-axis component of the coplanar plane rotation matrix. ok: 2D vector, principal point of camera k. okprime: 2D vector, principal point of camera k'. Limitations: Relies on accurate depth estimation; noisy depth in early training requires warm-up.
