name: Multi-scale PointNeRF++ Feature Aggregation
head: Hierarchical point cloud feature extraction, PointNeRF++ multi-scale approach
body: Multi-scale PointNeRF++ is a method for obtaining radiance (\rhoq) and density (\sigmaq) for a query point q by operating on a sparse, hierarchical point cloud representation at multiple granularity levels. It solves the problem of rendering in empty regions without relying on failure-prone region-growing heuristics. Unlike its sibling PointNeRF, this method naturally fills empty regions by averaging feature embeddings over valid scale levels where neighbors exist. It builds on NeRF Network Query with Hashed Embeddings by replacing hash grids with a multi-scale point cloud hierarchy. Inputs: Query point q \in \mathbb{R}^3. Hierarchical point cloud \{Ps\}{s=1}^{S}, where S=5 is the total number of scale levels. Feature maps \{Fs\}{s=1}^{S} associated with each scale level. Outputs: Radiance \rhoq \in \mathbb{R}^3 (color). Density \sigmaq \in \mathbb{R} (opacity). Point Cloud Hierarchy: The input is a set of 5 scale levels \{Ps\}. Global Scale (s=1): Represents the entire scene. Points are derived from a global voxel grid. Coarse Scales (s=2, 3): Intermediate granularity. Fine Scales (s=4, 5): Finest granularity, closest to the original point cloud density. Feature Storage: Features are stored differently depending on the scale level s: 1. Tri-plane Representation (Coarsest levels): Used for the global scale and the two largest (coarsest) remaining levels. Each point p at these levels is associated with three orthogonal feature planes: fp^{XY}, fp^{YZ}, fp^{XZ}. Resolution: Global scale: 512 \times 512 per plane. Coarsest two remaining levels: Each plane is a two-layer pyramid with 4 \times 4 and 2 \times 2 grids. Dimension: 32-dimensional feature vectors per plane. Query: Values are retrieved via bilinear interpolation at local coordinates. 2. Point Features (Finest levels): Used for the two finest scales. Each point p has a direct 32-dimensional feature vector fp. Decoder MLP (M): Density: One linear layer. Color: Four-layer MLP with 64 neurons per hidden layer. Feature Extraction MLP: Applied after tri-plane query or point feature retrieval. Architecture: Four-layer MLP with 64 neurons per hidden layer. \tau: Threshold ratio for neighborhood radius. The search radius at scale s is \tau Vs, where Vs is the voxel size at scale s. \epsilon: Small constant added to distance to avoid division by zero. Value not explicitly given in sources [G: typical value 10^{-6} or 10^{-8}]. Max Neighbors: 8 for ScanNet and NeRF Synthetic datasets. 6 for KITTI-360 dataset. Ray Sampling Points: 400 points per ray for ScanNet and NeRF Synthetic. 1,000 points per ray for KITTI-360. Positional Encodings: 5 frequencies augmented to global scale features. 1. Determine Valid Scale Levels: For a query point q and hierarchy \{Ps\}, identify the set of valid scale levels \mathcal{S}(q, \{Ps\}): \mathcal{S}(q, \{Ps\}) = \{ s \mid \mathcal{N}(q, Ps) \neq \emptyset \} where \mathcal{N}(q, Ps) is the set of neighbors at scale s. 2. Find Neighbors: For each scale s, find neighbors \mathcal{N}(q, Ps): \mathcal{N}(q, Ps) = \{ p \mid p \in Ps \land \|p - q\|2 \le \tau Vs \} Implementation note: Use voxel-grid-based approximate nearest neighbors to speed up search. Limit the number of neighbors to maxneighbors (8 or 6) to limit GPU memory. 3. Compute Feature Embedding per Scale: For each valid scale s \in \mathcal{S}(q, \{Ps\}), compute the feature embedding Es = \text{PointNeRF}{feature}(q | Ps, Fs): Es = \frac{\sum{p \in \mathcal{N}(q, Ps)} w(p, q) \cdot \text{MLP}{feature}(fp, up)}{\sum{p \in \mathcal{N}(q, Ps)} w(p, q)} where: w(p, q) = (\|p - q\|2 + \epsilon)^{-1}. up = (q - p) / (\tau Vs) is the local 3D coordinate relative to point p. \text{MLP}{feature}(fp, up) depends on the scale: If scale s uses Tri-planes: \text{MLP}{feature}(fp, up) = \text{MLP}{extract} \left( fp^{XY}[up] + fp^{YZ}[up] + fp^{XZ}[up] \right) where fp^{}[up] denotes querying the tri-plane at position up with bilinear interpolation, and \text{MLP}{extract} is the 4-layer, 64-neuron MLP. If scale s uses Point Features: \text{MLP}{feature}(fp, up) = \text{MLP}{extract} (fp) where fp is the 32-dim feature vector of point p. 4. Aggregate Features: Average the feature embeddings from all valid scales: E{avg} = \mathbb{E}{s \in \mathcal{S}(q, \{Ps\})} [ Es ] = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}(q, \{Ps\})|} \sum{s \in \mathcal{S}(q, \{Ps\})} Es 5. Decode Radiance and Density: Pass the aggregated feature E{avg} through the decoder MLP M: \rhoq, \sigmaq = M(E{avg}) \sigmaq is the output of the single linear layer. \rhoq is the output of the 4-layer, 64-neuron MLP. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def querypointnerfplusplus(q, hierarchy, params): """ Query radiance and density for point q using Multi-scale PointNeRF++. Args: q: Query point (3,) hierarchy: List of 5 scale levels. Each level s is a dict: {'points': list of (3,) points, 'features': list of features (either 32-dim vectors or tri-plane data), 'voxelsize': Vs} params: Dict containing tau, epsilon, maxneighbors, etc. Returns: rho: Radiance (3,) sigma: Density (scalar) """ tau = params['tau'] epsilon = params['epsilon'] maxneighbors = params['maxneighbors'] validscales = [] scaleembeddings = [] for s in range(len(hierarchy)): level = hierarchy[s] points = level['points'] features = level['features'] voxelsize = level['voxelsize'] istriplane = level['istriplane'] # True for coarsest 3 levels, False for finest 2 # Step 1 & 2: Find neighbors # Use voxel-grid-based approximate nearest neighbors in practice. # Here we simulate a ball query for clarity. neighbors = [] neighborfeatures = [] # Optimization: In implementation, use spatial hashing or voxel grid for O(1) lookup # rather than brute force O(N). for i, p in enumerate(points): distsq = sum((q[j] - p[j])2 for j in range(3)) dist = math.sqrt(distsq) radius = tau voxelsize if dist <= radius: neighbors.append(p) neighborfeatures.append(features[i]) if len(neighbors) >= maxneighbors: break if not neighbors: continue validscales.append(s) # Step 3: Compute feature embedding for this scale weightedsum = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # For 3D feature vector weighttotal = 0.0 for p, f in zip(neighbors, neighborfeatures): dist = math.sqrt(sum((q[j] - p[j])2 for j in range(3))) w = 1.0 / (dist + epsilon) # Compute local coordinate u = [(q[j] - p[j]) / (tau voxelsize) for j in range(3)] # Get feature value based on scale type if istriplane: # Tri-plane query: fp^XY[u] + fp^YZ[u] + fp^XZ[u] # Assuming f is structured as [XYdata, YZdata, XZdata] # Each data is a 2D grid or pyramid. # Bilinear interpolation is performed at u. # Note: u might be outside [0,1] depending on normalization. # Standard practice: clamp or handle boundaries. valxy = bilinearinterpolate(f['XY'], u[0], u[1]) valyz = bilinearinterpolate(f['YZ'], u[1], u[2]) valxz = bilinearinterpolate(f['XZ'], u[0], u[2]) triplanefeat = [valxy[j] + valyz[j] + valxz[j] for j in range(32)] # Apply 4-layer MLP with 64 neurons featmlpout = applymlp4x64(triplanefeat) else: # Point feature: direct 32-dim vector featmlpout = applymlp4x64(f) # Accumulate weighted sum for j in range(32): weightedsum[j] += w featmlpout[j] weighttotal += w if weighttotal > 0: avgfeat = [weightedsum[j] / weighttotal for j in range(32)] scaleembeddings.append(avgfeat) # Step 4: Aggregate features across valid scales if not scaleembeddings: # Fallback or error handling if no neighbors found at any scale #: Return zero or background color depending on context return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 0.0 avgscalefeat = [0.0] 32 numscales = len(scaleembeddings) for sfeat in scaleembeddings: for j in range(32): avgscalefeat[j] += sfeat[j] avgscalefeat = [x / numscales for x in avgscalefeat] # Augment with positional encodings if global scale is involved? # The source says "augment the features extracted from the global tri-plane # with positional encodings". This implies the augmentation happens # before the final averaging or during the global scale embedding calculation. # Re-reading: "augment the features extracted from the global tri-plane...". # This suggests the input to the MLP for the global scale includes PE. # However, the formula shows MLPfeature taking fp and u. # Let's assume the MLPfeature for the global scale internally handles PE # or the feature vector is concatenated with PE before the MLP. # Given the formula structure, we assume the MLPfeature output is the result. # If PE is separate, it would be concatenated to avgscalefeat before Decoder. # Source: "augment the features extracted from the global tri-plane with positional encodings...". # This likely means the input to the decoder or the feature embedding includes PE. # Let's stick to the formula: MLPdecoder takes the averaged feature. # If PE is needed, it's part of the feature representation. # For simplicity, we assume the 32-dim feature is sufficient as per the main formula, # and PE is an implementation detail of the global scale's MLPfeature or pre-processing. #: If PE is required, concatenate 5 frequencies of positional encoding to avgscalefeat. # Step 5: Decode # Density: Linear layer sigma = linearlayerdensity(avgscalefeat) # Color: 4-layer MLP with 64 neurons rho = mlpcolor(avgscalefeat) return rho, sigma def bilinearinterpolate(grid, u, v): """ Simple bilinear interpolation for a 2D grid. Assumes grid is normalized to [0,1]x[0,1]. """ # Clamp u, v to [0,1] u = max(0.0, min(1.0, u)) v = max(0.0, min(1.0, v)) # Get grid dimensions H, W, C = grid.shape # Map u, v to indices uidx = u (W - 1) vidx = v (H - 1) x0 = int(math.floor(uidx)) y0 = int(math.floor(vidx)) x1 = min(x0 + 1, W - 1) y1 = min(y0 + 1, H - 1) dx = uidx - x0 dy = vidx - y0 # Interpolate val00 = grid[y0, x0] val01 = grid[y0, x1] val10 = grid[y1, x0] val11 = grid[y1, x1] res = (1 - dx) (1 - dy) val00 + \ (1 - dx) dy val01 + \ dx (1 - dy) val10 + \ dx dy val11 return res def applymlp4x64(inputfeat): """ 4-layer MLP with 64 neurons. Input: 32-dim Hidden 1: 64 Hidden 2: 64 Hidden 3: 64 Output: 64 """ #: Standard ReLU activations assumed for hidden layers h1 = relu(linear(inputfeat, 32, 64)) h2 = relu(linear(h1, 64, 64)) h3 = relu(linear(h2, 64, 64)) return linear(h3, 64, 64) def linearlayerdensity(inputfeat): """ Single linear layer for density. """ return linear(inputfeat, 64, 1) def mlpcolor(inputfeat): """ 4-layer MLP with 64 neurons for color. Input: 64-dim (from feature extraction MLP) Hidden 1: 64 Hidden 2: 64 Hidden 3: 64 Output: 3 (RGB) """ h1 = relu(linear(inputfeat, 64, 64)) h2 = relu(linear(h1, 64, 64)) h3 = relu(linear(h2, 64, 64)) return linear(h3, 64, 3) def relu(x): return max(0.0, x) def linear(x, indim, outdim): #: Placeholder for actual weight matrix multiplication # In a real implementation, this would be a matrix multiply. # Here we assume a simplified linear transformation. # Since we cannot define weights, we return a dummy value for structure. # This function must be implemented with actual weights in the model. pass Empty Regions: If no neighbors are found at any scale, the query returns no valid embedding. The method avoids region-growing heuristics by relying on the multi-scale hierarchy to naturally fill gaps. If a query point is completely isolated, the result is undefined by this method alone [G: typically handled by background or fallback]. Numerical Stability: The weight calculation w(p, q) = (\|p - q\|2 + \epsilon)^{-1} requires \epsilon > 0 to prevent division by zero when p=q. Per-Point Weights: The original PointNeRF used per-point weights, but these were experimentally found to not improve rendering quality and are omitted in PointNeRF++. Bounding Box: For points outside the bounding box of the point cloud, the contraction function from [2] is used. Sky Modeling: For outdoor scenes like KITTI-360, a separate four-layer MLP mapping ray direction to color is used to model the sky, separate from the point cloud query. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of neighbors and scales. Neighborhood search is accelerated using voxel-grid-based approximate nearest neighbors. The number of neighbors is capped (6 or 8) to limit computation. Memory Complexity: Determined by the storage of tri-planes and point features. Tri-planes are 512 \times 512 for the global scale and pyramids for coarser levels, with 32-dim features. Performance: Trained on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU for 200k iterations. Strengths: Naturally fills empty regions without region-growing heuristics. Tri-plane representation at coarse levels increases representation power without excessive computational cost. Effective for large scenes (e.g., KITTI-360). Limitations: Requires a hierarchical point cloud input. Performance depends on the quality of the initial point cloud. When to Use: Suitable for novel view synthesis from sparse point clouds, especially in large outdoor scenes where empty regions are common. When Not to Use: If high-density point clouds are available and empty regions are not a concern, simpler methods like standard PointNeRF might suffice. Origin: PointNeRF++ was introduced in the paper "PointNeRF++: A Multi-scale, Point-Based Neural Radiance Field". Development: It extends PointNeRF [53] by introducing a multi-scale hierarchy and tri-plane features at coarse levels. Usage: Evaluated on ScanNet, NeRF Synthetic, and KITTI-360 datasets. It is used for novel view synthesis in both indoor and outdoor settings. name: FourieRF
head: FourieRF: Few-Shot NeRFs via Progressive Fourier Frequency Control, Fourier Parameterization for Few-Shot NeRFs
body: FourieRF is a few-shot Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) estimation method that prevents high-frequency artifacts and catastrophic overfitting by parameterizing grid-based features with a Fourier Transform prior. Unlike sibling methods that rely on external data priors or complex occlusion regularization, FourieRF uses an explicit curriculum training procedure to progressively increase the maximum learnable Fourier frequency, ensuring stable convergence on sparse data. It builds on NeRF Network Query with Hashed Embeddings by applying frequency control to the feature grids of grid-based NeRFs (specifically TensoRF) rather than MLP positional encodings. Inputs: A set of V sparse input images (typically 3–9 views) with known camera poses; a grid-based NeRF representation (CP or VM decomposition) initialized with feature tensors. Outputs: A trained radiance field model capable of novel view synthesis. Data Structures: The scene is represented by a 3D feature tensor \mathbf{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{I \times J \times K}. FourieRF operates on the factorized components of this tensor. 1. CP Decomposition: \mathbf{T} is decomposed into a sum of rank-1 tensors. The method applies frequency control to the 1D feature vectors \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^d. 2. VM Decomposition: \mathbf{T} is decomposed into a sum of outer products of a vector and a matrix (e.g., \mathbf{v}{r1} \circ \mathbf{M}{r2,3}). The method applies frequency control to: 1D feature vectors \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^d. 2D feature matrices \mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^{d1 \times d2}. Parameters: N: Total number of training iterations (typically 10,000). f0: Initial clipping threshold, representing the percentage of Fourier coefficients allowed. Default: 0.01\% (0.0001) for real scenes, 0.3\% for synthetic scenes. \Delta: Increment per iteration, calculated as \Delta = \frac{1 - f0}{N}. ft: Clipping threshold at iteration t. Optimizer: AdamW with \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.98. Weight Decay: 0.2 for synthetic scenes, 0 for real scenes. w{TV}: Total Variation loss weight for appearance and density features. Value: 1.0. w{L1}: L1 loss weight for density features (real scenes only). Value: 10^{-4}. Algorithm: The core mechanism is a progressive Fourier frequency control loop applied at the start of every training iteration, before gradient accumulation. 1. Initialization: Initialize feature vectors and matrices in the spatial domain. Set f0 and calculate \Delta. 2. Threshold Update: At the start of iteration t, update the clipping threshold: ft = f{t-1} + \Delta This update must occur before any gradients are computed to maintain differentiability. 3. Feature Transformation: For each feature component in the grid decomposition, apply the Fourier clipping: 1D Features (\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^d): Compute the mask \alpha(ft) of length df (dimension of FFT). The mask is defined as: \alphai(ft) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } i < t\alpha(ft) \\ t\alpha(ft) - \lfloor t\alpha(ft) \rfloor & \text{if } i = t\alpha(ft) \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where t\alpha(ft) = df \times ft. Transform the feature: \hat{\mathbf{v}} = \text{IFFT}(\text{FFT}(\mathbf{v}) \odot \alpha(ft)) 2D Features (\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^{d1 \times d2}): (Used only in VM decomposition) Compute the circular mask \beta(ft). The mask is a circle centered at c = (\lfloor d1/2 \rfloor, \lfloor d2/2 \rfloor) with radius r = ft \sqrt{\frac{\max(d1, d2)^2}{2}}. Coefficients outside the circle are set to 0. Transform the feature: \hat{\mathbf{w}} = \text{IFFT}(\text{FFT}(\mathbf{w}) \odot \beta(ft)) 4. Network Forward Pass: Use the smoothed features \hat{\mathbf{v}} and \hat{\mathbf{w}} to query the NeRF network for density and color. 5. Loss Computation: Compute the photometric loss (L2 or L1) between rendered and input images. Add regularization losses: Total Variation loss on features with weight w{TV} = 1.0. L1 loss on density features (w{L1} = 10^{-4}) for real scenes. Weight decay (synthetic scenes) or L1 density loss (real scenes) to remove floaters. 6. Backward Pass: Compute gradients and update parameters using AdamW. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def fourierfstep(features1d, features2d, iteration, totaliterations, f0): """ Applies Fourier frequency control to NeRF grid features. Args: features1d: List of 1D feature tensors [v] in R^d. features2d: List of 2D feature tensors [w] in R^(d1d2). iteration: Current training iteration t. totaliterations: Total number of iterations N. f0: Initial clipping threshold percentage (e.g., 0.0001 for 0.01%). Returns: Smoothed features1d, features2d. """ # 1. Update clipping threshold # Delta is the linear increment per iteration delta = (1.0 - f0) / totaliterations ft = f0 + iteration delta # 2. Process 1D Features smoothed1d = [] for v in features1d: # FFT along the feature dimension (last dim) vfft = torch.fft.fft(v, dim=-1) # Create 1D mask alpha(ft) df = vfft.shape[-1] talpha = df ft # Create indices array indices = torch.arange(df, device=v.device) # Apply mask definition: 1 if i < talpha, fractional if i == talpha, 0 otherwise mask = torch.zeroslike(vfft.real) mask[indices < talpha] = 1.0 mask[indices == talpha] = talpha - torch.floor(talpha) # Apply mask and IFFT vsmoothedfft = vfft mask.unsqueeze(-1) # Ensure broadcasting works if mask is 1D vsmoothed = torch.fft.ifft(vsmoothedfft, dim=-1).real smoothed1d.append(vsmoothed) # 3. Process 2D Features (VM decomposition only) smoothed2d = [] for w in features2d: # FFT along spatial feature dimensions (last two dims) wfft = torch.fft.fft2(w) d1, d2 = w.shape[-2], w.shape[-1] centerc1 = torch.floor(d1 / 2).to(w.device) centerc2 = torch.floor(d2 / 2).to(w.device) # Create coordinate grids for the frequency domain y, x = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(d1, device=w.device), torch.arange(d2, device=w.device), indexing='ij') # Calculate distance from center dist = torch.sqrt((x - centerc1)2 + (y - centerc2)2) # Radius r = ft sqrt(max(d1, d2)^2 / 2) maxdim = max(d1, d2) radius = ft torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(maxdim2 / 2.0, device=w.device)) # Create 2D mask beta(ft): 1 inside circle, 0 outside mask2d = (dist <= radius).float() # Apply mask and IFFT wsmoothedfft = wfft mask2d.unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1) wsmoothed = torch.fft.ifft2(wsmoothedfft).real smoothed2d.append(wsmoothed) return smoothed1d, smoothed2d def trainfourierf(inputimages, cameraposes, gridfeatures, optimizer, totaliterations=10000, f0=0.0001): """ Main training loop for FourieRF. """ features1d, features2d = gridfeatures # Unpack CP/VM components for t in range(totaliterations): # Step 1: Update features with Fourier control BEFORE gradient computation features1d, features2d = fourierfstep(features1d, features2d, t, totaliterations, f0) # Step 2: Forward pass through NeRF using smoothed features # (Assuming a standard NeRF query function that takes feature tensors) # This step depends on the specific grid-based NeRF implementation (e.g., TensoRF) renderedcolors, densities = querynerf(features1d, features2d, cameraposes, inputimages) # Step 3: Compute Loss # Photometric loss (e.g., L2) photometricloss = F.mseloss(renderedcolors, inputimages) # Regularization tvloss = computetotalvariationloss(features1d + features2d) tvloss = tvloss 1.0 # wTV = 1.0 l1densityloss = torch.tensor(0.0) # Apply L1 on density for real scenes (not synthetic) # This check depends on dataset type, assumed handled externally or via flag # l1densityloss = F.l1loss(densities, target) 1e-4 totalloss = photometricloss + tvloss + l1densityloss # Step 4: Backward pass optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() # Step 5: Optimizer step (AdamW) optimizer.step() # Note: Weight decay is handled by the optimizer configuration (0.2 for synthetic, 0 for real) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Differentiability: The threshold update ft must be applied at the start of the iteration, before any gradient is accumulated. Applying it during the backward pass or after gradient computation breaks differentiability. Overfitting to Views: In few-shot settings, models may overfit to directional information. FourieRF mitigates this by using a simplified decoder that does not use positional encodings for features or view directions. Occlusion: In real scenes, matter appearing in front of the camera can cause overfitting. FourieRF applies FreeNeRF's occlusion regularization without modification. Under-constrained Scenes: In severely under-constrained scenarios with significant view occlusion, FourieRF may still produce reconstruction errors. Synthetic vs. Real Scenes: Synthetic scenes (white background) require a higher initial f0 (0.3\%) compared to real scenes (0.01\%). Synthetic scenes use weight decay (0.2) for floater removal, while real scenes use L1 density loss (10^{-4}). Time Complexity: Training time is approximately 10 minutes for convergence on the Blender dataset (6 views, 10k iterations). Speed Comparison: FourieRF achieves 0.93\times the training time of TensoRF, 5.181\times faster than ZeroRF, and 35.71\times faster than FreeNeRF on the Blender dataset. It is slightly faster than vanilla TensoRF because it does not predict "useless" floaters. Memory Complexity: Inherits the memory complexity of the underlying grid decomposition (CP or VM). VM decomposition reduces space complexity from O(n^3) to O(n^2) compared to CP. Strengths: Fast convergence, robust on both synthetic and real scenes, no computational overhead per iteration, avoids complex occlusion regularization required by FreeNeRF. Limitations: May fail in severely under-constrained scenarios with heavy occlusion. Performance depends on the choice of \Delta (increment speed), though the linear schedule is generally robust. When to use: Few-shot novel view synthesis (3–9 views) where training speed is critical and external data priors (depth, diffusion) are unavailable. When not to use: Dense-view settings where standard NeRFs perform adequately, or scenarios with severe unobserved geometry where even frequency control cannot resolve ambiguities. FourieRF was introduced by Diego Gomez, Bingchen Gong, and Maks Ovsjanikov from LIX, École Polytechnique, IP Paris, in February 2025. The method addresses the "few-shot rendering problem," where high-frequency artifacts and catastrophic overfitting occur early in optimization due to sparse supervision. It builds upon TensoRF and compares against baselines like FreeNeRF and ZeroRF. The approach is inspired by the observation that low frequencies are easier to learn correctly and provide a robust base for subsequent higher frequencies. name: Appearance Matching
head: Block-NeRF Appearance Consistency, NeRF Analogy Training
body: Appearance matching is a post-training optimization procedure used in multi-block neural radiance field frameworks to ensure visual consistency across block boundaries. It solves the problem of appearance discontinuities that arise when independent Block-NeRFs are trained with randomly initialized appearance latent codes, which yield different colors for the same semantic code in adjacent blocks. It sets itself apart from standard training by freezing network weights and optimizing only latent codes or specific appearance parameters, whereas siblings like HybridNeRF Model Architecture or VoxNeRF integrate appearance handling into the primary forward pass without separate consistency post-processing. The method operates in two distinct contexts: global consistency for Block-NeRFs and example-based transfer for NeRF Analogies. Inputs: Two adjacent Block-NeRFs: a Target Block-NeRF (with a fixed, desired appearance) and an Adjacent Block-NeRF (with inconsistent appearance). A 3D matching location p in world coordinates. The appearance latent code c{target} of the Target Block-NeRF. The appearance latent code c{adj} of the Adjacent Block-NeRF. Data Structures: Block-NeRF Network: A neural network f\theta parameterized by \theta. Inputs: position x, viewing direction v, and appearance code c. Outputs: radiance r and density \sigma. Visibility Predictor: A function V(x) estimating the probability that a point x is visible and within the bounds of a specific Block-NeRF. Steps: 1. Select Matching Location: Identify a 3D point p located between the Target and Adjacent blocks. The selection criterion is that the visibility prediction V{target}(p) and V{adj}(p) must both be high for their respective blocks. 2. Freeze Weights: Freeze the network weights \theta{target} and \theta{adj} of both Block-NeRFs. Only the appearance latent code c{adj} is treated as an optimization variable. 3. Render Target Appearance: Compute the target radiance r{target} using the fixed code: r{target} = f{\theta{target}}(p, v, c{target}) where v is the viewing direction at p. 4. Render Adjacent Appearance: Compute the current radiance of the adjacent block: r{adj} = f{\theta{adj}}(p, v, c{adj}) 5. Optimize: Minimize the difference between r{adj} and r{target} by updating c{adj}. The loss function is typically the L1 or L2 norm of the radiance difference: \mathcal{L} = \| r{adj} - r{target} \|1 Gradient descent updates c{adj} until the appearance in the Adjacent block matches the Target block at location p. Inputs: Target 3D positions P{target}. Target surface normals N{target}. Target viewing directions V{target}. Source appearance mapping function \phi. Source appearances A{source} and source viewing directions V{source} derived from semantic correspondences. Data Structures: Target NeRF Network: A network f\theta taking inputs (x, n, v), where n is the surface normal. Outputs radiance r. Mapping Function \phi: Maps source appearance and viewing direction to the target domain. Steps: 1. Query Target Network: Input the target position pi, normal ni, and viewing direction vi into the target NeRF network to get predicted radiance r{pred}: r{pred} = f\theta(pi, ni, vi) Note: The density is assumed to be a Dirac delta distribution (surface), so volume rendering is skipped; the network outputs radiance directly at the surface point. 2. Compute Source Appearance: Apply the mapping function to the source appearance and viewing direction to get the target appearance r{source}: r{source} = \phi(A{source}, V{source}) 3. Calculate Loss: Compute the L1 loss between the predicted radiance and the mapped source appearance, averaged over all target indices i: \mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}{i} \left[ \| f\theta(pi, ni, vi) - \phi(A{source}, V{source}) \|1 \right] 4. Optimize: Update network parameters \theta to minimize \mathcal{L}. Parameters: Surface Normals: Added to the network input for NeRF Analogy to provide a high-frequency signal for recovering high-frequency color changes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Random Initialization: Without appearance matching, randomly initialized appearance codes lead to different appearances in different blocks, causing visible inconsistencies during compositing. Visibility: The matching location must have high visibility in both blocks; otherwise, the optimization may fail or produce artifacts due to occlusion or out-of-bounds queries. Dirac Delta Assumption: NeRF Analogy assumes the target density is a Dirac delta distribution. If the target is a volumetric field rather than a surface, the direct radiance query may not be valid without volume rendering integration. A method to train a target NeRF's appearance parameters such that the target's radiance matches the source's appearance under the source viewing direction, using semantic correspondences. It differs from Block-NeRF matching by using semantic mappings and surface normals rather than latent code optimization between adjacent blocks. It is chosen when transferring visual attributes (e.g., season, style) from a source image to a target NeRF. It assumes the target density is a Dirac delta distribution (surface), so no volume rendering is required. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of optimization steps and the number of matching points. For Block-NeRF, it is O(N{steps} \cdot N{points} \cdot D{network}), where D{network} is the cost of a forward pass. Since weights are frozen, gradients do not flow through the entire network depth for the base features, only through the appearance embedding layer or final output layer depending on implementation. Memory Complexity: Low. Only the appearance latent codes or network parameters need to be stored in the optimizer's state. No additional large data structures are required. Strengths: Ensures seamless compositing of large scenes split into blocks; enables style transfer without retraining the entire geometry. Limitations: Requires high visibility at matching locations; NeRF Analogy requires accurate semantic correspondences and surface normals. When to use: When compositing multiple Block-NeRFs or when transferring appearance attributes from a source image to a target NeRF. When not to use: When real-time rendering is required without pre-computation, or when the scene is a single monolithic Block-NeRF. Block-NeRF appearance matching was introduced in "Block-NeRF: Scalable Large Scene Neural View Synthesis" (CVPR 2022) to address scalability issues in large scenes by splitting them into blocks, which inadvertently caused appearance inconsistencies. NeRF Analogy Training was introduced in "NeRF Analogies: Example-Based Visual Attribute Transfer for NeRFs" (CVPR 2024) to enable example-based visual attribute transfer using semantic correspondences. name: Hash-grid anti-aliasing and regularization
head: Hash-grid regularization, Hash-grid anti-aliasing
body: This family encompasses techniques that modify the hash-grid encoding mechanism in neural radiance fields to mitigate artifacts such as high-frequency aliasing and sparse-view floaters. It differs from standard hash-grid encoding by introducing either capacity constraints (smaller hash tables) to enforce feature sharing and geometric consistency, or statistical down-weighting factors to suppress high-frequency noise during rendering. The core mechanism relies on the multi-resolution hash grid encoding where a 3D query point \mathbf{x} is mapped to feature vectors via hash table lookups and trilinear interpolation. The shared principles across this family involve altering the standard query process to improve generalization or visual quality: 1. Capacity Reduction for Regularization: Reducing the hash table size T forces feature sharing across distinct 3D points. This prevents the decoding MLP from learning discontinuities in volume density that manifest as floaters or incorrect object placement, particularly in sparse input scenarios. 2. Domain Constraints: Constraining the sampling domain (e.g., s \in [s{near}, 1] instead of s \in [0, 1]) ensures that the regularized model does not learn geometry arbitrarily close to the camera, which is a common failure mode in unbounded scenes. 3. Statistical Down-Weighting: Applying a multiplicative factor \Delta\ell to the interpolated features at hash-grid level \ell to approximate the integration of texture over the pixel footprint, thereby suppressing aliasing artifacts. Simple-ZipNeRF is a regularized variant of ZipNeRF designed to mitigate floater artifacts in sparse input scenarios by introducing an auxiliary "augmented" model with reduced capacity [7424-simple-zipnerf]. It differs from standard ZipNeRF by training a smaller hash-table model in parallel to provide depth priors that regularize the main model, whereas siblings like HybridNeRF or VoxNeRF use different architectural constraints or multi-resolution grids without this specific dual-model depth regularization mechanism [7424-simple-zipnerf]. Instant-NGP is a method that accelerates neural radiance field training and rendering by replacing positional encoding with a multiresolution hash grid encoding [13315-instant-ngp]. It offloads the representational burden from a deep multi-layer perceptron (MLP) to efficient hash-table lookups and trilinear interpolation, achieving training speeds three orders of magnitude faster than vanilla NeRF [13315-instant-ngp]. Definition: An augmented version of ZipNeRF designed to prevent overfitting and distortions (floaters, incorrect object placement) when trained with sparse input views by reducing hash table size and constraining the sampling domain. Steps: 1. Reduce the size of the hash table from T to T^s < T to encourage feature sharing across more 3D points, preventing the MLP N1 from learning discontinuities in volume density. 2. Sample 3D points pi along the ray in the s-domain in the range s \in [s{near}, 1] instead of s \in [0, 1] to ensure objects are placed at least at a certain distance away from the camera. 3. Use the depth estimates from the augmented model to supervise the main model. Pitfalls: Reducing the hash table size allows ZipNeRF to avoid collisions and map nearby points to independent entries, enabling the MLP to learn sharp depth edges and floaters. Employing the s-domain modification in the main model is detrimental to learning or rendering objects that are truly close to the camera. Definition: An implementation strategy using Per-Scene Hash (PSH) encoding to balance memory efficiency and rendering speed by caching the diffuse component and querying the specular network online. Steps: 1. Build an initial hash table to store features only for voxels surrounding the hit points, allowing finer grid resolution with acceptable parameter scale. 2. Decouple the neural network into a diffuse encoder and a specular encoder (Es). 3. Cache the diffuse component in the hash grid to avoid online querying. 4. Apply PSH encoding exclusively to the specular encoder (Es) and query it online for each ray. Parameters: Query Frequency: The specular network is queried online, while the diffuse is cached. The text notes querying the network twice to avoid additional time overhead in the context of this encoding. Definition: A down-weighting strategy applied to hash-grid queries to suppress high-frequency aliasing artifacts during rendering, derived from a statistical approximation of the pixel footprint. Steps: 1. During rendering, query the hash-grid at level \ell by hashing s\ell x^ and applying trilinear interpolation. Multiply the interpolated result by the precomputed down-weighting factor \Delta\ell before feeding it to the MLP. Formulas: The down-weighting factor for hash-grid level \ell is: \Delta\ell = 1 - \exp(-f^2 / (2\pi s\ell t^)^2). Here, f is the focal length, s\ell is the scale factor for level \ell, and t^ is the depth along the ray. The pixel footprint in world space is modeled as a 2D isotropic normal distribution \mathcal{N} with mean x^ = o + t^d (where o is origin, d is direction) and standard deviation t/f, parallel to the image plane. The integrated texture is approximated by evaluating the hash-grid at the ray intersection point x^ and scaling by \Delta\ell: \mathbb{E}[H\ell(s\ell x)] \approx \Delta\ell \cdot H\ell(s\ell x^). Comparison: Differs slightly from the original ZipNeRF down-weighting factor proposed by Barron et al., but achieves the same artifact suppression with a simpler derivation. Hash-grid encoding was introduced in Instant-NGP to accelerate NeRF training and rendering by replacing positional encoding with multi-resolution hash tables [13315-instant-ngp]. The concept of using hash tables for neural radiance fields was further explored in ZipNeRF, which utilized large hash tables to avoid collisions and support unbounded scenes. However, ZipNeRF was observed to incorrectly place multiple copies of objects close to the camera in sparse settings. Simple-RF addressed this by introducing an augmented model with reduced hash table capacity and domain constraints to regularize the main model. Anti-aliasing techniques for hash grids were later developed to suppress high-frequency artifacts, with methods like Nexels proposing down-weighting factors derived from pixel footprint statistics. name: Simple-ZipNeRF
head: Augmented ZipNeRF, Simple-RF ZipNeRF
body: Simple-ZipNeRF is a regularized variant of ZipNeRF designed to suppress floaters and improve geometry reconstruction in sparse input scenarios. It operates by training an auxiliary "augmented" model with reduced hash table capacity alongside the main model, using the augmented model's depth estimates to supervise the main model. Unlike the parent method which applies general anti-aliasing and regularization principles, Simple-ZipNeRF specifically targets the overfitting caused by large hash tables in sparse settings by forcing feature sharing through capacity reduction. Simple-ZipNeRF trains two models simultaneously: a main ZipNeRF model and an augmented ZipNeRF model. The augmented model serves as a regularizer by providing depth priors that guide the main model toward simpler, more geometrically consistent solutions. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sparse set of input images (typically 4–36 views), camera poses, and intrinsics. Outputs: A trained main ZipNeRF model capable of rendering novel views with reduced floaters. Data Structures: The architecture mirrors ZipNeRF, utilizing multi-resolution hash grids for spatial encoding. The key difference lies in the hash table size of the augmented model: Main Model: Uses the standard ZipNeRF hash table size T = 2^{21}. Augmented Model: Uses a reduced hash table size Ts = 2^{11}. MLPs: Both models use identical Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) for decoding features into color and density. Training Procedure: The training loop minimizes a combined loss function. Let Lm be the photometric loss for the main model, La be the photometric loss for the augmented model, and L{aug} be the regularization loss derived from the augmented model's depth. 1. Initialize the main ZipNeRF model with standard parameters and the augmented ZipNeRF model with Ts = 2^{11}. 2. Iterate for K iterations (typically 50k+): a. Sample Rays: For each pixel, sample a set of points along the ray using the main model's proposal network. b. Query Main Model: Compute color Cm and density \sigmam for the sampled points using the main hash grid and MLP. c. Query Augmented Model: Compute color Ca and density \sigmaa for the same points using the reduced hash grid and MLP. d. Compute Depth: Estimate depth Da from the augmented model's volume rendering. e. Validate Depth: Check if Da is reliable by reprojecting the 3D point to the closest training view and verifying consistency. If the depth is unreliable (e.g., in regions visible in only one view), discard it. f. Compute Losses: Lm = \| Cm - C{gt} \|^2. La = \| Ca - C{gt} \|^2. L{aug} is applied only if the depth Da is validated. The specific form of L{aug} is not detailed in the provided notes, but it utilizes the accurate depth estimates to supervise the main model. Note: Sparse depth loss L{sd} is not used, as COLMAP often fails or provides noisy sparse depth in these scenarios. g. Total Loss: L{total} = \lambdam Lm + \lambdaa La + \lambda{aug} L{aug}. h. Update: Perform gradient descent on both models. Parameters: Hash Table Size (Augmented): Ts = 2^{11}. Hash Table Size (Main): T = 2^{21}. Loss Weights: \lambdam = 1, \lambdaa = 1, \lambda{aug} = 10. Other Losses: \lambda{sd} = 0, \lambda{cfc} = 0, \lambda{mc} = 0. Regularization Start: L{aug} is imposed after 5k iterations. Hyperparameters: k=5, e\tau=0.2 (used in the regularization mechanism, exact definition not provided in notes). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. mainmodel = ZipNeRF(hashtablesize=221) augmodel = ZipNeRF(hashtablesize=211) optimizer = Optimizer([mainmodel.parameters(), augmodel.parameters()]) for iteration in range(totaliterations): # Sample rays rays = samplerays(batchsize) # Forward pass Main Model mainoutputs = mainmodel.forward(rays) colormain = mainoutputs.color densitymain = mainoutputs.density # Forward pass Augmented Model augoutputs = augmodel.forward(rays) coloraug = augoutputs.color densityaug = augoutputs.density # Compute Depth from Augmented Model depthaug = computedepth(densityaug) # Validate Depth Reliability # Reproject 3D points to closest training view and check consistency validmask = validatedepthconsistency(depthaug, rays, trainingviews) # Compute Photometric Losses lossmain = mse(colormain, gtcolors) lossaug = mse(coloraug, gtcolors) # Compute Regularization Loss (only on valid depths) if iteration > 5000: # Laug uses depthaug to supervise main model geometry # Exact formula for Laug not provided in sources lossaugreg = computedepthregularizationloss(depthaug, mainoutputs, validmask) else: lossaugreg = 0.0 # Total Loss lambdam = 1.0 lambdaa = 1.0 lambdaaug = 10.0 totalloss = (lambdam lossmain) + (lambdaa lossaug) + (lambdaaug lossaugreg) # Backpropagate and Update optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Blur: The reduced hash table size introduces blur in the augmented model, which may not be reflected in quantitative metrics like PSNR despite visual improvements. Sparse Depth: Sparse depth loss is ineffective because COLMAP often fails or provides noisy depth in sparse settings. Performance Limits: The augmentation does not help if the base model has very few input images (performance too low) or a large number of input views (performance saturated). Persistent Floaters: Some translucent floaters may persist even with Simple-ZipNeRF, particularly in regions visible in only one training view where reliable depth supervision is unavailable. Training Time: Simple-ZipNeRF takes approximately twice the training time of standard ZipNeRF because it employs a single augmentation with exactly the same number of queries as the main model. On an NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti 11GB GPU, ZipNeRF takes ~2.0 hours, while Simple-ZipNeRF takes ~4.2 hours. Inference Time: At inference time, Simple-ZipNeRF takes exactly the same time and memory as ZipNeRF because the augmentations are disabled. Inference time is ~13 seconds per frame. Memory: Training memory is higher due to the second model. ZipNeRF uses ~6.7 GB, while Simple-ZipNeRF uses ~8.6 GB. Inference memory is identical (~4.8 GB). Performance: MipNeRF360 (12 views): PSNR 17.60, SSIM 0.5245, LPIPS 0.4876. MipNeRF360 (20 views): PSNR 21.03, SSIM 0.6456, LPIPS 0.3421. MipNeRF360 (36 views): PSNR 24.19, SSIM 0.7458, LPIPS 0.2390. NeRF-Synthetic (4 views): PSNR 11.50, SSIM 0.7715, LPIPS 0.3878. NeRF-Synthetic (8 views): PSNR 15.88, SSIM 0.8063, LPIPS 0.2461. NeRF-Synthetic (12 views): PSNR 20.51, SSIM 0.8531, LPIPS 0.1532. Strengths: Significantly reduces floaters and improves geometry in sparse input scenarios. Limitations: Increased training time and memory; ineffective when input views are extremely sparse or extremely dense; may introduce blur. Simple-ZipNeRF is part of the "Simple Radiance Fields" (Simple-RF) family of models, which regularize radiance fields to choose simpler solutions over complex ones. The method was proposed to address the issue of floaters caused by large hash tables in ZipNeRF when trained with sparse inputs. The approach was evaluated on forward-facing scenes (NeRF-LLFF), unbounded forward-facing scenes (RealEstate-10K), unbounded 360° scenes (MipNeRF360), and bounded 360° scenes (NeRF-Synthetic). name: Instant-NGP
head: Instant Neural Graphics Primitives with a Multiresolution Hash Encoding
body: Instant-NGP is a method for real-time training and rendering of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) that achieves speedups of three orders of magnitude over vanilla NeRF by replacing positional encoding with a multi-resolution hash encoding. It solves the bottleneck of slow neural network queries and inefficient sampling by offloading representational burden to hash-table lookups, using an occupancy grid to skip empty space, and employing a fully-fused small MLP. Unlike its siblings, it prioritizes training throughput (seconds) and interactive rendering (milliseconds) over the high-quality, slow optimization of original NeRF. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D spatial coordinates \mathbf{x}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and camera parameters. Output: Volume density \sigma and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}. Data Structures: 1. Multi-resolution Hash Grids: A set of L hash tables. Each table l \in \{0, \dots, L-1\} contains T entries. Each entry is a trainable feature vector of dimension F. 2. Occupancy Grids: A set of multiscale voxel grids (coarse to fine) storing a single bit per voxel indicating occupancy (empty vs. non-empty). These are updated during training based on density predictions. Parameters: L: Number of resolution levels. T: Number of feature vectors (hash table size) per level. F: Dimensionality of feature vectors. Typical values: Training time 5–30 seconds; Rendering time tens of milliseconds at 1920×1080. Algorithm Steps: 1. Occupancy Culling: For a ray segment, check the occupancy grids. If the occupancy bit is low (empty), skip sampling in that region. If the accumulated transmittance is low (behind high density), skip sampling. This increases sampling speed by 10-100x. 2. Hash Encoding Query: For each sampled 3D point \mathbf{x}: a. Voxel Identification: For each resolution level l, identify the enclosing voxel in the grid at that resolution. b. Vertex Hashing: Map the 8 vertices of the enclosing voxel to hash indices. The hash function uses the input hash table size (l, b) and scaling factors (1/Na, 1/Nb). c. Feature Lookup: Retrieve the F-dimensional feature vectors from the hash table using the computed indices. d. Trilinear Interpolation: Interpolate the 8 retrieved feature vectors based on the continuous position of \mathbf{x} within the voxel to obtain the interpolated feature vector \mathbf{f}l for level l. e. Concatenation: Concatenate the interpolated features \mathbf{f}l from all L levels. f. Direction Encoding: Encode the viewing direction \mathbf{d} using spherical harmonics. g. Joint Vector: Concatenate the hashed spatial features and the encoded direction into a joint feature vector. 3. Neural Network Prediction: Feed the joint feature vector into a small, fully-fused MLP (typically 4 layers with 64 neurons each, or 1-2 layers for the final regression head depending on implementation specifics cited) to predict density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def queryinstantngp(x, d, hashgrids, occupancygrids, L, T, F): """ Query the Instant-NGP encoding and MLP for density and color. Args: x: 3D coordinate (float3) d: Viewing direction (float3) hashgrids: List of L hash tables, each of size T x F occupancygrids: List of L occupancy grids (bitmasks) L: Number of resolution levels T: Hash table size F: Feature dimension Returns: sigma: Volume density (float) color: RGB color (float3) """ # 1. Occupancy Culling (Simplified for single point query) # In practice, this is done during ray marching to skip segments. # For a single point query, we assume the point is valid. # 2. Hash Encoding concatenatedfeatures = [] for l in range(L): # a. Identify enclosing voxel at level l # Resolution scales with l. Let voxelsizel be the side length. voxelsizel = getvoxelsize(l, L) voxelcoords = floor(x / voxelsizel) # b. Get 8 vertices of the voxel vertices = getvoxelvertices(voxelcoords, voxelsizel) # c. Hash vertices and lookup features # Hash function: h(v) = hash(v) % T # Note: Hash collisions are not explicitly handled; gradients dominate optimization featurevectors = [] for v in vertices: index = hashfunction(v, T) featurevectors.append(hashgrids[l][index]) # d. Trilinear interpolation # Compute local coordinates within the voxel localcoords = (x - voxelcoords voxelsizel) / voxelsizel interpolatedfeature = trilinearinterpolate(featurevectors, localcoords) concatenatedfeatures.append(interpolatedfeature) # e. Concatenate features from all levels spatialfeatures = concatenate(concatenatedfeatures) # f. Encode viewing direction using spherical harmonics directionfeatures = encodesphericalharmonics(d) # g. Joint feature vector jointvector = concatenate([spatialfeatures, directionfeatures]) # 3. MLP Prediction # Fully-fused MLP: 4 layers, 64 neurons each # Or shallow MLP (1-2 layers) for final regression # Implementation depends on specific framework (e.g., tinycudann) sigma, color = mlpforward(jointvector) return sigma, color def hashfunction(vertex, T): # Standard hash function modulo table size # Exact hash function details not specified in sources return hash(vertex) % T def trilinearinterpolate(features, localcoords): # features: list of 8 vectors (F-dim) # localcoords: (x, y, z) in [0, 1] # Perform trilinear interpolation x, y, z = localcoords # Interpolate along x f000 = features[0] f100 = features[1] f010 = features[2] f110 = features[3] f001 = features[4] f101 = features[5] f011 = features[6] f111 = features[7] # Interpolate along x f00 = lerp(f000, f100, x) f01 = lerp(f010, f110, x) f10 = lerp(f001, f101, x) f11 = lerp(f011, f111, x) # Interpolate along y f0 = lerp(f00, f01, y) f1 = lerp(f10, f11, y) # Interpolate along z result = lerp(f0, f1, z) return result def lerp(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hash Collisions: Not explicitly handled. Multiple vertices may map to the same hash index. The trainable nature of the features allows the most important vertices to dominate optimization via gradients. Precision: Trilinear interpolation requires precise local coordinate calculation. Boundaries: The method assumes a bounded spatial domain for the hash grids. Time Complexity: Training time is reduced to seconds (5–30s for typical scenes). Rendering time is tens of milliseconds at 1920×1080. Memory Complexity: Determined by L \times T \times F. Trade-off between quality, memory, and performance. Performance: 1000x speedup over vanilla NeRF. Occupancy grid sampling increases speed by 10-100x. Fully-fused MLP is 5-10x faster than TensorFlow implementations. Strengths: Real-time training and rendering; efficient memory usage via hash encoding; robust to sparse input via regularization principles inherited from parent methods. Limitations: Quality may be lower than high-quality NeRF variants; hash collisions can cause artifacts if T is too small. When to use: Real-time applications, interactive editing, rapid prototyping. When not to use: High-fidelity offline rendering where training time is not a constraint. Instant-NGP was introduced by Müller et al. in 2022. It builds on the principles of hash-grid anti-aliasing and regularization [Parent]. The method breaks NeRF training into three pillars: improved ray marching with occupancy grids, a fully-fused small MLP, and multi-resolution hash encoding. It was the first practical NeRF for production, enabling real-time training and rendering. name: Instant-NGP with Scale-Space Augmentation
head: Instant-NGP adapted NeRF, NeRF with Instant-NGP extensions and scale-space augmentation, NeRF2Real NeRF
body: This method adapts the Instant-NGP architecture for robust reconstruction from short mobile videos, specifically targeting sim2real transfer scenarios where compact geometry and anti-aliased rendering are critical. It differs from standard NeRF by replacing dense grids with multi-scale spatial hash grids for O(1) lookup, adding a distortion loss for compactness, decomposing color into specular/diffuse components, and injecting scale-space variance as an MLP input for anti-aliasing. It builds on Hash-grid anti-aliasing and regularization by explicitly providing the integrated scale variance \Sigma to the decoder, allowing the network to interpolate samples in scale-space. Inputs: A short video (\sim 5-6 minutes) captured with a mobile camera (e.g., Google Pixel 6 rear camera). Camera intrinsics and keyframe extrinsics estimated via COLMAP. N \sim 1000 keyframes extracted from the video. Video resolution \ge 1080p. Outputs: A trained NeRF model capable of novel view synthesis and collision geometry extraction. Rendering speed of \sim 6ms per frame on a V100 GPU. Data Structures: Multi-scale Spatial Hash Grid: A set of hash tables, one per resolution level \ell. Each table maps hashed 3D coordinates to feature vectors. The layout follows the standard Instant-NGP structure: a global hash function maps a 3D point to an index in a flat feature array, with trilinear interpolation used for feature retrieval. MLP Decoder: A multi-layer perceptron that takes concatenated features from the hash grids and an additional scale variance input \Sigma to predict volume density \sigma and diffuse/specular color components. Numbered Steps: 1. Data Acquisition and Preprocessing: Capture a short video of the static scene using a mobile camera. Ensure slow, even camera movement to reduce motion blur and minimize drastic viewpoint changes. Fix white balance and brightness to ensure consistent lighting. Extract N \sim 1000 keyframes from the video. Use COLMAP to estimate camera intrinsics and keyframe extrinsics. 2. Network Architecture Setup: Initialize multi-scale spatial hash grids for feature encoding. Initialize the MLP decoder with Swish activations instead of ReLU. Add Layer Normalization before the final MLP layer. Configure the output to predict separate specular and diffuse color components to improve reconstructed geometry. 3. Training Loop (Per Ray): For each training ray, sample points along the ray using a proposal network. Scale-Space Augmentation: Sample a random blur variance \sigma{\text{blur}} from the range [\sigma{\min}, \sigma{\max}]. Compute the base sample variance \Sigma{\text{sample}} associated with the current sampling distribution. Calculate the injected scale-space variance \Sigma using the formula: \Sigma = \Sigma{\text{sample}} \times (1 + (\sigma{\text{blur}} - \sigma{\min})) where \Sigma is the scale-space variance injected as an extra MLP input, \Sigma{\text{sample}} is the base sample variance, \sigma{\text{blur}} is the random Gaussian blur variance, and \sigma{\min} is the minimum blur variance. Rendering: Use the trained model to render novel views or extract collision geometry (e.g., by coarsening the mesh and replacing the floor with a flat primitive). Parameters: \sigma{\text{blur}} \in [\sigma{\min}, \sigma{\max}]: Random variance for Gaussian blur augmentation applied to training samples. N \sim 1000: Number of keyframes extracted from the captured video. Video resolution \ge 1080p: Minimum resolution required for better localization and improved NeRF reconstruction results. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Motion Blur: Rapid camera movement during capture introduces motion blur, which degrades reconstruction quality. Slow, even movement is required. Lighting Consistency: Variable lighting (e.g., auto white balance) can confuse the model. Fixed white balance and brightness are necessary. Resolution: Low-resolution videos lead to poorer localization and reconstruction. Resolution \ge 1080p is recommended. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: NeRF-W
head: NeRF in the Wild
body: NeRF-W extends Neural Radiance Fields to handle unconstrained internet photo collections by modeling temporal modifications, specifically variable illuminations and transient objects (people, cars, occlusions). It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF by introducing per-image appearance embeddings to handle photometric variations and a secondary transient MLP head to model dynamic content, allowing the rendering of static geometry while accounting for scene changes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N with known camera poses (intrinsics and extrinsics). Outputs: A continuous 3D representation capable of rendering novel views of the static scene geometry, independent of transient objects and lighting conditions. Data Structures: 1. Appearance Embedding (Li^{(a)}): A learnable vector of fixed dimension associated with each input image i. This vector captures per-image lighting, exposure, and white balance variations. 2. Transient Embedding (Li^{(\tau)}): A learnable vector of fixed dimension associated with each input image i. This vector controls the appearance of transient objects specific to that view. 3. Networks: \text{MLP}{\theta1}: Takes 3D position \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z) as input. Outputs density \sigma and the appearance latent vector Li^{(a)}. \text{MLP}{\theta2}: Takes viewing direction \mathbf{d} and the appearance latent vector Li^{(a)} as input. Outputs the RGB color \mathbf{c} for the static scene. \text{MLP}{\theta3}: Takes the transient latent vector Li^{(\tau)} (and potentially position/direction, though sources emphasize Li^{(\tau)}) as input. Outputs the color and density for transient objects. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize \text{MLP}{\theta1}, \text{MLP}{\theta2}, \text{MLP}{\theta3} and the set of appearance embeddings \{Li^{(a)}\}{i=1}^N and transient embeddings \{Li^{(\tau)}\}{i=1}^N. 2. Ray Sampling: For each training image i, generate rays through each pixel. Sample Nc coarse points and Nf fine points along each ray. 3. Static Feature Query: For each sample point \mathbf{x}n on a ray from image i: Query \text{MLP}{\theta1}(\mathbf{x}n) to obtain density \sigman and appearance embedding Li^{(a)}. Query \text{MLP}{\theta2}(\mathbf{d}n, Li^{(a)}) to obtain static color \mathbf{c}n^{\text{static}}. 4. Transient Feature Query: For each sample point \mathbf{x}n on a ray from image i: Query \text{MLP}{\theta3}(Li^{(\tau)}) (or combined with position/direction if implied by architecture, but sources specify Li^{(\tau)}) to obtain transient color \mathbf{c}n^{\text{transient}} and transient density \sigman^{\text{transient}}. 5. Volume Rendering (Static): Compute the expected static color Ci^{\text{static}}(\mathbf{r}) for ray \mathbf{r} using alpha compositing over the static samples: Ci^{\text{static}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{n=1}^{N} Tn \alphan \mathbf{c}n^{\text{static}} where \alphan = 1 - \exp(-\sigman \deltan), Tn = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{n-1} \sigmaj \deltaj), and \deltan is the distance between samples. 6. Volume Rendering (Transient): Compute the expected transient color Ci^{\text{transient}}(\mathbf{r}) similarly using transient densities and colors: Ci^{\text{transient}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{n=1}^{N} Tn^{\text{trans}} \alphan^{\text{trans}} \mathbf{c}n^{\text{transient}} where \alphan^{\text{trans}} = 1 - \exp(-\sigman^{\text{transient}} \deltan) and Tn^{\text{trans}} is the transmittance for transient components. 7. Combined Rendering: The final expected color Ci(\mathbf{r}) is the sum of the static and transient components: Ci(\mathbf{r}) = Ci^{\text{static}}(\mathbf{r}) + Ci^{\text{transient}}(\mathbf{r}) Note: Sources indicate that at test time, the transient component is discarded, rendering only Ci^{\text{static}}(\mathbf{r}). 8. Uncertainty Weighting: Predict per-ray uncertainty \beta to downweight unreliable pixels during training. The loss function incorporates this uncertainty to handle photometric inconsistencies and transient artifacts. 9. Optimization: Minimize the difference between rendered colors Ci(\mathbf{r}) and ground truth image pixels Ii(\mathbf{r}), updating network weights and embeddings. Formulas: Image-Dependent Radiance: NeRF-W replaces image-independent radiance with image-dependent radiance Ci(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}), introducing dependency on image index i. Alpha Compositing: The standard volume rendering integral approximation used for both static and transient components. Uncertainty: Per-ray uncertainty \beta is predicted and used to weight the loss or compositing. Parameters: Nc: Number of coarse samples. Not given in the sources. Nf: Number of fine samples. Not given in the sources. Embedding Dimension: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Views: Degraded quality in rarely observed areas (e.g., ground surfaces) and poor reconstruction for oblique viewing angles. Camera Calibration: Blurry artifacts occur if camera poses are inaccurate, inheriting NeRF's sensitivity to calibration errors. Residual Artifacts: May leave residual artifacts when removing occlusions; uncertainty estimation can mask static scene errors. Specular Surfaces: Struggles with specular/reflective surfaces. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class NeRFW: def init(self, numimages, embeddingdim, hiddendim=256): """ Initialize NeRF-W model.:param numimages: Number of input images N:param embeddingdim: Dimension of appearance and transient embeddings:param hiddendim: Hidden layer size for MLPs """ super().init() # Network 1: Position -> Density + Appearance Embedding self.mlptheta1 = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(3, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1 + embeddingdim) # 1 for sigma, rest for La) # Network 2: Direction + Appearance Embedding -> Static Color self.mlptheta2 = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(3 + embeddingdim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 3) # RGB) # Network 3: Transient Embedding -> Transient Color + Density # Note: Source says MLPtheta3 takes Li^(tau). # Source implies it renders transient objects. # We assume it outputs color and potentially density for compositing. self.mlptheta3 = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(embeddingdim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 4) # RGB + sigma for transient) # Learnable Embeddings self.appearanceembeddings = nn.Embedding(numimages, embeddingdim) self.transientembeddings = nn.Embedding(numimages, embeddingdim) # Uncertainty head (predicted per ray or pixel, simplified here as a scalar per ray for weighting) self.uncertaintyhead = nn.Linear(1, 1) # Placeholder for uncertainty prediction mechanism def querystatic(self, positions, directions, imageindices): """ Query static component of the scene.:param positions: (Nrays, Nsamples, 3):param directions: (Nrays, Nsamples, 3):param imageindices: (Nrays,):return: sigmastatic (Nrays, Nsamples), colorstatic (Nrays, Nsamples, 3) """ # Get appearance embedding for each ray's image # imageindices shape: (Nrays,) # appearanceembeddings shape: (Nimages, embeddingdim) # We need to broadcast to (Nrays, Nsamples, embeddingdim) # Since embedding is per-image, it is constant along the ray for a given image appemb = self.appearanceembeddings(imageindices) # (Nrays, embeddingdim) appembexpanded = appemb.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, positions.shape[1], -1) # (Nrays, Nsamples, embeddingdim) # MLPtheta1: Position -> (sigma, appemb) # Note: Source says MLPtheta1 outputs density AND appearance latent vector. # However, we already have the appearance embedding from the embedding table. # The source implies MLPtheta1 outputs Li^(a). This suggests Li^(a) might be # predicted or refined by the network, or the embedding is an initial guess. # Standard interpretation: The embedding is learned, and MLPtheta1 uses it. # But Source says "MLPtheta1... outputs density sigma and appearance latent vector Li^(a)". # This implies the network predicts the embedding or refines it. # Let's follow Source strictly: MLPtheta1 outputs Li^(a). # This means we don't use self.appearanceembeddings directly in the forward pass of MLPtheta1? # Or does MLPtheta1 output the residual? # Re-reading: "MLPtheta1 takes 3D position... and outputs density sigma and appearance latent vector Li^(a)". # This contradicts the "learnable embedding vector" description if it's purely positional. # Usually, in NeRF-W, the embedding is an input to the color network. # Let's assume the standard NeRF-W architecture: # 1. Embedding is looked up. # 2. Position goes to MLPtheta1 to get sigma. # 3. Direction + Embedding goes to MLPtheta2 to get color. # Source phrasing is slightly ambiguous: "MLPtheta1... outputs... Li^(a)". # It might mean the system outputs Li^(a) via the embedding table, and MLPtheta1 outputs sigma. # Or MLPtheta1 predicts the embedding. # Given "Each image gets an appearance embedding vector (trained alongside the model)", # it is a learnable parameter. # If MLPtheta1 outputs it, it would be position-dependent, which contradicts "per-image". # Therefore, MLPtheta1 likely outputs sigma, and the embedding is separate. # However, to be safe and follow literally: # If MLPtheta1 outputs Li^(a), then Li^(a) is a function of x. # But says "dependency on image index i". # Let's stick to the most common implementation which aligns with 's "image-dependent radiance": # The embedding is per-image. # We will assume MLPtheta1 outputs sigma, and the embedding is retrieved. # If the source strictly means MLPtheta1 outputs the embedding, it would be weird. # Let's look at again: "MLPtheta1 connects a 3D position to a density value sigma and MLPtheta2 predicts a RGB color from a viewing direction d and a latent vector MLPtheta1 (x, y, z)." # This sentence structure is broken in the source. "latent vector MLPtheta1 (x,y,z)" likely means "latent vector produced by MLPtheta1". # But then MLPtheta2 takes that latent vector. # If the latent vector is produced by MLPtheta1 from position, it is position-dependent. # But says "per-image appearance embedding". # Resolution: The "latent vector" in refers to the appearance embedding Li^{(a)}. # The source likely means: The system provides Li^{(a)} (via embedding table). # MLPtheta1 outputs sigma. MLPtheta2 takes d and Li^{(a)}. # We will implement it this way, as it is the standard NeRF-W approach and consistent with. # Get sigma from position sigmainput = positions # (Nrays, Nsamples, 3) out1 = self.mlptheta1(sigmainput) # (Nrays, Nsamples, 1 + embeddingdim) sigma = out1[:,:, 0:1] # (Nrays, Nsamples, 1) # Get static color # Concatenate direction and appearance embedding # directions: (Nrays, Nsamples, 3) # appembexpanded: (Nrays, Nsamples, embeddingdim) concatinput = torch.cat([directions, appembexpanded], dim=-1) # (Nrays, Nsamples, 3 + embeddingdim) colorstatic = self.mlptheta2(concatinput) # (Nrays, Nsamples, 3) return sigma, colorstatic def querytransient(self, imageindices): """ Query transient component.:param imageindices: (Nrays,):return: sigmatransient (Nrays, Nsamples, 1), colortransient (Nrays, Nsamples, 3) Note: Transient embedding is per-image. """ transemb = self.transientembeddings(imageindices) # (Nrays, embeddingdim) # Expand to match ray samples if needed, or assume transient is constant along ray? # Usually transient objects are spatial, so we might need position. # Source says "MLPtheta3 takes transient latent vector Li^(tau)". # It does not mention position. This implies transient appearance is view-dependent only? # Or it's a simplified model. We follow the source. # If no position, we can't do spatial compositing easily. # However, says "renders both static and transient components (density + color)". # If MLPtheta3 only takes Li^(tau), it outputs a single color/density per ray? # Or per sample? If per sample, it needs position. # Let's assume MLPtheta3 takes Li^(tau) and outputs color/density for the whole ray or per sample if position is added. # Given the ambiguity, and saying "MLPtheta3 takes... Li^(tau)", we will pass only the embedding. # This implies the transient component is uniform along the ray or the network handles it implicitly. # This is a significant simplification. # Alternative: MLPtheta3 takes Li^(tau) and position. # Source does not explicitly say "and position" for MLPtheta3. # We will implement as taking only Li^(tau) as per source text, but note this is unusual. # Actually, looking at: "MLPtheta3 is introduced to render scenes with transient objects... thanks to Li^(tau)". # It doesn't specify inputs beyond Li^(tau). # We will assume it outputs color and density. # Expand embedding to (Nrays, Nsamples, embeddingdim) for consistency with ray sampling transembexpanded = transemb.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, 1, -1) # (Nrays, 1, embeddingdim) # If we assume transient is constant along ray, we can just use this. # If we need per-sample, we might need to repeat or use position. # Let's assume per-sample query is not supported by this specific source description for MLPtheta3. # We will return constant values along the ray for transient. out3 = self.mlptheta3(transembexpanded) # (Nrays, 1, 4) # Expand to Nsamples out3 = out3.expand(-1, positions.shape[1], -1) # (Nrays, Nsamples, 4) sigmatransient = out3[:,:, 3:4] colortransient = out3[:,:, 0:3] return sigmatransient, colortransient def render(self, rays, imageindices): """ Render a batch of rays.:param rays: Dictionary containing 'positions', 'directions', 'distances':param imageindices: Indices of the images for each ray:return: Rendered color, uncertainty """ positions = rays['positions'] directions = rays['directions'] dists = rays['distances'] # (Nrays, Nsamples) # Query Static sigmastatic, colorstatic = self.querystatic(positions, directions, imageindices) # Query Transient sigmatransient, colortransient = self.querytransient(imageindices) # Alpha Compositing for Static alphastatic = 1.0 - Rendering time is similar to NeRF but involves an extra query for transient components during training. Memory Complexity: Increased memory usage due to the storage of appearance and transient embeddings for each image, and the additional network parameters. Performance: Achieves better performance on unconstrained PhotoTourism datasets compared to standard NeRF. Strengths: Handles photometric variations and transient objects effectively. Limitations: Sensitive to camera calibration errors. Struggles with sparse views and oblique angles. High computational cost. Limited generalization to unseen viewpoints. name: UniSDF-based Latent NeRF
head: Latent NeRF Model with UniSDF
body:
UniSDF-based Latent NeRF is a geometry estimator and appearance model that utilizes UniSDF, a signed distance function (SDF) based volume rendering approach, to decouple geometry from appearance. It solves the problem of generating relightable 3D assets by extracting a mesh from the SDF for radiance cue computation via a standard rendering engine, while optimizing a latent NeRF for appearance. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly leveraging SDF-based mesh extraction to compute physically-based shading normals and radiance cues, rather than relying solely on differentiable volume rendering for all geometric cues. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Input images, camera poses, and a mask. Outputs: A mesh representing the geometry, a latent NeRF model for appearance, and radiance cues (shading normals, depth, etc.) rendered from the mesh. Data Structures: UniSDF Model: Parameterized similarly to the original UniSDF for the DTU dataset, with specific modifications to proposal sampling and encoding. Hash Grid Encoding: An additional hash grid encoding with 15 scales between a resolution of 32 and 4096, used exclusively for outputting predicted normals. GLO Embeddings: Applied via an MLP that predicts element-wise scale and shift values for the 'bottleneck' feature of UniSDF. Numbered Steps: 1. Geometry Estimation: Optimize the UniSDF model on the input images. The number of proposal sampling rounds is reduced from two to one, using 64 proposal samples. 2. Normal Prediction: Use the additional hash grid encoding (15 scales, resolution 32 to 4096) to output predicted normals. 3. Loss Computation: Compute the asymmetric predicted normal loss Lp and the smoothness loss Ls during optimization. 4. Mesh Extraction: Convert the optimized SDF representation to a mesh using marching cubes with a threshold set to zero. 5. Radiance Cue Rendering: Import the extracted mesh into a standard rendering engine (Blender Cycles) with predefined materials based on the GGX material model to render radiance cues. 6. Latent NeRF Optimization: Optimize the latent NeRF model. Incorporate GLO embeddings by using an MLP to predict element-wise scale and shift values applied to the UniSDF 'bottleneck' feature. Formulas: The asymmetric predicted normal loss Lp is defined as: Lp = \sumi \left( \lambda1 \omegai \|
abla ni - 
abla n'i \|2 + \lambda2 
abla \omegai \| ni - n'i \|2 + \lambda3 
abla \omegai \|
abla ni - n'i \|2 ight) where: \omegai is the volume rendering weight of the i-th sample. 
abla denotes the stop-gradient operator. ni is the i-th sample's density normal. n'i is the i-th sample's predicted normal. \lambda1 = 10^{-3}, \lambda2 = 10^{-3}, \lambda3 = 10^{-2}. The smoothness loss Ls is defined as: Ls = \lambda4 \sumi \omegai \| n'(xi + \epsilon) - n'(xi) \|2^2 where: xi is the 3D position of the i-th sample. \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I) is an isotropic Gaussian random variable used to perturb the sample locations. \lambda4 = 0.1. \sigma = 0.01. Parameters: Optimizer: Adam with  eta1 = 0.9,  eta2 = 0.99, and \epsilon = 1 	imes 10^{-15}. Learning Rate: Decayed logarithmically from 5 	imes 10^{-3} to 5 	imes 10^{-4} over 25k training iterations. Warmup: Cosine-scheduled warmup in the first 500 steps. Proposal Samples: 64 samples, with one round of proposal sampling. Hash Grid: 15 scales, resolution range 32 to 4096. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. model = UniSDFModel() hashgrid = HashGrid(numlevels=15, resolutionmin=32, resolutionmax=4096) optimizer = Adam(params=model.parameters(), lr=5e-3, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.99, eps=1e-15) warmupsteps = 500 totalsteps = 25000 for step in range(totalsteps): # Learning rate scheduling if step < warmupsteps: lr = cosinewarmup(step, warmupsteps, initiallr=5e-3, finallr=5e-4) else: lr = logarithmicdecay(step - warmupsteps, totalsteps - warmupsteps, startlr=5e-3, endlr=5e-4) optimizer.setlearningrate(lr) # Forward pass samples = samplerays(numproposalsamples=64, numrounds=1) sdfvalues, densities = model.forward(samples.positions) predictednormals = hashgrid.forward(samples.positions) # Additional hash grid for normals # Compute losses densitynormals = computedensitynormals(densities) lossp = computeasymmetricnormalloss( weights=samples.weights, densitynormals=densitynormals, predictednormals=predictednormals, lambda1=1e-3, lambda2=1e-3, lambda3=1e-2) # Smoothness loss epsilon = samplegaussiannoise(samples.positions, sigma=0.01) perturbednormals = hashgrid.forward(samples.positions + epsilon) losss = 0.1 meansquarederror(perturbednormals, predictednormals, weights=samples.weights) totalloss = lossp + losss # Backward pass optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() mesh = marchingcubes(sdf=model.sdffield, threshold=0.0) radiancecues = renderwithblendercycles(mesh, materialmodel='GGX') bottleneckfeature = model.getbottleneckfeature() scaleshift = glomlp.predict(bottleneckfeature) bottleneckfeature = bottleneckfeature scaleshift.scale + scaleshift.shift latentnerf.optimize(radiancecues, bottleneckfeature) Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Decouples geometry from appearance, allowing fixed geometry weights and optimized appearance weights. Enables mesh extraction for radiance cue computation. Modifications result in better and smoother geometry necessary for relighting objects with specular highlights. Limitations: Relies on external rendering engine (Blender Cycles) for radiance cues. When to use: When relightable 3D assets with specular highlights are required. When not to use: When end-to-end differentiable volume rendering without external tools is required. UniSDF-based Latent NeRF is based on the IllumiNeRF paper. It uses UniSDF [56] as the geometry estimator and Latent NeRF model. The method was implemented using JAX [11].
