name: RawNeRF
head: NeRF in the Dark
body: RawNeRF is a method for High Dynamic Range (HDR) view synthesis and denoising that adapts Mip-NeRF to train directly on raw linear images, preserving the scene's full dynamic range and enabling post-processing tasks like exposure adjustment and tonemapping after rendering. Unlike standard NeRF variants that use tonemapped low dynamic range (LDR) images, RawNeRF optimizes the neural radiance field in the linear raw domain, allowing it to recover correct colors in dark regions and unclipped highlights that are lost in standard camera pipelines. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A collection of N posed input raw images (typically 25–200 per scene), where N is the number of training images. Each image Ii has an associated shutter speed ti and camera pose. The raw images are 12-bit DNG files, converted to floating point by normalizing with white and black levels. Outputs: A trained NeRF model representing the scene in linear HDR color space. Novel views are rendered as raw linear HDR images, which can subsequently be tonemapped, exposed, or defocused. Data Structures NeRF Model: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) that takes a 3D position \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} as input and outputs volume density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. The color output is modified from a sigmoid to an exponential function to better parameterize linear radiance values. Exposure Parameters: For each unique shutter speed t present in the training set, a learned per-color-channel scaling factor \alpha{tc} is maintained, where c indexes the color channels (R, G, B). Numbered Steps 1. Preprocessing: Camera poses are calculated using full-resolution postprocessed JPEG images via COLMAP, as COLMAP does not support raw images directly. Inputs are not undistorted or downsampled to avoid affecting the raw noise distribution. Camera intrinsics are used to account for radial distortion when generating rays. Raw images are mosaicked (one color value per pixel). The loss is applied only to the active color channel for each pixel, effectively demosaicing the input during optimization. 2. Ray Marching and Integration: For each training image, rays are generated through the camera center. The NeRF is queried along the ray to sample points. Volume rendering is performed to accumulate color and opacity along the ray, producing a raw linear output color \hat{y}i for the pixel. 3. Exposure Scaling: To match the brightness of the input image Ii with shutter speed ti, the network's linear output \hat{y}i is scaled by ti and a learned per-channel scaling factor \alpha{ti c}. The final scaled value is clipped at 1 to account for pixel saturation in overexposed regions: \tilde{y}{ic} = \min(\hat{y}{ic} \cdot ti \cdot \alpha{ti c}, 1) The scaling factor for the longest exposure shutter speed t{max} is constrained to 1 (\alpha{t{max} c} = 1). 4. Loss Computation: A gradient supervision loss is applied. The loss uses a linearization of the tone curve \psi(z) = \log(z + \epsilon) with \epsilon = 10^{-3}. The loss for a pixel i is: Li = \left( \frac{\tilde{y}i - yi}{\text{sg}(\tilde{y}i) + \epsilon} \right)^2 where yi is the input raw pixel value, \text{sg}(\cdot) is the stop-gradient operator, and the denominator stabilizes training. Regularization: A regularization loss is applied to the variance of the weight distribution used to accumulate color values along the ray. This prevents partially transparent "floater" artifacts in extremely noisy scenes. 5. Optimization: The NeRF parameters and exposure scaling factors \alpha{tc} are jointly optimized using gradient descent. The Adam optimizer is used with a learning rate decaying from 10^{-3} to 10^{-5} over 500k steps. Batches consist of 16k random rays sampled across all training images. 6. Post-Processing (Inference): Rendered raw outputs are processed after training. This includes tonemapping, exposure adjustment, or synthetic defocusing. Synthetic Defocus: RGBA depth layers are precomputed from the trained model. A varying blur kernel is applied to different depth layers and composited together. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim class RawNeRF: def init(self, numshutterspeeds, channels=3): """ Initialize RawNeRF model and exposure parameters.:param numshutterspeeds: Number of unique shutter speeds in training set.:param channels: Number of color channels (3 for RGB). """ self.neuralfield = MipNeRF() # Assumes MipNeRF architecture from parent article # Learned per-channel scaling factors for each shutter speed # Shape: [numshutterspeeds, channels] self.alpha = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(numshutterspeeds, channels)) # Constraint: alpha for the longest exposure (index 0 assumed) is fixed to 1 self.alpha.data[0] = 1.0 self.epsilon = 1e-3 self.optimizer = optim.Adam(list(self.neuralfield.parameters()) + [self.alpha], lr=1e-3) self.scheduler = optim.lrscheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(self.optimizer, Tmax=500000, etamin=1e-5) def getexposurescaledcolor(self, rawcolor, shutterspeedindex): """ Apply exposure scaling and clipping to raw color output.:param rawcolor: Tensor of shape [..., 3] representing NeRF output color.:param shutterspeedindex: Integer index into self.alpha.:return: Scaled and clipped color tensor. """ # Get scaling factors for the specific shutter speed and all channels # alpha shape: [numshutterspeeds, 3] # rawcolor shape: [..., 3] # We need to broadcast alpha to match rawcolor dimensions alphafactors = self.alpha[shutterspeedindex] # Shape: [3] # Scale by shutter speed and learned factor # rawcolor ti alpha scaled = rawcolor shutterspeed alphafactors # Clip at 1 clipped = torch.clamp(scaled, max=1.0) return clipped def computeloss(self, predictedcolor, targetcolor, shutterspeedindex, shutterspeed): """ Compute the gradient supervision loss with regularization.:param predictedcolor: Scaled and clipped predicted color (from getexposurescaledcolor).:param targetcolor: Target raw pixel value (mosaicked, single channel active).:param shutterspeedindex: Index for alpha lookup.:param shutterspeed: Float shutter speed value ti.:return: Scalar loss value. """ # 1. Exposure Scaling # Note: In training loop, we usually pass raw NeRF output, then scale here or in forward pass. # Assuming predictedcolor here is the raw NeRF output before scaling for clarity of formula, # but the loss formula uses the scaled value. Let's follow the paper's flow: # The paper applies scaling before loss. # Re-calculate scaled value for loss computation consistency alphafactors = self.alpha[shutterspeedindex] scaledpred = torch.clamp(predictedcolor shutterspeed alphafactors, max=1.0) # 2. Gradient Supervision Loss # L = sum( ( (scaledpred - target) / (sg(scaledpred) + eps))^2) # Note: target is mosaicked. We only compute loss on the active channel. # This requires knowing which channel is active per pixel. # For simplicity, assuming targetcolor has 0s in inactive channels and we mask accordingly. denominator = torch.stopgradient(scaledpred) + self.epsilon lossperpixel = ((scaledpred - targetcolor) / denominator) 2 # Masking for mosaicked data: only sum over active channels # Assuming targetcolor is 0 in inactive channels, this naturally zeros out inactive channels # if we sum over channels. However, standard MSE sums all. # The paper says: "We only apply the loss to the active color channel". # Implementation detail: Multiply loss by a mask indicating active channel. # For this pseudocode, we assume targetcolor is structured such that inactive channels are 0 # and we sum over channels. pixelloss = torch.sum(lossperpixel, dim=-1) # Sum over RGB meanloss = torch.mean(pixelloss) # 3. Regularization Loss (Variance of weight distribution) # This requires access to the weights used in volume rendering. # Assuming a method getrenderingweights() exists in the NeRF forward pass. weights = self.getrenderingweights() # Shape: [numsamples] regularization = torch.var(weights) totalloss = meanloss + 0.1 regularization # Weight for regularization not specified, assumed small return totalloss def trainstep(self, batch): """ Perform one training step.:param batch: Dictionary containing rays, target colors, shutter speeds, and shutter speed indices. """ self.optimizer.zerograd() # Forward pass through NeRF # rays: [numrays, 3] (origin, direction) # shutterspeeds: [numrays] # shutterspeedindices: [numrays] # targets: [numrays, 3] (mosaicked) rawcolors = self.neuralfield(batch['rays']) # Shape: [numrays, 3] totalloss = 0 for i in range(len(batch['rays'])): shutterspeed = batch['shutterspeeds'][i] shutteridx = batch['shutterspeedindices'][i] target = batch['targets'][i] # Get scaled color scaledcolor = self.getexposurescaledcolor(rawcolors[i:i+1], shutteridx) # Compute loss loss = self.computeloss(scaledcolor, target, shutteridx, shutterspeed) totalloss += loss totalloss.backward() self.optimizer.step() self.scheduler.step() Parameters Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: Decays from 10^{-3} to 10^{-5} over 500k steps. Batch Size: 16k random rays. Log Tonemap Epsilon: \epsilon = 10^{-3}. Exposure Constraint: \alpha{t{max}} = 1. Input Count: 25–200 images per scene. Shutter Speeds: Simulated speeds include 1/7, 1/15, 1/30, 1/60, 1/120, 1/240 seconds. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Sensor Miscalibration: Varying exposures cannot be precisely aligned using shutter speed alone due to sensor miscalibration. This is corrected by the learned per-color-channel scaling factor \alpha{tc}. LDR Bias: Training on LDR images corrupts the noise distribution, causing NeRF to recover incorrect colors in dark regions and clip highlights. RawNeRF avoids this by training on raw data. Preprocessing: Applying single-image denoisers to inputs before training RawNeRF results in oversmoothed renderings. Wide Baseline: RawNeRF handles wide-baseline captures where camera movement is larger than in typical burst video, unlike multi-image denoisers that assume small motion. Time Complexity: Optimization requires 500k steps of gradient descent on batches of 16k rays. Memory Complexity: Depends on the NeRF architecture and the number of training images stored for pose calculation. Raw images are large (12MP), requiring significant storage. Measured Performance: On a real dataset with 101 noisy images, RawNeRF achieved a PSNR of 28.76 at 1/240s simulated shutter speed, compared to LDR NeRF's 14.51. In synthetic ablation on the Lego scene with 120 training images, RawNeRF achieved 32.11 PSNR at 1/240s shutter speed, while LDR NeRF achieved 18.27. On affine-aligned sRGB, RawNeRF achieved PSNR 23.53, SSIM 0.536, and LPIPS 0.501, outperforming LDR NeRF (PSNR 19.43) and Un+RawNeRF (PSNR 23.35). Strengths: Robust to noise; recovers HDR information; enables post-processing (exposure, focus, tonemapping); handles wide-baseline captures. Limitations: Requires raw images (large storage); dependent on COLMAP for pose estimation (fails in very low light); cannot handle dynamic scenes. When to Use: High dynamic range view synthesis, denoising scenes captured in near-darkness, HDR view synthesis tasks like changing focus and exposure. When Not to Use: When storage is limited; when camera poses cannot be reliably estimated by COLMAP; for dynamic scenes. RawNeRF was introduced by Mildenhall et al. in November 2021. It adapts Mip-NeRF to train directly on linear raw HDR input data, exploiting NeRF's robustness to zero-mean noise distribution when aggregated across frames. The method was developed to address the limitations of standard NeRF, which uses tonemapped LDR images that clip highlights and bias dark regions. It is used for high dynamic range view synthesis and denoising. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28 NeRF in the Dark: High Dynamic Range View Synthesis from Noisy Raw Images, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.01571, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Neural Duplex Radiance Field
head: Duplex Radiance Field
body: The Neural Duplex Radiance Field is a real-time view synthesis method that replaces dense volumetric ray marching with a two-surface proxy representation. It solves the computational bottleneck of evaluating deep MLPs for every sample point by learning to map the two endpoints of a ray segment (defined by intersections with inner and outer meshes) and the view direction to the final pixel color. It sets itself apart from its parent NeRF Network Query with Hashed Embeddings by abandoning per-point MLP queries in favor of vertex-attached features interpolated via hardware rasterization, and from siblings like HybridNeRF Model Architecture by relying on explicit mesh proxies rather than hybrid voxel/grid structures for the primary geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pretrained NeRF density field (used to generate proxies), camera parameters (view direction \mathbf{d}), and two proxy meshes (inner \mathcal{T}i and outer \mathcal{T}o). Output: Pixel color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Data Structures: 1. Inner Mesh (\mathcal{T}i): Extracted from the density field using a threshold of 10^{-4}. Contains vertices Vi and triangles Ti. 2. Outer Mesh (\mathcal{T}o): Extracted from the density field using a threshold of 10^{-2}. Contains vertices Vo and triangles To. 3. Vertex Features: Each vertex vk in both meshes has an associated learnable feature vector \mathbf{f}k \in \mathbb{R}^N. N=20 for CUDA implementation. N=8 for WebGL implementation. Numbered Steps: 1. Mesh Extraction: Extract \mathcal{T}i and \mathcal{T}o from a pretrained NeRF density field using marching cubes at the specified density thresholds. 2. Feature Initialization: Initialize learnable feature vectors \mathbf{f}k for every vertex vk in \mathcal{T}i and \mathcal{T}o. 3. Ray Intersection: For each pixel, cast a ray with direction \mathbf{d}. Compute the depth-sorted intersection points \mathbf{x}1 with the outer mesh \mathcal{T}o and \mathbf{x}2 with the inner mesh \mathcal{T}i. 4. Feature Interpolation: For each intersection point \mathbf{x} \in \{\mathbf{x}1, \mathbf{x}2\}, determine the containing triangle and compute barycentric coordinates. Interpolate the vertex features to obtain \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}). This is performed via hardware rasterization. 5. Color Aggregation: Pass the interpolated features and view direction through a shallow aggregation network F\Theta to predict the color. Formula: The rendering equation is defined as: \mathbf{c} = F{\Theta}(\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}1), \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}2), \mathbf{d}) where: \mathbf{x}1 \in \mathcal{T}o is the intersection with the outer mesh. \mathbf{x}2 \in \mathcal{T}i is the intersection with the inner mesh. \mathbf{d} is the view direction vector. F{\Theta} is a shallow network (3-layer convolutional network in CUDA, simplified in WebGL). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, innermesh, outermesh, aggregationnet): """ Renders a single ray using the Neural Duplex Radiance Field. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector (x, y, z) raydirection: 3D vector (x, y, z), normalized innermesh: Object containing vertices Vi, triangles Ti, and features Fi outermesh: Object containing vertices Vo, triangles To, and features Fo aggregationnet: Function FTheta taking (f1, f2, d) -> color Returns: color: 3D vector (R, G, B) """ # Step 1: Find intersections with outer mesh # Returns intersection point x1 and barycentric coordinates (u, v, w) # If no intersection, x1 is None x1, bary1 = raytriangleintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, outermesh) # Step 2: Find intersections with inner mesh # Returns intersection point x2 and barycentric coordinates (u, v, w) # If no intersection, x2 is None x2, bary2 = raytriangleintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, innermesh) # Step 3: Interpolate features # Initialize feature vectors to zero or a default value if intersection fails f1 = zeros(N) f2 = zeros(N) if x1 is not None: # Interpolate features from outer mesh vertices using barycentric coords f1 = interpolatefeatures(outermesh.vertices, outermesh.features, x1, bary1) if x2 is not None: # Interpolate features from inner mesh vertices using barycentric coords f2 = interpolatefeatures(innermesh.vertices, innermesh.features, x2, bary2) # Step 4: Aggregate color # The aggregation network handles cases where one intersection is missing # by relying on the view direction and available features color = aggregationnet(f1, f2, raydirection) return color def raytriangleintersection(origin, direction, mesh): """ Finds the closest intersection of a ray with any triangle in the mesh. Returns the intersection point and barycentric coordinates. """ closestdist = infinity closestpoint = None closestbary = None for triangle in mesh.triangles: # Perform ray-triangle intersection test dist, barycentric = intersectraytriangle(origin, direction, triangle) if dist is not None and dist < closestdist: closestdist = dist closestpoint = origin + direction dist closestbary = barycentric return closestpoint, closestbary def interpolatefeatures(vertices, features, point, barycentric): """ Interpolates feature vector using barycentric coordinates. """ # barycentric is (w0, w1, w2) corresponding to vertices 0, 1, 2 v0, v1, v2 = vertices[0], vertices[1], vertices[2] f0, f1, f2 = features[0], features[1], features[2] return f0 barycentric[0] + f1 barycentric[1] + f2 barycentric[2] Parameters: Feature Dimension (N): 20 (CUDA), 8 (WebGL). Inner Mesh Density Threshold: 10^{-4}. Outer Mesh Density Threshold: 10^{-2}. Aggregation Network: 3-layer convolutional network (CUDA); simplified network without final convolution layer (WebGL). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Missing Intersections: Not all rays hit both proxy surfaces. The view direction \mathbf{d} is appended to the input of F\Theta to allow the network to handle cases where one intersection is missing. Occlusion Artifacts: Local sampling around a single surface suffers from missing geometry or visible occlusions, leading to hole artifacts. The duplex field mitigates this by learning to combine locations on two estimated surfaces. High-Frequency Artifacts: Training from scratch fails to match the fidelity of original NeRFs. Multi-view distillation from a pretrained teacher model (e.g., TensoRF) is required to guide optimization. Time Complexity: O(1) per ray for feature lookup and aggregation, dominated by rasterization and ray-triangle intersection. Significantly faster than dense volumetric sampling O(N) where N is the number of samples. Memory Complexity: O(V) where V is the number of vertices in the proxy meshes. Much lower than storing dense voxel grids or large hash tables for every sample point. Performance: On an NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti, achieves real-time FPS (specific FPS values depend on resolution and scene complexity, but cited as comparable to KiloNeRF/SNeRG in terms of efficiency class). WebGL implementation offers cross-platform compatibility with some performance degradation. Strengths: Real-time rendering capability, reduced memory footprint compared to dense volumetric methods, handles view-dependent appearance via the aggregation network. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the proxy meshes; poor mesh extraction leads to artifacts. Requires a pretrained teacher model for stable training. May struggle with complex internal structures not captured by the two surface proxies. When to use: Real-time view synthesis where high fidelity is needed but dense volumetric rendering is too slow. When not to use: Scenes with highly complex internal geometry that cannot be approximated by two surfaces, or when training from scratch without distillation is required. The Neural Duplex Radiance Field was introduced in "Learning Neural Duplex Radiance Fields for Real-Time View Synthesis" (CVPR 2023). It addresses the computational cost of densely evaluating deep MLPs in NeRF-based methods. By leveraging two geometric proxy meshes and hardware rasterization, it enables real-time rendering. The method builds on the concept of using explicit geometry to guide neural rendering, contrasting with implicit volumetric approaches. It uses multi-view distillation from a pretrained teacher model (like TensoRF) to overcome the lack of high-frequency details when training from scratch. name: Chunked Network Evaluation
head: Batched NeRF Evaluation, Neural Network Chunking
body: Chunked Network Evaluation is a memory-management technique that evaluates a NeRF network on batched points in chunks to avoid out-of-memory errors during training or rendering. It partitions the total set of query points into smaller subsets processed sequentially, rather than attempting to process all points in a single forward pass. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: pts (tensor of shape (N{rays}, N{samples}, 3)), viewdirs (tensor of shape (N{rays}, 1, 3)), model (the NeRF network function), and netchunk (integer specifying the maximum number of points per chunk). Outputs: rgb (tensor of shape (N{rays}, N{samples}, 3)) and sigma (tensor of shape (N{rays}, N{samples}, 1)). Data Structures: allrgb and allsigma: Lists of tensors storing intermediate results from each chunk. Steps: 1. Flatten Inputs: Reshape pts and viewdirs into 2D tensors where the first dimension is the total number of points (N{total} = N{rays} \times N{samples}). pts{flat} = pts.reshape(-1, 3) viewdirs{flat} = viewdirs[:, None,:].expandas(pts).reshape(-1, 3) 2. Initialize Storage: Create empty lists allrgb and allsigma to store results from each chunk. 3. Iterate and Evaluate: Loop through the flattened points in steps of netchunk. For each chunk index i: Extract chunkpts from ptsflat[i: i + netchunk] and chunkdirs from viewdirsflat[i: i + netchunk]. Call model(chunkpts, chunkdirs) to get chunkrgb and chunksigma. Append chunkrgb to allrgb and chunksigma to allsigma. 4. Concatenate and Reshape: Concatenate all lists along dimension 0 and reshape back to the original 3D structure. rgb = concatenate(all\rgb, dim=0).reshape(N{rays}, N{samples}, 3) sigma = concatenate(all\sigma, dim=0).reshape(N{rays}, N{samples}, 1) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def chunkednetworkevaluation(pts, viewdirs, model, netchunk): ptsflat = pts.reshape(-1, 3) viewdirsflat = viewdirs[:, None,:].expandas(pts).reshape(-1, 3) Ntotal = ptsflat.shape[0] allrgb = [] allsigma = [] for i in range(0, Ntotal, netchunk): chunkpts = ptsflat[i: i + netchunk] chunkdirs = viewdirsflat[i: i + netchunk] chunkrgb, chunksigma = model(chunkpts, chunkdirs) allrgb.append(chunkrgb) allsigma.append(chunksigma) rgb = concatenate(allrgb, dim=0).reshape(pts.shape[0], pts.shape[1], 3) sigma = concatenate(allsigma, dim=0).reshape(pts.shape[0], pts.shape[1], 1) return rgb, sigma def concatenate(tensors, dim=0): # Standard tensor concatenation along dimension dim return tensors[0] if len(tensors) == 1 else tensors[0] + sum(tensors[1:], tensors[0]) Parameters: netchunk: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. A variant used in Point-NeRF to compute volume density for rays by querying a neural network with ray points and pre-computed density features, processed in chunks to manage memory. It differs from standard chunked evaluation by incorporating pre-computed features (densityfeature) into the query function. Definition: Computes density for rays in a Point-NeRF by querying a neural network with ray points and pre-computed density features, processed in chunks. Steps: 1. Initialize an empty list densities and determine the device from densityfeature. 2. Iterate over rayspts in chunks of size chunk (default 5120). 3. For each chunk index i, extract inputfeat = rayspts[i:i + chunk] and move it to the device. 4. Call networkqueryfn with inputfeat, None, densityfeature[i:i + chunk], and networkfn to get the density for the current chunk, and append it to densities. 5. Concatenate all density tensors in the densities list along the default dimension and return the result. Time Complexity: O(N{rays} \times N{samples}). Memory Complexity: O(netchunk) for the network inputs and outputs, instead of O(N{rays} \times N{samples}). Strengths: Enables processing large point sets without exceeding memory limits. Limitations: Sequential processing introduces loop overhead compared to a single forward pass. When to use: When the full batch of points exceeds available memory. Chunked Network Evaluation appears in open-source NeRF implementations and tutorials, such as "NeRF from Scratch". The technique is also adapted in variants like Point-NeRF, where it is used to manage memory during density queries with pre-computed features. damn8daniel/nerf-from-scratch, https://github.com/damn8daniel/nerf-from-scratch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Xharlie/pointnerf, https://github.com/Xharlie/pointnerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Point-NeRF Density Query
head: Chunked Density Query
body: A method to compute volume density for rays in a Point-NeRF by querying a neural network with ray points and pre-computed density features, processed in chunks to manage memory. It builds on Chunked Network Evaluation by specifically handling the density component of the radiance field query, separating it from RGB or feature queries to optimize memory usage during training. Inputs and Outputs: Input: rayspts (tensor of sample points along rays), densityfeature (pre-computed density features corresponding to the points), chunk (integer, default 5120), networkqueryfn (callable that queries the network), networkfn (network function). Output: Tensor of density values for all input points. Data Structures: rayspts: Tensor of shape (N, D), where N is the number of sample points and D is the spatial dimension (typically 3). densityfeature: Tensor of shape (N, Fd), where Fd is the dimension of the density feature. densities: List of tensors, each of shape (C, 1) or (C,), where C is the chunk size. Steps: 1. Initialize an empty list densities. 2. Determine the device (CPU/GPU) from the densityfeature tensor. 3. Iterate over rayspts in chunks of size chunk. For each chunk index i: a. Extract inputfeat = rayspts[i:i + chunk]. b. Move inputfeat to the device. c. Extract densityfeatchunk = densityfeature[i:i + chunk]. d. Call networkqueryfn(inputfeat, None, densityfeatchunk, networkfn) to get the density for the current chunk. e. Append the result to densities. 4. Concatenate all tensors in densities along the default dimension (usually the first dimension) and return the result. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pointnerfdensityquery(rayspts, densityfeature, chunk=5120, networkqueryfn=None, networkfn=None): """ Compute volume density for rays in a Point-NeRF using chunked evaluation. Args: rayspts: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing sample points along rays. densityfeature: Tensor of shape (N, Fd) containing pre-computed density features. chunk: Integer, size of chunks for processing (default 5120). networkqueryfn: Callable that queries the network for density. networkfn: The neural network function. Returns: Tensor of density values for all input points. """ densities = [] device = densityfeature.device # Iterate over rayspts in chunks for i in range(0, rayspts.shape[0], chunk): # Extract chunk of points inputfeat = rayspts[i:i + chunk].to(device) # Extract corresponding density features densityfeatchunk = densityfeature[i:i + chunk].to(device) # Query network for density # Note: The exact signature of networkqueryfn may vary, but it typically takes # input features, optional other features (None here), density features, and the network. chunkdensity = networkqueryfn(inputfeat, None, densityfeatchunk, networkfn) # Append to list densities.append(chunkdensity) # Concatenate all density tensors if densities: return torch.cat(densities, dim=0) else: return torch.empty((0, 1), device=device) Parameters: chunk: Default value is 5120 (1024 5). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If rayspts is empty, the function should return an empty tensor. Precision issues may arise if the density values are very small or very large; ensure appropriate data types are used. Boundary conditions for the last chunk (if the total number of points is not a multiple of chunk) are handled by slicing, which naturally handles the remainder. A helper function used by ray marching to query density and optionally RGB at sample points along rays. It converts rayindices to long type, extracts ray origins and directions, computes sample positions as the midpoint between tstarts and tends along the ray direction, queries geometry for density (and feature if needed), and returns density as a tensor with an extra dimension. This function is used to return both RGB and density for use in rendering. Time and Memory Complexity: Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of sample points, as each point is processed once in a chunked manner. Memory Complexity: O(C), where C is the chunk size, as only a chunk of points and features is processed at a time. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of sample points. Chunk size can be adjusted to balance memory usage and processing speed. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Efficient memory usage due to chunked processing, suitable for large-scale Point-NeRF training. Limitations: May introduce slight overhead due to chunking and concatenation. When to Use: Use when training Point-NeRF models with large numbers of sample points to avoid out-of-memory errors. When Not to Use: Not suitable for scenarios where memory is not a constraint and simpler, non-chunked evaluation is preferred for simplicity. Originated in the Point-NeRF project by Xharlie. It is used in the context of differentiable and inverse volume rendering, specifically in radiance-field optimization procedures. The method is part of the NeRF Training Loop, focusing on training ray marching and integration, and is an extension of chunked network evaluation techniques. name: Differentiable Volume Rendering Pipeline
body: The Differentiable Volume Rendering Pipeline orchestrates the training loop for Neural Radiance Fields by generating rays, sampling points through an implicit volume, evaluating the neural network, and aggregating results via differentiable alpha compositing. It solves the problem of optimizing 3D scene representations from 2D images by computing gradients of the rendered image loss with respect to network parameters. It differs from standard volume rendering by explicitly maintaining the computational graph through the sampling and integration steps to enable end-to-end backpropagation. Inputs: Camera parameters (intrinsics, extrinsics) for a batch of views. Ground truth images Ci for the corresponding pixel coordinates. Neural network model (implicit volume representation) with parameters \theta. Sampler configuration (number of samples per ray, hierarchical sampling settings). Training configuration cfg.training.batchsize (N), defining the number of random pixels sampled per iteration. Outputs: Rendered feature/color images \hat{C}i. Rendered depth maps. Data Structures: Ray Bundle: A tensor of shape (N, 3) containing the origin and direction for each ray in the batch. Sample Points: A tensor of shape (N, K, 3) containing the 3D coordinates of K samples along each ray. Network Outputs: Tensors of shape (N, K, 4) containing the predicted color (RGB) and density (\sigma) for each sample. Steps: 1. Ray Generation: Loop over cameras, generate NDC grids, and create ray bundles. 2. Sampling: Pass the ray bundle through model.sampler to generate sample points. 3. Network Evaluation: Call model(raybundle) to evaluate the implicit volume and aggregate results. 4. Alpha Compositing: Compute transmittance Tk and weight wk for each sample: \deltak = t{k+1} - tk \hat{\sigma}k = \sigmak \deltak \alphak = 1 - \exp(-\hat{\sigma}k) Tk = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{k-1} \hat{\sigma}j\right) wk = \alphak Tk The rendered color \hat{C} is the weighted sum: \hat{C} = \sum{k=1}^{K} wk \mathbf{c}k 5. Loss Calculation: Compute the loss between the rendered color \hat{C}i and the ground truth color Ci for the batch of N pixels: \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (\hat{C}i - Ci)^2 6. Reshape & Return: Extract rendered features and depth, reshape to image dimensions, and save/return them. Parameters: cfg.training.batchsize (N): Number of random pixels sampled per training iteration. Controls memory usage and gradient noise. Number of samples per ray (K): Typically 64–256. Learning rate: Typically 10^{-4} to 10^{-3}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting: If the network is too expressive or view-dependence is not handled carefully, it may overfit to training images. Precision: Floating-point precision in transmittance calculation can lead to artifacts if not handled correctly (Standard practice: clamp \hat{\sigma}k or use log-space accumulation). Boundaries: Rays intersecting the bounding box of the scene must be clipped (Standard practice: use near/far planes or AABB intersection). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderimages(model, cameras, gtimages, cfg): """ Orchestrates the differentiable volume rendering pipeline. """ batchsize = cfg.training.batchsize renderedimages = [] depthmaps = [] totalloss = 0.0 for cam in cameras: # 1. Ray Generation raybundle = generateraybundle(cam, batchsize) # 2. Sampling samplepoints = model.sampler(raybundle) # 3. Network Evaluation colors, densities = model(samplepoints) # 4. Alpha Compositing deltas = [] for i in range(len(samplepoints) - 1): deltas.append([samplepoints[i+1][j] - samplepoints[i][j] for j in range(3)]) deltas.append(deltas[-1]) dists = [math.sqrt(sum(d2 for d in delta)) for delta in deltas] sigmadeltas = [densities[i] dists[i] for i in range(len(dists))] alphas = [1.0 - math.exp(-s) for s in sigmadeltas] transmittances = [] t = 1.0 for a in alphas: transmittances.append(t) t = (1.0 - a) weights = [a t for a, t in zip(alphas, transmittances)] renderedcolors = [sum(w c for w, c in zip(weights, colors[i])) for i in range(len(colors))] rendereddepth = sum(w p[2] for w, p in zip(weights, samplepoints)) # 5. Loss Calculation gtcolors = samplegtcolors(gtimages, raybundle) loss = sum((rc - gc)2 for rc, gc in zip(renderedcolors, gtcolors)) / len(gtcolors) totalloss += loss renderedimages.append(renderedcolors) depthmaps.append(rendereddepth) # 6. Reshape & Return renderedimages = reshapetoimage(renderedimages, cameras) depthmaps = reshapetoimage(depthmaps, cameras) return renderedimages, depthmaps, totalloss / len(cameras) def generateraybundle(cam, batchsize): return [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(batchsize)] def samplegtcolors(gtimages, raybundle): return [[1.0, 1.0, 1.0] for in range(len(raybundle))] def reshapetoimage(images, cameras): return images A method to optimize camera poses and NeRF parameters jointly by using event data as a constraint to model non-uniform camera motion during exposure. It differs from standard NeRF training by incorporating event cameras and motion blur constraints. Choose this method when dealing with scenes captured with event cameras or significant motion blur. It renders virtual sharp images C(Ti, x) for each learnable pose Ti. Converts rendered colors to grayscale G(Ti, x) by averaging RGB channels. Transforms to log domain \mathcal{L}(Ti, x). Computes event loss \mathcal{L}{event} by comparing simulated events \hat{E} with real events E. Computes blur loss \mathcal{L}{blur} by comparing simulated blurry image \hat{B} with input blurry image B. Optimizes NeRF parameters \theta and learnable poses Ti by minimizing the final loss \mathcal{L}{total}. Simulated events are \hat{E}(x, ti, t{i+1}) = \frac{\mathcal{L}(T{i+1}, x) - \mathcal{L}(Ti, x)}{\Theta} with sign handling. Event loss is \mathcal{L}{event} = \frac{1}{m(p-1)} \sum{i=1}^{p-1} \sum{x \in X} \| \hat{E}(x, ti, t{i+1}) - E(x, ti, t{i+1}) \|2^2. Blur loss is \mathcal{L}{blur} = \frac{1}{m} \sum{x \in X} \| \hat{B}(x) - B(x) \|2^2. Final loss is \mathcal{L}{total} = \lambda \mathcal{L}{event} + \mathcal{L}{blur}^f + \mathcal{L}{blur}^c. Gradients are computed via chain rule: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}{event}}{\partial \theta} = \frac{1}{m} \sum{x \in X} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}{event}}{\partial \hat{E}(x)} \frac{\partial \hat{E}(x)}{\partial C(x)} \frac{\partial C(x)}{\partial \theta}. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with cfg.training.batchsize (number of random pixels sampled per iteration). Strengths: End-to-end differentiable rendering pipeline. Limitations: Computationally expensive, prone to overfitting if not regularized. When to use: Training NeRF from images, handling motion blur with event data. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The Differentiable Volume Rendering Pipeline is based on the NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) method proposed by Mildenhall et al. in 2020. It has been extended to handle event cameras and motion blur through methods like Event-Driven Bundle Adjustment (EBAD). It is widely used in 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis. samirangode/Volume-Rendering-and-Neural-Radiance-Fields, https://github.com/samirangode/Volume-Rendering-and-Neural-Radiance-Fields, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Deblurring Neural Radiance Fields with Event-driven Bundle Adjustment, https://doi.org/10.1145/3664647.3680569, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Active Learning Strategy for NeRF Distillation
head: Important camera poses selection, Important sample points selection, Important sample rays selection, PVD-AL active learning
body: This method bridges the performance gap between teacher and student Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) models during knowledge distillation by actively selecting challenging camera poses, sample rays, and sample points rather than processing all data uniformly. It distinguishes itself from standard uniform distillation by dynamically prioritizing difficult samples based on loss metrics, enabling student models to outperform those trained from scratch. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Teacher NeRF model, Student NeRF model, batch of training rays, camera poses, and hyperparameters for selection percentages and loss weights. Outputs: Updated Student NeRF parameters; sets of selected important poses, rays, and points for the next iteration. Data Structures lossrgb: Tensor of shape (Nrays,) storing the L2 loss per ray between teacher and student RGB outputs. lossimg: Tensor of shape (Nposes,) storing the accumulated image-level loss. Wt, Ws: Vectors of point weights for teacher and student, respectively, derived from density and distance. TSP: Set of indices for important sample points. TSR: Set of indices for important sample rays. TCP: Set of indices for important camera poses. Formulas The weight W^ for a sampling point i along a ray with N points is calculated as: W^ = \sum{i=1}^{N} (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) where \sigmai is the density and \deltai is the distance interval at point i. The density loss L{\sigma^2} constrains the numerical range of density \sigma to [a, b] for both teacher (\sigmat) and student (\sigmas): L{\sigma^2} = \| \min(\max(\sigmat, a), b) - \min(\max(\sigmas, a), b) \|2 This restriction avoids optimizing \sigma directly on \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), which is inefficient due to gradient saturation and high exponential computation cost during block-wise implementation. Parameters Distillation Loss Rates: Volume-aligned: 2 \times 10^{-3}, Density: 2 \times 10^{-3}, Color: 2 \times 10^{-3}, RGB: 1. Important Rays Percentage: 10\% of rays selected per iteration. Important Points Percentage: 30\% of sample points selected per iteration. Important Poses Percentage: 10\% of camera poses selected per epoch. Training Schedule: Stage 1 (3k steps), Stage 2 (5k steps), Stage 3 (remaining steps). Active learning is incorporated after Stages 1 and 2. Algorithm The active learning strategy operates within the training loop as follows: 1. Forward Pass & Loss Calculation: Compute the RGB loss between teacher and student outputs: \text{loss\rgb} = \text{L2}(\text{tea\out}['\text{rgb}'], \text{stu\out}['\text{rgb}']). Compute other losses (e.g., density, sigma) using the constrained density loss formula. 2. Record Image-Level Loss: Accumulate ray losses to their corresponding image indices: \text{loss\img}[\text{RaysMapToImgIdx}(\text{batch\rays})] += \text{loss\rgb}. 3. Backward Pass: Perform the optimization step. 4. Select Important Sample Rays (TSR): Sort rays by lossrgb in descending order. Select the top N{sr} rays (where N{sr} is 10\% of total rays) as important rays. 5. Select Important Camera Poses (TCP): Sort camera poses by lossimg in descending order. Select the top N{cp} poses (where N{cp} is 10\% of total poses) as important poses for the next epoch. 6. Select Important Sample Points (TSP): Calculate point weights W^ for both teacher and student using the density and distance. Concatenate teacher weights Wt and student weights Ws. Select the top N{sp} points (where N{sp} is 30\% of total sample points) with the largest combined weight values as important points. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def activelearningstep(teachermodel, studentmodel, batchrays, poses, hyperparams): # 1. Forward pass and loss calculation teaout = teachermodel(batchrays) stuout = studentmodel(batchrays) # Per-ray L2 loss between teacher and student RGB outputs lossrgb = [] for tr, sr in zip(teaout['rgb'], stuout['rgb']): lossrgb.append(sum((t - s) 2 for t, s in zip(tr, sr)) / len(tr)) # Density loss using constrained range [a, b] to avoid exp saturation a, b = hyperparams['sigmamin'], hyperparams['sigmamax'] teasigmac = [min(max(s, a), b) for s in teaout['sigma']] stusigmac = [min(max(s, a), b) for s in stuout['sigma']] lossdensity = sum((t - s) 2 for t, s in zip(teasigmac, stusigmac)) / len(teasigmac) # Other losses (volume-aligned, color) combined with specified rates lossother = lossdensity hyperparams['ratedensity'] # 2. Record image-level loss lossimg = [0.0] len(poses) for rayidx, poseidx in enumerate(batchrays['poseindices']): lossimg[poseidx] += lossrgb[rayidx] # 3. Backward pass totalloss = sum(lossrgb) hyperparams['ratergb'] + lossother optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() # 4. Select Important Sample Rays (TSR) sortedrayindices = sorted(range(len(lossrgb)), key=lambda i: lossrgb[i], reverse=True) nrays = len(batchrays) nimportantrays = int(nrays hyperparams['pctrays']) # 10% importantrayindices = sortedrayindices[:nimportantrays] # 5. Select Important Camera Poses (TCP) sortedposeindices = sorted(range(len(lossimg)), key=lambda i: lossimg[i], reverse=True) nposes = len(poses) nimportantposes = int(nposes hyperparams['pctposes']) # 10% importantposeindices = sortedposeindices[:nimportantposes] # 6. Select Important Sample Points (TSP) # Calculate point weights W = 1 - exp(-sigma delta) per point teaweights = [1.0 - math.exp(-teaout['sigma'][i] batchrays['delta'][i]) for i in range(len(teaout['sigma']))] stuweights = [1.0 - math.exp(-stuout['sigma'][i] batchrays['delta'][i]) for i in range(len(stuout['sigma']))] # Concatenate weights combinedweights = teaweights + stuweights # Select top N points npoints = len(teaweights) nimportantpoints = int(npoints hyperparams['pctpoints']) # 30% sortedpointindices = sorted(range(len(combinedweights)), key=lambda i: combinedweights[i], reverse=True) importantpointindices = sortedpointindices[:nimportantpoints] return { 'importantrays': importantrayindices, 'importantposes': importantposeindices, 'importantpoints': importantpointindices } Edge Cases and Pitfalls Gradient Saturation: Optimizing \sigma directly on \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) is inefficient because the gradient of the exponential function saturates easily, and computing exponentials increases calculation cost during block-wise implementation. The constrained density loss L{\sigma^2} is used to avoid this. Time Complexity: The active learning strategy adds overhead for sorting rays, poses, and points, and calculating point weights. By focusing computation on a subset of important samples (10% rays, 30% points), it improves the signal-to-noise ratio of gradient updates. Memory Complexity: Requires storing loss tensors for all rays and poses, and weight tensors for all sample points. This is O(N{rays}) and O(N{points}) respectively. Performance: PVD-AL yields student models that outperform those trained from scratch, breaking the upper limit of student capabilities. Strengths: Bridges the performance gap between teacher and student models; effectively transfers knowledge by focusing on challenging cases; flexible as a plugin for various methods. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained teacher model; adds complexity to the training loop with selection logic; performance depends on the quality of the teacher model. When to use: When distilling knowledge from a high-capacity teacher to a lower-capacity student, especially when the student struggles with specific views or details. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and the overhead of selection is prohibitive, or when the teacher model is not significantly better than the student. The method originates from the "Progressive Volume Distillation with Active Learning for Efficient NeRF Architecture Conversion" paper. It was developed to address the inefficiencies and performance gaps in NeRF architecture conversion via distillation. The authors found that uniformly sampling data for distillation leads to suboptimal student performance, particularly under certain camera poses. By actively selecting challenging poses, rays, and points, the method improves the student's understanding of crucial knowledge. The approach has been validated on benchmark datasets using NVIDIA V100 GPUs, demonstrating significant advantages in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS metrics. Progressive Volume Distillation with Active Learning for Efficient NeRF Architecture Conversion, https://doi.org/10.1007/s11263-026-02815-1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Direct Matching Alignment Loss
head: Direct Alignment
body: Direct Matching Alignment Loss (L{align}) is a regularization term used during NeRF training to align a reference image with a set of surrogate views, thereby reducing overfitting and improving pose estimation accuracy. Unlike standard rendering losses that only compare rendered pixels against ground truth, this method enforces geometric consistency between different camera viewpoints by projecting 3D points from a reference view into surrogate views and comparing their appearance. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Reference image Ir with pixel domain \Omega(Ir), camera intrinsics K (3 \times 3), rotation Rr (3 \times 3), translation \mathbf{t}r (3 \times 1); set of surrogate views \mathcal{N}r with poses (K, Rs, \mathbf{t}s); NeRF model parameters \Theta for depth estimation; depth threshold \deltad; Huber parameter \epsilon. Outputs: Scalar loss value L{align}. Data Structures: Pixel coordinates \mathbf{u} = [u, v]^T. Estimated depth \bar{d}(\mathbf{u}) (scalar). Image intensities \mathcal{I}r(\mathbf{u}), \mathcal{I}s(\mathbf{u}s) (RGB vectors). Numbered Steps: 1. Sample Reference Frame and Points: Randomly select a reference frame r from the training set and pixel coordinates \mathbf{u} \in \Omega(Ir). Unless specified, the entire training set serves as \mathcal{N}r. 2. Estimate Reference Depth: Compute \bar{d}(\mathbf{u}) as the weighted sum of sampled depths d{sample} along the ray, weighted by the ray termination distribution h: \bar{d}(\mathbf{u}) = \sum {d{sample}} h(\mathbf{u},d{sample}) d{sample} 3. Project to Surrogate View: For each surrogate view s \in \mathcal{N}r, compute the corresponding pixel coordinate \mathbf{u}s by back-projecting \mathbf{u} to 3D using \bar{d}(\mathbf{u}), transforming to the surrogate camera frame, and projecting back to 2D: \mathbf{u}s = \Pi \left( K Rs \left( R{r}^{-1} K^{-1} [\mathbf{u}, 1]^T \bar {d}(\mathbf{u}) - \mathbf{t}r \right) + \mathbf{t}s \right) where \Pi ([X,Y,Z]^T) = [X/Z, Y/Z]^T. 4. Check Occlusion (Visibility Indicator): Determine visibility using \mathcal{V}(\mathbf{u}s,\mathbf{u}): \mathcal{V}(\mathbf{u}s,\mathbf{u}) = \mathbbm {1}[ \bar {d}(\mathbf{u}s) < \mathcal {T}s (\mathbf{u}, \bar {d}(\mathbf{u})) - \delta d ] where \mathcal {T}s (\mathbf{u}, \bar {d}(\mathbf{u})) is the depth of the projected 3D point in the surrogate camera frame, calculated as the Z-component of the transformed point: \mathcal {T}s (\mathbf{u}, \bar {d}(\mathbf{u})) = \omega \left( K \left( Rs \left( R{r}^{-1} K^{-1} [\mathbf{u}, 1]^T \bar {d}(\mathbf{u}) - \mathbf{t}r \right) + \mathbf{t}s \right) \right) and \omega ([X,Y,Z]^T) = Z. 5. Compute Alignment Loss: Sum the Huber penalty between \mathcal{I}{r}(\mathbf{u}) and \mathcal{I}s (\mathbf{u}s), weighted by visibility: L{align} = \sum {r=1}^{F} \sum {s \in \mathcal {N}r} \sum {\mathbf {u} \in \Omega (Ir)} \mathcal {V}(\mathbf {u}s,\mathbf {u}) \| \mathcal {I}s (\mathbf {u}s) - \mathcal {I}{r}(\mathbf {u}) \|\epsilon where \| \cdot \|\epsilon is the Huber penalty. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computedirectalignmentloss(Ir, K, Rr, tr, surrogateviews, nerfmodel, deltad, epsilon): """Computes Direct Matching Alignment Loss per.""" totalloss = 0.0 H, W = Ir.shape[:2] # Step 1: Sample pixels u on reference image for v in range(H): for u in range(W): # Step 2: Estimate depth d(u) dsamples = nerfmodel.getsampledepths((u, v), (K, Rr, tr)) hvalues = nerfmodel.getterminationdistribution((u, v), (K, Rr, tr)) dest = sum(h d for h, d in zip(hvalues, dsamples)) # Step 3: Project to surrogate view uhom = [u, v, 1.0] # Pcam = inv(K) @ uhom dest Pcam = vecscale(matvecmul(inv3x3(K), uhom), dest) # Pworld = Rr.T @ (Pcam - tr) Pworld = vecadd(vecscale(Rr.T, Pcam), vecscale(-Rr.T, tr)) for Is, Ks, Rs, ts in surrogateviews: # Transform to surrogate camera frame Pscam = vecadd(vecscale(Rs, Pworld), ts) if Pscam[2] <= 0: continue # Behind camera # Project to us us = [Pscam[0] / Pscam[2], Pscam[1] / Pscam[2]] if not isinbounds(us, Is.shape): continue # Step 4: Occlusion Reasoning # Ts is depth of projected point in surrogate frame Ts = Pscam[2] # Query NeRF at us in view s dsampless = nerfmodel.getsampledepths(us, (Ks, Rs, ts)) hvaluess = nerfmodel.getterminationdistribution(us, (Ks, Rs, ts)) dests = sum(h d for h, d in zip(hvaluess, dsampless)) vis = 1.0 if dests < (Ts - deltad) else 0.0 if vis > 0: # Step 5: Compute Loss Isus = bilinearsample(Is, us) Iru = Ir[v, u] diff = Isus - Iru totalloss += vis huberpenalty(diff, epsilon) return totalloss def huberpenalty(diff, epsilon): absdiff = abs(diff) return epsilon (absdiff - 0.5 epsilon) if absdiff > epsilon else 0.5 diff2 def bilinearsample(img, uv): u, v = uv u0, v0 = int(u), int(v) u1, v1 = min(u0 + 1, img.shape[1]-1), min(v0 + 1, img.shape[0]-1) wu, wv = u - u0, v - v0 top = img[v0, u0](1-wu) + img[v0, u1]wu bot = img[v1, u0](1-wu) + img[v1, u1]wu return top(1-wv) + botwv def isinbounds(uv, shape): return 0 <= uv[0] < shape[1] and 0 <= uv[1] < shape[0] def vecscale(M, v): return [sum(M[i][j]v[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] def vecadd(v1, v2): return [a+b for a,b in zip(v1, v2)] def inv3x3(M): # Standard 3x3 matrix inversion invdet = 1.0 / (M[0][0](M[1][1]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][1]) - M[0][1](M[1][0]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][0]) + M[0][2](M[1][0]M[2][1]-M[1][1]M[2][0])) return [ [(M[1][1]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][1])invdet, (M[0][2]M[2][1]-M[0][1]M[2][2])invdet, (M[0][1]M[1][2]-M[0][2]M[1][1])invdet], [(M[1][2]M[2][0]-M[1][0]M[2][2])invdet, (M[0][0]M[2][2]-M[0][2]M[2][0])invdet, (M[0][2]M[1][0]-M[0][0]M[1][2])invdet], [(M[1][0]M[2][1]-M[1][1]M[2][0])invdet, (M[0][1]M[2][0]-M[0][0]M[2][1])invdet, (M[0][0]M[1][1]-M[0][1]M[1][0])invdet] ] def matvecmul(M, v): return [sum(M[i][j]v[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] Parameters: \deltad: Depth threshold for occlusion reasoning. Value not given in the sources. \epsilon: Huber penalty parameter. Value not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The projected pixel \mathbf{u}s is defined as the projection of the intersection point of the two rays by definition, ensuring geometric consistency for the occlusion check. Floating-point inaccuracies in depth estimation or projection can lead to incorrect occlusion decisions. Boundaries: Projected pixels \mathbf{u}s may fall outside the image boundaries of the surrogate view; these should be handled by skipping the pixel or assigning zero visibility. Degenerate Input: If the estimated depth \bar{d}(\mathbf{u}) is zero or negative, the back-projection is invalid; such rays should be skipped. This variant explicitly models visibility between views using a depth-based indicator. It calculates the depth of the 3D point projected from the reference view into the surrogate view and compares it with the NeRF's estimated depth at the corresponding pixel in the surrogate view. If the surrogate view's surface is closer than the projected point (minus a threshold \deltad), the point is considered occluded and excluded from the loss. This prevents the loss from penalizing the model for correct occlusions where the reference point is hidden in the surrogate view. This variant aligns the real-time camera viewpoint with the reconstructed model's observation vector to enhance spatial coherence and immersion. The alignment objective is defined as the squared L2 norm of the difference between perspective projections of the camera viewpoint V{cam} and the NeRF observation vector V{NeRF}: L{align} = \| \text{Proj}(V{cam}) - \text{Proj}(V{NeRF}) \|^2 where \text{Proj}(\cdot) is the perspective projection function. V{cam} is the real-time camera viewpoint from the user device, and V{NeRF} is the observation vector of the reconstructed model. This optimization improves spatial coherence between the user viewpoint and the virtual model, particularly for mobile and AR-enabled devices. Time Complexity: The loss calculation is O(F \cdot |\mathcal{N}r| \cdot |\Omega(Ir)|), where F is the number of reference frames, |\mathcal{N}r| is the number of surrogate views, and |\Omega(Ir)| is the number of pixels sampled. Since the entire training set is often used as surrogate views, this can be computationally expensive. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the NeRF model and the training images, with no additional large data structures beyond the ray samples. Measured Performance: On the Fern sequence, using alignment increased PSNR from 23.06 to 24.50 and SSIM from 0.72 to 0.75. On the Trex sequence, it increased PSNR from 21.82 to 21.90 and SSIM from 0.76 to 0.78. Strengths: Reduces overfitting to training data, improves pose estimation, and enforces geometric consistency across views. Limitations: Computationally intensive due to cross-view projections and depth queries; relies on accurate depth estimation from the NeRF. When to use: When training NeRFs on datasets with significant overfitting or when pose estimation accuracy is critical. When not to use: When computational resources are limited or when the dataset is very large, making the O(N^2) cross-view comparison prohibitive. The Direct Matching Alignment Loss was proposed by R. Garg et al. in the paper "Direct Alignment for Robust NeRF Learning" presented at ACCV 2024. The work addresses the issue of NeRFs overfitting to training data, even with multiple views, by introducing a direct alignment term that encourages consistency between different camera viewpoints. The method builds on the standard NeRF rendering pipeline and integrates with the training loop using SGD. name: Volume Rendering Integration and Forward Pass
head: Alpha Compositing, Volume Rendering Integral Discretization, Ray Marching Integration
body: This family defines the forward pass that synthesizes a 2D image pixel color from a 3D implicit scene representation by integrating radiance along camera rays. It solves the problem of differentiable volume rendering by approximating the continuous volume rendering integral as a discrete weighted sum, where weights are determined by the probability of the ray terminating at each sample point. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like NeRF Evaluation and Metric Calculation by focusing strictly on the geometric integration and compositing logic rather than loss computation or metric evaluation. All methods in this family compute the expected color \hat{C}(r) for a ray r by discretizing the medium interaction interval into steps and accumulating emission weighted by transmittance. The core mathematical formulation relies on the Beer-Lambert law to convert volume density \sigma into opacity \alpha and transmittance T. The discrete volume rendering equation is: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci Where: N is the number of samples along the ray. \sigmai is the volume density at sample i. ci is the emitted color at sample i. \deltai is the distance between sample i and i+1. Ti is the accumulated transmittance up to sample i: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) is the opacity of sample i. Numerical Stability: To prevent NaNs during gradient computation, a small epsilon \epsilon (typically 10^{-10}) is added to (1 - \alphaj) before the cumulative product or exponential calculation. Background Handling: If a background color c{bg} (typically white (1,1,1)) is assumed, the final color includes the contribution of rays that pass through the scene without terminating: \hat{C}{final}(r) = \hat{C}(r) + \left(1 - \sum{i=1}^{N} wi\right) c{bg} where wi = \alphai Ti is the weight of sample i. Depth Estimation: Expected depth \hat{D}(r) is computed analogously to color: \hat{D}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi ti where ti is the distance of sample i from the camera origin. NeRF Rendering (Alpha Compositing) is the forward pass method that synthesizes a 2D image pixel color from a 3D implicit scene representation by integrating radiance along camera rays. It solves the problem of differentiable volume rendering by approximating the continuous volume rendering integral as a discrete weighted sum, where weights are determined by the probability of the ray terminating at each sample point. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like NeRF-style Volume Rendering Integrator by explicitly defining the standard multi-layer perceptron (MLP) query pipeline, stratified sampling strategy, and the specific alpha-compositing formulation (\alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) that underpins the original NeRF architecture. This method computes the expected color \hat{C}(r) for a ray r by discretizing the medium interaction interval into fixed steps and accumulating emission weighted by transmittance. It differs from its sibling NeRF Rendering (Alpha Compositing) by using a fixed-step marching loop with explicit throughput tracking and jittering, rather than bin-based stratified sampling. It is designed for dense grid-based media where direction-dependent emission is not required. This variant extends the standard forward pass by incorporating alpha masking and NDC (Normalized Device Coordinates) ray sampling. It handles rays that hit empty space in an alpha mask by marking them invalid. It adjusts distances by ray norm and normalizes view directions if NDC simulation is enabled. Density features are converted to sigma using feature2density if not component-wise, and alpha weights are computed using raw2alpha with distance scaling. The depth map is computed as a weighted sum of z-values, adjusted by background weight and ray direction Z component, and clamped if NDC Euclidean depth simulation is enabled. The volume rendering integral was formalized by Kajiya and later adapted for neural implicit representations by Mildenhall et al. in the original NeRF paper. The specific alpha-compositing formulation and stratified sampling strategy described in NeRF Rendering (Alpha Compositing) are central to the NeRF architecture. The fixed-step integrator described in NeRF-style Volume Rendering Integrator appears in implementations such as Joint-TensoRF. name: NeRF Rendering (Alpha Compositing)
head: Alpha Compositing in NeRF, NeRF Integration, NeRF Rendering Equation, NeRF Rendering Process, Neural Radiance Field Volume Rendering
body: NeRF Rendering (Alpha Compositing) is the differentiable forward pass that synthesizes a pixel's color and depth by integrating the volume density and emitted radiance predicted by a neural network along a camera ray. It solves the problem of mapping a continuous 5D implicit function (mapping spatial coordinates and view directions to density and color) to a 2D image by discretizing the ray integral. Unlike deterministic ray tracing which follows specific light paths, NeRF leverages a probabilistic density function to compute the expected color, handling view-dependent effects (non-Lambertian materials) that standard photogrammetry often assumes as diffuse. It sets itself apart from its sibling NeRF-style Volume Rendering Integrator by explicitly defining the standard alpha-compositing formulation with stratified sampling and background handling as the baseline for training and inference. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera ray r(t) = o + td, where o is the camera origin and d is the unit viewing direction. Near bound tn (camera center) and far bound tf (scene boundary). Number of samples N (typical value: 64 for both coarse and fine networks). Neural network model F\Theta (MLP) taking positional encoding of (x, d) and outputting density \sigma and color c. Optional background color c{bg}. Outputs: Rendered RGB color \hat{C}(r). Expected depth \hat{D}(r). Data Structures: Sample Points: Array of N distances ti along the ray. Predictions: Tensor of shape (N, 4) containing N samples, each with 3 RGB channels and 1 density channel. Deltas: Array of interval lengths \deltai = t{i+1} - ti for i=1 \dots N-1, plus a large value (e.g., 10^{10}) for the final segment to infinity. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel in the target image, generate a ray r(t) = o + td using the camera's intrinsic and extrinsic parameters. 2. Sampling: Divide the interval [tn, tf] into N equally spaced bins. Draw one sample ti uniformly at random from each bin (non-deterministic stratified sampling): ti \sim U\left[tn + \frac{i-1}{N}(tf - tn), tn + \frac{i}{N}(tf - tn)\right]. 3. Querying: For each sample point ti, compute the 3D position xi = o + ti d. Input xi and the ray direction d (often with positional encoding \gamma) into the MLP F\Theta to predict volume density \sigmai and color ci: [\sigmai, ci] = F\Theta(\gamma(xi), \gamma(d)). Apply ReLU to \sigmai and Sigmoid to ci to constrain ranges. 4. Delta Calculation: Compute the distance between adjacent samples: \deltai = t{i+1} - ti \quad \text{for } i=1 \dots N-1. Append a large value \delta\infty = 10^{10} (or tf - tN if bounded) for the last segment to handle rays that do not terminate within the scene. 5. Opacity Calculation: Compute the opacity \alphai for each sample using the Beer-Lambert law: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai). 6. Transmittance Calculation: Compute the accumulated transmittance Ti, representing the probability that the ray travels from tn to ti without being intercepted. Use a cumulative product with a small epsilon \epsilon (typically 10^{-10}) added to (1 - \alphaj) for numerical stability to prevent NaNs during gradient computation: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj + \epsilon). Note: T1 = 1. 7. Weight Calculation: Compute the weight wi for each sample, representing the probability that the ray terminates at sample i: wi = \alphai Ti. 8. Color Integration: Compute the final rendered color \hat{C}(r) as the weighted sum of colors: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi ci. 9. Background Handling (Optional): If a background color c{bg} is assumed, add the contribution of rays that pass through the scene without terminating. Let W = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi be the total accumulated opacity. The final color is: \hat{C}{final}(r) = \hat{C}(r) + (1 - W) c{bg}. 10. Depth Estimation: Compute the expected depth \hat{D}(r) analogously to color, using the sample distances ti as the value: \hat{D}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi ti. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def nerfrendering(rayso, raysd, tvals, model, whitebackground=True, cbg=np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0]), eps=1e-10): """ Render RGB and Depth for a batch of rays using NeRF alpha compositing. Args: rayso: (B, 3) Camera origins. raysd: (B, 3) Ray directions (unit vectors). tvals: (B, N) Sample distances along rays. model: Function that takes (points, directions) and returns (sigma, rgb). whitebackground: Boolean, whether to add background color. cbg: (3,) Background color. eps: Float, epsilon for numerical stability. Returns: rgb: (B, 3) Rendered colors. depth: (B,) Expected depths. """ B, N = tvals.shape # 1. Compute 3D points # points shape: (B, N, 3) points = rayso[:, np.newaxis,:] + raysd[:, np.newaxis,:] tvals[:,:, np.newaxis] # 2. Query model # model returns sigma (B, N) and rgb (B, N, 3) # Note: In practice, positional encoding is applied inside or before model call. # Here we assume model handles input or we pass raw coords. # For strict adherence to NeRF, positional encoding is applied to x and d. # We assume 'model' expects encoded inputs or handles them. # To be self-contained, we denote the query as: sigma, rgb = model(points, raysd) # 3. Apply activation functions if not done in model # sigma = np.maximum(sigma, 0) # ReLU # rgb = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-rgb)) # Sigmoid (if raw logits) # Assuming model outputs valid sigma >= 0 and rgb in [0,1] or logits. # Standard implementation applies sigmoid to rgb and relu to sigma. sigma = np.maximum(sigma, 0) rgb = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-rgb)) # 4. Compute deltas # deltas shape: (B, N-1) deltas = tvals[:, 1:] - tvals[:,:-1] # Append infinity for the last segment # deltainf shape: (B, 1) deltainf = np.ones((B, 1)) 1e10 # Concatenate to get (B, N) deltas = np.concatenate([deltas, deltainf], axis=1) # 5. Compute opacity alpha # alpha shape: (B, N) alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigma deltas) # 6. Compute transmittance T # Ti = product{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - alphaj) # Use cumulative product with exclusive=True # (1 - alpha + eps) shape: (B, N) term = 1.0 - alpha + eps # cumprod along axis=1 (samples) # T shape: (B, N), T[:,0] = 1.0 T = np.cumprod(term, axis=1, exclusive=True) # 7. Compute weights # wi = alphai Ti # weights shape: (B, N) weights = alpha T # 8. Compute RGB # rgbfinal = sum(weights rgb) # weights needs to be broadcasted to (B, N, 1) rgbfinal = np.sum(weights[:,:, np.newaxis] rgb, axis=1) # 9. Background handling if whitebackground: # Total opacity W = sum(weights) W = np.sum(weights, axis=1) # (B,) # Add (1 - W) cbg rgbfinal = rgbfinal + (1.0 - W[:, np.newaxis]) cbg[np.newaxis,:] # 10. Compute Depth # depth = sum(weights tvals) depth = np.sum(weights tvals, axis=1) return rgbfinal, depth Parameters: N: Number of samples per ray. Typical value: 64. \epsilon: Epsilon for stability. Typical value: 10^{-10}. c{bg}: Background color. tn, tf: Integration bounds. tn is camera center, tf is scene boundary. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Stability: Without \epsilon, the cumulative product of (1-\alpha) can underflow to 0, causing NaNs in gradients. \epsilon = 10^{-10} is standard. Infinity Handling: The last segment \deltaN must be large enough to capture rays that exit the scene. Using 10^{10} ensures \alphaN \approx 1 if \sigmaN > 0, effectively terminating the ray. View-Dependent Effects: NeRF handles non-Lambertian materials by conditioning color on view direction d. Computational Cost: Original NeRF requires high computing power and long training times due to dense sampling and MLP queries. The complete workflow including data loading, ray generation, coarse/fine network sampling, and loss computation. Uses predicted depth maps to bias sample placement toward surfaces, reducing redundant sampling in free space. Uses rendered depth to warp images for consistency regularization, distinct from sampling strategies. Replaces uniform sampling with depth-prior guided stratified sampling to focus on likely surfaces. Uses SDFs instead of density, concentrating weight at the zero-level set for precise surface extraction. Models blur as a distribution of rays using a two-stage module. Approximates integrated positional encoding by treating rays as cones to solve aliasing. Simulates event camera data for motion blur supervision. A method for scaling NeRF rendering across multiple GPUs. It performs global composition by aggregating transmittance and color contributions from segments processed on different GPUs. Step: Initialize global transmittance T{1 \to i} = 1 and global color C{1 \to N+1} = 0. For each segment s in the GPU order list I, if the segment's GPU i \neq k (current GPU), gather T{i \to i+1} and C{i \to i+1}. Update global color: C{1 \to N+1} += T{1 \to i} \times C{i \to i+1}. Update global transmittance: T{1 \to i^} = T{i \to i+1}. Pitfall: During inference, data gathering is only required on a single GPU (e.g., GPU 0) to render the final image, reducing data transfer compared to training. Approximates the volume rendering integral by summing contributions from sampled spheres inside the cone using numerical quadrature. Formula: \text{Color} = \sumi Ti (1 - \exp(-\text{density}i (t{i+1} - ti))) \text{color}i, with Ti = \exp(-\sum{k<i} \text{density}k (t{k+1} - tk)). A rendering procedure using RM-LSTM to predict a single intersection point and output RGB directly, skipping volume rendering. Step: Extract latent features from PixelNeRF CNN encoder, feed into RM-LSTM. RM-LSTM predicts step length and updates depth for 10 steps with 512 feature channels. Pass final depth point through PixelNeRF network to obtain RGB. Comparison: ~80 times faster than baseline but slightly lower quality (PSNR 23.02 vs 23.34). Maps low-resolution feature maps to final images using upsampling and 2D convolution to alleviate multi-view inconsistent artifacts. Formula: \text{Upsample}(X) = \text{Conv2D}(Y, K), where Y = \text{Pixelshuffle}(\text{repeat}(X, 4) + \beta\zeta(X), 2). Parameter: Convolution kernel size is 1x1 to avoid multi-view inconsistencies. Real-time NeRF-based parametric head model inference. Step: Sample 64 points per ray, compute volume rendering to get feature map IF, pass IF through 2D neural rendering module (upsampling + 1x1 Conv) to get final image I. Performance: >40 fps on NVIDIA 3090 GPU. Extracts 3D point-cloud data by estimating depth where transmittance changes significantly. Formula: t{surface} \approx \arg \mint \left| \frac{dT(t)}{dt} \right|. Produces approximate rendering (RGB and features) at a target pose using input images. Step: Pass N input images through 2D U-Net to create feature images. Cast rays, sample 128 points (uniform up to distance 1, then linear in disparity). Reproject 3D points into input cameras, gather features. Append positionally-encoded 3D locations and statistics. Layout: Output tensor 64x64x131 (3 RGB + 128 features). Standard NeRF rendering using coarse and fine sampling. Step: Discretize integral using stratified sampling. Coarse sampling uses uniform distribution. Fine sampling uses volume density weights. Loss: Sum of squared errors for coarse and fine samples against ground truth. Models image motion blur by discretizing exposure time into p poses, rendering sharp images, and averaging them. Parameter: p (number of poses), typical value 5. Pitfall: Assumes uniform motion or linear interpolation for intermediate poses. Measured Performance: Original NeRF is slow; Instant NGP reduces processing time significantly using multi-resolution hash encoding. HeadNeRF achieves >40 fps on NVIDIA 3090 with 2D neural rendering module. Strengths: Handles view-dependent effects, high-quality novel view synthesis, fine details. Limitations: High computational cost, neither a point cloud nor a mesh (continuous voxels). When to Use: When high-quality novel view synthesis is required, especially for complex scenes with view-dependent effects. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical without acceleration techniques, or when explicit geometry (mesh/point cloud) is required. NeRF was first presented by Mildenhall et al. in 2020. It represents a static scene as a continuous 5D function outputting volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance. The method was initially presented at CVPR 2020. Subsequent developments include Instant NGP by Müller et al. (2022) which introduced multi-resolution hash encoding. It is used in Cultural Heritage for reconstruction of metallic, translucent, and transparent surfaces. Implemented in platforms like Instant NGP, Nerfstudio, and Luma AI. name: NeRF Rendering Pipeline
head: NeRF Rendering Path
body: The NeRF Rendering Pipeline orchestrates the generation of novel views from a trained Neural Radiance Field by iterating over a sequence of camera poses and invoking the volume rendering primitive for each. It handles data preparation, resolution scaling, and output assembly. It differs from the core NeRF Rendering (Alpha Compositing) method by managing the external loop of pose traversal, I/O, and metric computation rather than the per-ray integration itself. Inputs: renderposes: Array of shape (N, 4, 4) or (N, 3, 4) representing camera-to-world matrices. H, W: Integer height and width of the target image. focal: Scalar focal length in pixels. renderkwargs: Dictionary containing the model and rendering configuration passed to the volume renderer. renderfactor: Integer downsampling factor (default 0, meaning no downsampling). chunk: Integer number of rays to process in parallel (default 32768). gtimgs: Optional array of ground truth images for PSNR calculation. savedir: Optional directory path to save rendered images. Outputs: rgbs: List or array of rendered RGB images. disps: List or array of rendered depth/disparity maps. Data Structures: rgbs: List of numpy arrays, each shape (H', W', 3), where H' = H/render\factor and W' = W/render\factor. disps: List of numpy arrays, each shape (H', W'). Steps: 1. Initialize Output Containers: Create empty lists rgbs and disps. 2. Iterate Poses: For each camera pose c2w in renderposes: a. Downsample Resolution: If renderfactor > 0, compute effective height H{eff} = \lfloor H / render\factor \rfloor and width W{eff} = \lfloor W / render\factor \rfloor. Update focal by dividing by renderfactor. If renderfactor is 0, H{eff}=H, W{eff}=W. b. Render: Call the volume rendering function with arguments (H{eff}, W{eff}, focal, chunk, c2w, \text{render\kwargs}). This returns rgb (shape H{eff} \times W{eff} \times 3) and disp (shape H{eff} \times W{eff}). c. Store Results: Append rgb.numpy() to rgbs and disp.numpy() to disps. d. Compute PSNR (Optional): If gtimgs is not None and renderfactor == 0: i. Compute Mean Squared Error: MSE = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (rgbi - gt\imgi)^2. ii. Compute PSNR: PSNR = -10 \cdot \log{10}(MSE). e. Save Image (Optional): If savedir is not None: i. Convert rgb to 8-bit unsigned integer format (clamping values to [0, 255]). ii. Save as PNG file named '{:03d}.png' in savedir. 3. Return: Stack rgbs and disps along axis 0 and return them. Parameters: renderfactor: Controls rendering speed vs. resolution. Typical values: 4 or 8 for previews. Default: 0. chunk: Controls memory usage during rendering. Default: 32768. Decrease if out-of-memory errors occur. Edge Cases: Memory Limits: If chunk is too large for the GPU, the rendering call may fail. Reduce chunk size. Precision: PSNR calculation requires renderfactor == 0 to match ground truth resolution exactly. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot H \cdot W), where N is the number of poses. The constant factor depends on the number of samples per ray in the underlying volume renderer. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot H{eff} \cdot W{eff}) for storing output images. The rendering process itself uses O(chunk \cdot S) memory per batch, where S is samples per ray. Performance: Rendering speed is linearly proportional to the number of rays. Downsampling by renderfactor reduces ray count by render\factor^2. Strengths: Simple, modular pipeline that separates pose management from the rendering primitive. Limitations: Not optimized for real-time; relies on batched ray processing. The pipeline is derived from the original NeRF implementation by Mildenhall et al., specifically the render.py script in the official repository. It standardizes the evaluation and novel view synthesis workflow for neural radiance fields. bmild/nerf, https://github.com/bmild/nerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)
