name: ViiNeuS Hybrid Volume Rendering
head: Hybrid alpha composition, ViiNeuS Volume Rendering
body: ViiNeuS Hybrid Volume Rendering is a progressive training strategy for implicit neural surface reconstruction that transitions from pure volumetric density representation to signed distance field (SDF) representation during the optimization loop. It solves the initialization instability and slow convergence of pure SDF methods in complex scenes by initially leveraging a robust volumetric estimator, then gradually introducing SDF-based alpha compositing. Unlike standard NeRF rendering which uses only density-based alpha, or pure NeuS which uses only SDF-based alpha, this method dynamically assigns each sample's alpha value to either \alpha^{iv} or \alpha^{if} based on training stage and sample density, ensuring stable surface extraction. Inputs: Ray r defined by origin and direction. Sample points xi along the ray. Network outputs for each sample xi: Density \sigmai (from MLP F^h\Theta). Signed Distance Field value f(xi) (from MLP F^h\Theta). Color ci (from MLP F^c\Theta, using direction, latent vector, and normal). Current training step t and total training steps T{total}. Outputs: Rendered pixel color \hat{C}(r). The method relies on two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): 1. Geometry MLP (F^h\Theta): Input: Positional embedding embx(x). Output: Tuple (\sigma, f(x), h), where \sigma is density, f(x) is SDF value, and h is a latent vector. Architecture: 2 layers, 64 hidden units. 2. Color MLP (F^c\Theta): Input: Directional embedding embd(d), latent vector h, and normal vector -\vec{n}. Output: Color c. Architecture: 2 layers, 64 hidden units. Normal \vec{n} is computed as the gradient of the SDF: \vec{n} = \nabla f(x). Volumetric Stage Duration: First 100 training steps. Hybrid Stage End: 35% of total training time (0.35 \times T{total}). Sharpness Parameter (s): Controls the standard deviation of the SDF density distribution \phis (std = 1/s). Regularized during training with weight decay from 10^{-3} to 10^{-5}. Sample Spacing (\deltai): Distance between adjacent samples along the ray. 1. Volumetric Alpha (\alpha^{iv}): Computed from predicted density \sigmai and sample spacing \deltai: \alpha^{iv} = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) 2. SDF-based Alpha (\alpha^{if}): Computed using the sigmoid function \Phis and its derivative \phis. Let \Phis(z) = (1 + e^{-sz})^{-1} and \phis(z) = \frac{se^{-sz}}{(1 + e^{-sz})^2}. For sample i at position pi and next sample i+1 at p{i+1}, the alpha is: \alpha^{if} = \max\left( \frac{\Phis(f(pi)) - \Phis(f(p{i+1}))}{\Phis(f(pi))}, 0 \right) Note: The sources define \alpha^{if} using the difference of sigmas at section points. In implementation, f(pi) is the SDF value at sample i. 3. Final Rendered Color: Alpha compositing along the ray: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi ci where: wi = Ti \alphai is the weight of sample i. Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the accumulated transmittance. \alphai is the blending factor, determined by the training stage (see Steps). 1. Determine Training Stage: If current step t < 100: Volumetric Stage. If 100 \le t < 0.35 \times T{total}: Hybrid Stage. If t \ge 0.35 \times T{total}: Surface Stage. 2. Compute Network Outputs: For each sample xi on the ray: Compute embx(xi) using hash encoding. Query F^h\Theta(embx(xi)) to get \sigmai, f(xi), hi. Compute normal \vec{n}i = \nabla f(xi). SDF-Gradient Normalization: During the Hybrid Stage, normalize \vec{n}i to prevent large gradient values from compensating for alpha distribution differences. name: Depth-Guided Sampling
head: Local Sampling Strategies
body: Depth-Guided Sampling is a ray sampling strategy for neural radiance fields that focuses scene sampling on estimated surface regions using depth priors from input views to increase sample density in relevant areas, thereby improving synthesis quality and allowing a reduction in the number of samples per ray. It sets itself apart from uniform or hierarchical stratified sampling by explicitly leveraging predicted depth maps (and their uncertainties) to bias the placement of query points toward likely object surfaces, reducing redundant sampling in free space or occluded regions. The method operates by estimating depth and uncertainty for each pixel in the input views, projecting candidate points along camera rays onto these depth maps to compute surface likelihoods, and then selecting or generating sample points based on these likelihoods. Inputs: Camera rays r(t) defined by near plane t{near} and far plane t{far}. For each input view i: Input image I^{(i)}. Estimated depth map D^{(i)} (mean depth). Estimated standard deviation map D{std}^{(i)} (depth uncertainty). Camera projection matrix K^{(i)}. Depth map normals (derived from D^{(i)}). Outputs: A set of 3D sample points \{xj\} along the ray r(t), optimized for surface presence. Candidate Samples: A list of N{cand} points uniformly distributed along the ray interval [t{near}, t{far}]. Likelihood Fields: Per-view probability density values p^{(i)}(x) for each candidate point x. Occlusion-Aware Likelihoods: Values p{oa}(x) representing the probability that x is the first surface point encountered along the ray. 1. Candidate Generation: Uniformly sample N{cand} candidate points \{x\} along the ray r(t) within the interval [t{near}, t{far}]. \{x\} = \{r(t) \mid t \sim [t{near}, t{far}]\} The step size \delta for these candidates is defined as: \delta = (t{far} - t{near}) / N{cand} 2. Backface Culling: Calculate normals from the depth map D^{(i)}. For each candidate point x, project it into the i-th camera space to get x^{(i)}. Discard x if the angle between the ray direction and the projected normal is smaller than 90 degrees. 3. Per-View Surface Likelihood Calculation: For each input view i and each candidate point x: a. Calculate the difference \Delta z between the sample's z-component in the i-th camera space and its corresponding projected depth value: \Delta z = D^{(i)}(K^{(i)} \circ x^{(i)}) - x^{[z]} where x^{[z]} is the z-component of x in camera space. b. Determine the likelihood p^{(i)}(x) of x being a surface point for view i by integrating a Gaussian PDF over the sample interval \delta: p^{(i)}(x) = \int{z-\delta/2}^{z+\delta/2} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma} e^{-\frac{1}{2}(\frac{z'-\mu}{\sigma})^2} dz' where: \mu = D^{(i)}(K^{(i)} \circ x^{(i)}) \sigma = D{std}^{(i)}(K^{(i)} \circ x^{(i)}) z = x^{[z]} 4. Multi-View Likelihood Aggregation: Determine the multi-view likelihood p(x) by performing view-wise max-pooling over all input views: p(x) = \maxi p^{(i)}(x) 5. Shortlisting: Shortlist N{samples} candidates with the highest likelihoods p(x) for sampling the NeRF. 6. Gaussian Boosting: a. Calculate the occlusion-aware likelihood p{oa}(x) for each candidate x along the ray r(t): p{oa}(x) = p(x) \cdot \prod{\tilde{x} < x} (1 - p(\tilde{x})) where \tilde{x} denotes candidates with a smaller ray parameter t (closer to the camera) than x. b. Fit a Gaussian distribution against the occlusion-aware likelihoods p{oa}(x) along the ray. c. Sample N{gauss} points from this fitted Gaussian distribution and add them to the shortlisted candidates. Some implementations simplify the process by skipping coarse sampling and blank areas, directly sampling M points uniformly from the confidence interval [d-s, d+s] of the estimated depth d with confidence interval s. The depth tj of the j-th query point (j=1..M) is calculated as: tj = d - s + \frac{2s}{M - 1} (j - 1) In stereo settings, points are drawn from a normalized impulse distribution centered at the stereo depth prior Di[u, v]. The transfer function is: \delta(s; u, v, i) = \exp \left( -(s - Di[u, v])^2 / 2\xi^2 \right) Steps sj are drawn from \frac{1}{\xi\sqrt{2\pi}} \delta(s; u, v, i). The hyperparameter \xi is set to a small value to mimic a Dirac delta impulse. N{cand}: Number of initial candidate samples. Not given in the sources. N{samples}: Number of shortlisted candidates. Not given in the sources. N{gauss}: Number of points sampled during Gaussian boosting. Not given in the sources. M: Number of points in uniform interval sampling. Not given in the sources. d: Estimated depth. Not given in the sources. s: Confidence interval. Not given in the sources. \xi: Hyperparameter controlling the width of the Gaussian impulse in stereo depth-cueing. Set to a small value to mimic a Dirac delta impulse. \delta: Step size for candidate samples, (t{far} - t{near})/N{cand}. Large Confidence Interval: If the confidence interval s is large, sampling might still cover blank areas, although this method reduces this occurrence compared to uniform camera-space sampling. Occlusion Ordering: The occlusion-aware likelihood calculation assumes a specific ordering of samples along the ray; incorrect ordering leads to incorrect p{oa} values. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.stats import norm def depthguidedsampling(rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, depthmaps, depthstdmaps, cameramatrices, Ncand=100, Nsamples=20, Ngauss=10): """ Implements Depth-Guided Sampling as described in. Args: rayorigin: (3,) array, origin of the ray. raydirection: (3,) array, direction of the ray. tnear: float, near plane distance. tfar: float, far plane distance. depthmaps: list of (H, W) arrays, depth maps D^(i). depthstdmaps: list of (H, W) arrays, depth std maps Dstd^(i). cameramatrices: list of (3, 4) or (4, 4) arrays, projection matrices K^(i). Ncand: int, number of initial candidates. Nsamples: int, number of shortlisted samples. Ngauss: int, number of Gaussian boosted samples. Returns: samples: (Ntotal, 3) array of 3D points. """ # 1. Candidate Generation delta = (tfar - tnear) / Ncand tcandidates = tnear + np.arange(Ncand) delta candidates = rayorigin + tcandidates[:, np.newaxis] raydirection # Helper to project point to camera space and get depth/std def getprojecteddepthandstd(point, K, D, Dstd): # Transform point to camera coordinates pointh = np.append(point, 1.0) camcoords = (K @ pointh)[:3] u, v, zcam = camcoords[0], camcoords[1], camcoords[2] # Check if point is within image bounds if not (0 <= u < D.shape[1] and 0 <= v < D.shape[0]): return None, None, None # Interpolate depth and std at (u, v) # Using nearest neighbor for simplicity; bilinear is better mu = D[int(v), int(u)] sigma = Dstd[int(v), int(u)] return mu, sigma, zcam # 2. Per-View Likelihood Calculation # Initialize likelihood array likelihoods = np.zeros(Ncand) for i in range(len(depthmaps)): D = depthmaps[i] Dstd = depthstdmaps[i] K = cameramatrices[i] viewlikelihoods = np.zeros(Ncand) for j in range(Ncand): x = candidates[j] mu, sigma, zcam = getprojecteddepthandstd(x, K, D, Dstd) if mu is None: viewlikelihoods[j] = 0.0 continue # Step size delta delta = (tfar - tnear) / Ncand # Calculate likelihood by integrating Gaussian PDF over interval [z-delta/2, z+delta/2] # PDF: 1/(sqrt(2pi)sigma) exp(-0.5 ((z' - mu)/sigma)^2) # We integrate this from zcam - delta/2 to zcam + delta/2 lower = zcam - delta / 2.0 upper = zcam + delta / 2.0 # Using scipy norm.cdf for efficiency pi = norm.cdf(upper, loc=mu, scale=sigma) - norm.cdf(lower, loc=mu, scale=sigma) viewlikelihoods[j] = pi # Max-pooling across views if i == 0: likelihoods = viewlikelihoods else: likelihoods = np.maximum(likelihoods, viewlikelihoods) # 3. Shortlisting # Get indices of top Nsamples likelihoods topindices = np.argsort(likelihoods)[-Nsamples:][::-1] shortlistedsamples = candidates[topindices] # 4. Gaussian Boosting # Calculate occlusion-aware likelihoods # Sort candidates by distance (t value) tsortedindices = np.argsort(tcandidates) tsorted = tcandidates[tsortedindices] candidatessorted = candidates[tsortedindices] likelihoodssorted = likelihoods[tsortedindices] # Calculate product of (1 - p(xtilde)) for xtilde < x oneminusp = 1.0 - likelihoodssorted # Handle cases where p=1 to avoid log(0) or negative probs oneminusp = np.clip(oneminusp, 1e-7, 1.0) cumprod = np.cumprod(oneminusp) # Shift cumprod to align with current point (exclude current point's contribution) # For the first point, product is 1.0 occlusionaware = np.zeros(Ncand) occlusionaware[0] = likelihoodssorted[0] for k in range(1, Ncand): occlusionaware[k] = likelihoodssorted[k] cumprod[k-1] # Fit Gaussian to occlusionaware likelihoods along the ray # We treat tsorted as the domain and occlusionaware as the PDF # Normalize occlusionaware to be a valid PDF occlusionawarepdf = occlusionaware / np.sum(occlusionaware) # Calculate mean and std of this distribution meant = np.sum(tsorted occlusionawarepdf) stdt = np.sqrt(np.sum((tsorted - meant)2 occlusionawarepdf)) # Sample Ngauss points from this Gaussian if Ngauss > 0: gaussiant = np.random.normal(meant, stdt, Ngauss) # Clip to [tnear, tfar] gaussiant = np.clip(gaussiant, tnear, tfar) gaussiansamples = rayorigin + gaussiant[:, np.newaxis] raydirection finalsamples = np.vstack([shortlistedsamples, gaussiansamples]) else: finalsamples = shortlistedsamples return finalsamples Pixel Region and Depth Guided Ray Sampling is a ray sampling strategy that increases sampling probability in pixel areas exhibiting significant color and depth variation, reducing redundant rays in flat regions to accelerate network convergence and improve geometry perception. Unlike conventional NeRF which uses uniform distribution, this method samples varying ray densities based on depth boundaries and pixel regions to simultaneously accelerate convergence and improve geometry perception. It builds on Depth-Guided Sampling by explicitly incorporating color variation alongside depth estimates. Truncated Depth-Based Sampling (TDBS) is a ray sampling strategy that utilizes monocular depth priors informed by the truncated normal distribution to optimize ray point sampling, improving convergence speed and accuracy of pose estimation. It differs from siblings like NoPe-NeRF by explicitly using the truncated normal distribution for sampling to fully exploit depth priors, whereas NoPe-NeRF considers overall depth distortion and does not fully exploit the potential of monocular depth maps. It builds on Depth-Guided Sampling by replacing uniform or heuristic sampling with a probabilistic model centered on the estimated depth. Surface-Based Sampling is a strategy that restricts 3D sample point generation to a narrow band around the estimated surface of an object, rather than sampling throughout the entire volume or free space. It solves the problem of quality degradation caused by standard NeRF sampling in irrelevant regions (free space or occluded areas) by concentrating computational resources where the radiance field actually varies. It differs from its siblings by explicitly using depth priors to define this sampling band: Pixel Region and Depth Guided Ray Sampling uses pixel-region constraints, Truncated Depth-Based Sampling truncates rays based on depth, while Surface-Based Sampling defines a symmetric range around the depth value. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: reports improved synthesis quality and allows reduction of samples per ray on the FaceScape dataset. reports skipping coarse sampling and reducing sampling in blank areas. reports concentrating points near tissue surfaces for robotic surgery scenes. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of input views and candidate points. Depth-Guided Sampling was introduced in the DINER paper (2023) as part of a depth-aware image-based neural radiance field framework. It builds on pixelNeRF and uses TransMVSNet for depth estimation. The method was developed to address the inefficiency of uniform sampling in NeRF by focusing computation on relevant surface regions. Variants like NeRF-SDP and Stereo Depth-Cueing have adapted the core idea for generalizable NeRFs and stereo surgical reconstruction, respectively. name: Pixel Region and Depth Guided Ray Sampling
body: Pixel Region and Depth Guided Ray Sampling is a ray sampling strategy that increases sampling probability in pixel areas exhibiting significant color and depth variation, reducing redundant rays in flat regions to accelerate network convergence and improve geometry perception. Unlike conventional NeRF which uses uniform distribution, this method samples varying ray densities based on depth boundaries and pixel regions to simultaneously accelerate convergence and improve geometry perception. It builds on Depth-Guided Sampling by explicitly incorporating color variation alongside depth estimates. Inputs: A set of N training source images Ii with height Hi and width Wi. A neural radiance field network F\Theta parameterized by \Theta, mapping 3D position p and viewing direction d to volume density \sigma and emitted color c. Estimated depth information for each pixel, obtained from a depth estimation module (specifically the cost volume from the ENeRF framework). True color values ci^k for the pixels. Outputs: A set of sampled rays \mathbb{R}i with non-uniform density per image. Rendered pixel colors V\Theta(ri^k). Data Structures: Sampling Probability Map: A 2D array of size Hi \times Wi storing the probability P(u, v) for each pixel (u, v) to be sampled. Cost Volume: A 3D tensor used to derive depth estimates, as utilized in the ENeRF framework. Steps: 1. Depth Estimation: Obtain rough depth information for the scene using the depth estimation module from the ENeRF framework. Specifically, leverage the cost volume to obtain depth information for each pixel (u, v). 2. Probability Calculation: Calculate the sampling probability for each pixel (u, v) based on its color value and the estimated depth information. The probability is higher in areas with substantial color variation and marked geometric depth variation. 3. Ray Sampling: During ray sampling, sample additional rays in pixel areas exhibiting substantial color variation from the source view images. Similarly, guided by the depth-based sampling strategy, sample more rays in regions where geometric depth varies markedly. This replaces the uniform distribution ri(u, v) \sim U(Ii). 4. Volume Rendering: Perform volume rendering using the network to output colors and densities along the sampled rays to render the final pixel color. 5. Optimization: Optimize the network parameters \Theta by minimizing the volume rendering loss. Formulas: The optimization goal minimizes the volume rendering loss: \min{\Theta} \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{NM} \sum{ri^k \in \mathbb{R}i} \|V{\Theta}(ri^k) - ci^k\|2^2 where: ci^k is the true color of pixels. M is the number of sampled rays per image. N is the number of trained images. ri^k is the k-th ray from the i-th training image. V{\Theta} is the volume rendering function. Uniform ray sampling assumes rays follow a uniform distribution, which this method replaces: ri(u, v) \sim U(Ii), \quad u \in [0, Hi], \quad v \in [0, Wi] where Hi and Wi are the height and width of image Ii. Parameters: N: The number of trained images (source views). M: The number of sampled rays per image. \Theta: The network parameters optimized by minimizing the color error. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on the accuracy of the depth estimation module (ENeRF cost volume). Inaccurate depth estimates may lead to suboptimal sampling probabilities. Boundaries: The method specifically targets regions with "significant" variation. Flat regions with no variation receive fewer rays, which is intended to reduce redundancy but requires careful handling to ensure global scene coherence is maintained through the remaining samples. Degenerate Input: If the depth estimation fails or the cost volume is ambiguous, the depth-guided component may provide misleading probabilities. A sampling method for learning neural fields from large input images that optimizes pixel-level ray sampling by segmenting the error map into superpixels and dynamically updating their errors to increase ray sampling in areas with higher rendering errors. It segments the input image into various superpixels using the SLIC algorithm, treating superpixels as the smallest processing unit. It sets different sampling probabilities for various superpixels based on their rendering errors and continuously updates them during training. Unlike quadtree or fixed-shape patch sampling methods which may cause fragmented image information, superpixels reduce redundancy while considering local information. Unlike color-guided ray sampling which does not simultaneously consider rendering errors, SES uses rendering errors to guide sampling. Time and Memory Complexity: The method reduces the number of redundant rays, thereby accelerating network convergence and reducing training time. It achieves the same convergence effect in minutes through fine-tuning reconstructions from given views. Measured Performance: Applied to the ENeRF framework, it achieves state-of-the-art performance on both view synthesis and training time. Scaling: The strategy can directly transfer to existing NeRF models because ray sampling is ubiquitous in NeRF. Strengths: Accelerates per-scene optimization, improves efficiency, and better perceives spatial geometry, especially for rich-texture regions. Limitations: The method is described primarily in the context of static or dynamic scenes using the ENeRF framework; specific scalability limits to extremely high resolutions are not detailed, though it is noted that current acceleration methods predominately focus on static scenes. When to use: When faster per-scene optimization is desired and the scene contains rich textures or significant depth variations. When not: When uniform coverage is strictly required or when depth estimation is unreliable. The method was introduced in the paper "Efficient ray sampling for radiance fields reconstruction". It addresses the inefficiency of uniform ray sampling in NeRF, which fails to capture the non-uniform distribution of color differences and contextual information in images. The authors hypothesize that training with fewer, more informative rays can accelerate scene fitting. The method is applied to the ENeRF framework [15] to demonstrate its effectiveness. name: Truncated Depth-Based Sampling
body: Truncated Depth-Based Sampling (TDBS) is a ray sampling strategy that utilizes monocular depth priors informed by the truncated normal distribution to optimize ray point sampling, improving convergence speed and accuracy of pose estimation. It differs from siblings like NoPe-NeRF by explicitly using the truncated normal distribution for sampling to fully exploit depth priors, whereas NoPe-NeRF considers overall depth distortion and does not fully exploit the potential of monocular depth maps. It builds on Depth-Guided Sampling by using a coarse monocular depth map as a prior to sample points from a truncated normal distribution, assuming the real surface is near the estimated depth. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of input images, camera poses (initially unknown or coarse), and a pre-trained monocular depth network (DPT). Outputs: Sampled 3D points along rays, estimated color c and density \sigma, rendered RGB and depth images, and optimized radiance field parameters \theta and camera poses P. Data Structures: Depth Map: A 2D array of depth values D(u,v) for each pixel (u,v) in the input image, estimated by DPT. Ray: Defined as r(t) = o + td, where o is the camera origin and d is the viewing direction. Sampling Points: A set of N points \{t1, t2,..., tN\} along the ray, where N=128. Parameters: Truncation Interval: [a, b] = [0.001, 1.0]. Variance: \bar{\sigma} = 0.1. Number of Samples: N = 128. Steps: 1. Depth Estimation: Use a pre-trained monocular depth network (DPT) to estimate a coarse depth map for each input image. Let \bar{\mu} be the depth value at the current pixel's location in this map. 2. Ray Casting: For each pixel, cast a camera ray r(t) = o + td into the scene. 3. Sampling Distribution Definition: Define the probability density function (PDF) \psi(\bar{\mu}, \bar{\sigma}, a, b; x) of the truncated normal distribution: \psi(\bar{\mu}, \bar{\sigma}, a, b; x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x \le a \\ \frac{\phi(\bar{\mu}, \bar{\sigma}^2; x)}{\Phi(\bar{\mu}, \bar{\sigma}^2; b) - \Phi(\bar{\mu}, \bar{\sigma}^2; a)} & a < x < b \\ 0 & b \le x \end{cases} where \phi(\cdot) and \Phi(\cdot) denote the probability density and distribution function of the standard normal distribution, respectively. 4. Inverse Transform Sampling: Use inverse distribution sampling to obtain N sampling points along the ray from the truncated normal distribution defined by mean \bar{\mu}, variance \bar{\sigma}, and interval [a, b]. 5. Network Evaluation: Feed the sampled points into an MLP F\theta to estimate color c and volume density \sigma. 6. Volume Rendering: Render RGB and depth images by integrating color c and density \sigma via volume rendering. The color C(r) is computed as: C(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigma(r(t)) c(r(t), d) dt where T(t) = \exp\left(-\int{tn}^{t} \sigma(r(s)) ds\right) is the accumulated transmittance. 7. Optimization: Optimize the radiance field by supervising the rendered depth and RGB against targets. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.stats import norm def truncatednormalpdf(x, mu, sigma, a, b): z = (x - mu) / sigma za = (a - mu) / sigma zb = (b - mu) / sigma cdfdiff = norm.cdf(zb) - norm.cdf(za) pdfunnormalized = norm.pdf(z) / sigma return np.where((x > a) & (x < b), pdfunnormalized / cdfdiff, 0.0) def inversetransformsamplingtruncatednormal(mu, sigma, a, b, nsamples): za = (a - mu) / sigma zb = (b - mu) / sigma cdfa = norm.cdf(za) cdfb = norm.cdf(zb) u = np.random.uniform(cdfa, cdfb, nsamples) zsamples = norm.ppf(u) tsamples = zsamples sigma + mu return np.sort(tsamples) def evaluateradiancefield(points, direction): # Radiance field network Ftheta(points, direction) -> (colors, densities) # Implementation details of Ftheta are not provided in the sources. return np.zeroslike(points), np.zeros(points.shape[0]) def tdbsrendering(rayorigin, raydirection, depthprior, nsamples=128, a=0.001, b=1.0, sigma=0.1): tsamples = inversetransformsamplingtruncatednormal(depthprior, sigma, a, b, nsamples) points = rayorigin + tsamples[:, np.newaxis] raydirection colors, densities = evaluateradiancefield(points, raydirection) dt = np.diff(tsamples) alphas = 1.0 - np.exp(-densities[:-1] dt) transmittances = np.cumprod(1.0 - alphas) transmittances = np.insert(transmittances, 0, 1.0) weights = alphas transmittances renderedcolor = np.sum(weights[:, np.newaxis] colors[:-1], axis=0) rendereddepth = np.sum(weights tsamples[:-1]) return renderedcolor, rendereddepth A training strategy that progressively improves depth precision to circumvent local minima and refine depth geometry. It sets itself apart from standard single-stage training by decoupling the optimization into distinct phases: an initial phase focused on global convergence using robust priors, followed by a phase focused on local precision or error correction. This approach accelerates convergence and enhances the accuracy of pose estimation and scene reconstruction. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Improves convergence speed and accuracy of pose estimation compared to methods that do not fully exploit depth priors. Strengths: Explicitly uses truncated normal distribution to sample near the estimated depth, reducing the search space for the surface. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the coarse depth map. Coarse depth maps from pre-trained networks (e.g., DPT) fail to capture fine details and may be inaccurate or incorrect in many details, which can degrade rendering quality if used directly in a full-stage manner. When to Use: When monocular depth priors are available and the goal is to improve convergence and pose estimation accuracy in NeRF optimization. When Not to Use: When high-fidelity depth details are critical and the monocular depth prior is significantly inaccurate, as this can lead to local minima and degraded quality. Truncated Depth-Based Sampling (TDBS) was proposed in the TD-NeRF paper. It addresses the challenge of jointly optimizing neural radiance fields and camera poses without given camera poses. The method explicitly utilizes monocular depth priors through three key advancements: 1) TDBS, 2) a coarse-to-fine training strategy, and 3) a robust inter-frame point constraint. It improves upon previous state-of-the-art methods like NoPe-NeRF by fully exploiting the potential of monocular depth maps. name: Coarse-to-Fine Training Strategy
head: Coarse-to-Fine TDBS
body: A training strategy that progressively improves depth precision to circumvent local minima and refine depth geometry. It sets itself apart from standard single-stage training by decoupling optimization into distinct phases: an initial phase focused on global convergence using robust priors, followed by a phase focused on local precision or error correction. This approach accelerates the convergence of pose optimization and enhances the precision of pose estimation, while the Gaussian Splatting variant improves global consistency and manages large-scale scenes. The strategy manifests in two distinct variants depending on the underlying representation: a NeRF variant using Truncated Depth-Based Sampling (TDBS), and a Gaussian Splatting variant (CAG-GS) using a divide-and-conquer approach. Both variants share the core principle of dividing training into a "coarse" stage for global stability and a "fine" stage for local refinement. Inputs: Training images, initial camera poses, monocular depth priors (TDBS variant), or initial anchor positions and semantic features (CAG-GS variant). Outputs: Optimized radiance field and refined camera poses (TDBS variant), or optimized 3D Gaussians/anchors and final rendered images (CAG-GS variant). TDBS Variant: Epoch counter, threshold epoch Ts. CAG-GS Variant: Scene bounding box derived from coarse model anchors, block grid partitioning the bounding box (e.g., 4 \times 4 or 2 \times 4), local models per block containing MLP decoders and semantic mapping modules, anchor list with positions, features, and importance scores, and view assignment map. This variant uses TDBS to converge density values and Uniform Sampling to recompute erroneous depth values. 1. Initialize: Set up the NeRF model and training loop. Define threshold epoch Ts. 2. Coarse Stage (Epoch < Ts): For each training iteration, sample points along rays using Truncated Depth-Based Sampling (TDBS). TDBS utilizes monocular depth priors informed by a truncated normal distribution to optimize ray point sampling. Render the image and compute loss (photometric, depth, pose constraints). Update model parameters. 3. Transition: Check if current epoch \ge Ts. 4. Fine Stage (Epoch \ge Ts): For each training iteration, sample points along rays using Uniform Sampling. The purpose is to recompute erroneous depth values based on the already optimized majority of points, avoiding local minima caused by noisy depth priors. Render the image and compute loss. Update model parameters. This variant consists of three stages: coarse global model training, scene division, and block-wise local fine-tuning. 1. Coarse Global Model Training: Optimize a single global model for 60,000 iterations using the combined loss function (photometric, semantic feature alignment, normal consistency). This stage establishes a rough global consistency and provides anchor positions for scene division. 2. Scene Division: Estimate Bounding Box: Determine the scene bounding box based on the positions of anchors in the trained coarse model. Divide Scene: Sequentially divide the scene along the two axes of the bounding box into blocks. Ensure each block contains an approximately equal number of training views to balance optimization workload. Typical Grid: SmallCity scene divided into 4 \times 4 blocks; other scenes (Building, Rubble, Residence, Sci-Art) divided into 2 \times 4 blocks. Assign Views: Initially assign training views within each block boundary to the corresponding block. Blending Weight Calculation: Compute the blending weight \hat{\alpha}i(x') for Gaussian Gi when querying pixel x': \hat{\alpha}i(x') = \sigmai G'i(x') \prod{k=1}^{i-1} (1 - \sigmat G't(x')) where \sigmai is density, G'i is the Gaussian contribution, and the product term represents opacity accumulation. Importance Score: Compute the importance score s(Aj) for anchor Aj by accumulating blending weights over all pixels x' and Gaussians i \in Ij constructed by Aj: s(Aj) = \sum{i \in Ij} \sum{x' \in X} \hat{\alpha}i(x') Threshold Check: Compute the ratio of the sum of importance scores of anchors within the block boundary to the total importance score. If this ratio exceeds threshold \epsilon (set to 0.1), assign the training view to the target block. 3. Block-wise Local Fine-Tuning: Instantiate Local Models: Create a local model for each block. Initialize modules and anchors from the coarse model. Inherit parameters of MLP decoders and semantic mapping modules from the coarse model. Initialize Anchors: Iterate over assigned training views. Select anchors with positive importance scores as initial anchors. This process may introduce out-of-boundary anchors, which help provide reliable estimates for neighboring regions. Fine-Tune: Optimize each local model for another 60,000 iterations. 4. Block Merging: Discard Outliers: Discard anchors falling outside the block boundaries. Merge Borders: Merge remaining anchors along shared borders. Fuse Features: Fuse features of merged anchors with semantic features queried from their corresponding semantic mapping modules. Finalize: Discard semantic mapping modules of all local models. Retain MLP decoders for predicting Gaussian attributes. Sampling Strategy Switch (TDBS Variant): S(r) = \begin{cases} S{TDBS}(r) & \text{if epoch} < Ts \\ S{uni}(r) & \text{if epoch} \ge Ts \end{cases} Where S{TDBS}(r) is TDBS, S{uni}(r) is Uniform Sampling, and Ts is the threshold epoch. Blending Weight (CAG-GS Variant): \hat{\alpha}i(x') = \sigmai G'i(x') \prod{k=1}^{i-1} (1 - \sigmat G't(x')) Where x' is the queried pixel, I(x') represents sorted indices of contributing Gaussians. Importance Score (CAG-GS Variant): s(Aj) = \sum{i \in Ij} \sum{x' \in X} \hat{\alpha}i(x') Where Ij is the set of indices of Gaussians constructed by anchor Aj. Ts (Threshold Epoch): Set to 1000 epochs (corresponding to the epoch at which learning rate begins to schedule). \epsilon (Importance Score Ratio Threshold): Set to 0.1. Iterations: 60,000 iterations for coarse stage, 60,000 iterations for fine stage per block. Block Grid Dimensions: 4 \times 4 for SmallCity; 2 \times 4 for other scenes (Building, Rubble, Residence, Sci-Art). Loss Weighting (CAG-GS): \lambda = 0.2 (photometric), \lambda1 = 1.0, \lambda2 = 100.0, \lambda3 = 0.015. Semantic Feature Dimension (d): 32. Number of Gaussians per Anchor (K): 10. Noisy Depth Priors: If monocular depth priors are inaccurate, full-stage TDBS can degrade rendering quality. The coarse-to-fine strategy mitigates this by switching to Uniform Sampling in the fine stage to correct erroneous depth values. Out-of-Boundary Anchors: In the CAG-GS variant, initial anchor selection may include anchors outside the block boundary. These are intentionally kept during fine-tuning to provide reliable estimates for neighboring regions but must be discarded during the final merge. View Assignment Imbalance: If views are not assigned based on blending weights, some blocks may lack sufficient supervision. The threshold \epsilon controls the importance score ratio to assign additional views outside boundaries, ensuring adequate supervision per block. A two-stage training strategy for NeRF that uses TDBS in the coarse stage to converge density values and Uniform Sampling in the fine stage to recompute erroneous depth values and avoid local minima. It is chosen when using monocular depth priors that may contain noise, requiring a transition from prior-guided sampling to uniform sampling for refinement. The threshold Ts is set to 1000 epochs. A sampling strategy to capture ground truth depth by starting with a large interval around current depth estimation and gradually reducing it, keeping sampling density constant. It iterates over rays corresponding to foreground pixels and samples points uniformly in [d{ij} - o, d{ij} + o]. The offset parameter o defines the interval size. If the real depth falls outside this interval, appearance cannot guide geometry optimization effectively. Time Complexity: The CAG-GS variant increases total training time due to the multi-stage process (60,000 + 60,000 iterations) and scene division overhead, though block fine-tuning can be parallelized across GPUs. The TDBS variant follows standard NeRF training iteration costs, with sampling determined by the epoch threshold. Memory Complexity: The CAG-GS variant requires memory for multiple local models during fine-tuning but enables large-scale scene processing by partitioning the scene. The TDBS variant maintains memory complexity proportional to the number of sampled points per ray. Performance: Accelerates pose optimization convergence and enhances pose estimation precision. Improves global consistency and manages large-scale scenes effectively. Strengths: Circumvents local minima, refines depth geometry, handles noisy depth priors, scales to large scenes. When to Use: When using noisy monocular depth priors (TDBS variant) or rendering large-scale scenes requiring high global consistency (CAG-GS variant). The Coarse-to-Fine Training Strategy was introduced in the context of TD-NeRF (Truncated Depth Prior for Joint Camera Pose and Neural Radiance Field Optimization) to improve the joint optimization of camera poses and radiance fields using monocular depth priors. It was proposed to address the issue of noisy depth priors degrading rendering quality by progressively improving depth precision. A separate variant was introduced in CAG-GS (Consistent Anchor Guided Gaussian Splatting) to incorporate semantic guidance and improve global consistency under a divide-and-conquer strategy for large-scale scene rendering. TD-NeRF: Novel Truncated Depth Prior for Joint Camera Pose and Neural Radiance Field Optimization, https://doi.org/10.1109/iros58592.2024.10802634, fetched 2026-10-26 CAG-GS: Consistent Anchor Guided Gaussian Splatting for Large-scale Scene Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v40i14.38120, fetched 2026-10-29 Multi-View Reconstruction Using Signed Ray Distance Functions (SRDF), https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.01602, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Surface-Based Sampling
head: Near-Surface Sampling
body: Surface-Based Sampling is a strategy that restricts 3D sample point generation to a narrow band around the estimated surface of an object, rather than sampling throughout the entire volume or free space. It solves the problem of quality degradation caused by standard NeRF sampling in irrelevant regions (free space or occluded areas) by concentrating computational resources where the radiance field actually varies. Inputs: d: The depth value for a pixel/ray, representing the distance from the camera to the surface. \alpha: Half of the specified sampling range (bandwidth). N: The number of sample points per ray. Ray origin and direction (implicit in the calculation of sample positions along the ray). Outputs: A set of N sample locations \{S{r,1}, \dots, S{r,N}\} along the ray, clustered around the surface. Data Structures: The method generates a 1D array of N scalar distances from the camera origin. No complex spatial data structures are required for the sampling step itself, though the source notes mention an offline point cloud generation step for novel view depth estimation. Parameters: \alpha: Determines sampling density. Typical values: 1/2, 1/16. N: Number of samples. Typical value: 8. \gamma: A random number for stratified sampling, uniformly distributed in [0, 2\alpha/N). Steps: 1. Calculate the starting distance of the sampling range from the camera: S{r,0} = d - \alpha where S{r,0} is the location of the point nearest to the camera within the sampling range. 2. Generate N sample points using stratified sampling within the range [S{r,0}, S{r,0} + 2\alpha]: S{r,n} = S{r,0} + (n - 1) \frac{2\alpha}{N} + \gamma, \quad n = 1, \dots, N where \gamma is a random number uniformly generated between 0 and \frac{2\alpha}{N}. 3. Use the resulting points \{S{r,1}, \dots, S{r,N}\} to query the NeRF network for color and density. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def uniform(a, b): """Returns a random float uniformly distributed in [a, b).""" # Implementation depends on the language's standard PRNG; # here it represents the standard uniform random generator. pass def surfacebasedsampling(depthd, alpha, N): """ Generates N sample points along a ray, centered around the surface depth. Args: depthd (float): Depth value from the camera to the surface. alpha (float): Half of the specified sampling range. N (int): Number of sample points. Returns: list[float]: List of N sample distances from the camera origin. """ # Step 1: Calculate the start of the sampling range startdist = depthd - alpha # Step 2: Calculate bin width for stratified sampling binwidth = (2.0 alpha) / N samples = [] for n in range(1, N + 1): # Generate random offset gamma within 0, binwidth) gamma = uniform(0, binwidth) # Sr,n = Sr,0 + (n - 1) (2alpha/N) + gamma sampledist = startdist + (n - 1) binwidth + gamma samples.append(sampledist) return samples Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Accuracy: If the depth d is poorly estimated, using a small \alpha degrades rendering quality because the sampling band misses the actual surface. Parameter Selection: The value of \alpha must be set considering the accuracy of the input depth images. A larger \alpha provides a wider band, tolerating depth errors but reducing density near the surface. Accelerates [neural rendering by sampling only on the primary surface using a point cloud distribution, avoiding redundant sampling of multiple surfaces or empty space. The method computes N sample locations per ray using a constant number of arithmetic operations per sample. Restricting sampling to the near-surface area prevents quality degradation caused by sampling in free space or occluded regions, potentially improving rendering accuracy (PSNR) even without a fine sampling process. Strengths include improved rendering performance by focusing on the object surface and allowing denser sampling near the surface with fewer total samples when \alpha is small. Limitations include heavy dependence on the accuracy of the depth images, where poor depth estimation leads to degraded quality especially with small \alpha. The method requires depth images during training or a mechanism to generate them for novel views, such as point cloud refinement. The method was introduced in "Improving Neural Radiance Fields Using Near-Surface Sampling with Point Cloud Generation". It addresses the inefficiency of standard NeRF, which samples uniformly or hierarchically across the entire volume, including empty space. By leveraging depth information (either from training data or estimated for novel views), the method confines the search space to the object's vicinity. Improving Neural Radiance Fields Using Near-Surface Sampling with Point Cloud Generation, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11063-024-11654-5, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Adaptive Primary Surface Sampling
head: APS, HashPoint Sampling
body: Adaptive Primary Surface Sampling is a technique that accelerates neural rendering by adaptively sampling 3D points only on the primary surface (the first surface encountered by a camera ray), avoiding redundant sampling of multiple surfaces or empty space. It distinguishes itself from Depth Map Sampling by not requiring dense depth inputs, and from Multi-Surface Sampling by focusing exclusively on the front-most surface to balance precision and efficiency. It builds on Surface-Based Sampling by using a point cloud distribution to guide this selection rather than explicit depth maps. Inputs: Camera parameters: optical center \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, focal length f, pixel center \mathbf{p}o. Point cloud data \mathcal{P} stored in a Hashed-Point Searching structure (hash table mapping 2D image plane regions to 3D points). Hyperparameters: K (number of neighbors for pseudo-UDF calculation), \gamma (sampling range control), \beta (density-dependent scaling), r{min} (minimum search radius at t{near}), t{near}, t{far}. Outputs: A set of definitive sample points \{xj^{sp}\} located on the primary surface along the ray. Rendered color c for the pixel. Data Structures: Hashed-Point Searching Structure: A hash table that maps 2D pixel coordinates (or regions on the image plane) to lists of 3D point cloud indices. This allows O(1) lookup of points near a ray. Sample Point Candidate List: A temporary list of projected points xj^{sp} derived from neighboring points. Steps: 1. Ray Cone Definition and Search Kernel Construction: Define a ray cone from the optical center \mathbf{o} through the pixel center \mathbf{p}o. To mitigate holes caused by point cloud sparsity, expand the search kernel radius r dynamically based on distance t along the ray. The radius r at distance t is computed as: r(t) = \|\mathbf{p}o - \mathbf{o}\|2 \cdot \sqrt{\left(\sqrt{\|\mathbf{p}o - \mathbf{o}\|2^2 - f^2} - \ddot{r}\right)^2 + f^2} where \ddot{r} is the base radius of the searching kernel. The magnitude of the searching kernel s is deduced as s = 2 \cdot \ddot{r} + 1. The search is performed by traversing pixels in the search kernel and looking up associated points in the hash table. 2. Point Projection: Identify point clouds near the camera ray using the Hashed-Point Searching structure. Project these neighboring points onto the camera ray. Each projected point becomes a sample point candidate xj^{sp}, defined as: xj^{sp} = \mathbf{o} + tj \mathbf{d} where tj is the intersection parameter of the projection. 3. Pseudo-UDF Calculation: For each candidate xj^{sp}, calculate the average distance dj to its K nearest neighboring points in the point cloud \mathcal{P}. This distance is termed "pseudo-UDF" because it adheres to Unsigned Distance Function (UDF) principles but is not a strict UDF: dj = \frac{1}{K} \sum{i=1}^{K} \|xj^{sp} - xi^{pc}\|2 where xi^{pc} are the coordinates of the K nearest neighbors. 4. Confidence and Weight Calculation: Transform the distance dj into a confidence value \alphaj using a Gaussian-like function dependent on point cloud density \beta and sampling range \gamma: \alphaj = \gamma \exp \left( -\frac{dj^2}{\betaj^2} \right) Here, \beta is a hyperparameter depending on the local density of the point cloud; a smaller dj (proximity to surface) necessitates a reduced \beta to ensure distinct differentiation in confidence. To ensure occlusion awareness (prioritizing points closer to the viewpoint), define the weight wj for each candidate: wj = \alphaj \prod{k=1}^{j-1} (1 - \alphak) This formula ensures that if a candidate has high confidence (\alpha), it contributes significantly, while subsequent candidates are weighted by the transmittance of previous ones. 5. Sample Selection: Retain sample point candidates with wj > 0. These candidates are located near the primary surface. The number of retained samples is adaptive, ranging from 0 to n, depending on the point cloud distribution and ray path. 6. Rendering Integration: Sample between t{near} and t{far} using the selected definitive sample points. Simulate radiance using volume density accumulation: c = \sum{j=1}^{N} \tauj \left( 1 - \exp(-\sigmaj \Deltat) \right) cj^{sp} where: N is the number of selected sample points. \tauj = \exp(-\sum{k=1}^{j-1} \sigmak \Deltak) is the volume transmittance. \sigmaj is the density predicted by an MLP or estimated from point features for sample point j. cj^{sp} is the color for sample point j. \Deltat is the distance between adjacent sample points. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptiveprimarysurfacesampling(rayorigin, raydirection, cameraparams, pointcloudhashtable, K, gamma, beta, tnear, tfar): """ rayorigin: 3D vector o raydirection: 3D vector d cameraparams: dict containing focallength f, pixelcenter po, opticalcenter o pointcloudhashtable: Hash table mapping 2D regions to 3D points K: int, number of neighbors for pseudo-UDF gamma: float, sampling range control beta: float, density-dependent scaling tnear: float, near plane distance tfar: float, far plane distance """ f = cameraparams['focallength'] po = cameraparams['pixelcenter'] o = cameraparams['opticalcenter'] # Step 1: Determine search radius at tnear (rmin) # Note: The formula in source uses d for distance from origin to pixel center dpoo = np.linalg.norm(po - o) # Base radius rtilde is derived from input hyperparameters or kernel size s # Assuming rtilde is provided or calculated from kernel size s = 2 rtilde + 1 # For implementation, we assume rtilde is known or passed. # If not given, we use the dynamic radius formula for any t. samplecandidates = [] # Step 2: Identify points near the ray using Hashed-Point Searching # This involves querying the hash table for points within the expanded ray cone. # The cone radius r(t) expands with t. # We iterate through relevant pixels in the search kernel and retrieve points. nearbypoints = queryhashtable(pointcloudhashtable, rayorigin, raydirection, cameraparams) # Project nearby points onto the ray to form candidates for point in nearbypoints: # Project point onto ray direction # tj = dot(point - o, d) / dot(d, d) # Assuming d is normalized, dot(d,d) = 1 tj = np.dot(point - o, raydirection) # Only consider points within the rendering range if tj < tnear or tj > tfar: continue xsp = o + tj raydirection samplecandidates.append({'point': xsp, 't': tj, 'originalpoint': point}) # Step 3 & 4: Calculate Pseudo-UDF and Weights weightedsamples = [] # Sort candidates by distance from viewpoint (t) to ensure occlusion order samplecandidates.sort(key=lambda x: x['t']) for i, cand in enumerate(samplecandidates): xsp = cand['point'] # Find K nearest neighbors in the original point cloud # In a real implementation, this uses the hash table or a KD-tree neighbors = findknearestneighbors(pointcloudhashtable, xsp, K) # Calculate pseudo-UDF (average distance to K neighbors) dists = [np.linalg.norm(xsp - n) for n in neighbors] dj = np.mean(dists) # Calculate confidence alpha # beta might be local; here we use the passed beta parameter # If beta is density-dependent, it should be computed per point. # Source says "beta is a hyperparameter which depends on the density of the point cloud" # and "lesser dj necessitates a reduced beta". # For simplicity, we use the passed beta, but in practice betaj might vary. alphaj = gamma np.exp(-(dj2) / (beta2)) # Calculate weight wj # wj = alphaj product(1 - alphak) for k < j # We need to accumulate the product of (1 - alpha) from previous steps if i == 0: transmittancesofar = 1.0 else: # Recalculate or store previous transmittance # To avoid O(N^2), we can maintain a running product # However, the formula is explicit. We assume we have access to previous alphas. # Let's assume we store previous alphas in a list or compute on the fly. # For O(N) efficiency, we maintain a running product. pass # Efficient calculation of wj # We need the product of (1 - alphak) for all k < i # Let's assume we have a variable prevtransmittance updated in the loop wj = alphaj prevtransmittance if wj > 0: weightedsamples.append({ 'point': xsp, 't': tj, 'alpha': alphaj, 'weight': wj }) # Update transmittance for next iteration # The term (1 - alphaj) is the transmittance through this "layer" # Note: The weight formula uses product(1-alphak). # So for the next step, we multiply current transmittance by (1 - alphaj) prevtransmittance = (1 - alphaj) # Step 6: Render # Sort selected samples by t (they should already be sorted) weightedsamples.sort(key=lambda x: x['t']) color = 0.0 currenttransmittance = 1.0 for i, sample in enumerate(weightedsamples): # Predict density sigma and color csp for this sample point # This depends on the specific neural rendering method (e.g., MLP) sigmaj = predictdensity(sample['point']) cspj = predictcolor(sample['point']) # Distance to next sample or tfar if i + 1 < len(weightedsamples): deltat = weightedsamples[i+1]['t'] - sample['t'] else: deltat = tfar - sample['t'] # Volume rendering contribution # c = sum( tauj (1 - exp(-sigmaj deltat)) cspj) # tauj is the transmittance arriving at sample j # In the loop, currenttransmittance represents tauj contribution = currenttransmittance (1 - np.exp(-sigmaj deltat)) cspj color += contribution # Update transmittance for the next sample currenttransmittance = np.exp(-sigmaj deltat) # Early termination if transmittance is negligible if currenttransmittance < 1e-4: break return color Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Point Cloud Sparsity: If no points fall within the ray cone, rendering holes may occur. This is mitigated by modifying the ray cone for broader coverage using a larger disc radius for the searching kernel. Beta Parameter: The hyperparameter \beta depends on point cloud density. A smaller distance dj (proximity to surface) necessitates a reduced \beta to ensure distinct differentiation in confidence \alphaj across sample points. Zero Samples: The number of sample points can range from 0 to n. If 0 points are selected, the pixel may remain black or require a fallback strategy (not specified in source, but implied by "holes" mitigation). Time Complexity: The hash table lookup for point searching is O(1) per query. The overall complexity depends on the number of points in the search kernel and the K-nearest neighbor search, which is typically efficient with spatial hashing. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the point cloud and the hash table structure. Performance: Demonstrates significant acceleration in rendering process with similar or better accuracy compared to traditional methods on synthetic, real, indoor, and outdoor datasets. Strengths: Avoids redundant sampling on multiple surfaces (unlike Multi-Surface Sampling) and does not require dense depth maps (unlike Depth Map Sampling). Limitations: Performance depends on the quality and density of the input point cloud. Sparsity can lead to holes if not mitigated by the expanded search kernel. Adaptive Primary Surface Sampling was introduced in the paper "HashPoint: Accelerated Point Searching and Sampling for Neural Rendering". It is part of the HashPoint method, which aims to accelerate neural rendering by optimizing point searching and sampling strategies. The method was validated on various benchmark datasets, including NeRF-Synthesis. name: Rendered Depth-Guided Warping
head: Depth-Guided Warping
body: Rendered Depth-Guided Warping is a consistency regularization technique used during NeRF training to enforce geometric coherence between observed and unobserved viewpoints without the computational cost of full-resolution rendering. It generates a warped image from a source view using a low-resolution rendered depth map from a target view, enabling the computation of a consistency loss that encourages globally consistent geometry and appearance. Unlike Depth-Guided Sampling which uses depth to guide ray sampling, this method uses rendered depth to warp existing image data for loss calculation. Inputs: Source view image Ii at known viewpoint i. Target view (unseen) parameters: camera intrinsics K, rotation R{j \to i} relative to source. NeRF model f\theta capable of outputting density \sigma. Outputs: Warped image patch I{i \to j} aligned with the target view j. Data Structures: Strided Ray Grid: A 2D grid of ray origins and directions sampled with stride s (typically s=2) over the image dimensions. Low-Resolution Depth Map Dj: Rendered depth values corresponding to the strided ray grid. Upsampled Depth Map: Full-resolution depth map obtained via bilinear interpolation of Dj. Steps: 1. Strided Ray Sampling: Sample rays on a grid with stride s=2 to create low-resolution patches. This reduces the number of rays processed per iteration, significantly lowering computational cost. 2. Low-Resolution Depth Rendering: For each sampled ray, query the NeRF model for density \sigma and integrate along the ray to render a depth value Dj(pj) for pixel pj in the target view. The depth is formulated as a weighted composition of density values. 3. Depth Upsampling: Upsample the low-resolution depth map Dj back to the original image resolution using bilinear interpolation. This yields a full-resolution depth map required for precise inverse warping. 4. Coordinate Transformation: For each pixel pj in the target view, compute the corresponding coordinate p{j \to i} in the source view Ii using the camera intrinsics K, the viewpoint difference R{j \to i}, and the rendered depth Dj(pj): p{j \to i} \sim K R{j \to i} Dj(pj) K^{-1} pj where \sim indicates approximate equality and p{j \to i} is a continuous coordinate. 5. Inverse Warping: Use a differentiable sampler to extract color values from the source image Ii at the projected coordinates p{j \to i} to generate the warped image I{i \to j}: I{i \to j}(pj) = \text{sampler}(Ii; p{j \to i}) 6. Consistency Loss: Compare the rendered target view image Ij with the warped source image I{i \to j} using pixel-wise reconstruction loss or feature-level consistency loss to regularize the NeRF training. Parameters: Stride s: Typically set to 2 to balance computational efficiency and geometric accuracy. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusions: The warping assumes visibility. If the target view sees geometry occluded in the source view, the warped image will contain incorrect background colors. The source notes mention an "Occlusion mask" in Figure 3 of, implying masking strategies may be required to handle these regions, though the specific algorithm is not detailed in the text. Depth Precision: Errors in the rendered depth Dj propagate directly into the projected coordinates p{j \to i}. Low-resolution rendering may lack fine geometric detail, leading to misalignment artifacts. A strategy used in hybrid optimization pipelines (e.g., HO-Gaussian) to simulate images from virtual viewpoints by perturbing existing poses and querying colors from a grid-based volume. It helps align colors in multi-camera systems with limited overlapping areas and reduces overfitting to specific viewpoints. Process: Perturb an existing pose [Re, Te] by rotating around the current position xp with random angles in the range [-10, 10] to generate a virtual pose [Rv, Tv]. Projection: Project the image point pi to the warped point pv using the intrinsic matrix K and the virtual pose: p{v}=K(R{v}(p{i})+T{v}) Color Query: Obtain the color of the warped image at position xp and direction d using the grid-based volume MLP f\theta: cv^\theta = f\theta (xp, d) Computational Cost: Significantly reduced compared to full-resolution rendering. Rendering a full image can take tens of seconds per iteration; strided sampling with s=2 reduces this cost to a fraction, enabling efficient consistency regularization during training. Accuracy: The method relies on the accuracy of the rendered depth. Low-resolution depth may lack fine details, potentially causing warping artifacts in high-frequency regions. Bilinear upsampling helps mitigate this but does not recover true high-frequency geometry. Use Case: Best suited for few-shot NeRF training where geometric consistency is critical and full-resolution rendering is too slow for frequent consistency checks. Rendered Depth-Guided Warping was introduced in the context of GeCoNeRF (Geometric Consistency NeRF) for few-shot neural radiance fields. The method addresses the computational bottleneck of rendering full images for consistency regularization by leveraging low-resolution depth maps and inverse warping. It builds on the alpha compositing principles of NeRF Rendering (Alpha Compositing) to generate the depth priors necessary for the warping process. GeCoNeRF: Few-Shot Neural Radiance Fields via Geometric Consistency, https://core.ac.uk/works/309257742, fetched 2026-11-01 (unofficial) HO-Gaussian: Hybrid Optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting for Urban Scenes, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-73027-62, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Depth-Prior Guided Stratified Sampling
head: Confidence-bounded sampling, Priors-guided sampling
body: Depth-Prior Guided Stratified Sampling replaces uniform depth sampling in volume rendering by using predicted depth priors and associated confidence bounds to focus sampling on likely object surfaces. Inputs: depthpriors: Tensor of shape [N{rays}], containing the predicted depth for each ray. depthconfidences: Tensor of shape [N{rays}], containing the uncertainty width for each ray. nearbound: Scalar float, the minimum allowed depth offset multiplier. farbound: Scalar float, the maximum allowed depth offset multiplier. lindisp: Boolean flag. If True, samples linearly in inverse depth; otherwise, linearly in depth. perturb: Float. If non-zero, stratified random sampling is applied. Nsamples: Integer, number of samples per ray. Outputs: zvals: Tensor of shape [N{rays}, N{samples}], containing the sampled depths along each ray. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Compute Bounds: Calculate the near and far depth limits for each ray using the depth prior and confidence, clamped to the global bounds. near = depth\priors \times (1 - \text{clamp}(depth\confidences, min=near\bound, max=far\bound)) far = depth\priors \times (1 + \text{clamp}(depth\confidences, min=near\bound, max=far\bound)) Here, \text{clamp}(v, min, max) restricts v to the range [min, max]. 2. Generate Linear Spacing: Create a 1D tensor tvals of shape [N{samples}] linearly spaced from 0 to 1. 3. Interpolate Depths: If lindisp is False: z\vals = near \times (1 - t\vals) + far \times t\vals If lindisp is True: z\vals = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{near}(1 - t\vals) + \frac{1}{far}t\vals} This results in zvals of shape [N{rays}, N{samples}]. 4. Stratified Sampling (if perturb > 0): Compute midpoints between adjacent samples: mids = 0.5 \times (z\vals[..., 1:] + z\vals[...,:-1]) Construct upper and lower bounds for each interval: upper = \text{concatenate}(mids, z\vals[..., -1:]) lower = \text{concatenate}(z\vals[...,:1], mids) Generate random values: t\rand = \text{random\uniform}(shape=z\vals.shape) Sample new depths: z\vals = lower + (upper - lower) \times t\rand All steps follow the source implementation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def depthpriorguidedstratifiedsampling( depthpriors: torch.Tensor, depthconfidences: torch.Tensor, nearbound: float, farbound: float, lindisp: bool, perturb: float, Nsamples: int) -> torch.Tensor: # Step 1: Compute bounds clampedconf = torch.clamp(depthconfidences, min=nearbound, max=farbound) near = depthpriors (1.0 - clampedconf) far = depthpriors (1.0 + clampedconf) # Step 2: Generate tvals tvals = torch.linspace(0, 1, Nsamples) # Step 3: Interpolate tvalsexpanded = tvals.unsqueeze(0) nearexpanded = near.unsqueeze(1) farexpanded = far.unsqueeze(1) if lindisp: invnear = 1.0 / nearexpanded invfar = 1.0 / farexpanded denom = invnear (1.0 - tvalsexpanded) + invfar tvalsexpanded zvals = 1.0 / denom else: zvals = nearexpanded (1.0 - tvalsexpanded) + farexpanded tvalsexpanded # Step 4: Stratified Sampling if perturb > 0 if perturb > 0: mids = 0.5 (zvals[..., 1:] + zvals[...,:-1]) upper = torch.cat([mids, zvals[..., -1:]], dim=-1) lower = torch.cat([zvals[...,:1], mids], dim=-1) trand = torch.rand(zvals.shape) zvals = lower + (upper - lower) trand return zvals Parameters: lindisp: bool. If True, sampling occurs in inverse depth space. perturb: float. If non-zero, stratified random sampling is used. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: In lindisp=True mode, if near or far is zero, invnear or invfar becomes infinite. The source does not specify a guard, but numerically, 1/0 should be handled by clamping near/far to a small epsilon. Clamping Logic: The confidence is clamped to nearbound and farbound. Shape Broadcasting: Care must be taken to broadcast tvals correctly against near and far tensors of shape [Nrays] to produce [Nrays, Nsamples]. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Focuses sampling on high-probability regions defined by the depth prior. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of depthpriors and depthconfidences. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. weiyithu/NerfingMVS, https://github.com/weiyithu/NerfingMVS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Neus SDF Volume Rendering
head: Neus rendering, SRDF Volume Rendering, Volume Rendering of SRDF
body: Neus SDF Volume Rendering is a technique that renders 3D scenes represented as Signed Distance Functions (SDF) or Signed Ray Distance Functions (SRDF) by accumulating color and depth along rays using alpha compositing. It solves the problem of precisely extracting geometric surfaces from implicit representations by replacing the standard NeRF density field with an SDF-based weighting scheme. It differs from standard NeRF rendering by using a trainable S-density function to concentrate weight at the zero-level set of the SDF, ensuring the surface contributes most to the image, and adapts this theory to SRDF by treating surface normals as irrelevant to the value distribution. Inputs: Ray origin o and direction v. SDF field f(x) or SRDF field. Color field c(p(t), v) sampled at points along the ray. Number of sampled points M (sum of coarse N{coarse} and fine N{fine} samples). Trainable hyperparameter b. Outputs: Rendered color \hat{C}. Rendered depth \hat{D}. Ray Samples: A sequence of M points tj along the ray p(t) = o + tv, sorted from near to far. SDF Values: f(p(tj)) for each sample point. Color Values: \hat{c}j for each sample point. 1. S-Density Function The S-density \phib(f(x)) is defined as: \phib(f(x)) = \frac{b e^{-b f(x)}}{(1 + e^{-b f(x)})^2} where b is a trainable hyperparameter that gradually increases to a large number as network training converges. 2. Surface Extraction The surface S is extracted by finding the zero-level set of the SDF: S = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid f(x) = 0\} 3. Continuous Volume Rendering The continuous color C(o, v) is accumulated along the ray: C(o, v) = \int0^{+\infty} w(t)c(p(t), v)dt where the weight w(t) is rebuilt using the S-density to guarantee surface contribution: w(t) = \frac{\phis(f(p(t)))}{\int0^{+\infty} \phis(f(p(u)))du} Here, \phis is the S-density function used for weighting. 4. Discrete Opacity The discrete opacity \alphaj at sample j is defined by integrating the opaque density \rho(t) over the interval [tj, t{j+1}]: \alphaj = 1 - \exp\left(-\int{tj}^{t{j+1}} \rho(t) dt\right) For SRDF, \rho(t) uses the SRDF value instead of SDF, but the distribution is treated as equivalent to SDF where surfaces are perpendicular to the ray. 5. Discrete Accumulative Transmittance Tj = \prod{k=1}^{j-1} (1 - \alphak) with T1 = 1. 6. Rendered Color \hat{C} = \sum{j=1}^{M} Tj \alphaj \hat{c}j where \hat{c}j is the color at sample j. 7. Rendered Depth \hat{D} = \sum{j=1}^{M} Tj \alphaj tj where tj is the distance of sample j from the origin. b: Trainable hyperparameter for S-density sharpness. M: Total number of sampled points (N{coarse} + N{fine}). Typical values: N{coarse}=64, N{fine}=64. \delta: Threshold for image space consistency in geometric consistency filtering. Default: 1. \varepsilon: Threshold for depth consistency in geometric consistency filtering. Default: 0.01. 1. Emit Ray: Define ray p(t) = o + tv from pixel origin o and direction v. 2. Sample Points: Uniformly sample N{coarse} points and importance sample N{fine} points to get M total points tj along the ray. 3. Evaluate SDF/SRDF: Query the neural network for f(p(tj)) at each sample point. 4. Compute S-Density: Calculate \phib(f(p(tj))) using the current value of b. 5. Compute Opacity: Calculate \alphaj based on the integral of the density derived from \phib. Note: For SRDF, the method assumes the distribution of SRDF values along the ray is the same as SDF with surfaces perpendicular to the ray, allowing the use of the same SDF volume rendering theory. 6. Compute Transmittance: Calculate Tj using the product of (1-\alphak) for previous samples. 7. Accumulate Color: Compute \hat{C} = \sum{j=1}^{M} Tj \alphaj \hat{c}j. 8. Accumulate Depth: Compute \hat{D} = \sum{j=1}^{M} Tj \alphaj tj. SRDF vs SDF Normals: For SRDF, surface normal vectors are set to be random at intersection points because the distribution of SRDF is irrelevant to the surface normal. For SDF, surfaces are assumed perpendicular to the ray. The method adopts SDF rendering for SRDF based on the equivalence of their distributions under this assumption. Hyperparameter b: b must be trained and gradually increased to ensure the surface contribution is sharp and accurate. Geometric Consistency: When using multi-view aggregation, depth estimates should be filtered using geometric consistency with thresholds \delta=1 and \varepsilon=0.01 to reject unreliable views. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def neussdfvolumerendering(rayorigin, raydirection, sdfnetwork, colornetwork, b, numcoarse=64, numfine=64): """ Renders color and depth using NeuS SDF volume rendering. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, origin of the ray. raydirection: 3D vector, direction of the ray. sdfnetwork: Function returning SDF/SRDF value f(x) for point x. colornetwork: Function returning color c(x, v) for point x and direction v. b: Trainable hyperparameter for S-density. numcoarse: Number of coarse samples. numfine: Number of fine samples. Returns: renderedcolor: Scalar, accumulated color. rendereddepth: Scalar, accumulated depth. """ # 1. Sample points along the ray # Hierarchical sampling: uniform coarse, then importance fine tcoarse = uniformsample(numcoarse, tmin=0.0, tmax=raylength) # Importance sampling based on coarse SDF values would go here tfine = importancesample(numfine, sdfnetwork, rayorigin, raydirection, tcoarse) # Combine and sort tsamples = sort(concatenate(tcoarse, tfine)) M = len(tsamples) # 2. Evaluate SDF and Color at each sample points = [rayorigin + t raydirection for t in tsamples] sdfvalues = [sdfnetwork(p) for p in points] colors = [colornetwork(p, raydirection) for p in points] # 3. Compute S-Density and Opacity # S-density: phib(f(x)) = b exp(-b f(x)) / (1 + exp(-b f(x)))^2 sdensities = [] for fval in sdfvalues: expnegbf = exp(-b fval) phi = (b expnegbf) / ((1 + expnegbf) 2) sdensities.append(phi) # Compute opacity alphaj # alphaj = 1 - exp(- integral{tj}^{t{j+1}} rho(t) dt) # rho(t) is derived from S-density. # Note: In discrete implementation, often alphaj is approximated directly from phi or integrated density. # Based on NeuS, the weight w(t) is rebuilt by S-density. # The discrete opacity formula uses opaque density rho(t). # We approximate the integral of rho(t) over the interval. # A common approximation in NeRF/Neus is: alphaj = 1 - exp(-sigmaj deltaj) # where sigmaj is the density at tj and deltaj is the distance to next point. # Here, sigmaj is related to phib. alphas = [] for j in range(M): tj = tsamples[j] tnext = tsamples[j+1] if j < M-1 else tj + 0.01 # Handle last point deltat = tnext - tj # Approximate integral of rho(t) as phib deltat # This is a simplification; exact integration depends on the specific density formulation # NeuS uses the S-density directly in the weight formulation for continuous rendering, # but discrete alpha compositing requires opacity. # We use the S-density as the density proxy. rhointegral = sdensities[j] deltat alpha = 1.0 - exp(-rhointegral) alphas.append(alpha) # 4. Compute Transmittance transmittances = [1.0] M for j in range(1, M): transmittances[j] = transmittances[j-1] (1.0 - alphas[j-1]) # 5. Accumulate Color and Depth renderedcolor = 0.0 rendereddepth = 0.0 for j in range(M): weight = transmittances[j] alphas[j] renderedcolor += weight colors[j] rendereddepth += weight tsamples[j] return renderedcolor, rendereddepth Time Complexity: Linear in the number of samples M per ray. Memory Complexity: Linear in M for storing sample values. Performance: Depends on the resolution of the global feature volume and the number of samples. In experiments, N{coarse}=64, N{fine}=64 were used. Strengths: Precisely extracts geometric surfaces via the zero-level set of the SDF. Handles SRDF by leveraging the equivalence of value distributions with perpendicular SDF surfaces. Limitations: Not suitable for very large-scale scenes due to the low resolution of the global feature volume. Requires careful tuning of the hyperparameter b. Origin: The method is based on the NeuS paper [49] (Sitzmann et al., or similar, cited as [49] in S1, [38] in S2) which introduced SDF-based volume rendering for NeRF. Development: It was adapted for Signed Ray Distance Functions (SRDF) in VolRecon to handle multi-view reconstruction where surface normals are not explicitly defined or reliable. It is also used in Instant-NSR for accelerated training with Hash encoding. Usage: Used in multi-view stereo reconstruction (DTU, ETH3D datasets) for high-fidelity 3D reconstruction. VolRecon: Volume Rendering of Signed Ray Distance Functions for Generalizable Multi-View Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.01601, fetched 2026-10-26 High-fidelity 3D Reconstruction of Plants using Neural Radiance Field, https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.04154v1, fetched 2026-10-27
