name: Progressive Blur Estimation
head: two-stage blur estimation
body: Progressive Blur Estimation (PBE) is a two-stage implicit function module that estimates defocus and motion blur by predicting multiple ray origins, directions, and blending weights for each pixel. It solves the problem of rendering blurry observations from a radiance field by modeling blur as a distribution of rays rather than a single ray. It sets itself apart from single-stage blur models by using a coarse stage to predict initial kernel locations and a refinement stage that incorporates ray features for fine-grained blur modeling, which is more accurate and efficient than a single-stage approach with ray features. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: x: 2D pixel coordinate. o: Ray origin. d: Ray direction. l: View embedding for the current view. V: Number of source views. P: Number of rays (kernel size) estimated per pixel. Outputs: \{r{xk}\}{k=1}^P: Final set of P rays. \{h(xk)\}{k=1}^P: Blending weights for each ray. Data Structures: Canonical blur kernel location (x'k): Learnable parameter, shape \mathbb{R}^{V \times P \times 2}. Normalized to be at most \pm 10 pixels from x. View embedding (l): Learnable parameter, shape \mathbb{R}^{V \times K}. Implicit Function (H): A four-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with channel size 64 and ReLU activation. Ray Feature (f{ray}): Aggregated per-voxel features from the underlying radiance field, dimension 15. Parameters: P: Kernel size. Typical values: 5 or 10. K: View embedding size. Value: 32. H: Architecture: 4-layer MLP, channel size 64, ReLU. f{ray} dimension: 15. Steps: 1. Coarse Stage: Query implicit function H with view embedding l, 2D coordinate x, and canonical kernel location x'k to predict offsets \Delta o{x'k}, \Delta x'k and initial weights h'(x^k). Formula: \Delta o{x'k}, \Delta x'k, h'(x^k) = H(l, x, x'k, \emptyset) where \emptyset is a zero vector placeholder for additional features. Compute refined location x^k = x'k + \Delta x'k and origin o{x^k} = o + \Delta o{x'k}. Compute coarse ray r{x^k} = o{x^k} + t d{x^k}. 2. Feature Aggregation: Trace ray r{x^k} through the coarse radiance field to aggregate per-voxel features into f{ray}(r{x^k}). Note: The exact formulation for aggregation is elaborated in the underlying radiance field rendering equations (e.g., Eq. 7 in), typically involving alpha compositing of features along the ray. 3. Refinement Stage: Query implicit function H with view embedding l, 2D coordinate x, coarse location x^k, and ray feature f{ray}(r{x^k}) to predict offsets \Delta o{x^k}, \Delta x^k and final weights h(xk). Formula: \Delta o{x^k}, \Delta x^k, h(xk) = H(l, x, x^k, f{ray}(r{x^k})) Compute final location xk = x^k + \Delta x^k and origin o{xk} = o + \Delta o{x^k}. Compute final ray r{xk} = o{xk} + t d{xk}. 4. Rendering: Use the final set of rays \{r{xk}\} and weights \{h(xk)\} to render the blurry observation using Eq. (3) from the source. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def progressiveblurestimation(x, o, d, l, xprime, H, radiancefield, P): """ x: 2D pixel coordinate (float, shape (2,)) o: Ray origin (float, shape (3,)) d: Ray direction (float, shape (3,)) l: View embedding (float, shape (K,)) xprime: Canonical blur kernel locations (float, shape (P, 2)) H: Implicit function (MLP) radiancefield: Coarse radiance field for feature aggregation P: Number of rays per pixel """ # Coarse Stage # H predicts offsets and initial weights # Input to H: l, x, xprime, empty feature vector deltaocoarse, deltaxcoarse, hcoarse = H(l, x, xprime, np.zeros(xprime.shape)) # Compute coarse ray parameters xstar = xprime + deltaxcoarse ostar = o + deltaocoarse # dxstar is the direction vector corresponding to 2D coordinate xstar # Computed via standard pinhole projection from camera intrinsics dxstar = computedirectionfrom2d(xstar) # Feature Aggregation # Trace ray rx through radiance field to aggregate per-voxel features # Exact formulation uses alpha compositing of features along the ray fray = aggregatefeaturesalongray(radiancefield, ostar, dxstar) # Refinement Stage # H predicts final offsets and weights # Input to H: l, x, xstar, fray deltaorefined, deltaxrefined, hfinal = H(l, x, xstar, fray) # Compute final ray parameters xfinal = xstar + deltaxrefined ofinal = o + deltaorefined dxfinal = computedirectionfrom2d(xfinal) # Final rays and weights rays = [] weights = [] for k in range(P): rays.append((ofinal[k], dxfinal[k])) weights.append(hfinal[k]) return rays, weights def computedirectionfrom2d(x2d): # Standard pinhole camera projection to 3D direction pass def aggregatefeaturesalongray(radiancefield, origin, direction): # Standard volume rendering integration to aggregate per-voxel features pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: When observations are sharp, offsets \Delta o and \Delta x'k should converge to similar spatial locations. When observations are blurry, offsets \Delta o and \Delta x'k should be dissimilar to account for blur. The two-stage design is preferred over a single-stage design with ray features because the coarse stage computes quickly and provides an accurate x^ for a more informative f{ray} in the refinement stage. Time Complexity: The two-stage design is efficient because the coarse stage (Eq. 4) computes quickly, and the refinement stage benefits from a more accurate initial estimate. Memory Complexity: The model size for a single scene is 160MB in PDRF, which is smaller than TensoRF's 200MB for forward-facing scenes. Strengths: Can clearly distinguish foreground details from blurry background pixels, as shown by variance of predicted offsets. Limitations: Tracing multiple rays is costly, so the kernel size P should be minimal. Progressive Blur Estimation (PBE) was introduced in the PDRF (Progressively Deblurring Radiance Field) paper. It builds on prior works by introducing an implicit function H to model blur. name: MipNerfModel
head: Mip-NeRF 360 Model
body: The MipNerfModel is a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) architecture that approximates integrated positional encoding by treating rays as cones or cylinders rather than infinitesimally thin lines, thereby solving aliasing artifacts caused by high-frequency scene details. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF implementations by using multi-level sampling (coarse and fine) and integrated positional encoding to model the frequency content of the signal along the ray, which is essential for training on unbounded, outdoor scenes. The model implements a differentiable rendering pipeline that processes rays defined by origins, directions, radii, and viewing parameters. It utilizes a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to predict density and color, conditioned on integrated positional encodings of the sampled points. Inputs: rays: A structure containing: origins: 3D coordinates of ray origins. directions: Normalized ray direction vectors. viewdirs: View direction vectors, explicitly passed for conditioning. radii: The radius of the ray at the sample points (used for integrated encoding). near: Near plane distance for each ray. far: Far plane distance for each ray. temperature: Camera temperature parameter for ISP. exposure: Camera exposure parameter for ISP. coc: Circle of Confusion parameter (used to scale ray radii during training). rng: Random number generator state. whitebkgd: Boolean indicating if the background is white (affects alpha compositing). traincoc: Circle of Confusion multiplier for ray radii during training. randomized: Boolean indicating whether to use randomized sampling. Outputs: comprgb: Computed RGB color per ray. distance: Expected distance along the ray. acc: Accumulated alpha (opacity) along the ray. weights: Per-sample weights used for resampling in subsequent levels. The rays object holds batched arrays: origins: Shape (B, 3). directions: Shape (B, 3). viewdirs: Shape (B, 3). radii: Shape (B,) initially, representing the radius at the pixel, scaled by coc. near: Shape (B,). far: Shape (B,). numsamples: int, number of samples per level. Default: 128. numlevels: int, number of sampling levels (coarse and fine). Default: 2. resamplepadding: float, Dirichlet/alpha padding added to weights before normalization during resampling. Default: 0.01. stoplevelgrad: bool, if True, gradients do not backpropagate across levels. Default: True. useviewdirs: bool, if True, view directions are used as a condition for the MLP. Default: True. lindisp: bool, if True, sampling is linear in disparity (1/z) rather than depth (z). Default: False. rayshape: str, shape of cast rays, must be 'cone' or 'cylinder'. Default: 'cone'. mindegpoint: int, minimum degree of positional encoding for 3D points. Default: 0. maxdegpoint: int, maximum degree of positional encoding for 3D points. Default: 16. degview: int, degree of positional encoding for view directions. Default: 4. densityactivation: Callable, density activation function. Default: softplus. densitynoise: float, standard deviation of noise added to raw density. Default: 0.0. densitybias: float, shift added to raw densities pre-activation. Default: -1.0. rgbactivation: Callable, RGB activation function. Default: sigmoid. rgbpadding: float, padding added to RGB outputs. Default: 0.001. disableintegration: bool, if True, use Point-wise Positional Encoding instead of Integrated Positional Encoding. Default: False. 1. Initialization: Initialize the MLP and Image Signal Processing (ISP) modules. Create an empty result list ret. 2. Level Loop: Iterate ilevel from 0 to numlevels - 1. 3. Randomness: Split the random number generator rng into key and a new rng. 4. Sampling: If ilevel == 0 (Coarse): Perform stratified sampling along rays. Calculate effective radius: effectiveradius = rays.radii traincoc. Call samplealongrays(key, rays.origins, rays.directions, effectiveradius, numsamples, rays.near, rays.far, randomized, lindisp, rayshape). This returns tvals (sample positions along the ray) and samples (3D coordinates and radii at those positions). If ilevel > 0 (Fine): Resample along rays based on previous weights. Call resamplealongrays(key, rays.origins, rays.directions, effectiveradius, tvals, weights, randomized, rayshape, stoplevelgrad, resamplepadding). This returns updated tvals and samples. 5. Integration Check: If disableintegration is True, replace samples with (samples[0], jnp.zeroslike(samples[1])) to disable integrated encoding (effectively reverting to point-wise PE). 6. Positional Encoding: Compute integrated positional encoding for the 3D samples using integratedposenc(samples, mindegpoint, maxdegpoint). This function accounts for the cone/cylinder shape of the ray segment by integrating the standard positional encoding over the interval defined by the sample's radius. If useviewdirs is True, compute view direction encoding using posenc(rays.viewdirs, mindeg=0, maxdeg=degview, appendidentity=True). 7. MLP Forward Pass: Concatenate point encoding and view direction encoding (if used) to form the input to the MLP. The MLP outputs rawdensity and rawrgb. If randomized is True and densitynoise > 0, add Gaussian noise: rawdensity += densitynoise random.normal(key, rawdensity.shape, dtype=rawdensity.dtype). 8. Activations: Apply RGB activation: rgb = rgbactivation(rawrgb). Apply RGB padding: rgb = rgb (1 + 2 rgbpadding) - rgbpadding. Apply density activation: density = densityactivation(rawdensity + densitybias). 9. Volume Rendering: Perform volumetric rendering using volumetricrendering(rgb, density, tvals, rays.directions, whitebkgd). This step computes the final color comprgb, expected distance, accumulated alpha acc, and per-sample weights weights using alpha compositing. 10. ISP: Apply the learned Image Signal Processing pipeline to comprgb using isp(comprgb, rays.temperature, rays.exposure) to get rgbout. 11. Result Storage: Append (rgbout, distance, acc) to ret. 12. Return: Return the list ret. Unverified code. Returns tvals and samples (points, radii). # Implementation not provided in sources. pass def resamplealongrays(key, origins, directions, radii, tvals, weights, randomized, rayshape, stoplevelgrad, resamplepadding): # Resampling based on previous weights. Returns updated tvals and samples. # Implementation not provided in sources. pass def integratedposenc(samples, mindeg, maxdeg): # Integrates positional encoding over the cone/cylinder defined by samples. # Implementation not provided in sources. pass def posenc(dirs, mindeg, maxdeg, appendidentity): # Standard positional encoding for view directions. # Implementation not provided in sources. pass def volumetricrendering(rgb, density, tvals, directions, whitebkgd): # Alpha compositing along rays. Returns comprgb, distance, acc, weights. N = tvals.shape[-1] deltas = tvals[..., 1:] - tvals[...,:-1] # Handle last delta delta = jnp.concatenate([deltas, jnp.array([1e10], dtype=deltas.dtype)], axis=-1) alpha = 1.0 - jnp.exp(-density delta) T = jnp.exp(-jnp.cumsum(density delta, axis=-1)) T = jnp.concatenate([jnp.oneslike(T[...,:1]), T], axis=-1) weights = alpha T[...,:-1] comprgb = jnp.sum(weights[..., None] rgb, axis=-2) distance = jnp.sum(weights tvals, axis=-1) acc = jnp.sum(weights, axis=-1) if whitebkgd: comprgb = comprgb + (1.0 - acc[..., None]) return comprgb, distance, acc, weights def isp(rgb, temperature, exposure): # Image Signal Processing for tone mapping and color correction. # Implementation not provided in sources. pass class MipNerfModel: def init( self, numsamples: int = 128, numlevels: int = 2, resamplepadding: float = 0.01, stoplevelgrad: bool = True, useviewdirs: bool = True, lindisp: bool = False, rayshape: str = 'cone', mindegpoint: int = 0, maxdegpoint: int = 16, degview: int = 4, densityactivation: Callable = jnp.softplus, densitynoise: float = 0.0, densitybias: float = -1.0, rgbactivation: Callable = jnp.sigmoid, rgbpadding: float = 0.001, disableintegration: bool = False,): self.numsamples = numsamples self.numlevels = numlevels self.resamplepadding = resamplepadding self.stoplevelgrad = stoplevelgrad self.useviewdirs = useviewdirs self.lindisp = lindisp self.rayshape = rayshape self.mindegpoint = mindegpoint self.maxdegpoint = maxdegpoint self.degview = degview self.densityactivation = densityactivation self.densitynoise = densitynoise self.densitybias = densitybias self.rgbactivation = rgbactivation self.rgbpadding = rgbpadding self.disableintegration = disableintegration # Standard MLP forward pass (implementation not provided in sources) self.mlp = None def call( self, rays: Any, rng: Any, traincoc: float = 1.0, whitebkgd: bool = False, randomized: bool = True,) -> List[Tuple[Any, Any, Any]]: ret = [] effectiveradii = rays.radii traincoc prevtvals = None prevweights = None for ilevel in range(self.numlevels): key, rng = random.split(rng) if ilevel == 0: tvals, samples = samplealongrays( key=key, origins=rays.origins, directions=rays.directions, radii=effectiveradii, numsamples=self.numsamples, near=rays.near, far=rays.far, randomized=randomized, lindisp=self.lindisp, rayshape=self.rayshape,) else: tvals, samples = resamplealongrays( key=key, origins=rays.origins, directions=rays.directions, radii=effectiveradii, tvals=prevtvals, weights=prevweights, randomized=randomized, rayshape=self.rayshape, stoplevelgrad=self.stoplevelgrad, resamplepadding=self.resamplepadding,) if self.disableintegration: samples = (samples[0], jnp.zeroslike(samples[1])) pointencoding = integratedposenc(samples, self.mindegpoint, self.maxdegpoint) if self.useviewdirs: viewencoding = posenc(rays.viewdirs, mindeg=0, maxdeg=self.degview, appendidentity=True) mlpinput = jnp.concatenate([pointencoding, viewencoding], axis=-1) else: mlpinput = pointencoding rawdensity, rawrgb = self.mlp(mlpinput) if randomized and self.densitynoise > 0: rawdensity += self.densitynoise random.normal(key, rawdensity.shape, dtype=rawdensity.dtype) rgb = self.rgbactivation(rawrgb) rgb = rgb (1 + 2 self.rgbpadding) - self.rgbpadding density = self.densityactivation(rawdensity + self.densitybias) comprgb, distance, acc, weights = volumetricrendering( rgb=rgb, density=density, tvals=tvals, directions=rays.directions, whitebkgd=whitebkgd,) rgbout = isp(comprgb, rays.temperature, rays.exposure) ret.append((rgbout, distance, acc)) prevtvals = tvals prevweights = weights return ret Precision: The integrated positional encoding involves integration over the cone/cylinder. Numerical stability depends on the radius size. Very small radii may lead to precision issues in the integration. Boundaries: The near and far planes must be correctly set for each ray. Incorrect bounds can lead to sampling outside the scene or missing geometry. Degenerate Input: If radii are zero (e.g., at the camera origin), the cone shape degenerates to a line. The integratedposenc function should handle this gracefully, typically by falling back to point-wise encoding or ensuring the integration interval is non-zero. Gradient Flow: If stoplevelgrad is True, gradients do not flow from the fine level to the coarse level. This is a design choice to stabilize training but must be respected in the implementation. Uses depth estimates to guide sample placement, focusing on areas of interest. Depth-Guided Sampling Combines stratified sampling with depth priors for more efficient sampling. Depth-Prior Guided Stratified Sampling Estimates blur parameters to improve rendering quality in out-of-focus regions. Progressive Blur Estimation Time Complexity: O(L \cdot N), where L is the number of levels and N is the number of samples per level. The integrated positional encoding adds a constant factor overhead per sample. Memory Complexity: O(L \cdot N) for storing samples, encodings, and intermediate rendering results. Measured Performance: The model is designed for unbounded, outdoor scenes (Mip-NeRF 360 dataset). It provides higher quality images with fewer artifacts compared to standard NeRF, especially at high frequencies. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of samples and levels. Strengths: Reduces aliasing, handles high-frequency details better, suitable for unbounded scenes. Limitations: More complex implementation, slightly higher computational cost per sample due to integration. When to Use: When training on unbounded scenes or scenes with high-frequency details where standard NeRF exhibits aliasing. When Not to Use: For simple, bounded scenes with low-frequency content, standard NeRF may be sufficient and faster. The MipNerfModel was introduced in the Mip-NeRF paper by Barron et al. (2021) and extended in Mip-NeRF 360 (Barron et al., 2022). It addresses the issue of aliasing in NeRF by modeling rays as cones/cylinders and integrating positional encodings over these volumes. https://github.com/CPREgroup/CaSE-NeRF, https://github.com/CPREgroup/CaSE-NeRF, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Event Simulation from NeRF
head: Log-Difference Event Model, Virtual Event Generation
body: Event Simulation from NeRF generates virtual event data from a NeRF model to supervise training using real event camera observations. It solves the problem of motion blur in NeRF reconstruction by modeling the temporal integration of light during camera exposure. It differs from sibling methods like Depth-Guided Sampling by explicitly simulating asynchronous event streams rather than static depth or color, allowing for event-driven bundle adjustment to refine camera poses and recover sharp geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: NeRF model parameters \theta, a set of p evenly sampled poses \{Ti\}{i=1}^p representing the camera trajectory during exposure, and real event data E(x, ti, t{i+1}). Outputs: Virtual event count \hat{E}(x, ti, t{i+1}) and gradients for optimizing \theta and Ti. Data Structures: Poses: Ti \in SE(3), learnable variables representing camera poses at time ti. Events: E(x, ti, t{i+1}) is the count of real events at pixel x between time ti and t{i+1}. Log-Intensity: \mathcal{L}(T, x), the log-transformed grayscale intensity of the rendered image at pose T and pixel x. Steps: 1. Render Sharp Images: For each sampled pose Ti, render the color C(Ti, x) using standard volume rendering (see NeRF Rendering (Alpha Compositing)). 2. Convert to Grayscale: Average the RGB channels of C(Ti, x) to obtain grayscale intensity G(Ti, x). 3. Log Transform: Compute log-intensity \mathcal{L}(Ti, x) = \log(G(Ti, x)). 4. Simulate Events: Calculate the virtual event count \hat{E}(x, ti, t{i+1}) using the log-difference model. 5. Compute Loss: Calculate the L2 loss between virtual and real events. Formulas: The virtual event count is defined as: \hat{E}(x, ti, t{i+1}) = \begin{cases} \frac{\mathcal{L}(T{i+1}, x) - \mathcal{L}(Ti, x)}{\Theta} & \text{if } \mathcal{L}(T{i+1}, x) \le \mathcal{L}(Ti, x) \\ \frac{\mathcal{L}(T{i+1}, x) - \mathcal{L}(Ti, x)}{\Theta} & \text{if } \mathcal{L}(T{i+1}, x) > \mathcal{L}(Ti, x) \end{cases} Note: The source formula presents identical expressions for both cases, implying a linear difference scaled by \Theta. The threshold \Theta handles the polarity in standard event models, but here it acts as a scaling factor for the log-intensity change. Parameters: \Theta: Event generation threshold. Typical value: 0.3. p: Number of sampled poses. Typical value: 5. \lambda: Weight for event loss. Typical value: 0.005. Pitfalls: Event loss is calculated only between adjacent poses (ti, t{i+1}). Calculating between non-adjacent poses causes fluctuation and instability. A coarse initial pose is required for each view to start training. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def simulateevents(nerfmodel, poses, theta): """ Simulates virtual events from NeRF renders. Args: nerfmodel: Function rendering color C(T, x) given pose T and pixel x. poses: List of p SE(3) poses [T1,..., Tp]. theta: Event threshold (0.3). Returns: virtualevents: Tensor of shape (p-1, H, W) containing simulated event counts. """ virtualevents = [] for i in range(len(poses) - 1): Tcurr = poses[i] Tnext = poses[i+1] # Render sharp images for current and next pose # C is RGB color tensor [H, W, 3] Ccurr = nerfmodel.render(Tcurr) Cnext = nerfmodel.render(Tnext) # Convert to grayscale by averaging RGB channels Gcurr = mean(Ccurr, axis=-1) # Shape [H, W] Gnext = mean(Cnext, axis=-1) # Shape [H, W] # Log transform # Add small epsilon to avoid log(0) if necessary Lcurr = log(Gcurr + 1e-8) Lnext = log(Gnext + 1e-8) # Calculate log difference deltaL = Lnext - Lcurr # Simulate events (linear scaling by theta as per source formula) # Note: Source shows identical formulas for both cases. Ehat = deltaL / theta virtualevents.append(Ehat) return stack(virtualevents) def computeeventloss(virtualevents, realevents): """ Computes L2 loss between virtual and real events. Args: virtualevents: Tensor [p-1, H, W] realevents: Tensor [p-1, H, W] Returns: loss: Scalar L2 loss. """ # Sum over all pixels and pose intervals # p-1 intervals, m pixels loss = mean((virtualevents - realevents) 2) return loss The Event Loss is the L2 loss between simulated events \hat{E} and real events E, summed over all pixels x \in X and pose intervals i=1 \dots p-1. It serves as an intensity-change metric to supervise NeRF parameters and optimize adjunctive poses Ti and T{i+1} via event-driven bundle adjustment. The formula is: L{event} = \frac{1}{p-1} \sum{i=1}^{p} \frac{1}{m} \sum{x \in X} \| \hat{E}(x, ti, t{i+1}) - E(x, ti, t{i+1}) \|2^2 where p is the number of sampled poses and m is the number of pixels. Time Complexity: Adds overhead proportional to the number of sampled poses p per view, as p renders are required per exposure interval. Training time is reported to be close to standard BAD-NeRF. Memory Complexity: Requires storing intermediate renders for p poses per view. Performance: Improves PSNR, SSIM, and reduces ATE compared to baselines like BAD-NeRF. Strengths: Enables joint optimization of NeRF parameters and camera poses using asynchronous event data, handling motion blur effectively. Limitations: Requires synchronized event data and blurry images. Stability depends on adjacent pose intervals. Originated in the paper "Deblurring Neural Radiance Fields with Event-driven Bundle Adjustment" (EBAD-NeRF) by Yunshan Qi et al.. It builds on NeRF volume rendering and event-based vision models to address motion blur in dynamic scenes. Deblurring Neural Radiance Fields with Event-driven Bundle Adjustment, https://doi.org/10.1145/3664647.3680569, fetched 2026-10-27

name: NeRF-style Volume Rendering Integrator
head: NeRF forward raymarching, NeRFIntegrator
body: This method computes the expected color \hat{C}(r) for a ray r by discretizing the medium interaction interval into fixed steps and accumulating emission weighted by transmittance. It differs from its sibling NeRF Rendering (Alpha Compositing) by using a dense grid-based density representation with no direction-dependent emission, and by employing a fixed-step marching loop with optional jittering rather than adaptive sampling or neural network queries. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray r (origin, direction), scene geometry (for exit intersection), density grid (scalar field \sigma), emission field (vector field c), parameters: queriesperray, densitynoisestd, jitteringenabled, activation, hideemitters. Output: Rendered color \hat{C}(r), accumulated weights, and optionally depth. Data Structures: Density Grid: Dense 3D array of scalar values \sigma. Layout is not specified in sources. Emission Field: Dense 3D array of RGB values c. Layout is not specified in sources. State Variables: result (color accumulator), throughput (transmittance T), weightssum (accumulated opacity weight), stepj (current step index), ta (previous sample position), tb (current sample position). Parameters: queriesperray: Number of steps for ray marching. Default: 128. densitynoisestd: Standard deviation for noise added to density. Default: 0. jitteringenabled: Boolean flag enabling jittering for step positions. Default: True. activation: Activation function type for density ('identity', 'relu'). Default: 'identity'. hideemitters: Boolean flag to hide background emitters if weightssum is zero. Default: Not specified. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize result = 0, throughput = 1, weightssum = 0, stepj = 0, ta = 0. Determine primal mode (forward vs. adjoint). 2. Exit Intersection: Intersect ray with scene geometry to find medium exit distance t{exit}. Update active mask to include only rays that hit the exit. 3. Step Size Calculation: Calculate stepsize using stepsizeformarching(queriesperray, 0, t{exit}, jitteringenabled). Sample jittersample from sampler. 4. Marching Loop: While stillwalking (mask: stepj < queriesperray): a. Calculate tb using querytforstep(stepj + 1, stepsize, jittersample, jitteringenabled). b. Calculate actualstep = tb - ta. c. Calculate alpharecip: If stepj + 1 < queriesperray: alpharecip = \exp(-\sigma \cdot \text{actual\step}). Else: alpharecip = 1.0. d. Numerical Stability: Add \epsilon = 10^{-10} to alpharecip to prevent NaNs. e. Calculate weight = (1.0 - \text{alpha\recip}) \cdot \text{throughput}. f. Accumulate Color: If primal: result += weight emission. If adjoint: result -= weight emission. g. Increment stepj. Update ta = tb. h. Update Throughput: throughput = alpharecip. i. Update Weights Sum: weightssum += weight. 5. Background Contribution: Calculate contribution = (1 - \text{weights\sum}) \cdot c{bg}. Add to result for active pixels. If hideemitters is true and weightssum is zero, do not add background emission. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nerfintegrator(ray, scene, densitygrid, emissiongrid, params): """ NeRF-style volume rendering integrator. Args: ray: Ray object with origin and direction. scene: Scene object for intersection. densitygrid: 3D array of density values. emissiongrid: 3D array of emission values. params: Dictionary of parameters. Returns: result: Rendered color. """ # Parameters queriesperray = params.get('queriesperray', 128) densitynoisestd = params.get('densitynoisestd', 0) jitteringenabled = params.get('jitteringenabled', True) activation = params.get('activation', 'identity') hideemitters = params.get('hideemitters', False) # Initialization result = 0.0 throughput = 1.0 weightssum = 0.0 stepj = 0 ta = 0.0 # Exit Intersection texit = scene.intersect(ray) if texit is None: return 0.0 # Ray misses scene # Step Size Calculation stepsize = stepsizeformarching(queriesperray, 0, texit, jitteringenabled) jittersample = sampler.sample() # Marching Loop while stepj < queriesperray: # Calculate current sample position tb = querytforstep(stepj + 1, stepsize, jittersample, jitteringenabled) actualstep = tb - ta # Query density and emission sigma = querydensity(densitygrid, ray, tb) c = queryemission(emissiongrid, ray, tb) # Apply activation if needed if activation == 'relu': sigma = max(0, sigma) elif activation == 'identity': pass else: raise ValueError(f"Unknown activation: {activation}") # Add density noise if enabled if densitynoisestd > 0: sigma += randomnoise(std=densitynoisestd) # Calculate alpharecip if stepj + 1 < queriesperray: alpharecip = math.exp(-sigma actualstep) else: alpharecip = 1.0 # Numerical stability alpharecip += 1e-10 # Calculate weight weight = (1.0 - alpharecip) throughput # Accumulate color result += weight c # Update throughput and weightssum throughput = alpharecip weightssum += weight # Update step variables stepj += 1 ta = tb # Background contribution cbg = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # Default white background if not hideemitters or weightssum > 0: result += (1.0 - weightssum) cbg return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Adding \epsilon = 10^{-10} to alpharecip is critical to prevent NaNs during gradient computation. Boundaries: Rays missing the scene return 0. Rays hitting the exit are processed up to queriesperray steps. Degenerate Input: If queriesperray is 0, the loop does not execute, and only background is returned. If densitynoisestd is large, noise may dominate the signal. Time Complexity: O(N) per ray, where N is queriesperray. Total time is O(N \cdot R), where R is the number of rays. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the density and emission grids, where V is the volume of the grid. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Linear with respect to queriesperray and number of rays. Strengths: Simple implementation, deterministic (with fixed jitter), easy to differentiate. Limitations: Fixed step size may lead to aliasing or inefficiency in sparse regions. No direction-dependent emission. When to Use: When a dense grid representation is sufficient and direction-dependent effects are not required. When Not to Use: When adaptive sampling is needed for efficiency or accuracy, or when direction-dependent emission is required. Origin: The method is based on the NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) framework. History: Developed as part of the unbiased inverse volume rendering project. Usage: Used in differentiable rendering for inverse problems, such as scene reconstruction and optimization. Unbiased Inverse Volume Rendering, https://github.com/rgl-epfl/unbiased-inverse-volume-rendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Lightning-NeRF Rendering and Training Loop
head: Lightning NeRF
body: Lightning-NeRF is a neural rendering method that accelerates training and inference by combining a hybrid density representation (voxel grid with hash encoding) with a decomposed view-independent/view-dependent MLP architecture. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF implementations by employing adaptive sampling warmup schedules and dynamic occupancy grid updates to prune empty space, enabling efficient training on large-scale real-world scenes. Inputs: Camera poses and intrinsics. Ground truth RGB images. Optional point cloud file (.ply) for initialization. Configuration parameters (see Parameters). Outputs: Rendered RGB image. Accumulated opacity (accumulation). Depth map. Number of samples per ray. Optional residual RGB loss. Data Structures: Occupancy Grid: A multi-resolution hash grid storing occupancy probabilities. Updated dynamically based on density thresholds. Density Grid: A hybrid structure using a base voxel grid and hash encoding for density values. Color Grid: A multi-resolution hash grid for color features. MLPs: Two separate networks: View-Independent (VI) MLP: Encodes spatial position to intermediate features. View-Dependent (VD) MLP: Encodes viewing direction and VI features to final RGB color. Parameters: nearplane: Near clipping plane. Default: 0.01. farplane: Far clipping plane. Default: 6.0 (KITTI-360), 10.0 (Argoverse2). alphathre: Alpha threshold for occupancy culling. Default: 0.01 (KITTI-360), 0.02 (Argoverse2). occnumsamplesperray: Coarse samples per ray. Default: 750. pdfnumsamplesperray: Fine samples per ray. Default: 8. pdfsampleswarmupstep: Steps to keep max fine samples. Default: 100,000 (notes) / 500 (code). Note: Sources disagree on this value. The notes cite 100,000, while the source code defines 500. Implementers should verify against the specific configuration file used. pdfsamplesfixedstep: Steps after which fine sampling ratio stabilizes. Default: 100,000 (notes) / 2,000 (code). Note: See discrepancy above. pdfsamplesfixedratio: Final ratio of fine samples. Default: 0.5. occgridupdatewarmupstep: Steps before occupancy grid updates. Default: 256 (KITTI-360), 2 (Argoverse2). bgcolor: Background color strategy. Options: "black" ([0,0,0]), "white" ([1,1,1]), "random" (sampled at runtime). initdensityvalue: Initial density for pretraining. Default: 10.0. frontalaxis: Axis for background augmentation. Default: "x". Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the occupancy grid and sampler. Initialize the collider with nearplane and farplane. If a pointcloudpath is provided: Load vertices from the.ply file. Transform vertices to normalized space using metadata transformation and scale. Split vertices into pretrainfgvertices (inside the scene bounding box) and pretrainbgvertices (outside). Generate pretrainaugvertices by sampling points on the surfaces of the background bounding box, offset by 0.05 units. 2. Pretraining (Optional but typical): Foreground Density: Optimize the density encoding to match initdensityvalue at pretrainfgvertices locations for 20 iterations. Update the occupancy grid every iteration using densityfn(x) renderstepsize. Background Density: Optimize the background density encoding to match initdensityvalue at pretrainbgvertices and pretrainaugvertices locations for 40 iterations. Set gridinitialized = True. 3. Training Loop Callbacks: Step Increment: Increment trainingstep after each iteration. Occupancy Update: Before each training iteration, update the occupancy grid if trainingstep > occgridupdatewarmupstep. The update function uses occevalfn = lambda x: field.densityfn(x) renderstepsize and threshold alphathre. 4. Ray Marching and Integration (Forward Pass): Determine Fine Samples: Calculate numfinesamples based on trainingstep: If trainingstep < pdfsampleswarmupstep: numfinesamples = pdfnumsamplesperray. If pdfsampleswarmupstep <= trainingstep < pdfsamplesfixedstep: \text{ratio} = \frac{\text{training\step} - \text{pdf\samples\warmup\step}}{\text{pdf\samples\fixed\step} - \text{pdf\samples\warmup\step}} \text{max\ratio} = 1 - \text{pdf\samples\fixed\ratio} \text{num\fine\samples} = \text{round}(\text{pdf\num\samples\per\ray} \times (1 - \text{max\ratio} \times \text{ratio})) If trainingstep >= pdfsamplesfixedstep: \text{num\fine\samples} = \text{round}(\text{pdf\num\samples\per\ray} \times \text{pdf\samples\fixed\ratio}) Sampling: Sample rays using the sampler with raybundle, nearplane, farplane, renderstepsize, alphathre, coneangle, and numfinesamples. Returns raysamples and rayindices. Field Query: Query the neural field with raysamples to obtain densities (\sigma) and colors (C). Weight Computation: Compute ray weights from densities: wi = \sigmai \Delta ti \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \Delta tj\right) Implemented via nerfacc.renderweightfromdensity using frustum starts/ends and packed info. Accumulation: RGB: C{comp} = \sum wi Ci using nerfacc.accumulatealongrays. Opacity: A = \sum wi using nerfacc.accumulatealongrays with values=None. Background Compositing: Determine background color C{bg}: If bgcolor is "black": [0, 0, 0]. If bgcolor is "white": [1, 1, 1]. If bgcolor is "random": Sample C{bg} \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1) per pixel. Final RGB: C{final} = C{comp} + C{bg} (1 - A). If not training, clamp C{final} to [0, 1]. Depth Estimation: Compute step centers: ti = \frac{t{start, i} + t{end, i}}{2}. Weighted sum: D = \frac{\sum wi ti}{A + \epsilon}, where \epsilon = 10^{-10}. Clip D to [t{min}, t{max}]. 5. Loss and Metrics: Compute PSNR between C{final} and ground truth image. If residual RGB loss is enabled, compute mean residual and add to total loss with coefficient losscoefficients["resrgbloss"]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lightningnerfrenderandtrain(config, raybundle, gtimage, trainingstep): # 1. Determine number of fine samples based on warmup schedule if trainingstep < config.pdfsampleswarmupstep: numfinesamples = config.pdfnumsamplesperray elif trainingstep < config.pdfsamplesfixedstep: ratio = (trainingstep - config.pdfsampleswarmupstep) / \ (config.pdfsamplesfixedstep - config.pdfsampleswarmupstep) maxratio = 1.0 - config.pdfsamplesfixedratio numfinesamples = round(config.pdfnumsamplesperray (1.0 - maxratio ratio)) else: numfinesamples = round(config.pdfnumsamplesperray config.pdfsamplesfixedratio) # 2. Sample rays # Uses occupancy grid for pruning if enabled raysamples, rayindices = sampler.sample( raybundle=raybundle, nearplane=config.nearplane, farplane=config.farplane, renderstepsize=config.renderstepsize, alphathre=config.alphathre, coneangle=config.coneangle, numfinesamples=numfinesamples) # 3. Query Neural Field # Returns densities (sigmas) and colors (RGB) sigmas, colors = field.query(raysamples) # 4. Pack info for efficient accumulation packedinfo = nerfacc.packinfo(rayindices, numrays=len(raybundle)) # 5. Compute weights from density # Uses frustum starts/ends from raysamples weights = nerfacc.renderweightfromdensity( tstarts=raysamples.frustums.starts[..., 0], tends=raysamples.frustums.ends[..., 0], sigmas=sigmas[..., 0], packedinfo=packedinfo) # 6. Accumulate RGB comprgb = nerfacc.accumulatealongrays( weights=weights, values=colors, rayindices=rayindices, nrays=len(raybundle)) # 7. Accumulate Opacity accumulation = nerfacc.accumulatealongrays( weights=weights, values=None, rayindices=rayindices, nrays=len(raybundle)) # 8. Composite with Background if config.backgroundcolor == "black": bgcolor = torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, 0.0], device=colors.device) elif config.backgroundcolor == "white": bgcolor = torch.tensor([1.0, 1.0, 1.0], device=colors.device) else: # Random background bgcolor = torch.randlike(comprgb) rgb = comprgb + bgcolor (1.0 - accumulation) if not trainingstep: # Inference mode rgb = torch.clamp(rgb, 0.0, 1.0) # 9. Compute Depth steps = (raysamples.frustums.starts + raysamples.frustums.ends) / 2.0 depth = nerfacc.accumulatealongrays( weights=weights, values=steps, rayindices=rayindices, nrays=len(raybundle)) depth = depth / (accumulation + 1e-10) depth = torch.clamp(depth, steps.min(), steps.max()) # 10. Return Outputs outputs = { 'rgb': rgb, 'accumulation': accumulation, 'depth': depth, 'numsamplesperray': raysamples.numsamples } # Optional: Residual Loss if trainingstep and hasattr(config, 'resrgb') and config.resrgb is not None: resrgbloss = torch.mean(torch.abs(outputs['rgb'] - config.resrgb)) outputs['resrgbloss'] = resrgbloss return outputs Computes PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS for quality assessment. Details the TCNN-based hash encoding used for density and color features. Handles memory constraints by evaluating rays in chunks. The underlying differentiable integration framework. Uses uncertainty to select rays for distillation. Loss function for aligning distilled features. General volume rendering math. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays and samples per ray. The hash encoding lookup is approximately O(1) average case. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the hash grids for density and color. The size is determined by densitylog2hashmapsize (24) and colorlog2hashmapsize (19), allowing for high-resolution representations in limited memory. Performance: Significantly faster training than standard NeRF due to occupancy grid pruning and adaptive sampling. The hybrid representation reduces the number of MLP queries required for empty space. Strengths: Efficient training on large-scale real-world datasets (KITTI-360, Argoverse2). Good generalization with point cloud initialization. Limitations: Performance depends heavily on the quality of the input point cloud. The adaptive sampling schedule parameters require tuning for different scenes. When to use: Large-scale outdoor or indoor scenes where standard NeRF is too slow or memory-intensive. When not to use: Small-scale synthetic scenes (e.g., Blender) where coneangle should be 0.0 and simpler representations may suffice. Lightning-NeRF was introduced by the Vision-SJTU group as an efficient neural rendering method for large-scale scenes. It builds upon the principles of Instant-NGP (hash encoding) and NeRF (volume rendering) but introduces specific optimizations for real-world data, including point cloud initialization and background augmentation. name: Training Configuration
head: Hyperparameter Configuration, Implementation Parameters, Optimization Configuration, Optimization Setup, Optimizer Settings, Training Details, Training Hyperparameters, Training Settings
body: Training Configuration defines the hyperparameters, optimization strategies, and architectural settings required to train neural radiance fields or implicit surface representations. It solves the problem of reproducibly managing the state required for differentiable volume rendering optimization by standardizing how models, optimizers, and datasets are loaded and how gradients are applied. It differs from Learning Rate Scheduling and Mixed Precision Training by focusing on the structural orchestration of the training state rather than numerical precision or adaptive step sizing. The training configuration establishes the execution environment for the optimization loop. It specifies the optimizer type, learning rates, batch sizes, sampling strategies, and loss function weights. Inputs: Scene data (images, poses), network architecture definition, hyperparameter dictionary (learning rates, batch sizes, iteration counts), and device specification (GPU/CPU). Outputs: Trained model weights (MLP parameters, voxel grid values, latent codes) and optionally checkpoints for resume training. The configuration is typically stored in a dictionary or object containing: optimizer: String identifier (e.g., "Adam", "AdamW", "RMSProp") and parameters (betas, eps, weight decay). lr: Initial learning rate, potentially split by parameter group (e.g., embeddings vs. networks). batchsize: Number of rays or pixels per iteration. iterations: Total number of training steps. lossweights: Dictionary mapping loss terms (e.g., L2, SSIM, regularization) to scalar multipliers. sampling: Parameters for ray marching (e.g., number of coarse/fine samples, step sizes). 1. Initialization: Initialize the model parameters (MLP weights, voxel grids, latent codes) using specific schemes (e.g., Gaussian noise for density, specific initialization for alpha values). 2. Optimizer Setup: Instantiate the optimizer with specified hyperparameters (e.g., Adam with \beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.99, \epsilon=10^{-15}). 3. Data Loading: Load training images and camera poses. Create a data loader that samples pixels or rays. 4. Iteration Loop: a. Sample a batch of rays/pixels from the training set. b. Perform forward pass (ray marching and integration) to render predicted colors. c. Compute loss (e.g., L2 + 0.2 LSSIM). d. Backpropagate gradients. e. Update model parameters using the optimizer. f. Apply learning rate schedule if configured. g. Apply regularization or pruning if scheduled (e.g., every 300 iterations). 5. Checkpointing: Save model state periodically for resume training or evaluation. Loss Function: L = L2 + 0.2 \cdot L{SSIM}, where L2 is the L2-loss and L{SSIM} is the perceptual loss. Dynamic Frequency Masking (FreeNeRF): \alphai(t, T, L) denotes the i-th bit value of the mask \alpha(t, T, L): \alphai(t, T, L) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } i \le \lfloor \frac{t \cdot L}{T} \rfloor \\ \frac{t \cdot L}{T} - \lfloor \frac{t \cdot L}{T} \rfloor & \text{if } \lfloor \frac{t \cdot L}{T} \rfloor < i \le \lfloor \frac{t \cdot L}{T} \rfloor + 3 \\ 0 & \text{if } i > \lfloor \frac{t \cdot L}{T} \rfloor + 6 \end{cases} where t is current iteration, T is total iterations, and L is the tensor component length. Optical Flow Loss: L = L{color} + M \cdot L{flow}, where L{color} = \sum{r \in R(p)} ||\hat{C}c(r) - C(r)||^2 + ||\hat{C}r(r) - C(r)||^2. Optimizer: Adam is most common. Betas: (0.9, 0.99) or (0.9, 0.999). Epsilon: 10^{-15}. Learning Rate: Varies by method. Common values: 10^{-3}, 5 \times 10^{-4}, 0.1 for voxel grids. Batch Size: Ranges from 1 ray to 256 rays to 25,000 rays or 256 pixels. Iterations: 20,000, 25,000, 30,000, 200,000. Weight Decay: 0.1 for hash grid values, 2 \times 10^{-5}, 10^{-9}. Inaccurate Optical Flow: Can cause errors in later training phases; handled by disabling multi-sampling and using vanilla sampling with fewer but accurate data points. Overfitting: Mitigated by dynamic frequency masking or regularization. Narrow-Baseline Poses: COLMAP may struggle; treat camera pose parameters (focal length, parallax offset) as trainable variables. Non-determinism: GPU hashgrid optimization is nondeterministic; fixing seed does not guarantee bitwise-identical trajectories. Unverified code. Sample batch rays, gtcolors = next(trainloader) rays = rays.to(device) gtcolors = gtcolors.to(device) # 2. Forward pass # Render colors using current model parameters predcolors = model.render(rays) # 3. Compute Loss # Example: L2 loss loss = torch.mean((predcolors - gtcolors) 2) # Optional: Add regularization or other losses # loss += 0.2 ssimloss(predcolors, gtcolors) # 4. Backward pass optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() # 5. Update parameters optimizer.step() # 6. Update learning rate if scheduler: scheduler.step() # 7. Checkpointing (every N steps) if step % 1000 == 0: savecheckpoint(model, optimizer, step) Establishes the execution environment, handling initialization, data loading, and checkpoint management. Dynamically adjusts the optimizer's step size to balance convergence speed and quality. Replaces fixed background with random samples to prevent semi-transparent artifacts. Uses FP16 for forward/backward passes and FP32 for weights to accelerate training. Applies component-specific learning rate multipliers to address disparate convergence speeds. Restores optimization state from disk to continue training. Selects context and target camera views during training. Defines loss for high-resolution refinement after coarse stage convergence. Hyperparameters for specific NeRF variants (e.g., Mip-NeRF, DONeRF). Constraints beyond photometric reconstruction for physical plausibility. Conditions NeRF on image features for sparse-view reconstruction. Initializes network weights from previous frame to reduce flickering in animated scenes. Maps 3D coordinates to attenuation coefficients for X-ray imaging. Reference training protocols for differentiable volume rendering. Configures Region Proposal Network for object detection in NeRFs. Uses uncertainty estimation for active learning sample selection. Handles outlier poses during training. A technique to mask tensor components (density or appearance feature) based on training iteration to enhance high-frequency details in later stages and mitigate overfitting. It calculates mask values using integer and fractional parts for smooth transition during training (t < T) and returns ones after training (t \ge T). Introduced in FreeNeRF and used in Few TensoRF. Pitfall: May struggle with intricate details and hidden angles in complex scenes like 'Drums'. Configures training for object detection in NeRFs. Involves random flipping (x, y axes, prob 0.5), random rotation (z-axis, \pi/2, prob 0.5), and slight rotation (\alpha \in [-\pi/18, \pi/18], prob 0.5). Uses AdamW optimizer with LR 0.0003 and weight decay 0.001. Loss weights: \lambda = 5.0 for Eq. (3) and \lambda = 1.0 for Eq. (6). Balances performance and efficiency by adjusting the ratio of past task rays (mp) to current task rays (mc). mp = mc/2 is chosen as optimal trade-off (e.g., PSNR 22.14 / MS-SSIM 0.836 on Tanks and Temples/Barn with mc=4096). Alternately removes and re-samples particles to manage count and convergence. Re-sampled count gradually decreases to zero as model converges (e.g., after 10K steps on D-NeRF). Specific to joint thermodynamic reconstruction. Uses Multiresolution hash grid (2^{20} hashmap, \times 2 features, 20 levels), AdamW optimizer (LR 5 \times 10^{-4}, weight decay 10^{-5}). Trains 60k steps for joint reconstructions (1024 rays/batch) and 30k for density-only. Uses asinh loss with specific scale coefficients for different X-ray lines. Notes non-determinism in GPU hashgrid optimization. Initializes NeRF for structured light fields where camera pose parameters (focal length f, parallax offset \Delta) are trainable to handle narrow-baseline cases where COLMAP struggles. Defines loss functions such as L = L{color} + M \cdot L{flow}, where L{color} combines coarse and refined network predictions against ground truth. Time Complexity: Training time varies significantly by method and hardware. Typical ranges: 15 minutes, 20 hours, 1-2 days, few hours to one day. Memory Complexity: Depends on batch size and model size. GPU memory usage can be ~10.5 GB. Mixed precision training reduces memory bandwidth requirements. Scaling: Performance generally increases with more training iterations and larger batch sizes, but with diminishing returns and higher computational cost. Strengths: Flexible configuration allows optimization for various scenes and constraints (e.g., sparse views, dynamic scenes). Limitations: Hyperparameter tuning is often empirical and method-specific. Some methods are sensitive to initialization and learning rate schedules. When to Use: Standard NeRF optimization requires generic hierarchical sampling with Adam [Parent]. Specific variants (e.g., Mip-NeRF, DONeRF) require tailored configurations. Originating from the NeRF paper [37], training configuration has evolved to address challenges in convergence speed, memory efficiency, and generalization. Early methods used simple Adam optimization with fixed learning rates. Subsequent works introduced adaptive scaling, mixed precision, and dynamic sampling strategies. The field continues to develop specialized configurations for specific applications like object detection, dynamic scenes, and X-ray tomography. name: Training Loop Setup
head: IDR Baseline, PixelNeRF Training and Rendering Pipeline, Training Loop Configuration & Checkpointing, Training Step Execution
body: The Training Loop Setup establishes the execution environment for differentiable volume rendering optimization, handling initialization, data loading, checkpoint management, and the core iteration logic. It solves the problem of reproducibly managing the state required to train neural radiance fields or implicit surface representations by standardizing how models, optimizers, and datasets are loaded and how gradients are applied. It differs from Learning Rate Scheduling and Mixed Precision Training by focusing on the structural orchestration of the training state rather than numerical precision or adaptive step sizing. The method executes a single training iteration or configures the global training environment. It involves initializing random seeds, loading scene data and camera poses, managing checkpoint resumption, and performing the forward-backward pass sequence. Inputs: Configuration arguments (args): dataset type, paths, random seed, learning rate, batch size, GPU IDs, and checkpoint paths. Scene data: Images, camera poses, bounding boxes, and focal lengths. Model parameters: Neural network weights (coarse and optional fine networks). Optimizer state: Adam moments (expavg, expavgsq) if resuming. Outputs: Updated model weights. Loss metrics (RGB, SSIM, etc.) for logging. Checkpoint files saved at specified intervals. Ray Data: Generated per view using camera intrinsics and extrinsics. Shape: (NV, H, W, 8) where NV is number of views, H height, W width. Each ray vector contains 8 dimensions (typically origin xyz, direction xyz, and potentially view index or other metadata). Image Data: Input images shape: (SB, NV, 3, H, W) where SB is batch size. Source images selected shape: (SB, NS, 3, H, W) where NS is number of source views. Pixel values normalized to [0, 1] range via images 0.5 + 0.5. Checkpoint State: Weights stored as.npy files. Filename pattern includes step number: model.npy. Step number extracted from filename: int(ftweights[-10:-4]). 1. Environment Initialization: Set random seeds for reproducibility: np.random.seed(args.randomseed) and tf.compat.v1.setrandomseed (if using TensorFlow). Create log directory: os.makedirs(os.path.join(basedir, expname), existok=True). 2. Data Loading: Load images and transformation matrices from disk based on args.datasettype (e.g., llff, blender, deepvoxels). Transform poses and images to the target device (GPU). Normalize image values to [0, 1]. Generate camera rays for all views using util.genrays(poses, W, H, focal, znear, zfar). 3. Checkpoint Management: Check for existing checkpoints in the log directory. If args.ftpath is provided or latest checkpoint exists: Load weights: model.setweights(np.load(ftweights, allowpickle=True)). Set start step: start = int(ftweights[-10:-4]) + 1. If fine network exists, load corresponding fine weights. 4. View Selection (for multi-view methods like PixelNeRF): Randomly select currnviews source views from available views: np.random.choice(NV, currnviews, replace=False). Index into images and poses using util.batchedindexselectnd. Note: This selection is noted as "somewhat inefficient" in some implementations. 5. Network Encoding (if applicable): Encode source views into the network: net.encode(srcimages, srcposes, allfocals, c=allc). 6. Forward Pass: Render the scene by calling the parallel renderer on selected rays: renderdict = renderpar(allrays, wantweights=True). Outputs include coarse RGB, fine RGB (if enabled), and weights. 7. Loss Computation: Calculate RGB loss for coarse output: losscoarse = self.rgbcoarsecrit(coarse.rgb, allrgbgt). If fine rendering is used (len(fine) > 0), add fine RGB loss weighted by lambdafine: lossfine = lambdafine self.rgbfinecrit(fine.rgb, allrgbgt). Total loss: loss = losscoarse + lossfine. Normalize loss by lossInvN = 1.0 / (height width 3). 8. Backward Pass and Update: Compute gradients: loss.backward(). Step optimizer: optimizer.step(). Zero gradients: optimizer.zerograd(). 9. Logging and Checkpointing: Print metrics every iprint steps (default 100). Save weights every iweights steps (default 10000). Image Normalization: \text{images}{[0,1]} = \text{images} \times 0.5 + 0.5 Loss Normalization Factor: \text{lossInvN} = \frac{1.0}{\text{height} \times \text{width} \times 3} Scaling Factor for Bounding Box: \text{sc} = \begin{cases} 1. & \text{if } \text{bd\factor is None} \\ \frac{1}{\min(\text{bds}) \times \text{bd\factor}} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{coarse}} + \lambda{\text{fine}} \mathcal{L}{\text{fine}} where \lambda{\text{fine}} is loaded from config, default 1.0. iprint: Frequency of console printout and metric logging, default 100. iweights: Frequency of weight checkpoint saving, default 10000. lambdacoarse: Weight for coarse RGB loss, loaded from config. lambdafine: Weight for fine RGB loss, default 1.0. nobboxstep: Integer parameter; if globalstep >= nobboxstep, bbox sampling is disabled. randomseed: If not None, sets np.random.seed and tf.compat.v1.setrandomseed. Inefficient View Selection: Randomly selecting source views for each object in the batch loop is noted as inefficient. Checkpoint Resumption: Ensure step number extraction logic matches filename format exactly to avoid incorrect start steps. Device Placement: Ensure all data (images, poses, rays) are moved to the specified GPU device before computation. Precision: Use float32 for poses and images as specified. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainingloopsetup(args, model, optimizer, dataset, renderer): # 1. Environment Initialization if args.randomseed is not None: np.random.seed(args.randomseed) # tf.compat.v1.setrandomseed(args.randomseed) # If using TF os.makedirs(os.path.join(args.basedir, args.expname), existok=True) # 2. Data Loading images, poses, bds, focals = loaddata(args.datasettype, args.datadir) images = images.astype(np.float32) poses = poses.astype(np.float32) # Normalize images to [0, 1] images0to1 = images 0.5 + 0.5 # Move to device device = util.getcuda(args.gpuid[0]) images = torch.tensor(images0to1).to(device) poses = torch.tensor(poses).to(device) # Generate rays rays = util.genrays(poses, images.shape[-1], images.shape[-2], focals, znear, zfar) # rays shape: (NV, H, W, 8) # 3. Checkpoint Management startstep = 0 ckpts = sorted([f for f in os.listdir(args.logdir) if f.startswith('model') and f.endswith('.npy')]) if ckpts and not args.noreload: ftweights = ckpts[-1] print('Reloading from', ftweights) model.setweights(np.load(ftweights, allowpickle=True)) startstep = int(ftweights[-10:-4]) + 1 if model.hasfinenetwork(): # Load fine weights similarly pass # 4. Training Loop for step in range(startstep, args.maxsteps): # 5. View Selection (for multi-view) currnviews = args.currnviews NV = images.shape[0] sourceindices = np.random.choice(NV, currnviews, replace=False) srcimages = util.batchedindexselectnd(images, sourceindices) srcposes = util.batchedindexselectnd(poses, sourceindices) # 6. Network Encoding (if applicable) if model.hasencoder(): model.encode(srcimages, srcposes, focals) # 7. Forward Pass renderdict = renderer.bindparallel(model, args.gpuid).eval()(rays, wantweights=True) coarsergb = renderdict.coarse.rgb finergb = renderdict.fine.rgb if renderdict.hasfine else None # 8. Loss Computation losscoarse = computergbloss(coarsergb, images[sourceindices]) loss = losscoarse if finergb is not None: lossfine = computergbloss(finergb, images[sourceindices]) loss = loss + args.lambdafine lossfine # Normalize loss loss = loss (1.0 / (images.shape[-1] images.shape[-2] 3)) # 9. Backward Pass and Update optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() # 10. Logging and Checkpointing if step % args.iprint == 0: print(f"Step {step}, Loss: {loss.item()}") if step % args.iweights == 0: np.save(os.path.join(args.logdir, f"model{step:06d}.npy"), model.getweights()) Training Ray Batching is a data loading strategy for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that selects a random subset of pixel coordinates (and their corresponding rays) from the full training image grid per optimization iteration, rather than rendering complete images. It reduces the GPU memory footprint during the backward pass of gradient descent by processing only N{rand} rays per step, which controls gradient noise and enables efficient training. It differs from Training Loop for Refractive Index Field and Training Loop by explicitly managing the pre-computation, shuffling, and batch-slicing of ray tensors across multiple training images, whereas those siblings focus on the network forward/backward passes or specific physical models. This method defines the optimization loop for training a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to represent a 3D refractive index (IOR) field and associated emission field, using differentiable ray tracing. It distinguishes itself by combining Eikonal ray tracing with luminance integration, optimizing the IOR field via boundary regularization and luminance reconstruction loss, specifically implemented in JAX for multi-device sharding. It builds on Training Loop Setup and Training Ray Batching. The Training Loop is the core optimization procedure for NeRF and related radiance field methods, orchestrating data loading, ray sampling, model forward passes, loss calculation, and parameter updates. It solves the problem of iteratively refining a scene representation to minimize the difference between rendered views and ground truth images. It sets itself apart from its siblings by defining the high-level control flow (epochs, batches, validation, checkpointing) rather than the specific ray batching strategies Training Ray Batching or specialized guidance mechanisms like Diffusion-Based Guidance for Radiance Field Optimization. Computes gradients of the reconstruction loss with respect to the rotation and translation components of a camera view matrix. The main entry point for the training experiment, which loads configuration, sets up global parameters, loads the scene and sensors, renders reference images, and initializes the SDF for optimization. It loads configuration from a JSON file, updates experiment parameters (name, scene, epochs, lr, sensor counts, batch size) and rendering parameters (integrator, resolution, spp, SDF mode) using command-line args or config defaults. It loads the scene using mi.loadfile with the specified scene XML and hide environment flag. It sets sensor parameters (radius, height) based on scene name: 'hotdog' (h=0.5), 'lego' (h=0.35), 'chair' (h=0.6, r=1.5), else (h=0.4, r=1.3). It initializes the SDF for optimization as a SphereSDF with specified resolution and radius, enabling gradients on the SDF grid tensor. It checks if albedo, roughness, and metallic volumes are present in the scene parameters to determine optimization targets. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of rays per step and network depth. IDR baseline takes 0.2 sec/iteration. NeRF takes 0.40 sec/iteration. NLR takes 2.21 sec/iteration. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of rays processed per step. Ray batching reduces memory footprint by processing only a subset of rays. Measured Performance: Training time varies significantly by method and dataset. IDR: 0.2 sec/iteration, 0.025 sec/frame rendering. Scaling: Scales with number of GPUs via parallel binding. Strengths: Flexible configuration, supports resumption, handles multi-view inputs. Limitations: View selection can be inefficient. Memory intensive for full-image rendering. The Training Loop Setup is a fundamental component of differentiable volume rendering pipelines, originating from the NeRF paper and adapted in subsequent works like PixelNeRF and IDR. It provides the infrastructure for iterative optimization of neural scene representations. name: Training Ray Batching
head: Random Ray Batching, Random Ray Batching for NeRF Training, Random Ray Sampling, batch ray selection, partial ray sampling
body: Training Ray Batching is a data loading strategy for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that selects a random subset of pixel coordinates (and their corresponding rays) from the full training image grid per optimization iteration, rather than rendering complete images. It reduces the GPU memory footprint during the backward pass of gradient descent by processing only N{rand} rays per step, which controls gradient noise and enables efficient training. It differs from Training Loop for Refractive Index Field and Training Loop by explicitly managing the pre-computation, shuffling, and batch-slicing of ray tensors across multiple training images, whereas those siblings focus on the network forward/backward passes or specific physical models. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Training images tensor images of shape (N{img}, H, W, 3); camera poses tensor poses of shape (N{img}, 3, 4); camera intrinsic matrix K of shape (3, 3); image dimensions H, W; batch size N{rand}; boolean flag usebatching (default True). Outputs: A batch tensor batch of shape (3, N{rand}, 3) containing ray origins, ray directions, and target RGB values, ready for the NeRF forward pass. Data Structures: The core data structure is a flat tensor raysrgb of shape (N{total\rays}, 3, 3), where N{total\rays} = N{train} \times H \times W. The first dimension indexes the specific ray (image index, row, column). The second dimension indexes the component: index 0 is ray origin (x, y, z), index 1 is ray direction (dx, dy, dz), and index 2 is target RGB color (r, g, b). The third dimension is the coordinate value (3 floats). Data type is float32. Steps: 1. Generate Rays: For each training image, call getraysnp(H, W, K, p) for each pose p in poses[:,:3,:4] and stack them into a tensor rays of shape (N{img}, ro+rd, H, W, 3), where ro+rd=2 represents ray origins and directions. 2. Concatenate Targets: Concatenate rays with images[:,None] along axis 1 to create raysrgb of shape (N{img}, ro+rd+rgb, H, W, 3). 3. Transpose: Transpose raysrgb using [0,2,3,1,4] to shape (N{img}, H, W, ro+rd+rgb, 3). 4. Filter Training Set: Stack only the images in the training index list i{train} into raysrgb, resulting in shape (len(i{train}), H, W, ro+rd+rgb, 3). 5. Flatten: Reshape raysrgb to (-1, 3, 3), resulting in shape (N{train} \times H \times W, 3, 3). 6. Cast and Shuffle: Cast raysrgb to np.float32. Randomly shuffle the order of rays in raysrgb using np.random.shuffle(raysrgb) to ensure random sampling during training. 7. Batch Sampling (Per Iteration): Maintain a global index ibatch initialized to 0. Slice raysrgb[ibatch:ibatch+Nrand] to get the batch. Transpose the batch to shape (2+1, N{rand}, 3) where the first dimension represents ray origins, ray directions, and target values. Increment ibatch by N{rand}. If ibatch >= raysrgb.shape[0], shuffle raysrgb again using torch.randperm and reset ibatch to 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import torch def getraysnp(H, W, K, pose): # pose is (3, 4) [R|t] i, j = np.meshgrid(np.arange(W, dtype=np.float32), np.arange(H, dtype=np.float32), indexing='xy') dirs = np.stack([(i - K[0, 2]) / K[0, 0], (j - K[1, 2]) / K[1, 1], np.oneslike(i)], axis=-1) dirs = dirs / np.linalg.norm(dirs, axis=-1, keepdims=True) R = pose[:,:3] t = pose[:, 3] dirsworld = np.sum(np.expanddims(dirs, -2) R, axis=-1) origins = np.dot(-R.T, t) originsworld = np.broadcastto(origins, (H, W, 3)) rays = np.stack([originsworld, dirsworld], axis=0) return rays def prepareraybatch(images, poses, K, itrain, H, W, Nrand): Nimg = len(images) rays = np.stack([getraysnp(H, W, K, p) for p in poses[:Nimg]], axis=0) raysrgb = np.concatenate([rays, images[:, None]], axis=1) raysrgb = np.transpose(raysrgb, [0, 2, 3, 1, 4]) raysrgb = np.stack([raysrgb[i] for i in itrain], axis=0) raysrgb = raysrgb.reshape(-1, 3, 3) raysrgb = raysrgb.astype(np.float32) np.random.shuffle(raysrgb) raysrgb = torch.Tensor(raysrgb) return raysrgb def samplebatch(raysrgb, ibatch, Nrand): Ntotal = raysrgb.shape[0] batchflat = raysrgb[ibatch: ibatch + Nrand] batchtransposed = torch.transpose(batchflat, 0, 1) batchrays = batchtransposed[:2] targets = batchtransposed[2] newibatch = ibatch + Nrand if newibatch >= Ntotal: randidx = torch.randperm(Ntotal) raysrgb = raysrgb[randidx] newibatch = 0 return batchrays, targets, newibatch, raysrgb Parameters: Nrand: Number of rays per batch. Default value is 32 \times 32 \times 4 = 4096. Controls memory footprint and gradient noise. usebatching: Boolean flag. If True, rays are sampled from all training images globally. If False, rays are sampled from a single random image per iteration. K: Camera intrinsic calibration matrix, shape (3, 3). Simplified form: \begin{bmatrix} f{camera} & 0 & W/2 \\ 0 & f{camera} & H/2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. imagesize: Resolution of the target image, determines the search space for random sampling. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: When ibatch reaches the end of the tensor, a full shuffle is required to maintain randomness for the next epoch. Precision: The tensor is explicitly cast to float32 during preparation to match standard training requirements. Memory: Pre-computing all rays consumes memory proportional to the number of training pixels, which can be significant for high-resolution datasets. This method prepares training and validation data for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by loading synthetic Blender dataset scenes, parsing JSON metadata for camera poses and images, and precomputing rays and RGB values. It differs from LLFF Dataset Loading by assuming known, precise camera poses provided in JSON rather than estimating them, and by using fixed depth bounds (near: 2.0, far: 6.0) instead of NDC normalization. It differs from NeRF Dataset Loading by explicitly handling the specific preprocessing steps for the Blender synthetic dataset, including focal length computation from cameraanglex and RGBA compositing. Batch Ray Sampling is a data loading strategy for training neural radiance fields (NeRF) that generates batches of random rays from training images per optimization iteration, rather than rendering complete images. It solves the memory bottleneck of full-image rendering by processing only a subset of pixels (e.g., 1024–8192 rays) per step, enabling efficient gradient updates and better memory utilization. It differs from image-based training by sampling randomly across the entire image pool, which allows for different training dynamics compared to frameworks like I-NGP that sample every pixel of n images. body: This method prepares training and validation data for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by loading synthetic Blender dataset scenes, parsing JSON metadata for camera poses and images, and precomputing rays and RGB values. It differs from LLFF Dataset Loading by assuming known, precise camera poses provided in JSON rather than estimating them, and by using fixed depth bounds (near: 2.0, far: 6.0) instead of NDC normalization. It differs from NeRF Dataset Loading by explicitly handling the specific preprocessing steps for the Blender synthetic dataset, including focal length computation from cameraanglex and RGBA compositing. Inputs: transforms{split}.json: JSON file containing metadata for a specific split (train/val/test). Image files: Corresponding to the paths in the JSON. Configuration parameters: batchimagesampling (boolean), trainnumrays (integer), backgroundcolor (string: 'white' or 'random'). Outputs: rays: Tensor of shape (N, 6) containing ray origins (N, 3) and normalized directions (N, 3). rgb: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing target RGB colors. fgmask: Tensor of shape (N, 1) containing foreground masks. backgroundcolor: Tensor of shape (3,) for compositing. Data Structures: rays: Concatenated [rayo, rayd] where rayo is origin and rayd is unit direction. c2w: Camera-to-world transformation matrix, typically (4, 4) or (3, 4). Steps: 1. Load Metadata and Compute Focal Length: Parse transforms{split}.json. Extract cameraanglex (in radians). Compute focal length f: f = \frac{0.5 \times W}{\tan(0.5 \times \text{camera\angle\x})} where W is the image width. 2. Select Images: If stage is 'train' and batchimagesampling is true: Sample trainnumrays random indices from self.dataset.allimages. If stage is 'train' and batchimagesampling is false: Sample 1 random index. If stage is 'val' or 'test': Use the first camera for the index. 3. Load and Preprocess Images: Load the image for the selected index. Convert to RGBA. Resize to (W, H). Composite onto a white background: \text{rgb} = \text{rgba}[:,:,:3] \times \text{rgba}[:,:, 3:] + (1 - \text{rgba}[:,:, 3:]). 4. Generate Rays: Get camera-to-world matrix c2w for the selected index. Generate ray origins rayo and directions rayd using getraysnp(H, W, focal, c2w). getraysnp computes pixel coordinates (i, j), camera-space directions, and transforms them to world space using c2w. Normalize ray directions: \text{ray\d} = \text{normalize}(\text{ray\d}). Concatenate origins and directions: \text{rays} = \text{concat}([\text{ray\o}, \text{ray\d}], \text{dim}=-1). 5. Sample Pixels (Training): If training, sample random pixel coordinates (x, y) within image dimensions w, h. Extract RGB values and foreground masks for these pixels using the precomputed rays. If validation/testing, use all directions and full image RGB/masks. 6. Set Background Color: If backgroundcolor is 'white', set self.model.backgroundcolor to torch.ones((3,), dtype=torch.float32). If 'random', initialize randomly. Parameters: near: 2.0. far: 6.0. WHITEBG: Always True for Blender dataset. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np import json from PIL import Image def loadblenderdata(jsonpath, split, config): """ Loads and preprocesses Blender dataset data. Args: jsonpath: Path to transforms{split}.json split: 'train', 'val', or 'test' config: Configuration object with batchimagesampling, trainnumrays, backgroundcolor Returns: rays: Tensor (N, 6) rgb: Tensor (N, 3) fgmask: Tensor (N, 1) """ with open(jsonpath, 'r') as f: meta = json.load(f) # Compute focal length W = meta['w'] H = meta['h'] cameraanglex = meta['cameraanglex'] focal = 0.5 W / np.tan(0.5 cameraanglex) # Load images and poses images = [] poses = [] for frame in meta['frames']: img = Image.open(frame['filepath']).convert('RGBA') img = img.resize((W, H), Image.Resampling.LANCZOS) images.append(np.array(img)) poses.append(np.array(frame['transformmatrix'], dtype=np.float32)) images = np.array(images) poses = np.array(poses) # Select indices if split == 'train': if config.batchimagesampling: indices = np.random.choice(len(images), config.trainnumrays, replace=False) else: indices = np.random.choice(len(images), 1, replace=False) raysolist, raysdlist, rgblist, fgmasklist = [], [], [], [] for idx in indices: c2w = poses[idx] rayo, rayd = getraysnp(H, W, focal, c2w) # Sample random pixel coordinates for training x = np.random.randint(0, W) y = np.random.randint(0, H) raysolist.append(rayo[y, x]) raysdlist.append(rayd[y, x]) rgba = images[idx].astype(np.float32) / 255.0 rgb = rgba[y, x,:3] rgba[y, x, 3:] + (1 - rgba[y, x, 3:]) rgblist.append(rgb) fgmasklist.append(rgba[y, x, 3]) rayso = np.stack(raysolist) raysd = np.stack(raysdlist) rgb = np.stack(rgblist) fgmask = np.stack(fgmasklist) else: # Validation/testing uses first camera and full image idx = 0 c2w = poses[idx] rayo, rayd = getraysnp(H, W, focal, c2w) rgba = images[idx].astype(np.float32) / 255.0 rgb = rgba[:,:,:3] rgba[:,:, 3:] + (1 - rgba[:,:, 3:]) fgmask = rgba[:,:, 3:] rayso = rayo.reshape(-1, 3) raysd = rayd.reshape(-1, 3) rgb = rgb.reshape(-1, 3) fgmask = fgmask.reshape(-1, 1) # Normalize directions raysd = raysd / np.linalg.norm(raysd, axis=-1, keepdims=True) rays = np.concatenate([rayso, raysd], axis=-1) # Convert to tensors rays = torch.fromnumpy(rays).float() rgb = torch.fromnumpy(rgb).float() fgmask = torch.fromnumpy(fgmask).float() return rays, rgb, fgmask def getraysnp(H, W, focal, c2w, cx=None, cy=None): """NumPy version for dataset preprocessing.""" if cx is None: cx = W / 2.0 if cy is None: cy = H / 2.0 i, j = np.meshgrid(np.arange(W, dtype=np.float32), np.arange(H, dtype=np.float32), indexing='xy') # Camera-space direction (OpenCV convention: z-forward, y-down, x-right) dirs = np.stack([ (i - cx) / focal, -(j - cy) / focal, # flip y (image y-down -> camera y-up) -np.oneslike(i), # looking down -z in camera space (Blender/NeRF convention) ], axis=-1) # (H, W, 3) # Rotate directions to world space rayd = (dirs @ c2w[:3,:3].T) # (H, W, 3) # All rays share the camera centre as origin rayo = np.broadcastto(c2w[:3, 3], (H, W, 3)) # (H, W, 3) return rayo, rayd Loads real-world LLFF (Local Light Field Fusion) dataset scenes, parsing COLMAP poses from posesbounds.npy, correcting axis conventions, and applying NDC (Normalized Device Coordinates) normalization. It differs from general NeRF dataset loading by enforcing forward-facing scene assumptions and specific axis corrections required for the LLFF capture rig. This method loads the NeRF-Synthetic (Blender) dataset by parsing JSON metadata for camera poses and images, handling half-resolution resizing, and returning normalized RGBA images and camera parameters. It differs from LLFF Dataset Loading by assuming known, precise camera poses provided in JSON rather than estimating them from images, and by using a fixed scene bounding box.
