name: Masked Local-Global Ray Sampling
head: MLG Ray Sampling
body: Masked Local-Global (MLG) ray sampling is a strategy for X-ray volume rendering that extracts contextual and geometric information by segmenting informative foreground regions and sampling rays on specific patches and outside regions. It combines patch-level sampling on foreground regions with pixel-level sampling on the rest of the foreground to capture local semantic information and global contextual representations while avoiding uninformative background rays. Unlike standard uniform sampling, it explicitly partitions the foreground mask into non-overlapping windows to prioritize local structure perception for the Lineformer backbone. Inputs: Projection image I \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W}. Threshold T \in \mathbb{R} for binarization. Window size S (integer) for patch partitioning. Number of windows for patch sampling Nl. Number of pixels for global sampling Ng. Outputs: A set of rays \mathcal{R} comprising local rays \mathcal{R}l and global rays \mathcal{R}g. Data Structures: Binary mask M \in \{0, 1\}^{H \times W}. Set of non-overlapping windows \mathcal{W} \in \{0, 1\}^{\frac{HW}{S^2} \times S \times S}. Set of foreground windows \mathcal{W}f \subseteq \mathcal{W}. Selected local windows \mathcal{W}l \subseteq \mathcal{W}f. Set of selected global pixels Pg. Steps: 1. Binarize Projection: Create the binary mask M by comparing the projection image I against the threshold T: M = \mathbb{1}{I > T} where \mathbb{1}{condition} is 1 if the condition is true, 0 otherwise. 2. Partition into Windows: Partition the mask M into a set \mathcal{W} of non-overlapping windows of size S \times S. The total number of windows is \frac{HW}{S^2}. 3. Identify Foreground Windows: Define \mathcal{W}f as the subset of windows \mathbf{w} \in \mathcal{W} that are entirely contained in the foreground regions (i.e., all pixels in the window are 1 in M): \mathcal{W}f = \{ \mathbf{w} \in \mathcal{W} \mid \mathbf{w} = \mathbb{1}{S \times S} \} where \mathbb{1}{S \times S} denotes an S \times S matrix of ones. 4. Patch-Level Sampling (Local): Randomly select Nl windows \mathcal{W}l = \{ \mathbf{w}1, \dots, \mathbf{w}{Nl} \} from \mathcal{W}f. Construct the set of local rays \mathcal{R}l by sampling rays for all pixels p within the selected windows: \mathcal{R}l = \bigcup{i=1}^{Nl} \bigcup{p \in \mathbf{w}i} \text{Ray}(p) where \text{Ray}(p) maps pixel p to its corresponding X-ray. 5. Pixel-Level Sampling (Global): Randomly select Ng pixels Pg from the foreground regions of M, excluding the pixels covered by the windows in \mathcal{W}l, to avoid repeated sampling. Construct the set of global rays \mathcal{R}g by sampling rays for these pixels: \mathcal{R}g = \{ \text{Ray}(p) \mid p \in Pg \} 6. Combine: The final ray batch is \mathcal{R} = \mathcal{R}l \cup \mathcal{R}g. Parameters: T: Threshold for binarizing the projection image. Value not specified in sources. S: Size of the non-overlapping windows. Value not specified in sources. Nl: Number of windows selected for patch-level sampling. In implementation, 1024 rays are from patch-level sampling. Ng: Number of pixels selected for pixel-level sampling. In implementation, 1024 rays are from pixel-level sampling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def maskedlocalglobalsampling(I, T, S, Nl, Ng): """ I: Projection image, shape (H, W) T: Threshold for binarization S: Window size (integer) Nl: Number of windows for local sampling Ng: Number of pixels for global sampling Returns: List of ray indices or coordinates """ H, W = I.shape # Step 1: Binarize M = (I > T).astype(int) # Step 2: Partition into windows # Calculate number of windows numwindowsh = H // S numwindowsw = W // S totalwindows = numwindowsh numwindowsw # Create window indices windowindices = np.arange(totalwindows) # Step 3: Identify foreground windows # A window is foreground if all pixels in it are 1 # Reshape M to (numwindowsh, S, numwindowsw, S) Mreshaped = M[:numwindowshS,:numwindowswS].reshape(numwindowsh, S, numwindowsw, S) # Check if all pixels in each window are 1 windowisfg = np.all(Mreshaped == 1, axis=(1, 3)) # Flatten to 1D boolean array windowisfgflat = windowisfg.flatten() # Get indices of foreground windows fgwindowindices = np.where(windowisfgflat)[0] # Step 4: Patch-level sampling # Randomly select Nl windows from foreground windows if len(fgwindowindices) < Nl: # If not enough foreground windows, take all and pad or handle error # Based on source, we assume sufficient foreground exists selectedlocalwindowindices = fgwindowindices else: selectedlocalwindowindices = np.random.choice(fgwindowindices, Nl, replace=False) # Map window indices to pixel coordinates localpixels = [] for widx in selectedlocalwindowindices: # Convert flat index to 2D window index wh, ww = divmod(widx, numwindowsw) # Generate all pixel coordinates in this window for dy in range(S): for dx in range(S): py = wh S + dy px = ww S + dx localpixels.append((py, px)) # Step 5: Pixel-level sampling # Create a mask of pixels already sampled in local step localpixelset = set(localpixels) # Find all foreground pixels fgpixels = np.argwhere(M == 1) # Convert to set for fast lookup fgpixelset = set(map(tuple, fgpixels)) # Exclude local pixels availableglobalpixels = list(fgpixelset - localpixelset) if len(availableglobalpixels) < Ng: # If not enough pixels, take all selectedglobalpixels = availableglobalpixels else: selectedglobalpixels = np.random.choice(availableglobalpixels, Ng, replace=False) # Step 6: Combine # Ray(p) is assumed to be a function that returns ray data for pixel p # Here we return the pixel coordinates as a proxy for rays allrays = localpixels + selectedglobalpixels return allrays Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the number of foreground windows is less than Nl, the algorithm cannot select Nl unique windows. The sources do not specify the fallback behavior. If the number of available global pixels (foreground minus local) is less than Ng, the algorithm cannot select Ng unique pixels. The sources do not specify the fallback behavior. The threshold T is critical for defining the foreground mask but its value is not specified. The window size S must divide H and W for the partitioning to be exact, or the sources do not specify how to handle remainders. Time Complexity: The binarization and partitioning steps are O(HW). Identifying foreground windows is O(\frac{HW}{S^2}). Selecting windows and pixels is O(Nl + Ng) assuming efficient data structures. The dominant cost is likely the ray generation if \text{Ray}(p) is expensive, but the sampling logic itself is efficient. Memory Complexity: Storing the mask M is O(HW). Storing the windows \mathcal{W} is O(\frac{HW}{S^2} \cdot S^2) = O(HW). The output ray set is O(Nl \cdot S^2 + Ng). Measured Performance: In SAX-NeRF, the batch size is 2048 rays, with 1024 from patch-level and 1024 from pixel-level sampling. The method improves novel view synthesis and CT reconstruction performance compared to previous NeRF-based methods. Strengths: Avoids uninformative background rays, captures local semantic information via patches, and captures global shape via pixel-level sampling. Limitations: Requires a reliable foreground mask (dependent on T). Performance depends on the choice of S, Nl, and Ng. MLG ray sampling was proposed in the SAX-NeRF paper for sparse-view X-ray 3D reconstruction. It is designed to work with the Lineformer backbone, which captures internal structures by modeling dependencies within line segments of X-rays. The method addresses the problem of learning from uninformative background rays which degrade model efficiency. name: Training Ray Shuffling
head: Batch Index Generator, Ray Sampling and Shuffling, ray initialization, shuffleRays
body: Training Ray Shuffling generates random batch indices for training and transfers shuffled indices to the GPU. It differs from its parent Batch Ray Sampling by explicitly managing the permutation state and handling the CPU-to-GPU transfer. Inputs: Training cameras, ground truth images, scene data, dataset size N, batch size BS, and configuration flags MaskAreaOnly and whiteBG. Outputs: Shuffled ray indices on the GPU. Data Structures: idx (1D integer array storing a permutation of 0, N)), top (integer tracking the current position in idx), ray (GPU [array for ray data), and sampleRaysIndexGPU (GPU array for shuffled indices). Steps: 1. Initialize idx as a random permutation of 0, N) and top to 0. 2. Create a temporary object and call initialSelf with training cameras, ground truth, scene data, dataset size, MaskAreaOnly, false, whiteBG, and idx. 3. Call shuffleRays with temp.totalRays, false, and configs->shuffleRays. 4. Call temp.shuffleTo to transfer data to this->ray and this->sampleRaysIndexGPU. 5. Call temp.freeSelf() and regenerateSamples(). 6. In an infinite [training loop, check if top + BS > N. 7. If true, reset idx to a new random permutation and top to 0. 8. Yield the slice idx[top:top+BS] and increment top by BS. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np class TrainingRayShuffler: def init(self, N, BS, traincameras, groundtruth, scene, config): self.N = N self.BS = BS self.traincameras = traincameras self.groundtruth = groundtruth self.scene = scene self.config = config self.idx = None self.top = 0 self.ray = None self.sampleRaysIndexGPU = None self.initialize() def initialize(self): # Step 1: Initialize idx as a random permutation of [0, N) and top to 0 self.idx = np.random.permutation(self.N) self.top = 0 # Steps 2-6: Setup temporary object, initialize ray data, shuffle, transfer to GPU, cleanup # temp.initialSelf(traincameras, groundtruth, scene, N, MaskAreaOnly, False, whiteBG, idx) # temp.shuffleRays(temp.totalRays, False, config.shuffleRays) # temp.shuffleTo(&self.ray, self.sampleRaysIndexGPU) # temp.freeSelf() # regenerateSamples() # Note: The exact implementation of temp and regenerateSamples is not provided in the sources. def getnextbatch(self): # Step 7: Infinite training loop while True: # Check if current batch exceeds total samples if self.top + self.BS > self.N: # Reset idx to a new random permutation and top to 0 self.idx = np.random.permutation(self.N) self.top = 0 # Yield the slice idx[top:top+BS] and increment top by BS batch = self.idx[self.top:self.top + self.BS] self.top += self.BS yield batch Parameters: MaskAreaOnly (boolean flag for masked area sampling), whiteBG (boolean flag for background color assumption), and shuffleRays (configuration flag enabling the shuffle operation). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: torch.randperm may produce incorrect results on certain CUDA hardware; np.random.permutation is recommended instead. Ensure top is reset correctly when top + BS > N to avoid out-of-bounds access. Permutes ray data across GPU arrays using an index mapping array to improve training order or batch distribution. It sets itself apart by operating directly on GPU memory layouts rather than CPU-side index generation. Choose this variant when fine-grained control over GPU memory access patterns is required for performance optimization. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance and scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple implementation and effective randomization for training stability. Limitations: Potential platform-specific bugs with PyTorch primitives and CPU-to-GPU transfer overhead if not optimized. When to use it and when not to use: Not given in the sources. Originating from implementations in DirectVoxGO and Clear-plenoxels, this method is part of the broader NeRF training loop setup. sjtuytc/UnboundedNeRFPytorch, https://github.com/sjtuytc/UnboundedNeRFPytorch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) sunset1995/DirectVoxGO, https://github.com/sunset1995/DirectVoxGO, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) nortonBryan/Clear-plenoxels, https://github.com/nortonBryan/Clear-plenoxels, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

head: shuffleRays, shuffleToNewGroup
body: Ray Shuffling & Reordering permutes ray data across GPU arrays using an index mapping array to improve training order or batch distribution. Inputs: Source ray arrays (src) containing device arrays for cameraCenterXDevice, cameraCenterYDevice, cameraCenterZDevice, directionXDevice, directionYDevice, directionZDevice, neartDevice, fartDevice, gtMaskDevice, and color channels (gtGrayDevice if grayscale, else gtRedDevice, gtGreenDevice, gtBlueDevice). Destination ray arrays (dest) with an identical layout. shuffledIndexArray: A host or device array of integers mapping destination indices to source indices. src.totalRays: Total number of rays. src.graylized: Boolean flag indicating grayscale mode. Outputs: Destination ray arrays (dest) with rays reordered according to shuffledIndexArray. Data Structures: Rays are stored in Structure of Arrays (SoA) format on the GPU, with each attribute as a separate device array of size totalRays. Steps: 1. Host function allocates destination memory for ray attributes. 2. Host function calls ShuffleRank to generate shuffledIndexArray (implementation not provided in the sources). 3. Host function copies shuffledIndexArray to GPU. 4. Host function launches the shuffleToNewGroup kernel with grid/block dimensions sized to src.totalRays. 5. Each thread computes its global destRayIndex from block and thread indices. 6. If destRayIndex < src.totalRays, the thread reads the source index from shuffledIndexArray[destRayIndex]. 7. The thread copies all ray attributes from the source arrays to the destination arrays using the mapped source index. 8. If src.graylized is true, copy gtGrayDevice; otherwise, copy gtRedDevice, gtGreenDevice, and gtBlueDevice. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def shuffletonewgroup(src, dest, shuffledindexarray, totalrays, graylized, blockIdx, gridDim, threadIdx, blockDim): # Each thread executes this block once for its assigned destrayindex destrayindex = (blockIdx.y gridDim.x + blockIdx.x) blockDim.x blockDim.y + threadIdx.y blockDim.x + threadIdx.x if destrayindex >= totalrays: return srcindex = shuffledindexarray[destrayindex] dest['cameraCenterXDevice'][destrayindex] = src['cameraCenterXDevice'][srcindex] dest['cameraCenterYDevice'][destrayindex] = src['cameraCenterYDevice'][srcindex] dest['cameraCenterZDevice'][destrayindex] = src['cameraCenterZDevice'][srcindex] dest['directionXDevice'][destrayindex] = src['directionXDevice'][srcindex] dest['directionYDevice'][destrayindex] = src['directionYDevice'][srcindex] dest['directionZDevice'][destrayindex] = src['directionZDevice'][srcindex] dest['neartDevice'][destrayindex] = src['neartDevice'][srcindex] dest['fartDevice'][destrayindex] = src['fartDevice'][srcindex] dest['gtMaskDevice'][destrayindex] = src['gtMaskDevice'][srcindex] if graylized: dest['gtGrayDevice'][destrayindex] = src['gtGrayDevice'][srcindex] else: dest['gtRedDevice'][destrayindex] = src['gtRedDevice'][srcindex] dest['gtGreenDevice'][destrayindex] = src['gtGreenDevice'][srcindex] dest['gtBlueDevice'][destrayindex] = src['gtBlueDevice'][srcindex] Parameters: shuffledIndexArray: Host or device array of integers mapping destination indices to source indices. maxIndex: Total number of rays to shuffle (equivalent to src.totalRays). initialized: Boolean controlling host memory allocation for indices. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If destRayIndex >= src.totalRays, the thread returns immediately to prevent out-of-bounds memory access. Precision and boundary conditions for non-unit cell sizes or negative directions are not addressed by this method, as it operates purely on index permutation. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance, scaling, strengths, limitations, and usage conditions: Not given in the sources. The method is implemented in the nortonBryan/Clear-plenoxels repository. Origin details, broader history, and specific usage contexts beyond the provided code: Not given in the sources. nortonBryan/Clear-plenoxels, https://github.com/nortonBryan/Clear-plenoxels, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Training Ray Masking and Caching
head: Mask-Cached Ray Sampling
body: Training Ray Masking and Caching filters the set of candidate training rays to retain only those that intersect the coarse geometry of the scene, storing the valid rays and their associated RGB values in contiguous buffers for efficient training. It differs from sibling methods like Pixel Batching by explicitly discarding rays that miss the geometry (background or empty space) before the training loop begins, thereby reducing the number of rays processed per iteration. Inputs: rgbtrori: List of training image tensors (RGB values). cfg.data: Configuration object containing H, W, K (camera intrinsics), c2w (camera-to-world matrices), ndc (boolean for NDC coordinate normalization), inversey, flipx, flipy. model: The neural rendering model instance, specifically its hitcoarsegeo method. renderkwargs: Dictionary of arguments passed to model.hitcoarsegeo. DEVICE: Target device (e.g., torch.device('cuda')). Outputs: rgbtr: Tensor of shape [Nvalid, 3] containing RGB values for valid rays. raysotr: Tensor of shape [Nvalid, 3] containing ray origins. raysdtr: Tensor of shape [Nvalid, 3] containing ray directions. viewdirstr: Tensor of shape [Nvalid, 3] containing view directions. imsz: List of integers, where imsz[i] is the number of valid rays from image i. batchindexsampler: A lambda function that yields indices for sampling batches from the cached valid rays. Data Structures: mask: Boolean tensor of shape [H, W] indicating which pixels in the current image hit the coarse geometry. rgbtr, raysotr, raysdtr, viewdirstr: Pre-allocated float tensors of shape [N, 3] (where N is the sum of all pixels across all images) to store results before trimming. Steps: 1. Calculate the total number of pixels N across all training images: N = \sum{i} (\text{height}i \times \text{width}i) 2. Initialize the output tensors rgbtr, raysotr, raysdtr, and viewdirstr with shape [N, 3] on the DEVICE. Initialize a counter top = 0 and an empty list imsz. 3. For each training image with pose c2w, image img, dimensions (H, W), and camera matrix K: a. Compute ray origins rayso, ray directions raysd, and view directions viewdirs using getraysofaview(H, W, K, c2w, ndc, inversey, flipx, flipy). b. Initialize a boolean mask tensor mask of shape [H, W] on the DEVICE. c. Iterate over the height of the image in chunks of size CHUNK (64). For each chunk starting at row h: i. Extract raysochunk = rayso[h:h+CHUNK] and raysdchunk = raysd[h:h+CHUNK]. ii. Call model.hitcoarsegeo(raysochunk, raysdchunk, renderkwargs) to obtain a boolean tensor of shape [CHUNK, W] indicating which rays in the chunk hit the coarse geometry. iii. Update the mask: mask[h:h+CHUNK] = model.hitcoarsegeo(...).to(DEVICE). d. Calculate the number of valid pixels n = \text{mask.sum()}. e. Copy the data for valid rays into the global buffers starting at index top: rgbtr[top:top+n].copy(img[mask]) raysotr[top:top+n].copy(rayso[mask].to(DEVICE)) raysdtr[top:top+n].copy(raysd[mask].to(DEVICE)) viewdirstr[top:top+n].copy(viewdirs[mask].to(DEVICE)) f. Append n to imsz and update top += n. 4. Trim the output tensors to the actual number of valid pixels: rgbtr = rgbtr[:top] raysotr = raysotr[:top] raysdtr = raysdtr[:top] viewdirstr = viewdirstr[:top] 5. Create an index generator for the valid rays: indexgenerator = batchindicesgenerator(len(rgbtr), cfgtrain.Nrand). 6. Define the batch sampler: batchindexsampler = lambda: next(indexgenerator). 7. Print the ratio of kept rays to total rays: top / N. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def getraysofaview(H, W, K, c2w, ndc, inversey, flipx, flipy): # Standard ray generation from camera intrinsics and extrinsics i, j = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(W, device=c2w.device), torch.arange(H, device=c2w.device), indexing='xy') dirs = torch.stack([(i - K[0][2]) / K[0][0], -(j - K[1][2]) / K[1][1], torch.oneslike(i)], dim=-1) if ndc: dirs = (dirs - 0.5) / 0.5 rayso = c2w[:3, 3].expand(H, W, 3) raysd = (dirs @ c2w[:3,:3].T).to(dirs.device) if inversey: raysd[:,:, 1] = -1 if flipx: raysd[:,:, 0] = -1 if flipy: raysd[:,:, 1] = -1 viewdirs = raysd / torch.norm(raysd, dim=-1, keepdim=True) return rayso, raysd, viewdirs def batchindicesgenerator(totalrays, batchsize): # Standard cyclic index generator for training batches idx = 0 while True: yield idx % totalrays idx += 1 def gettrainingraysinmaskcachesampling(rgbtrori, cfg, model, renderkwargs, DEVICE): # Step 1: Calculate total pixels N N = sum(im.shape[0] im.shape[1] for im in rgbtrori) # Step 2: Initialize output tensors rgbtr = torch.zeros((N, 3), device=DEVICE) raysotr = torch.zeros((N, 3), device=DEVICE) raysdtr = torch.zeros((N, 3), device=DEVICE) viewdirstr = torch.zeros((N, 3), device=DEVICE) top = 0 imsz = [] CHUNK = 64 # Step 3: Process each image for i, (c2w, img, H, W, K) in enumerate(zip(cfg.data.c2w, rgbtrori, cfg.data.H, cfg.data.W, cfg.data.K)): # 3a: Compute rays rayso, raysd, viewdirs = getraysofaview( H, W, K, c2w, cfg.data.ndc, cfg.data.inversey, cfg.data.flipx, cfg.data.flipy) # 3b: Initialize mask mask = torch.zeros((H, W), dtype=torch.bool, device=DEVICE) # 3c: Chunked geometry check for h in range(0, H, CHUNK): hend = min(h + CHUNK, H) raysochunk = rayso[h:hend] raysdchunk = raysd[h:hend] # Call model to get hit mask for this chunk hitmaskchunk = model.hitcoarsegeo( raysochunk, raysdchunk, renderkwargs) # Update global mask mask[h:hend] = hitmaskchunk.to(DEVICE) # 3d: Count valid pixels n = mask.sum() # 3e: Copy valid data to global buffers if n > 0: rgbtr[top:top+n].copy(img[mask]) raysotr[top:top+n].copy(rayso[mask].to(DEVICE)) raysdtr[top:top+n].copy(raysd[mask].to(DEVICE)) viewdirstr[top:top+n].copy(viewdirs[mask].to(DEVICE)) # 3f: Update indices imsz.append(n) top += n # Step 4: Trim tensors rgbtr = rgbtr[:top] raysotr = raysotr[:top] raysdtr = raysdtr[:top] viewdirstr = viewdirstr[:top] # Step 5 & 6: Create sampler indexgenerator = batchindicesgenerator(len(rgbtr), cfgtrain.Nrand) batchindexsampler = lambda: next(indexgenerator) # Step 7: Print ratio print(f"Ratio of kept rays: {top / N}") return rgbtr, raysotr, raysdtr, viewdirstr, imsz, batchindexsampler Parameters: CHUNK: Integer, size of the ray chunk processed in each iteration of the geometry check loop. Typical value: 64. renderkwargs: Dictionary passed to model.hitcoarsegeo. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Images: If an image has no rays hitting the geometry (n=0), the copy operations are skipped, and imsz records 0. Geometry Definition: The mask correctness depends entirely on model.hitcoarsegeo returning accurate intersection results. Device Consistency: Tensors must be allocated and updated on the same device (DEVICE) to prevent runtime errors. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the total number of pixels across all training images, dominated by the model.hitcoarsegeo calls performed in chunks. Memory Complexity: O(N) for pre-allocated output tensors before trimming, plus O(H \times W) per image for the mask. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with training images and resolution; chunking manages GPU memory during geometry checks. Strengths: Reduces rays processed per training iteration by filtering background/empty space rays before the loop begins. Limitations: Requires an initial pass over all training rays to build the cache. When to use: When the scene has significant empty space or background, and a coarse geometry model is available. When not to use: When the geometry is unknown or highly dynamic, or when memory is extremely constrained due to N-sized tensor pre-allocation. This method is part of the DirectVoxGO and related NeRF optimization pipelines, specifically designed to optimize training efficiency by focusing on occupied voxels. It was introduced in the context of differentiable volume rendering optimization loops. The approach leverages a coarse geometry representation to pre-filter rays before the main training loop begins. name: Memory-Saving Ray Sampling
head: Full-Ray Training Optimization
body: Memory-Saving Ray Sampling is a technique that enables training neural radiance fields (NeRF) on all rays simultaneously, avoiding the need to downsample ray counts due to out-of-memory (OOM) constraints. Unlike sibling methods that may require sparse sampling or precomputed buffers, this approach allows full-resolution ray processing without degradation in stylization quality. It specifically addresses the trade-off where reducing sampled ray numbers to save memory increases noise and degrades results. The method relies on the assumption that the primary memory bottleneck in training is the storage of intermediate features or embeddings for all rays in a batch, rather than the ray geometry itself. By ensuring that all rays are processed, it avoids the noise introduced by sparse sampling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A batch of rays covering the full image resolution (e.g., W \times H rays). Output: Gradients and loss values computed using all rays. Data Structures: Ray buffer: Stores origin and direction for all pixels in the current image. Feature embeddings: 3D or 2D embeddings associated with the scene representation. Steps: 1. Select an image from the training dataset. 2. Generate rays for every pixel in the image (full resolution). 3. Sample points along these rays. 4. Compute radiance and density using the neural network. 5. Render the image and compute the loss. 6. Backpropagate gradients. Parameters: Ray count: Equal to the total number of pixels in the source image (W \times H). Typical values: Not specified in sources, but implied to be full resolution (e.g., 512 \times 512 or higher). Edge cases and pitfalls: OOM errors may occur if the system does not have sufficient VRAM to hold all intermediate activations for all rays. Reducing ray counts to fit memory leads to increased noise and degraded stylization quality. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def memorysavingraysampling(image, nerfmodel, optimizer): # Get image dimensions height, width = image.shape[:2] # Generate rays for ALL pixels (full resolution) # This is the key difference from sparse sampling methods rays = generateraysforallpixels(height, width) # Sample points along rays points = samplepointsalongrays(rays) # Forward pass densities, colors = nerfmodel(points) # Render image renderedimage = raymarch(rays, densities, colors) # Compute loss loss = computeloss(renderedimage, image) # Backward pass optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return loss A strategy to prevent OOM errors during training by randomly sampling feature vectors instead of feeding all embeddings. For 3D embeddings with F=8, randomly sample 150K feature vectors \thetas per iteration. For 3D embeddings with F=1, 2, 4, randomly sample 200K feature vectors \thetas per iteration. For 2D embeddings, feed all embeddings together in one iteration without random sampling. This is used in conjunction with memory-saving techniques to manage VRAM usage. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Significantly reduced compared to naive full-batch training by avoiding OOM, but higher than sparse sampling methods. Measured Performance: In NeRF-Art, this method achieved better stylization quality than AvatarCLIP, which used sparse rays (112 \times 112) due to OOM constraints. Scaling: Scales with image resolution; requires sufficient VRAM to hold all ray intermediates. Strengths: Avoids noise from sparse sampling; enables full-resolution training. Limitations: Requires high VRAM; may still require auxiliary strategies like feature vector sampling for very large scenes. When to use: When VRAM allows full-ray processing and high-quality stylization is critical. When not: When VRAM is severely limited and sparse sampling is unavoidable. Originated in the context of text-driven NeRF stylization, specifically in NeRF-Art. It was developed to overcome the limitations of methods like AvatarCLIP, which suffered from noise due to sparse ray sampling. The technique is part of a broader effort to optimize memory usage in NeRF training. name: Texture-Space Sampling
head: Texture-space batch sampling, UV-space sampling for training
body: Texture-space sampling is a method for forming training batches in differentiable inverse volume rendering and radiance-field optimization by sampling unknowns (texture variables) uniformly directly in texture space, rather than sampling a random subset of views. This approach reduces gradient noise by ensuring that batches of observations are directly relevant to the selected unknowns, providing even coverage within an iteration compared to standard image-based sampling. It sets itself apart from Batch Ray Sampling by prioritizing the uniformity of the latent representation (texture) over the uniformity of the input data (images), and from Texture-Space Differentiable Rendering by focusing on the batch formation strategy rather than the gradient computation mechanics alone. The method constructs a training batch by selecting texture variables first, then determining which camera observations are relevant to those variables. Inputs: Texture space representation (e.g., UV map of a mesh or implicit surface). Inverse UV mapping function U^{-1}: (u, v) \rightarrow \mathbf{p}, mapping texture coordinates to 3D surface positions. Set of reference camera views (intrinsics, extrinsics, and RGB frames). Batch size N, adjustable based on GPU memory. Outputs: A batch of rays connecting sampled 3D positions to reference camera centers. Corresponding target pixel values from reference frames. Gradients for the texture parameters. Data Structures: Sampled Points: A list of N texture coordinate pairs (ui, vi). 3D Positions: A list of N 3D points \mathbf{p}i = U^{-1}(ui, vi). Valid Rays: A subset of rays (\mathbf{o}j, \mathbf{d}j) where \mathbf{o}j is the camera center and \mathbf{d}j is the direction to \mathbf{p}i, filtered for visibility. Steps: 1. Sample Texture Coordinates: At the start of each iteration, select N points uniformly at random over the texture space domain [0, 1] \times [0, 1]. Let these be \{(ui, vi)\}{i=1}^N. 2. Map to 3D: Use the precomputed inverse UV mapping to lookup the corresponding 3D positions on the scene surfaces: \mathbf{p}i = U^{-1}(ui, vi). 3. Connect to Views: For each sampled 3D position \mathbf{p}i, determine connections to a set of reference view positions. This involves checking if \mathbf{p}i is visible from the camera frustum and not occluded by other geometry. 4. Filter Occlusions: Discard connections where the ray from the camera center to \mathbf{p}i is occluded by geometry or where \mathbf{p}i falls outside the camera’s frustum. 5. Fetch Targets: For the remaining valid 3D positions, fetch the corresponding pixel values from the reference RGB frames. 6. Render: Estimate the current radiance values for the batch using differentiable path tracing. 7. Compute Loss and Gradients: Compute the per-pixel loss (averaged over all rays in the batch). Backpropagate through the rendering algorithm to obtain gradients. 8. Update: Update scene parameters (texture values) with an optimizer step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def texturespacesamplingiteration(texturemap, inverseuvmap, cameras, rgbframes, batchsize, optimizer): """ Performs one iteration of texture-space sampling. Args: texturemap: Current state of texture parameters. inverseuvmap: Function mapping (u, v) to 3D point p. cameras: List of camera objects with intrinsics, extrinsics, and RGB frames. rgbframes: List of reference RGB images corresponding to cameras. batchsize: Number of texture samples to draw. optimizer: Optimization object with step method. Returns: Updated texturemap. """ # Step 1: Sample uniform texture coordinates usamples = random.uniform(0, 1, batchsize) vsamples = random.uniform(0, 1, batchsize) texturecoords = list(zip(usamples, vsamples)) # Step 2: Map to 3D positions # Note: inverseuvmap may return None for invalid UVs (e.g., holes in mesh) points3d = [] validindices = [] for i, (u, v) in enumerate(texturecoords): p = inverseuvmap(u, v) if p is not None: points3d.append(p) validindices.append(i) # If no valid points, skip iteration or reduce batch size if not points3d: return texturemap points3d = np.array(points3d) # Step 3 & 4: Connect to views and filter occlusions # For each point, find visible cameras rays = [] targets = [] for p in points3d: for camera, frame in zip(cameras, rgbframes): # Check if point is in frustum if not camera.isinfrustum(p): continue # Check for occlusion # Ray from camera center to p rayorigin = camera.center raydirection = p - rayorigin raydirection = raydirection / np.linalg.norm(raydirection) if not isoccluded(rayorigin, raydirection, p, scenegeometry): # Fetch pixel value # Project p to image plane to get pixel coordinates pixelcoords = camera.project(p) if pixelcoords is validpixel(pixelcoords, frame.shape): targetvalue = frame[pixelcoords] rays.append((rayorigin, raydirection)) targets.append(targetvalue) if not rays: return texturemap rays = np.array(rays) targets = np.array(targets) # Step 6: Differentiable rendering # Estimate radiance for the batch # Note: This assumes a differentiable renderer that can handle batched rays renderedradiance = differentiablepathtrace(rays, texturemap) # Step 7: Loss and Gradients loss = meansquarederror(renderedradiance, targets) gradients = computegradients(loss, texturemap) # Step 8: Update optimizer.step(gradients) return texturemap def isoccluded(origin, direction, target, geometry): """ Checks if the ray from origin to target is occluded by geometry. Returns True if occluded, False if visible. """ # Simple ray intersection test # In a real implementation, this would use a BVH or similar structure closesthit = geometry.rayintersect(origin, direction) if closesthit is None: return False distancetohit = np.linalg.norm(closesthit - origin) distancetotarget = np.linalg.norm(target - origin) # If the hit is significantly closer than the target, it's occluded # Use a small epsilon to avoid self-intersection issues return distancetohit < (distancetotarget - 1e-6) Parameters: Batch Size (N): The number of texture samples per iteration. Adjustable based on available GPU memory. Inverse UV Mapping: Precomputed mapping from texture space to 3D surface. Must handle degenerate cases (e.g., UVs outside mesh bounds). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Invalid UVs: Some texture locations may not map to any scene surface (e.g., holes in the mesh or UV islands outside the geometry). These result in zero gradients for those locations. The implementation must handle None or invalid returns from the inverse UV map. Occlusion: Connections discarded due to occlusion reduce the effective batch size. If too many are discarded, the gradient signal may become weak. Frustum Culling: Points outside the camera frustum are discarded, ensuring only relevant observations are used. A rendering and optimization approach where sampling and gradient computation occur in texture space rather than image space, ensuring even coverage and avoiding Jacobian factors that cause exploding gradients or uneven convergence. It selects texels uniformly at random and connects them to camera positions to form rays for path tracing. Gradients are computed by omitting Jacobian factors (the derivative of the mapping from texture to image space) to prevent exploding gradients when distance d approaches zero and to obtain gradients of comparable magnitude regardless of observation distance or angle. Unlike standard image-based differentiable rendering, which leads to nonzero gradients only within the frusta of cameras selected for the iteration, texture-space sampling provides even coverage within an iteration. Some texture locations may not be mapped to any scene surface, resulting in zero gradients for those locations. Time Complexity: Dominated by the differentiable path tracing step for the batch size N. The UV lookup and visibility checks are O(N) but depend on the complexity of the scene geometry for occlusion testing. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the batch of rays and targets, plus the memory for the texture map and scene geometry. Performance: More efficient than sampling a random subset of views because it reduces noise in gradients by proceeding with batches of observations directly relevant to the selected unknowns. Strengths: Even coverage of texture space within an iteration; avoids exploding gradients from Jacobian factors; reduces gradient noise. Limitations: Requires a precomputed inverse UV mapping; some texture locations may have zero gradients if not mapped to surface; performance depends on the efficiency of the differentiable path tracer. When to Use: When optimizing texture parameters for a scene with known geometry (e.g., mesh-based rendering); when even coverage of the texture space is desired. When Not to Use: When the scene geometry is unknown or implicit; when memory is extremely limited and N must be very small. Originated in the context of material and lighting reconstruction for complex indoor scenes. The method was proposed to address the inefficiencies of standard image-based differentiable rendering, where gradients are sparse and unevenly distributed. It builds on the idea of sampling unknowns directly in their native space (texture space) to improve optimization stability and convergence. name: Training Loop for Refractive Index Field
head: Neural Field Training Loop, Refractive Index Field Training Procedure
body: This method defines the optimization loop for training a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to represent a 3D refractive index (IOR) field and associated emission field, using differentiable ray tracing. It distinguishes itself by combining Eikonal ray tracing with luminance integration, optimizing the IOR field via boundary regularization and luminance reconstruction loss, specifically implemented in JAX for multi-device sharding. It builds on Training Loop Setup and Training Ray Batching. Inputs: rays: Batched ray initial conditions (positions and directions). raylumtarget: Ground truth luminance values for the rays. Xreg: Boundary points for regularization. lumfield: 3D grid of true luminance values for interpolation. svals: Integration sample points along rays. imgsplane: Target image plane parameters. planelocs: Plane locations for rendering. etatrue: Ground truth IOR field (for testing/plotting). sourcelocs, covs: Light source locations and covariance matrices for emission modeling. Outputs: Optimized MLP parameters for predicteta (IOR) and predictlum (emission). Checkpoints of the trained model and predicted IOR field (eta). Training logs (loss, images, IOR slices) via TensorBoard. Data Structures: MLP (MLPact): Inputs are positional encoded coordinates. Hidden layers have depth netdepth (default 4) and width netwidth (default 128). Activation is ReLU. Skip connections are enabled (doskip=True). Output is a scalar IOR value. Positional encoding uses degree degpoint (default 4) with vectorized safesin computation. Optimizer State: Managed by Optax Adam with a cosine learning rate schedule. Loss Function: Partial application of lossfn with parameters lam (weight) and bdval (boundary value). Numbered Steps: 1. Data Preparation: Load Xtest, rays, svals, lumfield, raylumtarget, etatrue. Interpolate emission: predictlum = interpgrid(lumfield, cval=0.). Compute boundary points: Xreg = getXbd(16). Shard data across available JAX devices. 2. Initialization: Initialize MLP parameters with seed=0. Create Adam optimizer with cosine learning rate decay from lrinit to lrfinal over numiters. Initialize loss function with lam (0.1 for gas, 1.0 for NF) and bdval (1.0003 for gas, 1.0 for NF). Initialize render function with svals, imgsplane, planelocs. 3. Training Loop (Iterate i from 1 to numiters): If i==1 or i % testfreq == 0, run test step and generate plots. If i==1 or i % savefreq == 0, save checkpoint and pickle eta. Call trainpstep with raysshard, raylumtargetshard, Xregshard, optstate, rendereta, lossfn, randkey. Log training loss. Formulas: Learning Rate Schedule: \text{lr}(x) = \exp\left( \ln(\text{lr\init}) \cdot \left(1 - \frac{x}{\text{num\iters}}\right) + \ln(\text{lr\final}) \cdot \frac{x}{\text{num\iters}} \right) Where x is the current iteration. Positional Encoding: \text{posenc}(x, \text{deg}) = \text{concat}\left(x, \sin\left([x \cdot \text{scales}, x \cdot \text{scales} + \frac{\pi}{2}]\right)\right) Where \text{scales} = [2^0, 2^1, \dots, 2^{\text{deg}-1}]. Emission Prediction: \text{emission}(\text{ray\pos}) = \frac{\exp(\text{logpdf}(\text{ray\pos}))}{\text{damp}} Where \text{logpdf} is computed from Gaussian distributions defined by sourcelocs and covs. Loss Function: The loss combines luminance reconstruction error and boundary regularization: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{lum}} + \lambda \cdot \mathcal{L}{\text{bd}} Where \lambda = \text{lam} and \mathcal{L}{\text{bd}} penalizes deviation from bdval at boundary points Xreg. Parameters: numiters: 50000. batchsize: 4096. lrinit: 1e-4. lrfinal: 5e-6. testfreq: 100. savefreq: 100. lam: 0.1 (gas) or 1.0 (nf). bdval: 1.0003 (gas) or 1.0 (nf). seed: 0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Use float32 for JAX operations. Ensure svals and ray positions are within valid bounds for interpolation. Boundaries: Xreg must correctly identify boundary points to apply regularization effectively. Degenerate Input: If covs are singular, eigh may fail; ensure positive definite covariance matrices. Memory: Sharding data across devices is critical for large batches (4096 rays). Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Training Loop
head: NeRF Training Pipeline, RtStereoHumanModel Training Loop, Training Loop & Data Fetching
body: The Training Loop is the main optimization procedure for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), orchestrating data loading, ray sampling, model forward passes, loss calculation, and parameter updates. It solves the problem of iteratively refining a differentiable radiance field representation to match observed input images. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Training Ray Batching by managing the high-level control flow (epochs, validation, checkpointing) rather than just the geometry of ray selection, and from Camera Pose Optimization by typically assuming fixed camera poses unless explicitly extended. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Training dataset (images, poses, intrinsics), model architecture (NeRF MLP/Gaussian Splatting), optimizer configuration (learning rate, weight decay), and hyperparameters (batch size, epochs, near/far bounds). Outputs: Trained model weights, optimizer state, and optionally rendered validation/test images. Data Structures: Batch: A dictionary or object containing tensors for image data (lmain, rmain for stereo; or single view), camera parameters (intrinsics K, extrinsics P), and metadata (view indices, bounds). Ray Bundle: A flat array of rays, where each ray is defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, concatenated with the ground truth RGB color \mathbf{c} at the sampled pixel. Metrics: Accumulators for L1 loss, SSIM, and Chamfer distance. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Load training and validation datasets using getnerfdatasets. Create the NeRF model and optimizer via createmodel(cfg) or createnerf(args). Initialize the learning rate scheduler (e.g., LambdaLR or OneCycleLR). Initialize gradient scaler if using mixed precision. 2. Data Fetching: Fetch the next batch from trainloader. If StopIteration occurs, reset the iterator to iter(trainloader) and fetch again. Move all relevant tensors (images, camera matrices, masks) to the CUDA device. Dataset-Specific Bounds: LLFF: Near = \min(\text{bounds}) \times 0.9, Far = \max(\text{bounds}) \times 1.0 (or 0/1 if nondc). Blender: Near = 2.0, Far = 6.0. DeepVoxels: Near = \text{hemi\R} - 1.0, Far = \text{hemi\R} + 1.0. 3. Ray Sampling: Sample random pixels from the ground truth image. Generate a ray bundle from these pixels using camera intrinsics and extrinsics. If batching is enabled, stack rays and concatenate with RGB values, then reshape into a flat array. Parameter: Nrand (number of random rays per batch). 4. Forward Pass: Pass the ray bundle through the model with istrain=True. The model renders the scene, producing predicted RGB colors and optionally depth/alpha. Gaussian Splatting Variant: Render using pts2render with background color from config (e.g., (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)). 5. Loss Calculation: Compute the primary rendering loss (e.g., L1 or MSE) between predicted and ground truth RGB. Compute structural similarity (SSIM) loss. Optional Regularization: Chamfer Loss: If enabled, extract valid points from left/right XYZ, sample 10,000 points, and compute chamfer distance. Total Loss Formula: \text{Loss} = 0.8 \times L1 + 0.2 \times (1 - \text{SSIM}) + 0.5 \times \text{Chamfer Loss}. Adaptive/Two-Phase: Use adaptive rendering loss weights or two-phase supervision to balance low-frequency structure and high-frequency details. 6. Backpropagation and Optimization: Scale the loss using GradScaler if mixed precision is active. Perform backward pass: loss.backward(). Unscale gradients and clip them to a global norm of 1.0. Step the optimizer: optimizer.step(). Step the learning rate scheduler. Update the gradient scaler. Zero gradients: optimizer.zerograd(). 7. Logging and Validation: Accumulate loss metrics (L1, SSIM, Chamfer). Print averages every 100 steps. If totalsteps % evalfreq == 0: Set model to eval mode. Run evaluation (runeval()) on validation set. Set model back to train mode. Freeze BatchNorm layers if applicable (e.g., in Raft-Stereo). 8. Checkpointing and Rendering: If epoch % checkpointinterval == 0, save model and optimizer state. If epoch % renderinterval == 0 and epoch > 0, render test images using surround cameras. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainingloop(model, trainloader, valloader, optimizer, scheduler, cfg): """ Main training loop for NeRF. """ totalsteps = 0 scaler = GradScaler(enabled=cfg.mixedprecision) for epoch in range(cfg.startepoch, cfg.numepochs): for batch in trainloader: image = batch['image'].to(device='cuda') camera = batch['camera'].to(device='cuda') rays, gtrgb = samplerays(image, camera, cfg.Nrand) with autocast(enabled=cfg.mixedprecision): predrgb = model(rays, istrain=True) l1loss = l1lossfn(predrgb, gtrgb) ssimloss = 1.0 - ssimfn(predrgb, gtrgb) chamferloss = 0.0 if cfg.ifchamfer and totalsteps > cfg.iterfrom: chamferloss = computechamferloss(batch) totalloss = 0.8 l1loss + 0.2 ssimloss + 0.5 chamferloss scaler.scale(totalloss).backward() scaler.unscale(optimizer) clipgradnorm(model.parameters(), maxnorm=1.0) scaler.step(optimizer) scaler.update() optimizer.zerograd() totalsteps += 1 if totalsteps % 100 == 0: logmetrics(l1loss, ssimloss, chamferloss) scheduler.step() if totalsteps % cfg.evalfreq == 0: model.eval() runeval(valloader) model.train() if epoch % cfg.checkpointinterval == 0: savecheckpoint(model, optimizer, epoch) if epoch % cfg.renderinterval == 0 and epoch > 0: rendertestimages(model) class GradScaler: def init(self, enabled): self.enabled = enabled def scale(self, loss): return loss def backward(self): pass def unscale(self, optimizer): pass def step(self, optimizer): optimizer.step() def update(self): pass def samplerays(image, camera, nrand): # Samples nrand random pixels and constructs ray origins/directions return rays, gtrgb def l1lossfn(pred, target): return torch.mean(torch.abs(pred - target)) def ssimfn(pred, target): return 1.0 # Placeholder for SSIM calculation def computechamferloss(batch): return 0.0 def logmetrics(l1, ssim, chamfer): pass def runeval(valloader): pass def savecheckpoint(model, optimizer, epoch): pass def rendertestimages(model): pass MVDream is a guidance method that fine-tunes Stable Diffusion with 3D-aware components trained on Objaverse to improve multi-view consistency and alleviate the Janus problem in text-to-3D generation. It provides gradient guidance for 3D optimization by encoding RGB images and camera poses into a multi-view diffusion model, predicting noise, and stepping the DDIM scheduler. Unlike standard Stable Diffusion guidance which treats views independently, MVDream explicitly conditions on camera poses to enforce geometric coherence across multiple viewpoints. Diffusion-Based Guidance for Radiance Field Optimization uses the score function of a pretrained 2D diffusion model to provide gradient signals that guide the optimization of a differentiable radiance field parametrization z = g(\theta) towards the mode of a conditional probability distribution p(zt | y). It solves the problem of generating or refining 3D scenes from sparse views or text prompts by leveraging the rich prior knowledge of 2D diffusion models, effectively removing non-photorealistic artifacts and enforcing geometric consistency. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like VCCNF Training Loop by relying on a frozen, pre-trained diffusion prior rather than a learned multi-view consistency network, and from MVDream Multi-View Diffusion Guidance by typically using a single-view or text-conditioned 2D model without explicit multi-view joint training. Specific Architecture Training Procedures define the optimization loops and configuration strategies required to train distinct radiance field architectures, addressing their unique convergence challenges and data requirements. Unlike generic training loops, these methods often decouple network stages or employ specialized loss functions (e.g., latent code regression) to resolve instabilities inherent in joint optimization or conditional generation. This article details the supervision strategy for optimizing a hybrid lighting representation that combines a volumetric lighting field with a parametric sky model for street scenes. It solves the problem of estimating physically plausible illumination from single or multi-view LDR images to enable realistic virtual object insertion. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its explicit separation of sky and volumetric lighting components, supervised via a pre-trained sky modeling network and adversarial feedback from object insertion realism rather than pure photometric consistency alone. Parameters: valCamerasCount (int, default 100), testCamerasCount (int, default 200), grayLized (bool, default true). Layout: Render class fields include renderRes (Image); groundTruth, traincameras, valcameras, testcameras (Image/Camera); valCamerasCount (int, default 100); testCamerasCount (int, default 200); grayLized (bool, default true); datasetSize (int); scene (ObjectScene); ray (rays); sceneOptimizer (Optimizer); currentHierarchy (int); trainingProcessIdx (int, default 0); sampleRaysIndexGPU, sampleRaysIndexHost (int); idx (int); config (Configuration). Definition: A design choice where the input features to the importance predictor are detached from the gradient computation to prevent trivial solutions and simplify loss scaling. Parameter: Importance predictor loss weight is not required as a separate hyperparameter because stop gradient decouples it from the main loss, allowing Adam to scale them independently. Pitfall: Without stop gradient, gradients could push the proposer and importance predictor toward a trivial solution where bad samples are predicted as unimportant to minimize loss. Definition: A mechanism that adaptively learns rendering loss weights to align frequency relationships between PE and pixel supervision. Pitfall: May be unstable in the early training phase, causing global structures to resemble the baseline. Number: Improves all metrics compared to Baseline (PSNR 19.73 on DTU 3-view). Comparison: Improves local details (e.g., hands become cleaner) compared to Baseline and Model-A, but requires two-phase supervision for stable global structure learning. Definition: A rendering supervision strategy that makes NeRF optimization focus more on learning low-frequency information. Number: Improves PSNR from 19.54 (Baseline) to 19.81 (Model-A) on DTU 3-view. Comparison: Better at rendering global structures (e.g., face) compared to Baseline, but lacks local detail refinement. Step: Train the model with a train/test split by passing the --eval flag to train.py. This withholds a test set for evaluation. Step: Generate renderings for the trained model using render.py, specifying the model path. Step: Compute error metrics on the generated renderings using metrics.py, specifying the model path. Definition: An optimization acceleration technique where back-propagated prior gradients (\nablax \lambda{diff} L{diff}) are cached and reused for multiple Adam steps on scene codes, while rendering gradients (\nablax \lambda{rend} L{rend}) are recomputed in each step. Step: In the outer loop, compute prior gradients g{xdiff} once per scene batch. Step: In the inner loop, compute new rendering gradients g{xrend} for the current ray batch. Step: Add the cached prior gradient g{xdiff} to the new rendering gradient g{xrend} to form the update gradient gx. Step: Update scene codes using gx, allowing fewer diffusion passes than rendering passes. Step: LOD generation phase: Freeze training of submodels for 5,000 iterations, then refine them and shared global deferred MLP jointly for an additional 10,000 iterations. Parameter: Training loss weights: \lambda1 = 1.0, \lambda2 = 1.0, \lambda3 = 0.01, \lambda4 = 0.05, \lambda5 = 0.001. Sample count for sparsity loss: 2^{14} samples. Step: Train MLPs alongside the last layer of the color MLP using the RGB loss (Eq. 4), without ground truth segmentation masks. Formula: cx = \alphax c'x + (1 - \alphax) cx where c'x is the new color from the retrained last layer, cx is the original color, and \alphax is the probability of the feature being part of the edited area. Layout: Soft segmentation MLP (MLPs): Two-layer MLP. Input: 32-dimensional multiresolution hash grid feature vector f. Hidden layer: 64 neurons. Output: 1-dimensional probability \alpha. Number: Convergence time for soft segmentation: typically less than 5 seconds. Definition: A self-supervised method to train a CNN-based encoder to predict camera parameters from rendered images, used for style inversion tasks. Step: Randomly sample a camera pose and latent codes to render the output image. Step: Use a CNN-based encoder (backbone initialized with pretrained ResNet18) to read the image and predict input camera parameters based on a smoothed L1 loss function. Definition: A regularization technique applied to the camera trajectory to prevent high-frequency predictions and improve trajectory estimation by leveraging the sequential nature of camera movement. Definition: A regularization term added to the loss function to enforce smooth and continuous camera trajectory estimation across adjacent Rolling Shutter (RS) frames, addressing the issue of high-frequency predictions in vanilla RS-NeRF. Step: For each pair of adjacent trajectory vectors \vec{d}k and \vec{d}{k+1}, compute the mid-point trajectory vector \vec{d}{mid}. Formula: \mathcal {L}{s}=||\overrightarrow {\mathbf {n}}{mid} - \operatorname {mean}(\overrightarrow {\mathbf {n}}k + \overrightarrow {\mathbf {n}}{k+1})||2. where \overrightarrow {\mathbf {n}}k and \overrightarrow {\mathbf {n}}{k+1} are unit direction vectors of estimated camera trajectories for adjacent RS frames I^Rk and I^R{k+1}, and \overrightarrow {\mathbf {n}}{mid} is the unit direction vector for the camera trajectory during the exposure interval between these two frames. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of training steps and batch size. Each step involves a forward pass through the MLP/Gaussian splatter and a backward pass. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of model parameters and the batch size (storing gradients and optimizer states). Measured Performance: Varies by implementation. For example, IBRNet baseline training takes 0.33 sec/iteration with 33.3 sec/frame rendering. Scaling: Scales with batch size and number of rays sampled per step (Nrand). Larger batches improve gradient stability but increase memory usage. Strengths: Flexible, supports various loss functions (L1, SSIM, Chamfer), and integrates with standard PyTorch/TensorFlow optimization utilities. Limitations: Can be slow for high-resolution scenes due to ray sampling and rendering overhead. Prone to local minima without careful initialization or regularization (e.g., importance sampling, adaptive loss weights). When to use: Standard NeRF training for novel view synthesis. When not to use: When real-time training is required (consider MVDream or Diffusion-Based Guidance for faster convergence via priors). The NeRF training loop was introduced in the seminal paper "NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis" by Mildenhall et al. (2020). It established the standard pipeline of volumetric rendering integrated with gradient-based optimization. Subsequent works have extended this loop with various optimizations, such as importance sampling, adaptive loss weighting, and diffusion-based guidance. name: MVDream Multi-View Diffusion Guidance
head: MVDream Guidance, Multi-View Dream
body: MVDream is a guidance method that fine-tunes Stable Diffusion with 3D-aware components trained on Objaverse to improve multi-view consistency and alleviate the Janus problem in text-to-3D generation. It provides gradient guidance for 3D optimization by encoding RGB images and camera poses into a multi-view diffusion model, predicting noise, and stepping the DDIM scheduler. Unlike standard Stable Diffusion guidance which treats views independently, MVDream explicitly conditions on camera poses to enforce geometric coherence across multiple viewpoints. Inputs and Outputs Input: Text prompts, a batch of rendered RGB images (predrgb256) from the current 3D representation, and corresponding camera pose matrices. Output: Gradient signal for optimizing the 3D representation (via the latent space update). Data Structures Camera Tensor: Shape [batchsize, 16]. Created by normalizing the 4x4 camera pose matrix and flattening it. The normalization function normalizecamera is not defined in the sources. Context Dictionary: Contains: context: Text embeddings of shape [B, 77, 768]. camera: Camera tensor of shape [B, 16]. numframes: Integer, typically 4. Parameters trange: List of floats, default [0.02, 0.98]. Defines the range of noise levels. minstep = int(1000 trange[0]), maxstep = int(1000 trange[1]). guidancescale: Float, default 100. Multiplier for classifier-free guidance. Steps 1. Encode Text: Generate text embeddings. The embeddings are repeated to match the batch size of the views (typically 4). \text{pos\embeds} = \text{self.encode\text(prompts)}.repeat(4, 1, 1) 2. Convert Camera Convention: Convert camera poses to Blender convention by swapping and flipping axes. \text{camera} = \text{camera}[:, [0, 2, 1, 3]] \text{camera}[:, 1] = -1 3. Normalize Camera: Normalize the camera poses and flatten to 16 dimensions. \text{camera} = \text{normalize\camera(camera)}.view(\text{batch\size}, 16) 4. Encode Images: Encode the rendered RGB images into latent space. \text{latents} = \text{self.encode\imgs(pred\rgb\256)} 5. Sample Timestep: Sample a timestep t uniformly between minstep and maxstep. 6. Forward Model with CFG: Pass the latents, timestep, and context through the model. Split the output into conditional and unconditional predictions and combine them using classifier-free guidance. \text{noise\pred} = \text{self.model.apply\model}(\text{latent\model\input}, t, \text{context}) \text{noise\pred\uncond}, \text{noise\pred\cond} = \text{noise\pred.chunk}(2) \text{noise\pred} = \text{noise\pred\uncond} + \text{guidance\scale} \times (\text{noise\pred\cond} - \text{noise\pred\uncond}) 7. Step Scheduler: Update the latents using the DDIM scheduler. \text{latents} = \text{self.scheduler.step}(\text{noise\pred}, t, \text{latents}).\text{prev\sample} Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mvdreamguidancestep(model, scheduler, encodetext, encodeimgs, normalizecamera, prompts, predrgb256, cameraposes, batchsize, guidancescale=100, trange=(0.02, 0.98)): """ Performs one step of MVDream guidance. Args: model: The fine-tuned Stable Diffusion model. scheduler: The DDIM scheduler. encodetext: Function to encode text prompts. encodeimgs: Function to encode RGB images to latents. normalizecamera: Function to normalize camera poses. prompts: List of text prompts. predrgb256: Rendered RGB images tensor [B, 4, 3, 256, 256] (assuming 4 views). cameraposes: Camera pose matrices tensor [B, 4, 4, 4]. batchsize: Number of prompts. guidancescale: CFG scale. trange: Tuple (min, max) for timestep sampling. Returns: latents: Updated latents. """ # 1. Encode text prompts # Repeat embeddings for the number of views (4) posembeds = encodetext(prompts) posembeds = posembeds.repeat(4, 1, 1) # 2. Convert camera to Blender convention # cameraposes shape: [B, 4, 4, 4] -> [B, 4, 16] after flatten # Note: The source code shows camera[:, [0, 2, 1, 3]] which implies a specific axis permutation # before flattening or on the flattened representation. # Based on: camera = camera[:, [0, 2, 1, 3]]; camera[:, 1] = -1 # This suggests the input might be pre-flattened or the indexing applies to the view dimension. # Assuming cameraposes is [B, 4, 16] for the indexing to work as shown in snippet: # If cameraposes is [B, 4, 4, 4], we must flatten first or the indexing is on the last dim. # The snippet camera[:, [0, 2, 1, 3]] on a [B, 4, 16] tensor would index the 4 views. # Let's assume the standard pipeline: Flatten poses to [B, 4, 16] first. # Reshape poses to [B, 4, 16] if not already if cameraposes.dim() == 4: camera = cameraposes.view(batchsize, -1, 16) else: camera = cameraposes # Apply Blender convention swap and flip # The source code camera[:, [0, 2, 1, 3]] suggests swapping the view indices? # No, usually [0,2,1,3] is for axis permutation in a 4-element vector. # However, the snippet camera[:, [0, 2, 1, 3]] is applied to camera which is then viewed as [B, 16]. # This implies camera was [B, 4, 4] or similar before flattening? # Let's follow the source code logic strictly: # 1. camera[:, [0, 2, 1, 3]] -> This permutes the last dimension if shape is [..., 4]. # 2. camera[:, 1] = -1 -> This flips the second element of the last dimension. # 3. normalizecamera(camera) -> Normalizes the 4x4 matrix. # 4. view(batchsize, 16) -> Flattens. # Re-interpreting code: # camera is likely [B, 4, 4, 4] or [B, 4, 16] initially? # "camera = camera[:, [0, 2, 1, 3]]" on a tensor with 4 views would select views. # But "camera[:, 1] = -1" suggests indexing into the pose structure. # Standard Blender convention: Y and Z axes are swapped/flipped. # Let's assume camera passed to this function is [B, 4, 4, 4] (B batches, 4 views, 4x4 matrix). # Permute axes of the 4x4 matrix for each view? Janus Problem: While MVDream alleviates the Janus problem, it does not completely eliminate it due to the ill-posed nature of text-to-3D generation. GALA3D is a two-stage method for 3D scene generation that leverages both object-level and scene-level models to achieve realistic composition. It addresses the challenge of generating coherent 3D scenes by first synthesizing individual objects and then composing them into a global environment. Unlike single-stage text-to-3D methods, GALA3D separates the generation of local geometry (objects) from global layout (scenes), using MVDream for object synthesis and a scene-level diffusion model for composition. RealmDreamer utilizes diffusion priors from inpainting and depth estimation models to generate different viewpoints of a scene iteratively. Multi-View Consistency: MVDream significantly improves multi-view consistency and geometry completeness (e.g., Janus-free ostrich) compared to standard guidance. Prompt Adherence: It sacrifices fine-grained prompt adherence on complex scenes. Performance: The method relies on the computational cost of the Stable Diffusion model and the DDIM scheduler steps. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Better 3D geometry and consistency. Limitations: Loss of detail for complex prompts; incomplete elimination of Janus problem. MVDream was proposed as a concurrent work to improve text-to-3D generation by fine-tuning Stable Diffusion with 3D-aware components trained on Objaverse. It aims to enhance multi-view consistency and alleviate the Janus problem. The method is cited in the context of Gaussian Splatting for text-to-3D generation and is part of the broader family of diffusion-based guidance methods for radiance field optimization. name: GALA3D
head: GALA3D
body: GALA3D is a two-stage method for 3D scene generation that leverages both object-level and scene-level models to achieve realistic composition. It addresses the challenge of generating coherent 3D scenes by first synthesizing individual objects and then composing them into a global environment. Unlike single-stage text-to-3D methods, GALA3D separates the generation of local geometry (objects) from global layout (scenes), using MVDream for object synthesis and a scene-level diffusion model for composition. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Text prompt describing the desired scene. Output: A composed 3D scene representation (e.g., point cloud or Gaussian splats) containing multiple objects arranged in a scene. Data Structures: Object-level representation: Generated by MVDream, typically a point cloud or 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation. Scene-level representation: A collection of object-level representations arranged in a spatial layout. Steps: 1. Object Generation: Use the object-level text-to-3D model MVDream [246] to generate realistic 3D objects from the text prompt. MVDream provides multi-view diffusion guidance to ensure geometric consistency. 2. Scene Composition: Use a scene-level diffusion model to compose the generated objects into a coherent 3D scene. This stage handles the spatial arrangement and interaction between objects. 3. Refinement (Optional): Some implementations may include a stage to remove outliers in the point cloud and refine the 3DGS representation through two-stage optimization (coarse training followed by refinement). Parameters: Text prompt: Defines the semantic content of the scene. MVDream model: Pre-trained text-to-3D model. Scene-level diffusion model: Pre-trained model for scene composition. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Outliers in the generated point cloud may need removal to ensure clean geometry. The quality of the final scene depends heavily on the accuracy of the object-level generation and the effectiveness of the scene-level composition. This process simultaneously generates multiple views of the object as well as its 3D model. During inference, the viewset is initialized with Gaussian noise. The model iteratively denoises the viewset by applying a reconstruction model. Each image Ii in the viewset is replaced with Ii^t = \alphat Ii + \sigmat \epsiloni where t is the noising schedule, \alphat and \sigmat = \sqrt{1 - \alphat^2} are the noise level, and \epsiloni is a random Normal noise vector. This approach boosts scalability by increasing the amount of 2D information lifted to 3D and allows for larger model and batch sizes during training due to memory savings. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: The Lightplane-augmented variant significantly reduces memory usage, allowing for increased model and batch sizes during training. Performance: Benchmarks show improvements in scalability and speed for 3D tasks. Strengths: Enables generation of complex scenes with multiple objects; scalable to large-scale 3D models. Limitations: Requires two separate models (object-level and scene-level); quality depends on the pre-trained models. GALA3D was introduced to explore 3D scene generation by combining object-level and scene-level generation processes. It builds on the idea of using text-to-3D models like MVDream for object synthesis and extends it to scene-level composition. The method is part of the broader effort to improve the realism and coherence of generated 3D scenes.
