name: Diffusion-Based Guidance for Radiance Field Optimization
head: SDS-like, Score Distillation Sampling, Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) Loss, Stable Diffusion Training Guidance
body:
Diffusion-Based Guidance for Radiance Field Optimization uses the score function of a pretrained 2D diffusion model to provide gradient signals that guide the optimization of a differentiable radiance field parametrization z = g(	heta) towards the mode of a conditional probability distribution p(zt | y). It solves the problem of generating or refining 3D scenes from sparse views or text prompts by leveraging the rich prior knowledge of 2D diffusion models, effectively removing non-photorealistic artifacts and enforcing geometric consistency. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like VCCNF Training Loop by relying on a frozen, pre-trained diffusion prior rather than a learned multi-view consistency network, and from MVDream Multi-View Diffusion Guidance by typically using a single-view or text-conditioned 2D model without explicit multi-view joint training. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A differentiable radiance field parametrization 	heta (e.g., NeRF weights or 3D Gaussian splatting parameters G), a text prompt y (or reference image), and a diffusion model \epsilon\phi (typically Stable Diffusion). Outputs: Updated parameters 	heta that minimize the SDS loss, resulting in a refined radiance field. Data Structures: Radiance Field Parameters (	heta): For NeRF: Network weights defining density and color fields. For 3DGS: Position \mathbf{x}, covariance \Sigma (or scale/rotation), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic coefficients for color. Diffusion Model State: Frozen weights \phi of a UNet-based diffusion model (e.g., Stable Diffusion 2.1). Latent Space: For latent diffusion models, images are encoded into latents \mathbf{z}0 of shape [B, 4, 64, 64] (for 512x512 input) via a VAE encoder. Numbered Steps: 1. Viewpoint Sampling: Sample random viewpoints around the center of the scene estimated from input cameras. For 3DGS, \kappa is sampled uniformly in a region (e.g., 6m^2) around the origin with random rotation about the vertical axis. 2. Rendering: Render an image \hat{I}p (or latent \mathbf{z}0) from the current radiance field parameters 	heta at the sampled viewpoint p. 3. Noise Addition: Add noise to the rendered image/latent. In pixel space: \hat{I} = N(\hat{\alpha} I', (1-\hat{\alpha})I), where N is noise addition, \hat{\alpha} is the cumulative product of one minus the variance schedule, I' is the noisy image, and I is the clean image. In latent space: Sample noise \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) and compute \mathbf{z}t = \sqrt{ ar{\alpha}t} \mathbf{z}0 + \sqrt{1 -  ar{\alpha}t} \epsilon. 4. Noise Prediction: Pass the noisy latent/image \mathbf{z}t (and timestep t, text embedding y) to the frozen diffusion model to predict the noise component \hat{\epsilon}\phi(\mathbf{z}t, y, t). If using Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG), duplicate inputs for conditional and unconditional branches. Compute \hat{\epsilon} = \hat{\epsilon}{uncond} + s (\hat{\epsilon}{cond} - \hat{\epsilon}{uncond}), where s is the guidance scale (default 100). 5. Gradient Computation: Compute the SDS gradient with respect to the radiance field parameters 	heta. The core formula is: 
abla	heta L{SDS} = \mathbb{E}{t, \epsilon} [\gamma(t) (\hat{\epsilon}\phi(\mathbf{z}t, y, t) - \epsilon)  rac{\partial \mathbf{z}0}{\partial 	heta}] where \gamma(t) is a weighting function dependent on timestep t, \hat{\epsilon}\phi is the predicted noise, \epsilon is the actual sampled noise, and  rac{\partial \mathbf{z}0}{\partial 	heta} is the gradient of the rendered output with respect to 	heta. Alternative formulation in z0 space: 
abla	heta L{SDS} = \gamma(t) \sqrt{ rac{ ar{\alpha}t}{1 -  ar{\alpha}t}} (\mathbf{z}0 - \hat{\mathbf{z}}0)  rac{\partial \mathbf{z}0}{\partial 	heta} where \hat{\mathbf{z}}0 = (\mathbf{z}t - \sqrt{1 -  ar{\alpha}t} \hat{\epsilon}\phi) / \sqrt{ ar{\alpha}t} is the one-step denoised estimate. For 3DGS parameters G: L{SDS} = 
ablaG \mathbb{E}[(\epsilon\phi(\hat{I}p; 	ilde{I}p) - \epsilon)  rac{\partial \hat{I}p}{\partial G}] where 	ilde{I}p is the denoised image. 6. Parameter Update: Perform gradient descent on 	heta using the computed gradient. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesdsloss(radiancefield, textprompt, diffusionmodel, vaeencoder, vaedecoder, timestepsampler, guidancescale): """ Computes the Score Distillation Sampling loss for a radiance field. """ # 1. Sample viewpoint viewpoint = samplerandomviewpoint(radiancefield.scenecenter) # 2. Render image from current radiance field renderedimage = radiancefield.render(viewpoint) # 3. Encode to latent space (if using Latent Diffusion) # If using pixel-space diffusion, skip encoding/decoding or treat image as latent latents = vaeencoder(renderedimage) # 4. Sample timestep and noise t = timestepsampler.sample() noise = torch.randnlike(latents) # 5. Add noise to latents # Assuming scheduler provides addnoise method consistent with DDIM/DDPM noisylatents = diffusionmodel.scheduler.addnoise(latents, noise, t) # 6. Prepare inputs for Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) # Duplicate latents and timesteps latentmodelinput = torch.cat([noisylatents, noisylatents]) timesteps = torch.cat([t, t]) # Prepare text embeddings # Positive embedding from textprompt posembed = diffusionmodel.textencoder(textprompt) # Negative embedding (empty string or null) negembed = diffusionmodel.textencoder("") # Concatenate embeddings for CFG embeddings = torch.cat([posembed, negembed]) # 7. Predict noise using UNet noisepred = diffusionmodel.unet(latentmodelinput, timesteps, encoderhiddenstates=embeddings).sample # 8. Apply Classifier-Free Guidance noisepredcond, noisepreduncond = torch.chunk(noisepred, 2, dim=0) noisepred = noisepreduncond + guidancescale (noisepredcond - noisepreduncond) # 9. Compute Gradient # Weighting factor w(t) w = (1 - diffusionmodel.scheduler.alphas[t]).view(1, 1, 1, 1) # Gradient signal: w (predictednoise - actualnoise) grad = w (noisepred - noise) # Handle numerical instability (NaNs) grad = torch.nantonum(grad) # 10. Compute Target for MSE Loss (equivalent to gradient step) # Target is the denoised latent target = (latents - grad).detach() # 11. Compute Loss # MSE between current latents and target loss = 0.5 F.mseloss(latents.float(), target, reduction='sum') / latents.shape[0] # 12. Backpropagate to radiance field parameters # Note: In practice, we compute grad w.r.t latents, then chain rule through rendering # gradlatents = dloss / dlatents # gradradiance = gradlatents dlatents / dradiance # Here we assume the framework handles the chain rule via autograd # If implementing manually: # gradlatents = (latents - target) / latents.shape[0] # renderedimage.backward(gradlatents) # This updates radiancefield parameters return loss Parameters: guidancescale: CFG scale multiplier. Default value in code: 100. trange: List [0.02, 0.98] used to compute minstep and maxstep as fractions of numtraintimesteps. stepratio: Float controlling timestep selection. 1.0 maps to minstep (early diffusion), 0.0 maps to maxstep (late diffusion). SDS Loss Weight: Typical value: 5 	imes 10^{-4}. Diffusion Model: Stable-Diffusion version 2.1 is commonly used. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: NaN Values: Gradient computation can produce NaN values due to numerical instability in the diffusion process or guidance scaling. The code explicitly clamps NaNs to 0 using torch.nantonum(grad). Over-saturation and Over-smoothing: SDS is known to encounter issues such as over-saturation and over-smoothing, leading to "melted" or blurry details. Local Patch Optimization: Directly applying SDS on NeRF renders may produce blurred details and fail to converge on detailed reconstructions because supervision is only provided over a small local patch of rays in each training step. This method addresses quality impairments in 3D generation caused by the discrepancy between the diffusion prior and the training process of the diffusion model. It sets itself apart from standard diffusion-guided approaches by introducing an iterative optimization loop that jointly updates the 3D model and specific learnable parameters within the diffusion guidance mechanism, rather than treating the diffusion model as a static prior. SKED is a method for editing a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) scene using guidance from 2D sketches provided from multiple views, in addition to an input text prompt. It addresses the problem of localized 3D editing, specifically object insertion and replacement, by ensuring that edits are confined to sketched regions while preserving the unedited parts of the original scene. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Inpainting SDS Loss by its explicit use of multi-view 2D sketches as spatial priors to define the edit region, rather than relying solely on text prompts or single-view masks. Diffusion-Based 3D Inpainting is a method that utilizes a self-trained 2D inpainting diffusion model to reconstruct missing or masked regions in a 3D scene represented by a radiance field. It solves the problem of 3D scene completion or object removal by combining explicit reconstruction constraints for visible areas with implicit diffusion priors for occluded areas. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Inpainting SDS Loss by its specific reliance on a self-trained 2D inpainting model rather than a generic pre-trained one, and from SKED by its focus on distilling 2D inpainting results into a single 3D scene via iterative refinement. This method performs 3D inpainting of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) by substituting a single reference view with a diffusion-generated target view, then optimizing the NeRF to match the new view while maintaining consistency with the remaining input views. It solves the problem of inserting or modifying objects in a 3D scene without requiring multi-view supervision for the target content. It differs from Inpainting SDS Loss by using a deterministic 2D inpainting prior (Stable Diffusion) followed by a bilateral solver for residual smoothing, rather than relying solely on gradient-based SDS guidance during optimization. This method defines the data preprocessing pipeline and training configuration for a fine-tuned Stable Diffusion 1.5 model used as a semantic prior in Street View Synthesis (SGD). It solves the problem of adapting a 2D diffusion model to guide 3D radiance field optimization by ensuring the input data distribution matches the model's expectations and by enabling classifier-free guidance. It sets itself apart from general diffusion training by specifically addressing the aspect ratio distortion of wide-angle street view images (KITTI-360) and enforcing a perspective gap between reference and training views to improve robustness. Two-Plane Diffusion Model (TPDM) is a method for solving 3D inverse problems and generating 3D voxel volumes by training two separate 2D diffusion models on perpendicular planes and alternating their usage during the denoising process to maintain 3D consistency. It avoids the curse of dimensionality by assuming a 3D distribution is the product of 2D distributions, allowing it to handle 3D volumes without using a 3D diffusion model. Unlike Diffusion-Based Guidance for Radiance Field Optimization which guides optimization via gradients, TPDM performs conditional sampling directly on the volume using a primary model for measurement consistency and an auxiliary model for cross-plane consistency. Score Distillation Loss Modifications are techniques that adapt the standard Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) gradient signal to address specific artifacts such as "black holes" in masked regions, incomplete object geometry, or limited high-frequency detail in super-resolution tasks. They set themselves apart from the parent Diffusion-Based Guidance for Radiance Field Optimization by altering the conditioning inputs (masks, background prompts), the diffusion trajectory (interval steps, renoising schedules), or the loss formulation itself to improve geometric consistency and texture fidelity. Uses a reference image as a condition alongside the text prompt to guide generation, allowing the radiance field to adopt visual characteristics (e.g., material, style) from the reference image. A text-to-image guidance approach using DeepFloyd IF, which features an Imagen-like architecture and a T-5 text encoder for stronger text understanding. It requires downsampling the input image to 64×64 pixels before passing it to the model due to its modular cascaded design. This produces better text-3D alignment than StableDiffusion but yields blurrier assets because of the mandatory downsampling. Incorporates fine-grained language features through MaskCLIP and FeatUp to enable open-vocabulary querying. It introduces Coherent Score Distillation Sampling (CSD) to ensure edits remain consistent across multiple views. Maps each edited 2D image to a latent edit code vector to characterize diverse edits and control NeRF-to-NeRF translation. It extracts a 64-dimensional latent edit code from an edited 2D image using a fixed, pre-trained VAE encoder from Stable Diffusion, passed through a 3-layer MLP network that estimates the mean and variance of a Gaussian distribution. The edit code z \in \mathbb{R}^{64} is sampled from this distribution and used to condition the translated NeRF for novel view synthesis. It is integrated into the GenN2N pipeline for text-driven editing, super-resolution, inpainting, and colorization tasks. Iteratively updates initially generated voxels V by rendering viewpoints and applying SDS loss on each image independently. For latent diffusion models, the noise prediction step is applied after encoding r(V, \kappa) to the LDM’s latent space. It optimizes L{SDS} with negative guidance using classifier-free guidance, where the unconditional embedding is replaced by an artifact conditioning embedding to sample away from images with artifacts. The viewpoint \kappa is sampled uniformly in a 6m^2 region around the origin with random rotation about the vertical axis. Utilizes a ControlNet-based network for texture refinement and ensures consistency between different viewpoints with view-consistent geometric guidance. Replaces the pre-trained diffusion model used in SDS loss by Zero-1-to-3 XL for image condition. It adds losses between the input image and the corresponding rendered image in the input view to make generation more consistent with the input image. Time Complexity: Each optimization step requires a forward pass through the radiance field (rendering), a forward pass through the diffusion model (UNet), and a backward pass through the diffusion model to compute the gradient w.r.t. the latent/image. The complexity is dominated by the diffusion model inference, which is typically O(N{timesteps} 	imes N{UNet\layers}). Memory Complexity: Requires storing the radiance field parameters, the diffusion model weights (frozen), and intermediate activations for the diffusion process. For latent diffusion, memory is reduced compared to pixel-space diffusion. Measured Performance: SDS has demonstrated remarkable results in Text-to-3D generation. However, it is known to encounter issues such as over-saturation and over-smoothing. Enabling SDS loss after two-thirds of the total iterations helps stabilize the scene structure before applying the prior. Scaling: Performance scales with the quality of the 2D diffusion prior. Using models with stronger text understanding (e.g., DeepFloyd IF with T-5) improves text-3D alignment but may reduce texture sharpness due to input resolution constraints. Strengths: Leverages powerful 2D priors; works with sparse input views; enables text-driven generation. Limitations: Prone to over-saturation and over-smoothing; computationally expensive due to diffusion model inference; may suffer from local patch optimization issues in NeRFs. When to use: When generating 3D scenes from text prompts or sparse views, or when refining existing radiance fields with a 2D diffusion prior. When not to use: When high-frequency detail preservation is critical without post-processing, or when computational resources are severely limited. Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) was introduced as an optimization objective that uses the score function of pretrained diffusion models to guide the optimization of a differentiable image parametrization. It has demonstrated remarkable results in Text-to-3D generation. The method relies on the relationship between the predicted noise component \epsilon and the score function 
abla{zt} \log p(zt | y). It is commonly implemented using Stable Diffusion models. name: Iterative Optimization with Learnable Parameters for Diffusion-Guided Radiance Fields
head: Iterative Optimization with Learnable Parameters
body: This method addresses quality impairments in 3D generation caused by the discrepancy between the diffusion prior and the training process of the diffusion model. It sets itself apart from standard diffusion-guided approaches by introducing an iterative optimization loop that jointly updates the 3D model and specific learnable parameters within the diffusion guidance mechanism, rather than treating the diffusion model as a static prior. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A frozen pre-trained diffusion model (e.g., Stable Diffusion), a 3D radiance field representation (e.g., 3D Gaussian Splatting or NeRF), and a text prompt. Output: An optimized 3D radiance field. Data Structures: Learnable Unconditional Embedding (e{uncond}): A vector parameter replacing or augmenting the standard unconditional embedding in the classifier-free guidance formula. Network Parameters (\theta{net}): Additional parameters added to the diffusion network, such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) weights. 3D Model Parameters (\theta{3D}): The parameters defining the radiance field (e.g., Gaussian centers, covariances, colors). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the 3D model parameters \theta{3D}, the learnable unconditional embedding e{uncond}, and the additional network parameters \theta{net} (e.g., LoRA matrices). 2. Sampling: Render an image from the current 3D model \theta{3D} from a random viewpoint. 3. Diffusion Guidance: Pass the rendered image and the text prompt into the frozen diffusion model. Compute the noise prediction using classifier-free guidance, but substitute the standard unconditional embedding with the learnable e{uncond} and apply the updated network parameters \theta{net}. 4. Loss Calculation: Calculate the Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) or similar loss based on the difference between the predicted noise and the actual noise added to the image. 5. Optimization: Perform gradient descent to update \theta{3D}, e{uncond}, and \theta{net} simultaneously. 6. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-5 until convergence. Formulas: The classifier-free guidance formula is modified to include the learnable parameters. Let \epsilon\theta be the noise prediction network. The guidance signal typically involves: \epsilon{pred} = \epsilon\theta(zt, c, t) + w \cdot (\epsilon\theta(zt, c, t) - \epsilon\theta(zt, u, t)) Where: zt is the noisy latent/image at timestep t. c is the conditional text embedding. u is replaced by the learnable unconditional embedding e{uncond}. The network \epsilon\theta includes the additional parameters \theta{net} (e.g., LoRA). w is the guidance scale. Parameters: Guidance scale w: Not given in the sources. Learning rates for \theta{3D}, e{uncond}, and \theta{net}: Not given in the sources. LoRA rank: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Not given in the sources. Degenerate Input: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Render image from 3D model image = render(theta3D, viewpoint) # 2. Encode image to latent space (if using latent diffusion) zt = encode(image) # 3. Add noise for diffusion step noise = samplenoise() znoisy = addnoise(zt, noise, timestep) # 4. Predict noise using diffusion model with learnable parameters # The unconditional embedding is replaced by euncond # The network uses thetanet (e.g., LoRA) epsiloncond = diffusionmodel.predictnoise(znoisy, textprompt, timestep, unconditionalembedding=euncond, networkparams=thetanet) # 5. Compute SDS Loss # Standard SDS formula using epsiloncond loss = computesdsloss(epsiloncond, noise, timestep) # 6. Backpropagate and update all learnable parameters loss.backward() optimizer.step(theta3D, euncond, thetanet) optimizer.zerograd() Uses SDS for inpainting tasks. Uses kernelized expected distance for guidance. Uses EG3D synthetic data for supervision. Uses masks and background prompts for SDS. Focuses on relighting capabilities. Details on sampling algorithms. 3D inpainting using diffusion. Uses reference images for inpainting. Setup details for diffusion models. Renoises the image at each step to reduce over-saturation. Strengths and Limitations: Addresses quality impairment from diffusion prior mismatches. Not limited to 3DGS; can be applied to NeRF-based methods like VSD and CSD. When to Use: When standard diffusion guidance leads to quality issues due to prior-training mismatches. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The method was proposed by Yang et al.. It is part of the broader effort to improve 3D generation quality by aligning the diffusion prior with the 3D model training process. It is applicable to various 3D representations, including 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and NeRF-based methods. name: LucidDreamer
head: Scene Generation via Diffusion and 3DGS
body: LucidDreamer is a scene generation method that extends a single reference image (user-specified or text-generated) outward to create a full 3D environment. It distinguishes itself by combining Stable Diffusion for view inpainting with Interval Score Matching (ISM) to stabilize the optimization process, initializing a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation from a depth-aligned point cloud. Inputs: A reference image I{ref} (either user-uploaded or text-to-image generated) and a set of target camera viewpoints for scene extension. Outputs: A 3D Gaussian Splatting scene representation. Data Structures: 1. Point Cloud: A set of 3D points P = \{pi\} derived from monocular depth estimation and alignment. 2. 3DGS Representation: Defined by Gaussian parameters: mean \mu, covariance \Sigma (or scale/rotation), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color c. Steps: 1. View Synthesis via Inpainting: For each target camera view vk not covered by the reference image, generate an inpainted image I{inpaint}^k using Stable Diffusion. This fills in the "unseen regions" of the scene relative to the reference view. 2. Depth Estimation and Alignment: Perform monocular depth estimation on the inpainted views I{inpaint}^k. Align these depth maps to establish a consistent 3D point cloud P that represents the geometry of the extended scene. 3. Initialization: Use the aligned point cloud P as the initial value for the 3D Gaussian centers \mu. 4. Optimization with Interval Score Matching (ISM): Train the 3DGS representation by minimizing the rendering loss between the projected 3DGS and the inpainted images I{inpaint}^k. To stabilize training and avoid large errors associated with one-step reconstruction in standard Score Distillation Sampling (SDS), LucidDreamer replaces the standard DDPM noise prediction with DDIM inversion and introduces supervision from interval steps of the diffusion process. This technique is referred to as Interval Score Matching (ISM). The optimization minimizes a loss function \mathcal{L}: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{render} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{ISM} Where \mathcal{L}{render} is the standard photometric rendering loss and \mathcal{L}{ISM} is the interval score matching loss derived from the diffusion process. Parameters: Diffusion model: Stable Diffusion. Optimization target: 3D Gaussian Splatting. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Alignment: Inconsistent depth estimation across views can lead to geometric artifacts in the initial point cloud. One-Step Reconstruction Error: Standard SDS can suffer from large errors; ISM is specifically introduced to mitigate this. Time Complexity: High, due to iterative diffusion sampling for inpainting and 3DGS optimization. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of Gaussians and the resolution of the inpainted views. Strengths: Enables scene extension from a single image; ISM improves stability over standard SDS. Limitations: Relies on the quality of monocular depth estimation and Stable Diffusion inpainting; may struggle with complex occlusions or inconsistent geometry. When to use: When a full 3D scene is needed from a single reference image. When not to use: When high-fidelity geometry is required without diffusion-based approximations. LucidDreamer was introduced as a method for 3D scene generation based on a reference image. It is cited in recent surveys on 3D Gaussian Splatting as a key approach for extending scenes outward. The method leverages Stable Diffusion for inpainting and 3DGS for representation. name: Diffusion Sampling and Denoising Mechanisms
body: This family defines the iterative algorithms and neural architectures used to reverse the diffusion process, transforming random noise into structured radiance field representations or refining existing NeRF renderings. It sets itself apart from direct optimization methods by leveraging pre-trained 2D diffusion priors (like Stable Diffusion) to guide the 3D generation or reconstruction, using noise prediction and classifier-free guidance to enforce photorealistic textures and geometry [8117-diffusion-based-guidance-for-radiance-field-optimization]. All methods in this family operate within the reverse diffusion process, where a noisy latent representation xt at timestep t is iteratively denoised to estimate the clean latent x0. The core mechanism involves a denoiser network (or a frozen pre-trained model) predicting the noise component \epsilon\theta(xt, t) or the score \nabla{xt} \log p(xt). This prediction is combined with conditional information (e.g., text embeddings or image features) via Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) to steer the generation towards the desired semantic content. The update rule generally follows the form: x{t-1} = \mu\theta(xt, t) + \sigmat \epsilon where \mu\theta is the mean estimate derived from the noise prediction and the diffusion schedule parameters (\alphat, \bar{\alpha}t), and \sigmat \epsilon represents stochastic noise (which may be zero for deterministic samplers like DDIM). In the context of radiance fields, the "latent" may be a 2D image latent (for 2D-to-3D consistency) or a 3D voxel/triplane latent (for direct 3D generation). DDIM Sampling with Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) is a deterministic (or stochastic with \eta > 0) reverse diffusion algorithm that generates samples or refines existing ones by iteratively denoising latent variables [8118-ddim-sampling-with-classifier-free-guidance.md]. It sets itself apart from standard DDPM sampling by skipping intermediate noise steps to allow for fewer sampling iterations, and by combining unconditional and conditional model predictions via a guidance scale to enhance fidelity [8118-ddim-sampling-with-classifier-free-guidance.md]. In the context of radiance field optimization, it serves as a denoising mechanism to refine NeRF renderings or guide 3D generation by leveraging 2D diffusion priors [8118-ddim-sampling-with-classifier-free-guidance.md]. The DDPM Denoise Function Network is a 3D convolutional neural network that predicts the noise to be removed from a latent radiance field representation during the reverse diffusion process. It serves as the core denoiser in diffusion-based radiance field optimization, enabling the generation of 3D structures from noisy latent codes. It differs from sibling methods like DDIM Sampling with Classifier-Free Guidance by relying on a fixed architectural prior for noise prediction rather than explicit classifier gradients or deterministic sampling trajectories [11102-ddpm-denoise-function-network.md]. A sampling method that guides the denoising process of a diffusion model using gradients of the rendering loss against known observations to reconstruct 3D scenes from images. Combine guidance gradients g with unconditional score prediction as a correction to the denoising output \hat{x}: \hat{x} \leftarrow \hat{x} - \lambda{gd}(t) g. Use a predictor-corrector sampler to solve for x(0) by alternating between a DDIM step and multiple Langevin correction steps. \omega: Hyperparameter for SNR-based weighting, chosen as 0.5 or 0.25. \lambda{gd}: Guidance scale used to combine guidance gradients with unconditional score prediction. The integration of diffusion models into volume rendering originated from the need to enforce photorealistic priors in 3D generation and reconstruction tasks where data is sparse or ambiguous. Early works like Single-Stage Diffusion NeRF demonstrated that joint optimization of scene codes and diffusion priors could improve reconstruction quality. The use of DDIM for efficient sampling and the application of Classifier-Free Guidance [8118-ddim-sampling-with-classifier-free-guidance.md] became standard techniques to balance fidelity and diversity. The development of 3D-specific denoising networks [11102-ddpm-denoise-function-network.md] allowed for direct manipulation of volumetric latents, bridging the gap between 2D diffusion priors and 3D geometric representations. name: DDIM Sampling with Classifier-Free Guidance
head: Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models, DDIM Sampling, DDIM Sampling Step (with CFG & v-parameterization)
body: DDIM Sampling with Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) is a deterministic (or stochastic with \eta > 0) reverse diffusion algorithm that generates samples or refines existing ones by iteratively denoising latent variables. It sets itself apart from standard DDPM sampling by skipping intermediate noise steps to allow for fewer sampling iterations, and by combining unconditional and conditional model predictions via a guidance scale to enhance fidelity. In the context of radiance field optimization, it serves as a denoising mechanism to refine NeRF renderings or guide 3D generation by leveraging 2D diffusion priors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: xT: Initial latent tensor (random noise if generating; existing latent if refining). Shape: (B, C, H, W). c: Conditional embedding (e.g., text or image features). Shape: (B, D). timesteps: Sequence of timesteps to traverse, typically reversed from T to 0. unconditional\guidance\scale: Scalar multiplier for CFG (default 1.0). ddim\eta: Stochasticity parameter (default 0.0). mask: Optional inpainting mask tensor. x0: Optional original image for inpainting. Outputs: x0: Final denoised latent tensor. Intermediates: Optional list of xt and predicted \hat{x}0 at logging intervals. Data Structures: The scheduler maintains several precomputed buffers registered as CUDA tensors (float32) indexed by timestep: alphascumprod (\alphat): Cumulative product of \alpha values. alphascumprodprev (\alpha{t-1}): Previous cumulative alpha. sqrtalphascumprod (\sqrt{\alphat}): Square root of cumulative alpha. sqrtoneminusalphascumprod (\sqrt{1-\alphat}): Square root of one minus cumulative alpha. ddimsigmas (\sigmat): DDIM-specific noise scale. ddimalphas (\alphat^{DDIM}): Adjusted alphas for the DDIM schedule. ddimalphasprev (\alpha{t-1}^{DDIM}): Previous adjusted alphas. ddimsqrtoneminusalphas: \sqrt{1-\alphat^{DDIM}}. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: If xT is not provided, sample xT \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) with shape (B, C, H, 8, W, 8). Initialize the schedule: Compute ddimtimesteps using makeddimtimesteps (default discretization: uniform). Calculate derived buffers (sqrtalphascumprod, etc.) from the model's DDPM parameters. Set the scheduler timesteps: scheduler.settimesteps(numinferencesteps). 2. Conditioning Preparation: Concatenate positive and negative embeddings for CFG: \text{embeddings} = \text{concat}([\text{embeddings}{pos}, \text{embeddings}{neg}]) where each is expanded to batch size B. If unconditionalguidancescale > 1, prepare conditional and unconditional inputs for the model. 3. Iteration Loop: Iterate through timesteps in reverse order (from T to 0). Let i be the index in the reversed list, and t be the current timestep value. Dynamic Guidance (Optional): If ucgschedule is provided, set unconditionalguidancescale to ucgschedule[i]. Inpainting Mask (Optional): If mask is not None, assert x0 is provided. Compute img{orig} = q\sample(x0, t). Update current image: img = img{orig} \cdot mask + (1 - mask) \cdot img. Model Prediction: Duplicate latents for CFG: x{in} = \text{cat}([xt, xt]). Duplicate timesteps: t{in} = \text{cat}([t, t]). Pass through UNet to get predictions for unconditional and conditional branches: [e{t, uncond}, e{t, cond}] = \text{chunk}(\text{model}(x{in}, t{in}, c{in}), 2) Apply Classifier-Free Guidance: et = e{t, uncond} + \text{unconditional\guidance\scale} \cdot (e{t, cond} - e{t, uncond}) If parameterization == "v", convert model output to noise prediction: et = \text{model.predict\eps\from\z\and\v}(xt, t, \text{model\output}) Otherwise, et is the direct noise prediction. Score Correction (Optional): If scorecorrector is not None, modify et (requires parameterization == "eps"). Select Timestep Parameters: Retrieve at, a{prev}, \sigmat, \sqrt{1-at} from the precomputed buffers at index i. Predict Clean Image (\hat{x}0): If parameterization == "eps": \hat{x}0 = \frac{xt - \sqrt{1-at} \cdot et}{\sqrt{at}} If parameterization == "v": \hat{x}0 = \text{model.predict\start\from\z\and\v}(xt, t, \text{model\output}) If quantizedenoised is True, quantize \hat{x}0 via the first stage model. Compute Direction to x{t-1}: \text{dir\xt} = \sqrt{1 - a{prev} - \sigmat^2} \cdot et Sample Noise: \text{noise} = \sigmat \cdot \mathcal{N}(0, I) \cdot \text{temperature} Apply dropout if noisedropout > 0. Update Latent (x{t-1}): x{t-1} = \sqrt{a{prev}} \cdot \hat{x}0 + \text{dir\xt} + \text{noise} Record Intermediates: If i \% \text{log\every\t} == 0 or i is the last step, append x{t-1} and \hat{x}0 to intermediates. 4. Final Output: Return the final x0 (or x{t-1} after the last step). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def ddimsamplewithcfg(model, scheduler, xT, c, timesteps, unconditionalguidancescale=7.5, ddimeta=0.0, parameterization="eps", temperature=1.0, noisedropout=0.0, mask=None, x0=None, ucgschedule=None): """ Perform DDIM sampling with Classifier-Free Guidance. Args: model: UNet model with applymodel method. scheduler: Scheduler object with precomputed buffers (alphas, sigmas, etc.). xT: Initial latent tensor (B, C, H, W). c: Conditional embedding tensor (B, D). timesteps: List of timesteps to traverse (reversed order). unconditionalguidancescale: CFG scale. ddimeta: Stochasticity parameter. parameterization: "eps" or "v". temperature: Noise scaling factor. noisedropout: Probability of zeroing noise. mask: Optional inpainting mask. x0: Optional original image for inpainting. ucgschedule: Optional list of guidance scales per step. Returns: x0: Final denoised latent. """ device = xT.device b = xT.shape[0] x = xT.clone() intermediates = {'xinter': [], 'predx0': []} # 1. Prepare conditioning for CFG cin = torch.cat([c, c]) # [2B, D] for i, t in enumerate(timesteps): ts = torch.full((b,), t, device=device, dtype=torch.long) # Dynamic guidance scale if ucgschedule is not None: currentguidance = ucgschedule[i] else: currentguidance = unconditionalguidancescale # Inpainting mask application if mask is not None: assert x0 is not None, "x0 must be provided for inpainting" # qsample adds noise to x0 at timestep t sqrtalpha = scheduler.sqrtalphascumprod[t] sqrtoneminusalpha = scheduler.sqrtoneminusalphascumprod[t] noisex0 = torch.randnlike(x0) imgorig = sqrtalpha x0 + sqrtoneminusalpha noisex0 x = imgorig mask + (1. - mask) x # 2. Model Prediction with CFG xin = torch.cat([x, x]) # Duplicate for unconditional/conditional tin = torch.cat([ts, ts]) # Get raw predictions for unconditional and conditional branches modeloutput = model.applymodel(xin, tin, cin) noisepreduncond, noisepredcond = torch.chunk(modeloutput, 2) # Apply CFG formula noisepred = noisepreduncond + currentguidance (noisepredcond - noisepreduncond) # Handle v-parameterization if parameterization == "v": noisepred = model.predictepsfromzandv(x, ts, modeloutput) # 3. Select timestep parameters at = scheduler.alphas[i] aprev = scheduler.alphasprev[i] sigmat = scheduler.sigmas[i] sqrtoneminusat = scheduler.sqrtoneminusalphas[i] # 4. Predict x0 if parameterization == "eps": predx0 = (x - sqrtoneminusat noisepred) / at.sqrt() else: # v predx0 = model.predictstartfromzandv(x, ts, modeloutput) # Quantize if needed if getattr(scheduler, 'quantizedenoised', False): predx0 = model.firststagemodel.quantize(predx0) # 5. Compute direction dirxt = (1. - aprev - sigmat2).sqrt() noisepred # 6. Sample noise noise = sigmat torch.randnlike(x) temperature if noisedropout > 0: masknoise = torch.bernoulli(torch.oneslike(noise) (1 - noisedropout)) noise = noise masknoise # 7. Update x xprev = aprev.sqrt() predx0 + dirxt + noise # 8. Record intermediates if i % 10 == 0 or i == len(timesteps) - 1: intermediates['xinter'].append(xprev) intermediates['predx0'].append(predx0) x = xprev return x, intermediates Parameters: numinferencesteps: Number of sampling steps. Default: 50. unconditionalguidancescale: CFG scale. Default: 1.0 (disables guidance). Typical values: 7.5 for sampling, 100 for refinement. ddimeta: Controls stochasticity. Default: 0.0. temperature: Scales injected noise. Default: 1.0. noisedropout: Dropout probability for noise. Default: 0.0. quantizedenoised: Quantize \hat{x}0. Default: False. useoriginalsteps: Use DDPM timesteps instead of DDIM timesteps. Default: False. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Masking Requires x0: Inpainting requires the original image x0 to compute the noisy version via q\sample. Dynamic Thresholding: Not implemented; raises NotImplementedError if enabled. Score Corrector: Only supports eps parameterization; raises assertion error otherwise. UCG Schedule Length: Must exactly match the length of timerange. A procedure to generate smooth transitions between 3D samples by interpolating in the diffusion latent space before deterministic decoding. It samples two initial latents x^{(T)} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), interpolates them using spherical linear interpolation (SLERP), and passes them through a deterministic solver. Standard Gaussian diffusion models often yield non-smooth interpolation; however, models trained with early stopping for sparse-view reconstruction (as in SSDNeRF) preserve a smoother prior, yielding better generalization and smoother transitions than long unconditional training schedules. Used in SSDNeRF for interpolating generated 3D samples. Adds noise to an initial image x0 according to the diffusion process at timestep t, using either DDPM or DDIM schedule parameters. It selects schedule parameters based on useoriginalsteps (DDPM vs DDIM alphas), generates noise, and computes the noisy latent: xt = \sqrt{\alphat} x0 + \sqrt{1-\alphat} \epsilon. Decodes a latent representation x{latent} into a sample by running the DDIM sampling process from a starting timestep t{start} down to 0. It selects timesteps (DDPM or DDIM based on useoriginalsteps), reverses them, and iteratively calls psampleddim to update the latent. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot T), where N is the number of sampling steps and T is the cost of one UNet forward pass. Memory Complexity: O(C \cdot H \cdot W) for latents, plus O(T) for precomputed schedule buffers. Measured Performance: With numinferencesteps=50 and guidancescale=7.5, it produces high-quality images suitable for NeRF refinement. Strengths: Deterministic sampling (when \eta=0) allows for reproducible results and fewer steps. CFG enhances conditional fidelity. Limitations: Stochasticity (\eta > 0) can introduce variance. Inpainting requires x0. Dynamic thresholding is not supported. DDIM (Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models) was introduced as a deterministic sampling method for diffusion models that skips intermediate noise steps, allowing for fewer sampling steps than DDPM while maintaining sample quality. It has been adapted for classifier-free guidance to enhance conditional generation. In the context of volume rendering, it is used in frameworks like GaussianObject for refining 3D Gaussians and in SSDNeRF for 3D interpolation and generation. dreamgaussian/dreamgaussian, https://github.com/dreamgaussian/dreamgaussian, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) chensjtu/GaussianObject, https://github.com/chensjtu/GaussianObject, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Single-Stage Diffusion NeRF: A Unified Approach to 3D Generation and Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv51070.2023.00229, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Conditional Generator for NeRF Refinement
head: 2D Post-processing Generator, Conditional Generator, GANeRF Generator Stage
body: The Conditional Generator is a 2D post-processing module that refines NeRF renderings by acting as a stochastic denoiser. It takes a raw NeRF rendering and an auxiliary random vector as input to produce a cleaned image, addressing artifacts that remain after 3D optimization. Unlike 3D discriminator-based methods that guide the radiance field directly, this method operates in image space, leveraging a StyleGAN2-inspired architecture to enhance perceptual quality without altering the underlying 3D representation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A raw NeRF rendering R{\perp\theta}(rP) (patch or full image) and an auxiliary random vector z. Output: A refined, cleaned image patch. Data Structures and Architecture: The generator G\omega is a fully convolutional network inspired by StyleGAN2 but adapted as a conditional generator, omitting the mapping network. Feature Extraction Pyramid: Consists of six blocks operating at multiple resolutions. Multi-scale Conditioning: The input patch is bilinearly downsampled 6 times by a factor of 2. Each downscaled version is encoded via a convolutional layer into 32 feature channels. These features are concatenated to the output of the corresponding generator layer at that scale. Generative Blocks: Starting from a 4 \times 4 down-sampled patch, convolutional blocks extract level-specific features. Features are upsampled and added with generative noise to the next level. Normalization and Activation: Uses normalization layers and leaky ReLU activations. Noise Injection: Additive noise is injected after normalization layers, scaled by a learnable per-layer factor. Skip Connections: Input and output skip connections are used. Resolution: The final output resolution matches the input resolution (typically 256 \times 256 during training). Training Objective: The generator is trained in a regularized adversarial setting alongside a discriminator D\psi. The loss function for the generator is: L{rgb}^G(\omega | \theta) = \mathbb{E}{q,n} \|G\omega(R{\perp\theta}(rP), z) - cP\|1 + \lambda{perc}^G \mathcal{L}{perc} + \lambda{adv}^G \max{\psi \in \Psi} L{adv}(\omega, \psi | \theta) Where: R{\perp\theta}(rP) is the NeRF rendering of patch P using optimized parameters \theta. cP is the ground truth color for patch P. \mathcal{L}{perc} is the perceptual loss. L{adv} is the adversarial loss. \lambda{perc}^G = 1.0, \lambda{rgb}^G = 3.0, \lambda{adv}^G = 5.0, and \lambda{gp}^G = 0.1 are loss weights. The saddle-point problem is coped with by alternating updates of the generator and discriminator. Parameters: Initial Training Patch Size: 256 \times 256. Batch Size: 8 for the generator. Discriminator Batch Size: 32 (the adversarial loss subdivides each 256 \times 256 patch into 4 non-overlapping 128 \times 128 patches). Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 2 \times 10^{-3} for both generator and discriminator. Epochs: 3000. Inference: At inference time, the generator runs fully convolutionally on high-resolution images to refine NeRF renderings. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Inspired by StyleGAN2, adapted as conditional generator. """ def init(self, inchannels=3, outchannels=3, latentdim=512): super().init() # Architecture inspired by StyleGAN2 generator blocks # Omitting mapping network; noise z is injected directly self.pyramid = StyleGAN2Pyramid(inchannels, outchannels, latentdim) def forward(self, nerfrendering, z): """ Args: nerfrendering: Tensor of shape (B, C, H, W) z: Random noise vector of shape (B, latentdim) Returns: Refined image of shape (B, C, H, W) """ # Multi-scale conditioning: 6 times bilinearly downsampled by factor of 2 # This enables multi-scale analysis scales = [] current = nerfrendering for in range(6): scales.append(current) current = F.interpolate(current, scalefactor=0.5, mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False) # Encode downscaled patches into 32 feature channels # Concatenate to generator layer output of corresponding scale # Note: Implementation details of StyleGAN2Pyramid are assumed standard # but adapted to accept these multi-scale features refined = self.pyramid(current, z, scales) return refined class StyleGAN2Pyramid(nn.Module): def init(self, inch, outch, latentdim): super().init() # Simplified representation of the 6-block pyramid # Starts from 4x4 down-sampled patch self.initconv = nn.Conv2d(inch, 512, 3, padding=1) self.noisescale = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1)) #... other StyleGAN2 blocks (Conv, UpSample, Noise, Add, LeakyReLU, Norm)... # Input/Output skip connections are used def forward(self, lowres, z, scales): # Process through pyramid # Inject additive noise after normalization layers, scaled by learnable factor # Concatenate encoded multi-scale features pass def trainstep(generator, discriminator, nerfrendering, groundtruth, z, optimizerg, optimizerd): """ Alternating update of generator and discriminator. """ # Generator Update optimizerg.zerograd() refined = generator(nerfrendering, z) # L1 color loss lrgb = torch.mean(torch.abs(refined - groundtruth)) # Perceptual loss (not detailed in sources, assumed standard LPIPS or VGG) lperc = computeperceptualloss(refined, groundtruth) # Adversarial loss (maximizing discriminator error) # Ladv is defined in the adversarial setting dfake = discriminator(refined.detach()) ladv = -torch.mean(dfake) # Simplified GAN loss formulation lossg = lrgb + 1.0 lperc + 5.0 ladv lossg.backward() optimizerg.step() # Discriminator Update optimizerd.zerograd() dreal = discriminator(groundtruth) dfake = discriminator(refined) # Adversarial loss for discriminator (minimizing discriminator error on real, maximizing on fake) # Plus gradient penalty lambdagp = 0.1 ladvd = torch.mean(dfake) - torch.mean(dreal) lgp = computegradientpenalty(discriminator, groundtruth, refined) lossd = ladvd + 0.1 lgp lossd.backward() optimizerd.step() Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Evaluated on ScanNet++ indoor scenes (office, lab, apartment) with spatially out-of-distribution test views. Compared against Mip-NeRF 360, Instant NGP, and Nerfacto variations. Strengths: Improves rendering quality in 2D post-processing; handles high-resolution images fully convolutionally at inference; stochastic nature helps with denoising. Limitations: Requires additional training of a GAN; operates in 2D, so it cannot fix 3D inconsistencies directly (though it complements 3D discriminator guidance). When to use: When NeRF renderings have perceptual artifacts that 3D optimization alone cannot resolve, and high-resolution refinement is needed. When not: When 3D consistency is paramount and 2D post-processing might introduce view-dependent inconsistencies not present in the 3D model. The Conditional Generator is part of the GANeRF framework, which leverages discriminators to optimize Neural Radiance Fields. It was introduced to address artifacts by repairing them in 2D post-processing after 3D optimization. The architecture is inspired by StyleGAN2 [Karras et al. 2020] and the conditional GAN setting of pix2pix [Isola et al. 2017]. name: DDPM Posterior Sampling with Adaptive Step Size
head: Joint Denoising and Material Optimization, Posterior Score Sampling
body: This method performs inverse rendering by jointly denoising an environment map using a Diffusion Posterior Sampling (DPS) prior while simultaneously optimizing material parameters (base color, roughness, metallic) to fit observed input images. It differs from standard denoising by interleaving the diffusion sampling steps with gradient-based material optimization, using an adaptive step size parameter \rho to balance the trade-off between the realism of the generative prior and the fidelity to the input observations. Inputs: Input images \hat{y}i for i=1 \dots m. Corresponding camera poses \mathbf{c}i. A pre-trained DDPM model for seamless spherical environment maps (architecture from [Nichol and Dhariwal 2021]). A differentiable renderer R(\cdot) capable of path tracing environment maps. Outputs: Optimized material parameters \mathbf{k}{arm} (base color, roughness, metallic texture maps). A clean, seamless environment map x0. Data Structures: Environment map xt: A spherical texture representing the illumination at diffusion step t. Initialized via Mitsuba3 reconstruction. Material parameters \mathbf{k}{arm}: Texture maps for base color, roughness, and metallic. Optimizer: Adam. Parameters: Learning rate: 1 \times 10^{-2} for all parameters during initialization. Denoising steps: 1000. Refinement iterations: 200. Hyper-parameter \rho: Balances generation realism vs. observation faithfulness. For t > 500: \rho = 0.1. For t < 500: \rho varies between 0.1 and 1. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Initialize environment map x using Mitsuba3 reconstruction. Initialize material parameters \mathbf{k}{arm} (base color, roughness, metallic). Run a preliminary optimization using the loss: L{init}(\mathbf{k}{arm}, x) = \sum{i=1}^{m} || \hat{y}i - R(x, \mathbf{k}{arm}, \mathbf{c}i)||^2 using Adam with learning rate 1 \times 10^{-2} for metallic, roughness, environment map, and base color. Reset: Keep the optimized roughness and metallic texture maps. Reset base color to zero. This serves as the initialization for the joint optimization. 2. Joint Denoising and Material Optimization: Iterate t from T down to 1 (1000 steps). In each step, perform one step of DDPM posterior sampling on xt to obtain x{t-1}, using the posterior score function defined in Eq. 13 of. The step size \rho is selected based on t. Simultaneously, optimize \mathbf{k}{arm} (base color, roughness, metallic) by minimizing the denoising loss: L{denoise}(\mathbf{k}{arm}, t) = \sum{i=1}^{m} || \hat{y}i - R(\hat{x}t, \mathbf{k}{arm}, \mathbf{c}i)||^2 where \hat{x}t is the current environment map estimate at step t. Note: The sources describe this as "interleaved" optimization. The pseudocode below reflects the joint update per step. 3. Refinement: After generating the clean environment map x0, refine the material parameters \mathbf{k}{arm} for 200 additional iterations using the refinement loss: L{refine}(\mathbf{k}{arm}) = \sum{i=1}^{m} || \hat{y}i - R(x0, \mathbf{k}{arm}, \mathbf{c}i)||^2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ddpmposteriorsamplingadaptive(inputimages, cameraposes, renderer, ddpmmodel, numsteps=1000, numrefine=200): """ Jointly denoise environment map and optimize materials using DDPM posterior sampling with adaptive step size. """ # 1. Initialization # Initialize environment map x using Mitsuba3 reconstruction x = initializeenvironmentmapmitsuba3() # Initialize material parameters (base color, roughness, metallic) karm = initializematerialparameters() # Preliminary optimization to initialize roughness/metallic optimizerinit = Adam([x, karm], lr=1e-2) for in range(initializationiterations): # Not specified, run until convergence lossinit = sum(norm(inputimages[i] - renderer(x, karm, cameraposes[i]))2 for i in range(len(inputimages))) optimizerinit.zerograd() lossinit.backward() optimizerinit.step() # Reset base color to zero, keep optimized roughness and metallic karm.basecolor = 0.0 # x remains as initialized by Mitsuba3 or the result of the init step # 2. Joint Denoising and Material Optimization optimizerjoint = Adam([x, karm], lr=1e-2) # Learning rate not explicitly specified for joint step, assume similar or default for t in range(numsteps, 0, -1): # Determine adaptive step size rho if t > 500: rho = 0.1 else: # rho varies between 0.1 and 1 for t < 500 # Exact schedule not given, assume linear interpolation or fixed value from context rho = interpolaterho(t, start=0.1, end=1.0, totalsteps=500) # Perform one step of DDPM posterior sampling on x # This uses the posterior score function from Eq. 13 in # x is updated to x{t-1} x = ddpmposteriorstep(x, t, ddpmmodel, rho) # Optimize material parameters jointly with the denoising loss # Note: The source says "in every denoising step, we optimize... jointly with the loss" # This implies an inner optimization loop or a single gradient step per diffusion step. # Given the timing (630ms for material opt vs 290ms for denoising), it likely involves multiple inner steps or a full optimization pass. # We assume a single optimization step per diffusion step for the pseudocode structure, # but in practice, this might be an inner loop. optimizerjoint.zerograd() lossdenoise = sum(norm(inputimages[i] - renderer(x, karm, cameraposes[i]))2 for i in range(len(inputimages))) lossdenoise.backward() optimizerjoint.step() # 3. Refinement # After generating clean environment map x0 (which is x after the loop) optimizerrefine = Adam([karm], lr=1e-2) # Only optimize materials for in range(numrefine): optimizerrefine.zerograd() lossrefine = sum(norm(inputimages[i] - renderer(x, karm, cameraposes[i]))2 for i in range(len(inputimages))) lossrefine.backward() optimizerrefine.step() return x, karm def interpolaterho(t, start, end, totalsteps): # t goes from 500 down to 1 # Map t to [0, 1] progress = (500 - t) / 499.0 return start + progress (end - start) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Choice of \rho: If \rho is too small, sampling ignores input observations in favor of realism. If \rho is too large, results are faithful to observations but have inferior realism. Local Minima: The adaptive schedule (low \rho early, high \rho late) prevents the material optimization from getting stuck in local minima by using the realistic prior to guide final noise reduction. Initialization: Resetting base color to zero while keeping optimized roughness/metallic is critical for faster convergence. Time Complexity: Obtaining a single sample takes approximately 20 minutes. Breakdown: This includes 1000 iterations of interleaved denoising (290 ms per iteration) and material optimization (630 ms per iteration). Hardware: Tested on four A100 GPUs for training the generative model; inference timing reported without specific hardware, but implied to be GPU-accelerated. Strengths: Produces realistic and seamless environment maps while fitting observations; the adaptive \rho balances realism and fidelity. Limitations: Computationally expensive (20 mins per sample); requires a pre-trained DDPM model. Origin: Proposed in "Diffusion Posterior Illumination for Ambiguity-Aware Inverse Rendering" (2023) by Linjie Lyu et al.. Context: Part of a pipeline for inverse rendering that uses generative models to resolve ambiguities in material and illumination estimation. Development: Builds on Diffusion Posterior Sampling (DPS) techniques and uses a DDPM architecture from [Nichol and Dhariwal 2021]. name: DDPM Denoise Function Network
head: 3D Convolutional Denoiser, DDPM Denoiser
body: The DDPM Denoise Function Network is a 3D convolutional neural network that predicts the noise to be removed from a latent radiance field representation during the reverse diffusion process. It serves as the core denoiser in diffusion-based radiance field optimization, enabling the generation of 3D structures from noisy latent codes. It differs from sibling methods like DDIM Sampling with Classifier-Free Guidance by relying on a fixed architectural prior for noise prediction rather than explicit classifier gradients or deterministic sampling trajectories. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A noisy latent radiance field representation (voxel grid) at time step t, and optionally a time embedding. Output: The predicted noise component \epsilon\theta or the denoised estimate \tilde{f}0^t. Data Structures: The network is an 8-layer 3D convolutional encoder-decoder. Layer Widths: The channel dimensions for the 8 layers are \{32, 64, 128, 256, 256, 128, 64, 32\}. Resolution Mapping: Encoder (Layers 1-4): Reduces spatial resolution from 32^3 to 4^3. Each of the first four layers applies a 3D convolution with stride 2. Decoder (Layers 5-8): Increases spatial resolution from 4^3 to 32^3. Each of the last four layers applies a 3D transposed convolution (convolution transpose) with stride 2. Algorithm Steps: 1. Time Embedding: Encode the current diffusion time step t into a vector (implementation detail not specified in sources, standard practice). 2. Forward Pass: Pass the noisy latent field and time embedding through the 8-layer 3D convolution network. Layers 1-4 downsample the input volume. Layers 5-8 upsample the latent representation. 3. Noise Prediction: The output of the final layer is the predicted noise \epsilon\theta(xt, t). 4. Denoising Estimate: Compute the denoised field estimate \tilde{f}0^t using the standard DDPM reverse step formula: \tilde{f}0^t = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alphat}} \left( xt - \frac{1-\alphat}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}t}} \epsilon\theta(xt, t) \right) where xt is the noisy input, \alphat and \bar{\alpha}t are diffusion schedule parameters. 5. Guidance (Optional): For image-to-volume synthesis, the predicted denoised field \tilde{f}0^t is further updated by minimizing photometric error. Render the current estimate \tilde{I}t from a given pose and compare it with the foreground-masked target image I. Compute the gradient \nabla{\tilde{f}t} (\tilde{I}t, I) via volumetric rendering and update the field: \tilde{f}0^t \leftarrow \tilde{f}0^t - \lambda \nabla{\tilde{f}t} (\tilde{I}t, I) where \lambda is a small guidance weight. Parameters: Learning Rate: 10^{-2} for the Adam optimizer when updating latent codes. L2 Regularization: Weight 5 \times 10^{-2} on the code. Guidance Weight (\lambda): Described as "small". Exact value not given. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: The use of stride 2 convolutions requires careful handling of input dimensions divisible by powers of 2. The source specifies starting at 32^3 and ending at 32^3, implying padding or specific boundary handling is used to maintain resolution. Photometric Gradient Stability: Volumetric rendering gradients can be noisy. The guidance step requires stable rendering and appropriate \lambda to prevent divergence. This variant uses the denoiser output to steer the sampling process towards a target image. It computes the gradient of the photometric error between the rendered view of the current denoising estimate and the foreground-masked target image, then updates the latent field by stepping in the negative gradient direction with a small guidance weight \lambda. Time Complexity: Determined by the 8-layer 3D convolution network. Each layer involves O(C{in} C{out} k^3) operations per voxel, where k is kernel size (not given). Memory Complexity: Dominated by the voxel grid storage and intermediate activations. The network processes volumes up to 32^3 resolution. Strengths: Provides a structured prior for 3D noise prediction, enabling coherent 3D generation. Limitations: Requires significant memory for 3D convolutions at higher resolutions. Performance depends on the quality of the photometric gradient in guidance steps. When to Use: When generating 3D radiance fields from noise with a need for 3D structural coherence, especially when guided by 2D image inputs. The method originates from the work on DiffRF (Diffusion Radiance Fields) and Neural Volumetric Mesh Generator. It was introduced to enable diffusion-based generation of 3D radiance fields by using a 3D convolutional network as the denoising function. The approach builds on standard DDPM frameworks but adapts the denoiser to operate directly on 3D voxel representations. name: Diffusion-Based 3D Inpainting
head: Inpaint3D
body: Diffusion-Based 3D Inpainting utilizes a self-trained 2D inpainting diffusion model to reconstruct missing or masked regions in a 3D scene represented by a radiance field. It solves the problem of 3D scene completion or object removal by combining explicit reconstruction constraints for visible areas with implicit diffusion priors for occluded areas. It differs from sibling methods like Inpainting SDS Loss by explicitly training the 2D inpainting model on inpainted data before applying it to the 3D optimization loop. Inputs: A 3D radiance field representation (e.g., NeRF) initialized from a set of input images. Per-view binary masks indicating regions to be inpainted (masked) and regions to be preserved (unmasked). A self-trained 2D inpainting diffusion model. Optional text prompts describing the content to be generated in masked regions. Outputs: An optimized 3D radiance field where masked regions are filled with semantically consistent and view-consistent geometry and texture. Data Structures: Radiance Field Parameters: Standard NeRF MLP weights or voxel grid densities/colors. Diffusion Model: Frozen U-Net parameters for noise prediction \epsilon\theta. Masks: Binary tensor M \in \{0,1\}^{H \times W} per view, where 1 indicates masked region. Parameters: Reconstruction Weight (\lambda{rec}): Weight for the unmasked region loss. SDS Weight (\lambda{sds}): Weight for the masked region loss. Diffusion Steps: Number of denoising steps for the 2D inpainter. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the 3D radiance field from the input images. Train the self-trained 2D inpainting diffusion model using a dataset of inpainted images. 2. Sampling: For each training iteration, sample a camera pose and render an RGB image I{render} from the current radiance field. 3. Unmasked Supervision: Apply the mask M to separate the image into observed (I{obs}) and masked (I{mask}) regions. Compute a reconstruction loss between the rendered unmasked pixels and the ground truth input pixels I{gt}: \mathcal{L}{rec} = \| (1 - M) \odot I{render} - (1 - M) \odot I{gt} \|1 4. Masked Supervision (SDS): Encode the masked region of the rendered image into latent space. Pass the latent through the frozen 2D inpainting diffusion model to predict noise \epsilon\theta. Compute the Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss to optimize the masked regions by backpropagating the difference between predicted and actual noise from the diffusion model. This gradient signal encourages the rendered masked region to match the distribution of the 2D inpainting model. 5. Optimization: Update the radiance field parameters by minimizing the combined loss: \mathcal{L}{total} = \lambda{rec} \mathcal{L}{rec} + \lambda{sds} \mathcal{L}{sds} 6. Refinement: Iterate steps 2–5 until convergence. The self-trained nature of the 2D model ensures it is specialized for the specific inpainting task, improving consistency. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: View Inconsistency: Standard 2D inpainting may produce inconsistent textures across views. The method relies on the 3D optimization loop to enforce consistency, but large view variations may still cause artifacts. Mask Boundaries: Sharp transitions between masked and unmasked regions can cause visible seams if the diffusion prior does not align with the existing geometry. Precision: The SDS gradient computation requires careful handling of the latent space scaling factors to avoid vanishing or exploding gradients. Nerfiller focuses on scene completion with arbitrary masks rather than object removal with tight masks. It utilizes a grid-based prior where images are shuffled into 2×2 grids and fed into 2D inpainting diffusion models to generate 3D consistent outputs. It further introduces an iterative framework to distill these 2D inpainting results into a single 3D scene. InFusion is a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) inpainting method that integrates depth completion based on diffusion models. It selects a reference image for inpainting, employs a self-trained depth completion model to predict the depth map of the inpainting region, and projects it back into point clouds for accurate initial completion. It designs a progressive strategy to resolve complex cases that could not be completed from a single view. 3D-Aware Inpainting inpaints masked 2D regions of an image while simultaneously reconstructing the underlying 3D shape, using a 3D-aware diffusion model to find a latent 3D structure consistent with observed parts and plausible in masked regions. It differs from RePaint [37] by replacing the 2D denoiser architecture with a 3D denoiser, enabling simultaneous 3D shape reconstruction alongside 2D inpainting. It is suitable when simultaneous 2D inpainting and 3D shape reconstruction are required, though it may produce blurrier outputs than GAN-based methods and requires training images with camera extrinsics. Time Complexity: High. Requires multiple forward passes through the radiance field and the diffusion model per iteration. Not given in the sources for exact scaling. Memory Complexity: Moderate to High. Requires storing the radiance field, the diffusion model weights (frozen), and intermediate latent states during SDS computation. Measured Performance: Produces high-quality, semantically consistent inpainting results, especially for large missing regions. Not given in the sources for specific hardware or resolution benchmarks. Strengths: Leverages powerful 2D diffusion priors; self-training allows adaptation to specific inpainting tasks. Limitations: Computationally expensive; sensitive to mask boundaries; may struggle with complex multi-view inconsistencies without additional mechanisms (like the multi-view scoring in MVIPNeRF). When to use: When high-fidelity semantic completion is required for large masked regions in 3D scenes. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical or when masks are very small and simple geometric interpolation suffices. The method originates from the application of 2D inpainting diffusion models to 3D radiance fields. It builds on the general framework of Diffusion-Based Guidance for Radiance Field Optimization [8117-diffusion-based-guidance-for-radiance-field-optimization.md]. The specific approach of using a self-trained 2D inpainting model for 3D inpainting is attributed to Inpaint3D. Recent advancements have also extended these techniques to 3D Gaussian Splatting, such as InFusion. name: Nerfiller
head: Grid-based Diffusion Inpainting for NeRF
body: Nerfiller is a method for 3D scene completion using arbitrary masks, leveraging a grid-based prior and an iterative distillation framework. It differs from sibling methods like Reference-guided Controllable Inpainting of Neural Radiance Fields and Masked Completion via GAN Inversion by explicitly shuffling rendered images into 2x2 grids to feed into 2D inpainting diffusion models, thereby enforcing 3D consistency through multi-view scoring. While Masked Completion via GAN Inversion relies on GAN inversion for completion, Nerfiller uses diffusion priors to generate harmonious completions for large, arbitrary masked regions. Inputs: A pre-trained 2D inpainting diffusion model. A text description of the scene content to be completed. A 3D mask defining the region to be completed. An initial NeRF representation (or empty scene). Outputs: A completed 3D radiance field (NeRF) consistent with the text description and unmasked regions. Data Structures: NeRF Grid: Standard multi-resolution hash grid or voxel grid storing density and color features. Image Grid: A temporary structure where N rendered images are shuffled and arranged into 2 \times 2 composite grids. Parameters: Text Prompt: Describes the desired content for the masked region. Diffusion Model: A 2D inpainting model capable of conditional generation. Multi-view Scoring Weight: Balances consistency across different views. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the NeRF parameters. Typically random initialization or from a coarse reconstruction. 2. Rendering: Render a set of views of the current NeRF from various camera poses. 3. Grid Construction: Shuffle the rendered images and arrange them into 2 \times 2 grids. This shuffling helps break view-specific biases and encourages the diffusion model to learn 3D-consistent features rather than 2D artifacts. 4. Diffusion Inpainting: Feed the 2 \times 2 grids into the 2D inpainting diffusion model, conditioned on the text prompt and the mask. The model generates inpainted images for the masked regions. 5. Distillation/Update: Distill the 2D inpainted results back into the 3D NeRF representation. This is done by minimizing a loss function that aligns the rendered views of the NeRF with the inpainted images from the diffusion model. 6. Multi-view Scoring: Apply a multi-view scoring mechanism to evaluate the consistency and sharpness of the generated content across different views, particularly under large view variations. This score guides the optimization to ensure 3D coherence. 7. Iterative Refinement: Repeat steps 2-6 iteratively. The framework distills the 2D inpainting results into a single 3D scene over multiple iterations. Formulas: The specific loss function for distillation is not explicitly detailed in the provided notes, but it leverages Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) to align rendered views with diffusion priors. Let I{rendered} be the rendered image, I{inpainted} be the diffusion-generated image, and L be the distillation loss. The optimization minimizes L(I{rendered}, I{inpainted}). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Large View Variations: The method is designed to handle large view variations, but consistency may still be challenging if the text prompt is ambiguous. Arbitrary Masks: The method supports arbitrary masks, but complex mask shapes may require more iterations for convergence. A technique to synthesize a completion of a masked region in a radiance field that harmonizes with the non-masked region, given an input radiance field and a 3D mask. It is distinct from Nerfiller's grid-based approach by using a conditional diffusion sampling process directly on the voxel grid. Choose this when a direct voxel-level completion is preferred over iterative distillation from 2D models. Steps: 1. Conditional Guidance: Perform conditional completion by gradually guiding the unconditional sampling process in the known region to the input radiance field f{in} using the update rule: f{t-1} = \bar{\alpha}t (m \tilde{f}t + (1 - m) f{in}) where m is a binary mask applied to the input voxel grid, \tilde{f}t is the denoised estimate at step t, and \bar{\alpha}t is the cumulative noise schedule coefficient. 2. Sampling: Sample the noisy latent at step t-1 from the distribution: f{t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}(f0, (1 - \bar{\alpha}t)I) where f0 is the initial noise. 3. Fusion: Iteratively fuse the non-masked input region with the estimated denoising \tilde{f}0^t and apply the diffusion process on the resulting f0^{t-1} to obtain the completion. Parameters: m: A binary mask applied to the input voxel grid, indicating known (1) and masked (0) regions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Iterative nature implies multiple forward passes through the diffusion model and NeRF renderer. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Depends on the NeRF grid size and the batch size of rendered images. Strengths: Handles arbitrary masks effectively; leverages strong 2D diffusion priors for high-quality texture; multi-view scoring improves consistency. Limitations: Not given in the sources for Nerfiller specifically, though related diffusion methods note limitations compared to GAN-based approaches in terms of diversity or fidelity. When to use: When scene completion with arbitrary masks is required, and high-quality texture synthesis is prioritized over geometric precision. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical, or when the mask is very small and tight (object removal), where other methods might be more efficient. Nerfiller was introduced as a method for 3D scene completion with arbitrary masks, building on the capabilities of 2D inpainting diffusion models. It was developed to address the limitations of previous methods that struggled with large, arbitrary masks. The method is part of the broader trend of using diffusion models for 3D editing and completion.
