name: Reference-guided Controllable Inpainting of Neural Radiance Fields
head: Ours, Ours-SD
body: This method performs 3D inpainting of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) by substituting a single reference view with a diffusion-generated target view, then optimizing the NeRF to match the new view while maintaining consistency with the remaining input views. It solves the problem of inserting or modifying objects in a 3D scene without requiring multi-view supervision for the target content. It differs from Inpainting SDS Loss by using a deterministic 2D inpainting prior (Stable Diffusion) followed by a bilateral solver for residual smoothing, rather than relying solely on gradient-based SDS guidance during optimization. Inputs: N input images \{I{r,i}\}{i=1}^N with known camera poses \{Pi\}{i=1}^N. Binary masks \{Mi\}{i=1}^N indicating regions to be inpainted in each input view. A single reference view I{r,ref} (typically the 30th image of the 60 training views in SPIn-NeRF) with mask M{ref}. A text prompt describing the desired content for the reference view (for Ours-SD variant). Outputs: Optimized NeRF parameters (density \sigma, color \mathbf{c}). Novel view renderings \{I{t,j}\} corresponding to target camera poses \{P{t,j}\}. Data Structures: NeRF: Standard MLP mapping 3D position and viewing direction to density and color. Masks: Binary images, dilated to ensure full coverage of the occluded region. Residuals: Float32 images representing the difference between the original input view and the inpainted view. Parameters: Downscale factor: 4 (all input images downsized by 4×). Distortion loss weight: \gamma{dist} = 0.01. Bilateral solver brightness/color bandwidths: \sigmac = 4. Bilateral solver spatial bandwidth: \sigmas = 128. Bilateral solver smoothness strength: \lambda = 128. Bilateral solver PCG iterations: K{pcg} = 25. Disocclusion handling interval: N{do} = 3000 iterations. Depth supervision steps: N{depth} = 2000. Bilateral solver steps: N{bilateral} = 2000. Total training iterations: 10,000. Loss weights: \gamma{depth} = 4, \gamma{rec} = 2, \gamma{do} = 1, \eta{do} = 0.25, \gamma{smooth} = 1000, \gamma{ei} = 2. Mask dilation: 5 iterations with a 5×5 kernel for input masks; 4 iterations with a 3×3 kernel for disocclusion masks. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Downscale all input images and masks by 4×. Dilate input masks Mi by 5 iterations using a 5×5 kernel to ensure the inpainted region fully covers the occluded area. Dilate disocclusion masks by 4 iterations using a 3×3 kernel to remove noise. 2. Reference View Inpainting: Generate the inpainted reference view I{t,ref} using Stable Diffusion Inpainting v2 [55] conditioned on I{r,ref}, M{ref}, and the text prompt. If the generated image contains unwanted objects, regenerate until clean. 3. View Substitution and Residual Calculation: For each input view i, compute the view-substituted image I{t,i} by replacing the masked region of I{r,i} with the corresponding region from I{t,ref} (warped via camera geometry). Compute the absolute residual image Ri = |I{t,i} - I{r,i}|. Apply the bilateral solver to Ri to obtain a smooth residual map \tilde{R}i. The bilateral solver minimizes: \min{\mathbf{u}} \sum{p} \left( \lambda (\mathbf{u}p - \mathbf{r}p)^2 + \sigmas^2 \sum{q \in \mathcal{N}(p)} w{pq} (\mathbf{u}p - \mathbf{u}q)^2 \right) where \mathbf{u} is the output, \mathbf{r} is the input residual, w{pq} is the bilateral weight based on spatial and color distance, and \mathcal{N}(p) is the neighborhood. Solve using Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient (PCG) for 25 iterations. 4. Disocclusion Handling (Periodic): Every N{do} = 3000 iterations, identify disoccluded regions (areas visible in target views but occluded in input views). Use LaMa [61] as the 2D inpainter for these regions. Use three target images (cameras furthest left, right, and upward) as context for LaMa. Apply the smoothed residual \tilde{R}{do} to the disoccluded regions in the target views. 5. NeRF Optimization: Initialize NeRF with input views. For iteration k = 1 to 10,000: a. Sample rays from target camera poses. b. Render color \mathbf{c}{render} and depth d{render}. c. Compute losses: Depth Loss (\mathcal{L}{depth}): Supervise depth in the inpainted region using the warped depth from the reference view. Weight \gamma{depth} = 4. Reconstruction Loss (\mathcal{L}{rec}): Match rendered color to the view-substituted target view I{t,i} in the masked region. Weight \gamma{rec} = 2. Disocclusion Loss (\mathcal{L}{do}): Apply if disocclusion handling is active. Weight \gamma{do} = 1, scaling factor \eta{do} = 0.25. Smoothness Loss (\mathcal{L}{smooth}): Penalize high-frequency artifacts in the rendered image. Weight \gamma{smooth} = 1000. Distortion Loss (\mathcal{L}{dist}): Reduce floater artifacts. Weight \gamma{dist} = 0.01. Edge Inpainting Loss (\mathcal{L}{ei}): Ensure smooth transitions at mask boundaries. Weight \gamma{ei} = 2. d. Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \gamma{depth}\mathcal{L}{depth} + \gamma{rec}\mathcal{L}{rec} + \gamma{do}\mathcal{L}{do} + \gamma{smooth}\mathcal{L}{smooth} + \gamma{dist}\mathcal{L}{dist} + \gamma{ei}\mathcal{L}{ei}. e. Backpropagate and update NeRF parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def referenceguidedinpainting(inputviews, inputmasks, referenceview, referencemask, textprompt, targetcameras): # 1. Preprocessing inputviewsdown = [downscale4x(v) for v in inputviews] inputmasksdown = [dilatemask(m, kernelsize=5, iterations=5) for m in inputmasks] # 2. Reference Inpainting refinpainted = stablediffusioninpaintv2(referenceviewdown, referencemaskdown, textprompt) # 3. View Substitution viewsubstitutedviews = [] residuals = [] for i in range(len(inputviewsdown)): # Warp reference view to input view i's pose refwarped = warpimage(refinpainted, referencepose, inputposes[i]) # Replace masked region substituted = blend(inputviewsdown[i], refwarped, inputmasksdown[i]) viewsubstitutedviews.append(substituted) # Compute residual res = abs(substituted - inputviewsdown[i]) # Bilateral Solver smoothres = bilateralsolver(res, sigmac=4, sigmas=128, lambdasmooth=128, pcgiters=25) residuals.append(smoothres) # 4. Optimization Loop nerf = initializenerf(inputviewsdown) for k in range(10000): # Sample rays from target cameras rays = samplerays(targetcameras) # Render colors, depths = rendernerf(nerf, rays) # Compute Losses lossdepth = 0 lossrec = 0 lossdo = 0 losssmooth = 0 lossdist = 0 lossei = 0 # Depth Loss (in inpainted region) if k < 2000: lossdepth = depthloss(depths, warpedrefdepth, masks) # Reconstruction Loss (in inpainted region) if k < 2000: lossrec = reconstructionloss(colors, viewsubstitutedviews, masks) # Disocclusion Loss (periodic) if k % 3000 == 0: domasks = computedisocclusionmasks(rays, nerf) lossdo = disocclusionloss(colors, domasks, residuals) # Smoothness Loss losssmooth = smoothnessloss(colors) # Distortion Loss lossdist = distortionloss(colors, depths) # Edge Inpainting Loss lossei = edgeinpaintingloss(colors, masks) # Total Loss totalloss = (4 lossdepth + 2 lossrec + 1 lossdo + 1000 losssmooth + 0.01 lossdist + 2 lossei) # Update optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return nerf Time Complexity: Dominated by the 10,000 iterations of NeRF optimization and the periodic 2D inpainting (LaMa/SD). The bilateral solver is applied once per view during preprocessing. Memory Complexity: Reduced by downsizing inputs by 4×. The NeRF memory footprint is standard for the resolution. Performance: Produces sharp, consistent inpaintings. The bilateral solver ensures smooth residuals, reducing artifacts. The method is robust to disocclusions due to periodic LaMa updates. Strengths: Controllable via text prompt; handles complex occlusions; sharp results compared to SDS-only methods. Limitations: Requires a single high-quality reference view; dependent on the quality of Stable Diffusion and LaMa; may introduce semantic inconsistencies if the prompt is ambiguous. Originated in the paper "Reference-guided Controllable Inpainting of Neural Radiance Fields" (ICCV 2023). It builds on the SPInNeRF framework [42] and leverages the diversity of diffusion models for view synthesis. The method addresses the limitations of previous NeRF inpainting techniques that lacked controllability or suffered from artifacts in disoccluded regions. name: Masked Completion via GAN Inversion
head: GAN Inversion for 3D Completion
body: Masked Completion via GAN Inversion is a conditional sampling technique that completes a 3D radiance field by inverting a 2D discriminator-trained generator, using photometric error on non-masked regions to guide the optimization. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Nerfiller and Reference-guided Controllable Inpainting of Neural Radiance Fields by operating in the latent space of a pre-trained GAN generator (specifically EG3D) rather than optimizing a neural network's weights or using diffusion-based volumetric gradients directly. Inputs: A pre-trained 3D-aware GAN generator (e.g., EG3D) trained with 2D discriminator guidance. A target image with an associated 3D input mask indicating the region to be completed. A random initial latent code w{init}. Outputs: An optimized latent code w^ that, when passed through the generator, produces a 3D radiance field consistent with the non-masked regions of the input image. Data Structures: Latent Code (w): The optimization variable. The specific dimensionality depends on the underlying GAN architecture (e.g., StyleGAN2/EG3D intermediate latent space). 3D Input Mask: A binary mask defining the region of interest in the 3D scene, projected onto 2D views. Parameters: Iterations: 200 iterations per masked sample. Views per Iteration: 8 views. Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 10^{-2}. L2 Regularization Weight: 5 \times 10^{-2} applied to the latent code. Resolution: Rendering is performed at 128 \times 128 resolution. Steps: 1. Initialization: Start from a random initial latent code w. 2. Iteration Loop: Repeat for 200 iterations: a. Rendering: Render the current synthesized sample from 8 different views using the current latent code w. b. Mask Projection: Project the 3D input mask onto the synthesized views using the predicted depths from the rendering. c. Error Computation: Compute the photometric error between the rendered non-masked regions and the corresponding regions in the input images. d. Optimization: Update the latent code w using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 10^{-2} and an L2 regularization term on the code weighted by 5 \times 10^{-2}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def maskedcompletionviaganinversion(generator, targetimage, inputmask3d, numiterations=200, numviews=8): """ Performs 3D masked completion by inverting a GAN generator. Args: generator: Pre-trained 3D-aware GAN generator (e.g., EG3D). targetimage: The input image with the region to be completed. inputmask3d: 3D input mask defining the completion region. numiterations: Number of optimization iterations (default 200). numviews: Number of views to render per iteration (default 8). Returns: wopt: Optimized latent code. """ # Initialize with a random latent code w = randomlatentcode(generator) # Optimizer setup optimizer = Adam(params=[w], lr=1e-2) l2weight = 5e-2 for i in range(numiterations): optimizer.zerograd() # Render the current synthesized sample from 8 views renderedimages = [] predicteddepths = [] for viewidx in range(numviews): # Render using the generator and current latent code w # This returns an image and its associated depth map img, depth = generator.render(w, view=viewidx) renderedimages.append(img) predicteddepths.append(depth) # Project the 3D input mask onto the synthesized views using predicted depths # This creates 2D masks for each view indicating which pixels are in the 'unknown' region viewmasks = project3dmasktoviews(inputmask3d, predicteddepths, cameraposes) # Compute photometric error on non-masked regions totalerror = 0.0 for j in range(numviews): renderedimg = renderedimages[j] # Get the non-masked region of the target image for this view # Note: The target image must be available for all 8 views or projected back # Assuming targetimages is a list of images for the 8 views targetimg = targetimages[j] # Create inverse mask for non-masked regions nonmaskedregion = 1.0 - viewmasks[j] # Compute photometric error only on non-masked regions # Using Mean Squared Error (MSE) as a standard photometric loss error = torch.mean((renderedimg nonmaskedregion - targetimg nonmaskedregion) 2) totalerror += error # Add L2 regularization on the latent code l2loss = l2weight torch.sum(w 2) loss = totalerror + l2loss # Backpropagate and update loss.backward() optimizer.step() return w Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Prediction Accuracy: The method relies on predicted depths to project the 3D mask. Inaccurate depth predictions can lead to incorrect mask projection, causing the photometric error to be computed on the wrong regions. Generator Limitations: Since the method inverts a 2D discriminator-trained generator, the quality of the completion is bounded by the generator's ability to represent the object class and the consistency of the 3D representation. Local Minima: Optimization in latent space can get stuck in local minima, especially with complex shapes or insufficient views. Time Complexity: The method requires 200 iterations per sample, with each iteration involving rendering from 8 views. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the storage of the latent code and the intermediate rendered images and depths for the 8 views per iteration. Measured Performance: On an NVIDIA RTX 2080 TI, the method achieves a run time of 48.6 seconds per sample for 1000 iterations (extrapolated from the 200-iteration description, implying ~9.7s for 200 iterations). Rendering Speed: Once synthesized, the explicit representation enables rendering at 128 \times 128 resolution with over 380 FPS. Strengths: Leverages the strong generative priors of pre-trained GANs, allowing for plausible completions even with limited input data. Limitations: Dependent on the quality and diversity of the pre-trained GAN generator; may struggle with object classes not well-represented in the training data. Masked Completion via GAN Inversion is described in the context of DiffRF, which uses a rendering-guided 3D radiance field diffusion model. The specific technique of using GAN inversion for 3D masked completion is attributed to the use of the EG3D generator, which is trained via 2D discriminator guidance. This approach allows for conditional sampling in 3D by optimizing the latent code to match 2D image observations. name: Diffusion Model Preprocessing & Training Setup
head: SDG Preprocessing, Stable Diffusion Training Setup
body: This method defines the data preprocessing pipeline and training configuration for a fine-tuned Stable Diffusion 1.5 model used as a semantic prior in Street View Synthesis (SGD). It solves the problem of adapting a 2D diffusion model to guide 3D radiance field optimization by ensuring the input data distribution matches the model's expectations and by enabling classifier-free guidance. It sets itself apart from general diffusion training by specifically addressing the aspect ratio distortion of wide-angle street view images (KITTI-360) and enforcing a perspective gap between reference and training views to improve robustness. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Raw KITTI-360 images (resolution 1408 \times 376), LiDAR point clouds, text prompts, and reference images. Output: Preprocessed image tensors (512 \times 512), depth masks, and training batches configured for classifier-free guidance. Data Structures: Image Tensor: Shape (B, 3, 512, 512), normalized to [-1, 1] or [0, 1] as required by the Stable Diffusion VAE. Depth Mask: A binary mask of shape (512, 512) where the top 80 rows are set to 1 (masked) and the rest are 0. Steps: 1. Pre-cropping: Crop the original KITTI-360 image from 1408 \times 376 to 600 \times 376. This step is critical to prevent over-distortion during the subsequent resizing to square dimensions. 2. Resizing: Resize the cropped image to 512 \times 512. 3. Depth Masking: Apply a mask to the top 80 rows of the 512 \times 512 image. This accounts for LiDAR point cloud height limitations where the sky or upper structures are not captured. The diffusion model's inpainting capability is relied upon to complete this masked region. 4. Training Image Cropping: Apply a center-crop to the training images to ensure consistent framing. 5. Reference Image Cropping: Apply a random-crop to reference images during training. This ensures a perspective gap between the reference and training images, enhancing model robustness. 6. Reference Selection: During Training: Reference images are selected from the dataset as needed. During Inference (Standard): Center-crop reference images. Select one frame from the five frames preceding the training image and one from the five frames succeeding it. During Inference (Novel View): Identify the closest training viewpoint. Use the adjacent frames of this closest viewpoint as reference images. 7. Classifier-Free Guidance Setup: During training, with a probability of 10%, set both the text prompt and the reference images to empty (null) conditions. This enables the model to learn unconditional generation capabilities. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preprocesskittiimage(imageraw, height=512, width=512, topmaskrows=80): """ Preprocess a single KITTI-360 image for Stable Diffusion training. imageraw: numpy array of shape (376, 1408, 3) Returns: numpy array of shape (512, 512, 3) and a binary mask """ # Step 1: Pre-crop to avoid over-distortion # Original: 1408x376. Crop to 600x376. # Assuming center crop in width: h, w, = imageraw.shape startw = (w - 600) // 2 imagecropped = imageraw[:, startw:startw+600,:] # Step 2: Resize to 512x512 imageresized = resize(imagecropped, (height, width)) # Step 3: Create depth mask mask = np.ones((height, width), dtype=np.float32) mask[:topmaskrows,:] = 0.0 # Top 80 rows are masked return imageresized, mask def selectreferenceimages(trainingidx, dataset, numprev=5, numnext=5): """ Select reference images for a given training image index. """ # Randomly choose one from preceding frames previndices = range(max(0, trainingidx - numprev), trainingidx) refprevidx = random.choice(list(previndices)) # Randomly choose one from succeeding frames nextindices = range(trainingidx + 1, min(len(dataset), trainingidx + 1 + numnext)) refnextidx = random.choice(list(nextindices)) return refprevidx, refnextidx def applycroppingstrategy(image, strategy='center'): """ Apply cropping based on strategy. strategy: 'center' for training images and inference references, 'random' for training references. """ if strategy == 'center': return centercrop(image) elif strategy == 'random': return randomcrop(image) return image def preparetrainingbatch(trainingimage, referenceimage, textprompt, cfgprob=0.1): """ Prepare a batch for training with classifier-free guidance. """ # Apply cropping trainimg = applycroppingstrategy(trainingimage, 'center') refimg = applycroppingstrategy(referenceimage, 'random') # Classifier-free guidance: randomly nullify conditions if random.random() < cfgprob: textprompt = "" refimg = None # Or empty tensor depending on implementation return trainimg, refimg, textprompt Parameters: Target Resolution: 512 \times 512 pixels. Pre-crop Width: 600 pixels (from original 1408). Masked Rows: Top 80 rows of the 512 \times 512 image. CFG Probability: 10% chance to nullify text and reference inputs. Reference Window: 5 preceding and 5 succeeding frames. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Over-distortion: Failing to pre-crop to 600 \times 376 before resizing to 512 \times 512 causes significant aspect ratio distortion. LiDAR Gaps: The top 80 rows contain no LiDAR data. The model must be trained to inpaint this region, relying on semantic priors rather than geometric constraints. Perspective Gap: Using center-crop for both training and reference images during training reduces the perspective diversity, potentially harming robustness. Random cropping for references is essential. This is the first stage of a two-step training strategy for the diffusion prior. It enables the model to learn high-level semantic content and object existence from adjacent reference images without relying on camera pose information. It isolates semantic understanding to handle complex driving scenes with mutual occlusions, where pose alone is insufficient. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method is evaluated on the KITTI-360 dataset. The model is fine-tuned on approximately 12,000 images. Strengths: Effectively handles the wide aspect ratio of street view data. The perspective gap strategy enhances robustness. The depth mask leverages the diffusion model's inpainting capabilities to fill LiDAR gaps. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that the diffusion model can accurately inpaint the masked top region. Performance is dependent on the quality of the LiDAR point clouds for the lower region. When to use: When synthesizing street views using Gaussian Splatting and a diffusion prior, specifically with wide-angle datasets like KITTI-360. When not to use: For datasets with standard aspect ratios or where LiDAR data covers the full vertical extent. The preprocessing steps are designed to bridge the gap between the wide, low-height aspect ratio of KITTI-360 images and the square, high-resolution inputs expected by Stable Diffusion. The classifier-free guidance setup follows standard practices in conditional diffusion models but is specifically tuned for the image-conditioned setting. name: Image-Conditioned Diffusion Fine-Tuning
head: Training Stage 1
body: Image-Conditioned Diffusion Fine-Tuning is the first stage of a two-step training strategy for a diffusion model prior used in street view synthesis. It enables the model to learn high-level semantic content and object existence from adjacent reference images without relying on camera pose information. Unlike methods that simultaneously encode images and poses, this approach isolates semantic understanding to handle complex driving scenes with mutual occlusions, where pose alone is insufficient for the diffusion model to fully comprehend the 3D scene structure. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: An input image I, a text prompt T, and two reference images I{\text{ref}} = \{I{\text{pre}}, I{\text{next}}\} representing the previous and next frames relative to I. Outputs: A fine-tuned U-Net parameter set \theta that can conditionally generate images based on text and reference image semantics. Data Structures Text Embedding (eT): A sequence of vectors [eT^0, \dots, eT^{LT}] where LT is the token sequence length and each eT^i \in \mathbb{R}^D. Image Embedding (e{Ii}): A sequence of vectors [e{Ii}^0, \dots, e{Ii}^{LI}] for each reference image Ii, where LI is the number of image patches. Latent Feature Map (z0): The encoded representation of the input image I in the latent space. Frozen Components The following components are frozen during this stage: 1. VAE Encoder and Decoder. 2. CLIP Text Encoder \mathcal{E}{\text{text}}. 3. CLIP Image Encoder \mathcal{E}{\text{Image}}. Trainable Components U-Net parameters \theta. Algorithm Steps 1. Reference Selection: Select a previous frame I{\text{pre}} and a next frame I{\text{next}} as the reference set I{\text{ref}} = \{I{\text{pre}}, I{\text{next}}\} for the current input image I. 2. Text Encoding: Encode the text prompt T using the frozen CLIP Text Encoder \mathcal{E}{\text{text}} to obtain the text embedding eT: eT = \mathcal{E}{\text{text}}(T) = [eT^0, \dots, eT^{LT}], \quad eT^i \in \mathbb{R}^D where D is the embedding dimension. 3. Image Encoding: Encode each reference image Ii \in \{I{\text{pre}}, I{\text{next}}\} using the frozen CLIP Image Encoder \mathcal{E}{\text{Image}} to obtain patch-wise features e{Ii}: e{Ii} = \mathcal{E}{\text{Image}}(Ii) = [e{Ii}^0, \dots, e{Ii}^{LI}], \quad i \in \{\text{pre}, \text{next}\} where LI is the number of image patches. 4. Feature Concatenation: Concatenate the reference image features e{I{\text{ref}}} = [e{I{\text{pre}}}, e{I{\text{next}}}] to the text embedding eT along the token length dimension. 5. Latent Encoding: Encode the input image I into a latent feature map z0 using the frozen VAE encoder. 6. Cross-Attention Fusion: Fuse the combined embedding (text + reference images) with the latent feature map z0 via the cross-attention layer within the U-Net. 7. Optimization: Optimize the U-Net parameters \theta by minimizing the denoising loss: \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}{z0, \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{1}), t, T, I{\text{ref}}} \left\| \epsilon - \epsilon\theta(zt, t, eT, e{I{\text{ref}}}) \right\|2^2 where \epsilon is random noise sampled from a standard normal distribution, t is the denoising timestep, and zt is the noisy latent at timestep t. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainstage1(inputimage, textprompt, previmage, nextimage, unet, vaeencoder, cliptextencoder, clipimageencoder, optimizer): """ Trains the U-Net parameters theta using image-conditioned diffusion loss. Assumes vaeencoder, cliptextencoder, and clipimageencoder are frozen. """ # 1. Encode Text # eT shape: (1, LT, D) eT = cliptextencoder(textprompt) # 2. Encode Reference Images # eIpre and eInext shape: (1, LI, D) eIpre = clipimageencoder(previmage) eInext = clipimageencoder(nextimage) # 3. Concatenate Reference Features to Text Embedding # Combined embedding shape: (1, LT + 2LI, D) # Note: The source concatenates eIref to eT along token length. # Assuming eIref is [eIpre, eInext] combinedembedding = concatenate([eT, eIpre, eInext], dim=1) # 4. Encode Input Image to Latent # z0 shape: (1, C, Hlat, Wlat) z0 = vaeencoder.encode(inputimage) # 5. Training Loop (Iterative) for iteration in range(totaliterations): # Sample noise and timestep epsilon = torch.randnlike(z0) t = samplerandomtimestep() # Create noisy latent zt # zt = alphat z0 + sigmat epsilon (Standard DDPM/DDIM noise schedule) zt = addnoise(z0, epsilon, t) # Predict noise using U-Net with cross-attention # The U-Net takes zt, t, and the combined embedding predictednoise = unet(zt, t, combinedembedding) # Calculate Loss loss = mseloss(predictednoise, epsilon) # Backpropagate and update U-Net parameters optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return unet.parameters() Parameters CLIP Image Encoder Input Size: 224 \times 224 \times 3. CLIP Image Encoder Hidden State Dimension: 1 \times 50 \times 768, where 50 is the token length (1 cls token + 49 patch tokens). Training Iterations: 625,000 iterations. Hardware: 4 NVIDIA V100 GPUs (32GB VRAM each). Batch Size: 4. A second fine-tuning stage that adds a ControlNet module to the frozen Stage 1 model to incorporate spatial relationships via depth maps derived from LiDAR point clouds. It derives depth maps for reference and input images by projecting 3D LiDAR point clouds onto the image plane and completing them using an off-the-shelf depth completion model. The ControlNet is initialized as a trainable copy of the U-Net’s encoder block from Stage 1. Depth features are encoded using a pre-trained depth encoder (structure identical to CLIP Image Encoder) and fused with CLIP image features via average pooling: \tilde{e}{Ii} = \text{AvgPool}(e{Ii}, e{Di}) for i \in \{\text{pre}, \text{next}\}. These fused features are concatenated with the text embedding and injected into the ControlNet via cross-attention. The ControlNet parameters \tilde{\theta} are trained using the loss: \mathcal{L}(\tilde{\theta}) = \mathbb{E}{z0, \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{1}), t, T, \{I{\text{ref}}, D{\text{ref}}\}} \left\| \epsilon - \epsilon\theta(zt, t, cD, eT, \tilde{e}{I{\text{ref}}}) \right\|2^2. Training iterations for this stage are 125,000 steps. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method is evaluated on KITTI and KITTI-360 datasets. Specific quantitative metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) are not provided in the source text, though ablation studies are referenced. Strengths: Effectively learns high-level semantic information and object existence from adjacent frames without requiring pose information, addressing the challenge of mutual occlusion in complex driving scenes. Limitations: Does not inherently capture spatial relationships between objects; this requires the subsequent Stage 2 (ControlNet). When to Use: When synthesizing street views where semantic consistency across adjacent frames is critical, and pose information is either unavailable or insufficient for the diffusion model to understand scene content. When Not to Use: When spatial accuracy and depth consistency are the primary requirements without additional depth conditioning (Stage 2). The method originates from the paper "SGD: Street View Synthesis with Gaussian Splatting and Diffusion Prior". It is part of a pipeline that uses a fine-tuned Stable Diffusion 1.5 model as a prior for optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting representations. The two-stage training strategy was developed to address the limitations of previous methods like ReconFusion, which introduced images and poses simultaneously, finding that pose alone was insufficient for diffusion models to fully understand 3D scenes with complex occlusions. The CLIP Image Encoder used is taken from clip-vit-B-32. The depth encoder is pre-trained using contrastive learning as proposed in [11] (not cited in the provided source list). The ControlNet module is based on the architecture described in [50] (not cited in the provided source list). name: Two-Plane Diffusion Model (TPDM)
head: Solving 3D Inverse Problem with TPDM, TDPM, TPDM (Two-Perpendicular Diffusion Models), TPDM Conditional Sampling, Two-Perpendicular Diffusion Models
body: Two-Plane Diffusion Model (TPDM) is a method for solving 3D inverse problems and generating 3D voxel volumes by training two separate 2D diffusion models on perpendicular planes and alternating their usage during the denoising process to maintain 3D consistency. It avoids the curse of dimensionality by assuming a 3D distribution is the product of 2D distributions, allowing it to handle 3D volumes without using a 3D diffusion model. Unlike Diffusion-Based Guidance for Radiance Field Optimization which guides optimization via gradients, TPDM performs conditional sampling directly on the volume using a primary model for measurement consistency and an auxiliary model for cross-plane consistency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Observed 3D measurement data Y \in \mathbb{R}^{N^{d1 \times d2 \times d3}}, forward operator A(\cdot): \mathbb{R}^{N^{d1 \times d2}} \to \mathbb{R}^{N^{d1 \times d2}}, pre-trained primary score model s{\theta^}, pre-trained auxiliary score model s{\phi^}, noise schedule \{\sigmai\}{i=0}^{10}, number of denoising steps N, integer hyperparameter K, and measurement consistency strength \lambda. Output: Reconstructed 3D volume X0 \in \mathbb{R}^{N^{d1 \times d2 \times d3}}. Data Structures: Xi: Tensor of shape N^{d1 \times d2 \times d3} representing the volume at denoising step i. Y: Tensor of shape N^{d1 \times d2 \times d3} representing the measurement data. s{\theta^}: Primary 2D diffusion model (score function). s{\phi^}: Auxiliary 2D diffusion model (score function). Parameters: K: Integer controlling the ratio of primary to auxiliary model usage. If K=4, the primary model is used 3 times and the auxiliary 1 time (ratio 3:1). \lambda: Hyperparameter controlling the strength of measurement consistency in the Data Consistency (DPS) step. N: Number of denoising steps. Typical value: 2000. \sigmat: Noise schedule parameter. Scheduled by a geometric sequence from \sigma0 = 0.01 to \sigma1 = 378. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the noisy volume XN by sampling from a Gaussian distribution N(0, \sigma1^2 I) with shape N^{d1 \times d2 \times d3}. 2. Iterate backwards from i = N-1 down to 0: a. Set time step t = i/N. b. Initialize an empty tensor Xi with the same shape as XN. c. Determine if the primary model is used. If K is an integer, use the condition mod(i, K) != 0. If true, use the primary model s{\theta^}; otherwise, use the auxiliary model s{\phi^}. (For non-integer K, sample from a Bernoulli distribution with probability p = 1 - 1/K). d. If using the primary model: i. Loop j from 1 to d3 (slicing along the Z-axis, or the axis perpendicular to the primary plane): 1. Extract current slice x = X{i+1}[:,:, j] and corresponding measurement slice y = Y[:,:, j]. 2. Compute the predicted clean sample \hat{x}0 = x + \sigmat^2 \cdot s{\theta^}(x, t). 3. Perform one step of the 2D Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DPM) using x, s{\theta^}, \sigmat, and t to get x'. 4. Apply data consistency correction: x'' = x' - \lambda \nablax \|A(\hat{x}0) - y\|2^2. 5. Assign the corrected slice to Xi[:,:, j] = x''. e. If using the auxiliary model: i. Loop j from 1 to d1 (slicing along the X-axis, or the axis perpendicular to the auxiliary plane): 1. Extract current slice x = X{i+1}[j,:,:]. 2. Perform one step of the 2D DPM using x, s{\phi^}, \sigmat, and t to get x'. 3. Assign the denoised slice to Xi[j,:,:] = x'. 3. Return X0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tpdmsample(Y, A, sthetastar, sphistar, sigmaschedule, N, K, lambdaval): """ Solves 3D inverse problem using Two-Plane Diffusion Model. Args: Y: Observed 3D measurement data, shape (N, d1, d2, d3) or (d1, d2, d3). Note: Source uses N^{d1xd2xd3} notation, implying batch N or dimension N. We assume shape (d1, d2, d3) for the volume tensor based on slicing logic. A: Forward operator function. Takes a 2D slice (d1, d2) and returns measurement. sthetastar: Primary 2D score model function. sphistar: Auxiliary 2D score model function. sigmaschedule: List of noise levels sigmat. N: Number of denoising steps. K: Integer controlling primary/auxiliary ratio. lambdaval: Strength of measurement consistency. Returns: X0: Reconstructed 3D volume. """ # Initialize XN ~ N(0, sigma1^2 I) # sigma1 is the largest noise level in the schedule sigma1 = sigmaschedule[0] # Assuming index 0 is sigma1=378 based on geometric sequence desc d1, d2, d3 = Y.shape Xnext = torch.randn(d1, d2, d3) sigma1 for i in range(N - 1, -1, -1): t = i / N sigmat = sigmaschedule[i] # Map step i to sigmat Xcurr = torch.emptylike(Xnext) # Determine model usage # If K is integer, use mod(i, K) != 0. # If K is float, use Bernoulli(1 - 1/K). # We assume integer K for standard implementation. useprimary = (i % K) != 0 if useprimary: # Primary model: slices along d3 (Z-axis) for j in range(d3): # Extract slice x from Xnext at [:,:, j] x = Xnext[:,:, j] # Extract measurement y from Y at [:,:, j] y = Y[:,:, j] # Predict x0hat # sthetastar returns score sthetastar(x, t) score = sthetastar(x, t) x0hat = x + (sigmat 2) score # Perform one step of 2D DPM # This is a black-box step function provided by the DPM sampler xprime = step2ddpm(x, sthetastar, sigmat, t) # Data consistency correction # A(x0hat) computes forward projection of the predicted clean slice # y is the observed measurement slice # We need gradient w.r.t x (the noisy slice input to the step) # However, the formula uses x'' = x' - lambda gradx ||A(x0hat) - y||^2 # Note: x' is the output of the DPM step. The gradient is typically # applied to the current estimate. In DPS, it's applied to the sample. # Here, the source defines x'' based on x'. # Compute residual # A is applied to x0hat. # We need to compute gradient of ||A(x0hat) - y||^2 w.r.t x? # Or w.r.t x'? The source says gradx. # In standard DPS, gradient is w.r.t the current noisy sample x. # But here x' is the denoised version. # Let's follow the source formula strictly: x'' = x' - lambda gradx ||...|| # This implies we need the gradient of the data term w.r.t x. # However, x0hat depends on x. # To implement this, we need to compute the gradient. # Let's assume we can compute gradx. residual = A(x0hat) - y loss = torch.sum(residual 2) gradx = torch.autograd.grad(loss, x, retaingraph=True)[0] xdoubleprime = xprime - lambdaval gradx Xcurr[:,:, j] = xdoubleprime else: # Auxiliary model: slices along d1 (X-axis) for j in range(d1): # Extract slice x from Xnext at [j,:,:] x = Xnext[j,:,:] # Perform one step of 2D DPM xprime = step2ddpm(x, sphistar, sigmat, t) Xcurr[j,:,:] = xprime Xnext = Xcurr return Xnext def step2ddpm(x, scoremodel, sigmat, t): """ Performs one step of the 2D Diffusion Probabilistic Model. This is a placeholder for the specific predictor-corrector or Euler-Maruyama step defined in the underlying DPM implementation (e.g., ncsnpp with VE-SDE). Since the source cites ncsnpp [40] and predictor-corrector sampling, this function encapsulates that logic. """ # Standard DPM step logic (e.g., Euler step for SDE) # This is a generic implementation of a DPM step. # The exact formula depends on the SDE (VE-SDE in this case). # For VE-SDE, the reverse process is: # x{t-1} = xt + (sigma{t-1}^2 - sigmat^2) scoremodel(xt, t) + sqrt(sigma{t-1}^2 - sigmat^2) z # where z ~ N(0, I). # However, the source just says "step 2D DPM". # We will implement a standard Euler-Maruyama step for VE-SDE. # Get next sigma # t is continuous index 0..1. We need to map to sigma schedule. # Assuming sigmaschedule is sorted descending. # t=0 is sigma1 (large), t=1 is sigma0 (small). # In the loop, i goes N-1 to 0. t = i/N. # So t=0 is step N-1 (sigma1), t=1 is step 0 (sigma0). # We need sigma{tnext} and sigmat. # This function requires access to the sigma schedule. # For simplicity, we assume the caller handles sigma mapping or this is a high-level step. # Given the constraint "valid Python", we must define it. # But we don't have the sigma schedule here. # We will assume a standard DPM step is called. # To make it self-contained, we need the sigma values. # Let's assume the caller passes sigmanext. pass Note: The pseudocode above uses a placeholder for step2ddpm. In a real implementation, this would be the specific sampling step (e.g., Euler-Maruyama for VE-SDE) defined in the underlying DPM library (ncsnpp). The core TPDM logic is the alternating slice processing and the DPS correction. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The noise schedule spans a large range (\sigma0=0.01 to \sigma1=378). Floating-point precision may affect the score estimation at high noise levels. Boundaries: The slicing loops assume the volume dimensions d1, d2, d3 are accessible. If the volume is not cubic, the slicing logic must adapt to the chosen primary/auxiliary planes. Degenerate Input: The method assumes the forward operator A is differentiable to compute the gradient \nablax \|A(\hat{x}0) - y\|2^2. TPDM can generate 3D voxel volumes without measurement guidance by skipping the DPS step and only using the alternating 2D DPM steps. This demonstrates that 3D consistency arises from the alternative denoising algorithms, not just measurement guidance. The two 2D models are trained on 2D slices extracted from 3D volumes. The primary model is trained on slices along one axis (e.g., d3), and the auxiliary model on slices along a perpendicular axis (e.g., d1). Time Complexity: The method iterates N times (typically 2000). In each step, it processes all slices of the volume. For the primary model, it processes d3 slices; for the auxiliary, d1 slices. The complexity is O(N \cdot (d1 + d3)) 2D DPM steps per volume. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the 3D volume X and the measurement Y. The 2D models are loaded once. Memory is O(d1 \cdot d2 \cdot d3). Measured Performance: SV-CT (36-view): TPDM achieved PSNR 38.25 and SSIM (Axial) 0.947, outperforming DPS (38.20, 0.942) and score-CT (37.56, 0.951). CS-MRI (×48 acceleration): TPDM achieved PSNR 37.17 and SSIM (Axial) 0.966, outperforming DiffusionMBIR (34.83, 0.950) and DPS (35.30, 0.951). Strengths: Avoids artifacts in the batch direction that plague 2D solvers like DPS when applied to 3D. Works in an unsupervised manner without fine-tuning for individual inverse problems. Limitations: Performance on non-primary planes (e.g., Coronal/Sagittal in SV-CT) can be lower than the primary plane, though still competitive. Requires pre-training of two 2D models. TPDM was introduced in the paper "Improving 3D Imaging with Pre-Trained Perpendicular 2D Diffusion Models" (ICCV 2023). It addresses the limitations of 2D diffusion models (like DPS) when applied to 3D inverse problems, which suffer from artifacts in the batch direction. The method leverages the assumption that a 3D distribution can be approximated by the product of 2D distributions on perpendicular planes, allowing it to solve general 3D inverse problems (such as CS-MRI, SV-CT, and MRI ZSR) and generate 3D volumes without a 3D diffusion model. name: Score Distillation Loss Modifications
body: This family comprises modifications to the Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) objective used in diffusion-guided radiance field optimization. While standard SDS predicts noise at a single timestep to guide optimization, these modifications introduce mechanisms such as multi-step interval supervision, inpainting conditioning, background semantic prompting, and latent-space re-noising to address specific artifacts like floating objects, black holes, and low-resolution details. They set themselves apart from the parent Diffusion-Based Guidance for Radiance Field Optimization by altering the loss computation or the conditioning inputs to the diffusion model rather than changing the core gradient backpropagation mechanism. All methods in this family operate within the differentiable rendering loop where a radiance field \Theta is optimized to minimize a loss derived from a frozen diffusion model. The core mechanism involves: 1. Rendering an image I (or latent z0) from the current parameters \Theta. 2. Adding noise \epsilon to obtain a noisy sample xt (or zt) at timestep t. 3. Querying the frozen diffusion model \epsilon\theta to predict the noise \hat{\epsilon}. 4. Computing a gradient signal based on the residual \hat{\epsilon} - \epsilon and backpropagating it through the differentiable renderer to update \Theta. The shared mathematical foundation is the SDS gradient: \nabla\Theta L = \mathbb{E}{t,\epsilon} \left[ \omega(t) \cdot (\hat{\epsilon}\theta(xt, \cdot) - \epsilon) \frac{\partial xt}{\partial \Theta} \right] where \omega(t) is a weighting function dependent on the diffusion schedule. The modifications in this family alter the inputs to \hat{\epsilon}\theta (e.g., masks, background prompts), the set of timesteps t considered (intervals, schedules), or the space in which the optimization occurs (latent residuals). Interval Score Matching (ISM) modifies the standard single-step SDS by incorporating supervision from multiple interval steps of the diffusion process [8995-interval-score-matching.md]. It replaces the standard DDPM forward process with DDIM inversion to determine noise levels for these intervals, mitigating high reconstruction error inherent in single-step prediction [8995-interval-score-matching.md]. It is chosen when single-step SDS yields poor geometric consistency or high error. Link: Interval Score Matching. Inpainting SDS Loss (iSDS) conditions the diffusion model on a binary mask M and a masked version of the rendered image IM to generate content that harmonizes with existing scene context [11185-inpainting-sds-loss.md]. Unlike vanilla SDS, which often produces floating objects, iSDS ensures proper pose and geometry integration by providing visual context to the inpainting model [11185-inpainting-sds-loss.md]. It is primarily used for inserting new objects into existing NeRFs or inpainting missing regions [11185-inpainting-sds-loss.md]. Link: Inpainting SDS Loss. Mask+SDS with Background Prompt addresses the "black hole" artifact in NeRF editing by explicitly providing a background description P{bg} alongside the object prompt P{obj} [14382-mask-sds-with-background-prompt.md]. It concatenates these into a single prompt (e.g., "object in background") to guide the diffusion model's text encoder, ensuring the surrounding environment is semantically consistent [14382-mask-sds-with-background-prompt.md]. It sets itself apart from standard Mask+SDS by adding semantic context and from Mask+SDS+CLIP by relying on the diffusion model rather than a separate CLIP loss for background filling [14382-mask-sds-with-background-prompt.md]. Link: Mask+SDS with Background Prompt. Renoised Score Distillation (RSD) is designed for 2D image resolution and super-resolution within iterative 3D synchronization [16424-renoised-score-distillation-rsd.md]. It optimizes learnable latent residuals h\theta by combining ancestral sampling and SDS, guiding optimization towards intermediate denoised latents z{t-1} over a linearly decreasing time schedule [16424-renoised-score-distillation-rsd.md]. Unlike standard SDS (limited details) or ancestral sampling (structural inconsistency), RSD generates sharp, high-resolution details consistent with low-resolution conditioning [16424-renoised-score-distillation-rsd.md]. Link: Renoised Score Distillation (RSD). A baseline method using per-scene text prompts to guide masked region generation via SDS loss. It improves quality by gradually and uniformly decreasing the maximum noise step t{max} to the minimum noise step t{min} during fitting, leveraging high noise levels for global structure and low noise levels for detail refinement. Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) was introduced in DreamFusion as a method to optimize 3D representations using 2D diffusion priors. The modifications in this family emerged to address specific limitations of DreamFusion, such as the "slimy" appearance, floating objects, and lack of background coherence. Inpainting SDS and Mask+SDS variants were developed to enable controllable editing and object insertion in NeRFs. Renoised Score Distillation was introduced to handle super-resolution tasks where standard SDS fails to preserve high-frequency details. Interval Score Matching was proposed to reduce reconstruction error by utilizing multiple diffusion steps. Reference-guided Controllable Inpainting of Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/ICCV51070.2023.01633, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Interval Score Matching
head: LucidDreamer (ISM)
body: Interval Score Matching (ISM) is a modification to Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) that replaces the standard Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) forward process with Denoising Diffusion Implicit Model (DDIM) inversion. It introduces supervision from multiple interval steps within the diffusion process to mitigate the high reconstruction error associated with single-step updates. This approach is primarily associated with the LucidDreamer method. Inputs: A frozen diffusion model \epsilon\theta, a radiance field \Theta, a prompt, and a diffusion schedule. Outputs: Gradients \nabla\Theta L for updating \Theta. Data Structures: x0: The rendered image (or latent) from \Theta. xt: The noisy sample at timestep t. \hat{\epsilon}: The noise prediction from the frozen model. Steps: 1. Render an image x0 from the current radiance field parameters \Theta. 2. Instead of using the standard DDPM forward noising process, apply DDIM inversion to generate the noisy samples xt from x0. This allows for deterministic inversion of the diffusion process. 3. Select a set of interval timesteps t rather than a single timestep. 4. For each interval step t, query the frozen diffusion model \epsilon\theta to predict the noise \hat{\epsilon}\theta(xt, \cdot). 5. Compute the gradient signal using the residual between the predicted noise and the actual noise added during inversion, weighted by a schedule function \omega(t). 6. Backpropagate the gradient through the differentiable renderer to update \Theta. The core distinction from standard SDS is the use of DDIM inversion and interval supervision. Standard SDS typically uses DDPM forward noising and may rely on a single timestep or a specific schedule. ISM leverages the deterministic nature of DDIM to ensure consistency across interval steps, reducing the error that arises when approximating the gradient with a single step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def intervalscorematching(renderfn, diffusionmodel, prompt, theta, timesteps, weights): # 1. Render current image x0 = renderfn(theta) # 2. DDIM Inversion to get noisy samples # Note: Exact inversion algorithm details are not provided in sources noisysamples = ddiminvert(x0, diffusionmodel, timesteps) gradients = 0 # 3. Iterate over interval steps for t, weight in zip(timesteps, weights): xt = noisysamples[t] # 4. Predict noise epsilonpred = diffusionmodel.predictnoise(xt, t, prompt) # 5. name: Inpainting SDS Loss
head: Inpainting-based Score Distillation Sampling, SDS loss with scene context
body: Inpainting SDS Loss (LiSDS) is a modification of the Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss that uses a pre-trained or fine-tuned 2D inpainting diffusion model to generate 3D content conditioned on existing scene context. It solves the problem of incomplete geometry and poor compositional harmony when inserting objects into existing scenes, which vanilla SDS often fails to achieve by generating isolated parts (e.g., only a head) that do not align with the background. Unlike vanilla SDS, which conditions only on a text prompt, LiSDS conditions the diffusion model on a masked version of the rendered image and a binary mask, ensuring the generated object seamlessly integrates with the established scene. The method operates within the standard differentiable rendering loop Parent. It replaces the standard noise prediction \epsilon\theta(xt; y, t) with an inpainting-aware noise prediction \epsilon\phi(xt; y, IM, M, t), where the model predicts noise for the masked region while preserving the unmasked region IM. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current radiance field parameters \Theta, camera pose, text prompt y, binary mask M, and the rendered image I (or latent z0). Output: Gradient \nabla\Theta L to update \Theta. Data Structures: Mask M: A binary mask of the same spatial dimensions as the rendered image. It is derived by projecting the 3D bounding box of the target object into the current camera viewpoint. Pixels inside the box are 1 (masked/inpainting region), and pixels outside are 0 (context region). Masked Image IM: The rendered image I where pixels outside the mask M are preserved, and pixels inside M are typically zeroed out or replaced with a neutral value before adding noise, depending on the specific inpainting model implementation. Steps: 1. Render: Render the current image I from \Theta using the current camera pose. 2. Mask Generation: Compute the binary mask M by projecting the 3D bounding box of the object being optimized onto the image plane. 3. Masked Input Preparation: Create the masked image IM by applying M to I. The specific handling of the masked region (e.g., zeroing) depends on the diffusion model's requirements. 4. Noise Addition: Sample a timestep t and Gaussian noise \epsilon. Add noise to IM to obtain the noisy sample xt. 5. Inpainting Noise Prediction: Query the frozen inpainting diffusion model \epsilon\phi with inputs: noisy image xt, text embedding y, masked image IM, mask M, and timestep t. The model outputs the predicted noise \hat{\epsilon} = \epsilon\phi(xt; y, IM, M, t). 6. Gradient Computation: Compute the SDS gradient using the residual between the predicted noise and the actual noise, weighted by \omega(t), and backpropagate through the renderer. Formula: The gradient for the radiance field parameters \Theta is: \nabla\Theta L{SDS} = \mathbb{E}{t,\epsilon,C} \left[ \omega(t) \cdot (\epsilon\phi(It; y, IM, M, t) - \epsilon) \frac{\partial It}{\partial \Theta} \right] where: \epsilon\phi is the inpainting diffusion model. It is the noise-perturbed masked image at timestep t. y is the text prompt embedding. IM is the masked image (context). M is the binary mask derived from the projected 3D bounding box. \epsilon is the sampled Gaussian noise. \omega(t) is the weighting function Parent. Alternative Formulation (LiSDS): In some implementations (e.g., DITTO-NeRF), the loss is formulated as a mean squared error between the predicted noise and the actual noise, used to optimize latent vectors or rendered latents: L{iSDS}(\phi, g(\theta)) = \mathbb{E}{t,\epsilon} \left[ ||\epsilon\phi(xt; y, t, M) - \epsilont||^22 \right] where xt is the noise image, \epsilont is the actual noise, and M is the binary mask. This is often combined with a Reliability-guided loss LR for in-boundary regions and sparsity loss L{sp}. Parameters: Mask M: Derived from projecting the 3D bounding box. Training Schedule: In some variants, a refinement step is applied during the last 10% of training, where random foreground patches are masked and optimized with LiSDS to improve texture continuity. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Mask Precision: The accuracy of the projected 3D bounding box directly affects the quality of the inpainting. Incorrect projection leads to misaligned generation. Context Leakage: If the mask M is too small or the inpainting model does not properly condition on IM, the generated object may not harmonize with the scene. Incomplete Generation: Vanilla SDS may generate incomplete objects; LiSDS mitigates this by conditioning on the scene context. MVIP-NeRF is a diffusion-based method for multiview-consistent inpainting of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs). It solves the problem of reconstructing missing geometry and texture in masked regions of a scene while maintaining consistency across multiple camera views. Unlike prior approaches that rely on independent 2D inpainting per view—often resulting in inconsistencies and poor geometry—MVIP-NeRF jointly optimizes across views. It employs Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) with a text-conditioned diffusion model to guide inpainting in masked regions, alongside RGB reconstruction in visible areas. RefFusion inpaints one reference image using an inpainting Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) on both global and locally cropped versions of the reference view. It utilizes SDS loss to distill learned priors from the adapted LDM into the scene, incorporating a discriminator loss and depth loss to improve quality. Quantitatively, RefFusion surpassed all baselines in LPIPSdir (0.4283) compared to NeRF-In (0.4884), SPIn-NeRF (SD) (0.5701), SPIn-NeRF (LaMa) (0.4654), Inpaint3D (0.5150), Reference-guided inpainting (SDV2) (0.4532), and Reference-guided inpainting (SDXL) (0.4453). A refinement step applied during the last 10% of training to improve texture and color continuity by masking foreground patches and optimizing them with LiSDS, excluding the Reliability-guided loss (LR). During this phase, if an in-boundary view is sampled, LR is excluded, and a random patch mask is applied to the foreground to refine the corresponding part using LiSDS. Time Complexity: Similar to vanilla SDS, as it involves one forward pass through the diffusion model per gradient step. However, the need to project 3D bounding boxes to generate masks adds a small overhead. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the mask M and potentially the masked image IM. Performance: Generates complete objects with proper poses that seamlessly integrate with the scene, outperforming vanilla SDS which often generates incomplete parts. Strengths: Ensures harmonized composition and complete geometry by leveraging scene context. Limitations: Requires accurate 3D bounding box estimation for mask generation. May require fine-tuning of the diffusion model for specific inpainting tasks. When to use: When inserting objects into existing scenes or inpainting missing regions in NeRFs. When not to use: When generating objects from scratch without scene context, vanilla SDS may be sufficient. Inpainting SDS Loss was introduced to address the limitations of vanilla SDS in scene composition tasks. Vanilla SDS often generates incomplete objects that fail to composite well with the background. By conditioning the diffusion model on masked images and masks, LiSDS leverages the generative priors of 2D inpainting models to guide 3D optimization. The concept has been explored in works such as DITTO-NeRF and GO-NeRF, and is related to methods like RefFusion and MVIP-NeRF. name: MVIP-NeRF
head: MVIPNeRF
body: MVIP-NeRF is a diffusion-based method for multiview-consistent inpainting of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs). It reconstructs missing geometry and texture in masked regions while maintaining consistency across multiple camera views. Unlike prior approaches that rely on independent 2D inpainting per view—often resulting in inconsistencies and poor geometry—MVIP-NeRF jointly optimizes across views. It employs Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) with a text-conditioned diffusion model to guide inpainting in masked regions, alongside RGB reconstruction in visible areas. Inputs: An initial NeRF representation (implicitly or explicitly parameterized). An RGB sequence of images corresponding to the camera poses. Per-frame binary masks indicating visible (unmasked) and missing (masked) regions. A text description of the scene content. Outputs: An optimized NeRF model with inpainted geometry and texture in masked regions. Data Structures: NeRF: Standard volumetric representation storing density (\sigma) and color (c) at query points. Diffusion Model: A pre-trained 2D text-conditioned diffusion model used for score estimation. Normal Map: Distilled geometric consistency signal derived from the NeRF. Parameters: Text Prompt: Describes the semantic content to be inpainted. Mask: Binary mask per view distinguishing observed from unobserved pixels. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Rendering: For each view i, render the RGB image Ii and normal map Ni from the current NeRF using standard volume rendering. 2. Loss Formulation: Compute the total loss as a combination of reconstruction and inpainting terms: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rec} + \mathcal{L}{inpaint} 3. Reconstruction Loss (\mathcal{L}{rec}): Compute the pixel-wise difference between the rendered image and the ground truth image only in the unmasked (visible) regions. 4. Inpainting Loss (\mathcal{L}{inpaint}): Compute the Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss in the masked regions. Sample noise \epsilon and add it to the rendered image representation. Pass the noisy input through the text-conditioned diffusion model to predict the noise \hat{\epsilon}. Compute the SDS gradient based on the difference between sampled and predicted noise, weighted by the mask. 5. Multi-View Scoring: Incorporate a multi-view scoring mechanism to improve consistency and sharpness, especially under large view variations. 6. Geometric Distillation: Distill normal maps to enforce geometric consistency. 7. Optimization: Update the NeRF parameters jointly across all views. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainmvipnerf(nerf, images, masks, textprompt, numsteps): """ Optimizes NeRF for multiview-consistent inpainting. Args: nerf: Neural Radiance Field model. images: List of RGB images for each view. masks: List of binary masks for each view (1 for visible, 0 for masked). textprompt: String describing the scene. numsteps: Number of optimization steps. """ for step in range(numsteps): totalloss = 0.0 for viewidx in range(len(images)): # 1. Render current NeRF renderedrgb, renderednormals = nerf.render(viewidx) # 2. Compute Reconstruction Loss (visible regions) visiblemask = masks[viewidx] == 1 if visiblemask.any(): recloss = sum((renderedrgb[visiblemask] - images[viewidx][visiblemask]) 2) / visiblemask.sum() totalloss += recloss # 3. Compute Inpainting Loss (masked regions) maskedmask = masks[viewidx] == 0 if maskedmask.any(): # Sample noise for SDS noise = random.normal(renderedrgb.shape) noisyrgb = renderedrgb + noise # Pre-trained 2D diffusion model forward pass predictednoise = diffusionmodel(noisyrgb, textprompt) # Standard SDS gradient term sdsterm = (noise - predictednoise) totalloss += sum(sdsterm) / sdsterm.numel() # 4. Geometric consistency via normal distillation # Geometric consistency prior for normal maps normalloss = sum((renderednormals - geometricnormalprior(renderednormals)) 2) / renderednormals.numel() totalloss += normalloss # 5. Joint optimization across views # Standard automatic differentiation gradients = computegradients(totalloss, nerf.parameters) nerf.step(gradients) def diffusionmodel(noisyrgb, textprompt): # Pre-trained 2D text-conditioned diffusion model forward pass return model.predict(noisyrgb, textprompt) def geometricnormalprior(normals): # Geometric consistency prior for normal maps return normals def computegradients(loss, params): # Standard automatic differentiation (backpropagation) return autograd.grad(loss, params, retaingraph=True) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Large View Variations: Inconsistencies may arise if the multi-view scoring mechanism is not robust to large angular differences. Mask Boundaries: Sharp transitions between masked and unmasked regions can cause artifacts if the diffusion prior does not align well with the visible geometry. Text Prompt Ambiguity: Incorrect or vague text prompts can lead to semantically incorrect inpainting. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of views, diffusion steps, and NeRF optimization iterations. Joint optimization across views ensures consistency but requires processing all views per step. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the NeRF representation, intermediate rendered images/normals, and the diffusion model state. Strengths: Ensures multiview consistency, handles large view variations better than independent 2D inpainting, produces high-fidelity results without high-resolution training data. Limitations: Requires a text prompt. Relies on a pre-trained diffusion model and joint optimization across views. When to use: When multiview consistency is critical and the scene has significant missing regions. When not to use: When text prompts are unavailable or independent per-view processing is sufficient. MVIP-NeRF was introduced in May 2024. It addresses limitations of prior NeRF inpainting methods that relied on independent 2D inpainting, which often resulted in inconsistencies and poor geometry. It builds on the concept of Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) and extends it to a multi-view setting with a specific formulation for consistency. It is used for NeRF inpainting tasks. name: Mask+SDS with Background Prompt
head: Mask+SDS+BGT
body: Mask+SDS with Background Prompt is a differentiable rendering optimization method that addresses the "black hole" artifact in masked NeRF editing, where occluded regions lack supervision and collapse to empty space. It distinguishes itself from standard Masked SDS by explicitly appending a background description to the diffusion model's text prompt, guiding the generation of surrounding content while the mask restricts changes to the target object. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A radiance field \Theta (NeRF parameters), a binary mask M identifying the editable region, an object text prompt P{obj}, and a background text prompt P{bg}. Output: Optimized radiance field \Theta'. Data Structures: Mask M: A 2D tensor of the same resolution as the rendered image, where M{ij}=1 if pixel (i,j) is in the editable region, and 0 otherwise. Text Prompts: Strings P{obj} and P{bg}. Steps: 1. Render: Render an image I from the current radiance field \Theta using the current camera pose. 2. Combine Prompt: Construct the full text prompt P{full} by concatenating the object and background prompts. For example, if P{obj} is "a lego man head" and P{bg} is "leaves", then P{full} is "a lego man head in leaves". 3. Noise: Add noise \epsilon to the rendered image I to obtain the noisy sample xt at timestep t. 4. Diffusion Query: Query the frozen diffusion model \epsilon\theta with xt and P{full} to predict the noise \hat{\epsilon}. 5. Compute Loss: Calculate the SDS loss. To prevent unwanted content generation in the unmasked region, a strong weighting is applied to the unmasked pixels. The loss is defined as: L = \mathbb{E}{t,\epsilon} \left[ \omega(t) \cdot (\hat{\epsilon}\theta(xt, P{full}) - \epsilon) \frac{\partial xt}{\partial \Theta} \right] where the gradient is masked such that only the unmasked region contributes significantly to the loss to avoid altering the background, or conversely, the mask is used to restrict the object deformation while the background prompt guides the surroundings. Note: The source indicates Eq. 10 is used to strongly control the unmasked part to avoid unwanted content. 6. Backpropagate: Backpropagate the gradient through the differentiable renderer to update \Theta. Parameters: Mask Weight (\lambda{unmask}): A hyperparameter controlling the strength of the constraint on the unmasked region. The source compares different values of \lambda{unmask} in Eq. 14. Text Prompts: P{obj} and P{bg} are user-defined. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Black Holes: Previously occluded or covered regions may develop into black holes (empty space) due to the lack of explicit supervision for those areas when only the object prompt is used or when the background prompt is insufficiently integrated. A variant that removes the background prompt from the diffusion model's text prompt and instead uses CLIP with a background prompt to fill occluded regions. It provides a view of the unmasked region to CLIP along with a background prompt to supervise and fill the black hole. While CLIP fills the black hole with reasonable texture, the generated shapes retain artifacts from the original occluded geometry (e.g., petal shapes). The final combined editing configuration that uses SDS with a full prompt (object + background) and CLIP with a background prompt on unmasked views. It sets the diffusion model text prompt to include both object and background (e.g., "object in background") and simultaneously feeds unmasked views to CLIP with the background prompt to supervise the surroundings. This produces normal shapes and fills black holes with appropriate background material (e.g., green leaves around a blue rose). Strengths: Explicitly guides the generation of surrounding content, resulting in more reasonable shapes for the edited object compared to using only an object prompt. Limitations: Without additional mechanisms (like CLIP), the previously covered parts of the object can become "black holes". Performance: Not given in the sources. Originated in the paper "RePaint-NeRF: NeRF Editing via Semantic Masks and Diffusion Models". The method was developed to improve NeRF editing by leveraging semantic masks and diffusion models, specifically addressing the issue of generating coherent backgrounds and avoiding artifacts in masked regions. name: Renoised Score Distillation (RSD)
body:
Renoised Score Distillation (RSD) is a score-distillation objective designed for 2D image resolution and super-resolution, specifically within the context of refining latent vectors during the upscaling stage of iterative 3D synchronization. It combines features from ancestral sampling and Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) to generate sharp, high-resolution images that remain consistent with low-resolution (LR) conditioning. Unlike standard SDS which optimizes in the z0 space, RSD formulates the loss in the latent space of intermediate timesteps, guiding the image towards the predicted denoised latent \hat{z}{t-1} over multiple noise predictions. This approach produces sharper details than SDS while maintaining better LR consistency than default ancestral sampling. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Latent z0: The encoded latent of the interpolated low-resolution image (shape H 	imes W 	imes C). Conditioning y: A concatenation of text prompt embeddings (y{text}), noise level embeddings (y{noise\level}), and the LR image embedding (I{lr}). Timestep bounds: t{min} and t{max}. Hyperparameters: Learning rate, number of super-resolution iterations (max\sr\iter). Outputs: Refined latent residuals h	heta: A zero-initialized tensor of the same shape as z0, containing the high-resolution details. Data Structures: h	heta: Learnable latent residuals, initialized to zero. z'0: Refined latent, computed as z0 + h	heta. \epsilon\phi: The noise prediction network (UNet backbone of SD	imes4), parameterized by \phi.  ar{\alpha}t: The cumulative noise schedule coefficient at timestep t. \sigmat: The standard deviation of Gaussian noise samples at timestep t. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize learnable latent residuals h	heta = 0 with the same shape as z0. 2. Loop for sr\iter from 0 to max\sr\iter: a. Sample noise \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I). b. Construct conditioning y = y{text} + y{noise\level} + I{lr}. c. Calculate current timestep t using a linearly decreasing schedule: t = t{max} - (t{max} - t{min}) \cdot  rac{sr\iter}{max\sr\iter} d. Compute the refined latent z'0: z'0 = \sqrt{z0 + h	heta} (Note: The source notation \sqrt{z0 + h	heta} is used verbatim. In standard diffusion contexts, this typically implies element-wise addition z0 + h	heta, but the square root symbol is present in the source equation.) e. Apply the forward noising process (Eq. 1 in) to z'0 at timestep t to obtain z't: z't = \sqrt{ ar{\alpha}t} z'0 + \sqrt{1 -  ar{\alpha}t} \epsilon f. Apply the forward noising process to z'0 at timestep t-1 to obtain z'{t-1}: z'{t-1} = \sqrt{ ar{\alpha}{t-1}} z'0 + \sqrt{1 -  ar{\alpha}{t-1}} \epsilon g. Pass z't and conditioning y to the UNet \epsilon\phi to predict the noise residual: \hat{\epsilon}\phi = \epsilon\phi(z't, y, t) h. Construct the predicted denoised latent \hat{z}{t-1} using the DDPM reverse process equation (Eq. 3 in): \hat{z}{t-1} = \sqrt{ rac{1}{ ar{\alpha}t}} \left( z't - \sqrt{1 -  ar{\alpha}t} \hat{\epsilon}\phi ight) + \sigmat \epsilon (Note: The source formula in Algorithm 2 line 9 is written as \hat{z}{t-1} = \sqrt{ rac{1}{ ar{\alpha}t}} z't - \sqrt{ rac{1}{1- ar{\alpha}t}} \hat{\epsilon}\phi(z't, y, t) + \sigmat \epsilon. This is mathematically equivalent to the standard DDPM denoising step if \sigmat = \sqrt{ rac{1- ar{\alpha}{t-1}}{1- ar{\alpha}t}} \sigmat^{standard}, but we follow the source's explicit formula.) i. Compute the L1 loss between the current noised latent z'{t-1} and the predicted denoised latent \hat{z}{t-1}: L{RSD} = \| z'{t-1} - \hat{z}{t-1} \| j. Backpropagate gradients through z'{t-1} towards h	heta and take a gradient descent step: h	heta \leftarrow h	heta - \eta 
abla{h	heta} L{RSD} 3. Return the refined latent residuals h	heta. Formulas: RSD Loss: L{RSD} = \| z{t-1} - \hat{z}{t-1} \| where z{t-1} is the current noised latent at t-1 and \hat{z}{t-1} is the predicted denoised latent from zt. Gradient: 
abla	heta L{RSD} =  rac{\partial \| z{t-1} - \hat{z}{t-1} \|}{\partial z{t-1}}  rac{\partial z{t-1}}{\partial 	heta} Relation to SDS: RSD can be interpreted as a renoised variant of SDS. While SDS optimizes in z0 space as 
abla	heta L{SDS} = \gamma(t) \sqrt{ rac{1}{1- ar{\alpha}t}} (z0 - \hat{z}0)  rac{\partial z0}{\partial 	heta}, RSD applies the forward noising process to both z0 and \hat{z}0 towards time t-1. Parameters: Scheduler: DDPM scheduler. Time Schedule: Linearly decreasing time schedule following ancestral sampling, from t{max} to t{min}. Patch Sampling: Uniform random crops of 128 	imes 128 resolution in latent space (corresponding to 512 	imes 512 image patches) are used for optimization. Text Prompt: Fixed prompt: <subject>, high resolution, 4K, photo, where <subject> is the scene name. Learning Rate: Constant 1 	imes 10^{-2} for all learnable parameters. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Inconsistency: Default ancestral sampling can generate details structurally inconsistent with the conditioned LR image, aggravating multi-view inconsistency. Detail Limitation: SDS produces LR-consistent features but with limited details. Implementation Note: In practice, \hat{z}{t-1} can be obtained directly from \hat{\epsilon}\phi(zt, y, t) using the DDPM denoising equation instead of renoising \hat{z}0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def RSD(z0, ytext, ynoiselevel, Ilr, tmin, tmax, maxsriter, lr): """ Renoised Score Distillation optimization loop. Args: z0: Initial latent (H, W, C) ytext: Text prompt embeddings ynoiselevel: Noise level embeddings Ilr: Low-resolution image embedding tmin: Minimum timestep tmax: Maximum timestep maxsriter: Number of super-resolution iterations lr: Learning rate Returns: htheta: Refined latent residuals (H, W, C) """ # Initialize learnable latent residuals htheta = torch.zeroslike(z0) # Precompute schedule coefficients if available, otherwise compute on fly # Assuming access to alphabar schedule array alphabar for sriter in range(maxsriter): # 1. Sample noise epsilon = torch.randnlike(z0) # 2. Construct conditioning y = concatenate([ytext, ynoiselevel, Ilr]) # 3. Calculate timestep t (linearly decreasing) t = tmax - (tmax - tmin) (sriter / maxsriter) # 4. Compute refined latent z'0 # Note: Source uses sqrt(z0 + htheta). Interpreted as element-wise sqrt of sum. z0prime = torch.sqrt(z0 + htheta) # 5. Forward noising at t alphat = alphabar[t] ztprime = torch.sqrt(alphat) z0prime + torch.sqrt(1 - alphat) epsilon # 6. Forward noising at t-1 alphatminus1 = alphabar[t - 1] ztminus1prime = torch.sqrt(alphatminus1) z0prime + torch.sqrt(1 - alphatminus1) epsilon # 7. Predict noise using UNet # epsilonphi is the noise prediction network epsilonphi = UNet(ztprime, y, t) # 8. Construct predicted denoised latent zhat{t-1} # Formula from source Algorithm 2 line 9: # zhat{t-1} = sqrt(1/alphat) zt' - sqrt(1/(1-alphat)) epsilonphi + sigmat epsilon # Note: sigmat is the standard deviation of Gaussian noise samples at t. sigmat = getsigmat(t) # Implementation detail for DDPM sigmat zhattminus1 = (torch.sqrt(1 / alphat) ztprime) - \ (torch.sqrt(1 / (1 - alphat)) epsilonphi) + \ (sigmat epsilon) # 9. Compute L1 loss loss = torch.mean(torch.abs(ztminus1prime - zhattminus1)) # 10. Backpropagate and update loss.backward() # Gradient descent step on htheta # Note: Gradients accumulate in htheta.grad with torch.nograd(): htheta -= lr htheta.grad htheta.grad.zero() return htheta A framework that alternates between upscaling LR rendered images with diffusion models (using RSD) and updating the underlying 3D representation (NeRF) with standard training. RSD is the specific upscaling method used within this framework. The overall method that utilizes I3DS and RSD to achieve high-quality super-resolution NeRF using only LR training images and a pretrained 2D diffusion upscaler (SD	imes4). Time Complexity: The optimization time for DiSR-NeRF (which includes RSD) is longer than standard NGP or NeRF-SR due to the RSD optimization steps, but it is faster than DreamFusion-SDS because I3DS segregates upscaling and synchronization stages. Memory Complexity: Uses dynamic ray sampling to increase ray count when the occupancy grid is pruned, optimizing GPU memory usage. Patch sampling (128 	imes 128 latent space) is used to further optimize speed and memory compared to full image optimization. Performance: RSD produces sharper details compared to SDS and better LR consistency compared to ancestral sampling. Quantitative results on synthetic and real-world datasets show DiSR-NeRF outperforms existing baselines (NGP, SD	imes4, NeRF-SR, DreamFusion, IN2N) in PSNR and SSIM. Strengths: Generates sharp, high-resolution images consistent with LR conditioning; alleviates the need for high-resolution reference images or large-scale multi-view HR datasets. Limitations: Requires a pretrained 2D diffusion upscaler (SD	imes4); optimization time is increased compared to non-diffusion methods. Origin: Introduced in the paper "DiSR-NeRF: Diffusion-Guided View-Consistent Super-Resolution NeRF". History: Developed to address the limitations of standard NeRF super-resolution methods, which either lack detail (SDS) or suffer from multi-view inconsistency (ancestral sampling). Usage: Used in the upscaling stage of the I3DS framework for super-resolving NeRFs from low-resolution inputs.
