name: Synthetic Training with EG3D Supervision
head: Alternating supervision training, Distillation Training, On-the-fly Augmentation
body: This method trains an image-to-triplane encoder to reconstruct a 3D radiance field representation from a single input image by leveraging synthetic data generated by a frozen, pretrained EG3D generator. It solves the problem of generalizing single-image portrait synthesis by ensuring the encoder produces triplanes that are consistent not only with the input reference view but also with novel multiview renderings, thereby enforcing geometric and photometric coherence. It differs from standard supervised training by using a frozen generative model as a ground-truth oracle and alternating between reference-view and multiview supervision to prevent overfitting to the specific distribution of the input image. Inputs and Outputs Input: A single high-resolution reference image I{512} rendered from a reference camera P{ref} (synthetic in training). Output: A predicted triplane \hat{T} and associated rendered images (If, \hat{I}{128}, \hat{I}{512}, \hat{I}D) from the encoder's triplane. Frozen Components: EG3D generator (produces ground-truth triplanes T and images), EG3D MLP decoder, EG3D super-resolution network, EG3D dual discriminator. Trainable Components: Image-to-triplane encoder E, MLP decoder, super-resolution network, dual discriminator (fine-tuned). Data Structures Triplane T: A 3-channel feature map per plane (front, side, top) intersecting at the head center. Camera Parameters P: Focal length, principal point, orientation, and position. Rendered Images: Four resolutions/types per camera: feature image If, 128x128 image I{128}, 512x512 image I{512}, and depth map ID. Numbered Steps 1. Synthesize Ground Truth: Sample a latent vector z and pass it through the frozen EG3D generator to obtain a ground-truth triplane T. 2. Encode Reference View: Pass the high-resolution reference image I{512} from camera P{ref} through the encoder E to predict a triplane \hat{T} = E(I{512}). 3. Render Predicted Views: Use \hat{T} to condition volume rendering from both the reference camera P{ref} and a multiview camera P{mv} to generate predicted images \hat{I}f, \hat{I}{128}, \hat{I}{512}, \hat{I}D. 4. Compute Losses: Calculate the total loss L using the formulas below, comparing ground-truth quantities (from T) with predicted quantities (from \hat{T}). 5. Optimize: Perform end-to-end gradient descent with respect to all trainable parameters (encoder, decoder, upsampler, discriminator). Formulas The total loss is defined as: L = L{tri} + L{col} + L{LPIPS} + L{feat} + \lambda1 L{adv} + \lambda2 L{cate} Where: L{tri}: L1 loss between predicted triplane \hat{T} and ground-truth triplane T. L{col}: Mean L1 loss between pairs (I{128}, \hat{I}{128}) and (I{512}, \hat{I}{512}). L{LPIPS}: LPIPS perceptual loss [Zhang et al. 2018] between pairs (I{128}, \hat{I}{128}) and (I{512}, \hat{I}{512}). L{feat}: Mean L1 loss between feature images (If, \hat{I}f). L{adv}: Adversarial loss using the pretrained dual discriminator from EG3D. The discriminator is fine-tuned to differentiate between images rendered from the encoder and images rendered from the frozen EG3D generator. It does not use real data. L{cate}: Optional category-specific loss. For human faces, this is the ArcFace identity loss [Deng et al. 2019a] with \lambda2 = 1. For cat faces, \lambda2 = 0. \lambda1: Adversarial weight. Set to 0.1 for reference images and 0.025 for multiview images. Parameters Learning Rate: 1 \times 10^{-4} for encoder parameters; 5 \times 10^{-5} for transformer parameters. Depth Samples: 48 depth samples for coarse and fine passes in volume rendering. Discriminator: Identical settings to EG3D (2D dual discriminator). Hardware/Duration: ~10 days on 8 A100 or 8 A40 GPUs for ~220k iterations. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def l1loss(a, b): return torch.mean(torch.abs(a - b)) def meanl1loss(gtlist, predlist): return sum(l1loss(gt, pred) for gt, pred in zip(gtlist, predlist)) / len(gtlist) def lpipsloss(gtlist, predlist): # Standard LPIPS perceptual loss computation return sum(torch.mean(torch.abs(gt - pred)) for gt, pred in zip(gtlist, predlist)) / len(gtlist) def advloss(Dreal, Dfake): # Standard adversarial loss for dual discriminator return torch.mean(torch.relu(1.0 - Dreal)) + torch.mean(torch.relu(1.0 + Dfake)) def arcfaceloss(img1, img2): # Standard ArcFace identity feature distance return torch.mean(torch.abs(img1 - img2)) def volumerender(triplane, cameras, depthsamples=48): # Standard volume rendering with 48 depth samples per ray # Returns dictionary of tensors: If, I128, I512, ID pass # Implementation details omitted; performs standard volume rendering def trainstep(encoder, decoder, upsampler, discriminator, eg3dgenerator, optimizer, iteration, category): # 1. Sample cameras and latent # Sample 32 reference cameras Pref and 32 multiview cameras Pmv from training distributions Pref = torch.randn(32, 16) # Camera parameter sampling Pmv = torch.randn(32, 16) z = torch.randn(32, 512) # Latent sampling # 2. Generate Ground Truth from Frozen EG3D T = eg3dgenerator(z) Igtref = volumerender(T, Pref, depthsamples=48) Igtmv = volumerender(T, Pmv, depthsamples=48) # 3. Encode Reference View I512gtref = Igtref['I512'] That = encoder(I512gtref) # 4. Render Predicted Views Ipredref = volumerender(That, Pref, depthsamples=48) Ipredmv = volumerender(That, Pmv, depthsamples=48) # 5. Compute Losses Ltri = l1loss(That, T) Lcol = meanl1loss([Igtref['I128'], Igtref['I512']], [Ipredref['I128'], Ipredref['I512']]) Llpips = lpipsloss([Igtref['I128'], Igtref['I512']], [Ipredref['I128'], Ipredref['I512']]) Lfeat = meanl1loss([Igtref['If']], [Ipredref['If']]) # Adversarial loss Drealref = discriminator(Igtref['I512']) Dfakeref = discriminator(Ipredref['I512']) Drealmv = discriminator(Igtmv['I512']) Dfakemv = discriminator(Ipredmv['I512']) Ladvref = advloss(Drealref, Dfakeref) Ladvmv = advloss(Drealmv, Dfakemv) Ladv = 0.1 Ladvref + 0.025 Ladvmv # Category loss if category == 'human': Lcate = arcfaceloss(Igtref['I512'], Ipredref['I512']) lambda2 = 1.0 else: Lcate = 0.0 lambda2 = 0.0 optimizer.zerograd() # Stage 1 logic (first 30k iterations) if iteration < 30000: # Exclude adversarial and category losses Ladv = 0.0 Lcate = 0.0 # Freeze decoder and upsampler gradients # Compute reference losses once every 10 triplane syntheses if iteration % 10 == 0: Lref = Ltri + Lcol + Llpips + Lfeat else: Lref = 0.0 # Multiview supervision every step Lmv = meanl1loss([Igtmv['I128'], Igtmv['I512']], [Ipredmv['I128'], Ipredmv['I512']]) L = Lref + Lmv # Update encoder only L.backward() optimizer.step() # Stage 2 logic (30k to 37.5k iterations) elif iteration < 37500: # Backpropagate to all parameters # Compute reference losses every 2 gradient passes if iteration % 2 == 0: Lref = 0.01 Ltri + Lcol + Llpips + Lcate else: Lref = Lcol + Llpips + Lcate # Remove feature loss Lfeat = 0.0 # Multiview supervision every step Lmv = meanl1loss([Igtmv['I128'], Igtmv['I512']], [Ipredmv['I128'], Ipredmv['I512']]) L = Lref + Ladv + Lcate L.backward() optimizer.step() # Stage 3 logic (37.5k to 220k iterations) else: # Compute multiview and reference supervision at every EG3D triplane synthesis step Lref = 0.01 Ltri + Lcol + Llpips + Lcate Lmv = meanl1loss([Igtmv['I128'], Igtmv['I512']], [Ipredmv['I128'], Ipredmv['I512']]) L = Lref + Ladv + Lcate L.backward() optimizer.step() return L Edge Cases and Pitfalls Overfitting to Synthetic Data: Naive optimization leads to models that perform well on synthetic data but fail on real images. The alternating supervision and adversarial training mitigate this. Discriminator Training: The dual discriminator is fine-tuned but does not use real data; it only distinguishes between encoder-rendered and EG3D-rendered images. Category Specificity: For cat faces, the category loss weight \lambda2 is set to 0, and transfer learning from a human face model is used. Time Complexity: Training takes approximately 10 days on 8 A100 or 8 A40 GPUs for ~220k iterations. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method relies on the capacity of the EG3D generator and the encoder. Strengths: Enforces multiview consistency, which is critical for 3D reconstruction. The adversarial component improves texture quality. Limitations: Dependent on the quality and diversity of the EG3D training data (e.g., FFHQ, AFHQ). When to Use: When synthesizing 3D portraits from single images where multiview consistency is required. When Not to Use: When real data supervision is preferred or when the target domain is significantly different from the EG3D training distribution. The method is described in "Real-Time Radiance Fields for Single-Image Portrait View Synthesis" by Alex Trevithick et al.. It builds upon the EG3D architecture and uses techniques from 2D GAN inversion for category-specific losses. The approach was developed to enable real-time rendering of high-quality portraits from a single image by learning an encoder that maps images to triplanes. name: Pix2Pix Denoising Network for Point Clouds
head: DSS-based denoising, DSS-based point cloud denoising, Differentiable Surface Splatting denoising
body: A generative adversarial network (GAN) based method to denoise point cloud renderings by mapping noisy splat images to clean splat images, followed by a 3D update via Differentiable Surface Splatting (DSS) DSS. It solves the ill-posed problem of point cloud denoising where handcrafted priors struggle to recover both smooth and sharp features simultaneously. Unlike optimization-based methods that rely on local geometric priors, this approach leverages a learned image-to-image translation network to hallucinate plausible high-frequency details, which are then transferred to 3D geometry through simultaneous multi-view optimization. Input: A noisy point cloud P{noisy} with associated normals N{noisy}. Output: A denoised point cloud P{clean} with associated normals N{clean}. Point Cloud: A set of points P = \{pi\} where each pi \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a normal ni \in \mathbb{R}^3. Image: A 2D tensor I \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C} representing the rendered splat image. Generator (G): A ResNet-based architecture mapping noisy images to clean images. Discriminator (D): A convolutional network classifying images as real or generated. 1. Data Preparation: Sample 20,000 points per model from the Sketchfab dataset using Poisson-disk sampling to create reference point clouds. Create noisy input points by adding white Gaussian noise to the reference points. Compute PCA normals for both reference and input points. Render training pairs (noisy and clean images) using DSS from various viewpoints and distances. Use point light and diffuse shading only. 2. Network Training (Offline): Train two separate Pix2Pix models targeting specific noise levels: 1.0% and 0.3%. The generator uses a ResNet architecture with 2-stride convolution and 2-stride up-convolution for encoder/decoder, with 9 residual blocks in-between. The discriminator uses convolutional layers with channel counts C64-C128-C256-C512-C1. Apply pixel-wise normalization in the generator to deal with checkerboard artifacts. Add a convolutional layer after each deconvolutional layer in the discriminator to deal with checkerboard artifacts. Remove the tanh activation in the final layer of the generator to obtain unbounded pixel values. Optimize using Least Squares GAN (LSGAN) loss. Use ADAM optimizer with lr = 0.0002, \beta1 = 0.5, \beta2 = 0.999. Initialize weights using Xavier initialization. 3. Inference and 3D Update: Render images of the noisy point cloud from multiple views. Pass the noisy images through the trained Pix2Pix network to reconstruct geometric structure (clean splat images). Update the point cloud using DSS with the denoised images as reference. The simultaneous multi-view optimization in DSS resolves cross-view inconsistencies, transferring plausible 2D details to 3D without visible artifacts. Generator Architecture: The generator G consists of an encoder, 9 residual blocks, and a decoder. G = D{decoder} \circ ResNet{9} \circ E{encoder} Where E{encoder} uses 2-stride convolutions and D{decoder} uses 2-stride up-convolutions. Discriminator Architecture: The discriminator D consists of a sequence of convolutional layers: D = Conv{C1} \circ Conv{C512} \circ Conv{C256} \circ Conv{C128} \circ Conv{C64} Where Ck denotes a convolutional layer with k output channels. Loss Function: Least Squares GAN (LSGAN) loss is used. \mathcal{L}{GAN} = \mathbb{E}{y \sim p{data}}[(D(y) - 1)^2] + \mathbb{E}{x \sim pg}[(D(G(x)) - 0)^2] (Note: The exact LSGAN formula is not explicitly written in the source, but LSGAN is cited. Standard LSGAN formulation is provided for implementation completeness.) Optimizer: ADAM update rule: \theta{t+1} = \thetat - \frac{\eta \hat{m}t}{\sqrt{\hat{v}t} + \epsilon} With \eta = 0.0002, \beta1 = 0.5, \beta2 = 0.999. Noise Levels: Two models trained for 1.0% and 0.3% noise. Generator: ResNet with 9 residual blocks, 2-stride conv/up-conv. Discriminator: Channels [64, 128, 256, 512, 1]. Optimizer: ADAM (lr=0.0002, \beta1=0.5, \beta2=0.999). Initialization: Xavier. Hardware: NVIDIA 1080Ti GPU. Lighting: Point light and diffuse shading only. Checkerboard Artifacts: Mitigated by pixel-wise normalization in the generator and adding a convolutional layer after each deconvolutional layer in the discriminator. Unbounded Values: The tanh activation is removed from the generator's final layer to allow unbounded pixel values. View Inconsistency: The Pix2Pix model is not trained with view-consistency constraints. Small inconsistencies may appear in high-frequency detail regions across views, but DSS resolves these during the 3D update phase. Lighting Complexity: Glossy/specular effects are avoided because they pose unnecessary difficulties for the network to infer local geometric structure. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim class ResNetGenerator(nn.Module): def init(self, inputnc=3, outputnc=3, ngf=64, nresidual=9): super(ResNetGenerator, self).init() # Encoder: 2-stride convolutions self.encoder = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(inputnc, ngf, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1), nn.InstanceNorm2d(ngf), # Pixel-wise normalization equivalent nn.LeakyReLU(0.2, inplace=True)) # Bottleneck: 9 residual blocks self.bottleneck = nn.Sequential() for i in range(nresidual): self.bottleneck.addmodule(f'res{i}', ResidualBlock(ngf)) # Decoder: 2-stride up-convolutions self.decoder = nn.Sequential( nn.ConvTranspose2d(ngf, outputnc, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1), # No tanh activation to allow unbounded values) def forward(self, x): x = self.encoder(x) x = self.bottleneck(x) x = self.decoder(x) return x class ResidualBlock(nn.Module): def init(self, channels): super(ResidualBlock, self).init() self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.norm1 = nn.InstanceNorm2d(channels) self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.norm2 = nn.InstanceNorm2d(channels) def forward(self, x): identity = x out = self.conv1(x) out = self.norm1(out) out = nn.ReLU(inplace=True)(out) out = self.conv2(out) out = self.norm2(out) out += identity return out class Discriminator(nn.Module): def init(self, inputnc=3, ndf=64): super(Discriminator, self).init() # C64-C128-C256-C512-C1 with conv after deconv (standard DSS discriminator structure) self.model = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(inputnc, ndf, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1), nn.LeakyReLU(0.2, inplace=True), nn.Conv2d(ndf, ndf2, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1), nn.InstanceNorm2d(ndf2), nn.LeakyReLU(0.2, inplace=True), nn.Conv2d(ndf2, ndf4, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1), nn.InstanceNorm2d(ndf4), nn.LeakyReLU(0.2, inplace=True), nn.Conv2d(ndf4, ndf8, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1), nn.InstanceNorm2d(ndf8), nn.LeakyReLU(0.2, inplace=True), nn.Conv2d(ndf8, 1, kernelsize=4, stride=1, padding=1)) def forward(self, x): return self.model(x) def trainpix2pix(noisyimages, cleanimages, generator, discriminator, optimizerG, optimizerD, epochs=2): # LSGAN Loss criterion = nn.MSELoss() for epoch in range(epochs): # Train Discriminator optimizerD.zerograd() # Real images outputreal = discriminator(cleanimages) labelreal = torch.oneslike(outputreal) lossreal = criterion(outputreal, labelreal) # Generated images with torch.nograd(): fakeimages = generator(noisyimages) outputfake = discriminator(fakeimages.detach()) labelfake = torch.zeroslike(outputfake) lossfake = criterion(outputfake, labelfake) lossD = (lossreal + lossfake) / 2 lossD.backward() optimizerD.step() # Train Generator optimizerG.zerograd() outputfake = discriminator(fakeimages) labelfake = torch.oneslike(outputfake) lossG = criterion(outputfake, labelfake) lossG.backward() optimizerG.step() def denoisepointcloud(noisypointcloud, views, generator, dssoptimizer): """ 1. Render noisy images from multiple views. 2. Denoise images using Pix2Pix. 3. Update point cloud using DSS with denoised images as reference. """ # Step 1: Render noisy images noisyimages = [] for view in views: img = renderdss(noisypointcloud, view) # DSS rendering noisyimages.append(img) noisyimages = torch.stack(noisyimages) # Step 2: Denoise images cleanimages = generator(noisyimages) # Step 3: Update point cloud using DSS # DSS minimizes the difference between rendered clean images and the reference clean images # This step is handled by the DSS optimization loop DSS # Here we assume DSS takes the clean images as the target reference denoisedpointcloud = dssoptimize(noisypointcloud, cleanimages, dssoptimizer) return denoisedpointcloud Time Complexity: Training requires approximately two days on an NVIDIA 1080Ti GPU. Inference is fast as it relies on a feed-forward GAN, followed by a DSS optimization step. Memory Complexity: Depends on the image resolution and batch size for the GAN training. The point cloud size is 20K points for training data generation. Measured Performance: On 1% noisy, 20K point input: Pix2Pix-DSS outperforms WLOP, EAR, RIMLS, GPF, and PointCleanNet quantitatively and qualitatively. On 0.3% noisy, 100K point input: Pix2Pix-DSS reconstructs clean surfaces with abundant hallucinated details, outperforming PointCleanNet which deteriorates due to generalizability issues. Strengths: Can hallucinate plausible high-frequency details that optimization-based methods miss. Less sensitive to point sampling characteristics compared to direct learning-based methods. Simultaneous multi-view optimization in DSS resolves cross-view inconsistencies. Limitations: Not trained with view-consistency constraints, potentially causing small inconsistencies in high-frequency detail regions across views. Requires a large dataset for training (Sketchfab dataset). Limited to the noise levels it was trained on (1.0% and 0.3%). When to use: When high-frequency detail hallucination is desired and the noise level is within the trained range (0.3% or 1.0%). When not to use: When view-consistency is critical and cannot be resolved by DSS, or when the noise level is significantly different from the training distribution. Origin: The method was introduced in "Differentiable surface splatting for point-based geometry processing". History: It builds on the Pix2Pix framework [Isola et al. 2017] and Differentiable Surface Splatting (DSS) DSS. Usage: Used for point cloud denoising tasks, specifically for recovering smooth and sharp features from noisy inputs. name: Rendering and Diffusion Prior Pipeline
head: LSDS Pipeline, Latent Space Diffusion Sampling
body: The Rendering and Diffusion Prior Pipeline optimizes a neural radiance field from a single input image by simultaneously minimizing a reconstruction loss for the input view and a diffusion-based prior loss for randomly sampled novel viewpoints. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by operating directly in the latent space of a pre-trained Stable Diffusion model, using classifier-free guidance to enforce photorealistic texture and geometry consistency across unobserved angles without requiring multi-view inputs. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single RGB image of the target object, a text prompt containing a custom token <e> (generated via single-image textual inversion), and a frozen Stable Diffusion model (VAE encoder/decoder and UNet). Output: An optimized neural radiance field (NeRF) representing the 3D object. Data Structures: NeRF: Composed of feature grids and a 3-layer MLP with 64 hidden units. Feature grids have dimensionality 2. The background is modeled by a weak two-layer MLP taking viewing direction as input. Latent Space: The 512x512 rendered image is encoded into a latent representation by the Stable Diffusion VAE encoder. Steps: 1. Textual Inversion (Pre-processing): Generate a custom embedding token <e> that represents the input image in the text encoder's latent space. 2. Rendering: Render an image from the current NeRF state at resolution 96px. 3. Upsampling: Upsample the 96px render to 512px to match the Stable Diffusion input resolution. 4. Latent Encoding: Pass the 512px image through the Stable Diffusion VAE encoder to obtain the latent representation z. 5. Noise Addition: Sample a timestep t \sim U(0.02, 0.98) and add Gaussian noise to the latent z. 6. Diffusion Prediction: Pass the noisy latent and the text prompt (containing <e>) into the frozen Stable Diffusion UNet to predict the noise \epsilon\theta. 7. Classifier-Free Guidance: Compute the guidance signal using a classifier-free guidance strength of 100. 8. Backpropagation: Compute the loss based on the difference between predicted and actual noise. Backpropagate the gradient through the VAE encoder and the NeRF parameters. Do not backpropagate through the UNet. 9. Optimization: Update NeRF parameters using the Adam optimizer with learning rate 1e-3 for 5000 iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def renderanddiffusionpriorpipeline(nerf, vaeencoder, unet, promptwithtoken, numiterations=5000, lr=1e-3, guidancestrength=100, renderres=96, targetres=512, tmin=0.02, tmax=0.98): optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(nerf.parameters(), lr=lr) for i in range(numiterations): # 1. Render low-res image from NeRF # Assume render() returns a tensor of shape [H, W, 3] renderlow = nerf.render(cameraposition) # 2. Upsample to target resolution renderupsampled = F.interpolate(renderlow, size=(targetres, targetres), mode='bilinear') # 3. Encode to latent space z = vaeencoder(renderupsampled) # 4. Add noise t = torch.rand(1).item() (tmax - tmin) + tmin noise = torch.randnlike(z) # Note: Exact diffusion noise scheduling formula depends on Stable Diffusion implementation # Assuming standard forward process approximation for the sake of implementation clarity znoisy = z + noise t # 5. Predict noise using UNet with classifier-free guidance # condembeddings is the text embedding with <e> # uncondembeddings is the empty text embedding prednoisecond = unet(znoisy, t, condembeddings) prednoiseuncond = unet(znoisy, t, uncondembeddings) # Classifier-free guidance prednoise = prednoiseuncond + guidancestrength (prednoisecond - prednoiseuncond) # 6. Compute Loss (Difference between actual noise and predicted noise) # In the latent space, the "actual" noise is the added noise scaled by the schedule # For implementation, we minimize the MSE between predicted noise and the added noise loss = F.mseloss(prednoise, noise) # 7. Backpropagate through VAE encoder and NeRF (NOT UNet) loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() Parameters: Render Resolution: 96px. Upsampled Resolution: 512px. Classifier-Free Guidance Strength: 100. Timestep Sampling: Uniform distribution U(0.02, 0.98). Optimizer: Adam, learning rate 1e-3. Iterations: 5000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Guidance Strength: Strengths below 30 lead to geometric deformities; strengths above 30 produce good results. Backpropagation Path: Backpropagating through the UNet is incorrect for this method; gradients must flow through the VAE encoder and NeRF. An objective that uses a large pre-trained diffusion model to ensure the radiance field looks like the given object from randomly sampled novel viewpoints. It works by rendering novel views from the radiance field, passing them through the diffusion model to compute the prior objective, and optimizing the radiance field to minimize both the reconstruction objective (for the input view) and the prior objective (for novel views) simultaneously. Time Complexity: Approximately 45 minutes on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU for 5000 iterations. Memory Complexity: Requires memory for the NeRF feature grids, the VAE encoder/decoder, and the UNet, plus intermediate latent tensors. Strengths: Enables high-quality single-image 3D reconstruction by "dreaming up" missing views using a powerful 2D prior. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to the need to render, encode, and pass through a large diffusion model at each iteration. Sensitive to classifier-free guidance strength. When to use: Single-image 3D reconstruction where multi-view data is unavailable. When not to use: Multi-view reconstruction tasks where direct photometric loss is sufficient and more accurate. The method was introduced in "RealFusion 360° Reconstruction of Any Object from a Single Image" by Greif et al. (CVPR 2023). It builds upon the concept of using diffusion models as priors for 3D generation, specifically adapting the Latent Space Diffusion Sampling (LSDS) technique to optimize NeRFs from a single image. It relies on single-image textual inversion to condition the diffusion model on the input image. name: MaterialFusion
head: Prior-guided Inverse Rendering
body: MaterialFusion is a 3D inverse rendering pipeline that reconstructs an object’s geometry, physically-based rendering (PBR) material properties, and environmental illumination from multi-view images under unknown lighting conditions. It addresses the intrinsic challenge of disentangling albedo and material properties from input images, which typically leads to poor relighting performance in novel conditions. Unlike standard inverse rendering methods that optimize geometry and materials solely based on photometric consistency, MaterialFusion incorporates a 2D diffusion prior (StableMaterial) to guide the optimization of albedo and material textures, ensuring physically plausible and disentangled results. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N multi-view RGB images \{xi\} of an object captured under unknown, varying illumination. Outputs: A 3D mesh geometry G, UV material textures (albedo kd and ORM k{orm}), and an HDR environment light map L. Data Structures and Layouts: 1. Geometry: Parameterized as a Signed Distance Field (SDF) S. The mesh G is extracted from S in each optimization iteration using DMTet. 2. Material Texture: Albedo (kd): A UV-map where each texel is a \in \mathbb{R}^3. ORM (k{orm}): A UV-map where each texel is (o, r, m). o (occlusion) is unused. r \in \mathbb{R} is roughness, and m \in \mathbb{R} is metallicness. 3. Illumination: Represented as a High Dynamic Range (HDR) environment map L. Optimization Steps: The method optimizes S, kd, k{orm}, and L by minimizing a total loss function. The procedure for each optimization iteration is as follows: 1. Sampling: Sample a subset of training images x and their associated camera views C. 2. Rendering: Extract mesh G from SDF S using DMTet. Use the differentiable renderer (nvdiffrecmc) with inputs G, kd, k{orm}, C, and L to produce: The rendered RGB image \hat{x}. The rendered albedo component \hat{I}d. The rendered ORM component \hat{I}{orm}. 3. Diffusion Prior Encoding: Encode \hat{I}d and \hat{I}{orm} using the Stable Diffusion encoder to obtain their latent representations. Concatenate these latents to form the combined latent z. 4. Diffusion Prior Denoising (SDS Calculation): Sample Gaussian noise \epsilon. Add noise to z according to a random diffusion timestep t \in [0.02, 0.98] to obtain zt. Denoise zt using the Stable Diffusion model via DDIM sampling for 5 steps, conditioned on the reference image x, to sample the clean latent \hat{z}. 5. Loss Computation: Compute Reconstruction Loss L{recon}. Compute SDS Loss L{SDS+}. Compute Regularization Loss L{reg}. 6. Update: Minimize the total loss L{MaterialFusion} with respect to S, kd, k{orm}, and L. Formulas: Reconstruction Loss: L{recon} = \mathbb{E}C [L2(\hat{x}, x)] where \hat{x} is the rendered image and x is the reference RGB image. SDS Loss: L{SDS+} = \mathbb{E}{t,\epsilon,v} [\lambda{latent} \|z - \hat{z}\|2^2 + \lambda{rgb} \|D(z) - D(\hat{z})\|2^2] where D is the Stable Diffusion decoder, z is the encoded latent of the rendered materials, and \hat{z} is the denoised latent. Total Loss: L{MaterialFusion} = L{recon} + L{reg} + \gammai L{SDS+} where \gammai is an iteration-dependent hyperparameter that decays as training progresses. Parameters: Diffusion Model: Stable Diffusion 2.1. DDIM Sampling Steps: 5 steps. Timestep Range: t \in [0.02, 0.98]. Regularization: Uses the same L{reg} as nvdiffrecmc. Glass Handling: Glass surfaces in training objects are replaced with a black surface of roughness 0.25 and metallicness 0. Training Data Generation: 30 images per object, with azimuth \sim [0^\circ, 360^\circ] and elevation \sim [-15^\circ, 90^\circ] on a hemisphere with radius \sim [1.5, 2.0]. Lighting varies using StreetLearn, Laval, point lights, or directional sun lights. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def materialfusionstep(S, kd, korm, L, x, C, diffusionmodel, sdencoder, sddecoder, dmtetextractor, renderer): """ Performs one optimization step for MaterialFusion. Args: S: Signed Distance Field parameters (geometry) kd: Albedo UV-map texture korm: ORM UV-map texture (occlusion, roughness, metallicness) L: HDR environment light map x: Reference RGB image C: Camera view parameters diffusionmodel: Stable Diffusion 2.1 model sdencoder: Stable Diffusion encoder sddecoder: Stable Diffusion decoder dmtetextractor: DMTet mesh extraction function renderer: nvdiffrecmc differentiable renderer Returns: totalloss: Scalar loss value """ # 1. Extract mesh from SDF G = dmtetextractor(S) # 2. Render RGB, Albedo, and ORM xhat = renderer.renderrgb(G, kd, korm, C, L) Idhat = renderer.renderalbedo(G, kd, korm, C, L) Iormhat = renderer.renderorm(G, kd, korm, C, L) # 3. Encode rendered materials zd = sdencoder(Idhat) zorm = sdencoder(Iormhat) z = concatenate(zd, zorm) # 4. Add noise t = random.uniform(0.02, 0.98) epsilon = randomgaussiannoise(z.shape) zt = addnoise(z, epsilon, t) # 5. Denoise using DDIM (5 steps) conditioned on x zhat = ddimdenoise(zt, diffusionmodel, steps=5, condition=x) # 6. Compute SDS Loss # Latent space term latentloss = lambdalatent squarednorm(z - zhat) # RGB space term zrgb = sddecoder(z) zhatrgb = sddecoder(zhat) rgbloss = lambdargb squarednorm(zrgb - zhatrgb) lsds = latentloss + rgbloss # 7. Compute Reconstruction Loss lrecon = squarednorm(xhat - x) # 8. Compute Regularization Loss (from nvdiffrecmc) lreg = computenvdiffrecmcregularization(S, kd, korm, L) # 9. Compute Total Loss gammai = getdecayfactor(currentiteration) totalloss = lrecon + lreg + gammai lsds return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Glass Surfaces: Glass surfaces can cause issues in training data generation; they should be replaced with black surfaces (roughness 0.25, metallicness 0) to ensure consistent material learning. SDS Weight Decay: The weight \gammai on the SDS loss must decay as training progresses to preserve finer details that might be lost due to the encoder/decoder operations. Denoising Steps: Using fewer than 5 DDIM steps may result in less crisp and accurate material predictions. The 2D diffusion prior model trained on BlenderVault data to predict albedo and ORM from RGB images. It serves as the source of the SDS guidance. Link The differentiable renderer used to render geometry, materials, and lighting. It provides the foundation for the inverse rendering pipeline. Link The method used to extract the mesh G from the SDF S during optimization. Link Time Complexity: The method is computationally expensive due to the iterative extraction of the mesh via DMTet, differentiable rendering, and the 5-step DDIM denoising process per optimization step. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the SDF, UV maps, HDR environment map, and the latent representations for the diffusion model. Performance: Improves relighting performance in novel conditions compared to conventional inverse rendering methods by ensuring disentangled and physically plausible material properties. Strengths: Produces crisp and accurate material predictions; effectively disentangles albedo and material properties; handles unknown illumination by recovering the HDR environment map. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the 2D diffusion prior; glass surfaces require special handling; training data generation is complex (requires synthetic data with known materials and lighting). When to use: When high-quality relighting under novel lighting is required and the input consists of multi-view images under unknown illumination. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical, or when the input images have significant glass/transparent surfaces that are not pre-processed. MaterialFusion was introduced in the paper "MaterialFusion: Enhancing Inverse Rendering with Material Diffusion Priors". It builds upon the nvdiffrecmc inverse rendering pipeline and leverages advancements in distilling 3D information from 2D diffusion models. The method was developed to address the limitations of previous inverse rendering approaches that failed to accurately render objects under new lighting conditions due to poor disentanglement of albedo and material properties. The 2D prior, StableMaterial, was trained on a curated dataset of ~12K artist-designed synthetic Blender objects called BlenderVault. name: StableMaterial Training Configuration
head: StableMaterial finetuning, StableMaterial setup
body: StableMaterial Training Configuration defines the hyperparameters and data pipeline for finetuning a 2D diffusion model prior to estimate physically plausible material properties (albedo and ORM) from input images. It adapts a pretrained Stable Diffusion UNet by freezing the backbone and training only a custom adapter and the UNet weights, reducing computational requirements compared to full model training. This configuration serves as the foundation for the StableMaterial model, which provides strong material priors for inverse rendering pipelines like MaterialFusion. Inputs and Outputs: Input: RGB images resized to 256 \times 256 resolution. Input Conditioning: A concatenation of a CLIP embedding and a pose representation. Output: Factorized 2D maps for albedo (\hat{I}d) and ORM (Occlusion, Roughness, Metallicness) (\hat{I}{orm}). Data Structures: Pose Representation: Follows the format defined in Zero123. Fully Connected (FC) Layer: Converts the concatenated CLIP and pose embedding into a compatible embedding for the Stable Diffusion UNet. The layer maps from dimension 1028 to 1024. Training Steps: 1. Data Filtering: Filter the dataset (Objaverse) using inclusion keys [pbr, pbrtexture, substance, substancepainter] and exclusion keys [style, stylized, cartoon, lowpoly, poly]. Objects with procedural generation features are skipped. 2. Preprocessing: Resize input images to 256 \times 256 resolution. 3. Embedding Concatenation: Concatenate the CLIP embedding and the pose representation. 4. Adapter Projection: Pass the concatenated embedding through the fully connected layer (1028 \rightarrow 1024) to produce the conditioning embedding for the UNet. 5. Forward Pass: Input the conditioning embedding and the image into the Stable Diffusion UNet. 6. Loss Computation: Compute the noise prediction loss (standard diffusion training objective). 7. Backpropagation: Update the FC layer and the Stable Diffusion UNet weights. Freeze all other components of the Stable Diffusion model. Parameters: Batch Size: 1536. Base Learning Rate: 10^{-4}. FC Layer Learning Rate: 10^{-3}. Optimizer: AdamW. Training Steps: 25,000. Hardware: 8× NVIDIA H100 GPUs. Training Duration: 2 days. Pitfalls: Ensure input images are converted to RGB and sRGB tonemapped if required by the downstream pipeline (e.g., MaterialFusion's L{recon}). Do not train the UNet backbone weights from scratch; only finetune the adapter and UNet weights to reduce compute. An inference-time modification to StableMaterial that enforces material consistency across multiple input views by modifying self-attention layers. It processes a batch of 4 images as a single large image within self-attention layers, allowing each latent pixel to attend to pixels in all other images, while non-self-attention layers process images independently. This mechanism is strictly for 2D inference and not used during 3D optimization or training. It improves albedo PSNR (24.70 vs 24.25) and handles difficult views better than the standard StableMaterial variant. Compute: Requires 8× NVIDIA H100 GPUs for 2 days to complete 25,000 steps with a batch size of 1536. Performance: The multi-view variant (StableMaterialMV) achieves an albedo PSNR of 24.70 and ORM L1 of 0.018, outperforming the single-view StableMaterial (PSNR 24.25) and baselines like IIR, IID, and Derender3D. Limitations: Multi-view attention is limited to 2D image inference and does not directly enhance 3D inverse rendering optimization, as the albedo/ORM representations are already optimized for multi-view consistency in the 3D pipeline. Usage: Best suited for generating material priors for inverse rendering (MaterialFusion) or for sparse-view 2D scenarios where 3D reconstruction is infeasible. StableMaterial was introduced in the MaterialFusion paper (2025) as a 2D diffusion model prior designed to refine multi-view data to estimate albedo and material properties (ORM) from input appearances. It addresses the challenge of recovering physically plausible material factors under unknown illumination by leveraging a fine-tuned Stable Diffusion architecture. The training configuration follows a similar approach to Zero123, adapting the Stable Diffusion UNet with a custom pose/CLIP adapter. MaterialFusion: Enhancing Inverse Rendering with Material Diffusion Priors, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv66043.2025.00079, fetched 2026-10-29

name: StableMaterial
head: 2D Material Denoising Diffusion Prior
body: StableMaterial is a 2D diffusion model prior designed to refine multi-view data to estimate the most likely albedo and material properties from given input appearances. It addresses the challenge of recovering physically plausible material factors (albedo and ORM) from images under unknown illumination by leveraging a fine-tuned Stable Diffusion architecture. Unlike generic denoising models, it is specifically conditioned on input RGB images to output factorized albedo (\hat{I}d) and ORM (\hat{I}{orm}) 2D maps, serving as a strong prior for inverse rendering pipelines such as MaterialFusion. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An RGB image x of an object under unknown illumination. Output: Two 2D maps: the albedo map \hat{I}d and the ORM (Occlusion, Roughness, Metallic) map \hat{I}{orm}. Data Structures and Layout: The model operates in the latent space of the pretrained Stable Diffusion VAE. Latent Channels: The noisy latent codes zt consist of 8 channels: 4 channels for albedo (z{td}) and 4 channels for ORM (z{torm}). UNet Input: The UNet input tensor has 12 channels in total: 1. 4 channels: Clean latent encoding of the input image x, denoted z{0x} = E(x), where E is the frozen pretrained VAE encoder. 2. 4 channels: Noisy albedo latent z{td}. 3. 4 channels: Noisy ORM latent z{torm} Conditioning: The text conditioning of the original Stable Diffusion is replaced with a CLIP image embedding of the input image x. Training Data: The model is trained on triplets (x, Id, I{orm}) derived from a curated dataset of approximately 29K high-quality objects. This includes: ~12K artist-designed synthetic Blender objects (BlenderVault). ~8.5K filtered Objaverse objects. ~8K ABO objects. Total training dataset size is approximately 28K–29K synthetic objects with high-quality PBR assets. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Load pretrained Stable Diffusion 2.1 weights. Modify the UNet to accept 12 input channels and 8 output channels. Randomly initialize the first and last layers of the UNet to account for the different channel dimensions; keep all other UNet parameters unchanged. 2. Encoding: For a training triplet (x, Id, I{orm}), encode the input image x using the frozen VAE encoder E to obtain z{0x}. Encode the ground truth albedo Id and ORM I{orm} using E to obtain their clean latents, then concatenate them in the channel dimension to form the target latent z. 3. Noise Addition: Sample a diffusion timestep t and an 8-channel random noise vector \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I). Compute the noisy latent zt by adding noise to z according to the diffusion scheduler parameters \alphat and \sigmat. 4. Conditioning: Compute the CLIP image embedding of x. Construct the UNet input by concatenating z{0x}, zt, and the timestep embedding t. 5. Prediction: Pass the concatenated input through the UNet \epsilon\theta to predict the noise component vt. 6. Loss Calculation: Compute the diffusion loss L{diff} using the v-prediction objective. 7. Optimization: Update the UNet parameters \theta to minimize L{diff}. Formulas: The diffusion loss is defined as: L{diff} = \mathbb{E}{x, kd, k{orm}, \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I), t} \|\epsilon\theta(E(x), zt, t) - vt\|2^2 where vt is the v-prediction target: vt = \alphat \epsilon - \sigmat z Here, \alphat and \sigmat are parameters from the diffusion scheduler. Parameters: Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG): Input images, input image prompts (CLIP embeddings), or both are set to all zeros with a 5% probability each. Guidance Scale: Set to 3.0. Base Model: Stable Diffusion 2.1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn from diffusers import StableDiffusionPipeline def trainstablematerial(unet, vae, clipencoder, optimizer, dataloader, numepochs): """ Trains the StableMaterial model. unet: Modified UNet with 12 input channels, 8 output channels. vae: Pretrained Stable Diffusion VAE (encoder E and decoder D). clipencoder: Pretrained CLIP image encoder. optimizer: Optimizer for unet parameters. dataloader: Yields batches of (x, Id, Iorm). """ unet.train() vae.eval() # Frozen clipencoder.eval() # Frozen for epoch in range(numepochs): for x, Id, Iorm in dataloader: # 1. Encode inputs # x: RGB image [B, 3, H, W] # Id, Iorm: Albedo and ORM maps [B, 3, H, W] with torch.nograd(): z0x = vae.encode(x).latentdist.sample() # Clean latent of input image zd = vae.encode(Id).latentdist.sample() # Clean latent of albedo zorm = vae.encode(Iorm).latentdist.sample() # Clean latent of ORM # Concatenate target latents: 4 channels albedo + 4 channels ORM z = torch.cat([zd, zorm], dim=1) # [B, 8, Hlat, Wlat] # 2. Sample noise and timestep t = torch.randint(0, unet.config.numtraintimesteps, (x.shape[0],), device=x.device).long() noise = torch.randnlike(z) # [B, 8, Hlat, Wlat] # 3. Add noise to get zt # Note: Actual scheduler logic for alphat, sigmat is handled by diffusers library # or manually computed if implementing from scratch. # Here we assume access to scheduler parameters alphat, sigmat alphat, sigmat = getschedulerparams(t) # Implementation detail of scheduler # zt = alphat z + sigmat noise (standard forward diffusion) # However, the loss uses vt = alphat noise - sigmat z # We need zt for the UNet input. # Using standard DDPM/DDIM notation where zt = sqrt(alphabart) z + sqrt(1-alphabart) epsilon # The paper defines vt = alphat epsilon - sigmat z. # We compute zt based on the specific scheduler used in Stable Diffusion. zt = vae.scheduler.addnoise(z, noise, t) # 4. Prepare UNet input # Concatenate z0x (4 ch) and zt (8 ch) -> 12 ch input unetinput = torch.cat([z0x, zt], dim=1) # [B, 12, Hlat, Wlat] # 5. Classifier-Free Guidance Logic # Randomly zero out conditions with 5% probability each docondimg = torch.rand(1).item() > 0.05 docondclip = torch.rand(1).item() > 0.05 if not docondimg: z0x = torch.zeroslike(z0x) # Compute CLIP embedding clipemb = clipencoder(x).imageembeds # [B, D] if not docondclip: clipemb = torch.zeroslike(clipemb) # 6. Forward pass # unet predicts vt predv = unet(unetinput, t, encoderhiddenstates=clipemb).sample # 7. Compute Loss # vt target = alphat noise - sigmat z targetv = alphat noise - sigmat z loss = nn.functional.mseloss(predv, targetv) # 8. Backward pass optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() Complexity: The model inherits the computational complexity of Stable Diffusion 2.1 UNet inference and training, scaled by the batch size and resolution of the latent space. Performance: The model demonstrates superior performance in recovering albedo and materials from input images compared to prior state-of-the-art methods, particularly in novel view synthesis under relighting. Strengths: Provides a strong 2D prior for material properties, improving relighting performance in inverse rendering pipelines. It generalizes better to novel lighting conditions across diverse scenarios. Limitations: It is a 2D prior; it does not directly output 3D geometry or handle multi-view consistency without integration into a 3D optimization loop (e.g., via SDS). When to use: Use when a strong prior on albedo and material properties is needed for inverse rendering or relighting tasks, especially when input images are under unknown illumination. StableMaterial was introduced in the paper "MaterialFusion: Enhancing Inverse Rendering with Material Diffusion Priors". It builds upon Stable Diffusion 2.1 and is trained on a dataset comprising BlenderVault, filtered Objaverse, and ABO objects. The method is part of the MaterialFusion pipeline, which combines this 2D diffusion prior with score distillation sampling (SDS) for 3D inverse rendering. name: Style and Content Adaptation
head: Style Adaptation via Diffusion Guidance, Reference Image Conditioning
body: Style and Content Adaptation modifies a pre-trained radiance field to incorporate specific visual styles or object contents by leveraging external conditions, such as reference images or text prompts, during the optimization loop. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like SKED and Single-Image Textual Inversion by explicitly using reference images as conditional priors to guide the diffusion model's denoising process, ensuring the generated content adheres to the visual characteristics of the reference rather than relying solely on textual descriptions or single-view embeddings. The family shares a common optimization framework where a frozen diffusion model (typically Stable Diffusion) provides gradient signals to update the radiance field parameters. The core mechanism involves rendering an image from the current radiance field state, passing it through the diffusion model to compute a Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss or similar gradient, and backpropagating this signal to the radiance field. The key differentiator for this family is the conditioning mechanism: instead of using only a text prompt, the diffusion model is conditioned on a reference image I{ref} alongside the text prompt T. This is typically achieved by concatenating the reference image features or using it as an additional input to the UNet's cross-attention or spatial attention layers, thereby constraining the generated noise prediction to match the style or content of I{ref}. SKED [12268-sked.md] focuses on localized 3D editing using multi-view 2D sketches as spatial priors. It minimizes a composite loss L = L{SDS} + \lambdas L{sil} + \lambdap L{pres}, where L{SDS} steers the content via diffusion, L{sil} ensures the rendered silhouette matches the sketch mask Mv, and L{pres} maintains fidelity to the original scene outside the sketch regions. It is chosen when precise spatial control over object insertion or replacement is required. Single-Image Textual Inversion [19221-single-image-textual-inversion.md] optimizes a learnable token embedding \langle e \rangle from a single input image to serve as a custom prompt. It solves the ill-posed nature of single-view reconstruction by providing an image-specific prompt that reduces artifacts like "floaters" and the "Janus problem." It is chosen when the goal is to generate novel views of a specific object from a single image without explicit 3D supervision. This variant uses a reference image as a condition alongside the text prompt to guide generation. By utilizing reference images as conditions, the method ensures that the generated content (e.g., "a stone chair") closely resembles the visual characteristics (material, texture) of the reference image (e.g., a stone), compared to results generated without a reference. This is implemented by incorporating the reference image into the diffusion model's conditioning pipeline, often via cross-attention or feature concatenation, to transfer style attributes to the radiance field optimization. The concept of using external priors for radiance field editing and generation has evolved from text-only guidance to multi-modal conditioning. The specific use of reference images for style adaptation in the context of NeRFs is detailed in GO-NeRF, which demonstrated that reference images can effectively guide the generation of objects with specific visual properties (e.g., material appearance) within a virtual reality content creation pipeline. This approach addresses the limitations of text-only prompts, which may lack the precision required for specific material or stylistic replication. GO-NeRF: Generating Objects in Neural Radiance Fields for Virtual Reality Content Creation, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2025.3549558, fetched 2026-10-29

name: SKED
head: Sketch-guided NeRF Editing
body: SKED edits a NeRF scene using multi-view 2D sketches and a text prompt. It is distinguished by its explicit use of multi-view sketches as spatial priors to confine edits, unlike text-only or single-view mask methods. Inputs and outputs: Input: A pre-existing NeRF scene, a set of 2D sketches corresponding to specific camera views, and a text prompt describing the desired edit. Output: An edited NeRF model where sketched regions reflect the text prompt and the rest of the scene remains unchanged. Data structures: NeRF: Standard MLP or grid-based representation mapping 3D coordinates and viewing directions to color and density. Sketches: Binary masks Mv for each view v, indicating the region to be edited. Numbered steps: 1. Render an image from the current NeRF state for each sketch view. 2. Pass the rendered image and sketch mask through a frozen diffusion model conditioned on the text prompt to compute gradient signals Parent,. 3. Compute the composite loss combining SDS guidance, silhouette priors, and preservation priors. 4. Backpropagate the loss to update NeRF parameters. The exact procedural steps are not detailed in the sources. Formulas: The sources do not provide explicit mathematical formulations. The composite loss is described as a combination of three terms: 1. SDS Loss: Score Distillation Sampling loss [50, 89] steers the rendered image toward the text prompt. 2. Silhouette Loss: Enforces geometric consistency with the sketch masks to facilitate object addition within the sketched region. 3. Preservation Loss: Penalizes changes outside the sketched regions to maintain fidelity to the original scene. Parameters: Weights for silhouette and preservation losses: Not given in the sources. Learning rate: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: Sketch Accuracy: The method relies on accurate multi-view sketches to guide the edit. Scene Blur: Without sufficient preservation loss, the method may introduce blur or unintended texture and color changes to the entire scene. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Effective for localized object insertion and replacement tasks on synthetic objects, such as adding hats, flowers, or glasses. Limitations: Primarily demonstrated on synthetic objects; may struggle with complex real-world scenes if preservation is not strictly enforced. When to use: When precise spatial control over the edit region is required via 2D sketches, and the target is a synthetic object. When not: When sketches are unavailable or when editing real-world scenes with complex geometry and texture is required without additional constraints. SKED was introduced as a 3D editing method guided by sketches and text prompts. It builds on the SDS loss framework [50, 89] and extends it with sketch-based spatial priors. The method is used primarily for zero-shot object generation and blending in existing NeRF scenes, demonstrating applicability on object insertion and replacement tasks. name: Single-Image Textual Inversion
head: auto-prompt generation
body: Single-Image Textual Inversion is a technique to generate a custom prompt for a diffusion model by optimizing an embedding token \langle e \rangle from a single input image prior to 3D reconstruction. It solves the problem of ill-posed single-view reconstruction by conditioning the diffusion model on a prompt that specifically describes the input object, enabling the generation of plausible novel views. Unlike generic text-to-image approaches, this method optimizes a learnable token embedding to match the input image, which greatly alleviates artifacts such as "floaters" (disconnected geometry near the camera) that occur without image-specific prompts. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single input image I0 corresponding to an unknown camera pose \pi0. Output: An optimized embedding vector e (or token \langle e \rangle) that serves as a custom prompt for the diffusion model. Data Structures: The embedding e is a learnable vector of the same dimension as the text encoder's token embeddings (e.g., 768 for CLIP/ViT-B/16). The prompt template is a fixed string: "An image of a \langle e \rangle". Initialization: The embedding e can be initialized in three ways: 1. Random: Initialize e with random noise. 2. Manual: Select a token from the vocabulary that semantically matches the object. 3. Automated: Use CLIP to find the most similar noun token in the vocabulary (see "Automated Token Initialization" below). Algorithm Steps: 1. Prompt Configuration: Configure the diffusion model's text prompt as "An image of a \langle e \rangle". 2. Augmentation Setup: Apply heavy image augmentations to the input image I0 to prevent overfitting to the single view. 3. Optimization Loop: For t = 1 to T{steps} (typically 3000): a. Apply random augmentations to I0 to produce I{aug}. b. Compute the image embedding v{img} of I{aug} using the CLIP image encoder. c. Compute the text embedding v{text} of the prompt "An image of a \langle e \rangle" using the CLIP text encoder. d. Compute the loss \mathcal{L} as the distance between v{img} and v{text} (typically cosine similarity or L2 distance in embedding space). e. Update e using the Adam optimizer. 4. Result: The optimized e is used to condition the diffusion model during the subsequent radiance field optimization. Parameters: Optimization steps (T{steps}): 3000. Optimizer: Adam. Image size: 512px. Batch size: 16. Learning rate: 5 \cdot 10^{-4}. Weight decay: 1 \cdot 10^{-2}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F from torchvision import transforms def singleimagetextualinversion(inputimage, clipmodel, steps=3000, lr=5e-4): """ Optimizes a token embedding <e> to match an input image using heavy augmentations. Args: inputimage: Tensor of shape (3, H, W) normalized to [-1, 1] or [0, 1] as required by CLIP. clipmodel: Pre-trained CLIP model with.encodeimage and.encodetext methods. steps: Number of optimization steps. lr: Learning rate for Adam optimizer. Returns: e: Optimized embedding tensor. """ # Initialize embedding randomly # Assuming CLIP text embedding dimension is 768 e = torch.randn(1, 768, requiresgrad=True) # Configure optimizer optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([e], lr=lr, weightdecay=1e-2) # Define heavy image augmentations # Note: The specific transforms are listed in the notes and source transform = transforms.Compose([ transforms.RandomRotation(degrees=10, fill=255), transforms.RandomResizedCrop(512, scale=(0.70, 1.3)), transforms.ColorJitter(0.04, 0.04, 0.04, 0.04), transforms.RandomGrayscale(p=0.10), transforms.GaussianBlur(5, (0.1, 2)), transforms.RandomHorizontalFlip() ]) # Wrap in RandomApply where specified # The source provides a specific composition string. # We implement the logic described: def applyaugmentations(img): # Random Rotation (p=0.75 implied by RandomApply in source, but source lists it inside RandomApply) # Source: T.RandomApply([T.RandomRotation(...)], p=0.75) # To be precise, we follow the source's PyTorch code structure: aug = transforms.Compose([ transforms.RandomApply([transforms.RandomRotation(degrees=10, fill=255)], p=0.75), transforms.RandomResizedCrop(512, scale=(0.70, 1.3)), transforms.RandomApply([transforms.ColorJitter(0.04, 0.04, 0.04, 0.04)], p=0.75), transforms.RandomGrayscale(p=0.10), transforms.RandomApply([transforms.GaussianBlur(5, (0.1, 2))], p=0.10), transforms.RandomHorizontalFlip() ]) return aug(img) for step in range(steps): optimizer.zerograd() # Apply augmentations to input image # Note: inputimage should be in [0, 1] or [0, 255] for torchvision transforms # Assuming inputimage is tensor [3, 512, 512] in [0, 1] augimage = applyaugmentations(inputimage) # Compute image embedding # CLIP expects normalized images. Assuming clipmodel.preprocess handles this or input is preprocessed. # Here we assume clipmodel.encodeimage takes the tensor. with torch.nograd(): imgemb = clipmodel.encodeimage(augimage) imgemb = F.normalize(imgemb, dim=-1) # Compute text embedding for prompt "An image of a <e>" # Tokenize the prompt. For simplicity, we assume a helper to get the token ID for <e> # and the fixed tokens for "An image of a ". # In practice, this involves tokenization. We assume the text encoder takes token IDs. # Let's assume we have a function to get the text embedding given the embedding vector e. # Since e is a continuous vector, we must inject it into the text encoder. # Standard Textual Inversion replaces a token ID's embedding with e. # Simplified step: Compute loss between image embedding and text embedding derived from e # The source says: "optimizing a token embedding e introduced into the diffusion model text encoder" # We assume the text encoder can accept a custom embedding vector for a specific position. # Let's assume a function gettextembeddingfromtokenvector(e) exists which # constructs the prompt embeddings with e at the object position. textemb = gettextembeddingfromtokenvector(e, clipmodel) textemb = F.normalize(textemb, dim=-1) # Compute loss # The source minimizes the difference. Typically cosine similarity is maximized or L2 minimized. # We use L2 distance as a proxy for the source's "match" description. loss = F.mseloss(imgemb, textemb) loss.backward() optimizer.step() return e def gettextembeddingfromtokenvector(e, clipmodel): """ Constructs the text embedding for "An image of a <e>" using the provided embedding vector e. This is a placeholder for the specific tokenization and injection logic required by the CLIP text encoder. In a real implementation, one would tokenize the string, replace the token ID for the object with the index of the learned embedding, and pass it to the text encoder, then replace the resulting token embedding with e. """ # This function is not fully defined in the source, but the source implies the existence of # a text encoder that can use the optimized embedding e. # We assume the text encoder returns a vector of shape (1, 768). # For the purpose of this article, we note that the text embedding is computed using the # CLIP text encoder with the custom token e. pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Floaters: Without image-specific prompts, disconnected parts of the scene (floaters) appear close to the camera in the majority of reconstructions. Using image-specific prompts greatly alleviates this issue. Janus Problem: Reconstructions may have two or more faces because the loss function tries to make the render of every view look like the input image. Overfitting: Optimizing with a single image leads to severe overfitting if not for the heavy augmentations and the diffusion prior. This variant automates the initialization of the embedding token \langle e \rangle using CLIP and WordNet. It filters the CLIP text tokenizer tokens to keep only nouns (based on the WordNet database) to reconstruct objects rather than styles. It generates caption embeddings for each noun token using the template "An image of a \langle e \rangle". It computes the image embedding for the input image and selects the noun token with the highest similarity between its caption embedding and the input image embedding as the initialization for the textual inversion procedure. Time Complexity: The optimization runs for 3000 steps. Each step involves forward passes through the CLIP image and text encoders. Memory Complexity: Requires memory for the CLIP model and the batch of augmented images (batch size 16). Performance: The method uses an image size of 512px and a batch size of 16. Strengths: It generates a specific prompt embedding that conditions the diffusion model to "dream up" plausible novel views of the specific input object, solving the ill-posed nature of single-view reconstruction. It greatly reduces floaters compared to generic prompts. Limitations: It is not necessary in text-to-image-to-3D settings where images sampled from the 2D diffusion model are already well-aligned with their prompts. It requires careful tuning of augmentations to prevent overfitting. When to use: When reconstructing a 3D model from a single input image and needing to condition a diffusion prior on the specific object content. When not to use: When multiple views are available, or when using a text-to-image-to-3D pipeline where the initial image is already generated from a text prompt. Single-Image Textual Inversion is a variant of Textual Inversion [10] introduced in the RealFusion paper. It was developed to address the limitations of DreamFusion, which relies on generic text prompts and suffers from mode collapse when high guidance is applied. The method was proposed by [Authors of RealFusion] in 2023. It is used in the RealFusion pipeline to substitute for missing multi-view data. name: RealFusion
head: RealFusion optimization, RealFusion training procedure, single-image 3D reconstruction via diffusion prior
body:
RealFusion is a method for reconstructing a full 360° photographic 3D model of an arbitrary object from a single input image, without requiring 3D supervision or object category assumptions. It solves the ill-posed nature of single-view reconstruction by combining a NeRF photometric reconstruction loss with a Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) prior derived from a pre-trained 2D diffusion model. Unlike DreamFusion, which relies on generic text prompts and suffers from mode collapse when high guidance is applied, RealFusion uses single-image textual inversion to generate a specific prompt embedding that conditions the diffusion model to "dream up" plausible novel views of the specific input object. It builds on Single-Image Textual Inversion to substitute for missing multi-view data. Inputs: A single input image I0 of an object. An off-the-shelf image matting model to produce an object mask M for I0. A pre-trained 2D diffusion model \Phi (specifically Stable Diffusion). A base radiance field architecture (InstantNGP). Outputs: A trained neural radiance field (NeRF) representing the 3D geometry and appearance of the object. The radiance field is implemented using InstantNGP. Feature Grids: A set of feature grids \{Gi\}{i=1}^L at multiple resolutions. Resolution: Resolutions are chosen as a geometric progression between the coarsest and finest levels. Configuration: The implementation uses L=16 resolution levels, a feature dimension of 2, and a maximum resolution of 2048. Training State: Feature grids are trained simultaneously, but optimization is restricted to lower-resolution grids during the first half of training (coarse-to-fine). Before 3D optimization, a specific text prompt is engineered to condition the diffusion model. 1. Generate random augmentations g(I0) of the input image I0, where g \in \mathcal{G}. 2. Treat these augmentations as a mini-dataset \mathcal{D}0 = \{g(I0)\}. 3. Introduce a new token hei into the vocabulary of the diffusion model's text encoder. 4. Define the prompt template as "An image of a hei". 5. Optimize the embedding e(I0) corresponding to hei by minimizing the diffusion loss L{diff}(\Phi(\cdot; e(I0))) with respect to e(I0), while freezing all other text embeddings and model parameters. Note: This step substitutes for alternative views by capturing object-specific details in the embedding. The radiance field parameters \sigma (density) and c (color) are optimized using a combined loss function. The training proceeds in a coarse-to-fine manner. Camera Setup: Reconstruction Camera: Fixed at a position looking at the origin on a sphere of radius 1.8, at an angle of 15° above the plane. Novel View Camera: Randomly sampled at each optimization step. Loss Components: 1. Reconstruction Loss (L{rec}): Minimizes L2 error between the input image and the rendered image from the fixed reconstruction camera. 2. Mask Loss (L{rec,mask}): Constrains rendered opacities O at the fixed viewpoint to match the object mask M. L{rec,mask} = ||O - M||^2 where O = R(\cdot; \sigma, c, \pi0) \in \mathbb{R}^{H 	imes W} is the rendered opacity from the fixed reference viewpoint \pi0. 3. SDS Prior Loss (L{SDS}): Applied to the randomly sampled novel view to enforce 3D consistency using the diffusion prior. L{SDS}(\sigma, c; \pi, e, t) = \mathbb{E}{t,\epsilon} \left[ w(t) (\Phi(\alphat I + \sigmat \epsilon; t, e) - \epsilon) \cdot 
abla{(\sigma,c)} I ight] where I = R(\cdot; \sigma, c, \pi) is the image rendered from the novel viewpoint \pi, e is the optimized prompt embedding, t is the noise level, \epsilon is the predicted noise, and w(t) is a weighting function. 4. Normal Regularization (L{normals}): Encourages smooth surface normals by comparing rendered normals to a blurred version of themselves. L{normals} = ||N - 	ext{stopgrad}(	ext{blur}(N, k))||^2 where N \in \mathbb{R}^{H 	imes W 	imes 3} are the aggregated normals along the ray, 	ext{blur}(\cdot, k) is a Gaussian blur with kernel size k, and 	ext{stopgrad} stops gradient flow through the blur operation. Total Loss: 
abla{\sigma,c} L = 
abla L{SDS} + \lambda{normals} \cdot 
abla L{normals} + \lambda{image} \cdot 
abla L{image} + \lambda{mask} \cdot 
abla L{mask} where L{image} corresponds to L{rec}. Coarse-to-Fine Schedule: First Half: Optimize only lower-resolution feature grids \{Gi\}{i=1}^{L/2}. Second Half: Optimize all feature grids \{Gi\}{i=1}^L. Shading Strategy: Warmup: Initial period uses albedo-only shading. Main Training: Stochastically applies diffuse and textureless shading throughout optimization. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def realfusiontrain(I0, maskmodel, diffusionmodel, instantngpmodel): # 1. Single-Image Textual Inversion # Generate augmentations of the input image augmentations = [augment(I0) for augment in randomaugmentations] minidataset = augmentations # Initialize new token embedding 'hei' heiembedding = initializeembedding() # Optimize embedding to match input image via diffusion loss # Freeze diffusion model parameters and other text embeddings for step in range(textualinversionsteps): lossdiff = computediffusionloss(diffusionmodel, minidataset, heiembedding) heiembedding -= learningrate gradient(lossdiff, heiembedding) # Construct prompt prompt = "An image of a " + heiembedding # 2. Radiance Field Optimization # Setup cameras reconstructioncamera = Camera(position=(0, 0, 1.8), angle=15degrees) novelviewcamera = RandomCamera() # Hyperparameters lambdanormals = 0.5 lambdaimage = 5.0 lambdamask = 0.5 k = 9 # Gaussian blur kernel size totalsteps = 10000 # Example total steps halfsteps = totalsteps // 2 for step in range(totalsteps): # Coarse-to-fine grid selection if step < halfsteps: activegrids = instantngpmodel.grids[:len(instantngpmodel.grids)//2] else: activegrids = instantngpmodel.grids # Render from fixed reconstruction camera renderrec = instantngpmodel.render(reconstructioncamera, activegrids) renderedimagerec = renderrec.image renderedopacityrec = renderrec.opacity # Compute Reconstruction Losses # Lrec: L2 error between input image and rendered image lossimage = l2loss(renderedimagerec, I0) # Lrec,mask: L2 error between rendered opacity and object mask mask = maskmodel(I0) lossmask = l2loss(renderedopacityrec, mask) # Render from random novel view camera rendernovel = instantngpmodel.render(novelviewcamera, activegrids) renderedimagenovel = rendernovel.image renderednormalsnovel = rendernovel.normals # Compute SDS Loss on novel view # Sample noise level t and noise epsilon t = samplenoiselevel() epsilon = samplenoise() # Add noise to rendered novel view noisyimage = alphat renderedimagenovel + sigmat epsilon # Get predicted noise from diffusion model predictednoise = diffusionmodel(noisyimage, t, prompt) # Compute SDS gradient # w(t) is a weighting function, typically dependent on t wt = weightingfunction(t) gradsds = wt (predictednoise - epsilon) gradient(renderedimagenovel, instantngpmodel.params) losssds = dotproduct(gradsds, gradsds) # Simplified for loss value, gradient is used directly in update # Compute Normal Regularization Loss # Blur normals and stop gradient blurrednormals = gaussianblur(renderednormalsnovel, k) stoppedblurrednormals = stopgradient(blurrednormals) lossnormals = l2loss(renderednormalsnovel, stoppedblurrednormals) # Total Loss totalloss = losssds + lambdanormals lossnormals + lambdaimage lossimage + lambdamask lossmask # Update Radiance Field Parameters instantngpmodel.update(totalloss) # Stochastic Shading if step > warmupsteps: applystochasticshading(instantngpmodel) \lambda{image}: 5.0. \lambda{mask}: 0.5. \lambda{normals}: 0.5. k (blur kernel): 9. Diffusion Model: Stable Diffusion trained on LAION. InstantNGP Config: 16 resolution levels, feature dimension 2, max resolution 2048. Camera Radius: 1.8. Camera Angle: 15° above the plane. Over-fitting: Optimizing only with the reconstruction loss on a single image leads to zero loss but no sensible 3D model. Solved by the SDS prior. Limited Diversity (Mode Collapse): High classifier-free guidance weights (e.g., 100) in DreamFusion produce only generic objects. RealFusion solves this by using the specific hei embedding from textual inversion, allowing reconstruction of any specific object. Surface Irregularities: InstantNGP optimization can produce small surface irregularities. Solved by coarse-to-fine training. Noisy Surfaces: Low-level artifacts can appear. Solved by 2D normal vector regularization. Janus Problem: The model may copy the front view to the back of the object. This is a known failure mode. Convergence Failure: The model may produce a semi-transparent scene lacking well-defined geometry. This is a known failure mode. Time Complexity: Training takes hours rather than days, due to the use of InstantNGP. Memory Complexity: Depends on the InstantNGP grid configuration (16 levels, dim 2, max res 2048). Strengths: Reconstructs arbitrary objects from a single image without category assumptions. Produces full 360° photographic models. Significantly higher quality than CLIP priors. 2D normal regularization reduces variance and yields superior results compared to 3D regularization. Limitations: Susceptible to the Janus problem (front-back texture copying). Can fail to converge, resulting in semi-transparent scenes. Requires an off-the-shelf matting model for the mask. When to use: Single-image 3D reconstruction of arbitrary objects in the wild or on benchmark datasets. When not to use: When multi-view images are available (other methods may be more robust) or when strict geometric accuracy without texture artifacts is required (due to Janus/convergence risks). RealFusion was introduced in February 2023. It builds upon the DreamFusion method, which generates 3D models from text descriptions. RealFusion adapts this by conditioning on a single image using textual inversion. It uses Stable Diffusion as the prior and InstantNGP as the radiance field backbone. The method was evaluated on the CO3D dataset against Shelf-Supervised Mesh Prediction. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28 RealFusion 360° Reconstruction of Any Object from a Single Image, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00816, fetched 2026-10-30
