name: Specific Architecture Training Procedures
body: Specific Architecture Training Procedures define the optimization loops and configuration strategies required to train distinct radiance field architectures, addressing their unique convergence challenges and data requirements. Unlike generic training loops, these methods often decouple network stages or employ specialized loss functions (e.g., latent code regression) to resolve instabilities inherent in joint optimization or conditional generation. The training procedures for these architectures share the following mechanisms: Iterative Optimization: Both child methods utilize stochastic gradient descent (or Adam) over epochs or fixed step counts, minimizing a composite loss function \mathcal{L} that typically combines reconstruction error with architecture-specific regularization or matching terms. State Management: Both methods require explicit management of model checkpoints and loss histories, saving parameters (e.g.,.param files) and metrics (e.g.,.npy arrays) at regular intervals to allow for monitoring and resumption. Device Placement: Inputs (voxel data, images, indices) and model parameters are explicitly moved to the target device (e.g., GPU) before forward passes. Scheduler Application: Learning rate scheduling is applied periodically (e.g., per epoch) to stabilize convergence, using standard schedulers like StepLR. The VCCNF Training Loop is a supervised optimization procedure for a Voxelized Continuous Coordinate Normalizing Flow (VCCNF) [4736-vccnf-training-loop.md]. It learns to map Gaussian noise to shape latent codes conditioned on voxel data by minimizing the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between predicted and target latent codes. It is chosen when training conditional generative models for 3D shapes where voxel data is available. It differs from diffusion-based guidance by directly optimizing a normalizing flow in a latent space rather than guiding a radiance field with a diffusion prior. Two-Stage Training for Learnable Proposer divides network optimization into two distinct stages to resolve the chicken-and-egg problem inherent in learning to sample for radiance fields [8685-two-stage-training-for-learnable-proposer.md]. Training the proposer requires a good fine network to provide a useful training signal, but the fine network can only improve if sampled at informative locations. This method sets itself apart from joint training approaches by decoupling proposer initialization from radiance field fine-tuning to ensure stable convergence. It is chosen when using learnable sampling strategies that depend on coarse network features. The IBRNet Baseline Training Loop involves learning a generalized model for 250,000 solver steps on 15 training DTU scenes, followed by fine-tuning the pre-trained model on seven training views of a specific test scene for another 60,000 steps. This two-phase approach allows the model to learn generalizable features before adapting to specific scenes. The training time is approximately 0.33 seconds per iteration, with a rendering time of 33.3 seconds per frame. The VCCNF and Two-Stage Training procedures are described in unofficial notes associated with the source. The IBRNet training configuration is detailed in the source, which compares training times and steps against other methods like NeRF and IDR. Fast Training of Neural Lumigraph Representations using Meta Learning, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2106.14942, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: VCCNF Training Loop
head: VCCNF Training Procedure
body: The VCCNF Training Loop is a supervised optimization procedure for a Voxelized Continuous Coordinate Normalizing Flow (VCCNF). It learns to map Gaussian noise to shape latent codes conditioned on voxel data by minimizing the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between predicted and target latent codes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A dataset of voxel grids and corresponding shape indices, along with pre-trained embeddings loaded from embeddingdir/embeddingsepoch{embeddingepoch}.param. Output: A trained VCCNF model checkpoint (vccnfepoch{e}.param) and a loss history array (lossesvccnf.npy). Data Structures: Voxel Data: Loaded from.npz files as torch.fromnumpy(data["voxeldata"]).float(). Latent Codes: Retrieved via embeddings(indices). Gaussian Latents: Generated as torch.randnlike(latentcodes). Parameters: Loss Function: nn.MSELoss, computed between predicted and target latent codes. Scheduler: StepLR with stepsize=100 and gamma=0.5, applied after each epoch. Dataset Split: 0.8 train / 0.2 validation, initialized with manualseed(42). Steps: 1. Split the dataset into 0.8 train / 0.2 validation using manualseed(42) and load pre-trained embeddings from embeddingdir/embeddingsepoch{embeddingepoch}.param. 2. For each epoch e from startepoch to epochs: a. Set model.train(). b. Iterate over batches (voxeldata, indices). c. Move indices to the target device. d. Retrieve target latent codes: L{\text{target}} = \text{embeddings}(\text{indices}). e. Generate Gaussian noise: L{\text{noise}} = \mathcal{N}(0, I) with the same shape as L{\text{target}}. f. Compute predicted latent codes: L{\text{pred}} = \text{VCCNF}(voxel\data, L{\text{noise}}). g. Compute loss: \mathcal{L} = \text{MSE}(L{\text{pred}}, L{\text{target}}). h. Zero gradients, perform backward pass, and step the optimizer. i. Accumulate loss, step the scheduler, and append the epoch loss to the losses list. j. If (e+1) \pmod{100} == 0, print progress, save lossesvccnf.npy, and save vccnfepoch{e+1}.param. k. Yield e and losses. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import numpy as np def trainvccnf(model, embeddings, dataloader, startepoch, epochs, embeddingepoch, device): # Load pre-trained embeddings from embeddingdir/embeddingsepoch{embeddingepoch}.param lossfn = nn.MSELoss() optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters()) # Optimizer not specified in sources; using standard Adam scheduler = torch.optim.lrscheduler.StepLR(optimizer, stepsize=100, gamma=0.5) losses = [] for e in range(startepoch, epochs): model.train() epochloss = 0.0 for voxeldata, indices in dataloader: indices = indices.to(device) voxeldata = voxeldata.to(device) latentcodes = embeddings(indices) gaussianlatents = torch.randnlike(latentcodes) latentpred = model(voxeldata, gaussianlatents) loss = lossfn(latentpred, latentcodes) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() epochloss += loss.item() scheduler.step() losses.append(epochloss) if (e + 1) % 100 == 0: print(f"Epoch {e+1}, Loss: {epochloss}") np.save("lossesvccnf.npy", np.array(losses)) torch.save(model.statedict(), f"vccnfepoch{e+1}.param") yield e, losses Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Resuming Training: The function latestepoch() computes the epoch as len(losses)//100100. No existence check for the weight file is performed before loading, unlike DeepSDFTraining. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple MSE-based supervision; leverages pre-trained embeddings. Limitations: No validation loss tracking mentioned; potential crash on resume if weights are missing. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The VCCNF Training Loop is a training procedure for a Voxelized Continuous Coordinate Normalizing Flow (VCCNF) that learns to map Gaussian noise to shape latent codes conditioned on voxel data. It builds on Training Loop. TurtleJayWang/VC-SDFGen, https://github.com/TurtleJayWang/VC-SDFGen, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Two-Stage Training for Learnable Proposer
body: Two-Stage Training for Learnable Proposer divides network optimization into two distinct stages to resolve the chicken-and-egg problem inherent in learning to sample for radiance fields. Training the proposer requires a good fine network to provide a useful training signal, but the fine network can only improve if sampled at informative locations. This method sets itself apart from joint training approaches by decoupling proposer initialization from radiance field fine-tuning to ensure stable convergence. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of training images with known camera poses. A coarse radiance field network (Nc). A fine radiance field network (Nf). A trainable proposer network (P). A heuristic proposer (H) (e.g., uniform or stratified sampling). Outputs: Optimized parameters for Nc, Nf, and P. Rendered images. Data Structures: Proposals: A set of 1D positions along the ray. Let Nc be the number of coarse samples and Nf be the number of fine samples. Heuristic Proposals: ZH generated by H. Learned Proposals: ZP generated by P. Parameters: Training Duration: The number of SGD steps for Stage 1 equals the number of SGD steps for Stage 2. The total training time is kept constant to allow fair comparison with vanilla NeRF. Steps: 1. Stage 1: Proposer Mimicry 1. Train Nc and Nf using the heuristic proposer H to generate samples ZH, following vanilla NeRF training procedures. 2. Simultaneously train the trainable proposer P to predict proposals ZP that match ZH. 3. Match the sets of proposals ZP and ZH in a greedy fashion for computational speed. 4. Minimize the sum of squared L2 distances between the greedily matched proposal pairs. 5. At the end of Stage 1, Nc and Nf match vanilla NeRF weights, and P mimics H. 2. Stage 2: End-to-End Optimization 1. Swap the heuristic proposer H with the learned proposer P so the fine network receives samples from P. 2. Train the entire system (Nc, Nf, P) end-to-end. 3. Minimize the reconstruction loss of the fine network to improve image quality. 4. Add the reconstruction loss of the coarse network to prevent divergence. 5. Optimize the coarse network to minimize its reconstruction loss AND produce features that enable P to provide informative samples to Nf. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def twostagetraining(images, poses, Nc, Nf, numstepsperstage): # Initialize networks Nc = CoarseNetwork() Nf = FineNetwork() P = ProposerNetwork() H = HeuristicProposer() # e.g., uniform sampling # Stage 1: Mimic Heuristic Proposer for step in range(numstepsperstage): # 1. Train Coarse and Fine with Heuristic Proposer (Vanilla NeRF style) ZH = heuristicsample(poses, Nc) Cf, Tf = render(Nf, ZH) lossrec = computeloss(Cf, images[step]) # 2. Train Proposer to match Heuristic Proposer ZP = propose(P, poses, Nc) ZPmatched, ZHmatched = greedymatch1d(ZP, ZH) lossprop = sumsquaredl2(ZPmatched, ZHmatched) # Total loss for Stage 1 loss = lossrec + lossprop updateparameters([Nc, Nf, P], loss) # Stage 2: End-to-End Optimization with Learned Proposer for step in range(numstepsperstage): # 1. Generate samples using Learned Proposer ZP = propose(P, poses, Nc) # 2. Render with Coarse and Fine networks using ZP Cc, Tc = render(Nc, ZP) Cf, Tf = render(Nf, ZP) # 3. Compute reconstruction losses lossfine = computeloss(Cf, images[step]) losscoarse = computeloss(Cc, images[step]) # Total loss for Stage 2 loss = lossfine + losscoarse updateparameters([Nc, Nf, P], loss) def heuristicsample(poses, Nc): # Standard uniform or stratified sampling along rays return sorted(random.uniform(0, 1, Nc)) def propose(P, poses, Nc): # Forward pass of trainable proposer to predict Nc positions return sorted(P.forward(poses, Nc)) def render(N, samples): # Standard volume rendering: query network at samples, accumulate color/alpha colors = [N.query(s) for s in samples] alphas = [0.5 for in samples] # Placeholder for standard alpha return accumulate(colors, alphas) def computeloss(renderedcolor, targetimage): # Standard L2 or L1 pixel-wise reconstruction loss return sum((renderedcolor - targetimage) 2) def greedymatch1d(ZP, ZH): # Sort both sets by position and match i-th to i-th for speed return sorted(ZP), sorted(ZH) def sumsquaredl2(A, B): return sum((a - b) 2 for a, b in zip(A, B)) def updateparameters(networks, loss): # Standard gradient descent update for net in networks: net.zerograd() loss.backward() net.step() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Training from Scratch: Jointly training Nc, P, and Nf from scratch can fail to reach good performance or fail badly (e.g., -5 PSNR on Blender: Ship) due to weak supervision (only final ray color). Divergence: In Stage 2, omitting the coarse network's reconstruction loss can lead to system divergence. Time Complexity: The total training time is kept constant compared to vanilla NeRF, as the two stages are of equal duration. Memory Complexity: Requires storing parameters for Nc, Nf, and P. No additional significant memory overhead compared to standard NeRF, assuming the proposer architecture is lightweight. Strengths: Solves the chicken-and-egg problem of learning to sample and prevents failure modes associated with joint training from scratch. Limitations: Requires two distinct training phases and the proposer initially mimics a heuristic method which may not be optimal for the final radiance field. When to Use: When training a learnable proposer for radiance field optimization, especially if joint training leads to poor convergence. The method originates from research on learning to sample for view synthesis. The proposer concept draws resemblance to two-stage object detectors such as Faster R-CNN, where a first network produces proposals and a second refines them. Unlike object detection, radiance field training lacks direct supervision via object bounding box annotations, necessitating the two-stage approach. The method also relates to DETR-inspired Transformer proposers. NeRF in detail: Learning to sample for view synthesis, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2106.05264, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Training and Supervision
head: Hybrid Lighting Supervision, Sky Modeling and Object Insertion Losses
body: This article details the supervision strategy for optimizing a hybrid lighting representation that combines a volumetric lighting field with a parametric sky model for street scenes. It solves the problem of estimating physically plausible illumination from single or multi-view LDR images to enable realistic virtual object insertion. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its explicit separation of sky and volumetric lighting components, supervised via a pre-trained sky modeling network and adversarial feedback from object insertion realism rather than pure photometric consistency alone. Inputs: LDR input images: Perspective crops I{crop} from panoramas or single images. Ground truth data: Captured images I{gt}, depth maps D{gt}, sky masks M{sky}, sun direction f{dir} (for panoramas), and camera poses/intrinsics. 3D Assets: High-quality 3D models (e.g., cars) for insertion. Outputs: Predicted lighting parameters: Sky peak intensity \hat{f}{intensity}, sky direction \hat{f}{dir}, sky latent code \hat{f}{latent}, and a lighting volume representation. Reconstructed HDR sky \hat{I}{pano}. Edited image \hat{I}{edit} containing inserted objects. Sky Mask (M{sky}): Binary mask indicating sky regions in panoramic images. Pseudo Labels: HDR estimates (\tilde{f}{intensity}, \tilde{f}{latent}) generated by a fixed pre-trained sky modeling network from LDR inputs. The total loss is a weighted sum of the following components. All vector norms are Euclidean (L2) unless specified. 1. Log-Encoded L2 Loss: Used for intensity and HDR reconstruction to handle high dynamic range. \text{LogEncodedL2}(\hat{x}, x) = \| \log(1 + \hat{x}) - \log(1 + x) \|2^2 where \hat{x} is the prediction and x is the target. 2. Sky Modeling Supervision (Pre-training): Applied to an encoder-decoder network trained on LDR-HDR pairs (I{LDR}, I{HDR}). I{LDR} is derived from I{HDR} via gamma correction and intensity clipping. Peak Direction Loss (L{dir}): L1 angular error between predicted and ground-truth sun direction. Peak Intensity Loss (L{intensity}): Log-encoded L2 error between predicted and ground-truth peak intensity. HDR Reconstruction Loss (L{hdr}): Log-encoded L2 error between reconstructed and ground-truth HDR panorama. 3. Hybrid Lighting Prediction Losses: HDR Sky Branch: Input: Perspective crop I{crop}. Targets: Pseudo labels \tilde{f}{intensity}, \tilde{f}{latent} from the pre-trained sky network; ground-truth sun direction f{dir}; LDR panorama I{pano} within sky mask M{sky}. L{intensity}: Log-encoded L2 between \hat{f}{intensity} and \tilde{f}{intensity}. L{latent}: L1 loss between \hat{f}{latent} and \tilde{f}{latent}. L{dir}: L1 angular loss between \hat{f}{dir} and f{dir}. L{sky\recon}: L1 reconstruction loss between \hat{I}{pano} \odot M{sky} and I{pano} \odot M{sky}. Lighting Volume Branch: Render radiance along camera rays using the predicted lighting volume and sky dome. L{vol}: L2 loss between rendered radiance and captured ground-truth image I{gt}. L{depth}: Consistency loss between rendered alpha-channel depth map and ground-truth depth D{gt}. Sky Separation Loss: Prevents the lighting volume from occluding the sky. L{sep}: Binary cross-entropy loss supervising sky transmittance \tauK (from Eq. 1 in source) against sky mask M{sky}. 4. Adversarial Supervision (Object Insertion): Insert a 3D asset into the scene using estimated lighting. Check collision/occlusion using depth maps. L{adv}: Adversarial loss -D(\hat{I}{edit}), where D is a discriminator judging the realism of the edited image \hat{I}{edit} against real car images. Unverified code. Assumes normalized vectors. """ # Cosine similarity cossim = torch.sum(preddir targetdir, dim=-1) # Clip to avoid numerical instability in acos cossim = torch.clamp(cossim, -1.0, 1.0) angle = torch.acos(cossim) return torch.mean(angle) class TrainingLoop: def init(self, skymodel, lightingnet, discriminator, optimizer): self.skymodel = skymodel # Pre-trained, fixed self.lightingnet = lightingnet self.discriminator = discriminator self.optimizer = optimizer def step(self, batch): """ Performs one training step. batch contains: Icrop: LDR perspective crop Ipano: LDR panorama (for sky branch supervision) Msky: Sky mask fdir: Ground truth sun direction Igt: Ground truth captured image Dgt: Ground truth depth camerapose, intrinsics """ self.optimizer.zerograd() # 1. Predict Lighting Parameters # lightingnet outputs: fhatintensity, fhatdir, fhatlatent, lightingvolume, Ihatpano fhatintensity, fhatdir, fhatlatent, lightingvolume, Ihatpano = self.lightingnet(Icrop) # 2. Sky Modeling Supervision (Pseudo Labels) # Use pre-trained sky model to get targets from LDR panorama with torch.nograd(): # Sky model takes LDR panorama, outputs HDR pseudo labels ftildeintensity, ftildelatent = self.skymodel(Ipano) # 3. Compute Sky Branch Losses lossintensity = logencodedl2(fhatintensity, ftildeintensity) losslatent = F.l1loss(fhatlatent, ftildelatent) lossdir = angularloss(fhatdir, fdir) # L1 reconstruction within sky mask skymaskedpred = Ihatpano Msky skymaskedgt = Ipano Msky lossskyrecon = F.l1loss(skymaskedpred, skymaskedgt) # 4. Compute Lighting Volume Branch Losses # Render radiance along camera rays renderedradiance = renderradiance(lightingvolume, Ihatpano, camerapose, intrinsics) lossvol = F.mseloss(renderedradiance, Igt) # Render depth from alpha channel rendereddepth = renderdepthfromalpha(renderedradiance) # Implementation detail lossdepth = F.mseloss(rendereddepth, Dgt) # 5. Sky Separation Loss # Supervise sky transmittance tauK with binary cross entropy against Msky # tauK is derived from lightingvolume and sky model (Eq 1 in source) tauK = computeskytransmittance(lightingvolume) losssep = F.binarycrossentropy(tauK, Msky.float()) # 6. Adversarial Loss (Object Insertion) # Insert 3D asset using estimated lighting # Assume objectinsertionmodule handles placement, collision, and rendering Ihatedit = objectinsertionmodule( scenelighting=(lightingvolume, Ihatpano), camerapose=camerapose, depthmap=rendereddepth, assetpath="carmodel.obj") # Discriminator output Doutput = self.discriminator(Ihatedit) lossadv = -torch.mean(Doutput) # 7. Total Loss # Weights are hyperparameters not specified in source totalloss = ( lossintensity + losslatent + lossdir + lossskyrecon + lossvol + lossdepth + losssep + lossadv) totalloss.backward() self.optimizer.step() return { "lossintensity": lossintensity.item(), "losslatent": losslatent.item(), "lossdir": lossdir.item(), "lossskyrecon": lossskyrecon.item(), "lossvol": lossvol.item(), "lossdepth": lossdepth.item(), "losssep": losssep.item(), "lossadv": lossadv.item(), "totalloss": totalloss.item() } Degenerate Sky Occlusion: Without the sky separation loss, the lighting volume may completely occlude the sky, leading to incorrect illumination. The binary cross-entropy loss on transmittance \tauK prevents this. Unrealistic Object Insertion: If adversarial supervision is omitted, the lighting may be photometrically consistent but produce incorrect shadows or specular highlights on inserted objects. The discriminator D detects these errors. Precision: Log-encoded L2 is used to handle the wide dynamic range of HDR data, preventing saturation issues in standard L2 losses. Time Complexity: Training involves rendering radiance fields and depth maps for every batch, which is computationally expensive. The adversarial step adds the cost of a discriminator forward pass. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the lighting volume representation and sky model parameters. Pseudo-label generation for sky supervision requires storing the pre-trained sky model in memory (though fixed). Strengths: Enables realistic virtual object insertion by ensuring lighting consistency with both the environment and inserted objects. Handles HDR estimation from LDR inputs effectively. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the pre-trained sky modeling network for pseudo-labels. Requires 3D assets and depth maps for adversarial training. When to use: When the goal is not just scene reconstruction but also editing (e.g., inserting virtual objects) with physically plausible lighting. When not to use: For simple view synthesis where editing is not required, or when HDR ground truth is available and no sky/volume separation is needed. The method originates from "Neural Light Field Estimation for Street Scenes with Differentiable Virtual Object Insertion". It addresses the limitation of previous radiance field methods that struggled with realistic object insertion due to inaccurate lighting estimation. The approach combines a parametric sky model with a neural volumetric light field, supervised by a combination of photometric, geometric, and adversarial losses. It utilizes datasets like nuScenes and HoliCity, which provide LDR street-level imagery, and lifts them to HDR pseudo-labels using a pre-trained sky network. name: Camera Pose Optimization
head: NeDDF Localization
body: Camera pose optimization refines the extrinsic parameters (rotation and translation) of a camera by minimizing a reconstruction loss, enabling accurate localization in neural radiance fields when initial poses are noisy or unavailable. It distinguishes itself from standard Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines by directly optimizing pose parameters through differentiable rendering gradients, often using hybrid schedules of photometric and reprojection errors to handle large initial errors. Unlike LocalRF which restricts sampling to valid pixels for sparse views, or SMPL Refinement via Soft Rasterization which targets human meshes, this method is a general procedure for arbitrary scene geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Initial camera pose P = [\mathbf{R} | \mathbf{t}] (rotation matrix \mathbf{R}, translation vector \mathbf{t}), neural scene representation (e.g., NeDDF, NeRF, Gaussian Splatting), and input image \mathbf{I}. Outputs: Refined camera pose P^. Data Structures: Pose Parameterization: The pose gradient is parameterized as a 6D vector in the Lie algebra \mathfrak{se}(3), corresponding to the local SE(3) update. Ray Sampling: Rays are sampled from the camera frustum. In specific implementations (NeDDF), "interest region sampling" selects a subset of rays (e.g., 256 rays) to focus optimization on regions with high gradient significance or correspondence reliability. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: Set initial pose P0 with potential noise. Define optimization schedule (e.g., photometric-only, reprojection-only, or hybrid). 2. Iterate: For each iteration k: a. Sample Rays: Select rays using interest region sampling or uniform frustum sampling. b. Render: Compute rendered image \hat{\mathbf{I}} or feature maps using the current pose Pk and the scene representation. c. Compute Loss: Calculate loss \mathcal{L} based on the chosen error metric (photometric or reprojection). d. Compute Gradients: Calculate gradients of the loss with respect to the pose parameters. For Gaussian Splatting (NeDDF context), gradients are computed with respect to translation \mathbf{t} and rotation \mathbf{R} using the chain rule through the Gaussian centers \tilde{\mu}n: \frac{\delta \mathcal{L}}{\delta \mathbf{t}} = - \sumn \frac{\delta \mathcal{L}}{\delta \tilde{\mu}n} \frac{\delta \mathcal{L}}{\delta \mathbf{R}} = - \left[ \sumn \frac{\delta \mathcal{L}}{\delta \tilde{\mu}n} (\mun - \mathbf{t})^\top \right] \mathbf{R} where \mun is the mean of the n-th Gaussian and \tilde{\mu}n is the transformed center. For general NeRF/NeDDF, gradients are computed via backpropagation through the differentiable renderer. e. Update Pose: Update the pose increment using the Adam optimizer with exponential decay learning rate schedule. The 6D gradient vector is converted to an SE(3) matrix update and applied to Pk. 3. Terminate: Stop after a fixed number of iterations or when convergence criteria are met. Parameters: Optimization Schedule: Photometric error only: 300 iterations. Reprojection error only: 300 iterations. Hybrid: 100 iterations reprojection error followed by 200 iterations photometric error. Batch Size: 256 rays per iteration (for interest region sampling). Optimizer: Adam with exponential decay. Thresholds: Photometric error optimization is accurate only if initial position error \le 0.5 m and angular error \le 10^\circ. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizecamerapose(initialpose, scenemodel, image, schedule='hybrid'): """ Optimizes camera pose using photometric and/or reprojection error. Args: initialpose: SE(3) matrix [R|t] scenemodel: Differentiable radiance field or Gaussian splatting model image: Target image tensor schedule: 'photometric', 'reprojection', or 'hybrid' Returns: refinedpose: Optimized SE(3) matrix """ pose = initialpose.clone() optimizer = Adam([pose], lr=0.001) # Exponential decay handled by scheduler # Determine iteration counts based on schedule if schedule == 'photometric': itersreproj = 0 itersphoto = 300 elif schedule == 'reprojection': itersreproj = 300 itersphoto = 0 elif schedule == 'hybrid': itersreproj = 100 itersphoto = 200 else: raise ValueError("Unknown schedule") totaliters = itersreproj + itersphoto for i in range(totaliters): # 1. Sample Rays # Use interest region sampling if supported, else uniform rays = sampleinterestregion(pose, numrays=256) # 2. Render renderedimage = scenemodel.render(rays, pose) # 3. Compute Loss if i < itersreproj: # Reprojection error # Requires correspondence matching (e.g., color similarity) # Note: This step is prone to mismatches loss = computereprojectionloss(renderedimage, image, rays) else: # Photometric error loss = computephotometricloss(renderedimage, image) # 4. Compute Gradients # For Gaussian Splatting, explicit gradient formulas may be used # Otherwise, standard autograd optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() # 5. Update Pose optimizer.step() return pose Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Photometric Error Limitations: Photometric error provides reasonable gradients only in regions with smooth color changes. Large initial errors lead to erroneous local solutions. Reprojection Error Limitations: Reprojection error alone fails to significantly improve residuals because correspondence point calculation based on color similarity lacks uniqueness, causing many mismatches. Wrong Correspondences: Incorrect correspondence points (e.g., in textureless or repetitive regions) negatively impact optimization. Mitigation strategies include reducing ray weights for these regions or using features with higher uniqueness instead of raw color. This method refines noisy initial camera poses by learning a per-camera correction conditioned on 2D image coordinates, jointly optimizing the neural radiance field and camera extrinsics. It models pose corrections as a continuous function of pixel location to achieve spatially coherent refinement. It sets itself apart from standard coarse-to-fine optimization methods by using a dedicated MLP to predict local SE(3) warps rather than relying solely on frequency-based positional encoding schedules. A preprocessing step to refine noisy SMPL parameters and camera estimates by minimizing the difference between predicted and rendered silhouettes and projected 3D joints. It regresses 2D joints and segmentation masks using HigherHRNet and DensePose, estimates an SMPL mesh using ROMP, and minimizes a loss combining silhouette and joint projection errors. It is specifically designed for human body modeling and differs from general scene pose optimization by targeting articulated human parameters. A method used to estimate camera poses for sparse views when standard Structure-from-Motion (SfM) tools like COLMAP fail, specifically by restricting ray sampling to valid color pixels. It is suitable for application in sparse views where the number of images to be determined is limited. It differs from general optimization by focusing on feasibility in extremely sparse scenarios where other methods fail, albeit at a substantial computational cost (e.g., 75 hours for 1392 images). Time Complexity: Depends on the number of iterations and ray sampling. Hybrid schedules require 300 iterations. LocalRF is substantially slower than COLMAP (speedup factor of 8-26.5 for 310-1392 frames) but necessary for sparse views. Memory Complexity: Low, as it primarily stores pose parameters and gradients, plus the scene representation. Strengths: Can recover poses from noisy initializations; integrates directly into the training loop of neural radiance fields. Limitations: Photometric error is sensitive to initial pose accuracy (requires <0.5m position error and <10° angle error). Reprojection error is prone to correspondence mismatches. When to Use: When initial poses from SfM are inaccurate or unavailable, and the scene has sufficient texture for photometric or reprojection gradients. When Not to Use: When initial errors are large (>0.5m, >10°) and only photometric error is used, or when computational resources are extremely limited and sparse views are not the primary constraint. Camera pose optimization in the context of neural radiance fields has been developed to address the sensitivity of NeRF training to initial camera poses. The NeDDF (Neural Density-Distance Fields) method explicitly details optimization schedules using photometric and reprojection errors, demonstrating the limitations of each when used in isolation. The Gaussian Splatting literature (gsplat) provides efficient gradient computations for pose optimization in 3D Gaussian splatting, enabling real-time or near-real-time refinement. Applications extend to human modeling (NeuMan) using soft rasterization for SMPL refinement, and sparse view reconstruction (LocalRF) where traditional SfM fails. name: Learnable Pose Refinement via Local SE(3) Warp
head: Embedding-Based Warp MLP, Local SE(3) Pose Correction
body: This method refines coarse camera poses by learning a per-camera correction in the SE(3) Lie algebra space, conditioned on 2D image coordinates and a learnable embedding. It addresses the problem of pose inaccuracies in sparse or noisy initial estimates by jointly optimizing the pose corrections alongside the radiance field, avoiding the instability of direct global pose optimization. Unlike methods that rely solely on geometric consistency or robust PnP variants, this approach uses a differentiable neural network to predict local SE(3) warps, allowing for end-to-end training with photometric and multi-view losses. The method optimizes camera poses by predicting a local SE(3) transformation for each view, which is composed with the initial pose estimate. The refinement is driven by a neural network (Warp MLP) that takes 2D pixel coordinates and a per-camera embedding as input. Inputs: Initial camera poses P{init} \in SE(3)^{N} (rotation R{init}, translation t{init}). Inverse intrinsics K^{-1}. Ray indices or pixel coordinates. Per-camera embeddings E \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d{emb}}. Outputs: Refined camera poses P{refined} \in SE(3)^{N}. Gradients for pose embeddings, MLP weights, and initial pose parameters. The implementation relies on the following structures: 1. Warp Embedding: Type: torch.nn.Embedding Layout: weight tensor of shape (numcameras, embeddingdim). Purpose: Stores a learnable vector ei for each camera i to capture view-specific pose biases. 2. Warp MLP: Type: localWarp (custom neural network module). Input: Concatenation of 2D coordinates (u, v) and embedding ei. Output: 6-dimensional vector representing the SE(3) Lie algebra \xi \in \mathbb{R}^6. 3. Camera Coordinates Grid: Precomputed or dynamically gathered 3D coordinates of camera centers or ray origins, used to derive 2D projections. 1. Initialization: Initialize initial poses R0, t0 from a coarse estimator (e.g., COLMAP). Initialize per-camera embeddings E randomly or with zeros. Initialize Warp MLP weights. 2. Ray Sampling: For each optimization step, sample N{rays} pixel rays per image. Typical values: 1024 rays for DTU/Replica, 2048 rays for LLFF. 3. Coordinate Extraction: Gather 3D camera coordinates for the sampled rays: C{3D} = \text{gather\camera\cords\grid\3D}(opt, batch\size, K^{-1}, ray\idx). Extract 2D coordinates from the 3D grid: C{2D} = C{3D}[:,:,:2]. 4. Embedding Retrieval: Retrieve the embedding for the current camera i: ei = E[i]. Expand ei to match the number of sampled rays: E{expanded} = \text{expand}(ei, (-1, N{rays}, -1)). 5. Local SE(3) Prediction: Concatenate 2D coordinates and embedding: Input = \text{concat}(C{2D}, E{expanded}, dim=-1). Pass through Warp MLP: \xi = \text{WarpMLP}(Input), where \xi \in \mathbb{R}^{N{rays} \times 6}. 6. SE(3) Matrix Conversion: Convert the Lie algebra vector \xi to an SE(3) matrix M{local}: M{local} = \text{SE3\exp}(\xi) where \text{SE3\exp} is the exponential map from Lie algebra to Lie group. 7. Pose Composition: Compose the local refinement with the initial pose P{init}: P{refined} = M{local} \times P{init} Note: The composition order depends on the convention (world-to-camera or camera-to-world). The source specifies compose([localposerefine, pose]). 8. Rotation Matrix Reconstruction (Alternative/Specific Variant): In some implementations (e.g., SPARF), the rotation is updated using a Gram-Schmidt-like process. Input: 4D vector r = [a1^T, a2^T]^T. Compute basis vectors: b1 = \frac{a1}{\|a1\|} b2 = \frac{a2 - (b1 \cdot a2)b1}{\|a2 - (b1 \cdot a2)b1\|} b3 = b1 \times b2 Construct Rotation Matrix: R = [b1, b2, b3] Update parameters: \hat{R}{w2c} = f(\hat{r}{w2c} + \Delta r) \hat{t}{w2c} = t{w2c} + \Delta t where f is the function defined above. Learning Rates (Adam Optimizer): Network Weights: DTU/Replica: Initial 5 \times 10^{-4}, decaying to 1 \times 10^{-4}. LLFF: Initial 1 \times 10^{-3}, decaying to 1 \times 10^{-4}. Camera Poses: DTU/Replica: Initial 1 \times 10^{-3}, decaying to 1 \times 10^{-4}. LLFF: Initial 3 \times 10^{-3}, decaying to 1 \times 10^{-5}. Image Resolution: DTU: 300 \times 400. Replica: 340 \times 600. LLFF: 378 \times 504. Ray Sampling: DTU/Replica: 1024 rays per step. LLFF: 2048 rays per step. Embedding Dimension: Defined by opt.arch.embeddingdim. Not given in the sources. Background Artifacts: In LLFF joint optimization, applying multi-view correspondence and depth consistency losses from the start can cause the background to appear in front of the foreground. It is recommended to use only photometric loss for the first 1,000 iterations. Hierarchical Sampling: For LLFF, hierarchical sampling provides no significant benefit over a single MLP and increases training time. A single MLP is preferred for efficiency. Precision: The Gram-Schmidt process for rotation reconstruction requires careful normalization to avoid numerical instability, especially when a1 or the residual vector is near zero. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class LocalSE3WarpRefinement: def init(self, numcameras, embeddingdim, warpmlp): """ Initialize the pose refinement module. Args: numcameras (int): Number of camera views. embeddingdim (int): Dimensionality of the per-camera embedding. warpmlp (nn.Module): Neural network mapping (2D coords + embedding) -> 6D Lie algebra. """ self.numcameras = numcameras self.warpembedding = nn.Embedding(numcameras, embeddingdim) self.warpmlp = warpmlp # Initialize embeddings nn.init.zeros(self.warpembedding.weight) def refinepose(self, initialpose, cameraindices, rayindices, intrinv, batchsize): """ Compute refined poses for a batch of cameras. Args: initialpose (torch.Tensor): Initial SE(3) poses of shape (numcameras, 4, 4). cameraindices (torch.Tensor): Indices of cameras in the batch. rayindices (torch.Tensor): Indices of rays to sample. intrinv (torch.Tensor): Inverse intrinsic matrix. batchsize (int): Number of rays per camera. Returns: torch.Tensor: Refined SE(3) poses of shape (numcameras, 4, 4). """ # 1. Gather 3D camera coordinates for sampled rays # Assuming a helper function exists to map ray indices to 3D coordinates # using inverse intrinsics. cameracordsgrid3D = gathercameracordsgrid3D( initialpose, intrinv, rayindices, batchsize) # 2. Extract 2D coordinates cameracordsgrid2D = cameracordsgrid3D[...,:2] # Shape: (batchsize, numrays, 2) # 3. Retrieve per-camera embeddings # cameraindices shape: (batchsize,) embeddings = self.warpembedding(cameraindices) # Shape: (batchsize, embeddingdim) # Expand embeddings to match ray dimensions # embeddings shape: (batchsize, 1, embeddingdim) -> (batchsize, numrays, embeddingdim) numrays = cameracordsgrid2D.shape[1] embeddingsexpanded = embeddings.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, numrays, -1) # 4. Concatenate 2D coords and embeddings inputtensor = torch.cat((cameracordsgrid2D, embeddingsexpanded), dim=-1) # 5. Pass through Warp MLP # Output: localse3refine of shape (batchsize, numrays, 6) localse3refine = self.warpmlp(inputtensor) # 6. Convert SE(3) Lie algebra to SE(3) matrix # Assuming a helper function for SE3 exponential map localposerefine = se3toSE3(localse3refine) # Shape: (batchsize, numrays, 4, 4) # 7. Compose local refinement with base pose # initialpose shape: (numcameras, 4, 4) # We need to gather the specific initial pose for each camera in the batch baseposes = initialpose[cameraindices] # Shape: (batchsize, 4, 4) # Expand base poses to match ray dimensions baseposesexpanded = baseposes.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, numrays, -1, -1) # Compose: localpose = localposerefine baseposes # Note: Matrix multiplication order depends on convention (left vs right multiplication) # The source says compose([localposerefine, pose]), implying localposerefine @ pose localpose = torch.matmul(localposerefine, baseposesexpanded) # 8. Aggregate poses (e.g., by averaging or selecting a representative ray) # Since the refinement is per-ray, we might average the resulting poses or # use the median. For simplicity, we average the 4x4 matrices. refinedpose = localpose.mean(dim=1) # Shape: (batchsize, 4, 4) return refinedpose def gathercameracordsgrid3D(initialpose, intrinv, rayindices, batchsize): """ Helper function to gather 3D coordinates. This is a placeholder for the specific implementation details of ray generation. """ # This function would typically: # 1. Generate 2D pixel coordinates from rayindices. # 2. Unproject them to 3D using intrinv and the camera pose. # For the purpose of this article, we assume this helper exists. pass def se3toSE3(liealgebra): """ Convert SE(3) Lie algebra vector to SE(3) matrix. """ # This function implements the exponential map from se(3) to SE(3). # Input: (N, 6) # Output: (N, 4, 4) pass This variant, associated with Robust SG-NeRF, enhances the pose refinement process by distinguishing between inlier and outlier poses based on confidence estimation. For inlier poses, it applies additional geometric constraints to improve consistency: Re-projection Loss: A loss term based on the current Signed Distance Function (SDF) and pose estimations is applied to inliers to strengthen constraints between matching image pairs. Intersection-of-Union (IoU) Loss: This loss is applied to further strengthen constraints between matching image pairs for inliers. Outlier Handling: For outlier poses, a Monte Carlo re-localization method is used to find better initializations, and a scene graph updating strategy is employed to eliminate incorrectly matched pairs. This approach avoids the instability of optimizing all poses equally and improves reconstruction quality on datasets like SG-NeRF and DTU. Time Complexity: The addition of multi-view correspondence loss and depth consistency objectives adds a factor of approximately 1.5 to the optimization time, regardless of the number of views. The PDC-Net for predicting matches runs at 10fps on 300 \times 400 images. Memory Complexity: The method introduces memory overhead for storing per-camera embeddings and the Warp MLP. The embedding dimension is a hyperparameter. Performance: The method has been validated on DTU, Replica, and LLFF datasets. It effectively corrects outlier poses and improves reconstruction quality. Strengths: Joint optimization of poses and radiance fields. Learnable per-camera embeddings allow for view-specific corrections. Local SE(3) warps provide a stable optimization landscape compared to global pose updates. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of learning rates for network weights vs. poses. May suffer from background artifacts if multi-view losses are applied too early in LLFF scenes. Relies on the quality of initial poses; poor initializations may require robust outlier handling. When to Use: Suitable for sparse and noisy pose scenarios where initial estimates are inaccurate but sufficient for coarse alignment. When Not to Use: Not recommended for dense pose scenarios with high-quality initial estimates, as the overhead may not be justified. Also, avoid if computational resources are severely limited due to the added complexity of the Warp MLP and embedding storage. The method originates from research on optimizing Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) from sparse and noisy poses. Key contributions include: SPARF (2023): Introduced a method for optimizing NeRF from sparse and noisy poses using a Gram-Schmidt-like process for rotation reconstruction and specific learning rate schedules for DTU, Replica, and LLFF datasets. Joint-TensoRF (Unofficial): Proposed an embedding-based warp MLP approach for local SE(3) pose correction, leveraging per-camera embeddings and 2D coordinate conditioning. Robust SG-NeRF (2024): Enhanced the pose refinement process with geometric constraints for inliers and Monte Carlo re-localization for outliers, improving robustness in scene graph-aided reconstruction. name: Camera Pose Refinement
head: Pose Refinement
body: Camera Pose Refinement addresses inaccuracies in coarse camera poses estimated by scene regressors or initial registration steps by minimizing a point-to-camera ray consistency loss. It serves as a post-initialization or iterative optimization step to align the estimated camera extrinsics with the reconstructed scene geometry. Unlike methods that jointly optimize poses and scene parameters via end-to-end differentiable rendering (e.g., BARF [33]), this approach often relies on geometric consistency or robust reprojection errors to avoid training instability. It is distinct from robust PnP variants which estimate poses independently per view before photometric polishing. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Coarse camera poses Pk (or Ck), 3D scene points (e.g., Gaussian means \mathbf{g}{kj} or reconstructed points \mathbf{X}i), and 2D image observations (e.g., patch centers \mathbf{u}i or ray directions). Outputs: Refined camera poses Pk. Data Structures: Camera pose Pk: A 4 \times 4 SE(3) transformation matrix or a tuple (R, t). 3D Points: A set of points \{\mathbf{X}i\} or Gaussian means \{\mathbf{g}{kj}\} associated with image patches. Correspondences: A mapping from 3D points to 2D image coordinates \mathbf{u}i. Steps: 1. Initialization Constraints: Fix the camera pose of the seed image to an identity matrix to resolve gauge ambiguity. Fix the scaling factor between the seed image and its most similar adjacent image to resolve scale ambiguity. Ensure the initial poses are normalized to the same scale as the scene points. 2. Correspondence Establishment: Identify 2D-3D correspondences. For each view n, find Gaussians j of token k with supporting patch i \in Ck that are visible in view n. Alternatively, use RANSAC and PnP to estimate initial correspondences between 3D points \mathbf{X}i and camera centers \mathbf{C}k. 3. Pose Optimization: Method A (Ray Consistency): Minimize a point-to-camera ray consistency loss. The loss measures the discrepancy between the ray from the camera center to a 3D point and the observed ray direction. \mathcal{L} = \sum{i,k} \rho(\| d{i,k} \cdot \nu{i,k} - (\mathbf{X}i - \mathbf{C}k) \|2) where \mathbf{C}k is the camera center, d{i,k} is the scaling factor, and \nu{i,k} is the ray direction. Method B (Robust Reprojection): Minimize robust reprojection error for each pose Pn independently: E{\mathrm{cam}}(Pn) = \sum{(k,j,i)} \rho \left( \| \pi(Pn, \mathbf{g}{kj}) - \mathbf{u}i \| \right) where \pi is the projection function, \mathbf{g}{kj} is the Gaussian mean, and \rho is a robust penalty function (e.g., Huber or Cauchy). Optimize Pn using gradient descent or iterative solvers (e.g., graduated non-convexity). 4. Photometric Polish (Optional): Perform a short photometric optimization to reduce patch-center quantization errors after geometric refinement. Parameters: Batch Size: Limited to 1 for transformer-based scene regressors on consumer GPUs (e.g., 24GB) to prevent divergence. Robust Penalty \rho: Not specified in detail, but typically a robust norm like Huber or Cauchy. Seed Image: One image is fixed as the reference. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Divergence with MLP Refiners: Using an MLP-based pose refiner (like ACE0) with a transformer-based scene regressor causes divergence. This is because the transformer limits batch size to 1, preventing the mixing of multi-view constraints that MLPs rely on for stable training. Gauge Ambiguity: Must fix at least one pose and one scale factor to avoid trivial solutions. Quantization Error: Patch-center quantization can introduce errors, mitigated by photometric polish. Refines camera poses using Gaussian-patch correspondences by minimizing robust reprojection error, estimated independently by robust PnP with graduated non-convexity. Each pose is estimated independently by minimizing the reprojection error over all its correspondences, followed by a short photometric polish to reduce patch-center quantization. Choose this when independent view refinement is preferred over joint optimization, or when 2D-3D correspondences are reliably established via token associations. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of correspondences and the optimization solver. Robust PnP is typically fast per view. Memory Complexity: Low, as it operates on correspondences rather than full batches of pixels. Performance: Improves pose accuracy significantly over coarse regressor outputs. ZipSplat demonstrates sharp renders with refined poses. Strengths: Avoids training instability associated with joint optimization in memory-constrained settings. Limitations: Requires reliable initial correspondences. Not suitable for MLP-based scene regressors due to batch size constraints. When to Use: When using transformer-based scene regressors with limited batch sizes, or when independent view refinement is sufficient. When Not to Use: When using MLP-based scene regressors that benefit from multi-view constraint mixing. Originated in the context of training 3D Gaussian Splatting from unposed images, specifically in ZeroGS and ZipSplat. ZeroGS proposed minimizing point-to-camera ray consistency to address inaccuracies from scene regressors, noting the failure of MLP-based refiners (ACE0) with transformers. ZipSplat introduced robust PnP refinement using Gaussian-patch correspondences. These methods address the challenge of initializing and refining camera poses without ground-truth poses, building on earlier work like BARF [33] and ACE0 [9]. name: Learning Rate Scheduling
head: Exponential Learning Rate Decay, LR Scheduling, LR decay, LambdaLR Scheduler, Learning Rate Decay, Learning Rate Scheduler
body: Learning Rate Scheduling (LRS) dynamically adjusts the optimizer's step size during the training of radiance fields to balance convergence speed and final reconstruction quality. It solves the problem of optimization instability and slow convergence by decaying the learning rate from an initial high value to a lower final value, often with specific phases for warm-up or delay. It differs from Training Schedule by adjusting only the scalar step size rather than the active set of losses or structural representation state, and from Adam Optimisation with Adaptive Scaling by providing the external schedule that modulates the base step size used by the adaptive optimizer. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current optimization step i (or epoch), initial learning rate lr{init}, final learning rate lr{final}, maximum steps max\steps, and optional delay parameters (lr{delay\steps}, lr{delay\mult}). Output: The current learning rate lr(i). Data Structures: No persistent data structures are required for the core scheduling logic; it is a stateless function of the step count. However, implementations may cache the schedule or use a scheduler object that tracks the last epoch/step. Formulas and Steps: 1. Log-Linear Exponential Decay (Standard): The most common schedule decays the learning rate log-linearly from lr{init} to lr{final} over max\steps. Calculate the normalized progress t: t = \text{clip}\left(\frac{i}{max\steps}, 0, 1\right) Calculate the base learning rate using log-linear interpolation: lr{base}(i) = \exp\left( \ln(lr{init}) \cdot (1 - t) + \ln(lr{final}) \cdot t \right) If a delay phase is enabled (lr{delay\steps} > 0), calculate a delay multiplier delay\rate: delay\rate = lr{delay\mult} + (1 - lr{delay\mult}) \cdot \sin\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \cdot \text{clip}\left(\frac{i}{lr{delay\steps}}, 0, 1\right) \right) If lr{delay\steps} \le 0, delay\rate = 1.0. The final learning rate is: lr(i) = delay\rate \cdot lr{base}(i) Edge case: If i < 0 or both lr{init} and lr{final} are 0.0, return 0.0. 2. Power-of-2 Batch Decay: In some implementations, the learning rate is divided by a power of 2 after each batch, dependent on the batch count and epoch. lr{new} = \frac{lr{old}}{2^{\frac{1}{batchCount \cdot (epoch + 1)}}} This applies separately to the main learning rate and the Spherical Harmonics (SH) learning rate. 3. LambdaLR (PyTorch Style): A generic exponential decay can be defined via a lambda function for use with torch.optim.lrscheduler.LambdaLR: \lambda(epoch) = \gamma^{\frac{epoch}{step\size}} where \gamma is the gamma value and step\size is the interval. 4. Piecewise Schedules: Complex schedules can be composed of multiple sub-schedules applied sequentially at milestone steps. Layout: A list of Schedule objects and a 1D array of cumulative milestones. Lookup: Given a step, find the index idx using searchsorted on milestones. The base step for the sub-schedule is step - milestones[idx-1] (or step if idx=0). 5. Per-Parameter Scheduling: Different parameter groups (e.g., means, features, scale, rotation) can have distinct learning rates. For 3D Gaussians, the mean positions (Adam group 0) often use an exponential decay from meanslrinit to meanslrfinal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def getlearningrate(step, maxsteps, lrinit, lrfinal, lrdelaysteps=0, lrdelaymult=1.0): """ Computes the learning rate using log-linear decay with optional delay. Args: step (int): Current optimization step. maxsteps (int): Total number of optimization steps. lrinit (float): Initial learning rate. lrfinal (float): Final learning rate. lrdelaysteps (int): Number of steps for the initial delay phase. lrdelaymult (float): Multiplier for the learning rate during the delay phase. Returns: float: The computed learning rate. """ # Edge case: invalid step or zero rates if step < 0 or (lrinit == 0.0 and lrfinal == 0.0): return 0.0 # Calculate normalized progress t t = np.clip(step / maxsteps, 0, 1) # Log-linear interpolation loglrinit = np.log(lrinit) loglrfinal = np.log(lrfinal) loglerp = np.exp(loglrinit (1 - t) + loglrfinal t) # Calculate delay multiplier if lrdelaysteps > 0: # Sinusoidal delay ramp delayt = np.clip(step / lrdelaysteps, 0, 1) delayrate = lrdelaymult + (1 - lrdelaymult) np.sin(0.5 np.pi delayt) else: delayrate = 1.0 return delayrate loglerp def getpiecewiseschedule(step, schedules, milestones): """ Retrieves the learning rate from a piecewise schedule. Args: step (int): Current step. schedules (list): List of schedule objects, each with a get(step) method. milestones (list): Cumulative step counts where each sub-schedule begins. Returns: float: The learning rate from the active sub-schedule. """ # Find the index of the schedule active at this step # searchsorted returns the index where step could be inserted while maintaining order # side='right' ensures we pick the schedule that starts at or before the step idx = np.searchsorted(milestones, step, side='right') # Get the active schedule schedule = schedules[idx] # Calculate the relative step within this sub-schedule if idx >= 1: baseidx = milestones[idx - 1] else: baseidx = 0 return schedule.get(step - baseidx) Parameters: lrinit: Initial learning rate. Typical values: 2 \cdot 10^{-3}, 10^{-3}. lrfinal: Final learning rate. Typical values: 2 \cdot 10^{-5}, 5 \cdot 10^{-5}. maxsteps: Total optimization steps. Default: 1,000,000. lrdelaysteps: Steps for initial delay. Default: 0. lrdelaymult: Delay multiplier. Default: 1.0. gamma: Exponential decay factor for LambdaLR. stepsize: Interval for LambdaLR decay. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Rates: If both initial and final rates are zero, the function must return zero to avoid division by zero or invalid log operations. Negative Steps: Steps before training begins should return zero. Precision: Log-linear interpolation preserves the geometric mean of the rates, which is often preferred over linear interpolation for multiplicative decay. Boundary Conditions: Ensure t is clamped to [0, 1] to handle steps outside the training range. This method defines the standard iterative optimization protocol for training Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), specifically tailored for sparse input scenarios. It solves the problem of converging a differentiable volume rendering model to match target images by combining ray-batched stochastic gradient descent with a two-phase loss schedule and exponential learning rate decay. It differs from sibling methods like FreeNeRF by using simpler auxiliary models for depth supervision rather than annealing positional encoding frequencies, and it explicitly manages regularization weights that decay alongside the learning rate. A training schedule defines the temporal progression of hyperparameters, loss functions, and structural updates during the optimization of a radiance field or implicit surface. It solves the problem of slow convergence and instability by decoupling coarse geometric alignment from fine detail refinement. Unlike Learning Rate Scheduling, which adjusts only the optimizer's step size, or Regularization and Priors, which adds static penalty terms, a training schedule actively changes the active set of losses and the structural state of the representation (e.g., enabling densification or freezing updates) over specific iteration intervals. This article defines the hyperparameter configuration required to optimize differentiable rendering methods using first-order (OurG, OurH) and second-order (OurHVP, OurHVPA) stochastic gradient estimators. It solves the problem of selecting optimal sampling, learning rate, and trust region parameters for inverse rendering tasks such as caustic optimization, shape reconstruction, and texture mapping. What sets this configuration apart from standard NeRF training is the explicit use of Sigma annealing for distribution bandwidth control and antithetic sampling to reduce variance, alongside distinct parameter sets for first-order versus second-order optimization loops. An exponentially decaying schedule that transitions a learning rate from an initial value to a final value using a base raised to a normalized step exponent. It differs from Linear Learning Rate Schedule by applying multiplicative reductions rather than additive ones, and from Step Decay Learning Rate Schedule by providing a continuous curve rather than discrete uniform reductions at specific boundaries. XYZ Learning Rate Scheduling adjusts the learning rate specifically for the 3D Gaussian point locations (xyz) during radiance-field optimization to balance training speed and rendering quality. It distinguishes itself from general scalar schedules by targeting the spatial parameters of the Gaussian primitives, addressing the sensitivity of point positions to large learning rates which can degrade rendering quality. Per-Parameter Learning Rate Scheduling adjusts the learning rates for specific parameter groups (scaling, opacity, rotation, and features) independently during each training iteration. It addresses the need to tune convergence speed and final rendering quality by allowing distinct optimization dynamics for different geometric and radiometric properties, setting it apart from uniform scheduling methods that apply a single rate to all parameters. Annealing Schedules provide a unified framework for decaying or maintaining hyperparameter values, primarily learning rates, during the training of neural radiance fields. Unlike specialized schedules that implement only one decay strategy, this framework supports constant, linear, and exponential interpolation between initial and final values. It is distinct from Exponential Decay Learning Rate Schedule by using interpolation between bounds rather than a fixed decay rate, and from Linear Learning Rate Schedule by offering multiple decay modes within a single class. A learning rate schedule that transitions from an initial value to a final value over a specified number of steps using linear interpolation. It provides a deterministic, monotonic decay path for optimization parameters in radiance-field training. Unlike exponential decay, which changes rate proportionally to the current value, this method changes the rate by a constant absolute amount per step. Adjusts learning rates based on a view-count prior. Without the view-count prior, PSNR can degrade up to -1.22 in the worst case. A technique to increase the learning rate of specific model parameters (instant NGP weights and vertex coordinates) after a densification event to allow rapid accommodation for changes. After densification at iteration I, the learning rate is increased by adding a spike function with duration L on top of the decay function l(i). The spike function increases the decaying learning rate back up to its maximum (initial) value, before decaying it back down in L iterations. Formula: \mathbb{1}\{i - I > 0\} (l(0) - l(I)) \exp\left(-\frac{6(i-I)}{L}\right) where i is the current iteration, I is the iteration of densification, l(0) is the initial learning rate, l(I) is the learning rate at iteration I, and L is the duration of the spike. If iteration is in upsamplist, pop target voxel count nvoxels = Nvoxellist.pop(0). Compute resolution resocur = Ntoreso(nvoxels, tensorf.aabb). Limit samples nSamples = min(args.nSamples, calnsamples(resocur,args.stepratio)). Call tensorf.upsamplevolumegrid(resocur). If args.lrupsamplereset is true, set lrscale = 1. Otherwise, compute lrscale = args.lrdecaytargetratio (iteration / args.niters). Get optimizer groups gradvars = tensorf.getoptparamgroups(args.lrinitlrscale, args.lrbasislrscale) and reinitialize optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(gradvars, betas=(0.9, 0.99)). Training for 15K iterations instead of 30K, compensated by learning rate schedules for scale, rotation, and SH DC coefficients, and increased SH higher-order LR. Train for 15K or 7.5K iterations instead of 30K. Apply additional learning rate schedules to enable rapid initial growth, compensating for the reduced iteration count. SH higher-order coefficient learning rate is increased 5x to 0.000625. Performance: 15K Iterations: PSNR 26.47, LPIPS 0.236, Opt Time 05:40. 30K Iterations: PSNR 26.51, LPIPS 0.243, Opt Time 10:24. 15K iterations + LR schedules: PSNR 26.47, SSIM 0.819, LPIPS 0.236, Opt Time 05:40, FPS 248, Final Avg Scale 0.0166. 7.5K iterations + LR schedules: PSNR 26.23, SSIM 0.817, LPIPS 0.238, Opt Time 02:58, FPS 229, Final Avg Scale 0.0153. A training strategy to gradually increase the Spherical Harmonics (SH) degree to improve image quality, as higher degrees do not significantly contribute if used from the start. During the coarse training course, increase the SH degree from 0 to 1. During fine training, gradually increase the degree from 1 to the target degree n. Each increase in degree happens after 10% of the total fine training iterations have completed. The default SH degree used in experiments is 1. The target degree n is chosen based on scene requirements. A schedule composed of multiple sub-schedules applied sequentially at specified milestone steps. Initialize schedules from config and compute cumulative milestones. On get(step), find index idx using searchsorted on milestones. Determine baseidx from previous milestone. Return schedule[idx].get(step - baseidx). Layout: schedules: list of Schedule objects. milestones: 1D array of cumulative step counts where each sub-schedule begins. Code: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. idx = jnp.searchsorted(self.milestones, step, side='right') schedule = self.schedules[idx] baseidx = self.milestones[idx - 1] if idx >= 1 else 0 return schedule.get(step - baseidx) Optimize networks using Adam optimizer. Warm up learning rate linearly from 0 to 10^{-3} over the first 5,000 iterations. Cosine decay learning rate to a minimum of 5 \times 10^{-5} after warmup. Apply coarse-to-fine strategy: optimize 100 \times 100 low-resolution images for first 5,000 iterations, then progressively upscale to 800 \times 800. Eikonal loss weight is 0.01 (lower weights lead to thinner reconstructed structures). Initialize Adam optimizer. Set initial learning rate to 2 \cdot 10^{-3} and decay it exponentially to 2 \cdot 10^{-5} over the course of training. During the first 512 training steps, apply a warm-up strategy by multiplying the learning rate by 0.01. Clip gradients by value at 0.1 and normalize them to 0.1 to ensure stability. A strategy to gradually enlarge the uncertainty parameter epsilon during training, providing more freedom for the radiance field to explore as training proceeds, opposite to learning rate decay. Formula: \epsilon' = \gamma \epsilon where \epsilon' is the updated uncertainty, and \gamma is the exponential growth rate. Loss: L = L{rgb} + \lambdad L{gd} + \lambdav Lv where L is the total loss, L{rgb} is the RGB loss, L{gd} is ground density supervision, Lv is multi-view consistency supervision, \lambdad = 0.2, and \lambdav = 0.5. Parameter: \gamma (gamma): Exponential growth rate for uncertainty tempering. Set to 1.0005 in experiments. Time Complexity: The scheduling calculation itself is O(1) per step. The impact on training time is indirect; effective scheduling reduces the number of iterations required for convergence. For example, halving iterations with proper scheduling reduced training time from 10:24 to 05:40 (approx. 2x speedup) with minimal quality loss. Memory Complexity: O(1) for stateless schedules. Piecewise schedules require storing the list of sub-schedules and milestones, which is negligible compared to model parameters. Measured Performance: On standard NeRF datasets, log-linear decay with warm-up/delay stabilizes training and improves final PSNR compared to constant learning rates. In 3D Gaussian Splatting, per-parameter scheduling allows for faster convergence of geometry (xyz) while maintaining stability in features. Scaling: Schedules scale with the total number of iterations. For ultra-large scale scenes, schedules may need to be adjusted to account for longer training times or different convergence dynamics. Strengths: Prevents divergence in early training, allows fine-tuning in later stages, and can be tailored to specific parameter groups (e.g., xyz vs. SH coefficients). Limitations: Requires careful tuning of initial/final rates and decay curves. Poorly chosen schedules can lead to suboptimal local minima or slow convergence. When to Use: Standard practice for almost all radiance field optimizations. Use log-linear or cosine decay for general MLPs. Use per-parameter schedules for Gaussian Splatting. Use piecewise schedules for complex multi-phase training (e.g., coarse-to-fine). When Not to Use: Not applicable for methods that use adaptive optimizers exclusively without external scheduling (though even Adam often benefits from LR decay). Learning rate scheduling is a fundamental technique in deep learning optimization, originating from the need to stabilize gradient descent and improve convergence. In the context of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting, it has been adapted to handle the unique challenges of differentiable volume rendering, such as the sensitivity of geometry parameters and the need for multi-scale optimization. The specific variants listed (e.g., log-linear decay, per-parameter scheduling, learning rate spikes) have emerged from various research groups and open-source implementations to address specific convergence issues in radiance field training. head: NeuS2 Training Details
body: Training schedules define the temporal progression of optimization hyperparameters, loss functions, and structural updates during differentiable volume rendering training. They solve unstable convergence and slow training by decoupling coarse geometry acquisition from fine detail refinement, actively managing scene representation complexity and optimization sensitivity over time. The implementation of a training schedule depends on the specific radiance field representation (Neural Implicit, 3D Gaussians, Surfel-based, etc.). Inputs: Static scene: Multi-view images. Dynamic scene: Multi-view image sequences. Camera poses (known or optimized). Outputs: Optimized SDF field, color field, and deformation field (for dynamic). Numbered steps: 1. Static Scene: Train for 15,000 iterations. 2. Dynamic Scene - First Frame: Train from scratch for 2,000 iterations (4,000 for Lego). 3. Dynamic Scene - Subsequent Frames: For each subsequent frame, optimize the global transformation independently for the first 100 iterations. Fine-tune network parameters and global deformation together for the remaining iterations. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Static training iterations: 15,000. Dynamic first frame iterations: 2,000 (4,000 for complex geometry like Lego). Dynamic subsequent frame iterations: 1,100. Global transformation optimization: First 100 iterations of subsequent frames. Edge cases and pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Inputs: Multi-view images. Optional ground-truth foreground masks. Initial point cloud (e.g., 50k surfels from depth estimation). Outputs: Optimized surfel positions, sizes, features, and camera parameters. Numbered steps: 1. Warm-up Phase: Activate only photometric and silhouette losses. Allow surfel set deformation under initial sparse coverage. 2. Densification Phase: Enable adaptive density control (splitting/pruning). Disable silhouette loss. Activate geometric regularizers (L{cons}, L{nc}). Perform densification every 4 epochs. If ground-truth masks are available, periodically remove floater surfels that project outside the foreground mask across a majority of views. 3. Refinement Phase: Freeze densification. Fine-tune with all remaining losses until convergence. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Total epochs scaled with volume size: 2,800 for small-medium, 1,600 for large, 800 for extremely large volumes. Densification interval: Every 4 epochs. Densification duration: Until 14–25% of the training process. Pruning interval: Structure-aware importance score pruning at 42–50% of the training process. BigBrain specific: Multi-stage pruning at epochs 200, 300, and 800 with ratios 0.8, 0.8, and 0.85. Edge cases and pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Inputs: Multi-view images. Outputs: Optimized point cloud, camera poses, and network weights. Numbered steps: 1. Warm-up: Train for 20 epochs at half image resolution. 2. Main Training: For epochs 51–600, randomly zoom in and out each epoch to train all convolution weights (which are not shared) to contribute to the final result. Use VGG-loss for epochs > 50. Use MSE+SSIM for epochs ≤ 50. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Total epochs: 600. Warm-up epochs: 20. Warm-up resolution: Half image resolution. Loss function: VGG-loss [JAF16] as primary criterion. Initial loss (first 50 epochs): Combination of MSE and SSIM [KKLD23] to speed up training by ~5%. Point size initialization: Average distance to the four nearest neighbors. Edge cases and pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Inputs: Photon field parameters. Target KNN radius r. Sequence of radii ri. Outputs: Optimized photon field. Numbered steps: 1. Define a sequence of increasing KNN query radii ri approaching the target radius r. 2. For each training step s, determine the current radius rs from the sequence. Query KNN with radius rs. If rs is small, k < K samples are returned; as rs increases, k \to K. 3. Update parameters using rMSE loss. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Training duration: 2,000–3,000 steps. Optimizer: Adam (\beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.99, no L2). Learning rate: 9 \times 10^{-4} with exponential decay of 0.92 starting at 70% of total steps, triggering every 25 steps. Loss: Relative Mean Square Error (rMSE) applied to each set of outputs individually. Edge cases and pitfalls: The exact design of the KNN schedule is an empirical matter that largely depends on the dataset, lighting conditions, and transfer function. Example Schedule (1M Photons): | Step Range | Radius | |------------|--------| | 0–36% | 25 | | 37–63% | 50 | | 64–90% | 50 | | 91–100% | 0 (Target) | Inputs: Deformation field \mathcal{D}. Current timestep t. Current iteration i. Total iterations \tau. Noise scaling factor \beta. Timestep interval \Delta t. Outputs: Perturbed Gaussian parameters for sensitivity estimation. Numbered steps: 1. During sensitivity estimation, compute the perturbed timestamp t' = t + \mathcal{N}(0,1)\beta\Delta t(1 - i/\tau). 2. Query deformation field \mathcal{D} with t' to get perturbed parameters. 3. Use these parameters to identify and prune unstable Gaussians. Formulas: (\mu + \Delta\mu, r + \Delta r, s + \Delta s) = \mathcal{D}(\mu, r, s, t + \mathcal{N}(0,1)\beta\Delta t(1 - i/\tau)) Where \mathcal{N}(0,1) is standard normal noise. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: Floaters are unstable Gaussians that appear static in observed views but drift at unseen timestamps; TSS addresses this by revealing them early in training via timestamp jittering. Inputs: Current training step step. proposalwarmup: Number of initial steps with no updates. proposalupdateevery: Maximum update frequency (min steps between updates). Outputs: Not given in the sources. Numbered steps: 1. If step < proposalwarmup, do not update proposal networks. 2. Otherwise, interpolate the update frequency linearly from 0 to proposalupdateevery over the warmup range. 3. Clip the frequency to be at least 1 (update every step) and at most proposalupdateevery. Formulas: \text{update\freq} = \text{clip}\left(\text{interpolate}(\text{step}, [0, \text{warmup}], [0, \text{max\freq}]), 1, \text{max\freq}\right) Where maxfreq is proposalupdateevery. Render 162 multi-view images using icosphere sampling. 2. Optimize TexGS-VolVis using the specified per-attribute learning rates. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Learning rate for additional shading attributes and cpal: 0.01. Learning rate for texture attribute: 0.025. Learning rate for other attributes: Same as 2DGS. Optimizer: Adam. Multi-view image resolution for text-driven NPSE: 512x512. Hardware: NVIDIA RTX4090 GPU. Edge cases and pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Hierarchical Spherical Harmonics (SH) Optimization is a training schedule strategy that iteratively optimizes the scene representation by activating Spherical Harmonics bands sequentially, starting from a designated start band up to a target maximum band. It addresses the problem of optimizing high-frequency appearance details in radiance fields by decoupling the optimization of different frequency components, allowing the model to converge on coarse geometry and color before refining fine details. Unlike Coarse-to-Fine Model Initialization, which adjusts the spatial resolution or density of the scene representation, this method specifically targets the frequency domain of the radiance field's color representation. Coarse-to-Fine Model Initialization is a training strategy for differentiable volume rendering that initializes a high-resolution (fine) radiance field model using the optimized parameters of a lower-resolution (coarse) model. It solves the problem of geometric artifacts and slow convergence that occur when training directly at high resolution by establishing a coherent global structure before fitting high-frequency features. It differs from standard full-resolution training by deferring the fitting of fine features until the global geometry is established, and differs from simple two-stage pipelines by potentially using continuous or multi-stage resolution scaling rather than a single abrupt switch. Convergence Speed: Staggered KNN schedules provide 2–3× improvement in training speed compared to naïve training using the target radius directly. Stability: Warm-up phases (e.g., 20 epochs at half resolution in TRIPS or photometric-only losses in 3DSS) prevent early divergence. Memory: Progressive image acquisition (LiTe-GS) reduces oracle evaluations by 23.64% to 62.11% compared to static subsets, improving memory efficiency during view selection. Quality: Temporal Sensitivity Sampling (TSS) in SpeeDe3DGS allows for up to 11× fewer Gaussians with comparable image quality by suppressing floaters.
