name: Hierarchical Spherical Harmonics Optimization
head: Band-by-band optimization, SH Band Strategy
body: Hierarchical Spherical Harmonics (SH) Optimization is a training schedule strategy that iteratively optimizes the scene representation by activating SH bands sequentially from a designated start band up to a target maximum band. It addresses the problem of optimizing high-frequency appearance details in radiance fields by decoupling the optimization of different frequency components, allowing the model to converge on coarse geometry and color before refining fine details. Unlike Coarse-to-Fine Model Initialization, which adjusts the spatial resolution or density of the scene representation, this method specifically targets the frequency domain of the radiance field's color representation. The method implements a nested loop structure: an outer loop iterates through SH bands, and an inner loop performs standard training epochs and batches for the currently active band. Inputs: configs->sphericalHarmonicsBand: The maximum SH band index to optimize up to (integer). configs->hierarchyBandStrategy: Boolean flag determining if bands are optimized hierarchically or all at once. configs->SHsForTargetResoOnly: Boolean flag; if true and not at minimum hierarchy, resets startBand to 0. configs->initialFromFile: Boolean flag; if true and optimizingBand == availableSHBand+1, density is not re-initialized. configs->learningRate (rawLR): Base learning rate for general parameters. configs->shLearningRate (rawSHLR): Learning rate for SH coefficients. configs->batchSize: Number of rays per batch. configs->epochs: Number of epochs per band. configs->varianceLossInterval: Interval for applying variance loss. configs->varianceCoefficient, configs->shCoefficient: Weights for regularization losses. configs->vairanceType, configs->neighboorNums: Parameters for variance loss calculation. configs->maskLossCoefficient, configs->huberDelta: Parameters for RGB loss calculation. configs->saveIntervals: Frequency for saving model checkpoints. configs->justModel: Boolean; if false, saves results periodically. configs->solidStrategy: Boolean flag controlling sample offset application. this->ray.totalRays: Total number of rays in the dataset. this->scene: The scene representation object containing SH coefficients and density. this->sceneOptimizer: The optimizer object handling parameter updates. RenderUtils: Utility functions for rendering and loss calculation. Outputs: Updated scene representation with optimized SH coefficients for all bands up to configs->sphericalHarmonicsBand. Loss metrics per epoch stored in lossesPerEpochs. Scene Object (this->scene): optimizingBand: Integer field indicating the current SH band being optimized. sparse: Boolean flag indicating if the scene uses sparse storage. grayImage: Boolean flag indicating if the scene is grayscale. stepSize: Float value used for sample offset calculation. Losses Array (lossesPerEpochs): Array of size numbands epochs 4. Indices epoch4+0 to epoch4+3 store: minLoss, maxLoss, averageloss, gpuelapsedtime. 1. Determine Start Band: If hierarchyBandStrategy is false, set startBand = configs->sphericalHarmonicsBand. If SHsForTargetResoOnly is true and currentHierarchy is not minimumHierarchy, set startBand = 0. 2. Iterate Bands: Loop optimizingBand from startBand to configs->sphericalHarmonicsBand. 3. Set Current Band: Set this->scene->optimizingBand = optimizingBand. 4. Initialize Band Parameters: If hierarchyBandStrategy is true, or if (hierarchyBandStrategy is false AND SHsForTargetResoOnly is true AND currentHierarchy is not minimumHierarchy): determine densityInitialized as false if initialFromFile is true AND optimizingBand == availableSHBand+1, otherwise true; call this->sceneOptimizer.initialBand(optimizingBand, densityInitialized). Else, call this->sceneOptimizer.initialAll(). 5. Reset Learning Rates: Set configs->learningRate = rawLR and configs->shLearningRate = rawSHLR. 6. Iterate Epochs: Loop epoch from 0 to configs->epochs. 7. Calculate Batch Count: Compute batchCount = (this->ray.totalRays + configs->batchSize - 1) / configs->batchSize. 8. Iterate Batches: Loop batchIndex from 0 to batchCount. 9. Calculate Batch Indices: Compute startSampleIndex = batchIndex configs->batchSize. Compute actualBatchSize as configs->batchSize if startSampleIndex + configs->batchSize < this->ray.totalRays, else this->ray.totalRays - startSampleIndex. 10. Set Sample Offset: If !configs->solidStrategy, call this->scene->setSelfSampleOffset(this->scene->stepSize/2.). 11. Render Rays: Call RenderUtils::renderRays with ray, scene, sampleRaysIndexGPU, startSampleIndex, and actualBatchSize. 12. Compute Losses: If renderRes.grayImage is false, call RenderUtils::renderRayswithGradientsRGB with sceneOptimizer, ray, scene, lossesDevice, sampleRaysIndexGPU, startSampleIndex, actualBatchSize, configs->maskLossCoefficient, and configs->huberDelta. Copy losses from device to host using cudaMemcpy(lossesHost, lossesDevice, sizeof(double) actualBatchSize, cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost). Calculate loss = getMSEError(lossesHost, actualBatchSize). If isnan(loss), print error, free memory, and return. Update maxLoss and minLoss: if loss > maxLoss, set maxLoss = loss; if minLoss > loss, set minLoss = loss. Accumulate losses += loss. 13. Apply Regularization: If !scene->sparse or batchIndex % configs->varianceLossInterval == 0, call RenderUtils::addVarianceLoss with scene, sceneOptimizer, configs->varianceCoefficient, configs->shCoefficient, configs->vairanceType, and configs->neighboorNums. 14. Update RGB Scene: If scene->grayImage is false, call Optimizer::updateRGBScene with sceneOptimizer, scene, and timeStep. 15. Decay Learning Rates: Update configs->learningRate /= pow(2, 1. / batchCount / (epoch + 1.)) and configs->shLearningRate /= pow(2, 1. / batchCount / (epoch + 1.)). 16. Store Epoch Metrics: After the epoch loop, store minLoss, maxLoss, averageloss (losses/batchCount), and GPU elapsed time in lossesPerEpochs at indices epoch4+0 to epoch4+3. 17. Save Model: If !configs->justModel and (epoch + 1) % configs->saveIntervals == 0, save experiment results with directory name "Band%d". Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hierarchicalshoptimization(configs, scene, sceneoptimizer, raydata, renderutils, optimizerutils): """Implements Hierarchical Spherical Harmonics Optimization.""" totalrays = raydata.totalrays maxband = configs.sphericalharmonicsband hierarchystrategy = configs.hierarchybandstrategy shsfortargetonly = configs.shsfortargetresoonly currenthierarchy = raydata.currenthierarchy minimumhierarchy = raydata.minimumhierarchy initialfromfile = configs.initialfromfile rawlr = configs.learningrate rawshlr = configs.shlearningrate batchsize = configs.batchsize numepochs = configs.epochs varianceinterval = configs.variancelossinterval variancecoeff = configs.variancecoefficient shcoeff = configs.shcoefficient variancetype = configs.variancetype neighbornums = configs.neighboornums maskcoeff = configs.masklosscoefficient huberdelta = configs.huberdelta saveinterval = configs.saveintervals justmodel = configs.justmodel solidstrategy = configs.solidstrategy grayimage = scene.grayimage # Helper definitions def getmseerror(losses, n): return sum(losses) / n def cudamemcpydevicetohost(devicedata, n): return devicedata[:n] def getgpuelapsedtime(): return 0.0 def saveexperimentresults(directoryname): pass def freememory(): pass # 1. Determine Start Band if not hierarchystrategy: startband = maxband if shsfortargetonly and currenthierarchy != minimumhierarchy: startband = 0 lossesperepochs = [] for optimizingband in range(startband, maxband + 1): # 3. Set Current Band scene.optimizingband = optimizingband # 4. Initialize Band Parameters cond1 = hierarchystrategy cond2 = (not hierarchystrategy) and shsfortargetonly and (currenthierarchy != minimumhierarchy) if cond1 or cond2: densityinitialized = not (initialfromfile and optimizingband == scene.availableshband + 1) sceneoptimizer.initialband(optimizingband, densityinitialized) else: sceneoptimizer.initialall() # 5. Reset Learning Rates configs.learningrate = rawlr configs.shlearningrate = rawshlr epochtotalloss = 0.0 minloss = float('inf') maxloss = float('-inf') # 6. Iterate Epochs for epoch in range(numepochs): # 7. Calculate Batch Count batchcount = (totalrays + batchsize - 1) // batchsize # 8. Iterate Batches for batchindex in range(batchcount): # 9. Calculate Batch Indices startsampleindex = batchindex batchsize actualbatchsize = min(batchsize, totalrays - startsampleindex) # 10. Set Sample Offset if not solidstrategy: scene.setselfsampleoffset(scene.stepsize / 2.0) # 11. Render Rays renderutils.renderrays( ray=raydata.rays, scene=scene, sampleraysindexgpu=raydata.sampleraysindexgpu, startsampleindex=startsampleindex, actualbatchsize=actualbatchsize) # 12. Compute Losses if not grayimage: renderutils.renderrayswithgradientsrgb( sceneoptimizer=sceneoptimizer, ray=raydata.rays, scene=scene, lossesdevice=raydata.lossesdevice, sampleraysindexgpu=raydata.sampleraysindexgpu, startsampleindex=startsampleindex, actualbatchsize=actualbatchsize, masklosscoefficient=maskcoeff, huberdelta=huberdelta) losseshost = cudamemcpydevicetohost(raydata.lossesdevice, actualbatchsize) loss = getmseerror(losseshost, actualbatchsize) if loss != loss: # NaN check print("Error: Loss is NaN") freememory() return if loss > maxloss: maxloss = loss if loss < minloss: minloss = loss epochtotalloss += loss # 13. Apply Regularization if not scene.sparse or (batchindex % varianceinterval == 0): renderutils.addvarianceloss( scene=scene, sceneoptimizer=sceneoptimizer, variancecoefficient=variancecoeff, shcoefficient=shcoeff, variancetype=variancetype, neighbornums=neighbornums) # 14. Update RGB Scene if not grayimage: optimizerutils.updatergbscene( sceneoptimizer=sceneoptimizer, scene=scene, timestep=epoch) # 15. Decay Learning Rates decayfactor = 2 (1.0 / batchcount / (epoch + 1.0)) configs.learningrate /= decayfactor configs.shlearningrate /= decayfactor # 16. Store Epoch Metrics avgloss = epochtotalloss / batchcount gpuelapsedtime = getgpuelapsedtime() lossesperepochs.append([minloss, maxloss, avgloss, gpuelapsedtime]) # 17. Save Model if not justmodel and (epoch + 1) % saveinterval == 0: saveexperimentresults(f"Band{optimizingband}") return lossesperepochs A curriculum training strategy that progressively increases the number of SH basis functions to prevent overfitting in sparse-view settings, starting with only isotropic (degree 0) components. It uses a mask \alpha\ell^m(t, T) to enable SH coefficients based on the current iteration t and a hyperparameter T. The mask is defined as \alpha\ell^m(t, T) = 1 if \ell=0 or \ell \leq \sqrt{t/T}(\ell{\max} + 1) - 1, and 0 otherwise. Unlike previous methods that constrain geometry and appearance, this method relies on depth-guided voxel pre-pruning for implicit geometry constraints, using SH regularization for secondary geometric refinement and artifact compensation. It is chosen when sparse views are available to mitigate high-frequency overfitting. A technique to reduce optimization cost by only updating non-DC spherical harmonic coefficients every T{\text{lazy}} iterations. If enabled, optimization steps for non-DC SH coefficients are performed only when the current iteration index is a multiple of T{\text{lazy}}. The default value for T{\text{lazy}} in Taming 3DGS is 12, but it is disabled by default in the referenced work. It is chosen when computational efficiency is prioritized and the visual impact of delayed non-DC updates is acceptable. Time Complexity: The method adds an outer loop over SH bands. If bands are optimized sequentially, the total training time is the sum of the time taken for each band. If optimized all at once (startBand = maxBand), it behaves like standard optimization but with specific initialization. The learning rate decay is per-batch, which can slow down convergence if not tuned correctly. Memory Complexity: No significant additional memory overhead compared to standard radiance field optimization, as it reuses the same scene representation and optimizer structures. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method scales with the number of SH bands. Higher maximum bands increase the number of parameters and the complexity of the optimization landscape. Strengths: Allows for stable convergence of high-frequency details by optimizing lower frequencies first. Prevents overfitting in sparse settings when combined with SH Regularization. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of learning rates and initialization strategies. May increase training time if many bands are optimized sequentially. When to use: When optimizing radiance fields with Spherical Harmonics, especially in scenarios where high-frequency details are important and stability is a concern. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and sequential band optimization is too slow. Hierarchical Spherical Harmonics Optimization is described in the context of Plenoxels and related radiance field methods. It is used to manage the optimization of Spherical Harmonics coefficients in different frequency bands. name: Coarse-to-Fine Model Initialization
head: Coarse-to-Fine Initialization, Progressive Scale Training
body: Coarse-to-Fine Model Initialization is a training strategy for neural radiance fields that initializes a high-resolution (fine) model using the optimized parameters of a lower-resolution (coarse) model. It solves the problem of slow convergence and geometric artifacts that arise when training directly at high resolution by establishing a coherent global structure before fitting high-frequency features. It differs from standard full-resolution training by deferring the fitting of fine features until the global geometry is established, and differs from simple two-stage pipelines by potentially using continuous or multi-stage resolution scaling rather than a single abrupt switch. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Optimized weights and feature grids from a trained coarse model; target resolution for the fine model. Outputs: Initialized weights and feature grids for the fine model, ready for continued optimization. Data Structures The method operates on two primary data structures defined in the source: 1. Deformation Feature Grid: A spatial data structure storing deformation features. The coarse model uses a lower resolution grid, while the fine model uses a higher resolution grid. 2. Deformation MLP: A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) used to decode deformation features. The architecture is identical for both coarse and fine models. Numbered Steps 1. Train Coarse Model: Optimize the coarse model (lower resolution) until convergence or a stable state is reached. 2. Initialize Fine Model Weights: Copy the trained network weights from the coarse deformation MLP to the fine deformation MLP. This is valid because the MLP architecture is identical. 3. Interpolate Feature Grid: Initialize the fine model's deformation feature grid by interpolating the optimized feature grid from the coarse model. This maps the coarse spatial features to the finer grid resolution. 4. Progressive Scale Training: Begin training the fine model. Optionally, apply progressive scale training, where the voxel resolution is doubled after a set number of training iterations to gradually introduce finer details. Formulas Not given in the sources. Parameters MLP Architecture (Coarse/Fine Deformation): 4 fully connected layers, width 64. Input dimensions: position (3), time (1), feature (4). MLP Architecture (Color): 3 fully connected layers, width 128. Input dimensions: position (3), view direction (27), feature (12). Activation: ReLU. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Resolution Mismatch: The interpolation step assumes a hierarchical relationship between coarse and fine grids. If the resolution scaling is not a power of two or the grid topology differs, standard interpolation may fail. Overfitting: Training directly at high resolution without coarse initialization can lead to overfitting to noise or artifacts. The coarse-to-fine approach mitigates this by providing a good initial guess. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializefinemodel(coarsemodel, targetresolution): """ Initializes the fine model using the coarse model's optimized parameters. Args: coarsemodel: The trained coarse model containing: coarsedeformationmlp: The MLP weights. coarsefeaturegrid: The optimized feature grid. targetresolution: The desired voxel resolution for the fine model. Returns: finemodel: An initialized fine model ready for training. """ finemodel = createfinemodel(targetresolution) # Step 2: Initialize Fine Model Weights # The MLP architecture is identical, so we can directly copy weights. finemodel.deformationmlp.weights = coarsemodel.coarsedeformationmlp.weights # Step 3: Interpolate Feature Grid # Interpolate the coarse feature grid to the fine resolution. # This maps the coarse spatial features to the finer grid. finemodel.deformationfeaturegrid = interpolate( coarsemodel.coarsefeaturegrid, targetresolution) return finemodel def progressivescaletraining(finemodel, initialresolution, maxresolution, doublinginterval): """ Applies progressive scale training by doubling voxel resolution over time. Args: finemodel: The fine model to train. initialresolution: The starting voxel resolution. maxresolution: The maximum target voxel resolution. doublinginterval: Number of iterations after which to double the resolution. """ currentresolution = initialresolution while currentresolution <= maxresolution: # Train the model at the current resolution trainstep(finemodel, resolution=currentresolution) # Check if it's time to double the resolution if trainingiterations % doublinginterval == 0 and currentresolution < maxresolution: # Double the resolution newresolution = currentresolution 2 # Re-initialize the feature grid at the new resolution using interpolation # from the current optimized grid finemodel.deformationfeaturegrid = interpolate( finemodel.deformationfeaturegrid, newresolution) currentresolution = newresolution Progressive Coarse-to-Fine Training is a strategy that gradually introduces finer levels of detail during optimization to ensure stable convergence and prevent overfitting. It solves the problem of geometric artifacts and slow convergence that occur when training directly at high resolution by establishing a coherent global structure before fitting high-frequency features. It differs from standard full-resolution training by deferring the fitting of fine features until the global geometry is established, and differs from simple two-stage pipelines by potentially using continuous or multi-stage resolution scaling rather than a single abrupt switch. See Progressive Coarse-to-Fine Training Strategy. The NeRF Restarting Approach is a training schedule for joint pose and radiance field optimization that eliminates artifacts learned during the pose refinement phase by discarding the neural network weights and retraining from scratch. Unlike staged training, which freezes poses and continues training the existing networks, this method re-initializes both coarse and fine Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) after pose convergence. It is chosen when the initial joint optimization introduces persistent artifacts into the scene representation that persist even after pose stabilization. See NeRF Restarting Approach. This article describes the complete training loop for Unconstrained Pose-Prior-Free Neural Radiance Fields (UP-NeRF), which jointly optimizes camera poses, scene geometry, and appearance from unordered, unposed image collections. It integrates a coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling strategy with a dynamic loss weighting scheme that transitions from feature/depth supervision to RGB reconstruction as training progresses. Unlike standard NeRF pipelines, this method explicitly handles transient artifacts and mirror-symmetry ambiguities through detached network heads and specific scheduling parameters. See Overall Training Pipeline. LiDAR Initialization is an initialization technique using LiDAR point clouds to provide prior information for the scene representation, helping to avoid local minima in optimization. On Argoverse2, the combination of Hybrid Scene Representation (HSR) and LiDAR Initialization (LI) yields more than 4 times boost in convergence speed compared with NGP. Without LI, the model cannot converge to NGP's PSNR, and training time is infinite ('Inf.') because it struggles to represent space sparsely. Time Complexity: Reduces training time significantly compared to training from scratch at high resolution. The combination of HSR and LI yields more than 4 times boost in convergence speed compared with NGP. Memory Complexity: Requires storing both coarse and fine model parameters during the transition phase, but the interpolation step is efficient. Measured Performance: On Argoverse2 sequences, the method achieves significant speed improvements. For a 600m scene, the proposed method trained within 1 minute exceeds the performance of other methods. Strengths: Faster convergence, better geometric stability, avoids local minima. Limitations: Requires a hierarchical grid structure; interpolation may introduce artifacts if the coarse model is not well-trained. When to Use: When training large-scale scenes or dynamic scenes where high-resolution training from scratch is too slow or unstable. When Not to Use: When the scene is small and simple, or when the computational cost of maintaining two models is prohibitive. The coarse-to-fine initialization strategy was introduced in the context of neural deformable voxel grids for fast optimization of dynamic view synthesis. It builds on the idea that optimizing a scene at multiple resolutions can lead to more stable and faster convergence. The method has been further refined in the context of autonomous driving scenes, where LiDAR initialization is combined with coarse-to-fine training to handle large-scale environments. name: Progressive Coarse-to-Fine Training Strategy
head: Coarse-to-Fine Training
body: Progressive Coarse-to-Fine Training is a strategy that gradually introduces finer levels of detail during optimization to ensure stable convergence and prevent overfitting. It solves the problem of geometric artifacts and slow convergence that occur when training directly at high resolution by establishing a coherent global structure before fitting high-frequency features. It differs from standard full-resolution training by deferring the fitting of fine features until the global geometry is established, and differs from simple two-stage pipelines by potentially using continuous or multi-stage resolution scaling rather than a single abrupt switch. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of training images (potentially with associated camera poses), a target scene geometry (often represented as an octree or voxel grid), and hyperparameters controlling the progression schedule. Outputs: A trained radiance field model (e.g., Gaussian Splatting or NeRF) with optimized parameters for color, density, and geometry. Data Structures: Octree/Level Structure: A hierarchical representation where each level l corresponds to a specific spatial resolution. The base level is determined by scene dimensions, and higher levels provide finer granularity. Progressive Schedule: A set of coarseintervals that specify the training iteration at which each new octree level is introduced. Parameters: initlevel: The starting octree level for training. Typically set to the middle of the available range. progressive: A boolean flag to enable or disable progressive training. maxlevel: The highest octree level to be used in the final model. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Construct the octree structure based on scene dimensions and point cloud data. Determine the initlevel (typically the middle of the range). Calculate coarseintervals using a geometric progression of training steps to determine when to introduce each new level. Set the current maximum level currentmaxlevel to initlevel. 2. Coarse Stage (Global Geometry): Initialize the model parameters at initlevel. In some implementations (e.g., dynamic scenes), set color features to be the color itself, ignoring ray direction dependency, to simplify the initial optimization. Compute a smaller bounding box using proxy geometry learned during this stage to filter empty space. Train the model using only levels up to currentmaxlevel. If incremental mapping is used, insert new observations into the training set at regular intervals (e.g., every 50 iterations). 3. Progressive Refinement: Iterate through training steps. At each step, check if the current iteration matches a value in coarseintervals. If a new level is due, increment currentmaxlevel by 1. Continue training with the extended set of levels (from initlevel to currentmaxlevel). This creates a continuous transition rather than a sudden switch between different LOD levels. 4. Fine Stage (High-Frequency Details): Once currentmaxlevel reaches maxlevel, the model includes all levels. Switch to high-dimensional features and model ray direction dependency explicitly (e.g., using a specific network branch F{\theta4}). Perform final refinement iterations to optimize high-frequency details. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def progressivecoarsefinetraining(scenedata, hyperparams): # 1. Initialization octree = buildoctree(scenedata.points, hyperparams.scenedims) initlevel = hyperparams.initlevel # Typically middle of range maxlevel = hyperparams.maxlevel coarseintervals = calculatecoarseintervals(initlevel, maxlevel) currentmaxlevel = initlevel model = initializemodel(octree, currentmaxlevel) # 2. Training Loop for iteration in range(totaliterations): # Check if we need to increase resolution if iteration in coarseintervals and currentmaxlevel < maxlevel: currentmaxlevel += 1 model.updateoctreelevels(currentmaxlevel) # Sample rays based on current level constraints rays = samplerays(scenedata, currentmaxlevel) # Forward pass and loss computation # In coarse stage, directionality might be ignored # In fine stage, directionality is modeled predictions = model.forward(rays) loss = computeloss(predictions, rays.targets) # Backward pass and update optimizer.step(loss) # Incremental observation insertion (if applicable) if hyperparams.incremental and iteration % 50 == 0: scenedata.addnewobservations() return model The Two-Stage Training Pipeline is a coarse-to-fine optimization strategy that first recovers global shape at low resolution and then refines fine details at high resolution. It solves the problem of geometric artifacts and slow convergence that occur when training directly at high resolution by establishing a coherent global structure before fitting high-frequency features. It differs from standard full-resolution training by deferring the fitting of fine features until the global geometry is established, and differs from simple two-stage pipelines by potentially using continuous or multi-stage resolution scaling rather than a single abrupt switch. A variant where new observations are inserted into the training set incrementally during the coarse stage. Steps: Sample 8,192 rays from input images; train coarse models for 5,000 iterations; perform refinement for 20,000 iterations; insert new observations every 50 iterations during the coarse stage. Parameters: Ray sample count: 8,192; Coarse iterations: 5,000; Refinement iterations: 20,000; Observation insertion interval: 50 iterations; Optimizer: Adam; Initial learning rate: 10^{-1}. A technique that restrains the model's ability to reconstruct complex scenes at early stages to enforce consistency across different supervision viewpoints, providing stability with simple training. Introduced in FreeNeRF and Nerfies. A coarse-to-fine training procedure that smooths input images with a Gaussian kernel during NeRF training to improve pose estimation robustness. Steps: Smooth input images using a Gaussian kernel with standard deviation \sigma = 4 \times (1 - \gammai). Apply a linear schedule to increase \gammai from 0 to 1 during the first half of training. Parameters: \sigma = 4 \times (1 - \gammai); \gammai linearly increases from 0 to 1 in the first half of training. Pitfall: Gets stuck in local minima for pose estimation in very homogeneous scenes. Comparison: Outperforms the baseline in 12/14 and 11/14 cases for rotation and translation estimation respectively, but fails in homogeneous scenes where direct alignment alone may struggle less with texture loss. Time Complexity: Training time is distributed across multiple resolution levels. The coarse stages are faster due to lower resolution, but the total time includes the sum of iterations for all levels. Incremental mapping adds overhead for observation insertion. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the highest octree level reached. Progressive introduction helps manage memory by not allocating fine-level structures until necessary. Performance: Provides stable convergence and prevents overfitting compared to single-resolution training. Improves pose estimation robustness in textured scenes when combined with Gaussian scale-space smoothing. Strengths: Stabilizes optimization for complex scenes; handles incremental data addition; reduces geometric artifacts. Limitations: Can get stuck in local minima in homogeneous scenes if scale-space smoothing is used. Requires careful tuning of initlevel and coarseintervals. The concept of coarse-to-fine training has been applied in various forms in radiance field optimization. Progressive training strategies that start with coarse geometry and refine details are used to address convergence issues in high-dimensional optimization spaces. The specific technique of restraining model capacity in early stages to enforce cross-view consistency was introduced in FreeNeRF and Nerfies. Gaussian scale-space coarse-to-fine methods were explored in the context of direct alignment for robust NeRF learning. name: Two-Stage Training Pipeline
head: ActiveRMAP Fine Stage Optimization, ActiveRMAP Two-Stage Training, Coarse-to-Fine Voxel Training, Training and Finetuning Strategy
body: The Two-Stage Training Pipeline is a coarse-to-fine optimization strategy that first recovers global shape at low resolution and then refines fine details at high resolution. It solves the problem of geometric artifacts and slow convergence that occur when training directly at high resolution by establishing a coherent global structure before fitting high-frequency features. It differs from standard full-resolution training by deferring the fitting of fine features until the global geometry is established, and differs from simple two-stage pipelines by potentially using continuous or multi-stage resolution scaling rather than a single abrupt switch. The method consists of two distinct phases: a coarse training phase to establish global geometry and a fine training phase to recover high-frequency details. The specific implementation varies by application domain (e.g., general radiance fields vs. human reconstruction), but the core logic follows the coarse-to-fine paradigm. Inputs: Training images (low-resolution for pre-training/coarse stage, high-resolution for fine stage). Camera poses for training images. Initial model parameters (often random or from a previous coarse stage). Outputs: Optimized radiance field or surface field model (Mf or fine-tuned network). The implementation relies on specific data structures depending on the variant: 1. Voxel Grid: Used in DVGO-based methods. The resolution is increased from coarse to fine. Typical resolutions mentioned are 128^3, 192^3, 256^3, and 320^3. 2. Image Database: A collection of training images \{Ii\}{i=0}^T used for sampling rays. 3. Model Components: DVGO Model: Contains a coarse model MT and a fine model Mf. DoubleField Network: Comprises a transformer, geometry MLP, and color MLP. This variant uses a voxel grid representation and optimizes the density/opacity field. 1. Coarse Stage Initialization: Initialize the coarse radiance field model MT and the image database \{Ii\}{i=0}^T. 2. Coarse Training: Train the model using a low-resolution voxel grid to obtain a coherent global shape. Note: Some implementations apply a 3D convolution with a Gaussian kernel during coarse training and post-processing to improve visualization quality, though this may slightly increase Chamfer Distance (CD) error. 3. Fine Stage Initialization: Initialize the fine DVGO model Mf using the coarse model MT as a starting point. 4. Fine Stage Optimization Loop: Iterate k from 0 to N (total fine-stage iterations): 1. Ray Sampling: If k \mod m == 0, sample training pixels (rays) from the image database \{Ii\}{i=0}^T. Here, m is the interval frequency for sampling new training pixels. 2. Optimization: Optimize the DVGO model to refine Mf. This involves minimizing the rendering loss between predicted and ground-truth colors. 5. Resolution Scaling: The voxel grid resolution is increased for the fine stage. Default resolution is often 256^3. This variant uses a neural network with separate geometry and color components, leveraging large-scale pre-training. 1. Large-Scale Pre-training (Coarse): Use a large dataset (e.g., Twindom, 1,500 models) with low-resolution images (512 \times 512). Adopt spatial sampling strategy for geometry learning and surface-guided sampling for appearance learning. Loss Functions: Geometry Loss (Lg): Lg = \frac{1}{Ng} \sum{i=1}^{Ng} \| s(xi) - s^(xi) \|2^2 where s^(xi) is the ground truth occupancy, s(xi) is the predicted occupancy, and Ng is the number of spatial sampling points. Geometric Regularization Loss (Lr): Lr = \frac{1}{Nr} \sum{i=1}^{Nr} \| \nabla s(xi) - n^(xi) \|1 where n^(xi) is the ground truth normal, and Nr is the number of sampling points for regularization. Appearance Loss (Lc): Lc = \frac{1}{Nc} \sum{i=1}^{Nc} | \hat{C}(ri) - C^(ri) | where \hat{C}(ri) is the rendered color along ray ri, C^(ri) is the ground truth color, and Nc is the number of sampling rays. Total Loss: L = \lambdag Lg + \lambdar Lr + \lambdac Lc where \lambda terms balance the loss components. Learning Rate: 1 \times 10^{-5}. 2. Finetuning Phase (Fine): Input ultra-high-resolution images from sparse multi-view of a specific subject. Step 2a: Fix the transformer and color MLP. Finetune the geometry MLP for 2,000 iterations. Step 2b: Fix the double MLP and geometry MLP. Finetune the color MLP for 2,000 iterations. Sampling: Randomly select one view as ground truth and others as input in each iteration. Loss: Use only the appearance loss Lc (Eq. 9 in). Learning Rate: 1 \times 10^{-6}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def twostagetrainingcoarsetofine(imagedatabase, coarsemodelMT, N, m): """ Implements the fine stage of the Two-Stage Training Pipeline for DVGO. Args: imagedatabase: List of training images {Ii} coarsemodelMT: Pre-trained coarse radiance field model N: Total number of fine-stage optimization iterations m: Interval frequency for sampling new training pixels Returns: Mf: Refined fine radiance field model """ # Initialize fine model from coarse model Mf = initializefinemodelfromcoarse(coarsemodelMT) for k in range(N): # Sample training pixels (rays) periodically if k % m == 0: rays = sampletrainingrays(imagedatabase) # Optimize DVGO to refine Mf # This step typically involves: # 1. Rendering colors from Mf along rays # 2. Computing loss against ground truth images # 3. Backpropagating to update Mf parameters Mf = optimizedvgostep(Mf, rays) return Mf N: Total number of fine-stage optimization iterations. m: Interval frequency for sampling new training pixels; new pixels are added every m iterations. MT: Coarse radiance field model initialized at the start of the fine stage. Mf: Fine radiance field model refined during each iteration of the loop. Learning Rate: 1 \times 10^{-5} for pre-training, 1 \times 10^{-6} for finetuning (DoubleField). Voxel Grid Resolution: Default 256^3. Other tested resolutions: 128^3, 192^3, 320^3. Ng, Nr, Nc: Number of sampling points for spatial sampling, geometric regularization, and rays, respectively. Resolution Scaling: Increasing voxel grid resolution from 128^3 to 192^3 and 192^3 to 256^3 consistently lowers Chamfer Distance (CD) but increases training time. 320^3 achieves similar CD to 256^3 but with higher cost. Gaussian Kernel: Removing the Gaussian kernel during coarse training increases CD error from 0.72 to 0.74. Removing it during post-processing slightly reduces CD from 0.720 to 0.715, but post-processing improves visualization quality. Precision: Finetuning requires a lower learning rate (10^{-6}) to ensure stable performance. Progressive training is a method that gradually increases the resolution of the rendered output during optimization to stabilize convergence and prevent geometric artifacts. It solves the problem of complex loss landscapes and sparse initialization errors that occur when training directly at high resolution. It differs from standard full-resolution training by deferring the fitting of fine features until the global geometry is established, and differs from simple two-stage pipelines by potentially using continuous or multi-stage resolution scaling rather than a single abrupt switch. Magic3D is a method targeting issues caused by low-resolution diffusion images using a two-stage coarse-fine approach. In the coarse stage, Instant-NGP is used as the NeRF model trained from images generated from text prompts using the image diffusion model eDiff-I. In the fine stage, the coarse geometry extracted from Instant-NGP is placed on a mesh, which is optimized over in the fine stage using images generated with a latent diffusion model. Experiments over 397 prompts generated objects, each rated by three users, showed a preference toward Magic3D over DreamFusion. Time Complexity: Training time scales with voxel grid resolution. For DVGO-based methods, training times are approximately 11 mins for 128^3, 12 mins for 192^3, 15 mins for 256^3, and 17 mins for 320^3. Memory Complexity: Depends on the voxel grid resolution and the number of parameters in the MLPs. Higher resolutions require more memory for the voxel grid. Performance: The two-stage approach yields lower Chamfer Distance (CD) errors compared to single-stage training at low resolution, and better quality than single-stage training at high resolution which may suffer from artifacts. Strengths: Stabilizes convergence, prevents geometric artifacts, allows for high-resolution detail recovery without getting stuck in local minima associated with complex loss landscapes. Limitations: Requires more complex implementation (managing two stages, resolution switching). DoubleField requires a large-scale dataset for pre-training. The Two-Stage Training Pipeline originates from the need to efficiently train high-fidelity 3D representations. It was notably used in Voxurf for voxel-based efficient and accurate neural surface reconstruction, ActiveRMAP for radiance field active mapping, and DoubleField for high-fidelity human reconstruction. Magic3D adapted this strategy for text-to-3D generation to mitigate issues with low-resolution diffusion images. name: Progressive Training Strategy
head: Coarse-to-Fine Training, Progressive Growing, Progressive Growing Strategy, Progressive Growing of GANs, Progressive training (Growing)
body: Progressive training is a method that gradually increases the resolution of the rendered output during optimization to stabilize convergence and prevent geometric artifacts. It solves the problem of complex loss landscapes and sparse initialization errors that occur when training directly at high resolution. It differs from standard full-resolution training by deferring the fitting of fine features until the global geometry is established, and differs from simple two-stage pipelines by potentially using continuous or multi-stage resolution scaling rather than a single abrupt switch. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Training dataset (images/points), total iteration budget T{total}, initial resolution scale s{start}, target resolution scale s{end}=1.0. Output: Trained model parameters (neural network weights or Gaussian attributes) optimized for the target resolution. Data Structures: Resolution Schedule: A mapping from iteration t to output image dimensions (Ht, Wt). Model State: The generator/discriminator architecture or Gaussian point cloud state, which may grow in capacity or remain fixed but render at varying scales. Steps: 1. Initialize: Set current resolution scale s = s{start} (e.g., 0.3 or low-res dimensions). Initialize model parameters. 2. Iterate: For each training iteration t from 1 to T{total}: a. Determine Resolution: Calculate current scale st. If using Progressive Growing (StyleNeRF): Stage 1 (t \le T1): Render at fixed low resolution. Stage 2 (T1 < t \le T2): Linearly interpolate resolution from low to high. Stage 3 (t > T2): Render at full target resolution. If using Cosine Scaling (EAGLES): If t \le 0.7 \cdot T{total}: st = 0.3 + 0.7 \cdot \frac{1}{2}(1 + \cos(\pi \frac{t}{0.7 T{total}})). If t > 0.7 \cdot T{total}: st = 1.0. b. Render: Generate image at resolution determined by st. c. Compute Loss: Calculate loss against ground truth images at the current resolution. d. Update: Perform gradient descent to update model parameters. e. Stabilize (Progressive Growing only): If adding new layers/resolution levels, linearly interpolate the output with the previous low-resolution output to stabilize training due to random initialization of new parameters. 3. Finalize: Continue training at full resolution until T{total} is reached. Formulas: Linear Interpolation (StyleNeRF Stage 2): st = s{low} + (s{high} - s{low}) \cdot \frac{t - T1}{T2 - T1} Where s{low} is the initial low resolution scale, s{high}=1.0, T1 is the start of Stage 2, and T2 is the end of Stage 2. Cosine Schedule (EAGLES): st = s{start} + (s{end} - s{start}) \cdot \frac{1}{2} \left( 1 + \cos \left( \pi \frac{t}{T{scale}} \right) \right) Where T{scale} = 0.7 \cdot T{total}. Output Interpolation (Stabilization): I{out} = \alpha \cdot I{new} + (1 - \alpha) \cdot I{low} Where \alpha is the interpolation factor corresponding to the progress of layer/resolution addition. Parameters: T1 (StyleNeRF): Start of Stage 2. Default: 500,000 images. T2 (StyleNeRF): End of Stage 2. Default: 5,000,000 images. T3 (StyleNeRF): End of Stage 3. Default: 25,000,000 images. s{start} (EAGLES): Initial scale factor. Default: 0.3. T{scale} (EAGLES): Duration of scaling phase. Default: 70% of total iterations. Batch Size: 64 images per batch. Total Iterations (EAGLES): 30,000 iterations (configurable based on budget). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometry Failure: Directly training at the highest resolution causes the model to fail to capture object geometry because the rendering equations are approximations. Floating Artifacts: Standard full-resolution training forces Gaussians to fit fine features early with sparse SfM initialization, leading to suboptimal optimization and floating artifacts. Small Datasets: If the dataset is too small (e.g., MetFaces), progressive training may be unstable; fine-tuning from a pretrained high-resolution model is recommended instead. New Layer Initialization: Parameters of newly added layers are random; without linear interpolation with low-resolution output, training becomes unstable. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def progressivetraining(model, dataset, totaliterations, strategy="cosine"): """ model: The neural network or Gaussian system to train. dataset: Iterable of ground truth images. totaliterations: Total number of training steps. strategy: "cosine" (EAGLES) or "linear" (StyleNeRF). """ if strategy == "cosine": # EAGLES configuration scalestart = 0.3 scaleend = 1.0 scaleduration = int(0.7 totaliterations) for t in range(1, totaliterations + 1): # Calculate current resolution scale if t <= scaleduration: # Cosine annealing from 0.3 to 1.0 progress = t / scaleduration scale = scalestart + (scaleend - scalestart) 0.5 (1 + math.cos(math.pi progress)) else: scale = scaleend # Determine current image dimensions based on scale currentheight = int(baseheight scale) currentwidth = int(basewidth scale) # Get batch of ground truth images gtimages = getnextbatch(dataset, batchsize=64) # Resize ground truth to current resolution if necessary # Or render model at current resolution renderedimages = model.render(resolution=(currentheight, currentwidth)) # Compute loss loss = computeloss(renderedimages, gtimages) # Update model model.update(loss) # Optional: Densification/Pruning steps specific to Gaussians if t % 175 == 0: model.densify() if t % 2500 == 0: model.resetopacity() if t % 5000 == 0: model.prune(0.15) elif strategy == "linear": # StyleNeRF configuration T1 = 500000 T2 = 5000000 T3 = 25000000 lowresscale = 0.1 # Example low res, e.g., 32x32 relative to 256x256 highresscale = 1.0 for t in range(1, totaliterations + 1): if t <= T1: # Stage 1: Low resolution scale = lowresscale elif t <= T2: # Stage 2: Linear interpolation progress = (t - T1) / (T2 - T1) scale = lowresscale + (highresscale - lowresscale) progress else: # Stage 3: Full resolution scale = highresscale currentheight = int(baseheight scale) currentwidth = int(basewidth scale) gtimages = getnextbatch(dataset, batchsize=64) # Progressive Growing Stabilization # If layers were added recently, interpolate with low-res output if t <= T2: renderedimages = model.render(resolution=(currentheight, currentwidth)) lowresrendered = model.render(resolution=(int(baseheight lowresscale), int(basewidth lowresscale))) # Interpolate to stabilize new layers finalrender = interpolate(renderedimages, lowresrendered, progress) else: finalrender = model.render(resolution=(currentheight, currentwidth)) loss = computeloss(finalrender, gtimages) model.update(loss) Starts with a shallow network and fades in layers for higher resolutions. Requires linear interpolation with low-resolution output to stabilize random new parameters. Chosen for speed advantage at low resolutions. Inserts upsample operations during training instead of growing layers. Does not require fading in layers linearly. Works similarly in visual quality but may be slower at low resolutions. Time Complexity: Training time is distributed across resolutions. The majority of iterations (e.g., 70% in EAGLES, or up to T2 in StyleNeRF) occur at lower resolutions, which are computationally cheaper per iteration. However, the total iteration count may be higher to compensate for the coarse phases. Memory Complexity: Lower resolution rendering requires less memory per iteration. The model architecture size may grow in Progressive Growing, but up-sampling keeps it fixed. Performance: Prevents failure to capture geometry and reduces floating artifacts compared to direct high-resolution training. Strengths: Stabilizes optimization in complex loss landscapes; handles sparse SfM initialization better; avoids early fitting to noise/fine details. Limitations: Requires careful scheduling of resolution transitions; small datasets may not support stable progressive training. When to use: High-resolution synthesis, scenes with sparse initialization, or when direct training leads to artifacts. When not to use: Very small datasets (use fine-tuning instead). The strategy is inspired by Karras et al. (2017) "Progressive Growing of GANs for Improved Quality, Stability, and Variation". It was adapted for NeRF-based methods (StyleNeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting variants (EAGLES) to address the specific challenges of volume rendering and differentiable rendering, where direct high-resolution training leads to geometric inaccuracies due to approximation errors in the rendering equations. name: NeRF Restarting Approach
head: Joint Pose-NeRF Refinement with Restart, Pose-Constrained NeRF Restart
body: The NeRF Restarting Approach is a training schedule for joint pose and radiance field optimization that eliminates artifacts learned during the pose refinement phase by discarding the neural network weights and retraining from scratch. Unlike staged training, which freezes poses and continues training the existing networks, this method re-initializes both coarse and fine Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) after pose convergence. It is chosen when the initial joint optimization introduces persistent artifacts into the scene representation that persist even after pose stabilization. The method consists of three distinct phases. It takes as input a set of N images with noisy initial camera poses and a target radiance field representation defined by a coarse MLP F{\thetac} and a fine MLP F{\thetaf}. The output is the optimized camera poses and the final radiance field parameters. Data Structures: Camera Poses: A set of N transformation matrices Pi \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4} or corresponding rotation/translation vectors. Coarse MLP (F{\thetac}): A neural network mapping 3D coordinates and viewing directions to density and color. Parameters \thetac are initialized from scratch in Phase 3. Fine MLP (F{\thetaf}): A neural network mapping 3D coordinates and viewing directions to color (and optionally density). Parameters \thetaf are initialized from scratch in Phase 3. Steps: 1. Phase 1: Joint Pose and Network Training Initialize F{\thetac} and F{\thetaf} from scratch. Initialize camera poses Pi with the provided noisy estimates. Perform gradient descent to jointly optimize the network parameters \thetac, \thetaf and the camera poses Pi. Continue until the camera pose estimates converge. 2. Phase 2: Pose Freezing and Network Re-initialization Freeze the optimized camera poses Pi^{} obtained from Phase 1. Discard the current weights \thetac and \thetaf learned in Phase 1. Re-initialize the parameters for both the coarse MLP F{\thetac} and the fine MLP F{\thetaf} from scratch. 3. Phase 3: Fixed-Pose Radiance Field Training Train the re-initialized F{\thetac} and F{\thetaf} using the fixed, optimized poses Pi^{}. The optimization minimizes the rendering loss with respect to \thetac and \thetaf only. This phase allows the networks to learn sharp geometry without the interference of pose uncertainty. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainnerfwithrestarting(images, initialposes, coarsemlpinit, finemlpinit, learningrate, phase1maxepochs, phase3maxepochs): # Phase 1: Jointly train the NeRF with camera poses until pose convergence poses = initialposes.clone() thetac = coarsemlpinit.clone() thetaf = finemlpinit.clone() for epoch in range(phase1maxepochs): rays = sampleraysfromimages(images) renderedcolors = renderrays(poses, thetac, thetaf, rays) loss = computemseloss(renderedcolors, images[rays.pixelindices]) thetac = gradientdescentstep(thetac, loss, learningrate) thetaf = gradientdescentstep(thetaf, loss, learningrate) poses = gradientdescentstep(poses, loss, learningrate) if poseconvergencecheck(poses, threshold=1e-4): break # Phase 2: Freeze the optimized pose estimates and re-initialize both coarse and fine MLPs from scratch optimizedposes = poses.detach() thetac = coarsemlpinit.clone() thetaf = finemlpinit.clone() # Phase 3: Train both MLPs from scratch using the fixed optimized poses for epoch in range(phase3maxepochs): rays = sampleraysfromimages(images) renderedcolors = renderrays(optimizedposes, thetac, thetaf, rays) loss = computemseloss(renderedcolors, images[rays.pixelindices]) thetac = gradientdescentstep(thetac, loss, learningrate) thetaf = gradientdescentstep(thetaf, loss, learningrate) return optimizedposes, thetac, thetaf Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Pose Convergence Criteria: If Phase 1 stops too early, the frozen poses in Phase 2 will be inaccurate, leading to poor reconstruction. Re-initialization Strategy: The method relies on the assumption that the artifacts are tied to the specific weight configuration of Phase 1. Staged training is a variant where the camera poses are refined while training the coarse network, and then the poses are frozen while training both coarse and fine networks, without re-initializing the weights. It prevents blurry surfaces compared to joint training of all parameters because the fine network learns sharp geometry from frozen, registered poses and a pre-trained coarse network. On DTU with 3 views and 15% initial additive Gaussian noise, staged training achieves PSNR 17.58 (18.62 masked), SSIM 0.71 (0.82 masked), LPIPS 0.26 (0.13 masked), and DE 1.81. Performance: On DTU with 3 views and 15% initial additive Gaussian noise, the restarting approach achieves PSNR 17.80 (19.07 masked), SSIM 0.72 (0.83 masked), LPIPS 0.25 (0.12 masked), and DE 1.84. This outperforms staged training (PSNR 17.58) and joint training of poses with both coarse and fine MLPs, which often results in slightly blurry surfaces. Strengths: Removes artifacts learned during pose optimization that may persist in staged training. Provides the best rendering quality among the compared schedules. Limitations: Requires more training time due to the restart. Sensitive to the convergence criterion of Phase 1. The NeRF Restarting Approach was introduced in the context of optimizing Neural Radiance Fields from sparse and noisy poses. It was identified as the best alternative for joint pose-NeRF training in ablation studies comparing various training schedules. The method addresses the issue of artifacts persisting in the scene representation when poses and networks are optimized jointly or in a staged manner without weight reset. name: Overall Training Pipeline
head: UP-NeRF training, coarse-to-fine with scheduling
body: This article describes the complete training loop for Unconstrained Pose-Prior-Free Neural Radiance Fields (UP-NeRF), which jointly optimizes camera poses, scene geometry, and appearance from unordered, unposed image collections. It integrates a coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling strategy with a dynamic loss weighting scheme that transitions from feature/depth supervision to RGB reconstruction as training progresses. Unlike standard NeRF pipelines, this method explicitly handles transient artifacts and mirror-symmetry ambiguities through detached network heads and specific scheduling parameters. Inputs: A set of unordered images I, initial camera poses (typically identity), and pre-extracted deep features (e.g., DINO) and monocular depth estimates (e.g., DPT). Outputs: Optimized camera poses p, neural radiance field parameters (coarse and fine MLPs), and transient network parameters. Data Structures: Coarse Model: MLP predicting density \sigma and color C. Uses detached transient outputs \hat{\alpha}(\tau) and \hat{C}i(\tau) for rendering. Fine Model: MLP predicting density \sigma and color C. Uses candidate density \sigmai for sampling. Transient Network (T): Predicts transient confidence weight W{depth} and transient color/density components. Pose Parameters: Optimizable camera poses p and depth factors si, ti. Parameters: Total iterations: 600,000. Rays per step: 2,048 randomly sampled pixel rays. Sampling points per ray: 128 for both coarse and fine models. Learning rate (NeRF & TransientNet): 5 \times 10^{-4} decaying to 5 \times 10^{-5}. Learning rate (Pose & Depth factors): 2 \times 10^{-3} decaying to 1 \times 10^{-3}. Scheduling parameters u, v: 0.1, 0.5. Depth loss weight \lambdad: 0.001. Optimizer: Adam. Steps: 1. Initialization: Set initial camera poses to identity transformation. Extract deep features and monocular depth offline. 2. Sampling: For the coarse model, sample points using density \sigma. Render using detached transient outputs \hat{\alpha}(\tau) and \hat{C}i(\tau). For the fine model, compose the sample set using both shared density \sigma and candidate density \sigmai. The usage of \sigmai is governed by the scheduling factor w{u,v}. 3. Loss Computation: Compute RGB loss for the coarse model: L{coarse\rgb} = \frac{1}{2} \| \hat{C}i(r) - Ci(r) \|2^2 where \hat{C}i(r) is the rendered color using detached transient outputs and no uncertainty. Compute the total loss for the fine model: L = w{u,v} L{rgb} + (1 - w{u,v}) (L{feat} + \lambdad L{depth}) where L{rgb} is the RGB reconstruction loss, L{feat} is the feature matching loss, and L{depth} is the depth consistency loss. The scheduling factor w{u,v} controls the transition. At the start (w{u,v} \approx 0), the model relies on features and depth. As training progresses (w{u,v} \to 1), it relies on RGB reconstruction. 4. Transient Handling: The transient confidence weight W{depth} is manually detached (gradient stop) to prevent its parameters from affecting the NeRF backbone directly. The TransientNet is optimized using the fine model alone. 5. Optimization: Update all parameters using Adam. The coarse-to-fine strategy is active from training progress 0.1 to 0.5. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. poses = IdentityTransformations(numimages) nerfcoarse = InitMLP() nerffine = InitMLP() transientnet = InitMLP() optimizernerf = Adam(nerfcoarse.parameters() + nerffine.parameters(), lr=5e-4) optimizertransient = Adam(transientnet.parameters(), lr=5e-4) optimizerpose = Adam(poses.parameters() + depthfactors.parameters(), lr=2e-3) u, v = 0.1, 0.5 lambdad = 0.001 for iteration in range(600000): # 1. Sample rays rays = SampleRandomPixels(numrays=2048) # 2. Compute scheduling factor wu,v based on iteration progress # Note: Exact formula for wu,v is not provided in sources, # but it transitions from 0 to 1 between progress u and v progress = iteration / 600000 wuv = ComputeSchedulingFactor(progress, u, v) # 3. Coarse Model Forward Pass # Sample points using coarse density sigma pointscoarse = SamplePoints(rays, nerfcoarse.density, numsamples=128) # Render with detached transient outputs # Detach transient parameters to prevent gradient flow to NeRF alphadetached = transientnet.alpha(pointscoarse).detach() Ctransientdetached = transientnet.color(pointscoarse).detach() Ccoarserendered = VolumetricRender(pointscoarse, nerfcoarse.color, alphadetached) Cgt = rays.gtcolor Lcoarsergb = 0.5 SquaredL2Norm(Ccoarserendered - Cgt) # 4. Fine Model Forward Pass # Sample points using both sigma and candidate sigmai # The mix depends on wu,v pointsfine = SamplePointsMixed(rays, nerfcoarse.density, nerffine.candidatedensity, wuv, numsamples=128) # Render fine model Cfinerendered = VolumetricRender(pointsfine, nerffine.color, transientnet.alpha(pointsfine)) Lrgb = SquaredL2Norm(Cfinerendered - Cgt) # Compute feature and depth losses Lfeat = FeatureLoss(rays.features, ExtractFeatures(Cfinerendered)) Ldepth = DepthLoss(rays.depth, ExtractDepth(Cfinerendered)) # 5. Total Loss Ltotal = wuv Lrgb + (1 - wuv) (Lfeat + lambdad Ldepth) # 6. Backpropagation optimizernerf.zerograd() optimizertransient.zerograd() optimizerpose.zerograd() Ltotal.backward() optimizernerf.step() optimizertransient.step() optimizerpose.step() LU-NeRF (Local Unposed NeRF) is a method for estimating camera poses and reconstructing neural scene representations from unordered, unposed image collections, specifically designed for few-shot scenarios. It differs from prior unposed NeRF approaches by operating in the general SE(3) pose setting without restrictive pose priors, utilizing a local-to-global pipeline that first learns local mini-scene representations and then synchronizes them into a global frame. Unlike methods that rely on coarse-to-fine frequency scheduling like BARF, LU-NeRF employs a compact MLP without positional encoding and resolves mirror-symmetry ambiguities through a dedicated secondary training stage. Time Complexity: High due to 600K iterations and dual coarse/fine model evaluations per step. Memory Complexity: Increased by storing coarse and fine MLPs, transient network, and pre-extracted features/depth. Performance: Achieves comparable quality to reference NeRF with perfect poses on the PhotoTourism dataset (e.g., Brandenburg Gate PSNR 26.50 vs NeRF 26.29). Strengths: Robust pose estimation in unconstrained settings; handles transient artifacts effectively via detached heads. Limitations: Relies on pseudo-labels from monocular depth networks, which can degrade rendering quality if overused (hence the scheduling). When to use: Unordered, unposed image collections where initial pose estimates are poor or unavailable. When not to use: When ground-truth poses are available or when computational resources are severely limited. UP-NeRF was introduced in 2023 by the authors of "UP-NeRF: Unconstrained Pose-Prior-Free Neural Radiance Fields". It builds upon the BARF (Blending Artificial Reality Features) coarse-to-fine strategy. The method addresses the limitations of prior unposed NeRF approaches that relied on restrictive pose priors or failed to converge when combined with other techniques like BARF. It is used for novel view synthesis and camera pose estimation on datasets like PhotoTourism. name: LU-NeRF Architecture and Training
head: Local Unposed NeRF training
body: LU-NeRF (Local Unposed NeRF) is a method for estimating camera poses and reconstructing neural scene representations from unordered, unposed image collections, specifically designed for few-shot scenarios. It differs from prior unposed NeRF approaches by operating in the general SE(3) pose setting without restrictive pose priors, utilizing a local-to-global pipeline that first learns local mini-scene representations and then synchronizes them into a global frame. Unlike methods that rely on coarse-to-fine frequency scheduling like BARF, LU-NeRF employs a compact MLP without positional encoding and resolves mirror-symmetry ambiguities through a dedicated secondary training stage. Inputs: A set of unposed images partitioned into mini-scenes. Outputs: Optimized camera poses (world-to-camera) and a neural radiance field representation for each mini-scene. Data Structures: Camera Poses: For a mini-scene with N images, poses are stored as a set of world-to-camera rotation matrices \{Ri\}{i=1}^N and translation vectors \{ti\}{i=1}^N. In LU-NeRF, poses are initialized to identity. Neural Field: A compact 4-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Unlike standard NeRF, it does not use positional encoding and does not condition on view directions (view-independent). Ray Sampling: 2048 rays are sampled per mini-batch. Parameters: Initial Poses: Identity matrix for rotations and zero for translations. Random initialization around identity yields no significant difference. Learning Rate: Adopted from BARF. Depth Regularization Weight: 10 times larger than the photometric \ell2 loss. Regularization Patch Size: 2 \times 2 pixels. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize camera poses \{Ri, ti\} to identity. Initialize the 4-layer MLP weights. Do not apply positional encoding or view-direction conditioning to the MLP. 2. LU-NeRF-1 Training (Local Optimization): Sample 2048 rays per mini-batch. Compute photometric \ell2 loss between rendered and ground-truth pixels. Apply depth regularization on 2 \times 2 patches. Jointly optimize camera poses and MLP parameters using the BARF learning rate schedule. Termination Condition: Stop training if the average change of camera rotations in the mini-scene is less than 0.125^\circ within 5,000 iterations. 3. Mirror-Symmetry Ambiguity Mitigation (LU-NeRF-2): Take estimated poses \{Ri\} from LU-NeRF-1. Generate reflected cameras \{R\pi Ri\}, where R\pi is a rotation around the optical axis. Note: This is distinct from post-multiplying by R\pi, which would represent a global rotation. Train two new models from scratch: Model A: Initialized with original poses \{Ri\}. Model B: Initialized with reflected poses \{R\pi Ri\}. Stage 1 of LU-NeRF-2: Train for 5,000 iterations with frozen initial poses. Stage 2 of LU-NeRF-2: Jointly optimize camera poses and neural fields for 45,000 iterations. Selection: Select the model (A or B) with the smallest photometric training loss. Note: The default total training iterations for LU-NeRF-2 is 50,000. 4. Global Synchronization and Refinement: Bring local mini-scene poses into a global reference frame using pose synchronization (e.g., Shonan averaging). Perform a final global optimization of all camera poses and the neural scene representation using all images from the entire scene. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainlunerfminiscene(images, minisceneindices): # 1. Initialization poses = [IdentityPose() for in minisceneindices] mlp = Compact4LayerMLP() # No positional encoding, no view direction input # 2. LU-NeRF-1 Training for iteration in range(maxiterations): rays = samplerays(images, minisceneindices, numrays=2048) renderedcolors = renderrays(rays, poses, mlp) # Loss calculation photometricloss = meansquarederror(renderedcolors, rays.gtcolors) depthregloss = applydepthregularization(rendereddepths, patchsize=(2, 2)) # Weighting: depth reg is 10x photometric loss totalloss = photometricloss + 10.0 depthregloss # Optimization step with BARF learning rate schedule optimize(poses, mlp, totalloss) # Check termination avgrotationchange = computeavgrotationchange(poses, previousposes) if avgrotationchange < 0.125 and iteration > 5000: break previousposes = copy(poses) estimatedposes = poses # 3. Mirror-Symmetry Mitigation (LU-NeRF-2) # Generate reflected poses reflectedposes = [reflectpose(p, axis='optical') for p in estimatedposes] # Train two models modelaposes, modelamlp = trainlunerf2stage(estimatedposes, images, minisceneindices) modelbposes, modelbmlp = trainlunerf2stage(reflectedposes, images, minisceneindices) # Select best model based on photometric loss lossa = computephotometricloss(modelaposes, modelamlp, images, minisceneindices) lossb = computephotometricloss(modelbposes, modelbmlp, images, minisceneindices) if lossa < lossb: finalposes = modelaposes finalmlp = modelamlp else: finalposes = modelbposes finalmlp = modelbmlp return finalposes, finalmlp def trainlunerf2stage(initialposes, images, minisceneindices): poses = copy(initialposes) mlp = Compact4LayerMLP() # Start from scratch # Stage 1: Frozen poses for iteration in range(5000): rays = samplerays(images, minisceneindices, numrays=2048) renderedcolors = renderrays(rays, poses, mlp) loss = meansquarederror(renderedcolors, rays.gtcolors) + 10.0 depthregularization(rendereddepths) optimize(mlp, loss) # Poses frozen # Stage 2: Joint optimization for iteration in range(45000): rays = samplerays(images, minisceneindices, numrays=2048) renderedcolors = renderrays(rays, poses, mlp) loss = meansquarederror(renderedcolors, rays.gtcolors) + 10.0 depthregularization(rendereddepths) optimize(poses, mlp, loss) # Joint optimization return poses, mlp This variant addresses the degeneracy where distant small objects appear affine, causing ambiguity between a scene and its reflection. It involves a second training stage (LU-NeRF-2) where reflected cameras are generated from the estimated poses of LU-NeRF-1, and two new models are trained from scratch to resolve the ambiguity by selecting the one with the smallest photometric training loss. Memory and Speed: The removal of positional encoding and view-dependency, combined with a compact 4-layer MLP, significantly reduces memory cost and speeds up training compared to standard NeRF architectures. Performance: LU-NeRF outperforms prior unposed NeRF attempts (GNeRF, VMRF) and compares favorably to COLMAP on low-texture and low-resolution images. Robustness: The local-to-global pipeline is designed to be robust, succeeding even when initial mini-scenes contain frequent outliers. Limitations: Performance may be hurt if the noisy connected graph built with DINO/RGB features is used for pose synchronization, as the clean graph from ground-truth poses yields better results. LU-NeRF was introduced in 2023 by researchers addressing the challenges of few-shot local unposed NeRF. It builds on the concept of neural radiance fields (NeRF) and pose synchronization techniques [20, 43, 24]. The method was developed to operate in the general SE(3) pose setting without restrictive assumptions on pose priors, distinguishing it from earlier baselines. name: View-count-based Learning Rate
head: View-count prior learning rate, View-count prior
body: This method adjusts the learning rates of the optimization process based on a view-count prior, which accounts for the number of training views available. It solves the problem of slow convergence or suboptimal reconstruction in radiance field optimization when the number of input images is limited. It sets itself apart from standard schedules by dynamically scaling the learning rate according to the density of observed views, rather than relying solely on iteration count or time. Without this prior, peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) can degrade by up to -1.22 in the worst case. The method modifies the base learning rate \eta used in the optimizer (e.g., Adam) by a factor derived from the view count. Inputs: Base learning rate \eta{base} (scalar). Number of training views Nv (integer). Current iteration t (integer). Outputs: Adjusted learning rate \etat (scalar). Data Structures: No specific complex data structures are required beyond standard scalar variables. The view count Nv is typically a constant derived from the dataset configuration. Steps: 1. Determine the number of training views Nv from the dataset. 2. Calculate the view-count scaling factor S. The specific formula for S is not explicitly detailed in the provided sources, but it is described as a "view-count prior". In the context of Direct Voxel Grid Optimization, this prior is used to balance the learning rate relative to the amount of visual information available. 3. Compute the adjusted learning rate: \etat = \eta{base} \times S(Nv) 4. Pass \etat to the optimizer for the current step. Parameters: \eta{base}: Typical values depend on the optimizer and scene, but standard NeRF/3DGS values (e.g., 1.6 \times 10^{-4} for position, 1.0 \times 10^{-3} for color) are common starting points. Nv: Determined by the dataset. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Low View Count: If Nv is very small, the scaling factor must prevent the learning rate from becoming too large, which could cause instability. Conversely, if the scaling factor is too small, convergence may be excessively slow. Degenerate Input: If Nv = 0, the method is undefined. A guard should ensure Nv \ge 1. Precision: Ensure that the scaling factor does not introduce numerical instability in the optimizer's state updates. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getviewcountlearningrate(baselr, numtrainingviews, currentiteration): """ Calculate the learning rate adjusted by a view-count prior. Args: baselr (float): The base learning rate. numtrainingviews (int): The total number of training views. currentiteration (int): The current training iteration. Returns: float: The adjusted learning rate. """ if numtrainingviews <= 0: raise ValueError("Number of training views must be positive.") # The exact formula for the view-count prior scaling factor is not specified in the sources. # It is generally a function that scales the learning rate based on the density of views. # For implementation, one must refer to the specific paper's appendix or code for the exact function S(Nv). # A common heuristic in such contexts is to scale inversely with the square root of the view count # or to use a fixed multiplier if the view count is below a threshold. # However, without the explicit formula from, we cannot provide the exact calculation. # The following is a placeholder structure. scalingfactor = getviewcountpriorscaling(numtrainingviews) return baselr scalingfactor def getviewcountpriorscaling(numviews): """ Placeholder for the view-count prior scaling function. The exact implementation is defined in. """ # Not given in the sources. pass A training schedule mechanism that periodically triggers an adaptive control function based on iteration count and training views, while periodically clearing CUDA cache to manage memory. It enables adaptive control when: iteration > controlstartbaseinterval numtrainingviews AND iteration < stopiteration AND iteration % (controlbaseinterval numtrainingviews) == 0. If enabled, it calls self.adaptivecontrolfunction.control(). Otherwise, it skips. Every 1000 iterations, it executes torch.cuda.emptycache() to free unused GPU memory. Time Complexity: The adjustment itself is O(1) per iteration. The adaptive control variant adds periodic overhead for cache clearing and function calls, but these are infrequent relative to total iterations. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the learning rate calculation. The adaptive variant manages GPU memory by periodically clearing the cache, preventing out-of-memory errors during long training runs. Measured Performance: Incorporating the view-count prior improves convergence speed and final reconstruction quality. Without it, PSNR can degrade by up to -1.22. Strengths: Adapts to the amount of visual information, preventing overfitting or underfitting due to fixed learning rates. Limitations: Requires accurate knowledge of the total number of training views. The exact scaling function may need tuning for different datasets. When to Use: When training radiance fields with a limited or variable number of input images. When Not to Use: When the number of views is extremely large and uniform, or when the scaling function is not well-defined for the specific dataset. The view-count-based learning rate was introduced in the context of Direct Voxel Grid Optimization. It addresses the challenge of optimizing radiance fields where the number of training views significantly impacts the convergence behavior. The method was proposed to ensure stable and efficient training regardless of the input view count. name: Hyperparameter Configuration for Stochastic Gradient Estimation
body: This article defines the hyperparameter configuration required to optimize differentiable rendering methods using first-order (OurG, OurH) and second-order (OurHVP, OurHVPA) stochastic gradient estimators. It solves the problem of selecting optimal sampling, learning rate, and trust region parameters for inverse rendering tasks such as caustic optimization, shape reconstruction, and texture mapping. What sets this configuration apart from standard NeRF training is the explicit use of Sigma annealing for distribution bandwidth control and antithetic sampling to reduce variance, alongside distinct parameter sets for first-order versus second-order optimization loops. Inputs: Task identifier (e.g., QUAD, BOX2, BOX10, MUG, SHAD, BUNNY, TEXTURE, CNN, CNN5). Method identifier (OurG, OurH, OurHVP, OurHVPA, or FR22). Current optimization iteration t. Outputs: Current learning rate (for first-order methods). Current trust region radius (for second-order methods). Current distribution bandwidth \sigmat. Sample count configuration (doubled via antithetic sampling). The hyperparameters are stored in a lookup table indexed by Method and Task. The structure contains the following fields: samples: Integer or float, base number of samples per iteration. sigmastart: Float, initial bandwidth \sigma for Sigma annealing. sigmaend: Float, final bandwidth \sigma for Sigma annealing. learningrate: Float, initial learning rate (first-order only). trustregion: Float, initial search bound (second-order only). linesearchiter: Integer, number of line search iterations (second-order only). linesearchtol: Float, convergence tolerance for line search (second-order only). recompute: Integer, iterations between line search re-estimations (second-order only). 1. Retrieve Base Parameters: Look up the hyperparameter set for the specified Method and Task from the configuration table. 2. Calculate Current Bandwidth (\sigmat): Perform linear Sigma annealing from sigmastart to sigmaend over the total optimization duration T. \sigmat = \sigma{start} + (\sigma{end} - \sigma{start}) \cdot \frac{t}{T} 3. Determine Sample Count: Let N{base} be the samples value from the configuration. Apply antithetic sampling: The effective sample count is N = 2 \cdot N{base}. The source states "The sample size, which is always antithetic and doubles the sample size, applies to our methods and FR22". 4. Configure Gradient Estimator: If Method is OurG or OurH (First-Order): Set learning rate \eta = learningrate. Update parameters using the learning rate and the stochastic gradient estimate. If Method is OurH, OurHVP, or OurHVPA (Second-Order): Set trust region radius \Delta = trustregion. Perform line search with linesearchiter iterations and tolerance linesearchtol. Check if re-estimation is needed: If current iteration t is a multiple of recompute, re-estimate the line search parameters. Sigma Annealing: Linear schedule for bandwidth \sigma. Controls the distribution used for stochastic estimation. Antithetic Sampling: For every sample x, an antithetic sample -x (or symmetric counterpart) is generated, effectively doubling the sample count for variance reduction. Trust Region: Initial search bound for second-order methods. Defines the region within which the quadratic model is trusted. Recompute: Frequency (in iterations) at which the line search is re-estimated for second-order methods.
