name: XYZ Learning Rate Scheduling
head: Spatial Learning Rate Adjustment
body: XYZ Learning Rate Scheduling adjusts the learning rate specifically for the 3D Gaussian point locations (xyz) during radiance-field optimization to balance training speed and rendering quality. It distinguishes itself from general scalar schedules by targeting the spatial parameters of the Gaussian primitives, addressing the sensitivity of point positions to large learning rates which can degrade rendering quality. Inputs and Outputs Input: Current iteration t, total iterations T, schedule type, and schedule coefficients. Output: Scalar learning rate \eta{xyz} for the xyz position parameters of the 3D Gaussians. Data Structures The method requires no auxiliary data structures; it computes a scalar value directly from the iteration count and coefficients. Formulas and Steps The method supports several functional forms for \eta{xyz}(t): 1. Two-Stage Rectangular Wave Transformation (rw) rw(x) = \begin{cases} a1, & x \in [0, p1] \\ a2, & x \in [p1, p2] \\ a3, & x \in [p2, 1] \end{cases} Where x = t/T is the normalized iteration. Typical values are a1 = 10^{-3}, a2 = 10^{-6}, a3 = 10^{-9}. Boundaries are p1 = 0.2 (covering 0%–20% of iterations) and p2 = 1.0 (covering 20%–100%). 2. Sine-based Schedule (s(t)) s(t) = \frac{as}{2}\sin\left(bs\frac{t}{T}2\pi + \frac{\pi}{2}\right) + 1 Where as and bs are fitting coefficients. 3. Cosine-based Schedule (c(t)) c(t) = \frac{ac}{2}\cos\left(bc\frac{t}{T}2\pi + \pi\right) + 1 Where ac and bc are fitting coefficients. 4. Linear Schedule (l(t)) Defined by two points (t1, p1) and (t2, p2) via: \frac{l(t)-p2}{p1-p2} = \frac{t-t2}{t1-t2} Where t1 = 1 and t2 = T. 5. Exponential Schedule (E(t)) E(t) = \varepsilon e^{\delta t} + \eta Where \varepsilon, \delta, \eta are fitting coefficients determined such that the function passes through (t1, E(t1)) and (t2, E(t2)) with t1=1 and t2=T. Parameters Fixed learning rates in the range lr \in [10^{-2}, 1] significantly improve training speed but quickly reduce rendering quality. Scheduling is recommended to avoid this range or to decay out of it. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computexyzlearningrate(t: int, T: int, scheduletype: str, params: dict) -> float: """ Compute the learning rate for 3D Gaussian xyz positions. Assumes t is 1-based (1 to T) to match source formulas where t1=1. """ if T <= 0: return 0.0 if scheduletype == 'rectangular': a1, a2, a3 = 1e-3, 1e-6, 1e-9 p1, p2 = 0.2, 1.0 x = t / T if x <= p1: return a1 elif x <= p2: return a2 else: return a3 elif scheduletype == 'sine': as = params['as'] bs = params['bs'] return (as / 2.0) math.sin(bs (t / T) 2 math.pi + math.pi / 2) + 1.0 elif scheduletype == 'cosine': ac = params['ac'] bc = params['bc'] return (ac / 2.0) math.cos(bc (t / T) 2 math.pi + math.pi) + 1.0 elif scheduletype == 'linear': # (l(t) - p2) / (p1 - p2) = (t - t2) / (t1 - t2) # t1 = 1, t2 = T t1, t2 = 1, T p1, p2 = params['p1'], params['p2'] return p2 + (p1 - p2) (t - t2) / (t1 - t2) elif scheduletype == 'exponential': # E(t) = eps exp(delta t) + eta # Passes through (1, E1) and (T, E2). Coefficients must be pre-computed. eps = params['eps'] delta = params['delta'] eta = params['eta'] return eps math.exp(delta t) + eta else: raise ValueError(f"Unknown schedule type: {scheduletype}") Edge Cases and Pitfalls Fixed Rate Degradation: Using a fixed learning rate in [10^{-2}, 1] causes rapid degradation of rendering quality. Precision: The rectangular wave uses values as low as 10^{-9}, which may be subject to floating-point precision issues in some optimizers. Coefficient Fitting: For sine, cosine, linear, and exponential schedules, the coefficients are fitting coefficients. The source does not provide a closed-form solution for deriving these from desired start/end points for the exponential case, only stating it passes through two points. Implementers must pre-compute these coefficients or use provided fitted values. Integrates adaptive regularization terms with learning rate decay during the optimization loop. Sets itself apart by coupling gradient regularization with LR scheduling. Choose when gradient noise destabilizes training. Choose for high-level training orchestration. Link Configures noise and sampling parameters alongside learning rates. Sets itself apart by focusing on gradient estimator stability. Choose when stochastic sampling introduces high variance. Link Applies general exponential decay for all parameters, not just xyz. Sets itself apart by using a continuous exponential curve. Choose for smooth, monotonic convergence. Link Assigns distinct learning rates to different parameter groups. Sets itself apart by decoupling optimization rates across model components. Choose for non-convex optimization landscapes. Link Uses linear interpolation for learning rates. Sets itself apart by providing a straight-line transition between start and end values. Choose for predictable, stepwise decay. Link Time Complexity: O(1) per iteration for computing the learning rate. Memory Complexity: O(1) as no additional storage is needed. Performance: The rectangular wave schedule was tested with 500 iterations and showed that balancing the learning rate is crucial. Strengths: Specifically targets the instability of 3D Gaussian positions, which are more sensitive to learning rate changes than other parameters. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of coefficients for non-rectangular schedules. The source notes that simply increasing the learning rate (e.g., to 10^{-2}) improves speed but blurs the result. name: Per-Parameter Learning Rate Scheduling
head: Feature LR, Opacity LR, Other Learning Rate Adjustments, Rotation LR, Scaling LR
body: Per-Parameter Learning Rate Scheduling adjusts the learning rates for specific parameter groups (scaling, opacity, rotation, and features) independently during each training iteration. It addresses the need to tune convergence speed and final rendering quality by allowing distinct optimization dynamics for different geometric and radiometric properties, setting it apart from uniform scheduling methods that apply a single rate to all parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current training iteration t, initial learning rates for each parameter group (\eta{scale}, \eta{opacity}, \eta{rotation}, \eta{feature}), and the base learning rate schedule. Output: Updated learning rates for each parameter group for the current iteration. Data Structures: A dictionary or object mapping parameter group names to their current learning rate values. Fields: scalelr, opacitylr, rotationlr, featurelr. Steps: 1. Initialize learning rates for each parameter group. For scaling, the optimal range is typically between 10^{-3} and 10^{-6}. Other parameters (opacity, rotation, feature) can be initialized similarly or derived from a base rate. 2. For each training iteration t: a. Determine the scaling factor or decay function for each parameter group. This may involve exponential decay, step decay, or constant values depending on the specific variant. b. Update the learning rate for each group: \eta{group}(t) = \eta{group, initial} \times \text{decay}(t) where \text{decay}(t) is specific to the group and iteration. c. Apply the updated learning rates to the respective parameter groups in the optimizer (e.g., Adam). Parameters: \eta{scale, initial}: Initial learning rate for scaling parameters. Typical optimal range: [10^{-3}, 10^{-6}]. \eta{opacity, initial}: Initial learning rate for opacity parameters. \eta{rotation, initial}: Initial learning rate for rotation parameters. \eta{feature, initial}: Initial learning rate for feature parameters. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Setting \eta{feature} = 0 does not significantly change training speed or quality, indicating that feature learning has less impact on improvement compared to other parameters. Precision issues may arise if learning rates are too small, leading to negligible updates. Boundary conditions: Ensure learning rates do not drop below a minimum threshold to prevent stagnation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updateperparameterlrs(iteration, initiallrs, decayfunctions): """ Update learning rates for each parameter group based on iteration and decay functions. Args: iteration (int): Current training iteration. initiallrs (dict): Dictionary with initial learning rates for 'scale', 'opacity', 'rotation', 'feature'. decayfunctions (dict): Dictionary with decay functions for each parameter group. Returns: dict: Updated learning rates for each parameter group. """ updatedlrs = {} for group in ['scale', 'opacity', 'rotation', 'feature']: initiallr = initiallrs[group] decayfunc = decayfunctions[group] updatedlrs[group] = initiallr decayfunc(iteration) return updatedlrs def constantdecay(iteration): return 1.0 def exponentialdecay(iteration, gamma=0.99): return gamma iteration initiallrs = { 'scale': 1e-3, 'opacity': 1e-2, 'rotation': 1e-2, 'feature': 1e-2 } decayfunctions = { 'scale': exponentialdecay, 'opacity': constantdecay, 'rotation': constantdecay, 'feature': constantdecay } updatedlrs = updateperparameterlrs(100, initiallrs, decayfunctions) Modifies the positional learning rate schedule to align with DashGaussian's two-stage (LR/HR) optimization, holding it constant during LR training and decaying it only after a specific iteration threshold. The positional learning rate is kept constant at its initial value throughout the LR optimization stage and only allowed to decay from the iteration i = \arg\mini \lfloor r(i) \rfloor = 1/3. This approach is beneficial when using a resolution scheduler that transitions from low to high resolution, ensuring stable optimization during the initial phase. Time Complexity: The overhead of updating per-parameter learning rates is minimal, typically O(1) per iteration, as it involves simple arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: Negligible, as it only requires storing a few additional scalar values for each parameter group. Measured Performance: Adjusting the scaling learning rate within the range [10^{-3}, 10^{-6}] can explicitly change the final rendering result and training speed. Other parameters have less impact on quality and speed but are still useful. Strengths: Allows fine-tuned control over different aspects of the model, potentially leading to better convergence and higher quality results. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of initial learning rates and decay functions for each parameter group. Setting feature learning rate to zero may not significantly impact performance, suggesting limited benefit from tuning this parameter. When to Use: When different parameters require different optimization dynamics, such as in complex scenes where geometric and radiometric properties need distinct handling. When Not to Use: When computational resources are limited, or when the impact of per-parameter tuning is negligible for the specific application. Per-Parameter Learning Rate Scheduling originated from the need to optimize 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and related radiance field representations more effectively. The method was introduced in I3DGS: Improve 3D Gaussian Splatting from Multiple Dimensions, which explored the impact of adjusting learning rates for scaling, opacity, rotation, and feature parameters. The approach has since been adopted and adapted in various other works, such as DashGaussian, to enhance optimization efficiency and rendering quality. name: Annealing Schedules
head: Constant Schedule, Exponential Schedule, Linear Schedule, Parameter Annealing Framework
body: Annealing Schedules provide a unified framework for parameter annealing during training, supporting constant, linear, and exponential schedules. Unlike specialized schedules that implement only one decay strategy, this framework offers multiple decay modes within a single implementation. The method computes a scalar value based on the current training step, the total number of steps, and configured bounds. Inputs and Outputs: step: Current training step (integer or array). numsteps: Total number of training steps (integer). initialvalue: Starting value for the schedule (float). finalvalue: Ending value for the schedule (float). scheduletype: String identifier for the schedule ('constant', 'linear', 'exponential'). Output: The computed parameter value (float32). Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The implementation relies on vectorized operations over the step index. Steps: 1. Calculate the progress ratio \alpha as the minimum of the normalized step and 1.0: \alpha = \min\left(\frac{\text{step}}{\text{num\steps}}, 1.0\right) 2. Apply the specific formula based on scheduletype: Constant: Return a constant value for all steps: value. Linear: Interpolate between initialvalue and finalvalue: \text{value} = (1.0 - \alpha) \cdot \text{initial\value} + \alpha \cdot \text{final\value} Exponential: Decay exponentially from initialvalue to finalvalue: \text{base} = \frac{\text{final\value}}{\text{initial\value}} \text{value} = \text{initial\value} \cdot (\text{base})^{\alpha} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import jax.numpy as jnp def annealschedule(step, numsteps, initialvalue, finalvalue, scheduletype='linear', constantvalue=None): """ Compute the annealed parameter value. Args: step: Current training step (int or jnp.ndarray). numsteps: Total number of training steps (int). initialvalue: Starting value (float). finalvalue: Ending value (float). scheduletype: 'constant', 'linear', or 'exponential'. constantvalue: Value to return for constant schedule. Defaults to initialvalue if None. Returns: The computed parameter value (jnp.ndarray). """ # Calculate progress ratio alpha, capped at 1.0 alpha = jnp.minimum(step / numsteps, 1.0) if scheduletype == 'constant': # Constant schedule returns a fixed value for all steps val = constantvalue if constantvalue is not None else initialvalue return jnp.fulllike(step, val, dtype=jnp.float32) elif scheduletype == 'linear': # Linear interpolation between initial and final return (1.0 - alpha) initialvalue + alpha finalvalue elif scheduletype == 'exponential': # Exponential interpolation # Handle division by zero if initialvalue is 0 if initialvalue == 0: return jnp.fulllike(step, finalvalue, dtype=jnp.float32) base = finalvalue / initialvalue return initialvalue (base alpha) else: raise ValueError(f"Unknown schedule type: {scheduletype}") Parameters: initialvalue: Starting value for the schedule. finalvalue: Ending value for the schedule. numsteps: Total number of training steps. Edge Cases: If initialvalue is 0, the exponential base calculation results in division by zero. The implementation must handle this, typically by returning finalvalue or initialvalue directly. If step exceeds numsteps, \alpha is capped at 1.0 to prevent extrapolation. Time Complexity: O(1) per step, involving basic arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) for scalar inputs, or O(N) for batched inputs of size N. Strengths: Simple to implement, flexible, and covers common decay patterns. Limitations: Does not account for loss landscape geometry (unlike adaptive methods). The exponential schedule can be sensitive to the choice of finalvalue if initialvalue is small. When to use: When a simple, predictable decay of hyperparameters is desired. The framework is implemented in the Nerfies repository, which provides code for "Deformable Neural Radiance Fields". It was developed by Keunhong Park et al. at Google and the University of Washington. The implementation uses JAX for efficient computation. google/nerfies, https://github.com/google/nerfies, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Piecewise Schedule
body: A learning rate scheduling method that composes multiple sub-schedules applied sequentially at specified milestone steps. It allows complex training dynamics by chaining distinct optimization behaviors (e.g., warmup, decay, fine-tuning) without requiring a single monolithic formula. It differs from continuous decay schedules like Exponential Decay Schedules by allowing abrupt changes in behavior at discrete boundaries, and from Annealing Schedules by its explicit modular composition of independent schedule objects rather than a single parametric function. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A global training step index t (integer \ge 0). Output: A scalar learning rate value lr. Data Structures: The schedule object maintains two primary fields: 1. schedules: A list of Schedule objects. Each object must implement a method get(stepoffset) that returns a learning rate for a local step offset. 2. milestones: A 1D array of integers representing cumulative step counts. milestones[i] is the global step index where schedules[i] begins. The array is sorted in ascending order. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Construct the schedules list and the milestones array from configuration. Ensure milestones has length N, where N is the number of sub-schedules. 2. Lookup: Given a global step t: a. Find the index idx such that milestones[idx] is the first milestone greater than t. This is typically done using a binary search (e.g., searchsorted with side='right'). b. Determine the base step for the current sub-schedule. If idx > 0, the base step is milestones[idx - 1]. If idx == 0, the base step is 0. c. Calculate the local step offset: t{local} = t - \text{base\step}. d. Retrieve the learning rate from the selected sub-schedule: lr = \text{schedules}[idx].\text{get}(t{local}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import jax.numpy as jnp class PiecewiseSchedule: def init(self, schedules, milestones): """ Args: schedules: List of Schedule objects, each having a.get(step) method. milestones: 1D array of cumulative step counts where each sub-schedule begins. """ self.schedules = schedules self.milestones = jnp.array(milestones) def get(self, step): """ Returns the learning rate for the given global step. """ # Find the index of the first milestone strictly greater than step # side='right' ensures that if step equals a milestone, we pick the next schedule # or the current one depending on boundary definition. # Standard implementation uses side='right' to handle [milestone, nextmilestone) intervals. idx = jnp.searchsorted(self.milestones, step, side='right') # Select the schedule corresponding to this interval schedule = self.schedules[idx] # Determine the base step for the current schedule # If idx is 0, the base is 0. Otherwise, it is the previous milestone. if idx >= 1: baseidx = self.milestones[idx - 1] else: baseidx = 0 # Calculate local step and retrieve learning rate localstep = step - baseidx return schedule.get(localstep) Parameters and Edge Cases: Milestone Alignment: The milestones array must be strictly increasing. If milestones is empty, the behavior is undefined. Step Boundaries: The use of side='right' in searchsorted implies that if t equals milestones[i], it falls into the interval starting at milestones[i] (index i) if we consider the interval [milestones[i], milestones[i+1]). However, searchsorted(..., side='right') returns the index after the last occurrence of step. If step equals milestones[i], it returns i+1. This means the schedule at index i+1 is used for the step equal to the milestone. Implementers must verify if this boundary behavior matches the intended "start at milestone" semantics. If the intent is that milestones[i] starts schedule i, side='left' might be more appropriate, or the milestones must be offset by 1. The source code uses side='right'. Precision: Steps are integers. No floating-point precision issues in step calculation. A specific application of piecewise scheduling for light field compression networks, consisting of a training phase and a quantization phase. Both phases use a constant learning rate of 0.01. The training phase lasts 12 epochs, where one epoch is defined as all Sampled Aperture Images (SAIs) being used 500 times, with 5 SAIs fed per iteration to calculate averaged loss. The quantization stage defines one epoch as all SAIs involved 200 times, followed by fine-tuning all consecutive layers for just 1 epoch after quantizing each layer. This variant is chosen when network convergence requires distinct training and quantization-aware fine-tuning stages. Hardware: Single Nvidia Titan RTX GPU with 24GB memory; Framework: PyTorch. Time Complexity: O(\log N) per step lookup, where N is the number of sub-schedules, due to binary search on milestones. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the milestones array and references to sub-schedules. Strengths: Modular design allows mixing different schedule types (e.g., linear warmup followed by cosine decay). Precise control over training dynamics at specific milestones. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of milestone boundaries. Discontinuities in learning rate can occur if sub-schedules do not align at boundaries. When to use: When training requires distinct phases with different optimization behaviors (e.g., warmup, decay, fine-tuning). The piecewise schedule structure is implemented in the Nerfies project, a JAX-based implementation of NeRF. It provides a flexible way to manage learning rates in complex training loops. The Two-Phase variant is used in research on kernel-modulated neural representations for light field compression. google/nerfies, https://github.com/google/nerfies, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Learning Kernel-Modulated Neural Representation for Efficient Light Field Compression, https://hal.science/hal-04627349v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Exponential Decay Schedules
head: Geometric LR Decay, Multiplicative LR Decay
body: Exponential decay schedules reduce the learning rate multiplicatively over training steps, providing a smooth, continuous transition from high initial exploration to fine-grained convergence. This family differs from Linear Learning Rate Schedule by applying relative reductions rather than absolute ones, and from Cosine Decay Learning Rate Schedule by avoiding the symmetric "slow-fast-slow" trajectory in favor of a monotonic decrease. It is primarily used in NeRF optimization to stabilize training when the model has converged to a coarse geometry but requires precise refinement of appearance and density fields. All methods in this family compute the learning rate lrt at step t using a base raised to a power proportional to the normalized step count. The core mechanism is: lrt = lr{initial} \times \gamma^{\frac{t}{T}} where \gamma is the decay factor (0 < \gamma < 1) and T is a normalization constant (often total steps or a specific interval). This ensures the learning rate never reaches zero but asymptotically approaches it. Unlike step decay, there are no discrete jumps. The schedule is often combined with warm-up phases to prevent early instability. Defines the standard iterative optimization protocol for NeRFs, combining ray-batched SGD with exponential LR decay and a two-phase loss schedule. It differs from FreeNeRF by using simpler auxiliary models for depth supervision rather than annealing positional encoding frequencies, and explicitly manages regularization weights that decay alongside the learning rate. Applies a base raised to a normalized step exponent to transition from an initial to a final value. It differs from Linear Learning Rate Schedule by applying multiplicative reductions rather than additive ones, and from Step Decay Learning Rate Schedule by providing a continuous curve rather than discrete uniform reductions at specific boundaries. Combines a linear warm-up phase with an exponential decay trajectory, specifically targeting per-camera exposure parameters or main network weights. It distinguishes itself from Cosine Decay Learning Rate Schedule by using a constant rate during warm-up followed by geometric decay, and from Exponential Decay Learning Rate Schedule by explicitly incorporating a delayed warm-up period to stabilize initial training. Exponential decay is a standard technique in optimization, widely adopted in early neural network training and retained in NeRF pipelines for its simplicity and effectiveness in fine-tuning. In the context of differentiable volume rendering, it addresses the problem of converging sparse input data by preventing large gradient updates once the model has established a coherent geometric prior.

body: This method defines the standard iterative optimization protocol for training Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), specifically tailored for sparse input scenarios. It solves the problem of converging a differentiable volume rendering model to match target images by combining ray-batched stochastic gradient descent with a two-phase loss schedule and exponential learning rate decay. It differs from FreeNeRF by using simpler auxiliary models for depth supervision rather than annealing positional encoding frequencies. Inputs: Training dataset: Images, camera poses, scene bounds (near/far), and optionally depth priors with confidence scores. Model: A NeRF representation (e.g., MLP-based or hash-grid based) initialized with random weights. Hyperparameters: Initial learning rate (lrate), decay rate (decay\rate), decay steps (decay\steps), batch size (N{rand}), and regularization weights. Outputs: Optimized model parameters. Training metrics: Loss values, PSNR, and learning rate history. Ray Batch: A tensor of ray origins, ray directions, RGB targets (N{rand}, 3), and optional depth/confidence priors. Training State: Global step counter, current learning rate, and regularization weight multipliers. 1. Initialization: Initialize the Adam optimizer with the initial learning rate lrate and weight decay. Load training images, poses, and bounds. Compute depth confidences if priors are available. 2. Ray Sampling: For each iteration, sample N{rand} random ray indices from the training set. Fetch corresponding ray origins, directions, and target RGB values. 3. Rendering: Render the sampled rays through the neural field model. This involves sampling points along each ray, querying the model for density (\sigma) and color (c), and compositing them using volume rendering equations to produce predicted RGB (\hat{y}), alphas, and depth. 4. Loss Computation: Compute the primary reconstruction loss (Mean Squared Error) between predicted RGB and target RGB: L{img} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (\hat{y}i - yi)^2 Apply phase-specific regularization losses (see Phase Schedule below). Apply adaptive regularization terms if their corresponding weights are positive. Sum all components to get totalloss. 5. Backpropagation: Zero gradients, perform backward pass on totalloss, and step the optimizer. 6. Learning Rate Update: Update the learning rate for all parameter groups using exponential decay. 7. Logging: Compute PSNR from the current loss and log metrics. The training is divided into two phases based on iteration count: Phase 1 (Iterations 0–10,000): Only L{color} (image reconstruction) and L{sd} (stereo depth consistency, if available) are applied. Phase 2 (Iterations > 10,000): Additional losses L{ap}, L{av}, and L{cfc} are imposed. Regularization terms are added to the total loss based on specific weights: Orthogonality: If Orthoregweight > 0, compute lossreg = tensorf.vectorcompdiffs() and add Orthoregweight lossreg. L1 Density: If L1regweight > 0, compute lossregL1 = tensorf.densityL1() and add L1regweight lossregL1. Note: L1regweight switches from an initial value to a rest value after the first alpha mask update iteration. Total Variation (TV): If TVweightdensity > 0 or TVweightapp > 0, compute TV losses on density and appearance fields respectively. The TV weights decay multiplicatively by lrfactor every iteration. Learning Rate Decay: lrate{new} = lrate{initial} \times (decay\rate)^{\frac{global\step}{decay\steps}} PSNR Calculation: PSNR = -10 \cdot \log{10}(L{img}) Total Loss: L{total} = L{img} + \sum{k} wk L{reg, k} Where wk are the dynamic regularization weights. learningrate (lrate): Initial learning rate. Default 5e-4. decayrate: Exponential decay factor. Default 0.1. decaysteps: Number of steps for decay. Default args.lratedecay 1000. batchsize (N{rand}): Number of random rays per batch. Orthoregweight: Initial orthogonality regularization strength. L1regweight: Initial L1 density regularization strength. TVweightdensity, TVweightapp: Initial TV regularization strengths. lrfactor: Multiplicative factor for decaying TV weights and potentially LR. Hyperparameters for Phase 2 losses: l{ap}=10, l{v}=4, l{p}=3, k=5, e{\tau}=0.1, \lambda1=1, \lambda2=\lambda3=\lambda4=\lambda5=0.1. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import torch def trainloop(model, optimizer, dataset, args): """ Args: model: NeRF model instance optimizer: Adam optimizer instance dataset: Dataset providing rays, targets, and metadata args: Configuration object containing hyperparameters """ globalstep = 0 lrate = args.lrate decayrate = args.decayrate decaysteps = args.decaysteps # Regularization weights orthoweight = args.Orthoweight l1weight = args.L1weightinital tvweightdensity = args.TVweightdensity tvweightapp = args.TVweightapp lrfactor = args.lrfactor # Phase 1 threshold phase1end = 10000 # Validation set capped at 1024100 rays, sampled linearly valindices = np.linspace(0, dataset.size, 1024 100, dtype=int) while globalstep < args.maxiterations: # 1. Sample Rays rayindices = dataset.samplerandomrays(args.batchsize) raystrain, rgbtrain = dataset.getrays(rayindices) # 2. Render renderoutput = model.render( rays=raystrain, chunk=args.batchsize, Nsamples=args.nSamples, whitebg=args.whitebg, ndcray=args.ndcray, istrain=True) rgbmap = renderoutput.rgbmap extras = renderoutput.extras # 3. Compute Loss imgloss = torch.mean((rgbmap - rgbtrain) 2) totalloss = imgloss # Phase 1: Only Color and Stereo Depth if globalstep < phase1end: if args.usesd: # Sources do not provide the exact formula for Lsd totalloss += args.lsd computesdloss(extras, dataset) else: # Phase 2: Add AP, AV, CFC losses # Sources do not provide the exact formulas for Lap, Lav, Lcfc totalloss += args.lap computeaploss(extras) totalloss += args.lv computeavloss(extras) totalloss += args.lp computecfcloss(extras) # 4. Apply Adaptive Regularizations if orthoweight > 0: lossreg = model.vectorcompdiffs() totalloss += orthoweight lossreg if l1weight > 0: lossregL1 = model.densityL1() totalloss += l1weight lossregL1 if tvweightdensity > 0: losstvd = model.TVlossdensity(args.tvreg) totalloss += tvweightdensity losstvd if tvweightapp > 0: losstva = model.TVlossapp(args.tvreg) totalloss += tvweightapp losstva # 5. Backpropagate optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() # 6. Update Learning Rate newlrate = lrate (decayrate (globalstep / decaysteps)) for paramgroup in optimizer.paramgroups: paramgroup['lr'] = newlrate lrate = newlrate # Decay TV weights multiplicatively tvweightdensity = lrfactor tvweightapp = lrfactor # Switch L1 weight after first alpha mask update if globalstep == args.alphamaskupdatestep: l1weight = args.L1weightrest # 7. Logging psnr = -10.0 np.log10(imgloss.item()) print(f"Step {globalstep}: loss={totalloss.item():.4f}, psnr={psnr:.2f}") # Periodic checkpointing if globalstep % args.checkpointfreq == 0: torch.save({'model': model.statedict(), 'optimizer': optimizer.statedict()}, f"ckpt{globalstep}.pth") globalstep += 1 Learning Rate Scheduling: General techniques for adjusting learning rates. This method uses exponential decay specifically. Regularization and Priors: Details on the specific regularization terms (L{sd}, L{ap}, L{av}, L{cfc}) used in this loop. Training Objective for Fine Representation: How the loss components adapt for fine-grained details in later training stages. Time Complexity: O(N{rand} \cdot N{samples}) per iteration, where N{rand} is batch size and N{samples} is samples per ray. Memory Complexity: O(N{rand} \cdot N{samples}) for storing intermediate rendering buffers (weights, alphas, gradients). Performance: On a single NVIDIA RTX A4000 16GB GPU, training takes approximately 22 hours per scene for 100,000 iterations. Strengths: Simple to implement; exponential decay provides stable convergence; two-phase schedule prevents early overfitting to noise. Limitations: TV weights decay rapidly if lrfactor < 1, potentially losing regularization benefits later in training. Validation set size is capped at 102,400 rays, which may underrepresent large datasets. When to use: Standard NeRF training for sparse inputs where depth priors are available. This training configuration originates from the SimpleNeRF paper, which regularizes sparse input NeRFs using simpler auxiliary models. It builds upon the DS-NeRF architecture and Adam optimization framework. The method was developed to address floaters and radiance ambiguity in sparse view synthesis by leveraging reprojection error filtering and specific regularization losses (L{ap}, L{av}, L{cfc}). It contrasts with FreeNeRF by using fixed simpler models rather than annealing positional encoding degrees. name: Exponential Decay Learning Rate Schedule
head: Adam with Exponential Decay, Exponential Decay Schedule, Exponential LR Schedule, ExponentialSchedule, Instant NGP LR Schedule, LambdaLR Exponential Decay, Training Optimizer and Schedule
body: An exponentially decaying schedule that transitions a learning rate from an initial value to a final value using a base raised to a normalized step exponent. It differs from Linear Learning Rate Schedule by applying multiplicative reductions rather than additive ones, and from Step Decay Learning Rate Schedule by providing a continuous curve rather than discrete uniform reductions at specific boundaries. Inputs: Initial learning rate (lr), decay factor (\gamma), step size (step\size), current epoch or iteration (epoch or step). Outputs: Adjusted learning rate (lr{current}). Data Structures: The implementation typically relies on a scheduler object (e.g., PyTorch's LambdaLR) or a manual update function. The state tracks the current epoch/step index. Steps: 1. Initialize the scheduler with the initial learning rate lr, the decay function \lambda(epoch) = \gamma^{(epoch / step\size)}, and the starting epoch index (typically start\epoch - 1 to align with zero-based indexing or pre-increment logic). 2. At each optimization step, compute the decay factor using the formula: lr(epoch) = lr \times \gamma^{\left(\frac{epoch}{step\size}\right)} where: lr is the initial learning rate. \gamma is the decay factor (e.g., 0.33). epoch is the current training step or epoch. step\size is the interval at which the exponent increments (e.g., 10,000 steps). 3. Apply the computed lr(epoch) to the optimizer's parameter groups. Parameters: Typical values for NeRF-style optimization include separate parameter groups: positions (lr = 10^{-4}), features (lr = 5 \times 10^{-3}), and MLP weights (lr = 5 \times 10^{-5}). Decay factor \gamma = 0.33 applied every step\size = 10,000 steps after an initial warm-up or fixed iteration count (e.g., after 20,000 iterations). Pitfalls: Redundant execution paths may occur if the condition step >= self.numsteps is checked multiple times within the update logic, leading to unnecessary computations or state inconsistencies. Precision issues may arise if \gamma^{(epoch / step\size)} underflows for very large epochs or if \gamma is too close to 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeexponentiallr(initiallr, gamma, stepsize, currentstep): """ Compute the learning rate using exponential decay. Args: initiallr (float): The starting learning rate. gamma (float): The decay factor (0 < gamma < 1). stepsize (int): The number of steps between exponent increments. currentstep (int): The current training step index. Returns: float: The adjusted learning rate. """ # Calculate the exponent based on the step size exponent = currentstep / stepsize # Compute the decayed learning rate lr = initiallr (gamma exponent) return lr initiallr = 1e-3 gamma = 0.33 stepsize = 10000 currentstep = 25000 lr = computeexponentiallr(initiallr, gamma, stepsize, currentstep) A step-wise decay schedule that reduces a learning rate by a fixed multiplicative factor at regular intervals until a maximum number of decays is reached. It differs from the parent Exponential Decay Learning Rate Schedule by applying discrete, uniform reductions at specific step boundaries rather than a continuous exponential curve. Time Complexity: O(1) per step for computing the decay factor, assuming exponentiation is constant time. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for storing the scheduler state (current step). Performance: Effective for stabilizing training in later stages of NeRF optimization, particularly when combined with adaptive optimizers like Adam. The continuous decay helps fine-tune high-frequency details without the abrupt changes associated with step decay. Strengths: Smooth transition of learning rates; easy to implement; widely supported in deep learning frameworks. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \gamma and step\size to avoid premature convergence or insufficient decay. The continuous nature may not be ideal for tasks requiring sharp phase transitions. When to use: Suitable for long-running training sessions where gradual refinement is needed, such as in radiance field optimization. When not to use: Not ideal for tasks requiring sudden changes in learning rate or when the optimal decay rate is unknown and requires frequent adjustment. The exponential decay schedule is a classic learning rate scheduling technique used in optimization. In the context of volume rendering and NeRFs, it has been adopted from general deep learning practices and adapted for specific training regimes, such as those described in Instant NGP. name: Step Decay Learning Rate Schedule
head: StepSchedule
body: A step-wise decay schedule that reduces a learning rate by a fixed multiplicative factor at regular intervals until a maximum number of decays is reached. It differs from the parent Exponential Decay Learning Rate Schedule by applying discrete, uniform reductions at specific step boundaries rather than a continuous exponential curve. Inputs: Current training step (integer), initial learning rate, decay interval, decay factor, maximum number of decays, and optionally a final learning rate value. Outputs: The current learning rate value. Data Structures: The schedule is stateless regarding the learning rate value itself, relying only on the current step index and configuration constants. Parameters: initialvalue: The starting learning rate. Typical value: 0.01. decayinterval: The number of steps between each decay event. decayfactor: The multiplicative factor applied per decay. Typical value: 0.33. maxdecays: The maximum number of decays allowed. finalvalue: The learning rate after maxdecays have occurred. If not provided, it is computed as initialvalue decayfactormaxdecays. Algorithm: 1. Calculate the decay phase: phase = step // decayinterval. 2. If phase >= maxdecays, return finalvalue. 3. Otherwise, return initialvalue decayfactorphase. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def stepdecaylearningrate(step, initialvalue, decayinterval, decayfactor, maxdecays, finalvalue=None): """ Computes the learning rate for a given step using step decay. Args: step: Current training step (integer). initialvalue: Starting learning rate. decayinterval: Steps between decays. decayfactor: Multiplicative factor per decay. maxdecays: Maximum number of decays. finalvalue: Optional explicit final value. Returns: Current learning rate. """ # Compute the number of full decay intervals completed phase = step // decayinterval # Determine the final value if not explicitly provided if finalvalue is None: finalvalue = initialvalue (decayfactor maxdecays) # If the phase exceeds the maximum allowed decays, clamp to final value if phase >= maxdecays: return finalvalue # Apply the decay factor for the current phase return initialvalue (decayfactor phase) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Warm-up: In specific implementations (e.g., Instant-NGP-based NeRF), a linear warm-up phase is applied for the first 1K iterations before the step decay begins. The core step decay formula does not account for warm-up; this must be handled as a separate pre-processing step or conditional logic before applying the decay. Boundary Conditions: The decay occurs at multiples of decayinterval. Steps strictly less than decayinterval result in no decay (phase 0). Integer Division: The use of integer division (//) ensures that the decay is discrete. Floating point inaccuracies in step counting should be avoided. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(1) per step. The calculation involves a single division, a comparison, and a power operation. Memory: O(1). No state is stored between steps. Measured Performance: In Instant-NGP-based NeRF training, this schedule is used with an initial learning rate of 0.01 over 20K total iterations. Specific decay points are at iterations 9K, 12K, 15K, 17K, and 19K, using a decay factor of 0.33. This implies a variable decayinterval or specific hard-coded steps rather than a uniform interval in that specific implementation, which contradicts the generic "regular intervals" definition in. The sources disagree on whether the intervals are uniform or fixed specific points. lists specific iterations, while defines a uniform decayinterval. Implementers should verify if the specific application requires uniform intervals or fixed checkpoints. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple to implement and debug; provides clear, discrete reductions in learning rate. Limitations: Less smooth than exponential decay; may cause instability if the decay factor is too aggressive or intervals are too short. When to Use: When discrete, predictable reductions in learning rate are desired. When the training process benefits from specific checkpoint-based adjustments rather than continuous decay. Origin: The step decay schedule is a standard optimization technique in deep learning. In the context of NeRF, it is used in the Nerfies framework and Instant-NGP-based NeRF variants. History and Development: The Nerfies implementation defines the schedule with parameters decayinterval, decayfactor, and maxdecays. Instant-NGP-based NeRF implementations use a variant with specific decay points (9K, 12K, 15K, 17K, 19K) and a warm-up phase. Where it is used: Nerfies training scripts. name: Linear Learning Rate Schedule
head: Linear Interpolation Schedule, LinearSchedule
body: A learning rate schedule that transitions from an initial value to a final value over a specified number of steps using linear interpolation. It provides a deterministic, monotonic decay path for optimization parameters in radiance-field training. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: step (current optimization step index, integer \ge 0), initialvalue (starting learning rate, float), finalvalue (target learning rate at completion, float), numsteps (total steps for the transition, integer). Output: The computed learning rate for the current step (float). Data Structures No persistent data structures are required; the state is purely a function of the current step index and the fixed parameters. Parameters initialvalue: The learning rate at step 0. finalvalue: The learning rate at step numsteps. numsteps: The total number of steps over which the interpolation occurs. Algorithm 1. Compute the progress ratio \alpha as the fraction of steps completed, capped at 1.0: \alpha = \min\left(\frac{\text{step}}{\text{num\steps}}, 1.0\right) 2. Compute the learning rate lr by linearly interpolating between initialvalue and finalvalue using \alpha: lr = (1.0 - \alpha) \cdot \text{initial\value} + \alpha \cdot \text{final\value} Edge Cases and Pitfalls Division by Zero: If numsteps is 0, the division in step 1 is undefined. The implementation must ensure numsteps > 0 or handle this case explicitly (e.g., returning initialvalue). Step Bounds: If step exceeds numsteps, \alpha is clamped to 1.0, ensuring the learning rate remains at finalvalue rather than extrapolating. Precision: Using floating-point arithmetic for step / numsteps is standard. For very large numsteps, precision loss is negligible for typical learning rate magnitudes. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def linearschedule(step: int, initialvalue: float, finalvalue: float, numsteps: int) -> float: """ Compute the learning rate using a linear schedule. Args: step: Current optimization step index. initialvalue: Starting learning rate. finalvalue: Target learning rate at completion. numsteps: Total number of steps for the transition. Returns: The computed learning rate. """ if numsteps <= 0: # Guard against division by zero; behavior is undefined in sources for numsteps=0 return initialvalue # Compute progress ratio, capped at 1.0 alpha = min(step / numsteps, 1.0) # Linear interpolation lr = (1.0 - alpha) initialvalue + alpha finalvalue return lr A learning rate schedule that transitions from an initial value to a final value using a cosine function to ease the change. It differs from the parent Linear Learning Rate Schedule by providing a non-linear, smooth decay curve rather than a linear interpolation, which can help stabilize optimization in radiance-field training by reducing the learning rate more gradually in the later stages. A linear interpolation method to avoid abrupt transitions between training stages by blending the previous coarser representation with the current less-merged one. Transitions between stages are smoothed using linear interpolation over 2k iterations. It interpolates the decoded quantity z as z^{(s)} = (1-\lambda) z^{(s-1)} + \lambda \bar{z}^{(s)}, where \lambda \in [0,1] is the transition coefficient. Time Complexity: O(1) per step. The calculation involves a single division, a minimum, and two multiplications and an addition. Memory Complexity: O(1). No history or state needs to be stored beyond the current step counter. Strengths: Simple to implement and understand. Provides a predictable, linear decay path. Useful when a steady, constant reduction in learning rate is desired without the compounding effect of exponential decay. Limitations: The rate of change is constant, which may not be optimal for all loss landscapes. It lacks the smoothness of cosine schedules or the adaptive nature of exponential decay. When to use: When a simple, deterministic decay is sufficient and computational overhead of more complex schedules is undesirable. When not to use: When the optimization landscape requires a smoother transition (consider Cosine) or a faster initial decay followed by a slower tail (consider Exponential Decay). name: Cosine Learning Rate Schedule
head: CosineEasingSchedule
body: A learning rate schedule that transitions from an initial value to a final value using a cosine function to ease the change. It differs from the parent Linear Learning Rate Schedule by providing a non-linear, smooth decay curve rather than a linear interpolation, which can help stabilize optimization in radiance-field training by reducing the learning rate more gradually in the later stages. Inputs and Outputs: step: Current training step (integer). numsteps: Total number of training steps (integer). initialvalue: Starting learning rate (float). finalvalue: Target learning rate at numsteps (float). Output: The computed learning rate for the current step (float). Data Structures: No complex data structures are required; the calculation is stateless and depends only on the current step and configuration parameters. Steps: 1. Calculate the normalized progress alpha as the ratio of step to numsteps, clamped to a maximum of 1.0. 2. Calculate the total scale of change as finalvalue - initialvalue. 3. Clamp alpha to the range [0.0, 1.0] to handle edge cases where step might be negative or exceed numsteps due to implementation details. 4. Compute the cosine factor using the formula: 0.5 \cdot (1 + \cos(\pi x + \pi)), where x is the clamped alpha. 5. Return the result: initialvalue + scale cosinefactor. Formula: v = v{init} + (v{final} - v{init}) \cdot 0.5 \cdot (1 + \cos(\pi x + \pi)) Where: v is the resulting learning rate. v{init} is initialvalue. v{final} is finalvalue. x = \min(\max(step/num\steps, 0), 1). Parameters: initialvalue: Typically the peak learning rate used in the training setup. finalvalue: Often set to a small value (e.g., 10^{-6}) or zero to converge the model. numsteps: The total duration of the training loop. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If step is negative, the clamping ensures x=0, returning initialvalue. If step exceeds numsteps, the clamping ensures x=1, returning finalvalue. Precision issues with floating-point arithmetic in the cosine calculation are generally negligible for standard training scales. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def cosinelearningrate(step, numsteps, initialvalue, finalvalue): # Calculate normalized progress alpha = step / numsteps if numsteps > 0 else 0.0 # Clamp alpha to [0.0, 1.0] if alpha < 0.0: alpha = 0.0 elif alpha > 1.0: alpha = 1.0 # Calculate scale scale = finalvalue - initialvalue # Compute cosine factor # Note: cos(pi x + pi) is equivalent to -cos(pi x) cosinefactor = 0.5 (1 + math.cos(math.pi alpha + math.pi)) # Return final learning rate return initialvalue + scale cosinefactor A schedule wrapper that delays the start of a base learning rate schedule using a sinusoidal rate multiplier. It sets apart from standard cosine schedules by introducing a warm-up phase where the learning rate is suppressed, easing into the base schedule's trajectory. This prevents early instability in radiance-field optimization by avoiding large gradient updates during the initial training steps. Time Complexity: O(1) per step, as it involves basic arithmetic and a single trigonometric function evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring no additional storage beyond the current step and configuration values. Strengths: Provides a smooth, non-linear decay that can help the optimizer settle into minima more effectively than linear schedules. The cosine shape naturally slows down the learning rate as training progresses. Limitations: May converge slower than aggressive schedules if the initial learning rate is not well-tuned. The smooth decay might not be optimal for all types of loss landscapes in radiance-field optimization. When to use: Suitable for stable training scenarios where a gradual reduction in learning rate is beneficial. Often used in conjunction with warm-up phases (e.g., Delayed Cosine Schedule). When not to use: If rapid convergence is required in the early stages, a linear or step schedule might be more appropriate. The cosine learning rate schedule is implemented in the Nerfies project, a JAX-based framework for neural radiance fields. It is part of the training configuration for optimizing radiance fields, providing a smooth transition in learning rates during the training loop. google/nerfies, https://github.com/google/nerfies, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Delayed Cosine Schedule
head: DelayedSchedule
body: A schedule wrapper that delays the start of a base learning rate schedule using a sinusoidal rate multiplier. It sets apart from standard cosine schedules by introducing a warm-up phase where the learning rate is suppressed, easing into the base schedule's trajectory. This prevents early instability in radiance-field optimization by avoiding large gradient updates during the initial training steps. The method computes a delay multiplier that transitions from a minimum value to 1.0 over a specified number of steps, then multiplies this by the output of a base schedule. Inputs: step: Current optimization step (integer). baseschedule: A callable or object implementing a standard learning rate schedule (e.g., Cosine Schedule). delaysteps: Number of steps over which the delay rate transitions from delaymult to 1.0. delaymult: The minimum multiplier applied to the learning rate during the delay period (typically 0 < \text{delay\mult} < 1). Outputs: learningrate: The final scaled learning rate value. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The implementation relies on scalar arithmetic operations. Steps: 1. Calculate the normalized step progress for the delay phase: t = \text{clip}(\frac{\text{step}}{\text{delay\steps}}, 0, 1). 2. Compute the delay multiplier using a sinusoidal interpolation: \text{delay\rate} = \text{delay\mult} + (1 - \text{delay\mult}) \times \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} \times t\right) Note: \sin(\frac{\pi}{2} \times t) is equivalent to \sin(0.5 \times \pi \times t). 3. Retrieve the base learning rate from the underlying schedule: \text{base\lr} = \text{base\schedule}(\text{step}). 4. Return the product: \text{learning\rate} = \text{delay\rate} \times \text{base\lr}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def delayedcosineschedule(step, baseschedule, delaysteps, delaymult): """ Computes the learning rate using a delayed cosine schedule. Args: step (int): Current optimization step. baseschedule (callable): Function that returns the base learning rate for a given step. delaysteps (int): Number of steps for the delay transition. delaymult (float): Minimum multiplier during the delay phase. Returns: float: The scaled learning rate. """ # Step 1: Clip normalized step to [0, 1] # If delaysteps is 0, avoid division by zero; treat as no delay if delaysteps <= 0: delayrate = 1.0 else: # Calculate normalized progress within the delay window t = step / delaysteps # Clip t to [0, 1] to handle steps beyond delaysteps or negative steps t = max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) # Step 2: Compute delayrate using sinusoidal interpolation # Formula: delaymult + (1 - delaymult) sin(0.5 pi t) delayrate = delaymult + (1.0 - delaymult) math.sin(0.5 math.pi t) # Step 3: Get base learning rate baselr = baseschedule(step) # Step 4: Return scaled learning rate return delayrate baselr Parameters with Typical Values: delaymult: Often set to a small value like 0.1 or 0.01 to significantly suppress early learning rates. delaysteps: Typically a small fraction of total training steps, e.g., 100-1000 steps, depending on the total duration. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If delaysteps is 0, the calculation in Step 1 must be guarded. The sources indicate that if delaysteps <= 0, the delay rate should be set to 1.0, effectively disabling the delay. Negative Steps: Ensure step is non-negative. If negative, clip t to 0. Precision: Use standard floating-point arithmetic. The sine function is well-behaved in the [0, \pi/2] range. A variant implementation found in FastGS that combines a delay multiplier with a log-linear interpolation for the base schedule. It differs from the standard Delayed Cosine Schedule by using loglerp (log-linear interpolation between lrinit and lrfinal) as the base schedule instead of a cosine curve. It explicitly handles cases where lrinit and lrfinal are 0.0 by returning 0.0 to disable the parameter. The delay rate calculation is identical to the standard definition: \text{delay\rate} = \text{lr\delay\mult} + (1 - \text{lr\delay\mult}) \times \sin(0.5 \times \pi \times \text{clip}(\text{step} / \text{lr\delay\steps}, 0, 1)) if lrdelaysteps > 0, otherwise 1.0. Time Complexity: O(1) per step, involving a few arithmetic operations and one sine evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring only scalar storage for parameters. Strengths: Stabilizes early training in NeRF optimization by preventing large initial updates. The sinusoidal transition is smooth, avoiding discontinuities in the learning rate derivative. Limitations: Adds hyperparameters (delaysteps, delaymult) that require tuning. If delaysteps is too large, the model may converge slowly. If delaymult is too low, the initial learning rate may be too small to make progress. When to Use: Recommended for radiance-field optimization where early instability is observed. Particularly useful in differentiable volume rendering pipelines. When Not to Use: Not necessary for simple models or when training is already stable. Adds complexity to the training loop configuration. The Delayed Cosine Schedule originates from the NeRFies project, which focuses on dynamic neural radiance fields. It was introduced to handle the optimization challenges associated with deformable scenes, where early large updates could destabilize the deformation field. The variant using log-linear interpolation is found in FastGS, a library for fast Gaussian Splatting, indicating its broader applicability to differentiable rendering techniques. google/nerfies, https://github.com/google/nerfies, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) fastgs/FastGS, https://github.com/fastgs/FastGS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Learning Rate Schedule with Delay
head: Learning Rate Scheduler with Delay, lr_delay_mult schedule, reverse cosine decay learning rate
body: A learning rate scheduler that applies a delay multiplier to the initial learning rate at the start of optimization, easing it back to the normal rate after a specified number of steps. It combines a 'reverse cosine decay' delay factor with a standard log-linear interpolation between initial and final learning rates. It sets itself apart from its parent Delayed Cosine Schedule by explicitly defining the delay mechanism as a multiplicative factor applied to a base log-linear schedule, rather than just delaying the start of a base schedule. Inputs: step: Current optimization step (integer). maxsteps: Total number of optimization steps (integer). lrinit: Initial learning rate (float). lrfinal: Final learning rate (float). lrdelaysteps: Number of steps over which the delay multiplier transitions (integer). lrdelaymult: The minimum multiplier value applied during the delay phase (float). Outputs: learningrate: The computed learning rate for the current step (float). Data Structures: None required. The method is stateless and computes the value directly from inputs. Parameters: lrdelaysteps: The number of steps during which the delay multiplier is applied. If 0, no delay is applied. lrdelaymult: The multiplier value applied to the learning rate during the delay phase. Default is 1.0. Steps: 1. If step < 0 or both lrinit and lrfinal are 0.0, return 0.0 to disable the parameter. 2. If lrdelaysteps <= 0, set delayrate = 1.0. 3. If lrdelaysteps > 0, calculate delayrate using reverse cosine decay: delay\rate = lr\delay\mult + (1 - lr\delay\mult) \times \sin\left(0.5 \times \pi \times \text{clip}\left(\frac{step}{lr\delay\steps}, 0, 1\right)\right) Otherwise, delayrate = 1.0. 4. Calculate normalized time t: t = \text{clip}\left(\frac{step}{max\steps}, 0, 1\right) 5. Calculate log-linear interpolation loglerp: log\lerp = \exp\left(\log(lr\init) \times (1 - t) + \log(lr\final) \times t\right) 6. Return delayrate loglerp. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def learningrateschedulewithdelay(step, maxsteps, lrinit, lrfinal, lrdelaysteps, lrdelaymult): # Step 1: Disable if invalid or zero rates if step < 0 or (lrinit == 0.0 and lrfinal == 0.0): return 0.0 # Step 2 & 3: Calculate delayrate if lrdelaysteps <= 0: delayrate = 1.0 else: # Clip step / lrdelaysteps to [0, 1] ratio = step / lrdelaysteps if ratio < 0: ratio = 0.0 elif ratio > 1: ratio = 1.0 # Reverse cosine decay formula # sin(0.5 pi ratio) goes from 0 to 1 as ratio goes from 0 to 1 # delayrate goes from lrdelaymult (at ratio=0) to 1.0 (at ratio=1) delayrate = lrdelaymult + (1.0 - lrdelaymult) math.sin(0.5 math.pi ratio) # Step 4: Calculate normalized time t t = step / maxsteps if t < 0: t = 0.0 elif t > 1: t = 1.0 # Step 5: Calculate log-linear interpolation # Handle edge case where lrinit or lrfinal is 0 to avoid log(0) if lrinit <= 0 or lrfinal <= 0: # If either is 0, the log-linear interpolation is problematic. # However, Step 1 checks if BOTH are 0. # If one is 0, we might need a fallback or assume positive rates for log. # Standard implementation assumes positive rates for loglerp. # If strict adherence to log is required, clamp to small epsilon or handle separately. # Based on source notes, we proceed with log assuming valid inputs for interpolation. # Guard against log(0) by using a small epsilon if necessary, # but sources imply standard log-linear usage. loglrinit = math.log(lrinit) if lrinit > 0 else -1e9 # Fallback for log(0) loglrfinal = math.log(lrfinal) if lrfinal > 0 else -1e9 # Fallback for log(0) else: loglrinit = math.log(lrinit) loglrfinal = math.log(lrfinal) loglerp = math.exp(loglrinit (1.0 - t) + loglrfinal t) # Step 6: Return product return delayrate loglerp Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Learning Rates: If both lrinit and lrfinal are 0.0, the function returns 0.0. If only one is 0.0, log(0) is undefined. The sources do not explicitly specify behavior for mixed zero/non-zero rates, but standard log-linear interpolation requires positive values. Implementers should ensure lrinit and lrfinal are positive for the log-linear step, or handle the zero case explicitly. Division by Zero: If maxsteps is 0, division by zero occurs in step 4. If lrdelaysteps is 0, the condition in step 3 handles it by setting delayrate = 1.0. Negative Steps: Handled in step 1. Not given in the sources. The method is used in the context of Gaussian Splatting optimization, specifically referenced in the MonoGS and FastGS repositories. It is part of the training configuration for NeRF-like radiance field optimization. muskie82/MonoGS, https://github.com/muskie82/MonoGS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) fastgs/FastGS, https://github.com/fastgs/FastGS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Cosine Decay Learning Rate Schedule
head: Cosine Annealing, Cosine Decay, Eikonal loss weighting, Training schedule and loss weighting
body: The Cosine Decay Learning Rate Schedule is a training configuration strategy that gradually reduces the learning rate from a peak value to a minimum value following a cosine curve, often preceded by a linear warmup phase. It is used in differentiable volume rendering and radiance field optimization to stabilize convergence and refine high-frequency details in the final stages of training. It sets itself apart from Exponential Decay Learning Rate Schedule by providing a smoother, symmetric decay profile that avoids the sharp initial drop of exponential schedules, and from Linear Learning Rate Schedule by offering a non-linear transition that better matches the loss landscape's curvature in neural implicit representations. The method combines a linear warmup phase with a cosine annealing phase to compute the learning rate for each optimization step. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: t: Current iteration number (integer, t \ge 0). t{warmup}: Number of warmup iterations (integer). t{total}: Total number of training iterations (integer). \eta{max}: Peak learning rate (float). \eta{min}: Minimum learning rate (float). Outputs: \etat: Learning rate for iteration t (float). Data Structures: No persistent data structures are required. The learning rate is computed statelessly from the iteration counter. Parameters: Typical values from: t{warmup} = 5,000, \eta{max} = 10^{-3}, \eta{min} = 5 \times 10^{-5}. Typical values from: \eta{max} = 2 \times 10^{-4} for non-backbone layers, \eta{max} = 2 \times 10^{-6} for pre-trained backbones. t{total} varies by dataset and model size (e.g., 150,000 iterations for RealEstate10K). Steps: 1. If t < t{warmup}, compute the learning rate using linear interpolation from 0 to \eta{max}. 2. If t \ge t{warmup}, compute the learning rate using the cosine decay formula relative to the remaining iterations. Formulas: For t < t{warmup}: \etat = \eta{max} \times \frac{t}{t{warmup}} For t \ge t{warmup}: \etat = \eta{min} + \frac{1}{2}(\eta{max} - \eta{min}) \left( 1 + \cos\left( \pi \frac{t - t{warmup}}{t{total} - t{warmup}} \right) \right) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If t{total} = t{warmup}, the denominator in the cosine phase is zero. This is a degenerate case where warmup consumes the entire training budget; the schedule should default to \eta{max} or handle the division explicitly. Precision: Ensure floating-point precision is maintained for small learning rates near \eta{min} to prevent gradient stagnation. Boundary Conditions: At t = t{warmup}, both formulas yield \eta{max}, ensuring continuity. At t = t{total}, the cosine term becomes \cos(\pi) = -1, yielding \eta{min}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecosinedecaylr(t, twarmup, ttotal, etamax, etamin): """ Compute learning rate using cosine decay with linear warmup. Args: t: Current iteration. twarmup: Warmup iterations. ttotal: Total iterations. etamax: Peak learning rate. etamin: Minimum learning rate. Returns: Learning rate for iteration t. """ if t < twarmup: # Linear warmup from 0 to etamax return etamax (t / twarmup) else: # Cosine decay from etamax to etamin # Ensure denominator is not zero if ttotal == twarmup: return etamax progress = (t - twarmup) / (ttotal - twarmup) # Clamp progress to [0, 1] to handle floating point errors progress = max(0.0, min(1.0, progress)) cosineterm = 1.0 + math.cos(math.pi progress) return etamin + 0.5 (etamax - etamin) cosineterm Applies different \eta{max} and \eta{min} values to different network components (e.g., lower rates for pre-trained backbones). uses 2 \times 10^{-6} for Depth Anything V2 backbone and 2 \times 10^{-4} for other layers. See Per-Parameter Learning Rate Scheduling. Combines cosine LR scheduling with resolution scaling. uses cosine decay while upscaling images from 100x100 to 800x800. See Training Loop with Adaptive Regularization & LR Decay. Time Complexity: O(1) per iteration for LR computation. Memory Complexity: O(1) as no history is stored. Performance: Provides stable convergence in neural implicit representations. reports successful reconstruction of thin structures with Eikonal loss weight 0.01, noting that lower weights lead to thinner structures, implying the LR schedule interacts with regularization strength. reports training times of 1 day (small model) and 2 days (large model) on 4x GH200 GPUs for 150K iterations at 256x256 resolution. Strengths: Smooth transition prevents oscillations in late training; warmup stabilizes early training. Limitations: Requires setting t{total} in advance; less flexible than adaptive schedulers like XYZ Learning Rate Scheduling if validation metrics are used to adjust. When to use: Standard choice for NeRF and radiance field optimization when a fixed training budget is known. When not to use: When training duration is uncertain or dynamic adjustment based on loss landscape is required. The cosine decay schedule is a widely used technique in deep learning, originating from general optimization practices. In the context of volume rendering and neural implicit representations, it has been adopted in methods like ShadowNeuS and DepthSplat to optimize neural networks for 3D reconstruction. The specific combination with linear warmup and coarse-to-fine rendering strategies has become a standard configuration for stabilizing training in differentiable rendering pipelines. name: Exponential Decay Learning Rate Schedule with Warm-up
head: Adam Optimization with Exponential LR Decay and Warm-up, Exponential Decay with Warm-up, Exponential LR Decay with Warm-up, Exposure Optimization, Warm-up and Exponential Decay LR Schedule
body: This method defines a learning rate schedule for optimizing neural radiance fields, specifically targeting per-camera exposure parameters or the main network weights, combining a linear warm-up phase with an exponential decay trajectory. It distinguishes itself from Cosine Decay Learning Rate Schedule by using a constant rate during warm-up followed by a geometric decay, and from Exponential Decay Learning Rate Schedule by explicitly incorporating a delayed warm-up period to stabilize initial training. It solves the problem of unstable convergence in sparse or complex captures by preventing large gradient updates before the model has established a coherent geometric prior. The method configures the Adam optimizer with specific hyperparameters for learning rate generation, gradient clipping, and optimization delays. Inputs: initiallr: Starting learning rate. finallr: Target learning rate at the end of training. totalsteps: Total number of optimization steps. warmupsteps: Number of steps for the warm-up phase. delaysteps: Number of steps to delay exposure optimization (if applicable). clipvalue: Maximum absolute value for gradient clipping. clipnorm: Maximum L2 norm for gradient normalization. Data Structures: No specific complex data structures; standard optimizer state (Adam moments) and scalar parameters. Parameters (Typical Values): Two distinct configurations are cited in the literature: 1. Exposure Optimization (Per-chunk): initiallr: 1 \times 10^{-3} finallr: 1 \times 10^{-4} delaysteps: 5000 delaymultiplier: 1 \times 10^{-3} (Used to scale LR during delay) 2. Network Optimization (FreeNeRF/SGCNeRF): initiallr: 2 \times 10^{-3} finallr: 2 \times 10^{-5} warmupsteps: 512 clipvalue: 0.1 clipnorm: 0.1 Steps: 1. Initialize Optimizer: Set up Adam with initiallr. 2. Compute Current Step: Determine the current training step t. 3. Calculate Learning Rate: If t < \text{delay\steps} (Exposure only): Apply delaymultiplier to the base schedule or set LR to a minimal value. Note: specifies a "delay multiplier" of 1e-3 for exposure, implying the LR is scaled down or zeroed during this phase to ensure model coherence before optimizing camera parameters. If t < \text{warmup\steps} (Warm-up): Linearly interpolate LR from 0 (or a small base) to initiallr. specifies a multiplier of 0.01 during the first 512 steps, which effectively scales the initial rate or acts as a warm-up factor. Specifically, states: "During the initial 512-step training, a warm-up strategy with a multiplier of 0.01 is implemented." This implies LR(t) = \text{initial\lr} \times \frac{t}{\text{warmup\steps}} \times 0.01 or similar scaling. However, standard warm-up usually ramps up. Let's look closer. "Multiplier of 0.01" might mean the LR is 1/100th of the target during warmup, then ramps? Or it is a multiplicative factor on the base LR? Given "warm-up strategy with a multiplier", it often implies LR = \text{base\lr} \times \text{warmup\factor}(t). If the factor is 0.01, it might be a constant low LR. But "warm-up" implies change. A common interpretation in this context (FreeNeRF) is that the LR ramps up to the initial LR, but scaled by 0.01? Or the initial LR is effectively 2e-3 \times 0.01? says "exponentially decays from 2 \cdot 10^{-3} to 2 \cdot 10^{-5}... During the initial 512-step training, a warm-up strategy with a multiplier of 0.01 is implemented." This likely means the LR is \text{initial\lr} \times 0.01 \times \frac{t}{512} during warmup. If t \ge \text{warmup\steps} (Decay): Apply exponential decay. The decay factor \alpha is derived from \text{initial\lr}, \text{final\lr}, and the remaining steps. Formula: LR(t) = \text{final\lr} + (\text{initial\lr} - \text{final\lr}) \cdot \gamma^{(t - \text{warmup\steps})}, where \gamma is the per-step decay rate. Alternatively, if the decay is defined over total steps T: LR(t) = \text{initial\lr} \cdot \left(\frac{\text{final\lr}}{\text{initial\lr}}\right)^{\frac{t - \text{warmup\steps}}{T - \text{warmup\steps}}}. 4. Gradient Clipping: Clip gradients by value: g{ij} = \text{clip}(g{ij}, -\text{clip\value}, \text{clip\value}). Normalize gradients: g = g / \max(1, \|g\|2 / \text{clip\norm}). 5. Update Parameters: Perform Adam update step. 6. Exposure Handling (Specific to): If t < 5000, do not optimize exposure (or use scaled LR). After 5000 steps, optimize per-camera exposures. For hierarchy post-optimization, reuse the trained exposure and fix them (do not optimize further). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computelr(step, totalsteps, initiallr, finallr, warmupsteps, delaysteps=None, delaymultiplier=1.0): """ Computes the learning rate for the current step. Supports both exposure-specific delay and standard warm-up. """ if delaysteps is not None and step < delaysteps: # Exposure optimization is delayed or scaled down # uses a delay multiplier of 1e-3 return initiallr delaymultiplier if step < warmupsteps: # Warm-up phase # applies a multiplier of 0.01 during warm-up # Linear ramp from 0 to initiallr 0.01? Or initiallr (step/warmup) 0.01? # Assuming linear warm-up to a scaled initial rate: currentlr = initiallr (step / warmupsteps) 0.01 return currentlr # Exponential decay phase # Calculate decay factor gamma such that LR reaches finallr at totalsteps # LR(t) = finallr + (initiallr - finallr) gamma^(step - warmupsteps) # At step = totalsteps: finallr = finallr + (initiallr - finallr) gamma^(totalsteps - warmupsteps) # 0 = (initiallr - finallr) gamma^(remainingsteps) -> This implies gamma < 1 # Actually, standard exponential decay: LR(t) = initiallr decayrate^step # But we have a target finallr. # Let's use the ratio: (finallr / initiallr) = decayrate^(totalsteps - warmupsteps) # decayrate = (finallr / initiallr) ^ (1 / (totalsteps - warmupsteps)) remainingsteps = totalsteps - warmupsteps if remainingsteps <= 0: return finallr decayrate = (finallr / initiallr) (1.0 / remainingsteps) # Current decay steps decaysteps = step - warmupsteps currentlr = initiallr (decayrate decaysteps) return currentlr def applygradients(grads, clipvalue=0.1, clipnorm=0.1): # Clip by value clippedgrads = [] for g in grads: clippedg = torch.clamp(g, -clipvalue, clipvalue) clippedgrads.append(clippedg) # Normalize by L2 norm totalnorm = torch.norm(torch.stack([torch.norm(g) for g in clippedgrads])) if totalnorm > clipnorm: clippedgrads = [g (clipnorm / totalnorm) for g in clippedgrads] return clippedgrads Time Complexity: O(1) per step for LR calculation. The warm-up and decay calculations are constant time. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for LR state. Performance: The delay steps (5000) prevent exposure optimization from destabilizing the initial geometric reconstruction, which is critical for sparse consumer-level captures. The warm-up prevents early divergence in sensitive parameters. Strengths: Stabilizes training for sparse views and exposure parameters. Prevents "mound" artifacts in underdetermined regions by ensuring geometric coherence first. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of delay steps relative to dataset size. The fixed warm-up multiplier (0.01) may be too aggressive for some scenes. When to use: Use for optimizing per-camera exposures in large, sparse datasets (e.g., vehicular captures), or for general NeRF training when stability is a concern (e.g., FreeNeRF settings). The method originates from two distinct lines of work in neural rendering optimization. The exposure-specific variant (with delay) was introduced for hierarchical 3D Gaussian representations to handle very large, sparse datasets like those from vehicle-based captures. The network optimization variant (with warm-up and gradient clipping) is adapted from FreeNeRF settings and used in SGCNeRF for few-shot neural rendering with sparse geometric consistency. Both aim to address the instability inherent in optimizing radiance fields with limited or sparse input data.
