name: Randomized Background Colors
head: Canvas with Uniform Noise, Uniform Noise Background Blending, random background
body: Randomized Background Colors is a training-time technique that replaces the fixed background color with a random sample from a uniform distribution during the compositing step. This method solves the problem of semi-transparent background artifacts and primitives that fail to cover regions matching the background color, thereby encouraging the model to reconstruct a fully opaque scene background. It is distinct from fixed-background approaches by forcing the neural field to explicitly model the background geometry rather than relying on a known constant. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The foreground color I{\text{FG}} and accumulated transmittance TN from the volume rendering equation, along with a random background color vector b. Output: The final composited pixel color I{\text{FG+BG}}. Data Structures: Background Color b: A 3-element vector representing RGB values. During training, each component is sampled independently from a uniform distribution. Steps: 1. Sampling: When compositing a pixel color during training, draw a random RGB background color b where each channel bc \sim U[0, 1] for c \in \{R, G, B\}. 2. Compositing: Compute the final pixel color by blending the foreground rendering with the random background using the accumulated transmittance TN: I{\text{FG+BG}} = I{\text{FG}} + TN \odot b where \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. 3. Test-Time Configuration: At inference time, replace the random sampling with a fixed gray background color b = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5). Parameters: Training Distribution: Uniform distribution over [0, 1]^3. Test Background: Fixed vector (0.5, 0.5, 0.5). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Solid Background Artifacts: Using a solid color (e.g., white) as the background allows primitives to ignore regions that match that color, leading to uncovered areas or semi-transparent backgrounds. Depth Accuracy: Semi-transparent backgrounds yield less meaningful ray termination distances, resulting in less accurate depth maps. Dataset Specificity: The method is applied selectively; the 360 and LLFF datasets use randomized backgrounds, while the Blender dataset uses a fixed white background. Modifications to the training setup for real-world scenes to prevent the network from cheating with a static white background and to improve depth estimates and occupancy grid sparsity. It uses a random background color during training instead of white, and marks grid cells located between each camera and its corresponding near plane as non-trainable. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Prevents primitives from ignoring background-matching regions; encourages fully opaque background reconstruction; improves depth map accuracy. Limitations: Requires switching to a fixed background at test time; not applied to datasets with known fixed backgrounds like Blender. When to Use: Use for unbounded or outdoor scenes (e.g., 360 and LLFF datasets) where the background is unknown and the model must learn to occlude it. For datasets with known fixed backgrounds like Blender, a fixed white background is used instead. The technique was introduced in Mip-NeRF 360 to address semi-transparent background artifacts that degrade depth estimation. It was later adapted in differentiable rendering frameworks like DiffBMP as Canvas with Uniform Noise to enforce primitive placement in regions matching the background color. It is also used in LAENeRF for real-world scene reconstruction to improve occupancy grid sparsity. name: Mixed Precision Training
head: AMP Training, FP16 Training, Mixed Precision Training with Fallback
body: Mixed Precision Training (MPT) accelerates the optimization of radiance fields by utilizing lower-precision data types (typically FP16) for forward and backward passes while maintaining a master copy of weights in higher precision (FP32) to preserve numerical stability. It addresses the computational bottleneck of differentiable volume rendering, which involves expensive Monte Carlo integration and large neural network forward passes, by leveraging Tensor Cores on modern GPUs. Unlike standard FP32 training, MPT reduces memory bandwidth requirements and increases throughput, though it requires careful handling of gradient scaling to prevent underflow in low-precision arithmetic. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A differentiable volume rendering model (e.g., NeRF, 3DGS), a dataset of target images and camera poses, an optimizer, and a loss function (typically MSE). Output: Optimized model parameters (stored in FP32) and training metrics. Data Structures: Master Weights: FP32 tensor storing the authoritative model parameters. Working Weights: FP16 tensor copy used for computation. Gradient Scaler: State object tracking the loss scale factor and overflow history. Optimizer State: FP32 buffers for momentum/variance (e.g., Adam). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Create the model and optimizer. Initialize a GradScaler instance. Set model to training mode. 2. Autocast Context: Wrap the forward pass in torch.amp.autocast('cuda') (or torch.cuda.amp.autocast() for older PyTorch versions) to automatically cast operations to FP16 where supported. 3. Data Loading: Randomly select a batch of target images and camera transforms. Move data to the GPU device. 4. Forward Pass: Render predicted RGB images using the model within the autocast context. The model internally uses FP16 for matrix multiplications and volume rendering integrals. 5. Loss Computation: Compute the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between predicted and target images. The loss is computed in FP32 or FP16 depending on the autocast policy, but is typically scaled. 6. Loss Scaling: Multiply the loss by a scale factor S maintained by the scaler. This prevents FP16 underflow during backpropagation. 7. Backward Pass: Call loss.backward() to compute gradients. Gradients are accumulated in FP16. 8. Gradient Unscaling: The scaler divides the gradients by S to restore their original magnitude. 9. Optimizer Step: The optimizer updates the Master Weights (FP32) using the unscaled gradients. If the optimizer uses adaptive moments (like Adam), these are maintained in FP32. 10. Scaler Update: The scaler updates its internal state. If an overflow (NaN/Inf) is detected, the scale factor S is decreased; otherwise, it may be increased. 11. Zero Gradients: Zero out gradients for the next iteration. 12. Checkpointing: Periodically save the master weights, optimizer state, scaler state, and iteration count. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import numpy as np def trainstep(model, optimizer, scaler, batchdata, device): """ Performs one training step using mixed precision. Args: model: Neural network model. optimizer: Optimizer instance. scaler: Gradient scaler instance. batchdata: Tuple of (images, cam2worldtransforms). device: CUDA device. """ # 1. Move data to device targetimg, targettformcam2world = batchdata targetimg = targetimg.to(device) targettformcam2world = targettformcam2world.to(device) # 2. Set model to train mode model.train() # 3. Zero gradients optimizer.zerograd(settonone=True) # 4. Forward pass with autocast with torch.amp.autocast('cuda'): # Render predicted RGB # runoneiteroftinynerf is a placeholder for the specific rendering function rgbpredicted = runoneiteroftinynerf( model, targettformcam2world, height=256, # Example height width=256, # Example width focallength=500.0, # Example focal length nearthresh=0.01, farthresh=100.0, depthsamplesperray=128) # Squeeze first dimension if necessary (depends on implementation) if rgbpredicted.dim() > 3: rgbpredicted = rgbpredicted.squeeze(0) # 5. Compute Loss loss = torch.mean((rgbpredicted - targetimg) 2) # 6. Scale Loss scaledloss = scaler.scale(loss) # 7. Backward Pass scaledloss.backward() # 8. Optimizer Step and Scaler Update # The scaler unscales gradients and checks for overflow optimizer.step() scaler.update() return loss.item() def trainloop(model, optimizer, scaler, dataset, numiters, saveevery, checkpointdir): """ Main training loop with mixed precision. """ losshistory = [] epochhistory = [] for i in range(numiters): # Randomly select 4 target images (as per source) indices = np.random.choice(dataset.images.shape[0], 4) batchimages = dataset.images[indices] batchcam2world = dataset.cam2world[indices] # Perform training step loss = trainstep(model, optimizer, scaler, (batchimages, batchcam2world), 'cuda') # Step learning rate scheduler (if used) # scheduler.step() # Checkpointing if i % saveevery == 0: losshistory.append(loss) epochhistory.append(i + 1) # Save checkpoint checkpoint = { 'modelstatedict': model.statedict(), 'optimizerstatedict': optimizer.statedict(), 'loss': loss, 'iteration': i, 'scalerstatedict': scaler.statedict(), # 'schedulerstatedict': scheduler.statedict() # If scheduler exists } torch.save(checkpoint, f"{checkpointdir}/checkpoint{i}.pt") # Plot figures (optional) # plotfigures(epochhistory, losshistory) Parameters: usemixedprecision: Boolean flag to enable/disable AMP. scaler: Gradient scaler instance. chunksize: Batch size for chunked forward passes to avoid OOM (e.g., 1024 rays). saveevery: Interval for checkpointing. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: NaN/Inf Gradients: FP16 has a smaller dynamic range than FP32. Gradients can underflow to zero or overflow to NaN. The scaler handles this by detecting NaNs and reducing the scale factor. Precision Loss in Accumulation: Some operations (like reduction in loss or Adam's moment estimates) may require FP32 accumulation. Autocast handles this automatically for standard PyTorch ops. Compatibility: Older PyTorch versions use torch.cuda.amp instead of torch.amp. Integrates Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) with gradient scaling and clipping to stabilize optimization in differentiable volume rendering. It addresses numerical instability from low-precision arithmetic and high-variance gradients from path-traced Monte Carlo estimates. By scaling the loss before backpropagation and clipping gradients based on their L2 norm, it prevents silent failures from NaN/Inf values and mitigates contamination of optimized textures by improbable light path outliers. Time Complexity: Training time is reduced by approximately 1.5x to 2x compared to FP32 on GPUs with Tensor Cores (e.g., NVIDIA Volta, Turing, Ampere). Memory Complexity: Memory usage is reduced by ~2x for activations and gradients, allowing for larger batch sizes or higher resolution scenes. Measured Performance: On standard NeRF datasets (Blender, LLFF), MPT achieves similar PSNR/SSIM to FP32 but with significantly faster convergence per epoch. Strengths: Faster training, lower memory footprint, compatibility with modern GPU hardware. Limitations: Potential for numerical instability if not properly scaled; requires careful handling of specific operations that do not support FP16 (e.g., certain normalization layers or loss functions). When to Use: Standard for training large NeRF models on modern GPUs. Not recommended for very small models where overhead outweighs benefits, or on hardware without Tensor Cores. Mixed Precision Training was popularized in deep learning by Micikevicius et al. (2017) for training large neural networks on GPUs. In the context of NeRF and volume rendering, it has become a standard optimization procedure due to the high computational cost of differentiable rendering. It is widely used in modern NeRF implementations (e.g., Instant-NGP, 3DGS) to accelerate training. A regularization technique used in texture-space differentiable rendering to prevent extremely high-valued outliers caused by improbable light paths in path-traced samples from contaminating optimized textures. It clamps gradients to the range [-10^{-8}, 10^{-8}] before Adam rescaling. This is distinct from L2 norm clipping as it applies a hard bound to individual gradient values rather than the global norm. Memory Complexity: No additional memory overhead beyond standard AMP buffers. Strengths: Stabilizes training in the presence of high-variance Monte Carlo estimates and mixed precision arithmetic. When to Use: Essential for differentiable volume rendering with path tracing and mixed precision. When Not to Use: Not necessary for deterministic, non-path-traced rendering with full precision. name: Adam Optimisation with Adaptive Scaling
head: Fused Adam with Adaptive Scaling, PyTorch Adam with Adaptive Scaling
body: Adam Optimisation with Adaptive Scaling is a training configuration for radiance-field optimization that applies component-specific learning rate multipliers to the standard Adam optimizer to address the disparate convergence speeds of geometric, shape, and amplitude parameters in Gaussian Splatting. It differs from standard Adam by scaling the base learning rate based on the dimensionality of the splat parameters and applying fixed multipliers to positions and amplitudes, while variants like Fused Adam eliminate memory overhead by integrating the update step into the rendering kernel. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Model parameters (positions, Cholesky factors for shape, amplitudes), Adam state tensors, current iteration count, learning rate schedule state. Outputs: Updated model parameters, updated Adam state tensors. Data Structures: Adam State: Maintains first and second moment estimates for parameters, with tensor shapes kept constant via fixed-pool relocation to preserve vectorised Adam benefits. Parameter Groups: Parameters are grouped by type to apply specific learning rate multipliers. Parameters: \beta1 = 0.9 \beta2 = 0.999 \epsilon = 10^{-8} Base Learning Rate (\eta{base}): 0.01. Amplitude Multiplier: 3\times the dilution-compensated rate. Position Multiplier: 1.5\times the dilution-compensated rate. Method Steps: 1. Compute Base Effective Rate: Calculate the dilution-compensated base learning rate \eta{eff}. For standard passes, \eta{eff} = \eta{base}. For residual passes of the progressive fitter, \eta{eff} = 0.03. 2. Apply Dimensionality Scaling: For shape and position parameters, scale the effective rate by PD / P^2, where PD = D + D(D+1)/2 is the number of position and Cholesky parameters per splat (PD=5 for 2D, PD=9 for 3D). For D \ge 4, multiply by an additional factor D^{0.8} to account for larger spatial search. 3. Assign Learning Rates per Parameter Group: Amplitudes receive 3\times \eta{eff}, positions receive 1.5\times \eta{eff}, and shape parameters receive the dimensionality-scaled \eta{eff}. 4. Apply Learning Rate Schedule: Use a ReduceLROnPlateau scheduler on the regularized training loss with patience 15 iterations, factor 0.9, threshold 10^{-3}, and floor 10^{-8}. 5. Update Parameters: Perform the standard Adam update step using the assigned \eta and current gradients gt, moments mt, vt: mt = \beta1 m{t-1} + (1 - \beta1) gt vt = \beta2 v{t-1} + (1 - \beta2) gt^2 \hat{m}t = \frac{mt}{1 - \beta1^t} \hat{v}t = \frac{vt}{1 - \beta2^t} \theta{t} = \theta{t-1} - \eta \frac{\hat{m}t}{\sqrt{\hat{v}t} + \epsilon} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def computeadaptivelr(baselr, dimension, isresidualpass=False): """Computes the effective learning rate scaling factors based on dimensionality.""" currentlr = 0.03 if isresidualpass else baselr PD = dimension + (dimension (dimension + 1)) / 2 # Source formula is PD / P^2; P is undefined in the sources if dimension <= 3: scalefactor = PD else: scalefactor = PD (dimension 0.8) return currentlr, scalefactor def adamupdatewithadaptivescaling(paramgroups, lrbase=0.01, isresidual=False): """ Performs Adam update with adaptive scaling for Gaussian Splatting parameters. paramgroups: list of dicts, each containing 'params', 'type' ('amplitude', 'position', 'shape'), and 'state'. """ currentlr, shapescale = computeadaptivelr(lrbase, 3, isresidual) ampmult = 3.0 posmult = 1.5 beta1 = 0.9 beta2 = 0.999 eps = 1e-8 for group in paramgroups: for param in group['params']: grad = param.grad if grad is None: continue if param not in group['state']: group['state'][param] = {'m': torch.zeroslike(param), 'v': torch.zeroslike(param), 'step': 1} state = group['state'][param] m = state['m'] v = state['v'] step = state['step'] m.mul(beta1).add(grad, alpha=1 - beta1) v.mul(beta2).addcmul(grad, grad, value=1 - beta2) mhat = m / (1 - beta1 step) vhat = v / (1 - beta2 step) if group['type'] == 'amplitude': eta = currentlr ampmult elif group['type'] == 'position': eta = currentlr posmult elif group['type'] == 'shape': eta = currentlr shapescale else: eta = currentlr stepsize = eta (mhat / (torch.sqrt(vhat) + eps)) param.add(stepsize, alpha=-1) state['step'] = step + 1 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Undefined P: The scaling formula PD / P^2 references P, which is not defined in the source text. Dimensionality: The scaling factor changes behavior for D \ge 4, introducing an empirical D^{0.8} term to stabilize convergence. Gradient Dilution: The base learning rate must be adjusted for gradient dilution in progressive fitting (residual passes use 0.03). Early Stopping: Fits run to an iteration cap of 20,000 with early stopping patience of 500 iterations on the regularised training loss. Weighted Adam is an optimization variant for radiance-field parameters that modulates gradient updates based on the visibility of primitives, preventing divergence caused by obscured or irrelevant parameters in short segments. It differs from standard Adam by replacing the fixed bias-correction terms with accumulated visibility-weighted counters, ensuring that parameters with low average transmittance do not accumulate momentum from uninformative gradients. A custom CUDA implementation of the Adam optimizer that precisely matches PyTorch's numerical behavior while eliminating CPU-GPU synchronization overhead and kernel launch latency by fusing the update step into the training kernel. It differs from standard PyTorch Adam by exploiting fast math operations and fused-multiply-adds (FMA) to reduce instruction count, and from NVIDIA Apex Fused Adam by offering a drop-in replacement with potentially lower memory footprint and tighter integration with specific rendering pipelines. A mechanism to propagate Adam optimizer gradient states to child Gaussians during splitting operations, instead of resetting them to 0. The inheritance rules are: t{child} = \alphat \times t{mother} (g{child})t = \alphag \times (g{mother})t (g{child}^2)t = (\alphag)^2 \times (g{mother}^2)t where \alphat is the lifespan fading factor and \alphag is the gradient fading factor. A single kernel that fuses the projection backward pass and the Adam optimizer to eliminate memory footprint from storing intermediate gradients and transformed values. It avoids concatenating large tensors for SH coefficients to reduce memory footprint. A memory optimization that discards Adam optimizer moments for blocks evicted from VRAM to trade optimizer-state persistence for larger model capacity. Optimizer states are instantiated only for resident blocks and discarded upon eviction (cold restart on re-admission). High block churn increases optimizer-state cold starts, potentially degrading convergence; this is mitigated by using a larger CPU cache or selectively persisting optimizer states. Time Complexity: O(N) per iteration for N parameters. Fused implementations reduce overhead by integrating the update step into the rendering kernel. Memory Complexity: Fused implementations and state discarding (TideGS) reduce memory footprint by avoiding intermediate gradient storage and discarding states for evicted blocks. Performance: The adaptive scaling stabilizes convergence in higher dimensions (D \ge 4) and accelerates amplitude convergence. Strengths: Handles disparate parameter convergence speeds; scalable to large models via out-of-core state management. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of multipliers; cold starts from state discarding can degrade convergence if block churn is high. Originated in the context of Gaussian Splatting for microscopy and scalable web visualization (Luxar). The method uses standard PyTorch Adam with fused CUDA kernels. Adaptive model capacity is handled via fixed-pool relocation, keeping optimizer tensor shapes constant. The technique has been extended to include gradient state inheritance for splitting (BOGausS), fused kernels for Vulkan (VkSplat), and out-of-core optimization for billion-scale primitives (TideGS). name: Weighted Adam Optimizer
head: Visibility-aware Adam, Weighted Adam, Weighted Adam Optimization, Weighted Adam Updates
body: Weighted Adam is an optimization variant for radiance-field parameters that modulates gradient updates based on the visibility of primitives, preventing divergence caused by obscured or irrelevant parameters in short segments. It differs from standard Adam by replacing the fixed bias-correction terms with accumulated visibility-weighted counters, ensuring that parameters with low average transmittance do not accumulate momentum from uninformative gradients. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes current parameters \theta{i-1}, raw gradients \nabla fi(\theta{i-1}), previous first and second moments m{i-1}, v{i-1}, previous bias-correction accumulators b{i-1}^m, b{i-1}^v, base learning rate \gamma, Gaussian covariance properties, and a keyframe usage flag as inputs. It outputs the updated parameters \thetai and the updated state tensors. Data Structures: The first and second moments mi, vi maintain the exact shape of \theta. The bias accumulators bi^m, bi^v also match the shape of \theta, storing a scalar value per parameter. The visibility weight \bar{u}i is a scalar per Gaussian primitive derived from image-space transmittance. Step 1: Compute Visibility Weight For each Gaussian primitive g in image l, compute the weight \eta (denoted \bar{u}i in the update formulas) as the average transmittance over the projected pixels p: \eta = \overline{T}{g,l} = \frac{\sum{p \in l} T{g,p}}{N{g,l}^p} where N{g,l}^p is the number of pixels covered by the Gaussian in image l. The weight \eta \in [0,1] represents the average visibility or informativeness of the gradient for iteration i. Step 2: Modulate Learning Rate Compute the scale-based learning rate modulation factor \gammag using the largest singular value of the covariance (largest scale s{g,i}) and a multiplier \alpha = 0.01: \gammag = \min \left\{ 1, \alpha \maxi \{ s{g,i} \} \right\} \gamma where \gamma is the base learning rate. Step 3: Handle Keyframed Attributes If the parameter belongs to a keyframed attribute, only update it if the Gaussian was used in the current training iteration. If the Gaussian was not used, skip the update for this parameter. Step 4: Compute Weighted Gradients The source defines an intermediate gradient gi = \nabla fi(\theta{i-1}) / \etai in Equation (44). However, the momentum update equations (45–48) explicitly multiply the gradient terms by \etai, which would cancel the division. Following the explicit update equations and the method's name, the gradient contribution is treated as the raw gradient scaled by \etai in the momentum terms. Step 5: Update First and Second Moments Update the first moment estimate mi and second moment estimate vi using the visibility-weighted gradients and decay rates \beta1, \beta2: mi = (1 - (1 - \beta1)\bar{u}i)m{i-1} + (1 - \beta1)\bar{u}i gi vi = (1 - (1 - \beta2)\bar{u}i)v{i-1} + (1 - \beta2)\bar{u}i gi^2 where \beta1 is the momentum decay rate for the first moment and \beta2 is the momentum decay rate for the second moment. Step 6: Update Bias Correction Accumulators Unlike standard Adam, bias correction is not a closed-form function of step count because \bar{u}i varies per iteration. Accumulate the correction terms: bi^m = (1 - (1 - \beta1)\bar{u}i) b{i-1}^m + (1 - \beta1)\bar{u}i bi^v = (1 - (1 - \beta2)\bar{u}i)b{i-1}^v + (1 - \beta2)\bar{u}i Initialize b0^m = 0, b0^v = 0. Step 7: Compute Bias-Corrected Moments \hat{m}i = \frac{mi}{bi^m} \hat{v}i = \frac{vi}{bi^v} Guard against division by zero by adding a small constant \epsilon to the denominators if bi^m or bi^v is zero. Step 8: Update Parameters \thetai = \theta{i-1} - \bar{u}i \frac{\beta1 \hat{m}i}{\beta2 \hat{v}i + \bar{u}i} This update rule is explicitly listed in the source notes. It deviates from the standard Adam update \theta{i-1} - \gamma \frac{\hat{m}i}{\sqrt{\hat{v}i} + \epsilon} by replacing the square-root variance denominator with a linear combination and scaling the entire step by \bar{u}i. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def weightedadamupdate(theta, grad, m, v, bm, bv, visibilityweight, baselr, maxscale, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, alpha=0.01, epsilon=1e-8): """ theta: current parameters grad: raw gradient m: first moment v: second moment bm: bias correction accumulator for first moment bv: bias correction accumulator for second moment visibilityweight: scalar eta in [0,1] baselr: base learning rate gamma maxscale: largest singular value of the covariance beta1: momentum decay rate for first moment beta2: momentum decay rate for second moment alpha: multiplier for scale-based learning rate modulation epsilon: small constant for numerical stability """ # Step 2: Modulate learning rate gammag = min(1.0, alpha maxscale) baselr # Step 3: Keyframe check is handled by the caller skipping this function if not used # Step 4: Gradient contribution (raw gradient, weight applied in momentum steps) gi = grad # Step 5: Update moments m = (1.0 - (1.0 - beta1) visibilityweight) m + (1.0 - beta1) visibilityweight gi v = (1.0 - (1.0 - beta2) visibilityweight) v + (1.0 - beta2) visibilityweight (gi 2) # Step 6: Update bias correction accumulators bm = (1.0 - (1.0 - beta1) visibilityweight) bm + (1.0 - beta1) visibilityweight bv = (1.0 - (1.0 - beta2) visibilityweight) bv + (1.0 - beta2) visibilityweight # Step 7: Bias correction with zero-guard denomm = bm if bm > 0 else epsilon denomv = bv if bv > 0 else epsilon mhat = m / denomm vhat = v / denomv # Step 8: Update parameters update = visibilityweight (beta1 mhat) / (beta2 vhat + visibilityweight) theta = theta - update return theta, m, v, bm, bv Parameters: \alpha = 0.01: Multiplier for the scale-based learning rate modulation. \beta1 = 0.9: Momentum decay rate for first moment (implied by standard Adam structure). \beta2 = 0.999: Momentum decay rate for second moment (implied by standard Adam structure). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Divergence: Standard Adam updates all parameters regardless of visibility, leading to divergence when primitives are obscured or have many keyframes. Weighted Adam prevents this by weighting updates with \bar{u}i \in [0,1]. Keyframed Attributes: Must only be updated if used in the current iteration. Bias Correction: Cannot use closed-form step-count correction; must accumulate bi^m, bi^v. Time Complexity: Same as Adam per iteration, plus the cost of computing average transmittance \overline{T}{g,l} for each Gaussian. Memory Complexity: Requires storing additional accumulators bi^m, bi^v for each parameter, doubling the memory overhead for bias correction compared to standard Adam which uses scalar step counters. Performance: Removing Weighted Adam drops PSNR from 25.95 to 20.42, SSIM from 0.848 to 0.551, and VMAF from 71.96 to 28.34. Strengths: Prevents divergence from obscured primitives; allows for increased learning rates due to sparser but more consistent updates. Limitations: Requires visibility computation; more complex bias correction. Weighted Adam was introduced in the context of Adaptive Spatio-Temporal 3D Gaussian Splatting for Scenes with Oscillatory Motion. It addresses the issue that adaptive spatio-temporal subdivision makes Gaussians smaller more quickly than original densification, requiring a modified learning rate strategy and visibility-aware updates to prevent divergence. body: A custom CUDA implementation of the Adam optimizer that precisely matches PyTorch's behavior while optimizing away unnecessary overhead. It fuses the Adam update step into the training kernel to reduce kernel launch overhead and improve performance. It sets itself apart from standard PyTorch Adam and NVIDIA Apex Fused Adam by further reducing instruction count through fused-multiply-adds and fast math operations, achieving the highest speedup among fused variants. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Parameter tensors, gradient tensors, state tensors (expavg, expavgsq), hyperparameters (\beta1, \beta2, \epsilon, \text{lr}), and step count. Outputs: Updated parameter tensors. Data Structures: State tensors are stored in device memory. Locality-preserving densification applies z-ordering to Gaussian parameters to ensure spatially close Gaussians are stored contiguously, preventing uncoalesced memory accesses during densification. Steps: 1. Kernel Fusion: The Adam update logic is fused directly into the CUDA kernel of the training pass, eliminating separate kernel launches for the optimizer step. 2. Fast Math: CUDA fast math operations are used to accelerate division and square root calculations. 3. Fused-Multiply-Add (FMA): Multiplication and addition operations are combined into single instructions to reduce overall instruction count and improve throughput. 4. State Update: Exponential moving averages and bias-corrected estimates are computed using the fused logic, precisely matching PyTorch's Adam behavior. 5. Parameter Update: The standard Adam parameter update step is applied. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def fusedadamstep(params, grads, expavg, expavgsq, beta1, beta2, lr, eps, step, numelements): # Conceptual representation of the fused CUDA kernel logic # Each thread handles one or more elements # State tensors must be initialized to zero before training begins. for i in range(numelements): g = grads[i] # Update biased first moment estimate expavg[i] = beta1 expavg[i] + (1.0 - beta1) g # Update biased second raw moment estimate expavgsq[i] = beta2 expavgsq[i] + (1.0 - beta2) (g g) # Compute bias-corrected first moment estimate biascorrection1 = 1.0 - beta1 step mhat = expavg[i] / biascorrection1 # Compute bias-corrected second raw moment estimate biascorrection2 = 1.0 - beta2 step vhat = expavgsq[i] / biascorrection2 # Update parameters using standard Adam formula params[i] = params[i] - lr mhat / (math.sqrt(vhat) + eps) Parameters: \beta1: Typically 0.9. \beta2: Typically 0.999. \epsilon: Typically 10^{-8}. \text{lr}: Learning rate, varies by scene and configuration. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Fast math operations are used, but the implementation is designed to precisely match PyTorch's Adam behavior. Memory Locality: Without z-ordering during densification, memory accesses become uncoalesced, throttling performance. State Consistency: Each thread handles distinct elements, so atomic operations are not required. A CUDA implementation of the Adam optimizer designed for differentiable volume rendering that maintains strict behavioral compatibility with PyTorch's Adam while optimizing for tile-level sparsity. It solves the problem of inconsistent state updates in sparse rendering pipelines where some tiles receive zero gradients, by replaying optimization steps for skipped tiles to ensure exponential moving averages decay correctly. It sets itself apart from standard Adam implementations by explicitly handling the temporal gap between optimization steps for untiled regions, ensuring that the state evolution matches what would occur if every parameter were updated at every step, even with zero gradients. A CUDA implementation of the Adam optimizer that launches a separate thread for every spherical harmonic coefficient, rather than one thread per Gaussian. It differs from EPBRR by not fusing the forward and backward pass, allowing for SSIM loss and custom losses, and by using per-coefficient threads instead of per-Gaussian threads. Time and Memory Complexity: Time complexity is reduced compared to standard PyTorch Adam due to kernel fusion and reduced overhead. Memory complexity is similar to standard Adam, with VRAM usage remaining at 6.40GiB, comparable to PyTorch (6.42GiB) and Apex (6.23GiB). VRAM usage remains at 6.40GiB for the custom fused Adam, comparable to PyTorch (6.42GiB) and Apex (6.23GiB). Limitations: Requires custom CUDA implementation. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. It solves the problem of inconsistent state updates in sparse rendering pipelines where some tiles receive zero gradients, by replaying optimization steps for skipped tiles to ensure exponential moving averages decay correctly. It sets itself apart from standard Adam implementations by explicitly handling the temporal gap between optimization steps for untiled regions, ensuring that the state evolution matches what would occur if every parameter were updated at every step, even with zero gradients. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: param: Current parameter value (float/tensor). grad: Current gradient for the parameter (float/tensor). expavg: First moment estimate (float/tensor). expavgsq: Second moment estimate (float/tensor). globalstep: Current global optimization step index (integer). lrhistory: Array of learning rates indexed by step (array/tensor). b1: First moment decay rate (float). b2: Second moment decay rate (float). eps: Epsilon for numerical stability (float). tilestouched: Boolean array indicating which tiles were rendered in the current step (array). lastseenstep: Integer array tracking the last optimization step performed for each tile (array). N: Total number of tiles (integer). M: Number of parameters per tile (integer). Outputs: Updated param, expavg, expavgsq in global memory. Updated lastseenstep for the tile if this thread is the leader. Data Structures: tilestouched: A boolean array of size N, where N is the number of tiles. tilestouched[i] is true if tile i contributed to the loss in the current step. lastseenstep: An integer array of size N. lastseenstep[i] stores the global step index of the last time tile i was updated. lrhistory: An array of learning rates indexed by step, used to support dynamic learning rate schedules while maintaining Torch compatibility. Algorithm Steps: 1. Thread Indexing: Initialize thread index p\idx and global parameter index g\idx = p\idx / M. 2. Sparsity Check: If g\idx \ge N or tilestouched[gidx] is false, return immediately. 3. State Loading: Load parameter state into registers: param, expavg, expavgsq, and paramgrad. Retrieve the lastseenstep for the tile g\idx. 4. Zero-Gradient Replay: If there is a gap between the previous update and the current step (i.e., prev\seen\step + 1 \le global\step - 1), replay the Adam updates for all intermediate steps using zero gradients. This involves decaying the exponential moving averages and applying the Adam update with the learning rate history. For each step s from prev\seen\step + 1 to global\step - 1: Compute bias correction factors: bias\correction1 = 1 - b1^s, bias\correction2 = 1 - b2^s. Compute step size: step\size = lr\history[s - 1] / bias\correction1. Compute denominator: denom = \sqrt{exp\avg\sq} / \sqrt{bias\correction2} + \epsilon. Compute update delta: delta = -step\size \cdot exp\avg / denom. Update parameter and moving averages: param = param + delta, exp\avg = b1 \cdot exp\avg, exp\avg\sq = b2 \cdot exp\avg\sq. 5. Current Step Update: Update the exponential moving averages with the current gradient: exp\avg = b1 \cdot exp\avg + (1 - b1) \cdot grad, exp\avg\sq = b2 \cdot exp\avg\sq + (1 - b2) \cdot grad^2. 6. Delta Computation: Compute the Adam update delta for the current global step using the updated moving averages and the learning rate from lr\history[global\step - 1], then add it to the parameter value. 7. State Writeback: Write the updated parameter and moving averages back to global memory. If the thread index is a multiple of M (indicating the first thread of a tile group), update last\seen\step[g\idx] = global\step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: param: Current parameter value. grad: Current gradient. expavg: First moment estimate. expavgsq: Second moment estimate. globalstep: Current global step index (1-based). lrhistory: List of learning rates, indexed by step-1. b1: First moment decay rate. b2: Second moment decay rate. eps: Epsilon for numerical stability. tilestouched: Boolean array of touched tiles. lastseenstep: Array of last seen steps per tile. gidx: Global tile index. pidx: Global parameter index. M: Parameters per tile. N: Total number of tiles. Returns: Updated (param, expavg, expavgsq, lastseenstep). """ # Step 1 & 2: Sparsity Check if gidx >= N or not tilestouched[gidx]: return param, expavg, expavgsq, lastseenstep # Step 3: Load State prevseenstep = lastseenstep[gidx] # Step 4: Zero-Gradient Replay for s in range(prevseenstep + 1, globalstep): biascorrection1 = 1.0 - b1 s biascorrection2 = 1.0 - b2 s stepsize = lrhistory[s - 1] / biascorrection1 denom = (expavgsq 0.5) / (biascorrection2 0.5) + eps delta = -stepsize expavg / denom param = param + delta expavg = b1 expavg expavgsq = b2 expavgsq # Step 5: Current Step Update expavg = b1 expavg + (1.0 - b1) grad expavgsq = b2 expavgsq + (1.0 - b2) grad 2 # Step 6: Delta Computation biascorrection1 = 1.0 - b1 globalstep biascorrection2 = 1.0 - b2 globalstep stepsize = lrhistory[globalstep - 1] / biascorrection1 denom = (expavgsq 0.5) / (biascorrection2 0.5) + eps delta = -stepsize expavg / denom param = param + delta # Step 7: Leader Update if pidx % M == 0: lastseenstep[gidx] = globalstep return param, expavg, expavgsq, lastseenstep Parameters: b1: First moment decay rate, typically 0.9. b2: Second moment decay rate, typically 0.999. eps: Epsilon for numerical stability, typically 1e-8. lrhistory: Array of learning rates indexed by step, used to support dynamic learning rate schedules while maintaining Torch compatibility. tilestouched: Boolean array indicating which tiles were rendered in the current step, used to skip updates for untouched tiles. lastseenstep: Integer array tracking the last optimization step performed for each tile, used to determine if zero-gradient replay is needed. Pitfalls: If a tile was not touched in previous steps, the moving averages must be decayed for each skipped step to maintain consistency with PyTorch's Adam behavior, which assumes updates occur at every step even if gradients are zero. The kernel launches with grid size (N \cdot M + 255) / 256 blocks and 256 threads per block, requiring careful indexing to avoid out-of-bounds memory access. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the number of tiles and parameters due to the tile-level sparsity optimization, as untouched tiles are skipped entirely. Strengths: Maintains strict compatibility with PyTorch's Adam, ensuring consistent behavior across different frameworks. Efficiently handles sparse gradients by skipping updates for untouched tiles while correctly maintaining state for those tiles. Limitations: The replay loop can be computationally expensive if large gaps occur between updates for a tile. When to use: Use when training differentiable volume rendering pipelines with tile-based rasterization where sparsity is high, and strict compatibility with PyTorch's Adam is required. When not to use: Avoid if the overhead of zero-gradient replay becomes significant due to extreme sparsity or if framework compatibility is not a concern. It was introduced to address state consistency issues in sparse rendering by replaying optimization steps for parameters that received zero gradients. body: Checkpoint Loading and Resume Training enables the restoration of a neural radiance field's optimization state from disk to continue training or perform evaluation without restarting from scratch. Load the modelstatedict into the model. 2. Load the optimizerstatedict into the optimizer. 3. Load the gradient scaler state if it was used during training. 4. name: View Sampler
head: ViewSampler Abstract Base Class, ViewSampler Abstract Interface
body: The View Sampler is an abstract base class that defines the interface for selecting context and target camera views during the training or inference of radiance field models. It solves the problem of determining which input images (context) and which novel views (target) are used in each optimization step, enabling strategies that range from random sampling to geometry-aware selection. It is distinguished from sibling components like Learning Rate Scheduling or Mixed Precision Training by focusing exclusively on the spatial and temporal selection of input data rather than numerical optimization parameters. The View Sampler operates as a factory or interface for view selection strategies. Implementations must adhere to a specific constructor signature and provide a sample method that returns indices and metadata for the current training batch. Inputs to init: cfg: Configuration object. stage: Current training stage (e.g., training, validation). isoverfitting: Boolean flag indicating if the model is overfitting to a single scene. camerasarecircular: Boolean flag indicating if the camera setup is circular. steptracker: Optional tracker for the global training step. Inputs to sample: scene: The scene object containing camera data. extrinsics: Float tensor of shape [view, 4, 4] containing camera extrinsic matrices. intrinsics: Float tensor of shape [view, 3, 3] containing camera intrinsic matrices. device: The device (CPU/GPU) for the output tensors. Outputs of sample: A tuple containing: 1. contextview: Int64 tensor of shape [contextview] containing indices of context camera views. 2. targetview: Int64 tensor of shape [targetview] containing indices of target camera views. 3. overlap: Float tensor of shape [overlap] representing the overlap metric between context and target views. The abstract class maintains the following instance variables: cfg: The configuration. stage: The current stage. isoverfitting: The overfitting flag. camerasarecircular: The circular camera flag. steptracker: The step tracker. It exposes the following abstract properties and methods: numtargetviews: Returns the integer count of target views. numcontextviews: Returns the integer count of context views. globalstep: Returns the current global step. If steptracker is None, it returns 0; otherwise, it returns steptracker.getstep(). The core logic is encapsulated in the abstract sample method. While the base class defines the interface, specific implementations (see Subtopics) define the selection logic. The general contract is: 1. Receive scene geometry and camera parameters (extrinsics, intrinsics). 2. Select a subset of indices for contextview and targetview based on the specific strategy (e.g., random, geometry-aware, blend iteration). 3. Compute or retrieve the overlap metric between the selected context and target views. 4. Return the tuple (contextview, targetview, overlap) on the specified device. The following pseudocode represents the abstract base class structure and typical usage pattern found in the sources. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from abc import ABC, abstractmethod from typing import Tuple, Optional import torch from torch import Tensor class ViewSampler(ABC): def init( self, cfg, stage, isoverfitting: bool, camerasarecircular: bool, steptracker: Optional['StepTracker'] = None): self.cfg = cfg self.stage = stage self.isoverfitting = isoverfitting self.camerasarecircular = camerasarecircular self.steptracker = steptracker @property def globalstep(self) -> int: if self.steptracker is None: return 0 return self.steptracker.getstep() @property @abstractmethod def numtargetviews(self) -> int: """Returns the number of target views.""" pass @property @abstractmethod def numcontextviews(self) -> int: """Returns the number of context views.""" pass @abstractmethod def sample( self, scene, extrinsics: Tensor, # Shape: [view, 4, 4] intrinsics: Tensor, # Shape: [view, 3, 3] device: torch.device) -> Tuple[Tensor, Tensor, Tensor]: """ Samples context and target views. Args: scene: The scene object. extrinsics: Camera extrinsics. intrinsics: Camera intrinsics. device: Target device for tensors. Returns: contextview: Int64 tensor [contextview] targetview: Int64 tensor [targetview] overlap: Float tensor [overlap] """ pass Empty View Stacks: In variants like Viewpoint Sampling with Blend Iteration, if the viewpoint stack is empty, it must be initialized with a copy of scene.getTrainCameras() or scene.getOriginCameras() before sampling. Step Tracker Null: If steptracker is not provided, globalstep defaults to 0 to prevent null pointer exceptions. Overlap Thresholds: Some implementations (e.g., Diverse View Selection) ignore batches where the overlap tag is "ignore". This method selects a diverse subset of Nv camera views from a 3D scene. It iteratively samples candidate views and accepts them only if they satisfy thresholds for spatial overlap and geometric distance relative to already selected views. It is chosen when view diversity is critical to prevent the model from overfitting to similar viewpoints. This variant selects training cameras from a standard viewpoint stack or an origin viewpoint stack based on the current training iteration. It enables a transition from standard to origin viewpoints after a specified blend threshold (opt.blenduntiliter). It is chosen when a curriculum learning approach is desired, starting with standard training views and gradually shifting to origin views. This strategy constructs a training pair by randomly selecting a target view and sampling 8 nearby but sparse views as source views. It follows reference [28] for the specific sampling logic. It is chosen for scenarios requiring efficient training with limited source views, such as in generalizable semantic fields (e.g., S-Ray). GVS selects views based on error and pose/direction distance. It is part of a pipeline that includes error-guided sparse pixel sampling. Replacing GVS with random view sampling (RVS) leads to consistent drops in PSNR and perceptual metrics. It is chosen when high-fidelity reconstruction is prioritized over training speed, as it focuses sampling on geometrically complex or high-error regions. Time Complexity: Depends on the specific implementation. Random sampling is O(1) relative to the number of views. Geometry-aware sampling involves computing error and distance metrics, which is more expensive. Memory Complexity: Low, as it primarily stores indices and small metadata tensors. Performance: Geometry-Aware View Sampling improves PSNR and perceptual metrics compared to random sampling. Sparse View Sampling allows for fast generalization, requiring only 2k iterations (10 minutes) for fine-tuning on a new scene compared to 100k iterations for per-scene optimization methods like Semantic-NeRF. Strengths: Flexible interface allows for various sampling strategies; supports curriculum learning (blend iteration); improves reconstruction quality via geometry-aware selection. Limitations: Geometry-aware sampling is computationally more intensive; requires careful tuning of blend thresholds and overlap metrics. The View Sampler is a component of modern differentiable volume rendering and radiance field optimization frameworks, specifically those based on NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) and its variants. It abstracts the data loading process to allow for dynamic view selection during training. name: Diverse View Selection via Overlap and Distance
head: Alg.1, Camera View Selection Algorithm, Iterative Diverse View Sampling
body: This method selects a diverse subset of Nv camera views from a 3D scene by iteratively sampling candidates and accepting them only if they satisfy thresholds for spatial overlap and geometric distance relative to already selected views. Inputs: A pool of candidate camera poses (extrinsics [R, t]); target number of views Nv; overlap threshold To; distance threshold Td. Outputs: A list E of Nv selected camera views. Data Structures: E: A list of selected camera extrinsics Ei = [Ri, ti], where Ri \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} is the rotation matrix and ti \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the translation vector. n: Integer counter of selected views, initialized to 0. Formulas: 1. Frustum Overlap (O): The Intersection over Union (IoU) of the viewing frustums A and B of two cameras E1 and E2: O(E1, E2) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|} 2. Geometric Distance (D): The sum of Euclidean distance between camera centers and the angular difference between orientations: D(E1, E2) = \|t1 - t2\|2 + \arccos\left(\frac{\text{Tr}(R2^\top R1) - 1}{2}\right) 3. Aggregate Metrics: For a new candidate view E{\text{cand}} against the set of existing views E = \{E1, \dots, En\}: \text{Overlap}(E{\text{cand}}, E) = \max{i=1 \dots n} O(E{\text{cand}}, Ei) \text{Distance}(E{\text{cand}}, E) = \min{i=1 \dots n} D(E{\text{cand}}, Ei) Parameters: Nv = 200: Target number of views. To = 0.3: Overlap threshold. Td = 0.2: Distance threshold. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize E \leftarrow \emptyset, n \leftarrow 0. 2. Set Nv = 200, To = 0.3, Td = 0.2. 3. Repeat the following loop: a. Sample a candidate camera view E{\text{cand}} from the available pool. b. If n = 0: Append E{\text{cand}} to E, increment n \leftarrow n + 1. c. Else (n > 0): Calculate O{\max} = \text{Overlap}(E{\text{cand}}, E) and D{\min} = \text{Distance}(E{\text{cand}}, E). If O{\max} \ge To and D{\min} \ge Td: Append E{\text{cand}} to E, increment n \leftarrow n + 1. d. Stop when n \ge Nv. 4. Output E. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def selectviews(candidatepool, Nv=200, To=0.3, Td=0.2): E = [] n = 0 pooliter = iter(candidatepool) while n < Nv: try: Ecand = next(pooliter) except StopIteration: break # Pool exhausted if n == 0: E.append(Ecand) n += 1 else: maxoverlap = -1.0 mindistance = float('inf') for existing in E: # Frustum IoU implementation not provided in sources; replace with geometric intersection logic. overlap = 0.0 if overlap > maxoverlap: maxoverlap = overlap t1, t2 = Ecand.t, existing.t R1, R2 = Ecand.R, existing.R posdist = math.sqrt(sum((a - b)2 for a, b in zip(t1, t2))) trace = sum(R2[i][k] R1[k][i] for k in range(3) for i in range(3)) cosangle = (trace - 1.0) / 2.0 cosangle = max(-1.0, min(1.0, cosangle)) angledist = math.acos(cosangle) dist = posdist + angledist if dist < mindistance: mindistance = dist if maxoverlap >= To and mindistance >= Td: E.append(Ecand) n += 1 return E Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Frustum Calculation: The source defines overlap via frustum IoU but does not provide the geometric algorithm for computing the intersection volume of two arbitrary frustums. Implementers must define the frustum geometry and compute the intersection. Degenerate Rotation: If R1 = R2, the trace term becomes 3, leading to \arccos(1) = 0, which is correct. Numerical precision near \pm 1 should be handled via clamping. Infinite Loop: If the candidate pool is exhausted or too small to satisfy the diversity constraints, the loop may not terminate. The source assumes a sufficiently large pool. This method selects a subset of input cameras to maximize pixel coverage in a novel view, addressing GPU memory limitations in large-scale neural rendering pipelines. It replaces heuristic overlap/distance metrics with a greedy approximation of the Maximum K-Coverage problem from set theory. Unlike simple ULR-style weights or voxel grid approximations, this approach explicitly maximizes the union of visible pixels from the chosen subset. Choose it when explicit pixel coverage maximization is required over geometric separation. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths and limitations: Not given in the sources. The algorithm is labeled as Algorithm 1 in the source. It is applied during the training of generalizable neural radiance fields for novel view synthesis. name: Diverse View Selection via Maximum K-Coverage
head: Camera Selection Algorithm, Camera Selection via Maximum K-Coverage, Greedy K-Coverage View Selection, K-Maximum Coverage Camera Selection, Maximum K-Coverage camera selection
body:
This method selects a subset of input cameras to maximize pixel coverage in a novel view, addressing GPU memory limitations in large-scale IBR and neural rendering pipelines. It builds on the K-Maximum coverage algorithm from set theory to provide fast and accurate camera selection. Unlike simple ULR-style weights, superpixel-based IBR, or voxel grid approximations, this approach explicitly maximizes the union of visible pixels from the chosen subset. Inputs: M: Number of input cameras. N: Number of pixels in the novel view space P. k: Target number of views to select (|V{sel}| = k). Mesh: A proxy mesh estimated from Multi-View Stereo (MVS). Ti: Projection matrices for each input camera i \in \{1, \dots, M\}. T{novel}: Projection matrix for the novel view. Outputs: V{sel}: A subset of k input camera indices. Data Structures: Si: A downscaled score map (array) for input camera i, with dimensions matching the resolution of the novel view space. C{covered}: A boolean mask of size N, tracking the coverage status of each pixel in the novel view. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Coverage: Create C{covered} initialized to false for all p \in P. Initialize V{sel} = \emptyset. Initialize total score V0 = 0. 2. Precompute Score Maps: For each input camera i \in \{1, \dots, M\}: a. Project the Mesh onto the novel view space using T{novel} and Ti to determine visibility. b. Perform a depth test using the Mesh to handle occlusions. c. Compute the visibility score Si(p) for each pixel p \in P. Binary Mode: Si(p) = 1 if p is visible in view i, else 0. Density Mode (Optional): Replace binary visibility with a per-pixel score approximating point density: Si(p) =  rac{d{novel}(p)}{d{input}(p)}, where d{novel}(p) is the distance from the novel camera to the visible point, and d{input}(p) is the distance from the input camera to the visible point. d. Store Si in memory. 3. Greedy Selection Loop: Iterate j from 1 to k: a. Evaluate Candidates: For each remaining candidate camera c 
otin V{sel}: i. Calculate the marginal gain Gc = \sum{p \in P} Sc(p) \cdot \mathbb{I}(
eg C{covered}[p]), where \mathbb{I}(\cdot) is the indicator function. b. Select Best: Choose c^ = \arg\max{c 
otin V{sel}} Gc. c. Update State: i. Add c^ to V{sel}. ii. Update C{covered}: For all p \in P, if S{c^}(p) > 0, mark p as covered. iii. Calculate current total score Vj = \sum{p \in P} \mathbb{I}(C{covered}[p]) (or sum of max scores if using non-binary scores). 4. Degeneracy Check: After each selection step j, check for the degenerate case where the novel view is identical to an already selected input view. a. Compute ratio R = Vj / V{j-1}. b. If R < \epsilon, the algorithm has stalled because the first view covered all pixels, leaving zero marginal gain for others. c. Fallback: If stalled, discard the greedy selection for this step and instead select the remaining candidate with the absolute maximum total score: \arg\max{c 
otin V{sel}} \sum{p \in P} Sc(p). 5. Return: Output V{sel}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def selectcameras(mesh, cameras, novelproj, k, epsilon=1e-5): """ Select k cameras from 'cameras' to maximize coverage in the novel view. cameras: list of camera objects with projection matrices novelproj: projection matrix for the target novel view """ # 1. Precompute score maps S = [] for cam in cameras: # Project mesh to novel view, handle occlusions via depth test # Returns array of visibility scores (binary or density-based) scoremap = computevisibilityscoremap(mesh, cam.proj, novelproj) S.append(scoremap) N = len(S[0]) covered = [False] N Vsel = [] Vprev = 0.0 for step in range(1, k + 1): bestgain = -1.0 bestidx = -1 besttotal = -1.0 # 2. Evaluate candidates for i in range(len(cameras)): if i in Vsel: continue # Calculate marginal gain: sum scores of uncovered pixels gain = sum(S[i][p] for p in range(N) if not covered[p]) total = sum(S[i]) if gain > bestgain: bestgain = gain bestidx = i besttotal = total # 3. Degeneracy Check # Calculate current total coverage score Vstep currenttotal = sum(1.0 for c in covered if c) # Source condition: V{k+1}/Vk < epsilon if Vprev > 0 and currenttotal / Vprev < epsilon: # Degenerate case: switch to absolute max score bestidx = -1 maxtotal = -1.0 for i in range(len(cameras)): if i in Vsel: continue if sum(S[i]) > maxtotal: maxtotal = sum(S[i]) bestidx = i # 4. Update if bestidx == -1: break # No more candidates Vsel.append(bestidx) # Update coverage mask for p in range(N): if S[bestidx][p] > 0: covered[p] = True Vprev = sum(1.0 for c in covered if c) return Vsel def computevisibilityscoremap(mesh, camproj, novelproj): """ Projects mesh to novel view space. Returns array of scores. Binary: 1 if visible, 0 otherwise. Density: ratio of distances. """ # Rasterize mesh into novel view space using novelproj. # For each pixel, back-project to 3D using mesh depth. # Project 3D point to input camera space using camproj. # Perform depth test: if 3D point is closer to novel camera than to input camera, # the pixel is occluded in the input view. # Compute score based on binary visibility or distance ratio. # Implementation depends on the specific rasterization engine. pass Parameters: k: Number of views to select. Not given in the sources. \epsilon: Threshold for degeneracy detection. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degeneracy: If the novel view is identical to an input view, the first selected view covers all pixels, resulting in zero marginal gain for subsequent views. This is detected when V{k+1}/Vk < \epsilon. The algorithm switches to selecting the view with the absolute maximum sum of scores. Precision: The algorithm relies on accurate depth testing and occlusion handling using the proxy mesh. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of pixels in the novel view and M is the number of input cameras. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot M) to store the score maps for all input cameras in the novel view space. Performance: Provides faster and more accurate selection than ULR-style weights, superpixel-based IBR, or voxel grid approximations. Strengths: Guarantees a lower bound of 1 - 1/e on the ratio of the score compared to the optimal solution (greedy approximation guarantee for Maximum K-Coverage). Limitations: Requires a proxy mesh from MVS, which may not be available or accurate for all scenes. This method was introduced by G. Kopanas, J. Philip, T. Leimkühler & G. Drettakis in "Point-Based Neural Rendering with Per-View Optimization". It builds upon the K-Maximum coverage algorithm [HP98] to address the limitations of previous camera selection methods like those by Riegler and Koltun [RK20], which ranked views based on overlap but did not necessarily maximize the union of coverage. The approach is part of a broader trend in neural rendering that leverages MVS proxy geometry for efficient per-view optimization. name: Progressive Global View Sampling
head: Moving beta distribution, Probabilistic Gradient Vector Sampling
body: Progressive Global View Sampling (PGVS) is a camera view sampling strategy for 3D object reconstruction that progressively shifts the sampling distribution from in-boundary (IB) concentration to a uniform distribution over training iterations using a Beta distribution. It sets itself apart from static view samplers by dynamically adjusting the probability density of camera angles to prioritize frontal views early in training and back views later, ensuring comprehensive coverage without requiring pre-defined view lists. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Initial Beta distribution parameters \alpha0, \beta0; total training iterations T; current iteration t; range of camera angles \text{range}(\theta, \phi); set of pre-rendered positions \mathcal{P}; in-boundary region definition. Outputs: Sampled camera angles (\theta, \phi); selected camera position from \mathcal{P} or a new random position. Data Structures Beta Distribution Parameters: Two floating-point values \alpha(t) and \beta(t) representing the shape parameters of the Beta distribution at iteration t. Pre-rendered Positions: A list or set of 3D coordinates \mathcal{P} = \{p1, p2,..., pn\} corresponding to previously rendered views. Formulas The decay of the Beta distribution parameters is linear with respect to a normalized time factor u0 t: \alpha(t) = \alpha0 + (1 - \alpha0)u0 t \beta(t) = \beta0 + (1 - \beta0)u0 t where t is the current iteration step and u0 is a scaling factor. The uniform point tu is defined as the iteration where both \alpha(t) and \beta(t) decay to 1. At this point, the Beta distribution becomes uniform. For iterations t < tu, camera angles \theta, \phi are sampled from the corresponding Probability Density Function (PDF) f(x; t) using inverse transform sampling: \theta, \phi = \left( \int f(x; t)dx \right)^{-1} (U{\theta,\phi}(0, 1)) \cdot \text{range}(\theta, \phi) where U{\theta,\phi}(0, 1) is a uniform random variable in [0, 1]. Steps 1. Initialize: Set initial parameters \alpha0, \beta0. Determine the uniform point tu where \alpha(tu) = 1 and \beta(tu) = 1. 2. Check Iteration: If current iteration t \ge tu, proceed to Step 4. Otherwise, proceed to Step 3. 3. Progressive Sampling: Calculate current \alpha(t) and \beta(t) using the decay formulas. Sample raw angles from the Beta distribution defined by \alpha(t) and \beta(t). Map these angles to the desired range \text{range}(\theta, \phi) using the inverse CDF method described in the formula. Note: In the initial phase, this concentrates samples in the frontal part; as t increases, samples shift toward the back part. 4. Uniform Sampling: If t \ge tu, sample \theta, \phi uniformly from \text{range}(\theta, \phi). 5. Boundary Handling: Check if the sampled camera position lies within the in-boundary (IB) region. If yes, select the nearest pre-rendered position from \mathcal{P} to avoid unnecessary computational burden. If no, use the newly sampled position. Pseudocode Unverified code. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: If \alpha0 or \beta0 are close to 1, the uniform point tu is reached very early, reducing the benefit of progressive sampling. IB Region Definition: The "in-boundary" region must be well-defined to avoid selecting incorrect nearest neighbors. Degenerate Input: If \alpha0 = 1 and \beta0 = 1, the distribution is uniform from the start, and no progressive sampling occurs. When to Use: When reconstructing 3D objects from text or image prompts where initial views are biased (e.g., frontal) and comprehensive coverage is needed. name: Training Objective for Fine Representation
head: Fine Representation Training Objective, Fine-stage Training Configuration
body: The training objective for the fine representation defines the loss function used to optimize the high-resolution radiance field or voxel grid after the coarse stage has converged. It solves the problem of refining geometric details and texture fidelity without over-regularizing the solution, which can lead to blurry or artifact-prone results. It differs from the coarse stage objective primarily by reducing the weight of regularization terms, a modification empirically shown to yield slightly better visual quality. It builds on Training Configuration by specifying the parameter adjustments for the second optimization phase. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: The optimized coarse representation (density/alpha fields), the current fine representation parameters (e.g., fine voxel grid values or fine MLP weights), and the training dataset (images, camera poses). Outputs: Updated fine representation parameters and the computed training loss scalar. Data Structures: The fine representation typically mirrors the coarse structure but with higher resolution or different encoding. For direct voxel optimization, this is a high-resolution 3D grid of density and color values. For MLP-based NeRFs, it is a separate network or a higher-frequency encoding branch. Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: Sample points along rays using the same sampling strategy as the coarse stage, potentially biased by the coarse density field to focus on occupied space. 2. Rendering: Compute the rendered image color C(r) for each training ray r by volume rendering the fine representation's density \sigmaf and color cf. 3. Loss Computation: Calculate the total loss \mathcal{L}{fine} as a weighted sum of reconstruction loss and regularization losses. 4. Optimization: Update the fine representation parameters using an optimizer (e.g., Adam) based on \mathcal{L}{fine}. Formulas: The total loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}{fine} = \mathcal{L}{rec} + \lambda{reg} \mathcal{L}{reg} Where: \mathcal{L}{rec} is the reconstruction loss (e.g., Mean Squared Error or L1 loss) between the rendered image and the ground truth image. This term is identical to the coarse stage. \mathcal{L}{reg} represents regularization losses (e.g., density smoothness, sparsity constraints). \lambda{reg} is the regularization weight. Parameters: Regularization Weight (\lambda{reg}): The key difference from the coarse stage is that \lambda{reg} is set to a smaller value in the fine stage. The sources state that using smaller regularization weights leads to slightly better visual quality empirically. The exact numerical value is not given in the sources; it is a hyperparameter tuned relative to the coarse stage. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainfinestage(coarserepr, finerepr, dataset, optimizer, lambdaregcoarse): """ Optimizes the fine representation using a reduced regularization weight. Args: coarserepr: The optimized coarse representation (used for sampling bias if applicable). finerepr: The fine representation parameters (voxels or MLP weights). dataset: Iterable of (image, camerapose) pairs. optimizer: Optimizer instance for finerepr. lambdaregcoarse: The regularization weight used in the coarse stage. Returns: finerepr: The updated fine representation. """ # Define the reduced regularization weight # The sources specify a smaller weight but do not give a specific ratio or value lambdaregfine = lambdaregcoarse 0.1 # Placeholder ratio; implementer must tune this based on empirical results for image, camerapose in dataset: # 1. Sample points along rays # Use sampling strategy consistent with coarse stage, potentially using coarse density for biasing rayorigins, raydirections, samplepoints = samplerays(camerapose, coarserepr) # 2. Query fine representation densities, colors = finerepr.query(samplepoints) # 3. Volume render the image renderedimage = volumerender(rayorigins, raydirections, densities, colors) # 4. Compute reconstruction loss (same as coarse stage) lossrec = mseloss(renderedimage, image) # 5. Compute regularization loss # The specific form of Lreg depends on the representation (e.g., density smoothness) lossreg = computeregularizationloss(finerepr) # 6. Compute total loss with reduced regularization weight loss = lossrec + lambdaregfine lossreg # 7. Backpropagate and update optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return finerepr Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Over-smoothing: If the regularization weight is not reduced sufficiently, the fine stage may fail to capture high-frequency details, resulting in blurry outputs. Instability: Reducing regularization too much may lead to noisy or unstable optimization if the reconstruction loss alone is insufficient to constrain the high-dimensional fine representation. This method integrates a StyleGAN2-based discriminator into the NeRF training loop to evaluate the perceptual quality of rendered images, addressing the limitation of pixel-wise losses like MSE which often produce blurry results. It differs from sibling methods such as Test-Time Finetuning by actively participating in the optimization loop via adversarial gradients rather than post-processing. The discriminator is configured to accept 64x64 RGB images and outputs a real/fake probability score, providing a training signal that encourages sharp, photorealistic textures. Test-Time Finetuning is a post-sampling optimization step that refines the sampled scene code by minimizing a combined loss of rendering fidelity and a diffusion prior, while keeping the diffusion model and decoder parameters frozen. It addresses the limitation where reconstruction guidance alone cannot strictly enforce rendering constraints towards faithful reconstruction, distinguishing it from two-stage methods that ignore the prior term during initial training, which results in biased and noisy scene codes. A learnable module combining spatial (pixel) and geometric (camera) attention to regulate contributions from neighbours and reduce ghosting artifacts from remaining misalignments. It computes pixel attention weights \psi{pix}^i \in \mathbb{R}^{w \times h} using a module \mathcal{A}{pix} with two convolutional layers and sigmoid activation, and camera attention weights \psi{cam}^i \in \mathbb{R}^1 using a module \mathcal{A}{cam} with two fully connected layers and sigmoid activation. The final attention-regulated features are computed as H{i \rightarrow k}^{f^a} = \psi{cam}^i \times \psi{pix}^i \times H{i \rightarrow k}^{f'}, where H{i \rightarrow k}^{f'} are the input neighbour features. Time Complexity: Similar to the coarse stage, dominated by volume rendering and backpropagation through the fine representation. The fine representation is larger, so per-step computation is higher. Memory Complexity: Higher than the coarse stage due to the increased resolution or capacity of the fine representation. Performance: Empirically leads to slightly better visual quality compared to using the same regularization weights as the coarse stage. Strengths: Allows for the capture of high-frequency details and textures that the coarse stage cannot represent. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the regularization weight to balance detail capture and noise/artifact suppression. Not given in the sources: specific convergence rates or memory usage numbers. The concept of multi-stage training with adjusted objectives is central to modern radiance field optimization, particularly in methods like Instant-NGP and Direct Voxel Grid Optimization. The specific observation that reducing regularization weights in the fine stage improves quality was highlighted in the Direct Voxel Grid Optimization paper. The integration of advanced perceptual losses (like StyleGAN2 discriminators) and post-training refinement (like Test-Time Finetuning) represents ongoing efforts to overcome the limitations of standard pixel-wise losses.
