name: ProbeSDF
head: Light Field Probes For Neural Surface Reconstruction
body: ProbeSDF is a neural surface reconstruction method that decouples spatial and angular light field components using two volumetric grids of different resolutions to achieve real-time rendering and accelerated training. It addresses the computational bottleneck of standard SDF-based neural fields by replacing the core appearance MLP with a lightweight model that uses spherical harmonic light field probes for angular variation and planar factorized features for spatial texture. Unlike Plenoxels or 3D Gaussian Splatting which require significantly more parameters per voxel (27 and 48 respectively), ProbeSDF uses as few as four parameters per voxel while maintaining high expressiveness. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images, camera poses, and an initial sparse voxel grid structure. Outputs: A signed distance function (SDF) field, spatial feature grid, angular feature grid (probes), and optionally per-camera bias vectors. The final output is rendered images via volume rendering. Data Structures: 1. SDF Grid: Implicit representation of 3D shape. Stores SDF values and derived surface normals \mathbf{n}. 2. Spatial Feature Grid (Fs): High-resolution grid using planar factorization. Each 16^3 tile contains three orthogonal planes of resolution 16 \times 16. Each plane stores ns coefficients. 3. Angular Feature Grid (Fa): Coarser grid storing light field probes. Each probe consists of spherical harmonic coefficients. Probes are stored at the corners of the spatial tiles. Probes at shared corners of adjacent tiles are duplicated in memory but maintain shared values to benefit from hardware-accelerated interpolation. Each probe stores l^2 \times na coefficients, where l is the spherical harmonic order and na is the number of angular features per coefficient. 4. MLP: A small neural network with 2 hidden layers, 32 neurons per layer, ReLU activations, and a sigmoid activation for the final output layer. Parameters: ns: Number of spatial coefficients per probe dimension. Typical value: 4 or 8. na: Number of angular features. Typical value: 4 or 8. l: Spherical harmonic order. Up to 16 coefficients (l=4). Typical value: 4. Per-camera bias vectors: Optional MLP bias vectors trained per camera to handle inconsistent shadows or large exposure changes (used for DTU and BMVS). Method Steps: 1. Ray Marching and SDF Evaluation: For a given camera ray, sample points \mathbf{x} along the ray. Query the SDF grid to get s(\mathbf{x}). Compute the surface normal \mathbf{n} = \nabla s(\mathbf{x}) / \|\nabla s(\mathbf{x})\|. Note: The conversion from SDF s(\mathbf{x}) to density \sigma(\mathbf{x}) follows the standard differentiable rendering pipeline principles defined in the parent article. 2. Spatial Feature Extraction (Fs): For point \mathbf{x}, identify the containing 16^3 tile. Retrieve the three orthogonal planes (Fx, Fy, Fz) for that tile. Compute the spatial feature vector via planar factorization (outer product): Fs = Fx \otimes Fy \otimes Fz This reduces dimensionality by storing three orthogonal planes per tile instead of a dense 3D grid. 3. Angular Feature Extraction (Fa): Compute the reflected vector \mathbf{r} based on the view direction \mathbf{v} and surface normal \mathbf{n} (typically \mathbf{r} = 2(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v})\mathbf{n} - \mathbf{v} or similar reflection geometry, though the text specifies evaluating at \mathbf{r}). Retrieve the 8 corner probes of the containing tile in the angular grid. Tri-linearly interpolate the spherical harmonic coefficients from these 8 corners to obtain the angular feature vector Fa(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{r}). 4. Incidence Angle Embedding: Compute the power terms of the cosine angle between the view direction and the surface normal to account for grazing angle reflectivity (Fresnel approximation): \text{incidence} = [(1 - \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v})^0, (1 - \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v})^1, \dots, (1 - \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v})^5] The term (1 - \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v}) approximates \cos \theta where \theta is the angle of incidence. 5. Radiance Decoding: Concatenate Fs, Fa, and the incidence angle embeddings. Pass them through the tiny MLP to predict the outgoing radiance C: C = MLP(Fs(\mathbf{x}), Fa(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{r}), (1 - \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v})^0, \dots, (1 - \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v})^5, \dots) The MLP acts as a minimal BRDF decoder. 6. Volume Rendering: Integrate the predicted radiance C and the density derived from the SDF along the ray to produce the final pixel color. 7. Optimization: Optimize the SDF grid values, spatial features, angular probe coefficients, and optionally per-camera bias vectors using gradient descent to minimize the difference between rendered and input images. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def probesdfrender(rayorigin, raydirection, sdfgrid, spatialgrid, angulargrid, tilesize=16, ns=4, na=4, l=4, mlpweights=None): """ Renders a single ray using ProbeSDF. Args: rayorigin: (3,) array, camera ray origin. raydirection: (3,) array, camera ray direction. sdfgrid: Sparse voxel grid storing SDF values. spatialgrid: Dictionary mapping tileid to (3, 16, 16, ns) tensor. angulargrid: Dictionary mapping cornerid to (l^2, na) tensor. tilesize: Size of the spatial tile in voxels. ns: Number of spatial coefficients. na: Number of angular features. l: Spherical harmonic order. mlpweights: Weights for the 2-layer MLP. Returns: color: (3,) array, rendered color. """ # 1. Ray Marching (Standard SDF approach) # Sample points along ray, query SDF, compute density and normal # This part relies on the parent article's SDF rendering logic [Parent] samples = [] for t in range(numsamples): x = rayorigin + t raydirection sval = querysdf(sdfgrid, x) normal = computenormal(sdfgrid, x) density = sdftodensity(sval) # Implementation from parent article samples.append({'x': x, 'normal': normal, 'density': density}) # 2. Volume Integration color = np.zeros(3) alphaaccum = 0.0 for sample in samples: x = sample['x'] n = sample['normal'] sigma = sample['density'] # 3. Spatial Features tileid = gettileid(x, tilesize) # Retrieve 3 planes for this tile Fx = spatialgrid[tileid][0] # (16, 16, ns) Fy = spatialgrid[tileid][1] Fz = spatialgrid[tileid][2] # Interpolate within tile to get Fx, Fy, Fz at local coordinates Fxlocal = interpolate3d(Fx, getlocalcoords(x, tilesize)) Fylocal = interpolate3d(Fy, getlocalcoords(x, tilesize)) Fzlocal = interpolate3d(Fz, getlocalcoords(x, tilesize)) # Planar factorization: Outer product # Fs is a vector of size ns Fs = np.outer(np.outer(Fxlocal, Fylocal), Fzlocal).flatten() # 4. Angular Features # Compute reflected vector r # Note: Standard reflection r = 2(n.v)n - v, but ProbeSDF uses r for SH evaluation v = raydirection r = 2 np.dot(n, v) n - v # Get 8 corner IDs of the tile containing x cornerids = gettilecorners(x, tilesize) # Tri-linear interpolation of SH coefficients # Each corner has l^2 na coefficients # Interpolate to get Fa vector of size l^2 na Fa = interpolateangularprobes(angulargrid, cornerids, x) # 5. Incidence Angle Embedding costheta = np.dot(n, v) incidence = np.array([(1 - costheta)i for i in range(6)]) # 0 to 5 # 6. MLP Decoding # Concatenate Fs, Fa, incidence inputvec = np.concatenate([Fs, Fa, incidence]) # Tiny MLP: 2 hidden layers, 32 neurons, ReLU, Sigmoid output # Assuming inputdim = ns + l^2na + 6 # Layer 1 h1 = relu(np.dot(inputvec, mlpweights['W1']) + mlpweights['b1']) # Layer 2 h2 = relu(np.dot(h1, mlpweights['W2']) + mlpweights['b2']) # Output C = sigmoid(np.dot(h2, mlpweights['W3']) + mlpweights['b3']) # 7. Composite alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigma dt) # dt is step size weight = alpha (1.0 - alphaaccum) color += weight C alphaaccum += weight if alphaaccum > 0.99: break return color def interpolateangularprobes(angulargrid, cornerids, x): """ Tri-linearly interpolates spherical harmonic coefficients from 8 corners. """ # Get local coordinates within the tile for interpolation weights localcoords = getlocalcoords(x, tilesize) # Retrieve coefficients for each corner # Each corner has shape (l^2, na) coeffs = [angulargrid[cid].flatten() for cid in cornerids] # Tri-linear interpolation weights based on localcoords w = computetrilinearweights(localcoords) # Weighted sum Fa = np.zeros(len(coeffs[0])) for i, c in enumerate(coeffs): Fa += w[i] c return Fa def computetrilinearweights(localcoords): """ Computes 8 weights for trilinear interpolation. localcoords is normalized [0, 1] within the tile. """ x, y, z = localcoords # Weights for corners (0,0,0) to (1,1,1) w000 = (1-x)(1-y)(1-z) w100 = x(1-y)(1-z) w010 = (1-x)y(1-z) w110 = xy(1-z) w001 = (1-x)(1-y)z w101 = x(1-y)z w011 = (1-x)yz w111 = xyz return [w000, w100, w010, w110, w001, w101, w011, w111] Time Complexity: Training converges in minutes (e.g., ~1 min for MVMannequins, ~150s for DTU) compared to hours for baselines like Voxurf or NeuS2. Rendering is real-time (200-400 Hz on RTX A6000). Memory Complexity: Highly memory efficient. Probes require 1/6th of the memory taken by spatial features when l=4 and ns=na. Model sizes are small (e.g., 30MB for MVMannequins, 56-88MB for DTU). VRAM usage is low (e.g., 5GB for MVMannequins). Performance: MVMannequins: PSNR 36.81-36.90, Chamfer 1.03-1.04mm. ActorsHQ: PSNR 37.48 (r/1), 36.62 (r/4). Model size 232MB (r/1), 57MB (r/4). DTU: PSNR 37.03-37.74, Chamfer 0.68-0.71mm. Twice as fast as NeuS2. BlendedMVS: PSNR 35.19-35.89, Chamfer 2.22-2.37mm. Strengths: Real-time rendering, fast training, low memory footprint, high PSNR and geometric accuracy on generic objects and humans with mild specularities. Limitations: Lighting encoded locally degrades extrapolation capabilities, causing shadow artifacts when looking from above or below on datasets with limited camera overlap along latitude (e.g., ActorsHQ legs). Local minima due to shape-radiance ambiguities because light transport is not explicitly simulated. Relighting and material editing are not supported. Targets objects with mild specularities; cone tracing methods are better for strong reflections but require >10 GPU-hours. ProbeSDF was introduced in the paper "ProbeSDF: Light Field Probes For Neural Surface Reconstruction". It builds on the hypothesis that angular components (lighting/environment) are predominantly extrinsic to the surface and locally invariant to parallax, allowing them to be encoded at a lower spatial resolution than intrinsic spatial texture. The method uses a sparse voxel grid based on Voxurf with targeted modifications to implement probes. It is evaluated on four representative datasets: MVMannequins, ActorsHQ, DTU, and BlendedMVS. name: Generalizable Implicit Reconstruction with SRDF
head: VolRecon, Volume Rendering of Signed Ray Distance Functions for Generalizable Multi-View Reconstruction
body: VolRecon is a generalizable implicit reconstruction method that predicts a Signed Ray Distance Function (SRDF) to reconstruct scenes with fine details and minimal noise from multi-view images. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like SparseNeuS by combining local projection features aggregated via a view transformer with global shape priors from a coarse feature volume, processed by a ray transformer to resolve surface ambiguity. Unlike standard SDF approaches that define distance in any direction, SRDF constrains the distance measurement to the specific ray direction, enabling more robust surface localization along the viewing ray. Inputs: A set of N source images I = \{I1, \dots, IN\} where Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}, and camera parameters for the source views and the target (reference) view. Outputs: Rendered color image, depth map, and implicitly, a mesh or point cloud representing the scene surface. Data Structures: 1. Feature Maps: \{Fi\}{i=1}^N \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4} \times C}, extracted from source images. 2. Global Feature Volume: Fv \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times K \times K \times C{vol}}, a 3D grid of voxels. 3. Learnable Token: f0 \in \mathbb{R}^C, a single vector used for aggregation in the view transformer. Parameters: N: Number of source views. M: Number of sampled points along a ray. K: Dimension of the global feature volume grid (K^3 voxels). C: Channel dimension of the feature maps. v: Unit ray direction vector (\|v\|2 = 1). o: Ray origin. Step 1: Feature Extraction For each source image Ii, extract feature maps Fi using a Feature Pyramid Network (FPN). The resolution is reduced to H/4 \times W/4. Step 2: Global Feature Volume Construction 1. Define the scene bounding volume and divide it into K^3 voxels. 2. For each voxel center pk, project it onto the feature map Fi of each source view i \in \{1, \dots, N\} using bilinear interpolation to obtain features f{k,i}. 3. Compute the mean \muk and variance \sigmak^2 of the N features \{f{k,i}\}{i=1}^N. 4. Concatenate \muk and \sigmak^2 to form the initial voxel feature. 5. Pass the volume of voxel features through a 3D U-Net to regularize and aggregate information, resulting in the global feature volume Fv. 6. For any 3D point p, the volume feature fv(p) is obtained by trilinear interpolation from Fv. Step 3: Ray Sampling and Projection Feature Extraction For a pixel in the reference view, define a ray p(t) = o + tv for t \ge 0. Sample M points \{pm\}{m=1}^M along this ray. For each sampled point pm: 1. Project pm onto the feature map Fi of each source view i. 2. Extract the color c{m,i} and feature vector f{m,i} using bilinear interpolation. Step 4: View Transformer Aggregate the multi-view features for each point pm into a single projection feature f{p,m}. 1. Initialize the input sequence with the learnable aggregation token f0 and the N multi-view features \{f{m,i}\}{i=1}^N. 2. Apply a self-attention transformer with linear attention. 3. Do not use positional encoding, as the order of source views is not assumed. 4. Compute the projection feature f{p,m} and updated multi-view features \{f'{m,i}\}{i=1}^N: f{p,m}, \{f'{m,i}\}{i=1}^N = \text{ViewTrans}(f0, \{f{m,i}\}{i=1}^N) Step 5: Ray Transformer and SRDF Prediction Compute the SRDF values for all sampled points along the ray. 1. For each point pm, concatenate its projection feature f{p,m} and its volume feature fv(pm). 2. Input the sequence of concatenated features for all M points into a Ray Transformer. 3. The Ray Transformer allows each point to attend to features of other points on the same ray, capturing long-range dependencies. 4. Output the predicted SRDF value \tilde{d}m for each point pm. Step 6: Volume Rendering Render the color and depth using the predicted SRDF values, following the NeuS approach for SDF volume rendering. 1. Convert SRDF \tilde{d}m to density \sigmam. The specific conversion function is not detailed in the sources. Standard practice involves a sigmoid-like function dependent on a learnable scale parameter, but the exact formula is not provided in the text. 2. Compute the accumulated alpha \alpham and transmittance Tm along the ray: \alpham = 1 - \exp(-\sigmam \deltam) Tm = \prod{j=1}^{m-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \deltam is the distance between adjacent samples. 3. Render the color C and depth D: C = \sum{m=1}^M Tm \alpham cm D = \sum{m=1}^M Tm \alpham tm where cm is the color at pm and tm is the depth coordinate. Formulas: The Signed Ray Distance Function (SRDF) \tilde{d}\Omega(p, v) for a point p and direction v is defined as: \tilde{d}\Omega(p, v) = (-1)^{1\Omega(p)} \min{p^ \in M, \|p^ - p\| = v} \|p - p^\|2 where M is the surface boundary, \Omega is the space, and 1\Omega(p) is the indicator function: 1\Omega(p) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } p \in \Omega \\ 0 & \text{if } p \notin \Omega \end{cases} The standard Signed Distance Function (SDF) d\Omega(p) is the minimum absolute SRDF over all directions v: d\Omega(p) = (-1)^{1\Omega(p)} \minv (|\tilde{d}\Omega(p, v)|) In the implementation, the network directly predicts \tilde{d}\Omega(p, v) for the specific ray direction v. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class VolRecon: def init(self, N, K, C, M, H, W): self.N = N self.K = K self.C = C self.M = M self.H = H self.W = W # Feature Pyramid Network for feature extraction self.fpn = FeaturePyramidNetwork(inchannels=3, outchannels=C) # 3D U-Net for global feature volume regularization self.globalvolumenet = UNet3D(inchannels=2C, outchannels=C) # Learnable aggregation token self.f0 = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(1, 1, C)) # View Transformer: Self-attention with linear attention self.viewtransformer = LinearAttentionTransformer(dim=C, heads=8) # Ray Transformer self.raytransformer = RayTransformer(dim=C, heads=8) # MLP to predict SRDF from ray transformer output self.srdfmlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(C, C), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(C, 1)) def extractfeatures(self, images): """ images: [N, 3, H, W] returns: [N, C, H/4, W/4] """ return self.fpn(images) def buildglobalvolume(self, featuremaps, voxelcenters): """ featuremaps: [N, C, H/4, W/4] voxelcenters: [KKK, 3] returns: [KKK, C] """ N, C, Hf, Wf = featuremaps.shape numvoxels = voxelcenters.shape[0] # Project voxel centers to each view and interpolate # Assuming camera projection matrices are available externally # This is a placeholder for the projection logic featurespervoxel = [] # [KKK, N, C] for i in range(N): # Project voxelcenters to view i # uvcoords: [KKK, 2] uvcoords = projecttouv(voxelcenters, featuremaps[i], Hf, Wf) # Bilinear interpolation # gridsample expects normalized coordinates [-1, 1] # Assuming uvcoords are normalized feat = F.gridsample(featuremaps[i].unsqueeze(0), uvcoords.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), mode='bilinear', paddingmode='border').squeeze() # feat: [N, C, KKK] -> [KKK, N, C] featurespervoxel.append(feat.permute(0, 2, 1)) featurespervoxel = torch.stack(featurespervoxel, dim=1) # [KKK, N, C] # Compute mean and variance meanfeat = featurespervoxel.mean(dim=1) # [KKK, C] varfeat = featurespervoxel.var(dim=1) # [KKK, C] # Concatenate voxelfeatures = torch.cat([meanfeat, varfeat], dim=1) # [KKK, 2C] # Reshape for 3D U-Net voxelfeatures3d = voxelfeatures.view(K, K, K, 2C).permute(3, 0, 1, 2) # [2C, K, K, K] # Regularize out = self.globalvolumenet(voxelfeatures3d) # [C, K, K, K] out = out.permute(1, 2, 3, 0).view(-1, C) # [KKK, C] return out def getvolumefeature(self, volume, points): """ volume: [KKK, C] points: [M, 3] returns: [M, C] """ # Reshape volume to 3D grid vol3d = volume.view(self.K, self.K, self.K, self.C).permute(3, 0, 1, 2) # [C, K, K, K] # Normalize points to [-1, 1] based on bounding box # Assuming bounding box is known normpoints = normalizepoints(points, bbox) # Trilinear interpolation # gridsample expects [N, C, D, H, W] and grid [N, P, D, H, W, 3] grid = normpoints.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # [1, 1, M, 1, 1, 3] feat = F.gridsample(vol3d.unsqueeze(0), grid, mode='trilinear', paddingmode='border').squeeze() # feat: [1, C, M, 1, 1] -> [M, C] return feat.permute(0, 2, 1).squeeze() # [M, C] def viewtransform(self, features): """ features: [M, N, C] returns: [M, C] (projection feature) """ M, N, C = features.shape # Expand f0 to match M f0expanded = self.f0.expand(M, 1, C) # Concatenate f0 and features # Input to transformer: [M, N+1, C] inputseq = torch.cat([f0expanded, features], dim=1) # Apply View Transformer # Output: [M, N+1, C] out = self.viewtransformer(inputseq) # The first token is the aggregated projection feature projectionfeatures = out[:, 0,:] # [M, C] return projectionfeatures def raytransform(self, projectionfeatures, volumefeatures): """ projectionfeatures: [M, C] volumefeatures: [M, C] returns: [M, 1] (SRDF values) """ # Concatenate features combined = torch.cat([projectionfeatures, volumefeatures], dim=1) # [M, 2C] # Wait, the paper says Ray Transformer takes concatenated features of all M points. # The input to Ray Transformer should be [M, C] if the projection of features is done before. # Re-reading: "concatenated features of all M points (projection features and volume features)" # This implies the input to Ray Transformer is [M, 2C] or the transformer handles the concatenation internally. # Let's assume the input is [M, 2C] and the transformer outputs [M, C] which is then passed to MLP. # However, standard transformers expect [Seq, Batch, Dim] or [Batch, Seq, Dim]. # Let's assume [M, 2C] is the sequence. # Apply Ray Transformer # Output: [M, C] out = self.raytransformer(combined) # Predict SRDF srdf = self.srdfmlp(out).squeeze(-1) # [M] return srdf def forward(self, images, rayorigins, raydirections, voxelcenters, bbox): """ images: [N, 3, H, W] rayorigins: [H, W, 3] raydirections: [H, W, 3] voxelcenters: [KKK, 3] bbox: bounding box of the scene """ # 1. Feature Extraction featuremaps = self.extractfeatures(images) # [N, C, H/4, W/4] # 2. Global Feature Volume globalvol = self.buildglobalvolume(featuremaps, voxelcenters) # [KKK, C] # 3. Ray Sampling # Sample M points along each ray # t values are sampled, e.g., uniform or importance sampling # For simplicity, assume uniform sampling between near and far planes tvals = torch.linspace(near, far, self.M) # [M] # Expand for all pixels # rayorigins: [H, W, 3], raydirections: [H, W, 3] # points: [H, W, M, 3] points = rayorigins.unsqueeze(2) + raydirections.unsqueeze(2) tvals.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(3) # Flatten for processing H, W, M, = points.shape pointsflat = points.view(-1, M, 3) # [HW, M, 3] # 4. Projection Feature Extraction # For each point, project to N views # This is complex to vectorize without specific projection functions # Placeholder: getfeaturesfromviews(pointsflat, featuremaps) # Returns: [HW, M, N, C] multiviewfeatures = getfeaturesfromviews(pointsflat, featuremaps) # 5. View Transformer # Aggregate N views for each point # Input: [HW, M, N, C] # Output: [HW, M, C] projectionfeatures = self.viewtransform(multiviewfeatures) # 6. Volume Feature Extraction # Get volume features for all points # Input: globalvol, pointsflat # Output: [HW, M, C] volumefeatures = self.getvolumefeature(globalvol, pointsflat.view(-1, 3)).view(HW, M, C) # 7. Ray Transformer and SRDF Prediction # Input: projectionfeatures, volumefeatures # Output: [HW, M] srdfvalues = self.raytransform(projectionfeatures, volumefeatures) # 8. Volume Rendering # Convert SRDF to density and render # This part depends on the specific NeuS implementation details not fully provided # Placeholder for rendering logic color, depth = volumerendersrdf(srdfvalues, pointsflat, raydirections, featuremaps) return color, depth Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusions: The view transformer aggregates multi-view features, which helps mitigate occlusion issues, but extreme occlusion may still lead to ambiguous features. Textureless Surfaces: The global feature volume provides shape priors, which is crucial for textureless regions where local projection features are unreliable. Large-Scale Scenes: The method is not suitable for very large-scale scenes due to the memory consumption of the global feature volume and the low resolution of the volume leading to decreased representation performance. Rendering Efficiency: The method is computationally expensive, taking approximately 30 seconds to render an 800x600 image and depth map. Time Complexity: Rendering is slow, taking ~30s for an 800x600 image. This is attributed to the volume rendering process and the transformer operations. Memory Complexity: Depends on the global feature volume size K^3 and the number of sampled points M. The method is not suitable for very large scenes due to memory constraints. Performance: On the DTU dataset, VolRecon outperforms SparseNeuS by ~30% in sparse view (N=3) reconstruction and 22% in full view reconstruction. It achieves comparable accuracy to MVSNet in full view reconstruction and better depth evaluation. Strengths: Generalizable to new scenes without per-scene optimization; produces fine details and less noise compared to SparseNeuS; good generalization to large-scale scenes (ETH3D) without fine-tuning. Limitations: Slow rendering speed; not suitable for very large-scale scenes; reconstruction quality improves with more images but is limited by the global feature volume resolution. When to Use: Generalizable implicit reconstruction from multi-view images, especially in sparse view scenarios or when fine details are required. When Not to Use: Real-time applications due to slow rendering; very large-scale scenes due to memory and resolution limits. VolRecon was introduced in 2023 by researchers from the IVRL lab. It builds upon the concept of neural implicit reconstruction, which typically optimizes per-scene parameters, lacking generalizability. The method addresses this by using a generalizable architecture that incorporates multi-view features and a global feature volume. It is based on the Signed Ray Distance Function (SRDF), which defines distance along a ray direction, differing from standard SDF. The method is compared against SparseNeuS, which uses only global feature volumes and an MLP, leading to over-smoothed surfaces. VolRecon is available at https://github.com/IVRL/VolRecon/. name: SDF-based Neural Volume Rendering with PBR
head: Neural volume rendering based on PBR and neural implicit surfaces, SDF-NeRF with PBR
body: This method integrates Signed Distance Function (SDF) representations for geometry with Physically Based Rendering (PBR) material models to achieve smoother geometric structures and accurate specular reflections, overcoming the coarse detail and foggy artifacts typical of standard NeRF. Unlike sibling methods such as ProbeSDF or SDF-based Neural Fields which may focus primarily on geometry or general neural fields, this approach specifically decouples geometry (via SDF) from material appearance (via PBR), providing interpretable parameters for reflection and diffuse components. It builds on Signed Distance Function (SDF) Representations by converting the SDF into a density field for volumetric integration while using the SDF gradient for surface normals required by the PBR model. Inputs: Camera poses and pixel information (images). Outputs: Rendered image colors C(r) for each ray r. Data Structures: 1. Spatial MLP: An N-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron. Input: Positional Encoded (PE) 3D coordinates \mathbf{x}. Output: Intermediate features used to derive SDF value f(\mathbf{x}), normal vector \mathbf{n}, volume density \tau(\mathbf{x}), and diffuse color Cd. 2. Directional MLP: (Implied by "directional MLP" in source for prefiltering, though details are sparse). Input: Surface normal \mathbf{n}, viewing direction \omegao, roughness \rho. Output: Prefiltered specular color f{prefilteredColor}. 3. BRDF LUT: A precomputed lookup table indexed by \cos\theta and roughness \rho. Fields:.r (red channel),.g (green channel). 4. Ray Sampling Buffer: Stores sampled points \mathbf{x}i, densities \sigmai, and colors ci along a ray. Parameters: \alpha: Learnable parameter controlling the transition between volume and surface density. Large \alpha implies a surface with low transmittance (e.g., metal); \alpha \to 0 implies a homogeneous medium (e.g., fog). \beta: Scale parameter for the Laplace distribution. In VolSDF, it is fixed as \alpha^{-1}. \rho: Surface roughness. F0: Reflectance at a perpendicular angle. \lambda: Weight for the SDF loss term. Steps: 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel, generate a ray \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the camera origin, \mathbf{d} is the direction, and t is incrementally adjusted to sample points along the ray path. 2. Positional Encoding: Apply one round of positional encoding (PE) to the sampled 3D points \mathbf{x}. 3. Spatial Feature Extraction: Feed the encoded points into the Spatial MLP to generate perspective-independent intermediate values. The MLP outputs: The SDF value f(\mathbf{x}). The volume density \tau(\mathbf{x}) derived from f(\mathbf{x}). The diffuse color Cd. The normal vector \mathbf{n} is derived from the SDF gradient \nabla f(\mathbf{x}). 4. Density Conversion: Convert the SDF value f(\mathbf{x}) to volume density \sigma(\mathbf{x}) (denoted as \tau in the source formula context, but used as \sigma in the rendering equation) using the cumulative distribution function \Psi\beta of a zero-mean Laplace distribution with scale \beta > 0: \sigma(\mathbf{x}) = \alpha \Psi\beta(f(\mathbf{x})) where \Psi\beta is the CDF of the Laplace distribution. 5. Diffuse Color Retrieval: Obtain Cd directly from the Spatial MLP output. This simulates irradiance with low angular correlation, representing subsurface scattering or air impurities. 6. Specular Color Calculation (PBR): a. Prefiltering: Calculate the prefiltered specular color f{prefilteredColor} using a Directional MLP or sampling. The incident direction \omegai for the prefiltering is the reflection of the viewing direction \omegao about the normal \mathbf{n}: \omegai = 2 (\omegao \cdot \mathbf{n}) \mathbf{n} - \omegao The prefiltered color depends on roughness \rho, position \mathbf{p}, and \omegai. b. BRDF Integration Approximation: Use the split sum approximation to separate the integration into a prefiltering texture part and a BRDF LUT part: L0(\mathbf{p}, \omegao) \approx \int{\Omega} Li(\mathbf{p}, \omegai) \, d\omegai \int{\Omega} fr(\mathbf{p}, \omegai, \omegao) \cos \theta d\omegai The right side (BRDF integration) is approximated using the BRDF LUT: \text{BRDF Term} = F0 \text{brdfLUT}.r + \text{brdfLUT}.g where the LUT is indexed by \cos\theta and roughness \rho. c. Final Specular Term: Calculate the specular color Cs: Cs = f{prefilteredColor} (F0 A + B) where A and B correspond to the.r and.g outputs of the BRDF LUT respectively. 7. Composite Color: Compute the total color ci at each sample point: ci = Cd + Cs 8. Volume Rendering: Render the final pixel color C(r) using the discrete volume rendering equation: C(r) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci where \sigmai is the volume density at sample point i, \deltai is the distance between sample point i and i+1, and Ti is the cumulative transmittance: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) with T1 = 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def laplacecdf(x, beta): """ Cumulative distribution function of zero-mean Laplace distribution with scale beta. """ if beta == 0: return 0.5 if x == 0 else (1.0 if x > 0 else 0.0) return 0.5 (1.0 + math.copysign(1.0, x) (1.0 - math.exp(-abs(x) / beta))) def getnormalfromsdf(sdfmlp, x): """ Computes the normal vector as the gradient of the SDF. Uses finite differences for gradient estimation. """ eps = 1e-4 xvec = np.array(x) sdfval = sdfmlp(xvec) grad = np.zeros(3) for i in range(3): xplus = xvec.copy() xminus = xvec.copy() xplus[i] += eps xminus[i] -= eps grad[i] = (sdfmlp(xplus) - sdfmlp(xminus)) / (2 eps) return grad / np.linalg.norm(grad) def getbrdflutvalue(costheta, roughness, lut): """ Retrieves A and B values from the precomputed BRDF LUT. lut is a 2D array indexed by [costhetabin, roughnessbin]. """ # Binarize indices based on resolution of LUT # Implementation detail: mapping continuous values to discrete indices idxcos = int(costheta (lut.shape[0] - 1)) idxrough = int(roughness (lut.shape[1] - 1)) # Clamp indices idxcos = max(0, min(idxcos, lut.shape[0] - 1)) idxrough = max(0, min(idxrough, lut.shape[1] - 1)) A = lut[idxcos, idxrough, 0] #.r channel B = lut[idxcos, idxrough, 1] #.g channel return A, B def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, spatialmlp, directionalmlp, brdflut, alpha, beta, numsamples): """ Renders a single ray using SDF-based Neural Volume Rendering with PBR. """ # 1. Sample points along the ray # Assuming a fixed range or adaptive sampling based on SDF zero-crossing # For simplicity, assume uniform sampling in a bounding box or near-surface region tvalues = np.linspace(0.0, 10.0, numsamples) # Placeholder range points = rayorigin + raydirection tvalues[:, np.newaxis] # 2. Positional Encoding (Placeholder for actual PE function) encodedpoints = positionalencoding(points) # 3. Spatial MLP Inference # Output: SDF values, Diffuse Color, and potentially other features # Note: Source says MLP outputs normal and density. # We compute normal from SDF gradient explicitly as per formula (4). sdfvalues = spatialmlp(encodedpoints) # Shape: (N,) diffusecolors = spatialmlpgetdiffuse(encodedpoints) # Shape: (N, 3) # 4. Compute Density from SDF # tau(x) = alpha Psibeta(f(x)) densities = alpha np.array([laplacecdf(f, beta) for f in sdfvalues]) # 5. Compute Normals from SDF Gradient normals = np.zeros((numsamples, 3)) for i in range(numsamples): normals[i] = getnormalfromsdf(spatialmlp, points[i]) # 6. Compute Colors finalcolors = np.zeros((numsamples, 3)) for i in range(numsamples): x = points[i] n = normals[i] Cd = diffusecolors[i] # Specular Component # View direction is opposite to ray direction for BRDF # However, in NeRF context, raydirection is from camera to scene. # Viewing direction omegao is from surface to camera = -raydirection omegao = -raydirection # Prefiltering: Incident direction is reflection of view direction # omegai = 2 (omegao. n) n - omegao dotno = np.dot(omegao, n) omegai = 2 dotno n - omegao # Get roughness (assumed to be a parameter or learned per point) # Source implies roughness rho is an input to the directional MLP/LUT # For this implementation, we assume a global or per-point roughness roughness = 0.5 # Placeholder, typically learned or input # Directional MLP for prefiltered color # fprefilteredColor = f(rho, p, omegai) # We assume directionalmlp takes encoded normal, view, roughness etc. # Simplified: assume it returns the prefiltered color directly fprefiltered = directionalmlp(n, omegao, roughness) # Shape: (3,) # BRDF LUT lookup # costheta is the angle between omegao and n? # In split sum, the integral is over the hemisphere. # The LUT is indexed by cos(theta) where theta is the angle between # the half-vector and normal? Or viewing angle? # Source formula 10 uses cos(theta) in LUT index. # Standard PBR LUTs use cos(thetav) (view angle) and roughness. costheta = max(0.0, dotno) # omegao. n A, B = getbrdflutvalue(costheta, roughness, brdflut) # F0 is reflectance at perpendicular angle (input or learned) F0 = 0.04 # Default dielectric, or learned # Cs = fprefilteredColor (F0 A + B) Cs = fprefiltered (F0 A + B) finalcolors[i] = Cd + Cs # 7. Volume Rendering # C(r) = sum Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai deltai)) ci # Ti = exp(-sum{j=1}^{i-1} sigmaj deltaj) deltat = np.diff(tvalues) deltat = np.insert(deltat, 0, 0.0) # Delta for first point is 0 or handled by T1=1 # Calculate optical depth # sigmai deltai opticaldepths = densities deltat # Cumulative transmittance # Ti = exp(-sum{j=0}^{i-1} opticaldepths[j]) # Note: Source uses 1-based indexing j=1 to i-1. # T1 = 1 (sum is empty). T = np.ones(numsamples) currenttransmittance = 1.0 renderedcolor = np.zeros(3) for i in range(numsamples): # Ti is already computed from previous step # Contribution: Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai deltai)) ci # Note: deltai is distance between i and i+1. # For the last point, delta is 0 or handled by boundary. # If i is the last point, delta might be 0, making contribution 0. # Standard NeRF rendering handles this by assuming infinite tail or fixed range. if i < numsamples - 1: sigmai = densities[i] deltai = tvalues[i+1] - tvalues[i] alphai = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigmai deltai) weight = T[i] alphai renderedcolor += weight finalcolors[i] # Update transmittance for next point T[i+1] = T[i] (1.0 - alphai) else: # Last point contribution is typically negligible or handled by background pass return renderedcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: SDF Gradient Noise: Computing normals via finite differences on noisy SDF outputs can lead to jittery specular highlights. Smoothing or analytical gradients (if the MLP structure allows) are recommended. Density Interpretation: The parameter \alpha controls the "sharpness" of the surface. If \alpha is too small, the volume appears foggy; if too large, it may become too opaque too quickly, losing volumetric details. LUT Resolution: The accuracy of the specular term depends on the resolution of the BRDF LUT. Low resolution can cause banding artifacts in reflections. Roughness Input: The source mentions roughness \rho as an input to the prefiltering and LUT lookup but does not specify if it is a global constant, per-pixel input, or learned. In practice, it is often a learnable parameter per object or global. Time Complexity: Rendering time is dominated by the MLP evaluations for each sample point along the ray. The PBR calculation adds overhead for normal computation and LUT lookups compared to standard NeRF's view-dependent radiance MLP. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the Spatial MLP, Directional MLP (if used for prefiltering), and the BRDF LUT. The LUT is small (typically 256 \times 64 or similar). Performance: Achieves better reconstruction quality than prior methods, particularly for specular reflections and geometric structures, overcoming the "foggy artifacts" of standard NeRF. Strengths: Interpretable parameters (SDF for geometry, PBR for materials), smoother normals, accurate speculars. Limitations: Complexity of PBR integration; potential for artifacts if SDF is not well-regularized; requires careful tuning of \alpha and \beta. This method was proposed by Chenyang Lv et al. in the paper "Volume rendering based on PBR and neural implicit surfaces". It addresses the limitations of NeRF, such as coarse detail and foggy artifacts in specular regions, by integrating SDF representation with PBR material models. It contrasts with Ref-NeRF (which uses reflected radiance interpolation) and NeRFReN (which uses an additional MLP for speculars) by providing interpretable parameters and smoother normals through the SDF-PBR combination. name: RS-Recon
head: Ray-Distance Volume Rendering for Neural Scene Reconstruction
body: RS-Recon is a neural scene reconstruction method that replaces the standard Signed Distance Function (SDF) with a Signed Ray Distance Function (SRDF) to model volume density, specifically addressing noise and inaccuracies in multi-object indoor scenes. Unlike SDF-based methods which consider surface points across the entire scene and may exhibit fluctuations leading to local minimum values, SRDF measures the shortest distance to the surface along a specific camera ray, eliminating the influence of surrounding surfaces not located on that ray. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Multi-view RGB images of an indoor scene. Output: Reconstructed 3D geometry and synthesized novel views. Data Structures: The method utilizes three distinct Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) and associated feature tensors: 1. Geometry MLP (fg): Input: Encoded position \mathbf{x} (and optionally grid features). Output: SDF value s{SDF}(\mathbf{x}) and geometry features \mathbf{F}g. 2. SRDF MLP (fs): Input: Encoded position \mathbf{x} and camera ray direction \mathbf{d}. Output: Signed Ray Distance value s{SRDF}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) and visibility probability v(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}). 3. Color MLP (fc): Input: Geometry features \mathbf{F}g and viewing direction \mathbf{d}. Output: Color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}). Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: For each pixel, cast a ray through the scene and sample points \mathbf{x}i along the ray. 2. SRDF Prediction: Pass each point \mathbf{x}i and the ray direction \mathbf{d} into the SRDF MLP (fs) to predict the signed ray distance s{SRDF} and visibility probability v. 3. SDF Prediction: Pass each point \mathbf{x}i into the Geometry MLP (fg) to predict the signed distance s{SDF} and geometry features \mathbf{F}g. 4. Density Conversion: Convert the SRDF value s{SRDF} into a ray-conditioned volume density \sigma using a differentiable mapping that concentrates density near the zero-level set. 5. Color Prediction: Use the geometry features \mathbf{F}g and viewing direction \mathbf{d} in the Color MLP (fc) to predict the color \mathbf{c} for each point. 6. Volume Rendering: Render the final image by integrating the predicted colors and densities along the ray using standard differentiable volumetric rendering. 7. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss using photometric consistency, SRDF-SDF consistency, and self-supervised visibility tasks. Formulas: SRDF-SDF Consistency Loss (\mathcal{L}{con}): Constrains the signs of the SRDF and SDF outputs to ensure they share the same sign indicating spatial occupancy. The exact mathematical formulation is not provided in the sources. It enforces \text{sign}(s{SRDF}) = \text{sign}(s{SDF}). Visibility Task: A self-supervised visibility task predicts the probability of whether sampled points are physically visible along the ray. It combines priors from predicted SRDF and SDF as pseudo labels. Parameters: SRDF MLP (fs): Dedicated MLP for SRDF values. Geometry MLP (fg): MLP for SDF and geometry features. Color MLP (fc): MLP for color prediction. Typical values for hyperparameters (e.g., learning rate, MLP depth) are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multi-object Scenes: Standard SDF may introduce noise due to fluctuations from surrounding surfaces. SRDF mitigates this by being ray-specific. Visibility Ground Truth: Unlike methods like VIP-NeRF that depend on multi-view geometry computation for visibility labels, RS-Recon's self-supervised visibility task requires minimal computational increase and does not depend on multi-view geometry for ground truth generation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def convertsrdftodensity(srdfvalues): # Standard differentiable mapping concentrates density near sSRDF=0. # Implementation varies; here is a common sigmoid-based approximation. return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-srdfvalues)) def mseloss(pred, target): return np.mean((pred - target) 2) def signconsistencyloss(sdf, srdf): # Not given in sources. Enforces sign agreement. return np.mean(np.abs(np.sign(sdf) - np.sign(srdf))) def visibilityloss(visprobs): # Not given in sources. Typically binary cross-entropy against pseudo labels. # Pseudo labels are derived from SRDF/SDF priors. return np.mean(-visprobs np.log(visprobs + 1e-8) - (1 - visprobs) np.log(1 - visprobs + 1e-8)) def rsreconforward(positions, raydirections, geometrymlp, srdfmlp, colormlp): """ Forward pass for RS-Recon. Args: positions: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing 3D points along rays. raydirections: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing ray directions for each point. geometrymlp: MLP predicting SDF and geometry features. srdfmlp: MLP predicting SRDF and visibility. colormlp: MLP predicting color. Returns: colors: Tensor of predicted colors. densities: Tensor of predicted densities. visibilityprobs: Tensor of visibility probabilities. sdfvalues: Tensor of SDF values. srdfvalues: Tensor of SRDF values. """ # Step 2: SRDF Prediction srdfvalues, visibilityprobs = srdfmlp(positions, raydirections) # Step 3: SDF Prediction sdfvalues, geometryfeatures = geometrymlp(positions) # Step 4: Density Conversion densities = convertsrdftodensity(srdfvalues) # Step 5: Color Prediction colors = colormlp(geometryfeatures, raydirections) return colors, densities, visibilityprobs, sdfvalues, srdfvalues def rsreconloss(colors, visibilityprobs, sdfvalues, srdfvalues, gtimages): """ Compute the total loss for RS-Recon. Args: colors: Predicted colors. visibilityprobs: Predicted visibility probabilities. sdfvalues: Predicted SDF values. srdfvalues: Predicted SRDF values. gtimages: Ground truth images. Returns: totalloss: Scalar loss value. """ # Photometric consistency loss (standard NeRF loss) photometricloss = mseloss(colors, gtimages) # SRDF-SDF Consistency Loss consistencyloss = signconsistencyloss(sdfvalues, srdfvalues) # Self-supervised visibility loss visibilitylossval = visibilityloss(visibilityprobs) totalloss = photometricloss + consistencyloss + visibilitylossval return totalloss Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Validated on indoor datasets, achieving improved performance in both reconstruction and view synthesis compared to SDF-based methods. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Eliminates influence of surrounding surfaces not on the camera ray; aligns density distribution with local maxima near intersected surfaces; self-supervised visibility task requires minimal computational increase. Limitations: Specific conversion from SRDF to density is not detailed; relies on consistency between SRDF and SDF which may require careful tuning. When to use: Indoor scene reconstruction with multi-object scenes where standard SDF may introduce noise. When not: Scenes where ray-specific distance is not the dominant geometric prior. RS-Recon was proposed in the paper "Ray-Distance Volume Rendering for Neural Scene Reconstruction". It addresses the issue of noise and inaccuracies in multi-object indoor scene reconstruction by modeling the volume density function using the Signed Ray Distance Function (SRDF) instead of the Signed Distance Function (SDF). The method was validated on indoor datasets, demonstrating improved performance in reconstruction and view synthesis. name: Volume-Augmented NeRF
head: Fluid volume augmented NeRF, Volume-Augmented Radiance Field
body: Volume-Augmented NeRF is a neural radiance field architecture designed for dynamic fluid scenes by binding explicit fluid volume values to sample points, allowing the renderer to learn density and color based on an explicit fluid distribution provided by a simulator. Unlike standard NeRF which assumes static scenes, this method augments the input with a fluid volume field V to handle temporal changes in density and color caused by fluid flow. It serves as the rendering component in a joint differentiable framework that infers fluid dynamics by matching observed images, avoiding the spatial and temporal ambiguities inherent in particle-based representations like NeuroFluid. The method combines a neural Euler fluid simulator with a neural renderer. The simulator provides a 3D volume field V representing the fluid distribution, which is interpolated at sample points to guide the NeRF network. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sample point position \mathbf{x}i, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and fluid volume value vi at \mathbf{x}i. Outputs: Volume density \sigmai and view-dependent RGB color \mathbf{c}i. Data Structures: Fluid Volume Field V: A 3D grid defined by the Euler simulator. For generated datasets: Grid size 40 \times 40 \times 40. For DPI Dam Break dataset: Grid size 54 \times 60 \times 32. Initialization: Volume value is 1.0 if the grid center is inside the initial fluid mesh, otherwise 0.0. Neural Network F\Psi: A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with specific layer widths and activation functions. Network Architecture Layout: 1. Positional Encoding: Input position \mathbf{x} is encoded using positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}). 2. Concatenation: \gamma(\mathbf{x}) is concatenated with the interpolated fluid volume vi. 3. Position MLP: The concatenated vector passes through 8 fully-connected ReLU layers, each with 256 channels. Skip Connection: The initial input (\gamma(\mathbf{x}) and vi) is concatenated to the activation of the 5th layer. 4. Density/Feature Layer: The output of the 8th layer passes through an additional fully-connected layer. Density \sigmai: Output is rectified using ReLU to ensure non-negativity. Feature Vector \mathbf{h}i: A 256-dimensional vector is output. 5. Directional Encoding: Viewing direction \mathbf{d} is encoded using positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{d}). 6. Shading MLP: The feature vector \mathbf{h}i is concatenated with \gamma(\mathbf{d}). This concatenated vector passes through a fully-connected ReLU layer with 128 channels. 7. Color Output: A final fully-connected layer with sigmoid activation outputs the RGB radiance \mathbf{c}i. Rendering Formula: The final pixel color \hat{C}(r) for a ray r is computed using standard volume rendering integration over N samples: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where: Ti = \exp \left( -\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj \right) is the accumulated transmittance from the near bound to sample i. \sigmai is the density predicted by the network. \mathbf{c}i is the color predicted by the network. \deltai is the distance between adjacent samples along the ray. Algorithm Steps: 1. Simulator Rollout: The neural Euler simulator computes the fluid volume field V for the current time step. 2. Ray Sampling: For each camera ray, sample N 3D points \mathbf{x}i between near and far bounds. 3. Volume Interpolation: For each sample point \mathbf{x}i, perform trilinear interpolation on the fluid volume field V to obtain the scalar volume value vi. 4. Network Forward Pass: Compute \gamma(\mathbf{x}i) and \gamma(\mathbf{d}). Concatenate \gamma(\mathbf{x}i) and vi. Pass through the 8-layer Position MLP (with skip connection at layer 5) to get \sigmai and \mathbf{h}i. Concatenate \mathbf{h}i and \gamma(\mathbf{d}). Pass through the 128-channel Shading MLP to get \mathbf{c}i. 5. Volume Rendering: Integrate \sigmai and \mathbf{c}i along the ray using the formula above to produce the image. Parameters: Position MLP hidden size: 256 channels. Shading MLP hidden size: 128 channels. Image resolution: 256 \times 256. A training procedure where the volume-augmented NeRF is jointly trained with a differentiable fluid simulator to infer fluid dynamics from images. Unlike particle-based methods (e.g., NeuroFluid) that overfit to single sequences, this approach uses the Eulerian volume field to allow generalizable learning across multiple sequences by avoiding spatial and temporal ambiguities. Training involves pre-training the NeRF on the first frames of all sequences for 20k iterations (learning rate 5 \times 10^{-4}, decay 0.5 every 5k iterations), followed by joint training of the simulator and renderer for 60k iterations (simulator LR 5 \times 10^{-5}, renderer LR 1 \times 10^{-6}, both decay 0.5 every 10k iterations). Complexity: The method adds a trilinear interpolation step per sample point to retrieve the fluid volume value vi from the Euler grid. The computational cost of the NeRF itself remains comparable to standard NeRF, with the addition of the volume input dimension. Performance: The method achieves significantly better rendering and simulation results compared to particle-based counterparts (NeuroFluid) in transfer settings (training on multiple sequences, testing on unseen ones). Strengths: Handles dynamic fluid scenes; avoids ambiguities of particle-based representations; enables generalizable learning across multiple sequences; differentiable bridge between simulator and renderer. Limitations: Requires a differentiable fluid simulator to provide the volume field; performance on single-sequence overfitting may be lower than complex particle-based methods (though this is a feature for generalization, not a limitation of the method's intent). Hardware: Demonstrated on 4 NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPUs. The method was introduced in the paper "Inferring Fluid Dynamics via Inverse Rendering". It addresses the limitation of original NeRF (Mildenhall et al., 2020) which works only on static scenes. By binding fluid volume values to sample points, it extends NeRF to dynamic scenes where density and color change with fluid flow. It is part of a broader effort to infer fluid dynamics using inverse rendering, contrasting with Lagrangian (particle-based) approaches like NeuroFluid (Guan et al., 2022). Inferring Fluid Dynamics via Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2304.04446, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Neural-PIL Decomposition Architecture
head: Coarse and Decomposition Networks, Neural-PIL Decomposition
body:
The Neural-PIL Decomposition Architecture addresses the problem of reflectance decomposition in novel view synthesis under varying illumination, where standard NeRF models fail to disentangle geometry, material, and lighting. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly modeling the rendering pipeline as a two-stage process: a coarse network that predicts view- and illumination-conditioned colors, and a decomposition network that estimates density, BRDF parameters, and surface normals, utilizing a learned Neural Pre-Integrated Lighting (Neural-PIL) module to efficiently compute shading. Unlike standard volume rendering that integrates color samples along a ray, this method computes an expected ray termination point and renders only at that specific location, leveraging explicit BRDF and normal estimates. Inputs: 3D spatial position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3, viewing direction  oldsymbol{\omega}o \in \mathbb{R}^3, and an illumination embedding \mathbf{z}l. Outputs: Volume density \sigma, view-dependent color \mathbf{c}, BRDF embedding \mathbf{z}b \in \mathbb{R}^4, and surface normal \mathbf{n}. The architecture consists of two primary neural networks and two frozen auto-encoder modules: 1. Coarse Network (\Phi{coarse}): An MLP taking (\mathbf{x},  oldsymbol{\omega}o, \mathbf{z}l) and outputting (\sigma, \mathbf{c}). It predicts illumination-conditioned colors. 2. Decomposition Network (\Phi{decomp}): An MLP taking \mathbf{x} and outputting density \sigma and BRDF embedding \mathbf{z}b \in \mathbb{R}^4. 3. Light-SMAE: A frozen auto-encoder that maps environment maps to a latent manifold. 4. BRDF-SMAE: A frozen auto-encoder that maps BRDF parameters to a latent manifold \mathbf{z}b. 5. Neural-PIL: A network trained to approximate pre-integrated lighting 	ilde{L}i( oldsymbol{\omega}r, \mathbf{b}), conditioned on roughness and viewing geometry. The rendering process differs from standard volumetric integration by decoupling geometry estimation from shading calculation. 1. Ray Termination Estimation: Compute the expected termination distance t^ along a camera ray by integrating sample densities \sigma(t) along the ray, similar to computing a depth map. t^ =  rac{\sumi ti \sigmai \Delta ti}{\sumi \sigmai \Delta ti} (Note: The exact weighting formula is not specified in the source text beyond "similar to depth map", but standard expected distance is implied.) 2. Normal Estimation: At the termination position \mathbf{x}^, estimate the surface normal \mathbf{n} by computing the gradient of the density output by the decomposition network with respect to the input position: \mathbf{n} =  rac{
abla{\mathbf{x}} \sigma(\mathbf{x})}{\|
abla{\mathbf{x}} \sigma(\mathbf{x})\|} Gradients are computed by passing backpropagation through \Phi{decomp}. 3. BRDF Parameter Extraction: Convert the BRDF embedding \mathbf{z}b predicted by \Phi{decomp} into explicit BRDF parameters \mathbf{b} using the decoder of the frozen BRDF-SMAE. 4. Illumination Computation (Neural-PIL): Compute the pre-integrated illumination 	ilde{L}i( oldsymbol{\omega}r, \mathbf{b}) using the Neural-PIL network. This network approximates the costly numerical integration of incoming light over the hemisphere, conditioned on the BRDF parameters \mathbf{b} and the reflection direction  oldsymbol{\omega}r. 5. Shading: Render the final color \mathbf{c} using the estimated BRDF \mathbf{b}, normal \mathbf{n}, and pre-integrated illumination 	ilde{L}i. The source references "Equation 2" for this step, which typically corresponds to a standard rendering equation form: \mathbf{c} = fr( oldsymbol{\omega}o,  oldsymbol{\omega}r, \mathbf{b}) \cdot 	ilde{L}i( oldsymbol{\omega}r, \mathbf{b}) where fr is the BRDF defined by parameters \mathbf{b}. The training occurs in distinct phases to manage memory and stability: 1. Pre-training Manifolds: Train Light-SMAE and BRDF-SMAE independently using datasets of environment maps and BRDFs, respectively. Freeze these networks after training. 2. Neural-PIL Training: Train the Neural-PIL network using the latent manifold created by the frozen Light-SMAE encoder. This separates the lighting approximation learning from the scene-specific optimization. 3. Joint Scene Optimization: Jointly optimize the Coarse Network and Decomposition Network on scene images. Optimization Variables: The illumination embedding \mathbf{z}l is optimized via the decomposition network. Constraint: The loss signal is not backpropagated to the illumination inputs in the coarse network. Only \mathbf{z}l is updated. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderraycoarse(rayorigin, raydirection, coarsenet, zl): """ Standard coarse network evaluation for initial color/density prediction. Note: This network does not receive gradient updates for zl during joint optimization. """ # Sample points along the ray points = samplepointsalongray(rayorigin, raydirection) # Flatten for MLP input pointsflat = points.reshape(-1, 3) directionsflat = np.tile(raydirection, (len(points), 1)) # Forward pass through Coarse Network # Input: x, omegao, zl sigma, c = coarsenet(pointsflat, directionsflat, zl) return sigma, c def renderraydecomposition(rayorigin, raydirection, decompnet, brdfsmaedecoder, neuralpilnet, zl): """ Decomposition-based rendering with Neural-PIL. """ # 1. Estimate density along ray to find termination points = samplepointsalongray(rayorigin, raydirection) pointsflat = points.reshape(-1, 3) # Forward pass through Decomposition Network # Input: x sigma, zb = decompnet(pointsflat) # 2. Compute expected termination distance (depth-like) # Assuming uniform step size dt dt = points[1] - points[0] # Approximate step size weights = sigma dt tstar = np.sum(points weights) / np.sum(weights) # 3. Get position at termination xstar = rayorigin + tstar raydirection # 4. Estimate Normal via gradient of density w.r.t x # Compute gradient numerically or via autograd sigmaxstar, = decompnet(xstar.reshape(1, -1)) # Gradient of sigma w.r.t x gradsigma = computegradient(decompnet, xstar, outputindex=0) n = gradsigma / np.linalg.norm(gradsigma) # 5. Convert BRDF embedding to parameters b = brdfsmaedecoder(zb) # 6. Compute Pre-Integrated Illumination # Neural-PIL takes roughness (from b) and reflection direction # omegar is the reflection of view direction about normal omegar = reflect(raydirection, n) Ltilde = neuralpilnet(omegar, b) # 7. Render Color using BRDF and Illumination # Equation 2: c = fr(omegao, omegar, b) Ltilde # fr is the BRDF function defined by parameters b c = brdfeval(b, raydirection, omegar) Ltilde return c, sigma, n def trainjointly(sceneimages, coarsenet, decompnet, brdfsmaedecoder, neuralpilnet, lightsmaeencoder): """ Joint optimization step. """ for image in sceneimages: # Forward pass through decomposition network to get zl update # Note: zl is treated as a learnable parameter per scene or per ray group # The source specifies optimizing zl via decomposition network # Render using decomposition method cpred, sigma, n = renderraydecomposition(...) # Compute loss against ground truth image loss = computeloss(cpred, image) # Backpropagate loss # CRITICAL: Do NOT backpropagate to illumination in coarse network # Only optimize zl via decomposition network loss.backward() # Update zl zl -= learningrate zl.grad # Update Coarse and Decomposition network weights coarsenet.step() decompnet.step() BRDF Embedding Size: \mathbf{z}b \in \mathbb{R}^4. Illumination Embedding: \mathbf{z}l is optimized per scene or per ray group, not backpropagated to the coarse network's input layer. Normal Estimation: Relies on the density gradient from the decomposition network. Degenerate cases where 
abla \sigma \approx 0 will result in undefined normals; a small epsilon guard is required. Ray Termination: The method assumes a dominant surface or thin geometry where a single termination point is sufficient. Thick volumes or participating media are not explicitly handled by the single-point termination strategy. Time Complexity: Rendering is faster than Monte Carlo integration because it avoids sampling the light hemisphere. However, it requires two network forward passes (coarse for initial estimate, decomposition for shading) and gradient computation for normals. Memory Complexity: Higher than standard NeRF due to the additional decomposition network, Neural-PIL network, and the storage of BRDF embeddings \mathbf{z}b and illumination embeddings \mathbf{z}l. Strengths: Explicitly handles varying illumination by decoupling lighting from geometry and material. The Neural-PIL module provides a differentiable, efficient approximation of pre-integrated lighting. Limitations: The single-point termination strategy may fail for complex volumetric scenes or thick objects. The reliance on frozen SMAE manifolds limits the range of representable BRDFs and lighting conditions to those seen in the pre-training datasets. The Neural-PIL Decomposition Architecture was introduced in the paper "Neural-PIL: Neural Pre-Integrated Lighting for Reflectance Decomposition". It extends the standard NeRF framework by incorporating reflectance decomposition techniques. The method builds on the concept of separating illumination, geometry, and material properties, which is challenging in standard NeRF where these are entangled in the color output. The use of Smooth Manifold Auto-Encoders (SMAE) for BRDF and lighting representation is a key innovation from this work.
