name: MINE
head: Continuous Depth MPI, MINE (Continuous Depth MPI), MINE: Towards Continuous Depth MPI with NeRF for Novel View Synthesis, Multiplane Image with Neural Radiance Fields
body: MINE is a method for novel view synthesis that models the frustum of the source camera using continuous depth Multiplane Images (MPI), conditioned on input images via a fully-convolutional decoder. It differs from pixelNeRF and GRF, which model the entire 3D space per ray, by reconstructing the source camera's frustum per plane, allowing rendering of any target view via homography warping after a single encoder pass and a fixed number of decoder passes, independent of the number of target views. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single source image (or multiple images for GRF, but MINE uses single image conditioning by default). Output: A rendered novel view image and optionally a disparity map. Data Structures: The method relies on a continuous depth MPI representation. The MPI consists of N{\text{planes}} planes. Each plane is represented by a 4-channel image: 3 channels for RGB color and 1 channel for volume density \sigma. The RGB values are bounded by a Sigmoid activation, and \sigma is the absolute value of the last channel. Network Architecture: 1. Encoder: A standard ResNet50. Feature maps are extracted from layers conv1, layer1, layer2, layer3, and layer4. 2. Decoder: A fully-convolutional depth decoder based on [12], modified with two additional downsampling blocks and two upsampling blocks to increase receptive fields. The decoder takes the encoder features and disparity encoding as input and outputs a 4-channel RGB-\sigma image. Decoder Layer Layout: The decoder is a multiscale architecture with outputs at four scales (output1 to output4). The layers are defined as follows (all convolutions are 3x3 unless specified, batch normalization is applied after convolutions in upconv blocks, ELU activation is used unless specified): Downsampling Path: downconv1: Input channels 2048 -> Output 512. downconv2: Input channels 512 -> Output 256. Upsampling Path (with Skip Connections): upconv1 extra: Input 256 -> Output 256. upconv2 extra: Input 256 -> Output 2048. upconv5: Input cat(upconv2extra, disparityencoding) (2048 + 21) -> Output 256. iconv5: Input cat(upconv5, encoderlayer3, disparityencoding) (256 + 1024 + 21) -> Output 256. output4: Input iconv5 (128 channels? Note: Source table says input 128, but iconv5 output is 256. The table lists output4 input as 128. Let's follow the table's explicit channel counts for the input to the output layer, which implies a preceding 1x1 conv or similar not explicitly named, or a typo in the source table's input column vs previous layer output. The source table explicitly lists output4 input channels as 128. We will use the explicit channel counts provided in the "Input" column of Table 5 in for the final output layers) -> Output 4 (RGB + \sigma). upconv4: Input 256 -> Output 128. iconv4: Input cat(upconv4, encoderlayer2, disparityencoding) (128 + 512 + 21) -> Output 128. output3: Input iconv4 (Input column says 64) -> Output 4. upconv3: Input 128 -> Output 64. iconv3: Input cat(upconv3, encoderlayer1, disparityencoding) (64 + 256 + 21) -> Output 64. output2: Input iconv3 (Input column says 32) -> Output 4. upconv2: Input 64 -> Output 32. iconv2: Input cat(upconv2, encoderconv1, disparityencoding) (32 + 64 + 21) -> Output 32. output1: Input iconv2 (Input column says 16) -> Output 4. upconv1: Input 32 -> Output 16. iconv1: Input 16 -> Output 16. Note on Channel Counts: The source table lists specific input channel counts for the output layers (16, 32, 64, 128) which differ from the output of the preceding iconv layers (32, 64, 128, 256). This implies a 1x1 convolution or projection step is applied before the final output activation, or the table describes the effective input to the final block. For implementation, one must ensure the channel dimension matches the expected input of the output layer as specified in the table. Numbered Steps: 1. Encode: Pass the input image through the ResNet50 encoder. Extract feature maps from conv1, layer1, layer2, layer3, and layer4. 2. Decode Frustum: Pass the encoder features through the fully-convolutional decoder N{\text{planes}} times. Each inference reconstructs one plane of the MPI frustum. 3. Warp: To render a novel view, apply homography warping to the reconstructed frustum (the set of N{\text{planes}}). 4. Render: Composite the warped planes using standard volume rendering equations (alpha compositing) to produce the final image. Formulas: The number of network forward passes P required for MINE is: P{\text{MINE}} = 1 + N{\text{planes}} where N{\text{planes}} is the number of planes in the MPI representation. For comparison, the forward passes for pixelNeRF and GRF are: P{\text{pixelNeRF}} = 1 + N{\text{targets}} \times N{\text{points}} \times H \times W P{\text{GRF}} = N{\text{views}} + N{\text{targets}} \times N{\text{points}} \times H \times W where N{\text{targets}} is the number of novel views, N{\text{points}} is the number of points per ray, and H \times W is the output resolution. Parameters: N{\text{planes}}: The number of planes in the MPI representation. Typical values are not explicitly given in the notes, but the method requires a fixed number of decoder passes equal to this value. Viewing Direction: MINE does not take viewing direction as input by default. It can be integrated by concatenating per-ray viewing directions with the output feature maps at the target view (after warping) and using a lightweight fully convolutional network to predict view-dependent radiance. Loss Functions: Multiscale training losses are used. L{L1} and L{SSIM} are applied only on output1. L{smooth} (edge-aware smoothness loss) is applied on all outputs (output1, output2, output3, output4). Flowers Light Fields Specifics: Disparity range: [3.0, 0.03]. Grid distance: 0.00128 between adjacent grids. Camera Intrinsics: fx = 0.868056, fy = 1.250000. Principal point shift is modeled as c{xij} = 0.5 + 0.002667 \times i, c{yij} = 0.5 + 0.002667 \times j, where [i, j] is the index in the extracted 8x8 grid and [0, 0] is the top-left view. Pitfalls: Principal Point Shift: In datasets like Flowers Light Fields (Lytro Illum camera), there is a shift in the principal point between different views. If metadata is unavailable, this shift must be approximated (e.g., as a constant value based on grid index). View-Dependence: The base MINE architecture does not model view-dependent effects. To support them, additional network passes are required, increasing complexity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class MINE: def init(self, nplanes, encoder, decoder): """ Initialize MINE.:param nplanes: Number of planes in the MPI representation.:param encoder: ResNet50 encoder model.:param decoder: Fully-convolutional decoder model. """ self.nplanes = nplanes self.encoder = encoder self.decoder = decoder def encode(self, image): """ Encode the input image and extract multi-scale features.:param image: Input image tensor of shape (B, 3, H, W).:return: Dictionary of feature maps from conv1, layer1, layer2, layer3, layer4. """ # Standard ResNet50 forward pass x = self.encoder.conv1(image) x = self.encoder.bn1(x) x = self.encoder.relu(x) x = self.encoder.maxpool(x) l1 = self.encoder.layer1(x) l2 = self.encoder.layer2(l1) l3 = self.encoder.layer3(l2) l4 = self.encoder.layer4(l3) # conv1 output is typically after maxpool or before? # Source says "conv1, layer1...". ResNet conv1 output is before maxpool usually, # but feature extraction often happens after. We assume standard feature map extraction. # For implementation, one must hook the specific layers. features = { 'conv1': x, # Assuming x is conv1 output before maxpool, or adjust based on actual hook 'layer1': l1, 'layer2': l2, 'layer3': l3, 'layer4': l4 } return features def decodefrustum(self, features): """ Reconstruct the MPI frustum by running the decoder Nplanes times.:param features: Dictionary of encoder feature maps.:return: List of Nplanes MPI planes, each of shape (B, 4, H, W). Channels are RGB (Sigmoid) and Sigma (Abs). """ planes = [] for in range(self.nplanes): # The decoder takes features and potentially disparity encoding. # In MINE, the decoder is run Nplanes times. # The source implies the decoder reconstructs the frustum per plane. # It is unclear if the decoder state changes or if it's a fixed mapping # for each depth plane. Assuming the decoder takes a depth/planar index # or the loop implies generating the full frustum volume. # However, the source says "Nplanes forward passes of the fully-convolutional decoder". # This suggests the decoder might take a depth coordinate or the loop # generates the planes sequentially. # Given it's a "depth decoder", it likely outputs a depth map or plane. # We assume the decoder outputs a 4-channel image per pass. # Note: The exact mechanism of "N planes forward passes" generating # a continuous depth MPI is slightly ambiguous in the text. # Standard MPI generation from a single image usually involves # predicting depth/disparity and then sampling. # MINE's specific "N planes forward passes" likely refers to # predicting the properties for each discrete plane in the discrete MPI approximation. planeoutput = self.decoder(features) # Apply output activations as per source: # RGB: Sigmoid, Sigma: Abs rgb = torch.sigmoid(planeoutput[:,:3,:,:]) sigma = torch.abs(planeoutput[:, 3:,:,:]) plane = torch.cat([rgb, sigma], dim=1) planes.append(plane) return planes def rendernovelview(self, planes, targethomography): """ Render a novel view by warping the reconstructed frustum.:param planes: List of Nplanes MPI planes (B, 4, H, W).:param targethomography: Homography matrix to warp the frustum to the target view.:return: Rendered image tensor (B, 3, H, W). """ # Warp each plane to the target view warpedplanes = [] for plane in planes: # Extract RGB and Sigma rgb = plane[:,:3,:,:] sigma = plane[:, 3:,:,:] # Warp RGB and Sigma using the homography # Homography warping is a geometric transformation warpedrgb = F.warpaffine(rgb, targethomography, dsize=(rgb.shape[2], rgb.shape[3])) warpedsigma = F.warpaffine(sigma, targethomography, dsize=(sigma.shape[2], sigma.shape[3])) warpedplanes.append((warpedrgb, warpedsigma)) # Composite the warped planes using volume rendering (alpha compositing) # Standard alpha compositing from front to back finalcolor = torch.zeroslike(warpedplanes[0][0]) accsigma = torch.oneslike(warpedplanes[0][1]) for rgb, sigma in warpedplanes: # Convert sigma to transmittance/opacity # Assuming sigma is density. Opacity alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma delta) # For simplicity, if sigma is already opacity-like or delta is 1: alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma) # Composite finalcolor = finalcolor (1.0 - alpha) + rgb alpha accsigma = accsigma (1.0 - alpha) return finalcolor def forward(self, image, targethomography): features = self.encode(image) planes = self.decodefrustum(features) renderedimage = self.rendernovelview(planes, targethomography) return renderedimage Time Complexity: The number of network forward passes is P{\text{MINE}} = 1 + N{\text{planes}}. This complexity is independent of the number of target views (N{\text{targets}}) and the spatial resolution (H \times W) of the output, unlike pixelNeRF and GRF where complexity is proportional to N{\text{targets}} \times N{\text{points}} \times H \times W. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Significantly more efficient than pixelNeRF and GRF for rendering multiple novel views. Allows for dense supervision signals (SSIM, edge-aware smoothness) during training because the full target image and disparity map can be rendered at training time. Generalizes well to large-scale real-world datasets (KITTI, NYU-V2, RealEstate10k, Flowers Light Fields, iBims-1). Limitations: Does not natively support view-dependent effects without additional network passes. Requires careful handling of camera intrinsics, especially for light field cameras with principal point shifts. When to use: When efficient novel view synthesis from a single (or few) input images is required, especially for multiple target views. Suitable for large-scale real-world scenes. When not to use: When view-dependent effects are critical and computational budget for additional passes is low. When the scene geometry is not well-suited for MPI representation (e.g., highly transparent or non-Lambertian surfaces without proper density modeling). MINE (Multiplane Image with Neural Radiance Fields) was introduced in the paper "MINE: Towards Continuous Depth MPI with NeRF for Novel View Synthesis". It was verified on datasets including KITTI, NYU-V2, RealEstate10k, Flowers Light Fields, and iBims-1. The method builds on the concept of Multiplane Images (MPI) and integrates it with neural network-based conditioning, differing from prior work like pixelNeRF and GRF by modeling the source camera frustum directly. MINE: Towards Continuous Depth MPI with NeRF for Novel View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv48922.2021.01235, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Voxel and Sparse Grid Representations
head: Grid-based NeRF, Voxel Grid NeRF, Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) NeRF, Hash Encoding NeRF, Triplane NeRF
body: Voxel and Sparse Grid Representations replace the continuous Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) of standard Neural Radiance Fields with structured spatial data structures (voxel grids, hash tables, or triplanes) to store scene features, enabling real-time differentiable volume rendering by eliminating heavy feed-forward network computations. Unlike hash-based or dense MLP approaches, this method limits learnable parameters strictly to grid values, offering a memory-efficient framework suitable for tasks such as extreme motion blur reconstruction. The core task of a NeRF network architecture is to learn a continuous volumetric scene representation F\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the spatial position, \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the viewing direction, \sigma is the volume density, and \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the view-dependent color. The rendering process integrates these outputs along rays using standard volume rendering equations. The shared mechanism involves: 1. Spatial Discretization: The 3D space is partitioned into a grid structure (dense voxels, sparse octrees, or hash tables). 2. Feature Storage: Each grid element stores learnable parameters, typically density \sigma and color features (e.g., spherical harmonic coefficients or RGB values). 3. Interpolation: For any query point \mathbf{x}, features are retrieved via interpolation (trilinear or bilinear) from the nearest neighboring grid elements. 4. View-Dependent Shading: View-dependent color is computed by projecting the viewing direction \mathbf{d} into a basis (e.g., Spherical Harmonics) and combining it with the interpolated spatial features. 5. Rendering: The retrieved \sigma and \mathbf{c} are used in the standard differentiable volume rendering equation to compute pixel color \hat{C}(r). Voxel-based Radiance Fields replace the MLP with structured voxel grids to store volume density and spherical harmonic coefficients, enabling real-time differentiable volume rendering. Unlike hash-based approaches, this method limits learnable parameters strictly to grid values, offering a memory-efficient framework suitable for tasks such as extreme motion blur reconstruction. This method performs neural multi-view image reconstruction and novel view synthesis by combining a hash-encoded geometry representation with a separate light field network. It solves the problem of reconstructing high-frequency geometric details and accurate textures from multi-view images, addressing the noise and roughness often found in density-based methods like NeRF and the poor performance in textureless areas seen in SDF-based baselines like NeuS and IDR. It is distinguished from its siblings by its use of a hierarchical sampling strategy combined with SDF thresholding to eliminate invalid points, and by its specific architecture where geometry and color are predicted by separate but connected MLPs. G-NeLF is a grid-based Neural Light Field (NeLF) method for novel view synthesis that predicts ray color directly without point-wise volume density modeling. It represents a ray as a sequence of spatial-aware features extracted from a hash-based multi-resolution tri-plane, which is decoded by an LSTM network to predict color. Unlike standard NeRF methods that model density and color per point, G-NeLF bypasses explicit volume density, allowing it to achieve performance comparable to state-of-the-art grid-based NeRFs (e.g., Instant-NGP, TensoRF) with approximately one-tenth the parameters and significantly lower storage overhead. It is distinct from its sibling Voxel-based Radiance Fields by replacing the volumetric integration step with a recurrent sequence decoding process, and from Neural Multi-View Image Reconstruction with Hash Encoding by utilizing a tri-plane structure and LSTM decoder rather than a single hash grid with an MLP. SCALAR-NeRF is a coarse-to-fine framework for scalable large-scale neural scene reconstruction that structures the neural representation as an encoder-decoder architecture to avoid the 'foggy' issue in Block-NeRF and enable training on a single GPU. It decomposes expansive scenes into manageable blocks, trains a shared decoder from a coarse global model, and fuses local results using the global model to avoid foggy reconstructions. Unlike Block-NeRF, which blends images using an inverse distance weighting function causing foggy appearance when block centroids are close, SCALAR-NeRF fuses local block outputs with a reference image from the coarse global model. TriDF is a hybrid explicit–implicit 3D representation designed for few-shot novel view synthesis (NVS) in remote sensing, specifically addressing the challenges of overfitting and slow convergence when trained on as few as three input views. It decouples scene representation into explicit triplanes for high-frequency color prediction and implicit continuous density fields for volume density, reducing the computational burden on implicit radiance fields and accelerating reconstruction by 30× compared to standard NeRF-based methods. Unlike sibling methods that jointly model color and geometry or rely on dense pretraining priors, TriDF leverages image-based rendering (IBR) features within the density branch and sparse depth supervision from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point clouds to stabilize optimization. The Tile and Slide Framework (Snake-NeRF) is an out-of-core method that scales Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) to massive 3D scenes (e.g., 10km x 10km) by partitioning the volume into non-overlapping 3D tiles, each trained with its own independent NeRF. Unlike sibling methods that dispatch multiple NeRFs across multiple GPUs or require pre-training a global model, this framework operates on a single GPU device, eliminating the need to load all images or network weights simultaneously. It solves the problem of catastrophic forgetting and memory overflow in large-scale training by using a 2x2 sliding window progression and a segmented ray sampler to ensure seamless rendering across tile boundaries. A real-time rendering pipeline that stores a NeRF model in a sparse 3D voxel grid, using an indirection grid to skip empty regions and a deferred MLP to compute view-dependent color from accumulated diffuse and specular features. Raymarch along r(t) = o + td. For occupied voxels, set step size \deltai equal to the voxel width. Concatenate accumulated diffuse color Cd, accumulated specular feature Fs, and positional encoding PE(\mathbf{d}) of the ray's view direction \mathbf{d}. Pass through a lightweight deferred MLP \Phi to produce a view-dependent residual color. wi = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) \alphai, where wi is the accumulated weight for sample i. Distills a large teacher NeRF into a spatially partitioned grid of tiny MLPs to enable fast, adaptive evaluation by mapping 3D positions to local student networks. Initialize a dictionary mapping 3D grid cell indices (i,j,k) to TinyMLP instances. For each training iteration, sample a random ray and generate numsamples stratified samples along it. Compute the grid cell index for each sample by normalizing its position within the bounding box and scaling by grid resolution. Accumulate L2 loss between student and teacher outputs across all samples. Update all grid MLPs using the accumulated loss and the configured learning rate. gridresolution: 3D tuple defining the number of cells per axis, e.g., (16,16,16). numdistilliterations: Number of distillation optimization steps, e.g., 1000. numsamples: Number of stratified samples per ray, e.g., 384. learningrate: Optimization step size for grid MLP updates, e.g., 1e-3. bmin, bmax: Axis-aligned bounding box defining the scene bounds, e.g., [0,0,0] and [1,1,1]. The shift from MLP-based NeRFs to grid-based representations was driven by the need for real-time rendering and scalability. SNeRG precomputed and stored a NeRF model in a sparse 3D voxel grid, using an indirection grid to enhance rendering by skipping empty regions. MERF presented a significant reduction in memory requirements by leveraging hybrid low-resolution sparse voxels and 2D high-resolution triplanes. KiloNeRF introduced grid distillation, mapping 3D positions to local student networks for fast evaluation. City-on-Web extended these concepts to large-scale web rendering, while Snake-NeRF addressed out-of-core training for massive scenes. name: Voxel-based Radiance Fields
head: Voxel NeRF, Voxel Radiance Fields
body: Voxel-based Radiance Fields replace the multi-layer perceptron (MLP) of standard NeRF with explicit voxel grids to store volume density and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients, enabling real-time volume rendering by eliminating heavy feed-forward neural computations. Unlike hash-based or dense MLP approaches, this method limits learnable parameters strictly to grid values, allowing for memory-efficient training via coarse-to-fine sparse voxel reconstruction and pruning. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D spatial position \mathbf{X}k and viewing direction \mathbf{d} for a sample point k on a ray. Output: Volume density \sigmak and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}k. Data Structures: Two separate voxel grids are maintained: 1. Density Grid (G\sigma): Maps \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}. Stores scalar volume density values. 2. SH Coefficient Grid (G{sh}): Maps \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{9 \times 3}. Stores degree-2 spherical harmonic coefficients for RGB color. Each spatial location stores a vector of 9 coefficients per color channel (total 27 values per voxel). Interpolation: For any query point \mathbf{X}k, features are retrieved via trilinear interpolation from the nearest 8 neighboring voxels in both G\sigma and G{sh}. Formulas: The volume density is computed as: \sigmak = \mathcal{G}\sigma(\mathbf{X}k) where \mathcal{G}\sigma denotes trilinear interpolation from G\sigma. The color is computed as: \mathbf{c}k = S(\mathbf{d})^\intercal \cdot \mathcal{G}{sh}(\mathbf{X}k) where: S(\mathbf{d}): \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^9 is the spherical harmonic function mapping the viewing direction \mathbf{d} to a 9-dimensional basis vector. \mathcal{G}{sh}(\mathbf{X}k) is the trilinearly interpolated vector of SH coefficients from G{sh} at \mathbf{X}k. The dot product combines the direction basis with the spatial features to produce the RGB color vector \mathbf{c}k. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: Xk: 3D spatial position (float32[3]) d: Viewing direction (float32[3]) Gsigma: Density grid (3D tensor) Gsh: SH coefficient grid (3D tensor, last dim 27) Returns: sigmak: Volume density (float32) ck: Color RGB (float32[3]) """ # 1. Trilinear interpolation for density # Gsigma is assumed to be a 3D array indexed by [x, y, z] # Trilinear interpolation from nearest 8 voxels sigmak = trilinearinterpolate(Gsigma, Xk) # 2. Trilinear interpolation for SH coefficients # Gsh stores 27 values (9 SH coeffs 3 RGB channels) per voxel shcoeffs = trilinearinterpolate(Gsh, Xk) # Returns float32[27] # 3. Compute SH basis vector for direction d # Degree 2 SH basis has 9 components shbasis = computeshbasis(d) # Returns float32[9] # 4. Compute color # Reshape shcoeffs to [3, 9] or [9, 3] depending on storage layout. # Standard layout implies shcoeffs[i] corresponds to channel i // 9? # Or shcoeffs is [9, 3] where row is SH order, col is RGB. # Based on formula ck = S(d)^T. Gsh(Xk), Gsh(Xk) must be [9, 3] or [3, 9] transposed. # Assuming Gsh stores [9, 3] (9 SH coeffs, 3 RGB channels): # shcoeffs shape: [9, 3] # Dot product: [1, 9] @ [9, 3] -> [1, 3] ck = shbasis @ shcoeffs.T # If shcoeffs is [9, 3], this is wrong. # Correct: ck = S(d)^T. V, where V is [9, 3]. Result is [3]. # ck[j] = sumi S(d)[i] V[i, j] ck = np.dot(shbasis, shcoeffs) # If shcoeffs is [9, 3], dot([9], [9,3]) -> [3] return sigmak, ck def trilinearinterpolate(grid, point): """ Perform trilinear interpolation from a 3D grid at a continuous point. """ # Get fractional coordinates x, y, z = point # Get integer base coordinates ix, iy, iz = floor(x), floor(y), floor(z) # Get fractional offsets fx, fy, fz = x - ix, y - iy, z - iz # Retrieve 8 corner values # Handle boundary conditions (clamp or wrap) v000 = grid[ix, iy, iz] v100 = grid[ix+1, iy, iz] v010 = grid[ix, iy+1, iz] v110 = grid[ix+1, iy+1, iz] v001 = grid[ix, iy, iz+1] v101 = grid[ix+1, iy, iz+1] v011 = grid[ix, iy+1, iz+1] v111 = grid[ix+1, iy+1, iz+1] # Interpolate along x v00 = lerp(v000, v100, fx) v01 = lerp(v010, v110, fx) v10 = lerp(v001, v101, fx) v11 = lerp(v011, v111, fx) # Interpolate along y v0 = lerp(v00, v01, fy) v1 = lerp(v10, v11, fy) # Interpolate along z return lerp(v0, v1, fz) def lerp(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) def computeshbasis(d): """ Compute degree 2 spherical harmonic basis vector for direction d. Returns float32[9]. """ # Standard degree 2 SH basis functions evaluated at d # x, y, z are components of normalized direction d x, y, z = d # Basis functions (unnormalized constants omitted or included in grid weights) # Typically: [1, x, y, z, x^2, xy, xz, y^2, yz] or similar ordering # Exact ordering must match training. Standard order implies 9 coeffs. # Common order: Y0, Y1, Y2, Y3, Y4, Y5, Y6, Y7, Y8 # Y0 ~ 1 # Y1 ~ x, Y2 ~ y, Y3 ~ z # Y4 ~ x^2, Y5 ~ xy, Y6 ~ xz, Y7 ~ y^2, Y8 ~ yz (simplified) # Note: Precise normalization factors are usually absorbed into the grid weights return np.array([1.0, x, y, z, xx, xy, xz, yy, yz]) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Handling: Trilinear interpolation requires handling coordinates outside the grid bounds. Clamping or wrapping must be defined. SH Basis Ordering: The ordering of the 9 SH coefficients in G{sh} must match the implementation of computeshbasis exactly. Memory: While more efficient than MLPs, dense voxel grids still consume significant memory for high-resolution scenes. Sparse reconstruction and pruning are required for scalability. Time Complexity: Rendering is significantly faster than MLP-based NeRF because it replaces expensive fully-connected layer computations with simple memory lookups and trilinear interpolation. This enables real-time volume rendering. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of voxels. It is more memory-efficient than dense MLPs for comparable resolution but less efficient than sparse hash grids for highly sparse scenes. Strengths: Real-time rendering capability; memory-efficient parameterization; compatible with differentiable volume rendering. Limitations: Resolution is limited by voxel grid size; aliasing artifacts may occur at high frequencies if grid resolution is insufficient; requires coarse-to-fine strategies and pruning for large scenes. When to Use: Applications requiring real-time rendering and moderate resolution, such as blurred view reconstruction or interactive applications. When Not to Use: Scenes requiring extremely high frequency details without massive grid sizes, or highly sparse environments where hash-based or octree methods are superior. Voxel-based Radiance Fields were introduced as a memory-efficient alternative to MLP-based NeRF, replacing the neural network with voxel grids for density and spherical harmonic coefficients. This approach was notably applied in ExBluRF for efficient radiance field optimization in the presence of extreme motion blur. The method leverages differentiable volume rendering while eliminating feed-forward operations to achieve real-time performance. body: This method performs neural multi-view image reconstruction and novel view synthesis by combining a hash-encoded geometry representation with a separate light field network. It solves the problem of reconstructing high-frequency geometric details and accurate textures from multi-view images, addressing the noise and roughness often found in density-based methods like NeRF and the poor performance in textureless areas seen in SDF-based baselines like NeuS and IDR. It is distinguished from its siblings by its use of a hierarchical sampling strategy combined with SDF thresholding to eliminate invalid points, and by its specific architecture where geometry and color are predicted by separate but connected MLPs. The method consists of a geometry network that predicts signed distance functions (SDF) and a light field network that predicts color. The geometry is represented by a hash grid, while the color is predicted using Fourier positional encoding of view direction and surface normal. Inputs: Multi-view images of a scene. Camera parameters (intrinsics and extrinsics) for the input views. Camera parameters for novel view synthesis. Outputs: Reconstructed 3D geometry (extracted as a mesh). Synthesized novel view images. name: G-NeLF
head: Grid-based Neural Light Field, Memory- and Data-Efficient Hybrid Neural Light Field
body: G-NeLF is a grid-based Neural Light Field (NeLF) method for novel view synthesis that predicts ray color directly without point-wise volume density modeling. It represents a ray as a sequence of spatial-aware features extracted from a hash-based multi-resolution tri-plane, which is decoded by an LSTM network to predict color. Unlike standard NeRF methods that model density and color per point, G-NeLF bypasses explicit volume density, allowing it to achieve performance comparable to state-of-the-art grid-based NeRFs (e.g., Instant-NGP, TensoRF) with approximately one-tenth the parameters and significantly lower storage overhead. It is distinct from its sibling Voxel-based Radiance Fields by replacing the volumetric integration step with a recurrent sequence decoding process, and from Neural Multi-View Image Reconstruction with Hash Encoding by utilizing a tri-plane structure and LSTM decoder rather than a single hash grid with an MLP. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}), training images, and hyperparameters (hash table size T, number of resolutions N, grid sizes si, feature dimension D{feat}, LSTM hidden size H{dim}). Outputs: Predicted ray color (r, g, b). Data Structures: 1. Hash Table: A lookup table mapping integer coordinate pairs to feature vectors. Size: T entries (typically 2^{14} for small/medium models, 2^{16} for large models). Content: Each entry stores a feature vector of dimension D{feat} (typically 2). Hash Function: For a 2D projected coordinate (x, y) at resolution level i, the index is calculated as: \text{Index} = (x \cdot a + y \cdot b) \pmod T where a=1 and b=2,654,435,761. 2. Tri-Plane: Three orthogonal feature planes \{\pi{xy}, \pi{xz}, \pi{yz}\}. Each plane contains N resolution levels. For small/medium models, N=8 with grid sizes ranging from 16 to 1024. For large models, N=16 with grid sizes ranging from 16 to 2048. Each resolution level has its own hash table of size T. 3. Point Feature Vector (\mathbf{F}): Constructed by concatenating features from all N resolutions across all 3 planes. Total dimension: 3 \times N \times D{feat}. For N=8, D{feat}=2, the dimension is 48. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Emission: For each pixel in the target image, emit a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} based on the camera model. 2. Bounding Box Intersection: Determine the intersection of the ray with the scene bounding box to define the sampling range [t{min}, t{max}]. 3. Point Sampling: Sequentially sample K points along the ray within the bounding box. K=256 for 360° scenes. K=128 for forward-facing scenes (using NDC coordinates). Let the sampled points be \{\mathbf{x}1, \mathbf{x}2, \dots, \mathbf{x}K\}, ordered from near to far. 4. Feature Extraction (Point Feature Acquirement): For each sampled point \mathbf{x}k: a. Projection: Project \mathbf{x}k onto the three orthogonal planes to obtain 2D coordinates \mathbf{x}{k}^{\pi} \in \mathbb{R}^2 for each plane \pi \in \{\pi{xy}, \pi{xz}, \pi{yz}\}. b. Hash Lookup and Interpolation: For each resolution level i \in \{1, \dots, N\} in each plane \pi: i. Calculate grid indices for the four corners of the cell containing \mathbf{x}{k}^{\pi}: u = \lfloor x{k}^{\pi}[0] / si \rfloor, \quad v = \lfloor x{k}^{\pi}[1] / si \rfloor The four corner indices are (u, v), (u, v+1), (u+1, v), (u+1, v+1). ii. Retrieve feature vectors from the hash table using the hash function: \mathbf{f}{tl} = \text{Hash}(\pi, i, u, v) \mathbf{f}{tr} = \text{Hash}(\pi, i, u, v+1) \mathbf{f}{bl} = \text{Hash}(\pi, i, u+1, v) \mathbf{f}{br} = \mathbf{f}{br} = \text{Hash}(\pi, i, u+1, v+1) iii. Perform bilinear interpolation to obtain the feature vector \mathbf{f}{k}^{\pi, i} for this resolution and plane: \mathbf{f}{k}^{\pi, i} = (1-\deltax)(1-\deltay)\mathbf{f}{tl} + \deltax(1-\deltay)\mathbf{f}{tr} + (1-\deltax)\deltay\mathbf{f}{bl} + \deltax\deltay\mathbf{f}{br} where \deltax = (x{k}^{\pi}[0] / si) - u and \deltay = (x{k}^{\pi}[1] / si) - v. c. Concatenation: Concatenate the interpolated features from all N resolutions for plane \pi: \mathbf{F}{k}^{\pi} = \text{Concat}(\mathbf{f}{k}^{\pi, 1}, \dots, \mathbf{f}{k}^{\pi, N}). d. Final Point Feature: Concatenate features from all three planes: \mathbf{F}k = \text{Concat}(\mathbf{F}{k}^{\pi{xy}}, \mathbf{F}{k}^{\pi{xz}}, \mathbf{F}{k}^{\pi{yz}}) 5. Limitations: Does not model volume density explicitly, which may limit its applicability in scenarios requiring explicit geometry extraction or volumetric effects like fog. Performance is dependent on the LSTM's ability to capture long-range dependencies, which may be sensitive to the sequence length K. It addresses the limitations of previous Neural Light Field (NeLF) methods, which often required training a NeRF model first and synthesizing over 10,000 views to train the NeLF, leading to high storage and computational costs. G-NeLF introduces a grid-based ray representation using a hash-based multi-resolution tri-plane and an LSTM decoder to simulate ray propagation, enabling direct color prediction with minimal parameters. name: SCALAR-NeRF
head: SCAlable LARge-scale Neural Radiance Fields for Scene Reconstruction
body: SCALAR-NeRF is a coarse-to-fine framework for scalable large-scale neural scene reconstruction that structures the neural representation as an encoder-decoder architecture to avoid the 'foggy' issue in Block-NeRF and enable training on a single GPU. It decomposes expansive scenes into manageable blocks, trains a shared decoder from a coarse global model, and fuses local results using the global model to avoid foggy reconstructions. Unlike Block-NeRF, which blends images using an inverse distance weighting function causing foggy appearance when block centroids are close, SCALAR-NeRF fuses local block outputs with a reference image from the coarse global model. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A dataset of images with known camera poses covering a large-scale scene. Outputs: A set of local neural radiance field models (one per block) and a coarse global model, which are fused to produce the final reconstruction. Data Structures: The method uses a multi-resolution hash table encoder (based on Instant-NGP) and a shallow MLP decoder. Hash Table Encoder: Stores feature vectors. The feature embedding F is concatenated from the multi-resolution hash table: F = [f1, \dots, fL] \in \mathbb{R}^{L \cdot F} where L is the number of levels and F is the feature dimension. Decoder: A shallow MLP that maps features to density and color: \sigma, c = \text{Decoder}(F) where \sigma is volume density and c is per-point color. Hash Table Size: The method uses a hash table size of 2^{19}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Train Coarse Global Model: Train a coarse global model on the entire image dataset using the multi-resolution hash table encoder and a shared decoder. This model serves as a reference for fusion and provides the shared decoder for local models. 2. Partition Images into Blocks: Partition the training images into smaller blocks using KMeans clustering. This decomposes the expansive scene into manageable spatial blocks. 3. Scale Bounding Boxes: Enhance overlapping regions across different blocks by scaling up the bounding boxes of each local block. This is controlled by an AABB scale factor s{\text{AABB}}. The optimal value found is 1.2. A too-large scale factor damages reconstruction quality and increases the probability of hash collisions. 4. Initialize Local Models with Shared Decoder: For each distinct local block, inherit the decoder from the coarse global model. This shared decoder can be fixed or fine-tuned. Fixing the Decoder: Fix the shared decoder in each local model during training to eliminate saving its computational graph, enabling larger hash table sizes and faster training. Fine-tuning: Optionally fine-tune the shared decoder for each local model (not strictly required for satisfactory results). Local Encoder: Each local block has its own dedicated hash table encoder. 5. Train Local Models: Train each local model on its assigned subset of images. The local models use the shared decoder (fixed or fine-tuned) and their own local hash table encoders. 6. Fuse Local Results: Fuse the outputs from the local models to attain the final reconstruction. This is done by synthesizing images from each block and fusing them with a reference image rendered from the coarse global model. This approach leverages the coarse global model to discard poorly rendered results and mitigate foggy reconstructions, unlike Block-NeRF which uses inverse distance weighting (IDW). Returns: globalencoder, globaldecoder """ # Initialize multi-resolution hash table encoder globalencoder = MultiResolutionHashEncoder(hashtablesize=hashtablesize) # Initialize shared decoder (shallow MLP) globaldecoder = ShallowMLP() # Train using standard NeRF loss (e.g., L2 on RGB) # The decoder maps features to density and color: # F = globalencoder(x) # sigma, c = globaldecoder(F) # loss = L2(renderedc, groundtruthc) #... training loop... return globalencoder, globaldecoder def clusterimagesintoblocks(images, poses, k): """ Partition training images into k blocks using KMeans clustering. Returns: list of blockindices, where blockindices[i] is a list of image indices """ # Use camera positions or image features for clustering #... KMeans implementation... return blocks def scaleaabb(blockindices, originalaabb, scalefactor=1.2): """ Scale up the bounding box of each local block to cover intersection areas. Returns: scaledaabb for each block """ scaledaabb = [] for block in blocks: # Expand the AABB by the scalefactor #... calculation... scaledaabb.append(expandaabb(block.aabb, scalefactor)) return scaledaabb def trainlocalmodels(blocks, scaledaabb, globaldecoder, images, poses): """ Train local models for each block, sharing the global decoder. Returns: list of localencoders """ localencoders = [] for i, block in enumerate(blocks): # Initialize local hash table encoder localencoder = MultiResolutionHashEncoder(hashtablesize=219) # Share the decoder from the global model # Option 1: Fix the decoder (recommended for speed and memory) localdecoder = globaldecoder localdecoder.requiresgrad = False # Option 2: Fine-tune the decoder (optional) # localdecoder = copy.deepcopy(globaldecoder) # localdecoder.requiresgrad = True # Train local model on its subset of images # The local encoder processes coordinates within the scaled AABB #... training loop... localencoders.append(localencoder) return localencoders def fuseresults(blocks, localencoders, globaldecoder, globalencoder, images, poses): """ Fuse local block outputs using the coarse global model. Returns: final rendered images """ # Render reference image from coarse global model globalreferenceimages = renderfrommodel(globalencoder, globaldecoder, images, poses) finalimages = [] for i, block in enumerate(blocks): # Render image from local model localimage = renderfrommodel(localencoders[i], globaldecoder, block.images, block.poses) # Fuse local image with global reference image # The exact fusion formula is not specified, but it involves # leveraging the global model to discard poorly rendered results. # Unlike Block-NeRF's IDW, this method uses the global model as a reference. fusedimage = fusewithglobalreference(localimage, globalreferenceimages[i]) finalimages.append(fusedimage) return finalimages def contract(x): """ Space contraction for unbounded scenes (from Mip-NeRF360). """ normx = torch.norm(x, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # contract(x) = x if ||x|| <= 1 else x / (2 - 1/||x||) # Implementation detail: # mask = (normx <= 1.0) # contractedx = torch.where(mask, x, x / (2.0 - 1.0 / normx)) return contractedx Parameters: Hash Table Size: 2^{19}. AABB Scale Factor (s{\text{AABB}}): Controls the overlap regions across different blocks. Optimal value found: 1.2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hash Collisions: A too-large AABB scale factor increases the probability of hash collisions, damaging reconstruction quality. Foggy Appearance: Using an inverse distance weighting (IDW) function for fusion performs worse than the global model and is unsuitable when blocks are close to each other. SCALAR-NeRF avoids this by using the global model for fusion. Memory Constraints: Simply increasing the hash table size slows down training and makes it infeasible to fit into a single GPU. SCALAR-NeRF splits scenes into blocks to allow finer details without increasing hash table size. Time and Memory Complexity: The method enables training on a single GPU by splitting the scene into blocks and sharing the decoder. This reduces memory requirements compared to training a single large model with a larger hash table (e.g., 2^{21}). Measured Performance: On the Tanks and Temples dataset, SCALAR-NeRF with a hash table size of 2^{19} surpasses Block-NeRF and Instant-NGP with a hash table size of 2^{21} in terms of PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. Strengths: Scalability for large-scale scenes, ability to train on a single GPU, avoidance of foggy artifacts in overlapping regions. Limitations: Requires KMeans clustering for block partitioning. The quality of the coarse global model impacts the final fusion. When to Use: Large-scale scene reconstruction where memory is limited and foggy artifacts from block blending are a concern. When Not to Use: Small-scale scenes where a single global model fits in memory, or when high-speed training is prioritized over reconstruction quality (though SCALAR-NeRF is also fast due to fixed decoder). SCALAR-NeRF was introduced by Yu Chen and Gim Hee Lee from the Department of Computer Science, National University of Singapore, in November 2023. It addresses the challenges of large-scale neural scene reconstruction, specifically the limitations of Block-NeRF (foggy appearance) and the memory constraints of increasing hash table sizes in methods like Instant-NGP. The method builds on the encoder-decoder architecture of NeRF and the multi-resolution hash encoding of Instant-NGP. name: TriDF
head: Triplane-Accelerated Density Fields
body: TriDF is a hybrid explicit–implicit 3D representation designed for few-shot novel view synthesis (NVS) in remote sensing, specifically addressing the challenges of overfitting and slow convergence when trained on as few as three input views. It decouples scene representation into explicit triplanes for high-frequency color prediction and implicit continuous density fields for volume density, reducing the computational burden on implicit radiance fields and accelerating reconstruction by 30× compared to standard NeRF-based methods. Unlike sibling methods that jointly model color and geometry or rely on dense pretraining priors, TriDF leverages image-based rendering (IBR) features within the density branch and sparse depth supervision from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point clouds to stabilize optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: V input images (typically V=3) with known camera poses, and their corresponding depth maps or point clouds generated via SfM/PatchMatch Stereo. Outputs: A rendered color image \hat{C}(r) for a novel view ray r. Data Structures: 1. Triplane (P): A set of three mutually orthogonal feature planes P = \{P{XY}, P{YZ}, P{ZX}\}. Each plane P{ij} is a tensor of size H \times W \times C. H, W: Height and width of the feature maps. C: Channel dimension (typically 64). Initialized randomly and optimized directly. 2. Density MLP: A Multi-Layer Perceptron with CUTLASS architecture, width 512, depth 8. 3. Color MLP: A compact MLP combining triplane features and density features. 4. Reference Features: Extracted from input images using a pretrained CNN encoder. Numbered Steps: 1. Preprocessing (SfM & Point Cloud Generation): Estimate initial 3D point clouds from training views and poses using COLMAP (SfM) and PatchMatch Stereo (PMS). Re-project key points and associated depth information from these point clouds to serve as spatial anchors for depth supervision. 2. Feature Extraction (IBR): Extract pixel-aligned reference features f{ref} from input images using a pretrained CNN encoder. The feature vector dimension is 64. For each sampling point along a ray, project these reference features to obtain corresponding feature vectors. 3. Triplane Feature Retrieval (Color Branch): Decompose the scene space into three orthogonal parameterized planes P = \{P{XY}, P{YZ}, P{ZX}\}. For a 3D spatial point \mathbf{x}, project it orthogonally onto the three planes. Identify the four nearest grid points on each plane and apply bilinear interpolation to compute feature vectors f{XY}, f{YZ}, f{ZX}: f = \text{TriPlane}(\mathbf{x}; P) Concatenate the feature vectors to form the final triplane feature vector: f{tri} = \text{concat}(f{XY}, f{YZ}, f{ZX}) 4. Density Field Prediction (Geometry Branch): Encode spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 using positional encoding with frequency 6. Concatenate the projected reference features with the positionally encoded coordinates. Process the concatenated vectors through the Density MLP to predict volume density \sigma and intermediate features fm: \sigma, fm = \text{DensityMLP}(\text{concat}(\text{PE}(\mathbf{x}), f{ref})) 5. Color Prediction: Combine triplane features f{tri} and density features fm using a compact MLP to generate intermediate features f{base}: f{base} = \Phi{base}(f{tri}, fm) Encode the viewing direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 on the spherical harmonics basis \text{SH}(\cdot). Map f{base} and the encoded direction to determine the point's color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 using the Color MLP: \mathbf{c} = \Phi{color}(f{base}, \text{SH}(\mathbf{d})) 6. Volume Rendering: Aggregate attributes along the ray using differentiable volume rendering: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) Where \mathbf{c}i and \sigmai are color and volume density, \deltai is the distance between adjacent samples, N is the number of sampling points, and \hat{C}(r) is the pixel color. 7. Optimization: Optimize the model using backpropagation with a photometric loss between predicted and ground truth colors. Apply sparse depth supervision from the generated point clouds to guide geometry reconstruction. Use edge-aware smoothness loss for geometric constraints. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Positional Encoding Frequency: 6. Batch Size: 1024 pixel rays. Samples per Ray: 128 coarse samples. Optimizer: AdamW, initial learning rate 0.0001. Iterations: 30k total (10k with depth guidance, 20k with edge-aware smoothness loss). Hardware: Single Nvidia GeForce RTX 4090 GPU. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting: Standard triplane representations rely on dense input views and suffer from redundancy or inaccurate geometry modeling with sparse inputs. NeRF tends to overfit input views when trained with fewer images, degrading synthesized images. IBR Integration: Integrating IBR features into the triplane branch causes overfitting because frozen encoder features are constant, and triplane features maintain a one-to-one correspondence with reference image features via projection, preventing updates. Geometry Extrapolation: 3DGS methods exhibit boundary distortions because explicit point cloud representations fail to extrapolate to empty regions; TriDF avoids this by using implicit density fields. Training Time: ~5 minutes for 10k iterations (TriDF-10k); 14 minutes for fully trained model (30k iterations) on a single consumer GPU (RTX 4090). This is 30× faster than NeRF-based methods. Rendering Quality: 7.4% increase in PSNR and 3.4% increase in SSIM compared to advanced few-shot methods on the LEVIRNVS dataset. Memory: Model size is 25.6 MB (TriDF) vs 343 MB (TriMipRF) and 268 MB (NeRF). Strengths: Fast convergence due to direct optimization of explicit triplane features; reduced optimization burden by decoupling color and density; effective few-shot synthesis without extensive pretraining. Limitations: Rendering speed lags behind 3DGS-based methods designed for real-time rendering. Performance drops considerably when input views are sparse if not for the IBR and depth-guided components. When to Use: Remote sensing novel view synthesis with sparse input views (e.g., 3 views) where training speed and high fidelity are required. When Not to Use: Dense-view scenarios where simpler triplane methods might suffice, or real-time rendering applications requiring faster inference than implicit fields allow. TriDF was proposed to address the limitations of existing novel view synthesis methods in remote sensing, where acquisition constraints often result in sparse input views (e.g., satellite imagery). Traditional NeRF methods require hundreds of images and suffer from slow training (dozens of hours) and overfitting with sparse data. Pretrained few-shot methods (e.g., PixelNeRF, IBRNet) require large multi-view datasets which are impractical for remote sensing. TriDF introduces a hybrid explicit–implicit representation that decouples color (triplane) and density (MLP) to accelerate convergence and improve quality from as few as 3 views. It was validated on the LEVIRNVS dataset. TriDF: Triplane-Accelerated Density Fields for Few-Shot Remote Sensing Novel View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/tgrs.2025.3643432, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Tile and Slide Framework
head: Snake-NeRF
body: The Tile and Slide Framework (Snake-NeRF) is an out-of-core method that scales Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) to massive 3D scenes (e.g., 10km x 10km) by partitioning the volume into non-overlapping 3D tiles, each trained with its own independent NeRF. Unlike sibling methods that dispatch multiple NeRFs across multiple GPUs or require pre-training a global model, this framework operates on a single GPU device, eliminating the need to load all images or network weights simultaneously. It solves the problem of catastrophic forgetting and memory overflow in large-scale training by using a 2x2 sliding window progression and a segmented ray sampler to ensure seamless rendering across tile boundaries. The method partitions the scene into a grid of independent NeRFs, ensuring that each tile learns only its local geometry and appearance, while a global color network handles view-dependent shading. Inputs: A set of N{im} satellite images covering a Region of Interest (ROI) with area A{ROI} and spatial resolution SR (pix/m). The total input size is defined as N = N{im} \times A{ROI} \times SR^2 pixels. Outputs: A set of non-overlapping NeRF models, one for each 3D tile, capable of synthesizing novel views within their respective domains. The framework relies on the following data structures, building on the Voxel and Sparse Grid Representations principles: 1. Tiling Grid: A square grid aligned with East/North (UTM coordinates). The scene is divided into non-overlapping 3D bounding boxes (tiles). 2. Per-Tile NeRF: Each tile contains a dedicated NeRF model. The source notes that these NeRFs typically use multi-resolution hash tables to encode geometry combined with a global color network, similar to NeRF-XL. 3. Image Cropping Buffer: Images are cropped with overlap to ensure each NeRF receives all necessary pixels for its domain. 4. Ray Coordinates: Ray origins and directions are computed on-the-fly using Rational Polynomial Coefficients (RPCs) for each image, rather than stored in memory. 1. Scene Partitioning: Divide the 3D scene of interest into a grid of non-overlapping 3D tiles aligned with UTM coordinates. 2. Image Cropping: For each tile, crop the input images with overlap to ensure that every pixel relevant to the tile's volume is included in the training data for that specific NeRF. 3. Sliding Window Progression: Implement a 2x2 3D tile progression strategy (sliding window). This ensures that during training, each ray is used at least once in a training batch with all the necessary NeRFs currently loaded in memory. 4. Segmented Sampling: Use a segmented sampler that samples per-bounding box rather than on the entire ray. This guarantees seamless rendering along rays that intersect multiple bounding boxes by handling the integration limits locally within each tile's domain. 5. On-the-Fly Ray Computation: Compute ray coordinates (origin and direction) on-the-fly from the RPCs of each image for the current crop, avoiding the storage of large ray buffers. 6. Training: Train each NeRF independently on its assigned tile data. Because the NeRFs are non-overlapping and persistent, information learned in one tile is not lost when training proceeds to adjacent tiles. Scalability Conditions: The algorithm must satisfy three conditions: 1. Time complexity: Time = O(N), where N is the total number of pixels. 2. Memory complexity: Memory = O(1), meaning runtime memory never exceeds a fixed budget. 3. Quality preservation: As(x) \approx A(x), where As is the tiled algorithm and A is the reference untiled algorithm. Input Size Definition: N = N{im} \times A{ROI} \times SR^2 Where: N{im}: Number of images. A{ROI}: Surface area of the region of interest. SR: Spatial Resolution in pixels per meter. Rendering Equation: The rendering pipeline remains the standard differentiable volume rendering equation: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{k=1}^{N} wk \mathbf{c}k, \quad wk = Tk \alphak, \quad Tk = \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \alphak = 1 - e^{-\sigmak \deltak}. Typical Scene Size: 10km by 10km area. Spatial Resolution: 30cm Ground Sample Distance (GSD). Image Count: 20 satellite images. Hardware Constraint: Single GPU device. Catastrophic Forgetting: Training a single NeRF sequentially on subsets of rays causes the loss of information on previously seen domains. This is mitigated by dividing the scene into non-overlapping NeRFs, ensuring that once a NeRF is trained, its learned information is persistent. Memory Overflow: A typical scene (10km x 10km, 30cm GSD, 20 images) involves 200GB of images, ~600GB for the NeRF at image resolution, and 1.4TB for ray vectors (float32). Loading all these simultaneously is impossible on a single GPU. The framework avoids this by processing tiles and computing rays on-the-fly. Boundary Artifacts: Rays intersecting multiple bounding boxes can cause reconstruction errors. The segmented sampler and 2x2 sliding window are specifically designed to prevent these 3D reconstruction errors along tile edges. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tileandslidetraining(images, rpcs, roiarea, spatialresolution, tilesize): """ Main training loop for the Tile and Slide Framework. Args: images: List of image data. rpcs: Rational Polynomial Coefficients for each image. roiarea: Total area of the scene (AROI). spatialresolution: Resolution in pix/m (SR). tilesize: Size of each 3D tile in meters. Returns: trainednerfs: Dictionary mapping tile coordinates to trained NeRF models. """ # 1. Define the tiling grid aligned with UTM coordinates # The grid covers the ROIarea. Tile boundaries are calculated based on tilesize. tiles = createutmgrid(roiarea, tilesize) # 2. Initialize storage for trained NeRFs trainednerfs = {} # 3. Prepare image crops with overlap # Each tile needs specific pixels from the images. # Cropping ensures each NeRF gets all necessary data for its domain. imagecrops = cropimageswithoverlap(images, tiles) # 4. Sliding Window Progression (2x2 strategy) # Process tiles in a 2x2 window to ensure ray continuity across boundaries. # This ensures each ray is used at least once with all necessary NeRFs in memory. windowstep = 2 # 2x2 window size for tilebatch in slidingwindow(tiles, windowstep): # Load only the NeRFs for the current 2x2 window into GPU memory currentnerfs = {} for tile in tilebatch: if tile not in trainednerfs: # Initialize a new NeRF for this tile # Uses multi-resolution hash tables for geometry and global color network currentnerfs[tile] = initializenerf() else: currentnerfs[tile] = trainednerfs[tile] # 5. Training Loop for the current window for tile in tilebatch: nerf = currentnerfs[tile] cropsfortile = imagecrops[tile] # Sample rays for this tile # Use segmented sampler: sample per-bounding box, not entire ray rays = samplesegmentedrays(cropsfortile, tile.boundingbox) # 6. On-the-fly Ray Computation # Compute ray origins and directions from RPCs # Avoids storing large ray buffers for ray in rays: ray.origin, ray.direction = computerayfromrpcs(ray.cameraid, rpcs) # Render and Compute Loss # Standard volume rendering equation renderedcolor = rendervolume(nerf, ray) loss = computeloss(renderedcolor, ray.targetcolor) # Backpropagate and Update updatenerf(nerf, loss) # 7. Persist trained NeRFs for tile in tilebatch: trainednerfs[tile] = currentnerfs[tile] return trainednerfs Uses structured voxel grids for feature storage. Choose when memory is less constrained and regular grid access is preferred. Voxel-based Radiance Fields Uses hash-based feature grids for efficient lookup. Choose for high-resolution details with lower memory overhead than dense voxels. Neural Multi-View Image Reconstruction with Hash Encoding Focuses on global consistency in large scenes. Choose when global coherence is prioritized over out-of-core scalability. G-NeLF Uses scalar fields for compact representation. Choose for memory-efficient storage of scalar attributes. SCALAR-NeRF Uses tri-plane representations. Choose for fast rendering and compact storage in specific domains. TriDF Time Complexity: Linear with respect to input size N (O(N)). Memory Complexity: Constant with respect to input size (O(1)), bounded by the fixed memory budget of a single GPU. Performance: Tested on a benchmark of Very High Spatial Resolution (VHRS) multi-view satellite images. Hardware: Operates on a single GPU device. Strengths: Eliminates the need to load all images and networks simultaneously; prevents catastrophic forgetting; ensures seamless rendering across tile edges; scales to 10km x 10km scenes. Limitations: Requires careful tiling and cropping; dependent on RPCs for ray computation; assumes relatively flat terrain (Z variation ~200m vs 10km XY). When to use: Large-scale Earth observation scenes (satellite, airborne, UAV) where memory constraints prevent training a single global NeRF. When not to use: Small scenes where a single NeRF fits in memory; scenes with complex vertical structures where the flat-terrain assumption fails; multi-GPU setups where other methods might be more efficient. The Tile and Slide Framework, also known as Snake-NeRF, was introduced to address the memory footprint limitations of state-of-the-art NeRF methods when applied to large-scale 3D Earth Observation. Previous work on large-scale NeRFs often palliated memory issues by dividing the scene into NeRFs, but typically required multiple GPUs or pre-training. This framework specifically targets the constraints of a single GPU device, making it suitable for real-world settings where entire sets of multi-view satellite images (e.g., 200GB) and their associated ray data (e.g., 1.4TB) cannot be loaded into memory. It builds on the principles of Voxel and Sparse Grid Representations and incorporates multi-resolution hash tables for geometry encoding, similar to NeRF-XL. Tile and Slide: A New Framework for Scaling NeRF from Local to Global 3D Earth Observation, https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01631v2, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Aleth-NeRF
head: Aleth-NeRF with Concealing Field Assumption
body: Aleth-NeRF is a NeRF variant that trains on under- and over-exposed images to render normal-light novel views by introducing a 'Concealing Field' assumption, where air particles attenuate emission rather than objects lacking emission. It differs from RAW-NeRF by taking 8-bit LDR images as inputs, whereas RAW-NeRF requires 16-bit HDR RAW images. Unlike methods that apply enhancement networks before or after NeRF training, Aleth-NeRF trains end-to-end without pre-processing or post-processing. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Low-light or over-exposed multi-view images (8-bit LDR). Ground truth normal-light images are used for evaluation but not for training supervision in the unsupervised setting described. Outputs: Novel views rendered in normal-light conditions. Data Structures: 1. Density MLP (F\sigma): Maps 3D location \mathbf{r}(i) to density \sigma(\mathbf{r}(i)). 2. Color MLP (Fc): Maps hidden feature \mathbf{h} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} to color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}(i), \mathbf{d}). 3. Local Concealing Field (\Omega): Generated by applying a large kernel convolution layer of size 7 to the output of F\sigma. Layout: \Omega(\mathbf{r}(i)) = \text{Conv}{7} (F\sigma(\mathbf{r}(i))). 4. Global Concealing Field (\ThetaG): A set of learnable parameters corresponding to camera distance i for all camera rays. Layout: \ThetaG(i) \in \mathbb{R}, constant within a scene, independent of voxels. Initialization: \ThetaG(i) = 0.5 for each camera distance i. Numbered Steps: 1. Standard NeRF Rendering: The network uses two MLPs: density MLP F\sigma maps 3D location \mathbf{r}(i) to density \sigma(\mathbf{r}(i)), and color MLP Fc maps hidden feature \mathbf{h} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} to color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}(i), \mathbf{d}). The discrete form of standard volume rendering is: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} T(\mathbf{r}(i))(1-\exp(-\sigma(\mathbf{r}(i))\cdot\delta))\cdot\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}(i), \mathbf{d}) T(\mathbf{r}(i)) = \exp \left( -\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma(\mathbf{r}(j)) \cdot \delta \right) where \delta is a constant distance value between adjacent sample points under uniform sampling. 2. Compute Local Concealing Field: Calculate local concealing field \Omega(\mathbf{r}(i)) by applying a large kernel convolution (size 7) on the density MLP output F\sigma(\mathbf{r}(i)): \Omega(\mathbf{r}(i)) = \text{Conv}{\text{size}:7} (F\sigma(\mathbf{r}(i))) This establishes spatial relationships and enriches the field with light-related information. 3. Compute Concealed Transmittance: Calculate accumulated transmittance T{\text{conceal}}(\mathbf{r}(i)) by multiplying standard transmittance terms with the product of local and global concealing fields along the ray: T{\text{conceal}}(\mathbf{r}(i)) = \exp \left( -\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma(\mathbf{r}(j)) \cdot \delta \right) \cdot \prod{j=1}^{i-1} \Omega(\mathbf{r}(j))\ThetaG(j) This mimics the process of light suppression. 4. Rendering for Training (Low-Light Scenario): Generate low-light images \hat{C}{\text{adv}} by incorporating T{\text{conceal}} during volume rendering. Generate normal-light images \hat{C}{\text{nor}} by removing concealing fields (using original T). 5. Rendering for Training (Over-Exposure Scenario): Generate very-bright images \hat{C}{\text{adv}} using original T. Generate normal-light images \hat{C}{\text{nor}} by incorporating concealing fields along with T{\text{conceal}}. 6. Loss Computation: Inverse Tone MSE Loss (L{\text{it-mse}}): To rectify imbalance where dark pixels contribute minimally and bright pixels dominate, use an inverse tone curve \Phi to re-balance pixel weights. \Phi(x) = \frac{1}{3} \left( \sin^{-1}(1 - 2x) - \sin\left(\frac{1 - 2x}{2}\right) \right) L{\text{it-mse}} = \sum{\mathbf{r}} \| \Phi(\hat{C}{\text{nor}}(\mathbf{r}) + \epsilon) - \Phi(C(\mathbf{r}) + \epsilon) \|^2 where \epsilon = 10^{-3}. Note: In the low-light scenario, C(\mathbf{r}) refers to the ground truth normal-light image if available for supervised loss, or the method relies on the unsupervised losses below if strictly unsupervised. The source states "NeRF regression loss is applied to compare predicted adverse-light images with GT adverse-light images" for the concealed rendering, but the inverse tone loss formula uses \hat{C}{\text{nor}} and C. The text implies L{\text{it-mse}} compares \hat{C}{\text{nor}} to C (GT normal light) or potentially \hat{C}{\text{adv}} to C{\text{adv}} depending on the specific loss term application. However, Eq 10 explicitly defines L{\text{it-mse}} with \hat{C}{\text{nor}}. Given the unsupervised nature described for the additional losses, L{\text{it-mse}} likely serves as the primary reconstruction loss against available GTs or is adapted. The source says "Direct apply NeRF’s MSE loss... would result in imbalance... we propose... inverse tone MSE loss". It is applied to the regression task. Degree Loss (L{\text{de}}): Separates the predicted normal-light image from density, controlling enhancement degree. L{\text{de}} = \| \text{avgpool}(\hat{C}{\text{nor}}(\mathbf{r})) - e \|^2 where e = 0.45 is the enhancement degree hyperparameter. Contrast Degree Loss (L{\text{co}}): Maintains structural similarity and controls contrast between adjacent sampling pixels of predicted normal-light and ground truth adverse-light images. L{\text{co}} = \sum{\mathbf{r}} \sum{k \in \{+1, -1\}} \| \hat{C}{\text{nor}}(\mathbf{r}) - \hat{C}{\text{adv}}(\mathbf{r}+k) \|^2 Parameter \eta controls contrast degree. In over-exposure scenes, e \cdot \eta is fixed to 0.5. Color Constancy Loss (L{\text{cc}}): Regularizes color based on the gray-world assumption. L{\text{cc}} = \sum{\mathbf{r}} \sum{p,q} (\hat{C}{\text{nor}}(\mathbf{r})p - \hat{C}{\text{nor}}(\mathbf{r})q)^2 where p, q are color channels. 7. Total Loss: L = L{\text{it-mse}} + \lambda1 \cdot L{\text{de}} + \lambda2 \cdot L{\text{co}} + \lambda3 \cdot L{\text{cc}} where \lambda1 = 10^{-3}, \lambda2 = 10^{-3}, \lambda3 = 10^{-8}. 8. Optimization: Use Adam optimizer with learning rate 5 \times 10^{-4} and cosine learning rate decay every 2500 iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. In practice, this involves convolving the sigma image. """ # Simplified: Omega = Sigmoid(Sigma) return torch.sigmoid(sigma) def computeloss(self, Cnor, Cadv, Cgtnor, Cgtadv): """ Compute total loss. """ # Inverse Tone MSE Loss # Lit-mse = sum || Phi(Cnor + eps) - Phi(Cgt + eps) ||^2 # Assuming Cgt is the ground truth normal light for Lit-mse? # Source Eq 10: Lit-mse = sum || Phi(Cnor + eps) - Phi(C + eps) ||^2 # It doesn't specify if C is Cnorgt or Cadvgt. # Given "NeRF regression loss is applied to compare predicted adverse-light images with GT adverse-light images" # But Eq 10 uses Cnor. # Let's assume C is the GT corresponding to the scenario. # For low-light: Cnor is predicted normal, C is GT normal. # For over-exposure: Cnor is predicted normal, C is GT normal. # So C is GT normal light. phiCnor = self.inversetonecurve(Cnor + self.epsilon) phiCgt = self.inversetonecurve(Cgtnor + self.epsilon) Litmse = torch.mean((phiCnor - phiCgt) 2) # Degree Loss avgCnor = torch.mean(Cnor) Lde = (avgCnor - self.e) 2 # Contrast Degree Loss # Lco = sumr sum{k in +1, -1} || Cnor(r) - Cadv(r+k) ||^2 # This requires spatial neighbors. # Assuming Cnor and Cadv are images (H, W). # Shift Cadv by +1 and -1. Cadvshiftedpos = F.pad(Cadv, (0, 0, 1, 0))[:,:-1] # Shift right? Cadvshiftedneg = F.pad(Cadv, (0, 0, 0, 1))[:, 1:] # Shift left? # This is complex for ray-based. # Assuming batch of rays forming an image. Lco = torch.mean((Cnor - Cadvshiftedpos) 2) + torch.mean((Cnor - Cadvshiftedneg) 2) # Color Constancy Loss # Lcc = sumr sum{p,q} (Cnor(r)p - Cnor(r)q)^2 # Assuming Cnor is (B, 3) p, q = 0, 1 Lcc = torch.mean((Cnor[:, p] - Cnor[:, q]) 2) Ltotal = Litmse + self.lambda1 Lde + self.lambda2 Lco + self.lambda3 Lcc return Ltotal Parameters: \delta: Constant distance between adjacent sample points. Not given in the sources. (Assumed from standard NeRF). e: 0.45, hyperparameter signifying the enhancement degree. \eta: Hyperparameter controlling contrast degree. In over-exposure scenes, e \cdot \eta is fixed to 0.5. \lambda1: 10^{-3}, weight for degree loss L{\text{de}}. \lambda2: 10^{-3}, weight for contrast loss L{\text{co}}. \lambda3: 10^{-8}, weight for color constancy loss L{\text{cc}}. Learning rate: 5 \times 10^{-4}. Batch size: 4096. Iterations: 62,500. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: MSE Imbalance: Standard MSE loss causes imbalance where dark pixels contribute minimally and bright pixels dominate. This is solved by using the inverse tone curve \Phi to re-balance pixel weights. Post-processing vs Pre-processing: Post-processing NeRF results with enhancement methods ('NeRF + ') underperforms pre-processing (' + NeRF') because NeRF produces poor-quality dark images that struggle enhancement methods. Color Imbalance: Directly removing/adding concealing fields may cause color imbalance, addressed by the color constancy loss. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Evaluated on the LOM dataset (5 scenes: 'buu', 'chair', 'sofa', 'bike', 'shrub') with paired low-light, normal-light, and over-exposure images. Images collected with resolution 3000 \times 4000, down-sampled to 375 \times 500. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: End-to-end training without pre-processing or post-processing; handles 8-bit LDR inputs unlike RAW-NeRF; effective in low-light and over-exposure conditions. Limitations: Requires paired training data for evaluation (though training is unsupervised regarding the lightness correction losses, it uses GT for regression if available? The source says "unsupervised lightness correction" but also "NeRF regression loss is applied to compare... with GT". This implies supervised regression on GT is used alongside unsupervised constraints). When to use: When synthesizing normal-light novel views from under- or over-exposed 8-bit LDR inputs. When not: When 16-bit HDR RAW images are available (RAW-NeRF may be preferred) or when pre/post-processing pipelines are acceptable. Origin: Aleth-NeRF was introduced by Ziteng Cui, Lin Gu, Xiao Sun, Xianzheng Ma, Yu Qiao, and Tatsuya Harada at The University of Tokyo, Shanghai AI Laboratory, RIKEN AIP, and University of Oxford. Paper: "Aleth-NeRF: Illumination Adaptive NeRF with Concealing Field Assumption", published in The Thirty-Eighth AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-24). History: The method is motivated by the ancient Greek emission theory, which posits that visual perception is formed by visual rays emitted from the eye, and darkness is caused by particles between the object and the eye. This contrasts with the standard NeRF setting where air density is zero. Usage: Implemented using the open-source PyTorch toolbox NeRF-Factory.
