name: Transformer and Vision Model Integration
head: Vision-Transformer NeRF, ViT-NeRF family
body: This family integrates Vision Transformers (ViT) and other vision backbones into Neural Radiance Fields to improve feature extraction from input images. It solves the limitation of standard NeRF architectures, which rely on simple positional encoding and lack semantic understanding, by providing rich global or local image features to condition the radiance field. Unlike pure geometric methods, these models leverage the self-attention mechanism of Transformers to capture long-range dependencies, addressing issues like self-occlusion and inconsistent appearance in novel view synthesis. The core mechanism replaces or augments the standard positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}) and directional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{d}) with features extracted from a pre-trained or fine-tuned vision model. 1. Feature Extraction: An input image I is processed by a vision backbone (ViT, CNN, or hybrid) to produce feature maps or tokens. 2. Spatial Alignment: For a 3D point \mathbf{x} sampled along a ray, its 2D projection \pi(\mathbf{x}) on the input image plane is computed. 3. Feature Query: The feature value F(\pi(\mathbf{x})) is sampled from the extracted feature maps at the projected location. 4. Conditioning: The radiance field MLP takes the spatial position \mathbf{x}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and the sampled feature F(\pi(\mathbf{x})) as input to predict density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Combines a ViT for global shape information and a 2D CNN for local appearance. It fuses these into a hybrid feature map to condition rendering. It is chosen when single-view synthesis requires both global semantic consistency and local detail, avoiding the inconsistent appearance of pure global methods. Infers a 3D radiance field from a single unposed image. It uses ViT self-attention to retrieve features for occluded regions, mitigating self-occlusion degradation. It is chosen when camera poses are unknown and occlusion handling is critical. A generalizable method that learns a generic scene representation from multiple source views without per-scene optimization. It uses an encoder-decoder Transformer to explore deep relationships among source views. It is chosen for cross-scene generalization where per-scene training is prohibitive. Transfers visual attributes (appearance) from a source NeRF to a target NeRF using dense semantic correspondences from ViT features. It is chosen for appearance transfer without requiring geometric alignment between scenes. The integration of Transformers into NeRFs emerged to address the inability of standard MLPs to leverage high-level semantic information from input images. Early works like ViT-NeRF demonstrated that combining global ViT features with local CNN features improved rendering quality over pure global or local approaches. Subsequent works extended this to unposed single-view synthesis VisionNeRF and generalizable multi-view settings TransNeRF. The use of semantic features for cross-scene manipulation, such as in NeRF Analogies, further expanded the utility of vision models beyond direct rendering. Transformer and Vision Model Integration Notes, 2023

name: ViT-NeRF
head: Global-Local Feature NeRF, Hybrid ViT-CNN NeRF, Vision Transformer for NeRF (ViT-NeRF)
body: ViT-NeRF is a view synthesis method that combines a Vision Transformer (ViT) to encode global shape information and a 2D CNN to extract local appearance features, conditioning volume rendering on hybrid per-pixel features. It addresses the limitation of pure global feature methods (which suffer from inconsistent appearance near input views) and pure local feature methods (which lack long-range semantic consistency) by fusing both representations. Unlike CodeNeRF and DISN, it does not require a canonical coordinate system to utilize global features, and compared to SRN and PixelNeRF, it produces sharper edges and clearer structures, particularly on invisible parts like chair legs. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single input image Is \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}, where H and W are height and width. Output: A rendered 2D image \hat{C}(r) for a target viewpoint defined by ray origin o and direction d. Data Structures: Image Tokens: Sequence of flattened 2D patches P \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times P^2 \times 3}, where N = \frac{HW}{P^2} is the number of patches and P is the patch size. Latent Features: Set of latent features f extracted by the ViT encoder. Multi-level Feature Maps: A set of global feature maps W^0G,..., W^JG at different resolutions. Local Feature Map: WL \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{2} \times \frac{W}{2} \times DL} extracted by the CNN. Hybrid Feature Map: W, the fused result of global and local features. Per-pixel Feature: W(\pi(x)), sampled from W at the 2D projection \pi(x) of a 3D point x. Numbered Steps: 1. Tokenization: Reshape input image Is into a sequence of flattened 2D patches. Linearly project each patch to an image token Pl. 2. Global Encoding: Input image tokens and learnable positional embeddings e into the Transformer Encoder to extract global latent features f. 3. Class Token Dropping: Define operation O: \mathbb{R}^{(N+1) \times D} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{N \times D} to drop the class token from f. The class token is useful for self-attention but has no physical meaning when unflattened. 4. Unflattening: Define operation U: \mathbb{R}^{N \times D} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{P} \times \frac{W}{P} \times D} to unflatten the remaining tokens into feature patches Pf = \{P^0f,..., P^Jf\}, where P^jf \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{P} \times \frac{W}{P} \times D}. 5. Global Feature Map Generation: For each level j \in \{0,..., J\}, generate global feature maps W^jG using a convolutional decoder D: W^jG = (D \circ U \circ O)(f^j) The decoder D: \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{P} \times \frac{W}{P} \times D} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{Hj \times Wj \times Dj} performs: (i) 1 \times 1 convolution, (ii) resampling via strided or transposed convolution to size Hj \times Wj, and (iii) 3 \times 3 convolution to Dj channels. 6. Local Feature Extraction: Extract local features WL using a 2D CNN module GL: WL = GL(Is) GL consists of three ResBlocks. WL \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{2} \times \frac{W}{2} \times DL}. 7. Hybrid Feature Fusion: Fuse multi-level global features W^0G,..., W^JG and local feature WL using a convolutional layer G to produce the hybrid feature map W: W = G(W^0G, W^1G,..., W^JG; WL). 8. Ray Sampling: For a target view, sample a ray r(t) = o + td bounded by near plane t{near} and far plane t{far}. Pick equally distributed samples xc along the ray. 9. Feature Sampling: For each 3D sample location xc, compute its 2D projection \pi(x) on the input image plane and sample the hybrid feature W(\pi(x)). 10. Positional Encoding: Encode the 3D location xc using positional encoding \gamma(xc) with M=10 frequency bases: \gamma(p) = (\sin(2^0 \pi p), \cos(2^0 \pi p),..., \sin(2^{M-1} \pi p), \cos(2^{M-1} \pi p)). 11. MLP Prediction: Input \gamma(xc), viewing direction dc, and per-pixel feature W(\pi(x)) into an MLP to output density \sigma and color c: (\sigma, c) = \text{MLP}(\gamma(xc); dc; W(\pi(x))). 12. Volume Rendering: Render the target view using standard volume rendering integral: \hat{C}(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t)\sigma(t)c(t)dt where T(t) = \exp(-\int{tn}^{t} \sigma(r(s))ds) is the accumulated transmittance. Approximate the integral with quadrature. Parameters: Frequency bases (M): 10. Learning Rate: 10^{-4} for the NeRF MLP; 10^{-5} for the ViT and CNN modules. Batch Size: 8 instances, with 512 rays per instance. ViT Initialization: Initialized from pretrained weights of reference [55] and fine-tuned. Warm-up: Linear warm-up from 0 learning rate for the first 10k steps. Pitfalls: Using only global ViT features compromises rendering quality for views close to the input view (inconsistent color/appearance). This is solved by adding the local CNN branch. The class token in ViT has no physical meaning when unflattened into spatial feature maps and must be dropped before decoding. Hardware: Evaluated on 16 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Training Time: Converges at 500K iterations. Strengths: Produces sharper edges and clearer structures than SRN and PixelNeRF, avoiding blurriness on invisible parts like chair legs. Combines the advantage of 2D-based methods (local detail) and 1D-based methods (global information). Limitations: Volume-based methods are computationally intensive and require more memory when increasing grid size. ViT-NeRF was introduced in the paper "Vision Transformer for NeRF-Based View Synthesis from a Single Input Image". It builds on the success of Vision Transformers in learning long-range dependencies between features, applying this to the NeRF framework to improve reconstruction quality in unseen regions. Vision Transformer for NeRF-Based View Synthesis from a Single Input Image, https://doi.org/10.1109/wacv56688.2023.00087, fetched 2026-10-27

name: VisionNeRF
head: Vision Transformer for NeRF
body: VisionNeRF is a novel view synthesis method that infers a 3D radiance field representation from a single unposed input image, addressing the degradation in rendering quality caused by self-occlusion when target views are distant from the source. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like ViT-NeRF and TransNeRF by explicitly combining global semantic features from a Vision Transformer (ViT) with local appearance features from a 2D CNN, enabling the retrieval of relevant features for occluded regions via self-attention rather than relying on geometric alignment or canonical coordinate systems. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single unposed image Is captured at camera s. No camera pose information is required. Output: A rendered novel view image for a target viewpoint defined by a camera pose and intrinsic parameters. Data Structures: 1. Feature Tokens: A sequence of vectors resulting from the ViT encoder. If the input image is H \times W and patch size is P \times P, the number of tokens is N = (H/P) \times (W/P). Each token has dimension D (the ViT embedding dimension). 2. Multi-level Feature Maps: A set of 2D feature maps at different resolutions (coarse-to-fine) derived from the unflattened and resampled tokens. These maps store global information aligned with spatial coordinates. 3. Local Feature Maps: 2D feature maps extracted directly from a CNN backbone, capturing high-frequency local details. 4. Radiance Field MLP: A multi-layer perceptron that takes concatenated global and local features as input and outputs volume density \sigma and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}. Numbered Steps: 1. Global Feature Extraction: Divide the input image Is into non-overlapping patches of size P \times P. Linearly embed each patch into a D-dimensional vector. Add positional embeddings to the patch embeddings. Pass the sequence of embedded patches through a Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder consisting of L transformer blocks. Each block applies multi-head self-attention and a feed-forward network. The output is a sequence of feature tokens \mathbf{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}, where N is the number of patches. 2. Feature Resampling: Unflatten the feature tokens \mathbf{T} into a 2D grid of shape (H/P, W/P, D). Resample these features into multi-level feature maps \{\mathbf{F}g^k\} at various resolutions (e.g., 1/4, 1/8, 1/16 of the original image size) using interpolation or learned upsampling layers. This creates a coarse-to-fine global representation. 3. Local Feature Extraction: Pass the input image Is through a 2D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) backbone (e.g., ResNet). Extract feature maps \mathbf{F}l at corresponding resolutions to the global feature maps. These maps capture local appearance details and high-frequency textures. 4. Volume Rendering: For a target viewpoint, sample points \mathbf{x}i along each camera ray. For each point \mathbf{x}i, query the global feature maps \mathbf{F}g and local feature maps \mathbf{F}l at the 2D projection of \mathbf{x}i onto the input image plane. Note: Since the input is unposed, the projection is implicit or handled via the learned correspondence established by the transformer's attention mechanism during training. Note: The source states the method uses an "explicit mapping between the input image and the 3D point query" via per-pixel information from feature maps, but does not specify the exact geometric projection formula for unposed inputs. It relies on the learned global-local conditioning. Concatenate the sampled global features \mathbf{f}g and local features \mathbf{f}l. Feed the concatenated vector [\mathbf{f}g; \mathbf{f}l] into the Radiance Field MLP. The MLP outputs density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i for each point. Compute the final pixel color C using standard differentiable volume rendering integration: C = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) is the accumulated transmittance, and \deltai is the distance between adjacent samples. Parameters: Input Image Resolution: Not given in the sources. Patch Size (P): Not given in the sources. ViT Depth (L): Not given in the sources. Embedding Dimension (D): Not given in the sources. MLP Layers: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-occlusion: Standard image-conditioned models (e.g., PixelNeRF) query features along the ray corresponding to the visible surface in the input view. If a target view pixel is invisible from the input view (e.g., a car's wheel occluded by the car body), the model incorrectly uses features from other visible surfaces (e.g., the car's window). VisionNeRF mitigates this by using self-attention to find long-range dependencies, retrieving relevant features from distant parts of the source view for occluded regions. Coordinate System: The method uses a viewer-centered coordinate system and does not enforce constraints like symmetry or canonical coordinate systems. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class VisionNeRF: def init(self, vitmodel, cnnbackbone, mlp, patchsize=16): """ Initialize VisionNeRF.:param vitmodel: Pre-trained or initialized Vision Transformer encoder.:param cnnbackbone: 2D CNN backbone for local features.:param mlp: Radiance field MLP.:param patchsize: Size of patches for ViT. """ self.vit = vitmodel self.cnn = cnnbackbone self.mlp = mlp self.patchsize = patchsize # Resampling layers for global features to multi-level maps self.globalresampler = GlobalFeatureResampler() # Resampling layers for local features to match global levels self.localresampler = LocalFeatureResampler() def extractglobalfeatures(self, image): """ Lift 2D image to feature tokens and apply ViT.:param image: Input image tensor of shape (B, C, H, W).:return: Global feature maps at multiple levels. """ # 1. Patch Embedding # Assuming ViT expects (B, N, D) patches = image.unfold(2, self.patchsize, self.patchsize).unfold(3, self.patchsize, self.patchsize) patches = patches.permute(0, 2, 3, 1, 4, 5).reshape(image.shape[0], -1, self.patchsize self.patchsize image.shape[1]) # Linear projection to D dimensions (simplified) tokens = self.vit.patchembedding(patches) # 2. ViT Encoder tokens = self.vit.encoder(tokens) # 3. Unflatten and Resample # Unflatten to (B, H/P, W/P, D) h, w = image.shape[2] // self.patchsize, image.shape[3] // self.patchsize gridtokens = tokens.reshape(image.shape[0], h, w, -1) # Resample to multi-level feature maps (e.g., 1/4, 1/8, 1/16) globalmaps = self.globalresampler(gridtokens) return globalmaps def extractlocalfeatures(self, image): """ Extract local features using CNN.:param image: Input image tensor.:return: Local feature maps at multiple levels. """ localmaps = self.cnn(image) # Resample to match global map levels localmapsresampled = self.localresampler(localmaps) return localmapsresampled def render(self, globalmaps, localmaps, rayorigins, raydirections, near, far): """ Render novel view using volume rendering.:param globalmaps: List of global feature maps at different levels.:param localmaps: List of local feature maps at different levels.:param rayorigins: Tensor of ray origins (B, N, 3).:param raydirections: Tensor of ray directions (B, N, 3).:param near: Near plane distance.:param far: Far plane distance.:return: Rendered image colors. """ # Sample points along rays tvals = torch.linspace(0., 1., 128) # 128 samples per ray zvals = near (1. - tvals) + far tvals points = rayorigins.unsqueeze(1) + raydirections.unsqueeze(1) zvals.unsqueeze(2) # Query features at points # Note: The exact projection from 3D points to 2D feature maps for unposed input is implicit # in the training process via the learned correspondence. Here we assume a query function # that retrieves features based on the learned mapping. globalfeatures = self.queryfeatures(globalmaps, points) localfeatures = self.queryfeatures(localmaps, points) # Concatenate features combinedfeatures = torch.cat([globalfeatures, localfeatures], dim=-1) # MLP to predict density and color density, color = self.mlp(combinedfeatures) # Volume rendering weights = density torch.sigmoid(-density) # Approximation for alpha transmittance = torch.cumprod(torch.cat([torch.oneslike(weights[...,:1]), 1. - weights + 1e-10], dim=-1)[:,:-1], dim=-1) colors = (weights transmittance color).sum(dim=-2) return colors def queryfeatures(self, featuremaps, points): """ Query feature maps at 3D points. This is a placeholder for the specific projection logic used in VisionNeRF which maps 3D points to 2D input image coordinates implicitly via the transformer's attention. """ # In practice, this involves projecting 3D points to the 2D input image plane # and sampling from the feature maps. Since the input is unposed, the projection # is learned or approximated. For implementation, one might use a learned # projection head or assume a canonical view during training. # Here we assume a simple trilinear interpolation for demonstration. # The actual VisionNeRF paper does not provide the explicit projection formula # for unposed inputs, relying on the end-to-end training of the MLP with the # feature maps as conditioning. pass class GlobalFeatureResampler(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # Define upsampling layers for coarse-to-fine maps self.upsample1 = nn.Upsample(scalefactor=2, mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False) self.upsample2 = nn.Upsample(scalefactor=2, mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False) def forward(self, tokens): # tokens: (B, H, W, D) f1 = self.upsample1(tokens.permute(0, 3, 1, 2)).permute(0, 2, 3, 1) f2 = self.upsample2(f1.permute(0, 3, 1, 2)).permute(0, 2, 3, 1) return [tokens, f1, f2] class LocalFeatureResampler(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() self.upsample1 = nn.Upsample(scalefactor=2, mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False) self.upsample2 = nn.Upsample(scalefactor=2, mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False) def forward(self, features): # features: list of CNN feature maps at different scales # Resample to match global map levels f1 = self.upsample1(features[0]) f2 = self.upsample2(f1) return [features[0], f1, f2] Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On the ShapeNet dataset, VisionNeRF achieves LPIPS: 0.09 and PSNR: 21.03 for novel views. This compares to PixelNeRF's LPIPS: 0.20 and PSNR: 21.85. Strengths: Handles self-occlusion better than local-feature-only models by using global attention to retrieve features from distant parts of the source view. Renders richer details and more accurate structure in unseen regions. Generalizes across multiple object categories using a single model. Works on real-world images. Limitations: PSNR is slightly lower than PixelNeRF (21.03 vs 21.85), though LPIPS is significantly better (0.09 vs 0.20), indicating better perceptual quality. Does not enforce geometric constraints like symmetry, which might limit performance in highly symmetric scenes if not learned from data. When to use: When novel view synthesis is required from a single unposed image, especially when occluded regions are present and perceptual quality is prioritized over raw PSNR. When not to use: When camera poses are known and high-precision geometric alignment is possible, or when PSNR is the primary metric and occlusion is minimal. VisionNeRF was proposed by Wei-Sheng Lai, Ravi Ramamoorthi, and Tsung-Yi Lin, with work done while interning at Google and at NVIDIA. It was published in the IEEE Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV) in 2023. The method builds on the principles of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [31] and Vision Transformers (ViT) [11], addressing the limitations of existing image-conditioned models like PixelNeRF [59] and SRT [42] in handling self-occlusion and generalizing from single unposed images. It was trained and evaluated on the ShapeNet dataset [6] including 13 object categories, as well as real-world images. name: TransNeRF
head: Generalizable Neural Radiance Fields for Novel View Synthesis with Transformer
body: TransNeRF is a generalizable neural radiance field method that learns a generic scene representation from multiple source views without requiring per-scene optimization. It replaces the pooling-based multi-view fusion of previous methods with an encoder-decoder Transformer framework that explores deep relationships among source views and enforces local consistency along rays. Unlike ViT-NeRF and VisionNeRF which focus on single-scene reconstruction with ViT backbones, TransNeRF is designed for cross-scene generalization, rendering novel views for unseen scenes directly from a pre-trained model. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of M source views \{Im\}{m=1}^M with corresponding camera parameters \{\Thetam\}{m=1}^M (poses, intrinsics, scene bounds), and a query 3D point location (x, y, z) with viewing direction d. Outputs: Differential volumetric density \sigma and directional emitted color c for the query point. Data Structures and Layouts: Query Embeddings: Learnable embeddings for the query point. Density query: x^0\sigma (initial), x^L\sigma (final). Color query: Y0 (initial), YL (final). Color ray query: z^0i (initial), z^Li (final). Source View Embeddings: Initial: x^0m derived from U-Net features and viewing direction d^m{src}. Final: x^Lm from the Density-ViewDecoder. Ray Neighbors: For a query point qi on a target ray, neighbors are q{i-n}, \dots, q{i-1}, q{i+1}, \dots, q{i+n}. Positional Encodings: E{pos} added to ray-space inputs, computed via sine/cosine functions of different frequencies. Parameters: Nq: Number of queries stacked in Q. N{kv}: Number of key-value pairs stacked in K. dv: Dimension of V. H: Number of attention heads. dh: Feature dimension per head, such that H \times dh = dk. n: Number of neighboring points on each side along the ray. L: Number of Transformer blocks. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Feature Extraction: For each source view m, extract a feature volume using a pre-trained U-Net. Retrieve spatial-aligned 2D-pixel features for the query 3D point (x, y, z) to form the initial source-view feature x^0m. Record the viewing direction d^m{src} for the projected pixel. 2. Density-ViewDecoder (Surrounding-view Space): Input: X0 = [x^0\sigma; x^01; x^02; \dots; x^0M]. Process: Apply L blocks of self-attention. Each block l computes: \tilde{X}l = \text{Norm}(\text{Density-ViAttn}(X{l-1}) + X{l-1}) Xl = \text{Norm}(\text{FFN}(\tilde{X}l) + \tilde{X}l) Where \text{Density-ViAttn}(X) = \text{MH-Attn}(X, X, X). Output: XL = [x^L\sigma; x^L1; \dots; x^LM]. The latent density representation is derived from x^L\sigma and the 3D coordinates (x, y, z). 3. Density-RayDecoder (Ray-cast Space): Input: Initial density representations of neighbors \sigma^0{i-n}, \dots, \sigma^0{i+n} plus positional encodings: D0 = [\sigma^0{i-n}; \dots; \sigma^0{i+n}] + E{pos}. Note: The initial density \sigma^0 for each point is computed by a linear function of the Density-ViewDecoder output: \sigma^0 = FC(x^L\sigma(x, y, z)). Process: Apply L blocks of self-attention. Each block l computes: \tilde{D}l = \text{Norm}(\text{Density-Attn}(D{l-1}) + D{l-1}) Dl = \text{Norm}(\text{FFN}(\tilde{D}l) + D{l-1}) Where \text{Density-Attn}(D) = \text{MH-Attn}(D, D, D). Output: The final density \sigma for the query point is obtained by projecting the output embedding \sigma^Li via a linear function. 4. Color-ViewDecoder (Surrounding-view Space): Input Query: Y0 = FC(\sigma^Li) \oplus d{tgt}, where \sigma^Li is the latent density from Density-RayDecoder and d{tgt} is the target viewing direction. Input Keys: X{src} = [FC(x^L1) \oplus d^1{src}; \dots; FC(x^LM) \oplus d^M{src}]. Input Values: C{src} = [\gamma(c^1{src}); \dots; \gamma(c^M{src})], where \gamma(\cdot) is an embedding function and c^m{src} is the RGB color of the source view. Process: Apply L blocks of cross-attention. Each block l computes: \tilde{Y}l = \text{Norm}(\text{Color-ViAttn}(Y{l-1}, X{src}, C{src}) + Y{l-1}) Yl = \text{Norm}(\text{FFN}(\tilde{Y}l) + \tilde{Y}l) Where \text{Color-ViAttn}(Y, X{src}, C{src}) = \text{MH-Attn}(Y, X{src}, C{src}). Output: Latent color representation YL. 5. Color-RayDecoder (Ray-cast Space): Input: Initial color embeddings of neighbors z^0{i-n}, \dots, z^0{i+n} plus positional encodings: Z0 = [z^0{i-n}; \dots; z^0{i+n}] + E{pos}. Note: The latent color representation YL from Color-ViewDecoder is assigned to the corresponding z^0i. Process: Apply L blocks of self-attention. Each block l computes: \tilde{Z}l = \text{Norm}(\text{Color-Attn}(Z{l-1}) + Z{l-1}) Zl = \text{Norm}(\text{FFN}(\tilde{Z}l) + Z{l-1}) Where \text{Color-Attn}(Z) = \text{MH-Attn}(Z, Z, Z). Output: The predicted color c is obtained by projecting the output embedding z^Li via a linear function. 6. Volume Rendering: Use classical differentiable volume rendering to compute the rendered color C(r) for a camera ray r(t) = o + td with bounds [tn, tf]: C(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t)\sigma(r(t))c(r(t), d)dt T(t) = \exp\left(-\int{tn}^{t} \sigma(r(s))ds\right) The model is trained end-to-end by minimizing the MSE loss between rendered and ground truth colors: \mathcal{L} = \sum{r \in R(\Theta)} \|\hat{C}(r) - C(r)\|2^2. Multi-Head Attention Implementation: \text{MH-Attn}(Q, K, V) = \text{Concat}(A1, \dots, AH)W Ah = \text{Attention}(Qh, Kh, Vh) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{Qh Kh^T}{\sqrt{dh}}\right)Vh Where Qh = QW^qh, Kh = KW^kh, Vh = VW^vh. Pitfalls: Pooling-based fusion models fail to explore complex relationships across multiple views and ignore local consistency of the 5D radiance field. The method assumes a pre-trained U-Net is available for feature extraction. Generalization: TransNeRF generalizes to unseen scenes without per-scene finetuning after training on a large dataset of diverse scenes. Complexity: The use of Transformer attention mechanisms allows for exploring deep relationships among views, but introduces higher computational complexity compared to simple pooling or CNN-based fusion, particularly in the view-decoder stages where attention is computed over M source views. Strengths: Captures global semantic context and local geometric consistency simultaneously. Invariant to permutations of source views. Limitations: Requires a large dataset for training the generalizable prior. Relies on the quality of the pre-trained U-Net encoder. TransNeRF was proposed to address the limitations of per-scene NeRF optimization and the inability of previous generalizable methods to model complex multi-view relationships. It builds on the success of Transformers in NLP and Vision. The method was introduced in a paper titled "Generalizable Neural Radiance Fields for Novel View Synthesis with Transformer". name: NeRF Analogies
head: Example-Based Visual Attribute Transfer, NeRF Analogies: Example-Based Visual Attribute Transfer
body: NeRF Analogies is a method for transferring visual attributes (appearance) from a source NeRF to a target NeRF by establishing dense semantic correspondences using Vision Transformer (ViT) features. It solves the problem of appearance transfer without requiring geometric alignment between scenes, relying instead on semantic similarity. It differs from sibling methods like ViT-NeRF and VisionNeRF by focusing on cross-scene attribute transfer via semantic key-component matching rather than single-scene reconstruction or local appearance editing. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A source NeRF (representing the appearance to transfer) and a target NeRF (representing the geometry to retain). Input images for both scenes are used to extract features. Outputs: A modified target NeRF that renders the target geometry with the source's appearance. Data Structures: NeRF MLP: A fully connected Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with 8 hidden layers of 256 neurons, followed by a single layer of 128 neurons, and an output layer activated by a Sigmoid function. ViT Features: Extracted using DiNO-ViT with a ViT-8B backbone. Patch Size: 8 pixels. Stride: 4 pixels. Resolution Enhancement: To achieve pixel-granularity correspondences, DiNO is queried on vertically and horizontally translated versions of the image (four subsequent translations by one pixel in the -x and -y directions). Feature Map Resolution: For 400p images, the resulting feature maps have a resolution of 392x392, with 384 features per pixel. Feature Source: The output of the deepest (11th) attention layer is used, specifically the key-component of the attention maps, which correlates well with semantic similarity. Training Procedure: 1. Feature Extraction: Extract dense semantic features from input images of the source and target scenes using the configured DiNO-ViT setup. 2. Correspondence Establishment: Compute semantic similarity between source and target features to establish dense correspondences. 3. Optimization: Train the target NeRF to minimize a combined loss function: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}c + \lambda \, \mathcal{L}G Where: \mathcal{L}c is the color loss (standard NeRF rendering loss). \mathcal{L}G is the Difference of Gaussians (DoG) loss, used to enforce edge consistency and alleviate noisy correspondences. \lambda is the weight for the DoG loss. 4. Loss Weighting Schedule: For the first 20,000 iterations, \lambda = 0. After 20,000 iterations, \lambda is gradually faded in, increasing up to a maximum of 50. 5. Convergence: Training runs for a total of 60,000 iterations. Parameters: Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 1 \times 10^{-4}. Batch Size: 512. Total Training Time: Less than two hours on a single GPU, including feature extraction. Evaluation Setup: Data Split: 200 images sampled randomly from a sphere around the object: 100 for training, 20 for validation, 80 for testing. Metrics: Evaluated on unseen test views. The CLIP direction consistency metric uses 80 images rendered in a circular trajectory with a constant elevation of 30°. Baseline Comparison: Compared against NeRFStudio Instant-NGP models trained for 10,000 iterations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noisy Correspondences: DiNO features can produce noisy mappings where two points on the target mesh map to different points in the source NeRF. This is mitigated by using the L1 loss component of the color loss to encourage sparsity. Feature Granularity: Using DiNO-v2 is avoided because its larger patch size results in coarser feature granularity, which is unsuitable for dense pixel-granularity correspondences. Alternative Features: SIFT features perform poorly as they do not capture semantic similarities. Diffusion (hyper-) features double computation time without significantly improving correspondence quality. Time Complexity: Feature extraction and training can be completed in less than two hours on a single GPU. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables appearance transfer between semantically related objects without geometric alignment; robust semantic correspondence using ViT key-components. Limitations: Performance degrades on semantically unrelated objects, though plausible outcomes may still occur if shapes are similar. When to use: When transferring appearance between scenes with similar semantic content but different geometry or lighting. When not to use: When high-frequency detail preservation is critical without semantic guidance, or when computational resources are extremely limited (though faster than diffusion-based alternatives). NeRF Analogies was introduced by Michael Fischer, Zhengqin Li, Thu Nguyen-Phuoc, Aljaž Božič, Zhao Dong, Carl Marshall, and Tobias Ritschel from University College London and Meta Reality Labs. The method leverages the semantic understanding capabilities of Vision Transformers (specifically DiNO) to bridge the gap between different 3D representations. It builds on the principles of Transformer and Vision Model Integration by utilizing ViT features for semantic correspondence. name: Human and Specific Subject Modeling
head: Human Avatar Modeling, Dynamic Human NeRF, SMPL-NeRF Hybrids
body: This family of methods extends static NeRF architectures to model dynamic human subjects, enabling novel view synthesis and pose extrapolation for animatable avatars. It addresses the limitations of standard NeRF, which overfits to static scenes and lacks the structural priors necessary to generalize across different poses or unseen subjects. By integrating parametric body models (like SMPL) or deformable mesh representations with neural radiance fields, these methods decouple geometry and appearance, allowing for high-fidelity rendering of complex human dynamics and clothing details that implicit fields alone struggle to capture. The core task of a NeRF network architecture is to learn a continuous volumetric scene representation F\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the spatial position, \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the viewing direction, \sigma is the volume density, and \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the view-dependent color. The rendering process integrates these outputs along rays using standard volume rendering equations. UVA is a neural radiance field representation for dynamic human avatars that enables local and independent editing of both geometry and texture while supporting novel view synthesis and pose rendering. It distinguishes itself from methods relying on pre-defined UV mapping or two-stage distillation by anchoring structured latent codes to a deformable canonical mesh, allowing direct manipulation of 3D space without 3D-to-2D projection ambiguities. HumanNeRF is a generalizable neural representation for high-fidelity free-view synthesis of dynamic humans that generalizes to unseen subjects and camera settings using sparse RGB inputs, avoiding per-scene training through aggregated pixel-alignment features and a pose-embedded non-rigid deformation field. It differs from its siblings by combining image-based rendering with NeRF-based volume rendering into a novel neural blending scheme to address artifacts and lack of high-frequency details in synthesized textures, which are common in methods relying solely on implicit texture representation. HumanNeRF-SE is a method for synthesizing novel pose images of humans from monocular video inputs by combining explicit SMPL shape priors with an implicit NeRF representation. It solves the problem of overfitting and high computational complexity inherent in previous deformable NeRF methods that learn blending weights from scratch or fine-tune SMPL weights. Unlike siblings such as HumanNeRF and Unified Volumetric Avatar (UVA), which often rely on frame-level features or learnable weight volumes prone to pose leakage and overfitting, HumanNeRF-SE uses frozen SMPL blending weights for rigid deformation and point-level spatial-aware features for non-rigid refinement. This ensures pose generalization without requiring multi-camera data. Definition: A method targeting the modeling of hands by approximating human hands with a collection of rigid parts. Step: Query points are input into MLPs, which are used to predict geometry (via SDFs) and color. Definition: A NeRF architecture consisting of a coarse sub-model and a fine sub-model for the scene, and a single sub-model for the human NeRF model, leveraging SMPL geometry priors. Layout: Architecture visualization (Fig. 10): Blue boxes are raw inputs, green boxes are positional encoded values, black boxes are hidden layers, pink boxes are final outputs. Numbers indicate feature dimensions. '+' indicates concatenation. ReLU is applied after each hidden layer. Comparison: Unlike NeuralBody which overfits to training observations and produces poor rendering on the back of the subject, NeuMan generalizes better and faithfully renders the back. The modeling of dynamic human subjects in neural radiance fields emerged as a distinct sub-area following the success of static NeRF. Early works like NeuralBody demonstrated the potential but suffered from overfitting and poor generalization to unseen poses. Subsequent research focused on animating subjects under novel poses, with notable contributions including NeuMan and TAVA. The field expanded to include face avatars with constraints based on animating expressions or face topology, building upon pioneering research in HyperNeRF and NeRFies. Impactful works in this domain include Neural Head Avatar (December 2021) [219], IMAvatar (December 2021) [220], and INSTA (November 2022) [221]. By 2022, the area saw further diversification with LISA targeting hand modeling and the emergence of diffusion-based 3D avatar generation powered by neural fields, such as DreamAvatar (April 2023) [222], DreamHuman (June 2023) [223], and AvatarVerse (August 2023). name: Unified Volumetric Avatar (UVA)
body: Unified Volumetric Avatar (UVA) is a neural radiance field representation for dynamic human avatars that enables local and independent editing of both geometry and texture while supporting novel view synthesis and pose rendering. It distinguishes itself from methods relying on pre-defined UV mapping or two-stage distillation by anchoring structured latent codes to a deformable canonical mesh, allowing direct manipulation of 3D space without 3D-to-2D projection ambiguities. Inputs: Target observation point \mathbf{x}t (sampled from a ray in the current pose). Current pose parameters \thetat (defining the skeleton and mesh deformation). Canonical mesh \mathcal{M} (T-pose reference). Top-K parameter for nearest-neighbor search. Outputs: Final pixel color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}) for the ray \mathbf{r}. Data Structures: 1. Canonical Mesh \mathcal{M}: A deformable mesh in canonical space with N anchor nodes. 2. Latent Codes: Two sets of learnable vectors anchored to the mesh nodes: \mathbf{l}{geo} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d{geo}}: Geometry latent codes. \mathbf{l}{rgb} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d{rgb}}: Appearance (texture) latent codes. 3. Neural Deformation Field: An MLP \phi{def} that predicts non-rigid displacement. 4. Radiance MLP: An MLP \phi{rad} that predicts density \sigma and base color \mathbf{c}0. 5. Shading MLP: An MLP \phi{shade} that predicts a pose-dependent shading factor s. Steps: 1. Compute LBS Weights: For a target point \mathbf{x}t, find the Top-K nearest neighbors on the current posed mesh. Interpolate the Linear Blending Skinning (LBS) weights \mathbf{w}b from the neighbors' weights. 2. Transform to Canonical Space: Invert the LBS transformation using \mathbf{w}b and the current pose \thetat to get an initial canonical position. Refine this position using a neural deformation field \phi{def} conditioned on the interpolated appearance latent code \mathbf{l}{rgb}. The transformation is defined as: \mathbf{x}c = \text{LBS}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}t, \mathbf{w}b, \thetat) + \phi{def}(\mathbf{l}{rgb}) (Note: The exact composition of the LBS inversion and deformation field addition is described as combining the NN motion field with the neural deformation field.) 3. Interpolate Latent Codes: In canonical space, find the Top-K nearest neighbors of \mathbf{x}c on the canonical mesh \mathcal{M}. Interpolate the geometry and appearance latent codes \mathbf{l}{geo} and \mathbf{l}{rgb} from the anchored nodes using nearest-neighbor interpolation. 4. Compute Signed Height Indicator: Calculate a local signed height indicator \tilde{\mathbf{h}} for \mathbf{x}c. This consists of UV coordinates (u, v) and the point-to-surface distance \bar{d} relative to the canonical mesh: \tilde{\mathbf{h}} = [u, v, \bar{d}] This indicator resolves spatial ambiguity caused by discrete latent code interpolation. 5. Predict Density and Base Color: Pass the interpolated latent codes and the signed height indicator through the radiance MLP: [\sigma, \mathbf{c}0] = \phi{rad}(\mathbf{l}{geo}, \mathbf{l}{rgb}, \tilde{\mathbf{h}}) 6. Modulate Color: Predict a pose-dependent shading factor s using the shading MLP and the current pose \thetat. Modulate the base color: \mathbf{c}{mod} = \mathbf{c}0 \otimes s (Note: \otimes denotes element-wise multiplication or modulation as per the source diagram description.) 7. Volume Rendering: Integrate the modulated colors and densities along the ray \mathbf{r} using standard volume rendering to produce the final color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}). Parameters: Top-K: The number of nearest neighbors used for interpolating LBS weights and latent codes. Typical values are not explicitly stated in the provided notes, but the method relies on this for spatial interpolation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Spatial Ambiguity: Using discrete latent codes defined on mesh nodes diffused via nearest-neighbor interpolation leads to spatial query indistinguishability (blocky artifacts or discontinuities). This is mitigated by the signed height indicator \tilde{\mathbf{h}}. UV Mapping Limitations: Unlike methods using pre-defined UV mapping, UVA avoids the difficulty of local texture editing because it operates in 3D canonical space with mesh-anchored codes. Editing Capability: Enables local and independent editing of geometry and texture, which is not possible with standard NeRF or UV-mapped methods. Training: End-to-end trainable from scratch, jointly optimizing the skinning field and radiance field, unlike two-stage distilling methods that require manual parameter tuning. Performance: Achieves competitive results in novel view synthesis and novel pose rendering on human avatars. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Unified Volumetric Avatar (UVA) was proposed to address the challenges of editing dynamic human avatars. Previous methods either lacked editing capabilities or relied on static meshes and two-stage processes. UVA introduces a mesh-guided canonical radiance field with structured latent codes and a signed height indicator to enable all-in-one solutions for view synthesis, pose rendering, and local editing. name: HumanNeRF
head: HumanNeRF: Efficiently Generated Human Radiance Field from Sparse Inputs
body: HumanNeRF is a generalizable neural representation for high-fidelity free-view synthesis of dynamic humans that generalizes to unseen subjects and camera settings using sparse RGB inputs, avoiding per-scene training through aggregated pixel-alignment features and a pose-embedded non-rigid deformation field. It differs from its siblings by combining image-based rendering with NeRF-based volume rendering into a novel neural blending scheme to address artifacts and lack of high-frequency details in synthesized textures, which are common in methods relying solely on implicit texture representation. Inputs and Outputs: The input consists of K synchronized videos of a performer captured at different viewpoints (preferably 360°) with T frames, denoted as I = \{I{k,t}\}, where each image Ik \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 4} includes a mask as the last channel. The output is a synthesized free-viewpoint video of the performer, generalizing motion to an arbitrary person. Data Structures and Network Architectures: The method employs five main neural components. All linear layers use ReLU activation unless specified. Positional Encoding (PE) is applied to specific inputs as detailed below. 1. Feature Extractor Network U: A U-Net structure extracting 2D image features. Layers: 8 layers of CRB2D (ConvBnReLU2D: Convolution + BatchNorm + ReLU 2D). Parameters: Kernel size k=3, stride s=1, dilation d=1 for all layers. Channel Layout: Down0: 4/32 Down1: 32/64 Down2: 64/128 Down3: 128/256 Up1: 256/256 Up2: 256/128 Up3: 128/64 Final: 64/32 2. Feature Blending Network MLPB: Estimates blending weights for aggregating features from multiple views. Layers: PE0, LR0-LR6 (Linear + ReLU). Input: View direction \vec{v}, angle \theta, PE0 output, features f. Channel Layout: PE0: 6/54 (for \vec{v}), 3/27 (for \theta). LR0: (54 + 27 + 32 \times 6)/256. LR1-4: 256/256. LR5: 256/128. LR6: 128/6. 3. Deformation Network MLPd: Learns non-rigid displacements from the observation space to the canonical space. Input: Rd (distances between sample point p and 24 SMPL joints), Rv (directions between p and 24 SMPL joints), F (blended feature). Layers: PE0, LR0-LR5. Channel Layout: PE0: 24/216. LR0: (216 + 72 + 32)/256. LR1-4: 256/256. LR5: 128/3. 4. Generalizable Dynamic Neural Radiance Field \Phi: Predicts density and color in canonical space. Input: Position x, view direction d, PE0, LR2, PE0, LR2, PE1, F, LR7, LR8. Layers: PE0, LR0-LR8, Density \sigma, PE1, LR7, LR8, Color c. Channel Layout: PE0: 3/63. LR0: 63/256. LR1-4: 256/256. LR5: (27 + 256)/256. LR6: 256/256. Density \sigma: 256/1. PE1: 3/27. LR7: (256 + 27 + 32)/256. LR8: 256/128. Color c: 128/3. 5. Appearance Blending Network MLPA: Refines texture details by aggregating colors from neighboring views. Input: f{r,0}^r, f{l,0}^l (two adjacent image features and occlusion maps). Layers: LR0-LR6, Blending weights W. Channel Layout: LR0: ((32 + 3) \times 2)/256. LR1-5: 256/256. LR6: 256/128. W: 128/3. Numbered Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: For each input image I^k, extract 2D feature maps f^k using the U-Net network U: f^k = U(I^k) 2. Pixel Alignment and Aggregation: For a spatial point p \in \mathbb{R}^3, project it into view k at qk \in \mathbb{R}^2 and fetch the corresponding feature vector f{qk}^k. Compute the aggregated pixel alignment feature Fp as a weighted summation: Fp = \sum{k=1}^{K} wq^k f{qk}^k where the blending weights wq^k are estimated by the feature blending network MLPB: wq^k = MLPB(\vec{v}, \thetaq^k, fq^k) Here, \vec{v} is the viewing direction and \thetaq^k is the angle of the viewing direction relative to the query ray of the source view. 3. Deformation to Canonical Space: Use the parametric human body model SMPL to estimate a basis model. Compute Rd \in \mathbb{R}^{24} and Rv \in \mathbb{R}^{72} representing distances and directions between sample point p and the 24 joints of the SMPL skeleton. Deform the point p to canonical space p' using the rigid transformation \mathcal{S} (based on SMPL mesh \mathcal{M} and skinning weights w^s) and the non-rigid displacement predicted by MLPd: p' = \mathcal{S}(p, \mathcal{M}, w^s) + MLPd(Rd, Rv, Fp) 4. Radiance Field Query: Query the generalizable dynamic neural radiance field \Phi at location p' in canonical space with the viewing direction d and the aggregated feature Fp to regress volume density \sigma and RGB radiance c, along with blending features F. 5. Appearance Blending (Optional Fine-tuning): To refine texture details and address artifacts, use the appearance blending network MLPA. Input two adjacent image features and occlusion maps (f{r,0}^r, f{l,0}^l) to predict blending weights W. Aggregate colors from neighboring views to produce the final high-frequency appearance. 6. Rendering: Perform standard volume rendering using the predicted density \sigma and color c to synthesize the image. Parameters: SMPL Skeleton Joints: 24 joints are used for computing distances (Rd) and directions (Rv). Fine-tuning Duration: 300 frames for a specific performer using only an hour to generate improved results. Input Views: The method is designed for sparse inputs, with experiments conducted on 2, 4, and 6 views. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multi-person/Human-Object Interaction: The method uses a regressed parametric human model, limiting it to single-person setups. It fails on multi-person or human-object interaction situations. Lighting Variation: No explicit lighting model is used. Significant brightness or color changes between views cause severe artifacts. Switching nearest views during appearance blending causes jumping artifacts, especially with high brightness variance. Generalization Limits: Capability is limited because human dataset distributions only cover a small portion of human dynamics and appearances. Time Complexity: The method is significantly more efficient than per-scene methods. On the 'batman' video (300 frames, multi-view dataset), full training takes 1.2 hours, compared to Neural Body (6.7h), Neural Volumes (8.4h), and ST-NeRF (9.5h). Ablation studies show that removing the feature aggregation (F) reduces time to 22.44 min, and removing the deformation network (MLPd) reduces it to 25.88 min, while removing appearance blending (MLPA) keeps it at 1.2h. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On six input views, the method achieves PSNR = 32.59, SSIM = 0.9817, and LPIPS = 0.0304. Strengths: Efficient generalization to unseen identities and poses without per-scene fine-tuning; high-fidelity free-view synthesis from sparse inputs; combines image-based rendering with NeRF for better texture details. Limitations: Limited to single-person setups; sensitive to lighting variations; generalization is constrained by the distribution of training datasets. When to Use: Dynamic human rendering from sparse multi-view inputs, specifically targeting unseen identities and poses with efficient generalization. When Not to Use: Multi-person scenes, scenes with significant lighting changes between views, or when human-object interactions are present. HumanNeRF was introduced by in 2022. It addresses the limitations of existing neural human representations that require dense multi-view inputs and costly per-scene training, which limits them to static models. The method builds on the idea of generalizable neural radiance fields, analogous to how IBRNet assists NeRF, by employing aggregated pixel-alignment features across multi-view inputs and a pose-embedded non-rigid deformation field. HumanNeRF: Efficiently Generated Human Radiance Field from Sparse Inputs, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.00759, fetched 2026-10-26

name: HumanNeRF-SE
head: HumanNeRF with SMPL Explicit vertices
body: HumanNeRF-SE is a method for synthesizing novel pose images of humans from monocular video inputs by combining explicit SMPL shape priors with an implicit NeRF representation. It solves the problem of overfitting and high computational complexity inherent in previous deformable NeRF methods that learn blending weights from scratch or fine-tune SMPL weights. Unlike siblings such as HumanNeRF and Unified Volumetric Avatar (UVA), which often rely on frame-level features or learnable weight volumes prone to pose leakage and overfitting, HumanNeRF-SE uses frozen SMPL blending weights for rigid deformation and point-level spatial-aware features for non-rigid refinement. This ensures pose generalization without requiring multi-camera data. Inputs: Monocular video frames \{In\}, corresponding camera poses, and SMPL parameters (shape \beta, pose J) for each frame. Outputs: Synthesized images of the human in novel poses and viewpoints. Data Structures: Voxel Volume V: A 3D grid representing the SMPL space. Layout: Each voxel stores a tuple (nv, w1, w2, \dots, w{24}). nv: Occupancy count (number of SMPL vertices in the voxel). w{1\dots24}: The Linear Blending Skinning (LBS) weights from the SMPL model corresponding to the vertices in that voxel. Empty voxels store (0, 0, \dots, 0). Spatial-Aware Features Fs: Output of channel-by-channel convolution on V. Sampling Points: xr: Human-related points (kept). xo: Irrelevant points (filtered out, density forced to 0). Parameters: vs: Voxel size used to scale the bounding box of the SMPL model. \lambda: Weight for the MSE loss term. Ns: Number of samples per ray. Algorithm Steps: 1. Voxelization: For a set of SMPL vertices v: a. Calculate the bounding box min/max on coordinate axes. b. Scale the bounding box to the set voxel size vs. c. Find the least common multiple of the axes dimensions and 32. d. Scale vertices down by vs after subtracting the minimum value. e. Construct voxel volume V using Sparse Convolution Sp: V = Sp(v, vs, W) Where W represents the SMPL weights. 2. Conv-Filter (Feature Extraction & Filtering): a. Initialize convolution kernel to one. b. Perform channel-by-channel convolution on V to obtain spatially-aware features Fs. For the i-th channel: Fs^i = \sum{m=h}^{h'} \sum{n=w}^{w'} \sum{t=d}^{d'} \nu{m,n,t,i} \cdot \vartheta{m,n,t,i} Where \nu is the voxel value and \vartheta is the kernel weight. c. Query Fs for each sampling point x. d. Filter points: xo \text{ (filter out), } d(xo) = 0 \quad \text{if } Fs(x) = 0 xr \text{ (remain)} \quad \text{if } Fs(x) > 0 3. Point Canonicalization: a. name: OPONeRF
head: One-Point-One NeRF
body: OPONeRF is a neural rendering method that personalizes the parameters of the plenoptic mapping function for each sampled 3D point, rather than using a single shared set of parameters for the entire scene. It solves the problem of handling test-time scene changes, such as motion, illumination variations, or contamination, by conditioning the renderer's weights on a global scene representation and a local point feature. Unlike generalizable NeRFs that concatenate geometry-aware features with fixed parameters, OPONeRF dynamically generates candidate parameters and selects from them based on the point's context, allowing for discriminative response to local variations. OPONeRF consists of a Geometry Encoder that extracts a global scene representation, a set of Parameter Candidate Decoders (PCD) that generate layer-specific parameter pools, and a personalized renderer that selects parameters for each point using probabilistic modeling. Inputs: A set of K posed support images \{Ik\}{k=1}^K. For each ray, a set of sampled 3D points \mathbf{x} and viewing directions \mathbf{d}. Outputs: Predicted radiance \mathbf{c} and volume density \sigma for each point, which are integrated via volume rendering to produce pixel colors. 1. Overall Scene Representation (\mathbf{F}) Source: Extracted from support images via the Geometry Encoder. Layout: A 3D feature grid. Construction: 1. Extract 2D feature maps Fk from each support image Ik using a shared CNN T(\cdot). 2. Construct a cost volume by warping Fk to a reference view (k=1) using homographic warping matrix Hk(z) at depth z. The warped feature at pixel (u,v) and depth z is F{k,z}(u,v). 3. Compute the view-wise variance of these warped features. 4. Pass the cost volume through a 3D CNN B(\cdot) to obtain \mathbf{F}. \begin{aligned} Fk &= T(Ik) \\ F{k,z}(u,v) &= Wk\bigl(\mathcal{H}k(z)[u,v,1]^T\bigr) \\ \mathbf{F} &= B\Bigl(\text{Var}\bigl(\{F{k,z}(u,v)\}\bigr)\Bigr) \end{aligned} 2. Point-wise Feature (f\mathbf{x}) Source: Interpolated from the gridded scene representation \mathbf{F} at the location of sampled point \mathbf{x}. Layout: A feature vector associated with \mathbf{x}. Probabilistic Modeling: f\mathbf{x} is modeled as a Gaussian distribution with mean \mu\mathbf{x} and variance \sigma\mathbf{x}. These are predicted by MLPs (\mu MLP, \Sigma MLP) taking f\mathbf{x} as input. \mathcal{L}{\mu\mathbf{x}, \sigma\mathbf{x}}(f\mathbf{x}) \approx \frac{1}{B}\sum{i=1}^B \ln p\theta(f\mathbf{x}^i|f\mathbf{x}^{Vi}) + \frac{1}{2B}\sum{i=1}^B\sum{j=1}^D \left(1 + \ln((\sigma^{(j)}{\mathbf{x}i})^2) - (\mu^{(j)}{\mathbf{x}i})^2 - (\sigma^{(j)}{\mathbf{x}i})^2\right) 3. Parameter Candidate Decoders (PCD) Structure: For each target layer l (where l=1, \dots, L), a PCD consists of two parallel decoders: Parameter Decoder D^lw(\cdot): Outputs base parameter matrix \mathbf{W}^ld \in \mathbb{R}^{Ci^l \times Co^l}. Mask Decoder D^lm(\cdot): Outputs a soft mask, which is quantized to a hard binary mask M^l \in \{0,1\}^{Ci^l \times Co^l}. Layer-Variant Codes: Learnable matrices \mathbf{Z}^l \in \mathbb{R}^{Ci^l \times Co^l}, initialized randomly and updated during training. Candidate Parameters \mathbf{W}^la: \mathbf{W}^la = (J - M^l) \mathbf{W}^ld + M^l \mathbf{Z}^l where J is an all-ones matrix and denotes the Hadamard product. 4. Adaptiveness Factor (A\mathbf{x}) Source: A vector of length L (number of target layers) computed for each point \mathbf{x}. Function: Determines how to fuse the parameter candidates \mathbf{W}^la for each layer l. It allows the renderer to select from the parameter pool in a layer-wise manner rather than element-wise. 1. Geometry Encoding: Input: Posed support images \{Ik\}{k=1}^K. Process: Extract features Fk, warp to reference view, compute variance, and pass through 3D CNN B(\cdot) to get \mathbf{F}. Output: Global scene representation \mathbf{F}. 2. Point Feature Interpolation: Input: Sampled 3D point \mathbf{x}. Process: Interpolate f\mathbf{x} from \mathbf{F}. Output: Point-wise feature f\mathbf{x}. 3. Parameter Candidate Generation: Input: Global scene representation \mathbf{F}. Process: For each target layer l: Compute \mathbf{W}^ld = D^lw(\mathbf{F}). Compute soft mask, quantize to hard binary mask M^l = D^lm(\mathbf{F}). Compute candidate parameters \mathbf{W}^la = (J - M^l) \mathbf{W}^ld + M^l \mathbf{Z}^l. Output: Pool of candidate parameters \{\mathbf{W}^la\}{l=1}^L. 4. Discriminative Parameter Personalization: Input: Point-wise feature f\mathbf{x}, candidate parameters \{\mathbf{W}^la\}. Process: Compute adaptiveness factor A\mathbf{x} from f\mathbf{x} (details of A\mathbf{x} calculation are not fully specified in the provided text, but it is discriminative to \mathbf{x}). Use A\mathbf{x} to select/fuse parameters from \mathbf{W}^la for each layer l. Output: Personalized layer weights for point \mathbf{x}. 5. Rendering: Input: Personalized weights, point \mathbf{x}, direction \mathbf{d}. Process: The renderer (Ray Transformer) uses the personalized weights for target layers (Q, K, V projection MLPs and feedforward layer) and shared weights for others. Output (\mathbf{c}, \sigma). Process: Volume rendering integrates (\mathbf{c}, \sigma) along rays. Output: Pixel colors. Mapping Function: \mathcal{M}\Theta^{opo}(\mathbf{x}): (\mathbf{x}, f\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}, \mathbf{F}) \longrightarrow (\mathbf{c}, \sigma) Reconstruction Loss: \mathcal{L}{rec} = \frac{1}{B}\sum{i=1}^B ||Enc(f\mathbf{x}^i) - Dec(F\mathbf{x}^i)||2 where Enc and Dec are encoder/decoder MLPs mapping to latent space. Diversity Loss: \mathcal{L}{div} = -\frac{1}{|R|}\sum{r=1}^{|R|} ||\mu{r,\cdot} - \tilde{\mu}{r,\cdot}|| - \frac{1}{N}\sum{s=1}^N ||\mu{\cdot,s} - \tilde{\mu}{\cdot,s}|| where \mu{r,\cdot} = \frac{1}{N}\sum{s=1}^N a{r,s}(x), \mu{\cdot,s} = \frac{1}{|R|}\sum{r=1}^{|R|} a{r,s}(x), and \tilde{\mu} are randomly shuffled versions to suppress trivial solutions. Gradient Approximation for Binary Quantization: The step function S(x) for binary mask quantization is non-differentiable. Its gradient is approximated by a long-tailed estimator H(x): \frac{d}{dx}S(x) \approx H(x) = \begin{cases} 2-4|x|, & -0.4 \le x \le 0.4 \\ 0.4, & 0.4 < |x| \le 1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Total Loss: \mathcal{L}{opo} = \mathcal{L}{pho} + \mathcal{L}{appr} + \gamma \mathcal{L}{rec} + 1e^{-5}\mathcal{L}{div} where \mathcal{L}{pho} is the photometric loss. L: Number of target layers in the OPONeRF renderer. Typically all linear layers except the last regression heads. \mathbf{Z}^l: Layer-variant codes for layer l, shape \mathbb{R}^{Ci^l \times Co^l}. Initialized randomly. \mathbf{W}^la: Candidate parameters for layer l, shape \mathbb{R}^{Ci^l \times Co^l}. Threshold Matrix: A learnable threshold matrix is used for binary quantization instead of a fixed scalar. Computational Cost of PCD: Generating full-sized output matrices for large layer widths (Ci^l, Co^l > 1000) is expensive. Mitigation: Generate a down-sized output, apply linear layers to upscale dimensions, then element-wise multiply with randomly initialized full-sized matrices that are iteratively optimized. Non-differentiability of Binary Quantization: The step function S(x) is non-differentiable. Mitigation: Use the long-tailed estimator H(x) for gradient computation. Unverified code. """ def init(self, sharedcnn, costvolumecnn): super().init() self.sharedcnn = sharedcnn # T(.) self.costvolumecnn = costvolumecnn # B(.) def forward(self, supportimages): # supportimages: [K, H, W, 3] K = supportimages.shape[0] features = [] for k in range(K): Fk = self.sharedcnn(supportimages[k]) # [H, W, C] features.append(Fk) # Construct cost volume # Note: Homographic warping Hk(z) and variance computation are assumed to be handled # by a custom CUDA kernel or specific library function not detailed in the source. # We assume a function warpandvariance(features, poses) exists. costvolume = warpandvariance(features, supportimages.poses) F = self.costvolumecnn(costvolume) # [H, W, D, Cout] return F class ParameterCandidateDecoder(nn.Module): """ Generates parameter candidates Wa and masks M for a target layer. """ def init(self, inchannels, outchannels, layerid): super().init() self.layerid = layerid # Three consecutive fully-connected layers for Dw and Dm self.Dw = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(inchannels, 512), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(512, 512), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(512, outchannels) # Output shape depends on target layer dims) self.Dm = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(inchannels, 512), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(512, 512), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(512, outchannels)) # Layer-variant codes Z^l self.Z = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(outchannels)) # Learnable threshold for binary quantization self.threshold = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(outchannels)) def forward(self, F): # F is the global scene representation, interpolated or pooled to match input dim Wd = self.Dw(F) softmask = self.Dm(F) # Binary quantization with straight-through estimator # S(x) is step function, H(x) is gradient estimator M = binaryquantize(softmask, self.threshold) # Candidate parameters: Wa = (J - M) Wd + M Z J = torch.oneslike(Wd) Wa = (J - M) Wd + M self.Z return Wa, M def binaryquantize(x, threshold): """ Binary quantization with long-tailed gradient estimator. """ # Forward pass: hard binary mask M = (x > threshold).float() # Backward pass: gradient approximation H(x) # Note: In PyTorch, this requires a custom autograd function or using straight-through # if the gradient is simply passed through. The source specifies H(x) for the gradient. # Here we simulate the gradient flow for the sake of the pseudocode structure. # In practice, this would be implemented as a custom Function. return M class LongTailedEstimator(torch.autograd.Function): @staticmethod def forward(ctx, x): return (x > 0).float() @staticmethod def backward(ctx, gradoutput): # H(x) approximation # 2-4|x| if -0.4 <= x <= 0.4 # 0.4 if 0.4 < |x| <= 1 # 0 otherwise absx = torch.abs(x) grad = torch.zeroslike(x) mask1 = (absx <= 0.4) mask2 = (absx > 0.4) & (absx <= 1.0) grad[mask1] = 2 - 4 absx[mask1] grad[mask2] = 0.4 return gradoutput grad class OPONeRFRenderer(nn.Module): """ Personalized renderer using Ray Transformer architecture. Placeholder for homographic warping and variance computation return torch.randn(100, 100, 10, 64) def RayTransformer(layerdims): # Placeholder for Ray Transformer implementation pass Concatenate geometry-agnostic [\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}] with geometry-aware f\mathbf{x} but keep parameters \Theta fixed. OPONeRF conditions parameters on \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{F}. Models static appearance as stochastic variables. OPONeRF targets the sampled point itself, subdividing the scene and personalizing point-wise parameters. Time Complexity: The computational cost of the Parameter Candidate Decoders (PCD) is high for full-sized outputs, especially when layer widths are large (Ci^l, Co^l > 1000). The mitigation strategy (down-sized output + linear upscaling + element-wise multiplication) reduces this cost but adds complexity. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the global scene representation \mathbf{F}, layer-variant codes \mathbf{Z}^l, and candidate parameters \mathbf{W}^la for all target layers. Strengths: Handles test-time scene changes (motion, illumination, contamination) robustly by personalizing parameters per point. More expressive and flexible than fixed-parameter NeRFs. Limitations: High computational overhead due to the need to generate and select parameters for each point. The probabilistic modeling and diversity loss add to the training complexity. When to use: When robustness to test-time perturbations is critical and computational resources allow for the overhead of per-point parameter generation. When not to use: When real-time performance is required and scene changes are minimal or non-existent. OPONeRF (One-Point-One NeRF) was introduced by Yu Zheng, Yueqi Duan, Kangfu Zheng, Hongru Yan, Jiwen Lu, and Jie Zhou. The method addresses the limitations of standard NeRFs and generalizable NeRFs in handling dynamic or perturbed scenes. It builds on the Ray Transformer architecture and incorporates ideas from probabilistic modeling and parameter-efficient fine-tuning. The method was presented in the paper "OPONeRF: One-Point-One NeRF for Robust Neural Rendering". name: Mixer-NeRF
head: Hybrid Spatial Feature NeRF, MLCA-NeRF
body: Mixer-NeRF is a neural radiance field architecture that addresses the loss of local information and blurry details in standard NeRF by integrating a hybrid spatial feature learning module (MLCA) and a squeeze-and-excitation (SE) network module. It differs from the baseline NeRF [Parent] by explicitly mixing spatial and channel features via fully connected layers before the main density/color prediction MLP, and by dynamically weighting features between sampling and inference layers. Mixer-NeRF modifies the standard NeRF pipeline [Parent] by inserting two specific modules: the MLCA module and the SE module. The method retains the standard volume rendering equation and stratified sampling strategy. Inputs: 3D spatial position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and viewing direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Outputs: Volume density \sigma and view-dependent color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3. The network processes features through fully connected (linear) layers. The feature vectors are dense real-valued tensors. Position Encoding: The input \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{d} are expanded using positional encoding \text{PE}(\cdot) with L layers. For \mathbf{x}, L=10. For \mathbf{d}, L=4. The encoded vectors are concatenated: X{\text{input}} = \text{Concat}(\text{PE}(\mathbf{x}), \text{PE}(\mathbf{d})). 1. Positional Encoding: Compute the positional encoding for the 3D location \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d}. The encoding function is defined as: \text{PE}(\mathbf{v}) = [\sin(2^i \pi \mathbf{v}), \cos(2^i \pi \mathbf{v})]{i=0}^{L} where \mathbf{v} is either \mathbf{x} or \mathbf{d}, and L is the number of encoding layers. Note: The source text contains a typo in the formula for \text{PE}(\mathbf{d}), writing \mathbf{x} instead of \mathbf{d} inside the trigonometric functions; the correct variable is \mathbf{d}. 2. Concatenation: Concatenate the encoded position and direction features to form the initial input tensor X{\text{input}}: X{\text{input}} = \text{Concat}(\text{PE}(\mathbf{x}), \text{PE}(\mathbf{d})) 3. Hybrid Spatial Feature Learning (MLCA Module): This module is inserted after positional encoding and before the main MLP backbone. It consists of two sub-layers: Spatial Feature Capturing Layer: Mixes spatial features using a fully connected layer with GELU activation: X{\text{token}} = \text{GELU}(W{\text{token}} X{\text{input}} + b{\text{token}}) where W{\text{token}} and b{\text{token}} are the weight matrix and bias vector, respectively. Hybrid Feature Channel Layer: Mixes feature channels to capture relationships between different channel features (e.g., color and density) at each spatial location using another fully connected layer with GELU activation: X{\text{channel}} = \text{GELU}(W{\text{channel}} X{\text{token}} + b{\text{channel}}) where W{\text{channel}} and b{\text{channel}} are the weight matrix and bias vector. 4. MLP Backbone Processing: The output X{\text{channel}} from the MLCA module is passed into the standard NeRF MLP backbone (Position MLP and Shading MLP as defined in the parent article). The backbone predicts the raw density and color features. 5. Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) Module: The SE module is constructed between the sampling layer (feature extraction) and the inference layer (final prediction) of the feature extraction network. Its purpose is to filter out high-weight information and dynamically weight features to aid detail restoration and light color handling in complex scenes. Note: The source describes the placement and purpose of the SE module but does not provide the explicit mathematical formulas for the squeeze and excitation operations (typically global average pooling followed by two fully connected layers with a gating mechanism). The implementation must follow the standard SE-net architecture. 6. Inference: The weighted features are passed to the final layers to predict volume density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. 7. Volume Rendering: The predicted \sigma and \mathbf{c} are integrated along rays using standard volume rendering equations [Parent]. Unverified code. """ def init(self, featuredim=256, hiddendim=256, pedimx=10, pedimd=4): super().init() # Positional Encoding parameters self.pedimx = pedimx self.pedimd = pedimd # Input dimension after concatenation of PE(x) and PE(d) # PE(x) has dim 2 (pedimx + 1) if i goes 0..L inclusive? # Source says L layers, formula sum i=0 to L. # Standard NeRF uses L=10 for x, L=4 for d. # The formula [sin(2^i pi x), cos(2^i pi x)] for i=0..L # implies 2(L+1) dimensions per vector. self.inputdim = 2 (pedimx + 1) + 2 (pedimd + 1) # MLCA Module self.mlca = MLCAModule(self.inputdim, featuredim) # Standard NeRF Backbone (Simplified representation) # In practice, this includes the Position MLP and Shading MLP # defined in the parent article [Parent]. # Here we assume a placeholder MLP that takes featuredim and outputs sigma, c. self.backbone = StandardNeRFBackbone(featuredim) # SE Module # Standard SE-net structure self.semodule = SENet(featuredim) def positionalencoding(self, v, L): """ Computes positional encoding as per. PE(v) = [sin(2^i pi v), cos(2^i pi v)] for i in 0..L """ freqbands = 2.0 torch.arange(L + 1, device=v.device).float() # v is shape (..., 3) # We need to apply this to each dimension of v # Reshape for broadcasting v = v.unsqueeze(-1) # (..., 3, 1) freqbands = freqbands.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # (1, 1, 1, L+1) scaledv = v freqbands math.pi sinvals = torch.sin(scaledv) cosvals = torch.cos(scaledv) # Concatenate sin and cos along the last dimension # Result shape: (..., 3, 2(L+1)) pe = torch.cat([sinvals, cosvals], dim=-1) # Flatten the spatial dimensions if necessary, but typically # we keep the batch/ray dimensions and flatten the feature dim return pe.view(v.shape[:-2], -1) def forward(self, x, d): """ x: (N, 3) 3D positions d: (N, 3) Viewing directions """ # 1. Positional Encoding pex = self.positionalencoding(x, self.pedimx) ped = self.positionalencoding(d, self.pedimd) # 2. Concatenation Xinput = torch.cat([pex, ped], dim=-1) # 3. MLCA Module Xtoken = self.mlca.spatialcapture(Xinput) Xchannel = self.mlca.channelmix(Xtoken) # 4. Backbone # The backbone processes Xchannel to get intermediate features # Note: Standard NeRF backbone usually takes PE(x) and PE(d) separately # or concatenated. Mixer-NeRF feeds the mixed features here. # We assume the backbone expects the featuredim sized input. backbonefeatures = self.backbone(Xchannel) # 5. SE Module # Applied between sampling/feature extraction and inference weightedfeatures = self.semodule(backbonefeatures) # 6. Inference # Final layers to predict sigma and color sigma, color = self.backbone.predict(weightedfeatures) return sigma, color class MLCAModule(nn.Module): """ Hybrid Spatial Feature Learning Module (MLCA). """ def init(self, inputdim, hiddendim): super().init() # Spatial Feature Capturing Layer self.spatialfc = nn.Linear(inputdim, hiddendim) # Hybrid Feature Channel Layer self.channelfc = nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim) def forward(self, x): # Xtoken = GELU(Wtoken Xinput + btoken) Xtoken = F.gelu(self.spatialfc(x)) # Xchannel = GELU(Wchannel Xtoken + bchannel) Xchannel = F.gelu(self.channelfc(Xtoken)) return Xchannel class SENet(nn.Module): """ Squeeze-and-Excitation Network Module. Standard SE-net implementation. """ def init(self, channels, reduction=16): super().init() self.avgpool = nn.AdaptiveAvgPool1d(1) self.fc = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(channels, channels // reduction, bias=False), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.Linear(channels // reduction, channels, bias=False), nn.Sigmoid()) def forward(self, x): # x shape: (N, C) or (N, C, L) depending on backbone output # Assuming x is (N, C) for simplicity as per MLP output b, c = x.size() # Squeeze y = self.avgpool(x.view(b, c, 1)).view(b, c) # Excitation y = self.fc(y).view(b, c, 1) # Scale return x y.expandas(x) class StandardNeRFBackbone(nn.Module): """ Placeholder for the standard NeRF MLPs defined in the parent article [Parent]. For viewing direction \mathbf{d}: L=4. Activation Function: GELU is used in the MLCA module. Sampling: Stratified sampling is used, consisting of coarse sampling and fine sampling stages. This is identified as a typo; the implementation must use \mathbf{d}. MLCA Integration: The MLCA module replaces the direct input to the MLP. The standard NeRF architecture separates position and direction inputs into different MLPs. Mixer-NeRF concatenates them first, processes them through MLCA, and then feeds the result into the backbone. name: Sparse View and Few-Shot Optimization
head: Few-shot NeRF
body: Sparse View and Few-Shot Optimization addresses the severe artifacts, overfitting, and geometry breakdown that occur when training Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) with a drastically reduced number of input viewpoints (|S| < 20). It sets itself apart from standard NeRF training by introducing specialized regularization, data densification, or geometric constraints to mitigate the ambiguity inherent in limited observations, rather than relying on large-scale pre-training or external depth priors. The core task of a NeRF network architecture is to learn a continuous volumetric scene representation F\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the spatial position, \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the viewing direction, \sigma is the volume density, and \mathbf{c} is the view-dependent color. The rendering process integrates these outputs along rays using standard volume rendering equations. Simple-NeRF is a regularization method for sparse-input Neural Radiance Fields that employs two simpler augmented NeRF models (points and views augmentations) to provide depth supervision to the main NeRF, mitigating overfitting and implausible geometries caused by high capacity and sparse views [7371-simple-nerf.md]. It sets itself apart from prior works by obtaining depth supervision through augmented models without requiring pre-training on large datasets or external depth models [7371-simple-nerf.md]. Unlike RegNeRF, which uses depth smoothness priors and may fuse objects at different depths, Simple-NeRF mitigates both floaters and incorrect depth issues by learning in-situ depth priors [7371-simple-nerf.md]. WaH-NeRF is a training framework for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) from sparse inputs that mitigates rendering confusion by addressing two root causes: sample-position confusion ("WHERE to Sample?") and prediction confusion ("HOW to Predict?") [11548-wah-nerf.md]. It differs from sibling methods like Simple-NeRF and Deceptive-NeRF/3DGS by analyzing the sample-render process and mitigating confusion before volume rendering, rather than relying on regularization for rendered color and depth images after volume rendering [11548-wah-nerf.md]. Unlike FlipNeRF which uses geometric consistency via flipped rays, WaH-NeRF uses a Deformable Sampling strategy for seen viewpoints and a Semi-Supervised NeRF paradigm based on pose perturbation for unseen viewpoints [11548-wah-nerf.md]. Deceptive-NeRF/3DGS is a sparse-view reconstruction method that overcomes the artifacts and overfitting inherent in standard NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines by densifying the input data. Unlike methods that use diffusion models as per-step regularizers (e.g., SDS), this approach generates photorealistic pseudo-observations (RGB-D images) from coarse renders and treats them as real training views [11859-deceptive-nerf-3dgs.md]. This "view densifier" strategy avoids the computational cost of inferring a large diffusion model at every optimization step, resulting in nearly tenfold faster training while improving reconstruction quality [11859-deceptive-nerf-3dgs.md]. FlipNeRF is a regularization method for few-shot novel view synthesis that generates auxiliary "flipped reflection rays" from original input rays and estimated surface normals to improve rendering quality and surface normal accuracy with sparse inputs [12967-flipnerf.md]. Unlike existing regularization methods that focus on accurate depth estimation or pre-training methods requiring large datasets, FlipNeRF is optimized per scene without pre-training and derives rays from estimated normals without heuristic factors [12967-flipnerf.md]. It sets itself apart from Ref-NeRF by generating additional training rays rather than reparameterizing the radiance field's input viewing direction [12967-flipnerf.md]. NeRF represents a scene as a continuous function F\theta(\cdot) implemented by a neural network with parameters \theta, taking 3D coordinates \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} with positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) to output color \mathbf{c} and density \sigma. Few-shot NeRF setting: number of input viewpoints |S| is drastically reduced to a few viewpoints, specifically |S| < 20. The term "Few-shot NeRF" was introduced to describe scenarios where the number of input viewpoints is drastically reduced from the standard hundreds to fewer than 20, leading to high divergent behaviors such as geometry breakdown and artifacts. The DaRF paper explores this setting, noting that existing frameworks applied regularization techniques at unknown viewpoints to constrain NeRF with additional 3D priors, though with limited performance. DaRF: Boosting Radiance Fields from Sparse Inputs with Monocular Depth Adaptation, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2305.19201, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)
