name: Object Decomposition and Composition
head: Object Decomposition, Compositional NeRF, Scene Decomposition
body: Object Decomposition and Composition refers to a family of NeRF architectures that explicitly separate a scene into distinct semantic or geometric entities (objects) to enable instance-level editing, manipulation, and analysis. Unlike standard NeRFs that treat the scene as a monolithic volume, these methods introduce mechanisms to identify, isolate, and recombine individual objects. This family is distinguished from siblings like Signed Distance Function (SDF) Representations by its focus on semantic/instance separation rather than just boundary representation, and from Mixture-of-Experts and Modular Architectures by its specific goal of compositional scene editing rather than just computational efficiency. The core task of a NeRF network architecture is to learn a continuous volumetric scene representation F\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the spatial position, \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the viewing direction, \sigma is the volume density, and \mathbf{c} is the view-dependent color. The rendering process integrates these outputs along rays using standard volume rendering equations. Simultaneously reconstructs geometry, decomposes objects, and supports manipulation via a learnable object field. Two-stage framework using a coarse global field to guide a fine-grained decomposed field, re-composed via differentiable one-hot weights. Divides scenes by object detail frequency, assigning high-frequency objects to individual NeRFs and low-frequency ones to a joint NeRF. Scene composition model for object interpolation and amodal segmentation using two separate NeRF models for foreground and background. Use an appearance NeRF conditioned on latent codes for the background model. Use two photometric losses, one for the foreground and one for the background. The concept of decomposing scenes into compositional parts emerged early in NeRF research. Fig-NeRF (April 2021) focused on object interpolation and amodal segmentation using separate NeRFs for foreground and background. Object-NeRF (September 2021) introduced a hybrid voxel-based approach with separate NeRFs for objects and the scene, conditioned on interpolated voxel features. These works laid the groundwork for later methods that integrate decomposition directly into the optimization loop for editing. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Fig-NeRF
head: FigNeRF
body: Fig-NeRF is a scene composition model designed for object interpolation and amodal segmentation by decomposing a scene into distinct foreground and background components. It differs from monolithic NeRFs by employing two separate neural radiance field models: a deformable model for the foreground object and a latent-conditioned appearance model for the background, enabling explicit manipulation of object shape and appearance. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Training images of objects from a specific category; a latent code z representing the object instance. Outputs: Rendered images of the foreground object and the background scene, allowing for amodal segmentation and object interpolation. Data Structures: Foreground Model: A deformable NeRF architecture (specifically the Nerfies model). It maps 3D coordinates and viewing directions to density and color, but includes a deformation field conditioned on the latent code z. Background Model: An appearance NeRF conditioned on latent codes. It represents the static or semi-static background environment. Latent Code z: A vector that conditions both the foreground deformation and the background appearance. Steps: 1. Latent Encoding: Encode the input object instance into a latent code z. 2. Foreground Deformation: Use the latent code z to condition a template shape of the object category, generating a deformation field that warps the canonical coordinates of the foreground object. This allows the network to explain shape variations as intuitive deformations of a template. 3. Background Appearance: Use the latent code z to condition the appearance of the background model. 4. Rendering: Render the foreground and background separately using volume rendering equations. 5. Loss Calculation: Compute two separate photometric losses: one for the foreground rendering and one for the background rendering. 6. Optimization: Optimize the parameters of both NeRF models and the latent code z to minimize the combined photometric losses. Formulas: Foreground Rendering: I{fg} = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \mathbf{c}{fg}(\mathbf{x}(t), \mathbf{d}) \alpha(t) dt, where \mathbf{x}(t) is deformed by the latent-conditioned deformation field. Background Rendering: I{bg} = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \mathbf{c}{bg}(\mathbf{x}(t), \mathbf{d}, z) \alpha(t) dt, where \mathbf{c}{bg} is conditioned on z. Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{photometric}(I{fg}, I{fg}^{gt}) + \mathcal{L}{photometric}(I{bg}, I{bg}^{gt}). Parameters: Latent Dimension: Not given in the sources. Deformation Field Complexity: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Amodal Segmentation: The method assumes the background model can effectively segment the object from its background, which may fail if the object and background have similar appearances or if the latent code does not sufficiently disentangle them. Deformation Artifacts: The deformable foreground model may produce artifacts if the latent code z leads to extreme or unrealistic deformations of the template shape. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Achieves good results for amodal segmentation and object interpolation on datasets such as ShapeNet, Gelato, and Objectron. Strengths: Enables explicit control over object shape and appearance through latent codes; supports object interpolation and amodal segmentation. Limitations: Requires separate models for foreground and background, increasing complexity; relies on the effectiveness of the latent code in disentangling object and background features. Fig-NeRF was introduced in April 2021. It builds on the NeRFies deformable NeRF model and focuses on scene composition, specifically object interpolation and amodal segmentation. It models an object category as a template shape conditioned on a latent code, which undergoes a deformation also conditioned on the same latent variable. This approach allows the network to explain shape variations as intuitive deformations. The method was applied to datasets including ShapeNet, Gelato, and Objectron. name: DM-NeRF
body: DM-NeRF is a pipeline that simultaneously reconstructs continuous 3D scene geometry, decomposes all individual objects in 3D space, and supports flexible object shape manipulation (translation, rotation, size adjustment, deformation) from 2D images only. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF by introducing an explicit object field that predicts a one-hot object code for every 3D point, enabling instance-level editing without explicit mesh extraction. It builds on Object Decomposition and Composition by using a learnable object code conditioned on spatial position rather than fixed segmentation masks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of L images for a static scene with known camera poses and intrinsics, denoted as \{(I1, \xi1, K1) \dots (IL, \xiL, KL)\}. Output: Volume density \sigma, object code \mathbf{o}, and color \mathbf{c} for any queried 3D point \mathbf{p} and viewing direction \mathbf{v}. Data Structures: Object Code: A one-hot vector of dimension H+1, where H is the predefined number of objects and the extra dimension represents the background/empty space. Ground Truth Labels: 2D object masks of dimension T, where T is the number of ground truth objects. Prediction Tensors: 2D object prediction images of size U \times V \times (H+1), where U, V are spatial width and height. Network Architecture: The pipeline consists of three components: 1. NeRF Backbone: Learns volume density and appearance. 2. Object Field: Learns a unique object code for every 3D point. 3. Object Manipulator: Edits the shape of specified objects and handles occlusions. The network takes positional encoding \text{PE}(x,y,z) for location and \text{PE}(\theta,\phi) for viewing direction as input. The architecture is an MLP with the following layer dimensions: 128 \rightarrow 256 \rightarrow 256 \rightarrow 256 \rightarrow 256 \rightarrow 256 \rightarrow 256 \rightarrow 256 \rightarrow 256 \rightarrow 256 \rightarrow 128 Formulas and Definitions: Positional Encoding: \text{PE}(\cdot) is applied to coordinates (x,y,z) and directions (\theta,\phi). Outputs: Density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}^1: Function of location only. Object Code \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^{H+1}: Function of location only. Color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Function of location and viewing direction. Training Procedure: 1. Forward Pass: For each ray, sample points. Compute \text{PE}(\mathbf{p}) and \text{PE}(\mathbf{v}). Feed into MLP to get \sigma, \mathbf{o}, \mathbf{c}. 2. Rendering: Render 2D images using standard volume rendering integration of \sigma and \mathbf{c}. 3. 2D Object Matching: Generate L images of 2D object predictions \{I1 \dots IL\}, where Il \in \mathbb{R}^{U \times V \times (H+1)}. Reshape the first H solid object predictions of Il to M \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times H}, where N = U \times V. Reshape ground truth labels \bar{I}l \in \mathbb{R}^{U \times V \times T} to \bar{M} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times T}. Use the Hungarian algorithm to associate every ground truth 2D object mask with a unique predicted 2D object mask based on Soft Intersection-over-Union (sIoU) and Cross-Entropy Score (CES). sIoU cost between predicted box h and ground truth box t: C^{sIoU}{h,t} = \frac{\sum{n} \dots}{\dots} (Note: The exact summation formula is truncated in the source text) 4. Loss Functions: Standard NeRF rendering loss (color difference). \ell{3d}^{empty} and \ell{3d}^{obj}: Jointly learn correct codes for empty 3D points and object points. These are crucial for accurate decomposition. Object Manipulation: 1. Inverse Query: Use a lightweight inverse query algorithm to edit the scene geometry. This avoids evaluating dense 3D points from implicit fields explicitly. 2. Tackle Visual Occlusions: Explicitly handle occluded regions during manipulation to prevent artifacts. 3. Apply Transformation: Translate, rotate, resize, or deform the specified object's coordinates. 4. Re-render: Render the novel view with the manipulated object. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.optimize import linearsumassignment def positionalencoding(x, mindeg=0, maxdeg=10, scale=1): """Standard NeRF positional encoding.""" scales = np.array([scale (2i) for i in range(mindeg, maxdeg)]) xb = np.expanddims(x, axis=-1) scales xb = np.reshape(xb, (-1, len(scales))) pe = np.concatenate([np.sin(xb), np.cos(xb)], axis=1) return pe def dmnerfforward(p, v, modelweights): """ Forward pass of DM-NeRF. p: (N, 3) query points v: (N, 2) viewing directions modelweights: parameters of the MLP Returns: sigma, objectcode, color """ # Compute positional encodings pepos = positionalencoding(p) peview = positionalencoding(v) # Concatenate inputs # Note: The source specifies PE(x,y,z) and PE(theta,phi) as inputs. # The exact concatenation strategy (e.g., direct concat vs. separate branches) # is not fully detailed in the text, but Figure 7 implies a shared backbone # with PE inputs. We assume standard concatenation for the MLP input. inputvec = np.concatenate([pepos, peview], axis=1) # MLP Forward Pass # Layers: 128 -> 256 (x9) -> 128 # Output heads: Density (1), Object Code (H+1), Color (3) h = inputvec for i in range(9): h = relu(linear(h, modelweights[f'W{i}'], modelweights[f'b{i}'])) # Final layer to 128 h = linear(h, modelweights['Wfinal'], modelweights['bfinal']) # Split outputs # Assuming the last 128 units are split into sigma, o, c # The source says sigma and o are functions of location, c of location+view. # However, the architecture diagram shows a single MLP outputting all three. # We assume the network is trained to output these jointly. # The exact split of the 128 output units is not specified. # Assuming a standard split: first 1 for sigma, next H+1 for o, last 3 for c. # This is a guess as the source does not specify the output head dimensions explicitly # other than the layer sizes. sigma = h[:, 0:1] objectcode = h[:, 1:1+H+1] color = h[:, 1+H+1:1+H+1+3] return sigma, objectcode, color def traindmnerf(images, poses, intrinsics, gtmasks, H, T, numepochs): """ Training loop for DM-NeRF. images: List of L images poses: List of L camera poses intrinsics: List of L camera intrinsics gtmasks: List of L ground truth 2D object masks H: Predefined number of objects T: Number of ground truth objects """ modelweights = initializeweights() for epoch in range(numepochs): for l in range(L): Il = images[l] xil = poses[l] Kl = intrinsics[l] Ibarl = gtmasks[l] # Sample rays rays = samplerays(Il, xil, Kl) # Forward pass sigma, objectcode, color = dmnerfforward(rays.p, rays.v, modelweights) # Render image renderedcolor = volumerender(rays, sigma, color) # Compute rendering loss lossrender = mse(renderedcolor, Il) # 2D Object Matching # Reshape predictions to M # Note: objectcode is per point. We need to aggregate to 2D mask. # Standard approach: project points to 2D and average/argmax object codes. # The source mentions "2D object predictions" derived from the object field. # We assume a projection step exists. pred2dmasks = projectobjectcodesto2d(objectcode, rays, Kl) # Hungarian Algorithm Matching # Reshape pred2dmasks to M (N x H) and Ibarl to Mbar (N x T) N = U V M = pred2dmasks.reshape(N, H) Mbar = Ibarl.reshape(N, T) # Compute cost matrix using sIoU and CES # The exact cost matrix computation is truncated in source. # We assume a standard sIoU cost. costmatrix = computesioucost(M, Mbar) rowind, colind = linearsumassignment(costmatrix) # Compute object loss based on matched pairs lossobj = computeobjectloss(M, Mbar, rowind, colind) # Compute empty space loss lossempty = computeemptyloss(sigma, objectcode) # Total Loss loss = lossrender + lossobj + lossempty # Backpropagate updateweights(modelweights, loss) def manipulateobject(scenemodel, objectid, transformation): """ Manipulate a specific object in the scene. objectid: Index of the object to manipulate transformation: Transformation matrix or parameters """ # Inverse Query Algorithm # The source mentions a "lightweight inverse query algorithm". # This likely involves querying the object field to find points belonging to objectid, # applying the transformation, and then re-rendering. # 1. Identify points belonging to the object # Sample points in the scene volume points = samplescenevolume(), objectcodes, = dmnerfforward(points, directions, scenemodel) # Select points with high probability for the target object objectmask = np.argmax(objectcodes, axis=1) == objectid # 2. Apply transformation transformedpoints = applytransformation(points[objectmask], transformation) # 3. Tackle Visual Occlusions # The source emphasizes this step. It likely involves checking if the # transformed points are occluded by other objects in the new view. # If occluded, the density/color might need to be adjusted or the points # might be hidden during rendering. occlusionmask = checkocclusions(transformedpoints, scenemodel, newview) # 4. Re-render # Use the transformed points and original model parameters to render renderedimage = renderwithtransformedgeometry(transformedpoints, scenemodel, newview) return renderedimage Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Ground Truth 3D Codes: Learning the object code faces the issue of no ground truth 3D object codes for full supervision. Variable Number of Objects: The number of total objects is variable and there is no fixed order for objects. Empty Space: Non-occupied (empty) 3D space must be taken into account, but there are no labels for supervision. Occlusion Artifacts: Manipulating originally occluded objects or parts may produce artifacts due to inaccuracies in the learned radiance fields. Lighting Discrepancies: Lighting factors are not decomposed, causing illumination discrepancies on edited objects compared to non-manipulated scenes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Novel view rendering quality is clearly better than PointNeRF, though it decreases after manipulation compared to non-manipulation baselines. Strengths: Simultaneously reconstructs, decomposes, manipulates, and renders complex 3D scenes in a single pipeline from 2D images. Accurately decomposes all 3D objects from 2D views. Limitations: Manipulation of originally occluded objects may produce artifacts. Lighting factors are not decomposed. When to Use: When 3D scene geometry decomposition and manipulation from 2D images is required. When Not to Use: When lighting decomposition is required or when high-fidelity manipulation of heavily occluded objects is critical without artifacts. DM-NeRF was published as a conference paper at ICLR 2023. It is among the first methods to simultaneously reconstruct, decompose, manipulate, and render complex 3D scenes in a single pipeline. It builds on the successful NeRF framework but adds an object field component to decompose the entire space into object fields. name: Unified Decompositional and Compositional NeRF
head: Joint decomposition and composition framework, Two-stage NeRF for joint decomposition and composition, UDC-NeRF, Unifed decompositional and compositional NeRF
body: Unified Decompositional and Compositional NeRF (UDC-NeRF) is a two-stage framework that jointly learns object-level and scene-level implicit representations to enable both novel view synthesis and instance-level scene editing. Unlike sibling methods such as DM-NeRF or Detail-based Segmentation which may treat decomposition and composition as separate or loosely coupled tasks, UDC-NeRF unites them in a single pipeline where a coarse global field guides the sampling for a fine-grained decomposed field, which is then re-composed using differentiable one-hot activation weights. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N multi-view posed images \{xi\}{i=1}^N and their corresponding instance semantic masks \{s{ij}\}{i=1, j=1}^{N, K+1} for a static scene, where K is the number of object instances and the background is treated as instance index 1. Outputs: A composited radiance field (c{comp}, \sigma{comp}) for novel view synthesis, and individual object/background radiance fields (c^k{object}, \sigma^k{object}) for editing. Data Structures: 1. Shared Backbone: A 4-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Input: 3D point coordinate p=(x,y,z) and view direction d. Output: Generic implicit scene feature vector f with dimension 256. Positional Encoding: 10 levels for coordinates, 4 levels for ray directions. 2. Guidance Head: Several MLPs following the backbone. Output: Global RGB color c{guidance} and volume density \sigma{guidance}. 3. Object/Background Heads: Separate 3-layer MLPs. Input: Feature vector f concatenated with learnable object codes (one per instance k \in [1, K+1]). Output: RGB color c^k{object} and volume density \sigma^k{object} for instance k. 4. Learnable Object Codes: A set of vectors, one for each of the K objects and the background. Numbered Steps: 1. Coarse Stage (Global Guidance): Sample points along camera rays. Pass points and directions through the Shared Backbone and Guidance Head to predict c{guidance} and \sigma{guidance}. Use the distribution of \sigma{guidance} to guide point sampling for the fine stage (coarse-to-fine sampling). 2. Fine Stage (Decomposition): Sample points along rays using the guidance from Step 1. Pass points and directions through the Shared Backbone to get feature f. For each instance k \in [1, K+1]: Concatenate f with the learnable code for instance k. Pass through the specific Object/Background Head (separate heads for background and objects) to predict c^k{object} and \sigma^k{object}. 3. One-Hot Activation (Composition Weights): To determine which instance dominates at each point, compute soft probabilities pi using Gumbel-Softmax on the predicted densities: pi = \frac{\exp((\sigma^i{object} + gi)/\tau)}{\sumj \exp((\sigma^j{object} + gj)/\tau)} where gi are i.i.d. samples from Gumbel(0,1) and temperature \tau = 0.1. Compute one-hot composition weights M{obj} using a stop-gradient operation to allow backpropagation through the soft probabilities P (where P is the vector of pi): M{obj} = fh(\arg\max[gi + \log \sigma^i{object}]) - f{sp}(P) + P where fh is the one-hot function and f{sp} is the stop-gradient operator. 4. Residual Composition: Compute the composited radiance field (c{comp}, \sigma{comp}) by weighting the individual instance fields with M{obj}. Combine (c{comp}, \sigma{comp}) with the residual radiance field (c{guidance}, \sigma{guidance}) from the coarse stage using point-wise average pooling on color and density. Render the final image from this combined field. Formulas and Losses: Binary Occupancy Mask: Determines if foreground objects occupy a point: Mc = [\arg\max([\sigma^1{object}, \sigma^2{object},..., \sigma^{K+1}{object}]) > 1] Note: The source uses index 1 for background in the regularization context, but the argmax compares all K+1 instances. 3D One-Hot Density Regularization: Constrains the background field (index 1) in regions occupied by foreground objects: L{one-hot} = Mc \|\sigma^1{object} - \sigma0\|^22 where \sigma0 = -0.01. ReLU is applied to \sigma during rendering to ensure positivity. 2D In-painting Pseudo Supervision: Handles occluded background regions using a pre-trained Lama model: L{color pseudo} = M^1b(r) \|\hat{C}^1{object}(r) - C^1{pseudo}(r)\|^22 where M^1b(r) is a 2D spatial weight map (value 0.05 for uncertain background regions) and C^1{pseudo} is the inpainted color. Intermediate Local Object Rendering: Renders color and opacity for each instance k: \hat{C}^k{object}(r) = \sum{i=1}^N T^ki (1 - \exp(-\sigma^k{object} \deltai)) c^k{object} \hat{O}^k{object}(r) = \sum{i=1}^N T^ki (1 - \exp(-\sigma^k{object} \deltai)) where T^ki = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma^k{object} \deltaj) is the transmittance, N is the number of sampled points, and \deltai is the distance between adjacent points. Object Loss: Enforces color and opacity consistency using semantic masks: L{object} = \sum{k=1}^{K+1} Mo(r)^k \|\hat{C}^k{object}(r) - C(r)\|^22 + \lambdab Mb(r)^1 \|\hat{O}^1{object}(r) - Mo(r)^1\|^22 where Mo(r)^k and Mb(r)^1 are 2D spatial weight maps derived from semantic masks. Overall Optimization Loss: L{overall} = L{comp} + \lambda1 L{object} + \lambda2 L{color pseudo} + \lambda3 L{one-hot} where \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 are balancing weights. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class UDCNeRF: def init(self, numobjects, hiddendim=256, numcoarsesamples=64, numfinesamples=48): """ Initialize the UDC-NeRF model. Args: numobjects (int): K, number of object instances. Background is index 1, objects 2..K+1. hiddendim (int): Dimension of the shared backbone output. numcoarsesamples (int): Number of points sampled in the coarse stage. numfinesamples (int): Number of points sampled in the fine stage. """ self.K = numobjects self.numinstances = numobjects + 1 # K objects + 1 background # Positional Encoding parameters self.freqcoords = 10 self.freqdirs = 4 # Shared Backbone: 4-layer MLP self.backbone = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(6 + 6 self.freqcoords + 6 self.freqdirs, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim)) # Guidance Head: Predicts global scene properties for sampling self.guidancehead = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 4) # 3 for color, 1 for density) # Learnable Object Codes self.objectcodes = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(self.numinstances, hiddendim)) # Separate Heads for Background (index 0 in code, but conceptually 1) and Objects # Note: Source says separate background head and object head. # We implement a generic head that takes the code as input. self.heads = nn.ModuleList([ nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(hiddendim 2, hiddendim), # Concat feature + code nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 4) # 3 for color, 1 for density) for in range(self.numinstances) ]) # Hyperparameters self.tau = 0.1 self.sigma0 = -0.01 self.lambda1 = 1.0 # Placeholder for Lobject weight self.lambda2 = 1.0 # Placeholder for Lcolorpseudo weight self.lambda3 = 1.0 # Placeholder for Lonehot weight def positionalencoding(self, x, numfreqbands, useidentity=True): """Standard positional encoding.""" f = [1.0] for i in range(1, numfreqbands): f.append(2i x) return torch.cat(f, dim=-1) def forward(self, rayso, raysd, semanticmasks=None, pseudocolors=None): """ Forward pass for training. Args: rayso: Origin of rays [Nrays, 3] raysd: Direction of rays [Nrays, 3] semanticmasks: Semantic masks for supervision [Nrays, Ninstances] pseudocolors: Pseudo colors from inpainting for background [Nrays, 3] Returns: renderedcolor: Final rendered color [Nrays, 3] losses: Dictionary of loss components """ Nrays = rayso.shape[0] # 1. Fine Stage Sampling # Use sigmaguidance to sample points (importance sampling) # For this pseudocode, we assume we have sampled points pointsfine # and their corresponding t values tfine # Encode fine points # pointsfine, dirsencoded = encode(pointsfine, raysd) # Get generic feature from backbone # f = self.backbone(pointsfine) # Shape: [Nrays, Nsamples, hiddendim] # 3. Instance-specific Prediction # Expand object codes to match batch and samples # codes = self.objectcodes # [Ninstances, hiddendim] # Predict color and density for each instance # cobjects, sigmaobjects = [], [] # for i in range(self.numinstances): # inputtohead = torch.cat([f, codes[i].unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).expandas(f)], dim=-1) # out = self.headsi # cobjects.append(out[...,:3]) # sigmaobjects.append(out[..., 3:]) # 4. Loss Calculation # losses = self.computelosses(renderedcolor, cfinal, sigmafinal, semanticmasks, pseudocolors) # Return renderedcolor and losses pass def computelosses(self, renderedcolor, cfinal, sigmafinal, semanticmasks, pseudocolors): """ Compute the total loss. """ # Lcomp: Color loss between rendered and ground truth # Lcomp = F.mseloss(renderedcolor, gtcolor) # Lobject: Color and opacity consistency # Requires rendering intermediate object fields # Lobject =... # Lcolorpseudo: In-painting supervision for background # Requires identifying background pixels and comparing with pseudo colors # Lcolorpseudo =... # Lonehot: Density regularization # Requires computing occupancy mask Mc # Lonehot =... # Loverall = Lcomp + lambda1 Lobject + lambda2 Lcolorpseudo + lambda3 Lonehot return {} Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Backpropagation with Argmax: The \arg\max operation is non-differentiable. This is addressed by using the Gumbel-Softmax function on volume density as a continuous approximation, combined with a stop-gradient operation on the soft probabilities to allow gradients to flow through the one-hot mask. Occluded Background Regions: Regions occluded by objects in all training views are ambiguous. This is handled by using a pre-trained Lama in-painting model to provide pseudo-color supervision for these uncertain 2D background regions. In-painting Ambiguity: 2D in-painting may introduce ambiguity in regions seen in other views, but this is suppressed by strong multi-view consistency supervision. Density Positivity: Volume density \sigma must be non-negative for rendering. ReLU is applied to \sigma during the rendering process. Time Complexity: The method involves two stages (coarse and fine) and multiple MLP passes per instance (K+1). The fine stage requires computing Gumbel-Softmax and one-hot weights for all instances, adding overhead compared to single-field NeRF. Memory Complexity: Requires storing learnable codes for K+1 instances and separate MLP heads for each instance (or a shared head with code conditioning). The source does not specify exact memory usage in MB/GB. Measured Performance: On the ToyDesk2 scene, the full model achieved an SSIM of 0.8126 and LPIPS of 0.4488. Ablations show that removing 3D One-hot Density Regularization drops SSIM to 0.8116, removing Gumbel-Softmax Activation drops it to 0.7217, and removing 2D In-painting pseudo Supervision drops it to 0.8127 (SSIM) and increases LPIPS to 0.4516. Removing Residual Radiance Composition drops SSIM to 0.8003. Strengths: Enables joint novel view synthesis and object editing in a unified pipeline. The one-hot regularization and in-painting supervision improve rendering and editing quality, especially for occluded regions. Limitations: Relies on semantic masks for supervision. The method assumes a static scene. The two-stage process adds complexity compared to single-stage NeRF. When to use: When both high-quality novel view synthesis and instance-level editing (removal, addition, transformation) are required for a static scene with known object instances. When not to use: For dynamic scenes, or when semantic masks are not available. Origin: Proposed in "Learning Unified Decompositional and Compositional NeRF for Editable Novel View Synthesis" (2023). History: Builds upon ObjectNeRF, which learns separate networks for global scene and local object branches without modeling interactions. UDC-NeRF unites decomposition and composition to model interactions and correlations between these tasks. Usage: Used for joint scene decomposition and composition to effectively learn object-level and scene-level implicit representations for effective scene modeling, allowing object editing and novel view synthesis in a unified pipeline. Learning Unified Decompositional and Compositional NeRF for Editable Novel View Synthesis, https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.02840v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Detail-based Segmentation
head: Detail-based NeRF Segmentation, Frequency-based Object Segmentation
body: Detail-based Segmentation is a divide-andconquer strategy for representing complex scenes using multiple Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) by partitioning objects based on their detail frequency. It assigns high-frequency objects to individual NeRFs while grouping low-frequency objects into a joint NeRF, thereby reducing the learning burden on each network and improving rendering quality for detailed regions. Unlike sibling methods that may use instance codes or density-based activation, this method relies on a frequency threshold derived from object detection masks to determine segmentation. Inputs: A set of original training images, a pre-trained object detection model, and a user-defined frequency threshold. Outputs: A collection of segmented training datasets, where each dataset corresponds to a specific object or group of objects, ready for individual NeRF training. Data Structures: Object Metadata: For each detected object instance in each image, store: objectid: Unique identifier for the object instance. mask: Binary mask covering the object's pixels. maxfrequency: The maximum detail frequency recorded for this object across all images. Segmentation Groups: A mapping from objectid to a nerfid (integer index of the NeRF responsible for rendering it). Steps: 1. Object Detection and Masking: Apply an object detection algorithm to all original training images. For each detected object, generate a binary mask covering all pixels occupied by the object. 2. Frequency Calculation: For each detected object in each image, calculate its "detail frequency". The specific formula for detail frequency is not provided in the sources, but it is a metric quantifying the complexity or high-frequency content of the object within that specific image view. Record this value for every object-instance-image triplet. 3. Determine Maximum Frequency: For each unique object instance, determine its maximum recorded frequency across all images in the training set: F{max}(o) = \max{i \in Images} (F(o, i)) where F(o, i) is the detail frequency of object o in image i. 4. Segmentation Decision: Compare F{max}(o) against the user-defined threshold T: If F{max}(o) > T, assign object o to a dedicated NeRF (new nerfid). If F{max}(o) \le T, assign object o to the joint NeRF (shared nerfid) along with other low-frequency objects. Note: The method uses maximum frequency rather than average frequency because the maximum frequency better reflects the importance of an object to the user's viewing experience, particularly focusing on complex or high-frequency regions. 5. Extraction and Scaling: For each object assigned to a dedicated NeRF: Extract the object from each image using its mask, using the outermost pixels of the mask as boundaries. Apply interpolation scaling to enlarge the segmented object within the image frame, retaining the original image dimensions. This process reduces the relative frequency of details the network needs to learn, improving rendering quality. For objects in the joint NeRF, the extraction and scaling process is not explicitly detailed, implying they may be processed collectively or left in their original context depending on the specific implementation of the joint NeRF. 6. Training Set Creation: Create separate training datasets for each NeRF. The dataset for a dedicated NeRF contains only the scaled, segmented images of that object. The dataset for the joint NeRF contains images of the grouped low-frequency objects. Parameters: Threshold Frequency (T): A user-adjustable value used to decide which objects warrant individual NeRF representations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The accuracy of the segmentation depends heavily on the quality of the object detection masks. Poor masks may lead to incorrect frequency calculations or incomplete object extraction. Boundary Artifacts: Using the outermost pixels of the mask as boundaries may introduce artifacts if the mask is noisy or if the object is partially occluded. Threshold Selection: The choice of T significantly impacts the number of NeRFs and the distribution of objects. A threshold that is too high may group too many complex objects together, degrading quality; a threshold that is too low may create too many NeRFs, increasing resource usage. Time Complexity: The initial object detection and frequency calculation are performed once per training image. The complexity depends on the object detector and the frequency calculation method. The subsequent NeRF training is parallelized across multiple NeRFs, potentially reducing total training time compared to training a single large NeRF, depending on the scene complexity and the number of segments. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is distributed across multiple NeRF models. Each NeRF stores its own weights, which may be smaller than a single monolithic NeRF, but the total memory is the sum of all individual NeRFs plus the overhead of managing multiple models. Strengths: Improves rendering quality for high-frequency details by dedicating network capacity to specific objects. Reduces the learning burden for each NeRF. Flexible and can be applied to various NeRF variants without modification. Limitations: Requires an external object detection step. The quality of segmentation is dependent on the detector. The threshold T requires manual tuning or heuristic selection. May not handle dynamic scenes or objects with significant appearance changes well if the frequency metric does not account for them. When to use: Scenes with distinct, high-frequency objects that benefit from dedicated representation, and where computational resources allow for multiple NeRFs. When not to use: Scenes with many small, low-frequency objects where the overhead of multiple NeRFs is not justified, or scenes with significant dynamic elements where static segmentation is inappropriate. Detail-based Segmentation was introduced in the NeRFlex system, a resource-aware real-time high-quality rendering framework for complex scenes on mobile devices. The method was designed to address the limitations of single NeRF models in learning high-frequency details, which often result in lower rendering quality. By segmenting objects based on their detail frequency, NeRFlex aims to optimize rendering performance and quality for mobile hardware. NeRFlex: Resource-aware Real-time High-quality Rendering of Complex Scenes on Mobile Devices, https://doi.org/10.1109/icdcs63083.2025.00067, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Neural Articulated Radiance Field (NARF)
head: NARFP, Part-Wise NARF
body: Neural Articulated Radiance Field (NARF) models articulated objects by decomposing them into rigid parts, each represented by a separate Rigidly Transformed Neural Radiance Field (RT-NeRF). Unlike sibling methods that may learn implicit dependencies or holistic representations, NARF explicitly estimates rigid transformations via forward kinematics to ensure each part maintains a consistent radiance field across different 3D pose configurations. It avoids the "part dependency" issue found in earlier approaches like P-NeRF by combining part-wise estimates into a unified global density and color using a differentiable softmax operation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of pose-annotated images; a kinematic 3D pose configuration defined by a root transformation T0, joint angles \theta, and shape parameters \zeta. Outputs: Rendered color C(\mathbf{r}) for a camera ray \mathbf{r}; optionally, a foreground mask M(\mathbf{r}) and part segmentation masks \mathbf{S}^i(\mathbf{r}). Data Structures: The method utilizes P separate RT-NeRF models, denoted as F{\Theta^i}^{l^i, \boldsymbol{\zeta}} for i \in \{1, \dots, P\}. Each model takes encoded local position, local viewing direction, local shape parameters, and global shape parameters as input and outputs density \sigma^i and feature vector \mathbf{h}^i (which is subsequently decoded to color \mathbf{c}^i). Steps: 1. Compute Global Rigid Transformations: For each rigid part i, compute the global rigid transformation li = \{R^i, \mathbf{t}^i\} using forward kinematics based on the input pose configuration \{T0, \zeta, \theta\}. 2. Transform Coordinates: For a global 3D location \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d}, compute the local coordinates for each part i: \mathbf{x}^i = R^{i-1}(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{t}^i) \mathbf{d}^i = R^{i-1}\mathbf{d} 3. Query Part-Wise RT-NeRFs: For each part i, query the corresponding RT-NeRF to obtain density and color estimates. The input to the i-th RT-NeRF consists of the encoded local position \gamma(\mathbf{x}^i), encoded local direction \gamma(\mathbf{d}^i), encoded local shape parameters \gamma(\boldsymbol{\xi}^i), and encoded global shape parameters \gamma(\boldsymbol{\zeta}): F{\Theta^i}^{l^i, \boldsymbol{\zeta}}: (\gamma(\mathbf{x}^{l^i}), \gamma(\mathbf{d}^{l^i}), \gamma(\boldsymbol{\xi}^i), \gamma(\boldsymbol{\zeta})) \rightarrow (\mathbf{c}^i, \sigma^i) 4. Combine Densities and Colors: Combine the estimates \{\sigma^i, \mathbf{c}^i\}{i=1}^P from all P parts into a single global density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} using a differentiable weighted sum via softmax over the densities, controlled by temperature parameter \tau: \sigma = \frac{\sum{i=1}^P \exp(\sigma^i/\tau)\sigma^i}{\sum{i=1}^P \exp(\sigma^i/\tau)}, \quad \mathbf{c} = \frac{\sum{i=1}^P \exp(\sigma^i/\tau)\mathbf{c}^i}{\sum{i=1}^P \exp(\sigma^i/\tau)} Note: The max operation for selecting the highest density is not differentiable, so the softmax approximation is used to allow gradient flow to all RT-NeRF models during training. 5. Volume Rendering: Perform standard volume rendering using the combined density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} to generate the rendered color C(\mathbf{r}) along the camera ray \mathbf{r}. 6. Optional Outputs: Foreground Mask: Estimate the foreground mask M(\mathbf{r}) as the integral of opacity along the ray: M(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{j=1}^N Tj(1 - \exp(-\sigmaj \deltaj)) Segmentation Masks: Render a segmentation image \mathbf{S}^i(\mathbf{r}) for part i by identifying the part with the greatest density at each sample point j: sj(\mathbf{r}) = \arg \maxi \{\sigmaj^i | i \in [1, P]\} \mathbf{S}^i(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{j=1}^N Tj(1 - \exp(-\sigmaj \deltaj))(sj(\mathbf{r}) == i) Parameters: \tau: Temperature parameter for the softmax function. Typical values are not specified in the sources. P: Number of rigid object parts. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Density Samples: Training is dominated by zero density point samples because a surface point belongs to only one part, resulting in zero density for all other parts. This leads to inefficient training as parts with small densities do not significantly affect the final value but still require calculation. Non-Differentiable Max: Using a hard max operation to select the highest density prevents gradient flow to all RT-NeRF models. The softmax approximation is required for effective training. Computational Cost: The cost is proportional to P, limiting representation capacity for complex articulated objects with many parts. Holistic NARF (NARFH) combines the inputs of the RT-NeRF models from Part-Wise NARF and feeds them as a whole into a single NeRF model for direct regression of final density and color. Unlike Part-Wise NARF, NARFH does not satisfy Part Dependency because all parameters are considered for each 3D location, and object part segmentation masks cannot be generated using Eq. 18. However, NARFH has computational cost almost constant to the number of object parts and naturally avoids the zero density problem. Time Complexity: The computational cost of Part-Wise NARF (NARFP) is proportional to the number of object parts P. Holistic NARF (NARFH) has a computational cost that is almost constant with respect to the number of object parts. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Explicitly estimated rigid transformations via forward kinematics avoid implicit transformation issues and part dependency. It allows for novel view synthesis, depth estimation, and body part segmentation by manipulating poses. Limitations: NARFP suffers from inefficient training due to zero density samples and high computational cost for complex objects. NARFH loses part dependency, preventing explicit part segmentation masks. When to use: Use NARFP when explicit part segmentation and strict part dependency are required, and the number of parts is small. Use NARFH when computational efficiency is prioritized over explicit part segmentation capabilities. Neural Articulated Radiance Field (NARF) was introduced in 2021 by Nian et al.. It builds on the concept of Rigidly Transformed Neural Radiance Fields (RT-NeRF) to model articulated objects. The method was developed to address issues in previous approaches like P-NeRF, specifically the part dependency problem where the network learns erroneous dependencies between parts. NARF is trained via pose-annotated images, decomposing the articulated object into rigid parts with local coordinate systems and global shape variations. Neural Articulated Radiance Field, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv48922.2021.00571, fetched 2026-10-26 Advances in Neural Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2111.05849, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Lighting and Appearance Models
body: Lighting and Appearance Models extend the standard NeRF architecture [11313-model-architecture-modifications.md] to explicitly model illumination, material properties, or stylistic variations, rather than predicting view-dependent color directly from position and direction. These methods solve the problem of disentangling geometry from appearance, enabling capabilities such as explicit relighting, physically-based rendering, or controllable style synthesis. They differ from siblings like DoF-NeRF by introducing specific parameterizations for light transport or style, rather than focusing on depth-of-field or sparse-view constraints. The standard NeRF architecture [11313-model-architecture-modifications.md] learns a continuous volumetric scene representation F\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}). Lighting and Appearance Models modify this mapping to output intermediate physical or stylistic quantities (e.g., albedo, normal, pre-integrated light, or style vectors) which are then combined with explicit lighting or style conditions during the rendering step. The rendering process still integrates these outputs along rays using standard volume rendering equations, but the final color \mathbf{C} is derived from a more complex composition of these intermediate fields and external parameters. Neural-PIL replaces costly numerical integration of incoming light with a neural network query, predicting pre-integrated light \tilde{L}i(\omegar, br) directly from an illumination embedding, view direction, and material roughness [13783-neural-pre-integrated-lighting-neural-pil.md]. It sets itself apart from Spherical Harmonics NeRF by using an MLP to represent finer illumination details efficiently, avoiding the lack of fine details or high memory costs associated with SH bases [13783-neural-pre-integrated-lighting-neural-pil.md]. Choose this method when physically-based relighting with roughness-dependent specular highlights is required. Spherical Harmonics NeRF replaces the standard view-dependent color prediction head with an explicit 2nd-order Spherical Harmonics (SH) illumination model, allowing for explicit relighting by varying learnable SH coefficients [14480-spherical-harmonics-nerf.md]. It differs from siblings like Neural-PIL by decoupling geometry (density) and appearance (albedo) into separate accumulations, then applying a global, per-image SH lighting model to the accumulated screen-space albedo and normals, rather than predicting color directly per sample [14480-spherical-harmonics-nerf.md]. Choose this method when global, consistent relighting of a scene is the primary goal. StylizedNeRF (also known as StyleNeRF) integrates a style-based generator into the NeRF architecture for high-resolution 3D-aware image synthesis [14882-stylizednerf.md]. It solves the problem of generating high-fidelity, view-consistent 3D objects with controllable appearance styles, addressing the limitations of standard NeRF which lacks explicit style conditioning [14882-stylizednerf.md]. It sets itself apart from siblings like Neural-PIL by using a GAN-based mutual learning strategy with a 2D stylization network, rather than optimizing for physical lighting parameters [14882-stylizednerf.md]. Choose this method for artistic style transfer or synthesis of specific subject appearances. The baseline NeRF architecture employs two MLPs: a Position MLP \Phi{pos} and a Shading MLP \Phi{shade}. Lighting and Appearance Models emerged to address the limitations of this monolithic color prediction, enabling explicit control over lighting and style. Neural-PIL and Spherical Harmonics NeRF focus on physical illumination, while StylizedNeRF focuses on generative style synthesis. Neural Pre-Integrated Lighting for Neural Radiance Fields, https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.00721, 2021-12-01 StyleNeRF: Stylizing Neural Radiance Fields, https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.14634, 2021-04-28

name: Neural Pre-Integrated Lighting (Neural-PIL)
head: Neural-PIL
body: Neural-PIL replaces the costly numerical integration of incoming light with a simple neural network query, predicting pre-integrated light \tilde{L}i(\omegar, br) directly from an illumination embedding, view direction, and material roughness. Unlike Spherical Harmonics NeRF which suffers from lack of fine details or high memory costs for high-frequency illumination, Neural-PIL uses an MLP to represent finer illumination details efficiently. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Illumination embedding \mathbf{z}l \in \mathbb{R}^{128}, incoming light direction (mirrored view direction) \omegar \in \mathbb{R}^3, and roughness br (scalar). Output: Pre-integrated light \tilde{L}i(\omegar, br). Data Structures: The method employs a coordinate-based Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) architecture based on pi-GAN with FiLM-SIREN layers. FiLM-SIREN Layer: A linear layer followed by a sine activation, modulated by parameters. The transformation is defined as: \phi(y) = \sin(\lambda0 \gamma \odot y + \beta) where y is the output of the linear layer, \odot denotes the Hadamard product, and \lambda0, \gamma, \beta are modulating parameters. Mapping Networks: Two separate mapping networks predict the modulating parameters (\gamma, \beta) for the FiLM-SIREN layers. 1. The first mapping network generates parameters for the first few layers from the illumination embedding \mathbf{z}l. 2. The second mapping network generates parameters for the penultimate layer from the roughness br. Algorithm Steps: 1. Encode the environment map into a 128-dimensional illumination embedding \mathbf{z}l using a frozen Light-SMAE (Smooth Manifold Auto-encoder). 2. For a given surface point, obtain the mirrored view direction \omegar and material roughness br. 3. Pass \mathbf{z}l through the first mapping network to generate modulating parameters (\gamma, \beta) for the initial FiLM-SIREN layers. 4. Pass \omegar through the initial FiLM-SIREN layers (modulated by parameters from step 3) to decode illumination information for the given direction. 5. Pass br through the second mapping network to generate modulating parameters for the penultimate layer. 6. Pass the output from step 4 through the remaining FiLM-SIREN layers (modulated by parameters from step 5) to perform light integration conditioned on roughness. 7. Output the final pre-integrated light value \tilde{L}i(\omegar, br). Rendering Equation Integration: The predicted \tilde{L}i is used in the split-sum approximation of the rendering equation: Lo(x, \omegao) \approx (bd/\pi)\tilde{L}i(n, 1) + bs (F0(\omegao, n)B0(\omegao \cdot n, br) + B1(\omegao \cdot n, br))\tilde{L}i(\omegar, br) where: bd, bs are diffuse and specular albedo weights. F0(\omegao, n) = (1 - \omegao \cdot h)^5 with h = (\omegai + \omegao)/\|\omegai + \omegao\|. B0, B1 are 2D lookup textures indexed by (\omegao \cdot n) and roughness br. \tilde{L}i(n, 1) is queried for the diffuse part (parameterized by normal n and diffuse roughness 1). \tilde{L}i(\omegar, br) is queried for the specular part. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The illumination embedding \mathbf{z}l must be derived from a dataset of environment maps to capture regularities (e.g., brighter light from above, tinting). Training the Neural-PIL requires a frozen Light-SMAE to ease memory requirements; joint training is not described. A baseline approximation method that splits the specular term into two factors: one involving the light integral and one involving the BRDF terms (D, G, F), allowing the light integral to be pre-integrated into a neural network. The specular term is split as: \int{\Omega+} L(\hat{x}, l)(\hat{n} \cdot l) dl \int{\Omega+} \frac{DGF}{4(\hat{n} \cdot v)(\hat{n} \cdot l)} (\hat{n} \cdot l) dl The rendering equation becomes: \tilde{L}\hat{\mathbf{c}}b + (\pi\tilde{L}) \int{\Omega+} \frac{DGF}{4(\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{v})(\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{l})} (\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{l}) d\mathbf{l} where \tilde{L} is the pre-integrated neural network representing the light integral factor divided by \pi. This approach is used as a baseline in NDJIR. Time Complexity: Replaces costly numerical integration with a simple network query, making it faster than direct integration or convolution on environment maps. Memory Complexity: Lower memory cost compared to high-band spherical harmonic or spherical Gaussian representations required for fine illumination details. Strengths: Represents finer illumination details than SG or SH representations; efficient for differentiable rendering engines. Limitations: Requires training a separate Light-SMAE; performance depends on the quality of the illumination embedding space. When to use: When high-fidelity illumination details are needed and standard basis functions (SH/SG) are insufficient or too expensive. Neural-PIL was introduced in "Neural-PIL: Neural Pre-Integrated Lighting for Reflectance Decomposition". It addresses the impracticality of costly numerical accumulation or convolution on complete environment maps within differential rendering engines. The method leverages a pi-GAN-like architecture with FiLM-SIREN layers. It builds on the split-sum approximation technique. Neural-PIL: Neural Pre-Integrated Lighting for Reflectance Decomposition, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2110.14373, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) NDJIR: Neural Direct and Joint Inverse Rendering for Geometry, Lights, and Materials of Real Object, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2302.00675, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Spherical Harmonics NeRF
head: NeRF with Spherical Harmonics, SH-NeRF
body: Spherical Harmonics NeRF replaces the standard view-dependent color prediction head of a NeRF with an explicit 2nd-order Spherical Harmonics (SH) illumination model, allowing for explicit relighting by varying learnable SH coefficients. It differs from sibling methods like Neural-PIL and StylizedNeRF by decoupling geometry (density) and appearance (albedo) into separate accumulations, then applying a global, per-image SH lighting model to the accumulated screen-space albedo and normals, rather than predicting color directly per sample or using learned style embeddings. The method separates the neural network outputs into density \sigma, albedo \mathbf{A}, and normal gradients, accumulating them along rays. The final color is computed by multiplying the accumulated albedo by the SH illumination evaluated at the accumulated normal. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray samples \{\mathbf{x}i\}{i=1}^{N{\mathrm{depth}}}, where \mathbf{x}i are 3D positions; per-image learnable SH coefficients \mathbf{L} \in \mathbb{R}^{9\times3}; neural network parameters for density \sigma(\mathbf{x}) and albedo \mathbf{A}{\mathrm{sample}}(\mathbf{x}). Outputs: Rendered color \mathbf{C} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Data Structures: \mathbf{L}: A matrix of shape (9, 3) storing the 9 SH coefficients for each of the 3 RGB channels. This is stored as a learnable parameter per image. \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{n}): A vector of shape (9,) containing the 2nd-order SH basis functions evaluated at normal \mathbf{n}. These are fixed, non-learnable values. Numbered Steps: 1. Accumulate Density and Albedo: For each ray, sample points \mathbf{x}i. Query the density MLP for \sigma(\mathbf{x}i) and the albedo MLP for \mathbf{A}{\mathrm{sample}}(\mathbf{x}i). Compute transmittance T(ti) and opacity \alpha(\sigma(\mathbf{x}i)\deltai) as in standard volume rendering. Accumulate the weighted albedo: \mathbf{A} = \sum{i=1}^{N{\mathrm{depth}}} \mathbf{A}{\mathrm{sample}}(\mathbf{x}i) T(ti) \alpha(\sigma(\mathbf{x}i)\deltai) where \mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the accumulated screen-space albedo. 2. Accumulate Unnormalized Normal: Compute the gradient of the density with respect to the sample positions \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{x}i}\sigma(\mathbf{x}i). Accumulate these gradients weighted by the visibility term T(ti)\alpha(\sigma(\mathbf{x}i)\deltai): \mathbf{\hat{N}} = \sum{i=1}^{N{\mathrm{depth}}} \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{x}i}\sigma(\mathbf{x}i) \right) \odot T(ti)\alpha(\sigma(\mathbf{x}i)\deltai) where \mathbf{\hat{N}} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the unnormalized normal vector. 3. Normalize Normal: Normalize the accumulated vector to a unit sphere to obtain the final normal \mathbf{N}: \mathbf{N} = \frac{\mathbf{\hat{N}}}{\|\mathbf{\hat{N}}\|^2} Note: The source formula uses \|\mathbf{\hat{N}}\|^2 in the denominator, which is mathematically equivalent to normalizing to unit length if interpreted as dividing by the squared magnitude to achieve a unit vector (though standard normalization divides by \|\mathbf{\hat{N}}\|). We follow the source's explicit formula. 4. Evaluate SH Basis: Evaluate the 2nd-order SH basis functions at the normal \mathbf{N} to get \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{N}) \in \mathbb{R}^9. 5. Compute Illumination: Multiply the per-image SH coefficients \mathbf{L} by the basis vector: \mathbf{L}{\mathrm{illuminated}} = \mathbf{L} \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{N}) This results in a vector in \mathbb{R}^3 representing the incident lighting color. 6. Render Color: Compute the final color by element-wise multiplying the accumulated albedo \mathbf{A} by the illuminated lighting term: \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{A} \odot (\mathbf{L} \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{N})) Formulas: Rendering Equation: \mathbf{C}\left (\{\mathbf {x}i\}{i=1}^{N\mathrm {depth}},\textbf {L}\right)= \mathbf {A}\left (\{\mathbf {x}i\}{i=1}^{N\mathrm {depth}}\right)\odot \mathbf {L}\mathbf {b}\left (\mathbf {N}\left (\{\mathbf {x}i\}{i=1}^{N\mathrm {depth}}\right)\right) Normal Extraction: \mathbf {N}\left (\{\mathbf {x}i\}{i=1}^{N\mathrm {depth}}\right) = \frac {\mathbf {\hat {N}}\left (\{\mathbf {x}i\}{i=1}^{N\mathrm {depth}}\right)}{\left \|\mathbf {\hat {N}}\left (\{\mathbf {x}i\}{i=1}^{N\mathrm {depth}}\right)\right \|^2} Unnormalized Normal: \mathbf {\hat {N}}\left (\{\mathbf {x}i\}{i=1}^{N\mathrm {depth}}\right) = \sum {i=1}^{N\mathrm {depth}}\left (\frac {\partial }{\partial \mathbf {x}i}\sigma (\mathbf {x}i)\right)\odot T(ti)\alpha (\sigma (\mathbf {x}i)\delta i) Parameters: \mathbf{L} \in \mathbb{R}^{9\times3}: Per-image learnable SH coefficients for illumination. \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{n}) \in \mathbb{R}^9: SH basis vector evaluated at normal \mathbf{n}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Shadow Generation: The model lacks direct shadow generation, which is crucial for modeling and subsequent relighting of outdoor scenes. A dedicated shadow model S can be introduced to extend the rendering equation, but the base SH-NeRF method does not include it. Normal Normalization: The source specifies dividing by \|\mathbf{\hat{N}}\|^2 rather than \|\mathbf{\hat{N}}\|. Implementers should verify this specific normalization convention, as it differs from standard unit vector normalization. Single Shading Calculation: The method performs a single shading calculation per ray using accumulated albedo and normals, rather than shading each sample point individually. This reduces noise and aids convergence but assumes the lighting is consistent across the accumulated depth. Time Complexity: The additional cost per ray is the evaluation of the SH basis \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{N}) and the matrix-vector multiplication \mathbf{L}\mathbf{b}(\mathbf{N}), which is constant time O(1) relative to the number of samples, as the order of SH is fixed at 2nd order (9 coefficients). Memory Complexity: Requires storing \mathbf{L} for each image, which is 9 \times 3 = 27 floats per image. This is negligible compared to the neural network weights. Strengths: Allows explicit relighting by varying \mathbf{L}; separates geometry and appearance; reduces noise in albedo and normal estimates through accumulation. Limitations: Cannot model direct shadows without an additional shadow network; assumes Lambertian shading (implied by the albedo \times lighting model). When to use: When explicit relighting of outdoor or indoor scenes is required and the scene can be approximated as Lambertian. When not to use: When accurate shadow modeling is critical and an additional shadow network is not feasible; when view-dependent specular effects are dominant and cannot be captured by 2nd-order SH. The method was introduced by V. Rudnev et al. in "NeRF for Outdoor Scene Relighting". It builds on the standard NeRF framework by replacing the view-dependent color prediction with an explicit SH illumination model to allow for relighting. The approach addresses the limitation of standard NeRFs, which do not have semantic meaning of underlying scene intrinsics or direct control over lighting. NeRF for Outdoor Scene Relighting, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-19787-135, fetched 2026-10-26

name: StylizedNeRF
head: StyleNeRF
body: StylizedNeRF (also known as StyleNeRF) is a method for high-resolution 3D-aware image synthesis that integrates a style-based generator into the Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) architecture. It solves the problem of generating high-fidelity, view-consistent 3D objects with controllable appearance styles, addressing the limitations of standard NeRF which lacks explicit style conditioning and struggles with high-resolution details. It sets itself apart from siblings like Neural Pre-Integrated Lighting by using a GAN-based mutual learning strategy with a 2D stylization network, rather than optimizing for physical lighting parameters. Unlike Spherical Harmonics NeRF, it does not decompose lighting into spherical harmonics but instead uses latent codes to modulate the radiance field's appearance. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 2D images (typically face datasets like FFHQ, AFHQ, CompCars) resized to a target resolution (e.g., 256^2). Outputs: A 3D radiance field model capable of rendering novel views of the synthesized object with a specific style. Data Structures: 1. Latent Code (\mathbf{w}): A vector sampled from a standard Gaussian distribution \mathcal{N}(0, I). 2. Mapping Network: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) that maps \mathbf{w} to a style vector \mathbf{w}'. 3. Synthesis Network (NeRF++ Backbone): Foreground MLP: Predicts density \sigma and feature vectors for points within a unit sphere. Background MLP: Predicts density \sigma for points outside the unit sphere using inverted sphere parameterization; has fewer parameters than the foreground MLP. Shared Color MLP: Predicts color \mathbf{c} based on position, view direction, and style-modulated features. 4. Style-Conditioned Block: Consists of an affine transformation layer and a 1 \times 1 Convolution layer. Algorithm Steps: 1. Latent Sampling: Sample a latent code \mathbf{w} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I). 2. Style Mapping: Pass \mathbf{w} through the Mapping Network to obtain the style vector \mathbf{w}'. 3. Ray Sampling: For a given camera pose, sample points \mathbf{x}i along the ray. 4. Feature Extraction: Pass \mathbf{x}i through the Foreground or Background MLP to get density \sigmai and intermediate features. 5. Style Modulation: Apply affine transformation to the style vector \mathbf{w}' to generate modulation parameters. Modulate the convolution weights in the Style-Conditioned Block using these parameters. Demodulate the convolution output for stability. Apply Leaky ReLU activation. 6. Color Prediction: Pass the modulated features and view direction \mathbf{d} into the Shared Color MLP to predict color \mathbf{c}i. 7. Volume Rendering: Compute the rendered color C(r) using the standard volume rendering integral: C(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i where \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj), and \deltai is the distance between samples. 8. Mutual Learning Optimization: Optimize the Stylized NeRF and a 2D Stylization Network simultaneously. Use learnable latent codes to handle ambiguities in 2D stylized results, ensuring 3D geometry consistency. Apply a NeRF path regularization to enforce 3D consistency. Use a non-saturating GAN objective with R1 regularization. Parameters: Input Resolution: Fixed at 32^2 for the training process. Target Resolution: Images are resized to 256^2 for evaluation. Batch Size: 64 images per batch. Training Steps: T1 = 500k, T2 = 5000k, T3 = 25000k images. Activation: Leaky ReLU. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Small Datasets: If the dataset is too small (e.g., etFaces), stable training is difficult; fine-tuning from a pretrained model (e.g., FFHQ) is required. 3D Inconsistency: Without proper regularization (like the NeRF path regularization), the model may produce artifacts where shape and appearance change constantly as the camera moves. This method integrates a physically constrained imaging model into the NeRF optimization loop to decompose illumination into direct sunlight and ambient skylight, using spherical harmonics to model the latter. It differs from standard NeRF by explicitly separating albedo, surface normals, and lighting to provide auxiliary supervision, thereby reducing lighting ambiguity and improving reconstruction fidelity in shadowed or radiometrically inconsistent regions. Physical Imaging Model with Spherical Harmonics StyleRF-VolVis is a framework for editing the style (appearance) of a DVR scene represented by a NeRF model without losing original content (geometry) information. It supports both photorealistic (PSE) and non-photorealistic (NPSE) editing in a single pipeline by separating content and appearance, allowing explicit assignment of different styles to different DVR regions via a Palette Color Network (PCN) and an Unrestricted Color Network (UCN), while preserving view-dependent lighting. It differs from prior works by supporting both photorealistic and non-photorealistic editing in a single framework, whereas others focus on one or the other. StyleRF-VolVis Non-Photorealistic Style Editing (NPSE) is a style transfer process for volume rendering that assigns specific styles to distinct regions of a scene using an unrestricted color network and Nearest Neighbor Feature Matching (NNFM) loss. Unlike StylizedNeRF which assigns one style to the whole scene, NPSE allows explicit assignment of different styles to different DVR regions. Unlike ARF and StylizedNeRF which discard view directions to ensure consistency, NPSE removes view direction input only in the Unrestricted Color Network (UCN) optimization to preserve lighting while ensuring consistency. Non-Photorealistic Style Editing StyleNeRF extends the original Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) architecture by integrating a style-based generator to handle illumination changes and synthesize high-resolution images]. It differs from standard NeRF by introducing a low-dimensional appearance code and style-based MLPs, setting it apart from siblings like StylizedNeRF which may use different stylization mechanisms [14882-stylizednerf.md]. StyleNeRF Architecture Configuration Time Complexity: Training involves mutual learning between the 3D NeRF and a 2D stylization network, which increases computational cost compared to standard NeRF. The use of NeRF++ (foreground/background split) adds complexity to the density prediction step. Memory Complexity: The architecture uses two MLPs for density (foreground and background) and a shared MLP for color, along with a Mapping Network and Style-Conditioned Blocks. The input resolution is fixed at 32^2 during training, which limits memory usage during the initial stages, but the target resolution is 256^2. Measured Performance: On datasets like FFHQ, AFHQ, and CompCars, StyleNeRF achieves high-quality and 3D-consistent results, outperforming baselines like HoloGAN, GARF, and \pi-GAN which suffer from severe artifacts or 3D inconsistency. Strengths: High-resolution synthesis, 3D consistency, style controllability, and ability to handle unbounded backgrounds via NeRF++. Limitations: Requires large datasets for stable training; small datasets require fine-tuning from pretrained models. Computationally intensive due to GAN training and mutual learning. When to use: When high-fidelity, 3D-consistent, stylized 3D object synthesis is required, particularly for face datasets. When not to use: When computational resources are limited, or when the dataset is small and fine-tuning is not feasible. StylizedNeRF (StyleNeRF) was introduced in the paper "StyleNeRF: A Style-based 3D-Aware Generator for High-resolution Image Synthesis". It builds upon the original NeRF architecture and StyleGAN2, integrating style-based generators into 3D-aware models to enable high-resolution image synthesis with style control. The method addresses the limitations of previous 3D-aware generators that struggled with 3D consistency and high-resolution details. It is part of the broader family of NeRF-based 3D editing and synthesis methods. A survey on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11704-025-41176-9, fetched 2026-10-28 StyleNeRF: A Style-based 3D-Aware Generator for High-resolution Image Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2110.08985, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Physical Imaging Model with Spherical Harmonics
head: Lambertian reflectance-based physical imaging model
body:
This method integrates a physically constrained imaging model into the NeRF optimization loop to decompose illumination into direct sunlight and ambient skylight, using spherical harmonics to model the latter. It differs from standard NeRF by explicitly separating albedo, surface normals, and lighting to provide auxiliary supervision, thereby reducing lighting ambiguity and improving reconstruction fidelity in shadowed or radiometrically inconsistent regions. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Density field \sigma(P) and its gradient 
abla\sigma(P) at a 3D point P=(x,y,z). Camera origin op for the current view. Surface albedo hoi (RGB) at point i. Illumination coefficients Lk for k=0..8. Outputs: Synthesized image intensity I{p2}^i at point i. Data Structures Illumination Coefficients: A vector of 9 coefficients L = [L0, L1,..., L8] representing the second-order spherical harmonic expansion of the ambient skylight field. Basis Functions: A vector of 9 values b = [b0,..., b8] computed from the surface normal components. Steps 1. Extract Density Gradient: Calculate the gradient of the density field \sigma at point P: 
abla\sigma(P) = \left[  rac{\partial\sigma}{\partial x},  rac{\partial\sigma}{\partial y},  rac{\partial\sigma}{\partial z} ight] 2. Normalize Gradient: Compute the unit normal vector n(P): n(P) =  rac{
abla\sigma(P)}{\|
abla\sigma(P)\|} 3. Constrain Normal Direction: Calculate the ray direction from the surface point P to the camera origin op: d{obs} = 	ext{normalize}(P - op) Compute the inner product n(P) \cdot d{obs}. If n(P) \cdot d{obs} < 0, reverse the normal vector: n(P) \leftarrow -n(P). Otherwise, retain n(P). This ensures the normal faces the camera (angle < 90^\circ). 4. Compute Spherical Harmonic Basis Functions: Evaluate the second-order basis functions bk using the components nx, ny, nz of the constrained unit normal n(P): b0 = \sqrt{ rac{1}{4\pi}} b1 = \sqrt{ rac{3}{4\pi}} nz b2 = \sqrt{ rac{3}{4\pi}} nx b3 = \sqrt{ rac{3}{4\pi}} ny b4 = \sqrt{ rac{5}{12\pi}} (3nz^2 - 1) b5 = \sqrt{ rac{15}{4\pi}} nx nz b6 = \sqrt{ rac{15}{4\pi}} ny nz b7 = \sqrt{ rac{15}{4\pi}} (nx^2 - ny^2) b8 = \sqrt{ rac{15}{4\pi}} nx ny 5. Synthesize Intensity: Compute the intensity I{p2}^i for each RGB channel: I{p2}^i = hoi \sum{k=0}^{8} Lk bk Here, hoi is the surface albedo (RGB), Lk are the illumination coefficients, and bk are the basis functions. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computephysicalimagingintensity(densitygradient, cameraorigin, pointp, albedo, illuminationcoeffs): """ Computes synthesized intensity using physical imaging model with spherical harmonics. Args: densitygradient: Array [dx, dy, dz] representing nabla sigma(P). cameraorigin: Array [ox, oy, oz] representing op. pointp: Array [x, y, z] representing P. albedo: Array [r, g, b] representing rhoi. illuminationcoeffs: Array [L0,..., L8] of length 9. Returns: intensity: Array [r, g, b] representing Ip2^i. """ # Step 1 & 2: Normalize gradient to get unit normal normmagnitude = sqrt(densitygradient[0]2 + densitygradient[1]2 + densitygradient[2]2) if normmagnitude == 0: # Guard against zero gradient; return zero intensity or handle as degenerate case. return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] nx = densitygradient[0] / normmagnitude ny = densitygradient[1] / normmagnitude nz = densitygradient[2] / normmagnitude # Step 3: Constrain normal direction # Calculate ray direction from surface point to camera origin dx = pointp[0] - cameraorigin[0] dy = pointp[1] - cameraorigin[1] dz = pointp[2] - cameraorigin[2] raylen = sqrt(dx2 + dy2 + dz2) if raylen == 0: # Guard against point coincident with camera origin return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] dobsx = dx / raylen dobsy = dy / raylen dobsz = dz / raylen # Inner product dotproduct = nx dobsx + ny dobsy + nz dobsz # If negative, reverse normal if dotproduct < 0: nx = -nx ny = -ny nz = -nz # Step 4: Compute Spherical Harmonic Basis Functions (Second Order, k=0..8) sqrt4pi = sqrt(4 3.141592653589793) sqrt12pi = sqrt(12 3.141592653589793) b0 = sqrt(1 / (4 3.141592653589793)) b1 = sqrt(3 / (4 3.141592653589793)) nz b2 = sqrt(3 / (4 3.141592653589793)) nx b3 = sqrt(3 / (4 3.141592653589793)) ny b4 = sqrt(5 / (12 3.141592653589793)) (3 nz2 - 1) b5 = sqrt(15 / (4 3.141592653589793)) nx nz b6 = sqrt(15 / (4 3.141592653589793)) ny nz b7 = sqrt(15 / (4 3.141592653589793)) (nx2 - ny2) b8 = sqrt(15 / (4 3.141592653589793)) nx ny basisfunctions = [b0, b1, b2, b3, b4, b5, b6, b7, b8] # Step 5: Synthesize Intensity # Sum over k=0 to 8 of Lk bk totalirradiance = 0.0 for k in range(9): totalirradiance += illuminationcoeffs[k] basisfunctions[k] # Apply albedo intensity = [albedo[0] totalirradiance, albedo[1] totalirradiance, albedo[2] totalirradiance] return intensity Parameters Spherical Harmonic Order: Second-order, resulting in 9 coefficients (k=0 to 8). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Zero Gradient: If 
abla\sigma(P) is zero, the normal cannot be normalized. Camera Coincidence: If P = op, the ray direction is undefined. Normal Ambiguity: Without the camera-view constraint, NeRF-predicted density gradients may point in the opposite direction of the actual surface normal. The inner product check resolves this. Time Complexity: The computation involves a constant number of operations (gradient, normalization, 9 basis evaluations, dot product, and sum) per sample point, making it O(1) per sample relative to scene size, but adds overhead to the per-point shading calculation during training. Memory Complexity: Requires storing 9 illumination coefficients Lk per view or globally, and the basis functions are computed on the fly. Strengths: Reduces lighting ambiguity and improves reconstruction fidelity in shadowed or radiometrically inconsistent regions by separating illumination from albedo. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the density gradient for normal estimation; assumes distant illumination sources (sunlight and skylight). When to Use: Satellite imaging conditions with complex lighting where radiometric decomposition is needed for accurate 3D reconstruction. When Not to Use: Scenes with complex local lighting or non-distant light sources where spherical harmonics may not adequately capture the illumination field. This method was introduced in the context of NeRF reconstruction for multi-view satellite images, specifically to handle radiometric decomposition under complex satellite imaging conditions. It was proposed by researchers publishing in Remote Sensing in 2026. The approach integrates the physical imaging module directly into the NeRF optimization process rather than applying it post-reconstruction. Shading and Geometric Constraint Neural Radiance Field for DSM Reconstruction from Multi-View Satellite Images, https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18071091, fetched 2026-11-05

name: StyleRF-VolVis
body: StyleRF-VolVis is a framework for editing the style (appearance) of a DVR scene represented by a NeRF model without losing original content (geometry) information. It supports both photorealistic (PSE) and non-photorealistic (NPSE) editing in a single pipeline by separating content and appearance, allowing explicit assignment of different styles to different DVR regions via a Palette Color Network (PCN) and an Unrestricted Color Network (UCN), while preserving view-dependent lighting. It differs from prior works by supporting both photorealistic and non-photorealistic editing in a single framework, whereas others focus on one or the other. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images of the scene, an initial Transfer Function (TF) defining opacity ranges, and optionally reference images for style transfer. Outputs: A stylized DVR scene represented by the optimized networks, allowing for interactive PSE and NPSE. Data Structures: 1. Base NeRF Model: Uses Instant-NGP architecture. Density MLP: Takes position x and hash-grid encoded features; outputs density \sigma(x). Hash-grid Encoder: Multiresolution hash-grid encoding for efficient optimization. Note: Parameters are frozen after Stage 1. 2. Palette Color Network (PCN): Composed of two branches: Specular Branch (Lighting MLP): Inputs: Geometry features (from density MLP) and spherical harmonics (SH) encoded view direction d. Output: Grayscale specular color cs(x, d). Diffuse Branch (Palette MLP): Inputs: Features from palette hash-grid encoder Ep. Outputs: Intensity I(x), weights \omegai(x) for NP palette colors, and color offsets \deltai(x). Palette Colors: P = \{P1,..., P{NP}\}, extracted and refined from input images. 3. Unrestricted Color Network (UCN): Architecture: Similar to the diffuse branch but without palette constraints. Inputs: Geometry features (no view direction d during optimization to ensure cross-view consistency). Output: Diffuse color cd(x). Numbered Steps: 1. Stage 1: Base NeRF Optimization Optimize the base NeRF model (Instant-NGP) to reconstruct scene geometry using the loss L{BASE}: L{BASE} = ||c(r) - \hat{c}(r)||2^2 where c(r) is ground-truth color and \hat{c}(r) is predicted color. Freeze all parameters of the base NeRF (density MLP and hash-grid encoder) to prevent style editing from affecting geometry. 2. Palette Refinement Extract initial palette colors P{CONVEX} using the RGB convex hull method from multi-view images. Refine the palette by removing similar colors. Calculate the distance between colors in HSB space using only the hue component. If the distance is below a threshold, remove the color. Determine the final number of palette colors NP. 3. Stage 2: PCN Optimization (PSE) Initialize the PCN. Initialize shallow layers of the palette MLP with hidden parameters from the base NeRF’s color function. Optimize PCN parameters and palette colors P using the loss L{PALETTE}: L{PALETTE} = ||c(r) - \hat{c}(r)||2^2 + \lambda\delta \sum{i=1}^{M} \sum{j=1}^{NP} ||\deltaj(xi)||2^2 where \lambda\delta = 0.1 is the regularization strength. The predicted color c(x, d) is computed as: c(x, d) = cs(x, d) + I(x) \sum{i=1}^{NP} \omegai(x)(Pi + \deltai(x)) Render \hat{c}(r) using the standard NeRF volume rendering equation: \hat{c}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{M} \alphai (1 - \omegai) c(xi, d) where \omegai = \exp(-(ti - t{i-1})\sigma(xi)) is transmittance, \alphai = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} \omegai is attenuation, and r=(o,d) is the ray. 4. Photorealistic Style Editing (PSE) Setup For PSE, compute the difference \Delta P between the original palette P and target palette P' in HSB space. Add \Delta Pi to Pi + \deltai(x) in the color equation. For opacity/lighting editing, multiply \sigma(x{Pi}) or cs(x{Pi}, d) by a scalar. 5. Stage 3: UCN Optimization (NPSE) via Knowledge Distillation (KD) Initialization: Perform color transfer in the PCN (teacher) to match target style colors. This ensures the UCN (student) color representation matches selected styles before NPSE. Optimization: Optimize the UCN using KD to transfer color knowledge from the PCN.
