Remove view direction input in UCN optimization to ensure cross-view consistency during NPSE. Optimize on a single camera view by rendering different regions independently to map a style to a region. Utilize the additional lighting MLP (optimized in Stage 2) to preserve DVR lighting during NPSE, keeping view directions for lighting calculation. 6. Inference For partial stylization, combine color representations: regions preserving original appearance use colors from PCN; stylized regions use UCN. Perform additional feedforward steps of the lighting MLP to provide lighting information. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. LAMBDADELTA = 0.1 def renderneRF(rayo, rayd, densitymlp, hashgrid, colorfn): # Standard volume rendering implementation pass def trainbasenerf(images, tf): densitymlp, hashgrid = initinstantngp() optimizer = Adam([densitymlp.parameters(), hashgrid.parameters()]) for epoch in epochs: for image in images: rayo, rayd = samplerays(image) # Sample points along ray points, depths = samplepoints(rayo, rayd, densitymlp) # Get density sigma = densitymlp(points, hashgrid) # Get color (initially from base NeRF color function, but not used for final stylization) cpred = renderneRF(rayo, rayd, densitymlp, hashgrid, basecolorfn) cgt = image.color loss = mse(cgt, cpred) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return densitymlp, hashgrid def trainpcn(densitymlp, hashgrid, images, refimages): # Extract initial palette Pconvex = extractconvexhullcolors(refimages) # Refine palette P = refinepalette(Pconvex, threshold=0.1) # Threshold based on hue distance NP = len(P) lightingmlp = initlightingmlp() palettemlp = initpalettemlp() # Initialize shallow layers of palettemlp with base NeRF hidden params initpalettemlpshallow(palettemlp, densitymlp) optimizer = Adam([lightingmlp.parameters(), palettemlp.parameters(), P]) for epoch in epochs: for image in images: rayo, rayd = samplerays(image) points, depths = samplepoints(rayo, rayd, densitymlp) # Get geometry features geofeatures = densitymlp(points, hashgrid) # Specular branch viewdirsh = encodesphericalharmonics(rayd) cs = lightingmlp(geofeatures, viewdirsh) # Diffuse branch palettefeatures = palettemlp(points, hashgrid) # Uses palette hash-grid encoder Ep I = intensity(palettefeatures) weights = softmax(paletteweights(palettefeatures)) # NP weights delta = coloroffsets(palettefeatures) # NP offsets # Compute diffuse color cd = I sum(weights[i] (P[i] + delta[i]) for i in range(NP)) # Total color c = cs + cd # Render sigma = densitymlp(points, hashgrid) cpred = renderneRF(rayo, rayd, densitymlp, hashgrid, lambda x, d: c) cgt = image.color # Loss mseloss = mse(cgt, cpred) regloss = LAMBDADELTA sum(norm(delta[i])2 for i in range(NP)) loss = mseloss + regloss optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return lightingmlp, palettemlp, P def trainucn(pcnlightingmlp, pcnpalettemlp, pcnP, images, targetstyleref): # Color transfer in PCN to match target style pcnP = transferstylecolors(pcnP, targetstyleref) ucn = initucn() # KD: UCN learns to match PCN output optimizer = Adam(ucn.parameters()) for epoch in epochs: for image in images: # Optimize on single view for region mapping rayo, rayd = samplerays(image) points, depths = samplepoints(rayo, rayd, densitymlp) # PCN (Teacher) geofeatures = densitymlp(points, hashgrid) csteacher = pcnlightingmlp(geofeatures, encodesphericalharmonics(rayd)) # PCN diffuse It = intensity(pcnpalettemlp(points, hashgrid)) wt = softmax(pcnpaletteweights(pcnpalettemlp(points, hashgrid))) dt = pcnpaletteoffsets(pcnpalettemlp(points, hashgrid)) cdteacher = It sum(wt[i] (pcnP[i] + dt[i]) for i in range(NP)) cteacher = csteacher + cdteacher # UCN (Student) - No view direction input ucnfeatures = ucn(points, hashgrid) # Or similar encoder cdstudent = ucnoutput(ucnfeatures) # KD Loss: Match student to teacher kdloss = mse(cdstudent, cdteacher) # Optional: Add reconstruction loss if needed, but primary is KD loss = kdloss optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return ucn def renderstylized(rayo, rayd, densitymlp, hashgrid, lightingmlp, palettemlp, P, ucn, regionmask): points, depths = samplepoints(rayo, rayd, densitymlp) geofeatures = densitymlp(points, hashgrid) # Lighting (Preserved) cs = lightingmlp(geofeatures, encodesphericalharmonics(rayd)) # Diffuse: Mix PCN and UCN based on region mask # If regionmask indicates stylized, use UCN. Else use PCN. # Note: UCN does not take view direction cducn = ucnoutput(ucn(points, hashgrid)) # PCN Diffuse Ip = intensity(palettemlp(points, hashgrid)) wp = softmax(paletteweights(palettemlp(points, hashgrid))) dp = paletteoffsets(palettemlp(points, hashgrid)) cdpcn = Ip sum(wp[i] (P[i] + dp[i]) for i in range(NP)) # Combine cd = where(regionmask, cducn, cdpcn) c = cs + cd sigma = densitymlp(points, hashgrid) return renderneRF(rayo, rayd, densitymlp, hashgrid, lambda x, d: c) Parameters: \lambda\delta = 0.1: Regularization strength for color offsets. Initial Transfer Function (TF): Defines opacity ranges. Regions with opacity equal to zero in the initial TF cannot be represented by NeRF and thus cannot undergo PSE or NPSE. Palette Refinement Threshold: Hue distance threshold in HSB space for removing similar colors. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Opacity: If the initial TF sets opacity to zero for certain regions, NeRF cannot represent these values, and PSE/NPSE cannot be applied to them. Similar Colors: If colors among different regions in the input DVR scene are similar, palette refinement may not separate them correctly. Users must manually adjust the number of palette colors and their RGB values. Lighting Direction: Lighting direction cannot be modified because no normal information is available, although lighting intensity can be adjusted. NPSE Consistency: Discarding view direction in UCN is necessary for cross-view consistency but requires careful initialization via PSE color transfer to avoid inaccurate style matching. Time Complexity: Training is slower than ARF but faster than SNeRF. The process involves three stages: Base NeRF, PCN, and UCN (KD). NPSE optimization on a single camera view requires rendering different regions independently, slowing the stylization process. Memory Complexity: Uses Instant-NGP hash-grid encoding, which is memory efficient compared to dense voxel grids. Additional memory for PCN and UCN parameters. Measured Performance: Inference time on combustion dataset: 564 ms. Training time on combustion dataset: 1.2 h. Training time on vortex dataset: 29.7 m. Inference time on vortex dataset: 373 ms. Cross-view consistency: Achieves best short- and long-range cross-view consistency (MSE and LPIPS) compared to AdaIN, ReReVST, ARF, and SNeRF. Strengths: Supports both PSE and NPSE in a single framework; preserves view-dependent lighting; allows explicit assignment of different styles to different regions; better cross-view consistency than image-based methods. Limitations: Slower training than ARF; interactive PSE supported but not interactive NPSE; cannot modify lighting direction; sensitive to similar colors in input. When to use: When high-quality, cross-view consistent stylization of DVR scenes is required, especially when mixing PSE and NPSE or applying different styles to different regions. When not to use: When real-time interactive NPSE is required, or when lighting direction modification is needed. StyleRF-VolVis is the first work in VolVis that targets style transfer in the NeRF space. It builds on NeRF representation and Instant-NGP architecture. It adapts NeRF's palette-based recoloring strategy and uses Knowledge Distillation (KD) to transfer color knowledge. It differs from prior works like ARF and SNeRF by supporting both photorealistic and non-photorealistic editing in a single framework and preserving view-dependent lighting. StyleRF-VolVis: Style Transfer of Neural Radiance Fields for Expressive Volume Visualization., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2024.3456342, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Non-Photorealistic Style Editing
body: Non-Photorealistic Style Editing (NPSE) is a style transfer process for volume rendering that assigns specific styles to distinct regions of a scene using an unrestricted color network and Nearest Neighbor Feature Matching (NNFM) loss. Unlike SNeRF which assigns one style to the whole scene, NPSE allows explicit assignment of different styles to different DVR regions. Unlike ARF and SNeRF which discard view directions to ensure consistency, NPSE removes view direction input only in the Unrestricted Color Network (UCN) optimization to preserve lighting while ensuring consistency. Inputs: A base NeRF model (with frozen density \sigma(\mathbf{x}) and pre-trained color network), one or multiple reference images S = \{S1, S2, \dots, S{NP}\} representing desired styles for NP regions, and camera views. Outputs: A stylized volume representation defined by the optimized Unrestricted Color Network cu(\mathbf{x}). Data Structures: Base NeRF: Frozen density field \sigma(\mathbf{x}). Unrestricted Color Network (UCN): Optimizable color network cu(\mathbf{x}). It outputs diffuse colors. Palette Weights: \omegai(\mathbf{x}) for each style region i \in \{1, \dots, NP\}. Feature Extractor: Pre-trained VGG-16 model \phi, specifically using the conv3 block. Steps: 1. Region Segmentation: If the number of reference images is less than NP or for local patterns, segment reference images into localized style regions using the Segment Anything Model (SAM) with optional point prompts. 2. Network Construction: Construct a new Radiance Field (RF) using the optimizable unrestricted color cu(\mathbf{x}) and the frozen density \sigma(\mathbf{x}) from the base NeRF. 3. Rendering: Compute NP rendering images R = \{R1, R2, \dots, R{NP}\} for each camera view. For a sample point \mathbf{x}, it contributes to rendering Ri only if its palette weight \omegai(\mathbf{x}) is greater than other palette weights. 4. Background Handling: Extract the luminance value from each style Si to use as the background color for the corresponding rendering Ri to handle transparency artifacts. 5. Loss Computation: Compute the stylization loss using NNFM loss between renderings R and styles S via VGG-16 features. Omit content loss between original and stylized images due to suboptimal outcomes. 6. Optimization: Update cu(\mathbf{x}) parameters using the computed loss. Formulas: The NNFM loss is formulated as: L{NNFM}(R, S) = \frac{1}{NF NP} \sum{i=1}^{NP} \sum{fj \in \phi(Ri)} \min{fk \in \phi(Si)} d(fj, fk) where: \phi(Ri) and \phi(Si) are the feature vectors extracted from the VGG-16 model \phi for rendering Ri and style Si respectively. NF is the number of feature vectors for \phi(Ri). NP is the number of style regions. d is the cosine distance between feature vectors fj and fk. Parameters: VGG-16 Block: conv3. Iterations: 210. Views per Iteration: One of 42 uniformly sampled camera views. Learning Rate: Fixed, following the ARF setting (Adam optimizer with \beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.999, initial LR 0.01, decayed to 0 for other stages, but fixed for NPSE). Batch Size: 4,096 rays. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainnpse(basenerf, referenceimages, numstyles, numviews=42, iterations=210): """ Trains the Unrestricted Color Network (UCN) for Non-Photorealistic Style Editing. Args: basenerf: Base NeRF model with frozen density sigma(x). referenceimages: List of reference images/styles. numstyles: Number of distinct style regions NP. numviews: Number of uniformly sampled camera views for training. iterations: Number of optimization iterations. Returns: Optimized UCN parameters. """ # 1. Segment reference images if necessary # If len(referenceimages) < numstyles or for local patterns, use SAM styleregions = [] for img in referenceimages: # Use SAM with optional point prompts to divide image into localized style regions # This step is external; assume styleregions contains the segmented masks/styles pass # 2. Initialize UCN with base NeRF color network weights, but make it optimizable ucn = copyweights(basenerf.colornetwork) ucn.requiresgrad(True) # 3. Setup feature extractor vggconv3 = getvgg16conv3block() # 4. Setup optimizer (Fixed LR as per ARF setting) # Adam with lr=0.01, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, but LR does not decay during NPSE optimizer = Adam(ucn.parameters(), lr=0.01, betas=(0.9, 0.999)) # 5. Sample camera views uniformly cameraviews = sampleuniformviews(numviews) for iteration in range(iterations): optimizer.zerograd() # Select one view for this iteration viewidx = random.randint(0, len(cameraviews) - 1) camera = cameraviews[viewidx] # 6. Render NP images for this view # For each sample point x, it contributes to Ri only if omegai(x) is max renderings = [] for i in range(numstyles): # Render using frozen sigma(x) and optimizable cu(x) # Apply palette weight logic: only contribute if omegai(x) > others renderingi = rendervolume(basenerf.sigma, ucn, camera, styleindex=i) renderings.append(renderingi) # 7. Set background colors based on luminance of styles for i in range(numstyles): bgcolor = extractluminance(referenceimages[i]) renderings[i] = setbackground(renderings[i], bgcolor) # 8. Compute NNFM Loss loss = 0.0 for i in range(numstyles): # Extract features from VGG-16 conv3 featr = vggconv3(renderings[i]) feats = vggconv3(referenceimages[i]) # Assuming referenceimages[i] corresponds to style i # Compute min cosine distance for each feature in rendering to style features # LNNFM = (1/(NFNP)) sumi sumj mink d(fj, fk) nf = featr.shape[0] # Number of feature vectors for j in range(nf): mindist = float('inf') for k in range(feats.shape[0]): dist = cosinedistance(featr[j], feats[k]) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist loss += mindist loss = loss / (numstyles nf) # 9. Backpropagate loss.backward() optimizer.step() return ucn Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Transparency Artifacts: Using incorrect background colors (e.g., black or white) leads to unsatisfactory stylization. Extracting luminance from the style image is required. Content Loss: Including content loss between original and stylized images yields suboptimal outcomes and should be omitted. Memory: Deferred backpropagation is employed to update UCN parameters for the entire image under limited GPU memory. A workflow to indirectly control NPSE stylization by iteratively refining reference image selections using negative point prompts and UCN retraining. If the initial style selection includes undesired styles, apply negative point prompts for SAM to the reference image to exclude them, then retrain the UCN to achieve the desired stylization. This is necessary because NPSE does not support direct control over the stylization process once initiated. Time and Memory Complexity: Training Time: For the "vortex" dataset, NPSE takes 29.7 minutes. For the "combustion" dataset, it takes 1.2 hours. This is faster than SNeRF (3.6 h and 3.8 h respectively) but slower than ARF (14.6 m and 20.1 m respectively). Inference Time: For the "vortex" dataset, NPSE takes 373 ms. For the "combustion" dataset, it takes 564 ms. This is slower than ARF (204 ms and 210 ms) and SNeRF (173 ms and 195 ms). Memory: Uses deferred backpropagation to handle limited GPU memory. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Allows explicit assignment of different styles to different DVR regions. Preserves view-dependent lighting by removing view direction input only in UCN optimization, unlike ARF and SNeRF which discard view directions entirely. Offers higher flexibility and robustness compared to conventional NPR methods by transferring arbitrary styles within a unified framework. Limitations: Does not support direct control over the stylization process; requires iterative refinement via SAM prompts. Relies on NNFM loss which focuses on negligible local style, mitigated by color transfer to align region color with overall style color. When to Use: Use when distinct styles are needed for different regions of a volume scene and view-dependent lighting preservation is important. Originated in the paper "StyleRF-VolVis: Style Transfer of Neural Radiance Fields for Expressive Volume Visualization". It is part of the StyleRF-VolVis framework for expressive volume visualization. StyleRF-VolVis: Style Transfer of Neural Radiance Fields for Expressive Volume Visualization., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2024.3456342, fetched 2026-10-26

name: StyleNeRF Architecture Configuration
head: StyleNeRF hyperparameters
body: StyleNeRF extends the original Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) architecture by integrating a style-based generator to handle illumination changes and synthesize high-resolution images. It differs from standard NeRF by introducing a low-dimensional appearance code and style-based MLPs, setting it apart from siblings like StylizedNeRF which may use different stylization mechanisms [14882-stylizednerf.md]. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera parameters, 3D coordinates, and a latent style vector. Outputs: Volume density (\sigma) and view-dependent color (c). Data Structures: Appearance Code: A 16-dimensional vector (z{app} \in \mathbb{R}^{16}) stored and optimized individually for every frame. Mapping Network: 8 fully connected layers. Latent/Style Dimensions: 512. Foreground Field MLP: Hidden units = 256. Background Field MLP: Hidden units = 128. Fourier Features: Dimension L=10. Network Layout: The architecture follows the StyleGAN2 configuration for layers after 2D aggregation. Feature sizes decrease from 512 (for 32x32 resolution) down to 32 (for 1024x1024 resolution). Parameters: Learning Rate: The mapping network uses a learning rate 100\times lower than the default. Batch Size: 64. Training Iterations: 25,000 images. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class StyleNeRF: def init(self): # Mapping network: 8 FC layers, latent/style dim 512 self.mappingnet = MappingNetwork(layers=8, latentdim=512, styledim=512) # Appearance code: 16-dim, per-frame optimization self.appearancecodedim = 16 # Fourier feature dimension self.L = 10 # MLP hidden units self.foregroundhiddenunits = 256 self.backgroundhiddenunits = 128 # Feature sizes for 2D aggregation layers # Decreases from 512 (32x32) to 32 (1024x1024) self.featuresizes = { 32: 512, 64: 256, # Example interpolation 128: 128, 256: 64, 512: 32, 1024: 32 } def getappearancecode(self, frameindex): """ Retrieve or initialize the 16-dimensional appearance code for a specific frame. This code is optimized individually per frame. """ # Implementation detail: Store as a learnable parameter tensor # Shape: (1, 16) return self.appearancecodes[frameindex] def buildmlp(self, inputdim, hiddenunits, outputdim): """ Build the style-based MLP for foreground or background fields. """ # Uses Fourier features with L=10 # Hidden units: 256 for foreground, 128 for background pass def configurelearningrate(self, baselr): """ Set mapping network learning rate to 1/100th of base. """ return baselr / 100.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The low dimensionality (16) of the appearance code is critical to learning global effects without deteriorating the benefits of relative encoding. Using higher dimensional codes (e.g., 128 as in NeuralBody baselines) may lead to suboptimal learning of global effects. Uses a different approach to stylization; StyleNeRF uses a style-based generator. Uses spherical harmonics for lighting; StyleNeRF uses appearance codes. Focuses on volume visualization; StyleNeRF focuses on high-resolution image synthesis. General style editing; StyleNeRF is a specific architecture for 3D-aware generation. Time Complexity: Training takes approximately three days on 8 Tesla V100 GPUs for 25,000 images. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles illumination changes effectively; generates high-resolution images (up to 1024x1024). Limitations: Requires careful tuning of appearance code dimensionality. When to use: When high-resolution, style-controlled 3D-aware synthesis is needed. When not to use: When computational resources are limited or real-time inference is required. StyleNeRF was proposed in "StyleNeRF: A Style-based 3D-Aware Generator for High-resolution Image Synthesis". It builds on the original NeRF architecture [42] and concurrent works on handling illumination changes [36, 49]. The architecture reuses parameters from StyleGAN2. StyleNeRF: A Style-based 3D-Aware Generator for High-resolution Image Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2110.08985, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) A-NeRF: Articulated Neural Radiance Fields for Learning Human Shape, Appearance, and Pose, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2102.06199, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Dual-Branch Hash Encoder NeRF for Stylization
head: Instant Photorealistic Neural Radiance Fields Stylization method, Two-branch Instant-NGP, Instant Neural Radiance Fields Stylization, Instant-NGP Stylization, InstantNeRF-Stylization
body: A method for multi-view image stylization of 3D scenes that uses a hash table-based position encoder (Instant-NGP) split into content and style sub-branches, applying Adaptive Instance Normalization (AdaIN) to position encoding features during inference to transfer style from a target (image or scene set) to novel views without retraining. It solves the problem of transferring style from a target scene/image to a content scene while preserving geometry, using an efficient hash encoder instead of a standard MLP for position encoding. Unlike previous works where style targets are only images, this method extends the style target to 3D scene image sets. Compared to using two independent Instant-NGP networks, the dual-branch approach with shared MLP RGB preserves geometry consistency better and avoids noise. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of images of a content 3D scene; a style target, which is either a single style image or a set of images of a style 3D scene. Outputs: Stylized novel view images of the content scene, preserving its geometry but adopting the appearance of the style target. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Grid (V): A 3D grid representing the spatial domain for style representation. Layout: V \in \mathbb{R}^{NV \times NV \times NV}. NV: Voxel resolution. Typical values: 32, 64, 128, 256. Default: 128. 2. Content Hash Encoder: A hash-based position encoder mapping 3D coordinates to feature vectors for the content scene. 3. Style Hash Encoder: A hash-based position encoder mapping 3D coordinates to feature vectors for the style scene. 4. Shared Direction Encoder: A spherical encoder mapping view directions to feature vectors. 5. Shared MLPRGB: A multilayer perceptron taking concatenated features from position encoders and the direction encoder to output color (C) and density (\sigma). 6. MLPDensity: A separate MLP (part of the content branch architecture) that outputs density based on content position encoder features. Numbered Steps: Training Process: 1. Initialize two position encoder branches (Content Hash Encoder, Style Hash Encoder) and one shared direction encoder (Spherical Encoder). Initialize the shared MLPRGB and content-specific MLPDensity. 2. For each training step, sample rays for both the content target and the style target. If the style target is a single image, treat it as a 3D scene by placing 3D colored voxels representing the 2D image pixels in the center of the 3D space. If the style target is an image set, treat it as a normal 3D scene. 3. Encode 3D coordinates (x, y, z) using both the Content Hash Encoder and the Style Hash Encoder to obtain content features (fc) and style features (fs). 4. Encode view direction (d) using the shared Direction Encoder. 5. Concatenate features and pass through the shared MLPRGB to predict color and density for both targets. For the content target, use content features (fc) and direction features. For the style target, use style features (fs) and direction features. 6. Compute loss using Huber loss for both content and style targets. Huber Loss Formula: L = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} rel^2, & \text{for } rel \le \delta \\ \delta(rel - \frac{1}{2}\delta), & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where rel = |C{predict} - C{target}|, C{predict} is the rendered color, C{target} is the target color, and \delta is a hyperparameter. 7. Optimize the Content Position Encoder based on the content target loss. 8. Optimize the Style Position Encoder based on the style target loss. 9. Optimize the Shared MLPRGB based on the combined content and style target losses. Inference (AdaIN Stylization): 1. Calculate content position encoder features (fc(x, y, z)) using voxel grid positions as input. 2. Calculate style position encoder features (fs(x, y, z)) using the same voxel grid positions. 3. Compute the mean (F\muc, F\mus) and standard deviation (F\sigmac, F\sigmas) of the content and style voxel grid features respectively. 4. Apply AdaIN transformation to the content features using the style statistics as reference: AdaIN(f(x, y, z)) = F\sigmas \left( \frac{f(x, y, z) - F\muc}{F\sigmac} \right) + F\mus where f(x, y, z) is the content voxel grid feature, F\muc, F\sigmac are the mean and std of content voxel grid features, and F\mus, F\sigmas are the mean and std of style voxel grid features. 5. Use the adjusted (stylized) features for color prediction via the shared MLPRGB. 6. Use the unadjusted (content) features for density prediction via the content MLPDensity to preserve geometry consistency. 7. (Optional) Control the degree of stylization using a style weight \alpha \in [0, 1]: AdaINc(f(x, y, z)) = (1-\alpha)f(x, y, z) + \alpha AdaIN(f(x, y, z)) where \alpha=0 is no style and \alpha=1 is full style. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def huberloss(predictedcolor, targetcolor, delta=0.01): """ Computes the Huber loss between predicted and target colors. """ rel = np.abs(predictedcolor - targetcolor) loss = np.where(rel <= delta, 0.5 rel2, delta (rel - 0.5 delta)) return np.mean(loss) def adaintransform(contentfeatures, stylemean, stylestd, contentmean, contentstd): """ Applies Adaptive Instance Normalization to content features using style statistics. """ normalized = (contentfeatures - contentmean) / contentstd stylized = stylestd normalized + stylemean return stylized def traindualbranchnerf(contentimages, styleimagesorimage, numsteps, learningrate): """ Trains the Dual-Branch Hash Encoder NeRF. """ # Initialize encoders and MLPs contenthashencoder = HashEncoder() stylehashencoder = HashEncoder() shareddirencoder = SphericalEncoder() sharedmlprgb = MLPRGB() contentmlpdensity = MLPDensity() # If style is a single image, convert to 3D colored voxels if issingleimage(styleimagesorimage): stylevoxels = create3dcoloredvoxels(styleimagesorimage, center=True) else: stylevoxels = styleimagesorimage # Treat as 3D scene image set for step in range(numsteps): # Sample rays for content and style contentrays = samplerays(contentimages) stylerays = samplerays(stylevoxels) # Encode content contentposfeat = contenthashencoder(contentrays.positions) contentdirfeat = shareddirencoder(contentrays.directions) contentcolor, contentdensity = sharedmlprgb(concat(contentposfeat, contentdirfeat)) # Encode style styleposfeat = stylehashencoder(stylerays.positions) styledirfeat = shareddirencoder(stylerays.directions) stylecolor, styledensity = sharedmlprgb(concat(styleposfeat, styledirfeat)) # Compute losses contentloss = huberloss(contentcolor, contentrays.targetcolors) styleloss = huberloss(stylecolor, stylerays.targetcolors) totalloss = contentloss + styleloss # Backpropagation and Optimization # Optimize content position encoder based on contentloss # Optimize style position encoder based on styleloss # Optimize shared MLPRGB based on totalloss # Optimize content MLPDensity based on contentloss (implied by architecture) optimizestep([contenthashencoder, stylehashencoder, sharedmlprgb, contentmlpdensity], totalloss, learningrate) def inferstylizedview(contenthashencoder, stylehashencoder, shareddirencoder, sharedmlprgb, contentmlpdensity, contentvoxelgrid, stylevoxelgrid, querypositions, querydirections, alpha=1.0): """ Infers a stylized view using AdaIN on position encoder features. """ # 1. Calculate content features contentposfeat = contenthashencoder(querypositions) # 2. Calculate style features styleposfeat = stylehashencoder(querypositions) # 3. Compute statistics from voxel grids # Note: In practice, these are pre-computed or computed on-the-fly from the grid features contentmean = np.mean(contentvoxelgrid) contentstd = np.std(contentvoxelgrid) stylemean = np.mean(stylevoxelgrid) stylestd = np.std(stylevoxelgrid) # 4. Apply AdaIN stylizedposfeat = adaintransform(contentposfeat, stylemean, stylestd, contentmean, contentstd) # 5. Content-style trade-off blendedposfeat = (1 - alpha) contentposfeat + alpha stylizedposfeat # 6. Encode direction dirfeat = shareddirencoder(querydirections) # 7. Predict Color (using blended/stylized features) color = sharedmlprgb(concat(blendedposfeat, dirfeat)) # 8. Predict Density (using unadjusted content features for geometry consistency) density = contentmlpdensity(contentposfeat) return color, density Time Complexity: Training is extremely fast, completing in less than 10 minutes on modern GPU hardware (e.g., Nvidia 3080). Memory Complexity: Increases storage compared to a single scene NeRF due to the two position encoder branches, but the hash encoder architecture keeps it efficient. Strengths: Fast training; preserves geometry consistency better than independent networks; handles both single image and 3D scene image set style targets; no retraining required for inference. Limitations: Does not handle stylization on illumination and reflection because AdaIN is only executed on position encoder features, leaving direction encoder features unchanged. Details of results vary with random encoding parameters, requiring fixed MLP weights for stable results across different scene pairs. When to use: When fast stylization of 3D scenes is required, especially when the style target is a 3D scene image set rather than just a single image. When not to use: When stylization of lighting/reflection effects is critical, or when consistent random initialization is required without fixing MLP weights. Originated in the paper "Instant Photorealistic Neural Radiance Fields Stylization". It builds on Instant-NGP Parent: [Instant Neural Graphics Primitives] and NeRF [Parent: Neural Radiance Fields]. It extends previous NeRF stylization methods (like SNeRF) by leveraging the hash encoder for speed and extending style targets to 3D scene image sets. Instant Photorealistic Neural Radiance Fields Stylization, https://doi.org/10.1109/icassp48485.2024.10446082, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Optimization and Training Procedures
body: This article defines the optimization and training procedures for NeRF-based architectures, focusing on hyperparameter configurations, learning rate schedules, and specific training loops for model editing or acceleration. It sets itself apart from sibling articles by detailing the numerical parameters (learning rates, batch sizes, iterations) and optimizer choices required to converge specific variants, rather than describing the architectural topology or rendering equations. Not given in the sources. This method accelerates NeRF inference by skipping the expensive fine-pass MLP evaluation for rays determined to be empty or background, based on intermediate activation values from the coarse pass [12277-activation-informed-coarse-to-fine-rendering.md]. It sets itself apart from standard coarse-to-fine rendering by using a data-driven mask derived from hidden layer statistics rather than a fixed geometric threshold or uniform sampling, achieving significant speedups on synthetic scenes with transparent backgrounds [12277-activation-informed-coarse-to-fine-rendering.md]. Last Layer Re-training is a technique to instantly propagate a color edit from a single view to the entire Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) by selectively retraining only the last layer of the color Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) [13532-last-layer-re-training.md]. It solves the problem of efficient NeRF editing by reducing the number of parameters requiring modification compared to full retraining, while preserving existing view-dependent information [13532-last-layer-re-training.md]. It sets itself apart from full MLP retraining by avoiding the loss of useful pre-trained information and from methods like ICE-NeRF by preventing color bleeding at object boundaries [13532-last-layer-re-training.md]. Definition: The optimization process for Rip-NeRF involves training the tiny MLP weights and the ripmaps R. Steps: The learning rate schedule is reduced by 0.6x at steps 60K, 90K, 100K, and 108K, over a total of 120K iterations. The batch size is dynamically adjusted to maintain approximately 256K spheres per batch. Parameters: MLP weights are initialized following Glorot and Bengio (2010). Ripmaps R are initialized from a uniform distribution over [-0.01, 0.01]. The optimizer is AdamW. The base learning rate for R is scaled by 10x due to its direct scene representation role. The base learning rate is 2 \times 10^{-3}. The specific optimization configurations for Rip-NeRF are derived from. General NeRF training principles, such as the use of AdamW and dynamic batch sizing, follow [Müller et al. 2022] as cited in. The activation-informed skipping method is detailed in [12277-activation-informed-coarse-to-fine-rendering.md]. The last layer re-training technique is detailed in [13532-last-layer-re-training.md]. name: Activation-Informed Coarse-to-Fine Rendering
head: Activation-based early exit, Masked fine pass
body: This method accelerates NeRF rendering by skipping the expensive fine-pass MLP evaluation for rays determined to be empty or background, using intermediate activation values from the coarse pass. It sets itself apart from standard coarse-to-fine rendering by introducing a data-dependent mask derived from hidden layer statistics rather than a fixed geometric or density threshold, specifically targeting synthetic scenes with transparent backgrounds. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A trained NeRF model with two MLPs: a coarse network \Theta{\text{coarse}} and a fine network \Theta{\text{fine}}. The coarse network outputs predicted density \sigma and radiance. The fine network outputs final radiance. Outputs: Final rendered image pixels. Data Structures Activation Tensor A^{(\ell)}: For a single ray, after linear layer \ell, the activation tensor has size Ns \times Nh, where Ns is the number of samples along the ray and Nh is the number of hidden units in layer \ell. The values are taken after the ReLU activation function is applied. Activation Image V\ell: A 2D image (or array) where each element corresponds to a pixel (x,y) and stores the scalar activation v\ell for that ray. Parameters \ell: Layer index for activation analysis. Typical values are 1, 2, or 3. Earlier layers provide greater acceleration. \tau: Threshold for skipping the fine pass. Defined as \tau = \mu(V\ell), the mean of the activation image V\ell across all rays/pixels. Steps 1. For each pixel (x, y), generate a ray r and apply positional encoding \gamma(\cdot). 2. Pass Ns samples along ray r through the coarse MLP \Theta{\text{coarse}} to obtain predicted densities \sigma and intermediate activations A^{(\ell)} at layer \ell. 3. Compute the scalar activation v\ell for the ray by summing all elements of A^{(\ell)} and dividing by the total number of elements (Ns \times Nh): v\ell = \frac{1}{Ns} \sum{i=1}^{Ns} \sum{j=1}^{Nh} A^{(\ell)}{i,j} 4. Calculate the threshold \tau as the mean activation \mu(V\ell) of the activation image V\ell across all rays/pixels. 5. Identify the set of rays P where v\ell < \tau. These rays are treated as having no significant scene content (background). 6. For rays r \in P, evaluate the fine MLP \Theta{\text{fine}} to compute the final radiance. 7. For rays r \notin P, use the coarse radiance \hat{C}c as the final output. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def activationinformedrendering(rays, thetacoarse, thetafine, layerindex): """ Renders an image using activation-informed coarse-to-fine strategy. Args: rays: List of ray objects, each containing origin, direction, and sample points. thetacoarse: Coarse NeRF MLP. thetafine: Fine NeRF MLP. layerindex: Integer index of the hidden layer to analyze. Returns: renderedimage: Array of final pixel colors. """ numrays = len(rays) # Step 1 & 2: Coarse pass for all rays coarseradiance = [] activations = [] for ray in rays: # Apply positional encoding and pass through coarse MLP # Assume thetacoarse returns (sigma, color) for each sample samples = ray.samplepoints() encodedsamples = positionalencoding(samples) # Forward pass through coarse MLP # We need intermediate activations at layerindex # Implementation detail: thetacoarse must expose intermediate layer outputs sigma, color, intermediateA = thetacoarse(encodedsamples, layerindex) # Compute radiance for coarse pass (standard volume rendering) # wi = Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai deltai)) # Cc = sum(wi colori) cc = volumerendercoarse(sigma, color, ray.sampledistances()) coarseradiance.append(cc) activations.append(intermediateA) # Step 3: Compute scalar activation vl for each ray # A^(l) is of size Ns x Nh # vl = (1 / (Ns Nh)) sum(all elements) scalaractivations = [] for A in activations: # A shape: (Ns, Nh) vl = np.sum(A) / (A.shape[0] A.shape[1]) scalaractivations.append(vl) # Step 4: Calculate threshold tau # tau = mean of scalaractivations across all rays tau = np.mean(scalaractivations) # Step 5 & 6 & 7: Determine final output renderedimage = [] for i, ray in enumerate(rays): vl = scalaractivations[i] if vl < tau: # Ray is in set P (background/empty) # Evaluate fine MLP samples = ray.samplepoints() encodedsamples = positionalencoding(samples) sigmaf, colorf = thetafine(encodedsamples) cf = volumerenderfine(sigmaf, colorf, ray.sampledistances()) renderedimage.append(cf) else: # Ray is not in set P # Use coarse radiance renderedimage.append(coarseradiance[i]) return np.array(renderedimage) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Real-world scenes: The method relies on transparent backgrounds found in synthetic scenes (e.g., Blender dataset). It fails on real-world scenes with detailed backgrounds, as the activation threshold may incorrectly classify background pixels as empty. Precision: The method uses standard floating-point arithmetic for activation summation. No specific precision constraints are noted, but ReLU application is required for consistent histograms. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of fine-pass evaluations. On the Blender 'lego' scene (800x800), using layer 1 achieved a 34.69% speedup with 40% of rays processed by the fine pass. Using layer 3 achieved a 55% speedup with 47% of rays processed by the fine pass. Memory Complexity: Requires storing intermediate activations A^{(\ell)} for all rays during the coarse pass to compute the threshold. This adds memory overhead proportional to N{rays} \times Ns \times Nh for the specific layer \ell. Quality Trade-offs: Slight drop in rendering quality. For the 'lego' scene with layer 1: PSNR 29.66, SSIM 0.93, LPIPS 0.04. With layer 3: PSNR 31.21, SSIM 0.95, LPIPS 0.02. The full NeRF baseline had PSNR 32.20, SSIM 0.96, LPIPS 0.02. Strengths: Significant performance improvement on synthetic scenes with transparent backgrounds. Early layers accelerate inference more substantially. Limitations: Not applicable to real-world scenes with complex backgrounds without modification (e.g., density approximation methods). Origin: Proposed in "Analyzing the Internals of Neural Radiance Fields" (CVPRW 2024). History: The method builds on the observation that intermediate activations in NeRF MLPs contain structural information about density. It specifically targets the inference time reduction for synthetic datasets like Blender. Usage: Applied to NeRF and Mip-NeRF models. Also applicable to proposal network samplers (e.g., nerfacto with Mip-NeRF 360 proposal sampler). Analyzing the Internals of Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvprw63382.2024.00288, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Last Layer Re-training
head: Instant NeRF Editing, Last Layer Fine-tuning
body: Last Layer Re-training is a technique to instantly propagate a color edit from a single view to the entire Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) by selectively retraining only the last layer of the color Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). It solves the problem of efficient NeRF editing by reducing the number of parameters requiring modification compared to full retraining, while preserving existing view-dependent information. It sets itself apart from full MLP retraining by avoiding the loss of useful pre-trained information and from methods like ICE-NeRF by preventing color bleeding at object boundaries. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained NeRF model (specifically its color MLP weights \phic and density MLP weights \phi\sigma) and a single edited view image I{edit} \in \mathbb{R}^{W \times H \times 3}. Output: Updated NeRF parameters where the last layer of the color MLP is replaced by \phi'{last}, producing a new rendered color c'{x,\theta}. Data Structures: The color MLP takes as input the concatenation of multiresolution hash grid features fx and a view direction encoding \gamma(\theta). The feature encoding fx is a concatenation of features from each resolution level L: fx = \{f{x,0} \oplus f{x,1} \oplus \dots \oplus f{x,L}\} where \oplus denotes concatenation. The last layer maps the penultimate layer output h{x,\theta} to the final color. Numbered Steps: 1. Extract Penultimate Output: For each ray sampled from the edited view, compute the hidden vector h{x,\theta} from the penultimate layer of the pre-trained color MLP. This vector depends on the position x and view direction \theta. 2. Initialize Last Layer: Initialize a new set of parameters \phi'{last} for the last layer of the color MLP. The rest of the network (density MLP and earlier layers of the color MLP) remains frozen. 3. Compute Loss: Render the color C'{ij} for each pixel (i,j) in the edited view using the volume rendering equation with the updated last layer. Compute the photometric loss against the ground truth edited image C{ij}: L = \sum{i,j} \| C{ij} - C'{ij} \|^2 where C{ij} is the original RGB value from the training image (the edited view) and C'{ij} is the volume rendered RGB value. 4. Optimize: Minimize L with respect to \phi'{last} using the Adam optimizer. 5. Update Model: Replace the original last layer weights \phic with the optimized \phi'{last}. Formulas: The naive approach would retrain the full color MLP: MLPc(hx, \gamma(\theta), \phi'c) = c'{x,\theta} However, Last Layer Re-training uses: MLP{last}(h{x,\theta}, \phi'{last}) = c'{x,\theta} where h{x,\theta} is the output of the penultimate layer. Parameters: Learning Rate: 0.01. Optimizer: Adam. Iterations: 200 iterations per scene. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Color Bleeding: Since the information encoded in the color MLP is global, modifying only the last layer may lead to undesired edits in regions not targeted by the user edit. This is addressed by IReNe using a soft 3D segmentation step to restrict edits to target regions. View-Dependent Effects: Editing only the last layer must preserve view-dependent effects (e.g., specularities) present in the pre-trained NeRF. The method relies on the view-dependent information already present in the pre-trained model's earlier layers. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lastlayerretraining(pretrainednerf, editedimage, numiterations=200, learningrate=0.01): """ Retrain only the last layer of the color MLP to match the edited image. Args: pretrainednerf: Pre-trained NeRF model with frozen density MLP and color MLP layers except last. editedimage: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) representing the single edited view. numiterations: Number of optimization steps. learningrate: Learning rate for Adam optimizer. Returns: updatednerf: NeRF model with updated last layer weights. """ # Extract the last layer of the color MLP colormlp = pretrainednerf.colormlp lastlayer = colormlp[-1] # Freeze all parameters except the last layer for param in colormlp.parameters(): param.requiresgrad = False for param in lastlayer.parameters(): param.requiresgrad = True # Initialize optimizer for the last layer only optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(lastlayer.parameters(), lr=learningrate) # Render rays for the edited image to get ground truth colors # Assume getrenderedcolors returns tensor of shape (H, W, 3) # using the current last layer weights def rendercolors(): # Sample rays from camera poses corresponding to editedimage # Compute penultimate layer output hxtheta for each sample # Apply last layer to get c'xtheta # Volume render to get C'ij return pretrainednerf.render(editedimage.cameraposes) for step in range(numiterations): optimizer.zerograd() # Forward pass Cprime = rendercolors() Cgt = editedimage # Ground truth edited image # Compute loss loss = torch.mean((Cgt - Cprime) 2) # Backward pass loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Update the pretrainednerf with the new last layer weights updatednerf = pretrainednerf updatednerf.colormlp[-1] = lastlayer return updatednerf IReNe is a method for instant 360-degree recoloring of pre-trained Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) using a single user-edited image. It addresses the limitations of prior methods by preventing color bleeding at object boundaries and ensuring multi-view consistency for view-dependent effects, such as specularities. Unlike ICE-NeRF, which suffers from color bleeding, or Palette-NeRF, which requires hours to train, IReNe achieves high-quality edits in under 5 seconds by selectively fine-tuning only the diffuse neurons in the last layer of the color MLP. Time Complexity: Significantly faster than full MLP retraining because only the last layer parameters are optimized. Memory Complexity: Lower memory footprint during training compared to full retraining as gradients are only computed for the last layer. Measured Performance: Achieves high-quality edits in under 5 seconds per scene. Strengths: Rapid edits, preserves view-dependent information, prevents color bleeding (when combined with segmentation). Limitations: May still suffer from global color bleeding if not combined with segmentation techniques. When to use: When instant editing of a pre-trained NeRF is required, and view-dependent effects must be preserved. When not to use: When the edit requires changes to the underlying geometry or density structure, or when the edit is complex and requires global feature retraining. Last Layer Re-training was introduced in the IReNe paper (Mazzucchelli et al., CVPR 2024) as a method for instant recoloring of Neural Radiance Fields. It builds on the Instant-NGP implementation. The method was developed to address the challenges of near real-time NeRF editing, specifically the trade-off between edit speed and quality. IReNe: Instant Recoloring of Neural Radiance Fields, https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2024/papers/MazzucchelliIReNeInstantRecoloringofNeuralRadianceFieldsCVPR2024paper.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: IReNe
head: Instant Recoloring of Neural Radiance Fields
body: IReNe is a method for instant 360-degree recoloring of pre-trained Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) using a single user-edited image. It addresses the limitations of prior methods by preventing color bleeding at object boundaries and ensuring multi-view consistency for view-dependent effects, such as specularities. Unlike ICE-NeRF, which suffers from color bleeding, or Palette-NeRF, which requires hours to train, IReNe achieves high-quality edits in under 5 seconds by selectively fine-tuning only the diffuse neurons in the last layer of the color MLP. Inputs: A pre-trained NeRF model (specifically Instant-NGP), consisting of a density MLP \sigma, multiresolution hash features f, and a color MLP c. A single training image I{edit} containing user-applied color edits. Outputs: An edited image I{render} generated via volumetric rendering. Data Structures: Multiresolution Hash Grid Features (fx): The feature vector for a 3D point x is a concatenation of features from L levels of a multiresolution hash grid. fx = \{f{x,0} \oplus f{x,1} \oplus \dots \oplus f{x,L}\} where \oplus denotes concatenation. Density MLP (MLP\sigma): Takes feature fx and outputs density \sigmax and hidden feature hx. MLP\sigma(fx, \phi\sigma) = \sigmax, hx Color MLP (MLPc): Takes hidden feature hx and encoded view direction \gamma(\theta) to output color c{x,\theta}. MLPc(hx, \gamma(\theta), \phic) = c{x,\theta} Instant-NGP uses spherical harmonics for the view direction encoding \gamma(\cdot). Segmentation MLP (MLPs): A lightweight, trainable MLP ruled by features f to estimate a volumetric soft-segmentation \alpha of the edited region. Neuron Classification: Neurons in the last layer of MLPc are classified as either "diffuse" or "view-dependent". Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: Load the pre-trained Instant-NGP NeRF. 2. Detect Diffuse Neurons: Automatically detect diffuse neurons in the last layer of the color MLP c. This is done by analyzing the activations of the last layer neurons across different view directions. Diffuse neurons exhibit color consistency across views, while view-dependent neurons (e.g., specularities) change color with the viewing angle. 3. Train Segmentation: Train the segmentation MLP MLPs using the multiresolution hash features f to estimate the volumetric soft-segmentation mask \alpha for the edited region. The optimization minimizes the RGB loss between the rendered image and the user-edited image I{edit}. 4. Fine-tune Diffuse Neurons: Fine-tune only the weights corresponding to the identified diffuse neurons in the last layer of MLPc. The view-dependent neurons remain frozen to preserve view-specific effects. 5. Compute Blended Color: For any 3D point x and view direction \theta, compute the final color C{final} as a linear combination of the color predicted by the frozen weights (c{x,\theta}) and the color predicted by the retrained weights (c'{x,\theta}), blended using the segmentation mask \alphax: C{final} = (1 - \alphax) c{x,\theta} + \alphax c'{x,\theta} where c{x,\theta} is the output of the original frozen MLPc and c'{x,\theta} is the output of the MLPc with the fine-tuned last layer. 6. Volumetric Rendering: Perform standard volumetric rendering using the density \sigmax and the blended color C{final} to obtain the edited image I{render}. Optimization: The segmentation MLP MLPs and the trainable last-layer diffuse neurons are optimized simultaneously. The loss function is the standard RGB loss between the rendered image I{render} and the user-edited image I{edit}: L = \sum \| C{ij} - C'{ij} \|^2 where C{ij} is the pixel value in I{edit} and C'{ij} is the rendered pixel value. Parameters: Optimization Time: Approximately 5 seconds. Input Resolution: Depends on the input image I{edit}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Color Bleeding: Without the segmentation module \alpha, color edits bleed into adjacent objects. The trainable segmentation module prevents this by providing spatial control over the edit. View-Dependent Consistency: If all neurons in the last layer were fine-tuned, view-dependent effects like specularities would be distorted or lost. Classifying and freezing view-dependent neurons ensures multi-view consistency. Complex 360-Degree Scenes: Unlike methods relying on reprojection which fail in complex 360-degree scenes, IReNe handles them consistently by operating directly in the 3D volume representation. Time Complexity: Extremely fast optimization, typically under 5 seconds per edit. This is 5× to 500× faster than competitors like Palette-NeRF (hours) and ICE-NeRF (seconds, but with quality issues). Memory Complexity: Low additional memory overhead due to the lightweight segmentation MLP and the fact that only a subset of the last layer weights are trained. Strengths: Near real-time interactive editing, prevention of color bleeding, multi-view consistency for specularities, and support for partial and multi-object edits. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained Instant-NGP model; relies on the accuracy of the automatic diffuse neuron classification. When to use: When instant, high-quality color editing of a NeRF is required, especially for scenes with complex boundaries or view-dependent effects. When not to use: When the underlying NeRF is not trained with Instant-NGP or when global scene reconstruction (not just color editing) is needed. IReNe was introduced by Mazzucchelli et al. in 2024. It builds upon the Instant-NGP architecture and addresses limitations in previous NeRF editing methods such as Palette-NeRF and ICE-NeRF. The method was validated on a new dataset with edited object colors, demonstrating significant quantitative and qualitative advancements. IReNe: Instant Recoloring of Neural Radiance Fields, https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2024/papers/MazzucchelliIReNeInstantRecoloringofNeuralRadianceFieldsCVPR2024paper.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Image Enhancement and Restoration Methods
body: Image Enhancement and Restoration Methods address the degradation of input data in NeRF training by modeling blur, transient occlusions, or missing geometry, enabling the synthesis of sharp, clean novel views from uncontrolled or low-quality inputs. Unlike sibling methods that modify the neural field's internal capacity or density representation, these methods explicitly model the imaging process (e.g., blur kernels) or separate static scene components from transient artifacts using external 2D priors and inpainting networks. The core task of a NeRF network architecture is to learn a continuous volumetric scene representation F\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the spatial position, \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the viewing direction, \sigma is the volume density, and \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the view-dependent color. The rendering process integrates these outputs along rays using standard volume rendering equations. The baseline architecture employs two MLPs: 1. Position MLP (\Phi{pos}): Takes \mathbf{x} and positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}) to produce a feature vector \mathbf{h}. 2. Shading MLP (\Phi{shade}): Takes \mathbf{h} and directional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{d}) to predict \sigma and \mathbf{c}. Reconstructs a sharp NeRF from blurry images by jointly optimizing a sharp NeRF and a Deformable Sparse Kernel (DSK) module. It physically approximates blur as a sparse mixture of deformed rays, handling camera motion and defocus blur without external clean data. Enhances novel view synthesis in uncontrolled environments by separating static scene rendering from transient occlusions (e.g., moving people). It predicts a 2D transient mask per image and uses a pre-trained inpainting network (LaMa) to generate a "clean" static supervision signal, avoiding dual NeRF pipelines. Renders clean, sharp images from blurry inputs by modeling spatially varying blur using discrete learnable kernels and a sharpness prior. It replaces neural network-based kernel generators with a fixed set of discrete kernels indexed by a precomputed sharpness map, significantly reducing training time. A 3D inpainting method that leverages LaMa for color and depth inpainting, replacing pixel loss with perceptual loss for visual coherence and using depth inpainting to supervise 3D geometry. It replaces pixel loss with perceptual loss. It struggles in tasks where 2D inpainting results are perceptually inconsistent. The baseline NeRF architecture employs two MLPs: 1. Position MLP (\Phi{pos}): Takes \mathbf{x} and positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}) to produce a feature vector \mathbf{h}. 2. Shading MLP (\Phi{shade}): Takes \mathbf{h} and directional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{d}) to predict \sigma and \mathbf{c}. A survey on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11704-025-41176-9, fetched 2026-10-28

name: DeblurNeRF
head: DeRF, Deblur-NeRF, Deblur-NeRF: Neural Radiance Fields from Blurry Images
body: DeblurNeRF is a framework that reconstructs a sharp Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) from blurry input images by explicitly modeling the blurring process via an analysis-by-synthesis approach. Unlike standard NeRF which assumes sharp inputs, DeblurNeRF jointly optimizes the NeRF parameters and a Deformable Sparse Kernel (DSK) module to simulate the blur, allowing the NeRF to recover sharp geometry and appearance during training. It sets itself apart from siblings like IE-NeRF and Sharp-NeRF by using a pixel-wise independent deformable sparse kernel to approximate spatially varying blur, rather than relying on global scene priors or post-processing. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of blurry multi-view images. Camera poses are assumed to be known (e.g., from COLMAP). Outputs: A sharp NeRF representation F\Theta and the DSK module parameters \Phi. At inference, the DSK is discarded, and the NeRF renders sharp novel views. Data Structures: 1. NeRF (F\Theta): Standard MLP mapping (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}). 2. DSK Module (G\Phi): An MLP parameterized by \Phi. Structure: 4 fully-connected hidden layers, each with 64 channels and ReLU activations. Includes a shortcut connection from the first layer to the last layer. Inputs: Pixel coordinate \mathbf{p}, canonical kernel location \mathbf{q}^0, and a learned view embedding \mathbf{l} (length 32). Outputs: For each of the N sparse locations, a tuple (\Delta \mathbf{o}q, \Delta \mathbf{q}, wq). \Delta \mathbf{o}q \in \mathbb{R}^3: Ray origin translation. \Delta \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^2: Kernel location deformation (2D image plane offset). wq \in \mathbb{R}: Composition weight. 3. Canonical Kernel: A set of N fixed 2D locations N^0(\mathbf{p}) = \{\mathbf{q}^0i\}{i=0}^{N-1} distributed around the pixel \mathbf{p}. Parameters: N: Number of sparse kernel locations per pixel. Default: 5. L: Highest frequency in positional encoding. Controls smoothness. \epsilon: Initialization gain. Default: 0.1. \lambdao: Alignment loss weight. Default: 10. \lambdaa: Reconstruction loss weight. Default: 0.1. Learning Rate: Starts at 5 \times 10^{-4}, decays exponentially to 8 \times 10^{-5}. Batch Size: 1024 rays. Sampling: 64 coarse samples, 64 fine samples. Formulas: Positional Encoding: \gammaL(\mathbf{x}) = [\sin(\pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(\pi \mathbf{x}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1}\pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^{L-1}\pi \mathbf{x})]^T. NeRF Rendering: \hat{c}p = \sum{i=1}^D T^{(i)} (1 - \exp(-\sigma^{(i)} \delta^{(i)})) c^{(i)}, where \delta^{(i)} = t^{(i+1)} - t^{(i)} and T^{(i)} = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma^{(j)} \delta^{(j)}). Blur Approximation: The blurry color bp is approximated by a sparse sum: bp = \sum{q \in N(\mathbf{p})} wq cq, subject to \sum{q \in N(\mathbf{p})} wq = 1. Ray Generation: Optimized rays are generated as rq = (\mathbf{o} + \Delta \mathbf{o}q) + t \mathbf{d}q, where \mathbf{d}q is derived from the deformed location \mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}^0 + \Delta \mathbf{q}. Gamma Correction: Applied to compensate for non-linear Camera Response Function (CRF): \hat{b}p = g(\sum{q \in N(\mathbf{p})} wq c^0q), where g(c^0) = (c^0)^{1/2.2}. Alignment Loss: L{align} = \|\mathbf{q}^0 - \mathbf{p}\|2^2 + \lambdao \|\Delta \mathbf{o}{q^0}\|2^2, where \mathbf{q}^0 is a fixed element in N(\mathbf{p}). Total Loss: L = L{reconstruct} + \lambdaa L{align}, where L{reconstruct} = \sum{\mathbf{p} \in R} \|\hat{b}p - b^{gt}p\|2^2. Steps: 1. Initialize: Initialize the DSK module such that optimized rays are close to the input ray. Multiply the output tuples (\Delta \mathbf{o}q, \Delta \mathbf{q}, wq) by a small gain \epsilon = 0.1. 2. Predict Deformations: For each pixel \mathbf{p} in the batch, forward the MLP G\Phi N times (once for each canonical location \mathbf{q}^0) to predict (\Delta \mathbf{o}q, \Delta \mathbf{q}, wq). 3. Generate Rays: Compute deformed locations \mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}^0 + \Delta \mathbf{q} and generate optimized rays rq = (\mathbf{o} + \Delta \mathbf{o}q) + t \mathbf{d}q. 4. Render: Render each optimized ray rq using the NeRF F\Theta to obtain color c^0q and density. 5. Composite: Blend the rendered colors using the predicted weights and apply gamma correction to compute the synthetic blurry pixel \hat{b}p. 6. Compute Loss: Calculate the reconstruction loss L{reconstruct} against the ground truth blurry image and the alignment loss L{align}. 7. Optimize: Update NeRF parameters \Theta and DSK parameters \Phi using the total loss L. 8. Inference: Discard the DSK module. Render rays directly from the camera center \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} using the trained NeRF F\Theta to produce sharp novel views. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class DeblurNeRF: def init(self, nerfmodel, numkernelpoints=5, viewembeddingdim=32): """ Initialize DeblurNeRF.:param nerfmodel: The NeRF MLP (FTheta).:param numkernelpoints: N, number of sparse kernel locations.:param viewembeddingdim: Length of the view embedding vector. """ self.nerf = nerfmodel self.numkernelpoints = numkernelpoints self.viewembeddingdim = viewembeddingdim # DSK Module: MLP with 4 hidden layers, 64 channels, ReLU, shortcut self.dskmlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(4 + 32 + 2, 64), # Input: p(2) + q0(2) + l(32) -> 4+32+2=38? # Note: Source says inputs are p, q0, l. p is 2D, q0 is 2D, l is 32D. Total 36. # Let's correct input dim based on source description: p(2) + q0(2) + l(32) = 36. nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 3 numkernelpoints) # Output: (do, dq, w) for N points) # Add shortcut from first layer to last layer manually or via structure # Source: "shortcut that connects the first layer to the last layer" # We will implement the forward pass to handle this explicitly. # Initialize view embeddings for each view (stored externally or here) # For simplicity, assume view embedding is passed in forward pass or managed externally. # Canonical kernel locations N0(p) # In practice, these are relative offsets around p. # Source says "canonical kernel locations... distributed around p". # We assume a fixed set of relative offsets is used. self.registerbuffer('canonicaloffsets', torch.zeros(numkernelpoints, 2)) # Initialize offsets to be close to 0 (small range) # Source: "randomly initialized canonical coordinates within a specific small range" # We'll use small random values. self.canonicaloffsets.data = torch.randn(numkernelpoints, 2) 0.01 def forwarddsk(self, p, q0, viewembedding): """ Forward pass of DSK MLP with shortcut.:param p: Pixel coordinates (B, 2):param q0: Canonical kernel locations (B, N, 2):param viewembedding: View embedding (B, 32):return: (deltao, deltaq, weights) """ # Concatenate inputs: p, q0, viewembedding # p needs to be broadcasted to (B, N, 2) pexpanded = p.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, self.numkernelpoints, -1) inputtensor = torch.cat([pexpanded, q0, viewembedding.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, self.numkernelpoints, -1)], dim=-1) # It differs from rigid kernel methods by allowing pixel-wise independent transformations, which can lead to 3D inconsistency. Choose when computational efficiency is prioritized over strict 3D geometric consistency. [Link to DSK if available, otherwise link to DeblurNeRF]. Alignment Loss: A regularization term that constrains the NeRF to align with observations by forcing one of the optimized rays to be similar to the input ray. It prevents non-rigid distortion of the NeRF during joint optimization. Time Complexity: Training is computationally intensive as it requires rendering N rays per pixel instead of 1. With N=5, this is 5x the rendering cost of standard NeRF per step. Memory Complexity: Requires storing parameters for the NeRF and the DSK MLP. The DSK MLP is small (4 layers, 64 channels). Scaling: Quality improves as N increases, but improvement is less substantial beyond N=5. Strengths: Can handle both camera motion blur and defocus blur. Recovers sharp novel views from blurry inputs. Efficient approximation for moderate blur. Limitations: Pixel-wise independent optimization can incur inconsistency in 3D geometry and appearance. May suffer from non-rigid distortion if not constrained by alignment loss. When to use: When input images are blurry (motion or defocus) and sharp novel views are desired. Suitable for moderate blur. When not to use: When severe motion blur requires physically grounded formulations for better pose accuracy (use BAD-NeRF instead). When 3D geometric consistency across views is critical and pixel-wise blur modeling is too inconsistent. DeblurNeRF (also known as DeRF) was proposed by Xiaoyu Li, Jing Liao, Qi Zhang, Jue Wang, Pedro V. Sander, and Li Ma from The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Tencent AI Lab, and City University of Hong Kong. It was published in CVPR 2022 (arXiv:2111.14292). It is the first method to recover a sharp NeRF from blurry input images using an analysis-by-synthesis approach. It was tested on synthetic scenes generated with Blender and real-world scenes captured with a Canon EOS RP. name: IE-NeRF
head: IE-NeRF Pipeline, Image-dependent NeRF with transient mask inpainting, Inpainting Enhanced NeRF
body: IE-NeRF is a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) variant designed to enhance novel view synthesis in uncontrolled, "in-the-wild" environments by separating static scene rendering from transient occlusions (e.g., moving people, vehicles) using an image-dependent inpainting module. Unlike sibling methods such as DeblurNeRF or Sharp-NeRF which focus on blur or sharpness, or NeRF-W which uses a 3D transient field, IE-NeRF predicts a 2D transient mask per image via its MLPs and uses a pre-trained inpainting network (LaMa) to generate a "clean" static supervision signal, avoiding the need for dual NeRF pipelines or external semantic segmentation priors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of uncontrolled images Ii with known camera poses (position o and direction d). Outputs: A static radiance field representation (density \sigma and image-dependent color c) and novel views of the static scene free from transient occlusions. Data Structures and Layout: 1. CNN Encoder (EE): Encodes input image Ii into a feature latent vector \elli \in \mathbb{R}^k. 2. NeRF MLPs: MLP{\theta1}: 8 fully connected layers, 256 hidden units. Input: Positional encoded ray position \gammax(r(t)). Output: Density \sigma(t) and intermediate feature zi(t). MLP{\theta2}: Input: Directional encoding \gammad(d), intermediate feature zi(t), and original position (x,y,z). Output: Image-dependent radiance ci(t) and transient mask embedding \ellt. Transient Mask Head: A fully connected layer with 128 channels and Sigmoid activation. Input: Transient embedding \ellt and 2D pixel location l{ij}=(u,v). Output: Transient mask probability M{ij}. Static Color Head: A fully connected layer with 128 channels and Sigmoid activation. Input: Output of MLP{\theta2}. Output: Static RGB color c. 3. Inpainting Module (G\Delta): Uses the LaMa model. Input: Concatenated tensor x' = \text{stack}(Ii \odot M{ij}, M{ij}) (4 channels). Output: Restored static image I{ri} and repaired depth map D{ri}. Numbered Steps: 1. Image Encoding: Encode each input image Ii into a feature latent vector \elli using the CNN encoder EE. 2. Ray Sampling: For a camera ray r(t) = o + td, sample points tk along the ray. Apply Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE) to positions and directions. 3. Static Feature Prediction: Pass the positional encoding \gammax(r(t)) through MLP{\theta1} to obtain density \sigma(t) and intermediate feature zi(t): [\sigma(t), zi(t)] = \text{MLP}{\theta1}[\gammax(r(t))] 4. Radiance and Mask Embedding: Pass the viewing direction \gammad(d), intermediate feature zi(t), and original position into MLP{\theta2} to predict image-dependent radiance ci(t) and transient mask embedding \ellt: ci(t) = \text{MLP}{\theta2}[\gammad(d), zi(t)] 5. Transient Mask Generation: Map the 2D pixel location l{ij} and the transient embedding \ellt through linear layers E\phi to generate a 2D pixel-wise transient mask probability M{ij}: M{ij} = E\phi(l{ij}, \ellt) 6. Volumetric Rendering (Static): Compute the approximated pixel color \hat{C}i(r) using the static density \sigma(t) and image-dependent radiance ci(t): \hat{C}i(r) = \sum{k=1}^{K} T(tk) \cdot \alpha(\sigma(tk)\deltak) \cdot ci(tk) where T(tk) = \exp\left(-\sum{k'=1}^{k-1} \sigma(t{k'}) \cdot \delta{k'}\right) is the accumulated transmittance. 7. Inpainting Supervision Generation: Threshold M{ij} to create a binary mask. Apply the mask to the original image Ii to create a masked image. Feed the masked image and mask into the pre-trained LaMa inpainting network G\Delta to produce the restored static image I{ri}. Render depth maps D{si} from the static NeRF. Inpaint the rendered depth maps using LaMa guided by the transient mask to produce restored depth maps D{ri}. 8. Optimization: Minimize the total loss function L combining static photometric loss, transient loss, perceptual loss (LPIPS), and depth loss. Formulas: Static Photometric Loss (Ls): Ls = \sum{ij} ||C(r{ij}) - \hat{C}s(r{ij})||^2 where C(r{ij}) is the observed color outside the transient mask, and \hat{C}s is the rendered static color. Transient Loss (Lt): Lt = \sum{ij} (1-M{ij})||C(r{ij}) - \hat{C}s(r{ij})||^2 + \lambda M{ij} ||Cs(r{ij}) - \hat{C}s(r{ij})||^2 The first term handles occlusion error (comparing rendered static to original where no transient exists). The second term handles reconstruction error inside the mask, comparing rendered static to the inpainted static color Cs (derived from I{ri}), weighted by \lambda. Perceptual Loss (L{LPIPS}): Calculated between the rendered static image and the inpainted static image I{ri} within the masked region. Depth Loss (L{depth}): L{depth} = \frac{1}{|R|} \sum{r \in R} ||\hat{D}{si}(r) - D{ri}(r)||^2 where \hat{D}{si} is the rendered static depth and D{ri} is the inpainted depth. Total Loss: L = \alpha \sum{ij} Ls + \beta \sum{ij} Lt + \gamma \sumi L{LPIPS} + \rho \sumi L{depth} where \alpha, \beta, \gamma, \rho are weights. Frequency Regularization (RegFre-IPE): \gamma'L(t, T; x) = \gammaL(x) \odot \omega(t, T, L) where \omega is a linearly increasing frequency mask based on current iteration t, max iteration T, and max frequency L. The i-th bit \omegai is defined as: \omegai(t, T, L) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } i \le \lfloor \frac{t \cdot L}{T} \rfloor \\ 0 & \text{if } i > \lfloor \frac{t \cdot L}{T} \rfloor + 6 \end{cases} (Note: The source provides a piecewise function involving r, the transient mask factor, but the core mechanism is the gradual introduction of high frequencies). Parameters: MLP Architecture: 8 layers, 256 hidden units for density; 128 hidden units for color/mask heads. Activation: ReLU for density \sigma; Sigmoid for transient mask M{ij} and static color c. LaMa Input: 4-channel tensor \text{stack}(Ii \odot M{ij}, M{ij}). \lambda: Balances static/transient components in transient loss. \alpha, \beta, \gamma, \rho: Weights for static, transient, perceptual, and depth losses. L: Maximum encoded frequency in positional encoding. r: Transient mask factor (ratio of transient pixels to total image area). Training Data: 2x downsampled images. Pre-filtering: Discards images with NIMA score < 3 or transient objects > 80% of frame. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Small Datasets/Sparse Inputs: The method struggles when the transient mask lacks sufficient information to guide inpainting reliably. Inpainting Artifacts: LaMa may produce blurry results or view inconsistencies. Mitigated by LPIPS loss inside the mask and depth supervision. High-Frequency Instability: High-frequency signals cause instability in transient separation. Mitigated by RegFre-IPE, starting training without positional encoding and incrementally boosting frequency. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class IENeRF: def init(self, numlayers=8, hiddendim=256, maskheaddim=128, colorheaddim=128): # MLP for density and intermediate features self.mlpdensity = nn.ModuleList([ nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim) for in range(numlayers) ]) # MLP for radiance and mask embedding self.mlpradiance = nn.ModuleList([ nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim) for in range(numlayers) ]) # Transient mask head self.maskhead = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1) # Output 1 channel for probability # Static color head self.colorhead = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 3) # Output RGB # CNN Encoder for image features (simplified placeholder for EE) self.imageencoder = nn.Conv2d(3, 256, kernelsize=3, padding=1) # LaMa Inpainting Module (Pre-trained, frozen during NeRF training) self.inpaintingmodule = LaMaModel() def forward(self, rayso, raysd, imagefeatures, pixelcoords, tvals): """ rayso: (N, 3) origin raysd: (N, 3) direction imagefeatures: (N, H, W, C) or latent vector li pixelcoords: (N, 2) 2D pixel location (u, v) tvals: (N, K) sample distances along ray """ # 1. Ray points pts = rayso.unsqueeze(1) + raysd.unsqueeze(1) tvals.unsqueeze(2) # (N, K, 3) # 2. Encode positions and directions (IPE) # Note: IPE implementation details depend on mip-NeRF library, # but conceptually maps 3D points to higher-dimensional space. posenc = integratedposencoding(pts) direnc = integratedposencoding(raysd) # 3. Predict density and intermediate feature zi x = posenc for layer in self.mlpdensity: x = F.relu(layer(x)) sigma = x[...,:1] # Density zi = x[..., 1:] # Intermediate feature # 4. Predict radiance ci and transient mask embedding lt # Concatenate direnc, zi, and original position if required by specific variant # Source says: "Feed the directional vector d..., intermediate feature zi(t), # and the original position (x,y,z) into MLPtheta2" xradiance = torch.cat([direnc, zi, pts], dim=-1) for layer in self.mlpradiance: xradiance = F.relu(layer(xradiance)) lt = xradiance[...,:1] # Transient mask embedding (simplified dimension) ci = xradiance[..., 1:] # Radiance features # 5. Generate Transient Mask Mij # Map 2D pixel location lij and transient embedding lt # Source: Mij = Ephi(lij, lt) # Assuming lt is broadcasted or aggregated per pixel maskinput = torch.cat([pixelcoords, lt], dim=-1) Mij = torch.sigmoid(self.maskhead(maskinput)) # 6. Generate Static Color c cstatic = torch.sigmoid(self.colorhead(ci)) # 7. Volumetric Rendering for Static Scene # T(tk) = exp(-sum(sigma delta)) deltas = tvals[:, 1:] - tvals[:,:-1] deltas = torch.cat([deltas, torch.oneslike(deltas[:,:1])], dim=-1) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-F.relu(sigma) deltas) transmittance = torch.cumprod(torch.exp(-F.relu(sigma) deltas), dim=1) transmittance = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(transmittance[:,:1]), transmittance[:,:-1]], dim=1) weights = alpha transmittance Crendered = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) cstatic, dim=1) # Render Depth Drendered = torch.sum(weights tvals, dim=1) return Crendered, Drendered, Mij, cstatic def computeloss(self, Crendered, Drendered, Mij, Ioriginal, Irestored, Drestored): """ Crendered: Rendered static color Drendered: Rendered static depth Mij: Transient mask probability Ioriginal: Original input image Irestored: Inpainted static image (from LaMa) Drestored: Inpainted depth (from LaMa) """ # Static Photometric Loss (outside mask) # Masked out transient regions staticmask = 1.0 - Mij Ls = torch.mean(staticmask (Crendered - Ioriginal)2) # Transient Loss # Term 1: Occlusion error (outside mask) # Term 2: Reconstruction error (inside mask) comparing rendered static to inpainted static # Note: Source uses Cs(rij) which is the color from Irestored Ltocclusion = torch.mean((1 - Mij) (Crendered - Ioriginal)2) Ltrecon = torch.mean(Mij (Crendered - Irestored)2) lambdaparam = 1.0 # Example weight Lt = Ltocclusion + lambdaparam Ltrecon # Perceptual Loss (LPIPS) inside mask # Implemented via external LPIPS metric between Crendered and Irestored masked Llpips = computelpips(Crendered Mij, Irestored Mij) # Depth Loss Ldepth = torch.mean((Drendered - Drestored)2) # Total Loss alpha, beta, gamma, rho = 1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0 # Weights Ltotal = alpha Ls + beta Lt + gamma Llpips + rho Ldepth return Ltotal Time and Memory Complexity: The method uses a standard NeRF MLP architecture (8 layers, 256 units) plus a CNN encoder and a LaMa inpainting network. The LaMa model is pre-trained and frozen, adding inference time for the inpainting step but not training memory for the NeRF weights. The dual-network (coarse/fine) strategy from NeRF can be applied for sampling efficiency. Measured Performance: On the Phototourism dataset (Brandenburg Gate), IE-NeRF achieved PSNR 25.33, SSIM 0.898, and LPIPS 0.158, outperforming NeRF (18.90/0.816/0.232), NeRF-W (24.17/0.891/0.167), and Ha-NeRF (24.04/0.877/0.139). Scaling: Performance degrades on small datasets and sparse inputs because the transient mask lacks sufficient information for reliable inpainting. Strengths: Effectively removes transient objects without requiring 3D transient fields or external semantic segmentation models. The frequency regularization strategy (RegFre-IPE) stabilizes training and improves early convergence. Limitations: Inpainting modules may produce blurry results or view inconsistencies. The method relies on the accuracy of the transient mask generated by the MLPs; if the mask is inaccurate, the inpainting supervision is flawed. IE-NeRF was proposed by Wang et al. from Sun Yat-sen University and Pengcheng Laboratory, published in Neurocomputing in 2024 (arXiv:2407.10695v2). It addresses the limitations of standard NeRF and NeRF-W in uncontrolled "in-the-wild" settings where transient objects (people, cars) and varying illumination degrade novel view synthesis. Unlike NeRF-W which uses a 3D transient field, IE-NeRF introduces an image-dependent 2D mask map and leverages the expertise of image inpainting (specifically the LaMa model) to restore static scene content.
