name: Sharp-NeRF
head: Grid-based Fast Deblurring Neural Radiance Fields using Sharpness Prior
body: Sharp-NeRF is a grid-based NeRF framework designed to render clean, sharp images from input blurry images by modeling spatially varying blur using discrete learnable kernels and a sharpness prior. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like DeblurNeRF and IE-NeRF by replacing neural network-based kernel generators with a fixed set of discrete kernels indexed by a precomputed sharpness map, significantly reducing training time to approximately half an hour while maintaining high-quality deblurring. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of blurry training images (views) and their corresponding camera poses. Outputs: A grid-based neural field representation of the scene and a set of discrete blur kernels. At inference, the system outputs sharp novel views. Data Structures: 1. Grid-based Neural Field: A decomposed-grid representation (e.g., Tri-Plane or Hash Grid) storing density and color information, replacing the standard MLP. 2. Sharpness Level Map (L): A 2D map per view where each pixel value is an integer index k \in \{0, \dots, Nk-1\} representing the quantized sharpness level of that pixel. 3. Discrete Blur Kernels (B): A set of Nk learnable 2D convolution kernels. Each kernel Bk has a fixed size (e.g., 3\times3 or 5\times5, though exact size is not specified in sources, the operation is convolution). 4. Ray Patch: A K \times K grid of rays sampled from the camera frustum, corresponding to a K \times K pixel patch in the image plane. Preprocessing (Offline): 1. For each training view, compute a defocus map (sharpness measure) for every pixel. 2. Quantize the continuous sharpness values into Nk discrete levels to create the sharpness level map L. This step is performed once before training and is not part of the differentiable graph. Training Steps: 1. Ray Patch Sampling: Sample a K \times K patch of rays from the training view. 2. Sharp Rendering: Query the grid-based neural field with the ray patch inputs to render a sharp image patch Ic'. 3. Kernel Indexing: Retrieve the sharpness level map L corresponding to the current view. For each pixel (u,v) in the patch, obtain its sharpness index k = L(u,v). 4. Kernel Selection: Select the discrete blur kernel Bk from the set B based on index k. 5. Blurring Synthesis: Apply the selected kernel Bk as a convolution operation over the sharp patch Ic' to produce the blurred patch Ib. Note: The sources describe this as a "weighted sum of per-pixel weights wx and the rendered sharp image patch," which in the context of discrete kernels and convolution implies applying the kernel weights to the neighborhood of pixels in Ic'. 6. Loss Computation: Compare the synthesized blurred patch Ib with the input blurry training image patch I{blur} using a reconstruction loss (e.g., L1 or L2). 7. Optimization: Backpropagate through the blurring operation (assuming the convolution is differentiable with respect to the kernel weights and the grid parameters) to update the grid parameters and the discrete kernels B. Inference: 1. Sample rays for the target novel view. 2. Query the grid-based neural field to render the sharp image Ic directly. 3. The blur kernel module is bypassed; the output is the sharp image Ic. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. Nk = 16 # Number of discrete kernels, typical value not explicitly given but implied by "few" K = 5 # Patch size, typical value not explicitly given but implied by "5 or 6" neighbors B = LearnableKernels(Nk, kernelsize=3) # Set of Nk kernels Grid = DecomposedGridRepresentation() # Grid-based NeRF backbone def computesharpnessmap(blurryimage): # Compute defocus map using a sharpness measure operator (e.g., variance of Laplacian) sharpnessvalues = SharpnessMeasureOperator(blurryimage) # Quantize to Nk levels sharpnesslevels = Quantize(sharpnessvalues, Nk) return sharpnesslevels for batch in trainingdata: blurryimages = batch.images cameraposes = batch.poses # Get precomputed sharpness maps for the current views sharpnessmaps = [computesharpnessmap(img) for img in blurryimages] for i, (blurryimg, sharpnessmap, pose) in enumerate(zip(blurryimages, sharpnessmaps, cameraposes)): # 1. Sample a KxK patch of rays rays = SampleRayPatch(pose, patchsize=K) # 2. Render sharp patch from grid sharppatch = Grid.Render(rays) # Shape: (K, K, 3) # 3. Get sharpness indices for the patch # sharpnessmap is aligned with the image coordinates patchcoords = GetPatchCoordinates(rays) sharpnessindices = sharpnessmap[patchcoords] # Shape: (K, K) # 4. Select kernels for each pixel in the patch # B is indexed by sharpnessindices kernels = B[sharpnessindices] # Shape: (K, K, kernelh, kernelw, channels) # 5. Apply convolution to blur the sharp patch # This step simulates the camera blur blurredpatch = Convolve2D(sharppatch, kernels) # Shape: (K, K, 3) # 6. Compute loss against the actual blurry image patch targetpatch = GetImagePatch(blurryimg, patchcoords) loss = L1Loss(blurredpatch, targetpatch) # 7. Backpropagate loss.backward() optimizer.step() Parameters: Nk: The number of discrete blur kernels. The sources do not specify the exact value used in experiments, only that it is a "few" to handle spatially varying blur. K: The size of the ray patch. The sources mention rendering 5 or 6 neighboring pixels, implying a patch size likely around 5\times5 or 6\times6. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory: Storing a unique blur kernel for every pixel is impractical for high-resolution, multi-view images. Sharp-NeRF avoids this by quantizing sharpness levels into Nk discrete kernels. Training Time: Rendering multiple neighboring pixels for a single pixel increases training time proportionally. Sharp-NeRF mitigates this by rendering a patch and applying convolution, which is more efficient than per-pixel ray batching. Preprocessing Dependency: The sharpness level map L is computed offline. If the input images have varying blur characteristics not captured by the initial quantization, the discrete kernels may not fully represent the blur. Time Complexity: Training time is significantly reduced compared to MLP-based methods. The sources state training takes approximately half an hour. This is achieved by using a grid-based representation and discrete kernels instead of MLPs for kernel generation. Memory Complexity: Lower than MLP-based NeRFs due to the grid representation. The memory for kernels is O(Nk \cdot k^2) where k is kernel size, which is negligible compared to MLP weights. Strengths: Fast training time; handles spatially varying blur effectively using discrete kernels; high-quality sharp novel view synthesis. Limitations: Relies on accurate precomputed sharpness maps; discrete kernels may not capture complex, continuous blur variations as well as learned continuous kernels. When to use: When training time is a constraint and the blur is primarily defocus-based. When not to use: When the blur is motion-based or complex non-defocus blur that requires more flexible kernel generation. Sharp-NeRF was proposed to address the high computational cost of MLP-based NeRF deblurring methods like Deblur-NeRF and DP-NeRF. It builds on the idea of using grid-based representations for speed. The method was introduced in the paper "Sharp-NeRF: Grid-based Fast Deblurring Neural Radiance Fields using Sharpness Prior". name: Modular, Hierarchical, and Latent Architectures
body: This family of architectures modifies the standard Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) MLP to handle complex scene properties—such as topological changes, hierarchical structures, or non-rigid deformations—that standard continuous coordinate-based networks struggle to represent due to band-limited interpolation artifacts. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like DoF-NeRF or NeRF-VPT by explicitly introducing auxiliary latent spaces (ambient dimensions or discrete codes) to decouple structural complexity from the primary radiance field, rather than relying solely on input augmentation or view-dependent pose conditioning. The core mechanism involves augmenting the input space of the radiance field MLP with auxiliary latent variables. These variables are either continuous (e.g., ambient coordinates in a higher-dimensional space) or discrete (e.g., vector-quantized codes). The radiance field F is conditioned on these latents to produce density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. The latents are typically generated by a separate lightweight network (encoder/generator) that maps 3D positions or observation indices to the latent space. This allows the main radiance field to remain relatively simple while the latent mechanism handles the complexity of the scene's structure or deformation. HyperNeRF models non-rigidly deforming scenes with topological variations by embedding the scene in \mathbb{R}^{3+W}. It sets itself apart from siblings like Strata-NeRF by explicitly addressing topological discontinuities via ambient dimensions rather than stratified sampling or hierarchical structures. Strata-NeRF models "stratified scenes" with distinct hierarchical levels using discrete Vector Quantized (VQ) latent codes. It sets itself apart from siblings like HyperNeRF by using discrete codes to explicitly represent scene hierarchy, allowing for sharp transitions between levels within a single unified network. The Strata-NeRF architecture includes a Latent Generator (LG) and a Latent Router (LR). Design choice comparisons indicate that using two parallel dense layers in the LR outperforms individual dense layers. The full LR architecture is superior to directly concatenating the generated embedding with the input positional encoding (D3) or replacing the VQ-VAE with a VAE (D4). Disabling the second router (D1) or the first router (D2) in the LR also impacts performance, with the full configuration being optimal. HyperNeRF was introduced to address the limitations of continuous deformation fields in modeling topological changes, such as openings and closings, which are difficult for band-limited MLPs. Strata-NeRF was developed to handle stratified environments (e.g., interior/exterior of buildings) where standard NeRFs produce cloudy artifacts due to an inability to model sudden structural discontinuities. These methods extend the foundational NeRF architecture to support more complex scene priors. name: HyperNeRF
head: Hyper-Space Template, Hyper-space Neural Radiance Fields, HyperNeRF (2021), HyperNeRF Template
body: HyperNeRF is a method for modeling non-rigidly deforming scenes with topological variations (e.g., mouth opening/closing, peeling) by extending the canonical NeRF input space to include higher-dimensional ambient coordinates. It addresses the limitation of continuous deformation fields, which cannot model discontinuities required for topological changes, by representing each observation frame as a non-planar slice through a hyperdimensional radiance field. Unlike strictly deformation-based approaches like Nerfies, HyperNeRF uses these additional dimensions to capture topology changes while retaining a deformation field to fuse information across observations. HyperNeRF builds on Modular, Hierarchical, and Latent Architectures by embedding the template NeRF in a higher-dimensional space. The method combines deformation-based and modulation-based approaches: it uses deformations to model motion for well-behaved optimization and extends the 3D input coordinate space to take additional higher-dimension coordinates as input. Inputs: Set of N images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N with known camera poses Pi and view directions d. Spatial positions x \in \mathbb{R}^3 and view directions d \in \mathbb{R}^3. Per-observation latent deformation codes \omegai and latent appearance codes \psii. Outputs: Density \sigma and color c for volume rendering. The method relies on three primary neural networks (MLPs): 1. Deformation Field (W): Input: (x, \omegai) where x \in \mathbb{R}^3 and \omegai is the latent deformation code. Output: (r, v) \in \mathfrak{se}(3), encoding rotation and translation parameters for the spatial deformation. 2. Slicing Surface Field (H): Input: (x, \omegai) where x \in \mathbb{R}^3 and \omegai is the latent deformation code. Output: w \in \mathbb{R}^W, the position along the ambient axes. 3. Template NeRF (F): Input: (x', w, d, \psii) where x' is the deformed spatial coordinate, w is the ambient coordinate, d is view direction, and \psii is the latent appearance code. Output: (c, \sigma). W: Number of higher (ambient) dimensions. Typical value: 2. m: Hyper-parameter for positional encoding bandwidth. m=1 for hyper-coordinate input w to the template; m=6 for spatial position input x to the slicing surface field H. \alpha: Window function parameter for coarse-to-fine optimization, linearly increased from 0 to 1 over 10k iterations. 1. Positional Encoding: Apply sinusoidal positional encoding \gamma\alpha(x) to inputs. For the spatial position x and view direction d, use standard encoding with bandwidth controlled by \alpha. For the ambient coordinate w, use m=1. \gamma(x) = [\sin(x), \cos(x), \dots, \sin(2^{m-1}x), \cos(2^{m-1}x)]^T The windowed encoding \gamma\alpha(x) weights frequency bands j \in \{0, \dots, m-1\} with: wj(\alpha) = \frac{1 - \cos(\pi \text{clamp}(\alpha - j, 0, 1))}{2} \gamma\alpha(x) = [w0(\alpha)\sin(x), \dots, w{m-1}(\alpha)\cos(2^{m-1}x)]^T 2. Deformation: Compute the spatial deformation field W(x, \omegai) to obtain rotation r and translation v. Transform the observation-space coordinate x to the canonical space x' using the rigid transformation defined by (r, v). 3. Slicing Surface Query: Compute the deformable slicing surface H(x, \omegai) to obtain the ambient coordinate w. This allows different spatial locations to reference different parts of the ambient coordinate space, creating a non-planar slice. 4. Radiance Field Evaluation: Query the template NeRF F with the concatenated canonical coordinate (x', w), view direction d, and appearance code \psii: F: (x', w, d, \psii) \rightarrow (c, \sigma) The SDF is effectively queried at the coordinate obtained by concatenating x' and H(x, \omegai). 5. Volume Rendering: Perform standard volume rendering along the ray using the sampled (c, \sigma) pairs. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import jax.numpy as jnp from jax import grad, jit def positionalencoding(x, m, alpha): """ Computes windowed sinusoidal positional encoding. x: (..., D) input coordinates m: int, number of frequency bands alpha: float, window parameter [0, m] """ # Generate frequency bands freqbands = jnp.arange(m) # Compute window weights # clamp(alpha - j, 0, 1) ensures the window slides correctly windowweights = (1 - jnp.cos(jnp.pi jnp.clip(alpha - freqbands, 0, 1))) / 2 # Expand dimensions for broadcasting # x shape: (..., D), freqbands shape: (m,) # We want to compute sin(2^j x) and cos(2^j x) for each j scales = 2 freqbands # Reshape for broadcasting: x -> (..., 1, D), scales -> (m, 1) xexpanded = x[..., jnp.newaxis,:] scalesexpanded = scales[jnp.newaxis,:, jnp.newaxis] # Compute sin and cos terms sinterms = jnp.sin(scalesexpanded xexpanded) costerms = jnp.cos(scalesexpanded xexpanded) # Apply window weights # windowweights shape: (m,) -> (1, m, 1) wexpanded = windowweights[jnp.newaxis,:, jnp.newaxis] sinencoded = wexpanded sinterms cosencoded = wexpanded costerms # Concatenate along the last axis encoded = jnp.concatenate([sinencoded, cosencoded], axis=-1) return encoded def deformationfieldW(x, omegai, paramsW): """ MLP W: (x, omegai) -> (r, v) in se(3) x: (..., 3) spatial coordinate omegai: (..., Dw) latent deformation code Returns: (r, v) rotation and translation parameters """ # Implementation of MLP W # Input concatenation inputfeat = jnp.concatenate([x, omegai], axis=-1) #... MLP layers... # Output (r, v) return r, v def slicingsurfaceH(x, omegai, paramsH): """ MLP H: (x, omegai) -> w x: (..., 3) spatial coordinate omegai: (..., Dw) latent deformation code Returns: w (..., W) ambient coordinate """ # Implementation of MLP H inputfeat = jnp.concatenate([x, omegai], axis=-1) #... MLP layers... return w def templatenerfF(xprime, w, d, psii, paramsF): """ MLP F: (x', w, d, psii) -> (c, sigma) xprime: (..., 3) deformed spatial coordinate w: (..., W) ambient coordinate d: (..., 3) view direction psii: (..., Dpsi) latent appearance code Returns: (c, sigma) """ # Concatenate inputs inputfeat = jnp.concatenate([xprime, w, d, psii], axis=-1) # Apply positional encoding if needed (typically applied before MLP) #... MLP layers... return c, sigma def hypernerfforward(x, d, omegai, psii, paramsW, paramsH, paramsF, mw, mx, alpha): """ Forward pass for HyperNeRF. x: (..., 3) observation-space spatial coordinates d: (..., 3) view directions omegai: (..., Dw) latent deformation code for frame i psii: (..., Dpsi) latent appearance code for frame i """ # 1. Deformation r, v = deformationfieldW(x, omegai, paramsW) # Transform x to canonical space xprime using SE(3) parameters (r, v) # Assuming a standard rigid transformation function applyse3 xprime = applyse3(x, r, v) # 2. Slicing Surface w = slicingsurfaceH(x, omegai, paramsH) # 3. Positional Encoding # Encode spatial position xprime for the template NeRF # Note: The paper specifies m=6 for spatial position input to H, # but for the template NeRF F, it uses m=1 for w and presumably standard for x'. # We encode xprime, w, and d. encxprime = positionalencoding(xprime, m=6, alpha=alpha) # Using m=6 as per H's spatial input spec, or standard NeRF m encw = positionalencoding(w, m=1, alpha=alpha) encd = positionalencoding(d, m=6, alpha=alpha) # Standard NeRF view direction encoding # 4. Radiance Field Evaluation c, sigma = templatenerfF(encxprime, encw, encd, psii, paramsF) return c, sigma Topological Changes: Continuous deformation fields (e.g., Nerfies) struggle with topological changes because they require discontinuities in the deformation field, which coordinate-based MLPs with positional encoding cannot model easily due to band-limited kernel interpolation. HyperNeRF avoids this by using higher dimensions. Regularization: The elastic regularization loss from Nerfies, which penalizes non-unit singular values of the Jacobian of the deformation field, is ill-suited for scenes with topological variations because these variations directly violate its assumptions. Camera Registration: HyperNeRF is dependent on camera registration; poor registration leads to artifacts or degraded performance. Occlusion and Rapid Motion: The method is limited to observed data and cannot faithfully reconstruct rapid motion or occluded regions. Real-world Photos: HyperNeRF fails on real-world photos with varying illumination and transient occluders. A sibling method that uses stratified sampling for efficient volume rendering. It differs from HyperNeRF by focusing on sampling efficiency rather than topological variation modeling. Choose Strata-NeRF for static scenes requiring faster rendering or better sampling; choose HyperNeRF for dynamic scenes with topological changes. Strata-NeRF Time Complexity: Training is computationally intensive. Training at half 1080p resolution (960x540) for 250k iterations takes roughly 8 hours on 4 TPU v4s. Full-HD training for 1M iterations takes roughly 64 hours. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: HyperNeRF reduces average error rates by 4.1% for interpolation and 8.6% for novel-view synthesis compared to Nerfies, as measured by LPIPS. Strengths: Capable of synthesizing views in scenes with topological changes (e.g., human mouth opening, banana peeling). Uses an optimization strategy that encourages smooth behavior in higher dimensions, enabling high-quality geometry reconstruction even with limited angle views. Limitations: Dependent on accurate camera registration; limited to observed data; fails with varying illumination and transient occluders; computational overhead. When to use: When modeling dynamic scenes with topological variations (e.g., facial expressions, deformable objects) where continuous deformation fields fail. When not to use: For static scenes, scenes with significant illumination changes, or scenes with transient occluders. HyperNeRF was introduced by Keunhong Park et al. in June 2021. It is inspired by level set methods pioneered in the late 1980s by Osher and Sethian, which model moving scenes as static objects in a higher-dimensional ambient space. The method builds on Nerfies by extending the canonical space to a higher dimension and using a slicing MLP to describe how to return to the 3D representation using ambient space coordinates. It is used for reconstructing human avatars and dynamic scenes, particularly in virtual/augmented reality and digital entertainment, where facial expressions and deformable objects require handling topological changes. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28 HyperNeRF, https://doi.org/10.1145/3478513.3480487, fetched 2026-10-28 Lecture 7 – Neural Radiance Fields Prof. Dr., https://virtualhumans.mpi-inf.mpg.de/3DVision25/slides25/pdf/Lecture07NeuralRadianceFields.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Strata-NeRF
head: Neural Radiance Fields for Stratified Scenes
body: Strata-NeRF is a neural radiance field method designed to implicitly capture scenes with multiple hierarchical levels (stratified scenes) by conditioning the radiance field on Vector Quantized (VQ) latent representations. Unlike standard NeRFs which assume continuous scene geometry and fail to model sudden structural changes between levels (producing cloudy artifacts or haziness), Strata-NeRF uses discrete latent codes to handle discontinuities in scene structure. It builds on Modular, Hierarchical, and Latent Architectures by introducing a Latent Generator and Latent Router to compress 3D positional information into discrete codes that condition the MLP. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D point coordinates \mathbf{x} along a ray, integrated positional encoding \boldsymbol{\gamma}(\mathbf{x}), and camera parameters. Output: Density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} for volume rendering. Data Structures: 1. Codebook \mathbf{E}: A lookup table of size N \times D. In the reference implementation, N=1024 and D=48. 2. Latent Generator Encoder: Two linear layers with hidden size 48. 3. Latent Generator Decoder: One linear layer with hidden size 96. 4. Latent Router: Two linear layers with hidden size 256. 5. Radiance Field MLP: The base network (based on Mip-NeRF 360) where the first two layers are conditioned by the routed latent. Algorithm Steps: 1. Positional Encoding: Compute the integrated positional encoding \boldsymbol{\gamma}(\mathbf{x}) for the 3D point \mathbf{x}. 2. Latent Generation: a. Pass \boldsymbol{\gamma}(\mathbf{x}) through the Latent Generator Encoder to get the continuous latent vector \mathbf{z}. b. Find the nearest neighbor in the Codebook \mathbf{E} to \mathbf{z}. Let \mathbf{z}e be the quantized latent code (the vector from \mathbf{E}). c. Pass \mathbf{z}e through the Latent Generator Decoder to get the reconstructed output \mathbf{y}. 3. Latent Routing: a. Pass the quantized latent code \mathbf{z}e through the Latent Router MLP. b. The output of the Latent Router is used to condition the first two layers of the Radiance Field MLP. 4. Radiance Field Evaluation: a. Compute density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} using the Radiance Field MLP, conditioned by the routed latent. 5. Volume Rendering: Render the color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}, t) along the ray \mathbf{r} using standard volume rendering integration. Loss Functions: The total loss is a combination of reconstruction, distortion, and VQ losses: L{total} = L{recon}(\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}, t), \mathbf{c}^(\mathbf{r})) + \lambda1 L{dist}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{w}) + \lambda2 L{vq} Where: L{recon} is the photometric reconstruction loss between estimated color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}, t) and ground truth \mathbf{c}^(\mathbf{r}). L{dist} is the distortion loss between normalized ray distances \mathbf{s} and weight vector \mathbf{w}. L{vq} is the Vector Quantization loss: L{vq} = ||\boldsymbol{\gamma}(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbf{y}||2^2 + ||sg(\mathbf{z}e) - \mathbf{z}||2^2 + \beta||\mathbf{z}e - sg(\mathbf{z})||2^2 Where: \mathbf{z} is the encoder output (continuous latent). \mathbf{z}e is the quantized latent code from the codebook. \mathbf{y} is the decoder output (reconstructed position). sg(\cdot) denotes the stop-gradient operator. \beta is a hyperparameter for the commitment loss. Parameters: \lambda1 (distortion loss weight): 0.01. \lambda2 (VQ loss weight): 0.1. \beta (commitment loss weight): 1.0. Codebook size: 1024 vectors. Codebook dimension: 48. Training iterations: 150,000. Optimizer: Adam with learning rate 1 \times 10^{-6}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class StrataNeRF: def init(self, codebooksize=1024, codebookdim=48, hiddenencoder=48, hiddendecoder=96, hiddenrouter=256): # Codebook: N x D self.codebook = nn.Embedding(codebooksize, codebookdim) # Latent Generator Encoder: 2 linear layers, hidden 48 # Input dim matches IPE output dim (let's assume Din for generality, # but decoder output matches IPE dim, so encoder output is codebookdim) self.encoder = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(codebookdim, hiddenencoder), # Assuming input is already encoded or mapped to D nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddenencoder, codebookdim)) # Latent Generator Decoder: 1 linear layer, hidden 96 # Output dim matches IPE output dim self.decoder = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(codebookdim, hiddendecoder), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendecoder, codebookdim) # Output matches codebook dim for reconstruction of latent space? # Note: Source says "output dimension of our decoder matches the output from Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE) block". # If IPE dim != codebookdim, this mapping needs adjustment. # However, Lvq uses ||gamma(x) - y||. If gamma(x) is high-dim, y must be high-dim. # But encoder output z is codebookdim. # Let's assume the "input" to encoder is gamma(x) and it projects to codebookdim. # And decoder projects codebookdim back to IPEdim. # Re-reading: "encoder has two linear layers... decoder has one... output dimension... matches IPE". # This implies: gamma(x) [IPEdim] -> Encoder -> z [codebookdim] -> Codebook -> ze [codebookdim] -> Decoder -> y [IPEdim]. pass ] # Correction for dimensions based on text: # Encoder input: gamma(x) [IPEdim]. Output: z [codebookdim]. # Decoder input: ze [codebookdim]. Output: y [IPEdim]. self.encoder = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(codebookdim, hiddenencoder), # Wait, input to encoder is gamma(x). # The text says "encoder has two linear layers of hidden size 48". # It doesn't explicitly state input dim, but it processes gamma(x). # Let's assume the first layer maps IPEdim to 48. nn.Linear(codebookdim, hiddenencoder), # Placeholder for IPEdim -> 48 nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddenencoder, codebookdim)) self.decoder = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(codebookdim, hiddendecoder), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendecoder, codebookdim) # Placeholder for 96 -> IPEdim) # Latent Router: 2 linear layers, hidden 256 self.router = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(codebookdim, hiddenrouter), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddenrouter, hiddenrouter)) # Radiance Field MLP (Base MipNeRF 360) # The first two layers are conditioned by the router output. self.radiancefield = MipNeRF360Base() def forward(self, x, rayparams): # 1. Get Integrated Positional Encoding gammax = getintegratedpositionalencoding(x) # Returns vector of dim IPEdim # 2. Latent Generator # Encode gamma(x) to z z = self.encoder(gammax) # Quantize: Find nearest codebook entry # Calculate distances between z and all codebook entries # z shape: [B, D], codebook shape: [N, D] distances = torch.cdist(z, self.codebook.weight, p=2) indices = torch.argmin(distances, dim=1) # Get quantized code ze ze = self.codebook(indices) # Decode ze to y y = self.decoder(ze) # 3. Latent Router # Route ze to condition the MLP routedlatent = self.router(ze) # 4. Radiance Field # Condition first two layers of MLP with routedlatent # This requires modifying the base MLP to accept conditioning. # For the purpose of this article, we assume the base MLP has a method to inject this. sigma, color = self.radiancefield(x, rayparams, conditioning=routedlatent) return sigma, color, indices, z, ze, y def computeloss(self, colorpred, colorgt, sigma, rayweights, raydistances, gammax, z, ze, y): # Lrecon lrecon = F.mseloss(colorpred, colorgt) # Ldist ldist = computedistortionloss(raydistances, rayweights) # Lvq # sg denotes stop-gradient zesg = ze.detach() zsg = z.detach() lvq = (torch.norm(gammax - y, dim=1)2).mean() + \ torch.norm(zesg - z, dim=1)2).mean() + \ 1.0 torch.norm(ze - zsg, dim=1)2).mean() lambda1 = 0.01 lambda2 = 0.1 ltotal = lrecon + lambda1 ldist + lambda2 lvq return ltotal Note on Pseudocode: The dimension mapping in the encoder/decoder is inferred from the loss function L{vq} which compares \boldsymbol{\gamma}(\mathbf{x}) and \mathbf{y}. Thus, the decoder output \mathbf{y} must have the same dimension as the Integrated Positional Encoding \boldsymbol{\gamma}(\mathbf{x}). The encoder maps \boldsymbol{\gamma}(\mathbf{x}) to the codebook dimension D=48. The router takes the codebook dimension D=48 as input. Time Complexity: Training requires 150k iterations. The addition of the Latent Generator and Router adds minimal computational overhead compared to training independent NeRFs for each level. Memory Complexity: The method uses significantly fewer parameters than training an independent NeRF model for each level, leading to reduced memory usage. The codebook size is 1024 vectors of dimension 48. Strengths: Effectively captures stratified scenes with sudden structural changes (e.g., exterior/interior of a building) where standard NeRFs fail. Reduces artifacts like haziness and white clouds seen in jointly trained continuous NeRFs. Limitations: Requires a stratified scene structure (discrete levels). Performance on non-stratified scenes is not the primary focus, though it builds on Mip-NeRF 360. When to use: When rendering scenes with distinct hierarchical levels (e.g., inside/outside a structure) and standard NeRFs produce artifacts due to continuous assumptions. When not to use: For simple, non-stratified scenes where standard NeRFs or Instant-NGP are sufficient and faster. Strata-NeRF was introduced in 2023 by Ati et al.. It addresses the limitation of existing neural radiance fields (like Mip-NeRF 360) which struggle to model scenes that can be deconstructed into several tiers or groupings of structure, termed "Stratified Scenes". Standard NeRFs produce unsatisfactory results (cloudy/sub-optimal views) when trained on images from all hierarchical levels together because their continuous nature is unsuitable for modelling sudden changes. The method was evaluated on a synthetic Stratified Scenes dataset (spheres, cubes, complex geometry) and the real-world RealEstate10K dataset. It builds upon the principles of Modular, Hierarchical, and Latent Architectures by using discrete VQ latents to handle scene complexity. name: NeuralEditor
head: NeuralEditor: Editing Neural Radiance Fields via Manipulating Point Clouds
body: NeuralEditor is a method for editing neural radiance fields (NeRFs) by exploiting an explicit point cloud representation as the underlying structural backbone. Unlike traditional NeRFs that lack native shape-editing capabilities, or mesh-based editing methods that separate mesh optimization from NeRF modeling, NeuralEditor intrinsically integrates point clouds with the implicit neural representation. It interprets NeRF rendering as a process that projects or "plots" an associated 3D point cloud to a 2D image plane, enabling users to manipulate scene geometry by moving points and re-plotting. This approach supports general shape deformation and scene morphing tasks with high-fidelity results, offering both zero-shot inference and fast fine-tuning capabilities. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of input images with known camera poses; an initial point cloud representation of the scene (generated via the model's own optimization or provided externally); camera parameters. Outputs: A trained NeuralEditor model capable of rendering novel views; an editable point cloud where points can be moved to deform the scene; rendered images of the edited scene. Data Structures 1. Point Cloud (\mathcal{P}): A set of 3D points \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Each point stores: Position: \mathbf{p}i Normal vector: \mathbf{n}i (extracted to guide rendering and editing). Color/Reflection parameters: Used to model view-dependent color via the Phong reflection model. 2. K-D Tree: A spatial data structure built over \mathcal{P} to organize points into density-adaptive voxels. This enables efficient neighbor search and stable rendering by handling varying point densities. 3. Neural Network (F\Theta): An MLP that maps point attributes and viewing direction to color. While the standard NeRF uses position \mathbf{x} and direction \mathbf{d}, NeuralEditor uses the associated point's features and direction. Method Steps 1. Point Cloud-Guided Model Construction: The method constructs a NeRF model guided by the point cloud. Instead of querying density at arbitrary 3D positions \mathbf{x}, the rendering process is tied to the explicit points \mathbf{p}i. Build a K-D tree from the current point cloud \mathcal{P}. For each ray, identify the relevant points using the K-D tree to define density-adaptive voxels. 2. Deterministic Integration Strategy: Standard NeRF uses stochastic sampling along rays. NeuralEditor employs a deterministic integration strategy based on the point cloud structure. For a ray r, find the intersection or proximity to points in \mathcal{P} using the K-D tree. Compute the contribution of each point to the ray. The opacity and color of a point are functions of the viewing direction. Integrate these contributions deterministically along the ray to produce the final pixel color. This ensures stable gradients and precise point cloud reconstruction during optimization. 3. Phong Reflection Modeling: To enhance color fidelity and geometric detail, the color output is modeled using the Phong reflection model. Decompose the color \mathbf{c} into diffuse and specular components. The specular component depends on the view direction \mathbf{d}, the surface normal \mathbf{n} (derived from the point cloud geometry), and the light direction (assumed or estimated). This decomposition allows the model to better represent scene geometry and handle specular highlights, which are difficult for standard NeRFs. 4. Optimization: Optimize the point cloud positions \mathcal{P}, normals \mathcal{N}, and neural network parameters \Theta to minimize the difference between rendered images and input images. Use a pruning and growing strategy to maintain an optimal point density. The optimization yields a precise point cloud that accurately represents the scene geometry. 5. Shape Editing: Editing is performed by manipulating the point cloud. Zero-shot Inference: Move points in \mathcal{P} to new positions \mathbf{p}'i to deform the shape. Re-render the scene using the same trained network F\Theta and the new point positions. No retraining is required. Fast Fine-tuning: For higher visual quality and consistency with ambient lighting after editing, perform a short fine-tuning phase on the edited point cloud and network parameters. 6. Scene Morphing (Optional Extension): Guided by a point cloud diffusion model, the method can be extended to smooth scene morphing across multiple scenes. This involves interpolating or transforming the point cloud structure between different scenes. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np class NeuralEditor: def init(self, pointcloud, kdtree): """ Initialize NeuralEditor with a point cloud and a pre-built K-D tree. pointcloud: List of points, each with position (3,), normal (3,), and color params. kdtree: K-D tree structure for efficient neighbor search. """ self.points = pointcloud self.kdtree = kdtree # Neural network parameters for Phong reflection and color prediction # Not shown: FTheta is an MLP taking point features and view direction self.networkparams = None def renderray(self, rayorigin, raydirection, numpointssampled): """ Render a single ray using deterministic integration over the point cloud. """ # 1. Find relevant points using K-D tree # Find points within a certain distance or along the ray path # This replaces stochastic sampling with point-based integration relevantpoints = self.kdtree.querynearby(rayorigin, raydirection) # 2. Sort points by distance along the ray relevantpoints.sort(key=lambda p: np.dot(p.position - rayorigin, raydirection)) accumulatedcolor = np.zeros(3) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 T = 1.0 # Transmittance for point in relevantpoints: # 3. Compute point contribution # Distance from ray to point dist = self.raypointdistance(rayorigin, raydirection, point.position) # Opacity depends on distance and point density # Simplified: Gaussian falloff based on distance opacity = self.computeopacity(dist, point) if opacity < 1e-5: continue # 4. Compute Color using Phong Reflection Model # Normal is assumed to be stored in point or computed from neighbors normal = point.normal viewdir = raydirection # Assume light direction is fixed or estimated lightdir = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]) color = self.phongreflection(normal, viewdir, lightdir, point.colorparams) # 5. Alpha Compositing alpha = opacity T accumulatedcolor += alpha color accumulatedalpha += alpha T = (1.0 - opacity) if T < 1e-5: break return accumulatedcolor def raypointdistance(self, origin, direction, pointpos): """Compute distance from a point to a ray.""" # Vector from ray origin to point v = pointpos - origin # Project v onto direction proj = np.dot(v, direction) # Closest point on ray closest = origin + proj direction return np.linalg.norm(pointpos - closest) def computeopacity(self, dist, point): """Compute opacity based on distance and point attributes.""" # Simplified Gaussian opacity sigma = point.sigmaparam return 1.0 - np.exp(-sigma dist2) def phongreflection(self, normal, viewdir, lightdir, colorparams): """Compute color using Phong reflection model.""" # Diffuse component diffuse = np.dot(normal, lightdir) diffuse = max(0, diffuse) # Specular component reflection = 2 np.dot(normal, lightdir) normal - lightdir specular = np.dot(reflection, -viewdir) specular = max(0, specular) shininess = colorparams.shininess specularcolor = colorparams.specular (specular shininess) # Combine ambient = colorparams.ambient diffusecolor = colorparams.diffuse diffuse return ambient + diffusecolor + specularcolor def editshape(self, pointindices, newpositions): """ Edit the shape by moving specific points. pointindices: List of indices of points to move. newpositions: List of new 3D positions for those points. """ for idx, newpos in zip(pointindices, newpositions): self.points[idx].position = newpos # Rebuild K-D tree if necessary, or update incrementally self.kdtree.update(self.points) def finetune(self, optimizer, lossfn, numiterations): """ Fast fine-tuning after editing to improve visual quality. """ for i in range(numiterations): # Sample rays from edited scene rays = self.samplerays() renderedcolors = [self.renderray(r.origin, r.direction) for r in rays] # Compute loss against ground truth loss = lossfn(renderedcolors, rays.gtcolors) # Backpropagate and update network params and point attributes optimizer.step(loss) Parameters K-D Tree Depth: Not given in the sources. Opacity Falloff Rate (\sigma): Not given in the sources. Phong Shininess: Not given in the sources. Pruning/Growing Thresholds: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Traditional NeRFs lack user-adjustable shape editing capabilities, requiring complex space deformation or mesh conversion which may lack precision. NeuralEditor avoids this by using explicit points. Boundary Conditions: The deterministic integration strategy must handle rays that do not intersect any points. The sources do not specify the fallback behavior for empty space. Normal Estimation: Accurate normal vectors are crucial for the Phong reflection model and editing. The sources do not specify how normals are initially estimated or updated during optimization. Time Complexity: Rendering is deterministic and based on point cloud queries via K-D trees. Complexity depends on the number of points sampled per ray and the efficiency of the K-D tree traversal. Memory Complexity: Stores the point cloud, normals, and neural network parameters. More memory than standard NeRF due to explicit point storage, but less than mesh-based methods if the mesh is complex. Measured Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art performance in shape deformation and scene morphing tasks. High-fidelity rendering results are produced. Scaling: Supports zero-shot inference, meaning editing does not require retraining, which is computationally efficient. Fast fine-tuning can be applied for higher quality. Strengths: Native shape editing via point manipulation; intrinsic integration of point clouds and NeRF; high-fidelity rendering; supports general scene editing operations difficult to achieve with mesh-guided deformation. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial point cloud; requires careful tuning of the pruning and growing strategy; Phong reflection model assumes simple lighting conditions. When to Use: When native shape editing of NeRFs is required, especially for general deformation and morphing tasks. When Not to Use: When simple novel-view synthesis without editing is needed (standard NeRF is sufficient); when complex lighting environments require more advanced shading models than Phong. NeuralEditor was proposed by Jun-Kun Chen, Jipeng Lyu, and Yu-Xiong Wang from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and Peking University. The paper was published in 2023 (arXiv:2305.03049v1, CVPR 2023). The work addresses the fundamental challenge of editing the shape of scenes in NeRFs, which traditionally lack this capability. It builds on the insight that NeRF rendering can be interpreted as plotting a 3D point cloud to a 2D image plane. The method is used in applications such as visual simulation, movie, and game industries, where free-form editing of 3D objects and scenes is required. name: MuRF (Multi-Baseline Radiance Fields)
head: Multi-Baseline Radiance Fields
body: MuRF is a feed-forward neural network method for sparse view synthesis that addresses the failure of prior methods on large baseline settings by constructing a target view frustum volume aligned with the novel view, rather than a reference input view. Unlike ray-based rendering methods that process rays independently (e.g., IBRNet, MatchNeRF), MuRF uses a 3D context-aware convolutional decoder to regress a radiance field from this volume, enabling effective information aggregation even when overlap between input and target views is small. MuRF is an encoder-decoder architecture. The encoder extracts multi-view features from input images. The decoder constructs a volume aligned with the target camera frustum, samples features and colors into this volume, and uses a (2+1)D CNN to regress density and color, which are then rendered via standard volume rendering [18]. Inputs: A set of K input images \{Ik\}{k=1}^K with known camera poses. A target camera pose (view direction and position) for which a novel view is to be synthesized. Outputs: A synthesized RGB image of resolution H \times W. 1. Input Images: \{Ik\}{k=1}^K, where each Ik \in \mathbb{R}^{Hk \times Wk \times 3}. 2. Multi-scale Features: Extracted by the CNN encoder at resolutions 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 of the input image dimensions. 3. Target View Frustum Volume (z): A 4D tensor representing the discretized 3D space aligned with the target view. Layout: z \in \mathbb{R}^{8 \times 8 \times D \times C}. Dimensions: Spatial: 8 \times 8 (subsampled from H \times W). Depth: D (number of equidistant samples per ray). Channel: C (concatenated sampled features, colors, and cosine similarities). 4. Radiance Field: Predicted density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} for each voxel in the upsampled volume. K: Number of input views (K \ge 2). H, W: Resolution of the target image. D: Number of equidistant points sampled on each ray within the target view frustum volume. Spatial Subsampling Factor: 8\times. The volume is constructed at H/8 \times W/8 resolution. CNN Encoder Depth: 6 residual blocks. Downsampling Stride: Stride-2 convolution applied every 2 residual blocks. 1. Multi-View Feature Extraction: For each input image Ik: Pass Ik through a weight-sharing 2D CNN encoder consisting of 6 residual blocks [12]. Apply stride-2 convolutions after every 2 residual blocks to downsample features. Obtain feature maps at 1/2, 1/4, and 1/8 resolutions. Feed the 1/8 resolution features from all K views into a joint multi-view Transformer (based on GMFlow [34, 35]) to perform cross-attention across all views simultaneously. Output: Multi-scale feature maps \{Fk^{(1/2)}, Fk^{(1/4)}, Fk^{(1/8)}\}{k=1}^K. 2. Target View Frustum Volume Construction: Define the target view frustum based on the target camera pose and the bounding volume of the scene (or input views). Cast rays from the target camera center through the target image grid. Perform 8\times subsampling in the spatial dimension. This means rays are cast only through a grid of size (H/8) \times (W/8). For each ray, uniformly sample D equidistant points along the ray within the frustum. Let \mathbf{x}i be the 3D coordinates of the i-th sample point. 3. Volume Element Sampling: For each sample point \mathbf{x}i at spatial index (u, v) in the subsampled grid: Color Sampling: Sample the RGB color from each input image Ik at the projected 2D coordinates of \mathbf{x}i. Feature Sampling: Sample the multi-scale features \{Fk^{(1/2)}, Fk^{(1/4)}, Fk^{(1/8)}\} from each input view at the projected 2D coordinates. Cosine Similarity Calculation: Compute the cosine similarity between the sampled feature vectors from different input views. Specifically, for a point \mathbf{x}i, compute the cosine similarity between features sampled from view j and view k. This provides multi-view consistency cues for density prediction. Concatenation: Concatenate the sampled colors, sampled features (from all scales and views), and computed cosine similarities to form the channel vector zi. The resulting volume z has shape 8 \times 8 \times D \times C. 4. Radiance Field Regression: Input the volume z into a (2+1)D CNN decoder. The (2+1)D CNN factorizes the 3D convolution: A 2D 3 \times 3 \times 1 convolution operates on the spatial dimensions (8 \times 8). A 1D 1 \times 1 \times 3 convolution operates on the depth dimension (D). This factorization reduces computational cost while modeling 3D context. Output: A low-resolution radiance field tensor of shape 8 \times 8 \times D \times 4 (density \sigma and RGB color \mathbf{c}). 5. Upsampling: Apply a lightweight 8\times upsampler [25] to the low-resolution radiance field. Output: Full-resolution radiance field tensor of shape H \times W \times D \times 4. 6. Volume Rendering: Render the target image using standard volumetric rendering [18] on the full-resolution radiance field. For each pixel (u, v), integrate the density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} along the ray: C(u, v) = \sum{i=1}^D Ti (1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai}) \mathbf{c}i where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) is the accumulated transmittance, and \deltai is the distance between sample points. Define target rays with 8x spatial subsampling # Target grid size: H/8 x W/8 hsub = self.H // 8 wsub = self.W // 8 # Generate ray origins and directions for the target view # This depends on the specific camera model (e.g., pinhole) # For simplicity, assume we have ray origins O and directions Dray # Shape: (hsub, wsub, D, 3) for origins and directions origins, directions = castrays(targetcameras, hsub, wsub, self.D, scenebounds) # 2. Sample features and colors from input views # Project 3D points to 2D image coordinates for each input view # This requires inverse projection matrices of input cameras sampledcolors = [] sampledfeatures = [] cosinesimilarities = [] for k in range(self.K): # Project 3D points to 2D for view k # Get 2D coordinates (u, v) for each of the D points on each ray # Shape: (hsub, wsub, D, 2) coords2d = projecttoimage(origins, directions, inputcameras[k]) # Sample color from input image Ik # Use bilinear interpolation color = sampleimage(inputimages[k], coords2d) sampledcolors.append(color) # Sample features from feature map Fk # Feature map shape: (K, C, Hin/8, Win/8) feat = features[k] feature = sampleimage(feat, coords2d) sampledfeatures.append(feature) # Compute cosine similarities between features from different views # For simplicity, compute similarity between view k and view 0 if k > 0: sim = cosinesimilarity(sampledfeatures[k], sampledfeatures[0]) cosinesimilarities.append(sim) # Concatenate all sampled data # sampledcolors: (hsub, wsub, D, 3) # sampledfeatures: List of (hsub, wsub, D, C) # cosinesimilarities: List of (hsub, wsub, D, 1) allchannels = [sampledcolors] allchannels.extend(sampledfeatures) allchannels.extend(cosinesimilarities) # Concatenate along channel dimension # Shape: (hsub, wsub, D, Ctotal) volume = torch.cat(allchannels, dim=-1) # Permute to (8, 8, D, C) if necessary volume = volume.permute(2, 0, 1, 3) return volume def decoderadiancefield(self, volume): """ volume: Tensor of shape (8, 8, D, C) Returns: Radiance field of shape (H, W, D, 4) """ # Apply (2+1)D CNN # 2D convolution on spatial dimensions x = self.decoder2d(volume) # 1D convolution on depth dimension x = self.decoder1d(x) # x shape: (8, 8, D, 4) # Upsample to full resolution # x shape: (H, W, D, 4) radiancefield = self.upsampler(x) return radiancefield def render(self, radiancefield): """ radiancefield: Tensor of shape (H, W, D, 4) Returns: Rendered image of shape (H, W, 3) """ # Extract sigma and color sigma = radiancefield[..., 0] color = radiancefield[..., 1:4] # Standard volume rendering # Assume uniform spacing delta delta = 1.0 # Placeholder for actual distance between samples # Compute transmittance # alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma delta) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma delta) # Ti = product(1 - alphaj) for j < i # T = exp(-sum(sigmaj delta) for j < i) T = torch.cumprod(torch.exp(-sigma delta), dim=-2) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[..., 0:1,:]), T[...,:-1,:]], dim=-2) # Weighted sum weights = alpha T image = torch.sum(weights color, dim=-2) return image def forward(self, images, targetcameras, scenebounds): features = self.extractfeatures(images) volume = self.samplevolume(features, targetcameras, scenebounds) radiancefield = self.decoderadiancefield(volume) image = self.render(radiancefield) return image Large Baselines: Using a reference view volume (aligned with an input view) for large baselines causes failure because the overlap between the reference and target view is small, leading to missing information outside the epipolar lines of the reference view. MuRF avoids this by aligning the volume with the target view. Information Loss: The 8\times spatial subsampling risks losing information if only a single sample is taken per pixel. The method compensates by sampling features and colors from multiple views and computing cosine similarities. Precision: The cosine similarity computation requires normalized feature vectors to be meaningful. Time Complexity: The method is feed-forward, so inference time is constant for a given input size. The (2+1)D CNN is more computationally efficient than full 3D convolutions. The 8\times subsampling reduces the number of rays processed by 64\times compared to full resolution, significantly speeding up feature sampling and volume construction. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the volume z and the intermediate feature maps. The subsampling reduces memory requirements for the volume. The multi-view Transformer scales with K^2 for cross-attention, but the method uses a joint multi-view architecture to mitigate this. Performance: MuRF achieves state-of-the-art performance on small baseline datasets (DTU, LLFF) and large baseline datasets (RealEstate10K). It also shows promising zero-shot generalization on Mip-NeRF 360. Strengths: General applicability to multiple baseline settings; effective 3D context modeling via CNN; efficient handling of high-resolution images via subsampling. Limitations: Requires known camera poses for input and target views. Performance may degrade if the scene bounds are poorly estimated. MuRF was introduced by Haofei Xu et al. in 2024. It addresses the limitations of previous sparse view synthesis methods that were specialized for either small or large baselines. By constructing a target view frustum volume and using a 3D context-aware CNN, MuRF provides a general solution for sparse view synthesis across different baseline settings. name: Gaussian and Primitive-Based Representations
head: Explicit Primitive Representations, Differentiable Primitives, Point-Based Radiance Fields
body: This family replaces the global implicit coordinate-to-radiance mapping of standard NeRF with explicit, learnable 3D primitives (Gaussians, quadrics, or neural points) to improve rendering efficiency and geometric fidelity. Unlike grid-based or pure MLP approaches, these methods represent the scene as a discrete set of elements, enabling differentiable rasterization or local neighborhood aggregation. This approach is distinct from Signed Distance Function (SDF) Representations by avoiding signed distance field constraints, and from Voxel and Sparse Grid Representations by using continuous or parametric primitives rather than discrete volumetric cells. All methods in this family share the following core mechanism: 1. Explicit Representation: The scene is defined by a set of N learnable primitives \mathcal{P} = \{pi\}{i=1}^N. Each primitive pi carries geometric parameters (e.g., position, covariance, quadric coefficients) and appearance parameters (e.g., color, opacity, feature vectors). 2. Differentiability: The rendering process is differentiable with respect to the primitive parameters. This allows gradients from the photometric loss to flow back to the primitive attributes, enabling end-to-end optimization via gradient descent. 3. Local or Explicit Evaluation: Unlike global NeRFs that query a single MLP for any coordinate, these methods evaluate appearance based on local context (neighborhood aggregation) or explicit projection (rasterization). 4. Alpha Compositing: The final pixel color is computed via volume rendering equation: C = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} ci \alphai \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj) where ci is the color, \alphai is the opacity, and the product term is the transmittance. The set \mathcal{N} contains primitives intersecting the ray or projected to the pixel, sorted by depth. Models geometry as an assembly of learnable quadric primitives using differentiable Boolean operations (intersection/union). Chosen for structured abstraction of complex topologies like holes and thin structures. Combines 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization with a neural network that modulates Gaussian opacity based on viewing direction. Chosen to resolve view-dependent artifacts (e.g., glass reflections) while maintaining real-time rendering speeds. Uses a discrete neural point cloud where density and radiance are regressed from local neighborhood features via inverse distance weighting. Chosen to avoid inefficient ray sampling in empty space and spectral bias of global MLPs. Uses an Adaptive Frequency Net (AFNet) to modulate implicit radiance signals with local texture frequency encoding. Chosen for high-frequency detail reconstruction in point-based rendering, overcoming spectral bias. The shift from implicit to explicit representations in radiance fields began as a response to the computational bottlenecks of ray-marching dense MLPs. Early work like Point-NeRF demonstrated that point clouds could approximate scene geometry more efficiently than grids. Subsequent developments, such as 3D Gaussian Splatting derivatives and quadric assemblies, leveraged differentiable rasterization to achieve real-time performance. These methods are widely used in real-time rendering, SLAM, and scenes requiring high-frequency detail or complex topology. name: Differentiable Primitive Assembly
head: DPA-Net Primitive Assembly, Quadric Primitive Assembly
body: Differentiable Primitive Assembly (DPA) models 3D shapes as an explicit assembly of learnable quadric primitives, utilizing differentiable set operations (intersection and union) to construct the scene geometry. Unlike implicit neural representations that query a continuous field, DPA defines the scene via a discrete set of primitives \mathcal{P} and a selection matrix \mathbf{T} that groups them into convexes, enabling end-to-end optimization of both geometry and appearance from image-space losses alone. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Gaussian Splatting by its use of algebraic quadric surfaces and Boolean CSG operations rather than spherical harmonics and rasterized Gaussians. Inputs: A set of N query points \mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3} sampled along camera rays; fused image features \mathbf{f} (typically from a multi-view network); ground truth color \mathbf{C} and mask \mathbf{M} images. Outputs: Primitive parameters \mathbf{P}, selection matrix \mathbf{T}, weights \mathbf{w}, and rendered pixel colors \mathbf{C}{hat}. Data Structures: 1. Primitive Parameters Matrix \mathbf{P}: Shape \mathbb{R}^{P \times 7}. Each row p contains coefficients (ap, bp, cp, dp, ep, fp, gp). The first three coefficients (a, b, c) are constrained to be non-negative to ensure convexity. 2. Selection Matrix \mathbf{T}: Shape \mathbb{R}^{P \times C}. Entries T{p,c} indicate the assignment of primitive p to convex c. During training, \mathbf{T} contains floating-point values in [0, 1]; in Phase 3, it is binarized. 3. Weight Vector \mathbf{w}: Shape \mathbb{R}^{C}. Learnable weights for the soft union operation, initialized close to 1. Parameters: P = 4,096: Number of primitives. C = 256: Number of convexes. Optimizer: Adam, learning rate 10^{-4}. Batch size: 4 object instances. Step 1: Primitive Parameterization Compute the query matrix \mathbf{Q} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 7} where the i-th row is (xi^2, yi^2, zi^2, xi, yi, zi, 1) for query point (xi, yi, zi). Compute the distance matrix \mathbf{D} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times P}: \mathbf{D} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{P}^T D{i,p} < 0 if point i is inside primitive p, and D{i,p} > 0 if outside. Step 2: Primitive Intersection (Convex Construction) Compute the convex occupancy matrix \mathbf{O} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C}: \mathbf{O} = \text{ReLU}(\mathbf{D})\mathbf{T} O{i,c} = 0 if point i is inside convex c (intersection of selected primitives), and O{i,c} > 0 if outside. Step 3: Union of Convexes (Occupancy Field) Compute the exact occupancy field \mathbf{a}^ \in \mathbb{R}^N via min-pooling (union): a^i = \min{1 \leq c \leq C} O{i,c} a^i = 0 if inside the shape, > 0 if outside. Compute the soft occupancy \mathbf{a}^+ \in \mathbb{R}^N for gradient flow: a^+i = \mathcal{L} \left( \sum{c=1}^{C} wc \mathcal{L} (1 - O{i,c}) \right) where \mathcal{L}(\cdot) clips input to [0, 1]. a^+i \approx 1 if inside, < 1 if outside. Step 4: Differentiable Rendering For each pixel, accumulate color along the ray with R sampled points: Cb = \sum{i=1}^{R} ti \alphai c{b,i} where ti = \prod{k=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphak) is the transmittance, c{b,i} is the color at point i, and \alphai is the opacity. Render the mask: Mc = \sum{i \in \Omega} ti \alphai where \Omega is the set of points contributing to the pixel. Step 5: Training Phases The method employs a multi-phase training strategy: Pretraining / Phase 1: Opacity: \alpha = a^+. Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{ph} + \mathcal{L}T + \mathcal{L}w. \mathcal{L}{ph} = \frac{1}{B} \sum{j=1}^B ||\hat{\mathbf{C}}j - \mathbf{C}j||2^2 + \frac{1}{B} \sum{j=1}^B ||\hat{\mathbf{M}}j - \mathbf{M}j||2^2. \mathcal{L}T = \sum{i,j} \max(-T{i,j}, 0) + \max(T{i,j} - 1, 0) (keeps \mathbf{T} \in [0,1]). \mathcal{L}w = \sumj |wj - 1| (keeps \mathbf{w} \approx 1). Parameters optimized: Network, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{w}. Phase 2: Opacity: \alpha = \exp(-10 a^). Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{ph} + \mathcal{L}T (\mathcal{L}w omitted). Parameters optimized: Network, \mathbf{T}. Overlapping Loss \mathcal{L}{over} is introduced here for regularization (see below). Phase 3: Selection Matrix: Binarize \mathbf{T} with threshold 0.01 and freeze. Opacity: \alpha = \exp(-10 a^). Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{ph} + \mathcal{L}{over}. Parameters optimized: Network only. Overlapping Loss \mathcal{L}{over}: Defined to discourage excessive overlap between convexes. For a point i, let hi = \sum{c=1}^C \exp(-10 O{i,c}). hi is large if the point lies in multiple convexes. \mathcal{L}{over} = \sum{i \in \Omega} \max(hi, 1.9) where \Omega is the set of points inside the shape (a^i < 0.01). In practice, 40,960 points are sampled surrounding the shape to compute this. Silhouette-aware Pixel Sampling: To handle complex topologies, sample 256 pixels randomly and 1,000 pixels around object contours (obtained via morphological closing on the mask + Gaussian noise). Primitive Dropout (Phase 3): Applied every 400 iterations. For each primitive p, set the p-th row of \mathbf{T} to zero. Compute new occupancy \mathbf{b}^. Quantify variation: v = K \sum{i=1}^P \mathbb{I}(\text{XOR}(b^i < 0.1, a^i < 0.1)) where K=40,960. If v \approx 0, keep the row zero (primitive removed); else restore. Unverified code. name: Viewing Direction Gaussian Splatting
body: Viewing Direction Gaussian Splatting (VDGS) is a hybrid neural rendering method that combines the explicit geometric representation of 3D Gaussian Splatting with the view-dependent appearance modeling of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). It solves the limitation of classical Gaussian Splatting, where color and opacity are static per primitive, by introducing a neural network that modulates opacity (and optionally color) based on the viewing direction. This allows VDGS to accurately model view-dependent phenomena such as glass reflections, transparency, and specular highlights without the computational overhead of full NeRF ray-marching. VDGS represents the scene as a set of N 3D Gaussians, where each Gaussian i is defined by a mean position \mathbf{m}i, a covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma}i, a base color \mathbf{c}i, and a base opacity \sigmai. Unlike standard Gaussian Splatting, the effective opacity of each Gaussian is dynamically adjusted by a neural network conditioned on the viewing direction. Inputs: A set of initial 3D Gaussian parameters (initialized from Structure from Motion points), camera poses, and viewing directions \mathbf{d} for each pixel ray. Outputs: Rendered pixel colors C(\mathbf{p}) for each camera view. 1. Gaussian Set \mathcal{G}: A collection of N primitives. Each primitive i stores: \mathbf{m}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean position. \mathbf{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Covariance matrix (parameterized as a rotation matrix \mathbf{R} and scaling vector \mathbf{s}, such that \mathbf{\Sigma} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^T \mathbf{R}^T). \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Base color (RGB). \sigmai \in \mathbb{R}: Base opacity (transparency). 2. Neural Network F{VDGS}: A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) that takes hashed Gaussian positions and viewing directions as input and outputs a density update \Delta \sigma. Hash Grid: A 3D structured hash grid with 12 levels of embedding (resolutions 16 to 512), a maximum hash table size of 2^{14} (16384), and a feature dimension of 2. MLP Architecture: 2-layer MLP with LeakyReLU activation. The vanilla NeRF model is defined as F{NeRF}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}; \Theta) = (c, \sigma), where \mathbf{x} is spatial location, \mathbf{d} is viewing direction, and \Theta are MLP parameters. In VDGS, the neural network F{VDGS} takes the Gaussian mean \mathbf{m} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} to produce a volume density update \Delta \sigma(\mathbf{d}): F{VDGS}(\mathbf{m}, \mathbf{d}; \Theta) = \Delta \sigma(\mathbf{d}) The effective opacity \alphai for a sample i along a ray is calculated using the base opacity \sigmai, the distance between adjacent samples \deltai, and the NeRF-based density update \Delta \sigmai(\mathbf{d}): \alphai = 1 - \exp\left( -\sigmai \cdot F{VDGS}(\mathbf{m}i, \mathbf{d}; \Theta) \cdot \deltai \right) The final pixel color C(\mathbf{p}) is computed by blending N ordered overlapping Gaussian samples using alpha compositing: C(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} \mathbf{c}i \alphai \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj) where \mathcal{N} is the set of Gaussians intersecting the ray, sorted by depth. Hash Grid Levels: 12. Hash Table Size: 2^{14} (16384). Feature Dimension: 2. Activation Function: LeakyReLU. MLP Layers: 2. 1. Initialization: Initialize the model with Structure from Motion (SfM) points, sourced from COLMAP or generated randomly, to establish the initial positions and covariances of the 3D Gaussians. 2. Hash Encoding: Encode the mean position \mathbf{m}i of each Gaussian using the 3D structured hash grid. 3. Density Update: Feed the hashed Gaussian mean \mathbf{m}i and the viewing direction \mathbf{d} into the MLP F{VDGS} to compute the density update \Delta \sigmai(\mathbf{d}). 4. Opacity Calculation: Compute the effective opacity \alphai for each Gaussian sample using the formula \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \cdot \Delta \sigmai(\mathbf{d}) \cdot \deltai). 5. Rasterization: Use a differential Gaussian rasterization pipeline to project the Gaussians to 2D, sort them by depth, and compute the pixel color C(\mathbf{p}) via alpha compositing. 6. Optimization: Jointly optimize all parameters (Gaussian means, covariance matrices, base colors, base opacities, and MLP weights) using gradient descent to minimize the difference between rendered and reference images. 7. Pruning and Densification: Every 100 iterations, eliminate Gaussians with opacity below a specific threshold and generate new Gaussians in unoccupied areas of 3D space to fill vacant regions. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class HashGrid: """ 3D Structured Hash Grid for encoding Gaussian positions. """ def init(self, numlevels=12, resolutionrange=(16, 512), tablesize=214, featuredim=2): self.numlevels = numlevels self.resolutionrange = resolutionrange self.tablesize = tablesize self.featuredim = featuredim # Implementation details of hash grid lookup omitted as per standard libraries # Assumes a standard hash grid implementation exists that maps 3D coords to feature vectors. class VDGSMLP(nn.Module): """ 2-layer MLP with LeakyReLU for computing density updates. """ def init(self, inputdim, hiddendim=256, outputdim=1): super(VDGSMLP, self).init() self.net = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(inputdim, hiddendim), nn.LeakyReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.LeakyReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, outputdim)) def forward(self, x): return self.net(x) class VDGS: def init(self, gaussians, hashgrid, mlp): self.gaussians = gaussians # List of Gaussian objects self.hashgrid = hashgrid self.mlp = mlp def getdensityupdate(self, gaussian, viewdirection): """ Computes the density update Deltasigma for a Gaussian given its mean and view direction. """ # Encode Gaussian mean using hash grid hashedpos = self.hashgrid.encode(gaussian.mean) # Concatenate hashed position and view direction # View direction is typically normalized. inputtensor = torch.cat([hashedpos, viewdirection], dim=-1) # Pass through MLP deltasigma = self.mlp(inputtensor) return deltasigma def computeopacity(self, baseopacity, deltasigma, deltaz): """ Computes effective alpha from base opacity, density update, and sample distance. alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma Deltasigma deltaz) """ effectivedensity = baseopacity deltasigma alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-effectivedensity deltaz) return alpha def render(self, rays): """ Renders the scene for a batch of rays. """ renderedcolors = [] for ray in rays: # 1. Intersect ray with Gaussians to get sorted list of samples samples = self.intersectray(ray) # Returns list of (gaussianidx, depth, deltaz) # 2. Compute transmittance and color T = 1.0 color = torch.zeros(3) for sample in samples: gidx, depth, deltaz = sample gaussian = self.gaussians[gidx] # Get view direction for this ray viewdir = ray.direction # Get density update from MLP deltasigma = self.getdensityupdate(gaussian, viewdir) # Compute opacity alpha = self.computeopacity(gaussian.baseopacity, deltasigma, deltaz) # Alpha compositing weight = T alpha color += weight gaussian.color T = (1.0 - alpha) # Early exit if T is very small if T < 1e-5: break renderedcolors.append(color) return torch.stack(renderedcolors) def optimizestep(self, rays, targetimages): """ Performs one optimization step. """ # Forward pass predictedcolors = self.render(rays) # Loss calculation (e.g., L1 or L2) loss = torch.mean((predictedcolors - targetimages) 2) # Backward pass loss.backward() # Update parameters # Assumes an optimizer (e.g., Adam) is attached to the model parameters. optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() # Pruning and Densification every 100 iterations # This logic is typically handled by the rasterization backend or a separate manager. if currentiteration % 100 == 0: self.prunelowopacitygaussians() self.densifyunoccupiedareas() Joint Color and Opacity Update: While VDGS can update both color and opacity, ablation studies show that updating only opacity yields more consistently high-quality results on real scenes. Updating both simultaneously can be less effective due to the dependency of opacity on color. Opacity Multiply vs. Color Multiply: The "Opacity Multiply" variant (VDGS Opacity Multiply) achieves the best scores on real scenes, while "Color Multiply" performs best on the NeRF Synthetic dataset. Precision: The hash grid provides fast queries but requires careful tuning of table size and levels to avoid collisions or insufficient resolution. Time Complexity: Training and inference times are comparable to standard Gaussian Splatting, significantly faster than NeRF-based methods. On an NVIDIA RTX 3090, VDGS-30K training times are approximately 46 minutes for Mip-NeRF360, 30 minutes for Tanks & Temples, and 41 minutes for Deep Blending. Memory Complexity: The memory footprint is dominated by the Gaussian primitives and the hash grid. The hash grid uses 2^{14} entries with feature dimension 2, which is relatively small compared to dense voxel grids. Performance: Mip-NeRF360: SSIM 0.813, PSNR 27.64, LPIPS 0.220. Tanks and Temples: SSIM 0.851, PSNR 24.02, LPIPS 0.176. Deep Blending: SSIM 0.906, PSNR 29.54, LPIPS 0.243. Shiny Blender: Avg PSNR 30.62. Inference FPS: On RTX 3090, VDGS-30K achieves 41.35 FPS (Mip-NeRF360), 38.53 FPS (Tanks & Temples), and 44.72 FPS (Deep Blending). Strengths: Fast training and inference; ability to model view-dependent effects (reflections, transparency) without increasing training time significantly compared to GS. Limitations: Requires tuning of hash grid parameters; joint optimization of color and opacity may be unstable. Viewing Direction Gaussian Splatting (VDGS) was proposed by researchers from the Jagiellonian University and the University of Cambridge. It was introduced to address the limitations of both Gaussian Splatting (which lacks view-dependent appearance) and NeRF (which is slow to train and render). The method leverages the fast differentiable rasterization of Gaussian Splatting while incorporating the view-dependent encoding capabilities of NeRF via a neural network. It is implemented using PyTorch and TinyCUDA frameworks. Gaussian Splatting with NeRF-based Color and Opacity, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2312.13729, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Point-NeRF Representation
head: Neural point cloud, Point-based radiance field
body: Point-NeRF is a method that represents a continuous volumetric radiance field using a discrete neural point cloud, avoiding the computational cost of ray sampling in empty space by leveraging classical point clouds to approximate scene geometry. It differs from global MLP-based NeRFs by regressing density and radiance from local neighborhood features rather than querying a single global network, and from Gaussian Splatting by using point-based aggregation with inverse distance weighting rather than explicit Gaussian projection. Inputs: A set of N neural points \mathcal{P}, a camera ray defined by origin and direction, and rendering parameters (number of shading samples M, neighborhood radius R, number of neighbors K). Outputs: Pixel color C computed via volume rendering. Data Structures: The scene is represented by a neural point cloud \mathcal{P} = \{ (pi, fi, \gammai) \mid i = 1, \dots, N \}: pi \in \mathbb{R}^3: The 3D spatial location of the i-th point. fi \in \mathbb{R}^D: A neural feature vector encoding local scene content (dimension D is a hyperparameter). \gammai \in [0, 1]: A scale confidence value representing the likelihood that the point is near an actual scene surface. Algorithm: 1. Ray Marching: For each pixel, march a ray through the scene. Sample M shading points \{xj \mid j = 1, \dots, M\} along the ray. 2. Neighborhood Query: For each shading point xj and viewing direction dj, query the K nearest neural points from \mathcal{P} within a radius R. Let this set be \mathcal{N}j. 3. Per-Point Processing: For each neighbor i \in \mathcal{N}j, compute a processed feature vector f{i,xj} using an MLP F: f{i,xj} = F(fi, xj - pi) The input to F is the concatenation of the point's feature fi and the relative position vector xj - pi. This makes the network invariant to point translation. 4. Feature Aggregation: Aggregate the processed features f{i,xj} into a single feature f{xj} using inverse distance weighting, weighted by the confidence \gammai: f{xj} = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}j} \gammai \frac{wi}{\sum{k \in \mathcal{N}j} wk} f{i,xj}, \quad \text{where } wi = \frac{1}{\|pi - xj\|} If \sum wk = 0 (e.g., no neighbors found), f{xj} is undefined or handled as a default (e.g., zero vector). 5. Radiance Regression: Regress the view-dependent radiance rj and volume density \sigmaj from the aggregated feature f{xj} and viewing direction dj using an MLP R: rj = R(f{xj}, dj) Note: The source defines the regression function as (\sigma, r) = \text{Point-NeRF}(x, d, \dots). Typically, \sigma is derived from f{xj} via a separate head or MLP, while r is derived from f{xj} and dj. The source explicitly states r = R(fx, d). The density \sigma is not explicitly defined by a separate formula in the provided text but is part of the regression output. 6. Volume Rendering: Accumulate the radiance using the volume rendering equation: C = \sum{j=1}^{M} \tauj (1 - \exp(-\sigmaj \Deltaj)) rj where \tauj = \exp\left(-\sum{t=1}^{j-1} \sigmat \Deltat\right) is the transmittance, and \Deltaj is the distance between adjacent shading samples. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, origin of the ray. raydirection: 3D vector, direction of the ray. neuralpoints: List of tuples (pi, fi, gammai). M: Number of shading samples along the ray. R: Radius for neighborhood query. K: Number of neighbors to query. MLPF: Neural network for per-point processing. MLPR: Neural network for radiance regression. Returns: Pixel color C. """ # 1. Sample shading points along the ray # Assume a fixed step size or adaptive sampling. # For simplicity, assume uniform sampling over a range [tmin, tmax]. tvalues = linspace(tmin, tmax, M) shadingpoints = [rayorigin + t raydirection for t in tvalues] pixelcolor = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 for j, xj in enumerate(shadingpoints): # 2. Query K nearest neighbors within radius R neighbors = queryneighbors(xj, neuralpoints, K, R) if not neighbors: # No neighbors found, contribution is zero or background continue # 3. Per-point processing and 4. Feature aggregation aggregatedfeature = 0.0 weightsum = 0.0 for (pi, fi, gammai) in neighbors: # Relative position relpos = xj - pi # Process feature fix = MLPF(concat(fi, relpos)) # Inverse distance weight dist = norm(pi - xj) if dist == 0: wi = infinity # Handle degenerate case, e.g., clamp or use epsilon else: wi = 1.0 / dist # Weighted aggregation weightsum += gammai wi aggregatedfeature += gammai wi fix if weightsum == 0: continue aggregatedfeature = aggregatedfeature / weightsum # 5. Radiance regression # Note: Source defines r = R(fx, d). Density sigma is also predicted. # Assuming MLPR outputs both sigma and r, or separate heads. # For this pseudocode, assume MLPR returns (sigma, r). sigmaj, rj = MLPR(concat(aggregatedfeature, raydirection)) # 6. Volume rendering accumulation # Deltaj is distance to next sample. For last sample, assume small delta or 0. if j < M - 1: deltaj = norm(shadingpoints[j+1] - shadingpoints[j]) else: deltaj = 0.0 # Or a small epsilon alphaj = 1.0 - exp(-sigmaj deltaj) pixelcolor += transmittance alphaj rj transmittance = (1.0 - alphaj) return pixelcolor Parameters: M: Number of shading samples per ray. Not given in the sources. R: Neighborhood query radius. Not given in the sources. K: Number of neighbors to query. Not given in the sources. D: Dimension of feature vector fi. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Neighbors: If a shading point has no neighbors within radius R, the aggregation step fails. A fallback (e.g., zero feature, background color) is needed. Zero Distance: If a shading point coincides with a neural point (pi = xj), the inverse distance weight becomes infinite. This should be handled by clamping or using a small epsilon. Precision: Floating-point precision in distance calculations and exponentiation in volume rendering can affect stability. Time Complexity: Rendering time depends on M (samples per ray), K (neighbors), and the cost of MLP evaluations. Querying neighbors is O(N \log N) or O(N) depending on spatial indexing. Aggregation is O(K). MLP evaluation is constant per point. Overall, it is generally faster than global NeRFs for sparse scenes because it avoids sampling empty space. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot D) to store the neural point cloud. Strengths: Faster optimization and rendering than global NeRFs; leverages existing point cloud reconstruction methods (e.g., COLMAP); can prune/grow points to fix holes and outliers. Limitations: Quality depends on the initial point cloud quality; may struggle with highly complex geometry if K is small or R is inappropriate. When to use: When fast per-scene optimization is desired, and a good initial point cloud is available. When not to use: When no initial point cloud is available, or for scenes with very dense, complex geometry where local neighborhoods are insufficient. Point-NeRF was introduced by Qiangeng Xu, Zexiang Xu, Julien Philip, Sai Bi, Zhixin Shu, Kalyan Sunkavalli, and Ulrich Neumann from USC and Adobe Research. It was presented at CVPR 2022.
