name: Frequency-Modulated Point Cloud Rendering
head: AFNet, Adaptive Frequency Net, Adaptive Frequency Net (AFNet) based rendering, FreqPCR, Frequency-Modulated Radiance Mapping
body: Frequency-Modulated Point Cloud Rendering is a real-time rendering pipeline that represents scenes as explicit point clouds and uses an Adaptive Frequency Net (AFNet) to modulate implicit radiance signals with local texture frequency encoding. It solves the problem of high-frequency detail reconstruction in point-based rendering, where standard MLPs suffer from spectral bias towards low-frequency signals. Unlike sibling methods that use fixed activation functions or global frequency encoding, AFNet predicts local frequency and phase parameters for each point via a hypernetwork, allowing the network to adaptively handle varying texture complexities (high frequency for textured regions, low for smooth regions). This approach enables high-fidelity local detail reconstruction, real-time rendering speeds, and user-friendly object-level editing. The method consists of three main components: point cloud geometry optimization, the AFNet radiance mapping module, and a rendering pipeline that supports editing and composition. Input: A set of N 3D points \mathcal{P} = \{\mathbf{p}i\}{i=1}^N, where each point \mathbf{p}i has a position \mathbf{x}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. The points may be initialized from sparse reconstructions or optimized via volume rendering. Output: A rendered image C \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} for a given camera pose. 1. Point Cloud: A list of N points. Each point stores: Position: \mathbf{x}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Opacity: \alphai \in [0, 1], learned during geometry optimization. Feature Vector: \mathbf{f}i \in \mathbb{R}^C, the input feature to the AFNet (initially derived from position or learned). 2. AFNet Model: Hypernetwork: A two-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) that takes point position \mathbf{x}i as input and outputs adaptive frequency \omegai \in \mathbb{R} and phase \phii \in \mathbb{R}. AF Layers: A sequence of layers within the radiance mapping network. Each layer i contains a linear transformation, an Adaptive Frequency (AF) activation layer, and potentially another linear transformation. Radiance Head: A final linear layer mapping the output feature to RGB color. To address the limitation where previous surface point-based works kept only the closest point per ray (preventing geometry optimization), this method uses volume rendering as a preprocessing module. 1. Initialize a dense point cloud. 2. During training, keep multiple points in the pixel buffer for each ray. 3. Learn the opacity \alphai of each point based on volume rendering. 4. This step improves rendering PSNR by 2-4dB for poorly reconstructed scenes and avoids artifacts. For each point \mathbf{p}i with position \mathbf{x}i and input feature \mathbf{X}^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^C (where C is the feature dimension): 1. Frequency Estimation: Pass \mathbf{x}i through the two-layer MLP hypernetwork to predict scalar frequency \omega^{(i)} and phase \phi^{(i)}. 2. Feature Propagation: The radiance mapping network processes features through L layers. Let \mathbf{X}^{(l)} be the input feature to layer l. 3. Adaptive Frequency Activation: For each layer l, compute the output \mathbf{Y}^{(l)} using the adaptive frequency activation layer: \mathbf{Y}^{(l)} = \mathbf{X}^{(l)} \circ \sin(\omega^{(l)} \circ \mathbf{X}^{(l)} + \phi^{(l)}) where \circ denotes the Hadamard (element-wise) product. The scalars \omega^{(l)} and \phi^{(l)} are broadcast to the dimension C. Note: The hypernetwork predicts \omega and \phi for each point. In the context of the layer-wise operation, \omega^{(l)} and \phi^{(l)} refer to the parameters associated with the point's contribution to that specific layer's modulation, or the hypernetwork outputs are used directly if the AFNet structure implies a single modulation per point per layer. The source specifies the hypernetwork infers parameters from the spatial point, and these are injected into the AF layers. 4. Linear Transformation: Apply a linear layer to \mathbf{Y}^{(l)} to produce the input for the next layer \mathbf{X}^{(l+1)}. 5. Final Output: After the last AF layer, apply a final linear layer to map the feature to RGB color \mathbf{c}i. 1. For each pixel, cast a ray and find the set of points \mathcal{N} intersecting the ray or projected to the pixel. 2. Sort points by depth. 3. Compute pixel color using alpha compositing: C = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} \mathbf{c}i \alphai \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj) where \mathbf{c}i is the color predicted by AFNet for point i, and \alphai is its learned opacity. Editing: For rigid object editing, users edit the point cloud directly. The deformation field between the original and deformed 3D space is obtained by querying the transformations performed on the point cloud. Composition: To combine multiple scenes, a masking strategy based on the depth buffer is used at the pixel level to avoid cross-scene training. Unverified code. """ def init(self, featuredim, hiddendim, numlayers, numhyperlayers=2): super().init() self.numlayers = numlayers self.featuredim = featuredim # Hypernetwork: Two-layer MLP to predict omega and phi from position # Input: x (3,), Output: omega (1,), phi (1,) hyperlayers = [] for i in range(numhyperlayers): indim = 3 if i == 0 else hiddendim outdim = hiddendim if i < numhyperlayers - 1 else 1 hyperlayers.append(nn.Linear(indim, outdim)) if i < numhyperlayers - 1: hyperlayers.append(nn.ReLU()) self.hypernetwork = nn.Sequential(hyperlayers) # Radiance Mapping Network # Consists of Linear -> AF Layer -> Linear -> AF Layer... -> Linear self.layers = nn.ModuleList() for i in range(numlayers): indim = featuredim if i == 0 else hiddendim outdim = hiddendim self.layers.append(nn.Linear(indim, outdim)) # AF Layer is implemented as a function, not a module with weights # The modulation parameters come from the hypernetwork # Final output layer self.outputlayer = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 3) # RGB def forward(self, points, features): """ Args: points: Tensor of shape (N, 3), 3D coordinates of points features: Tensor of shape (N, featuredim), input features for each point Returns: colors: Tensor of shape (N, 3), predicted RGB colors """ N = points.shape[0] # 1. Projects points to 2D, sorts by depth, and composites. """ # 1. Sort points by depth (front to back) sortindices = torch.argsort(depth) u = u[sortindices] v = v[sortindices] depth = depth[sortindices] opacities = opacities[sortindices] colors = colors[sortindices] # 4. Rasterize # Create an image buffer image = torch.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3), device=colors.device) alphabuffer = torch.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth), device=colors.device) # Iterate over points (in front-to-back order) for i in range(len(u)): px = int(u[i].item()) py = int(v[i].item()) if 0 <= px < imagewidth and 0 <= py < imageheight: alpha = opacities[i].item() color = colors[i] # Alpha compositing # Cnew = Cold (1 - alpha) + color alpha # Anew = Aold + alpha (1 - Aold) # Using tensor operations for efficiency would be better, # but this loop illustrates the logic. # In practice, this is done via scatteradd or similar. # Update color and alpha at pixel (px, py) # Note: This is a simplified single-point update. # Multiple points may map to the same pixel. # We need to accumulate. # Let's assume we process all points and use a scatter operation. pass # Efficient rasterization using scatter # This part is implementation-specific and depends on the graphics API or PyTorch3D/MinkowskiEngine. # The core logic is the alpha compositing equation provided in the parent article. return image Hypernetwork: Two-layer MLP. Rendering Speed: 39.27 FPS on NeRF-Synthetic dataset. Performance: 1700x faster than NeRF. Geometry Optimization: Improves PSNR by 2-4dB for poorly reconstructed scenes. Spectral Bias: Standard MLPs with ReLU have strong spectral bias towards low-frequency signals, limiting high-frequency reconstruction. AFNet mitigates this by adapting frequencies locally. Geometry Optimization: Previous surface point-based works could not optimize point cloud geometry because they kept only the closest point as surface estimation for each ray. This method avoids that by using volume rendering with multiple points per ray in the buffer. Cross-Scene Training: When composing scenes, failure to use a depth-based masking strategy can lead to cross-scene training artifacts. Time Complexity: Real-time rendering speed of 39.27 FPS on NeRF-Synthetic. It is 1700x faster than NeRF and 37x faster than CCNeRF. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of points N and the feature dimension C. The hypernetwork is small (two-layer MLP), adding negligible computational overhead. Strengths: High-fidelity local detail reconstruction, real-time rendering, user-friendly object-level editing, and scene composition. Limitations: Performance on poorly reconstructed scenes can still be improved by the geometry optimization module (2-4dB PSNR gain). The method relies on the quality of the initial point cloud. When to use: When real-time rendering and editable point-based representations are required, especially for scenes with varying texture frequencies. When not to use: When global consistency is more important than local detail, or when the scene is too large for the point cloud representation to be efficient. Frequency-Modulated Point Cloud Rendering was proposed by Zhang et al. in 2023. It addresses the limitations of Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) and standard MLPs in point cloud rendering, specifically the spectral bias towards low-frequency signals. The method builds on the concept of HyperNetworks [11] and Frequency Modulation Networks (MFN) [7] to create an adaptive frequency modulation mechanism. It is part of the broader effort to make neural rendering editable and real-time, competing with methods like CCNeRF and Object-NeRF. name: Neural Proxy
head: Neural Proxy Model
body: Neural Proxy is a neural rendering method that represents photo-realistic targets as animatable proxies to enable the rendering of unseen animations without temporal learning. It solves the limitation of standard NeRF, where content is tied to continuous Cartesian coordinates, making animation difficult, and Neural Texture, which requires animated training samples to render unseen animations. By combining neural volume rendering with neural texture, it mimics the typical CG pipeline of using a 3D mesh for geometry and a texture for appearance. The method constructs a volumetric proxy from reference geometry, wraps it with a neural texture, and uses a hybrid sampling strategy to render scenes containing both animatable targets and static surroundings. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Reference geometry (mesh \bar{M}), UV coordinates for the mesh, offset parameters for shell extrusion (\epsilon, \bar{\epsilon}), and a neural texture \Omega{Tex}. Outputs: Rendered image I. Data Structures: 1. Coarse Geometry (\bar{M}): Defined by vertices \mathbf{v}i and smoothed normals \mathbf{n}i. \bar{M} = \{\mathbf{v}i\}{i=1}^{Nv}, where Nv is the number of vertices. 2. Proxy Shell: A volume enclosing the target, formed by an outward surface \overrightarrow{M} and an inward surface \overleftarrow{M}. Outward vertices: \overrightarrow{\mathbf{v}}i = \mathbf{v}i + \mathbf{n}i \cdot \epsilon Inward vertices: \overleftarrow{\mathbf{v}}i = \mathbf{v}i - \mathbf{n}i \cdot \bar{\epsilon} Conditions: \epsilon, \bar{\epsilon} \ge 0 and \epsilon + \bar{\epsilon} > 0. The shell must enclose the photo-realistic target. 3. Proxy UV Coordinates: Lifted 2D UV coordinates to 3D to define depth within the shell. \overrightarrow{\mathbf{u}}i = (u{2D}, \overrightarrow{w}) where \overrightarrow{w} = 1 (outward shell label). \overleftarrow{\mathbf{u}}i = (u{2D}, \overleftarrow{w}) where \overleftarrow{w} = 0 (inward shell label). The full proxy vertex set is \{\overrightarrow{\mathbf{v}}i\}{i=1}^{Nv} \cup \{\overleftarrow{\mathbf{v}}i\}{i=1}^{Nv}. 4. Neural Texture (\Omega{Tex}): A learnable feature map. 5. Neural Renderer (f{NR}): Parameters \theta{NR}. Steps: 1. Proxy Construction: Retrieve reference geometry \bar{M} (e.g., via COLMAP or manual low-res mesh). Compute outward and inward surfaces using the extrusion formulas above. Assign UV coordinates to the original mesh vertices. Lift these to 3D proxy UVs using the depth labels \overrightarrow{w}=1 and \overleftarrow{w}=0. 2. Tetrahedralization for Barycentric Sampling: The extrusion of triangles forms prisms. Break each prism into three tetrahedra using the method from [PBFJ05] to enable Barycentric coordinate sampling. 3. Wrapping with Neural Texture: Wrap the proxy shell with the neural texture \Omega{Tex}. 4. Particle Sampling (Hybrid): For animatable targets: Use a Neural Proxy Sampler (Sp). Map a Cartesian point \mathbf{x} to Barycentric coordinates within the proxy shell. Sample features from \Omega{Tex} using a bilinear sampler f{Bi} based on the UV coordinates. Input the sampled features to the neural renderer: (\mathbf{c}, \sigma) = Sp(\mathbf{x}). Note: The view direction \mathbf{d} is dropped for simplicity in the proxy sampler definition, relying on local texture features. For static surroundings: Use a Static Sampler (standard NeRF-style Cartesian sampling). Mixture: Combine the outputs from the neural proxy sampler and static sampler for the final ray integration. 5. Rendering: Render the image using the neural renderer f{NR} and the sampled features. The rendering equation follows the standard neural volume rendering approximation: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) \approx \sum{i=1}^{Ns} Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \Delta tj), \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \Delta ti), and (\mathbf{c}i, \sigmai) are the color and density outputs from the respective sampler for particle i along ray \mathbf{r}. Parameters: \epsilon, \bar{\epsilon}: Offset parameters for shell extrusion. Set such that the shell encloses the target object. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Shell Enclosure: The shell must fully enclose the photo-realistic target to ensure relevant particles are contained. If the target moves outside the shell during animation, rendering artifacts will occur. Prism Tetrahedralization: Correctly breaking prisms into tetrahedra is required for valid Barycentric coordinate sampling. Failure here leads to incorrect texture lookups. Animation Capability: Unlike NeRF, it allows particles to move with the animation by animating the proxy geometry, enabling unseen animation synthesis without temporal learning. Training Data: Does not require animated training samples, unlike Neural Texture. Performance: The sources do not provide specific time/memory complexity metrics or measured performance benchmarks. Neural Proxy was proposed to address the lack of discussion on enabling neural rendering for synthesizing frames for unseen animations. It combines components from Neural Volume Rendering (specifically NeRF [MST 20]) and Neural Texture [TZN 19]. It was introduced in a paper by the author(s) of in 2021. name: ViSNeRF
head: Efficient Multidimensional Neural Radiance Field Representation for Visualization Synthesis of Dynamic Volumetric Scenes
body: ViSNeRF is a hybrid neural radiance field method designed for the efficient visualization synthesis of dynamic volumetric scenes with arbitrary adjustable parameters (e.g., time, isovalue, transfer functions). It combines explicit feature grids with implicit feature decoders to achieve high-quality, 3D-consistent renderings while minimizing model size and GPU memory cost. Unlike standard NeRFs that treat scenes as static 3D volumes, ViSNeRF factorizes the representation into a 3D spatial tensor and a K-dimensional parameter tensor, allowing it to interpolate across parameter spaces without retraining. It distinguishes itself from fully explicit methods (like PlenOctrees) and fully implicit methods (like CoordNet) by using vector-matrix decomposition for spatial features and small MLPs for decoding, offering a balance between rendering speed, storage efficiency, and visual fidelity. Inputs: A set of training images (DVR or IR) with known camera poses and associated scene parameters (e.g., timestep, isovalue). Ray origins and directions cast from screen pixels toward the scene. Sampling positions (x, y, z) along the rays. Scene parameters (p0, p1, \dots) defining the specific frame or state to visualize. Outputs: Predicted color \hat{C}(r) and density \sigma for each ray r. Synthesized visualization images for novel viewpoints and interpolated parameter values. 1. Spatial Feature Grid (T^3): Layout: A 3D tensor of size N \times N \times N (or non-cubic X \times Y \times Z based on bounding box). Factorization: Decomposed into vector-matrix pairs using block-term tensor decomposition. Density features: Depth R\sigma = 16. Appearance (color) features: Depth Rc = 48. Total low-rank components Rs = 64. Components: Three spatial matrices: M^X{XY,r}, M^Y{XZ,r}, M^Z{YZ,r} representing XY, XZ, and YZ planes. Three spatial vectors: v^Zr, v^Yr, v^Xr along the X, Y, Z axes. Initialization: Starts at N=128. For complex scenes (e.g., Tangaroa), resolution increases to 300^3 at iterations 2,000, 4,000, 6,000, and 8,000. 2. Parameter Feature Grid (T^K): Layout: A K-dimensional tensor M^K, where K is the number of adjustable parameters. Dimensions: M^k corresponds to the number of distinct values for parameter k in the training set. Example: 5 jets (timestep) K=1, M^1=11; Tangaroa (isovalue) K=1, M^1=13; Vortex (TF-1) K=2, M^2=36 (6 \times 6); Nyx (simulation params) K=3, M^3=45 (3 \times 3 \times 5). Factorization: Decomposed using CANDECOMP/PARAFAC (CP) decomposition into Rp one-rank components. Components: v^1r, v^2r, \dots, v^Kr. Number of components Rp = 4. 3. Feature Decoders (MLPs): Two small MLPs: g\sigma for density and gc for color. Architecture: One hidden layer, 128 channels per layer. Inputs: g\sigma: Density features f\sigma and positional encoding EP(x). gc: Color features fc and spherical harmonic encoding E{SH}(d) of viewing direction d. 4. Ray Data Structure: Each ray stores: Origin (3 floats), Direction (3 floats), RGB values (3 floats), and Parameters (1 float per parameter). Total: ~10 floats per pixel. 1. Ray Casting: Cast rays from screen pixels toward the scene from camera locations. 2. Stratified Sampling: Estimate the volume rendering integral using n samples along each ray. Step size \deltai = t{i+1} - ti. Transmittance Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right). Predicted color \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{n} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci. 3. Feature Retrieval: For each sample point (x,y,z) and parameters (p0, \dots), retrieve features from the spatial and parameter grids. Spatial features are combined via element-wise multiplication of vector-matrix pairs: V = \sum{r=1}^{Rs} \left( M^X{XY,r} \circ v^Zr + M^Y{XZ,r} \circ v^Yr + M^Z{YZ,r} \circ v^Xr \right) Parameter features are combined via element-wise multiplication of parameter vectors: P = \sum{r=1}^{Rp} v^1r \circ v^2r \circ \dots \circ v^Kr Concatenate the outcomes of these multiplications to form the final feature vector. 4. Decoding: Compute density: \sigma(x) = g\sigma(f\sigma(x), EP(x)). Compute color: c(x) = gc(fc(x), E{SH}(d)). 5. Rendering: Compose the visualization by collecting sampled points and applying the volume rendering equation. 6. Optimization: Minimize the loss function L = L{REC} + \lambda1 L{L1} + \lambda2 L{TV}. L{REC}: MSE between predicted and ground truth color. L{L1}: L1 norm regularization on grid weights (initialized to 1 for parameter vectors). L{TV}: Total Variation loss on vectors and matrices to reduce noise. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class ViSNeRF: def init(self, spatialres, paramdims, Rsigma=16, Rcolor=48, Rparam=4): """ Initialize ViSNeRF model. spatialres: int, N for N x N x N grid (or tuple for non-cubic) paramdims: list of ints, M^k for each parameter dimension Rsigma: int, low-rank components for density Rcolor: int, low-rank components for color Rparam: int, low-rank components for parameter space """ super().init() # Spatial Feature Grids (Block-Term Decomposition) # Density: Rsigma components self.MXYsigma = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rsigma, spatialres[0], spatialres[1])) self.MXZsigma = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rsigma, spatialres[0], spatialres[2])) self.MYZsigma = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rsigma, spatialres[1], spatialres[2])) self.vZsigma = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rsigma, spatialres[2])) self.vYsigma = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rsigma, spatialres[1])) self.vXsigma = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rsigma, spatialres[0])) # Color: Rcolor components self.MXYcolor = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rcolor, spatialres[0], spatialres[1])) self.MXZcolor = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rcolor, spatialres[0], spatialres[2])) self.MYZcolor = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rcolor, spatialres[1], spatialres[2])) self.vZcolor = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rcolor, spatialres[2])) self.vYcolor = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rcolor, spatialres[1])) self.vXcolor = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rcolor, spatialres[0])) # Parameter Feature Grid (CP Decomposition) # K dimensions, each with M^k entries self.paramvectors = [] for kdim in paramdims: # Rparam vectors of length kdim vec = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rparam, kdim)) self.paramvectors.append(vec) # MLP Decoders # Density MLP: input dim = Rsigma, output dim = 1 (sigma) self.gsigma = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(Rsigma, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 1)) # Color MLP: input dim = Rcolor, output dim = 3 (RGB) # Note: SH encoding is applied to direction d before input self.gcolor = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(Rcolor, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 3)) # Hyperparameters self.Rsigma = Rsigma self.Rcolor = Rcolor self.Rparam = Rparam self.paramdims = paramdims self.spatialres = spatialres def getspatialfeatures(self, x, featuretype='sigma'): """ Retrieve spatial features for position x using block-term decomposition. x: Tensor of shape (..., 3) containing (x, y, z) """ if featuretype == 'sigma': MXY = self.MXYsigma MXZ = self.MXZsigma MYZ = self.MYZsigma vX = self.vXsigma vY = self.vYsigma vZ = self.vZsigma R = self.Rsigma else: MXY = self.MXYcolor MXZ = self.MXZcolor MYZ = self.MYZcolor vX = self.vXcolor vY = self.vYcolor vZ = self.vZcolor R = self.Rcolor # Extract coordinates xcoord = x[..., 0] ycoord = x[..., 1] zcoord = x[..., 2] # Interpolate features from matrices and vectors # Note: In implementation, interpolation functions (e.g., gridsample or trilinear) # would be used. Here we assume a helper 'interpolate' that handles the indexing. # MXY: shape (R, X, Y) -> sample at (x, y) featXY = interpolate(MXY, xcoord, ycoord) # Shape (..., R) # MXZ: shape (R, X, Z) -> sample at (x, z) featXZ = interpolate(MXZ, xcoord, zcoord) # Shape (..., R) # MYZ: shape (R, Y, Z) -> sample at (y, z) featYZ = interpolate(MYZ, ycoord, zcoord) # Shape (..., R) # vX: shape (R, X) -> sample at x featX = interpolate(vX, xcoord) # Shape (..., R) # vY: shape (R, Y) -> sample at y featY = interpolate(vY, ycoord) # Shape (..., R) # vZ: shape (R, Z) -> sample at z featZ = interpolate(vZ, zcoord) # Shape (..., R) # Element-wise multiplication and summation # V = sumr ( MXYr vZr + MXZr vYr + MYZr vXr) # featXY is (..., R), featZ is (..., R) -> element-wise mult term1 = featXY featZ term2 = featXZ featY term3 = featYZ featX features = term1 + term2 + term3 return features def getparamfeatures(self, params): """ Retrieve parameter features using CP decomposition. params: Tensor of shape (..., K) containing parameter values """ K = len(self.paramdims) # Initialize feature accumulation # We need to sum over Rp components # Each component is the outer product of K vectors # Reshape params to (..., K, 1) for broadcasting paramsexpanded = params.unsqueeze(-1) # (..., K, 1) # For each parameter dimension k, interpolate the corresponding vector paramfeats = [] for k in range(K): # self.paramvectors[k] shape (Rparam, M^k) # paramsexpanded[..., k,:] shape (..., 1) # Since all are (..., Rparam), we can multiply them element-wise combined = paramfeats[0] for k in range(1, K): combined = combined paramfeats[k] # Sum over Rp components features = torch.sum(combined, dim=-1) # Shape (...,) return features def forward(self, rays, params): """ Forward pass for a batch of rays. rays: Tensor of shape (B, 3) -> (originx, originy, originz) for sampled points params: Tensor of shape (B, K) -> scene parameters for the frame """ # 1. Get Spatial Features fsigma = self.getspatialfeatures(rays, 'sigma') fcolor = self.getspatialfeatures(rays, 'color') # 2. Get Parameter Features fparam = self.getparamfeatures(params) # 3. Training Iterations: 30,000 for static, 90,000 for dynamic. Noise: Without L1 and TV regularization, excessive noise and film grains appear in spatial matrices and images. Memory: High-resolution datasets (e.g., 1024x1024) require significant RAM (~29 GB for raw ray data) and VRAM. Filtering rays outside the bounding box is necessary. Hardware: Minimum 32 GB RAM / 10 GB VRAM; 64 GB RAM / 16 GB VRAM recommended. Convergence: Static scenes converge at 30,000 iterations; dynamic scenes require triple this. Time and Memory Complexity: Spatial complexity reduced from O(N^3) to O(N^2). Parameter space complexity reduced from O(M^K) to O(M). Overall complexity reduced from O(N^3 M^K) to O(N^2 M). Measured Performance: Inference Speed: At least 1.86 FPS for 256x256 images; drops substantially for 1024x256. Slower than InSituNet/StyleGAN2 but faster than CoordNet/EG3D for low-res. Training Time: Fastest among compared methods (e.g., 1.43 hours for five jets). Model Size: Compact (e.g., 15.43 MB for five jets, 69.91 MB for Tangaroa). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: High quality (PSNR 27.51 on five jets vs 22.74 for EG3D), supports parameter interpolation, reduces training data by 95% compared to InSituNet, super-resolution capability. Limitations: Slow inference for high resolutions, high initial memory requirement for loading ray data, requires GPU training. Origin: ViSNeRF was introduced in the paper "ViSNeRF: Efficient Multidimensional Neural Radiance Field Representation for Visualization Synthesis of Dynamic Volumetric Scenes". History and Development: It builds on the NeRF framework and TensoRF, adapting tensor factorization techniques (block-term and CP decomposition) to handle dynamic scenes with arbitrary parameters. It addresses the limitations of fully explicit methods (limited expressiveness) and fully implicit methods (slow training/inference) by using a hybrid approach. Usage: Used for visualization synthesis of dynamic volumetric scenes, including super-resolution synthesis and parameter-space exploration (time, isovalue, transfer functions). name: EBAD-NeRF
head: Event-driven Bundle Adjustment for Deblurring Neural Radiance Fields
body: EBAD-NeRF is a method for reconstructing sharp 3D radiance fields from motion-blurred images by jointly optimizing learnable camera poses and NeRF parameters using hybrid event-RGB data. It distinguishes itself from prior works like BAD-NeRF and E2 NeRF by modeling complex camera motion trajectories using multiple learnable poses (rather than linear interpolation or fixed poses) and explicitly supervising the motion blur via an intensity-change-metric event loss alongside a photo-metric blur loss. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of motion-blurred RGB images B, corresponding event data E (intensity changes), and the exposure start/end times t{start}, t{end} for each image. Outputs: A trained NeRF network F\Theta representing the sharp static scene, and the optimized camera poses P(t) for each exposure interval. Data Structures: NeRF Network F\Theta: A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) taking encoded 3D position \mathbf{o} and view direction \mathbf{d} as input, outputting volume density \sigma and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}. Camera Poses: For each view v, a sequence of p learnable poses \{Pi\}{i=1}^p representing the camera trajectory during the exposure time, mapped to SE(3) space. Sampling Points: N points sampled along a ray segment [l{near}, l{far}] using stratified sampling. Numbered Steps: 1. Trajectory Modeling: For each blurred image view, define p learnable camera poses \{Pi\}{i=1}^p sampled evenly over the exposure time interval [t{start}, t{end}]. These poses represent the camera motion trajectory in SE(3) space. 2. Ray Sampling: For a pixel \mathbf{x} in the image plane, generate a ray \mathbf{r} based on the current camera pose. Divide the ray segment from l{near} to l{far} into N equal parts and sample one point \mathbf{o}i in each part. 3. Positional Encoding: Encode the 3D coordinate \mathbf{o} and view direction \mathbf{d} using positional encoding \gammaK: \gammaK(\mathbf{x}) = \{\sin(2^k \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^k \pi \mathbf{x})\}{k=0}^K This maps inputs to K+1 dimensions. 4. NeRF Query: Input the encoded coordinates and directions into the NeRF MLP F\Theta to obtain density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i for each sampled point: (\mathbf{c}i, \sigmai) = F\Theta(\gammao(\mathbf{o}i), \gammad(\mathbf{d}i)). 5. Volume Rendering (Sharp Image): Compute the color C(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{x}) for a sharp view using volume rendering: C(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \deltai = l{i+1} - li is the distance between adjacent points, and Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) is the accumulated transparency. 6. Blurred Image Formation: Model the motion blur by averaging the rendered sharp colors across the p poses in the trajectory: \hat{B}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{p} \sum{i=1}^p C(P(ti), \mathbf{x}) where P(ti) is the i-th pose in the trajectory. 7. Loss Computation: Photo-metric Blur Loss: Compare the rendered blurred image \hat{B} with the observed blurred image B. Intensity-change-metric Event Loss: Supervise the pose changes during exposure using event data. The event data measures intensity changes with high temporal resolution, providing explicit connection between camera motion trajectory and the target sharp NeRF. 8. Joint Optimization: Update both the NeRF parameters \Theta and the learnable camera poses \{Pi\} using the combined loss. Parameters: N: Number of stratified samples per ray. Not given in the sources. p: Number of poses used to model the motion trajectory. Not given in the sources. K: Degree of positional encoding. Not given in the sources. l{near}, l{far}: Near and far clipping planes for ray sampling. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Complex Motion: Linear interpolation of start and end poses (as in BAD-NeRF) fails to model complex motion blur; EBAD-NeRF addresses this by using multiple learnable poses. Pose Initialization: Unlike E2 NeRF which uses fixed poses from COLMAP, EBAD-NeRF learns poses, requiring careful initialization or regularization to avoid degenerate trajectories. Event Data Alignment: Requires spatially and temporally aligned event-RGB data. Misalignment can lead to incorrect intensity-change supervision. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples N, poses p, and network depth. Each iteration requires rendering p views per pixel and backpropagating through the NeRF and pose parameters. Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Stores the NeRF parameters and p poses per view. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Can recover accurate camera trajectories and sharper 3D representations from blurry images by leveraging event data for explicit motion supervision. Limitations: Requires event-RGB data, which is not always available. Joint optimization of poses and NeRF parameters can be computationally expensive and sensitive to initialization. When to use: When reconstructing 3D scenes from motion-blurred images and event data is available, especially for complex camera motions. When not to use: When only RGB images are available, or when the scene is static and sharp images are captured. EBAD-NeRF was proposed by Yunshan Qi, Lin Zhu, Yifan Zhao, Nan Bao, and Jia Li. It builds upon previous works like Deblur-NeRF, BAD-NeRF, and E2 NeRF, which attempted to address motion blur in NeRF using deformable kernels, linear pose interpolation, and fixed poses with event data, respectively. EBAD-NeRF introduces event-driven bundle adjustment to jointly optimize poses and NeRF parameters, leveraging the high temporal resolution of event cameras to model motion blur explicitly. name: NeurMiPs
head: NeurMiPs, Neural Mixture of Planar Experts, Neural Mixture of Planar Experts for View Synthesis
body: NeurMiPs represents a 3D scene as a mixture of K learnable rectangular planar surfaces, where each surface acts as an independent "expert" containing a small neural radiance field that predicts view-dependent color and transparency. It solves the frontal-parallel limitation of traditional Multi-Plane Imagery (MPI) and the high memory/compute costs of dense volume rendering by leveraging closed-form ray-plane intersections and local MLPs, achieving real-time rendering speeds while maintaining superior extrapolation capabilities compared to voxel-based methods. Inputs: Sparse 3D point cloud \{xi\} from Structure-from-Motion (SfM). Training images with known camera poses. Number of planar experts K (500 for Replica, 1000 for Tanks & Temples). Outputs: Rendered image color c(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r}. Estimated depth d(\mathbf{r}). Baked alpha textures Ak for each plane k (optional, for acceleration). Planar Expert Geometry Parameter sk Each planar expert k is defined by a tuple sk = (pk, nk, uk, wk, hk): pk \in \mathbb{R}^3: The 3D center coordinate of the rectangle. nk \in \mathbb{R}^3: The normalized 3D normal vector of the plane. uk \in \mathbb{R}^3: The normalized up vector defining the y-axis direction of the plane's local coordinate system. wk \in \mathbb{R}: The width of the rectangle. hk \in \mathbb{R}: The height of the rectangle. Neural Radiance Field fk Each expert k has an associated MLP fk: Architecture: 3 fully-connected hidden layers with ReLU activation; final output layer with sigmoid activation. Input: 3D coordinate \mathbf{x}k on the plane and normalized ray direction \mathbf{d} \in S^2. The direction \mathbf{d} is transformed into a higher-dimensional space using high-frequency positional encoding before input. Output: Color \mathbf{c}k \in \mathbb{R}^3 and transparency \alphak \in \mathbb{R}. Alpha Texture Ak A 2D texture map of size w \times h storing pre-computed, view-independent alpha values for plane k. Phase 1: Plane Initialization 1. Initialize plane centers pk using farthest point sampling on the SfM point cloud \{xi\}. 2. Initialize normals nk and up vectors uk based on local point sets around pk. 3. Optimize geometric parameters \{sk\} by minimizing the geometry loss \mathcal{L}g: \mathcal{L}g = \sumi \mink d(xi, sk) + \lambda \sumk (wk hk)^2 where d(xi, sk) is the distance from point xi to the closest rectangular surface sk, and (wk hk)^2 is an area regularization term to prevent arbitrarily large rectangles. \lambda is a weighting factor. Phase 2: Teacher Model Training 1. Train a large-capacity standard NeRF (Teacher) as a reference model. 2. Sample points along rays using the current NeurMiPs ray-plane intersection logic. 3. Jointly optimize the planar experts' geometric parameters and the teacher model using the total loss: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}g + \mathcal{L}c where \mathcal{L}c is the photometric loss: \mathcal{L}c = \sum{\mathbf{r}} \|c(\mathbf{r}) - c{\text{gt}}(\mathbf{r})\|2^2. Phase 3: Distillation 1. For each planar expert k, draw random points uniformly from its rectangle and random view directions from the half unit sphere. 2. Evaluate the Teacher model at these points to get target color \mathbf{c}{teacher} and alpha \alpha{teacher}. 3. Update the student network fk parameters by minimizing the L2 loss between the student's output (\mathbf{c}k, \alphak) and the teacher's output. Phase 4: Fine-Tuning 1. Fix the plane geometry parameters \{sk\}. 2. Fine-tune the student radiance field models fk to improve rendering quality by minimizing the photometric loss \mathcal{L}c between rendered pixel color and ground-truth color. Rendering Pipeline (Inference) 1. Ray-Plane Intersection: For a ray r = \{o, d\} and plane k with normal nk and center pk, compute the intersection point xk: xk = o + \frac{(pk - o) \cdot nk}{d \cdot nk} d Keep only rectangles where the intersection lies within the bounds defined by wk, hk and the local coordinate system defined by nk, uk. 2. Radiance Evaluation: For each intersecting planar expert k, evaluate fk(x{p,k}, d) to obtain transparency \alphak and color ck. If alpha baking is used, retrieve \alphak via bilinear interpolation from texture Ak. 3. Alpha Composition: Collect all intersecting points \{xj, cj, \alphaj\}. Sort points from closest to furthest relative to the eye o. Compute final ray color: c(r) = \sumj \left( \prodi^{j-1} (1 - \alphai) \right) \alphaj cj Compute expected depth: d(r) = \sumj \left( \prodi^{j-1} (1 - \alphai) \right) \alphaj tj where tj is the depth of sampled point j. 4. Early Ray Termination: If the accumulated transmittance \prod (1 - \alphai) is close to zero, stop evaluating further planes. Re-normalize if the sum of alpha values is smaller than 1. Returns distance t along ray, or None if parallel or behind ray. """ denom = np.dot(rayd, planenormal) if abs(denom) < 1e-8: return None t = np.dot(planecenter - rayo, planenormal) / denom if t < 0: return None return t def pointinrectangle(point, planecenter, planenormal, planeup, width, height): """ Checks if point lies within the rectangle defined by center, normal, up, width, height. """ optimizer = Adam(learningrate=5e-4) # Phase 1: Initialization (Optimize plane geometry only) for epoch in range(1000): # Placeholder for initialization steps # Minimize Lg lossg = computegeometryloss(planes, pointscloud) lossg.backward() optimizer.step() # Phase 2: Teacher Training & Joint Optimization # Train Teacher NeRF for epoch in range(epochsteacher): # Standard NeRF training loop pass # Distillation: Jointly optimize geometry and distill for epoch in range(epochsdistill): # Sample rays # Intersect with planes # Evaluate Teacher # Compute Lg and Lc # Update planes and experts pass # Phase 3: Fine-Tuning # Fix planes for epoch in range(epochsfinetune): # Sample rays # Intersect with planes # Evaluate Experts # Compute Lc # Update experts only pass K (Number of Planar Experts): 500 for Replica dataset, 1000 for Tanks & Temples dataset. Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 5 \times 10^{-4}. Training Epochs: Teacher Model: 6,000 epochs. Distillation: 1,500 epochs. Fine-Tuning: 2,500 epochs. \lambda (Geometry Loss Weight): Not given in the sources. Finite Plane Size: Planes may not cover all regions in extreme viewpoints, leading to higher depth errors for background scenes. Solution: Adopt multiple-layer boxes. SfM Dependency: Performance degrades if sparse point clouds are noisy or unavailable. Unbounded Scenes: The method currently cannot handle unbounded scenes. Solution: Incorporate techniques from NeRF++ to model background texture with non-Euclidean coordinates. Alpha Baking Artifacts: Applying alpha baking directly during inference may bring a minor rendering performance drop or quality drop due to discretization of the continuous radiance field. Time Complexity: Rendering is accelerated by closed-form ray-plane intersection and early ray termination. Only a small fraction of planes intersect a given ray. Memory Complexity: Significantly lower than voxel-based approaches due to the compact representation of planes and tiny MLPs. Alpha baking increases memory usage for textures. Measured Performance: Replica: 19.16 FPS on a single TITAN RTX using a custom CUDA kernel. Tanks & Temples (Truck scene, 1000 planes, 1920x1080): 976 FPS on a single RTX 3090 using texture baking. Strengths: More efficient in memory and computation than NeRF. More sample-efficient with better extrapolation than NeRF. Captures detailed textures on planar surfaces with sharp boundaries, avoiding the blurriness of NeRF in large-scale scenes. Better geometry reflection than Multi-Plane Imagery (MPI). Generalizes better in view extrapolation than voxel-based methods (PlenOctrees, KiloNeRF) which prune redundant voxels and cannot estimate appearances of unseen regions. Avoids "fog-like" artifacts of NeRF and "stack-of-cards" effects of NeX. Limitations: Cannot handle unbounded scenes natively. Relies heavily on SfM point clouds. Depth error increases in extreme viewpoints due to finite plane size. NeurMiPs was introduced in the paper "NeurMiPs: Neural Mixture of Planar Experts for View Synthesis". It builds upon the success of neural rendering [44, 73] and MPI. The method addresses the limitations of dense volume rendering and standard MPI by using a mixture of learnable planar experts. It is used for view synthesis on datasets like Tanks & Temples and Replica. name: Dynamic Scene and Temporal Modeling
head: Dynamic NeRF, 4D Radiance Fields, Temporal NeRF
body: Dynamic Scene and Temporal Modeling extends static Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) to reconstruct 4D radiance fields R(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}, t) from multi-view video sequences where scene geometry and appearance change over time. It solves the ambiguity between camera and object motion by explicitly conditioning the network on temporal coordinates, employing deformation fields, or using particle-based representations. Unlike static NeRF, which suffers from severe ghosting and blurriness on dynamic data, these methods separate or warp dynamic elements to enable novel view synthesis at arbitrary times. All methods in this family aim to predict volume density \sigma and view-dependent color \mathbf{c} for a ray \mathbf{r}(s) = \mathbf{o} + s\mathbf{d} at time t using the standard volume rendering integral: C(\mathbf{r}, t) = \int{sn}^{sf} T(s, t) \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s), t) c(\mathbf{r}(s), \mathbf{d}, t) ds where T(s, t) = \exp \left( -\int{sn}^{s} \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s'), t) ds' \right) is the accumulated transmittance. The core challenge is modeling the temporal variation of \sigma and \mathbf{c}. Common strategies include: 1. Direct Conditioning: Concatenating time t (often with positional encoding) to the input of an MLP alongside spatial coordinates \mathbf{x}. 2. Deformation Fields: Learning a displacement \Delta \mathbf{x} that warps dynamic points \mathbf{x} to a canonical static space \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} + \Delta \mathbf{x}, where a static radiance field is queried. 3. Hybrid Representations: Superimposing a static grid-based field with a dynamic component (e.g., particles or sparse latent codes) weighted by a mask wt(\mathbf{x}). Replaces the unified 4D field with stratified "gears" (feature volumes) assigned by semantic motion scale. High-motion regions use higher-resolution sampling. Choose for object tracking and high-fidelity dynamic synthesis. A baseline that concatenates time t to the spatial input of a standard MLP. Choose for simplicity; it lacks detailed dynamic reasoning and suffers from blurriness compared to deformation-based methods. Models a static canonical field and forward warps it to target times using differentiable splatting and an inpaint network. Choose for handling many-to-one mapping difficulties in dynamic scenes. Superimposes a static grid with a dynamic particle field for monocular video. Choose for single-view dynamic reconstruction where particles model only moving elements. Uses a Kalman filter to combine history-based motion prediction with current observations for deformation estimation. Choose for leveraging inductive smoothness bias of deformation fields over feature interpolation. Uses sparse latent codes aggregated via attention and a deformation field. Choose for reducing parameters while maintaining high quality by abandoning direct coordinate-to-feature mapping. Definition: A Conditional NeRF framework for high-accuracy dynamic portrait creation synchronized with audio. Steps: Utilizes spatial regions' distinct contributions to steer dynamic head modeling; develops a Tri-Plane Hash Representation; introduces Adaptive Pose Encoding to separate head and torso. Pitfall: Additional fine-tuning may be necessary for poses outside the training dataset. Performance: Attains instantaneous rendering and rapid convergence with a compact model size. Definition: A method that diminishes vagueness in visual alterations using a ternary loss to standardize visual code spread. Steps: Suggests a temporary decomposition unit to distinguish still scenes from dynamic objects. Pitfall: May struggle with significant sequence discrepancies, such as severe lighting changes. Performance: Attains cutting-edge results in multi-sequence scenarios, enhancing efficiency and minimizing ghost effects. The extension of NeRF to dynamic scenes emerged to address the "ghosting" artifacts inherent in static models when applied to video data. Early approaches treated time as an additional input dimension to the MLP, serving as a baseline for more complex deformation-based methods. Subsequent developments introduced canonical space warping, particle systems, and sparse latent representations to better handle the many-to-one mapping ambiguities and computational costs of 4D reconstruction. These methods are primarily used in 3D perception, dynamic portrait reconstruction, and novel view synthesis for video. name: Gear-NeRF
head: Gear-NeRF: Free-Viewpoint Rendering and Tracking with Motion-aware Spatio-Temporal Sampling
body: Gear-NeRF is a dynamic scene representation method that stratifies a 4D scene into multiple "gear" levels based on semantic motion scales, allowing for region-specific spatio-temporal sampling resolution. It differs from sibling methods like NeRF with Time Parameter by using semantic embeddings to drive adaptive resolution rather than uniform time-conditioning, and from KFD-NeRF by avoiding explicit deformation fields in favor of semantic-aware gear assignment. The method solves the inefficiency of uniform sampling in dynamic scenes by allocating higher resolution to regions with larger motion scales. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of W input videos V = \{V1, V2, \dots, VW\} of a dynamic scene with calibrated camera poses. Output: Volume density \sigma and view-dependent color \mathbf{c} for a ray \mathbf{r}(s) at time t, computed via the standard volume rendering integral. Data Structures: The representation consists of a series of 4D feature volumes, one for each gear level G \in \{1, \dots, N{\text{gear}}\}. Shared Spatial Features: Functions hj(\cdot, \cdot) map 2D coordinate tuples to features. These are shared across all gears. Gear-Specific Temporal Features: Functions k^Gj(\cdot, \cdot) map 2D coordinate tuples to M-dimensional feature vectors. Each gear G has its own set of these embeddings. Linear Transforms: Matrices Bj map the element-wise products to feature vectors of dimension M. Semantic Embedding: A 4D semantic embedding is optimized using features from a powerful image segmentation model (specifically SAM) to profile the scene into semantic regions. Formulas: The feature vector f^G(\mathbf{x}, t) for gear G at space-time coordinate (\mathbf{x}, t) is computed as: f^G(\mathbf{x}, t) = B1 (h1(x, y) \bowtie k^G1(z, t)) + B2 (h2(x, z) \bowtie k^G2(y, t)) + B3 (h3(y, z) \bowtie k^G3(x, t)) Where: \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z) are spatial coordinates. t is the time coordinate. hj(\cdot, \cdot) and k^Gj(\cdot, \cdot) are evaluated via bilinear interpolation on regularly spaced 2D feature grids. \bowtie denotes element-wise product. Bj denotes a linear transform. The gear level g(\mathbf{x}, t) at any spatio-temporal coordinate is computed from a planar-factorized 4D feature volume: g(\mathbf{x}, t) = \mathbf{1}^\top (h'1(x, y) \bowtie k'1(z, t) + \dots) (Note: The source provides the start of this formula but truncates the remaining terms. The structure implies a similar planar factorization to the feature vector, summed and projected to a scalar score.) Parameters: N{\text{gear}}: The total number of gear levels used to stratify the scene representation based on motion scales. M: The dimension of the feature space for the temporal embeddings k^Gj. Steps: 1. Semantic Embedding Optimization: Optimize a 4D semantic embedding for the scene using features extracted from a powerful image segmentation model (e.g., SAM). 2. Gear Assignment: Determine the gear level g(\mathbf{x}, t) for each space-time coordinate based on the semantic embedding and motion scale. Regions with larger motion scales are assigned higher gear levels. 3. Feature Computation: For a given coordinate (\mathbf{x}, t) and assigned gear G, compute the feature vector f^G(\mathbf{x}, t) using the formula above. 4. Density and Color Prediction: Pass the feature vector f^G(\mathbf{x}, t) through a tiny MLP to predict volume density \sigma and view-dependent color \mathbf{c} given the viewing direction \mathbf{d}. 5. Spatio-Temporal Sampling: Perform spatio-temporal sampling for ray integration. Higher gear levels (larger motion) receive higher-resolution sampling. 6. Rendering: Compute the final color C(\mathbf{r}, t) using the volume rendering integral. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Determine gear level for each point # Note: The exact formula for g(x,t) is truncated in sources. # Implementation requires the full planar factorization sum. gearlevel = computegearlevel(xyz, t, sharedparams['hprime'], sharedparams['kprime']) # 2. Retrieve gear-specific temporal embeddings and compute features # f^G(x,t) = B1(h1(x,y) k1G(z,t)) + B2(h2(x,z) k2G(y,t)) + B3(h3(y,z) k3G(x,t)) # Extract spatial coordinates x, y, z = xyz[:, 0], xyz[:, 1], xyz[:, 2] # Initialize feature vector features = torch.zeroslike(xyz) for G in range(len(gearparams)): # Get gear-specific temporal grids k1G = gearparams['k1'] k2G = gearparams['k2'] k3G = gearparams['k3'] # Get shared spatial grids h1 = sharedparams['h1'] h2 = sharedparams['h2'] h3 = sharedparams['h3'] # Get shared linear transforms B1 = sharedparams['B1'] B2 = sharedparams['B2'] B3 = sharedparams['B3'] # Interpolate spatial features # h1(x, y) -> (N, M) feath1 = interpolate2d(h1, x, y) feath2 = interpolate2d(h2, x, z) feath3 = interpolate2d(h3, y, z) # Interpolate gear-specific temporal features # k1G(z, t) -> (N, M) featk1 = interpolate2d(k1G, z, t) featk2 = interpolate2d(k2G, y, t) featk3 = interpolate2d(k3G, x, t) # Element-wise product and linear transform term1 = B1 @ (feath1 featk1).T # Assuming B1 is (M, M) or similar term2 = B2 @ (feath2 featk2).T term3 = B3 @ (feath3 featk3).T # Accumulate features for the assigned gear # In practice, only the features for the specific gear G assigned to each point are used # This loop structure is illustrative; actual implementation would mask by gearlevel features = term1 + term2 + term3 # Select features based on assigned gear level finalfeatures = features[range(len(xyz)), gearlevel] # 3. Predict density and color # tiny MLP maps feature vector to sigma and c sigma, color = predictsigmacolor(finalfeatures, direction) return sigma, color def computegearlevel(xyz, t, hprime, kprime): """ Computes the gear level g(x,t) for each point. Implementers must infer the remaining terms based on the symmetry of the feature vector formula or consult the full paper. Semantic Dependency: The method relies on a powerful image segmentation model (SAM) for semantic embedding. Errors in segmentation may propagate to incorrect gear assignments. Gear Assignment Ambiguity: The exact thresholding or soft-assignment mechanism for determining gear levels from the semantic embedding is not detailed in the provided notes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art rendering and tracking performance on multiple challenging datasets. Strengths: Enables free-viewpoint tracking of objects of interest almost for free; improves photo-realistic dynamic novel view synthesis through motion-aware sampling. Limitations: Requires calibrated camera poses and input videos; relies on external semantic segmentation models. When to use: When high-quality dynamic novel view synthesis is required for scenes with varying motion scales, and free-viewpoint tracking is desired. When not to use: For static scenes or scenes with uniform motion where uniform sampling is sufficient. Gear-NeRF was introduced in the paper "Gear-NeRF: Free-Viewpoint Rendering and Tracking with Motion-aware Spatio-Temporal Sampling". The method builds on the principles of differentiable volume rendering and radiance field optimization. It addresses the limitations of existing NeRF-based methods in handling dynamic scenes by introducing a semantic-aware stratification of the scene into motion-based "gears". name: NeRF with Time Parameter
head: NeRF + time, NeRF with Time Parameter Baseline, Time-NeRF
body: This method adapts the static Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) architecture to model dynamic scenes by explicitly conditioning the network on a temporal coordinate t. It solves the problem of reconstructing time-varying geometry and appearance, which vanilla NeRF cannot handle due to its static assumption. It differs from deformation-based siblings like Gear-NeRF by avoiding explicit spatial warping; instead, it learns the temporal variation directly in the latent space, making it a simpler baseline that often suffers from blurriness and ghosting compared to methods that reason about scene dynamics. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D spatial coordinate \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3, a viewing direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3, and a scalar time parameter t. Output: Volume density \sigma and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}. Data Structures: The model consists of two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), identical in structure to the standard NeRF: 1. Density MLP: Takes encoded spatial coordinates and outputs density \sigma. 2. Color MLP: Takes encoded spatial coordinates, viewing direction, and outputs color \mathbf{c}. Steps: 1. Positional Encoding of Time: Apply the same positional encoding function \gammat used for spatial coordinates to the time parameter t. \gammat(t) = \text{PE}(t) 2. Positional Encoding of Space: Apply positional encoding \gammax to the spatial coordinate \mathbf{x}. \gammax(\mathbf{x}) = \text{PE}(\mathbf{x}) 3. Concatenation: Concatenate the encoded time and encoded spatial coordinates to form the input vector for the density MLP. \mathbf{v}{\sigma} = [\gammax(\mathbf{x}), \gammat(t)] 4. Density Prediction: Pass \mathbf{v}{\sigma} through the density MLP to obtain \sigma. \sigma = \text{MLP}{\sigma}(\mathbf{v}{\sigma}) 5. Feature Extraction: Pass \gammax(\mathbf{x}) through the intermediate layers of the density MLP (or a shared feature network) to obtain a feature vector \mathbf{f}. [G: In standard NeRF, this is the output of the hidden layers before the density head]. 6. Color Input Preparation: Concatenate the feature vector \mathbf{f}, the viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and the encoded time \gammat(t). \mathbf{v}{c} = [\mathbf{f}, \mathbf{d}, \gammat(t)] 7. Color Prediction: Pass \mathbf{v}{c} through the color MLP to obtain \mathbf{c}. \mathbf{c} = \text{MLP}{c}(\mathbf{v}{c}) 8. Volume Rendering: Render the image using the standard volume rendering integral, integrating over the ray \mathbf{r}(s) = \mathbf{o} + s\mathbf{d} for the specific time t of the input image. Parameters: Training Configuration: Use the configuration reported for NeRF's real forward-facing experiments. Specific hyperparameters (learning rate, number of samples per ray, etc.) are not detailed in the sources beyond this reference. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Blurriness: The method lacks detail and suffers from blurry predictions because it does not explicitly model the motion or deformation of objects. Ghosting: Even small changes in camera pose lead to slightly different viewing directions for spatial points across frames, causing severe ghosting artifacts in static regions. Dynamic Reasoning: The model fails to reason about scene dynamics, meaning it cannot accurately reconstruct novel scene compositions or complex temporal interactions. A compression strategy for sequences of NeRF models that exploits temporal redundancy by treating the first model as a key-frame and compressing only the deltas between successive models. It is chosen when storage or transmission bandwidth for a sequence of dynamic NeRFs is constrained. Initialization: Train the NeRF for the first frame from scratch. Subsequent Frames: Initialize the NeRF for frame i using the weights of the trained NeRF from frame i-1 to encourage temporal redundancy and save training time. Delta Calculation: Calculate the delta \Delta W between the current frame's NeRF weights Wi and the previous frame's weights W{i-1}: \Delta W = Wi - W{i-1}. Compression: Apply exponent-based quantization and Huffman coding to the delta weights \Delta W. Restoration: To restore a model, accumulate the decoded deltas to the reference model (the previous frame's model). Time Complexity: Training time is comparable to standard NeRF per frame, but slightly reduced for subsequent frames if initialization from the previous frame is used (in the context of compression). Rendering time is identical to standard NeRF. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is identical to standard NeRF for a single time step. For a sequence, the compression variant reduces storage by storing only deltas. Performance: On KITTI dynamic scenes, "NeRF + time" achieves a PSNR of 24.18, SSIM of 0.677, and LPIPS of 0.425, which is better than vanilla NeRF (PSNR 23.34, SSIM 0.662, LPIPS 0.415) but significantly worse than dynamic scene graph methods (PSNR 26.66, SSIM 0.806, LPIPS 0.186). Strengths: Simple to implement; requires no modification to the core NeRF architecture other than input concatenation. Limitations: Produces blurry results; fails to handle complex dynamics; suffers from ghosting artifacts. When to use: As a baseline for dynamic scene reconstruction; when computational resources for complex deformation fields are unavailable. When not to use: When high-fidelity detail is required; when accurate novel view synthesis of dynamic objects is needed. The method was introduced as a baseline modification to demonstrate the limitations of simple time-conditioning in implicit neural representations for dynamic scenes. It was proposed in the context of comparing against "Neural Scene Graphs for Dynamic Scenes". The approach builds on the original NeRF architecture. name: Forward Warping for Novel View Synthesis
head: Canonical Field Forward Warping, Forward Flow
body: Forward Warping for Novel View Synthesis is a method for rendering dynamic scenes by modeling a static scene at a canonical time step and forward warping the entire canonical radiance field to other time steps. It addresses the many-to-one and one-to-many mapping difficulties inherent in dynamic scene reconstruction by employing differentiable forward warping with average splatting and an inpaint network. Unlike backward flow methods such as NDVG, this approach leverages a smooth trajectory field to achieve superior performance, particularly for canonical frames. The method uses a coarse-to-fine training strategy to learn a canonical radiance field and a deformation field, then warps the canonical field to target times for rendering. Inputs: A set of images \{It\} with known camera poses and timestamps t. The canonical time t{can} is selected (first frame for D-NeRF, middle frame for HyperNeRF). Outputs: Rendered images C(\mathbf{r}, t) for novel views and intermediate times. The method maintains several voxel grids and neural networks: 1. Canonical Radiance Feature Grid (VRf): Voxel grid containing radiance features. Feature dimension is 12. 2. Canonical Coordinate Grid (VrCan): Voxel grid containing the coordinate of each voxel. 3. Canonical Density Grid (V\sigma^{Can}): Voxel grid containing canonical density. 4. Canonical Color Feature Grid (Vcf^{Can}): Voxel grid containing canonical color features. Dimension is 3 or 12 depending on the training stage. 5. Canonical Deformation Feature Grid (VDf^{Can}): Voxel grid containing canonical deformation features. Dimension is 0 for D-NeRF, 12 for HyperNeRF. 6. Trajectory Grid (VT^t): Voxel grid containing DCT parameters of each voxel's trajectory. 7. Deformation Flow Grid (Vflow): Voxel grid containing deformation flow of each voxel from canonical to time t. 8. Warped Radiance Field (VR^t): Radiance field at time t warped from VR^{Can}. 9. Inpainted Radiance Field (VR^{t}{Inp}): Radiance field at time t after inpainting by F{\theta3}. 10. Upsampled Radiance Field (VR^{t}{Up}): Upsampled radiance field at time t. 1. Canonical Radiance Network (F{\theta1}): Structure: 3-layer MLP, width 128, ReLU activation. Input: Radiance feature from VRf (dim 12) and embedded position (dim 33). Output: Density (dim 1) and color feature (dim 3 or 12). 2. Canonical Deformation Network (F{\theta2}): Structure: 4-layer MLP, width 64. Input: Deformation feature (dim 0 or 12) and embedded position (dim 33). Output: Trajectory parameters (DCT coefficients). 3. View Dependent Color Network (F{\theta4}): Structure: 2-layer MLP, width 64. Input: Embedded view direction (dim 27) and color feature (dim 12). Output: RGB color (dim 3). 4. Inpaint Network (F{\theta3}): Structure: UNet with 4 encode layers and 3 decode layers, plus an upsample layer. Each encode layer has one max pooling layer and two convolution layers (Instance Norm + Conv + ReLU). Each decode layer has one up-sample interpolation layer and two convolution layers (Instance Norm + Conv + ReLU). Input: Warped radiance field features. Output: Inpainted radiance field features. D-NeRF: 15. HyperNeRF: 25. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def positionalencoding(x, numfreqs=15): """ Standard positional encoding for NeRF. x: (..., 3) coordinates. Returns: (..., 3 2 numfreqs + 3) encoded vector. """ # Implementation details omitted for brevity, assumed standard NeRF PE pass def initializegrids(voxelsize, bounds): """ Initialize voxel grids. """ # VRf: (N, 12) # VrCan: (N, 3) # VsigmaCan: (N, 1) # VcfCan: (N, 12) # or 3 # VDfCan: (N, 0 or 12) # VTt: (N, 2 numdctbases) # Vflow: (N, 3) pass def traincoarsestage(): """ Coarse stage: Learn proxy geometry. Voxel number: 6^3. Iterations: 20,000. No inpaint network used. """ pass def trainfinestage(): """ Fine stage: Refine radiance and deformation. Voxel number: 8^3 (D-NeRF) or 7^3 (HyperNeRF). Iterations: 100,000. Progressive training: Start with 10 images closest to canonical step, add one image with closest time step every 60 iterations. """ pass def forwardwarping(VRf, VrCan, VsigmaCan, VcfCan, VDfCan, VTt, Vflow, t): """ Warp canonical field to time t. """ # 1. Compute deformation flow from canonical to time t # Vflow is pre-computed or updated based on trajectory grid VTt # Flow = f(VDfCan, VTt, t) # 2. Average Splatting # Instead of softmax splatting, use average splatting to handle # many-to-one and one-to-many mappings. # VRt = AverageSplatting(VRf, VrCan, Vflow) # 3. Inpainting # VRtInp = Ftheta3(VRt) # 4. Upsampling # VRtUp = Upsample(VRtInp) return VRtUp def renderray(ray, VRtUp): """ Volume rendering from the warped and inpainted field. """ # Sample points along ray # Query VRtUp for density and color features # Compute color using Ftheta4 # Accumulate using standard volume rendering integral pass def computelosses(renderedcolor, gtcolor, VsigmaCan, Vflow, D): """ Compute total loss. """ # Lptc: Point-wise Color Loss # Lbg: Background Entropy Loss # Ltv: Total Variation Losses # Lflow, Lvdiff: Flow and velocity difference losses (if applicable) # Lphoto: Photometric loss # Weights for Fine Stage: # w1=1e-2, w2=1e-3, w3=1e-5, w4=1e-5, w5=1e-6, w6=1e-3, w7=1e-1 pass def optimize(): """ Main training loop. """ # Initialize grids and networks # Train Coarse Stage # Train Fine Stage with progressive image addition pass 1. Point-wise Color Loss (\mathcal{L}{ptc}): Supervises the color of sampled points weighted by their accumulation. \mathcal{L}{ptc} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{C}{\text{Inp}}(\mathbf{r})) + \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{C}{\text{Up}}(\mathbf{r})) where \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r})) = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^{K} A{\text{accum}}(k) \|\mathbf{c}(wk) - \mathbf{C}{\text{gt}}(\mathbf{r})\|2^2 and A{\text{accum}}(k) = T(wk) \, \sigma(wk) \deltak \mathbf{C}{\text{Inp}} and \mathbf{C}{\text{Up}} are colors from inpainted and upsampled fields. 2. Background Entropy Loss (\mathcal{L}{bg}): Encourages densities to concentrate on foreground or background. \mathcal{L}{bg} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{A}{\text{Inp}}(\mathbf{r})) + \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{A}{\text{Up}}(\mathbf{r})) where \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r})) = -\frac{1}{K-1} \sum{k=1}^{K-1} [ A{\text{accum}}(k)\log(A{\text{accum}}(k)) + (1-A{\text{accum}}(k))\log(1-A{\text{accum}}(k)) ]. 3. Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{photo} + w1\mathcal{L}{ptc} + w2\mathcal{L}{bg} + w3\mathcal{L}{flow} + w4\mathcal{L}{vdiff} + w5\mathcal{L}{tv}(\mathbf{V}{\sigma}^{\text{Can}}) + w6\mathcal{L}{tv}(\mathbf{V}{\text{flow}}^t) + w7\mathcal{L}{tv}(\mathbf{D}) where w1..w7 are balancing weights. Coarse Stage: Voxel Number: 6^3. Inpaint Scale: 1.5. Iterations: 20,000. Weights: w1=10^{-1}, w2=10^{-2}, w3=10^{-5}, w4=0., w5=10^{-6}, w6=10^{-3}, w7=10^{-1}. Fine Stage: Voxel Number: 8^3 for D-NeRF, 7^3 for HyperNeRF. Inpaint Scale: 2.0. Iterations: 100,000. Weights: w1=10^{-2}, w2=10^{-3}, w3=10^{-5}, w4=10^{-5}, w5=10^{-6}, w6=10^{-3}, w7=10^{-1}. Learning Rate: 10^{-1} for voxel grids, 10^{-3} for networks. Progressive Training: In fine stage, start with 10 images closest to canonical step, add one image with closest time step every 60 iterations. Canonical Time: First frame for D-NeRF, middle frame for HyperNeRF. Memory Consumption: High, especially for real scenes. Training Speed: Slow, approximately one day per scene on GeForce RTX 3090. Coarse Stage Importance: Removing the coarse stage causes significant performance drop because the voxel grid covers bigger space without proxy geometry filtering. Inpaint Network Importance: Removing the inpaint network significantly reduces performance (e.g., Hell Warrior PSNR drops from 27.71 to 27.15). Splatting Choice: Average splatting is used instead of softmax splatting. Softmax splatting with predicted weights showed no obvious improvement and introduced too much complexity. Time Complexity: Training is slow, taking approximately one day per scene on a GeForce RTX 3090 GPU. Memory Complexity: High memory consumption, particularly for real scenes. Model Size: 260M parameters for D-NeRF, 440M for HyperNeRF. Rendering Speed: 7s per image for D-NeRF, 15s per image for HyperNeRF. Strengths: Achieves SOTA performance on public datasets, especially for canonical frames. Clear advantage over backward flow based methods like NDVG. Limitations: High memory usage and slow training speed. Forward Warping for Novel View Synthesis was proposed in the paper "Forward Flow for Novel View Synthesis of Dynamic Scenes". The method builds on the idea of canonical representations but introduces forward warping with average splatting and an inpaint network to handle dynamic scenes. It was evaluated on the D-NeRF and HyperNeRF datasets, as well as a newly built Lego Complete Dataset.
