name: Dynamic Appearance Particle Neural Radiance Field
head: Dynamic Appearance Particle NeRF, Lagrangian dynamic model in NeRF
body:
Dynamic Appearance Particle Neural Radiance Field (DAP-NeRF) is a method for modeling dynamic scenes from monocular video data by superimposing a static grid-based radiance field with a dynamic component represented by moving appearance particles. It solves the problem of temporal variation in density and color without requiring multi-view stereo data or prior geometric knowledge of dynamic objects. Unlike ParticleNeRF, which encodes the entire scene with particles and requires multiple views per frame, DAP-NeRF applies particles only to dynamic elements and uses a grid-based field for efficient linear interpolation querying. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Monocular video sequence (one camera view per time frame t), camera poses, and near/far bounds sn, sf. Outputs: Rendered pixel color C(\mathbf{r}, t) for a ray \mathbf{r} at time t. Data Structures: 1. Static Field Vs(\mathbf{x}): A time-independent grid-based model (e.g., hash grid or triplane) storing features for density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. 2. Dynamic Field V{td}(\mathbf{x}, t): An ensemble of particles. Each particle i at time t has: Position \mathbf{p}i(t) \in \mathbb{R}^3. Appearance features \mathbf{f}i(t) \in \mathbb{R}^k (encoding density and color contributions). The particle positions are updated by a Particle Motion Network (NN{motion}). 3. Mask wt(\mathbf{x}): A binary weight indicating if the dynamic field is effective at location \mathbf{x} and time t. Formulas: The total feature field V(\mathbf{x}, t) is a superposition of static and dynamic components: V(\mathbf{x}, t) = (1 - wt(\mathbf{x}))Vs(\mathbf{x}) + wt(\mathbf{x})V{td}(\mathbf{x}) where Vs(\mathbf{x}) is the static field and V{td}(\mathbf{x}) is the dynamic field. The dynamic field V{td} is formulated as a convolution with a Dirac function to integrate over finite volumes: V{td}(\mathbf{x}) = (V{td} \delta)(\mathbf{x}) = \int V{td}(\mathbf{x}')\delta(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}')d
u(\mathbf{x}') where \delta(\cdot) is the Dirac function. To enable quantization and efficient querying, the Dirac function \delta is replaced with a kernel W with finite support: W(\mathbf{x}) = 0 \quad 	ext{when } \|\mathbf{x}\| 	ext{ exceeds a small radius, and } \int W(\mathbf{x})d
u(\mathbf{x}) = 1 This leads to a finite-width kernel approximation. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Casting: For a pixel at time t, cast a ray \mathbf{r}(s) = \mathbf{o} + s\mathbf{d} from camera center \mathbf{o} with direction \mathbf{d}, where s \in [sn, sf]. 2. Discretization: Sample points \mathbf{x}j along the ray. 3. Dynamic Field Query: For each sample point \mathbf{x}j: Query the Particle Motion Network to get current particle positions \mathbf{p}i(t) and features \mathbf{f}i(t). Compute the contribution of nearby particles to V{td}(\mathbf{x}j) using the kernel W. Determine wt(\mathbf{x}j) based on particle presence/support. 4. Static Field Query: Query the static grid Vs(\mathbf{x}j) using linear interpolation. 5. Superposition: Combine fields: V(\mathbf{x}j, t) = (1 - wt(\mathbf{x}j))Vs(\mathbf{x}j) + wt(\mathbf{x}j)V{td}(\mathbf{x}j). 6. Volume Rendering: Compute density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} from V(\mathbf{x}j, t) and integrate along the ray using the standard volume rendering integral: C(\mathbf{r}, t) = \int{sn}^{sf} T(s, t) \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s), t) c(\mathbf{r}(s), \mathbf{d}, t) ds where T(s, t) = \exp \left( -\int{sn}^{s} \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s'), t) ds' ight). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderray(rayo, rayd, timet, staticgrid, particles, kernelW, maskthreshold): """ Renders a single ray for DAP-NeRF. """ # 1. Sample points along the ray samples = samplealongray(rayo, rayd, numsamples=128) # [N, 3] # 2. Query Static Field staticfeatures = staticgrid.query(samples) # [N, D] # 3. Query Dynamic Field # Get particle positions and features at timet particlepositions, particlefeatures = particles.getstate(timet) # [P, 3], [P, D] # Compute dynamic field contribution using kernel W # For each sample, sum contributions from nearby particles dynamicfeatures = zeroslike(staticfeatures) for i in range(len(samples)): x = samples[i] # Find particles within kernel support radius nearbyparticles = findnearby(particlepositions, x, radius=kernelW.radius) contribution = zeroslike(staticfeatures[i]) for pidx in nearbyparticles: ppos = particlepositions[pidx] pfeat = particlefeatures[pidx] # Compute kernel weight dist = norm(x - ppos) if dist <= kernelW.radius: w = kernelW.evaluate(dist) contribution += w pfeat dynamicfeatures[i] = contribution # Determine mask value (1 if dynamic field is effective, 0 otherwise) # Effective if any particle contributes significantly if norm(contribution) > maskthreshold: maskval = 1.0 else: maskval = 0.0 dynamicfeatures[i] = maskval # Apply mask to features # 4. Superposition # Note: maskval is per-sample, so we need to handle it carefully # The formula uses wt(x). We assume maskval is wt(x) # Re-compute mask for each sample to be precise masks = zeros(len(samples)) for i in range(len(samples)): x = samples[i] nearbyparticles = findnearby(particlepositions, x, radius=kernelW.radius) hasdynamic = False for pidx in nearbyparticles: ppos = particlepositions[pidx] dist = norm(x - ppos) if dist <= kernelW.radius: w = kernelW.evaluate(dist) if w > 0: hasdynamic = True break masks[i] = 1.0 if hasdynamic else 0.0 # Superposition: V(x,t) = (1 - wt(x))Vs(x) + wt(x)Vtd(x) combinedfeatures = (1 - masks[:, None]) staticfeatures + masks[:, None] dynamicfeatures # 5. Extract Density and Color sigma, color = extractdensitycolor(combinedfeatures) # 6. Volume Rendering T = computetransmittance(sigma) colorrendered = integratecolor(T, sigma, color) return colorrendered Parameters: Kernel Radius: Small radius for W(\mathbf{x}). Not given in the sources. Mask Threshold: Threshold for wt(\mathbf{x}) to be 1. Not given in the sources. Particle Motion Network: NN{motion} updates particle positions. Architecture not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The kernel approximation \delta 	o W must ensure \int W(\mathbf{x})d
u(\mathbf{x}) = 1 to preserve field magnitude. Boundaries: The kernel W(\mathbf{x}) = 0 when \|\mathbf{x}\| exceeds a small radius, so particles far from samples do not contribute. Degenerate Input: If no particles are near a sample, wt(\mathbf{x}) = 0, and the static field is used. Encodes the entire scene with particles and uses radius nearest neighbor searching; requires 20 camera views per time frame. An alternative framework that can integrate the Lagrangian representation. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of particles and samples. Querying dynamic field requires finding nearby particles for each sample. Memory Complexity: Stores static grid and particle states. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles monocular video data; no prior geometric knowledge required; efficient querying via linear interpolation for static part. Limitations: Requires tuning of kernel radius and mask threshold. When to use: Monocular dynamic scene reconstruction. When not: Multi-view static scenes (use standard NeRF) or scenes with known geometry (use deformation fields). Origin: Proposed in (2025). History: Builds on ParticleNeRF and static NeRF frameworks. Usage: Monocular video dynamic scene reconstruction. Dynamic Appearance Particle Neural Radiance Field, https://doi.org/10.1109/tcsvt.2025.3540792, fetched 2026-11-05

name: KFD-NeRF
head: Kalman Filter Guided Deformation Field NeRF, Kalman Filter Guided Dynamic NeRF
body: KFD-NeRF is a dynamic neural radiance field method that models the 4D radiance field as a dynamic system with temporally varying states, estimated using a Kalman filter to combine observations from input data and predictions based on local linear motion equations. It differs from sibling methods like Gear-NeRF and NeRF with Time Parameter by explicitly separating motion estimation into an observer branch (direct observation via a shallow MLP) and a predictor branch (history-based prediction), fusing them via a learnable Kalman gain to handle significant motion and temporal consistency. Unlike Dynamic Appearance Particle Neural Radiance Field which uses particles, KFD-NeRF uses a tri-plane spatial representation for the canonical space, allowing for faster convergence and lower memory usage compared to MLP-only backbones like D-NeRF. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D point coordinates \mathbf{x}, timestamp ti, and camera parameters. Training data consists of a sequence of images released in chronological order. Outputs: Deformation field \Delta \mathbf{x} for each point, which warps real-space points to a canonical space. The canonical space is queried for density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} using a tri-plane representation. Data Structures: 1. Tri-Plane Representation: Three mutually orthogonal 2D planes encoding the canonical space. Features from these planes are concatenated with raw coordinate inputs to handle coordinate shift errors. 2. Observer MLP: A two-layer shallow MLP that takes \mathbf{x} and ti as input and outputs the mean observation y{ti} and noise-related terms \varepsilon{ti}. 3. Kalman Gain Network: A linear layer f that takes \varepsilon{ti}, \varepsilon{t{i-1}} and ti, t{i-1} as input to compute the Kalman gain K{ti}. Algorithm Steps: The deformation estimation for a point \mathbf{x} at time ti follows these steps: 1. Observer Query: Query the observer MLP with \mathbf{x} and ti to get observation y{ti} and noise terms \varepsilon{ti}. 2. Velocity Calculation: If ti is not the first frame, approximate velocity v{ti} using deformations from the previous two frames: v{ti} = (d\mathbf{x}{t{i-1}} - d\mathbf{x}{t{i-2}}) / \Delta ti where d\mathbf{x}{t} is the deformation at time t. 3. Prediction: Calculate the predicted deformation \hat{d\mathbf{x}}{ti}^{-} using the local linear motion model: \hat{d\mathbf{x}}{ti}^{-} = d\mathbf{x}{t{i-1}} + \Delta ti \cdot v{ti} = 2d\mathbf{x}{t{i-1}} - d\mathbf{x}{t{i-2}}. 4. Kalman Gain Calculation: Compute K{ti} using the linear layer f: K{ti} = f(\varepsilon{ti}, \varepsilon{t{i-1}}, ti, t{i-1}). 5. Update: Combine observation and prediction: \hat{d\mathbf{x}}{ti} = \hat{d\mathbf{x}}{ti}^{-} + K{ti} (y{ti} - \hat{d\mathbf{x}}{ti}^{-}). 6. Warping: Warp \mathbf{x} to canonical space \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} + \hat{d\mathbf{x}}{ti}. 7. Rendering: Query the tri-plane representation at \mathbf{x}' to obtain features, which are processed to yield \sigma and \mathbf{c} for volume rendering. Pseudocode: def kfdnerfdeformation(x, ti, observermlp, kalmangainnet, prevdeformations): """ Computes the deformation for point x at time ti using Kalman Filter guidance. Args: x: 3D point coordinates (tensor) ti: Current timestamp (float) observermlp: Two-layer MLP returning (observation, noiseterms) kalmangainnet: Linear layer returning Kalman gain prevdeformations: Dictionary mapping timestamp to deformation tensor Returns: deformation: Estimated deformation vector """ # Step 1: Observer yti, epsti = observermlp(x, ti) # Step 2 & 3: Prediction if ti in prevdeformations and (ti - 1) in prev

name: SLS4D
head: Sparse Latent Space for 4D Novel View Synthesis
body: SLS4D is a sparse latent space representation for 4D novel view synthesis that replaces dense voxel grids with learnable latent codes to reduce parameters while capturing global dynamics. It achieves state-of-the-art dynamic novel view synthesis results using approximately only 6% of the parameters of the previous SOTA work V4D. Unlike methods that rely on direct coordinate relationships or dense grids, SLS4D abandons direct use of coordinate relationships to determine final features, relying instead on relative relationships in the latent feature space, which is more compact and informative. SLS4D represents the 4D space in a sparse, compact and informative latent feature space. The method separates the temporal and spatial dimensions using a deformation field and a sparse spatial latent space, respectively. Inputs: A set of input images with known camera poses and timestamps t. The timestamps are normalized to the range [0, 1] or mapped to discrete time slots. Outputs: Volume density \sigma and view-dependent color \mathbf{c} for a ray \mathbf{r}(s) = \mathbf{o} + s\mathbf{d} at time t, computed via the standard volume rendering integral. 1. Time Slots (T): A dense set of learnable features representing the temporal space. The number of time slots is denoted by T. In the reported experiments, T = 512. 2. Spatial Latent Codes (B): A sparse, finite set of globally learnable latent codes representing the spatial features. The number of latent codes is denoted by B. In the reported experiments, B = 512. 3. Deformation Field MLP: A 7-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). 4. Interpolator Decoder: A network using GeGLU (bilinear Gated Linear Unit) activation. 1. Time Slot Encoding: The input timestamp t is mapped to a specific time slot feature from the dense set of learnable time slots. This ensures smoothness of dense temporal information and smooth transition while separating deformation fields for each timestamp. 2. Deformation Field Prediction: The 4D coordinate (x, y, z, t) is passed through the deformation field MLP. The MLP takes the spatial coordinates (x, y, z) and the time-dependent information (derived from the time slots associated with t) as input. The output is a 3D displacement vector \Delta \mathbf{x} = (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z). The deformed coordinate is computed as \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} + \Delta \mathbf{x}. This step decouples time and space, allowing the model to handle dynamic motion. 3. Spatial Feature Querying: The deformed coordinate \mathbf{x}' is used to query the sparse spatial latent space. A query feature \mathbf{q} is generated from \mathbf{x}' (implementation detail: typically via a small MLP or embedding, though the source describes the attention mechanism directly on the position feature). The weights for each latent code are determined using an attention mechanism. The weight wi for the i-th latent code \mathbf{L}i is computed using the inner product of the query feature \mathbf{q} and the key value \mathbf{K}i of the latent code. The spatial feature \mathbf{f}{spatial} is the weighted sum of the latent codes: \mathbf{f}{spatial} = \sum{i=1}^{B} \text{softmax}(\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{K}i) \mathbf{V}i where \mathbf{V}i is the value vector associated with the i-th latent code. The source states the latent code implicitly learns its position, making it adaptive to 4D scenes. 4. Radiance Field Prediction: The spatial feature \mathbf{f}{spatial} and the view direction \mathbf{d} are passed to the Interpolator Decoder. The decoder uses GeGLU activation. The output is the volume density \sigma and the view-dependent color \mathbf{c}. Deformation: \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} + \text{DeformationMLP}(\mathbf{x}, t). name: NeRF-Casting
head: NeRF-Casting: Improved View-Dependent Appearance with Consistent Reflections
body: NeRF-Casting is a method for synthesizing photorealistic specular appearance and reflections in real-world scenes by integrating ray tracing into the Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) rendering pipeline. It solves the problem of view-dependent appearance modeling by replacing expensive neural network queries for outgoing radiance with reflection rays cast into the NeRF geometry, which allows for consistent reflections of nearby and distant content. Unlike Ref-NeRF, which requires a large MLP to encode the entire environment at every point, or inverse rendering methods that perform expensive Monte Carlo integration over the hemisphere, NeRF-Casting renders accurate reflections with low computational overhead by using a small MLP to decode features sampled from traced reflection rays. NeRF-Casting improves upon the standard NeRF architecture Parent by decoupling the representation of geometry/density from the representation of view-dependent specular appearance. Instead of predicting color \mathbf{c} directly from position \mathbf{x} and view direction \mathbf{d} via a large MLP, it predicts a feature vector \mathbf{f} and decodes it into color using a small MLP, where \mathbf{f} is obtained by casting reflection rays into the scene. Inputs: Camera ray origin \mathbf{o}, camera ray direction \mathbf{d}, scene geometry (density \tau), and a pre-trained or concurrently trained NeRF representation. Outputs: Volume-rendered color \bar{\mathbf{c}} for the pixel. The method relies on the standard NeRF data structures but modifies the query logic: 1. NeRF Representation: A function F\Theta that maps a 3D position \mathbf{x} to volume density \tau(\mathbf{x}). In NeRF-Casting, this representation is used to trace reflection rays. 2. Color Decoder: A small Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), denoted as D, that maps a feature vector \mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{R}^k to RGB color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3. This MLP is significantly smaller than the standard NeRF shading MLP. To give higher representational capacity to points near the cameras, NeRF-Casting employs a spatial contraction function C: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3 that maps all points in \mathbb{R}^3 to a sphere of radius 2. C(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} \mathbf{x} & \text{if } \|\mathbf{x}\| \le 1 \\ \frac{1}{2 - \|\mathbf{x}\|} \frac{\mathbf{x}}{\|\mathbf{x}\|} & \text{if } \|\mathbf{x}\| > 1 \end{cases} This contracted coordinate C(\mathbf{x}) is used as the input to the NeRF density query when tracing reflection rays. The rendering process for a single camera ray proceeds as follows: 1. Sample Points: Sample N points t^{(i)} along the camera ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} for i = 1, \dots, N. 2. Query Density: For each sample point \mathbf{x}^{(i)} = \mathbf{o} + t^{(i)}\mathbf{d}, query the NeRF to obtain the volume density \tau^{(i)} = \tau(C(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})). 3. Cast Reflection Rays: For each sample point \mathbf{x}^{(i)} with non-negligible density, cast a reflection ray. The direction of the reflection ray \mathbf{d}{refl}^{(i)} is determined by the surface normal at \mathbf{x}^{(i)}. In the absence of an explicit normal field, the normal is typically approximated by the gradient of the density field or the view direction relative to the camera. The reflection direction is calculated as: \mathbf{d}{refl}^{(i)} = \mathbf{d} - 2(\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{n}^{(i)})\mathbf{n}^{(i)} where \mathbf{n}^{(i)} is the normal at \mathbf{x}^{(i)}. 4. Trace Reflection: Trace the reflection ray \mathbf{r}{refl}(t) = \mathbf{x}^{(i)} + t\mathbf{d}{refl}^{(i)} through the NeRF geometry. Sample points along this reflection ray and use the standard volume rendering equation to compute a feature vector \mathbf{f}^{(i)}. The feature vector represents the anti-aliased content of the reflected scene. Note: The specific feature dimensionality and encoding are implementation details not fully specified in the source, but the core idea is that \mathbf{f}^{(i)} captures the view-dependent appearance of the reflected environment. 5. Decode Color: Pass the feature vector \mathbf{f}^{(i)} through the small Color Decoder MLP D to obtain the color \mathbf{c}^{(i)} = D(\mathbf{f}^{(i)}). 6. Volume Render: Combine the colors \mathbf{c}^{(i)} and densities \tau^{(i)} using the standard volume rendering equation to produce the final pixel color \bar{\mathbf{c}}. The weight w^{(i)} for the i-th sample is calculated as: w^{(i)} = \left( 1 - \exp\left(-\tau^{(i)} \left( t^{(i+1)} - t^{(i)} \right) \right) \right) \exp\left( -\sum{j < i} \tau^{(j)} \left( t^{(j+1)} - t^{(j)} \right) \right) The final color is: \bar{\mathbf{c}} = \sumi w^{(i)} \mathbf{c}^{(i)} Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def spatialcontraction(x): """ Maps points in R^3 to a sphere of radius 2. x: numpy array of shape (3,) """ norm = np.linalg.norm(x) if norm <= 1.0: return x else: return (1.0 / (2.0 - norm)) (x / norm) def querydensity(nerfmodel, xcontracted): """ Queries the NeRF model for density at the contracted position. nerfmodel: function or object that takes contracted coordinates and returns density. xcontracted: numpy array of shape (3,) """ # Implementation detail: The NeRF model is queried at xcontracted. # The source does not specify if the NeRF also outputs features for the main ray, # but NeRF-Casting specifically uses reflection rays for features. # We assume the NeRF model provides density. return nerfmodel.getdensity(xcontracted) def tracereflectionray(nerfmodel, origin, direction, numsamples=64): """ Traces a reflection ray through the NeRF to render a feature vector. nerfmodel: function or object that takes contracted coordinates and returns density. origin: numpy array of shape (3,) direction: numpy array of shape (3,) numsamples: int Returns: feature vector (numpy array) """ # Sample points along the reflection ray tvals = np.linspace(0.0, 10.0, numsamples) # Range depends on scene bounds points = origin[:, np.newaxis] + direction[:, np.newaxis] tvals[np.newaxis,:] # Contract points contractedpoints = np.array([spatialcontraction(p) for p in points.T]) # Query densities densities = np.array([querydensity(nerfmodel, cp) for cp in contractedpoints]) # Standard volume rendering to get a feature vector. # Note: The source states "samples properly anti-aliased features". # It does not specify if the NeRF outputs features along the reflection ray # or if the feature is derived from the density/color of the reflection ray. # Given the description "render feature vectors which are decoded into color", # we assume the reflection ray trace produces a feature vector. # For the purpose of this implementation, we assume the NeRF model # can also output a feature vector along the ray, or we use a placeholder # for the feature extraction logic which is not fully detailed in the source. # However, the source emphasizes that the reflection ray renders the feature. # Let's assume the NeRF model has a method to render features along a ray. # Since the source doesn't give the exact feature rendering code for the reflection ray, # we use a standard volume render of a 'feature' channel if available, # or simply return a placeholder indicating the trace result. # To be implementable, we assume the NeRF model supports feature rendering. # Pseudocode for feature rendering along a ray: # weights = computeweights(densities, tvals) # features = renderfeatures(nerfmodel, contractedpoints, weights) # return features # As the source does not specify the feature rendering mechanism for the reflection ray, # we note this as a gap. However, the core innovation is the casting of the ray. # We will return a dummy feature vector to satisfy the structure, # noting that in practice, this would be the result of volume rendering # the scene content along the reflection ray. return np.zeros(32) # Placeholder for feature vector dimension def rendercameraray(nerfmodel, origin, direction, numsamples=64): """ Renders a single camera ray using NeRF-Casting. """ tvals = np.linspace(0.0, 10.0, numsamples) points = origin[:, np.newaxis] + direction[:, np.newaxis] tvals[np.newaxis,:] contractedpoints = np.array([spatialcontraction(p) for p in points.T]) densities = np.array([querydensity(nerfmodel, cp) for cp in contractedpoints]) # Compute weights # tau = densities # delta = np.diff(np.concatenate(([0], tvals))) # alpha = 1 - np.exp(-tau delta) # T = np.cumprod(1 - alpha + 1e-10) # T = np.concatenate(([1], T[:-1])) # weights = alpha T # Standard weight calculation delta = np.diff(np.concatenate(([0], tvals))) alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-densities delta) T = np.cumprod(1.0 - alpha + 1e-10) T = np.concatenate(([1.0], T[:-1])) weights = alpha T finalcolor = np.zeros(3) for i in range(numsamples): if weights[i] > 1e-5: x = points[:, i] # Approximate normal from density gradient or view direction # Source does not specify normal estimation method exactly. # We use a placeholder for normal estimation. normal = estimatenormal(nerfmodel, x) # Calculate reflection direction # d is the camera ray direction d = direction drefl = d - 2 np.dot(d, normal) normal # Trace reflection ray to get feature feature = tracereflectionray(nerfmodel, x, drefl) # Decode feature to color color = colordecoder(feature) finalcolor += weights[i] color return finalcolor def estimatenormal(nerfmodel, x): """ Estimates surface normal at x. Source does not specify. Common approach: gradient of density. """ # Numerical gradient of density eps = 1e-4 xcontracted = spatialcontraction(x) d = querydensity(nerfmodel, xcontracted) grad = np.zeros(3) for axis in range(3): xplus = x.copy() xplus[axis] += eps xpluscontracted = spatialcontraction(xplus) dplus = querydensity(nerfmodel, xpluscontracted) xminus = x.copy() xminus[axis] -= eps xminuscontracted = spatialcontraction(xminus) dminus = querydensity(nerfmodel, xminuscontracted) grad[axis] = (dplus - dminus) / (2 eps) return grad / np.linalg.norm(grad) def colordecoder(feature): """ Small MLP to decode feature to color. """ # Placeholder for the small MLP return feature / np.linalg.norm(feature) # Placeholder normalization Spatial Contraction: The sphere radius is fixed at 2. Reflection Ray Sampling: The number of samples along the reflection ray is not specified in the source, but the method implies it is sufficient to capture anti-aliased features. Color Decoder Size: Described as "small" and "inexpensive" compared to the standard NeRF MLP. Exact dimensions are not given. Normal Estimation: The source does not specify how surface normals are estimated for reflection ray casting. Using density gradients can be noisy in sparse regions. Reflection Ray Tracing: Tracing reflection rays adds significant computational cost per sample compared to standard NeRF, although it is cheaper than Monte Carlo integration. Feature Dimensionality: The dimensionality of the feature vector \mathbf{f} is not specified. Time Complexity: Higher than standard NeRF due to the additional ray tracing for reflections, but significantly lower than inverse rendering methods that use hundreds to thousands of samples per point. Memory Complexity: Similar to standard NeRF, as it does not require storing large environment maps or complex light transport data structures. Strengths: Synthesizes photorealistic specular appearance and reflections in real-world scenes; consistent reflections of nearby and distant content; comparable optimization time to state-of-the-art view synthesis models. Limitations: Requires ray tracing integration; performance depends on the accuracy of normal estimation for reflection directions. When to use: When view synthesis of scenes containing shiny objects is required, and photorealistic specular appearance is needed. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and specular reflections are not important. NeRF-Casting was introduced in 2024 by the authors of the paper "NeRF-Casting: Improved View-Dependent Appearance with Consistent Reflections". It addresses the limitations of prior NeRF methods that rely on large neural networks to model outgoing radiance, which limits optimization and rendering speed. It is distinct from Ref-NeRF and other inverse rendering approaches by using ray tracing to naturally synthesize reflections. name: RoseNeRF
head: Refracting Once is Enough, Refracting once is enough for NeRF
body: RoseNeRF is a method for high-fidelity novel view synthesis of real refractive objects that simplifies complex ray interactions inside objects to a single refraction event. It models refraction by predicting a single refracted ray using a 4D light field representation and a refraction network, avoiding the need for Index of Refraction (IoR) fields or detailed surface reconstructions. Unlike deformation field methods that predict position offsets for each sampling point, RoseNeRF predicts the refracted ray and uses hierarchical sampling, avoiding the need for point-by-point deformation and additional priors like IoR. It is designed for seamless integration into most NeRF-like frameworks, specifically implemented on top of MS-NeRF. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera rays defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Ground truth images \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}). Output: Synthesized pixel color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}). Data Structures and Layout: The method builds on the standard NeRF architecture Parent but introduces three specific components: 1. RefNet (Refraction Network): An MLP that maps incident rays to refracted rays. Student RefNet (\Thetas): 2-layer MLP, 64 hidden units. Input: 4D light field coordinates (u, v, s, t). Output: 4D refracted ray coordinates (u{nr}, v{nr}, s{nr}, t{nr}). Teacher RefNet (\Thetat): 3-layer MLP, 128 hidden units. Input: 5D vector (u, v, s, t, \mathbf{N}), where \mathbf{N} is the surface normal. Output: 4D refracted ray coordinates. 2. Decoder MLP (\ThetaD): Fuses density features from original and refracted rays. Architecture: 2-layer MLP, 256 hidden units, ReLU activations. Input: Densities \sigmai (from original ray) and \sigma{ir} (from refracted ray). Output: Complete density \sigma{ic}. 3. Base NeRF: Spatial MLP: 256 hidden units. Input: Positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}). Output: Density \sigma and intermediate features. Directional MLP: 256 hidden units. Input: Decoded density \sigma{ic} and direction \mathbf{d} (direction input last). Output: View-dependent color \mathbf{c}. Ray Parameterization (4D Light Field): Rays are parameterized by their intersections with two planes at Z0=0 and Z1=1. A ray is represented by 4D coordinates (u, v, s, t), where (u, v) is the intersection with Z0 and (s, t) is the intersection with Z1. The Cartesian direction \mathbf{d} is derived as: \mathbf{d} = (Z1 - Z0, u - s, v - t) = (1, u - s, v - t) Numbered Steps: 1. Initial Sampling (Warm-up Phase): For the first 5,000 iterations, only the base NeRF density \sigma is queried along the original ray. The Decoder is not used. Sample points \mathbf{x} along the original ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Estimate the surface normal \mathbf{N} at these points using the gradient of the predicted density (standard NeRF normal estimation). 2. Refracted Ray Prediction: Convert the original ray to 4D light field coordinates (u, v, s, t). Teacher Network (Distillation Target): Compute refracted coordinates using the teacher network: (u{nr}, v{nr}, s{nr}, t{nr}) = \Thetat(u, v, s, t, \mathbf{N}) Student Network (Inference): Compute refracted coordinates using the student network (without normal input): (u'{nr}, v'{nr}, s'{nr}, t'{nr}) = \Thetas(u, v, s, t) Convert the predicted 4D coordinates back to Cartesian direction \mathbf{d}r and origin \mathbf{o}r. The origin \mathbf{o}r is set at the intersection of the refracted ray with the camera plane Z = zc (where zc is the camera's Z-coordinate). The specific choice of starting point does not affect the final outcome. 3. Hierarchical Sampling: Phase 1 (Stratified): Sample along the original ray. Use the results to estimate normals \mathbf{N}. Phase 2 (Importance/Uniform): Predict the refracted ray \mathbf{r}r = \mathbf{o}r + t\mathbf{d}r using \Thetas. Query density \sigmai at points along the original ray using the Spatial MLP. Query density \sigma{ir} at points along the refracted ray using the Spatial MLP. Apply importance sampling based on Phase 1 results to the original ray. Uniformly sample the refracted ray. Subsequent Stages: Both original and refracted rays undergo independent importance sampling. 4. Feature Decoding: Feed the densities \sigmai and \sigma{ir} into the Decoder MLP \ThetaD: \sigma{ic} = \ThetaD(\sigmai, \sigma{ir}) Feed \sigma{ic} and the original viewing direction \mathbf{d} into the Directional MLP to obtain color \mathbf{c}c. 5. Rendering: Compute the final pixel color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) using volume rendering (alpha compositing): \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigma{ic,i} \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma{ic,j} \deltaj) and \deltai = ti - t{i-1}. Loss Functions: The total loss \mathcal{L} is a weighted sum: \mathcal{L} = \lambda1 \mathcal{L}{dist} + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{ref} + \mathcal{L}{NeRF} 1. Photometric Loss (\mathcal{L}{NeRF}): Standard MSE between predicted color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) and ground truth \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}). 2. Refraction Loss (\mathcal{L}{ref}): Ensures reversibility and physical consistency. It penalizes deviations from the teacher's prediction (using normal) and enforces reversibility (incident direction vs. predicted refracted direction): \mathcal{L}{ref} = \sumi (1 - \mathbf{d}i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{d}}{ri}) + \sumi (1 - \mathbf{d}i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{d}}{rni}) where \hat{\mathbf{d}}{ri} is the direction from the student network, and \hat{\mathbf{d}}{rni} is the direction from the teacher network. 3. Distillation Loss (\mathcal{L}{dist}): Encourages the student network (no normal) to match the teacher network (with normal): \mathcal{L}{dist} = \sumi (1 - \hat{\mathbf{d}}{ri} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{d}}{rni}) Parameters: \lambda1 = 0.003 (Distillation weight). \lambda2 = 0.003 (Refraction weight). L: Highest frequency in positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}) = [\sin(\mathbf{x}), \cos(\mathbf{x}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1}\mathbf{x}), \cos(2^{L-1}\mathbf{x})]. Batch size: 1024 rays. Iterations: 200,000. Warm-up: First 5,000 iterations use only density query without Decoder. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class RoseNeRF: def init(self, config): # Base NeRF components self.spatialmlp = SpatialMLP(hiddendim=256) self.directionalmlp = DirectionalMLP(hiddendim=256) # RoseNeRF specific components # Student RefNet: 4D -> 4D self.studentrefnet = RefNetMLP(layers=2, hidden=64) # Teacher RefNet: 5D -> 4D (used for distillation target) self.teacherrefnet = RefNetMLP(layers=3, hidden=128) # Decoder: 2 densities -> 1 density self.decoder = DecoderMLP(layers=2, hidden=256, activation='relu') # Hyperparameters self.lambdadist = 0.003 self.lambdaref = 0.003 self.warmupiters = 5000 self.currentiter = 0 # Positional Encoding parameters self.L = config.L # Highest frequency def positionalencoding(self, x, L): """Standard NeRF positional encoding.""" # x shape: (..., 3) # Output shape: (..., 2L3) scales = torch.tensor([2i for i in range(L)], device=x.device) xb = torch.reshape((x scales[:, None]), (x.shape[0], -1)) freqbands = torch.cat([torch.sin(xb), torch.cos(xb)], dim=-1) return freqbands def raytolightfield(self, origin, direction): """ Convert ray (o, d) to 4D light field (u, v, s, t). Planes at Z0=0, Z1=1. d = (1, u-s, v-t) => u-s = dx/dz, v-t = dy/dz Intersection with Z=0: x = ox - oz (dx/dz) Intersection with Z=1: x = ox + (1-oz) (dx/dz) """ # direction is normalized or unnormalized? # Formula d = (1, u-s, v-t) implies dz = 1. # We must normalize direction such that dz = 1 for this specific parameterization # or scale the coordinates. The paper defines d = (Z1-Z0, u-s, v-t). # Assuming d is the vector from origin to intersection. # Let's assume standard ray r(t) = o + td. # Intersection with Z=0: oz + t0dz = 0 => t0 = -oz/dz # u = ox + t0dx = ox - oz (dx/dz) # v = oy + t0dy = oy - oz (dy/dz) # Intersection with Z=1: oz + t1dz = 1 => t1 = (1-oz)/dz # s = ox + t1dx = ox + (1-oz) (dx/dz) # t = oy + t1dy = oy + (1-oz) (dy/dz) dz = direction[:, 2:3] # Avoid division by zero dz = torch.clamp(dz, min=1e-6) ratiox = direction[:, 0:1] / dz ratioy = direction[:, 1:2] / dz u = origin[:, 0:1] - origin[:, 2:3] ratiox v = origin[:, 1:2] - origin[:, 2:3] ratioy s = origin[:, 0:1] + (1.0 - origin[:, 2:3]) ratiox t = origin[:, 1:2] + (1.0 - origin[:, 2:3]) ratioy return torch.cat([u, v, s, t], dim=-1) def lightfieldtoray(self, lightfield, cameraz): """ Convert 4D light field (u, v, s, t) back to ray (origin, direction). Origin is set at intersection with Z = cameraz. """ u, v, s, t = lightfield[:, 0:1], lightfield[:, 1:2], lightfield[:, 2:3], lightfield[:, 3:4] # Direction components # dz = 1 (by definition of the parameterization space) # dx = u - s # dy = v - t direction = torch.cat([u - s, v - t, torch.oneslike(u)], dim=-1) direction = F.normalize(direction, dim=-1) # Origin calculation: # The ray passes through (u, v, 0) and (s, t, 1). # We want the point on this line where Z = cameraz. # Line equation: P(Z) = (u, v, 0) + Z ((s-u), (t-v), 1) # x = u + Z(s-u) # y = v + Z(t-v) # z = Z originx = u + cameraz (s - u) originy = v + cameraz (t - v) originz = cameraz origin = torch.cat([originx, originy, originz], dim=-1) return origin, direction def getnormal(self, spatialmlp, points): """Estimate normal from density gradient.""" points.requiresgrad(True) with torch.enablegrad(): sigma = spatialmlp(points) grad = torch.autograd.grad( sigma, points, gradoutputs=torch.oneslike(sigma), creategraph=True, retaingraph=True, onlyinputs=True)[0] normals = F.normalize(grad, dim=-1) return normals def forward(self, rayso, raysd, gtimages, spatialmlp, directionalmlp, studentrefnet, teacherrefnet, decoder, optimizer): """ Training step. """ self.currentiter += 1 # 1. Initial Sampling for Normal Estimation (Phase 1) # Sample along original ray tvals = torch.linspace(0, 1, 64) # Example Nsamples pointsorig = rayso[:, None,:] + raysd[:, None,:] tvals[None,:, None] # Get normals from density gradient normals = self.getnormal(spatialmlp, pointsorig.reshape(-1, 3)) normals = normals.reshape(rayso.shape[0], 64, 3) # 2. Predict Refracted Rays # Convert original rays to 4D light field lightfieldorig = self.raytolightfield(rayso, raysd) # Teacher prediction (with normal) # Concatenate lightfield (4) and normal (3) -> 5D input # Note: Normal needs to be associated with the ray. # The paper implies using the estimated normal N. # We can use the mean normal or the normal at the first intersection. # Let's use the normal at the first sample point for simplicity, # or average if needed. The paper says "local surface normal". # We'll assume N is passed as a tensor of shape (B, 3). # For this example, let's use the normal at the first sample point. N = normals[:, 0,:] teacherinput = torch.cat([lightfieldorig, N], dim=-1) lightfieldrefractedteacher = teacherrefnet(teacherinput) # Student prediction (without normal) lightfieldrefractedstudent = studentrefnet(lightfieldorig) # Convert refracted light fields to rays # Camera Z coordinate (assuming camera at Z=0 or similar, # paper says Zc is camera center Z. Let's assume Zc = 0 for simplicity # or pass it as a parameter. Standard NeRF often has camera at origin. # If camera is at origin, Zc = 0. cameraz = 0.0 or, dr = self.lightfieldtoray(lightfieldrefractedstudent, cameraz) # 3. Hierarchical Sampling # Phase 2: Sample along both rays # Original ray: Importance sampling based on Phase 1 density # Refracted ray: Uniform sampling # Query densities # Points on original ray pointsorigsample = rayso[:, None,:] + raysd[:, None,:] tvals[None,:, None] sigmaorig = spatialmlp(pointsorigsample.reshape(-1, 3)).reshape(rayso.shape[0], 64, 1) # Points on refracted ray pointsrefrsample = or[:, None,:] + dr[:, None,:] tvals[None,:, None] sigmarefr = spatialmlp(pointsrefrsample.reshape(-1, 3)).reshape(rayso.shape[0], 64, 1) # 4. Decoding # If warm-up, skip decoder if self.currentiter < self.warmupiters: sigmacombined = sigmaorig color = directionalmlp(sigmacombined, raysd) else: # Decoder takes sigmaorig and sigmarefr # Shape: (B, N, 1) -> (B, N, 2) for decoder input? # Decoder MLP usually takes concatenated features. decoderinput = torch.cat([sigmaorig, sigmarefr], dim=-1) sigmacombined = decoder(decoderinput) # Directional MLP takes sigmacombined and direction # Paper: "feed the decoded density and direction into the directional MLP" # "Inputting the direction into the network last" color = directionalmlp(sigmacombined, raysd) # 5. Rendering # Alpha compositing # delta = t[i] - t[i-1] deltas = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] deltas = torch.cat([deltas, torch.tensor([1e10], device=deltas.device)], dim=0) # Ti = exp(-sum(sigma delta)) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmacombined deltas[:, None]) transmittance = torch.cumprod(torch.exp(-sigmacombined deltas[:, None]), dim=1) transmittance = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(transmittance[:, 0:1]), transmittance[:,:-1]], dim=1) weights = alpha transmittance renderedcolor = torch.sum(weights color, dim=1) # 6. Loss Calculation lossneurf = F.mseloss(renderedcolor, gtimages) if self.currentiter >= self.warmupiters: # Refraction Loss # Convert student and teacher lightfields to directions dstudent = self.lightfieldtoray(lightfieldrefractedstudent, cameraz)[1] dteacher = self.lightfieldtoray(lightfieldrefractedteacher, cameraz)[1] # Lref = sum(1 - di. dhatri) + sum(1 - di. dhatrni) # di is original direction lref = torch.mean(1 - torch.sum(raysd dstudent, dim=-1)) + \ torch.mean(1 - torch.sum(raysd dteacher, dim=-1)) # Distillation Loss # Ldist = sum(1 - dhatri. dhatrni) ldist = torch.mean(1 - torch.sum(dstudent dteacher, dim=-1)) loss = self.lambdadist ldist + self.lambdaref lref + lossneurf else: loss = lossneurf optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return loss.item() Time Complexity: The method adds the cost of two additional MLP evaluations (Student and Teacher RefNet) and one Decoder MLP evaluation per ray per iteration. The RefNet is shallow (2-3 layers), so the overhead is low compared to the base NeRF. Memory Complexity: Requires storing parameters for Student RefNet, Teacher RefNet, and Decoder. Student: 2 \times 64 \times 4 + 64 (bias) \approx small. Teacher: 3 \times 128 \times 5 + 128. Decoder: 2 \times 256 \times 2 + 256. Total extra parameters are minimal compared to the base NeRF. Measured Performance: On the Eikonal Fields dataset (Ball, Glass, Pen, WineGlass) and Shiny dataset, RoseNeRF demonstrates state-of-the-art performance without additional information. It outperforms Ref-NeRF and NeX (which has 500x more parameters) in detail and competitive specular highlights. Strengths: No need for IoR fields or surface masks. Simplifies complex refraction to a single event, reducing computational load. Avoids floater artifacts common in standard NeRF on refractive objects. Easy integration with other NeRF variants. Limitations: Assumes a single refraction event; may not handle complex internal reflections or multiple refractions accurately. Performance depends on the accuracy of the initial normal estimation. Removing the refraction loss disrupts training. Using origin/direction instead of 4D light field worsens accuracy. RoseNeRF (Refracting Once is Enough for NeRF) was introduced in 2024 by Xiaoqian Liang et al.. It addresses the challenge of novel view synthesis for real-world refractive objects, where standard NeRF fails due to floater artifacts caused by incorrect sampling along bent ray paths. The method is inspired by Han et al. [20] (Eikonal Fields), who demonstrated the feasibility of reconstructing transparent objects by immersing them in liquid, but RoseNeRF simplifies this by not requiring detailed simulations of light interactions or assumptions about object shapes. It builds on MS-NeRF [59] for the decoding strategy. Refracting Once is Enough: Neural Radiance Fields for Novel-View Synthesis of Real Refractive Objects, https://doi.org/10.1145/3652583.3658000, fetched 2026-11-06

name: Semantic and Feature Field Extensions
head: Feature Fields, Semantic NeRF, DINO-NeRF, NeRF-Det, S-Ray
body: Semantic and Feature Field Extensions generalize the Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) formulation to predict arbitrary per-point feature signals \mathbf{f} in addition to color \mathbf{c} and density \sigma [12995-feature-fields.md]. This allows the representation of semantic labels, physical properties, or latent embeddings within the 3D volume [12995-feature-fields.md]. Unlike standard NeRF which only models appearance, this family lifts 2D observations into a consistent 3D representation, enabling tasks such as zero-shot segmentation, object manipulation, and view-dependent reflection modeling [12995-feature-fields.md, 12404-nerf-for-object-segmentation.md, unofficial]. The core mechanism modifies the radiance field function F\Theta to map input coordinates (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) to a tuple (\mathbf{f}, \mathbf{c}, \sigma), where \mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{R}^d is a feature vector [12995-feature-fields.md]. The rendering of these features follows the same volume integration principle as color. For a ray r, the rendered feature \hat{\mathbf{F}}(r) is computed as: \hat{\mathbf{F}}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai \mathbf{f}(xi) where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) is the accumulated transmittance and \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) is the opacity weight [12995-feature-fields.md]. Supervision is performed by comparing the rendered feature \hat{\mathbf{F}}(r) against ground-truth 2D feature maps or teacher network outputs projected onto the image plane [12995-feature-fields.md]. This process lifts 2D observations into a consistent 3D representation [12995-feature-fields.md]. Generalizes NeRF to predict arbitrary feature vectors \mathbf{f} alongside color and density. Enables zero-shot segmentation and object manipulation by lifting 2D features into 3D. Exploits instance masks from Visual Foundation Models to enhance surface estimation for transparent objects. Jointly optimizes a semantic field to enforce view-independent surface densities, producing sharper depth estimates and diffuse colors suitable for robotic grasping. Integrates pre-trained DINO vision features into the NeRF radiance field to enhance few-shot 3D reconstruction. Leverages self-supervised transformer features rather than generic learned feature fields. A joint "NeRF-and-Det" paradigm for indoor 3D object detection. Explicitly models scene geometry as an opacity field by jointly training a NeRF branch with a 3D detection pipeline, integrating multi-view geometry constraints into detection. Learns a generalizable semantic field for novel viewpoints across unseen scenes. Uses a Cross-Reprojection Attention module to exploit semantic context from multiple source views, decomposing dense attention into intra-view radial and cross-view sparse components. A NeRF variant that integrates pre-trained DINOv2 features by projecting them to match NeRF input dimensions and concatenating them with positional encodings before feeding into the NeRF MLP. The DINO model is pre-trained on ImageNet and frozen during training. Features are bilinearly sampled at projected 2D coordinates (ui, vi) = \Pi(Pi, x) for each 3D point x. These features are aggregated across all views into a single feature vector f(x). To interface with the NeRF MLP, the DINO features are projected using a learned linear transformation: f'(x) = Wf \cdot f(x) + bf where f(x) is the aggregated feature vector, and Wf, bf are learned linear transformation parameters. The transformed feature is concatenated with positional encodings and fed into the NeRF model: F\theta([\gamma(x), \gamma(d), f'(x)]) \rightarrow (c, \sigma) where f'(x) is projected to 256 dimensions. The DINOv2-base model outputs 768-dimensional features. The concept of extending NeRF with feature fields was introduced to enable semantic understanding and other auxiliary tasks beyond color rendering [12995-feature-fields.md]. SAID-NeRF was developed to address the ambiguity of transparent objects in NeRF by leveraging semantic masks [13619-said-nerf.md]. DINO-enhanced NeRF methods were proposed to improve few-shot reconstruction by utilizing self-supervised vision features [15497-dino-enhanced-nerf.md]. NeRF-Det was introduced to combine 3D detection and novel view synthesis in a joint framework [15549-nerf-det.md]. Semantic Ray (S-Ray) was developed to generalize semantic field learning to unseen scenes [15552-semantic-ray-s-ray.md]. Limitations of NERF with pre-trained Vision Features for Few-Shot 3D Reconstruction, https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.18208v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Feature Fields
head: Generalized NeRF, Semantic Fields
body: Feature Fields generalize the Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) formulation to predict arbitrary per-point feature signals \mathbf{f} in addition to color \mathbf{c} and density \sigma. This allows the representation of semantic labels, physical properties, or latent embeddings within the 3D volume. Unlike standard NeRF which only models appearance, this family lifts 2D observations into a consistent 3D representation, enabling tasks such as zero-shot segmentation, object manipulation, and view-dependent reflection modeling [12095-semantic-and-feature-branches.md, 12404-nerf-for-object-segmentation.md, 12072-nrff.md]. It sets itself apart from direct NeRF interpretation methods by requiring per-scene optimization before semantics can be exploited, limiting scalability for large datasets or real-time use. Siblings include SAID-NeRF, DINO-enhanced NeRF, NeRF-Det, and Semantic Ray (S-Ray). Children include Multi-Space Neural Radiance Field (MS-NeRF), NRFF, Semantic and Feature Branches, NeRF for Object Segmentation, Semantic-NeRF, and Augmented Features (Avg, Var, Color). See Semantic and Feature Field Extensions for shared principles. MS-NeRF addresses the failure of standard NeRF methods to render reflective and refractive objects, which violate multi-view consistency in Euclidean space and result in blurry or distorted images. It differs from single-space NeRF by representing the scene using a group of feature fields in parallel sub-spaces rather than a single radiance field, allowing virtual images to be placed in sub-spaces visible only from specific viewpoints. This approach automatically handles mirror-like objects without manual labeling, unlike vanilla NeRF which treats virtual images as textures on reflective surfaces. Choose it when rendering complex reflective/refractive scenes without manual mask annotation. NRFF encodes view-dependent effects in radiance fields by replacing Ref-NeRF's positional encoding and roughness/IDE inputs with a structured latent representation of specular reflections. It differs from its siblings like Multi-Space Neural Radiance Field (MS-NeRF) and Semantic-NeRF by explicitly modeling anisotropic reflections using Anisotropic Spherical Gaussians (ASG) and a custom Rendering Equation Encoding (REE) in the latent space, rather than relying on isotropic roughness or precomputed environment maps. Choose it for high-fidelity specular reflection synthesis. This method extends the standard NeRF formulation by adding a feature branch to the radiance field function, which outputs an arbitrary high-dimensional feature vector \mathbf{f} in addition to density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. It solves the limitation of standard NeRF, which only models appearance, by enabling the representation of semantic, geometric, or perceptual attributes within the 3D volume. Unlike sibling methods that may use fixed semantic labels or specific geometric constraints, this family generalizes the output space to support diverse downstream tasks such as zero-shot segmentation, pose estimation, and scene editing. Choose it for general-purpose auxiliary signal prediction. This method extends the standard NeRF formulation to perform object segmentation by simultaneously estimating scene geometry and predicting semantic occlusion masks. It introduces "area encoding" to represent the probability that a sampling point belongs to an occluded area, leveraging the strong correlation between geometry estimation and semantic label prediction. Unlike sibling methods that predict arbitrary feature vectors, this approach specifically targets binary or probabilistic occlusion masks to enable view-consistent segmentation and subsequent inpainting of occluded regions. Choose it when view-consistent segmentation and inpainting of occluded regions are required. Semantic-NeRF synthesizes semantic labels for novel views by extending the NeRF formulation with an additional direction-independent MLP branch. It integrates RGB images and corresponding 2D semantic labels to train the network, recovering semantic information from sparse or noisy annotations. It is distinguished from its siblings by being the first work to integrate semantic information directly into the NeRF framework using a dedicated semantic output branch. Choose it for dense 3D semantic understanding from sparse 2D annotations. Augmented Features (Avg, Var, Color) enhances neural radiance fields for 3D object detection by augmenting the feature or cost volume with mean, variance, and color information. It addresses insufficient geometric detail in standard NeRF opacity fields by explicitly leveraging statistical moments and low-level color cues as geometry priors. Choose it when geometric priors are needed for 3D detection tasks. Definition: A function f(\mathbf{p}) that maps a 3D point \mathbf{p} to an object code vector \mathbf{o}, representing object ownership independent of viewing angles. Parameters: H: Predefined maximum number of solid objects the network predicts. A relatively large value is chosen in practice. The function f is parameterized by a series of MLPs. Pitfall: Variable number of objects and large non-occupied volumes. Solved by fixing dimension to H+1, reserving the last dimension for empty space to handle occlusion/collision. Definition: A method that learns additional feature fields to realize self-supervised 3D segmentation. Definition: A method that learns additional feature fields to realize self-supervised 3D segmentation. Definition: Variance of color features describes occupancy: low variance implies occupied 3D location (Lambertian assumption), high variance implies free space (different appearances from different views). Steps: 1. Sample points along the ray originated from the camera: r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t \times \mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the ray origin and \mathbf{d} is the view direction. 2. Augment sampled features with variance from multiple views to describe occupancy. Compute variance: V{var}(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i=1}^{Mp} (Vi(\mathbf{p}) - \bar{V}(\mathbf{p}))^2 / Mp. 3. Compute mean and variance for pixel RGB values in the same way as for deep features. 4. Pass sampled augmented features into NeRF MLPs to generate density and color. Formula: Density and latent features are computed as: \sigma(\mathbf{p}), \hat{\mathbf{h}}(\mathbf{p}) = \text{G-MLP}(\bar{V}(\mathbf{p}), \gamma(\mathbf{p})), where \bar{V}(\mathbf{p}) is ray features aggregated and augmented from multi-view features, and \gamma(\mathbf{p}) is position encoding. Color is computed as: \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{d}) = \text{C-MLP}(\hat{\mathbf{h}}(\mathbf{p}), \mathbf{d}). Parameters: Grid resolution for 3D detection: 40 \times 40 \times 16. Source image feature map resolution: typically 160 \times 120. Layout: Augmented feature \bar{V} is a concatenation of \{V{avg}, V{var}, \text{RGB}{avg}, \text{RGB}{var}\}. Definition: Sampling point features along the ray from multi-view image features instead of low-resolution volume features to address the need for high-resolution images in NeRF. Number: Sampling from image features achieves 20.51 PSNR for novel-view synthesis compared to 18.93 with volume sampling. The concept of feature fields generalizes the original NeRF formulation, which maps (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\mathbf{c}, \sigma), to (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\mathbf{f}, \mathbf{c}, \sigma). This allows the network to predict arbitrary per-point feature signals, including semantics, physical properties, or latent descriptors. Semantic-NeRF was the first work to introduce semantic fields within the NeRF framework, using ground-truth semantic segmentation maps to augment the radiance field with per-point semantic logits. Subsequent works have expanded this to include self-supervised segmentation using teacher networks like DINO, object manipulation via object fields, and geometric priors for 3D detection. From reconstruction to reasoning: neural radiance fields for comprehensive 3D scene understanding, https://theses.hal.science/tel-05693528v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) DM-NeRF: 3D Scene Geometry Decomposition and Manipulation from 2D Images, https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.07227v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) A survey on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11704-025-41176-9, fetched 2026-10-28 NeRF-Det: Learning Geometry-Aware Volumetric Representation for Multi-View 3D Object Detection, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv51070.2023.02131, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Multi-Space Neural Radiance Field (MS-NeRF)
head: MS-Mip-NeRF 360, MS-NeRFB, Multi-space NeRF
body: MS-NeRF addresses the failure of standard NeRF methods to render reflective and refractive objects, which violate multi-view consistency in Euclidean space and result in blurry or distorted images. It differs from single-space NeRF by representing the scene using a group of feature fields in parallel sub-spaces rather than a single radiance field, allowing virtual images to be placed in sub-spaces visible only from specific viewpoints. This approach automatically handles mirror-like objects without manual labeling, unlike vanilla NeRF which treats virtual images as textures on reflective surfaces. MS-NeRF operates as an enhancement module that replaces the original output layer of a backbone NeRF method (MLP-based or grid-based) with a multi-space module. It builds on the Feature Fields principle, modifying the radiance field function to output multiple feature fields in parallel sub-spaces. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray r defined by origin and direction; backbone features/densities from the underlying NeRF architecture. Output: Final rendered color \hat{C}(r) for the pixel. Data Structures and Parameters: K: Hyperparameter for the total number of sub-spaces. d: Hyperparameter for the feature dimension of the neural feature field. \{\sigma{ik}\}: Density at sample point i in sub-space k. \{f{ik}\}: Feature vector of dimension d at sample point i in sub-space k. \ThetaD: Decoder MLP with one hidden layer. \ThetaG: Gate MLP with one hidden layer. Numbered Steps: 1. Multi-Head Output: Replace the backbone's final output layer with a multi-head layer. For each sample point i along the ray, the network outputs K densities \{\sigma{ik}\} and K feature vectors \{f{ik}\} of dimension d, where each pair corresponds to a specific sub-space k \in \{1, \dots, K\}. 2. Per-Subspace Volume Rendering: Integrate features along the ray in each sub-space independently to collect K feature maps. For a ray r, the rendered feature \hat{F}^k(r) for sub-space k is calculated as: \hat{F}^k(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} T{ik} (1 - \exp(-\sigma{ik} \deltai)) f{ik} where T{ik} = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma{jk} \deltaj) is the accumulated transmittance for sub-space k, and \deltai is the distance between sample points. 3. Decoder and Gate Processing: The aggregated features \{\hat{F}^k\} for all K sub-spaces are passed through two separate MLPs: The Decoder MLP \ThetaD takes \{\hat{F}^k\} as input and outputs RGB color vectors \{Ck\} for each sub-space: \ThetaD\{\hat{F}^k\} \rightarrow \{Ck\} The Gate MLP \ThetaG takes \{\hat{F}^k\} as input and outputs scalar weights \{wk\} that control the visibility of each sub-space: \ThetaG\{\hat{F}^k\} \rightarrow \{wk\} Both \ThetaD and \ThetaG are MLPs with one hidden layer. 4. Softmax Weighting: Apply the softmax function to the gate weights \{wk\} to determine the contribution of each sub-space to the final color. The final rendered color \hat{C}(r) is computed as: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \frac{\exp(wk)}{\sum{i=1}^{K} \exp(wi)} Ck Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method requires no additional loss terms compared to vanilla NeRF, relying on standard photometric loss. Computational overhead is small for training and inference. The composition weights of sub-spaces change dynamically according to spatial location and view direction, allowing the model to handle complex light paths. Time and Memory Complexity: The method introduces small computational overheads for training and inferring the extra-space outputs compared to single-space NeRF methods. Measured Performance: On the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset, MS-NeRF improves PSNR by 4.15 dB on reflective regions with only 0.5% extra parameters, without degrading rendering quality on other regions. On TensoRF, it improves PSNR by 2.71 dB on reflective regions with 0.046% extra parameters. Strengths: Automatically handles mirror-like objects in 360-degree rendering without manual labeling; overcomes multi-view consistency violations by placing virtual images in specific sub-spaces; works as a general enhancement for both MLP-based (NeRF, Mip-NeRF, Mip-NeRF 360) and grid-based (TensoRF, iNGP) methods. Limitations: Rendering quality on non-reflective regions is not degraded. Accurately modeling complex reflective and refractive scenes may require increasing the number of sub-spaces K. MS-NeRF was proposed to address the limitations of existing NeRF methods in handling reflective and refractive objects, which often result in blurry or distorted rendering due to violated multi-view consistency in Euclidean space. Existing datasets like RFFR and Shiny lacked sufficient coverage of 360-degree rendering with mirror-like objects, prompting the construction of a novel dataset with 33 synthetic and 7 real captured scenes. The method was published in IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence in 2025, with a preliminary version appearing at CVPR. MS-NeRF: Multi-Space Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/tpami.2025.3540074, fetched 2026-10-26 Neural Radiance Field-based Visual Rendering: a Comprehensive Review, https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/11455380, fetched 2026-10-30

name: NRFF
head: Neural Radiance Feature Field
body: NRFF encodes view-dependent effects in radiance fields by replacing Ref-NeRF's positional encoding and roughness/IDE inputs with a structured latent representation of specular reflections. It differs from its siblings like Multi-Space Neural Radiance Field (MS-NeRF) and Semantic-NeRF by explicitly modeling anisotropic reflections using Anisotropic Spherical Gaussians (ASG) and a custom Rendering Equation Encoding (REE) in the latent space, rather than relying on isotropic roughness or precomputed environment maps. It builds on Feature Fields. Inputs: Camera rays defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; ground-truth color images; optional ground-truth feature maps or teacher network outputs for supervision. Outputs: Rendered color images \hat{\mathbf{C}} and rendered feature maps \hat{\mathbf{F}} [12995-feature-fields.md]. Data Structures: 1. Spatial MLP: Takes 3D position \mathbf{x}. Uses Multiscale Tensor Decomposition (MTD) for input representation. Outputs a vector of 128 values representing N=8 \times 16 ASG lobes. 2. ASG MLP: Takes the 128 ASG feature vector. Outputs bottleneck coefficients \mathbf{a}, and scalar bandwidth coefficients \boldsymbol{\lambda}, \boldsymbol{\mu} (all of length N), where \lambdai, \mui > 0 model the ASG shape in orthogonal directions. 3. Directional MLP: Takes the REE vector (size 8 \times 16 \times 2) and view direction \mathbf{d}. Outputs color \mathbf{c} and density \sigma. Rendering Equation Encoding (REE): The REE integrates specular contributions in the latent space. For a reflection direction \hat{\omega}r, the encoding is computed as: \text{REE}(\hat{\omega}r, \mathbf{a}, \boldsymbol{\lambda}, \boldsymbol{\mu}) = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} ai S(\hat{\omega}r; \omegai) \exp\left(-\lambdai (\hat{\omega}r \cdot \omega{\lambdai})^2 - \mui (\hat{\omega}r \cdot \omega{\mui})^2\right) Where: N = 128 is the number of ASG lobes. ai is the bottleneck coefficient of the i-th ASG. S(\hat{\omega}r; \omegai) = \max(\hat{\omega}r \cdot \omegai, 0) is a smooth term. \lambdai, \mui > 0 are bandwidth coefficients related to orthogonal axes \omega{\lambdai}, \omega{\mui}. The set of directions \omegai covers the unit sphere (360 degrees). Algorithm Steps: 1. Sample points \mathbf{x}i along the ray. 2. Pass \mathbf{x}i through the Spatial MLP (using MTD) to get ASG features. 3. Pass ASG features through the ASG MLP to obtain coefficients \mathbf{a}, \boldsymbol{\lambda}, \boldsymbol{\mu}. 4. Compute the REE vector for the view direction \mathbf{d} using the formula above. 5. Pass the REE vector and \mathbf{d} through the Directional MLP to get \mathbf{c}i, \sigmai. 6. Render color and features using standard volume integration [12995-feature-fields.md]. 7. Compute loss: Color loss (standard MSE/SSIM). Feature loss (if available). Regularization loss Lf to enforce sparsity: Lf = \frac{\beta}{M} \sum{i=0}^{M-1} \frac{|\mathbf{F}\tau^i|}{\tau} Where M is the number of features in the density field representation, \mathbf{F}\tau is the density field feature map, \tau is a threshold, and \beta is a coefficient. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def samplepoints(rayorigin, raydirection, numsamples, tnear=0.0, tfar=1.0): """Uniformly samples points along a ray segment.""" tvals = [tnear + i (tfar - tnear) / (numsamples - 1) for i in range(numsamples)] return [rayorigin + raydirection t for t in tvals] def volumerender(colors, densities, deltas): """Standard alpha compositing for volume rendering.""" alpha = [1.0 - math.exp(-d dt) for d, dt in zip(densities, deltas)] transmittance = 1.0 rendered = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for c, a in zip(colors, alpha): rendered = [rendered[j] + transmittance a c[j] for j in range(3)] transmittance = (1.0 - a) return rendered def computeree(viewdirection, a, lambdacoeffs, mucoeffs, lobedirections, lobelambdaaxes, lobemuaxes): """Computes the Rendering Equation Encoding vector per lobe.""" reevalues = [] for i in range(len(a)): omegai = lobedirections[i] omegalambdai = lobelambdaaxes[i] omegamui = lobemuaxes[i] dotri = sum(v d for v, d in zip(viewdirection, omegai)) dotrl = sum(v d for v, d in zip(viewdirection, omegalambdai)) dotrm = sum(v d for v, d in zip(viewdirection, omegamui)) term = a[i] max(dotri, 0.0) term = math.exp(-lambdacoeffs[i] dotrl 2) term = math.exp(-mucoeffs[i] dotrm 2) reevalues.append(term) return reevalues def nrffforward(rayorigin, raydirection, spatialmlp, asgmlp, directionalmlp, numsamples, tnear, tfar, lobedirections, lobelambdaaxes, lobemuaxes): """Renders a single ray using the NRFF architecture.""" points = samplepoints(rayorigin, raydirection, numsamples, tnear, tfar) deltas = [math.dist(points[i], points[i-1]) if i > 0 else 0.0 for i in range(len(points))] colors = [] densities = [] for x in points: asgfeatures = spatialmlp(x) a, lambdacoeffs, mucoeffs = asgmlp(asgfeatures) reevalues = computeree(raydirection, a, lambdacoeffs, mucoeffs, lobedirections, lobelambdaaxes, lobemuaxes) # Reshape flat 128 values to 8x16x2 as required by the directional MLP reevector = [reevalues[i2:(i+1)2] for i in range(0, len(reevalues), 2)] c, sigma = directionalmlp(reevector, raydirection) colors.append(c) densities.append(sigma) return volumerender(colors, densities, deltas) Parameters: N: Number of ASG lobes, set to 8 \times 16 = 128. \mathbf{a}: Bottleneck coefficients vector, length N. \lambda, \mu: Scalar coefficients modeling ASG shape, must be > 0. \beta: Coefficient for regularization term Lf. \tau: Threshold in regularization term. Edge Cases: \lambdai, \mui must be strictly positive to ensure valid Gaussian shapes. Not given in the sources. Complexity: Uses Multiscale Tensor Decomposition (MTD) for efficiency in reconstructing scene geometry and appearance compared to standard Positional Encoding. Performance: Shows proficiency in encoding view-dependent effects and superior rendering quality on diverse datasets compared to Ref-NeRF. Strengths: Explicit modeling of anisotropic reflections; sparse feature representation enhances interpretability and mitigates overfitting. Limitations: Requires auxiliary ASG MLP and REE computation, increasing architectural complexity over standard NeRF. NRFF was proposed by Albert Barreiro, Roger Marı́, Rafael Redondo, Gloria Haro, Carles Bosch, and David Berga from Eurecat and Universitat Pompeu Fabra. It was submitted on 2024-07-09, accepted on 2025-01-17, and published in Image Processing On Line on 2025-03-12. It builds on the Ref-NeRF formulation.
