name: NeRF-Det
head: NeRF-then-Det
body: NeRF-Det is a method for indoor 3D object detection using posed RGB images that explicitly models scene geometry as an opacity field by jointly training a NeRF branch with a 3D detection pipeline. Unlike "NeRF-then-Det" approaches (e.g., NeRF-RPN) that treat geometry estimation and detection as separate stages, NeRF-Det is a joint "NeRF-and-Det" paradigm that integrates multi-view geometry constraints from the NeRF branch into 3D detection through a shared geometry MLP. This allows the method to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on multi-view indoor RGB-only 3D detection while enabling generalizable novel view synthesis on new scenes without per-scene optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of T posed RGB frames Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{Hi \times Wi \times 3} with corresponding intrinsic matrix K \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} and extrinsic matrix Ri \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 4} for i = 1, \dots, T. Output: 3D bounding boxes for object detection. Optionally, novel views and depth maps. Data Structures: 1. 2D Feature Map (Fi): Extracted from Ii using a Feature Pyramid Network (FPN). Fi \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times H/4 \times W/4}. 2. 3D Grid: A voxel grid of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz, where the z-axis denotes height and x/y denote horizontal dimensions. 3. 3D Volume Features (Vi(p)): For each voxel center p = (x, y, z)^T, features are assigned from the 2D feature maps. 4. Shared Geometry MLP (G-MLP): A neural network that predicts the density field \sigma(p). 5. Detection Head: Consumes geometry-aware volume features to regress 3D bounding boxes. Steps: 1. 2D Feature Extraction: Pass each input image Ii through an FPN backbone to extract high-resolution features Fi \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times H/4 \times W/4}. 2. 3D Feature Volume Construction: For each voxel center p = (x, y, z)^T in the 3D grid: a. Project p to view i to obtain 2D coordinates. The projected homogeneous coordinates are computed as: \begin{pmatrix} u'i, v'i, di \end{pmatrix}^T = K' \times Ri \times \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{p}, 1 \end{pmatrix}^T where K' is the scaled intrinsic matrix accounting for feature map downsampling. b. The pixel coordinates are (ui, vi) = (u'i/di, v'i/di). c. Assign 3D features using nearest neighbor interpolation: Vi(p) = \text{interpolate}((ui, vi), Fi) d. Boundary Handling: If p is projected outside the image boundary or behind the image plane (di \le 0), discard the feature and set Vi(p) = 0. 3. Multi-View Aggregation: Aggregate features from all Mp effective 2D projections (where Mp is the number of views where Vi(p) \neq 0) by averaging: V{\text{avg}}(p) = \frac{1}{Mp} \sum{i=1}^{Mp} Vi(p). 4. Geometry-Aware Feature Modulation (NeRF Branch): a. Feed the voxel coordinates p into the shared G-MLP to predict the density field \sigma(p). b. Transform the density field into an opacity field \alpha(p). The source text states: "transform the density field into an opacity field and multiply it with the volume features". While the exact formula for \alpha is not explicitly written as \alpha = 1 - e^{-\sigma \delta} in the NeRF-Det section, it follows the standard volume rendering opacity definition implied by the context of NeRF. c. Multiply the opacity with the volume features to reduce weights of empty space: V{\text{geo}}(p) = \alpha(p) \cdot V{\text{avg}}(p). 5. Detection: Feed the geometry-aware volume features V{\text{geo}}(p) to the detection head for 3D bounding box regression. 6. Inference: Remove the NeRF branch (G-MLP and associated computations) to minimize overhead. The detection head operates on the pre-computed or efficiently computed volume features. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nerfdetforward(images, poses, intrinsics, voxelgrid, gmlp, detectionhead, fpn): """ images: List of T RGB images Ii poses: List of T extrinsic matrices Ri intrinsics: Intrinsic matrix K voxelgrid: 3D grid of voxel centers p gmlp: Shared Geometry MLP detectionhead: 3D detection head fpn: Feature Pyramid Network backbone """ T = len(images) C, Hf, Wf = 256, 64, 64 # Example dimensions for Fi # Step 1: Extract 2D features F = [] for i in range(T): Fi = fpn(images[i]) # Fi in R^{C x H/4 x W/4} F.append(Fi) # Step 2 & 3: Construct 3D Volume and Aggregate # Vavg shape: (Nx, Ny, Nz, C) Vavg = torch.zeros((Nx, Ny, Nz, C)) counts = torch.zeros((Nx, Ny, Nz)) for i in range(T): Ri = poses[i] # Scale K for feature map downsampling (factor of 4) Kprime = intrinsics 0.25 # Project voxel centers to 2D # p is (Nx Ny Nz, 3) phomogeneous = torch.cat([voxelgrid, torch.oneslike(voxelgrid[:,:1])], dim=1) projected = Kprime @ Ri @ phomogeneous.T # (3, Nvoxels) uprime = projected[0,:] vprime = projected[1,:] d = projected[2,:] # Valid pixels: inside image bounds and in front of camera valid = (d > 0) & (uprime >= 0) & (uprime < Wf) & (vprime >= 0) & (vprime < Hf) u = uprime[valid] / d[valid] v = vprime[valid] / d[valid] # Nearest neighbor interpolation # Note: In implementation, this requires mapping 2D coords to grid indices # and gathering from Fi. Here we assume a gather function. Vivalid = gathernearest(F[i], u, v) # Update Vavg # This is a simplified representation of the aggregation logic # In practice, scatteradd is used counts[validindices] += 1 Vavg[validindices] += Vivalid # Average counts = torch.clamp(counts, min=1) Vavg = Vavg / counts.unsqueeze(-1) # Step 4: Geometry-Aware Modulation # Predict density for all voxels sigma = gmlp(voxelgrid) # (Nvoxels,) # Convert density to opacity # Assuming uniform step size delta or standard NeRF opacity formula # alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma delta) # Since delta is not explicitly given, we assume standard volume rendering opacity # or that the G-MLP output is directly used as a weight if delta is normalized. # The paper says "transform the density field into an opacity field". # We use the standard definition [12995-feature-fields.md] delta = 0.1 # Placeholder for voxel size, or derived from grid bounds alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma delta) # Modulate features Vgeo = alpha.unsqueeze(-1) Vavg # Step 5: Detection boxes = detectionhead(Vgeo) return boxes def nerfdetinference(images, poses, intrinsics, voxelgrid, detectionhead, fpn): """ Inference removes the NeRF branch. """ # Steps 1-3 are identical # Step 4 is skipped (no G-MLP, no alpha modulation) # Vgeo is effectively Vavg or a simpler aggregation # However, the paper implies the volume features are pre-computed or # the detection head is trained to work with the geometry-aware features. # During inference, the NeRF branch is removed. # This implies the detection head might rely on the volume structure # learned during joint training, but without the dynamic alpha modulation # at inference time? # The paper states: "during inference, the NeRF branch is removed, which minimizes the additional overhead". # It does not explicitly say Vgeo is replaced by Vavg at inference. # It likely means the G-MLP is not called, but the volume features Vavg # are still used, possibly with a fixed opacity or just Vavg. # Given the ablation "disabling the detection branch brings 0.43dB improvement", # the NeRF branch is the G-MLP. # We will assume Vgeo = Vavg at inference if G-MLP is removed, # or that the detection head was trained to expect Vgeo but # the "removal" refers to not computing sigma/alpha dynamically. # However, standard practice for "removing a branch" implies using the # remaining features. Let's assume Vgeo = Vavg for inference simplicity # unless specified otherwise. # Actually, the paper says "multiply it with the volume features... # Then, the geometry-aware volume features are fed to the detection head". # If the NeRF branch is removed, we don't have alpha. # So we likely use Vavg. # Re-run Steps 1-3 #... (same as forward) # Use Vavg directly boxes = detectionhead(Vavg) return boxes Parameters: Density Activation: ReLU. Color Activation: Sigmoid. Feature Interpolation: Nearest neighbor. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Projection: Voxels projected outside the image boundary or behind the image plane must have their features set to 0. Depth Estimation Errors: Using predicted depth maps from external geometry reconstruction (e.g., NeuralRecon) significantly degrades detection performance (by 2.3 mAP@.50 compared to plain ImVoxelNet) because depth estimation errors propagate inaccuracy through the detection pipeline. Detection Branch Impact: The detection branch negatively impacts the NeRF branch's novel view synthesis quality because it is prone to erasing low-level details required for NeRF rendering. Disabling the detection branch brings a 0.43dB improvement in PSNR. A shared geometry MLP that enables the constraint of multi-view consistency to be propagated from the NeRF branch to the detection branch. Without the shared G-MLP, performance drops from 50.1 to 48.1 mAP@.25, as the influence of multi-view consistency is only propagated into the image backbone. Time Complexity: The joint training is end-to-end. Inference latency is significantly lower than NeRF-then-Det methods. NeRF-Det-R50 has a latency of 0.554s on one V100, compared to NeRF-RPN's ~846.8s. Memory Complexity: Requires storing 3D feature volumes and the G-MLP parameters. The 3D grid size (Nx \times Ny \times Nz) determines memory usage for the volume features. Performance: Improves state-of-the-art by 3.9 mAP on ScanNet and 3.1 mAP on ARKITScenes benchmarks. On ScanNet, NeRF-Det-R50 achieves 35.13 AP50. Novel View Synthesis: Achieves an average PSNR of 20+ for novel view synthesis and an RMSE of 0.756 for depth estimation on 312 scenes in the validation set, without per-scene training. Strengths: Generalizable to unseen scenes without per-scene optimization; explicitly models geometry; faster than NeRF-then-Det. Limitations: The detection branch can degrade the NeRF branch's rendering quality by erasing low-level details. NeRF-Det was introduced by Chenfeng et al. (Meta) in 2023. It addresses the limitations of existing indoor 3D detection methods that struggle to model scene geometry and the high latency of per-scene NeRF optimization. It builds on the principles of Feature Fields by using a shared geometry MLP to connect the NeRF and detection branches. NeRF-Det: Learning Geometry-Aware Volumetric Representation for Multi-View 3D Object Detection, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv51070.2023.02131, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Semantic Ray (S-Ray)
head: S-Ray
body: Semantic Ray (S-Ray) is a method for learning a generalizable semantic field that infers semantic labels on novel viewpoints across unseen scenes, addressing the overfitting and lack of generalization inherent in single-scene methods like Semantic-NeRF. It distinguishes itself by using a Cross-Reprojection Attention module to exploit semantic context from multiple source views, decomposing dense attention into intra-view radial and cross-view sparse components to efficiently model semantic dependencies along reprojected rays. Inputs: A set of N{views} input views with known camera poses and semantic labels; a query ray r defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} for a novel viewpoint. Outputs: Rendered semantic feature map \hat{\mathbf{S}} and density \sigma for the novel view. Data Structures: Contextual Space M: A matrix of shape (N{views}, N \times C), where N is the number of quadrature points and C is the channel dimension. M = [\mathbf{F}1, \mathbf{F}2, \dots, \mathbf{F}{N{views}}]^T. Radial Feature \mathbf{F}i: A matrix of shape (N, C) representing features sampled along the reprojected ray in the i-th source view. \mathbf{F}i = [\mathbf{f}i(r^(z1)), \dots, \mathbf{f}i(r^(zN))]. Parameters: N: Number of random quadrature points between near plane tn and far plane tf. H: Number of heads in the intra-view radial attention module. C: Channel dimension of the extracted features. Steps: 1. Build Initial 3D Contextual Space: For each source view i \in \{1, \dots, N{views}\}: a. Reproject the query ray r to the i-th view. Since the ray is virtual in the novel view, it maps to a reprojected ray r^ in the source view, representing a line of possible positions rather than a single point. b. Sample N points \{zk\}{k=1}^N along r^ within the view's depth bounds. c. Apply a CNN-based module to extract contextual features for each sampled point, forming the radial feature matrix \mathbf{F}i \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C}. d. Assemble M = [\mathbf{F}1, \dots, \mathbf{F}{N{views}}]^T. 2. Cross-Reprojection Attention: Decompose M to learn dense semantic connections efficiently. a. Intra-view Radial Attention: For each view i, compute attention among the N points in \mathbf{F}i. Let \mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V} be derived from \mathbf{F}i. The attention for head h is: \text{Attention}h(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V}) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^T}{\sqrt{dk}}\right)\mathbf{V} where dk is the key dimension. The outputs of H heads are concatenated and linearly projected to produce the refined radial features \mathbf{F}'i. b. Cross-view Sparse Attention: Distinguish the same 3D point across different viewpoints and score the semantic contribution of each view. This module operates on the refined features \mathbf{F}'i to produce the refined contextual space M'. 3. Semantic Ray Construction: Use a Semantic-Aware Weight Net to learn the significance of each view. This net takes the refined contextual space M' and outputs view-specific weights wi that determine the contribution of each source view's semantic information to the final semantic ray. 4. Semantic Ray Rendering: a. Use a Geometry-Aware Net to predict density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} for the query ray points. b. Compute the accumulated transmittance Tk = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{k-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) and opacity \alphak = 1 - \exp(-\sigmak \deltak), where \deltak = t{k+1} - tk. c. Render the semantic feature \hat{\mathbf{S}} by aggregating the semantic information from the refined contextual space, weighted by the view significance and opacity: \hat{\mathbf{S}}(r) = \sum{k=1}^{N} Tk \alphak \mathbf{S}k where \mathbf{S}k is the semantic feature at sample k derived from the weighted combination of source views. d. Render color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(r) = \sum{k=1}^{N} Tk \alphak \mathbf{c}k. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def semanticrayrendering(inputviews, queryray, model): """ inputviews: List of Nviews images and camera poses. queryray: Tuple (origin, direction) for the novel view. model: Contains CNN, CrossReprojectionAttention, SemanticAwareWeightNet, GeometryAwareNet. """ N = model.numquadraturepoints Nviews = len(inputviews) # Step 1: Build Initial 3D Contextual Space # M shape: (Nviews, N, C) M = [] for i in range(Nviews): viewimg, viewpose = inputviews[i] # Reproject query ray to view i to get reprojected ray rstar rstar = reprojectray(queryray, viewpose) # Sample N points along rstar zsamples = samplepointsalongray(rstar, N) # Extract features using CNN # Features shape: (N, C) Fi = model.cnnextractor(viewimg, zsamples) M.append(Fi) M = torch.stack(M, dim=0) # Shape: (Nviews, N, C) # Step 2: Cross-Reprojection Attention # Intra-view Radial Attention # For each view, compute attention among its N points Frefinedviews = [] for i in range(Nviews): Fi = M[i] # Shape: (N, C) # Q, K, V derived from Fi Q, K, V = model.intraviewattention.getqkv(Fi) # Compute attention with H heads # Output shape: (N, C) Firefined = model.intraviewattention(Q, K, V) Frefinedviews.append(Firefined) Frefinedviews = torch.stack(Frefinedviews, dim=0) # Shape: (Nviews, N, C) # Cross-view Sparse Attention # Distinguish points across views and score contributions # Output shape: (Nviews, N, C) Mrefined = model.crossviewattention(Frefinedviews) # Step 3: Semantic Ray Construction # Learn view significance weights # Output shape: (Nviews,) viewweights = model.semanticawareweightnet(Mrefined) # Step 4: Semantic Ray Rendering # Get density and color from Geometry-Aware Net # Sample points along the original query ray in the novel view tsamples = samplequadraturepoints(queryray.origin, queryray.direction, N) xsamples = queryray.origin + tsamples queryray.direction # Predict density and color for these samples # sigma shape: (N,), c shape: (N, 3) sigma, c = model.geometryawarenet(xsamples) # Compute transmittance and opacity deltas = tsamples[1:] - tsamples[:-1] # Add a small epsilon to avoid division by zero or log(0) deltas = torch.cat([deltas, torch.tensor([1e-10])]) alphas = 1 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) transmittances = torch.cumprod(torch.exp(-sigma deltas), dim=0) transmittances = torch.cat([torch.tensor([1.0]), transmittances[:-1]]) # Aggregate semantic features # Mrefined is (Nviews, N, C). We need to aggregate over views first, then along ray. # However, the paper suggests constructing the semantic ray from the refined contextual space. # The semantic feature at sample k is a weighted sum of features from all views. # Let's assume the semantic feature for sample k is derived from Mrefined[:, k,:] # weighted by viewweights. # Semantic feature for each sample k: (N, C) # Mrefined[:,:,:] is (Nviews, N, C) # viewweights is (Nviews,) # We want to sum over views: sumi (wi F'ik) # This results in (N, C) semanticfeaturespersample = torch.einsum('v, vnc -> nc', viewweights, Mrefined) # Render semantic output # Shat = sumk Tk alphak Sk # Shat shape: (C,) weights = transmittances alphas Shat = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) semanticfeaturespersample, dim=0) # Render color Chat = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) c, dim=0) return Shat, Chat, sigma Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Computational Cost: Directly performing dense attention over sampled points on each reprojected ray of multiple views is computationally expensive. The decomposition into intra-view and cross-view attention is critical to mitigate this. Reprojection Uncertainty: Since the emitted ray from the query point is virtual, the network cannot obtain the exact reprojected point on each view, but a reprojected ray showing possible positions. The network must model this uncertainty within each view. Overfitting: Unlike Semantic-NeRF, which relies on positional encoding prone to overfitting the current scene, S-Ray is designed to generalize to unseen scenes by training on multiple scenes. Time Complexity: The method reduces computational cost compared to dense multi-view attention by decomposing it into intra-view radial and cross-view sparse attentions. Memory Complexity: The contextual space M scales with N{views} \times N \times C. The decomposition helps keep memory usage manageable. Performance: S-Ray achieves comparable quality to Semantic-NeRF's result for 100k iterations per-scene optimization by fine-tuning on more images for only 10 min (2k iterations). Strengths: Generalizes to unseen scenes; exploits rich semantic context from multiple views; efficient attention mechanism. Limitations: Requires multiple input views; relies on accurate camera poses for reprojection. When to use: When generalization to unseen scenes is required and multiple source views are available. When not to use: When only a single view is available or when per-scene optimization with unlimited time is feasible and generalization is not needed. Origin: Introduced by Fangfu Liu, Chubin Zhang, Yu Zheng, and Yueqi Duan from Tsinghua University in March 2023. History: S-Ray was proposed to address the limitations of Semantic-NeRF, which trains one specific model for each scene and relies on positional encoding prone to overfitting. S-Ray trains one unified model on multiple scenes and generalizes to unseen scenes. Usage: Evaluated on synthetic scenes from the Replica dataset and real-world scenes from the ScanNet dataset. Semantic Ray: Learning a Generalizable Semantic Field with Cross-Reprojection Attention, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.01668, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Neural Density-Distance Fields
head: Neural Density-Distance Fields (NeDDF) Architecture
body:
Neural Density-Distance Fields (NeDDF) is a neural network architecture that represents a scene using a reciprocally constrained distance and density field, extending the signed distance field formulation to adapt to arbitrary density distributions. Unlike standard NeRF which predicts density directly, NeDDF predicts a distance field D and derives density \sigma from its first spatial derivative, allowing for boundaryless scenes and complex shapes while providing stable mesh extraction. It sets itself apart from siblings like Signed Distance Function (SDF) Representations by handling translucent and thin surfaces through volumetric depth rather than hard boundaries, and from DoF-NeRF by explicitly linking the distance gradient to the viewing direction for reprojection-based localization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D position \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and viewing direction \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Outputs: Distance field value D(\mathbf{p}), auxiliary gradient component  rac{\partial D}{\partial w}, and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}). Density \sigma(\mathbf{p}) is derived from D and 
abla D. Data Structures and Layout: The network consists of two parallel MLP branches with a width of 256 neurons per hidden layer. 1. Distance Branch: Input: Concatenated positional encodings (size 144). Layers: Dense(256) ightarrow Activation ightarrow Dense(256) ightarrow Activation ightarrow Dense(256) ightarrow Activation. Output: D (scalar) and  rac{\partial D}{\partial w} (scalar). 2. Color Branch: Input: Concatenated positional encodings (size 144). Layers: Dense(256) ightarrow Activation ightarrow Dense(256) ightarrow Activation ightarrow Dense(256) ightarrow Activation ightarrow Dense(128) ightarrow Activation. Output: \mathbf{c} (vector, size 3). Positional Encoding (PE): Standard PE \gamma(\mathbf{p}) and damped PE \gamma'(\mathbf{p}) are used. Let L be the number of frequency bands. Standard PE \gamma(\mathbf{p}) (size 2 	imes 3 	imes L = 6L): \gamma(\mathbf{p}) = [\sin(\mathbf{p}), \cos(\mathbf{p}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1}\mathbf{p}), \cos(2^{L-1}\mathbf{p})]^T Damped PE \gamma'(\mathbf{p}) (size 6L): \gamma'(\mathbf{p}) = [\sin(\mathbf{p}), \cos(\mathbf{p}), \dots,  rac{1}{2^{L-1}}\sin(2^{L-1}\mathbf{p}),  rac{1}{2^{L-1}}\cos(2^{L-1}\mathbf{p})]^T High-frequency terms are dampened by 1/2^{L-1} to maintain scale consistency in the differentiation hierarchy. Directional PE \gamma(\mathbf{d}) (size 6L) is concatenated for the color branch. The input to the MLPs is the concatenation: [\gamma(\mathbf{p}), \gamma(\mathbf{d}), \gamma'(\mathbf{p})]. Note: The source diagram shows \gamma(\mathbf{p}) size 60, \gamma(\mathbf{d}) size 24, \gamma'(\mathbf{p}) size 60, implying L=10 for position and L=4 for direction, or specific configurations. We use the general formula. Activation Function: The network uses tanhExp activation, chosen because its second derivative is continuous, which is required for the objective function involving density field gradients. Density Calculation: Density \sigma(\mathbf{p}) is derived from the distance field D(\mathbf{p}) and its gradient 
abla D(\mathbf{p}). 1. Compute the gradient 
abla D(\mathbf{p}) = [ rac{\partial D}{\partial px},  rac{\partial D}{\partial py},  rac{\partial D}{\partial pz}]^T. 2. Calculate density using the approximation (assuming near field tn \approx 0): \sigma(\mathbf{p}) \simeq  rac{1 - \|
abla D(\mathbf{p})\|2}{D(\mathbf{p})} Auxiliary Gradient for Cusp Handling: To handle discontinuities in the distance field gradient at cusps, the domain is extended to 4D hyperspace [x, y, z, w] with an auxiliary gradient axis w. The slice at w=0 is the distance field. The network outputs  rac{\partial D}{\partial w}. The optimal view direction \mathbf{v}n is recovered from the gradient: \mathbf{v}n = - rac{
abla D(\mathbf{p})}{\|

abla Di}{\|

The reprojection error is the distance between the pixel coordinate \mathbf{q} and the projected pseudo-correspondence point \hat{\mathbf{q}}. Training Objectives: 1. Photometric Loss: Standard color difference between rendered and observed images. 2. Auxiliary Gradient Constraint (L{const}): L{\mathrm{const}} =  rac{\lambda{\mathrm{const}}}{M} \sum{\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{P}}  eta \left[ rac{\partial^2 D}{\partial t \partial w} -  rac{\alpha}{D(\mathbf{p})}  rac{\partial D}{\partial w}ight]^2 where  eta = D \left( rac{\partial D}{\partial t}ight)^2  rac{\partial D}{\partial w} is separated from the calculation graph (stop-gradient). 3. name: LAENeRF
head: Local Appearance Editing for Neural Radiance Fields
body: LAENeRF is a unified framework for the photorealistic and non-photorealistic local appearance editing of pre-trained Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs). It solves the problem of applying recoloring or stylization to arbitrary 3D regions while minimizing background artifacts and maintaining interactivity. Unlike methods that rely on semantic segmentation or global style transfer, LAENeRF uses a 3D edit grid for spatial selection and learns a palette-based color decomposition mapped from estimated ray terminations. It is distinguished by its ability to model smooth transitions between edited and unedited regions using a growing queue mechanism and its efficient distillation process that transfers edits back to the original radiance field parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained NeRF model \Theta{NeRF} (parameterized by MLPs predicting density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}), a set of training rays R, and a user-defined selection mask E (the edit grid). Output: An edited radiance field where the region defined by E is recolored or stylized, with smooth transitions to the surrounding geometry. Data Structures: 1. Edit Grid (E): A 3D voxel grid of resolution 128^3. It acts as a bitfield where bits are set to 1 for voxels containing selected content. It is a subset of the occupancy grid O from Instant-NGP. 2. Growing Queue (G): A queue storing direct neighbors of voxels in E to facilitate region growing and smooth transition modeling. 3. Growing Grid (\mathcal{G}): A grid constructed from the final state of G, used to compute transition weights. 4. LAENeRF Module Parameters (\Theta{LAENeRF}): Color Palette (\hat{P}): A learnable tensor of shape \mathbb{R}^{NP \times 3}, where NP is the number of base colors (initialized to 8). Hash Grid Encoder: A trainable multi-resolution hash grid (from Instant-NGP) encoding spatial positions. MLPs: Shallow networks taking encoded positions and view directions to predict weights \hat{w} and offsets \hat{\delta}. Numbered Steps: 1. Region Selection: The user scribbles on the 2D projection of the scene. For each selected pixel, a ray is cast through the pre-trained NeRF. The estimated ray termination x{term} is computed (see Formula 1). Each x{term} is mapped to the nearest voxel in E, setting the corresponding bit in the underlying bitfield to 1. 2. Region Growing: To enable smooth transitions, a growing queue G stores direct neighbors of voxels in E. During region growing, the current voxel is added to E and its neighbors to G if the occupancy grid O is set (O=1). This process continues until the user stops or a condition is met, creating a boundary zone for blending. 3. Featurization and Color Prediction: For rays intersecting E, the estimated ray termination x{term} is featurized using the trainable multi-resolution hash grid to produce \xi(x{term}). This is passed to shallow MLPs along with a spherical harmonics encoding of the viewing direction d to predict: Per-ray barycentric weights \hat{w} \in [0, 1]^{NP}. View-dependent offsets \hat{\delta} \in [-1, 1]^3. The predicted color \hat{c} is composed using the learnable palette \hat{P}: \hat{c} = \text{clamp}(\hat{w}^T \hat{P} + \hat{\delta}) where \text{clamp}(\cdot) restricts values to [0, 1]. 4. Optimization: The LAENeRF module is optimized by minimizing a composite loss function over a set of rays R. The pipeline is fully differentiable. The total loss includes: Content Loss: L{content} = \|\hat{c} - \mathcal{C}(r)\|2^2, where \mathcal{C}(r) is the ground truth color. Style Loss (Optional): L{style} = \lambda{style} \|G(s) - G(\hat{c})\|2^2, where s is a style image and G(\cdot) is the Gram matrix of features from a semantic encoder (e.g., VGG19 conv5, conv6, conv7). Total Variation Loss: L{TV} = \lambda{TV} \|\nabla \hat{c} \cdot (1 - \text{depth\guide})\|2^2, restricting smoothing to regions without depth discontinuities. Depth Discontinuity Loss: L{depth-disc} = -\lambda{depth-disc} \|\nabla \hat{c} \cdot \text{depth\guide}\|2^2, encouraging gradients at depth edges. Offset Loss: L{offset} = \lambda{offset} \|\hat{\delta}\|2^2, preventing extreme high-frequency offsets. Palette Regularization: L{palette} = \|\lfloor \hat{P} \rfloor \cdot \hat{P}\|2^2, ensuring valid RGB colors. Weight Loss: L{weight} = \lambda{weight} (1 - \|\hat{w}\|\infty), encouraging sparse weight usage. Smooth Transition Loss (Optional): L{smooth} = \lambda{smooth} \|(\hat{c} - c)^2 \cdot d{trans}\|1, applied when d{trans} \in (0, 1]. 5. Distillation/Transfer: After training \Theta{LAENeRF}, changes are transferred to \Theta{NeRF} via distillation. A modified training dataset is created where the target color is T\alpha \hat{c} + (1-T\alpha)\mathcal{C}(r). Rays not intersecting E use the ground truth color \mathcal{C}(r). The pre-trained NeRF is fine-tuned using this dataset for 7 \times 10^4 iterations. Formulas: 1. Estimated Depth: \zeta = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) t{i+1} where Ti is transmittance, \sigmai is density, \deltai = t{i+1} - ti, and t{i+1} is the next sample position. 2. Ray Termination: x{term} = o + \zeta d where o is the camera position and d is the viewing direction. 3. Accumulated Alpha in Edit Grid: T\alpha = \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbbm{1}(o + ti d \in E) Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) where \mathbbm{1}(\cdot) is the indicator function. Rays are only processed if T\alpha > \tau{edit} (default 0.5). 4. Transition Weight: d{trans} = 1 - \frac{\min(d{min}, \tau{dist})}{\tau{dist}} where d{min} is the minimum distance from x{term} to the growing grid \mathcal{G}, and \tau{dist} controls transition size (default 1 \times 10^{-2}). 5. Depth Guide: (\text{depth\guide}){i,j} = \left( |\text{depth}{i,j+1} - \text{depth}{i,j}|, |\text{depth}{i+1,j} - \text{depth}{i,j}| \right) Used to mask Total Variation and Depth Discontinuity losses. Parameters: Edit Grid Resolution: 128^3. Initial Palette Size (NP): 8. Edit Threshold (\tau{edit}): 0.5. Transition Size (\tau{dist}): 1 \times 10^{-2}. Learning Rate: 1 \times 10^{-3} for all components except \hat{P} (1 \times 10^{-2}). LAENeRF Training Iterations: 1 \times 10^5. Distillation Iterations: 7 \times 10^4. Style Weight (\lambda{style}): 1.3 \times 10^2 for stylization, 0 for recoloring. TV Weight (\lambda{TV}): 1 \times 10^{-4}. Depth Disc Weight (\lambda{depth-disc}): 5 \times 10^{-4}. Weight Loss (\lambda{weight}): 1 \times 10^{-7}. Offset Loss (\lambda{offset}): 5 \times 10^{-5}. Smooth Loss (\lambda{smooth}): 1 \times 10^{-3}. Pitfalls: Small Structure Loss: Naive stylization using only L{content} and L{style} eliminates small structures. Geometry Noise: Imperfect geometry in the pre-trained NeRF causes noise in x{term}, requiring regularization (L{TV}, L{offset}). Boundary Discontinuities: Sharp color changes occur at the boundary of E if adjacent cells are occupied; mitigated by the growing queue and L{smooth}. Palette Pruning: Color palettes that do not contribute significantly should be removed after 1.5 \times 10^3 iterations. A stylization technique that respects the learned geometry of the pre-trained NeRF by performing depth estimation to counteract the removal of small structures common in naive 2D style transfer. It achieves this by training LAENeRF without L{style}, L{offset}, and L{TV} for the first 1000 iterations to achieve a well-initialized palette \hat{P} before applying geometry-aware losses. Time Complexity: The method is interactive, with previews available after \sim 20 seconds of LAENeRF optimization. Distillation takes no longer than 5 minutes on an NVIDIA RTX 4090. Memory Complexity: Uses a lightweight NeRF-like network and a 128^3 edit grid, significantly reducing memory requirements compared to full scene re-optimization. Performance: LAENeRF reduces background MSE error rates by 59% compared to PaletteNeRF with semantic guidance on the LLFF dataset. It introduces fewer background artifacts than Ref-NPR and is the only compared method capable of modeling smooth transitions between original and edited content. Strengths: Interactive local editing, smooth transitions, low background artifacts, unified recoloring/stylization. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the pre-trained NeRF's geometry; imperfect geometry leads to noise in ray terminations. LAENeRF was proposed by Lukas Radl, Michael Steiner, Andreas Kurz, and Markus Steinberger from Graz University of Technology. It was published in CVPR 2024 (arXiv:2312.09913v2, March 25, 2024). The method builds on NeRFShop for region selection and Instant-NGP for the hash grid encoder, implementing on the torch-ngp framework. It is evaluated on NeRF-Synthetic, LLFF, and mip-NeRF 360 datasets. name: ExtremeNeRF
head: Few-shot NeRF under varying-illumination, NeRF Extreme
body: ExtremeNeRF is a few-shot view synthesis framework designed to generate novel views from sparse multi-view images captured under unconstrained, varying illumination. Unlike standard NeRF methods that require dense input views and consistent lighting, ExtremeNeRF achieves illumination robustness by enforcing multi-view albedo consistency, supported by geometric alignment. It distinguishes itself from other few-shot methods (e.g., RegNeRF, FreeNeRF) by utilizing a two-stage intrinsic decomposition pipeline (FIDNet and PIDNet) to guide NeRF optimization, allowing it to work effectively with significantly fewer input images (e.g., 3 views) while maintaining high geometric fidelity. ExtremeNeRF builds on the standard NeRF architecture Parent by integrating an intrinsic decomposition module that separates albedo (illumination-invariant surface color) from shading (illumination-dependent effects). The method operates in two stages: an offline intrinsic decomposition of input images and an online patch-wise decomposition during NeRF training. Inputs: A set of N input images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N with known camera poses (Ki, Ti) and intrinsics Ki, captured under varying illumination. The number of views N is small (e.g., N=3). Outputs: A trained NeRF model F\Theta capable of rendering novel views \hat{c}(x) and depth maps \hat{d}(x) for arbitrary camera poses, along with estimated albedo maps. 1. NeRF Model (F\Theta): Standard MLP mapping 3D position \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} to density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} [Parent]. 2. FIDNet: A pre-trained Full-image Intrinsic Decomposition Network (based on IIDWW) used offline. It takes an input image I and outputs a pseudo-albedo map a{gt}(x). 3. PIDNet: A Patch-wise Intrinsic Decomposition Network used online. It takes a patch of synthesized color \hat{c}(x) and outputs estimated albedo \hat{a}(x) and shading \hat{s}(x). 4. Camera Parameters: Intrinsics K \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} and extrinsics T \in SE(3) for each view. 1. Offline Albedo Extraction (FIDNet): For each input image Ii, apply FIDNet to extract the global context-aware pseudo-albedo ground truth a{gt}(x). This step is performed before NeRF training begins. 2. NeRF Optimization Loop: For each training iteration: a. Ray Sampling: Sample rays from novel view camera poses. Render color \hat{c}(x) and depth \hat{d}(x) using the NeRF model. b. Color Loss: Compute the mean squared error between rendered color \hat{c}(x) and ground-truth color c{gt}(x) for sampled pixels S: L{color} = \sum{x \in S} \|\hat{c}(x) - c{gt}(x)\|^22 c. Patch-wise Intrinsic Decomposition (PIDNet): Extract patches of size S{patch} \times S{patch} from the rendered novel view color \hat{c}(x). Feed these patches into PIDNet to estimate albedo \hat{a}(x) and shading \hat{s}(x). d. Albedo Consistency Loss (L{ac}): Enforce that the albedo extracted from the novel view \hat{a}(x) matches the pseudo-albedo a{gt}(x') from the corresponding input view pixel x'. This requires geometric alignment (Step 3) to find the correspondence x'. e. Geometric Alignment: Map pixel x in the novel view to pixel x' in the input view using the rendered depth \hat{d}(x): xw = T \hat{d}(x) K^{-1} \bar{x} x' = (K' T'^{-1} T) \hat{d}(x) K^{-1} \bar{x} where \bar{x} = [x^T, 1]^T is the homogeneous coordinate, T, K are the novel view pose/intrinsics, and T', K' are the input view pose/intrinsics. f. Visibility Mask Weight (\omega(x)): Calculate a weight to exclude invalid correspondences caused by occlusions or large projection errors. Define projection error E{proj}(x') as the squared difference between rendered depth \hat{d}(x) and projected depth \tilde{d}(x'): E{proj}(x') = (\hat{d}(x) - \tilde{d}(x'))^2 The weight is: \omega(x) = re \left( 1 - \frac{E{proj}(x')}{M{proj}} \right) where re is an error rate coefficient that diminishes toward the end of training, and M{proj} is the maximum projection error. g. Depth Consistency Loss (L{dc}): Regularize the projection error between adjacent pixels to prevent smoothing of unrelated surfaces due to occlusions: L{dc} = \sum{x' \in P'} \sum{y \in N(x')} (E{proj}(y) - E{proj}(x'))^2 where P' is the set of pixels in the input view and N(x') are the 4-neighbor adjacent pixels of x'. h. Total Loss: Combine L{color}, L{ac} (weighted by \omega(x)), L{dc}, and additional regularizations (L{ds}, L{edge}, L{pid}, L{chrom}, frequency regularization). i. Update: Update NeRF parameters \Theta and PIDNet parameters using the total loss. Intrinsic Decomposition (Lambertian): \log c(x) = \log a(x) + \log s(x). Intrinsic Decomposition (Real-world): \log c(x) = \log a(x) + \log s(x) + l + R, where l is light color vector and R is non-Lambertian residuals. Projection Error: E{proj}(x') = (\hat{d}(x) - \tilde{d}(x'))^2. Visibility Mask Weight: \omega(x) = re (1 - E{proj}(x')/M{proj}). Pixel Correspondence: x' = (K' T'^{-1} T) \hat{d}(x) K^{-1} \bar{x}. 3D Point Projection: xw = T \hat{d}(x) K^{-1} \bar{x}. Inverse Projection: x = K T^{-1} xw. Spatch: Patch size for PIDNet input/output, set to 32 \times 32. Training Resolution: Image size used for training is 300 \times 400. Training Duration: 70,000 iterations per scene. Hardware: 4 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Error Rate Coefficient (re): Diminishes toward the end of training to reduce the number of pairs enforced for cross-view consistency as geometry improves. Maximum Projection Error (M{proj}): Threshold for visibility mask calculation. Projective Transformation Errors: Incorrect synthesized depth values lead to projection errors. The visibility mask \omega(x) handles cases where alignment fails. Occlusions: Projection errors caused by scene geometry (occlusions) must be distinguished from floating artifacts. The weight \omega(x) diminishes re toward the end criteria to rectify inaccurate geometry alignments while occlusions persist. Direct Minimization of E{proj}: Directly minimizing projection error is counterproductive due to occlusion smoothing unrelated surface depths. Instead, L{dc} regularizes the projection error between adjacent pixels. FIDNet Substitution: Replacing FIDNet with other intrinsic decomposition models (e.g., Das, Karaoglu, and Gevers 2022) shows degraded performance, indicating FIDNet is a suitable guide for cross-view consistency. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainextremeneRF(inputimages, inputposes, inputintrinsics, novelviewposes, novelviewintrinsics): """ Trains ExtremeNeRF using the two-stage intrinsic decomposition pipeline. """ # Stage 1: Offline Albedo Extraction pseudoalbedogroundtruths = [] for img in inputimages: # FIDNet extracts global context-aware pseudo-albedo agt = FIDNet(img) pseudoalbedogroundtruths.append(agt) # Initialize NeRF and PIDNet nerfmodel = NeRF() pidnet = PIDNet() # Parameters spatch = 32 trainingiterations = 70000 re = 1.0 # Error rate coefficient, diminishes over time Mproj = 100.0 # Maximum projection error (example value) for iteration in range(trainingiterations): # Decay re toward end of training currentre = re (1.0 - iteration / trainingiterations) # Sample rays from novel views rays = samplerays(novelviewposes) # Render color and depth renderedcolor, rendereddepth = nerfmodel.forward(rays) # Compute Color Loss Lcolor = meansquarederror(renderedcolor, groundtruthcolor) # Patch-wise Intrinsic Decomposition patches = extractpatches(renderedcolor, size=spatch) estimatedalbedo, estimatedshading = pidnet.forward(patches) # Geometric Alignment and Visibility Mask Lac = 0.0 Ldc = 0.0 for x in novelviewpixels: # Map novel view pixel x to input view pixel x' xhomogeneous = [x.x, x.y, 1.0] xw = transformtoworld(novelviewposes, novelviewintrinsics, rendereddepth[x], xhomogeneous) xprime = transformtoinputview(inputposes, inputintrinsics, xw) # Calculate Projection Error projecteddepth = getprojecteddepth(inputposes, inputintrinsics, xw) Eproj = (rendereddepth[x] - projecteddepth) 2 # Visibility Mask Weight if xprime is withinfov(inputimages) and Eproj < Mproj: omega = currentre (1.0 - Eproj / Mproj) # Albedo Consistency Loss agtprime = pseudoalbedogroundtruths[inputviewindex][xprime] aest = estimatedalbedo[x] Lac += omega (aest - agtprime) 2 else: omega = 0.0 # Depth Consistency Loss (for adjacent pixels) if xprime is valid: for neighbor in get4neighbors(xprime): Eprojneighbor = calculateprojectionerror(inputposes, inputintrinsics, neighbor) Ldc += (Eprojneighbor - Eproj) 2 # Total Loss Ltotal = Lcolor + Lac + Ldc + Lregularization # Update parameters update(nerfmodel, Ltotal) update(pidnet, Ltotal) Training Time: ExtremeNeRF requires approximately 1.5 hours for 3 views on 4 NVIDIA A100 GPUs, compared to 2.4 hours for RegNeRF and 2 hours for FreeNeRF. Most other few-shot NeRF methods require 10 to 20 hours. Memory: Uses standard NeRF memory plus overhead for FIDNet and PIDNet. Strengths: Works with very few input images (few-shot) under unconstrained illumination; achieves better geometry details than baselines that struggle with inconsistent illumination. Limitations: Relies on the quality of FIDNet; replacing FIDNet with other intrinsic decomposition models degrades performance. Performance may be limited by the accuracy of depth estimation in the presence of occlusions. When to Use: When input data is sparse (few views) and illumination varies significantly across views. When Not to Use: When dense input views are available and illumination is consistent (standard NeRF is sufficient); when real-time inference is required (training time is non-trivial). ExtremeNeRF was introduced in the paper "Few-Shot Neural Radiance Fields under Unconstrained Illumination" presented at the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence in 2024. It addresses the limitation of existing NeRF methods that require extensive multi-view images under constrained illumination. The method builds upon the concept of intrinsic image decomposition, separating albedo and shading, and applies it to the NeRF optimization process to handle varying illumination in few-shot settings. It utilizes the NeRF Extreme benchmark, the first in-the-wild benchmark for novel view synthesis under varying illumination. name: Conditional and Latent Representations
head: Conditional NeRF, Disentangled Conditional NeRF, CLIP-NeRF
body: Conditional and Latent Representations extend the standard NeRF Parent to model an entire object category (e.g., chairs) rather than a single static scene, using instance-specific latent vectors for shape and appearance. This approach solves the problem of efficiently representing diverse 3D instances within a unified model, enabling editing and generation without training separate models per instance. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly decoupling shape and appearance into separate learned codes, often utilizing a shared shape branch or deformation networks to enforce geometric consistency and prevent mutual interference between geometry and color. The core mechanism involves a neural network F that maps a 3D location \mathbf{x}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and instance-specific latent codes to volumetric density \sigma and radiance \mathbf{c}. The latent codes are typically split into a shape code \mathbf{z}^{(s)} and an appearance/color code \mathbf{z}^{(c)}. 1. Latent Code Injection: The latent codes are injected into the network to condition the output. In standard conditional formulations, \mathbf{z}^{(s)} and \mathbf{z}^{(c)} are concatenated with positional and directional encodings. In disentangled variants, \mathbf{z}^{(s)} is used to deform the positional encoding of \mathbf{x}, while \mathbf{z}^{(c)} is deferred to the radiance prediction to ensure shape and appearance are independent. 2. Rendering: The rendering process follows standard volume rendering Parent. For a ray r, Nc points \{ti\} are sampled. Density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i are computed using F. The pixel color \hat{C} is computed via alpha compositing: \hat{C}(r, \mathbf{z}^{(s)}, \mathbf{z}^{(c)}) = \sum{i=1}^{Nc} \mathbf{c}i \alphai \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) where \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) and \deltai = t{i+1} - ti. 3. Disentanglement: The density output \sigma is designed to be independent of the viewing direction \mathbf{d}, while radiance \mathbf{c} depends on both \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{d}. Disentanglement is achieved either by architectural separation (shared shape branch vs. instance-specific branches) or by deformation networks that map \mathbf{z}^{(s)} to displacement vectors for positional encodings. A method for modeling shape and appearance variations across multiple 3D instances by training a single unified radiance field conditioned on instance-specific latent codes. It solves the problem of efficiently representing a dataset of diverse objects without training separate NeRF models for each, while maintaining rendering quality comparable to independent per-instance models. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly decoupling shape and appearance into separate learned codes and utilizing a shared shape branch to enforce geometric consistency across instances. The Conditional Radiance Field with Shared Branch is a neural radiance field architecture designed for shape and color disentanglement, enabling efficient editing by allowing specific submodules to be finetuned. It maps a 3D location \mathbf{x}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and instance-specific shape code \mathbf{z}^{(s)} and color code \mathbf{z}^{(c)} to radiance \mathbf{c} and scalar density \sigma. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF Parent by introducing a modular structure with a shared shape branch and instance-specific branches, rather than a single monolithic MLP or simple input concatenation. Conditional NeRF is a generative model for a specific object category that maps 5D coordinates (spatial position \mathbf{x} and view direction \mathbf{v}) along with dedicated latent vectors for shape (\mathbf{z}s) and appearance (\mathbf{z}a) to volumetric density \sigma and view-dependent radiance \mathbf{c}. It differs from standard NeRF by replacing the single-scene optimization with a category-level generative process controlled by explicit latent codes, and it distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Conditional Radiance Field Training by enforcing disentanglement: shape conditioning is applied via volumetric deformation of positional encodings, while appearance conditioning is deferred to the radiance prediction network to prevent mutual interference between shape and color. Definition: A neural network representation that extends NeRF to model an entire object class (e.g., chairs) rather than a single scene, using latent vectors for shape and appearance to allow editing. The network F takes a 3D location \mathbf{x}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and instance-specific latent vectors \mathbf{z}^{(s)} and \mathbf{z}^{(c)} to output radiance \mathbf{c} and density \sigma. The density output \sigma is independent of the viewing direction, while the radiance output \mathbf{c} depends on both position and viewing direction. The network F is parametrized as a multi-layer perceptron (MLP). Step: Sample Nc 3D points \{ti\}{i=1}^{Nc} along a cast ray r from pixel location, ordered near to far. Compute radiance \mathbf{c}i and density \sigmai at each sampled point ti using network F. Formula: Alpha compositing value: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), where \deltai = t{i+1} - ti is the distance between adjacent samples. Parameter: \mathbf{x}: 3D location vector (x, y, z); \mathbf{d}: viewing direction vector (\phi, \theta); \mathbf{z}^{(c)}: latent color (appearance) vector. Definition: A technique to achieve gradual editing of shape and appearance by scaling the editing direction vectors in the latent space using a scalar factor. Formula: \mathbf{z}s = s \times \Delta \mathbf{z}s + \mathbf{z}{s0}, \mathbf{z}a = s \times \Delta \mathbf{z}a + \mathbf{z}{a0}, where s is a scalar, \mathbf{z}s and \mathbf{z}a are the updated shape and appearance codes, \mathbf{z}{s0} and \mathbf{z}{a0} are the original codes, and \Delta \mathbf{z}s and \Delta \mathbf{z}a are the manipulation directions provided by the code mappers. Parameter: Scalar s: Controls the intensity of the edit. Typical range: 0 to 1.6 with step 0.2. Effect: Manipulation strength increases as s increases. Usage: Used for continuous editing of both shape and appearance given a single text prompt or exemplar, allowing users to adjust the degree of change. Step: 1. Extract CLIP feature embedding from input text prompt or exemplar image. 2. Feed embedding into two separate feed-forward code mappers (shape mapper and appearance mapper). 3. Mappers output local displacements in the latent space to update \mathbf{z}s and \mathbf{z}a. 4. Render image with updated codes. 5. Train mappers using a CLIP-based matching loss to enforce CLIP space consistency between input constraint and output renderings. Comparison: Differs from optimization-based editing (e.g., EditNeRF) by using learned feed-forward networks mapping user edits to latent codes, enabling fast inference for interactive editing instead of slow iterative optimization per sample. Step: Stage 2: Fix generator weights and train CLIP manipulation parts (shape mapper Ms and appearance mapper Ma). Sampling for mapper training: Randomly sample \mathbf{z}s from Zs, \mathbf{z}a from Za, \mathbf{v} from Zv, and text prompt t from pre-defined text library T. All network weights except mappers are fixed (denoted with hat). Formula: Shape mapper loss L{shape}: L{shape} = f(\hat{D}(\hat{F}\theta(\mathbf{v}, Ms(\hat{E}t(t)) + \mathbf{z}s), \mathbf{z}a)) + \lambdac D{CLIP}(\hat{F}\theta(\mathbf{v}, Ms(\hat{E}t(t)) + \mathbf{z}s), \mathbf{z}a, t). Appearance mapper loss L{appear}: L{appear} = f(\hat{D}(\hat{F}\theta(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{z}s, Ma(\hat{E}t(t)) + \mathbf{z}a))) + \lambdac D{CLIP}(\hat{F}\theta(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{z}s, Ma(\hat{E}t(t)) + \mathbf{z}a), t). Parameter: \lambdac is the weight for the CLIP distance term in the mapper losses. Conditional NeRF was introduced by Chan et al. in 2021, building upon the original NeRF representation [45] to enable editing over entire shape classes like "chairs". The method learns a conditional radiance field model extended with latent vectors over shape and appearance, trained over a set of shapes belonging to a class. CLIP-NeRF, introduced in 2022, extended this framework by integrating the CLIP model [34] to learn code mappers that map CLIP features to the latent space, enabling text-and-image driven manipulation. This allowed for fast inference for interactive editing and supported global deformation, differing from previous methods like EditNeRF [21] which relied on user scribbles and iterative optimization. The approach has been used for high-resolution NeRF manipulation and text-driven 3D content generation. name: Conditional Radiance Field Training
head: Conditional NeRF, Instance-conditioned NeRF
body: Conditional Radiance Field Training is a method for modeling shape and appearance variations across multiple 3D instances by jointly optimizing a single neural radiance field with instance-specific latent codes. It differs from standard NeRF by replacing the implicit instance identity with explicit, learnable shape and color codes that condition the network's output, allowing for efficient multi-instance reconstruction and editing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A dataset of K instances, where each instance k has a set of training rays Rk. Each ray r consists of origin, direction, and ground truth color C(r). Output: A conditional radiance field model consisting of two networks (F{coarse}, F{fine}) and K pairs of latent codes (\mathbf{z}k^{(s)}, \mathbf{z}k^{(c)}). Data Structures: Latent Codes: For each instance k \in \{1, \dots, K\}, two learned vectors are maintained: Shape code \mathbf{z}k^{(s)}: 32-dimensional. Color code \mathbf{z}k^{(c)}: 32-dimensional. Note: An ablation variant uses a single 64-dimensional code for both. Networks: Two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), F{coarse} and F{fine}, each 4 layers deep with 256 channels. They use ReLU activations. F{coarse}: Estimates density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} for coarse sampling. F{fine}: Estimates density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} for fine sampling. Architecture details: The networks use skip connections from the input position to the output. The shape code is embedded and concatenated with the positional encoding. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize F{coarse}, F{fine}, and the latent codes \mathbf{z}k^{(s)}, \mathbf{z}k^{(c)} for all k=1 \dots K. 2. Iteration Loop: Repeat until convergence (average 1M iterations): 1. Sample Instance: Randomly select an instance index k \in \{1, \dots, K\}. 2. Retrieve Codes: Obtain the shape code \mathbf{z}k^{(s)} and color code \mathbf{z}k^{(c)} for instance k. 3. Sample Rays: Sample a batch of training rays r from the set Rk belonging to instance k. 4. Coarse Rendering: For each ray r, use stratified sampling to generate points. Compute positional encodings for the points. Concatenate the shape code \mathbf{z}k^{(s)} and color code \mathbf{z}k^{(c)} with the encoded position and viewing direction \mathbf{d}. Pass through F{coarse} to get density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Render coarse color \hat{C}{coarse}(r, \mathbf{z}k^{(s)}, \mathbf{z}k^{(c)}) using volume rendering. 5. Hierarchical Sampling: Use the density outputs from F{coarse} to sample a hierarchical volume (importance sampling) for the fine network. 6. Fine Rendering: Pass the fine samples through F{fine} using the same conditioning codes \mathbf{z}k^{(s)}, \mathbf{z}k^{(c)}. Render fine color \hat{C}{fine}(r, \mathbf{z}k^{(s)}, \mathbf{z}k^{(c)}). 7. Loss Calculation: Compute the photometric loss L{train}: L{train} = \sum{k=1}^{K} \sum{r \in Rk} \left( \|\hat{C}{coarse}(r, \mathbf{z}k^{(s)}, \mathbf{z}k^{(c)}) - C(r)\|2^2 + \|\hat{C}{fine}(r, \mathbf{z}k^{(s)}, \mathbf{z}k^{(c)}) - C(r)\|2^2 \right) 8. Optimization: Update F{coarse}, F{fine}, and all latent codes \mathbf{z}k^{(s)}, \mathbf{z}k^{(c)} using the Adam optimizer. Parameters: Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 10^{-4} for training. Adam Hyperparameters: \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.999, \epsilon = 10^{-8}. Training Duration: Until convergence, averaging 1M iterations. Code Dimensionality: 32 dimensions for shape and 32 for color. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Disentanglement: The method relies on separate shape and color codes to prevent appearance from affecting geometry estimation. Using a single combined code (64-dim) yields lower performance than separate codes. Parameter Count: Ablation studies must increase layer widths to keep the total parameter count approximately equal across different architectural choices (e.g., shared vs. separate branches) to ensure fair comparison. Editing Stability: During editing, the coarse network is kept fixed, and only the fine network and codes are optimized with a higher learning rate (10^{-2}) for 100 iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def trainconditionalnerf(instances, raysperinstance, numiterations=1000000): """ instances: List of K instance objects. raysperinstance: Function or list providing rays Rk for each instance k. """ K = len(instances) # Initialize networks (4 layers, 256 channels, ReLU, skip connections) Fcoarse = initializemlp(4, 256) Ffine = initializemlp(4, 256) # Initialize latent codes (32-dim each) zshape = np.random.randn(K, 32) zcolor = np.random.randn(K, 32) # Optimizer state for Adam optimizer = Adam(Fcoarse.parameters(), lr=1e-4, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, eps=1e-8) optimizer.addparameters(Ffine.parameters()) optimizer.addparameters(zshape) optimizer.addparameters(zcolor) for iteration in range(numiterations): # 1. Sample instance k = np.random.randint(0, K) # 2. Retrieve codes zks = zshape[k] zkc = zcolor[k] # 3. Sample rays for instance k batchrays = samplerays(raysperinstance[k]) totalloss = 0.0 for r in batchrays: # 4. Coarse Rendering # Stratified sampling for coarse points coarsepoints = stratifiedsampleray(r) # Encode position and direction posenc = positionalencoding(coarsepoints) direnc = directionalencoding(r.direction) # Condition with latent codes # Concatenate shape code with posenc, color code with direnc/posenc as per standard NeRF injection # Note: Source says "injected wherever positional or directional embeddings are injected" inputcoarse = concatenate(posenc, zks, direnc, zkc) sigmacoarse, ccoarse = Fcoarse(inputcoarse) Chatcoarse = volumerendering(coarsepoints, sigmacoarse, ccoarse) # 5. Hierarchical Sampling # Use sigmacoarse to sample fine points finepoints = hierarchicalsample(r, sigmacoarse) # 6. Fine Rendering posencfine = positionalencoding(finepoints) inputfine = concatenate(posencfine, zks, direnc, zkc) sigmafine, cfine = Ffine(inputfine) Chatfine = volumerendering(finepoints, sigmafine, cfine) # 7. Loss gtcolor = r.color loss = np.sum((Chatcoarse - gtcolor)2) + np.sum((Chatfine - gtcolor)2) totalloss += loss # 8. Optimization optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return Fcoarse, Ffine, zshape, zcolor Performance: On the PhotoShapes dataset, the method matches the performance of training independent NeRF models for each instance. Scalability: The method scales well to large numbers of instances; training with all 626 instances of the PhotoShapes dataset achieves high reconstruction quality. Metrics: Evaluated using PSNR and LPIPS. Strengths: Jointly models shape and appearance differences; allows for editing by optimizing latent codes. Limitations: Requires joint optimization of codes and network weights, which can be sensitive to hyperparameters. Origin: Introduced in "Editing Conditional Radiance Fields" (ICCV 2021). Development: The method builds upon the original NeRF architecture and ablates various conditioning strategies (single code vs. separate shape/color codes, shared vs. separate branches). Usage: Used for modeling multi-instance 3D objects (e.g., chairs) and enabling appearance editing. name: Conditional Radiance Field with Shared Branch
head: CRF with Shared Branch, Modular Conditional Radiance Field
body: The Conditional Radiance Field with Shared Branch is a neural radiance field architecture designed for shape and color disentanglement, enabling efficient instance-specific editing by allowing specific submodules to be fine-tuned independently. It maps a 3D location \mathbf{x}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and instance-specific latent codes to volumetric density \sigma and radiance \mathbf{c}. Unlike standard conditional formulations that concatenate all latent codes with positional encodings, this method separates the shape representation into a category-specific shared branch and an instance-specific branch, improving view synthesis quality and scalability to multiple instances. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D position \mathbf{x}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, instance-specific shape code \mathbf{z}^{(s)}, instance-specific color code \mathbf{z}^{(c)}. Outputs: Scalar density \sigma, radiance vector \mathbf{c}. Data Structures: The network consists of five Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), all configured identically unless specified: F{\text{share}}: Shared shape network. F{\text{inst}}: Instance-specific shape network. F{\text{fuse}}: Fusion shape network. F{\text{dens}}: Output density network (Linear layer). F{\text{rad}}: Output radiance network. Each MLP (F{\text{share}}, F{\text{inst}}, F{\text{fuse}}) has 4 hidden layers, 256 channels per layer, and ReLU activations. The output of these MLPs is a 256-dimensional feature vector. F{\text{dens}} is a linear layer mapping 256 dimensions to 1 (scalar density). F{\text{rad}} is a 2-layer MLP (implied by "two-layer MLP" in source, typically meaning 2 hidden layers or 2 linear layers; standard NeRF convention suggests 2 hidden layers for radiance, but source says "two-layer MLP... to get radiance". Given F{\text{share}} is 4 layers deep, "two-layer" likely refers to hidden layers or total linear layers. Source states: "passed through a two-layer MLP, the output radiance network F{\text{rad}}". In deep learning literature, "2-layer MLP" often means 2 linear layers (1 hidden). However, NeRF [45] uses 8 layers for the main body. Let's look at the context. F{\text{share}} is 4 layers deep. F{\text{rad}} is described as "two-layer". We will assume 2 hidden layers for consistency with typical MLP depth descriptions, or strictly follow "two-layer" as 2 linear transformations. Given the ambiguity, we define it as 2 linear layers with ReLU, outputting 3 (RGB). Correction: Standard NeRF [45] uses 8 layers. The source explicitly says "two-layer MLP". We will implement 2 hidden layers (3 linear layers total) or 2 linear layers (1 hidden). Let's stick to the text: "two-layer MLP". In many contexts, this means 2 hidden layers. Let's assume 2 hidden layers, 256 width, output 3. If it meant 2 linear layers, it would likely say "single hidden layer". We will use 2 hidden layers for F{\text{rad}} to be safe, or simply state it is a 2-layer MLP. Let's define it as 2 hidden layers, 256 width, ReLU, output 3. Latent codes \mathbf{z}^{(s)} and \mathbf{z}^{(c)} are 32-dimensional vectors. Numbered Steps: 1. Positional Encoding: Compute the positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}) for the input position \mathbf{x} and \gamma(\mathbf{d}) for the viewing direction \mathbf{d} using the standard NeRF positional encoding scheme. 2. Shared Shape Representation: Pass the positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}) through the shared shape network F{\text{share}} to obtain the shared shape feature \mathbf{f}{\text{share}}: \mathbf{f}{\text{share}} = F{\text{share}}(\gamma(\mathbf{x})) 3. Instance-Specific Shape Representation: Concatenate the shape code \mathbf{z}^{(s)} with the positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}). Pass the concatenated vector through the instance-specific shape network F{\text{inst}} to obtain the instance shape feature \mathbf{f}{\text{inst}}: \mathbf{f}{\text{inst}} = F{\text{inst}}([\mathbf{z}^{(s)}; \gamma(\mathbf{x})]) 4. Fusion: Add the shared and instance-specific shape features, then pass the sum through the fusion shape network F{\text{fuse}} to obtain the fused shape feature \mathbf{f}{\text{fuse}}: \mathbf{f}{\text{fuse}} = F{\text{fuse}}(\mathbf{f}{\text{share}} + \mathbf{f}{\text{inst}}) 5. Density Prediction: Pass the fused shape feature \mathbf{f}{\text{fuse}} through the linear density network F{\text{dens}} to obtain the scalar density \sigma: \sigma = F{\text{dens}}(\mathbf{f}{\text{fuse}}) 6. Radiance Prediction: Concatenate the fused shape feature \mathbf{f}{\text{fuse}}, the color code \mathbf{z}^{(c)}, and the encoded viewing direction \gamma(\mathbf{d}). Pass this concatenated vector through the radiance network F{\text{rad}} to obtain the radiance \mathbf{c}: \mathbf{c} = F{\text{rad}}([\mathbf{f}{\text{fuse}}; \mathbf{z}^{(c)}; \gamma(\mathbf{d})]) Rendering: The rendering process follows standard volume rendering Parent. For a ray r, Nc points \{ti\} are sampled. Density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i are computed using the network defined above. The pixel color \hat{C} is computed via alpha compositing: \hat{C}(r, \mathbf{z}^{(s)}, \mathbf{z}^{(c)}) = \sum{i=1}^{Nc} \mathbf{c}i \alphai \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) where \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) and \deltai = t{i+1} - ti. Parameters: Shape code dimension: 32. Color code dimension: 32. MLP depth for F{\text{share}}, F{\text{inst}}, F{\text{fuse}}: 4 layers. MLP width: 256 channels. Activation: ReLU. Optimizer: Adam. Training learning rate: 10^{-4}. Edit learning rate: 10^{-2}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Standard float32 precision is assumed for latent codes and network weights. Boundaries: The method assumes valid positional encodings. Degenerate inputs (e.g., identical positions for different instances) are handled by the instance-specific branch. Caching: During optimization, the set of training rays is small, allowing caching of intermediate representations to accelerate editing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class ConditionalRadianceFieldSharedBranch(nn.Module): def init(self, posencdim, viewencdim, latentdim=32, hiddendim=256, numhiddenlayers=4): super().init() # Fshare: 4 layers, 256 channels, ReLU self.fshare = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(posencdim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim)) # Finst: 4 layers, 256 channels, ReLU # Input: [zs; gamma(x)] self.finst = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(latentdim + posencdim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim)) # Ffuse: 4 layers, 256 channels, ReLU self.ffuse = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim)) # Fdens: Linear layer self.fdens = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1) # Frad: Two-layer MLP (2 hidden layers, 256 channels, ReLU) # Input: [ffuse; zc; gamma(d)] self.frad = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(hiddendim + latentdim + viewencdim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 3) # RGB) def forward(self, x, d, zs, zc): # 1. Shared shape representation fshare = self.fshare(x) # 2. Instance-specific shape representation # Concatenate zs and x xinstinput = torch.cat([zs, x], dim=-1) finst = self.finst(xinstinput) # 3. Fuse representations ffuse = self.ffuse(fshare + finst) # 4. Predict density sigma = self.fdens(ffuse) # 5. Predict radiance # Concatenate ffuse, zc, and d radinput = torch.cat([ffuse, zc, d], dim=-1) c = self.frad(radinput) return sigma, c General training procedures for conditional radiance fields, including loss functions and optimization strategies. Conditional Radiance Field Training Specific implementation details for Conditional NeRF, such as data loading and preprocessing. Conditional NeRF Implementation Details Time and Memory Complexity: The shared branch reduces the number of parameters that need to be updated during editing, accelerating color edits by 3.2× and shape edits by 1.9× compared to non-modular approaches. Caching of intermediate representations is feasible due to the small set of training rays during optimization. Measured Performance: On the PhotoShapes dataset, the model with the shared shape branch achieves a PSNR of 35.79, compared to 33.91 for a model without the shared shape branch. Strengths: Improves view synthesis quality, enables efficient editing by isolating shape and color updates, and scales better to multiple instances. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of latent codes and network architecture to maintain disentanglement. When to Use: When efficient instance-specific editing (shape or color) is required, and the dataset contains multiple instances of similar objects. When Not to Use: When editing efficiency is not a priority, or when the dataset contains highly diverse objects where a shared shape representation is not beneficial. The Conditional Radiance Field with Shared Branch was introduced in the paper "Editing Conditional Radiance Fields" (2021). The method builds on the original NeRF architecture [45] and aims to provide modular inductive biases for better shape and color disentanglement. It was developed to address the limitations of single-instance NeRF models and to enable efficient editing of 3D objects represented as radiance fields. name: Conditional NeRF Implementation Details
head: Conditional NeRF, Conditional NeRF Architecture, Conditional NeRF Model Specs
body: Conditional NeRF is a generative model for a specific object category that maps a 5D coordinate (spatial position \mathbf{x} and view direction \mathbf{v}) along with instance-specific latent codes to volumetric density \sigma and view-dependent radiance \mathbf{c}. It differs from standard per-scene NeRF by conditioning the neural field on latent vectors that dedicatedly control shape and appearance, enabling the generation of novel instances within a category. It builds on Conditional and Latent Representations by providing the specific architectural and training configurations required to implement the conditional mapping and latent injection mechanisms. Inputs and Outputs: The model F\theta takes as input: 1. Spatial position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. 2. View direction \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (normalized). 3. Shape latent code \mathbf{z}s \in \mathbb{R}^{128}. 4. Appearance latent code \mathbf{z}a \in \mathbb{R}^{128}. The output is: 1. Volumetric density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}. 2. View-dependent radiance \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (RGB). Data Structures and Layout: The core component is an 8-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Hidden Units: 256 per layer. Activations: ReLU for all hidden layers. Input Dimension: 64. This dimension is composed of the concatenated positional encodings of \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{z}s, and \mathbf{z}a. Output: A single scalar for \sigma and three scalars for \mathbf{c}. Positional Encoding: The positional encoding function \Gamma(\mathbf{p}) projects each coordinate p of a vector \mathbf{p} into a high-dimensional space using sinusoidal functions. For a frequency band parameter m, the encoding has 2m dimensions. The k-th dimension (k \in \{0, \dots, 2m-1\}) is defined as: \gamma(\mathbf{p})k = \begin{cases} \sin(2^k \pi p), & \text{if } k \text{ is even} \\ \cos(2^k \pi p), & \text{if } k \text{ is odd} \end{cases} The input to the MLP is the concatenation: \Gamma(\mathbf{x}) \oplus \mathbf{z}s, \Gamma(\mathbf{v}) \oplus \mathbf{z}a. Note that in the disentangled variant, \Gamma(\mathbf{x}) is replaced by a deformed encoding \Gamma^(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}s) (see Subtopics). Deformation Network (Disentangled Variant): To achieve disentanglement, a deformation network maps the shape code \mathbf{z}s to displacement vectors \Delta \mathbf{x}. Architecture: 4-layer MLP. Hidden Units: 256 per layer. Activations: ReLU. Input: \mathbf{z}s \in \mathbb{R}^{128}. Output: Displacement vectors \Delta \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 2m} corresponding to each band of the positional encoding \Gamma(\mathbf{x}). Deformed Encoding: \Gamma^(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{z}s) = \{ \gamma^(\mathbf{p}, \Delta \mathbf{p}) \}, where \Delta \mathbf{p} are the displacements derived from \mathbf{z}s. Rendering: The rendering process follows standard volume rendering Parent. For a ray r, Nc points \{ti\} are sampled. Density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i are computed using F. The pixel color \hat{C} is computed via alpha compositing: \hat{C}(r, \mathbf{z}s, \mathbf{z}a) = \sum{i=1}^{Nc} \mathbf{c}i \alphai \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) where \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) and \deltai = t{i+1} - ti. Training Optimization: The network is trained using the Adam optimizer. Initial Learning Rate: 10^{-4}. Decay: By 0.5 every 50,000 steps. Inversion Optimization: When optimizing latent codes for a specific input image (inversion), Adam is used with an initial learning rate of 10^{-3}, decreasing by 0.75 every 100 steps. Loss Weights: In the inversion process, regularization weights are \lambdar = 0.5, \lambdav = 0.1, \lambdas = 0.2, and \lambdaa = 0.2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. This ensures that changes to \mathbf{z}a do not influence \sigma. It is used in the disentangled variant to maintain shape integrity during appearance editing. The complexity is dominated by the MLP forward pass per sample point. Memory usage is proportional to the number of parameters in the MLPs and the storage of latent codes per instance. Measured Performance: The model was trained on an NVIDIA V100 GPU. It was evaluated on the Photoshapes and Carla datasets. For the Carla dataset, 10K cars were rendered at 256x256 resolution. The method requires only one view per instance for training, unlike EditNeRF which requires multiple views. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths include the ability to generate novel instances from a single view and text-driven manipulation without per-sample optimization (in the CLIP variant). Limitations include the potential for mutual intervention in the standard conditional formulation if disentanglement is not used. The inversion process (optimizing latent codes for a specific image) can be time-consuming and requires careful tuning of learning rates and regularization weights. When to Use: Use when generating multiple instances of a category with controlled shape and appearance is required. Use the disentangled variant when independent editing is critical. Use the CLIP-driven variant for text-based generation. Conditional NeRF was introduced in the paper "CLIP-NeRF: Text-and-Image Driven Manipulation of Neural Radiance Fields" by Can Wang et al., published in CVPR 2022. It builds upon the original per-scene NeRF [24] and addresses the need for generative models of 3D objects that can be manipulated via latent codes or text prompts. The work extends previous methods like EditNeRF by allowing generation of new instances rather than just editing existing ones, and by using a single view for training.
