name: Sparse Latent Space for 4D Novel View Synthesis (SLS4D)
body: SLS4D is a method for 4D novel-view synthesis that represents dynamic radiance fields using a learnable sparse latent space, reducing network parameters compared to dense grid discretizations while maintaining high-frequency detail via attention-based interpolation. It differs from dense grid methods (like TiNeuVox) by avoiding the O(N^3TF) space complexity of 4D grids, and from per-image latent code methods by offering better generalization across time through continuous temporal interpolation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D spatial coordinates \mathbf{p} = (x, y, z), time t, and view direction \mathbf{d}. Outputs: Color \mathbf{c} and density \sigma for volume rendering. Data Structures: 1. Sparse Latent Space (Vs): A set of learnable global features Vs = \{f1, f2,..., fB\} \in \mathbb{R}^{F \times B}, where B is the number of feature vectors and F is the feature dimension. 2. Latent Time Slots (H): A set of learnable time-dependent features H = \{h0, h1,..., h{T-1}\}, where T is the number of time slots. 3. Deformation MLP (\Phid): A 7-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron. 4. Interpolator Decoder: A 4-layer MLP mapping to dimension 512, with GeGLU activation in the second layer. 5. Color/Decoding MLPs: A 1-layer MLP for color and a 3-layer MLP for density. Numbered Steps: 1. Temporal Interpolation: For a given timestamp t, obtain the corresponding time-dependent high-frequency feature ht by linearly interpolating between the nearest learnable latent time slots \{hi\}{i=0}^{T-1}. 2. Deformation Prediction: Encode input coordinates (x, y, z, t) into a higher dimension. Concatenate the encoded coordinates with the interpolated time feature ht. Decode the concatenated features using the Deformation MLP (\Phid) with a \tanh activation function to compress deformations to the range [-1, 1]. Compute the deformation displacement (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z) = \Phid(x, y, z, t). 3. Feature Query via Attention: Compute the query vector q(\mathbf{p}) using a frequency encoder: q(\mathbf{p}) = \phiq((\sin(2^0 \mathbf{p}), \cos(2^0 \mathbf{p}),..., \sin(2^{L-1} \mathbf{p}), \cos(2^{L-1} \mathbf{p}))) where L is the max frequency and \phiq is a linear projection. Pass q(\mathbf{p}) through a small projection matrix to transform from coordinate frequency space to dot-product space. Compute the feature f\mathbf{p} for the 3D position \mathbf{p} using multi-head attention: f\mathbf{p} = \frac{E(Q(\mathbf{p})^T K(Vs)) V(Vs)}{\sqrt{d}} where Q, K, V are query, key, and value projections; d is the feature dimension; E(\cdot) is the softmax function; and Vs represents the key/value pairs from the sparse latent space. 4. Radiance Field Decoding: Pass the interpolated feature f\mathbf{p} through the Interpolator Decoder (4-layer MLP with GeGLU in the second layer). Feed the output into separate small MLPs to decode color \mathbf{c} (1-layer) and density \sigma (3-layer). Feed viewpoint information \mathbf{d} into the decoding MLPs. The final radiance field query is: (\mathbf{c}, \sigma) = \Phic(x + \Delta x, y + \Delta y, z + \Delta z, \mathbf{d}) where (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z) is the displacement computed in Step 2. Formulas: GeGLU Activation: \text{GeGLU}(x, W, V, b, c) = \text{GELU}(xW + b) \otimes (xV + c) where \text{GELU}(x) = x \cdot [1 + \text{erf}(x/\sqrt{2})] and \text{erf} is the error function. Temporal Continuity Loss (TV Loss): Lt = \sum{i=0}^{T-1} ||h{i+1} - hi|| This ensures temporal continuity over time for latent time slots. Learning Rate Schedule: F{sc}(s) = \begin{cases} \frac{s}{Nw} & \text{if } s \le Nw \\ \exp\left(\frac{s-Nw}{Nm}\right) \left(1 + \cos\left(\pi \frac{s-Nw}{Nm}\right)\right) & \text{if } s > Nw \end{cases} where s is the current step, Nw is the warm-up step, and Nm is the max step. Optimization Loss: L = wc \frac{1}{|R|} \sum{r \in R} ||C(r) - \hat{C}(r)||^22 + wt Lt where C(r) is ground truth color, \hat{C}(r) is predicted color, and R is the set of rays. Parameters (Typical Values): B (number of latent features): 256 for D-NeRF, 512 for HyperNeRF. F (feature vector dimension): 64. T (time slots size): 256 for D-NeRF, 512 for HyperNeRF. Transformer heads: 8 heads with context dimension 32. Learning rate: 0.0001 for feature space, interpolation transformer, and first three MLP layers; 0.001 for subsequent MLP layers. Training iterations (Nm): 30,000. Warm-up steps (Nw): 2,000. Loss weights: wc = 1, wt = 0.0001. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dense grids neglect the sparsity of 3D radiance fields and have extremely high parameter counts for 4D space. Standard bilinear/trilinear interpolation cannot simultaneously focus on low-frequency and high-frequency information when used with frequency encoders. The method uses a strategy similar to the "empty grid" approach in HexPlane to focus training on specific parts of the target object. Time and Memory Complexity: The space complexity of dense 4D grids is O(N^3TF), whereas the sparse latent space reduces parameters significantly since B \ll N^2. Measured Performance: On the D-NeRF dataset, SLS4D achieves a PSNR of 32.67, SSIM of 0.963, and LPIPS of 0.034, outperforming methods like D-NeRF, TiNeuVox, and HexPlane. Hardware: Experiments were conducted on an Nvidia 4090 server. Strengths: Reduces parameter count significantly compared to dense grids and Tensor4D; more generalizable than per-image latent codes; handles high-frequency dynamic information effectively. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Suitable for 4D novel-view synthesis on synthetic (D-NeRF) and real-world (HyperNeRF) datasets where high fidelity and parameter efficiency are required. SLS4D was introduced in the paper "SLS4D: Sparse Latent Space for 4D Novel View Synthesis". It builds on the concept of implicit radiance fields and deformation fields (as in D-NeRF) but addresses the limitations of dense grid discretizations and standard interpolation methods by introducing a sparse latent space with attention-based feature interpolation. SLS4D: Sparse Latent Space for 4D Novel View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2024.3429421, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Neural Feature Fusion Fields (N3F)
head: Neural Distillation of Self-Supervised 2D Image Representations
body: Neural Feature Fusion Fields (N3F) is a method that distills dense 2D image features from a pre-trained teacher network into a 3D neural field (student) via differentiable volumetric rendering, enabling 3D-aware feature representation. Unlike Semantic NeRF or Panoptic NeRF which fuse discrete semantic labels, N3F fuses continuous dense feature vectors, allowing for open-world applications without manual labels. It differs from standard feature distillation because the student operates in 3D world space (ensuring spatial consistency) while the teacher operates in 2D image space. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of input images It \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W} defined on lattice \Omega = \{1, \dots, H\} \times \{1, \dots, W\} for t=1 \dots T, with known camera parameters. A pre-trained 2D feature extractor (teacher) \Phi. Outputs: A 3D neural feature field defined by occupancy \sigma: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^+ and a color/feature function c: \mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^{3+C}, where C is the number of feature channels. The rendered outputs are color images \hat{I}t and feature images \hat{\Phi}t \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times H \times W}. Data Structures: The student network implements the pair (\sigma, c). The function c is decomposed into c = (c{rgb}, c{\Phi}), where c{rgb} outputs 3 color values and c{\Phi} outputs C feature values. For dynamic scenes (e.g., using NeuralDiff), the architecture decomposes the scene into static, dynamic (time-dependent), and actor (camera-anchored) fields, each with its own feature prediction head (MLP followed by tanh). Preprocessing: 1. Teacher features \Phi(It) are pre-computed using public weights (e.g., DINO, MoCo-v3, DeiT). 2. Features are L2-normalized and reduced to 64 dimensions via Principal Component Analysis (PCA) before distillation. 3. Images are down-sampled to 480 \times 270 pixels; 2D features are up-sampled to match using nearest-neighbor interpolation. Numbered Steps: 1. Teacher Forward Pass: Compute 2D feature maps \Phi(It) for each input image It using the frozen teacher network \Phi. Apply stop-gradient (sg) to prevent teacher updates. 2. Ray Casting: For each pixel u in image It, cast a ray r through the scene. Sample points X{tu}(r) along the ray. 3. Student Forward Pass: Query the student network for each point X to obtain occupancy \sigma(X) and the concatenated vector (c{rgb}(X), c{\Phi}(X)). 4. Volumetric Rendering: Compute the rendered feature vector \hat{\Phi}t^u for pixel u by accumulating feature outputs weighted by density and transmittance, analogous to color accumulation: \hat{\Phi}t^u = \sum{i=1}^{N} c{\Phi}(X{tu}(ri)) \alphai where \alphai is the weight derived from density \sigma and transmittance Ti = e^{-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma(X{tu}(rj)) \deltaj}. 5. Loss Computation: Calculate the total training loss \mathcal{L} as the sum of image reconstruction loss and feature reconstruction loss: \mathcal{L} = \sumt \| \hat{I}t - It \|2^2 + \lambda \| \hat{\Phi}t - \Phi(It) \|2^2 where \lambda is the feature distillation loss weight. 6. Optimization: Update student parameters using Adam optimizer with cosine annealing schedule. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class N3FStudent(nn.Module): def init(self, featuredim=64): super().init() # Student network implementing sigma and c = (crgb, cphi) # crgb outputs 3 channels, cphi outputs featuredim channels self.network = NeuralFieldNetwork() self.featuredim = featuredim def forward(self, rayso, raysd, tnear, tfar, numsamples): """ rayso: (B, 3) ray origins raysd: (B, 3) ray directions (normalized) tnear, tfar: (B,) near and far clip distances numsamples: int, number of points per ray """ # Sample points along rays tvals = torch.linspace(0, 1, numsamples).to(rayso.device) tsamples = tnear + tvals (tfar - tnear) points = rayso.unsqueeze(1) + raysd.unsqueeze(1) tsamples.unsqueeze(2) # Query student network # points shape: (B, numsamples, 3) # directions shape: (B, numsamples, 3) sigma, colorandfeatures = self.network(points, raysd.unsqueeze(1).expandas(points)) # Split output color = colorandfeatures[...,:3] features = colorandfeatures[..., 3:] # Compute weights for volume rendering # delta = tsamples[i+1] - tsamples[i] deltas = tsamples[:, 1:] - tsamples[:,:-1] # Add infinite delta for last point deltas = torch.cat([deltas, torch.tensor([1e10]).to(rayso.device)], dim=1) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) transmittance = torch.cumprod(torch.exp(-alpha), dim=1) transmittance = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(transmittance[:,:1]), 1.0 - transmittance[:,:-1]], dim=1) weights = alpha transmittance # Render color and features renderedcolor = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) color, dim=1) renderedfeatures = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) features, dim=1) return renderedcolor, renderedfeatures, sigma def computeloss(renderedcolor, renderedfeatures, targetimage, targetfeatures, lambdafeat): """ targetimage: (B, 3, H, W) targetfeatures: (B, C, H, W) """ # Image reconstruction loss colorloss = F.mseloss(renderedcolor, targetimage) # Feature reconstruction loss featureloss = F.mseloss(renderedfeatures, targetfeatures) totalloss = colorloss + lambdafeat featureloss return totalloss Parameters: \lambda: Weight for feature reconstruction loss. Typical values: 0.001 for NeRF/LLFF experiments; 1.0 for NeuralDiff/EPIC-KITCHENS experiments. C: Number of feature channels. Depends on teacher (e.g., reduced to 64 via PCA). Learning Rate: 5 \times 10^{-4} with cosine annealing. Batch Size: 1024. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Teacher Freezing: The teacher network weights must be frozen (stop gradient) during student training. Feature Normalization: Features should be L2-normalized and PCA-reduced before distillation to stabilize training. Dynamic Scenes: For egocentric videos, standard NeRF is insufficient; NeuralDiff architecture is required to handle static, dynamic foreground, and actor components. Finds occurrences of an object across views using feature similarity. Uses mean feature descriptor of a query region Rt and matches against rendered features \hat{\Phi}t using threshold \tau. Localizes objects in 3D space by querying the student field for points X where feature similarity to a query descriptor is high and density \sigma(X) exceeds threshold \tau\sigma. Removes objects by setting occupancy \sigma(X)=0 for 3D points matching the object's feature descriptor. Renders features through occluders by disabling occupancy \sigma for regions dissimilar to the query descriptor, revealing the full extent of occluded objects. Time Complexity: Training time depends on the base neural rendering architecture. For NeuralDiff on EPIC-KITCHENS, single scene training takes ~24 hours for RGB reconstruction and ~2 hours for feature distillation (20 epochs, 500 iterations) on an NVIDIA Tesla P40. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the 3D neural field parameters and pre-computed 2D teacher features for all views. Performance: N3F consistently improves over 2D self-supervised baselines. On LLFF dataset, N3F with DINO [ViT-B/8] achieved mAP 76.26 vs teacher 64.35 (+11.91); with DINO [ViT-B/16] 78.84 vs 60.15 (+18.69); with MoCo-v3 76.15 vs 57.51 (+18.64); with DeiT 74.53 vs 47.51 (+26.82). Strengths: Enables 3D-aware feature representation, viewpoint independence, and occlusion awareness. Improves generalization compared to 2D teachers. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of teacher features. Performance depends on the quality of the 2D teacher network (SSL models generalize better than supervised ones like DeiT). N3F was introduced in the paper "Neural Feature Fusion Fields: 3D Distillation of Self-Supervised 2D Image Representations". It builds on the student-teacher distillation paradigm (Hinton et al.) but applies it to 3D neural fields via differentiable rendering. It is evaluated on static scenes (LLFF dataset with vanilla NeRF) and egocentric videos (EPIC-KITCHENS dataset with NeuralDiff). Neural Feature Fusion Fields: 3D Distillation of Self-Supervised 2D Image Representations, https://doi.org/10.1109/3DV57658.2022.00056, fetched 2026-10-30

name: CLNeRF Architecture with Embeddings
head: Appearance and Geometry Embeddings, Compact Continual NeRF
body: CLNeRF is a model architecture modification for NeRF that enables continual learning by incorporating scene changes (appearance and geometry) over time within a single model, preventing model size growth as new scans are added. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like MIMO-DONeRF and SLS4D by using explicit, trainable per-scan embedding vectors rather than latent space compression or multi-instance networks, allowing for efficient updates and low overhead for generative replay. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A spatial location \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3, a viewing direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3, and a time step index t identifying the current scan in a continual sequence. Output: Color c and volume density (opacity) \sigma. Data Structures: Feature Vector \mathbf{f}: The encoded representation of spatial location \mathbf{x}. For NGP backbone: \mathbf{f} is produced by a grid-based hash encoder. For Vanilla NeRF backbone: \mathbf{f} is produced by an MLP. Appearance Embedding ea: A trainable vector encoding appearance changes (e.g., lighting, weather). Dimension: 48. Layout: A single vector per time step t. Geometry Embedding eg: A trainable vector encoding geometry changes (e.g., new objects, construction). Dimension: 16. Layout: A single vector per time step t. Decoders: Dc: Color decoder (MLP). D\sigma: Opacity decoder (MLP). Numbered Steps: 1. Encode Spatial Location: Given a spatial location \mathbf{x}, encode it into a feature vector \mathbf{f}. If using NGP, use the grid-based hash encoder; if using vanilla NeRF, use an MLP. 2. Compute Color: Decode color c using the color decoder Dc. The inputs are the feature vector \mathbf{f}, the viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and the trainable appearance embedding ea corresponding to the current time step t. c = Dc(\mathbf{f}, \mathbf{d}, ea) 3. Compute Opacity: Decode opacity \sigma using the opacity decoder D\sigma. The inputs are the feature vector \mathbf{f} and the trainable geometry embedding eg corresponding to the current time step t. \sigma = D\sigma(\mathbf{f}, eg) 4. Embedding Assignment: For each new time step t (scan) in the continual learning sequence, add one new appearance embedding ea and one new geometry embedding eg to the model. These embeddings are distinct per time step. Parameters: Appearance embedding dimension: 48. Geometry embedding dimension: 16. Pitfalls: Transient Objects: The architecture does not automatically filter transient objects (e.g., moving pedestrians) within a single scan. Using a transient MLP with NGP causes the non-transient network to overfit to transient objects and fail to filter them. Transient objects must be filtered using segmentation masks. Backbone Choice: Using vanilla NeRF as the backbone results in worse performance and efficiency compared to NGP for CLNeRF, particularly regarding model updates and generative replay overhead. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class CLNeRF(nn.Module): def init(self, usengp=True, appearancedim=48, geometrydim=16): super().init() self.usengp = usengp self.appearancedim = appearancedim self.geometrydim = geometrydim # Encoders if usengp: # NGP grid-based hash encoder self.spatialencoder = HashEncoder() # Implementation details of NGP hash encoder else: # Vanilla NeRF MLP encoder self.spatialencoder = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(3, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256)) # Decoders # Color decoder takes f, d, ea self.colordecoder = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(256 + 3 + appearancedim, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 3) # RGB) # Opacity decoder takes f, eg self.opacitydecoder = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(256 + geometrydim, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 1) # Sigma) # Embeddings are stored in lists, one per time step self.appearanceembeddings = [] self.geometryembeddings = [] def addtimestep(self): """Add new embeddings for a new scan/time step t.""" ea = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(1, self.appearancedim)) eg = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(1, self.geometrydim)) self.appearanceembeddings.append(ea) self.geometryembeddings.append(eg) def forward(self, x, d, t): """ x: (N, 3) spatial coordinates d: (N, 3) viewing directions t: int, current time step index """ # 1. Encode spatial location f = self.spatialencoder(x) # (N, 256) # 2. Get embeddings for time step t # Note: In a real implementation, embeddings would be registered as parameters # or stored in a buffer. Here we assume they are accessible. ea = self.appearanceembeddings[t] # (1, 48) eg = self.geometryembeddings[t] # (1, 16) # Expand for batch ea = ea.expand(x.size(0), -1) eg = eg.expand(x.size(0), -1) # 3. Compute Color # Concatenate f, d, ea colorinput = torch.cat([f, d, ea], dim=-1) c = self.colordecoder(colorinput) # (N, 3) # 4. Compute Opacity # Concatenate f, eg opacityinput = torch.cat([f, eg], dim=-1) sigma = self.opacitydecoder(opacityinput) # (N, 1) return c, sigma Uses multiple instances of NeRF to handle dynamic scenes. Choose when scene changes are complex and multi-instance representation is feasible. [16217-mimo-donerf.md] Compresses 4D data into a sparse latent space. Choose when memory efficiency for 4D data is critical. [18112-sparse-latent-space-for-4d-novel-view-synthesis-sls4d.md] Fuses neural features from multiple views. Choose when multi-view consistency is paramount. [18114-neural-feature-fusion-fields-n3f.md] Time and Memory Complexity: The model size increases linearly with the number of time steps t, but the increase is minimal due to the small embedding dimensions (48 and 16). Measured Performance: Using NGP as the backbone provides better performance and efficiency compared to vanilla NeRF for CLNeRF, enabling efficient model updates and low overhead for generative replay. Strengths: Compact model size, efficient updates, handles appearance and geometry changes separately. Limitations: Requires segmentation masks for transient object filtering; not compatible with transient MLPs for automatic filtering. When to use: When continual learning of a scene with appearance and geometry changes is required, and model size must remain compact. When not to use: When transient objects within a single scan are present and segmentation masks are unavailable. CLNeRF was introduced in the paper "CLNeRF: Continual Learning Meets NeRF". It addresses the challenge of continual learning in NeRFs, where the model must adapt to new scans without forgetting previous ones or growing indefinitely in size. The method builds on the Instant Neural Graphics Primitives (NGP) architecture. CLNeRF: Continual Learning Meets NeRF, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv51070.2023.02119, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Mutual Information Gradient Shaping
head: J-NeRF, MI-shaping NeRF, NeRF shaping with mutual information gradients, mutual information shaped NeRF
body: Mutual Information Gradient Shaping (MIGS), implemented as JacobiNeRF, is a training regularization technique that shapes the tangent space of a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) to encode semantic correlations between scene entities. Unlike first-order approaches that distill 2D features into 3D radiance channels or treat labels as separate output channels, MIGS aligns the Jacobians of correlated entities to maximize their mutual information under random weight perturbations, enabling efficient sparse label propagation and semantic consensus. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A standard NeRF model \Phi parameterized by weights \theta \in \mathbb{R}^D; a set of labeled source pixels/points S = \{s1, \dots, sK\} with semantic labels; unlabeled target pixels/points T = \{t1, \dots, tM\}; camera parameters for rendering. Outputs: A trained NeRF \Phi where the Jacobian of rendered values with respect to weights encodes semantic similarity; propagated semantic labels for target entities. Data Structures NeRF Weights (\theta): Vector of size D. Jacobian (\partial \Phi): Gradient vector of the same size D, representing \frac{\partial I(p)}{\partial \theta} for a pixel/point p. Perturbation (n): Vector of size D, sampled from a uniform distribution on the unit sphere S^{D-1}. Method Steps 1. Compute Jacobians: For each labeled source pixel sk and target pixel ti, compute the Jacobian of the rendered value with respect to the NeRF weights \theta at the current training state. Let \partial \Phi^{J,sk} and \partial \Phi^{J,ti} denote these gradients. 2. MI-Shaping Loss Calculation: Align the Jacobians of correlated entities using contrastive learning. The Mutual Information (MI) between two entities is approximated by the cosine similarity of their Jacobians. Define the MI approximation: I(I(pi), I(pj)) \propto \cos(\partial \Phii, \partial \Phij) = \frac{\partial \Phii \cdot \partial \Phij}{\|\partial \Phii\| \|\partial \Phij\|} where \alpha is the angle between Jacobians, and I(I(pi), I(pj)) = \log(1/\sqrt{1 - \cos^2 \alpha}) + \text{const}. Construct positive pairs (entities known to be correlated, e.g., same semantic class) and negative pairs (different classes). Compute the MI-Shaping Loss (L{MIG}) using InfoNCE: L{MIG} = -\log \frac{\exp(\|\cos(\partial \Phii, \partial \Phi{i+})\|/\tau)}{\sum{j \in \{i^+\} \cup \{i^-\}} \exp(\|\cos(\partial \Phii, \partial \Phij)\|/\tau)} where \tau is a temperature parameter, i+ denotes positive pairs, and i- denotes negative pairs. The notation \|\cos(\cdot)\| is used to handle the absolute cosine similarity as per the source's convention for magnitude. 3. Gradient Normalization: Apply a regularization term to compact gradients onto a unit sphere, improving training efficiency and facilitating label propagation: L{norm} = \gamma (1.0 - \|\partial \Phii\|)^2 where \gamma is a weighting factor. 4. Total Loss: Combine the standard photometric reconstruction loss (L{NeRF}) with the shaping terms: L{TM} = L{NeRF} + \lambda L{MIG} + L{norm} where \lambda controls the strength of the mutual information shaping. 5. Label Propagation (Inference/Post-Training): For a target pixel ti, select the best source pixel k^ based on Jacobian alignment: k^ = \arg\maxk \frac{\|\partial \Phi^{J,sk} \cdot \partial \Phi^{J,ti}\|}{\|\partial \Phi^{J,sk}\| \|\partial \Phi^{J,ti}\|}. Alternatively, propagate labels via perturbation response: Perturb weights: \thetaD' = \theta + \sigma n, where n \sim \text{Uniform}(S^{D-1}). Render perturbed image Ik using weights perturbed along the gradient of source pixel k (i.e., \theta + \sigma \partial \Phi^{J,sk}). Compute response: Rk(ti) = |Ik(ti) - I(ti)|. Assign label: l{ti} = \arg\maxk Rk(ti), treating Rk as logits for K-way classification. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computejacobian(nerfmodel, pixelcoords, cameraparams, weights): """ Computes the gradient of the rendered pixel value with respect to network weights. Returns a vector of size D (number of weights). """ # Use automatic differentiation to compute d(renderedvalue) / d(weights) # renderedvalue = nerfmodel(pixelcoords, cameraparams, weights) return grad(renderedvalue, weights) def cosinesimilarity(vec1, vec2): """Computes cosine similarity between two vectors.""" dotproduct = np.dot(vec1, vec2) norm1 = np.linalg.norm(vec1) norm2 = np.linalg.norm(vec2) if norm1 == 0 or norm2 == 0: return 0.0 return dotproduct / (norm1 norm2) def trainjacobinerf(nerfmodel, dataloader, labeledsources, unlabeledtargets, lambdami, gammanorm, tau, numepochs): """ Trains NeRF with Mutual Information Gradient Shaping. """ for epoch in range(numepochs): for batch in dataloader: # 1. Standard NeRF forward pass and photometric loss renderedimages = nerfmodel(batch.rays) lnerf = photometricloss(renderedimages, batch.gtimages) # 2. Compute Jacobians for labeled sources and targets jacobianss = {} for s in labeledsources: jacobianss[s] = computejacobian(nerfmodel, s.coords, s.camera, nerfmodel.weights) jacobianst = {} for t in unlabeledtargets: jacobianst[t] = computejacobian(nerfmodel, t.coords, t.camera, nerfmodel.weights) # 3. Compute MI-Shaping Loss (LMIG) # Assume we have defined positive pairs (s, t) based on ground truth or self-supervised features lmig = 0.0 count = 0 for t in unlabeledtargets: for spos in labeledsources: # Positive pair cossimpos = cosinesimilarity(jacobianss[spos], jacobianst[t]) exppos = np.exp(np.abs(cossimpos) / tau) sumexp = exppos for sneg in labeledsources: # Negative pairs if sneg != spos: cossimneg = cosinesimilarity(jacobianss[sneg], jacobianst[t]) sumexp += np.exp(np.abs(cossimneg) / tau) lmig -= np.log(exppos / sumexp) count += 1 if count > 0: lmig /= count # 4. Compute Normalization Loss (Lnorm) # Regularize the norm of target Jacobians to be close to 1.0 lnorm = 0.0 for t in unlabeledtargets: normt = np.linalg.norm(jacobianst[t]) lnorm += (1.0 - normt)2 lnorm /= len(unlabeledtargets) # 5. Total Loss totalloss = lnerf + lambdami lmig + gammanorm lnorm # 6. Backpropagation and update nerfmodel.backwardandupdate(totalloss) def propagatelabelsjacobinerf(nerfmodel, labeledsources, targetpixels, sigma=0.01): """ Propagates semantic labels from labeled sources to target pixels using perturbation response. """ propagatedlabels = {} # Pre-compute perturbed models for each source # Perturb weights along the gradient of the source pixel perturbedmodels = {} for s in labeledsources: grads = computejacobian(nerfmodel, s.coords, s.camera, nerfmodel.weights) # Create a temporary model with perturbed weights # thetaperturbed = theta + sigma grads perturbedmodels[s] = nerfmodel.clone() perturbedmodels[s].weights += sigma grads for t in targetpixels: responses = [] for s in labeledsources: # Render target pixel with model perturbed along source s's gradient # Ik(t) = Phi(ot, vt; theta + sigma grads) renderedval = perturbedmodels[s].render(t.coords, t.camera) originalval = nerfmodel.render(t.coords, t.camera) # Response is absolute difference rk = np.abs(renderedval - originalval) responses.append(rk) # Label is the argmax of responses (treating responses as logits) bestsourceidx = np.argmax(responses) bestsource = labeledsources[bestsourceidx] propagatedlabels[t] = bestsource.label return propagatedlabels Parameters \lambda (lambda): Weight for L{MIG}. Not given in the sources. \gamma (gamma): Weight for gradient normalization. Not given in the sources. \tau (tau): Temperature parameter for InfoNCE loss. Not given in the sources. \sigma: Scale for weight perturbation. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The Jacobian computation requires accurate gradients with respect to all network weights. Numerical instability may occur if weights are large; the normalization term helps mitigate this. Boundaries: The method assumes the NeRF is differentiable with respect to its weights. Discontinuities in the scene representation (e.g., hard cutoffs) may break gradient flow. Degenerate Input: If labeled sources are not semantically distinct or if the scene has no correlated entities, the contrastive loss may not provide meaningful gradients. Propagates labels in the 2D image domain by computing perturbation differences after volume rendering. Suitable for pixel-wise semantic segmentation. Propagates labels in 3D space by estimating perturbation differences for 3D points along rays before volume rendering. Suitable for instance segmentation and 3D entity selection. Time Complexity: Training requires computing Jacobians for all labeled and target pixels, which is O(N \cdot D) where N is the number of pixels/points and D is the number of weights. Label propagation requires rendering with K perturbed models, costing O(K \cdot M \cdot R) where M is the number of targets and R is the number of samples per ray. Memory Complexity: Requires storing Jacobians for all entities, O(N \cdot D), and potentially K copies of the NeRF weights for perturbation-based propagation, O(K \cdot D). Strengths: Enables efficient label propagation from extremely sparse annotations; encodes semantic consensus in the tangent space rather than output channels; supports view-invariant propagation. Limitations: Requires computing second-order information (Jacobians), which is more expensive than first-order methods; performance depends on the quality of self-supervised features used for contrastive pairs. When to use: Sparse label propagation for semantic/instance segmentation; entity selection by clicking a single point; appearance edit propagation. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and only photometric reconstruction is needed; when dense annotations are available and first-order methods suffice. Mutual Information Gradient Shaping was introduced by Xiaomeng Xu, Yanchao Yang, Kaichun Mo, Boxiao Pan, Li Yi, and Leonidas Guibas in "JacobiNeRF: NeRF Shaping with Mutual Information Gradients" (arXiv:2304.00341v1, April 2023). The method addresses the limitation of traditional NeRFs that only capture appearance, by explicitly regularizing learning dynamics to align Jacobians of correlated entities, thereby encoding mutual information in the NeRF tangent space. It is used for sparse label propagation, entity selection, and scene modifications. JacobiNeRF: NeRF Shaping with Mutual Information Gradients, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.01583, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Multi-Level Neural Scene Graph
head: NSG
body: Multi-Level Neural Scene Graph (NSG) is a scene representation that decomposes an environment into a graph of static, dynamic, and temporal nodes to model urban environments with moving objects and appearance variations. It distinguishes itself from sibling architectures by explicitly separating the radiance field into a static component \phi and a dynamic component \psi, conditioned on sequence-level and object-level latent vectors respectively, enabling the disentanglement of scene-dependent appearance from object texture. Inputs: A set of training rays \mathcal{R}, where each ray is defined by (r, t, s): ray direction/origin parameters, time t, and sequence s. Ground truth colors \hat{C}(r, t, s) and depths \hat{D}(r, t, s). LiDAR point clouds and ego-vehicle poses P for space contraction bounds. Initial ego-vehicle poses P{ts} \in SE(3) and object poses \xi{ot} \in SE(3). Outputs: Rendered color C(r, t, s) and expected depth D(r, t, s) for each ray. Optimized radiance field parameters \theta, including MLP weights, latent vectors, and pose residuals. Scene Graph G = (V, E): Nodes V: Root node vr: Defines the global coordinate system. Associated latent vector \omegar (not used for conditioning fields in the described method). Camera nodes \{vc\}{c \in C}: Associated with camera calibration. Sequence nodes \{v{st}\}{s \in S, t \in Ts}: Associated with latent vector \omega{st}. Dynamic object nodes \{vo\}{o \in Os}: Associated with latent vector \omegao. Edges E: Oriented rigid transformations between coordinate frames. e{v{st} vr} = P{ts}: Transformation from global frame to sequence frame (ego-vehicle pose). e{vc v{st}} = Tc: Transformation from ego-vehicle frame to camera frame (fixed calibration). e{vo v{st}} = \xi{ot}: Transformation from sequence frame to object local frame. Bounding Boxes: Each dynamic object node vo has an associated 3D bounding box b{to} in its local coordinate frame. Latent Vectors: \omega{st} = [As F(t), Gs F(t)]: Sequence-level latent vector. As: Appearance matrix for sequence s. Gs: Transient geometry matrix for sequence s. F(\cdot): 1D basis function of sines and cosines with linearly increasing frequencies at log-scale. \omegao: Object-level latent vector conditioning the dynamic field. Coordinate System Contraction: Unbounded scene space is contracted into a unit cube. Bounds are computed from LiDAR point clouds and ego-vehicle poses P. Any 3D position x is normalized to this unit cube before processing. 1. For a given ray (r, t, s), traverse the graph to identify relevant dynamic object nodes vo present in sequence s at time t. 2. Retrieve the 3D bounding box b{to} for each dynamic object node. 3. Compute the ray origin o and direction d in the global coordinate system: o = R{ts} tc + t{ts} d = R{ts} Rc Kc^{-1} (px, py, 1)^T where R{ts}, t{ts} are the rotation and translation from P{ts}, Rc, tc are from Tc, and Kc is the camera intrinsic matrix. 4. For each dynamic object node, transform the ray into the object's local coordinate frame using the edge transformation \xi{ot} and the sequence pose P{ts}: x{local} = (P{ts} \xi{ot})^{-1} I3 \frac{1}{\max(so)} x{global} (Note: The source formula (P{ts} \xi{ot})^{-1} I3 (1/\max(so)) implies scaling by the inverse of the maximum object size \max(so) for normalization, applied to the position vector). 5. Compute the entry u{in} and exit u{out} points of the ray intersecting the local bounding box b{to}. Evaluate the static field \phi and dynamic field \psi at sampling location r(u) along the ray. Static Field \phi(x, d, \omega{st}): 1. Compute multi-scale 3D hash grid features: fx = H3(x). 2. Compute density feature and density: (h{\sigma\phi}, \sigma\phi) = \text{MLP}{\sigma\phi}(fx). 3. Compute color: c\phi = \text{MLP}{c\phi}(h{\sigma\phi}, \gamma{SH}(d), As F(t)). \gamma{SH}(\cdot) is spherical harmonics encoding. 4. Compute transient geometry feature and color: (\sigmaG, cG) = \text{MLP}G(h{\sigma\phi}, Gs F(t)). 5. Combine static and transient outputs to get final \phi color and density (mixture analogous to Eq. 12 in source, but specifically for static part). Dynamic Field \psi(x, d, \omega{st}, \omegao): 1. Transform position x and direction d to local object coordinates (as in Step 1.4). 2. Compute density feature and density: (h{\sigma\psi}, \sigma\psi) = \text{MLP}{\sigma\psi}(\gamma{PE}(x), \omegao). \gamma{PE}(\cdot) is positional encoding. 3. Compute color: c\psi = \text{MLP}{c\psi}(h{\sigma\psi}, \gamma{PE}(d), \omegao, \omega{st}). Composite Rendering: 1. If the sampling location r(u) is not within the interval [u{in}, u{out}] of any dynamic node's bounding box, set \sigma\psi = 0 and c\psi = 0. 2. Compute composite density and color: \sigma = \sigma\phi + \sigma\psi c = \frac{\sigma\phi}{\sigma\phi + \sigma\psi} c\phi + \frac{\sigma\psi}{\sigma\phi + \sigma\psi} c\psi 1. Proposal Density: Distill the static density \sigma\phi into a proposal density \sigma{prop}(r(u), \omega{st}). 2. Sampling Strategy: Use two iterations of ray sampling. Iteration 1 (Uniform): Sample uniformly along the ray. Iteration 2 (Inverse Transform): Sample based on the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) F(u) = 1 - U(u), where U(u) = \exp\left(-\int{u{in}}^u \sigma(u') du'\right). 3. Joint Sampling: Sample jointly from \sigma{prop} and \sigma\psi. Constrain sampling from \sigma\psi to the interval [u{in}, u{out}] of the relevant dynamic nodes. 1. Optimize pose residuals \delta P{ts} \in \mathfrak{se}(3) for ego-vehicle poses and \delta \xi{ot} \in \mathfrak{se}(2) for object poses. 2. Update ego-vehicle pose: \hat{P}{ts} = \text{expmap}(\delta P{ts}) P{ts}. 3. Update object pose: \hat{\xi}{ot} = \text{expmap}(\delta \xi{ot}){SE(2) \to SE(3)} \xi{ot}. Note: Object pose residuals are constrained to \mathfrak{se}(2) (ground plane motion) and mapped to SE(3). 4. Keep camera extrinsics Tc fixed. Total loss \mathcal{L} is the sum of: \mathcal{L} = \sum{(r,t,s) \in \mathcal{R}} \left( \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambda{dist} \mathcal{L}{dist} + \lambda{prop} \mathcal{L}{prop} + \lambda{dep} \mathcal{L}{dep} + \lambda{entr} \mathcal{L}{entr} \right) Photometric Loss: \mathcal{L}{rgb}(r, t, s) = \| C(r, t, s) - \hat{C}(r, t, s) \|2^2. Expected Depth Loss: \mathcal{L}{dep}(r, t, s) = \| D(r, t, s) - \hat{D}(r, t, s) \|2^2, where \hat{D}(r, t, s) = \int{u{in}}^{u{f}} u U(u) \sigma(r(u), t, s) du. Entropy Regularization: Encourages separation between \phi and \psi densities within bounding boxes: \mathcal{L}{entr}(r, t, s) = \int{u{in}}^{u{f}} H\left( \frac{\sigma\psi(r(u), t, s)}{\sigma\phi(r(u), s) + \sigma\psi(r(u), t, s)} \right) du where H(\cdot) is Shannon entropy. Distillation/Proposal Loss: \mathcal{L}{dist} and \mathcal{L}{prop} follow the method in [2] (Instant-NGP/NeRF), supervising \sigma{prop} with \sigma\phi. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computebasisfunction(t, numfrequencies=10): """ 1D basis function of sines and cosines with linearly increasing frequencies at log-scale. t is normalized to [-1, 1]. """ # Implementation detail: Standard positional encoding basis # F(t) = [sin(2^k pi t), cos(2^k pi t)] for k in 0..numfrequencies-1 # Note: Source cites [61, 69] for log-scale frequencies. # For implementation, we use standard NeRF positional encoding as proxy if exact log-scale # implementation is not specified, but strictly following "linearly increasing frequencies at log-scale" # usually implies geometric progression. frequencies = np.logspace(0, np.log10(2numfrequencies), numfrequencies) texpanded = t[:, np.newaxis] frequencies[np.newaxis,:] return np.concatenate([np.sin(texpanded), np.cos(texpanded)], axis=1) def contractspace(x, bounds): """ Contract unbounded scene space into a unit cube. bounds: computed from LiDAR and ego-vehicle poses. """ # Normalize x to [-1, 1] based on bounds xcenter = (bounds.min + bounds.max) / 2 xscale = (bounds.max - bounds.min) / 2 return (x - xcenter) / xscale def evaluatestaticfield(x, d, omegast, hashgrid, mlpsigmaphi, mlpcphi, mlpG): """ Evaluate static radiance field phi. omegast = [As F(t), Gs F(t)] """ # 1. Hash grid features fx = hashgrid.query(x) # 2. Density hsigmaphi, sigmaphi = mlpsigmaphi(fx) # 3. Color # gammaSH is spherical harmonics encoding dsh = sphericalharmonicsencoding(d, degree=3) # Standard degree 3 for NeRF AsFt = omegast['appearance'] cphi = mlpcphi(hsigmaphi, dsh, AsFt) # 4. Transient geometry GsFt = omegast['geometry'] sigmaG, cG = mlpG(hsigmaphi, GsFt) # Mixture of static and transient (analogous to Eq 12 structure for static part) # Source says "final colors and densities are computed as a mixture... analogous to Eq 12" # Assuming simple additive mixture for static part components before combining with dynamic sigmastatic = sigmaphi + sigmaG cstatic = (sigmaphi cphi + sigmaG cG) / (sigmastatic + 1e-8) return sigmastatic, cstatic def evaluatedynamicfield(xlocal, dlocal, omegao, omegast, mlpsigmapsi, mlpcpsi): """ Evaluate dynamic radiance field psi. xlocal, dlocal are in object coordinate frame. """ # 1. Density # gammaPE is positional encoding xpe = positionalencoding(xlocal, numfrequencies=10) hsigmapsi, sigmapsi = mlpsigmapsi(xpe, omegao) # 2. Color dpe = positionalencoding(dlocal, numfrequencies=10) cpsi = mlpcpsi(hsigmapsi, dpe, omegao, omegast) return sigmapsi, cpsi def rayboxintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, boxmin, boxmax): """ Compute entry (uin) and exit (uout) of ray with AABB. Returns None if no intersection. """ # Standard AABB-ray intersection tmin = (boxmin - rayorigin) / raydirection tmax = (boxmax - rayorigin) / raydirection tenter = np.maximum(tmin, tmax).min() texit = np.minimum(tmin, tmax).max() if tenter > texit or texit < 0: return None, None return tenter, texit def renderray(rayparams, graph, timet, sequences, hashgrid, models): """ Render a single ray using the Multi-Level Neural Scene Graph. """ # 1. Coordinate Transformation # Get ego-vehicle pose Pts and object poses xiot Pts = graph.getpose(sequences, timet) # Ego-vehicle pose Tc = graph.cameracalibration # Fixed # Ray origin and direction in global frame oglobal = Pts.R @ Tc.t + Pts.t # o = Rts tc + tts (Note: source uses tc for cam extrinsic translation) # d = Rts Rc Kc^-1 (px, py, 1) # Assuming rayparams provides (px, py) or direction in camera frame dcam = rayparams.directionincam dglobal = Pts.R @ Tc.R @ dcam dglobal = dglobal / np.linalg.norm(dglobal) # 2. Traverse Graph for Dynamic Objects dynamicnodes = graph.getdynamicnodes(sequences, timet) # 3. Composite Sampling and Rendering # Use composite ray sampling strategy # Distill static density for proposal sigmaprop = distillstaticdensity(rayparams, sequences, hashgrid, models['mlpsigmaphi']) # Sample points # Two iterations: 1. Uniform, 2. Inverse Transform Sampling samples = compositesample(rayparams, sigmaprop, dynamicnodes, timet, sequences) sigmatotal = 0.0 colortotal = np.zeros(3) for u, weight in samples: xglobal = rayparams.origin + u rayparams.direction # Contract space xcontracted = contractspace(xglobal, graph.bounds) # Evaluate Static Field sigmaphi, cphi = evaluatestaticfield( xcontracted, rayparams.direction, graph.getsequencelatent(sequences, timet), hashgrid, models['mlpsigmaphi'], models['mlpcphi'], models['mlpG']) # Evaluate Dynamic Field sigmapsi = 0.0 cpsi = np.zeros(3) # Check intersection with dynamic nodes for node in dynamicnodes: # Transform ray to local object frame # Edge evovst = xiot xiot = graph.getobjectpose(node, timet) # Local transform: (Pts xiot)^-1 # Note: Source formula includes scaling 1/max(so). # Assuming xiot includes scale or we normalize by object size. # For simplicity, assume xiot is SE(3) and we handle scale in coordinate transform if needed. # The source says: (Pts xiot)^-1 I3 (1/max(so)) # Let's assume we transform xglobal to localx localx = inversetransform(Pts @ xiot) @ xglobal localx = localx / node.maxsize # Scale normalization locald = inverserotation(Pts @ xiot) @ rayparams.direction # Check if within bounding box uin, uout = rayboxintersection(localx, locald, node.boxmin, node.boxmax) # Check if current u (in global) maps to interval [uin, uout] in local # This requires mapping u back to local distance or transforming uglobal to local ray parameter # Simplified: if global point is within transformed box if ispointinbox(localx, node.boxmin, node.boxmax): sigmapsi, cpsi = evaluatedynamicfield( localx, locald, node.latentvector, graph.getsequencelatent(sequences, timet), models['mlpsigmapsi'], models['mlpcpsi']) break # Assume only one dynamic object per sample for simplicity or accumulate # Composite sigma = sigmaphi + sigmapsi if sigma > 1e-8: c = (sigmaphi cphi + sigmapsi cpsi) / sigma else: c = np.zeros(3) # Alpha compositing alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigma ustep) # ustep is distance between samples colortotal += weight alpha c # Note: Standard NeRF compositing: C = sum Ti alphai ci # Here 'weight' from sampling might already account for Ti, or we compute Ti explicitly. # Source uses standard volumetric rendering integral. return colortotal def optimizeposeresiduals(graph, lossgradients): """ Hierarchical pose optimization. """ # Optimize ego-vehicle pose residuals deltaPts in se(3) deltaPts = computese3residual(lossgradients, 'egovehicle') Ptsnew = expmapse3(deltaPts) @ graph.getpose('egovehicle') graph.setpose('egovehicle', Ptsnew) # Optimize object pose residuals deltaxiot in se(2) for node in graph.dynamicnodes: deltaxiot = computese2residual(lossgradients, node) # Map se(2) to SE(3) xiotnew = expmapse2tose3(deltaxiot) @ graph.getobjectpose(node) graph.setobjectpose(node, xiotnew) Dynamic Node Boundary: When computing composite rendering, \sigma\psi must be set to zero if the sampling location r(u) does not lie within the 3D bounding box of a dynamic node. Failure to do so results in incorrect density mixing in empty space. Coordinate Transformation: The transformation of 3D position x and viewing direction d into the local object coordinate frame uses (P{ts} \xi{ot})^{-1} I3 (1/\max(so)). The scaling factor 1/\max(so) is critical for normalizing the object size, likely to match the training distribution of the MLP. Pose Constraints: Object pose residuals are constrained to \mathfrak{se}(2) (ground plane motion), assuming objects are upright. Optimizing them in full \mathfrak{se}(3) may lead to instability. Time Normalization: Time t must be normalized to [-1, 1] using the maximum sequence length to ensure the basis function F(t) operates correctly. Time Complexity: Rendering involves evaluating two MLPs (\phi and \psi) and a hash grid lookup per sample. The composite sampling strategy reduces the number of samples needed compared to dense sampling, as \sigma{prop} skips empty space. Memory Complexity: The scene graph structure is lightweight, storing only latent vectors and poses. The primary memory cost is the 3D hash grid for \phi and the MLP weights for \phi and \psi. Strengths: Disentangles static and dynamic components, allowing for better generalization across sequences and objects. Handles appearance variations (e.g., auto-exposure) and transient geometry (e.g., tree leaves) via sequence-level latents. Efficient rendering via composite sampling and space contraction. Limitations: Requires accurate initial poses and bounding boxes for dynamic objects. Complexity increases with the number of dynamic objects and sequences. When to Use: Suitable for dynamic urban environments with multiple sequences, moving objects, and appearance variations. When Not to Use: Static scenes or scenes with very few dynamic objects may not benefit from the complexity of the graph structure. Origin: Multi-Level Neural Scene Graphs were introduced in "Multi-Level Neural Scene Graphs for Dynamic Urban Environments" (CVPR 2024). Development: The method builds upon previous work in neural radiance fields (NeRF) and dynamic scene representations, incorporating ideas from hash grids, pose optimization, and composite sampling. Usage: Designed for novel view synthesis in dynamic urban environments, leveraging LiDAR and camera data. name: NAN (Noise-Aware NeRFs)
head: IBRNet-based architecture with noise-aware extensions, NAN method
body: NAN is a burst-denoising method that extends the IBRNet architecture to handle degraded noisy images, such as those captured in low-light conditions, by modifying feature extraction, aggregation, and color blending to be noise-aware. Unlike standard NeRFs that synthesize novel views, NAN fixes an existing view image by leveraging multiple noisy inputs of the same scene. It distinguishes itself from its sibling MIMO-DONeRF and Point-NeRF Adaptation for Object Manipulation by explicitly modeling spatial noise statistics through 3D blending kernels and cross-view variance features, rather than relying solely on single-pixel cross-view consistency. Inputs: A burst of N noisy RGB images of the same scene, captured from different viewpoints. Each image is associated with its camera pose. The noise model is assumed to be additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) in linear space, potentially with per-pixel variance estimates. Outputs: A single denoised RGB image corresponding to a target viewpoint (which may be one of the input views or a novel view, though the primary application is burst denoising of an existing view). Pre-Net Layer: A single convolutional layer at the entry point of the network. Kernel Size: 3 \times 3. Output Channels: 3 (RGB). Activation: None. Initialization: Gaussian per-channel filters. Function: Preserves spatial and channel dimensions; reduces input noise efficiently. Feature Aggregation Input: Pixel feature embedding vectors are expanded by concatenation to include cross-view mean and variance feature vectors for the specific pixel. Additionally, estimated noise variances per-pixel per-color channel are concatenated to the global features. Transformer Module: A standard single 5-head self-attention transformer is added to the feature aggregation stage to capture intricate relations and statistics of cross-view features. Color Blending Weights: Instead of outputting N blending scalars, the network outputs N vectors, each of dimension k^2 \times 3. This represents a per-pixel per-view k \times k spatial kernel of blending weights, with separate weights per color channel. 1. Preprocessing: Linearize input images by applying inverse gamma correction and inverse random white balancing. This ensures the noise model, which refers to linear images, is correctly applied. 2. Pre-Net Processing: Pass the linearized input images through the Pre-Net layer (single 3 \times 3 convolution, no activation) to perform initial noise reduction while preserving spatial resolution. 3. Feature Extraction: Extract pixel feature embeddings from the Pre-Net outputs using the truncated ResNet34 encoder-decoder network from IBRNet. 4. Ray Projection: For each pixel in the target image, project a ray into the scene. Sample points along the ray. 5. Cross-View Projection: Project each 3D sample point onto each of the N input views to retrieve corresponding features. 6. Feature Aggregation: Compute cross-view mean and variance feature vectors for the specific pixel. Concatenate these statistics to the pixel feature embedding vectors. Concatenate estimated noise variances (per-pixel per-color channel) to the global features. Process the aggregated features through the 5-head self-attention transformer to capture intricate cross-view relations. 7. Density and Color Estimation: Predict the point color cm and density \rhom for each sample m along the ray. Calculate the probability wm that an object exists at sample m: wm = 1 - e^{-\rhom / \sum{j=1}^{M} \rhoj} where \rhom is the density and M is the total number of samples. 8. Noise-Aware Color Blending (Spatial Kernel): Instead of a single scalar weight per view, predict a k \times k spatial kernel of blending weights for each view and each color channel. The output is N vectors, each of dimension k^2 \times 3. Normalize the weights per channel to sum to 1 using a softmax operation prior to blending. Apply these kernels to the k \times k spatial neighborhood of each projected pixel to gather spatial context. 9. Rendering: Integrate the weight-color pairs along the ray to produce the final color \hat{C}(r): \hat{C}(r) = \sum{m=1}^{M} wm cm where wm is the weight, cm is the color, and M is the total samples. 10. Coarse/Fine Sampling: Repeat the sampling process in two stages. The 'fine' stage refines sampling around depth values that most influence rendering (visible surfaces). 11. Post-processing: Apply the respective gamma correction and white balancing to the output linear denoised image to return it to display space. Apply a simple bilateral filtering post-process to the main network output. Spatial Kernel Size (k): Set to 3. This provides a balance between quality gain and increase in network complexity. Transformer Heads: 5. Original IBRNet Feature Extraction: The original IBRNet uses a 7 \times 7 kernel size and immediate spatial resolution reduction by a factor of two at the entry point. This makes the layer incapable of performing simple noise filtering, necessitating the addition of the Pre-Net layer. Standard Blending Insufficiency: Standard IBRNet blending gathers only cross-view (single pixel) information without spatial extent. This is insufficient for noise filtering, as noise is a spatial phenomenon. The introduction of k \times k spatial kernels addresses this. Clean vs. Noisy Regimes: In clean images, IBRNet ignores feature statistics (mean/variance) because variance is low for surface points. In noisy regimes, individual features become more significant than joint statistics, necessitating the transformer module. Signal-Dependent Noise: The separation of blending weights per color channel is important, especially in the case of signal-dependent noise, which can vary across color channels. Not given in the sources. The addition of the Pre-Net layer, transformer module, and spatial kernels increases network complexity compared to standard IBRNet, but the exact computational cost is not quantified. Not given in the sources. The paper demonstrates improved denoising performance on the LLFF-N dataset compared to baseline IBRNet-N, but specific metrics (PSNR, SSIM) are not detailed in the provided notes. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Effectively handles degraded noisy images (e.g., low-light) by leveraging spatial context via 3D blending kernels and cross-view statistics via transformers. The Pre-Net layer efficiently reduces input noise without losing spatial resolution. Limitations: The method is designed for burst denoising of existing views rather than novel view synthesis. The reliance on accurate noise variance estimation may be a limitation if noise statistics are unknown or misestimated. Use NAN when the goal is to denoise a burst of noisy images of the same scene (burst denoising) rather than synthesizing novel views. It is particularly suitable for low-light conditions where noise is significant. Do not use NAN if the primary task is novel view synthesis from clean images, as standard IBRNet or other NeRF variants may be more appropriate. It is also not designed for single-image denoising without a burst of inputs. NAN was introduced in the paper "NAN: Noise-Aware NeRFs for Burst-Denoising". It extends the IBRNet architecture [29] to address the challenges of burst denoising, which differs from novel view synthesis in its focus on degraded noisy images and fixing existing views. The method builds upon IBRNet, which was designed for novel view synthesis with significant camera motion and complex 3D geometry. The authors observed that standard IBRNet performs poorly on noisy inputs due to its feature extraction and blending mechanisms. They introduced the Pre-Net layer, cross-view statistics aggregation, a transformer module, and 3D blending kernels to adapt IBRNet for noise-aware rendering. NAN is used for burst denoising of images captured in low-light conditions, where multiple noisy views of the same scene are available. It is evaluated on the LLFF-N dataset, which consists of noisy versions of the LLFF dataset. name: Multi-input MLP (mi-MLP)
head: mi-MLP, per-layer inputs incorporation
body: The multi-input MLP (mi-MLP) is a network architecture modification for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) designed to prevent overfitting in few-shot view synthesis without sacrificing the capacity to synthesize high-frequency details. Unlike the standard NeRF architecture Parent, which relies on a single deep path from input embeddings to output predictions, mi-MLP incorporates the positional encoding of the 3D location and viewing direction into every layer of the MLP. This creates shorter paths between inputs and outputs, allowing the model to learn flexible mappings that alleviate overfitting while maintaining the original model capacity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 5D coordinate vector \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^5, composed of the 3D spatial position \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and the 2D viewing direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^2 (normalized). Note: Standard NeRF uses \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3, but the source formulation for mi-MLP explicitly references 2D viewing direction in the definition of inputs, though the positional encoding \gammaL is applied to the combined input \mathbf{x}. Output: Volume density \sigma \in \mathbb{R} and view-dependent color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Data Structures: The network consists of N layers. Each layer i (for i > 1) contains: Weight matrix components \mathbf{w}i^{j0} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times d1} connecting the input embedding to the j-th neuron. Weight matrix components \mathbf{w}i^{j1} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times d2} connecting the previous layer's output to the j-th neuron. Bias vector \mathbf{b}i \in \mathbb{R}^{d2 \times 1}. Activation function \epsilon (default: ReLU). Parameters: L: Hyperparameter controlling the number of frequencies in the positional encoding. d1: Dimension of the encoded input embedding \gammaL(\mathbf{x}). d2: Hidden dimension of the MLP layers. Weight Initialization: Default PyTorch initialization is used, which satisfies the condition \|\mathbf{w}i^{j1}\|1 \in (0, 1]. Positional Encoding: The input \mathbf{x} is transformed using positional encoding \gammaL(\mathbf{x}): \gammaL(\mathbf{x}) = (\sin(2^0 \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^0 \mathbf{x}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^{L-1} \mathbf{x})) This results in an embedding vector of size 2 \cdot L \cdot \dim(\mathbf{x}). Algorithm: The output of layer i, denoted as fi, is computed by applying the layer function \phii to the previous layer's output f{i-1} and the positional encoding of the input \gammaL(\mathbf{x}). 1. Compute the positional encoding of the input: \mathbf{e} = \gammaL(\mathbf{x}) 2. Initialize the first layer output f1: f1 = \phi1(\mathbf{e}) Where \phi1 is the first layer function. 3. For each subsequent layer i from 2 to N: fi = \phii(f{i-1}, \mathbf{e}) The j-th element of the output feature fi, denoted \phii^j, is calculated as: \phii^j(\mathbf{e}) = \epsilon\left( \mathbf{w}i^{j0} \mathbf{e} + \mathbf{w}i^{j1} f{i-1} + \mathbf{b}i \right) Where: \epsilon is the activation function (default ReLU). \mathbf{w}i^{j0} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times d1} are the weights connecting the input embedding to the neuron. \mathbf{w}i^{j1} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times d2} are the weights connecting the previous layer's output to the neuron. \mathbf{b}i \in \mathbb{R}^{1} is the bias for the neuron. 4. The final layer outputs \sigma and \mathbf{c} are derived from fN. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import math class PositionalEncoding(nn.Module): def init(self, L): super(PositionalEncoding, self).init() self.L = L def forward(self, x): # x shape: (..., D) # Output shape: (..., 2 L D) # Note: The source defines gammaL(x) as sin/cos of 2^k x # We assume x is already scaled or the frequencies are applied directly. # Standard NeRF uses frequencies 2^0 to 2^(L-1). freqbands = 2.0 torch.arange(self.L, device=x.device).float() # Expand dimensions for broadcasting # x: (..., D) -> (..., 1, D) # freqbands: (L,) -> (L, 1, 1) scaledx = x.unsqueeze(1) freqbands.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(-1) # Apply sin and cos # scaledx: (..., L, D) sinvals = torch.sin(scaledx) cosvals = torch.cos(scaledx) # Concatenate along the last dimension # Result: (..., L D 2) out = torch.cat([sinvals, cosvals], dim=-1) return out class MiMLP(nn.Module): def init(self, inputdim, hiddendim, numlayers, L): super(MiMLP, self).init() self.inputdim = inputdim self.hiddendim = hiddendim self.numlayers = numlayers self.L = L # Input dimension for positional encoding is 5 (3 pos + 2 view dir as per source text) # However, standard NeRF uses 3 for view dir. The source text says "2D viewing direction". # We follow the source text's explicit mention of 2D for the input definition, # but note that standard NeRF uses 3D. If 3D is required, adjust inputdim. # The source formula uses gammaL(x) where x is 5D. self.posenc = PositionalEncoding(L) # Calculate encoded input dimension # x is 5D. gammaL produces 2 L 5 dimensions. self.encodedinputdim = 2 L inputdim # Layer 1: Takes only encoded input self.layer1 = nn.Linear(self.encodedinputdim, hiddendim) # Layers 2 to N: Take previous output AND encoded input self.layers = nn.ModuleList([ nn.Linear(hiddendim + self.encodedinputdim, hiddendim) for in range(numlayers - 1) ]) # Output layer self.outputlayer = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 4) # 1 for sigma, 3 for color def forward(self, x): # x: (..., 5) # 1. Encode inputs e = self.posenc(x) # (..., 2 L 5) # 2. First layer h = self.layer1(e) h = torch.relu(h) # 3. Subsequent layers for i in range(len(self.layers)): # Concatenate previous hidden state with encoded input # h: (..., hiddendim) # e: (..., encodedinputdim) combined = torch.cat([h, e], dim=-1) h = self.layersi h = torch.relu(h) # 4. Output out = self.outputlayer(h) sigma = out[..., 0:1] color = out[..., 1:4] return sigma, color Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Amplitude: During early training, vanilla MLPs result in similar gradient amplitudes for all layers. mi-MLP ensures that deeper layers (close to outputs) are updated with large gradients while shallower layers are updated with extremely small ones. This behavior is theoretically supported by the ratio of gradient amplitudes between adjacent layers. Weight Initialization: The condition \|\mathbf{w}i^{j1}\|1 \in (0, 1] is critical for the gradient ratio property. Default PyTorch initialization satisfies this. Input Dimension: The source explicitly states "2D viewing direction" in the definition of inputs for mi-MLP, which differs from the standard 3D viewing direction in vanilla NeRF. Implementers should verify if the specific dataset requires 2D or 3D direction encoding. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The mi-MLP boosts the PSNR of the baseline from 14.73 to 24.23 on few-shot view synthesis benchmarks. Strengths: Prevents overfitting in few-shot view synthesis without reducing model capacity. Allows synthesis with fewer parameters in an end-to-end way due to shorter paths between inputs and outputs. Keeps inputs and outputs unchanged, making it a plug-and-play solution for current NeRF-based pipelines. Limitations: Rendered novel views may still contain noticeable artifacts if colors and volume density are not modeled separately. When to use: When performing few-shot view synthesis and experiencing overfitting with a standard vanilla MLP architecture. The multi-input MLP (mi-MLP) was proposed by in 2024. It addresses the overfitting issue in few-shot view synthesis by modifying the network structure to incorporate inputs into each layer. The method is orthogonal to parameter reduction techniques, as it maintains model capacity while improving generalization. name: Regularization Techniques
body: Regularization techniques in NeRF training are strategies applied to the optimization objective or the model parameters to mitigate artifacts such as floaters, blur, and overfitting, particularly in sparse-view or ill-posed reconstruction scenarios. They set themselves apart from general hyperparameters (like learning rate or batch size) by directly modifying the geometry, density distribution, or view-dependency of the radiance field to enforce physical plausibility or structural consistency. The family shares the goal of constraining the solution space of the neural radiance field to prevent degenerate solutions (e.g., empty space filled with noise, or "floaters") that fit the training images but do not represent the true 3D scene. Common mechanisms include: 1. Density Constraints: Penalizing non-zero density in regions where no geometry should exist (e.g., near the camera or in the background) to suppress floaters. 2. Consistency Losses: Enforcing agreement between different representations of the scene (e.g., coarse vs. fine NeRFs, or predicted vs. geometry normals) to stabilize optimization. 3. Frequency/Complexity Control: Restricting the model's capacity to learn high-frequency details too early or in noisy conditions, often via curriculum learning or simplified architectures. 4. Geometric Priors: Using surface normals or edge-aware constraints to guide the shape of the reconstructed geometry. Spherical Harmonics Regularization restricts the maximum degree of Spherical Harmonics (SH) during early optimization to prevent high-frequency overfitting and improve coarse geometry reconstruction. It stabilizes optimization in harsh input conditions by allowing the model to learn diffuse reflectance (low-frequency SH) before view-direction-sensitive components (high-frequency SH). It sets itself apart by applying frequency regularization directly to SH coefficients in a voxel grid representation, rather than to positional encodings or Fourier coefficients. Bilateral Edge-Aware Constraint is a geometric regularization technique for NeRF-based volume rendering that suppresses high-frequency noise while preserving sharp geometric discontinuities such as building roofs and shadow boundaries. Unlike standard smoothness constraints that blur distinct edges, this method dynamically weights geometric penalties using photometric differences between neighboring rays, ensuring that significant color changes are not penalized as geometric errors. It addresses the lack of fixed neighborhood connectivity in implicit radiance fields by sampling neighbors via image-plane offsets. Definition: The total loss function used to train the Simple-RF models, combining multiple regularization terms to mitigate floaters and improve geometry in sparse input scenarios. Step: During the first 10k iterations of training, only impose Lm, La, and L{sd}. Do not impose L{aug} and L{cfc}. After 10k iterations, impose all loss terms including L{aug} and L{cfc}. Formula: L = \lambdam Lm + \lambdaa La + \lambda{sd} L{sd} + \lambda{aug} L{aug} + \lambda{cfc} L{cfc} + \lambda{mc} L{mc}. Parameter: \lambda{sd}: Weight for the smoothness/depth loss. Value: 0.1. \lambda{aug}: Weight for the augmentation loss. Value: 0.1. \lambda{cfc}: Weight for the consistency/contrastive loss (main NeRF only). Value: 0.1. Pitfall: L{cfc} and L{mc} are imposed only for the main NeRF and augmented TensoRF models respectively, not for all variants simultaneously in the same way. Definition: A regularization technique that minimizes the density of early samples along a ray to suppress background misplaces and floaters, adapted with a black/white prior for uniform backgrounds. Step: When a pixel value is either black or white, minimize the density of the first M+10 samples along the ray instead of the first M samples. Number: On the DTU dataset (3/6/9 views), RING-NeRF with density loss and continuous coarse-to-fine achieves 16.18/20.47/23.19 PSNR, 0.713/0.808/0.847 SSIM, 0.200/0.127/0.085 LPIPS. Comparison: Using only the density loss yields correct metrics but produces a slightly less precise 3D reconstruction and lower stability compared to using continuous coarse-to-fine alone. The combination of both provides the best trade-off between 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis quality. Definition: A regularization technique to prevent blur in rendered images caused by inconsistencies between coarse and fine NeRF depth estimates in few-shot settings. It drives the two NeRFs to be consistent in their solutions. Formula: L{cfc} = \mathbb{1}{\{m{cfc}=1\}} \odot \|zc - \tau(zf)\|^2 + \mathbb{1}{\{m{cfc}=-1\}} \odot \|\tau(zc) - zf\|^2, where zc and zf are depths estimated by coarse and fine NeRFs, \tau is a transformation function, and m{cfc} is a mask determined by reliability estimation. Pitfall: Without this loss, dense sampling may not be employed around the region where the fine NeRF predicts the object surface, leading to blur in rendered images. Number: Disabling L{cfc} leads to a drop in performance and increases training time by almost 2× due to the inclusion of augmentations for the fine NeRF. Definition: Apply an asymmetric predicted normal loss to tie predicted normals \tilde{n} to geometry normals n and rendering weights w, allowing separate multipliers for gradients flowing from geometry normals and weights to predicted normals, and vice versa. Formula: Compute asymmetric loss L{pred} = \lambdan Lp(w, n, \text{sg}(\tilde{n})) + \lambda{\tilde{n}} Lp(\text{sg}(w), \text{sg}(n), \tilde{n}), where Lp(w, n, \tilde{n}) = \sum w^{(i)} \|n^{(i)} - \tilde{n}^{(i)}\|^2 and \text{sg}(\cdot) is stop-gradient. Parameter: \lambdan: Multiplier for the term tying predicted normals to geometry normals. Typical value: 10^{-3}. Pitfall: Using standard symmetric predicted normal loss tends to oversmooth or underconstrain geometry, preventing normal vectors from converging to the correct solution. Definition: A regularization method that models input rays with mixture density models to achieve promising results with sparse inputs. Step: Minimize the negative log-likelihood (NLL) to learn the density distribution effectively with sparse inputs. Formula: Mixture coefficient \pii = wi / \sum{m=1}^{M} wm = Ti(1-\exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) / \sum{m=1}^{M} Tm(1-\exp(-\sigmam \deltam)), where wi is alpha blending weight, \deltai is sample interval, Ti is transmittance, \sigmai is volume density, and M is number of samples. Definition: A regularization term to prevent 'floater' or 'walls' artifacts in sparse-view training by constraining near-camera density to zero. It operates effectively where geometry regularization cannot due to missing correspondences. Formula: Total loss: L(\theta, t) = L{color}(\theta) + L{geo}(\theta, t) + \lambda{occ} L{occ}(\theta), where \lambda{occ} is a pre-defined weighting factor. Parameter: Occlusion regularization weight (\lambda{occ}): 0.01 across all experiments. Regularization in NeRFs emerged as a response to the inherent ill-posedness of the inverse rendering problem, particularly when training data is sparse or noisy. Early NeRF implementations often produced "floaters" (spurious geometry in empty space) or blurry reconstructions. Simple-RF and SimpleNeRF introduced simplified augmentation strategies and consistency losses to address these issues in sparse settings. RING-NeRF highlighted the importance of density losses combined with coarse-to-fine sampling for stability. FreeNeRF formalized occlusion regularization to suppress near-camera artifacts. Ref-NeRF and subsequent works like NeRF-Casting introduced normal-based regularization to improve surface detail and specular consistency. MixNeRF utilized mixture density models to handle ambiguity in sparse inputs. name: Spherical Harmonics Regularization
head: SH coefficient masking, SH curriculum training, SH degree regularization
body: Spherical Harmonics (SH) Regularization is a training strategy that restricts the maximum degree of Spherical Harmonics during the early stages of optimization to prevent high-frequency overfitting and stabilize geometry reconstruction. It addresses the problem where high-frequency SH coefficients cause inaccurate geometry and "floaters" (noise artifacts) when the model attempts to learn view-dependent effects before the coarse geometry is established. It sets itself apart from general density constraints by specifically targeting the frequency content of the radiance representation, acting as a curriculum learning mechanism for view-dependent appearance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A voxel grid representation of the scene where each voxel stores opacity and Spherical Harmonics coefficients for color/radiance. The SH coefficients are typically organized by degree l and order m. Output: A trained radiance field with stabilized geometry and reduced high-frequency artifacts, achieved by gradually unlocking high-frequency SH coefficients during training. Data Structures: The radiance field uses a voxel grid. Each voxel v contains: Opacity \alphav (scalar). SH Coefficients c{l,m} for color channels. For a maximum degree L, there are (L+1)^2 coefficients per color channel. The coefficients are indexed by degree l \in \{0, \dots, L\} and order m \in \{-l, \dots, l\}. Parameters: L{max}: The maximum SH degree supported by the representation (e.g., L{max}=3 or 4). E{curriculum}: The number of epochs for the curriculum schedule. Sources specify E{curriculum}=5. L{start}: The initial maximum SH degree allowed. Sources imply starting with low degrees (e.g., l=0 or l=1) to capture diffuse reflectance. Masking Rate Decay: The rate at which the masking constraint is relaxed. Sources specify a decay of 1/5 per epoch for the first 5 epochs. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the voxel grid with SH coefficients. Set the current maximum allowed SH degree L{curr} = L{start} (typically 0 or 1). 2. Masking Definition: Define a binary mask M{l,m} for each SH coefficient. If l > L{curr}, then M{l,m} = 0 (masked); otherwise, M{l,m} = 1. 3. Gradient Application: During backpropagation, compute gradients \nabla c{l,m} for all coefficients. Apply the mask to the gradients or the coefficients themselves: c{l,m}^{new} = c{l,m}^{old} + \eta \cdot M{l,m} \cdot \nabla c{l,m} where \eta is the learning rate. This ensures that coefficients with l > L{curr} do not update. 4. Curriculum Schedule: For each epoch e: If e < E{curriculum}: Gradually increase L{curr}. Sources describe decreasing the "rate of SH masking" by 1/5 per epoch. This implies a linear relaxation of the constraint. Specifically, if the mask initially blocks all coefficients above a certain degree, the threshold for L{curr} increases. A precise interpretation from is that the masking is relaxed such that by epoch 5, full SH degrees are allowed. If e \ge E{curriculum}: Set L{curr} = L{max}. All SH coefficients are updated with full rate. 5. Optimization: Continue optimizing opacity, SH coefficients, and other parameters (e.g., white balance) using the standard reconstruction loss. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sphericalharmonicsregularization( voxelgrid, maxshdegree: int, curriculumepochs: int = 5, learningrate: float): """ Applies SH regularization during training. Args: voxelgrid: Object containing SH coefficients c[l][m] for each voxel. maxshdegree: The maximum SH degree Lmax (e.g., 3). curriculumepochs: Number of epochs for the curriculum (Ecurriculum). learningrate: Base learning rate for SH coefficients. Returns: Updated voxelgrid after one training step. """ # Determine current max degree based on epoch # Note: The exact epoch counter is assumed to be available in the training loop context. # Here we assume 'currentepoch' is passed or tracked externally. # For the purpose of this self-contained function, we define the logic for a given epoch. # Placeholder for current epoch from outer loop # currentepoch =... # Calculate current allowed degree # Source: "decrease the rate of SH masking by 1/5 per epoch during the early five epochs" # This implies a linear ramp-up. # If we start at degree 0 (only l=0), and end at degree Lmax after 5 epochs. # A simple interpretation: Lcurr = floor(currentepoch (maxshdegree / curriculumepochs)) # However, mentions masking degrees 2 and 3 specifically in the context of HDR-Plenoxels. # Let's implement a general linear schedule from 0 to maxshdegree. if currentepoch < curriculumepochs: # Linear interpolation: at epoch 0, degree 0; at epoch 5, degree maxshdegree # Using float division for smoothness, then clamping progress = currentepoch / curriculumepochs currentmaxdegree = int(progress maxshdegree) else: currentmaxdegree = maxshdegree # Apply masking to gradients or coefficients for voxel in voxelgrid: for l in range(0, maxshdegree + 1): for m in range(-l, l + 1): # Get gradient for this coefficient grad = getgradient(voxel, l, m) # Apply mask: if l > currentmaxdegree, mask is 0 if l > currentmaxdegree: maskedgrad = 0.0 else: maskedgrad = grad # Update coefficient voxel.c[l][m] += learningrate maskedgrad return voxelgrid Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: SH coefficients can vary in magnitude. Masking high-frequency terms prevents them from dominating the loss gradient early on, which can cause instability if not masked. Boundary Conditions: The transition from masked to unmasked coefficients must be smooth to avoid sudden changes in radiance representation. The linear schedule in helps mitigate this. Degenerate Input: In scenes with very high-frequency view-dependent effects (glossy materials), early masking might slow down convergence for those specific materials, but it stabilizes the overall geometry. Time Complexity: Adds negligible computational overhead. The masking operation is a simple conditional check per coefficient per voxel per step. Memory Complexity: No additional memory required beyond storing the SH coefficients and the epoch counter. Performance: Improves geometry accuracy and reduces floaters, especially in few-shot or harsh input conditions. It stabilizes optimization by decoupling geometry learning (low frequency) from appearance learning (high frequency). Strengths: Simple to implement, no extra hyperparameters beyond the curriculum length, effective at preventing high-frequency overfitting. Limitations: Requires a fixed curriculum schedule; may not adapt well to scenes with varying frequency content across different regions. Spherical Harmonics Regularization was introduced in the context of Plenoxels and related voxel-based radiance field methods. It was inspired by frequency regularization techniques used in FreeNeRF (positional encoding) and FourieRF (Fourier coefficients). The specific application to SH coefficients was detailed in HDR-Plenoxels and F2Plenoxels. It is used in few-shot view synthesis and high-dynamic-range radiance field reconstruction.
