name: UE4-NeRF
body: UE4-NeRF is a neural rendering system designed for the real-time interactive rendering of large-scale 3D scenes by integrating Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) with the Unreal Engine 4 (UE4) rasterization pipeline. It partitions large environments into sub-NeRFs, representing each block using textured polygonal meshes initialized from regular octahedra, and utilizes a Level of Detail (LOD) hierarchy to maintain high frame rates at varying observation heights. Unlike Block-NeRF, which is limited to grid structures, UE4-NeRF supports diverse terrains including mountainous areas, and unlike Mobile-NeRF, it handles tilted surfaces and semi-transparent objects more effectively. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of posed camera images (typically drone-captured) with GPS metadata; camera intrinsics and extrinsics; a large-scale scene bounding box. Outputs: A set of textured polygonal meshes (shading meshes) for each scene block at multiple Levels of Detail (LOD); a neural shader (HLSL fragment shader) deployed in UE4; real-time rendered RGB images. Data Structures 1. Scene Partitioning: The large scene is divided into overlapping blocks. Each training area is slightly larger than the corresponding scene area to ensure smooth transitions at boundaries. 2. Mesh Representation: Each block is represented by a textured polygonal mesh. The mesh is initialized from a grid and optimized during training. The texture atlas stores feature vectors and opacity information. 3. Coordinate System: X-axis: East. Y-axis: South. Z-axis: Up. Scale: 100:1 (UE4 units to real-world units). 4. Network Architecture: Encoder: A 4-layer MLP with dimensions 32 \times 64, 64 \times 64, 64 \times 64, 64 \times 8. It takes multi-resolution hash-encoded position features and outputs an opacity scalar \alpha and an 8-dimensional feature vector \mathbf{m}. Decoder: A 3-layer MLP with dimensions 17 \times 16, 16 \times 16, 16 \times 3. It takes the feature vector \mathbf{m} and spherical harmonics coefficients of the view direction to predict the final RGB color \mathbf{c}. Method Steps 1. Preprocessing and Coordinate Transformation: Convert GPS-captured drone imagery coordinates to the UE4 coordinate system (X=East, Y=South, Z=Up) and apply the 100:1 scale conversion. 2. Block Partitioning: Partition the large-scale scene into multiple blocks (sub-NeRFs). Train a coarse model for sub-region segmentation to capture overall terrain and building outlines. Filter images associated with each sub-region and apply a mask to exclude pixels outside the specific scene area. 3. Mesh Initialization: Initialize a 128 \times 128 \times 128 grid for each block. Select the center point of each grid cell along with its six neighboring grids (front, back, left, right, top, bottom) to form the initial polygonal mesh structure. Use regular octahedra with 20 faces (8 exterior, 12 interior) instead of the Mobile-NeRF approach to address slow/unstable convergence on tilted surfaces. 4. Training (Optimization): For each block, optimize the Encoder-Decoder network parameters and the vertex positions of the meshes simultaneously. Encoding: Use multi-resolution hash encoding (from Instant-NGP) for the position input pi to accelerate training. View Direction: Represent the viewing direction d using spherical harmonics SH(d). Forward Pass: Compute opacity and feature vector: \mathbf{m}i, \alphai = E(\text{hash}(pi); \thetaE) Compute color: \mathbf{c}i = D(\mathbf{m}i, SH(di); \thetaD) Where E is the Encoder MLP and D is the Decoder MLP. Loss: Minimize the difference between rendered colors and ground truth images using PSNR/SSIM and LPIPS metrics. Hardware: Implement computationally intensive portions using CUDA on NVIDIA GPUs (e.g., RTX 3090). Iterations: Train for 80,000 epochs per block to achieve convergence. 5. Shading Mesh Extraction: Extract coarse polygonal meshes without textures during training. Apply vertex optimization results. Encode texture maps (feature vectors and opacity) into the network outputs. 6. Level of Detail (LOD) Generation: Train meshes with varying levels of detail for different observation heights. Coarser meshes are used for higher observation heights to ensure real-time performance. Extract pre-rendered polygonal meshes at different LODs for the final rendering module. 7. Rendering in UE4: Deploy the Encoder-Decoder network as an HLSL fragment shader in UE4. The shader takes feature vectors (from the texture atlas) as input and outputs colors. Combine the extracted LOD meshes with the UE4 rasterization pipeline. UE4 handles occlusion automatically; if traditional 3D models (e.g.,.obj,.fbx) are imported, the neural shader computation is skipped for occluded regions. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class UE4NeRFBlock: def init(self, scenebounds, gridsize=128): self.scenebounds = scenebounds self.gridsize = gridsize # Initialize mesh vertices from 128x128x128 grid neighbors self.vertices = initializeoctahedronmesh(gridsize) # 20 faces: 8 exterior, 12 interior self.faces = getoctahedronfaces() # Network Parameters # Encoder: 4-layer MLP (32->64->64->64->8) self.encoderweights = initmlpweights([32, 64, 64, 64, 8]) # Decoder: 3-layer MLP (17->16->16->3) # Input: 8 (features) + 9 (SH coefficients) = 17 self.decoderweights = initmlpweights([17, 16, 16, 3]) # Multi-resolution hash grid (from Instant-NGP) self.hashgrid = inithashgrid() def encodeposition(self, position): # Apply multi-resolution hash encoding to position # position is in UE4 coordinate system (X=East, Y=South, Z=Up) # Scale is 100:1 hashedfeatures = hashencode(position, self.hashgrid) return hashedfeatures def sphericalharmonics(self, direction): # Compute SH coefficients for view direction # direction is normalized vector shcoeffs = computeshcoefficients(direction, degree=3) # 9 coefficients return shcoeffs def forwardencoder(self, hashedpos): # E(hash(pi); thetaE) -> Mi, alphai # Input: hashedpos (dim 32) # Output: featurevector (dim 8), opacity (scalar) x = hashedpos for layer in self.encoderlayers: x = relu(layer(x)) featurevector = x[:,:8] opacity = sigmoid(x[:, 8]) # Assuming last output is opacity return featurevector, opacity def forwarddecoder(self, featurevector, shcoeffs): # D(Mi, SH(di); thetaD) -> ci # Input: featurevector (dim 8) + shcoeffs (dim 9) = 17 # Output: color (RGB, dim 3) inputvec = concat(featurevector, shcoeffs) x = inputvec for layer in self.decoderlayers: x = relu(layer(x)) color = sigmoid(x) # Output RGB return color def renderray(self, rayorigin, raydirection): # Calculate intersection with polygonal mesh # Ray: r(t) = o + td intersectionpoint, normal = intersectmesh(rayorigin, raydirection, self.vertices, self.faces) if intersectionpoint is None: return backgroundcolor # Encode position at intersection hashedpos = self.encodeposition(intersectionpoint) # Get view direction SH coefficients shcoeffs = self.sphericalharmonics(raydirection) # Get features and opacity featurevector, opacity = self.forwardencoder(hashedpos) # Get color color = self.forwarddecoder(featurevector, shcoeffs) return color def trainstep(self, images, poses, optimizer): # Filter images for this block using mask blockimages, blockposes = filterimagesbymask(images, poses, self.scenebounds) for image, pose in zip(blockimages, blockposes): # Generate rays for each pixel rays = generaterays(pose, image.shape) renderedcolors = [] for ray in rays: color = self.renderray(ray.origin, ray.direction) renderedcolors.append(color) # Compute Loss (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) loss = computeloss(renderedcolors, image) # Backpropagate to update network weights and vertex positions optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Update mesh vertices based on gradient updatemeshvertices(self.vertices, self.faces, gradients) def extractmeshforlod(self, lodlevel): # Extract coarse polygonal meshes without textures # Apply vertex optimization results # Encode texture maps (feature vectors and opacity) mesh = self.vertices textureatlas = generatetextureatlas(self.encoderweights, self.decoderweights) return mesh, textureatlas def ue4renderloop(mesheslod, textureatlases, camerapose): # Select LOD based on camera height lodindex = selectlod(camerapose.height, mesheslod) mesh = mesheslod[lodindex] texture = textureatlases[lodindex] # Deploy neural shader (HLSL fragment shader) # Shader takes feature vectors from texture atlas # Outputs colors renderedimage = rasterizewithneuralshader(mesh, texture, camerapose) # Handle occlusion with imported 3D models (.obj,.fbx) # UE4 automatically skips neural shader for occluded regions finalimage = handleocclusion(renderedimage, importedmodels) return finalimage Parameters Grid Initialization Size: 128 \times 128 \times 128. Octahedron Faces: 20 total (8 exterior, 12 interior). Encoder MLP Dimensions: 32 \times 64, 64 \times 64, 64 \times 64, 64 \times 8. Decoder MLP Dimensions: 17 \times 16, 16 \times 16, 16 \times 3. Training Hardware: 1 Nvidia RTX 3090 GPU. Training Iterations: 80,000 epochs per block. Coordinate System: X=East, Y=South, Z=Up. World Scale: 100:1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Tilted Surfaces: Mobile-NeRF suffers from slow/unstable convergence on tilted surfaces; UE4-NeRF addresses this by using regular octahedra. Semi-transparent Objects: Mobile-NeRF cannot handle transparent/semi-transparent objects (water, glass, plastic) due to opacity binarization. UE4-NeRF stores opacity in texture maps to mitigate this, though semi-transparent objects (e.g., vegetation) increase computational overhead and reduce frame rates. Pre-rendering Gaps: Pre-rendering cannot capture rays from all viewing angles, potentially resulting in gaps or holes in the final rendered scene. Exposure Matching: Consistent exposure matching with original images is difficult in UE4, causing evaluation metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) to underestimate actual reconstruction quality. Memory Overhead: Rendering large scenes (square kilometers) incurs significant memory overhead, especially when using CUDA and NVIDIA GPUs. Increasing accuracy further amplifies memory consumption. Training Speed: 1000× faster than Mobile-NeRF. Training time per block: 40 minutes on 1×RTX 3090. Training time for full scene (n blocks): 1 hour + (40 minutes × n/4) on 1×RTX 3090. Rendering Performance: Real-time rendering at 4K resolution with up to 43 FPS. 50 FPS on full scene at 2K resolution. ≥70 FPS on individual blocks at 2K resolution. Memory: Significant memory overhead for large scenes (square kilometers). Requires NVIDIA GPUs and CUDA. Strengths: Real-time interactive rendering of large-scale scenes; handles tilted surfaces and semi-transparent objects better than Mobile-NeRF; supports scene editing with traditional 3D models; suitable for diverse terrains (mountainous, farmland) unlike Block-NeRF. Limitations: Pre-rendering gaps/holes; exposure matching issues in UE4; high memory consumption; semi-transparent objects reduce frame rates; requires NVIDIA GPUs. When to Use: Real-time interactive rendering of large-scale outdoor scenes (e.g., digital twins, VR, games) where high fidelity and editability are required. When Not to Use: Scenes requiring perfect ray-casting from all angles without pre-rendering artifacts; environments with extremely high densities of semi-transparent objects where frame rate is critical; hardware without NVIDIA GPUs/CUDA support. UE4-NeRF was introduced in the paper "UE4-NeRF: Neural Radiance Field for Real-Time Rendering of Large-Scale Scene". It was developed to address the limitations of existing NeRF methods in real-time rendering of large-scale scenes, such as high training costs, slow rendering speeds, and lack of editability. The method combines NeRF with the Unreal Engine 4 (UE4) rasterization pipeline, leveraging LOD techniques and multi-resolution hash encoding to achieve real-time performance. It is used in UE4 for real-time interactive rendering and scene editing/manipulation, particularly for drone-captured large-scale scenes like farmlands, construction sites, and industrial parks, and has been evaluated on the Mega-NeRF public dataset. name: Multi-view Aggregation with Skeletal Features
head: Multi-view aggregation of skeletal and query features
body: This method aggregates complementary geometric and appearance information from multiple camera views to enhance the radiance field representation of dynamic humans. It combines time-augmented skeletal features, which provide robust geometric priors via a SMPL model, with pixel-aligned image features, which capture high-frequency visual details. By using a cross-attention mechanism to weigh these features based on their compatibility, the method resolves ambiguities in single-view observations and improves rendering quality for articulated subjects. It differs from standard NeRF by explicitly integrating skeletal priors and multi-view consistency through attention, rather than relying solely on positional encoding of raw coordinates. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A 3D query point x \in \mathbb{R}^3 in world space; a set of C input images I{c,t} at time t; camera parameters for each view; a SMPL model instance at time t; and the viewing direction d \in \mathbb{R}^3. Outputs: Volume density \tilde{\sigma}t(x) and RGB color \tilde{r}^g{bt}(x) for the query point. Data Structures: Skeletal Features (s^0{c,t}): A dense 3D volume of features d-dimensional, defined on the SMPL mesh vertices and interpolated into space. Pixel-aligned Features (p^x{c,t}): A d-dimensional feature vector extracted from the image I{c,t} corresponding to the 2D projection of x. Attention Weights (mv\att^x): A C \times C matrix representing cross-view compatibility. Steps: 1. Retrieve Skeletal Feature: Map the query point x to the local coordinate space of the SMPL model at time t. Retrieve the skeletal feature s^0{c,t} at this location using trilinear interpolation within the SparseConvNet representation of the SMPL volume. This feature is time-augmented, encoding geometric deviations of the SMPL vertices. 2. Sample Pixel-aligned Feature: Project the query point x onto the 2D image plane of each camera view c to obtain pixel coordinates. Sample the feature p^x{c,t} from the image I{c,t} at these coordinates. This feature is time-specific and represents the exact visual appearance at the query location. 3. Construct Multi-view Cross-Attention: Let s^0{1:C,t} = \{s^0{c,t} \mid c=1,\dots,C\} and p^x{1:C,t} = \{p^x{c,t} \mid c=1,\dots,C\} be the sets of skeletal and pixel-aligned features across all C views. Compute keys k(\cdot) and values v(\cdot) for both feature types using learned linear layers (independent from temporal transformers). Calculate the attention weights mv\att^x \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times C} using the dot product between skeletal keys and pixel-aligned keys, scaled by dimension: mv\att^x = \psi \left( \frac{k(s^0{1:C,t}) \cdot k(p^x{1:C,t})^T}{\sqrt{d}} \right) where \psi is the softmax operator applied along the second axis (columns). This highlights confident observations where skeletal and image features are compatible. 4. Compute View-wise Representation: Aggregate the values from both feature types using the attention weights: z^x{1:C,t} = mv\att^x \cdot v(p^x{1:C,t}) + v(s^0{1:C,t}) Here, z^x{c,t} \in \mathbb{R}^d is the view-wise representation for view c. The term mv\att^x \cdot v(p^x{1:C,t}) re-weights the pixel-aligned features based on skeletal compatibility, while v(s^0{1:C,t}) adds the skeletal value directly. 5. Compute Meta-time and Meta-view Representation: Average the view-wise representations across all C views to obtain a single robust feature vector z^xt \in \mathbb{R}^d: z^xt = \frac{1}{C} \sum{c=1}^{C} z^x{c,t} This step fuses multi-view information into a meta-representation. 6. Predict Density: Pass z^xt through a Multi-Layer Perceptron MLP\sigma consisting of four linear layers to predict the volume density: \tilde{\sigma}t(x) = MLP\sigma(z^xt) 7. Predict Color: Compute the mean of the pixel-aligned values across views: \bar{v}p = \frac{1}{C} \sum{c=1}^{C} v(p^x{c,t}). Apply positional encoding \gammad(d) to the viewing direction d (using 2 \times l basis functions as in [28]). Concatenate the mean pixel-aligned value and the encoded direction, then pass through MLP{rgb} (two linear layers): \tilde{r}^g{bt}(x) = MLP{rgb} \left( [\bar{v}p; \gammad(d)] \right) Note: The source formula shows MLP{rgb} taking the mean of values and the direction encoding. Parameters: d: Feature dimension (Not given in the sources). C: Number of input views. l: Number of frequency bands for directional encoding (Not given in the sources). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion: If a query point is occluded in some views, the pixel-aligned features p^x{c,t} may be noisy. The attention mechanism mitigates this by down-weighting incompatible views, but extreme occlusion may require robust skeletal priors. SMPL Accuracy: The skeletal feature retrieval depends on the accuracy of the SMPL pose estimation. Errors in SMPL pose will propagate to s^0{c,t}, potentially misleading the attention weights. Trilinear Interpolation: Sampling from the SparseConvNet volume requires careful handling of boundaries outside the SMPL mesh. Points outside the SMPL volume should be handled with a fallback or clamping to avoid NaNs. This method samples time-augmented skeletal features at arbitrary 3D query points by diffusing discrete skeletal features into a continuous 3D volume using sparse convolutions. It differs from dense voxelization by processing only occupied voxels, significantly improving efficiency for large 3D spaces. It is chosen when computational efficiency is critical and the scene contains large empty regions. See SparseConvNet-based Skeletal Feature Sampling. Time Complexity: Dominated by the multi-view attention mechanism, which is O(C^2 \cdot d) for the attention weights and O(C \cdot d) for the aggregation, plus the MLP inference. The SparseConvNet sampling is efficient due to sparsity. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the SparseConvNet volume for skeletal features and the image features for all views. The attention matrix is C \times C. Strengths: Effectively combines geometric priors (SMPL) with visual details (images). Handles multi-view inconsistencies via attention. Improves rendering quality for articulated humans. Limitations: Relies on accurate SMPL pose estimation. Computationally more expensive than standard NeRF due to multi-view processing and attention. When to use: Dynamic human rendering where multi-view consistency and geometric priors are beneficial. When not to use: Static scenes without articulated subjects, or resource-constrained environments where SMPL inference and multi-view attention are too costly. The method originates from the "Neural Human Performer" paper, which introduces a framework for learning generalizable radiance fields for human performance rendering. It builds on the idea of using skeletal priors (SMPL) to regularize the radiance field, extending it with multi-view aggregation to handle dynamic scenes and multiple viewpoints. The multi-view pose refinement variant is described in "A-NeRF," which focuses on articulated neural radiance fields for learning human shape, appearance, and pose, incorporating multi-view constraints for pose refinement. Neural Human Performer: Learning Generalizable Radiance Fields for Human Performance Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2109.07448, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) A-NeRF: Articulated Neural Radiance Fields for Learning Human Shape, Appearance, and Pose, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2102.06199, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: SparseConvNet-based Skeletal Feature Sampling
head: 3D sparse convolution feature diffusion, SparseConvNet sampling
body: This method samples time-augmented skeletal features at arbitrary 3D query points by diffusing discrete skeletal features into a continuous 3D volume using sparse convolutions, enabling spatially aware feature retrieval for NeRF input. It differs from dense voxelization by using sparse convolutions to process only occupied voxels, improving efficiency for large 3D spaces. Inputs: SMPL parameters defining the human body pose and shape. Discrete skeletal features s{01:C,t} \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times C \times d} associated with the skeleton at time t. A 3D query point x in world coordinates. Outputs: A sampled skeletal feature vector s{01:C,t}^x \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times 128}. Data Structures: Input Volume: A 3D grid of dimensions D0 \times H0 \times W0 representing the 3D bounding box of the human body. The grid is sparse, containing features only at voxel locations corresponding to the skeleton. SparseConvNet Architecture: A sequence of sparse convolutional layers with batch normalization and ReLU activation. The architecture is defined as follows: Layer 1: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 64 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 1) \times 2 Layer 2: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 64 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 2) Layer 3: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 64 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 1) \times 2 Layer 4: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 64 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 2) Layer 5: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 64 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 1) \times 3 Layer 6: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 64 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 2) Layer 7: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 128 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 1) \times 3 Layer 8: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 128 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 2) Layer 9: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 128 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 1) \times 3 Layer 10: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 128 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 2) Layer 11: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 128 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 1) \times 3 Layer 12: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 128 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 2) Layer 13: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 128 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 1) \times 3 Layers 14-17: Resize and concatenate outputs of layers 5, 9, 13, and 17. Steps: 1. Bounding Box Computation: Compute the 3D bounding box of the human body based on the SMPL parameters. 2. Voxelization: Divide the 3D bounding box into voxels of size 5\text{mm} \times 5\text{mm} \times 5\text{mm}, resulting in a volume of dimensions D0 \times H0 \times W0. 3. Coordinate Transformation: Transform skeletal feature locations and the query location x to the SMPL coordinate system to ensure invariance to world position and orientation. 4. Feature Diffusion: Pass the input volume through the SparseConvNet architecture. The network consists of 3D sparse convolutions that diffuse the skeletal features into the nearby 3D space. 5. Multi-scale Aggregation: Resize and concatenate the multi-scale outputs from layers 5, 9, 13, and 17 to form the output feature. The output feature dimensions are D'/16 \times H'/16 \times W'/16 \times 384 before reduction, where D', H', W' correspond to the dimensions after the respective strided convolutions. 6. Interpolation: Sample the corresponding skeletal feature at query location x via trilinear interpolation from the concatenated output volume. 7. Channel Reduction: Pass the sampled feature through a fully-connected layer to reduce the channel size to 128. Parameters: Voxel size: 5\text{mm} \times 5\text{mm} \times 5\text{mm}. Output channel size after reduction: 128. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method relies on the accuracy of the SMPL parameters to define the bounding box and coordinate transformation. Incorrect SMPL fitting may lead to misaligned features. Sparse convolutions require efficient data structures to handle sparsity. Inefficient implementation may negate the performance benefits. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves efficiency for large 3D spaces by processing only occupied voxels. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When spatially aware feature retrieval for NeRF input is required, and efficiency in large 3D spaces is a concern. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method is described in "Neural Human Performer: Learning Generalizable Radiance Fields for Human Performance Rendering". It builds on Parent. name: Lightning-NeRF Model Configuration
head: LightningNeRFModelConfig
body: Lightning-NeRF is a configuration framework for efficient radiance field optimization, designed to accelerate training and rendering through specific architectural choices and initialization strategies. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF implementations by utilizing a density grid with hash encoding for the density branch and a separate MLP for color, alongside specific hyperparameters for ray marching and background handling. The method defines the hyperparameters and structural configuration for the Lightning-NeRF neural network. It separates the representation of density and color, using a hash-encoded density grid and a view-dependent MLP for appearance. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Camera parameters (intrinsics, extrinsics), scene bounding box, optional point cloud for initialization, and hyperparameters defined in LightningNeRFModelConfig. Outputs: Predicted volume density \sigma and RGB color \mathbf{c} for sampled points along rays. Data Structures The configuration is encapsulated in a class or dictionary structure with the following fields: | Field | Type | Default Value | Description | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | nearplane | float | 0.01 | Start distance for ray sampling. | | farplane | float | 6.0 | End distance for ray sampling. | | vimlpnumlayers | int | 3 | Number of layers in the view-independent MLP. | | vimlphiddensize | int | 64 | Hidden dimension of the view-independent MLP. | | vdmlpnumlayers | int | 2 | Number of layers in the view-dependent MLP. | | vdmlphiddensize | int | 32 | Hidden dimension of the view-dependent MLP. | | appearanceembeddingdim | int | 0 | Dimension of appearance embedding. 0 disables it. | | useaverageappearanceembedding | bool | True | Use average appearance embedding for inference. | | backgroundcolor | str | 'random' | Background color mode: 'random', 'black', or 'white'. | | alphathre | float | 0.01 | Opacity threshold for skipping raymarching steps. | | coneangle | float | 0.004 | Cone angle for adaptive raymarching. 0.0 for synthetic, 1./256 for real. | | pointcloudpath | str | None | Path to a point cloud file (e.g.,.ply) for initialization. | | frontalaxis | str | 'x' | Axis for scene bounding box background augmentation ('x' or 'y'). | | initdensityvalue | float | 10.0 | Initial density value for occupied regions in the density grid. | | densitygridbaseres | int | 256 | Base resolution for the density grid. | | densitylog2hashmapsize | int | 24 | Log2 size of the hash map for density encoding. | | bgdensitygridres | int | 32 | Resolution for the background density grid. | | bgdensitylog2hashmapsize | int | 18 | Log2 size of the hash map for background density. | Optimization Configuration The training loop uses specific optimizers and schedulers for different components: Density Encoder (denencoder): RAdam optimizer with learning rate 1.0. Exponential decay scheduler: warmup 10 steps, linear ramp to final LR 0.01 over 10,000 steps. Color Encoder (colencoder): RAdam optimizer with learning rate 1.0. Exponential decay scheduler: warmup 10 steps, linear ramp to final LR 0.01 over 10,000 steps. Network (network): Adam optimizer with learning rate 10^{-2} and \epsilon=10^{-15}. Exponential decay scheduler: final LR 10^{-4} over 30,000 steps. Pseudocode The following Python-like pseudocode illustrates the configuration structure and initialization logic. It assumes standard libraries for math and file I/O. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class LightningNeRFModelConfig: def init(self): # Ray Sampling Parameters self.nearplane = 0.01 self.farplane = 6.0 self.alphathre = 0.01 self.coneangle = 0.004 # 0.0 for synthetic, 1./256 for real # MLP Architecture self.vimlpnumlayers = 3 self.vimlphiddensize = 64 self.vdmlpnumlayers = 2 self.vdmlphiddensize = 32 # Appearance self.appearanceembeddingdim = 0 self.useaverageappearanceembedding = True self.backgroundcolor = 'random' # Density Grid & Hash Encoding self.pointcloudpath = None self.frontalaxis = 'x' self.initdensityvalue = 10.0 self.densitygridbaseres = 256 self.densitylog2hashmapsize = 24 self.bgdensitygridres = 32 self.bgdensitylog2hashmapsize = 18 # Optimization Hyperparameters (stored for trainer) self.optimizers = { "denencoder": { "optimizertype": "RAdam", "lr": 1.0, "schedulertype": "ExponentialDecay", "warmupsteps": 10, "lrfinal": 0.01, "maxsteps": 10000 }, "colencoder": { "optimizertype": "RAdam", "lr": 1.0, "schedulertype": "ExponentialDecay", "warmupsteps": 10, "lrfinal": 0.01, "maxsteps": 10000 }, "network": { "optimizertype": "Adam", "lr": 1e-2, "eps": 1e-15, "schedulertype": "ExponentialDecay", "lrfinal": 1e-4, "maxsteps": 30000 } } def initializedensitygrid(self, gridresolution): """ Initializes the density grid with the specified initial density value. """ # Create a 3D grid of zeros grid = [0.0] (gridresolution 3) # Fill occupied regions with initdensityvalue # Note: Exact occupancy mask depends on point cloud or bounding box # This is a placeholder for the actual initialization logic for i in range(len(grid)): grid[i] = self.initdensityvalue return grid def getraysamplingrange(self, scenedepth): """ Determines the near and far planes based on scene properties. """ # Clip height (z-axis) to avoid underground areas if using Argoverse2-like data # This is specific to certain datasets as noted in sources minz = -5.0 near = self.nearplane far = self.farplane # If scene depth exceeds farplane, adjust or clip if scenedepth > far: far = scenedepth return near, far Edge Cases and Pitfalls Cone Angle: Setting coneangle to 0.0 is required for synthetic scenes (e.g., Blender), while real-world scenes (e.g., KITTI-360, Argoverse2) require a non-zero value (typically 1./256) for adaptive raymarching. Background Augmentation: The frontalaxis parameter affects how background points are generated for augmentation. Incorrect axis selection may lead to artifacts in background regions. Point Cloud Initialization: If pointcloudpath is provided, the density grid is initialized based on the point cloud occupancy. If not, the grid may be initialized uniformly or based on the bounding box. Precision: The Adam optimizer uses a small \epsilon=10^{-15}, which may require careful handling of numerical stability in gradient computation. Time Complexity: Training time is reduced compared to standard NeRF due to the use of hash encoding for density and optimized raymarching with alphathre skipping. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is determined by the hash map sizes (densitylog2hashmapsize and bgdensitylog2hashmapsize). A size of 24 corresponds to 2^{24} entries, which is memory-intensive but allows for high-resolution detail. Performance: The configuration is tuned for efficient training on large-scale real-world datasets like KITTI-360 and Argoverse2. Strengths: Fast training, good reconstruction quality for real-world scenes, flexible background handling. Limitations: High memory usage for large hash maps; requires careful tuning of coneangle for different scene types. Lightning-NeRF was introduced by VISION-SJTU as an efficient method for training and rendering neural radiance fields. It builds upon the original NeRF architecture but introduces optimizations such as hash encoding for density and specific initialization strategies to handle large-scale real-world scenes. The method is implemented in the Nerfstudio framework. Lightning-NeRF, https://github.com/VISION-SJTU/Lightning-NeRF, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Residual-NeRF
head: Residual-NeRF-S (ablation variant)
body: Residual-NeRF is a method for improving depth perception and training speed for transparent objects in mostly static scenes by leveraging a static scene prior. It solves the ambiguity of depth estimation for transparent objects, where standard NeRFs struggle due to multiple surfaces radiating light along a ray, leading to noisy depth maps and perceived holes that hinder robotic grasp planning. Unlike methods that require pre-defined spatial areas for fusion (e.g., Block-NeRF, NeRFusion), Residual-NeRF learns to mix a pre-trained background NeRF and a residual NeRF at every point in space using a learned Mixnet, resulting in fewer holes and less noise in depth maps. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: I{bg}: Set of images of the scene without transparent objects (used to train the background NeRF). I{res}: Set of images of the scene with transparent objects present (used to train the residual NeRF and Mixnet). Camera poses P for I{bg} and I{res}. Ray parameters r(\lambda) = o + \lambda d for rendering. Outputs: Rendered color \hat{C}(r) for a given ray. Depth map \hat{D}(r) for the scene. Data Structures The method utilizes three Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): 1. Background NeRF (\Phi{bg}): Input: Encoded position and view direction h(x, y, z, \theta, \phi). Output: Pre-activation color \mathbf{c}'{bg} and volume density \sigma{bg}. 2. Residual NeRF (\Phi{res}): Input: Encoded position and view direction h(x, y, z, \theta, \phi). Output: Pre-activation color \mathbf{c}'{res} and volume density \sigma{res}. 3. Mixnet (\Phi{mix}): Input: Encoded position h(x, y, z). The sources specify a "location-dependent multi-resolution hash encoding" is used for the Mixnet input. Output: Mixing weight \beta \in [0, 1]. Numbered Steps 1. Train Background NeRF: Train \Phi{bg} on images I{bg} (scene without transparent objects) to infer \sigma{bg} and \mathbf{c}'{bg}. 2. Train Residual NeRF and Mixnet: Train \Phi{res} and \Phi{mix} on images I{res} (scene with transparent objects). The background NeRF \Phi{bg} is frozen and not updated during this phase. 3. Compute Mixing Weight: For each point along a ray, the Mixnet infers \beta using the encoded position. 4. Render Color: Combine the outputs of \Phi{bg} and \Phi{res} using \beta in the volumetric rendering equation to render the final color. 5. Compute Depth: Estimate depth using a density threshold m. Formulas The rendering process combines the background and residual fields. The final color \hat{C}(r) is computed by integrating along the ray: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-((1 - \beta)\sigma{bg} + \beta\sigma{res})i \deltai)) (\mathbf{c}{bg} + \mathbf{c}{res})i Where: Ti = \exp \left( -\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj \right) is the accumulated transmittance up to sample i. \deltai = t{i+1} - ti is the segment length between samples. \sigma{bg} and \sigma{res} are the densities from the background and residual NeRFs, respectively. \beta is the mixing weight from the Mixnet. (\mathbf{c}{bg} + \mathbf{c}{res})i is the combined color at sample i. The combined color is a sigmoid-weighted sum of the pre-activation colors: \mathbf{c}{bg+res} = S((1.0 - \beta)\mathbf{c}'{bg} + \beta\mathbf{c}'{res}) The mixing weight \beta is the sigmoid output of the Mixnet MLP applied to the encoded position: \beta = S(\Phi{mix}(h(x, y, z))) The sigmoid function S(x) is defined as: S(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}} The individual network outputs are defined as: (\mathbf{c}'{bg}, \sigma{bg}) = \Phi{bg}(h(x, y, z, \theta, \phi)) (\mathbf{c}'{res}, \sigma{res}) = \Phi{res}(h(x, y, z, \theta, \phi)) Depth Estimation Standard depth estimation using the expected distance is inaccurate for transparent objects due to multiple surfaces radiating light. Instead, the method finds the point closest to the camera where the density exceeds a threshold m: \hat{D}(r) = tn \quad \text{where} \quad \sigman \ge m \quad \text{and} \quad \forall j < n, \sigmaj < m Parameters m: A tunable parameter for depth estimation threshold. It is used to find the closest point to the camera where density \sigmai \ge m. A single tuned value is reused across scenes. Typical value: 3.0 for Blender scenes; tuned per real environment. \beta: The mixing weight inferred by the Mixnet, constrained to [0, 1] via sigmoid activation. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class ResidualNeRF: def init(self, bgmlp, resmlp, mixmlp, mthreshold=3.0): """ Initialize Residual-NeRF. Args: bgmlp: Background NeRF MLP (Phibg). resmlp: Residual NeRF MLP (Phires). mixmlp: Mixnet MLP (Phimix). mthreshold: Density threshold for depth estimation (m). """ self.bgmlp = bgmlp self.resmlp = resmlp self.mixmlp = mixmlp self.mthreshold = mthreshold # Note: In training, bgmlp is frozen after Step 1. def encodeposition(self, x, y, z): """ Encode position coordinates. Note: The sources specify a 'location-dependent multi-resolution hash encoding' for the Mixnet, and standard positional encoding for the NeRFs. This function is a placeholder for the specific encoding implementation (e.g., NeRF positional encoding or Hash grid lookup). """ # Standard NeRF positional encoding is assumed for bg/res inputs. # Hash encoding is assumed for mix input. pass def forward(self, rayorigins, raydirections, numsamples, near, far): """ Render a batch of rays. Args: rayorigins: Tensor of shape (..., 3). raydirections: Tensor of shape (..., 3). numsamples: Number of samples per ray. near: Near plane distance. far: Far plane distance. Returns: color: Rendered color tensor. depth: Estimated depth tensor. """ # 1. Sample points along rays tvals = torch.linspace(0., 1., numsamples) zvals = near (1. - tvals) + far tvals points = rayorigins.unsqueeze(-2) + raydirections.unsqueeze(-2) zvals.unsqueeze(-1) # 2. Encode inputs # Position encoding for bg/res posenc = self.encodeposition(points[..., 0], points[..., 1], points[..., 2]) # Direction encoding (standard NeRF) direnc = self.encodedirection(raydirections) # Standard NeRF dir encoding # Mixnet uses only position encoding (hash grid) mixposenc = self.encodepositionhash(points[..., 0], points[..., 1], points[..., 2]) # Hash encoding # 3. Query Background and Residual NeRFs # bgmlp and resmlp take (posenc, direnc) bgoutput = self.bgmlp(torch.cat([posenc, direnc], dim=-1)) resoutput = self.resmlp(torch.cat([posenc, direnc], dim=-1)) cprimebg, sigmabg = bgoutput[...,:3], bgoutput[..., 3] cprimeres, sigmares = resoutput[...,:3], resoutput[..., 3] # 4. Query Mixnet # mixmlp takes mixposenc beta = torch.sigmoid(self.mixmlp(mixposenc)) # 5. Compute combined density and color # Density: weighted sum sigmacombined = (1.0 - beta) sigmabg + beta sigmares # Color: sigmoid-weighted sum of pre-activation colors ccombined = torch.sigmoid((1.0 - beta) cprimebg + beta cprimeres) # 6. Volumetric Rendering # Compute transmittance deltas = zvals[..., 1:] - zvals[...,:-1] deltainf = 1e10 torch.oneslike(deltas[...,:1]) deltas = torch.cat([deltas, deltainf], -1) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmacombined deltas) T = torch.cumprod(torch.exp(-alpha), dim=-2) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[...,:1]), T], -1) weights = alpha T[...,:-1] color = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) ccombined, dim=-2) # 7. Depth Estimation # Find closest point where sigma >= m # Implementation detail: This requires finding the first index i where sigmacombined[i] >= mthreshold # along each ray. depth = self.computedepth(zvals, sigmacombined) return color, depth def computedepth(self, zvals, sigma): """ Compute depth as the first point where density >= mthreshold. """ # Logic to find the first index i where sigma[i] >= mthreshold # If no such point exists, return far or handle appropriately. # This is a simplified representation of the logic described in. mask = sigma >= self.mthreshold # Find the first True in each row indices = torch.argmax(mask.float(), dim=-1) # Check if any mask was True anymask = torch.any(mask, dim=-1) depths = zvals[torch.arange(zvals.shape[0]), indices] # Handle cases where no point exceeds threshold depths = torch.where(anymask, depths, zvals[..., -1]) return depths def encodedirection(self, directions): """ Standard NeRF positional encoding for directions. """ # Standard implementation of gamma(p) for directions pass def encodepositionhash(self, x, y, z): """ Multi-resolution hash encoding for Mixnet. """ # Torch-NGP hash grid lookup implementation pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls Transparent Objects: Standard depth estimation (expected distance) is inaccurate for transparent objects because multiple surfaces radiate light along the ray. Mixnet Necessity: Without the Mixnet (using simple addition, referred to as Residual-NeRF-S), the residual NeRF must deduce the background NeRF's predictions in previously empty regions. This leads to unpredictable behavior, significant noise in view reconstruction, and holes in depth maps. Depth Map Holes: Perceived holes in depth maps can lead to robot collisions, while hallucinating non-existent surfaces may lead to no available grasp location. Threshold Tuning: The parameter m must be tuned. Increasing m beyond the optimal point leads to more noise without additional gains in hole filling. Time and Memory Complexity: The method uses three MLPs (\Phi{bg}, \Phi{res}, \Phi{mix}). The Mixnet uses a multi-resolution hash grid (via Torch-NGP), which typically offers faster training and inference compared to standard MLPs. Measured Performance: On synthetic data, Residual-NeRF achieves 46.1% lower RMSE and 29.5% lower MAE compared to baselines (NeRF, Dex-NeRF). RMSE on 'Bowl' scene: NeRF 0.1900, Dex-NeRF 0.1065, Residual-NeRF 0.0699. MAE on 'Bowl' scene: NeRF 0.1453, Dex-NeRF 0.0195, Residual-NeRF 0.0140. Scaling: The method is designed for mostly static scenes where the background can be extensively observed (e.g., 100 images) while the foreground (transparent objects) is observed with fewer viewpoints (e.g., 50 images). Strengths: Improves depth perception of transparent objects, reduces holes and noise in depth maps, speeds up training compared to training a single NeRF on the complex scene, and facilitates robust grasp planning for robots. Limitations: Requires a static background scene. Performance depends on the quality of the background NeRF prior. The threshold m requires tuning. When to use: When depth perception of transparent objects is required in a mostly static environment, particularly for robotic manipulation tasks. When not to use: In highly dynamic scenes where the background changes significantly, or when transparent objects are not the primary focus of depth estimation. Residual-NeRF was proposed by Ichnowski et al. in 2024. It addresses the challenge of dexterous manipulation of transparent objects, where common depth sensors struggle. The method builds on the observation that robot work areas (kitchens, shelves) are mostly static and opaque, allowing a background NeRF to serve as a strong prior. It is implemented using Torch-NGP (PyTorch version of InstantNGP) with multi-resolution hash grids, running on hardware such as RTX 4090 and AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 5965WX. The method is compatible with grasp planners like Dex-Net. name: MZEN (Multi-zoom Enhanced NeRF)
head: Multi-zoom Enhanced NeRF
body: MZEN is a framework for 3-D reconstruction from images with unknown camera poses where the optical zoom level varies significantly across views. It solves the problem of geometric inconsistency in pose-free NeRFs when magnification changes, which typically couples translation, scale, and focal length in an unidentifiable way. Unlike Mip-NeRF 360 MLP Architecture or CamP which rely on high-resolution image pyramids or external pose initialization, MZEN keeps every frame at native resolution and explicitly models optical zoom as a learnable intrinsic parameter. MZEN represents the radiance field using a standard NeRF MLP and introduces a zoom-aware camera model optimized through a three-phase training schedule. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of N images \mathcal{I} = \{Ik\}{k=1}^N. The set is partitioned into N{out} zoomed-out images (indices i=1 \dots N{out}) and N{in} zoomed-in images (indices j=N{out}+1 \dots N). Each image has a rough initial estimate of its zoom parameter \xik (e.g., from a dial reading or apparent size comparison). Outputs: NeRF network parameters \Theta, camera poses \Pi = \{Rk, tk\}{k=1}^N, and zoom parameters \{\xik\}{k=1}^N. Data Structures Camera Pose \Pik: A tuple (Rk, tk, f, c, \xik) where Rk \in SO(3) is rotation, tk \in \mathbb{R}^3 is translation, f=(fx, fy) is the shared base focal length, c=(cx, cy) is the principal point, and \xik \ge 1 is the zoom parameter. Effective Intrinsic Matrix: K{eff}^k = \text{diag}(\xik fx, \xik fy, 1). NeRF Parameters \Theta: Weights of the MLP representing the radiance field. Numbered Steps 1. Phase A: Global Pose Bootstrap Initialize zoom parameters for the N{out} most zoomed-out images: \xii = 1 for i=1 \dots N{out}. Randomly initialize NeRF parameters \Theta^{(A)}, rotations Ri, translations ti, and focal lengths f^{(A)}. Withhold all zoomed-in images (j > N{out}) from training. Optimize \Theta^{(A)}, Ri, ti, and f^{(A)} by minimizing the coarse loss L{coarse} over the N{out} images. The coarse loss is defined as: L{coarse} = \sum{i=1}^{N{out}} \| F{\Theta^{(A)}}(\Theta^{(A)}, \Pi^{(A)}) - Ii \|2^2 where \Pii = (Ri, ti, f, c, \xii) and F{\Theta} is the differentiable volume renderer. Output: Coarse NeRF parameters \Theta^{(A)} and globally consistent poses for zoomed-out views. 2. Cross-Zoom Pose Registration (Initialization for Phase B) For each zoomed-in image Ij (j > N{out}): Find the best matching zoomed-out image g^(j) from the set of N{out} images. Extract the central 1/\xij crop from the zoomed-out image I{g^(j)}. Bilinearly resize the crop to the native resolution of Ij to create a surrogate view \tilde{I}{g^(j) \to j}. Select g^(j) that minimizes the RGB mean-squared error between Ij and \tilde{I}{g^(j) \to j}. Pose Priming: Initialize the pose \Pij for each zoomed-in image j by copying the rotation R{g^(j)}, translation t{g^(j)}, and focal length f from the matched zoomed-out image g^(j). The zoom parameter \xij is initialized from the rough estimate. 3. Phase B: Zoom-in Pose Registration Freeze NeRF parameters at \Theta^{(A)}. For each zoomed-in image j, optimize only the rotation Rj, translation tj, and zoom parameter \xij. Intrinsics f and c remain fixed from the surrogate initialization. Minimize the pose loss L{pose}: L{pose} = \sum{j=N{out}+1}^{N} \| F{\Theta^{(A)}}(\Theta^{(A)}, \Pi^{(B)}) - Ij \|2^2 where \Pij = (Rj, tj, f, c, \xij). Output: Provisional full pose set \Pi^{(B)} = \{\Pii^{(A)}\}{i=1}^{N{out}} \cup \{\Pij^{(B)}\}{j=N{out}+1}^{N}. 4. Phase C: Joint Refinement Initialize NeRF parameters \Theta^{(C)} = \Theta^{(A)}. Unfreeze all NeRF parameters and all camera pose parameters (including all \xik). Optimize jointly over all N images by minimizing the fine loss L{fine}: L{fine} = \sum{k=1}^{N} \| F{\Theta^{(C)}}(\Theta^{(C)}, \Pi^{(B)}) - Ik \|2^2 Output: Final NeRF parameters and pixel-accurate poses. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mzentraining(images, initialzoomestimates, Nout): """ images: List of N images [I1,..., IN] initialzoomestimates: List of N initial zoom estimates [xi1,..., xiN] Nout: Number of zoomed-out images """ # Phase A: Global Pose Bootstrap # Initialize zoom for out-views to 1 zoomparams = [1.0] Nout + initialzoomestimates[Nout:] # Random initialization of NeRF and poses for out-views thetaA = randominitnerf() posesA = randominitposes(Nout) focallength = randominitfocallength() principalpoint = [0.0, 0.0] # Or fixed center # Minimize Lcoarse for iteration in range(PhaseAiterations): loss = 0.0 for i in range(Nout): # Construct camera parameters for image i pii = (posesA[i].R, posesA[i].t, focallength, principalpoint, zoomparams[i]) # Render image renderedi = volumerenderer(thetaA, pii) # Compute photometric loss loss += l2norm(renderedi - images[i]) # Backpropagate and update thetaA, posesA, focallength updateparameters(thetaA, posesA, focallength, loss) thetastar = thetaA # Cross-Zoom Pose Registration (Preparation for Phase B) posesB = list(posesA) # Copy out-views poses zoomparamsB = list(zoomparams) for j in range(Nout, len(images)): bestmatchidx = -1 minmse = infinity # Find best matching zoomed-out image for g in range(Nout): # Extract central 1/zetaj crop from zoomed-out image Ig # Note: zoomparams[g] is 1.0 for out-views, but we use the estimate for j crop = extractcentercrop(images[g], scale=1.0/initialzoomestimates[j]) # Resize to native resolution surrogate = bilinearresize(crop, targetsize=images[j].size) # Compute MSE between Ij and surrogate mse = l2norm(images[j] - surrogate) if mse < minmse: minmse = mse bestmatchidx = g # Pose Priming: Copy pose from best match matchedpose = posesA[bestmatchidx] posesB.append((matchedpose.R, matchedpose.t)) zoomparamsB.append(initialzoomestimates[j]) # Phase B: Zoom-in Pose Registration # Freeze thetastar # Optimize only poses for j > Nout and their zoom params for iteration in range(PhaseBiterations): loss = 0.0 for j in range(Nout, len(images)): pij = (posesB[j].R, posesB[j].t, focallength, principalpoint, zoomparamsB[j]) renderedj = volumerenderer(thetastar, pij) loss += l2norm(renderedj - images[j]) # Backpropagate only through posesB[j] and zoomparamsB[j] updateparameters(posesB, zoomparamsB, loss, freezenerf=True) # Phase C: Joint Refinement thetaC = thetastar posesfinal = posesB zoomfinal = zoomparamsB for iteration in range(PhaseCiterations): loss = 0.0 for k in range(len(images)): pik = (posesfinal[k].R, posesfinal[k].t, focallength, principalpoint, zoomfinal[k]) renderedk = volumerenderer(thetaC, pik) loss += l2norm(renderedk - images[k]) # Backpropagate through all parameters updateparameters(thetaC, posesfinal, zoomfinal, loss, freezenerf=False) return thetaC, posesfinal, zoomfinal Parameters Zoom parameter \xik: Learnable intrinsic parameter. \xik=1 for zoomed-out, \xik > 1 for zoomed-in. Step size \eta: Must satisfy \eta \in (0, 1/L] where L is the Lipschitz constant of the gradients. PL constant \mu: Positive constant defining the local Polyak-Łojasiewicz condition. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Simultaneous optimization of NeRF parameters and camera poses across all zoom levels is unstable; the three-phase schedule is required. Standard NeRF formulations assume fixed or small zoom-level perturbations; significant magnification changes break these assumptions, coupling translation, scale, and focal length. Pose priming converges faster than random initialization because the initial error is O(\delta^2) (crop misregistration) compared to O(\sigma{rand}^2) (random noise), where \delta \ll \sigma{rand}. Time Complexity: The method requires three sequential optimization phases. Phase A scales with N{out}, Phase B with N{in}, and Phase C with N. Theoretical analysis shows linear convergence rate e^{(t+1)} \leq (1 - \eta\mu) e^{(t)} for Phase B under the PL condition. Memory Complexity: Standard NeRF memory usage plus storage for camera poses and zoom parameters. Strengths: Does not require high-resolution images or external pose initialization (unlike Mip-NeRF 360 MLP Architecture or CamP). Handles non-overlapping zoomed-in and zoomed-out views via cross-zoom registration. Limitations: Requires a rough initial estimate of zoom parameters (e.g., from dial readings). Performance degrades if Phase B (cross-zoom matching) is skipped or if wide-field views are absent. When to use: Industrial imaging systems (microscopes, SEMs) where exact calibration is unavailable and stage movement is minimal. MZEN was introduced to address the failure of classical Structure-from-Motion (SfM) and standard pose-free NeRFs in industrial imaging contexts where optical zoom changes significantly. It explicitly models optical magnification as a learnable intrinsic parameter and uses cross-zoom pose registration to align views. The method is designed for scenarios where the specimen stage moves only microns, making traditional pose estimation unreliable. name: UV Volumes
head: UV Volume Representation
body: UV Volumes is a method for real-time, editable free-view rendering of human performers that decouples smooth 3D geometry/density from high-frequency appearance. It differs from standard NeRF by encoding smooth density and UV coordinates in a 3D feature volume (the UV volume) while storing detailed appearance in a 2D Neural Texture Stack (NTS), enabling real-time performance and retexturing. Inputs: Multi-view videos of a human performer, a posed SMPL model parameterized by pose \theta, and latent codes \mathbf{z} anchored to SMPL vertices. Outputs: A rendered RGB image for a given camera view. Data Structures: 1. UV Volumes: A 3D feature volume generated by a 3D sparse CNN. It stores feature vectors f(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}, \theta) at 3D points \mathbf{x}. 2. Neural Texture Stack (NTS): A set of 2D texture representations \mathcal{E}k for each body part k, generated by a CNN texture generator G. 3. SMPL Model: Provides the posed mesh structure used for ray sampling bounds. Steps: 1. Generate UV Volumes: Voxelize the latent codes \mathbf{z} anchored on the SMPL vertices. Input these voxels into a 3D sparse CNN to produce the 3D feature volume (UV volumes). 2. Ray Sampling: For a camera ray \mathbf{r}, sample N points \{\mathbf{x}i\}{i=1}^N along the ray between near and far bounds. The bounds are determined by the intersection of the ray with the posed SMPL model. 3. Feature Query and Density Prediction: For each sample point \mathbf{x}i, query the feature vector f(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{z}, \theta) from the UV volumes. Predict the volume density \sigma(\mathbf{x}i) using a shallow MLP M\sigma: \sigma(\mathbf{x}i) = M\sigma(f(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{z}, \theta)) where M\sigma is a shallow MLP. 4. Volume Rendering of Feature Map: Render the feature volume into a 2D feature map \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{r}) using standard volume rendering. Calculate the accumulated transmittance Ti and the weighted sum of features: Ti = \exp \left( - \sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma(\mathbf{x}j) \deltaj \right) \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigma(\mathbf{x}i) \deltai)) f(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{z}, \theta) where \deltai = \|\mathbf{x}{i+1} - \mathbf{x}i\|2 is the distance between adjacent sampled points. 5. UV Image Generation: Decode the feature map \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{r}) pixel-by-pixel using an MLP M{uv} to predict part assignments \hat{\mathcal{P}} and UV coordinates \hat{\mathcal{U}}, \hat{\mathcal{V}}: \left(\hat{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbf{r}), \hat{\mathcal{U}}(\mathbf{r}), \hat{\mathcal{V}}(\mathbf{r})\right) = M{uv}(\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{r})) The part assignments satisfy \sum{k=1}^{Nk} \hat{\mathcal{P}}k(\mathbf{r}) = 1. 6. Generate Neural Texture Stack (NTS): Use a CNN texture generator G conditioned on the pose \theta and one-hot labels \mathbf{k} for each body part to generate the NTS \mathcal{E}: \mathcal{E}k = G(\theta, \mathbf{k}) The body surface is subdivided into Nk = 24 parts. 7. Color Reconstruction: Interpolate texture embeddings from the NTS using the predicted UV coordinates and part assignments. For each pixel, the final color is recovered by querying the NTS at the predicted UV coordinates weighted by the part assignments. Parameters: Nk = 24: Number of body parts used to subdivide the body surface for the NTS. N: Number of samples along the ray. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: SMPL Dependency: Ray sampling bounds rely on the accuracy of the posed SMPL model. Incorrect pose estimation may lead to incorrect sampling bounds. Part Assignment: The part assignments \hat{\mathcal{P}} must sum to 1. Incorrect normalization or prediction can lead to artifacts in color reconstruction. Performance: Renders 960 × 540 images at an average of 30 FPS on CMU Panoptic, ZJU Mocap, and H36M datasets. Strengths: Real-time rendering, editability (retexturing), and better generalization on novel poses and shapes due to the mapping between the parameterized human model and smooth texture coordinates. Limitations: Relies on the SMPL model for geometry and sampling. High-frequency appearance is separated from the 3D volume, which may limit its applicability to non-human or non-parametric scenes. UV Volumes was introduced to address the high computational costs of real-time free-view human rendering in VR/AR applications. It builds on the idea of separating smooth 3D properties from high-frequency appearance, leveraging the SMPL model for pose-dependent texture generation. name: Low-Light NeRF (LLNeRF)
body: Low-Light NeRF (LLNeRF) is an unsupervised method that synthesizes normal-light novel views directly from low-dynamic-range (LDR) sRGB images captured in low-light conditions. It solves the problem of training Neural Radiance Fields on camera-finished sRGB data, where the Image Signal Processor (ISP) introduces non-linearity, low signal-to-noise ratio, and color distortion that standard NeRF cannot handle. Unlike HDR-NeRF, which requires RAW data with exposure metadata, LLNeRF decomposes the radiance field into view-dependent lighting and view-independent color components, allowing for joint enhancement and reconstruction without ground-truth supervision. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of N low-light sRGB images (8-bit/channel, LDR) with known camera intrinsics and extrinsics. Output: A radiance field model capable of rendering normal-light, enhanced novel views. Data Structures and Network Architecture The model replaces the standard NeRF MLP with a decomposed architecture consisting of two branches: 1. View-Dependent Branch (F1): Predicts a single-channel intensity value v. This branch captures lighting-related intensity variations. Input: Encoded position \tau and view direction d. Output: v \in \mathbb{R}^1. Architecture: As shown in Figure 3(c) of, this involves a Feature MLP (8x256), a Coeff MLP (1x128), and an Enhancement Model \phi. 2. View-Independent Branch (F2): Predicts the intrinsic color basis r. Input: Encoded position \tau. Output: r \in \mathbb{R}^3 (RGB). Architecture: As shown in Figure 3(c) of, this involves a Feature MLP (8x256), a Color MLP (1x128), and a Direction MLP (1x128). The final color c is the element-wise product of these components: c = v \bullet r. Numbered Steps 1. Ray Sampling: For each pixel, generate a ray r(\lambda) = o{world} + \lambda d{world} using camera intrinsics and extrinsics. Sample K points along the ray within the near/far range. 2. Positional Encoding: Apply hierarchical positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) to the 3D position \mathbf{x} and view direction \mathbf{d}. Let \tau denote the concatenated encoded position features. 3. Decomposition Forward Pass: Compute the view-dependent intensity: vi = F1(\taui, di; \Theta{F1}) for each sample i. Compute the view-independent color: ri = F2(\taui; \Theta{F2}) for each sample i. Compute the raw color: ci = vi \bullet ri. 4. Enhancement: Apply an enhancement function \phi to the view-dependent component v to produce the enhanced intensity \hat{v} = \phi(v). The enhanced color is then \hat{c}i = \hat{v}i \bullet ri. The function \phi is part of the learnable network parameters, allowing the model to learn the inverse ISP mapping and noise reduction jointly with the scene representation. 5. Volume Rendering: Render the pixel color \hat{c}r using the standard volume rendering integral with the enhanced colors \hat{c}: \hat{c}r = \sum{i=1}^{K} \alphai \hat{c}i where \alphai = (1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai}) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} e^{-\sigmaj \deltaj}, \sigmai is the volume density predicted by the density branch (standard NeRF density MLP), and \deltai = t{i+1} - ti. 6. Optimization: Minimize the photometric loss between the rendered enhanced image \hat{c}r and the input low-light image I. The optimization is unsupervised, relying on the consistency of the decomposition and the enhancement capability of \phi. Formulas Decomposition: v = F1(\tau, d; \Theta{F1}) r = F2(\tau; \Theta{F2}) c = v \bullet r \hat{c} = \phi(v) \bullet r Where \bullet denotes element-wise multiplication. Rendering: \hat{c}r = \sum{i} \left( P{1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai}} e^{-\sum{j<i} \sigmaj \deltaj} \hat{c}i \right) (Note: The source provides the standard NeRF rendering equation Eq. 2, substituting ci with \hat{c}i). Parameters Input images: 8-bit/channel sRGB. Network depths/widths: Specific layer dimensions are provided in Figure 3(c) of (e.g., Feature MLP 8x256, Coeff MLP 1x128). Not given in the text body. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Non-linearity: Standard NeRF assumes linear radiance. sRGB images are non-linear due to ISP gamma correction and tone mapping. LLNeRF handles this by learning the enhancement \phi within the network, effectively inverting the ISP effects. Noise: Low-light sRGB images have low signal-to-noise ratio. NeRF is robust to zero-mean noise in RAW data but not to the blended noise in sRGB. The decomposition helps isolate noise into the view-dependent component, which is then suppressed by the enhancement model \phi. View Inconsistency: Applying 2D enhancement before NeRF training causes view inconsistency. LLNeRF avoids this by performing enhancement implicitly during 3D optimization. Time Complexity: Comparable to standard NeRF training, but requires additional forward passes for the decomposition branches and the enhancement function \phi. Memory Complexity: Slightly higher than standard NeRF due to the additional MLPs for F1 and F2. Strengths: Works directly on camera-finished sRGB images without RAW data or exposure metadata; unsupervised; jointly enhances illumination and reconstructs geometry. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that lighting variations are primarily view-dependent and can be separated from intrinsic color; performance depends on the capacity of the enhancement model \phi to generalize to in-the-wild scenes. When to use: When only low-light sRGB images are available and RAW data is not accessible. When not to use: When RAW data with exposure metadata is available (HDR-NeRF may be more appropriate) or when high-dynamic-range scenes are not the primary focus. LLNeRF was proposed in "Lighting up NeRF via Unsupervised Decomposition and Enhancement" (ICCV 2023). It addresses the limitations of previous methods like HDR-NeRF, which require RAW data, and standard NeRF, which fails on low-light sRGB images due to ISP-induced non-linearity and noise. The method builds on the observation that lighting intensity is often view-dependent, while intrinsic color is view-independent, allowing for a product decomposition of the radiance field. name: Compression and Model Efficiency
head: Low-rank NeRF, Tensor Train NeRF, CCNeRF, ADMM NeRF
body: This family addresses the excessive memory footprint and computational cost of standard Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by reducing model size through low-rank approximations, tensor decompositions, and pruning. It differs from sibling methods that modify architecture for specific tasks (e.g., Binary Radiance Fields or Mip-NeRF 360 MLP Architecture) by focusing strictly on compressing the existing radiance field representation while preserving rendering quality. The core mechanism involves approximating high-dimensional parameters (typically fully connected layer weights in the MLP renderer or the radiance field tensor itself) using low-rank structures. This reduces the number of trainable parameters from O(N^2) or O(N^3) to O(N \cdot r) or O(N \cdot r^2), where r is the target rank. The rendering equation remains standard volume rendering, but the query function \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) is computed via decomposed components rather than a dense MLP. A hybrid tensor rank decomposition method that models the radiance field only with tensor components, avoiding MLPs in the rendering path to preserve low-rank properties. It supports dynamic model size adjustment via rank truncation and arbitrary composition via rank concatenation. Choose this when you need a purely tensor-based representation that allows for scene composition and dynamic compression without retraining. This method reduces the model size of a trained NeRF by decomposing fully connected layer weights into a Tensor Train (TT) format. It solves the resulting rank-constrained optimization problem using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to minimize reconstruction error while enforcing low-rank structure. It is distinguished from sibling methods like CCNeRF by its specific use of ADMM for rank-constrained weight decomposition rather than other compression or clustering techniques. A pruning-based continual learning approach applied to NeRF for multiple scenes. Pruning rate: 0.5. The motivation for compression arises from the quadratic or cubic scaling of NeRF parameters with respect to network depth and width. Early works like NSVF [MST21] and TensoRF [CLBL22] explored hybrid tensor-MLP approaches. CCNeRF was introduced to provide a purely tensor-based alternative that avoids the MLP bottleneck, enabling better composition and truncation. The ADMM-based approach addresses the difficulty of directly optimizing low-rank constraints by using augmented Lagrangian methods. PackNet [ML18] was adapted to NeRF for continual learning scenarios, demonstrating that pruning can maintain performance across multiple scenes. SCARF: Scalable Continual Learning Framework for Memory‐efficient Multiple Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.15255, fetched 2026-10-26

name: CCNeRF
head: Rank-residual Decomposition NeRF
body: CCNeRF is a neural field representation that models 3D scenes using hybrid tensor rank decomposition (CP and triple-plane variants) without neural networks for rendering, enabling dynamic compression via rank truncation and arbitrary composition via rank concatenation. Unlike NeRF variants that rely on shared MLP renderers (e.g., NSVF) or hybrid tensor-MLP approaches (e.g., TensoRF), CCNeRF preserves the low-rank approximation property of the radiance field, allowing model size and detail levels to be adjusted post-training without retraining. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 2D images with known camera poses (o, d) for a 3D scene. Output: A compressed radiance field representation consisting of rank components (vectors or matrices) and a weight matrix, capable of rendering colors \hat{C}(r) for any ray r. Data Structures: The model structure consists of two main parts: 1. Rank Components: A set of decomposed components representing the scene. These are either: Vector-based (CP): Factor matrices U^x, U^y, U^z for spatial dimensions. Matrix-based (Triple Plane): Factor matrices for 2D planes (e.g., U^{xy}, U^{yz}, U^{xz}). The ratio of vector- to matrix-based components is controllable. 2. Weight Matrix: A matrix storing rank weights for different feature channels, mapping the decomposed components to the final output (density and color). Querying a 3D Coordinate: To query a 3D coordinate \mathbf{x}: 1. Project the coordinate to the decomposed vectors or matrices. 2. Perform weighted interpolation using the stored rank weights. Rendering Equation: The color \hat{C}(r) for a ray r is computed using standard volume rendering: \hat{C}(r) = \sumi Ti \alphai ci where: Ti = \prod{j<i} (1 - \alphai) is the transmittance. \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) is the opacity. \deltai = t{i+1} - ti is the distance between sample points. \sigmai is the density and ci is the color at sample point i along ray r from origin o with direction d. Training and Rank-Residual Learning: The model is trained to learn a hybrid tensor rank decomposition. A rank-residual learning strategy is employed to encourage lower ranks to preserve more important information of the whole scene. This allows the model to maintain high quality even when truncated to lower ranks. Compression (Rank Truncation): Model size is dynamically adjusted by rank truncation: 1. An empirical sort-and-truncate strategy is used. 2. Components are sorted based on their importance (derived from the weight matrix and rank-residual learning). 3. The least important components are removed to achieve a targeted rank r. 4. This achieves near-optimal low-rank approximation at any targeted rank without retraining, allowing a trade-off between model size and rendering quality. Note: Standard truncated Higher-Order SVD (HOSVD) does not hold the optimal property of truncated SVD but yields a quasi-optimal solution sufficient for practical use. Composition (Rank Concatenation): Different models (objects) are composed into a single scene by concatenating their rank components along the rank dimension: 1. Each object model is stored with its own rank components. 2. A transformation matrix is recorded for each object to control its position and orientation in the composed scene. 3. Concatenation is performed along the rank dimension. 4. The growth of storage cost can be mitigated by compressing (truncating) less important objects in the composed scene. Args: x: 3D coordinate (x, y, z). rankcomponents: List of decomposed components. Each component is either a set of vectors (CP) or matrices (Triple Plane). weightmatrix: Matrix storing weights for feature channels. Returns: density: Scalar density value. color: 3D color vector. """ # 1. Project coordinate to decomposed vectors/matrices # For CP components: # projectedvalues = [dot(x, Udim) for Udim in rankcomponents] # For Triple Plane components: # projectedvalues = [interpolate2dplane(x, Uplane) for Uplane in rankcomponents] # 2. Perform weighted interpolation # Combine projected values using the weight matrix # combinedfeatures = matmul(projectedvalues, weightmatrix) # 3. Extract density and color from combined features # density = combinedfeatures[..., 0] # color = combinedfeatures[..., 1:] # Note: Exact projection and interpolation details depend on # whether the component is vector-based or matrix-based. # The weight matrix maps the rank dimension to the output channels. pass def compressccnerf(rankcomponents, weightmatrix, targetrank): """ Compress the model by truncating rank components. Args: rankcomponents: List of decomposed components. weightmatrix: Matrix storing weights for feature channels. targetrank: The desired number of rank components to keep. Returns: compressedcomponents: List of truncated rank components. compressedweightmatrix: Truncated weight matrix. """ # 1. Sort components based on importance # Importance is determined by the rank-residual learning strategy # and the weight matrix. sortedindices = sortbyimportance(rankcomponents, weightmatrix) # 2. Truncate to target rank # Keep the top 'targetrank' components selectedindices = sortedindices[:targetrank] # 3. Return compressed components and corresponding weights compressedcomponents = [rankcomponents[i] for i in selectedindices] compressedweightmatrix = weightmatrix[selectedindices,:] return compressedcomponents, compressedweightmatrix def composeccnerf(models, transformations): """ Compose multiple CCNeRF models into a single scene. Args: models: List of CCNeRF models (each with rankcomponents and weightmatrix). transformations: List of transformation matrices for each model. Returns: composedmodel: A single CCNeRF model representing the composed scene. """ # 1. Concatenate rank components along the rank dimension # Note: Transformations are stored separately and applied during querying # or rendering, not by modifying the rank components themselves. allcomponents = [] for model in models: allcomponents.extend(model.rankcomponents) # 2. Concatenate weight matrices # The weight matrices must be aligned or transformed appropriately. # In CCNeRF, the weight matrix maps rank components to output. # Concatenation along rank dimension implies stacking the components. # The weight matrix needs to be expanded to cover the new rank dimension. # This part requires careful handling of the weight matrix structure. # For simplicity, we assume the weight matrix is concatenated or expanded. # In practice, the weight matrix might need to be reshaped or padded. # 3. Store transformations # The transformations are recorded for each object to control position/orientation. # They are not part of the rank components but are metadata for the composed scene. composedmodel = { 'rankcomponents': allcomponents, 'weightmatrix': expandweightmatrix(models), # Placeholder for exact logic 'transformations': transformations } return composedmodel Compression: Achieves near-optimal low-rank approximation at any targeted rank without retraining. Lower ranks preserve primary information due to rank-residual learning. Composition: Supports arbitrary composition of different models without retraining or compatibility constraints, as there are no MLP renderers. Storage: Model size is dynamically adjustable. Storage cost growth in composed scenes can be mitigated by compressing unimportant objects. Limitations: Standard truncated HOSVD is quasi-optimal, not strictly optimal. The method relies on the low-rank assumption of the scene; scenes with high-frequency details or complex structures may require higher ranks, increasing storage. CCNeRF was introduced by Jiaxiang Tang, Xiaokang Chen, Jingbo Wang, and Gang Zeng in 2022. It addresses the difficulty of manipulating NeRF models (like compression and composition) caused by their implicit representation and shared MLP renderer. The method is motivated by the low-rank approximation property of the SVD algorithm and the use of tensor decomposition in vision tasks. It builds on the idea that neural radiance fields can be modeled using tensor rank decomposition, similar to image compression.
