name: PAC-NeRF
head: Physics Augmented Continuum Neural Radiance Fields
body: PAC-NeRF is a method for geometry-agnostic system identification that estimates the unknown geometry and physical parameters of highly dynamic objects from multi-view videos. It solves the problem of recovering physical properties (e.g., Young’s modulus, viscosity) without assuming prior object geometry or topology. It differs from standard dynamic NeRFs by enforcing continuum mechanics conservation laws via a differentiable Material Point Method (MPM) simulator, rather than learning dynamics from scratch. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of posed multi-view video frames \{\hat{C}(r, ti)\} of a dynamic scene. Output: An explicit geometric representation (voxel grid) and physical parameters (e.g., material constants) that minimize the difference between rendered and observed images. Data Structures: The method uses a hybrid Eulerian-Lagrangian representation: 1. Eulerian Grid: Stores the NeRF fields. Density Grid (G\sigma): Stores volume density \sigma(x, t). Layout: \mathbb{R}^{I \times J \times K}. Appearance Grid (Gc): Stores latent features for color prediction. Layout: \mathbb{R}^{I \times J \times K \times P}, where P is the number of feature channels. 2. Lagrangian Particles: A set of particles that advect the field values. Each particle carries state information used in the MPM simulation. Query Mechanism: For a query point p in world space at time t, grid values are retrieved via trilinear interpolation: f(p) = \text{trilinear\interp}(p, G) This yields scalar density \sigma(p, t) and feature vector f(p, t). Decoding: The feature vector f(p, t) and viewing direction \omega are passed to a decoding MLP \mathcal{S} to predict color \mathbf{c}: \mathbf{c} = \mathcal{S}(f(p, t), \omega) Simulation and Advection (MPM): The core innovation is the enforcement of physical conservation laws using the Material Point Method (MPM): 1. Material Derivative: The density \sigma and color field c are assumed to be conserved along particle trajectories: \frac{D\sigma}{Dt} = 0, \quad \frac{Dc}{Dt} = 0 where \frac{D\phi}{Dt} = \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial t} + \mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla \phi and \mathbf{v} is the velocity field. 2. Momentum Conservation: The velocity field evolves according to: \frac{D\mathbf{v}}{Dt} = \frac{1}{\rho} \nabla \cdot \mathbf{T} + \mathbf{g} where \rho is physical density, \mathbf{T} is the internal Cauchy stress tensor, and \mathbf{g} is gravity. 3. Differentiable Physics: The MPM simulator computes the velocity field \mathbf{v} and updates particle positions. The stress tensor \mathbf{T} is computed based on physical parameters (e.g., Young’s modulus). Optimization Loop: 1. Initialize Eulerian voxel NeRF for density \sigma and color c. 2. Bind renderable quantities to Lagrangian particles via a sampling scheme. 3. Simulate particle dynamics using differentiable MPM. 4. Convert particle states back to the Eulerian grid via Grid-to-Particle (G2P) and Particle-to-Grid (P2G) transforms. 5. Render images from the Eulerian voxel NeRF using the volume rendering integral: C(r, t) = \int{sn}^{sf} T(s, t) \sigma(r(s), t) c(r(s), \omega, t) ds + c{bg} T(sf, t) where T(s, t) = \exp\left(-\int{sn}^{s} \sigma(r(\bar{s}), t) d\bar{s}\right). 6. Compute loss against ground truth video frames: L{render} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=0}^{N-1} \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \| C(r, ti) - \hat{C}(r, ti) \|^2 where N is the number of frames and \mathcal{R} is the set of rays. 7. Optimize geometry (grid values) and physical parameters via gradient-based optimization. Parameters: Physical parameters to estimate: Young’s modulus, fluid viscosity, friction angles, etc.. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Topology Changes: Standard mesh-based methods fail here; PAC-NeRF uses MPM to naturally handle topology changes and frictional contacts. Unknown Geometry: The method does not require watertight mesh representations or known object geometries. Time Complexity: Accelerates NeRF rendering by two orders of magnitude compared to MLP-based dynamic NeRFs due to the Eulerian voxel representation. Memory Complexity: Depends on the voxel grid resolution (I \times J \times K) and the number of Lagrangian particles. Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Validated on elastic bodies, plasticine, sand, Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluids. Strengths: Data-efficient, physically plausible, interpretable, handles complex dynamics and topology changes. Limitations: Requires multi-view video input; relies on the accuracy of the differentiable MPM simulator. When to use: When estimating physical properties of dynamic objects from video without prior geometric knowledge. When not to use: When single-view input is available or when the scene does not involve continuum mechanics (e.g., rigid body kinematics only). PAC-NeRF was introduced to address the challenge of inferring geometric and physical properties from visual observations without assuming object geometry. It builds on the concept of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and the Material Point Method (MPM) for physics simulation. It differs from D-NeRF and other dynamic NeRFs by using a prescriptive physics model rather than learning dynamics from scratch. It also differs from existing system identification methods by not requiring known object geometries. PAC-NeRF: Physics Augmented Continuum Neural Radiance Fields for Geometry-Agnostic System Identification, https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.05512v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Dynamic and Articulated Scene Modeling
head: Dynamic NeRF, Articulated NeRF, Human NeRF
body: Dynamic and Articulated Scene Modeling extends static radiance fields to handle time-varying geometry and non-rigid deformations, primarily in human performance capture. It solves the ill-posed problem of mapping dynamic 3D points to a static representation by introducing canonical spaces, skeletal constraints, or surface-relative encodings. Unlike static methods, these approaches must jointly optimize or infer pose, deformation, and appearance from monocular or sparse multi-view video inputs. All methods in this family map a 3D query point \mathbf{x} observed at time t to a canonical space \mathbf{x}c where the radiance field is static. The rendering process remains volume rendering, but the density \sigma and color c are conditioned on the deformation state. 1. Canonical Transformation: A transformation function T(\mathbf{x}, t) maps observation space to canonical space. Common strategies include: Skeleton-based: Using inverse Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) or skeletal relative coordinates. Surface-based: Using signed distances to nearest neighbors in a reconstructed surface mesh [18160-selfnerf]. Residual-based: Predicting radiance residuals in the canonical space conditioned on pose [16197-moco-nerf]. 2. Conditioning: The radiance field MLP F\omega takes the canonical point \mathbf{x}c, view direction \mathbf{v}, and often a pose or identity code as input. 3. Optimization: Training typically involves minimizing photometric loss \| C{rendered} - I{gt} \|. Articulated methods often include regularization terms for pose smoothness and consistency with initial pose estimates [18108-a-nerf]. MoCo-NeRF models non-rigid body motions as radiance residual fields rather than spatial offsets [16197-moco-nerf]. It separates the rigid canonical representation from pose-dependent non-rigid residuals, allowing for direct color supervision of the dynamic components. Unlike sibling methods that rely on spatial deformation fields, MoCo-NeRF reduces learning complexity by predicting residuals in the radiance space conditioned on a rigid prior [16197-moco-nerf]. It uses a skeletal weights volume decoder to predict canonical skinning weights w^ck for K joints [16197-moco-nerf]. The canonical point is computed via inverse linear blend skinning: \mathbf{x}c = \sum{k=1}^K w^ok (Rk \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{t}k) where observation weights w^ok are derived from canonical weights [16197-moco-nerf]. Non-rigid features are generated using cross-attention between a learnable base code and sinusoidal-encoded joint positions [16197-moco-nerf]. A-NeRF learns a user-specific neural 3D body model and underlying skeleton pose from unlabelled monocular videos by extending NeRFs with a skeleton to apply to time-varying and articulated motion [18108-a-nerf, unofficial]. It solves the ill-posed inverse problem of mapping dynamic 3D points to a static radiance field by defining spatial latent variables relative to the pose of body parts, effectively overparameterizing the representation with one embedding per bone [18108-a-nerf, unofficial]. Unlike explicit surface models that use forward kinematics, A-NeRF learns an implicit volumetric model that jointly refines pose and appearance without requiring ground truth labels for shape or pose [18108-a-nerf, unofficial]. It employs a "Rel. Ray" encoding combining bone-relative distance, direction, and the angle between the ray and the joint vector [18108-a-nerf, unofficial]. SelfNeRF is a novel view synthesis method for human performance that trains from scratch using monocular self-rotating video inputs, achieving high-fidelity results in approximately twenty minutes [18160-selfnerf, unofficial]. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like MoCo-NeRF by utilizing a surface-relative hash encoding to aggregate inter-frame information, enabling rapid convergence without multi-view inputs [18160-selfnerf, unofficial]. It relies on external reconstruction methods (e.g., VideoAvatar) to recover surface shape point clouds \{Tt\} and maps query points to canonical space via K-nearest neighbor signed distances [18160-selfnerf, unofficial]. A feed-forward method for synthesizing novel-view videos of arbitrary human performers from sparse multi-view camera inputs (3-4 views) by learning generalizable neural radiance fields using a parametric 3D body model (SMPL) and transformer-based aggregation of spatio-temporal features. It constructs time-augmented skeletal features by leveraging SMPL and aggregates temporal information using a temporal transformer, followed by a multi-view transformer for cross-attention. A novel 360° free-view rendering method capable of reconstructing dynamic human-object-scene neural radiation fields from a single monocular video. It estimates complex object motion during human-object interaction by introducing new object skeletons into the traditional human skeletal hierarchy and uses two learnable object state embeddings for different interaction contexts. It significantly outperforms existing techniques on challenging datasets, with a 40% to 50% improvement on the LPIPS metric. A method for learning generic dynamic radiation fields from monocular video. It learns both point features and scene streams through video feature extraction, implicit velocity fields, and stream-based feature aggregation modules. It supports new applications such as scene editing, unseen frame synthesis, and fast new scene adaptation. The extension of NeRF to dynamic scenes originated with the need to capture human performance and articulated objects from limited camera views. Early works like [18108-a-nerf] addressed the ill-posed nature of monocular dynamic reconstruction by introducing skeletal-relative encodings and joint optimization of pose and appearance. Subsequent methods like [16197-moco-nerf] and [18160-selfnerf] refined this by decoupling rigid and non-rigid components or leveraging surface geometry for faster convergence. Generalizable approaches like Neural Human Performer and HOSNeRF further expanded the domain to sparse multi-view and single-view human-object interactions, respectively. Neural Human Performer: Learning Generalizable Radiance Fields for Human Performance Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2109.07448, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Neural Radiance Field-based Visual Rendering: a Comprehensive Review, https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/11455380, fetched 2026-10-30

name: MoCo-NeRF
head: Motion-Oriented Compositional Neural Radiance Fields
body: MoCo-NeRF is a framework for free-viewpoint rendering of monocular human videos that models non-rigid body motions as radiance residual fields rather than spatial offsets, using rigid skeletal transformations as a prior. It separates the canonical radiance representation from pose-dependent non-rigid residuals, allowing direct supervision from ground-truth pixel colors to optimize both components simultaneously. Unlike sibling methods like A-NeRF which may rely on spatial offsets or surface-based deformations, MoCo-NeRF avoids the high computational complexity and misaligned learning objectives associated with unbounded spatial offset prediction by operating directly in the radiance space. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Monocular video frames I, camera poses, and skeletal joint positions J for each frame. Outputs: Rendered RGB images C{final} for arbitrary viewpoints and times. Data Structures: 1. Skeletal Weights Volume Decoder: An explicit volume decoder optimized to store canonical skinning weights w^ck for K joints. 2. Multi-Resolution Hash Encoding (MHE): A hash grid \psi{hash} with 16 levels and feature dimension H=2 per level. For multi-subject training, a global MHE \psi^G{hash} (4 levels, H=2) and Ns local MHEs \{\psi^i{hash}\} are used. 3. Learnable Base Code: A tensor S \in \mathbb{R}^{64} initialized randomly. 4. MLP Decoders: M{rigid}: Predicts rigid color and density. M{nr}: Predicts non-rigid color and density residuals. 5. Projection Matrices: Wp, WQ, WK, WV for pose-embedded feature generation. Numbered Steps: 1. Canonical Transformation: Transform an observation point \mathbf{x} at time t to canonical space \mathbf{x}c using inverse linear blend skinning: \mathbf{x}c = \sum{k=1}^K w^ok (Rk \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{t}k) where Rk, \mathbf{t}k are the rotation and translation of bone k, and observation weights w^ok are computed from canonical weights w^ck: w^ok = \frac{w^ck(Rk \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{t}k)}{\sum{j=1}^K w^cj(Rj \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{t}j)} The canonical weights w^ck are optimized via an explicit volume decoder. 2. Rigid Branch Feature Query: Query multiresolution volumetric features \mathbf{f}{\mathbf{x}c} from the MHE \psi{hash} (or global/local MHEs in multi-subject mode): \mathbf{f}{\mathbf{x}c} = \psi{hash}(\mathbf{x}c) Slice the first half (H dimensions) of \mathbf{f}{\mathbf{x}c} at each resolution level to compute \mathbf{f}^{:H}{\mathbf{x}c}. 3. Rigid Radiance Prediction: Predict rigid color \mathbf{c} and density \sigma using decoder M{rigid}: \mathbf{c}, \sigma = M{rigid}(\mathbf{f}^{:H}{\mathbf{x}c}) Note: In multi-subject mode, concatenate global features, sliced local features, and subject ID code \mathbf{S}i: \mathbf{c}, \sigma = M{rigid}(\psi^G{hash}(\mathbf{x}c) \oplus (\psi^i{hash}(\mathbf{x}c))^{:H} \oplus \mathbf{S}i) \quad \text{} 4. Non-Rigid Feature Preparation: Use the full feature \mathbf{f}{\mathbf{x}c} but freeze the first half representing canonical radiance. Denote the remaining optimized half as \mathbf{f}^{\mathbf{x}c}. 5. Pose-Embedded Implicit Feature Generation: a. Initialize learnable base code \mathbf{S} \in \mathbb{R}^{64}. b. Apply sinusoidal positional encoding \gamma to 23 joint positions \mathbf{J} = \{\mathbf{j}i\}{i=1}^{23} with L=10 frequency bands: \gamma(\mathbf{j}i) = [\mathbf{j}i, \sin(2^0 \pi \mathbf{j}i), \cos(2^0 \pi \mathbf{j}i), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{j}i), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{j}i)] Resulting in \gamma(\mathbf{J}) \in \mathbb{R}^{23 \times 63}. c. Project encoded joints to raw pose-embedded code \mathbf{P}{raw} using projection matrix Wp: \mathbf{P}{raw} = Wp \cdot \gamma(\mathbf{J}) d. Generate query \mathbf{P}q from \mathbf{S}, and key \mathbf{P}k, value \mathbf{P}v from \mathbf{P}{raw} via linear projections: \mathbf{P}q = WQ \cdot \mathbf{S}, \quad \mathbf{P}k = WK \cdot \mathbf{P}{raw}, \quad \mathbf{P}v = WV \cdot \mathbf{P}{raw} e. Compute final implicit feature \mathbf{P}{nr} using cross-attention: \mathbf{P}{nr} = \text{softmax}(\mathbf{P}q \cdot \mathbf{P}k^\top) \cdot \mathbf{P}v 6. Non-Rigid Radiance Residual Prediction: Predict color \Delta \mathbf{c} and density \Delta \sigma residuals using decoder M{nr} conditioned on \mathbf{f}^{\mathbf{x}c} and \mathbf{P}{nr}: \Delta \mathbf{c}, \Delta \sigma = M{nr}(\mathbf{f}^{\mathbf{x}c}; \mathbf{P}{nr}) 7. Compositional Rendering: For each ray \mathbf{r}, query M samples. Compute transmittance Tm and final RGB color C{final} using stratified sampling: Tm = \exp\left(-\sum{n=1}^{m-1} \sigman \deltan\right) C{final}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{m=1}^M Tm (1 - \exp(-(\sigmam + \Delta \sigmam)\deltam)) (\mathbf{c}m + \Delta \mathbf{c}m) where \deltam is the distance between adjacent samples. Similarly, compute C{rigid} from (\mathbf{c}, \sigma) for loss calculation. 8. Optimization: a. Sample Np patches per iteration. b. Render patches \hat{P}^rk from C{rigid} and \hat{P}^fk from C{final}. c. Compute LPIPS loss using pre-trained VGGNet against ground truth patch P^{GT}k: \mathcal{L}{LPIPS} = \text{LPIPS}(\text{VGG}(\hat{P}), \text{VGG}(P^{GT}k)) d. Compute MSE losses \mathcal{L}^r{MSE} and \mathcal{L}^f{MSE} for rigid and final patches. e. Compute SSIM loss \mathcal{L}^f{SSIM} only for final patches. f. Compute total loss \mathcal{L}^o with hyperparameter \lambda = 0.2: \mathcal{L}^r = \mathcal{L}^r{LPIPS} + \mathcal{L}^r{MSE} \mathcal{L}^f = \mathcal{L}^f{LPIPS} + \mathcal{L}^f{MSE} + \mathcal{L}^f{SSIM} \mathcal{L}^o = \lambda \mathcal{L}^r + (1-\lambda) \mathcal{L}^f Parameters: K: Total number of joints (23). L: Number of frequency bands in positional encoding (10). \lambda: Loss balancing hyperparameter (0.2). Optimizer: Adam with betas (0.9, 0.99). Learning Rate: 5 \times 10^{-5} for skeletal weights volume decoder; 5 \times 10^{-3} for all other components. MHE Configuration: 16 levels, H=2 per level; Global MHE: 4 levels, H=2. Sampling: 6 patches of size 32 \times 32 per iteration; 256 samples per ray. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Spatial offset strategies suffer from high computational complexity because a single spatial offset spans an unbounded range and is unique for every 3D point across all input frames and body poses. Spatial offset strategies suffer from misaligned learning objectives because the learning objective of spatial offsets is not directly aligned with conventional RGB-based supervision. MoCo-NeRF avoids these by modeling residuals directly. Time Complexity: Training is significantly faster than offset-based methods. Single-subject training takes 1–2 hours on an RTX 3090 GPU. Multi-subject training (6 subjects) takes ~2 hours on one RTX 3090. This is much faster than HumanNeRF (38.9h single-subject) and NHP (~123h multi-subject). Memory Complexity: Uses a single MHE for single-subject, or global + local MHEs for multi-subject. Feature dimension H=2 is small. Performance: On ZJU-MoCap single-subject (subjects 377, 386, 387, 392, 393, 394), achieves PSNR 31.06, SSIM 0.9734, LPIPS 28.83. On multi-subject (377, 386, 392), achieves PSNR 31.97, SSIM 0.9781, LPIPS 24.54. Strengths: Direct color supervision for non-rigid motions; efficient training; supports multi-subject training in a single framework. Limitations: Requires skeletal joint positions as input. Performance depends on the accuracy of the skeletal transformation. MoCo-NeRF was proposed by J. Kim et al. in 2024. It addresses the limitations of conventional spatial offset modeling in dynamic human rendering, which suffers from high learning complexity and misaligned objectives. The method builds on the principles of canonical transformation and conditioning described in Parent, specifically utilizing inverse linear blend skinning for rigid transformations. It is evaluated on the ZJU-MoCap and MonoCap datasets. Motion-Oriented Compositional Neural Radiance Fields for Monocular Dynamic Human Modeling, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72933-127, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Neural Scene Graphs
head: NSG
body: Neural Scene Graphs (NSG) is a method for decomposing dynamic, multi-object scenes into a learned hierarchical scene graph with decoupled object transformations and scene representations. It solves the problem of novel view synthesis and rendering of unseen arrangements in dynamic scenes by lifting the assumption of static scene consistency required by existing neural rendering methods. Unlike methods that encode the entire scene into a single, static network, NSG uses a hierarchical scene-graph model with object-level implicit representations, allowing for the learning of object representations directly from video frames and tracking data. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of video frames and corresponding tracking data (labels for object instances, classes, and poses). Camera intrinsics and extrinsics are required for ray generation. Outputs: A rendered image for a given camera pose and a scene graph S containing learned object representations, transformations, and background models. Data Structures The scene is defined as a directed acyclic graph S: S = \langle W, C, F, L, E \rangle W: The root node representing the global world space. C: The camera node. F: A set of representation nodes. This includes a static background node F{\theta{bckg}} and dynamic object nodes F{\thetao}. L: Latent descriptors lo associated with object nodes to encode instance-specific appearance. E: A set of edges representing affine transformations or property assignments. Edges and Transformations Edges E represent affine transformations from node u to node v or property assignments: E = \{ e{u,v} \in \{ [\cdot], M{uv} \} \} where M{uv} is a 4 \times 4 affine transformation matrix: M{uv} = \begin{bmatrix} R & t \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad R \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, t \in \mathbb{R}^3 For all edges originating from the root node W, transformations T^Wv are assigned between the global world space and the local object or camera space. The background node has no assigned transformation as it is already aligned with W. To represent different scales of the same object type, a non-uniform scaling matrix So is computed and assigned at the edge e{o,f} between an object node and its shared representation model F. Representation Models Representation models are shared and defined in a shared, unit-scaled frame. 1. Background Node (F{\theta{bckg}}): Approximates all static parts of the scene. It maps a point x and viewing direction d to volumetric density \sigma and color c. Unlike standard volumetric NeRF, this representation lives on sparse planes instead of a volume. It uses Fourier encodings [37] to aid learning high-frequency functions in the MLP model. 2. Object Nodes (F{\thetao}): Scene objects are represented as augmented implicit neural radiance fields following Mildenhall et al. [22]. To generalize across a class of objects, a latent vector z (or lo) is added to the input 3D query point, allowing similar objects to be modeled using the same network. Rendering Algorithm 1. Graph Traversal: To retrieve an object’s local transformation and position po = [x, z, y]o, traverse from the root node W, applying transformations until the desired object node F{\thetao} is reached, ending in the frame of reference defined by the accumulated transformations. 2. Ray Sampling: Generate rays r(\lambda) = o{world} + \lambda d{world} based on camera intrinsics and extrinsics. 3. Evaluation: For background points, query F{\theta{bckg}}(x, d). For object points, transform the query point x from world space to the object's local unit-scaled space using the accumulated transformation from the graph traversal. Query the shared representation model F with the transformed point and the latent descriptor lo. 4. Compositing: Perform standard volume rendering integration along the ray using the sampled densities and colors. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderneuralscenegraph(camerapose, scenegraph, rayorigin, raydirection): """ Renders a single ray through a Neural Scene Graph. Args: camerapose: Extrinsics (R, t) and intrinsics of the camera. scenegraph: The scene graph S = <W, C, F, L, E>. rayorigin: World space origin of the ray. raydirection: World space direction of the ray. Returns: color: Rendered RGB color. depth: Rendered depth. """ # 1. Initialize accumulation variables accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedweight = 0.0 accumulateddepth = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 # 2. Sample points along the ray # Assume samples are pre-computed along the ray within near/far bounds samples = samplepointsalongray(rayorigin, raydirection) for sample in samples: worldpoint = sample.position localtransform = identitymatrix() isbackground = True objectnode = None latentcode = None # 3. Determine which node represents this point # In a full implementation, this involves spatial partitioning or # querying the graph structure to find the relevant object node. # For NSG, we assume a mechanism exists to identify if a point # belongs to a specific object's bounding volume or the background. # Check if point belongs to any dynamic object node for objnode in scenegraph.dynamicnodes: # Get transformation from root W to this object node # This involves traversing edges E from W to objnode transformtoobj = gettransformationfromroot(scenegraph, objnode) # Transform world point to object's local unit-scaled frame localpoint = transformpoint(worldpoint, inverse(transformtoobj)) # Apply scaling if defined on edge eo,f if hasscaling(scenegraph, objnode): scalematrix = getscaling(scenegraph, objnode) localpoint = scalematrix localpoint # Check if localpoint is within the object's representation domain # (e.g., within the unit-scaled bounding box) if isinsidedomain(localpoint, objnode): isbackground = False objectnode = objnode localtransform = transformtoobj latentcode = getlatentdescriptor(scenegraph, objnode) break # 4. Query the appropriate representation model if isbackground: # Background lives on sparse planes density, color = querybackgroundmodel(scenegraph.backgroundnode, worldpoint, raydirection) else: # Object representation is an augmented implicit neural radiance field # Input: localpoint + latentcode, raydirection density, color = queryobjectmodel(objectnode.model, localpoint, latentcode, raydirection) # 5. Volume Rendering Integration alpha = 1.0 - exp(-density sample.distance) weight = transmittance alpha accumulatedcolor += weight color accumulateddepth += weight sample.depth accumulatedweight += weight transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) # Early termination if transmittance is negligible if transmittance < 1e-4: break # Final color finalcolor = accumulatedcolor + transmittance backgroundcolor return finalcolor, accumulatedweight Parameters Latent Vector Dimension: Not given in the sources. Number of Frequency Bands for Fourier Encoding: Not given in the sources. MLP Architecture: Follows Mildenhall et al. [22] (standard NeRF MLP) for object nodes; specific architecture for background sparse planes not detailed beyond "Fourier encodings" and "MLP model". Edge Cases and Pitfalls Scale Normalization: Objects are represented in a shared, unit-scaled frame. Non-uniform scaling So must be correctly computed and applied to handle objects of different physical sizes within the same class. Tracking Data Dependency: The method relies on labeled and generated tracking data to learn object representations and transformations. Poor tracking data quality may degrade performance. Background Representation: The background uses sparse planes instead of a volume. This requires careful handling of the plane geometry and sampling to avoid artifacts. Uses a continuous angular representation to handle multi-scale features. Choose when high-frequency details are critical across varying distances. Choose when interactive visualization is required. UE4-NeRF Extends NeRF to panoptic segmentation. Choose when semantic understanding of the scene is needed alongside rendering. Strengths: Allows for novel view synthesis and rendering of unseen arrangements in dynamic scenes; facilitates 3D object detection using inverse rendering; decouples object transformations and scene representations. Limitations: Relies on tracking data; less interpretable than explicit methods due to the use of MLPs. When to use: When dealing with dynamic, multi-object scenes where novel views and unseen arrangements are required, and tracking data is available. When not to use: When the scene is static and a simpler NeRF variant is sufficient; when tracking data is unavailable or unreliable. Neural Scene Graphs was introduced by Park et al. in 2021. The method builds on the success of implicit neural representations for static scenes, specifically NeRF by Mildenhall et al. [22], and extends it to dynamic scenes by introducing a hierarchical scene-graph model. name: A-NeRF
head: Articulated Neural Radiance Fields
body: A-NeRF learns a user-specific neural 3D body model and underlying skeleton pose from unlabelled monocular videos by extending Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) with a skeleton to apply to time-varying and articulated motion. Its core technical novelty is defining spatial latent variables relative to the pose of body parts to overcome ill-posed inverse operations with an overparameterization, embedding domain knowledge of how humans move. Unlike MoCo-NeRF which uses residual-based conditioning, A-NeRF uses skeleton-relative embeddings; unlike SelfNeRF which uses surface-based SDFs, A-NeRF uses volumetric density conditioned on bone-relative coordinates. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of N images Ik \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} of the same person. Initial pose estimates \hat{\theta}k from an off-the-shelf estimator (e.g., SPIN [26]). Outputs: Refined skeleton poses \thetak, neural network parameters \phi (defining shape and appearance), and rendered images C\phi(\thetak). Data Structures: 1. Skeleton Representation: Rest pose: 3D joint locations \tilde{a}m for m=1..24, root at 0, connected via B bones. Pose \thetak: Vector containing relative rotations of 24 joints \tilde{\theta}{k,m} to parents and global position \tilde{\theta}{k,0}. 2. Neural Network Architecture (F\phi): Follows original NeRF [42] structure. Inputs: Positional Encoded (PE) query point \Gamma(q), PE view direction \Gamma(d), appearance code, and Relative Ray encoding. Hidden Layers: 10 fully-connected layers with sizes [256, 256, 256, 256, 256, 256, 256, 256, 256, 256, 128]. Activations: ReLU for all layers except the last two. Sigmoid for the final output layer. Specific Injection: Appearance code and Relative Ray encoding are concatenated into the network at the second-to-last fully-connected layer (before the final 128-unit layer) to prevent them from affecting body geometry. Outputs: Density \sigma \in \mathbb{R} and color c \in \mathbb{R}^3. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize camera intrinsics, bone lengths am, and pose \thetak using SPIN [26] for every frame k. 2. Encoding: Map input scene point q and view direction d to higher dimensional space using Positional Encoding \Gamma. 3. Skeleton-Relative Encoding (Rel. Ray): For a query point q and frame k, compute the vector from q to each joint m: \tilde{q}{k,m} = q - \tilde{a}m(\thetak). Compute the angle between the ray direction \tilde{d}k and the vector to joint m: d'{k,m} = \arccos(\tilde{d}k \cdot \tilde{q}{k,m}). Concatenate these angles for all 24 joints to form the Relative Ray encoding. 4. Network Forward Pass: Feed \Gamma(q), \Gamma(d), appearance code, and Rel. Ray encoding into F\phi to obtain \sigma and c. 5. Volume Rendering: Render the image C\phi(\thetak) via classical ray-marching using coarse-to-fine importance sampling. Restrict samples to be within a coarse human silhouette estimated with [10] unless the background is monochrome. 6. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss L{SV}: L{SV}(\theta, \phi) = \sumk \| C\phi(\thetak) - Ik \|1 + \lambda\theta \sumk d(\thetak - \hat{\theta}k) + \lambdat \sumk \left\| \frac{\partial^2 \thetak}{\partial t^2} \right\|^2 Where: Data term: L1 distance between generated and input images. Pose regularizer: d(x) = \min(\|x\|2 - \epsilon, 0) with \epsilon = 0.01. Encourages solution to stay close to initial pose \hat{\theta}k. Smoothness prior: Penalizes acceleration \frac{\partial^2 \thetak}{\partial t^2} between consecutive frames. 7. Optimization Loop: Form a training batch by randomly sampling N{batch} = 3072 rays from all available images. Accumulate gradient update \nabla \theta for G \times (30 \times N{batch}) / N iterations so that each \thetak is expected to be sampled 30 times before update. Optimize poses \thetak and neural parameters \phi for 500k iterations on objective Eq. 2. Stop optimizing pose and continue training \phi with only the data term for additional 200k iterations. Parameters: \lambdat: Hyperparameter balancing the smoothness prior term. \lambda\theta: Hyperparameter balancing the pose regularizer term. \epsilon: Tolerance for small shifts in the pose regularizer, value 0.01. Cutoff distance t: 500mm, with exponential decay over 250k iterations. Cutoff temperature \tau: Starts at -20, decays exponentially to -200 over 500k iterations. Coarse samples: 64. Fine samples: 16. Positional encoding frequencies for input (L{input}): 7. Positional encoding frequencies for view (L{view}): 4. Learning rate for \phi: Starts at 5 \times 10^{-4}, decays exponentially over 200k iterations. Learning rate for \phi (finetune): 2 \times 10^{-4} decaying to 5 \times 10^{-5}. Gradient accumulation steps G: 20 for Mixamo, 50 for Human 3.6M, 10 for MonoPerfCap. Pitfalls: Using World Ray direction causes overfitting in static/estimated camera settings, leading to flickering results for novel view rendering (e.g., bullet-time effect). Encoding world coordinates directly fails on motions and has large memory consumption. Encoding positions relative to skeleton has high dimensionality. Straightforward baselines conditioning directly on pose (World Position + Joint Position + \theta) perform worst, achieving 0.7 SSIM by simply rendering background colors. Time Complexity: Training takes approximately 60 hours on 2 Nvidia Tesla V100 32GB GPUs. Memory Complexity: High due to per-bone embeddings and large MLP. Encoding positions relative to the skeleton has high dimensionality compared to world coordinates. Measured Performance: On Human 3.6M S9 Protocol II: PSNR 26.64, SSIM 0.9192, PA-MPJPE 41.00 with per-image code and Rel. Ray. On SURREAL: PSNR 29.10, SSIM 0.9655, compared to NeuralBody PSNR 23.86, SSIM 0.9304. Rendering Time: 1-4 seconds per 512x512x3 image on a single Nvidia Tesla V100 GPU. Strengths: Works better than NeuralBody for longer sequences and retargeting to diverse poses. Can be trained with only a single view; adding more views does not help if poses are not diverse enough. One long video with diverse poses is comparable to multiple shorter multi-view recordings. Limitations: Requires rough 3D pose estimates for initialization. Does not require surface supervision or initialization, but relies on off-the-shelf predictors which may be inaccurate. A-NeRF builds on NeRF [42] and uses appearance code design from [36, 49]. It was proposed to learn a generative neural body model from unlabelled monocular videos by extending Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) with a skeleton to apply to time-varying and articulated motion. The method addresses the ill-posed inverse problem of mapping 3D world coordinates to a canonical space for articulated bodies by overparameterizing with one embedding per bone. A-NeRF: Articulated Neural Radiance Fields for Learning Human Shape, Appearance, and Pose, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2102.06199, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Pixel-aligned Volumetric Avatars (PVA)
body: Pixel-aligned Volumetric Avatars (PVA) is a method for estimating a volumetric 3D avatar of a human head from only a few input images, enabling view synthesis for unseen identities and expressions. It generalizes across identities by combining a neural radiance field with local, pixel-aligned features extracted directly from input images, avoiding the information loss associated with global latent codes. Unlike mesh-based methods, PVA captures arbitrary topology and high-frequency details (e.g., hair, expressions) without requiring explicit 3D supervision or voxel grids. Inputs: One or more conditioning images vi of dimensions h \times w \times 3, along with their camera intrinsics Ki and extrinsics [R|t]i. Outputs: A radiance field function that predicts color \mathbf{c} and volume density \sigma for any 3D point \mathbf{X} and view direction, allowing novel view synthesis. Data Structures: 1. Feature Map (f^{(i)}): A 2D tensor of size h \times w \times C, where C is the feature dimension. This is the output of the encoder-decoder network N{feat}. 2. Radiance Field Network (N): A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) taking encoded position and pixel-aligned features as input. 3. Positional Encoding (\phi): A hierarchical sinusoidal encoding function applied to 3D coordinates. Numbered Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: For each conditioning view vi, compute the pixel-aligned feature map f^{(i)} by passing the image through the shallow convolutional encoder-decoder network N{feat}: f^{(i)} = N{feat}(vi) 2. Feature Interpolation: For a 3D point \mathbf{X} in world space, determine its corresponding pixel location \mathbf{x} in the conditioning view vi using perspective projection \Pi: \mathbf{x} = \Pi(\mathbf{X}) Extract the feature vector \mathbf{f}\mathbf{X} by bilinearly interpolating the feature map f^{(i)} at location \mathbf{x}: \mathbf{f}\mathbf{X} = F(f^{(i)}, \mathbf{x}) where F denotes bilinear interpolation. 3. Radiance Field Query: Pass the positional encoding of the 3D location, \phi(\mathbf{X}), and the extracted feature vector \mathbf{f}\mathbf{X} into the radiance field network N to predict color \mathbf{c} and opacity/density \sigma: \{\mathbf{c}, \sigma\} = N(\phi(\mathbf{X}), \mathbf{f}\mathbf{X}) Note: The positional encoding \phi(\cdot) follows the standard hierarchical sinusoidal encoding defined in the parent article [Parent]. 4. Ray Marching for Rendering: For a target view j with camera intrinsics Kj and extrinsics [R|t]j, march rays into the scene. For a pixel \mathbf{p}, compute the ray direction \mathbf{d}: \mathbf{d} = \frac{P^{-1} \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{r}0}{\| P^{-1} \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{r}0 \|} where P^{-1} = [Ri | ti]^{-1} Ki^{-1} is the inverse projection matrix relative to the conditioning view i (or target view if self-conditioning), and \mathbf{r}0 is the ray origin. All camera extrinsics are relative to the computed head pose to help the network focus on scene content. 5. Sampling: Uniformly sample a set of ns points t along the ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{r}0 + t\mathbf{d} for t \in [t{near}, t{far}]. Set \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{r}(t). 6. Volume Rendering: Use the quadrature rule to approximate the integral of color along the ray, accumulating the color and occupancy produced by N at each sample point. The predicted color I\alpha(\mathbf{p}) is computed as: I\alpha(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i=1}^{ns} Ti \left( 1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai} \right) \mathbf{c}i where Ti = e^{-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj} is the accumulated transmittance, \deltai is the distance between samples, and \{\mathbf{c}i, \sigmai\} are the outputs of N at sample i. Parameters: ns: The number of uniformly sampled points along the ray for volume rendering. Value not given in the sources. t{near}, t{far}: The near and far clipping planes for ray sampling. Value not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Global Latent Codes: Using global latent codes (as in SRNs) summarizes image information and discards details, making it difficult to generalize to local changes like facial expressions and failing to recover high-frequency details. PVA avoids this by using local pixel-aligned features. 3D Supervision: PVA does not require explicit 3D supervision during training, relying solely on photometric re-rendering loss. Methods requiring 3D supervision may fail to generalize to unseen identities if not trained on a multi-identity corpus. Time Complexity: Rendering time depends on the number of sampled points ns and the cost of the radiance field network N and encoder-decoder N{feat}. Interpolation is O(1) per sample. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the feature maps f^{(i)} for all conditioning views. This avoids the high memory cost of 3D voxel grids. Strengths: Captures arbitrary topology (e.g., hair, expressions) and high-frequency texture details better than mesh-based methods. Generalizes to unseen identities and expressions. Does not require 3D supervision. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the input images and the accuracy of the head pose estimation. Performance may degrade if the input images do not cover the necessary viewpoints for the target view. When to use: Virtual telepresence applications, specifically for generating photo-realistic human heads from a small number of example views. When not to use: When explicit 3D geometry is required for downstream tasks that cannot be derived from the volumetric representation, or when computational resources are extremely limited and real-time rendering is critical without optimization. PVA was introduced in the paper "PVA: Pixel-aligned Volumetric Avatars". It builds on insights from NeRF [Parent] and PIFu/PIFuHD, which use pixel-aligned features to retain high-frequency detail. Unlike PIFu/PIFuHD, PVA does not require explicit 3D supervision. It addresses the limitations of Scene Representation Networks (SRNs) and GRAF by using local pixel-aligned features to handle multiple identities and local deformations, rather than global latent codes or disentangled global shape/appearance codes. The method is used for virtual telepresence applications. PVA: Pixel-aligned Volumetric Avatars, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2101.02697, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: SelfNeRF
head: SelfNeRF: Fast Training NeRF for Human from Monocular Self-rotating Video
body: SelfNeRF is a novel view synthesis method for human performance that trains from scratch using monocular self-rotating video inputs, achieving high-fidelity results in approximately twenty minutes. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like MoCo-NeRF and A-NeRF by eliminating the need for multi-view inputs or explicit skeletal priors, instead relying on a surface-relative hash encoding to aggregate inter-frame information and accelerate training. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A monocular self-rotating video of a human performer consisting of Nt frames. Output: A trained neural radiance field model capable of rendering novel views of the performer. Data Structures: Surface Shape \{Tt\}: A set of point clouds representing the human surface for each frame t \in \{0, \dots, Nt - 1\}. These are recovered using external reconstruction methods (e.g., VideoAvatar or SelfRecon). Body Mask \{Mt\}: Binary masks for each frame t, identifying the human region. Hash Grid: A multi-resolution hash encoding structure storing high-dimensional feature vectors. MLP F\omega: A neural network with weights \omega that maps encoded features to density \sigma and color c. Numbered Steps: 1. Preprocessing: For the input video, recover the surface shape Tt and body mask Mt for each frame t using existing reconstruction algorithms. 2. Surface-Relative Representation: For a query point \mathbf{x} at frame t: Find the K-nearest neighbor points on the current frame's point cloud Tt. Calculate the signed distances from \mathbf{x} to these neighbors. Map these neighbors and their signed distances to the corresponding points and signed distances in the canonical space (Frame 0). 3. Encoding: Encode the resulting surface-relative representation using multi-resolution hash encoding to produce a high-dimensional feature vector. 4. Radiance Prediction: Feed the encoded feature vector into the MLP F\omega to regress the density \sigma and color c. 5. Rendering: Render the image using volume rendering to calculate the pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) for each ray \mathbf{r}. 6. Optimization: Train the model by minimizing photometric loss and geometric guidance loss. Formulas: The volume rendering equation for a ray \mathbf{r} is: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} \alpha(\mathbf{x}i) \left( \prod{j<i} (1 - \alpha(\mathbf{x}j)) \right) c(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{v}) where: \alpha(\mathbf{x}i) = 1 - \exp(-\sigma(\mathbf{x}i) \deltai) is the transmittance-derived opacity. \mathbf{x}i = \mathbf{o} + ti \mathbf{v} are the sample points on the ray. \deltai = u{i+1} - ui is the distance between adjacent sample points. c(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{v}) is the color predicted by F\omega. Parameters: Nt: Total number of frames in the input monocular video. K: Number of nearest neighbors used to calculate the surface-relative representation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def selfnerfrender(rayo, rayd, frameidx, surfaceclouds, hashgrid, mlp, K): """ Render a single ray for SelfNeRF. Args: rayo: Origin of the ray. rayd: Direction of the ray. frameidx: Index of the current frame t. surfaceclouds: List of point clouds {Tt} for all frames. hashgrid: Multi-resolution hash encoding structure. mlp: Neural network Fomega. K: Number of nearest neighbors. Returns: color: Rendered color for the ray. """ # 1. Sample points along the ray # Note: Specific sampling strategy (e.g., uniform, stratified) is not detailed in sources. # Assume standard NeRF sampling is used. tvals = samplepoints(rayo, rayd) xsamples = rayo + tvals[:, None] rayd # 2. Compute Surface-Relative Representation for each sample features = [] for x in xsamples: # Get surface cloud for current frame currentcloud = surfaceclouds[frameidx] # Find K-nearest neighbors in current frame's cloud # Note: Exact NN search algorithm (e.g., KD-Tree) is implementation detail. kneighbors, distances = findknearestneighbors(currentcloud, x, K) # Map neighbors and distances to canonical space (Frame 0) # Note: The source states "take the corresponding point of the k-nearest neighbor # points on the canonical space". This implies a correspondence mapping exists # between frame t and frame 0. canonicalneighbors, canonicaldistances = maptocanonical(kneighbors, distances, frameidx) # Encode the relative representation # Note: Hash encoding function details are abstracted. feature = hashencode(canonicalneighbors, canonicaldistances) features.append(feature) features = torch.stack(features) # 3. Predict density and color # Note: View direction v is constant for the ray. sigma, color = mlp(features, rayd) # 4. Volume Rendering # Compute opacity alpha # Note: deltai calculation requires tvals[i+1] - tvals[i] deltas = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] # Pad delta for last point if necessary, or assume N samples deltas = torch.cat([deltas, torch.zeroslike(deltas[:1])]) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) # Compute transmittance # Ti = product{j<i} (1 - alphaj) transmittance = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha, dim=0) transmittance = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(transmittance[:1]), transmittance[:-1]]) # Composite color weights = alpha transmittance color = torch.sum(weights[:, None] color, dim=0) return color Training Time: Approximately 20 minutes for convergence. Input Requirements: Monocular self-rotating video; no multi-view setup required. Strengths: Fast training speed due to hash encoding; ability to train from scratch with minimal input. Limitations: Relies on accurate surface reconstruction from monocular video, which can be challenging for complex motions or occlusions. When to use: When only monocular video is available and rapid training is desired. When not to use: When multi-view data is available and higher fidelity is required, or when explicit skeletal animation is needed. SelfNeRF was proposed by Bo Peng, Jun Hu, Jingtao Zhou, and Juyong Zhang from the University of Science and Technology of China. It was published on arXiv in October 2022. The method addresses the challenge of high-fidelity novel view synthesis for human performance using only monocular inputs, a common scenario in practical applications like sports broadcasts and VR/AR. name: CLA-NeRF
head: Category-Level Articulated Neural Radiance Field
body: CLA-NeRF is a differentiable representation for articulated objects that explicitly models part and joint attributes, disentangling camera pose, part pose, part segmentation, and joint attributes to allow independent control during rendering. It solves the problem of rendering deformable articulated objects at unseen poses and estimating their articulated pose from RGB images, without requiring CAD models or depth data. Unlike standard NeRF formulations which model camera poses but ignore object articulation, CLA-NeRF predicts a part segmentation field alongside density and color, enabling the inference of joint attributes via line-fitting on the segmentation field. It differs from sibling methods like NARF by focusing on general articulated objects without assuming known joint attributes (e.g., bone length) at test time, and by using part segmentation labels for supervision rather than explicit joint attributes. Inputs and Outputs: Training Inputs: A set of RGB images with ground truth camera poses and part segmentation labels for a specific object category. Inference Inputs: A few RGB views (few-shot) of an unseen 3D object instance within the known category, along with an articulated pose input. Outputs: Rendered RGB images, part segmentation maps, and estimated articulated pose (via inverse rendering). Data Structures: MLP Backbone (F\Theta): A multilayer perceptron parameterized by weights \Theta. Positional Encoding (\gamma): High-frequency positional encoding applied to 3D positions. Segmentation Logits (\mathbf{s}): A vector of dimension P + 1, where P is the number of parts and the extra dimension represents the background. Numbered Steps: 1. Feature Retrieval and Conditioning: Retrieve features from input RGB images to condition the NeRF model. 2. Deformation Matrix Calculation: Calculate a deformation matrix based on the input articulated pose. 3. Ray Deformation: Deform the sampled rays along the camera ray using the calculated deformation matrix. 4. Field Prediction: For each 3D location \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d}, predict volumetric density \sigma, RGB color \mathbf{c}, and part segmentation logits \mathbf{s} using the MLP backbone: (\sigma, \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{s}) = F\Theta(\gamma(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{d}) where \mathbf{s} has P + 1 dimensions. 5. Articulation-Aware Volume Rendering: Render the deformed visual image using the learned framework via volume rendering. The rendered color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} is computed as: \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} Tk \alphak \mathbf{c}k where \alphak = 1 - \exp(-\sigmak(t{k+1} - tk)) and Tk = \exp(-\sum{k'<k} \sigma{k'}(t{k'+1} - t{k'})). 6. Segmentation Rendering: Predict the part segmentation map \hat{\mathbf{S}}(\mathbf{r}) following the volume rendering procedure: \hat{\mathbf{S}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} Tk \alphak \mathbf{s}k where \mathbf{s}k is the predicted part segmentation of the sampled point \mathbf{r}(tk). 7. Joint Attribute Inference: Infer joint attributes by performing line-fitting on the predicted part segmentation field. 8. Inverse Rendering (Pose Estimation): Estimate the articulated pose via inverse rendering by minimizing the residual between rendered and observed pixels. Formulas: Segmentation Rendering: \hat{\mathbf{S}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} Tk \alphak \mathbf{s}k Tk = \exp\left(-\sum{k'<k} \sigma{k'}(t{k'+1} - t{k'})\right) where \mathbf{s}k is the predicted part segmentation of sampled point \mathbf{r}(tk). Color Loss (\mathcal{L}{color}): \mathcal{L}{color} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathbf{R}} \left( \|\hat{\mathbf{C}}c(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r})\|2^2 + \|\hat{\mathbf{C}}f(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r})\|2^2 \right) where \mathbf{R} is the set of rays, and the subscripts c and f likely refer to different components or views as per the source notation. Segmentation Loss (\mathcal{L}{seg}): \mathcal{L}{seg} = -\sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathbf{R}} \sum{i=1}^{P+1} \left( pi(\mathbf{r}) \log \hat{p}i(\mathbf{r}) + pi(\mathbf{r}) \log \hat{p}i(\mathbf{r}) \right) where \hat{p}i(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{\exp(\hat{\mathbf{S}}i(\mathbf{r}))}{\sum{j} \exp(\hat{\mathbf{S}}j(\mathbf{r}))} is the softmax probability for part i. Note: The source formula for \mathcal{L}{seg} appears to have a typo or specific notation where pi(\mathbf{r}) is used for both ground truth and predicted terms in the log expression; standard cross-entropy would use pi^{gt} \log \hat{p}i. The source text is reproduced as cited. Parameters: P: The number of parts in the articulated object, determining the dimensionality of the segmentation logits (P + 1 including background). Pitfalls: Standard NeRF formulations explicitly model camera poses but do not consider object articulation, making them unable to render deformable articulated objects at different poses. The method assumes revolute joints causing 1D rotational motion (e.g., eyeglasses) in the experiments. Not given in the sources. CLA-NeRF was proposed by Wei-Cheng Tseng, Hung-Ju Liao, Lin Yen-Chen, and Min Sun. It was published in the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) in 2022. The work addresses the challenge of modeling general articulated objects (composed of rigid parts connected by joints) without relying on instance-level CAD models or depth data, enabling few-shot inference on unseen 3D object instances within a known category. It is the first method to model general articulated objects with neural radiance fields, allowing for view synthesis, part segmentation, and articulated pose estimation.
