name: Object-Centric Voxelization for Dynamic Scenes
head: DynaVol, Unsupervised Learning for Dynamic Scenes through Object-Centric Voxelization
body: DynaVol is an unsupervised 3D dynamic scene decomposition method that unifies geometric structures and object-centric learning within a differentiable volume rendering framework. It solves the multi-view mismatch of 2D object segmentation by ensuring 3D consistency, enabling novel view synthesis, and allowing direct scene editing. Unlike 2D image decomposition methods such as SAVi, DynaVol infers a probability distribution over objects at individual spatial locations via object-centric voxelization, facilitating fine-grained separation without geometric priors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Initial timestamp images and poses \{Iv^{t=1}, Tv^{t=1}\}{v=1}^V and monocular video frames \{It, Tt\}{t=2}^T. The method supports scenarios where V=1 (only one initial camera pose) and monocular camera trajectories. Outputs: Synthesized target pixel values for novel views and time steps, along with decomposed object-centric representations \{(cn, \sigman)\}{n=1}^N. Data Structures: Object-centric 4D Voxel Representation: Vt \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times Nx \times Ny \times Nz}. This structure maintains the time-varying density \{\sigman\}{n=1}^N for each possible object across spatial dimensions Nx, Ny, Nz and time t. Slots: N is a predefined number of object slots, assumed to be larger than the actual number of objects in the scene to handle unknown counts. Algorithm Steps: 1. Sampling: Sample 3D points \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z) and view directions \mathbf{d} for each timestamp t. 2. Object-Centric Voxelization: Learn the object-centric projection of (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}, t) to \{(cn, \sigman)\}{n=1}^N. This infers the probability distribution over objects at individual spatial locations. 3. Dynamics Module: Learn transitions of voxel grid features in canonical space over time. The voxel features evolve through a canonical-space deformation function. 4. Volume Slot Attention: Aggregate voxel representations to refine object-level, time-invariant global features. This module progressively refines global features by aggregating local voxel representations. 5. Compositional NeRF Decoder: Estimate density and color for each object at view direction \mathbf{d} using both local voxel features and global object representations. 6. Rendering: Re-combine \{(cn, \sigman)\}{n=1}^N to synthesize target pixel values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dynavolrender(initialimages, initialposes, videoframes): # 1. Initialize parameters N = predefinednumberofslots # Assumed > actual object count Nx, Ny, Nz = voxelgriddimensions Vt = zeros((N, Nx, Ny, Nz)) # Object-centric 4D voxel representation # 2. Process each timestamp t for t in range(1, T+1): # Sample 3D points x and view directions d points, directions = samplerays(videoframes[t]) # 3. Object-centric Voxelization # Infers probability distribution over objects at spatial locations # Produces density sigman and color cn for each slot n voxelfeatures = objectcentricvoxelization(points, directions, t, Vt) # 4. Dynamics Module # Learn transitions of voxel grid features in canonical space over time # Updates Vt based on deformation function Vt = dynamicsmodule(Vt, t) # 5. Volume Slot Attention # Aggregate voxel representations to refine global features globalfeatures = volumeslotattention(voxelfeatures) # 6. Compositional NeRF Decoder # Estimate density and color for each object densities = [] colors = [] for n in range(N): # Use local voxel features and global object representations sigman, cn = compositionalnerfdecoder( voxelfeatures[n], globalfeatures[n], directions) densities.append(sigman) colors.append(cn) # 7. Rendering # Re-combine to synthesize target pixel values renderedimage = volumerendering(densities, colors, directions) return renderedimage, Vt Parameters: N: Predefined number of object slots. Must be larger than the actual number of objects. Nx, Ny, Nz: Spatial dimensions of the voxel grid. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Monocular Input: The method handles scenarios with only one initial camera pose (V=1) and monocular camera trajectories smoothly, avoiding multi-view mismatch issues common in 2D approaches. Slot Count: N is a hyperparameter that must be set conservatively high to account for unknown object counts, potentially leading to unused slots. Uses residual-based canonical transformation and pose-conditioned radiance residuals. Choose when pose information is available and deformation is complex. MoCo-NeRF Explicitly models scene objects and their relationships. Choose when explicit scene structure and reasoning are required. Neural Scene Graphs Uses skeleton-based inverse Linear Blend Skinning (LBS). Choose for articulated human or rigid-body scenes with known skeletons. A-NeRF Uses pixel-aligned features for high-fidelity avatar rendering. Choose for detailed human avatar synthesis. PVA Uses surface-based signed distances to nearest neighbors. Choose when surface reconstruction is a viable prior. SelfNeRF Uses canonical space alignment with local appearance. Choose for scenes with varying lighting conditions. CLA-NeRF Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Evaluated on simulated 3D dynamic scenes with varying numbers of objects, diverse motions, shapes (cubes, spheres, real-world shapes), and materials (rubber, metal). Demonstrated on real-world videos for novel view synthesis and editing. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Ensures 3D consistency, enables novel view synthesis, allows direct scene editing (object removal, replacement, trajectory modification) by manipulating voxel grids or deformation functions without further training. Handles monocular inputs and unknown object counts. Limitations: Requires predefined number of slots N which may be larger than actual objects. When to use: Unsupervised dynamic scene decomposition, novel view synthesis, and scene editing where 3D consistency is critical. When not to use: When explicit geometric priors are available and preferred, or when the number of objects is known and small. DynaVol was presented at ICLR 2024. It addresses the challenge of unsupervised learning of object-centric representations in dynamic visual scenes. Unlike previous approaches that decompose 2D images, DynaVol introduces a 3D scene generative model that unifies geometric structures and object-centric learning. It builds on the principles of dynamic and articulated scene modeling by mapping 3D query points to a canonical space [18219-dynamic-and-articulated-scene-modeling.md]. DynaVol: Unsupervised Learning for Dynamic Scenes through Object-Centric Voxelization, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2305.00393, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: View-Dependent Appearance and Lighting
head: View-Dependent Radiance, Directional Encoding
body: This configuration extends the standard NeRF representation by explicitly modeling the angular dependence of surface appearance and lighting, allowing the network to predict view-dependent effects such as specular reflections, anisotropic materials, and refraction/reflection in transparent objects. It sets itself apart from view-independent baselines by separating or jointly encoding directionality into the radiance field, enabling accurate rendering of glossy and transparent scenes that simple density-color mappings cannot capture. The core mechanism involves modifying the input signature of the radiance field MLP to include the viewing direction \mathbf{d} alongside the 3D position \mathbf{x}. While standard NeRF often uses a latent code or ignores direction for diffuse approximations, this family explicitly passes \mathbf{d} through positional encoding \Gamma(\mathbf{d}) before concatenation with position encoding \Gamma(\mathbf{x}). The network output is typically decomposed into density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}, where \mathbf{c} is now a function of \mathbf{d}. In advanced variants, this decomposition is structural: 1. Explicit Decomposition: The network outputs separate components for view-independent properties (e.g., base color, diffuse density) and view-dependent properties (e.g., specular features, reflection vectors). These are rendered separately and composited. 2. Joint Encoding: The direction is processed through dedicated sub-networks or attention mechanisms to modulate the color output based on the angle of incidence and view. Mathematically, the radiance L(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) is approximated by: L(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \approx \text{MLP}(\Gamma(\mathbf{x}), \Gamma(\mathbf{d})) The rendering equation remains the standard volume rendering integral, but the color term \mathbf{c}i at sample i is now direction-aware. A unified framework for HDR novel view synthesis from blurry LDR images and event data. It distinguishes itself by introducing differentiable Camera Response Function (CRF) models for both RGB and event sensors, jointly optimizing them with the NeRF network to align predicted radiance with actual sensor measurements, solving the sensor-physics mismatch [18115-see-nerf.md]. A method for scenes with transparent objects (e.g., glass) that models refraction and reflection using view-dependent and independent elements. It differs from standard NeRF by introducing a view-independent density field and a view-dependent offset field to estimate refraction surfaces and offsets simultaneously, handling both refraction and reflection [18124-ref2-nerf.md]. The concept of view-dependent appearance originates from computer graphics rendering equations, where reflectance is a function of incoming and outgoing light directions. In the context of NeRF, the original work used a simple MLP mapping position and direction to color, implicitly capturing view dependence. Subsequent works like and explored explicit separation of diffuse and specular components or used hierarchical encoding to better capture high-frequency directional variations. This configuration represents the generalization of those specific architectural choices into a training configuration category. Mildenhall, B., Srinivasan, P. P., Tancik, M., Barron, J. T., Ramamoorthi, R., & Ng, R. (2020). NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis. ECCV. Niemeyer, M., Barron, J. T., Mildenhall, B., Sajjadi, M. S., Geiger, A., & Radwan, N. (2020). RegNeRF: Regularizing Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis from Sparse Inputs. CVPR. Wang, P., Liu, Y., Liu, Y., Theobalt, C., Koltun, V., & Zhou, K. (2021). NeRF-X: Efficient Scene Representation with View-Dependent Appearance for Unconstrained Photogrammetry. ICCV.

name: See-NeRF
head: See-NeRF framework, Sensor-Physics Grounded Deblurring HDR NeRF
body: See-NeRF is a unified sensor-physics grounded NeRF framework for sharp High Dynamic Range (HDR) novel view synthesis from single-exposure blurry Low Dynamic Range (LDR) images and corresponding event data. It solves the problem of recovering sharp 3D radiance from degraded inputs by explicitly modeling the physical imaging process of both RGB and event sensors, rather than applying tone mapping directly to 3D points. Unlike sibling methods like REF2-NeRF or EvHDR-NeRF which ignore sensor-physics mismatches, See-NeRF bridges the gap between physical scene dynamics and sensor output using differentiable Camera Response Function (CRF) models for both RGB and event streams. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A single blurry LDR RGB image \mathcal{I}{LDR}, corresponding event data B, camera poses p(t), and exposure time \Delta t{exp}. Outputs: Sharp HDR novel view images and LDR images at arbitrary exposures. Data Structures: NeRF Network (F\theta): A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with parameters \theta. It takes positional encodings of 3D position \mathbf{o} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} as input. Input: \gammao(\mathbf{o}), \gammad(\mathbf{d}). Output: Raw HDR radiance \mathbf{e} and density \sigma. RGB CRF Model: Three separate MLPs (f{crf}), one for each color channel (R, G, B). Event CRF Model: Delay Coefficient MLP (f{ev}): Outputs scalar \epsiloni. Offset Estimator (h): Estimates temporal delay offset from input events. Positional Encoding (\gammaM): \gammaM(x) = \{\sin(2^m\pi x), \cos(2^m\pi x)\}{m=0}^{M} Numbered Steps: 1. Scene Representation: For a 3D point \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, compute raw HDR radiance \mathbf{e} and density \sigma using the NeRF network: (\mathbf{e}, \sigma) = F{\theta}(\gammao(\mathbf{o}), \gammad(\mathbf{d})) 2. Time Discretization: Discretely sample b+1 time points \{ti\}{i=0}^b within the exposure interval [t{start}, t{end}]. The parameter b is typically set to 4. 3. Volume Rendering (Latent HDR): For each time point ti, render the latent sharp HDR radiance E(x,y,p(ti)) at pixel (x,y) using standard volume rendering: E(x,y,p(t)) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1-\exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{e}i where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) is the accumulated transmittance, \deltai is the distance between adjacent sampled 3D points, and N is the number of samples per ray. 4. Raw HDR Pixel Calculation: Calculate the predicted raw HDR pixel value by summing the weighted radiance values at the sampled time points: \hat{\mathcal{I}}{HDR}(x,y) = \sum{i=0}^{b} wi Ei(x,y,p(ti)) where wi are weights calculated based on the time points \{ti\}. 5. RGB CRF Application: Convert the raw HDR pixel value to LDR using the learned RGB CRF models in the log domain. For each color channel c \in \{R, G, B\}: \hat{\mathcal{I}}{LDR}^c(x,y) = f{crf}^c(\ln(\hat{\mathcal{I}}{HDR}^c(x,y) \Delta t{exp})) where \Delta t{exp} = t{end} - t{start} is the exposure time. 6. Event CRF - Bayer Adaptation: Input the b+1 scene radiance values \{E(x,y,p(ti))\}{i=0}^b into an RGGB Bayer pattern to obtain event sensor pixel radiance values E{ev}(x,y,p(ti)). 7. Event CRF - Delay Coefficient: Calculate the delay coefficient \epsiloni for each time step using the event CRF MLP: \epsiloni = f{ev}(E{ev}(x,y,p(ti))) 8. Event CRF - Latency Synthesis: Synthesize event latency using a second-order low-pass filter. Initialize L^0{lp} = E{ev}(p(t0)). For i > 0: L^i{lp} = (1-\epsiloni)L^{i-1}{lp} + \epsiloni E{ev}(p(ti)) 9. Event CRF - Ideal Event Count: Calculate the estimated number of events \hat{B}'(ti, t{i+1}) between time steps ti and t{i+1} using the contrast threshold \Theta: \hat{B}'(ti, t{i+1}) = \text{floor}\left(\frac{\ln(L^{i+1}{lp}) - \ln(L^{i}{lp})}{\Theta}\right) 10. Event CRF - Delay Compensation: Compensate for temporal delay by estimating an offset h(B(ti, t{i+1})) from the input events and subtracting it to get the final estimated event count: \hat{B}(ti, t{i+1}) = \hat{B}'(ti, t{i+1}) - h(B(ti, t{i+1})) 11. Optimization: Jointly optimize the NeRF network parameters \theta and the CRF model parameters by minimizing the combined loss function: \mathcal{L} = \lambda \mathcal{L}{evs} + \mathcal{L}{ldr} where: \mathcal{L}{ldr} = \sum{(x,y)\in \mathcal{X}} ||\hat{\mathcal{I}}{LDR}(x,y) - \mathcal{I}{LDR}(x,y)||^22 \mathcal{L}{evs} = \sum{(x,y)\in \mathcal{X}} \sum{i=0}^{b-1} ||\hat{B}(ti, t{i+1}) - B(ti, t{i+1})||^22 \mathcal{X} denotes all pixels of the camera sensor. Parameters: b: Number of time intervals minus one. Value: 4. \lambda: Weight for event loss. Value: 0.005. \Theta: Contrast threshold in event generation. Definition: Minimum detectable brightness change lower bound. \Delta t{exp}: Exposure time (t{end} - t{start}). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sensor-Physics Mismatch: Traditional methods apply tone mapping directly to 3D points, ignoring that CRFs apply to pixel-level integrals. This leads to suboptimal HDR and deblurring results. Low-Light Delay: Event generation exhibits significant delay and uncertainty in low-light regions where brightness changes are below the threshold \Theta. Pose Estimation: Camera poses p(t) change during exposure in handheld scenarios. The method relies on event-guided COLMAP for pose estimation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art HDR and deblurring novel view synthesis results on synthetic and real datasets compared to EvHDR-NeRF and HDR-NeRF. Strengths: Physically consistent 3D representation; handles single-exposure blurry LDR images and events; explicitly models sensor physics for both RGB and event cameras. Limitations: Requires corresponding event data; relies on accurate pose estimation (event-guided COLMAP); joint optimization of multiple networks may be computationally intensive. When to use: When reconstructing sharp HDR scenes from single-exposure blurry images and event streams, particularly in extreme lighting conditions. When not to use: When only standard LDR images are available without events, or when real-time performance is critical and the overhead of joint CRF optimization is prohibitive. See-NeRF was proposed by researchers from iCVTEAM. It addresses the limitations of prior works like EvHDR-NeRF, which extended HDR-NeRF by applying tone mapping to 3D points without considering event generation characteristics. The method builds on the physical imaging principles of RGB and event sensors, leveraging spatial and temporal dynamic information in events to enhance sharp HDR 3D representation learning. Seeing through Light and Darkness: Sensor-Physics Grounded Deblurring HDR NeRF from Single-Exposure Images and Events, https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.15475v4, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: REF2-NeRF
head: Reflection and Refraction aware Neural Radiance Field
body: REF2-NeRF is a NeRF-based modeling method designed for scenes containing transparent objects, specifically glass cases, where it models refraction and reflection using elements dependent and independent of the viewer's perspective. It estimates surfaces where refraction occurs and separates direct (view-independent) and reflected (view-dependent) light components. Unlike methods that assume straight light rays or only handle reflections, REF2-NeRF handles both refraction and reflection in scenes with multiple transparent objects by using two independent MLPs: a glass network for refraction offsets and a decomposition NeRF for rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of n images \{Ik\} taken from different viewpoints, with predetermined camera poses (often acquired via a robotic arm). Output: A rendered image C(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r}, composed of view-independent and view-dependent components. Data Structures and Network Layout: The method uses four main MLPs: 1. Glass Network (\Theta{gl}): Input: Concatenation of positional encoding of position \Gamma(\mathbf{x}) and view direction \Gamma(\mathbf{d}). Output: Glass density \sigma{gl} \in \mathbb{R} and offset vector \Delta \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Architecture: Input layer [6 \times 256], Output layer [256, 128] (implied by diagram labels, though text specifies output values). 2. Decomposition NeRF (\Theta{nf}): Input: Concatenation of positional encoding of adjusted position \Gamma(\mathbf{x}') and view direction \Gamma(\mathbf{d}). Output: View-independent density \sigma{vi} \in \mathbb{R}, view-independent color \mathbf{c}{vi} \in \mathbb{R}^3, view-dependent density \sigma{vd} \in \mathbb{R}, and view-dependent feature vector \mathbf{f}{vd} \in \mathbb{R}^\theta. Architecture: Input layer [8 \times 256], Output layer [256, 128]. 3. Decoder MLP (\Theta{dc}): Input: Rendered feature vector \mathbf{F}{vd}. Output: Reflection color \mathbf{C}{vd}. 4. Gate MLP (\Theta{gt}): Input: Rendered feature vector \mathbf{F}{vd}. Output: Blending parameter \alpha. Parameters: Feature vector dimension \theta = 64. Regularization weight \epsilon = 10^{-5}. Sampling points: Coarse 128, Hierarchical Fine 64, Glass Density 32, View-Independent Density 32. Total fine model points: 192. Numbered Steps: 1. Sampling: For a ray \mathbf{r}, sample N points \mathbf{x}i at uniform intervals (coarse). Then, sample additional points hierarchically based on density (fine). Specifically, sample 32 points using glass density \sigma{gl} and 32 points using view-independent density \sigma{vi}. 2. Glass Network Forward Pass: For each sampled point \mathbf{x}i and view direction \mathbf{d}i, compute glass density \sigma{gl,i} and offset \Delta \mathbf{x}i using \Theta{gl}: F{\Theta{gl}}: \Gamma(\mathbf{x}i), \Gamma(\mathbf{d}i) \rightarrow \sigma{gl}(\mathbf{x}i), \Delta \mathbf{x}(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{d}i) 3. Refraction Weight Calculation: Calculate the weight wi for each sampling point i using glass density \sigma{gl,i} and distance \delta{gl,i} between adjacent points. Ti is the transmittance from previous points: wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigma{gl,i} \delta{gl,i})), \quad Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma{gl,j} \delta{gl,j}\right) 4. Position Adjustment: Adjust the position \mathbf{x}'i by cumulatively adding the weighted offset vectors along the ray: \mathbf{x}'i = \mathbf{x}i + wi \Delta \mathbf{x}i 5. View-Independent Rendering: Perform volume rendering on the adjusted positions \mathbf{x}' using view-independent density \sigma{vi} and color \mathbf{c}{vi} to get view-independent color \mathbf{C}{vi}. Note that T{vi,i} calculation uses \sigma{vi}: \mathbf{C}{vi}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} T{vi,i} (1 - \exp(-\sigma{vi,i} \delta{vi,i})) \mathbf{c}{vi,i} 6. View-Dependent Feature Rendering: Perform volume rendering on adjusted positions \mathbf{x}' and view directions \mathbf{d} using view-dependent density \sigma{vd} and feature vector \mathbf{f}{vd} to get feature vector \mathbf{F}{vd}: \mathbf{F}{vd}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigma{vd,i} \delta{vd,i})) \mathbf{f}{i} 7. View-Dependent Color and Blending: Decode the rendered feature vector \mathbf{F}{vd} into reflection color \mathbf{C}{vd} using decoder MLP \Theta{dc} and determine blending parameter \alpha using gate MLP \Theta{gt}: \mathbf{C}{vd}(\mathbf{r}) = F{\Theta{dc}}: \mathbf{F}{vd}(\mathbf{r}) \rightarrow \mathbf{C}{vd}(\mathbf{r}) \alpha(\mathbf{r}) = F{\Theta{gt}}: \mathbf{F}{vd}(\mathbf{r}) \rightarrow \alpha(\mathbf{r}) 8. Final Image Composition: The final pixel color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) is the sum of the view-independent color and the blended view-dependent color: \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \mathbf{C}{vi}(\mathbf{r}) + \alpha(\mathbf{r})\mathbf{C}{vd}(\mathbf{r}) Training and Loss: The method is trained by minimizing the total loss \mathcal{L}, which is the sum of the rendering loss \mathcal{L}{render} (L2 distance between rendered color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) and input image \bar{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r})) and a regularization loss \mathcal{L}{offset}: \mathcal{L}{render} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \|\bar{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r})\|^2 \mathcal{L}{offset} = \sum{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}} (\Delta \mathbf{x})^2 \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{render} + \epsilon \mathcal{L}{offset} where \mathcal{R} is a batch of sampled rays and \epsilon = 10^{-5}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import math class PositionalEncoding(nn.Module): def init(self, numfreqbands=6, includeinput=True): super().init() self.numfreqbands = numfreqbands self.includeinput = includeinput # Standard NeRF positional encoding frequencies self.frequencies = 2.0 torch.linspace(0, numfreqbands - 1, numfreqbands) def forward(self, x): # x: (..., 3) if self.includeinput: out = [x] else: out = [] for freq in self.frequencies: out.append(torch.sin(x freq)) out.append(torch.cos(x freq)) return torch.cat(out, dim=-1) class GlassNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self, inputdim=6256, hiddendim=256): super().init() # Simplified MLP structure based on source description # Input: Gamma(x), Gamma(d) -> Output: sigmagl, deltax self.fc1 = nn.Linear(inputdim, hiddendim) self.fcsigma = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1) self.fcoffset = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 3) self.relu = nn.ReLU() def forward(self, xenc, denc): x = torch.cat([xenc, denc], dim=-1) h = self.relu(self.fc1(x)) sigmagl = self.fcsigma(h) deltax = self.fcoffset(h) return sigmagl, deltax class DecompNeRF(nn.Module): def init(self, inputdim=8256, hiddendim=256, featuredim=64): super().init() # Input: Gamma(x'), Gamma(d) -> Output: sigmavi, cvi, sigmavd, fvd self.fc1 = nn.Linear(inputdim, hiddendim) self.fcsigmavi = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1) self.fccvi = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 3) self.fcsigmavd = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1) self.fcfvd = nn.Linear(hiddendim, featuredim) self.relu = nn.ReLU() def forward(self, xprimeenc, denc): x = torch.cat([xprimeenc, denc], dim=-1) h = self.relu(self.fc1(x)) sigmavi = self.fcsigmavi(h) cvi = self.fccvi(h) sigmavd = self.fcsigmavd(h) fvd = self.fcfvd(h) return sigmavi, cvi, sigmavd, fvd class DecoderMLP(nn.Module): def init(self, inputdim=64, hiddendim=128): super().init() self.fc1 = nn.Linear(inputdim, hiddendim) self.fcout = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 3) self.relu = nn.ReLU() def forward(self, fvd): h = self.relu(self.fc1(fvd)) cvd = self.fcout(h) return cvd class GateMLP(nn.Module): def init(self, inputdim=64, hiddendim=128): super().init() self.fc1 = nn.Linear(inputdim, hiddendim) self.fcout = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1) self.relu = nn.ReLU() self.sigmoid = nn.Sigmoid() def forward(self, fvd): h = self.relu(self.fc1(fvd)) alpha = self.sigmoid(self.fcout(h)) return alpha def renderref2nerf(rayorigins, raydirections, glassnet, decompnet, decodernet, gatenet, numcoarse=128, numfine=192, epsilon=1e-5): """ Renders a single ray using the REF2-NeRF method. """ # 1. Sampling # Coarse sampling: 128 points at uniform intervals tcoarse = torch.linspace(0, 1, numcoarse).to(rayorigins.device) xcoarse = rayorigins.unsqueeze(1) + raydirections.unsqueeze(1) tcoarse.unsqueeze(0) # Fine sampling: 192 points total (64 hierarchical + 32 glass + 32 view-ind) # Note: Source says "Total points for fine model: 192". # Implementation detail: Hierarchical sampling usually replaces or adds to coarse. # We assume standard NeRF coarse-to-fine where fine samples are added. # For simplicity in this self-contained code, we generate fine samples based on density. # In practice, this requires forward pass of coarse model to get densities. # Here we simulate the fine sampling positions xfine. tfine = torch.linspace(0, 1, numfine).to(rayorigins.device) xfine = rayorigins.unsqueeze(1) + raydirections.unsqueeze(1) tfine.unsqueeze(0) # 2. Glass Network Forward Pass # Encode positions and directions posenc = PositionalEncoding(numfreqbands=6, includeinput=True) xfineenc = posenc(xfine) denc = posenc(raydirections) sigmagl, deltax = glassnet(xfineenc, denc) # 3. Refraction Weight Calculation # Calculate distances between adjacent points deltas = torch.diff(xfine, dim=1) deltalengths = torch.norm(deltas, dim=2, keepdim=True) # Pad the last delta to match size deltalengths = torch.cat([deltalengths, deltalengths[:, -1:,:]], dim=1) # Transmittance Ti # Ti = exp(-sum{j=1}^{i-1} sigmagl,j deltagl,j) # sigmagl is (N, 1), deltalengths is (N, 1, 1) -> need to handle dimensions # sigmagl: (batch, N, 1) # deltalengths: (batch, N, 1) # Cumulative sum of sigma delta # sigmagl deltalengths -> (batch, N, 1) sigmadelta = sigmagl deltalengths # Cumulative sum from start to i-1 # Using cumsum, then shifting cumsigmadelta = torch.cumsum(sigmadelta, dim=1) # Ti corresponds to sum up to i-1. For i=0, sum is 0. # Shift cumsum to right by 1, fill with 0 cumsigmadeltashifted = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(cumsigmadelta[:,:1,:]), cumsigmadelta[:,:-1,:]], dim=1) T = torch.exp(-cumsigmadeltashifted) # Weights wi w = T (1 - torch.exp(-sigmagl deltalengths)) # 4. Position Adjustment # x'i = xi + wi deltaxi # w: (batch, N, 1), deltax: (batch, N, 3) xprime = xfine + w deltax # 5. View-Independent Rendering xprimeenc = posenc(xprime) sigmavi, cvi, sigmavd, fvd = decompnet(xprimeenc, denc) # View-independent volume rendering # Cvi(r) = sum Tvi,i (1 - exp(-sigmavi,i deltavi,i)) cvi,i # Tvi,i uses sigmavi sigmadeltavi = sigmavi deltalengths cumsigmadeltavi = torch.cumsum(sigmadeltavi, dim=1) cumsigmadeltavishifted = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(cumsigmadeltavi[:,:1,:]), cumsigmadeltavi[:,:-1,:]], dim=1) Tvi = torch.exp(-cumsigmadeltavishifted) alphavi = 1 - torch.exp(-sigmadeltavi) Cvi = torch.sum(Tvi alphavi cvi, dim=1) # 6. View-Dependent Feature Rendering # Fvd(r) = sum Ti (1 - exp(-sigmavd,i deltavd,i)) fi # Note: Source uses Ti (from glass density) for view-dependent feature rendering? # Source Eq 8: Fvd(r) = sum Ti (1 - exp(-sigmavd,i deltavd,i)) fi # Yes, it uses Ti from glass density. sigmadeltavd = sigmavd deltalengths alphavd = 1 - torch.exp(-sigmadeltavd) Fvd = torch.sum(T alphavd fvd, dim=1) # 7. View-Dependent Color and Blending Cvd = decodernet(Fvd) alphablend = gatenet(Fvd) # 8. Final Image Composition C = Cvi + alphablend Cvd return C Time Complexity: Training requires 200,000 iterations, taking approximately 10 hours per scene on an Nvidia RTX 4080 GPU. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method uses a coarse-to-fine sampling strategy with a total of 192 points for the fine model (128 coarse + 64 hierarchical + 32 glass density + 32 view-independent density). Strengths: Handles both refraction and reflection in scenes with multiple transparent objects (e.g., glass cases). Separates view-independent and view-dependent components effectively. Limitations: Requires predetermined camera poses, which can be difficult to acquire in scenes with glass objects. When to use: Scenes with glass objects where both refraction and reflection need to be modeled accurately. When not: Scenes without transparent objects or where camera poses are unknown. REF2-NeRF was proposed in 2024 by authors publishing in the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS). It addresses the challenge of modeling scenes with multiple glass objects, such as objects in a glass showcase, where existing methods struggle with multiple reflection and refraction effects. It builds on LB-NeRF, which simplifies refraction as an offset, but introduces view-independent density and view-dependent offset fields to estimate refraction surfaces and offsets simultaneously. It also differs from MS-NeRF, which uses multiple explicit spaces for mirrors, by using a single view-dependent feature field to handle reciprocal reflections from multiple glass plates. name: Lighting and Intrinsic Decomposition
head: Inverse Rendering, Intrinsic Decomposition, Relightable NeRF
body: Lighting and Intrinsic Decomposition refers to methods that separate a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) into view-independent intrinsic properties (such as albedo, normals, and density) and view-dependent lighting components, enabling realistic relighting and scene understanding [16200-urbanir.md]. Unlike standard NeRFs that bake lighting into the observed color, these methods explicitly model the illumination environment (e.g., sun, ambient, sky) or decompose color into lighting and reflectance bases to solve the ill-posed inverse rendering problem [16200-urbanir.md, 18127-unsupervised-decomposition-and-nerf.md]. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of decomposing the radiance field output into distinct semantic or physical components rather than a single RGB color value. 1. Intrinsic Representation: The scene is represented by attributes \mathbf{A} (e.g., albedo \mathbf{a}, normal \mathbf{n}, semantics \mathbf{s}, density \sigma) or a decomposition of color into a lighting component v and a reciprocal color basis r [16200-urbanir.md, 18127-unsupervised-decomposition-and-nerf.md]. 2. Volume Rendering of Intrinsics: These attributes are accumulated along rays using standard alpha-composition weights wi [16200-urbanir.md, 18127-unsupervised-decomposition-and-nerf.md]: wi = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) The rendered intrinsic value \mathbf{I}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} is: \mathbf{I}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi \mathbf{A}i 3. Lighting Model Integration: The final color is computed by combining rendered intrinsics with a lighting model \mathcal{L} [16200-urbanir.md]. For example, UrbanIR uses a sun, ambient, and sky model [16200-urbanir.md], while Unsupervised Decomposition uses a neural enhancement function \phi to modify the lighting component v [18127-unsupervised-decomposition-and-nerf.md]. 4. Ill-posed Constraint: Since decomposition is ill-posed, these methods rely on priors (e.g., gray-world, smoothness, multi-view consistency) to constrain the optimization [16200-urbanir.md, 18127-unsupervised-decomposition-and-nerf.md]. UrbanIR is a method for the inverse rendering of large-scale, unbounded urban scenes from a single monocular video under single illumination [16200-urbanir.md]. It infers shape, albedo, surface normals, semantics, and sun/sky illumination to enable realistic relighting and night simulation [16200-urbanir.md]. Unlike standard NeRFs that bake lighting into color, or methods requiring LiDAR/multiple cameras (e.g., FEGR, LightSim) or multiple light sources (e.g., NeRF-OSR), UrbanIR uses only RGB video and known camera poses [16200-urbanir.md]. It distinguishes itself by using a spatial hash-based voxel representation (Instant-NGP) for scalability and a visibility estimation technique that avoids per-scene optimized MLP heads for shadows, allowing the sun position to change during relighting [16200-urbanir.md]. This method decomposes the view-dependent color in a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) into a view-dependent lighting component v and a view-independent reciprocal color basis r, then enhances v using a neural network to produce an enhanced image Ie without ground truth supervision [18127-unsupervised-decomposition-and-nerf.md]. It sets itself apart from 2D Retinex-based methods by leveraging 3D geometry and multi-view consistency to constrain the ill-posed decomposition, allowing for unsupervised training [18127-unsupervised-decomposition-and-nerf.md]. Inverse rendering in NeRFs emerged as a way to move beyond static appearance synthesis to scene understanding and relighting. UrbanIR [16200-urbanir.md] adapted these concepts to large-scale urban environments using hash-based representations for efficiency. Unsupervised Decomposition [18127-unsupervised-decomposition-and-nerf.md] addressed low-light enhancement by decomposing color into lighting and reflectance components, leveraging 3D consistency to avoid the need for paired low/high-light training data. UrbanIR and Unsupervised Decomposition notes provided in the prompt.

name: UrbanIR
head: Urban Scene Inverse Rendering
body: UrbanIR is a method for inverse rendering of large-scale urban scenes from a single monocular video under single illumination, inferring shape, albedo, visibility, and sun/sky illumination to enable relighting and night simulation. It differs from standard NeRFs by learning intrinsic attributes (albedo, normal) independent of lighting, solving the problem that standard NeRFs bake shading and shadows into observed color, making them non-relightable. Unlike methods requiring multiple lighting sources (e.g., NeRF-OSR) or LiDAR/multi-camera setups (e.g., FEGR, LightSim), UrbanIR uses only single illumination RGB video. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A multi-frame video of a scene under single illumination with known camera motion. Defined as \{Ii, Ei, Ki\}, where Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} is the RGB image, Ei \in SE(3) is the camera pose, and Ki is the camera intrinsic matrix. Output: A neural scene model encoding albedo, normal, semantics, and density, along with inferred lighting parameters (sun, ambient, sky), enabling rendering of novel views under novel lighting conditions. Data Structures: The scene representation is built on Instant-NGP, a spatial hash-based voxel NeRF representation. Dense Feature Hash Table: Represents the scene geometry and attributes. It maps 3D coordinates to dense feature vectors. MLP Headers: Individual Multi-Layer Perceptrons are used to decode each attribute (albedo \mathbf{a}, normal \mathbf{n}, semantics \mathbf{s}, density \sigma) given a queried feature at point \mathbf{x}. Lighting Model \mathcal{L}: Encodes outdoor illumination as \mathcal{L} = \{ (\mathbf{L}{\text{sun}}, \psi{\text{sun}}, \phi{\text{sun}}), \mathbf{L}{\text{amb}}, \mathbf{L}{\text{sky}} \}. Sun: 5-DoF representation encoding sun color \mathbf{L}{\text{sun}} and azimuth/zenith angles \psi{\text{sun}}, \phi{\text{sun}}. Ambient: 3-DoF Lambert model \mathbf{L}{\text{amb}}. Sky: Sky dome model inferring sky texture from viewing direction \mathbf{L}{\text{sky}}. Numbered Steps: 1. Scene Query: For a query point \mathbf{x} and direction \mathbf{d}, retrieve the dense feature vector from the hash table. Pass this feature through individual MLP headers to predict intrinsic attributes \mathbf{F}\theta(\mathbf{x}) = (\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{s}, \sigma). 2. Volume Rendering of Intrinsics: Sample N points along a ray \mathbf{r}. Compute alpha-composition weights wi and accumulate intrinsic values: wi = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) where \deltai = ti - t{i-1}. The rendered intrinsic values are: \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi \mathbf{a}i, \quad \mathbf{N}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi \mathbf{n}i, \quad \mathbf{S}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi \mathbf{s}i 3. Visibility Estimation: To model shadows without per-scene optimized MLP heads (which are impractical for changing sun positions), compute an estimate \hat{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{r}) of the 3D point being shaded by volume rendering depth (substituting \hat{t} = \sum wi ti). Compute visibility V(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \text{sun}) by calculating the transmittance along the ray segment between \hat{\mathbf{x}} and the light source using volume rendering. 4. Final Color Computation: Combine rendered intrinsics with the lighting model \mathcal{L} and shadow visibility V using a shading function \texttt{Shade}: \mathbf{C} = \texttt{Shade}(\texttt{Intrinsic}(\mathbf{F}\theta, \mathbf{r}), \texttt{Shadow}(\mathbf{F}\theta, \mathbf{r}, \mathcal{L}), \mathcal{L}) 5. Joint Optimization: Optimize scene parameters \theta and lighting parameters \mathcal{L} jointly using a loss function \mathcal{L}{\text{render}} and additional constraints \lambda1 \mathcal{L}1 + \dots. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def urbanirrender(rayorigin, raydirection, scenehashtable, lightingparams, numsamples): """ Renders a single ray using UrbanIR's inverse rendering pipeline. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, origin of the camera ray. raydirection: 3D vector, direction of the camera ray. scenehashtable: Data structure mapping 3D coords to feature vectors. lightingparams: Dict containing suncolor, sunangles, ambientcolor, skymodel. numsamples: Integer, number of points to sample along the ray. Returns: finalcolor: 3D vector, RGB color. albedomap: 3D vector, rendered albedo. normalmap: 3D vector, rendered normal. depth: Float, rendered depth. """ # 1. Sample points along the ray tmin, tmax = getraybounds(rayorigin, raydirection) tvals = linspace(tmin, tmax, numsamples) points = rayorigin + outerproduct(tvals, raydirection) # 2. Query scene attributes for each point # Retrieve features from hash table and decode via MLP headers # Returns: albedos (N,3), normals (N,3), semantics (N,C), densities (N,1) features = queryhashtable(scenehashtable, points) albedos, normals, semantics, densities = decodeattributes(features) # 3. Compute alpha-composition weights # deltai = ti - t{i-1} deltas = diff(tvals) # Transmittance Ti = exp(-sum{j=1}^{i-1} sigmaj deltaj) # Weights wi = Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai deltai)) # Note: Standard NeRF alpha composition assumes sigma is density. # UrbanIR uses Instant-NGP density. sigma = densities transmittance = exp(-cumsum(sigma deltas[:-1])) weights = transmittance (1 - exp(-sigma deltas)) # 4. Volume render intrinsics albedomap = sum(weights albedos, axis=0) normalmap = sum(weights normals, axis=0) semanticmap = sum(weights semantics, axis=0) # 5. Estimate depth for shadow visibility # that = sum(wi ti) depth = sum(weights tvals) shadedpoint = rayorigin + raydirection depth # 6. Compute shadow visibility # Trace ray from shadedpoint to sun sundirection = getsundirection(lightingparams) # Compute transmittance along shadow ray # This approximates visibility V(shadedpoint, sun) shadowraypoints = sampleshadowray(shadedpoint, sundirection) shadowfeatures = queryhashtable(scenehashtable, shadowraypoints) shadowsigma = decodedensity(shadowfeatures) shadowtransmittance = computetransmittance(shadowsigma) visibility = shadowtransmittance # 7. Compute final color using shading model # C = Shade(Intrinsic, Shadow, Lighting) finalcolor = shademodel(albedomap, normalmap, visibility, lightingparams) return finalcolor, albedomap, normalmap, depth Parameters: Hash Table Resolution: Not given in the sources. Number of Samples: Not given in the sources. Loss Weights: \lambda1 and others are used in joint optimization but specific values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visibility Estimation: Modeling visibility with a per-scene optimized MLP head is impractical because the sun position changes during relighting, but training data only has one sun position. UrbanIR avoids this by estimating visibility via transmittance from the shaded point to the light source. Large-Scale Scenes: Standard NeRFs are not suitable for large-scale urban scenes due to memory and consistency issues. Instant-NGP is used to provide compactness and consistency. Time and Memory Complexity: Instant-NGP offers low memory consumption and high efficiency in training and rendering compared to standard MLP-based NeRFs. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Designed for expansive outdoor scenes. Strengths: Works with single monocular video; does not require LiDAR or multiple cameras; enables relighting and night simulation. Limitations: Assumes single illumination during training; relies on monocular cues (shadows, normals) which can be ambiguous. UrbanIR was introduced by Chih-Hao Lin, Bohan Liu, Yi-Ting Chen, Kuan-Sheng Chen, David Forsyth, Jia-Bin Huang, Anand Bhattad, and Shenlong Wang from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and University of Maryland, College Park. The paper "UrbanIR: Large-Scale Urban Scene Inverse Rendering from a Single Video" was published in 3DV 2025 (arXiv:2306.09349v4, 14 Jan 2025). It addresses the limitation of existing relightable NeRF methods that focus on small bounded indoor environments or require multiple lighting sources/LiDAR. UrbanIR: Large-Scale Urban Scene Inverse Rendering from a Single Video, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv66043.2025.00052, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Unsupervised Decomposition and Enhancement in NeRF
head: LLNeRF, Lighting up NeRF
body: This method decomposes the view-dependent color of a neural radiance field into a view-dependent lighting component v and a view-independent reciprocal color basis r, then enhances v using a neural network to produce an enhanced image without ground truth supervision. It sets itself apart from 2D Retinex-based methods by leveraging 3D geometry and multi-view consistency to constrain the ill-posed decomposition, avoiding the need for paired low-light/high-light training data. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of uncalibrated, low-light RGB images (or RAW images) of a scene. Outputs: A trained radiance field model capable of rendering novel views, and an enhanced version of those views Ie. Data Structures: The model consists of three main neural network components: 1. Radiance Field Model: Density MLP (F{density}): Input: spatial coordinate \tau. Output: scalar density \sigma. Direction MLP: Input: view direction d. Output: feature vector. Feature MLP: Concatenates density and direction features. Output: view-dependent color c (3 channels). Note: The standard NeRF architecture is modified to output v and r separately instead of c directly. 2. Decomposition Networks: F1 (Lighting MLP): Input: spatial coordinate \tau, view direction d. Output: scalar lighting component v. F2 (Color Basis MLP): Input: spatial coordinate \tau. Output: 3-channel reciprocal color basis r. 3. Enhancement Model \phi: Feature MLP 1: Input: v. Output: 8x256 feature vector. Feature MLP 2: Input: Feature from MLP 1. Output: 1x256 feature vector. Coeff MLP: Input: Feature from MLP 2. Output: Coefficients \alpha (scalar) and \gamma (3D vector). Color MLP: Input: Feature from MLP 2. Output: 3-channel color correction (used in some variants, but primary enhancement uses \alpha, \gamma). Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: For each pixel in a training image, cast a ray \mathbf{r} through the scene. Sample N points along the ray at spatial coordinates \taui and view directions di. 2. Decomposition: For each sample i, compute the lighting component vi and color basis ri: vi = F1(\taui, di; \Theta{F1}) ri = F2(\taui; \Theta{F2}) The unenhanced color is ci = vi \circ ri, where \circ is pixel-wise multiplication. 3. Enhancement: Apply the enhancement function \phi to vi to get \hat{v}i: \hat{v}i = \phi(vi) = \left( \frac{vi}{\gamma0} \right)^{\alpha} \circ \gamma \alpha is a scalar output by the Coeff MLP, adjusting global lighting gain. \gamma is a 3D vector output by the Coeff MLP, correcting color distortion. \gamma0 is a fixed initialization value for the non-linear transform. The enhanced color sample is \hat{c}i = \hat{v}i \circ ri. 4. Volume Rendering: Render the enhanced image Ie and the standard image I using alpha-composition. Compute weights wi = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)). Enhanced pixel color: \hat{c}r = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi \hat{c}i = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi \phi(vi) \circ ri. Standard pixel color: cr = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi ci. 5. Loss Computation: Calculate the total loss \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}c + \mathcal{L}s + \mathcal{L}d. Gray-world Prior Loss (\mathcal{L}c): Constrains the enhanced color to have natural statistics. \mathcal{L}c = \mathbb{E}[(\hat{c}r - e)^2] + \lambda1 \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\text{var}c(\hat{c}r)}{\beta1 + \text{var}c(rr)}\right] + \lambda2 \|\gamma\|^2 e = 0.55: Target brightness for the gray-world prior. \text{var}c(\cdot): Channel-wise variance. \beta1, \lambda1, \lambda2: Hyper-parameters. The term \frac{\text{var}c(\hat{c}r)}{\beta1 + \text{var}c(rr)} relaxes the gray-world constraint for highly saturated colors (high variance in rr). Smoothness Loss (\mathcal{L}s): Constrains the gradients of the enhancement coefficients with respect to the integrated lighting component to preserve local structure. \mathcal{L}s = \mathcal{L}{s\alpha} + \mathcal{L}{s\gamma} \mathcal{L}{s\alpha} = \frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{(\alphar - \alpha{rh})^2}{(vr - v{rh})^2 + \epsilon1} + \frac{(\alphar - \alpha{rv})^2}{(vr - v{rv})^2 + \epsilon1} \right] \alphar, vr: Integrated \alpha and v for the current ray. \alpha{rh}, v{rh}: Integrated values for the horizontally neighboring ray. \alpha{rv}, v{rv}: Integrated values for the vertically neighboring ray. \epsilon1: Small constant to prevent division by zero. \mathcal{L}{s\gamma} is computed similarly for \gamma. Data Loss (\mathcal{L}d): Supervises the radiance field geometry using the observed RAW pixel values \tilde{c}r. \mathcal{L}d = \mathbb{E}[\eta(\tilde{c}r) - \eta(cr)] \eta(y) = \log(y + \epsilon2): Tone mapping function to amplify errors in dark regions. \epsilon2: Small constant. 6. Optimization: Update parameters \Theta{F1}, \Theta{F2}, \Theta{\phi} (for \mathcal{L}c, \mathcal{L}s) and \Theta{density} (for \mathcal{L}d) via gradient descent. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class EnhancementModel(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # Feature MLP 1: 1 -> 256 -> 256 (8x256 output in paper implies 8 layers or features, # but standard implementation uses sequential layers. # Based on "Feature MLP 1 has 8x256 channels", this likely refers to depth/width. # We implement a standard MLP structure as described in Fig 3c. self.featuremlp1 = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(1, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256) # Output 256) self.featuremlp2 = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU() # Output 256) self.coeffmlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(256, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 4) # Output: alpha (1), gamma (3)) self.colormlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(256, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 3) # Output: 3 channels) def forward(self, v): # v shape: (batch, 1) feat1 = self.featuremlp1(v) feat2 = self.featuremlp2(feat1) coeffs = self.coeffmlp(feat2) alpha = coeffs[:, 0:1] # (batch, 1) gamma = coeffs[:, 1:4] # (batch, 3) colorcorr = self.colormlp(feat2) return alpha, gamma, colorcorr def enhancev(v, alpha, gamma, gamma0=1.0): """ Apply dynamic gamma correction. v: (batch, 1) alpha: (batch, 1) gamma: (batch, 3) """ # vhat = (v / gamma0) ^ alpha gamma # Note: Element-wise power and multiplication. # gamma is a 3D vector, v is scalar per channel? # In the paper, v is 1-channel (intensity). gamma is 3-channel. # The operation implies broadcasting or channel expansion. # Assuming v is expanded to 3 channels for multiplication with gamma. vexp = v.repeat(1, 3) # (batch, 3) vhat = (vexp / gamma0) alpha.repeat(1, 3) gamma return vhat def renderray(samples, densitymlp, f1mlp, f2mlp, enhancementmodel, gamma0): """ samples: (N, 3) spatial coords, (N, 3) view dirs Returns: enhancedcolor, standardcolor, alphavals, gammavals, vvals """ # 1. Decomposition v = f1mlp(samples.spatial, samples.viewdir) # (N, 1) r = f2mlp(samples.spatial) # (N, 3) # 2. Enhancement alpha, gamma, = enhancementmodel(v) vhat = enhancev(v, alpha, gamma, gamma0) c = v r # (N, 3) chat = vhat r # (N, 3) # 3. Volume Rendering (Standard Alpha Compositing) # Assuming densitymlp outputs sigma sigma = densitymlp(samples.spatial) delta = samples.distances # (N-1,) or similar alphaweights = torch.exp(-torch.cumsum(sigma delta, dim=0)) (1 - torch.exp(-sigma delta)) standardcolor = torch.sum(alphaweights.unsqueeze(-1) c, dim=0) enhancedcolor = torch.sum(alphaweights.unsqueeze(-1) chat, dim=0) return enhancedcolor, standardcolor, alpha, gamma, v def computelosses(enhancedcolor, standardcolor, observedraw, alpha, gamma, v, neighbors): """ neighbors: dict containing alphah, alphav, vh, vv for current ray """ # Data Loss epsilon2 = 1e-6 eta = lambda y: torch.log(y + epsilon2) lossd = torch.mean(eta(observedraw) - eta(standardcolor)) # Gray-world Prior Loss e = 0.55 beta1 = 1e-3 lambda1 = 1.0 lambda2 = 1e-4 varcenh = torch.var(enhancedcolor, dim=0, unbiased=False) # Channel-wise var varcr = torch.var(standardcolor / (enhancedcolor / vhat + 1e-6), dim=0, unbiased=False) # Approx var of r # Note: rr is the integrated r. rr = cr / vr (if vr != 0). # In implementation, we might track integrated r directly or approximate. # Using the formula from paper: varc(rr). lossc = torch.mean((enhancedcolor - e)2) + \ lambda1 torch.mean(varcenh / (beta1 + varcr)) + \ lambda2 torch.mean(gamma2) # Smoothness Loss epsilon1 = 1e-6 alphah = neighbors['alphah'] alphav = neighbors['alphav'] vh = neighbors['vh'] vv = neighbors['vv'] losssa = 0.5 ( (alpha - alphah)2 / ((v - vh)2 + epsilon1) + (alpha - alphav)2 / ((v - vv)2 + epsilon1)) # Similar for gamma (Lsg) gammah = neighbors['gammah'] gammav = neighbors['gammav'] losssg = 0.5 ( (gamma - gammah)2 / ((v - vh)2 + epsilon1) + (gamma - gammav)2 / ((v - vv)2 + epsilon1)) losss = torch.mean(losssa) + torch.mean(losssg) return lossd, lossc, losss Parameters: \alpha: Scalar output by \phi, global lighting gain. \gamma: 3D vector output by \phi, color distortion correction. \gamma0: Fixed initialization value for the non-linear transform. e: Hyper-parameter for gray-world prior, set to 0.55. \lambda1, \lambda2, \beta1: Hyper-parameters for \mathcal{L}c. \epsilon1: Small constant in \mathcal{L}s denominator. \epsilon2: Small constant in tone mapping \eta. Pitfalls: RAW Image Noise Bias: In RAW images, non-linear ISP processes change the noise distribution. If not accounted for, the predicted color cr converges to a biased value \bar{c} + b instead of the true color \bar{c}, leading to color distortions. The method assumes zero-mean noise in RAW images, but ISP non-linearity violates this, necessitating the gray-world prior and smoothness constraints. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples per ray and the depth of the MLPs. The enhancement network adds a small overhead to the standard NeRF rendering step. Memory Complexity: Requires storing parameters for F1, F2, and \phi. No additional large data structures. Strengths: Unsupervised; works with low-light images without paired ground truth; leverages 3D geometry for robust decomposition; handles color distortion via \gamma. Limitations: Sensitive to noise in RAW images; requires careful tuning of hyper-parameters (\lambda1, \lambda2, e); decomposition is still ill-posed and relies on priors. Origin: Proposed in "Lighting up NeRF via Unsupervised Decomposition and Enhancement" (ICCV 2023). History: Builds on the NeRF framework [22] and RawNeRF [21] for RAW image processing. It addresses the limitations of 2D Retinex methods [28, 9, 31, 38] which require ground truth and lack 3D consistency. Usage: Used for low-light novel view synthesis and enhancement in indoor and outdoor scenes. Lighting up NeRF via Unsupervised Decomposition and Enhancement, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv51070.2023.01161, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Generative and GAN-Based Methods
head: Generative Radiance Fields, 3D GANs, GAN-based NeRF
body: Generative and GAN-Based Methods synthesize novel 3D objects or scenes by optimizing a radiance field to match the distribution of a pretrained 2D Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) or by directly training a generative radiance field with adversarial losses. Unlike standard NeRF which reconstructs a specific static scene from images, these methods generate new instances by sampling latent codes, enabling data augmentation and novel view synthesis of unseen objects. They differ from their siblings by incorporating adversarial training objectives or by lifting 2D GAN priors into 3D representations, rather than relying solely on photometric reconstruction losses. The core mechanism involves a generator network g\theta that maps a latent code z and camera pose \xi to a radiance field representation, which is then rendered into 2D images. The training process typically involves an adversarial loop where a discriminator distinguishes between real and generated images, guiding the generator to produce photorealistic outputs. Latent Space Conditioning: The radiance field is conditioned on a latent code z sampled from a prior distribution (e.g., Gaussian \mathcal{N}(0, I)). In methods lifting 2D GANs, the latent space is often disentangled into pose and shape components. Adversarial Loss: A discriminator D is trained to classify rendered images as real or fake. The generator minimizes the adversarial loss \mathcal{L}{adv}, often combined with photometric losses (e.g., L1) to ensure consistency with ground truth or template data. Rendering: Standard volume rendering is used to synthesize images from the radiance field: C(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigma(r(t)) c(r(t), d) dt where \sigma is density and c is color. Generative Occupancy Fields (GOF) is a 3D-aware image synthesis method that combines radiance fields with occupancy representations to learn compact object surfaces without impeding training convergence. It solves the problem of diffused surfaces in prior generative radiance fields (like pi-GAN) and the sparse gradient convergence issues in direct occupancy networks by transitioning from cumulative volume rendering to surface-point rendering. Unlike its siblings that predict volume densities, GOF predicts alpha values interpreted as occupancy, enabling surface-aware synthesis via root-finding. See Generative Occupancy Fields (GOF) for implementation details. This method distills 3D structural knowledge from a pretrained 2D Generative Adversarial Network (StyleGAN2) into a shared conditional Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) to generate novel 3D objects with arbitrary poses for data augmentation. It differs from naive isolated NeRF reconstruction by jointly optimizing a shared NeRF and latent codes for all objects simultaneously (Generative Latent Optimization), thereby learning shared category priors and mitigating noise from imperfect GAN interpretation. See Lifting 2D GAN to 3D Radiance Field for implementation details. An inverted 2D-to-3D generation framework that synthesizes 3D training data by lifting a pretrained 2D GAN to a 3D generative radiance field, achieving high-resolution synthesis and accurate 3D annotations. Step 1: Use a well-disentangled 2D GAN (StyleGAN2) to generate multi-view images with corresponding pseudo pose annotations. Step 2: Lift the generated multi-view images to a 3D representation using NeRF reconstruction. Step 3: Distill from the pretrained 2D GAN to achieve high-quality synthesis comparable to SOTA 2D generative models. Step 4: Decouple 3D generation from generative image synthesis to generate images tightly aligned with sampling labels. Step 5: Synthesize images in any resolution by accumulating single-ray evaluation, avoiding 2D upsamplers. Latent code z: Sampled from a Gaussian distribution Z ~ N(0, I) with dimension R^512. Unlike previous 3D GANs that rely on a 2D upsampler and suffer from trade-offs between high-resolution synthesis and 3D consistency, Lift3D inverts the pipeline to 2D-to-3D, allowing arbitrary rendering resolution and object pose sampling. The field emerged from the need to generate diverse 3D data for tasks like autonomous driving and object detection, where labeled 3D data is scarce. Early 3D GANs suffered from resolution limits and 3D inconsistency. Lift3D introduced the "inverted" pipeline of lifting 2D GANs to 3D, while GOF addressed surface ambiguity in generative radiance fields by using occupancy-based rendering. These methods are primarily used for data augmentation in 3D perception tasks. name: Generative Occupancy Fields (GOF)
body: Generative Occupancy Fields (GOF) is a 3D-aware image synthesis method that combines generative radiance fields with occupancy representations to learn compact object surfaces without impeding training convergence. It solves the problem of diffused surfaces in methods like GRAFs and the sparse gradient convergence issues in direct occupancy networks by transitioning from cumulative volume rendering to surface-point rendering. Unlike its sibling Lifting 2D GAN to 3D Radiance Field which may predict diffused surfaces, GOF concentrates rendering weights closely around object surfaces, resulting in compact and smooth geometry. GOF predicts alpha values (interpreted as occupancy) instead of volume densities to resolve shape-color ambiguity and enable surface-aware image synthesis. The method locates the surface via root-finding on these alpha values and gradually shrinks the sampling region during training to enforce compactness. Inputs: Latent code z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), camera pose \xi (origin o, direction d). Outputs: Rendered image color C(r) for rays r(t) = o + td. Generator g\theta: A neural network (e.g., FiLMed-SIREN backbone) that takes position x and latent code z as input and outputs alpha value \alpha\theta(x, z) \in [0, 1] and color c\theta(x, d, z) \in \mathbb{R}^3. Discriminator D{\thetaD}: A neural network that classifies images as real or fake. N: Number of rendering samples per ray. Typical value: 12. M: Number of root-finding bins. Typical value: 12. ms: Number of secant iterations for surface refinement. Typical value: 3. \tau: Threshold for root-finding. Typical value: 0.5. \Delta{init}: Initial sampling interval half-width. Set to (tf - tn)/2. \Delta{min}: Minimal sampling interval half-width. Not given in the sources. \gamma: Decay rate for shrinking interval. Not given in the sources. \lambda{normal}: Weight for normal regularization. Not given in the sources. \lambda{opacity}: Weight for opacity regularization. Not given in the sources. 1. Surface Location via Root-Finding: Sample M evenly-spaced points xk partitioning the volume [tn, tf] along the ray. Query the generator for alpha values \alpha\theta(xk, z) for all k=1 \dots M. Find the bin kS where the alpha value crosses the threshold \tau: kS = \arg\mink (\alpha\theta(xk, z) < \tau \le \alpha\theta(x{k+1}, z)) Apply the secant method iteratively ms times within the bin [x{kS}, x{kS+1}] to find the precise surface point xs and its distance ts. Note: The M points are used only for root-finding and do not require gradient computation. 2. Shrinking Sampling Region: Initialize sampling interval \Delta{init} = (tf - tn)/2. At training step n, compute the current interval half-width: \Deltan = \max(\Delta{init} \exp(-\gamma n), \Delta{min}) Sample N points uniformly in the region [ts - \Deltan, ts + \Deltan] using: ti \sim U\left[ts - \Deltan + \frac{2i-2}{N}\Deltan, ts - \Deltan + \frac{2i}{N}\Deltan\right] for i=1 \dots N. If the region exceeds [tn, tf], shift it back to fit within bounds. 3. Rendering: Compute the integrated color \tilde{C}(r, z) using alpha composition: \tilde{C}(r, z) = \sum{i=1}^{N} \alpha\theta(xi, z) \left( \prod{j<i} (1 - \alpha\theta(xj, z)) \right) c\theta(xi, d, z) Here, \alpha\theta(xi, z) is the predicted alpha (occupancy) and c\theta(xi, d, z) is the predicted color. 4. Inference: Fetch truncated latent code \hat{z}. Locate surface xs using steps 1-2 with \Delta{min}. Render using either: Cumulative rendering with N points in [ts - \Delta{min}, ts + \Delta{min}]. Single-point surface rendering with N=1 at xs for speed. Unverified code. """ fa = f(a) fb = f(b) for in range(iterations): if abs(fb - fa) < 1e-8: break xnew = b - fb (b - a) / (fb - fa) a, b = xnew, b # Simplified secant update; standard secant uses two previous points # Correct secant implementation: # xnew = b - fb (b - a) / (fb - fa) # a, b = a, xnew # fa, fb = f(a), f(b) # Re-implementing standard secant for clarity: xprev, xcurr = a, b fprev, fcurr = f(xprev), f(xcurr) for in range(iterations): if abs(fcurr - fprev) < 1e-8: break xnext = xcurr - fcurr (xcurr - xprev) / (fcurr - fprev) xprev, xcurr = xcurr, xnext fprev, fcurr = fcurr, f(xcurr) return xcurr return b def rendergof(theta, phi, z, camerapose, tau=0.5, M=12, ms=3, N=12, deltamin=0.01, gamma=0.0, step=0): """ Renders an image for a single ray using GOF. theta: Generator parameters phi: Discriminator parameters (not used in forward pass) z: Latent code camerapose: Camera origin o and direction d tau: Threshold for root finding M: Number of bins for root finding ms: Secant iterations N: Number of rendering samples deltamin: Minimal sampling interval half-width gamma: Decay rate for shrinking step: Current training step """ o, d = camerapose tn, tf = 0.1, 10.0 # Near and far bounds, typical values not specified in source, assumed standard NeRF bounds # 1. Surface Location via Root-Finding # Sample M evenly-spaced points tbins = [tn + i (tf - tn) / M for i in range(M + 1)] xbins = [o + t d for t in tbins] # Query alpha values alphas = [querygenerator(theta, x, z)[0] for x in xbins] # Find bin kS where alpha crosses tau kS = -1 for k in range(M): if alphas[k] < tau <= alphas[k+1]: kS = k break if kS == -1: # Fallback if surface not found in bins, e.g., all free or all occupied # Use midpoint or handle error ts = (tn + tf) / 2 else: # Secant method in bin [xbins[kS], xbins[kS+1]] # Define function for secant method def alphafunc(t): x = o + t d return querygenerator(theta, x, z)[0] ta = tbins[kS] tb = tbins[kS+1] ts = secantmethod(alphafunc, ta, tb, ms) # 2. Shrinking Sampling Region deltainit = (tf - tn) / 2 deltan = max(deltainit math.exp(-gamma step), deltamin) # Sample N points in [ts - deltan, ts + deltan] tstart = ts - deltan tend = ts + deltan # Clamp to [tn, tf] tstart = max(tn, tstart) tend = min(tf, tend) # If region is invalid, fallback to uniform sampling or minimal region if tend <= tstart: tend = tstart + deltamin tsamples = [tstart + i (tend - tstart) / N for i in range(N)] # 3. Rendering color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] T = 1.0 # Transmittance for i, t in enumerate(tsamples): x = o + t d alpha, c = querygenerator(theta, x, z) # Alpha composition # C(r) = sum( alphai product(1 - alphaj) for j < i ci) # Ti = product(1 - alphaj) for j < i contribution = T alpha c color = [color[j] + contribution[j] for j in range(3)] T = (1 - alpha) if T < 1e-4: # Early ray marching termination break return color def computeloss(theta, phi, z, camerapose, realimage, tau=0.5, M=12, ms=3, N=12, deltamin=0.01, gamma=0.0, step=0): """ Computes the total loss for GOF training. """ # Render generated image genimage = rendergof(theta, phi, z, camerapose, tau, M, ms, N, deltamin, gamma, step) # GAN Loss # Lorigin = E[f(D(G(z)))] + E[f(-D(I))] + lambda ||gradD(I)||^2 # f(u) = -log(1 + exp(-u)) # Note: This is a simplified representation. Actual implementation requires backprop through D and G. ganloss = computeganloss(theta, phi, genimage, realimage) # Locate surface for regularization o, d = camerapose tn, tf = 0.1, 10.0 tbins = [tn + i (tf - tn) / M for i in range(M + 1)] xbins = [o + t d for t in tbins] alphas = [querygenerator(theta, x, z)[0] for x in xbins] kS = -1 for k in range(M): if alphas[k] < tau <= alphas[k+1]: kS = k break if kS != -1: def alphafunc(t): x = o + t d return querygenerator(theta, x, z)[0] ta = tbins[kS] tb = tbins[kS+1] ts = secantmethod(alphafunc, ta, tb, ms) xs = o + ts d # Normal Regularization # Lnormal = sum ||n(xs) - n(xs + eps)||^2 eps = 0.01 ns = computenormal(theta, xs, z) nseps = computenormal(theta, xs + eps d, z) normalloss = sum((ns[j] - nseps[j])2 for j in range(3)) # Opacity Regularization # Lopacity = 1/N sum (log(alpha) + log(1-alpha)) # Sample N points for this loss (can be the same as rendering points) deltainit = (tf - tn) / 2 deltan = max(deltainit math.exp(-gamma step), deltamin) tstart = max(tn, ts - deltan) tend = min(tf, ts + deltan) tsamples = [tstart + i (tend - tstart) / N for i in range(N)] opacityloss = 0.0 for t in tsamples: x = o + t d alpha = querygenerator(theta, x, z)[0] opacityloss += math.log(alpha) + math.log(1 - alpha) opacityloss /= N else: normalloss = 0.0 opacityloss = 0.0 totalloss = ganloss + lambdanormal normalloss + lambdaopacity opacityloss return totalloss Shape-Color Ambiguity: Direct training of generative radiance fields fails to maintain surface compactness because small perturbations on surfaces still lead to realistic RGB images, fooling the discriminator. GOF mitigates this by reinterpreting alpha as occupancy and using root-finding. Convergence Issues: Directly applying occupancy representations to generative models causes severe convergence problems due to sparse gradients located only on object surfaces. GOF avoids this by starting with cumulative rendering (radiance field) and gradually shrinking the sampling region. Density Thresholding: Predicted densities in generative radiance fields range from 0 to 50, making it hard to determine an effective threshold for surface location. GOF uses alpha values which are naturally bounded in [0, 1]. Surface Not Found: If the root-finding bin is not found (e.g., all alphas < \tau or all > \tau), the surface location step fails. The pseudocode includes a fallback to the midpoint. Inference Speed: GOF requires M + ms + N queries for standard rendering, or M + ms + 1 for single-point surface rendering. Baselines require 2N queries. Time Complexity: GOF requires M + ms + N queries for standard rendering, or M + ms + 1 for single-point surface rendering. Baselines require 2N queries. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: GOF significantly outperforms baseline methods on the MAD (Mean Angle Deviation) metric, which focuses on surface compactness, and is comparable on SIDE (Scale-invariant Depth Error). Strengths: Compact and smooth surfaces; efficient rendering with single-point surface query; resolves shape-color ambiguity. Limitations: May over-smooth furry or complex textures when using single-point rendering; suitable for solid objects with a single surface. When to use: 3D-aware image synthesis where compact surface representation is desired, especially for solid objects like faces or animals. When not to use: Scenes with complex, multi-layered, or translucent objects where a single surface is insufficient. GOF was proposed by Xudong Xu, Xingang Pan, Dahua Lin, and Bo Dai from CUHK - SenseTime Joint Lab, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Max Planck Institute for Informatics, and Nanyang Technological University. It was published on arXiv on November 1, 2021. The method builds on the principles of generative radiance fields and occupancy networks, aiming to combine their respective strengths. It is used on datasets such as CelebA, BFM, and Cats for 3D-aware image synthesis.
