name: Lifting 2D GAN to 3D Radiance Field
head: GAN-to-NeRF Lifting, Lift3D
body: This method distills 3D structural knowledge from a pretrained 2D Generative Adversarial Network (specifically StyleGAN2) into a shared conditional Neural Radiance Field (NeRF). It solves the problem of generating photorealistic 3D objects with arbitrary poses for data augmentation in downstream tasks (e.g., autonomous driving perception) by jointly optimizing the NeRF parameters and latent codes. Unlike naive isolated NeRF reconstruction which fails to capture category priors and is hindered by noisy GAN sampling, this approach uses Generative Latent Optimization (GLO) to learn shared shape and appearance priors across all objects simultaneously. Inputs: 1. Pretrained 2D GAN: StyleGAN2 trained on a specific category (e.g., LSUN Car). 2. Template Data: A set of 3D models (e.g., from ShapeNet) rendered under 200 viewpoints to establish pose-latent mappings. 3. Ground Truth Masks: Binary masks for objects, extracted using a segmentation network like PointRend. 4. Environment Layout: 2D images with drivable area annotations, processed via HRNet and Inverse Perspective Mapping (IPM). Outputs: 1. Shared Conditional NeRF (\Phi\theta): A 3D radiance field representation conditioned on latent codes. 2. Optimized Latent Codes (\hat{Z}): A set of latent vectors for each object in the asset bank. 3. Synthetic 3D Assets: Novel views of generated objects with consistent geometry and appearance. 1. Disentangled Latent Space (w^): The StyleGAN2 latent space z is mapped to an intermediate space w^ = (w1^,..., w{16}^) via 16 affine transformations. Pose Latents (wp): The first 8 layers (w1^... w8^) control camera viewpoint/pose. Shape/Appearance Latents (ws): The remaining 8 layers (w9^... w{16}^) control shape, texture, and background. 2. Tri-Plane NeRF Representation (\Phi\theta): The NeRF is represented using three axis-aligned orthogonal feature planes (XY, YZ, XZ). Feature Planes: Generated by a 2D CNN mapping a constant input conditioned on latent code z. Point Query: For a 3D point x \in \mathbb{R}^3, features are retrieved by projecting x onto the three planes and performing bilinear interpolation. MLP Head: The summed feature vector is fed into a single-layer SIREN-based MLP conditioned on z to output density \sigma and color c. 3. Pose Label (P): Defined by azimuth \alpha \in 0, 360^\circ) and elevation \beta \in [0, 20^\circ), representing a unit sphere looking at the origin. 1. Disentangle StyleGAN2: Map the input latent code z to w^ using the StyleGAN2 generator's affine layers. Separate w^ into pose latents wp (first 8 layers) and shape/appearance latents ws (remaining 8 layers). 2. Obtain Latent-Label Pairs: Select a 3D model (e.g., from ShapeNet). Render the model under 200 different viewpoints P. Use optimization-based GAN inversion to find the template latent code corresponding to the rendered image. Associate the first 8 layers of this template latent with the pose label P. 3. Generate 2D Training Data: Sample pose latents wp from the obtained pose-latent pairs. Sample shape/appearance latents ws randomly from a Gaussian distribution \mathcal{N}(0, I). Combine wp and ws to generate 2D images I with associated pose labels P. Filter out generated objects that fall outside drivable areas by projecting 2D drivable area masks (from HRNet) to Bird's-Eye-View (BEV) via IPM. 4. Joint Optimization (GLO): Initialize a shared NeRF \Phi\theta and a set of latent codes Z for all objects in the asset bank. Minimize the total loss \mathcal{L} with respect to \theta and Z simultaneously. 5. Volumetric Rendering: For a camera ray r(t) = o + td, compute the expected color C(r): C(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigma(r(t)) c(r(t), d) dt Compute transmittance T(t): T(t) = \exp\left(-\int{tn}^{t} \sigma(r(s)) ds\right) tn and tf are the nearest and furthest sampling bounds. 6. Shadow Generation: Cast a pre-computed shadow map at the bottom of each object to simulate lighting interactions. 7. Binary Mask Prediction: Extract the foreground mask \hat{M} based on accumulated transmittance at the furthest bound tf: \hat{M} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } T(tf) \geq 0.5 \\ 0 & \text{if } T(tf) < 0.5 \end{cases} 8. Composition: Alpha blend the foreground image I2 and background image I1 using the smoothed mask M (smoothed via Gaussian filter): I{out} = I1 \cdot M + I2 \cdot (1 - M) [Optimization Objective: \hat{Z}, \hat{\theta} = \arg \min{z, \theta} \mathcal{L}(I, \Phi{\theta}(z, P)) where \hat{Z} is the concatenation of all latent codes, P is the pose label, and \mathcal{L} is the total loss. Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \sum{i=1}^{N} (\mathcal{L}{RGB} + \lambda{IoU}\mathcal{L}{IoU} + \lambda{perc}\mathcal{L}{perc}) where N is the number of image pairs, and \lambda{IoU}, \lambda{perc} are loss weights. Photometric Loss (L1): \mathcal{L}{RGB} = \frac{1}{CHW} |Ii - \Phi{\theta}(zi, Pi)| where C, H, W are channel, height, and width dimensions. Perceptual Loss: \mathcal{L}{perc} = \frac{1}{CHW} |VGG(Ii) - VGG(\hat{I}i)| where VGG is a 16-layer network pretrained on ImageNet. IoU Loss: \mathcal{L}{IoU} = 1 - \frac{\hat{M} \cap M^}{\hat{M} \cup M^} where \hat{M} is the predicted mask and M^ is the ground truth mask from PointRend. Pose Latent Layers: First 8 layers of w^. Shape/Appearance Latent Layers: Remaining 8 layers of w^. Mask Threshold: 0.5 (for binary mask prediction). Confidence Filter Threshold: 0.5 (during inference, images with confidence < 0.5 are filtered as noisy). Pose Sampling Range: Azimuth 0-360^\circ, Elevation 0-20^\circ. Viewpoints per Model: 200. Asset Bank Size: 1000 different vehicles (each with 200 multi-view images). Loss Weights: \lambda{IoU}, \lambda{perc} are hyperparameters; exact values not specified in sources. Noisy GAN Sampling: Generated images and pose labels can be noisy or corrupted. This is mitigated by filtering low-confidence images (confidence < 0.5) and using GLO to learn shared priors rather than isolated reconstruction. Drivable Area Constraints: Objects must be filtered if they fall outside drivable areas to maintain environmental consistency (e.g., vehicles not appearing inside buildings). Boundary Artifacts: Alpha blending with a Gaussian-filtered mask is required to smooth edges when composing foreground and background. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class TriPlaneNeRF(nn.Module): """ NeRF representation using Tri-Plane feature encoding. """ def init(self, latentdim, featuredim, hiddendim): super().init() # 2D CNN to map constant input to three orthogonal feature planes # conditioned on latent code z. self.featureextractor = FeatureExtractor(latentdim, featuredim) # Single-layer SIREN-based MLP conditioned on z self.mlp = SIRENMLP(featuredim 3, hiddendim) def forward(self, x, z): """ x: (N, 3) 3D points z: (N, latentdim) latent codes """ # Project x onto three planes and retrieve features via bilinear interpolation featuresxy = self.featureextractor.getplanefeature(x, 'xy', z) featuresyz = self.featureextractor.getplanefeature(x, 'yz', z) featuresxz = self.featureextractor.getplanefeature(x, 'xz', z) # Sum the three feature vectors combinedfeatures = featuresxy + featuresyz + featuresxz # Output density and RGB density, color = self.mlp(combinedfeatures, z) return density, color class StyleGAN2Disentangler: """ Disentangles StyleGAN2 latent space into pose and shape components. """ def init(self, stylegan2model): self.model = stylegan2model def getlatents(self, z): # Map z to w via 16 affine transformations wstar = self.model.mapping(z) # First 8 layers are pose latents wp = wstar[:,:8] # Remaining 8 layers are shape/appearance latents ws = wstar[:, 8:] return wp, ws def generatetrainingdata(stylegan2disentangler, numsamples=1000): """ Generates 2D training data by sampling pose and shape latents. """ images = [] poses = [] for in range(numsamples): # Sample pose latents from pre-computed pose-latent pairs wp = sampleposelatent() # Sample shape/appearance latents from Gaussian distribution ws = torch.randn(8) # Combine and generate image wfull = torch.cat([wp, ws], dim=0) img = stylegan2disentangler.model.synthesis(wfull) # Sample pose label P (Azimuth 0-360, Elevation 0-20) azimuth = torch.rand(1) 360 elevation = torch.rand(1) 20 pose = (azimuth, elevation) images.append(img) poses.append(pose) return images, poses def computevolumetricrendering(rayo, rayd, nerfmodel, z, tn, tf, numsamples=256): """ Renders a single ray using volumetric rendering. """ # Sample points along the ray tvals = torch.linspace(tn, tf, numsamples) xyz = rayo.unsqueeze(1) + rayd.unsqueeze(1) tvals.unsqueeze(0) # Query NeRF for density and color density, color = nerfmodel(xyz, z) # Compute transmittance # T(t) = exp(-int{tn}^{t} sigma(r(s)) ds) # Approximated using discrete sum deltas = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] alpha = 1 - torch.exp(-density deltas) transmittance = torch.cumprod(torch.exp(-density deltas), dim=0) transmittance = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(transmittance[:,:1]), transmittance], dim=1) # Compute expected color weights = alpha transmittance colorrendered = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) color, dim=0) # Compute accumulated transmittance at furthest bound for mask Ttf = transmittance[-1] return colorrendered, Ttf def computeloss(renderedimg, gtimg, renderedmask, gtmask, vggmodel): """ Computes the total loss: Photometric + IoU + Perceptual. """ # Photometric Loss (L1) lrgb = torch.mean(torch.abs(renderedimg - gtimg)) # IoU Loss intersection = torch.sum(renderedmask gtmask) union = torch.sum(renderedmask + gtmask) liou = 1 - (intersection / (union + 1e-6)) # Perceptual Loss vggrendered = vggmodel(renderedimg) vgggt = vggmodel(gtimg) lperc = torch.mean(torch.abs(vggrendered - vgggt)) # Total Loss lambdaiou = 1.0 # Placeholder, should be tuned lambdaperc = 1.0 # Placeholder, should be tuned totalloss = lrgb + lambdaiou liou + lambdaperc lperc return totalloss def trainlifting3d(stylegan2model, gtmasks, drivableareas, assetbanksize=1000): """ Main training loop for Lifting 2D GAN to 3D Radiance Field. """ # 1. Disentangle StyleGAN2 disentangler = StyleGAN2Disentangler(stylegan2model) # 2. Obtain Latent-Label Pairs (using ShapeNet templates) # This step is done offline to initialize pose-latent mappings poselatentpairs = getposelatentpairsfromshapenet() # 3. Generate 2D Training Data images, poses = generatetrainingdata(disentangler, numsamples=assetbanksize 200) # Filter out objects outside drivable areas # Convert 2D drivable areas to BEV via IPM and filter validindices = filterbydrivablearea(images, drivableareas) images = [images[i] for i in validindices] poses = [poses[i] for i in validindices] gtmasks = [gtmasks[i] for i in validindices] # 4. Initialize Shared NeRF and Latent Codes nerf = TriPlaneNeRF(latentdim=512, featuredim=64, hiddendim=256) latentcodes = [torch.randn(512) for in range(len(images))] # 5. Joint Optimization (GLO) optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(list(nerf.parameters()) + [nn.Parameter(code) for code in latentcodes], lr=1e-4) vggmodel = VGG16(pretrained=True) for epoch in range(numepochs): for i, (img, pose, mask) in enumerate(zip(images, poses, gtmasks)): # Sample rays for this image based on pose rayo, rayd = sampleraysfrompose(pose) # Render renderedcolor, Ttf = computevolumetricrendering(rayo, rayd, nerf, latentcodes[i], tn=0.0, tf=10.0) # Predict Binary Mask renderedmask = (Ttf >= 0.5).float() # Compute Loss loss = computeloss(renderedcolor, img, renderedmask, mask, vggmodel) # Backpropagate optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return nerf, latentcodes Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: The method uses a Tri-Plane representation, which is more memory-efficient than voxel grids or dense point clouds for high-resolution scenes. The memory usage scales with the number of feature planes and the resolution of the 2D CNN output. Time: The joint optimization (GLO) requires simultaneous updates of the NeRF parameters and all latent codes, which can be computationally intensive compared to isolated NeRF reconstruction. However, the Tri-Plane representation allows for efficient feature querying. Measured Performance: The method was evaluated on KITTI and nuScenes datasets for 3D object detection tasks. It generates high-quality synthetic data that improves the performance of downstream 3D detection models. Qualitative comparisons show superior visual quality compared to GIRAFFE and GIRAFFE HD, especially when increasing depth magnitude. Strengths: Data Augmentation: Enables the generation of novel 3D objects with arbitrary poses for training data augmentation. Shared Priors: Learns shared shape and appearance priors within a category, mitigating the noise from GAN sampling. Efficiency: Uses Tri-Plane representation for efficient 3D feature encoding. High Quality: Produces photorealistic images with consistent geometry and appearance. Limitations: Dependency on 2D GAN: Relies on the quality of the pretrained 2D GAN (StyleGAN2). Noisy Inputs: Generated images and pose labels can be noisy, requiring filtering and robust optimization. Environment Constraints: Requires accurate drivable area annotations to filter out invalid objects. When to Use: When generating large-scale synthetic 3D datasets for training perception models in autonomous driving or robotics. When high-quality, diverse 3D objects with consistent appearance are needed. When Not to Use: When precise geometric accuracy is more important than photorealism. When computational resources are limited for joint optimization. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Lift3D: Synthesize 3D Training Data by Lifting 2D GAN to 3D Generative Radiance Field". History and Development: The method builds on the success of StyleGAN2 in generating high-quality 2D images. It leverages the concept of GANSpace to disentangle pose and shape latents. It addresses the limitations of naive NeRF reconstruction by incorporating Generative Latent Optimization (GLO). The method was applied to the LSUN Car dataset and evaluated on KITTI and nuScenes datasets. Applications: Autonomous driving perception (3D object detection). Robotics simulation. Data augmentation for 3D vision tasks. Lift3D: Synthesize 3D Training Data by Lifting 2D GAN to 3D Generative Radiance Field, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00040, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Training Configuration and Optimization
body: This article defines the hyperparameter settings, optimization schedules, and loss function configurations required to train Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) models. It addresses the problem of converging the implicit representation to a high-fidelity 3D scene by specifying learning rates, sampling strategies, and regularization weights. It differs from sibling articles by focusing on the training dynamics (optimizer state, loss weights, schedule) rather than the network architecture (layer counts, encoding functions) or scene representation (static vs. dynamic, depth-guided vs. text-guided). The training process for NeRF variants generally follows a stochastic gradient descent loop where camera rays are sampled, rendered via volume integration, and compared against ground-truth observations. The core optimization mechanism involves minimizing a photometric loss (typically L1 or L2) between rendered and ground-truth colors. Key shared components include: 1. Optimizer: Adam is the standard optimizer, often with weight decay. 2. Learning Rate Schedule: A step decay or linear decay is commonly applied over a fixed number of iterations. 3. Ray Sampling: Points are sampled along rays using uniform or importance sampling, with distinct coarse and fine models often employed. 4. Loss Composition: The total loss is a weighted sum of color reconstruction loss and auxiliary losses (e.g., depth, uncertainty, or semantic constraints). A training configuration that incorporates depth priors to regularize optimization, addressing monocular depth ambiguity. It distinguishes itself by modifying the NeRF architecture with dropout layers (p=0.1 after the first eight FC layers) and introducing a weighted depth loss term [11916-depth-guided-nerf-training-configuration.md]. It is chosen when geometric consistency is critical and ground-truth depth maps are available. See Depth-Guided NeRF Training Configuration. A configuration for text-guided stylization that minimizes the negative cosine similarity between rendered images and text prompts in CLIP embedding space. name: Depth-Guided NeRF Training Configuration
head: Depth-Guided NeRF Training
body: This configuration defines the training protocol for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that incorporate depth priors to improve reconstruction quality, specifically addressing the ambiguity of scale and geometry in monocular settings. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF training by integrating a depth loss term weighted by a scene-specific hyperparameter and modifying the network architecture with dropout to prevent overfitting. It builds on Training Configuration and Optimization by adding specific depth-related auxiliary losses and architectural regularizers. Inputs: Ground-truth RGB images. Ground-truth depth maps (or depth estimates derived from stereo/multi-view consistency). Camera poses and intrinsics. Outputs: Optimized NeRF model parameters (MLP weights, positional encoding frequencies). Rendered RGB images and depth maps. Data Structures: NeRF Model: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) taking 5D input (3D position + 2D viewing direction). The architecture is based on the original NeRF [15] but with specific modifications. Depth Scale: A learnable scalar parameter used to align predicted depth with ground-truth depth scale. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the NeRF MLP. Initialize the depth scale parameter. 2. Sampling: Sample points along rays using uniform or importance sampling. Generate coarse and fine samples as per standard NeRF practices. 3. Forward Pass: Encode positions and viewing directions using positional encoding. Pass through the MLP. The first eight fully connected ReLU-activated layers encoding the positional encoding must have dropout applied with probability p=0.1. Output volume density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Compute depth from the volume density and transmittance. 4. Loss Computation: Compute photometric loss (e.g., L1 or L2) between rendered color and ground-truth color. Compute depth loss between predicted depth \hat{d} and ground-truth depth d. The depth loss is weighted by \lambda. Compute uncertainty loss weighted by \gamma. Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{color} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{depth} + \gamma \mathcal{L}{uncertainty}. 5. Optimization: Update NeRF parameters using Adam optimizer. Update depth scale parameter using Adam optimizer with a separate learning rate. 6. Learning Rate Schedule: Reduce the main learning rate to 5 \times 10^{-5} after 80% of the total training steps. Formulas: Depth Evaluation Metrics (for validation, not necessarily loss): RMSE(d, \hat{d}) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1,...,K} (dk - \hat{d}k)^2} RMSE{log}(d, \hat{d}) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1,...,K} (\log dk - \log \hat{d}k)^2} AbsRel(d, \hat{d}) = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1,...,K} \frac{|dk - \hat{d}k|}{dk} SqRel(d, \hat{d}) = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1,...,K} \frac{(dk - \hat{d}k)^2}{dk} Where K is the number of pixels with valid ground-truth depth. Uncertainty Threshold: \tau = (\text{max\depth} - \text{min\depth}) \cdot 0.0001 For ScanNet, \text{max\depth} = 10 and \text{min\depth} = 0.001. Parameters: Depth Loss Weight (\lambda): 0.007 for most scenes; 0.02 for scene 710. Uncertainty Weight (\gamma): 1. Optimizer: Adam. Initial Learning Rate: 5 \times 10^{-4}. Learning Rate Schedule: Reduce to 5 \times 10^{-5} after 80% of steps. Weight Decay: 1 \times 10^{-6}. Total Training Steps: 500,000. Depth Scale Learning Rate: 1 \times 10^{-7}. Dropout Probability: 0.1 applied after each of the first eight fully connected ReLU-activated layers that encode the positional encoding. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim class DepthGuidedNeRF(nn.Module): def init(self, inputdim=3, hiddendim=256, numlayers=8): super().init() self.layers = nn.ModuleList() for i in range(numlayers): layer = nn.Linear(inputdim if i == 0 else hiddendim, hiddendim) self.layers.append(layer) # Dropout applied only to the first 8 layers encoding positional encoding if i < 8: self.layers.append(nn.Dropout(p=0.1)) self.layers.append(nn.ReLU()) self.colorlayer = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 3) self.sigmalayer = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1) def forward(self, x): for layer in self.layers: x = layer(x) sigma = self.sigmalayer(x) color = self.colorlayer(x) return sigma, color def traindepthguidednerf(model, optimizer, depthscaleoptimizer, dataloader, numsteps=500000): model.train() depthscale = nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(1.0)) # Learnable depth scale # Hyperparameters lambdadepth = 0.007 # Default, adjust for scene 710 gammauncertainty = 1.0 lrmain = 5e-4 lrdepthscale = 1e-7 weightdecay = 1e-6 for step in range(numsteps): # Learning rate schedule if step > 0.8 numsteps: for paramgroup in optimizer.paramgroups: paramgroup['lr'] = 5e-5 # Get batch rays, gtcolors, gtdepths = next(dataloader) # Forward pass # Note: Actual NeRF rendering involves volume integration. # Simplified for illustration of loss components. predictedcolors, predicteddepths = renderrays(model, rays, depthscale) # Compute losses losscolor = torch.mean(torch.abs(predictedcolors - gtcolors)) lossdepth = torch.mean(torch.abs(predicteddepths - gtdepths)) lossuncertainty = computeuncertaintyloss(predicteddepths, gtdepths) # Implementation depends on specific uncertainty formulation totalloss = losscolor + lambdadepth lossdepth + gammauncertainty lossuncertainty # Backward pass optimizer.zerograd() depthscaleoptimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() depthscaleoptimizer.step() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Scene 710: Requires a higher depth loss weight (\lambda = 0.02) compared to other scenes (\lambda = 0.007). Depth Scale: The depth scale is a learnable parameter with a very small learning rate (1 \times 10^{-7}) to prevent instability. Uncertainty Threshold: The threshold \tau for evaluating depth uncertainty is scene-dependent, calculated as (\text{max\depth} - \text{min\depth}) \cdot 0.0001. Integrates the depth loss from the DS-NeRF official code base into the training pipeline. Due to missing configuration files for DTU in the official release, results for DTU are taken from the publication, while LLFF results are re-trained on specific train/test splits using released configuration files, as the original publication used a different split. Time Complexity: Training requires 500,000 steps. The addition of depth loss and uncertainty loss increases computational overhead per step compared to standard NeRF. Memory Complexity: The dropout layers add negligible memory overhead. The depth scale parameter is minimal. Strengths: Improves geometric accuracy and scale consistency by leveraging depth priors. Dropout prevents overfitting, especially important when using depth constraints. Limitations: Requires ground-truth depth maps or reliable depth estimates. Performance is sensitive to the choice of \lambda and \gamma. When to use: When monocular NeRF reconstruction suffers from scale ambiguity or poor geometry. When not to use: When depth information is unavailable or unreliable. This configuration originates from the work on Depth-Guided NeRF Training via Earth Mover’s Distance. It builds upon the original NeRF architecture [15] and incorporates techniques from DS-NeRF for depth loss integration. The method is designed to address the limitations of standard NeRF in reconstructing accurate 3D geometry from monocular images by explicitly incorporating depth information into the training loop. name: CLIPNeRF Training Configuration
head: Absolute Directional CLIP Loss, CLIPNeRF Hyperparameters, CLIPNeRF Implementation, Directional CLIP Loss, Relative Directional CLIP Loss, StyleGAN-NADA CLIP Loss
body: CLIPNeRF training configuration defines the optimization procedure for text-guided stylization of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) by minimizing the negative cosine similarity between rendered image embeddings and target text prompt embeddings. It distinguishes itself from standard photometric NeRF training by replacing or augmenting pixel-wise color loss with semantic constraints in the CLIP embedding space, enabling style transfer without requiring paired 3D data. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained NeRF model (MLP parameters), a source image I{src} (optional, for relative loss), a target text prompt t{tgt}, and a source text prompt t{src} (optional). Output: Updated NeRF parameters that stylize the rendered views to match the semantic direction of t{tgt} relative to t{src} or absolute style. Data Structures: NeRF Model: Standard MLP mapping 3D coordinates and viewing directions to color and density. Parameters are split into density-related and color-related sub-parameters. CLIP Encoder: ViT-B/32 architecture. Takes an image or text and outputs a normalized embedding vector. Patch Buffer: Stores rendered pixel values for a 128 \times 128 patch. Parameters: Iterations: 500. Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 0.0001. Patch Size: 128 \times 128 pixels. Ray Sampling Stride: 5 within the patch. This results in a receptive field of 640 \times 640 on the original image scale. Importance Sampling Points: 16 per ray during patch rendering. Fine MLP Total Samples: 80 (64 coarse + 16 fine). Steps: 1. Freeze Density: Freeze sub-parameters related to density in the NeRF to prevent structural changes during stylization. 2. Sample Ray: Randomly sample a camera pose from the training dataset. 3. Render Patch: Render a 128 \times 128 patch from the sampled pose. Rays are sampled with a stride of 5 to cover a wider area. Use importance sampling with 16 points per ray. The fine MLP uses 80 total samples (64 coarse, 16 fine). 4. Resize: Apply bilinear interpolation to resize the rendered patch to the input resolution required by the CLIP encoder. 5. Encode: Pass the resized patch through the CLIP ViT-B/32 image encoder to get \hat{e}i. Encode the target text prompt t{tgt} to get \hat{e}t. 6. Compute Loss: Calculate the loss based on the chosen directional strategy (see Formulas). 7. Optimize: Update the color-related NeRF parameters using Adam with learning rate 0.0001. Formulas: Two variants of the directional CLIP loss are used: 1. Absolute Directional CLIP Loss: Measures cosine similarity between the rendered image embedding and the target text embedding. \mathcal{L}{dir} = 1 - \langle \hat{e}i(I{tgt}), \hat{e}t(t{tgt}) \rangle Where \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle denotes the dot product of normalized vectors. This guides the NeRF with a global direction but ignores magnitude. 2. Relative Directional CLIP Loss: Transfers style from a source image I{src} to the target domain using a pair of text prompts (t{src}, t{tgt}). \mathcal{L}{dir} = 1 - \langle \hat{e}i(I{tgt}) - \hat{e}i(I{src}), \hat{e}t(t{tgt}) - \hat{e}t(t{src}) \rangle This enforces the correct stylization trajectory relative to the source. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Constraints: Naive differentiable rendering of high-resolution images is intractable due to memory limits. The patch-based approach mitigates this. Mode Collapse: Absolute directional CLIP loss can cause mode collapse of the generator and hurt generation diversity. Insufficient Magnitude: Directional loss alone struggles to reach sufficient stylization magnitude, resulting in weak style transfer. This is because it measures directional similarity but ignores actual distances in embedding space. Non-Uniform Stylization: Global contrastive loss may lead to excess stylization in some regions and insufficiency in others (e.g., eyes vs. faces). Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of iterations (500) and the number of rays sampled per patch. Patch rendering is significantly faster than full-image rendering. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the patch size (128 \times 128) and sampling points (80 per ray), rather than full image resolution. This allows training on hardware with limited VRAM. Strengths: Enables text-driven stylization without 3D ground truth; computationally efficient via patch rendering. Limitations: May produce non-uniform stylization across the scene; absolute loss risks mode collapse; relative loss requires a source image and prompt. When to use: When text-guided style transfer is required for NeRFs and computational resources are constrained. When not to use: When high-fidelity, uniform stylization magnitude is critical without additional global contrastive mechanisms. CLIPNeRF was introduced by Wang et al. in 2021. It extends the StyleCLIP [Patashnik et al. 2021] and StyleGAN-NADA [Gal et al. 2021] concepts to 3D neural radiance fields. The method was further refined in NeRF-Art to address issues with magnitude and uniformity. It is used for text-driven 3D scene stylization and editing. name: Triplane and Planar Representations
head: Triplanar Representation, Triplane NeRF, Hybrid Triplane
body: Triplane and Planar Representations model 3D scenes using a set of axis-aligned orthogonal 2D feature planes (typically xy, xz, and yz) to achieve full expressivity at scale while avoiding the cubic memory complexity of voxel-based representations. This approach projects image features into a 3D volume and aggregates them into 2D planes, allowing for efficient rendering and optimization compared to dense 3D grids. The core mechanism involves representing the scene geometry and appearance using a fixed number of 2D feature grids stored along canonical planes. Unlike the parent method's MLP-only approach, this representation explicitly stores features in a grid structure that is sampled via interpolation. Data Structure The scene is represented by a tensor S (or T) of shape \mathbb{R}^{3 \times C \times D \times D}, where the first dimension indexes the three planes (xy, xz, yz), C is the feature dimension, and D \times D is the spatial resolution of each plane. Feature Aggregation To query a point \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3, features are gathered by projecting \mathbf{x} onto each of the canonical planes and bilinearly interpolating the nearby features. Let \mathbf{f}{xy}, \mathbf{f}{xz}, \mathbf{f}{yz} be the features gathered from the respective planes. These are combined, often via a mean operator \Phi, and passed to a lightweight MLP to predict radiance field properties (color, density, or other features). Rendering The gathered features condition the neural volumetric rendering process. Points are sampled along rays, and their features are aggregated to render images, similar to the ray sampling defined in the parent article. Image-Conditional Triplanar Representation is a 3D scene representation that models scenes using three axis-aligned orthogonal planes (S = [S{xy}, S{xz}, S{yz}]) to achieve full expressivity at scale. It avoids the cubic memory complexity of voxel-based representations and the dimensionality limitations of 2D or Bird's Eye View (BEV) representations by projecting image features into a 3D volume and aggregating them into 2D planes. Inputs: Input image I \in \mathbb{R}^{Hi \times Wi \times 3}, camera pose \gammai, camera intrinsic Ki. Outputs: Triplanar feature tensor S \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times C \times D \times D}, where the first dimension indexes the planes (xy, xz, yz), C is the feature dimension, and D \times D is the spatial resolution of each plane. Data Structures: 1. Feature Map (FI): 2D tensor of shape \mathbb{R}^{Hi/2 \times Wi/2 \times C}. 2. 3D Feature Volume (VF): Implicitly constructed grid where features are projected along rays. 3. Depth-Encoded Features (VZ): Output of the depth MLP. 4. Triplane (S): Tensor \mathbb{R}^{3 \times C \times D \times D}. Steps: 1. Image Encoding: Extract low-resolution spatial features from the input image I using an ImageNet pre-trained ConvNet backbone E. This transforms I into a 2D feature map FI \in \mathbb{R}^{Hi/2 \times Wi/2 \times C}. 2. Back-Projection: Project local features from FI backwards along every ray to construct a 3D feature volume VF. This projection uses the camera pose \gammai and intrinsic Ki. 3. Depth Encoding: Encode the depth of individual features in the grid using an MLP VZ = Z(VF, xc, d). The MLP takes as input: Concatenated features in the grid (VF). Positions of the grid in the camera frame (xc). Directions from the world frame positions (xw) to the camera frame. The output is depth-encoded features VZ. 4. Triplane Aggregation: Obtain triplane features S{xy}, S{xz}, S{yz} by summing weighted depth-encoded features VZ. The weights are softmax scores from aggregation MLPs A{xy}, A{xz}, A{yz} conditioned on VZ and world coordinates. The specific formulas are: S{xy} = \sumi w{xyi} V{Zi}, \quad w{xy} = A{xy}(V{Zi}, x{wz}) S{xz} = \sumi w{xzi} V{Zi}, \quad w{xz} = A{xz}(V{Zj}, x{wy}) S{yz} = \sumi w{yzi} V{Zi}, \quad w{yz} = A{yz}(V{Zj}, x{wx}) where w{xy}, w{xz}, w{yz} are softmax scores obtained after summing over the z, y, and x dimensions respectively. 5. Upsampling and Convolution: Transform the built image-conditional triplanes into a new G-channel output using learned 2D convolutions. The number of output channels is G = C/4. The spatial dimension of the planes is upsampled from D \times D to the image feature space resolution (H/2 \times W/2). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def imageconditionaltriplanarrepresentation(I, gammai, Ki, E, Z, Axy, Axz, Ayz, C, D): """ I: Input image tensor (Hi, Wi, 3) gammai: Camera pose Ki: Camera intrinsic E: ImageNet pre-trained ConvNet backbone Z: Depth encoding MLP Axy, Axz, Ayz: Feature aggregation MLPs C: Feature dimension D: Spatial resolution of each plane """ # Step 1: Image Encoding # E transforms I to 2D feature map FI FI = E(I) # Shape: (Hi/2, Wi/2, C) # Step 2: Back-Projection # Project features from FI backwards along rays to 3D feature volume VF # Using camera pose gammai and intrinsic Ki # Note: Implementation details of volumetric projection are assumed standard VF = projectfeaturesbackwards(FI, gammai, Ki) # Step 3: Depth Encoding # VZ = Z(VF, xc, d) # xc: positions of grid in camera frame # d: directions from world frame positions xw to camera frame # For each point in the volume, compute xc and d VZ = Z(VF, xc, d) # Step 4: Triplane Aggregation # Sxy = sumi wxyi VZi, where wxy = softmax(Axy(VZi, xwz)) # Sxz = sumi wxzi VZi, where wxz = softmax(Axz(VZj, xwy)) # Syz = sumi wyzi VZi, where wyz = softmax(Ayz(VZj, xwx)) # Compute weights for xy plane wxy = softmax(Axy(VZ, xwz)) Sxy = sum(wxy VZ, dim=0) # Sum over feature dimensions # Compute weights for xz plane wxz = softmax(Axz(VZ, xwy)) Sxz = sum(wxz VZ, dim=0) # Compute weights for yz plane wyz = softmax(Ayz(VZ, xwx)) Syz = sum(wyz VZ, dim=0) # Stack into triplane S S = stack([Sxy, Sxz, Syz]) # Shape: (3, C, D, D) # Step 5: Upsampling and Convolution # Upsample spatial dimension from DD to H/2W/2 # Transform to G-channel output where G = C/4 G = C // 4 Supsampled = upsample(S, targetsize=(Hi/2, Wi/2)) Soutput = learned2dconvolution(Supsampled, outchannels=G) return Soutput Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The back-projection and interpolation steps require careful handling of floating-point precision to avoid artifacts in the feature volume. Boundaries: The projection relies on valid camera parameters; invalid poses or intrinsics may lead to incorrect feature placement. Degenerate Input: If the input image lacks sufficient texture or detail, the extracted features FI may be insufficient for accurate 3D reconstruction. The framework uses a triplane NeRF representation where scene codes are optimized jointly with a diffusion prior to handle sparse-view data and ensure end-to-end coherence. Parameter Prediction Format: v-parameterization \hat{v}\phi(x(t), t) from [43], such that \hat{x} = \alpha(t)x(t) - \sigma(t)\hat{v}. Weighting Function w(t): Uses SNR-based weighting w(t) = (\alpha(t)/\sigma(t))^2\omega from Eq. (5), instead of LSGM mechanisms. Layout Scene code xi: Shape \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 6 \times 128 \times 128}, representing a triplane NeRF representation. Denoising Network Input/Output: Noisy and denoised triplane features, with channels of all three planes stacked together. Denoising Network Architecture: U-Net with 122M parameters. EG3D learns unconditional 3D-aware image generation from a collection of single-view images and corresponding noisy camera poses, where each image has resolution 512 \times 512. Step Render feature image If \in \mathbb{R}^{32 \times 128 \times 128} and raw RGB image I{128} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 128 \times 128} by accumulating points along rays and performing volume rendering. Extract dense depth map ID \in \mathbb{R}^{128 \times 128} from the volume rendering. Feed If and I{128} into a 2D super-resolution network to yield final output I{512} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 512 \times 512}. Formula \text{SuperRes}(If, I{128}) = I{512} Parameter Image resolution: 512 \times 512 for input images and final output. Layout Triplane representation T: A tensor in \mathbb{R}^{256 \times 256 \times 96}, corresponding to 3 axis-aligned planes (xy, xz, yz), each with 32 channels and resolution 256 \times 256. Number Rendering speed: 42 fps on RTX 3090. On D-NeRF dataset, DoublePlane achieves PSNR 30.370, SSIM 0.961, LPIPS 0.054, Training Time 8m 04s. Triplane representations were introduced as an efficient alternative to dense voxel grids for 3D-aware image generation and NeRF optimization. The hybrid triplane representation was notably used in EG3D to enable fast rendering and high-quality 3D generation. Image-conditional triplanar representations were developed to generalize NeRF reconstruction from single or sparse views by conditioning the triplane features on input images. DoublePlane and HexPlane variants further optimized this structure for dynamic scenes. name: EG3D Triplane Representation
head: ConvONet / EG3D (Tri-plane), EG3D Triplane-Based 3D GAN, Hybrid Triplane Representation, Tri-plane Features, Tri-plane representation
body: The EG3D Triplane Representation is a 3D scene encoding method that stores features in three orthogonal 2D grids (xy, xz, yz) to enable efficient neural volumetric rendering. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D voxel grids by reducing memory footprint through 2D convolution and from MLP-only representations by explicitly storing spatial features, though it introduces axis-aligned bias that can complicate handling of complex structures. Inputs and Outputs Input: A noise vector z and camera pose parameters (in the generative context) or a 3D point \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (in the query context). Output: For a point query, a feature vector \mathbf{f}, color c, and volume density \sigma. For rendering, a feature image \mathbf{I}f \in \mathbb{R}^{32 \times 128 \times 128}, a raw RGB image \mathbf{I}{128} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 128 \times 128}, and optionally a depth map \mathbf{I}D \in \mathbb{R}^{128 \times 128}. Data Structures The scene is represented by a triplane tensor \mathbf{T} with shape \mathbb{R}^{3 \times C \times D \times D}. Dimensions: 3 axis-aligned planes (xy, xz, yz). Channels (C): 32. Resolution (D \times D): 256 \times 256. Total Size: 3 \times 32 \times 256 \times 256 elements. Feature Aggregation To query a point \mathbf{x}, features are gathered by projecting \mathbf{x} onto each canonical plane and bilinearly interpolating the nearby features. Let \mathbf{f}{xy}, \mathbf{f}{xz}, \mathbf{f}{yz} be the features gathered from the respective planes. These are combined using a mean operator \Phi and passed to a lightweight MLP to predict radiance field properties: (\mathbf{f}, c, \sigma) = \text{MLP}(\Phi(\mathbf{f}{xy}, \mathbf{f}{xz}, \mathbf{f}{yz})) The output values, including color, are independent of viewing direction and depend only on \mathbf{x}. Rendering Points are sampled along rays, and their features are aggregated to render images via volume rendering. 1. Accumulate points along rays using the queried (\mathbf{f}, c, \sigma) values. 2. Perform volume rendering [Max 1995] to produce a feature image \mathbf{I}f \in \mathbb{R}^{32 \times 128 \times 128} and a raw RGB image \mathbf{I}{128} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 128 \times 128}. 3. Extract a dense depth map \mathbf{I}D \in \mathbb{R}^{128 \times 128} from the volume rendering. 4. Feed \mathbf{I}f and \mathbf{I}{128} into a 2D super-resolution network to yield the final output \mathbf{I}{512} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 512 \times 512}: \text{SuperRes}(\mathbf{I}f, \mathbf{I}{128}) = \mathbf{I}{512} Parameters Image Resolution: Input images and final output are 512 \times 512. Intermediate Resolution: 128 \times 128. Pitfalls Axis-Aligned Bias: The orthogonal coordinate transformation can be challenging to handle complicated structures due to the axis-aligned bias of the representation. Optimization: Optimization is more easily affected by local minima compared to MLP representations that benefit from inductive smoothness bias. Memory: Requires high spatial resolution to represent fine details, leading to large memory usage. Performance: Rendering from a triplane achieves 42 fps on an RTX 3090. Quality: Provides comparable quality to state-of-the-art 2D GANs by FID. Memory: Significantly reduces memory footprint compared to standard 3D grids by using 2D convolutions. Limitations: The axis-aligned nature limits its ability to represent complex, non-axis-aligned structures efficiently. The triplane representation was used in ConvONet and EG3D to model 3D scenes by applying an orthogonal coordinate transformation to spatial points within a bounded scene. It is viewed as an instance of the Factor Fields framework with N=1, \gamma1(\mathbf{x}) = \text{Orthogonal-2D}(\mathbf{x}), f1(\mathbf{x}) = \text{2D-Maps}(\mathbf{x}), and P(\mathbf{x}) = \text{MLP}(\mathbf{x}). EG3D specifically learns unconditional 3D-aware image generation from single-view images and noisy camera poses. name: Image-Conditional Triplanar Representation
head: Tri-plane Features
body: Image-Conditional Triplanar Representation is a 3D scene representation that models scenes using three axis-aligned orthogonal planes (S = [S{xy}, S{xz}, S{yz}]) to achieve full expressivity at scale. It avoids the cubic memory complexity of voxel-based representations and the dimensionality limitations of 2D or Bird's Eye View (BEV) representations by projecting image features into a 3D volume and aggregating them into 2D planes. Inputs: Input image I \in \mathbb{R}^{Hi \times Wi \times 3}, camera pose \gammai, camera intrinsic Ki. Outputs: Triplanar feature tensor S \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times C \times D \times D}, where the first dimension indexes the planes (xy, xz, yz), C is the feature dimension, and D \times D is the spatial resolution of each plane. Data Structures: 1. Feature Map (FI): 2D tensor of shape \mathbb{R}^{Hi/2 \times Wi/2 \times C}. 2. 3D Feature Volume (VF): Implicitly constructed grid where features are projected along rays. 3. Depth-Encoded Features (VZ): Output of the depth MLP. 4. Triplane (S): Tensor \mathbb{R}^{3 \times C \times D \times D}. Steps: 1. Image Encoding: Extract low-resolution spatial features from the input image I using an ImageNet pre-trained ConvNet backbone E. This transforms I into a 2D feature map FI \in \mathbb{R}^{Hi/2 \times Wi/2 \times C}. 2. Back-Projection: Project local features from FI backwards along every ray to construct a 3D feature volume VF. This projection uses the camera pose \gammai and intrinsic Ki. 3. Depth Encoding: Encode the depth of individual features in the grid using an MLP VZ = Z(VF, xc, d). The MLP takes as input: Concatenated features in the grid (VF). Positions of the grid in the camera frame (xc). Directions from the world frame positions (xw) to the camera frame. The output is depth-encoded features VZ. 4. Triplane Aggregation: Obtain triplane features S{xy}, S{xz}, S{yz} by summing weighted depth-encoded features VZ. The weights are softmax scores from aggregation MLPs A{xy}, A{xz}, A{yz} conditioned on VZ and world coordinates. The specific formulas are: S{xy} = \sumi w{xyi} V{Zi}, \quad w{xy} = A{xy}(V{Zi}, x{wz}) S{xz} = \sumi w{xzi} V{Zi}, \quad w{xz} = A{xz}(V{Zj}, x{wy}) S{yz} = \sumi w{yzi} V{Zi}, \quad w{yz} = A{yz}(V{Zj}, x{wx}) where w{xy}, w{xz}, w{yz} are softmax scores obtained after summing over the z, y, and x dimensions respectively. 5. Upsampling and Convolution: Transform the built image-conditional triplanes into a new G-channel output using learned 2D convolutions. The number of output channels is G = C/4. The spatial dimension of the planes is upsampled from D \times D to the image feature space resolution (H/2 \times W/2). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def imageconditionaltriplanarrepresentation(I, gammai, Ki, E, Z, Axy, Axz, Ayz, C, D): """ I: Input image tensor (Hi, Wi, 3) gammai: Camera pose Ki: Camera intrinsic E: ImageNet pre-trained ConvNet backbone Z: Depth encoding MLP Axy, Axz, Ayz: Feature aggregation MLPs C: Feature dimension D: Spatial resolution of each plane """ # Step 1: Image Encoding # E transforms I to 2D feature map FI FI = E(I) # Shape: (Hi/2, Wi/2, C) # Step 2: Back-Projection # Project features from FI backwards along rays to 3D feature volume VF # Using camera pose gammai and intrinsic Ki # Note: Implementation details of volumetric projection are assumed standard VF = projectfeaturesbackwards(FI, gammai, Ki) # Step 3: Depth Encoding # VZ = Z(VF, xc, d) # xc: positions of grid in camera frame # d: directions from world frame positions xw to camera frame # For each point in the volume, compute xc and d VZ = Z(VF, xc, d) # Step 4: Triplane Aggregation # Sxy = sumi wxyi VZi, where wxy = softmax(Axy(VZi, xwz)) # Sxz = sumi wxzi VZi, where wxz = softmax(Axz(VZj, xwy)) # Syz = sumi wyzi VZi, where wyz = softmax(Ayz(VZj, xwx)) # Compute weights for xy plane wxy = softmax(Axy(VZ, xwz)) Sxy = sum(wxy VZ, dim=0) # Sum over feature dimensions # Compute weights for xz plane wxz = softmax(Axz(VZ, xwy)) Sxz = sum(wxz VZ, dim=0) # Compute weights for yz plane wyz = softmax(Ayz(VZ, xwx)) Syz = sum(wyz VZ, dim=0) # Stack into triplane S S = stack([Sxy, Sxz, Syz]) # Shape: (3, C, D, D) # Step 5: Upsampling and Convolution # Upsample spatial dimension from DD to H/2W/2 # Transform to G-channel output where G = C/4 G = C // 4 Supsampled = upsample(S, targetsize=(Hi/2, Wi/2)) Soutput = learned2dconvolution(Supsampled, outchannels=G) return Soutput Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The back-projection and interpolation steps require careful handling of floating-point precision to avoid artifacts in the feature volume. Boundaries: The projection relies on valid camera parameters; invalid poses or intrinsics may lead to incorrect feature placement. Degenerate Input: If the input image lacks sufficient texture or detail, the extracted features FI may be insufficient for accurate 3D reconstruction. Time Complexity: Avoids the cubic complexity of 3D CNNs and voxel-based representations. Memory Complexity: Linear in the number of planes and their resolution, avoiding cubic scaling with volume size. Expressivity: Full expressivity at scale, modeling all three dimensions unlike 2D or BEV representations. Strengths: Computationally efficient compared to 3D CNNs; more expressive than 2D/BEV methods; acts as a global feature representation. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial image features and camera parameters. When to Use: Sparse view synthesis of outdoor scenes where computational efficiency and expressivity are critical. When Not to Use: When high-resolution volumetric details are required that cannot be captured by planar projections. The Image-Conditional Triplanar Representation was introduced in "NeO 360: Neural Fields for Sparse View Synthesis of Outdoor Scenes". It builds on prior works involving volumetric reconstruction. The method is designed to address the limitations of voxel-based and 2D/BEV representations in modeling 3D scenes. name: Surface and SDF-Based Representations
head: SDF-based NeRF, Implicit Surface Rendering, Occupancy Fields
body: This family replaces the standard volume density \sigma output of canonical NeRF with a Signed Distance Function (SDF) or occupancy field to represent geometry. By modeling the scene as an implicit surface, these methods achieve sharper geometry extraction and better surface definition than density-based approaches, which often suffer from "fuzzy" boundaries. They differ from siblings like Voxel and Grid Representations by using continuous neural fields for geometry rather than discrete grids, and from Triplane and Planar Representations by explicitly optimizing for distance-to-surface metrics rather than just feature aggregation. The core mechanism involves predicting a scalar field f(\mathbf{x}) that represents the signed distance to the nearest surface (or occupancy) at position \mathbf{x}, rather than volume density. This scalar field is transformed into opacity \alpha or density \sigma for volume rendering integration. SDF to Opacity/Density Transformation The SDF value s(\mathbf{x}) is converted into a probability of occupancy or density using a distribution parameterized by a variance or sparsity term \beta [S1, 18174-sdf-based-volume-rendering-with-laplacian-cdf.md, unofficial]. 1. Laplacian CDF (Standard SDF): Used in SDF-based Volume Rendering with Laplacian CDF. The opacity \sigma is derived from the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) of a Laplacian distribution: \sigma = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} \exp\left(\frac{s}{\beta}\right) & \text{if } s \le 0 \\ 1 - \frac{1}{2} \exp\left(-\frac{s}{\beta}\right) & \text{if } s > 0 \end{cases} where \beta controls the tightness of the surface representation [18174-sdf-based-volume-rendering-with-laplacian-cdf.md]. 2. Piecewise Exponential (I2-SDF): Used in I2-SDF. The density \sigma is defined as: \sigma(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{\beta}(1 - \exp(d(\mathbf{x})/\beta)) & \text{if } d(\mathbf{x}) < 0 \\ \frac{1}{2\beta}\exp(-d(\mathbf{x})/2\beta) & \text{if } d(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0 \end{cases} where d(\mathbf{x}) is the SDF value and \beta is a learnable sparsity parameter [18170-i2-sdf.md]. Inverse CDF Sampling To sample points efficiently near the surface, methods like SDF-based Volume Rendering with Laplacian CDF use inverse CDF sampling. Random numbers ui \in [0, 1] are generated and transformed to sample distances ti using the inverse of the CDF \Phi^{-1}(ui), concentrating samples near the zero-crossing of the SDF [18174-sdf-based-volume-rendering-with-laplacian-cdf.md]. Stratification is applied by dividing the unit interval into bins [18174-sdf-based-volume-rendering-with-laplacian-cdf.md]. Occupancy Fields As seen in UniSurf, an occupancy field acts as an indicator of surface presence. For solid objects, the occupancy at the i^{th} sample corresponds to an indicator of whether the sample is inside the surface. I2-SDF is a neural implicit framework for complex indoor scenes that jointly recovers underlying shape, radiance, and material fields from multi-view images [18170-i2-sdf.md]. It distinguishes itself by decomposing the radiance field into spatially-varying material and emission components using surface-based, differentiable Monte Carlo raytracing, enabling physically based scene relighting and editing [18170-i2-sdf.md]. Unlike standard NeRF approaches that treat radiance as a monolithic field, I2-SDF employs a two-stage training scheme and error-guided adaptive sampling to resolve ambiguities and improve reconstruction quality on fine-grained small objects [18170-i2-sdf.md]. This method renders geometry by outputting a Signed Distance Function (SDF) value s and a variance parameter \beta from a neural network, then transforming s into opacity \sigma using a Laplacian Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) [18174-sdf-based-volume-rendering-with-laplacian-cdf.md]. It builds on Model Architecture and Encoding by integrating triplane features and SDF-based sampling. Unlike standard NeRF which outputs density directly, this approach enables tight surface extraction and inverse CDF sampling for more accurate depth estimation [18174-sdf-based-volume-rendering-with-laplacian-cdf.md]. A method unifying volume rendering (radiance fields) and surface rendering (implicit surfaces) to achieve high-quality geometry and sharp textures without mask supervision. Uses an occupancy field where the occupancy at the i^{th} sample corresponds to an indicator of surface presence. Uses volume rendering in the early stage for optimization without mask supervision. Uses surface rendering in the later stage to extract level-set surfaces. Unlike pure surface rendering which requires mask supervision and has blurry texture mapping, this method provides high-quality novel views and sharp textures/colors without mask supervision. The concept of unifying neural radiance fields with implicit surfaces was introduced by Oechsle et al. in "Unifying Implicit Surfaces and Radiance Fields" (ICCV 2021). Prior to this, surface extraction from NeRF relied on thresholding density fields, which resulted in inaccurate geometry and blurry textures. UniSurf demonstrated that treating the output as an occupancy field allows for the application of surface rendering techniques in later training stages, combining the best of both worlds: the robustness of volume rendering for optimization and the precision of implicit surfaces for geometry. This family has since evolved to include more sophisticated SDF transformations and sampling strategies, such as the Laplacian CDF approach and material decomposition in I2-SDF. Lecture 7 – Neural Radiance Fields Prof. Dr., https://virtualhumans.mpi-inf.mpg.de/3DVision25/slides25/pdf/Lecture07NeuralRadianceFields.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: I2-SDF
head: Intrinsic Indoor Scene Reconstruction and Editing via Raytracing in Neural SDFs
body: I2-SDF is a neural implicit framework for jointly reconstructing the geometry, material, and incident radiance of complex indoor scenes from multi-view images. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF approaches by modeling geometry as a Signed Distance Field (SDF) and decomposing the radiance field into spatially-varying material and emission components via surface-based, differentiable Monte Carlo raytracing. This decomposition enables physically based scene relighting and editing, which standard volume rendering cannot achieve directly. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images of an indoor scene. Optional geometry priors such as depth maps and surface normals. Outputs: Neural fields for geometry (Fd), radiance (Fc), material (Fa, F\rho), and emission (Fe, L[\cdot]); rendered novel views; decomposed intrinsic maps (albedo, roughness, emission). Data Structures: The method uses four Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) to represent implicit fields: 1. Fd: Maps 3D position \mathbf{x} to SDF value d(\mathbf{x}) and its gradient (normal). 2. Fc: Maps 3D position \mathbf{x} and view direction \mathbf{v} to radiance \hat{c}. 3. Fa, F\rho: Map \mathbf{x} to material parameters (e.g., albedo, roughness). 4. Fe: Maps \mathbf{x} to emitter semantic probability (identifying light sources). SDF to Density Transformation: The SDF value d(\mathbf{x}) is converted to volume density \sigma(\mathbf{x}) using a learnable sparsity parameter \beta: \sigma(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{\beta}(1 - \exp(d(\mathbf{x})/\beta)) & \text{if } d(\mathbf{x}) < 0 \\ \frac{1}{2\beta}\exp(-d(\mathbf{x})/2\beta) & \text{if } d(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0 \end{cases} Rendering: To render a pixel, a ray \mathbf{r} is cast from camera origin \mathbf{o} along direction \mathbf{v}. M points \mathbf{x}{ir} = \mathbf{o} + ti \mathbf{v} are sampled. The color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) is computed via numerical integration: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{M} T{ri} \alpha{ri} \hat{c}{ir} where: \hat{c}{ir} = Fc(\mathbf{x}{ir}, \mathbf{v}) is the predicted radiance. \alpha{ri} = 1 - \exp(-\sigma{ri} \delta{ri}) is the opacity, with \sigma{ri} = \sigma(\mathbf{x}{ir}) and \delta{ri} the distance to the next sample. T{ri} = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha{rj}) is the accumulated transmittance. Training Strategy: I2-SDF employs a two-stage training scheme to resolve ambiguities between geometry, material, and lighting: 1. Stage 1 (Geometry & Radiance): Train Fd, Fc, and the emitter semantic field Fe. The network learns the SDF and the total incident radiance (lighting + material). 2. Stage 2 (Material & Emission): Train the material fields (Fa, F\rho) and the emission field L[\cdot]. During this stage, Fd, Fc, and Fe are fixed and detached from gradient descent. The radiance field is decomposed using surface-based, differentiable Monte Carlo raytracing. Adaptive Sampling and Loss: To handle fine-grained small objects, I2-SDF introduces an error-guided adaptive sampling scheme and a "bubble loss". Standard uniform sampling often fails to capture high-frequency details of small objects because low-frequency large objects converge faster. The adaptive scheme concentrates samples where rendering error is high, and the bubble loss penalizes deviations from the expected SDF structure near small surfaces. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, cameraparams, model, stage): """ Renders a single ray using I2-SDF. stage: 'geometry' for Stage 1, 'material' for Stage 2. """ # 1. Sample points along the ray # In practice, I2-SDF uses error-guided adaptive sampling. # For simplicity, we assume M samples are selected. tvalues = getadaptivesamples(rayorigin, raydirection, model, stage) points = rayorigin + tvalues[:, None] raydirection # 2. Query Geometry and Radiance Fields # Fd predicts SDF and potentially normal sdfvalues, normals = model.Fd(points) # Transform SDF to density using learnable beta beta = model.beta density = computedensity(sdfvalues, beta) # Fc predicts radiance based on position and view direction radiance = model.Fc(points, raydirection) # 3. Volume Rendering Integration # Calculate opacity alpha from density and step size delta # delta is the distance between consecutive samples deltas = np.diff(tvalues, prepend=0) opacity = 1.0 - np.exp(-density deltas) # Calculate transmittance T # Ti = product(1 - alphaj) for j < i transmittance = np.cumprod(1.0 - opacity) # Shift transmittance for the first sample (T0 = 1) transmittance = np.roll(transmittance, 1) transmittance[0] = 1.0 # Weighted sum of radiance weights = transmittance opacity color = np.sum(weights[:, None] radiance, axis=0) return color, density, opacity def computedensity(sdf, beta): """ Converts SDF to volume density using the piecewise exponential function. """ density = np.zeroslike(sdf) maskneg = sdf < 0 maskpos = ~maskneg # For d(x) < 0: sigma = (1/beta) (1 - exp(d(x)/beta)) density[maskneg] = (1.0 / beta) (1.0 - np.exp(sdf[maskneg] / beta)) # For d(x) >= 0: sigma = (1/(2beta)) exp(-d(x)/(2beta)) density[maskpos] = (1.0 / (2.0 beta)) np.exp(-sdf[maskpos] / (2.0 beta)) return density def trainstage1(model, images, depths, normals): """ Stage 1: Train Geometry (Fd), Radiance (Fc), and Emitter Semantic (Fe). """ for image, depth, normal in zip(images, depths, normals): # Render image using current model renderedimage = renderimage(image.cameraparams, model, stage='geometry') # Compute loss against ground truth image lossrgb = mseloss(renderedimage, image.rgb) # Compute SDF loss against depth/normal priors if available losssdf = computesdfloss(model.Fd, depth, normal) # Compute emitter semantic loss lossemitter = computeemitterloss(model.Fe, image) totalloss = lossrgb + losssdf + lossemitter model.updategradients(totalloss) def trainstage2(model, images): """ Stage 2: Train Material (Fa, Frho) and Emission (L). Fd, Fc, Fe are frozen. """ for image in images: # Decompose radiance using Monte Carlo raytracing on the fixed SDF # This step separates material and emission from the total radiance materialmap, emissionmap = decomposeradiancemontecarlo( image.cameraparams, model.Fd, model.Fc, model.Fe) # Train material and emission fields to match the decomposed targets # and the original image lossmaterial = trainmaterialfields(model.Fa, model.Frho, materialmap) lossemission = trainemissionfield(model.L, emissionmap) totalloss = lossmaterial + lossemission model.updategradients(totalloss) Complexity: Training is iterative and requires multiple passes over the dataset. Stage 1 is similar to NeRF but with SDF regularization. Stage 2 involves Monte Carlo raytracing, which is computationally more expensive per sample than direct volume rendering but allows for physically based decomposition. Strengths: Superior reconstruction quality for complex indoor scenes with fine-grained small objects due to adaptive sampling and bubble loss. Enables intrinsic decomposition (relighting, editing) which standard NeRF lacks. Limitations: Requires a two-stage training process, increasing implementation complexity. The decomposition relies on the accuracy of the SDF and emitter semantics; errors in Stage 1 propagate to Stage 2. When to use: When the goal is not just novel view synthesis but also scene editing, relighting, or when the scene contains many small, high-frequency details that standard NeRF struggles to reconstruct. I2-SDF was introduced in 2023 by Jingen Zhu et al.. It builds upon the success of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [18] and neural SDF representations [43] but addresses their limitations in handling complex indoor scenes and intrinsic decomposition. The method was developed to enable physically based scene editing and relighting, which are difficult with standard volume rendering approaches. name: SDF-based Volume Rendering with Laplacian CDF
head: Laplacian opacity transformation, VolSDF variant
body: This method renders geometry by predicting a Signed Distance Function (SDF) value s and a variance parameter \beta from a neural network, then transforming s into volume opacity \sigma using the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) of a Laplacian distribution. It builds on Surface and SDF-Based Representations by providing a differentiable mechanism to extract tight surfaces while enabling efficient inverse CDF sampling. Unlike I2-SDF, which uses a piecewise exponential density definition, this approach explicitly models the opacity via the Laplacian CDF, allowing \beta to vary spatially to control surface tightness locally. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a viewing direction \mathbf{v}. Output: Opacity \sigma \in [0, 1], radiance color \mathbf{c}, and geometry features \mathbf{f}{geo}. Data Structures Triplane Features (\mathbf{T}x): Three aligned 2D feature grids (e.g., resolution 512 \times 512, feature size 32). For a point \mathbf{x}, features are gathered by projecting \mathbf{x} onto the three axis-aligned planes and taking the Hadamard product of the resulting vectors. MLP Architecture: MLPSDF: Takes positional encoding of \mathbf{x} and triplane features \mathbf{T}x. Outputs scalar SDF s, scalar variance \beta, and geometry feature vector \mathbf{f}{geo}. MLPc: Takes positional encoding of viewing direction \mathbf{v} and geometry features \mathbf{f}{geo}. Outputs radiance \mathbf{c}. Parameters \beta: The variance of the Laplacian distribution, governing the "tightness" of the surface representation. It is a learnable output of MLPSDF and varies spatially across the volume. N: Number of samples per ray. Step-by-Step Method 1. Positional Encoding: Compute the positional encoding \text{PosEnc}(\mathbf{x}) for the input point \mathbf{x}. 2. Feature Gathering: Retrieve triplane features \mathbf{T}x by projecting \mathbf{x} to the three axis-aligned planes and computing the Hadamard product of the three resultant vectors. 3. SDF Prediction: Pass (\text{PosEnc}(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{T}x) to MLPSDF to obtain the SDF value s, variance \beta, and geometry features \mathbf{f}{geo}: (s, \beta, \mathbf{f}{geo}) = \text{MLPSDF}(\text{PosEnc}(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{T}x) Initialize the ReLU activations in MLPSDF as in SAL to ensure an approximately spherical SDF in early training. 4. Opacity Transformation: Transform s and \beta into opacity \sigma using the Laplacian CDF: \sigma = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} \exp\left(\frac{s}{\beta}\right) & \text{if } s \le 0 \\ 1 - \frac{1}{2} \exp\left(-\frac{s}{\beta}\right) & \text{if } s > 0 \end{cases} where s is the SDF value and \beta is the variance. 5. Radiance Prediction: Compute radiance \mathbf{c} using the geometry features and viewing direction: \mathbf{c} = \text{MLP}c(\text{PosEnc}(\mathbf{v}), \mathbf{f}{geo}) 6. Inverse CDF Sampling: To sample points near the surface, generate random numbers ui \in [0, 1] and transform them to sample distances ti using the inverse CDF \Phi^{-1}: ti = \Phi^{-1}(ui) where \Phi is the CDF derived from the Laplacian distribution defined by s and \beta, and ui is sorted in increasing order. 7. Rendering: Approximate the volumetric rendering integral for a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} by summing the contributions of samples: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i where Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the transmittance, \alphai is the opacity \sigma at sample i, and \mathbf{c}i is the radiance. Stratification During training, stratify the random numbers ui by dividing the unit interval into bins and taking a sample from each bin to lower rendering variance, especially at low sample counts N. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import torch def laplaciancdf(s, beta): """ Transforms SDF value s and variance beta into opacity sigma using the Laplacian CDF. """ # Clamp beta to avoid division by zero beta = torch.clamp(beta, min=1e-6) sigma = torch.where( s <= 0, 0.5 torch.exp(s / beta), 1.0 - 0.5 torch.exp(-s / beta)) return sigma def inverselaplaciancdf(u, s, beta): """ Computes sample distance t from random number u, given SDF s and variance beta. Note: The exact inverse CDF formula for the Laplacian distribution centered at s with scale beta is required. The source defines ti = Phi^{-1}(ui) but does not provide the explicit closed-form inverse in the text. Implementation requires deriving the inverse of the piecewise exponential CDF defined in laplaciancdf. """ # Placeholder for the actual inverse CDF derivation # The CDF is: # F(t) = 0.5 exp((t-s)/beta) for t < s # F(t) = 1 - 0.5 exp(-(t-s)/beta) for t >= s # Inverting this for t given u requires solving for t. # This step is marked as because the explicit inverse # formula is not provided in the source text. raise NotImplementedError("Inverse Laplacian CDF formula not provided in source.") def renderray(x, v, triplanes, mlpsdf, mlpc, numsamples): """ Renders a single ray using SDF-based volume rendering with Laplacian CDF. """ # 1. Positional Encoding posencx = positionalencoding(x) # Standard NeRF positional encoding # 2. Feature Gathering # Project x to axis-aligned planes and take Hadamard product tx = gathertriplanefeatures(triplanes, x) # 3. SDF Prediction s, beta, fgeo = mlpsdf(posencx, tx) # 4. Opacity Transformation sigma = laplaciancdf(s, beta) # 5. Radiance Prediction posencv = positionalencoding(v) c = mlpc(posencv, fgeo) # 6. Sampling # Generate sorted random numbers u = torch.rand(numsamples) u = torch.sort(u).values # Stratification: divide unit interval into bins # ui = (i + rand()) / N # i = 0,..., N-1 # This is a common stratification technique mentioned in context indices = torch.arange(numsamples) ustratified = (indices + torch.rand(numsamples)) / numsamples # Sample distances using inverse CDF # t = inverselaplaciancdf(ustratified, s, beta) # Note: In practice, t represents the distance along the ray. # The source implies ti are sample distances derived from the CDF. # For a ray r(t) = o + td, we need to map these to 3D points. # 7. Rendering # Compute transmittance and accumulated color # This part depends on the specific sampling strategy (uniform vs adaptive) # The source mentions "uniform samples" for probing and "inverse CDF" for surface concentration. # The final rendering equation is provided as a sum. return c, sigma, s, beta Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples N and the cost of the MLP evaluations. The use of inverse CDF sampling concentrates samples near the surface, potentially reducing the number of samples needed for high-fidelity geometry compared to uniform sampling. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the triplane features (e.g., 3 \times 512 \times 512 \times 32 floats) and the MLP weights. Strengths: Tight surface extraction due to the SDF representation; efficient sampling near the surface via inverse CDF; lower rendering variance with stratification. Limitations: Requires careful initialization (e.g., SAL initialization) to avoid degenerate SDFs early in training. The spatially varying \beta requires regularization to prevent instability. When to use: When high-fidelity geometry extraction is prioritized over texture, and when training a 3D GAN or differentiable renderer. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and simple uniform sampling suffices, or when the scene does not have well-defined surfaces. This method is described in "What You See is What You GAN: Rendering Every Pixel for High-Fidelity Geometry in 3D GANs". It builds upon VolSDF [72] and StyleSDF [45], improving upon NeRF [38] and EG3D [7] by incorporating stratified sampling and a triplane-based SDF representation. The use of the Laplacian CDF for opacity transformation was previously explored in VolSDF [72], but this method extends it by allowing \beta to vary spatially and integrating it into a GAN framework with triplane conditioning.
