name: Skeleton-Relative Encoding
head: A-NeRF Skeleton-Relative Encoding, Relative Encoding, Skeleton-Relative Input Encoding
body: Skeleton-Relative Encoding transforms 3D query positions and view directions into local bone-relative coordinate systems before processing them through a neural radiance field, explicitly incorporating domain knowledge of human body part linkage. Unlike standard NeRF which treats space as continuous and unstructured, this method reparameterizes the input space to respect the piece-wise rigidity of articulated motion, making it suitable for dynamic human avatars where global coordinate systems are insufficient. It sets itself apart from siblings like Mip-NeRF 360 MLP Architecture by replacing global positional encoding with bone-centric relative metrics, and from SUDS by relying on explicit skeleton transforms rather than implicit deformation fields. Inputs: World-space query position q \in \mathbb{R}^3. World-space view direction d \in \mathbb{R}^3. Skeleton pose parameters \thetak for frame k, defining bone transformations T(\thetak, m) for each bone m. Outputs: Combined encoding vector ek \in \mathbb{R}^D, which serves as the input to the density/color MLP F\phi. Skeleton Representation: A set of M bones (typically M=24 for a standard human skeleton, indices 1 to 24). Bone Transformation: T(\thetak, m) is a 4 \times 4 homogeneous transformation matrix mapping local bone coordinates to world coordinates for bone m at pose \thetak. Encoding Components: Relative Distance \tilde{v}k \in \mathbb{R}^M: Scalar distance from q to each bone. Relative Direction \tilde{r}k \in \mathbb{R}^{3M}: Unit vector from q to each bone. Relative Ray Direction \tilde{d}k \in \mathbb{R}^{3M}: View direction rotated to local bone frame. 1. Compute Bone-relative Position: For each bone m \in \{1, \dots, M\}, transform the world query q into the local coordinate system of bone m using the inverse transformation: \tilde{q}{k,m} = T^{-1}(\thetak, m) q where \tilde{q}{k,m} \in \mathbb{R}^3. 2. Compute Relative Distance: Calculate the L2 norm of the bone-relative position to obtain the radial distance: \tilde{v}{k,m} = \| \tilde{q}{k,m} \|2 \in \mathbb{R} The vector of distances for all bones is \tilde{v}k = [\tilde{v}{k,1}, \dots, \tilde{v}{k,M}]. 3. Compute Relative Direction: Normalize the bone-relative position to capture orientation information: \tilde{r}{k,m} = \frac{\tilde{q}{k,m}}{\| \tilde{q}{k,m} \|2} \in \mathbb{R}^3 The vector of directions is \tilde{r}k = [\tilde{r}{k,1}, \dots, \tilde{r}{k,M}]. 4. Compute Relative Ray Direction: Rotate the incoming world-space view direction d by the rotational part of the inverse bone-to-world transformation: \tilde{d}{k,m} = [T^{-1}(\thetak, m)]{3\times3} d \in \mathbb{R}^3 where [T^{-1}(\thetak, m)]{3\times3} is the upper-left 3 \times 3 rotation submatrix. The vector of ray directions is \tilde{d}k = [\tilde{d}{k,1}, \dots, \tilde{d}{k,M}]. 5. Apply Cutoff Function: To prevent distant bones from influencing the prediction, apply a sigmoid-based cutoff function h(\cdot) to the distance and ray direction encodings: h(\tilde{v}{k,m}) = 1 - S(\tau (\tilde{v}{k,m} - t)) where S(\cdot) is the sigmoid function, t is the cutoff threshold, and \tau controls the sharpness of the cutoff. 6. Construct Final Encoding: Combine the components into the final input vector ek. Positional Encoding \Gamma(\cdot) is applied to the relative distance and relative ray direction, but not to the relative direction \tilde{r}k. ek = [h(\tilde{v}k) \odot \Gamma(\tilde{v}k), \quad \tilde{r}k, \quad h(\tilde{v}k) \odot \Gamma(\tilde{d}k)] Here, \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. \Gamma(\cdot) is the hierarchical sinusoidal positional encoding defined in the parent article Model Architecture and Encoding. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def skeletonrelativeencoding(q, d, bonetransformsinv, t=1.0, tau=10.0, L=10): """ Computes the skeleton-relative encoding for a query point and view direction. Args: q: np.array, shape (3,), world-space query position. d: np.array, shape (3,), world-space view direction. bonetransformsinv: list of np.array, shape (4, 4), inverse bone-to-world transforms for M bones. t: float, cutoff threshold for the sigmoid function. tau: float, sharpness of the cutoff. L: int, number of frequency bands for positional encoding. Returns: ek: np.array, the combined encoding vector. """ M = len(bonetransformsinv) # Lists to store components for each bone reldistances = [] reldirections = [] relraydirections = [] for m in range(M): # Step 1: Bone-relative position # Tinv is 4x4, q is (3,). We treat q as (3,1) for matrix mult or handle manually. # Tinv @ [q, 1] gives [x, y, z, w]. We take the first 3 components. qhomogeneous = np.append(q, 1.0) qlocalhomogeneous = bonetransformsinv[m] @ qhomogeneous qlocal = qlocalhomogeneous[:3] # Step 2: Relative Distance vm = np.linalg.norm(qlocal) reldistances.append(vm) # Step 3: Relative Direction # Avoid division by zero if q is exactly at the bone origin if vm < 1e-8: rm = np.zeros(3) else: rm = qlocal / vm reldirections.append(rm) # Step 4: Relative Ray Direction # Extract 3x3 rotation part of the inverse transform Rinv = bonetransformsinv[m][:3,:3] dlocal = Rinv @ d relraydirections.append(dlocal) # Convert to arrays vk = np.array(reldistances) # Shape (M,) rk = np.array(reldirections) # Shape (M, 3) dk = np.array(relraydirections) # Shape (M, 3) # Step 5: Cutoff Function # Sigmoid: 1 / (1 + exp(-x)) sigmoidinput = tau (vk - t) h = 1.0 - (1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-sigmoidinput))) # Step 6: Positional Encoding and Combination # Apply PE to distances # Gamma(v) returns a vector of size 2L for each scalar v # We apply it element-wise to the array vk vpe = positionalencoding(vk, L) # Shape (M, 2L) # Apply PE to ray directions # Gamma(d) is applied to each component of dk? # The source says Gamma(dk). In standard NeRF, PE is applied to each scalar component. # dk is (M, 3). We flatten to (3M,) or apply per component. # Standard PE: for scalar p, returns (sin(2^0 pi p), cos(2^0 pi p),...) # So for vector dk, we apply PE to each of the 3 components for each bone. dpeflat = positionalencoding(dk.flatten(), L) # Shape (3M, 2L) dpe = dpeflat.reshape(M, 3 2 L) # Shape (M, 6L) # Apply cutoff h to the PE outputs # h is (M,). vpe is (M, 2L). Broadcast h to (M, 1) vpecropped = vpe h[:, np.newaxis] dpecropped = dpe h[:, np.newaxis] # Concatenate: [h(v)Gamma(v), r, h(d)Gamma(d)] # r is (M, 3) # vpecropped is (M, 2L) # dpecropped is (M, 6L) ek = np.concatenate([vpecropped, rk, dpecropped], axis=1) return ek def positionalencoding(values, L): """ Applies hierarchical sinusoidal positional encoding to a 1D array of values. Args: values: np.array, shape (N,), scalar values to encode. L: int, number of frequency bands. Returns: encoded: np.array, shape (N, 2L). """ N = len(values) encoded = np.zeros((N, 2 L)) for i in range(L): freq = 2i np.pi encoded[:, 2i] = np.sin(values freq) encoded[:, 2i+1] = np.cos(values freq) return encoded Number of Bones (M): 24, corresponding to indices 1 to 24 of the human skeleton. Cutoff Threshold (t): Not given in the sources. Sharpness (\tau): Not given in the sources. Frequency Bands (L): Not given in the sources (inherited from parent Model Architecture and Encoding). Dimensionality Explosion: Using bone-relative position (\tilde{q}{k,m}) instead of relative distance (\tilde{v}{k,m}) increases the input dimensionality by an order of magnitude, which can hinder learning. The method prefers relative distance for lower dimensionality and better reconstruction accuracy. Relative Direction Encoding: The relative direction \tilde{r}k is passed directly into the final encoding ek without subsequent positional encoding (PE). Applying PE to direction vectors is not beneficial in this context. Ambiguity: While bone-relative position removes ambiguities of assigning a query to a single part, the radial distance encoding naturally captures spherically shaped limbs and is robust to the ill-posed association to a single part. Maps the query q to local coordinates of each bone. Sets itself apart by preserving full 3D local structure but suffers from high dimensionality. Choose when local geometric detail per bone is critical and computational budget allows. Computes the L2 norm from q to each bone. Sets itself apart by being lower-dimensional and capturing radial symmetry of limbs. This is the preferred encoding in the final A-NeRF model. Normalizes the bone-relative position vector. Sets itself apart by providing orientation information without PE. Always used in conjunction with distance encoding. Rotates the view direction into the local bone frame. Sets itself apart by enabling view-dependent appearance modeling relative to the body part. A sigmoid-based weighting mechanism. Sets itself apart by localizing the influence of each bone, preventing distant bones from affecting the prediction. Time Complexity: O(M \cdot L) per query point, where M is the number of bones and L is the number of frequency bands. The transformation T^{-1} is O(1) per bone. Memory Complexity: O(M \cdot L) for the encoding vector. The skeleton transforms must be stored or computed on the fly. Strengths: Incorporates explicit domain knowledge of human articulation. Invariant to global shift and rotation of the person. Preserves piece-wise rigidity of articulated motion. Lower dimensionality compared to full bone-relative position encoding. Limitations: Requires a skeleton pose estimator for initialization and runtime. Performance depends on the accuracy of the skeleton tracking. Does not model complex soft-tissue deformation (muscle bulging) as explicitly as parametric surface models, though it approximates it via the neural field. When to use: Dynamic human avatar rendering where pose information is available or can be estimated. When not to use: Static scenes, scenes without articulated structures, or when skeleton tracking is unreliable. Skeleton-Relative Encoding was introduced in A-NeRF: Articulated Neural Radiance Fields for Learning Human Shape, Appearance, and Pose by Gkioxari et al. (2021). The method was developed to address the limitations of standard NeRF in modeling dynamic humans, where global coordinates fail to capture the rigid motion of body parts. It inverts the approach of parametric models like SMPL: instead of deforming a surface, it deforms the query space. The work builds on the foundational NeRF architecture Model Architecture and Encoding and integrates it with articulated skeleton data. name: Random Offset Annealed Fourier Encoding
head: ROAFE
body: Random Offset Annealed Fourier Encoding (ROAFE) is a positional encoding scheme for 3D coordinates that combines Fourier basis functions with random Gaussian offsets and an annealing schedule to improve the optimization landscape for neural radiance fields. It addresses the axis-alignment artifacts and striping issues inherent in standard NeRF encoding by breaking symmetry through random shifts, while using a truncated Hann window to gradually introduce high-frequency details. It is primarily used in the SAMURAI framework. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D coordinate vector x \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: An encoded vector \gamma(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{3+6L}, where L is the number of frequency bands. Data Structures: R \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times 3}: Matrix of random Gaussian offsets, sampled from \mathcal{N}(0, 0.1). \alpha \in [0, L]: Annealing parameter, typically annealed from 0 to L over a fixed number of training steps (e.g., 50,000 steps). L: Number of frequency bands. Default value is 10. Formulas: The encoding is defined as: \gamma(x) = (x, \Gamma1(x; \alpha), \dots, \Gamma{L-1}(x; \alpha)) Note: The source notation uses indices 1 to L-1 for the frequency components, implying L total bands including the input or a specific indexing convention. However, the text states "10 Random Offset Annealed Fourier Frequencies" and the formula sums up to L components if we consider the range. The source formula (1) lists \Gamma1 \dots \Gamma{L-1}. Let us strictly follow the source's indexing: \gamma(x) = (x, \Gamma1, \dots, \Gamma{L-1}) Each frequency component \Gammak for k \in \{1, \dots, L-1\} is computed as: \Gammak(x; \alpha) = wk(\alpha) \left[ \sin(2^k x + 2^k Rk), \cos(2^k x + 2^k Rk) \right] where Rk is the k-th row of the offset matrix R (a vector in \mathbb{R}^3). The annealing weight wk(\alpha) is a truncated Hann window: wk(\alpha) = \frac{1 - \cos(\pi \cdot \text{clamp}(\alpha - k, 0, 1))}{2} Here, \text{clamp}(v, 0, 1) restricts v to the range [0, 1]. Parameters: L = 10: Number of frequency bands. R \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.1): Random offsets. \alpha: Annealing parameter, annealed over 50,000 steps. Direction encoding: 4 non-annealed and non-offset Fourier frequencies are used for the view direction d. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def randomoffsetannealedfourierencoding(x, L=10, alpha=0.0, R=None): """ Computes the Random Offset Annealed Fourier Encoding for a batch of 3D coordinates. Args: x: numpy array of shape (N, 3), batch of 3D coordinates. L: int, number of frequency bands. alpha: float, annealing parameter in [0, L]. R: numpy array of shape (L, 3), random offsets. If None, sampled from N(0, 0.1). Returns: numpy array of shape (N, 3 + 6(L-1)), the encoded vector. Boundary Conditions: The clamp function in the weight calculation ensures wk is 0 when \alpha < k and 1 when \alpha > k+1, providing a smooth transition. name: NeuRay
head: Neural Rays
body: NeuRay is an occlusion-aware image-based rendering method that represents a scene by estimating occlusion probabilities (hitting probabilities) from input views to arbitrary 3D points, enabling efficient novel view synthesis. Unlike standard radiance field methods that treat volume density as a continuous scalar, NeuRay explicitly models visibility to handle feature inconsistency caused by occlusions, particularly in sparse or 360-degree captures. It differs from sibling methods like IBRNet by integrating a visibility encoder and using spherical harmonics to fit anisotropic colors, allowing it to outperform baselines in generalization and fine-tuning settings where occlusions are prevalent. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of N input images with known camera poses (intrinsics and extrinsics). For rendering a test view, a subset of Nw neighboring input images (working views) is selected. Outputs: A synthesized RGB image for the test view, and optionally depth maps. Data Structures 1. Cost Volume: Constructed using Ns=3 neighboring source views. Dimensions are H/4 \times W/4 \times D, where D=64 is the number of disparity planes. 2. Visibility Feature: A feature map of size H/4 \times W/4 \times 32 generated by the Initialization Network and refined by the Visibility Encoder. 3. Spherical Harmonics Coefficients: For each sample point, a vector \boldsymbol{\theta}i \in \mathbb{R}^{16} representing SH coefficients up to degree 3. 4. Hitting Probability: A scalar \hat{h}i representing the probability that a point pi is visible from the test view, derived from a mixture of logistics distributions. Network Architecture The model consists of shared encoders and task-specific decoders for coarse and fine stages. 1. Image Encoder: A ResNet with 13 residual blocks, outputting a feature map with 32 channels. Convolution layers use ReLU; batch normalization is replaced by instance normalization. 2. Initialization Network: Inputs: Image feature (H/4 \times W/4 \times 64), Depth regression (H/4 \times W/4 \times 32), Cost Volume (H/4 \times W/4 \times 1). Structure: Conv3x3(32) \rightarrow ResBlock(32) \rightarrow Conv1x1(32). Output: Visibility Feature (H/4 \times W/4 \times 32). 3. Visibility Encoder: Inputs: Visibility Feature (H/4 \times W/4 \times 32), Image feature (H/4 \times W/4 \times 96). Structure: Conv3x3(32) \rightarrow ResBlock(32) \rightarrow Conv1x1(32). Output: Refined Visibility Feature (H/4 \times W/4 \times 32). 4. Decoder F (Distribution): Contains 5 sub-networks, each with 3 fully-connected layers. Predicts \mu1, \mu2, \sigma1, \sigma2 and mixing weight w0 (where w1 = 1 - w0). Uses ReLU for hidden layers, SoftPlus/Sigmoid for output. 5. Aggregation Networks (Coarse/Fine): Network \mathcal{M} (Feature Aggregation): Inputs are Visibility features (N \times K \times 32), View directions (N \times K \times 3), Image features (N \times K \times 3). Process: MLP(1,32,32) on visibility, MLP(3,32,32) on directions, MLP(32,32,1) on image features. Element-wise product. MLP(32,32,32). Element-wise plus. MLP(192,64,32). Transformer. MLP(16,1). Output: Aggregated feature. Network \mathcal{A} (Alpha): Inputs are Mean (N \times 1 \times 32) and Var (N \times 1 \times 32). MLP(35,16,8,1) followed by Softmax. Output: Alpha value \alphai \in [0,1]. Network \mathcal{B} (Blending): Inputs are Mean (N \times 1 \times 32) and Var (N \times 1 \times 32). MLP(64,32,16) followed by sigmoid. Output: Blending weights (N \times K \times 1). Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: Construct a cost volume using COLMAP patch-match stereo and Ns=3 source views. Pass image features through the Image Encoder, Initialization Network, and Visibility Encoder to obtain the Refined Visibility Feature. 2. Ray Sampling: For a test ray r(\lambda) = o + \lambda d, sample K{t,1} points for the coarse stage and K{t,2} points for the fine stage. Default values are K{t,1}=64, K{t,2}=64. Use the coarse model to estimate hitting probabilities \hat{h}i for all coarse points. Perform coarse-to-fine sampling: select fine points based on the distribution defined by the coarse hitting probabilities. 3. Visibility and Alpha Computation: For each sample point pi, compute the hitting probability \hat{h}i using the mixture of Nl=2 logistics distributions parameterized by the Decoder F. Compute the alpha value \alphai = \mathcal{A}(\mathbf{f}i), where \mathbf{f}i is the aggregated feature. The network \mathcal{A} assigns large \alphai when features from visible input views are consistent. 4. Color Computation (Radiance Field Rendering): Compute the color \mathbf{c}i for point pi using the color blending network \mathcal{B}: \mathbf{c}i = \mathcal{B}(\mathbf{f}i, \{\mathbf{f}{i,j}; \mathbf{r}{i,j} - \mathbf{r}; \mathbf{c}{i,j}; v{i,j}\}) where \mathbf{r}{i,j} is the view direction from the j-th input view to pi, \mathbf{c}{i,j} is the projected color, and v{i,j} is the visibility. Render the final pixel color \hat{c} using alpha compositing weighted by hitting probabilities: \hat{c} = \sumi \mathbf{c}i \hat{h}i (Note: The source describes direct rendering as \hat{c} = \sumi \hat{c}i \hat{h}i, but standard volume rendering composites alpha. The text states "compute output color by \hat{c} = \sumi \hat{c}i \hat{h}i" in the context of direct rendering, but for the main radiance field, it blends colors. We follow the explicit formula given for direct rendering and the blending description for the main method). 5. Spherical Harmonics Fitting (Direct Rendering / Anisotropic Color): To represent anisotropic colors, fit a function R(\mathbf{r}; \boldsymbol{\theta}i) on the sphere for each point pi using spherical harmonics. Solve the linear least squares problem for coefficients \boldsymbol{\theta}i: \min{\boldsymbol{\theta}i} \sumj \tilde{h}{i,j}(z{i,j}, z{i,j}+li) \|R(\mathbf{r}{i,j}; \boldsymbol{\theta}i) - \mathbf{c}{i,j}\|^2 + \boldsymbol{\theta}i^\intercal \boldsymbol{\Lambda} \boldsymbol{\theta}i where \tilde{h}{i,j} is the hitting probability, \boldsymbol{\Lambda} is a diagonal regularization matrix with elements (0, 0.001, 0.005, 0.01) for degrees 0 to 3, and R is the SH basis function. The color is then computed as \mathbf{c}i = R(\mathbf{r}; \boldsymbol{\theta}i). 6. Training and Loss: Depth Loss: \ell{depth} = \sum \|\mu1 - z{in}\|^2, where \mu1 is the mean of the first logistics distribution and z{in} is input depth from the cost volume. Color Loss: The difference between predicted and ground truth colors is weighted by hitting probabilities to prevent occluded rays from interfering. Visibility Memorization: During training, predicted hitting probabilities hi are memorized. If a point is invisible to view A, this is used to refine visibility predictions for other views (e.g., view D) in subsequent steps. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def neurayrender(inputimages, cameraposes, testviewpose, numworkingviews=8): """ Renders a test view using NeuRay. """ # 1. Select Working Views workingviews = selectnearestviews(testviewpose, cameraposes, numworkingviews) # 2. Construct Cost Volume # Uses Ns=3 source views and D=64 planes costvolume = constructcostvolume(workingviews, depthplanes=64) # 3. Encode Features # Image Encoder: ResNet-13 with Instance Norm imagefeatures = imageencoder(workingviews) # Depth Regression (from Cost Volume or COLMAP) depthregression = getdepthfromcostvolume(costvolume) # Initialization Network visibilityfeature = initializationnetwork(imagefeatures, depthregression, costvolume) # Visibility Encoder refinedvisibility = visibilityencoder(visibilityfeature, imagefeatures) # 4. Sample Points along Test Ray # Coarse stage: 64 points coarsepoints = sampleray(testviewpose, numsamples=64) # Compute Coarse Hitting Probabilities # Decoder F predicts params for mixture of 2 logistics distributions coarseparams = distributiondecoder(refinedvisibility, coarsepoints) coarsehittingprobs = computelogisticsmixture(coarseparams) # Fine stage: Sample based on coarse probabilities finepoints = samplefine(coarsepoints, coarsehittingprobs, numsamples=64) # 5. Compute Alpha and Color for Fine Points aggregatedfeatures = featureaggregationnetwork( refinedvisibility, finepoints, workingviews) # Alpha Network A alphavalues = alphanetwork(aggregatedfeatures) # Color Blending Network B colors = colorblendingnetwork( aggregatedfeatures, workingviews, finepoints) # 6. Render # Direct rendering formula from source: chat = sum(ci hi) # Note: Standard volume rendering uses alpha compositing. # The source explicitly states: "compute output color by chat = sum(ci hi)" # for direct rendering. For the main radiance field, it blends colors. # We implement the explicit sum formula provided for the final output. finalcolor = np.zeros(3) for i, point in enumerate(finepoints): hi = coarsehittingprobs[i] # Or refined hitting prob ci = colors[i] finalcolor += ci hi return finalcolor def sphericalharmonicsfit(point, workingviews, hittingprobs): """ Fits spherical harmonics to anisotropic color at a point. """ # Degree 3 SH, theta in R^16 # Lambda diagonal: [0, 0.001, 0.005, 0.01] lambdadiag = np.array([0, 0.001, 0.005, 0.01]) # Construct matrix A and vector b for least squares: (A^T A + Lambda) theta = A^T b # Sum over visible views j Amatrix = [] bvector = [] for j, view in enumerate(workingviews): hij = hittingprobs[j] rij = viewdirection(view, point) cij = projectcolor(view, point) # SH basis evaluation basis = evaluateshbasis(rij, degree=3) # Weighted by hitting probability Amatrix.append(hij basis) bvector.append(hij cij) Amat = np.array(Amatrix) bvec = np.array(bvector) # Regularization matrix Lambda = np.diag(lambdadiag) # Solve (A^T A + Lambda) theta = A^T b ATA = Amat.T @ Amat ATb = Amat.T @ bvec theta = np.linalg.solve(ATA + Lambda, ATb) return theta def evaluateshbasis(direction, degree): """ Evaluates spherical harmonics basis functions up to given degree. Returns vector of size (degree+1)^2. """ # Standard SH basis evaluation # x, y, z = direction # Degree 0: 1 # Degree 1: y, z, x # Degree 2: xy, yz, z^2-1, xz, x^2-y^2 # Degree 3:... # Implementation details omitted for brevity, standard math operation pass Parameters D=64: Number of planes in cost volume. Nl=2: Number of logistics distributions. K{t,1}=64, K{t,2}=64: Sample points in coarse/fine stages. Ns=3: Neighboring source views for cost volume. SH Degree: 3, resulting in \boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^{16}. Regularization \boldsymbol{\Lambda}: Diagonal elements (0, 0.001, 0.005, 0.01). Optimizer: Adam (\beta1=0.999, \beta2=0.9). Batch Size: 512 rays per step. Learning Rate: Generalization 2 \times 10^{-4} (decay half every 100k steps); Finetuning 1 \times 10^{-4} (decay half every 100k steps). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Invisible Regions: NeuRay cannot render regions invisible to all working views, even if visible in other input views, because it is image-based. Textureless/Cluttered Regions: Feature matching struggles in textureless or cluttered complex regions (e.g., Ficus), leading to view inconsistency and artifacts. Generalization Speed: In generalization settings, predicted visibility is often inaccurate, preventing high-quality rendering with very few sample points. Speeding up rendering requires accurate surface location estimation, which is only reliable in finetuned models. Direct Rendering Artifacts: Direct rendering produces meaningful results but artifacts occur on edges. Time Complexity: Rendering time is significantly reduced compared to NeRF. On the DTU 'birds' dataset, using 4-8 fine sample points speeds up rendering from 30s to ~3s (10x speedup). Memory Complexity: Uses a cost volume of size H/4 \times W/4 \times 64 and feature maps of size H/4 \times W/4 \times 32. The image encoder is lighter than IBRNet. Performance: NeRF Synthetic (Lego): NeuRay-Ft achieves 30.63 PSNR in ~32 minutes, comparable to NeRF's 30.27 PSNR in ~9.5 hours. LLFF (Nw=8): NeuRay 27.06 PSNR vs IBRNet 26.87 PSNR. LLFF (Nw=2): NeuRay 24.86 PSNR vs IBRNet 21.72 PSNR. Generalization (Lego, N=100): NeuRay 28.41 PSNR vs IBRNet 25.64 PSNR. Strengths: Occlusion-aware, handles sparse 360-degree captures better than IBRNet, recovers details more clearly than NeRF with fewer training steps, fast finetuning. Limitations: Fails on regions invisible to all working views, struggles with textureless regions, generalization mode requires more samples for high quality. When to Use: Novel view synthesis with sparse or 360-degree input views, especially where occlusions are present. Suitable for scenarios requiring fast finetuning. When Not to Use: Scenes with large invisible regions relative to working views, or highly textureless environments. NeuRay was introduced in the paper "Neural Rays for Occlusion-aware Image-based Rendering". It addresses the limitations of existing image-based rendering methods like IBRNet, which suffer from feature inconsistency due to occlusions in sparse captures. By explicitly modeling occlusion probabilities, NeuRay refines scene representation and provides better occlusion inference during finetuning. It is used on datasets such as LLFF, NeRF synthetic (Lego), and DTU. Neural Rays for Occlusion-aware Image-based Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.00767, fetched 2026-10-26

name: SAMURAI
head: Joint optimization of shape, BRDF, cameras, and illuminations, Shape and Material from Unconstrained Real-World Arbitrary Image Collections
body: SAMURAI is a joint optimization framework that estimates 3D shape, BRDF material properties, per-image illumination, camera poses, and camera intrinsics from unconstrained in-the-wild image collections with varying backgrounds and illuminations. It addresses the limitations of prior methods like NeRF and Neural-PIL by handling imperfect segmentation masks, arbitrary camera distances, and multiple illumination conditions without requiring correspondences or GAN-style training. Unlike SUDS which focuses on differentiable rendering for inverse problems, SAMURAI specifically targets the decomposition of radiance into shape, material, and illumination from single-view-like unconstrained data. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A collection of q object images Cj \in \mathbb{R}^{sj \times 3} with varying resolutions, backgrounds, and illuminations. Rough camera pose quadrants annotated with 3 binary questions: Left vs. Right, Above vs. Below, Front vs. Back. Automatically estimated foreground segmentation masks Mj \in \{0, 1\}^{s \times 1} (e.g., via U2-Net), which may be noisy. Outputs: A 3D neural volume representing shape and material. Explicit meshes with BRDF textures extracted from the volume. Per-image camera poses and intrinsics. Per-image latent illumination vectors. Data Structures and Network Architecture The method uses a single fine/decomposition network (no coarse network) implemented as an MLP with 8 layers of 128 features. Input Encoding: Input coordinates \mathbf{x} and view directions \mathbf{d} are processed using hierarchical positional encoding \gamma(\cdot). To prevent axis-aligned artifacts, Gaussian distributed noise is added to the Fourier embedding frequencies as offsets to the logarithmically spaced frequencies. Output Heads: Density: A layer with 1 feature output predicts volume density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}. BRDF/Normal: The main network features are compressed to 16 features and expanded to predict BRDF parameters \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^5 (base color \mathbf{bc} \in \mathbb{R}^3, metallic \mathbf{bm} \in \mathbb{R}^1, roughness \mathbf{br} \in \mathbb{R}) and unit-length surface normal \mathbf{n} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Radiance: An MLP with a hidden layer predicts view-dependent radiance \tilde{\mathbf{c}}. Illumination: Per-image latent illumination vectors \mathbf{z}{jl} \in \mathbb{R}^{128} are estimated. Camera Parameterization: Uses a 'look-at' parameterization stored as offsets to initial parameters: 3D look-at vector \mathbf{r}j \in \mathbb{R}^3, scalar up rotation uj \in [-\pi, \pi], 3D camera position \mathbf{t}j \in \mathbb{R}^3, and focal length fj \in \mathbb{R}. Vertical focal length offsets are compressed as \hat{f}j = fj / \sqrt{h}, where h is image height. Ray Sampling and Bounds Sampling: 128 points are sampled along the ray in fixed steps. Bounds: Unlike fixed near/far planes, bounds are defined by a world-space sphere with radius v (diameter 1). For a camera origin \mathbf{o}, the near bound is |\mathbf{o}| - v and the far bound is |\mathbf{o}| + v. This allows arbitrary camera distances. Optimization Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize camera poses based on quadrant annotations and an initial Field of View of 53.13 degrees. Initialize Fourier frequencies with logarithmic spacing plus Gaussian noise offsets. 2. Camera Multiplex Optimization: For each image, optimize 4 randomly jittered poses around the quadrant center. Compute mask reconstruction loss L{Mask{ij}} for each camera i in the multiplex for image j. Calculate multiplex weights \mathbf{S}j \in \mathbb{R}^4: \mathbf{S}j = \text{softmax}(-\lambdas L{Mask{ij}}) where \lambdas is a scalar gradually increased during optimization. Update weights \mathbf{S}j using a memory bank and momentum across batches. Dynamically re-weight network losses: L{Networkj} = \sumi S{ji} L{Network{ij}}. 3. Posterior Scaling: Maintain a circular buffer of ~1000 elements containing recent mask and rendered image losses. Calculate mean \mul and standard deviation \sigmal of losses. Compute loss scalar spj: spj = \max\left(\tanh\left(\frac{\mul - (L{Maskj} + L{Imagej})}{\sigmal}\right) + 1, 1\right). Apply scaling: L{Networkj} = spj L{Networkj}. 4. Network and Camera Update: Optimize networks using Adam (LR 10^{-4}, decay order of magnitude every 300k steps). Optimize cameras using Adam (LR 3 \times 10^{-3}, decay order of magnitude every 70k steps). Camera optimization uses the same loss structure but does not apply posterior scaling, allowing badly initialized poses to recover. 5. Scheduling: Use fading variables \lambdab (fade direct color to BRDF), \lambdaa (scale specific losses), and \lambdac (increase resolution, reduce active multiplex cameras). Perform Fourier frequency annealing (BARF) in early stages. Delay focal length optimization to later stages. Loss Functions The total network loss is: L{Network} = \lambdab L{Image}(Cs, \tilde{\mathbf{c}}) + (1 - \lambdab) L{Image}(Cs, \hat{\mathbf{c}}) + L{Mask} + \lambdaa L{Init} + \lambda{ndir} L{ndir} + \lambda{Smooth} L{Smooth} + \lambda{Dec\Smooth} L{Dec\Smooth} + \lambda{Dec\Sparsity} L{Dec\Sparsity}. Image Loss: Charbonnier loss L{Image}(g, p) = \sqrt{(g - p)^2 + 0.001^2} between input color Cs and predicted color. Mask Loss: L{Mask} = L{BCE} + L{Background}, where L{BCE} is binary cross-entropy and L{Background} forces background samples to 0 (from NeRD). Initialization Loss: L{Init} = L{MSE}(Cs, \mathbf{bc}) to prevent illumination local minima. Normal Direction Loss: L{ndir} constrains normals to face the camera. BRDF Sparsity: L{Dec\Sparsity} = \frac{1}{N} \sumi |ei|, where ei is the BRDF embedding. BRDF Smoothness: L{Dec\Smooth} = \frac{1}{N} \sumi |f(\theta; ei) - f(\theta; ei + \epsilon)|, where \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.01^2). Camera Constraints: L{lookat}: L1 loss on look-at vector \mathbf{r}j. L{Bounds} = \max((v - |\mathbf{t}j|)^2, 0) to prevent cameras from going too far into the volume bound. Update Scheduling self.lambdas = min(self.lambdas + 0.001, 10.0) # Gradually increase # Update lambdab, lambdaa, lambdac based on stepcount # 2. Camera Multiplex Weight Update Lmaskmultiplex = [] for j in range(self.numimages): for i in range(self.nummultiplex): camparams = self.cameramultiplex[j][i] # Render rays for this camera color, alpha,,, = self.forward(...) Lmask, = self.computelosses(...) Lmaskmultiplex.append(Lmask) # Calculate weights Sj Lmasktensor = torch.stack(Lmaskmultiplex).view(self.numimages, self.nummultiplex) self.S = torch.softmax(-self.lambdas Lmasktensor, dim=1) # Update memory bank and momentum for S (simplified) self.updatemultiplexmemory() # 3. Posterior Scaling # Calculate recent loss stats from buffer meanloss, stdloss = self.getlossstats() sp = torch.clamp(torch.tanh((meanloss - Lmasktensor.mean(dim=1)) / stdloss) + 1, min=1.0) # 4. Network Optimization self.optimizernet.zerograd() totalloss = 0 for j in range(self.numimages): for i in range(self.nummultiplex): # Only optimize active cameras (controlled by lambdac) if torch.rand(1) < self.lambdac: camparams = self.cameramultiplex[j][i] # Forward pass color, alpha, density, brdf, normal = self.forward(...) # Compute losses Lnet, Lmask = self.computelosses(...) # Apply multiplex weight and posterior scaling Lnet = Lnet self.S[j, i] sp[j] totalloss += Lnet totalloss.backward() self.optimizernet.step() # 5. Camera Optimization self.optimizercam.zerograd() # Do NOT apply posterior scaling for camera optimization totalcamloss = 0 for j in range(self.numimages): for i in range(self.nummultiplex): camparams = self.cameramultiplex[j][i] # Forward pass with current cam params color, alpha,,, = self.forward(...) Lnet, = self.computelosses(...) # Add camera specific losses Lcam = Lnet + Llookat + Lbounds totalcamloss += Lcam.mean() # Mean loss for recovery totalcamloss.backward() self.optimizercam.step() def updatemultiplexmemory(self): # Update memory bank with recent losses and momentum for S pass def extractmesh(self): # Extract explicit mesh with BRDF texture from the learned neural volume pass Time Complexity: Rendering samples 128 points per ray. Optimization involves multiple cameras per image (multiplex), increasing memory and compute per step compared to single-camera NeRF. Adam optimizer is used for both network and cameras. Memory Complexity: Stores 4 camera poses per image in the multiplex. Requires a circular buffer of ~1000 elements for posterior scaling statistics. Performance: Handles in-the-wild images with varying illumination and background. Outperforms BARF on coarse poses and NeRD/Neural-PIL on unconstrained datasets. Strengths: Robust to noisy masks, arbitrary camera distances, and multiple illuminations. Does not require correspondences or GAN training. Limitations: Requires manual quadrant annotation (3-5 minutes per 80 images). Optimization is complex due to multiplex and posterior scaling. SAMURAI was proposed to tackle the challenge of estimating 3D shape, BRDF, and per-image camera pose and illumination from unconstrained in-the-wild online image collections. It addresses limitations of NeRF (fixed near/far planes, no BRDF) and Neural-PIL (requires perfect camera poses and segmentation). It is distinct from SCNeRF (no correspondences), BARF (handles extremely coarse poses), NeRF-- (no double training), and GNeRF (no GAN). name: AReT (Anatomy-Regularized TensoRF)
head: AReT NeRF, AReT framework, AReT model, Anatomy-Regularized TensoRF, Prior TensoRF v2, proposed AReT model
body: AReT is a scene-specific (patient-specific) inverse solver that reconstructs 3D lung nodule volumes from only three orthogonal Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs (DRRs: coronal, sagittal, axial) using a Tensorial Radiance Field (TensoRF) representation. It solves the problem of sparse-view medical reconstruction where standard TensoRF fails due to a density-parameterization dead zone that suppresses gradients. Unlike generative-prior approaches like MedNeRF, AReT is prior-free during training, relying instead on a corrected density initialization and anatomy-aware regularization (\ell1 sparsity and Total Variation smoothness) to enforce physiologically plausible attenuation distributions in the air-dominated thoracic cavity. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Three orthogonal DRRs (coronal, sagittal, axial) generated from a patient's ground-truth CT volume via Beer-Lambert forward projection. Camera poses are assigned based on the orthogonal projection directions. Outputs: A reconstructed 3D density field (linear attenuation coefficient \mu) and a segmented nodule volume. Data Structures: TensoRF Representation: A VM-rank-16 TensoRF model. The scene is represented by a set of low-rank tensor factors. Grid Resolution: A 64^3 grid is used for density queries. The voxel spacing is approximately [3.75, 1.875, 2.1875] mm. Memory: A 64^3 VM-rank-16 TensoRF requires approximately 14 GB VRAM (including gradient buffers) on an NVIDIA T4. Parameters: Density Shift (\Delta): Set to 0 (default in standard TensoRF is -10). This is critical to prevent gradient suppression. Scale (s): Set to 1 (default in standard TensoRF is 25). Regularization Weights: \lambda1 = 1 \times 10^{-4} (sparsity), \lambda2 = 1 \times 10^{-5} (TV smoothness). Optimizer: Adam. Learning rate 0.02 for grid parameters, 0.002 for MLP. Batch Size: 2048 rays per iteration. Iterations: 3000 total iterations. Alpha Mask Updates: Deterministic updates at iterations 1500 and 2500 to prune near-empty voxels. Random Seeds: torch.manualseed(0) and numpy.random.seed(0). Numbered Steps: 1. CT Preprocessing and HU Calibration: Load DICOM slices and sort by ImagePositionPatient Z-coordinate. Convert Hounsfield Units (HU) using RescaleSlope and RescaleIntercept. Apply lung-window clipping and linear normalization: v{norm} = \frac{HU - (-1000)}{400 - (-1000)} 2. DRR Simulation and Camera Pose Assignment: Generate three orthogonal DRRs (coronal, sagittal, axial) from the normalized CT volume using the Beer-Lambert forward model: I(r) = I0 \cdot \exp \left( - \int \mu(x) \, dx \right) where \mu(x) is approximated by summing normalized HU values along the projection direction. Assign camera poses corresponding to the orthogonal directions. 3. AReT Training: Initialize the TensoRF model with \Delta = 0 and s = 1. For each iteration i from 1 to 3000: Sample 2048 rays randomly. Render DRRs from the current TensoRF model. Compute Photometric Loss (L{photo}): Mean Squared Error (MSE) between rendered DRRs and input DRRs. Compute Regularization Losses: Sparsity Loss (L{sparse}): \ell1 norm of the density field. Smoothness Loss (L{TV}): Total Variation of the density field. Compute Total Loss: L = L{photo} + \lambda1 L{sparse} + \lambda2 L{TV} Update TensoRF parameters using Adam optimizer. If i \in \{1500, 2500\}, update the alpha occupancy mask to prune near-empty voxels. 4. Volumetric Reconstruction and Nodule Extraction: Query the converged density field on a 64^3 grid using getDenseAlpha. Perform a percentile threshold sweep on the non-zero density distribution for p \in \{85, 88, 90, 91, \dots, 99\}. For each threshold: Remove connected components with fewer than 10 voxels. Apply binary closing with a radius-2 spherical structuring element to fill boundary gaps. Identify connected components with equivalent sphere diameters in [5, 80] mm. Select the candidate whose equivalent sphere diameter is closest to the LIDC-IDRI annotated diameter for that patient. Compute physical volume: V = N{voxels} \times \prod \Delta xk where \Delta xk are the per-axis voxel spacings. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np def trainarect(ctvolume, annotations, patientid): # 1. Preprocessing ctnormalized = normalizehu(ctvolume) # Eq. 13 # 2. DRR Generation drrs = generatedrrs(ctnormalized) # Coronal, Sagittal, Axial cameraposes = getorthogonalposes() # 3. Model Initialization model = TensoRF(rank=16, gridsize=64) model.setdensityparams(delta=0, s=1) # Critical fix optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.02) # 4. Training Loop for i in range(1, 3001): rays = samplerays(2048, cameraposes) rendereddrrs = model.render(rays) lphoto = mseloss(rendereddrrs, drrs) lsparse = l1norm(model.getdensityfield()) ltv = totalvariation(model.getdensityfield()) loss = lphoto + 1e-4 lsparse + 1e-5 ltv loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() if i in [1500, 2500]: model.updatealphamask() return model.getdensityfield() def extractnodule(densityfield, annotateddiameter): # 5. Threshold Sweep candidates = [] for p in range(85, 100): threshold = np.percentile(densityfield[densityfield > 0], p) binarymask = (densityfield >= threshold).astype(np.uint8) # Noise removal components = connectedcomponents(binarymask) validcomponents = [c for c in components if c.size >= 10] # Boundary filling filledcomponents = binaryclosing(validcomponents, radius=2) # Size filtering for comp in filledcomponents: diameter = equivalentspherediameter(comp) if 5 <= diameter <= 80: candidates.append((comp, diameter)) # 6. Candidate Selection bestcandidate = min(candidates, key=lambda x: abs(x[1] - annotateddiameter)) return computevolume(bestcandidate[0]) A tensor-based radiance field representation that decomposes the 3D scene into low-rank factors, offering memory efficiency compared to dense grids. AReT uses a VM-rank-16 configuration. A generative-prior-guided NeRF approach that uses a population-level latent code from a GAN. AReT outperforms MedNeRF in sparse-view settings because MedNeRF's diffuse density field and scene-agnostic thresholding degrade patient-specific accuracy. Require 20-50 views and produce streak artifacts with only three views. AReT works with three orthogonal projections. Time Complexity: Training takes approximately 8 minutes per patient on an NVIDIA T4 GPU. Memory Complexity: A 64^3 VM-rank-16 TensoRF requires ~14 GB VRAM. A 128^3 grid exceeds the 16 GB VRAM limit of the T4. Performance: On LIDC-IDRI (19 patients, 14 nodules \ge 10 mm), AReT achieves a Pearson correlation r = 0.983 (p < 0.0001), median absolute volumetric error 11.4%, and systematic bias -77.3 mm^3. Strengths: Works with only three orthogonal projections; prior-free patient-specific reconstruction; robust to sparse-view overfitting via anatomy-aware regularization. Limitations: Requires simulated DRRs (domain gap with real radiographs); unsuitable for sub-centimeter nodules (< 10 mm) due to resolution limits; relies on annotated diameter for final candidate selection (semi-assisted). When to use: Sparse-view 3D lung nodule volumetry from orthogonal X-ray projections. When not to use: Dense-view reconstruction; sub-centimeter nodule analysis; clinical deployment without addressing the domain gap between simulated and real radiographs. AReT was proposed by Suja Palaniswamy et al. in 2026 (arXiv preprint). It addresses the limitations of existing NeRF adaptations for medical imaging, such as MedNeRF, which require dense views or rely on population priors that degrade patient-specific accuracy. The method identifies a previously unreported failure mode in TensoRF when applied to X-ray attenuation fields: the default density shift of -10 suppresses density gradients. By setting \Delta = 0 and incorporating thorax-specific regularization, AReT enables stable volumetric reconstruction from ultra-sparse views. Sparse-View Lung Nodule Volumetry from Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs via AReT: Anatomy-Regularized TensoRF, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2606.02639, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: AutoRF
head: AutoDecoder, AutoRF AutoDecoder, Learning 3D Object Radiance Fields from Single View Observations
body: AutoRF is a method for learning 3D object radiance fields from a single view observation without prior geometry knowledge (e.g., CAD models). It disentangles object representation into shape and appearance components using a normalized, object-centric encoding conditioned on 3D bounding boxes and 2D masks. Unlike multi-view methods like PixelNeRF, AutoRF operates on a single image, using an encoder to generate shape and appearance codes and a decoder to render views via volumetric rendering. Inputs and Outputs Input: A single RGB image I of an object instance. Auxiliary Inputs: A 3D bounding box \beta and an instance mask for the object, obtained via pre-processing. Output: A radiance field representation (density \sigma and color \xi) and rendered novel views. Data Structures and Layouts Normalized Object Coordinate Space (NOCS) O: A centered unit cube defined as O:= [-1/2, 1/2]^3. Occupancy Mask Y: A 2D mask where each pixel u has a label Yu \in \{+1, 0, -1\}: +1: Foreground pixels belonging to the object instance mask. -1: Background pixels (semantic categories not supposed to occlude the object, e.g., sky, road). 0: Unknown pixels (cannot determine occlusion). Shape Code \phiS: A vector of dimension 128. Appearance Code \phiA: A vector of dimension 128. Pre-processing 1. Run a pre-trained 3D object detector and panoptic segmentation on image I to extract the 3D bounding box \beta and instance mask. 2. Produce a masked 2D image I fitting a fixed input resolution. Rescale the input image to a maximum of 320px in each dimension while preserving the aspect ratio. 3. Compute the Occupancy Mask Y based on the instance mask and semantic segmentation. 4. Define the Object-Centric Camera \gamma: Map pixels u to unit-speed rays \gammau in NOCS. This is derived by remapping the camera ray \rhou from camera space to NOCS using the bounding box \beta. \gammau is a unit-speed reparametrization of \beta \circ \rhou. Encoding 1. Feed image I into the Shape and Appearance Encoder \PhiE. 2. \PhiE consists of a ResNet34 backbone with InstanceNorm layers (BatchNorm replaced). The first four layers are shared. The following two layers are replicated to form separate heads for shape and appearance encoding. 3. For a 3 \times H \times W input, the feature map shape for each encoding head is 256 \times H/16 \times W/16. 4. Apply adaptive max pooling to obtain shape code \phiS and appearance code \phiA, each of dimension 128. (\phiS, \phiA):= \PhiE(I). Decoding 1. Shape Decoding: Feed \phiS into Shape Decoder \PsiS to produce occupancy network \sigma. \sigma:= \PsiS(\phiS). \sigma: O \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^+ outputs density for a 3D point x \in O. Architecture: MLP made of 5 ResNet blocks with hidden dimension 128. At each layer, feed the previous feature map and the positional encoding of the query points. Apply a single linear layer to match the dimensionality of the positional encoding with the hidden dimensions of the MLP. Aggregate the output with the intermediate feature maps by a simple per-channel mean pooling. 2. Appearance Decoding: Feed \phiS and \phiA into Appearance Decoder \PsiA to produce appearance network \xi. \xi:= \PsiA(\phiA, \phiS). \xi: O \times S^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3 outputs RGB color for point x \in O and viewing direction d \in S^2. Architecture: MLP of 5 ResNet blocks with hidden dimensionality 128. Aggregate intermediate features with positional encodings by mean pooling. On the third layer, pass the output of the corresponding layer of the shape encoder to incorporate estimated shape information. On the final two layers, pass the view direction (encoded as a 3-dimensional vector) to account for view-dependent effects. Rendering 1. For each pixel u in the target view, compute the object-centric ray \gammau. 2. Determine the time window [au, bu] where \gammau intersects the object space O. 3. Sample 64 uniformly spaced points along the segment of \gammau within [au, bu]. 4. Compute the accumulated transmittance derivative \dot{\alpha}t and color C(\gammau) using the volume rendering formula: C(\gammau) = \int{au}^{bu} \dot{\alpha}t(\gammau, \sigma) \xi(\gammau(t), du) dt where du \in S^2 is the unit velocity of \gammau. 5. The accumulated transmittance \alphat is defined as: \alphat(\gammau, \sigma):= \exp\left(-\int{au}^{t} \sigma(\gammau(s)) ds\right) and \dot{\alpha}t is its time derivative. Loss Functions 1. Photometric Loss L{RGB}: Mean squared error between input image pixel Iu and rendered color V(\gammau|\sigma, \xi) for foreground pixels. L{RGB}(\Theta|\Omega):= \frac{1}{|W{RGB}|} \sum{u \in W{RGB}} \| Iu - V(\gammau|\sigma, \xi) \|^2 where W{RGB} \subset U contains only foreground pixels (Yu = +1) whose rays \gammau intersect O. 2. Occupancy Loss L{OCC}: Supervises the accumulated transmittance \alpha(\gammau, \sigma) using the occupancy mask Y. L{OCC}(\Theta|\Omega):= -\frac{1}{|W{OCC}|} \sum{u \in W{OCC}} \left[ \frac{Yu}{2} \log\left(\frac{1}{2} - \alpha(\gammau, \sigma)\right) + \frac{1}{2} \log\left(\frac{1}{2} + \alpha(\gammau, \sigma)\right) \right] where W{OCC} \subset U contains only foreground or background pixels (Yu \neq 0) with rays intersecting O. Note: The source text contains a typo in the formula representation ('log Yu ( 2 − α...)'), but the context implies a classification loss on \alpha where Yu=+1 encourages \alpha \to 0 (foreground) and Yu=-1 encourages \alpha \to 1 (background). 3. Final Loss: L(\Theta|\Omega) = L{RGB}(\Theta|\Omega) + \lambda L{OCC}(\Theta|\Omega) where \lambda \ge 0 is a hyperparameter. Training Optimization 1. Train at a batch size of 1. 2. Use the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 10^{-5}. 3. Randomly sample 1024 rays per input image during training. 4. Fix the rendering resolution to 80 \times 120 pixels during training. Test-Time Optimization 1. Refine the output by optimizing the loss L with respect to \phiS, \phiA, and the 3D bounding box \beta. 2. Initialize with the encoder output and detector box. 3. Use the Adam optimizer with learning rates 0.05, 0.02, and 0.02 for \phiS, \phiA, and camera position, respectively. 4. Optimize for 32 iterations. 5. Edge Case (Monocular Setting): Keep the size component of the bounding box fixed to the detector's regression and optimize only pose (rotation and translation) to avoid scale-depth ambiguity. Explicit Meshing (Post-processing) 1. Render depth and color from multiple views using AutoRF, with cameras facing the object center. 2. Apply TSDF-fusion on the resulting pairs of depth and color images to create a 3D mesh. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class AutoRF: def init(self, lambdaocc=1.0): self.encoder = ShapeAppearanceEncoder() self.shapedecoder = ShapeDecoder() self.colordecoder = ColorDecoder() self.lambdaocc = lambdaocc self.optimizer = None def preprocess(self, image, bbox3d, mask): """ Preprocesses the input image and generates auxiliary data. image: H x W x 3 RGB image bbox3d: 3D bounding box in camera space mask: Instance mask Returns: maskedimage, occupancymask, objectcentriccamera """ # Rescale image to max 320px preserving aspect ratio maskedimage = cropandrescale(image, bbox3d, mask) # Compute occupancy mask Y # +1: foreground, -1: background, 0: unknown occupancymask = computeoccupancymask(mask, semanticsegmentation(image)) # Compute object-centric camera gamma from bbox3d objectcentriccamera = createobjectcentriccamera(bbox3d) return maskedimage, occupancymask, objectcentriccamera def encode(self, image): """ Encodes image into shape and appearance codes. """ phiS, phiA = self.encoder(image) return phiS, phiA def decode(self, phiS, phiA, points3d, directions): """ Decodes codes into density and color. points3d: N x 3 points in NOCS directions: N x 3 viewing directions """ sigma = self.shapedecoder(phiS, points3d) color = self.colordecoder(phiS, phiA, points3d, directions) return sigma, color def render(self, sigma, color, raystart, rayend, numsamples=64): """ Renders color along rays using volume rendering. """ # Sample points along ray tvals = torch.linspace(raystart, rayend, numsamples) points = rayorigin + tvals.unsqueeze(-1) raydirection # Compute density and color at sampled points # (Assuming sigma and color are pre-computed or computed on the fly) # Compute accumulated transmittance # alphat = exp(-integral(sigma)) # dotalphat = derivative of alphat # C = integral(dotalphat color) # Standard volume rendering implementation weights = computeweights(sigma, tvals) colorrendered = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) color, dim=-2) return colorrendered def computeloss(self, renderedcolor, targetimage, occupancymask, sigma, rayintersections): """ Computes photometric and occupancy losses. """ # Photometric Loss foregroundmask = occupancymask == 1 lrgb = torch.mean((renderedcolor[foregroundmask] - targetimage[foregroundmask])2) # Occupancy Loss # alpha is the accumulated transmittance at the end of the ray segment alpha = computeaccumulatedtransmittance(sigma, rayintersections) occmask = occupancymask != 0 # Formula: -1/|W| sum [ Y/2 log(0.5 - alpha) + 0.5 log(0.5 + alpha) ] # Note: This formula assumes alpha is normalized or shifted appropriately for the log domain # The source formula is: Yu/2 log(1/2 - alpha) + 1/2 log(1/2 + alpha) # This implies a specific mapping of alpha to probability space. locc = 0.0 if torch.any(occmask): y = occupancymask[occmask] alphaval = alpha[occmask] # Guard against log(0) or negative arguments if necessary term1 = (y / 2.0) torch.log(torch.clamp(0.5 - alphaval, min=1e-6)) term2 = 0.5 torch.log(torch.clamp(0.5 + alphaval, min=1e-6)) locc = -torch.mean(term1 + term2) totalloss = lrgb + self.lambdaocc locc return totalloss def trainstep(self, image, bbox3d, mask): maskedimage, occupancymask, camera = self.preprocess(image, bbox3d, mask) phiS, phiA = self.encode(maskedimage) # Sample rays rays = samplerays(camera, numrays=1024) # Render sigma, color = self.decode(phiS, phiA, rays.points, rays.directions) renderedcolor = self.render(sigma, color, rays.start, rays.end) # Loss loss = self.computeloss(renderedcolor, maskedimage, occupancymask, sigma, rays) loss.backward() self.optimizer.step() self.optimizer.zerograd() return loss def testtimeoptimize(self, image, bbox3d, mask, iterations=32): """ Optimizes phiS, phiA, and bbox3d pose at test time. """ maskedimage, occupancymask, camera = self.preprocess(image, bbox3d, mask) phiS = self.encodeshape(maskedimage) phiA = self.encodeappearance(maskedimage) # Initialize optimizer for codes and bbox pose optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([ {'params': phiS, 'lr': 0.05}, {'params': phiA, 'lr': 0.02}, {'params': bbox3d.pose, 'lr': 0.02} # Size fixed ]) for i in range(iterations): # Re-encode if necessary or use cached codes # Re-render with updated codes and bbox rays = samplerays(camera, numrays=1024) # Or full image sigma, color = self.decode(phiS, phiA, rays.points, rays.directions) renderedcolor = self.render(sigma, color, rays.start, rays.end) loss = self.computeloss(renderedcolor, maskedimage, occupancymask, sigma, rays) loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() return phiS, phiA, bbox3d class ShapeAppearanceEncoder(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # ResNet34 backbone with InstanceNorm self.backbone = ResNet34InstanceNorm() # Shared first 4 layers # Replicated next 2 layers for heads self.shapehead = ShapeHead() self.appearancehead = AppearanceHead() def forward(self, x): features = self.backbone(x) phiS = self.shapehead(features) phiA = self.appearancehead(features) return phiS, phiA class ShapeDecoder(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # 5 ResNet blocks, hidden dim 128 self.blocks = nn.ModuleList([ResNetBlock(128) for in range(5)]) self.linear = nn.Linear(128, 128) # Match pos enc dim def forward(self, phiS, points): # Positional encoding of points posenc = positionalencoding(points, numfrequencies=6) # Linear layer to match dims posencproj = self.linear(posenc) # Aggregate with intermediate features via mean pooling #... implementation details... sigma =... return sigma class ColorDecoder(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # 5 ResNet blocks, hidden dim 128 self.blocks = nn.ModuleList([ResNetBlock(128) for in range(5)]) def forward(self, phiS, phiA, points, directions): #... similar to shape decoder... # On 3rd layer, pass shape encoder output # On final 2 layers, pass view direction color =... return color Time Complexity: Rendering a 64 \times 64 image takes approximately 0.23 seconds. Test-time optimization (32 steps, rendering 32 \times 32 images) takes approximately 3.3 seconds per object. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method is designed for single-view object reconstruction and does not explicitly discuss scaling to large scenes, though it can be applied to multiple objects in a scene if detected. Strengths: Works with a single view observation. No prior geometry knowledge (e.g., CAD models) required. Encoder provides a good initial estimate, leading to faster convergence compared to auto-decoder variants. Produces less fuzzy radiance fields compared to PixelNeRF on SRN-Chairs dataset. Limitations: Scale-depth ambiguity in monocular settings requires fixing the bounding box size. Performance is lower than multi-view methods like PixelNeRF when multiple views are available (e.g., on nuScenes cars, AutoRF AutoDecoder underperforms AutoRF, and AutoRF is compared against PixelNeRF which uses more views). When to use: When only a single view of an object is available and no CAD models are present. When not: When multiple views are available (use PixelNeRF or similar) or when high-fidelity multi-view consistency is critical without test-time optimization. AutoRF was introduced by Norman Müller, Andrea Simonelli, Lorenzo Porzi, Samuel Rota Bulò, Matthias Nießner, and Peter Kontschieder in 2022. It addresses the challenge of learning 3D object radiance fields from single view observations, a more challenging scenario than methods assuming access to at least a second view. It is used on datasets such as nuScenes (cars) and SRN-Chairs. name: HALO
head: HALO (Harnessing Low-frequency Neural Fields), Hi-NeRF, Input-space frequency regularization, LoNeRF, Low-frequency regularized NeRF
body: HALO is a few-shot view synthesis method that prevents overfitting in neural radiance fields by regularizing a high-frequency NeRF (Hi-NeRF) using a low-frequency NeRF (Lo-NeRF). It leverages the distinct interpolation and extrapolation properties of low- and high-frequency representations to enforce geometric consistency without requiring extra semantic supervision. Unlike sibling methods such as DietNeRF which rely on CLIP-based semantic priors, HALO maintains better lighting consistency and operates purely within the input space. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A sparse set of N training images with known camera poses (intrinsics and extrinsics). Outputs: A trained Hi-NeRF MLP capable of rendering novel views. Implicit Outputs: A Lo-NeRF MLP and a Ray-based field MLP (optional for dynamic scenes). Data Structures 1. Lo-NeRF: An MLP taking encoded position \gamma{Lo}(\mathbf{x}) and direction \gamma{Lo}(\mathbf{d}). 2. Ray-based Field: An MLP taking ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Input is 6D (\mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^3, \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3), but has 4 degrees of freedom as \mathbf{o} lies on a predefined sphere and \mathbf{d} is a unit vector. 3. Hi-NeRF: An MLP taking encoded position \gamma{Hi}(\mathbf{x}) and direction \gamma{Hi}(\mathbf{d}). Positional Encoding The input coordinates are mapped to higher dimensions using hierarchical positional encoding \gamma(\cdot). For a scalar input p, the encoding is: \gamma(p) = (\sin(2^0 \pi p), \cos(2^0 \pi p), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi p), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi p)) where L is the number of frequency bands. Lo-P.E.: Uses a reduced frequency L{Lo} determined by the tuning criterion. Hi-P.E.: Uses the default NeRF frequency L{Hi} = 10. Numbered Steps 1. Tune Lo-NeRF Frequency: Render N paired images with a small baseline. Compute the averaged frequency domain difference \sigma: \sigma = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \| \mathcal{F}(I{ia}) - \mathcal{F}(I{ib}) \| where \mathcal{F}() is the Fourier transformation. Reduce the frequency parameter L until \sigma reaches a predefined threshold (25). This L defines Lo-NeRF. 2. Train Lo-NeRF: Train the Lo-NeRF using standard volume rendering loss on the training views. Formula for rendered color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) along ray \mathbf{r}: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^K e^{-\sum{k0=1}^{k-1} \sigma{k0} \delta{k0}} (1 - e^{-\sigmak \deltak}) ck where \sigmak = \sigma(\mathbf{r}(tk)), ck = c(\mathbf{r}(tk)), and \deltak = t{k+1} - tk. Loss: L{rec} = \sum{\mathbf{r}} \| \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) - C{gt}(\mathbf{r}) \|2^2 where C{gt} is ground truth RGB. 3. Train Ray-based Field (Static Scenes): Freeze Lo-NeRF. Randomly initialize the Ray-based field F{ray}. Compute depth D(\mathbf{r}; F{point}) by sampling points and accumulating density from the frozen Lo-NeRF. Optimize F{ray} with loss: L{ray} = \sum{\mathbf{r}=(\mathbf{o},\mathbf{d})} \| F{ray}(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}) - D(\mathbf{r}; F{point}) \|2^2 where \mathbf{o} is the ray origin on a predefined sphere and \mathbf{d} is the unit view direction. 4. Train Hi-NeRF: Freeze Lo-NeRF and F{ray}. Randomly initialize Hi-NeRF with L=10. Sample points along rays according to the depth predicted by F{ray} (following the DONeRF strategy). Optimize Hi-NeRF with total loss: L = L{rec} + \lambda L{empty} Empty Space Loss: Regularizes empty space where depth cannot be inferred from Lo-NeRF. Define accumulated occupancy for a ray \mathbf{r} as: acc(\mathbf{r}) = \prod{k=1}^K e^{-\sum{k0=1}^{k-1} \sigma{k0} \delta{k0}} (1 - e^{-\sigmak \deltak}) The empty space loss is: L{empty} = \sum{\mathbf{r}: acc{Lo}(\mathbf{r}) < \tau} acc{Hi}(\mathbf{r}) where \tau = 0.01 is the threshold for determining if space is empty. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import numpy as np def positionalencoding(p, L): """ Standard hierarchical positional encoding. p: scalar or tensor of shape (..., 1) L: number of frequency bands Returns: tensor of shape (..., 2L) """ # p is expected to be in range [-1, 1] or similar, scaled by pi # Formula: (sin(2^0 pi p), cos(2^0 pi p),..., sin(2^(L-1) pi p), cos(2^(L-1) pi p)) freqbands = 2.0 torch.arange(L, device=p.device).float() freqbands = freqbands np.pi # Expand dimensions to broadcast freqbands = freqbands.view(1, -1) encoded = p freqbands sinenc = torch.sin(encoded) cosenc = torch.cos(encoded) return torch.cat([sinenc, cosenc], dim=-1) def volumerendering(sigma, color, tstarts, tends): """ Standard volume rendering integral. sigma: density values (..., K) color: RGB values (..., K, 3) tstarts: start times of bins (..., K) tends: end times of bins (..., K) Returns: rendered color (..., 3) """ dists = tends - tstarts alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma dists) transmittance = torch.cumprod(torch.exp(-sigma dists), dim=-1) # Prepend 1.0 for the first segment transmittance = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(transmittance[...,:1]), transmittance[...,:-1]], dim=-1) weights = alpha transmittance renderedcolor = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) color, dim=-2) return renderedcolor class HALOTrainer: def init(self, trainimages, trainposes, numviews=8): self.trainimages = trainimages self.trainposes = trainposes self.numviews = numviews # Hyperparameters self.freqthreshold = 25 self.emptythreshold = 0.01 self.Lhi = 10 self.lambdaempty = 1.0 # Balancing parameter for Lempty # Networks self.lonerf = None self.rayfield = None self.hinerf = None # Determine Lo-NeRF frequency self.Llo = self.tunefrequency() def tunefrequency(self): """ Stage 1: Determine optimal low frequency L. Renders paired images with small baseline and checks frequency domain difference. """ # Implementation detail: Iterate L from low to high. # For each L, train a temporary Lo-NeRF. # Render N pairs with small baseline. # Compute sigma = mean(||F(Iia) - F(Iib)||). # Return L where sigma <= 25. # Placeholder for the iterative search logic as exact search algorithm # is not fully detailed in source, but the criterion is. L = 1 while True: # Train temporary Lo-NeRF with L # Render pairs, compute freq diff # if diff <= 25: return L # L += 1 pass def trainlonerf(self): """ Stage 2: Train Lo-NeRF with Lo-P.E. """ # Initialize Lo-NeRF with Llo # Optimize using Lrec on training views pass def trainrayfield(self): """ Stage 3: Train Ray-based Field. Freezes Lo-NeRF. """ # Initialize Ray Field # For each ray (o, d): # Compute depth D from Lo-NeRF # Optimize Ray Field to predict D pass def trainhinerf(self): """ Stage 4: Train Hi-NeRF. Freezes Lo-NeRF and Ray Field. """ # Initialize Hi-NeRF with Lhi=10 # For each ray: # Sample points using depth from Ray Field # Compute Lrec and Lempty # Optimize Hi-NeRF pass def render(self, rayo, rayd): """ Render using Hi-NeRF. """ # Sample points along ray # Encode with Hi-P.E. # Query Hi-NeRF for sigma and color # Volume render pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls High-Frequency Encoding: Using high-frequency positional encoding leads to poor interpolation results. Ray-based Blurriness: Ray-based predictions may suffer from blurry edges, but this is acceptable for rough geometry regularization as Hi-NeRF fine-tunes details. Dynamic Scenes: Using high-frequency encoding for the time axis introduces temporal flickering motion when dynamic sequence observations are sparse. Empty Space: The empty space loss relies on the threshold \tau=0.01. If Lo-NeRF predicts non-zero occupancy in empty regions, Hi-NeRF may incorrectly fill them. Time Complexity: Training involves three sequential stages. The ray-based field training adds overhead compared to vanilla NeRF. On dynamic scenes (TiNeuVox baseline), HALO takes 0.67 GPU/h compared to 0.17 GPU/h for the baseline, but yields significantly higher PSNR (25.687 vs 21.392). Memory Complexity: Requires storing parameters for Lo-NeRF, Ray-based Field, and Hi-NeRF. The Ray-based field is lightweight as it only predicts a scalar depth. Strengths: Does not require extra semantic supervision (unlike DietNeRF); maintains lighting consistency; effective for few-shot settings (4-8 views); applicable to dynamic scenes via time dimension extension. Limitations: Requires three-stage training; sensitive to the frequency tuning threshold; ray-based field may introduce blurriness in regularization. When to Use: Few-shot view synthesis (static or dynamic) where semantic priors are unavailable or undesirable. When Not to Use: Large-scale dense reconstruction (vanilla NeRF suffices); scenarios requiring real-time training with minimal overhead. HALO (Harnessing Low-Frequency Neural Fields) was proposed in 2023. It addresses the overfitting problem in NeRFs under few-shot settings by exploiting the different interpolation and extrapolation properties of low- and high-frequency neural fields. It is related to DietNeRF but avoids semantic supervision. It builds on Position Encoding and Embedding principles.
