name: Neural LiDAR Fields
body: Neural LiDAR Fields reconstructs a 3D point cloud scene into an implicit continuous representation by redefining neural fields specifically for LiDAR sensors, modeling geometric depth, reflection intensity, and ray-drop probability. Unlike standard NeRFs that optimize for photometric RGB loss, this method adapts the radiance field formulation to LiDAR physics, enabling novel space-time view synthesis for dynamic driving scenarios. It distinguishes itself by combining coarse-resolution multi-planar features with high-resolution hash grid representations to mitigate hash collisions while maintaining efficiency. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: LiDAR point clouds (position, intensity, time), camera intrinsics/extrinsics (for ray generation), and temporal indices for dynamic scenes. Outputs: Predicted depth \hat{\mathcal{D}}, intensity \hat{\mathcal{I}}, and ray-drop probability \hat{\mathcal{P}} for synthesized rays. Data Structures The method employs a hybrid feature representation to handle large-scale dynamic scenes: 1. Multi-planar Features: Coarse-resolution features stored in planar grids. 2. Hash Grid: High-resolution feature grid using spatial hashing to avoid collisions. 3. Temporal Encoding: Time information is aggregated into the planar and hash features to support 4D (space-time) reconstruction. Positional Encoding Input coordinates undergo hierarchical positional encoding \gamma(\cdot). For a scalar input p, the encoding is: \gamma(p) = (\sin(2^0 \pi p), \cos(2^0 \pi p), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi p), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi p)) where L is the number of frequency bands. This is applied to position and direction vectors. Ray Generation Lasers are transmitted at specific angular intervals within the LiDAR's Field of View (FOV), using the sensor center as origin o. The direction \mathbf{d} is determined by azimuth angle \theta and elevation angle \phi in a polar coordinate system: \mathbf{d} = (\cos \theta \cos \phi, \ \sin \theta \sin \phi, \ \cos \phi)^T 3D points are sampled along these rays within a defined near/far range. Network Architecture and Prediction The neural field predicts density \sigma, intensity i, and ray-drop probability p for each sampled point. 1. Feature Query: Temporal aggregated planar features \mathbf{f}{\text{planar}} and hash features \mathbf{f}{\text{hash}} are retrieved based on the 3D position. 2. Intensity Prediction: A dedicated MLP takes the features and position-encoded viewpoint \gamma(\mathbf{d}) as input: i = \mathrm{MLP}{\text{intensity}}(\mathbf{f}{\text{planar}}, \mathbf{f}{\text{hash}}, \gamma(\mathbf{d})) 3. Ray-drop Prediction: A separate MLP predicts the ray-drop probability \rho (denoted as pi in rendering equations): \rho = \mathrm{MLP}{\text{raydrop}}(\mathbf{f}{\text{planar}}, \mathbf{f}{\text{hash}}, \gamma(\mathbf{d})) 4. Density: Density \sigma is predicted from the position features (standard NeRF branch). Rendering (Alpha Composition) The final outputs are computed by alpha-compositing along the ray \mathbf{r} with N samples: Opacity: \alphai = 1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai}, where \deltai is the distance between samples. Transmittance: Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). Depth: \hat{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai}) zi where zi is the depth value of the queried point. Intensity: \hat{\mathcal{I}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai ii Ray-drop Probability: \hat{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai pi where ii and pi are the point-wise outputs. Ray-drop Refinement To address noisy point-wise ray-drop predictions, a U-Net with residuals refines the global ray-drop mask using the full predicted depth, intensity, and ray-drop probability as inputs. The refinement loss is binary cross-entropy: \mathcal{L}{\text{refine}} = \mathrm{BCELoss}(\hat{\mathcal{M}}{\text{Pred}}, \mathcal{M}{\text{GT}}) where \hat{\mathcal{M}}{\text{Pred}} is the refined mask and \mathcal{M}{\text{GT}} is the ground truth. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def neurallidarfieldsrender(rayorigin, raydirection, timestep, planarfeatures, hashgrid, mlpintensity, mlpraydrop, mlpdensity, numsamples): """ Renders depth, intensity, and ray-drop probability for a single LiDAR ray. """ # 1. Sample points along the ray # Generate N points between near and far bounds tvalues = linspace(near, far, numsamples) points = rayorigin + tvalues raydirection # 2. Query features and predict properties densities = [] intensities = [] raydrops = [] for point in points: # Query hybrid features (planar + hash) at point location for given time fplanar = queryplanarfeatures(point, timestep, planarfeatures) fhash = queryhashfeatures(point, hashgrid) # Positional encoding of direction dencoded = positionalencoding(raydirection) # Predict density sigma = mlpdensity(fplanar, fhash, point) densities.append(sigma) # Predict intensity i = mlpintensity(fplanar, fhash, dencoded) intensities.append(i) # Predict ray-drop probability p = mlpraydrop(fplanar, fhash, dencoded) raydrops.append(p) # 3. Alpha composition densities = array(densities) intensities = array(intensities) raydrops = array(raydrops) # Calculate opacity and transmittance # delta is distance between consecutive samples deltas = diff(tvalues, prepend=near) alphas = 1.0 - exp(-densities deltas) # Transmittance Ti = product(1 - alphaj) for j < i # T1 = 1.0 transmittances = ones(numsamples) for i in range(1, numsamples): transmittances[i] = transmittances[i-1] (1.0 - alphas[i-1]) # Render Depth # D(r) = sum(Ti alphai zi) # Note: zi is the depth value (distance along ray) which is tvalues[i] depth = sum(transmittances alphas tvalues) # Render Intensity # I(r) = sum(Ti alphai ii) intensity = sum(transmittances alphas intensities) # Render Ray-drop Probability # P(r) = sum(Ti alphai pi) raydropprob = sum(transmittances alphas raydrops) return depth, intensity, raydropprob def positionalencoding(v, L=10): """ Hierarchical positional encoding. gamma(p) = (sin(2^0 pi p), cos(2^0 pi p),..., sin(2^{L-1} pi p), cos(2^{L-1} pi p)) """ encoded = [] for l in range(L): freq = 2l pi encoded.append(sin(freq v)) encoded.append(cos(freq v)) return array(encoded) Complexity: The use of hash grids provides efficient memory access and storage, scaling better than dense volumetric grids for large scenes. Multi-planar features reduce the memory footprint for coarse geometry. Performance: The method is designed for large-scale dynamic driving scenarios, balancing efficiency and reconstruction quality. Strengths: Avoids adverse effects of hash collisions through hybrid representation; explicitly models LiDAR-specific physics (intensity, ray-drop) rather than just RGB. Limitations: Ray-drop prediction at the point-wise level is inherently noisy and unreliable, requiring a separate U-Net refinement step. Neural LiDAR Fields, specifically implemented as LiDAR4D, was introduced to address the limitations of standard NeRFs when applied to LiDAR data. Standard NeRFs rely on photometric loss for RGB images, which does not directly translate to LiDAR's time-of-flight and intensity measurements. The method builds on the concept of neural radiance fields but redefines the output space to include geometric depth, reflection intensity, and ray-drop probability. It was developed to enable novel space-time view synthesis for dynamic driving scenarios, incorporating temporal information encoding to handle 4D scenes. LiDAR4D: Dynamic Neural Fields for Novel Space-Time View LiDAR Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.00492, fetched 2026-10-30

name: NeRF Optimization via SDS
body: NeRF Optimization via SDS (Score Distillation Sampling) optimizes the parameters of a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) to match a user-provided text prompt by leveraging gradients from a pretrained 2D text-to-image diffusion model. Unlike standard NeRF training which minimizes pixel-wise reconstruction error against ground-truth images, this method treats the NeRF as a differentiable renderer within an optimization loop, using the diffusion model as a perceptual prior to guide the generation of novel 3D geometry and appearance. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like SUDS or Rip-NeRF by explicitly incorporating view-dependent text conditioning based on camera azimuth angles and specific regularization terms for entropy and orientation. The method optimizes a NeRF network using SDS gradients derived from a latent diffusion model. The process involves initializing a NeRF, preparing text embeddings, and iteratively updating the NeRF weights by rendering images, encoding them into latent space, and computing the SDS loss. Inputs: Text prompt string. Optional negative prompt string. Camera poses and intrinsics (from NeRFDataset). Hyperparameters: learning rate (lr), optimizer settings, regularization weights (lambdaentropy, lambdaorient), iteration ratios (latentiterratio), and shading parameters. Outputs: Optimized NeRF model parameters (MLP weights). Rendered images matching the text prompt. NeRF Model (NeRFNetwork): A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) representing the radiance field. It takes encoded 3D position and view direction as input and outputs volume density (\sigma) and RGB color (\mathbf{c}). The architecture follows the standard shared-basis or multi-resolution hash encoding approach (see Model Architecture and Encoding). Text Embeddings: A dictionary mapping text conditions (e.g., "front", "side", "back", "default") to latent text embeddings generated by the diffusion model's text encoder. Dataset (NeRFDataset): Stores images, camera parameters (rotation R, translation T, focal length F, principal point C), and optional masks. 1. Initialize Text Embeddings: Prepare text embeddings using the diffusion model's encoder. If viewdependent is enabled, generate embeddings for different viewpoints (e.g., front, side, back) based on azimuth angles. \text{embeddings} = \text{prepare\embeddings}(\text{sds}, \text{prompt}, \text{neg\prompt}, \text{view\dependent}=\text{True}) 2. Initialize NeRF Model: Instantiate the NeRFNetwork and move it to the target device (e.g., GPU). 3. Configure Optimizer: Create an Adan optimizer with the following specific parameters: Learning rate: 5 \times \text{lr}, where \text{lr} = 10^{-3}. Epsilon: 10^{-8}. Weight decay: 2 \times 10^{-5}. Max gradient norm: 5.0. Scheduler: Constant LambdaLR. 4. Load Data: Load training and test datasets (NeRFDataset) specifying image height, width, and batch sizes. 5. Optimization Loop: Iterate through epochs and training batches. For each step: a. Calculate Iteration Ratio: \text{exp\iter\ratio} = \frac{\text{global\step} - \text{args.exp\start\iter}}{\text{args.exp\end\iter} - \text{args.exp\start\iter}} b. Set Shading and Background Parameters: If \text{exp\iter\ratio} \le \text{args.latent\iter\ratio}: Set ambientratio = 1.0. Set shading = "normal". Set bgcolor = None. Otherwise: Sample ambientratio uniformly between \text{args.min\ambient\ratio} and 1.0. Select shading: "textureless" with probability \text{args.textureless\ratio}, otherwise "lambertian". c. Set Background Color: If \text{args.bg\radius} > 0 and a random number > 0.5: Use a background network bgnet (returning None for color, implying alpha blending or specific background handling). Else: Use a random single-color background sampled from a uniform distribution: \mathbf{c}{bg} \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)^3. d. Render: Perform a forward pass through the NeRF model using the current ray parameters, MVP matrix, image dimensions (H, W), and shading/background settings. \text{pred\rgb} = \text{NeRF}(rays, \dots) Reshape output to [B, 3, H, W]. e. Select Text Conditioning: If args.viewdeptext is true: Calculate azimuth angle \phi of the camera. If |\phi| \le 45^\circ: Use embeddings["front"]. If 45^\circ < |\phi| \le 135^\circ: Use embeddings["side"]. Else: Use embeddings["back"]. Else: Use embeddings["default"]. f. Encode to Latent Space: Interpolate predrgb to 512 \times 512 using bilinear interpolation. Encode the image using the diffusion model's VAE encoder: \text{latents} = \text{sds.encode\imgs}(\text{interpolate}(\text{pred\rgb}, \text{size}=(512, 512))) g. Compute SDS Loss: Calculate the Score Distillation Sampling loss: \mathcal{L}{SDS} = \text{sds.sds\loss}(\text{latents}, \text{text\cond}, \text{text\uncond}) Where textcond is the selected text embedding and textuncond is the unconditional embedding (or negative prompt embedding). h. Entropy Regularization: If \text{args.lambda\entropy} > 0: Compute entropy loss on the alpha values (\alpha) from the rendering. Clamp \alpha to [10^{-5}, 1 - 10^{-5}]. \mathcal{L}{entropy} = -\mathbb{E}[\alpha \log2 \alpha + (1 - \alpha) \log2 (1 - \alpha)] Scale the loss: \mathcal{L}{entropy\scaled} = \mathcal{L}{entropy} \times \text{args.lambda\entropy} \times \min\left(1, \frac{2 \times \text{global\step}}{\text{args.iters}}\right) Add to total loss. i. Orientation Regularization: If \text{args.lambda\orient} > 0 and the NeRF output contains lossorient: \mathcal{L}{orient\scaled} = \text{args.lambda\orient} \times \text{loss\orient} Add to total loss. j. Backward Pass: Sum all loss components. Perform backward pass. If args.lossscaling is true, use GradScaler for mixed precision training; otherwise, use standard backward. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def optimizenerfsds( sdsmodel, nerfmodel, dataset, prompt, negprompt, args, device): """ Optimizes a NeRF model using SDS gradients. Args: sdsmodel: Pretrained diffusion model wrapper (provides encodeimgs, sdsloss, prepareembeddings). nerfmodel: NeRFNetwork instance. dataset: NeRFDataset instance. prompt: Text prompt string. negprompt: Negative prompt string. args: Configuration object containing hyperparameters. device: Torch device. """ # Step 1: Initialize Text Embeddings embeddings = sdsmodel.prepareembeddings( prompt=prompt, negprompt=negprompt, viewdependent=True) # Step 2: Initialize NeRF Model (Assumed already initialized and moved to device) # nerfmodel = NeRFNetwork().to(device) # Step 3: Configure Optimizer optimizer = torch.optim.Adan( nerfmodel.parameters(), lr=5e-3, # 5 lr where lr=1e-3 eps=1e-8, weightdecay=2e-5, maxgradnorm=5.0) scheduler = torch.optim.lrscheduler.LambdaLR(optimizer, lrlambda=lambda epoch: 1.0) # Step 4: Load Data (Assumed already loaded) # dataloader = DataLoader(dataset, batchsize=args.batchsize,...) globalstep = 0 totaliters = args.iters for epoch in range(args.epochs): for batch in dataloader: images, cameras, masks = batch # Step 5a: Calculate Iteration Ratio expiterratio = (globalstep - args.expstartiter) / (args.expenditer - args.expstartiter) # Step 5b: Set Shading and Background Parameters if expiterratio <= args.latentiterratio: ambientratio = 1.0 shading = "normal" bgcolor = None else: ambientratio = torch.rand(1).item() (1.0 - args.minambientratio) + args.minambientratio if torch.rand(1).item() < args.texturelessratio: shading = "textureless" else: shading = "lambertian" bgcolor = None # Placeholder, handled in Step 5c # Step 5c: Set Background Color if args.bgradius > 0 and torch.rand(1).item() > 0.5: bgcolor = None # Use bgnet else: bgcolor = torch.rand(3, device=device) # Step 5d: Render # Note: render function signature depends on specific NeRF implementation. # Assuming it returns predrgb, alphas, and potentially lossorient. predrgb, alphas, outputs = nerfmodel.render( cameras=cameras, imgsize=(args.height, args.width), ambientratio=ambientratio, shading=shading, bgcolor=bgcolor) # predrgb shape: [B, 3, H, W] # Step 5e: Select Text Conditioning if args.viewdeptext: # Extract azimuth angle from camera parameters # Assuming cameras object has azimuth attribute or can be computed from R/T azimuth = computeazimuth(cameras) if abs(azimuth) <= 45: textcond = embeddings["front"] elif abs(azimuth) <= 135: textcond = embeddings["side"] else: textcond = embeddings["back"] else: textcond = embeddings["default"] textuncond = embeddings.get("uncond", embeddings["default"]) # Fallback # Step 5f: Encode to Latent Space # Interpolate to 512x512 predrgbresized = F.interpolate(predrgb, size=(512, 512), mode="bilinear", aligncorners=False) latents = sdsmodel.encodeimgs(predrgbresized) # Step 5g: Compute SDS Loss loss = sdsmodel.sdsloss(latents, textcond, textuncond) # Step 5h: Entropy Regularization if args.lambdaentropy > 0: # Clamp alphas alphasclamped = torch.clamp(alphas, min=1e-5, max=1-1e-5) # Compute binary entropy entropy = -(alphasclamped torch.log2(alphasclamped) + (1 - alphasclamped) torch.log2(1 - alphasclamped)) lossentropy = entropy.mean() # Scale factor scalefactor = min(1.0, 2 globalstep / totaliters) loss += args.lambdaentropy scalefactor lossentropy # Step 5i: Orientation Regularization if args.lambdaorient > 0 and "lossorient" in outputs: loss += args.lambdaorient outputs["lossorient"] # Step 5j: Backward Pass if args.lossscaling: scaler = torch.cuda.amp.GradScaler() with torch.cuda.amp.autocast(): scaler.scale(loss).backward() scaler.step(optimizer) scaler.update() else: loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() scheduler.step() globalstep += 1 lr: Base learning rate, typically 10^{-3}. args.expstartiter, args.expenditer: Iteration range for exponential scheduling. args.latentiterratio: Threshold for switching shading/background strategies. args.minambientratio: Minimum ambient ratio for later training stages. args.texturelessratio: Probability of using "textureless" shading. args.bgradius: Radius for background network usage. args.viewdeptext: Boolean flag for view-dependent text conditioning. args.lambdaentropy: Weight for entropy regularization. args.lambdaorient: Weight for orientation regularization. Precision: Mixed precision training (GradScaler) is recommended to handle potential numerical instability in SDS gradients. Boundaries: Alpha values must be clamped to [10^{-5}, 1-10^{-5}] before computing entropy to avoid \log(0). Degenerate Input: If the text prompt is empty or invalid, the embedding preparation step may fail. Ensure negprompt is handled correctly to avoid unconditional bias if not intended. View-Dependent Conditioning: Incorrect calculation of azimuth angles can lead to mismatched text conditioning. Ensure camera coordinate systems are consistent. Time Complexity: Each iteration involves a forward pass through the NeRF, a forward pass through the diffusion encoder, and a backward pass through the SDS loss. The complexity is dominated by the diffusion model inference, which is significantly more expensive than standard NeRF rendering. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the NeRF model, the diffusion model (encoder and UNet), and intermediate activations for backpropagation. Memory usage is high due to the large size of the diffusion model. Measured Performance: On the "Truck" dataset, the method achieved a Mean PSNR of 27.717 and Mean SSIM of 0.926. Strengths: Enables text-driven 3D generation without requiring 3D ground-truth data. Can produce high-quality, semantically consistent 3D assets. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to diffusion model usage. May suffer from "over-saturation" or "over-saturation" artifacts common in SDS optimization. Requires careful tuning of regularization parameters. When to Use: When generating 3D scenes from text prompts is required, and computational resources are sufficient for diffusion-based optimization. When Not to Use: When fast training is required, or when ground-truth images are available (standard NeRF training is more efficient and stable). The method was introduced by Shashwat Chawla in the repository "Diffusion-guided-3D-Representations". It builds upon the concept of Score Distillation Sampling (SDS), adapting it for NeRF optimization. The approach incorporates view-dependent text conditioning and specific regularization techniques to improve the quality of the generated 3D models. name: NeX-MPI
head: NeX, NeX MPI with Neural Basis Expansion, Neural Basis Expansion MPI
body: NeX-MPI is a real-time view synthesis method that combines Multiplane Image (MPI) parameterization with a neural scene representation to model view-dependent effects. It solves the limitation of standard MPIs, which assume brightness constancy and fail on non-Lambertian surfaces (e.g., glass, ceramics) by appearing dull or breaking down. Unlike NeRF, which renders slowly via volumetric integration, NeX-MPI caches a 3D MPI grid optimized via MLPs, enabling real-time rendering in fragment shaders. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of calibrated, undistorted input images Ii with known camera intrinsics and extrinsics. Outputs: A cached 3D MPI grid (alphas and view-dependent colors) that can be rendered in real-time via OpenGL/WebGL. Data Structures The scene is represented as a 3D MPI grid with D layers (planes). Each layer d \in \{1, \dots, D\} has: 1. Alpha (\alpha): Per-pixel transparency, predicted by MLP F\theta. 2. Color Coefficients (K): View-dependent color parameters. To reduce memory, every M consecutive planes share the same set of coefficients \{K0, \dots, KN\}, but have distinct alphas. K0: Base color, stored explicitly as a learnable parameter tensor (not predicted by MLP). Kn (n=1 \dots N): Reflectance parameters for basis functions, predicted by MLP F\theta. Networks Two MLPs are used: 1. F\theta (Spatial): Maps pixel coordinates x=(x,y,d) to \alpha and K1 \dots KN. Encoding: Positional encoding. Input x,y encoded to 20 dims each; depth d to 16 dims. Total input dim: 56. Architecture: 6 fully-connected layers, 384 hidden nodes, LeakyReLU activations. Output: \alpha uses Sigmoid; Kn use Tanh. 2. G\phi (Directional): Maps normalized viewing direction v to global basis function values H1 \dots HN. Encoding: Positional encoding. Input vx, vy encoded to 6 dims each. Total input dim: 12. Architecture: 3 fully-connected layers, 64 hidden nodes, LeakyReLU activations. Output: 8 dimensions of H (number of basis functions N=8). Formulas The color Cp(v) for pixel p at viewing direction v is: Cp(v) = K{0p} + \sum{n=1}^{N} K{np} Hn(v) where K{0p} is the explicit base color, K{np} \in \mathbb{R}^3 are coefficients from F\theta, and Hn(v) are basis function values from G\phi. The rendering equation for an MPI layer i with alpha Ai and color Ci is standard alpha blending: \hat{I}i = O(Wi(A), Wi(C)) where O denotes the differentiable MPI rendering operator. Training Algorithm 1. Initialize parameters \theta, \phi, K0. Pre-compute pixel coordinates X. 2. Loop for maxIter epochs: a. Sample a training image Ii. b. Compute viewing direction Vi for each pixel: Vi = \frac{X - \text{center of projection of } Ii}{\|X - \text{center of projection of } Ii\|} c. Compute coefficients: (A, \tilde{K}) = F\theta(X), where \tilde{K} = [K1, \dots, KN]. d. Compute basis functions: \tilde{H} = G\phi(Vi). e. Compute view-dependent color: C = K0 + \tilde{K} \cdot \tilde{H}. f. Render predicted image: \hat{I}i = O(Wi(A), Wi(C)). g. Compute loss: L = L{rec}(\hat{I}i, Ii) + \gamma \cdot TV(K0) where L{rec} is the reconstruction loss (Eq. 6 in) and TV is Total Variation regularization on K0. h. Update \theta, \phi, K0 using Adam optimizer. Parameters MPI Layers (D): 192. Coefficient Sharing (M): 12 planes share one set of \{K0, \dots, KN\}. Basis Functions (N): 8. Loss Weights: \omega = 0.05 (gradient loss weight in L{rec}), \gamma = 0.03 (TV weight). Optimizer: Adam. Learning rate: 0.01 for K0, 0.001 for \theta, \phi. Decay factor 0.1 every 1,333 epochs. Sampling: 8,000 pixels sampled per iteration. Epochs: 4,000. Pitfalls Standard MPIs fail on non-Lambertian surfaces due to brightness constancy violation. MLPs predicting coefficients (Kn) lack high-frequency detail, resulting in blurry images. Explicitly storing K0 mitigates this. Direct optimization of MPI parameters leads to overfitting and noise; deep priors (MLPs) are required for regularization. Boundary distortions may occur near image edges. Speed: Real-time rendering (>300 FPS on RTX 2080Ti via WebGL). Training takes ~18 hours on a single NVIDIA V100 for 17 images. Efficiency: 0.16 MFLOPs/pixel for rendering, compared to NeRF's 226 MFLOPs/pixel. Quality: Outperforms NeRF, LLFF, and SRN on Real Forward-Facing and Shiny datasets in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. Limitations: May exhibit boundary distortions; relies on pre-computed cache for real-time speed. NeX-MPI was introduced in "NeX: Real-time View Synthesis with Neural Basis Expansion" (CVPR 2021). It builds on the MPI framework to address the lack of view-dependent modeling in traditional MPIs, which struggle with reflections and refractions. It leverages the "deep prior" concept, using MLPs to regularize MPI parameters, similar to techniques used in image synthesis. name: AS-NeRF
head: Adaptive Scaled Neural Radiance Field, Adaptive Scaled Neural Radiation Field with Conditional Diffusion, Conditional Diffusion Model for Sparse-View Reconstruction
body: AS-NeRF is a 3D reconstruction method designed to improve accuracy and quality from single or few views by integrating multi-task learning feature extraction, adaptive scale adjustment with spectral sensing, and a conditional diffusion model. It addresses the limitations of existing methods that either focus solely on feature extraction (e.g., Transformer-based NeRF) or sparse viewpoint fusion (e.g., SparseFusion) by explicitly modeling local details and geometric consistency. Unlike SparseFusion which distills viewpoint information, or PixelNeRF which relies on feature reprojection, AS-NeRF uses a composite feature vector to guide both the NeRF rendering and a diffusion process for synthesizing unobserved viewpoints. Inputs and Outputs Input: A single 2D toy view (or few views, 1–5) sampled uniformly from an ellipsoidal cone trajectory. Output: A rendered RGB image for a target viewpoint and a 3D radiance field representation. Data Structures The method comprises three main components: 1. MTL-FeatureNet: Based on a Vision Transformer (ViT). Encoder: 12 layers, 768 embedding dimensions, 12 attention heads (64 dimensions each). Task Relevance Scoring Module: An MLP with 2 layers, hidden size 256, ReLU activation, applied independently per task (texture, shape, color, depth). 2. NeRF Model: An improved NeRF that integrates adaptive scaling and spectral sensing. Adaptive Scale Parameter: \beta, initialized to 1.0, automatically adjusted by backpropagation. Spectral Sensing Parameters: N = 31 (covering wavelengths 400–700 nm at 10 nm intervals). \mun = 1.0 for each wavelength bin. \deltan^2 = 15 (uniformly set for spectral response smoothness). Gn = 1.0 (initialized to learn wavelength contribution). 3. Conditional Diffusion Model: Condition Vector: c, a high-dimensional vector compressed from global semantic vectors. Numbered Steps 1. Feature Extraction: Input a single 2D image into MTL-FeatureNet. Extract local feature maps and global semantic vectors. The local maps guide density and color prediction in NeRF; the global vectors are used for adaptive scale selection, spectral decoding, and diffusion conditioning. 2. NeRF Rendering with Adaptive Scale and Spectral Sensing: For each camera ray, sample 3D points. Adaptive Scale: Use the global semantic vectors to select an adaptive scale. The sensitivity of this function is optimized via \beta. Spectral Decoding: Map the scene properties to spectral responses using N=31 bins. The spectral response for bin n is modulated by \mun=1.0 and variance \deltan^2=15, with learnable weights Gn initialized to 1.0. Ray Marching: Compute volume density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} using the local feature maps and the encoded position/direction (as per Model Architecture and Encoding). 3. Diffusion Conditioning: Compress the global semantic vectors from Step 1 into a conditional vector c. Input c into the conditional diffusion model to constrain the generation of new viewpoints. 4. Training Loop (Pseudo-Supervision): Generate new viewpoints using the conditional diffusion model. Project these generated viewpoints back to the NeRF as pseudo-supervision signals. Minimize the composite loss \mathcal{T}(\theta): \mathcal{T}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}{q(Ot|O0)}\left[\log\frac{q(O{t-1}|Ot, O0)}{\rho\theta(O{t-1}|Ot, c)}\right] where O0 is the clean image, Ot is the noisy image at step t, q is the true posterior, and \rho\theta is the learned reverse transition conditioned on c. Multi-Task Loss Balancing: Task weights \lambdak: Texture=1.0, Shape=1.0, Color=0.8, Depth=1.0. Balance parameter \mu = 0.1 to balance individual task performance and inter-task synergy. Task relevance v{ij}: Dynamically adjusted, initialized to 0.5. Scaling factor \gamma{task}: Initialized to 1.0, learned via training. 5. Inference: Perform one feature extraction via MTL-FeatureNet. Render real viewpoints via NeRF using the extracted features. Simultaneously synthesize arbitrary unobserved viewpoints via the diffusion model using the same global features. The two paths share features without blocking each other. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class ASNeRF: def init(self): # MTL-FeatureNet (ViT-based) self.mtlfeaturenet = MTLFeatureNet( encoderlayers=12, embeddim=768, numheads=12, headdim=64) # Task Relevance Scoring Module (MLP) self.taskscoring = TaskRelevanceMLP(hiddensize=256) # NeRF Model self.nerf = NeRFWithAdaptiveScaleAndSpectral() # Conditional Diffusion Model self.diffusion = ConditionalDiffusionModel() # Parameters self.lambdak = {'texture': 1.0, 'shape': 1.0, 'color': 0.8, 'depth': 1.0} self.mu = 0.1 self.vijinit = 0.5 self.betainit = 1.0 self.N = 31 self.mun = 1.0 self.deltansq = 15 self.Gninit = 1.0 def extractfeatures(self, image): """ Step 1: Extract local feature maps and global semantic vectors. """ localmaps, globalvectors = self.mtlfeaturenet(image) return localmaps, globalvectors def computetaskrelevance(self, localmaps): """ Compute dynamic task relevance scores. """ # Apply MLP independently per task scores = self.taskscoring(localmaps) return scores def renderneRF(self, rayorigins, raydirections, localmaps, globalvectors): """ Step 2: Render using NeRF with adaptive scale and spectral sensing. """ # Sample points along rays (as per parent article) points = samplepointsalongrays(rayorigins, raydirections) # Encode position and direction (as per parent article) encodedpos = positionalencoding(points) encodeddir = positionalencoding(raydirections) # Adaptive Scale Adjustment # beta is learned via backpropagation, initialized to 1.0 scalefactor = self.applyadaptivescale(globalvectors, beta=self.betainit) # Spectral Sensing # N=31 bins, 400-700nm, 10nm intervals spectralweights = self.computespectralresponse(self.N, self.mun, self.deltansq, self.Gninit) # Predict density and color using local maps and encoded features density, color = self.nerf.forward(encodedpos, encodeddir, localmaps, scalefactor, spectralweights) # Volume rendering (as per parent article) renderedcolor = volumerendering(density, color) return renderedcolor def generatediffusionview(self, globalvectors, targetviewpoint): """ Step 3 & 4: Generate new viewpoint via diffusion. """ # Compress global vectors into conditional vector c c = self.compressglobalvectors(globalvectors) # Sample noise and run reverse diffusion conditioned on c # Loss minimization: T(theta) = E[log(q(O{t-1}|Ot, O0) / rhotheta(O{t-1}|Ot, c))] generatedimage = self.diffusion.sample(c, targetviewpoint) return generatedimage def trainstep(self, image, rayorigins, raydirections, targetview): """ Step 4: Training loop with pseudo-supervision. """ # 1. Extract features localmaps, globalvectors = self.extractfeatures(image) # 2. Render NeRF view nerfrender = self.renderneRF(rayorigins, raydirections, localmaps, globalvectors) # 3. Generate pseudo-supervision via Diffusion pseudoview = self.generatediffusionview(globalvectors, targetview) # 4. Compute Losses # Image reconstruction loss (e.g., MSE/SSIM) imgloss = computeimageloss(nerfrender, pseudoview) # Multi-task loss with balancing taskscores = self.computetaskrelevance(localmaps) multitaskloss = self.computemultitaskloss( localmaps, taskscores, self.lambdak, self.mu, self.vijinit) # Diffusion loss (as per formula) diffusionloss = self.computediffusionloss(globalvectors) totalloss = imgloss + multitaskloss + diffusionloss # Backpropagate to update beta, Gn, and network weights totalloss.backward() return totalloss def infer(self, image, targetviews): """ Step 5: Inference. """ localmaps, globalvectors = self.extractfeatures(image) results = {} for view in targetviews: # Render real viewpoint via NeRF nerfimg = self.renderneRF(view.origins, view.directions, localmaps, globalvectors) # Synthesize arbitrary viewpoint via Diffusion diffimg = self.generatediffusionview(globalvectors, view) results[view.id] = { 'nerf': nerfimg, 'diffusion': diffimg } return results class MTLFeatureNet(nn.Module): def init(self, encoderlayers, embeddim, numheads, headdim): super().init() # ViT Encoder self.encoder = nn.TransformerEncoder( nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(dmodel=embeddim, nhead=numheads), numlayers=encoderlayers) self.embeddim = embeddim def forward(self, x): # x: [B, C, H, W] -> [B, HW, C] # Return local feature maps and global semantic vector # Implementation details of ViT specific to AS-NeRF are not fully specified in sources # Placeholder for ViT forward pass pass class TaskRelevanceMLP(nn.Module): def init(self, hiddensize): super().init() self.net = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(hiddensize, hiddensize), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddensize, hiddensize)) def forward(self, x): return self.net(x) class NeRFWithAdaptiveScaleAndSpectral(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # Standard NeRF MLPs for density and color pass def applyadaptivescale(self, globalvectors, beta): # Adaptive scale selection based on global vectors # beta is adjusted by backpropagation pass def computespectralresponse(self, N, mun, deltansq, Gn): # Compute spectral weights for N bins # mun=1.0, deltansq=15, Gn=1.0 pass class ConditionalDiffusionModel(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # Diffusion model architecture pass def compressglobalvectors(self, globalvectors): # Compress to conditional vector c pass def sample(self, c, targetview): # Reverse diffusion process pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The spectral sensing uses 31 bins for 400-700 nm. Precision in wavelength mapping is critical for color accuracy. Boundaries: The camera trajectory is an ellipsoidal cone (elevation 10°–70°, azimuth 0°–360°). Views outside this range may not be well-supported by the training data. Degenerate Input: Single-view input is the primary use case. Performance degrades if the input image lacks sufficient texture or geometric cues, as the method relies on MTL-FeatureNet to extract these. AS-NeRF is specifically designed for 1–5 input views, outperforming SparseFusion and PixelNeRF in PSNR and SSIM on the Co3D dataset. Uses MTL-FeatureNet to extract texture, shape, color, and depth features simultaneously, balancing them with task relevance scores. Incorporates wavelength-based rendering (400-700 nm) to improve color fidelity, distinct from standard RGB NeRFs. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Hardware: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 (24GB VRAM), Intel Core i9-10900K, 64GB RAM. Resolution: Training 512×512 px (randomly cropped/scaled); Test 768×768 px. Dataset: Co3D Toys dataset (80% train, 20% test). Metrics (1 View): PSNR 2.4 dB higher than SparseFusion, 5.4 dB higher than PixelNeRF. SSIM 0.05 higher than SparseFusion, 0.10 higher than PixelNeRF. Chamfer distance 4.6 (0.4 lower than SparseFusion, 0.8 lower than PixelNeRF). Metrics (2 Views): PSNR 35.0 dB (1.4 dB higher than SparseFusion, 5.3 dB higher than PixelNeRF). SSIM 0.80 (0.08 higher than SparseFusion, 0.10 higher than PixelNeRF). Chamfer distance 4.2 (0.5 lower than SparseFusion, 0.9 lower than PixelNeRF). Perceptual Loss: Lower than SparseFusion and PixelNeRF at 256, 512, and 768 resolutions. Scaling: Performance improves with more viewpoints (1 to 5) but shows diminishing returns after 2 views. Strengths: High accuracy in single-view reconstruction; handles complex illumination and depth; generates consistent pseudo-supervision via diffusion. Limitations: Computationally intensive due to the combination of NeRF, MTL-FeatureNet, and Diffusion Model; specialized for toy objects with complex information. AS-NeRF was proposed by Lin et al. in 2023. It was developed to address the challenges of 3D reconstruction for toy objects with complex details, where existing methods like Transformer-based NeRF and SparseFusion fell short in modeling local details and geometric consistency. The method integrates multi-task learning, adaptive scaling, spectral sensing, and conditional diffusion to achieve high-quality reconstruction from sparse views. 3D reconstruction of toys based on adaptive scaled neural radiation field., https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.3053, fetched 2026-10-26

name: CoNeRF
head: Controllable NeRF, Controllable Neural Radiance Field
body: CoNeRF extends the HyperNeRF framework to enable intuitive, interpretable, and sparse supervision of localized scene attributes (e.g., facial expressions) by treating them as latent variables. Unlike HyperNeRF, which learns an arbitrary attribute space, or domain-specific methods like A-NeRF that rely on SMPL models, CoNeRF provides direct control over localized appearance using only sparse 2D mask annotations and attribute values, without requiring dense 3D supervision or heavy engineered control models. Inputs and Outputs Input: A collection of C color images \{Cc\} \in [0, 1]^{W \times H \times 3}. Sparse Supervision: For a subset of images and attributes, the user provides: Attribute values \alpha{c,a} \in [-1, 1] for the a-th attribute in the c-th image. Mask annotations M{c,a}^{gt} \in [0, 1]^{W \times H} specifying the image region controlled by the a-th attribute. Output: A radiance field model capable of rendering novel views and synthesizing attribute combinations not seen during training (e.g., closed eyes with a smiling mouth). Data Structures The model consists of three neural networks and a set of latent codes: 1. Canonicalizer K: Maps query point x to canonical space. Parameters \thetaK. K(x) \equiv K(x | \beta, \theta). 2. Hyper Map H: Maps the latent code \beta to a hyperspace field \beta(x). Parameters \thetaH. \beta(x) \equiv H(x | \beta, \theta). 3. Radiance Field R: Takes canonical coordinates K(x) and hyperspace features \beta(x) to output density \sigma(x) and color c(x). Parameters \thetaR. c(x), \sigma(x) = R(K(x), \beta(x) | \theta). 4. Regressors A and M: Map the latent code \beta to attribute values \alpha and mask fields m(x) respectively. Parameters \thetaA, \thetaM. \alpha = A(\beta | \thetaA). m(x) = M(x | \beta, \thetaM). 5. Latent Codes: A set of latent codes \{\betac\}{c=1}^C, one per input image, optimized jointly with network parameters. Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize parameters \theta = \{\thetaK, \thetaH, \thetaR, \thetaA, \thetaM\} and latent codes \{\betac\}. 2. Canonicalization: For a query 3D point x and image c, compute canonical coordinates: K(x) = K(x | \betac, \theta) 3. Hyperspace Lifting: Compute the hyperspace feature field for the attribute: \beta(x) = H(x | \betac, \theta) 4. Attribute and Mask Regression: Regress the attribute value \alphac from the latent code: \alphac = A(\betac | \thetaA) Regress the 3D volumetric mask field ma(x) for attribute a: ma(x) = M(x | \betac, \thetaM) 5. Radiance Field Evaluation: Compute density and color: \sigma(x), c(x) = R(K(x), \beta(x) | \theta) 6. Volume Rendering: Render the color C(r) and mask M(r) for a ray r parameterized by t \in [tn, tf]: C(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigma(r(t)) c(r(t), v) dt M(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigma(r(t)) m(r(t)) dt where transmittance T(t) = \exp\left(-\int{tn}^t \sigma(r(s)) ds\right). 7. Loss Computation: Calculate the total loss (see Formulas). 8. Optimization: Update \theta and \{\betac\} to minimize the total loss. Formulas The total optimization objective is: \arg \min{\theta=\{\theta, \betac\}} L{rep}(\theta | \{Cc\}) + L{ctrl}(\theta | \{M{c,a}^{gt}\}, \{\alpha{c,a}\}) Reconstruction Loss (L{rep}): L{rep}(\cdot) = L{recon}(\theta, \{\betac\} | \{Cc\}) + L{enc}(\{\betac\}) Photometric Reconstruction Loss (L{recon}): L{recon}(\cdot) = \sum{c} \mathbb{E}{r \sim Cc} \| C(r | \betac, \theta) - C{gt}(r) \|^2 Latent Code Regularization (L{enc}): L{enc}(\cdot) = \sum{c} \| \betac \|^2 Control Loss (L{ctrl}): L{ctrl}(\cdot) = L{mask}(\theta, \{\betac\} | \{M{c,a}^{gt}\}) + L{attr}(\theta, \{\betac\} | \{\alpha{c,a}\}) Attribute Loss (L{attr}): L{attr}(\cdot) = \sum{c} \sum{a} \delta{c,a} \| \alpha{c,a} - \alpha{c,a}^{gt} \|^2 where \delta{c,a} = 1 if annotation is provided, else 0. Mask Loss (L{mask}): L{mask}(\cdot) = \sum{c} \sum{a} \delta{c,a} \mathbb{E}{r} \text{CE}(M(r | \betac, \theta), M{c,a}^{gt}(r)) where \text{CE} is the cross-entropy loss between the rendered mask and the ground truth mask. Parameters Attribute Values \alpha{c,a}: Constrained to [-1, 1]. Mask Annotations M{c,a}^{gt}: Values in [0, 1]^{W \times H}. Frequency Bands: Not given in the sources. MLP Layers: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Quasi-Conditional Independence: The method assumes spatial quasi-conditional independence of attributes, allowing the synthesis of attribute combinations never seen in training data (e.g., closed eyes with a smiling mouth). Sparse Supervision: Attributes are supervised only when annotations are provided (\delta{c,a}=1). For frames without annotations (\delta{c,a}=0), attributes are discovered automatically by the framework during training. Domain Agnosticism: Unlike methods relying on SMPL, CoNeRF does not require domain-specific control models, making it applicable to general scenes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows fine-grained, direct, and interpretable control over attributes with as little as two annotations per attribute. Does not require dense 3D supervision or heavily engineered control models. Limitations: Relies on the assumption of spatial quasi-conditional independence of attributes. Requires sparse manual annotations for training. CoNeRF was introduced in the paper "CoNeRF: Controllable Neural Radiance Fields". It builds upon the HyperNeRF framework. The method addresses the limitations of existing works that either enable only compositional control of object location or rely on domain-specific models like SMPL for human bodies. CoNeRF was designed to allow intuitive and interpretable user control over scene attributes via few-shot supervision. CoNeRF: Controllable Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.01807, fetched 2026-10-26

name: NARFD with Autoencoder for Appearance Variation
head: NARF-based autoencoder
body: This method extends the Neural Articulated Radiance Field (NARFD) framework by integrating a 2D CNN-based autoencoder to model shape and appearance variations across multiple articulated objects (specifically human bodies). It solves the problem of single-view reconstruction and appearance transfer by learning a disentangled latent representation from a single input RGB image, allowing for the independent control of camera viewpoint, bone parameters, pose, and color appearance. Unlike standard NeRF variants that optimize per-scene, this approach learns a global generative model capable of reconstructing novel instances and poses from limited input. Inputs and Outputs Input: A single RGB image I of an articulated object (human body). Outputs: Reconstructed RGB image, depth map, and segmentation map. Latent Codes: The method produces a shape latent vector \mathbf{z}s and an appearance latent vector \mathbf{z}a. Data Structures Latent Vector \mathbf{z}: A vector generated by the encoder, decomposed into \mathbf{z}s and \mathbf{z}a. Bone Parameters \zeta: Parameters defining the skeletal configuration. Local Transformation \xi: Local transformation parameters for parts. Part Mask/Weight p^i: Weight associated with part i. Number of Parts P: Total number of articulated parts. Network Architecture The system consists of two main components: 1. Encoder: A 2D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) that maps the input image to a latent vector \mathbf{z}. 2. Decoder: An NARF-based decoder comprising two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): Density Network (F{\Theta,\sigma}^{t,\zeta,\mathbf{z}}): Predicts volume density \sigma and an intermediate feature vector \mathbf{h}. Color Network (F{\Theta,c}^{t,\zeta,\mathbf{z}}): Predicts RGB color c using \mathbf{h}. Step-by-Step Method 1. Encoding: The 2D CNN encoder processes the input image to generate the latent vector \mathbf{z}. 2. Latent Decomposition: The latent vector \mathbf{z} is split into the shape latent \mathbf{z}s and the appearance latent \mathbf{z}a. 3. Density Network Input Preparation: Compute positionally encoded locations \gamma(\mathbf{x}^{t^i}) for each part i \in [1, P], weighted by part mask p^i. Compute positionally encoded bone parameters \gamma(\zeta). Concatenate these with \mathbf{z}s: \text{Cat}(\{\gamma(\mathbf{x}^{t^i}) p^i | i \in [1, P]\}, \gamma(\zeta), \mathbf{z}s). 4. Density Prediction: The density network F{\Theta,\sigma}^{t,\zeta,\mathbf{z}} takes the concatenated input from Step 3 and outputs density \sigma and feature vector \mathbf{h}. 5. Color Network Input Preparation: Compute positionally encoded view directions \gamma(\mathbf{d}^{t^i}) for each part i \in [1, P], weighted by p^i. Compute positionally encoded local transformations \gamma(\xi^i) for each part i \in [1, P], weighted by p^i. Concatenate \mathbf{h}, the encoded direction/transformation pairs, and \mathbf{z}a: \text{Cat}(\mathbf{h}, \{(\gamma(\mathbf{d}^{t^i}) p^i, \gamma(\xi^i) p^i) | i \in [1, P]\}, \mathbf{z}a). 6. Color Prediction: The color network F{\Theta,c}^{t,\zeta,\mathbf{z}} takes the concatenated input from Step 5 and outputs the color c. 7. Rendering: Standard volume rendering is performed using \sigma and c to generate the output image. 8. Training: The encoder and decoder are trained jointly using the loss function defined in the base NARFD paper (Eq. 25 in). Formulas The core mapping functions are defined as: F{\Theta,\sigma}^{t,\zeta,\mathbf{z}}: \text{Cat}(\{\gamma(\mathbf{x}^{t^i}) p^i | i \in [1, P]\}, \gamma(\zeta), \mathbf{z}s) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{h}) F{\Theta,c}^{t,\zeta,\mathbf{z}}: \text{Cat}(\mathbf{h}, \{(\gamma(\mathbf{d}^{t^i}) p^i, \gamma(\xi^i) p^i) | i \in [1, P]\}, \mathbf{z}a) \rightarrow (c) Where: \text{Cat}(\cdot) denotes concatenation. \gamma(\cdot) is the positional encoding function (see Model Architecture and Encoding). \mathbf{x}^{t^i} is the position for part i at time/pose t. \mathbf{d}^{t^i} is the view direction for part i at time/pose t. \xi^i is the local transformation for part i. p^i is the part mask or weight for part i. \zeta represents bone parameters. \mathbf{z}s is the shape latent vector. \mathbf{z}a is the appearance latent vector. \sigma is volume density. \mathbf{h} is the intermediate feature vector. c is the predicted color. Parameters Image Resolution: 128 × 128 pixels. Dataset: Synthetic human body dataset derived from THUman. Subjects: 112 male subjects. Poses: 35 poses on average per person. Training Images: 35,450 images (10 images per pose with randomly sampled viewpoints). Evaluation Images: 3,940 images. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Disentanglement: The method relies on the successful decomposition of \mathbf{z} into \mathbf{z}s and \mathbf{z}a. Failure to disentangle may lead to coupled control of shape and appearance. Single-View Ambiguity: Reconstructing 3D structure from a single 2D image is ill-posed; the model relies on learned priors from the training dataset. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method successfully reconstructs RGB, depth, and segmentation maps from a single input RGB image. It effectively models appearance variation across multiple objects using a single autoencoder. Strengths: Allows individual control of camera viewpoint, bone parameters, human pose, and color appearance via the disentangled representation. Enables appearance transfer by replacing \mathbf{z}a with that of another person. Limitations: Limited to articulated objects (humans) and requires a dataset of articulated objects for training. When to use: Single-view reconstruction of articulated objects where appearance variation across instances is significant. When not to use: Static scenes or non-articulated objects where a single instance NeRF is sufficient. This method was introduced in the paper "Neural Articulated Radiance Field". It builds upon the NARFD framework, which learns disentangled representations of camera viewpoint, bone parameters, and pose. The autoencoder extension was developed to handle shape and appearance variations among multiple articulated objects, specifically humans, using a synthetic dataset derived from THUman. Neural Articulated Radiance Field, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv48922.2021.00571, fetched 2026-10-26

name: MTL-FeatureNet
head: Multi-Task Learning Feature Network
body: MTL-FeatureNet is a feature extraction network designed for multi-task learning that improves the accuracy and relevance of features extracted from a single 2D input view. It addresses the challenge of adapting a unified feature representation to diverse task requirements by integrating task dynamic attention modulation and a dynamic adapter layer. Unlike standard NeRF encodings which map coordinates to radiance properties directly, MTL-FeatureNet operates on 2D image features to support multiple downstream tasks simultaneously, distinguishing it from sibling architectures like SUDS or Rip-NeRF which focus on 3D coordinate encoding for volume rendering. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 2D image I and a set of tasks \{T1, T2, \ldots, Tn\}. Output: A set of task-specific features \{F{task1}, F{task2}, \ldots, F{taskn}\}. Data Structures Initial Features (Ci): Extracted from image I for each task Ti. Task Relevance (TRi): A scalar score computed for each task. Global Features (F{global}): The aggregated feature representation after attention modulation. Task-Specific Features (F{taski}): The final output features for task i. Parameters \gamma{task}: A learnable scaling factor customized for each task, adjusted during learning to optimize transformation efficiency. W{task}: A task-specific weight matrix. b{task}: A task-specific bias term. \sigma: An activation function. \lambdak: Weight for the loss of task k. \mu: Weight for the cross-task consistency loss. v{ij}: A dynamically adjusted weight based on the correlation between tasks i and j. dk: The dimension of the key vectors in the attention mechanism. Formulas 1. Task Dynamic Attention Modulation: The attention mechanism is modulated by the task relevance score TRi: A{ti}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{dk}} \cdot \exp(TRi)\right) \cdot V where Q, K, V are the query, key, and value matrices. 2. Task-Specific Feature Transformation: Task-specific features are derived from global features using a dynamic adapter layer: F{task} = \sigma(\gamma{task} \cdot W{task} \cdot F{global} + b{task}) where \gamma{task} scales the transformation. 3. Composite Loss Function: The total loss combines individual task losses and a cross-task consistency term: L = \sumk \lambdak \cdot Lk + \mu \cdot L{cross}(F{task1}, F{task2}, \ldots) where Lk is the loss for task k. 4. Cross-Task Consistency Loss: This loss encourages consistency or appropriate divergence between task features based on their correlation: L{cross}(F{task1}, F{task2}, \ldots) = \sum{i \ne j} v{ij} \cdot \|F{taski} - F{taskj}\|^2 where v{ij} is the dynamically adjusted weight. Numbered Steps 1. Feature Extraction and Task Relevance: For each task Ti, extract initial features Ci from the input image I. Compute the task relevance score TRi using a task-specific MLP: TRi = \text{MLP}{task}(Ci). 2. Task Dynamic Attention Modulation: For each task Ti, adjust the attention weights using the computed relevance score TRi via the formula A{ti}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}((QK^T/\sqrt{dk}) \cdot \exp(TRi)) \cdot V. 3. Dynamic Adapter Layer (DAL): Process the modulated features through the DAL to compute task-specific features F{taski} using the transformation F{task} = \sigma(\gamma{task} \cdot W{task} \cdot F{global} + b{task}). 4. Loss Computation: Compute the composite loss L using the individual task losses Lk and the cross-task consistency loss L{cross}. 5. Output Features: Return the set of task-specific features \{F{task1}, F{task2}, \ldots, F{taskn}\}. Pseudocode Unverified code. Args: imageI: Input 2D image. tasks: List of task identifiers {T1, T2,..., Tn}. Returns: List of task-specific features {Ftask1, Ftask2,..., Ftaskn}. """ n = len(tasks) initialfeatures = [] taskrelevancescores = [] # Step 1: Feature Extraction and Task Relevance for i, task in enumerate(tasks): # Extract initial features Ci from image I Ci = extractfeatures(imageI, task) initialfeatures.append(Ci) # Compute task relevance TRi using a task-specific MLP TRi = mlptask(Ci) taskrelevancescores.append(TRi) # Step 2: Task Dynamic Attention Modulation # Note: Q, K, V are derived from initial features or a shared projection # The exact construction of Q, K, V is not specified in the source # Assuming a standard self-attention setup where Q, K, V are projections of Ci modulatedfeatures = [] for i, task in enumerate(tasks): Ci = initialfeatures[i] TRi = taskrelevancescores[i] # Project to Q, K, V (implementation detail not in source) Q = projectquery(Ci) K = projectkey(Ci) V = projectvalue(Ci) # Adjust attention using TRi # Ati(Q, K, V) = softmax((QK^T/sqrt(dk)) exp(TRi)) V dk = Q.shape[-1] # Dimension of key vectors attentionweights = softmax((Q @ K.T) / sqrt(dk) exp(TRi)) Ati = attentionweights @ V modulatedfeatures.append(Ati) # Step 3: Dynamic Adapter Layer (DAL) # Fglobal is assumed to be the aggregated or concatenated modulated features # The source implies Fglobal is used for all tasks, likely derived from the # modulated features Fglobal = aggregatefeatures(modulatedfeatures) taskspecificfeatures = [] for i, task in enumerate(tasks): # Ftask = sigma(gammatask Wtask Fglobal + btask) gammatask = getscalingfactor(task) Wtask = getweightmatrix(task) btask = getbias(task) # Linear transformation with scaling transformed = gammatask (Wtask @ Fglobal) + btask # Apply activation function Ftaski = activation(transformed) taskspecificfeatures.append(Ftaski) # Step 4: Loss Computation (for training) # L = sum(lambdak Lk) + mu Lcross # This step is part of the training loop, not inference # Lcross = sum(vij ||Ftaski - Ftaskj||^2) # Step 5: Output Features return taskspecificfeatures Edge Cases and Pitfalls Task Correlation: The weight v{ij} in the cross-task loss depends on the correlation between tasks. If tasks are highly correlated, v{ij} should reflect this to prevent redundant feature learning; if uncorrelated, it should allow divergence. The method for dynamically adjusting v{ij} is not specified in the sources. Attention Modulation: The term \exp(TRi) scales the attention logits. If TRi is large, this can lead to numerical instability or overly sharp attention distributions. Proper scaling or normalization of TRi may be required. Global Feature Aggregation: The source mentions F{global} but does not specify how it is constructed from the modulated features A{ti} (e.g., concatenation, averaging, or attention pooling). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method is reported to improve rendering accuracy and color reproduction fidelity for toy 3D models compared to standard NeRF approaches. Strengths: Handles multiple tasks efficiently by dynamically modulating attention and adapting features via the DAL. Limitations: Designed for 2D toy views, which may limit its applicability to complex 3D scenes without modification. When to use: When a single 2D view needs to support multiple downstream tasks with shared but distinct feature requirements. When not to use: For standard single-task volume rendering where direct coordinate-to-radiance mapping is sufficient. It was proposed to address the challenges of high complexity scenes and complex lighting conditions by combining adaptive scale adjustment with spectral perception. name: Attention-Based Volumetric Rendering
head: AB Transformer, ABLE-NeRF, Attention-based Neural Radiance Fields
body: Attention-Based Volumetric Rendering (ABLE-NeRF) replaces the physics-based volumetric rendering equation with a self-attention mechanism to handle view-dependent effects, glossy surfaces, and translucent objects. Unlike standard NeRF variants that rely on normal prediction or regularization to exclude back-facing points, ABLE-NeRF uses masked attention to implicitly enforce front-to-back accumulation, avoiding the ill-posed nature of predicting normals in an object's interior. It incorporates Learnable Embeddings (LE) to memorize scene lighting information, similar to light probes in game engines, allowing for accurate relighting and specular effect rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera ray r(t) = o + td (origin o, direction d), camera pose for view token. Output: Predicted RGB color \mathbf{y} for the ray. Data Structures: 1. Conic Frustum Volumes: N samples along the ray. Each volume is encoded using Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE). 2. Volume Embeddings (vi): Latent vector of dimension D. Generated by passing each conic volume through a Volume Embedding Block (4 MLP layers). 3. Ray Token (R): Learnable vector of dimension D, prepended to the sequence. 4. Learnable Embeddings (LE): K learnable memory tokens of dimension D (e.g., K=32). 5. View Token (V): Derived from camera pose, used to query LEs. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: Cast a camera ray r(t) = o + td into the scene. Sample N conic frustum volumes along the ray between near and far boundaries. The positions are encoded using Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE). 2. Volume Embedding: Pass each conic volume i through a Volume Embedding Block consisting of four MLP layers with ReLU activations and hidden dimension D. This generates a sequence of volume embeddings v1, v2, \dots, vN, where i denotes the position from the camera. 3. Sequence Initialization: Prepend the Ray Token R to the sequence to form the input for the first transformer layer: Z0 = \{R, v1, v2, \dots, vN\} where R and all vi have dimension D. 4. Attention-Based Rendering Transformer (AB Transformer): Process the sequence through L transformer encoder layers. For layer l (1 \le l \le L): Masked Self-Attention for Volumes: Each volume embedding vi^l attends only to itself, the Ray Token, and volume embeddings vj where j < i (in front of it). It excludes volumes behind it (j > i). This is implemented by setting the scaled-dot product attention scores to -\infty for illegal connections before the softmax operation. vi^l = \text{Att}(Z^{l-1} \setminus \{v^{l-1}{i+1}, \dots, v^{l-1}N\}) Unmasked Attention for Ray Token: The Ray Token R^l attends to all elements in the sequence Z^{l-1} (all volumes and previous tokens). R^l = \text{Att}(Z^{l-1}) Note: The set notation Z^{l-1} represents the sequence of tokens at layer l-1. The output of the attention mechanism is typically followed by Layer Normalization and a Feed-Forward Network (FFN) as in standard Transformers, though the specific FFN structure is not detailed beyond the hidden unit ratio. 5. Color Prediction: After the final layer L, attach a single MLP classification head to the final Ray Token RL to predict the ray color \mathbf{y}. \mathbf{y} = \text{MLP}(RL) 6. Learnable Embeddings (LE) Integration (Optional/Extended): To capture view-dependent effects, K Learnable Embeddings are introduced. Cross-attention is applied where the LEs attend to the volume embeddings (or the output of the AB Transformer) to memorize scene information. A directional View Token V, comprising the camera pose, queries the LEs to decode view-dependent effects. Note: The core AB Transformer logic (Steps 1-5) defines the replacement of the VR equation. The LE component is an additional module for handling complex lighting/specularities. Formulas: Input Sequence: Z0 = \{R, v1, v2, \dots, vN\} \quad Volume Update (Masked): vi^l = \text{Att}(Z^{l-1} \setminus \{v^{l-1}{i+1}, \dots, v^{l-1}N\}) \quad Ray Token Update (Unmasked): R^l = \text{Att}(Z^{l-1}) \quad Output: \mathbf{y} = \text{MLP}(RL) \quad Parameters: N: Number of conic frustum volumes sampled along the ray. Typical value: 96 per network (192 total for coarse+fine). L: Number of transformer layers. Typical value: 2 for coarse network, 6 for fine network. D: Latent dimensional size of volume embeddings and ray token. Typical value: 192. K: Number of Learnable Embeddings. Typical value: 32 (standard Blender), 16 (Shiny Blender). Pitfalls: Masking: Without masking, the ray is treated as bi-directional, causing the network difficulty in predicting correct surface appearance. Normal Prediction: Unlike Ref-NeRF, this method does not predict normals. Relying on normal prediction for excluding back-facing points is ill-posed for interior points. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class VolumeEmbeddingBlock(nn.Module): """4 MLP layers to generate volume embedding from conic frustum.""" def init(self, D=192): super().init() # Implementation details of 4 MLP layers with ReLU and dim D # Not fully specified in source, assumed standard MLP stack self.layers = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(D, D), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(D, D), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(D, D), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(D, D)) def forward(self, x): return self.layers(x) class AttentionBasedVolumetricRendering(nn.Module): def init(self, N=96, L=6, D=192, numheads=8): super().init() self.N = N self.L = L self.D = D # Ray Token self.R = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(1, 1, D)) # Volume Embedding Block self.volumeembedder = VolumeEmbeddingBlock(D) # Transformer Layers self.transformerlayers = nn.ModuleList([ TransformerEncoderLayer(D, numheads) for in range(L) ]) # Output MLP self.outputmlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(D, D), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(D, 3) # RGB) def createattentionmask(self, N): """ Create causal mask for volume embeddings. vi can attend to vj where j <= i. Shape: (N, N) """ # Create a mask where 1 means allowed, 0 means blocked # We want vi to attend to 0..i # Standard causal mask is upper triangular 0s, lower triangular 1s # But here index 0 is closest to camera? # Source says: "vi can only attend to itself... and other volume embeddings lying in front of it (indices < i)" # And "Exclude conic volumes sequenced behind vi" # Assuming sequence is [v1,..., vN] from camera to far. # v1 (closest) attends to v1. # v2 attends to v1, v2. # Mask should allow attention to indices <= i. mask = torch.tril(torch.ones(N, N, dtype=torch.bool)) return mask def forward(self, volumefeatures): """ volumefeatures: (B, N, D) - Embedded conic frustums """ B, N, D = volumefeatures.shape # Prepend Ray Token # R shape: (1, 1, D) -> broadcast to (B, 1, D) Rexpanded = self.R.expand(B, 1, -1) Z = torch.cat([Rexpanded, volumefeatures], dim=1) # Z shape: (B, N+1, D) # Index 0 is R, Indices 1..N are v1..vN # Create mask for the N volume embeddings # We need to mask attention among the volume embeddings only. # The Ray Token (index 0) is unmasked. for layer in self.transformerlayers: # Get attention scores for all tokens # Assuming layer handles multi-head attention internally # We need to inject the mask # Extract volume embeddings part for masking logic # Z[:, 0,:] is R # Z[:, 1:,:] are volumes # Standard Transformer Layer forward would compute Q, K, V # Then apply mask to attention scores # Since we can't easily modify internal layer without subclassing, # we assume a custom TransformerEncoderLayer that accepts a mask # for specific token interactions. # Simplified: Pass Z and a mask that blocks volume-to-volume rear attention # Mask shape: (B, numheads, seqlen, seqlen) # Construct mask: # R (idx 0) can attend to all. # vi (idx i+1) can attend to R (idx 0) and vj (idx j+1) where j <= i. seqlen = N + 1 mask = torch.ones(seqlen, seqlen, dtype=torch.bool) # Mask for volume-to-volume # vi (row i+1) can attend to vj (col j+1) if j <= i # i ranges 0..N-1 (indices in volume list) # Tensor indices in Z are 1..N for i in range(N): rowidx = i + 1 for j in range(N): colidx = j + 1 if j > i: mask[rowidx, colidx] = False # R (row 0) is all True. # Columns for R (col 0) are all True (volumes can attend to R? # Source says "vi can only attend to itself, the ray token...") # So yes, volumes attend to R. # Apply mask in layer Z = layer(Z, mask=mask) # Final Ray Token is at index 0 Rfinal = Z[:, 0,:] y = self.outputmlp(Rfinal) return y class TransformerEncoderLayer(nn.Module): def init(self, D, numheads): super().init() self.selfattn = nn.MultiheadAttention(D, numheads, batchfirst=True) self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(D) self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(D) self.ffn = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(D, D 3), # FF hidden unit ratio 1:3 nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(D 3, D)) def forward(self, x, mask=None): # Self Attention attnoutput, = self.selfattn(x, x, x, attnmask=mask) x = self.norm1(x + attnoutput) # FFN ffnoutput = self.ffn(x) x = self.norm2(x + ffnoutput) return x Uses a different sampling strategy. Satellite and Remote Sensing NeRFs Time Complexity: Depends on the number of transformer layers L and samples N. The self-attention mechanism is O(N^2) per layer. With L=6 and N=96, this is computationally heavier than standard NeRF's MLP evaluation per point, but avoids the iterative alpha-compositing loop of VR. Memory Complexity: Stores N volume embeddings and L transformer states. The Learnable Embeddings add K \times D memory. Measured Performance: On the Blender dataset, ABLE-NeRF achieves SOTA results, surpassing Ref-NeRF in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. Strengths: Handles glossy and translucent objects better than standard NeRF and Ref-NeRF. Does not require normal prediction, avoiding ill-posed interior normal estimation. Limitations: Requires careful masking to prevent bi-directional ray issues. The attention mechanism may be slower to train than simple MLPs. When to use: When rendering scenes with significant specular highlights, glossy surfaces, or translucency where standard NeRF fails. When not to use: For simple diffuse scenes where standard NeRF is sufficient and faster. Attention-Based Volumetric Rendering, specifically implemented as ABLE-NeRF, was introduced by Zhe Jun Tang, Tat-Jen Cham, and Haiyu Zhao in the paper "ABLE-NeRF: Attention-Based Rendering with Learnable Embeddings for Neural Radiance Field" (arXiv:2303.13817v1, March 2023). The method was developed to address the "Achilles' heel" of NeRF: its difficulty in rendering view-dependent effects like glossy and transparent surfaces, which often appear murky. It draws inspiration from modern game engines' use of light probes for caching indirect lighting.
