name: Adaptive-Scale and Spectral-Aware NeRF
head: NeRF combining adaptive scaling with spectral perception
body: Adaptive-Scale and Spectral-Aware NeRF is a variant of Neural Radiance Fields that integrates an adaptive scale function to modulate sample point contributions and a spectral decoder to handle multispectral information (including infrared and ultraviolet) for improved color fidelity. It builds on Model Architecture and Encoding by replacing the standard color prediction with a wavelength-aware mechanism and adjusting density integration weights via local feature analysis. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: 2D toy image I, camera parameters P, global features G extracted from I using MTL-FeatureNet, and spectral components \varepsilon. Outputs: Rendered 3D image C(r). Data Structures Global Features (G): Extracted from input image I using MTL-FeatureNet. Local Features (Q): Derived from 3D position x(t) and global features G via function FA. Adaptive Scale (S): A scalar value computed from local features and global features. Spectral Components (\varepsilon): Wavelength values for which color is estimated. Method Steps 1. Initialize Model: Load MTL-FeatureNet to extract global features G from input image I. Define the volume density network \sigma(x) and the color network c(x, \varepsilon, S). 2. Compute Adaptive Scale: Extract local features Q from 3D position x(t) using FA(G, x(t)). Compute the adaptive scale S using the formula: S(FA(G, x(t)), G) = \sigma(\beta \cdot D{complex}(CT(FA(G, x(t)), G))) Where D{complex} is a depth network, CT is a feature combination function, and \beta is a parameter. 3. Spectral-Aware Color Estimation: Estimate color c(x, \varepsilon) at position x and wavelength \varepsilon using the spectral decoder: c(x, \varepsilon) = \text{softmax}\left(\sum{n=1}^N Gn \cdot e^{-\frac{(\varepsilon - \mun)^2}{2\deltan^2}}\right) \cdot MLP{color}(F(x, \varepsilon)) Where N is the number of spectral components, Gn is the weight of the n-th component, \mun is the center wavelength, \deltan^2 is the variance, MLP{color} is a multilayer perceptron, and F(x, \varepsilon) are spectral features. 4. Rendering: Render the image C(r) by integrating along the ray r: C(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \cdot \sigma(p(x(t))) \cdot c(x(t), S(FA(G, x(t)), G)) \, dt Where T(t) is the accumulated transmittance, \sigma(p(x(t))) is the spectral-aware volume density, and c is the color modulated by the adaptive scale S. 5. Output: Return the final rendered image C(r). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivescalespectralnerf(I, P, G, epsilon): """ Render an image using Adaptive-Scale and Spectral-Aware NeRF. Args: I: Input 2D toy image. P: Camera parameters. G: Global features from MTL-FeatureNet. epsilon: Spectral components (wavelengths). Returns: C: Rendered 3D image. """ # Step 1: Initialize # MTL-FeatureNet is assumed to be loaded and G is provided. # Define networks: sigmanetwork, colornetwork, fafunction, dcomplex, ctfunction, mlpcolor # Step 2 & 3 & 4: For each ray r in camera parameters P renderedimage = emptyimage() for ray in P.rays: # Sample points along the ray tvalues = samplepoints(ray.origin, ray.direction, near=ray.near, far=ray.far) accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 raycolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for t in tvalues: # 3D position x(t) xt = ray.origin + t ray.direction # Step 2: Adaptive-Scale Function # Extract local features Q from 3D position x(t) using FA(G, x(t)) localfeatures = FA(G, xt) # Compute adaptive scale S # S = sigma(beta Dcomplex(CT(localfeatures, G))) combinedfeatures = CT(localfeatures, G) depthoutput = Dcomplex(combinedfeatures) S = sigma(beta depthoutput) # Step 3: Spectral-Aware Color Estimation # c(x, epsilon) = softmax(sum(Gn exp(-((epsilon - mun)^2) / (2 deltan^2)))) MLPcolor(F(x, epsilon)) # Calculate spectral weights spectralweights = 0.0 for n in range(N): # Gn is the weight of the n-th component # mun is the center wavelength # deltan^2 is the variance gaussianweight = exp(-((epsilon - mun)2) / (2 deltan2)) spectralweights += Gn gaussianweight softmaxweight = softmax(spectralweights) # Get spectral features F(x, epsilon) spectralfeatures = F(xt, epsilon) # Apply MLP for color color = mlpcolor(spectralfeatures) # Combine with softmax weight cxepsilon = softmaxweight color # Step 4: Rendering Integration # sigma(p(x(t))) is the spectral-aware volume density density = sigma(xt) # Contribution contribution = accumulatedtransmittance density cxepsilon raycolor += contribution # Update transmittance # T(t) = exp(-sum(sigma deltat)) # Note: Standard NeRF transmittance update accumulatedtransmittance = exp(-density (tvalues[1] - tvalues[0])) # Approximation for discrete steps renderedimage[ray.id] = raycolor return renderedimage Parameters \beta: Parameter in the adaptive scale computation. N: Number of spectral components. Gn: Weight of the n-th spectral component. \mun: Center wavelength of the n-th component. \deltan^2: Variance of the n-th component. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Spectral Range: The method supports infrared and ultraviolet information, requiring appropriate handling of \varepsilon outside the visible spectrum. Feature Extraction: The quality of G depends on MTL-FeatureNet; poor extraction may degrade adaptive scaling. Depth Network: D{complex} requires accurate depth estimation; errors here affect the adaptive scale S. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves color fidelity and visual effects by handling multispectral data and adapting sample contributions. Limitations: Increased complexity due to additional networks (MTL-FeatureNet, D{complex}) and spectral decoding. The method was proposed to improve 3D toy reconstruction by integrating adaptive scaling and spectral perception into NeRF models. It utilizes MTL-FeatureNet for global feature extraction and combines this with a conditional diffusion model for generating high-quality viewpoint images. 3D reconstruction of toys based on adaptive scaled neural radiation field., https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.3053, fetched 2026-10-26

name: HIVE (HIerarchical Volume Encoding)
head: HIerarchical Volume Encoding
body: HIVE is a plug-and-play module for neural implicit surface reconstruction that explicitly encodes spatial information using hierarchical feature volumes to capture high-frequency details and enforce spatial consistency. It replaces or augments the implicit encoding of MLPs by concatenating features from multiple low-to-high resolution volumes, avoiding the global incoherence of single high-resolution volumes and the hash collisions of hash-table encodings. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N and corresponding camera poses. A point x \in \mathbb{R}^3 and viewing direction v \in S^2. Outputs: A reconstructed 3D surface S defined by the zero-level set of an SDF, and rendered images. Data Structures: Feature Volumes: A set of K 3D grids (volumes). In the basic setting, K=8. Resolutions: The volumes have resolutions increasing from 2 \times 2 \times 2 to 256 \times 256 \times 256. The source text specifies the sequence ends at 256 for the initial stage, but mentions high-resolution volumes of 512 or 1024 for the second stage. Feature Dimension: Each volume stores a small number of feature channels (e.g., 4 channels as implied by the progression description, though exact channel count per volume is not explicitly fixed in the text, the concatenation implies a fixed total input dimension to the MLP). Sparse High-Resolution Volumes: High-resolution volumes (512 or 1024) are stored as sparse structures, keeping only voxels near the surface. Numbered Steps: 1. Stage 1 (Coarse Reconstruction): Compute an initial surface reconstruction using features from low-to-medium resolution volumes (resolutions 2 to 256). For a query point x, trilinearly interpolate features from all K volumes. Concatenate these features to form F(x). Input F(x) to the SDF network to predict the SDF value. Render images and minimize the difference between rendered and input images, plus two regularization terms for smoothness. 2. Sparsification: Based on the preliminary surface from Stage 1, sparsify the high-resolution volumes (512 or 1024). Keep only voxels located near the surface of the preliminary result. Discard empty or distant voxels to reduce memory consumption. 3. Stage 2 (Fine Reconstruction): Finalize the result using features from the sparsified high-resolution volumes. Query features from the sparse high-resolution volumes (if the point is within the sparse structure) and the dense low-resolution volumes. Concatenate and input to the SDF network. Optimize the network and volume features to minimize rendering loss and smoothness regularization. Formulas: Rendering Equation: C(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \rho(t) c(p(t), v) dt where T(t) is the accumulated transmittance, \rho(t) is the density, and c(p(t), v) is the color. Weighting Function: w(t) = T(t)\rho(t) T(t) = e^{-\int0^t \rho(u) du} Density from SDF: \rho(t) = \max\left(-\frac{d\Phi}{dt}(\text{sdf}(p(t))), 0\right) where \Phis(x) = (1 + e^{-sx})^{-1} is the sigmoid function with sharpness parameter s. SDF Definition: S = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid \text{sdf}(F(x)) = 0\} Parameters: Number of Volumes: 8 in the basic setting. Resolutions: 2, 8, 32, 128, 256 (dense); 512, 1024 (sparse, high-res). Sharpness s: Not given in the sources. Regularization Terms: Two smoothness terms are used, but their specific mathematical forms are not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hivereconstruct(images, cameras): # Initialize 8 dense feature volumes with resolutions [2, 8, 32, 128, 256, 512, 1024,...] # Note: Source specifies 8 volumes, resolutions 2 to 256 for stage 1. # High-res volumes (512, 1024) are initialized but will be sparsified. volumes = initializefeaturevolumes(resolutions=[2, 8, 32, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048]) # 8 volumes total sdfmlp = initializemlp() colormlp = initializemlp() # Stage 1: Coarse Optimization for epoch in range(coarseepochs): for image, camera in zip(images, cameras): rays = generaterays(camera) points = samplepointsalongrays(rays, near, far) # Get features from all volumes (dense) features = [] for vol in volumes: feat = trilinearinterpolate(vol, points) features.append(feat) # Concatenate features Fx = concatenate(features, dim=-1) # Predict SDF and Color sdfval = sdfmlp(Fx) # Color prediction typically uses direction and intermediate features color = colormlp(Fx, rays.direction) # Render density = computedensity(sdfval) transmittance = computetransmittance(density) renderedcolor = integratedensitycolor(transmittance, density, color) # Loss loss = imageloss(renderedcolor, image) + smoothnessregularization(sdfval) optimize(loss) # Sparsify High-Resolution Volumes # Identify voxels near the surface from Stage 1 surfacepoints = extractsurface(sdfmlp, volumes) sparsemask = createsparsemask(volumes, surfacepoints, threshold=1.0) volumes[highresindices] = applysparsity(volumes[highresindices], sparsemask) # Stage 2: Fine Optimization for epoch in range(fineepochs): for image, camera in zip(images, cameras): rays = generaterays(camera) points = samplepointsalongrays(rays, near, far) features = [] for i, vol in enumerate(volumes): if i in highresindices: # Only interpolate if point is within sparse structure if isinsidesparsestructure(vol, points): feat = trilinearinterpolate(vol, points) else: feat = zerovector() # Or fallback to lower res else: feat = trilinearinterpolate(vol, points) features.append(feat) Fx = concatenate(features, dim=-1) sdfval = sdfmlp(Fx) color = colormlp(Fx, rays.direction) density = computedensity(sdfval) transmittance = computetransmittance(density) renderedcolor = integratedensitycolor(transmittance, density, color) loss = imageloss(renderedcolor, image) + smoothnessregularization(sdfval) optimize(loss) return extractmesh(sdfmlp, volumes) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Consumption: High-resolution volumes (512+) consume significant memory if dense. Sparsification is critical. Hash Collisions: Avoided by using hierarchical volumes instead of hash tables. Global Incoherence: Avoided by low-resolution volumes enforcing spatial consistency. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Reduced compared to single high-resolution dense volumes due to sparsification and the use of low-dimensional features in high-resolution volumes. Measured Performance: DTU dataset: NeuS error reduced by 25% (0.84 mm to 0.63 mm). DTU dataset: VolSDF error reduced by 23% (0.86 mm to 0.66 mm). DTU dataset: NeuralWarp error reduced by 10% (0.68 mm to 0.61 mm). EPFL dataset: NeuralWarp error reduced by 31% (full metric). Strengths: Captures high-frequency details, enforces spatial consistency, avoids hash collisions, plug-and-play. Limitations: Requires multi-stage optimization, sparsification adds complexity. When to use: When high-frequency detail and smoothness are both required, and memory is a constraint for high-res volumes. When not to use: If single-stage optimization is required, or if memory is extremely limited even for sparse structures. HIVE was introduced in the paper "HIVE: HIerarchical Volume Encoding for Neural Implicit Surface Reconstruction". It addresses limitations in existing methods where single high-resolution volumes lead to incoherent shapes and hash-table encodings suffer from collisions. It is demonstrated on DTU, EPFL, and BlendedMVS datasets. name: Panoptic Radiance Field
head: Panoptic Lifting
body: Panoptic Lifting learns a 3D panoptic radiance field from posed RGB images and machine-generated 2D panoptic segmentation masks, lifting noisy 2D labels into a consistent 3D representation of color, density, semantics, and instance identifiers. Unlike Panoptic NeRF or DM-NeRF which require manual ground truth or coarse meshes, this method requires only pre-trained 2D segmentation outputs, making it robust to in-the-wild scenes. It sets itself apart by using a linear assignment to resolve 2D instance inconsistencies and specific gradient-stopping techniques to prevent noisy labels from corrupting geometry. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Posed RGB images \{I\} and corresponding machine-generated 2D panoptic segmentation masks. Each training ray r has an associated RGB color \hat{c}r \in \mathbb{R}^3, semantic class \hat{k}r \in K, and 2D instance ID \hat{h}r \in HI (defined only for thing classes \hat{k}r \in KT). Outputs: A panoptic radiance field \Phi(x, d) that, for a 3D point x \in \mathbb{R}^3 and direction d \in S^2, predicts density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}{\ge 0}, semantic class distribution \kappa over K, distribution \pi over surrogate identifiers J, and RGB color c \in \mathbb{R}^3. From novel views, it renders color images and 3D-consistent panoptic masks. Data Structures The representation \Phi comprises four components: 1. Color and Density: Leverages a TensoRF [4] representation (lines and planes). 2. Semantic Field: A small MLP predicting \kappa. 3. Instance Field: A small MLP predicting \pi. 4. Surrogate Identifiers: A fixed set J of class-agnostic, 3D-consistent identifiers. Parameters K: Set of semantic classes, partitioned into thing classes KT and stuff classes KS. J: Fixed number of surrogate identifiers held by the instance MLP. H{3D}: Set of all possible 3D instances, H{3D}:= KT \times J. Loss weights: \lambda{con} = 1.35, \lambda{ins} = 1, \lambda{sem} = 1, \lambda{RGB} = 1. Optimizer: Adam. Learning rates: 5 \times 10^{-4} for MLPs, 1 \times 10^{-2} for TensoRF lines and planes. Hardware: 1 NVIDIA A6000, 450k iterations (~10 hours). Preprocessing: Confidence Estimation To handle noisy 2D labels, test-time augmentations (horizontal flip, scale, brightness, contrast) are applied to input images. The resulting segmentations are fused by segment clustering to obtain a semantic class distribution \hat{\kappa}r and a confidence estimate wr for each pixel (ray r). Training Steps 1. Ray Sampling: Sample rays r from training images. Let RS be rays randomly sampled across the scene and RI be rays sampled from a single image. 2. Forward Pass: For each ray, query \Phi(x, d) to get \sigma, \kappa, \pi, c. 3. Rendering: Compute rendered fields using the volumetric rendering equation: R[f |r, \sigma]:= \int0^\infty \alphat (r)\sigma(rt)f (rt, d{rt})dt where \alphat (r):= \exp \left(-\int0^t \sigma(rs)ds\right) is the transmittance. Rendered color: cr = R[c|r, \sigma]. Rendered semantic distribution: \kappar = R[\kappa|r, \sigma]. Rendered instance distribution: \pir = R[\pi|r, \sigma]. Constraint: The semantic and instance fields must output bounded probability distributions, not logits, to prevent unbounded signals in low-density areas. 4. Instance Assignment: For rays in RI, map the 2D instance ID \hat{h}r to a 3D surrogate identifier j \in J by solving a linear assignment problem. The cost is based on the model's current predictions and the 2D masks, ensuring consistent lifting of 2D instances to 3D. 5. Loss Computation: Semantic Loss (L{sem}): Cross-entropy between rendered \kappar and 2D label \hat{\kappa}r, weighted by confidence wr: L{sem}(R):= -\frac{1}{|R|} \sum{r \in R} wr \sum{k \in K} \hat{\kappa}r(k) \log \kappar(k) Instance Loss (L{ins}): Log-loss of the rendered instance distribution \pir against the mapped surrogate identifiers from the 2D instances. Segment Consistency Loss (L{con}): Guides semantic supervision to avoid fragmenting objects due to label inconsistencies. Photometric Loss (L{RGB}): L2 loss between rendered color cr and ground truth \hat{c}r. 6. Total Loss: L{tot}(R):= \lambda{ins} L{ins}(RI) + \lambda{con} L{con}(RI) + \lambda{RGB} L{RGB}(RS) + \lambda{sem} L{sem}(RS) 7. Gradient Blocking: Stop gradients from the semantic and instance branches back to the density field \sigma to prevent noisy labels from corrupting geometry. 8. Update: Update parameters using Adam. Inference For a novel view ray r: 1. Render \kappar and \pir. 2. Determine semantic class k^r:= \arg \max{k \in K} \kappar(k). 3. If k^r \in KT, determine surrogate ID j^r:= \arg \max{j \in J} \pir(j). 4. Form 3D instance ID (k^r, j^r) \in H{3D}. Scene Editing Deletion: Set density \sigma to zero for points where the predicted instance matches the target instance. Duplication: Manipulate rays passing through a new region to query the original instance region. Manipulation: Combine deletion and duplication. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainstep(rays, gtcolors, gtsemantics, gtinstances, semanticmlp, instancemlp, tenorfrmodel, optimizer, lambdacon=1.35, lambdains=1.0, lambdasem=1.0, lambdargb=1.0): optimizer.zerograd() # 1. Forward Pass # TensoRF provides sigma and color c sigma, cpred = tenorfrmodel(rays.positions, rays.directions) # Semantic and Instance MLPs provide distributions # Note: Outputs must be bounded probabilities, not logits kappapred = semanticmlp(rays.positions) pipred = instancemlp(rays.positions) # 2. Volumetric Rendering # Render color, semantic distribution, and instance distribution # R[f|r, sigma] = integral(alpha sigma f) crendered = rendervolumetric(rays, sigma, cpred) kapparendered = rendervolumetric(rays, sigma, kappapred) pirendered = rendervolumetric(rays, sigma, pipred) # 3. Loss Computation # A. Photometric Loss (on RS - rays sampled across scene) # Assuming rays are split or weighted appropriately in the batch # LRGB = L2(crendered, gtcolors) lossrgb = mseloss(crendered, gtcolors) # B. Semantic Loss (on RS) # Weighted Cross Entropy # Lsem = - sum(wr khat log(kapparendered)) # Note: gtsemantics should be the distribution khatr from TTA # and weights wr from TTA losssem = weightedcrossentropy(kapparendered, gtsemantics, rays.confidence) # C. Instance Loss (on RI - rays from single image) # Map 2D instance IDs to 3D surrogate IDs via linear assignment # This step resolves inconsistencies mappedsurrogates = solvelinearassignment( rays.instances, pipred, instancemlp.numsurrogates) lossins = crossentropy(pirendered, mappedsurrogates) # D. Segment Consistency Loss # Guides semantic field to avoid fragmenting objects losscon = computesegmentconsistencyloss(kapparendered, rays.instances) # 4. Total Loss # Gradients from semantic and instance branches are STOPPED before reaching sigma # This is implemented by detaching sigma from the computation graph # for the semantic/instance branches or using stopgradient ops. sigmadetached = sigma.detach() # Or equivalent stopgradient # Re-render or compute losses using detached sigma if necessary, # but typically the rendering equation integrates sigma. # The key is that d(Lsem)/d(sigma) = 0. totalloss = (lambdains lossins + lambdacon losscon + lambdargb lossrgb + lambdasem losssem) # 5. Backpropagation totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return totalloss.item() Time Complexity: Training is lengthy, requiring ~10 hours on a single NVIDIA A6000 for 450k iterations. It runs offline due to pre-processing (pose estimation, 2D segmentation) and optimization. Memory Complexity: Uses TensoRF for density/color (compact) plus two small MLPs for semantics and instances. Performance: Improves scene-level Panoptic Quality (PQ) by 8.4% on Hypersim, 13.8% on Replica, and 10.6% on ScanNet over state-of-the-art methods. Maintains comparable PSNR for novel view synthesis. Strengths: Robust to noisy, machine-generated 2D labels; requires no manual 3D ground truth; enables scene editing. Limitations: Limited to classes supported by the pre-trained 2D segmenter (e.g., Mask2Former); offline processing; performance depends on the quality of the 2D segmentation model. Panoptic Lifting was introduced in "Panoptic Lifting for 3D Scene Understanding with Neural Fields" (CVPR 2023). It addresses the limitation of previous panoptic NeRF methods (like Panoptic NeRF and DM-NeRF) which required manual ground truth or coarse meshes. It builds on TensoRF for efficient density/color representation and uses Mask2Former as the pre-trained 2D segmenter. name: Panoptic Neural Fields (PNF)
body: Panoptic Neural Fields (PNF) is an object-aware neural scene representation that decomposes a dynamic 3D scene into a set of discrete objects ("things") and an amorphous background ("stuff"), predicting a panoptic-radiance field for color, density, instance, and category labels at any point in time. Unlike Panoptic Radiance Field and Category-Level Semantic NeRF, which are not object-aware and cannot handle dynamic scenes, PNF explicitly models moving objects using separate MLPs per instance within dynamic bounding boxes, enabling joint optimization of 3D shape, appearance, semantics, and object poses from RGB images alone. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A sequence of RGB images. No 3D supervision or ground-truth semantic labels are required during training. Off-the-shelf algorithms provide camera parameters, 2D semantic segmentations, and 3D object detections (oriented bounding boxes with category labels). Outputs: For a query (x, d, t) where x \in \mathbb{R}^3 is position, d \in \mathbb{R}^3 is view direction, and t \in \mathbb{R} is time, the model outputs color c, density \sigma, semantic label s, and instance label i. Data Structures The scene is composed of two types of neural functions: 1. Things (Foreground Objects): Represented by a separate, time-invariant MLP for each object instance k. Each MLP operates within a local domain defined by a dynamic 3D oriented bounding box. The bounding box track Tk is parameterized by a sequence of transformation matrices at discrete timestamps. For each timestamp, parameters include a rotation matrix R \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, a translation vector t \in \mathbb{R}^3, and a time-invariant box extent s \in \mathbb{R}^3. 2. Stuff (Background): Represented by a single static MLP (or separate foreground/background MLPs for large scenes). Architecture is similar to NeRF but includes an additional direction-invariant head for semantic logits. Numbered Steps 1. Input Preparation: Employ off-the-shelf algorithms to predict camera parameters, 2D semantic segmentations for all images, and a set of 3D object detections with 3D oriented bounding boxes and category labels. 2. Initialization: Initialize the weights of the MLPs for the panoptic neural field model. This can be done using object category-specific meta-learned initialization or a simple biased initialization of density activation layers. 3. Track Interpolation: To determine the coordinate frame of an object at an arbitrary real-valued timestamp t, interpolate the discrete track steps (rotation R, translation t, extent s). 4. Coordinate Transformation: For a query point x and time t, transform the position from the world frame to the bounding box frame of the relevant object instance k using the interpolated track Tk^{-1}. 5. Field Evaluation: Query the respective MLPs (thing or stuff) to obtain density, color, semantic, and instance outputs. 6. Aggregation: Combine outputs from all active bounding boxes and the background field to form the final panoptic-radiance field. 7. Optimization: Jointly optimize the bounding box parameters (poses) and MLP weights to minimize analysis-by-synthesis style losses measuring differences in synthesized color and semantic images. Formulas The final panoptic-radiance field for any output channel (e.g., color c) is computed by aggregating contributions from bounding box hits, defaulting to the stuff output if there is no intersection: c(x | \theta) = \mathbb{1}S(x) cs(x | \theta) + \sumk ck(Tk^{-1} x | \theta) Where: \mathbb{1}S(x) is 1 if and only if the point x intersects no bounding boxes, and 0 otherwise. cs is the stuff color field. ck is the thing color field for object instance k. Tk^{-1} is the inverse transformation of the bounding box track for object k at the query time. \theta denotes the MLP weights for both stuff and thing MLPs. For other fields (density, semantic, instance), substitute radiance c with the respective function. Parameters Optimization Targets: MLP weights and bounding box parameters (object poses). Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Pitfalls Rotation Orthogonality: Optimizing rotation matrices requires maintaining orthogonality. After each gradient descent step, orthogonalize R using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to project it back onto the special orthogonal group SO(3). Shared MLPs: Previous methods that share MLPs for multiple objects limit the ability to reproduce specific discrete instances. PNF avoids this by using separate MLPs per instance, which allows each MLP to be smaller and faster, leveraging category-specific priors via meta-learned initialization. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def orthogonalizeR(R): """ Orthogonalize a rotation matrix R using SVD to project back onto SO(3). """ U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(R) return U @ Vt def interpolatetrack(track, t): """ Interpolate the discrete track steps to find the transformation at time t. track is a list of dicts, each containing 'R', 't', 's' at specific timestamps. Returns the interpolated R, t, s for time t. Note: Specific interpolation method (e.g., linear, spline) is not detailed in sources. """ # Placeholder for interpolation logic # Find surrounding timestamps and interpolate R, t, s pass def querypnf(x, d, t, things, stuffmlp): """ Query the Panoptic Neural Field for color, density, semantic, and instance. things: List of dicts, each containing 'mlp', 'track', 'instanceid', 'category'. stuffmlp: The MLP for the background stuff. """ # Check intersection with bounding boxes intersectingthings = [] for thing in things: # Get interpolated transform for this thing at time t R, trans, s = interpolatetrack(thing['track'], t) # Transform point to local box frame # xlocal = R^T (x - trans) # Note: Source uses Tk^-1 x. Assuming Tk is the transform from local to world. # Tk^-1 involves rotation transpose and translation negation. xlocal = R.T @ (x - trans) # Check if xlocal is within box extent s if np.all(np.abs(xlocal) <= s): intersectingthings.append((thing, xlocal)) # Aggregate results # Default to stuff if no intersection if not intersectingthings: return stuffmlp.query(x, d) # Sum contributions from intersecting things # Note: Source formula sums ck(Tk^-1 x). # In volumetric rendering, this usually implies alpha compositing, # but the formula provided is a direct sum for the field value itself. # We follow the formula strictly. finalcolor = np.zeros(3) finaldensity = 0.0 finalsemantic = np.zeros(numclasses) finalinstance = -1 for thing, xlocal in intersectingthings: # Query thing MLP ck, sigmak, sk, ik = thing['mlp'].query(xlocal, d) # Accumulate finalcolor += ck finaldensity += sigmak # Semantic and instance aggregation logic depends on specific rendering setup # Source formula implies direct sum for the field definition finalsemantic += sk finalinstance = ik # Overwrite or handle conflict; source doesn't specify conflict resolution # Add stuff contribution if no intersection (handled by if/else above) # If there are intersections, the formula implies the stuff term is 0 (1S(x) = 0) return finalcolor, finaldensity, finalsemantic, finalinstance def optimizepnf(images, semanticpreds, things, stuffmlp, optimizer): """ Jointly optimize bounding box and MLP parameters. """ for image, semanticpred in zip(images, semanticpreds): # Render image from current camera pose renderedcolor, renderedsemantic = renderimage(image.camerapose, things, stuffmlp) # Compute losses colorloss = lossfunction(renderedcolor, image.rgb) semanticloss = lossfunction(renderedsemantic, semanticpred) totalloss = colorloss + semanticloss # Backpropagate totalloss.backward() # Update parameters optimizer.step() # Orthogonalize rotation matrices for all things for thing in things: thing['track'].R = orthogonalizeR(thing['track'].R) optimizer.zerograd() A method for panoptic segmentation in radiance fields. PNF differs by being object-aware and handling dynamic scenes, whereas Panoptic Radiance Field is not object-aware and cannot handle dynamic scenes. A method for semantic NeRF. PNF differs by explicitly decomposing scenes into dynamic objects and background with separate MLPs, whereas Category-Level Semantic NeRF is not object-aware and cannot handle dynamic scenes. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. However, using separate MLPs per instance allows each MLP to be smaller and faster than shared MLPs, speeding inference in scenes with many objects. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Object-aware representation handles multiple moving objects; separate MLPs per instance allow overfitting to specific novel objects; smaller MLPs per instance speed up inference; uses meta-learned initialization for category-specific priors. Limitations: Requires off-the-shelf algorithms for initial camera poses, semantic segmentations, and 3D object detections; optimization of rotation matrices requires SVD orthogonalization after each step. When to use: Novel view synthesis, 2D panoptic segmentation, 3D scene editing, and multiview depth prediction on dynamic scenes. When not: Static scenes without semantic requirements may not benefit from the complexity; scenes where off-the-shelf detection/segmentation fails may lead to poor initialization. Panoptic Neural Fields were introduced by Google Research, Georgia Tech, Simon Fraser University, and Stanford University in a paper presented at CVPR 2022. The work addresses limitations of previous object-aware frameworks that do not produce panoptic segmentations, learn from scratch for every scene, and share MLPs for multiple objects, limiting their ability to reproduce specific instances. It builds on NeRF [37] and extends it to semantic and panoptic understanding in dynamic scenes. name: Category-Level Semantic NeRF
head: CLA-NeRF (Category-Level Articulated NeRF)
body: Category-Level Semantic NeRF extends the standard NeRF framework to predict part segmentation logits in addition to density and color, enabling category-level generalization for articulated objects. It differs from sibling methods like Panoptic Radiance Field by conditioning the neural field on image features extracted from input views, allowing the model to generalize across instances of the same category rather than optimizing for a single specific object. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of multi-view images I of articulated objects belonging to the same category, relative camera poses, and part segmentation labels for supervision. Outputs: For a 3D location \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d}, the model outputs density \sigma, color \mathbf{c}, and segmentation logits \mathbf{s}. Data Structures: Segmentation Logits: A vector \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^{P+1}, where P is the number of object parts and the extra dimension represents the background. Image Feature Map: W = E(I), where E is an image encoder. Projected Coordinates: \pi(\mathbf{x}), the 2D coordinate of 3D point \mathbf{x} projected onto the input image plane. Method Steps: 1. Image Encoding: Extract a feature map W from the input image I using an image encoder E. 2. Coordinate Projection: For each sampled 3D point \mathbf{x} along a ray, project it to the input image plane to obtain the coordinate \pi(\mathbf{x}). 3. Neural Field Forward Pass: Query the MLP backbone F\Theta with the positional encoding of the 3D point \gamma(\mathbf{x}), the viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and the augmented feature W(\pi(\mathbf{x})) to predict density, color, and segmentation logits: (\sigma, \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{s}) = F\Theta(\gamma(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{d}, W(\pi(\mathbf{x}))) 4. Volume Rendering of Segmentation: Compute the rendered segmentation \hat{\mathbf{S}}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} by summing over K samples, weighted by transmittance and density, similar to RGB rendering: \hat{\mathbf{S}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \hat{T}k (1 - \exp(-\sigmak(t{k+1} - tk))) \mathbf{s}k where \mathbf{s}k is the segmentation logit vector at sample k, and \hat{T}k is the accumulated transmittance: \hat{T}k = \exp\left(-\sum{k' < k} \sigma{k'}(t{k'+1} - t{k'})\right) 5. Probability Conversion: Convert logits \hat{\mathbf{S}}(\mathbf{r}) to probabilities \hat{p}i(\mathbf{r}) using the softmax function: \hat{p}i(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{\exp(\hat{S}i(\mathbf{r}))}{\sum{j=1}^{P} \exp(\hat{S}j(\mathbf{r}))} 6. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss as a weighted sum of color and segmentation losses. 7. Optimization: Jointly train the model on a collection of articulated objects from the same category using relative camera poses and part segmentation labels. Formulas: Color Loss (\mathcal{L}{color}): Mean squared error between ground truth color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) and predictions from coarse (\hat{\mathbf{C}}c) and fine (\hat{\mathbf{C}}f) networks: \mathcal{L}{color} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \frac{||\hat{\mathbf{C}}c(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r})||^2 + ||\hat{\mathbf{C}}f(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r})||^2}{2} Segmentation Loss (\mathcal{L}{seg}): Multi-class cross-entropy loss encouraging consistency between rendered semantic labels and provided labels, computed for both coarse and fine networks: \mathcal{L}{seg} = - \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \sum{i=1}^{P+1} \left( pi(\mathbf{r}) \log \hat{p}i^c(\mathbf{r}) + pi(\mathbf{r}) \log \hat{p}i^f(\mathbf{r}) \right) where pi(\mathbf{r}) is the ground truth probability of part i. Total Loss: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{color} + \lambda \cdot \mathcal{L}{seg} Parameters: \lambda: A coefficient modulating the segmentation loss during training. Typical value: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def categorylevelsemanticnerfforward(image, cameraposes, points3d, directions): # 1. Extract image features # E is the image encoder W = imageencoder(image) # 2. Project 3D points to image plane # pi is the projection function based on camera intrinsics and poses projectedcoords = projecttoimage(points3d, cameraposes) # 3. Sample feature from image feature map W at projected coordinates # This requires interpolation (e.g., bilinear) features = samplefeaturemap(W, projectedcoords) # 4. Query the MLP backbone # gamma is positional encoding # FTheta is the neural network # Inputs: positional encoding of x, viewing direction d, and image feature sigma, color, seglogits = neuralnetwork( gamma=positionalencoding(points3d), direction=directions, imagefeature=features) return sigma, color, seglogits def computesegmentationloss(renderedseglogits, groundtruthprobs, numparts): # Convert logits to probabilities using softmax # Note: The denominator sum in the source is over P parts, # but the logit vector has P+1 dimensions (including background). # Assuming the source formula implies softmax over the relevant classes. renderedprobs = softmax(renderedseglogits, axis=-1) loss = 0 for i in range(numparts + 1): # Cross-entropy term # Add epsilon to log to avoid log(0) term = groundtruthprobs[:, i] log(renderedprobs[:, i] + 1e-8) loss -= sum(term) return loss def trainstep(image, cameraposes, groundtruthcolor, groundtruthseg, lambdaseg): # Cast rays and sample points rays = castrays(cameraposes) points3d, directions = samplepointsalongrays(rays) # Forward pass sigma, colorcoarse, colorfine, seglogitscoarse, seglogitsfine = \ categorylevelsemanticnerfforward(image, cameraposes, points3d, directions) # Render color (standard volume rendering) renderedcolorcoarse = volumerendercolor(sigma, colorcoarse, rays) renderedcolorfine = volumerendercolor(sigma, colorfine, rays) # Render segmentation (volume rendering of logits) renderedsegcoarse = volumerenderseg(sigma, seglogitscoarse, rays) renderedsegfine = volumerenderseg(sigma, seglogitsfine, rays) # Compute Color Loss lcolor = (mse(renderedcolorcoarse, groundtruthcolor) + mse(renderedcolorfine, groundtruthcolor)) / 2 # Compute Segmentation Loss # groundtruthseg contains probabilities pi(r) lsegcoarse = computesegmentationloss(renderedsegcoarse, groundtruthseg) lsegfine = computesegmentationloss(renderedsegfine, groundtruthseg) lseg = lsegcoarse + lsegfine # Total Loss ltotal = lcolor + lambdaseg lseg return ltotal Time Complexity: Training requires joint optimization over a collection of objects, which may be more lengthy than single-object NeRF due to the additional segmentation head and feature conditioning. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the image feature map W and the segmentation logits for each sample, increasing memory usage compared to standard NeRF. Strengths: Enables category-level generalization for articulated objects; predicts part segmentation alongside geometry and appearance. Limitations: Requires part segmentation labels for supervision; optimization can be lengthy. When to use: When the goal is to reconstruct and segment articulated objects from a category (e.g., chairs, tables) given limited views, and part-level understanding is required. When not to use: For single-instance reconstruction without semantic needs, or when category-level generalization is not required. Category-Level Semantic NeRF (CLA-NeRF) was introduced in 2022 by the authors of "CLA-NeRF: Category-Level Articulated Neural Radiance Field". It builds upon the NeRF framework and previous works on category-level reconstruction. The method is used for rendering articulated objects at unseen poses and estimating joint attributes (rotation axis and pivot point) from the predicted segmentation field. name: Sat-NeRF
head: Sat-NeRF model, Satellite Neural Radiance Field
body: Sat-NeRF is a neural rendering method adapted for multi-view satellite photogrammetry that simultaneously learns the geometry and appearance of permanent structures while explicitly modeling shadows and transient objects (e.g., vehicles, vegetation). It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF variants by assuming a Lambertian surface, omitting viewing-angle dependence, and using native Rational Polynomial Camera (RPC) models for ray casting instead of pinhole approximations. Unlike indoor NeRFs, it incorporates a shadow-aware irradiance model and uncertainty weighting to handle multi-date imagery where lighting and transient occlusions vary significantly. Inputs and Outputs The model takes a set of multi-date satellite images as input. For each training iteration, rays are cast into the scene volume. The network function F takes three inputs: 1. \mathbf{x}: A 3-valued vector of spatial coordinates of a point on the ray. 2. \boldsymbol{\omega}: A 3-valued direction vector encoding the direction of solar rays, extracted from the azimuth and elevation angles in the image metadata. 3. \mathbf{t}j: An N(t)-valued learned embedding vector specific to image index j, used to featurize transient elements not explained by the sun's position. In the source, N(t)=4. The network outputs a tuple (\sigma, ca, s, a, \beta): \sigma: Scalar volume density at \mathbf{x}. ca: Albedo RGB color, dependent only on geometry (\mathbf{x}). s: Shadow-aware shading scalar, dependent on \mathbf{x} and \boldsymbol{\omega}, taking values in [0, 1]. a: Ambient RGB color, independent of geometry, dependent on \boldsymbol{\omega}. \beta: Uncertainty coefficient related to the probability that the color is explained by a transient object. Data Structures and Network Layout The architecture consists of three parts: 1. Main Block: A fully-connected block with h channels per layer. It predicts \sigma and ca. It uses SIREN layers with the initialization from [46]. 2. Secondary Head: Fewer layers with h/2 channels per layer. It estimates s based on \boldsymbol{\omega} and the h-dimensional geometry features from the main block. 3. Single-Layer Heads: One head predicts \beta from \mathbf{t}j and \boldsymbol{\omega}. One head predicts a from \boldsymbol{\omega}. Typical value for h is 512, adjusted based on resolution and area size. Activation Functions \sigma: Softplus. \beta: Softplus (yields smoother optimization than ReLU). ca, s, a: Sigmoid (outputs are normalized RGB values in [0, 1]). Ray Casting and Sampling Rays are cast using the Rational Polynomial Camera (RPC) model of each input image directly in object space, providing independence from the specific satellite system. Prior to training, a bundle adjustment is applied to the RPC models to boost performance and optionally extract a sparse point cloud for depth supervision. Each ray \mathbf{r} is discretized into 64 uniformly distributed 3D points. Color Rendering The color c(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}, \mathbf{t}j) at point \mathbf{x} is computed using a shadow-aware irradiance model: c(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}, \mathbf{t}j) = ca(\mathbf{x}) \cdot s(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}) + (1 - s(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega})) \cdot a(\boldsymbol{\omega}) where s \approx 1 for sun-lit points and s \approx 0 for shadowed points. Loss Function The total loss combines image reconstruction, solar correction, and optional depth supervision. 1. Main Image Loss with Uncertainty: \mathcal{L}{img} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in R} \sum{i=1}^{Nr} \betai (\mathbf{c}i - \hat{\mathbf{c}}i)^2 where R is the batch of viewing rays, \mathbf{c}i is the ground truth color, \hat{\mathbf{c}}i is the rendered color, and \betai is the uncertainty coefficient. Note: The source text describes \beta as weighting the impact of transient objects to minimize their contribution to the loss, effectively down-weighting inconsistent pixels. The specific formula in the source notes refers to equation (8) incorporating \beta. 2. Solar Correction Term (Optional): \mathcal{L}{SC}(\mathcal{R}{SC}) = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}{SC}} \sum{i=1}^{N{SC}} (Ti - si)^2 + \sum{i=1}^{N{SC}} \left(1 - \sum{i=1}^{N{SC}} Ti \alphai si \right)^2 where \mathcal{R}{SC} is a secondary batch of rays following the solar direction \boldsymbol{\omega}, Ti is transmittance, \alphai is opacity, and si is shading. 3. Depth Supervision Term (Optional): Uses sparse 3D points from the bundle adjustment. Weight \lambda{DS}. Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{img} + \lambda{SC} \mathcal{L}{SC} + \lambda{DS} \mathcal{L}{DS} Pseudocode Unverified code. Typical value: 512. \lambda{SC}: Weight for solar correction. Value: 0.05/3 (if only SC added to S-NeRF baseline) or 0.1/3 (otherwise). \lambda{DS}: Weight for depth supervision. Value: 1000/3. Learning Rate: 5 \times 10^{-4}. Scheduler: Step scheduler, decrease by factor \gamma = 0.9 every epoch. Batch Size: 1024 rays. Points per Ray: 64 uniformly distributed points. Iterations: 300k to converge. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Sparse Point Cloud Outliers: The sparse point cloud from bundle adjustment may contain outliers, especially in multi-date collections, leading to slightly worse altitude Mean Absolute Error (MAE) in some areas compared to plain Sat-NeRF loss. Uncertainty Limitations: The uncertainty coefficient \beta can only absorb occasional inconsistencies. It does not account for roofs under construction or roofs unusually free of parked cars, which may cause holes in the Digital Surface Model (DSM). Solar Direction Extrapolation: The shading scalar s can produce unrealistic results for solar ray directions not seen in training data. This is mitigated by the solar correction term. A variant for sparse single-date satellite imagery using Semi-Global Matching (SGM) depth supervision. Choose when only 2-3 images are available and standard Sat-NeRF fails due to insufficient geometric constraints. Time Complexity: Training takes approximately 10 hours for 300k iterations with a single batch of rays, or ~20 hours if solar correction or depth supervision terms are added. Memory: Requires a GPU with 16 GB RAM. Performance: Sat-NeRF provides higher PSNR/SSIM and similar or smaller altitude MAE compared to S-NeRF without requiring solar correction. Adding solar correction decreases altitude MAE further. Geometry Quality: Sat-NeRF DSMs have more detailed structures and sharper edges than traditional stereo pipelines (S2P), but S2P provides more regular surfaces. Sat-NeRF produces more local irregularities (less flat roofs/roads) but is free of single-point outliers. Strengths: Robust to shadows and transient objects; uses native RPC models; high-quality novel view synthesis and 3D modeling. Limitations: Local irregularities in flat surfaces; potential holes in DSM for dynamic structures not captured by \beta; sensitive to outliers in bundle adjustment point clouds. Sat-NeRF was introduced by Roger Marí, Gabriele Facciolo, and Thibaud Ehret from Université Paris-Saclay and Centre Borelli in 2022. It extends the S-NeRF method by incorporating modeling of transient objects similar to NeRF-W and using RPC camera models more adapted to satellite data. It was evaluated on the 2019 IEEE GRSS Data Fusion Contest data, using Maxar WorldView-3 images over Jacksonville, Florida. name: SpS-NeRF
head: SparseSat-NeRF (SpS-NeRF)
body: SpS-NeRF is a variant of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) adapted for novel view synthesis and 3D geometry reconstruction from sparse, single-date satellite imagery. It solves the problem of reconstructing high-quality Digital Surface Models (DSM) and photorealistic views when only a few (2-3) satellite images are available, a scenario where standard NeRF and its predecessor Sat-NeRF fail due to insufficient geometric constraints. Unlike learning-based depth completion methods used in indoor scenes, SpS-NeRF leverages traditional Semi-Global Matching (SGM) to generate dense, albeit noisy and incomplete, depth maps which serve as supervision. It distinguishes itself by incorporating an uncertainty metric derived from SGM cross-correlation maps to guide ray sampling and weight depth losses, allowing the network to refine depth in occluded or textureless areas while maintaining sharp building outlines. SpS-NeRF builds on the architecture of Sat-NeRF. It omits the modeling of transient objects and solar correction found in Sat-NeRF because it targets synchronous satellite acquisitions where lighting and scene content are consistent across views. The method jointly optimizes RGB color and depth geometry by integrating dense depth supervision derived from traditional computer vision techniques. Inputs: 1. A set of N satellite images (typically N=2 or N=3) with known camera intrinsics and extrinsics. 2. Dense depth maps and corresponding cross-correlation confidence maps generated by Semi-Global Matching (SGM). The depth maps are computed from images downsampled by a factor of 4, resulting in a Ground Sample Distance (GSD) that is 4\times larger than the original image resolution. The depth maps are incomplete (due to occlusions) and imprecise. 3. A margin parameter m defining the acceptable deviation from the input depth. Outputs: 1. Rendered RGB images for novel viewpoints. 2. A refined, dense Digital Surface Model (DSM). The method relies on the standard NeRF volumetric representation but augments it with external supervision data structures: SGM Depth Map: A 2D array D{SGM} of size H \times W (where H, W are the downsampled image dimensions). Values represent depth in meters. Invalid pixels (occlusions/no texture) are marked with a specific invalid value (e.g., 0 or NaN). SGM Correlation Map: A 2D array C{SGM} of size H \times W. Values represent the cross-correlation similarity score between matched pixels in the stereo pair. Higher values indicate higher confidence. NeRF Network F\Theta: A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) taking encoded position \mathbf{x} and view direction \mathbf{d} as input, outputting volume density \sigma and RGB color \mathbf{c}. 1. Preprocessing (SGM): For each pair of input satellite images, compute dense depth maps and cross-correlation maps using Semi-Global Matching (SGM) on images downsampled by a factor of 4. 2. Ray Sampling (Guided): For each pixel in a target view, cast a ray r(\lambda) = o + \lambda d. Sample N points along the ray within the near/far bounds. The sampling strategy is "guided" by the input depth and uncertainty. Calculate the uncertainty weight w(r) for the ray based on the SGM correlation map at the corresponding 2D pixel location. The uncertainty measure intervenes in three ways: 1. As a weight applied to the final depth loss. 2. As a threshold to determine whether the depth loss should be activated for a specific sample. 3. In guided ray sampling to concentrate samples near the expected depth surface. 3. Forward Pass (NeRF): For each sampled point xi on the ray: Encode position \mathbf{x}i and direction \mathbf{d} using hierarchical sinusoidal positional encoding \gamma(\cdot). Pass encoded features through the MLP F\Theta to predict volume density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i. 4. Volume Rendering (RGB): Compute the rendered color C(r) for the ray using standard volume rendering integration: C(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i where: \alphai = 1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai} Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) \deltai = t{i+1} - ti Here, \alphai is the opacity of the i-th sample, Ti is the transmittance (probability that the ray reaches xi without being blocked), and \deltai is the distance between samples. 5. Depth Estimation: Compute the rendered depth D(r) for the ray. This is typically the expected distance of the samples weighted by their opacity: D(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai ti where ti is the distance of the i-th sample from the camera origin. 6. Loss Calculation: The total loss \mathcal{L} is a weighted sum of the RGB loss and the Depth loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambdad \mathcal{L}{depth} RGB Loss (\mathcal{L}{rgb}): Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the rendered color C(r) and the ground truth image color C{gt}(r). Depth Loss (\mathcal{L}{depth}): Formulated similarly to DDPNeRF but using the SGM-derived uncertainty. Let D{gt}(r) be the input depth from SGM at the pixel location. The loss is activated only if the predicted depth D(r) is within a margin m of the input depth D{gt}(r): \text{Condition: } |D(r) - D{gt}(r)| < m If the condition is met, the loss is computed as the absolute difference, weighted by the uncertainty w(r) derived from the SGM correlation map C{SGM}: \mathcal{L}{depth} = w(r) \cdot |D(r) - D{gt}(r)| The weight w(r) is higher for pixels with high correlation confidence (low uncertainty). Note: The exact formula for w(r) as a function of C{SGM} is not explicitly defined in the text, but it is described as an "uncertainty measure" based on correlation maps. 7. Optimization: Minimize \mathcal{L} with respect to the network parameters \Theta using an optimizer (e.g., Adam). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def spsnerftrainingloop(images, poses, sgmdepths, sgmcorrelations, numviews, numsamples, marginm, lambdad): """ Simulates the training loop for SpS-NeRF. Args: images: List of input satellite images (H, W, 3). poses: List of camera poses (extrinsics) for each image. sgmdepths: List of dense depth maps from SGM (H/4, W/4). sgmcorrelations: List of SGM cross-correlation confidence maps (H/4, W/4). numviews: Number of input views (e.g., 2 or 3). numsamples: Number of points sampled along each ray. marginm: Margin for depth loss activation. lambdad: Weight for depth loss. Returns: Trained NeRF network parameters. """ # Initialize NeRF MLP parameters Theta # Architecture: Input (posenc(x) + direnc(d)) -> MLP -> (sigma, color) Theta = initializemlpparameters() for epoch in range(maxepochs): totalloss = 0 for viewidx in range(numviews): img = images[viewidx] pose = poses[viewidx] depthmap = sgmdepths[viewidx] corrmap = sgmcorrelations[viewidx] # Get image dimensions (original resolution) H, W, = img.shape # Downsample factor for SGM data scale = 4 # Iterate over pixels in the image for y in range(H): for x in range(W): # 1. Ray Generation # Compute ray origin and direction from camera intrinsics/extrinsics # dcam = ((x - cx)/fx, (y - cy)/fy, 1) # dworld = R dcam # oworld = t rayo, rayd = generateray(pose, x, y) # 2. Guided Ray Sampling # Map pixel (x,y) to SGM coordinate space sgmx = x // scale sgmy = y // scale # Get SGM depth and correlation for this pixel # Handle invalid pixels (occlusions) if isinvalid(depthmap[sgmy, sgmx]): # Standard sampling or skip depth loss samplest = samplealongray(rayo, rayd, numsamples) depthlossval = 0.0 uncertaintyweight = 0.0 else: # Guided sampling: concentrate samples near the SGM depth # The text mentions "guided ray sampling borrowed from Roessle et al." # and that uncertainty is used in sampling. # We assume samples are clustered around the SGM depth value. sgmdepthval = depthmap[sgmy, sgmx] samplest = guidedsamplealongray(rayo, rayd, sgmdepthval, numsamples) # 3. Uncertainty Weight Calculation # Based on SGM correlation map corrval = corrmap[sgmy, sgmx] uncertaintyweight = computeuncertaintyweight(corrval) # 4. Depth Loss Condition # We need the predicted depth to compare against SGM depth # This requires a forward pass first, or simultaneous calculation. # For clarity, we separate forward pass. pass # 5. Forward Pass (NeRF) # Sample points along the ray points = rayo + samplest[:, np.newaxis] rayd[np.newaxis,:] # Encode positions and directions # Using hierarchical positional encoding gamma(p) posenc = hierarchicalposenc(points) direnc = hierarchicalposenc(rayd) # MLP Forward # Density branch and Color branch as per parent article sigma, color = mlpforward(posenc, direnc, Theta) # 6. Volume Rendering (RGB) # Compute opacities and transmittance deltas = np.diff(np.concatenate(([0], samplest))) # Distance between samples alphas = 1 - np.exp(-sigma deltas) transmittances = np.cumprod(np.concatenate(([1], 1 - alphas[:-1]))) # Rendered Color renderedcolor = np.sum(transmittances alphas color, axis=0) # Rendered Depth (Expected distance) rendereddepth = np.sum(transmittances alphas samplest) # 7. Loss Calculation # RGB Loss gtcolor = img[y, x] rgbloss = np.mean((renderedcolor - gtcolor) 2) # Depth Loss depthlossval = 0.0 if not isinvalid(depthmap[sgmy, sgmx]): sgmdepthval = depthmap[sgmy, sgmx] # Check margin condition if abs(rendereddepth - sgmdepthval) < marginm: # Apply uncertainty weight depthlossval = uncertaintyweight abs(rendereddepth - sgmdepthval) else: depthlossval = 0.0 # Loss not activated outside margin else: depthlossval = 0.0 # Total Loss for this pixel pixelloss = rgbloss + lambdad depthlossval totalloss += pixelloss # Backpropagation and Optimization Step updateparameters(Theta, totalloss) return Theta def hierarchicalposenc(p, L=10): """ Hierarchical positional encoding as defined in parent article. gamma(p) = (sin(2^0 pi p), cos(2^0 pi p),..., sin(2^{L-1} pi p), cos(2^{L-1} pi p)) """ encodings = [] for i in range(L): freq = 2i np.pi encodings.append(np.sin(freq p)) encodings.append(np.cos(freq p)) return np.concatenate(encodings) def computeuncertaintyweight(corrval): """ Computes weight based on SGM correlation. Higher correlation -> Higher weight (more trust). Exact formula not given in sources, but concept is defined. Assuming a linear or sigmoidal mapping from correlation [0,1] to weight. """ # Placeholder for the specific mapping function not detailed in text # Typically, weight = corrval or 1 - corrval depending on definition of "uncertainty" # Text says "uncertainty measure... as a weight applied to the final depth loss" # and "corr(r)=1... deactivate uncertainty metric". # If corr=1 (high confidence), weight should be high. return corrval def guidedsamplealongray(origin, direction, targetdepth, numsamples): """ Samples points along the ray, clustering around the targetdepth. Target depth is in world units. """ # Project target depth to ray parameter lambda # lambda = targetdepth / dot(direction, normalofplaneatorigin?) # In standard NeRF, depth is often Euclidean distance from origin. # Assuming targetdepth is the Euclidean distance along the ray. lambdatarget = targetdepth / np.linalg.norm(direction) # Generate samples around lambdatarget # The text mentions "m margin" and "guided ray sampling". # We assume a Gaussian or uniform distribution centered at lambdatarget. spread = 0.1 lambdatarget # Heuristic spread samples = np.random.normal(loc=lambdatarget, scale=spread, size=numsamples) return samples Downsample Factor: 4 (SGM is run on images with 1/4 resolution). Margin (m): Not explicitly given in the text, but referenced as a threshold for depth loss activation (Equation 5). Number of Views: 2 (DFC2v, Dji2v) or 3 (DFC3v, Dji3v). Optimizer: Not explicitly named, but standard NeRF optimization uses Adam. Flat Surface Regularization: SpS-NeRF lacks regularization on flat surfaces, leading to local irregularities (noise) in the reconstructed DSM. This is a common problem in NeRF. Adding semantic information is suggested as a potential solution. SGM Outliers: SGM is susceptible to outliers. The Ground Truth DSM in the Djibouti dataset was generated using the same SGM method, potentially biasing the evaluation and corrupting the GT with erroneous depth estimations. Occlusions: Input depth maps are incomplete due to occlusions. SpS-NeRF handles this by jointly optimizing RGB and depth losses, allowing it to complete missing information, but performance depends on the quality of the SGM correlation map in these regions. Comparison Bias: SpS-NeRF is less accurate than full-resolution SGM (SGMscl1) on valid pixels (MAEin) due to lack of regularization, but better in occluded/poorly textured areas (MAEout). Time Complexity: Not explicitly given. Depends on the number of views, samples per ray, and MLP size. Training involves joint optimization of RGB and depth losses. Memory Complexity: Not explicitly given. Depends on the resolution of the SGM depth maps and the NeRF MLP size. Measured Performance: DFC2019 (2 views): PSNR 20.2, SSIM 0.87, MAEin 3.02, MAEout 7.77. DFC2019 (3 views): PSNR 19.06, SSIM 0.86, MAEin 4.63, MAEout 2.05. Djibouti (2 views): PSNR 32.85, SSIM 0.92, MAEin 1.57, MAEout 1.15. Djibouti (3 views): PSNR 36.26, SSIM 0.95, MAEin 1.35, MAEout 0.81. Scaling: The method is designed for sparse views (2-3 images). It outperforms standard NeRF and Sat-NeRF in these scenarios. Strengths: Effective for sparse satellite imagery. Better than SGM in occluded and poorly textured areas (MAEout). Produces sharper building outlines than vanilla Sat-NeRF. Free of SGM outliers. Limitations: Lacks regularization on flat surfaces, causing local irregularities. Less accurate than full-resolution SGM on valid pixels (MAEin). Relies on the quality of SGM; if SGM fails (e.g., textureless areas), supervision is weak. SpS-NeRF (SparseSat-NeRF) was introduced by Zhang et al. in 2023. It is an extension of Sat-NeRF (Marí et al., 2022) and incorporates ideas from DDPNeRF (Roessle et al., 2022). The method was developed to address the challenges of 3D reconstruction from sparse satellite imagery, where traditional NeRF variants require many views to produce convincing geometries. It was tested on the DFC2019 dataset and the Djibouti dataset (obtained via the CNES ISIS framework). Numerical computations were performed on the SCAPAD cluster at the Institute de Physique du Globe de Paris. name: Sampling and Rendering Pipeline Configuration
body: This configuration defines the parameters and logic for generating rays and querying the neural radiance field during training and inference. It solves the problem of balancing rendering fidelity with computational cost by controlling sample density, noise injection, and multi-resolution strategies. It differs from sibling configurations by focusing specifically on the ray-sampling mechanics and the structure of the rendering kwargs dictionary, rather than initialization weights, architecture, or regularization terms. The core mechanism involves constructing a renderkwargs dictionary that is passed to the volumetric rendering function. This dictionary controls how rays are discretized into samples and how the network outputs are processed. Key shared concepts include: Ray Discretization: Rays are sampled at discrete points along their length. The number of samples (N{samples}) and the distribution (linear vs. inverse depth) determine the spatial resolution of the query. Noise Regularization: Random noise is added to the sampled depths or the network's raw density output (\sigma) to prevent the network from memorizing the training views and to encourage smoothness. Multi-Stage Rendering: High-fidelity rendering often involves a coarse network for initial sampling and a fine network for denser sampling in promising regions. Determinism vs. Stochasticity: Training typically uses stochastic sampling (perturbation, noise) to improve generalization, while testing uses deterministic sampling to ensure consistent evaluation metrics. Definition: A configuration that sets up the rendering arguments to support a two-stage sampling process involving a coarse network and a fine network, along with noise regularization for the density output. Step: 1. Create a dictionary renderkwargstrain containing: networkqueryfn, perturb, Nimportance, networkfine, Nsamples, networkfn, useviewdirs, whitebkgd, and rawnoisestd. 2. Determine NDC and linear depth settings: If the dataset type is not 'llff' or args.nondc is true, set ndc=False and lindisp=args.lindisp. 3. Create renderkwargstest by copying renderkwargstrain, but override perturb=False and rawnoisestd=0. to ensure deterministic output. Parameter: Nsamples: Number of coarse samples per ray. Default: 64. Nimportance: Number of additional fine samples per ray. Default: 0. perturb: Jitter factor for sampling depths. Default: 1.0. rawnoisestd: Standard deviation of noise added to the raw sigma output. Default: 0.0. Code: python renderkwargstest['perturb'] = False renderkwargstest['rawnoisestd'] = 0. Pitfall: Test rendering must disable perturbation and raw noise to ensure deterministic output for evaluation. Definition: A training strategy divided into warm-up and finetuning phases to optimize efficiency, accelerate convergence, minimize early overfitting artifacts, and learn intricate details via denser sampling in high-complexity areas. Step: 1. Divide training into two phases: warm-up and finetuning. 2. During the warm-up phase, start with a small number of samples per ray and increase steadily to a target number. 3. During the finetuning phase, set the base number of samples per ray to match the final count of the warm-up phase. 4. Add an additional small number of sample points to the finetuning count. 5. Sample these additional points using an importance sampling technique. Parameter: Initial warm-up samples per ray: 64. Additional finetuning samples: 64. Definition: A ray sampling strategy that excludes rays passing through the black outer areas of laparoscopic images to prevent artifacts caused by overlapping images where black areas intersect with valid color regions of other views. Step: 1. Create a single circular mask centered on the image. 2. Calculate the radius of the circular mask based on the circular view of the laparoscope. 3. Sample rays only from pixels that fall within the mask (i.e., pixels with color values), excluding rays from the black peripheral areas. 4. Allow the NeRF model to infer the content of the masked black areas based on color information from overlapping regions in other images. Parameter: Mask shape: Circular. Mask position: Centered on the image. Pitfall: Artifacts occur at intersections between valid color lines of one image and black area lines of overlapping images if rays are sampled from the black areas. The configuration of sampling and rendering pipelines is fundamental to Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and its variants. The original NeRF paper introduced the concept of importance sampling and multi-resolution coarse/fine networks to improve rendering quality. Subsequent works have adapted these pipelines for specific domains, such as dynamic volumetric scenes using two-phase progressive sampling and medical laparoscopy using mask-based sampling to handle non-circular fields of view. name: Method-Specific Training Pipelines
body: This family encompasses specific training configurations and optimization loops for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that deviate from standard baseline implementations to address specific challenges such as motion blur, single-image synthesis, or stratified scene structures. Unlike generic NeRF training, these methods integrate domain-specific constraints—such as physical image formation models for blurred inputs or generative adversarial networks for unsupervised learning—directly into the optimization loop. The articles in this family share the core mechanism of optimizing NeRF parameters (\theta) via gradient descent, typically using the Adam optimizer. However, they differ fundamentally in the loss functions, input data structures, and auxiliary variables optimized. Commonalities include: 1. Differentiable Rendering: All methods rely on the differentiability of the volume rendering equation to backpropagate gradients from image space to scene representation. 2. Iterative Optimization: Training proceeds over a fixed number of iterations or until convergence, updating parameters to minimize a specific loss metric (photometric, adversarial, or perceptual). 3. Ray Sampling: All methods involve sampling points along camera rays to query the NeRF density and color fields. The number of samples and sampling strategy (e.g., stratified, uniform) are hyperparameters tuned per method. BAD-NeRF reconstructs 3D scenes and recovers camera poses from motion-blurred images. It differs from standard NeRF by explicitly modeling the camera's exposure time. Instead of assuming sharp images, it jointly optimizes the NeRF parameters and the continuous camera motion trajectory (start and end poses) for each image. It synthesizes blurred images by rendering and averaging a sequence of sharp intermediate views along the interpolated trajectory. Choose this method when inputs are motion-blurred and accurate pose estimation is required. Pix2NeRF is an unsupervised method for translating a single input image into a NeRF using a pre-trained \pi-GAN. It differs from inverse rendering methods like BAD-NeRF by not requiring multi-view supervision or test-time optimization against ground-truth views. It achieves a super-resolution effect by training at 64×64 resolution while rendering at 128×128. Choose this method for single-image 3D reconstruction where multi-view data is unavailable. Strata-NeRF optimizes NeRFs for stratified scenes (e.g., multi-level buildings) using a specific configuration derived from Mip-NeRF 360. It uses the "360.gin" configuration file, which employs a contract function to map input coordinates onto a ball of radius 2, handling large scenes better than the "blender 256.gin" configuration. It uses a vector codebook in a "Latent Generator" network. Choose this method for large-scale, multi-level synthetic or real-world scenes where standard NeRF configurations fail to capture global structure. The concept of method-specific training pipelines emerged as NeRF applications expanded beyond simple synthetic scenes to complex real-world scenarios involving motion blur, single-image synthesis, and large-scale stratified environments. BAD-NeRF was introduced to handle the physical reality of camera exposure times, which standard NeRF ignores. Pix2NeRF addressed the lack of multi-view data by leveraging generative priors. Strata-NeRF adapted Mip-NeRF 360's architecture to handle the specific challenges of stratified scenes, such as occlusion and scale variations across levels.
