name: AR-NeRF Training Configuration
head: AR-NeRF Implementation Details, AR-NeRF architecture and training configuration
body: AR-NeRF is a method for unsupervised learning of depth and defocus effects from natural images by combining aperture rendering with neural radiance fields. It solves the problem of generating photorealistic images with controllable depth-of-field effects without requiring explicit 3D scene reconstruction or ground-truth depth labels. It differs from standard NeRF variants by integrating a GAN-based training framework (specifically adapted from pi-GAN) to handle the ill-posed nature of single-view synthesis, while explicitly modeling aperture size and focus distance as continuous control parameters. The method trains a generative model that maps a latent code to a radiance field, which is then rendered via volume rendering with aperture control. The training minimizes a combination of GAN loss, R1 regularization, and an identity regularizer to maintain consistency across viewpoints. Inputs: A dataset of unposed natural images (e.g., flowers, birds, faces). A random latent code z sampled from a standard normal distribution. Outputs: Synthesized images with controllable defocus strength (aperture size s) and focus distance (f). The architecture consists of three main components: a Mapping Network, a Synthesis Network (split into Foreground and Background), and a Discriminator. 1. Mapping Network: Structure: Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Hidden Layers: 3 layers. Units per Layer: 256. Activation: Leaky ReLU (LReLU) with negative slope 0.2. Latent Code Dimension: 256. Purpose: Propagates information from the latent code to the synthesis network layers. 2. Synthesis Network: Structure: MLP using FiLM-SIREN (Fourier Feature SIREN with Feature-wise Linear Modulation). Foreground Synthesis Network: Hidden Layers: 8 layers. Units per Layer: 128. Note: Reduced from 256 (used in original pi-GAN) to allow more points per ray, improving performance without significant quality loss. Background Synthesis Network: Hidden Layers: 8 layers. Units per Layer: 64. Rationale: Fewer parameters are used under the assumption that the background is simpler than the foreground. 3. Discriminator: Structure: Convolutional network with residual blocks. For FFHQ (Faces): Includes CoordConv layers followed by residual blocks. For Oxford Flowers and CUB-200-2011: Same as FFHQ but without CoordConv layers. CoordConv was found to have negative effects on these datasets likely due to the lack of strict alignment (unlike facial landmarks in FFHQ). The training process uses the non-saturating GAN loss with real gradient penalty (R1) regularization. 1. Optimization Setup: Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 0.00006. Total Iterations: 200,000. R1 Regularization Weight: 0.2. Identity Regularizer Weight: 15. The identity regularizer ensures that the generated content remains consistent (preserves identity) across different viewpoints. 2. Ray Sampling and Rendering: The synthesis network outputs density and color. Ray sampling involves querying the network at points along the ray. The number of points per ray is increased to improve performance, facilitated by the reduced unit count (128) in the foreground network. Defocus parameters (aperture size s, focus distance f) are integrated into the rendering process to simulate camera optics. 3. Loss Function: The total loss L is a weighted sum: L = L{GAN} + \lambda{R1} L{R1} + \lambda{ID} L{ID} Where: L{GAN} is the non-saturating GAN loss. L{R1} is the R1 gradient penalty regularization. \lambda{R1} = 0.2. L{ID} is the identity regularizer loss. \lambda{ID} = 15. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainarnerf(dataset, numiterations=200000): # 1. Initialize Networks mappingnet = MLP(hiddenlayers=3, units=256, activation='LReLU', slope=0.2) foregroundnet = MLP(hiddenlayers=8, units=128, activation='FiLM-SIREN') backgroundnet = MLP(hiddenlayers=8, units=64, activation='FiLM-SIREN') # Discriminator setup depends on dataset if dataset == 'FFHQ': discriminator = Discriminator(withcoordconv=True) else: # Oxford Flowers, CUB-200-2011 discriminator = Discriminator(withcoordconv=False) # 2. Initialize Optimizer optimizer = Adam(learningrate=0.00006) # 3. Hyperparameters lambdar1 = 0.2 lambdaid = 15 # 4. Training Loop for iteration in range(numiterations): # Sample batch of real images realimages = dataset.nextbatch() # Sample latent codes z = samplefromnormaldistribution(batchsize) # Generate images via AR-NeRF rendering # Note: Defocus parameters s and f are controlled during rendering generatedimages = renderarnerf(z, foregroundnet, backgroundnet, mappingnet) # Compute GAN Loss ganloss = computeganloss(realimages, generatedimages, discriminator) # Compute R1 Regularization r1loss = computer1gradientpenalty(realimages, discriminator) # Compute Identity Regularization # Ensures consistency across viewpoints idloss = computeidentityloss(generatedimages, mappingnet) # Total Loss totalloss = ganloss + (lambdar1 r1loss) + (lambdaid idloss) # Update weights optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() CoordConv Usage: Using CoordConv layers in the discriminator for non-aligned objects (flowers, birds) degrades performance. Ray Density: Processing time and memory increase with the number of rays. While 10 rays were found sufficient for comparable performance to stratified sampling with fewer rays, higher resolutions may require more points per ray. Unit Reduction: Reducing synthesis network units from 256 to 128 is critical for allowing more points per ray, which improves performance. A defocus renderer trained on AR-NeRF-generated images that allows continuous and intuitive manipulation of defocus strength and focus distance given an input image. Unlike AR-GAN-DR, where defocus parameters are uniquely determined by the input image, AR-NeRF-R allows interactive adjustment via auxiliary inputs. Definition: A conditional U-Net that takes an image and auxiliary parameters (aperture size s, focus distance f) to output a defocused image. Training Steps: 1. Generate training images at 128×128 resolution using AR-NeRF by increasing input point density. 2. Train a conditional U-Net on these images. 3. Feed aperture size s and focus distance f as auxiliary information to the U-Net. 4. Output defocused images by varying s and f continuously. Layout: U-Net architecture with two auxiliary scalar inputs (s, f) concatenated or injected as conditioning signals. Usage: Trained on Oxford Flowers dataset using 128×128 images generated by AR-NeRF; evaluated on iPhone2DSLR Flower dataset. An adaptation of RegNeRF using default DTU dataset settings with specific adjustments for compatibility with the AR-NeRF pipeline. Definition: A baseline configuration for RegNeRF used in comparative experiments. Steps: 1. Use default settings provided by authors for the DTU dataset. 2. Adjust the near and far planes and scene scaling. 3. Disable the loss from the appearance regularizer because the model is not available in this context. Performance: AR-NeRF achieves competitive FID and KID scores compared to baseline GANs (AR-GAN, AR-GAN++, RGBD-GAN) on Oxford Flowers, CUB-200-2011, and FFHQ datasets. Memory/Time: Processing time and memory usage scale with the number of rays and points per ray. The reduction in network units (128 vs 256) helps mitigate memory constraints, allowing for higher point density. Strengths: Unsupervised learning of depth and defocus; continuous control of defocus parameters; high-quality synthesis on natural images. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of discriminator architecture (CoordConv) based on dataset alignment; performance may degrade if ray density is insufficient for higher resolutions. AR-NeRF was introduced in 2022 by the authors of the paper "AR-NeRF: Unsupervised Learning of Depth and Defocus Effects from Natural Images with Aperture Rendering Neural Radiance Fields". It builds upon the pi-GAN framework, adapting it for unsupervised depth and defocus learning. The method was applied to three datasets: Oxford Flowers (8,189 images, 102 categories), CUB-200-2011 (11,788 images, 200 bird species), and FFHQ (70,000 face images). AR-NeRF: Unsupervised Learning of Depth and Defocus Effects from Natural Images with Aperture Rendering Neural Radiance Fields, https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.06100v1, fetched 2026-10-26 Preface: A Data-driven Volumetric Prior for Few-shot Ultra High-resolution Face Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv51070.2023.00315, fetched 2026-10-27

name: DP-based Configuration Selector
head: Multiple-Choice Knapsack Configuration Selection, Dynamic-programming-based configuration selection, MCK-based configuration selection, NeRFlex configuration selector
body:
The DP-based Configuration Selector is a method for selecting optimal neural radiance field (NeRF) configurations for multiple segmented objects under a strict global memory constraint H. It solves the configuration selection problem by formulating it as a Multiple-Choice Knapsack (MCK) problem, which is NP-hard. Unlike greedy approaches that rely on feasibility conditions often violated in multi-knob NeRF scenarios, this method uses dynamic programming to guarantee an optimal solution within the memory limit. It is specifically designed for mobile deployment where exceeding memory limits causes rendering failures or severe performance degradation. Inputs and Outputs Input: I: The set of segmented objects, with size n = |I|. Ci: The configuration space for object i, containing discrete configuration pairs 	heta. f{si}(	heta): A profiling function estimating the memory size (in bytes) of object i's NeRF representation given configuration 	heta. f{qi}(	heta): A profiling function estimating the rendering quality (e.g., SSIM or PSNR) of object i's NeRF representation given configuration 	heta. H: The maximum allowed total memory size for the multi-modal NeRF representation. Output: configs: A list of pairs (i, 	hetai^) representing the selected optimal configuration for each object i. Data Structures The algorithm utilizes three primary data structures: 1. q: A 1D array of size H+1. q[j] stores the maximum achievable total quality for the processed objects using exactly (or at most) capacity j. Initialized to 0. 2. choices: A 2D array of dimensions n 	imes (H+1). choices[i][j] stores the configuration pair 	heta selected for object i when the remaining capacity is j. Initialized to null/None. 3. configs: An empty list to store the final selected configuration pairs during backtracking. Parameters Configuration Pair 	hetai = (gi, pi): Represents the geometry resolution knob gi and texture parameter knob pi for object i. Memory Constraint H: Fixed memory size available on the target device. Typical values are 240MB for iPhone 13 and 150MB for Pixel 4. Baseline Configuration: For single NeRF or Block-NeRF baselines, the recommended pair is (128, 17). Algorithm Steps The algorithm proceeds in two phases: DP table filling and backtracking. 1. Initialization: For each object i \in I, initialize the minimum configuration 	hetai^ \leftarrow \min(Ci) = (\min(gi), \min(pi)). Initialize q as an array of zeros of length H+1. Initialize choices as a 2D array of nulls with dimensions n 	imes (H+1). Initialize configs as an empty list. 2. DP Table Filling: Iterate through each object i from 0 to n-1. For each object, iterate through the capacity j from H down to 0 (to ensure each object is selected at most once per capacity level in the knapsack formulation). For each configuration 	heta \in Ci: Calculate Threshold: Compute the minimum memory required by all other objects h 
eq i using their minimum configurations: ri = H - \sum{h=1, h 
eq i}^{n} \min{	hetat \in Ch} f{sh}(	hetat) Feasibility Check: If the size of the current configuration f{si}(	heta) \ge ri, skip this configuration. This ensures that selecting 	heta leaves enough room for the minimal configurations of all other objects, satisfying the feasibility condition. State Transition: If the current capacity j is sufficient for the configuration (j \ge f{si}(	heta)): Calculate the potential new quality: Q{new} = q[j - f{si}(	heta)] + f{qi}(	heta). If q[j] < Q{new}: Update q[j] \leftarrow Q{new}. Record the choice: choices[i][j] \leftarrow 	heta. 3. Backtracking: Initialize currentcapacity = H. Iterate from the last object index m = n-1 down to 0: If choices[m][currentcapacity] is not null: Let 	heta{selected} = 	ext{choices}[m][	ext{current\capacity}]. Add the pair (m, 	heta{selected}) to configs. Update currentcapacity \leftarrow 	ext{current\capacity} - f{sm}(	heta{selected}). Else: Assign the minimum configuration 	hetam^ to object m and add (m, 	hetam^) to configs. [G: The source algorithm description implies that if no choice was recorded, the object was not part of the optimal DP path for the remaining capacity, but since every object must be rendered, the fallback to the minimum configuration is necessary to ensure a valid solution. The source notes state "Initialize the minimum configuration... 	hetai^" at the start, implying this is the fallback.] Return configs. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dpconfigurationselector(objects, sizefunc, qualityfunc, H): """ Selects optimal NeRF configurations for a set of objects under memory constraint H. Args: objects: List of object identifiers I. sizefunc: Function fsi(theta) returning memory size for object i and config theta. qualityfunc: Function fqi(theta) returning quality for object i and config theta. H: Maximum allowed memory size. Returns: configs: List of tuples (objectindex, selectedconfigpair). """ n = len(objects) # Data structures # q[j] stores max quality for capacity j q = [0.0] (H + 1) # choices[i][j] stores the config theta selected for object i at capacity j choices = [[None] (H + 1) for in range(n)] # Precompute minimum configurations for all objects to calculate thresholds # Note: Ci is the configuration space for object i minconfigs = {} minsizes = {} for i, obj in enumerate(objects): Ci = getconfigurationspace(obj) # Helper to get Ci minconfigs[i] = min(Ci, key=lambda theta: sizefunc(i, theta)) minsizes[i] = sizefunc(i, minconfigs[i]) # DP Table Filling for i, obj in enumerate(objects): Ci = getconfigurationspace(obj) # Calculate the minimum memory required by all OTHER objects # Sum of min sizes for all h != i minothersize = sum(minsizes[h] for h in range(n) if h != i) ri = H - minothersize # Iterate capacity downwards to satisfy MCK constraints (each object picked once) for j in range(H, -1, -1): for theta in Ci: size = sizefunc(i, theta) # Feasibility check: ensure remaining capacity can fit min configs of others if size >= ri: continue # State transition if j >= size: newquality = q[j - size] + qualityfunc(i, theta) if newquality > q[j]: q[j] = newquality choices[i][j] = theta # Backtracking configs = [] currentcapacity = H for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1): selectedtheta = choices[i][currentcapacity] if selectedtheta is not None: configs.append((i, selectedtheta)) currentcapacity -= sizefunc(i, selectedtheta) else: # Fallback to minimum configuration if not explicitly chosen in DP path # This ensures all objects have a valid configuration configs.append((i, minconfigs[i])) return configs Edge Cases and Pitfalls Infeasibility of Greedy Conditions: The feasibility condition \sum{	hetaj \in Ci} f{si}(	hetaj) + \min{h 
eq i} \min{	hetat \in Ch} f{sh}(	hetat) \le H is often not met in NeRFlex due to the presence of two control knobs (g and p). Greedy algorithms fail here, necessitating DP. Memory Limits: On iPhone 13, exceeding 240MB causes the local WebGL rendering engine to fail to load data. On Pixel 4, exceeding 150MB causes average FPS to drop by ~15, leading to stuttering. Precision: The size function f{si} and quality function f{qi} are derived from profiling models. Inaccuracies in these models can lead to suboptimal selections or constraint violations if the estimated size is significantly lower than the actual runtime size. Time Complexity: O(nhc), where n is the number of objects, h is the memory constraint H, and c is the size of the configuration space C for an object. The threshold calculation takes O(n) per object, and the DP process takes O(hc) per object. Memory Complexity: O(nh) for the choices table and O(h) for the q array. Strengths: Guarantees an optimal solution to the MCK problem within the memory constraint, unlike greedy approaches which may fail or produce sub-optimal results when feasibility conditions are not met. Limitations: The problem is NP-hard. The pseudo-polynomial time complexity O(nhc) can be prohibitive if H or c is very large. It requires accurate profiling models for size and quality. When to Use: When deploying multi-NeRF systems on resource-constrained devices (e.g., mobile phones) where strict memory limits must be respected and optimal quality is desired. When Not to Use: When real-time configuration selection is required and n or H are too large for the O(nhc) complexity, or when profiling models are unavailable or inaccurate. The DP-based Configuration Selector was introduced in the NeRFlex paper. NeRFlex is a resource-aware real-time high-quality rendering system for complex scenes on mobile devices. The method addresses the challenge of managing memory for multiple segmented NeRF objects on devices with limited RAM, such as the iPhone 13 and Pixel 4. The problem is formulated as a Multiple-Choice Knapsack (MCK) problem, which is known to be NP-hard. Previous approaches for single-object NeRFs or those relying on greedy search were insufficient due to the multi-knob nature of the configuration space and the strict feasibility requirements of greedy algorithms. NeRFlex: Resource-aware Real-time High-quality Rendering of Complex Scenes on Mobile Devices, https://doi.org/10.1109/icdcs63083.2025.00067, fetched 2026-10-29

name: ActiveNeRF Training Configuration
head: Active Learning with Uncertainty Estimation, ActiveNeRF, ActiveNeRF optimization settings, NeRF training hyperparameters
body: ActiveNeRF is a learning framework that models a 3D scene with a constrained input budget by incorporating uncertainty estimation into a NeRF model and using an active learning scheme to select new training samples based on information gain. It supplements the existing training set with newly captured samples to improve model performance upper bounds under limited training budgets. Unlike NeRF-W which models uncertainty for transient objects across images, ActiveNeRF models uncertainty for inherent noise in training data to guide active sampling. Unlike S-NeRF which uses variational inference and requires multiple identical inferences, ActiveNeRF follows the volume rendering procedure strictly and does not require multiple inferences for uncertainty. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Initial set of posed images (training data), camera poses, and a budget for additional captures. Outputs: A trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) with uncertainty estimation, and a sequence of selected viewpoints for active capture. Data Structures: The model consists of two parallel Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): a coarse model and a fine model. Coarse Model: Identical to vanilla NeRF. Outputs density \sigma and feature vector f from positional encoding \gammax(x), and color c from f and direction encoding \gammad(d). [\sigma, f] = \text{MLP}{\theta1}(\gammax(x)) c = \text{MLP}{\theta2}(f, \gammad(d)) Fine Model: Includes an additional uncertainty branch. Outputs density \sigma, feature f, and variance \beta^2(r(t)) from coordinates. [\sigma, f, \beta^2(r(t))] = \text{MLP}{\theta1, \theta3}(\gammax(r(t))) The mean color \bar{c}(r(t)) is output by a separate MLP: \bar{c}(r(t)) = \text{MLP}{\theta2}(f, \gammad(d)). The variance is regularized via softplus to ensure validity: \bar{\beta}^2(r(t)) = \beta0^2 + \log(1 + \exp(\beta^2(r(t)))), where \beta0^2 ensures a minimum variance for all locations. Numbered Steps: 1. Train ActiveNeRF Model: Train the coarse and fine models using the initial observation data. The optimization minimizes the negative log-likelihood of rays in a batch B, combined with a regularization term for sparser density. Loss: \mathcal{L}^{uct} = \frac{1}{N}\sum{i=1}^N \left( \frac{\|C(ri) - \bar{C}(ri)\|2^2}{2\bar{\beta}^2(ri)} + \frac{\log \bar{\beta}^2(ri)}{2} + \frac{\lambda}{Ns}\sum{j=1}^{Ns} \sigmai(ri(tj)) \right) Total Loss: \mathcal{L}^{uct}(C(r), \bar{C}^f(r)) + \frac{1}{N}\sum{i=1}^N \|C(ri) - \hat{C}^c(ri)\|2^2. 2. Render Novel Views: Render novel views from the trained model to estimate uncertainty. The rendered color C(r) follows a Gaussian distribution \mathcal{N}(\bar{C}(r), \bar{\beta}^2(r)) where \bar{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{Ns} \alphai \bar{c}(r(ti)) and \bar{\beta}^2(r) = \sum{i=1}^{Ns} \alphai^2 \bar{\beta}^2(r(ti)). 3. Estimate New Viewpoint: Evaluate candidate views to find the one that most reduces uncertainty. Sample candidate views from a spherical space. For efficiency, evaluate new inputs with lower resolution by sampling H/r \times W/r rays instead of full H \times W rays, approximating the influence of the whole image with 1/r^2 time consumption. Calculate the information gain as the subtraction of the variance from the prior to posterior distribution. The acquisition function \mathcal{A}(D2) is defined as the sum of variance reductions for all sampled locations across all rays in an image: \mathcal{A}(D2) = \sum{ri \in D2} \sum{j=1}^{Ns} \left( \text{Var}^{(\text{pri})}(ri(tj)) - \text{Var}^{(\text{post})}(ri(tj)) \right) The posterior variance for a sampled location r2(tk) given a new ray r2 is: \text{Var}^{(\text{post})}(r2(tk)) = \left( \frac{1}{\bar{\beta}^2(r2(tk))} + \frac{\alphak^2}{\bar{\beta}^2(r2)} \right)^{-1} = \frac{\bar{\beta}^2(r2(tk))\bar{\beta}^2(r2)}{\alphak^2\bar{\beta}^2(r2(tk)) + \bar{\beta}^2(r2)} This is always less than the prior variance \bar{\beta}^2(r2(tk)). Choose the top-k candidates that score highest in the acquisition function as the supplementary of the current training set. 4. Capture and Add: Capture a new perception and add it to the training set. Two approaches exist for incorporation: Bayesian Estimation (BE): Compute the posterior distribution of scene locations using ground-truth values from new inputs, avoiding collateral training. The posterior mean is used as the estimate. \text{Mean} = \gamma \frac{C(r2) - b(tk)}{\alphak} + (1 - \gamma) \bar{c}(r2(tk)) where \gamma = \frac{\alphak^2 \bar{\beta}^2(r2(tk))}{\alphak^2 \bar{\beta}^2(r2(tk)) + \bar{\beta}^2(r2)} and b(tk) represents the contribution of unrelated sampled locations in the ray. Continuous Learning (CL): Add captured inputs to the training set and tune the model based on the current one. NeRF fails to generalize well from one or few input views and may collapse to trivial solutions in unobserved regions. The uncertainty estimation ensures robustness by providing larger variances in unobserved regions instead of collapsing. Unlike random view synthesis which may contain large redundancy, this policy selects samples with the most information gain. Time and Memory Complexity: Bayesian Estimation (BE): Saves 75% of time consumption compared to Continuous Learning (CL) because it avoids collateral training. When to Use: Use when the training data budget is constrained and the goal is to maximize performance with minimal additional resources. name: Meta-learning for Fast NeRF Reconstruction
head: Gradient-based Meta-learning with Local Conditioning
body:
This method enables the rapid reconstruction of a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) from a small number of input images by leveraging gradient-based meta-learning. Unlike standard NeRF training which requires hundreds of optimization steps to converge, this approach learns an initialization or adaptation strategy that allows the scene representation MLP to converge in significantly fewer steps. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like NeRF Hyperparameters by focusing on the initialization and meta-update phase rather than just static hyperparameter tuning, and differs from DONeRF by explicitly using meta-learning to capture priors rather than just dynamic sampling. The core objective is to optimize the weights W of an MLP scene representation such that it can fit a new scene's data D{new} in K steps, where K \ll K{standard}. Inputs: A set of meta-training scenes \mathcal{S}{meta} = \{S1,..., SM\} with associated image sets. A target scene with a small set of input images I{target}. A base MLP architecture \mathcal{M}	heta mapping (x, \omega) to (\sigma, c). Outputs: A meta-initialized parameter set 	heta^ or a meta-updated parameter set 	heta' for the target scene. Data Structures: MLP Parameters 	heta: Standard weights and biases for the density/color network. Meta-Gradient Buffer: Stores gradients accumulated over meta-training tasks. Algorithm Steps: 1. Meta-Training Phase (Learning the Prior): For each meta-task i from a meta-training dataset: a. Sample a scene Si and a support set of images I{support}. b. Compute the loss \mathcal{L}(	heta) on I{support} using differentiable volume rendering. c. Perform one or more gradient descent steps to obtain task-specific weights 	hetai': 	hetai' = 	heta - \alpha 
abla	heta \mathcal{L}i(	heta) where \alpha is the inner learning rate. d. Compute the loss \mathcal{L}i'(	hetai') on a query set (or the same support set for one-step meta-learning). e. Compute the meta-gradient: 
abla	heta \mathcal{L}i'(	hetai') f. Update the global meta-parameters 	heta: 	heta \leftarrow 	heta -  eta 
abla	heta \mathcal{L}i'(	hetai') where  eta is the meta-learning rate. Note: For Category-Specific Learned Initialization, this step uses FedAvg (equivalent to REPTILE). Specifically, independently optimize MLPs on separate shapes from a collection (e.g., ShapeNet), then average the weights across all models to form the new initialization. 2. Local Conditioning (Optional Enhancement): To account for local variations, image features can be extracted from the input images and used to condition the MLP initialization or the first few layers, allowing the model to adapt to specific lighting or texture details. 3. Target Scene Adaptation: a. Initialize the target scene MLP with the meta-learned weights 	heta^. b. Render images for the input views I{target}. c. Compute photometric loss against ground truth. d. Perform K gradient descent steps to refine 	heta for the target scene. Parameters: Inner Learning Rate (\alpha): Not given in the sources. Typical values range from 10^{-4} to 10^{-3}. Meta Learning Rate ( eta): Not given in the sources. Typically smaller than \alpha, e.g., 10^{-5} to 10^{-4}. Number of Meta-Steps: Not given in the sources. Often 1-5 steps for fast adaptation. Number of Views: Requires fewer views compared to standard neural radiance field training. Edge Cases: Degenerate Input: If the target scene is significantly out-of-distribution from the meta-training set, the meta-prior may hinder convergence rather than help. Precision: Gradient accumulation in meta-learning can suffer from precision issues if not carefully managed. This variant uses meta-learning to capture category-specific shape and appearance priors from a large shape collection (e.g., ShapeNet). It improves generalization and convergence for specific object categories. The process involves meta-learning category-specific initial weights by pre-training on ShapeNet using FedAvg. To perform one meta-step of FedAvg: independently optimize a set of MLPs, each on a separate ShapeNet shape. Average the model weights across all NeRF models, and start another meta-step. When reconstructing a full scene, initialize the MLPs for each instance track T to this initialization. FedAvg is equivalent to REPTILE meta-learning. Time Complexity: Training time is dominated by the meta-training phase, which is expensive as it requires many gradient steps across many tasks. However, inference (adaptation to a new scene) is extremely fast, requiring only a few gradient steps. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the meta-parameters and potentially intermediate gradients for the meta-update, which is higher than standard NeRF training but comparable to other meta-learning approaches. Performance: Significantly reduces the number of optimization steps required for convergence on novel scenes. Strengths: Fast reconstruction from few images; robust initialization. Limitations: Requires a large meta-training dataset; may not generalize well to out-of-distribution scenes. The concept of quickly optimizing MLP scene representations via gradient-based meta-learning was proposed to address the slow convergence of standard NeRF training. Bergman et al. [BKW21] leveraged this approach with local conditioning on image features. Category-specific initialization using FedAvg/REPTILE was introduced in the context of Panoptic Neural Fields. name: Category-Specific Learned Initialization
head: Category-specific prior initialization, Federated averaging initialization, Learned Initialization, Meta-learned Initialization
body: Category-Specific Learned Initialization uses meta-learning to capture shape and appearance priors from a large collection of objects within a specific category (e.g., cars on ShapeNet) to initialize the weights of instance-specific neural radiance field (NeRF) MLPs. It solves the problem of poor reconstruction quality and slow convergence when training on novel scenes with sparse input views, where standard random initialization fails to complete partial views. It sets itself apart from standard initialization by distilling category-level knowledge into the starting weights, allowing the model to generalize better and converge faster, particularly in data-sparse regimes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A large dataset of 3D models from a specific category (e.g., ShapeNet cars), rendered into 2D images. Output: A set of optimized MLP weights \theta{init} that serve as the initialization for instance-specific "thing" MLPs during novel scene reconstruction. Data Structures: \theta: The weights of the MLP (typically a "thing" MLP with 4 hidden layers and width 128, using positional encoding with L=6 frequencies for object coordinates). Dk: The dataset for client k, defined as a bundle of rays corresponding to every observed pixel of object instance k. \mathcal{B}: A set of local minibatches, where each batch contains B rays. Algorithm (Federated Averaging for Meta-Learning): The method employs Federated Averaging (FedAvg) to meta-learn the initialization. This process is equivalent to REPTILE meta-learning. 1. Server Initialization: Initialize global weights \theta0. 2. Outer Loop (Meta-Training): For each outer epoch t = 1, 2, \dots: a. Client Updates (Parallel): For each client k \in \{1, \dots, K\} (where K is the number of unique object instances): i. Receive current weights \thetat from the server. ii. Split Dk into batches of ray bundles of size B. iii. Perform local optimization for E inner epochs: For each inner epoch i = 1, \dots, E: For each batch b \in \mathcal{B}: \theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta \nabla\theta \ell(\theta; b) (Note: \eta is the learning rate, \ell is the loss function, typically reconstruction loss. The algorithm assumes simple SGD but can be adapted for other optimizers.) iv. Return the updated local weights \theta{t+1}^k to the server. b. Server Aggregation: Average the weights from all clients: \theta{t+1} = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^{K} \theta{t+1}^k 3. Final Initialization: The resulting \theta{final} is used as the initialization for the thing MLPs when training on a novel scene. Usage in Novel Scene Reconstruction: When reconstructing a novel scene containing instances of the trained category: 1. Initialize the MLP for each object instance track T with the meta-learned weights \theta{final}. 2. Train the inference-time scene representation network on the novel scene data, focusing only on the individual set of object instances present. Parameters: K: Number of clients (unique object instances in the meta-training set). B: Local minibatch size (number of rays per batch). E: Number of inner (local) epochs per client. \eta: Learning rate. \thetat: Network parameters after t outer epochs. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The algorithm description assumes simple SGD; adaptation for other optimizers requires modifying the CLIENTUPDATE step. Standard Xavier (Glorot) initialization fails to complete partial views with sparse inputs, whereas this method succeeds. A decentralized federated training algorithm used to realize category-specific learned initialization for thing MLPs by meta-learning from 2D rendered images of 3D models from ShapeNet. It allows for parallel processing of unique object instances. It is chosen when a large shape collection is available for a specific category (e.g., cars and vans) to distill priors into initialization weights. It is equivalent to REPTILE meta-learning. Time Complexity: The meta-training phase requires T outer epochs, each involving K parallel client updates of E inner epochs. The total computational cost is proportional to T \times K \times E. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the MLP weights \theta and the datasets Dk for each client. Performance: On ShapeNet cars, the model reconstructs novel object instances well even with just a single image input, outperforming standard initialization which fails to complete partial views. With dense input views (at least 50 views over two full epochs), it provides faster convergence compared to standard Xavier initialization. Strengths: Improves generalization and convergence; enables complete reconstruction from sparse views (1 or 3 images); efficient inference-time training as the network focuses only on present instances. Limitations: Requires a large shape collection for the specific category; other object categories not covered by the meta-learned prior use biased initialization. When to use: When reconstructing scenes with sparse input views for categories with available prior data (e.g., cars, vans). When not to use: For categories without a large shape collection or when dense views are available and standard initialization converges sufficiently (though learned initialization still offers faster convergence). Originated in the Panoptic Neural Fields paper (2022). The method leverages meta-learning [11] to capture category-specific shape and appearance priors. It uses the FedAvg algorithm [36], which is known to be equivalent to REPTILE [42] meta-learning [25]. The approach was evaluated on ShapeNet [5] cars (provided by [56]) and applied to cars and vans in dynamic KITTI scenes. It addresses the issue where dense content in "stuff" can suppress gradients from distant objects, making prior knowledge via initialization robust. """ # Initialize optimizer for volume and MLP weights optimizer = Adam([volume, mlpweights.parameters()], lr=0.001) # Learning rate not specified, standard NeRF is 5e-5 or similar. for iteration in range(numiterations): totalloss = 0 # Sample a batch of target views or all views for view in targetviews: # Get image dimensions height, width = view.imageheight, view.imagewidth # Initialize rendered image renderedimage = torch.zeros((height, width, 3)) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): # Cast ray rayorigin, raydirection = getray(view, x, y) # Sample points along the ray # Uniform sampling with small per-step randomness tvals = uniformsample(rayorigin, raydirection, pointsperray) points = rayorigin + tvals raydirection # Volume Rendering alphas = [] colors = [] ts = [] for i, point in enumerate(points): # 1. MLP Forward Pass # Concatenate PE and feature # Note: Source Table 3 suggests complex input dimensions. # We assume the MLP handles the concatenation internally or via a linear layer. inputtomlp = concatenate(pe, feat) sigma, color = mlpforward(mlpweights, inputtomlp) # 4. Compute alpha # Delta is distance between samples delta = distance(points[i], points[i+1]) if i < len(points)-1 else 0.01 # alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma delta) alphas.append(alpha) colors.append(color) ts.append(tvals[i]) # Composite color # Ti = exp(-sum{j=1}^{i-1} sigmaj deltaj) # C(r) = sum Ti alphai ci renderedcolor = compositecolor(alphas, colors) renderedimage[y, x] = renderedcolor # Compute Loss # Assuming target image is available for the view targetimage = view.image loss = l1loss(renderedimage, targetimage) totalloss += loss # Backpropagate totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() if iteration % 1000 == 0: print(f"Iteration {iteration}, Loss: {totalloss.item()}") return volume, mlpweights Training Iterations: 10,000. Points per Ray: 128 for standard scenes, 256 for challenging scenes (high gloss/specularity). Hardware: Single NVIDIA RTX 2080Ti GPU. Training Duration: ~15 minutes. 1. Out-of-Frustum Artifacts: If the scene is large, parts visible in novel views may lie outside the reference view's frustum. This causes artifacts because the volume is only initialized within the frustum. Solution: Pad the boundary voxels of the neural encoding volume to extend beyond the frustum. Pitfall: Padded voxels are not well-reconstructed initially and may require longer fine-tuning to achieve high quality. 2. Limited Viewing Range: The representation is initialized only for content seen by the reference view. Unseen parts (occluded or outside frustum) are not directly recovered, making 360-degree rendering challenging with a single volume. Solution: Combine multiple neural encoding volumes at multiple views for larger viewing ranges. 3. View-Dependent Shading: Highly challenging scenes with high glossiness or specularities are hard to recover via network inference alone. Solution: Use more points per ray (256) and potentially longer fine-tuning. Time Complexity: O(I \cdot N \cdot P), where I is the number of iterations (10,000), N is the number of points per ray (128-256), and P is the number of pixels. Memory Complexity: O(V \cdot C + M), where V is the volume size, C is the feature dimension, and M is the MLP size. Measured Performance: On the DTU and LLFF datasets, MVSNeRF's 15-minute fine-tuning (10k iterations) achieves quality comparable to or better than NeRF's 10.2-hour optimization (200k iterations). Scaling: Performance scales with the number of iterations. The 12k-iteration result (18 min) is already better than NeRF's 48k-iteration result (10.2h). Strengths: Significantly faster than from-scratch optimization (15 min vs 10.2 hours). High quality results quickly. Limitations: Limited viewing range with a single volume. Struggles with highly specular scenes without extended fine-tuning. Padding voxels require longer convergence. When to Use: When high-quality novel view synthesis is required for a specific scene and a generalizable initial reconstruction is available. Ideal for scenarios where training time is constrained but quality is critical. When Not to Use: When 360-degree rendering is required and multiple volumes cannot be combined. When scenes have extreme specularities and very short fine-tuning time is available. Origin: MVSNeRF was introduced by Sun et al. in 2021. Development: The method builds on the idea of generalizable radiance field reconstruction, using a CNN to predict a neural encoding volume and an MLP decoder. The per-scene fine-tuning step was introduced to refine the initial prediction, addressing the limitations of pure inference-based reconstruction. Usage: Used in view synthesis tasks on datasets like DTU and LLFF. name: Mip-NeRF Optimization and Activation Details
head: JaxNeRF Training Procedure, Mip-NeRF Misc. Changes
body: This article defines the specific hyperparameters, activation functions, and input preprocessing steps used to train Mip-NeRF and JaxNeRF models. These details address implementation-specific challenges such as training stability, catastrophic failure modes in density prediction, and optimization robustness, rather than introducing new geometric or rendering primitives. The method sets itself apart from standard NeRF configurations by replacing the identity concatenation in MLP inputs with pure Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE), using shifted softplus and widened sigmoid activations for density and color respectively, and employing a specific warmup learning rate schedule. It builds on Method-Specific Training Configurations. The training procedure minimizes photometric error using the Adam optimizer. The following details define the network input, activation functions, and optimization schedule. Input: Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE) of the ray mean and covariance. The original position and view direction are not concatenated with the encoding. View Direction: The ray direction d is normalized, positionally encoded with L=4, and injected into the last layer of the MLP after density \tau is predicted but before color c is predicted. Output: Density \tau and color c for each sample point. MLP Input: A vector containing only the IPE features. MLP Architecture: Standard MLP as defined in the parent Mip-NeRF method. The view direction encoding is added to the final layer weights/biases or concatenated before the final output layer. Standard ReLU and sigmoid activations are replaced to improve optimization stability. 1. Density Activation (\tau): A shifted softplus function is used instead of ReLU. This prevents catastrophic failure where the MLP outputs negative values everywhere, resulting in zero gradients for density. \tau = \log(1 + \exp(x - 1)) The shift by -1 is equivalent to initializing the biases producing \tau to -1, resulting in small initial density values. 2. Color Activation (c): A "widened" sigmoid is used instead of the standard sigmoid. This function saturates slightly outside the [0, 1] range to avoid optimization failure when explaining black or white pixels, which might otherwise cause the network to saturate activations excessively. c = \frac{1 + 2\epsilon}{1 + \exp(-x)} - \epsilon where \epsilon = 0.001. Training uses the Adam optimizer with a logarithmic learning rate annealing and a warmup phase. Total Iterations (n): 1,000,000. Batch Size: 4096. Learning Rate Annealing: Logarithmic interpolation from \eta0 = 5 \cdot 10^{-4} to \etan = 5 \cdot 10^{-6}. Warmup: The first nw = 2500 iterations use a warmup scale factor \lambdaw annealed from 0.01 to 1. The learning rate \etai at iteration i is calculated as: \etai = \left( \lambdaw + (1 - \lambdaw) \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} \operatorname{clip}\left(\frac{i}{nw}, 0, 1\right)\right) \right) \times \exp\left( \left(1 - \frac{i}{n}\right) \log(\eta0) + \frac{i}{n} \log(\etan) \right) where \lambdaw is the current warmup scale factor, which is linearly interpolated from 0.01 to 1 during the first nw iterations. """ i = iteration n = totaliterations nw = warmupiterations # Calculate warmup scale factor lambdaw # Annealed from 0.01 to 1 during warmup clipval = min(max(i / nw, 0.0), 1.0) lambdaw = 0.01 + (1.0 - 0.01) (0.5 (1 - math.cos(math.pi clipval))) # Note: The source uses sin(pi/2 clip). # sin(pi/2 x) goes from 0 to 1 as x goes from 0 to 1. # lambdaw = 0.01 + (1 - 0.01) sin(pi/2 clipval) # Let's stick strictly to the formula in: # lambdaw is annealed from 0.01 to 1. The term multiplying the base LR is: # (lambdaw + (1 - lambdaw) sin(...)) # Wait, the formula in is: # etai = (lambdaw + (1 - lambdaw) sin(...)) baselr # And lambdaw is annealed from 0.01 to 1. # This implies lambdaw is a variable that changes. # Let's re-read carefully: "scale factor that is smoothly annealed between lambdaw = 0.01 and 1" # The formula uses lambdaw inside. This suggests lambdaw in the formula IS the annealed value. # Let's define lambdawcurrent as the annealed value. # Re-evaluating the formula structure from: # etai = (lambdaw + (1 - lambdaw) sin((pi/2) clip(i/nw, 0, 1))) baselr # If lambdaw is the annealed value, it appears on both sides? No. # "we scale the basic learning rate by an additional scale factor that is smoothly annealed between lambdaw = 0.01 and 1" # This phrasing is slightly ambiguous. Usually, warmup is a multiplier. # Let's look at the formula again: # etai = (lambdaw + (1 - lambdaw) sin(...)) exp(...) # If lambdaw is constant 0.01, the term is 0.01 + 0.99sin(...). # If lambdaw is the current value being annealed, it's recursive? # Standard interpretation: lambdaw is a parameter that is annealed. # However, the text says "scale factor... annealed between lambdaw=0.01 and 1". # It is most likely that the term in the parenthesis IS the warmup multiplier. # Let's assume the formula defines the multiplier Mi. # Mi = lambdawcurrent + (1 - lambdawcurrent) sin(...) # But lambdawcurrent is defined as being annealed. # Actually, looking at JaxNeRF docs or standard practices: # Often lambdaw is a fixed hyperparameter for the warmup curve shape, or it's the value at the end. # Let's look at the limits. # If i=0, sin(0)=0. M0 = lambdaw. # If i=nw, sin(pi/2)=1. Mnw = lambdaw + (1-lambdaw) = 1. # So the multiplier goes from lambdaw to 1. # The text says "annealed between lambdaw = 0.01 and 1". # This implies lambdaw is the STARTING value of the multiplier, and it ends at 1. # So lambdaw is a constant 0.01 in the formula? # "we scale the basic learning rate by an additional scale factor that is smoothly annealed between lambdaw = 0.01 and 1" # This implies the SCALE FACTOR is the thing annealing. # The formula calculates the scale factor. # So lambdaw in the formula is the constant 0.01. lambdawconst = 0.01 # Warmup multiplier sinterm = math.sin((math.pi / 2) clipval) warmupmultiplier = lambdawconst + (1 - lambdawconst) sinterm # Base learning rate (logarithmic annealing) baselr = math.exp((1 - i / n) math.log(lrstart) + (i / n) math.log(lrend)) return warmupmultiplier baselr def densityactivation(x): """Shifted softplus for density.""" return math.log(1 + math.exp(x - 1)) def coloractivation(x, epsilon=0.001): """Widened sigmoid for color.""" return (1 + 2 epsilon) / (1 + math.exp(-x)) - epsilon Catastrophic Failure: Using standard ReLU for density can cause the MLP to emit negative values everywhere, leading to zero gradients and optimization failure. The shifted softplus prevents this. Black/White Pixel Saturation: Standard sigmoid saturation can cause optimization failure when trying to explain extreme pixel values. The widened sigmoid avoids this. Identity Concatenation: Keeping the identity concatenation (position/view direction appended to PE) makes the formalization of IPE features challenging and does not improve performance. It should be removed. Mip-NeRF 360 optimization setup defines the training configuration for unbounded neural radiance fields, specifically addressing the challenge of rendering large-scale urban scenes with limited video memory by warping the infinite scene domain into a finite sphere. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF training by combining a specific scene contraction function, a multi-stage proposal network sampling strategy, and a robust learning schedule that prevents aliasing artifacts in unbounded spaces. Mip-NeRF 360 Optimization Setup Scale-Dependent Downweighting is a technique to anti-alias trilinear interpolation in neural radiance fields by downweighting features interpolated from grid cells that are small relative to the sampling Gaussian's spread, preventing aliasing artifacts from high-frequency content. Unlike naive trilinear interpolation which causes aliasing at high frequencies, this method uses the Gaussian CDF to weight samples, similar to Mip-NeRF's IPE features but applied to grid-based representations. Scale-Dependent Downweighting for Grid Interpolation S-NeRF defines the specific hyperparameters, network architectures, and training schedules required to optimize neural radiance fields for dynamic street scenes using LiDAR and RGB data. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF variants by employing a coarse-fine training strategy with separate configurations for foreground vehicles and background street scenes, and by integrating confidence maps derived from multi-view geometric consistency to mitigate depth outliers. S-NeRF Training Configuration An alternative to Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE) involves concatenating the positional encodings of the mean and the (signed) square root of the covariance matrix elements. Specifically, positional encoding with L=12 is applied to the mean \mu, and positional encoding with L=2 is applied to \operatorname{vec}(\operatorname{triu}(\operatorname{sign}(\Sigma) \circ \sqrt{|\Sigma|})). This approach performs comparably to IPE in terms of PSNR and SSIM but is sensitive to the hyperparameters L and the covariance parameterization design. IPE is preferred because it is hyperparameter-free and more compact. A geometric derivation used in Mip-NeRF to handle reflections. To ensure consistent view-dependent appearance, the origin of the reflected ray \mathbf{o}' is shifted so that its cone radius matches the incident ray's cone radius at the intersection point \bar{\mathbf{x}}. The condition is: \dot{r}\|\bar{\mathbf{x}} - \mathbf{o}\| = \dot{r}'\|\bar{\mathbf{x}} - \mathbf{o}'\| where \dot{r} and \dot{r}' are the incident and reflected ray radius parameters, \mathbf{o} is the incident ray origin, and \mathbf{d}' is the reflected direction. This equation, along with the constraint that \mathbf{o}' lies on the reflected ray, determines the shifted origin. Training Speed: Mip-NeRF is 13x faster to train than a brute-force supersampling baseline (16 rays/pixel). Evaluation Speed: Mip-NeRF is 16x faster to evaluate than the supersampling baseline. Quality: Mip-NeRF outperforms the 16x supersampling baseline in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS metrics on multiscale Blender datasets. Stability: The specific activation functions and learning rate warmup improve training stability, particularly with large learning rates, though they do not significantly change the final accuracy or speed compared to standard NeRF settings. Memory: The use of IPE and unified multiscale models reduces memory overhead compared to separate per-scale models. The details described herein originate from the Mip-NeRF paper (Barron et al., 2021) and the JaxNeRF codebase documentation. The "miscellaneous" changes, including the activation functions and identity removal, were introduced to simplify the method's formalization and increase robustness during optimization without altering the core accuracy or speed. The reflected cone derivation is detailed in the NeRF-Casting paper (2024) as an extension for consistent reflections. name: Mip-NeRF 360 Optimization Setup
head: Gaussian Position Encoding, Mip-NeRF 360 Training Procedure, Position Warping for Unbounded Scenes
body: Mip-NeRF 360 optimization setup defines the training configuration for unbounded neural radiance fields, specifically addressing the challenge of rendering large-scale urban scenes with limited video memory by warping the infinite scene domain into a finite sphere. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF training by combining a specific scene contraction function, a multi-stage proposal network sampling strategy, and a robust learning schedule that prevents aliasing artifacts in unbounded spaces. The method optimizes a radiance field for unbounded scenes by warping coordinates, training a proposal network to guide sampling, and minimizing a composite loss function. Inputs: Camera poses \mathbf{t} (estimated via COLMAP), input images \mathbf{C}^, and scene coordinates \mathbf{x}. Outputs: Rendered color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{t}), depth maps, and optimized network weights for the proposal and NeRF MLPs. 1. Proposal MLP (\Theta{\text{prop}}): Architecture: 4 layers, 256 hidden units. Activations: ReLU for hidden layers, Softplus for density output \tau. 2. NeRF MLP (\Theta{\text{NeRF}}): Architecture: 8 layers, 1024 hidden units. Activations: ReLU for hidden layers, Softplus for density output \tau. 3. Scene Warping: Input: 3D coordinate \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: Warped coordinate \mathbf{x}{\text{encoding}} \in \mathbb{R}^3. 1. Scene Warping (Position Encoding): For every 3D point \mathbf{x} sampled along a ray, apply the contraction function to map unbounded space to a unit sphere: \mathbf{x}{\text{encoding}} = \begin{cases} \mathbf{x} & \text{if } \|\mathbf{x}\|2 \leq 1 \\ \left(2 - \frac{1}{\|\mathbf{x}\|2}\right) \frac{\mathbf{x}}{\|\mathbf{x}\|2} & \text{if } \|\mathbf{x}\|2 > 1 \end{cases} Points within the unit sphere (\|\mathbf{x}\|2 \leq 1) remain unchanged; points outside are contracted towards the boundary. 2. Proposal Network Sampling (Two Stages): Stage 0: Evaluate the proposal MLP using 64 samples along the ray to produce interval midpoints \hat{s}0 and weights \hat{w}0. Stage 1: Resample based on \hat{w}0 and evaluate the proposal MLP again with 64 samples to produce \hat{s}1 and \hat{w}1. 3. NeRF Network Sampling (One Stage): Resample based on the final proposal weights \hat{w}1. Evaluate the NeRF MLP using 32 samples to produce final interval midpoints s and weights w. 4. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} averaged over all rays in the batch: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}}(\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{t}), \mathbf{C}^) + \lambda \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{w}) + \sum{k=0}^1 \mathcal{L}{\text{prop}}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{w}, \hat{\mathbf{s}}^k, \hat{\mathbf{w}}^k) \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}}: Charbonnier loss \sqrt{(x - x^)^2 + \epsilon^2} with \epsilon = 0.001. \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}: Regularizer minimizing weighted interval size. \mathcal{L}{\text{prop}}: Interlevel loss supervising the proposal network. \lambda: Hyperparameter balancing data and regularizer, set to 0.01. 5. Gradient Stop-Gradient: Apply stop-gradient to \mathcal{L}{\text{prop}} to ensure the optimization of \Theta{\text{prop}} is independent from \Theta{\text{NeRF}}. 6. Optimization Update: Update weights using the Adam optimizer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def warpposition(x): """ Warps unbounded 3D coordinates into a unit sphere. Args: x: numpy array of shape (N, 3) Returns: xencoding: numpy array of shape (N, 3) """ norm = np.linalg.norm(x, axis=1, keepdims=True) # Points inside unit sphere remain unchanged mask = norm <= 1.0 xoutside = x[~mask] normoutside = norm[~mask] # Contract points outside unit sphere # Formula: (2 - 1/||x||) (x / ||x||) scale = 2.0 - (1.0 / normoutside) xencodedoutside = scale (xoutside / normoutside) xencoding = np.zeroslike(x) xencoding[mask] = x[mask] xencoding[~mask] = xencodedoutside return xencoding def computecharbonnierloss(pred, target, epsilon=0.001): """ Computes Charbonnier loss. """ return np.sqrt(np.square(pred - target) + epsilon2) def trainmipnerf360(rays, images, numiterations=250000, batchsize=16384): """ Main training loop for Mip-NeRF 360. """ # Initialize networks # Proposal MLP: 4 layers, 256 hidden, ReLU, Softplus for density thetaprop = initializemlp(layers=4, hidden=256, densityactivation='softplus') # NeRF MLP: 8 layers, 1024 hidden, ReLU, Softplus for density thetanerf = initializemlp(layers=8, hidden=1024, densityactivation='softplus') # Optimizer settings beta1 = 0.9 beta2 = 0.999 epsadam = 1e-6 lrstart = 2e-3 lrend = 2e-5 warmupiters = 512 gradclipnorm = 1e-3 lambdadist = 0.01 # Adam optimizer state initialization mprop, vprop = initadamstate(thetaprop) mnerf, vnerf = initadamstate(thetanerf) for i in range(numiterations): # 1. Sample batch of rays batchrays = samplerays(rays, batchsize) batchimages = getcorrespondingimages(batchrays, images) # 2. Learning Rate Schedule # Annealed log-linearly from 2e-3 to 2e-5 with warm-up of 512 iterations if i < warmupiters: lr = lrstart (i / warmupiters) else: # Linear interpolation in log space loglrstart = np.log(lrstart) loglrend = np.log(lrend) progress = (i - warmupiters) / (numiterations - warmupiters) lr = np.exp(loglrstart + progress (loglrend - loglrstart)) # 3. Forward Pass: Proposal Networks (2 stages) # Stage 0: 64 samples # Sample positions t0 uniformly or stratified along ray t0 = samplepositions(batchrays, numsamples=64) # Warp positions x0 = warpposition(transformraytoworld(batchrays, t0)) # Evaluate Proposal MLP density0, = evaluatemlp(thetaprop, x0) # Compute weights w0 from density0 w0 = computeweights(density0) # Compute interval midpoints s0 s0 = computemidpoints(t0) # Stage 1: Resample based on w0, 64 samples t1 = resamplepositions(batchrays, w0, numsamples=64) x1 = warpposition(transformraytoworld(batchrays, t1)) density1, = evaluatemlp(thetaprop, x1) w1 = computeweights(density1) s1 = computemidpoints(t1) # 4. Forward Pass: NeRF Network (1 stage) # Resample based on w1, 32 samples tnerf = resamplepositions(batchrays, w1, numsamples=32) xnerf = warpposition(transformraytoworld(batchrays, tnerf)) densitynerf, colornerf = evaluatemlp(thetanerf, xnerf) wnerf = computeweights(densitynerf) snerf = computemidpoints(tnerf) # 5. Compute Losses # Reconstruct color Crecon = volumerender(colornerf, wnerf) Lrecon = computecharbonnierloss(Crecon, batchimages) # Distortion loss Ldist(s, w) Ldist = computedistortionloss(snerf, wnerf) # Proposal losses Lprop for k=0, 1 # Stop-gradient on proposal loss terms to decouple optimization Lprop0 = computeinterlevelloss(snerf, wnerf, s0, w0, stopgrad=True) Lprop1 = computeinterlevelloss(snerf, wnerf, s1, w1, stopgrad=True) Ltotal = Lrecon + lambdadist Ldist + Lprop0 + Lprop1 # 6. Backpropagation and Update # Compute gradients gradprop = computegradients(Ltotal, thetaprop) gradnerf = computegradients(Ltotal, thetanerf) # Gradient clipping gradprop = clipgradients(gradprop, gradclipnorm) gradnerf = clipgradients(gradnerf, gradclipnorm) # Adam update thetaprop, mprop, vprop = adamupdate(thetaprop, gradprop, mprop, vprop, lr, beta1, beta2, epsadam) thetanerf, mnerf, vnerf = adamupdate(thetanerf, gradnerf, mnerf, vnerf, lr, beta1, beta2, epsadam) return thetaprop, thetanerf Optimizer: Adam. Beta 1: 0.9. Beta 2: 0.999. Epsilon: 10^{-6}. Learning Rate: Annealed log-linearly from 2 \times 10^{-3} to 2 \times 10^{-5}. Warm-up: 512 iterations. Gradient Clipping Norm: 10^{-3}. Training Iterations: 250,000. Batch Size: 2^{14} (16,384) rays. Lambda (\lambda): 0.01 for \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}. Charbonnier Epsilon (\epsilon): 0.001. Z-aliasing: The standard interlevel loss can cause the proposal MLP to learn non-smooth mappings, leading to rays "skipping" scene content, especially with high-capacity backends like iNGP. This is mitigated by the stop-gradient and the specific loss formulation, though variants like Anti-Aliased Interlevel Loss further smooth this. Unbounded Memory: Without warping, rendering large-scale scenes exhausts video memory due to the infinite domain. The contraction function ensures all points are mapped to a finite sphere, preventing this. Precision: The contraction function is continuous but has a derivative discontinuity at \|\mathbf{x}\|2 = 1. Implementations must handle the boundary condition carefully to avoid gradient issues. The Anti-Aliased Interlevel Loss is a proposal supervision loss function that measures the distance between a NeRF histogram and a proposal histogram by blurring the NeRF histogram into a piecewise-linear spline and resampling it into the proposal's interval endpoints. Unlike the piecewise constant loss used in mip-NeRF 360, which suffers from aliasing when NeRF histogram bins are narrow or translate relative to the proposal, this method produces a smooth loss surface that prevents aliasing artifacts during training. Isotropic Gaussian Scale Contraction is a technique for efficiently adapting the scale of isotropic Gaussians when a scene contraction function C(\mathbf{x}) is applied. It solves the problem of maintaining correct anti-aliasing properties in contracted coordinate spaces without the computational overhead of general multivariate Gaussian transformations. It sets itself apart from the standard mip-NeRF 360 approach by linearizing the contraction around each Gaussian center to derive an isotropic scale from the Jacobian determinant, rather than contracting a full covariance matrix. A method for 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis that distills a dense collection of indoor photos into a neural field to render photorealistic views from viewpoints not present in the original collection, specifically optimized for the scale, lighting variability, and privacy constraints of Google Maps Immersive View. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF implementations by integrating low-dimensional generative latent optimization (GLO) vectors and metadata-derived exposure conditioning into the radiance network, thereby resolving cloudy geometry artifacts caused by lighting changes without sacrificing interpretability. Unlike Anti-Aliased Interlevel Loss which focuses on sampling strategies, this method focuses on appearance modeling and capture constraints; it builds on Mip-NeRF 360 Optimization Setup as its architectural base. Progressively Optimized Local Radiance Fields (LocalRF) is a view synthesis method that jointly optimizes camera poses and multiple overlapping local radiance fields from a single long monocular video, avoiding Structure-from-Motion and scaling to unbounded scenes with fixed memory. It differs from global optimization approaches by dynamically allocating new local fields as the camera trajectory extends, preventing global failure from pose outliers and maintaining high resolution around the camera path. Unlike Mega-NeRF, it does not require pre-partitioned space, and unlike Mip-NeRF 360, it jointly estimates poses rather than relying on pre-computed ones. The method minimizes geometric and photometric loss together on a set of frames using differentiable rendering functions to optimize network weights. A method to resolve 'z-aliasing' artifacts in proposal networks by replacing the discrete interlevel loss with a continuous, smooth loss function that penalizes partial overlaps between proposal and NeRF histograms. It identifies z-aliasing artifacts where the proposal MLP learns a non-smooth mapping, causing rays to 'skip' scene content, especially when using iNGP backends for rapid optimization. The original Mip-NeRF 360 interlevel loss assigns equivalent loss to NeRF and proposal histogram bins regardless of overlap extent, penalizing only complete failures to overlap, leading to non-smooth density maps. The new loss prevents the proposal network from learning non-smooth mappings that occur with the previous loss, particularly when the proposal network has high capacity (e.g., iNGP backend). An unbounded extension of MipNeRF that uses a contract function to parameterize 3D Euclidean space within a ball of radius 2, allowing direct rendering of images and depth maps in the contracted space. It renders images and depth maps in the contracted space using standard NeRF equations (Eq. 1 and Eq. 2). A simplified module that outputs K scalars and K RGB-G vectors (4 dimensions: 3 RGB + 1 gating scaler) without efficient multi-space composition strategy, leading to over-smoothing. Rendering uses the same integral equation as NeRF to accumulate the K RGB-G vectors \{\hat{c}{ki}\} and get the RGB-G maps of each sub-space. It splits the RGB-G maps into RGB maps and sub-space composition maps (gating maps), applies softmax over the gating maps along the sub-space channels, and uses it as the weight to compose sub-space RGB maps to form the final rendering results. The number of sub-spaces K is set to 8. The lack of an efficient multi-space composition strategy introduces an over-smoothing problem. Uses the scene warping scheme identical to DVGO and Mip-NeRF360. Keeps other components (positional encoding, point sampling, etc.) identical to TensoRF. Uses 2 scales. Mip-NeRF360 results (Table 9): garden PSNR 24.13, room PSNR 28.11, Model Size avg 12.6MB. Implementing the MipNeRF-360 distillation mode replaces the default settings with a light proposal MLP, reducing training and inference time. The distillation mode runs 30% faster in training and 40% faster in inference than default settings, with a PSNR drop of 0.33. Time Complexity: The multi-stage sampling (2 proposal stages + 1 NeRF stage) increases per-iteration cost compared to single-stage NeRF, but the proposal network reduces the number of NeRF evaluations needed for high quality. The distillation mode variant reduces this overhead, running 30% faster in training and 40% faster in inference. Memory Complexity: The scene warping function allows the method to handle unbounded scenes without increasing memory usage proportional to scene size, as all geometry is confined to a unit sphere. This makes it suitable for large-scale urban scenes where standard 3DGS or NeRF would exhaust video memory. Performance: On the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset, the method achieves a PSNR of 24.13 on the "garden" scene and 28.11 on the "room" scene, with an average model size of 12.6MB. Strengths: Robust to unbounded scenes, prevents aliasing artifacts through specific loss formulations and warping, and provides stable optimization via the Charbonnier loss and gradient clipping. Limitations: Requires pre-computed camera poses (e.g., via COLMAP). The warping function introduces a discontinuity in the derivative at the unit sphere boundary, which can be challenging for gradient-based optimization if not handled carefully. Mip-NeRF 360 was introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2022. It extends the original mip-NeRF approach to handle "in the wild" photo collections with large scale variations. The optimization setup, including the specific MLP architectures, learning rate schedule, and scene warping, was designed to stabilize training for unbounded scenes. The scene warping technique, often referred to as Gaussian Position Encoding in subsequent works like HO-Gaussian, was inspired by this method to handle large-scale urban scenes. name: Anti-Aliased Interlevel Loss
head: Blurred NeRF Loss, Prefiltered Loss
body: The Anti-Aliased Interlevel Loss is a proposal supervision loss function that measures the distance between a NeRF histogram and a proposal histogram by blurring the NeRF histogram into a piecewise-linear spline and resampling it into the proposal's interval endpoints. Unlike the piecewise constant loss used in mip-NeRF 360, which suffers from aliasing when NeRF histogram bins are narrow or translate relative to the proposal, this method produces a smooth loss surface that prevents aliasing artifacts during training. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: NeRF histogram endpoints \mathbf{s} = \{s0, \dots, sN\} and weights \mathbf{w} = \{w0, \dots, w{N-1}\}, where si are normalized distances in [0, 1] and wi are accumulated weights for interval [si, s{i+1}]. Proposal histogram endpoints \hat{\mathbf{s}} = \{\hat{s}0, \dots, \hat{s}M\} and weights \hat{\mathbf{w}} = \{\hat{w}0, \dots, \hat{w}{M-1}\}. Convolution radius r. Outputs: Scalar loss \mathcal{L}{\text{prop}}. Resampled NeRF weights \hat{\mathbf{w}}^{\mathbf{s}}. Parameters r: The radius of the rectangular pulse used for convolution. Other parameters are not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps 1. Normalize: Divide NeRF weights \mathbf{w} by the size of each interval in \mathbf{s} to yield a piecewise constant PDF that integrates to \le 1. 2. Convolve: Convolve the piecewise constant PDF with a rectangular pulse of radius r (integrating to 1) to obtain a piecewise linear PDF. This is implemented by turning each endpoint si into two signed delta functions at si - r and si + r with values proportional to the change between adjacent PDF heights, sorting them, and integrating twice. 3. Integrate to CDF: Integrate the piecewise linear PDF to produce a piecewise-quadratic CDF. 4. Resample: Query the piecewise-quadratic CDF via piecewise quadratic interpolation at each location in \hat{\mathbf{s}}. 5. Compute Loss: Calculate resampled NeRF weights \hat{w}i^{\mathbf{s}} by taking the difference between adjacent interpolated CDF values at the proposal endpoints. Evaluate the loss as an element-wise function of \hat{\mathbf{w}}^{\mathbf{s}} and \hat{\mathbf{w}}. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def antialiasedinterlevelloss(s, w, shat, what, r): """ Computes the anti-aliased interlevel loss. Args: s: NeRF histogram endpoints, shape (N+1,) w: NeRF histogram weights, shape (N,) shat: Proposal histogram endpoints, shape (M+1,) what: Proposal histogram weights, shape (M,) r: Convolution radius Returns: loss: Scalar loss value """ N = len(w) M = len(what) # Step 1: Normalize to piecewise constant PDF # h[i] is the height of the step function in interval i intervals = s[1:] - s[:-1] # Guard against zero-width intervals intervals = np.maximum(intervals, 1e-8) h = w / intervals # Step 2: Convolve with rectangular pulse using delta functions # Create delta functions at s[i] - r and s[i] + r # The value is proportional to the change in h, scaled by 1/(2r) deltas = [] # At s[0], change is h[0] - 0 deltas.append((s[0] - r, h[0] / (2 r))) deltas.append((s[0] + r, -h[0] / (2 r))) # Internal boundaries for i in range(1, N): deltaval = (h[i] - h[i-1]) / (2 r) deltas.append((s[i] - r, deltaval)) deltas.append((s[i] + r, -deltaval)) # At s[N], change is 0 - h[N-1] deltas.append((s[N] - r, -h[N-1] / (2 r))) deltas.append((s[N] + r, h[N-1] / (2 r))) # Sort deltas by position deltas.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) # Step 3 & 4: Integrate twice to get CDF values at shat # Double integration of a delta at pos with value v yields v max(0, x - pos) # This computes the piecewise-quadratic CDF values at proposal endpoints cdfvalues = np.zeros(M + 1) for j in range(M + 1): x = shat[j] cdfval = 0.0 for pos, val in deltas: if pos <= x: cdfval += val (x - pos) cdfvalues[j] = cdfval # Step 5: Compute resampled weights # whats[i] = CDF(shat[i+1]) - CDF(shat[i]) whats = cdfvalues[1:] - cdfvalues[:-1] # Step 6: Evaluate loss # Lprop = sumi (1 / whati) max(0, stopgrad(whatsi) - whati)^2 # stopgrad is applied conceptually; gradients flow through whats to the NeRF, # but not to the proposal network diff = np.maximum(0, whats - what) # Guard against division by zero in what whatsafe = np.maximum(what, 1e-8) loss = np.sum(diff2 / whatsafe) return loss Edge Cases and Pitfalls Narrow Bins: Rasterizing the step function and performing convolution fails in the common case of extremely narrow histogram bins, necessitating the delta-function integration algorithm. Zero-Width Intervals: If s{i+1} - si = 0, the normalization step involves division by zero, so a small epsilon is added to the interval size. Zero Proposal Weights: If \hat{w}i = 0, the loss term involves division by zero, so a small epsilon is added to the proposal weights in the denominator. Strengths: Produces a smooth loss surface that is robust to aliasing when NeRF histogram bins are narrow or translate relative to the proposal. Limitations: More computationally expensive than the piecewise constant loss used in mip-NeRF 360 due to the convolution and resampling steps. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The Anti-Aliased Interlevel Loss was introduced in the Zip-NeRF paper. It builds on the proposal supervision approach from mip-NeRF 360. The key innovation is the use of a blurred, piecewise-linear representation of the NeRF histogram to enable smooth gradient flow during training, addressing the aliasing issues inherent in the piecewise constant comparison used in mip-NeRF 360. name: Isotropic Gaussian Scale Contraction
head: Isotropic scale contraction, Jacobian-based isotropic scale estimation
body: Isotropic Gaussian Scale Contraction is a technique for efficiently adapting the scale of isotropic Gaussians when a scene contraction function C(\mathbf{x}) is applied. It solves the problem of maintaining correct anti-aliasing properties in contracted coordinate spaces without the computational overhead of general multivariate Gaussian transformations. It sets itself apart from the standard mip-NeRF 360 approach by linearizing the contraction around each Gaussian center to derive an isotropic scale from the Jacobian determinant, rather than contracting a full covariance matrix. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of isotropic Gaussians defined by their means \mathbf{x}j and scales \sigmaj, and a scene contraction function C: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3. Output: The contracted means \mathbf{x}'j = C(\mathbf{x}j) and the contracted isotropic scales \sigma'j. Data Structures The method operates on scalar values for scale and 3D vectors for position. No complex covariance matrices are stored or manipulated. Steps 1. Contract Means: Evaluate the contraction function at the original Gaussian center: \mathbf{x}'j = C(\mathbf{x}j). 2. Compute Jacobian Determinant Factor: Calculate the scaling factor derived from the determinant of the Jacobian of the contraction function JC(\mathbf{x}j). For the specific contraction function used in Zip-NeRF, this factor has a closed-form solution: \text{scale\factor}j = \left| \det(JC(\mathbf{x}j)) \right|^{1/3} = \left( \frac{\sqrt[3]{2 \max(1, \|\mathbf{x}j\|) - 1}}{\max(1, \|\mathbf{x}j\|)} \right)^2. Here, \|\mathbf{x}j\| is the Euclidean norm of the original mean \mathbf{x}j. 3. Update Scale: Multiply the original isotropic scale \sigmaj by the computed factor: \sigma'j = \sigmaj \times \text{scale\factor}j. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def isotropicgaussianscalecontraction(means: np.ndarray, scales: np.ndarray) -> tuple: """ Contracts isotropic Gaussians using the Zip-NeRF specific closed-form Jacobian determinant. Args: means: Array of shape (N, 3) containing Gaussian centers xj. scales: Array of shape (N,) containing isotropic scales sigmaj. Returns: contractedmeans: Array of shape (N, 3) containing C(xj). contractedscales: Array of shape (N,) containing sigma'j. """ # Step 1: Contract means # Contract means: xj' = C(xj). The exact form of C(x) is not provided in the sources, # but is evaluated per Gaussian. contractedmeans = means.copy() # Placeholder for C(xj) evaluation # Step 2: Compute the closed-form scale factor from the Jacobian determinant norms = np.linalg.norm(means, axis=1) maxnorm = np.maximum(1.0, norms) numerator = np.cbrt(2.0 maxnorm - 1.0) scalefactor = (numerator / maxnorm) 2 # Step 3: Update scales contractedscales = scales scalefactor return contractedmeans, contractedscales Parameters \|\mathbf{x}j\|: Euclidean norm of the Gaussian mean. \max(1, \|\mathbf{x}j\|): Ensures stability for points near the origin. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Origin Singularity: The formula uses \max(1, \|\mathbf{x}j\|) in the denominator. If \|\mathbf{x}j\| < 1, the denominator is 1, avoiding division by zero. The numerator becomes \sqrt[3]{2(1)-1} = 1, so the scale factor is 1^2/1^2 = 1. This implies no scale change for points within the unit sphere, which is consistent with many contraction functions that leave the central region uncontracted. Naive Multivariate Approach: Contracting the scale by treating the Gaussian as a full multivariate Gaussian with covariance \sigma^2 I and then identifying the isotropic Gaussian with the same generalized variance is significantly more expensive. This method avoids that by using the linearized Jacobian approximation. Time and Memory Complexity The method is O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians. It requires only vector norm calculations and scalar multiplications, making it significantly less computationally expensive than the multivariate Gaussian contraction approach used in mip-NeRF 360. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: High computational efficiency; avoids matrix operations; closed-form solution for the specific Zip-NeRF contraction. Limitations: It is an approximation based on linearization. It assumes the contraction function is locally linear around \mathbf{x}j. For very large Gaussians or highly non-linear contractions, this approximation may introduce errors. It is specific to isotropic Gaussians. When to Use Use this method when rendering with isotropic Gaussians in a scene that has been contracted (e.g., for distant scene content allocation) and computational efficiency is a priority. It is particularly suitable for Zip-NeRF and similar architectures that use multisampled isotropic Gaussians. This technique was introduced in Zip-NeRF. It was developed to address the need for efficient anti-aliasing in neural radiance fields that use scene contraction to allocate model capacity proportional to disparity. The method improves upon the mip-NeRF 360 approach by reducing the computational cost of scale contraction while maintaining the necessary anti-aliasing properties.
