name: Google Immersive View NeRF
head: Indoor NeRF Reconstruction, NeRF Reconstruction for Immersive View
body: A method for 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis that distills a dense collection of indoor photos into a neural field to render photorealistic views from viewpoints not present in the original collection, specifically optimized for the scale, lighting variability, and privacy constraints of Google Maps Immersive View. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF implementations by integrating low-dimensional generative latent optimization (GLO) vectors and metadata-derived exposure conditioning into the radiance network, thereby resolving cloudy geometry artifacts caused by lighting changes without sacrificing interpretability. Unlike Anti-Aliased Interlevel Loss which focuses on sampling strategies, this method focuses on appearance modeling and capture constraints; it builds on Mip-NeRF 360 Optimization Setup as its architectural base. Inputs: 1. Capture Data: A dense collection of DSLR photographs of an indoor venue, captured within a short timeframe (typically <1 hour). 2. Metadata: Photo metadata including ISO, aperture, and white balance settings. 3. Camera Parameters: Extrinsic (position, orientation) and intrinsic (focal length) parameters solved via Structure-from-Motion (SfM). Outputs: 1. NeRF Model: A trained neural radiance field specific to the location. 2. Immersive Video: 360° rendered video along a smoothed flight path. The method utilizes the standard Mip-NeRF 360 architecture. The key structural modification is in the Radiance Network inputs: Positional/Orientation Encodings: Standard positional and angular encodings for the 3D point and view direction. GLO Vectors: A set of learned real-valued latent vectors, one per input image, appended to the radiance network inputs. Exposure Conditioning: Scalar or vector values derived directly from photo metadata (ISO, etc.), appended to the radiance network inputs. 1. Capture: Photograph the venue using DSLR cameras. Ensure every surface is observed from multiple directions. Keep camera properties (white balance, aperture) fixed. Freeze the scene (no movement, stable lighting). 2. Privacy Processing: Automatically scan uploaded photos and blur personally identifiable content (faces, license plates). 3. Structure-from-Motion (SfM): Run an SfM pipeline to solve for each photo's camera parameters (position, orientation, focal length). Associate each pixel with a 3D point and direction. 4. Scale Calibration: Capture pairs of images exactly 3 meters apart during the session. Use this known distance to scale the generated 3D model for consistent video velocity. 5. Model Initialization: Initialize a new NeRF model from scratch for the location, using Mip-NeRF 360 as the base architecture. 6. Latent Vector Assignment: Assign a unique low-dimensional generative latent optimization (GLO) vector to each input image. These vectors are learned during training. 7. Exposure Conditioning Extraction: Extract exposure values from the photo metadata for each image. 8. Radiance Network Input Construction: For each ray sampled during training, construct the input vector for the radiance network comprising: Standard positional/oriental encodings. The GLO vector corresponding to the source image of the ray. The exposure conditioning value corresponding to the source image. 9. Training: Train the model from scratch using the Mip-NeRF 360 optimization loop, minimizing rendering loss against the input photos. 10. Video Rendering: Define a flight path by interpolating keyframe positions computed during SfM. Render 360° videos by ray casting through a virtual spherical camera along this path. The sources do not provide explicit mathematical formulas for the GLO vector integration or exposure conditioning. The radiance network function \mathcal{F} can be conceptually described as: (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}, \mathbf{z}i, \mathbf{e}i) Where: \mathbf{x} is the 3D position. \mathbf{d} is the view direction. \mathbf{z}i is the GLO vector for image i. \mathbf{e}i is the exposure conditioning for image i. \sigma is the density. \mathbf{c} is the color. Note: Exact architectural details of the Mip-NeRF 360 base are assumed from the parent article [3426-mip-nerf-360-optimization-setup.md]. Capture Timeframe: < 1 hour. Calibration Distance: 3 meters between image pairs. Hardware: TPUs or GPUs. Lighting Changes: If lighting changes during capture, reconstruction quality suffers significantly. Cloudy Geometry: Without GLO vectors or exposure conditioning, casual NeRF captures exhibit "cloudy geometry" artifacts when handling lighting variations. Scene Movement: The scene must be frozen in time; any movement degrades reconstruction. Privacy: Failure to blur personally identifiable content violates privacy requirements. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainimmersivenerf(photos, metadata, sfmresults): """ Trains a NeRF model for Immersive View using GLO and Exposure conditioning. Args: photos: List of image arrays. metadata: List of metadata dicts containing 'iso', 'aperture', etc. sfmresults: Dict mapping image index to camera parameters (position, orientation, focallength). Returns: trainedmodel: The trained NeRF model. """ # 1. Privacy Processing blurredphotos = [blurpii(photo) for photo in photos] # 2. Initialize Mip-NeRF 360 Base Model # Assumes base architecture from parent article model = MipNeRF360Base() # 3. Initialize GLO Vectors # One latent vector per image numimages = len(blurredphotos) glovectors = initializelatentvectors(numimages, dimension=16) # Dimension not specified, assumed small # 4. Extract Exposure Conditioning exposurevalues = [extractexposure(meta) for meta in metadata] # 5. Scale Calibration # Use 3m pairs to scale the scene coordinates scalefactor = computescalefactor(sfmresults, calibrationdistancemeters=3.0) sfmresults = scalesfmresults(sfmresults, scalefactor) # 6. Training Loop for epoch in range(maxepochs): for i in range(numimages): image = blurredphotos[i] cameraparams = sfmresults[i] glovec = glovectors[i] exposureval = exposurevalues[i] # Sample rays for this image rays = sampleraysfromimage(image, cameraparams) # Render using Radiance Network with auxiliary inputs # The radiance network receives: position, direction, glovec, exposureval renderedcolors = renderrays(model, rays, glovec, exposureval) # Compute Loss loss = computerenderingloss(renderedcolors, image) # Backpropagate updatemodel(model, loss) updatelatentvectors(glovectors, loss) # GLO vectors are learned parameters return model def renderimmersivevideo(model, keyframeindices, sfmresults, videolengthframes): """ Renders a 360 video by interpolating keyframes. """ # 1. Define Flight Path # Interpolate camera positions from SfM results of keyframes path = interpolatepath(sfmresults[keyframeindices], videolengthframes) # 2. Render Frames frames = [] for camerapos in path: # Ray cast through virtual spherical camera rays = castsphericalrays(camerapos) # Render using the trained model # Note: For video rendering, GLO and Exposure might be averaged or set to neutral if not tied to a specific source image # The source does not specify how GLO/Exposure are handled for novel view video rendering, # only for training against source images. color = renderrays(model, rays) frames.append(color) return frames The base architecture used for the radiance field, providing anti-aliased cone tracing and positional encoding. Mip-NeRF 360 Optimization Setup A loss function technique often associated with mip-NeRF variants to reduce aliasing artifacts. Anti-Aliased Interlevel Loss A technique for handling scale invariance or contraction in neural fields, potentially relevant for the latent space or encoding. Isotropic Gaussian Scale Contraction Time Complexity: Training is computationally intensive. The method uses Mip-NeRF 360, which is noted as "more computationally intensive" than Nvidia's Instant NGP. Memory Complexity: Requires storing GLO vectors for each image and the full Mip-NeRF 360 network weights. Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Produces fewer artifacts and higher reconstruction quality than Instant NGP. Strengths: Handles lighting changes and varying exposure without cloudy geometry artifacts. Provides interpretable exposure control (ISO/brightness) at inference time. Consistent quality across diverse indoor venues (dimly-lit bars to cafes). Limitations: Requires strict capture constraints (frozen scene, fixed camera properties). High computational cost compared to faster alternatives like Instant NGP. GLO vectors are uninterpretable latent codes, though they solve the artifact problem. When to use: When high-quality, artifact-free indoor reconstruction is required for user-facing products like Immersive View, and computational resources are available. When not to use: For real-time applications requiring lower latency (use Instant NGP), or when capture constraints cannot be met (lighting changes, movement). The method was developed by Google to power the "Immersive View" feature in Google Maps, which provides indoor views of restaurants, cafes, and other venues. It was described in a blog post in June 2023. The work builds on Alphabet's recent advances in neural radiance fields, specifically incorporating techniques from "NeRF in the Wild" (GLO vectors) and "Block-NeRF" (exposure conditioning). It was chosen over Instant NGP for its superior reconstruction quality despite higher compute requirements. Reconstructing Indoor Spaces with NeRF, https://ai.googleblog.com/2023/06/reconstructing-indoor-spaces-with-nerf.html, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Progressively Optimized Local Radiance Fields
head: LocalRF
body: Progressively Optimized Local Radiance Fields (LocalRF) is a view synthesis method that jointly optimizes camera poses and multiple overlapping local radiance fields from a single long monocular video, avoiding Structure-from-Motion and scaling to unbounded scenes with fixed memory. It differs from global optimization approaches by dynamically allocating new local fields as the camera trajectory extends, preventing global failure from pose outliers and maintaining high resolution around the camera path. Unlike Mega-NeRF, it does not require pre-partitioned space, and unlike Mip-NeRF 360, it jointly estimates poses rather than relying on pre-computed ones. Inputs and Outputs Input: A sequence of P monocular video frames \{\mathbf{C}k\}{k=1}^P with unknown camera poses. Output: A set of M local radiance fields \{\Thetaj\}{j=1}^M and their corresponding camera poses \{[R|t]k\}{k=1}^P. Data Structures Camera Pose: Each pose [R|t]k is a continuous 6D representation of rotation and translation. Local Radiance Field: Each field \Thetaj is implemented using TensoRF, a factorized 4D tensor representation mapping 3D position \mathbf{x} to volume density \sigma and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}. Resolution: TensoRF resolution starts at 64^3 and upsamples to 640^3 during refinement. Supervision Subset: For each local field, the supervision set includes frames active during the field's lifetime plus the preceding 30 frames for overlap. Formulas Scene Contraction: Maps points \mathbf{x} to [-2, 2] space using L-infinity norm to handle unbounded scenes: \text{contract}(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} \mathbf{x} & \text{if } \|\mathbf{x}\|\infty \leq 1 \\ \left (2 - \frac {1}{\| \mathbf{x} \|{\infty }}\right) \left (\frac {\mathbf{x} }{\| \mathbf{x} \|{\infty }}\right) & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} Local Field Query: The j-th radiance field is centered at translation tj: (\mathbf{c}i, \sigmai) = \text{RF}{\Thetaj}(\mathbf{x}i - \mathbf{t}j) Volume Rendering: Renders color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) along ray \mathbf{r} with N samples: \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti(1-\text{exp}(-\sigmai\deltai))\mathbf{c}i, \quad Ti = \text{exp}\left (-\sum{j=1}^{i-1}\sigmaj\deltaj\right) where \deltai is the distance between sample points. Photometric Loss:: \mathcal{L} = \left \| \hat {\mathbf {C}}(\mathbf {r}) - \mathbf {C}(\mathbf {r}) \right \|{2}^{2} Depth Rendering:: \hat {\mathbf {D}}(\mathbf {r}) = \sum {i=1}^{N} Ti(1-\text {exp}(-\sigma i\delta i))di where di is distance to ray origin. Depth Normalization: For a depth map \mathbf{D} with M samples, compute shift t(\mathbf{D}) and scale s(\mathbf{D}): t(\mathbf{D}) = \text{median}(\mathbf{D}), \quad s(\mathbf{D}) = \frac {1}{M} \sum{1}^{M} |\mathbf{D} - t(\mathbf{D})| Normalized depth: \mathbf{D}^ = (\mathbf{D} - t(\mathbf{D}))/s(\mathbf{D}). Depth Loss:: \mathcal{L}d = \left | {\hat {\mathbf {D}}^} - {\mathbf {D}^}\right | Rendered Flow: Computes optical flow \hat{\mathcal{F}}{k\rightarrow k+1} between consecutive frames using relative pose [R|t]{k\rightarrow k+1} = [R|t]k^{-1}[R|t]{k+1}, projection \Pi, and unprojection \Pi^{-1}: \hat {\mathcal {F}}{k\rightarrow k+1} = (u,v) - \Pi \left ([R|t]{k\rightarrow k+1}\Pi ^{-1}(u,v,\hat {D})\right) Flow Loss:: \mathcal{L}f = \left \| \hat {\mathcal {F}}{k\rightarrow k+1} + \mathcal {F}{k\rightarrow k+1} \right \|1 where \mathcal{F}{k\rightarrow k+1} is RAFT-estimated flow. Parameters Optimizer: Adam with \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.99. Learning Rates: Initial rotation LR 5 \cdot 10^{-3}, translation LR 5 \cdot 10^{-4}. Loss Weights: Flow loss weight 1, Depth loss weight 0.1. Frame Addition: Every 100 iterations. Refinement: 600 iterations per frame addition step. Overlap: Preceding 30 frames included in local supervision. Batch Size: 16 images for depth normalization statistics. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize optimization with the first 5 frames. Set their poses [R|t]k to identity. Initialize the first TensoRF model \Theta1 with resolution 64^3 centered at t1 = \mathbf{0}. 2. Iterative Frame Addition: For k = 6 to P: a. Append Frame: Add frame k to the supervision set. b. Pose Initialization: Initialize the new pose [R|t]k using the previous pose [R|t]{k-1} to enforce locality prior: [R|t]k \leftarrow [R|t]{k-1} c. Joint Optimization: Jointly optimize the new pose [R|t]k and the current radiance field parameters \Thetaj using the photometric, depth, and flow losses for 100 iterations. 3. Boundary Check: Monitor the estimated camera pose relative to the boundary of the high-resolution uncontracted space of the current local radiance field. Check if \|\mathbf{t}p - \mathbf{t}j\|\infty \geq 1, where \mathbf{t}p is the last registered frame's translation and \mathbf{t}j is the current field's center. 4. Refinement: If the boundary is reached (or after every 100 iterations if not yet reached, though the text specifies refinement after reaching boundary or as part of the cycle): a. Stop adding frames. b. Refine the current TensoRF \Thetaj and camera poses for 600 iterations. c. Apply exponential decay to loss weights towards 0.1 factor. d. Upsample TensoRF resolution up to 640^3. 5. Allocation: If the pose exceeds the boundary: a. Allocate a new TensoRF radiance field \Theta{j+1} centered at the last estimated pose \mathbf{t}p. b. Freeze the previous field \Thetaj (disable supervision). c. Clear unneeded supervising frames from memory. d. Increment j. 6. Repeat: Repeat steps 2-5 until all input frames are registered. 7. Blending: At inference, blend rendered colors \hat{\mathbf{C}}j(\mathbf{r}) of all overlapping radiance fields using per-frame linear blending weights within the overlap region. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def localrfoptimization(frames, numframes): # Initialization poses = [IdentityPose() for in range(numframes)] fields = [] currentfieldidx = 0 # Initialize first field field = TensoRF(resolution=64) fields.append(field) # Supervision set includes first 5 frames supervisionframes = frames[:5] # Initial optimization of first 5 frames optimize(poses[:5], field, supervisionframes, iterations=500) for k in range(5, numframes): # Append frame supervisionframes.append(frames[k]) # Initialize new pose from previous poses[k] = poses[k-1].copy() # Joint optimization for 100 iterations optimize(poses[:k+1], field, supervisionframes, iterations=100) # Check boundary lastpose = poses[k] currentcenter = field.center if norminf(lastpose.translation - currentcenter) >= 1.0: # Refine for 600 iterations optimize(poses[:k+1], field, supervisionframes, iterations=600) # Upsample field.upsampleto(640) # Allocate new field newfield = TensoRF(resolution=64, center=lastpose.translation) fields.append(newfield) currentfieldidx += 1 # Freeze previous field field.frozen = True # Clear old frames from memory if needed (logic implied by "clear unneeded") # In practice, keep overlap frames # supervisionframes = recentframeswithoverlap # Switch to new field for next iterations field = newfield return fields, poses Subtopics TensoRF Representation: A factorized 4D tensor representation used as the base for LocalRF, offering quality and reasonable training speed. Mip-NeRF 360 Optimization Setup: The parent method that LocalRF builds upon, specifically regarding contraction and unbounded scene handling, but LocalRF differs by jointly estimating poses. Time Complexity: Optimization takes 30-40 hours for 1000 frames on a single NVIDIA TITAN RTX. Memory Complexity: Fixed memory usage due to dynamic allocation and freezing of previous fields, allowing scaling to arbitrarily long videos. Performance (Tanks and Temples): PSNR 22.40, SSIM 0.667, LPIPS 0.494. Performance (Self-Calibrated): PSNR 22.85, SSIM 0.676, LPIPS 0.708. Strengths: Robust to pose outliers, handles long unbounded scenes, no SfM required. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of overlap and refinement steps; slower than methods with known poses. LocalRF was introduced in 2023 by Andreas et al.. It addresses the limitations of global radiance field optimization, which fails on long videos due to misestimation impact and fixed capacity blur. It builds on TensoRF and Mip-NeRF 360's contraction. Progressively Optimized Local Radiance Fields for Robust View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.01587, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Mip-NeRF RGB-D Volume Rendering and Loss
head: Mip-NeRF RGB-D Loss, RGB-D Optimization in Mip-NeRF
body: This method optimizes a neural radiance field using RGB-D data by minimizing a combined geometric and photometric loss. It differs from standard NeRF by incorporating depth variance into the geometric loss to handle uncertainty and using integrated positional encoding for conical frustums to address aliasing. It builds on Mip-NeRF 360 Optimization Setup but replaces the standard depth loss with a variance-normalized geometric loss and utilizes RGB-D specific sampling bounds. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of RGB-D frames, each containing color image C, depth map D, and camera pose. Network parameters \theta. Outputs: Optimized network weights \theta, rendered color \hat{C}(r), and rendered depth \hat{D}(r) for each ray r. Data Structures Network Architecture: A single MLP with 4 hidden layers, each of feature size 256. Layer 1-2: Hidden layers. Layer 3: Hidden layer with a skip connection from the input position. Layer 4: Hidden layer. Viewing direction is concatenated to the output of Layer 3 before entering Layer 4. Output: Color c and volume density \tau. Positional Encoding: Position: Integrated positional encoding applied to the conical frustum (16 frequency bands). Direction: Standard positional encoding with frequency 4 applied to viewing directions. Volume Rendering Formulas For a ray r(t) = o + td with near bound tn and far bound tf: 1. Accumulated Transmittance: T(t) = \exp\left(-\int{tn}^{t} \tau(r(s)) ds\right) Discretized with N samples: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \tauj \deltaj\right) where \tauj is volume density, \deltaj is segment length, and T1 = 1. 2. Discrete Color Estimate: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\taui \deltai)) ci where ci is the predicted color at sample i. 3. Discrete Depth Estimate: \hat{D}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\taui \deltai)) ti where ti is the sample position. 4. Depth Variance: \hat{D}{var}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\taui \deltai)) (\hat{D}(r) - ti)^2 This represents the variance of the depth distribution along the ray. Loss Function The total loss combines geometric loss lg and photometric loss lp with a scale factor \lambdap: \min\theta (lg + \lambdap lp) 1. Photometric Loss (lp): L1-norm between predicted and ground truth color: lp = \sum{r \in R} |\hat{C}(r) - C(r)| 2. Geometric Loss (lg): Absolute difference between predicted and true depth, normalized by depth variance: lg = \sum{r \in R} \frac{|\hat{D}(r) - D(r)|}{\sqrt{\hat{D}{var}(r)}} Normalization discourages weights with high uncertainty. Parameters \lambdap = 100 (default photometric scale factor). Near/Far bounds: tn = D - \alphan and tf = D + \alphaf, where D is the depth value and \alphan, \alphaf are empirically chosen based on depth uncertainty. Standard deviation for Gaussian sampling: 0.3. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computetransmittanceandweights(tau, delta): """ Compute accumulated transmittance Ti and weights Wi for volume rendering. tau: array of shape (N,) volume densities delta: array of shape (N,) segment lengths Returns: T (transmittance), W (weights) """ # Ti = exp(-sum{j=1}^{i-1} tauj deltaj) # We compute cumulative sum of tau delta taudelta = tau delta cumsum = np.cumsum(taudelta) # Shift for Ti: T1 = 1, Ti = exp(-cumsum[i-2]) for i > 1 # Using padding to handle index alignment cumsumshifted = np.concatenate(([0.0], cumsum[:-1])) T = np.exp(-cumsumshifted) # Weight Wi = Ti (1 - exp(-taui deltai)) W = T (1.0 - np.exp(-taudelta)) return T, W def renderray(positions, directions, networkforward, depthmap, camerapose): """ Render a single ray using Mip-NeRF RGB-D volume rendering. positions: array of shape (N,) sample positions along the ray directions: array of shape (3,) viewing direction networkforward: function that takes (positions, directions) -> (color, density) depthmap: scalar or array containing ground truth depth D for the ray origin camerapose: camera pose information (used to determine bounds) Returns: renderedcolor, rendereddepth, depthvariance """ # 1. Determine near and far bounds based on depth uncertainty # D is the depth value from the depth map for this pixel D = depthmap alphan = 0.1 # Example empirical value, typically chosen based on uncertainty alphaf = 0.1 # Example empirical value tn = D - alphan tf = D + alphaf # 2. Sample points within [tn, tf] # In practice, this uses stratified or Gaussian sampling around D # Here we assume 'positions' are already sampled within bounds N = len(positions) # 3. Query network # Network expects integrated positional encoding for positions and standard PE for directions colors, densities = networkforward(positions, directions) # 4. Compute segment lengths # Assuming sorted positions deltas = np.diff(positions) # Pad the last delta or handle boundary. Standard NeRF uses deltai = ti - t{i-1} # For the last sample, delta is often estimated or set to a small value. # Here we assume deltas is computed correctly for the N samples. # Note: deltas usually has length N-1 if computed from diff. # For volume rendering, we need delta for each sample. # Standard approach: deltai = ti - t{i-1} for i>1, delta1 = t1 - tn. # This requires tn. Let's assume 'positions' includes tn or deltas are precomputed. # For this pseudocode, we assume 'deltas' is provided or computed as: # deltas = np.zeros(N) # deltas[0] = positions[0] - tn # deltas[1:] = np.diff(positions) # 5. Compute Transmittance and Weights T, W = computetransmittanceandweights(densities, deltas) # 6. Compute Rendered Color renderedcolor = np.sum(W colors, axis=0) # 7. Compute Rendered Depth rendereddepth = np.sum(W positions) # 8. Compute Depth Variance # Dvar = sumi Wi (Dhat - ti)^2 depthvariance = np.sum(W (rendereddepth - positions)2) return renderedcolor, rendereddepth, depthvariance def computeloss(renderedcolor, rendereddepth, depthvariance, gtcolor, gtdepth): """ Compute Mip-NeRF RGB-D loss. """ # Photometric Loss (L1) lp = np.sum(np.abs(renderedcolor - gtcolor)) # Geometric Loss (Normalized L1) # Avoid division by zero epsilon = 1e-6 lg = np.sum(np.abs(rendereddepth - gtdepth) / (np.sqrt(depthvariance) + epsilon)) # Total Loss lambdap = 100.0 totalloss = lg + lambdap lp return totalloss, lg, lp Edge Cases and Pitfalls Division by Zero: Depth variance \hat{D}{var}(r) can be zero if all samples are at the same depth or if transmittance is zero. Add a small epsilon to the denominator in the geometric loss. Depth Uncertainty: The choice of \alphan and \alphaf significantly impacts the sampling bounds. If depth uncertainty is high, bounds may need to be wider to avoid empty space, but this increases computational cost. Precision: The exponential terms in transmittance and weights can suffer from underflow or overflow. Use stable log-space computations if necessary. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples N per ray and the number of rays. The network is smaller (4 layers, 256 features) than original NeRF, leading to faster training and prediction. Memory Complexity: Lower than original NeRF due to the reduced network size. Performance: Adaptive sampling performs best among proposed sampling strategies, improving underlying geometry compared to NeRF. Strengths: Faster training/prediction, better geometry estimation with RGB-D data, handles aliasing via integrated positional encoding. Limitations: Requires depth data. Performance depends on accurate depth uncertainty estimation for bounds. When to Use: When RGB-D data is available and faster training is desired without significant quality loss. When Not to Use: When only RGB data is available, or when depth uncertainty is poorly estimated. Origin: Proposed in "Mip-NeRF RGB-D: Depth Assisted Fast Neural Radiance Fields". name: Scale-Dependent Downweighting for Grid Interpolation
head: Gaussian CDF Downweighting, Interpolation Weighting
body: Scale-Dependent Downweighting is a technique to anti-alias trilinear interpolation in neural radiance fields by downweighting features interpolated from grid cells that are small relative to the sampling Gaussian's spread, preventing aliasing artifacts from high-frequency content. Unlike naive trilinear interpolation which causes aliasing at high frequencies, this method uses the Gaussian CDF to weight samples, similar to Mip-NeRF's IPE features but applied to grid-based representations. Inputs: A set of multisampled isotropic Gaussians, each defined by a mean coordinate \mathbf{x}j and standard deviation \sigmaj. A set of feature grids \{V\ell\} at different resolution levels \ell, where each grid has a linear size (resolution) n\ell. Outputs: A concatenated feature vector provided as input to the subsequent MLP, consisting of downweighted interpolated features \{\mathbf{f}\ell\} and featurized downweighting factors \{\omega{j,\ell}\}. Data Structures: V\ell: A 3D tensor (or hash grid) storing feature vectors of dimension c\ell. \mathbf{x}j: A 3D coordinate vector representing the mean of the j-th Gaussian. \sigmaj: A scalar representing the standard deviation of the j-th Gaussian. n\ell: A scalar representing the linear size (resolution) of grid level \ell. Parameters: n\ell: The linear size (resolution) of the grid at level \ell. Used to scale the coordinate \mathbf{x} before interpolation. \sigmaj: The standard deviation of the isotropic Gaussian for multisample j. Represents the spatial extent of the sample. Steps: 1. For each multisample j with mean \mathbf{x}j and standard deviation \sigmaj, and for each grid level \ell with linear size n\ell and feature grid V\ell: a. Compute the downweighting factor \omega{j,\ell} based on the fraction of the Gaussian's PDF inside the grid cell. The formula is: \omega{j,\ell} = \sqrt{\operatorname{erf}\left(\frac{1}{8\sigmaj^2 n\ell^2}\right)} where \omega{j,\ell} \in [0, 1]. b. Scale the coordinate \mathbf{x}j by the grid's linear size n\ell to get \mathbf{x}'j = n\ell \cdot \mathbf{x}j. c. Perform trilinear interpolation on grid V\ell at coordinate \mathbf{x}'j to obtain the interpolated feature vector \mathbf{f}{j,\ell}. d. Compute the downweighted feature for this sample and level as \omega{j,\ell} \cdot \mathbf{f}{j,\ell}. 2. Approximate the expected grid feature for level \ell by taking the mean over all multisamples j: \mathbf{f}\ell = \operatorname{mean}j\left( \omega{j,\ell} \cdot \operatorname{trilerp}(n\ell \cdot \mathbf{x}j; V\ell) \right) This approximation relies on the assumption that grid values are zero-mean and normally distributed due to weight decay, allowing the expected feature to be approximated as \omega{j,\ell} \cdot \mathbf{f}{j,\ell} + (1 - \omega{j,\ell}) \cdot 0 = \omega{j,\ell} \cdot \mathbf{f}{j,\ell}. 3. Concatenate the downweighted features \{\mathbf{f}\ell\} from all levels and the featurized versions of \{\omega{j,\ell}\} to form the input for the subsequent MLP. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def scaledependentdownweighting(xmeans, sigmas, grids, gridsizes, featuredim): """ Compute scale-dependent downweighted features for grid interpolation. Args: xmeans: Array of shape (N, 3) containing mean coordinates for N multisamples. sigmas: Array of shape (N,) containing standard deviations for N multisamples. grids: List of 3D arrays Vl for each level l. gridsizes: List of scalars nl for each level l. featuredim: Integer dimensionality of the feature vectors stored in the grids. Returns: finalinput: Concatenated feature vector for the MLP input. """ N = len(xmeans) numlevels = len(grids) alllevelfeatures = [] allweightscalars = [] for l in range(numlevels): Vl = grids[l] nl = gridsizes[l] downweightedfeaturessum = np.zeros(featuredim) count = 0 for j in range(N): xj = xmeans[j] sigmaj = sigmas[j] # Step 1a: Compute downweighting factor arg = 1.0 / (8.0 (sigmaj 2) (nl 2)) omega = math.sqrt(math.erf(arg)) # Step 1b & 1c: Scale coordinate and interpolate scaledx = nl xj fjl = trilinearinterpolation(scaledx, Vl) # Step 1d: Downweight downweightedf = omega fjl # Accumulate for mean downweightedfeaturessum += downweightedf count += 1 # Step 2: Mean over samples if count > 0: fl = downweightedfeaturessum / count else: fl = np.zeros(featuredim) alllevelfeatures.append(fl) # Step 3: Featurize weights # The source mentions concatenating "featurized versions of {ωj,ℓ}" but does not specify the exact transformation. # We concatenate the scalar omega for each sample as a direct representation. weightvec = np.array([math.sqrt(math.erf(1.0 / (8.0 (sigmas[k] 2) (nl 2)))) for k in range(N)]) allweightscalars.append(weightvec) # Concatenate all level features concatenatedfeatures = np.concatenate(alllevelfeatures) # Concatenate weight scalars concatenatedweights = np.concatenate(allweightscalars) finalinput = np.concatenate([concatenatedfeatures, concatenatedweights]) return finalinput def trilinearinterpolation(coord, grid): """ Standard trilinear interpolation. coord: (3,) array, scaled coordinates. grid: 3D array. """ x, y, z = coord ix, iy, iz = int(math.floor(x)), int(math.floor(y)), int(math.floor(z)) fx, fy, fz = x - ix, y - iy, z - iz Dx, Dy, Dz = grid.shape # Clamp indices to valid range [0, D-2] for interpolation ix = np.clip(ix, 0, Dx - 2) iy = np.clip(iy, 0, Dy - 2) iz = np.clip(iz, 0, Dz - 2) c000 = grid[ix, iy, iz] c100 = grid[ix+1, iy, iz] c010 = grid[ix, iy+1, iz] c110 = grid[ix+1, iy+1, iz] c001 = grid[ix, iy, iz+1] c101 = grid[ix+1, iy, iz+1] c011 = grid[ix, iy+1, iz+1] c111 = grid[ix+1, iy+1, iz+1] c00 = c000 (1-fx) + c100 fx c01 = c001 (1-fx) + c101 fx c10 = c010 (1-fx) + c110 fx c11 = c011 (1-fx) + c111 fx c0 = c00 (1-fy) + c10 fy c1 = c01 (1-fy) + c11 fy result = c0 (1-fz) + c1 fz return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the Gaussian is much larger than the grid cell, the interpolated feature is unreliable. The downweighting factor \omega approaches 0, effectively discarding this unreliable sample. The approximation relies on the assumption that grid values are zero-mean and normally distributed due to weight decay. If this assumption does not hold, the approximation \omega{j,\ell} \cdot \mathbf{f}{j,\ell} may be inaccurate. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Effectively reduces spatial aliasing artifacts caused by high-frequency content when using multisampling with trilinear interpolation. Limitations: Relies on the assumption of zero-mean, normally distributed grid values, which is encouraged by weight decay but may not always be perfectly met. When to use: When training grid-based neural radiance fields (like iNGP or Zip-NeRF) with multisampling to prevent aliasing artifacts. When not to use: Not given in the sources. This technique is described in the context of Zip-NeRF, an anti-aliased grid-based neural radiance field method. It is inspired by Mip-NeRF's IPE features but adapted for grid-based representations. name: S-NeRF Training Configuration
head: S-NeRF Optimization Setup, S-NeRF Hyperparameters
body: S-NeRF defines the specific hyperparameters, network architectures, and training schedules required to optimize neural radiance fields for dynamic street scenes using LiDAR and RGB data. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF variants by employing a coarse-fine training strategy with separate configurations for foreground vehicles and background street scenes, and by integrating confidence maps derived from multi-view geometric consistency to mitigate depth outliers. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sparse LiDAR points (consecutive frames t-1, t, t+1), RGB images, camera poses, and intrinsics. Outputs: Optimized MLP weights for density and color fields, and confidence maps for filtering outliers. Data Structures: The method uses two distinct MLP architectures depending on the scene component: 1. Foreground Vehicle MLP: 4 layers, 256 hidden units per layer. 2. Background Density MLP: 8 layers, 1024 hidden units per layer. 3. Background Color MLP: 3 layers, 128 hidden units per layer. Note: The background coarse and fine networks share parameters. Training Procedure: The training is split into foreground and background phases. 1. Foreground Vehicle Training: Sampling: 64 samples per ray. Iterations: 30,000. Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 5 \times 10^{-4}. Batch Size: 1024. Loss Weights: Depth loss weight \lambda1 = 1, Smooth loss weight \lambda2 = 0.15. Hardware: Single RTX 3090 GPU. 2. Background Street Scene Training: Scene Parameterization: Radius r = 3. Sampling: 128 samples per ray in log scale. Iterations: 100,000. Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate Schedule: Log-linear decay from 5 \times 10^{-4} to 5 \times 10^{-6} with a warm-up phase of 2,500 iterations. Batch Size: 2048. Loss Weights: Depth loss weight \lambda1 = 0.2, Smooth loss weight \lambda2 = 0.01. Confidence Threshold: \tau = 20\% for confidence measurement. Hardware: Two RTX 3090 GPUs. Confidence Map Computation (Minor Variant): To reduce the influence of depth outliers, S-NeRF computes geometry and projection confidence maps. 1. Reprojection: Project 3D LiDAR points from time t-1 and t+1 to time t using the displacement \Delta P between frames. 2. Consistency Check: Remove moving object outliers using optical flow and depth projection consistency. 3. Feature Consistency: Compute RGB, SSIM, and VGG confidence maps to measure photometric and feature consistency. 4. Aggregation: Combine depth, flow, RGB, SSIM, and VGG components via learnable aggregation to produce final confidence maps. Parameters Summary: Foreground samples: 64 Background samples: 128 Foreground iterations: 30,000 Background iterations: 100,000 Foreground LR: 5 \times 10^{-4} Background LR: 5 \times 10^{-4} to 5 \times 10^{-6} Background Batch Size: 2048 Foreground Loss \lambda1: 1 Foreground Loss \lambda2: 0.15 Background Loss \lambda1: 0.2 Background Loss \lambda2: 0.01 Confidence Threshold \tau: 20% Scene Radius r: 3 This method distinguishes inlier and outlier camera poses by using a detached color network that omits the viewing direction as input, minimizing the impact of shape-radiance ambiguities that cause high PSNR for wrong poses. It solves the issue where outliers might have higher PSNR than inliers due to shape-radiance ambiguity, which traditional rendering metrics fail to detect. Unlike previous works using rendering metrics directly, this approach uses a detached network to provide reliable confidence scores for pose filtering. Training Time: ~2 hours per vehicle on a single RTX 3090 GPU; ~17 hours per background scene (250 images, 1280×1920) on two RTX 3090 GPUs. Parameter Count: 8.76M learnable parameters, similar to other SOTA methods (8.7–9.9M). Performance: On Waymo dataset, S-NeRF achieves 23.60 PSNR and 0.743 SSIM, outperforming Mip-NeRF 360 (22.10 PSNR, 0.724 SSIM). Scaling: Training time scales with scene complexity and number of images; background scenes require more iterations and larger batch sizes than foreground vehicles. Limitations: Training is slower than Mip-NeRF 360 due to the requirement of coarse rendering for supervision, though this can be accelerated by removing coarse supervision. S-NeRF was introduced in the paper "S-NeRF: Neural Radiance Fields for Street Views" published at ICLR 2023. It builds on the Mip-NeRF optimization and activation details [3409-mip-nerf-optimization-and-activation-details.md] to handle dynamic street scenes with LiDAR data. The method was developed to address the challenges of reconstructing large-scale urban environments with moving objects and depth outliers. name: Confidence Updating with Detached Color Network
head: Cn-based confidence scoring, Color Network w/o View Direction, Detached Color Network for Confidence, Isolated Color Network, PSNR-based confidence update
body: This method distinguishes inlier and outlier camera poses by using a detached color network that omits the viewing direction as input, minimizing the impact of shape-radiance ambiguities that cause high PSNR for wrong poses. It solves the issue where outliers might have higher PSNR than inliers due to shape-radiance ambiguity, which traditional rendering metrics fail to detect. Unlike previous works using rendering metrics directly, this approach uses a detached network to provide reliable confidence scores for pose filtering. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of training images V, initial camera poses, a scene graph, and a primary NeRF model (including geometry SDF f and traditional color network Co). Outputs: Updated confidence scores CS(vi) for each view vi \in V, used to guide ray sampling. Data Structures: Confidence Score (CS(vi)): A scalar value representing the reliability of pose vi. Initialized based on keypoint matches and updated iteratively. Detached Color Network (Cn): A shallow Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) identical in architecture to the primary color network Co but without viewing direction input. PSNR Estimates: PSNRo: PSNR estimated using the primary color network Co. PSNRn: PSNR estimated using the detached color network Cn. Parameters: \lambdac: Weight for PSNR contribution to confidence update. Typical value not explicitly given in sources; assumed to be a small positive constant (e.g., 1.0 or normalized weight) based on standard additive update rules. \tau1: Inlier-outlier threshold for PSNR discrepancy between Co and Cn. Set to 9. \lambda: Weight for regularization term in loss. Set to 0.1. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Confidence Scores: Calculate initial confidence scores CS(vi) based on keypoint matches from the scene graph. Let |Mi| be the total number of edges (matches) for view vi. Normalize these scores to form a probability distribution: CS(vi) = \frac{|Mi|}{\sum{v \in V} |Mv|} (Note: The source describes normalizing based on match counts initially, then updating additively). 2. Construct Detached Color Network (Cn): Create a color network Cn that takes only geometry features (from the SDF network) as input, explicitly excluding the viewing direction vector. Use the same sampling points and geometry features as the original color network Co. 3. Detach Optimization Graph: Detach all computations involving Cn from the main pose-NeRF optimization graph. This ensures that the loss calculated from Cn does not backpropagate to the SDF network or the primary color network Co, maintaining the performance of the NSR backbone. 4. Compute Rendering Losses: For each training image i: Render the image using Co to get \hat{C}o. Compute photometric loss L{color}(Co) = \|\hat{C}o - C\|1. Render the image using Cn to get \hat{C}n. Compute photometric loss L{color}(Cn) = \|\hat{C}n - C\|1. Estimate PSNRo from L{color}(Co) and PSNRn from L{color}(Cn). 5. Update Confidence Scores: Update the confidence score for each view vi using the PSNR estimated by the detached network Cn: CS(vi) = CS(vi) + \lambdac \cdot PSNRn(vi) where PSNRn(vi) is the PSNR value for view vi estimated by Cn. 6. Normalize Confidence Scores: After updating, normalize the confidence scores to form a probability distribution for ray sampling: CS(vi) = \frac{CS(vi)}{\sum{v \in V} CS(v)} This distribution guides the training to sample more rays from poses with higher confidence. 7. Identify Outliers (Optional Filtering): Monitor the discrepancy between PSNRo and PSNRn. If |PSNRo - PSNRn| > \tau1 (where \tau1 = 9), the pose is identified as an outlier. This discrepancy indicates shape-radiance ambiguity where the view-dependent network Co overfits to the wrong pose while the view-independent network Cn fails to render accurately. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializeconfidence(views, scenegraph): """ Initialize confidence scores based on keypoint matches. views: List of view indices. scenegraph: Graph structure containing match counts. """ confidencescores = {} totalmatches = 0 for v in views: # |Mv| is the number of matching pairs/edges for view v matchcount = scenegraph.getedgecount(v) confidencescores[v] = matchcount totalmatches += matchcount # Normalize to form initial probability distribution for v in views: confidencescores[v] /= totalmatches return confidencescores def traindetachedcolornetwork(Cn, geometryfeatures, groundtruthimages, lr=0.001): """ Train the detached color network Cn independently. Cn: MLP taking only geometry features. geometryfeatures: Features from SDF network at sampled points. groundtruthimages: GT RGB images. """ optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(Cn.parameters(), lr=lr) for epoch in range(numepochs): optimizer.zerograd() renderedcolors = Cn(geometryfeatures) loss = torch.mean(torch.abs(renderedcolors - groundtruthimages)) loss.backward() optimizer.step() return loss def updateconfidence(views, confidencescores, psnrnvalues, lambdac=1.0): """ Update confidence scores using PSNR from detached network. psnrnvalues: Dict mapping view index to PSNRn. """ for v in views: psnrn = psnrnvalues[v] confidencescores[v] += lambdac psnrn # Normalize totalconfidence = sum(confidencescores.values()) for v in views: confidencescores[v] /= totalconf return confidencescores def identifyoutliers(psnrovalues, psnrnvalues, threshold=9.0): """ Identify outliers based on discrepancy between Co and Cn PSNR. """ outliers = [] for v in psnrovalues: discrepancy = abs(psnrovalues[v] - psnrnvalues[v]) if discrepancy > threshold: outliers.append(v) return outliers Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Shape-Radiance Ambiguity: Traditional color networks Co (with view direction) can render high-PSNR images even for wrong poses, leading to incorrect sampling if used for confidence. Overfitting: The detached network Cn must not be coupled with the main optimization to prevent it from learning pose-specific artifacts that defeat its purpose. Computational Cost: While Cn adds overhead, using a shallow MLP minimizes the impact on training time. Time Complexity: Adds minimal computational overhead because Cn is a shallow MLP, similar to the existing color network. Training time increases slightly but remains comparable to baseline NeuS/SG-NeRF (e.g., 13 hours for 150k iterations on SG-NeRF, 22 hours for 300k iterations on DTU on RTX 3090). Memory Complexity: Requires storing parameters for an additional shallow MLP Cn. Exact memory footprint not given, but described as not substantially increasing costs. Performance: Effectively differentiates inliers and outliers, leading to higher quality 3D reconstructions and accurate pose rectification. Strengths: Robust against shape-radiance ambiguity; simple rule-based thresholding (\tau1=9) for outlier detection; does not complicate the joint pose-NeRF optimization. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that view-independent rendering quality correlates better with pose correctness than view-dependent rendering; requires careful tuning of \lambdac and \tau1. Origin: Introduced in "Robust SG-NeRF: Robust Scene Graph Aided Neural Surface Reconstruction". History: Addresses limitations in SG-NeRF where heuristic confidence updating based solely on PSNR failed to distinguish inliers from outliers due to shape-radiance ambiguity. Usage: Used in object-level 3D surface reconstruction from unorganized inward-facing images, specifically on datasets like SG-NeRF and DTU. name: NeRF-SR Training Configuration
head: NeRF-SR, NeRF-Supersampling
body: NeRF-SR is a training configuration designed to generate high-resolution (HR) novel views from low-resolution (LR) input images by optimizing a neural radiance field to match the LR observations while implicitly learning HR details through a supersampling strategy. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF training by decoupling the training resolution from the rendering resolution, allowing the model to learn fine-grained texture details that are lost in standard LR training, and from post-processing upsampling methods by maintaining 3D consistency across views. Unlike Super-NeRF, which couples the NeRF with a GAN-based 2D super-resolution backbone and per-view latent codes, NeRF-SR relies on a deterministic supersampling strategy and a optional patch-based refinement network to enhance texture sharpness. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N LR images \{In\} with known camera intrinsics Kn and extrinsics Tn. The target output is an HR image at a specified scale factor (e.g., \times 2 or \times 4). Outputs: A trained MLP representing the radiance field and the synthesized HR images. Data Structures: MLP: Two identical Multi-Layer Perceptrons (Coarse and Fine) mapping 3D coordinates and viewing directions to density and color. The architecture and size are identical to the baseline NeRF. Sampling: Hierarchical sampling is used. Coarse samples: 64 points per ray. Fine samples: 64 points per ray. Total samples per ray: 128. Training Steps: 1. Data Preparation: Select N{train} views for training and N{test} views for evaluation. The standard split uses 100 training views and 200 held-out test views. 2. Ray Generation: For each training image, generate rays. Unlike standard NeRF which samples pixels at the input resolution, NeRF-SR samples rays corresponding to the target HR resolution. This is the "supersampling" step. The ray origins and directions are calculated based on the camera parameters of the LR input image, but the pixel grid is denser. 3. Volume Rendering: Query the Coarse MLP for density \sigmac and color cc at 64 sampled points. Compute weights wi based on \sigmac and transmittance. Query the Fine MLP for density \sigmaf and color cf at 64 sampled points. Render the final color C using the fine samples and weights. 4. Loss Calculation: Compute the photometric error between the rendered HR image and the ground truth HR image. Note: Since HR ground truth is not available, the rendered HR image is downsampled to LR resolution and compared against the input LR image, or the method relies on the consistency of the supersampled rays against the LR input constraints. The source notes indicate evaluation against ground truth for metrics, but training minimizes the difference between the rendered image (upsampled or supersampled) and the input. Specifically, the method exploits 3D consistency from the supersampling strategy. 5. Optimization: Update MLP parameters using the Adam optimizer. Parameters: Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: Exponentially decayed from 5 \cdot 10^{-4} to 5 \cdot 10^{-6}. Batch Size: 2048 rays per batch. Epochs: 20 epochs for Blender dataset; 30 epochs for LLFF dataset. Hyperparameters: \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.999. Refinement Network (Ours-Refine): For real-world datasets like LLFF, supersampling alone may not be sufficient for photorealistic textures. A refinement network is applied post-training or during inference to boost edge sharpness and texture details. Definition: A network that takes patches from the rendered image and reference patches to enhance details. Reference Patch Selection: K=8 reference patches are selected. The reference image is typically the first image in the dataset. Patch Extraction: For a pixel i,j on a patch P, the 3D world coordinate is computed using the estimated depth d{i,j} and camera parameters: P{i,j}^{REF} = K{REF}^T (Kn^{-1} d{i,j} P{i,j}^e) where Tn is the transformation between camera extrinsics from In to I{REF}, and K{REF}, Kn are intrinsic matrices. Points falling outside I{REF} are discarded. Inference: Input images are divided into non-overlapping 64 \times 64 patches. These patches are refined using the reference patches and stitched together. Performance: On a single 1080Ti, rendering a 1008 \times 756 image takes ~48 seconds, with an additional 1.3 seconds for refinement. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainnerfsr(model, lrimages, lrintrinsics, lrextrinsics, targetscale, epochs, batchsize, lrstart, lrend): optimizer = Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lrstart, betas=(0.9, 0.999)) for epoch in range(epochs): # Exponential learning rate decay currentlr = lrstart (lrend / lrstart) (epoch / epochs) for paramgroup in optimizer.paramgroups: paramgroup['lr'] = currentlr for batch in getbatches(lrimages, batchsize): optimizer.zerograd() renderedhrimages = [] for i, (img, K, T) in enumerate(batch): # Generate rays at HR resolution rays = generatehrrays(img.shape, K, T, targetscale) # Hierarchical sampling coarsesamples = samplecoarse(rays, 64) coarsedensity, coarsecolor = model.query(coarsesamples) weights = computeweights(coarsedensity) finesamples = samplefine(rays, coarsesamples, weights, 64) finedensity, finecolor = model.query(finesamples) # Volume rendering hrcolor = volumerender(finesamples, finedensity, finecolor, weights) renderedhrimages.append(hrcolor) # Loss computation: Compare rendered HR with ground truth HR # Note: In NeRF-SR, the "ground truth" for loss is often the # downsampled input or the method relies on the consistency # of the supersampled rays. The source evaluates against GT # for metrics, but training minimizes photometric error. loss = computeloss(renderedhrimages, batch.gthrimages) loss.backward() optimizer.step() def refinepatches(hrimage, referenceimage, k=8, patchsize=64): """ Refine HR image using reference patches. """ refinedimage = np.zeroslike(hrimage) h, w = hrimage.shape[:2] # Divide into non-overlapping patches patches = extractpatches(hrimage, patchsize) refpatches = extractpatches(referenceimage, patchsize) for i, patch in enumerate(patches): # Compute 3D coordinates and backproject to reference # Pref = Kref^T (Kn^-1 d Pe) # Extract corresponding patch from reference refpatch = getrefpatch(patch, refpatches, k) # Apply refinement network refinedpatch = refinementnetwork(patch, refpatch) # Stitch back refinedimage = stitch(refinedimage, refinedpatch, i) return refinedimage Super-NeRF is a method for NeRF super-resolution that generates plausible, 3D-consistent high-resolution (HR) details using only low-resolution (LR) observations, without requiring HR ground truth. It distinguishes itself from NeRF-SR by coupling the NeRF with a GAN-based 2D super-resolution backbone and per-view latent codes to explicitly search the latent space of a powerful SR prior, rather than relying on simple linear formulations or HR refinement via per-patch warping. The method employs a Consistency Controlling Super Resolution (CCSR) module and mutual learning between a fixed LR NeRF and a learnable HR NeRF to ensure view consistency. Time Complexity: Training time is comparable to training an HR NeRF, as it involves rendering at HR resolution. Inference time for a 1008 \times 756 image is ~48 seconds on a single 1080Ti, with an additional 1.3 seconds if the refinement network is used. Memory Complexity: Higher than standard NeRF due to the larger number of rays sampled per batch (HR resolution) and the storage of the refinement network if used. Performance: On the LLFF dataset at \times 4 scale, NeRF-SR with refinement (Ours-Refine) achieves PSNR 25.59, SSIM 0.759, and LPIPS 0.165. At \times 2 scale, it achieves PSNR 27.34, SSIM 0.842, and LPIPS 0.103. Strengths: Generates photorealistic HR details without external data or HR ground truth. Maintains 3D consistency. Limitations: Does not support arbitrary-scale super-resolution (fixed scales like \times 2, \times 4). Introduces extra computational cost compared to LR NeRF, though less than training a full HR NeRF from scratch. Supersampling alone may be insufficient for real-world complex structures, requiring the refinement network. NeRF-SR was introduced by Wang et al. in the paper "NeRF-SR: High-Quality Neural Radiance Fields using Supersampling". It addresses the limitation of standard NeRF, which often produces blurry results when trained on LR inputs. The method leverages the implicit representation of NeRF to learn HR details by optimizing the radiance field against LR inputs while rendering at HR resolution. It is used for high-quality novel view synthesis in both synthetic (Blender) and real-world (LLFF) datasets. head: Super-NeRF: View-Consistent Detail Generation for NeRF Super-Resolution
body: Super-NeRF is a method for NeRF super-resolution that generates plausible, 3D-consistent high-resolution (HR) details using only low-resolution (LR) observations, without requiring HR ground truth. It distinguishes itself from NeRF-SR by coupling the NeRF with a GAN-based 2D super-resolution backbone and per-view latent codes to explicitly search the latent space of a powerful SR prior, rather than relying on simple linear formulations or HR refinement via per-patch warping. The method employs a Consistency Controlling Super Resolution (CCSR) module and mutual learning between a fixed LR NeRF and a learnable HR NeRF to ensure view consistency. Inputs: A set of low-resolution (LR) images C{LR,i} with corresponding camera poses. A pre-trained LR NeRF (fixed during Super-NeRF training). A pre-trained 2D SR backbone (ESRGAN). Outputs: A high-resolution (HR) NeRF model capable of rendering novel views at super-resolved resolution. A Consistency Controlling Latent Code (CCLC) for each view, which guides the 2D SR module. 1. LR NeRF: Lightweight MLP structure, approximately 1/4 the size of the HR NeRF. Uses lower-dimensional positional encoding to capture coarse details. Pre-trained on LR images and kept fixed during Super-NeRF optimization. 2. HR NeRF: Standard NeRF structure with higher-dimensional positional encoding to capture fine details. Learnable parameters optimized during training. 3. CCSR Module Components: CCLC (Consistency Controlling Latent Code): A learnable latent code for each view. For an LR image of size H \times W, the CCLC is a tensor of dimensions 3 \times (sH) \times (sW), where 3 corresponds to the image channels and s is the super-resolution multiplier. 2D SR Module: A pre-trained ESRGAN backbone. CEM (Consistency Enforcing Module): A post-processing step that enforces consistency with the LR input. 4. Parameters: s: Super-resolution multiplier. Set to 4 for the 4x SR backbone. 1. Pre-training: Train the LR NeRF on LR images for approximately 30 minutes. Pre-train the ESRGAN backbone. 2. Initialization: Initialize the HR NeRF and the CCLC for each training view. 3. Training Iteration: For each iteration: a. Randomly select a training viewpoint i. b. SR Generation: Concatenate the LR input C{LR,i} to a random CCLC and pass it to the ESRGAN backbone to generate an initial super-resolved image \tilde{C}{HR,i}. c. Consistency Enforcement: Apply the Consistency Enforcing Module (CEM) to \tilde{C}{HR,i} to produce the final CCSR output C{HR,i}, ensuring it matches the LR input after blurring. d. Ray Sampling: Upsample rays for viewpoint i to match the HR resolution. e. LR Rendering: Query the fixed LR NeRF with the upsampled rays to obtain the rendered image C{LN,i}. f. HR Rendering: Query the learnable HR NeRF with the same rays to obtain the rendered image C{HN,i}. g. Loss Computation: Calculate the total loss L using C{HR,i}, C{LN,i}, and C{HN,i}. h. Optimization: Update the HR NeRF parameters and the CCLC for view i using gradient descent. 1. Consistency Enforcing Module (CEM) Objective: Find a solution C{HR,i} that minimizes the distance to the SR output \tilde{C}{HR,i} while satisfying the constraint that blurring H yields the LR image C{LR,i}: \arg \min | \tilde{C}{HR,i} - C{HR,i} |, \quad \text{s.t.} \quad H C{HR,i} = C{LR,i} where H is the blur kernel. 2. CEM Output Adjustment: The final CCSR output C{HR,i} is calculated by mapping LR content via orthogonal projection and ESRGAN output via the remainder matrix: C{HR,i} = (I - H^T (H H^{-1} H)) \tilde{C}{HR,i} + H^T (H H^{-1}) C{LR,i} Note: The source notation H H^{-1} H implies a pseudo-inverse operation or specific matrix algebra defined in the cited reference [1] within. The term H^T (H H^{-1}) maps the LR content to the HR space. 3. Mutual Learning Loss (L{SR}): Combines constraints from the LR NeRF (C{LN,i}) and HR NeRF (C{HN,i}) against the CCSR output (C{HR,i}) using a trade-off function \alpha(t): L{SR} = \alpha(t) | C{LN,i} - C{HR,i} | + (1 - \alpha(t)) | C{HN,i} - C{HR,i} | where t is the iteration time, \alpha(0) = 1, and \lim{t\to\infty} \alpha(t) = 0. This gradually shifts supervision from the LR NeRF (view consistency) to the HR NeRF (detail generation). 4. Range Penalty Loss (L{range}): Penalizes CCSR output colors exceeding the valid range [0, 1]: L{range} = \frac{1}{N} \sumx | \hat{x} - \text{truncate}{0,1}(\hat{x}) |1 where N is the number of pixels, and \text{truncate}{0,1}(\hat{x}) is defined as: \text{truncate}{0,1}(\hat{x}) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } \hat{x} < 0 \\ 1 & \text{if } \hat{x} > 1 \\ \hat{x} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}. 5. Total Loss: L = L{SR} + L{range}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class SimpleNeRF(nn.Module): def init(self, dimin, dimhidden, dimout): super().init() self.net = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(dimin, dimhidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(dimhidden, dimhidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(dimhidden, dimout)) def forward(self, x): # x: (N, dimin) return self.net(x) class ESRGANBackbone(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # Placeholder for pre-trained ESRGAN self.model = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(6, 64, 3, 1, 1), # Input: LR image (3) + CCLC (3) nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(64, 3, 3, 1, 1) # Output: HR image (3)) def forward(self, lrimg, cclc): # Concatenate LR image and CCLC along channel dim x = torch.cat([lrimg, cclc], dim=1) return self.model(x) class CEM: def init(self, blurkernel): self.blurkernel = blurkernel # H def forward(self, sroutput, lrinput): # CEM Output Adjustment Formula: # CHR = (I - H^T (H H^-1 H)) CtildeHR + H^T (H H^-1) CLR # Note: The exact matrix inversion/pseudo-inverse implementation depends on H. # For simplicity in pseudocode, we assume a function applycem exists # that performs the linear algebra described in. # In practice, this might involve solving a least-squares problem or # using specific matrix properties of the blur kernel. return applycem(sroutput, lrinput, self.blurkernel) def truncate01(x): return torch.clamp(x, 0.0, 1.0) def computerangepenalty(pred, target): # Lrange = 1/N sum |x - truncate(x)|1 # Here, target is not explicitly used in the formula, only the prediction # is penalized if it exceeds [0,1]. The formula uses xhat which is the prediction. truncated = truncate01(pred) diff = pred - truncated return torch.mean(torch.abs(diff)) def computel1loss(pred, target): return torch.mean(torch.abs(pred - target)) def alphaschedule(t, totaliters): # alpha(0) = 1, lim t->inf alpha(t) = 0 # Linear decay as a simple implementation of the trade-off function return 1.0 - (t / totaliters) def trainsupernerf(lrimages, poses, lrnerf, esrgan, cem, hrnerf, cclcs, numiters, blurkernel): """ lrimages: List of LR images, shape (N, 3, H, W) poses: List of camera poses for each view lrnerf: Pre-trained LR NeRF (fixed) esrgan: Pre-trained ESRGAN backbone cem: Consistency Enforcing Module hrnerf: HR NeRF (learnable) cclcs: List of CCLC tensors, shape (N, 3, sH, sW) numiters: Total training iterations blurkernel: Blur kernel H """ optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(list(hrnerf.parameters()) + [cclcs], lr=1e-4) for t in range(numiters): # 1. Randomly choose training viewpoint i i = torch.randint(0, len(lrimages), (1,)).item() lrimg = lrimages[i] # (3, H, W) pose = poses[i] cclc = cclcs[i] # (3, sH, sW) # 2. Super-resolve LR image with CCSR (ESRGAN) # Concatenate LR input to random CCLC # Note: In the paper, CCLC is learnable, so we use the current cclc # The input to ESRGAN is LR image + CCLC cclcexpanded = cclc.unsqueeze(0) # (1, 3, sH, sW) lrimgexpanded = lrimg.unsqueeze(0) # (1, 3, H, W) # ESRGAN takes concatenated input # Assuming ESRGAN expects (B, 6, H, W) if CCLC is resized or (B, 6, sH, sW) # The paper says CCLC is 3x(sH)x(sW). ESRGAN outputs HR. # We assume ESRGAN handles the upsampling or CCLC is already at HR size. # Based on "CCLC is a 3 x (sH) x (sW) dimensional latent code", # and ESRGAN is a 4x SR backbone, the CCLC is likely at the HR resolution scale. # Concatenate along channel dim: LR (3) + CCLC (3) -> (6) # But LR is HxW, CCLC is sHxsW. We need to upsample LR or assume CCLC # is the latent code for the HR space. # The paper says: "concatenate the LR input to the random CCLC". # This implies spatial alignment. Usually, this means upsampling LR to HR # or CCLC is at LR size and ESRGAN upsamples. # Given "CCLC is 3x(sH)x(sW)", it is at HR size. # So we likely upsample LR to HR size to concatenate, or the ESRGAN # architecture handles multi-scale input. # For pseudocode, we assume a helper upsamplelrtohr exists. lrimghr = F.interpolate(lrimg.unsqueeze(0), size=(cclc.shape[1], cclc.shape[2]), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False).squeeze(0) # Concatenate LR (HR size) and CCLC (HR size) esrganinput = torch.cat([lrimghr, cclcexpanded], dim=1) # (1, 6, sH, sW) # Forward ESRGAN tildeCHR = esrgan(esrganinput) # (1, 3, sH, sW) tildeCHR = tildeCHR.squeeze(0) # (3, sH, sW) # 3. Refine tildeCHR by CEM to get CHR CHR = cem(tildeCHR, lrimg) # (3, sH, sW) # 4. Upsample rays for viewpoint i and query LR NeRF # Assume rendernerf function handles ray sampling and volume rendering # It returns an image of size (sH, sW) CLN = rendernerf(lrnerf, pose, resolution=(cclc.shape[1], cclc.shape[2])) # (3, sH, sW) # 5. Query HR NeRF with same rays CHN = rendernerf(hrnerf, pose, resolution=(cclc.shape[1], cclc.shape[2])) # (3, sH, sW) # 6. Compute loss alpha = alphaschedule(t, numiters) # Mutual Learning Loss losssr = alpha computel1loss(CLN, CHR) + (1 - alpha) computel1loss(CHN, CHR) # Range Penalty Loss lossrange = computerangepenalty(CHR, None) # Total Loss loss = losssr + lossrange # 7. Train HR NeRF and CCLC optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() if t % 100 == 0: print(f"Iter {t}, Loss: {loss.item()}, Alpha: {alpha}") def rendernerf(nerfmodel, pose, resolution): """ Renders an image from a NeRF model given a pose and resolution. This is a simplified placeholder for the actual volume rendering code. """ # Generate rays for the given pose and resolution # Sample points along rays # Query NeRF for color and density # Perform volume rendering # Return image tensor (3, H, W) pass Precision: The CEM formula involves matrix operations (H^T (H H^{-1} H)) which may be sensitive to the properties of the blur kernel H. Numerical stability should be considered. Boundaries: The range penalty loss handles colors outside [0, 1], but the CEM assumes the LR input is within a valid range. Degenerate Input: If the LR images are extremely noisy or have severe artifacts, the ESRGAN may generate inconsistent details, which the CEM may not fully correct if the LR constraint is weak. Training Time: The method requires significant training time (10 hours for Super-NeRF on a single RTX 3090). Time Complexity: Training involves iterative optimization of the HR NeRF and CCLC. The average training time for Super-NeRF is 10 hours on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU. Pre-training the LR NeRF takes 30 minutes. Memory Complexity: The method requires storing the LR NeRF, HR NeRF, and CCLC for each view. The LR NeRF is lightweight (1/4 size of HR NeRF). Measured Performance: Super-NeRF achieves 4x super-resolution of NeRFs on various datasets (LLFF, Synthesis360, Blender, FaceScape). Scaling: The method is designed for 4x super-resolution (s=4). Strengths: Generates plausible 3D-consistent HR details without HR ground truth; explores the SR solution space using CCLC for better view consistency compared to NeRF-SR. Limitations: Relies on a pre-trained 2D SR prior (ESRGAN); training time is longer than standard NeRF training. When to use: When HR ground truth is unavailable and high-quality, view-consistent super-resolution of NeRFs is required. When not to use: When computational resources are limited or real-time training is required. Super-NeRF was proposed in the paper "Super-NeRF: View-Consistent Detail Generation for NeRF Super-Resolution". It addresses the limitations of NeRF-SR, which uses a simple linear formulation from LR to HR causing aliasing at edges and relies on HR refinement via per-patch warping. Super-NeRF focuses on generating plausible 3D-consistent HR details based on LR observations only, exploring the SR solution space using CCLC. It was published in IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence in 2024.
