name: NARF Training
head: NARF Optimization
body: NARF (Neural Articulated Radiance Field) training optimizes a neural network to represent the radiance field of articulated 3D objects by minimizing photometric and mask errors between rendered images and ground truth inputs. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF training by incorporating known kinematic pose configurations \{T0, \zeta, \theta\} into the rendering pipeline, allowing the model to disentangle geometry from articulation. Among its variants, Disentangled NARF (NARFD) is preferred for its balance of computational efficiency and ability to generate segmentation masks, outperforming Part-Wise and Holistic variants in novel pose/view settings. Inputs: Set of training images with known camera poses. Kinematic 3D pose configuration for the articulated object: global rigid transformation T0, bone parameters \zeta, and joint angles \theta. Ground truth pixel colors \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) and foreground masks \mathbf{M}(\mathbf{r}). Outputs: Rendered color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) and mask \hat{\mathbf{M}}(\mathbf{r}) for each ray \mathbf{r}. Optimized network parameters \Theta. Data Structures: NARF Model: A single Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) mapping spatial coordinates and viewing directions to density \sigma, feature vector \mathbf{h}, and color C. Selector S (NARFD only): A set of P lightweight sub-networks, one for each object part. Each sub-network O\Gamma^i is a two-layer MLP with 10 hidden nodes. Input: Local 3D position \mathbf{x}^i and bone parameter \zeta. Output: Logit o^i, normalized to probability p^i via softmax. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: Randomly sample a batch of camera rays \mathcal{R} from all pixels. 2. Hierarchical Sampling: For each ray, query N samples using the hierarchical volume sampling strategy from original NeRF. 3. Coordinate Transformation: For each sample at global position \mathbf{x} and direction \mathbf{d}, compute local coordinates for each part i using the known kinematic pose \{T0, \zeta, \theta\}: \mathbf{x}^i = R^{i-1}(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{t}^i), \quad \mathbf{d}^i = R^{i-1}\mathbf{d} where R^{i-1} and \mathbf{t}^i are the rotation and translation of part i. 4. Positional Encoding: Apply positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) to inputs. Dimensions are set to 10 for 3D location \mathbf{x} and 4 for other parameters (directions, bone parameters). 5. Selector Probability (NARFD only): For each part i, compute the probability p^i that \mathbf{x} belongs to part i: O\Gamma^i: (\gamma(\mathbf{x}^i), \gamma(\boldsymbol{\zeta})) \rightarrow (o^i), \quad p^i = \frac{\exp(o^i)}{\sum{k=1}^P \exp(o^k)}. 6. Network Forward Pass: Construct the input vector by concatenating the masked local features. For each part i, mask the encoded local position and direction with the selector probability p^i: \text{Input}\sigma = \text{Cat}(\{\gamma(\mathbf{x}^i) p^i \mid i \in [1, P]\}, \gamma(\zeta)) \text{Input}c = \text{Cat}(\mathbf{h}, \{(\gamma(\mathbf{d}^i) p^i, \gamma(\boldsymbol{\xi}^i) p^i) \mid i \in [1, P]\}) where \mathbf{h} is the intermediate feature vector from the density network. Query the NARF model to obtain density \sigma, feature \mathbf{h}, and color C. 7. Volume Rendering: Render the color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) and mask \hat{\mathbf{M}}(\mathbf{r}) for the ray using standard volume rendering equations (Eq. 5 and Eq. 16 in). 8. Loss Computation: Compute the total squared error loss: \mathcal{L} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \|\hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r})\|2^2 + \|\hat{\mathbf{M}}(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{M}(\mathbf{r})\|2^2 where \mathbf{C} and \mathbf{M} are ground truth color and foreground mask. 9. Optimization: Update network parameters using gradient descent. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainnarf(batchrays, poses, gtcolors, gtmasks, nerfmodel, selector=None, numsamples=64): """ One iteration of NARF training. Args: batchrays: List of rays, each defined by origin and direction. poses: Kinematic pose configuration {T0, zeta, theta} for the current frame. gtcolors: Ground truth color images. gtmasks: Ground truth foreground mask images. nerfmodel: The NARF MLP model. selector: Optional selector S (list of P MLPs) for NARFD. numsamples: Number of samples per ray (N). Returns: loss: Scalar loss value. """ totalloss = 0.0 for ray, gtcolor, gtmask in zip(batchrays, gtcolors, gtmasks): # 1. Hierarchical sampling samples = hierarchicalsampleray(ray, numsamples) # 2. Transform coordinates based on kinematic pose localcoords = [] localdirs = [] for partidx in range(numparts): # Compute local position and direction for part i # Ri, ti derived from poses {T0, zeta, theta} xlocal = transformtolocalpart(ray.origin, partidx, poses) dlocal = transformdirection(ray.direction, partidx, poses) localcoords.append(xlocal) localdirs.append(dlocal) # 3. Positional Encoding # Dimensions: 10 for x, 4 for others encodedlocals = [posenc(x, dim=10) for x in localcoords] encodeddirs = [posenc(d, dim=4) for d in localdirs] encodedzeta = posenc(poses.zeta, dim=4) # 4. Selector Probabilities (if NARFD) probs = [] if selector is not None: for i in range(numparts): # OGamma^i takes local pos and zeta logit = selector[i].forward(encodedlocals[i], encodedzeta) probs.append(logit) # Softmax normalization probs = softmax(probs) # 5. Construct Concatenated Input # Mask local features with probabilities maskedlocalinputs = [] maskeddirinputs = [] for i in range(numparts): # Masking: element-wise multiplication maskedlocalinputs.append(encodedlocals[i] probs[i]) maskeddirinputs.append(encodeddirs[i] probs[i]) # Concatenate all masked local positions sigmainput = concatenate(maskedlocalinputs + [encodedzeta]) # Forward pass for density and features sigma, h = nerfmodel.forwardsigma(sigmainput) # Concatenate features and masked directions for color # Note: gamma(xi) is assumed to be part of the direction encoding or similar auxiliary input colorinput = concatenate([h] + maskeddirinputs) color = nerfmodel.forwardcolor(colorinput) # 6. Volume Rendering renderedcolor, renderedmask = volumerender(samples, sigma, color) # 7. Loss Calculation colorloss = sum((renderedcolor - gtcolor) 2) maskloss = sum((renderedmask - gtmask) 2) totalloss += colorloss + maskloss return totalloss / len(batchrays) Parameters: Positional encoding dimension for 3D location \mathbf{x}: 10. Positional encoding dimension for other parameters (directions, bone parameters): 4. Number of samples per ray N: Not given in the sources. Selector network architecture: Two-layer MLP with 10 hidden nodes per part. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Input Concatenation: Although irrelevant parts are masked, the input remains a concatenation of all parts. This is intentional to allow the single NeRF to distinguish different bones via the dimensions of the concatenated vector, similar to part identity encoding. Selector Output: The selector outputs probabilities for all parts, even if a location belongs to only one. The softmax ensures normalization. An approach that shares the merits of both Part-Wise NARF (NARFP) and Holistic NARF (NARFH) while avoiding their weaknesses by introducing a selector S to identify which object part a global 3D location belongs to. It uses lightweight sub-networks to output part probabilities, which mask the concatenated inputs to the main NeRF. It outperforms other methods under all evaluation metrics and test data settings, exhibiting high performance under novel pose and/or novel view settings with low computational cost close to a single NeRF model. Time Complexity: Computational cost is close to a single NeRF model, as it uses one unified network rather than separate networks per part. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of elements to preserve during forward propagation per ray, which is similar to a single NeRF. Performance: NARFD outperforms NARFP and NARFH under all evaluation metrics and test data settings. It shows slight performance drop on SSIM (within 4%) in novel pose/view settings but maintains high performance. Strengths: Avoids the zero density problem of NARFH; satisfies Part Dependency unlike NARFH; generates segmentation masks; low computational cost. Limitations: Requires known kinematic 3D pose configuration \{T0, \zeta, \theta\}. When to use: When reconstructing articulated 3D objects with known kinematics and requiring efficient training with segmentation capabilities. When not to use: When kinematic poses are unknown or when the object is not articulated. NARF was introduced in the paper "Neural Articulated Radiance Field". It addresses the challenge of representing articulated 3D objects by combining neural radiance fields with kinematic models. The method was developed to overcome the limitations of Part-Wise and Holistic NARF approaches, offering a disentangled representation that is both efficient and accurate. Neural Articulated Radiance Field, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv48922.2021.00571, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Regularization and Priors
body: Regularization and Priors in NeRF training introduce constraints beyond photometric reconstruction to enforce physical plausibility, structural stability, and uncertainty awareness. This family addresses issues such as scale ambiguity in material decomposition, instability in dynamically growing networks, and overfitting to noisy observations. It is distinct from sibling methods like Learning Rate Scheduling or Adam Optimisation with Adaptive Scaling by modifying the loss landscape or network outputs directly rather than the optimization trajectory or parameter updates. The core mechanism involves augmenting the primary photometric loss \mathcal{L}{photo} with auxiliary terms \mathcal{L}{reg} derived from domain-specific assumptions (e.g., smoothness, intrinsic decomposition, or probabilistic uncertainty). The total training loss is typically a weighted sum: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{photo} + \sumk \lambdak \mathcal{L}{reg}^{(k)} where \lambdak are hyperparameters balancing the influence of each prior. These priors often operate on intermediate representations (such as reflectance/shading fields or uncertainty maps) rather than just the final rendered pixel values. This method balances photometric and uncertainty-based losses across multiple stages of a dynamically growing neural radiance field [2967-multi-scale-joint-training-parameters.md]. It addresses the instability of training deep, adaptive networks by jointly optimizing coarse and fine representations, ensuring that uncertainty estimates guide structural growth while maintaining fidelity. It is distinct from static loss weighting by coupling loss coefficients with a multi-stage optimization loop where the number of active stages D increases dynamically. This method enforces physical plausibility by decoupling rendered color into material reflectance \mathbf{R} and shading \mathbf{S} [4624-reflectance-and-shading-decomposition-priors.md]. It solves the problem of unstable material properties in novel view synthesis, particularly for object insertion or complex lighting. It distinguishes itself from standard photometric priors by explicitly regularizing intermediate decomposition components, mitigating scale ambiguity and ensuring consistent brightness levels. A technique to anneal proposal weights by raising them to a power that increases from 0 to 1 over training steps, encouraging exploration by presenting a wider range of proposal intervals early in training. The annealed weight \hat{\mathbf{w}}n at step n (out of N total steps) is computed as: \hat{\mathbf{w}}n \propto \hat{\mathbf{w}}^{\frac{bn/N}{(b-1)n/N+1}} where b is the bias hyperparameter. In experiments, b=10 is used. Ablating this annealing causes SSIM on the bicycle scene to decrease from 0.687 to 0.679. This method approximates the posterior distribution of network parameters as a multivariate Gaussian centered at the optimal weights \omega^, using the inverse Hessian of the negative log-posterior as the covariance matrix. The covariance is derived as \Sigma = -H(\omega^)^{-1}. However, directly applying this to NeRF parameters is impracticable due to high correlation between parameters, making accurate covariance estimation challenging, and the expensive sampling overhead. Regularization in NeRFs evolved from basic L2 losses to more sophisticated priors addressing specific failure modes. Weight annealing was introduced in mip-NeRF 360 to improve proposal network training stability. Intrinsic decomposition priors (reflectance/shading) were developed to handle lighting variations and object insertion [4624-reflectance-and-shading-decomposition-priors.md]. Uncertainty-aware losses in multi-scale training address the instability of dynamically growing architectures [2967-multi-scale-joint-training-parameters.md]. Bayesian approaches using Laplace approximation have been explored for uncertainty quantification but face scalability issues. name: Multi-scale Joint Training Parameters
head: Multi-scale joint training loss weights
body: Multi-scale joint training parameters refer to the specific hyperparameter configuration used to balance photometric and auxiliary losses across different stages or resolutions during the optimization of neural radiance fields. This method addresses the instability inherent in jointly optimizing complex, multi-component inverse rendering models by ensuring that gradient signals are appropriately weighted at each scale of the training hierarchy. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Surface Smoothness Regularization by explicitly tying loss weights to a multi-stage or multi-resolution progression rather than applying static priors to a single-stage network. The method defines a composite loss function that aggregates errors from multiple network stages or resolution levels. The primary inputs are the rendered images from each stage i and their corresponding ground truth images. The outputs are the scalar loss values used to update the network weights. The total loss \mathcal{L} is computed as a weighted sum over D stages (where D corresponds to the current number of stages or network growth depth): \mathcal{L} = \sum{i=1}^D \left( \beta1 \mathcal{L}{MSE}^i + \beta2 \mathcal{L}{unct}^i \right) Where: D: The current number of stages in the training hierarchy. In dynamic growth schemes, D-1 represents the number of previous network growth events. \mathcal{L}{MSE}^i: The Mean Squared Error (photometric) loss for the output image of stage i. \mathcal{L}{unct}^i: The uncertainty loss for the output image of stage i. This term typically derives from domain-specific assumptions about view-dependent noise or confidence in the rendered pixels. \beta1: The weight for the photometric (MSE) loss component. \beta2: The weight for the uncertainty loss component. \beta1 = 1.0 \beta2 = 0.1 These values are empirically determined to balance the contribution of pixel fidelity against the regularization provided by the uncertainty term. The following Python-like pseudocode illustrates the computation of the joint loss for a given batch of stages. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computemultiscalejointloss(renderedimages, groundtruthimages, uncertaintymaps, beta1=1.0, beta2=0.1): """ Computes the multi-scale joint training loss. Args: renderedimages: List of tensors, shape (N, H, W, 3), for each stage i. groundtruthimages: List of tensors, shape (N, H, W, 3), for each stage i. uncertaintymaps: List of tensors, shape (N, H, W, 1), for each stage i. beta1: Weight for MSE loss (default 1.0). beta2: Weight for uncertainty loss (default 0.1). Returns: totalloss: Scalar tensor. """ totalloss = 0.0 numstages = len(renderedimages) for i in range(numstages): # Calculate MSE loss for stage i # Note: Standard MSE implementation mseloss = torch.mean((renderedimages[i] - groundtruthimages[i]) 2) # Calculate uncertainty loss for stage i # Note: The exact formulation of Lunct is not specified in the source beyond its name. # In typical inverse rendering contexts, this may involve the variance or confidence # predicted by the network. Here we assume uncertaintymaps provides the necessary # scalar field for the loss term. # Assuming a standard uncertainty regularization term proportional to the map values. unctloss = torch.mean(uncertaintymaps[i]) # Weighted sum for this stage stageloss = beta1 mseloss + beta2 unctloss totalloss += stageloss return totalloss Precision: The uncertainty loss \mathcal{L}{unct} requires careful handling of numerical stability, particularly if the uncertainty maps contain near-zero values that could lead to division by zero or vanishing gradients if used in a probabilistic likelihood formulation. Stage Count (D): In dynamic growth scenarios, D changes as the network expands. The loss function must dynamically adjust the summation range to include only active stages. A coarse-to-fine training scheme that uses different camera intrinsic parameters to construct an image pyramid, enhancing multi-scale feature learning. It sets itself apart by modifying the camera projection matrix K at each scale rather than just the image resolution, thereby enforcing multi-view consistency through geometric constraints. Choose this method when training multi-view Gaussian Splatting or NeRF variants where view-dependent noise is significant and multi-view consistency is critical. Definition: Constructs a 4-layer image pyramid with downsampling factors S = \{2^{k-1} \mid k = 4, 3, 2, 1\}. Step 1: For each layer s \in S, reconfigure the intrinsic matrix K by dividing the focal length f and principal point coordinates cx, cy by s: K's = \begin{bmatrix} f/s & 0 & cx/s \\ 0 & f/s & cy/s \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} Step 2: Assign matched multi-view settings Ms = \{M4, M3, M2, M1\} to each layer. Larger downsampling factors (coarser layers) use more views to provide stronger multi-view constraints. Step 3: Run only a few thousand iterations per stage for the first three coarse stages (s=8, 4, 2). Then start fine training (s=1) to refine details. Parameters: S is the set of downsampling factors \{1, 2, 4, 8\}. The largest factor s=8 is empirically sufficient; s=1 means no downsampling. Pitfalls: Excessively large downsampling factors lead to blurry ground truth, decreasing fidelity and increasing refinement difficulty. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of stages D and the number of views per stage. In dynamic growth schemes, the cost increases as D grows. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the storage of intermediate rendered images and uncertainty maps for all active stages. Strengths: Stabilizes training in complex inverse rendering models by decoupling the optimization of geometry, appearance, and lighting across scales. Reduces view-dependent noise. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of stage counts and loss weights. Coarse stages may not capture sufficient detail, necessitating a fine-tuning phase. When to use: When training neural radiance fields or Gaussian Splatting models that exhibit instability due to interdependent modules or multi-view inconsistencies. The concept of multi-scale joint training parameters originates from Recursive-NeRF, which introduced an efficient and dynamically growing NeRF architecture. The specific weights \beta1=1.0 and \beta2=0.1 were proposed to balance MSE and uncertainty losses in this dynamic growth framework. The related Cross-intrinsic Guidance variant was introduced in MVGS (Multi-view-regulated Gaussian Splatting) to address multi-view consistency issues by leveraging camera intrinsic parameter variations. name: Multi-stage Training Protocol
head: Pretrain and Joint Train Strategy
body: Multi-stage training protocols decompose the optimization of complex neural radiance fields or inverse rendering models into sequential phases to stabilize convergence and manage conflicting gradients. Unlike single-stage end-to-end training, which often suffers from instability when optimizing heterogeneous components (e.g., geometry, appearance, and lighting) simultaneously, this method decouples the process into distinct steps such as pretraining, joint training, and fine-tuning. It addresses the problem of initializing dependent modules with reasonable values before introducing more complex interactions, ensuring that the model components act as expected during the final end-to-end optimization. The protocol generally follows a progressive scheme where specific submodules are trained, frozen, or jointly optimized in a defined order. The exact steps vary by implementation, but the core logic involves warming up coarse representations before refining high-frequency details or coupled variables. Inputs: Camera poses, images, and optionally auxiliary supervision (e.g., depth, normals, albedo). Outputs: Optimized neural field parameters (MLP weights, grid features, or volume densities) and associated attributes (lighting, material properties). Data structures depend on the specific variant (e.g., Direct Prediction Module vs. UV Volumes). Common structures include: Neural Networks: MLPs for direct prediction or lighting estimation. Volumetric/Grid Representations: 3D volumes (e.g., 128^3) or UV-metric grids for storing features. Loss Weights: Scalars \lambda for balancing multi-task losses. The general multi-stage protocol consists of the following phases: 1. Pretrain Direct Prediction Module: Train the albedo, normal, and depth branches of the Direct Prediction Module independently. Goal: Ensure these branches produce reasonable initial values, as they are dependencies for subsequent modules (e.g., Lighting Joint Prediction Module). Loss: Standard reconstruction or supervision losses for albedo, normal, and depth. 2. Joint Train Direct and Lighting Modules: Jointly optimize the Direct Prediction Module and the Lighting Joint Prediction Module. Loss: Multi-task loss L combining albedo, normal, depth, lighting, visibility, and regularization terms: L = \lambdaA L{albedo} + \lambdaN L{normal} + \lambdaD L{depth} + \lambdaL L{light} + \lambda{visible} L{visible} + \lambda{reg} L{reg} + \lambda{rerender} L{rerender} where \lambda are hyperparameters balancing the terms. 3. Train Joint Re-prediction Module: Freeze the weights of the Direct Prediction Module and Lighting Joint Prediction Module. Train the Joint Re-prediction Module to refine albedo, normals, and depth. Goal: Improve the consistency of intermediate outputs without disturbing the already learned lighting and direct appearance features. 4. End-to-End Finetune: Unfreeze all modules and jointly finetune the entire network end-to-end. Loss: Multi-task loss computed on both the joint prediction outputs (\hat{A}, \hat{N}, \hat{D}, \hat{L}) and the intermediate outputs (\tilde{A}, \tilde{N}, \tilde{D}). Goal: Refine the global consistency of the model. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multistagetraining(model, dataloader, config): # Step 1: Pretrain Direct Prediction Module # Train albedo, normal, and depth branches of Direct Prediction Module for epoch in range(config.pretrainepochs): optimizerdirect.zerograd() outputs = model.directpredictionmodule(data) loss = computedirectloss(outputs, data) loss.backward() optimizerdirect.step() # Step 2: Joint Train Direct and Lighting Modules # Freeze nothing yet, optimize both modules for epoch in range(config.jointepochs): optimizerjoint.zerograd() directout = model.directpredictionmodule(data) lightingout = model.lightingjointpredictionmodule(directout, data) loss = computemultitaskloss(directout, lightingout, data) loss.backward() optimizerjoint.step() # Apply learning rate decay if applicable adjustlearningrate(optimizerjoint, epoch, config.lrdecay) # Step 3: Train Joint Re-prediction Module # Freeze weights of Direct and Lighting modules freezemodel(model.directpredictionmodule) freezemodel(model.lightingjointpredictionmodule) for epoch in range(config.repredepochs): optimizerrepred.zerograd() # Only re-prediction module gradients flow repredout = model.jointrepredictionmodule(data) loss = computerepredloss(repredout, data) loss.backward() optimizerrepred.step() # Step 4: End-to-End Finetune # Unfreeze all modules unfreezemodel(model.directpredictionmodule) unfreezemodel(model.lightingjointpredictionmodule) unfreezemodel(model.jointrepredictionmodule) for epoch in range(config.finetuneepochs): optimizere2e.zerograd() # Forward pass through all modules directout = model.directpredictionmodule(data) lightingout = model.lightingjointpredictionmodule(directout, data) repredout = model.jointrepredictionmodule(data) # Loss on both joint predictions and intermediate outputs loss = computee2eloss(directout, lightingout, repredout, data) loss.backward() optimizere2e.step() adjustlearningrate(optimizere2e, epoch, config.lrdecay) Learning Rate Decay: Exponential decay is often used. For example, in UV Volume variants, decay rates \gamma are applied. Loss Weights: \lambdaA, \lambdaN, \lambdaD, \lambdaL, \lambda{visible}, \lambda{reg}, \lambda{rerender} balance the multi-task loss. Ray Sampling: 64 points sampled along each camera ray between near and far bounds. Optimizer: Adam optimizer. Dependency Violation: If the Direct Prediction Module is not pretrained, the Lighting Joint Prediction Module may receive unreasonable inputs, leading to poor convergence. Freezing Timing: Freezing modules too early may prevent necessary co-adaptation; freezing too late may lead to instability. The protocol specifies freezing after Step 2 and unfreezing in Step 4. UV Volume Warm-start: In UV-based methods, UV volumes must be learned first to warm-start coarse geometry before optimizing the Neural Texture Stack (NTS) for high-frequency signals. MobileNeRF Staged Training is a multi-stage optimization protocol designed to train the MobileNeRF neural field representation efficiently on mobile hardware constraints. It addresses the challenge of jointly optimizing geometry (vertices), appearance (MLPs), and acceleration structures (grids) by decoupling them into sequential phases. Unlike standard NeRF training which optimizes all parameters simultaneously, this method fixes geometry and acceleration structures in later stages to stabilize convergence and reduce computational overhead during the final refinement of appearance features. Multi-resolution Feature Grid Pre-train is a method that constructs a multi-resolution ground feature plane representation for large urban scenes, capturing density and appearance separately to reduce memory footprint and guide subsequent NeRF sampling. It differs from standard NeRF training by decoupling the initial scene representation into a compact, low-rank tensor factorization (the grid branch) that is pre-trained before joint optimization with a full 3D NeRF branch. This approach leverages the planar nature of urban environments to achieve robust performance with sparse view data.#### UV Volume Training Strategy The UV Volume Training Strategy uses two optimization strategies for UV volumes and the Neural Texture Stack (NTS) branch. UV volumes are learned primarily in early stages to warm-start coarse geometry, while NTS is optimized later to fit high-frequency signals. The learning rate for UV volumes is calculated as l{uv} = 1 \times 10^{-3} \beta^{epoch}, where \beta = 1 \times 10^{-1}. The learning rate for NTS is calculated as l{nts} = 5 \times 10^{-4} \beta^{epoch}, where \beta = 1 \times 10^{-1}. Ray sampling uses 64 points along each camera ray between near and far bounds, with scene bounds estimated based on the SMPL model. The Adam optimizer is used. Training on 26-view videos of 100 frames at 960 × 540 resolution takes approximately 20 hours (200k iterations) on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. Time Complexity: Multi-stage training increases total training time compared to single-stage methods due to sequential phases. For example, UV Volume training takes ~20 hours for 200k iterations. Memory Complexity: Depends on the representation (e.g., 128^3 volume or UV grids). Pretraining stages may require less memory if only subsets of parameters are active. Strengths: Stabilizes convergence for complex models with dependent components; allows for specialized optimization strategies for different parts of the network (e.g., geometry vs. appearance). Limitations: Increased training time; requires careful tuning of stage transitions and learning rates; potential for suboptimal solutions if stages are not well-coordinated. When to Use: When training complex inverse rendering models or neural fields with heterogeneous components (e.g., lighting, material, geometry) that conflict during joint optimization. When Not to Use: For simple NeRFs where single-stage training converges reliably; when computational resources are extremely limited and training time is a critical constraint. The multi-stage training protocol originated in the context of inverse rendering and neural radiance field optimization, where models often comprise multiple interconnected modules (e.g., direct prediction, lighting estimation, re-prediction). The approach was formalized in works such as "Learning Indoor Inverse Rendering with 3D Spatially-Varying Lighting" and "UV Volumes for Real-time Rendering of Editable Free-view Human Performance". It addresses the instability observed in end-to-end training of such complex systems by progressively introducing model complexity. name: MobileNeRF Staged Training
head: MobileNeRF Training Stages
body: MobileNeRF Staged Training is a multi-stage optimization protocol designed to train the MobileNeRF neural field representation efficiently on mobile hardware constraints. It addresses the challenge of jointly optimizing geometry (vertices), appearance (MLPs), and acceleration structures (grids) by decoupling them into sequential phases. Unlike standard NeRF training which optimizes all parameters simultaneously, this method fixes geometry and acceleration structures in later stages to stabilize convergence and reduce computational overhead during the final refinement of appearance features. The method optimizes the MobileNeRF representation through three distinct training stages, interleaved with specific acceleration grid optimization steps. The representation consists of a regular-grid mesh \mathbf{M} defined by vertices \mathbf{V}, an acceleration grid \mathbf{G}, and three Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): an opacity MLP with parameters \theta{OpacityMLP}, a features MLP with parameters \theta{FeaturesMLP}, and a shader MLP with parameters \theta{ShaderMLP} (also denoted as \thetaA). Inputs: Training images, camera poses, initial vertex positions \mathbf{V}, initial MLP weights, acceleration grid \mathbf{G} (initialized to zero or sparse values), and scene type (synthetic 360°, forward-facing, or unbounded 360°). Outputs: Optimized vertices \mathbf{V}, acceleration grid \mathbf{G}, and MLP parameters \theta{OpacityMLP}, \theta{FeaturesMLP}, \theta{ShaderMLP}. Vertices (\mathbf{V}): Defines the geometry of the regular-grid mesh \mathbf{M}. Acceleration Grid (\mathbf{G}): A 3D grid of size P \times P \times P used to prune voxels during ray marching. MLPs: Three separate networks for opacity, features, and shading. wd: Weight for the distance loss \mathcal{L}{dist}. Synthetic 360° scenes: 0.0. Forward-facing scenes: 0.01. Unbounded 360° scenes: 0.001. w{g1}, w{g2}: Weights for sparse and smooth grid losses. Value is 10^{-5} for both. \tauG: Threshold for pruning voxels in the acceleration grid. Value is 0.1. 1. Initialization: Initialize vertices \mathbf{V}, acceleration grid \mathbf{G}, and MLP parameters \theta{OpacityMLP}, \theta{FeaturesMLP}, \theta{ShaderMLP}. 2. Stage 1: Joint Optimization: Optimize all parameters jointly to minimize the Stage 1 loss: \mathcal{L}{Stage1} = \mathcal{L}{Color} + wd \mathcal{L}{dist} + \mathcal{L}{v} where \mathcal{L}{Color} is the color reconstruction loss, \mathcal{L}{dist} is the distance loss, and \mathcal{L}{v} is the volume loss. Acceleration Grid Optimization: Concurrently or interleaved, optimize \mathbf{G} to minimize: \mathcal{L}{Grid} = \mathcal{L}{Grid}^{bnd} + w{g1} \mathcal{L}{Grid}^{sparse} + w{g2} \mathcal{L}{Grid}^{smooth} where \mathcal{L}{Grid}^{bnd} is the boundary loss, \mathcal{L}{Grid}^{sparse} is the sparse loss, and \mathcal{L}{Grid}^{smooth} is the smooth loss. Ray Marching Adaptation: During the first quarter of Stage 1 iterations, \mathbf{G} is inaccurate. The ray marching algorithm keeps all 3P intersected voxels and intersection points regardless of \tauG. 3. Stage 2: Modified Color Loss: Optimize all parameters jointly again, but using a modified color loss \mathcal{L}{Color}^{stage2}: \mathcal{L}{Stage2} = \mathcal{L}{Color}^{stage2} + wd \mathcal{L}{dist} + \mathcal{L}{v} The acceleration grid \mathbf{G} is also optimized using the same grid loss as Stage 1. Ray Marching Adaptation: In the next quarter of training, \mathbf{G} is used to remove empty voxels. The algorithm keeps at most 3P/2 non-empty voxels and the 3P/2 intersection points closest to the camera. The training batch size is doubled. 4. Stage 3: Post-Convergence Refinement: When the loss converges, fix the weights of vertices \mathbf{V}, opacity MLP parameters \theta{OpacityMLP} (denoted \thetaA in some contexts, but notes specify fixing V, \thetaA, and G), and the acceleration grid \mathbf{G}. Optimize only the features MLP parameters \theta{FeaturesMLP} and shader MLP parameters \theta{ShaderMLP} to minimize the binarized color loss: \mathcal{L}{Stage3} = \mathcal{L}{Color}^{bin} Ray Marching Adaptation: In the remainder of the training, keep at most 3P/4 non-empty voxels and intersection points. The batch size is doubled again. Unbounded Scenes Exception: For concentric boxes in unbounded 360° scenes, compute intersections and keep all of them throughout the process. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mobilenrfstagedtraining(scenetype, images, poses, P, tauG): # Initialize parameters V = initializevertices() G = initializegrid(P) thetaOpacityMLP = initializemlp() thetaFeaturesMLP = initializemlp() thetaShaderMLP = initializemlp() # Set distance loss weight based on scene type if scenetype == "synthetic360": wd = 0.0 elif scenetype == "forwardfacing": wd = 0.01 elif scenetype == "unbounded360": wd = 0.001 else: wd = 0.0 # Default or error wg1 = 1e-5 wg2 = 1e-5 totaliterations = gettotaliterations() quarter = totaliterations // 4 for iteration in range(totaliterations): # Determine ray marching strategy based on training progress if iteration < quarter: # First quarter: G is inaccurate, keep all intersections maxvoxels = 3 P maxintersections = 3 P usegridpruning = False elif iteration < 2 quarter: # Second quarter: Use G to prune, keep 3P/2 maxvoxels = 3 P // 2 maxintersections = 3 P // 2 usegridpruning = True batchsize = initialbatchsize 2 elif iteration < 3 quarter: # Third quarter: Keep 3P/4 maxvoxels = 3 P // 4 maxintersections = 3 P // 4 usegridpruning = True batchsize = initialbatchsize 4 else: # Final quarter: Keep 3P/4 (same as third quarter logic for pruning) maxvoxels = 3 P // 4 maxintersections = 3 P // 4 usegridpruning = True batchsize = initialbatchsize 4 # Unbounded scenes exception: keep all intersections if scenetype == "unbounded360": maxvoxels = None # Keep all maxintersections = None # Keep all usegridpruning = False # Sample rays and render rays = samplerays(images, poses, batchsize) colors, depths = rendermobilenrf( V, G, thetaOpacityMLP, thetaFeaturesMLP, thetaShaderMLP, rays, tauG, usegridpruning, maxvoxels, maxintersections) # Compute losses based on stage if iteration < 2 quarter: # Stage 1 and 2 losscolor = computecolorloss(colors, images) if iteration < quarter: # Stage 1 loss = losscolor + wd computedistanceloss(depths) + computevolumeloss() else: # Stage 2 loss = computecolorlossstage2(colors, images) + wd computedistanceloss(depths) + computevolumeloss() # Optimize all parameters optimize(V, thetaOpacityMLP, thetaFeaturesMLP, thetaShaderMLP, loss) # Optimize Grid G lossgrid = computeboundaryloss(G) + wg1 computesparseloss(G) + wg2 computesmoothloss(G) optimize(G, lossgrid) else: # Stage 3: Post-convergence # Fix V, thetaOpacityMLP, G loss = computecolorlossbin(colors, images) # Optimize only Features and Shader MLPs optimize(thetaFeaturesMLP, thetaShaderMLP, loss) return V, G, thetaOpacityMLP, thetaFeaturesMLP, thetaShaderMLP Inaccurate Grid Early On: In the first quarter, the acceleration grid \mathbf{G} is not reliable. Failing to disable pruning or keep all 3P intersections will lead to missing geometry and poor convergence. Batch Size Scaling: The batch size must be doubled when the number of kept intersections is halved to maintain stable gradient statistics. Unbounded Scenes: Standard pruning logic fails for concentric boxes in unbounded 360° scenes; all intersections must be retained. Texture Constraints: Mobile hardware requires texture sizes to be powers of 2 and at most 4096 \times 4096. Large texture images must be split into multiple tiles. The core training objective minimizes \mathcal{L}{Color} + wd \mathcal{L}{dist} + \mathcal{L}{v} with respect to vertices \mathbf{V}, opacity MLP parameters \theta{OpacityMLP}, features MLP parameters \theta{FeaturesMLP}, and shader MLP parameters \theta{ShaderMLP}. This objective is used in the first stage. The distance loss weight wd varies by scene type, and the loss terms include color, distance, and volume components. Time Complexity: The ray marching complexity is O(P) for finding intersections on a regular grid of size P \times P \times P. The staged approach reduces the number of parameters optimized in later stages, potentially speeding up convergence. Memory Complexity: The acceleration grid \mathbf{G} requires O(P^3) memory. Vertices \mathbf{V} and MLP parameters also consume memory, but the fixed-parameter stages reduce gradient storage requirements in Stage 3. Strengths: Stabilizes training by decoupling geometry/acceleration from appearance refinement. Adapts ray marching efficiency based on training progress. Suitable for mobile hardware constraints. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of stage transitions and batch size scaling. The acceleration grid optimization adds complexity. When to Use: When training MobileNeRF on mobile devices or when standard joint optimization fails to converge due to geometry/acceleration instability. MobileNeRF was introduced to exploit the polygon rasterization pipeline for efficient neural field rendering on mobile architectures. The staged training protocol was developed to handle the joint optimization of geometry, acceleration structures, and neural appearance models under the computational and memory constraints of mobile GPUs. name: Multi-resolution Feature Grid Pre-train
head: Grid Branch Pre-training, Stage 1 Training
body: Multi-resolution Feature Grid Pre-train is a method that constructs a multi-resolution ground feature plane representation for large urban scenes, capturing density and appearance separately to reduce memory footprint and guide subsequent NeRF sampling. It differs from standard NeRF training by decoupling the initial scene representation into a compact, low-rank tensor factorization (the grid branch) that is pre-trained before joint optimization with a full 3D NeRF branch. This approach leverages the planar nature of urban environments to achieve robust performance with sparse view data. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of calibrated images of a large urban scene; camera poses. Outputs: Pre-trained multi-resolution density and appearance feature grids (\mathcal{G}\sigma, \mathcal{G}c) used to initialize the joint training stage. Data Structures: The method uses a multi-resolution feature grid composed of density and appearance tensors at various resolutions n. For a specific resolution n, the tensors are constructed from low-rank components: \mathbf{v}{\sigma, r}^{z}: A vector along the z-axis for density component r. \mathbf{M}{\sigma, r}^{xy}: A matrix in the xy-plane for density component r. \mathbf{v}{c, r}^{z}: A vector along the z-axis for appearance component r. \mathbf{M}{c, r}^{xy}: A matrix in the xy-plane for appearance component r. R\sigma: Number of density components. Rc: Number of appearance components. Formulas: The density and appearance tensors at resolution n are obtained by concatenating outer products of z-axis vectors and xy-plane matrices: \mathcal {G}{\sigma }^n = \oplus [ (\mathbf {v}{\sigma, r}^{z} \circ \mathbf {M}{\sigma,r}^{xy})]{R\sigma }, \quad \mathcal {G}{c}^n = \oplus [\mathbf {v}{c, r}^{z} \circ \mathbf {M}{c,r}^{xy})]{Rc} where \circ denotes the outer product and \oplus denotes concatenation over the R\sigma and Rc dimensions. Positional Encoding (PE) uses Fourier features: \text{PE}(x) = (\sin(x), \cos(x), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1}x), \cos(2^{L-1}x)) Parameters: Positional Encoding Frequency: The highest frequency is set to 2^{15}. Components: 8 components for density and 16 for appearance. Resolutions: The method uses a highest resolution feature plane plus downsampled resolutions at \times 4 and \times 16. MLP Head: A small MLP with 2 fully connected layers of 128 hidden units and ReLU activation is used as the output head for the grid branch. Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: Initial learning rate of 0.02 for tensor factors and 0.01 for MLP layers. Batch Size: 4096 rays. Pre-training Iterations: 10,000 iterations. Steps: 1. Scene Capture: Capture the scene with a pyramid of feature planes at the pre-train stage. 2. Coarse Sampling: Perform a coarse sampling of ray points (e.g., 64 coarse samples per ray). 3. Feature Interpolation: For each sampled point, interpolate features from the multi-resolution feature grids. 4. Prediction: Predict radiance values (density \sigma and color c) through a shallow MLP renderer (grid branch) using the interpolated features and positional encoding. 5. Loss Calculation: Compute the Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss between the predicted volumetrically integrated pixel colors and the ground truth. 6. Optimization: Update the tensor factors (\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{M}) and MLP weights to minimize the loss. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pretraingridbranch(images, poses, numiterations=10000): # Initialize multi-resolution feature grids # Resolutions: base, base/4, base/16 # Density components: 8, Appearance components: 16 Gsigma = initializemultiresolutiongrid(resolutions=[1, 0.25, 0.0625], numcomponents=8, type='density') Gc = initializemultiresolutiongrid(resolutions=[1, 0.25, 0.0625], numcomponents=16, type='appearance') # Initialize shallow MLP for grid branch gridmlp = ShallowMLP(hiddensize=128, numlayers=2) optimizer = Adam([Gsigma, Gc, gridmlp.parameters()], lr=0.02) # Note: MLP layers might have different lr, handled by optimizer groups in practice for iteration in range(numiterations): # Sample rays from images rays = samplerays(images, poses, numrays=4096, coarsesamples=64) # Get 3D coordinates for sampled points points = rays.origin + rays.direction rays.sampledistances # Interpolate features from multi-resolution grids # This involves selecting the appropriate resolution and bilinear interpolation featuressigma = interpolatefeatures(Gsigma, points) featuresc = interpolatefeatures(Gc, points) # Apply Positional Encoding to positions # Highest frequency 2^15 pepos = fourierpositionalencoding(points, maxfreq=15) # Concatenate features and PE # Fsigma and Fc are fusing functions (small MLPs) # In the grid branch, features are concatenated with PE and fed to MLP inputtomlp = concatenate(featuressigma, featuresc, pepos) # Predict density and color # The grid branch outputs sigma and c sigmapred, cpred = gridmlp(inputtomlp) # Volumetric rendering to get pixel color # Alpha compositing using predicted sigma and c colorpred = volumetricrender(rays, sigmapred, cpred) # Calculate MSE loss against ground truth image colors gtcolors = getpixelcolors(rays, images) loss = mseloss(colorpred, gtcolors) # Backpropagate and update optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return Gsigma, Gc def initializemultiresolutiongrid(resolutions, numcomponents, type): # Initialize tensor factors for each resolution # For density: vz (N, 1, D), Mxy (N, H, W, D) # For appearance: vz (N, 1, D), Mxy (N, H, W, D) # D is the component dimension (e.g., 128) grids = [] for res in resolutions: if type == 'density': # Initialize vsigma and Msigma v = torch.randn(numcomponents, 1, 128) M = torch.randn(numcomponents, 1, 1, 128) # Placeholder for spatial dims grids.append({'v': v, 'M': M}) else: # Initialize vc and Mc v = torch.randn(numcomponents, 1, 128) M = torch.randn(numcomponents, 1, 1, 128) grids.append({'v': v, 'M': M}) return grids def interpolatefeatures(grid, points): # For each point, find the closest resolution and interpolate # This is a placeholder for the actual interpolation logic # which involves mapping 3D points to 2D planes and z-axis vectors features = [] for g in grid: # Interpolate Mxy at (x,y) and vz at z # Outer product to get 3D feature # Concatenate over components pass return concatenatedfeatures Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse View Data: The method is designed to be robust to sparse view training data, but extremely sparse data may still lead to poor feature plane initialization. Urban Scene Assumption: The method relies on the assumption that large urban scenes are grounded on the xy-plane. Scenes with significant vertical structures or non-planar layouts may not benefit as much. Precision: The use of Fourier features with high frequencies (2^{15}) requires careful handling of numerical precision during optimization. A staged training approach for mobile devices, focusing on efficiency and quantization, whereas Multi-resolution Feature Grid Pre-train focuses on large-scale urban scenes and tensor factorization. The parent method that encompasses Multi-resolution Feature Grid Pre-train as its first stage. Time Complexity: The pre-training stage takes approximately 10,000 iterations, which is roughly 1/5 of the total training time (100k iterations for joint optimization). Memory Complexity: The low-rank tensor factorization significantly reduces the memory footprint compared to full 3D grids. For example, using 8/16 components for density/appearance with multi-resolution planes is more compact than the 16/48 components used in the TensoRF baseline. Performance: The method achieves robust performance on large urban scenes with sparse view data. Strengths: Reduced memory footprint, robustness to sparse views, suitability for large urban scenes. Limitations: Assumption of planar scene structure, potential sensitivity to sparse view data quality. The method was introduced in "Grid-guided Neural Radiance Fields for Large Urban Scenes". It builds on the observation that large urban scenes are primarily grounded on the xy-plane, allowing for efficient representation using 2D feature planes and 1D vectors. The approach is inspired by tensor factorization techniques like those used in TensoRF. name: Reflectance and Shading Decomposition Priors
head: Intrinsic Priors, Mean Reflectance Regularization, Shading Smoothness
body: Reflectance and Shading Decomposition Priors enforce physical plausibility in neural radiance fields by decoupling the rendered color into material reflectance (intrinsic to the surface) and shading (dependent on illumination and viewpoint). This method solves the problem of unstable or physically inconsistent material properties in novel view synthesis, particularly when inserting objects into scenes or handling complex lighting. It distinguishes itself from standard photometric priors by explicitly regularizing the intermediate decomposition components—reflectance and shading—rather than just the final pixel values, thereby mitigating scale ambiguity and ensuring consistent brightness levels across different scenes or inserted objects. The method augments the primary photometric reconstruction loss with specific regularization terms targeting the decomposed reflectance \mathbf{R} and shading \mathbf{S} fields. Inputs: \mathbf{R}(\mathbf{r}): Reflectance vector at ray \mathbf{r} (typically RGB). \mathbf{S}(\mathbf{r}): Shading scalar or vector at ray \mathbf{r}. \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{r}): Surface normal at ray \mathbf{r}. \mathbf{p}(\mathbf{r}): 3D position of the sample point on ray \mathbf{r}. \beta{avg,r}: Target mean reflectance hyperparameter. Outputs: \mathcal{L}{mean,r}: Mean reflectance regularization loss. \mathcal{L}s: Shading smoothness loss. \mathcal{L}{sn}: Shading-Normal consistency loss. The network outputs two primary channels per sample point: 1. Reflectance \mathbf{R}: A 3-channel vector (RGB) representing the material albedo. 2. Shading \mathbf{S}: A scalar or 3-channel vector representing the illumination factor. In the context of the mean reflectance loss, \mathbf{R}(\mathbf{r}).max refers to the maximum value among the three RGB channels of the reflectance vector. 1. Mean Reflectance Regularization (\mathcal{L}{mean,r}) This term constrains the reflectance magnitude to prevent unreasonable brightness changes, ensuring that inserted objects match the scene's brightness level. \mathcal{L}{mean,r} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \left| (\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{r}).max) - \beta{avg,r} \right| \mathcal{R}: The set of sampled rays in the current batch. \mathbf{R}(\mathbf{r}).max: The maximum value across the RGB channels of the reflectance vector \mathbf{R}(\mathbf{r}). \beta{avg,r}: A hyperparameter representing the target average reflectance. The source sets this to 0.6 for most scenes. |\mathcal{R}|: The number of rays in the batch. 2. Shading Smoothness Loss (\mathcal{L}s) This term enforces spatial coherence in the shading field, reducing noise in the estimated illumination. \mathcal{L}s = \text{Var}(\{\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{r}) \mid \mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}\}) Defined as the variance of shading values for all pixels (or sampled points) in a single batch. 3. Shading-Normal Consistency Loss (\mathcal{L}{sn}) This term leverages the correlation between shading and surface normals to enforce local smoothness, weighted by geometric proximity and orientation. \mathcal{L}{sn} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \omegan(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}') \cdot |\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{S}(\mathbf{r}')| \cdot (1 - \tanh(\text{Dis}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}'))) \mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}': Rays/samples. The summation iterates over \mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R} and aggregates contributions from neighboring samples \mathbf{r}'. \omegan(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}'): A weight measuring the cosine similarity between the surface normals \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{r}) and \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{r}'). \text{Dis}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}'): The Euclidean distance between the 3D points associated with rays \mathbf{r} and \mathbf{r}'. The term (1 - \tanh(\text{Dis}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}'))) acts as a distance decay factor, giving higher weight to closer points. 4. Total Training Loss The priors are combined with other intrinsic priors (chromaticity \mathcal{L}{chro}, sparsity \mathcal{L}{rs}, non-local sparsity \mathcal{L}{nrs}) and the base photometric loss \mathcal{L}: \mathcal{L}{train} = \lambda0 \mathcal{L} + \lambda1 \mathcal{L}d + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{mean,r} + \lambda3 \mathcal{L}{chro} + \lambda4 \mathcal{L}{rs} + \lambda5 \mathcal{L}{nrs} + \lambda6 \mathcal{L}s + \lambda7 \mathcal{L}{sn} \lambdai: Adjustable weights for each loss term. \mathcal{L}d: A decomposition loss term. Not given in the sources. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeintrinsicpriors(reflectancebatch, shadingbatch, normalsbatch, positionsbatch, betaavgr=0.6): """ Computes the Reflectance and Shading Decomposition Priors losses. Args: reflectancebatch: list of [r, g, b] floats for N rays. shadingbatch: list of floats for N rays. normalsbatch: list of [nx, ny, nz] floats for N rays. positionsbatch: list of [x, y, z] floats for N rays. betaavgr: Float, target mean reflectance (default 0.6). Returns: dict: Loss values for mean reflectance, shading smoothness, and shading-normal consistency. """ N = len(reflectancebatch) # 1. Mean Reflectance Regularization # R(r).max is the max value across the RGB channels for each ray maxreflectance = [max(rgb) for rgb in reflectancebatch] lmeanr = sum(abs(m - betaavgr) for m in maxreflectance) / N # 2. Shading Smoothness Loss # Variance of shading for all pixels in the batch means = sum(shadingbatch) / N ls = sum((s - means) 2 for s in shadingbatch) / N # 3. Shading-Normal Consistency Loss # Sum over rays r in R, comparing with neighbors r' lsn = 0.0 for i in range(N): r = positionsbatch[i] rnorm = normalsbatch[i] si = shadingbatch[i] pairsum = 0.0 for j in range(N): if i == j: continue rprime = positionsbatch[j] rprimenorm = normalsbatch[j] sj = shadingbatch[j] # Dis(r, r') is Euclidean distance dist = math.sqrt(sum((a - b) 2 for a, b in zip(r, rprime))) # omegan measures cosine similarity of normals dotprod = sum(a b for a, b in zip(rnorm, rprimenorm)) normi = math.sqrt(sum(a 2 for a in rnorm)) normj = math.sqrt(sum(a 2 for a in rprimenorm)) cossim = dotprod / (normi normj) if (normi normj) > 1e-8 else 0.0 # Shading difference sdiff = abs(si - sj) # Distance decay factor: (1 - tanh(Dis(r, r'))) decay = 1.0 - math.tanh(dist) pairsum += cossim sdiff decay lsn += pairsum lsn /= N return { "lmeanr": lmeanr, "ls": ls, "lsn": lsn } Scale Ambiguity: There is an inherent scale ambiguity between shading and reflectance; scaling reflectance by k and shading by 1/k yields the same observed image. The mean reflectance regularization helps constrain this by fixing the brightness level of reflectance, ensuring inserted objects match the scene's shading brightness. Sampling Sparsity: In scenes with large backgrounds and small objects, sampling points on objects may be sparse, leading to missing details or artifacts if not handled by specialized sampling strategies (e.g., segmented sampling). Hyperparameter Sensitivity: The value of \beta{avg,r} is critical. The source recommends 0.6 for most scenes, but this may need adjustment for scenes with significantly different average brightness. Strengths: Produces smoother normal maps and more physically plausible material properties, especially in complex scenes. Enables consistent object insertion by aligning shading levels. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of estimated normals and sampling density. Sparse sampling on small objects can degrade performance. This method originates from the work on "Relighting Scenes With Object Insertions in Neural Radiance Fields". It adapts traditional intrinsic image decomposition constraints (chromaticity, sparsity, non-local sparsity) into the NeRF backbone to improve the quality of rendered images and enable novel view synthesis with inserted objects. name: Surface Smoothness Regularization
head: Depth Smoothness Regularization, Surface Smoothness on Integrated Unobserved Rays
body: Surface Smoothness Regularization imposes piece-wise smoothness constraints on rendered depth from unobserved rays to alleviate spatial ambiguity and stabilize the joint optimization of blur kernels and radiance fields in sparse-view DeRF. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF regularization by integrating "hidden rays" derived from the estimated blur kernel alongside standard "unseen rays," specifically targeting the coupled uncertainty of defocus and geometry. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of target camera poses \{Pi^{target}\}, an estimated blur kernel h, and the current radiance field parameters. Outputs: A scalar loss value \mathcal{L}{ss} used in the total training loss. Data Structures Target Poses: Pi^{target} = [Ri^{target} | ti^{target}] \in SE(3). Sampled Poses: SP, a set of camera poses [R|t]. Integrated Unobserved Rays: r{iu}, a union of hidden rays rq and unseen rays r{us}. Depth Map: \hat{d}, computed per ray. Color Map: \hat{C}, computed per ray. Step-by-Step Method 1. Define Sample Space for Unseen Rays: Determine the bounding box for camera translation t based on target poses: t{min} = \min(\{ti^{target}\}), \quad t{max} = \max(\{ti^{target}\}) Sample translation t uniformly within [t{min}, t{max}]. 2. Compute Mean Focus Point: Calculate the mean focus point \bar{p}f by solving a least squares problem to find the central point of the scene. 3. Sample Camera Rotation: Calculate the normalized mean over the up axes of all target poses, denoted \bar{p}u. Sample a rotation matrix R using: SR|t = \{R(\bar{p}u, \bar{p}f + \epsilon, t) \mid \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.125)\} where \epsilon is a small jitter value added to the focus point to ensure the camera roughly focuses on the scene center. 4. Generate Unseen Rays (r{us}): Form the set of sampled camera poses: SP = \{[R|t] \mid R \sim SR|t, t \sim St\} Generate rays r{us} from these poses. 5. Generate Hidden Rays (rq): Derive rays rq from the estimated blur kernel h. The kernel transforms rays to approximate the color composition process of the blur. These rays are defined as: rq \sim h(r) where r represents the main rays. These hidden rays provide supplementary information exclusively present in blurry inputs. 6. Form Integrated Unobserved Rays: Combine the two sets: r{iu} = \{rq, r{us}\} Note that r{us} remains unchanged during training, while rq changes as the blur kernel h is optimized. 7. Compute Expected Depth and Color: For each ray r \in r{iu}, compute the expected depth \hat{d} and color \hat{C}: \hat{d} = \int{tn}^{tf} \sigma(r(t))t \, dt \hat{C} = \int{tn}^{tf} \sigma(r(t))c(r(t)) \, dt where \sigma is density, c is color, and tn, tf are near and far bounds. 8. Calculate Weighted Depth Differences: For a patch of size S{ptc} \times S{ptc} centered at ray r{i,j}, compute horizontal and vertical weighted depth differences: \Delta \hat{d}x(r{i,j}) = \omega{i+1,j} (\hat{d}(r{i+1,j}) - \hat{d}(r{i,j}))^2 \Delta \hat{d}y(r{i,j}) = \omega{i,j+1} (\hat{d}(r{i,j+1}) - \hat{d}(r{i,j}))^2 The weights \omega are based on pixel-wise color difference: \omega{i+k,j+l} = \exp(-|\hat{C}(r{i,j}) - \hat{C}(r{i+k,j+l})|) This ensures smoothness is enforced where colors are similar, preserving edges. 9. Compute Loss: Sum the differences over all rays in r{iu} and all positions in the patch: \mathcal{L}{ss}\{r{iu}\} = \sum{r \in r{iu}} \sum{i,j=1}^{S{ptc}-1} (\Delta \hat{d}x(r{i,j}) + \Delta \hat{d}y(r{i,j})) Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesurfacesmoothnessloss(targetposes, blurkernel, radiancefield, patchsize=5): """ Computes the Surface Smoothness Regularization loss. Args: targetposes: List of SE(3) poses [R|t] used for training. blurkernel: The current estimated blur kernel h. radiancefield: The radiance field model (NeRF/DeRF). patchsize: Integer size of the depth patch for smoothness calculation. Returns: Scalar loss value. """ # 1. Define Sample Space tmin = min(t for, t in targetposes) tmax = max(t for, t in targetposes) # 2. Compute Mean Focus Point (Least Squares) # Placeholder for specific least squares implementation details not provided in source. # Assuming a function solveleastsquaresfocus(targetposes) exists. pf = solveleastsquaresfocus(targetposes) # 3. Compute Mean Up Axis # Assuming normalized up axes are extracted from R matrices. upaxes = [getupaxis(R) for R, in targetposes] pu = normalize(mean(upaxes)) # 4. Generate Unseen Rays (rus) unseenrays = [] numsamples = 100 # Arbitrary sample count for implementation completeness; source does not specify N. for in range(numsamples): # Sample translation t = randomuniformvector(tmin, tmax) # Sample rotation with jitter epsilon = randomnormal(0, 0.125) R = generaterotation(pu, pf + epsilon, t) pose = [R, t] # Generate ray from pose ray = generaterayfrompose(pose) unseenrays.append(ray) # 5. Generate Hidden Rays (rq) # Implementation of ray transformation via blur kernel h. # Source states rq ~ h(r). We sample main rays r and transform them. mainrays = [generaterayfrompose(p) for p in targetposes] hiddenrays = [] for r in mainrays: rq = transformraybyblurkernel(r, blurkernel) hiddenrays.append(rq) # 6. Integrated Unobserved Rays integratedrays = hiddenrays + unseenrays # 7 & 8 & 9. Compute Loss totalloss = 0.0 # Iterate over rays in batches or patches. # Source sums over r in riu and i,j in patch. # We assume a grid structure or spatial hashing to find neighbors (i+1,j) and (i,j+1). # For simplicity, we assume rays are sorted/spatially indexed. # Create a spatial map for neighbor lookup raymap = {ray.id: ray for ray in integratedrays} for ray in integratedrays: # Placeholder for patch extraction logic. # In practice, rays are projected to image plane or voxel grid. # Here we assume we can access neighbors r{i+1,j} and r{i,j+1}. neighbors = getspatialneighbors(ray, integratedrays, patchsize) if not neighbors: continue # Compute depth and color for current ray dcurr, ccurr = radiancefield.integrate(ray) # Horizontal neighbor (i+1, j) rh = neighbors.get('right') if rh: dh, ch = radiancefield.integrate(rh) weighth = exp(-abs(ccurr - ch)) diffx = weighth (dh - dcurr)2 totalloss += diffx # Vertical neighbor (i, j+1) rv = neighbors.get('down') if rv: dv, cv = radiancefield.integrate(rv) weightv = exp(-abs(ccurr - cv)) diffy = weightv (dv - dcurr)2 totalloss += diffy return totalloss Parameters Jitter Standard Deviation: 0.125 for the normal distribution \mathcal{N}(0, 0.125). Patch Size (S{ptc}): Not given in the sources. Number of Unseen Ray Samples: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Blur Kernel Convergence: Hidden rays rq depend on the blur kernel h. If h is poorly estimated, hidden rays may provide misleading smoothness constraints. Spatial Ambiguity: The method specifically addresses ambiguity in sparse views; it may be redundant or computationally wasteful in dense-view settings where geometry is well-constrained. Boundary Conditions: The summation limits i,j=1 to S{ptc}-1 imply that boundary rays in the patch do not contribute to the loss in the same way, or require padding. Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Adds overhead proportional to the number of sampled unseen and hidden rays and the patch size. Requires additional ray marching for unobserved rays. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the set of integrated unobserved rays and their associated depth/color values during the backward pass. Strengths: Stabilizes joint optimization of blur and geometry in sparse-view DeRF; alleviates spatial ambiguity by leveraging unobserved rays. Limitations: Relies on accurate estimation of the blur kernel for hidden rays; requires careful sampling of the camera pose space. When to Use: Sparse-view DeRF training where spatial ambiguity is high and blur kernel optimization is coupled with radiance field optimization. When Not to Use: Dense-view settings where geometry is well-constrained by observed rays; non-blurry scenes where hidden rays provide no additional information. Originated in the context of Deblurred Neural Radiance Fields (DeRF) from sparse views. The method was introduced in "Sparse-DeRF: Deblurred Neural Radiance Fields From Sparse View" (2025) to address the difficulty of regularizing complex joint optimization in DeRF, where standard NeRF regularization fails. It builds on the concept of using unseen rays for regularization as seen in RegNeRF [6], but extends it with blur-kernel-derived hidden rays. name: Perceptual Distillation Module
head: Perceptual Loss for Deblurred Radiance Fields
body: The Perceptual Distillation Module (PDM) is a regularization technique designed for deblurring Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) trained on sparse views. It addresses the 3D geometric inconsistency inherent in independently deblurred multi-view images by using pre-deblurred images as a perceptual prior. Unlike standard photometric losses that may reinforce geometric artifacts, PDM transfers texture information from 2D deblurred priors to the implicit 3D radiance field via feature-space matching. It is distinct from Surface Smoothness Regularization (which enforces geometric smoothness) and Reflectance and Shading Decomposition Priors (which separates intrinsic image properties) by operating on high-level perceptual features rather than pixel values or geometric derivatives. The module augments the training loss by comparing features extracted from rendered patches against features extracted from pre-deblurred versions of the input blurry images. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Blurry training images I, camera poses, the current NeRF model (MLPs for color and density), a pre-trained image deblurring network \ThetaD, and a pre-trained feature extractor E. Outputs: A scalar perceptual loss value \mathcal{L}{pd} used for backpropagation. Data Structures Patch Rays (r{pd}^{ptc}): A set of rays sampled from the training view frustum corresponding to a specific image patch. Deblurred Image Patch (\bar{C}{ptc}): A 2D image patch of size S{ptc} \times S{ptc} extracted from the pre-deblurred image \bar{I}. Rendered Color Patch (\hat{C}{ptc}): A 2D image patch rendered from the NeRF using rays r{pd}^{ptc}. This rendering is performed without the blur kernel to produce "clean" radiance. Feature Maps (\hat{\phi}{ptc}, \bar{\phi}{ptc}): Multi-channel feature tensors extracted from \hat{C}{ptc} and \bar{C}{ptc} respectively. Numbered Steps 1. Generate Pre-deblurred Images: For each blurry training image I, compute the deblurred image \bar{I} using the pre-trained deblurring network \ThetaD: \bar{I} = \ThetaD(I) \quad 2. Sample Patch Rays: On the training views, sample a set of rays r{pd}^{ptc} that correspond to a square patch of size S{ptc} \times S{ptc} in the image plane. 3. Render Clean Patch: Render the color patch \hat{C}{ptc} from the sampled rays r{pd}^{ptc} using the NeRF MLPs. Crucially, this rendering does not apply the blur kernel, producing a "patch radiance". 4. Extract Features: Pass both the rendered patch \hat{C}{ptc} and the corresponding deblurred image patch \bar{C}{ptc} (extracted from \bar{I}) through the shared pre-trained feature extractor E: \hat{\phi}{ptc} = E(\hat{C}{ptc}) \quad \bar{\phi}{ptc} = E(\bar{C}{ptc}) \quad 5. Compute Perceptual Loss: Calculate the L2 norm between the extracted feature maps: \mathcal{L}{pd} = ||\hat{\phi}{ptc} - \bar{\phi}{ptc}||2^2 \quad Parameters Patch Size (S{ptc}): The dimension of the square patch. The source specifies S{ptc}=8 for one dimension and implies a total area or second dimension of 64, resulting in 8 \times 8 patches. Perceptual Loss Weight (\lambda{pd}): The weight applied to \mathcal{L}{pd} in the total loss function. Set to 0.01. Deblurring Network (\ThetaD): MPRNet. Feature Extractor (E): VGG19. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def perceptualdistillationloss( blurryimage: Tensor, rays: List[Ray], nerfmodel: NeRFModel, deblurringnet: Module, featureextractor: Module, patchsize: int = 8, lambdapd: float = 0.01) -> Tensor: """ Computes the Perceptual Distillation Loss. Args: blurryimage: Input blurry image tensor (H, W, 3). rays: List of Ray objects corresponding to the patch in the image. nerfmodel: The NeRF MLPs (color and density). deblurringnet: Pre-trained MPRNet for deblurring. featureextractor: Pre-trained VGG19 for feature extraction. patchsize: Size of the square patch (Sptc). lambdapd: Weight for the perceptual loss. Returns: Scalar tensor representing the weighted perceptual loss. """ # Step 1: Generate deblurred image using pre-trained network # Ibar = ThetaD(I) deblurredimage = deblurringnet(blurryimage) # Step 2 & 3: Render clean patch from NeRF (without blur kernel) # Chatptc is rendered from rays rpdptc # Note: rays must be sampled to correspond to an Sptc x Sptc region # in the blurryimage. The NeRF forward pass does not apply blur. renderedpatch = nerfmodel.render(rays) # Returns color tensor (Sptc, Sptc, 3) # Step 2 (continued): Extract corresponding patch from deblurred image # Cbarptc is the patch from Ibar at the same spatial location # Assuming rays provide spatial coordinates or indices to locate the patch deblurredpatch = extractpatch(deblurredimage, rays, patchsize) # Step 4: Extract features using shared pre-trained extractor (VGG19) # phihatptc = E(Chatptc) # phibarptc = E(Cbarptc) # VGG19 typically expects normalized inputs and returns intermediate layer features renderedfeatures = featureextractor(renderedpatch) deblurredfeatures = featureextractor(deblurredpatch) # Step 5: Compute L2 loss between features # Lpd = ||phihatptc - phibarptc||2^2 perceptualloss = torch.sum((renderedfeatures - deblurredfeatures) 2) # Return weighted loss return lambdapd perceptualloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls Geometric Inconsistency: The method relies on the assumption that the 2D deblurred image \bar{I} contains valid texture information consistent with the 3D scene. If \ThetaD hallucinates textures that do not exist in the 3D geometry, the NeRF may learn inconsistent geometry. Patch Alignment: The rays r{pd}^{ptc} must precisely correspond to the spatial location of \bar{C}{ptc} in \bar{I}. Misalignment leads to incorrect feature matching. Feature Normalization: VGG19 requires specific input normalization (mean/std). Failure to normalize \hat{C}{ptc} and \bar{C}{ptc} identically will result in meaningless feature differences. Time Complexity: Adds overhead proportional to the number of patch rays sampled per iteration. Requires two forward passes through \ThetaD (once per image, cached or pre-computed) and two forward passes through E per patch. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the pre-deblurred images \bar{I} or computing them on the fly. The feature extractor E (VGG19) is large, but only features for small patches are computed. Strengths: Effectively transfers high-frequency texture details from 2D priors to 3D fields, mitigating the blurriness and artifacts common in sparse-view deblurring. Limitations: Depends heavily on the quality of the pre-trained deblurring network \ThetaD and the feature extractor E. If the deblurring network fails on a specific image, the prior becomes misleading. When to use: Sparse-view deblurring scenarios where geometric consistency is compromised by independent 2D deblurring. When not to use: Dense-view settings where photometric loss alone is sufficient, or when computational budget is extremely limited due to the extra network evaluations. The Perceptual Distillation Module was introduced in the context of Sparse-DeRF (Deblurred Neural Radiance Fields From Sparse View). It addresses the problem of camera motion blur in sparse view settings, where traditional NeRF optimization fails to recover sharp details due to insufficient angular coverage and blur. The method is described as a "first attempt" at utilizing pre-deblurred images as an additional prior in deblurring radiance fields. It builds upon the observation that independently deblurred multi-view images suffer from 3D geometric inconsistency, which can be alleviated by distilling texture information from these 2D priors into the 3D field. The implementation uses MPRNet for deblurring and VGG19 for feature extraction, standard choices in perceptual loss literature. name: Warm-start Encoding
head: Temporal Coherency Encoding, Temporal warm-start, Temporally-Coherent Warm-Start Encoder, Warm-start Encoder
body: Warm-start encoding accelerates the training of neural volume representations for animated sparse volumes by initializing the network weights for each frame with the converged weights from the previous frame. It solves the problem of flickering artifacts caused by weight discontinuities in high-frequency details (e.g., thin smoke layers) when using naive cold-start training, while simultaneously reducing encoding time by a factor of 1.5–2.5 compared to independent frame training. Unlike standard cold-start methods, it leverages temporal coherency to preserve smooth transitions across frames. Inputs: A sequence of animated sparse volumes V1, V2, \dots, VN; a target learning rate \eta{\text{target}}; a neural network architecture. Outputs: A sequence of trained neural networks W1, W2, \dots, WN, where Wi encodes volume Vi. Data Structures: W{\text{prev}}: The converged network weights from the previous frame. For the first frame, W{\text{prev}} is initialized using standard random initialization. \eta{\text{current}}: The active learning rate for the current training phase. L1: The final loss of the first frame, used as a stopping threshold for subsequent frames. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize: Set W{\text{prev}} \leftarrow \text{RandomInit}(). Set \eta{\text{current}} \leftarrow \eta{\text{target}}. 2. Iterate Frames: For each frame i from 1 to N: a. Warm-Start Initialization: Initialize the current network weights W{\text{curr}} with W{\text{prev}}. b. First Frame Special Handling: If i == 1: i. Train W{\text{curr}} on V1 using learning rate \eta{\text{target}} until convergence, recording the final loss as L1. ii. Save W1 \leftarrow W{\text{curr}}. iii. Re-process frame 1: Set \eta{\text{fine}} \leftarrow \eta{\text{target}} / 100 (or smaller). Train W1 on V1 using \eta{\text{fine}} until convergence. iv. Update \eta{\text{current}} \leftarrow \eta{\text{fine}}. c. Subsequent Frames: If i > 1: i. Train W{\text{curr}} on Vi using \eta{\text{current}} for a single pass, stopping training iterations when the loss becomes lower than L1. ii. Save Wi \leftarrow W{\text{curr}}. d. Update Previous: Set W{\text{prev}} \leftarrow Wi. 3. Domain Decomposition Exception: If a new domain is added mid-sequence (e.g., via domain decomposition), repeat the "First Frame Special Handling" process for that new domain using \eta{\text{target}} followed by \eta{\text{fine}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def warmstartencode(volumes, targetlr, networkclass): prevweights = None currentlr = targetlr firstframefinalloss = None savednetworks = [] for i, volume in enumerate(volumes): # 1. Initialize network with previous frame's weights if prevweights is None: net = networkclass() net.weights = standardrandominit() # else: net = networkclass() net.weights = prevweights.copy() if i == 0: # 2. First frame: Train with target LR until convergence net.train(volume, lr=targetlr) # Standard training loop firstframefinalloss = net.getloss() # 3. First frame: Re-process with smaller LR to fix flickering finelr = targetlr / 100.0 net.train(volume, lr=finelr) # Standard training loop currentlr = finelr savednetworks.append(net) else: # 4. Subsequent frames: Train once with reduced LR # Stop when loss is lower than first frame's final loss net.train(volume, lr=currentlr, stoploss=firstframefinalloss) savednetworks.append(net) prevweights = net.getweights() return savednetworks Parameters: \eta{\text{target}}: Target learning rate for initial convergence. Typical value: Not given in the sources. \eta{\text{fine}}: Reduced learning rate for re-processing. Value: Up to 100 times smaller than \eta{\text{target}}. Stop Condition: Training iterations stop when loss becomes lower than the first frame's final loss. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Flickering: Naive cold-start encoding with a fixed learning rate causes discontinuities in network weights across frames, leading to flickering, especially in high-frequency details like thin smoke layers. Domain Decomposition: If new domains are added mid-sequence, the warm-start logic must be reset for that domain, re-running the target LR then fine LR process. It sets apart from warm-start by focusing on per-step optimization dynamics rather than frame-to-frame weight coupling. Choose it when training stability requires adaptive scaling. General strategies for adjusting learning rates over time. It sets apart from warm-start by applying global schedules rather than sequence-dependent initialization. Choose it for standard curriculum or decay-based training. Optimizes memory and compute by using lower-precision data types. It sets apart from warm-start by targeting hardware efficiency rather than temporal coherence. Choose it for memory-constrained or high-throughput training. An adaptive optimizer that adjusts step sizes per parameter. It sets apart from warm-start by focusing on gradient normalization rather than initialization state. Choose it for non-convex optimization with sparse gradients. Defines the overall timeline and phase transitions of training. It sets apart from warm-start by managing macro-level phases rather than micro-level weight transfers. Choose it for complex multi-stage training pipelines. Specifies loss functions for high-fidelity reconstruction. It sets apart from warm-start by defining the optimization target rather than the initialization strategy. Choose it when detail preservation is the primary goal. A collection of tailored settings for specific neural volume methods. It sets apart from warm-start by being a category header rather than a specific temporal technique. Choose it for method-specific tuning. Techniques to constrain the solution space and prevent overfitting. It sets apart from warm-start by applying explicit penalties rather than implicit temporal continuity. Choose it when model complexity needs control. A view-based neural rendering method using pixel-aligned implicit functions. It sets apart from warm-start by operating on image-space features rather than volume-space weights. Choose it for novel view synthesis from sparse images. Time Complexity: Accelerates encoding by a factor of 1.5–2.5 compared to cold-start training. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the network weights for each frame during sequential processing. Measured Performance: Tested on NVIDIA RTX A40 GPUs and AMD EPYC 7502 CPU. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Ensures temporal coherence; reduces flickering in high-frequency details; speeds up training. Limitations: Sequential dependency (frame i depends on i-1); requires careful LR tuning for the fine step. When to Use: Animated sparse volumes with high-frequency details (e.g., smoke, fire) where temporal coherence is critical. When Not to Use: Static volumes or sequences with no temporal coherence. Introduced in the NeuralVDB paper for encoding time-sequences of animated sparse volumes. It is similar to fine-tuning in transfer learning [Zhou et al. 2017], adapting to a new target without drifting too much from the old one. The method leverages the temporal coherency of input volumes to preserve coherency in output volumes.
