name: Regularization and Loss Functions
body: Regularization and Loss Functions define the objective landscape for optimizing Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) during differentiable volume rendering. While the parent NeRF Training Loop handles sampling strategies to balance training data, this family addresses the ill-posed nature of the inverse rendering problem by enforcing geometric plausibility, structural coherence, and semantic consistency beyond simple pixel-wise photometric reconstruction. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Training Ray Marching and Integration by focusing on the what to optimize (the loss terms and regularizers) rather than the how of the integration process. All methods in this family operate within the differentiable volume rendering framework where gradients flow from the loss \mathcal{L} back through the rendered color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) and depth \hat{\mathbf{D}}(\mathbf{r}) to the network parameters \theta (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}) [S1, 7475-geometric-baseline-regularization.md, 8582-regnerf.md]. The rendering process computes expected color and depth along rays r(t) = o + td using sample points ti with weights wi = T(ti)\rho(ti), where \rho(ti) = 1 - \exp(-\sigma(\mathbf{r}(ti))(t{i+1} - ti)) and T(ti) = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \rho(tj)). The rendering weights wi serve as the probability distribution of absorption along the ray, often denoted as h(t) = T(t)\sigma(t), which is used in distributional geometric losses. The rendered depth is typically the expected distance along the ray: \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N wi ti where wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) are the rendering weights, ti are sample depths, and Ti is the accumulated transmittance. Gradients are backpropagated through the differentiable volume rendering process to update the density and color field parameters. Diffusion-regularized NeRF improves geometric plausibility in limited-view scenarios by incorporating a Denoising Diffusion Model (DDM) as a learned prior. Unlike sibling methods that rely on hand-crafted geometric constraints, this method directly regularizes the density and color fields by backpropagating the score function of RGBD patches learned from synthetic data. It addresses the under-constrained nature of NeRFs, which often produce artifacts like "floaters" when trained on few views. RegNeRF synthesizes novel views from sparse input images by applying depth smoothness and color priors to constrain unobserved regions. It differs from sibling methods like DiffNeRF by using finite-difference approximations on patch-based dataloaders to compute depth gradients. Unlike Depth and Geometry Supervision which often requires explicit depth labels, RegNeRF employs generative priors (Normalizing Flows) and geometric smoothness constraints without requiring pretraining on the target dataset. This family incorporates geometric constraints—typically derived from sparse 3D points, monocular depth priors, or multi-view consistency—to resolve the shape-radiance ambiguity inherent in NeRFs. Unlike pure photometric methods, these methods enforce that the rendered depth distribution aligns with external geometric signals, accelerating convergence in sparse-view settings and suppressing artifacts such as "floaters" or translucent geometry in empty space. The family is distinguished by its direct manipulation of the ray termination distribution h(t) or the expected depth \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) via explicit loss terms, rather than relying on implicit structural priors or diffusion models. Multi-view SDS is a plug-and-play regularization method that addresses the "Janus problem" (inconsistent facial features or object orientations) inherent in standard Single-view Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) by enforcing consistency across multiple viewpoints simultaneously. Unlike standard SDS which optimizes one view at a time, this method stitches rendered images from multiple sampled views into a single composite image to compute gradients under multi-view normal map conditions, thereby improving the geometric coherence of the generated 3D asset. This family comprises specific objective functions used to optimize the parameters of a neural radiance field during differentiable volume rendering. While the parent family defines the general mechanism of gradient flow through the rendering integral, these specific formulations address distinct training goals: photometric fidelity (Final Loss Function), geometric plausibility via distortion minimization (NeRF-XL Multi-GPU Distortion Loss), representation efficiency (Rate-Distortion Optimization Loss), and structural or semantic constraints (Geometric and Structural Regularization). They are distinguished from sibling methods like Diffusion-regularized NeRF by their direct reliance on rendered pixel/depth statistics or explicit geometric priors rather than external generative priors. S3IM (Stochastic Structural SIMilarity) is a multiplex loss function for neural fields that captures non-local structural similarity by processing multiple data points (pixels/rays) as a whole set, rather than individually. It addresses the limitation of point-wise losses (like MSE) which fail to use collective supervision of distant pixels. Unlike conventional MSE loss which is computed pixel-wisely, S3IM cannot be expressed as the sum of any other loss computed over individual pixels from the batch. It diverges from conventional point-to-point loss functions by analyzing various data points collectively to obtain non-local structural details. Volumetric Supervision is a training strategy that leverages high-quality volumetric reconstructions from conventional tomography to supervise neural network training at intermediate time steps where only sparse projection data is available. It solves the problem of temporal interpolation in dynamic tomography by using dense ground-truth volumes at the start and end of an experiment to regularize the learning of the canonical model and deformation field. Unlike sibling methods that primarily enforce geometric consistency via depth or gradient losses, this method directly minimizes the discrepancy between the predicted 3D volume and a physically reconstructed 3D volume. Style Loss is a regularization term used in differentiable volume rendering to improve color and style coherence between generated objects (or rendered scenes) and a given reference image. It operates by minimizing the distance between feature representations of the rendered output and the reference in a pre-trained VGG feature space. Unlike Perceptual Loss, which minimizes the distance to a fixed reference feature to preserve geometric and semantic integrity, Style Loss focuses on texture statistics and local contextual matching to enforce stylistic similarity. It is distinct from(10895-s3im-stochastic-structural-similarity.md) and Semantic Consistency Loss by targeting low-level texture and color distribution rather than structural similarity or high-level semantic alignment. Confidence-Based Loss Calibration dynamically weights the optimization of NeRF parameters and camera poses using estimated reliability metrics, addressing the bas-relief ambiguity and registration failures in joint optimization. It sets itself apart from static regularization methods by using pose confidence to weight NeRF gradients and ray confidence to weight pose gradients, effectively decoupling error sources during training. Semantic Consistency Loss (SCL) is a regularization term that enforces semantic alignment between rendered images and text prompts or between unseen views by minimizing the distance between their embeddings in the CLIP latent space. Unlike standard photometric losses that optimize for pixel-wise intensity matching, SCL optimizes for high-level semantic consistency, making it robust to pixel-wise misalignment and enabling text-guided editing or zero-shot segmentation in radiance fields. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Diffusion-regularized NeRF by leveraging pre-trained vision-language models for global structure guidance rather than generative priors, and from RegNeRF by focusing on semantic rather than geometric or photometric constraints. Applies a depth bidirectional inconsistency prior in the background MLP to restore occlusion-free backgrounds via depth distance supervision. Pitfall: When the occluding object is a light-loss transparent glass body, reflection artifact noise pollution prevents generalization. Predict an additional output from the cache c{\text{irradiance}}(\mathbf{x}, \omegao) and supervise it to match irradiance from the physically-based model (computed by setting BRDF to perfectly Lambertian with a(\mathbf{x}) = 1). Formula: Appearance loss: Lp = \frac{1}{2|R|} \sum{r \in R} \| \hat{C}(r) - C(r) \|^2, where R are sampled rays in a training batch, C(r) is ground truth RGB, and \hat{C}(r) is predicted RGB. Query models to predict color via volume rendering. 3. Render image from random camera pose. 4. Encode rendered and original images with CLIP. 5. Compute L{hpg} and L{hsg}. 6. Optimize \Thetac, \Thetaf to minimize sum. Formula: \min{\Thetac, \Thetaf} (L{hpg} + \lambda L{hsg}), optimizing coarse and fine model parameters using combined photometric and semantic losses. The need for regularization in NeRFs arose from the observation that standard photometric reconstruction alone leads to ambiguous solutions, particularly in sparse-view settings, resulting in "floaters" (semi-transparent artifacts in empty space) and poor generalization. Early methods like RegNeRF introduced geometric smoothness and generative color priors to constrain unobserved regions. Subsequent work expanded this to include diffusion-based priors for better geometric plausibility, semantic consistency via CLIP for text-guided editing, and multi-view consistency to solve the Janus problem in 3D generation. The field has evolved from simple depth smoothness constraints to complex, multi-modal regularization strategies involving diffusion models, vision-language models, and physically-based rendering constraints. name: RegNeRF
head: Regularized NeRF
body: RegNeRF is a method for synthesizing novel views from sparse input images by applying depth smoothness and color priors to constrain the unobserved regions of the scene. It differs from sibling methods like DiffNeRF, which relies on automatic differentiation of the ray-based representation for gradient estimation, by using finite-difference approximations on patch-based dataloaders to compute depth gradients. Unlike Depth and Geometry Supervision which often requires explicit depth labels, RegNeRF employs generative priors (Normalizing Flows) and geometric smoothness constraints without requiring pretraining on the target dataset. RegNeRF operates within the differentiable volume rendering framework. It uses Mip-NeRF [48] as the backbone neural radiance field, which renders anti-aliased cones instead of rays to handle frequency aliasing. The method introduces three key components: sampled space annealing, depth smoothness regularization, and color regularization via Normalizing Flows. Inputs: A sparse set of N input images with known camera poses. Outputs: A trained NeRF model (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} fields) capable of rendering novel views. Patches: The method operates on image patches of size S{patch} \times S{patch} rather than single pixels or full images. A patch Pr is centered at pixel r. Normalizing Flow Model: A pre-trained bijection \phi mapping patches to \mathbb{R}^d where d = S{patch} \cdot S{patch} \cdot 3, trained on a large unposed dataset (e.g., JFT-300M). 1. Sampled Space Annealing: At the start of training, to prevent divergent NeRF modes with high density at the ray origin, the range of sample points along each ray is limited to a small volume defined by the bounding box of all input images. This volume is gradually extended to cover the full scene as training progresses. 2. Random View Sampling: For each training step, randomly sample unobserved viewpoints (camera poses) that are not in the input set. Render patches from these viewpoints using the current NeRF model. 3. Depth Smoothness Loss (\mathcal{L}{ds}): Compute the expected depth \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) for rays passing through the rendered patches. The smoothness loss encourages the world geometry to be piecewise smooth by penalizing depth differences between adjacent pixels in the patch: \mathcal{L}{ds} = \sum{i,j} \sum{\mathbf{r}} \left( (d(\mathbf{r}{i,j}) - d(\mathbf{r}{i+1,j}))^2 + (d(\mathbf{r}{i,j}) - d(\mathbf{r}{i,j+1}))^2 \right) where d(\mathbf{r}{i,j}) is the expected depth of the ray through pixel (i,j) of a patch of size S{patch} from a randomly sampled unobserved viewpoint. 4. Color Regularization Loss (\mathcal{L}{NLL}): Estimate the likelihood of the rendered color patches using a Normalizing Flow model. The flow model \phi maps the predicted RGB patch P{\mathbf{r}} (centered at \mathbf{r}) to a latent space where the distribution is assumed to be Gaussian pz. The loss is the negative log-likelihood: \mathcal{L}{NLL} = - \sum{\mathbf{r}} \log pz(\phi(P{\mathbf{r}})) where pz is a Gaussian distribution. 5. Optimization: Minimize the total loss (typically combining \mathcal{L}{ds}, \mathcal{L}{NLL}, and the standard photometric reconstruction loss on input views) with respect to the NeRF parameters using gradient descent. """ nerf = MipNeRF() # Backbone model optimizer = Adam(nerf.parameters()) # Annealing parameters minvolume = getboundingbox(inputimages) maxvolume = getscenebounds() for epoch in range(numepochs): # 1. Sampled Space Annealing # Gradually expand sample range from minvolume to maxvolume currentsamplerange = lerp(minvolume, maxvolume, epoch / numepochs) for batch in dataloader(inputimages, inputposes): optimizer.zerograd() # 2. Render input views (standard photometric loss) renderedcolorsinput = rendernerf(nerf, batch.poses, currentsamplerange) lossrecon = mseloss(renderedcolorsinput, batch.images) # 3. Sample random unobserved viewpoints randomposes = samplerandomposes(numviews=1) # 4. Render patches from unobserved views # Render at patch resolution to extract patches renderedcolorsrandom = rendernerf(nerf, randomposes, currentsamplerange) patches = extractpatches(renderedcolorsrandom, size=Spatch) depthsrandom = renderdepth(nerf, randomposes, currentsamplerange) depthpatches = extractpatches(depthsrandom, size=Spatch) # 5. Compute Depth Smoothness Loss lossds = 0 for patchdepth in depthpatches: # Compute differences between adjacent pixels in the patch diffx = patchdepth[:, 1:,:] - patchdepth[:,:-1,:] diffy = patchdepth[:,:, 1:] - patchdepth[:,:,:-1] lossds += mseloss(diffx, 0) + mseloss(diffy, 0) # 6. Compute Color Regularization Loss lossnll = 0 for patchcolor in patches: # Map patch to latent space using Normalizing Flow latent = flowmodel.encode(patchcolor) # Compute negative log-likelihood under Gaussian prior lossnll += -loglikelihoodgaussian(latent) # 7. Total Loss and Update totalloss = lossrecon + lambdads lossds + lambdanll lossnll totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() S{patch}: Patch size. Not given in the sources. \lambda{ds}: Weight for depth smoothness loss. Not given in the sources. \lambda{NLL}: Weight for color regularization loss. Not given in the sources. Backbone: Mip-NeRF. Divergent Modes: Without sampled space annealing, the NeRF may converge to modes with high density at the ray origin, failing to reconstruct the scene geometry. Sparse Views: The method is specifically designed for sparse input views; performance on dense views may be suboptimal compared to standard NeRF due to the overhead of regularization. Flow Model Dependency: The color regularization relies on a pre-trained Normalizing Flow model. If the flow model is not well-calibrated for the domain, the regularization may introduce artifacts. DiffNeRF is a regularization framework that uses differential geometry to improve robustness in few-shot scenarios by modifying the NeRF to represent continuous, infinitely differentiable functions. Unlike RegNeRF, which approximates gradients via finite differences on patch-based dataloaders, DiffNeRF uses automatic differentiation to compute depth gradients directly from the ray-based NeRF representation, allowing regularization of unseen views without specialized dataloader modifications. SS-NeRF employs an encoding function and two position decoding functions (one direction-dependent, one direction-independent) represented by MLPs to produce various scene properties. It trains the network to produce color, semantic labels, surface normal, shading, keypoints, and edges. It uses a combination of losses: MSE for color and surface normals; MAE for shading, keypoints and edges; and cross-entropy for semantic labels. Time Complexity: Training time is increased due to the additional loss computations (depth smoothness and flow likelihood) and the need to render from random unobserved viewpoints at each step. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the pre-trained Normalizing Flow model and its parameters, in addition to the NeRF model. Performance: RegNeRF outperforms models such as PixelNeRF, SRF, and MVSNeRF under sparse view conditions on DTU and LLFF datasets. It achieves comparable performance to models that require pretraining on DTU and fine-tuning per scene, without needing such pretraining. Strengths: Does not require pretraining on the target dataset; effective for sparse view synthesis; improves geometric smoothness and color consistency in unobserved regions. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the pre-trained Normalizing Flow model; may not generalize well to domains significantly different from the flow model's training data. RegNeRF was proposed in December 2021. It aimed to solve the problem of NeRF training with sparse input views by employing additional depth and color regularization, without requiring pretraining. It was tested on DTU and LLFF datasets. The method builds on the Mip-NeRF backbone [48]. name: DiffNeRF
head: RegNeRF differential formalization, Regularization of NeRFs using differential geometry
body:
DiffNeRF is a regularization framework for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that uses differential geometry to improve robustness when training with sparse or inconsistent data. It addresses MLP overfitting and unrealistic interpolation in few-shot scenarios by modifying the NeRF to represent continuous, infinitely differentiable functions. Unlike its sibling RegNeRF, which approximates gradients via finite differences on patch-based dataloaders, DiffNeRF uses automatic differentiation to compute depth gradients directly from the ray-based NeRF representation, allowing regularization of unseen views without specialized dataloader modifications. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A NeRF MLP F mapping spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and viewing direction \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^3 to color \mathbf{c} \in [0, 1]^3 and volume density \sigma \in 0, \infty), along with training images and camera parameters. Output: A regularized NeRF model and rendered images/depth maps. Data Structures: NeRF MLP: Uses Softplus activation instead of ReLU to ensure the function is continuous and infinitely differentiable. Ray Discretization: Each ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{v} is discretized into N 3D points \{\mathbf{x}i\}{i=1}^N, where \mathbf{x}i = \mathbf{o} + ti \mathbf{v} and ti are sampled between minimum and maximum depth. Transmittance: Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). Parameters: Regularization Weight (\lambda): 2 	imes 10^{-4} for both LLFF and DTU datasets. [Clipping Value (g{max}): 20 for LLFF; 5 for DTU. This parameter is used in a differentiable clipping function to preserve sharp edges that would otherwise be over-smoothed. Steps: 1. Modify Activation: Replace ReLU in the NeRF MLP with Softplus to enable direct training using gradients or higher-order operators. 2. Ray Sampling: For each training pixel, cast a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{v} and sample N points \mathbf{x}i along it. 3. Forward Pass: Query the MLP to obtain \sigmai and \mathbf{c}i for each point, compute transmittance Ti, and render the color \mathbf{c}(r) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i. 4. Depth Estimation: Compute the expected depth d(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{v}) for the ray. 5. Orthographic Assumption: Assume a local orthonormal basis (\mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}) of the image plane where the viewing direction \mathbf{v} is fixed and the origin shifts as \mathbf{C}(x, y) = x\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j}. 6. Gradient Computation: Compute the gradient of the depth with respect to the ray origin 
abla{\mathbf{o}} d(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{v}) using automatic differentiation. 7. Regularization Loss: Compute the depth regularization loss using the simplified form derived from the orthographic assumption. Since (\mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf{v}) is an orthonormal basis, the squared norm of the image-space gradient equals \|
abla{\mathbf{o}} d(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{v})\|^2 - \langle 
abla{\mathbf{o}} d(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{v}), \mathbf{v} angle^2. L{depth} = \sum{(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{v})} 	ext{clip}\left( \|
abla{\mathbf{o}} d(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{v})\|^2 - \langle 
abla{\mathbf{o}} d(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{v}), \mathbf{v} angle^2, g{max} ight) The sum is over the rays sampled for the current batch. This loss is applied to training views and can be applied to unseen views, though regularizing unseen views without data attachment may encourage "floaters". 8. Optimization: Minimize the total loss (including photometric loss and L{depth}) using gradient descent. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def softplus(x): return F.softplus(x) def computedepthandgrad(o, v, nerfmodel, samplet): """ Computes depth and its gradient w.r.t origin o using autograd. o: (batch, 3) ray origins v: (batch, 3) ray directions samplet: (batch, N) sampled depths """ o.requiresgrad(True) # Discretize ray x = o.unsqueeze(1) + samplet.unsqueeze(2) v.unsqueeze(1) # (batch, N, 3) # Query NeRF sigma, c = nerfmodel(x, v) # MLP forward pass returning sigma and color # Compute alpha delta = samplet[:, 1:] - samplet[:,:-1] delta = torch.cat([delta, delta[:, -1:]], dim=1) # Standard interval calculation for NeRF sampling alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma delta) # Compute transmittance T = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha, dim=1) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[:,:1]), T[:,:-1]], dim=1) # Compute rendered color and depth weights = T alpha.unsqueeze(2) # (batch, N, 3) renderedcolor = torch.sum(weights c, dim=1) rendereddepth = torch.sum(weights.squeeze(2) samplet, dim=1) # Compute gradient of depth w.r.t origin grado = torch.autograd.grad( rendereddepth.sum(), o, creategraph=True, retaingraph=True)[0] # (batch, 3) return renderedcolor, rendereddepth, grado def diffnerfdepthloss(o, v, grado, gmax): """ Computes the simplified depth regularization loss. """ # Norm squared of gradient w.r.t origin gradnormsq = torch.sum(grado 2, dim=1) # Projection onto viewing direction projv = torch.sum(grado v, dim=1) # Image-space gradient norm squared (orthographic approximation) # ||grado||^2 - <grado, v>^2 imggradnormsq = gradnormsq - projv 2 # Differentiable clipping loss = torch.clamp(imggradnormsq, max=gmax) return loss.mean() def trainstep(nerfmodel, o, v, gtcolor, samplet, lambdareg, gmax): # Forward pass predcolor, preddepth, grado = computedepthandgrad(o, v, nerfmodel, samplet) # Photometric loss photometricloss = F.mseloss(predcolor, gtcolor) # Regularization loss regloss = diffnerfdepthloss(o, v, grado, gmax) totalloss = photometricloss + lambdareg regloss # Backward pass totalloss.backward() return totalloss.item() The parent method that uses patch-based finite differences for depth regularization. DiffNeRF is a differential formalization of RegNeRF. Choose RegNeRF when patch-based sampling is acceptable and computational overhead must be minimized. See RegNeRF. An extension of DiffNeRF that regularizes Gaussian or mean curvatures using higher-order operators. Choose this variant when surface smoothness and curvature regularity are prioritized over raw rendering speed. See DiffNeRF. Time Complexity: DiffNeRF depth regularization is approximately 16% slower than RegNeRF on an NVIDIA V100 16GB GPU, with ~5000 rays/s vs ~6000 rays/s for RegNeRF (without appearance regularization). Normals regularization is much slower at ~1100 rays/s. Strengths: Improves PSNR of reconstructed unseen views by 1dB compared to equivalent RegNeRF and outperforms RegNeRF with appearance regularization by almost 0.5dB on LLFF. Produces smoother depth maps and better separates objects from background. Does not require patch-based dataloaders or sampling additional rays from unseen views. Limitations: Regularizing unseen views without data attachment encourages the creation of "floaters" (groups of points with non-zero density disjoint from the scene), particularly in textureless background regions or areas observed by a single camera. Computationally slower than finite-difference methods. When to use: When training NeRFs with sparse data (e.g., few views) and needing robust geometry estimation without modifying dataloaders for patch sampling. When not to use: When computational speed is critical and the slight performance drop is unacceptable, or when the scene has large textureless background regions where floaters are a significant issue. DiffNeRF was introduced by Thibaud Ehret et al. in the paper "Regularization of NeRFs using differential geometry" (arXiv:2206.14938, 2022). It builds on the observation that NeRFs can overfit with insufficient data, leading to poor geometry estimates. The method formalizes the depth regularization proposed in RegNeRF [23] using differential geometry, replacing finite differences with automatic differentiation. It was demonstrated on the LLFF and DTU datasets, showing improved performance in few-shot settings (e.g., 3 input views). name: Depth and Geometry Supervision
head: Geometric Regularization, Depth Priors
body: Depth and Geometry Supervision refers to a family of regularization techniques in differentiable volume rendering that incorporate geometric constraints—typically derived from sparse 3D points, monocular depth priors, or multi-view consistency—to resolve the shape-radiance ambiguity inherent in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs). Unlike pure photometric methods that rely solely on RGB reconstruction, these methods enforce that the rendered depth distribution aligns with external geometric signals, accelerating convergence in sparse-view settings and suppressing artifacts such as "floaters" or translucent geometry in empty space. The family is distinguished by its direct manipulation of the ray termination distribution h(t) or the expected depth \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) via explicit loss terms, rather than relying on implicit structural priors or diffusion models. All methods in this family operate within the differentiable volume rendering framework where gradients flow from the loss \mathcal{L} back through the rendered color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) and depth \hat{\mathbf{D}}(\mathbf{r}) to the network parameters \theta (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}) [S1, 7475-geometric-baseline-regularization.md, 8582-regnerf.md]. The rendering process computes expected color and depth along rays r(t) = o + td using sample points ti with weights wi = T(ti)\rho(ti), where \rho(ti) = 1 - \exp(-\sigma(\mathbf{r}(ti))(t{i+1} - ti)) and T(ti) = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \rho(tj)). The rendering weights wi serve as the probability distribution of absorption along the ray, often denoted as h(t) = T(t)\sigma(t), which is used in distributional geometric losses. The rendered depth is typically the expected distance along the ray: \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N wi ti where wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) are the rendering weights, ti are sample depths, and Ti is the accumulated transmittance. Gradients are backpropagated through the differentiable volume rendering process to update the density and color field parameters. Geometric Baseline Regularization is a composite loss function designed to prevent degenerate solutions in NeRF optimization, particularly in few-view settings where the network might collapse to copying training images [7475-geometric-baseline-regularization.md]. It serves as a strong baseline by combining photometric reconstruction with geometric priors that enforce compact depth distributions, full absorption, and multi-view consistency [7475-geometric-baseline-regularization.md]. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on external depth supervision or complex structural constraints, this method derives regularization directly from the probabilistic interpretation of the volume rendering weights [7475-geometric-baseline-regularization.md]. Guided Optimization of NeRF mitigates shape-radiance ambiguity in indoor scenes by constraining the sampling range of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) using adapted monocular depth priors [7496-guided-optimization-of-nerf.md]. Unlike standard NeRF, which samples uniformly between near and far bounds derived from sparse reconstruction, this method calculates adaptive bounds based on multi-view consistency errors of the depth priors, ensuring samples concentrate around plausible geometry even in textureless regions [7496-guided-optimization-of-nerf.md]. It sets itself apart from Depth and Geometry Supervision methods that apply explicit geometric losses by instead guiding the sampling distribution itself, thereby preventing the network from exploring degenerate geometric solutions that still fit the RGB data [7496-guided-optimization-of-nerf.md]. Depth-Supervised NeRF (DS-NeRF) is a training procedure for Neural Radiance Fields that incorporates sparse 3D depth supervision from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point clouds to accelerate convergence and improve reconstruction quality with fewer input views [8687-depth-supervised-nerf.md]. Unlike methods relying on category-specific priors or dense multi-view stereo (MVS) initialization, DS-NeRF treats the sparse keypoints generated during standard SfM preprocessing as "free" geometric constraints, enforcing that the rendered ray termination distribution aligns with these surface priors [8687-depth-supervised-nerf.md]. This approach reduces overfitting in sparse-view settings and typically achieves target quality in 2–3× fewer training iterations than standard NeRF [8687-depth-supervised-nerf.md]. Robust Depth Loss is a geometry supervision function designed to mitigate the degradation of extrapolation performance caused by inaccurate or noisy pseudo-depth maps in differentiable volume rendering [9368-robust-depth-loss.md]. It addresses the problem where standard L2 losses are overly sensitive to outliers, forcing the neural radiance field (NeRF) to fit erroneous geometry [9368-robust-depth-loss.md]. By using a loss function that is less sensitive to large errors than L2, it encourages the network to terminate rays near the pseudo-depth while retaining freedom to ignore inaccurate geometry when the error is very large or very small [9368-robust-depth-loss.md]. It is distinct from Geometric Baseline Regularization which focuses on baseline consistency, and Depth-Supervised NeRF which typically uses standard L1/L2 losses without this specific robust formulation. Depth Structural Consistency Regularization (RDSC) is a geometric regularization technique applied during Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) training to enforce continuity constraints on rendered depth maps, leveraging external depth priors such as those from DepthAnythingV2 [9371-depth-structural-consistency-regularization.md]. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Patch-Based Depth Regularization by explicitly modeling structural consistency through k-nearest neighbor (KNN) relationships in depth space rather than spatial proximity alone, ensuring that neighboring pixels in the prior map exhibit similar continuity in the rendered output [9371-depth-structural-consistency-regularization.md]. Novel View Regularization mitigates the shape-radiance ambiguity in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by incorporating rays from unobserved viewpoints into the training loop [10806-novel-view-regularization.md]. Unlike methods that rely solely on observed image supervision, this approach adds geometric guidance to prevent overfitting to sparse input views [10806-novel-view-regularization.md]. It sets itself apart by explicitly sampling and rendering novel views during optimization to enforce geometric consistency, whereas siblings like Depth and Geometry Supervision may rely on external depth priors or structural constraints without necessarily synthesizing new viewpoints [10806-novel-view-regularization.md]. Geometry and Opacity Regularization applies explicit penalties to the opacity parameters of a volume rendering model to enforce geometric compactness and binary opacity states. It solves the problem of "floaters" (spurious geometry in empty space) and translucent artifacts that arise when neural fields learn to distribute density across many samples rather than concentrating it on actual surfaces. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Geometric Baseline Regularization by operating directly on the opacity values O(i) or \alphai rather than relying on depth consistency or gradient penalties on the density field \sigma. Direct Depth Supervision is a regularization technique in differentiable volume rendering that minimizes the pixel-wise discrepancy between the depth map rendered by the neural radiance field and a provided ground truth depth prior [11396-direct-depth-supervision.md]. It explicitly constrains the geometric structure of the scene, distinguishing it from photometric losses that enforce color consistency. Unlike indirect methods that enforce geometric consistency through other signals, this approach directly penalizes errors in the expected depth value [11396-direct-depth-supervision.md]. This method minimizes the Euclidean distance between 3D points backprojected from rendered depth and ground-truth 3D points to enforce global geometric consistency during NeRF optimization [12693-3d-point-supervision-loss.md]. Unlike direct depth regression, which often fails to register camera poses in sparse-view regimes by favoring per-image local geometry, this loss explicitly connects training images to the underlying scene structure, enabling robust pose refinement [12693-3d-point-supervision-loss.md]. Generalized Ray Supervision is a framework for optimizing neural scene representations by treating arbitrary rays in a scene as "ray sensors" that record incoming radiance, extending the standard NeRF approach which only supervises camera rays [14127-generalized-ray-supervision.md]. It solves the problem of limited geometric and photometric constraints in standard multi-view optimization by allowing supervision signals from non-camera perspectives, such as shadow rays or rays from unseen viewpoints, to guide the learning of density and color fields [14127-generalized-ray-supervision.md]. Unlike standard NeRF which assumes light emission from scene particles, this generalization allows for physically correct modeling where the scene absorbs light from known sources or enforces semantic consistency across views [14127-generalized-ray-supervision.md]. Not given in the sources. S-NeRF Confidence Components is a selective confidence weighting mechanism for differentiable volume rendering that adapts the reliability of supervision signals based on scene content, specifically distinguishing between static background environments and dynamic foreground objects like vehicles [15152-s-nerf-confidence-components.md]. It sets itself apart from standard geometric regularization by decoupling confidence metrics per object class: it employs geometry and reprojection measurements for background learning, while restricting foreground vehicle learning to RGB and SSIM confidences, leveraging the higher quality of LiDAR depth maps available for foreground objects [15152-s-nerf-confidence-components.md]. Not given in the sources. A loss function that enforces consistency between depth estimates of the coarse and fine NeRF models to prevent ineffective hierarchical sampling and blur. The loss is defined as L{cfc} = \mathbb{1}{\{mf=1\}} \odot \|zc - \hat{\nabla}(zf)\|^2 + \mathbb{1}{\{mc=1\}} \odot \|\hat{\nabla}(zc) - zf\|^2, where zc and zf are coarse and fine depths, and mc/mf are reliability masks determined by reprojection. A regularization technique that uses depth priors to constrain the NeRF weights by aligning the probability distribution of rendering weights with the depth prior, specifically using KL divergence. The loss is defined as L{KL} = \sum{i}^{Nr} \sum{t=tn}^{tf} D(ri) - \epsilon \log wk \exp(-\frac{(t - D(ri))^2}{2\hat{\sigma}^2}) \Delta tk, where wk are rendering weights, tk are sampled points, \Delta tk are distances, D(ri) is ground truth depth, \epsilon is a kernel parameter, and \hat{\sigma} is a variance parameter. The kernel \epsilon(x) integrates to one (a distribution) with a bounded domain parameterized by \epsilon. The URF loss (Urban-NeRF) has no open-source implementation, so KL loss is selected as the representative for indirect supervision. An approach that uses data augmentation by rendering new training images with new noisy camera poses using DSNeRF as a baseline and using depth as regularization. The concept of using depth priors to regularize NeRF training emerged as a solution to the ambiguity inherent in single-view or sparse-view reconstruction, where RGB data alone is insufficient to determine unique geometry. Early work, such as DS-NeRF, demonstrated that sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) keypoints could serve as effective geometric constraints, significantly reducing the number of training iterations required for convergence [8687-depth-supervised-nerf.md]. Subsequent research expanded this to include monocular depth priors from deep learning models (e.g., DepthAnythingV2) and robust loss functions to handle noisy pseudo-depths [9371-depth-structural-consistency-regularization.md, 9368-robust-depth-loss.md]. The family has evolved to include confidence-weighted supervision for dynamic scenes [15152-s-nerf-confidence-components.md] and generalized ray supervision for physically based rendering [14127-generalized-ray-supervision.md]. name: Geometric Baseline Regularization
head: Geometric Baseline, Geometric Loss
body: Geometric Baseline Regularization is a composite loss function designed to prevent degenerate solutions in Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) optimization, particularly in few-view settings where the network might collapse to copying training images. It serves as a strong baseline by combining photometric reconstruction with geometric priors that enforce compact depth distributions, full absorption, and multi-view consistency. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on external depth supervision or complex structural constraints, this method derives regularization directly from the volume rendering process. The method optimizes the density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} fields by minimizing a total loss \mathcal{L}{\text{geom}} that combines a photometric term with three geometric regularizers. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Training images \mathcal{I}, camera poses, ray origins \mathbf{o} and directions \mathbf{d}, sample depths ti along rays, and hyperparameters \lambda{\text{fg}}, \lambda{\text{fr}}, \lambda{\text{dist}}. Outputs: Updated network parameters \theta = (\sigma, \mathbf{c}). Data Structures Rendering Weights: wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)), where Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \rhoj) is the accumulated transmittance, \rhoi = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) is the opacity, and \deltai = t{i+1} - ti. Expected Depth: \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{\sum{i=1}^N wi ti}{\sum{i=1}^N wi}. Formulas The total loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}{\text{geom}} = \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} + \lambda{\text{fg}} \mathcal{L}{\text{fg}} + \lambda{\text{fr}} \mathcal{L}{\text{fr}} + \lambda{\text{dist}} \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}} 1. Photometric Loss: L2 difference between input image Ii and rendered color \mathbf{C}i: \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}}(\sigma, \mathbf{c}) = \sum{i=1}^{\mathcal{I}} ||Ii - \mathbf{C}i||2 2. Foreground Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{fg}}): Encourages weights to sum to unity, ensuring rays are fully absorbed by scene geometry: \mathcal{L}{\text{fg}} = \left( 1 - \sum{i=1}^N wi \right)^2 3. Frustum Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{fr}}): Penalizes density placed in only one view frustum to prevent "image plane" collapse: \mathcal{L}{\text{fr}} = \sumi wi \mathbf{1}(ni \le 1) where ni is the number of training view frustums containing the point \mathbf{r}(ti), and \mathbf{1}(\cdot) is the indicator function. 4. Distribution Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}): Regularizes weights to have a compact distribution, deviating from the original formulation by dividing by expected depth to increase strength for geometry close to the camera: \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}} = \frac{1}{\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{r})} \left( \sum{i,j} wi wj \left| \frac{ti + t{i+1}}{2} - \frac{tj + t{j+1}}{2} \right| + \frac{1}{3} \sum{i=1}^N wi^2 (t{i+1} - ti) \right) Note: The source text contains a typo using wk in the pairwise sum; it is corrected here to wj to match the summation indices. Parameters \lambda{\text{fg}}, \lambda{\text{fr}}: Coefficients for foreground and frustum losses. Values not explicitly given in the sources. \lambda{\text{dist}}: Weight for the distribution regularizer. It is 0 for the first 3000 steps, then linearly increases to 1 \times 10^{-4} for the DTU dataset and 1.5 \times 10^{-5} for the LLFF dataset at 8000 steps. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def geometricbaselineloss(renderedcolors, targetimages, weights, depths, frustumcounts, lambdafg, lambdafr, lambdadist, step, maxsteps=8000, dataset='DTU'): """ Computes the Geometric Baseline Loss. weights: list of lists, shape [numrays, N] depths: list of lists, shape [numrays, N+1] (N sample depths + ray end) frustumcounts: list of lists, shape [numrays, N] """ # 1. Photometric Loss photoloss = 0.0 for img, pred in zip(targetimages, renderedcolors): photoloss += sum((x - y) 2 for x, y in zip(img, pred)) 0.5 # 2. Foreground Loss: Encourage sum of weights to be 1 fgloss = 0.0 for w in weights: fgloss += (1.0 - sum(w)) 2 # 3. Frustum Loss: Penalize weights in only one frustum frloss = 0.0 for w, n in zip(weights, frustumcounts): for wi, count in zip(w, n): if count <= 1: frloss += wi # 4. Distribution Loss distloss = 0.0 for w, d in zip(weights, depths): numerator = sum(wi di for wi, di in zip(w, d[:-1])) denominator = sum(w) # Avoid division by zero if denominator > 1e-8: D = numerator / denominator else: D = 1.0 # Fallback if D < 1e-8: continue # Term 1: Sum over pairs i, j of |midi - midj| wi wj pairsum = 0.0 numsamples = len(w) for i in range(numsamples): midi = (d[i] + d[i + 1]) / 2.0 for j in range(numsamples): midj = (d[j] + d[j + 1]) / 2.0 pairsum += w[i] w[j] abs(midi - midj) # Term 2: 1/3 sum(wi^2 deltai) deltasum = 0.0 for i in range(numsamples): delta = d[i + 1] - d[i] deltasum += (w[i] 2) delta raydist = (pairsum + (1.0 / 3.0) deltasum) / D distloss += raydist # Schedule lambdadist: starts at 3000 steps per source if step < 3000: currentlambdadist = 0.0 else: progress = (step - 3000) / (maxsteps - 3000) maxval = 1e-4 if dataset == 'DTU' else 1.5e-5 currentlambdadist = progress maxval totalloss = photoloss + lambdafg fgloss + lambdafr frloss + currentlambdadist distloss return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls Division by Zero: The distribution loss divides by expected depth \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{r}). If a ray has no absorption (sum of weights \approx 0), depth is undefined. Few-View Collapse: Without \mathcal{L}{\text{fr}}, NeRFs may collapse to copying training images. Depth Scaling: The division by \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{r}) in \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}} increases the regularizer's strength for geometry close to the camera, which is a deviation from the original formulation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides a robust baseline for few-view reconstruction without requiring external depth maps or point clouds. It effectively prevents degenerate solutions. Limitations: The effectiveness depends on careful tuning of \lambda{\text{dist}} schedule. The Geometric Baseline Regularization is a loss combination used as a strong baseline for NeRF optimization, detailed in the DiffusioNeRF paper. It addresses degenerate solutions in few-view settings by regularizing the density and color fields through derived ray metrics. name: Guided Optimization of NeRF
head: Confidence-Based Depth Filtering
body: Guided Optimization of NeRF mitigates shape-radiance ambiguity in indoor scenes by restricting the sampling range of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) along camera rays using adapted monocular depth priors. Unlike standard NeRF, which samples uniformly between near and far bounds derived from sparse reconstruction, this method computes adaptive bounds based on multi-view geometric consistency errors, ensuring samples concentrate around plausible geometry. It sets itself apart from siblings like Depth-Supervised NeRF by not requiring ground-truth depth labels during training, instead using the rendered RGB reconstruction error to derive confidence scores for post-processing depth refinement. Inputs: N input views with RGB images and camera intrinsics K. Initial adapted monocular depth priors \{D^i\}{i=1}^N for each view i, obtained from a finetuned monocular depth network. Relative poses T^{i \rightarrow j} between views. Parameters: K=4 (number of cross-view errors for consistency), \alphal = 0.05 (lower bound factor), \alphah = 0.15 (upper bound factor), M (number of samples per ray). Outputs: Optimized NeRF parameters \theta (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}). Refined depth maps for all views. Data Structures: Error Map e^i: A 2D array per view i, where each pixel value represents the average of the K minimum cross-view reprojection errors. Confidence Map S^i: A 2D array per view i, where each pixel value S^ij \in [0, 1] represents the confidence of the depth prediction at pixel j. Steps: 1. Acquire Adapted Depth Priors: Initialize depth priors \{D^i\}{i=1}^N using a pre-trained monocular depth network finetuned on the target scene. 2. Compute Geometric Consistency Error Maps: For each view i, project its depth map D^i to all other views j \neq i. Calculate the projected depth D^{i \rightarrow j} at 2D coordinates p^{i \rightarrow j} in view j: p^{i \rightarrow j}, D^{i \rightarrow j} = \text{proj}(K, T^{i \rightarrow j}, D^i) D^{j'} = D^j(p^{i \rightarrow j}) Compute the relative reprojection error for overlapping pixels. For each pixel in view i, calculate the error map value e^i as the average of the K minimum cross-view depth projection errors. 3. Calculate Adaptive Sample Ranges: For each ray \mathbf{r} corresponding to a pixel in view i, determine the near bound tn and far bound tf using the adapted depth prior D (the value of D^i at that pixel) and the error map value e (the value of e^i at that pixel): tn = D(1 - \text{clamp}(e, \alphal, \alphah)) tf = D(1 + \text{clamp}(e, \alphal, \alphah)) Here, \text{clamp}(x, a, b) restricts x to the interval [a, b]. 4. Stratified Sampling: Partition the interval [tn, tf] into M bins. For each bin k \in [1, M], sample a point tk uniformly from the bin interval: tk \sim \mathcal{U} \left[ tn + \frac{k-1}{M}(tf - tn), \,\, tn + \frac{k}{M}(tf - tn) \right] Query the NeRF at positions xk = o + tk d to obtain color \mathbf{c}k and density \sigmak. 5. Volume Rendering: Compute the accumulated transmittance Tk = \exp \left(-\sum{j=1}^{k-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right), where \deltaj = t{j+1} - tj. Render the color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) and depth \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) for the ray: \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{M} Tk (1 - e^{-\sigmak \deltak}) \mathbf{c}k \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{M} Tk (1 - e^{-\sigmak \deltak}) tk 6. Compute Confidence Scores: After rendering, compute the confidence score S^ij for pixel j in view i based on the L1 difference between the ground truth RGB image \mathbf{C}{gt}^i(j) and the rendered RGB image \hat{\mathbf{C}}^i(j) (values normalized to [0, 1] by dividing by 255): S^ij = 1 - \frac{1}{3} \|\mathbf{C}{gt}^i(j) - \hat{\mathbf{C}}^i(j)\|1 7. Depth Refinement: Apply plane bilateral filtering to the rendered depth map \hat{D}^i, weighted by the confidence scores S^i, to produce the final refined depth map. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def guidedoptimizationneRF(N, views, K=4, alphal=0.05, alphah=0.15, M=48): """ N: Number of input views views: List of view objects containing 'rgb', 'depthprior', 'Kintrinsics', 'pose' K: Number of minimum cross-view errors for consistency check alphal, alphah: Bounds for sample range expansion M: Number of samples per ray """ # Step 1: Adapted depth priors are assumed to be in views[i].depthprior # Step 2: Compute Error Maps errormaps = [] for i in range(N): viewi = views[i] depthi = viewi.depthprior errormapi = np.zeroslike(depthi) validpixels = [] # Project depthi to all other views for j in range(N): if i == j: continue viewj = views[j] # Project coordinates and depth # proj function handles K, T, and depth interpolation coordsj, projecteddepth = projectdepth(depthi, viewi.K, viewi.pose, viewj.pose, viewj.K) # Get ground truth depth from viewj at projected coordinates # Handle occlusions/non-overlaps by masking gtdepthj = sampledepth(viewj.depthprior, coordsj) # Compute relative error where valid validmask = (gtdepthj > 0) & (projecteddepth > 0) if np.any(validmask): relerror = np.abs(gtdepthj[validmask] - projecteddepth[validmask]) / gtdepthj[validmask] # Store errors for sorting later # Note: In implementation, accumulate errors in a list per pixel or use sparse structure # For simplicity, we assume a dense accumulation or mask-based update # Here we simulate the "K minimum" logic by storing all errors and sorting later # In practice, this is done efficiently using image processing libraries pass # Calculate ei as average of K minimum errors # This requires collecting all cross-view errors for each pixel # Simplified representation: errormapi = computekminaverageerrors(depthi, views, K) errormaps.append(errormapi) # Step 3-6: Optimization Loop # Initialize NeRF parameters theta theta = initializenerf() for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Sample a batch of rays rays = samplerays(views) # For each ray, determine bounds tn, tf = [], [] for ray in rays: viewidx = ray.viewindex pixel = ray.pixel D = views[viewidx].depthprior[pixel] e = errormaps[viewidx][pixel] clampede = np.clip(e, alphal, alphah) tn.append(D (1 - clampede)) tf.append(D (1 + clampede)) tn = np.array(tn) tf = np.array(tf) # Step 4: Stratified Sampling # Generate M samples per ray # tsamples shape: (batchsize, M) tsamples = stratifiedsample(tn, tf, M) # Query NeRF # positions shape: (batchsize, M, 3) positions = rayorigins + tsamples raydirections colors, densities = nerfquery(positions, theta) # Step 5: Volume Rendering # Compute weights and rendered values deltas = tsamples[:, 1:] - tsamples[:,:-1] # Handle last delta deltas = np.concatenate([deltas, np.zeroslike(deltas[:,:1])], axis=1) alpha = 1 - np.exp(-densities deltas) transmittance = np.cumprod(1 - alpha, axis=1) # Adjust transmittance for first sample transmittance = np.concatenate([np.oneslike(transmittance[:,:1]), transmittance[:,:-1]], axis=1) weights = transmittance alpha renderedcolors = np.sum(weights[:,:, None] colors, axis=1) rendereddepths = np.sum(weights tsamples, axis=1) # Compute Loss (RGB L1) gtcolors = getgtcolors(rays) loss = np.mean(np.abs(gtcolors - renderedcolors)) # Backpropagate to update theta updatenerf(theta, loss) # Step 6 & 7: Post-processing for final depth finaldepths = [] for i in range(N): # Render depth for all pixels in view i depthmap = renderdepthforview(views[i], theta) # Compute confidence gtrgb = views[i].rgb / 255.0 renderedrgb = renderrgbforview(views[i], theta) confidence = 1 - np.mean(np.abs(gtrgb - renderedrgb), axis=2) # L1 over channels # Apply plane bilateral filtering refineddepth = planebilateralfilter(depthmap, confidence) finaldepths.append(refineddepth) return theta, finaldepths def projectdepth(depth, Ksrc, posesrc, posedst, Kdst): """ Projects depth from source view to destination view. Returns 2D coordinates in dst and projected depth values. """ # 1. Unproject depth to 3D points in source camera frame # xcam = Ksrc^-1 [u, v, 1] depth # 2. Transform to world frame # xworld = posesrc^-1 [xcam, 1] # 3. Transform to destination camera frame # xdstcam = posedst [xworld, 1] # 4. Project to 2D # udst, vdst = Kdst xdstcam[:3] / xdstcam[2] # depthdst = xdstcam[2] pass def computekminaverageerrors(depth, views, K): """ Computes the error map ei for a view by averaging the K minimum cross-view reprojection errors. """ N = len(views) H, W = depth.shape errors = np.zeros((H, W, N-1)) # Store errors from other views for j in range(N): if j == views.index(views[0]): # Skip self, handled by index logic continue # Project depth from current view to view j #... implementation details... # Calculate relative error # Store in errors array pass # For each pixel, take K smallest errors and average them # If fewer than K valid projections, average all valid ones # This is a placeholder for the specific aggregation logic pass def stratifiedsample(tn, tf, M): """ Stratified sampling within [tn, tf] for M bins. """ # tn, tf are arrays of shape (batchsize,) # Returns array of shape (batchsize, M) bins = np.linspace(0, 1, M + 1) # Uniform sample within each bin samples = np.random.uniform(bins[:-1], bins[1:], size=(tn.shape[0], M)) # Map to [tn, tf] result = tn[:, None] + samples (tf[:, None] - tn[:, None]) return result def planebilateralfilter(depth, confidence): """ Applies plane bilateral filtering weighted by confidence. """ # Placeholder for the specific filtering algorithm from [51] pass Integrates pixel-region and depth-boundary-guided ray sampling into ENeRF to reduce GPU memory and improve sampling efficiency using monocular depth priors. Uses a discrete feature grid to guide NeRF sampling toward the scene surface, resolving shape-radiance ambiguity in large-scale urban scenes. Time Complexity: The method adds overhead to the standard NeRF training loop due to the initial multi-view consistency check (projection of depth maps) and the final bilateral filtering. The core training loop complexity remains similar to NeRF, O(N{rays} \cdot M), but the adaptive sampling may reduce the effective search space, potentially accelerating convergence in ambiguous regions. Memory Complexity: Requires storing N depth maps and N error maps. The projection step requires temporary storage for projected coordinates and depths. No significant additional memory is required for the NeRF model itself compared to standard NeRF. Performance: Outperforms original NeRF and other state-of-the-art methods on indoor datasets like ScanNet in terms of depth estimation accuracy (e.g., AbsRel, SqRel) and view synthesis quality (PSNR). Strengths: Effectively mitigates shape-radiance ambiguity in poorly textured indoor areas (e.g., walls) where standard NeRF fails. Does not require ground-truth depth supervision during training. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial monocular depth priors. Performance degrades if the priors are inaccurate. The method assumes sufficient multi-view overlap for the consistency check. When to use: Indoor multi-view stereo and depth estimation where texture is sparse and ground-truth depth is unavailable. When not to use: Outdoor scenes with rich textures where standard NeRF sampling is sufficient, or scenes with significant motion blur where monocular priors are unreliable. The method was introduced in "Depth-Guided Optimization of Neural Radiance Fields for Indoor Multi-View Stereo". It addresses the limitation of standard NeRF, which suffers from shape-radiance ambiguity in indoor environments, particularly in texture-less regions like walls. While NeRF can synthesize high-quality RGB images, the underlying geometry (depth) often deviates significantly from the ground truth. The authors observed that applying correspondence-based optimization directly to monocular depth priors degrades quality, motivating the guided optimization approach that uses the priors to constrain sampling rather than as direct supervision. name: ENeRF with Guided Sampling Training
head: ENeRF Depth-Guided Training, ENeRF Guided Sampling
body: ENeRF with Guided Sampling Training is a training procedure that integrates pixel-region and depth-boundary-guided ray sampling into the Efficient Neural Radiance Field (ENeRF) framework. It reduces GPU memory consumption and improves sampling efficiency by using fewer rays per iteration while maintaining or improving rendering performance. It builds on Guided Optimization of NeRF by actively guiding sampling locations using adapted monocular depth priors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A pre-trained ENeRF model (generalized from the DTU dataset), input images, and estimated depth maps for the input views. Outputs: Optimized radiance field parameters and rendered images for novel views. Data Structures: Ray Sampling Set: A subset of camera rays selected based on pixel region importance and depth boundary locations. Sampling Points: Points along the selected rays where the neural network is evaluated. The default configuration uses 8 points for the coarse stage and 2 points for the fine stage in a 2-stage NeRF setup. Training Steps: 1. Initialization: Load the ENeRF model pre-trained on the DTU dataset. 2. Ray Selection: Sample a reduced number of rays (Nr) per iteration. The selection is guided by prioritizing regions with high gradient or error, and prioritizing rays passing through depth discontinuities derived from monocular depth estimates. 3. Point Sampling: For each selected ray, sample points along the ray. The number of points is typically 8 for the coarse network and 2 for the fine network. 4. Rendering: Render the color \hat{C}i for each ray using volume rendering. 5. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} using the following components: MSE Loss: \mathcal{L}{mse} = \frac{1}{Nr} \sum{i=1}^{Nr} \| \hat{C}i - Ci \|^2 where Nr is the number of sampled rays, \hat{C}i is the rendered color, and Ci is the ground-truth color. Perceptual Loss: \mathcal{L}{perc} = \frac{1}{Ni} \sum{i=1}^{Ni} \| \Phi(\hat{I}i) - \Phi(Ii) \| where Ni is the number of image blocks, \Phi is the perceptual function defined in the original ENeRF paper, \hat{I}i is the rendered image block, and Ii is the ground-truth image block. Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{mse} + \lambda' \mathcal{L}{perc} where \lambda' is the weight for perceptual loss. 6. Optimization: Update the ENeRF model parameters using gradient descent on \mathcal{L}. 7. Fine-tuning: After pre-training on DTU, fine-tune the model on the target novel scenes for a few epochs. Parameters: \lambda': Weight for perceptual loss. Default value: 0.01. Sampling Points: 8 (coarse) and 2 (fine) for standard settings; 16 (coarse) and 4 (fine) for large-baseline adaptations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Estimation Quality: In large baseline settings with sparse view overlap, monocular depth estimation quality degrades, which negatively affects the NeRF rendering process. Memory Usage: While the method reduces GPU memory usage compared to standard ENeRF by sampling fewer rays, insufficient sampling points in low-quality depth scenarios can lead to poor results. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainenefrguidedsampling(model, images, depths, numepochs, lambdaprime=0.01, numcoarse=8, numfine=2): """ Trains ENeRF with guided sampling. Args: model: Pre-trained ENeRF model. images: List of input images. depths: List of estimated depth maps. numepochs: Number of fine-tuning epochs. lambdaprime: Weight for perceptual loss. numcoarse: Number of coarse sampling points per ray. numfine: Number of fine sampling points per ray. """ # Standard gradient-based optimizer (e.g., Adam) optimizer = Optimizer(model.parameters()) for epoch in range(numepochs): for image, depth in zip(images, depths): # 1. name: Grid-Guided NeRF Branch Training
head: Grid Pretrain, Grid branch, Grid-guided Neural Radiance Fields, NeRF Branch, Ours, Stage 2 Joint Learning
body: Grid-Guided NeRF Branch Training is a two-stage optimization procedure for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that integrates a discrete feature grid with a continuous MLP branch to resolve the shape-radiance ambiguity inherent in large-scale urban scene reconstruction. Unlike pure grid-based methods (e.g., TensoRF) that suffer from noise in continuous regions or pure NeRF methods that struggle with high-frequency details, this method uses a pre-trained grid to guide NeRF sampling toward the scene surface while the NeRF branch provides high-frequency regularization and detail recovery. It sets itself apart from siblings like ENeRF with Guided Sampling Training by explicitly coupling the grid's density/appearance features with the NeRF's positional encoding in a joint optimization loop, rather than using the grid solely for sampling density. Inputs: A set of calibrated camera poses and corresponding RGB images for a large-scale scene. A pre-trained multi-resolution feature grid (see Data Structures). Outputs: A refined feature grid and a NeRF branch network (MLP) that jointly predict volume density and color for any 3D point and viewing direction. Multi-Resolution Feature Grid: The 3D feature grid is stored as a plane-vector representation to reduce memory usage compared to a full 3D voxel grid. It consists of: 1. Ground Feature Planes: 2D planes representing the xy-plane. For each resolution level r, there are separate planes for density (R{\sigma}) and appearance (R{c}). 2. Z-Axis Encoding: Globally encoded feature vectors for the z-axis. 3. Resolution Levels: The grid uses multiple resolutions. The highest resolution is denoted as H^2 (e.g., 4096^2). Additional lower resolutions are included at downsampled scales of \times 4 and \times 16 relative to the highest resolution. 4. Channel Allocation: The highest resolution plane uses 8 components for density and 8 for appearance. Lower resolutions follow similar allocations scaled by the resolution factor. 5. Parameter Count: The total parameter count for this representation is approximately 3 \times 10^8, which is fewer than TensoRF's 4 \times 10^8 parameters. NeRF Branch Network: A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with D=4 layers (3 hidden layers + 1 output layer) and no skip connections. Hidden width W=256. Input dimension depends on the concatenation of grid features and positional encodings. 1. Stage 1: Grid Pretraining Train the feature grid branch independently for the first 10,000 iterations. Sample N points along each ray using a coarse sampling strategy (e.g., uniform or stratified sampling). For each sampled point X, retrieve grid features \mathcal{G}\sigma(X) and \mathcal{G}c(X) via bilinear interpolation on the multi-resolution feature planes. Predict volume density \sigma and color c using a small MLP head (same architecture as TensoRF's renderer). Render pixel colors via volumetric integration. Optimize the grid parameters using the Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss between rendered and ground truth pixel colors. 2. Stage 2: Joint Optimization Initialize the NeRF branch network. Optimize both the grid branch and the NeRF branch jointly for 100,000 iterations. Sampling Guidance: Use the density predictions from the pre-trained grid branch to guide the sampling of points along camera rays. The sampling concentrates on the scene surface approximated by the grid, allowing for denser sampling in relevant regions. Feature Extraction: For each sampled point X, infer grid features \mathcal{G}\sigma(X) and \mathcal{G}c(X) by bilinear interpolation on the multi-resolution feature planes. NeRF Input Construction: Concatenate the inferred grid features with positional encodings of the point coordinates X and viewing direction d. \text{Input} = [\mathcal{G}\sigma(X), \mathcal{G}c(X), \operatorname{PE}(X), \operatorname{PE}(d)] NeRF Prediction: Feed the concatenated input into the NeRF branch network F' to predict refined volume density \sigma' and color c': (\sigma', c') = F'(\mathcal{G}\sigma(X), \mathcal{G}c(X), \operatorname{PE}(X), \operatorname{PE}(d)) Rendering: Render fine-resolution pixel colors using the NeRF branch's density and color predictions via volumetric integration. Loss Calculation: Compute the reconstruction loss (MSE) for both the grid branch outputs and the NeRF branch outputs. Joint Update: Update both the grid parameters and the NeRF branch parameters using the combined loss. The loss weighting between the two branches is set to 1:1. Grid Feature Interpolation: For a point X = (x, y, z), the grid features are obtained by projecting X onto the ground feature planes and interpolating. Let P{xy} be the 2D coordinates on the ground plane. The feature F(X) at resolution r is: F(X) = \text{BilinearInterpolate}(P{xy}, \text{Plane}r) This is performed for each resolution level and combined (e.g., via summation or concatenation as per the specific implementation, though the text implies retrieval from the multi-resolution set). NeRF Branch Forward Pass: (\sigma', c') = F'(\mathcal{G}\sigma(X), \mathcal{G}c(X), \operatorname{PE}(X), \operatorname{PE}(d)) Where: \sigma' is the predicted volume density. c' is the predicted view-dependent color. F' is the 4-layer MLP without skip connections. \operatorname{PE}(\cdot) is the positional encoding function. Loss Function: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{grid}} + \mathcal{L}{\text{nerf}} Where \mathcal{L}{\text{grid}} is the MSE loss between the grid branch's rendered image and the ground truth, and \mathcal{L}{\text{nerf}} is the MSE loss between the NeRF branch's rendered image and the ground truth. The weights are equal (1:1). Pretraining Iterations: 10,000. Joint Optimization Iterations: 100,000. Time Fraction: Roughly 1:4 between pretraining and joint optimization stages. Loss Weighting: 1:1 between grid branch and NeRF branch during joint training. Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 0.02 for tensor factors (grid parameters), 0.01 for MLP layers (NeRF branch). Batch Size: 4096 rays. NeRF MLP Architecture: Depth D=4 (3 hidden layers), Width W=256, no skip connections. Positional Encoding (PE) Frequency: Standard configuration bandwidth ranges from 20 to 22. Ablation tests used up to 216. Grid Resolutions: Tested at 512^2, 2048^2, and 4096^2. Low-Resolution Grids: Using a low-resolution grid (e.g., 512^2) during pretraining results in blurry artifacts. While the NeRF branch can recover some details, the overall result lacks sharpness. High-Resolution Grids without NeRF: High-resolution grids (e.g., 2048^2) pre-trained without NeRF supervision produce fuzzy and noisy results in continuous regions (e.g., roads, walls) due to grid variation artifacts. Small NeRF Capacity: A NeRF branch with insufficient capacity (e.g., D=3, W=32) is unable to effectively translate grid features, leading to inaccurate geometry and scene contents. Training Speed: The joint optimization stage suffers from slow training times. Shuffled ray batch sampling is highly ineffective for large scenes without distributed training infrastructure. PE Frequency: Increasing PE frequency bandwidth beyond the standard range (20-22) provides little benefit if the NeRF model capacity is not sufficiently large (e.g., W=256). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def gridguidednerftraining(scenedata, gridconfig, nerfconfig): """ Main training loop for Grid-Guided NeRF Branch Training. Args: scenedata: Object containing camera poses and RGB images. gridconfig: Configuration for the feature grid (resolutions, channels). nerfconfig: Configuration for the NeRF branch (MLP layers, PE frequency). Returns: Trained grid parameters and NeRF branch weights. """ # Initialize Grid Branch grid = FeatureGrid(gridconfig) gridoptimizer = Adam(grid.parameters(), lr=0.02) # Initialize NeRF Branch nerfmlp = MLP(nerfconfig) # 4 layers, W=256, no skip connections nerfoptimizer = Adam(nerfmlp.parameters(), lr=0.01) # Stage 1: Grid Pretraining (10,000 iterations) for iteration in range(10000): rays = samplerays(scenedata, batchsize=4096) # Coarse sampling guided by nothing yet, or uniform points = samplepointsuniform(rays, numsamples=64) # Get grid features gridfeaturessigma = grid.interpolatedensity(points) gridfeaturescolor = grid.interpolateappearance(points) # Predict density and color using small MLP head (TensoRF style) # Note: The text implies a small MLP head for the grid branch during pretraining sigma, color = gridrenderer(gridfeaturessigma, gridfeaturescolor) # Render image renderedimage = volumerender(points, sigma, color, rays) gtimage = getgroundtruth(rays, scenedata) # Compute Loss loss = mseloss(renderedimage, gtimage) # Update Grid gridoptimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() gridoptimizer.step() # Stage 2: Joint Optimization (100,000 iterations) for iteration in range(100000): rays = samplerays(scenedata, batchsize=4096) # Guide sampling using grid density # 1. Get initial coarse density from grid to guide sampling coarsepoints = samplepointsuniform(rays, numsamples=32) coarsegridsigma = grid.interpolatedensity(coarsepoints) coarsesigma, = gridrenderer(coarsegridsigma, grid.interpolateappearance(coarsepoints)) # 2. Use coarsesigma to guide finer sampling (concentrate on surface) # Implementation detail: Use inverse CDF of coarsesigma to sample more points near surfaces finepoints = samplepointsguided(rays, coarsesigma, numsamples=128) # Get grid features for fine points finegridsigma = grid.interpolatedensity(finepoints) finegridcolor = grid.interpolateappearance(finepoints) # Get Positional Encodings pepoints = positionalencoding(finepoints, freqmin=20, freqmax=22) pedirs = positionalencoding(rays.directions, freqmin=20, freqmax=22) # Concatenate features nerfinput = concatenate([finegridsigma, finegridcolor, pepoints, pedirs]) # Predict density and color using NeRF branch sigmanerf, colornerf = nerfmlp(nerfinput) # Render image using NeRF branch renderedimagenerf = volumerender(finepoints, sigmanerf, colornerf, rays) gtimage = getgroundtruth(rays, scenedata) # Compute Loss for NeRF branch lossnerf = mseloss(renderedimagenerf, gtimage) # Also compute loss for Grid branch to maintain its quality # Re-render grid output for the same points or use a separate coarse render # The text says "grid branch outputs maintain being supervised... along with fine-rendering results" # We assume we render the grid branch output for the same points or a standard coarse set gridsigma, gridcolor = gridrenderer(finegridsigma, finegridcolor) renderedimagegrid = volumerender(finepoints, gridsigma, gridcolor, rays) lossgrid = mseloss(renderedimagegrid, gtimage) # Total Loss (1:1 weighting) totalloss = lossnerf + lossgrid # Update both branches gridoptimizer.zerograd() nerfoptimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() gridoptimizer.step() nerfoptimizer.step() return grid, nerfmlp def positionalencoding(x, freqmin, freqmax): """ Standard positional encoding. """ # x is (N, 3) scales = np.array([2i for i in range(freqmin, freqmax)]) scaledx = np.outer(x.flatten(), scales) encoded = np.sin(scaledx) return encoded.reshape(-1, 3 2 (freqmax - freqmin)) The initial phase where only the feature grid is trained using coarse sampling and a small renderer. It provides a coarse approximation of the scene density and appearance. It is chosen when a strong geometric prior is needed before refining with a complex MLP. Link: Grid Pretrain (conceptual link within the parent article). The continuous MLP component that takes grid features and positional encodings as input. It is chosen for its ability to recover high-frequency details and regularize the grid features. Link: NeRF Branch. Time Complexity: The joint optimization stage is computationally expensive. Training time is dominated by the 100,000 iterations of joint optimization, with a time fraction of roughly 1:4 compared to the pretraining stage. Memory Complexity: The plane-vector representation uses approximately 3 \times 10^8 parameters, which is memory-efficient compared to full 3D voxel grids and slightly better than TensoRF's 4 \times 10^8 parameters. Measured Performance: On large urban scenes, the method achieves a PSNR of 20.915, comparable to TensoRF's 21.075, but with fewer parameters. Scaling: The method is designed for extremely large-scale environments (e.g., urban scenes). However, shuffled ray batch sampling is ineffective for large scenes without distributed training, limiting scalability on single machines. Strengths: Mitigates shape-radiance ambiguity by guiding sampling to the scene surface. Reduces noise in continuous regions (roads, walls) through NeRF's implicit regularization. Achieves photorealistic quality with high visual fidelity. Limitations: Slow training times in the joint optimization stage. Ineffective batch sampling for large scenes without distributed training. Sensitive to grid resolution; low resolution causes blurriness, high resolution causes noise without NeRF supervision. When to Use: Large urban scene rendering where high visual fidelity is required and computational resources allow for long training times. When Not to Use: Real-time applications or scenarios with limited computational resources due to slow training. Grid-Guided NeRF Branch Training was proposed in the paper "Grid-guided Neural Radiance Fields for Large Urban Scenes". The work addresses the limitations of existing NeRF and grid-based methods when applied to large-scale urban environments. Pure NeRF methods suffer from blurry artifacts and slow convergence due to the difficulty of learning low-frequency functions in large scenes. Grid-based methods like TensoRF offer better performance but can produce noisy appearance and inaccurate shapes in continuous regions. The authors introduced this two-branch framework to combine the global structure capture of feature grids with the local detail recovery of NeRF, specifically targeting large urban scene rendering.
