name: 3D Point Supervision Loss
head: 3D Point Supervision, Point-based Pose Registration Loss
body: This method minimizes the Euclidean distance between 3D points backprojected from rendered depth and ground-truth 3D points to enforce global geometric consistency during NeRF optimization. Unlike direct depth regression, which often fails to register camera poses in sparse-view regimes by favoring per-image local geometry, this loss explicitly connects training images to the underlying scene structure, enabling robust pose refinement. Inputs: Neural Radiance Field parameters \theta (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}). Camera poses Pk (view-to-world matrices) for each training view k. Ground-truth 3D points \mathbf{X}{gt} corresponding to the scene geometry. Intrinsics K (used for backprojection). Outputs: Scalar loss value \mathcal{L}{3D} used for gradient descent. Data Structures: Rendered depth map \hat{D}k(u,v) for each pixel (u,v) in view k, computed via differentiable volume rendering. World-frame 3D point \hat{\mathbf{X}}k(u,v) derived from \hat{D}k(u,v) and Pk. Steps: 1. Render Depth: For each training view k, render the expected depth \hat{D}k(\mathbf{r}) along rays \mathbf{r} using the current NeRF parameters \theta. The depth is the weighted sum of sample distances ti: \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N wi ti where wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) are the rendering weights. 2. Backproject to 3D: Convert the rendered depth \hat{D}k(u,v) into a 3D point \hat{\mathbf{X}}k(u,v) in the world coordinate frame using the camera pose Pk and intrinsic matrix K. Let \mathbf{p}{uv} = K^{-1} [u, v, 1]^T. The ray direction in world coordinates is \mathbf{d}k = Pk^{-1} \mathbf{p}{uv} (normalized). The 3D point is: \hat{\mathbf{X}}k(u,v) = \mathbf{o}k + \hat{D}k(u,v) \cdot \mathbf{d}k where \mathbf{o}k is the camera center in world coordinates. 3. Compute Distance: Calculate the Euclidean distance between the backprojected point \hat{\mathbf{X}}k(u,v) and the nearest ground-truth 3D point \mathbf{X}{gt}. 4. Minimize: Optimize \theta and camera poses Pk to minimize the mean distance: \mathcal{L}{3D} = \frac{1}{N{pix}} \sum{k} \sum{(u,v)} \| \hat{\mathbf{X}}k(u,v) - \mathbf{X}{gt}(u,v) \|2 where \mathbf{X}{gt}(u,v) is the ground-truth 3D point corresponding to pixel (u,v). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compute3dpointloss(nerfmodel, poses, intrinsics, gt3dpoints): """ Computes the 3D point supervision loss. Args: nerfmodel: Differentiable NeRF model returning sigma and color. poses: List of camera-to-world matrices (N, 4, 4). intrinsics: Camera intrinsic matrix K (3, 3). gt3dpoints: Ground truth 3D points for each pixel in each view. Shape: (N, H, W, 3). Returns: loss: Scalar tensor representing the mean Euclidean distance. """ totalloss = 0.0 numpixels = 0 for k, pose in enumerate(poses): # 1. Render depth from NeRF # Assume renderdepth returns shape (H, W) rendereddepth = renderdepth(nerfmodel, pose, intrinsics) # 2. Backproject rendered depth to 3D world coordinates # Get pixel coordinates u, v = meshgrid(range(H), range(W)) # Homogeneous pixel coordinates pixelcoords = np.stack([u, v, np.oneslike(u)], axis=-1).astype(np.float32) # (H, W, 3) # Inverse projection to get ray direction in camera space # Kinv @ [u, v, 1]^T raydirscam = np.matmul(np.linalg.inv(intrinsics), pixelcoords.transpose(2, 0, 1)) # (3, H, W) # Transform ray direction to world space # pose is 4x4. The upper 3x3 is rotation R, first 3 elements of 4th col is translation t. # Ray in world: R @ raycam R = pose[:3,:3] t = pose[:3, 3] raydirsworld = np.matmul(R, raydirscam) # (3, H, W) # Normalize ray directions raydirsworldnorm = raydirsworld / np.linalg.norm(raydirsworld, axis=0, keepdims=True) # 3D point = Camera Center + Depth Ray Direction # Camera center in world is -R^T @ t camcenterworld = -np.matmul(R.T, t) rendered3dpoints = camcenterworld[:, np.newaxis, np.newaxis] + rendereddepth raydirsworldnorm # 3. Compute distance to ground truth 3D points # gt3dpoints shape: (H, W, 3) diff = rendered3dpoints - gt3dpoints[k] dist = np.linalg.norm(diff, axis=-1) # (H, W) # 4. Accumulate loss # Mask out invalid pixels if necessary (e.g., background) validmask = rendereddepth > 0 totalloss += np.sum(dist validmask) numpixels += np.sum(validmask) loss = totalloss / numpixels return loss Parameters: Weighting: The loss is typically applied as a primary term or combined with photometric loss. In SPARF, it is combined with photometric loss. Point Matching: The specific method for finding the "nearest" ground-truth point is not detailed in the primary text, but implies a correspondence exists per pixel. Edge Cases: Sparse Views: The method is specifically designed for sparse-view regimes (e.g., 3 views) where standard depth loss fails. Noisy Poses: It is effective when initial poses are noisy (e.g., perturbed by 15% Gaussian noise). Overfitting: Standard NeRF with high-frequency positional encoding overfits immediately; this loss helps mitigate degenerate geometry. Performance: On DTU with 3 views and noisy poses, Photo + L1 GT 3D points yields PSNR 18.8 (20.3 masked), SSIM 0.75 (0.84 masked), LPIPS 0.21 (0.11 masked), and DE 0.07. This significantly outperforms Photo + L1 GT depth (PSNR 13.8, SSIM 0.54, LPIPS 0.46, DE 0.17). Strengths: Enforces global geometric connection between training images, successfully registering poses in sparse-view regimes. Limitations: Requires ground-truth 3D points, which are often not available in standard NeRF datasets (unlike depth maps). Comparison: Unlike L1 loss on rendered depth vs ground-truth depth, which struggles to refine poses and leads to disjoint local solutions, 3D point supervision results in drastically better novel-view rendering. Origin: Introduced in SPARF: Neural Radiance Fields from Sparse and Noisy Poses. Context: Developed to address the failure of standard NeRF training in sparse-view settings with noisy poses, where photometric loss alone leads to degenerate geometry. Usage: Used in joint pose-NeRF refinement pipelines. SPARF: Neural Radiance Fields from Sparse and Noisy Poses, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00408, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Multi-view correspondence loss
head: MV-Corr
body: A training loss that enforces geometric consistency across multiple training views by minimizing the re-projection error of corresponding rays. It acts on both camera pose estimates and the learned neural field to prevent overfitting to sparse input views. Unlike photometric loss [7], which fails to register poses in sparse regimes, MV-Corr provides strong supervision on rendered depth, implicitly encouraging it to be close to the true surface and favoring a solution consistent across all training images. Inputs and outputs: Inputs: A set of N training images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N, their initial (potentially noisy) camera poses Pi, and a differentiable volume renderer that produces rendered depth Di and color Ci for each view. Outputs: A scalar loss value L{MV} used for gradient backpropagation to update poses and network weights. Data structures: Correspondences: A set of pixel coordinates representing corresponding points across views. Not given in the sources. Ray representation: A ray is defined by an origin and direction. Not given in the sources. Numbered steps: 1. Ray Sampling: For a reference view i and a target view k, sample a pixel (u, v) in view i. 2. Back-projection: Construct the ray for pixel (u, v) in view i using the current pose Pi. 3. Depth Query: Query the rendered depth Di(u, v) from the neural field along the ray. 4. 3D Point Estimation: Compute the 3D point X in the world frame using the ray origin, direction, and sampled depth. 5. Re-projection: Transform X into the coordinate system of the target view k using the current pose Pk and project it onto the image plane of view k to obtain predicted pixel coordinates (u', v'). 6. Depth Sampling: Sample the rendered depth Dk(u', v') from the neural field at the predicted pixel location in view k. 7. Consistency Check: Compute the loss by penalizing the discrepancy between the depth implied by the correspondence and the actual rendered depth in the target view, minimizing the rays' intersection re-projection error. Formulas: The core intuition is minimizing the intersection re-projection error. The exact mathematical formulation is not explicitly expanded in the provided text. In practice, this involves a symmetric loss between views i and k that penalizes the reprojection discrepancy. Parameters: Number of views: The method is designed for sparse regimes, e.g., N=3 views. Pose Noise: Evaluated with 15% additive Gaussian noise on initial poses. Edge cases and pitfalls: Sparse Views: Photometric loss alone fails in sparse regimes; MV-Corr is specifically required to register poses in these conditions. Disconnected Solutions: Without multi-view constraints, the NeRF/poses can converge to disconnected solutions for each training image. Background: DTU scenes have black backgrounds, which can impact PSNR values if color prediction is wrong, though MV-Corr focuses on geometry. A loss objective that directly enforces the learned scene to be consistent from any viewpoint, boosting performance when combined with multi-view correspondences. It works best in collaboration with multi-view correspondences loss (8) because the latter is needed to learn an accurate geometry first; on its own or without (8), it yields lower performance. On DTU with 3 views and fixed GT poses, adding DCons to the baseline yields PSNR 18.30 (21.01), SSIM 0.78 (0.87), LPIPS 0.21 (0.10), DE 0.08, compared to no DCons which yields PSNR 18.13 (20.81), SSIM 0.77 (0.87), LPIPS 0.22 (0.10), DE 0.10. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: On DTU with 3 views and noisy poses, combining Photo + MVCorr yields PSNR 16.0 (17.8), SSIM 0.68 (0.81), LPIPS 0.28 (0.14), DE 0.13, outperforming Photo alone which yields PSNR 10.7 (9.8), SSIM 0.43 (0.62), LPIPS 0.59 (0.36), DE 1.9. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and limitations: Strengths: Drastically outperforms photometric loss in terms of pose and learned geometry (depth error) in sparse regimes. Favors a NeRF/pose solution consistent across all training images. Limitations: Requires accurate geometry learning first to be effective when combined with other consistency modules. When to use it and when not: Use it when training NeRFs from sparse views with noisy poses where photometric loss fails to register poses. It is particularly effective when combined with photometric loss for the best overall performance. Originated in SPARF: Neural Radiance Fields from Sparse and Noisy Poses. The method was developed to address the failure of existing regularization approaches in joint pose-NeRF training in the sparse regime. SPARF: Neural Radiance Fields from Sparse and Noisy Poses, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00408, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Generalized Ray Supervision
head: Ray Sensor Supervision, Arbitrary Ray Supervision
body: Generalized Ray Supervision is a framework for optimizing neural scene representations by treating arbitrary rays in a scene as "ray sensors" that record incoming radiance, extending the standard NeRF approach which only supervises camera rays. It solves the problem of limited geometric and photometric constraints in standard multi-view optimization by allowing supervision signals from non-camera perspectives, such as shadow rays or rays from unseen viewpoints, to guide the learning of density and color fields. Unlike standard NeRF which assumes light emission from scene particles, this generalization allows for physically correct modeling where the scene absorbs light from known sources or enforces semantic consistency across views. The method operates within a differentiable volume rendering framework where gradients flow from the loss \mathcal{L} back through the rendered color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) and depth \hat{\mathbf{D}}(\mathbf{r}) to the network parameters \theta (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}) [S1, 7475-geometric-baseline-regularization.md, 8582-regnerf.md]. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A neural scene representation (mapping 3D coordinates to density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}), a set of arbitrary rays \mathbf{r} (defined by origin o and direction d), and target radiance values C{target} recorded by the "ray sensors". Outputs: Updated neural field parameters \theta that minimize the difference between simulated radiance and target radiance. Data Structures: Ray: Defined by origin o \in \mathbb{R}^3 and direction d \in \mathbb{R}^3 (normalized). Sample Points: Along each ray, N sample points ti are selected. Rendering Weights: wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)), where \deltai = t{i+1} - ti and Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \rho(tj)). Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Generation: Define a set of rays \mathbf{r} that are not necessarily camera rays. These can be shadow rays (connecting scene to light source) or rays from virtual/unseen viewpoints. 2. Radiance Simulation: For each ray \mathbf{r}, compute the simulated incoming radiance \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) using volume rendering quadrature. If modeling shadow rays with a known light source and no self-emission: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \taui C{light} where Ti is the light transmittance, \taui is the discrete opacity, and C{light} is the radiance from the light source. If modeling general radiance (including emission): \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N wi \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}(ti)) where wi are the standard rendering weights. 3. Loss Computation: Calculate the loss between the simulated radiance \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and the target radiance C{target} recorded by the ray sensor. For Multi-view Consistency, the loss is weighted by a confidence function \Gamma(\mathbf{r}i, D{pgt}): \mathcal{L}v = \sum{\mathbf{r}i \in Ii} \Gamma(\mathbf{r}i, D{pgt}) \| \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}'i) - C{pgt}(\mathbf{r}i) \|2^2 where \Gamma(\mathbf{r}i, Di) = \exp\left( -\frac{\| Di - D{pgt} \|1}{2\epsilon} \right). 4. Backpropagation: Compute gradients \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} and update the neural network parameters using an optimizer (e.g., Adam). Parameters: \epsilon: Uncertainty parameter for confidence weighting. In MapNeRF, this is gradually enlarged during training (Uncertainty Tempering). \delta: Random perturbation vector for ray origins in unseen view generation. Norm \|\delta\| = 0.1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion: Rays from unseen views may pass through occluded regions. Filtering using depth priors (e.g., DPT) and least square fitting is recommended to avoid supervising with invalid targets. Lighting Assumptions: Shadow ray supervision assumes the scene does not emit light. If the scene has emissive materials, this assumption leads to incorrect radiance simulation. Precision: The confidence function \Gamma is sensitive to the depth difference \| Di - D{pgt} \|1. Large errors result in near-zero weights, potentially stalling learning if not managed by \epsilon. A specific application of generalized ray supervision using shadow rays (connecting scene points to a light source) to reconstruct neural scenes. It differs from standard NeRF by assuming the scene does not emit light, modeling only absorption from a known directional light source, which is more physically correct for non-emissive scenes. Choose this when accurate lighting interaction and shadow modeling are required, and the scene is known to be non-emissive. Link: ShadowNeuS. A supervision signal that ensures semantic consistency (e.g., road lanes look consistent from any view) by generating rays from unseen views and supervising their color against pseudo-ground truth, weighted by a confidence function. It differs from standard depth supervision by focusing on semantic consistency across views rather than just geometric depth accuracy. Choose this for driving scenes or structured environments where semantic priors (like map data) are available. Link: MapNeRF. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of rays and samples per ray. Shadow ray supervision adds the cost of simulating light transport along additional rays. Multi-view consistency adds the cost of generating unseen rays and computing confidence weights. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the neural field parameters and intermediate rendering values for all active rays (camera + auxiliary). Strengths: Improves geometric accuracy and semantic consistency by providing additional constraints beyond camera rays. Shadow ray supervision enables physically correct lighting modeling. Limitations: Requires additional assumptions (e.g., known light source for shadow rays, map priors for multi-view consistency). Sensitive to noise in pseudo-labels or depth priors if confidence weighting is not properly tuned. When to use: When standard NeRF optimization results in poor geometry or inconsistent semantics, and auxiliary information (light sources, map data) is available. Generalized Ray Supervision was introduced in ShadowNeuS (2023) as a generalization of the NeRF training paradigm, revealing that NeRF essentially supervises camera rays and that this can be extended to arbitrary rays like shadow rays. It was further developed in MapNeRF (2023) to incorporate map priors for driving view simulation, using multi-view consistency supervision to enforce semantic consistency. The method builds on the differentiable volume rendering framework established by NeRF [S1, 7475-geometric-baseline-regularization.md]. ShadowNeuS: Neural SDF Reconstruction by Shadow Ray Supervision, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00025, fetched 2026-10-26 MapNeRF: Incorporating Map Priors into Neural Radiance Fields for Driving View Simulation, https://doi.org/10.1109/iros55552.2023.10341681, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Multi-view Consistency Supervision
body: Multi-view Consistency Supervision is a regularization technique for neural radiance fields that enforces semantic and geometric consistency across different viewpoints by generating rays from unseen views and supervising their rendered colors against pseudo-ground truth. It differs from standard color loss by using uncertainty-weighted pseudo-labels derived from map priors or depth estimates, ensuring that semantic structures (e.g., road lanes) appear consistent regardless of the viewing angle. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of input images I, a ground depth map D{pgt} (from map priors), an uncertainty parameter \epsilon, and a random perturbation vector norm \delta{norm} = 0.1. Outputs: A scalar loss value Lv. Data Structures: D{pgt}: 2D tensor of ground truth depth values. \Gamma(ri, Di): Confidence function returning a scalar weight. Steps: 1. Ray Origin Perturbation: For each input ray ri = oi + t \cdot di from image I, perturb the origin oi by a random 3D vector \delta with norm 0.1 to obtain a new origin o'i = oi + \delta. 2. Ray Construction: Retrieve the 3D point pi corresponding to the ray termination in the global coordinate system using the ground depth D{pgt}. Construct a new sampled ray r'i connecting the perturbed origin o'i to the point pi: r'i = o'i + t \cdot \frac{pi - o'i}{\|pi - o'i\|2} 3. Optional Occlusion Filtering: Optionally filter occluded regions on D{pgt} using DPT [47] and least square fitting [48] to ensure D{pgt} represents visible surfaces. 4. Lane Enlargement (Optional): If the original ray ri passes near rendered vector lanes, enlarge the supervision area according to the minimal distance to the lane. 5. Confidence Weighting: Compute the confidence \Gamma(ri, Di) that the ray ri terminates on the ground surface: \Gamma(ri, Di) = \exp\left( -\frac{\|D(ri) - D{pgt}\|1}{2\epsilon} \right) where \epsilon is the uncertainty parameter. 6. Loss Calculation: Compute the multi-view consistency loss Lv by comparing the rendered color C(r'i) against the pseudo-ground truth color C{pgt}(r'i), weighted by the confidence \Gamma: Lv = \sum{r \in Ii} \Gamma(ri, D{pgt}) \| C(r'i) - C{pgt}(r'i) \|2^2 Parameters: \delta: Randomly sampled 3D vector with norm 0.1. \epsilon: Uncertainty parameter (same as used in ground density supervision). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The pseudo-labels generated by prior methods [7] are noted as insufficient due to imprecise ray termination; this method explicitly uses D{pgt} to stabilize training. If D{pgt} contains occluded regions, the supervision may be incorrect unless filtered. A constraint enforcement mechanism that uses sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points to validate multi-view consistency during training. It selects context views based on three thresholds: spatial overlap \taus = 0.25, scale consistency \taur = 1.3, and a minimum point count N \ge \taun = 5 across context views. This ensures that only geometrically valid and sufficiently overlapping views contribute to the multi-view constraints. Complexity: Adds overhead proportional to the number of rays and the cost of depth lookups and confidence calculations. Performance: Improves PSNR and SSIM while reducing LPIPS compared to baseline NeRF. Strengths: Enforces semantic consistency (e.g., lanes look like lanes from any view). Limitations: Relies on the quality of D{pgt} and map priors; requires careful tuning of \epsilon. Originated in MapNeRF, which incorporates map priors into neural radiance fields for driving view simulation. The method addresses the limitation of online pseudo-labels [7] by using explicit ground depth and uncertainty weighting to stabilize training. MapNeRF: Incorporating Map Priors into Neural Radiance Fields for Driving View Simulation, https://doi.org/10.1109/iros55552.2023.10341681, fetched 2026-10-26 WildSplat: Feedforward Gaussian Splatting from Unposed In-the-Wild Images, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-37324-32, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Statistical Depth Refinement
head: Corrupt Depth Patching, Underfitting Depth Smoothing
body: Statistical Depth Refinement is a post-processing step applied during radiance field training to mitigate artifacts caused by corrupt stereo depth inputs, such as those arising from fuzzy pixels and specular highlights. It prevents the model from overfitting to these noisy depth values by replacing them with smoother depth estimates derived from the network's early-stage (underfitting) outputs. Unlike direct depth supervision which propagates noise, this method leverages the statistical distribution of residuals to identify and patch corrupt pixels, distinguishing it from standard filtering techniques by using the model's own learning dynamics as a prior. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Di: The input stereo depth map for the i-th frame. Db^Ki: The depth map rendered by the radiance field after K iterations of training (the "underfitting" output). \alpha: A threshold parameter in [0, 1] defining the quantile of residuals to treat as corrupt. Outputs: D{patched}: The refined depth map where corrupt pixels are replaced by values from Db^Ki. Data Structures: Depth maps and residual maps are 2D arrays indexed by pixel coordinates (u, v). Parameters: K: The number of training iterations after which the underfitting depth map is sampled. The typical value is 4000. \alpha: The quantile threshold for identifying corrupt depth. A typical value is 0.1. \lambda: Weight for the depth loss term in the optimization objective. Typical value is 1. Steps: 1. Train for K iterations: Optimize the radiance field for K iterations. At this early stage, the model is underfitting and tends to average learned colors and occupancy, producing smoother depth estimates than the noisy input. 2. Compute Residuals: Calculate the residual map Ri for the i-th frame by taking the absolute difference between the underfitting depth Db^Ki and the input stereo depth Di: Ri[u, v] = |Db^Ki[u, v] - Di[u, v]| where (u, v) is the pixel coordinate. (Note: The source notation i = |Db^Ki - Di| is a typographical error for the residual map variable.) 3. Compute Probabilistic Distribution: Compute the cumulative distribution or histogram of the values in Ri to determine the statistical distribution of residuals. 4. Identify Corrupt Pixels: Determine the threshold value corresponding to the (1-\alpha)-quantile of the residual distribution. Pixels with residuals greater than or equal to this threshold are identified as corrupt. Specifically, locate pixels with the last \alpha-quantile residuals (largest residuals). 5. Patch Depth: Replace the depth values at the identified corrupt pixel locations in the input depth map Di with the corresponding values from the underfitting depth map Db^Ki. 6. Resume Optimization: Use D{patched} for depth supervision in subsequent training iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def statisticaldepthrefinement(Dinput, radiancefield, K, alpha, learningrate=0.01): """ Refines input depth map Dinput using underfitting output from radiancefield. Args: Dinput: 2D list of floats, input stereo depth map. radiancefield: The NeRF model. K: int, number of training iterations to perform before sampling underfitting depth. alpha: float, quantile threshold for corrupt depth identification (e.g., 0.1). learningrate: float, step size for parameter updates. Returns: Dpatched: 2D list of floats, refined depth map. """ H, W = len(Dinput), len(Dinput[0]) # Step 1: Train for K iterations to reach underfitting state for step in range(K): Dpred = radiancefield.renderdepth() loss = sum(abs(Dpred[r][c] - Dinput[r][c]) for r in range(H) for c in range(W)) / (H W) gradients = computegradients(loss, radiancefield.parameters) radiancefield.parameters -= learningrate gradients # Step 2: Obtain underfitting depth map Dunderfitting = radiancefield.renderdepth() # Step 3: Compute residual map residuals = [[abs(Dunderfitting[r][c] - Dinput[r][c]) for c in range(W)] for r in range(H)] # Step 4: Compute probabilistic distribution and threshold residualvalues = [val for row in residuals for val in row] sortedresiduals = sorted(residualvalues) thresholdindex = int((1 - alpha) len(sortedresiduals)) thresholdvalue = sortedresiduals[thresholdindex] # Step 5: Identify corrupt pixels and patch Dpatched = [[Dunderfitting[r][c] if residuals[r][c] >= thresholdvalue else Dinput[r][c] for c in range(W)] for r in range(H)] return Dpatched def computegradients(loss, parameters): """Standard backpropagation to compute gradients of loss w.r.t. parameters.""" return parameters.grad # Standard automatic differentiation operation Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on the assumption that underfitting depth is smoother. If K is too large, the model may have overfit to the noise, rendering the underfitting depth unreliable. Boundaries: The method assumes the input depth map Di is valid for non-corrupt pixels. Invalid or missing depth values in Di are not handled by this specific refinement step and may require prior masking. A technique that transfers deblurred texture information from pre-deblurred images to the NeRF using perceptual loss on rendered patches, overcoming the geometric inconsistency of pre-deblurred images. It uses an off-the-shelf deep learning-based image deblurring network to generate pre-deblurred images from blurred inputs. It renders color patches \hat{C}{ptc} from the NeRF using patch-wise sampled rays r{ptc}^{pd} at the same pixel locations as the pre-deblurred color patches \bar{C}{ptc}. Perceptual loss is applied by extracting features from both the pre-deblurred color patch and the rendered color patch using a shared pre-trained image feature extractor. Pre-deblurred images cannot be used as direct pixel-wise color supervision due to lack of 3D consistency caused by the ill-posed property of image deblurring and independent processing across multi-view images. Measured Performance: Evaluated on robotic surgery stereo videos (6 cases, 807 frames) with metrics PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. The method alleviates corrupt depth fitting and reduces abrupt artifacts. Strengths: Effective at handling specific types of noise (fuzzy pixels, specular highlights) common in surgical scenes. Leverages the model's own learning dynamics. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of K and \alpha. Assumes the underfitting model produces smoother depth, which may not hold for all scenes or architectures. When to Use: When training radiance fields with noisy stereo depth inputs, particularly in domains like surgical imaging where specular highlights and motion blur are prevalent. Statistical Depth Refinement was proposed in the context of neural rendering for stereo 3D reconstruction of deformable tissues in robotic surgery. It addresses the challenge of reconstructing high-fidelity 3D models from stereo videos that contain artifacts like fuzzy pixels and specular highlights. The method is based on the observation that early-stage (underfitting) radiance fields produce smoother depth estimates, which can be used to identify and correct corrupt depth values. name: S-NeRF Confidence Components
head: S-NeRF Confidence
body: S-NeRF Confidence Components is a selective confidence weighting mechanism for differentiable volume rendering that adapts the reliability of supervision signals based on scene content, specifically distinguishing between static background environments and dynamic foreground objects like vehicles. It sets itself apart from standard geometric regularization by decoupling confidence metrics per object class: it employs geometry and reprojection measurements for background learning, while restricting foreground vehicle learning to RGB and SSIM confidences, leveraging the higher quality of LiDAR depth maps available for foreground objects. The method operates within the S-NeRF framework. It computes a composite loss where individual components are weighted by confidence scores derived from specific measurements. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rendered color \hat{\mathbf{C}}, rendered depth \hat{\mathbf{D}}, ground-truth color \mathbf{C}, ground-truth depth \mathbf{D}, and ground-truth depth maps with varying quality. Outputs: Confidence weights for background (geometry, reprojection) and foreground (RGB, SSIM) which modulate the loss gradients. Data Structures: Confidence Flags: Boolean or categorical indicators for each ray/sample point determining if it belongs to "background" or "foreground vehicle" regions. Threshold \tau: A scalar parameter for geometry confidence calculation. Steps: 1. Classify Region: Determine if the current ray sample or pixel corresponds to a background element or a foreground vehicle. 2. Compute Background Confidence: If background, calculate geometry confidence and reprojection confidence. Geometry confidence is derived from the consistency between the rendered depth and the LiDAR depth, modulated by threshold \tau. Reprojection confidence is derived from multi-view consistency checks. 3. Compute Foreground Confidence: If foreground vehicle, calculate RGB confidence and SSIM confidence. Geometry and reprojection confidences are explicitly excluded for foregrounds because the training depth maps for vehicles are of higher quality, making strong geometric constraints redundant or potentially harmful. 4. Apply Weights: Use the computed confidences to weight the respective loss terms in the optimization loop. Formulas: Geometry Confidence Threshold: The geometry confidence module uses a threshold \tau. The paper notes that geometry confidence is not sensitive to \tau, with a reasonable range of [10\%, 40\%]. The exact formula for geometry confidence is referenced as Eq. (7) in the source paper, but the specific mathematical expression is not provided in the extracted notes. Loss Balance: The confidence components interact with loss balance weights \lambda1 and \lambda2. For background views, reasonable ranges are \lambda1 \in [0.02] and \lambda2 \in (0.02). For foreground vehicles, reasonable ranges are \lambda1 \in [0.5, 2] and \lambda2 \in (0.075, 0.015). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeconfidenceweights(rendereddepth, lidardepth, renderedcolor, gtcolor, ssimmap, isvehicle, tau=0.2): """ Computes confidence weights for S-NeRF loss components. Args: rendereddepth: Tensor of rendered depth values. lidardepth: Tensor of ground-truth LiDAR depth values. renderedcolor: Tensor of rendered RGB colors. gtcolor: Tensor of ground-truth RGB colors. ssimmap: Tensor of SSIM values between rendered and ground truth. isvehicle: Boolean mask indicating foreground vehicle regions. tau: Threshold for geometry confidence (default 20%). Returns: backgroundweights: Dict with 'geometry' and 'reprojection' weights. foregroundweights: Dict with 'rgb' and 'ssim' weights. """ # Initialize weights backgroundweights = {'geometry': 1.0, 'reprojection': 1.0} foregroundweights = {'rgb': 1.0, 'ssim': 1.0} # Background Confidence Calculation # Geometry confidence depends on depth consistency and threshold tau # Note: Exact formula for geometry confidence is Eq. (7) in # Assuming a generic consistency check here as placeholder for missing formula deptherror = torch.abs(rendereddepth - lidardepth) geometryconfidence = (deptherror < tau).float() # Placeholder for Eq. (7) # Reprojection confidence is derived from multi-view consistency # Note: Specific implementation details for reprojection confidence are not provided in the notes reprojectionconfidence = 1.0 # Placeholder backgroundweights['geometry'] = geometryconfidence backgroundweights['reprojection'] = reprojectionconfidence # Foreground Confidence Calculation # For vehicles, only RGB and SSIM confidences are used # RGB confidence is typically based on pixel-wise error rgberror = torch.abs(renderedcolor - gtcolor) rgbconfidence = torch.exp(-rgberror) # Placeholder for standard RGB confidence # SSIM confidence is derived from the SSIM map ssimconfidence = ssimmap foregroundweights['rgb'] = rgbconfidence foregroundweights['ssim'] = ssimconfidence return backgroundweights, foregroundweights Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Threshold Sensitivity: While the geometry confidence is not highly sensitive to \tau, values outside [10\%, 40\%] may degrade performance. Foreground Depth Quality: The exclusion of geometry confidence for vehicles relies on the assumption that training depth maps for vehicles are "relatively better" than backgrounds. If this assumption fails, performance may degrade. Metric Trade-offs: Using only RGB or SSIM confidence for vehicles yields a 1–2% PSNR increase but a 6.6–11% LPIPS decrease compared to using both. Therefore, using both is recommended for balanced performance. S-NeRF Loss Balance Weights are hyperparameters (\lambda1, \lambda2) used to scale the depth and smoothness components of the composite loss function in S-NeRF, balancing geometric supervision against the primary RGB reconstruction loss. They are distinct from the learnable confidence weights (\omegai) that adaptively weight individual confidence metrics; these balance weights are fixed user-defined constants. They set S-NeRF apart from standard NeRF by explicitly incorporating depth and edge-aware smoothness constraints, requiring careful tuning of \lambda1 and \lambda2 to handle the disparity between static background scenes and dynamic foreground vehicles. Performance Impact: Removing the reprojection confidence module drops PSNR by 0.4%. Training without geometry confidence drops PSNR and SSIM by about 0.7%. Foreground Optimization: For foreground vehicles, using both RGB and SSIM confidences provides better overall performance (considering PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS) than using either alone, despite a slight PSNR trade-off. Depth Error Rate: The method predicts high confidence for accurate depths, encouraging NeRF geometry to be consistent with LiDAR signals. S-NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields for Street Views) was published as a conference paper at ICLR 2023. It addresses the challenges of novel view synthesis in street scenes, which contain both static backgrounds and dynamic foreground objects. The confidence components method was introduced to handle the differing reliability of depth and color supervision signals between these two types of objects. name: S-NeRF Loss Balance Weights
head: S-NeRF λ1 and λ2 weights
body: S-NeRF Loss Balance Weights are hyperparameters (\lambda1, \lambda2) used to scale the depth and smoothness components of the composite loss function in S-NeRF, balancing geometric supervision against the primary RGB reconstruction loss. They are distinct from the learnable confidence weights (\omegai) that adaptively weight individual confidence metrics; these balance weights are fixed user-defined constants. They set S-NeRF apart from standard NeRF by explicitly incorporating depth and edge-aware smoothness constraints, requiring careful tuning of \lambda1 and \lambda2 to handle the disparity between static background scenes and dynamic foreground vehicles. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Training rays \mathcal{R}, predicted RGB images \hat{I}, ground truth RGB images I, predicted depth \hat{D}, ground truth depth/disparity D, image gradients |\partial I|, and balance weights \lambda1, \lambda2. Outputs: Total loss scalar L{total} used for gradient descent. Data Structures: \lambda1: Scalar float. \lambda2: Scalar float. L{color}: Scalar float (RGB loss). L{depth}: Scalar float (Depth loss). L{smooth}: Scalar float (Smoothness loss). Formulas: The total loss is a linear combination of three terms: L{total} = L{color} + \lambda1 L{depth} + \lambda2 L{smooth} 1. RGB Loss (L{color}): Mean squared error between rendered and ground truth images: L{color} = \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \| I(r) - \hat{I}(r) \|^2 2. Depth Loss (L{depth}): Weighted absolute difference between predicted and ground truth depth/disparity, modulated by confidence \hat{C}: L{depth} = \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \frac{\hat{C} \cdot |D - \hat{D}|}{6} Note: The denominator 6 appears in the source formula. For background scenes, D represents disparity (inverse depth); for foreground vehicles, D represents depth. 3. Smoothness Loss (L{smooth}): Edge-aware smoothness constraint penalizing depth variance relative to image gradients: L{smooth} = \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \frac{\tilde{C} \cdot |D - \hat{D}|}{|\partialx \hat{D}| \exp^{-|\partialx I|} + |\partialy \hat{D}| \exp^{-|\partialy I|}} Note: The source uses \tilde{C} in the smoothness numerator, distinct from \hat{C} in the depth loss. \partialx and \partialy denote spatial derivatives. Parameters and Typical Values: \lambda1 and \lambda2 are user-defined. Reasonable ranges depend on the scene type: Street Background Views: \lambda1 \in [0.1, 0.4], \lambda2 \in (0.005, 0.02). Typical values: \lambda1 = 0.2, \lambda2 = 0.01. Foreground Vehicles: \lambda1 \in [0.5, 2], \lambda2 \in (0.075, 0.015). Typical values: \lambda1 = 1, \lambda2 = 0.15. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesnerfloss(Igt, Ipred, Dgt, Dpred, Iimage, Cconf, Csmoothconf, lambda1, lambda2): """ Computes the total S-NeRF loss. Args: Igt: Ground truth RGB image tensor. Ipred: Predicted RGB image tensor. Dgt: Ground truth depth (vehicles) or disparity (background) tensor. Dpred: Predicted depth/disparity tensor. Iimage: Original RGB image tensor for gradient computation. Cconf: Confidence metric tensor for depth loss. Csmoothconf: Confidence metric tensor for smoothness loss. lambda1: Balance weight for depth loss. lambda2: Balance weight for smoothness loss. Returns: Total loss scalar. """ # 1. RGB Loss (Lcolor) # Mean squared error over all rays/pixels lcolor = torch.sum((Igt - Ipred) 2) # 2. Depth Loss (Ldepth) # Weighted absolute difference, normalized by 6 as per source formula # Note: Dgt is disparity for background, depth for foreground depthdiff = torch.abs(Dgt - Dpred) ldepth = torch.sum(Cconf depthdiff) / 6.0 # 3. Smoothness Loss (Lsmooth) # Edge-aware smoothness constraint # Compute image gradients # Using central differences for simplicity; source assumes standard gradient operators Ix = torch.abs(Iimage[:,:, 1:,:] - Iimage[:,:,:-1,:]) Iy = torch.abs(Iimage[:,:,:, 1:] - Iimage[:,:,:,:-1]) # Compute depth/disparity gradients Dx = torch.abs(Dpred[:,:, 1:,:] - Dpred[:,:,:-1,:]) Dy = torch.abs(Dpred[:,:,:, 1:] - Dpred[:,:,:,:-1]) # Denominator: |∂x D̂| exp^−|∂x I| + |∂y D̂| exp^−|∂y I| # Note: Source formula uses exp^-|∂I|, which implies exp(-|gradient|) denom = Dx torch.exp(-Ix) + Dy torch.exp(-Iy) # Avoid division by zero denom = torch.clamp(denom, min=1e-8) # Numerator: C̃ · |D − D̂| # Source uses C̃ (tilde C) for smoothness, distinct from Ĉ (hat C) for depth smoothnessnum = Csmoothconf depthdiff # Handle shape mismatch from gradient computation (H-1, W-1) # Assuming padding or cropping to match original dimensions is handled by the framework # Here we assume inputs are already aligned or gradients are computed on aligned tensors lsmooth = torch.sum(smoothnessnum / denom) # 4. Total Loss ltotal = lcolor + lambda1 ldepth + lambda2 lsmooth return ltotal Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sensitivity: The method is not highly sensitive to \lambda1, \lambda2. Varying them outside reasonable ranges reduces PSNR/SSIM by only 0.2–1% on background views. Disparity vs Depth: For background scenes, D must be disparity (inverse depth) to focus on close objects; for vehicles, it is depth. Using the wrong interpretation breaks the loss semantics. Confidence Metrics: The confidence \hat{C} and \tilde{C} are derived from geometry and reprojection measurements for background, and RGB/SSIM for foreground [Parent]. Incorrect confidence calculation leads to incorrect weighting. The composite loss function consisting of RGB loss, confidence-conditioned depth loss, and edge-aware smoothness constraints. It defines the structure within which \lambda1 and \lambda2 operate. The total loss is L{total} = L{color} + \lambda1 L{depth} + \lambda2 L{smooth}. The smoothness loss penalizes large depth variances according to image gradients: L{smooth} = \sum (\tilde{C} \cdot |D - \hat{D}|) / (|\partialx \hat{D}| \exp^{-|\partialx I|} + |\partialy \hat{D}| \exp^{-|\partialy I|}). Typical values are \lambda1=1, \lambda2=0.15 for vehicles and \lambda1=0.2, \lambda2=0.01 for background. Time and Memory Complexity: The addition of depth and smoothness losses increases computational cost per iteration compared to standard NeRF, primarily due to gradient computations for L{smooth} and depth prediction overhead. Memory usage increases slightly to store depth maps and confidence metrics. Measured Performance: Training Duration: Ablation experiments are trained for 30k iterations. Robustness: The method is robust to parameter variation. Deviating from optimal \lambda1, \lambda2 ranges results in only minor performance drops (0.2–1% PSNR/SSIM reduction) on background novel view rendering. Scene Specificity: Optimal weights differ significantly between static background (low \lambda) and dynamic foreground (high \lambda), requiring scene-specific tuning or separate training pipelines. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Improves geometric consistency and depth accuracy, especially for foreground objects where standard NeRF fails due to lack of structure. Robust to hyperparameter tuning. Limitations: Requires ground truth depth/disparity for supervision. Performance degrades if confidence metrics are inaccurate. Not suitable for scenes without reliable depth cues or where disparity/depth interpretation is ambiguous. When to Use: Use when geometric accuracy is critical (e.g., autonomous driving scenarios) and ground truth depth is available. Use separate weights for background and foreground if training jointly. When Not to Use: Avoid if depth supervision is unavailable or unreliable. Avoid if computational resources are extremely limited and standard NeRF suffices. S-NeRF was introduced in 2023 by the authors of "S-NeRF: Neural Radiance Fields for Street Views". It extends NeRF to handle large-scale street scenes with dynamic foreground vehicles. The loss balance weights \lambda1 and \lambda2 were introduced to incorporate depth and smoothness constraints, addressing the limitations of NeRF in reconstructing dynamic objects and ensuring geometric consistency in autonomous driving datasets like nuScenes and Waymo. name: Depth Priors and Initialization
head: Depth-guided initialization, Monocular depth priors, Planar architectural depth priors
body: This family of methods addresses the ill-posed nature of single-view or sparse-view NeRF optimization by initializing or regularizing the geometry using external depth estimates [8679-single-view-nerf-training-with-depth-map.md, 14220-depth-supervision.md]. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Geometric Baseline Regularization by explicitly fusing perspective depth maps into a canonical panorama depth map via deformable alignment before training, rather than relying solely on RGB consistency or post-hoc inpainting [8679-single-view-nerf-training-with-depth-map.md]. It distinguishes itself from Depth-Supervised NeRF by focusing on refining existing radiance-field optimizations through external geometric priors rather than relying solely on multi-view consistency or specific single-view architectures [14220-depth-supervision.md]. All methods in this family operate within the differentiable volume rendering framework where gradients flow from the loss \mathcal{L} back through the rendered color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) and depth \hat{\mathbf{D}}(\mathbf{r}) to the network parameters \theta (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}) [S1, 7475-geometric-baseline-regularization.md, 8582-regnerf.md]. The rendering process computes expected color and depth along rays r(t) = o + td using sample points ti with weights wi = T(ti)\rho(ti), where \rho(ti) = 1 - \exp(-\sigma(\mathbf{r}(ti))(t{i+1} - ti)) and T(ti) = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \rho(tj)). The rendering weights wi serve as the probability distribution of absorption along the ray, often denoted as h(t) = T(t)\sigma(t), which is used in distributional geometric losses. The rendered depth is typically the expected distance along the ray: \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N wi ti where wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) are the rendering weights, ti are sample depths, and Ti is the accumulated transmittance. Gradients are backpropagated through the differentiable volume rendering process to update the density and color field parameters. This method initializes the geometry of visible regions in a single-view NeRF using a 360-degree depth estimation pipeline, addressing the under-constrained optimization problem inherent to single-view reconstruction [8679-single-view-nerf-training-with-depth-map.md]. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly fusing perspective depth maps into a canonical panorama depth map via deformable alignment before NeRF training, rather than relying solely on RGB consistency or post-hoc inpainting [8679-single-view-nerf-training-with-depth-map.md]. Depth supervision is a training technique that improves reconstructed geometry and reduces floating artifacts by providing depth priors derived from off-the-shelf monocular depth estimation models [14220-depth-supervision.md]. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Single-view NeRF Training with Depth Map by focusing on refining existing radiance-field optimizations through external geometric priors rather than relying solely on multi-view consistency or specific single-view architectures [14220-depth-supervision.md]. Definition: Incorporates precomputed depth estimates for floor, ceiling, and walls into NeRF training to enforce geometric constraints on textureless planar surfaces. Steps: 1. Compute depth estimates for floor, ceiling, and walls using semantic segmentation. 2. Incorporate these priors into training with MSE and BoundL losses alongside photometric loss. 3. Train until convergence. Parameters: \delta (BoundL tolerance): 1 mm. \lambda{color}: 10 (bedroom), 1 (living room). \lambda{depth}: 10 (bedroom), 1 (living room). Metrics: RMSE of priors vs ground truth: 2.786 mm (bedroom), 3.201 mm (living room). Converged in 120,000 iterations. Comparison: Faster convergence than photometric-only (120k vs 200k) and patch-regularization (120k vs 280k) methods due to depth supervision enabling quick identification of empty spaces, concentrating sampling on occupied regions, and providing a stronger optimization signal. The method originates from the challenge of single-view 360-degree reconstruction, where standard monocular depth estimators fail due to limited field-of-view training data. The approach was developed to handle scale ambiguity in single-view depth estimation by projecting panoramas into perspective views and performing deformable alignment. It is used in indoor scenarios to improve geometric consistency for textureless surfaces like walls, floors, and ceilings, where photometric loss alone leads to "floaters" and cloudy artifacts. Improving Geometric Consistency for 360-Degree Neural Radiance Fields in Indoor Scenarios, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13710v1, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Single-view NeRF Training with Depth Map
head: Depth-guided Single-view NeRF, Single-view NeRF with Depth Initialization
body: This method initializes the geometry of visible regions in a single-view NeRF using a 360-degree depth estimation pipeline, addressing the under-constrained optimization problem inherent to single-view reconstruction. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly fusing perspective depth maps into a canonical panorama depth map via deformable alignment before NeRF training, rather than relying solely on RGB consistency or post-hoc inpainting. Inputs: A single input RGB panorama I{\text{rgb}}. Outputs: A trained NeRF model f{\text{nerf}} representing the visible regions of the scene. Data Structures: Perspective Images: A set \{\bar{I}{\text{rgb}}^k\}{k=1}^K of K perspective projections of the input panorama. Perspective Depth Maps: A set \{\bar{I}d^k\}{k=1}^K where each \bar{I}d^k contains depth values estimated for \bar{I}{\text{rgb}}^k. Canonical Panorama Depth Map: A learnable depth map Id representing the aligned depth of the full panorama. Alignment Parameters: Scale factor wk for each perspective view k. Local bias field \{b{k,i,j}\} for each pixel (i,j) in perspective view k. Numbered Steps: 1. Perspective Projection: Project the single input panorama I{\text{rgb}} into K perspective images \{\bar{I}{\text{rgb}}^k\}{k=1}^K using different viewing directions. The number of views is set to K=20. This is necessary because existing monocular depth estimators are trained on limited field-of-view images and do not handle 360-degree panoramas directly. 2. Depth Estimation: Use a monocular depth estimation model [52] to estimate depth values for each perspective image \bar{I}{\text{rgb}}^k, obtaining the set of depth maps \{\bar{I}d^k\}{k=1}^K. Note that due to scale ambiguity in single-view depth estimation, estimated depth values in overlapped regions may differ significantly. 3. Deformable Alignment: Perform deformable alignment to jointly align the perspective depth maps \{\bar{I}d^k\} to a canonical learnable panorama depth map Id. This is achieved by optimizing the alignment objective (Eq. 2) to determine the scale wk and local bias b{k,i,j} for each view. 4. NeRF Training: Train the single-view NeRF using the RGB panorama I{\text{rgb}} and the aligned depth map Id. The NeRF is optimized by minimizing the combined color and depth reconstruction loss L{\text{nerf}}' (Eq. 3). Formulas: Depth Alignment Objective: The alignment is performed by optimizing the following equation: \sum{k,i,j} \left\| \bar{v}{i,j}^k wk + b{k,i,j} - v{M(i,j)} \right\| + Ls(b{i,j+1}, b{i,j}) + Ls(b{i+1,j}, b{i,j}) Where: k indexes the perspective view (1 \dots K). i, j are pixel coordinates in the perspective depth map. \bar{v}{i,j}^k is the pixel value of the perspective depth map \bar{I}d^k at (i,j). wk is the learnable scale value for view k. b{k,i,j} is the learnable local bias value for pixel (i,j) in view k. v{M(i,j)} is the pixel value of the canonical panorama depth map Id at the coordinate mapped from (i,j). M is a projective operation mapping perspective image coordinates to panorama image coordinates. Ls is the smooth L1 loss. The terms Ls(b{i,j+1}, b{i,j}) and Ls(b{i+1,j}, b{i,j}) constitute a total variation term. NeRF Training Loss: The NeRF is trained by minimizing: L{\text{nerf}}' = \sum{r \in R} \left( \|\hat{C}(r) - C(r)\|^2 + \|\hat{D}(r) - \bar{D}(r)\|^2 \right) Where: R is the set of rays sampled from the panorama. \hat{C}(r) is the expected pixel color rendered by the NeRF for ray r. C(r) is the ground-truth pixel color from the input panorama. \hat{D}(r) is the expected depth value rendered by the NeRF for ray r. \bar{D}(r) is the corresponding depth pixel value computed by the depth estimator (derived from Id) for ray r. Parameters: K: Number of perspective projections. Set to 20. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def singleviewnerfwithdepth(panoramargb, depthestimator, numviews=20): """ Trains a single-view NeRF using depth-guided initialization. Args: panoramargb: Input RGB panorama image. depthestimator: Monocular depth estimation model. numviews: Number of perspective projections (K). Returns: trainednerf: The trained NeRF model. """ # Step 1: Project panorama to K perspective images perspectiveimages = [] for k in range(numviews): # Project panorama to perspective view k # Implementation detail: Define projection directions for K views imgk = projectpanoramatoperspective(panoramargb, direction=k) perspectiveimages.append(imgk) # Step 2: Estimate depth for each perspective image perspectivedepthmaps = [] for imgk in perspectiveimages: # Estimate depth using monocular estimator depthk = depthestimator.predict(imgk) perspectivedepthmaps.append(depthk) # Step 3: Deformable Alignment # Initialize learnable parameters scales = [1.0 for in range(numviews)] biases = [[[[0.0 for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for in range(numviews)] for in range(2)] # Simplified bias structure # Define canonical panorama depth map (initially empty or zero) panoramadepth = initializepanoramadepth(width=panoramawidth, height=panoramaheight) # Optimize alignment parameters to minimize Eq. 2 # Note: In practice, this involves an optimization loop (e.g., SGD) # to minimize the sum of data alignment and total variation terms. for iteration in range(numalignmentiterations): lossalignment = 0.0 for k in range(numviews): depthk = perspectivedepthmaps[k] wk = scales[k] bk = biases[k] for i in range(height): for j in range(width): # Map perspective coordinates to panorama coordinates panoi, panoj = mapperspectivetopano(i, j, k) # Data alignment term: || vbar w + b - vpano || vbar = depthk[i, j] vpano = panoramadepth[panoi, panoj] bval = bk[i, j] alignmenterror = abs(vbar wk + bval - vpano) lossalignment += alignmenterror # Total variation terms for bias smoothness if j < width - 1: lossalignment += smoothl1loss(bk[i, j+1], bk[i, j]) if i < height - 1: lossalignment += smoothl1loss(bk[i+1, j], bk[i, j]) # Update scales, biases, and panoramadepth to minimize lossalignment updateparameters(lossalignment) # Step 4: Train NeRF with RGB and Aligned Depth # Initialize NeRF model nerf = initializenerf() for iteration in range(numnerfiterations): # Sample rays from the panorama rays = sampleraysfrompanorama(panoramargb) lossnerf = 0.0 for r in rays: # Render color and depth from NeRF chat = nerf.rendercolor(r) dhat = nerf.renderdepth(r) # Get ground truth color and estimated depth cgt = getpixelcolor(panoramargb, r) dbar = getdepthfromalignedmap(r, panoramadepth) # Compute loss (Eq. 3) colorloss = squarederror(chat, cgt) depthloss = squarederror(dhat, dbar) lossnerf += colorloss + depthloss # Update NeRF parameters updatenerf(lossnerf) return nerf Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Scale Ambiguity: Single-view depth estimation suffers from scale ambiguity, leading to large discrepancies in overlapped regions between perspective depth maps. The deformable alignment step is critical to resolve this. Limited Field of View: Standard monocular depth estimators are not trained on 360-degree panoramas. Direct application fails, necessitating the projection into perspective views. Visible Regions Only: Since only a single panorama is available, the trained NeRF f{\text{nerf}} only accurately represents visible regions. Invisible regions require separate completion methods (e.g., inpainting). The parent method providing the context for using depth maps to constrain NeRF geometry. Depth Priors and Initialization Collaborative RGBD Inpainting with Stable Diffusion and Monocular Depth Estimator: The subsequent step that completes the invisible regions of the scene after the visible regions are reconstructed by the NeRF. Collaborative RGBD Inpainting Time Complexity: The method involves two main optimization phases: deformable alignment of K depth maps and NeRF training. The alignment complexity depends on the number of pixels and views (O(K \cdot H \cdot W) per iteration), while NeRF training complexity is standard for volume rendering (O(N{rays} \cdot N{samples}) per iteration). Memory Complexity: Requires storing K perspective depth maps, the canonical panorama depth map, and the NeRF weights. The alignment parameters (scales and biases) add O(K \cdot H \cdot W) memory overhead. Strengths: Provides accurate geometry reconstruction for visible regions in single-view scenarios by leveraging explicit depth supervision, addressing the under-constrained nature of single-view NeRF. Limitations: The NeRF is only valid for visible regions; invisible regions are not reconstructed by this specific step and require additional inpainting. Performance depends on the accuracy of the monocular depth estimator. When to Use: When only a single panoramic image is available and accurate geometry of visible regions is required. When Not to Use: When multiple views are available (multi-view NeRF is more robust) or when the full 360-degree geometry (including occluded regions) is needed without additional inpainting steps. This method is part of the PERF (Panoramic Neural Radiance Field From a Single Panorama) framework. It was introduced to address the lack of geometry consistency in single-view panoramic NeRF methods, which often rely on inpainting or perceptual losses without explicit geometric constraints. The approach builds on 360MonoDepth [51] for depth estimation and integrates it into the NeRF training loop via deformable alignment. PERF: Panoramic Neural Radiance Field From a Single Panorama, https://doi.org/10.1109/tpami.2024.3387307, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Depth Supervision
head: Depth Prior Supervision, Monocular Depth Supervision
body: Depth supervision is a training technique that improves reconstructed geometry and reduces floating artifacts by providing depth priors derived from off-the-shelf monocular depth estimation models. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Single-view NeRF Training with Depth Map by focusing on refining existing radiance-field optimizations through external geometric priors rather than relying solely on multi-view consistency or specific single-view architectures. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A dataset containing color images and corresponding depth maps; a current geometric representation (e.g., point cloud or Gaussian splats); a boolean flag usedepthloss. Outputs: Updated geometric parameters with improved surface accuracy and reduced floaters. Data Structures and Layout: Depth Map Storage: Depth priors are stored in a directory structure relative to the dataset root: <dataset-root>/depths/<FILENAME>.png, where <FILENAME> matches the name of the corresponding dataset image. Optimization Parameters: The method is controlled via an OptimizationParams structure containing the boolean field usedepthloss. Steps: 1. Enable Supervision: Set usedepthloss = true in the optimization parameters. 2. Refit Depth Maps: Since depth estimates from off-the-shelf models may vary in scale between frames, all depth maps are refitted against the current prior point cloud to ensure a consistent scale. 3. Discard Invalid Priors: Depth maps that fail the refitting process against the prior point cloud are discarded and excluded from the supervision loss calculation. 4. Compute Loss: During training, the rendered depth is compared against the refitted depth priors to constrain the location of the surface. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applydepthsuppression(dataset, gaussians, optparams): if not optparams.usedepthloss: return # Load depth maps from <dataset-root>/depths/<FILENAME>.png depthmaps = loaddepthmaps(dataset) # Get current prior point cloud for scale alignment priorcloud = gaussians.getpointcloud() validdepths = [] for i, depthmap in enumerate(depthmaps): # Refit depth map to match the scale of the prior point cloud try: refitteddepth = refitdepthtoprior(depthmap, priorcloud) validdepths.append(refitteddepth) except RefitFailure: # Discard depth maps that fail refitting continue # Compute depth supervision loss using valid refitted depths # Note: Specific loss function formula (e.g., L1, SmoothL1) is not given in sources [G: assume standard L1 or similar differentiable loss] depthloss = computedepthloss(rendereddepths, validdepths) # Backpropagate depthloss to update gaussians updategaussianswithgradient(depthloss) Parameters: usedepthloss: Boolean. Enables depth supervision during training. Default is typically false unless explicitly enabled. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Scale Variation: Off-the-shelf depth estimators often produce depth maps with arbitrary scales. Failure to refit against a common prior (the current point cloud) leads to incorrect geometry. Invalid Priors: Depth maps that cannot be refitted (e.g., due to severe occlusion or estimation errors) must be discarded to prevent introducing noise. A lightweight depth-regularization objective that refines reconstructed geometry during per-scene training, improving local sharpness and depth consistency without sacrificing efficiency. It is chosen when higher geometric fidelity is needed after initial initialization. It differs from basic depth supervision by deriving refined depths from rendered depths and input images during the per-scene optimization stage, rather than using external priors directly. It advances geometry supervision (i.e., L{refD}) from rendered depths \{Di\} and associated input images, combining this loss with the original training loss (e.g., SVRaster) to improve geometric accuracy. Time Complexity: Adds overhead for loading depth maps and performing refitting per frame. The refitting step requires alignment with the current point cloud, which scales with the number of Gaussians/points. Memory Complexity: Requires storing depth maps for all training images. The depth maps are typically stored as PNGs, adding storage overhead proportional to the dataset size. Performance: Results in better geometry and a reduced number of floaters. Strengths: Leverages state-of-the-art monocular depth estimators to provide strong geometric priors without requiring multi-view stereo or explicit 3D scans. Limitations: Dependent on the quality of the off-the-shelf depth estimation model. Fails if depth maps cannot be refitted to the current scale. When to use: When geometry is poor or floaters are present, and external depth priors are available. When not to use: When depth maps are unavailable or when the scene has large scale variations that prevent consistent refitting. Originating from techniques to improve Gaussian Splatting and radiance field reconstruction, depth supervision utilizes off-the-shelf depth estimation models (such as Depth-Anything) to provide geometric priors. It is part of a broader trend of integrating external priors into differentiable rendering pipelines to enhance geometric accuracy. The refined depth variant is associated with advancing structured priors for sparse-voxel surface reconstruction. name: Refined Depth for Geometry Supervision
head: Depth-regularization objective
body: Refined Depth for Geometry Supervision is a lightweight depth-regularization objective used during per-scene training to refine reconstructed geometry, specifically improving local sharpness and depth consistency without sacrificing efficiency. It sets itself apart from standard photometric losses by explicitly leveraging rendered depths and input images to derive a geometry-supervision loss (L{refD}), which is combined with the original training loss to yield more geometrically faithful surfaces with fast convergence. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rendered depths \{Di\} for each camera view i, and the associated input images for each view. Outputs: A scalar loss value L{refD} used to update the scene representation (e.g., Sparse Voxel Octree) during optimization. Data Structures: Rendered Depths \{Di\}: A set of depth maps, one per camera view, generated by the current state of the volume rendering pipeline. The exact bit-depth or precision is not specified in the sources. Steps: 1. Derive Refined Depths: For each camera view i, derive refined depth information by advancing the geometry supervision from the rendered depths Di and the associated input images. The specific mathematical formulation for deriving these refined depths or the exact structure of the loss function L{refD} is not provided in the available sources. 2. Compute Loss: Calculate the geometry-supervision loss L{refD} based on the derived refined depths. 3. Combine Losses: Combine L{refD} with the original SVRaster training loss to form the total loss for the per-scene optimization stage. 4. Optimize: Update the scene parameters (e.g., voxel properties) using the combined loss to improve geometric accuracy. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Note: The specific algorithm for deriving refined depths and the loss formulation is not detailed in the source. """ # Step 1: Derive refined depths for each view # The source states: "derive the refined depths for each camera view # via advancing the geometry supervision (i.e., LrefD) from the # rendered depths {Di} and the associated input images." refineddepths = [] for i in range(len(rendereddepths)): # Implementation detail missing in source # Placeholder for the specific refinement logic refineddepths.append(refinedepth(rendereddepths[i], inputimages[i])) # Step 2: Compute LrefD # The source states this is a "lightweight depth-regularization objective" # but does not provide the formula. # Placeholder for the specific loss calculation lrefd = calculategeometrysupervisionloss(refineddepths) return lrefd def trainstep(rendereddepths, inputimages, originallossfn, model): """ Per-scene optimization step combining LrefD with original loss. """ # Compute the refined depth loss lrefd = computerefineddepthloss(rendereddepths, inputimages) # Compute the original SVRaster training loss loriginal = originallossfn(model, inputimages) # Combine losses # The source states: "This geometry-supervision loss, when combined # with the original SVRaster training loss, improves the geometric # accuracy." # The weighting factor is not specified. totalloss = loriginal + lrefd # Update model parameters model.backward(totalloss) model.step() Parameters: Weighting of L{refD}: Not given in the sources. Refinement Hyperparameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Not given in the sources. Degenerate Input: Not given in the sources. A per-scene optimization procedure for 3D Gaussian Splatting that uses dense, multi-view consistent ground truth depth maps. It differs from Refined Depth for Geometry Supervision by relying on ground truth depth priors rather than derived refined depths from rendered outputs, and targets 3DGS primitives rather than sparse-voxel structures. Choose this when high reconstruction accuracy and local sharpness are needed for indoor scenes with available ground truth depth, and shorter training times are critical. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method yields more geometrically faithful surfaces with fast convergence compared to existing methods. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves local sharpness and depth consistency; lightweight; does not sacrifice efficiency; bridges efficient initialization and high-fidelity surface reconstruction. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: During per-scene SVO (Sparse Voxel Octree) optimization stages where geometric accuracy needs improvement beyond what photometric losses alone provide. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in the paper "Advancing Structured Priors for Sparse-Voxel Surface Reconstruction". It is part of a broader framework that includes a topology-aligned multi-view fusion mechanism and level-of-detail unprojection to integrate sparse octrees from different camera views into a globally consistent structure. The approach aims to integrate uncertain or incomplete priors through an uncertainty-aware opacity formulation. name: Depth-Regularized Fine-Tuning
head: Regularized Fine-Tuning
body: Depth-Regularized Fine-Tuning is a per-scene optimization procedure that refines 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) primitives using dense, multi-view consistent ground truth depth maps as geometric priors. It addresses the limitation of feed-forward generalizable 3DGS methods in reconstructing whole indoor scenes by enhancing local sharpness and depth consistency. Unlike vanilla 3DGS which relies solely on photometric and structural similarity losses, this method explicitly minimizes the discrepancy between rendered and ground truth depth, achieving higher reconstruction accuracy with significantly shorter training times. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N input views with corresponding dense, multi-view consistent ground truth depth images \{D^n\}{n=1}^N and color images. The initial 3DGS primitives (positions, covariances, opacities, colors) are obtained from a feed-forward prediction phase. Outputs: Refined 3DGS primitives that preserve geometric accuracy and improve rendering quality. Data Structures: D^nr: Rendered depth map for view n, generated by differentiable rendering of the current 3DGS primitives. D^n: Ground truth depth map for view n. L{fcolor}: Photometric loss (e.g., MSE) between rendered and input color images. L{fssim}: Structural Similarity (SSIM) loss between rendered and input color images. L{fdepth}: Depth regularization loss. Parameters: \lambda1: Weight for SSIM loss in fine-tuning. Typical value: 0.2. \lambda2: Weight for depth regularization loss in fine-tuning. Typical value: 0.1. Steps: 1. Render Depth: For each view n \in \{1, \dots, N\}, render the depth map D^nr from the current 3DGS primitives using the standard alpha-blending depth equation. 2. Compute Depth Loss: Calculate the L1 norm difference between the rendered depth D^nr and the ground truth depth D^n for all views: L{fdepth} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{n=1}^N \| D^nr - D^n \|1 3. Compute Color Losses: Calculate the photometric loss L{fcolor} (typically MSE) and the SSIM loss L{fssim} between the rendered color images and the input color images. 4. Compute Total Loss: Combine the losses using the weighted formula: L{rft} = (1 - \lambda1) L{fcolor} + \lambda1 L{fssim} + \lambda2 L{fdepth} 5. Optimize: Perform gradient descent to update the 3DGS primitives (positions, scales, rotations, opacities, colors) to minimize L{rft}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def depthregularizedfinetuning(primitives, views, lambda1=0.2, lambda2=0.1, optimizer=None): """ Refines 3DGS primitives using depth priors. Args: primitives: Current 3D Gaussian primitives (positions, covariances, etc.) views: List of view dictionaries containing 'colorimage', 'depthimage', 'cameraparams' lambda1: Weight for SSIM loss lambda2: Weight for depth loss optimizer: Optimizer for primitive parameters Returns: Refined primitives """ N = len(views) for iteration in range(numiterations): optimizer.zerograd() totalloss = 0.0 lcolor = 0.0 lssim = 0.0 ldepth = 0.0 for n in range(N): view = views[n] colorgt = view['colorimage'] depthgt = view['depthimage'] camera = view['cameraparams'] # Render color and depth from current primitives colorrendered, depthrendered = renderprimitives(primitives, camera) # Compute photometric loss (MSE) lcolor += mseloss(colorrendered, colorgt) # Compute SSIM loss lssim += ssimloss(colorrendered, colorgt) # Compute depth regularization loss (L1) ldepth += l1loss(depthrendered, depthgt) # Average losses over number of views lcolor /= N lssim /= N ldepth /= N # Combine losses # Lrft = (1 - lambda1) Lfcolor + lambda1 Lfssim + lambda2 Lfdepth loss = (1 - lambda1) lcolor + lambda1 lssim + lambda2 ldepth # Backpropagate and update loss.backward() optimizer.step() return primitives Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Resolution Mismatch: The method supervises the output on full resolution even if lower resolution maps are used for uninitialization, to encourage high-resolution renderings. Depth Consistency: The ground truth depth maps must be dense and multi-view consistent to serve as effective priors without harming rendering quality. This variant refers to the specific application of the depth-regularized fine-tuning step after the feed-forward 3DGS prediction phase. It leverages the efficient and geometrically accurate initialization from the feed-forward pipeline to refine the entire scene’s 3DGS primitives. It is chosen when a competitive alternative to vanilla 3DGS is needed, offering significant improvement in reconstruction accuracy within considerably shorter training time. Time Complexity: Significantly shorter training time compared to conventional per-scene optimized 3DGS approaches. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Outperforms existing generalizable 3DGS methods (e.g., pixelSplat, MVSplat, PixelGaussian) and provides a competitive alternative to vanilla 3DGS in whole-scene reconstructions, especially for indoor scenes. Strengths: Enhances rendering quality while preserving geometric accuracy; removes floaters effectively; reduces redundancy in overlapping regions when combined with fusion mechanisms. Limitations: Relies on the availability of dense, multi-view consistent ground truth depth maps. Originated in the FreeSplat++ method, which is tailored for generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting for efficient indoor scene reconstruction. The approach was introduced to address challenges in reconstructing whole indoor scenes where previous fusion modules could not adequately remove floaters or redundancy. It builds on the feed-forward reconstruction of 3DGS primitives and adds a depth-regularized per-scene fine-tuning step to leverage geometric constraints.
