name: Volumetric Supervision
head: CT-Guided Training, Hybrid Supervision
body: Volumetric Supervision is a training strategy that leverages high-quality volumetric reconstructions from conventional tomography to supervise neural network training at intermediate time steps where only sparse projection data is available. It solves the problem of temporal interpolation in dynamic tomography by using dense ground-truth volumes at the start and end of an experiment to regularize the learning of the canonical model and deformation field. Unlike sibling methods that primarily enforce geometric consistency via depth or gradient losses, this method directly minimizes the discrepancy between the predicted 3D volume and a physically reconstructed 3D volume. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sparse projection data for intermediate time steps t \in (0, 1). Dense projection data at boundary time steps t=0 and t=1. Conventional tomography reconstructions (ground truth volumes) \mathbf{y} at t=0 and t=1. Neural network parameters \theta defining the canonical volume and deformation field. Outputs: Updated network parameters \theta. Predicted volume \hat{\mathbf{y}} at intermediate times. Data Structures: Target Volume \mathbf{y}: A 3D voxel grid representing the ground-truth density/attenuation field reconstructed via conventional tomography at t=0 or t=1. Predicted Volume \hat{\mathbf{y}}: A 3D voxel grid sampled from the neural network's canonical representation, warped by the deformation field to match the intermediate time step. Note: The exact resolution and bit-depth of these volumes are not specified in the sources. Steps: 1. Boundary Reconstruction: Obtain rich projection data at the start (t=0) and end (t=1) of the experiment. Reconstruct the 3D volumetric data \mathbf{y}0 and \mathbf{y}1 using conventional tomography algorithms. 2. Intermediate Prediction: For an intermediate time step t \in (0, 1) with sparse projections, query the neural network to predict the volume \hat{\mathbf{y}}t. This involves evaluating the canonical volume and applying the learned deformation field to account for temporal changes. 3. Correlation Calculation: Compute the normalized correlation coefficient C{cor} between the target volume \mathbf{y} (interpolated or selected from t=0 or t=1 based on temporal proximity or specific protocol) and the predicted volume \hat{\mathbf{y}}t. 4. Loss Computation: Calculate the volumetric loss \mathcal{L}{vol} as the negative normalized correlation coefficient: \mathcal{L}{vol} = -C{cor}(\mathbf{y}, \hat{\mathbf{y}}t) 5. Optimization: Minimize \mathcal{L}{vol} along with other task-specific losses (e.g., projection consistency) using gradient descent to update \theta. Formula: The normalized correlation coefficient C{cor} between two volumes \mathbf{y} and \hat{\mathbf{y}} is defined as: C{cor}(\mathbf{y}, \hat{\mathbf{y}}) = \frac{\sum{i} (yi - \bar{y})(\hat{y}i - \bar{\hat{y}})}{\sqrt{\sum{i} (yi - \bar{y})^2 \sum{i} (\hat{y}i - \bar{\hat{y}})^2}} where yi and \hat{y}i are the voxel values at index i, and \bar{y} and \bar{\hat{y}} are the mean values of the respective volumes. The volumetric loss is: \mathcal{L}{vol} = -C{cor}(\mathbf{y}, \hat{\mathbf{y}}) Parameters: Time Steps: t=0 and t=1 are the boundaries. Intermediate t values are not given specific typical values. Correlation Metric: Normalized correlation coefficient is used to handle scale differences in density levels between the canonical volume and the CT-reconstructed volume. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Scale Mismatch: Density levels may differ between the canonical volume and the CT-reconstructed volume. Using the normalized correlation coefficient mitigates this issue. Sparse Data: The method is specifically designed for the "sparse few-projection regime" at intermediate times. Performance may degrade if the sparse projections are insufficient to constrain the deformation field. Temporal Alignment: The method assumes that the deformation field can accurately warp the canonical volume to match the physical state at time t. Misalignment may lead to poor correlation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computevolumetricloss(targetvolume, predictedvolume): """ Computes the volumetric loss as the negative normalized correlation coefficient. Args: targetvolume (np.ndarray): 3D array of ground truth voxel values. predictedvolume (np.ndarray): 3D array of predicted voxel values. Returns: float: The volumetric loss value. """ # Compute means meantarget = np.mean(targetvolume) meanpred = np.mean(predictedvolume) # Compute deviations devtarget = targetvolume - meantarget devpred = predictedvolume - meanpred # Compute numerator and denominators numerator = np.sum(devtarget devpred) denomtarget = np.sqrt(np.sum(devtarget 2)) denompred = np.sqrt(np.sum(devpred 2)) # Handle division by zero (e.g., constant volume) if denomtarget == 0 or denompred == 0: correlation = 0.0 else: correlation = numerator / (denomtarget denompred) # Loss is negative correlation loss = -correlation return loss def trainstep(sparseprojections, targetvolume, network, optimizer): """ Single training step for Volumetric Supervision. Args: sparseprojections (list): List of sparse projection images at time t. targetvolume (np.ndarray): Ground truth volume from CT at t=0 or t=1. network: Neural network with canonical volume and deformation field. optimizer: Optimizer for updating network parameters. """ optimizer.zerograd() # 1. Predict volume at intermediate time t # Note: The exact warping mechanism is not detailed in the source predictedvolume = network.predictvolumeattime(t) # 2. Compute volumetric loss lossvol = computevolumetricloss(targetvolume, predictedvolume) # 3. Compute projection consistency loss (implied, not detailed in source) # lossproj = computeprojectionloss(sparseprojections, predictedvolume, network) # 4. Total loss (assuming only volumetric loss for this method's core definition) totalloss = lossvol # 5. Backpropagate and update totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return totalloss.item() An optimization strategy that approximates the dense voxel objective using a subset of voxels while preserving consistency with the full-volume optimization. It uses importance-weighted Monte Carlo estimation to approximate dense reconstruction objectives from sparse voxel subsets. Instead of computing the reconstruction loss over the full voxel grid, it uses the Monte Carlo estimator to approximate the objective. Importance-weighted sampling improves coverage of informative regions. This updates Gaussian parameters using more representative voxel samples and stabilizes optimization. However, without slice supervision, the model lacks structured planar constraints and shows lower performance in rendered views than methods combining sparse voxel sampling with slice-based sampling. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Directly supervises the 3D structure, which can improve the accuracy of the canonical model and deformation field in dynamic tomography. Handles scale differences between canonical and CT volumes via normalized correlation. Limitations: Requires high-quality volumetric reconstructions at the start and end of the experiment, which may not always be available. Relies on the quality of the conventional tomography reconstruction. When to Use: When dense volumetric ground truth is available at boundary time steps and sparse projections are available at intermediate times. When Not to Use: When no boundary volumetric data is available or when computational resources for conventional tomography reconstruction are limited. Volumetric Supervision was introduced in the context of dynamic tomography, where the goal is to reconstruct 4D (3D + time) volumes from sparse projections. The method builds on the idea that while intermediate time steps may have sparse data, the start and end states often have rich data that can be reconstructed using conventional tomography. This approach was proposed to improve the training of neural networks for dynamic tomography by providing strong volumetric constraints. name: Style Loss
head: VGG Style Loss
body: Style Loss is a regularization term used in differentiable volume rendering to improve color and style coherence between generated objects (or rendered scenes) and a given reference image. It operates by minimizing the distance between feature representations of the rendered output and the reference in a pre-trained VGG feature space. Unlike Perceptual Loss, which minimizes the distance to a fixed reference feature to preserve geometric and semantic integrity, Style Loss focuses on texture statistics and local contextual matching to enforce stylistic similarity. It is distinct from S3IM and Semantic Consistency Loss by targeting low-level texture and color distribution rather than structural similarity or high-level semantic alignment. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rendered image \hat{\mathbf{I}}, Reference image \mathbf{R} (typically the original captured image or a target style image), and a pre-trained VGG network. Output: Scalar loss value \mathcal{L}{STY} used for gradient backpropagation. Data Structures: VGG Features: Intermediate feature maps extracted from specific layers of the VGG network. Let F(\cdot) denote the feature extraction function. Gram Matrix: A statistical representation of texture, computed as the outer product of flattened feature vectors. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Pass both the rendered image \hat{\mathbf{I}} and the reference image \mathbf{R} through a pre-trained VGG network (e.g., VGG19) to obtain feature maps at selected layers. 2. Global Style Loss Calculation: Compute the mean and variance of the saturation values or the feature activations for both images. The global loss minimizes the difference between these statistical moments. Let \hat{G}{vgg} and R{vgg} be the feature representations of the rendered and reference images, respectively. The global component is defined as: \mathcal{L}{STY}^{global} = \| \hat{G}{vgg} - R{vgg} \|^2 + \| \hat{\hat{G}}{vgg} - \hat{R}{vgg} \|^2 where the second term typically refers to saturation statistics if explicitly modeled, or higher-order moments depending on the specific implementation variant. 3. Local Style Loss Calculation: Compute the contextual loss by finding the nearest neighbor in the feature space. This captures local texture details more effectively than global statistics. For each feature vector G{vgg}(i) in the rendered image's feature map, find the closest feature vector R{vgg}(i') in the reference image's feature map. The local loss is: \mathcal{L}{STY}^{local} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \min{i'} \| G{vgg}(i) - R{vgg}(i') \|^2 where N is the number of feature vectors. 4. Total Loss: Combine the global and local components: \mathcal{L}{STY} = \mathcal{L}{STY}^{global} + \mathcal{L}{STY}^{local}. Parameters: VGG Layers: Typically, features are extracted from 5 specific layers of VGG19, specifically the layers following each pooling operation. Reference Image: Unless specified otherwise, the rendered scene image itself or the original captured image serves as the reference \mathbf{R}. Pitfalls: Masking: Using arbitrarily-shaped regions with masks for VGG loss computation is less reliable than rectangular crops because masks often require case-dependent erosion to be effective. Gradient Noise: Alternative distribution-based losses (like Sliced Wasserstein) may introduce more noise into gradients compared to Gram matrix or contextual approaches. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def styleloss(renderedimg, referenceimg, vggmodel, layersindices): """ Computes the combined global and local style loss. Args: renderedimg: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) or (1, H, W, 3). referenceimg: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) or (1, H, W, 3). vggmodel: Pre-trained VGG19 model. layersindices: List of layer indices to extract features from. Returns: Scalar loss value. """ # 1. Extract features # Note: VGG expects normalized input (e.g., ImageNet stats) renderedfeatures = [vggmodel(renderedimg)[i] for i in layersindices] referencefeatures = [vggmodel(referenceimg)[i] for i in layersindices] # 2. Compute Global Loss (Statistical moments) # Simplified global loss based on feature mean/variance or saturation stats globalloss = 0.0 for frender, fref in zip(renderedfeatures, referencefeatures): # Flatten spatial dimensions frenderflat = frender.view(frender.size(0), -1) frefflat = fref.view(fref.size(0), -1) # Compute mean and variance for each channel meanr = torch.mean(frenderflat, dim=1) varr = torch.var(frenderflat, dim=1, unbiased=False) meanref = torch.mean(frefflat, dim=1) varref = torch.var(frefflat, dim=1, unbiased=False) # MSE between means and variances globalloss += torch.mean((meanr - meanref) 2) globalloss += torch.mean((varr - varref) 2) # 3. Compute Local Loss (Contextual/Nearest Neighbor) localloss = 0.0 for frender, fref in zip(renderedfeatures, referencefeatures): # Flatten spatial dimensions: (C, H, W) -> (C, HW) frenderflat = frender.view(frender.size(0), -1) frefflat = fref.view(fref.size(0), -1) # Normalize features for distance calculation (optional but common) # frenderflat = F.normalize(frenderflat, p=2, dim=0) # frefflat = F.normalize(frefflat, p=2, dim=0) # Compute pairwise distances # dist[i, j] = || frenderflat[:, i] - frefflat[:, j] ||^2 distmatrix = torch.cdist(frenderflat.T, frefflat.T) 2 # Find min distance for each rendered feature mindists, = torch.min(distmatrix, dim=1) # Average over all rendered features localloss += torch.mean(mindists) # 4. Combine totalloss = globalloss + localloss return totalloss A loss function based on Gram matrices of VGG layers, used for style or texture matching. It extracts deep features from 5 specific layers of VGG19 (the layers after each pooling operation), computes the Gram matrices of these features, flattens them, and concatenates them into a single vector descriptor for the crop texture. This descriptor size is independent of the input crop size, allowing comparison of differently-sized crops. It is preferred over masked VGG losses because rectangular crops are more robust and avoid the need for case-dependent erosion. Compared to Sliced Wasserstein loss, it is more reliable, whereas Sliced Wasserstein introduces more noise into gradients despite theoretically comparing distributions more accurately. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of VGG layers used and the spatial resolution of the images. Feature extraction is O(H \cdot W \cdot C) per layer, and Gram matrix computation is O(C^2 \cdot H \cdot W) or O(C^2) if flattened globally. Local loss involves nearest neighbor search, which is O(N^2) if brute-force, where N is the number of spatial locations. Memory Complexity: Requires storing intermediate feature maps for the VGG network and the reference image features. Strengths: Effective at enforcing color and style coherence; robust to rectangular crop variations; captures both global statistics and local texture details. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to VGG feature extraction and nearest neighbor search; sensitive to the choice of VGG layers; rectangular crops may not align perfectly with object boundaries compared to masked approaches (though masks have their own reliability issues). When to use: When style transfer or color coherence is critical, such as in object insertion or scene generation tasks. When not to use: When strict geometric fidelity is required without stylistic alteration, or when computational resources are severely limited. Style Loss originates from the application of deep learning features for image style transfer, pioneered by Gatys et al. [2016] using VGG Gram matrices. In the context of differentiable volume rendering, it has been adapted to guide the optimization of radiance fields, particularly for tasks like generating objects in 3D scenes (e.g., GO-NeRF) and inverse procedural material rendering (e.g., PSDR-Room). It addresses the problem of ensuring that generated or rendered content matches the stylistic and textural properties of a reference, which is crucial for seamless integration in virtual reality and scene editing applications. name: Perceptual Loss
head: Content-Preservation Loss, VGG Feature-based Content Loss
body: Perceptual loss is a regularization term used in differentiable volume rendering to preserve the structural content of the original scene during stylization. It operates by minimizing the distance between feature representations of the rendered stylized image and the original captured image in a pre-trained VGG feature space, balancing stylization and content preservation unlike Gram matrix-based style losses that average out details. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: I{tgt} (rendered stylized image), I{src} (original captured image), \Psi (set of pre-defined VGG layers), \psi (feature extractor for a layer in \Psi). Outputs: Scalar loss \mathcal{L}{per}. Data Structures The VGG network is used as a fixed feature extractor. Feature maps are 3D tensors of shape (channels, height, width). Steps 1. Feature Extraction: Pass I{tgt} and I{src} through the pre-trained VGG network to obtain feature maps. 2. Layer Selection: Select layers \psi \in \Psi for comparison. 3. Distance Calculation: Compute the squared Euclidean distance between the feature maps of I{tgt} and I{src} for each selected layer. 4. Aggregation: Sum the distances across all selected layers to produce the final loss. Formula The perceptual loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}{per} = \sum{\psi \in \Psi} \| \psi(I{tgt}) - \psi(I{src}) \|2^2 Where: \psi(I) denotes the output of the VGG network at layer \psi for input image I. \| \cdot \|2^2 is the squared L2 norm applied element-wise to the feature maps. \Psi is the set of chosen VGG layers. Parameters \lambda{per}: Weight for the perceptual loss term in the total objective function. In, the total loss is \mathcal{L} = (\mathcal{L}{dir} + \mathcal{L}{con}) + \lambda{per} \mathcal{L}{per} + \lambda{reg} \mathcal{L}{reg}. The specific value of \lambda{per} is not given in the sources. \Psi: The set of VGG layers. The sources do not specify the exact layers used, only that they are "pre-defined". Edge Cases and Pitfalls Memory Consumption: Backward gradient propagation through the VGG network combined with volumetric rendering consumes prohibitively huge memory, making it infeasible to train on all rays. Mitigation: Previous approaches mitigate this by rendering low-resolution images or sampling sparse rays/patches rather than full high-resolution images. Deferred Back-propagation: introduces deferred back-propagation to enable memory-efficient auto-differentiation of scene parameters with image losses, allowing optimization on high-resolution images without storing the full forward pass of the VGG network in memory. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: High when processing full-resolution images due to gradient storage requirements. Mitigated by low-resolution rendering, sparse ray sampling, or deferred back-propagation. Strengths: Effectively preserves content structure during stylization, preventing the "averaged-out" style details often seen with Gram matrix-based style losses. Limitations: Computationally expensive for full-resolution NeRF training. Perceptual loss was originally introduced for image style transfer. In the context of NeRF, it has been adapted for text-driven and artistic radiance field stylization. (NeRF-Art, 2023) uses it as a content-preservation term alongside text-guided stylization losses. (ARF, 2021) employs it to balance stylization and content preservation, noting that traditional Gram matrix style losses degrade quality in 3D artistic radiance fields. name: Nearest Neighbor Feature Matching Loss
head: NNFM Loss
body: Nearest Neighbor Feature Matching (NNFM) is a style loss function that minimizes the distance between local feature vectors of a rendered image and the nearest neighbor feature vectors in a style image's feature map. It solves the problem of capturing distinctive local details, such as brushstrokes, which global statistics (e.g., Gram matrices) fail to preserve faithfully. Unlike Perceptual Loss which typically minimizes the distance to a fixed reference feature, NNFM dynamically matches each rendered feature to its closest counterpart in the style feature space, enabling high-frequency detail transfer while maintaining multi-view consistency in 3D radiance fields. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: I{render}: The image rendered from the radiance field at a specific viewpoint. I{style}: The 2D style image. I{content}: The original content image (used for the content-preserving term). \lambda: Weight for the content-preserving loss. Outputs: Scalar loss value \ell to be minimized during optimization. Data Structures: Feature maps F{render}, F{style}, and F{content} are extracted using the conv3 block of a pretrained VGG-16 network. VGG-16 Structure: Consists of 5 layer blocks (conv1 to conv5). Each block begins with a max-pooling layer that downsamples the feature map by a factor of 2. Inside each block, feature maps share the same spatial resolution. Feature Map Layout: F{render} is a tensor of shape (H, W, C), where H and W are the height and width of the rendered image, and C is the number of channels in the conv3 block. The same dimensions apply to F{style} and F{content}. Feature Vector: F(i, j) denotes the feature vector at pixel location (i, j), with shape (C,). Numbered Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Extract feature maps F{render}, F{style}, and F{content} from their respective input images using the conv3 block of a pretrained VGG-16 network. 2. Nearest Neighbor Search: For each pixel location (i, j) in F{render}, find the pixel location (i', j') in F{style} that minimizes the cosine distance between their feature vectors. 3. Distance Calculation: Compute the cosine distance D between the rendered feature vector \boldsymbol{F}{render}(i, j) and its nearest neighbor \boldsymbol{F}{style}(i', j'). 4. Aggregation: Average the minimum distances over all pixels N in F{render} to compute the NNFM loss \ell{\textrm{nnfm}}. 5. Content Preservation: Compute the L2 difference between F{render} and F{content}. 6. Final Loss: Combine the NNFM loss and the content loss using the weight \lambda. Formulas: The NNFM loss is defined as: \ell {\textrm {nnfm}}({\boldsymbol {F}{\textrm {render}}}, \boldsymbol {F}{\textrm {style}})=\frac {1}{N}\sum {i, j} \min {i', j'} D\big ({\boldsymbol {F}{\textrm {render}}}(i, j),\boldsymbol {F}{\textrm {style}}(i',j')\big) where N is the number of pixels in F{render}. The cosine distance D between two feature vectors \boldsymbol{v}1 and \boldsymbol{v}2 is: D(\boldsymbol {v}1, \boldsymbol {v}2)=1-\frac{\boldsymbol {v}1^T\boldsymbol {v}2}{\sqrt {\boldsymbol {v}1^T\boldsymbol {v}1 \boldsymbol {v}2^T\boldsymbol {v}2}} The final loss combines the NNFM loss with a content-preserving L2 loss: \ell =\ell {\textrm {nnfm}}({\boldsymbol {F}{\textrm {render}}}, \boldsymbol {F}{\textrm {style}})+\lambda \cdot \ell 2({\boldsymbol {F}{\textrm {render}}}, \boldsymbol {F}{\textrm {content}}) where \ell 2({\boldsymbol {F}{\textrm {render}}}, \boldsymbol {F}{\textrm {content}}) is the L2 difference between the feature maps. Parameters: \lambda: Controls stylization strength. A larger \lambda preserves more content, while a smaller \lambda leads to stronger stylization. Typical value: \lambda = 0.001 for forward-facing captures. Typical value: \lambda = 0.005 for 360° captures. Scale: Stylization is applied only at the final scale (full resolution), not using a coarse-to-fine approach. Augmentations: Style image augmentations (rotation and/or scaling) are skipped. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Over-stylization: Using the NNFM loss alone can lead to overly strong stylization, making the content harder to recognize. The content-preserving loss term is necessary to balance this. Memory Constraints: Volumetric radiance field rendering consumes significant memory. Computing style losses on full-resolution rendered images is memory-intensive. A deferred back-propagation method is required: disable auto-differentiation to render the full-resolution image, compute the loss, and then back-propagate. View-Dependence: To ensure consistent stylization, view-dependent appearance modeling should be discarded (e.g., by zeroing out view directions in MLPs or keeping only the first spherical harmonic component). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def cosinedistance(v1, v2): """Computes cosine distance between two tensors of feature vectors.""" v1norm = torch.nn.functional.normalize(v1, p=2, dim=-1) v2norm = torch.nn.functional.normalize(v2, p=2, dim=-1) return 1.0 - torch.sum(v1norm v2norm, dim=-1) def nnfmloss(Frender, Fstyle, Fcontent, lambdaweight): """ Computes the Nearest Neighbor Feature Matching Loss. Args: Frender: Tensor of shape (H, W, C) containing rendered features. Fstyle: Tensor of shape (Hs, Ws, C) containing style features. Fcontent: Tensor of shape (H, W, C) containing content features. lambdaweight: Float, weight for the content loss. Returns: Scalar loss value. """ # Flatten spatial dimensions: (H, W, C) -> (N, C) Frenderflat = Frender.view(-1, Frender.shape[-1]) Fcontentflat = Fcontent.view(-1, Fcontent.shape[-1]) Fstyleflat = Fstyle.view(-1, Fstyle.shape[-1]) # Compute pairwise cosine distances: (N, C) and (Ns, C) -> (N, Ns) dist = cosinedistance(Frenderflat.unsqueeze(1), Fstyleflat.unsqueeze(0)) # Find minimum distance for each rendered feature vector mindists, = torch.min(dist, dim=1) # Average over all pixels to get NNFM loss nnfmlossval = torch.mean(mindists) # Compute L2 content loss (mean squared error) contentlossval = torch.mean((Frenderflat - Fcontentflat) 2) # Combine losses totalloss = nnfmlossval + lambdaweight contentlossval return totalloss A technique to handle memory-intensive style losses on full-resolution rendered images by disabling auto-differentiation during rendering and enabling it only for loss computation and back-propagation. The specific feature extractor used for NNFM, chosen empirically for capturing style details better than other blocks. Time Complexity: The nearest neighbor search requires computing distances between all rendered feature vectors and all style feature vectors, resulting in O(N \cdot Ns) complexity per iteration, where N is the number of pixels in the rendered image and Ns is the number of pixels in the style image. Memory Complexity: Requires storing full-resolution feature maps for the rendered image, style image, and content image simultaneously during the loss computation phase. The deferred back-propagation method is necessary to avoid out-of-memory errors during the rendering phase. Strengths: Captures high-frequency visual details and local structures (e.g., brushstrokes) more effectively than global statistics-based losses like Gram matrices. Maintains multi-view consistency when applied to radiance fields. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to the nearest neighbor search. Can lead to overly strong stylization if not balanced with a content loss. When to use: When high-fidelity transfer of local stylistic details (like texture and brushstrokes) is required, and computational resources allow for full-resolution feature matching. The Nearest Neighbor Feature Matching (NNFM) loss was introduced in the "ARF: Artistic Radiance Fields" paper by K. Zhang et al.. It was proposed to address the limitations of previous VGG-based style losses (which relied on Gram matrices) that produced blurry results and failed to capture faithful brushstrokes in 3D stylization. The method was adapted from 2D style transfer techniques but optimized for 3D radiance fields by applying stylization only at the final scale and skipping style image augmentations. name: Confidence-Based Loss Calibration
head: ICON, Incremental CONfidence
body: Confidence-Based Loss Calibration dynamically weights the optimization of NeRF parameters and camera poses using estimated reliability metrics, addressing the bas-relief ambiguity and registration failures in joint optimization. It sets itself apart from static regularization methods by using pose confidence to weight NeRF gradients and ray confidence to weight pose gradients, effectively decoupling error sources during training. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current NeRF parameters \Theta, current pose estimates \hat{P}, input images I, momentum factor \beta, re-initialization threshold \lambda, and window size K. Outputs: Calibrated loss values L{NeRF}, L{Pose}, and updated parameters \Theta, \hat{P}. Data Structures: Pose Confidence (\zetaP): A scalar value per pose, maintained as an exponential moving average. Ray Confidence (\zetar): A scalar value per ray, computed from the current step's consistency metrics. Steps: 1. Initialize: Set initial pose confidences \zetaP^{(0)} based on initial registration quality. 2. Sample Rays: For each pose Pi, sample a set of rays \{r{ji}\}{j=1}^B. 3. Compute Ray Confidence (\zetar): Calculate a confidence metric \zeta{r{ji}} for each ray based on consistency (e.g., photometric or geometric consistency). 4. Update Pose Confidence (\zetaP): Update the exponential moving average for pose Pi: \zeta{Pi}^{(t)} = \beta \zeta{Pi}^{(t-1)} + (1 - \beta) \frac{1}{B} \sum{j=1}^B \zeta{r{ji}} The momentum \beta is typically 0.9. 5. Compute Calibrated Losses: NeRF Loss: Weight the per-ray loss by the pose confidence \zeta{Pi}: L{NeRF}(\Theta|\hat{P}, I) = \frac{\sumi \sumj L(r{ji}) \zeta{Pi}}{\sumi \zeta{Pi}} Pose Loss: Weight the per-ray loss by the ray confidence \zeta{r{ji}}: L{Pose}(\hat{P}|\Theta, I) = \frac{\sumi \sumj L(r{ji}) \zeta{r{ji}}}{\sumi \sumj \zeta{r{ji}}} Total Loss: L{all}(\Theta, \hat{P}|I) = L{NeRF} + L{Pose} + L{conf} Where L{conf} is an additional confidence regularization term. 6. Optimize: Backpropagate gradients through L{all} to update \Theta and \hat{P}. 7. Pose Re-initialization (Guard): If a new pose Pi fails to register (abrupt confidence drop), restart from the previous pose. Failure is declared if: \zeta{Pi} \le \text{mean}(\{\zeta{Pj}\}{j=i-K}^{i-1}) - \lambda \cdot \text{std}(\{\zeta{Pj}\}{j=i-K}^{i-1}) Typical values: \lambda = 2, K = 10. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def confidencecalibratedstep(nerfparams, poses, images, beta=0.9, lam=2.0, K=10): LneRF = 0.0 Lpose = 0.0 sumposeconf = 0.0 sumrayconf = 0.0 raylosses = [] rayconfs = [] poseconfs = [] for i, Pi in enumerate(poses): # 1. Sample rays for current pose rays = samplerays(Pi, images[i]) # 2. Compute per-ray loss and raw confidence currentraylosses = [] currentrayconfs = [] for r in rays: # Render and compute basic loss L(r) lossr = computerenderingloss(nerfparams, Pi, r, images[i]) # Compute ray confidence (e.g., consistency metric) confr = computerayconfidence(nerfparams, Pi, r, images[i]) currentraylosses.append(lossr) currentrayconfs.append(confr) # Accumulate for Pose Loss (weighted by ray confidence) Lpose += lossr confr sumrayconf += confr # 3. Update Pose Confidence (Exponential Moving Average) meanrayconf = sum(currentrayconfs) / len(currentrayconfs) prevconf = poseconfs[i] if i < len(poseconfs) else meanrayconf newconf = beta prevconf + (1 - beta) meanrayconf poseconfs.append(newconf) # 4. Accumulate for NeRF Loss (weighted by pose confidence) for lossr in currentraylosses: LneRF += lossr newconf sumposeconf += newconf # 5. Normalize Losses if sumposeconf > 0: LneRF /= sumposeconf if sumrayconf > 0: Lpose /= sumrayconf # 6. Pose Re-initialization Check if i >= K: window = poseconfs[i-K:i] meanw = sum(window) / len(window) stdw = sqrt(sum((x - meanw)2 for x in window) / len(window)) if newconf < meanw - lam stdw: # Restart from previous pose poses[i] = poses[i-1] # Re-compute or reset confidence for this step pass # 7. Add Confidence Regularization (Lconf) Lconf = computeconfidenceregularization(poseconfs, rayconfs) totalloss = LneRF + Lpose + Lconf return totalloss, nerfparams, poses A variant that computes a robust confidence map by defining learnable weights \omegai for individual confidence metrics (e.g., RGB, SSIM, VGG, Depth, Flow) and jointly optimizing them during training. The final confidence map is \hat{C} = \sumi \omegai Ci, subject to \sumi \omegai = 1. This allows the model to automatically focus on the most reliable confidence signal for a given scene or region. Complexity: Adds minimal overhead to the training loop, primarily involving the computation of ray/pose confidence metrics and simple averaging operations. Strengths: Mitigates the bas-relief ambiguity by down-weighting ambiguous poses. Prevents error propagation from poorly registered images by re-initializing failed poses. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of hyperparameters \beta, \lambda, and K. Relies on the quality of the underlying confidence metrics. When to use: Joint pose and NeRF optimization where initial pose estimates may be noisy or registration fails. Introduced in the ICON (Incremental CONfidence) paper, this method draws inspiration from trial-and-error registration mechanisms in incremental SfM. It addresses the bas-relief ambiguity, a common issue in monocular NeRF optimization where depth and scale are coupled. name: Semantic Consistency Loss (CLIP-based)
head: Semantic Consistency Loss using CLIP-ViT, CLIP-ViT Feature Consistency Loss
body: Semantic Consistency Loss (SCL) is a regularization term that enforces semantic alignment between rendered images and text prompts or between unseen views by minimizing the distance between their embeddings in the CLIP latent space. Unlike standard photometric losses that optimize for pixel-wise intensity matching, SCL optimizes for high-level semantic consistency, making it robust to pixel-wise misalignment and enabling text-guided editing or zero-shot segmentation in radiance fields. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Diffusion-regularized NeRF by leveraging pre-trained vision-language models for global structure guidance rather than generative priors, and from RegNeRF by focusing on semantic rather than geometric or photometric constraints. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Training images I (or unseen views I1, I2), rendered images \hat{I} (or rendered views), and optionally text prompts T (for direction consistency variants). Outputs: A scalar loss value \mathcal{L}{SC} used to update the NeRF parameters \theta. Data Structures: CLIP-ViT Encoder (\phi): A pre-trained Vision Transformer that maps an image to a normalized embedding vector. The output \phi(I) is a unit vector in the CLIP latent space. Rendering Weights: As defined in the parent article, rendering weights wi determine the contribution of sample points to the final rendered image \hat{I}. Method Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Pass the ground-truth training image I and the rendered image \hat{I} through the CLIP-ViT encoder \phi to obtain normalized image embeddings \phi(I) and \phi(\hat{I}). Note: To reduce computational cost, volume rendering and subsequent CLIP feature extraction are often performed at a smaller resolution than the final output. 2. Loss Computation: Compute the loss based on the embeddings. Standard Formulation (DietNeRF): The loss is defined as the squared Euclidean distance between the normalized embeddings: \mathcal{L}{sc} = \frac{||\phi(I) - \phi(\hat{I})||2^2}{2} Since CLIP produces normalized embeddings (unit vectors), this simplifies to a cosine similarity loss. Unseen View Consistency (360FusionNeRF): For enforcing consistency between two unseen views I1 and I2, the loss is defined as the dot product of their embeddings, scaled by a factor \lambda: \mathcal{L}{SC}(I1, I2) = \lambda \phi(I1)^T \phi(I2) Because \phi(I) are unit vectors, this is equivalent to cosine similarity up to a constant. Direction Consistency (Blended-NeRF): For text-guided editing, the loss measures the similarity between the change in text descriptions and the change in image embeddings: L{direction} = \frac{\Delta T \cdot \Delta I}{|\Delta T| |\Delta I|} where \Delta T = ET(Te) - ET(To) and \Delta I = EI(Ie) - EI(Io). ET and EI are the text and image encoders of CLIP, Te and To are text captions for edited and original scenes, and Ie and Io are the corresponding views. 3. Optimization Scheduling: Since \mathcal{L}{SC} converges faster than photometric (\mathcal{L}{Color}) and geometric (\mathcal{L}{Geo}) losses, it is often minimized every k iterations, while the other losses are minimized every iteration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesemanticconsistencyloss(renderedimage, groundtruthimage, clipvitencoder, lambdaweight=1.0): """ Computes the Semantic Consistency Loss between a rendered image and a ground truth image using CLIP-ViT embeddings. Args: renderedimage (Tensor): Rendered image tensor of shape (H, W, 3). groundtruthimage (Tensor): Ground truth image tensor of shape (H, W, 3). clipvitencoder (Module): Pre-trained CLIP-ViT encoder. lambdaweight (float): Scaling factor for the loss. Returns: Tensor: Scalar loss value. """ # 1. Extract features using CLIP-ViT # Note: In practice, images may be resized to a smaller resolution before encoding # to reduce computational cost. featrendered = clipvitencoder(renderedimage) featgt = clipvitencoder(groundtruthimage) # 2. Normalize embeddings (if not already normalized by the encoder) # CLIP-ViT typically produces normalized embeddings. featrendered = featrendered / (torch.norm(featrendered) + 1e-8) featgt = featgt / (torch.norm(featgt) + 1e-8) # 3. Compute Cosine Similarity Loss # Formula: Lsc = ||phi(I) - phi(Ihat)||^2 / 2 # For unit vectors, this is equivalent to 1 - cosinesimilarity. # The implementation below uses the squared Euclidean distance form. diff = featrendered - featgt loss = torch.sum(diff diff) / 2.0 # 4. Apply scaling factor loss = lambdaweight loss return loss def computedirectionconsistencyloss(textencoder, imageencoder, textoriginal, textedited, imgoriginal, imgedited): """ Computes the CLIP Direction Consistency Loss for text-guided editing. Args: textencoder (Module): CLIP text encoder. imageencoder (Module): CLIP image encoder. textoriginal (str): Text caption for the original scene. textedited (str): Text caption for the edited scene. imgoriginal (Tensor): Original scene view. imgedited (Tensor): Edited scene view. Returns: Tensor: Scalar direction consistency loss. """ # 1. Encode text and images embtextoriginal = textencoder(textoriginal) embtextedited = textencoder(textedited) embimgoriginal = imageencoder(imgoriginal) embimgedited = imageencoder(imgedited) # 2. Compute deltas deltatext = embtextedited - embtextoriginal deltaimg = embimgedited - embimgoriginal # 3. Normalize deltas deltatext = deltatext / (torch.norm(deltatext) + 1e-8) deltaimg = deltaimg / (torch.norm(deltaimg) + 1e-8) # 4. Compute cosine similarity # Formula: Ldirection = (Delta T. Delta I) / (|Delta T| |Delta I|) loss = torch.dot(deltatext, deltaimg) return loss Parameters: \lambda (lambda): Scaling factor for the semantic loss. In, it is absorbed into the loss weight. Typical values are not explicitly given in the sources, but it is tuned relative to \mathcal{L}{Color} and \mathcal{L}{Geo}. k (iteration frequency): The interval at which \mathcal{L}{SC} is minimized. states it is minimized every k iterations because it converges faster. The exact value of k is not specified in the sources. Resolution: Semantic consistency is often computed over a smaller resolution to reduce computational cost. The exact resolution reduction factor is not specified. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Computational Cost: Volume rendering is expensive, and CLIP feature extraction adds further overhead. Computing LSC at full resolution is prohibitive; using a smaller resolution is recommended. Coarse Semantics: Vanilla CLIP image encoders produce coarse and noisy relevancy maps, particularly at object boundaries, because they are designed for image classification rather than dense prediction. This can lead to mixed semantics (e.g., colors blending incorrectly). View Inconsistency: Relevancy maps derived from CLIP may be inconsistent across different views. A method that distills knowledge from an off-the-shelf 2D feature extractor (CLIP-based) into 3D feature fields, optimized in conjunction with in-scene radiance fields to produce a NeRF model with semantic understanding. It sets itself apart from standard photometric NeRFs by enabling zero-shot segmentation from an open set of text labels or queries, and from direct supervision methods by using novel-view features as a teacher signal rather than ground-truth labels. CLIP Direction Consistency is a quantitative metric used to evaluate the temporal or spatial coherence of edits in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) by comparing the semantic trajectory of changes between adjacent views. It solves the problem of verifying that an edited scene evolves smoothly relative to the original scene, ensuring that the direction of semantic change in the edited views matches the direction of change in the original views. It is distinct from the CLIP Direction Similarity metric, which measures the alignment between the text prompt and the image features; instead, this metric focuses on the consistency of the delta (change) between consecutive frames. A regularization term that enforces semantic alignment between rendered images and text prompts by minimizing the distance between their embeddings in the CLIP latent space. It differs from photometric losses by optimizing for high-level semantic consistency rather than pixel-wise intensity matching, enabling text-guided editing and semantic constraints in radiance fields. A regularization technique that uses 2D mask proposals from the Segment Anything Model (SAM) to provide region-level semantic hints, correcting the coarse and noisy semantics produced by vanilla CLIP image encoders, particularly at object boundaries. It refines original relevancy maps from CLIP to produce more precise training relevancy maps for optimizing the semantic field. The regularization process is defined as \tilde{S}i = \Psi(Si), where Si is the original relevancy map and \tilde{S}i is the regularized map. The RSR loss is the sum of cross-entropy losses between the predicted semantic field output \hat{S}(r) and the regularized map \tilde{S}(r) for all rays r: L{RSR} = \sumr L{ce}(\hat{S}(r), \tilde{S}(r)). RSR is performed offline and does not introduce extra training time; during training, only the loss L{RSR} is employed. A key pitfall of vanilla CLIP relevancy maps is that they are coarse and noisy, mixing semantics (e.g., purple and green mixed in Table) and lacking fine boundaries because CLIP is designed for image classification rather than dense prediction. Time Complexity: High. Volume rendering is computationally expensive, and adding CLIP feature extraction further increases the cost. Mitigation strategies include computing LSC at a smaller resolution. Memory Complexity: Depends on the CLIP-ViT model size and the resolution of the input images. The embeddings themselves are small (e.g., 512 or 768 dimensions), but the intermediate feature maps from the ViT can be large. Measured Performance: DietNeRF, which introduced the semantic consistency loss, was benchmarked on a subsampled NeRF synthetic dataset and the DTU dataset, reaching results comparable to hours of baseline NeRF training within 15 minutes. 360FusionNeRF used 200,000 epochs with a batch size of 1,400 on a DGX A100 GPU. Scaling: Scales with the number of views and the resolution of the images. Using smaller resolutions for LSC computation helps scalability. Strengths: Robust to pixel-wise misalignment; enables zero-shot segmentation and text-guided editing; converges faster than photometric losses. Limitations: Coarse and noisy semantics from vanilla CLIP, especially at object boundaries; computationally expensive; requires careful tuning of the loss weight and iteration frequency. When to Use: When semantic understanding, text-guided editing, or zero-shot segmentation is required, and photometric losses alone are insufficient due to textureless regions or misalignment. When Not to Use: When computational resources are severely limited and high-fidelity photometric reconstruction is the only goal. The Semantic Consistency Loss based on CLIP-ViT was introduced by DietNeRF in June 2021. DietNeRF [51] proposed using CLIP-ViT [123] to extract image features and enforce semantic consistency in addition to standard photometric loss. The method was benchmarked on a subsampled NeRF synthetic dataset [1] and the DTU dataset [29]. The concept of using CLIP for semantic consistency in NeRFs was further explored in works like 360FusionNeRF and Blended-NeRF, which adapted the loss for panoramic scenes and text-guided editing, respectively. Region Semantic Ranking Regularization later addressed the limitations of vanilla CLIP relevancy maps by incorporating SAM [31].
