name: Incremental Registration
head: Incremental CONfidence (ICON) registration, Incremental Image Registration
body: Incremental Registration is a training strategy for joint pose and radiance field optimization that registers camera frames sequentially following their temporal order. It solves the problem of non-convex pose optimization and local minima by leveraging the intuition that adjacent camera poses in video sequences are spatially close. Unlike methods that optimize all poses simultaneously or rely on global initialization, this method incrementally adds frames to the training buffer, initializing new poses from previous ones and freezing older parameters to prevent disruption. The method operates in two primary modes depending on the underlying architecture: the ICON approach for NeRF-based radiance fields and the ZeroGS approach for 3D Gaussian Splatting. Both follow the shared principles of metric computation, expansion triggers, and re-optimization defined in Parent. Inputs: A sequence of unposed images \{I1, I2, \dots, IN\}; a scene regressor (NeRF or Gaussian Splatting); hyperparameters k (iteration interval), T{freeze} (freeze duration), and T{init} (initialization iterations). Outputs: Optimized radiance field parameters \Theta and camera poses \{P1, \dots, PN\}. Training Buffer: A set of registered images and their associated poses. Scene Regressor: The neural network (NeRF or 3DGS) representing the scene. Pose Parameters: A vector or matrix representing the 6-DoF pose Pi for each image Ii. ICON (NeRF): Jointly optimize NeRF parameters \Theta and poses \{P1, P2\} using the first two frames \{I1, I2\}. ZeroGS (3DGS): Select a seed image I{seed}. Initialize the scene regressor by passing I{seed} to itself: (Xi, Gi; Xj, Gj) = f{SCR}(I{seed}, I{seed}), fixing the camera pose as an identity matrix. Finetune the scene regressor for T{init} iterations (e.g., 500 iterations). Repeat the following until all images are registered: 1. Select Batch: Select a batch of unregistered images I{buf} = \{Ik\}. In ZeroGS, the reference image is selected from registered images that connects to the most unregistered images. 2. Pose Initialization: For each new frame Ii, initialize its pose Pi using the previous pose P{i-1}. 3. Add to Buffer: Add Ii and Pi to the training buffer. 4. Optimization: ICON: Freeze the learning rate on poses \{Pi\} and NeRF \Theta for T{freeze} iterations. ZeroGS: Fix camera poses registered in previous epochs and only optimize poses registered in the current epoch. Convergence: Train until convergence or for a fixed number of iterations (e.g., 1,000 for LLFF, 1,500 for Mip-NeRF360). 5. Trigger Check: If using a metric-based trigger (e.g., inlier count > s{inlier}), add the image to the buffer only if the metric is satisfied. ICON: After all frames are registered, apply a learning rate decay schedule. ZeroGS: Optimize all camera poses using the reprojection error loss: \arg \min{Xi, Ck} \sum{i,k} \rho(\|d{i,k} \cdot \nu{i,k} - (Xi - Ck)\|2) where Ck is the camera center, d{i,k} is the scaling factor, and \nu{i,k} is the ray direction. Fix the seed image pose and optimize all others. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def incrementalregistration(images, sceneregressor, k, Tfreeze, Tinit): # 1. Initialization # ICON: Optimize first two frames if method == "ICON": optimizejointly(sceneregressor, images[0:2]) registered = {1: images[0], 2: images[1]} else: # ZeroGS: Seed initialization seed = images[0] finetune(sceneregressor, seed, Tinit) registered = {1: seed} sceneregressor.setpose(1, Identity()) i = 2 while i <= len(images): # 2. Select Batch batch = selectbatch(images[i:i+k], registered) for frame in batch: # 3. Pose Initialization prevpose = sceneregressor.getpose(registered[-1].id) sceneregressor.setpose(frame.id, prevpose) # 4. Add to Buffer registered.append(frame) # 5. Optimization if method == "ICON": freezelearningrate(sceneregressor, poses=True, nerf=True) trainiterations(Tfreeze) unfreezelearningrate(sceneregressor) else: # ZeroGS: Fix old poses, optimize new fixoldposes(registered) optimizecurrentposes(sceneregressor, batch) trainiterations(Tinit) i += k # 3. Finalization if method == "ICON": applylrdecay() else: globalposeoptimization(sceneregressor, registered) k (Iteration Interval): Number of iterations between adding new frames. Value: 1,000 for CO3D/HO3D; 500 for LLFF. T{freeze} (Freeze Duration): Iterations to freeze learning rates. Value: 100,000 for HO3D/CO3D; 30,000 for LLFF. T{init} (Initialization Iterations): Finetuning iterations for scene regressor. Value: 500 for seed; 1,000 for LLFF; 1,500 for Mip-NeRF360. s{inlier} (Inlier Threshold): Minimum inlier count for registration. Value: 5,000. Local Minima: Optimizing poses and NeRF using photometric losses is highly non-convex. Incorrectly optimized poses can mislead the NeRF, causing re-registration on already registered viewpoints. Pose Drift: Errors accumulate during incremental training. Finalization stages are required to refine poses. Occlusion: Avoid sampling rays from occluded regions. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of frames, as each frame is processed once. However, the total training time is significantly higher than global optimization due to the iterative nature and freezing/unfreezing cycles. Memory Complexity: Bounded by the number of registered frames and the scene representation size. Freezing older parameters helps manage memory. Strengths: Provides good initialization for camera poses, avoiding the breaking point of 20-degree rotation difference observed in global optimization. Efficient for video sequences with smooth camera motion. Limitations: Not suitable for scenes with large, abrupt camera motions or non-sequential image sets. Requires careful tuning of k and T{freeze}. Incremental Registration was introduced in the ICON (Incremental CONfidence) paper and adopted in ZeroGS. It addresses the limitations of global pose optimization, which suffers from local minima and requires good initial poses. The method leverages the temporal coherence of video data. name: Online Incremental NeRF Optimization
head: Incremental NeRF Training, Online NeRF
body: Online Incremental NeRF Optimization addresses the problem of reconstructing 3D scenes from a continuous stream of incoming camera views, rather than a fixed, pre-collected dataset. Unlike offline methods such as DVGO, which optimize the scene representation based on a static set of images, this method updates the representation dynamically as new observations are collected. It enables active exploration by planning next-best views and integrating new data incrementally, allowing the model to build better 3D models with limited viewpoints while adapting to real-world navigation scenarios. The method operates as a continuous loop of perception, planning, and optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A current scene representation (e.g., a NeRF or grid-based model), a set of previously collected images/poses, and a new incoming image/pose from a sensor or agent. Output: An updated scene representation and a plan for the next viewpoint. Data Structures: Scene Representation: Typically a neural radiance field (MLP) or a grid-based representation (e.g., HashGrid, Voxel Grid). Training Buffer: A set of stored images and their corresponding camera poses. In online settings, this buffer may be bounded or managed to handle large environments. Steps: 1. Perception: The agent or system captures a new observation (image and pose) based on the current scene representation. 2. Incremental Update: The new observation is added to the training set. The scene representation is optimized using this expanded dataset. 3. Planning (Active): Based on the current representation, the system computes a metric (e.g., entropy or uncertainty) to determine the "next best view" for future exploration. 4. Iteration: Repeat steps 1-3 as new data arrives. Formulas and Parameters: Entropy-based Exploration: The method may use entropy to guide viewpoint selection, allowing the agent to explore diverse viewpoints. Thresholds: Specific thresholds for triggering growth or pruning are not explicitly defined in the provided sources for the general online method, but are discussed in the context of the parent family. Pitfalls: Catastrophic Forgetting: In vanilla NeRF, global MLP updates can cause previously reconstructed regions to degrade when new, unsupervised areas are optimized. Memory Usage: Large environments result in a high number of captured images, requiring strategies to discard older frames or manage memory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Plan next view based on current representation # Compute metric (e.g., entropy) over the scene nextview = plannextbestview(R, D) # 2. Capture new observation # Assume sensor provides image Inew and pose Pnew Inew, Pnew = captureobservation(nextview) # 3. Add to training buffer D.add((Inew, Pnew)) # 4. Optimize representation incrementally # Update R using all data in D R = optimize(R, D) # 5. Update current pose Pcurr = Pnew A strategy for online incremental reconstruction to address catastrophic forgetting, where the model integrates new viewpoints while preserving previously learned information. It employs pre-trained, scene-agnostic decoders that remain frozen during the feature grids optimization. This design enables new grid cells to represent unseen areas while preserving the integrity of already reconstructed regions. Vanilla NeRF suffers from catastrophic forgetting because every optimization step updates shared MLP weights globally, causing previously reconstructed regions not supervised anymore to degrade. Grid-based representations partially mitigate forgetting due to spatially localized feature storage, but forgetting still occurs due to the decoder and hashgrid dictionary. Time Complexity: Depends on the optimization frequency and the size of the training buffer. Incremental updates are generally faster than full re-optimization but require careful management of buffer size. Memory Complexity: Scales with the number of stored views and the complexity of the scene representation. Large environments may require discarding older frames to bound memory usage. Strengths: Enables real-time or near-real-time reconstruction; supports active exploration; adapts to dynamic or large-scale scenes. Limitations: Susceptible to catastrophic forgetting in vanilla architectures; requires careful management of training data and optimization steps. When to use: When data arrives continuously (e.g., robot navigation, AR/VR) and offline retraining is not feasible. When not to use: When a fixed, high-quality reconstruction from a static dataset is sufficient and computational resources allow for offline optimization. The concept of online incremental NeRF optimization arises from the need to adapt NeRFs to real-world scenarios involving imperfect data, large-scale scenes, and incremental reconstruction. Traditional NeRF methods optimize offline on fixed datasets, which is insufficient for active mapping and planning tasks. The method builds on the principles of progressive and dynamic scene growth, where the scene representation is expanded based on metrics of insufficiency. name: Sparse View and Initialization Methods
head: Sparse-View NeRF, Initialization Priors
body: This family addresses the instability, artifacts (floaters, blurring), and slow convergence inherent in Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) optimization when trained on sparse input views (typically fewer than 50–100 images). It solves the problem of insufficient geometric constraints by introducing external priors—such as geometry scaffolds, visibility maps, or semantic masks—to regularize the implicit density and color fields. What sets these methods apart from standard NeRF training is the explicit injection of structural or visibility information before or during optimization, rather than relying solely on photometric consistency across views. All methods in this family share the goal of stabilizing the optimization of the implicit function \sigma(\mathbf{x}) and \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) under data scarcity. They achieve this by: 1. External Priors: Utilizing data outside the raw RGB images (e.g., point clouds, depth maps, semantic masks, or inter-view consistency) to constrain the solution space. 2. Regularization: Adding loss terms or initialization biases that penalize physically implausible density distributions (e.g., floaters in empty space) or inconsistent geometry. 3. Initialization: Starting the NeRF parameters closer to a valid solution than random initialization, often by mapping geometric priors into the implicit space. A method for indoor scene free view synthesis that uses a geometry scaffold (pseudo depth maps) and view coverage information to guide optimization. It differs from siblings by specifically targeting the "free navigation" extrapolation problem in indoor scenes using a robust depth loss and dynamic view-coverage-based regularization, rather than static semantic weights. Choose this when robust 3D geometry is required for novel views in indoor environments with low-texture regions. A training procedure that introduces visibility priors to supervise density estimation, computed directly from input images using planar scanned volumes without pre-training. It differs from siblings by estimating pixel visibility between main and secondary views to regularize density, avoiding the need for pre-trained geometric priors or diffusion models. Choose this when input views are sparse (<50–100) and you need to prevent artifacts caused by insufficient data without external geometric models. A method that stabilizes implicit function learning by anchoring the scene structure with COLMAP-generated point clouds and refining optimization weights via Mask R-CNN semantic segmentation. It differs from siblings by mapping dense geometric priors into the implicit space and applying differentiated semantic weights to accelerate convergence and reduce initial MSE. Choose this for sparse view reconstruction (15–20 images) where semantic category information is available and high-fidelity detail preservation is critical. A neural field method for sparse-view CBCT reconstruction, used as a baseline in DiffVox evaluations. It is a traditional CBCT reconstruction algorithm, used as a baseline in DiffVox evaluations. Runtime: 10.3 h for 60-view reconstruction on RTX A6000. SAX-NeRF achieves higher PSNR than DiffVox for 30-60 views but is prohibitively slow for real-world deployment compared to DiffVox. A frame selection strategy that identifies maximally informative, non-redundant viewpoints from raw video footage to serve as input for NeRF training, addressing the challenge of sparse acquisition in field phenotyping. Sharpness metric (\psi{sharp}): Laplacian variance of the frame. Motion metric (\psi{motion}): Optical-flow magnitude. Coverage metric (\psi{coverage}): Penalizes geometric redundancy via inter-frame homography differences, calculated as the Frobenius norm of the difference matrix \|\Delta H\|F. Score each frame vt using the weighted sum: s(vt) = 0.4 \times \text{sharpness} + 0.3 \times \text{motion} + 0.3 \times \text{coverage}. Apply temporal non-maximum suppression with window size \omega = 5 to the scored frames. The challenge of sparse-view NeRF reconstruction has been a significant focus in computer vision, as standard NeRF requires dense sampling to resolve the ambiguity between density and color. name: NeRFVS
head: Neural Radiance Fields for Free View Synthesis via Geometry Scaffolds
body: NeRFVS is a method for indoor scene free view synthesis (FVS) that utilizes a geometry scaffold generated by off-the-shelf neural reconstruction methods to guide the optimization of a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF). It addresses the poor extrapolation performance of standard NeRF in sparse-view or low-texture regions by integrating holistic priors, specifically pseudo depth maps and view coverage information, into the training loop. Unlike standard NeRF, which suffers from distortions when rendering views significantly different from training views, NeRFVS minimizes per-pixel loss artifacts by enforcing 3D consistent geometry and regularizing density/color variance, distinguishing it from methods like SVS that rely on perceptual losses and suffer from noticeable distortions. Inputs: A collection of N RGB images \{Ii\}{i=0}^{N-1}. Camera intrinsic parameters Ki \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} for each view. Camera poses pi \in \mathbb{R}^6 for each view. A pre-generated geometry scaffold (pseudo depth maps and/or point cloud) derived from an off-the-shelf neural reconstruction method using the input images and camera parameters. Outputs: A trained NeRF model defined by volume density \sigma(\mathbf{x}) and emitted color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}), capable of rendering novel views with improved extrapolation quality. Data Structures: NeRF Model: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) or hash-grid based network (e.g., Instant-NGP compatible) mapping 3D coordinates \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} to density and color. View Coverage Map: An approximation V \in [1, N]^{H \times W \times 1} tracking the number of training views covering each pixel region, ignoring emitting directions. Formulas: 1. Volume Rendering: The expected color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} is computed as: \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) = \int{tn}^{tf} w(\mathbf{r}(t)) \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}(t), \mathbf{d}) dt where w(\mathbf{r}(t)) = T(t)\sigma(\mathbf{r}(t)) is the weight, T(t) = \exp(-\int{tn}^t \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s))ds) is the accumulated transmittance, and tn, tf are near and far bounds. 2. Depth Rendering: The expected depth \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) is: \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \int{tn}^{tf} w(\mathbf{r}(t)) t dt 3. Photometric Loss: The standard L2 loss between rendered color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) and ground truth \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}): \mathcal{L}{\text{color}}(\mathbf{r}) = \|\hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r})\|2^2 4. Robust Depth Loss: To alleviate the influence of scaffold errors (pseudo depth inaccuracies), a robust depth loss is applied. While the exact functional form of Eq. 4 in is not fully expanded in the provided text, it is described as replacing the standard L2 loss with a robust variant that handles outliers in the pseudo depth map, preventing artifacts such as the disappearance of objects like ceiling lamps. Implementer Note: A common robust loss for depth consistency in this context is the Huber loss or a truncated L2 loss, but the specific function must be sourced from the original paper's Eq. 4 if exact implementation is required. The text confirms it is distinct from standard L2. 5. Variance Loss: To decrease ambiguity in low-texture areas, the variance of the predicted density distribution and color values along each ray is regularized. This comprises two terms, Lw^{var}(\mathbf{r}) and L{var}(\mathbf{r}) (Eqs. 5 and 6 in). Implementer Note: The text states these constrain density and color distribution. Typically, this involves minimizing the variance of the weights w(t) and the color values \mathbf{c}(t) along the ray to force a single dominant surface interaction rather than a diffuse spread. The exact formulas for Eqs. 5 and 6 are not provided in the source text. 6. View Coverage Adjustment: The intensity of the depth and variance losses is dynamically adjusted based on the view coverage map V. Regions with low coverage (few-shot regions) receive weaker regularization to avoid over-constraining the geometry where data is scarce, while high-coverage regions receive stronger constraints. Numbered Steps: 1. Generate Geometry Scaffold: Use an off-the-shelf neural reconstruction method on the input images \{Ii\} and camera parameters to generate a 3D consistent geometry scaffold (pseudo depth maps). 2. Compute View Coverage: Generate the view coverage map V by counting the number of input views that observe each pixel/region, approximating the observation density. 3. Initialize NeRF: Initialize the NeRF model (e.g., Instant-NGP). 4. Render and Compute Losses: For each sampled ray \mathbf{r}: a. Render color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) and depth \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) using the volume rendering equations. b. Compute photometric loss \mathcal{L}{\text{color}}. c. Compute robust depth loss against the scaffold's pseudo depth. d. Compute variance loss Lw^{var} + L{var} to regularize density and color distributions. 5. Adjust Regularization: Scale the depth and variance loss terms based on the view coverage value V for the corresponding pixel/ray. Low coverage implies weaker regularization. 6. Optimize: Minimize the total loss (sum of photometric, adjusted robust depth, and adjusted variance losses) using gradient descent to update the NeRF parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: images: List of RGB images. poses: List of camera poses (R, t). intrinsics: Camera intrinsic matrices. scaffolddepths: Pre-computed pseudo depth maps from neural reconstruction. scaffoldcoverage: View coverage map V (H x W), count of views per pixel. numepochs: Number of training iterations. Returns: Trained NeRF model. """ # Initialize NeRF model (e.g., Instant-NGP) nerfmodel = initializenerf() for epoch in range(numepochs): totalloss = 0 for image, pose, scaffolddepth, coverage in zip(images, poses, scaffolddepths, scaffoldcoverage): # Sample rays for this image rays = samplerays(image, pose, intrinsics) # Render NeRF output # raycolors: (Nrays, 3) # raydepths: (Nrays,) # rayweights: (Nrays, Nsamples) - for variance calculation # raycolorssamples: (Nrays, Nsamples, 3) raycolors, raydepths, rayweights, raycolorssamples = rendernef(nerfmodel, rays) # 1. Photometric Loss gtcolors = getgtcolors(rays, image) losscolor = l2loss(raycolors, gtcolors) # 2. Robust Depth Loss # Align scaffold depth with rendered depth # Note: Exact robust loss function from Eq. 4 is not fully specified in text # Using a placeholder for robust depth loss (e.g., Huber or Truncated L2) scaffolddepthsaligned = aligndepths(scaffolddepth, rays) lossdepth = robustdepthloss(raydepths, scaffolddepthsaligned) # 3. Variance Loss # Regularize density (weights) and color distributions # Lwvar: Variance of weights along ray # Lvar: Variance of colors along ray lossvarw = varianceloss(rayweights) lossvarc = varianceloss(raycolorssamples) lossvariance = lossvarw + lossvarc # 4. View Coverage Adjustment # Dynamically adjust regularization strength based on coverage # Low coverage -> weaker regularization # High coverage -> stronger regularization # Note: The text says "weak depth and variance regularization where coverage is low" # This implies the loss terms are scaled by a factor derived from coverage. # Let's assume a scaling factor alpha(V) that is smaller for low V. # Implementer Note: The exact mapping from coverage count V to loss weight # is not provided. A common approach is inverse scaling or a sigmoid. # We will use a placeholder function adjustweight(coverage). coverageweight = adjustweight(coverage) # Apply adjustment to depth and variance losses # Photometric loss is typically not adjusted or adjusted differently adjustedlossdepth = lossdepth coverageweight adjustedlossvariance = lossvariance coverageweight # Total Loss batchloss = losscolor + adjustedlossdepth + adjustedlossvariance totalloss += batchloss # Backpropagate and update optimize(nerfmodel, totalloss) return nerfmodel Parameters: Geometry Scaffold Source: Off-the-shelf neural reconstruction method. View Coverage Approximation: Counts number of observations per region, ignoring emitting directions. Ablation Results (ScanNet Extrapolation): Full Model: PSNR 23.714, SSIM 0.829, LPIPS 0.414. Without Depth Loss: PSNR 23.187, SSIM 0.821, LPIPS 0.428. Without Var Loss: PSNR 23.435, SSIM 0.822, LPIPS 0.431. Without Adjustment: PSNR 23.172, SSIM 0.821, LPIPS 0.429. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Inaccurate Scaffold: If the geometry scaffold is inaccurate, extrapolation performance degrades significantly. Coverage Approximation: The view coverage map is an approximation that ignores emitting directions, which may degrade view-dependent appearance. It also fails in extreme cases like holes and thin objects. Few-Shot Regions: Reliance on pseudo depth in few-shot regions may cause poor extrapolation if the geometry is exceptionally poor. Low-Texture Areas: Without variance regularization, arbitrary density and color distributions can cause notable artifacts in extrapolation. Uses visual priors to improve NeRF optimization. Link Uses geometric and semantic priors for initialization. Link Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. However, the method can be integrated into Instant-NGP, which accelerates training and inference by a large margin without obvious performance degradation. Measured Performance: On the ScanNet dataset in an extrapolation setting, the full NeRFVS model achieved a PSNR of 23.714, SSIM of 0.829, and LPIPS of 0.414. It outperforms methods like SVS, NerfingMVS, and Dense, which suffer from artifacts or lack 3D consistency. Scaling: The method is designed for indoor scenes and room-scale free view synthesis. Strengths: Improves extrapolation ability of NeRF-based methods; reduces distortions and floaters; uses 3D consistent geometry scaffolds; robust to scaffold errors via robust depth loss; handles low-texture areas via variance regularization. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the geometry scaffold; view coverage approximation ignores emitting directions; may fail in extreme cases like holes and thin objects; poor extrapolation if geometry is exceptionally poor in few-shot regions. When to use: Indoor scene free view synthesis where extrapolation beyond training views is required, and a neural reconstruction scaffold is available. When not to use: Scenes with extreme geometry errors in the scaffold, or where view-dependent appearance is critical and the coverage approximation is insufficient. NeRFVS was introduced to address the poor extrapolation performance of NeRF in indoor scenes, particularly in low-texture and few-shot regions. It builds on the observation that while neural reconstruction methods can recover holistic scene geometry successfully, their synthesized images contain artifacts and are over-smoothed, whereas NeRF has good interpolation but poor extrapolation. The method was developed to enable free navigation in rooms by equipping NeRF with scene priors from neural reconstruction. It was evaluated on indoor datasets like ScanNet and compared against methods such as SVS, NerfingMVS, and Dense. The authors note that NeRFVS can be integrated into Instant-NGP to boost performance. name: ViP-NeRF
head: Visibility Prior NeRF
body: ViP-NeRF is a training procedure for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that introduces visibility priors to supervise density estimation, specifically designed to improve rendering quality under sparse input view conditions (fewer than 50–100 views). It prevents artifacts caused by insufficient training data by estimating whether pixels in a main view are visible in secondary views, using this information to regularize the NeRF density field. Unlike methods that rely on pre-trained geometric priors or diffusion models, ViP-NeRF computes these visibility priors using planar scanned volumes without requiring any pre-training. Inputs: A set of input images with known camera poses. For each "main view" image, a set of "secondary view" images. A NeRF model parameterized by \theta, mapping 3D coordinates \mathbf{x} and viewing directions \mathbf{d} to density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Outputs: A trained NeRF model. A visibility prior map for the main view. Data Structures: Plane Scan Volume: A list of 2D error maps. For a given main view and secondary view pair, this volume contains error maps corresponding to different depth planes. Visibility Prior Map: A 2D map of the same resolution as the main view image, where each pixel value indicates the likelihood of visibility (derived from thresholded minimum error). Algorithm: 1. Visibility Regularization Setup: The method integrates a visibility regularization term into the NeRF training loss. This term uses the visibility prior map to supervise the density \sigma of the NeRF. 2. Visibility Prior Estimation: For a specific main view I{\text{main}} and a secondary view I{\text{sec}}, estimate the visibility of each pixel in I{\text{main}} by checking if it is visible in I{\text{sec}}. 3. Effective Prediction of Visibility (Planar Scan): a. Define a set of depth planes D = \{d1, d2, \dots, dk\} relative to the camera frame of the secondary view. b. For each depth plane di \in D: i. Warp the image I{\text{sec}} to the coordinate system of the main view using the known camera poses and the depth di. Let the warped image be I{\text{warped}}^{(i)}. ii. Compute an error map E^{(i)} between the main view I{\text{main}} and the warped image I{\text{warped}}^{(i)}. c. Find the minimum error for each pixel across all depth planes: E{\min}(u, v) = \min{i} E^{(i)}(u, v) where (u, v) are pixel coordinates in the main view. d. Threshold the minimum error map E{\min} to obtain the visibility prior map V{\text{map}}: V{\text{map}}(u, v) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } E{\min}(u, v) < \tau \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where \tau is a predefined threshold. 4. NeRF Training with Visibility Prior: a. Render the main view using the current NeRF model. b. Compute the standard photometric loss between the rendered image and I{\text{main}}. c. Compute the visibility regularization loss. For pixels where V{\text{map}}(u, v) = 1, enforce that the accumulated density along the ray should correspond to a visible surface. d. Update NeRF parameters \theta using gradient descent. Parameters: \tau: Threshold for visibility prior map. Value not given in the sources. D: Set of depth planes. The number of planes and their range are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Interpolation methods that weigh Block-NeRFs based on per-pixel or per-image predicted visibility to improve sharpness of distant areas. On the Mission Bay dataset, Pixelwise Visibility achieved a PSNR of 27.39 and Imagewise Visibility achieved a PSNR of 27.41. These methods produce sharper reconstructions of far-away areas but are prone to temporal inconsistency, making them suitable only for still images. Time and Memory Complexity: The method requires computing planar scanned volumes for each main-secondary view pair during training, which adds computational overhead. The complexity depends on the number of depth planes and the resolution of the images. Measured Performance: On the RealEstate-10K dataset, ViP-NeRF achieves a PSNR index 3–4 points higher than the latest paper in 2, 3, and 4 input views. Strengths: Improves rendering quality under sparse view conditions without pre-training. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the threshold \tau and the set of depth planes. Performance may degrade if camera poses are inaccurate. When to use: When training NeRFs with very few input views (e.g., 2–4 views) and no external geometric priors are available. When not to use: When temporal consistency is required for video rendering, as related visibility-based interpolation methods are prone to temporal inconsistency. ViP-NeRF was introduced to address the challenge of novel view synthesis with sparse input views. It builds on the idea that visibility information from multiple views can provide a reliable estimate to supervise the density of the NeRF. The method was proposed in the context of improving the rendering quality of synthesized images from new viewpoints under sparse input view conditions. name: Sparse NeRF Reconstruction with Geometric and Semantic Initialization
head: Geometric initialization based on depth prior and semantic segmentation
body: This method addresses the blurred geometry, loss of detail, and slow convergence inherent in NeRF reconstruction when using sparse input (15–20 images). It stabilizes the optimization by combining COLMAP-derived geometric priors with Mask R-CNN semantic segmentation to guide the initialization of the implicit radiation field. Unlike standard NeRF which suffers from randomness in initialization, this approach anchors the scene structure with depth priors and applies differentiated semantic weights to accelerate convergence and improve fidelity. Inputs: 15–20 consumer-grade images (mobile phone or ordinary SLR) of the scene. The method tolerates up to 10% blurred images and does not require uniform camera winding. Outputs: A NeRF model with initialized density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} parameters, ready for joint optimization. Data Structures: 1. Sparse Point Cloud: Generated by COLMAP. Density: 10–15 points/mm². 2. Semantic Masks: Binary or categorical masks from Mask R-CNN. Categories: Product, Exhibition Stand, Background. Accuracy: 92%. 3. Dense Point Cloud: Generated by Poisson Surface Reconstruction. Density: \ge50 points/mm². Empty rate: \le5%. 4. NeRF Implicit Function: \sigma(\mathbf{x}) and \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}). Initialized based on the dense point cloud. Parameters: Semantic Optimization Weights: Product area weight wp = 0.7, Exhibition stand weight we = 0.2, Background weight wb = 0.1. Noise Filter Threshold: Density < 0.5 points/mm². Steps: 1. COLMAP Sparse Point Cloud Generation: Perform feature matching using the SIFT algorithm and camera pose estimation on the sparse input images to generate a sparse point cloud. This cloud serves as the initial geometric prior, covering the main structure (product, exhibition stand, background) with a density of 10–15 points/mm². 2. Mask R-CNN Semantic Segmentation: Input the sparse images into a pre-trained Mask R-CNN model to generate semantic masks. The masks divide the scene into three categories: product, exhibition stand, and background, with 92% accuracy. 3. Point Cloud Filtering and Completion: Filter noise points from the sparse point cloud using a statistical outlier filter, removing points with density < 0.5 points/mm². Apply the Poisson surface reconstruction algorithm to the filtered cloud to fill empty regions (empty rate \le5%). Generate a dense point cloud with density \ge50 points/mm², ensuring geometric continuity. 4. Initial Radiation Field Model Initialization: Map the dense point cloud to the implicit function space of NeRF. Initialize the spatial distribution parameters (density \sigma, color \mathbf{c}) of the radiation field based on this geometry. The semantic masks are used to assign the differentiated optimization weights (wp, we, wb) during subsequent training. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sparsenerfreconstruction(imagepaths): # Step 1: COLMAP Sparse Point Cloud Generation # Perform feature matching (SIFT) and camera pose estimation sparsecloud = colmapprocess(imagepaths) # sparsecloud density: 10-15 points/mm^2 # Step 2: Mask R-CNN Semantic Segmentation # Generate semantic masks for each image semanticmasks = maskrcnnsegment(imagepaths) # Categories: product, exhibition stand, background # Accuracy: 92% # Step 3: Point Cloud Filtering and Completion # Filter noise points (density < 0.5 points/mm^2) filteredcloud = statisticaloutlierfilter(sparsecloud, threshold=0.5) # Apply Poisson surface reconstruction to fill empty regions # Empty rate <= 5% densecloud = poissonsurfacereconstruction(filteredcloud) # densecloud density >= 50 points/mm^2 # Step 4: Initial Radiation Field Model Initialization # Map dense point cloud to NeRF implicit space # Initialize sigma and c based on geometry nerfmodel = initializenerf(densecloud) # Set semantic optimization weights for training # Product: 0.7, Exhibition stand: 0.2, Background: 0.1 semanticweights = { 'product': 0.7, 'exhibitionstand': 0.2, 'background': 0.1 } return nerfmodel, semanticweights Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Blurred Images: The method tolerates a fault rate of \le10% blurred images, but exceeding this may degrade the COLMAP reconstruction and semantic segmentation accuracy. Empty Regions: Poisson reconstruction is used to handle empty regions, but if the empty rate exceeds 5%, the geometric continuity may be compromised. Semantic Accuracy: The method relies on 92% accurate semantic masks. Misclassification could lead to incorrect weight assignment during optimization. A joint optimization algorithm that simultaneously enhances geometric accuracy and appearance realism by balancing convergence speed and precision through a hierarchical iterative process. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF training by explicitly decoupling geometry correction and appearance restoration into weighted phases within a single optimization loop, leveraging sparse geometric priors and semantic masks to accelerate convergence and improve detail fidelity under sparse input conditions. Performance: Initial MSE loss is reduced from 0.12–0.15 (original NeRF) to <0.05. Convergence speed is increased by 50%. Input Requirements: 15–20 consumer-grade images. No strict requirement for uniform winding. Fault tolerance rate \le10% blurred images. Strengths: Addresses blurred geometry and loss of detail under sparse input. Accelerates convergence. Differentiated optimization based on semantic characteristics. Limitations: Relies on external tools (COLMAP, Mask R-CNN). Performance depends on the accuracy of semantic segmentation (92%) and the quality of the initial sparse point cloud. When to use: VR advertising scenarios requiring fast generation and high fidelity from sparse data. When not to use: Dense input scenarios where standard NeRF may suffice, or scenes with significant motion blur exceeding the 10% fault tolerance. This method was proposed in "Efficient Sparse Input Scene Reconstruction and Real-Time Rendering for VR Advertising Using Optimized NeRF Framework" (Informatica 50, 2026). It addresses the core demands of VR advertising scenarios for data scarcity, fast generation, and high fidelity. The innovation lies in the bidirectional constraint initialization of depth priors and semantic-guided differentiated initialization, addressing the defect of traditional geometric initialization that emphasizes the whole over the part. name: Hierarchical Iterative Joint Optimization for Geometry and Appearance
head: Hierarchical Iterative Joint Optimization
body: A joint optimization algorithm that simultaneously enhances geometric accuracy and appearance realism by balancing convergence speed and precision through a hierarchical iterative process. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF training by explicitly decoupling geometry correction and appearance restoration into weighted phases within a single optimization loop, leveraging sparse geometric priors and semantic masks to accelerate convergence and improve detail fidelity under sparse input conditions. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Sparse input images (15-20 images), COLMAP sparse point clouds (geometric prior), Mask R-CNN semantic masks, initial MLP parameters. Outputs: Optimized NeRF implicit function parameters, refined depth map, rendered texture with enhanced contrast. Data Structures MLP Parameters: Initialized as random values within the range [-0.01, 0.01]. Geometric Parameters: Constrained by depth priors to avoid random initialization bias. Loss Weights: Scalars \alpha, \beta, \gamma summing to 1.0, adjusted per phase. Formulas The total loss function is defined as: L{total} = \alpha \cdot L{geo} + \beta \cdot L{app} + \gamma \cdot L{reg} Where: L{geo}: Geometric loss, calculated based on the difference between the depth prior point cloud and the NeRF predicted depth. L{app}: Appearance loss, calculated as the L1 pixel difference between the NeRF rendered image and the input image. L{reg}: Regularization loss, constraining the smoothness of implicit functions to avoid local overfitting. Parameters Optimizer: AdamW. Initial Learning Rate: 5 \times 10^{-4}. Learning Rate Decay: Attenuates by 10% every 1000 rounds. Convergence Threshold: Relative change of L{total} between consecutive 500 rounds < 10^{-5}. Post-Processing Gaussian Filter: \sigma = 0.5. Total Rounds: 5000 (base) + up to 1000 (extension). Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize the implicit function parameters of NeRF using geometric priors from COLMAP sparse point clouds and semantic masks from Mask R-CNN. Set MLP initial parameters to random values within [-0.01, 0.01]. Constrain geometric parameters by the depth prior. 2. Iterative Optimization Phase 1 (Rounds 0-2000): Focus on geometric structure correction. Set weights \alpha=0.5, \beta=0.4, \gamma=0.1. This prioritizes aligning the predicted depth with the depth prior to correct scene distortion. 3. Iterative Optimization Phase 2 (Rounds 2001-5000): Focus on appearance detail restoration. Adjust weights to \alpha=0.3, \beta=0.6, \gamma=0.1. This enhances texture detail fidelity (e.g., metal brushing, leather pores). 4. Convergence Judgment: Check if the relative change of L{total} between consecutive 500 rounds is less than 10^{-5}. If convergence is not achieved after 5000 rounds, reduce the learning rate to 10^{-5} and optimize for an additional 1000 rounds to avoid local optima. 5. Post-Processing: Filter the predicted depth map using a Gaussian filter (\sigma=0.5) to smooth geometric noise. Perform histogram equalization on the rendered texture to enhance contrast consistency. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hierarchicaljointoptimization(images, colmappoints, semanticmasks): # Step 1: Initialization mlpparams = [random.uniform(-0.01, 0.01) for in range(numparams)] geoparams = constrainbydepthprior(colmappoints) optimizer = AdamW(params=mlpparams, lr=5e-4) prevltotal = None converged = False # Step 2: Iterative Optimization for round in range(5000): # Adjust weights based on phase if round < 2000: alpha, beta, gamma = 0.5, 0.4, 0.1 else: alpha, beta, gamma = 0.3, 0.6, 0.1 # Decay learning rate every 1000 rounds currentlr = 5e-4 (0.9 (round // 1000)) optimizer.lr = currentlr # Forward pass and loss calculation predicteddepth = nerfpredictdepth(mlpparams, geoparams) renderedimage = nerfrender(mlpparams, geoparams) lgeo = calculategeoloss(predicteddepth, colmappoints) lapp = calculatel1loss(renderedimage, images) lreg = calculatesmoothnessloss(mlpparams) ltotal = alpha lgeo + beta lapp + gamma lreg # Backward pass optimizer.zerograd() ltotal.backward() optimizer.step() # Step 3: Convergence Judgment (every 500 rounds) if round % 500 == 0 and round > 0: if prevltotal is not None and abs(ltotal - prevltotal) / prevltotal < 1e-5: converged = True break prevltotal = ltotal # Handle non-convergence after 5000 rounds if not converged: optimizer.lr = 1e-5 for extraround in range(1000): predicteddepth = nerfpredictdepth(mlpparams, geoparams) renderedimage = nerfrender(mlpparams, geoparams) lgeo = calculategeoloss(predicteddepth, colmappoints) lapp = calculatel1loss(renderedimage, images) lreg = calculatesmoothnessloss(mlpparams) ltotal = alpha lgeo + beta lapp + gamma lreg optimizer.zerograd() ltotal.backward() optimizer.step() # Step 4: Post-Processing depthmap = filtergaussian(predicteddepth, sigma=0.5) texture = histogramequalization(renderedimage) return mlpparams, depthmap, texture def constrainbydepthprior(points): return points # Constrained by depth prior to avoid random initialization bias def nerfpredictdepth(params, geoparams): return computedepthfromimplicitfunction(params, geoparams) def nerfrender(params, geoparams): return volumerender(params, geoparams) def calculategeoloss(preddepth, priorpoints): return mean(abs(preddepth - priorpoints)) def calculatel1loss(rendered, inputimg): return mean(abs(rendered - inputimg)) def calculatesmoothnessloss(params): return mean(abs(diff(params))) def filtergaussian(depth, sigma): return convolve(depth, gaussiankernel(sigma)) def histogramequalization(texture): return equalizehistogram(texture) class AdamW: def init(self, params, lr): self.params = params self.lr = lr def zerograd(self): for p in self.params: p.grad = 0.0 def step(self): for p in self.params: p.data -= self.lr p.grad Edge Cases and Pitfalls Local Optima: If convergence criteria are not met by round 5000, the method explicitly extends training with a reduced learning rate to escape local optima. Initialization Bias: Random initialization of MLP parameters without geometric constraints can lead to bias; thus, geometric parameters are constrained by depth priors. Geometric Noise: Without post-processing, predicted depth maps may contain noise; a Gaussian filter is required to smooth this. Time Complexity: Total training rounds are 5000, which is 75% shorter than the original NeRF's 20,000 rounds. Performance: Under sparse input conditions, PSNR increased by 2.3 \pm 0.2 dB (mean \pm std over 10 trials) compared to baseline methods. Strengths: Balances convergence speed and optimization precision; effectively handles sparse input by leveraging geometric and semantic priors; reduces training time significantly. Limitations: Requires pre-processing steps (COLMAP, Mask R-CNN) to generate priors and masks; relies on specific hyperparameter tuning for loss weights and learning rate decay. When to Use: Suitable for sparse input scene reconstruction (15-20 images) where geometric accuracy and appearance realism are critical, such as in VR advertising. This method was proposed in the paper "Efficient Sparse Input Scene Reconstruction and Real-Time Rendering for VR Advertising Using Optimized NeRF Framework" by Y. Tao et al., published in Informatica 50 (2026). It addresses the challenges of blurred geometry, loss of detail, and slow convergence in sparse NeRF reconstruction by integrating geometric priors from COLMAP and semantic guidance from Mask R-CNN into a joint optimization framework. name: SAX-NeRF
head: Neural Attenuation Fields, NAF, Nesterov
body: SAX-NeRF is a neural field method for sparse-view Cone-Beam CT (CBCT) reconstruction that models the 3D volume as a continuous attenuation field. It solves the problem of reconstructing high-quality 3D volumes from a limited number of 2D X-ray projections, addressing sparse-view artifacts like floaters and aliasing. Unlike traditional iterative algorithms, it uses differentiable rendering to optimize neural network parameters directly against projection data. It is distinguished from its siblings NeRFVS and ViP-NeRF by its specific formulation as a baseline for differentiable voxel-based methods, often cited for its high reconstruction quality (PSNR) but prohibitive runtime. Inputs: K 2D X-ray projections (angles and pixel values); camera extrinsics and intrinsics for each view. Outputs: A neural network \mathcal{N} representing the attenuation coefficient field \mu(\mathbf{x}), where \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Data Structures: The core data structure is a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) \mathcal{N}. The inputs to the MLP are 3D coordinates \mathbf{x}, and the output is a scalar attenuation value \mu. The specific architecture details (hidden layers, activation functions, encoding) are not explicitly detailed in the provided sources, only that it is a "neural field method". Steps: 1. Sampling: For each training image, sample 3D points \mathbf{x}i along the rays corresponding to the 2D pixels. Typically, points are sampled uniformly or stratified along the ray segment within the volume bounds. 2. Network Evaluation: Query the neural network to get attenuation coefficients: \mui = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}i). 3. Differentiable Rendering: Compute the predicted 2D projection intensity I{pred} by integrating the attenuation along the ray. The sources mention Siddon's method as a differentiable rendering technique used in related baselines (DiffVox) for comparison, but do not explicitly specify the rendering integrator for SAX-NeRF itself, only that it is a neural field method. Standard NeRF-style volume rendering is implied: I{pred} = \sumi Ti (1 - e^{-\mui \deltai}), where Ti is transmittance and \deltai is step size. 4. Loss Computation: Compare I{pred} with the ground truth projection I{gt} using a loss function, likely Mean Squared Error (MSE) given PSNR reporting. 5. Optimization: Update the neural network parameters using gradient descent to minimize the loss. Parameters: Number of views K: Evaluated at 5, 10, 20, 30, 60 views. Hardware: RTX A6000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Runtime: The method is prohibitively slow for real-world deployment. Sparse Views: Performance degrades as the number of views decreases, though it outperforms traditional methods in PSNR for 30-60 views. DIF-Net is a supervised deep learning method for sparse-view Cone-Beam CT (CBCT) reconstruction that formulates the CT volume as a continuous intensity field g: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}, regressing the intensity value v of an arbitrary 3D point p from K 2D projections I. Unlike NeRF-based methods that require per-patient optimization, DIF-Net learns prior knowledge from a large dataset, enabling high-quality reconstruction from extremely sparse views (\le 10) without per-scan training. It differs from voxel-based methods by avoiding 3D CNNs for feature decoding, thereby reducing memory requirements and enabling scalable output resolutions without model retraining. Time Complexity: Prohibitively slow. Takes 10.3 hours to reconstruct a volume from 60 input views on an RTX A6000. This is orders of magnitude slower than traditional methods like Siddon's method or Nesterov, which take no more than 5 minutes. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: PSNR: Achieves higher PSNR than DiffVox for 30-60 views. Quality: Produces higher fidelity novel views with fewer stereotypical sparse-view artifacts (floaters, aliasing) compared to previous neural field methods. Strengths: High reconstruction quality (PSNR) for moderate sparse-view counts (30-60 views); effective at reducing sparse-view artifacts. Limitations: Extremely slow runtime (10.3h for 60 views), making it unsuitable for real-world clinical deployment compared to faster baselines. When to use: When reconstruction quality (PSNR) is prioritized over speed and sufficient time is available for per-scan optimization. When not to use: When real-time or near-real-time reconstruction is required, or when the number of views is very low (where DIF-Net may be preferable) or very high (where traditional methods are faster and comparable). SAX-NeRF (also known as Neural Attenuation Fields or NAF) is a neural field method for sparse-view CBCT reconstruction. It is used as a baseline in evaluations of differentiable voxel-based reconstruction methods, such as DiffVox. The method is cited in the context of comparing neural field approaches against traditional iterative algorithms (like Siddon's method, Nesterov) and other neural field methods (like NAF). The name "SAX-NeRF" appears to be a specific variant or alias used in the DiffVox paper, potentially referencing the "Neural Attenuation Fields" (NAF) work by Zha et al. [4] or a specific implementation detail. The sources do not provide the original publication date or authors for "SAX-NeRF" specifically, only citing the DiffVox paper which uses it as a baseline. name: DIF-Net
head: Continuous Intensity Field Representation, Deep Intensity Field Network
body: DIF-Net is a supervised deep learning method for sparse-view Cone-Beam CT (CBCT) reconstruction that formulates the CT volume as a continuous intensity field g: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}, regressing the intensity value v of an arbitrary 3D point p from K 2D projections I. Unlike NeRF-based methods that require per-patient optimization, DIF-Net learns prior knowledge from a large dataset, enabling high-quality reconstruction from extremely sparse views (\le 10) without per-scan training. It differs from voxel-based methods by avoiding 3D CNNs for feature decoding, thereby reducing memory requirements and enabling scalable output resolutions without model retraining. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: K 2D projection images I = \{I1, \dots, IK\}, where each Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W}. The projections correspond to scanning angles \alphai and imaging parameters \beta (distance, spacing). Outputs: A 3D volume of intensity values V, where each voxel's intensity is the output of the network for its corresponding 3D coordinate. Data Structures: Feature Maps: \{F1, \dots, FK\}, where Fi \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times H \times W}. C is the number of feature channels (default 128). Point Coordinates: A set of 3D points P = \{p1, \dots, pN\} in world coordinates, ranging from (0,0,0) to (sh H, sw W, sd D). Intensity Values: Scalar values v \in \mathbb{R}. Parameters: K: Number of sparse projection views. Typical value: \le 10. C: Number of output feature channels in the U-Net encoder. Value: 128. N: Number of points sampled per training iteration. Typical value: 10,000. s: Scaling ratio for output resolution. Condition: s > 1. Intensity Threshold: Value to distinguish foreground from background. Value: 10^{-5}. Optimizer: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with momentum 0.98 and initial learning rate 0.01. Learning Rate Schedule: Decreased by a factor of 0.001^{1/400} \approx 0.9829 per epoch. Batch Size: 4. Training Epochs: 400. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Feature Extraction: For each projection Ii, extract feature maps Fi using a shared 2D encoder. The encoder is a U-Net. Fi = \text{Encoder}(Ii), \quad Fi \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times H \times W} 2. View-Specific Querying: For a 3D point p \in \mathbb{R}^3 and view i with angle \alphai and parameters \beta: a. Compute 2D projection coordinates p'i \in \mathbb{R}^2 using the projection function \phi: p'i = \phi(p, \alphai, \beta) The projection function \phi transforms p from the world coordinate system to the scanner coordinate system via rotation matrix R(\alphai) \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}, projects onto the 2D imaging panel via projection matrix A(\beta) \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 4}, and applies homogeneous division H: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^2: \phi(p, \alphai, \beta) = H \left( A(\beta) R(\alphai) \begin{bmatrix} p \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \right) b. Query the view-specific feature fi \in \mathbb{R}^C from feature map Fi via bilinear interpolation \pi: fi = \pi(Fi, p'i) 3. Cross-View Fusion: Aggregate the list of K view-specific features F(p) = \{f1, \dots, fK\} into a single vector \bar{f} \in \mathbb{R}^C using a set function \delta(\cdot). Implementation (Uniform Angles): If training and test angles are uniformly sampled (e.g., 0^\circ to 180^\circ), F(p) is treated as an ordered list. \delta(\cdot) is implemented as a 2-layer MLP: \bar{f} = \text{MLP}{\text{fusion}}([f1, \dots, fK]) Architecture: K \times C \rightarrow \lfloor K/2 \rfloor \times C \rightarrow 1 \times C (Note: The source describes the MLP structure as K \rightarrow \lfloor K/2 \rfloor \rightarrow 1, implying the reduction happens on the view dimension, resulting in a vector of size C). Alternative (Non-Uniform Angles): If view angles are inconsistent, use max pooling or average pooling. 4. Intensity Regression: Apply a 4-layer MLP to the fused feature \bar{f} to regress the intensity value v \in \mathbb{R}: v = \text{MLP}{\text{reg}}(\bar{f}) Architecture: C \rightarrow 2C \rightarrow \lfloor C/2 \rfloor \rightarrow \lfloor C/8 \rfloor \rightarrow 1. 5. Training Sampling: To handle class imbalance (background air ~62%, foreground bones/organs ~38%): a. Identify foreground and background areas using an intensity threshold of 10^{-5} via binary classification on ground truth. b. Randomly sample N points (default 10,000) from the world coordinate range (0,0,0) to (sh H, sw W, sd D). c. Ensure balanced sampling: N/2 points from foreground and N/2 points from background. 6. Loss Calculation: Compute ground-truth intensity values \hat{V} = \{\hat{v}1, \dots, \hat{v}N\} for the sampled points using trilinear interpolation from the ground-truth CT volume. Calculate the Mean-Square-Error (MSE) loss: L(V, \hat{V}) = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (vi - \hat{v}i)^2 7. Inference/Reconstruction: a. Uniformly sample a dense point set covering all voxels. For a target resolution H \times W \times D, sample H \times W \times D points from (0,0,0) to (sh H, sw W, sd D). b. For scalable resolutions, sample \lfloor H/s \rfloor \times \lfloor W/s \rfloor \times \lfloor D/s \rfloor points to generate a coarse image (speed) or \lfloor sH \rfloor \times \lfloor sW \rfloor \times \lfloor sD \rfloor points for higher resolution, where s > 1. c. Input projections and points to DIF-Net to generate intensity values, reconstructing the CT volume. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class DIFNet(nn.Module): def init(self, K, C=128, H=256, W=256): super(DIFNet, self).init() self.K = K self.C = C # 2D Encoder (U-Net) self.encoder = UNet(inchannels=1, outchannels=C) # Cross-View Fusion MLP # Input: K C, Output: C # Architecture: (KC) -> (K//2)C -> C fusionhidden = (K // 2) C self.fusionmlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(K C, fusionhidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(fusionhidden, C)) # Intensity Regression MLP # Architecture: C -> 2C -> C//2 -> C//8 -> 1 reghidden1 = 2 C reghidden2 = C // 2 reghidden3 = C // 8 self.regmlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(C, reghidden1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(reghidden1, reghidden2), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(reghidden2, reghidden3), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(reghidden3, 1)) def forward(self, projections, points, angles, params): """ projections: Tensor of shape (K, H, W) points: Tensor of shape (N, 3) in world coordinates angles: Tensor of shape (K,) containing alphai params: Tensor of shape (K,...) containing beta (distance, spacing, etc.) """ # Step 1: Feature Extraction # projections shape: (K, 1, H, W) if encoder expects channel dim # Assuming encoder handles batch dim K features = self.encoder(projections) # Shape: (K, C, H, W) # Step 2: View-Specific Querying # Project points to 2D for each view # phi(p, alpha, beta) -> (N, 2) projectedcoords = [] for i in range(self.K): # Compute projection coordinates p'i for all N points # This requires the specific projection function phi # phi involves rotation R(alphai), projection A(beta), and homogeneous division pprimei = computeprojection(points, angles[i], params[i]) projectedcoords.append(pprimei) # Shape: (N, 2) # Query features using bilinear interpolation # features[i] is (C, H, W) # We need to sample from each feature map at the projected coordinates viewspecificfeatures = [] for i in range(self.K): # F.gridsample expects grid of shape (N, Hout, Wout, 2) # We want N points, so grid is (N, 1, 1, 2) grid = projectedcoords[i].unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1) # (N, 1, 1, 2) # features[i] is (C, H, W), unsqueeze to (1, C, H, W) for gridsample # Note: gridsample expects input (N, C, H, W) featmap = features[i].unsqueeze(0) # (1, C, H, W) sampled = F.gridsample(featmap, grid, aligncorners=True) # (1, C, 1, 1) fi = sampled.squeeze() # (C,) viewspecificfeatures.append(fi) # Stack to (N, K, C) viewspecificfeatures = torch.stack(viewspecificfeatures, dim=1) # (N, K, C) # Reshape for MLP: (N, KC) viewspecificfeaturesflat = viewspecificfeatures.view(-1, self.K self.C) # Step 3: Cross-View Fusion fusedfeatures = self.fusionmlp(viewspecificfeaturesflat) # (N, C) # Step 4: Intensity Regression intensities = self.regmlp(fusedfeatures) # (N, 1) return intensities.squeeze(-1) def computeprojection(points, angle, params): """ Computes 2D projection coordinates p' from 3D points p. phi(p, alpha, beta) = H(A(beta) R(alpha) [p; 1]) """ # points: (N, 3) # Add homogeneous coordinate pointshomo = torch.cat([points, torch.oneslike(points[:,:1])], dim=1) # (N, 4) # Rotation matrix R(alpha) # R(alpha) transforms world to scanner coordinates # Implementation depends on specific rotation convention R = getrotationmatrix(angle) # (4, 4) # Projected in scanner coordinates pointsscanner = torch.matmul(pointshomo, R.t()) # (N, 4) # Projection matrix A(beta) # A(beta) projects to 2D panel # Implementation depends on specific camera model A = getprojectionmatrix(params) # (3, 4) pointspanelhomo = torch.matmul(pointsscanner, A.t()) # (N, 3) # Homogeneous division H # Map homogeneous coordinates to Cartesian x = pointspanelhomo[:, 0] / pointspanelhomo[:, 2] y = pointspanelhomo[:, 1] / pointspanelhomo[:, 2] return torch.stack([x, y], dim=1) # (N, 2) def getrotationmatrix(angle): # Placeholder for specific rotation matrix implementation # Returns a (4, 4) matrix pass def getprojectionmatrix(params): # Placeholder for specific projection matrix implementation # Returns a (3, 4) matrix pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Class Imbalance: Uniform sampling leads to imbalanced prediction because background (air) occupies more space than foreground (bones/organs). Using an intensity threshold of 10^{-5} to balance foreground and background sampling is critical. Point Count: Using fewer points (e.g., 5,000) may destabilize the loss and gradient during training, leading to performance degradation. 10,000 points are sufficient for best performance. View Angle Consistency: The MLP fusion assumes uniformly sampled angles. If view angles are inconsistent across training/test data, max pooling is a more general solution. Encoder Choice: Using a pre-trained ResNet18 encoder instead of U-Net does not bring improvement (PSNR/SSIM: 29.2/0.92 vs 29.3/0.92), indicating U-Net is powerful enough for feature extraction in this task. Time Complexity: Reconstruction time is ultrafast, approximately 1.6 seconds for a 256³ resolution volume with 10 views (batch size 1). This is significantly faster than iterative methods like SART (106s) and NeRF-based methods like NAF (738s). Memory Complexity: Training memory cost is 7,617 MB for DIF-Net (10-view, 256³ resolution, batch size 1). This is lower than NAF (3,095 MB is listed for NAF?
