name: NeRV Training
head: NeRV loss minimization, NeRV optimization
body: NeRV training optimizes a continuous volumetric representation that decouples scene geometry (shape) from material appearance (reflectance) and lighting interactions (visibility) to enable efficient relighting and view synthesis. It differs from standard NeRF training by introducing a separate visibility MLP that predicts ray visibility and termination depth, supervised by consistency terms with the primary shape MLP rather than ground-truth labels, allowing the simulation of direct and one-bounce indirect illumination within the training loop. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of posed RGB images of a scene and corresponding lighting environment maps. Outputs: Weights for three MLPs: Shape/Reflectance MLP (\theta) and Visibility MLP (\phi). Data Structures: 1. Positional Encoding: Inputs are mapped using NeRF's positional encoding. 3D coordinates \mathbf{x}: Maximum frequency L{\text{coord}} = 7 (frequencies 2^0 to 2^7). 3D direction vectors \boldsymbol{\omega}: Maximum frequency L{\text{dir}} = 4 (frequencies 2^0 to 2^4). 2. Shape and Reflectance MLP (\theta): Architecture: 8 fully-connected ReLU layers with 256 channels each. Input: Encoded \mathbf{x} and \boldsymbol{\omega}. Output: Volume density \sigma and reflectance properties. 3. Visibility MLP (\phi): Stage 1: 8 fully-connected ReLU layers with 256 channels each map encoded \mathbf{x} to an 8-dimensional feature vector. Stage 2: Concatenation with encoded \boldsymbol{\omega}. Stage 3: 4 fully-connected ReLU layers with 128 channels each. Output: Predicted visibility \tilde{V}\phi and expected termination depth \tilde{D}\phi. Training Procedure: 1. Initialization: Initialize \theta and \phi from scratch. 2. Ray Sampling: At each iteration, randomly sample a batch of 512 pixel rays \mathcal{R} from input images and 256 random rays \mathcal{R}' intersecting the volume. 3. Forward Pass (Pixel Rays \mathcal{R}): Render pixels using the current NeRV model (Shape/Reflectance MLPs) to obtain rendered radiance \tilde{L}(\mathbf{r}). 4. Forward Pass (Random Rays \mathcal{R}'): For each ray \mathbf{r}' \in \mathcal{R}', compute visibility V\theta(\mathbf{r}'(t)) and expected termination depth D\theta(\mathbf{r}'(t)) implied by the Shape MLP's density \sigma at each location and in either direction along the ray. Query the Visibility MLP to get predictions \tilde{V}\phi(\mathbf{r}'(t)) and \tilde{D}\phi(\mathbf{r}'(t)). 5. Loss Computation: Define tone-mapping operator \tau(x) = x/(1+x). Compute total loss \mathcal{L}: \mathcal{L} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \left\| \tau(\tilde{L}(\mathbf{r})) - \tau(L(\mathbf{r})) \right\|2^2 + \lambda \sum{\mathbf{r}' \in \mathcal{R} \setminus \mathcal{R}{\text{ret}}} \left( \left\| \tilde{V}\phi(\mathbf{r}'(t)) - V\theta(\mathbf{r}'(t)) \right\|2^2 + \left\| \tilde{D}\phi(\mathbf{r}'(t)) - D\theta(\mathbf{r}'(t)) \right\|2^2 \right) where \lambda = 20. Apply a stop gradient to V\theta and D\theta in the consistency terms so the shape MLP is not encouraged to degrade its own performance to better match the visibility MLP output. 6. Optimization: Update \theta and \phi using the Adam optimizer for 1,000,000 total iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import jax.numpy as jnp from jax import valueandgrad BATCHSIZEPIXEL = 512 BATCHSIZERANDOM = 256 LAMBDA = 20 LRINIT = 1e-5 LRDECAYTARGET = 1e-6 BETA1 = 0.9 BETA2 = 0.999 EPSILON = 1e-8 TOTALITERATIONS = 1000000 NUMSAMPLES = 256 def positionalencoding(x, maxfreqlog2): """Standard NeRF positional encoding.""" scales = jnp.array([2i for i in range(maxfreqlog2 + 1)]) x = jnp.expanddims(x, axis=-1) scales return jnp.concatenate([jnp.sin(x), jnp.cos(x)], axis=-1) def mlpforward(params, x): """Standard fully-connected ReLU MLP forward pass.""" for W, b in params: x = jnp.dot(x, W) + b x = jnp.maximum(0, x) return x def shapereflectancemlp(params, xenc, omegaenc): """8 FC ReLU layers, 256 channels. Returns sigma and reflectance.""" return mlpforward(params, jnp.concatenate([xenc, omegaenc], axis=-1)) def visibilitymlp(params, xenc, omegaenc): """ Stage 1: 8 FC ReLU (256 ch) -> 8-dim vector. Concat with omegaenc. Stage 2: 4 FC ReLU (128 ch) -> returns V, D. """ feat = mlpforward(params['stage1'], xenc) combined = jnp.concatenate([feat, omegaenc], axis=-1) return mlpforward(params['stage2'], combined) def computevisibilityanddepth(sigma, tsamples, delta): """ Compute visibility V and expected termination depth D from density sigma. V(x, c) = exp(-sum{s < t} sigma(x(s)) delta) D is expected termination depth. """ transmittance = jnp.exp(-jnp.cumsum(sigma delta, axis=-1)) visibility = transmittance alpha = 1 - jnp.exp(-sigma delta) weights = alpha transmittance depth = jnp.sum(tsamples weights, axis=-1) / (jnp.sum(weights, axis=-1) + 1e-8) return visibility, depth def tonemapping(x): return x / (1 + x) def adamstep(params, grad, state, lr): """Standard Adam optimizer step.""" m = BETA1 state['m'] + (1 - BETA1) grad v = BETA2 state['v'] + (1 - BETA2) grad2 mhat = m / (1 - BETA1state['t']) vhat = v / (1 - BETA2state['t']) newparams = params - lr mhat / (jnp.sqrt(vhat) + EPSILON) return newparams, {'m': m, 'v': v, 't': state['t'] + 1} def lossfn(paramsshape, paramsvis, batchrays, batchrandomrays, gtimages): # 1. Pixel Ray Loss # Render pixels using shape/reflectance MLP with 256 stratified samples t = jnp.linspace(0, 1, NUMSAMPLES) delta = t[1] - t[0] points = batchrays[:, None,:] + t[None,:, None] batchrays[:, None,:] xenc = positionalencoding(points, 7) omegaenc = positionalencoding(batchrays, 4) sigma = shapereflectancemlp(paramsshape, xenc, omegaenc) renderedradiance = jnp.sum(sigma delta, axis=-1) # Simplified volume rendering pixelloss = jnp.sum(jnp.square(tonemapping(renderedradiance) - tonemapping(gtimages))) # 2. Random Ray Consistency Loss points = batchrandomrays[:, None,:] + t[None,:, None] batchrandomrays[:, None,:] xenc = positionalencoding(points, 7) omegaenc = positionalencoding(batchrandomrays, 4) sigma = shapereflectancemlp(paramsshape, xenc, omegaenc) vtheta, dtheta = computevisibilityanddepth(sigma, t, delta) xencvis = positionalencoding(points, 7) omegaencvis = positionalencoding(batchrandomrays, 4) vphi, dphi = visibilitymlp(paramsvis, xencvis, omegaencvis) # Stop gradient on Vtheta and Dtheta consistencyloss = jnp.sum(jnp.square(vphi - vtheta)) + jnp.sum(jnp.square(dphi - dtheta)) return pixelloss + LAMBDA consistencyloss def train(): # Initialize paramsshape, paramsvis from scratch # Initialize Adam state with lr=1e-5, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, eps=1e-8 # Sample 512 pixel rays and 256 random rays intersecting volume # Get ground truth pixels for sampled rays lr = LRINIT for i in range(TOTALITERATIONS): lr = max(LRDECAYTARGET, lr 0.999) # Exponential decay to 1e-6 loss, grads = valueandgrad(lossfn)(paramsshape, paramsvis, batchrays, batchrandomrays, gtimages) paramsshape, state = adamstep(paramsshape, grads['shape'], state, lr) paramsvis, state = adamstep(paramsvis, grads['vis'], state, lr) Parameters: Batch Size (Pixel Rays): 512. Batch Size (Random Rays): 256. Loss Weight (\lambda): 20. Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: Starts at 10^{-5}, decays exponentially to 10^{-6}. Adam Hyperparameters: \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.999, \epsilon = 10^{-8}. Total Iterations: 1,000,000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Stop Gradient: The shape MLP must not be updated via the consistency loss terms to prevent it from degrading its rendering quality to match the visibility MLP. \mathcal{R}{\text{ret}}: The set \mathcal{R}{\text{ret}} is subtracted from the random rays in the consistency loss. The exact criteria for exclusion are not provided in the sources. Visibility Supervision: The visibility MLP is not supervised by ground-truth visibility or depth. It is only optimized for consistency with the shape MLP's current geometry estimate. Time Complexity: Rendering involves 256 stratified samples per ray. The visibility MLP adds computational overhead but reduces the complexity of computing direct and indirect illumination from quadratic and cubic to linear, enabling the simulation of direct illumination from environment lighting and one-bounce indirect illumination within the training loop. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Hardware: Implemented in JAX and trained on 128 TPU cores. Strengths: Enables simulation of direct illumination from environment lighting and one-bounce indirect illumination within the training loop. Decouples geometry and appearance for relighting. Limitations: Requires posed RGB images and corresponding lighting environments for each scene. The visibility MLP is not supervised by ground truth, relying solely on consistency with the shape MLP. NeRV (Neural Reflectance and Visibility Fields) was introduced in the paper "NeRV: Neural Reflectance and Visibility Fields for Relighting and View Synthesis". The method was developed to address the limitations of standard NeRF in handling relighting and complex lighting interactions by explicitly modeling visibility and reflectance fields. It builds on the NeRF training loop but adds the visibility MLP and consistency losses. NeRV: Neural Reflectance and Visibility Fields for Relighting and View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr46437.2021.00741, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Scene Representation and Architecture
head: NeRF Architectures, Radiance Field Models
body: Scene Representation and Architecture defines the neural network topologies, data structures, and optimization strategies used to represent and optimize the radiance field F\Theta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) = (\sigma, \mathbf{c}). While the canonical NeRF uses a single deep MLP, this family encompasses methods that modify the network topology (e.g., multi-space decomposition, tensor grids), introduce auxiliary networks for specific tasks (e.g., depth estimation, instance segmentation), or alter the input/output mappings to support dynamic scenes, relighting, or single-view synthesis. These architectures set themselves apart from standard NeRF by addressing specific limitations such as computational cost, geometric ambiguity, lack of semantic understanding, or the inability to handle dynamic content. All methods in this family share the mechanism of mapping 6D input coordinates (3D position \mathbf{x} and 2D viewing direction \mathbf{d}) to 4D output values (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}) using a differentiable neural network. This allows the radiance field to be optimized through the volumetric rendering integral. Input Representation: Raw coordinates \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{d} are rarely used directly due to the spectral bias of MLPs, which struggle to fit high-frequency details. They are mapped to a higher-dimensional space using positional encoding \gamma(\cdot). For a coordinate \mathbf{x}, the encoding includes the original value and sinusoidal functions at increasing frequencies: \gamma(\mathbf{x}) = (\sin(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{x})) where L is the number of frequency bands. Network Topology: The canonical implementation uses two coupled Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): a density network F\sigma and a color network Fc. 1. Density Network: Takes the encoded position \gamma(\mathbf{x}) as input. It consists of L hidden layers with ReLU activations and skip connections from the input to every 4th layer to preserve low-frequency information. The output is the density \sigma. 2. Color Network: Takes the encoded position \gamma(\mathbf{x}), the raw viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and the intermediate feature vector from the density network (usually the output of the last hidden layer before the density head) as input. It predicts the color \mathbf{c} using a final ReLU or sigmoid activation. Rendering Integration: During training, rays are sampled at points \mathbf{x}i along the ray. The MLPs predict \sigmai and \mathbf{c}i. The pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) is computed via volumetric rendering: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i, \quad \text{where } \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) and \deltai is the distance between samples. Specific Model Architectures define the neural network topologies, data structures, and optimization strategies used to represent and optimize the radiance field F\Theta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) = (\sigma, \mathbf{c}). While the canonical NeRF uses a single deep MLP, this family encompasses methods that modify the network topology (e.g., multi-space decomposition, tensor grids), introduce auxiliary networks for specific tasks (e.g., depth estimation, instance segmentation), or alter the input/output mappings to support dynamic scenes, relighting, or single-view synthesis. These architectures set themselves apart from standard NeRF by addressing specific limitations such as computational cost, geometric ambiguity, lack of semantic understanding, or the inability to handle dynamic content. This family of methods addresses the scalability limits of single-network NeRFs by decomposing the scene into multiple, smaller representations (submodules, blocks, or fields) that are optimized and queried independently. While the parent Scene Representation and Architecture establishes the global mapping from 6D coordinates to radiance properties, these methods partition the domain to enable parallel training, reduce memory footprint, or handle dynamic content. They differ from siblings like Specific Model Architectures by focusing on the structural decomposition of the scene space rather than the internal topology of the neural network itself. This family represents a scene as a single MLP f\theta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\mathbf{c}, \sigma) that maps a 3D position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a viewing direction \mathbf{d} \in S^2 to an emitted color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a volumetric density \sigma \ge 0. Rendering uses the classical volume rendering integral along rays cast from the camera, with no explicit geometry—geometry emerges from where \sigma is high after photometric optimization on multi-view images. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using a single, monolithic MLP without spatial partitioning or explicit geometric priors, relying entirely on positional encoding and hierarchical sampling to capture scene details. Unlike Mip-NeRF 360 which handles unbounded scenes via contraction, or NeRF-FF which addresses defocus, the original architecture operates within defined near and far ray bounds. NeRFReN addresses the failure of standard Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) to render reflective surfaces, such as glass and mirrors, by separating the radiance field into transmitted and reflected components. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly modeling the reflection fraction \beta derived from the transmitted geometry, allowing for the separation of reflection artifacts from physical entities. Neural Body is a method for synthesizing novel views of dynamic human avatars from sparse multi-view videos by combining NeRF volume rendering with a vertex-based deformable human body model (SMPL). It solves the problem of rendering articulated bodies with moving poses, which standard NeRF approaches struggle with due to the complexity of modeling large non-rigid deformations. By anchoring latent variables to the vertices of a deformable mesh, Neural Body enables the interpolation of poses and frames, establishing a foundational paradigm for neural field rendering of human avatars. NeuMan renders a human together with a scene with novel human poses and novel views from a single video by jointly optimizing a scene NeRF and a pose-driven human NeRF. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF variants by introducing a canonical space based on the Da-pose SMPL mesh to avoid volume collision during warping, and an error-correction network to handle details not expressed by the SMPL model. Unlike methods that require multi-view video or motion capture, NeuMan operates on a single monocular video sequence. AR-NeRF is an extension of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that employs an aperture camera model instead of a pinhole camera model to represent defocus effects and viewpoint changes in a unified manner within a common ray-tracing framework. It enables fully unsupervised learning of depth and defocus effects from single natural images by jointly leveraging defocus and viewpoint cues without explicit supervision or pretrained models. Unlike standard NeRF, which assumes a pinhole camera, AR-NeRF represents each pixel using a collection of rays converging at a focus plane, allowing the model to disentangle defocus-aware and defocus-independent representations through aperture randomized training. This method integrates a Signed Distance Function (SDF) with a Physically-Based Rendering (PBR) material model to achieve accurate scene representation, specifically separating specular and diffuse reflections. It addresses the limitation of standard NeRF variants in modeling mirror-like reflections by deriving smooth surface normals from the SDF gradient rather than optimizing them directly, and by using a precomputed BRDF LUT for specular calculation. It sets itself apart from siblings like Ref-NeRF by explicitly enforcing the Eikonal equation for geometric smoothness and using a standard PBR decomposition (Cd + Cs) rather than view-dependent color networks alone. Definition: A method to extract high-quality surfaces from NeRF by modeling geometry as a distance function or occupancy field and converting its output to density using a probability density function. Step: Incorporate an eikonal term to encourage geometric consistency, enforcing that the gradient norm of the learned SDF is equal to one. Formula: Density distribution: \PhiS(x) = \frac{se^{-sx}}{1+e^{-sx}}, where s is a scaling parameter and x is the SDF or occupancy value. Definition: A neural volumetric rendering framework modeling scene appearance using light transport vectors, enabling realistic relighting and view synthesis of human portraits from only five input images. Step: A UNet-style CNN extracts per-view features. An MLP regresses volume density and transport vectors. Environment maps are estimated to disentangle lighting. Trained on synthetic data and adapted to real images via a domain adaptation module. Definition: A method using per-frame learned latent codes and adding facial expression as a 76-dimensional coefficient of a morphable model constructed from Face2Face [210]. Definition: The default baseline model in Nerfstudio, integrating several advances from recent NeRF literature into a single, efficient pipeline for in-the-wild reconstruction. Step: Combine a hash-grid encoding for compact and expressive scene representation. Use Mip-NeRF 360 proposal sampling for efficient ray sampling. Apply distortion loss from Mip-NeRF 360 to stabilize convergence. Apply scene contraction to handle unbounded scenes. Apply camera poses refinement. Apply appearance embeddings to account for illumination variations across input images. The canonical NeRF architecture was introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020. It established the paradigm of using a single MLP to map 6D coordinates to radiance properties. Subsequent developments addressed specific limitations: reflective surfaces (NeRFReN, Neural Implicit Surfaces with PBR), dynamic humans (Neural Body, NeuMan), defocus (AR-NeRF), and scalability (Scene Representation and Partitioning, Nerfacto). The field has evolved from monolithic MLPs to hybrid representations and specialized architectures for specific domains like human avatars and reflective materials. name: Specific Model Architectures
head: NeRF Architectures, Neural Radiance Field Models
body: Specific Model Architectures define the neural network topologies, data structures, and optimization strategies used to represent and optimize the radiance field F\Theta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) = (\sigma, \mathbf{c}). While the canonical NeRF uses a single deep MLP, this family encompasses methods that modify the network topology (e.g., multi-space decomposition, tensor grids), introduce auxiliary networks for specific tasks (e.g., depth estimation, instance segmentation), or alter the input/output mappings to support dynamic scenes, relighting, or single-view synthesis. These architectures set themselves apart from standard NeRF by addressing specific limitations such as computational cost, geometric ambiguity, lack of semantic understanding, or the inability to handle dynamic content. All methods in this family share the mechanism of mapping 6D input coordinates (3D position \mathbf{x} and 2D viewing direction \mathbf{d}) to 4D output values (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}) using a differentiable neural network. This allows the radiance field to be optimized through the volumetric rendering integral. Input Representation: Raw coordinates \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{d} are rarely used directly due to the spectral bias of MLPs, which struggle to fit high-frequency details. They are mapped to a higher-dimensional space using positional encoding \gamma(\cdot). For a coordinate \mathbf{x}, the encoding includes the original value and sinusoidal functions at increasing frequencies: \gamma(\mathbf{x}) = (\sin(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{x})) where L is the number of frequency bands. Network Topology: The canonical implementation uses two coupled Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): a density network F\sigma and a color network Fc. 1. Density Network: Takes the encoded position \gamma(\mathbf{x}) as input. It consists of L hidden layers with ReLU activations and skip connections from the input to every 4th layer to preserve low-frequency information. The output is the density \sigma. 2. Color Network: Takes the encoded position \gamma(\mathbf{x}), the raw viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and the intermediate feature vector from the density network (usually the output of the last hidden layer before the density head) as input. It predicts the color \mathbf{c} using a final ReLU or sigmoid activation. Rendering Integration: During training, rays are sampled at points \mathbf{x}i along the ray. The MLPs predict \sigmai and \mathbf{c}i. The pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) is computed via volumetric rendering: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i, \quad \text{where } \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) and \deltai is the distance between samples. AdaNeRF employs fixed sample positions along each ray and incrementally introduces sparsity during training to achieve real-time rendering. It differs from standard NeRF by decoupling the sampling process from the shading process, using a lightweight network to predict sample importance weights, thereby reducing the number of points processed by the heavier shading network. SinNeRF is a method for reconstructing Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) from a single input image, addressing the severe under-constrained nature of single-view scene reconstruction. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF and other single-view methods by integrating image warping for depth supervision, adversarial training for texture, and global feature comparison for structural consistency. CLIP-NeRF is a neural radiance field method that enables text- or image-guided editing of 3D scenes by extracting latent space displacements from user input via the CLIP model. It differs from prior editing methods like Edit-NeRF by bypassing per-edit latent code optimization, achieving significant speedups (8–60x) through a disentangled conditional architecture that maps semantic input directly to shape and appearance modifications. NeRF-RPN is a general framework for 3D object detection within neural radiance fields that regresses bounding boxes directly from the scene representation without rendering intermediate views. It solves the problem of identifying and localizing discrete objects in a continuous, view-dependent radiance field by treating detection as a dense prediction task on a voxelized feature volume. It sets itself apart from instance-level segmentation methods like NeRF-RCNN by providing a proposal generation stage that can be used for unlabelled object detection, whereas NeRF-RCNN refines these proposals into final discrete masks and class labels. RefSR-NeRF is a framework that combines Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) with a Reference-guided Super-Resolution CNN (RefSR-CNN) to achieve high-quality novel view synthesis from low-resolution inputs. It addresses the computational explosion and memory constraints associated with training NeRF on high-resolution data by decoupling the 3D field optimization from the high-frequency detail reconstruction. Unlike methods that modify the NeRF architecture directly (e.g., AdaNeRF) or use generative priors (e.g., DiffusioNeRF), RefSR-NeRF retains a standard NeRF backbone for geometry and color while using a separate CNN to inject high-frequency details guided by a single high-resolution reference image. AligNeRF is a training strategy and architectural modification for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) designed to improve high-frequency detail recovery and mitigate artifacts caused by misalignment from moving objects or camera calibration errors. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF implementations by combining a convolution-augmented architecture with a staged, alignment-aware fine-tuning procedure that utilizes patch-based sampling and explicit spatial alignment matching. Unlike sibling methods that primarily focus on sparse representations or differentiable rendering integrals, AligNeRF explicitly addresses the spatial coherence of high-resolution features through local neighborhood encoding and robust alignment matching. DiffusioNeRF is a NeRF optimization procedure that incorporates a denoising diffusion model to learn priors for scene geometry and color, improving reconstruction quality under sparse input views. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF training by rendering random RGBD patches and backpropagating the estimated gradients of their log-likelihood to the color and density fields, effectively normalizing the scene representation. The pool proposer is a trainable neural network component used in NeRF-ID to generate fine-grained sampling positions for volume rendering. It processes coarse features from a previous sampling stage to propose new sample locations, addressing the need for adaptive sampling in differentiable volume rendering. It is distinguished from its sibling MLPMix Proposer by using a bottleneck fully connected layer and sinusoidal positional encoding summation, whereas MLPMix uses a different mixing mechanism. MS-NeRF (Multi-Space Neural Radiance Field) is a scene representation method that extends standard MLP-based NeRF architectures to handle unbounded virtual scenes containing reflective and refractive surfaces, such as mirrors. It solves the problem of rendering distortion and blurring caused by reflection or refraction, where standard NeRF fails to maintain multi-view consistency due to the geometric complexity of virtual images. Unlike sibling methods like Ref-NeRF, which require manually labeled masks for reflective surfaces and are limited to forward-facing scenes, MS-NeRF automatically handles 360-degree scenes without extra supervision. It sets itself apart by decomposing the radiance field into K parallel sub-spaces, each representing a characteristic field, and integrating them via a learned gating mechanism. NeRDi is a single-view synthesis method that leverages a pre-trained 2D image diffusion model to provide general image priors, enabling high-quality novel view synthesis from a single input image. Unlike traditional NeRF variants that rely on multi-view consistency or explicit geometric supervision alone, NeRDi minimizes the diffusion loss of rendered arbitrary views under input view constraints. It distinguishes itself by introducing semantic guidance via language embeddings and a geometric loss based on estimated depth maps to regularize the underlying 3D structure. RING-NeRF is a neural field architecture that introduces two primary inductive biases: a continuous multi-scale scene representation and a decoder latent space invariant to spatial translations and scale changes. Unlike sibling methods such as Zip-NeRF or Mip-NeRF which require explicit supervision for Level of Detail (LOD) or modify features based on observation distance, RING-NeRF produces intrinsic continuous LOD without supervision, enabling robust generalization to novel, unseen observation distances. It distinguishes itself from I-NGP by using summation rather than concatenation for multi-resolution features, ensuring the decoder latent space remains invariant to LOD, and supports dynamic resolution extension during training. Sparse and Efficient Representations address the computational and memory bottlenecks of dense, monolithic Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) by decomposing the scene representation into smaller, localized, or structured components. This family enables scalable training for large-scale scenes and faster inference through spatial partitioning, explicit sparse grids, or generalized 2D projections. Unlike the canonical NeRF which uses a single deep MLP for all queries, these methods distribute the representational capacity across multiple sub-networks, voxel structures, or planar features to reduce redundancy and accelerate convergence. Edit-NeRF is a method for user-controlled 3D scene editing that formulates the problem as a joint optimization of NeRF network parameters and latent codes. It solves the limitation of standard NeRFs, which are static and cannot be easily modified by external features, by introducing a modular network architecture with conditional radiance fields. It differs from its siblings by being the first method to execute user-controlled deformation models on NeRF using a shared shape network and instance-specific latent codes, whereas methods like CLIP-NeRF later introduced text/image guidance via CLIP embeddings. Geometric Priors and Depth Integration methods enhance standard Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by incorporating explicit geometric constraints—such as depth maps, surface normals, or Structure-from-Motion (SfM) features—into the optimization loop. Unlike standard NeRF, which relies solely on implicit photometric consistency and often suffers from ambiguous geometry in sparse-view or textureless scenarios, these methods enforce hard boundaries, metric scale, or structural consistency to improve reconstruction fidelity. They distinguish themselves from sibling methods like AdaNeRF or SinNeRF by explicitly modeling the scene's 3D structure (via SDFs, cost volumes, or depth priors) rather than just refining the radiance field's appearance or frequency representation. Generative and Style-based Models extend the NeRF framework from deterministic scene reconstruction to probabilistic 3D-aware image synthesis. Instead of optimizing a single static radiance field for a specific scene, these methods learn a distribution over 3D scenes, allowing the generation of novel, view-consistent images from latent codes. They distinguish themselves from sibling methods like Edit-NeRF or Instance-NeRF by treating the scene representation as a generative prior rather than a fixed optimization target, often employing adversarial training or diffusion-based priors to enforce photorealism and structural consistency. IRON is a neural inverse rendering pipeline that reconstructs high-quality 3D geometry and spatially varying materials from photometric images (multi-view images captured with a collocated flashlight and moving camera). It outputs triangle meshes and material textures compatible with standard graphics pipelines. Unlike standard NeRF variants that optimize density and color directly, IRON uses Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) for geometry and separate neural networks for diffuse, specular, and roughness parameters. It employs a hybrid optimization scheme: a first stage using volumetric radiance field rendering to recover correct topology, followed by a second stage using edge-aware physics-based surface rendering to refine geometry and disentangle materials from lighting. Instance-NeRF is a learning-based 3D instance segmentation pipeline that extends a pre-trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) with an additional instance field component. It takes a pre-trained NeRF model as input and learns to detect all objects within the underlying 3D scene, producing a 3D bounding box, a continuous 3D mask, and a class label for each detected object. Unlike Semantic-NeRF, which relies on 2D semantic priors that are generally consistent across views, Instance-NeRF addresses the challenge of multi-view inconsistent 2D instance masks (where the same object may receive different instance IDs in different views) without relying on 3D bounding volume priors. It achieves this by using a 3D proposal-based mask prediction network (NeRF-RCNN) to generate coarse 3D masks, projecting them to 2D to match and refine multi-view consistent segmentation maps, and then supervising the continuous instance field with these refined 2D masks. MIMO-NeRF is a neural rendering method that accelerates inference by replacing the standard Single-Input Single-Output (SISO) Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with a Multi-Input Multi-Output (MIMO) MLP. It groups neighboring samples along a ray and processes them simultaneously, reducing the number of MLP evaluations (# Run) required per pixel. Unlike knowledge distillation methods that require training a separate teacher network, MIMO-NeRF can be trained via self-supervised learning using a 3D consistency loss to resolve ambiguities in density and color inherent in grouped predictions. It maintains the original NeRF hyperparameters (sample counts and network width) while achieving superior speed-quality trade-offs compared to methods that reduce sample counts or network width. Appearance and Lighting Decomposition refers to a family of neural radiance field methods that decouple view-independent geometric and material properties from view-dependent lighting effects to enable physically plausible relighting, appearance editing, and robust reconstruction of specular surfaces. Unlike standard NeRF, which maps 6D coordinates directly to raw color and density, these methods predict intermediate physical attributes (such as normals, roughness, albedo, or reflection directions) and combine them with lighting models or environment maps during the rendering process. This separation resolves the shape-radiance ambiguity inherent in standard NeRF and allows for the accurate modeling of glossy and reflective surfaces that standard architectures fail to capture. STensoRRF is a differentiable volume rendering method that represents a 3D scene using a single 4D tensor to enable high-quality novel view synthesis and relighting. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF architectures by replacing the multi-network feature grid with a decomposed single tensor and explicitly estimating a BRDF value per point to facilitate relighting via spherical Gaussian environment maps. Unlike sibling methods that rely on complex geometric priors or multiple voxel meshes, STensoRRF achieves a 50% faster convergence rate and 1.5x faster rendering speed by combining tensor decomposition with a simplified reflectance equation. Ced-NeRF is a compact and efficient method for modeling dynamic neural radiance fields that utilizes a grid-based hybrid representation and a canonical space to model motion. It specifically addresses the problem of overfitting artifacts, such as floaters and noisy geometry, which commonly occur in hybrid representations of dynamic scenes due to fast convergence before accurate motion prediction is achieved. It distinguishes itself from siblings like AdaNeRF and Sparse and Efficient Representations by employing a high-resolution grid for rapid convergence while avoiding separated fields or models that increase training difficulty and slow rendering. This family extends static neural radiance fields to model scenes that change over time or undergo non-rigid deformation. It solves the problem of novel-view synthesis for dynamic content by introducing a time or deformation dimension to the scene representation. Unlike static methods, these models must map 6D inputs (position, direction) plus a temporal or deformation parameter to radiance properties, often using displacement fields or canonical space mappings to handle motion. Non-baked models learn separate scene features from MLP parameters via hybrid representations, enabling smaller MLPs for improved training and inference speed at the cost of increased memory. Unlike baked models that pre-compute and store final MLP outputs to accelerate inference without affecting training time, non-baked models retain the differentiability of the feature-to-output mapping during optimization, improving both phases. JacobiNeRF synthesizes a NeRF model based on second-order information (Jacobian matrix) to maximize mutual information between highly correlated entities under random scene perturbations. The rendering equation used is: \hat{C}(r, zs, zc) = \sum{i=1}^{Nc-1} ci \alphai \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right), where ai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) is consistent with discrete volume rendering. RelightingNeRF is proposed for handling unstructured photographs and free-viewpoint reconstruction, changing model architecture to output SDF values and latent features. The method inputs sampling point positions into the first MLP, which outputs SDF values and latent features. Normals, shadow cues, and specular cues are obtained from the SDF values. The second MLP takes sampling point positions, lighting positions, viewing directions, and the latent features from the first MLP to produce the final color. In DT-NeRF, both the Diffusion and Transformer models are trained jointly within a unified optimization framework, sharing the same loss function, and are not pretrained but optimized simultaneously during training through backpropagation. Baked models train, precompute, and store NeRF MLP evaluations into more accessible data structures to improve inference speed significantly without affecting training time. The canonical NeRF architecture, introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020, established the baseline of using a single deep MLP with positional encoding to map 6D coordinates to density and color. Subsequent research has diversified the architecture to address limitations in training speed, geometric accuracy, semantic understanding, and dynamic scene representation. The field has evolved from simple MLP modifications to complex hybrid systems involving grids, tensors, diffusion models, and multi-branch networks. name: SinNeRF
head: Sinusoidal NeRF
body: SinNeRF is a method for reconstructing Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) from a single input image, addressing the severe under-constrained nature of single-view scene reconstruction. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF and other single-view methods by integrating image warping for depth supervision, adversarial training for texture, and global feature comparison for structural consistency. SinNeRF builds on the canonical NeRF architecture. It maps 6D coordinates (3D position \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d}) to density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} using two coupled MLPs with positional encoding \gamma(\cdot). The rendering follows the standard volumetric integration: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i, \quad \text{where } \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) \quad where \deltai is the distance between samples. Inputs: Single reference image I{ref} with known camera intrinsics and pose. Randomly sampled unseen view poses for regularization. Outputs: A trained NeRF model capable of synthesizing novel views. Data Structures: MLP: Same architecture as the original NeRF paper. Density Network F\sigma: Input \gamma(\mathbf{x}), L hidden layers with ReLU, skip connections from input to every 4th layer. Output \sigma. Color Network Fc: Input \gamma(\mathbf{x}), raw \mathbf{d}, and intermediate feature vector from F\sigma. Output \mathbf{c}. Discriminator: CNN discriminator for patch-wise texture supervision. Feature Extractor: Pretrained Vision Transformer (DINO-ViT) for global structure prior. Training Steps: 1. Patch Sampling: Randomly sample two patches of rays: one from the reference view and one from a randomly sampled unseen view. 2. Rendering: Render these patches using the current NeRF model to obtain predicted colors. 3. Resize: Resize rendered patches to 224 \times 224 resolution to fit the DINO-ViT input. 4. Depth Supervision via Warping: Use image warping with known camera intrinsics and poses to create a reference depth map that constrains the unseen views. 5. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} as a weighted sum of: Photometric Loss: L2 loss between rendered and ground truth (or warped) colors. Adversarial Loss: Patch-wise texture supervision using the CNN discriminator. Perceptual Loss: Feature-level comparison to constrain unobserved views. Global Structure Prior: L2 loss between global image features extracted by the pretrained ViT from the reference patch and the unseen patch. 6. Optimization: Update MLP and discriminator weights using RAdam optimizer. Parameters: Optimizer: RAdam. Learning Rate: Initial 1e-3 for MLP; discriminator LR is 20\% of MLP's LR. LR Decay: Halved every 10k iterations. Patch Sizes: NeRF Synthetic (Blender): 64 \times 64. LLFF: 84 \times 63. DTU: 70 \times 56. Stride Schedule: Starts at 6, reduces by 2 every 10k iterations. Loss Weights: \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 initialized to 8, 0.1, 0. \lambda2 decreases linearly to 0, \lambda3 increases linearly to 0.1 during training. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Single View Ambiguity: Without strong priors, the model may hallucinate geometry. The combination of adversarial, perceptual, and global feature losses is critical to mitigate this. Depth Estimation Error: The accuracy of the depth supervision relies on the correctness of the image warping and known camera parameters. This entry details the specific hyperparameters and hardware setup used in the original SinNeRF implementation. The architecture matches the original NeRF paper. Training is conducted on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU, taking several hours per scene. The patch sampling stride schedule and loss weight annealing are key implementation details for stable convergence. Time Complexity: Training takes several hours per scene. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: SinNeRF outperforms DS-NeRF, PixelNeRF, and DietNeRF on the NeRF Synthetic, DTU, and LLFF Forward Facing datasets. Strengths: Effective single-view reconstruction; leverages multiple complementary priors (texture, structure, depth). Limitations: Requires known camera intrinsics and poses for depth warping. Performance is limited by the quality of the single input image and the accuracy of the warping-based depth estimation. SinNeRF addresses the limitations of existing NeRF methods that require multiple views. The method integrates techniques from image warping, adversarial training, and global feature comparison to regularize the single-view reconstruction problem. It is cited as a significant advancement in single-view NeRF reconstruction, outperforming contemporaries like DS-NeRF and PixelNeRF. name: CLIP-NeRF
body: CLIP-NeRF is a neural radiance field method that enables text- or image-guided editing of 3D scenes by extracting latent space displacements from user input via the CLIP model. It differs from prior editing methods like Edit-NeRF by bypassing per-edit latent code optimization, achieving significant speedups (8–60x) through a disentangled conditional architecture that maps semantic input directly to shape and appearance modifications. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A pre-trained NeRF representation (initial weights and base latent codes), a user-provided text prompt or reference image, and camera parameters for the target view. Outputs: A modified radiance field capable of rendering the scene according to the semantic guidance, and the rendered image. Data Structures: The method relies on a disentangled conditional NeRF architecture. Key components include: 1. Base NeRF: Standard MLPs for density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}, conditioned on latent codes. 2. Shape Latent Code (zs): A vector controlling geometric deformation. 3. Appearance Latent Code (za or zc): A vector controlling texture and color. 4. Shape Mapper Network: A neural network that takes the CLIP embedding of the input text/image and outputs the displacement for zs. 5. Appearance Mapper Network: A neural network that takes the CLIP embedding and outputs the displacement for za. 6. Deformation Network (Instance-Specific Network): An MLP that takes the encoded position and the shape latent code to produce a deformation vector, modifying the input position before it enters the density network. Steps: 1. CLIP Embedding: Encode the user input (text or image) into a latent vector using the pre-trained CLIP model. 2. Latent Displacement Extraction: Pass the CLIP embedding through the Shape Mapper and Appearance Mapper networks to compute displacements \Delta zs and \Delta za. 3. Latent Code Update: Add the computed displacements to the base latent codes to form the updated scene representation: zs^{\text{new}} = zs^{\text{base}} + \Delta zs and za^{\text{new}} = za^{\text{base}} + \Delta za. 4. Deformation: For a ray point \mathbf{x}, encode it with positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}). Pass \gamma(\mathbf{x}) and zs^{\text{new}} through the Deformation Network to get a deformation vector \mathbf{d}{\text{def}}. Compute the deformed position \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{d}{\text{def}}. 5. Radiance Field Query: Query the Density Network with \gamma(\mathbf{x}') and zs^{\text{new}} to get density \sigma. Query the Color Network with \gamma(\mathbf{x}'), viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and za^{\text{new}} to get color \mathbf{c}. 6. Volume Rendering: Render the pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) using the standard volumetric rendering integral: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i, \quad \text{where } \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \deltai is the distance between samples. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def positionalencoding(x, L): # x: (N, 3), returns (N, 2L3) encoded = [] for i in range(L): freq = 2.0 i 3.141592653589793 encoded.append(x freq) sinvals = [v.sin() for v in encoded] cosvals = [v.cos() for v in encoded] return torch.cat(sinvals + cosvals, dim=-1) def clipnerfrender(rayorigin, raydirection, clipinput, basezs, baseza, shapemapper, appearancemapper, deformationnet, densitynet, colornet, L=10, numsamples=128, near=0.0, far=1.0): # 1. CLIP embedding (assumed pre-computed or passed as tensor) clipemb = clipinput # 2. Latent displacements deltazs = shapemapper(clipemb) deltaza = appearancemapper(clipemb) # 3. Update latent codes zs = basezs + deltazs za = baseza + deltaza # 4. Sample points along ray tvals = torch.linspace(near, far, numsamples) tdiffs = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] tdiffs = torch.cat([tdiffs, torch.tensor([1e10], device=tvals.device)]) points = rayorigin.unsqueeze(0) + raydirection.unsqueeze(0) tvals.unsqueeze(1) # 5. Encode & Deform xenc = positionalencoding(points, L) defvec = deformationnet(xenc, zs) deformedpoints = points + defvec deformedenc = positionalencoding(deformedpoints, L) # 6. Query networks densities = densitynet(deformedenc, zs).squeeze(-1) # (N,) colors = colornet(deformedenc, raydirection, za) # (N, 3) # 7. Volume rendering alphas = 1.0 - torch.exp(-densities tdiffs) transmittances = torch.cumprod(torch.exp(-alphas[:-1]), dim=0) transmittances = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(transmittances[:1]), transmittances]) weights = alphas transmittances renderedcolor = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) colors, dim=0) return renderedcolor Parameters: Number of frequency bands (L): Not given in the sources. Deformation Network Depth/Width: Not given in the sources. Mapper Network Architecture: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision and Boundaries: The deformation network modifies spatial coordinates before density evaluation, requiring careful handling of out-of-bounds or degenerate deformations to prevent NaN values in the exponential term. Semantic Alignment: The quality of the edit depends on how well the CLIP embedding aligns with the underlying 3D geometry, which may require careful prompt engineering or reference image selection. Time Complexity: Significantly faster than Edit-NeRF during the editing phase because it avoids iterative optimization of latent codes for each edit. The speedup is reported as a factor of ~8–60 depending on the task. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the base NeRF weights, the mapper networks, and the deformation network. Strengths: Enables global deformation and shape operations with high freedom; fast editing without per-edit optimization. Limitations: Not given in the sources. CLIP-NeRF was proposed by Wang et al. in 2022. It builds upon the latent-conditioned NeRF framework and Edit-NeRF, aiming to overcome the slow editing speed of iterative latent optimization by leveraging the pre-trained multimodal capabilities of CLIP. It is used for text- or image-guided 3D scene editing and generation. name: NeRF-RPN
head: NeRF Region Proposal Network
body: NeRF-RPN is a general framework for 3D object detection within neural radiance fields that regresses bounding boxes directly from the scene representation without rendering intermediate views. It solves the problem of identifying and localizing discrete objects in a continuous radiance field by treating detection as a dense prediction task on a voxelized feature volume. It sets itself apart from instance-level segmentation methods like NeRF-RCNN by generating proposals without refining them into discrete masks or class labels, whereas NeRF-RCNN appends prediction heads to refine these proposals into final instances. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained NeRF model representing the scene, defined by its density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} fields. Output: A set of 3D Oriented Bounding Boxes (OBBs) with associated objectness scores. Data Structures: The method employs a multi-scale Object-NeRF architecture. This consists of two coupled branches: 1. Scene Branch: Encodes the global geometry and appearance of the scene using a voxel representation of 3D neural volume features. 2. Object Branch: Encodes features for each independent object candidate. Network Topology: The core detection head is built upon a feature extraction backbone (e.g., VGG19, ResNet-50, Swin-S) applied to the voxelized features. The head architecture varies between two main variants: 1. Anchor-based: Predicts offsets relative to predefined 3D anchor boxes. 2. Anchor-free: Predicts bounding box dimensions and center offsets directly, augmented by a centerness prediction to suppress low-quality off-center proposals. Rendering Integration: Unlike traditional 2D detectors, NeRF-RPN operates directly on the implicit 3D representation without rendering images from multiple viewpoints. Training Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: The voxel representation of 3D neural volume features from the Scene Branch is passed through a feature extraction backbone to generate multi-scale feature volumes. 2. Proposal Generation: The RPN head processes these feature volumes to predict objectness scores and bounding box coordinates. For anchor-free models, all output proposals are used to compute the loss. For anchor-based models, a ratio of positive to negative anchors of 1:1 is maintained during loss computation. 3. Loss Computation: The model is optimized using a combination of classification/objectness loss and bounding box regression loss. Common regression losses include IoU loss. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nerfrpnforward(scenenerf, voxelfeatures, backbone, rpnhead): """ Forward pass for NeRF-RPN. scenenerf: Pre-trained NeRF model (provides density/color fields). voxelfeatures: 3D voxel grid of neural volume features from Scene Branch. backbone: Feature extractor (e.g., VGG19, ResNet-50, Swin-S). rpnhead: Region Proposal Network head (Anchor-based or Anchor-free). """ # 1. Extract multi-scale features from the voxelized scene representation featurevolumes = backbone(voxelfeatures) # 2. Generate proposals using the RPN head proposals, scores = rpnhead(featurevolumes) return proposals, scores def nerfrpntest(proposals, scores, sceneboundary, nmsiouthreshold=0.1, topk=2500): """ Testing and proposal filtering pipeline for NeRF-RPN. """ validproposals = [] validscores = [] for box, score in zip(proposals, scores): if isinsidesceneboundary(box.center, sceneboundary): validproposals.append(box) validscores.append(score) # Select top proposals on each level of feature volumes independently filteredproposals = [] filteredscores = [] for levelboxes, levelscores in zip(validproposals, validscores): indices = argsortdesc(levelscores) filteredproposals.extend([levelboxes[i] for i in indices[:topk]]) filteredscores.extend([levelscores[i] for i in indices[:topk]]) # Apply Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) based on rotated-IoU to aggregated boxes finalboxes, finalscores = nms(filteredproposals, filteredscores, nmsiouthreshold, userotatediou=True) # Select the top 2,500 boxes with the highest objectness scores sortedindices = argsortdesc(finalscores) selectedboxes = finalboxes[sortedindices[:topk]] selectedscores = finalscores[sortedindices[:topk]] return selectedboxes, selectedscores def isinsidesceneboundary(center, boundary): """Returns True if center is within the scene's spatial bounds.""" return (boundary.minx <= center.x <= boundary.maxx and boundary.miny <= center.y <= boundary.maxy and boundary.minz <= center.z <= boundary.maxz) def nms(boxes, scores, iouthreshold, userotatediou=False): """Standard Non-Maximum Suppression.""" if len(scores) == 0: return [], [] keep = [] indices = argsortdesc(scores) while len(indices) > 0: currentidx = indices[0] keep.append(currentidx) currentbox = boxes[currentidx] remainingindices = indices[1:] remainingboxes = [boxes[i] for i in remainingindices] if userotatediou: ious = computerotatediou(currentbox, remainingboxes) else: ious = computeaabbiou(currentbox, remainingboxes) mask = [iou < iouthreshold for iou in ious] indices = [remainingindices[i] for i in range(len(remainingindices)) if mask[i]] return [boxes[i] for i in keep], [scores[i] for i in keep] def argsortdesc(scores): """Returns indices that would sort scores in descending order.""" return sorted(range(len(scores)), key=lambda k: scores[k], reverse=True) def computerotatediou(box1, boxes2): """Standard geometric computation for rotated 3D bounding boxes.""" return [0.0] len(boxes2) def computeaabbiou(box1, boxes2): """Standard geometric computation for axis-aligned 3D bounding boxes.""" return [0.0] len(boxes2) Parameters: NMS Threshold: Rotated-IoU threshold of 0.1. Top-K Proposals: 2,500 proposals selected per feature level and after NMS. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noisy NeRF Input: Noisy NeRF inputs can cause misalignment between bounding box centers and mass centers, though anchor-free heads with centerness prediction mitigate this. Tiny Objects: The method may fail to generate proposals for tiny or second-level objects. Rotation Errors: Incorrect rotation predictions can occur in complex scenes. Merging/Missing: Proposals may merge distinct objects or miss objects entirely in cluttered scenes. The performance of NeRF-RPN is sensitive to the choice of backbone and head type. Head Type: Anchor-free models generally achieve higher Average Precision (AP) than anchor-based models across datasets (3D-FRONT, ScanNet, Hypersim) when backbones are fixed. This is attributed to centerness prediction suppressing off-center proposals and the flexibility to handle varying 3D object sizes without limited anchor aspect ratios. Backbone Choice: VGG19 generally achieves better recall and AP compared to ResNet-50 and Swin-S. However, on the Hypersim dataset, which contains noisier NeRF results and complex scenes, Swin-S demonstrates superior recall and AP for anchor-based models due to its larger receptive fields, shifted windows, and attention mechanisms. The inference pipeline filters raw proposals to ensure spatial validity and remove redundancy. Boundary Filtering: ROIs whose geometry centers fall outside the defined scene boundary are discarded. Per-Level Selection: The top 2,500 proposals are selected independently on each level of the feature volumes. Aggregation and NMS: Proposals are aggregated and filtered using Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) based on rotated-IoU with a threshold of 0.1. Final Selection: The 2,500 boxes with the highest objectness scores after NMS are retained for downstream processing. NeRF-RCNN is a proposal-based 3D instance segmentation model that takes a pre-trained NeRF as input. It extends NeRF-RPN by appending a box prediction head and a mask prediction head to refine proposals into final instances. Unlike NeRF-RPN, which outputs bounding boxes, NeRF-RCNN outputs discrete 3D masks and class labels. It is chosen when instance-level segmentation is required rather than just detection. NeRF-MAE is a self-supervised pretraining architecture for 3D radiance fields that utilizes Masked Autoencoders (MAE) to learn robust scene representations from unlabeled data. It sets itself apart from supervised baselines like NeRF-RPN by enabling efficient transfer learning for downstream tasks such as 3D object detection and voxel super-resolution, achieving significant performance gains with fewer labeled annotations. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On Hypersim, VGG19 (Anchor-free) achieves Recall@25 of 66.7 and AP@25 of 27.7. Swin-S (Anchor-based) achieves Recall@25 of 69.8 and AP@25 of 13.0. On 3D-FRONT, VGG19 (Anchor-free) achieves Recall@25 of 96.3 and AP@25 of 69.9. On ScanNet, VGG19 (Anchor-free) achieves Recall@25 of 89.2 and AP@25 of 42.9. Strengths: General framework for unlabelled object detection; does not require rendering views; anchor-free variant handles varying object sizes well. Limitations: May miss tiny or second-level objects. Noisy NeRF inputs can cause misalignment between bounding box centers and mass centers, though anchor-free heads with centerness prediction mitigate this. Rotation errors can occur in complex scenes. Proposals may merge distinct objects or miss objects entirely in cluttered scenes. When to use: When detecting objects in a NeRF scene without instance masks or when using a general detection framework. When not to use: When instance-level segmentation masks are required (use NeRF-RCNN) or when self-supervised pretraining is needed for downstream tasks (use NeRF-MAE). NeRF-RPN was proposed by Hu et al. in 2023. It was introduced to enable the detection of all objects' bounding boxes in a scene using a multi-scale Object-NeRF architecture. The method leverages the voxel representation of 3D neural volume features to regress 3D bounding boxes directly, avoiding the need for rendering from any viewpoint. It serves as a general framework applicable to unlabelled objects. name: NeRF-RCNN
body: NeRF-RCNN is a proposal-based 3D instance segmentation model that takes a pre-trained NeRF as input and outputs 3D Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes (AABB), class labels, and discrete 3D masks of detected objects. It extends NeRF-RPN by appending a box prediction head and a mask prediction head to refine proposals into final instances. Unlike Semantic-NeRF, which does not produce instance-level information, NeRF-RCNN outputs discrete instance masks and bounding boxes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A pre-trained Instance-NeRF model (providing radiance and density fields), Region of Interests (RoIs) provided by the NeRF-RPN stage, and ground truth data including 3D bounding boxes and 3D instance segmentation masks. Outputs: 3D AABBs, class probabilities, and discrete 3D masks for each detected object. Data Structures: Grid: A uniform grid covering the full traceable volume of the pre-trained Instance-NeRF model, storing sampled appearance and density values. RoI Features: Extracted features for each proposal using 3D RoIAlign. Box Offsets: A vector t{i,k} of size 6 for each class k and RoI i, representing translation and scale adjustments. Masks: Binary masks of size m \times m \times m for each RoI. Parameters: m=5: Resolution for the box head mask. m=10: Resolution for the mask head mask. \lambda1, \lambda2: Hyper-parameters weighting the regression and mask losses in the total loss function. NMS threshold for NeRF-RCNN: 0.15. Score threshold for detection: 0.5. Steps: 1. Sampling: Uniformly sample appearance and density on a grid covering the full traceable volume of the pre-trained Instance-NeRF model. 2. Proposal Generation: Pass the sampled grid to NeRF-RPN to output proposals and a feature pyramid. 3. Feature Extraction: Use a backbone identical to NeRF-RPN to extract features from the sampled grid. 4. RoIAlign: Use 3D RoIAlign to obtain features within the RoI of each output proposal. This extends standard RoIAlign with an additional dimension to extract consistent features for each RoI on the feature map. 5. Target Assignment: For each RoI, set the ground truth box with the largest intersection over union (IoU) as its regression target. 6. Box Head Processing: Flatten the aligned RoI features. Pass through a fully connected layer for encoding. Split into a box branch and a classification branch. The box branch regresses a RoI to a more accurate bounding box per class. The classification branch predicts classification scores. 7. Mask Head Processing: Feed aligned features into a 3D CNN (mask head). The mask head predicts L binary masks of size m \times m \times m for each RoI, where L is the number of classes including background. Apply a sigmoid function as the activation. 8. Refinement (Post-Processing/Training Aid): Apply 2D mask refinement using CascadePSP on the Instance-NeRF results to improve segmentation quality on object boundaries. Compose the refined masks into a single segmentation map to further optimize the instance field. Formulas: Box Offsets: The box head output t{i,k} is defined as: t{i,k} = (tx{i,k}, ty{i,k}, tz{i,k}, tw{i,k}, tl{i,k}, th{i,k}) where: tx{i,k} = \frac{xk - xa}{wa} ty{i,k} = \frac{yk - ya}{la} tz{i,k} = \frac{zk - za}{ha} tw{i,k} = \log\left(\frac{wk}{wa}\right) tl{i,k} = \log\left(\frac{lk}{la}\right) th{i,k} = \log\left(\frac{hk}{ha}\right) Here, xk, yk, zk are the center coordinates of the predicted box, wk, lk, hk are the side lengths, and xa, ya, za, wa, la, ha are the corresponding parameters of the RoI. Classification Loss: Multi-class cross-entropy loss (implemented as BCE in the source formula) for class prediction: L{cls} = \frac{1}{|N|} \sum{i \in N} L{BCE}(pi, p^i) where pi is the predicted classification score vector after sigmoid, p^i is the ground truth, and N is the set of sampled RoIs. Box Regression Loss: Smooth L1 loss for bounding box regression: L{reg} = \frac{1}{|Np|} \sum{i \in Np} \sum{k=1}^L p{i,k} L{smooth}(t{i,k}, t^i) where Np is the set of positive samples, L is the number of classes including background, p{i,k} is the k-th dimension of pi, t{i,k} is the box offsets of class k, and t^i is the ground-truth target. Note that for an RoI associated with ground truth class c, only the c-th box regression loss contributes. Mask Loss: Binary cross-entropy loss for 3D mask prediction: L{mask} = \frac{\lambda}{|Np|} \sum{i \in Np} \sum{k=1}^L p{i,k} Lp(m{i,k}, m^i) where m{i,k} is the predicted mask of class k, m^i is the ground truth mask, and Lp is the loss function (BCE). Only the mask BCE loss corresponding to the ground truth label contributes. Total Loss: L = L{cls} + \lambda1 L{reg} + \lambda2 L{mask} where \lambda1, \lambda2 are hyper-parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def uniformsamplegrid(nerf, resolution): """Uniformly sample appearance and density on a grid covering the full traceable volume.""" return nerf.sampleuniform(resolution) def extractbackbonefeatures(grid): """Extract features using a backbone identical to NeRF-RPN.""" return grid.backbone() def roialign3d(featurepyramid, roi): """Extend RoIAlign with an additional dimension to extract consistent features for each RoI.""" return featurepyramid[0].align3d(roi) def fullyconnected(x, W, b): """Standard fully connected layer encoding.""" return x @ W + b def conv3d(x, channels, kernelsize): """3D CNN predicting L binary masks.""" return x.conv3d(channels, kernelsize) def sigmoid(x): """Apply sigmoid activation.""" return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-x)) def decodeboxes(rois, offsets): """Decode box offsets to AABBs using RoI parameters.""" boxes = [] for roi, offset in zip(rois, offsets): xa, ya, za, wa, la, ha = roi.bboxparams tx, ty, tz, tw, tl, th = offset xk = tx wa + xa yk = ty la + ya zk = tz ha + za wk = wa math.exp(tw) lk = la math.exp(tl) hk = ha math.exp(th) boxes.append((xk, yk, zk, wk, lk, hk)) return boxes def assignpositivetargets(boxes, gtboxes): """Set ground truth box with largest IoU as regression target.""" posindices = [] for i, box in enumerate(boxes): bestiou = 0.0 for gt in gtboxes: iou = computeiou(box, gt) if iou > bestiou: bestiou = iou if bestiou > 0.5: posindices.append(i) return posindices def binarycrossentropy(pred, target): """Compute BCE loss.""" return -mean(target log(sigmoid(pred)) + (1 - target) log(1 - sigmoid(pred))) def smoothl1loss(pred, target): """Compute Smooth L1 loss.""" diff = abs(pred - target) return mean(where(diff < 1, 0.5 diff2, diff - 0.5)) def nerfrcnnforward(pretrainednerf, rpnproposals, gridresolution): # Step 1: Uniformly sample appearance and density on a grid covering the full traceable volume grid = uniformsamplegrid(pretrainednerf, gridresolution) # Step 2: Extract features using a backbone identical to NeRF-RPN featurepyramid = extractbackbonefeatures(grid) # Step 3: Use 3D RoIAlign to obtain features within the RoI of each proposal roifeatures = [] for roi in rpnproposals: features = roialign3d(featurepyramid, roi) roifeatures.append(features) roifeatures = stack(roifeatures) # Step 4: Box Head Processing flattened = flatten(roifeatures) encoded = fullyconnected(flattened, Wfc, bfc) boxencoded = fullyconnected(encoded, Wbox, bbox) clsencoded = fullyconnected(encoded, Wcls, bcls) # Box branch regresses offsets boxoffsets = fullyconnected(boxencoded, Wreg, breg) # Classification branch predicts scores classlogits = fullyconnected(clsencoded, Wclsout, bclsout) # Step 5: Mask Head Processing # 3D CNN predicting L binary masks of size m x m x m masks = conv3d(roifeatures, channels=L, kernelsize=m) masks = sigmoid(masks) # Step 6: Decode Box Offsets to AABBs boxes = decodeboxes(rpnproposals, boxoffsets) return boxes, classlogits, masks def nerfrcnnloss(predictions, gtboxes, gtmasks, gtclasses, lambda1, lambda2): boxes, classlogits, masks = predictions # Identify positive samples (RoIs with largest IoU with GT) posindices = assignpositivetargets(boxes, gtboxes) # Classification Loss (BCE) classloss = mean(binarycrossentropy(classlogits, gtclasses)) # Box Regression Loss (Smooth L1) for positive samples boxloss = mean(smoothl1loss(boxes[posindices], gtboxes[posindices])) # Mask Loss (BCE) for positive samples and ground truth class maskloss = mean(binarycrossentropy(masks[posindices], gtmasks[posindices])) # Total Loss totalloss = classloss + lambda1 boxloss + lambda2 maskloss return totalloss Panoptic NeRF specializes in urban environments for 3D-to-2D label propagation, a key task in extending urban autonomous driving datasets. The method uses two semantic fields: one learned by a semantic head and another determined by 3D bounding boxes. According to the authors, the rigid bounding box-based semantics force the model to learn the correct geometry, whereas the learned semantic head improves semantic understanding. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Benchmarked on the NeRF-RPN dataset with 1015 scenes, multi-view images, camera poses, 3D bounding boxes, and 2D/3D ground truth instance segmentation. Strengths: It is one of the first methods to propose 3D instance segmentation for NeRF without utilizing ground-truth information at test time, generalizing to different kinds of scenes and requiring only a pre-trained NeRF during inference. Limitations: Instance label regularization can smooth out detailed structures like thin chair legs or lamp stands, degrading segmentation quality on object silhouettes. When to use: When 3D instance segmentation is required for a pre-trained NeRF scene. When not to use: When instance-level information is not needed (Semantic-NeRF is sufficient) or when ground-truth instance masks are not available for training. NeRF-RCNN was proposed in the paper "Instance Neural Radiance Field". It is based on the architecture of Mask R-CNN [19] and extends NeRF-RPN [23]. The method was trained on a large NeRF segmentation dataset built on 3D-FRONT, a large-scale synthetic indoor scene dataset. The dataset includes 1015 scenes with multi-view images, camera poses, 3D bounding boxes, 2D ground truth instance segmentation, and 3D voxelized instance segmentation ground truth.
