name: NeRF-MAE Pretraining Architecture
head: NeRF-MAE
body: NeRF-MAE is a self-supervised pretraining method for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) that utilizes Masked Autoencoders (MAE) to learn robust 3D scene representations from unlabeled data. It differs from supervised baselines like NeRF-RPN by training an encoder-decoder architecture on masked input grids, enabling the transfer of general scene understanding (semantic and spatial structure) to downstream tasks such as 3D object detection and voxel super-resolution. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D radiance and density grid (volume) representing a scene. Output: Reconstructed color and density values for the masked patches, and latent features for the unmasked patches used by downstream heads. Data Structures: The architecture consists of an encoder and a decoder. Encoder: Based on the Swin-S Transformer backbone. It comprises four Swin blocks with specific depths and head counts: Block 1: Depth 2, 3 heads. Block 2: Depth 2, 6 heads. Block 3: Depth 18, 12 heads. Block 4: Depth 2, 24 heads. Decoder: A lightweight network that reconstructs the masked patches. It utilizes feature pyramids and includes skip connections from the encoder to improve representation learning. Parameters: Total parameter count: 70 million. Masking ratio: 75% of the input patches are masked during pretraining. This ratio was identified as optimal in ablation studies (comparing 65%, 75%, and 85%). Batch size: 32 for pretraining. Training Procedure: 1. Data Augmentation: Apply random flip, rotation, and scaling with a probability of 50% to the input grids. 2. Masking: Randomly select 75% of the patches in the input 3D grid to be masked. 3. Encoding: Pass the unmasked patches through the Swin-S Transformer encoder to extract latent features. 4. Decoding: Combine the latent features with mask tokens and pass them through the lightweight decoder with skip connections to reconstruct the missing patches. 5. Loss Calculation: Compute the masked color reconstruction loss against the ground-truth upsampled grid. 6. Optimization: Update weights using the Adam optimizer. Maximum learning rate: 3 \times 10^{-4}. Weight decay: 1 \times 10^{-3}. Learning rate schedule: One-cycle scheduling. Gradient clipping: Maximum normal gradient clip value of 0.1. 7. Iteration: Repeat for 1200 epochs. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Transfer Learning Strategy: Changing the learning rate or strategy during the transfer learning phase decreases performance for both NeRF-MAE and the NeRF-RPN baseline. The same learning rate and strategy as pretraining must be maintained. Convergence Metrics: Convergence determination varies by downstream task: AP50 for 3D OBB prediction, accuracy for 3D semantic voxel labeling, and PSNR for voxel super-resolution. A task to predict 3D Oriented Bounding Boxes (OBBs) by regressing bounding box offsets, objectness scores, and objectness probabilities for each voxel, functioning as an anchor-free Region Proposal Network (RPN). It differs from standard RPN implementations by utilizing the NeRF-MAE pre-trained encoder rather than training from scratch or using other baselines like NeRF-RPN. Complexity: The method uses a 70 million parameter network, which is efficient enough to train on diverse scenes. Performance: NeRF-MAE outperforms the NeRF-RPN baseline in downstream tasks. For example, on the Front3D dataset, it achieves higher AP25 and AP50 scores for 3D OBB prediction. On HM3D, it improves PSNR from 14.65 to 15.20 and reduces MSE from 0.035 to 0.030 for voxel super-resolution. Strengths: The pretraining weights capture general-purpose scene understanding, including semantic and spatial structure, which facilitates better transfer to specific tasks. The use of skip connections in the decoder further enhances representation learning. Limitations: Performance is sensitive to the learning rate strategy during transfer learning; deviating from the pretraining schedule degrades results. NeRF-MAE was introduced by M.Z. Irshad et al. in 2024. It builds upon the original 2D MAE work and adapts it to 3D radiance fields. The method is designed to leverage large amounts of unlabeled data (such as Front3D, Habitat-Matterport3D, and HyperSim) to learn better representations for downstream 3D tasks. NeRF-MAE: Masked AutoEncoders for Self-Supervised 3D Representation Learning for Neural Radiance Fields, https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.01300v3, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Downstream 3D Object Detection in NeRF
head: 3D OBB prediction, NeRF-MAE for 3D Object Detection
body: A task to predict 3D Oriented Bounding Boxes (OBBs) by regressing bounding box offsets, objectness scores, and objectness probabilities for each voxel, functioning as an anchor-free Region Proposal Network (RPN). It differs from standard RPN implementations by utilizing the NeRF-MAE pre-trained encoder rather than training from scratch or using other baselines like NeRF-RPN. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A voxel grid representation of the scene, processed through the NeRF-MAE pre-trained encoder. Output: For each voxel, a prediction vector t, an objectness score c, and a single objectness probability p. Data Structures: The prediction for each voxel is a vector t containing 8 components: t = (x0, y0, z0, x1, y1, z1, \Delta\alpha, \Delta\beta) Where: (x0, y0, z0) and (x1, y1, z1) represent the bounding box offsets (likely defining the center and dimensions or corners relative to the voxel). \Delta\alpha, \Delta\beta represent orientation offsets. c is the objectness score. p is the single objectness probability. Steps: 1. Encode the input voxel grid using the NeRF-MAE pre-trained encoder. 2. For each voxel in the grid, regress the bounding box offset vector t. 3. Simultaneously predict the objectness score c and the single objectness probability p for each voxel. 4. Aggregate these voxel-level predictions to form 3D OBB proposals, similar to an anchor-free RPN mechanism. Parameters: Voxel grid resolution: Not given in the sources. Encoder: NeRF-MAE pre-trained weights. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The quality of the initial 3D object detector bounding boxes can be inaccurate. Inaccurate poses may require refinement, guided by depth supervision and visual multiview constraints, to ensure robust training. A variant or subsequent step where inaccurate initial 3D object detector bounding boxes are corrected. It improves inaccurate poses by being guided by depth supervision and visual multiview constraints during the training of the scene representation (e.g., S-NeRF). It is chosen when the initial detection quality is insufficient for high-fidelity rendering or when robustness to detection errors is required. The quality of the 3D object detector does not significantly influence the final rendering quality if pose refinement is employed. The method is robust to varying detection qualities; bounding boxes with an Intersection over Union (IoU) greater than 0.5 are sufficient for training. Measured performance impacts on rendering quality (PSNR/SSIM) relative to ground truth bounding boxes when using different detector qualities (mIoU): mIoU 0.79 (default detector): PSNR drops by 0.23, SSIM drops by 0.04, LPIPS does not change. mIoU 0.67: PSNR drops by 0.49. mIoU 0.55: PSNR drops by 0.97. Strengths include robustness to imperfect detection inputs, allowing the use of existing 3D object detectors without strict accuracy requirements. Limitations include the dependency on the effectiveness of the pose refinement stage to mitigate initial detection errors. The task is defined in the context of NeRF-MAE, which applies masked autoencoder pre-training to 3D representation learning for Neural Radiance Fields. It builds on the concept of anchor-free Region Proposal Networks (RPN). The robustness of this approach to detection errors is further explored in S-NeRF, which focuses on neural radiance fields for street views. NeRF-MAE: Masked AutoEncoders for Self-Supervised 3D Representation Learning for Neural Radiance Fields, https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.01300v3, fetched 2026-10-26 S-NeRF: Neural Radiance Fields for Street Views, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2303.00749, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: RefSR-NeRF
head: Reference-guided super-resolution neural radiation field
body: RefSR-NeRF is a framework that combines Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) with a Reference-guided Super-Resolution CNN (RefSR-CNN) to achieve high-quality novel view synthesis from low-resolution inputs. It addresses the computational explosion and memory constraints associated with training NeRF on high-resolution data by decoupling the 3D field optimization from the high-frequency detail reconstruction. Unlike methods that modify the NeRF architecture directly (e.g., AdaNeRF) or use generative priors (e.g., DiffusioNeRF), RefSR-NeRF retains a standard NeRF backbone for geometry and color while using a separate CNN to inject high-frequency details guided by a single high-resolution reference image. Inputs: 1. A set of low-resolution input images with known camera poses. 2. A single high-resolution reference image of the scene (typically from one of the input viewpoints or a similar angle). 3. Ray origins and directions for rendering. Outputs: 1. A high-resolution rendered image for a target viewpoint. 2. The optimized NeRF parameters (density and color networks). Data Structures: NeRF Model: Standard MLP-based radiance field mapping 6D coordinates (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) to density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}, as defined in Specific Model Architectures. RefSR-CNN: A convolutional neural network containing: Detail-dominant information module. Degradation-dominant information module. Feature fusion layer. Algorithm: The method operates in two distinct stages. Stage 1: Low-Resolution NeRF Training The NeRF is trained using a modified sampling strategy to reduce memory usage and computational cost. 1. Patch Ray Sampling: Instead of sampling rays independently for batch processing, rays are sampled in patches corresponding to the high-resolution input image grid. This allows the system to generate a low-resolution image from the NeRF. 2. Optimization: The NeRF parameters are optimized by minimizing the difference between the rendered low-resolution image and the ground-truth low-resolution input images. The rendering equation remains: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i where \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) and Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). Stage 2: Reference-Guided Super-Resolution The low-resolution image rendered by the NeRF and the high-resolution reference image are processed by the RefSR-CNN. 1. Feature Extraction: The RefSR-CNN extracts features from both the low-resolution NeRF output and the high-resolution reference image. The detail-dominant module captures high-frequency textures and fine details from the reference image. The degradation-dominant module captures the structural and low-frequency information from the NeRF-rendered image. 2. Feature Fusion: The feature maps from both modules are fused. This step aligns the high-frequency details from the reference with the geometric consistency of the NeRF output. 3. Reconstruction: The fused features are upsampled and decoded to produce the final high-resolution image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainnerfstage1(inputimages, cameraposes): """ Stage 1: Train NeRF using patch ray sampling on low-resolution inputs. """ nerfmodel = initializenerf() optimizer = Adam(nerfmodel.parameters()) for epoch in range(numepochs): for patch in getpatches(inputimages): # Sample rays in patches to reduce memory rays = samplepatchrays(patch, cameraposes) # Render low-res image lowresrendered = rendernerf(nerfmodel, rays) # Compute loss against ground truth low-res patch loss = mseloss(lowresrendered, patch) # Backpropagate optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return nerfmodel def superresolvestage2(nerfmodel, lowrestargetview, refhighresimage): """ Stage 2: Refine the low-res NeRF output using RefSR-CNN and a reference image. """ # 1. Render the target view at low resolution using the trained NeRF lowresoutput = rendernerf(nerfmodel, getraysforview(lowrestargetview)) # 2. Initialize RefSR-CNN refsrcnn = initializerefsrcnn() # 3. Extract features from the degradation-dominant module (NeRF output) # This captures the structural/low-frequency info featdegradation = refsrcnn.degradationmodule(lowresoutput) # 4. Extract features from the detail-dominant module (Reference image) # This captures high-frequency textures featdetail = refsrcnn.detailmodule(refhighresimage) # 5. Fuse features fusedfeat = fusefeatures(featdegradation, featdetail) # 6. Reconstruct high-resolution image highresresult = refsrcnn.reconstructionhead(fusedfeat) return highresresult Parameters: Patch Size: Not specified in sources, but critical for memory management. Reference Image: Must be high-resolution and semantically aligned with the scene. Learning Rate: Standard NeRF optimization rates. Edge Cases: Misalignment: If the reference image is significantly misaligned with the target view, the detail injection may produce artifacts. The source notes that misalignment is a general challenge in high-resolution NeRF processing. Memory Explosion: The primary motivation for this method is the "explosion of parameters and computational complexity" when training NeRF on high-res data directly. A deterministic supersampling method that enforces sub-pixel multi-view consistency and uses a depth-guided patch warp network. It differs from RefSR-NeRF by not relying on an external CNN reference model but rather on 3D consistency and patch-based refinement. Memory Efficiency: Significantly reduces memory storage requirements compared to training NeRF directly on high-resolution images by using patch ray sampling in Stage 1. Speed: Improves training speed by lowering the resolution of the NeRF optimization phase. Quality: On the NeRF-LLFF dataset, the PSNR is nearly one point higher than the best competing paper at the time of publication. Limitations: Relies on the availability of a high-quality reference image. Performance may degrade if the reference image does not contain sufficient detail or is poorly aligned. RefSR-NeRF was introduced to address the challenges of high-resolution processing in Neural Radiance Fields, specifically the trade-off between image quality and computational resources. It builds on the standard NeRF framework Specific Model Architectures and integrates concepts from Reference-based Super-Resolution (RefSR) CNNs. The method is part of a broader trend of improving novel view synthesis quality through high-resolution processing techniques. Methods and Strategies for Improving the Novel View Synthesis Quality of Neural Radiation Field, https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2024.3382997, fetched 2026-10-30

name: NeRF-SR
head: NeRF-SR Refinement, NeRF-SR: High-Quality Neural Radiance Fields using Supersampling, Patch-Based Refinement
body: NeRF-SR is a super-resolution method that attacks the problem by deterministic supersampling that enforces sub-pixel multi-view consistency and by a depth guided patch warp and refine network that reuses one high-resolution reference image. It solves the problem of generating high-resolution novel views from mostly low-resolution inputs by exploiting the 3D consistency of NeRF, where an observed pixel absorbs information from nearby views. Unlike Super-NeRF which couples NeRF with a GAN based 2D super-resolution backbone, NeRF-SR stays closer to classical supersampling and patch based refinement. Unlike Mip-NeRF which only considers rendering with downsampled resolutions, NeRF-SR studies how to increase the resolution of NeRF. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Posed multi-view low-resolution images of the target scene; one high-resolution reference image (I{REF}). Outputs: High-resolution synthesized images (In) and depth maps for novel viewpoints. Data Structures: NeRF Model: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) predicting per-point density \sigma(\mathbf{x}) and color c(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) = (r, g, b) given 3D position \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d}. Refinement Network: A U-Net based convolutional network. Encoder: Consists of seven convolutional layers followed by ReLU activation. Decoder: Takes as input the nearest-neighbor upsampled features from previous layers concatenated with both the encoded features of the input SR patch and max-pooled features of reference patches. All convolutional layers are followed by a ReLU activation. Parameters: Supersampling Rays: Multiple rays are shot per pixel. The exact number is not specified in the sources [G: Typically 4-16 rays per pixel in supersampling contexts, but NeRF-SR sources do not specify]. Reference Patches (K): Number of reference patches sampled within a fixed window around the projected location. The exact value of K is not specified in the sources [G: The text mentions "sample K reference patches", but does not give a number]. Loss Weights (\lambdal): Reciprocal of the number of neurons in layer l of the pretrained VGG-19 network. Numbered Steps: 1. NeRF Training with Supersampling: Train the base NeRF using the low-resolution input images. During rendering for supervision, shoot multiple rays at each image pixel to enforce multi-view constraints at a sub-pixel level. Supervision: Compare the average color of sub-pixels, referred to as 'average kernel'. Note: The sources mention that while the method assumes an "average kernel" degradation, the actual Blender dataset uses Lanczos downsampling, which is asymmetric. Using a symmetric average kernel for degradation simulation improves results (e.g., PSNR 30.94 vs 29.77 for Blender \times 2 at 100x100). 2. Depth Estimation: Render the estimated depth map d{i,j} for the target view using the trained NeRF. 3. Reference Patch Extraction (Testing/Inference): For each pixel (i,j) in the synthesized SR patch Pe: a. Compute its 3D world coordinate using the estimated depth d{i,j} and camera parameters. b. Backproject this 3D coordinate to the high-resolution reference image I{REF} to find the corresponding pixel location. c. Extract patches around this location to form a set of reference patches \{P{REF}^k\}{k=1}^K. d. Points falling out of I{REF} are discarded. The transformation between camera extrinsic matrices from the target view In to I{REF} is denoted as T, and K{REF} and Kn refer to the camera intrinsic matrices. 4. Patch Refinement: For each SR patch Pe: a. Encode Pe and each reference patch P{REF}^k respectively using the encoder (7 conv layers + ReLU). b. The decoder generates the refined patch P from the concatenated features (nearest-neighbor upsampled features, encoded Pe, and max-pooled features of \{P{REF}^k\}). c. The refinement stage is efficient and introduces negligible running time compared with NeRF rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class RefinementEncoder(nn.Module): """Encoder consisting of seven convolutional layers followed by ReLU.""" def init(self): super().init() # Implementation detail: 7 conv layers. # Exact channel dimensions are not specified in sources [G: Standard U-Net encoder structure assumed, e.g., 64, 128, 256...] self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(3, 64, 3, padding=1) self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(64, 64, 3, padding=1) self.conv3 = nn.Conv2d(64, 128, 3, padding=1) self.conv4 = nn.Conv2d(128, 128, 3, padding=1) self.conv5 = nn.Conv2d(128, 256, 3, padding=1) self.conv6 = nn.Conv2d(256, 256, 3, padding=1) self.conv7 = nn.Conv2d(256, 256, 3, padding=1) def forward(self, x): x = F.relu(self.conv1(x)) x = F.relu(self.conv2(x)) x = F.relu(self.conv3(x)) x = F.relu(self.conv4(x)) x = F.relu(self.conv5(x)) x = F.relu(self.conv6(x)) x = F.relu(self.conv7(x)) return x class RefinementDecoder(nn.Module): """Decoder that generates refined patch from concatenated features.""" def init(self): super().init() # Implementation detail: Decoder layers not fully specified [G: Standard upsampling conv layers] self.convout = nn.Conv2d(256, 3, 3, padding=1) # Output 3 channels (RGB) def forward(self, features): # features: concatenated encoded features x = F.relu(self.convout(features)) return x class RefinementNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() self.encoder = RefinementEncoder() self.decoder = RefinementDecoder() def forward(self, Pe, PREFlist): """ Pe: SR patch tensor [B, 3, H, W] PREFlist: List of reference patch tensors [B, K, 3, H, W] """ # Encode SR patch feate = self.encoder(Pe) # Encode reference patches and pool reffeats = [] for Pref in PREFlist: featref = self.encoder(Pref) # Max pool at the same spatial resolution pooledref = F.maxpool2d(featref, kernelsize=featref.shape[2]) reffeats.append(pooledref) # Concatenate features # Note: Source says "concatenated with both the encoded features of Pe and max pooled features of PREF" # Assuming concatenation along channel dimension combined = torch.cat([feate] + reffeats, dim=1) # Decode refinedpatch = self.decoder(combined) return refinedpatch def trainrefinementnetwork(model, Pe, P, K, windowsize): """ Training step for the refinement network. Pe: SR patch sampled from SR image at camera pose of IREF P: HR patch from IREF at the same location K: Number of reference patches to sample windowsize: Fixed window around P to sample reference patches """ # Sample K reference patches within a fixed window around P PREFlist = [] for k in range(K): # Sample patch from IREF within window around P # Implementation detail: Exact sampling logic for window not specified [G: Random crop within window] Pref = samplepatchfromreference(P, windowsize) PREFlist.append(Pref) # Perform perspective transformations on Pe and P as during testing # (To account for different camera poses) Petransformed = perspectivetransform(Pe) Ptransformed = perspectivetransform(P) # Forward pass Prefined = model(Petransformed, PREFlist) # Loss function: Lrefine = Lrec + Lper # Lrec = ||Pe - P||1 # Lper = suml lambdal ||phil(P) - phil(Prefined)||1 # phil is a set of layers in a pretrained VGG-19 # lambdal is the reciprocal of the number of neurons in layer l lossrec = torch.mean(torch.abs(Prefined - Ptransformed)) # Perceptual loss calculation lossper = 0 philayers = getvgg19layers() for l, phil in enumerate(philayers): lambdal = 1.0 / phil.numneurons # Not given in sources, assumed definition lossper += lambdal torch.mean(torch.abs(phil(Prefined) - phil(Ptransformed))) loss = lossrec + lossper return loss def renderneRFSR(nerfmodel, cameraparams, numraysperpixel): """ Render NeRF with supersampling. """ # Shoot multiple rays at each image pixel rays = generaterays(cameraparams, numraysperpixel) # Query NeRF for density and color densities, colors = nerfmodel.query(rays) # Volume rendering to get pixel color pixelcolors = volumerender(densities, colors) # Supervision: Compare average color of sub-pixels (average kernel) # Implementation detail: The exact "average kernel" comparison is not defined as a standard loss [G: Likely comparing rendered sub-pixel averages to downsampled ground truth] return pixelcolors def refinepatch(nerfmodel, IREF, cameraparams, Pe, K): """ Refine a single SR patch using the reference image. """ # Get depth map from NeRF depthmap = nerfmodel.renderdepth(cameraparams) # Extract reference patches PREFlist = [] for i, j in pixellocations(Pe): # Compute 3D world coordinate x3d = backproject(depthmap[i, j], cameraparams) # Backproject to IREF uvref = projecttoreference(x3d, cameraparams, IREF) # Extract patch around uvref if uvref is within IREF bounds: Pref = extractpatch(IREF, uvref) PREFlist.append(Pref) # Refine Prefined = RefinementNetwork(Pe, PREFlist) return Prefined Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Arbitrary Scale: The method does not support arbitrary-scale super-resolution. Reference Out of Bounds: Points falling out of I{REF} during backprojection are discarded. Degradation Kernel: The method assumes an "average kernel" degradation for supervision, but real datasets (like Blender) use Lanczos. Using the correct kernel (symmetric average) improves results. Training Data: Training data for the refinement network is only available at the camera pose of I{REF}, requiring perspective transformations during training to generalize to other views. Time Complexity: The refinement stage is efficient and introduces negligible running time compared with NeRF rendering. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Blender \times 2 (100x100): PSNR 29.77, SSIM 0.946, LPIPS 0.045. Blender \times 4 (100x100): PSNR 28.07, SSIM 0.921, LPIPS 0.071. Blender \times 2 (200x200): PSNR 31.00, SSIM 0.952, LPIPS 0.038. Blender \times 4 (200x200): PSNR 28.46, SSIM 0.921, LPIPS 0.076. LLFF \times 2: PSNR 27.31, SSIM 0.838, LPIPS 0.139. LLFF \times 4: PSNR 25.13, SSIM 0.730, LPIPS 0.244. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Generates high-quality results for novel view synthesis at HR on both synthetic and real-world datasets without any external information. Outperforms baselines that require LR-HR pairs for training. Works even with only one HR reference. Limitations: Does not enjoy the nice arbitrary-scale property. Requires at least one HR reference image. Origin: NeRF-SR was presented by Wang et al. from Tsinghua University and Kuaishou Technology. Paper: "NeRF-SR: High-Quality Neural Radiance Fields using Supersampling" published in ACM Multimedia (MM '22), October 10–14, 2022, Lisboa, Portugal. History: It is the first framework that produces decent multi-view super-resolution results with mostly LR input images. Usage: Used for high-resolution novel view synthesis, particularly in VR and AR applications. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28 NeRF-SR: High-Quality Neural Radiance Fields using Supersampling, https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.01759v3, fetched 2026-10-26

name: AligNeRF
body: AligNeRF is a training strategy and architectural modification for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) designed to improve high-frequency detail recovery and mitigate artifacts caused by misalignment from moving objects or camera calibration errors. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF implementations by combining a convolution-augmented architecture with a staged, alignment-aware fine-tuning procedure that utilizes patch-based sampling and explicit spatial alignment matching. Unlike sibling methods that primarily focus on sparse representations or differentiable rendering integrals, AligNeRF explicitly addresses the spatial coherence of high-resolution features through local neighborhood encoding and robust alignment matching. AligNeRF builds on the standard NeRF representation [Parent] but modifies the architecture and training loop to support local spatial reasoning and misalignment correction. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D coordinates \mathbf{x}, viewing directions \mathbf{d}, and ground truth image patches. Outputs: Rendered RGB color images. Internally, the model outputs high-dimensional feature vectors during the pre-training stage. Data Structures and Layout: 1. Positional Encoding: As per [Parent], coordinates \mathbf{x} and directions \mathbf{d} are encoded using \gamma(\cdot) with L frequency bands. 2. MLP Backbone: Two coupled MLPs (density F\sigma and color Fc) with skip connections [Parent]. Modification: The output channel count of the final layer in the MLPs is changed from 3 (RGB) to a larger number N (feature space). 3. Convolutional Network: A 3-layer CNN with ReLU activations and 3 \times 3 kernels follows the volumetric rendering step. Padding: "Reflectance" padding is used for inputs to prevent checkerboard artifacts; padding values are removed from outputs. 4. Feed-Forward Perceptron: A final layer converts the CNN feature representation back to RGB space. Numbered Steps: 1. Pre-training (Normal Stage): Train the modified MLPs (outputting N-dimensional features) using standard volumetric rendering in the feature space. Use random ray sampling during this initial phase to establish a baseline density and feature field. 2. Architecture Augmentation: After pre-training, append the 3-layer CNN to the rendering pipeline. The CNN takes the rendered feature map (from the N-channel output) as input. The CNN output is passed to the feed-forward perceptron to produce the final RGB color. 3. Alignment-Aware Fine-Tuning: Sampling Switch: Change from random ray sampling to patch-based sampling. Gather a local image region (patch) during each iteration. Ground Truth Patch Size: Sample a larger ground truth patch G of size 48 \times 48 pixels. Rendered Patch Size: Render a smaller patch R of size 32 \times 32 pixels. Alignment Search: Search over every possible subpatch Gi within the larger ground truth patch G to find the best match with the rendered patch R. Loss Function: Minimize the alignment-aware loss L{PM}: L{PM}(G, R) = \min{i=1,...,N} \left( D(Gi, R) + \lambda \cdot D{coord}(Gi, R) \right) where: D(Gi, R) = \|Gi - R\|2^2 is the Euclidean distance between the subpatch and rendered patch. D{coord}(Gi, R) = \sqrt{\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2} is the coordinate offset penalty, where \Delta x and \Delta y are the horizontal and vertical offsets between Gi and R. \lambda is a regularization weight, empirically set to 0.01. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def alignerftraining(gtimage, numepochspre, numepochsfine, batchsize, N): # Helper: Standard volumetric rendering formula [Parent] def volumetricrendering(samples, sigmas, features): deltas = [samples[i+1] - samples[i] for i in range(len(samples)-1)] alphas = [1.0 - math.exp(-s d) for s, d in zip(sigmas, deltas)] transmittances = [math.prod(1.0 - a for a in alphas[:i]) for i in range(len(alphas))] rendered = [t a f for t, a, f in zip(transmittances, alphas, features)] return sum(rendered) # Helper: Feed-forward perceptron for feature-to-RGB conversion def featuretorgb(features): return [sum(f w for f, w in zip(feature, weights)) for feature in features] # 1. Initialize MLPs with N-channel output mlpdensity = MLP(outputdim=1) mlpcolor = MLP(outputdim=N) # 2. Pre-training: Standard volumetric rendering in feature space for in range(numepochspre): rays = samplerandomrays(batchsize) renderedfeatures = [] for ray in rays: samples = samplepointsalongray(ray) sigmas = mlpdensity(samples) features = mlpcolor(samples) renderedfeatures.append(volumetricrendering(samples, sigmas, features)) rgb = featuretorgb(renderedfeatures) loss = mseloss(rgb, gtimage) updateparameters(mlpdensity, mlpcolor, loss) # 3. Append CNN and Perceptron cnn = ConvNet(layers=3, kernelsize=3, padding='reflect') perceptron = LinearLayer(infeatures=N, outfeatures=3) # 4. Alignment-Aware Fine-Tuning for in range(numepochsfine): # Patch-based sampling gtpatch = gtimage.crop(size=(48, 48)) renderedpatch = renderpatch(mlpdensity, mlpcolor, cnn, perceptron, size=(32, 32)) bestloss = float('inf') bestoffset = (0, 0) # Search over all possible subpatches in the larger GT patch for i in range(gtpatch.height - renderedpatch.height + 1): for j in range(gtpatch.width - renderedpatch.width + 1): subpatch = gtpatch.crop(i, j, renderedpatch.height, renderedpatch.width) # Euclidean distance dist = sum((subpatch - renderedpatch) 2) # Coordinate offset penalty coordpenalty = math.sqrt(i2 + j2) # Total loss with lambda currentloss = dist + 0.01 coordpenalty if currentloss < bestloss: bestloss = currentloss bestoffset = (i, j) loss = bestloss updateparameters(mlpdensity, mlpcolor, cnn, perceptron, loss) Parameters: Patch size (rendered): 32 \times 32 pixels. Patch size (ground truth): 48 \times 48 pixels. Regularization weight \lambda: 0.01. CNN Kernel size: 3 \times 3. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Checkerboard Artifacts: Mitigated by using "reflectance" padding and removing padding values in CNN outputs. Multiview Inconsistency: The shallow CNN does not perform upsampling, which helps avoid introducing multiview inconsistencies. Blurry Renderings: If the rendered patch R is too blurry, it may match multiple subpatches equally well. The coordinate penalty D{coord} regularizes this by penalizing large offsets. Time Complexity: The alignment-aware fine-tuning stage involves searching over all possible subpatches, which adds a computational overhead proportional to the number of subpatches in the ground truth patch relative to the rendered patch. However, the CNN is shallow, and the method does not significantly increase training time compared to baseline NeRF. Memory Complexity: The modification increases memory usage slightly due to the larger output channel count N in the MLP and the storage of the CNN weights, but it reduces the total number of parameters compared to a pure high-resolution MLP approach by leveraging convolutional efficiency. Performance: On outdoor datasets, AligNeRF achieves a PSNR more than 3 points higher than standard NeRF and outperforms the best mip-NeRF results. It is particularly effective for high-resolution images and scenes with moving objects. Strengths: Improves high-frequency detail recovery; handles misalignment from moving objects; easy to plug into existing NeRF-like models (point-sampling or frustum-based). Limitations: Requires staged training (pre-training then fine-tuning); relies on patch-based sampling which increases memory bandwidth usage per iteration. AligNeRF was introduced by Yifan Jiang, Peter Hedman, Ben Mildenhall, Dejia Xu, Jonathan T. Barron, Zhangyang Wang, and Tianfan Xue in 2022. It was published at CVPR 2023. The method addresses limitations in training NeRF on high-resolution images, specifically the degradation of quality due to misalignment and the inability of standard MLPs to capture high-frequency details efficiently. It builds upon the mip-NeRF 360 baseline. name: DiffusioNeRF
head: Diffusion-guided NeRF, Diffusion Prior NeRF
body: DiffusioNeRF is a method that integrates a denoising diffusion model (DDM) as an initial learning factor to standardize the training of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). It utilizes the DDM to learn priors for scene geometry and color, normalizing these fields to achieve higher quality reconstruction, particularly under sparse input views. Unlike standard NeRF which relies solely on photometric consistency, DiffusioNeRF steers the optimization by backpropagating gradients derived from the diffusion model's likelihood estimates. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view RGB images (sparse or dense), camera poses, and a pre-trained denoising diffusion model trained on synthetic RGBD data (e.g., Hypersim). Outputs: Optimized NeRF parameters (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}) and rendered novel views. Data Structures: The method builds upon the standard NeRF architecture Parent. 1. NeRF MLPs: Two coupled Multi-Layer Perceptrons (F\sigma for density, Fc for color) taking positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}) and viewing direction \mathbf{d} as input [Parent]. 2. Diffusion Model: A denoising network D\theta trained to predict noise in RGBD patches. It outputs gradients of the log-likelihood of the joint probability distribution of color and depth. Algorithm Steps: 1. Diffusion Prior Training: Train the DDM on a large synthetic dataset (e.g., Hypersim) consisting of RGBD patches. The model learns the joint distribution P(\text{RGB}, \text{Depth}). 2. Ray Sampling: During NeRF training, sample points \mathbf{x}i along rays \mathbf{r} using the standard stratified sampling or importance sampling strategy [Parent]. 3. NeRF Prediction: Query the NeRF MLPs to obtain density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i for each sample point [Parent]. 4. Patch Rendering: Render random RGBD patches from the current NeRF state. This involves aggregating the sampled \sigmai and \mathbf{c}i into a depth map and color image. 5. Gradient Estimation: Compute the estimated gradients of the log-likelihood of the rendered RGBD patches with respect to the NeRF parameters, using the pre-trained DDM. Specifically, the DDM provides the gradient of the log-prior \nabla{\text{NeRF}} \log P{\text{diff}}(\text{RGBD}{\text{rendered}}). 6. Backpropagation: Backpropagate these estimated gradients to the NeRF's color and density fields. This step normalizes the geometry and color of the scene. 7. Optimization Update: Update NeRF parameters using an optimizer (e.g., Adam) with the combined loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{photometric}} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{\text{diffusion}} where \mathcal{L}{\text{diffusion}} is derived from the diffusion model's gradient guidance. Parameters: \lambda: Weight for the diffusion prior loss. Not given in the sources. Patch Size: Size of the RGBD patches rendered for diffusion guidance. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Views: The method is specifically designed to handle sparse views (e.g., 3 views) where standard NeRF fails due to ambiguity. Synthetic Bias: The diffusion prior is trained on synthetic data (Hypersim). Domain gap between synthetic and real data may affect performance. Gradient Noise: The gradients from the diffusion model may introduce noise if the rendered patches deviate significantly from the training distribution. SSDNeRF is a unified framework that jointly optimizes a NeRF auto-decoder and a latent diffusion model in a single training stage to learn generalizable 3D priors from multi-view images. Unlike two-stage approaches that pretrain auto-decoders without diffusion models, SSDNeRF blends generative and rendering biases coherently, enabling robust training on sparse-view data (as few as three views) and avoiding the noisy latent manifolds induced by inverse rendering uncertainty. It supports flexible test-time sampling for both unconditional 3D generation and reconstruction from arbitrary view counts. Time Complexity: Training time is increased due to the additional gradient computation from the diffusion model and the need to render RGBD patches for prior evaluation. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the NeRF parameters and the diffusion model parameters. No significant additional memory overhead compared to standard NeRF. Performance: On the LLFF dataset, DiffusioNeRF achieves PSNR improvements of 1-2 points over SOTA methods for 3, 6, and 9 input views. Specifically, with 3 input views, it is nearly 1 point higher than ViP-NeRF. It outperforms current methods on the DTU dataset as well. Strengths: Improved geometry and color quality in sparse-view scenarios; reduced artifacts in stratified scenes. Limitations: Reliance on synthetic data for prior training; potential domain gap; increased training complexity. DiffusioNeRF was introduced in 2023. It addresses the limitations of NeRF in handling sparse input views and complex geometries by incorporating generative priors from diffusion models. The method leverages the ability of diffusion models to capture complex data distributions, using them to guide the NeRF optimization process. It has been evaluated on the LLFF [33] and DTU [41] datasets. name: SSDNeRF
head: Single-Stage Diffusion NeRF
body: SSDNeRF is a unified framework that jointly optimizes a NeRF auto-decoder and a latent diffusion model in a single training stage to learn generalizable 3D priors from multi-view images. Unlike two-stage approaches that pretrain auto-decoders without diffusion models, SSDNeRF blends generative and rendering biases coherently, enabling robust training on sparse-view data (as few as three views) and avoiding the noisy latent manifolds induced by inverse rendering uncertainty. It supports flexible test-time sampling for both unconditional 3D generation and reconstruction from arbitrary view counts. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A dataset of multi-view images \{y{ij}\} for a set of scenes indexed by i, where j indexes the rays (pixels) and their corresponding camera poses r{ij}. Outputs: Optimized decoder parameters \psi, diffusion prior parameters \phi, and scene latent codes xi. Data Structures: Scene Code (xi): A latent representation for scene i. The source specifies a triplane NeRF representation where xi \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 6 \times 128 \times 128}. NeRF Decoder (p\psi): A network that maps the scene code xi and ray parameters r{ij} to predicted RGB color y{ij}. It uses spherical harmonic (SH) encoding for position features, Linear layers, SiLU activations, and Sigmoid/Exp activations for output. Diffusion Prior (p\phi): A U-Net based denoising network conditioned on time step t and scene code xi. It takes a noisy code xi^{(t)} and outputs a denoised estimate \hat{x}\phi(xi, t). Parameters: Time Step (t): Sampled uniformly from U(0, T). Weighting Function (w(t)): An empirical time-dependent weighting function for the diffusion loss. Minimum Views: Training requires at least 3 views per scene. Formulas: The total loss \mathcal{L} is a simplified variational upper bound on the negative log-likelihood (NLL), ignoring uncertainty in latent codes: \mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}i [-\log p\psi(\{y{ij}\}|xi, \{r{ij}\})] + \mathbb{E}i [-\log p\phi(xi)] Where: The first term is the rendering loss \mathcal{L}{rend}, measuring the likelihood of observed data given the scene code and ray parameters. The second term is the prior term, measuring the likelihood of the scene code under the diffusion prior. The diffusion loss component is typically formulated as: \mathcal{L}{diff} = \mathbb{E}{t, xi} [w(t) \| xi^{(t)} - \hat{x}\phi(xi, t) \|^2] where xi^{(t)} is the noisy code at step t and \hat{x}\phi(xi, t) is the denoised prediction. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize NeRF decoder parameters \psi, diffusion prior parameters \phi, and scene latent codes xi for all scenes in the dataset. 2. Forward Pass (Rendering): For each scene i and ray j: Encode position features using Spherical Harmonics (SH). Pass scene code xi and ray parameters r{ij} through the NeRF decoder p\psi to predict RGB color \hat{y}{ij}. Compute rendering loss \mathcal{L}{rend} between predicted \hat{y}{ij} and ground truth y{ij}. 3. Forward Pass (Diffusion): Sample a time step t \sim U(0, T). Add noise to scene code xi to obtain noisy code xi^{(t)}. Pass xi^{(t)} and t through the U-Net denoiser p\phi to predict the denoised code \hat{x}\phi(xi, t). Compute diffusion loss \mathcal{L}{diff} using the weighting function w(t). 4. Loss Combination: Compute total loss \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rend} + \mathcal{L}{prior}, where \mathcal{L}{prior} is derived from -\log p\phi(xi). 5. Optimization: Update \psi, \phi, and xi jointly using gradient descent on \mathcal{L}. 6. Test-Time Sampling (Unconditional): Sample random Gaussian noise x^{(T)}. Use a solver (e.g., DDIM) to recursively denoise x^{(t)} to x^{(0)} using the trained prior p\phi. Decode x^{(0)} using p\psi to generate a 3D scene. 7. Test-Time Sampling (Guided Reconstruction): Start with random noise or a prior sample. Guide the denoising process by computing gradients of the rendering loss with respect to the latent code xi against known observations y{ij}. Update xi during the reverse diffusion process to reconstruct the scene from arbitrary view counts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim class SSDNeRF: def init(self, numscenes, numviewsperscene, T=1000): """ Initialize SSDNeRF model.:param numscenes: Number of scenes in the dataset.:param numviewsperscene: Number of views per scene (min 3).:param T: Total number of diffusion timesteps. """ self.numscenes = numscenes self.numviews = numviewsperscene self.T = T # Initialize NeRF Decoder parameters psi # Structure: SH encoding, Linear, SiLU, Linear, Sigmoid/Exp self.decoder = NeRFDecoder() self.psi = self.decoder.parameters() # Initialize Diffusion Prior parameters phi (U-Net) self.diffusionmodel = UNetDenoiser() self.phi = self.diffusionmodel.parameters() # Initialize scene latent codes xi # Shape: [numscenes, 3, 6, 128, 128] self.x = torch.randn(numscenes, 3, 6, 128, 128) # Optimizer for joint optimization self.optimizer = optim.Adam(list(self.psi) + list(self.phi) + [self.x], lr=1e-4) # Time-dependent weighting function w(t) [G: Placeholder for specific empirical function] self.wt = self.getweightingfunction() def getweightingfunction(self): # Returns a tensor of weights for each timestep t # Implementation depends on the specific empirical function used in return torch.ones(self.T) def render(self, xi, rays): """ Render RGB colors from scene code xi and rays.:param xi: Scene code [3, 6, 128, 128]:param rays: Ray parameters rij [numrays,...]:return: Predicted RGB colors yhat [numrays, 3] """ # Encode position features using SH posfeats = encodesh(rays) # Pass through NeRF decoder yhat = self.decoder(xi, posfeats) return yhat def diffuse(self, xi, t): """ Add noise to scene code xi at timestep t.:param xi: Scene code:param t: Timestep:return: Noisy code xi^(t) """ # Standard Gaussian diffusion forward process # xi^(t) = sqrt(alphabart) xi + sqrt(1 - alphabart) epsilon # [G: Assume standard DDPM forward process implementation] return addnoise(xi, t) def denoise(self, xit, t): """ Predict denoised code from noisy code.:param xit: Noisy scene code:param t: Timestep:return: Denoised estimate xhatphi """ return self.diffusionmodel(xit, t) def computerenderingloss(self, yhat, ygt): """ Compute rendering loss Lrend.:param yhat: Predicted RGB:param ygt: Ground truth RGB:return: Scalar loss """ # Negative log-likelihood approximation (e.g., MSE or L1) return torch.mean((yhat - ygt) 2) def computepriorloss(self, xi, xit, t): """ Compute prior loss Lprior (diffusion loss).:param xi: Original scene code:param xit: Noisy scene code:param t: Timestep:return: Scalar loss """ xhat = self.denoise(xit, t) # Ldiff = w(t) || xi^(t) - xhatphi ||^2 # Note: The source formula uses -log pphi(xi), which is approximated by the diffusion loss weight = self.wt[t] return torch.mean(weight (xit - xhat) 2) def trainstep(self, batchdata): """ Single training step.:param batchdata: Dictionary containing images, rays, and scene indices:return: Total loss """ self.optimizer.zerograd() totalloss = 0.0 for i, sceneidx in enumerate(batchdata['sceneindices']): xi = self.x[sceneidx] rays = batchdata['rays'][i] ygt = batchdata['images'][i] # 1. Rendering Loss yhat = self.render(xi, rays) lrend = self.computerenderingloss(yhat, ygt) # 2. Prior Loss t = torch.randint(0, self.T, (1,)).item() xit = self.diffuse(xi, t) lprior = self.computepriorloss(xi, xit, t) # 3. Total Loss ltotal = lrend + lprior totalloss += ltotal totalloss.backward() self.optimizer.step() return totalloss.item() def sampleunconditional(self, numsamples=1): """ Unconditional 3D generation.:param numsamples: Number of samples to generate:return: List of scene codes x^(0) """ samples = [] for in range(numsamples): # Start from random Gaussian noise x^(T) xt = torch.randn(3, 6, 128, 128) # Recursively denoise using DDIM or similar solver for t in reversed(range(self.T)): xhat = self.denoise(xt, t) # [G: Implement DDIM update step from xt to x{t-1} using xhat] xt = updateddim(xt, xhat, t) samples.append(xt) return samples def reconstructguided(self, observations, rays, numguidancesteps=10): """ Guided reconstruction from arbitrary observations.:param observations: Known RGB images:param rays: Corresponding ray parameters:param numguidancesteps: Number of guidance steps per diffusion step:return: Reconstructed scene code x^(0) """ # Start from random noise or prior sample xt = torch.randn(3, 6, 128, 128) for t in reversed(range(self.T)): # Compute gradient of rendering loss w.r.t latent code # [G: This requires backpropagating through the renderer to the latent code] xt.requiresgrad = True yhat = self.render(xt, rays) lrend = self.computerenderingloss(yhat, observations) # Guidance step: update xt to minimize rendering loss # [G: Implement gradient ascent on lrend w.r.t xt] grad = torch.autograd.grad(lrend, xt)[0] xt = xt - guidancescale grad # Denoising step xhat = self.denoise(xt, t) xt = updateddim(xt, xhat, t) return xt A method that utilizes a denoising diffusion model to learn priors for scene geometry and color, normalizing the geometry and color of the scene to achieve better quality in reconstructed geometry under sparse input views. It serves as the parent method, focusing on geometry normalization, whereas SSDNeRF focuses on joint optimization for generalizable priors. DiffusioNeRF Approaches that pretrain auto-decoders or VAEs without diffusion models, then train diffusion models on the resulting latent codes. SSDNeRF differs by jointly optimizing both stages to avoid noisy latent manifolds. Time and Memory Complexity: Joint optimization of \psi, \phi, and xi increases memory usage compared to single-stage NeRF due to storing latent codes for all scenes and the diffusion model. Training time is longer than standard NeRF but avoids the separate pretraining phase of two-stage methods. Measured Performance: Demonstrates robust results comparable to or better than leading task-specific methods in unconditional generation and single/sparse-view 3D reconstruction. Scaling: Enables training on as sparse as three views per scene, which is previously infeasible for two-stage methods. Strengths: Blends generative and rendering biases coherently; supports flexible test-time sampling (unconditional and guided); robust to sparse-view input. Limitations: Requires joint optimization which may be computationally intensive; sensitive to the choice of weighting function w(t) and guidance scale in reconstruction. When to use: When generalizable 3D priors are needed from sparse multi-view data, or for unconditional 3D generation. When not to use: When high-fidelity reconstruction from dense views is the only goal and computational resources are limited, as standard NeRF may be more efficient. SSDNeRF was proposed in April 2023. It addresses the issue that previous two-stage approaches (pretraining auto-decoders/VAEs then training diffusion models) induce noisy patterns and artifacts in the latent code due to the uncertain nature of inverse rendering, particularly with sparse-view data. The method was developed during a remote internship with UCSD. It advances the field of 3D learning by providing a general-purpose framework for both generation and reconstruction. name: Pool proposer architecture
head: Pooling-based proposer
body: The pool proposer is a trainable neural network component used in NeRF-ID to generate fine-grained sampling positions for volume rendering. It processes coarse features from a previous sampling stage to propose new sample locations, addressing the need for adaptive sampling in differentiable volume rendering. It is distinguished from its sibling MLPMix Proposer by using a bottleneck fully connected layer and sinusoidal positional encoding summation, whereas MLPMix uses a different mixing mechanism. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of Nc = 64 coarse features, denoted as \mathbf{F}{coarse} \in \mathbb{R}^{Nc \times D}, where D = 256 is the feature dimension. Output: A set of Nf = 128 proposed sample features \mathbf{P} \in \mathbb{R}^{Nf \times D}. Data Structures: The proposer consists of a single bottleneck fully connected (FC) layer and a positional encoding module. Bottleneck Layer: A linear transformation W \in \mathbb{R}^{256 \times 256}. Positional Encoding: Sinusoidal positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) applied to the input features. Steps: 1. Positional Encoding: Apply sinusoidal positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) to the input coarse features \mathbf{F}{coarse}. 2. Summation: Sum the encoded features with the original coarse features: \mathbf{F}{sum} = \mathbf{F}{coarse} + \gamma(\mathbf{F}{coarse}). 3. Bottleneck Projection: Pass \mathbf{F}{sum} through the bottleneck fully connected layer: \mathbf{F}{out} = \mathbf{F}{sum} W. 4. Proposal Generation: The output \mathbf{F}{out} constitutes the features for the Nf = 128 proposed samples. The exact method for mapping these features back to spatial coordinates is not given in the sources. Parameters: Nc = 64: Number of coarse samples. Nf = 128: Number of fine proposals. Feature dimension: 256. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Blind Proposer: Ignoring input coarse features leads to poor performance, showing that a degenerate strategy of constant output is insufficient. No-position Proposer: Ignoring the positions of coarse samples along the ray performs badly on Blender scenes due to insensitivity to feature ordering (e.g., producing identical proposals for colinear rays of opposite directionality), but remains competitive on forward-facing LLFF-NeRF scenes. The MLPMix proposer is an alternative trainable proposer architecture that uses a mixing mechanism instead of pooling. It is preferred over the Transformer proposer due to the Transformer's inferior performance on specific scenes (Blender: Ficus, Blender: Lego, LLFF-NeRF: T-Rex) and unstable training curves. MLPMix and Pool are generally on par, but Pool has higher variance. Choose MLPMix over Pool when lower variance and consistent performance across challenging scenes are required. Complexity: The most expensive operations are applied to each of the Nc = 64 coarse features before the bottleneck. The bottleneck is a single 256 \times 256 FC layer. Performance: Pool and MLPMix tend to be the best performing proposers, but Pool has higher variance and is significantly worse on Blender: Materials and Blender: Mic scenes compared to MLPMix. Cost: The additional FC layer application on Nc = 64 vectors is negligible compared to the 8 FC layers in the NeRF backbone applied to Nc + Nc + Nf = 2048 vectors. The Transformer proposer is more expensive due to the lack of pooling operations. The pool proposer architecture was introduced in the context of NeRF-ID (NeRF with Importance Sampling) as part of a comparison between different trainable proposer architectures (Transformer, Pool, and MLPMix). The training procedure used differs slightly from the original NeRF, employing smaller batch sizes, fewer iterations (around 1.2 billion rays), and ensuring each ray passes through the center of its pixel rather than the corner.
